1963-01-11-shades-of-freud:
Shades of Freud

Robert Ashman interviews Philip Mansell

[The printed surname “Ashman” is a byline error for Robert Cushman.]

Philip Mansell, who produces The Winter's Tale for the ADC this term, is an habitual joker with a voice ranging between Peter Ustinov and David Frost, and a habit of fingering a guitar when at a loss for words.

His serious moments derive a contrasting intensity from the facetiousness that surrounds them. He can be very disarming, as when he blithely admitted that he wanted to produce the play because, having read the critics and seen the lamentable television production, “I thought it couldn't be as bad as that.”

Why Shakespeare for his first major production? He feels that he is more liable to understand a play that he has studied academically, and wishes to communicate his understanding to an audience. He dismisses previous productions as “lopsided and sentimental” and refuses to regard the play as a fairy-tale or Leontes' jealousy as incredible. His theory is at any rate ingenious.

“Leontes' marriage has been on the rocks for a long time before the play opens.” He sees Hermione as a frigid sophisticate whom Leontes is now unable to satisfy. Leontes projects on to their marriage a guilt-complex deriving from unconscious homosexual feelings for Polixenes, his inseparable companion in adolescence; Hermione's curiosity about their boyhood suggests that she suspects the memory is undermining her marriage.

Welcome change

The emphasis on Hermione's unsympathetic qualities is at least a welcome change from the traditional plaster-saint conception. Mansell brushes aside the suggestion that all this psychology would have surprised Shakespeare by referring to Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy.

“Elizabethan psychiatry,” he claims, “lacked our vocabulary, but not our insight.”

It is usual to regard the play as an allegory of the healing-power of youth; but for Mansell, Leontes is cured purely by instantaneous shock-therapy: the news of his wife's “death.” His essentially weak nature is easily led to religion as a consolation; he is more conscious of having sinned against his God than against his queen.

Sympathetic

This interpretation, regarding Leontes as basically sympathetic and the fulcrum of the play, places a great responsibility on the normally placid Tony Gooch: not the most obvious casting, but Mansell regards Gooch's range as extending far beyond the parts he has played hitherto.

Tony Palmer plays Autolycus, whom Mansell unexpectedly describes as “bitter—all thieves must be cynics”—a piquant piece of casting, perhaps. But certainly the comedy scenes can stand some freshening: it was heartening to hear Mansell inveigh against Gloucestershire accents for the shepherds.

He also rebels against the customary dewy-eyed treatment of Florizel and Perdita (played by Helen Kaswell). For him they represent “A type of Lawrentian uninhibited sex-relationship” which throws into relief the soured sexuality of the Sicilian court. The cast is predominantly young—more than three-quarters freshmen, culled from an influx which Mansell regards as exceptionally promising.

Perry Mason

I mentioned a rumour that he planned to equip the Sicilian court of justice with a stenographer. He remained non-committal, merely remarking that he wanted to achieve “A businesslike Perry Mason atmosphere.”

But no modern dress—“that's cheating.”

“The whole process of Shakespearean production,” he informed me with an oracular air, “should be simplification.”

This profession of faith is perhaps a rationalisation of his lack of confidence in his ability to handle mass movement. For him a crowd represents “an extra duty for the producer”—a duty which, unlike some other directors (he mentioned Mark Lushington), he prefers to forego.

Welcome approach

His own acting experience is fairly modest, but this does not worry him. As a director he wants to explain rather than demonstrate—an approach which most actors will welcome: nothing is more demoralising than a director who attempts to act a part by proxy. He refused to admit the possibility of an actor saying “I can't do this” but is prepared to tolerate “I can't see the way to do this.”

Twenty-seven actors have been warned.
1964-01-24-marching-song:
Marching Song

Reviewed by Robert Cushman

[Editorial note: One partly obscured word is supplied in square brackets below.]

Nobody in the contemporary theatre writes quite like John Whiting; Arden has inherited his moral preoccupation, but has added a flamboyance alien to his precursor. "The Devils" at least offers fancy dress and ear-catching rhetoric; "Saint's Day" has the manic wildfire of anybody's first play; but "Marching Song", which the Dryden Society mounted at the A.D.C. in the first week of term, is the bleakest bone of Whiting.

In one of those chilly ultra-modern rooms in one of those nameless European states, a defeated war-hero faces the alternatives of suicide or disgrace by public trial. Years of imprisonment have left him emotionally stripped; and the memory of his past, as exemplified in his elegantly-preserved mistress and a decayed film-director, holds no attraction for him. But the harsh uncommitted vitality of a waif-like young girl awakens a response in him, a belief that there may still be a present to live for.

Honourable Service

Dido's reference to her archaeologist father—"Always grubbing in the past. Disgusting occupation"—offers the clearest pointer to the [thematic] centre, but it is not the play's definitive voice. Rupert Forster has to come to terms with his past before his suicide can be, by his own questing standards, honourable. The young officer who will re-fight Forster's battles without Forster's scruples does not suggest an unconditional brief for starry-eyed youth.

The play is intellectually and atmospherically water-tight. But its very completeness within its own terms creates dangers. It is the coolest of plays, and unless its peculiar temperature can be re-created in performance, it reaches the danger-point and freezes. And ice is for falling through.

Parallel to the footlights

Michael Woosnam-Mills' production had the initial advantage of a good skeletal set and was pleasingly unpretentious. But a play which lives through its dialogue as completely as this one needs far more careful pacing than it received here. Ideas and images came at the audience in an undifferentiated heap which obscured the play's inner shape. The tension was never spun tight enough to justify the continuous presentation. Too many duologues were handled by lining up the actors parallel to the footlights and letting them speak through the back of each others' necks.

Understandably the characters who fared best were the weak recognisable ones: Liz Goodwin beautifully caught the mistress' frayed nerves and suppressed jealousy, and Christopher Pinfield, though his boyish appearance militated against belief, eased his way securely into the director. David Ross, attacking Forster with presence and intelligence, never latched on to the steely intellectuality of the text; his long speeches came over as nicely-prepared audition-pieces, poised between invisible quotation marks. The fault, perhaps, is Whiting's; in paring the play down to the bone, he neglected an audience's craving for human flesh.
1964-02-21-the-visit:
The Visit

Reviewed by Robert Cushman

Nobody could reasonably accuse 'The Visit' of obscurity. The greenbacks flourished in our faces at the end only make tangible what Durrenmatt has been drumming in our ears all along: that this is a play about selling-out. Obediently we switch on our collective-guilt reflexes and cower in our seats. It's microcosm time again, and Guellen, where money buys justice, is guaranteed to scorch our consciences.

But I am developing scorch-resistance. Neat little parables worked out by characters bizarre or generalised (the Schoolmaster, the Priest) are too easy, and soothe the wounds they pretend to mortify. Money goes hand in hand with deceit—even Claire's limbs are artificial, and she makes humanity her playthings. At which we all murmur 'How true' and go home untouched and unrepentant.

And yet, as a theatrical mechanism, the play works. The mixture of Grand Guignol and eccentric hilarity is its own reward and, feeding upon itself, sprouts vigorously throughout the evening. The effect is of a hectically sick cartoon, with built-in social significance.

As such, it presents its director with a formidable stylistic problem, which Rob Knights solves for the Mummers with something like triumph. He tends to over-build factitious climaxes, and cogency is lacking in the middle stretches, but his overall touch is masterfully sure. Sets, lighting, and sound—all unusually good—are integrated with a rare feeling for mood and tempo.

He is particularly successful with the visitors. Lis Rietberg's magnificent Claire suspends disbelief from exactly the right altitude, and her entourage—from Jeffrey Tate's doom-laden butler through the capering castrati to Tim Davies' comic precision as the husbands—runs the play's horror-comic gamut in miniature.

The Guelleners are fine in concert but lack conviction as individuals. David Lascelles and Ian Barritt get the right metallic ring in small parts, but Bernard Krichefski's querulous schoolmaster is the only wholly successful principal. The penalty of Durrenmatt's method is that approximations will not do; thus the control and assurance of Roger Gartland's Mayor are negated by his lack of weight. And David Collins plays Ill frankly against the grain of the play: he has some marvellous moments, but his attempts to make a three-dimensional hero out of a one-dimensional victim result inevitably in an uncentred performance.
1965-01-26-arts-theatre-the-alchemist:
Arts Theatre: The Alchemist

I am frankly at a loss for a critical approach to this competent, agreeable, workmanlike, desperately average production. In no mood, and with no right, to submit a coherently-reasoned critique, I offer instead a series of notes.

1) The Play. I was seeing it, it dawned on me as the intrigues piled relentlessly up, for the fourth time. I still laughed, so I suppose it must be good. And yet, the great comic masterpiece of received opinion? Almost invariably I have lost the will to cope with the increasingly convulsive plot. It becomes less a play than a music-hall bill; Subtle and Face in the chair presiding over a succession of gulled guests. The acts vary considerably in quality and has to stand on its own, so there are bound to be longueurs. It is a plot-necessity that the various dupes should never meet; hence, we do not see them played off against each other until the action is two-thirds over. When they do collide, all hell should break loose, but it doesn't quite. The sum of the entertainment-value is considerable, but it is not cumulative, as farce ideally should be.

2) Production. A very even pace—not a good idea. I heard more of Jonson than ever before—some throw-away lines caught the audience laughing off their guard, but the big obvious ones ("Thou look'st like Antichrist in that lewd hat") came through muffled, and there was very little climactic sense. Ananias' entry at the height of confusion with "Peace to this house" should raise the roof. I smiled. Surely the long reels of alchemical jargon were meant to be gabbled. The set was pleasant, atmospheric, cluttered and reduced blocking to a series of brisk walks round a small room down right centre.

3) Acting. Subtle (Alan MacNaughtan) rather heavy-handed. Belief in him as a con-man hindered by the fact that he used his real voice for his assumed persona, and vice versa; strain in the wrong places the natural result. In general, too mellow, not sharp enough. All this goes too for Face (John Turner) whose best moments are at the end when he reverts to his butler-identity, (for which he has another funny voice—sustained over all that time?) Both are reasonably genial company; both lack the force of personality to carry the audience with them. Here they are in marked contrast to Dol (Judi Dench) who aroused all the sympathetic enthusiasm normally generated by transparently nice young actresses trying roguishly to pretend they're not. Before I am wrathfully struck down I will admit that Miss Dench is still the most adorable actress in the world and that I duly adored her. Furthermore that when her overrated, under-written part gave her an opportunity (in her Queen of Fairy scene) to display the talents of a real comedienne, as opposed to a girl it's fun to have around, she took it. So much for the tricksters. The tricked:—Mammon (David Swift) a casualty. What is initially a pleasingly un-emphatic approach to the big speeches proves not to conceal a supply of power-in-reserve. The glorious character fades into gruff oblivion. Surly (Zia Mohyeddin) my big disappointment—not perhaps the ideal vehicle for his mercurial talents, but still what has happened to him? Drugger (Simon Ward) my big surprise in the other direction; a gauche, stolid, foursquare, thickly-spoken, slow-witted joy. My favourite character (in terms of laughter, not sympathy) came out tops again; Ananias (Julian Curry) has brought blinkered fanaticism to unwaveringly funny heights.

4) Why the hell doesn't someone do VOLPONE instead?

Robert Cushman
1965-03-09-arts-theatre-romeo-and-juliet:
Arts Theatre: Romeo and Juliet

In the programme-note to his Marlowe Society production Gareth Morgan lays great stress on the importance to the play of the Montague-Capulet feud, not merely as a convenient lever to set the love-story in motion, but as a positive fact in the play in its own right. His production brings this out almost too well. Despite an inappropriately chilly set the atmosphere of steamy discontent, erupting into violence, is most powerfully summoned. The small-part actors are uniformly good—they really look dangerous; a repulsively flippant Sampson and Gregory pave the way for a sleek, menacing Tybalt; not quite convincing as the fanatically punctilious duellist described by Mercutio, but admirably epitomising the perversity that turns nice young men into killers.

As a picture of strife-torn Verona the production is completely convincing; in other words, the first half (up to the death of Mercutio) is fine. At the interval I felt elated, by the end I was rather depressed. For the connection between the brawling environment and the love story it frames is never fully established. The droop is partially inherent in the play itself; Romeo offstage in Mantua for an act constitutes a formidable break in continuity which can only be bridged if the early love scenes have conditioned us to accept the protagonists as essentially inseparable. But in this production nobody is really in touch with anybody else. Marlowe tradition is flouted by the inclusion of a curtain call, but it seems curiously inapposite: it is a surprise to realise that all these disparate people have in fact been acting in the same play.

This fragmentary impression is echoed in the shape of individual performances. Juliet, in particular, is patchy. She gets the second half way off the ground with a reading of “Gallop apace, you fiery-footed steeds” whose unabashed relaxed eagerness engages completely and stamps her as a real actress of exceptional promise. Yet a moment later she is greeting the presumed death of her husband with, at unconvincing best, mild concern; the emotional complexities of the last scenes never get beyond hints. Her best moments—her first sight of Romeo, for example—are magic; the girl is really in love. More than can be said for her Romeo who, despite a certain morning freshness, is unremarkable, never really engaging with his own, or anyone else's character.

The best performance is probably Mercutio, who exudes all the necessary panache and manages to build his relationships with Romeo and Benvolio single-handed. The Nurse, too, after a shaky start which drowns her garrulous reminiscences in a sea of vocal fidgets, settles down into an enjoyable routine character study (though I felt that the same actress got unobtrusively to the heart of a similar character much more successfully in last year's Galileo). But the elders in general are not very successful: Lady Capulet pauses in the middle of an otherwise stiff and colourless performance to call down vengeance for Tybalt's death with stunning effect. Her husband fusses and chuckles his way through the play in the all-too-familiar manner. And there is an incredibly prim and platitudinous Friar Laurence whose broad grin at the idea of Juliet shut up in the Capulet tomb suggests disturbing tendencies unmentioned by Shakespeare. Unthinkable for him to belong to the same world as the richly-realised crowd. But that is the paradox of the whole production.

Robert Cushman
1967-06-01-o-casey-double-bill:
O'Casey Double Bill

Most reviews of this double-bill have ignored the curtain-raiser and it is not difficult to see why. A Pound on Demand is a blown-up revue sketch about the antics of two drunks in a post office which only the exotic tag of Irishness could possibly sell to an English audience. The writing presents the depressing spectacle of a first-rate comic talent at third-rate pressure; a piece of genuine mediocrity would be easier to accept, but the continual unavailing strain towards a higher level of whose existence author and audience are thoroughly aware is really punishing. If only the name attached were not O'Casey's there wouldn't have been so earnest an effort to laugh; as it is, all one can salvage is the memory of some virtuoso alcoholic sliding from Jack MacGowran.

He also reigns supreme in The Shadow of a Gunman, which nobody needs telling is a much better play. All the same, it adds to the creeping suspicion of the last few years that during his long period in the wilderness O'Casey was, paradoxically, oversold. I can only go on the plays I've actually seen, since phrasing that on the page appears overripe has always to be read with the mental proviso that it probably sounds marvellous in a Dublin brogue, and the sudden changes of gear on which his structures are based demand to be fleshed. But neither the National Theatre Juno nor the present production raise him above the “rather good” level; not to be sneered at, but not to be lauded either. The myth of his verbal genius needs careful examination. It holds good for some magnificent passages of sustained comedy (in this vein the jeep sequence in The Bishop's Bonfire seems to me to surpass anything in the acknowledged major parts) but the corresponding tragic effects are willed rather than created; instance the twice-repeated maternal lament in Juno: high-sounding verbiage to pressure-cook a situation. In The Shadow of a Gunman the shock effect of Minnie Powell's death is blanketed, not intensified, by the vaporous rhetoric with which the poseur Davoren greets it; and I don't think there's a dramatic point here—at this point, as far as one can tell, he has stopped posing.

Still, it's a sturdy play in which most of the elements add up; the Civil War appears by refraction in Davoren and the superstitious ex-patriot Seamus Shields, and then in grim earnest in the catastrophe to which their antics and their neighbours' war-obsession lead. But at the Mermaid the whole falters for lack of life in the parts. The episode of Mr Gallagher's petition drags laboriously, so that its eventual effect on the denouement is obscured; the loquacious drunk who should heighten the tension of the second half fatally dissipates it.

Through it all, Jack MacGowran perseveres with his usual ferrety expertise, though without ever reaching the heights of his recent work in Beckett. Seamus is no immortal but he's a sharp and funny creation and an obvious star part. Unfortunately, he's not the protagonist; and Davoren, who is, is in fact only the shadow of a character—his not being a gunman is the most positive thing about him. Brian Phelan lacks the exceptional magnetism that might hold the stage in such a wholly passive rôle. But Shivaun O'Casey, though rather too predestined a martyr, gives a haunting account of Minnie, and Terry Downes, no less, makes a most convincingly brutal Auxiliary, though the relationship to what is usually known as acting is remote.

O'Casey is an easy dramatist to love. I wish I were convinced.
1967-08-01-the-trial:
The Trial

Maybe we're going soft. Long before the days of World Theatre Seasons foreign companies visited us regularly, without benefit of simultaneous translation and we did our best to cope. The language barrier seldom deterred critics from writing detailed reviews, compounded in about equal proportions of faith, hope and charity. And yet, the burden of the notices received by the Czech Theatre on the Balustrade for their production of The Trial has been baffled indignation. Judgment has been self-righteously withheld (in a context of Kafka as an earlier Aldwych programme once had it, this must be catching) pending either a crash-course in Czech or the immediate employment of a bisexual pair of bi-linguists to synchronise as best they can with the dialogue on stage.

My Czech is no better than the next critic's but I thought I recognised in Jan Grossman's production the flawlessly efficient workings of a powerful theatrical imagination. It didn't quite tally with what I take to have been Kafka's intentions, or anyway with his ambience. Kafka's world was an ordinary one in which extraordinary things happened and were thereby rendered more terrifying; in Grossman's version much of the same extraordinary things happen (and then some—Josef K. does an unbelievable back-somersault in the brief interval between strangulation and demise) but in a context in which nothing else can be expected. It shrieks nightmare from the start; the murderers look like Laurel and Hardy but I don't see Stan and Ollie surviving ten minutes in this atmosphere; even Goldberg and McCann might have found it menacing beyond the call of comedy. There's a lot of organ music, which is very impressive as organ music invariably is. There's a set composed of tubular steel scaffolding which revolves smartly and reminded me strongly of at least one other set composed of tubular steel scaffolding; it's backed by a dazzling cyc and the overall effect bears out all the good things you ever heard about Czech designers except that, doubtless by some oversight, it's not by Svoboda. There's an impressive collection of nymphets, nymphomaniacs and just plain nymphs, by whom K was not, as far as I could tell, universally frustrated. Above all, there's speed and precision of movement; I've never seen a production as uncannily choreographed. The Piccolo Teatro seem, in comparison, showily virtuoso. These Czechs have other things on their mind beside their feet, but their springy swiftness, just one and a half times as fast as normal pace, was totally expressive; it concretely evoked a firmly believable dream-world (compare, unfavourably, Jonathan Miller's Alice in Wonderland, as slow as which no mortal man has surely ever dreamed).

The net result was sheer terror. With this I was well satisfied but I doubt if the director intended me to be, since he framed the play in what is, at first blush, a classic alienation device; a narrative voice to apprise us at intervals of what was going to happen, or had just happened, or was happening at this moment if we would kindly concentrate; for the Czechless, it was often anybody's guess which. This, of course, just made the whole thing even more terrifying, and less susceptible to the rational analysis which I take to be the goal of alienation. I got the picture of K versus the rest, but I found it difficult to tell the rest apart.

So, finally, I guess I join hands with everyone else. I wanted a translation. To say that everyone likely to see the production will have read the original anyway is no real answer; the last thing anyone ever bore away from The Trial is a clear plot-outline. The programme synopsis, unless you can memorise it before the lights go down, is no help either; though, by virtue of its being merely the baldest string of apparently unrelated incidents, it unnerved me more than either seeing the play or (yes, madam, my credentials are impeccable) reading the book.

Jan Preucil is a brilliant K, a good deal smoother than you'd expect and more interestingly doomed on that account; and, apart from a slight lack of weight, I couldn't fault the ensemble. The whole is a coolly thrilling experience and takes second place only to the Comédie Française in Marivaux in the Non-Tourist Class of this year's festival.
1968-05-01-open-on-sundays:
Open on Sundays

Ever alert for a chance to offer really constructive criticism, I would like to point out to would-be patrons the salient fact about Open on Sundays, namely that it isn't. I can now get round to explaining why, if you are a would-be patron, Sunday is the day to choose.

An actor I know who was appearing in an evening of folksy fun and not enjoying it very much was a little dashed after one performance by an enthusiastic spectator who informed him that it was just what she'd always imagined Jewish humour to be. The actor replied ruefully that he'd always assumed Jewish humour was funnier.

This crystallises my reaction to Open on Sundays, which is set in a timeless community of no fixed abode, where a few kopeks will buy you a tin of Heinz tomato soup. Waste no time on wondering whether you are in pre-1914 Odessa or the pre-1939 East End; the authors see no essential difference and have worked in guest appearances for Moses, Spinoza, Dai Francis and others. Groucho Marx even gets to heckle his uncle Karl in stray lines from his movies whose delivery here should kill the legend that he owed everything to his writers. The Hitler-Chaplin bit also turns up, done in the old flicker-flashback style.

Like much of the show, this sequence is briskly staged and excellently lit, and, to the extent that the entire cast looks unabashedly and unforcedly involved throughout, the group-improvisation method has obviously worked. They also look directed; Ron Pember always manages to keep attention focused on the right spot. But the goings-on in that spot hardly justify him; let a bunch of actors improvise on the general theme of how colourful and lovable they are, and astringent entertainment will not result. A one-act play by Michael Landy lies buried somewhere; what it can have been like is anybody's guess, and mine are all doleful.

Things happen in moderate quantity, but their running-order could easily be reversed, which is a working definition of bad dramaturgy. Between whiles, the actors sing, better than most of them act. The songs are standard traditional and have an unnerving habit of resembling, if you can imagine such a thing, pastiche Lionel Bart. The jokes are trad, too, and as such well below par.

The show's most crippling limitations are inherent in its premise. The Anglo-American theatre has benefited enormously from Jewish talent, but Yiddishness is not of itself enough. An excruciatingly protracted and sentimental anecdote about whether to put grandfather in the old folks' home seems to labour under the impression that this is a situation whose poignancy is peculiarly Jewish; it could happen anywhere and is of no dramatic moment unless the participants are individualised. Nor can I take seriously a self-styled “full-length experience of Jewish life and humour” which takes no account of assimilation, the state of Israel, or any Gentiles other than Hitler and an unspecified Tsar, and which equates the ghetto with the Garden of Eden. Jews are supposed to be the worst anti-Semites and I cannot forgive this production for the feelings it aroused in me.
1968-07-01-bunraku-national-theatre:
Bunraku National Theatre

Well, they are a civil company, I like them for that. They offer not to fleer, nor jeer, nor break jests, as the great players do; and then, there goes not so much charge to the feasting of them, or making them drunk, as to the other by reason of their littleness. Do they use to play perfect? Are they never flustered?

So Bartholomew Cokes, esquire of Harrow, to the puppet master of Bartholomew Fair. And the Bankside of his day, not having a Peter Daubeny to bring the wonders of the Orient to its friendly neighbourhood playhouse, he hadn't seen nothing. A civiller company of puppets than those of the Japanese Bunraku Theatre there can never have been; I work on the assumption that the essence of civility is restraint, and that of restraint, control. The Bunraku cross new frontiers of control, new for us, anyway. They use to play perfect, and they are never flustered. As to their propensity for fleering, jeering and breaking jests, I would not like to swear; they have a trick of mountainous eyebrow-raising before which the Aldwych audience, myself among them, had a tendency to cave in. But subsequent recourse to the programme synopses revealed that nothing particularly funny was going on at the time.

For long stretches the Bunraku—to a far greater degree than anything else seen in this year's World Theatre season—is a richly incomprehensible experience, that defies you to identify with its intended audience. That audience, however, has deserted it. Bunraku is dying in Japan, though acclaimed over here. It looks as if ignorance is bliss or do the Japanese find each other inscrutable?

I would not want to make too much of this point; I enjoyed the Bunraku's second programme more than the first, and this must in part have been due to growing familiarity. But I still remained a spiritual tourist; held, even hypnotised, but never involved, never fundamentally interested.

There is much to wonder at. Puppetry as we know it tends to be ingratiating, designed more often than not for children. Here, on the whole, it is endistancing, due to an unexpected eruption of the human element. The puppeteers are visible, one maestro and two hooded assistants to each four-foot doll; in prospect, this struck me as an impossibly cluttering device. In retrospect, I still cannot see how it failed to be. At the time, I just gasped at the spaciousness of it all. Nothing could have been less cluttered.

These puppets, though, operate on the grand scale, moving over most of the Aldwych stage (a segment stage left is reserved for the impassive musicians and storytellers) in front of grandiose Pollock-print sets. A moment at which the stage was occupied by only two dolls, both flopped face-down on the deck, reminded me irresistibly of Punch and Judy; this, I decided, was the Cinemascope version. But a second's awareness of the puppeteers' presence was enough to banish that idea; were ventriloquists perhaps a more fruitful parallel? But there was none of the chumminess of manipulator and dummy; there was, though, an open flaunting of the tension that must underlie any such art, and supplied the motive-power for such a nightmare film as Dead of Night (and, by extension, for the computer sequence of Kubrick's 2001): the sense of a continual battle for possession.

During moments of impending conflict (they were frequent) when puppets clawed to get at each other, their apparent struggle to escape their controllers almost supplied a sub-plot. The climax comes in the first programme with a puppet's suicide; with shocking abruptness, in the wake of a most delicate depiction of apparently autonomous misery, the doll is picked up and hurled to the ground. But there's a catch: resurrection follows. A Bunraku puppet cannot be killed that easily. When suicide is really final it is treated with respect; as in the stunning closing image of the second programme. Two lovers, who have chosen the sword in preference to separation, slump slowly, and with infinite grace, towards each other, the lights fading. The Bunraku may be ancient, incidentally, but they have nothing to learn about the use of electricity.

The sheer physical dexterity—the loving exact sewing, the shocking realism of the fights—need not be rehearsed here; it impressed but did not excite me. But the most compelling of the plays, The Subscription List, furnished a real virtuoso performance; Benkei, the servant who turns master in order to protect his lord. The mixture of joy in deceit and fear of detection was consummately conveyed by manipulator and reciter: the final dance of triumph brought the house down. Benkei (a creation of the Japanese Shakespeare, we were told, though not by the programme) belongs with Figaro and Truffaldino: he took his calls like the star he transparently is.
1968-07-01-the-queen-s-highland-servant:
The Queen's Highland Servant

I would hazard, gentle reader, that you get most of your kicks on the subsidised circuit and that theatreland for you is arc-shaped, extending down to Waterloo Road, over the bridge and round to the Aldwych. Do you, I wonder, ever cast fleeting glances of guilty longing up the Strand, Trafalgarwards? Well cheer up, you're not missing much. For before you have a chance to succumb to the Siren Song of Charlie Girl you must negotiate Scylla and Charybdis. On second thoughts, let's jack the classical bit in and come home to Bunyan for metaphors; I hereby rechristen the Adelphi the Slough of Despond, and name the Savoy and the Vaudeville twin projections of Doubting Castle.

Of late, Giant Despair has been having a ball—indeed, two balls—one being The Imaginary Invalid imported from Billingham (Where? Oh yes, of course, Billingham) and the other a morel of Victoriana from William Douglas-Home. When a crime has been committed you look for a motive, so here goes: Molière obviously counts as a revival and we all know about revivals, don't we? And the importation from Windsor (where presumably it counted as théâtre vérité) of The Queen's Highland Servant only makes sense as an attempt to cash in on the loyalist reaction to Edward Bond's Early Morning. Victoria has now been led out of the house of Bondage back into her ancestral stately Home; where were you all on that cold, empty second night?

John Brown, the faithful ghillie, is here seen pouring copious draughts of whisky down his sovereign's throat, and telling braw home truths about her and her ministers. She liked it (“You're such a comfort, Brown”)—they didn't. This point is reiterated at some length; of twelve scenes, about eight are built on a recurring pattern. The politicos chatter among themselves about the distressing effect of Brown on Queen and country; to them enter Brown who puts them to shame by talking to them as man to dog. First time round this is quite funny. Thereafter Brown is a bore, unsalvageable by any, except possibly Marianne Faithfull.
Due to his excessive zeal in chasing the Queen's enemies and detractors round the castle (what wouldn't he have done to Edward Bond?), Brown eventually catches his death. This is in Act Three Scene Two but both Queen and play proceed for two more scenes and become much sprightlier, and not above tossing the odd epigram. But up until the mouldering of John Brown's body, Victoria is not really much fun. She must, she tells us, always have a man to look up to, which is all very credible but not on her own lips. And however smoothly he may rationalise the relationship, Mr Home seems unable to dramatise it. For twenty whole years it stands still and inert. And platonic. Mr Home has, in fact, created a new genre—the royal non-scandal—but one, I fear, of limited fascination to any who do not bring an obsession with Victoria into the theatre with them. Others may find themselves mentally constructing a spicier play, tentatively entitled The Balmoralists.

For acting and production there can be nothing but praise, so let there be nothing.
1968-07-01-the-sleeping-prince:
The Sleeping Prince

Meanwhile there is perturbation but not much music in West Street where countless plays have loped in and out of the St Martin's in the sixteen heart-stopping years that The Mousetrap has stood immovable guard next door. One of these nights, confused by the rapid turnover, I shall wander into the Ambassadors (what can it be like?) by mistake. On occasions, I have felt very tempted.

The Sleeping Prince just misses being one of those occasions. When, a few months ago, I commanded in these pages that some Rattigan be revived forthwith, this play was not quite what I had in mind. Still, the West End is not so rich in good boulevard comedy that we can afford to sneer at even a second-rate example of the genre. The Sleeping Prince is a second-rate example of the genre, and I shall try to bear in mind that we cannot afford to sneer at it.

A Grand Duke, in London for the 1911 Coronation, picks up an American chorus-girl. Had he fancied an English one instead life would have been easier for most of the actresses likely to play the part and for those forced to hear them at it, but she has to be American for the sake of some wide-eyed lines about free speech and democracy. He entertains her to a champagne supper in the Royal Suite of the Carpathian Legation in Belgrave Square, London. At first she takes a dim view of his blandishments (I quote Walter Kerr quoting heaven knows what) but gradually the dim view brightens until, within hailing-distance of the crucial moment, it suffers total eclipse. She passes out (first-act curtain). I know this is predictable; so do you; so, luckily, does Rattigan, and most of the laughs derive from our mutual awareness.

But in Act Two the gurgling has to stop. Showgirl awakens in love with prince and hangs round his neck like a nubile albatross for the rest of the play. This and a spot of consummation apart, the relationship remains static and the play has to be fuelled by diplomatic complications involving the teenage king of Carpathia and determined mainly by the necessity of ensuring a decent time-lapse between interval and curtain-call.

George Baker, an actor who excels in exploring the nuances of stolidity, gives a workmanlike performance as the Grand Duke, which is fine if you like your Grand Dukes to be like workmen. His comic climaxes lack their final éclat but most of the time he has only to express various degrees of exasperation, which he manages with suspicious conviction, though as director and impresario he only has himself to blame. Anyway, the play depends on its leading lady, so sweet, so dumb, and yet so diabolically clever. Susan Hampshire is very sweet, but she is far from dumb, and her skilful endeavours to pretend otherwise weigh down what should be the most enjoyable portion of the play. In the second act, effortlessly disentangling the politics of Carpathia, she is far nearer her element. All the same, her stage appearances are too infrequent to be squandered like this.

The Grand Duke has a Grand Duchess whom Kenneth Tynan once aberrantly described as “the first exceptional human being Rattigan has invented”. She is, in fact, a traditional stage eccentric, absent-mindedly awaiting the services of some grande dame with time to kill. Martita Hunt created the part; it goes now to Jean Anderson, whose sturdy Scots good sense renders it effectively redundant. Two players are in key with their material: David Hutcheson whose English ADC is fortified by years of experience at this sort of thing, and Roger Davenport, the boy-king, who in the nature of things can hardly have been at it so long but never betrays the fact. If someone slips you some free tickets, I should go.
1968-08-01-the-foundations:
The Foundations

There is something unmistakably village-hall about beginning a production with a pop record, and even more so about reprising it at the beginning of each act. But The Foundations is or was a pretty village-hall production anyway, and the record was appropriate on several counts. It was the Beatles' “All You Need is Love”, or at any rate its trick opening; “The Marseillaise”, creaky but recognisable, giving way to the noble sentiments of the title-phrase.

Galsworthy's play is a weird but quite likeable relic, written in 1917 as a jokey forecast of what life was going to be like after the Great War. There was going to be a slump, and something in the nature of an insurrection, here represented by an offstage crowd of dynamic content (demonstrations were obviously not what they are) who indeed sing “The Marseillaise” and are countered by noble philanthropists who believe Dickensianly in kindness. And in love. “There bain't nothin' in life but a bit of lovin'.” Love is all you need. With unthinking brilliance the Beatles have compressed the whole play into fifteen seconds, and for all I know the revival has been staged purely because the record was ready at hand. True, the programme mumbles something about the Galsworthy centenary—but that was last year, wasn't it?

The play moves in neat pincer-fashion (Act 1 The Rich, Act 2 The Poor, Act 3 They Meet), the catalytic agent being the Press, lanky, cheerful and acting someway below its best. It lumbers less than much Galsworthy, and in its portrait of the stumbling, well-meaning aristocrat (Emrys Jones, smiling through) achieves a pleasing ironic balance, a quality for which confused liberals are always good. I hope that irony also underlies the scenes depicting the humble poor, which in this production are a sentimental morass, presided over by a serene Devonshire seamstress (“I sews,” she remarks simply and often) whom Mary Merrall probably makes as little irritating as is humanly possible. The only relief hereabouts comes, improbably, from a brash child unforgivably christened Little Aida, whom a Corona kid called Julie Booth punches across with infectious relish. “One of these days,” someone says, “you'll make an actress”, and I shouldn't be surprised. The others, regardless of rank, hang helpless in the limp grip of the production, which is as diabolical as I've seen in a reputable theatre, if that is what the Arts is. One or two of them deserve it.

Galsworthy's diagnosis of the way in which revolutions are disarmed—sweet words without and sentimentality within—is substantially that of his spiritual descendant Arnold Wesker, only more blandly expressed. It is the bland paternalism that sticks in the throat now. We had the slump and we had the strike (in the reverse order to Galsworthy's, incidentally) and they did not much resemble this genteel charade. If there is a sense of danger in the text, this production has bled it white. I would like to find an excuse for labelling the proceedings The Hindsyte Saga, but I can't, so we'll let it ride.
1968-09-01-revivals-and-the-west-end:
Revivals and the West End

Pendulums regularly swing, and the cry of the immediate post-war years—that the London theatre's mania for revivals was stifling a new generation of dramatists—is heard again in the land. It may be that our theatre moves in ten-year cycles—in the decade beginning 1955 revivals (Shakespeare doesn't count) were apologetic stop-gaps for the rare occasions when a new dramatist had absent-mindedly failed to get himself delivered. By 1961 he was failing with perturbing regularity; Kenneth Tynan noticed, and trouble was obviously in store. After rebuking the new wave for rejecting bourgeois tradition (you never knew where you were with Ken) he paused to remark that there were only three plays on in London more than ten years old, and what had happened to history? At that moment, perhaps, a Dramaturg was born. Anyway, before the appointed ten years were out, he was in a position to do something about it.

He has, too. Fashions may come and go but the English theatre's sacred mission remains what it has always been: to present the plays I want to see in the way I want to see them. The National Theatre has fulfilled the first half of the prescription to near-perfection. And, though it matters little in comparison, they have obviously been plays that a lot of other people have wanted to see as well; the greedy audiences accumulated by the National and the Royal Shakespeare Company probably contribute the most important theatrical phenomenon of the sixties. The commercial managements certainly think so: what lay back of the “dirty plays” row of 1964 but resentment of the fact? Over the last couple of years, they have taken on the subsidised companies at the game. Hence, the revival boom. Peter Bridge, the manager most prolifically responsible, declared flatly last month that revivals were an economic necessity, and no useful purpose is served by arguing with that. Go out and risk your own money instead.

Here, then, follows no diatribe: I myself am an avid consumer of revivals. And, being as honest as I can, I cannot see this as escapism—as being afraid of what new plays might do to me. Most of the time, they don't do anything to me, though as a rule the critics have promised that I will be lacerated, transported, elated, or irrevocably transformed to the marrow of my being. There are not, really, many plays able to do this to me but I live in hope. Such hope can have no foundation when I already know the text; I go without false expectations, and so cannot be disappointed. Add to this an Eng. Lit. grounding which makes the piecing together in performance of dramatic history a positive, pleasurable experience.

To take an example from Mr Bridge's current list: I knew beforehand that Justice was a pretty dead play, and pace Harold Hobson's genuflection to the valiant piety of doing it so as only just to miss the Galsworthy centenary, I knew from the ads (“by the author of The Forsyte Saga”) that it had been mounted as the merest cashing-in job. Never mind, it was heartening to find Galsworthy's programmatic humanitarianism still striking the occasional chord, a dim echo of the Dickensian power to send the reader striding round the room foaming at the iniquity of Chancery and framing passionate letters to the papers about it. Galsworthy has of course, nothing of Dickens' ability to transmute the law into an image of the impersonal inhumanity of society; a pity, since this was the effect he was aiming for—he tells us so, repeatedly, but without ever making us feel it. There is a hint of lumbering power in the pathetic victim's final suicide, but the mechanism that has crushed him is less social than theatrical. Richard Briers' performance is mechanical too, but unavoidably so, since the dramatist shies away from the character throughout—so the play turns into one of those lopsided affairs where the commentator becomes the protagonist; here it's the kindly managing clerk (a stock character, but quite healthy stock) whom Eric Portman underplays to great effect, though his high reputation was surely won in bloodier fields than this.

The dead play has been fitted out in a suitably dead production, but it's a solid funeral. The National would probably have done better by it, but I can't pretend to regret that they didn't bother. If they ever get those twin auditoria and that fifty-play repertory, then maybe; for Galsworthy's 150th. The trial scene at the St. Martin's, though ashen, is a mite lovelier than the glass-boothed one which formerly held that stage.

But though Justice is nice to have seen, if not to see, some of Mr Bridge's other choices jar. I am sufficiently a child of my generation not to be able to face Dear Octopus (largely out of a sneaking suspicion that I would thoroughly enjoy it), and I do not understand the general consensus that it is “brave” to revive Hay Fever so soon after the National Theatre triumph. Just shadow-boxing: and a significant indication of how little of Coward's massive output is revivable (four plays, and here we go round again). But Too True to Be Good—the production which started the whole thing off—was a genuine piece of creative impresage: obscure play, unlikely casting, and total success; in general, Peter Bridge's productions have escaped the tattiness that is endemic to large-cast plays in the West End. In the West End's recent collected edition of the minor plays of Oscar Wilde, his Ideal Husband positively shimmered in comparison with Tennents' erratic Lady Windermere's Fan and John Gale's desperate A Woman of No Importance—opportunism gone completely to seed. Tennents have of course redeemed themselves with The Importance of Being Earnest—had they failed with that play, an era would really have crumbled. I suspect Robert Chetwyn of being a talented director; faced with three out of four less than ideal lovers and a Chasuble and Prism splendidly capable of relegating them all to sub-plot status, he balanced the play impeccably.

Contrary to rumour, the West End has not become a hotbed of all-star classics. The actors have in general been featured second-rankers—married couples are especially popular, possessors of loyaller publics than accrue to most stars in their frantic passage from the film studios to prestige appearances with “the companies”. The plays have been pop favourites angling for the nostalgia of those who caught them first or last time around; the material, when thinned out a bit, of a future classic repertoire but not of ours. The Haymarket's attempt, with The Rivals and The Merchant of Venice to aim beyond this, was a startling reminder of time passed. I do not, Heaven help us, believe that divine inspiration has descended on the Aldwych and Waterloo Road, but how fussy, how thin, how unnecessary these productions seemed, and how slighting (not, maybe, that he bothered) to the great actor at their centre. To have given the finest Shakespearean performance in the worst Shakespearean production, of the last few years, is a paradox peculiarly befitting Richardson. The death of Donald Wolfit, while an inferior Volpone holds court at the Old Vic, should have rung ironic bells in somebody's ears. We still waste talent on a colossal scale.

More so, perhaps, than before. In that first era of revivals, just after the war, the big guns were firing in the West End (Gielgud worked consistently for Tennents and Olivier had a permanent lien on the now defunct St. James's) and, on the whole, at bigger targets. There were even excursions into the hinterland beyond Sheridan—a few Jacobeans and much Restoration, this largely in the hands of John Clements, an actor-manager whose career is a pattern of the whole period. As the Royal Court came in, he went out—in some glory, with a distinguished season of genuine classics at the Saville. During the fervent years, he confined his West End appearances to mainly second-rate modern plays: now he suddenly re-surfaces at Chichester, which under his influence surely counts as an annexe to the West End rather than to the subsidised belt—if only because he too is now concerned mainly with the recent past. Eliot and Wilder are on the bill for this year while last year, The Beaux' Stratagem, once his biggest success of all, went ignominiously under.

The inference is plain. Once it mattered that the West End's energies went into revivals: it mattered because the choice and execution of plays showed those energies to be the best there were. Now, the action is elsewhere; when the National or the Royal Shakespeare blunder (they often do, and this last year has been a honey) we are right to be concerned, for where else do we go? But passion forsook Shaftesbury Avenue long ago, leaving only a variegated collection of shows: when they are good, I applaud—when bad, I shrug. They are likelier to be good when old (to put it in instantly graspable form, the best reason for reviving The Boy Friend is The Four Musketeers!); when the present is arid, one can only cling to the past.

Robert Cushman
1968-11-01-close-the-coalhouse-door:
Close the Coalhouse Door

For me television drama is pre-eminently a dispensable alternative to whatever old movie is playing on the other channel, so all honour to Alan Plater who once hooked me for three successive Mondays with a trilogy called To See How Far It Is. At its best, which was somewhere around its middle, it displayed a notable talent for the elegant facing of painful truths and impressed upon the mind the necessity of judging its author's future work by high standards. Well then, judging by those standards, this particular example of its author's future work is quite disgraceful. It was also one of the half-dozen most entertaining evenings on offer in the London theatre. Let me argue myself out of that one.

It makes only limited sense to consider Close the Coalhouse Door as an Alan Plater play, or as an anyone play. It is the first example to reach London of the regional historical-documentary which is increasingly recommending itself to provincial reps as a means of proving that they are where they are because they want to be. It hails from Newcastle and traces, in the approved comic-strip cum music-hall manner, the fortunes and more especially, the misfortunes of the Northumbrian pit-man over the past two centuries. I wish that that were all it did.

But Mr Plater had to go and fix it up with a framework. He begins with (and rapidly drops) an oleaginous Southern expert who might have been expressly designed to bring out the worst in Ken Wynne; this talented comedian, presented with a weak script, can always be relied on to descend to it. By the quantity of his mugging shall ye know the quality of what he mugs. In this show he plays most of the Establishment-figures so he mugs much, though he does get in a not-bad Harold Wilson towards the end.

But I run ahead of myself. Mr Wynne's expertise is summarily dispensed with, and we are left with the real people who are celebrating a golden wedding, and taking the opportunity to reminisce. The writing here is amorphous and undistinguished, fit to reinforce anyone's prejudices about cosy TV dramatists straying beyond their proper limits. Then suddenly we are in the 1820s witnessing the birth of trade unionism in the pits. The treatment here is based starkly and sensibly on the proposition that a bare recital of the working-conditions of the time still makes the blood boil. Just as we are beginning to get stirred and interested, we are returned to the tedious 1960s, and soon afterwards the lights go up, leaving us to reflect on the wisdom of Shakespeare and Brecht and John Arden and all other dramatists who didn't reckon that the only way to make the past relevant was to keep cutting back to the present.

Occasional songs have helped Act One on its way; and in Act Two they become a good deal less occasional. The General Strike is the period covered, a source apparently of jolly good fun for all. This at any rate is the impression conveyed by the rather haphazard light-heartedness of the treatment, all fun and games and vaudeville. (Most would-be impersonators of Groucho Marx succeed with the walk but can't manage the voice; discuss, with special reference to Bryan Pringle at the Fortune Theatre, and attempt to explain what Groucho is doing in the show in the first place.) Of course the fun is meant to highlight the pain underneath but that would need a much subtler and more accurate counterpoint of theme and treatment than is aimed at here. We are thrown back on the fun as fun, in which capacity it is extremely successful. It only starts wearing thin in Act Three, where contemporary problems get on top of the play and leave it floundering. A paradox is (just about) adumbrated but never explored; if the pit is such a bloody awful job, why weep for its disappearance? The play stops being funny but can't seem to start being serious: the closing song (“It's only a story, a fanciful tale”—irony intended) tries to wipe from our faces a smile that has long since vanished but cannot summon up a scowl to replace it.

Meanwhile the family drama has limped on, partially sustained by an extremely strong performance from John White as a young pit-man half inclined to break out, and brought to the brink by the socially-conscious girl-friend of his college-bred brother.

There remain a mixed but largely enjoyable bunch of songs (by Alex Glasgow) and the riotous performances of three underrated character actors. Colin Douglas, previously known to me as the toughie of innumerable children's serials, turns the paterfamilias into a vastly endearing shambles of a man. He shares the burden of history with two mates who verge on the out-of-this-world. Of course I always knew that Bryan Pringle could gangle, but even expected pleasures sometimes acquire special intensity. I never knew that John Woodvine could sing, and years of watching him being dour, solid and invaluable at the Old Vic, the Mermaid and such had not prepared me for the warmth, passion and humour of his performance here. From now on I want to see him properly used.
1968-12-01-can-t-help-loving-you:
Can't Help Loving You

I don't know if I could cope with a masterpiece at lunchtime. Try me. In the meantime I have descended into Inter-Action's Queensway basement for a forgettable hour of harmless fun. Two workshop improvisations have been knocked up by author-director Neil Hornick into a pair of one-act plays.

Henry introduces us to a quintet of conscientious fun-lovers who discover that one of their number is missing and spend the bulk of the play reacting to the fact. A predictable gamut is run, developing from, roughly, “Henry was the life and soul of the party, how are we going to get along without him?” to “Henry was always the one who spoiled everything, we'd never take him back.” A superficial view might find this obvious and heavy-handed. A superficial view would, on the whole, be correct, but there should be some acknowledgement of the mechanical skill involved. The route is quite persuasively charted, and an impressive number of changes are rung on the simple phrase “I am having a good time”. I didn't have a bad one myself; but I was glad when it stopped. Most of the cast acted loyally. Sandy Macdonald acted well.

I can't be the only person to whom computer dating has seemed for some time a likely subject for a comedy. I know I can't because of Mr Hornick's Can't Help Loving You. In approved comic fashion this takes a potentially funny situation just one step beyond reality. The computer-matched couple arrive for their first date armed with tape-recorders which assume the burden of conversation for them, and are able to sustain it long after the humans have fled the scene and each other. Of course it's amusing to hear people talking in the style of questionnaires (“I am a white male Caucasian between twenty-five and thirty years old”) but it's only one joke. It is also tough on the actors; deprived of dialogue by the march of science they could only hop around trying vainly to achieve a convincing variety of reactions to a single situation. (The first play proved how much easier this is when you have something to say.) What we have here (why should I knock myself out trying to be original?) is an over-extended revue sketch. The comedy remains to be written.
1968-12-01-funny-sunday:
Funny Sunday

Sunday is funny, I spend it reviewing things,
Eating the hours when I could have been doing things.

Plays that are dead and, please God, won't get up again.
Some nervous theatre has purchased a pup again.
Death is a joke, and we all know how gay it is,
Joe Orton lives with the posthumous deities.
Little white wreaths of most flatt'ring sincerity,
Born to the manner but not the dexterity—
Funny Sunday.

“Somehow,” says Florence, in connection with her deceased spouse, “it spoilt the whole day, Alfred popping off like that.” That is the best possible summation of the mood of Funny People, the first of the two plays here, if you'll pardon the expression, commemorated. A casual understated reference to death is always good for a nervously approving titter, though I have yet to hear it raise a healthy laugh. As a comic ploy inter alia it no doubt has a legitimate function but it is thin nourishment for an entire play. It's too easily fabricated for one thing. Even echt Orton (particularly Entertaining Mr Sloane) seemed to me to place monotonous reliance on it, and in imitation Orton it becomes positively oppressive.

I'm a gullible fellow and if you were to tell me that Roy Minton was completely unacquainted with his presumptive master's voice, I would believe you. It is, after all, a small and funny world. But I could not credit such innocence to the management concerned; it is the theatre manager's unquestioned prerogative to be in tune with yesterday's zeitgeist. And really what, in the circumstances, could be more appropriate than a nice little play about necrophilia?

Florence keeps her husband's corpse in the bath, and being a lady of rigorous virtue, gives it not a lascivious thought. Alice, though, is made of frailer stuff, and is soon embarked on a round of what the girl in Black Comedy called “kinky games”. And not just with her own coffined husband, mark you; she covets her neighbour's as well. But it does wonders for releasing her inhibitions which, we are given to understand, were plentiful. They are also, I think, the point of the play. I reserve a particular corner of my loathing for plays whose characters have been called into existence purely as targets for their author's pity or disapproval—in fact, to feed his sense of superiority. (Please note “pity” as opposed to compassion; “disapproval” as opposed to hatred; either as opposed to love.)

For what it's worth, my notes include “Hazel Hughes arranges her clothes authoritatively”. Miss Hughes, of course, does everything authoritatively. More power to her, not that she needs it. Patricia Lawrence offered a remarkably sustained impersonation of Dora Bryan.

Come Sunday was better, even if its characters are called Mr and Mrs Seedy. Mr S is a tramp who speaks in the accents, though not the accent, of Pinter's caretaker. His wife drudges in an East End café and, desperate, has married him on an acquaintance of five minutes. This struck me as a trifle improbable, so a sign flashed up in my compartmentalised critic's mind: Theatre of the Absurd. However, what power the rest of the play had depended on its being taken literally.

Mrs Seedy is systematically humiliated, and sadism is not much fun unless you believe in the reality of the victim. That we did believe was largely due to Gwen Watford who raised the play's routine unpleasantness to the level of real pain as, endlessly battered, she kept returning for more.

The author has obviously worked hard, or hopefully, on the tramp's lines; they are painstakingly demotic, and one is left wondering why they seem so unreal. I can imagine no improvement on Alan Clarke's direction of either play.
1968-12-01-grass-roots:
Grass Roots

An American graduate student once advised me to visit some of her country's small towns instead of just city-hopping. That way, she said, I would understand what, or who, kept Johnson in power. I was irresponsible enough not to take her advice, but I have now been provided with a surrogate. And without having to go any further afield than the stockbroker belt. (And go you and do likewise if the opportunity offers, because it's a very pleasant theatre, easy of access to and from London, with—if this production is representative—a satisfyingly high standard of presentation.)

Grass Roots, which is not about marijuana and ran long and happily off-Broadway as Now Is the Time For All Good Men, which is indisputable if desperate, is not, in theme, style or content, the most original show you are ever going to see. But it has and makes its points. Its hero breezes in from swinging Philadelphia to take up a position as English teacher in Bloomdale, Indiana (population 973), and immediately sets about shocking the community with his new-fangled ideas. They didn't seem very shocking in Leatherhead or, I would imagine, off-Broadway, and what, I ask you, are the show's chances of being seen in Bloomdale, Indiana? This is the kind of question we should all be pondering but not too deeply, lest all our theatres close down at once.

Once upon a time, though it never trespassed upon ours, there was a musical called Bloomer Girl whose emancipated female chorus sang that it was good enough for grandma, that good old girl, but it wasn't good enough for them. In Grass Roots the male and female chorus are of the opinion that it was good enough for grandma (those very words) and that they have no quarrel with it either. At this moment in time, that scene is genuinely frightening. History has played into the authors' hands; the election of a bull-headed sports coach as man of the century becomes almost a metaphor for the barnstorming progress of George Wallace. This makes the indomitable right-minded liberal hero a little less difficult to take; the authors have cunningly employed the love-interest as a means of expressing their own doubts concerning his inflexibility. He frightens off the young widow who gets involved with him, and her point of view is stated with a sympathy that is even extended to the square head teacher who also loves her.

I would like to see a straight play about modern small-town America (not, that is, about a divided family who just happen to live there). Grass Roots goes about as deep as a musical decently can, and surprisingly enough never becomes portentous. There are no stentorian dreamers of impossible dreams. It is also the first musical I have encountered written entirely by women. (Female lyricists are common enough but composers, in this field, almost unheard of.) This is really about the only history it makes; verbally and musically, the songs are generally no more than a pleasant way of passing the time. Nancy Ford, says the programme, spent some time pounding a piano for The Fantasticks and it shows. Her tinkles are less resounding than her model's, though both scores, curiously enough, reach their peak with songs about the rain. This one (“Rain—It's April”) has a haunting title-phrase, and a resourceful structure.

So is the whole show. I don't know where they've been hiding all these years but the entire cast can sing and act. The hero (Stuart Damon) functions admirably in both departments, and the heroine (Eira Heath) even better. (In view of this I felt rather sorry when boy didn't, in the end, get girl. I can't remember when he last did in an American musical. Still, he doesn't die in this one.) Paul Maxwell is excellent as the head, and Bill Kerr, to my delight, plays the coach, and doesn't sound in the least like he used to do with Hancock. The town whore, for whose benefit the score goes mildly rock, is endowed by Marti Webb with a vivacious personality, a demeanour which if not sexy is nothing, and a very loud voice. Anton Rodgers' direction is the height of spruceness, and (I am requested to advertise) can be adjusted for larger halls. I don't think it's by any means sure-fire West End material but seeing it where it was, when it was, I was impressed.
1969-01-01-the-strange-case-of-martin-ri:
The Strange Case of Martin Richter

Every so often I get lucky. I don't suppose that I would have got out to Hampstead to see The Strange Case of Martin Richter had Plays and Players not pushed me into it. To you who were not pushed and so missed it, a treat was denied: the best new play (in itself, admittedly, no great praise) that I have had to review in the last two years.

Martin Richter's case is of a strangeness analogous to that of Jekyll and Hyde. He is a man sleek and civilised enough to be the perfect butler (which is what, in private life, he is) who, for his own purposes, assumes the mark of the beast. Unlike Jekyll's, though, his transformation involves no loss of control; it brings him in fact as near control as he can hope to come. In the name of an organisation known as the National Health Party he leads the domestics in a revolt against the master of the house, whom he proceeds to imprison in a cage, as Tamburlaine did Bajazeth. (I hope you're counting the literary echoes; they're important.) The scene is presumed to be Germany; at any rate, the characters all talk like stock Teutons. The only exceptions are the deposed sovereign (actually some kind of industrialist) and, in his butlering moments, Richter himself. This use of a frankly stagey accent to denote an assumed persona—a persona with which other characters in the play are stuck for real—has, incredibly, brought down on Stanley Eveling's head the accusation that he is dealing, in all seriousness, in racial stereotypes. Of course Brecht sincerely believed that all Caucasian landowners wore masks.

Richter has his own motives for involving himself with the National Health: partly fear (they outnumber him in the household) but more especially revenge. Unknown to them, he is a Swabian. For National Health of course we read National Socialist, and for Swabian Jew. In Eveling's piece the anti-Semitism is real and only the name has been changed to protect the play's comic identity, which could certainly not survive the intolerable emotive effect of the real words. As things are, it survives triumphant, recalling an early and superior Frisch play, The Fire Raisers, lingering in my memory as a blaze of candles on an ill-omened festive table. Martin Richter repeats the image and enriches it; a boar's head glowers out at the audience as the successful conspirators gobble, quaff, and remember the great days. In a moment Richter will proceed to secure his revenge by setting them against each other in approved classical style, and it is a tribute to this author's mastery that he can get us not just to swallow, but to relish, the hoary antecedents of the situation (which even extends to the casually murderous dropping of a knife within reach of two death-locked combatants).

Let me reiterate the levels on which the play has thus far (that is, for two-thirds of its length) succeeded: (a) as pungent political satire, or if you like as a rough allegory of neo-Nazism; (b) as a perfectly acceptable study of the behaviour of grotesque but believable characters—in this respect, Richter himself shows up The Man in the Glass Booth for the hollow conundrum he was; (c) as an essay in irony of language and situation—the writing in the scenes between Richter and his caged but still urbane master is of a quality to make you, if not roar with laughter, then purr with quiet delight; (d) as a brilliant literary exercise, impudently weaving familiar texts and situations into a new and individual fabric; and (e) as an exciting story for whose concluding third I could hardly wait.

In the concluding third, unfortunately, the narrative underpinning lets the structure down.

Michael Blakemore's production matches the play in wit, tension, and inventiveness, and actually surpasses it in narrative lucidity. Leonard Rossiter, whose attributes apparently include the enviable ability to walk effortlessly with his body arched back at an angle of forty-five degrees, solves the problems of playing an outsize character by going out and creating a world of his own, and daring the rest of the play to match up to it.

Tony Steedman, caged or enthroned, is the perfect complement; the poise of this duo probably accounts in some measure for my enthusiasm about the writing of their scenes together.
1969-02-01-mr-and-mrs:
Mr and Mrs

I see from the Sunday papers that Mr and Mrs is (or, if you like, Mr and Mrs are) to be retained for a second week in the West End. Heaven knows to what a pass this lamentable state of affairs may have attained by the time you read this; but, ever an optimist, I shall compose the remainder of this review in the past tense.

These, then, were attempts to musicalise what the programme, with unendearing vagueness, referred to as “the plays by Noël Coward”. Mr in fact derived from Fumed Oak and Mrs from Still Life, and there was no point in trying to disguise the fact, since the bones of each were quite clearly visible through the encrusting fat. You may skip the next paragraph, which is a digression on the advisability of turning plays into musicals.

One assumes that it is being done all the time but as a matter of fact it isn't, and for such forbearance the showmen of the world have only my admiration. Assuming the original to be a workable theatrical mechanism, it is going to get in the way. It can, of course, be spoofed—Shakespeare lends itself very well to this treatment as The Boys from Syracuse and Kiss Me Kate and (I assume) Your Own Thing will bear witness. It can be systematically and ruthlessly rebuilt—as we have seen this year in Cabaret and Golden Boy. But it gets you nowhere merely to punch a few holes in a previously viable structure and plug them with the odd bout of song and dance. My Fair Lady admittedly got away with doing just that but then it's never been one of my favourite musicals, possibly because it contravenes all my theories.

At all events it's a loner. Mr and Mrs was more representative of the results to be expected from slavish opportunism. Mr was the more endurable; at least its central joke—a seemingly docile, downtrodden husband rounding on and forsaking his horrible wife, daughter and mother-in-law—remained recognisable. It went off at half-cock though, for a variety of interlocked reasons.

One was the doughy quality of John Taylor's lyrics which—as is the way of musicals—took over from Mr Coward's original dialogue at crucial and climactic points. It would, of course, take a very brilliant lyricist (Noël Coward for example) to stand the implied comparison, but it's no use whimpering, Mr Taylor should have thought of that in the first place. Another was the acting. Honor Blackman and (surprisingly) Hylda Baker were only half-heartedly awful (or awfully half-hearted), and with such opposition the worm had not far enough to turn. And John Neville is hardly a wormlike actor; he might not have been able to eat that family for breakfast, but he could certainly have disposed of them long before lunch. So his moment of escape by becoming predictable was robbed of some of its glory—not all, since it resolved itself into a sprightly song-and-dance routine which the actor obviously loved doing, and with enough justification to make us enjoy it too. Only the chorus jarred, for their presence was a reminder of the shameless and snobbish inflationary tactics for which they had been utilised earlier; the programme dubbed them “The Faceless Society” and they were meant to illustrate the pitiful universality of the main characters and their drab little lives. They were also, of course, used as padding.

On which cue, enter Mrs, a protracted immolation of what was once Still Life, then became Brief Encounter and here wound up as a classic of shoddiness. Sizeable portions of the original duologues cropped pointlessly up, looking very lonely. It is just possible to see them as the basis of a chamber musical, given the right kind of bitter-sweet (I don't mean Bitter Sweet) score, and sensitive period staging. There is no point in dragging it into the 1960s while the memory of the film (which for most people, even those who haven't seen it, symbolises the entire British cinema of the forties) still remains potent. There is certainly no point in encumbering it with lachrymose ballads which are not even wholeheartedly schmaltzy enough to make good Humperdinck fodder. Above all, there is no point, having retained so much of the original, in harnessing it to a couple of other love-stories, thrown in for multiple audience appeal. For the mums and dads, the elderly courtship and eventual union of a station buffet lady and an engine-driver, enacted with many a knees-up. For the kids, and in some desperation, a much younger buffet lady and her teenage boyfriend, pretexts for the show to take a few tottering steps underground and to come up with a light-show of devastating feebleness: Sunday Night at the Palladium Turns On.

Still, all credit to author-composer-lyricist John Taylor and his triple pronged attack; not every show can manage to reach three separate nadirs in only an hour. As an anthology of all that is worst and apparently (despite the Beatles) irreducible in British pop, it had a certain point. Actually there were one or two moments when the score developed an appealing brassiness, and if I attribute these to the orchestrations of Johnnie Spence, one of the best big-band writers in the country, I am probably being unjust.

So I'm unjust.

I have no idea where Mr Taylor's musical heart may lie: possibly in the Billy Cotton Band Show. Certainly Alan Breeze as the engine-driver seemed more at ease than anyone else on stage. John Neville did his sensitive best by such stray gobbets of Coward as came his way. As a singer (rather than, as in the first half, a putter-over of numbers) he proved uneven; having sailed with apparently justified confidence through three-quarters of a phrase he would come up against a note outside his range and retire momentarily disconcerted. Honor Blackman, whose bounds are narrower yet and narrower, stayed at any rate well within them.

Still, Charlie Girl and The Four Musketeers! have outrun Cabaret, so there is obviously a public for good old British stuff. Certainly the creators of Mr and Mrs have worked hard to provide something for everybody so may I suggest, relapsing reluctantly into the present, that, whatever your taste in musicals, there is something to disappoint you at the Palace.
1969-02-01-the-man-with-a-load-of-mischi:
The Man with a Load of Mischief

Certain shows should be reviewed the morning after or not at all. Writing for a monthly the temptation to control yourself, contain yourself, and try to let tranquillity be your goal can be overwhelming. Having succumbed to it in this instance I find that tranquillity offers very little in the way of recollection. But then Man with a Load of Mischief offered very little in the way of emotion (that much I do remember), belonging as it does, or did, to the tinkly style of musical comedy, staking its all on fragile charm. That which aspires to the condition of gossamer has no kick coming if it is found to float, traceless, out of the mind. I am making the experience sound more agreeable than it was, but in the interim there has been Mr and Mrs, which has exhausted most of my spleen for this month. That was fish-and-chips theatre, and this one has perceptible inclinations towards caviare. They are not fulfilled but the show does occasionally reach the tinned salmon level.

It calls itself “a romantic New Musical” and the appellation has brought the name of Novello down on its head. But nothing so lush has been attempted. The real inspiration would appear to be The Fantasticks, the off-Broadway equivalent of Salad Days, though in longevity it now more resembles The Mousetrap. In its wake there have appeared such slender confections as the present one, small-scale costume intrigues which make no great claim to being funny or anything vulgar like that, but will be happy if you go away with your heart a little warmer and a little more wistfully wise in the ways of love and life.

The settings are mostly European (actually English in this case), thus imparting an air of inverted cultural snobbery, and confronting their original American performers with virtually insoluble problems. For they are being asked not just to adapt themselves to an alien style but to travesty it; to assume outward flourishes which are only meaningful as a means of conveying a corresponding inner substance in works from which the substance has been carefully removed.
