Every number showed a keen eye for specifics in character and situation and he met the challenge of providing seven Merman specialities in one score with great resource. The best lyric, however, goes not to Mama, but to the two daughters she forced on stage to gratify her own ambition, and who cannot wait to be rid of her.

[Song lyric excerpt omitted.]

Mama keeps pets. The deadpan cataloguing of apparently incongruous objects has become a Sondheim trademark.

In this song, too, Sondheim captures a tone of silky bitchiness he was later to explore in some depth. Here it is embryonic, as the girls exhort their already much-married mother:

[Song lyric excerpt omitted.]

During most of the dozen years that have elapsed since Gypsy's Broadway opening, there have been rumours that Merman would be repeating her triumph over here. Even last year they had not been finally stilled (though she was, strictly speaking, too old for the part even in 1959). Now, however, we are to see Angela Lansbury who opens in the show at the Piccadilly Theatre on May 29 with author Arthur Laurents directing.

We have a fair amount of catching-up to do with middle-period Sondheim. We have seen only one of the shows that came between Gypsy and Company - A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum, Sondheim's Broadway debut as a composer and a great success in both London and New York (where it was revived last year), though its music (lightweight, untroubled, easy to listen to and to forget) is both the least distinguished and the least typical he has written. He wrote a far more expansive score for a major flop, Anyone Can Whistle ("full of inventive stage techniques; but it was arch and it suffered from a certain condescension towards the audience"). Throughout all these projects Sondheim's talents were audibly maturing.

Company arrived in 1970, five years after Sondheim's last musical, Do I Hear a Waltz? In the interim Broadway had come up with its nearest approach yet to a serious (as opposed to a solemn or bloated) musical in Cabaret. Flawed though it was, this was a triumph for its ubiquitous producer-director Harold Prince who now performed the same dual function on Company. He and Sondheim, together with librettist George Furth, hit on the ideal form for a modern intelligent musical. Company is a comedy of manners. And, faithful to its genre, it details the capitulation to marriage of an apparently dedicated bachelor. Set, as all musicals really should be, in New York, it gets right to the heart of Manhattan, or at any rate of some variously monied segments of it.

The score is the peak of Sondheim's achievement. The music is sinuous, surprising, vertiginously modern. The wry fruit of Sondheim's own 41 years as a bachelor can be tasted when the hero's married lady friends cluck over his supposed loneliness:

[Song lyric excerpt omitted.]

The soothing accompaniment adds the final touch of patronage (or, possibly, matronage). Even more unnerving is the catalogue of his domestic virtues reeled off by the five ladies and their five husbands, who act both as an unofficial chorus to the show and as the vehicles for its examination of marriage.

Sondheim's own enthusiasm for it is greater than for any of his other shows: "I never get bored by a moment of it. It's full of life, point, joy, guts. It's always fresh to me."

Within a year Company had been joined on Broadway by Follies. As before, the production team comprised Hal Prince, choreographer Michael Bennett, and the superlative designer Boris Aronson, and all three surpassed themselves. Follies is a spectacular production in which the memory of the supposedly carefree musical productions of the Thirties is ironically counterpointed by the frustrations that have overtaken those of their performers who have survived into the Seventies. The setting, aptly enough is a Broadway Theatre on the eve of demolition.

Sondheim's talent for period pastiche is evident in Gypsy and in a couple of numbers in Company, but only in Follies is it given full exposure in a series of minutely accurate recreations of the show songs of the Twenties and Thirties:

[Song lyric excerpt omitted.]

The protectiveness and the preciousness - the sense that falling in love meant the right to try on long words as though they were long pants - are exactly right. And the tune which accompanies is one of its composer's proudest achievements: "I'd challenge anyone to distinguish it from authentic Jerome Kern."

Though he loves the songs of the period, Sondheim has little affection for the shows which encased them, and Follies is, if anything, an exaggerated attack on the cocksure values which the Ziegfeld spectaculars exemplified. Could I Leave You, the reaction of an embittered wife to a husband who has suggested divorce, is in Sondheim's best contemporary style:

[Song lyric excerpt omitted.]

Sondheim is not the first to try this kind of lyric but his predecessors have usually just spluttered in admiration of their own audacity. He is the first to keep his cool and his technique.

That technique amounts here, as in Company, to virtuosity. Consider the wit and economy that can reduce the masochistic ballad formula to the breeziness of a blues song. Or another of Sondheim's laconic catalogues summarising a classic Hollywood career. Or perhaps best of all, the accumulation of evocative detail with which two middle-aged men recall their youth as stage-door johnnies:

[Song lyric excerpt omitted.]

The principal characters of Follies, so richly depicted in the songs, are rather thinly drawn in James Goldman's book. Sondheim defends this on the ground that "they're not really characters, they're essences". But you could have said the same of the lovers in West Side Story, and maybe Follies too is best enjoyed as a celebration of theatre. The title, of course, is double-edged, referring to follies both Ziegfeld and human; in a few years' time, if the musical dates, it could have taken on a triple resonance, and we could be thinking of it as Sondheim's Folly. But follies can be magnificent buildings, and London should have been allowed a look at this one before it was finally dismantled.

Company and Follies have given Sondheim the same position for his generation as Rodgers and Hammerstein had for theirs.

He and his collaborators have broken down technical barriers and restored to the musical the fluidity that was its birthright and which was being buried under trundling narratives. Company has no plot-line and a bizarre time-scheme involving three 35th birthdays for its protagonist; Follies makes successful use of flashbacks and double exposure. They have also followed the path mapped out by the most successful parts of Cabaret and given the musical back to music; the numbers are once again the core of the show instead of having to sneak in between wedges of book.

Sondheim has now written his third show for Prince, A Little Night Music, which opened in New York on February 25 and has already picked up the Tony Award for the season's best musical. The team remains much the same as for Follies, with the addition of a new choreographer, Patricia Birch, and a new librettist, the playwright Hugh Wheeler. Wheeler, following a fashion for making musical plays out of non-musical films, has found his source in the classic Ingmar Bergman Smiles of a Summer Night. The film is comedy veering towards farce, an elegant bedroom pavane, set in turn-of-the-century Sweden. Again it is comedy of manners, though the manners are different from those of Company, and the score - though filled with waltzes, a new departure for Sondheim as a composer - can hardly accommodate the pastiche of Follies. Perhaps to ensure a proper tone, two English comediennes - Glynis Johns and Hermione Gingold - have been cast in the leads. When the show was tried out in Boston somebody was heard to remark in tones of respectful wonder, "It has a beginning, middle, and end, and no-one picks up a microphone." It sounds as though Sondheim has retained his complete technical assurance, and his sense of form.

He is, despite his refusal to write his own books, a natural dramatist, with the dramatist's delight in paradox, in character and in narrative (his declared ambition is "to go on finding new ways to tell stories"). But beyond this he has the great lyricist's delight in the sheer flavour of words and rhymes: Elaine Stritch's big belting number in Company may illustrate it best of all:

[Song lyric excerpt omitted.]
1973-06-03-gypsy-triumphant:
Gypsy triumphant

Something remarkable is currently happening at the Piccadilly Theatre. That is not opinion, it's fact: on Wednesday night I witnessed a standing ovation accorded to Angela Lansbury by a second night audience.

The cheers were provoked, I think, by the show's closing 15 minutes. For most of its length Gypsy is a very good musical; at its close, it reaches greatness. We have watched Miss Lansbury as a selfish and bone-stupid theatrical mother, steam-rollering her two luckless young daughters through the death throes of vaudeville. Gradually, but not grudgingly, we have come to admire her resilience, and to sympathise with her bewilderment as both girls desert her.

One runs off to become a real actress; the other achieves fake stardom as the stripper Gypsy Rose Lee, and immediately sets about banishing her mother from her dressing-room and her life.

Suddenly it's Mama's turn. A light-studded platform has been shunted across the orchestra pit, annihilating the distance that generally separates a musical from its audience. She strides on to it to try her own hand as a performer. She falters, weighted down by memories of the past, and her failure is Miss Lansbury's acting and singing triumph. She stops the show. The effect is devastatingly direct and as moving as anything to be seen in London.

Robert Cushman
1973-06-17-noh-to-vanbrugh:
Noh to Vanbrugh

THEATRE

Robert Cushman on a week of classic plays.

THERE has hardly been a play to be had this week much below the age of 300. It began, appropriately, with the Umewaka Noh Troupe, concluding their two-week season at the Aldwych.

I found them very restful, and less boring than many groups supposedly more accessible. It is heartening anyway, at a World Theatre Season, to meet with visitors so far outside our comprehension as to be beyond the reach even of simultaneous translation. Free of those crackling translations and their monotone messages, we could attend to the sound of the actors' stockinged feet upon the polished wooden floor, as much a part of the spectacle as the masks, the silken gowns, the chanting, and the guttural croakings that are the nearest these Japanese actors come to expressing recognisable emotion (though having once seen one of last week's plays in an English translation, I can testify that, divorced from its traditional presentation, Noh drama can be made to yield explicit emotional content).

While I doubt that the Umewaka troupe have taught our theatre much that it did not, in theory, know already about the strengths of formality and simplicity, it is pleasant to see the theories put so thoroughly into practice. It is pleasant, too, to have a demonstration of the basic principles of comic relief. Sandwiched between each pair of Noh dramas is a short farce; after half an hour of masked solemnity, the impact of a human face--emitting sounds that could only be human laughter--is almost physical.

Once there were modern-dress productions of Shakespeare. They were delightfully shocking, meticulously detailed (telephones always figured prominently) and only done occasionally, so as to jolt the audience out of their presumed complacency. They look, in photographs, extraordinarily dated. These days a new convention has taken hold. Pop has come among us, and, by introducing a style of clothing that is tied to no particular period, but thrives on joky anachronism, it has made casual, timeless Shakespeare a possibility. Two Gentlemen of Verona was cast in this mould, both at its most recent Stratford appearance and in the current rock version; so was As You Like It, first with an all-male cast at the National Theatre, and now in a new production at Stratford.

The style only obtrudes itself where, logically, it should be most useful. A unisex costume for Rosalind would seem to be the perfect solution to the problem of her male disguise. In her tight-fitting jacket and jeans, she could just as easily be a boy as a girl. She could, however, just as easily be a girl as a boy and I have never felt less inclination to suspend my disbelief.

Eileen Atkins has a wary, fine-drawn talent, and there is one corner of Rosalind--the mordant satirist of romantic attitudes--of which she takes complete possession. But the undertow of erotic abandon is barely there at all, and even the irony is muted. At moments, David Suchet's vigorous, confident Orlando (an understudy performance, calling for no indulgence whatever) was running rings round her and, in this play, that is the wrong way round for rings to be run.

Miss Atkins delivers the epilogue splendidly (with the houselights up as they should be), but the end of the play inevitably suffers at the moment from the ankle-injury which keeps her out of the final marriage-dance (as it nearly kept her out of the first night altogether). By this time, anyway, Buzz Goodbody's direction has run out of steam. She clearly recognises the importance of the marriage theme, but her methods of underlining it are tired. Grinning supers fling confetti into the house, and the audience gamely grins and wishes it would all go away.

These tactics spoil an agreeable lightweight production which has little to say on the play's main themes (court or country?--you choose), but makes good sense of individual scenes. The mod trappings are a great help to Brian Glover, puffing with professional pride as Charles the wrestler, and they work well, too, for Clement McCallin's icily capricious Duke Frederick. When we reach the forest, it is a great comfort to find it in the charge of Tony Church, a pipesmoking banished Duke, mercifully unembarrassed by his own pronouncement. Particularly telling is his rebuke to the cynically moralising Jaques: "For thou thyself hast been a libertine/As sensual as the brutish sting itself. . ."

Who would have guessed that Shakespeare had Malcolm Muggeridge's number so accurately?

In Richard Pasco's hands, Jaques becomes almost the central character of the play--paradoxically, really, since he spends most of his time prowling its periphery, peering at the action with beady distaste through rimless glasses. The mere sight of the amorous Touchstone and Audrey sends a visible shudder through him. I sympathised; they are played grossly enough for me to contribute a few winces myself.

For an even richer study of an Elizabethan malcontent, you go--reasonably enough--to The Malcontent; John Marston's play has now come from Nottingham to London's Bankside Globe Playhouse.

The experience is not without hazard, since neither playhouse nor play is innocent of chilly gaps in its structure. Shakespeare was almost unique among his contemporaries in knowing how to pace himself. In this piece, the work of an inchoate satirist whose quest for moral certainties finally took him into the Church, words and events tumble out, still knotted together and at breakneck speed.

Breakneck is the word. This is the conventional English idea of an Italian Renaissance Court, every man someone else's hired assassin, and yet--for once--every character ends up alive. The play is a comedy or, as Jonathan Miller has chosen to direct it, a satiric farce. His court is an assemblage of shadowy white-faced grotesques; setting and costumes suggest gorgeousness gone into decay. The treatment is sometimes too insistent; these dramatists were prone to sudden changes of gear, and Marston probably intended some of his twists of plot to be a good more than a giggle. The play, like many of its age, including the genuine revenge dramas of Webster and Tourneur, is apt to slide into parody with disconcerting speed; Mr Miller hardly ever lets it slide out. But he has accurately located the play's lunatic gusto and has, more surprisingly, done serious justice to its fits of morality.

Mr Miller's style is well suited to a cast generally stronger on enthusiasm than finesse. Hazel Hughes's old bawd is irreproachable, and there can be no reservations at all about Derek Godfrey. This malcontent is another banished duke, but one who has no intention of waiting for his supplanter to be converted by an old religious man (though he gets him to impersonate one). Mr Godfrey is always a witty, stylish actor; sometimes he lets loose a gleeful demon who, on this occasion, has one of his richest outings ever.

I would have welcomed his irruption during a leaden revival of Vanbrugh's The Provok'd Wife (Greenwich), which gets us as far as the 1690s. Next week I hope to venture into the twentieth century.
1973-06-24-two-from-the-critics:
Two from the critics

Theatre

by Robert Cushman

I CLOSED last week with a promise to drag this column into the twentieth century. I was not rash enough to specify the 1970s, but I had hopes. They were pinned to two of my fellow reviewers with plays of their own about to appear. Broken reeds. In The Houseboy (Open Space), Irving Wardle offers sensitive transportation to the nineteen-fifties; in Sing of the Times (Vaudeville), Jeremy Kingston exhibits some of the typical humours of the sixties.

Mr Kingston's is the lighter play but the more serious offence, since it clearly suffers from delusions of contemporaneity. (This despite a pianist in the pit tinkling out the message that this is the dawning of the age of Aquarius: Hair arrived here in 1968 and it was already receding then.) Mr Wardle at least matches form to content, and period to both.

His play has the feel of autobiography, like most works about gauche, serious young men. John, 25 years old, recently down from Oxford, currently a music student, works as a scullion in a London hotel run by two middle-aged homosexuals. Their relationship is fraying ("two old hot-water bottles wrinkling up together"), and John, foreseeably, serves them as a battleground. For the first time he finds himself possessed of power; he begins, not altogether amiably, to grow up.

Mr Wardle easily makes us free of John's mind--too easily since the play works best when he remains a sounding-board for his patrons. John is most satisfying when most opaque; Philip Donaghy's silences are far more compelling than the glimpses we are clumsily offered of his inner life. When he quotes Shakespeare, at moments both frequent and inopportune, we can--unless I am being fanciful--observe a drama critic in the making; Mr Donaghy makes this eventual metamorphosis seem a very likely prospect. But the real interest resides with the rival queens. Mr Wardle has given them some neat dialogue and a ration of emotional depth; Nicholas Selby (who explodes) and Timothy West (a slow fuse burning beneath an ominously level surface) handle them efficiently.

The play's period flavour has one piquant aspect. No actual English play of the fifties ever managed to treat homosexuality so unflappably. The club theatres of the period (which would surely have been patronised by Mr Wardle's odd couple had he not drawn them as ballet-fanciers) were full of shrill, martyred approaches to the subject. The West End was as rife with plays whose authors, by way of obeisance to the Lord Chamberlain, disguised or discarded any homosexual relationships among their characters, and gravely impaired their credibility-rating as a result. One of the last playwrights from whom this homage was extracted (over a play called No Concern of Mine) was Mr Kingston. In his new piece he makes sacrifice to another of the theatre's antique deities, the god (surely not Eros, despite his convenient location) of West End sex comedy.

Before word spread of sexual revolution, this genre had a certain point. The author's ingenuity, and the audience's presumed censoriousness, combined to keep the bedroom door closed, and the heroine outside it. Now she is allowed in but, since nothing else in the play has changed, her emancipation seems remarkably incongruous. The artificial, asexual ambience is not to be transformed merely by allowing Kenneth More to make jokes about virgins. It appears, if you please, that he knew one once who worked for The Observer.

A lot of the jokes concern newspapers. So, in a way, does the plot, which presupposes--with more confidence than is strictly justified--a universal craze for all things astrological. Even The Times gets itself a stargazer, in the comfortably crumpled shape of Mr More. But since he only takes the job in order to influence the ladies in his life, both of them avid horoscope-heads, the comedy of gullibility dies at birth, and another evening is spent hovering round the bedchamber without so much as a maidenhead at stake. Sometimes people come in and tell us about the exciting things happening in the outside world, like in Greek tragedy.

The sad thing is that Mr Kingston does have some comic gift (he goes for the smart rattle where Mr Wardle is more your sombre ironist) and that he must have known, from his own critical experience, the kind of stereotype to which his idea was being reduced. Mr More, who has brought the art of passive comedy to a very high pitch, is a continual consolation. He is that treasurable phenomenon, the straight man who gets all the laughs. Not even Frankie Howerd is more adept at thinking of an entendre and then doubling it.

  

Strictly speaking, there are more laughs to be had at the Vaudeville than in Nuts (Theatre Workshop), but the latter has a cleaner smell. This show defies criticism. Songs and sketches by Joan Littlewood's regular troupe alternate with personal appearances by real East London journalists, whose speeches--whether attacking property developers or just hawking the Socialist Worker--are the best things in the evening, and the only occasions on which those delivering the material display any faith in it. As community theatre, this is totally honest. There is no attempt to pass propaganda off as drama, and none of the masturbatory quality of actors trying earnestly to act local.

But the ineptitude of most of the numbers passes belief. Some of the sketches might be salvageable, but there is no telling since few of the performers are bothering anyway. Well, at least they're relaxed. Kent Baker does Mae West to a nice turn ("Where's your Danny La Rue this noo") and Bill Wallis, a bearded roly-poly pudding of an actor, alone displays the anarchic offhandedness which presumably is the goal throughout.

  

At the Young Vic, an evening of Beckett Shorts (presumably to be worn with Tom Stoppard's Jumpers) is most noteworthy for a performance of Play which discovers a vein of humour missing from the original National Theatre production, and for the transformation of Krapp's Last Tape into a videocassette. How could he possibly have afforded the equipment?

  

Back to the Aldwych, to round off the World Theatre Season, come the Zulus in Umabatha. The dancing is the thing, to be relished without much reference to the Macbeth storyline, though the ceremonial does make you understand why a man might kill to become king. The original is closely followed, so don't bother to hire a translation receiver. I picked mine up to check out the hero's state of mind and found him wondering if that was an assegai he saw before him. As I suspected.
1973-09-02-a-chekhovian-powerhouse:
IF THE author of The Wood Demon (Lyceum, Edinburgh) will just step along to my room, I shall explain to him how he may reassemble the elements of his immoderately exhilarating play into not just one masterpiece, as he might expect, but four. I shall do this (the author, one Chekhov, being safely dead) with the aid of an invaluable critical tool known as Hindsight.

In this Actors' Company production The Wood Demon, previously regarded only as a rough draft for Uncle Vanya, stands revealed as the great Chekhovian seed-bed. It foreshadows The Seagull in its alphabetical progression of broken hearts (A loves B who actually prefers C who is languishing for D); the luncheon party at which these emotional tangles are revealed to us looks like a trial run for the first act of Three Sisters. As for Dr Kruschov, the wood demon himself, his passion for forest preservation inaugurates the symbolic pattern that was to be completed with the laying of the first axe to that cherry orchard in which all Russia was prefigured.

But the play also looks backward, to the one-act farces on which Chekhov's playwriting skills were originally honed. The blustering soldier Theodore (who afterwards merged with the wood demon to produce Astrov, the hard-drinking medico-ecologist of Vanya) is a descendant of the tactless wooers of The Bear and The Proposal. There is nobody in the mature plays anything like as funny--or so I thought as I watched Robin Ellis, striking classical poses in bushy beard and blanket, and radically extending my view both of his range and of Chekhov's.

If the comedy in this play is more broadly conceived than in Vanya, the tragedy is more compressed, but also more direct. Where Uncle Vanya, at the climax of his desperation, tries unsuccessfully to shoot the Professor who has exploited him, his prototype here, Uncle George, tries successfully to shoot himself. Vanya spends the last act of his play in a hideous awareness of futility; George spends it in his grave, virtually forgotten by those who survived him. The play moves into a vein of romantic comedy; two elusive couples are hurriedly brought together at the final curtain. In David Giles's production these pairings are uproarious and slightly unreal, like Moliere's happy endings. Suddenly we remember that George is dead, and that the Professor's wife, Helen, who in this play makes a half-hearted attempt to escape her husband, has gone with docility back to her fate. Kruschov's diatribes (which included a generous measure of self-hatred) against the surrounding second-rateness ring ironically when we see him abruptly dismissed to happiness.

The irony is, of course, refined by our memories of the later play, which we can hardly expunge. They are actually encouraged by the quality of this production, the first Chekhov I have seen to approach the National Theatre Vanya of a decade ago. To watch the shooting scene in that production, or the reconciliation of Helen and Sonya, was like assisting at the realisation of a myth. In The Wood Demon the same episodes are played out almost word for word, but the diffuseness of the surrounding action prevents them from having a comparable effect.

However, if this dramatic powerhouse, which fuelled Chekhov for the rest of his career, has too much energy for its own immediate purposes, that is hardly a fault at which to repine--not, at any rate, with this cast. Tenniel Evans's hollering Uncle, Ian McKellen's mercurial forest-freak, and Robert Eddison's unreachable Professor constitute, with Mr Ellis's grandiloquent Cossack, as formidable a male quartet as I remember; John Woodvine, suave on the sidelines, comes in a good fifth. The girls are less impressive, but the sharp corners of action and dialogue (strongly emphasised in Ronald Hingley's translation) are negotiated with dashing adroitness. The craft of Mr Giles's direction is impeccable, but it is the performances that register.

Our National Theatre recently announced the engagement of half a dozen associate directors, with barely a word of who is to do the acting. The attitude this represents is now the theatrical norm; with this production, a year after their inception, the Actors' Company acquire the authority to supply a necessary corrective.

The other main Festival offering this week has been a version of Buchner's Woyzeck, offered matinees only in the Assembly Hall by the Young Lyceum Company, the junior branch of the Edinburgh Rep. Since Buchner himself died at 23, play and players might seem excellently matched, but Woyzeck is in spirit the oldest young play ever penned, and its ashen disillusion is beyond these actors' reach. As individuals, that is; when they function as anonymous members of a unit under the Romanian director, Radu Penciulescu, they can be numbingly impressive.

Early on, Mr Penciulescu has them lie down all over the stage, the field of the living dead. The only two actors left upright step among them, swapping images of gloom. As their conversation ends, drums sound: the prostrate cast beat an accelerating tattoo on the floor. For this effect, I felt I could forgive much; but as the afternoon ground on I began to repent of my charity. "Not so fast, Woyzeck," says the tyrant Captain at the start of the play, but he seems to have dictated the pacing throughout.

Buchner leads naturally (as he did historically) to early Brecht. Drums in the Night, poor B.B.'s second play, has been staged at the Traverse, whence it will shortly transfer to the Hampstead Theatre Club. I recommend it, though not without misgivings. Roland Rees's production seems imbued initially with the playful spirit which Brecht demanded but rarely obtains and which, if anything, intensifies his savagery. That savagery was still nihilistically indiscriminate when he wrote Drums; only when he revised it in East Berlin after the war did he point it in an approved political direction. But Brecht's second thoughts are not in the same league as Chekhov's. C. P. Taylor has adapted the play by following in the master's revisionist footsteps and then imprinting a few of his own, but thinking to sharpen the play's claws, he has actually pared them. There are residual ironies in the text which the relentlessly partisan production refuses to countenance; the acting meanwhile grows increasingly strident.

Dear old Uncle George attributed his downfall to his sense of irony; the contemporary theatre seems in little danger of succumbing to the same disease. Michael Almaz's Chicago Sunday School for Anarchists (Poole Theatre, lunchtime) is a possible exception; I assume Mr Almaz intends his schoolmistress with her dreams of dynamite (a left-wing Jean Brodie, or so it seems in Edinburgh) to share the responsibility for disaster with the fascist cop who opposes her.

The Poole and the Traverse are Edinburgh fixtures. The transient bulk of the Festival fringe is suffering this year from a bad attack of the Christopher Robins; everybody has gone down with Alice. Dodging all the plays by, from or about Lewis Carroll wound up with the Brontes. For the second time this year they failed to hold me past the interval, but Richard Crane's Thunder (Bradford University Drama Group), though fearfully overlong, has some good jokes and this time I forsook the sisterhood, if without regret, then also without malice.
1973-09-09-defeated-by-congreve:
Defeated by Congreve

THEATRE

Robert Cushman on a revival of 'Way of the World.'

FIRST it is necessary to mop up after the Edinburgh Festival. During their two weeks at the Lyceum the Actors' Company followed 'The Wood Demon' with The Way of the World; both productions are now embarked on a provincial tour (for the next two weeks they are at the Arts Theatre, Cambridge). Having been elevated by Chekhov, the company were brought down a few bumps by Congreve. Such has been the way of this world for a good two and a half centuries.

David William's production can claim an honourable place in the doom-stretching line of good tries. That is not nothing; and for its first scene I had even higher hopes of it. The action has been advanced from the close of the seventeenth century to the beginning of the twentieth; in the cool spaciousness of a St James's club, the sparring of Fainall and Mirabell has a deliberate casualness which is both dangerous and appropriate. Robin Ellis's Fainall is a robust schemer and hypocrite; Edward Petherbridge's Mirabell is barely more likeable or trustworthy, but his fastidious pallor commands respect. In a battle of styles he could be the one to back; and since that is largely what the play consists of, this establishment of the combatants should yield valuable dividends.

They fail, however, to accrue. It is difficult for any director to keep the thread of a personal duel through the labyrinth of Congreve's plotting, and Mr William gets lost with his predecessors. The antagonists prove unequally balanced, and the choice of period unduly favourable to the villains. Fainall's Victorian mustachios seem to grow curlier by the minute, while he plays a series of vigorous duets with Paola Dionisotti's striking Mrs Marwood. These two characters, traditionally dismissed as mechanical creatures of intrigue, are emerging as the most convincing in the play. We are no longer scared or sceptical of melodrama, and their disregard of finer feelings works positively to their advantage.

For this play's finer feelings are notoriously difficult to convey, wrapped up as they are in the sad brilliance of its style. Passion, say the critics, underlies it all, but the passion of the schemers is far easier to realise than that of the lovers. Mirabell figures in both guises: Mr Petherbridge is a curiously detached actor and the distance which he so effectively maintains in his dealings with Fainall or the play's various fops is scarcely reduced in his courtship of Millamant. Caroline Blakiston (who enters pastoral-fashion, carrying a shepherd's crook like a large Bo-Peep) brings warmth and poise on with her, but little sense of erotic challenge: 'What would you give that you could help loving me?'--that line, with its combination of cruelty and tenderness, is the heart of the play; their ability to feel and inspire such emotions constitutes the true victory of Millamant and Mirabell over their adversaries. Neither Miss Blakiston's delivery of the line nor Mr Petherbridge's response to it has left any impression on me. (She, at least, is battling against historic odds; radio be thanked, even junior citizens now know how Edith Evans sounded in the part.)

Other complaints: the later settings look both fussy and cheap, and the same adjectives may serve for the playing of the fops (especially Witwoud), whose scenes can and do drag horribly. Help is to hand in a lively posse of servants, and in John Woodvine's Salopian intruder who, in what Arnold Bennett called the great cause of cheering us all up, does noble battle with a tiger-skin rug.

  

Stanley Eveling is one of the few current dramatists to whom one turns with a positive expectation of pleasure: his Union Jack (and Bonzo) (Traverse) was predictably the brightest new play of the Festival. For much of its length I felt some resentment at its apparent slightness; I laughed but nothing grabbed me. By the end, however, Mr Eveling had fashioned from his Boy Scout extravaganza a chilling image of alienated youth. Very alienated and very young: just a couple of pubescent schoolkids knifing their piggish elders and gleefully shouting their four-letter word for the day.

The seniors nearly justify such blithe contempt; the only honest soul among them is the scoutmaster, Union Jack himself, a hung-up adolescent of 40 or so, depicted by Richard Ireson with a caricaturist's unflinching conviction. You can almost smell his 'halitosis.' Katy Manning makes a dazzling addition to Mr Eveling's impressive gallery of nymphets (fantasies of juvenile seduction almost invariably furnish the most persuasive scenes of his plays) and Susan Carpenter draws a sharp, resonant picture of a district nurse who, to judge from the debauched angle at which her cigarette slouches from her lips, is clearly in training for matron of St Trinian's. Mike Ockrent's production makes exuberant use of the Traverse stage.

  

Returning to London, I can add little to other critics' findings on An Inspector Calls (Mermaid); like them I responded to J. B. Priestley's mastery of traditional stagecraft, agog to know what happened next or, since this inspector is concerned to elucidate the truth of past events, what happened last. I responded, too, to much of the acting in Bernard Miles's production: Philip Stone, his entry fittingly preceded by a cry of 'Give us some more light,' is so perfectly the police inspector, so unassuming and yet so authoritative with his bald head, his raincoat and his gentle disdain for plutocratic pastimes, like golf, that we will willingly accept him as a symbol of anything the author chooses (and, man, he chooses). The family he investigates is notably tough at the top--Campbell Singer as the cocksure industrialist and especially Elizabeth Tyrrell as his genteel armour-plated wife.

The family smugness proves impenetrable; so much so that a second inspector is required, and is on the way as the play ends. Gogol closed The Government Inspector on an identical note, but for him it was a comic climax and his instinct was surely correct. Mr Priestley has had to work hard to keep laughter out of this piece (despite some facile ironies of the kind associated with his 'time' plays), and this, coupled with the relentlessness of his reiterated if humane message, makes for a thinness in texture.

  

Finishing Touches (Apollo) is an American comedy about a menopausal marriage, whose central role has been Anglicised for Wendy Craig; she should have declined the compliment since her lines are still recognisably American and she is landed with all the wrong rhythms. The author, Jean Kerr, once wrote a book called Please Don't Eat the Daisies, about how it felt to be the wife of a theatre critic; since I might one day be married to the wife of a theatre critic this seemed to me amusing and useful information. After Finishing Touches, which is neither amusing nor useful, I no longer want to know. The author's husband, Walter Kerr of the New York Times, once wrote, 'Some plays are so bad you don't even feel like a drink afterwards.' Finishing Touches is a play for abstainers.
1973-09-16-wolf-from-hungary:
Wolf from Hungary

I HAVE no wish to keep The Wolf from the door of any London theatre; indeed, the sooner this Oxford Playhouse production comes to town the brighter town will be. All the same, I have to present intending patrons with a stark choice: either you see the play or you read this review.

I cannot, I fear, discuss this play intelligibly without giving away its surprises. Its narrative twists are not the only pleasures it provides, but they are substantial--if that word may be permitted of a play which is largely concerned with manipulating levels of fantasy. In this connection the expertise of Ferenc Molnar, the Hungarian master of the boulevards who wrote this piece in 1914, prompts comparison with that of Jean Anouilh. I admire much of Anouilh's work, but despite his reputation for theatricality I have found no moment in his plays as arresting as the revelation at the end of Act II of The Wolf that the preceding scene has taken place inside the heroine's head. The information is craftily, economically conveyed. One is momentarily bewildered, then accepts it as a coup de theatre; only in the course of Act III does the psychological accuracy of this dream-sequence finally become apparent.

In the first act we have witnessed this heroine dining with her husband in a restaurant, and seen his jealousy aroused (not that it is ever exactly dormant) by the sight of one of her old admirers. After the interval we find the couple preparing to attend a diplomatic reception; and still embroiled. She unearths an old letter from her former swain in which he promises to return to her some day--as a soldier, a diplomat, an artist or a mere servant. We next meet her, duly arrived at the party, exposed and succumbing to the allurements of just such a quartet. Each appears in turn, and each exactly resembles her cast-off lover.

Here Molnar's manipulation of his audience is at its most magisterial. When the second suitor appears as the double of the first, we are bemused, and begin to hunt for realistic explanations. At the third appearance we think we see the dramatist's game and agree to play it with him. A similar stage of tacit connivance is reached in An Inspector Calls, but Molnar's strategy is more audacious than Mr Priestley's. There is a traditional understanding that running gags come in threes; when we are faced with the fourth mutation--the suitor as servant--we catch our breath. (We do; I heard us.) It is at this point that the dreamer awakes (and decides that it might be best after all not to go to the ball) and the release, though a theatrical shock, is as necessary for us as for her.

Frank Hauser's 17 years as director of the Playhouse (now sadly about to end) have never been notable for ensemble playing. His achievement has been to bring distinguished texts to the light, and to attract star players to their service. On this occasion the simultaneous (and well directed) presence of Judi Dench, Leo McKern and Edward Woodward renders the gaps below the top level fairly harmless.

Our theatre is not short of clever comediennes: Miss Dench is special because her brittleness is always an abstraction from a hard core of common-sense. She is thus able to combine the lady's languorous visions (happily flaunting her flunkey to the horror of Budapest society) with the practicality that can eventually send her lover on his way and out of town. She is, if you like, a classic bourgeois hypocrite, and the play could certainly be accused of coquetting with adultery while saving itself for marriage. The denouement on the surface could hardly be cosier; so why does the final curtain descend on the husband, alone and in tears?

The answer is supplied by Mr McKern, who plays the eternal cuckold in his own imagination, unable to credit his wife's fidelity in a world full of wenching hussars, seeking always to buy himself into her favour. He is a man of outward substance and inner vertigo. Finally confronted by his supposed rival he takes firm hold of the back of a chair and promptly loses his balance.

These are two consummate performances. When the wind is to Woodward the air is somewhat thinner; playing the lover in his various guises he is constrained to offer a string of what I can only call tours-de-farce. All are funny (a haughty impersonation of Mario Lanza brings the house down), but I still wait to see on stage the relaxed, compassionate, humorous actor who once shone out on television in an Evelyn Waugh trilogy.

  

The Actors' Company (currently at the Arts, Cambridge) offer at certain lunchtime and late-night showings a double bill of new plays. The first half did little to allay my suspicions, aroused by their Iris Murdoch premiere last year, of this company's susceptibility to the spuriously literary: Gabriel Josipovici's Flow intercuts five reminiscent monologues, a line at a time. Banality chopped up and counterpointed is still banal.

Edward Petherbridge's stage version of R. D. Laing's Knots is likewise fragmented, but here each segment makes a point. A wry, humorous and occasionally desperate image accumulates of the slippery delusions that clog up human relationships. Mr Petherbridge's brilliant production is a company showcase packed with surprises; we learn that he himself is a virtuoso mime, that Caroline Blakiston can play the organ, and that John Moreno can do almost anything.

  

There is more good company acting in And They Put Handcuffs on the Flowers (Open Space): Malcolm Storry, Anthony Milner and Ian McDiarmid hurl themselves with anthropoid abandon into Fernando Arrabal's demonstration that prison can be good sadomasochistic fun. The arresting title phrase is Garcia Lorca's; and due tribute is paid to his death at the hands of a Franco firing-squad. The play's intentions are of the best; Arrabal wrote it at the request of the Madrid prisoners whose incarceration he shared for 25 days in 1967, to tell the world of the conditions they endured. But, faced with the enticing prospect of actually writing about three men in a cell, this Peter Pan of the avant-garde goes all giggly. There are one or two passages of authentic horror, but there are many more (priest-baiting, excremental reveries and phallic frolics) which play like private jokes. Most unforgivable is the bonelessly reverential treatment accorded to the play's lone activist, who is most respectfully groomed for martyrdom. It seems that jail doesn't humiliate everyone after all; insulated from all the buffoonery he even gets to keep his clothes on. He represents the gesture to commitment of an apolitical talent, forcing itself to keep a straight face.

  

At least the production (by Arrabal himself) is physically and scenically striking. You look in vain for such attributes in The Cilla Black Show (Palladium), except in the performance of Philippe Genty & Co., invisible puppeteers who contrive a bewitching dance for a trio of emus, one of whom keeps burying his beak in the pink feather-duster that serves him for a body. Nobody else on stage evinces this becoming bashfulness. The star herself, as healthily winsome as ever, sings her older hits very well. Either that, or sixties nostalgia is on its way and I am its first victim.
1973-10-14-gay-times-for-the-cia:
Gay times for the CIA

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on two very different products of the American theatre.

FOR their new experimental season at The Place, the Royal Shakespeare Company have abandoned the steeply banked arena seating that they adopted there two years ago. The actors now face the audience conventionally head-on; most directly they face the critics who, on first nights, are lined up in front in what must look from the stage like Murderers' Row.

This week a new American comedy called Section Nine came up before the bench which was seen, at various points in the evening, to shake with laughter. There were other points, though, at which it trembled with irritation.

Philip Magdalany has given us the latest specimen of doomsday comedy, a genre whose rules were firmly established some years ago by Dr Strangelove. An apocalyptic global threat is posited, generally with a severe time limit, and the action consists of frantic attempts to defuse it. In this case an absentee scientist (a multiple Nobel prize winner and refuser; some kind of genius) has the vital formula tattooed on his penis. Since it is only legible when he has an erection, the CIA faces a double imperative: (a) to find him--no easy task since he has had plastic surgery (on his face, stupid, go wash your mind out with soap); and (b) to arouse him. This also is no cinch, since the discovery that his girl-friend of three years standing has been keeping elaborately mechanised government tabs on him has turned him off women and American Intelligence has apparently no homosexual agents to call upon. It has, however, a system for creating them--the eponymous Section Nine.

The induction into this bizarre training-scheme of three reluctant anti-heroes is, to some extent, the matter of the play, though to exactly what extent Mr Magdalany never quite decides. He has a lot of plot-threads to handle, and somehow he has to weave them all into a second-act situation out of Feydeau. All the characters are brought together in a bath-house (some more logically than others) and proceed to chase one another through its cubicles as unrestrainedly and amusingly as if they were in a French hotel. But Mr Magdalany cannot maintain this farcical vein for very long, and his ending, designed to establish a connection between sexual and political up-tightness, is a mess.

The crappiness of the text is reflected in Charles Marowitz's production, which is crisp and soggy by disconcerting turns. The cast, like many intelligent British actors, give off a generalised impression of knowing all about America (especially in its Terry Southern States), but fall down on embodying it in detail. Their performances are consequently patronising, as if they have pre-judged the characters. Harry Towb, who hits an accurate note of buttoned-down hysteria, is an exception; so, to an extent, is Geoffrey Hutchings as the most craven of the recruits. But even Colin Blakely, after a splendid introductory grin, makes a generalised sort of general. David Waller adapts his usual steam-rollering performance to a Senator from Texas (I go by the LBJ stetson rather than the accent), and two lady agents are turned into fair movie stereotypes by Judy Geeson, the ever-loving, and Margaret Whiting, the ever-lusting. Just about everyone in the play is some kind of spy, and the merest ashtray, daffodil, nipple or ear-lobe may hide a bugging device. The piece has post-Watergate ambitions, though hardly post-Watergate significance; coming out of The Place to be confronted by the billboards ('Bitter Battle for Agnew's Job') I realised that Mr Magdalany could hardly compete.

  

The King and I (Adelphi) belongs to an altogether more assured period of American theatre, and this is its strength. Oscar Hammerstein's well-carpentered succession of scenes, perfectly underpinned by Richard Rodgers's music, are the confident product of an age when musicals were generally expected to be good. Nowadays we go anticipating the worst and even the best musicals show the strain. (Consider the vertiginous brilliance of Company.) Roger Redfarn's production, brought down from Billingham and scenically and economically under-nourished, nevertheless communicates this authority; The King and I is a surprisingly homespun musical (and more accessible to a British cast than any other short of My Fair Lady), but it provides one spectacular opportunity--the Siamese children's ballet The Small House of Uncle Thomas--and this is excellently taken, both by the dancers and the designer Terry Parsons, who suddenly burgeons in silver and black.

By the standards of the 1950s the show took risks; by any standards it takes diabolical liberties, notably by persevering, a full half-hour after the last song has been sung, in killing off its hero as a lachrymose gesture towards artistic integrity. (Rodgers and Hammerstein, who have been mistakenly credited with bringing the Broadway musical to life, in fact came nearer bringing it to death; they were applauded for their daring in disposing of their villain in Oklahoma! and it went to their heads.)

Actually Peter Wyngarde's King dies as splendidly as he has lived, confronting the Western values in which his authors have such touching faith with dapper, bewildered authority. The scenes of his education suggest an unexpected source for Peter Shaffer's account of the meeting of two cultures in The Royal Hunt of the Sun. But if the King is excellent, a dignified clown, I is a definite disappointment. Anna should stand up to his majesty with the force proper to a Victorian governess, widow and mother--as Deborah Kerr did in the film, as Gertrude Lawrence must have done on Broadway. Sally Ann Howes never stands up to anyone; all her lines are sent straight into the auditorium while she smiles beatifically like a golden-haired doll from The Sound of Music. (That stage in the degeneration of Rodgers and Hammerstein--a path paved with the best of intentions--was still to come.) Still, she sings beautifully and the songs are the evening's real justification. Rodgers is the nonpareil of theatrical composers and the serene, floating waltz Hello Young Lovers represents him at his best (as the candid benevolence of Getting to Know You shows him at his worst).

  

The Howff in Regent's Park Road is probably London's pleasantest theatre; you sit at well-spaced tables, eat good food, listen to a balalaika duo and drink enough wine to forget the play, a dismal piece of domestic in-fighting called Wait till the Sun Shines, Nellie. The acting, though inevitably tarred by cliche, is efficient and the direction adroit.
1973-10-21-pinter-s-mixed-doubles:
Pinter's mixed doubles

THEATRE

Robert Cushman on a week of duologues.

NEXT week the Royal Shakespeare Company is finally permitting the critics to get their hands on its productions of Shakespeare's four Roman plays. But we must starve before we are stuffed, and the RSC has this week offered three duologues, one of them fleshed out by a mute third presence.

I refer to the mysterious Matchseller of A Slight Ache, which now forms the first half of a double bill of Harold Pinter plays at the Aldwych. Originally written for radio, it was first staged in 1961 along with one-acters by John Mortimer and N. F. Simpson. (That was our idea of an avant-garde evening back in 1961.) It has survived rather better than I would have expected.

There is a school of thought, examined and partially endorsed by Simon Trussler in his recent excellent study, that considers Mr Pinter's plays mainly as so many actors' exercises, composed of arbitrary tensions that spring to life when they are well performed, and sink back into meaninglessness thereafter. It is interesting to approach the Aldwych production from this point of view, and to note that if actors bring out the best in Pinter, he can do the same for them.

I referred last Sunday to David Waller as a steamrollering actor; he has always seemed best when most monstrously complacent--as, for example, a practically definitive Dogberry. The protagonist of A Slight Ache is also unhealthily prone to self-satisfaction, but--being a man of letters--he vents it in more refined, arcane terms than we usually expect of Mr Waller. He rises to the occasion magnificently, however. His jowls are as heavy as ever, but a trim grey moustache prickles above them; in his dealings with his wife, with the wasp that strays with fatal unwariness into his breakfast marmalade, and even, before panic sets in, with the intrusive decrepit matchseller (to whom he confides 'I was in commerce too') he contrives to be skittish, even dainty.

In the confrontation of Mr Waller (who finishes up a gibbering idiot) and his silent, victorious opposite (whom the author himself is alleged to have played in a radio production) is it fanciful--well, yes it is, but what the hell--to see Civilisation engulfed by its Discontents? Among the trophies which Mr Waller's Edward must yield to the invader is his wife Flora (a line about his biological interests suggests that he has somewhere a mistress called Fauna), who is beautifully played by Peggy Ashcroft. Flora is the prototype of those faithless females who have lolled or sauntered their way, usually in the person of Vivien Merchant, through Mr Pinter's later plays. Dame Peggy defies convention by giving her a housewifely practicality which melts into erotic surrender without a hint of tease.

Peter James's direction, refreshingly light-handed, ensures that we follow this study in capitulation with fascinated attention but, as far as I am concerned, without much belief. Why should Flora give herself, and why should Edward give himself away, the one so freely, the other so crassly? What's in a matchseller? Unless we can credit their reactions to him as a human being, he can only be an author's convenience, the laziest of symbols.

Landscape, which completes the evening, is less immediately compelling than A Slight Ache, but lingers more acceptably in the mind. Here are the same actors as another married couple with no need of a matchseller to prise them apart. Time has done the job. He rambles and reminisces; she merely remembers. He tries fumblingly to re-establish contact, but she is beyond him. It is the play's singular merit (which I failed to recognise at its first appearance four years ago) that it makes no attempt to generalise from this bleak vignette; here are merely two people, fastidiously particularised. Its weakness is the roseate sentimentality that clings to the character of the wife, even in the lovely simplicity of Dame Peggy's performance. We are on the side of her memories, and resent the clumsy intrusions of the man whose last speech, in Mr Waller's powerful delivery, amounts to verbal rape. She, however, is able to turn the assault aside, to ignore or to transcend it--choose your interpretation--by immersing herself in the seductive, see-saw rhythms of nostalgia.

Nostalgia plays a large, bitter part in the RSC's other duologue, Athol Fugard's Hello and Goodbye at The Place; here the son and daughter of an old Afrikaner railwayman chew up their past and spit it out at each other. We are confronted with inbred situations that need some exceptional dramatic spark to ignite them. In this early play, Mr Fugard gives us pages of earnest effortful writing, which establish beyond doubt that his characters are wretched, but fail to provide any motive for the audience--a notoriously unfeeling animal--to care. So Johnnie Smit is going out of his skull; so Hester has come in off the streets and will probably return there. So what?

That question can be briefly, affirmatively answered when Hester, ransacking the place for her father's money, comes upon a dress belonging to her dead mother and joyfully exclaims that it still carries her smell; or in some moments of graveyard wit, unsurprisingly akin to Jewish ghetto humour. Much of this seeps through Ben Kingsley's hopelessly defeated Johnnie; he seems at home in the Port Elizabeth shanty, stumbling around in his pyjamas. But Janet Suzman, though her tirades give the play a welcome lift, looks and sounds too smart to be credible.

If Frank Hauser's Meadow Players have to end their 17-year tenure of the Oxford Playhouse one would have liked them to go out in triumph with their production of The Wolf; their current version of Doctor Knock is a miserable pendant. There is no reason to assume that a satire on French medicine in the early 1920s is fatally dated; in the age of Need Your Doctor Be So Useless it is plainly still very topical. In conscience, though, Jules Romains, having conceived the masterful joke of a doctor who propagandised the healthy (and more particularly the wealthy) villagers of his district into sickbeds, took a long time to set it up. The greater the necessity, therefore, for the comic chances to be firmly seized when they occur. But Minos Volanakis's direction has no grip on them; gags sputter up out of nowhere, misfire, and are gone. Nor is the occasion redeemed by a dazzling central performance; Alfred Burke is a competent sharper where the text demands a great manic rogue, the intoxicated victim of his own deception. Only in the last act, when Knock has visions of hundreds of thermometers simultaneously taking rectal temperatures, does the mercury show any sign of rising on stage. James Cairncross gives a good anonymous performance as the town pharmacist, and there is a nice moment when an hotel chambermaid is metamorphosed into a nurse at the drop of a mob cap.

All in all, things were better in Salisbury, where the Playhouse offered, as its contribution to a mysterious event now deceased called the Festival of British Theatre, a competent reduction of What Maisie Knew. Denis Constanduros could hardly dramatise the novel's perceptions, but he hinted at their existence. A certain amount of vulgarity might have perplexed Henry James; when he spoke of the dramatic method as throwing the cargo overboard to save the ship I doubt if running gags about sea-sickness were quite what he had in mind.

 The Plays of Harold Pinter (Gollancz, £2.50).
1973-10-28-the-roman-invasion:
The Roman invasion

THEATRE

by ROBERT
CUSHMAN

I DID not see The Romans at Stratford last year, but I gathered from the publicity attending their transfer to the Aldwych that though the directorate intended to impose no pattern on the four plays they sort of hoped that one would emerge.

On the whole they hoped in vain; the only shape formed by this Shakespearean quartet turned out to be a downward spiral. For if these plays are to be viewed as a mirror of statecraft, their performance in chronological succession (which happens to be more or less the reverse of the order in which they were written) reveals a consistent narrowing of political scope. We begin in Coriolanus with a vibrant portrait of a city; the key to this is maybe the tribune's rhetorical question (thunderously echoed by the populace in this production), 'What is the city but the people?' In Julius Caesar the light shines even clearer on individuals, but the city has begun to recede; the crowd, a dramatic antagonist in Coriolanus, have shrunk to being a collective supernumerary. In Antony and Cleopatra they have vanished completely, and Rome itself is hardly more than a distant backdrop. (All critical cant to the contrary, this is as much a political play as Hamlet or Macbeth; that is to say, only marginally.)

Titus Andronicus returns us to Rome, but by now you would hardly know the place. It is in fact no longer a place, but only a symbol; the brick reality that Shakespeare found in Plutarch's chronicles has given way to the mere abstraction of Senecan theory. Characters spout Latin tags like tourists hoping to pass for natives. Within these severe limits Titus is a very good play, impeccable in its pace and logic (was not the Elizabethan phrase for a well-made play 'as tight as Andronicus'?), but it makes a strange end to the cycle. It is so palpably an early work, and its historical basis is so slight, that we seem to have been plunged abruptly far back in time, and to be witnessing the bloody birth of a State rather than its decadence.

So what we have are just four Shakespeare productions, considerably above the recent Stratford average, though still subject to the under-casting that remains the bane of the Royal Shakespeare Company. This is made all the clearer by the arrival of Nicol Williamson to play Coriolanus; his magnificent performance casts a long shadow over the other plays in which he does not appear. Like many actors in these productions he goes to emotional extremes, but he goes, it seems, of his own volition; he has not been visibly pushed there by his director.

This Coriolanus is a man whose upbringing has forced him to live unnaturally. If anything, Mr Williamson goes too far in denying the few grace-notes that Shakespeare has written into his part; he manifests for example very little affection for his wife, and the love which he unquestionably feels for his mother is only an inch removed from hatred. When she sends him to make his peace with the plebeians, he goes forward with little confidence; when at the last she begs him to spare Rome, she cracks him apart. Margaret Tyzack, whose hauteur in the early scenes is somewhat forced (like her oddly pasty make-up), now flares into life; her oration is a sustained act of will, the only force capable of bending his. She has to tap the suppressed emotion of a lifetime, to burst the dam she has herself constructed. His face works for an eternity before Shakespeare's most eloquent stage-direction, 'he holds her by the hand, silent.' I have rarely known such suspense; finally--and by a wonder they are no anti-climax--come the words 'Oh mother, mother,' and the voice rises to an agonised shout, 'What have you done?' The man becomes a naked boy.

The flight from human contact has hitherto been the key-note of Mr Williamson's performance. Banished from Rome, he runs out of the gate while his friends' backs are turned. The honours bestowed him at the siege of Corioli cause him to run through half a dozen shades of embarrassment; in sheer defensiveness he even makes a joke. More often he takes refuge in abrasiveness; he has scarcely more patience with his own party than with the despised tribunes of the people. Mr Williamson can sneer like nobody else, sneer passionately; certain lines ('You common cry of curs ...') might have been written for him. His effective political neutrality chimes with Trevor Nunn's impartial direction; the consul Cominius (Nicholas Selby) and the disgruntled First Citizen (Morgan Sheppard) are allowed equal eloquence. The citizens rather puzzlingly bring the tools of their trades with them to the consular elections; here Mr Nunn is himself truckling for a critical response that will delightedly murmur 'Brechtian' at the merest glimpse of a lathe. It spoils the flow of the scene. This week seekers after relevance should have found more nourishment in the scenes in the Volscian camp. 'What good condition can a treaty find/I'th' part that is at mercy.' The lines ache.

Julius Caesar is a tidier production, glorified by a brilliant staging of the Forum scene. Brutus and Antony are spotlit for their orations; as Antony wins the crowd over--and it is a seamless job in Richard Johnson's performance--they join him on stage. Earlier we have seen the murderers in revealing double focus; posing in their own imagination as saviours of their country (RSC grandiosity turned delightfully against itself) and then, after the interval, blood-boltered and thoroughly rattled. John Wood's performance of Brutus is so searching that virtually nothing of the poor man's pretensions is left standing; only his love for his wife (Miss Tyzack showing how unaffectedly fine she can be in her natural sympathetic mode) does him credit. By the close he is so deeply riven that he could almost play the quarrel scene on his own. Patrick Stewart's Cassius can hardly match him in temperament, and, like many of these actors, is given stressful pauses, often before perfectly innocuous words. Mark Dignam is Caesar, resonant and despite the abundant Fascist trimmings of the production, unresolvably ambiguous.

Antony and Cleopatra is comparatively disappointing. I can never get this play together in my mind and, though Mr Nunn has scrupulously assembled all the elements, the result has less bite than Tony Richardson's comparatively slapdash production at the Bankside this summer. Vanessa Redgrave's wholehearted blowsiness seems in retrospect preferable to Janet Suzman's carefully defined sluttishness; Miss Suzman sails more logically into the death-scene, but less affectingly. Mr Johnson's mastery of Antony's public face turns out not to conceal much inner life; physically impressive (particularly in single combat) the performance is vocally and emotionally monotonous.

Mr Nunn's triumph is Titus, played for the most part in pools of light amid engulfing darkness. The horrors have to be stylised for a modern audience, but not to the point of immobilising the play. There are mistakes here: a masked chorus that steals everybody's best lines and begins by wailing out the play's title in different keys, as if to try which sounds best, and a Tamora (Margaret Whiting) who never once touches ground (and who, having unwittingly devoured her two sons baked in a pie, demonstrates her Gothic ill-breeding by talking with her mouth full). But Mr Stewart's gleeful Aaron is his best performance, Judy Geeson is a sweet and touching Lavinia, and Colin Blakely's Titus is crumbling Rome incarnate. The downfall of his reason is beautifully marked; he congratulates his son on being banished. But this peak once passed, he lacks resource to sustain the endless blows rained upon him. Mr Nunn's ordering of the stage, his balance of ceremonial and narrative gusto, and his cultivation of a stern pity amid the savagery are admirable.

I have to add that the RSC have also to their credit an intriguing Sylvia Plath programme, well directed by Barry Kyle, at the Place; and that in the Young Vic's cheerful Much Ado About Nothing, Roy Hudd's Dogberry deserves to be written down an ass in letters of gold seven feet high.
1973-11-04-bowl-of-british-pasta:
I discovered last week that it is possible to enjoy oneself immensely, but not quite whole-heartedly. Eduardo de Filippo's Saturday, Sunday, Monday is the latest of the National Theatre's forays into an alien comic style. Paris (A Flea in Her Ear) and Chicago (The Front Page) have both fallen to this company, but Naples, as might have been expected, put up a tougher resistance. The terrain is less familiar and not even the recruitment of an Italian to direct the operation could solve all the problems.

Franco Zeffirelli is, by instinct and practice, a carnival director; he is apt to sign his work (as he does here) with a flamboyantly irresistible curtain-call, and he can imbue British players with an extrovert spirit which a British audience will immediately dub Italian. But Eduardo de Filippo, as several fine critics have testified and as we could see for ourselves when he brought his company to the Aldwych last year, is the soberest of comedians. He has a gift for simply existing on a stage, with minimum effort and maximum intensity, which no British actor can match. (Alan Webb, I think, comes nearest.) His plays may be Neapolitan family comedies, but they are not soap-operas; they have an acrid tang to them and I call to witness not only my memories of the black-market satire in which London saw him, but assorted comments in the Old Vic programme concerning the present piece.

It treats of a weekend in which a marriage and a family come near to breaking-point. The husband, a shopkeeper preoccupied with business, accuses his wife of infidelity; as Sunday fades into Monday he is made to realise that her supposed coolness is the reflection and the result of his own. The pressures of work leave him only one day a week into which to cram his private life and, not unnaturally, it cracks under the strain. This obsession with work runs through all the men in the family: from grandfather, nostalgic for the hat-trade and twisting every piece of headgear within reach into strange but doubtless therapeutic forms, to his favourite grandson, the proud and cocky proprietor of his own clothes store. The theme is explicitly stated in the play, but it seems bald and unsupported in a production which works far better as a celebration of life than as a critique.

Much of the celebration is centred on food, which is rendered as convincing in sight and smell as could be desired. A ragout is prepared, calamares are anatomised, onions are chopped (we were a hungry, lachrymose bunch in the front stalls); Sunday lunch is magnificently served, and it is only logical that the marital squabble should finally hinge on the disputed merits of a dish of macaroni alla Siciliana. Joan Plowright is the rightful queen of this kitchen and the fine, frayed duel she fights with Frank Finlay gives the evening its substance.

Mr Finlay, in de Filippo's own role, functions as the punchbag to his volatile friends and neighbours; there are many good jokes in this adaptation (by Keith Waterhouse and Willis Hall), but none better or more apposite than Mr Finlay's rebuke to an emotive compatriot: "You're spitting in my soup." Some of the wives he crosses are exceptionally live: Laurence Olivier, of course, plunging in and out of his own world as granddad; Nicholas Clay as the unquenchable infant capitalist; Denis Quilley, who looks continually on the brink of song; and, the choicest of all, Anna Carteret as an urchin-cropped maid, downtrodden, tearful and strangely resilient. Perhaps she glories in the possession of such a brother as Desmond McNamara, the ultimate skinhead, whose particular foible (baring his pate to all-comers as if it were a challenge) is integrated into the action by the hand of a master dramatist.

If this review has turned into a parade of National Theatre favourites it is merely reflecting the production; there are perilous moments at which the main interest lies in anticipating the effect of Italian vowels upon the next familiar voice. Weak performances here induce a kind of vertigo, and much of the enclosed family feeling has disappeared through the open spaces of Zeffirelli's inexplicable set. What survives, and places the show among the finest as well as the funniest in London, is a humanity and generosity comparable to that radiated by de Filippo's own troupe.

Our native family drama, David Storey's The Farm (now at the Mayfair) is pinched and jaded by comparison, despite its incidental humours and well-managed scene a faire; while the new American musical, Pippin (Her Majesty's) is merely loathsome. It does not lack talent. Tony Walton's sets, amusing in themselves, bring out the best in Bob Fosse's direction. A bolt of green silk billowing down from the flies, a double file of spotlights to simulate a curtain, or a talking head upon a battlefield, stimulate Mr Fosse to magical feats. But the show, having got its mileage out of magic, in the end professes to discard it; having gained its effects by split-second professionalism it makes a great parade of improvisation, also rehearsed to the last split second. The script sneers at the appeal of lovable stage children, brings one on (complete with animal), and exploits him, then sneers again for luck. The music and lyrics, as full of sunshine as a cereal commercial, refute the canard that after his score for Godspell, Stephen Schwartz had nowhere to go but up. As Pippin (mythical son of a pantomime Charlemagne, but bearing a strong resemblance to the timeless, witless hero of an Anthony Newley show) Paul Jones is likeable, but inexpert; Northern J. Calloway as an omnipresent evil genius is precisely the reverse. The authors have things to say about War, Revolution and Sex; none of it explains their choice of a mock-medieval setting.

Two plates of goulash: Molnar's The Wolf, over which I enthused at Oxford, has come to the Apollo; while a modern Hungarian play, Istvan Orkeny's Catsplay, serves at Greenwich as a vehicle for Elisabeth Bergner who, within a limited range, is an enchantress without flaw. She is a mistress of direct address, a necessary attribute for this play, in which she bends all ears to the tale of her one great love. She is, in fact, one of those suicidally dependent heroines from whom, it is to be hoped, Women's Lib may one day deliver us. Close of play finds her on all fours, miaowing, while Margaret Rawlings, hitherto immobilised and stately, unbends as far as is physically possible in a wheelchair and confesses that she has wet her knickers. This has been acclaimed as a great comic moment. Maybe I'm hard to please.

I could even resist Michael Elliott's largely impeccable staging of T. S. Eliot's The Family Reunion (69 Company, Manchester). The chorus of uncles and aunts were convincing in isolation and impressive in unison; the Eumenides, supposedly unstageable, were truly terrifying. Mr Elliott, greatly aided by his designer, Laurie Dennett, and the arena stage of his inviting temporary playhouse in the Royal Exchange, proved the play to be theatrical. What he could not do, despite the surly passion of Edward Fox's country-house Orestes, was to pierce the mists of its narrative of guilt once removed and render it dramatic.
1973-11-11-thoughts-of-footman-fritz:
Thoughts of footman Fritz

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

The scene of A Lesson in Blood and Roses (Royal Shakespeare Company at The Place), says the programme, is the library of the Villa von Kellig on the outskirts of Vienna in 1848, Europe's year of revolutions.

Farrah's set is something of a non-starter as a library, being completely devoid of books, but this conceivably is a comment on the essential illiteracy of the ruling classes; and otherwise the stage looks pleasing, an arrangement of plush curtains, plusher doors, and elegant furniture strategically placed to give the characters plenty of room to attack each other. One thing that John Wiles's play does not lack is conflict.

Fritz the footman is a revolutionary; he at any rate can read and does, aloud, from a suspiciously modern red book. He informs us, by way of prologue, that the art of the successful guerrilla lies in defeating the enemy with his own weapons. And though it takes more than an anachronistic reference to Mao to disconcert the hardened audiences of today, Fritz feels obliged to follow it with a joky reassurance that we are, in the right theatre. Even as he said it I began to wonder.

The objects of Fritz's guerrilla strategy are the children of the house. While daddy, a general, is away at the wars, they have been left in the charge of a governess who, despite a Miss Julie-ish passion for Fritz, believes in the established order. She, however, is on the way out, to be replaced by a male tutor from Paris. The Monsieur duly appears, to be greeted by the footman with considerably more warmth than he ever bestowed on the poor mademoiselle.

It seems that Monsieur is Fritz's half-brother and that his entry into the house has been arranged by machiavellian intrigues, whose full subtleties I cannot divulge since the author has neglected to. Monsieur sets about disorientating the boy and girl Von Kellig; beginning in a small but significant way with the casual assertion that sound travels faster than light, he goes on to instruct them in Archimedes's Premium, whereby two and two make at least five and preferably more, and to disabuse them of certain common geographical fallacies. One can see that if his ideas caught on, and the children of the rich all came to doubt that Rome and Florence were both in Italy, the popular cause might eventually benefit, particularly in the event of a pitched battle being fought near either city.

But this does not seem to be quite what Fritz wants (what he does want is another matter on which Mr Wiles keeps silence) and he remonstrates. Monsieur, however, is now unstoppable, fired by the memory of a public orgy (rather stirringly described), at which all the whores in town gave their services, freely and repeatedly, "for the people." He has seen the future and it fornicates: where his brother quoted Mao at us, he proffers de Sade. (And as the Marquis said to Jean Paul Marat, when they met one day in that house of Weiss near Charenton, "What's the good of a revolution without general copulation?") So he wreaks untold havoc on the children's bodies and, indeed, on their sexual identity; by the time he is through, they are wearing each other's clothes or none at all, little Annamarie is out killing rabbits, young Max-Ernst is cooking them, and the library is frankly a mess. Such is their decadent state that they are chopping up the furniture for firewood; could this have been what Fritz meant when he spoke of "turning the tables"? By this time Fritz has been shot for attempting to interfere with Monsieur's personal hedonistic revolution. But the more established puritanism represented by Mademoiselle (I bet you had forgotten about her) proves harder to beat and it is she who by a final turn of the screw (the apposite phrase) wins possession of the children. Or nearly final, because, but I must not deprive you of the pleasure of guessing for yourselves Mr Wiles's highly foreseeable surprise ending.

Schematic drama always has a certain built-in force and this is occasionally generated when Mr Wiles's representative figures are at each other's throats. But the higher melodrama is a risky and risible genre, and the author's verbal tactlessness, which first shows itself in the supposedly disarming prologue and grows steadily thereafter, finally scuppers it. Ben Kingsley puts his louring forehead and snarling delivery to good use as Fritz. One of the RSC's intensity specialists, he is here matched against their acknowledged leader, John Wood, bubbling over with intellectual bravura as Monsieur.
