English history takes a beating in the cause of youth in Paul Foster's Elizabeth I, mounted at the Theatre Upstairs in association with the Royal Court's Young People's Theatre Scheme. I am not too sure about the purport of this piece; I expected a straight piece of demystification, but though a savage opening song ("My God, what an age") suggests a critical approach, when Mr Foster gets up close to Elizabeth he finds he rather likes her. Carole Hayman plays her as an amiable fishwife (which is how she plays most parts) who wants to keep the peace, however funny it will make her look in the history books. The business of Mary Stuart is shadier (the play goes very heavy and reverent for her execution) and I didn't much care for Bess's councillors: Francis Bacon is thoroughly unsavoury and, besides, you can't understand a gnomic word he says. Still, nobody's immaculate or, as the delightful Charlotte Cornwell puts it with a soft rock backing: "The Queen of England is a virgin queen, ho, ho." Walter Donohue's production is lively, though the grouping (in an old-fashioned show one would have criticised the grouping) is definitely sub-standard.

  

The situation downstairs is altogether more reassuring: D. H. Lawrence is to the Court as Pinero to Chichester, a thoroughly reliable commodity, and The Merry-Go-Round is the most enjoyable exhumation yet. The loving care of Peter Gill's direction is again phenomenal, from the opening scene in which opposing characters are denoted by their approach to the making of a bed to the familiar set-piece of the coalminer's homecoming. At Mr Gill's stately pace the play's parade of lovers, tentatively pairing and repairing, is more of a processional than a carousel and the final burst of speed for a traditional comic finale jars horribly. But for most of the time Lawrence's style of playmaking is his own invention and it serves him well. So do the players: Marjorie Yates rampaging round her parents' cottage in a fury of young widowhood, George Malpas as an aged bashful suitor and, as the object of every man's attention, Mary Miller, a passionately sensible heroine who would have delighted Jane Austen. Derrick O'Connor is a towering presence and his major outburst of violence is amazing, but the casualness of his speech puts him out of place and period.

  

John Hopkins's Economic Necessity (at the new Haymarket, Leicester) is the victim of its own structure. Beginning with the familiar situation of a man who quits his job because it no longer makes sense to him, it wearily catalogues the reactions of his friends and relations and conscientiously charts the estrangement of his wife. Finally we are allowed a glimpse inside his mind, where an awareness of the world's cruelty is blotting out everything else. Whether this was the cause or the effect of his withdrawal is not stated; either way it bites and frightens, but it has no organic relation to the rest of the play, and the final effect is of laborious sentimentality.
1973-11-18-polish-apocalypse:
Polish apocalypse

Theatre

Robert Cushman in Paris.

I do not know whether Michel Guy, who runs the Paris Autumn Festival, regards himself as a prophet of environmental theatre. It is a fact, though, that the four Festival productions I saw last week derived part of their impact from their relationship to the buildings in which they were housed.

I applaud this approach less for its honesty (a questionable theatrical commodity, even when it is to be had) than for its expediency. I extend this commendation even to Jerzy Grotowski, the hallowed Polish experimentalist, the altitude of whose principles is hardly to be measured, let alone questioned.

When Grotowski's laboratory troupe visited London a few years back those of us permitted to see them were transported in secret coachloads to a City church. In Paris we again find Grotowski in church: in Sainte-Chapelle, celebrated for its stained glass and its tourists. Grotowski has exploited the former and banished the latter.

Seeking to establish what Peter Brook has called a holy theatre, Grotowski very properly latches on to sites with reverential potential. On the same principle, the audience at a musical is conditioned to gaiety by the overture. At Sainte-Chapelle, after a brief sojourn in an antechamber to read our programmes (afterwards removed, lest we succumb to the temptation of perusing them rather than watching the play), we were escorted in small groups up winding stairs, and finally ushered two by two into the chapel itself. There, on a raised wooden platform lit from ground level by a single powerful lamp, crouched the actors. It was an awesome sight, which would have been totally ruined had we been allowed to crowd in en masse.

The play, Apocalypsis Cum Figuris, was apparently worked up in improvisations stemming initially from the Book of Revelation, and shaped to lead up to a confrontation between the Christlike figure called the Innocent (played by the remarkable Ryszard Cieslak, Grotowski's superstar, acknowledged as such on the posters) and a Simon Peter who speaks in the voice of Dostoevsky's Grand Inquisitor. Not understanding the words, one's response must inevitably be an act of trust; feeling the presence of an undeviating line in the production I trusted Grotowski, as I failed earlier this year to trust his compatriot, Tadeusz Kantor, whose Lovelies and Dowdies was the buttered toast of the Edinburgh Festival fringe. The two are, as I fear I am not the first to observe, Poles apart: Kantor bullied his audience through an initial cloakroom ceremony, based on the assumption that every time we say goodbye to our coats we die a little. Those of us who are only too glad to shed them for the duration were inevitably suspicious, and the suspicion deepened when the performance proved to be a collection of unrelated and not particularly striking images. I believe that the theatre works through concentration, not dispersal, and it is for his adherence to this principle, as well as his engagingly practical attitude towards his venue and his public, that I salute Grotowski. His work may, as has been alleged, be humourless, but this is not a crippling disadvantage to a man who is not trying to make jokes.

It is on the other hand a grievous handicap to TSE, the Argentinian group now based in Paris, who attempt at the Palace, which certainly has the right ambiance, to burlesque the French music hall in a show called Luxe. It sounds, as indeed it is, a pointless exercise; effective parody of a form so effervescent would after all be indistinguishable from the real thing. Luxe can be distinguished from its models by the slowness of its performance, the uninventiveness of its routines, and the blankness of its stare; this finding aural equivalent in the dispiriting use of pre-recorded music throughout. I suppose the intention may have been to expose the spurious glamour of the halls, but I hesitate, without further evidence, to accuse TSE of anything so detestably high-minded.

Downstairs at the Palace, a long, mirrored rehearsal-room has been utilised for performances of Les Quatre Jumelles, a cheerful fable about four ladies who, for the sake of a whole heap of greenbacks, maim, blind and kill one another repeatedly.

Here, too, the author (Copi) is Argentinian; so is the director, Jorge Lavelli, who has staged the piece, all over the room, with flair and four good uninhibited actresses, in the grimly mischievous style which might be christened Arraballetic.

Grotowski apart, the jewel of the festival has been a reworking of an obscure Marivaux play, La Dispute, by the Theatre National Populaire: once, under Jean Vilar, the glory of French theatre and now reconstituted at Lyons under Roger Planchon, maestro of that parish. In the glittering confines of the Theatre de la Musique, Patrice Chereau, a young colleague of M. Planchon, has mounted the play as a mock opera. A burst of romantic music starts us off; smoke belches from the infernal depths of the orchestra pit. ("Hell," said Shaw's Don Juan, "is full of amateur musicians.") The main business of the play, a formal trial of the inconstancy of the sexes, which is also an expose of the myth of the noble savage, is despatched in chiaroscuro light against sumptuous pastoral decor. From his actors, many of them very young, M. Chereau has conjured performances of shattering force, not least in the Prologue, played in evening dress on the rim of the orchestra, in which a sardonic Prince broaches the play's argument to his self-pitying betrothed. Finally, he lures her, by way of a perilous plank flung across the abyss, to the stage where the action unfolds in illustration of his argument.

With productions as electrifying as this, the TNP could regain its former prestige, which has currently passed to the Theatre Municipale Populaire, established by Jean Mercure in the gutted Theatre Sarah Bernhardt, reconstituted and renamed the Theatre de la Ville. Straying from the festival, I visited Monsieur Mercure's production of Peter Nichols's The National Health, transported from an English to a French hospital and rather dashingly subtitled Les Amours Noires d'un Homme en Blanc. The ward (give a bottle of Lucozade and take one of Evian) is almost identical to the one we saw at the Old Vic; and Mr Nichols's humanity, which I have thought unalterably English, has crossed the Channel undamaged. Certainly a packed house thought so, and the Theatre de la Ville, where a single-tiered auditorium sweeps down a steep rake to confront an open stage, proved an ideal meeting place for audience and play. Puzzlingly the interpolated segments of soap opera (parodies of Doctor Finlay, et al.) were left in their English guise; this added to the confusion which overtakes the play in its second half, and which erupts helplessly, and topically, in the royal wedding finale.
1973-11-25-the-riddle-of-the-lake:
THEATRE/1: Robert Cushman on
Handke, Coward and convicts.

The riddle
of the lake

The legend goes, or so we are informed, that a horseman, lost on a winter night while looking for Lake Constance, unwittingly rode right over its thinly frozen surface. Arriving at a village he asked the locals the way to the lake, was told he had already crossed it, and promptly dropped dead from retrospective fright.

What has Peter Handke in his play The Ride Across Lake Constance (Hampstead Theatre Club) done with this extraordinarily haunting tale, beyond obliging each of his reviewers to expend a paragraph on retelling it? It serves, you will scarcely be surprised to learn, as a metaphor for the precious sustaining distance that separates our experience of life from its unbearable reality. I have to confess to some disappointment with a play which, having chosen so chilling a central image, leaves it sitting in a programme note. Nobody on the stage itself actually mentions Lake Constance (perhaps logic would demand that they dropped down dead if they did). But the evening provides a more than respectable quota of haunting moments, one of which, to my delight, does concern a lake. Alan Howard tells of how he sat beside one and noticed to his amazement that it was sparkling, just like a good lake should.

The play's main theme is, in fact, the relationship between objects (including people) and our preconceptions about them. Its major source of terror is the oppressive weight of those preconceptions: our first sight of something determines our subsequent behaviour. So when Mr Howard first comes upon the scene (which appears to be a drawing-room), accompanied by the resplendent Faith Brook and the mercilessly pretty Nicola Pagett, it is already occupied by Nigel Hawthorne and Nicky Henson. Mr Henson, having greeted the newcomers with a polite but ill-advised "What would you like?" is immediately tagged as a shop-assistant and treated as one; not surprisingly, he plays along. Mr Hawthorne tells of the ghastly day he had when a woman whom he took to be mad because she was trampling on eggshells disconcertingly proved to have good reason for her conduct. (I think Mr Hawthorne could afford to plumb murkier depths in his treatment of this speech; I have no other quarrel with his performance, and none at all with anybody else's.)

On at least one occasion the characters manage to escape from the tyranny of predetermined associations. If someone is flinching, they will not assume that he is suffering the pangs of conscience; he merely flinches. If a drawer is stuck halfway out of its chest, they will not, so to speak, look into it; they will just accept its stuckness. Not only accept, but celebrate: they sing about its stuckness, and as they sing they dance. This is their high point; retribution strikes at the end of the play when they are all scared rigid by a baby crying and Mr Henson, in what I take to be a propitiatory gesture, unsticks the drawer and pushes it firmly shut.

As social comment all this is very apt; I only jib at the implication (fostered, perhaps, less by Handke himself than by his critics) that it also has value as satire on the theatre. The revival of Noel Coward's Design for Living (Phoenix) provides more rewarding insights into the social and artistic connotations of the verb "to act."

Otto paints, Leo writes plays, Gilda decorates interiors; they are truly inseparable, but only discover this fact after they have tried coupling in each of the available permutations. In any other company they are outsiders; to underline this, Coward gives them Central European names while moving the action through Paris, London and New York. Each capital brings them greater material success, makes them more outrageous or, hopefully from the audience's point of view, more delightful.

Ideally, the audience should see them in double focus: as Gilda, Otto and Leo, who are insufferable, and know it, and tell each other so with murderous candour, and as the all-licensed stars of the show (at the premiere in 1933, Coward himself and the Lunts). Vanessa Redgrave, Jeremy Brett and John Stride hurl their knives and bare their wounds with great skill. Mr Stride, who has developed more steadily than any other actor I can think of, plays Leo the lionised with a silvery mane and a satisfyingly contemptuous growl. Mr Brett is maybe a little too open to fit into this jungle, but on the whole the play is mined as deeply for character values as it could ever be. In the third act Messrs Stride and Brett make a magnificent white-tie entrance like twin Fred Astaires, blending most harmoniously into the black-and-silver New York apartment.

Yet the suspicion that Leo and Otto are no more than insufferable little boys refuses to be shaken, and is powerfully reinforced by their final appearance in matching pyjamas. Even at their bohemian peak they have merely got drunk before breakfast on brandy chased by sherry. (If they had stayed sober on it, that might have been something.) They behave monstrously, but the text, which thins as the evening lengthens, cannot make them sacred; as always, Coward has trusted to his players' surpassing glamour to do that. Messrs Stride and Brett are very good actors, but so is their chief butt, Peter Bayliss. What gives them the right to patronise him?

Miss Redgrave, of course, is a different case. Hers is not the wittiest Gilda imaginable, but she radiates and intensifies and in thirties gowns shimmers. And this being a Michael Blakemore production the supporting players are given room to breathe: the solidity of Neil Wilson as a reporter, trudging through an automatic interview, and of the superb Hazel Hughes as one of Coward's disparaging domestics, is the best rebuke to the posturing of their tormentors, and contributes to the ambiguous texture of the play's fine second act.

A less intriguing triangle is tinkled to fleeting effect in Tina Brown's Under the Bamboo Tree (King's Head, Upper Street, N1): Carole Boyd and Olivia Mundy do spirited battle over the weary head of Ben Aris. This is half of a double bill, of which the remainder is actually called Triangle, but proves to be a monologue, well written (James Saunders), better acted (Michael Graham Cox) and again concerned with theatrical illusion, a subject of which you and I have had quite enough this week.

Steve Gooch's Female Transport (Half Moon, Alie Street, E1) has done two impossible things: he has written a believable historical play (not a documentary) and he has convincingly evoked an enclosed community of women. The enclosure is the hold of a convict ship, en route for Australia. Remember Mr Gooch's name for the future, but see his play now.
1973-12-02-end-of-a-genius:
End of a genius

THEATRE

by Robert Cushman

When I told the taxi-driver who was taking me to Exeter's fine and progressive Northcott Theatre that they were playing Bingo that night, he was bemused. "Aren't there cinemas for that kind of thing?"

The attraction in question has now run its course at Exeter but is on view this week at Plymouth. Brethren, be advised. This is a play, Edward Bond's account of the last days of William Shakespeare, who never got to shout anything as triumphant as "Bingo." In the eyes of the world, and especially of his own family, this successful playwright and Stratford property-owner has hit the jackpot; as death approaches, he comes increasingly to believe that the jackpot has hit him.

Visually, the Shakespeare presented by Mr Bond and his actor Bob Peck is the traditional egghead; the shell, however, is hollow. Mr Bond has seized on the most disconcerting fact about Shakespeare: that this overflowing genius should apparently have dried up. Has any other comparable figure ever truly retired? Mr Bond shows us Ben Jonson persuading him to make a comeback, failing and lapsing into criticism of the late romances. Just what, he asks, was The Winter's Tale about anyway? ("He is loth to make Nature afraid in his plays like those that beget Tales, Tempests, and suchlike drolleries," Jonson wrote in his induction to Bartholomew Fair.)

Shakespeare doesn't answer; mindful perhaps of the discrepancy between the idealised daughter-figures of those plays and the shrewishly unimaginative actuality of his own Judith (who on this showing was fittingly commemorated by my favourite Stratford landmark, now, alas, no more, the Judith Shakespeare Wimpy Bar).

Then again, the qualified optimism of those plays seems to have been decisively denied by the experiences of his affluence. Shakespeare, the one Elizabethan playwright to go into management and profitably invest the proceeds, finds himself in his capitalist role either the witness of cruelty or an accomplice to it. His assistance in protecting the interests of the enclosing landowners against those of the townspeople is sought and obtained by the local entrepreneur, the manner of whose speech Shakespeare might well find disturbingly familiar. "We needn't," he avers, "build a bridge if there's a ford downstream" (cf. Much Ado About Nothing: "What need the bridge much broader than the flood"). A homeless woman stumbles into his garden, is whipped for vagrancy, and eventually executed. Here, brought literally home to him, is the reality of those "poor naked wretches" apostrophised by King Lear.

When Mr Bond wrote his own Lear, he had the King die while attempting to destroy the society he had created. His Shakespeare dies partly of drink (Mr Bond having adopted the legend of the final, fatal carousal with Jonson) but more basically of disgust at his failure to act upon his own deepest insights, which should have prompted a similar revolt. I think that Mr Bond has underestimated the force of the Shakespearean Lear's great question, "Is there any cause in Nature (not society) that makes these hard hearts?" Shakespeare believed, as Mr Bond does not, in natural human evil; facing this, he could also face its opposite, as in Jonson's bugbear The Winter's Tale, which in many respects (notably the progress from court to country) both echoes and answers King Lear.

Still, every man has the right to his own Shakespeare; and Mr Bond's, once the first deep credulous breath has been taken, is powerfully convincing. Mr Peck, morose and haunted, rises to a funny and harrowing last scene, with Anne Hathaway (the unseen image of his greatest failure) beating hysterically on his bedroom door, under which, as a placating gesture, is finally slipped Will's will (with provision duly made, as he insists in Mr Bond's nearest approach to high camp, for the bed).

The action surrounding the central figure is less satisfactory, partly due to acting which, perhaps influenced by the laconic Royal Court style, is often cursory, underweight and thickly Mummerseted. It is frequently difficult to determine just what is going on, particularly in relation to the enclosure struggles; and the panoramic Northcott stage is, in more than one way, a barrier to concentration. At the moment I respond to the play with respect rather than enthusiasm. I would like an opportunity to change my mind.

I have already been made to change it with regard to Snoo Wilson, whose The Pleasure Principle is, in every respect but one, a great improvement on his last, Vampire. In this case the play is much helped by David Hare's witty and, in the context of the Theatre Upstairs, spectacular production, and by the acting of Julie Covington (her best performance to date), Ann Firbank, Dinsdale Landen, Brenda Fricker and a goat.

The play is inferior to Vampire only in its lack of any binding theme (which is all Vampire had). I could, if pressed, invent one (what else are critics for?) by slightly amending the title of an ancient American drama into They Got What They Wanted (And Much Good It Did Them). Miss Covington is careless of possessions, and is repeatedly burgled. She is also frigid, but dreams, Leda-like, of being possessed by a swan. Mr Landen eventually ravishes her, inside a hollow swan which happens to be lying around the circus tent in which he has taken up residence. (This is not, strictly considered, a realistic play.) Mr Landen has long fancied Miss Covington, so his desire has been realised too. Miss Firbank, once married to Mr Landen, longs to be reunited with him, but ends up sharing his tent. Miss Fricker, who is Irish, wants to go to England and does. Mr Landen's chauffeur, painfully illiterate in Act One, has learned by Act Three to read and write and to be a bailiff.

For all that the play begins in Ireland amid bombing and mutilation, it is totally devoid of pain. Laughter (and the play abounds in sharply angled comic dialogue and fantastic action) anaesthetises: that, I guess, is the pleasure principle in operation. This is one of the best plays of the seventies' heartless school; Coward's Design for Living is a fount of charity by comparison. A troupe of clowns arrive to engineer, for our benefit, a totally arbitrary happy ending, so our complicity is enlisted, too. Earlier, a couple of gorillas instruct us in the rules of enjoyment (nothing in excess). I thought they were sweet.

I would like to hear their opinion of Zorba (Greenwich), a musical whose pleasures are real but strictly limited. Alfred Marks's talents as actor, singer and clown are at last properly bestowed on the eponymous Greek, and he dances with dignity. Robin Phillips's production is smooth. Roger Butlin, who has imposed many ingenious shapes on the Greenwich platform, has surpassed himself with a huge ramp, scooped out of its nethermost recesses. John Kander's musical ingenuity survives the dire challenge of the bouzouki better than might be expected.

But if a musical is going to tell a dramatic story, it had better do so with more conviction than has been mustered here by Joseph Stein, whose melodramas lie fallow for long periods and then revive in inexplicable, indigestible bursts. Mr Stein also wrote the book for Fiddler on the Roof, a shaming comparison. Broadway of course can be Jewish from the inside; here everything is studied and external, down to the deployment of Dorothy Vernon (in good clarion voice) as a Chorus Leader. How Greek can you get?

Nicol Williamson's one-man show, Midwinter Spring (Aldwych, Sundays), is marvellous, especially the dirty bits.
1973-12-09-playing-it-for-laughs:
Playing it for laughs

THEATRE

Robert Cushman on the frontiers of comedy and farce.

The term "sex-farce" is beginning to be employed, shall we say, promiscuously in the London theatre. A title (and there are many) of the order of Bed and Bored will, of course, make any critic cower; we are none of us in favour of British rubbish. We cling, however, to the belief that they order these things better in France.

Or anywhere else on the Continent. One side-effect of the Feydeau fashion which spread so enjoyably a few years ago has been the labelling as farce of any reasonably jocular theatrical treatment of infidelity among the European middle-classes, at the end of the last century or the beginning of the present one. If the play includes a scene in an eating-house, the case is generally considered clinched.

I am referring as much to audience expectation as to managerial promises. As far as I know, Molnar's The Wolf has never been advertised as a farce, but when I revisited it this week (on the first flight of its abrupt transfer to the Queen's) the leisureliness of the comedy clearly took the house by surprise. After all, the setting is Hungarian, and the programme clearly locates the first act in "the dining-room of a fashionable hotel." In such a soil preconceptions prosper.

The production now goes some way towards meeting them. The fantasy sequence is more sharply stylised than before, so the audience twigs that it is a dream far earlier, and is deprived of the realisation which, at the Oxford Playhouse in September, only dawned when the curtain fell. This seems to me an improvement, but I have to admit that it detracts from the play far less than I would have expected. The weight now rests firmly on the evolving relationship of the married couple played by Judi Dench and Leo McKern.

Their performances have gained not so much in depth (which was there to begin with) as in ease and solidity. Both from time to time employ familiar comic effects, Mr McKern tactlessly raising his voice to his wife with waiters present, Miss Dench lovingly lengthening the vowels of her final "I adore you"; but the decoration always sits logically on the structure. A good test for comic acting is the ease with which it can support an occasional extravagance. In the last act Edward Woodward, released from a series of brash disguises, shyly emerges on the level of the other two. They make a very likeable trio; the evening is perhaps the most distinguished to be had in the West End.

Molnar shows us a husband who is unsure of his wife's love and so attempts to buy it. A faintly similar situation is presented in Georges Courteline's Home Life, at the Howff, in what is frankly billed as an evening of French farce. Here the husband attempts to blackmail his wife into submission by fining her every time she displeases him. The mechanics of this system are sufficiently emphasised for the play to qualify as farce; and there is one definitely zany moment when the lady threatens to commit suicide by jumping from a ground-floor window. But nothing so grand as adultery, real or suspected, is at issue; the relationship is compact of pettier aggravations, the kind that actually do make marriages miserable. The play in fact puts farcical techniques to seriously comic ends: a respectable bastardisation. Courteline is a bridge between Feydeau and Ionesco; one of his wilder pieces is composed mainly of a loving couple throwing the furniture at each other. But his success can hardly be judged from this production, in which the two performers seem hardly to be in the same play, let alone the same marriage.

Coupled with it, and far better done, is a genuine Feydeau, Respectable Women. The master's one-act plays are held by connoisseurs to be his masterpieces. The complications are distilled into a perfect symmetry, thoroughly predictable and mathematically pleasing. Given a little breathing-space, Feydeau develops the bilious view of character implicit in his full-length works; he virtually invents a miniature genre, the farce of bad manners. Philandering males and outrageously prim cocottes feed off each other (almost literally, thanks to the traditional restaurant setting); Christopher Benjamin and Christina Greatrex are a fine pair of mutual predators. Realism, though not of the Stanislavskyan kind, is the key to Feydeau; this truism is still neglected, not least in Paris where I recently saw a prettified version of L'Hotel du Libre Echange (Hotel Paradiso), which turned the play from a satire on bourgeois morality almost into a celebration of it. (The audience glowed.)

Type-casting has an ugly reputation, but it is a necessity in farce, and in much comedy. Intelligent approximations are not enough. The wittiest, cleverest performance in The Apple Cart (Bristol Old Vic) is given by Judy Parfitt as Orinthia, but it misfires since Orinthia exists in the play as the King's mistress and Miss Parfitt is one of the theatre's natural wives.

Ultimately, of course, Shaw's play depends on the presence of one of the theatre's natural monarchs and this it is granted. On the first night Peter O'Toole, creased and handsome in green corduroy, staked a good deal on charm (as, I suppose, royalty must) and won. Clearly under-rehearsed, he fluffed engagingly through his first scene, so that one's heart lurched at the thought of the marathon speech ahead. In the event (and really we might have known), he brought it off flawlessly; "You did speak that piece beautifully, sir," says one of the ladies in the Cabinet, and I expected to hear the auditorium echo in agreement.

There should have been applause, too, for Thelma Whiteley, whose delivery of the Powermistress's attack on the big business interests bit harder than anything else in the play, a circumstance for which Miss Whiteley and the state of the nation should perhaps share the credit. Nobody will begrudge Shaw his easy laughs at politicians, and Mr O'Toole makes the fleeting fantasy of kingly rule undeniably seductive. Perhaps that is because it remains a fantasy throughout; it might have been harder to swallow the reality.

The Bristol complex is currently booming. Mr O'Toole is packing them in at the Royal, the Little is celebrating its golden jubilee with Blithe Spirit (Peggy Ann Wood, who, with her husband, Ronald Russell, built this theatre up, plays Madame Arcati, the happy medium), and the New Vic Studio, more harshly occult, offers John Downie's collage version of Dracula. This begins in stock menace and ends in total obscurity: the middle, though, is scary. Howard Davies's rigorous and inventive production demands a high level of intrepidity from its actors and, especially from Roger Gartland and Gay Rose, receives it. The action is filtered through the mind of a madman, a popular device which gives the audience no means of checking the relevance of any section or the worth of the whole experience.
1973-12-16-o-sweet-o-lovely-wall:
O sweet, O lovely Wall!

THEATRE

Robert Cushman on 'Cockie'.

London's latest nostalgia trip is Cockie (Vaudeville), a tribute to the most celebrated of West End impresarios, Charles B. Cochran.

Since Cochran's speciality was revue, Peter Saunders (who hereby qualifies as the impresario's impresario) has chosen to commemorate him with a melange of songs and sketches on the pattern of the Mermaid's Cowardy Custard. What would be the equivalent culinary title? Cock-a-leekie, I guess. Thematic unity is not the evening's strongest point. The opening number, appropriately enough, is "Anything Goes," given a spirited, featureless song-and-dance rendition by a scrubbed, anonymous crew who apparently constitute the full company. At the prospect of being entertained all night by a bunch of chorines, male and female, the heart sinks.

It stays sunk as two young men detach themselves from the corps and start in on the biography. With stolid mid-Atlantic cheeriness, they dispatch some rhyming couplets which, since no author is named, might just have been dreamed up by Mr Saunders in his bath. Some of the terms in which they apostrophise Cochran are a little obscure. For a taste: "Reinhardt and Hackenschmidt were one to you." Not to me. I've heard of Reinhardt.

The narrators vanish, for good, having informed us that Cochran's early failure as a performer left him with no recourse but to turn manager. Just like that. C.B.'s conversation is informative rather than sparkling; unexpectedly rescued from bankruptcy, he tosses off, "I'm going straight into production at the Adelphi with Noel Coward's new revue Words and Music." That's telling us.

At other times continuity becomes the responsibility of disembodied voices reverently intoning the names of Cochran's leading ladies. Alice Delysia gets the fullest treatment; her euphonious surname is sent fairly echoing round the stage. I might have been more awestruck had I not recently seen the Bristol Old Vic's Dracula, where the same trick is played with the word Transylvania.

The ads for Cockie give top billing to the composers of the twenties and thirties. They can be sampled here in some quantity: eight numbers by Coward, four by Cole Porter, three by Rodgers and Hart, two each by Jerome Kern and Irving Berlin, and one by the Gershwins. The prospect waters the mouth, but the actuality dries it up a bit. I expect shows like this to introduce me to neglected material, but here most of the melodies are familiar, and there is little pleasure in hearing American standards given the English musical comedy treatment. Why shackle them with Palm Court arrangements and nondescript, interchangeable routines? (The Coward songs are far more dependent on a sense of period, so it is perverse to offer a beat arrangement of "Dance Little Lady" in a disco setting.)

What we hear of the Cochran lavishness is belied by what we see in William Chappell's production. Peter Rice's sets centre on a pair of rickety steps and a receding series of false proscenia; a starry sky-cloth is visible when romantic atmosphere is required. Four choreographers are listed, of whom Lionel Blair registers most strongly, having masterminded an invigorating tap trio danced to Kern's bouncy "She Didn't Say Yes." (Otto Harbach gets programme credit for his equally bouncy lyric, which is nice; it would be nicer still if somebody actually sang it.) But Mr Blair is also responsible for a sad staging of "Dancing on the Ceiling": in Lorenz Hart's lyric, the heroine clearly states that the hero "dances overhead / On the ceiling near my bed." Only the last three words appear to have been heeded by Mr Blair, whose danseur merely twirls about on the deck in unbecoming blue-grey pyjamas. There is nothing for it but to amend the lyric:

He dances round and round,  
Both feet firmly on the ground,  
Drably clad,  
Silly lad.  
I whisper "Get aloft, my lover,  
Climb the wall;  
And let me, snug beneath my cover,  
Watch you fall."  
I find my ceiling bare:  
Put the blame on Lionel Blair,  
And on my love.

Most of Cockie's faults are concentrated in the first act. After the interval it develops the elusive rhythm, essential to revue, whereby the good numbers give pleasure in themselves and build confidence for what follows. The orchestrations get richer, Mr Rice's costumes more opulent, and at last, in a medley from Bitter Sweet (another step towards the full-dress revival for which the whole West End scene has been softening us up over the last five years), a performer takes full possession of a song: Avril Angers quietly and steadfastly sings "If Love Were All," which is the one, probably Coward's best, about only having a talent to amuse, and stills the house until it roars again.

So, in a different way, does Max Wall, who comes on next to closing, ostensibly to sing "Birth of the Blues." If the bulk of the show suffers from its uncertainty of attitude, alternately lecturing and cajoling us, Mr Wall has no such problem. He treats us with outright disdain, a disdain all the deeper for being edged with dismay. Terrible things happen to Mr Wall while he is on stage. He is goosed from behind the curtain and he falls over. (He says) a hole in the stage, a misadventure which prompts him to put the dread, unanswerable question, "How desperate can a comedian be?" As it happens he cannot spare much of his hauteur for us since he needs it for the orchestra, an insubordinate assembly which is plainly trying to give premature birth to the blues; at least, they are finishing long before he is. With his staring eyes and death's-head grin, the patient mask of a man at the end of his tether, this Wall, this sweet and lovely Wall, is a genius. And since, forty years ago, he was a Cochran discovery, he justifies the show.

Won't You Stay for Breakfast? (Apollo), which is a good notch and a half above the recent run of commercial farce, enables Derek Nimmo to demonstrate the depths that can be found within a well-drawn stock character. He is a bumbler, but a bumbler of principle and no fool; within two minutes of curtain-rise we have seen him cook suki-yaki, soothe a troublesome sister, and circle a room all more or less at the same time. No one else in the play has the same opportunities, but Nimmo and his director, Ray Cooney, are model craftsmen, meticulous but without appearance of spontaneity. Mr Cooney also wrote the play, in collaboration with Gene Stone.

The Young Vic revival of Harold Pinter's The Caretaker is admirable in its lucidity and its avoidance of cheap laughs. But it also misses some perfectly legitimate ones, thereby reducing the play's range and in the end its stature. What remains is a tight, bleak tale without resonance.
1973-12-23-drag-gag:
Drag gag

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN at the 'Danny La Rue Show' and 'Jack and the Beanstalk'.

MUCH money has been spent, but will doubtless be recouped, on the new attractions at London's two premier show shops.

The Danny La Rue Show (Prince of Wales) is a splashier enterprise than Jack and the Beanstalk (Palladium). Neither show is remarkable for imaginative decor, but Berkeley Sutcliffe's creations at the Prince of Wales are more solidly lavish than Tod Kingman's for the Palladium panto. The latter, though, scores valuable points with its all too brief introduction of a large green fire-breathing dragon.

Freddie Carpenter's direction of the La Rue show is superior in terms of sheer efficiency. (One hardly expects artistry in these circumstances, and though one might reasonably demand dynamism it would be more prudent not to.) Here also may be found the better and punchier band: musical director, Derek New. As regards costuming, there is little to choose: Mr La Rue's gowns (designed by Mark Canter, executed by Isolyn) are justly famous, but they are hardly more delightful than the insect casings in which hordes of stage children scuttle fluorescently, if a little aimlessly, across the stage of the Palladium. Both shows are shoved at us through microphones, but whereas the La Rue team have taken the measure of their amplification system, the Palladium gang are nearly overwhelmed by theirs. This pantomime sounds distant and metallic.

Its performers, however, make it in the end the more rewarding entertainment. This is not to deny that all London will flock to see Mr La Rue. He has practically blackmailed us into it by announcing that this is our last chance to see him in drag. After this we must wear La Rue with a difference.

But will we want to? If he carries out his published threat to hang up his tits, he will presumably have to hang up all those dresses alongside them, thus depriving us and himself of the peaks of his acts. (And not just the peaks: think of the valleys.) The evening has very little to offer beyond the breathtaking series of entrances made by Mr La Rue in his multitudinous frocks. Since show-biz propriety demands that some pretext shall be furnished for each disguise, he is forced to dissipate the instant conviction of his appearance as Nell Gwyn, Princess Anne or Carol Channing in some feebly written song or sketch. The sung words are preferable to the spoken, but there is only one joke throughout: phallic double entendre.

Dispensing this material, Mr La Rue reveals himself to be a merely competent gag-man and a powerful but anonymous vocalist. He can do one limited thing supremely well, and is thus a speciality performer, no more suited than an accomplished juggler or trapeze artist to be the king-pin of a revue. (Compare him with Stanley Baxter, a comedian whose female impersonations disclose as much finesse and far more wit, and who can also be very funny in men's wear.) The Danny La Rue Show is monotonous; perhaps a book show, with a satirical plot that might utilise the star's transvestite skills, would have been a better idea.

  

One of the merits of Jack and the Beanstalk is that, despite the temptations that commonly beset a pantomime, it never quite loses sight of its story. The perils include the casting of two mid-road pop singers as Jack and his uncommonly tough little Princess; they, who should have the most vested of interests in keeping the action going, are in fact the likeliest of all to halt it. So quick are they to burst into unheralded song that their first duet suggests love before first sight.

The show is rich, however, in comic talent. Even too rich: Alfie Bass, cast as the King, is given nothing whatever to do. Perhaps it is the competition from the La Rue camp that has killed the idea of a male Dame (as of a female Principal Boy), but Dora Bryan makes Jack a good mother, winsome, agile, and very friendly with cows and people. Her Shirley Temple turn is a treat.

Frankie Howerd is the star, and a problem. One senses trouble when the familiar opening "ladies and gentlemen" has to be followed by "boys and girls." This is tampering with a sacred text, and spoils the rhythm besides. Pantomime, and indeed children, circumscribe (no, dear, circumscribe) Mr Howerd; he has to watch his language (though this script hardly repays such attention), but he sticks loyally by the occasion. He regularly sabotages the narrative, as a pantomime comic should, but never undermines the convention. Never, that is, until his final solo spot when he comes into something resembling his own. He rapidly disposes of the dreaded song sheet sequence by taking us phonetically into what purports to be the national anthem of the Common Market (as befits the commonness--let us face it, the dead commonness--of which Mr Howerd can convict all with whom he comes into contact).

Soon he is beseeching us to join in the chorus of the saga of the three little fishes who swam over the dam; yes, he knows we think it's childish. Actually I was more than willing to oblige him since his rendition of this ballad was a cherished part of my own childhood. I regret, though, that he has now shorn it of its tragic conclusion and savagely cautionary moral. In times like these we can hardly afford to shield our children from the harsher facts of life.

  

I must postpone until next week proper consideration of The Party, Trevor Griffiths's new play at the National. Let me in the meantime wrap up a few things for Christmas: the Actors' Company have brought their version of R. D. Laing's Knots, seen at the Edinburgh Festival and elsewhere, to the Shaw; while another Edinburgh original, Stanley Eveling's Union Jack (and Bonzo), has reached the Hampstead Theatre Club, whose previous incumbent, Peter Handke's The Ride Across Lake Constance, has transferred to the Mayfair. God bless them, every one.
1973-12-30-the-national-party:
The National Party

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Trevor Griffiths's new play about revolutionary politics.

TREVOR GRIFFITHS'S The Party is the final fruit of Kenneth Tynan's Literary Consultancy at the National Theatre. The National has in the past derived more sustenance from Tynan the showman than from Tynan the ideologue, but The Party, commissioned from our most explicitly political playwright, could be an attempt to even the score.

As ever, one searches for clues in the programme. There, amid a generous selection of revolutionary texts, one slogan from Paris 1968 claims attention: "When the National Assembly becomes a bourgeois theatre, all the bourgeois theatres must become National Assemblies."

Mr Griffiths has attempted to effect this transformation at the Old Vic. The central portion of his play is a debate between assorted radicals who, at the time of those same Paris explosions, sit at home in London and try to hammer out a programme for a new revolutionary party. If you detect a note of scorn in that sentence it is implicit in the situation, as the characters themselves testify by their fascination with the TV news; they are uneasily aware that the real action is going on elsewhere.

The discussion is inconclusive; theatrically, its main interest is that it throws up two marathon speeches. Their sustained seriousness suggests that Mr Griffiths wishes, straightforwardly, to educate his auditors; their length that he is daring them not to listen or even to fall asleep. The National Theatre audience, however, is a collective good sport, game as well as ripe for instruction. It swallowed Tom Stoppard philosophising, Peter Shaffer psychologising, and it will not strain at Mr Griffiths politicising. Nor should it; Mr Griffiths's tirades are extremely well written and superbly delivered.

Denis Quilley leads off as an LSE teacher who believes that nothing further can be expected from the Western proletariat and that the centres of revolutionary hope now lie exclusively in the Third World. He is thus inclined to regard much of his colleagues' activities as irrelevant. But there is a fair touch of irrelevance about him in Mr Quilley's performance: he is bland, a little prim, and his fingers, unzipping his briefcase to extract his notes and fastening it again once the lecture has been given, are deliciously self-satisfied.

But is this just jolly character detail or is it some kind of pointer to the play's theme? That the latter may be the case is suggested, though never positively established, by the treatment given to his antagonist, an old Glaswegian Trotskyist of majestic stature. In great tidal waves of rhetoric, artfully proportioned, he politely savages the middle-class trendies by whom he is surrounded: "You bite the hand that feeds you, but you'll never bite it off." Hear Olivier bark that last word; I have never seen him act better. Greater, but not better.

Few of the others present are more than caricatures, granted a couple of stereotyped lines apiece. Did Mr Griffiths intend his play to be merely a satire on the New Left? Or are they there because this is a National Theatre play, and should therefore have a large cast? Some of the best actors in the company and indeed the country are on view in this production (I hope Peter Hall is not intending to sack too many of them) and they do their best; but many of them are constrained to let their costumes do the work of characterisation. None of them is equipped to issue a direct challenge to Olivier's John Tagg, so this has to be done by underhand means. Not once but twice the instigator of the gathering, a television producer, is taken aside by his ex-wife (works for the Guardian, very forthright, understands him perfectly, God knows why they split up) and warned against succumbing to the old man's dangerous working-class sentimentality.

I am not sure whether this advice is meant to reflect on her or on Tagg or both; more damagingly, I am unsure of its effect on the recipient. He is the protagonist and what finally wrecks the evening is Mr Griffiths's failure to establish any relationship (even a negative one) between the play's public argument and the character's private life. He carries the full load of successful hang-ups: a refugee from his class, from his North-country background, and from commitment; he has a bitch of a wife, is maybe impotent, and certainly masturbates (the play begins with a sex-scene of cinematic explicitness). He also has a young brother who is touching him for 300 pounds to start a business. Initially he demurs at devoting his surplus cash to the furtherance of capitalism, though, to judge from John Napier's inordinately plush set - perhaps another necessary concomitant of National Theatre production - he has already invested so much in the consumer society that to scruple at this point is ridiculous; finally he delivers. But how, or whether, this decision relates to all that has gone before, or how we are to judge it, is never revealed.

In themselves, the scenes between the two brothers are good to watch: John Shrapnel is beautifully fresh, shy and bruisable as the nascent entrepreneur and Ronald Pickup brings his usual intelligence (subtly stepping up the Northern accent whenever he encounters a compatriot) to the vastly ungrateful central role, though he is physically too slight to compel attention when passive, which is most of the time. He has a further foil in Frank Finlay, playing, with appropriate richness, a successful and very drunk playwright several steps farther along the road to disillusion, who regularly punctures the pretensions of the other characters. This is often a superfluous exercise, but he has some very amusing lines.

Closing my eyes and holding on tight I would hazard that Tagg is the play's true hero and the others who disagree with him, deride him, ignore him, or put him down behind his back are meant to be condemned; in the words of John Lennon, "It ain't easy to be a working-class hero." But that is an abstraction from the play, not a response to it. To watch and listen to it is to be fogged and finally frustrated by directionless, inconclusive ironies. Overtopping them all, of course (and maybe it is the play's real subject - a gigantic escape-clause), is the presence of this author at this theatre, compounded by the casting of Olivier in such a role (and further compounded by his brilliance in it). John Dexter's production is excellent in its own terms; but they are glossy, prestigious terms. I am not blaming anyone; the machine goes into action and that is what it produces.

The result is another victory for showmanship. We take pleasure in the rhetoric; but in our attentiveness there is an element of self-congratulation by which Mr Griffiths might well be perturbed.

Still, if you're looking for a party the National is currently a better bet than the Roundhouse where Feast of Fools, a medieval frolic, is as uncontrollable as the Black Death and nearly as messy. For a really good group show try the Actors' Company, making an overdue London debut at the Shaw with their version of R. D. Laing's Knots. This company's egalitarian principles are their own affair; their standards are mine, and on this occasion are exhilaratingly high.
1974-01-06-antigone-in-south-africa:
Antigone in South Africa

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Fugard and Sherlock Holmes.

THE liaison between Athol Fugard and the Serpent Players of South Africa's Port Elizabeth is in some respects a strange one.

Mr Fugard is a dramatist of literary stamp, spare in construction, but sometimes over-ripe in expression. He is himself an actor and director, but it is difficult to imagine him working up his plays in collaboration with his casts. Yet this has been precisely his method with the Serpent Players.

There is, in fact, no author named for The Island (Royal Court). We are told it was "devised" by Mr Fugard and his two actors, John Kani and Winston Ntshona. By all accounts the process worked magnificently in Sizwe Bansi is Dead. But in The Island the joins show; it is streakily superb.

Messrs Kani and Ntshona are naturals. This is not to deny their technical skill, but watching them one thinks as little of acting as when watching Laurel and Hardy or Tony Hancock and Sid James. Can you imagine such performers engaged in acting out an existence in South Africa's maximum security political prison? Think for a moment of Mr Fugard's avowed master, Samuel Beckett. The cosmic, comic agonies of Mr Beckett's no-man's-land are those of Mr Fugard's everyday world. And in his two actors he has found or created or sparked off an immaculate Vladimir and Estragon: the primal double-act.

The lineage is particularly apparent when they begin a rehearsal-within-the-play. John and Winston share a cell. They are preparing a performance of the Antigone story for the prison concert, and John, the sharper of the two, has some difficulty in persuading Winston to go through with it.

Winston vents his misgivings in the very accents of Estragon refusing to recognise the advisability of waiting for Godot. He has a legitimate grievance: not only has it been kept from him until the last unguarded moment that Antigone and Creon probably never existed, but his assumption of the heroine's wig and padding has John falling about. Crushed and resentful, Winston foresees an eternity of teasing from the other prisoners. John's attempt to assert that the show must go on is met by a beleaguered rhetorical question: "You call laughing at me theatre?" John now shows himself a masterly persuader. "Let them laugh," he says, "so long as they listen at the end."

The implicit claim made for theatre is a huge one, but this show validates it. At its close we watch the Antigone performance: we see Winston come on stage, self-conscious in drag, and we don't laugh. So all right, we've been conditioned by what we have already seen. But when Creon, the State, sentences Antigone, the conscience of humanity, to be walled up within a rock, upon an island, with just enough food to keep her alive, we assist at the re-activation of a myth. It is possible to sense what the Antigone story may have meant to Sophocles's audience, to Jean Anouilh's during the Occupation, and indeed to Athol Fugard's when The Island was performed in Cape Town.

But between the Antigone rehearsal and performance a longish stretch of play intervenes and it is here that doubts arise. John is told that his 10-year sentence has been commuted; he will be out in three months. Winston, the lifer, seems delighted for him; in the face of such unselfishness we wonder if the play could actually be depicting imprisonment as an ennobling experience. But as John's elation grows (to the point where he asks, self-consciously, for his impending release not to be mentioned in the cell again), jealousy and desperation overcome Winston. Frantically, graphically, he describes the good times in store for his friend; the tirade is all the more bitter because it is with the relation of just such dreams as this that the two have taken it in turns to make life bearable for each other. But there is a difference in texture here which is more than a matter of context.

When John beguiled Winston with a long imaginary phone-call home the words seemed to flow from him, but by this later stage the playwright appears to have taken over. We are into Fine Writing, even momentarily into Fine Acting: good things in their place, but this is not it. We have also been uncomfortably reminded of the inert passages in Mr Fugard's more orthodox plays, though their concomitant sin - a thinness in characterisation - has vanished in the presence of these two players. Mr Ntshona, with his strength and his appalling vulnerability, seems to me marginally the finer of the two, but it is their interaction which we shall remember. This production, in both its style and its substance, is an affirmation of human interdependence (which encompasses human conflict); it takes us down to the roots of drama.

Sherlock Holmes (Aldwych) offers another rich relationship though not, as you might expect, between Holmes and Watson. In this melodramatisation (vintage 1899), adapted from Conan Doyle by the American actor William Gillette (with, naturally, razor sharpness) the good doctor is a shadow of his legendary self, skimpily written and rather callowly played. Holmes's true partner is his greatest adversary, Professor Moriarty. They even, after much brilliant fencing, suffer a similar decline, Moriarty crumbling into custody as bathetically as Holmes dwindles into a husband.

Wreathed in a truly Holmesian fog (regular Aldwych customers might deduce from the smoke that a Shakespearean battle was in progress), the evening proceeds on a rapturous course, in Carl Toms's sets which, for Victorian gusto and mechanical delight, have not been matched since Sean Kenny's for Oliver! (The Stepney gas-chamber is a masterpiece.) Frank Dunlop, a director who usually arouses my admiration and despair in equal proportions, here puts not a toenail wrong. His is not a totally straight-faced production - it begins with a funereal fiddling of the James Bond theme - but it plays a neat game with our responses: the actors' voices may waver ("Not Sherlock Holmes!"), but their eyelids remain in place.

John Wood's vocal technique is so developed that he can switch from burlesque to stern reality within a sentence; he is Holmes to the afterlife. Philip Locke's silky lisp is perfect for Moriarty, and his associates - Nicholas Selby, Barbara Leigh-Hunt, Harry Towb, Trevor Peacock - might have stepped up from Tussaud's basement. Mr Peacock, who plays a safe-breaker (with stethoscope), has a particular aptitude for what I would call mutton-chop acting.

So, though the onset of 1974 leaves me as cold as it does most of you (overcoats are currently de rigueur in theatres) it has, thus far, been a good year in my patch. A piece called Judies (Comedy: place and genre) let down the tone a bit, but we can live with that.

1974-01-13-drama-s-invalids:
Drama's invalids

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

IN the theatre, even more perhaps than in life, we flinch from illness and from physical pain. This is not due merely to queasiness. Dramatically it seems an unprofitable subject.

It leaves the playwright and his characters nowhere to go; a cry of rage, and then what follows? There is rarely anyone to blame, and hence no conflict. The earliest, and probably the greatest, play on the subject - Sophocles's Philoctetes - rather neatly sidestepped the problem. The hero's poisoned foot causes him atrocious suffering, expressed in some harrowing lyrics, but he is also provided with human enemies. (His comrades, unable to bear the stink of his wound, have marooned him on an uninhabited island, so a large part of his fury can be directed at them.) Finally he qualifies, through heavenly intervention, as one of the few curable invalids in world drama.

His successors have generally been less fortunate; the luckiest were hypochondriacs. They have not been able to call on divinely infallible physicians, and the human substitutes available, though frequently efficient, have not always been sympathetic. The rise of institutional medicine has triggered off as much resentment as gratitude; the cleaner the surroundings, the more degrading illness can seem. This helpless rage at physical decay throbs, I think, beneath a play like Peter Nichols's The National Health, only occasionally breaking surface.

It bursts right through in David Rudkin's Ashes (Open Space), which concerns a married couple who, though not precisely sick, are still the victims of their own malfunctioning bodies. They are mysteriously childless; medical opinion puts the blame on the husband's insufficient sperm-count. Cold water, taken externally, is the prescription ("Hands up," says our beleaguered hero to the audience, "who's tried bathing his balls"); the treatment grows more complicated as the doctors consulted become more specialised. At last, after some reorientation of their sex-life (they never seem quite at ease with canine-type coupling), the miracle happens: triumphal music and a golden light on the victorious urine-sample. But it proves an ironic respite. The balance of humiliation now shifts to the wife: she miscarries, losing both babies (yes, she was carrying twins) and her womb as well.

That is some hard-luck story. Mr Rudkin makes it convincing by getting the domestic tone accurate. We believe in this couple - in their love, in their tolerance (or I should say in hers, since he is the one with the interesting neuroses) and in their rows: when she is ill, and he brings her breakfast in bed and spills the milk, her edgy martyred exasperation ("I'll eat the cornflakes dry") is exactly right. Hence we believe in their pain as well, and do not begrudge them their self-pity. (I see no reason why self-pity should never be regarded as justly earned.) Paranoia, however, is another matter; I first suspected it when the grandest of the doctors, known as the Guru, brushed aside a suggestion that the couple might give up all idea of propagation by smugly admonishing them of their duty to continue the species. This strain continues to be heard in the play and damages it: as the victims of their own humanity the characters are tragic, but their predicament shrinks when it is blamed on bland officials or patronising relatives, however exasperating they may be. The limitations of the theme strike us all over again.

Much of Mr Rudkin's language is also, as the leader-writers say, grossly inflationary. Both protagonists soliloquise to excess; Peter McEnery and Lynn Farleigh play desperately well together in Pam Brighton's production, but turned loose on a monologue she congeals, searching too hard for natural pauses. He is more successful in riding the rhetoric, particularly at the end when he tells of a journey home. Home happens to be in Belfast, where his uncle has been killed by a bomb. Mr McEnery's long evocation of the battered city and his despair at its dedication to future bloodshed are as moving as anything in O'Casey. They have, however, no visible connection with the rest of the play except that they artificially increase the husband's isolation. He is now a two-way orphan: no future, no past.

I should add that there is a rumour going around the Open Space that the whole play is a metaphor for the Ulster situation. (Unnatural conceptions and bloody miscarriages: it might fit.) Since this rumour reached my ears only after I had seen the performance (a preview) on Monday, I cannot say how the play would stand up to detailed inspection from this angle. You might like to go along and try it.

Sizwe Bansi is Dead (Royal Court) will withstand inspection from any angle. Since this production is already legend may I register one small reservation? John Kani's opening monologue is too long. His devastating account of a day in a South African Ford factory is justly famous and a necessary introduction to the play's treatment of apartheid. But when Mr Kani, as Styles the photographer, began to re-enact his most memorable sessions I got restless. I was anxious, remembering The Island from the previous week, for Winston Ntshona to enter, both for his own sake and for that of the partnership.

On neither score was I disappointed. Mr Ntshona, posing for his photograph as a man of the world with a pipe in one hand and a cigarette in the other, is at first sweet, shy and bewildered. Later his bewilderment intensifies in the face of the damning stamp in his pass-book (which, by the way, as he reiterates in the most resonant line of the evening, he cannot read); then it burgeons into a towering assertion of his own manhood and finally settles into a mature hopefulness, infinitely qualified. Meanwhile the mockery that seethed behind Mr Kani's Louis Armstrong grin is released into the full bitterness of urban experience, painful to acquire but almost unfairly exhilarating to watch.

Messrs Kani and Ntshona devised the entertainment with their director, Athol Fugard. If we are to regard it as his play it is his best; there may be too many lines, but there is not a single false one. And truthfully, you have never seen such acting.
1974-01-20-breathing-life-into-ghosts:
Breathing life into 'Ghosts'

THEATRE

by ROBERT
CUSHMAN

WHEN Ibsen selected the title Ghosts he made an unconscious prophetic joke; none of his plays is harder to bring to life.

We are all, of course, far too sensitive and sophisticated to believe that the play lost its validity when science came up with a cure for syphilis. We have been told, and can appreciate, that the disease which destroys Oswald and which he inherited from his father is merely a figure for the destructive influence of heredity, tradition, conventional belief, and all those bequests from the past which are never likely to be vanquished by a shot of penicillin. We can see, too, that the true carrier of the disease is Oswald's mother, Mrs Alving; and that it is all the more virulent in her because she imagines that she has fought free of it.

We can see it, but in performance it is usually very difficult for us to feel it. We are aware instead of portentous dialogue, obviously heavy with symbolism; why else would the actors pace their lines so funereally, weight them so oddly, and look so intently past one another's shoulder-blades? Should we want something to look at, the stage will generally be heaped with heavy Victorian furnishings, though these may be somewhat obscured by the dim light that seems to have pervaded Norway throughout the last century. In these circumstances it is impossible to take the action seriously, let alone to admit its significance. The atmosphere becomes not so much obscure as oppressively muggy.

Jonathan Miller's enthralling production at Greenwich clears the air, as decisively as Ingmar Bergman's Hedda Gabler (and with rather more respect for the text). Like Bergman, he has refreshed our senses with a non-realistic set; Patrick Robertson has enclosed the play in a huge string cage, somewhat resembling Josef Svoboda's setting for the National Theatre's disappointing Three Sisters. The abstraction that proved fatal to Chekhov works wonders for Ibsen; uncluttered and clearly lit, the play is set free.

There is nothing abstracted, however, about the performance itself, even in the woollier passages of the script. Ibsen's exasperating vagueness concerning Mrs Alving's scandalously adventurous literary tastes (talking of Advanced Books as if they were an accredited series like Penguins) is generally underscored by a shocked inflection from Pastor Manders: "You read books of this kind?" In Robert Stephens's reading of this line, the emphasis is on the word "you"; attention is directed away from the author's mannerisms and on to the relationship of the characters.

This discreet understatement is wholly typical of Mr Stephens's performance, which amounts to a major job of rehabilitation. The author's credit is saved with the character's, for the tiresome old buffer we usually see could have been created only by another tiresome old buffer. Mr Stephens's Pastor is liable to clasp his hands at preacherly comments, but he is personable and intelligent enough to be forgiven that; only as the play progresses do we come to realise the abrupt and painful limits he has set to both his intellect and his emotions for the sake of his self-esteem. This being his ruling passion, a performance that has avoided caricature attains in the end to high comedy when he tumbles into Engstrand's blackmailer's trap. At this moment, too, Antony Brown - who has timed Engstrand's Dickensian hypocrisies with sly individuality - suddenly and memorably ceases to be funny.

A similar, though more complex, balance is struck between Manders and Mrs Alving in their long scenes together. Remembering the past they also relive it; Irene Worth is particularly acute when she recalls the Pastor's earlier rejection of her. A wiser woman now, she watches him (watchfulness is indeed the keynote of her performance) intently and amusedly. When he mentions ideals, she repeats the word, tastes it on her tongue, chews it over as a good Ibsen heroine should. When the Alving orphanage, the supposed embodiment of those ideals, burns down, she responds with an uncontrolled burst of bitter laughter: the boldest stroke in the production (and perhaps, all told, the most tactful way to greet such a bludgeoning stroke from one's dramatist). Only at the close does Miss Worth's intelligence betray her; invited to perform euthanasia upon her son she objects, "I gave you life," as if it were a reasoned debating-point rather than an instinctual cry.

The end still packs a Grand Guignol punch; Peter Eyre's Oswald is a young man with the gaunt looks of an old one (freezing rather than burning up) and he gets full value from his marvellous simile for softening of the brain: "Like cherry-red velvet curtains." Hardly less gruesome is the family carousal with Nicola Paget's Regina keeping a distrustful distance, stiffly nursing a glass of champagne; her inevitable progression into her father's brothel is one of the most clearly charted lines in the production.

  

Mr Miller's version of Measure for Measure (a National Theatre Mobile Production, which last week fetched up for a matinée at the Old Vic) is less admirable, though it boasts in Julian Curry's murderously prim Angelo a study in uptightness to rank almost with Mr Stephens's. Here too, as in Ghosts, are long duets played with a minimum of movement and a maximum of lucid flexibility. Mr Curry's attempted seduction of Gillian Barge's Isabella is hardly finer than her subsequent encounter with her brother (David Bradley), whose disobliging inclination to save his life at the expense of her honour is rewarded by a vicious swipe from her handbag.

This, you will gather, is a modern-dress production; its Vienna is not merely post-Shakespearean but post-Freudian. Escalus (a dignified performance by John Gregg) wears a frock-coat, Mariana is a 1920s vamp in black dress and beads (with matching cigarette) and Angelo is timeless in pin-stripes. Some characters are amusingly transformed: Mistress Overdone is not the usual raddled old bawd, but a chic, dykey coeval of Norma Levy, while Pompey (a sharp performance by Neil Cunningham) is, to match, a thin-lipped, red-tied Soho ponce.

The action passes in an all-purpose waiting-room, which is yet too detailed to be accepted as neutral territory; outdoor scenes look very odd there and the final dispensation of justice "without the city gate" is so cramped as to be meaningless. The show is cramped in other ways too: it is under-projected (only Mr Curry is compellingly audible throughout), over-solemn (our most revered directors, from Peter Brook on down, apparently regard Shakespeare's farce as beneath their notice) and under-populated (Juliet, the girl whose pregnancy sets the plot in motion, is reduced to an offstage voice).

The end is very strange; Isabella greets the Duke's proposal of marriage by backing away in horror, and the general mood is, in P. G. Wodehouse's phrase, if not actually disgruntled then far from being gruntled. I think myself that it should be almost wholly gruntled. Of course my views are governed by preconception and prejudice since I have dreamed of directing the play myself, but would it not make sense to see it as a progression by all the characters (notably the Duke, Angelo, and Isabella) towards an acceptance of the love they all reject at the beginning in the name of principle or ideals? Could it not be, in fact, that this is a play in which the lesson so grimly taught in Ghosts is actually learned?

Further performances of the touring Measure for Measure: Nuffield Theatre, Southampton University, 2 February; Old Vic, 5, 20, 21 February; Uppingham School, 16 February.
1974-02-03-bird-of-mystery:
Bird of mystery

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'The Seagull.'

YOU can generally have a good if tepid time at a Chekhov production by concentrating on the characters and not worrying about shapes or meanings. The Seagull (Greenwich) is an exception; it is colder in temper than his later plays and more obviously invites analysis. That bird, as Nina exasperatedly says, seems to be meant as some kind of symbol.

Lying all on its own, well forward on the wide apron, it looks exposed and a little ludicrous. Some yards away Trigorin is holding forth to Nina on the tribulations of the novelist. We listen as raptly as she does, but occasionally our eyes stray to that poor forlorn symbolic property. We - with my own puzzlement I associate the director Jonathan Miller and, I suspect, Chekhov himself - are not quite sure what to make of it.

We will just have to sidestep the seagull and omit it from our pattern. For there is a pattern, though it is slow to unravel. Only when the last act begins, moving us on two years in time, does it finally become apparent that this is a play about survival. All the characters but one are survivors, and they pay in various ways for the privilege. The one exception - the suicide, Konstantin - pays of course more heavily than anyone.

We realise he is doomed from the moment he announces that he has burned the manuscript of his unsuccessful play. Having seen it virtually jeered off the stage by his own mother, he has perhaps some excuse, but it is the act of a man who will always leave his wounds open; most importantly, it is the act of an amateur. All the other men in this play are professionals. Even useless old Sorin has managed to hold down a Civil Service post for years.

The two super-pros are the novelist Trigorin - who would never destroy or forget any piece of material until he had made use of it - and the doctor Dorn. For both, the price of futile marriages. Has Women's Lib discovered The Seagull yet?

Mr Miller's production is less complete than its companion-piece, Ghosts, but then that is a simpler play, more satisfactory, but less satisfying. It is nevertheless a rich experience. Peter Eyre comes nearest to duplicating his Ghosts performance, but his pallor, as of a boy never young, in fact suits Konstantin better than it did Oswald whose "joy of life" had to be taken rather on trust. He is, here, a natural pedant, dreadfully earnest, his faculty of self-criticism so highly developed as to lead quite logically to suicide. His happiest moment is his entry, lugging the dead seagull and radiating the satisfaction of a poet who has found his metaphor.

Strangely enough, considering the family bonds that are meant to link this season, his relationship with his mother is one of the least well realised aspects of the production. (The two players embark on their big confrontation with palpable self-consciousness, as if determined to do justice to the theme.) Irene Worth's Arkadina is a ruthless study of a ruthless woman, but - perhaps inevitably, given Miss Worth's undisguisable intelligence - it has to be a calculating ruthlessness. She gives little evidence of feeling, so her prolonged weeping, when she thinks Konstantin has shot himself, seems out of key.

Robert Stephens is again superb; his acting has taken on a new muscularity which, paradoxically, enables him to project all Trigorin's flabbiness while preserving the steel core that keeps him working and so existing. There are other fine performances: from Anthony Nicholls, the essence of impotent kindliness as Dorn; from Philip Lowrie as Medviedenko; and from George Howe, who is truly too old for Sorin, but whose huddled, wheel-chaired figure makes a powerful image to launch (and partially summarise) the last act.

Maureen O'Brien's Nina is fresh, but a little blank, yielding in interest to her shadow-sister Masha, endowed with Nicola Paget's hardest edge and marrying Medviedenko as much out of spite as desperation. Antony Brown deals nicely with Shamyarev's theatrical memories, but fails to establish that his sycophancy towards the great actress (a necessary aspect of Chekhov's presentation of the all-enveloping theatrical shallowness that helps to kill Konstantin) is the obverse of his tyrannical rudeness: Shamyarev is a boor as well as a bore.

It is, I think, understandable that Mr Miller's season of Hamlet variations has not found room for Adrian Mitchell's Mind Your Head (Shaw), which transforms the Prince to the driver of a No 24 bus (Hampstead to Pimlico), his mother to a clippie, and his villainous uncle Claude to a ticket-collector who turns out to be Hitler, a figure of whom, it is fair to say, Mr Mitchell thoroughly disapproves. His other attitudes are hardly less predictable and the show (a whimsical mini-musical) is often plain silly, and occasionally - as in a parodied TV quiz - much worse. But somehow it survives; we don't very often see plays set on double-decker buses and Peter James's production fills this one with nice energetic people like Nicky Henson and Lynda Marchal. Anyway I live on the 24 bus route and I cannot be too discourteous to the first play ever to pass my door.

  

David Edgar's Operation Iskra (Bush) works effectively as political melodrama, but its psychological structure is shaky. Since the play is fuelled by the dissensions among its revolutionary characters, it is unfortunate that they can hardly be told apart. The men in this Paradise Foundry production (well directed by Chris Parr) are more convincing politicos than the women, who come on strong like well-intentioned actresses.

  

The Grand Magic Circus, led by Jerome Savary of the uniquely mournful voice and visage, are back at the Roundhouse with From Moses to Mao, with better music than we get at the Shaw, a comic-strip world history which is fun to be at even when it ceases to be fun to watch.
1974-02-10-in-praise-of-chez-nous:
In praise of 'Chez Nous'

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

MEMORIAL ENTERPRISES, who are presenting Peter Nichols's Chez Nous (Globe), have asked the critics not to reveal a couple of surprise developments in the first act. After all, they reminded us, we kept mum about Sleuth and our forefathers did the same for The Mousetrap.

However Chez Nous is neither Sleuth nor The Mousetrap. It is the best new play in London and the best its author has written. It can withstand a few critical indiscretions, and, in the cause of intelligible discussion, it will have to. All I can do, as with The Wolf last year, is to issue a caveat: you may prefer to see the play first and read this review (which you will of course preserve, with reverence) later.

Well, how did you enjoy the play?

You will remember that it concerns Dick and Liz (I am not sure whether Mr Nichols intends mythological overtones), who invite their old friends Phil and Diana to stay with them in their farmhouse in the Dordogne. (The bit of it we see looks like a de luxe barn; it ranks as one of the two best sets in the West End, along with that created by the same artist, Michael Annals, for - most appropriately - Design for Living.)

The association of these two fortyish married couples stretches back to their single days. The only significant blemish on Robert Chetwyn's production is that it is sometimes difficult to accept this fact. Liz and Diana are said to have gone to school together, but Diana is the fastidiously mannered Geraldine McEwan, whom I cannot imagine at school with anyone except Glynis Johns, Joan Greenwood and Fenella Fielding, plus occasional trips to stay with Maggie Smith at weekends. She certainly seems to share no audible point of origin with Pat Heywood's determinedly placid and ordinary Liz.
