On second thoughts, and with an effort, I can accept that both these ladies, whatever they may have been like as young girls, are as we now see them because of a process of choice, conscious or unconscious. Diana, with her bleached, wire-drawn frame and her dreams of elegant ravishment by some suave Scott Fitzgerald playboy, forced herself to grow up into Geraldine McEwan; Liz settled for comfortable domesticity and wound up believing that, sunning herself down on the farm, she could feel like Mrs Tolstoy.

Given these predilections it is unfortunate that Liz's marriage should have turned out the remunerative one. Dick is a paediatrician who has struck it rich with a book which someone has providentially persuaded him to entitle The Nubile Baby (Mr Nichols's other jokes are better than that, but less easily quotable). His attitude to his success, and to its source, is complex. He professes to be pained by the title, and by the sexy schoolgirl photo which adorns its cover - of which, however, he keeps a large blow-up on the premises. He knows he should despise money and fame but he enjoys the attention, having always resented his own bashfulness. In particular he resents the fact that his wife is the only woman he has had; surely there must be more to sex than he has known with her. So in The Nubile Baby he rails against conventional sexual restraints and, of course, against the family. Which is ironic, since not only is his wife family personified, but they have three children of their own.

Only they have two. Their new baby son is actually their grandson begotten on their 14-year-old daughter (first surprise) by old pal and present guest, Phil (second surprise).

Now about Phil. He is an architect, though we don't hear much about that; we hear more about his habit of taking his wife to jazz clubs (not her idea of a glamorous good time), where he invariably ends up sitting in on banjo. He wants a child; when they married she was pregnant by another man, and after the birth she had herself sterilised. His discovery that he has a son sets up a battle for possession of the baby which comes to dominate the play. Given something to fight for, Albert Finney's roused performance takes on extraordinary strength; this is his definitive roaring boy.

But it is Dick on whom the play finally closes in; for funnier, for sadder, Mr Nichols has here developed and enriched the themes of loneliness and aching regret which he adumbrated in Forget Me Not Lane, and A Day in the Death of Joe Egg. Denholm Elliott gives him occasional surges of joy (as when, making a hopeful leap at adultery, he sings out - and him a specialist - that children are really very boring) rising from a sea of angst: the resigned agony of a man who has reached the middle of his life and the end of his tether simultaneously.

At least two scenes should make the history-books: a terminal silent solo by Mr Elliott, and a central quartet of recrimination which plays like classic comedy. I must mention Denis Carey's enchanting old villager who turns out to serve a purpose beyond local colour; and Mr Nichols's magisterial use of solid objects (the blown-up schoolgirl, a pram, a swing) to focus his themes. Formally this is his least obviously experimental play, and his most successful.

  

David Mercer's Duck Song (Aldwych) is, by contrast, vociferously unconventional and a failure. We were repeatedly told before the opening that this play represented Mr Mercer's break with naturalism and, more surprisingly, we continued to be told so on the first night. The break turned out to consist of the furniture which filled the stage in Act I disappearing, more or less in a puff of smoke, by the beginning of Act II.

From where I sat this was a distinct gain in terms of sight-lines, but the inexplicable catastrophe - to which the characters never ceased referring, as if they could hardly credit their author's audacity - proved less successful in clarifying the play's inner landscape. Regret and recrimination were again the themes; but it is difficult to take much interest in the baring of souls which have never inhabited credible bodies, whether of Socialist cracksmen or idle painters living on inherited wealth. The acting is nothing much, though David Waller is fruity, Elizabeth Spriggs creamy, and Gareth Hunt, as a Red Indian, impressively stony. David Jones's direction assumes some odd shapes, but they are probably unavoidable.

Adrian Mitchell's Mind Your Head, set on a bus, has now been furnished at the Shaw with an afterpiece, James Saunders's Double Double, set in a bus-drivers' cafe. I doubt if much of the dialogue would actually be encountered there, but it is very satisfying stage-rhetoric (the subject - again - the decay of youthful dreams), excellently delivered by Lesley Joseph and a memorably enraged Sam Kelly.
1974-02-24-triumph-for-harrison-rex:
Triumph for Harrison Rex

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a Pirandello revival.

NOT the least merit of Clifford Williams's production of Pirandello's Henry IV (Her Majesty's) is that it destroys the play's reputation as one of the clumsiest pieces of narrative ever to attain the status of a modern classic.

It really is quite easy to follow, even for those who arrive at the theatre sharing the delusion of the young man so fetchingly portrayed in this production by Robin Sachs; he imagines, until corrected, that the monarch of the title is Henry IV of England; whom Shakespeare so memorably bisected. In fact, as he rapidly learns, we are concerned with an earlier Henry, the twelfth-century German Emperor who opposed the Pope and was forced to expiate his defiance by kneeling in the snow at Canossa.

Not that the play is really about the historical Henry: its protagonist is a twentieth-century Italian who dressed up as the Emperor in a carnival procession, fell from his horse, was concussed and awoke in the belief that he was the man he had been impersonating. When the play begins he has been maintained in this illusion for 20 years, surrounded and humoured by servants in period costume. At this point he is visited by a group of people who believe that he may be restored to sanity, among them the woman whom he wooed in vain before his accident and his former rival, now her lover.

It is, though, too late for "Henry" to be cured; he has known the truth for eight years, during which he has enjoyed prolonging the masquerade. Rex Harrison projects this enjoyment quite magnificently. Always he preserves a careful distance from everyone else, alternately confounding them with his courtesy and his rudeness. At times it is difficult to distinguish the two; Mr Harrison is constantly cocking his head towards his interlocutors, a gesture which denotes simultaneously an earnest desire to hear what they have to say and an implicit dismissal of it. He knows who his visitors are, of course, and he derives a sharp-edged pleasure from their uneasiness in the disguises which they must adopt in order to be admitted to his presence; faced with his old rival Belcredi, unhappily attired as a Benedictine monk, he twits him with being one of the Emperor's historical enemies and cannot be persuaded otherwise. The feigning madman is traditionally the quickest-witted man on stage and Mr Harrison is the most mentally agile of actors.

He is also the most lucid; and here we are in trouble. We are not informed that Henry has recovered from his delusion until halfway through the play; up until then we should at least have been in doubt and the revelation should strike us like a thunderclap. Here there is no surprise; Mr Harrison's conscious manipulation of the situation has been too obvious, and despite his admirably uncompromising appearance, his rouged cheeks and greying hair, nothing in his personality suggests madness.

Shorn of its ambiguity, the play loses much else. Perhaps it is to the point that while Henry, by remaining for 20 years in the role of the young emperor abasing himself at Canossa, has made a futile attempt to conquer time (how futile those grey locks bear witness), Mr Harrison as an actor seems to have done precisely that; his perennial vigour is amazing. Pirandello's hero is an all-time loser; in the end, the play being in part an inverted revenge-tragedy, much indebted to Hamlet, Henry runs Belcredi through. The penalty here, though, is not death, but death-in-life; having apparently given proof of his relapse into madness he is cast back for all time into his fantasy, knowing it to be a fraud. It is an appalling prospect; but Mr Harrison looks as if he might squeeze some fun from it.

None of this criticism constitutes an excuse for missing the performance. Mr Harrison is almost a great actor--who fits, by a truly Pirandellian irony, into hardly any of the great parts--and his wit, authority and vocal resource are to be treasured. Besides, missing his Henry would entail missing the Donna Matilda of Yvonne Mitchell, an actress whose work has recently taken on a rare and rewarding boldness of outline without losing any of its accustomed truth; her portrayal of Henry's lost love is uncompromising in its vanity and self-pity, its uneasy regrets and final terror.

James Villiers's lounge-lizard Belcredi is expectedly expert, and Peter Cellier as the senior member of the imperial entourage has an unforced style and presence which recall standards that could once (though, alas, no longer) be taken for granted in the West End. This production, with its spacious sets by Farrah, comes nearer those standards than most: nearer, for example, than The Waltz of the Toreadors (and there is a part for Mr Harrison) across the road.

  

If I may just go back to where I came in, Jean Genet's The Maids makes very few concessions to those (me, for instance) who like a good story well told, and Minos Volonakis's production at Greenwich makes even fewer. Those who care may argue whether the play's psychological content has been sacrificed to its Black Mass aspect or vice versa (I have seen both views advanced); I would merely like to quote Pauline Kael's gloss on "ritual" as "a word that has come to stand for much of what I could happily do without in the theatre" and to endorse it, where Black Masses are concerned, in spades.

Yolanda Sonnabend's bedroom is, shell-like (it was only when the walls were referred to as "the ears of God" that I got the message); it is also geometrically floral, like the dance routines of Busby Berkeley. Indeed, when Vivien Merchant comes on as Madame, lamenting her jailed lover, it is briefly possible to see the whole thing as a transplanted Warner-Brothers musical; Miss Merchant actually looks very 1930s and might easily pass for the society dame in hopeless thrall to the cynical bootlegger. She sounds very sleepy throughout.

Nor is Glenda Jackson absolutely the life of the party as the more ferocious of the domestics, though she does her own intense thing to some effect towards the end. She is partnered, vibrantly if too relentlessly, by Susannah York who should appear on our stages more often, if only to learn how to husband her very impressive resources. Neither actress can escape from the stranglehold of their author, who is interested in them only as the vehicle of his own obsessions. (Madame, being satirised and therefore objectified, is a more rewarding role, and Miss Merchant does gather a few laughs.) Mr Volonakis's production is fittingly portentous (you might argue that the rhetoric should be played down, but I cannot see what would be left) and the run is already sold out.

  

That being so, hasten to the Hampstead Theatre Club which this week offers amazing reductions: prices slashed by half, since the play Bremen Coffee lasts only an hour (The Maids is 90 minutes), within which time its heroine plans and commits a dozen murders (the maids plan one, and bungle it). Though she flourished in Germany in the 1830s, her author (Rainer Werner Fassbinder) sees her as an extremist forerunner of Women's Lib, ready to poison anyone who denies her sexual satisfaction or the control of her own business. Linda Marlowe conveys the former obsession more powerfully than the latter, but the production, elegantly acted and set, testifies anew to the potential of multiple murder (especially when kept in the family, cf. Lizzie Borden) as a source of harmless theatrical fun.
1974-03-03-monty-mania:
Monty mania

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

IF Monty Python's First Farewell Tour (Drury Lane) were not the funniest show in London, something would be seriously amiss. Well, it is the funniest show in London, and something is still seriously amiss.

Two bits in the show made me weep with laughter. The first was an Olympiad which involved a Marathon race for men with weak bladders and an aquatic event for non-swimmers, who dived into the pool and did nothing else. Ever. The second was also of a sporting nature, being a football match, Ancient Greek philosophers v. modern German. (Rather a dull game, owing to the tendency of both teams to stand around arguing.) Both sequences were on film.

The experience of watching them was therefore not dissimilar to watching "Monty Python" on a very large colour television screen, in the company of a correspondingly large number of devotees. Though I malign them: they were not devotees, they were sycophantic maniacs.

Now, one of the charms of watching these film clips, as of watching television, is that you can mentally phase out your fellow viewers; but you can't ignore the audience during the live sketches. The skits are mostly familiar (though surprisingly few of them would rate inclusion in my personal anthology, the Pith of Python), loved and learned by rote from TV runs and reruns and from the movie. Like pop fans cheering the opening bars of a favourite song, so Tuesday's house howled when Eric Idle stressed, heavily, that he wanted to be a lumberjack or when John Cleese wandered on carrying a cage containing a dead parrot. (To be fair, the first time he does this he wanders straight off again, the celebrated parrot number being reserved for much later; this teaser is the only point at which the show recaptures the joyously eccentric continuity of its TV original.) However brilliant the material, it cannot survive transformation into a rite for initiates only.

Live comedy depends on danger, on contact, and on unpredictability: it demands an alert but critical audience. To have one's defences breached by a great clown is a marvellous experience, but the defences have to be there.

Anyway, with one and a half exceptions these are not really clowns; they are ideas-men who have conquered one medium, but look lost outside it. On stage the pecking order becomes unwontedly (and unwantedly) clear: Mr Cleese is very funny, and Mr Idle is quite funny, and Graham Chapman is a bit funny, and the others are indistinguishable and screech a lot. This last tendency is emphasised, and my antagonism exacerbated, by the murderous amplification and the cavernous incongruity of the theatre itself. Even Mr Cleese's personality loses some of its flavour under these circumstances.

  

Messrs Cleese and Idle might be amusingly cast in the opening scene of David Rudkin's No Title (presented by the Birmingham Repertory Theatre's Brum Studio), in which a nervous young man is shown round his new flat by a tall, beaky supercilious caretaker. Once his guide has departed, the tenant, Mr Bisthorpe, sets about altering those features of his lodging which are not to his taste. Principally he is affronted by some very drab lampshades; his ensuing battle with the light-fittings, permanently uncertain whether he has pulled the cord which operates them to the On or Off position, provides a delicious sequence of silent comedy.

The comedy continues, but grows less silent and less delicious. Though Bisthorpe's flat was advertised as being "self-contained," it affords no cooking facilities. The house to which it is attached boasts a communal kitchen, but when he wanders into it four cooks, already at work there, set upon him, apparently with murderous intent. They seem mad; and gradually it dawns upon him and upon us that he is indeed in an asylum, presided over by a formidable, and totally unsympathetic, lady doctor. His four assailants reappear as the Institution's board of governors.

Is Bisthorpe a sane man who, like Peer Gynt, has wandered into a madhouse where the inmates have taken control? Or has he actually been committed and are we seeing events as they appear to him in his mania? Mr Rudkin keeps his options open for a very long time, then reveals that neither is applicable and that we have here a dramatic metaphor for a Britain, out of control and devoted to dispossessing its inhabitants. Bisthorpe may think he has a tenant's rights, but in fact he has none: No Title.

I remember the kitchen scene from a television play some years back; the rest of it has fled my memory so I cannot say how much of the present work is really new. My impression is that Mr Rudkin rather hastily grafted a few topical jabs on to a scheme he had originally found unworkable. The board tell Bisthorpe that it does not matter if he can no longer afford meat; indeed it doesn't really matter if he starves. There is talk of power-cuts and of "the need for a human face."

The satire and the symbolism may be crude, but they are wrenchingly powerful. Mr Rudkin can stage action that lives in its own right and his verbal command is unmatched by any other current playwright. I prefer his punning here to his poeticising in Ashes; it creates a world and gives us an agonising involvement in Bisthorpe's struggles, trapped in a cage of words. "Oh witty . . . witty Dr Kings," he gasps at his chief tormentor, and tries to erect his own pedantic verbal barricade against her. Tormented by Muzak, he refers to it as an "intravenous assault on my auditory privacy." "Who," he asks, when finally reduced, "can have pity for a man who merely wakes up to find his value fallen in the night?" Colin Farrell has the full measure of his desperation, though some other roles could do with stronger playing; more particularly, with older playing. Don't tell me that this is difficult in rep; I know.

  

Like Mr Rudkin, Sam Shepard can create potent theatrical images; unlike him he has no gift for suspense; and though Geography of a Horse Dreamer (Theatre Upstairs) is a more accessible work, by word, than some of his previous work, its total import baffles me. It concerns an American prophet of horse-racing results, who is transported blindfold to England by a couple of gangsters and then ignominiously relegated to the dog-tracks. Finally mayhem erupts. Some warning may be intended about the dangers of uprooting a dreamer, or anyone else, from his nourishing native soil. One incompetent performance, and several effortful ones, perhaps render the play more portentous than it need be, but Bob Hoskins shines out as one of the few British actors one would happily cast in Guys and Dolls.
1974-03-10-the-national-s-great-tempest:
The National's great 'Tempest'

THERE is only one word to describe The Tempest, Peter Hall's first production for the National Theatre, and for once it can be employed literally. The word is fabulous.

Fabulous, but not by any means fanciful: Mr Hall's approach is, by the lights of this play, scrupulously realistic. He begins with a thoroughly convincing storm, the hard-working, hard-lurching sailors beset by a bunch of troublesome courtiers scrambling up from a cabin below decks. At the close of the scene the roof of their cabin slams shut; standing on it, the first of a series of inspired transformations, is Prospero, the controller of the tempest and of the play.

His control is not, in John Gielgud's performance, serene or untroubled. To work magic on this scale requires of him an enormous effort of concentration; his magician's robe weighs him down and it is a relief to him to shed it. He lays great stress on the line about "the most auspicious star" on whose influence, necessarily transient, his success depends. This Prospero is engaged in a race against time and this awareness colours the whole of his dispute with Ariel, whose demand for his liberty "before the time be out" endangers the whole scheme.

As it turns out it is only when the scheme is successful that Prospero's real troubles start. For the time being his charms work like a charm. The responsibility for showing this is not the actor's (since Prospero has a habit of not being around while his spells are operating), but the director's, and Mr Hall shirks none of it. Some of his coups-de-theatre are truly coups of grace: the appearance of Ariel as a water-nymph when we expect the lumbering entrance of Caliban (I know the play by heart and this moment still took me by surprise, so cunningly is it staged) and the arrival of Ferdinand on the spot where Caliban had stood only a second before.

This last trick is effected with the aid of sliding scenery. One of the prime qualities of the isle, as realised by John Bury, is its mobility: a theatrical delight, to be relished as such. The masque element in the production erupts in two set pieces: the vanishing banquet, borne by "strange shapes" like a bad baroque dream of fertility corrupted, and the show of goddesses, sung throughout (which I found excessive, but pardonable) with Iris perched aloft, somewhere under a rainbow.

All of these wonders are germane to the play; most of them are explicitly demanded by it, though few directors respond as generously as Mr Hall. His triumph in this vein is his treatment of Ariel: "an airy spirit" he apparently lives in the sky (I said that this was a literal-minded production) whence he regularly descends by pulley. (I came to think of this contraption as Ariel's aerial.) Nearly always he is in some disguise; by his constant changes of shape Michael Feast comes as close to incorporeality as can be asked of any actor. He has besides two voices (which makes him, as Stephano remarks in another context, a most delicate monster); he sings both tenor and counter-tenor, rendering, in the latter, the lovely original setting of "Full fathom five."

"But this rough magic I here abjure"; the effects can only furnish the groundwork of the play, and in the end everything depends on Gielgud. Approaching victory he approaches despair: "Our revels now are ended" is savage rather than lyrical. His renunciation of revenge is tremendous, though not marked by any weighty pause. His tormented outburst against the "born devil" Caliban is balanced at the end by a glimmering of tolerance; a tolerance more than deserved, since Denis Quilley's Caliban, though resembling a Hiawatha who has gone berserk with the tomahawk and scalped himself, yet contrives to appear attractive. His roar of freedom has amazing force (in every performance of Mr Quilley's there is one moment that makes me think him the most exciting actor in the world and this is it), so his abasement before Stephano is all the more poignant.

Arthur Lowe's Stephano is as funny as you would expect and more than twice as mean; his function in the play is brilliantly illuminated at his final appearance in his stolen regal robes, to be greeted by Prospero's wry "You'd be king of the isle, sirrah?" Suddenly the stage appears thronged with monarchs, true and false; not for nothing do mirrors feature heavily in Mr Bury's set.

One parallel stands out over all; in his ducal gown Prospero is a dead ringer for his usurping brother Antonio, who emerges, far more than Caliban, as the play's negative pole. The role has been unusually strongly cast with an actor, Cyril Cusack, who approximates to Gielgud's own stature; untouched by the forgiveness at the close (though when Miranda appears he looks as though he might be harbouring avuncular thoughts of rape), he breaks silence only to make a sour joke over Caliban. One glance between the brothers at the end establishes them as eternally unreconcilable.

Having absorbed both this blow and his effective desertion by Ariel (who, having finally gained his freedom, celebrates by taking an express lift upstairs), Gielgud speaks the Epilogue, and sets his seal on the role forever. His next appearance (in Edward Bond's Bingo) will be as Shakespeare himself. It seems logical.

A magnificent evening: not, however, a flawless one. The flaws are important, less for the harm they do to this play (which easily survives them) than for the future of the company. On this showing there is no company; despite the trendy and prestigious casting the remarkable performances are outnumbered (not outweighed) by the mediocre ones. The lovers are conventional; Jenny Agutter, in virtually her first stage role, does little more than obey orders. The courtiers (even Mr Cusack) are pallid; one of the play's crucial moments--Alonso's first access of guilt--goes, in Joseph O'Conor's amiable hands, for nothing.

Though the splendours of the South Bank will doubtless defy description, it becomes increasingly depressing to think of the National deserting the Old Vic, a perfect theatre. Not that all continuity with the past has been irretrievably lost. Intentionally or not, this Tempest bears some resemblance to Michael Blakemore's National version of Macbeth, which was also rooted in the Jacobean period and evinced the same enthusiasm for stage conjuring.

  

Mr Blakemore has this week come up with another virtuoso production, David Hare's new play Knuckle (Comedy).

Once again, as in his triumphant Front Page, he pays homage to the movies. The play's framework is that of a detective novel; the text refers to Mickey Spillane, but the ambience is more that of Raymond Chandler, a classic source for Hollywood, right down to The Long Goodbye last year. As often in Chandler a cynical loner investigates the case of a girl missing, believed murdered; only this time the girl is his own sister and the hero, an arms salesman, has lost all trace of Philip Marlowe's tattered chivalry. He is a sting-ray among sharks, the location having shifted from LA to the twisted depths of Guildford, Surrey.

The play moves from the only club in Guildford (fringed curtains and a tender-tough proprietress) to a sinister beach at Eastbourne to the home of a villainous merchant-banker (Douglas Wilmer, rock-solid and velvet-smooth), each transition accompanied by a surge of poisonously romantic theme music. Edward Fox's camel-coated hero has extraordinary style, a mocking grace of movement, and an unsettling smile; it looks deeply untrustworthy, but there is always a chance it might be genuine.

The writing is marked by wit, intelligence and a deepening sense of strain; the author becomes the captive of his own idea. Hollywood into Guildford is a good joke, but an imperfect equation, so when Mr Hare finally starts laying into the Home Counties capitalist ethic it is difficult to take him seriously; like his hero, he is not quite as tough as perhaps he would like to think. And the format presents insoluble narrative problems: in the book you would read the plot passages twice, in the film you would settle for incomprehension and get high on speed and action, but the stage allows neither alternative.

  

The Gershwin musical Oh Kay! which I enjoyed at Colchester last year has arrived at the Westminster, neat as ever if sometimes a little arch.
1974-03-17-more-cheers-for-chekhov:
More cheers for Chekhov

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

I RHAPSODISED at length over the Actors' Company production of The Wood Demon when it first appeared at last year's Edinburgh Festival; so I had not planned to bestow more than a final paragraph of benediction on its arrival at Wimbledon Theatre, the first in a season of five plays.

But this rare Chekhov (rare and yet formidably well done) is so vivid an experience that I have to dwell on it once more. It presents an almost ideal conjunction of material with interpreters; in time this company must obviously get to one of Chekhov's later, sterner, tidier plays, but at present such a challenge might hem them in. This extravagant malformed piece allows them to run free; but some tight residual discipline in the writing, in David Giles's direction, and in themselves prevents them from running wild.

The more they are together, the happier we can be. Wimbledon is a barn of a theatre (it goes, I suppose, with the common and the tennis courts) and for the first quarter of an hour, mainly duologues and, would it be, triologues, I feared that the production's vital juices had evaporated. But once the stage had filled for the first-act luncheon party misgivings fled; everything was as good as I had remembered it, except for some bits which were better.

Several characterisations have matured: Juan Moreno's hopelessly jittery suitor for one and Tenniel Evans's Uncle George for a definite other. No, he is not Uncle Vanya nor, whatever Chekhov may have decided afterwards, was he meant to be. I have seen great Vanyas, Redgrave and Scofield, and they were all over the place. Mr Evans is firm-set, upon a rock of bitterness and rancour. His insights, unlike Vanya's, are firm and undeviating; during the second act, which he plays barefoot, his very toes curl at the unfairness of it all.

The most dramatic advance has been made by Marian Diamond, who registers every gradation in Helen's response, and final capitulation, to the futility and vulgarity engulfing her in the Professor's 26 gloomy rooms. And for the benefit of posterity (which likes to know these things) I must record a joyous action-packed moment in which Robin Ellis tosses into the air what he believes to be a peppermint, catches it in his mouth, swallows it, gags, inspects the container whence it came and inquires with jovial insouciance: "Is the Professor ill, then?" Having last week lamented the impending departure of the National Theatre from the Old Vic, I would add my voice to those urging that the Actors' Company should take over there--though preferably for no more than six months in a year. To mount a year-round repertory they would have to inflate themselves, and they might easily burst.

  

Chekhov, being a doctor, is a welcome presence in a theatrical week rife with bugs and germs and uncleanliness generally. At the Vaudeville there is Snap!; if the author, Charles Laurence, had not lost his nerve it would have been Clap. (Or did he perhaps fear confusion with the recent musical hit Applause?)

Most of the characters are infected; the hero begins by wondering whether it's good old gonorrhoea or what he rather charmingly describes as "this new thing," non-specific urethritis.

The first 30 minutes of the play are in fact quite springy; after that the conventions close in and it becomes just another mechanical West End comedy. Outside the sun is shining (this is mentioned so often that you may well feel like going outside to enjoy yourself); within, the hero's apartment is got up like a 1930s liner, so that the other characters can make jokes about it. Other running gags stumble unrelatedly through the evening: one character is a lapsed Catholic, another an unlapsed lesbian, very hearty and a champion dog-breeder. (Jolly well done, Elspeth March.) VD and homosexuality in the same play--are there no taboos left? (Well, yes, there are; characters are allowed to be gay or diseased, but not both. There is one minor character who is neither, but is toothy and an opera-fanatic. I mention her while I am in this parenthesis because I would not like to see her get loose outside it.)

But there is reason in most things, and in this thing there is Maggie Smith. Miss Smith is timing of unholy perfection, a larynx that can droop over the unlikeliest lines (I will swear her vocal cords have limp wrists) and draw laughter from them, and a pair of knees that waddle in tune with the dialogue and can be drawn up to hide her face in moments of deep embarrassment; she is also a person, gleeful, superior, and very nervous. When she appears in good plays (which is usually) her battery of accomplishments can seem excessive, but to this one she can do nothing but good, except in the closing stages when she can do nothing. The director is William Gaskill; maybe this is the kind of work he really yearned to do during his years at the Royal Court.

  

Industrial rather than sexual disease is the form there; Peter Ransley's Runaway is the latest of the North Country family dramas that usually seem to be running in Sloane Square, and a fair specimen of its kind. Daughter (Susan Tracy) has come home after a broken marriage and takes out her frustrations on her 11-year-old son (Kevin Moreton, no drama-school monster, but a real, breathing, swearing kid). He, not surprisingly, is the runaway; but so, in a way, is his grandfather. (Bill Owen, too soft--in both senses--but a kindly presence none the less.) A union leader, he has partially betrayed his workmates by keeping quiet about the presence in the works of a poisonous chemical; and now he himself may have developed cancer from it. Mr Ransley strikes sparks from a number of themes and encounters, but he fails to weld them together.

  

Once again the most reviving thing in town is a revival. The West End is strewn with them, and Tennessee Williams's A Streetcar Named Desire (Piccadilly) is the best. This is a dream of a play, with dialogue that glows on actors' lips. I had not realised how much of it has passed into history: "Sometimes there's God so quickly"; "I have always depended on the kindness of strangers."

That last quivering line of broken Blanche Dubois is delivered by Claire Bloom with a marvellous dazed dignity. There is sweetness in it, and a hint of flirtatiousness, and a subtler hint of priggishness and the faintest memory of faded aristocracy. It is in fact Blanche, the southern schoolteacher as nymphomaniac, gathered together and placed before your eyes: the summation of the most moving performance I have seen in a year.

It is also a constantly surprising performance, since Miss Bloom's resources continually outpace expectation; she looks, at first glance, limited. Blanche's credo (and her undoing) is that she prefers magic to realism, "and if that is a sin, then let me be damned for it." Miss Bloom, like Mr Williams, gives us both magic and realism in generous measure. I have no intention whatever of damning them.

There is a slight atmospheric glibness about the play; the lighting and sound effects are written in (dead on cue), and any director must be grateful for a play set in New Orleans, a chance to fill the scene-breaks with a dreamy jazz cornet. Edwin Sherrin's production goes with the text, a rewarding journey and there are no weaknesses in his cast. Actually, there are amazing strengths: Martin Shaw, insolent and brutally honest as Stanley (only his bellowing lets him down), Morag Hood, whose Stella is incarnate sense to Blanche's sensibility, and as Mitch, a gentle shambles, Joss Ackland, whose ingratiatingly unexpected question "How much do you think I weigh?" is something else posterity should know about.
1974-03-24-king-barton-s-john:
King Barton's 'John'

THIS year's season at Stratford on Avon began on Wednesday with William Shakespeare's King John. So, at least, declared the programme, thereby exposing the Royal Shakespeare Company not merely to criticism, but to possible prosecution under the Trades Descriptions Act.

I doubt if more than 50 per cent of the lines spoken in this production could be found in the received text. For the rest the director, John Barton, has had recourse to an early Tudor morality play, King Johan, which depicts John as a Protestant hero, defying the Pope; to the anonymous Troublesome Reign of King John, which was Shakespeare's immediate source (a generous gesture, this, to give back to one's author much that he had already rejected); and, Mr Barton modestly adds, to "additions of my own." I would guess that among these is the allusion to the state of the nation made by some baron or other in justifying a change of allegiance: "The price of goods soars meteor-like to heaven."

A meteor was a favourite Elizabethan image for over-reaching ambition, and on this occasion Mr Barton has gone in for a certain amount of soaring himself. Apparently, he began with the intention of making a few interpolations to clarify the actions and significance of a muddled play with (in recent years) a spare and disappointing stage-history. The fit grew on him, and he found himself refashioning the entire piece. It is possible to sit at this production and relive the experience with him. We witness the enthronement of the adaptor-director, transformed as the contending princes of the play are transformed when they assume (as in this production they constantly do) the golden mask of kingship. The title acquires a double edge.

The process is gradual; the first half is easy and even familiar. The turbulent but monotonous rhetoric of the opposing forces of France and England is given a satiric twist; the self-interest that underlies their stately protestations is glaringly exposed. Mr Barton did the same thing 10 years ago in The Wars of the Roses and the main change since then has been in the mode of design, which is Brechtian in the airy, as opposed to the earthy, manner. Into this ironic context the cynical comments of the Bastard Faulconbridge fit quite naturally.

That is not necessarily a good thing, since he is meant to be an irritant; here, despite Richard Pasco's forceful performance, he seems redundant, deflating the already deflated. As the play proceeds he dwindles, and is finally reduced to reading the play's famous, uncuttable, but embarrassingly positive last lines on national unity from a hefty unidentified volume.

Before this point is reached, however, we have been through a great deal, much of it brilliant. Believing unity of style to be an overrated virtue (if it is a virtue at all), I was beguiled by Mr Barton's breezy mastery in alternating realpolitik with emblematic morality. Pictures multiply: young Arthur (excellently played by Benedict Taylor) sitting cross-legged and silent while his elders manipulate his future; a young couple, betrothed for reasons of State, disappearing into gunsmoke; the arrival of the Papal Legate (Jeffery Dench, also excellent), a walking skull encased in scarlet.

I do believe, however, in unity of idea; and I was thus dismayed by Mr Barton's attempts to turn King John into a play about everything. I suspect that rehearsals were partly fuelled by the company's memories of past productions and preoccupations. The self-justifying barons come straight out of Murder in the Cathedral. The proclamation "God save King Arthur" seems to have set off recollections (which can't have been altogether happy) of John Arden's Island of the Mighty and its musings, as of a cynical anthropologist, on the theme of monarchy. Almost for the first time I believed in the RSC's protestations about the influence of their modern work on their Shakespeare; usually it has seemed to me to be the other way about.

Kingship, with its disparity between the man and the office, the player and the role--as in last year's Richard II--seems to be on Mr Barton's mind; so does the state of England among the nations: at one point the play threatens to become an allegory of the EEC. There's a line about little Albion dodging in and out between "Holland, Denmark, Germany and Rome." The production takes on the quality of a brainstorm; it finally bursts when John's poisoning is staged as a tableau of the Last Supper. I flinched, not merely at the pretentiousness, but because the evening had already lasted three hours, and Last Suppers can take a long time. This one has carols.

Shakespeare's play, as several reviewers hastily remarked last week, is no masterpiece, but it does have its points: pace is one of them and humanity another. On the few occasions when the original script is employed at any length Mr Barton proves, infuriatingly enough, that he can still direct it better than anyone else. Constance's grief (Sheila Allen, subtly distanced, gives the most judicious performance of her career) is beautifully handled; so are John's tempting of Hubert and the Bastard's soliloquies. (Though even in the commodity speech there are interpolations, provoking audible, if probably unconscious, changes of gear in Mr Pasco's delivery.) John's great death-scene is more or less intact, but it is too late for us to take much interest in it. Emrys James is foxy, freakishly amoral, and thoroughly compelling, but he cannot hold this production together; nobody could. For once Stratford seems to have a company with personality and weight; they need a text to support them.

  

We know from Ghosts and The Seagull that Jonathan Miller has a strong company for his Family Romances at Greenwich but on the first night of Hamlet (which last week was a shorter play than King John) they were floundering in visible distress. Robert Stephens's Claudius will probably grow into a fine study of a beleaguered ruler, oppressed equally by the memory of his brother and the presence of his nephew, but on Tuesday it was difficult to distinguish the King's nervous mannerisms from the actor's.

Peter Eyre and Irene Worth strike sparks off each other in the closet scene (for which, after all, they have been warming up all season); otherwise the performers make no contact. Mr Eyre, a sulky prince, never talks to anyone, though his soliloquies make internal sense; at the end of his last one he just stops himself from launching into a self-defeating tirade and settles for quiet resolution instead. Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are as good as dead. Nicola Pagett is a notable and surprisingly straightforward Ophelia, regressing to babyhood in madness, Antony Brown a properly humourless Polonius and Anthony Nicholls a remarkably solid Ghost, who sits down beside his victims and chats them up in a most unnerving manner.

Mr Miller has no truck with atmospherics; he stages the duel and the play-scene well, though he cannot make a virtue out of the economic necessity of a small cast. I was sorry that the players were interrupted before we could see how the murderer got the love of Gonzago's wife; it would have been fascinating, since they are both the same actor.

  

George Kelly's The Show-Off (Hampstead Theatre Club) features a physically witty, but vocally overwrought performance from Al Mancini, and some compensating comic reality from Doreen Mantle. A respect for reality is the play's distinguishing feature; her daughter cannot visit her parents without mentioning that she was on her way to pay the electricity bill. If this occurred in a new play at the Royal Court I would dismiss it as a tiresome reflex; in this comedy, from 1920s Philadelphia, it strikes me as honest and delightful. This is known as critical bias.
1974-03-31-kemp-s-flower-show:
Kemp's flower show

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

LINDSAY KEMP'S Flowers, "a pantomime for Jean Genet," has opened at the Regent Theatre, Oxford Circus. When Flowers was first seen at the Bush it was reviewed by our dance critic, while the Regent itself was, until very recently, the Cameo-Poly Cinema. I am not sure whether to regard myself as a usurper or a simple trespasser.

Flowers is, as it happens, an outsiders' evening. Genet canonised the outcast, but then as a writer--a solitary animal--he had the right to do so; Mr Kemp's troupe have the strength of numbers--ten's a crowd in the theatre--and in creating a sealed-off stage equivalent of Genet's Catholic homosexual underworld they can afford the luxury of mocking their audience as well as defying them.

Though the show pays token tribute to Genet with mock-crucifixions, booming organ-music and such, it is most itself when it ventures into showbiz camp; in a seedy cabaret (a blend of gay bar and sad cafe) three transvestite singers bawl out a tortured version of "Over the Rainbow." Into this setting Mr Kemp makes a still, shy, imposing entrance in Dietrich drag, coyly fluttering a fan. He performs with great delicacy in an ambience that is often overstated to the point of tawdriness, and some of his staging--particularly his use of a gauze-curtain--is inspired. He also gives the impression of being the only person on stage who does not hate women.

  

A squarer misogyny pervades Royalty Follies (at the Royalty, which has also been a cinema in its short time, and might be happier that way). I had not realised how deeply sadistic is Paul Raymond's idea of Everyman's fantasy-life. Perhaps I should say how shallowly sadistic, and also how old-fashioned. The set-pieces in this show derive either from the Valentino era ("such a man of Destiny was Genghis Khan; the one thing he never had was Love") or from the even remoter myth of James Bond. The final number even recalls swinging London. Somehow it all figures, and I would not attempt to dispute the wisdom of Mr Raymond's diagnosis. The programme states that the phenomenal success of his play Pyjama Tops has confounded the critics. But really it wasn't the success that confounded us; just the play.

Nudity still flourishes, but striptease is dead. (It may be up to Mr Kemp to revive it.) At the Royalty there are always men around to take--or preferably tear--the girls' clothes off for them. The one thing they cannot remove is the uncertain smile that appears to be the English chorine's birthright. Even the lady in an adagio act, visibly gritting her teeth while she gets thrown around in profile, manages to register a brave grin when she faces front. The show also features a proficient conjuror and ventriloquist, but comedy is not even attempted.

In this respect it is impious for Mr Raymond to invoke the shades of Ziegfeld or George White, whose revues were probably just as rubbishy, but still acted as springboards for a Bert Lahr or Fanny Brice. They also of course introduced some great songs; John Taylor's music and lyrics here are desperately unoriginal and could interest nobody. One item, called "Black and White," is uncannily similar to an early Cole Porter thing called "That Black and White Baby of Mine." There are no real singers here either, only an overworked male vocalist with bizarre mid-Atlantic intonations. ("Diamonds are Forevore.")

  

Shorn of Mr Raymond's quaintly cosmopolitan orthography, Royalty Folies might make a good subtitle for King Lear, which is the second play in the Actors' Company season at Wimbledon. Contrary winds forced the company last month to open this production in New York without benefit of sets and costumes. This stroke of ill-luck seems, judging by what we see in Wimbledon, to have been the greatest good fortune. The hats and helmets are a particular affliction; aiming at barbaric grandeur, but suggesting the D'Oyly Carte, they gravely impair the authority and credibility of all who wear them.

David William's direction is not rigorous enough to compensate. Characters skip or scamper on when they might just as well walk; a table is laboriously introduced so that Robert Eddison's Lear, in the height of his fury, can mount an unfortunately feeble attack upon it. There is an intelligent attempt to link the play's cruelty with its eroticism; the blinding of Gloucester practically arouses Cornwall and Regan to orgasm, and there is unusual force in the sisters' involvement with Edmund. (Narrative clarity is the production's greatest virtue.) This theme should explode in Lear's Swiftian diatribes at Dover, but again Mr Eddison, mournful and mellifluous, lacks the strength to bring them off.

In other respects this scene finds him at his best; I have never heard the quicksilver associative transitions of Lear's derangement so fluently expressed. I had expected to be much moved by him in the reconciliation with Cordelia, but it means very little unless we can contrast it with the violence and intransigence of the king's earlier scenes. And these aspects of Lear, Mr Eddison simply cannot encompass. An occasional grace note finds him at his ease, but then he must be off again, tilting at windmills. His whimsy suits one aspect of Lear's madness, but he lacks the granite. Where is the actor who could give us both? (That is a rhetorical question. Anyone who has heard Ralph Richardson read Blake will know where to find Lear.)

With no centre to play to, the other actors necessarily flounder; the air is full of unpointed rhetoric. Definition returns--with a vengeance, I would say--in Ford's 'Tis Pity She's a Whore, the Actors' Company's third production at Wimbledon. David Giles has transferred this incest tragedy from a timeless Renaissance Italy to one firmly rooted at the end of the last century. A play whose host of characters and intrigues can easily become confusing in some neutral limbo gains enormously from the obligation which modern dress imposes to find a rationale for every scene.

Ian McKellen's moody schoolboy Giovanni, his voice even more tousled than his hair, has grown since I saw it two years ago; he now has the diabolism to sweep the play to its blood-boltered end. But this Giovanni is such a narcissist that his love for his sister--freshly and beguilingly played by Paola Dionisotti--is hard to credit. There is more believable passion in John Bennett's stony avenger, and in the jealous rage of Edward Petherbridge's bridegroom who, starting out chill and dapper, blows his cool to stunning effect. Margery Mason (with more than a hint of a moustache) and Tenniel Evans (ditto, with a trim beard) give rock-solid support, though I could wish that Mr Evans, when finally ordered to take Miss Mason away and burn her to ashes, would refrain from sobbing "It is poor dust." A simple assent would be far less risible.
1974-04-07-let-s-be-nice-to-aegisthus:
THREE of this week's plays are revivals; the fourth might just as well be. Indeed, Jean Anouilh's You Were So Sweet When You Were Little, though technically a British premiere, might almost count as a double revival. Based on and incorporating occasional chunks of Aeschylus's Libation Bearers, it also bears a startlingly close resemblance to M. Anouilh's Antigone of 30 years ago.

Once again there is a grubbily intransigent Greek heroine: Electra this time, spurring on her brother Orestes to murder their mother, Clytemnestra, and her lover, Aegisthus, in retribution for the death of Electra's father, Agamemnon, who had himself been guilty of the blood of his daughter Iphigeneia. (The family that slays together stays together.) Now Antigone's aims, you may remember, were more limited (her relatives were mostly dead already, she merely wanted to bury one of them), but it was clear that for her one pretext for revolt would be as good as any other. At the time of Antigone's premiere in Occupied France everyone, except presumably the Germans, applauded her, but in the years that have passed the arguments of her opponent, Creon, have come to seem increasingly reasonable, and his condemnation of her futile, selfish heroism increasingly persuasive.

The new play is perhaps an attempt to put the record straight: to show that Anouilh was rooting for Creon all along. Electra dwells lovingly on the martyrdom she has imposed upon herself, while the nicest character is Aegisthus, not only doomed but henpecked, and coated in puppy-fat. Anouilh is cunning enough, having aroused our sympathy for him, to turn it against us. When Orestes taunts him for the very stolidity of his long-suffering virtues ("Why not draw us a map of your varicose veins?") we wince, wondering if we have been had.

As you can see, and would expect, this is a well-written but redundant play. Nothing but historical accident makes it seem much inferior to Antigone; the change in emphasis reflects the times as much as the text. Once, when Anouilh's Chorus proclaimed that tragedy was a restful genre, we took it for an oblique commendation of Antigone, a tragic heroine; now it seems an ironic indictment of Electra, luxuriating in the same status. In general, I find Anouilh's mythical reworkings his least satisfactory plays; this business of debunking Aeschylus and Sophocles has been going on for millennia and none has done it so well as Euripides, who really had a stake in what he was attacking. The current production opens the Theatre at New End in Hampstead. I saw it at a preview, when it was rough but not ready. Angela Pleasence is good, obvious casting for Electra.

When I spoke last week of the misogyny variously evinced by Lindsay Kemp and Paul Raymond I should have added that they have plenty of exemplars in the classier spoken drama. M. Anouilh hints that things might have been all right, with the House of Atreus had Orestes and Aegisthus been able to get together out of reach of those awful Furies, women. A golden time-suspending drink scene works to much the same effect in the second offering from the Peter Hall regime at the National, J. B. Priestley's Eden End. Note the title; we have already had The Tempest, and are promised Heartbreak House and John Gabriel Borkman, further studies in finality, before the year is out. Mr Hall may be moving towards a concept of Terminal Theatre.

Eden End is the end of innocence; in October 1912 a North Country doctor, his son and two daughters come briefly together for what we, through hindsight and a certain amount of conscientious prodding from Mr Priestley, know will be the last time. The prodding is the play's most irritating feature; we get occasional hopeful speeches about how much better life is going to be in the 1930s, which happens to be when Mr Priestley was writing the play. He is thus able to attain by conscious effort the sort of effect which time and the Russian Revolution achieved for Chekhov.

But along with much that is takingly Chekhovian, the play offers a few things that are truly Chekhovian: the end -- the very end, the last few seconds -- and that drunk scene, here enacted by Paul Gregory and Michael Jayston. There is a lot of Mr Gregory -- length-wise, at any rate -- and it gets itself draped in helpless, intriguing shapes on chairs and sofas, while the face above it stares, gaunt and admiring, at Mr Jayston, whose inebriated oratory deserves the compliment, though elsewhere his portrait of a middle-aged boy actor is rather too restrained and solid. In one respect the play can be ranked with The Seagull; with no scenes in or near theatres, but with much talk of touring and of the Sunday train to London ("it's a brute"), it creates and paints a wholly convincing picture of the actor's life.

Laurence Olivier's production, which, again, I saw at a preview, is occasionally stiff, but more often rich and expansive. (The Mermaid's An Inspector Calls was brusque by comparison.) On this showing Mr Priestley writes the kind of flat dialogue from which the right actors can sculpt mountains or excavate hollows: Leslie Sands and Geoffrey Palmer are triumphantly the right actors here. Joan Plowright brings to the central role a captivating laconic wit and an undiminished gift for expressing momentary happiness; but she is also liable to swirl around in an undefined emotional wash.

Arnold Wesker's Roots has been accorded a moderate but enjoyable revival by the Young Vic, with Tamara Ustinov, a very perky Beatie Bryant. It is, in both senses, a funny play. It has acquired a reputation for buoyant optimism, but what lingers from it is a picture of family life which, if not quite as mordant as M. Anouilh's, is a good deal blacker than Mr Priestley's.

We all know that The Way of the World is a great text; the Actors' Company production at Wimbledon, with an Edwardian setting and immeasurably improved, since the Edinburgh Festival, reveals it as a great play, racy, cutting, dynamic, and very nearly comprehensible. "O man, man," howls Paola Dionisotti's Marwood in an ecstasy of jealous fury, and then relaxes into what is for her a melting mood (i.e. one of lingering self-contempt) to add "woman, woman!" Robin Ellis's Fainall is a more natural cynic, but in him too sexual nihilism is spurred on by self-hatred. What Millamant and Mirabell have to offer -- to each other and to us -- is self-respect: Edward Petherbridge, without losing any of his critical sense, has come far enough out of his shell to make a believable lover as well as a stylish schemer, and though Caroline Blakiston has been set (by herself, her director or the Millamant legend) the impossible task of acting radiance she succeeds surprisingly often; only she surrenders far too easily.

John Woodvine's ebullient Sir Wilful, formerly an isolated comic force, is now part of a triple alliance, flanked as he is by Margery Mason's agreeably vulnerable Lady Wishfort and by John Tordoff whose mannerisms (chiefly a falsetto sigh at the end of every line) remain the same from play to play, but are here used to expose young Witwoud's patronising pretensions, spiced by an insecurity that almost becomes endearing.
1974-05-05-fighting-it-out-in-the-suburb:
Fighting it out in the suburbs

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a new play at the National.

THERE is a curious innocence about John Hopkins's plays; at times they bleed like open wounds.

Their vulnerability can turn them into actors' feasts. From the television quartet Talking to a Stranger everyone remembers Judi Dench's exhilarating tirades. In New York last week I saw a remarkable young actor, Michael Moriarty, rising effortlessly, with no apparent build-up, to climax after climax as a volatile desperate homosexual in Mr Hopkins's Find Your Way Home, which flopped in London a couple of years ago.

His later plays are more secretive. It took us a long time to find out what was bugging the unfortunate husband in Economic Necessity. We learn even less about a similar figure in his new play at the National, Next of Kin. As James Laurenson plays him (eye-catchingly well), Brian Lloyd, suburban husband in his thirties, is hesitant, choked, withdrawn, and happiest when putting a toy tank together. He likes using his hands, is not at all happy in his job as a car salesman. So he walks out, in the first act, and to my regret is never seen again.

It could be that he leaves merely to avoid meeting his relatives. The occasion of the play is one of Mr Hopkins's Sunday afternoon family reunions. On their way to Brian's home are his two sisters (with their husbands); his brother, without his wife; and their widowed mother. All arrived, they settle down to a round of recrimination and intrigue as bloody-minded and protracted as you could find in several months of other dramatists' Sundays.

The innocence remains; Mr Hopkins approaches the horrors of family life as if nobody had ever dramatised them before. The naivete can be excruciating: the play yields a choice collection of lines you have wished never to hear again. "You want to hurt him," says A, to which B replies, "Naturally, I love him." A mother is informed that she resents her children "because you made them and they aren't everlastingly grateful." The nastiest of the women declares herself with the words, "I'm not responsible; I won't be made responsible." Occasionally the dialogue goes antiphonal. "He was himself," remarks somebody of the dead father; "a man to be remembered," caps somebody else. At moments like these Harold Pinter's production becomes suitably, if half-heartedly, hieratic.

There are compensations. Mr Hopkins may have overloaded his battlefield (all these crises in one afternoon?), but he knows his way round it, and he draws a subtle distinction between the ties of family and those of marriage. His siblings may hate one another, but they can still constitute a united force. Indeed, their hatred may be their strength; against it Brian's wife, Susan--their reluctant hostess--can muster only a cold dislike, related as she is by marriage, but not by blood. (The title really proclaims the play.) When the adult pressure falters, a suitably horrible brood of children can take over, confirming incidentally that the standard of juvenile acting in this country is improving out of recognition. Of the grown-ups Gemma Jones as Susan establishes herself slowly but irresistibly at the centre of the play; and, though I felt dubious about their claims to consanguinity, the others mostly justify their presence.

  

Having seen two first-rate musicals in New York (Candide and A Little Night Music), I approached London's two new offerings rather warily. It is probably kinder not to consider the Israeli Dominoes (Shaw) as a musical at all. Its tunes display an occasional piping charm; its lyrics may be assumed to have lost in translation. This charity might be extended to the play itself; its three characters converse in the kind of simple sentences to be found in a foreign phrase-book's early chapters. For the first act I was just about able to believe that this artlessness might conceal art; it was agreeable to watch John Bluthal, a doormat offering himself to every passing pair of feet, or to hear Richard Hampton, an apparently lucky lover, so exultant at having found someone who will weep at his funeral that he can hardly wait for that happy day to dawn.

The second act, in which these two are corralled with the lady of their choice, applies itself to larger themes, but with the same limited resources, and the result is grisly. The author, Khanoch Levin, is presented in the programme as among Israel's newest and finest; it is all the more depressing to find him offering us, in all seriousness, the stock Jewish figure of the castrating wife and mother. At least he has Dorothy Vernon, a splendid singing actress, to embody his harpy for him; were there a show she might have stopped it.

  

At Drury Lane there is unquestionably a show, as enormous as Dominoes is tiny. I trembled at it in prospect; it has become all too easy (all too common, anyway) to take a successful play and market it as a musical by chopping down its title to a single key word; this last season on Broadway A Raisin in the Sun and Two for the Seesaw have resurfaced as Raisin and Seesaw respectively. By American standards, Billy (ne Liar) probably rates as a formula musical; by ours it is something of a phenomenon.

It represents a successful compromise with the British theatrical genius in that its virtues belong as much to dramaturgy as to showbiz. Onna White's choreography is more notable for vigour than invention (and much of the dancing is leaden); the songs by Don Black and John Barry are all right, sometimes displaying a humour hardly to be expected from the men who once won an Oscar for Born Free, a terribly solemn ballad about (one had to assume) a lion. But the book (by Dick Clement and Ian La Frenais out of Keith Waterhouse and Willis Hall) and its direction (by Patrick Garland) are something else: funny, humane, and neatly structured. The production numbers, already an excellent device for representing Billy's fantasy life, gain from the finesse with which they are introduced. The opening routine, Ambrosia, introduces us to the hero's dream-world, and its brief reprise at the end is an apt and touching way of signifying his final retreat from reality.

Bryan Pringle and Avis Bunnage are shunted on and off stage to offer some vinegary vignettes of Billy's home life; Barry James, a short and pungent comedian, peers darkly out of dance halls and funeral parlours; and Lockwood West contributes some sterling memories of the North in the days before shopping precincts. Michael Crawford seems rather a winsome plant to have flowered in this rocky soil; having to do most of his acting through a throat-mike, on a vast and comfortless set, he is inhibited from making much contact with the life around him. He is happiest in his moments of solitary clowning, and as an appealing and energetic song-and-dance-man. A nimble mover he is, but no Fred Astaire. You would not expect him to be? Well, somebody does, because the first-half finale involves him in a top-hat routine which is not witty enough to pass as parody. Obviously we are meant to take it straight and Mr Crawford ("Ooh, isn't he clever") to our hearts. Yet again amateurism strikes the British musical, but the blow, for once, is not fatal.
1974-05-12-bewitched-bewildered:
Bewitched, Bewildered

SOMEWHERE towards the end of Peter Barnes's The Bewitched (Aldwych), Alan Howard, who for most of the evening has been impersonating a gibbering idiot, has a few lucid moments in which to lay a message on us.

The news he bears is that there is no news; events have no meaning and effects no causes. 'We stand alone at the mercy of chance.' In one respect I found this comforting; it excused my incomprehension of the dynastic and political intrigues that make up the bulk of the play. Bulky it is, going on for three and a half hours, after which it is hard to be informed that they might as well have been three and a half other hours.

We have come through so much; is all our pain to be of no account? We have watched Mr Howard expertly limping, hunching, screeching and snorting his way through the role of Carlos II of Spain, an object lesson in what can be achieved through generations of determined inbreeding. (In this case, at least, there seems to have been a quite recognisable link between cause and effect.) We have watched his wife, his mother and his councillors squabbling among themselves while trying every means to save Carlos from his biologically predestined role as the last of the Hapsburgs. So that he may beget an heir, heretics have been burned and witches hunted; we have spent much time in the torture-chamber, with an interlude, by way of sub-plot, in the dentist's chair. It is, please bear in mind, a seventeenth-century dentist's chair.

None of this suffering engages our sympathy nor, I imagine, is it intended to. Mr Barnes invites our shudders, our disgust, and our giggles. When, on the eve of an auto da fe, the officers of the Inquisition give out with a couple of choruses of 'That's Entertainment' they appear to have their author with them. Certainly this showman's view of death at the stake has been adopted by the director, Terry Hands, and his designer, Farrah, who have staged the scene in their most palatial style. As the victims (a joky bunch, considering) expire, the king and queen, done up as vast effigies of themselves, are united by a huge golden phallus. This is spectacular, but confusing. Are we meant to assume that such a symbolic protuberance really formed part of the ritual at therapeutic autos? Is it the author's and director's satiric comment on the superstition involved? Or is it a kind of theatrical shorthand to assure us that the magic actually worked and that on this occasion the royal couple, however fruitlessly, made it?

Mr Hands and his company -- with the glowing exception of Joe Melia -- are less at home with the occasional musical numbers. But I suspect the function of these anyway. Mr Barnes is a former programmer for the National Film Theatre, and he is obviously in thrall to the great MGM musicals. So am I, but though I enjoy hearing the old tunes I cannot feel that their introduction at climactic moments does much for the cause of popular theatre. (For one thing the joke works only if you recognise the songs and these days not too many people do.) Their use is really a form of pedantry. Mr Barnes can be a dreadfully earnest funster, breathing -- for all his command of scenic effect -- the thin air of closet-drama in which story and characters wither.

Of course, in so long an evening there are successful passages, more than in Mr Barnes's previous play, The Ruling Class, which had a modern setting. Fancy-dress seems to suit him better. There is a funny, surprising duel between a dwarf jester and a full-sized grandee, and there is the spectacle of a huge box gradually closing on a dying queen mother. A previous line of this lady's -- 'I hurt, therefore I am' -- taken with the torture scenes and the agonised deformity of Carlos himself, suggest -- though the theme is unfocused -- that pain, loneliness and death are the only realities. Mr Barnes has provided witty lines for Philip Locke, playing a sinister archbishop rather like (to be honest, exactly like) Mr Locke's Professor Moriarty; and has invented a period jargon (people saying 'casn't' as a compromise between 'canst not' and 'can't'), which is at any rate original. He aims for a Renaissance variety of tone by conscientiously laying contrasting styles end to end.

  

As far as I know Jason Miller is not Arthur Miller's son, but his play That Championship Season (Garrick) assaults one of the old man's favourite targets: the belief that success comes to the guy who plays ball -- foot, base, or in this case, basket. The team that once brought their town a cherished trophy have grown up to wealth and power (one of them is mayor) guided in work as they were in play by their revered and rednecked coach. However: they are all insecure, all unhealthy (one is an alcoholic, a rewarding disease for author and actor, since it is a theatrical rule that unbridled drinkers shall also be unbridled cynics) and it finally transpires that they couldn't even play clean basketball. This last is one twist too many; it suggests that if they had been decent sportsmen they would be perfectly fitted to run the town. Once again audiences on Broadway (where the play has been a huge success) have been taken in by the pretence of seriousness, but they have benefited from a shared understanding with their author; America (unlike England) is still a valid and palatable dramatic subject. Otherwise the play is fair to middlebrow, offering some thrills, more spills, wisecracks and effective acting. Broderick Crawford makes a fearsome coach, all jowls and scowls.

  

I remember Mr Crawford as the hero of television's Highway Patrol, alternately tracking down crooks and preaching homilies on road safety. Two other experienced TV cops, Stratford Johns and Lee Montague, duel to the death in the new thriller Who Saw Him Die? (Haymarket). I am not allowed to reveal the outcome, or even the substance, of their combat, but I can disclose that Mr Montague wins on acting.
1974-05-12-turning-up-at-tony-time:
Turning up at Tony-time

NEW YORK THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN reports on his recent visit to Broadway.

LONDON no longer has a definable theatre season, but Broadway still likes things to be official and that's why Tonys were born.

The Tony (Antoinette Perry Award) is Broadway's Oscar, presented in droves in mid-April to reward the best endeavours of the previous twelvemonth. The visiting critic arriving, as I fortuitously did, at Tony-time is thus provided with a handy official guide to what he should be seeing. (Shows presented off-Broadway--one step down the economic scale--or off-off-Broadway--where the unions are charitable and wages minimal--are not eligible.)

It has been, by most accounts, a dim season for musicals; the acknowledged best, Candide, was a revival and therefore ineligible for an award of its own. There were prizes, though, for several of its participants, including confusingly enough, its author--Hugh Wheeler having provided a new libretto to replace the one which was generally held to have sunk the show back in 1956.

Even Mr Wheeler's version is liable to sag; nor, despite the presence of many good voices, is full justice done to Leonard Bernstein's celebrated score. Mr Bernstein actually wrote a mock-opera, in a variety of parodied styles, and this is a form of sophistication for which Harold Prince's production has very little time. He has opted for calculated innocence, accepted that Voltaire's fable is too repetitive to be conventionally dramatic, and cunningly embraced the picaresque. Suspense consists not in wondering what is going to happen next, but where. There is a choice of half a dozen stages, situated all over the theatre; the audience sits in the middle. The method will be familiar to anyone who has seen the Grand Magic Circus, but Candide is both more expert and more fun. Mark Baker, guileless and curly-headed, is a model Candide and the music is still glorious.

When the Broadway musical is not battering its audiences with, or into, insensibility, Mr Prince's presence can generally be assumed. His production of Stephen Sondheim's A Little Night Music is now into its second year and, despite some signs of wear, was the best thing I saw in New York. Based on the Ingmar Bergman film Smiles of a Summer Night, it makes a conscious (sometimes a self-conscious) bid for high comedy tinged with farce, and is thus unusually dependent on its cast. On Broadway I was moved and enchanted by the performances of Glynis Johns and Hermione Gingold and by the dizzying splendour of Sondheim's lyrics, matched, on this occasion, by his tunes. A London version is due in the autumn.

Neither of these shows offers much scope to the choreographer, though what there is has been well seized by Patricia Birch. She and her dancers are the best reason for seeing Over Here, an attempted musical epic of the home front in World War II. It is, a little bewilderingly, a cosy epic, since it features the two surviving Andrews Sisters, chatting up their audiences with the matronly aplomb of an American Elsie and Doris Waters.

The Sisters still sound as they used to 25 years ago when there were three of them, which is some kind of achievement, and it is pleasant to watch the patrons enjoying them. (The American audience is one of the nicest things about the American theatre: kindly, earnest, homogeneous and recognisable. Nobody knows who goes to the theatre in London.) It would be easy to be offended (as some New Yorkers have been) by the show's general silliness (and even more by its attempts at intelligence), but an Englishman cannot help admiring its efficiency. It comes from the same producers as Grease (its rock 'n' roll equivalent, now the longest-running show on Broadway) and has a similar frenetic appeal.

Ulysses in Nighttown (originally seen off-Broadway and indeed in London in the late fifties) is not musical, but it is a similar kind of star vehicle, being an excuse for Zero Mostel to do his Leopold Bloom routine; sentences from Ulysses are read aloud and he (often hilariously) mimes to them. Mr Mostel's look of appalled distaste when instructed that Bloom "kisses the bedsores of a palsied veteran" is a sight, but it illustrates the extent to which he is commenting on the text rather than acting it.

With his button eyes, short and bristly moustache and battery of chins, Mr Mostel certainly looks like Bloom and he transmits a furious worship of Joyce, but he sounds like nothing on earth; certainly not on Irish earth. Burgess Meredith's production is decently imaginative, but the occasion hardly amounts to more than an animated literary recital. Molly Bloom's monologue, as delivered by the nude and supine Fionnula Flanagan, is, aurally and visually, the highlight of the evening; but it is out of context, only thrown in because it could hardly be left out.

The house rose (literally) to both play and star. But I became progressively appalled by what New York would accept in the way of seriousness (and a little surprised by what they would not accept: Tom Stoppard's Jumpers opened to apathy and bewilderment during my stay). Broadway's pride is a lethargic production of O'Neill's A Moon for the Misbegotten, not itself the snappiest of plays, but possibly possessed of a warmth which was here stamped into the ground in the name--presumably--of truth. Ten years ago it was claimed that such solemnity had very nearly murdered American acting, and the charge still holds.

In truth I saw no production of a native play as good as the current London version of A Streetcar Named Desire; directed--with an English cast--by the American Edwin Sherin. Obviously, though, Mr Sherin is good at transatlantic transplants; his was the Broadway production of John Hopkins's Find Your Way Home with the magnetic performance (at once controlled and overflowing) by Michael Moriarty to which I referred last week. But even in this cast there was some poor acting. Once the musicals are left behind, Broadway's performance standards can dip surprisingly.

So can off-Broadway's, though a lugubriously sentimental piece called The Sea Horse, much lauded by the Press, and offered by a prestigious group called the Circle Repertory, was well played throughout. It had a cast of two.

Off-off-Broadway seemed largely given over to revivals, though it can take first-night credit for an entertaining double-bill--Bad Habits by Terrence McNally--which has now made the full Broadway pilgrimage: off-off to off to on. I caught it off, and found it--at any rate its first half, which was, enragingly, the less well acted--a well-drawn cartoon of hung-up middle-class America, who of course filled the theatre and reacted with marvellous masochistic sportsmanship. The air was full--if you can imagine it--of rueful guffaws.
1974-05-12-the-making-of-alec-mccowen:
The making of Alec McCowen

by Robert Cushman

IN 1959 Alec McCowen went to play his first season at the Old Vic. He was 34, and was invariably, almost officially, referred to as "one of our most promising young actors". This reputation had been gained entirely in modern plays, and most recently in television, where he had played 18 parts in two years. He had virtually never appeared in the classics, had done hardly any Shakespeare. Within six months of joining the company he was the most accomplished actor in it, and critics were making respectful reference to his speaking of the verse.

Last year he returned to the Old Vic, appearing for the first time as a member of the National Theatre. It was hard to believe that the National could ever have got on without him. He is probably the most skilful actor of his generation.

Having said that, I have to admit that I am not too sure (and he couldn't tell me) quite which is his generation, theatrically. He fits in somewhere after Paul Scofield but before Albert Finney. Though he made his name in the 1950s he appeared only once in that decade's particular shrine, the Royal Court. He was sufficiently in tune with the zeitgeist to play Jimmy Porter in what he describes as "the last of the first lot of revivals of 'Look Back in Anger'." That production was directed by John Dexter, and the two didn't get on. Times and personalities have changed: Dexter directed McCowen's last two London performances--in The Misanthrope and Equus at the National--and he is also responsible for Pygmalion, in which McCowen is due to open at the Albery on Wednesday.

McCowen's peculiar position--on his own in a one-man generation--reflects the pattern of his career. He entered RADA at 16 ("far too young"). Then, without finishing his course, he went into repertory (at Macclesfield, Llandudno, York) full of what he recalls (again deprecatingly) as "the enthusiasm of youth", a confidence which inevitably evaporated by the time its possessor was 30. But the enthusiasm must have co-existed with considerable insecurity since it was, as much as anything, a mania for disguise. "For the first five, maybe 10 years, I was using acting as a means of disguising my personality. I was happier the more make-up I wore." His ultimate achievement here (and it must have taken nerve as well as nervousness to bring it off) came in York when at the age of 19 he essayed the title role in a popular piece of Spanish sentiment called A Hundred Years Old. The company's resident old man (aged 75) played his son--"He was furious."
