So when he began playing characters of his own age he felt "terribly naked". Ironically his first real London success, in Roger Macdougall's Escapade, came in the role of a schoolboy. He was then 27, and there then ensued 10 years as one of the theatre's most highly regarded juveniles. He refers to it as my "neurotic young man period". He was forever turning up on television as comically (occasionally tragically) shy youths, dangerously out of their accustomed depth. The first time I saw him on stage was at the Edinburgh Festival of 1958, at which he played the wastrel son of T. S. Eliot's Elder Statesman turning on his heel and demanding "What is my inheritance?"

The physical impact of that moment was electric (remembered, I think, by everyone who saw it at Edinburgh, or later at the Cambridge Theatre in London) and it exemplified some of the approach to acting that McCowen, by now soberly acclimatised to the theatre just as a way of making a living, had begun to work out for himself. "Ideally, in a performance the actor shouldn't know what he's like but what the character does. One is easily led into descriptive acting. You come on and say 'I am like this.' But really what you do should add up to what you're like."

The man most responsible for guiding him along this path was the actor-director Vivian Matalon (best known for his work as director of the Hampstead Theatre Club), who had himself been greatly influenced by working and studying in America. There has always been a strong transatlantic pull on McCowen's work. As far back as 1948 he visited New York (on holiday from a spell of repertory in Newfoundland) and saw A Streetcar Named Desire, which he describes today as "an eye-opening experience; wonderful and comforting. I have always loved naturalism, and it made me realise that what I'd seen in the West End was only stylised naturalism; if someone wanted to indicate worry he put his forefinger and thumb to the bridge of his nose. It was often brilliant, but not very human. When Brando came on in Streetcar he was so completely natural, I remember blushing. I thought for a moment that a beautiful stage-hand had wandered on by mistake."

The next major influence was also American: the great comedienne Ruth Gordon, with whom he worked in 1955 in Thornton Wilder's The Matchmaker. "She was the most inventive and dedicated actress I'd worked with up to that time. She was alive every night--she recreated the performance every night. I was bewildered by how she did it." Somehow, although they were in the same show, they never seemed to meet, so in the end McCowen wrote her a fan letter, asking her how she worked this nightly miracle. "We started a correspondence. She said the miracle was getting the job. After that it was work." What he finally learnt from her was the secret of comedy playing lay in "intensity of belief".

His first success at the Old Vic was in comedy--Touchstone in As You Like It--supposedly the unfunniest of Shakespeare's clowns, a supposition he decisively shattered, winning an award for the best supporting performance of the year, and curing himself of "the awful fear that you had to be a different kind of actor to play Shakespeare".

He stayed at the Vic for two years, playing Mercutio in the famous Zeffirelli Romeo and Juliet, Malvolio and the best Richard II I have seen. Then, after a slump, during which he appeared in two infinitesimal West End runs (a revue, and a play by Francoise Sagan), he went to the Royal Shakespeare Company. He played in two enormously successful productions--The Comedy of Errors and Peter Brook's King Lear--which kept him busy (at Stratford, in London, and on a world tour) for 18 months. He worked for the first time with Diana Rigg, who subsequently played opposite him in The Misanthrope at the National and is now his Eliza in Pygmalion. But it was not a very happy time for him. Playing the Fool to Scofield's Lear he drew, as he often does, on his own childhood: in this case of "waiting when I was five or six years old for my father to come home cross, wanting to relax him, and being physically frightened of him."

The result was a poignant, and supremely intelligent performance, but he felt that his "ultimate in character juvenile parts" had brought him to end of the road. "I couldn't go on trading on my juvenile appearance. I felt very played out and worried." His solution was to go out and buy a grey wig. "I played in that grey wig and glasses for the next three plays." The third of them was Hadrian the Seventh, a dramatisation of Baron Corvo's novel of the bitter, arrogant young man who became Pope. For McCowen, it was definitely third time lucky.

When offered the play he was at his lowest ebb, and accepted it without any great belief in its possibilities. He played it first in Birmingham, where it did terrible business. Nonetheless a London run was arranged: six weeks at the Mermaid. McCowen, by now thoroughly despondent, wondered whether it would not be better to settle for four.

He said at the time that he read the reviews, the morning after the Mermaid opening, "with a mixture of astonishment and pleasure. I began to have the guilty feeling that I'd written them myself." It became fashionable to say that, fine though the performance was, he had done many other things just as good to less applause. But that Mermaid opening was really memorable. It was exhilarating to see an actor rising so fully and surely to each successive climax (it's certainly one of the showiest parts in recent drama).

What difference did Hadrian finally make to him? "By giving me box-office success it stopped me chasing after it. And people started sending me scripts second or third rather than tenth on the list."

There were some other consequences. He found himself making a dreadful movie with Charlton Heston, called Master of the Islands, "with so much spirit gum on I couldn't speak. The character had to be 72; someone had said 'Get the Pope'." It made a change from the usual experience of an actor being refused the part of a 33-year-old because he was only 23.

In 1970, having played Hadrian in New York, McCowen returned to Birmingham to play a controversial Hamlet; one would have expected him to be a worrying if not exactly a gloomy Dane, but his performance was generally found to be surprisingly extrovert. He himself says that he was too old for the part, feeling that for a mature man to go on at his mother like that (why shouldn't she marry whomever she wants?) is fairly insufferable.

He returned to general favour (and incidentally to the Royal Court) as the word-obsessed hero of Christopher Hampton's The Philanthropist, trying desperately to lead a sheltered life; a much enriched version of the shy young men of his earlier days. Hampton deliberately planned this character to be the obverse of Alceste in Moliere's Misanthrope so it was logical that McCowen should eventually find himself at the National giving a volcanic account of Alceste himself. At the heart of the performance as of the play was a man's fury, not with society, but against himself for loving a woman he partially despises. He found Alceste's great outburst against Celimene (Diana Rigg) "as demanding as anything in drama--to come right in with that degree of passion. There was an old fire-bucket in the rehearsal room, and one day I gave it a great kick just before going on. John Dexter seemed to think that was just what the scene needed."

After this came one of his best performances ever as the greying psychiatrist in Peter Shaffer's Equus, from his point of view a problem of restraint. "My instincts are always to have a go, to act. But this character's mostly re-acting. I had to resist the temptation to colour the questions he asks." But being himself a conscientious workman McCowen has always seemed able to illuminate the work-processes of his characters; he emerged in Equus as a supreme exponent of the professional man in crisis. Again one savoured his ability to appear watchful, amused, detached, without ever being uninvolved. And still, beneath the tiredness and the coping with the unaccustomed brisk moustache, there was a trace of ineradicable boyishness. His face is slightly puffier than it used to be, but it is still possible to think--or even unguardedly to write--of him as "one of our best (not promising: that's been redeemed) younger actors". He's growing a beard for Pygmalion: perhaps that will finally age him.

The instinct to act is not confined to the stage. He is alert and responsive in conversation but he blazes into life when he gets out of his chair to illustrate a technical point, or to tell a story. If the story allows him to assume an American accent, so much the better; when I met him he had just returned from a solitary holiday discovering Oregon and was full of it. (Why Oregon? He was a bit vague; I think he liked the name.) On a smaller scale his favourite therapy when he needs to get away from the theatre is to get into a car and drive somewhere unlikely.

For the most part though he remains "steeped in the theatre; he only knows people in the theatre". So says one of his closest friends, the actress Patience Collier, who adds--though he himself fervently denies it--that "he hates emotional involvement. He likes to be fond of people--up to a limit. I couldn't understand when I met him--12 years ago--how anyone could be so un-vain. He used to dress terribly." (Miss Collier takes some credit for having partially cured him of that.) "He can be very generous but he always says he has a terribly mean, puritanical streak. He used to have just one 15-watt uncovered light bulb in his bedroom. Of course that's changed since he started making money."

The money has largely come from his two biggest film roles, in George Cukor's Travels with My Aunt and Alfred Hitchcock's Frenzy, and some of it has gone on a wholesale redecoration of his bachelor flat, several flights up in Notting Hill Gate. His instructions to the decorators are said to have been "You can do what you like with it--only don't ask me." Outside the theatre, says Miss Collier, "he doesn't know about personal tastes and wishes. He just about knows if he doesn't like something." She adds that he plays the piano "divinely" and displays great tact and skill in persuading unlikely ladies to sing along with him. (His selections always begin with Jerome Kern's "I'm Old Fashioned": conceivably a musical credo, certainly an assertion of good taste.)

Someone comes back to talking with him about performers, not necessarily straight actors. "I've found more inspiration and enjoyment from music-hall and from entertainers than from straight theatre; I learnt most from Sid Field, Max Miller, Jack Benny--because of their magical capacity to transmit thought from the stage to the audience. To remember Max Miller coaxing an audience to think the worst and then changing the subject is marvellous; or to watch Benny thinking."

Interviewed on the air in America, McCowen once described Benny as his favourite actor. The word spread and Benny, declaring that it had brought him $10,000 worth of publicity, made McCowen a present of a gold money-clip stamped with the comedian's unmistakable features. (Whether this confirms or belies Benny's own celebrated "puritanical streak" is a nice question.) So, standing on a bookcase filled with playscripts and surrounded by posters, there it is. Flanked majestically by two Evening Standard Drama Awards (for Hadrian VII and for The Misanthrope), a tribute from one professional to another: Alec McCowen's Benny Award.
1974-05-19-today-i-improvise:
Today I improvise

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Pirandello and 'Pygmalion.'

THE Chichester season began on Wednesday with a prolonged blackout. Out of the darkness came an unknown voice, requesting Keith Michell, the theatre's new artistic director, to report to the control box. We all laughed, Mr Michell being such a famous name and all.

His expedition to the sources of power proves successful and the lights go up, in the auditorium as well as on stage, allowing him to come before and among us in his own person. He tells us that the Chichester troupe is about to appear under his direction, improvising its way through a scenario devised from a short story by Luigi Pirandello.

A glance at the programme (easy enough with the houselights on) is enough to inform us that he is lying. Tonight We Improvise is indeed emblazoned there, but it seems to be less a statement of intent than the title of a play written by--rather than based on--Pirandello himself. Furthermore there is a director listed and it is Peter Coe, not Mr Michell, who is billed as an actor--and what is more looks and talks like one. He does not chat us up, he harangues us. This is a result partly of his own stage personality, partly of the lines he has been given to speak, which move on stilts in the manner of bad Pirandello translations.

This is disturbing. Mr Michell is pretending to be himself (and we know at least that this is his theatre, as he claims) and he is also proclaiming--in a very literary manner--a theory of drama that has no time for texts; obviously he is generously lending his own name to an acid caricature of a director who behaves in the manner he affects to condemn. But this will not quite do, because in time other actors appear, and though they do not pretend to be directors they talk as unnaturally as he does. They are in fact giving highly stylised performances of themselves as actors, but they do not seem aware of the fact; they think they're being informal. To be fair, one of them, Alfred Marks, profiting from a training in variety, succeeds.

Let me try to fight my way out of this. (Pirandello's influence on the style of subsequent playwrights is widely acknowledged; less so his effect on the style of subsequent reviewers. No wonder he gets bad notices.) Pirandello wrote a play purporting to explore the nature and validity of theatrical improvisation without actually employing it. From this paradox all else springs. He posits a director who wants to do without a text and then lets the text take its revenge. The more the actors try to improvise the more obscure the basic scenario becomes.

Deciding that the fault lies in the director, who is coming between them and the truth with all his effects, the actors banish him from the theatre. The scene they invent in his absence is certainly more concentrated than what has preceded it, but it is no less artificial, deriving much of its effect from make-up and lighting.

But--and here again it is maybe the translator rather than the dramatist who is to blame--there is an extra layer of artifice. These actors' improvisations hardly sound like improvisations (or like good dialogue either). Pirandello wins his case--chaos reigns, sometimes enjoyably, when the author is dethroned--by not strictly fighting it; given his method, he never could. If you are willing to accept that method (and to overlook such confusing extravagances as the leading lady's supposed death from a surfeit of identification), the play remains a useful airing of some basic theatrical questions: the kind that are best considered early and then forgotten. If ever a play was a candidate for sober academic revival this is it.

But of course no director could bear to treat it that way. Mr Coe can hardly be blamed for trying to create a Happening and for calling his director Keith Michell (Pirandello called him Dr Hinkfuss, not, as far as I know, the name of a real person). He could even claim that he is helping to make Pirandello's point, by showing us how calculated all this spontaneity must be; and by loading the evening with impressively boring set-pieces--processions but no progress and stylised cafe scenes--he supplies a convincing rationale for the actors' revolt.

Finally given the chance to act, Keith Baxter and June Ritchie take it very skilfully, but for all their intensity their big scene is still fairly tedious, since it is far too late for us to take any interest in the characters they are supposed to be portraying. And maybe that, too, is part of the point--but I could go on for ever apportioning praise and blame between author, translator, director, actors, and the Chichester audience, whose applause for each familiar face (Miriam Karlin and Annie Ross are also in the company) is an integral part of the occasion. I at least can make it all up as I go along.

  

AT THE Half Moon Theatre there is an endearing, brave, but ultimately unsuccessful attempt to confine Brecht's vast Saint Joan of the Stockyards within the limitations of a slender budget.

Set in the Chicago of 1929, the play recounts the story of a latter day St Joan who is converted from the pious do-goodery of the Salvation Army to a real dedication to the poor. She attempts to transform Pierpont Mauler, king of the meat industry, but her naivete cannot distinguish between his genuine spasms of good will and the hypocrisy which gets him a better deal. After throwing in her lot with the workers she dies of pneumonia, and is canonised by those she despises.

It is a heavy play, crammed with abstruse financial knowledge, and the Half Moon company's addition of new scenes of battle on the stock market floor does not in any way lighten things. Nor does their propensity to shout their way too quickly through the blank verse in American accents of varying accuracy. But the set--an opening up of the theatre to its rafters in a welter of sawdust and meathooks--is intelligent and right, and the performances, especially that of Philip McGough as Mauler, are spirited. It's not the Berliner Ensemble; but it's a play worth seeing.

  

Off the Peg, an all-male revue at the Arts Theatre Club, has a sketch from Mahagonny, an awesomely banal parody of the parody. The premise for this unremittingly vulgar evening seems to be that you put the boys in the band in girls' clothes (rather good girls' clothes), make-up and wigs (rather good as well), play some recordings (on a bad sound system), and get the boys/girls to mime to them precisely, but pointlessly; and the whole thing becomes instant amusement. Add frequent gropings at crotches (many of them sequinned) and the whole thing becomes instant hysteria.

A first-class drag artist, like the American Jim Bailey, who impersonates Judy Garland, can tell us a lot about the star, women in general and men's aptitudes to both. But in Off the Peg, impersonations of Ella Fitzgerald, Billie Holiday, Jessie Matthews, Gypsy Rose Lee, Marlene Dietrich and even David Bowie merely provide a supply of coathangers on which to hang some costumes and memories of movies.

  

Nobody expected the new production of Pygmalion (Albery) to be anything but a success, but in some respects expectation has been outpaced. This is particularly the case with Diana Rigg's Eliza, a rare comic creation, compact of dignity, fire and mischief. This flower-girl, having grown up with nobody to talk to, has necessarily spent much of her short lifetime mumbling to herself, and she carries the habit with her into Professor Higgins's laboratory, where her aggrieved determination to remain a good girl takes on the force of an obsession. As her education proceeds, she floats into Mrs Higgins's at-home, the most bewitching automaton imaginable, and in the last scene, with her full humanity achieved, plays a surpassing duet with Alec McCowen's Higgins. Eyes aflame he circles her, hardly daring to comprehend the enormity of the change that has taken place in his creation.

This Higgins is a man with all the jollity in the world and none of the humour; when--and it is the turning-point of the performance--he accuses Eliza of making him lose his temper for almost the first time in his life, it can be taken as the literal truth. A man so unthinkingly and habitually rude can usually do without emotional outlets. Perhaps taking a cue from the description of Eliza as Higgins's "live doll," John Dexter's production gives her a final door-slamming exit like Ibsen's Nora. The intention may have been to deromanticise the play, but so far as Higgins is concerned it has the reverse effect; she may not be in love, but he is, too late and unavailingly.

  

Stanley Eveling may never become the major dramatist we once hoped, but he remains among the most engaging of the minors. Shivvers (Theatre Upstairs), a fable of degradation, is intermittently eloquent, chilling and funny, but it suffers from making insecure moral judgments. Two characters pursue a similar downward course, but while one (a recalcitrant vicar, joyfully played by Bill Stewart) is acclaimed a saint, the other (Tony Haygarth, in another of his portrayals of Eveling man, timorous, tubby and lustful--Tony Hancock with metaphysical overtones) is condemned as a villain and left to despair. So one of the thieves was saved, but who holds the scales, and she is well and wearily played by Deirdre Costello.

Alan Ayckbourn's Table Manners (Greenwich) boasts at least one hilarious scene, garnering more laughs than could be believed from the spectacle of a dinner-guest sitting on a chair too low for him, his chin just clearing the board. Perhaps it has to do with timing; we only notice the situation at the precise moment we are intended to. This play is the first of a trilogy. I shall return.
1974-05-26-second-time-round:
Second time round

CONSIDER trilogies, and the authors who beget them. Think of Aeschylus, Shakespeare, O'Neill, Arnold Wesker. Now stop frowning and consider Alan Ayckbourn, the latest and, no contest, the funniest of the drama's triple threats.

Most trilogists devote their three evenings to the telling of a solemn story in chronological sequence. Mr Ayckbourn tells an hilarious story (his may not be the only comic trilogy in existence but at the moment it pleases me to think so) three times over. Each play takes us through the same weekend in the same troubled house, inhabited by the same six characters. All that changes is the room. Table Manners, which opened a fortnight ago at Greenwich, takes us into the dining-room. Very soon we are to go Round and Round the Garden; last week's instalment was called Living Together, from which you may draw your own conclusions.

The plays interlock. "They can be seen," says the author kindly, "in any order since, like a three-ended ball of string, it doesn't really matter where you start to unravel." Ever since reading that sentence in the programme I have been torturing myself trying to imagine a three-ended ball of string. The experience of watching the play is, however, quite painless.

It may even be more painless than the author intended. Sprinkled through the first two plays (and, for all I know, the third as well) are references to the unseen presence who rules the household--a selfishly sentimental bedridden matriarch. Somehow I could never believe in her existence, and my scepticism about her spread outwards to embrace all the darker aspects of Mr Ayckbourn's menage. Like John Hopkins in Next of Kin, he shows us a discordant set of brothers and sisters, husbands and wives. And my first response to him was to give thanks for a dramatist who could insinuate that family life could be hell rather than brazenly proclaiming it. But by the end of his second play I had changed my mind.

Mr Hopkins, however laboured and repetitious, writes like someone who believes what he is saying and has probably lived it; Mr Ayckbourn sounds his bass notes as if fulfilling an obligation. His dialogue is weightless; this does not make him a frivolous writer, but it does limit his capacity to convey pain. He is an unexcelled farcical architect; no other current writer could have invented this cycle, let alone ridden it. He has--this is a compliment--the most acutely mechanical mind of any dramatist since Feydeau; but unlike Feydeau, who could casually annihilate a character or a relationship in a line, he is not a natural misanthrope.

Mr Ayckbourn has time, and even charity, for all his characters: even for the bossy and beady-eyed lady played here (to perfection) by Penelope Keith, busying herself uninvited with other people's problems as a desperate means of avoiding facing her own. Asked pointblank whether she is happy she comes brightly back with "Yes, mostly"; amends that to "occasionally"; and finally settles for "now and then." I look forward to re-encountering Miss Keith in the garden though, not--except in terms of plot--in hopes of learning more about her. I want her to stay as she is. And I would be heartbroken were there to be any change at all in Michael Gambon, who plays a country vet, considerably more honest than the day is long and possessed of a sound but slow and excessively literal mind. He is all pause. As late as the last scene of the second play he is still wringing tears of laughter from us while he carefully considers someone's jocular suggestion that, by having made an unexpected entrance through the French windows, he might be a cat-burglar. He finally denies the charge but it is obviously an infinitely reasoned decision.

Gambon is not one of the family. He is on hand as the inactive wooer of Felicity Kendal, who is in danger of being left on the shelf. Though she looks dishevelled and keeps her hands plunged deep in the pockets of a pair of battered jeans, Miss Kendal cannot make this seem a likely prospect. Tom Courtenay, too, is a touch glamorous for his role. He is meant to be an assistant librarian, which may be a case of Mr Ayckbourn's whimsy getting the better of him, and might well benefit from a spot of character-development in the open air. At the moment his personality, meant to be pivotal, is ill-defined.

His name is Norman and the overall title of the series is The Norman Conquests.

  

This, since it sounds historical, is the best lead-in I can contrive to The Great Society (Mermaid), which is historical. It tells of how Sir Pierce of Exton broke into Richard II's cell and instead of immediately clobbering him, as in Shakespeare, tried instead to bore him to death. This he does, in Beverley Cross's play, by recalling the events of the Peasants' Revolt in which they had both been concerned 20 years before. The audience gets little out of this except a steady dosage of possibly useful information about the Middle Ages; the actors of Richard and Exton get less, being compelled to give lantern lectures when they obviously want to play at murderer and victim. Richard is allowed to roll about a bit, to denote fear.

  

The story and characterisation of Jennifer Phillips's Bodywork (Hampstead) are tenuous in a good light and non-existent in a bad. But it has thematic unity, denoted by the title. In the first act a girl, on a premarital Mediterranean fling, drops her bra as a come-on for any passing male; in the second a young man is dared into posing in the nude for a couple of girl painters, and feels very uncomfortable; in the third the female body is stretched out as a receptacle for impersonal impregnation, but is rescued just in time. The play leaves the slightest of aftertastes, but there is wit in it.
1974-06-02-nightmare-in-nottingham:
Nightmare in Nottingham

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

HOWARD BRENTON'S new play at Nottingham Playhouse begins chillingly. The body of Winston Churchill is lying in state in Westminster Abbey; four soldiers, dimly lit, flank the coffin. In a roaring monotone one of them begins to explain the situation to us. He tells us that his mother was moved to tears when she heard of his assignment to so honourable a post. For her Churchill was God.

His rage over her sentimentality--the two co-existing while threatening to cancel each other out--promises an evening which might equal Mr Brenton's Magnificence in richness of texture. The body, apparently, will not remain hearsed; Winston arises, but before he has a chance to say very much the stage becomes fully illuminated, and we find that we have been watching a play within a play. Or rather, a rehearsal within a play; a rehearsal now interrupted by stern outside pressures.

Mr Brenton's full title is The Churchill Play, "as performed in the winter of 1984 by the internees of Churchill Camp"; somewhere in England; Churchill Camp is where the Con-Lab coalition government dumps its political--predominantly working class--malcontents. Somebody describes it as "the English Dachau"; unless the word "English" is meant to convey a certain cynical moderation, that description, on the evidence of what we see and hear, is excessive. The camp hardly compares with the cellars of Orwell's Ministry of Love.

Mr Brenton's vision of the future involves less sadism than Orwell's but rather more practicality; he shows the Army mentality, hardened by years of what is known as peacekeeping work into the attitudes required for the efficient running of a camp. In one of his most memorable scenes a liberal officer is rendered effectively impotent by his contemptuous subordinates in the most proper manner; they simply bellow him into defeat, never once forgetting to call him "sir."

Some of Mr Brenton's best writing has gone into the depiction of Churchill Camp, as well as into the spare evocation of what lies beyond it. The prospect of escape is finally spurned by one inmate in the words "that outside there lies only more of the same"; the grey concrete world over. The bleakness is admirably realised in Richard Eyre's production and Hayden Griffin's set; but though the overall impact is powerful the details are blurred. On a wide and cavernous stage the voices boom and the characters elude our grasp. They may have eluded the author's as well.

For the whole structure is as unwieldy; the play is built on two resonant myths--Churchill and 1984 are talismanic labels--which finally fail to cohere. That Churchill-worship leads inexorably to Churchill Camp is a good debating-point, and one that Mr Brenton might well be capable of proving. All he does here, though, is to get his rocks off, passion declining into aggro (the distinguishing mark of most of his contemporaries). When the internees finally get to perform their play its upshot is that, whatever may be believed by soldiers' sentimental mothers, Churchill did not win the war; "People won the war." True or false, that makes little difference to one's view of concentration camps.

Mr Brenton manages one extraordinary image: "We are told that Churchill referred to his constant fits of depression as 'Black Dog,' and we see him actually communing with this animal (a large, shaggy creature, rather like Nana in Peter Pan)." The didactic point may be that supposed heroes are as vulnerable and pitiful as anyone else, but dramatically the scene wins our sympathy for Churchill (a marvellous ungainly performance by Paul Dawkins), in a manner with which the author cannot have reckoned. The final scene leaves him grappling with a pile of unrealised themes; they explode in violence, but the impression is of a dramatist's desperate expedient, rather than--as in Magnificence--of the action's inevitable resolution.

  

If Mr Brenton momentarily makes us warm to Churchill, David Cregan in The King (Shaw) makes no such mistake. He is out to debunk King Arthur and he does, remorselessly, for three hours. The trouble is that though he may dislike the Arthurian ethic he is obviously deeply in love with the legends themselves and cannot bear to pass any of them up. But from each one he wrings the same moral--that Arthur's idealism (and, by extension, all idealism) is merely a mask for human, and specifically sexual, inadequacy. He is probably right but I believed him the first time. Some of his jokes at the expense of Galahad, Gawain, and the rest of the Malory gallery are amusing, but not enough. The evening is whimsically interspersed with doggerel songs, in a manner which begins distressingly to resemble a Shaw Theatre house-style; in other respects, though, Peter James's direction is unimpeachable, being lucid, good-humoured, and thoroughly well-acted, with Geoffrey Hutchings a bouncy and resourceful Arthur. The seats are now free.

With Mr Eyre at Nottingham and Mr James about to take over at Sheffield the push reps may be in for a good time. Down from Edinburgh to prove the point comes Bill Bryden to direct Spring Awakening for the National Theatre. Triumphantly he creates an enclosed world. Geoffrey Scott's set is an open plane, occasionally decked by essential furnishings and always liable to be savagely shut off by vast, steely sliding doors. Just so are the pubescent schoolchildren of Wedekind's play crunched by the jaws of German society at the turn of the century.

Puberty in this world has been turned into a particularly forbidding exam; and from each year's crop of competitors the adult world claims a sacrificial quota of failures. That at least is how it appears to young Moritz Stiefel, the more unfortunate of the play's two heroes, whose ineptitude, both sexual and scholastic, finally drives him to suicide. His is a desperate progress, but there is something comic about it, too; at least there should be, but Michael Kitchen's performance is surprisingly stolid, and in general Mr Bryden's production underrates the volatility of the writing.

The only actor to do justice to Wedekind's savage elegance is, fittingly enough, Cyril Cusack, who appears at the end to give a wittily dandified account of the author's own role. (In two senses; the character speaks for the author and the author once played the character.) The other elders include a fine array of monstrous pedagogues, dominated by the rococo rhetoric of William Squire; a pair of equally horrific fathers (one of them sternly depicted by James Mellor in a single line); and two rather more human mothers. One of these is Susan Engel, exuding a gracious sexuality which helps to drive poor Moritz (she turns his head by calling him Herr Stiefel), over the edge.

Miss Engel's performance begins better than it finishes; but there is no falling off in Beryl Reid, whose frightened Hausfrau, hiding her daughter's head in her lap while she fails to tell her about sex, is the most achieved performance of the evening and of her career. Veronica Quilligan is a sweet sight as the girl; most especially when she awaits the fatal attentions of the local abortionist, her frightened eyes peeping above the sheets; Peter Firth is properly cocky as her seducer, the play's survivor.

  

So much for innocence. Experience is rampant in Vanbrugh's The Confederacy (Chichester) but to little effect. The production is roguish, frilly, expertly manoeuvred, and thoroughly dead.
1974-06-09-the-bard-s-board-game:
The Bard's board game

THEATRE

ROBERT
CUSHMAN
on 'Cymbeline'.

A STRANGE kind of record was set up at Stratford-on-Avon this week. Cymbeline became the thirty-seventh, ergo the last, Shakespeare play to be fitted out with its own magazine programme. These engaging publications, combining glossy texts and textual glosses, have been a Stratford feature since 1963. It happens that the last RSC Cymbeline was in 1962.

One can see why they have waited so long to bring it back. The play is a programme editor's nightmare. There is no question of summarising its plot, as is customary, in a couple of trenchant paragraphs. The legend (as our forefathers would most appropriately have designated it) is accorded a triple-page spread. The reader makes his way through 14 episodes linked together by a series of wavy lines, the whole resembling a particularly eventful Waddington's board game.

This concept of Cymbeline as a game any number can play is reflected in the tone of the production which is, for this company, unusually relaxed. The directors--referred to officially as "John Barton with Barry Kyle and Clifford Williams" and hereinafter as Mr Barton--tell their story clearly, relishing each stroke of fortune in the hope that blessedness will descend with the final curtain. There is an intense and poignant pleasure to be gleaned from the disposal of events at the end of a Shakespearean comedy, a pleasure amply afforded by Mr Barton's productions of Twelfth Night and All's Well that Ends Well, two of the richest evenings I have spent in the theatre.

Neither production, though, came into this glory until it arrived at the Aldwych. At their Stratford openings they were both muted; which leads me to hope that the consummation of this Cymbeline is yet to be achieved. On Tuesday the finale faced us with a long line of actors trying their best to look mystically radiant (this, after all, is one of the Last Romances), but succeeding only in looking determined. Ian Richardson as Iachimo came off best: he had a handy piece of scaffolding to lean on, which breeds relaxation, and besides he has uncommonly piercing eyes.

There is a surprising faintness about much of the acting in this scene at the moment. I suspect, too, that Mr Barton has attempted to put pressure on one of the aspects of the play least able to sustain it; Sebastian Shaw, playing the least rewarding title-role in Shakespeare, is decked out (for is he not King of Britain?) in the golden robe which our native monarchs are wearing at Stratford this year on ceremonial occasions. For Cymbeline there are few enough of these; most of the time he is under the thumb of his wicked Queen and is forced to wear a silvery-grey gown, whose main distinction is that it perfectly matches his beard; one flows into the other so that he looks like Father Time.

Finally released from marital tyranny, he celebrates his independence by re-establishing Britain as a fully paid-up tributary of the Roman Empire. This he does with his author's and directors' apparent approval. (When King John bound himself to Rome earlier this season, Mr Barton rewarded him with a custard pie in the face. Values change.) Heaven knows what the Jacobean audience made of this ending; perhaps their classical education outweighed their celebrated patriotism.

The point must be that fealty to Rome equals piety towards Jupiter, the play's presiding deity who makes a brief personal appearance, quelling the murmurings of lesser apparitions with a voice supposedly of thunder while stylishly riding inside a golden eagle. Meanwhile back on earth Sheila Allen as the Queen enjoys herself being evil (with a clear conscience, since nobody but her husband believes a word she says); Charles Keating as Cloten struts about like a rooster, his multi-coloured plumage gorgeous but diseased; Tony Church as Belarius watches proudly and resonantly over a couple of stolen princelings whom he has apparently brought up as Red Indians; and a new leading character takes the stage.

This is the physician Cornelius, for whom, in Jeffrey Dench's performance, medicine is the merest sideline; he also tells fortunes and is a most active First Gentleman, i.e., one who retails the story so far to a Second Gentleman, who responds with such concise and truthful remarks as "I am dumb." Cornelius so thrives on this persona that he begins to adopt the same tone towards us, and finally takes to reading the stage directions for the last-act battle, which is simultaneously being fought upstage and nearly invisible.

Here I quarrel with Mr Barton; the battle is a decisive factor in the action, and in the destinies of many of the characters, and whatever the difficulties (and they are immense) we need to get a good look at it. We need, for example, to see the disarming and partial repentance of Iachimo, if only so that we may be reminded of his existence before the end.

Earlier on Mr Richardson reveals that Iachimo's best scene (and perhaps the best in the play) is neither his attempted seduction of Imogen, nor his bedchamber soliloquy, but his baiting of Posthumus. This becomes a refined version of the central duet in Othello; Tim Piggott-Smith, a tightly confident Posthumus, burns towards jealousy on a slow fuse, though he lacks passion for the grossness of Iachimo's imaginings when once the fit is on him. What Susan Fleetwood's fiery, witty and radiant Imogen is supposed to see in him remains inexplicable. I expect her performance to grow with the production from meritorious to triumphant. She helps it to look good, as do a multitude of white and gold traverse curtains. The designers (another trio) only go berserk in the wilderness near Milford Haven, which they have backed with a large bent drainpipe and populated with small silvery mounds of the kind which traditionally house sinister visitors from outer space.

Charles Marowitz's version of The Shrew (Open Space) sets out to prove (in the teeth of Germaine Greer, among others) that Petruchio's conquest of Katherine was completely vicious. In his sneering threat to make her conformable as other household Kates, Tim Hardy's brutish Petruchio shows his true chauvinist mettle. I bet he could do electric things with a line like "Marry, peace it bodes and love and quiet life." The piece inhabits the limbo reserved for plays about other plays; interesting, even sparky, but unfulfilling and as academic as any stolid old revival.
1974-06-16-stoppard-run-wilde:
Stoppard run Wilde

TOM STOPPARD is the kindest of playwrights. He has written with compassion of Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, and even (in The Real Inspector Hound) of theatre critics. These are all characters who watch while others act; and in Mr Stoppard's world the on-stage spectator invariably misses most of the game.

Take Henry Carr, the hero of his new play, Travesties (Aldwych). Carr was, historically, employed in the British Consulate in Zurich during the latter part of the First World War; resident in the same city at the same time were such revolutionary figures as James Joyce, Lenin, and the daddy of Dada, Tristan Tzara. Though he briefly brushed with Joyce, there is no evidence that Carr ever met either of the other two: a waste, when he comes to think of it, of two splendid opportunities. But of course, as he insists in his reminiscent old age, he might have met them, no reason why not; and Travesties, which is a play-within-a-monologue, is largely devoted to his imaginative substantiation of this hypothesis.

Carr's acquaintance with Joyce was not happy. The novelist, on his accustomed uppers, inveigled Carr into appearing as Algernon in a production of The Importance of Being Earnest, for which he served as manager and then refused to reimburse him for the cost of a pair of trousers purchased for the performance. The matter ended in the courts. It caused great bitterness, but it did enable Carr to creep--by the seat of his pants--into the footnotes of Joyceana, thence into Mr Stoppard's ken and, so, into the centre of his play.

Making the most of the few facts at his disposal, Mr Stoppard has magnified Carr's known preoccupation with his trousers into such a passionate dress-sense as might actually befit a Wildean dandy. From here the obvious next step--given Mr Stoppard's taste and talent for pastiche--is to mould much of the play in the style, and even the shape, of The Importance. Looking back on his Zurich youth, Carr sees himself, even before Mr Joyce's fateful talent-scouting, as being a natural Algy, languidly inquiring of his manservant as to the state of the war, the wine-cellar and the Russian Revolution and attempting to protect his sister Gwendolen from the attentions of his anti-artistic friend, Mr Tzara, who drops in regularly and, as it might be earnestly, for tea. Joyce figures in this scheme as Lady Bracknell, though when he appears the dialogue temporarily abandons the epigram for the limerick. The pun remains a constant factor.

The surface of the play is one to revel in, and beneath it, ideas are shaping. The theme is self-justification; the play represents Carr's strategy to impart a retrospective dignity and glamour to his life, and the distinguished shades he conjures up are all embarked on their own ego-trips. Carr, being an English gentleman, extolling art while distrusting artists, serves them as an excellent sparring-partner; he has his author's facility for seeing and espousing any side of any question (an aspect of the Stoppard sensibility to which I, like many critics, am deeply sympathetic). When not arguing with Carr, Tzara, who draws fragments of Shakespeare sonnets at random from his hat, can clash directly with the literary purist Joyce (occasionally referred to as Doris).

Or again any one of them can argue with Lenin, though none of them actually does. He exists in his own corner of the play, sealed off as in the famous railway compartment in which he entered Russia. We are into Act II; Carr has sloped off to the city library to encounter a girl named, naturally, Cecily. There he is, in mid-Bunbury, when suddenly Lenin's wife commandeers the stage, introducing her husband in excerpts from his speeches on the responsibility of the artist to the State.

One sees the relevance to the previous pronouncements made by Joyce and Tzara, and notes with wry amusement that Vladimir and Tristan would each stigmatise the other as bourgeois. But Mrs Lenin's recollections can have no place within Henry Carr's, and the play's fantastic structure splits: a fatal mistake which Mr Stoppard has never, to my knowledge, made before. We may momentarily welcome the weightier texture of the Lenin speeches, but when the play begins to run Wilde again we have lost track of the farcical issues. The two girls' encounter, to the rollicking, infallible ragtime strains of Mr Gallagher and Mr Shean ("Oh, Gwendolen . . . oh, Cecilee") and their duet would be a delight, if only we could figure out what they were on about. By the end, Peter Wood's production is assuming more euphoria than it is generating.

It is hampered by performances that are generally undistinguished and occasionally clumsy. The exceptions are Frank Windsor, ambiguously massive as Lenin and, providentially if quite foreseeably, John Wood, who gives several brilliant performances as Carr. There is the young consul basking in Swiss neutrality ("the entente cordiality of it"); the blushing amateur actor, seduced by appeals to the memory of his brilliant Goneril at Eton into essaying the part of Algernon (though he looks, to be truthful, as though his name were Ernest); and, when his memories are done, the final unwilling return to old age, his hands and feet still obstinately going through the motions of a swaying, decelerating foxtrot, as the grin of youth fades from his face.
1974-06-23-norman-s-conquests:
Norman's conquests

IF people really laugh like drains, two London theatres must currently resemble sewers. One is the Aldwych, on the occasions when Tom Stoppard's Travesties is playing; the other is Greenwich which, like the Aldwych, is operating a repertoire system. However, since the repertoire consists entirely of Alan Ayckbourn's trilogy The Norman Conquests, you may be assured of a guffaw any night on which you can gain admittance.

I fear that last week I under-emphasised the sheer funniness of Mr Stoppard's play. It is--unless you have a deaf spot for puns and conceits--immense.

Mr Ayckbourn, too, deals in conceits (for how else would you describe the three-fold reiteration of the events of a single weekend). Norman is a man--or at any rate an Assistant Librarian--and his conquests sexual. His attempted conquests, I should say. Though he lays siege during the trilogy to all three of the women in the cast, only one of them actually capitulates, and that his own wife. His avowed intention is to seduce his sister-in-law. He is, however, thwarted by his other sister-in-law, a monitress. It was always a question whether Mr Ayckbourn could convincingly complete his scheme by contriving a plausible encounter between Norman and this last lady. He begged it, until the final play, Round and Round the Garden, and then he blew it.

Though it has always been difficult to fault Tom Courtenay's performance of this Norman, it has never been possible quite to believe in it. In the earlier plays he was a manic presence who promised to improve, and even to become comprehensible, on closer acquaintance.

This last and most schematic of the three drags him firmly but disappointingly into the centre. He propositions the ladies, and is rejected by them, more for the sake of his author's pattern than from internal logic.

Towards the close, Round and Round the Garden takes on the forced formality that for me maimed the finale of Mr Ayckbourn's Absurd Person Singular; while earlier the action is prolonged (and Michael Gambon's delightfully stolid vet distorted) beyond reason by the introduction of a contrived misunderstanding.

The level of incidental merriment remains intelligently high, and many lines still bruise the bone. The play offers pleasing variations on the basic form, without ever breaking faith with it. Though it scrupulously confines itself to the same weekend as its predecessors, it begins a little earlier in the day. We are thus slyly afforded an exposition, wherein Mr Ayckbourn may tell us things we already know and are only too delighted to hear again. And though, since the plot is unalterable, Norman's wife is still condemned to exist offstage until halfway through the evening, on this occasion her activities upon arrival allow the actress, Penelope Wilton, to come within reach of her acerbic own. Eric Thompson's direction is excellent, as it has been throughout; and the whole enterprise will shortly transfer, all three of it, to the West End.

Robert Cushman
1974-07-14-the-cut-throat-barber:
The cut-throat barber

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the National's Figaro.

LOUIS XVI was dismayed by Beaumarchais's The Marriage of Figaro, but aristocratic society in general laughed all the way to the scaffold: not such a long ride, since the play preceded the Revolution by only five years.

In one defiant line of Figaro's, Lytton Strachey, of whom more later, detected the voice of the guillotine. But this, the play's most oratorical moment, was presented, not in the dark and sparkling light of frivolity, but as the natural extension of intrigue and vapid lovemaking among the antiquated remains of feudal privileges and manners. The intrigue was the frivolity.

Some inconsistency there, but it faithfully reflects the play, which is more notable for comic energy than for unity of tone, or even of action. It is constructed like an old-time movie serial; there is a predestined goal--the marriage of Figaro and Suzanne--and a series of intrigues which run, not in parallel, but in series. Just when you think the plot is exhausted, it starts all over again.

Jonathan Miller's Old Vic Theatre production at the Old Vic does not so much solve these problems as override them. At times I have found his work over-solemn, as if he were trying to illuminate while dimming the lights. This, however, is one of his more joyous offerings, fun for both him and us.

Mr Miller's style occasionally recalls that of the late Tyrone Guthrie. He does not possess Guthrie's consummate showmanship, but he permits his small-part players a similar licence. The practical result--as in The School for Scandal--is a household full of eccentric domestics. One minor role--a justice's clerk--is played perfectly straight; lacking even a facial tic the actor looks startlingly naked, and one feels like ordering him back to his dressing-room.

Wily, experienced players profit most under this dispensation. The most successful of the "secondary characters" (Beaumarchais so described them in his stage directions, before the term was converted to the delicate treatment accorded them here) is the justice himself. In the person of Howard Goorney, he crawls across the stage bent double; an exit begun as the curtain falls on Act One nears completion as it rises on Act Two.

The principal characters have their eccentricities as well. The crucial opposition, as realised here, is the duel between Figaro and the Count: hard-worked wit against hereditary privilege. It is underlined in the casting; Derek Godfrey, an accomplished and experienced classical comedian, gives of his best as the Count, a scheming, ageing seducer excessively liable to accident and frustration. On this occasion, he admits with ruffled dignity, "I was wrong." I forget to which of his mishaps he refers; there are so many. Most characteristically he finds himself caught up in a peasant dance while attempting to pass a note to his intended; trying, for the sake of appearances, to enter into the spirit of the thing, he raises his hands gaily above his head and unconsciously adopts the formal posture of a trained dancer.

Matched against him is Gawn Grainger, who has done sturdy and versatile supporting work at the National, as Figaro. All he lacks is the ultimate turn of speed in soliloquy. Figaro, as everybody knows, entered theatrical history as a barber. With its eyes firmly on the past, Mr Miller has had him revert to his old trade. As his razor plays deftly around his master's chin, Mr Grainger scores for both role and for the company he is representing. It is a neat yet broadened world of catch-throat competition. The production, like the text, tends to sprawl; in the last act Gemma Jones as the Countess and Nicola Pagett as Suzanne are called on to engage in mutual impersonations, which may be a sly comment on The School for Scandal, or it could be carelessness. But the heart of the play--at least in this staging--beats strongly enough.

  

Johnny Mercer is one of the great men of our time; a new revue built around some of his own lyrics (from You Must Have Been a Beautiful Baby to Moon River and beyond) has cheered my week considerably. His contributions to The Good Companions (Her Majesty's) did less for me (as they will, I suspect, for him); his best work is steeped in Americana (rural-bucolic or urban-hip) and, though the Englishness of his current subject has not actually defeated him, it has cost him audible effort.

Indeed the J. B. Priestley novel has proved an unwieldy source for all concerned. The first act is all flashback, the second mostly wrap-up; the Good Companions themselves--a touring concert party--are squeezed out of the action, and as a backstage musical the show only fitfully takes off. Even the love-interest is belatedly introduced and perfunctorily dispatched. Judi Dench's charm and conviction, as always, are largely wasted (she is given ballads beyond her range instead of the belters she handled so well in Cabaret). John Mills, shyly and fetchingly, takes up where he left off in the film.

Still, Mercer can hardly help writing singable words (he would have done better with a different subject), and some of the numbers have their amiable moments. The production relies heavily on the all-purpose jollity which traditionally fuels the English musical.

  

The view from Dublin pier

E. A. WHITEHEAD'S The Sea Anchor (Theatre Upstairs) is a searing, sombre little play about the misery of sexual relationships, within and without marriage, in a society where there are no rules other than male/female archetypes.

The characters are four working-class Liverpudlians in Dublin for a dirty weekend: Les, apparently coarse and brutal; Sylvia, his naive, defenceless girlfriend; Andy, a romantic, gentle and self-deceiving; and Jean, affectedly cynical and inwardly hysterical. Out there is a fifth, Nick, Jean's lover, trying to cross from Liverpool to Dublin in a dinghy, not waving but drowning. Nick's hapless voyage, viewed by the quartet during the course of an afternoon, evening and the following morning as they wait for him on a pier, becomes the pivot for the way the characters see themselves and each other. It is an act of suicidal bravado for Nick, torn apart by the jealous devotion of the wife on one shore and the mistress on the other.

Both men see it as such: Les with contempt, Andy with admiration. For the women it is yet another unintelligible gesture of contempt from a man.

It is also a clever dramatic device which allows the quartet to assemble and reassemble on the pier in varying groups, illustrating the different sides of their sexual feelings and ideas. When the two men are together the talk is comradely crudeness; the two women alone are wary, united by a common understanding, but separated by sexual jealousy. Alone with Sylvia, Les is tender; in a group he treats her with brutality. When Les is about, Andy assumes some of his mocking misogyny; with the women he is generous, anxious to please and placate. Les and Jean, both strong-willed and firmly stuck in the prejudices of their sex, despise each other.

This is an intelligent, tight, and meticulously structured play. Jonathan Hales's direction gives it the maximum naturalism with the maximum economy, and John Tindale's lighting casts a bleak view from Dublin pier.
1974-07-21-oi-oi-it-s-oidipus:
Oi, oi--it's Oidipus

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

MOST of us, when reading Greek tragedy, must at times have felt disinclined to take it seriously. We have found the heroes sententious and self-important, and the chorus tireless and tiresome staters of the obvious.

Most directors attempt to overcome this reaction; Hovhanness I. Pilikian tries to capitalise on it. Last week at Chichester he gave us the play which I generally think of as 'Oedipus the King' but which now confronts us, with fearless phonetic fidelity to the original, as Oidipus Tyrannus.

There is more than pedantry behind this. Mr Pilikian is much concerned with the literal meaning of the title. As he writes in his voluminous programme note: "'Oidipus' means 'swollen-foot.' Every time the name is mentioned in the play, it spotlights the cruel tale of his birth." We are assured that Sophocles's text is full of puns on the name, puns which the present translation (by Gail Rademacher) resourcefully echoes. Oidipus, say the chorus congratulating themselves on the joke, is the man who put our city back on its feet.

I cannot quite follow the director's apparent assumption that Oidipus's deformity--which, strangely, is hardly noticeable in Keith Michell's performance--in some way diminishes him. On the evidence of Philoctetes, whose hero suffered with even worse feet, Sophocles was sympathetic to such ailments. But Mr Pilikian is out to get Oidipus. Hence perhaps his use of that jarring pronunciation (summoning memories of Frankie Howerd's evocation of Greek tragedy: Odtpns... oi, de naghty puss).

Hence, too, the insistence on the hero as--in the modern sense--a tyrant. Did the word 'Tyrannus' have the same emotive significance for the Greeks? I lack the expertise to answer that question. I think Mr Pilikian has a telling point when he reminds us that reactionary regimes have had, not merely to emasculate, but to ban the Greek classics outright. I know that in Antigone Sophocles unsparingly condemned the lawless ruler Creon: the same Creon who is seen ascending to Oidipus's power at the end of the present play, and is also seen to behave outrageously in Oedipus at Colonus.

He condemns Creon, but he did not mock. Mr Pilikian would have it that in the case of Oidipus he did both; and he does his utmost to ensure that we should too. After all, goes the theory, Oidipus and his people were Thebans; the Thebans had sided against Athens in the Persian wars; and no public-spirited Athenian writer could possibly treat them sympathetically. The argument is horribly specious; Aeschylus, every bit as patriotic as Sophocles, managed in The Persians to write with compassion of the barbarians themselves. Could we not credit Sophocles with a similar immunity to xenophobia?

Mr Pilikian's polemical preoccupations give him one practical advantage; he cares about the way his actors speak the lines. His chorus are a collection of crotchety old dotards (and when their director decides to put them through the odd choreographic hoop they are plain embarrassing), but at least it is possible to hear and understand them. A sensible conversational vigour also informs much of the dialogue. The Priest (David King) in the opening scene hardly disguises his contempt as Oidipus, all too consciously the saviour of the city, addresses his suffering 'children.'

Mr Michell's sneering narcissism at this point is his best piece of acting in years. Thereafter his performance goes into neutral and remains there, a victim of the irreconcilable demands of author and director. For Mr Pilikian's juiciest news is that the play concerns 'a Watergate-style cover-up of the truth.' Last year, in this very column, Robert Brustein bemoaned President Nixon's failure to come as clean as did the Theban king when confronted with his misdeeds. The comparison struck me as unreasonable (a live politician can hardly be blamed for falling short of standards set by a mythical hero), but the implicit assumptions about Oidipus himself was surely correct. Halfway through the play he suspects that he is the incestuous parricide who has ruined Thebes and he says so, out loud, in front of Iocasta and the chorus. Being, by his own lights, a textual purist, Mr Pilikian has left this passage intact, and so sacrificed any chance of proving Oidipus a scoundrel. (No critics, to my knowledge, have tried to prove him a saint, though Mr Pilikian seems convinced that they have.)

Having--to his own satisfaction--knocked his protagonist down the director proceeds to kick him. He decides that the final appearance of Oidipus's two daughters takes place only in their sightless father's self-pitying imagination. Since the Greeks left no stage-directions there is no way either of proving or refuting this theory, but Mr Pilikian is fooling himself if he believes that Mr Michell emoting into space is a harsher or less pathetic image than Mr Michell embracing two real live girls. If you want (and I suppose you do) an opinion of Diana Dors's Iocasta you must go to some less charitable critic; but I liked Willoughby Goddard's Teutonically gutteral account of the shepherd-messenger (who chomes from Chorinth).

  

Mustapha Matura's Play Mas (Royal Court) is a sparkling achievement, as elegantly sewn as the suits whose virtues the Trinidadian tailor (Indian) extols in the first act to his apathetic apprentice (African). Comes the revolution, and the second act: the apprentice has become Chief of Police, and his former employer is tolerated (just) as a quivering informer. And still the talk is of suits, and of films, on the aesthetics of which the tailor had also been accustomed to hold forth. (Sometimes he combines the two; his theory is that Robert Mitchum is no actor--his seams do all the work.)

The symmetry is beautiful, both in the writing and in the acting of Stefan Kalipha and Rudolph Walker. The carnival image, denoted by the title, is less successful in binding the play together, though it occasions some delightful moments. As it proceeds, the play sails into late Shavian waters which it lacks the weight to navigate; not, however, to worry. Grieve instead for the Cambridge Footlights, who have thudded into the West End with a revue called Chox (Comedy). As my favourite Toytown character used to say, it ought not to be allowed.
1974-07-28-on-the-slippery-slope:
On the slippery slope

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

I IMAGINE that the Mayfair is even more dependent than most West End theatres on the patronage of tourists. I wonder what the visitors, when they roll down from the hotel upstairs, will make of The Golden Pathway Annual.

For here, imported from the studio of Sheffield's Crucible Theatre, is the authentically English entertainment in whose possibility I had ceased to believe. On the first night a house filled with natives resounded to the laughter of recognition. The show-stopping moment arrived when Michael Peters, schoolboy of the 1950s, brandished a textbook at us, and announced: "We not only have to read these books; we have to put brown paper covers on them as well." Michael is in the first form of his grammar school: "Class," as he emphasises, "1A."

He has, perhaps, some reason to be proud; though he admits that his mother is quite capable of being proud enough for them both. She can introduce her son's scholastic achievements into any conversation, 45 seconds after the off. And behind this there lingers the memory of the morning on which his parents had crept respectfully into his bedroom ("quite a den you've got up here") to acquaint him with the awful significance of the approaching 11-plus. If he fails it, he will miss out on life's opportunities, just as his father always has. Not, as his mother hastily adds, that there's anything wrong with his father's life: it's just that...

Fill in the rest for yourself.

The complexities of the situation are endless and familiar, though in the theatre they have suffered from their association with turgid melodramas about declasse students. The virtue of this show is that it catches the process of alienation on the wing.

It is written by John Harding and John Burrows, two young actors who also comprise half the cast. The hybrid form they have adopted--half play, half revue--is both a strength and a weakness. The scenes are mainly self-contained sketches; some of them are funny and pointful, but when they fail to be either they can be partially excused as temporary lapses in the execution of a master-plan. When the plan itself falters we can concentrate on the individual jokes.

Two main images are employed to chart Michael's progress from conception (he is an immediate result of post-war euphoria) to post-graduation (brandishing an Honours Degree in English, no less, in a vain attempt to break into Fleet Street). First, awaiting us as we enter the theatre, is that huge immortal advertisement for children's shoes, in which two determined tots, pathetically isolated but immaculately shod, march away up a steeply dwindling perspective.

When I was their size this advertisement used to terrify me; its threat ("Children's shoes have far to go") seemed far more potent than its promise ("Startrite and they'll walk happily ever after"). I now know, thanks to Messrs Harding and Burrows, that my fears were fully justified and that the Golden Pathway they travelled would lead only to disillusion.

Which brings us to the second image. The Golden Pathway Annual is a 10-volume compilation, delivered to Michael in birthday instalments, and designed to foster general knowledge, intellectual curiosity, a sense of adventure, pride in our island story, and snobbery. It is the Children's Encyclopaedia, as it might have been edited by Enid Blyton.

The authors have a fine instinct for the potent nostalgic symbol. It was apparent in their previous collaboration, For Sylvia, which was hailed by some as a satiric view of World War II, and which I thought lovely and about as malevolent as The Boy Friend. On the simplest level here they can put on a record of "The Laughing Policeman" and flood the house with memories of "Children's Favourites," and Sunday mornings with Uncle Mac. The Golden Pathway Annual is one of their aptest creations, but having created it they seem none too certain of what to do with it. It does not control the action as it should. There are a couple of good scenes early on where its stories merge in Michael's mind with his real-life circumstances; he imagines himself caught up in a middle-class children's adventure story, where he is cast as the faithful dog and his father--a laundry-roundsman of whom, as his education progresses, he grows increasingly ashamed--as the villain.

As the show proceeds, however, the framework diminishes, occasionally vanishing altogether. When Michael, as a bob-a-jobbing Scout, retreats from the advances of a mature prospective mistress, his punch-line--"Can I come back when I'm a Rover?"--is transparent gag-writing, the product of the author's sensibility rather than the character's. So we stop believing in the play, settle for it as a revue, and have no response when the end arrives and the screws are tightened. Michael begins ineffectually to revolt against his conditioning, but by now the evening is out of control; even Volume 10 of the annual lies far in the past and we have forgotten it. A last-second attempt to remind us of it is devoid of resonance.

Mr Burrows plays Michael, and Mr Harding assumes a variety of roles, most of them figures of authority. Their relationship (which could trigger off a television series) is seen at its purest when Mr Harding briefly impersonates a chicken; oblivious of incipient incineration he stares haughtily down his beak, while Mr Burrows (who cannot be much more than three at the time) gazes back, bright-eyed and fascinated. Mark Wing Davey plays Dad, and Maggie McCarthy is all womankind; the director is Ed Thomason. Good people all.

  

The Sack Race (Ambassadors) is a business thriller about a firm which appears to be in a bad way; its walls shudder when touched, and it cannot afford three-dimensional box-files for its shelves, which are filled instead with painted replicas. I failed to follow the intrigues, but the minutiae of office life have a soap-opera fascination, and Michael Denison plays an excellent and conscientious managing clerk in a manner befitting.

  

Sherlock's Last Case (Open Space) is a graceless pastiche, whose author believes that a four-line doggerel may be described as a limerick. I do not think that a man possessed of such convictions should be trusted to create a text composed of epigrams, and the actors--to judge from the reluctance with which they let his phrases escape their lips--would agree with me.
1974-08-01-towards-the-mountain-top:
Towards the mountain top

PETER HALL talks to ROBERT CUSHMAN about his plans for the new National

ROBERT CUSHMAN: Why did you take on the job of Director of the National Theatre?

PETER HALL: When I left Stratford in 1968 I had a very firm conviction that I would never, under any circumstances, run a theatre again. I'd had it. I felt it was a dreadful strain, which is obvious, but more than anything, it was a liability on someone who's trying to be a director of plays. The unfortunate fact is that when you're directing a play is always the moment when news comes that the Arts Council grant cannot be increased or some member of the press accuses you of doing dirty plays or some actor finds he cannot honour his contract. One is very vulnerable. So I thought from now on I'm just going to be a director--swan around the world doing this and that. But it was a reaction against a central action. Whether I'm any good at running a theatre or not is for other people to say. I certainly don't know. But I do know that for 21 years my main motivation has been to try and create working conditions for other people which I myself can test and enjoy. It's selfish, but also altruistic. I think the two things go together. And the fact that the National has this extraordinary new building proved absolutely irresistible. I don't mean that buildings make theatres--I don't think they do--but good facilities are a considerable help in making good theatre. They're no guarantee of it. They can be a seduction. They can be a difficulty indeed. But I think the South Bank has three beautiful spaces. And it was a bit like being asked to go back to Go, and start again, with better resources and better opportunities. And it was therefore impossible to say no.

RC: If the building had been less attractive, would you still have been interested in the idea of running the company?

PH: No. If the building had been like most modern theatres that I've seen round the world, or indeed if the building was not there and if one was going to stay at the Old Vic, I would not have done it. No, I want to run a theatre again, but I want it to be one with good working and rehearsal conditions.

RC: Are you aware of a certain feeling around that people are going to miss the Old Vic a lot when the National Theatre leaves it?

PH: Oh yes of course. I mean the Old Vic is a very beautiful theatre to sit in, but hard to work in. It's nice to act in, but not to rehearse in. The actors never create their work on the stage where they're going to perform it. They are in dreadful rehearsal rooms which any factory worker would walk out of. I've spent many fine evenings there, as I'm sure you have, and it will be sad, it will be a pang, to leave it; but the National Theatre has reached its end point in Old Vic terms. It can't have enough activity, I think, to be a National Theatre while it remains there.

RC: Now, why is the National Theatre different from other new theatre buildings?

PH: Well, first of all, it was designed by an architect who listened to the brief of a group of theatre people. Denys Lasdun used the knowledge of the theatre that was available. The building committee of the National Theatre--I don't think there has been anything like enough comment or interest taken in this--under the chairmanship of Sir Laurence Olivier, was a very extraordinary cross section of people, including Peter Brook, Michel St Denis, George Devine, Bill Gaskill, Michael Elliott, Jocelyn Herbert, Tyrone Guthrie for a short period. It was a very wide section of theatre opinion, and things were really hammered out. It wasn't a question of A's prejudices against B's prejudices. We really set ourselves the task of defining what is the best possible theatre at this moment. That was the brief, and that's what was given to Denys Lasdun. So a number of very crucial decisions were taken. We concluded that although fashions in staging may come and go, the one thing that does not alter is the scale of the human figure. We decided that if any member of the audience is more than 65 feet away you have a dilution of experience. So we said 65 feet is the maximum, and that is a very very high standard of communication indeed. The back of the stalls at Stratford is I think 83 feet--a lot further. And we thought of servicing the actor, so that he could work in one place, not in a draughty rehearsal hall on the other side of London, but actually work on the stage with his props and actually create his work for the place where he was going to present it. These may seem luxuries but they make for better work.

RC: They don't seem like luxuries, but I imagine they're common to most of the new theatre buildings?

PH: No, they're common to some of the European theatres, they're not very common to most of the new buildings in America.

RC: Just mentioning America, are you frightened at all by what's happened at Lincoln Center? It seems to me a perfect example of an imposing building which has never managed to fill itself with anything very interesting.

PH: I think the problem with Lincoln Center has been that the building was designed without reference to a company, and there was no company either then or now. They keep struggling to make one. I think the virtue of Sir Laurence's philosophy was that he tried to form the National Theatre Company and the tradition of the Company before the building was designed or built.

RC: How much do you consider yourself as being Olivier's direct heir as far as that's concerned?

PH: Well, I was on the building committee, not as heir apparent, but as a member of the theatrical profession. We worked for many years, long hours. I think when it's all totted up in 30 or 40 years time there will be seen to be great similarities between the Olivier theatre at the National, and the Barbican Theatre of the RSC. They came out of the same decade, the same impulse of theatre. I certainly see myself as Sir Laurence's heir because I endorse these two buildings.

RC: I didn't so much mean that, you said yourself he committed himself to forming a company first. Listening to you talk for example, I get the impression you are now more excited by the idea of the building than by the idea of running a company as much.

PH: No. Why on earth should I want to run a building? I think the only way to work in the theatre is with a company. And decent facilities--such as this building provides makes a company more possible. In fact to answer your first question again, the reason why I accepted the job in the National Theatre is because being a freelance is so very wasteful as far as failure is concerned. If you fail as a freelance, you fail, that's it. Within a Company, failure can be as productive as success. There is a continuum. On the other hand I think that within our society the only kind of company you can make is one which is reasonably small in its numbers. I don't believe you can have a company if it's got a hundred actors in it. A company is about 30 or 40 people. I also believe that you have to recognise that actors in order to endorse membership of a group have to have their freedom as well. They do not want to be part of a corporation for ever and ever amen. The only way you can get them to stay is by positively encouraging them to go away. The new company system at the National is based on the fact that we will have three or four groups which will be encouraged to develop their own personalities--their own identities--and that they will be there for eight months and then away for eight months and then back for eight months so that they can do outside work if they so wish. I think that without a continuity of actor/designer/director you can't do anything at all in the theatre. But equally, you shouldn't kid yourself that you've got a permanent company when you haven't and I think we've all tended to do that.

RC: Well, obviously this is a difference from your philosophy when you started with the RSC?

PH: Yes. Nobody had tried when I started at the RSC to run a permanent company. I think that if I did nothing else, I proved that in fact you can't, in the sense of saying to an actor: "Here's a five-year contract. You're not to go away. If you want to do a television serial in order to educate your children privately, it is a betrayal of the company and the company's aesthetics and how dare you--you're a traitor". And all that. I've been through all that.

RC: Under your new scheme, how many plays in a year will you reckon a company actor to be doing?

PH: Well, a company actor will come for eight months and he will be in two main house productions in the Olivier as a minimum. Now, that's not very much for eight months. But he will also have the opportunity of being cast in the new writing seasons or the thematic seasons in the Lyttelton (which are short runs), or the short runs of new plays or of other work in the smallest house, the Cottesloe. So he will have a really wide variety of work which he must and will be drawn into. He has to evaluate his casting on his Olivier theatre offer, and then see how the rest develops. We're doing long term planning for the Olivier and deliberate short term planning in the others so that we can get things up quickly and respond to new plays and new events.

RC: So your first year and a half in the new theatre anyway presumably is mapped out by now?

PH: We're mapped out at the Olivier as we speak until November of next year but we're not mapped out at all in the two others.

RC: My own feeling about the work of the Old Vic so far is that though I've enjoyed most of the productions individually, I haven't had any sense of a corporate achievement at all.

PH: I think it's much too early to say that, if I may say so. Many of last year's company went off to Australia in The Front Page and will be returning to the National in the autumn. Others are going on the West End transfer of Saturday Sunday Monday.
