I think that the work that came out of The Tempest into Spring Awakening and is now going into Romeo and Juliet--I'm talking about the younger members of that company--is developing a corporate identity. I've no doubt about that at all. And I know that the Next of Kin/Marriage of Figaro group have in themselves, it may not be evident to you, a strong feeling of corporate identity. There are two groups who are in growth. You can't talk about company feeling until it happens. It happens by doing it. And after all we are under six months old. It took the RSC three years before I suddenly woke up and noticed that everybody was telling me we had a company in that sense.

RC: I think that may have been wrong. I think as far back as your first RSC season in 1960 one felt the quickening of something which isn't evident at the National as yet.

PH: I don't know how to answer that. I think you are forgetting the hostility to the idea of the RSC in 1960 and remembering only the praise. I can see it particularly in the Spring Awakening group where I think there's an enormous number of very talented young actors raring to work and to do things.

RC: On the other hand a lot of those talented young actors seem to be fairly uneasy about the prospect of committing themselves to more than one play, never mind about committing themselves for years.

PH: Yes, but they were griping and were encouraged to gripe by Plays and Players. At this moment they're working for a theatre with one auditorium, although they're programmed into a new theatre with 3 auditoriums. I don't blame some of them for being restless. They haven't got enough work to do. Although at the moment Plays and Players talked to them they were just doing The Tempest. Now that they're on tour with Spring Awakening and rehearsing Romeo, I'm getting cries from them that they're being worked too hard. The point I'm making is that the spectrum of work which we can offer an actor will not be there until next April. It can't be, we're not in the theatre.

RC: I'm thinking more of an actor like Michael Kitchen who said in P&P (May) he didn't feel like committing himself to more than one play at a time. I think this must be a fairly widespread feeling among young actors. Is it going to present difficulties for you?

PH: Yes, and I've got to convince them that they're wrong. But they're not going to come for one play at a time, that's all. If we are sitting here saying that the company is the most important thing, it behoves me to stick to the rules of making a company. And to convince the profession that this is a good way of working. And I'm not going to have, and I say this absolutely categorically, I'm not going to have guest visits, in the Olivier. I'm not going to work that way.

RC: Are any of the actors in your current season guests? Or put another way, how many of the actors you have at the moment do you see yourself taking with you as far as the end of this year and then into the summer?

PH: The majority. All the leading performers of The Tempest are returning. All the younger people, when they've done Romeo will be able to evaluate whether they want to go on or not. We couldn't run our eight months on, eight months off scheme when we are only at the Vic. We are in a transitional phase. But Gielgud, Arthur Lowe, Julian Orchard, Denis Quilley, they are all coming back when we do The Tempest again. That was part of the arrangement with them. Now this doesn't mean that someone will be contracted to play the doctor in Macbeth for 2 years and 4 months. He may change. But Macbeth and Lady Macbeth and Macduff and Banquo will not change. Otherwise, they won't play it in the first place. And an author knows his play will be current for a total of 16 months over 2 years, which isn't bad. It's better than anything that's happened so far because any play at the National or at the RSC up to date that's chalked up more than 100 performances has been doing jolly well for itself.

RC: But do you think the National Theatre by definition has to be so large?

PH: But the whole virtue of what I'm doing is that it isn't large. If we were going to take on that space, run 3 theatres 7 nights a week and tour we would need about 150/160 actors, and a repertoire of 40 plays. That is impossible.

RC: That's not what I'm saying. I'm saying really does the National Theatre need to have that number of spaces, that many touring commitments.

PH: No, I don't think it does, but I am glad in the event that it has. Let me explain. When I was on the building committee of the National, there was a minority group of us who believed very passionately that the National Theatre should not have two main auditoria--it should have one. And if we weren't prepared to commit ourselves to what a theatre was in 1970 we shouldn't be doing it at all. A minority of us thought that the proscenium theatre was an insurance which was not necessary. Sir Laurence felt very strongly that if the National Theatre was to be a continuing facility for future generations it had to have a proscenium Theatre as well. And I think on reflection that he was right. If I was thinking of running a theatre in the way that I ran the RSC which, although I don't mean in any way to diminish what my colleagues did to me and for me, was very much the expression of what I wanted, then I think one auditorium is enough. But I don't think that way now. I think the National Theatre in this day and age means a company of actors who are very prejudiced and develop a particular aesthetic. But I also think a National theatre must be an expression of the whole nation's theatre. Everybody who wants to should play there--other companies, other groups. The company itself should do a fairly small amount of work--there won't be more than 6 productions at the Olivier, plus the possibility of touring and seasonal work in the other houses. And most important there will be a great deal coming in from the rest of the nation's theatre or from overseas. That seems to me at this moment to represent National Theatre. I can of course be absolutely wrong about this. The company itself must be as small and lean as it possibly can be. And believe you me if I can do this with two groups instead of 4, I'll do it. But all the rest of it, the ferment of theatrical activity, the cross-fertilisation by going out to the regions and the regions coming in to us, that represents National Theatre to me. It's not an expression of my taste--it's a facility. And I think that the building is primarily a facility in which a small National theatre company can function and the nation's theatre can talk to the whole community. So that's why I now think Olivier's decision was right.

RC: With the great increase in the National's own activity is the Aldwych going to seem a little redundant?

PH: I wouldn't have thought so. It seems to me that there are whole areas of drama which are the concern and interest of the RSC at this moment and which will remain so. I thought when I went to the National that, possibly, there were only about 500 plays in the Western repertoire which merited revival. I think I was wrong. I've had the benefit of 2 years of study and thought. There's an enormous amount that needs to be done. German theatre's virtually unexplored in this country. French theatre's also unexplored in this country. As far as new writing is concerned I basically believe that the more opportunity there is to put on new writing, the more new writing will exist. Therefore if the Court, the Aldwych and the National are all presenting new plays there will be that much more new writing and the more new writing there is the more new writing there'll be. And there's one thing I would like to stress very strongly. There seems to be current, because the National Theatre is a modern theatre and it's therefore, and why shouldn't it be, full of modern equipment, that we are going to be engaged in large spectacular productions. That we will constantly be staging The Battle of Trafalgar with full scenic effects. The machinery that the National has been designed for one thing only: to make it possible for a play to be changed from the matinee to the evening performance and to make it possible for the actor to create his work on the stage in the set. There will therefore be more variety in the repertoire day by day. With the cost of raw materials and roaring inflation we are going to be driven and should be driven in my view into discovering ways of doing theatre with people in space and with light. No doubt about that whatsoever. And as two of our theatres out of the three are spaces where scenery is not necessary we are in a good position. I think there is hostility to the new National because it is the biggest and the glossiest and the most heavily endowed. I think also we're going through a national nervous breakdown with a consequent lack of confidence. We like to think that everything we're doing is disaster. I don't just speak of the theatre.

RC: Isn't there a more general disillusion with institutional theatre?

PH: Yes, and that is a swing of the pendulum. I think it's grossly exaggerated and wrong. I'd like to know what kind of life you'd lead as a critic if the institutional theatre did not exist.

RC: I'd lead a dreary life. You said yourself, about a year ago, that you thought all three of the institutional theatres had got to a stage where they were very predictable.

PH: Yes, I agree. I still do. I think everybody is looking for new paths. I don't expect that I'll find it and I don't expect anyone'll recognise I've found it until we're in that new building. I believe that the National must have a repertoire of plays which mean something to the moment--in other words I don't think there's much virtue in having a repertoire of classic revivals for scholastic or representational reasons or to show that we've all got a catholic taste. I think that you've got to believe that the repertoire should represent the collective obsessions of the actors and directors who are working in the National Theatre because they believe that the play will speak to their audiences. Our theme seasons in the Lyttelton will investigate areas of the repertoire which are entirely neglected.

RC: Which areas?

PH: Well, German expressionist drama is totally unknown in this country. It's just something we pay lip service to. I would think twice about doing a Toller play or a Kaiser play in the Olivier repertoire, but if I was going to do three of them together for a short season in the Lyttelton called German Expressionist Drama, with a few films at the NFT of German expressionism, some pictures in the foyers and a few talks about German expressionism, one could get something going. A further responsibility is obviously new writing and that will come from the writers who want to write for us. Pinter is there, he's an Associate Director. I hope he will write for us. We've commissioned plays from Howard Brenton and from David Hare of the younger dramatists, and all the heavyweight dramatists have been asked if they would like to write a play for the new National Theatre. They may or they may not. That's up to them.

RC: Let's keep for a moment to the idea of what the plays you yourself personally want to do as a Director. Do you feel very differently about that from what you did, say, when you were directing the RSC?

PH: Oh yes, because when I was in the RSC I was more than anything passionately concerned with Shakespeare and there are a number of plays I very much want to do, but they are not in the centre of my preoccupations at this moment. I would very much like to do Ibsen, and I'm going to try and do John Gabriel Borkman at the end of this year. Obviously if Pinter or Beckett write anymore I would hope that I would be involved because they speak to me and I feel very deeply about them.

RC: I made a joke about terminal theatre in The Observer, because I felt that it's a long way from The Wars of the Roses to All Over. I mean that's the direction in which you've been travelling. Are you conscious of this?

PH: No, I'm not actually. Do you think it's getting more depressive?

RC: Well I do, I think what I was actually on to was that your work is getting smaller.

PH: I can offset that by saying that I think the most important piece of work for me that I've done in the last few years was the Monteverdi Ulysses at Glyndebourne, which was a piece of epic theatre. That's why I want to do Tamburlaine in the Olivier. I find Borkman an epic play which starts small and opens up. It starts on a sofa and ends with the world.

RC: You've never done Ibsen before.

PH: No, never. Why I'm attracted to Borkman is precisely that sense of the iris opening out--you start in a claustrophobic tiny room and end on the mountain top looking at the world. In my mind it connects with Tamburlaine actually. On the other hand, I'm doing Beckett's Happy Days which is extremely terminal, I must agree. As a director, I would like to do farce, I've never done farce. I think I need it. I think I need the anarchy of farce, and the vigour of farce. But I think once I went into Opera, my theatre work tended to become more and more concerned with the head of a pin in a way, Pinter and Albee--very, very detailed. I left the larger gestures to the opera world. Well, I won't say I've finished with opera, but obviously opera is not going to play much part in my life in the next few years, but large emblematic statements of theatre like Tamburlaine I'm very keen to do. I'm very keen also to try and bring back some rhetoric, not in a pejorative sense, to classical acting. When I have to stand up and be counted I do think that the contribution of the RSC, which I was partly responsible for, was the reconsideration of what Shakespeare's verse meant intellectually and what its ambiguities were; how you spoke it wittily and lightly and quickly. I'm proud of all that. I think that was something that's made a mark. But the converse of it produced by its strength, is perhaps 300 actors who are extremely intellectual in their approach to Shakespeare in danger of being insufficiently physical and emotional.

RC: Isn't a National Theatre in a tricky position when another company has the first right to the national dramatist?

PH: I don't think so, there are 37 plays. The Stratford tradition is something which I honour and obviously have a terrific love for, and it will go on because the Stratford festival will go on. I believe that the National Shakespeare is going to take a little time to emerge. I know what it is and what we intend to do, but I'm not going to tell you because it has got to happen, not be talked about. We're not in competition with the RSC in any kind of "Hands off Hamlet" spirit.

RC: The National's Shakespeare has after all had 10 years to emerge already.

PH: Yes, but you see one of the interesting things about that is that they haven't done enough Shakespeare.

RC: That's one thing I'm getting at, they haven't done enough.

PH: Well I think we will do quite a lot but in different terms to the RSC situation. You're pushing me, and I don't want to be pushed. But I mean I take your point that the National can't ignore Shakespeare or it can't say "Thank God we don't have to do Shakespeare, there's the RSC", because actually inescapably the centre of our theatre tradition, whether you like it or not (and I do), is Shakespeare.

RC: Well, I wouldn't be interested in the theatre if it wasn't for Shakespeare.

PH: Nor would I, nor would I, you know, but on the other hand I would hate to run a theatre again whose main external purpose was Shakespeare. If you've got to do six plays a year they come round with great regularity.

RC: I'm beginning to find as a critic that's not true of just Shakespeare.

PH: You're not seeing enough Shakespeare?

RC: No, I'm seeing quite enough Shakespeare. I'm also seeing enough of a certain number of other classics. I don't know how big the classic repertoire is outside it. I find it quite significant that the Actors Company this year are doing two plays that the National have already done, one of them pretty recently. I do sometimes worry about there being too many companies, too many institutional or semi-institutional theatres chasing too few plays and too few actors.

PH: Yes, I worry about that too and it seems to me that one of the things that the National has got to do is broaden the repertoire. By looking, looking out, out, out. We've got to German expressionism, but we've got to do Marivaux.

RC: I'm glad you said that.

PH: Right, we just must. I mean we will of course have little help from the critics who are very stick in the mud as far as looking at the past repertoire is concerned.

RC: I would take that personally very badly indeed.

PH: There's too much received opinion trotted out. Too much of a feeling that if it's old, it must be boring. The reception of Spring Awakening was generally very good and the audience response has been splendid, it's packed and all that and there's a lot of young people there, because I think with reason young people find it a play which is about authority over the young, you know; but so many critics simply said "In this permissive age, who needs a play about sexual liberation", which is exactly like saying "In an age where countries are not ruled by hereditary monarchs, who needs Hamlet". I mean that's really not the issue.

RC: I quite agree, but I think one reason why they've been driven towards it is a feeling shared within the profession itself. Are we all a bit too hung up on relevance.

PH: I think we are. That's the cant of the last 10 years which has hardened into a kind of dogma.

RC: Do you find anything odd in the idea of writers like Trevor Griffiths or David Hare writing for an institutional theatre representing a society to which they are fundamentally opposed?

PH: Well, who says that these institutions represent their society in that sense. I feel certainly that I'm running a theatre which is supported by the society that I live in at this moment. But the society is not telling me what I shall do and shall not do. I had a great argument with Trevor, who I'm very fond of and think very highly of, not very long ago when he said to me "Yes, I'll maybe give you the play after next, but I'm not going to give you the next play because it wouldn't be good for you, you wouldn't do it." And I said that is the biggest bloody impertinence. If you say I won't do it, you are turning me into the sort of theatre that you want to turn me into and you're not giving me the chance to be anything else. Now why will I not do it? And he said, well you wouldn't it would be too controversial. I said well you're frightened I'll say yes, and it would then upset your dogma. We had a terrific carry on. It was good. If a dramatist is absolutely seeking to change his society, it seems to me he can decide either to use the institutional theatre in order to get the message across, or not. It's up to him isn't it, not up to me. But certainly this particular runner of an institutional theatre is not going to silence argument or controversy or unpopular opinion. I won't. Obviously there's going to be a good deal of this sort of discussion and argument. The last thing I want the National to do is to trendily run after the most insulting and revolutionary dramatists and do them in a desperate attempt to show that we are broadminded. I really think that would be odious in the extreme.

RC: How broad would you say your tastes were?

PH: I think they are getting a little broader. I managed to get through the period at the RSC without doing a single restoration play. As I was leaving we did The Relapse. Restoration drama has been for me for years something insignificant. Now I'm beginning to understand it. I must say for many years I have thought of Shaw as a sexless pamphleteer with very little passion. Over the last years I've been re-reading and re-thinking Shaw very much and I want to do a Shaw play very much now. Where the boundaries of my own taste lie, I don't know, they change a great deal. I suppose that I could be seen as a working class scholarship Cambridge-warped, media-altered, lefty trendy child of the 'sixties and that's my period, I suppose. But I refute that, I'm beginning again. The excitement of the 'seventies for me, is going to the National. I feel all sorts of new currents in myself. I'm excited at the prospect of working again in a theatre which must be part of the community. So I won't be labelled: it makes me indignant.
1974-08-04-turgenev-s-duets:
Turgenev's duets

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

TURGENEV'S A Month in the Country begins with a tableau: on one side of the stage three old people playing cards; on the other two young ones, a man reading and a woman embroidering.

In fact, the age distinction is not that clear-cut; two of the card players might fairly claim to be still only middle-aged, while their opposite numbers--he 30 and she 29--are already resigned to having lost their youth. This is a world where--psychologically, at any rate--age comes early and youth suffers. As the play proceeds we are introduced to two characters who are unequivocally young, and it becomes plain that this country-house society has no place for them. They are cast out.

Since the Chichester Festival Theatre has an open stage, the director, Toby Robertson, is unable to have his opening group discovered; instead he brings them on, formally, to music, so striking a satiric note which dominates the entire production. For the play revolves around Natalya Petrovna, the self-consciously languid lady of the house. She is more than something of a poseuse; so much the dialogue makes clear, but clarity becomes transparency when we see Dorothy Tutin, radiantly bored, walk on stage and scrupulously arrange herself in a becoming position.

A glass of water is proffered: she graciously sips it. The profferer is Rakitin, for four years her admirer, but no more than that: as he puts it, "I'm no Don Juan, I'm sorry to say." Miss Tutin knows exactly how to administer the degree of mild torment that will keep him in leading-strings. When she mentions that she has engaged a new tutor, and that he is young, she makes it sound like a comment on their own premature decay. She can render affection infinitely condescending. Taking Rakitin's hand, and addressing him as "My old friend," she reassures him that "it's only the good things we can have too much of."

In fact Natalya ends up losing most of the good things. Rakitin, not altogether of his own volition, finally forsakes her; she persuades herself that she is in love--at last--with the young tutor and he too has to leave; though not before Natalya has jealously and calculatingly manoeuvred her ward--aged 17 and a potential rival--into marriage with a fat, stupid landowner of 48.

This is a play largely composed of duologues, and Miss Tutin, presenting a narcissist desperate for contact but incapable of it, excels in them. She advances, feints, withdraws with consummate skill. And yet, somewhere, somehow, monotony creeps in. The fault, I think, is Turgenev's. He eventually gave up the theatre for the novel, convinced that he could not construct a play. In some respects he was too hard on himself; the play tells its story subtly, the scenes have their own momentum. But three-quarters of the way through the evening the abundance of two-handed scenes creates a log-jam. The characters--and the cast is large--queue up for their moments; some simply vanish. (Compare Chekhov, in some respects Turgenev's pupil, who knew how to keep his minor figures active and relevant.) These are hardly insufferable faults, but they glare quite ferociously on a frameless stage. Events at Chichester simply happen; a director can hardly hope to impose a shape.

He can of course impose a tone. There are occasions in this play when soliloquy sets in; these are heralded at Chichester by a sharpening of the lights and the distant sound of a horn, a near relation of the clarion employed at this theatre to summon the audience back from the bars. The monologue then proceeds, backed by mood music, which is likely--given the cynical mind of your contemporary playgoer--less to reinforce the speech than to undercut it. We are in fact invited to smile at the characters' self-dramatisation. This fits Miss Tutin's characterisation perfectly, but it seems ludicrously inappropriate when applied to John Turner as her honest unimaginative husband and a grave handicap to Derek Jacobi as Rakitin. Being short Mr Jacobi is apt to forfeit attention when not actually doing anything, and in his early scenes Rakitin does virtually nothing. One wonders why Natalya keeps him on, even as a butt.

Later, when suffering drives him to unclench his teeth and loose his accumulated bitterness, Mr Jacobi is very good. Natalya--in that charming way she has of delivering a compliment as if it were a rebuke--calls him "Mr Observer," but that title truly belongs (and the critic of this journal should surely be allowed to bestow it) to Timothy West's doctor, despising the household on which he battens and grimly aware that the feeling is returned. Narrowing his eyes he surveys the pack of them while ostensibly gazing into the distance; asked if he is staying to dinner he replies "If I may" with the respectful confidence of the accustomed freeloader. He is also extremely funny.

  

The Two Noble Kinsmen (Regent's Park), believed to be the joint work of Shakespeare and Fletcher, treats, like A Midsummer Night's Dream, of the delayed nuptials of Theseus and Hippolyta. While they hang about waiting for wedlock, two gallants, Palamon and Arcite, fall for the same girl and descend from courtly sentiment to mere squabbling. At length, after many vicissitudes--notably the death of Arcite--Palamon's pre-eminence ("I saw her first") is established and rewarded.

This, considering the omens, is in the nature of a surprise ending: on the eve of their last combat Arcite, praying to Mars, had been rewarded by a most impressive thunderclap; Palamon, taking Venus as his patroness, had been granted only a swarm of balloons. (The text actually calls for doves, but the director presumably felt the need of a laugh at this point; that at any rate is what he got.) The play calls out for a high fantastic style, as of the Royal Shakespeare Company at their most ceremonious; the approach in the Park oscillates between the raucous and the artlessly conversational. There is a bouncy jailer's daughter who, as has been the way of jailers' daughters down the ages, arranges the escape of her daddy's handsomest prisoner; she skips around a good deal, is condemned to deliver her best speech from impossibly far upstage and eventually goes mad, but were she to quieten down a bit she might be nice to know.
1974-08-11-young-lovers-of-verona:
Young lovers of Verona

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

LAST WEEK I saw a junior delegation from the National Theatre performing Romeo and Juliet in Harrogate. This week they will be at it in Ilminster and Exeter; and subsequently elsewhere.

Most of the young sprigs involved were first seen at the Old Vic this year in The Tempest as strange, and generally hideous, Shapes. They were first heard--at some length--in Spring Awakening; having mutely supported their elders in Shakespeare, they were supported by them in Wedekind's tragedy of maimed adolescence. In Romeo, most of the senior actors have vanished entirely. Here finally is the teen-and-twenty Verona for which the times so obviously clamour.

Hello, young lovers, you're
all under age,
And few of you are alive,
Wedekind only killed two of
his kids;
Shakespeare has finished off
five.

(Romeo, Juliet, Mercutio, Tybalt, Paris: count 'em.)

Well, the National have all these youngsters around; they made an uneven showing in Spring Awakening, but several of them are known to be talented, and there are not many plays in the repertoire to suit them. Have we not always known Romeo to be a tragedy, not merely of youth but of childhood, and have we not always lamented the maturity which our theatre has habitually lavished on it unasked? It seems, though, that we overlooked something. Consider.

Younger than you, says Lady Capulet, urging her 13-year-old onto the dance-floor and into the marriage bed, are made already mothers. The statistics of teenage maternity may be soaring but we have still to recapture that degree of social tolerance; not merely tolerance, but endorsement. Shakespeare emphasises Juliet's age at her first appearance, and then drops the subject. He does not seem to have felt it to be too much of an issue. But the precocious casting of Bill Bryden's production makes it the issue.

We are well aware that Veronica Quilligan, who plays Juliet here (and there, and everywhere, this being a Mobile Production), is a credible 13; indeed, in a kindly light she might pass for 12. So we become preoccupied less with the depth of Juliet's passion than with its piquancy; the more so since piquancy seems at this moment all that Miss Quilligan has to offer. Taking the production on its own terms we can agree that she looks right: gleeful or apprehensive as required. But, if we are concerned with naturalistic consistency, she would also have to sound right; and in fact she stresses nearly every line wrong. Some she stresses not at all; they slide uninflected into the wings.

I am not insisting on verbal music. Peter Firth, who plays Romeo, is no great melodist either, but he displays a startling ability to weight the words so that they will support a characterisation. (I call it startling since I am one of those who sneakily doubted Mr Firth's ability to redeem the promise he showed in Equus. A year from now I shall probably feel similarly shamefaced about Miss Quilligan.) He comes upon the scene a sulky self-absorbed 16. When he asks, "Is the day so young?" he is believably, indeed archetypally, the adolescent who doesn't know what time it is. For much of the play he remains the "boy" of Tybalt's taunt; never more so than when hounding his tormentor to death. He is called "man" by those who wish to stand well with him (his chums Mercutio and Benvolio, with their own insecure pretensions to maturity) or to shame him out of himself; this is the tactic of the Nurse and Friar when faced with the ground-battering hysteria that follows his banishment, an hysteria explicitly demanded by the text, shirked or muffed by most actors, but enthusiastically rendered by Mr Firth. He gives us some taste of his manhood early on--notably in his foreboding on the way to the ball--and attains it where he should; in his defiance of the stars.

Good Romeos are rare; and here at least Mr Bryden's emphasis on adolescence has paid off. His intelligence is never in doubt; he frequently illuminates the text, though he rarely sparks it. Marginal benefits in an uncomfortably cast are Gerard Ryder's resentful clown and a pleasantly embarrassed Benvolio from Michael Kitchen (who takes over as Romeo in September when Mr Firth goes to Broadway for the re-mounting of Equus); major ones are Peter Needham's magisterial Friar, and Beryl Reid's slow, sly Nurse.

  

I was much disappointed by the Low Moan Spectacular in Bullshot Crummond (Hampstead), having been convulsed by their El Coca Cola Grande two years ago. That benefited from hilarious mime and words that always hovered a few feet away from recognisable English. This time the Low Moaners' movements remain snappy, but their script and its performance struck me as laboured, gaining momentum only in the last 15 minutes. The show is, of course, a parody of the Bulldog Drummond books, and had I read any of them I might have laughed much more. As it was I felt the basic joke had been assumed rather than established.

  

On the other hand, I was a pushover for The Count of Monte Cristo Shaw (Theatre Workshop), which is not a parody at all but an extraordinarily inclusive rendering of the original, adorned, but by no means obscured, by the usual Stratford East curlicues. Prominent among these are a couple of luscious singing birds, and an enthusiastic audience. The night I went we were very good, but we deserved to be much bigger.
1974-08-18-desperate-lives:
Desperate lives

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on "Stallerhof," "Bingo" and the Beatles

The event of the week should have been the arrival in London of Edward Bond's Bingo (Royal Court), first seen in Exeter last year, but it has been overshadowed for me by a German play, Stallerhof, which has been at the Bush, and reopens this week at the Pool in Edinburgh, as a lunchtime offering on the Festival fringe.

It is the work of a young writer, Franz Xaver Kroetz, and it recalls Mr Bond's Saved in the spareness, frequently contracting into silence, of its dialogue and the brute (which is not to say brutal) realism of its action; we are shown characters living at the extremest edge of social and emotional deprivation. An ageing farmworker couples with his employer's spastic daughter, and gets her pregnant. Her parents' reaction is disgust: but then that has been their reaction to her throughout her life. When her mother describes her as "backward," the word is at worst an accusation; at best, this being a religious family, the acceptance of a cross.

The dramatist's satiric emphasis on Bavarian Catholicism is perhaps the play's weakest point; it leads him to conventionalise the presentation of the parents. He has little to say about farmers other than that he is a tyrant embittered by puritanism and poverty. As facts these are not disputable, but there is no surprise in them, and the man behaves strictly according to plan when he sourly dismisses the employee who has made him a grandfather.

His wife fares more interestingly. Declaring her intention to wash her daughter's filthiness away the same way it went in, she prepares, with a hosepipe and a pail of soapy water, to administer an abortion. It seems that she will go through with it, and certainly in a play which has already presented us, graphically but quite calmly and unsensationally, with defecation, masturbation and intercourse, there seems no aesthetic reason why she should not. But she draws back, respecting the girl's humanity, for perhaps the first time in her life.

Starkness is not in itself a guarantee of quality; to strip a scene of obvious emotion can be as short a cut to impressing an audience as striking up "Hearts and Flowers." Occasionally I suspected that David Mouchtar-Samurai's extraordinarily measured production was attempting to hypnotise us into admiration. But behind the evenness lies an infinity of concentration, most of all in the scenes between Celia Quicke as the retarded Beppi and Bill Stewart as her seducer. Is it in fact seduction? Is it rape? Maybe it qualifies as love. The man proceeds on the apparent assumption that the girl will not understand what is happening to her; and initially perhaps that is the truth. There is certainly little physical pleasure for her; but if part of her is an automaton, dropping her knickers whenever her partner approaches, a fragment is an awakened human being. Miss Quicke's performance, filtering emotional half-tones through incoherent murmurs and earnest bespectacled blinks, is uncanny. She is used, abused and yet, at the core, untouchable. She put me in mind of the first great tragedy of the inarticulate (and, more than incidentally, another German work): Buchner's Woyzeck. Both, as it happens, contain crucial scenes in fairgrounds, a potent image of mechanical gaiety offsetting desperate lives.

There is a similar feeling to two speeches in Mr Bond's Bingo. A crazed old man shudders in memory through the merrymaking associated with a public hanging. Another man - who unfortunately for his own peace of mind is not crazed - recalls the ingenious horrors of bear-baiting. This second man is Shakespeare; and however marginal biography may have been to Mr Bond's conscious concerns, the play stands as the most convincing picture of a genius - certainly of this genius - achieved by a contemporary dramatist.

One reason for this is that he shows us genius, but not creativity. This is Shakespeare in retirement, the central figure, ironically enough, of another tragedy of inarticulacy. The irony is compounded by the casting of John Gielgud, the most eloquent of actors, who here achieves his finest effects in silence, as he tries to distance himself from the acquisitive cruelty which he once denounced from behind the mad mask of King Lear (the play depends a good deal on our awareness of this literary fact), and in which, as a Stratford burgher, he is now acquiescing. Allegorically this is a most moving performance, for who in our time has been closer to Shakespeare than Gielgud? Naturalistically, it fails to convince; it is Shakespeare taken at his own valuation - as a man superior to avarice - rather than at Mr Bond's. It is a static performance, as melancholic at the beginning as at the end, and it thereby underlines the main flaw in the play, an impressive still life rather than a developing drama.

Jane Howell's production, still excessively low-keyed, has gained some good performances since its premiere in Exeter; most notably there is Arthur Lowe's Ben Jonson. Mr Lowe, with his uniquely inconsequential timing, could get a laugh on almost any line; the house expects it of him and he obliges, then stills the tumult with the declaration: "I hate. A short, hard word. Begins with a hiss and ends with a spit."

The London theatre is getting very chummy with its songwriters. The Mermaid has "Cole." Now at the Lyric are John, Paul, George, Ringo and Bert, who stayed behind in Liverpool, a happily dedicated fan, while the fab four were making it all over the world, and was finally disillusioned by their disillusion. All that money and success and London (Bingo). What, one wonders, will happen to the creators of this show, which also comes to us from Liverpool? To be honest, Bert might well have been left on Merseyside a second time; he must have meant more there. George Costigan, who plays him, gets on excellent terms with the audience, but his story interrupts that of the Beatles. Or vice versa.
1974-08-25-a-magnificent-hypocrite:
A magnificent hypocrite

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN
on 'Tartuffe' at the
Edinburgh Festival

MOLIERE took several risks in writing Tartuffe. His satire on religious poseurs and their dupes offended vested interests, which for a time at least succeeded in keeping the play off the boards and the playwright behind bars. To us, though, these liberties are trifling compared to the licence he took in keeping his principal character offstage for the first two of five acts.

Encore l'audace. Peter James, in his production for the Actors Company, keeps Tartuffe in the wings--if the gaunt, earthbound platform stage of the Assembly Hall can be said to have wings--for two acts and a 20-minute interval. For the entire first half of the show we are offered Tartuffe without the Hypocrite and sometimes without very much else either.

It takes nerve, in any case, to offer this play in this environment; not so much because of the place's ecclesiastical associations (God may not be mocked, but what of John Knox?) as because of its frightful acoustics, and yet more dreadful sightlines. (I may have got that the wrong way round.) It may be a great place for pageants and chronicles--the best thing I ever saw there was Richard II--but it bears hard on more civilised pastimes like comedy.

Nor is the situation improved if players and director simply attempt--as might initially seem reasonable--to conquer by sheer vigour. Tartuffe begins with a family row, which in Mr James's production is spread so thin and shouted so loud that I almost despaired of the evening ahead. Only when Sheila Burrell's black-lace Welsh widow came off the rampage, slowed down and summoned her forces for a concentrated lecture did I feel any confidence.

You may be able to bombast out a blank verse but you cannot rant a rhyming couplet. The form, if ingeniously retained in Richard Wilbur's translation which, it is pleasing to note, has attracted fewer sneers this year than when it was aired some time ago by the National Theatre; but it is not, of course, a mode of expression to which most British actors are accustomed. There are a couple of players in this company--one melodious Robert Eddison, or agile Edward Petherbridge--sufficiently smooth-tongued to wrap themselves around Mr Wilbur's phrases and still have energy to spare. But the majority are less nimble and need time to stand still and collect themselves.

When they do, the results are most gratifying. I think of Sharon Duce pleading earnestly with her father not to marry her to Tartuffe, and of Windsor Davies's surly response. Earlier Mr Davies hits a nicely unassertive basso note on his Orgon with his moved reiterated "Poor fellow" as Tartuffe's gluttonies and complacencies are unavailingly recounted to him. This, alas, is all the compliment I can bestow on this actor, whose performance has already, I see, been critically described as "bearish." If I could show you the jottings on my programme, I could prove to you that the same adjective had occurred, quite independently, to me. As it is, you will just have to take my word for it, together with my assurance that it constitutes a monotonous drag on the play.

Mr Davies sounds less Welsh than his supposed mother, Miss Burrell, but Mr James sees the entire family as aspiring provincials in Paris. There being no obvious social difference in this production between the family and their servant Dorine, her domination of them is robbed of its comic point. Hers is, as Mr James says, "the best part ever written for a maid" but Paola Dionisotti makes surprisingly little of it. She, more than most, gets lost in the uproar. Sheila Reid, however, endows Elmire with more wit and poise than she has ever shown before; and rises, red-haired and delectable, to her encounter with Tartuffe.

We have arrived at length--as the play does--at Charles Kay's gleaming, beaming protagonist; and if the production's greatest power lies in its moments of stillness they are multiplied tenfold whenever he is on the stage. He is stillness; one can see why Orgon takes him for a saint. An audience, marvelling at his presence, may feel impelled to offer similar devotion before reflecting that a man so completely in control of himself could only be a charlatan.

I have sometimes imagined a Tartuffe in whom there was no clear demarcation between sincerity and falsehood; who might, like Shakespeare's Angelo, half-believe in his own sanctity and occasionally despise himself for his lust. Maybe this is fanciful; certainly it is not Mr Kay's Tartuffe, whose every passion has been sublimated within his assumed persona. Moliere's strategy here--simple but immensely powerful--was to devise situations increasingly outrageous, while exempting their supposed originator not merely from compunction but from any hint of surprise. Mr Kay, seraphically glowing beneath the gold wig and matching spectacles, meets the challenge magnificently; nothing fazes, nothing throws him.

Awarded the deeds to his benefactor's house, he betrays his satisfaction by no more than a raised eyebrow; his hands stay devotionally clasped. Finally, very swiftly, he surveys the stage (for this scene Geoffrey Scott's handsome outdoor set has unexpectedly sprouted some wrought iron work which it shortly mysteriously sheds). But in that one look he takes possession. Seducing Elmire he glides noiselessly between professions of piety, of love, of contempt for her husband. (Mr Wilbur's couplets gild and undercut his sophistries simultaneously.) Here, Mr James turns the garden setting memorably to account; echoes from Eden sound as Elmire tempts Tartuffe with grapes, and they ring out as he returns to claim her, draped in satanic red. That an actor could be at once so unassuming and so majestic; the paradox persists, exhilaratingly and disturbingly right to the end of the play.

The production is an achievement, if an uneven one. Notice how rapidly--in the wake of the National's Misanthrope--we have come to expect as much proficiency from English Moliere as English Chekhov. The various companies will now please line up and offer us The School for Wives and Don Juan. After that they may proceed to Marivaux, beginning with Les fausses confidences.

  

At the Haymarket Icerink the Young Lyceum Company offer Sean McCarthy's The Fantastical Feats of Finn MacCool, he being a mythical celtic giant here cut--in the sturdy and subdued form of Tony Haygarth--very much down to size. The show is sustained by spectacle (Jeananne Crowley gives a magical, darting performance as a faun) and one or two of the jokes are as good as the title; but the overall tone--as of a jeering, pedantic pantomime--often grates.
1974-09-01-going-to-the-devil:
Going to the devil

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN reports from the Edinburgh Festival

MARLOWE'S Doctor Faustus is a rather shifty play, but if you can manage to look it straight in the eye you may be able to obtain from it a straight and extremely orthodox answer to the old question about the profits accruing to those who gain the world and lose their souls. The answer is, of course, that it profiteth them not at all.

This at least is the moral punched out at the end of the play: "Faustus is dead, regard his hellish fall" and do not be so impious as to seek forbidden knowledge. A dramatist committed to this treatment of the legend faces a tricky problem, not unlike that confronting Faustus himself: how to while away the time between initial commitment to the devil and ultimate damnation? It is a problem which Marlowe notoriously failed to solve.

The middle sections of the play are traditionally, and quite legitimately, dismissed as buffoonery. They show Faustus exercising his magic powers to ingratiate himself with neighbouring potentates or to play practical jokes, or both. It seems, on the face of it, rather a poor price to get for one's soul; but there is a self-congratulatory note about the writing of these scenes, thin as they are, which prevents one from assuming that this is necessarily what Marlowe meant.

Besides, we are told--though inevitably not shown--that Faustus also engaged in headier pastimes, driving through the heavens in dragon-drawn chariots. The higher they ride, the further they fall; and when the end is damnation (whether envisaged as an eternity of roasting, or more subtly as permanent exile from grace--again the play is undecided) the most exalted fancies are liable to look like meaningless pranks. Whatever Faustus does with the middle of his life, or Marlowe with the middle of his play, the upshot would be the same, but this thought is not much consolation to us while we are watching, even if we can believe that the play has whole-heartedly accepted it.

John Barton, directing his own adaptation at the Lyceum (and this week at the Aldwych), has added his own complications. He employs the play's diabolic trinity--Lucifer, Beelzebub and Mephistophilis--to speak the Chorus of the original text; in their mouths its traditional exhortations and moralisings sound decidedly wry. The intention may have been only to provide an ironic frisson; but if taken seriously it suggests that the whole moral system which Faustus transgresses is diabolically controlled.

But on this matter, as on much else, the play is inconsistent; and the most satisfying passages are certainly those which assume that the hero's fall is essentially his own work.

Mr Barton--himself no marvel of consistency on this occasion--reinforces this view with his presentation of the Good and Bad Angels who give explicit utterance to the protagonist's internal struggle. They are reduced to a couple of silent glove-puppets; Faustus himself appropriates their lines. The resulting dialectic puts an added edge on Ian McKellen's performance, which is pretty well barbed to begin with; profiting from the prologue's reference to his parents as "base of stock," Mr McKellen presents a thrusting arriviste scholar whom ambition has propelled to the top of every faculty in Wittenberg, and who now finds himself satiated and a little disgusted. He has perforce gone short on sensual pleasures, and it is for these as much as anything that he turns to the devil. In fact they do nothing to alleviate his distemper; his increasing sourness becomes the binding thread of the production. Only at the end is he seriously disappointing, employing vocal tricks which include the rendition of "O, I'll leap up to my God" as a practicable bright idea.

Emrys James adds a chilling imperturbable Mephistophilis to his fine line of theatrical fiends: there is a remarkable sureness about his colloquies with Mr McKellen. For this, perhaps, Mr Barton may be held responsible; a surpassing feeling for the space around, rather than between, Elizabethan words has generally distinguished his Shakespeare productions, and it is now obvious that he could help us all to deal with the other dramatists of the period.

The supporting playing--though Denis Holmes and Terence Wilton speak sturdily for the lower orders--is generally dull. There is a far more even acting level in the Actors' Company production of Euripides's The Bacchae (Assembly Hall), though its peaks are a good deal less exalted. The company deserve our thanks for letting us hear William Arrowsmith's tersely exciting translation (one of the brilliant Chicago versions which have languished on the shelves while our directors have sported with inferior models) whose economy is echoed in Edward Petherbridge's direction.

The bones of the play are there but they remain bare; the evening is gripping but never disturbing. On two occasions the production bit into my nerve-ends: when Charles Kay recounted the butchery of Pentheus (they played with scraps of his body) and when Sheila Burrell as Agave cradling her son's head was wrenched out of frenzy into a recognition of ultimate horror: "I feel as though my mind was somehow changing." The production works hard at establishing the bi-sexual tension between Dionysus and Pentheus, but the effort is more notable than the result.

Robin Ellis's Pentheus is gallant, but he only realises the full possibilities of drag in the afterpiece, a mimed version of Jack and the Beanstalk in which he plays Dame, walking with a pained and careful delicacy as if suffering from mild indigestion. This entertainment, sometimes coy, often delightful, features juggling, home musicianship, and a wholly entrancing interlude of shadow-puppetry, culminating in the cutting off of the giant's head. (Decapitation is the evening's unifying theme.)

This has been a festival full of notable acting: Mr Kay's Tartuffe, Mr McKellen's Faustus, and matching if not overtopping them Sven Wollter's electrically temperamental portrayal of Strindberg's Gustav III, presented by the Gothenburg City Theatre. On the fringe there has been Fulton Mackay's delicate double performance in McGonagall and the Murder at the Pool; John Spurling's study of two men differently obsessed by the image of Queen Victoria was a little infirm in establishing its premise and occasionally dilatory in developing it, but haunting and ingenious none the less. Mr Spurling has the expected fun with McGonagall's verse-forms; though he depends far less on pastiche than does Richard Crane in The Quest, presented by the Bradford University Group at Lauriston Hall.

I cannot see that The Quest reverberates much beyond the Arthurian myths of which it treats; but it approaches them with great buoyancy, and builds them into a remarkably stable structure. It is given a superb production by Chris Parr, the audience seated in two opposing ranks, as if watching a tournament: the best battle I have seen on any stage.
1974-09-29-lament-for-a-little-night-mus:
Lament for a 'Little Night Music'

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN casts a gloomy eye over the commercial theatre scene.

AFTER three weeks away I glance casually down the theatre lists and am horrified. I have never felt inclined to storm at the endless succession of West End farcical comedies; I see them one at a time, shrug, forget, and go on to other things. But I must acknowledge that the plays themselves refuse to follow my amiable example; they stay around, accumulate, taking up space.

The unsubsidised theatre currently offers a few things that are recommendable: two first-class revivals, a mass of plays by Alan Ayckbourn. There are also a couple of borderline musicals; "Billy" at any rate sleek, "The Good Companions" at any rate engaging. And with these modest virtues it seems we shall have to live, this week having brought the gloomy news that the London production of "A Little Night Music" has been cancelled.

The management were probably right in thinking that this musical would lose money; if it would be depressing to think that we are currently being given the theatre we deserve, it is hardly less so to reflect that we are getting the only theatre we can afford. The loss of "A Little Night Music" (as of its predecessor "Follies," a magnificent piece of stagecraft which has never even been announced for London) deprives us of the work of major talents: of Harold Prince, a fine if uneven director; of the superlative designer Boris Aronson; of Glynis Johns, whose frayed, affecting singing of "Send in the Clowns" could hardly be imagined by anyone who has not heard the song in context; and of Stephen Sondheim, whose music, and above all his lyrics, proclaim him the most important writer now active in the American theatre. No playwright can match him for wit, insight, irony or felicity of expression. Set in a high-comedy Sweden (and based on an Ingmar Bergman film), the show lacks the Manhattan bite of "Company" or "Follies"; an intermittent, uncomfortable sense of every one on their best behaviour trying to be stylish and European communicated itself to several of the performers in New York. For this very reason, though, it would have been fascinating to see it played by a British cast. Perhaps it is time for musicals (the few good ones) to move out of the private sector; "Follies" would have looked well in a World Theatre Season, and "A Little Night Music" might even be the musical that the National Theatre have coquetted so long with producing.

Why not? Over at the Aldwych bursts of good song have much enlivened the Royal Shakespeare productions of "The Bewitched" and "Travesties." Indeed, songwriters and musicians have contributed much to the London stage this year. "Cole" at the Mermaid is more or less of a delight; the Beatles play at the Lyric is (I realise with surprise) almost the best new play around, fragmentary but rueful, tough and acidulous like the music it celebrates. At the Mayfair--unless he has radically changed his act since I saw it a couple of years ago--John Gould is providing understated, bespectacled fun at and around a piano; and I believe all the good that I have heard of Sammy Cahn. And, saving the face of the West End this week, there is show business.

More or less to the tune (omnipresent at the moment) of "That's Entertainment" a toothy quintet called Dallas Boys, closing the first half of The Ken Dodd Laughter Show (Palladium), announce that "the stage is the place to see a real live show," thereby giving the lie to the rest of their act, which is a celebration of television. Presumably the aim is to make the audience feel at home--though home is precisely where they have paid a great deal of money not to be. Nobody, however, could feel at home in Mr Dodd's outlandish presence; we feel at ease (there's a phrase he could do something with), but that is quite different.

For a man who tells so many jokes (and never a one mistimed) he is surprisingly independent of the telly as a source of material. Nor does he merely bombard us with bad jokes, hoping that they and he will escape in the confusion. Many of his observations are original, perhaps profound; few others, confronted by a real and ham pie, would gaze at the egg in the middle and muse (it is of necessity a very quick muse) on the cleverness of some hens. Two surprising facts about Mr Dodd: he has not, except on his frequent ascents into falsetto, a very individual voice and, alone among our major clowns, his act is free of hidden aggression. (There is plenty of overt aggression, but it is harmless.) He seems very good-natured, free of the desperation of Max Wall, the scorn of Frankie Howerd or the off-hand humiliation that Morecambe inflicts on Wise. These are all comics whom I prefer, but this week at the Palladium (first house Wednesday, which is all I have so far seen) Mr Dodd would not have missed.

The Turning Point (Duke of York's) I saw, and the second half I actually did. I was driven away by the embarrassment of hearing the protagonist continually exclaim how stock the situation is. There is, as if the admission made them any better. The author, Francoise Dorin, is French, but the play has been anglicised. (One character is called Roderick Timms-Taylor.) David Tomlinson directs, and plays--seemingly in one continuous woebegone sentence--the leading role. He more or less survives, but his colleagues can only beat the empty air. The play concerns the conflict between boulevard drama, of whose decadence it is itself an uncomfortable specimen, and an avant-garde of which it seems spectacularly ignorant.

I particularly regretted this last deficiency, since a progressive bill at the Theatre at New End had put me in the mood for some good reactionary satire. We are given two pieces by Copi, an Argentinian playwright living in France. The curtain-raiser, The Four Twins, was done in Paris last year by Jorge Lavelli; it looked like spectacular rubbish, but in Hampstead the spectacle has departed. The main piece, Eva Peron, is an acrid cartoon of the lady's last day. It contains one arresting image--Eva, dying of cancer, is played by a man--and one effective twist. These are enough to stimulate interest in the playwright, but not in the play. Hatred might be able to fuel an entire evening, but contempt--of which this one is composed--exhausts itself in 10 minutes. Steven Darnell's direction is spruce; Cornelius Garnett is the best of the turns, and Murray Salem a haughty, muscular Eva.
1974-10-06-running-into-roadblocks:
Running into roadblocks

BEYOND the motorway The Freeway (Old Vic) lies in wait. By the uncertain future date at which Peter Nichols's new play is set, motorways (together with what are described with incredulous contempt as 'the old A roads') have been virtually abandoned by the progressive motorist; those who dare to use them are liable to become the prey of 'marauding lorry-drivers.'

The freeway, F1, which apparently runs the length of the country, north to south, is, nearly everyone agrees, the only way to travel. Such a consensus is, of course, liable to result in fearful traffic-jams, but probably, in the normal course of events, these would be philosophically accepted. Still, the particular jam which is the subject of this play would tax any philosopher; it stretches over 80 miles, and it lasts for three days.

It is also--and this is perhaps the most sinister thing about it--a symbol. In this it recalls Mr Nichols's earlier play, The National Health. Both titles set off reverberations which the author has been unable to resist exploiting, but which he has only sketchily followed through. Early on in the present piece someone speaks of 'the Free Way,' tentatively breaking up the syllables as if testing them for their weight-bearing capacity. By the end of the evening the metaphor is full-blown: a Minister of Movement has been brought on stage to inform the trapped and indignant travellers that the freeway is, in effect, their way of life. The dominion of the motor-car is what they voted for; if they wanted freedom, they now have (traffic conditions permitting) total liberty to drive to Scotland, the rest of Britain having been reduced to a gigantic by-pass.

The metaphor is neater than that of The National Health and I, a snug non-driver, found it reasonably convincing. It is not, though, dramatically interesting. There is no passion behind Mr Nichols's vision of the future, no real point of view, and not even very much indignation: just a generalised cynicism. It was possible during long passages of The National Health to forget the play's schematic pretensions and appreciate Mr Nichols's best features: his ear for dialogue (fully as acute as Harold Pinter's), his eye for realistic detail, his nose for character. An uncommitted satirist, he needs to fasten on a solidly contemporary situation. (When, as in Chez Nous earlier this year, he buttons down tight on an enclosed group, the result can be really memorable.) Futuristic fantasy loosens all the controls; he proves inventive in short bursts, never seeming to know where he is heading.

His main characters are the inhabitants of two adjacently stranded vehicles. From a huge and luxuriously appointed motor-caravan ('an Englishman's motor-home is his castle') there pour (oh, the irony) a Ford works supervisor and his family. From the small and battered car in front issue a peer, a close friend of the Prime Minister, and his fearsome mother. Forced into proximity the two groups are soon on first-name terms. For the time being they have much to offer each other. The workers have some food, some fuel, the expertise to repair his lordship's car, and--most important--a portable lavatory. The aristocrats have affability. The lady is admittedly reactionary (and makes several repetitive speeches to prove it), but she turns up trumps on the third day, when there is a baby to be delivered, rallying all the other girls to help. In the end, however, when the multitudes are ordered to walk home, she and her son are raised aloft to depart by helicopter. (How often have you seen gods getting into a machine?)

Mr Nichols pays acid tribute to the British class system (the play is not as futuristic as all that) but, though he may try hard to persuade himself, I doubt if he is really angered by it. This part of the play needs perhaps to be rewritten by Edward Bond; though he would probably have had his roadside castaways eating each other by the second act. Stretches of The Freeway are very funny, but it keeps running into road blocks. Some of these are the fault of the production; for its realisation the text demands clean technical virtuosity, the quality in which Jonathan Miller as a director is most notably deficient. A first act curtain, meant to be menacing, peters embarrassingly out; violence, though much talked of, conspicuously fails to impend. Some obstacles were hopefully peculiar to the first night, when the cast succumbed to hideous panic; nerves and memories collapsed. Subtracting the agony and adding a few days' worth of confidence, one can calculate several good performances.

Graham Crowden is all quizzical good-fellowship as the lord, bending over forwards (this being the angle at which Mr Crowden plays) to humour his inferiors; Rachel Kempson may be our stage's most terrifying gentlewoman, instinct with the insouciant vulgarity that only breeding can bestow. The caravan party is led by Paul Rogers, worryingly conscientious and so unobtrusively right that his full quality escaped me on the night, and only thudded home the following morning. Irene Handl is her good theatrical self as his wife; to her belongs the evening's most enchanting moment, as she recites a solid patch of 'Hiawatha', and its most hilarious when, tidying a monumentally messy grass verge, she tosses back on to it a piece of litter for which she takes no responsibility. Joan Hickson, as a predatory belle of the ballrooms, and Lionel Murton, as a visitor from Canada, warily play out the early stages of a courtship which the play proceeds to forget, though, as if in compensation, it bestows on Mr Murton the responsibility for a final curtain which is obviously significant and confusingly ill-prepared. Mark Dignam is unpersuasive as the Minister, but he is lumbered with the worst written scene.

  

Peter King's Away From It All (Terrace Theatre, ICA), is, I suppose, a serious comedy whose seriousness (amounting at times to tartness) worked better on a sparsely attended second night than its humour. The production seemed jerky, needing to be lubricated by laughter. This might make the play's technical contrivance (particularly as regards exits and entrances) a formal delight rather than an irritant. Zena Walker as an overworked wife is throatily enchanting (she always reminds me of Judi Dench, though historically she got there first) and her emotional generosity goes some way towards filling the house.
1974-10-13-back-to-the-kitchen:
Back to the kitchen

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

THE most urgent task confronting me this week is to estimate the profits and losses incurred by the National Theatre's Saturday Sunday Monday on its transfer from the Old Vic to the Queen's.

First, the theatres themselves. The Queen's, having a narrower proscenium opening, is able to offer the Priore family snugger, and therefore more convincing, accommodation than the Neapolitan mansion which they perplexingly inhabited in the Waterloo Road. Donna Rosa's kitchen is now on a scale befitting a conscientious housewife rather than an under-equipped restaurateur; and even though the dining-room is still decorated in the blood-red tones which I associate with symbolist productions of Ibsen, it too has contracted enough for the family to get properly to grips with each other.

They have a harder job, though, to get to grips with us. I missed the cosiness (not a pejorative word) of the Old Vic auditorium, and the friendliness engendered by a group of actors whom one had grown used to seeing on that stage for the past 18 months. Permanent companies are always being lauded for the benefits they bestow on their members; nobody ever mentions how pleasant (never mind about aesthetically rewarding) they can be for audiences.

Of that original team only six remain. (Higher figures have been reported in some newspapers, but do not be fooled.) The casualty-list includes Laurence Olivier's maniacal hatter and with him has departed much of the impact of the play's best running gag. Some glee has also departed with Denis Quilley's accountant, though his replacement, Stephen Greif, is still sharp and friendly enough for all reasonable purposes. Besides, Joan Plowright, ferociously fragmenting macaroni at the end of the first act, supplies as much culinary passion as any play could hold. Not that there is anything joyous about Miss Plowright at this point; her attack on the macaroni is a silent raging protest.

There is a fervour in Miss Plowright which was missing last year and which now offsets what I then took to be the excessive gaiety of Franco Zeffirelli's production. This remains full of excellent farcical routines, but they no longer camouflage the play's pain. They rather intensify it; most notably in Frank Finlay's performance of the head of the house, which I do not think the author himself, Eduardo de Filippo, could better. Mr Finlay plays a man hugging a grievance; he is accordingly quiet and watchful, darting thunderous glances at his many troublesome relatives. Sometimes he comes far enough out of himself to mount a verbal attack, short, stinging, and masterfully timed. The timing is of course the actor's accomplishment and we delight in it as such; part of the joy of the play is its utilisation of traditional theatrical skills. But the expertise never obscures the line of the performance, erupting into rage and scarcely subsiding even in regret.

The cast changes have blessed Mr Finlay with two suitably volatile offspring (Celia Gregory and John Hug) to maintain the illusion of a family out of the Commedia Napolitana and with a delightfully gangling nephew. (David Firth, his predecessor in the role, was also fairly delightful, but he did not, if my memory serves, gangle.)

  

The Taming of the Shrew (Shaw) also betrays the influence of the Italian commedia, a tradition of which the director, James Roose-Evans, obviously possesses much knowledge which he has used deftly but also a little pedantically; as if it were there to do us good rather than to make us laugh. It can be rather exhausting; Biondello, the play's comic messenger-boy, becomes a tight zany, smiling and skipping about the stage with a head full of bubble curls, like a half-crazed version of Fotherington-Thomas, the immortal swot of St Custard's.

The production, as is now customary, retains the introductory figure of Christopher Sly the tinker (Peter Bayliss, touchingly bemused), but departs from modern tradition by jettisoning him at the point where his role ends in the Shakespearean text (most productions go back to the source-play for material to keep Sly on stage throughout). This presumably is the moment for the main action to take on a life of its own, but it does so only fitfully. Nicky Henson is a splendid Petruchio, alternatively reflective and rumbustious; he goes into the taming business with some diffidence, scarcely fooled by his own bravado. Really, though, his fears are needless; there is little conviction in Susan Hampshire's shrewishness (though much in her ultimate surrender, which is subtly and tantalisingly played) and she scarcely needs subduing. So the action seems for once as sadistic as it is commonly, and groundlessly, held to be.

  

Another comic tradition was revived this week at the Royal Court, where it has been spasmodically at home these 20 years. Ken Campbell's The Great Caper belongs in a line of elaborate wordy farces with everything to recommend them except humour. They are generally concocted by dramatists earnestly dedicated to entertaining the populace, and it is sad to see Mr Campbell (whose Roadshows really were entertaining) fall into their company.

The play is set in the recent past (at any rate it begins with a scene in Strand Underground station, apparently fully operative) and it concerns a trio of characters with interlocking obsessions; since they truly do interlock it is useless to accuse Mr Campbell of formlessness. The themes--a fascinated abhorrence of technology, a compensating drift towards the occult--recall those of Heathcote Williams's AC/DC, which is drily referred to as "that lively piece." This seemed to me the drollest line of the evening, though there are other good throwaways up there with it: Richard O'Callaghan parenthetically remarks of his girl-friend's boy-friend that "he was away, but he was 6 ft 6 in. if he came back." The piece is terrifically well performed by Mr O'Callaghan, as lively, not to say febrile, an actor as ever twitched; by Mr Campbell, who looks lugubrious; and by Warren Mitchell, who hardly ever shouts. The sets (cut-outs among the cut-ups) are by Bob Ringwood and they are nice, too.
1974-10-20-problems-at-the-place:
Problems at the Place

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

IN the programme for the Royal Shakespeare Company's memorable Richard II at the Aldwych, the regular profile of the company has been reworded. Its gait is rather uncertain; it begins with a strut ('The Royal Shakespeare Company is probably the best known theatre company in the world') and ends ('For your support tonight the company is grateful') with a grovel. But it omits the customary roll-call of Associate Artists (an imposing line, most of whom can invariably be found acting somewhere else) and has also dropped the brazen declaration that 'the RSC occasionally give short experimental seasons in which they challenge accepted forms of acting, writing and directing.'

This is tactful, and suggests that the company may at last be dropping its dangerous habit of believing their own publicity. The RSC's initial two seasons at the Place in Euston challenged no accepted forms, but merely mishandled them. The first was disappointing and the second (particularly in choice of plays) disastrous. The third is now upon us, and two of its four productions have already opened.

First is Strindberg's Comrades, concerning marriage and taking -- even for Strindberg -- an extreme view of it. Axel is a saint and Bertha unspeakable. They are living the artistic life in Paris, and both have paintings up for acceptance by the Academy. Axel, well aware that he is the more talented of the two, and anxious to spare his wife the humiliation of rejection, switches the name-tags on the two pictures; so she gets in and he doesn't. She, however, has no wish to spare him any humiliation; she piles it on till eventually even his good nature is exhausted. He reveals the deception; she collapses, writhing; and he finds that he now has the strength to leave her.

Structurally, the play is a fine, tight melodrama buoyed up -- at any rate in Jeremy Brooks's snappy adaptation -- by a raciness rare in Strindberg. It is also, despite the rigidity of its attitudes, enticingly topical. Axel and Bertha are ostensibly trying to escape from traditional roles and turn their marriage into a companionship of equals; hence the title. Bertha and her friend Abel belong to a women's movement and ask awkward questions. Why shouldn't Bertha paint nude men if her husband can paint nude women?

A modern director perks up at moments like these; or so Barry Kyle has done at the Place. Strindberg, however, lets him down. As a capable dramatist he gives these revolutionary stirrings a momentary hint of conviction, but as an obsessed misogynist he regards them as works of the devil. (The brief glimpse we are given of Bertha's bunch in session does actually look uncommonly like a witches' coven.) Partnership in marriage is an unworkable fraud, a ruse by which the wife may undermine her husband and embezzle the housekeeping. Sex (and here Strindberg goes beyond ordinary male chauvinism to something more individual and unpleasant) is the worst tyranny of all. Axel really becomes free when Bertha offers him her body and he declines it. At last, he cackles, she will know the male agony of pursuit and refusal. An orthodox liberationist would probably say that Bertha, in using her sexuality as a weapon, has betrayed her own cause. Strindberg differs in regarding this betrayal as a biological inevitability rather than a lapse to be blamed on social conditioning. He refuses to believe in female solidarity; Abel, carrying her own bundle of neuroses, makes Bertha a most untrustworthy ally.

Susan Fleetwood and Rosemary McHale are a spirited pair of harpies, though Miss Fleetwood is inclined to play for sympathy where her author can only offer her a contemptuous pity. Peter Eyre's Axel is the production's undoing. Earlier this year in Ghosts Mr Eyre played another Scandinavian artist in Paris. That one had syphilis and this one doesn't look or sound much healthier. He droops and whines, so that his charity seems merely wet, and his final triumph incredible. I assume that Strindberg saw himself as Axel, and Mr Eyre's performance is probably a fair representation of what Strindberg was really like. But it is not what he thought he was like, however much a modern director may jib at such explicit sexism. Besides, the play already contains a frightening picture of a defeated male (a cringing author, unsparingly played by David Suchet) and it scarcely needs another.

Having fudged the play's central, central relationship, Mr Kyle, seemingly uncertain of how funny he wants the play to be, misjudges its tone and fumbles with its action; unwanted actors, left crouching over pieces of furniture, are apt to look exposed in so small an auditorium. And when a senior member of so distinguished a company is inaudible throughout a long scene, as was Clement McCallin (who admittedly had his back to me at the time), one wonders.

  

Having failed with a good play, the RSC has, after a fashion, succeeded with a bad one. Victor Lanoux's The Can Opener is a waste of everybody's time, notably that of its adaptor Charles Wood. But it is possible, while pondering that the existence of the only two men left alive after an unidentified holocaust would probably be as monotonous as M. Lanoux makes it seem, to admire the interplay of Roy Kinnear and Joe Melia. One may reflect that Mr Kinnear, despite his excesses (not too evident here), is still an actor, while Mr Melia, who seems to find his lines interesting but not convincing, is not; which does not mean that I would like to see him drummed out of Equity or even the RSC. It's a bleak life at the end of the world: just a couple of good jokes, any amount of whimsical philosophising, endless tins of processed peas, and Mr Kinnear has lost the opener.

  

There are good comedies that present almost intractable difficulties to a modern company. To make its audiences really understand The Tragedy of Tragedies or the Life and Death of Tom Thumb the Great, the Young Vic would first have to revive several of the forgotten eighteenth-century tragedies which Fielding, an energetic playwright before the imposition of censorship drove him to the novel, was here burlesquing: and I doubt if we could spare the time. Bernard Goss's production is hit or miss; it hits most often at the close when the narrative takes on its own momentum and heads hilariously for general massacre. The personages of the scene range from Thumb himself, a voluble conquering midget, to a stoical giantess; big girls don't cry. Spoiled princesses do, though, and Zoe Wanamaker, a languorous Huncamunca, acts accordingly and very well. She seems to have a better idea of what she is about than anyone else on stage, though Alfred Lynch and Christopher Timothy have between them a multitude of moments.

  

A sterner comedy, Schippel (Germany, pre-1914 vintage) by Carl Sternheim has reached the Open Space, adapted -- which is to say, softened, elongated and finally travestied -- by C. P. Taylor. On its own terms the version is amusing and we are to see more Sternheim soon, so it may not be fatal.
1974-10-27-good-dose-of-strychnine:
Good dose of Strychnine

EVER since I took on this job I have been waiting to see a West End comedy at which I could laugh consistently. It seems a modest ambition, but only this week with the arrival of Neil Simon's The Gingerbread Lady (Phoenix) was it gratified.

Mr Simon writes phenomenally good wisecracks; not since Tom Stoppard's Jumpers has any play in this city boasted so worthy an accumulation of laugh-lines. Mr Simon, to adapt Jean Hagen's defiant splutter in Singin' in the Rain, is funnier than Alan Ayckbourn put together. In this production he has Elaine Stritch to deliver his goods; and she is an incomparable mouthpiece.

Evy (Miss Stritch) may represent Mr Simon's means of exercising his own fearsome facility. She is a compulsive high-quality gagster; and her jokes are shown to be both the mask and the consequence of her own inadequacy. Psychologically this may be sound, but theatrically it has its drawbacks. After an immensely enjoyable two acts we are implicitly commanded to stop laughing in the third. Just what we are meant to do instead remains uncertain.

Evy is a woman with several pasts: in fact, a past-mistress (of a guitar player). Her other former occupations include nightclub singing, marriage, motherhood and alcoholism.
