When we meet her she has just returned from being dried out. Her friends hover around, hoping that the cure will last, but in fact helping to precipitate her fall from the wagon. For they are losers themselves, and their troubles are quite enough to drive Evy to drink; or at least to furnish her with the pretext which is all she requires. Meanwhile, however, another piece of her past has materialised. Her 17-year-old daughter has decided to adopt her, maybe even to save her from herself. At the final curtain it looks, precariously, as if she may stand a chance; Polly, says her mother, enunciating a standard piece of Broadway lore on the proper relationship of mother and daughter (cf, the close of Gypsy), "when I grow up I want to be just like you."

This aspect of the play is not so much false as ill-realised. The young are not a species with whom Mr Simon feels at home, and daughter Polly has been synthesised rather than created. ("I'm sticking with marriage" is her reaction to an experiment with booze; the time-lag between the play's American and British productions has not been kind to her.) She suffers, too, in the direction (we are not always allowed a clear view of her reactions to her mother's progress) and even in the playing. Jenny Quayle is clearly a strong and intelligent actress; but her personality, not just her voice, is ringingly English.

Evy's pals are given good if not outstanding performances. Sarah Marshall, with a set of vowels all her own, is an experienced man-eater who, having with fanatical conscientiousness kept young and beautiful, finds that on her fortieth birthday she is not loved, and her husband wants a divorce. Kevin Lindsay is a middle-aged actor, still dreaming of stardom while being fired from a bit part by a boy producer just out of college, but sensible enough to resist marriage with Evy on the grounds that he's an alcoholic nymphomaniac and he's homosexual and they'd have trouble getting their kids into a good school. From which it may be seen that in Mr Simon's world wit belongs not to Miss Stritch alone, but to all the desperate.

She none the less appropriates the lioness's share, to such effect that it is hard for us to wish her other than she is, no matter what it would do for her health. She comes on in a non-alcoholic daze and remarks on the change that sobriety has wrought on her view of her apartment: "I thought I had twice as much furniture." From then on I never wanted her to stop. Miss Stritch does as well by her lines as Maggie Smith but where Miss Smith teased, soothed and bandaged her words (some of them needed it), Miss Stritch, with richer, less vulnerable material, is a bouncer, occasionally a murderess. A furious self-deprecation ("I very nonchalantly got down on my knees") is her speciality; Max Factor should bottle her verbal acid and market it. They could call it Stritchnine. That it really is poisonous--suicidally poisonous--can be seen in her face: in the wrinkles, in the winces. There is one other performance as complete as hers and it comes complete as hers and it comes not in the smallest role in the play: from Lulie Callan as a Puerto Rican delivery boy.

  

Whatever else may be ailing in the West End, the star system, on first night's showing, still prospers. Miss Stritch speaks her first line from off stage and so on Wednesday she was applauded before entering. The previous night, in Alun Owen's The Male Of The Species (Piccadilly), Edward Woodward entered, was applauded, crossed the stage, wandered off, came back, and was applauded again. This I take to be the theatrical equivalent of double-entry bookkeeping; a practice initially profitable but ultimately hazardous. This is Mr Woodward's show; he plays three parts (as in The Wolf last year) and plays them most efficiently; if he wishes to prove that his range extends beyond Callan he has made his point. But versatility is not everything; Miss Stritch in The Gingerbread Lady is not essentially different from Miss Stritch in Company, but her full-length portrayal is far more satisfying than Mr Woodward's clever snippets.

Mr Owen's play is in fact three playlets, Mr Woodward portraying three men in the life of Michele Dotrice. The first two treat her rough; so she takes her revenge on the third. Now for the evening to work in any sustained way we would have to take an interest in Miss Dotrice, she being the only constant. But no actress should be asked to play the betrayed innocent twice in one evening; even once is pushing it. By the time the third play comes round we are attuned to watching Mr Woodward; and Miss Dotrice, as tough a cookie as she now is, may go hang. As it happens the third play is the only tolerable part of the bill. Its predecessors are soggy and soapy, but in the end Mr Owen gets down to frank and competent gag-writing (though it sounds a little hollow without canned laughter) with the acting and production stylised to match.
1974-11-03-a-famous-thane:
A famous Thane

I AM sorry to go on about the Royal Shakespeare Company's public relations but their latest display advertisement combines a puff for the famous Royal Shakespeare Theatre (gosh, not the Royal Shakespeare Theatre?) with the announcement for the Aldwych of Wedekind's celebrated comedy The Marquis of Keith. Just where these celebrations have been carried on I am unsure, but I doubt if you were invited.

Anyway, this week at Stratford they have given us William Shakespeare's famous tragedy of Macbeth, with the celebrated Scottish actor Nicol Williamson in the title role. Ever since he began astonishing us a decade ago we have awaited Mr Williamson's Macbeth for many reasons, not all of them ethical. Still, it was shrewd of Trevor Nunn, the director, to capitalise on his star's origins and present us with a Scotland fit for nationalists to speak in. All the gentlemen have a bash at the accent, the only southerner audibly present is Helen Mirren's Lady Macbeth, a sexy predator who has crossed the border to drain her husband of his virtue and allegiance as if they were North Sea oil.

Visually there is nothing particularly Caledonian about Mr Nunn's production, which appears to be going on partly in its hero's head and partly in church. As we enter the theatre we are faced by what appears to be an altar-table; doors at the back of the stage are able to blow open for processional entrances, as if the characters were coming at us down the nave of a cathedral.

At the beginning of the play we watch the coronation of Duncan, a paradigm of order; a pair of white curtains close across the scene, and, in shadow-play, we watch destruction sicken. Some kind of horned being appears to be breaking up the ceremony with a gigantic inverted crucifix; silhouettes can be peculiarly horrific. It looks as though three figures are levitating from the debris, and sure enough, when the curtains part, there are the witches, perched cosily on a giant chandelier. The conflict of good and evil established, we begin the play.

The theological emphasis enables Mr Williamson to give full value to passages that are generally skimped: 'the eternal jewel given to the common enemy of man' is a realisation that eats into his consciousness, and into ours as well. There is no more immediate actor on our stage and his performance develops through a series of breath-taking insights. At the beginning he is the most jovial of successful generals and at the close the most hopeless of forsaken tyrants.

Other actors have shown me desperation, but I do not believe I have ever had a clearer glimpse of despair (not, in fact, a condition encountered in many roles) than in Mr Williamson's last scenes, and in particular in his speaking--shorn of false, or any other, nobility--of 'tomorrow and tomorrow and tomorrow.' (Mr Nunn's production, which can be surprisingly literal in a symbolic sort of way, gives him an actual brief candle to blow out, just as earlier he has had a real poisoned chalice to put to his own lips.) It is time, by the way, to dispose of the assumption that this actor cannot speak verse. A Victorian critic, paying tribute to Irving's 'staccato, raven croak,' held that elocution was primarily the art of making yourself heard and understood. By that standard Mr Williamson, like Irving, is a superb elocutionist.

But he can be heavy-handed with it: literally. Climax after climax in this performance is accompanied by the steady pounding of fists on furniture. There is a heart-stopping moment when Macbeth first catches sight of Banquo's ghost, but the relentless percussion which follows can only cheapen it. Some of the power of his concluding scenes derives from their stillness, with Macbeth perched high and lonely on a devil's throne, itself perched on what appears to be several layers of table. By this time the subjective aspect of the production has become paramount, scenes in which Macbeth does not appear are cut to the quick (which does not mean played very fast), while minor characters are allowed as little time on stage as possible.

Still, an exclusive focus on the tragic hero is, at this stage of theatrical history, no bad direction in which to err. It chimes, too, with other RSC productions; Richard II to an extent, certainly Dr Faustus, even Tom Stoppard's Travesties, have all led us into their protagonists' minds; and have occasioned an unprecedented quantity of major acting. As far as the classics are concerned I am ready to subscribe to the cult of the individual. It may mean that the RSC, who have crested with the histories and never lacked for success in comedy, will finally be able to conquer the tragedies.

  

Robert Patrick is a hugely prolific off and off-off Broadway playwright; and if that intelligence makes you yawn you are hardly likely to be revived by the information that Kennedy's Children consists entirely of interconnected monologues delivered by five human casualties in a downtown New York bar, time the present. However, wake up and make straight for the King's Head. The play is fantastic. Its subject is the sixties, a decade which, according to one of the five, began with the death of Marilyn Monroe. More central is the Kennedy assassination; the first one, as another character carefully, ghoulishly, puts it.

One of the quintet is a JFK freak, she worshipped 'the Kennedy legend and time stopped for her on the day of the murder.' Her obsession could be ludicrous and Mr Patrick does get some laughs out of it, but his writing and the acting of Vivian Pickles, with her careful delivery and nervous eyes, are so finely balanced that ambivalence is triumphantly preserved. Don Parker plays a gay actor who traces for us the rise and fall of underground theatre. His evocations of Greenwich Village, icily hilarious, do a great deal to draw us into the play; his later speeches slightly outlive their interest. Jan Waters paints a bitter, not quite defeated picture of a glamour girl born after glamour had died.

Then there is a GI, finding cynicism in Vietnam. His is the weakest part in the piece. He takes us over unhappily familiar ground and his presence in the bar seems to be symbolic rather than actual; a play should abide by its own rules, however tenuous. But Deborah Norton throttles all doubts as a veteran of every protest, every movement of the decade, suffering a little from her own disillusion and a lot from that of her man; to be in the same small room with Mr Williamson's, and Miss Norton's, anguish has been a week I shall not forget.

At first I distrusted the play; then it began to tap my English nostalgia for New York (gratitude here to Clive Donner's direction and John Scully's set); by the time it had conducted its unsparing, unsneering progress through the heroes of the decade I grew up in (Kennedy only the figurehead and the title unfathomably ironic), it had grabbed me as very few plays ever have.

This has been a week for heroes; John Whiting was one, fashioning a wry, elegant victory from defeat. He wrote of them as well: I find his life, though, more appealing than his art. Marching Song, revived at Greenwich, proves to be no masterpiece, though it contains some bracing scenes and is worth checking out.
1974-11-10-golden-boy:
Golden Boy

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Peter Brook's `Timon.'

FOR some years now Peter Brook's theatrical headquarters has been Paris, whence he has emerged to stage gibberish spectaculars in Persepolis, or to tour African villages, before returning to base for another bout of secluded experiment with the actors of his International Centre for Theatrical Research. However, at this year's Paris Autumn Festival, he and his troupe have emerged to present their first classic: Shakespeare's Timon of Athens.

As a Shakespearean director Mr Brook has retained a scrupulous regard for the text. His celebrated version of A Midsummer Night's Dream was indeed exceptional in its refusal to cut a single line, even the most obscure. For this production of Timon some of the most oceanic of Elizabethan verse has been transmuted into crisp French prose, but I detected no actual excisions.

The production has been staged in a house--the Theatre des Bouffes-du-Nord--unused for 20 years and now virtually derelict. Both the stage and the original seating have been torn out; entering the auditorium we confront a gaping proscenium arch, which gives on to a bare peeling wall adorned by a perilous-looking catwalk. Between the arch and the wall, where the stage used to be, is now an abyss, out of which climb two or three stairways and, at various times, several presumably intrepid performers. Most of the action, however, takes place on the floor of what were once the stalls. Here the audience sit in a semicircle, awaiting the telling of a tale. The actors, sitting and strolling among them, detach themselves to do the telling.

Sometimes they form their own circles. This is the shape in which Mr Brook has staged the two banquets: the first at which the prodigal Timon showers his friends with gifts, and the second at which, bankrupt and appalled by their ingratitude, he showers them with dirty water. The production is not, from moment to moment, amazingly inventive, but every so often it comes up with an image that transfixes.

Two flattering lords, during Timon's prosperity, lie with their heads in his lap and he fondles them. These same lords, believing their benefactor ruined, arrive at his last surprise banquet bemused, frightened and huddling together for reassurance. And in the play's last movement, when Timon in a frenzy of disgust has retreated to the wilderness and, digging for roots to eat, finds gold, his discovery takes the form not of gold coin but of gold-dust, which Francois Marthouret's Timon blows out of his hand at all who come to visit him.

M. Marthouret constitutes no mean image himself. He may well be the handsomest young actor in Europe. His Timon, if you will forgive the dated reference, is one of the Beautiful People, innocently living up to a code of unreal generosity. To go back further, and more appropriately still, he is a Golden Boy. Gold is the chain around his neck, and golden too the sweater beneath his casual, dazzling white suit. Golden above all is his smile; he is, up until the moment at which he realises his betrayal, superlatively sunny. That moment, too, is well taken, the smile giving way to a snarl, and against all augury he succeeds at least part-way with the extended unforgiving rage of the last acts.

Apart from M. Marthouret there are 11 French actors in Mr Brook's troupe of 19; and the cosmopolitan remainder (including one Englishman, Bruce Myers, an RSC dropout) do not seriously interfere with the rewardingly native flavour of the whole. For, whatever rigorous and innovative motions they may have been through in the interests of Theatrical Research, this company preserve the strength of the French classic tradition. Even when acting in prose they know how to handle tirades; M. Marthouret's flights--particularly his first farewell to Athens--are an instance; the banished Alcibiades, defying the senate, is equally adept in the rhetoric.

What the production cannot do is to establish the play as a unity; the second half is sustained purely by magnificent invective, but it can pall in the original and does so sooner here. The notorious split in the play is not in its structure so much as in the balance of its characterisation. Timon is seen tragically, while his contemporaries are satirised; they, more than any other in the canon, belonging to the world of Ben Jonson. Mr Brook treats them accordingly and amusingly: the Athenian Senate convene in academic gowns; Timon's creditors arrive to hammer on his door like so many brokers' men--to each his own briefcase.
1974-11-10-touch-of-ogden:
Touch of Ogden

I WAS reading some of the poems of Ogden Nash before setting out for the Comedy, a theatre in London that I visit with a regularity that threatens to become monotonous;

Because nothing seems to run there and neither does the public, and Sunday critics are seated behind pillars which suggests that the management dislike or have forgotten us.

And this week's piece was called The Pay Off

And it was a comedy thriller written by William Fairchild, possibly when tired and in need of a lay-off.

And Nigel Patrick appeared in it as an eminent surgeon or slicer

Who had made so much money that he lived in a house full of borscht-coloured furniture whose aspect was applauded by the audience because they plainly could conceive of nothing nicer.

And this house was on the Sussex coast and the month was September and the day (for the play observed the unities) a Friday

Which turned out not to be Mr Patrick's day as neither indeed was it my day.

For it seems that this surgeon had antagonised the Treasury or rather incensed it

For he had placed his enormous earnings in a Swiss bank account without telling anyone, and there is a law, and what he was doing was against it.

And there were a famous actress and a pop singer (called, would you believe, Johnny Tomorrow) and they had done the same thing as Mr Patrick

Which made it a hat-trick.

And there was a fourth culprit played by the villainous Peter Vaughan and he was nastier than the others

Because they had invested their money abroad for noble reasons like trying to help their husbands and their secretaries and medical science and probably their grey-haired mothers.

Yes, they all claimed to have sinned with the best of intentions;

But Mr Vaughan was a money-grubber impure and simple and made no such pretensions.

In the first act they were all blackmailed by Peter Sallis, who is a very good actor, but in the second act we unfortunately saw much less of him

Because Mr Vaughan had made rather a mess of him.

Dulcie Gray played the actress and she kept delivering epigrams in the manner of the great Dame Edith

And they seemed inopportune and detrimental to suspense but you could not blame Miss Gray because the actress she followeth where her author and her director (who happened to be Mr Patrick) leadeth.

And the comedy was not comic and the thrills would not have excited the most secluded spinster

And I doubt if those responsible are going to be able to bank huge sums in Switzerland or even at their local branch of the National Westminster.

During the interval I asked one of my colleagues if the once respected firm of Tennents would have presented such stuff in the days of their late managing director Binkie Beaumont;

And he said he didn't think so for a meaumont.

Which seems to show where we are headed;

And makes one wonder just who can rescue the West End theatre from the mire in which it is embedded.

And Mr Fairchild's play does seem to contain a hint of the only possible measure:

We look to the Treasury however little it now has to treasure.

Robert Cushman
1974-11-17-motorbike-show-that-fails-to-:
Motorbike show that fails to start

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

With the rock musical virtually defunct, it seems gratuitously unkind of the Royal Court to offer us the Tokyo Kid Brothers in The City. This entertainment might reasonably be described as outlandish; it is surprising, at first blush, to hear Westernised pop belted at us in Japanese accents. But that first blush is the only one; it is for the most part an extremely pallid evening.

Accents apart, we have heard it all before. Come to think of it we have heard it all before, accents included. As far back as South Pacific we were thrilling to the titillating sound of the Oriental lisp. There was even a twenties hit called Nagasaki, whose lyrics ("Hot ginger and dynamite, There's nothing but that at night") sound kind of uncomfortable now. I have to report that the most appealing moment in the present show is provided by a Tokyo Kid Sister shyly confiding, "I think it would be fun to rip off a motorbike." How you say?

To be fair, the show is not always as ingenuous as that. The Tokyo Kid Brothers proclaim themselves to be the children of a Japanese culture fostered by American occupation; they listen to rock, eat Kentucky Fried Chicken, ride motorbikes. That last is most important; the show is subtitled "a motorcycle musical." It could conceivably be the aim of the Brothers - and even more of the Royal Court - to offer us an oblique but devastating view of our own values by showing us the effect they have had on alien lives.

Approached from this angle, however, the show is simply confusing. Its attitude to fried chicken is indeed somewhat caustic; it is remarkable how swiftly Colonel Sanders has come to be accepted as shorthand for imperialism. But rock and motorbikes are equally products of a commercial civilisation, and these The City celebrates.

Actually it is nearly crushed between them; what with the backing-group giving out upstage and Hondas and Suzukis lying around downstage, the cast have very little room to manoeuvre. For much of the time they are occupied performing characterless dance routines (as nearly static as choreography could be) to equally anonymous music, and performing them so stiffly that I could almost have sworn they were English.

The first of these numbers - an opening celebration by a motorbiking commune living just outside Tokyo - is interrupted by a couple of baton-swinging cops (the villains; they later double as the Kentucky chicken merchants) determined to put the kids in their place; I thought I heard the word "punks." (Half the dialogue is in Japanese, half in English.) The echoes of West Side Story are quite deafening, but in its later stages the show takes on a closer resemblance to Hair.

The kinship is particularly noticeable in the thinness - amounting nearly to invisibility - of the story-line and in the self-regarding sentimentality of the general conception. The land which the gang occupy is destined to be the site of a housing complex, an object which the bikers, opposed to all forms of mechanisation (with one rather obvious exception), dismiss as a "computer city." They want to protest; and one of them does so by riding his machine full-tilt against a newly erected barricade. He kills himself in the process, which is very sad since not 20 minutes before he has palpitatingly found Love.

A guard delivers a long and tearful monologue disclaiming responsibility; we must not assume, just because he built a barrier that he wanted young heroes to go dashing themselves against it. I believed him, but his extreme volubility lost him my sympathy. There is a great deal of violence in the show, and the Court may conceivably be hoping to siphon off some of the Kung Fu audience. Those who think fifth-rate musicals are redeemed by social comment, faraway places and strange-sounding names should also have a good time.

  

I cannot think whom to recommend to see The Highwayman (Roundhouse), despite its undoubted historic interest. This is the first English production of Schiller's Die Rauber, first published in 1781 and a seminal Romantic work. It concerns two brothers, one of whom, naturally base, contrives that his virtuous sibling shall be disinherited, said brother thereupon taking philosophically (everything in this play is done philosophically) to a life of crime. He proves in fact a singularly benevolent bandit, but Remorse weighs him down just the same.

The brothers never appear together; they may therefore be played by the same actor, in this case Derren Nesbitt, who manages a dual performance of staggering dullness. He is slightly more bearable as the good brother; the bad one is a cripple and his affliction elicits from Mr Nesbitt an unconscionable amount of plodding and grunting. He also has a nasty habit of nudging people with his hump.

Here, however, I must cease berating the actor and turn to the director. Hovhannes I. Pilikian's production is unbelievably graceless. Backs are slapped, fists clenched, elbows rubbed, laps fondled; the director appears to know no other way of establishing relationships between characters and he makes his actors look ridiculous. They are not safe even when dead; ramp-shaped traps open to receive them, and it is a pretty sight to see a performer in his final throes carefully rolling himself into the required position.

Mr Pilikian, who gave us such a rollicking production of Oedipus at Chichester, may possibly be out to prove that Schiller, like Sophocles, was a farceur under the skin (he mutters something in a programme note about the Theatre of the Absurd), but, like so many directors who reach about comedy, he lacks any recognisable sense of humour; and in this play, where melodrama (some of it rather stirring) is liable to topple into burlesque even without prodding, such a lack is fatal.

The leading actress, continually defending her virtue, is given a terrible time; not least by the translator, who requires her to say "I feel as strong as a horse" after niftily disarming her persecutor. Other characters litter the stage by tossing down books or papers in moments of passion. It is altogether an untidy occasion.
1974-11-24-con-tricks:
Con-tricks

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'The Marquis' and 'The Beast.'

ANY heavy theatre company is liable to expend much of its energies on the caprices of inordinate ambition. (I am referring, of course, to the characters we see on the stage, not to those we may imagine behind it.) This week from the Royal Shakespeare, the people who gave you--are still giving you--the fortunes of Faustus and the machinations of Macbeth--comes a further flurry of malevolent mountebanks.

At the Aldwych we are introduced to The Marquis Keith, a character imagined, written, and originally played by Frank Wedekind, and the hero of a play which here justifies its reputation as its author's best. Keith is an adventurer, floating in from nowhere and surfacing in Munich at the turn of the century, dispensing money in order to attract it. He distributes largesse to a horde of hangers-on, while touting for support for the Magidome, a project which appears to be nothing more nor less than an arts complex.

In view of this last item, Ronald Eyre, director and co-translator, is to be congratulated on his restraint in not taking the play and shoving it bodily into the 1970s. He has, however, while still maintaining in the programme that we are in 1899, prodded it slyly forwards as far as the twenties. With Carl Davis's estringent clarinet-haunted music besieging our ears, we may even ignore all references to Munich and dream ourselves into the Berlin of everybody's favourite decadence. The vast grotesques of German society, swathed in furs, move mountainous around the thin contorted figure of the Marquis himself. Clearly Mr Eyre owes a great deal to his designer, Voytek; but he must himself take credit for the swift, chill exuberance of the evening, the best of the various good things that have been seen at the Aldwych this year, and rich in off-handed wit.

Sara Kestelman has a new comic assurance (and a new feathery voice) as Anna, Keith's mistress, destined like the wife of Citizen Kane for stardom in his custom-built opera-house and dreading it. ("What happens," she asks, "when I, for want of a better word, sing?") A lower-grade whore is played with appealing scornful relish by Patti Love, who has become, at two strokes, our most experienced Wedekind actress: she played a similar role, less happily, in the National's Spring Awakening. Not all the girls have to have fun; Keith's, for want of a better word, wife is a wraith, knowing that she will possess him for only as long as he remains an outsider, killing herself when his success seems in sight.

This only shows how little she knows her man; Keith is destined always to glitter, never to arrive. He lacks solidity, above all he lacks solid cash (huge bank-notes are the binding symbol of this production); so, thinking to batten on polite society, he finds it battening on him, squeezing him dry, finally squeezing him out. The play is actually none too explicit as to what society sees in him in the first place; the details of his intrigues are left very murky. Perhaps Wedekind trusted to his own charm to carry it (certainly a Keithian thing to do); we have Brecht's testimony that he was an actor of limited accomplishment and amazing charisma.

Ian McKellen, who plays the part now, is an actor of outstanding accomplishment and, by common consent even of his detractors, as charismatic as they come. But he is not, in the traditional sense, a charmer; as a new kind of star actor he compels attention by insistently deglamourising his roles. Keith is a cripple; Mr McKellen bends and protrudes at incredible angles, outpacing Olivier's Richard III in deformity. And here reverberations begin. Reminded of Richard III one thinks, in this Brechtian setting, of Hitler; would that be a Chaplin moustache on Mr McKellen's upper lip? Suddenly the idea of a con-man at large in twenties Germany loses its appeal.

The play, I think, loses too; we do not have to like Keith, but we should be carried along with him--we should feel his defeat. Mr McKellen distances us altogether too much. Our sympathy goes instead to Ian Richardson, who plays his doppelganger Scholz, as encased in morality as Keith is indifferent to it, trying desperately to break out and enjoy something called Life, finally and frighteningly retreating into madness. Mr Richardson offers a delicious comic performance, in the English tradition that repression is endearing. If Mr McKellen is Chaplin, he is Keaton, never cracking a smile as he contemplates the delights of an early morning bicycle ride or propositions Anna when his every instinct is to propose to her.

The balance of these two Ians is wrong, though something asserts itself in their final encounter where Mr Richardson, buttoned up tight in an immaculate pearl-grey suit, confronts Mr McKellen in a golden-brown robe that once was glamorous and now is just dishevelled; and their costumes tell everything about them.

  

Insouciance is much, indeed very nearly all, in the theatre; as Mr McKellen demonstrates at the final curtain. Snoo Wilson's The Beast (the RSC at The Place) is heavy with its absence, though there is enough zip in it to make one wonder what it would be like in a less portentous production. Its subject--the week's second would-be superman--is Aleister Crowley, styled "the wickedest man in the world." Why did Mr Wilson write about him? Perhaps merely because he was there; for a long time. His career as magician, diabolist and spiritual leader is ingeniously jumped through, its roots perversely and persuasively discovered in his fundamentalist background and its flowering verbosely documented in a long inverted pastoral during which, if you doze, you do so to the soothing accompaniment of high-quality writing. The effects of magic may be theatrical and its renunciation (cf. Prospero) certainly is, but its processes--here endlessly discussed--are a bore. In his downfall, which is more or less continuous, Crowley is hauntingly portrayed by Richard Pasco; and Rosemary McHale, for the first time since joining the company, does justice to her own talent as his bitterly decaying mistress.

  

The Young Vic, having revived several plays acknowledged to be modern classics, has discovered one of its own in John Antrobus's wartime comedy Crete and Sergeant Pepper. Denise Coffey's production is the best at this house in ages.
1974-12-01-victims-of-parental-war:
Victims of parental war

ROBERT CUSHMAN on fringe plays in London, an Anouilh premiere in Bristol and 'The Party' on tour.

JOHNNIE QUARRELL'S Stakeout at the Half Moon is a play about baby-bashing. The statistics of the subject are frightening: 4,000 cases each year is the number quoted in the programme, and the implication is that it is these figures that have driven the author to write his play.

The implication is borne out by what we see on stage; there are in fact two characters but essentially this is a play about statistics. Mr Quarrell's embattled parents exist only as mechanisms for destroying one child, and conceiving another plainly destined for the same end. One or two traces of individuality they must be allowed in order to keep the play going, but these are arbitrary and unconvincing. The play is one half of a double bill, its companion piece being Homeworker by the young German playwright Franz Xaver Kroetz, whose Stallerhof made so deep an impression at the Bush a few months ago. The new play bears some superficial resemblances to Stakeout; it also depicts infanticide against a starkly underprivileged background. Like Mr Quarrell, Kroetz quotes statistics in his programme note (the English play seems, indeed, to have been specifically designed as a counterpart to the German one), but Mr Quarrell has fastened precisely on what is least valuable in Kroetz's work. Homeworker, whatever its inspiration may have been, is a play about people.

It has a real quirky shape. The title refers to a husband, debarred by illness from outside employment. His wife is periodically, joylessly unfaithful; she gets pregnant. At his suggestion she attempts to abort herself with a knitting needle. She fails; and when the baby is born it has a couple of lumps on its head, a deformity on which the husband--to the confusion of his own two children--continually and bitterly harps. She leaves him; eventually she returns but by this time the baby, left in his care, is dead.

Kroetz's characters, like Mr Quarrell's, live on the edge of desolation; the difference is that the German writer never quite pushes them over. Always there is some saving humanity; the play is bleak, but it is not mechanical. I will admit, though, that the memory of Stallerhof rather than anything apparent at the Half Moon persuaded me of this.

The production is considerably more crippled than any of its characters. The play, written in short scenes, constantly changing its locale, is here approached with a hopeless listless literalism. Long pauses for scene changes murder the dramatic rhythm--or would if any had been achieved within the episodes themselves. Much of Kroetz's drama is unspoken; in this production it is merely absent.

As damaging as anything else is the decision to abandon the play's German setting so as to give it an immediate local relevance. This surely is community theatre gone berserk; the idea that people can only respond to actions that are supposedly taking place on their own doorstep is destructive to the idea of drama, which is supposed to widen audiences' horizons, and patronising to the spectators themselves. The implicit assumption is that the plays are absolutely representative of local working-class life. That is insulting if false and self-defeating if true; anyone not aroused to protest by direct experience of such a situation is unlikely to be much affected by seeing it re-enacted on a stage. What actually happens, of course, is that the intended audience stays well away from the play, which ends up performed for us middle-class voyeurs. Even we, however, deserve a better deal.

  

Stephen Poliakoff is a 21-year-old writer who has written a stage-worthy play. That will do for compliments. Clever Soldiers (Hampstead Theatre Club) tells of a young man's progress from public school to Oxford and thence into the trenches of the First World War. It is a progress of disillusion. Young Teddy loses all faith in the values he has been taught but finds that they have gone too deep in him to permit any real change. He is fated to command and his men to obey; the only way out is death, which obstinately avoids him.

Intellectually the play is persuasive enough; structurally it is neat; its characters, like those of Stakeout, are all too obviously tailored to fit the thesis. Teddy is powerfully portrayed by Simon Ward in his best young subaltern manner, but his every action seems dictated. Perhaps the worlds he moves through are--from previous plays, films and books--just too familiar to us. We know all about World War I--at least we know as much as Mr Poliakoff is able to tell us. We know too the legend of pre-cataclysmic Oxford, divided between rampageous bloods and nervously epigrammatic aesthetes.

These last are represented by Michael Feast, splendidly tic-ridden, but required to bear too heavy a load of degeneracy. Opposed to him is Teddy's socialist tutor, and the two spend much of the play battling for the hero's affections and, by implication, for his soul. But the implications are difficult to swallow because the actual relationships are underwritten; there are huge gaps in the development. This is even more the case with the one girl in Teddy's life, an emergent liberated woman whom Sheila Ruskin plays--perhaps of necessity--on one barking note. Teddy ends by rejecting everybody, and this at least is painfully believable.

  

Trevor Griffiths's The Party looks considerably more persuasive in its National Theatre mobile production than it did last year at the Old Vic. The living room in which its collection of radical intellectuals assemble during the 1968 Paris uprisings now looks as if it might truly belong to a TV producer rather than a movie mogul. Several minor characters have been eliminated and those who remain have been fleshed out a bit, each being allowed some kind of response to the success ethic which the producer shamefacedly embodies, and which the Trotskyist Tagg attacks in the play's longest speech.

In its original venue half the play's energies seemed devoted to providing a bourgeois audience with an enforced lesson in political philosophy. The present production, touring mainly on a university circuit, more narrowly examines the psychology of the amateur revolutionary. The main conflict is no longer between Tagg and his LSE opponent, whose revisionist credo, delivered with such sparkle by Denis Quilley at the Vic, has been considerably damped down and seems in fact much longer than is justified by its significance to the argument. It is easily squelched by Fulton Mackay's Tagg, lacking Olivier's bravura, but substituting an unassuming intensity which establishes him almost unassailably at the play's moral centre.

Almost but not quite, since he comes under withering fire from the play's Thersites-figure, materially the most successful of them all. Jack Shepherd in this role lacks Frank Finlay's comic finesse (most actors do) but makes up for it in violence. It remains a weakness in the play that these two are permitted no real confrontation; their opposition is dramatised only by their effect on the producer and this is still bewilderingly inconclusive. (Intellectual ambivalence may be a sophisticated virtue, but here spills over into insecure dramaturgy.) Hugh Thomas nevertheless makes more of his focal role than I would have thought possible, aided by direction from David Hare which makes up in intelligence and clarity for what is lost in atmosphere.

  

I saw The Party in the studio theatre of the Bristol Old Vic, whose main house had on the previous night scooped the world premiere of Jean Anouilh's The Arrest, which title--or so I like to think--derives from Shakespeare. The Arrest is the strict one imposed by the fell sergeant Death, here promoted to the rank of superintendent and played unerringly by Michael Rothwell, a Bristol fixture for several years and among the most calmly skilful actors in the land. His victim is portrayed--simultaneously--by Alan Dobie (ageing and embittered), John Hurt (youthful and vulnerable), and a small boy (a small boy).

This is one of those plays about time--or rather (like all such from Priestley to Pinter) a play about memory; as ingenious and enjoyable as you would expect from Anouilh and not overburdened with significance. Applause for most of the cast, among whom Marilyn Taylerson and Charlotte Cornwell are particularly striking, for Alexander McPherson's spectacular sets, and for Val May's impeccably neat production.
1974-12-08-national-manoeuvres:
National manoeuvres

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on A. E. Ellis's new play about Dreyfus.

THE original title of the National Theatre's new play about the Dreyfus case was "The Jew of Mulhaus." It now comes before us as Grand Manoeuvres, a phrase used at one point by Esterhazy, the adventurer actually responsible for selling French military secrets to German intelligence, and applied, by ironic extension, to the gyrations of the French high command in their hideously successful efforts to send the wrong man to prison and keep him there. In general, though, irony is not this play's style. It is a slam-bang clamorous affair which might more frankly have been re-titled "The Dreyfus Show."

In this enjoyably phantasmagoric epic, cast and settings vie with each other in number and mobility. The movements of both are witty, intricate and precisely timed; one knows within minutes of the opening that everything and everyone will click into place. Only a full-time theatre critic, perhaps, can appreciate how refreshing that knowledge is; and I must stress that it is never allowed to relax into complacency. The surprises, for three whole hours, keep on coming.

I am inclined to attribute them to the director, Michael Blakemore, rather than to the author, A. E. Ellis, but this may be prejudice since I have known and admired Mr Blakemore's work for years while Mr Ellis's is new to me. I have not read his one novel, and this is his first play. As such it should probably not, in an ideal world, be accorded a full-scale National production unless it were either a masterpiece or the likely precursor of one. It is neither, but most of the new plays offered this year by our three major theatres have been so dismal that this one may be tolerated, even welcomed. An occasion for a virtuoso production is at least an occasion.

On the evidence before me I would judge Mr Ellis to be more of an editor than writer. Many of the play's speeches are evidently verbatim reproductions of what was said and written at the time; other aspects are less obviously derivative. I thought it at first an excellent idea to dramatise the divisive effect of the affair by showing a bourgeois dinner-party turned into a shambles at the mention of Dreyfus's name. I was therefore a little dashed when I opened the programme to find that what I had admired was merely an animation of a cartoon of the period; I had accordingly to divide my admiration between the original artist and the director, designer (John Bury) and choreographer (Sue Lefton) who had revivified him. Very little was left over for the author, whose accompanying dialogue is no more than efficient. An encounter between Esterhazy and two moustachioed intelligence officers disguised as ladies of leisure is wittier, but here, too, the programme discloses a less direct debt to a contemporary draughtsman.

It is an admirably honest thing, this programme, and well worth consulting. It enables Mr Ellis to fill in the details that are wanting from the play, to tell us why the France of the 1890s felt itself to be vulnerable, why it needed a scapegoat and why that scapegoat should have been a Jewish Army officer. It tells us a great deal about Edouard Drumont, an author and journalist who seems almost to have invented French anti-semitism and whose newspaper, Libre Parole, hysterically led the cry against Dreyfus.

The way Mr Ellis goes on about Drumont you expect him to be the villain of the piece. In fact he does not even appear in it, though his influence is to some degree felt; the officers who are the play's chief rogues are first seen ensconced behind copies of the Libre Parole, whence they emerge to embark on grand and petty manoeuvres designed to ruin Dreyfus and to camouflage their own corruption and incompetence. Their spokesmen--written and played with considerable spirit--is a Major Henry, risen from obscurity and rising still; Paul Rogers, charting his progress, runs through about three-and-a-half different accents before a temporary crest in Dreyfusard sentiment brings his career to an expedient and suicidal halt. But sentiment prevails, and children for his orphaned children is soon heard tinkling into the colonel's cap (I told you he'd risen) of the unfortunate deceased. Meanwhile Dreyfus continues to rot on Devil's Island.

I liked that moment. But what with his twitting of the soldiery and the politicians, and the necessity of conveying the events of a dozen years, and the tendency of the characters to address one another by name, rank and title so that we may have some idea who they are, Mr Ellis has left himself with very little time to examine the significance of the case to France, or to the outside world, in general. I think he kept meaning to, and, late on, he at any rate shows us the shocked, derisive reactions to Dreyfus's family of a trio of yokels made up as circus clowns.

It might have helped more if we had been allowed to judge the inroads made by anti-semitism on recognisable people. Here, however, we come up against the play's own grand manoeuvre, which is to deny sympathy, humanity and even a normal speaking-voice to practically everyone except Dreyfus himself. When Alan MacNaughtan first comes on, the contrast of his dapper quietude to the preceding rowdiness is quite breathtaking. Where the others are allowed no nobility, he is allowed no flaw, the play taking the reasonable if limiting view that his sufferings were so great as to make any judgment on his character irrelevant.

At the end of the play Mr MacNaughtan gives us one final, overwhelming shudder. Vindicated and released, Dreyfus is grudgingly awarded the Legion d'Honneur. He turns to the audience and we find he has been decorated with a yellow star. The sheer theatricality is almost irresistible; but I began resisting when the figure of a Nazi guard loomed upstage and have continued ever since. These are the prime horrors of our time and they must not be too easily used. They become cheapened; so do the artists responsible; so do we. Since the play never really examines the French anti-semitism of the 1890s, it can tell us nothing of its relation to the German of the 1930s. As far as it goes, however, the narrative is absorbing and (unless, like some learnedly dismissive critics, you know it all already) instructive.

  

Much of the 1950s seemed gathered at Greenwich to watch John Osborne's The Entertainer. This play has weathered 17 years and will certainly outlast Grand Manoeuvres. But, at least in the author's own reverently uncut production, it contains an inordinate amount of moaning and I found that the celebrated equation of Britain with a decaying music-hall rang no bells; it belongs firmly to its period. The evening is nearly wrecked by the length of the transitions from hall to home, and saved by Max Wall's Archie Rice. He has to rein himself in on Archie's awful early routines; he has after all convulsed audiences with material even more tenuous (though I wonder if Mr Osborne intended Archie's lyrics to be quite as bad as they are). But he excels in the extension of the act that constitutes his family life; it is here that Archie performs best, simultaneously wooing and excluding his audience as Mr Wall has always done: his last great, dismissive monologue, actor, role and play come resoundingly together.

  

In Barrie's What Every Woman Knows (Albery) some harsh unfashionable views on marriage are compromised by a compulsion to appear as pleasant as possible. This weakness, already present in the writing, is greatly intensified in Clifford Williams's production. Peter Egan, who breathes sensitivity, is cast as an unimaginative careerist who does not know when he is insulting his wife. A self-made Scot, he falls for an English aristocrat; credible enough if the lady were not recognisable as a twittering nonentity a mile off. Meanwhile his wife suffers from her lack of charm--which, since Dorothy Tutin plays the part, is plainly (or beautifully) absurd. Though the miscasting is monstrous (and could the right kind of actress ever get the part in the West End?), it is almost justified since Miss Tutin, who has the most eloquent eyes in the world, acts subtly and superbly.

  

In Sheffield, the Crucible Studio is showing an early Athol Fugard, Nongogo, which is certainly very promising and contains a good flash performance by Alton Kumalo.
1974-12-15-the-end-of-a-flying-angel:
The end of a flying angel

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

Perhaps it is more dramatic for women to be teases; that at any rate is how our dramatists seem to see them. Girls in plays only say No as preludes to saying Yes: this must be what is known as wish fulfilment. Last week, in David Mercer's television piece, Find Me, a young lady rejected Anthony Hopkins with such vehemence that one could only count the seconds before the camera found them in bed together. Sandra, the girl in Dennis Potter's Only Make Believe (Oxford Playhouse), holds out longer; she is working as a temp for Christopher, a playwright whom a burned hand has rendered incapable of typing his own scripts. His wife has left him, and he is taking it badly; his injury is self-inflicted, a gesture of annoyance and frustration.

For an act and a half Christopher pours out his woes, his needs, and even considerable stretches of his new television play to the nervously attendant Sandra; finally, she allows him to have her, and regrets it immediately after. Though Only Make Believe itself began life on television, the Oxford Playhouse puzzlingly claims that it is Mr Potter's first theatre play. (Why does Son of Man, which made a similar journey from screen to stage, not qualify?) In at least one respect I imagine that it worked better in the original medium; every time Christopher comes on to create, the stage darkens, half the set disappears, and with a creak, a groan and a trundle we are plunged into his imagined world.

The play within the play concerns a young man who claims to be an angel and dies in this belief, having attempted to fly out of a bedroom window, the bed being one in which a resentful housewife has attempted to give incontrovertible proof of his humanity by seducing him. Christopher's title for it is Angels Are So Few; which is also the name of one of Mr Potter's own previous works, from which the episodes we see have presumably been extracted. Nobody could accuse Mr Potter of profligacy and on most (not all) of the evidence given here quite the best thing he could have done with this earlier play was to camouflage it by writing another play round it.

In so doing, however, he has fallen into a trap. The scenes Christopher dictates and the ones in which he himself figures are written in precisely the same style; one we agree to accept as realistic, because it is plainly not aiming at stylisation and because we have been ground into expecting it of all literate mainstream playwrights. We accept it because not to do so would be too much trouble and would leave us with virtually nothing we could say we enjoyed. So we go along with the jokes that are too consciously prepared and the epigrams that never quite attain to wit and the intrusive imagery at moments of stress.

Sometimes, however, we rebel; and on this occasion Mr Potter has given us cause. He is not out to make portentous Pirandellian points about illusion and reality; the play's structure makes no pretence that Stage Left, where the angel gets unwillingly bedded, is as real as Stage Right, where Sandra meets the same fate. It offers us merely a good running gag about the words that fall so laboriously from their author's lips and so effortlessly from those of their actors. But the joke is spoiled because Christopher, when speaking for himself, is as conventionally glib as his characters. Or as most characters in most plays; I would not get at Mr Potter particularly if the situation he has conjured up did not demand something more believable.

Granted the style, he uses it rather well; Christopher has an opening monologue which crackles and a post-coital diatribe which propels the play out of its rut. It also propels John Fraser out of his; having offered an anonymous, generalised performance for most of the evening, he suddenly begins to bite. Brenda Cavendish has some good humorous moments, and some even better sullen ones, as Sandra; but both her authors (Christopher and Dennis) tend to patronise her and she seems inclined to go along with them. The best performance is given by Andre van Gyseghem as a doctor persuaded by the exigencies of one-act drama into bestowing a home call on an ambulant patient with nothing more mortal than a bandaged hand to recommend him.

It is the prerogative of children at pantomimes and other such things to despise the hero and love the clowns. Ken Campbell's Old King Cole (Shaw) pre-empts this reaction; Prince Charming is put firmly down and Buttons gets Cinderella. I have, of course, changed the names in the interests of clarity; on second thoughts, the lucky lover is less a Buttons than a junior broker's man. His main attraction is a capacious overcoat, stocked like a supermarket (with a particularly large confectionery counter) and presumably borrowed from Harpo Marx. Mr Campbell has a good memory for gags, and an unerring nose for audience participation. I would have liked a story as well, but the rest of the audience seemed happy to do without. The very bright five-year-old who accompanied me wants to go again, but someone else will have to take him.
1974-12-22-pantomime-pleasure:
Pantomime pleasure

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'Cinderella' and 'Hans Andersen.'

HAVING been numbed by West End pantomimes over the years I found Cinderella (London Casino) very refreshing. Essentially it is not of the West End at all, being a blown-up transfer of the last Christmas show at the Oxford Playhouse, written and directed by that theatre's former chieftain, Frank Hauser.

Mr Hauser has supplied an unusually witty script. I hesitate to call traditional because I am no longer sure what constitutes pantomime tradition. Metropolitan or provincial, few of our shows bear much relation to the Victorian extravaganzas seasonally exhumed by the Players' Theatre; and even Palladium pantomime may be said to have established some traditions of its own.

There is, for example, the convention that every opening scene shall be set in a village square, inhabited by a rollicking, mildly bucolic chorus. Cinderella gets there in its second scene, but it begins, in revolutionary fashion, in Baron Hardup's kitchen, where our heroine, in some kind of trance, is listening to the voices of her dead parents filling her in on her situation. This is undeniably getting down to business, and betrays a concern for narrative that might serve the entire evening, if only the Cinderella story had enough plot to be stretched that far. To help it along Mr Hauser has furnished a sub-plot: conceivably pantomime's first.

I have always thought of Prince Charming, when I have thought of him at all, as an orphan, but he turns out, like other theatrical princes, to have a mother and an uncle. His mother is all right, but his uncle is rotten and even stoops (literally) to stealing the slipper. He is in league with the nastier of the Ugly Sisters. There goes another tradition: when I was young no such gradations in villainy were permitted and both the Uglies were as bad as each other. The mould was first broken, I think, by Hugh Lloyd and Terry Scott; and their example is followed here. Hugh Paddick is prim, attenuated, with the makings of a conscientious objector; Roy Kinnear--in the governing performance of the evening--is more robust, physical, vocally and immorally, his behaviour towards the end earning him some thoroughly justified hisses. "Let us," he remarks on an early exit, "decamp--for a change," and he seems to have taken his own injunction to heart; his demeanour--considering his present context and past record--is quite remarkably straightforward.

Messrs Kinnear and Paddick are finely foiled by Nicky Henson, the most masterful actor in the country under 30; as Buttons he is nimble, tuneful, warm and precise. The only thing he lacks is pathos, but this is a notably unsentimental panto all round. Twiggy is certifiably magic when she arrives at the ball, but for most of the time she is a pretty tough Cinders ("an insolent chit with appalling vowel sounds" is Mr Kinnear's prejudiced estimate), who takes the stage with a shrugging assurance that blossoms in song and, more especially, dance.

Joyce Grant is an enchantingly arch Fairy Godmother, thrown, but not very far, by her inability to remember the appropriate spells and their effects. Her funny fairy makes up for a disappointing pair of Brokers' Men. Harry H. Corbett and Wilfrid Brambell have presumably been hired to reenact their TV relationship, but the script takes little account of this; so they are miscast, and since they are actors and not personality clowns (though Mr Corbett's mugging affords him some independent comic identity) they necessarily flounder.

They do in fact reflect a split in the enterprise. Pleasant though it is to have the Casino reclaimed after two decades of Cinerama, its size distorts a basically intimate show; the spaces have to be arbitrarily filled in with hunks of show biz. I do not expect classical consistency in a pantomime; when the company breaks into a number called "Australia" (for no better reason than that the Queen, the Prince and Dandini are all Aussies), the occasion has the pleasingly zany irrelevance of the production numbers in early Marx Brothers movies.

This song, some adapted music hall tunes, and Vivian Ellis's jaunty "Spread a Little Happiness" belong to one world (reflected in some pretty two-dimensional sets); a stupefyingly unnecessary ensemble about a fox belongs to another. So does the show's main ballad, "For All We Know," though song-buffs might like to note that this is the original song of that name, written by the immortal J. Fred ("You Go To My Head") Coots, and still surviving a prolonged pummelling from Ray Conniff.

  

The same enthusiasts are directed to this year's Palladium show, Hans Andersen, where they will find Frank Loesser's fifties film score in excellent nick. The songs, originally a fleet of vehicles for Danny Kaye, are now beguilingly handled by Tommy Steele; he does especially well with "The Ugly Duckling," though the rangy "Anywhere I Wander" nearly defeats him (a heavenly choir has to be called to the rescue) and he has been robbed of what should have been his main prize: the title song, which has been fed to an anonymous, semi-audible crowd. Somebody called Marvin Laird has furnished additional numbers, and they are horrible.

The production is in a far more advanced state of schizophrenia than Cinderella; to judge by the staging it is another pantomime. (This time we do get the village square opening, first glimpsed as always through a gauze; later on a coach is transformed into a ship through purely theatrical magic, which I'll admit is more fun than white mice and pumpkins.) However, Beverley Cross, who wrote the book, obviously sees the thing as an intelligent, or at least non-cretinous, musical, though the necessity of linking pre-existent songs causes some strain. The close, where Hans, rejected by his beloved Jenny Lind (a creditable performance by Colette Gleeson), realises he can write happy endings even if he can't live them, is very touching.

  

Off the festive track the Open Space continues its assault on the cold and glittering comedies of Carl Sternheim with The Snob. The conception is less of a travesty than its predecessor, Schippel's; the execution is considerably worse. The production is stylish, or rather attitudinised, when it remembers; and nondescript when it forgets.
1974-12-29-cymbeline-transported:
Cymbeline transported

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

Productions transported from Stratford to the Aldwych customarily improve in their acting but suffer in their looks. The current Cymbeline is an exception. The performances remain much as they were: Susan Fleetwood's Imogen is lovelier than ever, but an unexciting competence is the mark of most of those who surround her.

Physically, however, the comparatively cramped quarters of the Aldwych work to the play's advantage. A proscenium arch provides a frame excellently suited to this fantastic fairy-story. Certain aspects of John Napier's set still perturb me: when Imogen arrives in Wales she speaks of mountains but the stage is dotted with molehills. At the back of it, however, there is a charmingly artificial blue sky, complete with puffy clouds, which we see in a most satisfying perspective. And though the play is bound to ramble--that is its charm or its curse, depending on your temperament--it does it no harm for its wanderings to be more circumscribed than they were earlier this year.

An acceptance, not to say an enjoyment, of artifice is essential to either the staging or the understanding of Shakespeare's romances. It abundantly marked the recent National Theatre production of The Tempest; after that cornucopia this Cymbeline, chastely set in glowing white curtains, looks ascetic. But asceticism is not always a mark of virtue: and though our companies may from now on be forced to spend less money on their productions, we should not kid ourselves that there is any artistic merit in a diminished budget.

Cymbeline still suffers from the bloodlessness that has marred much of the RSC's work at Stratford, and has also affected their season at The Place, though it seems to have been eliminated from the recent run of plays at the Aldwych. A year ago, I chid them for their lack of humour; they have got merrier since then, or at any rate more knowing. But in Cymbeline this knowingness can be irritating. It permits, for example, Ian Richardson as Iachimo to assume a comic pose and destroy both the tension and the sexuality of the scene in which he steals Imogen's ring while she lies sleeping. I suspect that Mr Richardson could play this role--a sophisticated Italian villain--in his own sleep; it may be unfair that an actor's continual accomplishment should make one tire of him, but there are no surprises in this performance.

Even if one concedes him the right to his little joke in the bedchamber, the profusion of such moments in other performances eats away at the evening. Wit here becomes a matter of decoration rather than texture (as if the RSC were showing off a new selection of ill-fitting funny hats) so that the most nakedly theatrical moment in the play--the descent of Jupiter on his eagle--is greeted with giggles. The directors (three of them are listed, with Barry Kyle now given top billing) flunk this scene despite their obvious awareness of its importance: conceptually, theirs is a very intelligent production.

Background attractions include a courteous Philario (Malcolm Armstrong) and a disturbing buffoon of a Cloten (Charles Keating), at his best immediately before he meets his death. And there is Miss Fleetwood, who has had a good year: meritorious in Comrades, sharp and odd in Summerfolk, and meltingly triumphant here. The role seems to make a princess out of anyone who plays it; I have never heard of a bad Imogen.

  

In Autosacramentales (Roundhouse) I must declare a lack of interest; this is a 60-minute account of the Creation and Fall derived from the religious dramas of Calderon (the Renaissance Spanish master whom, in the English theatre, no great dramatist is more neglected than) and performed in Portuguese. Naturally, I found it incomprehensible; but not unpleasant to watch. Its cast of 15--totally and permanently nude--have been well drilled by Victor Garcia with, as far as I could tell, not a trace of directorial exploitation.
1975-01-01-best-of-1974-roundup:
ROBERT CUSHMAN

OBSERVER

Best New Play: KENNEDY'S CHILDREN

Best New Musical: COLE

Best Performance by an Actor: ROBERT STEPHENS in Ghosts

Best Performance by an Actress: CLAIRE BLOOM in A Streetcar Named Desire

Best Performance by an Actor in a Supporting Role: JOSS ACKLAND in A Streetcar Named Desire

Best Performance by an Actress in a Supporting Role: BERYL REID in Spring Awakening and Romeo and Juliet

Most Promising New Actor: MICHAEL FEAST in The Tempest

Most Promising New Actress: CELIA QUICK in Stallerhof

Best Production (Director): EDWIN SHERIN for A Streetcar Named Desire

Best Production (Designer): CARL TOMS for Sherlock Holmes

I HAVE one or two doubts about Kennedy's Children; I am enough of a traditionalist not to feel total confidence in a dramatist until he has made his characters talk to each other as well as to me. Still, you can only approach these annual contests determined to vote for whatever turns you on (posterity can sort out the ultimate values) and Mr Patrick's monologues, more than any conventionally structured play this year, sent me out of the theatre aching to tell my friends. It contains, by the way, the most stunning musical moment of any show this year; when the silent barman (as vital to the whole as the auditor of Beckett's Not I) crosses to the juke-box and selects Don McLean's American Pie. [Song lyric excerpt omitted.] Mr Patrick's achievement has been to assemble the generation, and find them the place.

Second best for me was Peter Nichols's Chez Nous; nice that he should have given us this in the same year as the tearing disappointment of The Freeway. If, as we are always being told, a dramatist's job is to get up the noses of his audience Chez Nous should have delighted everyone, since I met hardly a soul with a good word to say for the play. Either they didn't understand what the characters were about, or they understood all too well and winced. I liked Play Mas, The Island, Stallerhof, Travesties (if Tom Stoppard had really got it together it would have been the play of the year); and laughed at The Gingerbread Lady and sizeable sections of The Norman Conquests.

My pleasure in seeing Robert Stephens re-emerge as a major, unmannered actor puts him ahead of considerable competition, much of it emanating from the RSC, where the concentration of male talent at the top has been extraordinary. Nicol Williamson, Ian McKellen, John Wood, Richard Pasco, Ian Richardson, Emrys James and Alan Howard have all given major performances. Pasco's Richard II, which so brilliantly realised the king's ultimate triumph "in being nothing" might have had my vote if it were not a hold-over from the previous year. The same consideration debars Frank Finlay in Saturday Sunday Monday. I also admired Charles Kay in Tartuffe and (not really a contender but delightful nonetheless) Derek Godfrey in The Marriage of Figaro.

It is probably no accident that the best female performances were in American plays: Miss Bloom was hotly pursued by Elaine Stritch and Deborah Norton, though there might be a sui generis award for Maggie Smith in Snap. Joss Ackland only just outpaces Timothy West (in A Month in the Country), Arthur Lowe (in The Tempest and Bingo) and Stefan Kalipha in Play Mas. Mickey Feast may not be altogether new, but then who is? And Cole, being an anthology, may not be an ideal musical but then, this year, what was?

1974 began well (Sherlock Holmes was as nice a New Year present as you could hope for) but it got pretty horrible, particularly in the West End. The RSC did far better at the Aldwych than at Stratford; the new National got off to a splendid start with The Tempest, lost it, and are now apparently en route for Square One. Frustrating.
1975-01-05-on-the-beach:
On the beach

Caryl Churchill registers her Objections to Sex and Violence (Royal Court) on an English beach, but she has not crowded her stage with deck-chairs. The strip of sand we see is all but deserted, partly because it is rocky and exposed, partly because the play is set in an uncertain June. Miss Churchill's characters are taking their holidays ahead of the crowd, and they suffer for it.

Their situation does however permit their author to move them around in discussion groups of two or three. They have their exits and their entrances and these are not, by any realistic standards, plausibly managed. Still, they have not come to the seaside to tell us a story; they are there to decorate a couple of themes.

In the centre is Jule, who stands--in others' eyes if not her own--for a permissive attitude to both sex and violence. She is on the run, having apparently participated in a bombing. After her comes her sister Annie, a repressed, oppressed, depressed woman, accustomed to being sexually and socially exploited; her current job--cleaning house for an ex-lover and his wife--allows her to wallow in both conditions simultaneously. She regards her sister with a furious mixture ("all right, we all know you're the most liberated woman in the world") of envy and disapproval.

With Annie comes her boyfriend, Phil, who does not seem to be exploiting her; perhaps because he is a born victim himself. Half-way through the play she momentarily convinces him that to kill someone--even someone against whom he has no direct grudge--would be both a release and a relief. This provides an arresting if unconvincing first-act curtain. When we return from the bars we wait to see the matter taken further, but all that happens is that Phil backs down, somewhere off stage.

Also intermittently present are a middle-aged couple named Arthur and Madge. Madge, like the lady in the Canadian Club ads, disapproves of virtually everything; Arthur seeks consolation in soft-core porn, which she forces him to burn when she catches him with it. Two of Jule's young men also turn up. One of them spends the first act taunting Phil and Annie as the nearest available straights. The second act finds him less defiant, disguised so effectively that I took him for a new character; and an object of virulent scorn to Jule. He has betrayed their principles; what they are she never makes very clear, but her ex-husband turns up to clarify what they are not. He is a party-line Communist, and as alien to her as any bourgeois.

The play is a conversation-piece with annoying vestiges of plot. I tried approaching it as a Shavian fantasia, but kept stubbing my toes on doggedly naturalistic fragments of character and dialogue, fragments which refused to build into any kind of structure. Individual lines are witty and revealing. Phil's shuffling declaration that faced with a crisis he would always resort to non-violence, or Madge's ambiguous snort of "Young women today want to be whipped." On a larger scale Miss Churchill contrives a pleasing, even touching, imbroglio between Arthur, Madge and a passing old lady of whose general relevance I remained uncertain.

This is the only occasion on which the author makes action work for her as well as words. Even verbally the play never really coheres. The characters' sexual and political attitudes are mechanically aligned, rather than dramatically knotted. Each scene divides in half; first, let's talk about sex, then about violence. Intellectually we can see where the issues join, but then we always could. Madge abhors sex and wants to see the law upheld as forcefully--violently--as possible. Undoubtedly this kind of woman (or this combination of attitudes) exists, but I knew no more about her when I left the theatre than when I entered it. The only character not cut down to size is Jule, who remains in control, a sphinx in the sand, untouchable because inscrutable.

There could hardly be a better moment for a play that explored the motivation--psychological or ideological--of the urban guerrilla; hardly a worse to concentrate on a character who avows no goals and merely hints that killing might be therapeutic. Asked what kind of society he believes in, the pacific Phil can only stammer ludicrously. Jule never gets caught like that, but her magnificent opacity looks to me like dramatic miscalculation. The part calls for stamina, which Rosemary McHale supplies, and to which she adds grace and a touch of humour. Anna Calder-Marshall partners her with obsessive determination; like a highly strung terrier desperately sniffing round a statue. But the best performances are Stephen Moore's Phil and Ivor Roberts's Arthur, two sad sacks kept equally clear of compromise and condescension.
1975-01-12-bigots-and-barons:
Bigots and barons

HECTOR MacMILLAN'S The Sash was first presented by the Pool Theatre at the last Edinburgh Festival but one. It now fetches up a little late at the Hampstead Theatre Club.

The Sash is a displaced Irish play: a Protestant-Catholic conflict, set in Glasgow, with distant echoes of Romeo and Juliet. Towards its close a disaffected Protestant boy and a disillusioned Catholic girl, each living with a rabidly intolerant elder, seem to be reaching some kind of understanding.

Earlier on we get a fuller treatment of the crumbling relationship between the boy and the primly bigoted girl his father wants him to marry, so as to unite the two most zealously Protestant families in the neighbourhood. Dad's attitudes here are not beyond reproach, and young Georgina gives several loud squeals when she finds his hand up her kilt. All the same she seems a much better match for him, a widower, than for his son; at least she is willing and eager to march with him in the Orange Day parade on which the play centres. It is his son's abstention from this yearly outburst of anti-Papist jubilation that sparks off old Bill MacWilliam's bitterest fury. It is the day of his year, and his life centres around its symbols. He even enters drying himself with an orange towel.

Bill is given a towering, roaring performance by Andrew Keir: Scots acting at its strongest. Doreen Cameron's Georgina, pert and blinkered, is similarly archetypal. Her opposite number--the Irish girl from downstairs who has seen too much violence, but has acquired a wider perspective through suffering--is less convincing, perhaps because she comes nearer to having the author's blessing than any other character. Though he may be willing to call down a plague on both their houses, the Protestants get by far the greater share of Mr MacMillan's vitriol. I assume he is avenging himself on his own background; the mildly rebellious son has the look of an author's surrogate.

As domestic drama, The Sash works pretty well, even as domestic comedy. We are in Alf Garnett territory; the more reactionary the characters the more we laugh. Let us hope we are being purged. But the play's naturalism is too limited in scope for us to accept occasional excursions into song and dance or breathy, antiphonal dialogue, designed to heighten our awareness of the major issues. These sadly respond hardly more to miniaturist treatment than to the schematised debating of the previous week's Objections to Sex and Violence.

Perhaps the blame lies less with the material than with our expectations. The reason why new plays are usually less enjoyable than revivals is that we approach the latter knowing what to expect. We go to a new work unwisely hoping, even demanding, to be illumined and/or lacerated, the victims of years of extravagant promises from playwrights, reviewers and publicists. So herewith a warning: The Sash is not bad, but it will not change your life.

  

The Royal Shakespeare Company's King John (Aldwych) is now attributed to John Barton rather than, as at Stratford, to Shakespeare. This is honest; though it cannot hide the fact that the few extended bits of Bard remaining are the most gripping in the evening, and the only ones allowing the actors to express anything resembling full humanity. For the rest a rather brittle style (Jokey-Didactic) prevails, suitable to a lengthy morality which merely tells us that Death (who makes a personal appearance in the saturnine figure of Mike Gwilym, this company's most interesting new actor) comes even to kings.

To point this moral any king would serve; and Emrys James needs all his resources to keep us attentive to the fortunes of John, whom he portrays as an unstable clown, falling fecklessly into evil but scarcely deserving the opprobrium he attracts. Denis Holmes lends the evening a little depth as the most scrupulous of the barons; and Ian McKellen is ringingly attractive as the Bastard, whose honesty seems, in this jingling world, such an anachronism. Mr McKellen himself seems somewhat old-fashioned in this context; to put it another way, his is the best acting in the play.
1975-01-12-billy-gets-the-treatment:
Billy gets the treatment

EVERY collector of American show records knows that the best original cast LPs are made by CBS, and are generally produced by Goddard Lieberson. He has been imported to supervise the recording of Billy (CBS 70133), and the resulting album is as sleek as the Drury Lane original.

There is, however, nothing aurally remarkable about Michael Crawford's performance in the title role and John Barry's tunes are repetitive without being compulsive. The most pleasing is 'Any Minute Now,' a duet for two of Billy's birds which can turn wistful or brassy depending on which lady is singing. Don Black's lyrics survive respectably, though invention often gives way to trickiness. A couplet like 'I'll hang my hat in every part of the atlas / Most of the time I will be hopelessly hatless' is not worth the trouble it takes to sing.

Billy's West End competitor The Good Companions (EMI EMC 3042) is ramshackle by comparison. All the same it wins. John Mills and Judi Dench are authentic stars; talking or singing, Miss Dench captivates the moment she opens her mouth. Andre Previn's music is sometimes undistinguished, but never formless; the ballad Dance of Life distils an original, complex melancholy, and the production number A Little Travelling Music racily underlines some of Johnny Mercer's best syllabic juggling.

Mr Mercer is past his prime as a lyricist (though not as a singer, as two LPs recorded in London this year bear eloquent witness); he has a shaky grasp of English, as opposed to American, locutions, and he has never really been a theatrical writer. He is the genius of the one-shot song. In this show he is liable to move from inspiration to cliche within a single song. But he retains the lyricist's supreme gifts: a delight in the flavour of words and the ability to make them ride the music. I doubt if there is a rhythmically misplaced word in the score. The rhyming tag at the end of a song ('Agitate your tempo, professor / I taught the score to your predecessor') is unmistakable Mercer.

A consideration of his work leads us backwards, to where most of the best show records come from.
