The Mermaid's Cole has been recorded on two discs (RCA LRL2 5054), which preserve most of the songs and, less appealingly, some of the linking material in which the compilers attempt to father on Cole Porter their own nudgingly patronising view of Broadway and Hollywood. In the theatre the show is delightful, but when taken home most of the performers are audibly trying too hard; the exception is Kenneth Nelson, who expresses all the defiance of I Happen to Like New York and even made me listen afresh to Night and Day. Otherwise I shall treasure the album for the ensembles, for Ken Moule's tingling arrangements, and for nine or ten songs elsewhere unobtainable.

Porter has done better than any other composer out of the renewed interest in classic show songs. Though successive explorations of his neglected work have shown his musical range to be far wider than has been supposed -- and I rate him far higher now than I would have done five years ago -- his lyrics, even when impassioned, all speak with the same dryly ingenious voice. (When he ventures into Shakespearia, in Brush Up Your Shakespeare, the effect is ventriloquial, we cannot see the Manhattan sophisticate's lips moving.) His songs may belong to the supper-club to which no composer has bequeathed a larger catalogue of viable material rather than to the theatre.

More of it can be sampled on another double album, Cole Porter in London (World Records SHB 26), which collects original cast recordings of Porter shows (and of individual Porter songs included in revues) performed in London between 1919 and 1951. The gift inside the package is Gertrude Lawrence with her classic The Physician and I, neglected but rousingly cynical exercise called It's Bad for Me.

Miss Lawrence turns up on a companion record, George Gershwin in London, as does Claude Hulbert, rendering Clap Yo' Hands much as Bertie Wooster might have sung it in his bath; which -- since P. G. Wodehouse wrote the book for this as for dozens of other musicals in the twenties -- is bizarrely appropriate.

An astute A & R man can make a show LP an enjoyable entity, but films generally sound scrappy. This is particularly the case with the MGM double album of That's Entertainment (MGM 2659 033), a film which was scrappy to begin with, because of the producer's reluctance to stay with any number long enough for us to see it build. At full stretch On the Atchison, Topeka and the Santa Fe is irresistible; cut down it means little, and on this record virtually nothing. Far more satisfying are the soundtrack recordings of four Astaire-Rogers pictures: Swing Time and The Gay Divorce (EMI EMTC 101), Top Hat and Shall We Dance? (EMTC 102). These find space even for the RKO pipes (endearing like a distress signal) at the start of each movie, as well as for significant dialogue (mostly Ginger telling Fred that he'll never learn to dance). If you just want to hear the songs (Porter, Gershwin, Kern, Berlin), there are better versions available, including studio performances by Astaire himself. But as nostalgia objects these discs are irresistible and though you may weary of the sound of tapping feet in current versions of the continental so overwhelming.
1975-01-19-tragedy-of-the-hungry-tribe:
Tragedy of the hungry tribe

I WOULD like to proclaim Peter Brook's Théâtre des Bouffes-du-Nord as the most exciting playhouse in Britain. The fact that it is actually in Paris hinders me somewhat; but I cannot repress my delight that the greatest of living British directors should now, for the first time in his career, have his own theatre. His troupe may contain only one British actor (the origins of the others stretching from Africa to Japan) and it may perform in French; but chauvinism will out.

In this scooped-out shell of a theatre, formerly disused for 20 years, contact between actors and audience is unusually (though not, of course, unprecedentedly) close; Mr Brook exploited it in Timon of Athens, a play about hospitality and its collapse. Timon has now been followed by Les Iks, a more extreme treatment of the same theme.

Timon's disillusion caused him to pray for the destruction of every social bond, and this is the situation depicted in Les Iks. The title refers to a Ugandan mountain tribe, whom a governmental decree forced into an almost overnight change of life-style. Originally hunters, they were compelled to become farmers, a pursuit suited neither to their temperament nor their terrain. Drought compounded their plight; and they began to starve.

In the 1960s an English-born, American-based anthropologist, Colin Turnbull, spent two years among the Ik, subsequently describing his experiences in a book, The Mountain People. He tells of a world in which survival has become the only value and food the only good; a good man is in fact defined, not as one who gives food, but as one who has eaten it. The family has hardly any meaning; the young and the old are victims of the few who have somehow managed to attain a short-lived prime. Mr Turnbull devotes a final chapter to prophecy; his thesis is not merely that in similar circumstances we could become like the Ik (which few would dare dispute), but that in many ways we already have. Here he strains a bit; sending one's children to a day-school is not invariably the same as banishing them permanently from the household at the age of three, so that their only hope of survival lies in combining into predatory packs.

The tone of the book is surprisingly jocund; Mr Turnbull writes with cool detachment, not merely because this may be held to be scientifically appropriate, but because he realises that nothing is more shocking than unshockability--the characteristic of the Ik and eventually, he implies, of anyone who shares their life. He does not mock the Ik; indeed, he scrupulously records the occasions on which they mocked him, misleading outsiders being one of their few remaining pleasures. The anthropologist as fall-guy haunts the book; and comes to solid life in the play. The adaptation (by Colin Higgins and Denis Cannan) is remarkably faithful; but the fact of dramatisation inevitably alters the emphases. When we see Turnbull enacted, conscientiously capturing suffering for posterity with camera and cassette-recorder, he becomes ludicrously irrelevant in a way that may be hinted at, but is never embodied, in his own lucid prose.

I have mentioned suffering, a word sparingly employed by Mr Turnbull, but inescapably by Mr Brook and his actors. They have sacrificed the book's didacticism, reproduced its humour, and intensified its pain. A couple of paragraphs about the visit of two missionaries become a great tragi-comic set-piece; cracked voices desperately sing out "Rock of Ages," having been promised food in return for volume. The production never begs for pity; a woman announces that she has not eaten for three days and laughs; but not nobly--contemptuously. The Ik attitude is catching; when some of the lucky ones vomit up the food they have just swallowed, many of the audience laugh. I could not join in but I suspect that they were right. Probably the most powerful sequence shows a woman picking up a piece of orange peel, whimpering for a second, and beginning to eat; a child snatches the peel from her and is joined by two other children; the three of them conclude by jumping on the woman.

The cosmopolitan cast make no attempt to impersonate Africans; with superb cohesion they show us instead irreducible, nerveless, shuffling humanity. (The contrast to the gross and fumbling portrayal of Vietnamese in Mr Brook's US could hardly be more marked.) The barren theatre is the perfect environment: rungs fixed into the exposed back wall enable two of the actors to undertake a breathtaking mountain ascent; there is a recurring image of the Ik sitting with their backs to us, their legs dipping into the void that was once a stage. Brook wants to restage this production in London, in English; finding him the right venue may not be easy, but there is no more urgent quest confronting our theatre.

  

Tom Stoppard's Rosencrantz And Guildenstern Are Dead has returned to the Young Vic, from which indeed it has seldom been absent in two years. Mr Stoppard has written more engaging plays, but none so satisfyingly shaped; it dovetails and resolves every one of its preoccupations, philosophic, dramaturgic, or merely exuberantly verbal. (Mr Stoppard is an incurable semantic.) On the tongues of Christopher Timothy and Richard O'Callaghan not all of the wit emerges as trippingly as Lord Hamlet (or I) would desire; but their awareness of the characters' plight is admirable. As a bonus Graham Crowden has slipped across the road from the National to re-create his definitive First Player, resonant with remembered bravado, electric with contempt.

True love conquers all--as usual

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a new Osborne play and a Pinter revival.

JOHN OSBORNE'S The End of Me Old Cigar (Greenwich) is the latest paean to true love. This is a commendable preoccupation, but his view of it is uncomfortably proprietorial. One favoured couple per play appears to be his limit, and it may not be accidental that the lady in the present case is portrayed by the author's wife.

In this new play Jill Bennett (Mrs Osborne) and Keith Barron share a rhapsodic interlude in the midst of elegant squalor. They are guests at the house of Lady Regine Frimley, an exalted brothel-keeper out to screw her clients in all possible senses; she entertains a succession of prominent men so that she may eventually expose them and implicitly the whole male sex. It is all their ridiculousness (I apologise for the double entendre; they will keep coming). It is surprising to find Mr Osborne endorsing even so eccentric a brand of Women's Lib as this, but, of course, it turns out that he had no such intention. Lady Regine is morally defeated by the joy of Miss Bennett and Mr Barron, and practically by as feeble and arbitrary a plot-twist as a reputable dramatist can ever have employed to bring down his final curtain.

Though he may have little sympathy with the lady and her cohorts, Mr Osborne has found uses for them en route. On arrival, each is granted a streak or two of individuality, but they soon drop indistinguishably into the house-style, the frigid raillery -- spinsterish even when scabrous -- which dominates this author's worst plays, and disfigures even his best (though in A Sense of Detachment it was elevated, unencumbered by the complications of plot and character, into real humour, real passion). Rachel Roberts as Regine seems to have half the lines, and speaks them well, and the play, in Hayden Griffin's designs and Max Stafford-Clark's direction, looks as nice as any country-house comedy in years.

It was tough to be a theatre critic in 1958. That year saw the first production of Harold Pinter's The Birthday Party, and, though a couple of reviewers may now pride themselves on the lonely wisdom which they extended to the play, the rest simply rejected it must surely shudder. Truly, the oldest hath borne most; we that are young shall never see so much. It would be becoming in us to comfort our elders by deciding that really they did not miss so much; that the play, though very well for its time, seems in 1975 no more than a interestingly quaint. I anticipated that I would have some such response to the revival at the Shaw Theatre, but Kevin Billington's production confounded me. The play moves here with the confident autonomous gait of a classic.

It is almost possible to take it for a masterpiece, so astonishing is Mr Pinter's command of dialogue and stagecraft; indeed it is his wholly traditional technical expertise that makes the fifties response to this play seem so surprising. The humiliation of Stanley, the browbeating of Meg's seaside boarding-house at the hands of Goldberg and McCann, is totally hypnotic as a process. It is more than that because our interest, if hardly our sympathy, is proportion to Stanley himself, and almost as much by his external language as by his cross-talking persecutors.

At the birthday party itself, Stanley is momentarily exposed to the two simultaneously; Meg's speech of congratulation assaults his ears, while McCann's torch shines in his eyes. This hint that a man's protective shell may be used to destroy him is the most powerful moment in the play. But it never captures this unity of theme; the rest of the party is a bravura piece of atmospheric writing in which meaning evaporates. I may accept (though I do not really believe) that we need not be told why Stanley is finally reduced to zombiedom, but it seems an inexcusable failure to black out the stage and so we never even find out how. For the rest of the play, the emphasis switches to Goldberg, whose steady line of patter represents his hold on the world; when it falters, as, momentarily, does Petey, we see how close he comes to being as lost as Stanley. But this is a schematic demonstration, further undermined by the realisation that by the third act the play has outlasted its own narrative reserves. What Goldberg's reduction of Lulu or her whole character are meant to add I have never understood.

Mr Billington brilliantly unites the characters' isolation in playing, in pools of loneliness and bewilderment. John Alderton is a regally unsentimental Stan, gruff when he gets the chance, whining when he doesn't; in aspect a desiccated cross between John Lennon and Piggy of Lord of the Flies. (Fate fashions impasses for men who wear glasses.) Sydney Tafler as Goldberg looks, especially in moustache, exact, although neither he nor his director always makes the most of the jokes. Goldberg is, for an actor, the most munificent Jew since Shylock; Lee Montague's television performance remains indelible (it had a great deal to do with establishing the Pinter vogue) and it might be worth recalling that the part was created by John Slater who died just as this revival opened. Anna Wing strikes the proper cloying chord as Meg; and Basil Lord is nobly reserved as her husband Petey, who may represent the closest approximation to a moral force in the whole of Mr Pinter's work. Eliot would have made a guardian out of him.

Female conspiracy (Osborne) and male dementia (Pinter) collide in Laure (Theatre at New End). This is announced by its director, Steven Dartnell, as a modern adaptation of Strindberg's The Father, and it does indeed make a few fashionable lurches, emphasising (though hardly exploring) the theme of insanity, and hinting at incest. More to the point is that Mr Dartnell has drastically telescoped the action, gaining in sharpness if hardly in clarity. That the cast are catastrophically young for their roles (except for one who is too old) may, since there is no attempt to disguise it, be intentional.

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the National Theatre's new production of John Gabriel Borkman.

THE theatre's contribution to the Ibsen revival is Ibsen's John Gabriel Borkman at the Old Vic.

Ibsen's penultimate play is concerned, characteristically, with the hallucinatory effect on normal life of a man -- a "builder" who preceded him and the sculptor who was to follow. In When We Dead Awaken, J. G. Borkman, banker, expresses his author's fears of having sacrificed his life -- not to pay his wife -- to the demands of his art (or more brutally of his career) and of not having produced work of a quality to justify the sacrifice. Master builder Solness grew tired of building houses, and turned instead to spectacular towers; Ibsen increasingly forsook intricate domestic realism for prose poetry.

But since he was still telling stories about families he could not abandon his old skills altogether; and, in John Gabriel Borkman, he parades them before dismissing them. Borkman has dreamed and dared too much; more prosaically he has embezzled a vast amount of money, and been detected; eight years on, his career and his marriage lie in ruins. He is a recluse, never stirring from his room; one floor below, his unforgiving wife listens to the ceaseless pad of his feet; and dreams of getting their son to redeem the family name.

The situation is explained and developed in three rather tight acts with a decidedly exceptional event for Ibsen, and with a new limpid simplicity. The machinery is far less cumbrous than usual; Mrs Borkman's hopes are foredoomed to frustration, and there is something almost contemptuous about the ease with which her son is allowed to escape her, slipping off to a warmer climate with the local siren. We sense that the reason for the speedy dispatch of this business is that Ibsen is not really interested in it. The play exists for its final scene, in which Borkman begins an ascent to the mountaintops in order to survey the country which he has always believed to be his kingdom. He dies of exposure, according to his wife, but by the account of her sister whose love he had sacrificed to his ambition at the start of his career -- of guilt, clutching his heart like ice.

The mountain air may kill Borkman, but it makes the piece the most bracing, least stifling of Ibsen's after Peer Gynt. It is a play of extremes, beginning with a strange attractive combination of psychological tension and narrative relaxation, and bursting into poetic freedom; corroded love for her husband.

The seductress, Mrs Wilton, the only unillusioned character present, is played by Anna Carteret, most enlivening at her first appearance, rather too blatant at her second; and the smallest parts are done exceedingly well by Cheryl Campbell and Barbara Keogh. The production yields a surprising number of laughs, none forced, all justified, but I doubt if Mr Hall's view of the play is fundamentally comic. Grandeur seems to be the aim; and all three leading performances, though incomplete, sporadically attain it.

It is in the nature of Ralph Richardson's Borkman to play tricks with perspective; his is a typically quirky performance, allowing the character no mercy, half Ancient Mariner, half White Knight, he presents a florid, majestic fraud. His pacing of his room denotes nervousness rather than caged impatience; his gait, once freed from his wife, is as awkward as the iron I once dreamed of quarrying out of the mountains, is invested with all the mysterious conviction of which this actor is capable. Borkman dreams of a comeback, but Richardson never lets us believe in its possibility. The text may appear to support him; Ibsen is at his most self-lacerating, and Borkman's actual lines may suggest no more than wistful megalomania. But the architecture of the play seems to demand something more. For Borkman finally does confront his wife, does break free; both the confrontation and the release are under-written, but the actor must somehow find them within his own personality. They are nowhere prefigured in Richardson's performance, though he is magnificently rotund in the final speech; actor and character reach the heights together.

In his ascent he is beautifully partnered, selflessly served, by Peggy Ashcroft as his forsaken sister-in-law; beauty and selflessness, indeed, are everywhere apparent in her performance, sometimes too oppressively. She emphasises nobility as insistently as Sir Ralph denies it; it has grown on her as the play has proceeded, for at the beginning she has played a fine duet with Wendy Hiller's Mrs Borkman, suggesting that they remain sisters in selfishness; they have merely sublimated their bitterness in different ways. Miss Hiller is rocky, unforgiving and, like the production, rewardingly unafraid of melodrama; but she fails to convey her corroded love for her husband.

Statements is about South Africa's racial laws; and yet it is these that inevitably make the greater impact on an audience. I found the carefully fashioned dialogue more rewarding on a second hearing, but it means less than the cruel play of police torches on two naked, imperfect, vulnerable, human bodies.

Nudity here is more than a device, almost a dramatic subject; Miss Bryceland's shyness and pride under interrogation, Mr Kingsley's shame and anguish, are what will remain. Coupled with Statements in a daunting double-bill (probably the most dimly lit show in London) is Not I, Samuel Beckett's monologue for a frantic, disembodied mouth, white-lipped in the encircling blackness so that my thoughts strayed towards Al Jolson. This was probably reprehensible of them and certainly fatal; since, by the time I had refocused them, the play (11 minutes long) was over. Mr Fugard had exhausted my concentration; but two years ago I found Not I (voiced, as now, by Billie Whitelaw) riveting.

Howard Barker's Claw is the liveliest thing I remember at the Open Space: the engrossing story of a neglected schoolboy's rise to prosperity as a ponce and summary extinction at the hands of the ruling class. Act One is mordantly funny scene-setting; Act Three is a savage verdict. Act Two should assemble the evidence, but Mr Barker devotes it instead to a cartoon of sexual laxity at Ministerial level, racier but no more relevant than John Osborne's in The End of Me Old Cigar. Billy Hamon burns through the leading role in a tight, lucid production by Chris Parr in which everybody deserves praise and Roger Sloman, Rod Beacham and Isabel Dean hereby receive it.

Gosh, what improvising!

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on two plays from Stratford and Max Wall's one-man show.

THE 1974 season at Stratford was generally reckoned to be unfortunate, an estimate in which I concurred. I did not, however, see all the productions; and the two which arrived in London last week are gaps that I am glad to have filled. Last year on Avon was happier than I had realised.

Babies Grow Old brings the RSC to the ICA. It was first staged in Stratford's smallish Other Place and, like most of the work of its director, Mike Bogdanov, is composed through improvisation. Surprisingly, considering that this has been going on long enough perhaps for its actors to regard it as just another text, it retains its peculiar fascination, the overheard quality of a dramatic solution. There is an unusual quality of document in a theatre. It is not merely a matter of short or half-formed sentences; these certainly occur, but in the performance of one actor, Matthew Guinness, the form reaches out to incorporate great rolling cadences.

Mr Guinness plays a youngish doctor, an out-sider in what is otherwise a family group. He is eager and well meaning and out of his depth. He sits on a sofa, politely refusing and then consuming innumerable cups of tea and, as afternoon gives place to evening, glasses of Scotch. He seems reluctant to go home, though he often gestures towards it, and we may guess that he is not happy there. He finally breaks out into an extraordinary tirade about his own profession, lashing himself as a licensed drug-peddler, backtracking to reassure himself that after all he is a good deal charier with the prescriptions than most of his colleagues, then taking off again into horrible premonitions of the world his daughter will inherit.

Mr Guinness's tumbling eloquence (underlined by the elaborate unceasing gaucherie of his arms and legs, which betray him whenever he tries either to relax or to persuade) is a tribute to the improvisational method; no writer could set down the stops and starts, the furious emphases, that make up his speeches (or would even dare sprinkle them with the `goshes' and `supers' that seem so bashfully accurate here), and no actor could derive them from a conventional text. Emlyn Williams's The Corn is Green might have a young man rather like Mr Guinness's doctor, but he would use well-turned English and Shakespearean quotations, not such things as a child's `I don't know' transformed into a diagnosis of a life-style.

The home which Mr Guinness invades belongs to a half-crippled old woman who sits beneath her roof, but hardly to address a word to her. And by appropriating an unoccupied bed on the ground floor, they unintentionally confine her to an upper room. It is a symbol of exquisite injustice, and rather horrible because no one seems aware of it. The acting is mostly remarkable. Jane Lapotaire's Viola should address the audience, seeking a sounding-board rather than a mirror. When Robert Lloyd's Sebastian appears he is, as he should be, Viola's twin sister's gallant whirlwind opportunism.

Miss Lapotaire, who races round the stage as if taking possession of it before demanding what she should do in Illyria, is the most believable boy-girl since Barbara Jefford 17 years ago; and she has the advantage of a production which explores all the play's bisexual tensions. The atmosphere is, in Auden's phrase, a bit whiffy. Here is an Orsino (John Price) as apt to fondle a page as a mistress, who at one point addresses himself to the young twin, and says, "Most wonderful!" in a squeal of exquisite recognition, finding herself confronted with two apparent boy-girls.

The scenes in which one heroine woos the other are exemplary, Viola alternately retreating and raising as Mary Rutherford's Olivia (the best I remember) sheds her defences and goes on the attack. From her first appearance, indeed, she shows signs of life and humour; it is because she is inclined to speak well of fools that Nicol Williamson's Malvolio -- a Welsh precision machine -- might so jealously fur her soul and ultimately for her body.

All this brings out the interdependence of the play's two plots. It is Malvolio's contemptuous description of Viola that excites Olivia's desire to see her. Olivia, embracing Malvolio with Illyrian carelessness, unwittingly primes him for his downfall. Mr Williamson's dreams of lust in the garden are terrible to overhear, his smile a major climax. His enemies are formidable: David Waller a malcontent Sir Toby, living on the edge of his niece's tolerance and his own, and Ron Pember a tattered clown who accepts tips, plaudits and rebukes with the steely disdain of an over-seasoned entertainer, insisting out on us until the last word of the last song.

A seductive rumour has it that the part of Feste in this production was originally offered to Max Wall; and in fact his demeanor in his one-man show Aspects of Max Wall (Garrick) is not dissimilar to Mr Pember's. Mr Wall ("I'm an mourning for my material") exploits, but does not indulge, his new cult status. He is a sweetness itself as he remonstrates with the musicians who have beaten him to the end of a phrase ("you were too fond and far too quick and everything went wrong"), but he is liable, with a flash of his teeth and an upward thrust of his chin, to dismiss them and us and the whole business of being the last surviving star of the music-hall.

Mr Wall is a battered cheerful misanthrope, a singing guitarist of great charm, a man of strange and sudden pleasures, a Beckett figure. (Compare the delight he squeezes from the word "stool" with that taken by Krapp in "spool.") I have insufficient space for him, which is a shame; that I have none for the Oxford Playhouse's disinterment of The Vegetable, a cheery, weary comedy by Scott Fitzgerald, is a mercy.

Fighting off sharks

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

JOHN McGRATH's Fish in the Sea--presented by the 7:84 company at the Half Moon, Aldgate East, prior to a national tour, its first stop Lancaster--is an unclassifiable piece. It suggests a disturbing novel brought to the stage in the style of a dramatised documentary.

Like most stage documentaries it is a kind of musical revue. It is traditional enough in form: its first half has a title song, and for this number to be the highlight of the evening. It is a mixture of defiance and foreboding. The title, the feelings of a father and son-in-law, both involved in the workers' occupation of a Liverpool engineering factory; the foreboding in the three girls of the family. All of them are fish in the sea; the point at issue is whether they will manage to escape or defeat the sharks.

Song is a great crystalliser. It can concentrate meaning without debasing it, and the musical and dramatic impact of this one is tremendous. For it can also produce dangerous simplifications. Mr McGrath's convictions are militant but he is sceptical about the chances of being realised. The title-song expresses this division, but theatres and audiences being what they are, it is the optimistic rhythms that are uppermost in us at the interval.

When we return there is less music. The first half has contained some buoyant rock numbers which the band can carry even when the actors falter. In the second half Mr McGrath makes greater use of traditional tunes, Marching Through Georgia to bellow distrust of bosses and Two Lovely Black Eyes to cartoon a trio of Labour MPs. The songs are fun, but they are also a bit perfunctory. The heart of the play is now elsewhere.

The Labour delegation are the only caricatured figures in the piece; otherwise Mr McGrath solves the political playwright's eternal problem of how to treat his adversaries simply by excluding them. The real tensions are within the family, one of the three sisters marries a shop-floor activist, another is courted by a Marxist intellectual and emotionally besieged by an Ulster Protestant gunman. In this last character are concentrated reserves of bitterness that have less to do with sectarian struggles than with Mr McGrath's feelings over the wastage of working-class anger. Andy, the gunman, is one character who never sings.

He is Scots, not Irish, in origin; we are on the same ground with him as in Hector MacMillan's The Sash. That was a small, funny naturalistic play that ruptured itself whenever it reached out. This is a multi-layered chronicle, funnier still and almost an epic.

The qualification is necessary mainly because of the size of the Half Moon. Pam Brighton's production and Bill Dudley's designs are endlessly inventive at moving the action and the scene-changes along, but they have not been able to provide the framing devices that might make us glory in the form rather than merely accept it. As it is there are more strands of action than can be comfortably encompassed and at least one character--an atheistic, sentimental Welshman--whose inclusion seems, to put it benevolently, over-generous.

The play lasts three and a quarter hours and by its close acting, production and text were beginning to show signs of wear; only the audience still looked invigorated. Most of the performances are excellent: my favourite, for pace and geniality, is John Judd, an open-faced comedian with barbed wire on his tongue.

7:84 is a company whose minor technical lapses can be forgiven: it is not selling slickness, but it does not try to pass off muffed moves or mistimed lines as part of its charm.

  

This is the state to which, farther east at the Theatre Royal, Stratford, Theatre Workshop has now been reduced. Superficially Maxwell Shaw's production of Labiche's An Italian Straw Hat is smoother than some of its recent shows. But even its passing facilities are disastrous, destroying the sense of danger basic to this as to all classic farces.

Mr Shaw has at least given the play an agreeable spine: as Fadinard, the distraught bridegroom, traverses Paris in search of a straw hat with poppies (no substitute accepted), his in-laws follow him in eight horse-drawn cabs and it is pleasant to see them mime this progress, high-stepping across the stage. But Sylvester McCoy lacks all precision as Fadinard, and the male supporting acts range from a good imitation of Eric Morecambe to a terrible one of Bill Fraser. As ever at this theatre, the girls are attractive, physically and vocally; Melody Kaye is as valuable as Valerie Walsh is melodious.

  

Eastward still, but south of the river, lies Greenwich, whose platform stage affords a fairer haven for drawing-room sets than any proscenium arch: the acres of red plush in which Bernard Culshaw has framed The Picture of Dorian Gray are richly imposing, so long as they are left alone. When the stage hands or the lighting technicians begin to play tricks with them, to effect a change of scene, the results are clumsy. John Osborne's adaptation of the Wilde novella is faithful even unto death; he has invented no theatrical equivalent for the original narrative method of revealing Dorian's guilty secret to us, so the second half of the play should prove incomprehensible to many people. But it includes much entertaining material, as well heard or read, and really makes a better play than many of Wilde's own. Unfortunately Anne Blake is the only member of the cast who knows how to weight an epigram and she has very little to say.
1975-02-23-the-comedians-and-their-criti:
The comedians and their critic

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a new play by Trevor Griffiths and two Shakespeare productions.

THERE were three Englishmen, two Irishmen and a Jew, and they were learning how to be stand-up comics. They lived in the north, which made their immediate goal the working men's clubs. After that the Palladium and perhaps the world.

The plot of Trevor Griffiths's Comedians (Nottingham Playhouse) goes something like that. His six hopefuls are attending evening classes to receive instruction from an old star of the music halls. One night they are paraded at a club to do their stuff, in between bingo sessions, and to receive the judgment of a prestigious promoter from the south. He listens to them, signs a couple of them up, and dismisses the others with counsel and criticism.

Two decades ago, in The Entertainer, John Osborne was content to plant the dying music hall on the stage before us and trust to its power as an image. Mr Griffiths tries something more disturbing; the tradition he explores is, for better or worse, still alive. The implication of the play is that it is very much for worse; Mr Griffiths is far more concerned than was Mr Osborne with the quality of laughter. Nobody found Archie Rice funny; it was almost his dramatic point that he played only there for the nudes. But whatever the individual quality of Mr Griffiths's jesters, the breed they aspire to join is flourishing.

Their medium is one-line quick-change patter; the man from London castigates one aspirant for maintaining continuity in his material. People get bored, and they do not want to be burdened with a comic's individuality. So, goes the advice, fire your shots from as many angles as possible, but always at the same targets. We are now a multi-racial society, and afraid of it, so racist jokes go down well; if an anti-Irish joke is told by an Irishman, the savour, so long as he does not so to speak harp on it, is all the sweeter. We can even congratulate him and ourselves on our sportsmanship. We profess to be liberated about sex and are even more afraid of that; so jokes that manage to be both risque and evasive--elaborate euphemisms--are also in order.

Within his own terms, the visitor offers brilliant analyses of the turns presented to him, and the excellence of the writing and acting (by Ralph Nossek) of this role is matched by that of his subjects; one may not agree with his judgment of them, but one can see what has prompted it in each case. Richard Eyre's direction of the various comics can hardly be faulted, and several of the performances are memorable: Dave Hill an engaging loser, Stephen Rea a coruscating winner, and, in a category of his own, Jonathan Pryce.

Mr Pryce looks and snarls like an emaciated Nicol Williamson; he is lankier, nearly as powerful, and more controlled. His nose is long and sharp, his death's head shaven, his face, when he does his routine, white, and his body trim and grotesquely flexible. He plays the one clown who rebels, breaks taboos, and dredges up the undertow of all the other acts. He brings on two prosperously dressed cut-out figures and attacks them. "It's not envy, it's hate." His punchline is "National Unity? Up your sunshine." He naturally disgusts the agent (who has exhorted this crew of pawky or abrasive northerners to emulate Max Bygraves, the archetype of southern blandness) and shocks the old pro instructor who cautions that if you hate your audience, "you'll end up hating yourself."

Mr Pryce seems to me to prove him right (I didn't like his act much, either). But I hesitate to draw definite conclusions, since the scene in which they thunder out their differences, though powerful in a generalised way, is muddy. The acoustics of the Playhouse are unkind to unfocused rhetoric and Jimmy Jewel, though he looks suitably careworn, is over-ingenious casting for the teacher.

Mr Griffiths has, on this showing, written another impenetrably private play on a public theme; but one worth following as far as possible. He is, when he chooses, a very funny writer; while his protagonists knock themselves out for laughs, his minor characters effortlessly achieve them. A school caretaker (Richard Simpson) looks disapprovingly on, a bingo caller (John Joyce) stolidly announces the acts that have so rudely interrupted the real business of his evening, and a passing Pakistani (Talat Hussain), telling an adapted Jewish joke, wraps up the racial theme on which Mr Griffiths has played inventive variations throughout.

  

Both this week's Shakespeare productions begin with a sing-song: a favourite method among the several now in vogue for deferring as long as possible the awful moment at which the first line of text will have to be uttered. The Two Gentlemen of Verona (Young Vic) commences with a ballad which, though none too audible, seems to have something to do with fools and lovers, and probably with the frequent difficulty of distinguishing between the two. This makes it, of course, a very suitable opening for any of the early comedies, and Two Gentlemen is as early as a comedy could well be. The road away from it could lead nowhere but up, and the play is well furnished with signposts pointing in that direction.

The Tempest, at the other end of the canon, contains a large number of original vocal gems and most of them are preprised (the opposite of reprised) before the play begins. Sea shanties predominate, giving way to the catch "flout 'em and scout 'em" with its significant refrain "thought is free." The production which has come to Wyndham's from Leeds Playhouse clearly knows it to be significant, for the line is repeated several times; when the play proper begins all passages concerning freedom are reverentially delivered, the word itself isolated as if hung about with invisible quotation marks.

Paul Scofield is the most benevolent Prospero I've seen, marvellously tender with his daughter, but so lacking in bitterness that his passion at the end seems to spring from nowhere. It is, however, superbly rendered: "I'll break my staff" brought me literally out of my seat. It suggests incredible pressures, even if we are left uncertain what they are. Here, for moments, is the greatest of acting. Back in Verona, Pip Miller's Proteus is notably accomplished, while Alfred Lynch gives initial promise of being the first Launce in theatrical history not to be upstaged by his dog. This one, however (he is called Flicker and has traces of terrier), has tricks in reserve. None of your customary mournful tail-waggers, he knows when he is being insulted and barks to prove it.
1975-03-02-the-happiest-of-heartbreaks:
The happiest of Heartbreaks

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the National's new Shaw production.

THE National Theatre generally performs best in periods of retrenchment. At present it may be carrying this policy to extremes: the three plays in the current repertory have cast-lists of eight, ten and two, which suggests that the National is doing rather less than its bit to relieve theatrical unemployment. But those actors who are working are, as one would expect, extremely accomplished, and whatever may lie in wait in the new building, the last days at the Old Vic will probably be good ones.

The lavish insecurities of last year have given way to the imposing austerities of John Gabriel Borkman and to the full-scale triumph of Heartbreak House, a practically faultless production. It is the best account of the play that I have seen, and the others have all been good. That last consideration leads me to believe that Heartbreak House, though not an easy play to stage (no play is easy to stage), is not supernally difficult. It demands 10 good performances, but it offers 10 good parts and a prestigious company should be able to cast them. These performances have to be welded into an ensemble; but British actors are famously unselfish, and this -- far more than the plays of Chekhov that inspired it -- is a play that breeds co-operation. Its rhythms are imposed by the text; no sensitive actor could ignore them.

The play is by no means devoid of emotion -- that canard is hardly true of any of Shaw's work and of this least of all -- but all feeling is brought to the surface and carefully, often brilliantly, expressed. Here, of course, is the crucial difference from Chekhov, much of whose impact derives from what we sense behind the lines, but there can be powerful surprises in Shaw's explicitness. When Captain Shotover cries at the betrayal of his mental powers by his 88 years ('I must go in and out . . . I can't keep awake and alert') and goes on to detail the encroachments of sleep and 'the horrors of an old man drinking,' he is getting, quite literally, on his author's nerves.

A well-performed group play is a peculiarly soothing experience; the cohesion communicates itself to the audience. What dialogue and delivery cannot supply in the way of atmosphere may be supplemented by setting and lighting; Shaw was extremely canny in his requests for both. For the first two acts we are in Shotover's ship-shaped house, for the last in the garden on an autumnal night lit by an arc-lamp 'like the moon in its opal globe.' 'What a lovely night,' says Ariadne Utterword, leaving nothing to chance, 'it seems made for us.'

In John Schlesinger's production the night is actually less magical than I have known it, perhaps because Michael Annals, having done the interior up proud in a series of monumental curves interrupted on a journey to infinity, has all but given up out of doors. The ending of the dream is here less powerful than its beginning, though Mr Schlesinger adorns his author by bringing down the garden flagstaff in the final air-raid.

But the most decisive action of the evening comes before the first line has been spoken; when Ellie Dunn drops her volume of Shakespeare and falls asleep. The play is full of references to sleep, dreams, hypnotic trances. Either Mr Schlesinger has emphasised them or I was listening for them; at any rate, the play has a visionary unity that I have never found in it before. Ellie's experiences in its hackneyed; Kate Nelligan, initially ingenuous without being mawkish, goes on to give a heartbreakingly full-blooded account of her disillusion, her rage, and her metallic realism. This is a remarkably authentic performance. Ellie's infatuation for the romantic Hector -- the cause of her 'heartbreak' -- is treated by Shaw as if it had the resonance of a grand passion; this makes her one of the play's main problems, here decisively solved.

Another is the industrialist, Boss Mangan, so baited and condemned by the assembled company that he becomes sympathetic and almost lovable. Paul Rogers does his best to guard against this in the early scenes, playing down the vulnerability and pouring oil into his voice and smile, but when he too has his heart broken we cannot help warming to him. Shaw piled it on with Mangan (even his money is shown to be illusory), so that he hardly seems worth the extermination which his author has thoughtfully provided for him. Colin Blakely's Shotover, pungently timed and alarming in distress, is a major creation; so is Anna Massey's unshakeable Ariadne.

Eileen Atkins, though she lacks the overwhelming force that Irene Worth gave the role (very useful in shaping the last act), has a fine, clear-eyed gaiety as Hesione; Alan MacNaughtan brings to Mazzini his unexcelled gift for distinguishing greyness from greyness; and Graham Crowden is a fantastical Hector. The remainder -- Edward de Souza, Patience Collier, Harry Lomax -- do not miss a beat. This is posh theatre at its best.
1975-03-09-undermining-shakespeare:
Undermining Shakespeare

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'Macbeth' and a play from Australia.

WHEN Nicol Williamson, in the closing scenes of Trevor Nunn's production of Macbeth (Aldwych), harangues his doctor ("Throw physic to the dogs, I'll none of it"), he throws a cloak over the poor man's head, thereby adding greatly to his terror and confusion.

When he has had enough of this game, he brusquely orders the doctor to unhood himself. "Pull't off, I say" is the line, and this reading of it is certainly ingenious. It is generally taken to refer to Macbeth's armour, which only a few lines before he has ordered to be put on, and to denote his restlessness and general lack of purpose. There is, I suppose, no way of proving these things; the new interpretation seems to me laborious and unrevealing compared with the accepted one, but it could be that Mr Nunn has miraculously uncovered a significance long concealed.

I doubt it, though. When we see the new use to which he has put the old line we murmur "How clever", and this kind of congratulation is just what Mr Nunn is aiming for, though I doubt if he would admit it, least of all to himself. It is a perfect example of the paltry academicism which underlies--and undermines--so many Shakespearean productions. It glares with especial ferocity in this one, since so little energy is expended on bringing the characters alive. The supporting cast strut before us in grey plaids, sounding even duller than they look. The English scene, though considerably cut (the whole performance lasts less than two hours, without an interval), is an interminable conversation between two characters I hardly knew, so slight had been their previous impact. Gordon Jackson, who once played Horatio to Mr Williamson's Hamlet, now makes him a nice friendly Banquo who hints at stirrings of ambition within his own nature; and Ron Pember is an ingratiating porter. Otherwise everything depends on the two principals.

Helen Mirren's Lady Macbeth is firmer than at Stratford, she plunges into evil with gusto, goes arrestingly to pieces when the murder is discovered and somnambulates with style. Her tortured conversations with her husband on the subject of sleep are the most gripping exchanges of the evening. But her performance remains evanescent, a series of moments.

With Mr Williamson it is the same, only more so. He cuts a jagged and apparently heedless path through much of the verse, punctuating it eccentrically ("making the green one--red" recklessly tides the multitudinous seas for a set of traffic-lights) or not at all, until he arrives at a bit which interests him. Fortunately many of these are the peaks of the play; there are moments that take us--naturally and unfussily--straight inside Macbeth's world.

Advancing confidently enough towards Duncan's chamber, Mr Williamson suddenly stands still and forces us to see the visionary dagger, as he later compels us to see the ghost of Banquo and the show of kings--neither of which, in this production, actually materialises on stage. His reaction to his wife's death is extraordinary--half resigned sneer, half baffled growl, and wholly and properly ignoble; while his most sustained success is his briefing of Banquo's murderers. He tempts them with a staccato volley of words and when he is sure of them relaxes into a studiedly casual affability, like a coiled snake with a poisoned tongue at the ready.

Some unexpectedly beguiling passages even suggest--as, more consistently, does Paul Scofield's Prospero at Wyndham's--that old-style verbal music may be on its way back. But it is more characteristic of Mr Williamson to preface his lines with a kind of half-formed verbal shrug as who should say "I haven't quite got the words to express what I feel, but this is the best I can do." This mannerism has infected most of the cast, and it makes for a querulous evening. Sometimes the shrug becomes an actual syllable, the classical equivalent of the interjections which unsteady actors in modern plays employ to bolster up the pretence of naturalism ("look" is a favourite, much in evidence at the Royal Court this week) or the upward inflection with which Americans convert every statement into a question.

Mr Nunn has cut down on his setting--last year it was a church, this year a ruined church--and has also abandoned some of his striking opening effects: the Satanic shadow-play, the witches perched on a chandelier. Obviously he has been heeding the wrong critics; this is the only example I remember of a production and performance significantly deteriorating between Stratford and the Aldwych.

  

The week has been full of Williamsons. David of that name is the author of Don's Party, a ribald and ingenious sex comedy from Australia. That last fact probably explains its presence at the Court; the management would certainly sniff at a similar piece from Britain or (a likelier origin) America. But they have heard that there is an Australian dramatic renaissance and this piece offers some generalised social comment to reassure them.

Between lunges the characters--mainly lefty-trendies--watch the Australian election coverage on television; Labour is defeated and we are apparently meant to equate its failure with that of the characters' ideals. Neither sociologically nor psychologically does the play tell us enough to justify these pretensions; the characters are held up for our disapproval rather than our understanding. So the play depends on its lines and its mechanics. When these falter it goes fearfully flat. It is generally aerated by Michael Blakemore's production, which is witty, precise and inventive: the funniest sequence--in which Ray Barrett as a self-satisfied stud overhears the women in the cast discussing his prowess--does not appear in the printed text. The hatchet-faced Carol Macready, hapless Anthony Haygarth and drifting, delectable Barbara Ewing expertly pin down some of the other types.

It is probably unfortunate that we still automatically regard Australian plays as ethnic studies. The programme glossary is almost too anxiously helpful: a "panning" means "an unfavourable or hostile critical response" in this hemisphere too. Surely the Court knows that.

  

I try whenever I can to put in a plea for Jean Anouilh as a great comic dramatist, but Romeo and Jeanette (Yvonne Arnaud, Guildford) quite defeats me. It is a schoolgirl crush of a play, spineless and moony. Peter Coe's production does it justice.
1975-03-16-from-frayn-to-beckett:
From Frayn to Beckett

MICHAEL FRAYN'S Alphabetical Order (Hampstead Theatre Club) is the most likeable play to have appeared in London in months. Obviously it possesses a particular appeal for journalists--it is set in the cuttings library of a provincial daily and might conceivably be retitled The Back Page--but it is likely to mean as much to anyone who has ever worked in companionable chaos, which is to say to everyone.

The chaos in this instance may be attributed partly to institutional lethargy and partly to the personality of the central character, though the second cause could be regarded as merely an aspect of the first. Lucy, Mr Frayn's librarian, is as appealing as the play; she is also, especially as played by Billie Whitelaw, rather desirable--sufficiently disorganised for men to offer to protect her, strong and generous enough for them to hope that actually she will protect them. Even the lady features editor, fulsomely envious, admits that "everybody loves our Lucy." So it happens that at least three of the male staff are liable to spend whole afternoons hunting among the files.

All this changes when Lucy is supplied with a new assistant, a brisk Mancunian girl called Leslie (Barbara Ferris, forthright). Mr Frayn has dealt before with the impact of an ambitious, efficient newcomer on a cosily comatose section of the supposedly dynamic newspaper profession. Lucy is not as high a climber as the tele-bound whizz-kid of Towards the End of the Morning, any more than this play is the equal of that dazzling novel; but she and it are still pretty effective.

I would not like to be an assistant stage manager on Alphabetical Order; the tidying-up that has to be effected between the end of Act One (Leslie's first day at work) and the beginning of Act Two (Six Months Later) is monstrous. Lucy is still nominally in charge, but effectively Leslie rules. The difference in their regimes may be illustrated by their respective views on the proper limitations of their work. Lucy instructs Leslie only to extract cuttings that have to be fitted into existing folders, "otherwise we have to start a new file." Leslie instructs the world in general not to seek information before the library is officially open. "They know the rules" and "The rules are rules"; filling words are the deftest, most economical of the evening.

They are not, however, the most obviously quotable; I could fill the rest of my space with those that are. "I sometimes think I've got so little objective reality that people don't even talk about me behind my back": that is the plaint of John, a leader-writer who once held a philosophy fellowship at All Souls. He is thus what you would call highly qualified; even his briefest utterances--"Oh, as it might be, God"--have qualifications. He stoops and hovers round the library searching, with imperious vagueness, for a fugitive quotation; his attributes--which include the best first-act curtain line in London--are shown off to the fullest advantage by Dinsdale Landen. James Cossins and Bernard Gallagher are the other members of a splendidly seedy male trio, all, in some sort, suitors to Lucy; a tangled situation on which Leslie lavishes the same ruthless benevolence as characterises her professional activities. She really comes into her own as an organiser when the paper, all unexpected, folds.

This jars. We have had little warning of it, and its theatrical import is that Mr Frayn has tired of indulging his characters and proposes to test them. They go ape, unfolding the folders, defiling the files. This scene is intended as one of those striking theatrical images, of which we write so often and which you are quite right to distrust; they generally look effortful. Mr Frayn is not a theatrical storyteller and when he attempts to gather up the threads of his action he comes near to choking himself with them. The play is most alive in its details, mostly affectionate, occasionally lethal: as when Leslie breaks open a first-aid box while everybody else is hunting for the key. That is an image; I would call it meaningful.

  

Mr Frayn's play survives its narrative deficiencies. Anthony Shaffer's Murderer (Garrick) does not. Any thriller must play games with the audience's assumptions; Mr Shaffer's special characteristic is to include the assumptions we have derived from the billing. In Sleuth he succeeded; I actually believed that he had killed off one of his stars by the interval. But you cannot play that trick twice, and anyway there are limits to credulity. I did not believe that any management would engage an actress of the standing of Caroline Blakiston merely to be talked of in Act I, and to say a few offstage lines before being killed (also offstage) at the beginning of Act Two. Obviously she would appear as advertised; but I resented being kept waiting for her, since nobody else onstage was much fun.

This was not altogether the actors' fault; they were required to expend a great many words on a simple situation, and make them seem not merely functional but witty. Robert Stephens, playing an inept assassin with delusions of sophistication, looks apt: his head-movements are aptly obsessive. A police sergeant called, and I longed to dispatch him to Tom Stoppard for rewriting. Mr Stephens rushed frantically around carrying a nude body, and I wanted Joe Orton's mummy (from Loot). Murderer, a slack thriller with pretensions, goes beyond ordinary tedium; the boredom it engenders is actually painful.

  

The Case in Question (Haymarket) is much better: the drama of a disputed inheritance (how the old words come back) derived by Ronald Millar from a C. P. Snow novel. Zena Walker as the embattled claimant stills the stalls with a passionate plea for distressed gentility, later delivering a directly contradictory anti-materialist diatribe with equal conviction. John Clements goes through similar contortions, but his are more subtly plotted (though less well acted): beginning as a good-fairy tycoon of immense wealth and urbanity (jokes against Wedgwood Benn, an intimate acquaintance with Dr Barnard), he emerges as a selfish manipulator determined to make Miss Walker rich despite herself.

Mr Millar spoils everything by hinting that Sir John may be Miss Walker's father, but you may close your ears to the hint and concentrate instead on the amoral force of riches, a theme also powerfully embodied in Simon Cadell's debonair young opportunist. A jovial trial scene lightens the atmosphere, and an austere appeal hearing impressively stiffens it.

An uneven evening. Happy Days (Old Vic) is the thinnest of Samuel Beckett's major plays, its first act over-insistent and even patronising. But its second deepens to situation-tragedy, magnificently handled by Peggy Ashcroft in Peter Hall's production, desperately steering her eyes, her thoughts and her voice (Fortnum-and-Mason, gently overlaid with Irish) away from engulfing disaster. For much of the evening I wondered whether her husband (mostly silent or invisible or both) really needed the distinguished attentions of Alan Webb; when he finally appeared full-length, the way he wore his hat (a topper), shot his cuffs and preened his moustache gave me my answer.
1975-03-23-the-obscurity-of-miller-s-ear:
The obscurity of Miller's Earnest

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

A DIRECTOR who casts Irene Handl as Lady Bracknell is plainly not attempting a conventional production of The Importance of Being Earnest, but just what Jonathan Miller is after in his revival at Greenwich never becomes clear.

Miss Handl being nobody's grande dame, one assumes that he intended to take Wilde's characters down a few pegs, by both emphasising and undercutting their snobbery. The key line here becomes Algernon's "Really, if the lower orders don't set us a good example what on earth is the use of them?" and the key relationship is that between him and his manservant. Should Alan Hay's Lane wish to remain in domestic service, I can furnish him with a reference. He is meek but not obsequious when patronised or bullied and stands patiently, cynically by while the young master tears up the latest line of an obviously endless line of bills.

Greed is exposed as mercilessly as improvidence; the devouring of the muffins is as fine and furious a display as I have seen. Elsewhere the exchanges between David Leech's quite competent Jack and Robert Swann's Algy (whose nasal slur may be a gift from his director) are decidedly - or rather undecidedly - choppy. They fumble too many lines to be funny, but if it's laughter you're after, you don't go to Mr Miller in one of his Puritan moods. This bias might also account for Charlotte Cornwell's Cecily, not so much a pink rose as a big baby, so rude to everyone from the outset that her behaviour to Gwendolen loses all its surprise and half its comedy. This scene is, however, much enlivened by Angela Down, quelling with a shudder any suspicion that she might once have seen a spade.

Actually, by the time this point is reached any idea of sustained interpretation has long been abandoned, and both actors and audience are grabbing desperately at any passing joke. The chief beneficiary is Benjamin Whitrow's Chasuble, a rector whose ministry seems to be someone like that of Silly Walks and whose double-take at the news of Ernest's decease is quite stunning. No less memorable is Joan Sanderson's Miss Prism, passing judgment on the absent and the dead with the unanswerable precision of a spectacle-case snapping shut.

Why so formidable a female should cower before this Lady Bracknell is a mystery. In theory Mr Miller is entitled to treat a classic any way he chooses; in practice a director, if he wishes to offer anything more substantial than a parlour game, is obliged to make sense of a play. And in allowing Miss Handl to be described as a Gorgon, Mr Miller makes nonsense. There is, to be sure, some charm in her performance; she acts her way out of the legendary handbag with finesse, and (on the first night seemed compounded of nerves and little else) it is fascinating to count the lines that she can make work for her. She sounds mysteriously Central European, disarming opposition not through patrician obstinacy but by impenetrable gemutlich silliness. What Miss Handl does to Lady Bracknell is nothing to what the real Lady Bracknell would do to Miss Handl.

  

The Theatre at New End is liable to close, penniless, at the end of this month. On its past record I would not mourn it excessively, but the current production, Peter Handke's Kaspar, though it may not inspire a reprieve, certainly qualifies as a redemption. Actually it is rather surprising that one should have to go to Hampstead (to the Theatre Club for The Ride Across Lake Constance last year and now to New End) to find a Handke play; he should surely be in the repertories of our major companies. When these were founded there was an unspoken assumption that they would look to Germany for much of their modern work: to unperformed Brecht, to Max Frisch and Friedrich Durrenmatt. But the Brechtian supply ran out, and the plays of his successors no longer seemed very interesting. Handke is the first writer to fill the space they vacated: an authentic instant classic.

Kaspar Hauser was an autistic 16-year-old who appeared in Nuremberg in 1828 with the ability to speak a single sentence: "I would like to become a horseman such as my father once was." Handke strips him of even that much particularity. Kaspar's one sentence becomes "I want to be someone like somebody else was once"; the play shows how he is converted into someone like everyone else is now. The historical setting has been removed; the play takes place in a single, modernistic white room. For much of the time Kaspar is the only character on stage; in the later scenes he is joined by three silent replicas of himself. But his main antagonists are offstage voices; it is they who turn him into a model citizen. They pour words into his ears, so that he loses his hold on his one sentence; then set about teaching him new sentences, full of humane advice and cautious counsel. Not the least chilling aspect of the instruction process is that, for much of the time, it would be difficult to disprove that it is being done for Kaspar's own good.

The play demonstrates not the impossibility of communication (that hoary old dramatic alibi), but its fearful efficacy; language, the vehicle of thought, is also the most potent instrument for restricting it. What we call education can also be indoctrination, and in Kaspar history has presented Handke with the perfect metaphor. As enacted by Richard Tresson, he is his own dogged self, an individual before he is a symbol. At the beginning Mr Tresson flops about the stage, bumping into things and directing at them the only words he knows. At the close he is fully co-ordinated, but equally at the mercy of objects: he knows their names and the words oppress him. It is difficult to say which situation is the more poignant.

Handke's ability to give theatrical form to metaphysics is greater than that of any playwright since Samuel Beckett. Like Beckett's, his technique can be monotonous and the most conscientious spectator is likely to lose his grip somewhere. But he is also likely to recapture it; neither playwright generates the arid boredom of which I had cause to complain last week.

  

Events in an Upper Room (ICA) is a modern-dress version of the Easter story (Joseph of Arimathea, a confused liberal), which communicates mainly satisfaction at its own ingenuity. The actors helped to write it, but otherwise they have not done badly.
1975-03-30-catching-up-with-a-classic:
Catching up with a classic

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Schiller's Don Carlos.

As far as our theatres are concerned Friedrich von Schiller is missing, presumed dead, and hardly mourned. The German classics stand high among the plays which our major companies are always promising themselves and us to get around to, but the promises have yet to be redeemed.

It could be that the plays would not suit them. Schiller's historical plays are not amenable to presentation in serge or leather; they demand brocade. So his spiritual home among us might well be Chichester. He would make a palatable alternative to Robert Bolt.

The Cheltenham Everyman, which attracts an audience perhaps more modest than Chichester's but definitely akin to it, is currently staging, with casual but commendable enterprise, Don Carlos; which may well be Schiller's best play and is certainly as neglected as any classic need be. (This seems to be its English premiere.) Its titular hero is the son of Philip II of Spain, but Philip himself is the real centre of interest, as he seems to have been for every writer who has ever touched him. He is walled up in kingship, pursuing a repressive policy in Spain and in the Netherlands, but tempted away from it by a liberal idealism which, though it actually belongs some time in the future (to be exact to the 1780s, when Schiller wrote the play), here finds premature expression in Carlos and his friend, the Marquis of Posa. But Philip's is not the power that rules Spain--that belongs to the Inquisition which brings the king to his knees and seems prepared to bring Carlos to the stake. And for Philip the issue is complicated by jealousy; for Carlos is in love with his stepmother, Philip's young wife. It is rather like seeing Hamlet through the eyes of Claudius.

So at least it seems in Cheltenham, where Norman Wooland's throaty Philip, though somewhat monotonous (this is really a part for a Scofield) has a lonely authority which inevitably breeds sympathy. Carlos, on the other hand, alienates it. This happens to be historical truth (the real Carlos was murderously mad), but it has nothing to do with Schiller's text; whatever he wanted of his Carlos (and he is not very specific) it is hardly likely to have been the petulant inadequacy proffered in this production. Losing interest in Carlos, we inevitably stop following the struggles (half sexual, half political) which occupy the middle of the play; this despite an intelligent Queen (Valerie Holliman) and a sharp collection of courtiers.

The production sails out into the open only with the final confrontation between the King and the Inquisitor (Dennis Edwards), old, blind and implacable; this is recognisably the work of a great dramatist. At the very least the play--in a workable translation by James Kirkup--must rank among the most intelligent historical romances ever written. I was grateful to the Everyman for letting me see it; and my gratitude seemed shared by the audience.

A rep that can offer such a rarity between productions of 'Move Over Mrs Markham' and 'Equus' seems to me worth preserving. And as a colleague pointed out last week, disturbingly and authoritatively, it is the survival of the theatre that now concerns us. (Of course, there are even worthier, more desperate, claimants of public money, but nobody supposes that the cash saved by killing off the arts would ever reach them.) While we hope for the best, we might stop cutting one another's throats; the life of one kind of theatre ought not to necessitate the death of another. I doubt if there is much overlap between the Everyman audience and that for the touring company Belt and Braces (it might be healthier if there were), but both organisations give identifiable pleasure. B and B were at the Jeannette Cochrane last week with 'Weight', a collaboratively written show, which, like 'Don Carlos', builds to a grand confrontation at its close; this time between a one-time miner's strike leader, turned negotiator for the Coal Board, and his wife, left behind in the life he has largely deserted.

Both the writing and the acting here are tough and passionate; a question which should be central to socialist drama--how do you actually live while awaiting the revolution--is posed and, yet more wonderfully, explored. Like John McGrath's 'Fish in the Sea', 'Weight' is a long chronicle, less rich in human detail, but considerably more searching (and more humorous) in its treatment of politics; it also offers some excellent music (though less good lyrics), pleasingly sung by the girls of the company. The men, meanwhile, get to do most of the acting. Is this a new gloss on the old complaint that "men must work, while women must weep"? And does it count as sexism?
