The kiss in the cafe

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

THE way in which boy gets girl in Stephen Poliakoff's Hitting Town (Bush) is distinctly unusual.

Ralph and Claire sit in a Wimpy bar in Leicester - a doubly depressing experience - and service is not forthcoming. It is in fact non-existent and Ralph, a nervy exhibitionist, fills his plate with the contents of up-ended mustard-jars and bisected plastic tomatoes. Still he gets no attention - the one visible waitress is actually off-duty and merely sits at an adjacent table, blankly sipping a drink - but at least Claire takes notice. Perhaps his whimsical vandalism turns her on, perhaps it embarrasses her and she wants to deflect him from it; either way, she kisses him, forcefully and repeatedly on the mouth.

Ralph is excited; he feels like telling the world. At least he calls up the local radio station and informs the DJ on the phone-in programme that he and Claire are lovers. He adds a few circumstantial details: that they are both 11 years old and that they are brother and sister. Most of this is untrue; Ralph and Claire are both in their twenties and they are not yet lovers. But, yes, they are siblings; and by the end of the play they have indeed gone to bed together.

The play presents incest as a by-product of urban blight; what else, it seems to be asking, is there to do in Leicester? Mr Poliakoff's psychological build-up is cunning, but with hardly a hint of contrivance. Ralph is a student at Birmingham, and Claire awaits his trips home with a mixture of eagerness, trepidation and proprietorial concern; he is rootless and seems to need an older woman. Their kinship apart, they might very easily drift into a desultory spasmodic affair. So we have a play about incest which avoids both sensationalism and studied camp casualness. Indeed, I regret having to use the word "incest" at all; it has a flavour of melodrama, and this play is an honest comedy.

Ralph's shapeless, defiant hysteria is well conveyed by James Aubrey, but is less interesting than Claire's control. Everything in Judy Monahan's performance - compassion, humour, exasperation, fear - is contained; she is not hard, nor preternaturally cool, but she will survive. Tim Fywell's production is tightly atmospheric; multiple scene-changes paradoxically work far better in this tiny space than in a large one. The play is slightly too long; Ralph's memories of the Birmingham bombing seem like an artificial attempt to add resonance to a text that breeds its own. It is preceded by This Property is Condemned, an early Tennessee Williams, done slowly.

What can I say about the first night of The Exorcism (Comedy)? After a dilatory start, depicting a quartet of wealthy lapsed idealists settling down to Christmas dinner in a richly-appointed country cottage, it gathered momentum when the author Don Taylor turned on the horrors and the four found themselves trapped in space and time (doors and windows, clocks and watches, alike immovable) and rose to a chilling climax when the spirit of the house took possession of one of the four and spoke through her.

The chosen medium was played by Mary Ure and the scene has since proved - in the most literal, ghastly sense - to have been the climax of her career as well. She died on the following day and I can only record that her last speech was frighteningly well done, while earlier in the evening she had meshed excellently with Honor Blackman, Brian Blessed and Ronald Hines as Peter Coe's production steadily raised the temperature.

It was not admittedly until past the interval that their efforts were rewarded. The play, though short, appears padded and the early airing of Socialist guilt (though vigorously done in particular by Mr Blessed, the best-heeled and worst-conscienced of them all) is hardly anything new. But it proves in the end unexpectedly valid; the ghost that haunts the house died cursing the unfeeling rich, and it is this curse that Ure pronounced and that Mr Taylor's characters expiate. It may not be the subtlest of propaganda, but it is more powerful than you would expect in the West End and has greater emotional force than much that is preached on the fringe; it is the theatrical equivalent of an Oxfam ad as opposed to a Workers' Revolutionary pamphlet. It will do nothing to change society, but it could inspire the penning of a few well-aimed cheques.

  

The World Theatre season is upon us again, reinforcing Peter Brook's contention that drama in an alien tongue can be more impressive than drama understood. It can also be more boring, but such are the breaks. The Cracow Stary Theatre's production of Wyspianski's November Night (Aldwych) was in fact less tedious than frustrating; it dramatises the Polish uprising of 1830 against Tsarist rule in a style which it would be tempting, but over-indulgent, to describe as epic.

It gives us not episodes but large fragments - chunks, really. Some show the insurrectionaries (who, like all good conspirators, wear their collars turned up); others, the Tsar's deputy, single in will but divided in conscience (and smoulderingly played by Jan Nowicki, who has an individual - perhaps unique - line in stocky neurotics); others still, supernatural powers, alternately encouraging strife and symbolising it, and here given stunningly operatic treatment. Andrzej Wajda's direction has visual grandeur to match. If the imagery seems obvious (withered branches and decapitated statues in the field, huge isolated double doors revealing brilliant vistas at court) it is also rewardingly bold. But if there is any unity in this dislocated text it would have to be apprehended through verbal imagery, and while this may abound in the original little of it survived the customary sepulchral litany available on the simultaneous translation system.

There is the kind of play (such as Philadelphia Here I Come!) in which two actors embody a single divided psyche; and there is the kind of play (most recently Only Make Believe) in which a writer writes on one side of the stage while the results of his labours are acted out on the other. I don't like either kind, and Stanley Price's The Two of Me (Jeannetta Cochrane) is both kinds at once. Its hero is played by the brothers Clive and David Swift, a wheeze to be remarked more for its cuteness than its cohesion. You get a better class of incest at the Bush.
1975-04-13-a-good-case-for-kings:
HISTORICALLY kings may be outmoded, but dramatically we miss them. Drama being an instrument for the apprehension of man, a king interests us partly because exciting things are likely to happen to him, partly because both what he does and what he suffers may affect thousands of others. Most of all, perhaps, the king interests us because he knows all this: there is hardly a moment when he can forget it.

This, of course, is the burden and the magic of Shakespeare's histories, plays which change the country, returning always to a royal base. Its definitive statement is the ceremony speech in Henry V, which is now being given searching, imaginative expression by Alan Howard at Stratford. As it should be; this speech follows a debate on the monarch's responsibility to his subjects, it details obsessively the symbols of royalty, describes the concept as a proud dream, but offers no hope that it may be escapable. Henry by now is wedded to his office, nothing else of him is left.

This speech is the summation not only of the play and of Terry Hands's production, but of the whole season. It may seem a little early to pronounce this verdict since we have yet to see any of the other plays. But this year Stratford is running backwards: Henry V is to be followed by the two parts of Henry IV (though Part I will actually, if inconsistently, precede Part II). The education of a prince is beyond doubt the subject of Henry IV, and it can be demonstrated - though not conclusively proved - that it is that of Henry V as well.

As yet, however, we have only the last play to go on, and its first night set up some curious, muted reverberations. We could not (and were not, I think, intended to) respond to the play wholly for itself, but neither could we bring to it fully-formed memories of earlier episodes. In the comedy scenes I warmed to Tim Wylton's Bardolph, with his pickled-beetroot nose and bleary intimations of better days, but when Henry gave the order for his death the production made demands on me I could not meet; I was obviously meant to remember their former relationship, which won't even be happening for a month or so. When it does, it will doubtless be enriched by our knowledge of the end. We shall feel like the White Queen, blessed with perfect recall of the future.

Meanwhile Mr Hands's production (which, before I forget, is very good indeed, the best evening I have had at Stratford in ages) presents us with a fascinating, but not altogether convincing, conflict. On the one hand there is Emrys James as the Chorus acclaiming Harry, almost from the outset, as "the mirror of all Christian kings"; on the other there is Mr Howard having serious doubts. It takes him until the ceremony speech to become fully king in his own estimation, that he is king in Heaven's he cannot believe until after Agincourt, when he murmurs incredulously "Oh God, thy arm was here." The early conspiracy against him ("another fall of man") is greeted with agonised shock instead of the customary sanctimonious blandness. In other circumstances, he can put on a good show, a professional imitation of a hero-warrior. The interpretation suits Mr Howard almost too well, he can be rather an effortful actor himself, with a steely but over-obsessive grip on the verse. Like Henry he gets what he wants, which is fine, but you can see him trying, which isn't. Quibbling aside, he might loosen up a bit for the wooing of Katherine, by which time Henry is surely the man he wishes to be.

Mr James paints beautiful word-pictures (his seascapes are particularly seductive), and at the close of the play unexpectedly annexes the Duchy of Burgundy. I had noted that no Burgundy was named in the cast, and had rather expected his lines on the devastation of war to be given to Oliver Ford-Davies, a courteously forceful French Herald. Being emblematic, they would come better from a herald than a chorus. While in France, I must pay additional homage to Geoffrey Hutchings, whose petulant Dauphin, an unsuccessful candidate for heroism, counterbalances Henry; to Ludmilla Mikael (beshrew her eyes) as the princess, and to Yvonne Coulette, her amused, amusing attendant. On the home team Trevor Peacock's expectedly engaging Fluellen is partnered by a sturdily original Gower from Derek Smith. The same two actors in the first scene play at being bishops, Mr Smith more successfully than Mr Peacock. At this point, everybody is dressed in jeans and the stage is overhung by a large grey-green contraption with ungainly folds, looking like a giant upended artichoke. Once war has been declared it descends and reveals itself to be a dazzling stage-cloth in the pattern of a coat of arms. The general aspect becomes as pleasing as it is intelligent. It is worth going to Stratford merely to see the golden armour of the French catch the sun. The English, very properly, look to have cost much less. Farrar is the designer.

  

Henry V was the second royal to arrive last week, Gustav III having been brought to the Aldwych by the Gothenburg Stadsteater. Though no Englishman has written a tolerable play about kingship since the Jacobeans, the tradition survived several centuries in Europe (and still does in America if you stretch a few points to include Kennedy's Children). I might instance Schiller or Ibsen; and, as of this week, Strindberg, whose historical plays - if Gustav is typical - are superior to his exploitations of his marital hang-ups.

Gustav, reigning in Sweden while the French Revolution presaged the end of effective monarchy, scrapes under the wire as a dramatic subject, a powerless king being of little more than gossip-column interest. But, coming as late as he does, he recognises himself for a player-king more clearly even than Mr Howard's Henry and enjoys the role far more. Sven Wollter gave him, magnificently, the desperate impudence of a man who believes in the general doom but cannot in his heart accept its application to himself. His adversaries were equally sharply realised: grotesques but not caricatures. This was one of the most enjoyable of all World Theatre productions.

  

The ovation that greeted James Stewart when he sauntered on in Harvey (Prince of Wales) would have been well earned had he immediately sauntered off again. In fact he stayed to give an extremely good performance. As to how it has matured in the 30 years since it was first offered I cannot speak, but it seemed a good deal less sentimental than in the film.

The opposition should be stronger; the family from which Dowd (Elwood P.) takes alcoholic refuge in the company of his invisible six-foot rabbit lacks its provincial rectitude. Mona Washbourne is too plumply unpretentious an actress to save social face by having her brother committed; though this is a point on which the text itself is consistent. The other major flaw of Mary Chase's play is its attempt to bully rather than seduce us into believing in Harvey ourselves. For myself I never saw him; though I wanted to. There are, however, some outstandingly funny lines; when I laughed, I laughed loud and happy, particularly at Geoffrey Lumsden's psychiatrist.

A Family and its Fortune (Apollo), adapted by Julian Mitchell from the Compton-Burnett novel, leaves most of its actors floundering for air. I gasped with them, though I revived when Rachel Kempson held the stage. She dies untimely, but Alec Guinness survives, his face a mass of pouches, each one alternately inflated with judicious self-satisfaction and distended with ironic malice.

Our Treasury of Drama

Robert Cushman on our treasury of drama

Editorial note: The surviving family clipping is incomplete. Printed page 30 and a later concluding column are preserved, but the intervening portion is missing. The text below reproduces only the surviving material, and the break is marked where it occurs.

THE ENGLISH theatre is proverbially insular. We have—or so we are told—a glorious dramatic heritage, and we see no good reason to complicate it with the works of untranslatable Europeans. We do actually make a few exceptions; insularity is not, after all, the same thing as xenophobia. We have tolerated Ibsen, and we have virtually adopted Chekhov.

The situation may well change. The new National Theatre complex will gobble up quantities of plays and there are enough institutional or semi-institutional theatres to begrudge them every mouthful. We have half-a-dozen companies chasing the same plays (and to a large extent the same actors). They will have to discover some new ones; or, rather, some old ones. The golden and silver ages of English drama—the ‘Elizabethan’ and ‘Restoration’ periods—are likely to be extensively revisited. What follows is a sketch-map of the terrain, noting some recently discovered features, and others still neglected.

It should be noted that a single revival of a play proves nothing, except perhaps the intrepidity of the company responsible. A piece may really be considered to have entered the national repertory when a second revival is undertaken within, say, 15 years.

Some kind of relationship can usually be traced between a play’s academic prestige and its theatrical appearances. The school textbooks themselves remain in circulation. We see little medieval drama in our theatre, but when we do it is likely to be extracted from the biblical mystery cycles, originally performed by the craft-guilds. These are favoured less for their religious content than for their status as community drama; even their multiple authorship works in their favour in a culture where the individual is fashionably disprized.

The sheer size of the mystery cycles is another enticement; apart from Shakespeare’s histories, they are the nearest we have come to epic theatre. Of the four major cycles extant, those of York, Chester and Coventry have all in recent years been mounted in their cities of origin. The fourth cycle, that of Wakefield, has had to come south for recognition; it has been staged in London several times, by the Mermaid and the Young Vic, which have both cultivated (if that is the right word) an informal, broadly comic house-style ideal for the plays’ unsophisticated anachronistic humour, if not for their grandeur of scope.

The best of the Wakefield plays—those credited to an unknown ‘Wakefield master’—are, when read or seen in the context of the whole cycle, stunningly good. They detach themselves from their surroundings, rather as Shakespeare does from the work of his contemporaries. Suddenly the lines cease to be well-meaning doggerel and take on vigour and stage-presence; there is even a sense of dramatic (rather than just narrative) form. This is particularly evident in the celebrated Shepherds’ play, the first good play in the language.

The second is generally agreed to be the morality drama ‘Everyman’; it is probably the best known of all medieval plays. Best known, that is, by name (and possibly by association with Everyman’s Library, which derived from it both its name and its motto) and perhaps in its printed text. But it has had no recent stage history; it may take first place among the schoolbook classics on which our theatre has turned its back. The reason may be that the morality play, far more obviously than the mysteries, aims to do its audience good; it is schematically allegorical, the

[An intervening portion of the article is missing from the surviving clipping. The preserved concluding column resumes mid-sentence.]

a small candle for George Peele’s ‘The Old Wives’ Tale’, in which a bedtime story takes charm and spectacular shape before the astonished eye of its narrator.

And there remains one major dramatist whose development spanned the whole period and who has remained unstaged since the seventeenth century. George Chapman, whose translation of Homer inspired Keats’s sonnet, wrote some reflectively resonant tragedies, but it is his comedies that now suggest themselves for performance.

The major Restoration comedies have been fashionable since the 1920s. Critics who condemned them as immoral or (more astringently) as painfully frivolous, merely confirmed the theatrical view of the plays as a daring brand of escapism. Nowadays we are much soberer and have discovered social realism; the best productions in this vein have mercifully not neglected the acute and joyous sexual patternings that give the plays their life.

Modern criticism is at last getting to grips with the plays, and the theatre is helping, though it is still fighting shy of the most powerful writer of the period. William Wycherley’s ‘The Country Wife’ is theoretically a staple of the repertoire, and it may be only chance that has kept it out of London for nearly 20 years. But the savagery of ‘The Plain Dealer’ seems to frighten everybody off.

Of all our classic dramatists Wycherley is the one most urgently in need of reclamation. Unless you count Henry Fielding, the last writer of the great ages, who, at a time when Restoration comedy had long lost its celebrated raffishness and had given itself over to decent sentiment and indecent sentimentality, turned out topical squibs and burlesque tragedies, which are still funny to read, and which it must be possible to stage (though nobody has yet discovered how) so that we understand the jokes. There is one hilarious piece entitled ‘The Historical Register for the Year 1736’. The day some manager puts that in his bills, we shall really have a liberated repertoire.
1975-04-27-mr-pinter-s-spoonerisms:
Mr Pinter's Spoonerisms

THE last time we saw John Gielgud and Ralph Richardson together they were keeping each other company in David Storey's Home. In Harold Pinter's No Man's Land (Old Vic) they appear to be in Sir Ralph's home; Sir John has been invited in for a drink.

Sir Ralph plays a wealthy and successful literary man named Hirst, Sir John an extremely seedy one called Spooner. The contrast is piquant; we are used to seeing Richardson on the skids (and as this evening wears on he does take some tremendous alcoholic falls), and Gielgud aloof and dominant. Sir John's new role inspires in him some brilliant variations on his familiar stage persona. His suit and his face are equally crumpled; what with the faded pinstripes of the one and the furrows and wrinkles of the other, the actor wears as many lines as he speaks. But there remains a certain jauntiness, and the mellifluous voice has taken on a plaintiveness that makes it if anything more persuasive.

As a house-guest uncertain of how long his welcome will last, Spooner needs persuasiveness. His situation strongly recalls that of Davies, the intrusive cuckoo-man of The Caretaker. Like Davies, he finds his tenure of his new premises threatened by prior occupants. Hirst already retains a spiv and a thug (antique but useful terms) beneath his roof and their demeanour towards Spooner is not welcoming.

Like Davies, this minor poet is liable to endanger his own position with bursts of razored insolence. That which hath made Hirst drunk (and morosely silent) makes Spooner bold; learning, or sensing, that his host has had and lost a wife he taunts him with the loss; and in rhyme, which makes it sound no nicer. The following morning, when Hirst, now spruce and fresh and seemingly enjoying the opposite of a hangover, reappears and apparently takes him for someone else entirely, battle is joined on the subject of eternal betrayal. My own interpretation of this rather obscure passage is that Spooner, under cover of humouring Hirst's mistake, is having a good time flinging mud at his patron; doubtless, too, there are sexual indignities in his own past which he is pleased to have the opportunity of flaunting, and of blaming on someone else.

Altogether Spooner must rank in Gielgud's performing canon with Pinter's finest creations. Hirst, despite Sir Ralph's massive presence, may prove less memorable, but each has been neatly deposited at his own station (on the Northern Line). From Chalk Farm, where Spooner earns a crust by clearing pub tables, to Hampstead, where Hirst exists as a Beckettian recluse with added alcohol, is a short but steep ascent. One poor bohemian's attempt to climb up Haverstock Hill is here wittily documented.

But there is, unfortunately, more to it than that. Mr Pinter's titles are a good index to the progress of his art: once they referred to characters, objects or events, now to abstractions. No Man's Land may denote the area of ground -- Hirst's house -- in which the characters are struggling to gain or regain a footing. (Mr Pinter's plays are frequently described as territorial battles. The description holds good, as it does drama being conflict and stage spaces for most plays.) But when the phrase actually occurs in the dialogue it is used of a state of mind: a sense of time having ceased and all memories having jelled into a single immovable instant.

Pinter has treated of this instant before; the irony is that he defined it most clearly in Silence, a play which, however interesting philosophically, proved dramatically unsatisfactory and possibly unworkable. The references in No Man's Land, though climactically placed, are self-contained globules, failing to connect with the personal conflict that occupies us elsewhere. So what might have been a synthesis of the two main currents in his work looks more like a frayed rehash.

Certainly the two minor characters, despite Michael Feast's whinnying smoothness and Terence Rigby's threatening grunts, are like ghosts of more substantial figures in earlier plays. When Hirst remarks that he would like to change the subject (for the last time) they hold him to it. There will be no liberation in this status quo; and the play is stocked on a metaphysical quibble.

But the language yields much pleasure; among other things it amusingly characterises Spooner as a minor-league Eliot, parodying the Four Quartets ('now and in England and in Hampstead and for all eternity') and pronouncing sternly-chymed judgement as Hirst makes a drunken exit on all fours ('I have known this before. The exit through the door, by way of belly and floor'). Peter Hall delivers his usual (in these circumstances) impeccable production and benefits, again as usual, from a stylish enclosure of a setting designed by John Bury. (Future title for a Pinter play: Buried Alive.)

A word more of Sir Ralph: he could surely give the definitive performance of his namesake, surnamed Bloomfield Bonington, the consultant with the blood, healing voice in Shaw's The Doctor's Dilemma. James Villiers, who now plays B.B. at the Mermaid, is excellent, with all the required rotundity of voice and manner if not of shape. He only falls short of the ideal in being visibly too young and in failing to make the celebrated Shakespearean recitation at Dubedat's death as moving as it is funny.

His professional colleagues are equally admirable: Frank Thornton, Nigel Hawthorne, John Cairncross, Tony Jay and Derek Godfrey, whose watchful irony, finally and explosively punctured, in the pivotal part of Ridgeon suggests that he might play a definitive Duke in Measure for Measure. Lynn Farleigh similarly qualifies for Isabella with her direct unembarrassed passion as Mrs Dubedat, pleading for her husband's life. (Miss Farleigh, who was the wife longing for a child in David Rudkin's Ashes, has been having some tough times in doctors' surgeries.) Ken Cranham, whom I had thought an unalterably comic performer, surprised me with the accuracy of his Dubedat; he dies, as he lives, with the right mischievous ambiguity.

Mentioning everybody is my tribute to Robert Chetwyn's production, one of the best stagings of Shaw I have seen and hardly inferior to the National's Heartbreak House. It is neither a spuriously topical polemic nor an excuse for creating stars to romp easy paradoxes. Mr Chetwyn gets the right laughs by stamping on the wrong ones. Right at the start he refuses to let the old housekeeper (Ruby Head) be endearing; her dismissal of science -- 'you won't think much of it when you've lived as long with it as I have' -- is deadly serious. Deadly is the word throughout: a skeleton, with scythe and hour-glass, dominates Dubedat's studio. It is special.
1975-05-04-bertolt-out-brechted:
DAVID HARE'S Fanshen (Joint Stock Theatre Group at the ICA) is a play in the Brechtian manner on a Brechtian subject, though it hews far closer to the master's theories than he himself ever did in his practice.

I was reminded of this by the television production of The Caucasian Chalk Circle which, for a wonder (theatre critics not generally being allowed home in the evenings), I caught on its repeat showing last week. This play, you may remember, begins with a group of peasants discussing the proper use of a piece of land; but the discussion is not prolonged and is used only as the basis for a moral fairy-tale. Nor, along the way, are we left in much doubt of what the moral is, nor of the author's attitudes towards the characters. A storyteller is provided to make it all clear to us; and Brecht's vaunted objectivity has gone where it usually goes into abeyance.

Mr Hare's play also begins with a discussion among peasants; it ends with another and consists of little else in between. But there is no danger of Mr Hare sliding into obvious partisanship; if alienation was a discipline which Brecht had to invent in order to keep his feelings under control, for Mr Hare it appears to be a perfectly normal way of writing. His previous plays have been cold-blooded satirical comedies, surveying their characters and the society enclosing them with dispassionate loathing. Fanshen by contrast regards its characters with dispassionate approval and is not a comedy.

It does raise the occasional sour laugh: "Under the nationalists too many taxes, under the Communists too many meetings." Fanshen (based on a book by William Hinton) is the story of how one village in post-war China passed from the first state to the second. "Fanshen" (meaning a turning-over) is the name given to this process, and also to the many smaller changes, both within society and the individual, which it involves. As the only Chinese word in a script otherwise composed in good plain English it takes on mystical overtones as the evening proceeds. The Party becomes revered as the organisation that gave the people Fanshen: now and everlastingly. And it comes as no surprise (though still something of a culture-shock) to hear one conscience-stricken recalcitrant lamenting his probable fate: "I'll be thrown out of the Party--that's worse than being dead."

In one sense this is political drama of a rigour we rarely experience; the Joint Stock actors, under the direction of William Gaskill and Max Stafford-Clark, present and clarify arguments. They do not characterise. Once the landlords have been expropriated (and the production seems to take some joy in literally putting the boot in) all is sober dialectic. Each revolutionary step is scrutinised, the villagers agonise over their own decisions, and Party secretaries--themselves impeccably self-critical--pay periodic visits to keep them up to the mark; or to inform them where the mark now is. Mr Hare offers no authorial comment on the struggle, merely the assurance that it is worth waging--an assurance made explicit in the very last speech and implicit in his devoting three hours of dramatic time to it.

Granted that these hours are informative and occasionally gripping, doubts arise. Under the Communists too many meetings; so many that one wonders what time could be found actually to work the land so exhaustively discussed. Perhaps this is simply a reflection of what can and cannot be efficiently represented on a stage. But its effect is to provide both for the presenters and the audience a major exercise in wish-fulfilment; there is (especially if you actually live in an urban industrial society) more fun and more intellectual glamour in discussing agrarian activity, revolutionary or otherwise, than in actually performing it. Politics, divorced from any visible effect other than the humiliation of an unpleasant landlord or two, becomes an end in itself; for many people this is apparently an extremely seductive prospect.

Some years ago at the National Theatre Mr Gaskill gave us some extremely effective eighteenth-century comedies with Brechtian trimmings. It is commonly supposed that these productions showed us, once for all, the correct way to handle the genre; and it has become regulation critical drill to shoot down any director foolhardy enough to try another method.

Ian McKellen has directed Colman and Garrick's The Clandestine Marriage at the Savoy for H. M. Tennent; and has predictably, but groundlessly, been accused of eliminating the play's social comment. Now the comment in this play, as in so many others, is concerned with money, and it is particularly directed against the nouveau riche. The chief butt is Sterling, a merchant who, having made his pile, wishes to augment it with prestige by marrying his daughter into the aristocracy; the aristocracy, being impoverished, is willing to co-operate, but collectively rejects the merchant's plainer elder daughter in favour of his pretty younger one. She, however, is secretly married to her father's clerk. The merchant's lines are full of explicit greed. (He rejects the clerk because he has "no stuff, no money.")

In Mr McKellen's production Sterling's mercenary vulgarities are positively roared out by Ron Moody, and the landscape garden, which is his pride and joy, is as elaborately tasteless as the severest critic would desire. I do not see how Mr McKellen could have exposed the man more mercilessly without descending to the kind of over-emphasis (dressing the servants in rags for example) that we would surely all dismiss as vulgar. Mr Moody may even push Sterling a trifle too hard, but then he has a soft and exquisite foil in Alastair Sim's rheumaticky Lord Ogleby, contemplating with intrigued disbelief, slowly melting into charmed surprise, the unnatural sights that adorn Sterling's domain: "a spire ... without a church ... halfway up a tree." The gradualness is all.

For all this Mr McKellen's production is not very good: Messrs Sim and Moody would probably be much as they are (and neither is absolutely at his best) whoever directed and the other funnies lack inspiration. The straights (Kay Barlow, Peter Blythe) are better, but much of the play is tepid and it finally comes to the boil without our noticing. The last scene finds most of the cast assembled outside a bedroom. The man they suspect of being inside enters from the opposite direction. A comic climax, everyone aghast? Not a bit of it; the intruder sidles unobtrusively onto a reaction delayed, diffused, defeated.

  

The Stratford Love's Labour's Lost of two seasons ago has come to the Aldwych newly-charged. The dynamo is Ian Richardson, in virtuoso form as he has not been in Shakespeare these seven years; careering through the verse full tilt and full tremolo, able to brake or deepen on the instant. He would be invulnerable if Estelle Kohler's Rosaline were not part-mistress of the same weapons; she unseats him with lazy ease. There is, too, a new boy Moth (Martin Lev) who knows what he is about and why.

At Stratford itself Alan Howard, having scaled the Harfleur ladders as Henry V, slides down a snake or two to become Prince Hal in Henry IV, Part One: a moody but not moony lad driven to bad company (Brewster Mason's Falstaff, on my visit, was laryngitic) by the oppressiveness of the good. As represented by Emrys James, Henry Part One is the vile politician excoriated by Hotspur; he is perhaps storing up his nobler qualities for Part Two.
1975-06-15-meddle-for-measure:
Meddle for Measure

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

I MUST apologise for coming late to Charles Marowitz's production of Measure for Measure (Open Space), but it deserves more than a mention. It begins with the Viennese hierarchy--Duke, Deputy and Ancient Lord, plus a Bishop of the director's own invention--bestowing on each other the knowing winks and benevolent glances of the well-fed. Richard Mayes's Duke is, appropriately, the blandest of them all; his voice, as he hands over power to the precise Angelo, is coated with ozone. Such men are dangerous.

In Mr Marowitz's dispensation the Duke then vanishes till the end of the play. He does not lurk around the city, keeping tabs on everyone in the guise of a friar. Perhaps Mr Marowitz has something against friars: Shakespeare wrote a genuine pair into the play, but they have gone and the Bishop has seized upon their lines.

The Duke's absence shortens the play considerably; but apart from one other significant change, noticeable, we seem to be getting a quiet, bare, concentrated version of the original, which I was prepared to mark down as the best I had seen. (I have been unlucky in my 'Measures.') Certainly Ciaran Madden's Isabella outstrips (she gets down to her slip at one point) all others in my experience. Above all else, she is fresh; there are no wrinkles on her face, her mind or her sensibility. So her beauty can quite credibly topple a Puritan (Angelo was probably kinky for nuns, anyway); and she is sheltered enough to build her life on dogma, untroubled by doubt. Miss Madden, unlike most young actresses in Shakespeare, does not circle her emotions, or tunnel underneath them; she meets Isabella's rage, her horror, her forensic fire, her limited good sense, all head on; she conquers and embodies all of them. In all respects save one, this is the complete Isabella.

The omission, however, is crucial. In Mr Marowitz's version Isabella is still saddled with the notorious formulation 'More than our brother is our chastity.' But she does not have to commit herself to it since this Isabella, having thought the matter over, scampers off to bed with Angelo. She even shows momentary signs next morning of having fun.

This is the first of Mr Marowitz's departures from Shakespeare's plot; others follow. Claudio is executed, for real; there is no substitution of a convenient pirate's head. The Duke returns, hears the evidence, dismisses Isabella's pleas, protects Angelo. The play ends with the ruling class more frolicsome than ever.

Even by his own lights Mr Marowitz is inconsistent here: he has retained the early scene in which the Duke declares his intention of testing Angelo; why then does he set the results of the test aside? The latter end of Mr Marowitz's commonwealth forgets his beginning. But I am inclined to forgive him for several reasons. First for the ingenuity with which he reorders the old words to a new end; this is the cleverest of his Shakespearean jigsaws. Second, for the tautness of his production and the intelligence of its acting. Brian Gwaspari's Claudio is particularly good. Third, the sentimental cynicism with which Mr Marowitz concludes his self-proclaimed 'adaptation' has often been foisted on to the play by directors claiming to present the thing itself. The accepted mode of reinterpreting a classic is to make everyone in it as nasty (hence as uncomplicated) as possible. This makes the director feel tough and defiant, particularly when the characters represent authority. By a twisted logic it also allows him to express his dislike of his author (who is certainly part of the establishment) and his audience (who are presumed to be). Directors are often their own evidence that power corrupts.

  

The habit is world-wide. In America last month I was urged to visit the Yale School of Drama to see a production of A Midsummer Night's Dream, which, it was claimed, opened up a new era for American Shakespeare. The novelty turned out to reside in a stressing of the violence in the play. The squabbling of Oberon and Titania had real force, even real terror; you could believe that it would affect the course of the seasons. The forest itself was terrifying, not least in the demands it made on the actors. Oberon's ability to keep his footing on a nearly vertical ramp was proof enough of magic powers.

So far, excellent; but the director, Alvin Epstein, failed to justify his preoccupations in the rest of the play. The court scenes were backed by a giant battle-painting, after Uccello (very striking; design now ranks with dance among the highest skills of the American theatre). In front of it Theseus and Hippolyta attempted a quarrel unsupported by the text. The lovers thumped each other and fell about; but they always do that. The clowns were traditional, too. (There was even a deaf Starveling; I haven't seen one of those since 20 years ago in Regent's Park.) Sometimes the action froze while a chorus rendered excerpts from Purcell's Fairy Queen. This, in Bottom's words, was lofty (on this showing, they sing at Yale far better than they act), but it spun out the play to a length unheard-of since the days of Beerbohm Tree. As a combination of insight with insensitive silliness, the production would be hard to beat.

  

The Open Space's most lauded new play, David Rudkin's Ashes, has been revived at the Young Vic. The new cast hardly improve on their fine predecessors. Gemma Jones is flinty, glowering, ultimately moving as the wife condemned to childlessness, but Ian McKellen is all fuzzy rhetoric as her husband. He brings out the worst in the play; but I doubt if that worst could ever be fully obscured. Even the best--the detailed presentation of a wracked, infertile marriage under horrible stress--is weakened by self-pity. A play about physical incapacity can hardly avoid futility: where do you go and whom do you blame? The references to the man-made catastrophe in Ireland do not fit.

  

Gaston Leroux's The Phantom of the Opera is an exciting story; David Giles's adaptation for the Actors' Company, despite many infelicities, does not disguise that fact. Mr Giles cannot make us accept the Wimbledon Theatre as the Paris Opera (where, apparently, the artistes used to mime badly to distant records), but when the action shifts to the sewers beneath he gets a grip on himself and us. He is much assisted by Juan Moreno, a more than agreeable actor and an accomplished mime, playing a mysterious Persian more phantasmal than the Phantom; Jonathan Adams wins some legitimate laughs as a frightened manager. The others try hard and are likeable. Sheila Reid as a diva with a weird and wandering accent goes furiously gelid when subjected to phantom-mouse letters. I think that was the word.
1975-06-22-quixote-in-his-windmill:
Quixote in his windmill

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

KERRY Lee Crabbe's new play The Last Romantic (Actors' Company, Wimbledon) celebrates the union of this year's most compatible couple, Doom and the English. Having ogled each other for most of the evening, they get together at the end in a small flash of apocalyptic symbolism. Suddenly last summer, in a Suffolk cottage made over from a windmill, the lights go out in the routine warning that heralds a power cut. To be honest I don't remember there being any power cuts last summer but maybe East Anglia had problems the rest of us never knew about.

The cottage is inhabited by an old soldier, who now aspires to save the country with a private army, and his son, a hard-drinking homosexual ex-BBC drama producer (that's not a character, it's a case-history), who aspires to hardly anything. The son's inertia is in itself an affront to his father's briskness and he can arouse himself from it to issue a lazy, memorable political challenge to the effect that the Left must be right because they're so bloody dull. Faced with this kind of insubordination, or with a daughter who decamps to marry the local doctor, dad is liable to throw a heart attack. Which is how it comes to pass that in the last scene, with the lights going out all over Suffolk, the old man is discovered, at death's door and his own, by a lady who, conveniently for everybody including the author, is passing by, selling candles.

Opinions obviously differ as to the utility of candles in a national crisis. Sylvia Plath, at any rate, would not have approved. I mention her because the programme does. For her 'they should have gone out with balloon flights and the stereopticon, these candles.' What is more, 'they are the last romantics.' In fact, in their unassuming inanimate way, they join the small queue of characters trying out for the play's title role. For that title could as well apply to the uncaring son (it is very lonely to be uncommitted) as to the quixotic father. (I got that from the programme, too; I like the idea of a Quixote who lives in a windmill.) Ambiguity can be a rich and stylish thing, but this is confusion.

Mr Crabbe has worked hard at both characters; he has given them excellent things to say, but little to do and less to be; the old man, spouting science and philosophy, seems to have arrived by a circuitous route at a very commonplace reactionary stance.

So attention shifts to the lesser characters, the daughter and the doctor, and they provide solace. Their courtship is shy and brusque (just a quick embrace and the odd bird-impersonation), their disillusion not violent but speedy and merciless. Beyond doubt this is what would happen to the girl in Alan Ayckbourn's Norman Conquests should she ever marry her dull and faithful vet. Mr Crabbe's physician is a similar type less farcically conceived; Tenniel Evans masterfully conveys the agonies inflicted and suffered by the apologetic bore. He goes through the play in stoically ridiculous discomfort, as if condemned to stand for ever on one leg.

With Mr Evans in this form, and with Ralph Michael and Charles Kay rallying round in the heavier roles, it is possible to accept much of the play as domestic comedy, oddly shaped but sharply written. Larger resonances are muted; by the end they are ringing out all right, but hollow and none too easy to distinguish. Mr Crabbe's Plath quotation ends, 'This is no time for the private point of view.' That is a nonsensical position for a dramatist to adopt (even a play written in committee represents a private point of view from where its audience is sitting) and it does not square with Mr Crabbe's own talent. Conceivably he disapproves of his characters, but he never insults them.

  

Heading the week's batch of oldies is Pinero's The Gay Lord Quex (Albery), wrongly described in the text-books as a society drama. John Gielgud's immaculate production reveals it to be a social comedy with farcical interludes. The production sometimes changes tone because the play does, but since author and director both know what they are about the changes are not jarring but exhilarating. We continually underestimate the sophistication and complexity of Victorian drama. Tribute, sometimes grudging, is paid to Pinero's engineering skill; nobody acknowledges that he wrote very funny dialogue.

He offers us here a female Figaro; Sophy Fullgarney, who keeps a chocolate-coloured manicure parlour charmingly realised by Alan Tagg, has an understanding with the male palmist across the way. Both of them adopt alien manners and accents (his French, hers London-genteel) to deal with their clientele; they deceive everybody but themselves. The play's aristocrats, by contrast, are almost totally self-deluded. Sophy enters their world to break off her foster-sister's engagement to the eponymous Quex, believing her to be really in love with an Army captain. She succeeds, but there is one element in the situation unforeseen even by her. Everybody in this play is fooled, more or less; hence its comic eminence.

Most telling is the realisation of Quex, the ageing lecher, that it is his age for more than his lechery which counts against him. Daniel Massey takes this moment with a fine laughing melancholy; in the rest of his performance he hammers the point a little hard. Mr Massey has been a juvenile lead for most of his career, but he does not have to atone for it by ageing so remorselessly. He realises that Quex's vaunted gaiety is as much a fraud as any other comic mask, but his performance could be speedier. He rises admirably though to his long cat-and-mouse confrontation with Sophy; there is a satisfying whiff of sawmill melodrama about this scene and you may feel like cheering Judi Dench's final defiance. Miss Dench's capacity to delight is greater than that of any other player I know. Two witty exercises in style by Rosalind Shanks (a good girl) and Sian Phillips (a bad) dispose of the trickiest parts in the piece. This is the West End resurgent.

  

The chief ornament of Jean Anouilh's Ardele (Queen's) is Charles Gray, a walrus in knickerbockers. He plays the General who was later to flower in The Waltz of the Toreadors (which might itself have flowered last year had Mr Gray been around). He is related to a Countess, Coral Browne, and a Count, Vincent Price. We are back in high society; and history, if it still takes an interest, may well find M. Anouilh's view of it harsher and truer than Pinero's. Right now, however, the play's trappings have dated without acquiring period charm. Its centre is difficult to judge, consisting as it does of several speeches on the bitter-sweetness of love delivered by the Count. Mr Price has a witty, deprecating presence and a good pettish way with a one-liner (both reminiscent of Clifton Webb), but handed anything more complex he mumbles. Odd suggestions by the others that cynicism is afoot are hushed by a soft, pretty production. This is the West End recumbent.

  

In The Knight of the Burning Pestle, Beaumont (though not by scholarly consensus and pace the Greenwich Theatre programme, Fletcher) took the Elizabethan theatre gleefully apart with a contempt for illusion that anticipates Sheridan, Tom Stoppard and Monty Python. The play can be hilarious, as in a school production I remember; or regrettable, as here.
1975-06-29-crowning-of-prince-hal:
Crowning of Prince Hal

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN at Stratford.

WHEN Alan Howard as Prince Hal, the emergent Henry V, tried on the English crown for the first time, I thought the weight would kill him. It is a strange kind of agony that possesses his face; it shifts to accommodate hope, joy, triumph, without ever ceasing to be pain. Mr Howard has a broad, spacious face; there is room.

There is room all over Terry Hands's Stratford production of Henry IV Part 2; it is, like the play itself, marvellously inclusive and unfettered. It roams, but it does not wander. That agonised assumption of royalty is, in every sense, its crowning moment; and it nails, not just this play, but the triptych of which it is the centre. We have already seen Henry IV Part 1 and Henry V, the first of these done dimly and the second triumphantly. The new production falls between the other two in quality as well as in historic sequence; but the unity of the whole is beyond question.

It resides essentially of course in Mr Howard's performance. When we first meet him in this play he is what Rosalind called "a moonish youth." Military glory he has had; it has not turned him on much, but it has spoiled him for pub-crawling and brothel-creeping. (In this production the two activities are virtually synonymous.) Mr Howard has a trick, which I have often found irritating, of acting to himself; lucid and malleable in soliloquy, he freezes over in dialogue, intoning the verse in slabs instead of exploring it line by line. This season has found him more fluent than ever before; and it has also provided him with justification for his solitude. Henry V slaps many backs, but he looks into few faces; and the two Henry IV plays constitute a long practice-run for the eventual, inevitable isolation.

In Part Two, the process is far advanced. Hal's first scene is a weary (his word) colloquy with Poins, ostensibly his sole remaining confidant; Mr Howard aims most of his speeches somewhere past his companion's right ear. Trevor Peacock's Poins is quick-witted enough to deal with routine cynicism (it's his own stock-in-trade), but this disillusion, which we would call alienation, fazes him. Between them these two actors build a whole neglected relationship.

On to the tavern to spy on Falstaff. "How shall we disguise ourselves?" is the question, farcically bored, of someone who hardly cares to hear the answer. ("Drawers, if you're interested.") The Falstaff he beholds is, in Brewster Mason's performance, softer-centred than he might be; his bitching at Hal and Poins is mellow rather than tetchy. (It's backed by soothing lute-music and Mr Mason appears to be acting the music instead of the text.) So Hal's anger seems under-motivated, and the scene only catches alight when, at the words "his grace says that which his flesh and blood rebels against," Falstaff literally thrusts him into the arms of Doll Tearsheet.

For a moment Hal might succumb (body-contact must be a rare sensation for him), but military news calls him away, into the play's other world. Falstaff has made him look and feel a fool and there will be no forgiveness. The official rejection at the end of the play is the merest formal epilogue delivered by Hal, aloof and invulnerable (until the next play starts and presents him with fresh problems) in golden armour. Dear Arts Council: it was the only visual extravagance in the production and thoroughly justified.

Otherwise all is plain. The stage is backed by a cannon, which is removed when peace breaks out, and by a great tree with barren branches. For the scenes in Justice Shallow's orchard the floor is strewn with autumn leaves; nobody seems in any hurry to unstrew them, so they remain, an apt motif for a deciduous play. "Death, saith the Psalmist," (saith Shallow) "is certain; all shall die." Henry IV himself has nothing to do in the play but die. He does it with dignity, forsaking vanity; to put it less delicately, Emrys James no longer indulges in the overworked displays of hysterical meanness with which he sought, in Part One, to justify his son's aversion. He howls like a wolf at the thought of England under a King Hal; and it is only here that Mr Howard's defences really break. For a naked moment he is caught between roles (wanton prince, hero-king) and there is contact. It comes almost too late; but that's Shakespeare, and this is nearly tragedy.

Should Falstaff likewise smell of mortality? Should he have misgivings as to his ultimate success? I think so; but Mr Mason grants him a virtually unchecked progress, blind and hopeful, towards abrupt disillusion. The pox and the gout may gnaw at him, but his limp is not pronounced, and his voice still strides. That voice is as robust and authoritative an instrument as our theatre owns; what Mr Mason does, he does magisterially. In the tavern scene he even gets momentarily rattled, but mostly he is in command, genial and even benevolent. This is Falstaff seen through the eyes of Mistress Quickly; and when he cheats her we mind it as little as she does. This might be because Maureen Pryor is too tough an actress to encompass the hostess's loquacious silliness, to immerse herself in the woman's stream of consciousness. You cannot play Quickly slowly. But Sydney Bromley finds the right rhythm for Shallow's memories, while Mr Peacock, resurfacing as Silence, verges on the out-of-this-world, bent double and exploding into inexplicable, unquenchable carousal. Falstaff and the two justices, reminiscing in tempo, are the most amazing sight of an amazing play. Behind them stands Tim Wylton's Bardolph, a sodden batman, his voice a chuckling gravelly echo of his master's, his red-scarred pate giving him the look of a damaged samurai. If Bardolph is fathoms deep in drink, Mr Wylton is fathoms deep in Bardolph.

Fine small performances breed unstoppably; Oliver Ford-Davies as Wart, the ragged recruit pushed into musket-drill, distils a strange and frazzled dignity merely by standing still. Bob Peck as Mowbray, hard-boned and suspicious, vitalises the intractable rebellion scenes. Indeed, though Mr Hands's production lacks any overt political edge, the episodes of royal treachery stand out in the sharpest relief. And right back at the beginning of the play I remember Clement McCallin's direct force as Northumberland (a symbolist born, who says he'll throw away his staff of sickness and promptly does); and I remember (though I do not honestly approve) the division of the complex prologue spoken by Rumour among all the members of the company. This may do great things for their team-spirit but newcomers to the play (or is Stratford no longer concerned with them?) must find the words difficult to follow.

  

The Actors' Company have tamed their Tartuffe (Wimbledon) since its appearance at Edinburgh last year. The Orgon family play fewer games, and pull together more. Tenniel Evans is nicely bewildered at their head, but a touch of King Lear when his daughter gives him trouble might not come amiss. Tartuffe himself is now Edward Petherbridge, impenetrably wrapped in his devotee's disguise, unshakeable even in defeat. I found this credible and interesting, but just one flash of the diabolism Charles Kay gave the role would round the play out. Postscript to the Arts Council: the Actors' Company, tethered to no place and no ideology, may look dispensable. They are not.

  

And neither, really, are the group of improvisatory clowns known as Theatre Machine, though their current involvement with a scripted play, Kitty Hawk (Bush) -- by an American, Leonard Jenkin, and dealing with two crazies who think they are the Wright brothers -- is not too happy. Whimsy is piled on whimsy. Philip Sayer, the one outside actor involved, is the most in control.
1975-07-06-cruel-concert-party:
Cruel concert-party

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on "a terrifying theatrical experience."

I start from the assumption that any theatrical treatment of the Nazi murder of the Jews must be suspect. An Die Musik, presented by the newly reconstituted Pip Simmons Group at the ICA, is startlingly if unevenly conceived, brilliantly directed, acted with great skill and dedication, and hypnotically watchable. Apart from that, there is little to be said in its favour.

The framework is a concentration-camp concert, performed presumably to a mixed audience of prisoners and guards. An SS-man announces, curtly but politely, that the first offering will be an operetta. You could call it that.

There is no dialogue, and all the singing is done by the band, four wailing instrumentalists, whose words are generally drowned by the merciless percussive throbbing of their music. Meanwhile five actors mime the operetta's action. This, like the words, is hideous, but difficult to interpret precisely. A Jewish family meal is disrupted by the SS-man, whose truncheon, liberally applied, forces them into ever-weirder contortions. It is like watching a silent film with a screeching musical accompaniment; smiles get ghastlier, gestures jerkier, everything louder and faster. The situation is played for grotesquerie if not actually for laughs: the mother is a grinning female impersonator.

The operetta is entitled, for no obvious reason, "The Dream of Anne Frank." Presumably the real Anne, in hiding with her family in an Amsterdam garret before being discovered and sent to be killed in Belsen, often had nightmares like this; But I suspect that in using her name Pip Simmons is on to something else; the Anne Frank story is one of the few methods we have -- but a very effective one -- of sentimentalising the death-camps, and Mr Simmons will have none of it. The dream is succeeded by the reading of an extract from Anne's diary, the famous passage in which she declares her belief that, in spite of everything, people are good at heart. The production tries to show just what "everything" meant in her case and, by doing so, to disprove her.

The Anne Frank reading is the bridge-passage of An die Musik. The second part of the concert picks up from the first: one of the most dismaying moments of the operetta showed us the family forced into performing a high-kicking routine. This kind of humiliation is extended over the rest of the show; the actors and musicians are lined up and ordered sadistically through a series of exercises. There are blows and assorted other torments for those who weaken. Putting them through their paces is a second SS-guard, the first having changed costumes and identities with one of the prisoner-actors at the end of the operetta. What is meant by this transformation I cannot say; perhaps it is part of the treatment to put a prisoner into the jailer's uniform and force him to abuse his fellows, but this remains cloudy.

The commands change and the entertainment continues; the wretched musicians play Schubert, Liszt, Beethoven; two actors even more wretched are announced as "Jewish comics" and compelled to totter and wheeze through the remnants of music-hall routines. A girl playing the triangle is stripped; nothing in the evening is more piercing than the expression, desperately eager to please, on Sheila Burnett's face as her dress comes off. Before long all the others have joined her in nudity, but -- so it seems -- voluntarily and with dignity. The musicians, naked but serene, play a Beethoven dead march. Smoke fills the stage. Gas.

An Die Musik is unequivocally my most terrifying theatrical experience. It eats into the nerves; a shuffle in the seat behind and you wonder who is coming for you. There is no question here of welding the audience into a responsive unit; everybody who watches this is on his own. The ending is curiously soothing; maybe this is what catharsis means. Certainly there is enough pity and terror here (enough terror, anyway) to purge anybody's soul. Tragedy, as described in the books, is a much gentler discipline and less immediately effective.

But even while watching I rebelled. There were prisoners' orchestras in some of the camps -- a macabre decoration, if the decoration of death-camps interests you, but not a detail strong enough to bear the weight Mr Simmons puts upon it. He builds his whole conceit of a camp concert on it, and it shows the strain. Is the concert meant to absorb the whole action -- even the gassing? Is the metaphor meant to make us, as an audience, feel guilty? Where does that leave Mr Simmons, who carefully staged it for us?

There is a sense in which the camps were theatre -- to the guards who reduced the prisoners to objects in a spectacle, even to the prisoners who felt they were filling allotted roles. But that is an argument for shattering the image, not for perpetuating it. There is probably no legitimate way of dramatising this material; even novels on the subject end up between exploitative paper covers. The presence of live (or even filmed) actors emphasises the exploitation. It is degrading to watch actors being pummelled (some of them must really get hurt) while reflecting that millions went through far worse, far longer. And the scenes of explicit violence are actually less offensive than the beautifully choreographed bits -- those early high-kicks, for example, which suggest that the director has a real relish for dehumanisation.

"Lest we forget" is the usual excuse, but our memories could equally well be stirred by the recital of a few statistics. And in a few minutes, at most, of brutality make as strong a point as could be wished; to prolong it is to leave us with nothing to do except to admire the ingenuity of either the tormentors or the presenters. Besides, who needs reminding? Was it all news to the critic of Time Out, who called the show "essential stuff," or to those few of his readers who obeyed him and turned up on the second night? I suspect that the more people are told about this production, even about its merits, the less they will want to see it.

  

Stephen Poliakoff, the author of Heroes (Theatre Upstairs) is very young, very prolific, and very uneven. This is one of his lesser works, reordering some of the materials of Clever Soldiers and Hitting Town into this week's vision of apocalypse. He does not write well enough for the subject and his characters do not convince. Lines like "this is a mad and grotesquely lonely place" cry out to be swallowed, and David Dixon (playing Mr Poliakoff's perennial self-pitying dandy) answered the cry. Dressed in white, he was, on the first night, pallid, but Jonathan Pryce in the black corner loured fairly magnetically.
1975-07-20-double-death:
Double death

THEATRE
by ROBERT CUSHMAN

JOE ORTON'S last play, What the Butler Saw, was first staged in the West End in 1969, soon after its author's death. It flopped; and last week at the Royal Court it died its second London death. And yet I doubt if it will lie down. Of course every failed play has its bedraggled adherents; but in this case they--or rather we--have solid evidence to point to. In the years between its two metropolitan appearances audiences in reps all over the country have seen What the Butler Saw and have laughed even louder than he presumably did.

They were lucky; neither they nor the productions they enjoyed were intimidated by the play. Orton invented his own genre--epigrammatic, subversive farce--and this piece is its finest if not its firmest flower. The first production foundered in disordered extravagance; the new version is equally disordered, but far from extravagant. Like its two predecessors in the Court's Orton season, and worse than either of them, it tramples its author's wit into the ground.

Since Orton was never a Sloane Square playwright (he found his sponsors, to tell the awful truth, in the commercial theatre), there have been suggestions that in mounting the season at all the Court has betrayed its own traditions. This is to get the matter the wrong way round; as a theatre dedicated to the best new English writing the Court should have been presenting Orton in the sixties (very little of what it did present was of comparable interest) and it is decent of it to offer reparation now.

But though the will to recognise Orton as a serious, provocative writer may now be there, the spirit is still lacking. In the Court's formative days you knew when a writer was anti-Establishment because he told you so. Arnold Wesker preached, John Osborne grumbled, John Arden folkwove; they all tried hard. But Orton, homosexual and jailbird, never needed to raise his voice; cutting and insouciant, he effortlessly presented the complete outsider's view of society.

In What the Butler Saw it takes the form of a madhouse with a social conscience. "We've no privileged class here. It's democratic lunacy we practise." Those lines are the hook on which Orton hangs a gleeful indictment of Britain, and a device for embroiling the psychiatrists in the play's farcical action as inextricably as their patients. It is doubtful if Orton had any great interest in satirising psychiatry for its own sake; it served him as a metaphor for a system which operates by manipulating minds, and rarely doubts its own right to do so.

Dr Rance, the play's senior shrink, is as much civil servant as physician: "I represent Her Majesty's Government, your immediate superiors in madness" is the formula with which he introduces himself to his colleague Dr Prentice.

Prentice, a distinguished careerist, inaugurates the action by attempting to seduce his prospective secretary; surprised first by his wife, then by his superior, he spends the play rushing through doors, inventing plots, inveigling other characters into drag. He might, at any early stage, be willing to confess, but an account of the facts would disturb Dr Rance's own highly personal interpretation of them, and authority would not dream of allowing itself to be thus deflected.

Rance, by the way, is no stuffed shirt; faced by a situation that appears to involve fetishism, murder and incest, he dreams of turning it into a best-seller. He's cool ("someone should really write a book on these folk-myths," he remarks when presented with a standard view of heterosexuality) and desperately prurient. At one point Rance takes off into a denunciation of the avant-garde ("an instrument for inciting decent citizens to commit bizarre crimes against humanity and the State"); never afraid to underline the obvious, the director, Lindsay Anderson, has this speech delivered straight at the audience.

A running gag about a statue of Churchill with its private parts missing (the most blatant, dated thing in the play) is also given fearless prominence. Mr Anderson never stops reminding us that he knows what the play means, but he gives few signs of realising how it works. The pressure of farce is entirely absent; the pace is low and level, there is no energy in the exits and entrances. The sight-gags are clumsily handled, while most of the verbal humour is annihilated.

The play, like The Importance of Being Earnest, has too many funny lines; and a production must decide which it will capitalise on, which it will throw away. Here they are all left to take their chance; and since misreadings are rife that chance is a thin one. (On the first night a nervous cast displayed a tendency--unhelpful in a script crammed with mistaken identity--to get the names wrong.) Prentice is a role demanding great physical and verbal dexterity; after 10 years away from acting Michael Medwin was understandably floored. Betty Marsden as his wife came nearest to style and nearest to reality. The production as a whole, joyless and therefore toothless, is an impressive testimony to the continuing ravages of Royal Court blight. Other theatres suffer from other diseases.

  

At Chichester the audience's delight in simple trick effects must tempt any director to smother a play in whimsy. That is the course Wendy Toye has taken with Andrew Sachs's Made in Heaven, a play richly deserving to be smothered; sweets to the sweet, but why pour honey on sugar? Mr Sachs's comedy, a dissection of a marriage that had no dramatic existence to begin with, cannot even smirk with conviction. Chichester-kind cannot bear very much reality, though Patricia Routledge throws some in against the odds.

Attendance at Made in Heaven might prime you, though, for a visit to the Hampstead Theatre Club, now equipped with excellent air-conditioning, but still very hot on comic exposure of the bourgeoisie. Chichester, of course, goes in for comic reassurance. Hampstead's special subjects are those young bourgeois who kid themselves that they have escaped into Bohemia; Wolfgang Bauer's Ghost is interesting testimony that Hampstead plays are now being written in Austria. It offers amusing, cross-talking monologues, a mad monk who squeaks like a Monty Python housewife, a grand slam ending in which the characters degenerate to type and torment the maid; and good acting by a cast of the usual Hampstead weight. More than promising, less than stellar.

Trevor Nunn has prepared a sparkling translation of Hedda Gabler (a play by Ibsen, unlike Ghosts) and his production at the Aldwych is clear if, after its protracted world travels, a bit jaded. Particularly good is the evocation of the play's masculine world; Timothy West's solid, mischievous Judge Brack holds the ring for Patrick Stewart's fiery Lovborg and Peter Eyre's excellent Tesman. Mr Eyre, tall, young, and stooping, has the exact measure of Tesman's scholarly passion, of his myopia, and of his noble awareness of his own limitations; momentarily jealous, he finds lasting satisfaction in acknowledging his rival's genius. Glenda Jackson's Hedda is masculine too; if ladies rode to hounds in Norway her problems would be solved. She copes silently and well with the burning of Lovborg's manuscript and with suicide; but otherwise she is monotonous, conveying no belief in herself as a thwarted tragic heroine. This charmless Hedda is an unlikely lure for three men and a sad companion for the audience.
1975-07-27-comforting-crises:
Comforting crises

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

REVIEWING `The Norman Conquests' I said that Alan Ayckbourn was not a natural misanthrope. That accusation (or, if you like, that compliment) is firmly refuted by his latest comedy to reach London. Absent Friends (Garrick) is the title, and it turns out to be not a toast but a tautology. Friends are by definition absent.

Standing in for them on the stage of the Garrick are five comforters, comprising between them two and a half marriages. Their prey is Colin, a young man whose fiancee has recently drowned. His old acquaintances, Paul and Diana, invite him to their house for a cheering tea-party, and they summon other couples to make the going easier. There are Gordon and Marg: Gordon cannot make it on account of illness (there is always something wrong with Gordon) but Marg is conscientiously present. And John and Evelyn have come; though Evelyn is not a great hand at cheering. When Colin arrives she hardly talks to him, perhaps because she never knew him. Evelyn, actually, is the kind of girl who has never except in the Biblical sense known anybody.

Evelyn and Paul have had it off, once and dismally, in the back of Paul's car. John knows, but since, for business reasons, he needs to keep Paul sweet he shuts up. Diana suspects, and though she has always been tolerant of Paul's infidelities, thinking herself too boring to deserve his continued interest, on this occasion her patience snaps. So, indeed, does she; she pours cream over her husband's head as if he were a trifle (in a sense I suppose he is) and soon afterwards collapses in hysterics. Marriage was a commodity which she only bought because it came so highly recommended; now she would like to give it back.

Before the tea-party is even under way Mr Ayckbourn has managed to stage simultaneous crises for all three couples (Gordon phones in his contribution) but they pull themselves partially together to console Colin. The joke is that he doesn't need it; Colin is a gladhand artist and though he may have lost his love (`a perfect person,' he calls her in passing) he still has his memories. He is only too willing to pass around the photograph album. He is happy; and he is glutinously eager to make everybody share his happiness. He lectures, cajoles, reminisces; altogether he is a dangerous character. One marriage explodes in front of him; the others ominously smoulder.

One feature that distinguishes Mr Ayckbourn's play from previous West End successes is that nobody ever applauds their sets. His suburban interiors are hardly squalid, you might call them comfy, but they are decidedly not elegant. The same is true of the actors; the author and his director Eric Thompson have provided employment for a string of solid, mildly eccentric performers, of the kind you see in the best situation comedies on television. Once again they do the text proud.

Pat Heywood's Diana, plump and rosy, looks reassuring until you realise how badly she herself needs to be reassured; her breakdown is at once appalling and absurd. Cheryl Kennedy, who used to be a winsome actress, now perches on a stool at the side of the stage, chews gum, and is unreachable. Mr Ayckbourn writes particularly good parts for angular actresses, and Marg provides a splendid outing for Phyllida Law; teetering round the stage with knitting-needles protruding from her torso; looking beadily down a beaky nose, and growing steadily less benign.

Paul is Peter Bowles, who has an individual vocal register; atop his rotund crispness lies an anguished, incredulous squeak on which he draws increasingly often as Colin's amiable posturing becomes increasingly difficult to take. Paul fancies himself as an athlete but Mr Bowles's preliminary prancing is soon eclipsed by the ceaseless activity of Ray Brooks as John. Crawling with tics, he looks as if he needs either to relieve himself or to tapdance.

Mr Brooks's demeanour caps that of the entire quintet; there was once an American musical called `The Nervous Set,' and they might be auditioning for it. They are afraid of one another, of themselves, of Colin. Fearful of saying anything to upset him, they find him impervious to hurt but innocently capable of wounding them.

Colin is altogether a problem, and not only to the other characters. Despite Richard Briers's energetic, rabbity performance he fails (like his catalytic equivalent in `The Norman Conquests') to fill the space required. Either Mr Ayckbourn's nerve or his skill has failed him with Colin. There is no theatrical taboo on death, only on grief; when the bereaved character is as unaffected as Colin, the comedy is no more daring than `Arsenic and Old Lace.' The play's success lies with the married people; Mr Ayckbourn takes an excessive time to set them up, but their collective presence (individually, none of them goes very deep) produces comedy of an unsettling, even saddening kind. There are no belly-laughs, but there is tension.

  

Matters are contrariwise in Tarantara! Tarantara! (Westminster). This stage biography of Gilbert and Sullivan is the Bristol Old Vic's answer to the Liverpool Everyman's John, Paul (those names again), George, Ringo ... and Bert. It too begins spiritedly, with a rehearsal row between its protagonists; and then plunges into flashback. For Bert read Joe, a stagestruck stagehand who knows all the words and all the facts. But where Willy Russell dared to dramatise the Beatles throughout, Ian Taylor rushes as soon as possible for documentary safety; G (Christopher Scoular) and S (Timothy Kightley) read letters at each other from opposite sides of the stage to denote conflict. They also, along with the rest of the cast, sing songs from the shows; and here lies the evening's salvation.

Since much of the feuding between the collaborators seems to have resulted from the value each attached to his own contribution, it is amusing to find Mr Kightley projecting the lyrics with greater clarity and wit than Mr Scoular. They make a good duo, nicely varied in temperament and whiskers. Mr Kightley is small and beaverish, delighted to find himself in the chorus line, a situation which Mr Scoular endures with lofty disbelief. He imparts a Groucho touch to the girl-chasing judge whom he impersonates in a potted `Trial by Jury,' first and best of the musical excerpts. Though David Horlock's direction is racy, with much adroit changing of costume, the numbers become in time as predictable as the dialogue.

  

Nobody Knew They Were There (Bush) is ostensibly about three geriatric ladies abandoned in an isolation ward. What it is basically about I am not too sure. Self-delusion, the battle for precedence, and the role of sexual memories in both activities are all present; the richness of detail, even when the structure wobbles, makes Terence Greer the most interesting new writer to appear for some time. His words are well spoken, and his characters beautifully played, by Yvonne Gillan, Marion Fiddick and Gaye Brown projecting a fiery, raucous spirit which never cracks the fragile shell.
1975-08-03-the-truth-about-simon:
The truth about Simon

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

I DOUBT if there is a shapelier play on the London stage than Simon Gray's Otherwise Engaged (Queen's). Its two acts admirably rhyme, so that a mock suicide in the first is balanced by a genuine suicide in the second. This underlines the fact that in the first act we are concerned with characters to whom life and death are a sour joke, and in the second with people to whom they are a sour reality.

Between these two groups stands the play's central figure, so central that he never leaves the stage. His name, like his author's, is Simon, and he is a publisher, successful and extremely comfortable. The play shows him to us in two lights: our angle of vision changes abruptly at the interval. To begin with, he seems a good-natured, apparently passionless chap doing his best to accommodate everyone. He is scrupulously interested in the correct use of words. His friends, as friends will, use them sloppily, filling their conversation with unintentional ambiguities. Most of us would let these pass, but not Simon. His candour sweetly laced with irony, he tries to get the record straight by asking the questions we would all like to ask.

So we sympathise with him; we also laugh with him, his questions are so elegantly poised. And he seems so assured and with it all so kind; it seems very good of him to bother with people as grey as his brother, desperate for the assistant headmastership of a very minor public school, or as plain objectionable as his best friend, a drunken literary journalist who is having an affair with his own ex-wife and moans about having to write articles for the Radio Times. (It seems that all other publications are monopolised by versatile, hard-working Australians who don't care how little they're paid).

There are also the upstairs lodger, a sociology student who sponges on Simon without shame and is indulged without stint, and a girl who strips to the waist in an effort to get herself laid and published. Simon turns down her body (though not her manuscript) on the grounds that, though desirable, it cannot outweigh her appalling behaviour. Besides, he has a famously happy marriage.
