However, the implication that he therefore never plays around is dispelled at the first-act curtain when he receives a visit from an old schoolmate whose adored girlfriend, it turns out, Simon has seduced.

From then on it is all downhill for Simon. All the qualities for which we have esteemed him are turned against him. The man he has cuckolded recalls their schooldays; Simon was the golden boy, the beautiful bedmate of the sixth, while he himself was a plop; a quaint synonym for a drip, defined in later life as one who progresses from masturbation to marriage to monogamy. Simon's urbanity towards him, as towards his own brother, stands revealed as heartlessness. The lodger realises that his landlord's generosity barely conceals a lazy contempt.

Finally his marriage, the biggest prize of all, is shown to have its basis not in trust but in a kind of rootless tolerance; it goads his wife to take a lover (Mary Miller) which troubles his detachment hardly at all. The curtain falls on Simon, in the company of his writer chum, listening to a recording of Parsifal, for which he has been trying to find the time all day: portrait of a couple of creeps at rest.

I am not sure, though, that the play ever faces up to quite how creepy Simon is. According to his wife he should be envied for his serenity but pitied for the emptiness that makes it possible. But it is the serenity that makes the greater mark, since it finds its expression in wit. Alan Bates (who looks in this role appropriately like Cliff Richard, prototype of bland agelessness) corners virtually all of the evening's abundant laughs; one or two are left over for Julian Glover, in a good coarse performance of the journalist. But the other characters, Simon's victims, are allowed no spark; not once does a joke go against him. The play's structure and its style tell us different things; we only get round to feeling pity for Simon at the final curtain, by which time it seems disproportionate and sentimental.

Still, Otherwise Engaged, following the soupy Ardele into the Queen's, is, in Harold Pinter's icy production, a superior piece of comedie grincante. The actors, apart from one player whose words would sound as expressive delivered by a computer, are good; Mr Glover and Benjamin Whitrow match each other, soak for plop, and Mr Bates radiates glamorous unconcern. Whatever the author's intentions, audiences will go for Mr Bates for his insouciant put-downs and for the splendour of his living-room.

  

Topol's Othello at Chichester turns out surprisingly well. He can make little of his earlier scenes; what hampers him is not his voice, which is slow and painstaking but gets there in the end, but his appearance. His build seems unexpectedly light, he rocks on his feet, describes strange circles with one arm. The play goes to sleep. But the onset of jealousy transforms this Moor; an animal passion seizes him, at one point propelling him bodily down the steps of the platform stage and out through the auditorium. I have never seen an Othello throw a more convincing epileptic fit; even the arm gestures expand with his madness till the final scene finds him executing some spectacular underarm bowling. By this time his interpretation has worn thin again (unless you prefer an Othello permanently denuded of nobility), but he vitalises the middle of the play.

Keith Michell's Iago has an excellent moment as he gazes open-mouthed at the first eruption, wondering what he has let loose and whether he can control it. Iagos come in two categories; surly and glamorous. Mr Michell, naturally equipped for the latter, tries for the former. A sternly non-commissioned moustache vainly competes with a ringing Sandhurst voice. He carries no outer marks of villainy, which makes his dealings with the other characters brilliantly convincing, and none inner, which ruins the soliloquies. Peter Dews's production, accorded a nineteenth-century setting, is solidly attuned to plot and character. I doubt if Mr Dews would recognise an RSC Guiding Concept if he found one lurking in one of his own programme notes.

  

Agatha Christie's Murder at the Vicarage (Savoy) is about a Colonel who is found with a red rosette pinned to the back of his head. But the people on stage call it blood, and are distressed. They include an Artist, a Policeman, a Young Girl (who flounces; no other word for it, in token that she will come to no good), a Doctor, a Curate and, of course, a Vicar. Also a sweet old lady detective who solves the mystery by studying human nature, though where she finds it is unclear. Barbara Mullen plays her with much winsomeness, rotating both her arms even more ferociously than Topol. I thought Derek Bond as the vicar was the best, though I caught him gazing stolidly at the audience when he should have been humouring Miss Mullen. The younger members of the cast are unable to bring any conviction at all to their roles; which doubtless reflects great credit on them. Has not this play the cosiest of titles?
1975-08-31-rocky-road-for-bunyan:
Rocky road for Bunyan

I LIKE the Edinburgh Festival; I want it to go on. But I cannot feel so benevolent towards the three plays which opened in the official festival last week. I wanted them to stop.

Pilgrim is a rock musical based on Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress. It is what likes to be known as a life-enhancing show, very loud and bouncy. It is odd to father such a thing on a seventeenth-century Puritan allegorist, who presumably abhorred the theatre; piquant to encounter it in that august and uncomfortable pile, the Assembly Hall of the Church of Scotland (has it ever been so wired and bugged before?); and downright perverse to cut the story from its historical and theological moorings, so that it becomes a series of pointless episodes. Bunyan would have found it, in the literal sense, graceless; the odd inexplicable religious symbol may be glimpsed floating in a sea of spurious modernity.

Despite their choice of title, the Prospect Theatre Company have essentially dumped the Pilgrim but kept the Progress. Christian is still the star; obviously, since he is played by Paul Jones at his most worried and well-meaning. But he is a Christian without guilt, which is absurd.

This year the Assembly Hall stage is saucer-shaped. The cast begin by bounding on to it, all jeaned and jubilant, letting us know that they are happy (after all this is the opening number) and that they have no room for prophets of doom. Here, they say, while keeping their balance on the edge of the saucer with admirable aplomb, is their world spinning round and round. On this slender provocation Christian (a flat-earth man?) decides to leave home and to forsake what he calls 'this life of spiritual death.' Well, all right, some people don't like musicals, and it is probably very vexing to live next door to a juvenile chorus.

Given these austere tastes, it is odd that Christian should leave home, at the prompting of the somersaulting quick-change artist (name of Evangelist). But he does. Perhaps he merely wanted to get away from his wife, though she haunts him through the show, causing him to pause in his wanderings and participate in long-distance duets. She wants to know why she has been left alone, but he can't come up with an answer; maybe wedlock and salvation are incompatible and he's really an Early Christian.

No, he really is just one of the roving kind, a compulsive musical-comedy tripper. Keep on Travelling Life unrevelingly is his motto, often repeated (sometimes without accompaniment, which makes it sound worse). If travel broadens the mind, it conveniently lengthens the show, though when undertaken without a definite object it can be monotonous, and Christian does seem to keep having the same adventure everywhere he goes. His meeting with Apollyon differs little from his meeting with Giant Despair, neither of them having any noticeable allegorical significance and both of them being the same actor. And he can't get away from that chorus; they keep coming on looking devoutly dynamic or devoutly decadent or just devout. At Vanity Fair they give their androgynous slink and in Prating Row their Hilly Billy stomp, in which they are led by Mr Talkative.

Camped up by Paul Nicholas (who has earlier rendered the same service to Mr Worldly Wiseman), he makes rather a pleasing impression, though the script breaks into genuine Bunyanese to express its disapproval. All his heart lies in his tongue, and his religion is to make a noise therewith.

This seems a fair description of the entire show. When Christian finally gets to the Celestial City, the gang's all there, looking holy. The show washes its hands of religion, and Mr and Mrs Christian declare, in a closing-piece of rhythmic uplift, that there is a time for everything: a time to live, and a time to die, and you know the way they go on.

The production (Toby Robertson) has drive and the music (Carl Davis) has drive and even melody. But both are synthetic; if the authors have treated Bunyan cavalierly (of course he was used to that), they have stuck all too conscientiously to a book of theatrical rules already musty. For a youth-oriented -- indeed child-oriented -- musical, with some original life to it, I commend Venus and Superskid at the Roundhouse in London.

Unlike Pilgrim, Bill Bryden's production of How Mad Tulloch Was Taken Away (Lyceum) can't be accused of excessive brightness. Mr Bryden puts his actors in pools of light but surrounds them with darkness. This first play by Tom Morris is written in short scenes, to each of which Mr Bryden and his designer Hayden Griffin allot the necessary minimum of suggestive setting, whisked on and off the huge bare stage. Actors are disposed in sculptural groupings.

General murk, though soporific and ruinous to the legibility of critical notes, is meant, I would guess, to signify the darkness in Mad Tulloch's mind; he is a Scottish soldier who spends most of the play in inner turmoil, only achieving clarity in the last scene for which, sure enough, Mr Bryden switches the brights up. Tulloch is finally sure of his sanity; when other characters, strong in the opposite belief, approach him he calls out: "They're not coming for me, they're coming to me." That's good, but he adds: "What beautiful things human beings can be," suggesting that, if he has not gone crazy, he has at least gone Hollywood.

It is just such idealistic remarks that have earned Tulloch the reputation for insanity in his own circle. The Highland Infantry must be a singularly repressive organisation to be so roused by routine expressions of trust in common humanity and distrust of social mechanisation. That is about all the provocation Tulloch gives, though he does give it at extreme length. He is a particular bete noire of a punctilious sergeant who seems, in Rikki Fulton's performance, to have come from another, funnier play; the audience perceptibly cheered up whenever Mr Fulton came on, thereby giving Mr Morris counsel as good as any critic is likely to offer.

There is also an officer's wife who stands in the spotlight opposite Tulloch and addresses him in the frigid tones in which high-born ladies in plays are accustomed to address orderlies. She gets him to bed, no problem, but ultimately he is the death of him. Her husband, whom she has taunted for his homosexuality, shoots Tulloch, proclaiming: 'I had the right.' The production may be blamed for the play's portentousness; perhaps it seems naive.

The challenge of Andy Fuggard's play is persistently sounded too literary for his characters. In Dimetos (Church Hill) he solves this problem by placing everyone in a mythological void. The words are resonant but the combination of labour and narrative makes action slack, and setting abolishes action. Both Mr Morris and Mr Fuggard have heroines called Lydia; that exact property was sufficiently promising to have reached the Festival fringe. I shall report next week.
1975-09-07-rocking-at-the-court:
Rocking at the Court

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

Give us a play whose characters are young and we will take it to be a comment on a generation; give us a play about nothing at all and we will read in it as an allegory on the state of the nation. That is the way we have been programmed, over the last couple of years; and David Hare's Teeth 'n' Smiles (Royal Court), in some of its aspects, makes things easy for us. How else can we take a play that ends with a haunting chorus entitled "Last Orders on the Titanic"?

It is a fact, though, that this chorus (music by Tony Bicât) would sound just as haunting, and indeed just as meaningful, if heard completely out of context. The play is full of self-contained effects. They happen to be extremely effective effects, and your reaction to Teeth 'n' Smiles may well depend on whether you most value taste or aftertaste, on whether you want your gratification in the theatre or wherever you do your musing afterwards.

The production is crammed with life. Mr Hare joins the impressive line of dramatists (Howard Brenton, Trevor Griffiths, Snoo Wilson) whose plays have been shown off to best advantage when directed by Mr Hare. His staging here moves through a variety of tones with equal mastery: from a wild, captivating rock-and-roll chorus round a piano to a love-scene where visibility is reduced to--in the words of an older kind of song--two cigarettes in the dark.

The play, though, is concerned with a later variety of pop than either of these; it concerns a rock group, playing at a Cambridge May Ball in 1969. Much of its appeal is that of a backstage musical with superior dialogue; we watch the musicians before, between and after sets and enjoy their reactions--a mixture of incredulity and derision--to the surroundings in which their manager has landed them. Their weariness breeds wit; Mr Hare has a dashing way with one-liners and a rarer gift for building a gag over a period.

The band singer, Maggie, comes apart and doing her best to hurry the process along, living on alcohol, exhibitionism and contempt. Helen Mirren gives a terrific, lashing, frazzled performance, screeching her songs into the mike as if she hated herself and the whole world. Her performance is all that remains though it, too, is now poisoned. But the causes of her malaise are left muddy; the band are apt to remark, inaccurately, that it is no more than a pose that has got into the bone, and Mr Hare seems three-quarters inclined to agree with them. Alternately crying up Maggie's anguish and laughing it down, he ends up with what he probably most wants to avoid: sentimentality. The band's manager makes an overlong speech about a war-time bomb in the Cafe de Paris from which he finally draws a moral about the persistence of the class war. This, Maggie points out, is an idea that has for years saved him the risk and effort of action; but if she has an idea or a plan of action of her own she never lets on. Neither does the songwriter who discovered her and is trying to end their affair, furnished though he is with many of the play's best quips. Neither do the band, one of whom is going sparer than Maggie.

Occasionally a line like "the acid dream is over" suggests that we are in at the end of an era; 1969 was, no argument, the end of the sixties; but Teeth 'n' Smiles, unlike Kennedy's Children, cannot make this appear of more than statistical significance. Towards the close the play goes strident and a touch didactic, as if Mr Hare were trying to force us and himself into seeing a meaning. But he is defeated by his own eye (partly a satirist's eye) for the truth of the situation, and of the characters. If they behave like showbiz stereotypes (for Maggie read any suffering singer from Helen Morgan to Janis Joplin) that is what entertainers do; sticking a counter-culture label on them makes no difference. The manager and the tunesmith are stylishly played by Dave King and Jack Shepherd while the band, acting it up or laying it down, are marvellous.

  

The lack of any confrontation between rock and Cambridge is fair enough; rock presents no challenge and Cambridge is hardly present, though its one student is charmingly played by Antony Sher. (To have Mr Sher, last seen as Ringo Starr, as the only character from outside the music business, is a witty piece of casting; another is to bring on Heinz, one of the strange raves of the early sixties, as a projected star of the seventies.) There are moments in the play where the confrontation is presumed to have taken place but it is best to forget these and take the evening as a celebration--almost an embodiment--of musicians' cool, a perennial and generally uncommitted thing. On those terms, play and performance positively bulge with pleasures.

The highlight of the official Edinburgh Festival was, unexpectedly, the Nottingham Playhouse production of that chestnut As You Like It (Lyceum). Peter Gill's production begins slowly but forcefully; I have never known the battles in Oliver's orchard to be so determinedly fought. In the second scene the entry of Jane Lapotaire as Rosalind, resplendent in golden brown, destroys all doubts. She and Celia (Susan Tracy) appear almost like a couple of Moliere heroines as they discuss Rorqual, Nature and falling in love; from black and gold, straight-backed chairs, two elegant eminences on William Dudley's green box set.

Some Rosalinds drench themselves in love and then shower us with it; Miss Lapotaire is dryer, though as sensible of her own folly as of anyone else's. In the mock-wooing she describes ecstatic circles with her foot, the only outlet for her sense of the joy and absurdity of her situation. With her wit goes an unaccustomed gravity; no other Rosalind has spoken so seriously of her disguised meeting with her father or of her claims to be possessed of magic powers. These you may half believe; Mr Gill has arranged a cunningly magisterial exit for her on "I have left you commands." He has also dug into the relationship of Alun Armstrong's Touchstone, shining with city slickness, and Susan Porrett's Audrey, a large well-meaning girl trying to live up to a lover who, until the end, hardly deserves her; and he has achieved a consummate staging of "Blow, blow, thou winter wind," the singer spotlit and his hearers silhouetted.

The casting of old vaudevillian Leslie Sarony perhaps diverts more attention than is tactful to the faithful Adam (who goaded Shaw to exclaim "O, William Shakespeare, Esquire, you who died drunk, WHAT a moral chap you were!") but he doubles as a usefully befuddled Martext. Mr Gill's firm grip on the play expresses itself through the actors rather than bypassing them.

  

Moving towards the fringe, the Traverse, too, has an excellent company; Susan Carpenter, an actress at once sharp and sympathetic, governs a team notable for its pudgy vulnerability. This is a quality for which the Traverse's two tame playwrights offer much scope: Stanley Eveling's The Dead of Night comes over as a blend (not incongruous) of Peter Ustinov and Tom Stoppard. Little cosmopolitan soldiers debate on the roof of Hitler's bunker the night of his death. Only with Hitler himself, who emerges as rather a bore, does Mr Eveling falter. I preferred C. P. Taylor's Gynt to his reworkings of Sternheim and minor Brecht, the original Ibsen being so huge a work that it qualifies almost as a myth and so leaves plenty of room for retreading; it stays itself regardless. Mr Taylor's version requires that three actors be raised to the Peerage. Mike Ockrent's production is lovely.

On the fringe proper I was cast down by Instant Sunshine, four songster-pranksters dedicated to perpetuating the style of Flanders and Swann beyond its natural; I was cast up again by the Oxford Theatre Group's skilful and unpretentious production of Semmelweiss, a play by Garry O'Connor with a cracking good story (about surgical hygiene) and the wit to open out its implications. The University of Southern California, who regularly revive the very best musicals, lacked the guns for Gypsy, but were delightful in the more congenial Dames at Sea. Kimme Chaloukian might be Ruby Keeler incarnate (and she is a very touching Baby Gypsy). There were hundreds of other shows: I missed them.
1975-09-14-hail-to-britannica:
Hail to Britannica

REWORKING Racine's Phedre under the title Phaedra Britannica (Old Vic), Tony Harrison has moved the action forward from mythical Greece (where Racine found it in Euripides and where he left it) to nineteenth-century India.

Phaedra becomes the Memsahib (all three syllables pronounced in order to preserve the rhythms of Mr Harrison's couplets) lusting after her stepson Thomas Theophilus. Theseus is now her husband the Governor, working hard at slaying tigers, seducing native girls and attempting to stave off the Indian Mutiny. The divinities who tear Racine's characters are now the gods of India--or, as the baffled English characters habitually exclaim, merely "India" itself. The mythology has to be fed to us along with the narrative, which may be why the adaptation seems both longer and slower than the original.

There is nothing wrong with this; not, at least, in the National Theatre production. John Dexter, directing, has literally got Mr Harrison's measure; he has adopted the same hypnotic gait. Tanya Moiseiwitsch, the doyenne and quite possibly the best of British stage designers, has furnished a sweeping colonnade which seems to stretch further the longer you look at it; classical columns are interspersed with tropical blinds, while a menacing deity squats over a huge carved doorway. Within this baleful surround Mr Dexter has conjured performances of uncommon dignity, passion, discipline and weight.

We wait for the weather as much as the characters to break. "Could even come today, the first cloudburst/This damned hot weather's at its very worst," is among the earliest of Mr Harrison's couplets. The refrain develops in time with the fable; the lines that have stayed with me most surely are delivered by Michael Gough as the Governor, gazing through the blinds to summon the cataclysm: "I hope whatever happens happens soon/Then everything washed clean by the monsoon." He gets his wish.

Historically Mr Harrison's achievement is remarkable. We measure Shakespeare's maturity by his abandonment of rhyme for blank verse and even Dryden (whose preference for exotic settings may have influenced Mr Harrison) made the same transition in his one actable tragedy. Mr Harrison's may be the first serious success of any English dramatist in rhyming couplets. Sometimes his very ingenuity works against him; our delight in his adroit solution of his problems unduly lightens the texture of the experience. His cleverness cannot always escape the kind of frigidity endemic to English versions of classical drama, French or Greek.

He has built his edifice with enormous care and cunning. Just as the sea encircled Racine's play, so this version is surrounded by the jungle, Phedre's rejected nurse drowned herself; when similarly treated the Memsahib's Ayah (given a brilliantly incisive foxy performance by Alaknanda Samarth) heads for the woods. "The jungle swallowed her." What have initially seemed self-conscious references to the savage strangeness of the landscape have sharpened and strengthened to culminate in the horror of those four words. As with the country so with its inhabitants; beasts, monsters, brutes (tigers are obviously the least of it) stalk the text until the last arrives to destroy Thomas Theophilus as the sea-dragon put paid to Hippolytus.

The catastrophe is stunningly reported by Robert Eddison, a strange kind of great actor who flourishes on the edges and in the corners of great drama: witness his murderer at the tail-end of Edward II. His iron control of form allows him an untrammelled passage through the verse, a smooth flow which in the first scene combines with David Yelland's staccato attack as Thomas to demonstrate the resource of the production and the possibilities of the text; though Mr Yelland, while characterising excellently, betrays a weakness for forced, ingenuous pauses.

Fearful though Mr Harrison's jungle monster may be, he has not quite the logic of Racine's sea-beast; to ask a hostile sub-continent to devour your son is not quite the same as begging the favour of a marine god who happens to owe you a good turn. And a Phaedra who can find no peace even in death because her father is judge of the underworld must exert more force than one who merely trembles at the thought of what her daddy would say to her. Racine's heroine was of erotic lineage; she brought sex with her. Diana Rigg's Memsahib arrives an innocent and blames lust on the climate. To obscure her from half the audience when she declares her love is one of Mr Dexter's rare gaffes; but a significant one. The bias of the performance is towards justifying the woman's repression, which is done with ashen conviction, and towards expressing her jealousy, in which Miss Rigg is electric. Technically she matches Mr Eddison--surpasses him considering the demands made on her--and she is obviously our next-but-one Cleopatra (Dorothy Tutin being first in line), but as Phaedra she skirts eroticism; indeed her skirts, which make her look like a young Queen Victoria gone untimely into widowhood, may be to blame. The atmospherics finally count for more than the narrative and the adaptation could be self-defeating (even with our classical education in tatters we might find Venus more accessible than Shiva), but it aims higher and gets farther than anything else this year.

Certainly it dwarfs the National's two latest offerings at the ICA. Barry Collins's Judgement (to be restaged in the main house, wherever that turns out to be) is a two and a half hour monologue, undeniably well written but what of that, delivered by the only sane survivor of a group of men driven to cannibalism. We are supposed to judge him; though I would not dream of doing so, Colin Blakely plays with a fearful relaxed urgency, his voice like a stream of unwelcome thoughts pressing upon the brain. He impresses like a man, not an actor; few others have that gift. But he was so casual that little of what he said penetrated to my corner of the room, so I left dissatisfied. Out of the Mouth of Crabs, Ron Daniels's compilation on Sir Walter Raleigh, piling anachronism on inconsequence, is pretty well indefensible.

  

Happy as a Sandbag (Ambassadors) is an anthology of entertainment 1939-45, written by Ken Lee, though what he wrote is uncertain. Not the songs, which are standards, nor the best jokes, which were the property of Max Miller. They prove (as did Lenny) that first-class stand-up material may even outlast its original exponent, who is here lovingly and lovably impersonated by Roy Macready. Darlene Johnson gets several acute cameos; indeed the performance level, under Philip Hedley's precision direction, is captivatingly high. Much fun is to be had, but so is some discomfort. Not that anything nasty is shown on stage, apart from some rations. I would be happier if it were.

The evening ends with the cast singing (and the audience, berserk with nostalgia, joining in) "Here's to the Next Time." As the envoy to a show about war this strikes me as sinister.
1975-09-20-mr-welland-and-the-masculine-:
Mr Welland and the masculine mystique

It is a masculine world: beer, sweat and coachloads of rugger hearties. Its women live on the sidelines. But rugby makes separate demands on both players and their women, as a new drama series starting this week shows. Here Robert Cushman talks to playwright Colin Welland about the divided loyalties around the game

The Wild West Show
Friday 10.15 pm BBC2

'AS YOU KNOW we're a pretty motley crew. One of the great strengths of our game is that up here in the North, at least, it's not identified with any social stratum or class. If you want to play rugby, you're welcome.'

The speaker is the secretary of Cogdon rugby union club. Cogdon is a small town in the North, and imaginary. It has been created, though, as much through memory and observation as imagination. Television playwright Colin Welland played for just such a club in his home town of Newton-le-Willows in Lancashire -- played for it for 20 years from the time he was 16 until he was 36. He would even slip back for the odd game during the three years he was PC Graham in Z Cars, a formative experience.

Z Cars was a masculine world; women were on the sidelines, suffering and criticising. And this may also be the impression created initially by Welland's cycle of six plays about the Cogdon rugby players. It's even called The Wild West Show -- after the rugby song about being off to see the Wild West show.

Fear had been expressed that women may find the series unpalatably male -- or at any rate the first play, Good Lad Terry, which is concerned with the election of a new captain and focuses almost exclusively on the practice-field, the changing-room, the communal bath, the club bar. Welland himself is unworried. 'Let's woo 'em that way, let's get a bit of rile going.'

The clue to his approach is to be found in that speech of the secretary's and in his own reminiscences of playing for Newton. 'I can go back to that club now, I can meet fellers who I've known since I was eight.

'It's a complete cross-section. In our pack we had a schoolteacher hooking, two face-workers at the pit propping, in the second row would be a doctor and a corset-salesman.'

But all this camaraderie is based on a strictly limited view of the world, one which Welland himself has been compelled to discard. He got out of Newton when he was 26, probably just in time. (He went to Manchester to act in rep, played the lead in a Pinter play straight off, and discovered colloquial modern dialogue for the first time. The discovery was inspiring, and he began writing almost as soon as he had begun acting.) There are plenty of others who should have got out but didn't; and they appear in the plays. This image of a closed society which is part haven, part trap recurs in Welland's plays.

The role of the women in the plays steadily expands. In the electioneering of the first play they are, according to one of the stage-directions 'the female -- shut out from it all -- all the big decision-making -- handy for having it off with and helping serve food on special occasions'. But as the series proceeds they assume central roles in more complex situations. Mad Mick's wife has to choose between her distaste for rugby and the disintegration of her husband to whom the club means so much. In Oh Oh Antonio the captain's marriage reaches a crisis during an old friend's anniversary party. And in Melvyn's Marauders, a wife is faced with her portly husband's obsession to get back into trim for one more match.

While the men can escape reality at the rugby club, the women are left to cope at home. Welland is insistent that his rugby plays, unlike David Storey's The Changing Room (which he thinks belongs spiritually to the 50s), are happening now. 'The place isn't a sort of picturesque Lancashire pitch with a viaduct behind it and terraced houses -- it's got motorways round it and factories beside it. And all the attitudes and the problems that the lads are facing are today.'

He thinks in fact that both sexes are trapped by the system. But while the men can respond by trying to perpetuate their youth, the women have to retrace their steps because nothing individual is left for them to do. 'You go to Leeds on a Wednesday night, you go into a pub and it's packed with married women who have this night out. The system's easier on the men but it still sells them short.'

Welland has written about rugby before; in fact it was the subject of his first produced play Bangelstein's Boys which was such a success that London Weekend television entered for an Italia Prize. (It didn't win; 'they thought it was too disgusting.') The Wild West Show attempts to do justice to the material which was left unexplored in that early one-shot effort; it has the same producer, Kenith Trodd, and three of the six instalments have the same director, John Mackenzie. His career between these two works on rugby has been almost entirely, and very successfully, on television. There has been one stage play, Say Goodnight to Grandma, and as a theatre critic I would like more. He would, too (the theatre pays better for one thing), but he likes to keep his stories on the move ('I'm good at action and rows, I'm bad at philosophising') and he feels hampered by the restrictions of set and characters imposed on most stage playwrights. Certainly it's as a playwright that he wants to be remembered.

The Wild West Show is likely to exercise rather than exorcise his mixed feelings about his early years and the game that seems to symbolise them. 'The one thing you can't show is the thrill of actually playing. It's very much a communal game; it's probably very damaging to the maturing process but I've got great affection for it. I'd hate to see Newton Rugby Club go. But my wife, whenever she's really disgusted with me, will always say "Back we go to Newton rugby club." She sees me back again as one of those boozing chauvinist pigs.'
1975-09-21-brave-and-bracing:
Brave and bracing

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a Harley Granville Barker revival.

ONE of the more disturbing features of the theatre this year has been the extent to which our two most highly subsidised theatres have been encouraged to play safe.

The National Theatre can hardly have been expected to fail with Ibsen, Shaw, Beckett and Pinter--standard authors, infallibly cast. But a national theatre should not only protect, but extend the national repertory, and though we may be within our rights to pronounce the attempted resurrection of Gilbert's 'Engaged' a failure, it is chilling to hear it declared that the attempt should never have been made.

To their credit, the National proceeded undeterred to honour another of the obscurer dead, a foreigner too. After a week of brooding over their 'Phaedra Britannica,' my admiration for the technical skill of translator, director and performers remains immense, though in altering Racine's mythology they have sacrificed more logic than they have gained.

I cannot begrudge the Aldwych their safe period earlier in the year, if only because the revival of Tom Stoppard's 'Travesties,' with John Wood picking his way unerringly through a minefield of jokes and Lenin (Harry Towb) accorded his proper status like the other characters among history's clowns, possesses twice the sparkle of the first attempt and three times the logic. ('If only Tom Stoppard had got it together,' I pontificated last Christmas, 'it would have been the play of the year.' I see now that he had, and it was.) But I respect the RSC the more for their new kamikaze tactics. True there are limits (David Mercer's 'Duck Song' last year was beyond them, even as it was beyond most of us), but Charles Wood's 'Jingo' was a thoroughly honourable flop, whatever it cost. Suppose we agree to stop using the economic situation as a critical sanction.

From all of which it follows that I wish to hear no puling objections to the latest offering at the Aldwych, where on Thursday we assisted at the second performance (not production, performance) of Granville Barker's The Marrying of Ann Leete, the first having taken place on a Sunday night in 1902. How pleasant to be in virtually at the birth of a major dramatist.

The play was actually written in 1899, and is set a hundred years previously; it is one dying era's tribute to another. No, tribute is not the word; and Barker and his characters are very careful of their words, very jealous of how much they may be permitted to convey. He was 21 when he composed it, and the play has the harshness of youth, though not (compared with some of our infant prodigies) either its hysteria or its priggishness. It is also extraordinarily brave.

Ann Leete is a politician's daughter. Her elder sister has been married off for her father's advantage, and she is about to be sent the same way. At first she acquiesces, somewhat frightened but resigned. Only she overhears too much of the family cynicism, the family scheming and--particularly in reference to her sister's marriage--the bitterness of the family failure. The same day as her match is made she breaks it off, and offers herself as the wife of the gardener, the new self-reliant man, named--with heavy but not unpleasant symbolism--Abud. At the play's end, Ann, removed from spacious gardens to her husband's narrow cottage, contemplates an unromantic future. 'I'll do my part . . . something will come of it.'

The play presages change, not only historical (and its characters live in submerged awareness of revolution across the Channel) but theatrical. To us it may recall Chekhov--but the play it most resembles, 'The Cherry Orchard,' it actually antedates. The dialogue can be cryptic and allusive beyond anything in Pinter. It requires attention (and, if possible, a preliminary squint at the text), but magnificently rewards it. Sometimes the words are used, in Jamesian fashion, to polish thought (and to convey a period style with no recourse to archaism), sometimes to conceal it; the characters play devious games. Barker's plays are oddly angled; they tell their stories with a teasing disregard for the obvious.

This one begins with a kissing-game, before dawn, and the images of kissing, of play, of light and darkness reverberate through it, in action as well as dialogue. The Leetes' intrigues are harshly, classically illuminated; the final scene, candle-lit, implies both completion and progression. David Jones's production seems to me a rarer achievement than his Gorki plays (and will, hopefully, inaugurate a similar Barker cycle); Gorki's are juicy plays; obvious gifts for actors. This needs to be played with passion, but within a strict, witty convention. Here, as in 'Phaedra Britannica,' those demands are met. Mr Jones finds the rhythms of the play, and shapes them into personal encounters.

The casting of Mia Farrow as Ann proves an inspiration. She is opposed to a collection of hard stylish actors; Paul Rogers, Richard Pasco, Estelle Kohler at her brittlest and best; only Mike Gwilym, as a brother half out of the family, makes some humane concessions. Among them all Miss Farrow, fiercely vulnerable, has to work out her own stance. Hers is, in no derogatory sense, a very painstaking performance; she learns, and grows, we watch and grow with her. 'I must study politics,' she says with her head on one side (her voice, too, it seems) and the impact on her consciousness is precisely charted. Not all of Barker's ideas come off the page; a Hogarthian rout of wedding-guests remains an intention rather than a fact. But the evening is fresh, vital, bracing, and all things pertaining to iced water.

  

Steven Berkoff has in the past directed the London Theatre Group, acted with it, adapted Kafka for it. He now puts it, himself included, through its paces in his first original work. Unfortunately East (King's Head) seems to have been written for little reason beyond that of furnishing the group with a text of Mr Berkoff's own; it is aimless, with a tyro's idea of shape. That is, it ends with the same lines as it has begun, in the apparent belief that there is something profound about a loop. (I would have said a circle, but 'East' is not so well rounded.)

The subject matter, loosely assembled, is life in the East End; vignettes have been selected in order to allow scope for maximum aggression which, when it slackens, necessarily entails maximum sentimentality. Much of the dialogue is pastiche blank verse, delivered in the clipped Shakespearean tones made familiar by Peter Sellers, Benny Hill and Laurence Olivier. Some of the prose bits, though, are good; notably a hard-pressed mum's dreamy monologue of escape, delivered in drag by Robert Longden.

Barry Stanton has some huffy, rosy-faced moments as Dad; his off-beat timing suggests that they may be improvised. And as a work-out for its actors the show, fluently staged, is reasonably enjoyable; enabling them to shine as motor-bikes, dodgem-cars (Mr Berkoff's arrival tending to the mechanistic) and even, sometimes, as people.
1975-09-21-fey-lady-with-steel-nerves:
Fey lady with steel nerves

THE first time many people took Mia Farrow seriously was when she appeared in Rosemary's Baby. Before then she might have been seen in the TV serial Peyton Place or read of as Frank Sinatra's third wife: a short-lived marriage that seems more unlikely the further away it recedes.

Rosemary fixed a screen-image for her, one that has been difficult to shake off. In Roman Polanski's neo-Gothic melodrama she played a young wife impregnated by witchcraft, and she brought to the role a haunting mixture of fright and determination. As her knowledge of her plight grew, her nerves began almost to protrude through her skin, but hysteria never quite took over.

Miss Farrow, now playing the title role in the Royal Shakespeare Theatre production of Granville-Barker's The Marrying of Ann Leete in the Aldwych, recalls Rosemary's Baby now as "the most fun I ever had making a film." She speaks of the demands it made on her but these turn out, surprisingly, to have been more physical than psychological: dangerous things like walking across a real crowded New York street while cars screeched to a halt around her. "But Roman said it was all right, nobody would hit a pregnant woman."

After Rosemary she was, inevitably, offered a whole string of "hounded, neurotic, ailing women" in films. She only played one, in Joseph Losey's Secret Ceremony, giving an odd, haunting performance.

Her films since then have been undistinguished, culminating in the thumpingly bathetic Great Gatsby. Meanwhile she resumed her stage career.

In 1963, at the age of 18, she had made her Broadway debut as Cecily in The Importance of Being Earnest, a role in which she received influential applause but no Press reviews (there was a newspaper strike). Nine years later, in Manchester and later in London, she played the title role in Barrie's Mary Rose. Barrie would seem to be the ideal dramatist for her - all feyness without, all steel within - but the performance proved a little beyond the theatrical effectiveness of her bright, piercing Anglo-American voice.

It tended to isolate her on stage, and made her next stage appearances memorable. She went to Greenwich for a season of plays under the direction of Robin Phillips: Chekhov's Three Sisters and Lorca's House of Bernarda Alba. In both she was the youngest sister and she looked a frail, gawky adolescent harbouring private traumas, private joys and private rages, hugging them to her so intensely that the privacy itself became public. Now she comes back to the stage again in Granville-Barker's play, eighteenth-century in setting and allusive in dialogue to an extent that has daunted producers and kept it off the stage during Edwardian days. She describes her character as "the only member of a wealthy political family trying to create an honest life for herself."

Meanwhile she tries to create her own life as the wife of the most popular (at a guess) musician in the country. Since Andre Previn's chief job is conducting the London Symphony Orchestra, the life centres just outside London: in a handsome low-slung oak-beamed farmhouse in Surrey, called The Haven and standing in 20 acres. When he travels she goes with him whenever she can. The main restriction on her mobility now is obvious: the heroine of Rosemary's Baby having become one of the most publicised of mothers: three sons, plus two adopted daughters from Vietnam. "Whatever is small is ours," remarked Previn.

With the children surrounding her, climbing all over her, asking her when they'll see the musical Peter Pan which they've watched her shooting for television (Christmas, of course) it seems pointless to ask what occupies her time when she's not working. But I do ask and she says of course that the children do.

Otherwise: "I always aim for the sea when I want a frolic. As a child I grew up by the sea in Malibu, and I miss being near it and consulting it daily." Consulting it? Well, "our brain is over 90 per cent water so we ought to feel an affinity with it."

Her father is film director John Farrow and her mother the actress Maureen O'Sullivan (Johnny Weissmuller Tarzan, she Jane) but she doesn't cite any family influence on her choice of career. She makes it sound the most comprehensible of desires: "To be anything you wanted - it's an irresponsible way of living a lot of lives. It's a safe way to let things out emotionally - there's no real risk because you know how it's going to end."

Robert Cushman
1975-09-28-complex-simon:
Complex Simon

PROFILE

MOTOR-BICYCLES, TV tubes, motor cars, machine tools, ships, House of Commons crockery: Britain may be getting worse at all these things, but we are still good at playwrights. In recent weeks, another of them has broken through the mysterious barrier between obscurity and fame: Simon Gray.

He has had successes before now. Indeed, of all English dramatists to emerge since the war, few have a better commercial track-record. Both the Royal Shakespeare Company and the National Theatre have presented plays of his, but it is in the West End that he has scored. 'Wise Child,' in 1967, was a big hit; 'Butley,' in 1971, was even bigger. Now his new play, 'Otherwise Engaged,' looks as if it will outstrip them both; and it has at last made Gray's name known.

His popular success is not surprising. There has always been a good public for comedy of manners, and this is Gray's field. He specialises in bleakly comic accounts of the personal relations between professional people, highly intelligent and articulate, as they grate against and wound one another, often within some educational establishment.

Gray is a London don. It is a recurrent theme, especially in his later work, that the child is father to the man. In a new play he has written for television, to be shown this autumn, a character remembers a stroke he played in an under-15 cricket match, a late cut to the boundary. It was, he recalls, 'the one moment in my life when I felt a touch of sublimity.' This is a rare case of a Gray protagonist dropping his shield of self-protective wit and revealing the schoolboy still in there. To Gray, school is still uncommonly vivid: a time when anything was possible; when friends and brothers were choosing which route to take, before spending the rest of their lives wondering if it was the right one.

Gray is dark and chunky, with hair over his eyes. He was born in 1936, the second son of a physician of Canadian extraction. He spent the war years in Montreal where, freed from the parental grip, he acquired the habit of smoking 10 cigarettes a day and developed an ingenious form of street begging: this involved writing an address on an envelope and then bursting into tears until a kindly passer-by would prevail on the little chap to explain that he had lost the stamp for the letter he had been sent to post, and would cough up the necessary sum.

Aged 14, having returned with his brother to England at the age of eight, he became mixed up in the Great Tube Ticket Machine Swindle, whereby he inserted a Georgian penny, purchasable for twopence, instead of a florin, and thereby acquired a ticket and three sixpences change. He worked this racket until he and the rest of his gang were nabbed on Victoria station by three policemen.

He went to Westminster School in London, where he was very keen at games; then for three years to Dalhousie University in Canada, after his father took a job there as a pathologist; and then to Cambridge, chiefly because he wanted to study under F. R. Leavis.

He went to all Leavis's lectures and seminars, and Leavis was and continues to be an enormous influence. He regards Leavis as the greatest critic of the century and the greatest teacher he has ever met. He considers Leavis's direct influence to have been on his reading rather than on his writing, but there too it can be seen in the way that Butley or Simon in the new play both, so to speak, act as literary critics in life.

To others, the way they catch at words and phrases and play wittily with them may seem a device for distancing experience and protecting themselves from realities. But it is only through words that we can grasp realities, and it is only by using words precisely that we can properly engage with experience. That fuzzy language is not only fuzzy thinking but also fuzzy morality is one belief at least that Simon Gray's protagonists share with Dr Leavis.

There were some bright people around Cambridge in those days -- Peter Cook, David Frost, Andrew Sinclair, Ian McKellen, Margaret Drabble, and Jonathan Miller among them. But Gray made little effort to cut a figure in university society; he is remembered by his contemporaries chiefly for a lacerating attack on undergraduate writers, including Margaret Drabble.

One thing he had in common with that generation, though, was a feeling that if you were ever going to make it, you had better get started quickly. By the mid-sixties, he had published three novels, moved to London, married, and started teaching.

The first two novels were comedies, rather in the style of early Henry James. The third, 'Little Portia,' showed a considerable rise in temperature, which was maintained in his early TV plays. After a genial first effort about a man with an addiction to hot baths, these became increasingly violent, both physically and emotionally, culminating in 'Wise Child,' which, said the BBC, could not possibly be performed on television. It was thereupon commissioned as a stage play and associated Gray in many people's minds with the late Joe Orton; like an Orton play, it appeared to be a comedy of kinkiness, requiring its leading actor, Sir Alec Guinness, to spend most of the evening in skirts.

The subsequent plays have been, so to speak, straighter. Though there were plenty of intimations of homosexuality in 'Butley,' it was the hero's marriage which, however obliquely presented, lay at the core of the play. This is more plainly true of 'Otherwise Engaged'; the heroes of both these plays shun emotional commitment, and shelter behind walls of irony. In 'Butley' the audience could be fairly sure that this was a sign of the character's inadequacy, but 'Otherwise Engaged' is more unsettling. It almost dares us to reject its hero; where Butley was seedy, he is well set up and supremely witty. The precision of his language makes it clear why Harold Pinter, sensing a fellow-spirit, has been so eager to direct Gray's plays.

After a period in which the word was suspect in the theatre, our writers are rediscovering language; they use it sparely and sardonically, often as an instrument of judgment, and here Gray is in the mainstream.

While producing these plays he has remained a full-time lecturer in English at Queen Mary College, London. The Mile End Road is one of London's least attractive spots, and Queen Mary College is scarcely the intellectual powerhouse of the Western world. Someone who has long-running plays in the West End and Broadway can hardly be there for the money. Nor does he seem destined for great heights in the academic career structure. Though he has written some critical essays, he has had neither the time nor inclination for Eng. Lit. crit. of the kind that brings advancement.

In Academe it is not enough to write literature: you have to write about it. Gray once actually received a letter from some college committee which pointed out that his chances of promotion were being jeopardised by the fact that he had never published anything: this was at a time when he had brought out four novels and three plays.

Why, then, does he go on teaching? First, because he enjoys it. It also gives him a life outside the theatre and keeps him in touch with literature. 'You must have a grotesquely high opinion of yourself,' he says, 'to think that your contribution as a writer is more important than your contribution as a teacher.'

What time is left over from the theatre and the university is lived privately in North London in a big house with his wife, two children of nine and six, three cats, two dogs, a great many books and various lodgers and droppers-in. He works long hours, writes compulsively, and reads with ferocious concentration -- especially Dickens, which he goes through over and over again. He plays squash, watches cricket and football, and goes to the cinema -- often secretly in the afternoon, so that he can have the added pleasure of feeling guilty.

He usually gives the impression of being harassed and about to be overwhelmed by domestic crises and the complications and sheer busy-ness of his life. This is partly a protective device to preserve time to work in and to keep social predators at bay.

However, though he doesn't suffer fools gladly, he does alleviate the pain they cause by taking an almost clinical interest in what makes them such fools, and in why their folly takes the precise form it does. He is fascinated by the motives behind people's behaviour -- including his own -- and has a collector's interest in foibles, mannerisms, and obsessions.

His refusal to accept unthought-out or half-baked judgments, his quickness of mind, and a wit that is not always tempered by mercy, can make him intimidating. But when he is relaxed and with friends, he is excellent company and an extremely funny talker. Though none of the characters in his plays is a self-portrait, there are family resemblances between him and them. With a packet of cigarettes, some good whisky, and a great deal of wit and intelligence, they do their best to cope with the pleasures and pain inherent in the human condition.

Acts of rage and laughter

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

TO RECAP on Trevor Griffiths's Comedians, which the National Theatre has brought to the Old Vic from the Nottingham Playhouse: it deals with six young men, learning stand-up comedy at evening classes under the tuition of an old pro called Eddie Waters, played with increased authority and undiminished concern by Jimmy Jewel.

At the end of the course they perform, one after the other, in a Manchester club, between bingo sessions. The adjudicator is Bert Challenor, a big-time London agent and, by temperament and experience, an enemy of Eddie's. He believes in escapism, where Eddie takes it to be the comic's duty to reveal the truth. His pupils face a last-minute choice: to stand by what he has taught and they have prepared, or to jack it in and improvise in the hope of a metropolitan contract. In the event they divide equally; in one case the division cuts across a double-act, reducing it to chaos. Otherwise, those who go for the money achieve it. One of them is an Irishman and another a Jew.

`Comedians' is not a play about race, but one of the most fascinating things about it is the way in which ethnic themes, recurring in the dialogue and action, bind it together. It starts from the observation that racial jokes and racial stereotypes -- malicious or good-humoured and very often self-propagated -- are the staples of pop comedy. To Eddie they are anathema, and those of his pupils who adopt them prove him right. Sammie Samuels, one of the sellers-out, is very much a case in point; assailed by a staccato catalogue of stock anti-semitic jibes, he replies, lamely but by the book, `you must have met the wife's family.'

The most memorable lines in Sammie's act are spoken after a brace of Jewish jokes have died on him: `All right, forget the Jews, everyone else has.' He switches into characterless aimless gag-reeling, a transition much approved by Mr Challenor who believes in having a go at everything without actually hitting anything. This is the technique adopted in excelsis by the Irish winner; Bert really goes for him and such is the lightness and panache of Stephen Rea's performance that Bert's judgment in this instance is hard to dispute.

There is also an Irishman among those who remain loyal to Eddie; his humour is quiet and realistic, rooted in his origin -- and more particularly in his position as an Irishman in England -- but not exploiting it; Bert finds him monotonous and parochial, though Jim Norton endows the act with such an easy Dave Allen authority that it is possible to think that, even in his own terms, Bert may for once be making a mistake.

A progression begins to emerge: Jewishness is now too familiar to be anything more than a tired comic reflex, Irishness is going the same way, but its state is still critical enough to permit of thoughtful laughter. Later immigrants are still the butt of jokes, but have not yet learned to seize the jokes for themselves (which could be aggression or capitulation, depending). But Mr Griffiths slyly suggests that they are already on the move: a Pakistani who wanders into the class, looking for some other form of adult education, returns at the end to tell a joke of his own which Eddie recognises as old Jewish. Which wraps it all up.

There are darker echoes here. It was hearing a mild anti-Jewish joke shortly after visiting the site of a concentration camp which sickened Eddie of professional comedy. He has come to distrust the easy attractions of aggression and he detects them in the work of his star pupil, Gethin Price.

Gethin's act might have been tailored to upset the man from London (though it is technically too elaborate to have been whipped up on the instant for that purpose), but even Bert grants him `some talent as a mime.' That is poor praise for Jonathan Pryce's miraculously supple Gethin, whose body is as taut and plangent as a violin-string. He actually plays the violin -- a mocking tuneless version of `The Red Flag' -- and there is mockery too in his stance; at one point he executes a devastating ballet of sham abasement. Outside his act he can be funny as well as electrically angry. Within the act -- which is largely a diatribe against two cardboard (literally) middle-class figures -- a cold coherent rage takes over. Eddie's doubts about whether it can truly be called comic are justified; it is not funny, but more to the point it is not -- the defining mark of comedy -- oblique.

I am not sure that the play fully recognises this; and the uncertainty -- along with some cloudiness, and even a touch of sensationalism, in the argument about the camps -- must be held against it. Otherwise the evening (scheduled for only a few performances, but we can get it extended if we shout) is exceptionally rich.

Characterising his six aspirants, their teacher and their judge, Mr Griffiths sets up complex cross-currents which Richard Eyre's production masterfully navigates. He is witty, too, and it is piquant and instructive that while the vocational comics hammer away, the best lines go to outsiders -- a caretaker, a bingo caller -- who are unconscious of possessing them. Behind it all Mr Griffiths is giving us a re-handling, in immeasurably strengthened form, of his previous play, `The Party.' For comedy serves him as a metaphor of dissent, even of revolution; and the characters divide, without forcing, into those who accept or profit from it, those like Gethin who want to dynamite it, and those like Eddie who hate one side for its mendacity and fear the other for its violence. Mr Griffiths, I would guess, has split himself between Gethin and Eddie; but this time the ambiguity comes over not as an evasion of responsibility, but as a recognition of human complexity.

  

The National's season at the ICA has ended at its best with Richard Crane's Bloody Neighbours. The programme credits Mr Crane, the Ernie Wise of fringe playwrights, with 10 plays this year. Like Ern, he often draws on schoolroom classics; `Bloody Neighbours' is one of his rare modern subjects. It still has a touch of precocity about it; its first half featuring a suburban couple is beguiling at the time, but thin in retrospect. The second act, set among supposedly freer spirits, moves heavily, but lingers longer. Brenda Blethyn makes a nagging wife more than tolerable; when she describes a fantasised affair she is positively touching. Touching, too, is the homosexual next door, played by an actor improbably billed as C. J. Allen.

  

Mr Griffiths's scheme is big, but smaller than his play; Mr Crane's scheme defines his play, but confines it, too. Andrew Cruickshank's Games (Haymarket Studio, Leicester) is all scheme, and requires characters who have hardly been introduced (in either sense, theirs or ours) to strip one another loquaciously bare. Mr Cruickshank's own presence, a massively quizzical teddy-bear, is the chief compensation.

World of cads
and tuxedos

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on
a revival of Noel
Coward's 'The Vortex.'

WANDERERS in an Art Deco wilderness, Florence Lancaster and her son Nicky appear on the stage of the Greenwich Theatre like late arrivals to last year's series of 'Family Romances.' You may remember that that season, under the direction of Jonathan Miller, consisted of 'Hamlet,' 'The Seagull' and 'Ghosts'; and at one time it was rumoured that Noel Coward's The Vortex would be of their company.

It is as well perhaps that the rumour proved false, and that we have had to wait till now to see Coward's play at Greenwich, under the direction of James Roose-Evans. Mr Miller, once he had started work on it, would surely have got irritated by its thinness, and this irritation would have communicated itself to us. Compared with Chekhov's and Ibsen's Hamlet-variations, never mind with the thing itself, Coward's play lacks body. It suffers, too, from a facile ending, curing mother and cadging son happy in each other's arms at the final curtain. Chekhov and Shakespeare placed their equivalent clinches in the middle of the action; by the end of the show such easy reconciliations have been left far behind. In Ibsen the embrace is saved for the finale, but it is a ghastly parody of a happy ending.

'The Vortex,' however, closes with Florence, who has had lovers, and Nicky, who has taken drugs, both promising never to do it again. We can believe them or not as we choose, I found it difficult to care either way. In this respect the play is partly the victim of history; or at least of that small tributary of history called fashion. Its true element is the twenties, the cocktail and tuxedo twenties: the Noel Coward twenties in short, by our lights the cutest period that ever was. Mr Roose-Evans has tried to woo us into the play by initially emphasising twenties charm (so that cloche-hatted Jennifer Hilary, as Florence's confidante, never sits on a chair when she can perch on its arm or drape herself against its back), and subsequently fading it out so that the last scene leaves us with unadorned timeless emotion.

Here he echoes his author, who fills out his first two acts with the bitchy humours of his heroine's entourage before turning relentlessly to business in the last. The result, however, in both writing and production is that manner, or just mannerism, outbalances matter. Having become attuned to a Coward comedy, though not one of his best, we are dashed to find mother and son upbraiding each other in a modern closet scene. (When they start rolling on the bed it's really too much.)

The turning-point has been a moment of sheer melodrama, well-made melodrama, but no more convincing for that. Florence discovers her current gigolo kissing Nicky's fiancee. 'What does this mean?' she asks rhetorically. 'You are an utter cad,' she states, even more rhetorically. The following year Coward himself parodied this kind of thing in 'Hay Fever' where the inveterate performer Judith Bliss ('Is this a game?' 'Yes, and a game that must be played to the finish') makes every blameless intrusion the occasion for a scene. Judith is a more truthful as well as a funnier version of Florence. Each one of them is a Bright Middle-aged Thing, a sad phenomenon, as 'The Vortex' keeps insisting, but not overwhelmingly tragic. Where Judith is an actress, Florence merely moves in a theatrical ambience. We are already within sight of Coward's typical snobbery towards non-thespians, treating them as bizarre objects to be sniffed at, patronised and touched with tongs.

The milieu is too shallow to be worth storming at or preaching over, but Coward does both in 'The Vortex.' He is fair enough to make his mouthpiece Nicky more than slightly suspect, though little of this emerges in the performance of Timothy Dalton, who seems undernourished but thoroughly healthy. Vivien Merchant, all of a flutter as Florence, speaking low, slow and breathy like an enervated Fenella Fielding, pays the same price as the play and production, livening the early scenes at the expense of the conclusion. The freshest acting comes from Gabrielle Drake, the fiancee who acts as foil to Nicky's grand filial passion.

  

Toby Robins, a leading Canadian actress over two decades, looks startlingly youthful as the recidivist heroine of The Ecstasy of Rita Joe. She is a better advertisement for Canadian theatre than George Ryga's play (at the fallible Hampstead Theatre Club), which treats of the dispossessed Indian in a manner stolid, documentary at best and leadenly fanciful otherwise. (Red man speak with ornamental tongue; often he trip over it.) It must have seemed more urgent in its own time (1967) as well as its own place. Technically it plods in a manner we have outgrown on both sides of the Atlantic; its avoidance of character confrontation strains both the patience and the nerves. Its original production probably owed much to the presence of genuine Indians. (One staging featured Chief Dan George, the indestructible ancient of 'Little Big Man.') At Hampstead it falls an easy victim to a miserably unauthentic production, which closes with blanketed white actors stomping hard, perhaps to ward off the evil spirits of embarrassment. They materialised nonetheless.
1975-10-12-all-about-the-irish:
All about the Irish

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN at the Dublin Festival.

THE critic who has been properly chastened by Trevor Griffiths's `Comedians' is likely to feel nervous for several weeks about his response to racial stereotypes: particularly, in view of Mr Griffiths's preoccupation, Irish racial stereotypes. The Dublin Theatre Festival, it turns out, is no place to escape from them; here, however, when the Irish stock is boiling over, the polite phrase to reach for is not exploitation, but national consciousness.

At the Gaiety, for example, Hugh Leonard offers three one-act plays collectively entitled Irishmen. Imagine that on the bill in any other capital. Had Joyce not got in first, it might have been `Dubliners'; all the plays take place in the city, indeed in a single street, in the course of a single evening. And if Barbra Streisand, or her songwriters, had not staked their claim, Mr Leonard might simply have settled for `People.' For a street, as Granada television has spent years instructing us, is a universal thing and Mr Leonard's is not, in its essence, hopelessly remote from other streets.

Mr Leonard's position in Dublin rivals, for popularity and productivity, Alan Ayckbourn's in London or Neil Simon's in New York, but technically his range is greater than either of them. A bit of pathos, a bit of melodrama, a bit of farce, make up a pleasing, teasing mixture; if you tickle us, do we not bleed?

The pathos is served first: a late night drunk returns home to find `the house talking to itself' and proceeds to follow its example. On the whole we are his beneficiaries, especially as the monologue is played by the stalwart Godfrey Quigley. An exquisitely appropriate name that: a portmanteau of quick and wriggly. He is here extremely quigly, executing elaborate diagonals across the debris of his life and his living-room, but never relaxing into self-indulgence. With the fun and the pain goes an unsentimental evaluation of the man's plight and his own responsibility for it. His wife has left him, and so may his job; one can see the reason for both predicaments without quite losing sympathy for the victim. The playlet is over-long, but it has the most consistent writing of the three.

The best individual flashes, however, come in the melodrama. A young bourgeois, identified by his possessions (`a car that's fast and a wife that looks fast'), falls foul of two embittered activists; he is hated, and he suffers, less as an enemy than as a blundering neutral. The early dialogue, with the situation still mysterious, is charged with solid dread: dangerous banter on the surface and deadly grudge beneath. The later passages are less original, recalling `The Birthday Party' as the aggressors turn interrogators in the antiphonal style that is supposed to denote uncompromising realism. (Actually I have never heard anyone -- or any two -- speak antiphonally in real life, and I doubt if it could be done without a great deal of practice, even in Ireland.) This play comes nearest of the three to an honest justification of the overall title. Its concerns, bleakly realised, are native and organic -- notably in Donal McCann's chilling performance of a gunman.

In the farce, local colour is pasted on. A husband gets the chance to deceive his wife because she has gone on a pilgrimage; when she makes the expected unexpected return she mistakes his girl friend for a leprechaun. That sort of thing. There is no very good reason for the wife's gullibility, but in order to get his machinery moving Mr Leonard needs to keep most of his characters stupid and this blunts his comedy. Farce is a struggle between a man's wits and a malevolently logical fate. Fate has it too easy here; despite all that a bustling Mr Quigley can do for the husband, it is too obvious that he hasn't got a prayer.

Mr McCann also makes a solicitous return as a fey friend of Mr Quigley. I have never seen Irish camp before, and I laughed a great deal. But again my conscience, new moulded by Griffiths, troubled me; for assuredly Mr McCann is playing a homosexual stereotype, and the offence is not lessened but increased by having him deny that he is gay before milking hell out of the assumption that he is. And a similar, larger duplicity informs the whole piece. If Irish puritanism were as rampant as the plot assumes, then Mr Leonard's play would not be put on.

  

Probably there are subtleties I missed; certainly I felt completely out of touch with Thomas Murphy's The Sanctuary Lamp at the Abbey. An English dramatist who took loss of religious faith for his subject would need to work at it; he could not assume an interested audience. Even in Dublin Mr Murphy has been too confident in the demands he makes. All his dramatic skill goes on setting up the situation -- on getting Harry, a down and out with an unstamped card, into a church as keeper of the eponymous flame and general janitor.

But turning Harry loose in the midst of religion does him no good nor Mr Murphy either; the symbols sap their will to act and tempt them to the making of interminable speeches. The man who ran off with Harry's wife turns up, gets into the pulpit and talks longer still; I took him to be a satirical anti-Christ ranged, probably with his author's approval, against the presence in the lamp. But I could not feel that Mr Murphy had activated the conflict, or that the Abbey production, offering turbulence without excitement (in other words dullness), helped any.

  

And if this, the Irish National Theatre, is disappointing, what can be said of the Gate, the temple of Hilton Edwards and Micheal Mac Liammoir? In the days of its glory its likeness to a village hall was presumably forgotten the moment the curtains parted. But the amateurishness of its festival offering is extraordinary. It is called The Real Charlotte, but it is strictly apple sauce.
1975-10-19-laying-the-judge-bare:
Laying the judge bare

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

THE title-figure of Howard Barker's Stripwell (Royal Court) is a man of variable disposition, and this seems to be one of the things his author has against him. Different people know him as different things: to his wife and son he is Graham, to his mistress Strip, a name to which her profession lends a certain displaced appropriateness. She is a go-go dancer, and you do not have to delve very far into contemporary mythology to discover what kind of elderly man would be hanging around her. Stripwell is a judge.

We catch him at it - the judging, I mean - at the very beginning of the play. He is about to hand out to a young tearaway what may be the toughest sentence imposed for misappropriating a motor-car since the celebrated case of Mr Toad. Asked for his comments before sentence is passed, the prisoner offers the following: "If you put me away, I'll escape and murder you."

Hearing this, Strip takes a recess, during which he consults his girlfriend (who arranges her touring dates to coincide with his) and returns to administer a term of 12 months. "Will that," he inquires nervously, "be all right?" The accused says that it won't and reiterates his threat. At the end of the play he returns to carry it out, his reappearance charged with just the right blend of necessity and surprise.

The play thus boasts a witty start and a powerful finish; only the in-between, which is of course the longest bit, goes wrong. Stripwell's nervous behaviour in court has shown him not to have the courage of his convictions; the rest of the play denies him even the convictions.

The promise from the dock impels him to examine his threatened life. He determines to introduce some truth and decision into it; to begin with he will leave his wife. Unfortunately his go-go girl sees him mainly as material for her autobiography and ditches him, in the interest of youth and her next chapter; Stripwell's own son, a prankish drug-trafficker who smuggles heroin in the private parts of female elephants, supplants his father. Stripwell is left bemoaning his fate: "She didn't want me because she'd fallen for somebody else."

There is no escaping the indebtedness of that line and of the whole situation to a hundred matinee-dramas. On what Mr Barker has given us we can feel sorry for Stripwell or bored with him or (as in my case) a bit of both, but no more serious response is possible; we have not the evidence.

Strip and his wife converse for ages without giving us any sense of what their marriage was like; Constance Cummings is left being stylish in a vacuum. The two young characters - conventional caricatures of cool - carry even less conviction in the writing and, though Patricia Quinn jerks a mean abdomen, hardly any in the acting.

All our sympathies go to the leading character which, with Michael Hordern playing him, was probably inevitable. He has all the best lines or at least (an attribute common to most of Mr Hordern's roles) he sounds as if he has. At first the character seems likely to become another Hordern eccentric, victimised but jovial. With superb resource he lays this familiar spectre, but in doing so makes a better case for hesitant liberalism than Mr Barker can have envisaged. His good intentions count for more than his backslidings and his isolation for more than either. With his extraordinary face (indestructibly lean, for all its pouches), he becomes a figure of pathos, if not of tragedy: a sardonic Don Quixote with, unfortunately, nothing to tilt against.

  

Earlier this year, Mr Barker's play Claw, at the Open Space drew apocalyptic conclusions from cartooned premises; the imbalance was plain, but, since the apocalypse was gripping and the cartoon fairly funny, forgivable. Moving up to the Royal Court he has tried for greater density, but only achieved sobriety, which is far less interesting. It has infected the production too: Chris Parr's handling of Claw was beautifully fluid. At the Court, given sets to play with, he lets the brief scenes trundle.

  

The kaleidoscopic method works much better in the studio confines of the Bush, where Stephen Poliakoff's City Sugar puts a supermarket, a bed-sit and a local radio station simultaneously on stage and leaves us to decide which is the most depressing. The play itself - though it enlarges on the pessimistic view of life in Leicester propounded by Mr Poliakoff's Hitting Town - is far from depressing. It pits a disc-jockey who has known more hopeful times against a salesgirl for whom there is only now: hard to say which cynicism is the more corroding. Both are to an extent their author's puppets, but they give Lynne Miller and John Shrapnel enough to go on.

Mr Shrapnel indeed is given, and returns, rather more. On one level he obviously enjoys the DJ bit (as his author has enjoyed writing it: it's a generation's fantasy). On another his round owlish glasses and curving moustache give him an air at once appalled and appalling; his depression at the girl's ignorance of the Beatles is very real. So is his relationship with his nudgingly ambitious sound engineer (admirably played by Leon Vitali), his butt on and off the air.

  

Thomas and the King confirms that, after all their play and movie exposure, Henry II and Becket have passed as securely into showbiz folklore as Robin Hood - whom I kept expecting them to meet. They wander on, thoughtless playboy and tight-lipped retainer, for all the world like Bertie and Jeeves in the last musical shipwreck at Her Majesty's; this show is similarly maladroit and also (unlike 'Jeeves') plain stupid.
1975-11-02-down-in-the-country:
Down in the country

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on revivals of Chekhov and Synge.

THE THEATRE, a metropolitan art, is much given to proclaiming the tedium of life in the country. Two highly esteemed studies of what Wilde called agricultural depression turned up in London last week; at the Lyric a play puzzlingly billed as The Sea Gull (by Chek Hov?) took us among the rich rural Russians and the following night The Playboy of the Western World (Old Vic) exposed us to the indigent indigenous Irish.

In both societies we found heroines dreaming of escape and clutching at it in the shape of a possible lover from the outside world. It is possible that Chekhov and Synge did not mean these girls to be the precise centrepieces of their respective plays, but the performances of Helen Mirren as Nina and of Susan Fleetwood as Pegeen Mike make no other judgment possible. Both girls are a credit to the Royal Shakespeare Company, up through which they sprang.

Things in the theatre being as they are, i.e., confused, neither of them is acting in an RSC production; Miss Fleetwood is with the National Theatre, while Miss Mirren is a founder-member of the Lyric Theatre Company, a new attempt by H. M. Tennent to regain respectability if not their old prestige. The Lyric venture is true enough to West End tradition to list its players hierarchically rather than (as at the National or RSC) alphabetically; the star emphasis in advertising and publicity has been so strong that I had no idea who any of the supporting actors were until I opened my programme.

Doubtless the ensemble concept has in recent years been oversold and over-sentimentalised, and it would certainly be foolish to pretend that `The Playboy' is the work of a permanent company; none of the cast has appeared before with the National (two were in `Comedians,' but that was an importation from Nottingham) and few of them, if we look at the matter chauvinistically, have any right to be there at all.
