This production makes no attempt to test English actors in the disciplines -- if that's the word -- of Irish drama (as did the Olivier production of `Juno and the Paycock' with some success nine years ago), though it seems to have more faith in English actresses. And isn't it a grand thing to see Miss Fleetwood and Margaret Whiting the way they'd be exercisin' their art and thrustin' their voices into strange accents and breath-bereavin' sentences, and they surrounded by more well-thought-on Irish actors than a man could find on all the stages of the Dublin Festival not four weeks past.

The acting level in `The Playboy' -- despite the presence of such revered and authentic seniors as J. G. Devlin, Liam Redmond and Eddie Byrne -- is not in fact staggeringly high; the only outstanding supporting turn is Jim Norton's as Pegeen's hopeless suitor, prim, frightened and blushing to the roots of his sparse fair hair. The chorus of village girls go very prettily through all their motions, but are apt to look lost when called upon merely to stand still and respond. Still, much can be forgiven for our first sight of them, jammed together in the cottage doorway as they strain for a sight of Christy Mahon, playboy, potboy, and presumed parricide.

That is magic; and it is characteristic of Bill Bryden's production. He has the strongest visual sense of any of our young directors, and this is his best work that I have seen. It makes a surprisingly gentle evening; the farce of Christy's masquerade counts for considerably more than its inherent cruelty. Stephen Rea struts and cowers to the limits of the text, but never beyond them; since he never reaches very high, he has not very far to fall.

He lives less in his own right than as a thing in Pegeen's dream, and Miss Fleetwood is a beautiful dreamer. Lying barefoot before the fire at curtain-rise she spells out an order for bridal clothes with the languorous longing of a self-appointed fairy princess; confronted a moment later by a prince who, in Mr Norton's performance, bears definite traces of the frog, she unleashes her tongue to withering effect. She is a romantic scold -- a combination that encompasses her changing moods throughout the play; when it ends on a burst of anger succeeded instantly by grief, it is seen to have described a neat and satisfying circle.

Within it, Miss Whiting as Widow Quin commands considerable attention if not unvarying approval. She needs space; having discovered it -- and it is her first objective whenever she comes through the door -- she secures it by planting herself with her arms, and indeed her voice, akimbo, taking great care to melt and relax when her lines speak of loneliness. A disgracefully self-indulgent display, but not wholly resistible.

The play itself is not resistible at all; it is now the accepted thing to be bored by Synge's rhetoric, but since I was hearing it for the first time I have not had time to progress that far. Whatever the individual failings of the cast, collectively they are enchanting. But it is harder for a Chekhovian whole to be greater than the sum of its parts; and the subsidised team, unfairly confirming everyone's prejudices, make a better group showing than the commercial one.

Mr Bryden can legitimately drench his stage in atmosphere; at the Lyric, Lindsay Anderson, virtuously enough, has no truck with it. The Chekhovian texture is in fact wholly a matter of performance: the stronger the individuals, the better. They are all solitaries, but if they do not interact they at any rate bounce off one another and one weak performance -- as Kevin Stoney's Dorn here -- can dislocate several others. By the time the train of cause and effect has gone through, the whole undertow of life on the Arkadina estate has disappeared.

Only Patricia Healey's Masha, a dark rhapsody of self-pity, is fully realised.

Otherwise, our attention, in approved Shaftesbury Avenue fashion, goes to the stars, particularly -- and even more traditionally -- to the female stars. Of the men, Frank Grimes is an unusually firm Konstantin, a character who usually drowns in a wash of puppyish vulnerability -- as 10 years ago when Peter McEnery played the part just up the road. Mr McEnery is now Trigorin, but though several times the actor he was then he has not ripened into the novelist's full weariness. As Arkadina, however, Joan Plowright erupts into middle age with great spirit; her duel of affections with her son -- an encounter which reduces them to theatrical tears almost simultaneously -- is one of the production's brightest ironic episodes.

As for Miss Mirren, she begins almost as Alice in Wonderland, and is superbly unabashed about it. But along with Alice's wide-eyed hero-worship goes Alice's instinctive practicality. There is nothing distracted about her final scene; the famous antiphony (`I'm a seagull; no, I'm an actress') becomes a balancing of possibilities and there is no doubt that the second will win. She is not going to become a thing in anyone's dream. The part, though Miss Mirren finds a totally different style for it, is analogous to the rock-singer in `Teeth 'n' Smiles': both doomed in theory, both survivors in fact.

  

Farjeon Revue (Mermaid) is a tribute to a man announced as the best revue writer of the thirties. There must be some mistake. Caution: you may revive old songs (though these sound frail in the theatre), but old sketches are death. Revue is one form where stars are a necessity. Herbert Farjeon by all accounts had them. The Mermaid, painfully, does not.
1975-11-09-consumed-by-flames:
Consumed by flames

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

J. A. WHITEHEAD'S Old Flames (New Vic Studio, Bristol) might be subtitled "Memories of a Catholic Boyhood."

At least, that at any rate is its main character - a youngish man called Edward who recalls that his first ever crisis was over the Pope. Later it transferred its affections to women but ultimately, to its author's discontent, on to other, consequent objects.

Most of its story has to do with sex. It is concerned, if I identify him correctly, with Edward himself who says that he uses it as cover for seduction, but he means it. And he thinks that by declaring it he in some way absolves himself from guilt and can continue as before. The same firmness underlies his refusal to his current girl to stop him when he goes too far. He half means it, but when she takes him literally and slashes his face he more than half resents it. This repression of an uneasy conscience upon a character too light to carry it is a subtle achievement, both in the writing and in the shifting heartlessness of Gary Bond's performance: a deep voyage into shallow waters.

The play actually takes place on a boat. Sally, Edward's new love, lives on one and she has invited him home. But she has also invited a selection of his current entanglements: two wives and, as aforesaid, a mother. The Pope, alas, fails to appear, but his influence is felt enough to deflect the new metaphorical overtones of the watery setting, but the dialogue and action reek of stillness.

At the simplest, there is Edward's mother, who has herself suffered a long and unsuitable marriage, pouring tight-lipped disapproval of her son for welshing on his first wretched alliance; his second of course turned out equally badly. Edward himself, giving thanks (typically half-baked and, as it turns out, rather premature) for the sexual revolution, toasts the assembled ladies with a magnificent unconscious pun: "We've been through the flames and we've survived." He has been through several flames and here they are, still burning, ready to lick him to death. He does not survive.

At the end of the first act, with everyone present, Edward lightly asks what's for supper. He is told, "you are," and he is. He is absent from the second act, which is largely devoted to a lively, not to say scabrous, discussion of his shortcomings and those of men in general. At length you fall to wondering what has become of him. He is not asleep, or in the lavatory, or even overboard. He has been killed, and the ladies, who appear to be consuming tomato juice and chunks of rhubarb (I was sitting quite far back), are in fact consuming his body and blood; the play concludes appropriately with a solemn parody of Communion.

Even the mother, who has sat in shocked silence through the younger women's more uninhibited exchanges, acknowledges firmly that Edward "had to be put down." This may strain credulity, but the play has been so formally constructed that the question hardly arises. But other questions do: is Edward, so finely exposed to us at the outset, anything worse than an ordinary man with common weaknesses?

But no sooner do you rebel against these women's unfairness to men than you remember that the author is a man; such rebellion is in fact a considerable compliment to him. Is this how women behave when alone together? I wouldn't know, would I. But the actresses seem convinced: in the case of Judy Cornwell and Susan Tracy, superb as the two wives, not just convinced, but possessed. Jane Asher is cool and bleached as the mistress of the revels who turns her houseboat into a Whitehead sepulchre; and Anne Dyson supplies one of her embittered elderly Northern women.

  

Miss Dyson is the only player in Jonathan Hale's production who strikes recognisably regional notes, and the disparity points to an ambiguity in the play. The characters at some points appear to be products of a specific background and culture (I assume Liverpudlian, though this is never made explicit); at others to stand for all contemporary men and women. Sexual exploitation may be general, but it does not always take the forms Mr Whitehead depicts. But in other respects his play is rewardingly impersonal; you might take it for the most fervent of propaganda for or against the women's movement. This means, not that it does not know its own mind, but that it has access into everybody's.

If Mr Whitehead writes well enough of women to convince one that he might be a woman, what of Charles Pierce, the American female impersonator at the Fortune? It would be interesting to hear his material - whose treatment of female sexuality is something more than innuendo and less than acknowledgment - actually delivered by a woman. Not, I think, since Mae West has there been a comedienne whose humour was primarily sexual; and she, of course, had censorship problems.

Mr Pierce does Miss West of course; he also offers a delectable Carol Channing addressing her choicest remarks to the Dress Circle with a smile and a curtsey; indeed with a smile that is almost a curtsey. He is most celebrated for his Bette Davis, most striking from behind, raunchily swinging her shoulders. His facial transformations are more remarkable than his vocal; even his account of Miss Davis is a bit approximate. He can do Tallulah Bankhead, but then (to use his own terms) couldn't everybody? There is something ventriloquial about his technique; he sets his creations bitching against one another, but you have to be a rabid film-nostalgia freak (simultaneously loving and resenting the idols) to get an enormous charge out of that. Now, if it were the real thing... But they are creations all the same, quite a few of the jokes are good, and Mr Pierce is quite free of the single-track hypocrisy of Danny La Rue whose humour consists in nudging you about how butch he really is.

  

Aneurin Bevan: Struggles Against The Iron Heel, seen last week at the Sherman, Cardiff, is now touring Wales; this week Aberystwyth. The first half is compilation-theatre at its worst; minced slogans which the actors must try hopelessly to convert into conversation. The author, David Illingworth, appears to be another of the breed, currently represented in London by Ian Taylor of Taramtara Taramtara, claiming to be dramatists at minimal expense. But in the second act he spreads himself a bit. Confining himself to two subjects - the birth of the NHS and the nuclear disarmament traumas of the fifties - he begins to build a play, and lets Colin McCormack as Bevan build a character. But the attitude to other figures is skittish, refusing to name them but banking on our knowing who they are.

  

The Haymarket, Leicester, has attempted Ibsen's last play When We Dead Awaken, an almost immovable monument which needs casting similar to or identical with the National's John Gabriel Borkman. Michael Meacham's production got the outlines of the play boldly right, but Andrew Cruickshank and Renee Asherson could not bring to life the hollow artist-Ibsen, his very self - nor the model he once betrayed (and condemned to a lifetime of posing on the halls). While they agonised, Heather Sears, in the more approachable role of the young wife intent on freedom, strode off with the play.

  

At Hampstead a group called Foco Novo has a free adaptation of Brecht's A Man's A Man, supplying it, among other things, with a happy ending, but failing to camouflage its elephantine (there's an in-joke for Brechtians) development.
1975-11-14-multiple-exposure:
Multiple exposure

When is a wrestler not a wrestler? Answer: when his name is Brian Glover and he's an actor who writes television plays. As Leon Arras, he's a star of the wrestling circuit. As Brian Glover, he has played Shakespearean fops and telly convicts. This week sees Glover's latest play. It is set in a Yorkshire village based on his childhood home and stars two Alberts -- a pigeon and a man. Robert Cushman asked him about his triple life

Keep an Eye on Albert, Tuesday BBC1

ASKED TO NAME a time and place for the interview, Brian Glover was tempted to suggest tea at the Ritz. To my regret he thought better, or more modestly, of it, and so we met instead at a Soho patisserie, where the cakes are excellent but where there are no cucumber sandwiches. At first glance, Mr Glover, Yorkshire-born actor, playwright and all-in wrestler, is not a cucumber sandwich man, but he has a keen appetite for the good things of life. He certainly did a hearty job on those cakes.

Something funny happened to him just as he was parking his car in Old Compton Street. A couple of blokes came up to him, and one of them asked to shake his hand; hadn't he been in the telly play about the three friends who went up to Stratford by barge? This play, Peter Terson's Shakespeare or Bust, is now three years old, but it still remains fresh in many memories, and Brian Glover is used to being associated with it. So he took this approach calmly; he was less prepared for the handshake to be followed by a kick. Not at him, at his little four-year-old Volkswagen: 'It wasn't good enough for them, not their idea of what a successful actor should have. They decided I was pretty ordinary after all.'

Glover is 41 now; his acting career only really got started when he was 36, so it has taken him a fairly short time to reach this equivocal position of being simultaneously revered and resented by the fans (or, as he likes to call them when they're paying customers, 'the punters'). He wears it well and cheerfully, but then he's been some kind of a star for 20 years. That's the length of his wrestling career, but that fame has been won under another name. In the ring he is known as Leon Arras.

He has always been pulled in two directions. He grew up in a mining village just outside Barnsley; his parents kept the corner-shop. 'We were firmly at the top of the bottom drawer.' His mother had wanted him to get a nice, steady job: say, a draughtsman. He obliged her to the extent of winning a scholarship to Barnsley Grammar and then going to Sheffield University. But his father supplemented the earnings from corner-shop-keeping with a spot of wrestling which, he pointed out, could earn Brian more than any amount of education. So, with some exertion of influence from Glover Sr, Leon Arras was born.

L. Arras received so much more from the wrestling promoters than B. Glover did from the education authorities that at the end of a year Sheffield University lost a student. However, heedful of his mother's advice, he took a teachers' training course.

Actually though, he was still leading a double life: slipping off at weekends to throw and be thrown in Paris (Saturdays) and Zurich (Sundays), returning to Barnsley Sunday night just in time for a drink before closing time. So he was a jet-setter long before he was an actor, acquiring the confidence which one day was to enable him to negotiate with West End producer Binkie Beaumont for a higher fee than any agent could get.

Between the staff-room and the Haymarket Theatre had come Kes. The Ken Loach film was based on a novel by Barry Hines, who happened to be teaching at the same school as Glover. Glover browbeat -- his word -- Hines into getting him cast. It wasn't quite his professional debut; he'd done some commercials.

If his final capitulation to show business might have pleased his father, the solidity of his success should also have delighted his mother. 'I'm a very successful actor. Producers know what they're going to get when they get me. A big, square figure which should at least have a lot of presence, something definitely northern, and at times slightly humorous.' Add a pink, open-face with some fairish fuzz circling the back of a shiny dome, making him look at once tough and cherubic. He's very likable.

Television has always found him valuable, whether sharing a cell with Ronnie Barker in Porridge or as one of the three men in that Stratford barge. The year after doing that he was at Stratford himself, which he thinks may have had something to do with the fact that Janet Suzman, wife of Royal Shakespeare director Trevor Nunn, was in the Terson play. He pictures 'Trevor and our Janet' watching it at home on television and thinking, 'We could use him.' So they could: they happened to be doing the one play (As You Like It) that definitely calls for a real wrestler, as well as Richard II, in which he gave what you might call a regional performance as the Bishop of Carlisle. More recently he has worked a great deal with Lindsay Anderson at the Royal Court.

There have been films: Anderson's O Lucky Man and Brannigan, in which he got to be beaten up by John Wayne. Photographs of this encounter have come in very handy on his wrestling publicity.

He also writes plays, and received perhaps his most valuable advice from Tony Garnett: if somebody says they'd be interested to see a script of yours, have one in your pocket to show them, immediately. Operating in this way he was able to sell his first two plays to BBCtv simultaneously; they hit the screen within weeks of each other -- one of them, naturally, was a wrestling play and his greatest critical success. It was called A Drink Out of the Bottle -- 'that's a wrestler's term, that's used to give the word between rounds that no quarter is going to be given.'

Another play, Pig Bin, got him into trouble 'because it's the most truthful play I've written.' It depicted football hooligans and it upset people. Glover's new play, Keep an Eye on Albert, is about a shaky marriage in a northern village. Pigeon-racing is involved as well. 'What triggered off the play was watching miler pigeons; you try to release the cock when it's desperately wanting to fertilise the egg -- just when the hen is about to lay -- so it'll fly home like a bullet. If the hen has laid the night before, you've had it. And that, of course, can be a very potent sexual metaphor.' There are two Alberts in the play, one a bird and one a man.

I asked him why he wrote for television rather than the stage. 'I like to know how much I'm going to get from my effort. I've still got that Yorkshire sense.' His parents would be proud of him.
1975-11-16-critical-conclusions:
Critical conclusions

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

I WOULD like to save the English stage. It would make me feel good and after two-and-a-half years in this space I cannot help but feel that I owe the theatre a living.

The trouble is I'm bashful. Of course the trade of critic is a presumptuous one, but I reckon that I have reached the justified limits of presumption when I inform a dramatist that I do not want what he is offering me. It is not for me to tell him what I do want; in the first place he would then find me even more insufferable than he does now, and in the second I don't know.

I am not sure that I would recognise a piece of constructive criticism if I wrote it, but I do know, and dislike, prescriptive criticism -- criticism which instructs writers or theatres precisely what they should be producing. It occurs at a minor level, annoying but probably harmless, when we complain, as one reviewer did, that if the National Theatre wanted to do an Irish play something by O'Casey would have been much more relevant (I hate that word) than `The Playboy of the Western World.' Maybe they didn't want to do `an Irish play'; maybe they wanted to do `The Playboy.'

Prescriptive criticism on a larger scale has won its good name through its mistaken association with the two most brilliant of modern drama critics: Bernard Shaw and Kenneth Tynan, both of whom were spectacularly good at dismissing what they didn't want. As for what they did want: inveighing against `our drama's prevalent genre, the Loamshire play' (which, by the way, has made a triumphant return this year with `Murder at the Vicarage'), Mr Tynan proclaimed `we need plays about cabmen and demi-gods . . . warriors politicians and grocers.' That is the properly vague note of the theatrical prophet. It is true that when `Look Back in Anger' arrived two years later he had the wit and the taste to announce that this was what he had hoped for all along. Helpful journalism consists in being wise as soon after the event as possible. But being wise before it is the prerogative of the practitioners -- who themselves often only blunder into discovery.

Recently as in a time-warp, Mr Tynan has been at it again, this time on television and with the addition of a demagogically dictatorial note. Pinter and Simon Gray are castigated for concentrating on small middle-class agonies while the world around them crumbles. But unless you have a new cure for cancer (which is unlikely) you are not necessarily doing anything useful by expatiating on it and ignoring your own chilblains. (The terms are Mr Tynan's own.) I am not advocating escapism; civic problems can actually be an escape for a man immersed in his own. If Messrs Pinter and Gray were commanded to write on obviously public themes they might write very bad plays or no plays at all. That would be a loss. And unless they are actually hiding such plays -- in their heads or in their bottom drawers -- or are stopping other people from writing them, criticism should accept them as they are. If you hate them say so, but don't lecture them.

I feel the inadequacies of criticism with particular acuteness this week, having discovered a theatrical creator who can obviously do without all of us. Oh What! (Bush), an improvised show presented by the Hull Truck Theatre Company under the direction of Mike Bradwell, has defeated the negative critic, since there is so very little wrong with it, and as for explaining the play, Mr Bradwell has done that himself with perfect clarity.

In an interview handed to me with my programme he says that his object is to present characters living in Hull and confused by fashionable ideas. Thus Celia is `a rich university graduate who has discovered the drug culture eight years too late.' (It was always too late to discover the drug culture.) She lives in a country cottage and dreams of ecological self sufficiency. Yes, that's Celia; and if you detect affection as well as mockery in that dry summary you will be well prepared for Rachel Bell's performance.

One of the things she has acquired in her retreat is an appalling cold; or perhaps she was born with nasal constriction. Everything she says is on one note; when she is earnest (as she frequently is) she must rely on intensity rather than variations of pitch to make her points. When she protests that `Christmas is no excuse for eating dead animals,' you realise that there can be beauty even in catarrh. Miss Bell, protesting that just because she's a vegetarian people think she's fair game, is dumpy, solid and hilarious.

The timing of Miss Bell, David Hatton and Joseph Peters (like that of Matthew Guinness in Mike Leigh's `Babies Grow Old') is from a comic realm to which it seems only improvised performances have access. And though the evening, being mainly a series of conversations, lacks an obvious shape, a burst of anger from Mr Peters as a bullying soldier back from Belfast, clinging like the others to a threadbare code, rounds it off with peculiar conviction. Sometimes the dialogue slips from authentic to forced intimacy (like a radio phone-in); the relationship between Celia and her sister, a fashion-writer, only becomes believable when it is stylised by having the two of them step out of context to sing the Irving Berlin song `Sisters.' The show is musically very strong.

  

Its songs gave me more pleasure than those Carl Davis has composed for Cranford (Theatre Royal, Stratford), though these, like the rest of the show, maintain strict decorum. They have been composed, agreeably if too copiously, as pastiche; I did wonder why the absence of men in this Victorian village should be lamented to the tune, more or less, of `When Johnny Comes Marching Home.' If he did return he would be done for; the masculine mortality rate in Cranford is something shocking. One man is mown down by an emergent railway train; another returns from Paris fatally diseased; even a male cat cops it.

The village is mainly inhabited by spinsters making the show all of a-twitter and something of a-flutter. Penelope Lee is most tender and forbearing as the elderly heroine, and as her best friend (she says, though they hardly exchange a word) Jeanne Watts is contrastingly trim and tart. Much of the original novel's sharpness has been lost and some episodes in the second half are dull and dewy, but the evening (like Sandy Wilson's `Valmouth,' unsexed and decamped) has charm.
1975-11-16-playwright-for-today:
Playwright for today

HOWARD BRENTON, a tall, broad, and gentle man of 32, is the playwright of his generation. He may or may not be the best of them (I think he is) but he typifies them. This 'generation' (a word frequently on Brenton's own lips) is, at least in terms of its playwrights, a broad one. It stretches from Stephen Poliakoff, in his early twenties, to Trevor Griffiths, pushing 40. Besides their individual plays, these writers have often worked together. Brenton and David Hare's joint work 'Brassneck', seen at Nottingham two years ago, was as big a success as either has had. As far as Brenton is concerned the works of his peers are all-important, the only plays he can read with interest. 'I'm a bit of a Philistine,' he says. 'For me one play of David Hare's is worth more than the whole of Shaw.'

Brenton was the first playwright of his group to be commissioned by Peter Hall's new regime at the National Theatre, and the fruits of that commission, 'Weapons of Happiness', will open at the Lyttelton Theatre next June. His playwriting career began, disastrously, however, in 1965, in his last term as a Cambridge undergraduate. What he now calls 'a hopeless, huge, soggy, violent, joyless allegory' drove its audience out of the theatre in large numbers. To compensate he wrote another play, handling the same themes at half the length in a vein of 'savage, absurdist, black comedy. I discovered that I could tell jokes. The bedrock of my work is still, in a way, a delight in scabrous humour.

'Why scabrous? I've always felt like something of a bum; maybe that's the position a writer finds himself in. Believing nothing that's told you, moving on from theatre to theatre. So the sense of fun is a delinquent one.'

That 'believing nothing that's told you' may explain why Brenton, though a political writer, is not doctrinaire. He is a socialist, but he worries about not being affiliated to a specific party. Again, he describes his politicisation in terms of generational solidarity. In 1969 he visited Paris where he 'met many people who were survivors -- barely survivors -- of what had happened in '68. I began to think of political things for the first time. The sense of loss was enormous; something had been attempted by my generation and it had been smashed.'

Even before this Brenton had been preoccupied with questions of law and authority. Policemen and criminals recur in his plays. His first important play, 'Revenge', staged at the Royal Court's Theatre Upstairs in 1969, concentrated on one of each, played by the same actor. It was a sour, uproarious farce, elegantly written, elegance being a matter not of decoration but of efficiency: the ability to make words carry the maximum weight with the minimum effort. A one-act play, 'Christie in Love', probing the legend of the most celebrated of post-war murderers, moved more darkly over a similar area.

'Christie' was presented by the pioneer touring group Portable Theatre. Writing for them Brenton had to pare everything down; once a florid writer he was now charged and laconic. His clipped, disciplined sentences can give an extraordinary impression of pent-up fury.

In 1973 Brenton completed a year as resident dramatist at the Royal Court (an institution with which he has had, and maintains, an intense, amused love-hate relationship) with 'Magnificence'. The concluding scene showed a young revolutionary trying to find a rationale for throwing a bomb at a Tory Minister and finding himself trapped in a vortex of conflicting emotions. Involved rather than committed, it was the most honestly complex scene yet to appear in New Left drama.

Last year saw his 'Churchill Play' staged at Nottingham; this too may be done at the National. Again it is ambivalent since, whatever Brenton's private view of Churchill, as a playwright, 'I wanted to give him his full voice and passion -- horrible though I think it was'. He reckons that his plays are getting 'more real and more loving of people'. This may be due to the aging process though he takes the depressing view that 'most playwrights blow up by the time they're 35'. Or it could owe something to his marriage; it is from that event, five years ago, that he dates his ability to write about women. 'I was a fearfully sexist playwright before I met Jane; the women in my plays were lovely but fearsome creatures.'

He and his wife now own a house in Camberwell, have one child, live on what might be called a steady income. He reckons he's been able to make a living as a playwright since 1969. 'Sometimes you can go abroad, ride everywhere in taxis; sometimes you can't sell anything and the rats are coming up through the drain to get you.'

Robert Cushman
1975-11-23-bond-s-prisoners-of-greed:
Bond's prisoners of greed

EDWARD BOND'S The Fool (Royal Court) begins with a mummers' play. A group of East Anglian villagers perform outside the local lord's door: very imposing as designed by William Dudley and apparently free-standing. The gentry applaud politely. It seems a reasonably happy, peaceful scene--the only such scene, it turns out, in the entire play.

The Napoleonic Wars have just ended, and we are in at the death of agricultural England. The parson, in attendance on the squire, preaches an impromptu sermon on the new industrial age. "An iron age," he calls it, and the ambiguous phrase gives promise of a complex evening. The parson talks of working for the common good, we sit back and wait for exploitation.

Two scenes on, the mummers have turned rioters. Once again they come up against the parson, this time to strip him, partly for the loot that adorns his body and partly so that they can cry "Under that he's same as us." When he is raked, though, they decide that this is not quite true. His skin, white and uncalloused, seems another mask it hides. "Where you stole that flesh, boy? Your flesh is stolen goods"; the obvious next step is to flay him. This is prevented, but the violent (and in context irresistible) logic of Mr Bond's writing makes it a real momentary possibility. Meanwhile the parson whimpers that he is a powerless old man; and that's true, too.

His attackers are arrested and condemned to death. Then their sentences are commuted to life imprisonment. This grisly mercy sets them laughing in thankful joy: a powerful device that survives its own awareness of how powerful it is.

While in prison they are visited by a friend. We have glimpsed him before, in the mummers' show. It now transpires--nearly half-way through the play--that he is a poet and also ("scribblin' come to summat") that he has found a publisher and is off to London. In fact he is the fool of the title: John Clare, whom the last scene will find in the madhouse.

Part of his folly seems at first to be lovesickness; he has become smitten with a maid at the squire's house. He misses the stripping of the parson having rushed off in search of her, but she returns in time not merely to witness it, but to make off with much of the booty: the others are too busy with the ritual of humiliation to notice. But "Mary" remains a presence in his poems; his real wife he calls her when questioned by his fans--not an idea that commends itself to his legal wife, who is tormented besides by the painful realisation that poetry brings in even less money than labouring. She nags him at length, but with some virtuosity: "Sleep on your own--you have the pleasure of getting kids, you have the worry of feeding them." She has throughout this knack of yoking images: granting Clare his right to a drink, she defines the question as one of "letting your glass empty afore your purse."

Bridget Turner makes the most of such lines as she does of the character's whole progress--from brisk girl to stony shrew to stranger, visiting her husband just once in the asylum because someone has paid her fare. Some other actors are equally adept with good material: John Normington with the quaverings of the clergyman, Bill Fraser with the complacencies of a poetaster admiral, asserting that some of Clare's amorous verses are too warm ever for the bedroom, "and I've been round the world." The best of Mr Bond's writing has matchless stage presence; his carved prose must be the envy and the goal of half the playwrights in Britain.

For all that, the play halts; nothing binds it. A gamekeeper early declares the need for "keepers of people," anticipating Clare's incarceration by the best part of two acts. The lord, mellowed, or perhaps simply tired by the last scene, notes that his son has fulfilled the parson's prophecy: he is "in love with his factories." But these are literary felicities; they do not amount to a theatrical structure.

The play is meant, I think, as a panoramic indictment of greed; apart from Clare himself, all the characters are, with varying degrees of volition, its prisoner. Mary searching for silver while Clare searches for her, the villagers stripping the parson, the gentry stripping the villagers. On the fringes are prizefighters breaking themselves down for money; off-stage are Clare's publishers unloading on him his unsold books.

The protagonist of Mr Bond's last play Bingo was an earlier poet, Shakespeare, depicted as the victim of his own acquiescence in the rise of capitalism. Clare is a victim, period, and easy to sentimentalise. Lunatic, lover and poet, peasant and social critic: he has something for everyone. But he is too slim a character (and too tardily developed) to unite the action. So the play--which is considerably more varied than Bingo--appears even more static. Nor is it much activated by the grey performance of Tom Courtenay, cast fatally to sensitive type; or by Peter Gill's production in which the muttering subfusc style falsely fathered on Brecht--and now deemed suitable for all plays set in the past or in changing locales or both--begins to approach self-parody.

  

I thought we had done for the Theatre at New End, but no, here we trudge again to the playhouse opposite the hospital (and converted from a mortuary). Trudging is the mode on stage as well; hopeful new management or not, David Edgar's Death Story is rather less interesting than the Anouilh Electra play with which the old gang kicked off. This one too retells an old story, Romeo and Juliet, divided within a modern city in which the Montagues are craftsmen and the Capulets financiers. An alien military force tries cynically to keep them off the streets; Mr Edgar must mean us to think of Ulster, but he hardly explores the parallel (and a modern town disrupted just by two families is not very credible).

His best moments are sour jokes on Shakespeare: Juliet writhing in an exhibitionist nightmare while waiting for Romeo, Romeo impotent on the night; it is probably healthy to be reminded that the two had imperfect bodies as well as perfect voices. Mr Edgar manages a good Mercutio of suicidal impulse (well played by Terry Palmer) and winds up with a thrice-repeated version of the lovers' suicide to show us how easy it has always been for us to lap up personal tragedy instead of facing the real truth about sectarian warfare. I trust that makes you feel guilty.

  

Ronnie Scott's Jazz Haven in Soho has been temporarily captured for the theatre in the early evening, through the agency of the Sadista Sisters, four female persons who sing very well--and act less adroitly--pungent little rock-songs and sketches about feminine stereotypes. Particularly arresting is a stripper who turns out to be heavily anaphrodisiacally pregnant. The attitude towards men (equally trapped by stereotypes) is altogether less helpful than seems to have been intended.

The Greenwich revival of Coward's Fallen Angels is frothy, neatly set and over before you know it. This particularly applies to the two heroines' famous scene of alcoholic reminiscence; if you wait for the scandal, you wait all night. Eileen Atkins and Judy Parfitt do a conscientious job (Miss Atkins in particular is more fetching than she has been in ages, and more feathery than I would ever have imagined), but conscience, alas, cannot make Cowards of us all. Joyce Grant, at least, has no truck with it, turning what was written as modest scene-stealing into grand larceny. I missed this production's first night by going to watch Charles Pierce working over the queens of Hollywood; somehow I feel the two experiences might have been profitably and entertainingly combined.
1975-11-29-some-of-the-parts:
Play for Today - Through the Night, Tuesday 9.25 pm BBC1

When she discovers a lump in her breast, the heroine of Trevor Griffiths's new play does exactly what she should: she goes to her doctor then is taken into hospital for observation. From that moment her bewilderment and fear grow, not because she is ill but because she has become an object, a 'patient' instead of a person. The topic is a new departure for Griffiths, who talks here to Robert Cushman, theatre critic of The Observer

Some of the parts

WHEN I MET Trevor Griffiths he was resilient, talkative but tired. His home is in Leeds but he was down in London for a screening of his new BBC television play, Through the Night. The title must have been beginning to seem very apt; by his own account he hardly ever sleeps, and works an incredible 20-hour day, going to bed only between four and eight in the morning.

'I was one of those babies who didn't sleep so you could say I was learning from an early age. My daughter's the same.' Since she is an adopted daughter it must be an environmental trait, not a hereditary one. As far as Griffiths is concerned, early conditioning or not, the present routine is 'murder. I'm drawing on my equipment colossally. But it seems to be holding up -- I haven't had a heart attack yet.'

Through the Night is a new departure for him. His recent plays -- All Good Men on television, The Party on stage -- have had explicitly political subjects or, like his stage success this year, Comedians, have dealt in metaphors (does a comedian try to soothe his audience or unsettle it) which have been readily transferable into political terms. Through the Night is set entirely in a hospital and though Griffiths sees its terms of reference as wide ('the play will invite people to question what happens to them in surgeries, doctors' waiting-rooms, factories') the impact of the immediate subject could be so great that viewers will not look beyond it. The play touches on a very raw nerve indeed.

It concerns a woman who discovers a lump on her breast and is admitted into hospital for what she believes to be a routine check-up. She goes through much of the play in a state of terrified bewilderment; nobody will tell her anything. Griffiths saw his own father die of cancer without knowing what had hit him, and he has always, in his own words 'had a running battle with medicine.' What angers him is the profession's 'extraordinary insensitivity to the wholeness of human beings. Medicine treats people as just the sum of their parts. If you've ever been in hospital you'll know how you immediately regress to infantilism; because you're being treated as an infant, it's your only way of coping. And that's for you and me -- middle-class, professional, highly articulate, capable of aggression. What is it like for a woman with a potentially terminal condition who is used in precisely that way and without the resources, without the tradition of getting what you want that we have even if we don't exercise it?'

This is the first Griffiths play to have a woman at its centre. Comedians is an all-male play and the position of women in his other plays -- notably The Party -- can be marginal and a bit uneasy. He's aware of this; even a little sheepish about it. 'I've been trying to raise my own feminist consciousness -- certainly for the last seven years. It's very difficult if you've been brought up in Manchester with that heavy masculine conditioning, trained to assert the supremacy of the male. You can get it in your head, fine, but you can't pull it round to actually doing things. When I'm eating and finish a dish I still push the plate to one side -- that kind of thing. That's a terrible limitation on growth, on realising the things that collectively make you respectful of other persons who happen to be women.' He shudders. 'But I'm getting better.'

On a wider scale, this impulse towards 'personal aggressiveness' continued through his years as a student, still in Manchester. He describes himself at that stage as 'a social fascist. Everything in my life led that way. Total incapacity to handle my own emotions, overspill into violence, total unconcern about other people's feelings -- everything that made a man a man in Manchester 1951 -- that was me. The great symbol for that would be early Brando; I'm sure that thousands of young guys like me felt the same. It was years after that I discovered that inarticulateness is not necessarily a virtue.' Inarticulateness is about the last thing that anybody would accuse him of now.

Though he acknowledges some debts to his university training (particularly, and rather surprisingly, to having had to learn Anglo-Saxon) he obviously feels that the most important part of his education only came later -- when he discovered the Left, taking writers like Raymond Williams, Richard Hoggart and Dennis Potter as his mentors. He is now probably the playwright most aware of politicians, of political activists and political theorists. He has however broken away from the traditional method of dramatising politics; his plays are not struggles between Left and Right. They take that much for granted and focus instead on struggles between Left and Left; and this sometimes makes him unpopular.

But Griffiths's great strength (though critics, including myself, have sometimes been slow to realise it and have categorised him as a doctrinaire propagandist) is his ability to dramatise his own conflicts: 'I don't think I know where I'm going when I write a play. I do a tremendous amount of groundwork and I know that I'm scoring over my own fears, anxieties and beliefs -- and counter-beliefs. But the material itself impacts upon all that.' So when researching a play about Lenin in 1903 for the Fall of Eagles series he had no wish to jettison material merely because it was critical of Lenin and Leninism. 'Far from it; I wanted to incorporate it into the play to make it richer and darker and more difficult. I'm not for easy options anywhere.'

So that the Lenin piece is almost a case of distanced autobiography: 'I was getting at something very important in me, but also very important in terms of social and political process, to do with total commitment to a revolutionary perspective which will inevitably eliminate humane considerations -- of relationship, sympathy, care -- and that seems to me a problem that we face all the time.'

It is a problem that recurs in most of his plays. In Comedians (which for me was the stage play of the year) it was there in the conflict between the old comic who hated the cruelty of laughter and the brilliant young apprentice for whom laughter was an instrument of destruction; both represent parts of Griffiths himself. You can find it too in Through the Night with its attack on the impersonality of the medical profession. 'What they lose touch with is the freshness of suffering.' Isn't that inevitable? 'Well, that's arguable. They say it's necessary.' And it is this necessity that the play fiercely questions.
1975-11-30-in-the-company-of-turgenev:
In the company of Turgenev

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

SOMEBODY said to me last week that a new group of actors will always seize upon a Russian classic as their initiation rite. Chekhov and Turgenev are not merely playwrights; they signify comradeship, companies, unselfish teamwork and good parts for everybody. Company Theatre began its year's tenancy of Greenwich with "Three Sisters"; Lindsay Anderson's Lyric players launched themselves with "The Seagull"; and now the Prospect Theatre Company has come determinedly to town with A Month in the Country (Albery).

This, so far as its principal casting is concerned, is the same production we saw at Chichester last year. Robin Archer's sets remain, looking, as is the way when open-stage designs are placed behind a proscenium, ingenious but draughty. But there is another kind of nip in the air and it is considerably more bracing.

At Chichester, deprived of curtains, Toby Robertson brought his cast on formally to music, and the artificial note never quite departed the performance thereafter. The characters were all branded as poseurs, which, considering that one or two of them are honest, was both unsubtle and unjust. Now, however, the music is gone and with it the languor. Turgenev's comedy can never have seemed quite so hard, quite so funny, quite so English.

I find this admirable, since it is often complained that the English theatre's way with the Russians is droopy and lachrymose. This view seems to be based on productions of Chekhov that everybody knows about, but nobody has actually seen. Most of the English Chekhov I remember has been spruce and -- as far as the plays allowed -- cheerful. If they were not uproarious this may be because Chekhov was kidding us or himself when he claimed that they were.

The failed doctors of "Uncle Vanya" and "Three Sisters" get bitterly drunk; they do not, like their confrere in "A Month in the Country," blithely admit their incompetence ("If you get ill don't come to me") in the middle of a proposal of marriage. This scene -- which yields practically a laugh a line -- is not so much beyond Chekhov's mature range as irrelevant to it, but it fits easily into the tradition of Middleton, Wycherley and Maugham. The play's world is one of sexual and mercenary intrigue and the doctor is its prime survivor; he begins the play with two objectives -- a wife and a team of horses -- and ends in possession of both. Nearly everybody else has lost something.

Timothy West's medic has grown inward since Chichester; less weight is given to his contempt for others, more to his disgust with himself. Mr West, buoyantly enjoyable, makes his points lightly but firmly. In fact this is just about the best-acted play in the West End. "No Man's Land" is the only competition, and Dorothy Tutin's performance can rank with Gielgud's; it covers a similar range with a similar economy of means. Her Natalya, reaching for something she hopes may be passion and wounding everybody in the process, shelters behind a radiant, teasing, and almost continuous smile: a smile which refuses to budge. The charm which has been her refuge in the end becomes her prison; the mask usurps the face.

She is contrasted with the honest merriment of Jane Lapotaire's Vera, who has not yet learned to lie; Miss Lapotaire's beaky schoolgirl seems an excellent reading (it makes Natalya's jealousy the more ironic for being fundamentally unnecessary), though I imagine that when she proclaims "I'm a woman now" she is attempting an instant transformation which she fails to accomplish. Derek Jacobi, John Turner and Carol Gillies remain and have grown; and the tutor, Michael Howarth, shiny but unkempt, gives the production a new convincing centre, justifying both the women's emotions and his own bewilderment.

Turgenev turns his psychological screws exquisitely and often; too often really -- the middle of the play abounds in scenes that explore the characters without actually developing the drama. Theatrical narrative is always a problem to a novelist like Turgenev; so, it seems, is fictional narrative.

  

Oh, dear yes, the novel tells a story, said E. M. Forster, wishing it didn't; and Richard Cottrell's dramatisation of A Room with A View, which is Prospect's second Albery offering, copes as best as it can with this odious necessity.

The characters are sent sprinting (or strolling, or -- through some pleasant stylisation -- bicycling) after the narrative. Catching up with it, they get moral and start "placing" one another, as we used to say in Eng. Lit. This is another example of what cultivated actors are likely to wish upon themselves and their audience; if Bloomsbury lives, it lives in the theatre.

Those who have not read the book may miss much of the fun: may wonder, for example, what Lynn Farleigh is doing in such a strained and unsympathetic role, the guardian of a repressive morality that condemns itself in five minutes of stage time. In fact there is more to Miss Farleigh's character than that, but it is revealed, flatly and belatedly, in a conversation behind her back -- too late to give her performance any help. As the girl who escapes her influence (and, by implication, that of Edwardian polite society), Miss Lapotaire is fresh if oddly monotonous; Mr Jacobi as the suitor she almost accepts copes gamely and deliciously with his creator's disapproval. (There is no scorn like that of an English novelist for a character who transgresses his scheme of values.) Mr West, very kind, and Mr Howarth, very bright, do as well with the hardly less onerous burden of his good-will.

  

At the Young Vic two more books have been theatricalised: John Lennon's In His Own Write and A Spaniard in the Works are dished up by Denise Coffey as All Walks of Leg and house a major comic performance from Hugh Hastings as a school-mistress. School, rather than home (as in the more sentimental National Theatre version of a few years ago) is the centre of Miss Coffey's adaptation. But Mr Lennon's aimless punning is still very wearing; and the show, for all its energy, is shapeless. It also threatens to be endless, though the last line when it comes is very good.
1975-12-14-the-whole-of-hamlet:
The whole of Hamlet

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the National Theatre's new production.

ALBERT FINNEY is almost out of his thirties. His first Hamlet (National Theatre) is from one point of view an audition: we want to know if, after all this delay, he will redeem his promise. The answer, in thunder and spades, is Yes.

His success is one of presence and stagecraft, rather than of acute definition. And here the performance merges into the production, which is by Peter Hall, and which, though it is far from being entirely successful, is, in a double sense, revolutionary: it makes a change and it completes a cycle.

The cycle was begun at this same Old Vic in the twenties, when Shakespeare was presented in full texts and on bare stages, and when the production of 'Hamlet' in its entirety was almost an annual event. Almost as soon as that norm was established it began to shift; the plays were cut and they were scenically ornamented. Much of what we know as interpretation is reducible to just those two factors: what you dump on to the stage and what you gouge out of the text. And this is particularly true of 'Hamlet,' as Mr Hall's present uncut version reveals.

His line on the events onstage is no more readily identifiable than Mr Finney's; or, as it turns out, than Shakespeare's. But no critic that I know has yet offered any credible account of what 'Hamlet' is supposed to be about. Plainly it is not about its plot; Eliot was right, though ungrateful, when he complained that there is more play here than is needed to tell the story. As inherited from its source, it is a revenge drama; and what fascinates is the movement of the writer's mind around the idea of revenge, and indeed around the idea of writing a play about it. Hamlet's delays -- that gigantic alibi of 'The Murder of Gonzago' -- are so much fuel for author and character; they both create events and diversions (and it is typical of Shakespeare that he refuses to let things just happen to Hamlet) in order to think and talk about them.

Mr Finney's performance, though short on explicit characterisation, is compounded of raw irony and intelligence; and for once the soliloquies are as enjoyable as the banter. (His timing is marvellous; he can detonate a famous phrase before you have time to duck away from it.) And he meets the most basic condition of all for a Hamlet: he is an actor in whose company one is happy to spend four hours.

Agreed, he could range wider and dig deeper than he does. His Hamlet is pivoted on one moment; his reason jumps when the Ghost leaves him. His subsequent determination to put on an antic disposition is self-delusion (and treated as such by his hearers) since he is already wearing one. It serves him until the killing of Polonius when it is replaced by what Tom Stoppard's Rosencrantz or the other one called 'a high, not to say, homicidal excitement' which communicates itself -- the excitement, not the homicide -- to the audience. Throughout all this middle section of the play Mr Finney is dishevelled, with his stockings round his ankles, just as Ophelia describes him; I hope he gets away with this but reviewers are notoriously prone to pounce on actors for obeying Shakespeare's explicit instructions.

In the graveyard he effectively mocks the audience with Yorick's intimations of mortality, but the performance tails off in the last scene which is hurriedly staged, yielding no sense of a destiny accomplished or an action resolved. John Bury's set is dispiriting; if Denmark's a prison, this is the yard. There are other questions to put to Mr Hall. Why is Ophelia's madness witnessed by a semi-circle of yokels, whose expressions of solicitude look even falser than their beards? Why, having erected a stage within a stage for the players -- an apt image of the Chinese-boxiness of 'Hamlet' -- is he so tentative about letting Mr Finney mount it? Why do Polonius and Reynaldo enter from opposite sides when they are plainly in the middle of a conversation? Why are so many relationships rudimentary, which is not the same as fluid?

Mr Hall is not yet in control of his new method and it is a little ironic that he should be trying it at all, since it was he who perfected -- for what were at the time excellent reasons -- the highly detailed style, thick with props and intellectual concepts, against which he now seems to be reacting. It took time to get the first right and while the possibilities of the second are equally exciting its demands are even more rigorous.

Some of them are met. One of the play's major harmonies is thrillingly sounded in the varied treatment of the young avengers: Hamlet spinning webs, the callow Laertes daring damnation, the cool, victorious Fortinbras collecting a kingdom, and the bloody-handed Pyrrhus, inset in the Hecuba speech (delivered with predictable perfection by Robert Eddison, who also snares a good play-scene with Struan Rodger). The full text constantly assaults the ear with unexpected material.

The time goes by fast, and the counter-manoeuvrings of Hamlet and Claudius are gripping; Denis Quilley, in resplendent voice and excellent at plotting, reverses the new orthodoxy about Claudius being the nicer man of the two. Indeed many old verities are restored in this production: Polonius (Roland Culver) is back to being an old duffer after a few years living beyond his means as a subtle politician, while Laertes, who has always seemed like type-casting for Simon Ward, is revealed to be just that. Ophelia is Susan Fleetwood, for whose grace and power I am beginning to run out of superlatives. And the clowns are J. G. Devlin and Stephen Rea, who virtually reprise their father-and-son act from 'The Playboy of the Western World': a sequel suggests itself in which the Second Gravedigger, goaded beyond endurance by the riddles of the first, brains him with his own mattock and runs off to take refuge in a hostelry in Finland. (Title: 'Inn at the Finnish.')

Only with two performances does Mr Hall flout tradition. Angela Lansbury, gazing into space as if human contact would wrench her from her dream of queenship, valiantly attempts to do justice to Gertrude's stupidity: how could she sit through the play and not suspect? This is an area which most actresses, faced with an underwritten role, tactfully ignore; and Miss Lansbury, acting against her temperament and in an alien style, might have been happier if directed to follow their example. But Philip Locke, from his first wry words ('What is Horatio there?' -- 'A piece of him') makes brilliant sense of Hamlet's friend. Truly his fellow-student, he is also his censor; seeing far enough, he knows when, for safety's sake, to draw back. Complementing Mr Finney's performance he also lends it meaning; his is the watchful thought of the survivor while Hamlet's is the unbridled mind of the self-destructive hero.

  

I should have more space for two most likeable openings. Ben Travers, unquestionably our and everyone else's finest octogenarian dramatist, has a new comedy called, not too meaningfully, The Bed Before Yesterday (Lyric). Joan Plowright plays a woman who, after half a lifetime of revulsion from the flesh, rather suddenly takes to it; never an actress to do things by halves, she offers in effect two performances, one of vinegar and the other of honey. John Moffatt partners her with great skill. Mr Travers's plotting is uncertain, but his words coruscate and his feelings do him credit. Writing about sex from (forgive me) a missionary position is apt to impair a writer's sense of humour, but his appears to be inviolable. Of the 7:84 Company's Yobbo Nowt (Shaw) more, I hope, next week.
1975-12-21-in-the-marriage-trap:
LAST year I attacked a production of a Franz Kroetz play for transferring its action from Bavaria to London, on the apparent assumption that no audience can take any interest in a situation farther away than its own backyard. This adherence to fashionable dogma effectively destroyed much of the play's fibre.

Now at Hampstead there is another Kroetz play; and from its title Morecambe you may guess that it too has been given a local injection. And there goes one more critical theory, for in this case the text has been so resourcefully transplanted that the play stands and the critic kneels.

Today, of course, the name Morecambe has two connotations, and Jane Brenton's translation exploits both of them. The play concerns a young marriage, and the two partners begin the evening by expressing admiration for Morecambe, near Wise and, associated with this, a desire to visit Morecambe, near Lancaster. It is not made too clear whether this would mean popping into the next town, or taking a long trip by Inter-City. The second sounds more probable; the dialogue and its delivery, in Annabel Leventon's production, are very London.

Whatever the distance, it increases in the course of the play; Morecambe, which would once have been a nice place to visit, becomes an impossible goal. So do a lot of other things. He works as a delivery driver, she in a shop. But their finances are precariously balanced, and an accidental pregnancy is enough to unsettle them fatally. Almost the husband's first thought is of an abortion; the wife resists and though she lets him arrange an appointment she ends up refusing to keep it.

Despite this the tone of the relationship and of the play is remarkably cheerful. A happy marriage is a rare phenomenon in a good play, and given the acting of Lesley Joseph and Philip Sayer one would be tempted to call this a perfect match. Sometimes, of course, it frays; there is a memorable pub scene in which she has to seek him out in the gents (the only place she can get a word alone with him) in order to beg him to spend no more of their substance on drinks for his mates. The very brightness and kindness of the relationship makes the situation hurt the more. In the most memorable scene the two of them, accepting the inevitability of parenthood, go through their budget wondering which items are the most expendable, and knowing throughout that in fact nearly everything will have to be. I don't know how it sounds in Deutsch Marks but it rings fearfully true in sterling. (Though while immediacy is in question: I don't find that when a play touches on my own problems I concentrate on it harder; I am more likely to embark on trains of thought of my own.)

Kroetz may be sorrowing that his characters have wrapped up so much of their happiness in consumer goods, or he may be raging that so basic a thing as birth should prevent them from doing so any longer. Decide for yourselves; the important thing is that you will want to. Both the trap and its inmates are solid and inescapable; the play resonates accordingly.

  

The difference between Morecambe and John McGrath's Yobbo Nowt, presented by the 7:84 company at the Shaw, is the difference between a created work and an enjoyable piece of theatrical journalism. Mr McGrath also deals with a woman trapped by pregnancy: in her case, into marriage with a man who leaves her some 17 years later with two adolescent kids, no job and no qualifications. Her encounters with the National Assistance lady, very sweet and smiling and deadly, are excellently done as lemony revue-sketches. Eventually she lands work in a factory, finds she is being exploited, and decides to find out about the system that is doing it to her. The investigation becomes, as she says, her hobby; but the more questions she asks, the more predictable become the answers. Suspense disappears; and so, with the leaden cartooning of the one Establishment figure in the show, does conflict.

Meanwhile the vanished husband reappears and is dismissed, our heroine having had her consciousness raised in matters of sex as well as class. Altogether she shapes up into an indomitably faultless heroine, on the lines of The Mother; and though Mr McGrath's play lacks the odious sentimentality of Brecht's it is equally one-sided. It rambles, too, without attaining to the picaresque quality of his earlier Fish in the Sea. It is saved by the spirit of the cast, and especially by their musicianship. The evening is packed with songs, all of them well performed. Mark Brown's music happily utilises a collection of pop styles, and Mr McGrath's lyrics, in this instance, are sharper than his dialogue. An aggressive number disposing of the love generation (if any of it is still around) is particularly good.

  

The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (ICA) is, as you would expect from the Pip Simmons Group, more like a nightmare. Based, how faithfully I cannot say, on a Dostoevsky short story, it puts an intending suicide to sleep, conjures up for him a series of painful or pleasurable hallucinations, and lets him wake up to the conclusion that life is pretty good after all if approached in the right spirit: sentiments of a singalong, which in fact is how the show ends. All the same, anyone joining in will have been had. There are fangs behind the smile. Even more disturbingly there is a leer.

In the middle of the dream, blending wit and enchantment, is the most idyllic tableau to be found on a London stage: a Polynesian paradise, represented by palms, bare-breasted girls, a couple of doves, a fruit vendor and a zany but harmonious addition--an old man knitting in a deck-chair and a live chicken. The scene is, of course, created only to be destroyed--which would be fair enough except that the cynicism is cranked up in excess of the situation.

  

Lonsdale's On Approval, revived at the Haymarket, begins as dead drawing-room comedy. Then it moves its four characters to Scotland where the air is much more bracing. Two of them, a rich woman and an impoverished Duke, are intolerable; gradually the two others realise the fact. Edward Hardwicke and Jennie Linden manage decency without dullness (Miss Linden even runs to a little sparkle) but in Frank Hauser's snappy and thoroughbred production the running is naturally made by the two monsters. They differ in approach. Geraldine McEwan, unbelievably white of face and thin of limb, is a terror from the start; but then she can afford to be while Edward Woodward, with only blood to recommend him, has to lace his way into awfulness.

Miss McEwan is like a sea-creature, jealously guarding her own rock, thrashing out with her tentacles whenever someone comes too near for decorous comfort or absents himself too far for speedy service. She can stretch her voice like elastic; some of the things she does with it are indeed scarcely human.

Edward Woodward, with his odd mixture of threat and drawl, has never been funnier. The ending, which maroons the two of them for an indefinite period in a snowbound house, reveals that Lonsdale saw Hell in much the same terms as Jean-Paul Sartre. Concerning the influence of the English boulevardiers of the twenties on the French philosophers of the forties, much work has still to be done.
1975-12-28-danniella-and-the-dragon:
Danniella and the dragon

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the latest offerings from Danny La Rue and Charles Marowitz.

A YEAR ago the London Casino returned to live entertainment with a pantomime, Cinderella. Though excellent in most respects, this flunked the principal requirements of a modern Christmas show by failing to run until Easter. So this year no chances have been taken and the Casino has requisitioned the services of Danny La Rue, the surest draw in the West End. The show's title--though this is of the merest academic interest--is Queen Danniella.

For the past three Christmases I have been trying to explain the conventions of pantomime to my Canadian wife. I have had little success, and Queen Danniella makes the task harder than ever. It has virtually no story. Digression is of course the staple diet of pantomime, but this one has nothing to digress from. It has, to be sure, some stock situations: there is the usual quest in which all the good or funny characters venture into the castle of the bad or serious ones. Mr La Rue as Danniella, whose queendom is in hock, gets lost in a forest glade where she (I am running into trouble with personal pronouns) meets an admittedly sweet baby dragon. But the charm of irrelevant episodes like this is traditionally that of playing truant from the main action; when school has been closed up truancy loses much of its appeal.

Mr La Rue for the adults, fragments of narrative and slapstick for the kids, and some indeterminate pop for everyone or no one: that must have been the formula. It is, I suppose, only a logical culmination of the process which has been overtaking the cavernous West End panto for years. But at a matinee performance the calculations seemed upset; there were plenty of empty seats and those that were full were mainly full of children. Now whatever the advances of juvenile sophistication (signalised by a shrill cry of "Rape" from the back stalls when some villain made off with Sheila White's extremely tough Princess), Mr La Rue's characteristic double entendres are not likely to mean too much to the under-twelves. He went devoutly through his patter, and through Bryan Blackburn's lyrics (which contribute to theatrical history by rhyming "Gielgud" with "feel good" and don't ask me to explain the context or we'll never get home), but it was all done with subdued desperation.

In fact Mr La Rue was up against it; and in these circumstances he strangely seemed far more likeable than when playing to a full and sycophantic house at the Prince of Wales. His manner is always professional, and in this show his professionalism is manna. I have never seen a performer get through the community singing bit with more address or less embarrassment.

I even, when the panto-pretence was finally discarded for a prolonged star-turn, enjoyed his impersonations--done, remember, to an audience that can never have heard of Carmen Miranda or even of Marlene Dietrich. (He also does the Marilyn Monroe of Some Like It Hot, flanked by two other guys pretending to be Tony Curtis and Jack Lemmon pretending to be girls. Even Shakespeare never thought of that juxtaposition.) He has the legs for Grable and he wears the frocks as ever with superb panache--though the problem of how to occupy the stage while he is changing them has been solved even more miserably than usual. (By the way, could someone be hired before next Christmas to teach the pantomime chorus just one new step--or alternatively to drown them. Everybody knows these routines bore the kids; but whom are they supposed to entertain?)

The whole production stinks of compromise, but Mr La Rue--especially after you have spent an evening hearing Charles Pierce bitching at the ladies to whom he owes his livelihood--is very pleasant. He is, in fairness, less funny than Mr Pierce; next Christmas perhaps the two of them could do the Ugly Sisters.

  

Charles Marowitz, of all directors, respects his author. It takes only a workaday trust in Shakespeare to assume that his plays will make sense if the lines are delivered in the order their author set down, but to believe that they will still be effective with their running-order jumbled requires true fanaticism. It also requires of course that your audience, if they are to enjoy themselves, must bring prior knowledge to the theatre with them.

As this is true of Mr Marowitz's Shakespearean collages, so it is of his latest work. Artaud at Rodez (Open Space) is a phantasmagoric view of the French theatrical theorist and madman Antonin Artaud, Rodez being the asylum in which he spent some of the latest years of his life. That, and a deal else, I learned from Mr Marowitz's compilation but it was not enough. The production lacks flair, but it might succeed as an illustrated lecture if only we were told more; if, for example, some attempt were made to distinguish between Artaud's Theatre of Cruelty and its common interpretation as a theatre of sadism. The line is perhaps a thin one, and Artaud himself probably smudged it, but it ought at some stage of the evening to be drawn.

The show makes no bones, and a few good jokes, of the misinterpretation of Artaud's ideas by his disciples, but since those ideas are never presented to us he comes over as just another victim. As such he is well and feverishly played by Clive Merrison.

  

I missed Beetles and Buckman when they played the Mermaid this year, but I will do my best to catch them when they return to the boards in February at the Mayfair. Catch is the appropriate word; they are a pair of doctor-comedians, and for their current season at Quaglino's Beetles (Chris) has pulled the ultimate medical joke by going down with hepatitis, leaving Buckman (Robert) to carry the act on his own. This he does most appealingly, revealing himself as a unique commodity in Britain: an overtly literate stand-up clown, the first since Jonathan Miller.

His humour is far less surreal than was Mr Miller's; though it has a touch of what I can only call solid whimsy, in the most recent Cambridge tradition: hence a rousing sea-shanty about working in a public library. And though he does not actually cut anybody, he is sharp: he even creates an endearing critic, one who having left his concert tickets behind, nevertheless followed the pianist he was sent to review to the restaurant of his choice and there timidly admired the technique of a virtuoso "trained to be equally at home with spoon and fork." Geniality flows from Dr Buckman; go and see him, unless of course you are ill.
1976-01-04-return-of-annie-oakley:
IT IS always good to see an audience enjoying itself, and this is the main delight afforded by the Nottingham Playhouse production of Annie Get Your Gun.

It is cheering too to find that a major rep can fill its house with a modern classic. Actually revivals of the best post-war musicals have been a profitable commonplace for some time now; the regions have bristled with Kiss Me Kate and Guys and Dolls. But Annie is a comparative rarity, and I approached it warily.

The story goes that when somebody, during the show's original New York run, described it as old-fashioned, its composer, the imperturbable Irving Berlin, retorted: "That's right, a good old-fashioned smash." For him it certainly was; the score is justly considered his masterpiece. From "Doing What Comes Naturally" to "No Business Like Show Business" and on again to "They Say It's Wonderful," it seems to consist of nothing but hits.

But Annie is a comparative rarity, and I approached it warily. The Nottingham programme lists just one unfamiliar song-title, "I'll Share It All With You," whose obscurity must result from its being a holy terror to sing. Its complications, which happen very fast, are not what one expects of Mr Berlin: a reminder that this composer, so often taken for granted, in fact confounded expectation throughout his career.

Despite its technical originality, however, "I'll Share It All With You" is generally a very traditional kind of musical comedy number. It is a comedy love-song for the show's two second leads; there are numbers in Show Boat which fulfil exactly the same function. Annie came 20 years after Show Boat, but architecturally it has not advanced a step further. Modern enough to boast a story, it is still not sure what to do with it.

Annie Oakley, sharpest of shooters from the backwoods, becomes the heroine of a conventional backstage romance. She might, what is more, be back of just about any stage. (Not for nothing has "Show Business" become an all-purpose anthem.) Playhouse patrons, looking at the publicity and the programme covers, might be forgiven for thinking that they are off to see the Wild West show; but the book makes little of the ambience (beyond a few random jokes about Indians) and the production much less.

There is altogether a distressing baldness about the show at Nottingham; it consists of little more than the songs successively happening; and though they are enough to make a pleasant evening they also make an unsatisfying one. The script does remarkably little to set them up; the hero, Frank Butler, has hardly got his sights on Annie before he starts in about the girl that he marries having to be as pink and as white as a nurseree. I can imagine a production and performance so effervescent as to fill out the gaps, as the authors doubtless trusted they would; you can probably imagine it too; at the Playhouse you have to.

The most distinguished element of the evening is David Collis's open set, but this, though stark and stylish, is also a downer. It looks brilliantly economical; but brilliant economy is not really what one wants of a good old-fashioned smash. The one really joyous number, "I Got the Sun in the Morning," significantly deploys enough actors--virtually the entire cast--to obliterate the background. This, too, is the only point at which the band wakes up, spurred on perhaps by an arrangement which, like the tune itself, has not much to do with the Old West, but a great deal to do with swing. Annie is a forties musical and this song rejoices in the fact. It makes a lovely noise.

But this kind of volume and vivacity is noticeably absent from the other songs, most of them solos or duets for the leading couple. The show is essentially a duel for egomaniacs; shortcomings in staging, decor and choreography could all be redeemed by justified assurance from the performers. But John Price shambles apologetically through Frank Butler, his defences down from the start; and though Ursula Smith acts Annie rather well, this virtue, affecting only the dialogue, is of strictly limited use. Her voice is a throaty purr (at least it was last Monday), charming for a ballad like "I Got Lost in his Arms" (the best song in the score, incidentally, winding its melody up tight before releasing it), but fatally devoid of brass. So when the two of them square up to what should be a classic encounter ("anything you can do I can do better--no you can't--yes I can" and all that), nothing much happens.

The plot is interesting at this point though; Annie, having lost Frank by her irritating habit of outgunning him, purposely shoots below her best and gets him back. And this in a sex discrimination week: throw in the comic book Indians (a diminutive Sitting Bull must, to judge from his jokes, have been as much Jew as Sioux) and you have a stimulatingly reactionary entertainment.

  

The Oxford Playhouse, also in seasonal flight from tradition, has come up with an elaborate re-telling by Frank Marcus of Beauty and the Beast. Its comic diversions are mostly elephantine; a quasi-dame only just rescued by Hugh Paddick, a monstrously coy French fairy not rescued at all, a black postman who sings his messages. Others are potentially interesting: the postman is turned into a mountebank's symbol of the noble savage; this is obviously meant to illuminate the main plot, but it is difficult to see how. It comes over as filler; and the production has the heaviness which seems the hallmark of the new regime at Oxford.

But though Mr Marcus takes a long time to get to his real story, there is some magic in its eventual telling: in Terence Evans's bewilderment as Beauty's father lost in the Beast's castle and in the immaculate priggishness, not at all repellent, of Debbie Bowen's Beauty. There are her attempts to teach the Beast (Christopher Gable, piquant casting) to dance, and, most satisfyingly logical, her dismay when he turns into a prince. She misses his furriness.

  

In The Everest Hotel (Bush), Snoo Wilson transports three girl singers, rock-and-rolling in the service of the Lord and more particularly the Pope, from the Himalayas to Portugal by a route I found it difficult to follow.
