That the one sequence of clarity should be a prolonged account of death by torture is a comment certainly on the director, possibly on the author, and confessedly on the receptivity of us in the audience.

  

The Chairman (Globe), a comedy about the PR department of a large company, whose members demonstrate a similarly mystifying standard of behaviour, is mildly amusing and--given its theme of the corrupting force of a totalitarian organisation--one which might have raised a few ripples outside its little frogpond. Most of the performances do better than the script, especially Tony Britton's smooth, peacock-pleased David and Peter Blythe's waterfall torrent of breathy giggles and hyper-kinesis as Peter.
1976-03-28-the-pure-in-heart:
This week's musical is quite the most feathery and unperturbed of shows. In the escapist musicals of the twenties and thirties, some disturbance--a couple of gangsters, say, or a team of fortune hunters--was generally admitted to menace the well-being of the virtuous. But Very Good Eddie belongs to an earlier age when it seems the pure in heart had things entirely to themselves. It was first staged in New York in 1915, though the programme at the Piccadilly dates the action as two years earlier. Even in its cradle, it seems, the show relied on period charm.

It may have taken 60 years to cross the Atlantic, but of late it has been a fast mover. Last July it was revived in Connecticut at a place called, prophetically, Goodspeed. A few months later, David Merrick had it on Broadway. A few months more, and we have it here. At least five other current New York shows--all of them, on the face of it, demanding importation more urgently than this one--are still struggling to get through Customs. But then, they are heavier laden.

Very Good Eddie fits into the current West End scene with twofold neatness; it is light and it is old. To take the age first: I suspect that the omnipresence of revivals in the West End owes less to audience nostalgia than to managerial neurosis. No sane impresario could doubt that there is still a profit to be made on new plays, but how to choose them? Anyone can make a mistake, and play-readers doubtless make more than most. It is obviously safer to unearth a proven success from the past, even if you forfeit not only the good opinion of the critics but any chance of the big money. Please note that even in the last couple of years no old play has run as long as the new ones of Alan Ayckbourn and Simon Gray. The only revival that looks like challenging their longevity is Murder at the Vicarage, whose popularity has nothing to do with its age. I doubt if its audiences notice anything old-fashioned about it; it is timelessly terrible.

Very Good Eddie moves on a higher plane, so its survival cannot be guaranteed. It is a work of composite authorship: one composer, one librettist, and nine lyricists, among whom Schuyler Greene may be credited with the hardest work, Elsie Janis with the neatest joke, and P. G. Wodehouse with the most famous name. Wodehouse turns out to have been an early rhymer of "life" with "care and strife," but otherwise his "Bungalow in Quogue" (pronounced Quog) is one of the best numbers celebrating innocence with a touch of aerated fantasy. His colleagues are generally content just to smile, but at least their scansion is irreproachable.

The music is early Jerome Kern: post "They Didn't Believe Me," but pre everything else. It has plenty of grace but--like much of Kern's work before his brilliant flowering in the thirties--it lacks spice. "Good Night Boat" has a suave lilt and "I've Got to Dance" prefigures the Kern who wrote for Fred Astaire. It's good to have neglected songs in circulation (the real justification for productions like this one usually is the original cast recording), but at a first hearing these tunes, blandly arranged, are disappointing. They sound, in truth, strangely English.

Some of them have been interpolated from other Kern shows of the period: a succession of entertainments which were praised, in a period of inhuman extravaganzas, for their modesty and wit. The modesty is now more in evidence than the wit, and it is well preserved in Bill Gile's production, which itself contrasts refreshingly with the overblown style in which other old musicals have been revived. The performers never patronise their material, but it is difficult for the audience to avoid doing so. One wonders how they coped in 1915; did they too find it deliciously simple-minded, did they take it for real or for granted?

Nothing dates faster than realism in musicals (consider South Pacific) and the proper objection to Guy Bolton's script is not its lack of credibility but its lack of energy; it is half-hearted farce. The verbal humour is, on a strict count, awful; but it is the kind of awfulness that a bright vaudevillian--John Blythe in this case--can make irresistible. Mr Blythe's professionalism puts you in touch with the ages.

There is a deal of charm around, but it rarely makes any dramatic point. In fact it does so twice in the final revelation that the title of the show actually means something, and in a dance-duet which Richard Freeman and Prue Clarke turn into an enchantingly fleet-footed demonstration of falling in love. They play (if you can bear to hear the plot at this stage) two short people apparently condemned to marry two tall people. This is taken to be a particularly alarming kind of miscegenation; I don't know that I agree. Miss Clarke apart, the women in the show are inferior to the men. (What can be done about the British chorine?) Robert Swann is engaging as a chap who was at Yale with all the other chaps and who sings two songs, one at each end of the show, and both saying exactly the same thing. Act One takes place on a boat and Act Two in a honeymoon hotel. There you have plot and atmosphere.

  

Patrick Hamilton's Gaslight has both, but atmosphere is the more important. The plot is a drawn-out anecdote; what counts is Hamilton's relish for the details of his Victorian setting: the murk, the orotund speech, and the studied cruelty, class and connubial. Most of this is scuppered in the Criterion revival. There are three major roles, all radically miscast. A man is attempting to drive his wife mad; she fears and worships him. Anton Rodgers offers bloated sulks for calculated murderous caprice. His victim is Nicola Pagett, unalterably balanced and self-reliant; in the horrible final scene, where the worm turns, she has no reversal to make, and merely displays an anxiety to get the play over as soon as possible. An avuncular policeman, who adjures her to look into his face for comfort, is played by the greasily menacing Peter Vaughan.

  

Sur Le Fil (Greenwood, London Bridge) is the first Arrabal play I have seen which amounts to more than a heap of self-regarding neuroses. Usually his directors indulge him; Jorge Lavelli keeps him on a tight lead and, miraculously, he ceases to whoop, or to whimper. His dramatic landscape takes on a sculptural reality--a ghost town, the end of the line--excellently realised in Max Bignens's set, and in the performances of Daniel Ivernel, Pierre Constant and Georges Chorafas. Poise is not a quality I expected to grant an Arrabal work, but here it is (M. Constant walking the tightrope of the title) in abundance.
1976-04-04-simple-stratford:
Simple Stratford

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

ANNUALLY, it seems, Stratford remodels its stage and announces its longest season ever. The latter resource must soon die a natural death - not even the Arts Council can be relied on to provide a year with more than 52 weeks - but the former has indefinite possibilities. Having missed the Roman plays of 1972, I have often thought wistfully of the spectacular machinery installed for their benefit. Apparently I shall never see it in operation: Stratford, like everywhere else, is into simplicity.

This year it is into Elizabethan simplicity. The stage juts decisively into the auditorium, and the front stalls have been rearranged so that the audience may sit on either side of its protrusion. But one hardly thinks of it as an open stage in the manner of Stratford, Ontario, or its stunted child, Chichester. It is in fact very enclosed by terraces. The concentric circles - upper and dress - no longer stop precipitously in mid-wall. They reach round the sides of the acting area, becoming part of the set, and meet at the back to become once more the preserve of the audience. One thinks of this stage in terms of balconies, so it is appropriate that the first play given there should be Romeo and Juliet.

Actually the balcony in this play is a separate construction, standing out from the timbered surround but harmonising with it; the scene fits into this structure with unusual aptness. The full picture, designed by John Napier, is maybe the most cunning yet devised for this house. It is reminiscent, not only of Shakespeare's own stage, but of the tiered scaffolded settings devised at Stratford by Tanya Moiseiwitsch in the forties and fifties (I've seen photographs). But it has a warmth probably lacking then, and whose absence I mourn in the new Lyttelton on the South Bank.

For this we thank not only Mr Napier, but the patrons at the rear who complete the ring and must be rewarded by splendid views of the actors' backs and the crowns of their heads. Only David Waller as Friar Laurence is charitable enough ("we still have known thee for a holy man") to toss the odd fragment of soliloquy in their direction. I take it that their seats are cheap and that the company has tacitly adopted the principle expounded by Dame Edna Everage in addressing her audience, i.e., you get what you pay for.

This time round, you get a lot of it. When the chorus, a nice young man in denim, made the usual promise of "the two hours' traffic of our stage," someone near me uttered a disbelieving grunt. He must have been to a preview; the premiere lasted nearer four hours than two, which, for a supposedly fast-moving action on a permanent set, is a very long time. In a way, perhaps, Chorus tells the truth: one hour, if not two, seems taken up with traffic (as opposed to drama) and the jams are frequent.

In fact, for all its austerity, this is at heart a normally complicated RSC production, full of comings, goings and elaborate standing-still. Some of these are helpful. The opening brawl is excellent; the ball, which involves a masque of Cupid, presented by Romeo's party with Benvolio shooting toy arrows into the company, is festive, though it has made its point long before the lovers' meeting. Perhaps the directors (Trevor Nunn with Barry Kyle) have had their happiest inspiration when Juliet is discovered, doped on her bridal bed; her marriage escort arrives in full revelry, dancing and piping, turning ironically to lament.

The subsequent altercation between the unemployed musicians and the clown Peter is played with both parties in a foul temper and shouting a time-dishonoured method of dealing with Shakespeare's comedy when you cannot figure out how to make it funny. Earlier on, Richard Griffiths is rather good as Peter, doing his stuff with a burly perplexed intensity, not to say an accent, that amusingly recalls Albert Finney's Hamlet.

Mr Griffiths connects with the audience better than many of those in more obviously rewarding roles. The most regrettable quality of this production - and the most surprising, considering what a platform stage is supposed to do for a play - is its remoteness. Marie Kean, though in no way startling, sets the nurse's words snugly to Irish rhythms, Michael Pennington's Mercutio is dangerously alive at the approach of death, but his earlier scenes are casualties of the production's busy-ness: instead of building a relationship with Romeo and Benvolio, he has to go through exhausting routines for the entertainment of a crowd of extras. He is far more fantastical than the Tybalt whose affectations he despises. The best of the supports, by a long way, is John Woodvine's Capulet, hearty, possessive, tyrannic, and momentously forgiving. Largely through him, the reconciliation of the two families becomes unwontedly affecting.

Affecting, too, is Francesca Annis's Juliet, a slender flame but a true one. Her heights are the traditional ones of the potion, where she is really frightening, and the balcony, where she is really in love. While she is confident and generous, Ian McKellen's Romeo is bewildered by his luck: a blushing youth hoping for favour and then basking in it, surprised even by the mood that tips with silver all the fruit-tree tops.

An actor who in his mid-thirties essays Romeo must expect double-edged compliments: having acknowledged him the best adolescent of his generation, I must express familiar misgivings. He is given to sulks, which suit some of Romeo but not all; he defies the stars with a violent twist of his mouth, sounding like tragedy and looking like toothache. Like Miss Annis, he is good at dread, hurrying a line to its end with a kind of vocal shiver. Pillared sets are a permanent temptation to him, though I suppose that Romeo might well be given to posing in picturesque loops.

  

Having noted that last year's Merry Wives of Windsor has come to the Aldwych in, on the whole, improved fettle, I pass to our second most established provincial company. The Bristol Old Vic now has three auditoria: as many as the National, with the bonus that at Bristol all three are operational. All are currently given over to the work of Aleksei Arbuzov, monarch of the Moscow boulevards, whose The Promise also conquered London a few years back. That play is revived in Bristol's studio, while its two larger theatres are occupied by pieces strange to us.

I remember The Promise as unfulfilling; I was not much taken by the new lot either. Evening Light (Theatre Royal) is the more beguiling of the two; its appeal largely suggested by its title, it moves magically from a newspaper office to the porch of a country house to the river bank of the Volga, whose vistas have inspired John McMurray to design the most effective propaganda for the long-neglected backcloth that I have seen in years. The lighting is by a Mr Shakespeare (Robert A.) and worthy of the name.

Arbuzov's atmosphere and technique - though not, unfortunately, his vision - are Chekhovian. But Daniel Massey lacks energy (one of your mournful Russians) and Sheila Reid works too hard to convey automatic enchantment. Felicity Kendal cannot only convey it, she is it; and Arbuzov's Once Upon A Time (Little Theatre) is lucky to have her. It also has Michael Hordern, whose special line in beaming testiness, though not unfamiliar, ginger ups the text valuably. The play, about the invigorating effect of young Miss K on old Mr H, is set in a puppet shop; but it may just be memories of children's ballet that keep you waiting for the dolls, if nothing else, to spring into life.

  

The eighteenth-century Royal, by the way, remains a jewelled delight, effortlessly uniting the audience in just the manner Stratford has to strive for. The Little is not delightful. Nor is the Wimbledon Theatre, though it is far from little. It makes the Actors' Company look diminished. By the standards of two years ago, they may be anyhow, but they give a reasonable account of Widowers' Houses, which was Shaw's first play and, it occasionally seems to me, his best. Its satire is ruthless and absolutely unfused, its development - making an absolute virtue of its author's inexperience - as volatile as a jumping-cracker.
1976-04-09-dennis-potter-the-values-of-a:
Over the last ten years around 20 plays by Dennis Potter have been seen on television. He is probably the most highly regarded playwright working for the medium, and he has devoted most of his time and talent to it. When he has not been writing for it, he has been writing about it: first for the Sun, now for the New Statesman. He has also written a novel, but though three or four of his plays have been adapted for the stage, he has never, until now, written directly for the theatre. Now, it seems that his career may change direction.

His name has been missing from the screen for about a year - a year in which his work has kept accumulating, with the result that three plays were to be transmitted in quick succession. After I had talked with Potter and written this feature, it was decided that one of those plays would not be shown, but the transmission of the other two has more than a statistical significance; Potter says that the plays may (and he stresses the qualification) be among the last he writes for television. He feels despondent about the current state of television plays, finding they blend increasingly into programmes that surround them. 'More and more one talks of television as a thing, rather than of its constituent parts. I think the days of the television play are numbered; it will soon all be done on film, and it'll be a director's medium like the cinema. It only remains an author's medium at the moment because of British anachronisms. But before it ends I want to make a few defiant noises.'

Potter has been making defiant noises throughout his career. Both his plays and his journalism have been abrasive. (He had a spell as a book critic on The Times, and after he had written scathingly of a volume of military history one reader wrote in to say how interesting it was to hear Mr Potter's unfavourable opinion of the British army and now could The Times please print a review of the book.) So it is a surprise to visit his home, a three-storey house at Ross-on-Wye near the Welsh border, and to find his domestic life to be as charming (in the shapes of a wife, three children and a dog) as anyone could reasonably hope for. He talks quietly, considerately, and with exceptional lucidity.

Only he is ill. He has had arthritis for 14 years and he has often had to write in hospital. At the moment his condition is good but the constant undertow of depression and anxiety still makes itself felt. Obviously it has affected his work, making it darker but also funnier. As he says, 'a sense of the ludicrous emerges very strongly when you're not well.'

He has recently suffered another blow. His father has just died and he is still trying to come to terms with the loss. Equilibrium is harder to attain because his feelings for his father are bound up with his complicated emotions concerning the area in which he lives. Ross is the posh area of the Forest of Dean; Potter was born in the Forest, the son of a miner, and he grew up regarding 'Ross' with a mixture of distrust, amusement and presumably envy. (His wife Margaret comes from the same background; their fathers knew each other though the couple only met when Potter was an undergraduate.)

When he was 14 his parents made an abortive move to London - his mother was a Londoner and his father had wanted to get out of the pit for years - but it didn't work out. Dennis however remained in London, staying with relatives; he was attending St Clement Danes School in Hammersmith, and his 'O' Levels were in sight. (He had also become a Fulham fan; he still comes up to London to see them play.) School was succeeded by National Service, then by Oxford. He continued to spend his holidays in the Forest of Dean but returned to London to work: first for the BBC, then as a journalist.

His life has always been bounded in a small geographical compass; he has never travelled outside Britain, and now he is back nearly where he started: in a region which has served as a background for some of his plays, and for one of his novels. Plainly some of his work engages him in a wrestling-match with his roots. He refers to his home influences as 'soggy, blanket-like things' but adds that the writer's job is to make them concrete. 'As soon as you're compelled to wrestle daily with words you're immediately in contact with your childhood. There is an insight to be gained by living in a different relationship with your past, and one of the most dangerous ways is to return to near where you lived as a child. Everything I write comes out of those first ten to 14 years.' The retreat to the Forest of Dean was partly an escape but partly a search for something positive.

'The Forest of Dean is beginning to change because of the closing of all the pits but it was an extremely tightly-knit, rather weird community, wholly working-class.' He ticks off the characteristics - 'chapel, rugby football, male voice choir, many seemingly Welsh things.' Like many others he found that 'if accident and examination take you up the educational ladder you do lose many of these things along the way to a more general culture. But that cultural change, and all the insecurities accompanying it, was always there, waiting to be assessed by me, looked at again.'

The choir-and-chapel aspect of Potter's background has, in a strange way, caught up with him. From being a convinced atheist he has found himself in his work increasingly veering towards what he calls 'the traditional preoccupations of religious aspiration.' He is careful to put the word 'religious' in inverted commas and to emphasise that he does not mean the Church; he defines the object of his quest as 'the shape of an individual destiny, the uniqueness of an individual if that uniqueness is more than merely bio-chemical - and purpose, in terms of death, love, hate, beyond the merely political sense.'

The early Dennis Potter was very much concerned with 'the merely political'. While still at Oxford he worked on a scathing analysis of the society of the late 50s entitled The Glittering Coffin, which won him some notoriety. The book went beyond party to treat of politics 'in the whole New Leftish sense' and to undertake 'a sort of cultural analysis, a bastardised Marxism' addressed to problems of social mobility in an England which 'appeared to be changing very rapidly' but was as class-divisive as ever, and was inflicting 'casualties in terms of sensibility' on those who were moving. Such as Potter himself, who drew on his own experience both at Oxford and at home.

He in no way repudiates that analysis now; he feels 'very tender' towards the past self who wrote the book, and finds the political responses 'very healthy, very necessary'. One of its components was 'indignation and guilt' about the way in which his father's life had been wasted and misused. He found there were few ways in which British politics could answer such problems, but that the act of writing was in itself 'the first grappling with the permanent problems of human beings living together'. That, he agrees, sounds a Right-wing phrase 'and in a way it is instinctively right-wing to be concerned with those patterns which politics cannot change. In that sense,' he continues, 'I veer between a cast of mind which has many of the characteristics of right-wing thought, and a passion for justice which is, and must remain, intensely radical.' And in that tension lies drama.

His first drama grew almost literally out of that tension. The experience of standing as a Labour candidate in a safe Tory seat produced Vote, Vote, Vote for Nigel Barton and Stand Up, Nigel Barton - two plays about a Labour politician, a graduate from a working-class background, who finally retreats in disillusion from the crunches of the party machine. The plays were produced by the BBC in rapid succession back in 1965 and they established Potter as a television playwright. But already he was in transit, and his next play Emergency Ward Nine denoted a shift of interest. He had been in hospital, seen death for the first time, seen 'how sick bodies were'; and the play - a live Thirty-Minute Theatre planned rather cynically as a formula drama - became concerned with people's fantasies, and their inability to understand the shape of their own lives.

'All the time I've been writing for television I've been trying to break its endemic naturalism.' As he says, this is a very difficult undertaking: 'You can't beat it by, say, putting the camera in shot because all you have is another piece of naturalism in a slightly different convention. The only way you can beat it is by the strength of the play's whole metaphor.' As an example he proffers Follow the Yellow Brick Road which used the disparity between grimy reality and the sunlit world of television commercials as a fight between devils and angels. He adds though that this metaphor of 'a certain religious striving' was probably lost on the audience, as it certainly was on the critics. He says this without perceptible rancour; of my own disparaging review of the stage version of Only Make Believe he remarks mildly that it spoiled his Sunday, as he in his New Statesman television column, has spoiled other people's Fridays.

He regards his journalism both as a necessary job ('I need to keep in employment') and as a safety-valve: 'I'm saved from sounding off in a sterile way in my plays by being able to do it in my column.' When he sounds off in his plays he wants it to be for real. 'I have a solemn, serious, almost indecent sense of my own importance as a writer and an individual; it's odd that I should wrestle for 11 years in the one medium - television - which tends to modify that seriousness.' He recognises, and uses, the pervasive modern mode of irony but dreads it degenerating into nervous jokiness. 'We ought not to be so diffident that we can't say our plays are about these things. If you do that then you become diffident about everything and I'm damned if I'm going to be diffident or mocking about everything. Today it seems irony exists almost in its own right; it becomes a giggling, chuckling bog.'

As an example of a play which really satisfied him, Potter cites Moonlight On The Highway which used images of nostalgia (particularly records of the 30s crooner Al Bowlly - phrases from popular songs have often furnished Potter with springboards for plays) as a 'kind of fungoid growth' - on a contemporary study of sexual unease and fear. This creative use of nostalgia is a difficult feat; one I would have thought to be impossible.

The 'defiant noises' of the new plays are inherent in both technique and content. The religious concern, coupled with a determined wryness about dogma is evident in Where Adam Stood in which Alan Badel plays a Victorian naturalist who evolves a theory to reconcile Darwin and the Book of Genesis and whose young son learns to turn his father's belief to his own advantage. The characters are historical; the boy grew up to be the literary critic Edmund Gosse. Double Dare (another Al Bowlly title) explores the mind of a playwright by juxtaposing levels of reality in a manner with which Potter experimented in Only Make Believe and the novel Hide and Seek. The idea is not just 'to write about writing' but to define the link between the way a writer looks at the world and what he actually writes.

After reading the scripts, the play I had found the most fascinating of Potter's new work was the untransmitted third play, Brimstone and Treacle. It seemed to be nearest the author's own heart, bringing on a modern devil, working to what appears a perversely good end. The new plays continue on the road begun in Emergency Ward 9: they all concern what Potter calls 'the unconscious abstractions that make up our images of other people'.

In announcing that he may have come to the end of the road, at least as far as television is concerned, he is revolting as much as anything against the ephemerality of the medium. He feels a duty, as well as a desire, to leave a permanent mark, and accordingly he is writing his first stage play. He has long been wary of the theatre; its 'elitism' seems both to attract and repel him. His craftsman's interest in television remains unabated; and it is hard to believe that he will write no more original TV plays. I suppose that he can get on without television and television of course can get on without him. But it possesses few writers of his intelligence and ambition, and I hope it won't have to.
1976-04-11-much-ado-in-india:
Much Ado in India

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN at Stratford.

OBVIOUSLY the prospect of Donald Sinden and Judi Dench in Much Ado About Nothing (Stratford) was enticing, but it also prompted misgivings.

Miss Dench, we knew, would be funny and enchanting, but with so much going for her and virtually nothing going against her, it was difficult to imagine her as a plausible spinster. For this is what Beatrice is: not a bachelor girl, which would imply choice, but a woman who, both being of and living in a marriageable age, sees her contemporaries and juniors go to the world's end, accompanied by her own cry of "Heigh ho for a husband."

Miss Dench is not, on the face of her, a plausible occupant of any shelf anywhere. Stratford's last two Beatrices were, in different ways, alarming; they frightened off all but the exceptional man. In a world of Claudios they needed the Benedick. But Miss Dench is not a scarer; you could imagine her rejecting suitors, but never failing to attract them.

She copes unimaginably well. Her strategy is, at first, to damp herself down; her dress is drab and her wit sour rather than sparkling. Her gibes at Benedick are meant to hurt, not to entertain; their first encounter is played, unusually, without spectators. It yields intensity but not much laughter, and I began to fear that we would see another comedy crucified.

Relief and enlightenment came on a couple of lines, rather obscure and generally ignored, which hint at a previous, scarring involvement between the two protagonists. In John Barton's production, Miss Dench pulls this suggestion to the front of the play. We see what is gnawing her, sympathise and relax. When she melts, the effect is breathtaking. Miss Dench is always inspiring sentences like that, but her means for doing so seem simple enough; she merely injects into a hush a few lines denoting surrender and spoken with an unquestioning directness that inspires a kindred feeling in the audience. But I wish I knew how she created a hush in the first place; can there be more to it than concentration? I know, though, that while her spark and bubble make her a fine comic actress, it is these moments that silently proclaim her great.

We weep for happiness at Beatrice's conversion, having already laughed at Benedick's, which is enormously coy. Mr Barton has set the play in an outpost of the British Raj; there are gains and losses, but one of the gains is a dinner gong furiously struck by Miss Dench, when dispatched to summon Mr Sinden for tiffin. Benedick's desperate efforts to find signs of love in her ("There's a double meaning in that") have never, in my experience, been more hilarious.

His new passion is still, at this stage, a joke. It does not deepen until the church scene. Beatrice, enraged at Claudio's rejection of her cousin, falls--an inspirational touch--to sweeping up the confetti; she must, instinctively, do something. Benedick has to fight hard to reclaim her; has in fact to declare his love to her unyielding back; and his agreement to challenge Claudio is the natural development. He has been moved and stung into seriousness, and he grows. Mr Sinden conveys all these transformations beautifully.

With the happy ending secure, the two of them can afford to play a bit; in their mockery they almost return to first base. But this time it is a game, and if Benedick remains, in his airy way, something of a male chauvinist pig, he is obviously ripe--in the imagery of this production--for sticking. One mark of Miss Dench's supremacy in comedy is my invariable delight at seeing her get her man; Which, considering my feelings in the matter, is generous of me. The theatre must be an ennobling place.

Mr Barton's production is already fine and will probably be finer. The stage is thick with relationships: full of detail but not submerged in it. Some characters are dull, but others stand out as seldom before: the waiting women, for instance, with Margaret (Eliza Ward), the witty, flirtatious chambermaid, and Ursula (Marilyn Taylerson), a genteel lady's companion with an earnest enthusiasm for pleasures and plotting. Don John (Ian McDiarmid) is earnest too, and wholly original: curly-haired and studious, obviously sent out to the Army against his will and bitterly resenting it. Claudio (Richard Durden) is conventional but none the worse for it, convention being the key of his character.

In some ways the production is a companion to Mr Barton's Othello, also set in an outpost of the Empire; in others--notably its awareness that in Much Ado people are always awaiting, then attending, or recovering from a party--it resembles Franco Zeffirelli's National Theatre version. But it has wit and consistency of its own. (I have actually seen one Much Ado that wasn't set in the nineteenth century; it was something of a revelation.) The chosen medium has the drawback of making marriage seem the exception rather than the rule, which strikes at the play's ethos and diminishes Don Pedro's isolation at the end. I found myself, too, wondering precisely where on this subcontinent place names like Aragon and Messina might be found.

The lower orders are all loyal natives, which lends strange conviction to John Woodvine's Dogberry, both in his struggles with the English language and his pride in it. His friend Verges is a Briton, which seems inconsistent, but maybe the actor had trouble with the accent. Plainly the National's Phaedra has established a new route for the classics; they must all be shipped off to India at least once, so that they may learn what it means to be British.

  

Colonialism lingers on in The Soul of the White Ant (Bush), a brilliant play in which Snoo Wilson regains the lightness of touch which he--or perhaps his directors--seemed to have mislaid since The Pleasure Principle. Dusty Hughes's production hits the right note of hard insouciance; everything seems inconsequential as it happens, and then reveals its meaning. This is the first of Mr Wilson's plays in which I have known, from moment to moment, what was going on. Clive Merrison, fresh from impersonating Artaud at the Open Space, is now Eugene Marais, a South African writer with wide-ranging ideas about termites. Mr Wilson's interest in cracked theorists is greater than mine, but even if the idea of South Africa as a giant ant-heap fails to grab you, the rest of the play should. Example: two white women pregnant after bathing in a river full of a black house-boy's sperm thrown there after a spell in a fridge, where it had to be kept since the donor could hardly give it to his wife, she being, by law, miles away. Mr Wilson's characters are all sad, all white, all funny; Lynda Marchal, who builds a shapeless, battered character outwards from her accent, leads a cast in full control of style and meaning.

  

How the Other Half Loves has been regarded as a profitable skeleton in Alan Ayckbourn's cupboard; it rattled through a long West End run without actually pleasing anyone; least of all, it was rumoured, the author. The blame was placed on Robert Morley for turning a comedy of subtle social differences into a burlesque about the large gulf between himself and everybody else.

The Actors' Company at Wimbledon save the play's honour, revealing it as a trial run for Absurd Person Singular and in many ways its superior. It is more honestly farcical in its machinery, which is never allowed to run down but never obscures the characters.

  

At the Round House Downstairs, The Measures Taken is early Brecht adopting an aggressively anti-humanitarian stance in an attempt to prove himself more Communist than the Party chairman. His better feelings betray him; or maybe ours do. The Exception and the Rule, played second, is one of his best fables; several varieties of fear and self-interest accumulate through it to be exposed, with a sweet but mirthless smile, in one of the author's best ironic trial scenes. The Mutable Theatre Company, despite their name, do better with the direct statements of the first play than the inscrutable twists of the second.
1976-04-18-reviving-a-mixed-salad:
THE PRESS looked a bit sheepish as it filed into Salad Days (Duke of York's). Most of it was weighed down with memories. The Evening Standard had reviewed the original production; had disliked it, and had been regarded - until enlightened opinion caught up with him - as a notorious curmudgeon for his pains.

The Observer also recalled that production, which he had seen when he was about 12. He had loved it then, but he had come to believe that 12 was the optimum age for a spectator of this show and that reaction had long set in. Still, nostalgia is a strange bloom and he was perhaps as likely to be re-enchanted as disgusted. On the whole, it was a test he would rather not face; particularly as it was likely to have no definite outcome and to leave him sitting, dispiritedly as usual, on the fence.

It is in fact from that fence that I now address you. Parts of Salad Days hold up well; others do not. The present production has some pleasing performances, but is not very good.

Salad Days, as you too may remember, is about a boy and girl, just down from three suspiciously idyllic years at what seems to be Cambridge, which they follow up with a very similar month in London. The time is the early fifties, when the sun shone and birds sang in the park and that sort of thing. It is in the park that Jane and Timothy spend their time: he avoiding work, she (a reluctant deb fractionally before her time) avoiding marriage.

The first problem is solved when they take temporary possession of a magic piano, so constituted that all who hear it break into frenzied dance-steps which involve the transfer of money from their pockets into an upturned hat, thereby providing Jane and Timothy with a living wage. The second is settled by having the couple marry in the hope that they will subsequently fall in love; which, as the show proceeds, they unobtrusively do. (With each other.)

So far, you may be surprised to hear, so good: the romance is pleasant and uncomplicated, the magic piano is an inoffensive and efficient piece of whimsy, and the romance uncomplicated and likeable. It is buoyed up by three ballads which, to make no great claim for them, are as beguiling as anything heard in a British musical since the war. Thus far we have a piece of juvenilia as well worth your attention as Very Good Eddie.

But Julian Slade, though we have to look at their subsequent careers for proof of this, was no Jerome Kern. He filled this score out with chorus numbers of jigging, undistinguished cheerfulness; one or two of them (any one or two, really) would be all right, but a batch of them clogs up the evening. Such charm as they have is anyway destroyed in this production by the emergence from the pit of a droning mechanical noise, attributable to what the programme calls a Keyboard.

Something similar happens to the script, which is padded out with a succession of unrevivable revue sketches. These are now mainly entrusted to Elizabeth Seal, who looks alarmed, and Sheila Steafel, who looks dismissive (a more effective strategy). The leads, Adam Bareham and Christina Matthews, are unobjectionable, except on some of her high notes, and if there were still a great future in playing debs' delights, Osmund Bullock, as perfectly poised as named, would surely have one. But the honours on the first night went to Malcolm Rennie and Ian Talbot, playing policemen, for gallantry in the face of an unfunctioning property gramophone.

I trust their difficulties were real: I would hardly know what to think of a production which went to the lengths of faking inefficiency. It was anyway typical of the rest of the show, a rest frequently disturbed by the thudding of a remarkably graceless drop-curtain. The show kept stalling; it lacked flow. (That's a line I recall from the original; the reply was "I'm sorry, sir, it's Flo's day off." Why did they cut that? As bad remains behind.)

I remember the original as being more wittily performed; it had the benefit of a good rep cast. It began as an end-of-term romp in Bristol. But spiritually it was a transplanted Cambridge show; it reeks of the Footlights of the early fifties or even - to judge from their last offering to arrive in London - of the early seventies. Maybe, in this era of laissez-faire desperation in the West End, its time has come again.

  

Considering that it deals with a mad German writer of the eighteenth century rather than a sane English grocer of the twentieth, Mike Stott's Lenz (Hampstead) bears a surprising resemblance to his Funny Peculiar. In both, a supposedly adventurous spirit is set in the context of a remote village and found wanting. Mr Stott sets his German community to speaking modern (but never clangorously anachronistic) Yorkshire with remarkable success.

The play possesses abundant local life (my own salad days are receding, but I think I have the Eng. Lit. jargon right), but is gravely deficient in overall structure. Not even Jonathan Pryce, despite a new disturbing gentleness, can hold us merely by loosing off a series of unexplained tirades, though Lenz's frequent quotations from Hamlet afford a useful preview of what will plainly be one of the great inevitable performances of the next few years. There is an excellent sour and sturdy performance by Derek Smith, free of the sing-song mannerisms which have affected his work at Stratford.

  

The London theatre having conspired to deny me a chance of ever seeing The Country Wife, I went to the Cambridge Arts to see it done by the company from the Oxford Playhouse. Wycherley's comedy has always struck me in the text as surpassingly moral; none of its rakes, innocents, cuckolds, whores and hypocrites gets less than his due. This production did not exactly destroy this impression for me; indeed it did nothing exactly. It was an evening of approximations. It was a faithful production; unless, as I am inclined to do, you count sloth and dowdiness as betrayals. As Restoration comedies go, this one is beautifully constructed, but if it once slackens its grasp it can be interminable.
1976-05-09-the-innocent-troublemaker:
Lee Remick, like Audrey Hepburn and Shirley MacLaine - is one of those top movie actresses who really wanted to be dancers. As a 12-year-old at school she hated acting - 'a perfectly natural hatred for an awkward growing kid. Those who enjoy it have probably got a lot wrong with them. At that stage dancing, a purely technical discipline, requiring me to use my body but not my personality, was far more attractive.'

She got her first job by lying about her age. 'I was 16, said I was 18, actually looked about 11.' At the end of the season the choreographer confessed that she hadn't been fooled for a moment, but had gone ahead and engaged her anyhow.

Miss Remick, now 40, cool, sensible and obviously able to take care of herself, is as unfairly attractive off the screen as on it. She is married to Kip Gowans, a British assistant film director (living with them are her two teenage children, a girl and a boy, by a previous marriage). She moved to London from the States seven years ago. In that time she has made two incursions into British television: one of Tennessee Williams's neurotic Southerners - the repressed one - in a BBC production of 'Summer and Smoke' four years ago, and the notably unrepressed Lady Churchill, née Jerome, in the ITV serial 'Jennie' which brought her probably her biggest audience. She has also shot the odd film here, including 'The Severed Head'.

In 'Bus Stop', the story of a group of people temporarily stranded in a small café, she plays another Southern heroine, though of a very different kind from Tennessee Williams's Alma, or from the Faulkner girl of 'The Long Hot Summer' whom she played memorably almost at the outset of her film career back in 1957. For 'Bus Stop', this will, surprisingly, be its London premiere, though it is 20 years since it was a hit on Broadway and almost as long since it became one of the most memorable of Marilyn Monroe's screen vehicles. Lee Remick is unlikely to offer anything resembling that performance, though she too has a fondness for 'naive innocent women who create havoc around themselves without realising it'.

She was lucky in being able to break into films without having to break into Hollywood. It happened 15 years ago when Elia Kazan saw her in a television play, and asked her to read the script of 'A Face in the Crowd'. He even asked her what she thought of it. She seems to have thought enough, and well enough, to get the eye-catching part of Andy Griffith's baton-twirling girl-friend. The film had, as she says, 'nothing to do with Hollywood; it was shot in New York and Arkansas' and it afforded her not only 'a splashy entrance - being a dishy kind of sex-pot part' but a prestigious one.

Kazan remained an enormous influence as he has been, she thinks, on almost every actor who has worked for him. 'Actors on other movies are always harking back, or imagining what he might say in that situation.' He directed her again in 'Wild River', her favourite film. But probably the movie in which she made her most decisive impact was directed by Otto Preminger: it was 'Anatomy of a Murder', in which she played the prototype of those wide-eyed trouble-makers. Preminger she found, considering his fearsome reputation, 'amazingly benign; I'd just had a baby so maybe the feminine mystique was in my favour'.

The film was considered immensely daring at the time, though there was nothing indecorous about what was seen in this courtroom picture. Such shock as there was lay in the evidence. (One ruffled British critic said the picture might have been better called 'Anatomy of a Rape'.) She stresses that the girl in 'Long Hot Summer' was sexy and funny and that though 'Wild River' had 'a strong undercurrent of sexual drive, there was no conventional sex-symbol aspect'.

The subsequent move towards sexual explicitness in films leaves her a little cynical: she regards it as largely responsible for what she calls 'a certain paucity of interesting parts for women'. 'It's ironic,' she says, 'that women were more alive in films in the 1940s, years before women's lib, than they are now. All those ridiculous restrictions on sex meant that women had to be shown doing other things. So the Rosalind Russell heroine got to run factories, or work on newspapers. That's why Jennie was so fascinating: a chance to do something more than lie down in bed'.

Robert Cushman
1976-05-16-soldiers-upstairs:
Soldiers Upstairs

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

THE Royal Court's Theatre Upstairs is in business again, and the reopening production is worth the climb. Yesterday's News deals with the contribution of British mercenaries to the civil war in Angola. It is a show for talking heads and, in one or two cases, for some revealingly fidgety hands. Seven actors sit in a row, facing the audience, and deliver monologues which they themselves have culled (with the assistance of Jeremy Seabrook) from documentary material and interviews. Four of them represent actual mercenaries, of varying degrees of professionalism; the other three have more distant interests in Angola.

Only five of the cast are on stage to begin with. The two toughest soldiers arrive late, their looks uncompromising enough to suggest momentarily that this is a raid. They take their places at the end of the line and the central position accordingly shifts. Before it was occupied by a voluble lady journalist; now it belongs to Keith Jones, a 17-year-old recruit at first believed dead in Colonel Callan's massacre but later discovered to have survived.

He has, it seems, less to say than anyone; he sits hunched forward, and his ears, protruding before his cropped hair, seem to be propelling him further to the front. If he is the man in the middle, the others have all to some extent shaped his destiny: at one end his more hardened colleagues from the SAS and the paras, at the other, Roche, the man who recruited him. Nearer to him sit more domestic influences: a girlfriend, the reporter who got him into the papers having commandeered the rights to his story by moving in on his parents, and a stockbroker concerned with British investments in Africa.

These last two confuse the piece a bit. The girl has one bitter outburst about Keith's misguided ideas of playing at soldiers, but she seems too slight and too particular. The stockbroker, by contrast, seems too generalised; there is more to be said about economic interests in Angola than the play has time for, and his streaks of individuality--he was once an actor and may be one again--do not compensate. He never quite makes it as either a person or a type.

It is none the less an informative, scary and riveting evening: not about Angola but about Britain. The tone of the production (by William Gaskill and Max Stafford-Clark, for Joint Stock) is unremittingly level. Will Knightley's bewilderment as Keith becomes recognisable as native violence: a state which the real soldiers (Paul Kember and David Rintoul) have by now stonily transcended, their frustrations thickened into a way of life. Less reachable is Philip McGough's Roche, whose departure, in scowling fury, is as disconcerting as the arrival of the other two. Perhaps because these three characters are the least familiar, their performances are the most persuasively real. The others are actors' distillations, not larger but more insistently revealing than life; Gillian Barge, who excels in playing harried professional women, has her best and best-taken opportunity since The National Health as the journalist, alternately brandishing and tripping over her own nervousness.

  

This has been a good week for rooms above. The Bush (over a pub) offers Franz Xaver Kroetz's Geisterbahn, a sequel to his Stallerhof. Spastic Beppi, whom we saw impregnated by a farm-hand in the first play, has now had her baby, and the birth seems to have mellowed everyone considerably. This may partly be due to changes of cast: only Penelope Lee as Beppi's mother remains from before, even more creased and more desperately tired but with more sorrow than anger in her eyes. Her husband (Mike Pratt) looks positively benign, while Sepp (Peter Sproule), the discharged farm-worker, previously played as a man in whom gentleness occasionally surfaced, has been transformed by fatherhood, and dies a kindly martyr's death (to cancer and Social Security).

Beppi herself has more than doubled her output of words; she can not only talk to her baby but can deliver a poem over Sepp's body. This moment, and a couple of others, are unwontedly sentimental for Kroetz; he may be trying to get more out of these characters than they will render him, and some strain shows too in David Samourai's production, which is occasionally mannered in its stillness. Pictorially, though, it improves even on its predecessor: a series of bleak interiors takes shape, the actors harshly posed against walls that may once have been white. Harshly but not pitilessly: even when Kroetz appears to be wallowing in desolation, past the making of his points, there is some surprising human action at the end of it. He does not deal in automata.

Beppi's slow gyrations, as she fights against putting her child in a home, are touchingly executed by Jenny Twigge; hers is less of a virtuoso display than her predecessor's (if only because Beppi is now less of a case), but her decision to give the baby up--and her concern lest it should suffer for her negligence--is acted, as it is written, with stunning humanity. It is not the end of the play; what is, it would be worth your while to discover.

  

In the fifties, when they spoke of American playwrights, it was Tennessee Williams, Arthur Miller and William Inge. Inge's plays never reached London, except as films, and he is dead now; but his Bus Stop has finally arrived at the Phoenix as (appropriately) a vehicle ridden by Lee Remick and Keir Dullea: she as a Kansas City bar-room singer, he as the cowboy who fell for her at first glance and is abducting her to Montana on that basis (not to mention on that bus) but is temporarily halted, first by snow, and then by the suggestion that she may not actually like him.

They both do well, but the conventions of the play demand that we should will them to come together at the end, and I could not oblige. The film craftily began with the cowboy, and so got us on his side. The play starts with Cherie, stating her case, plaintively but firmly, against her boorish pursuer, and nothing that happened later persuaded me she was wrong. Other couples dispose themselves around Saul Radomsky's roadside diner (which looks as if it ought to be authentic) and Vivian Matalon's production takes good care of the counterpoint. The play really centres on a young waitress, watching it all as part of growing up; Jenny Quayle, who was promising but wrong in The Gingerbread Lady, is here fulfilling and right. The play is not badly contrived; but it is contrived.

  

At the Palladium last week Joel Grey did his MC numbers from Cabaret; their chill, their zest and their authority were undiminished. What was diminished was the rest of his act, which was compact of just the kind of showbiz bonhomie that Cabaret undercuts. Mr Grey does not need this kind of charm (just as well, since he hasn't actually got it); he has colossal energy, and is the fleetest performer I have ever seen, electric even when changing his shoes: one pair with taps and one without. He was supported by Johnny Hackett, a better than average Northern comic, and the Brotherhood of Man, a shiny gang of Eurovision song contestants for whom "slickening" would be the right portmanteau word.
1976-05-23-in-a-hellish-half-light:
THE LAST SLICE of Samuel Beckett's seventieth birthday cake, as served up at the Royal Court, is a triple-decker, Play and Other Plays.

Play comes first. It is the eldest, 13 years old. A good sprig. With the years it has grown funnier. It is the one about the three people - a man and two women - encased in funeral urns. Once they were husband, wife and mistress. Now they are dead. (I think. Many agree.) On each of them in turn, a light plays. When it shines, they jabber, of their past and one another. The light is cruel. Not only does it prod them to speak, it will never let them finish. Bored with one, it constantly moves on to the next, and back again. Having exhausted their supply of confessions, it starts again. "Repeat play exactly," says the stage-direction.

This repetition is purgatorial for them, but helpful for us. On the first hearing, we may grasp the shape of their affair; on the second, we can begin to take in the details, which are, in a high-class way, sordid. Love is not lovelier the second time around, and it gets progressively less so. Here are the remnants of a drawing-room comedy triangle laid out for us sub specie aeternitatis. Thus displayed, played, replayed, whose passions would not look ridiculous?

Mr Beckett shields us a bit by placing his characters outside the social circles to which most of us are accustomed. One of his ladies had a butler, whose fate she momentarily ponders. I might gawp at her at the Haymarket, but I will not identify with her at the Royal Court. I know my place, I was taught at the Court. However, when the poor adulterer expressed his distaste for the tea drunk by his entanglements ("personally I preferred Lipton's") when, as of course they would, they got together to discuss him - then I laughed.

Play impresses me too as a study in the psychology of interrogation. The trio complain of the light that oppresses them, but they fear, as much as anything, its going out. They have come to depend on it. They call it a "hellish half-light," but they fear that really this is not hell, not eternal. (Their philosophy seems to be somewhere between "confession is good for the soul" and "better the devil you know.") And maybe their fears are realised. Perhaps, when the light goes out at the end of Play, it goes out for ever, consigning them to a well-earned rest.

The first play, then, now looks a masterpiece. But not the second, That Time. Not this time. Like most of Mr Beckett's plays it deals with the horror of the past. (I except Waiting for Godot, which is concerned with the horror of the future, and Happy Days, which satirises those who are not horrified by the present.) Here is the haggard face of Patrick Magee, surrounded by flowing grey hair (like a monstrous halo) and otherwise surrounded by darkness. Here is Mr Magee's voice, prerecorded, through three speakers, sounding less like a circular saw than usual; softened but no more attractive, and decidedly soporific.

High on the list of the things which I can live, even die, without would be, had I ever thought of it, Mr Magee in three-track stereo. Faber and Faber, in the blurb to the published version (16pp., 50p) say of Magee and Magee and Magee: "The voices speak of the past; nostalgic, regretful, elegiac, poignant, fragmentary." The adjectives are not really deniable, and I might have used a couple of them myself. But the substance is only a rerun of Krapp's Last Tape without the props: a process of refinement but not necessarily of enrichment.

The third play, Footfalls, moves in the opposite direction. Yes, I said moves. This is another piece for one player (Billie Whitelaw, who is extraordinary) and not only is she visible - dimly, I admit - from her head to her foot, but she gets about. This is, in all respects, the nearest thing to a full-length portrait Mr Beckett has painted in years. Miss Whitelaw is even given a realistic situation, a woman in her forties looking after her bedridden mother (unseen but vocal). The relationship ("Would you like me to inject you again?" - "Yes, but it is too soon") is terrifyingly, and - need I say - sparely evoked. Mother does not really nag; she worries, over her daughter's ceaseless padding up and down. She never goes out, just remembers. And that, we can hear the author saying, is what motion gets you; don't ask me for it again.

Miss Whitelaw's memories take up half the play, and they lack nothing of skill in writing or performance. What they do lack is inevitability; the play does not have to tell this particular story to make this particular effect. Common to all three plays are the compulsive vomitings of the human voice and brain, and the hypnotic effect of thin white light. Mr Beckett, who provides rigorous instructions for them all and directed the last himself, is a gentleman and a showman.

  

The night before this triple bill, a quintuple one from Alan Ayckbourn: Confusions (Apollo). The last confusion is actually quite Beckettian: a cast of five telling one another their troubles and realising that "you might as well be talking to yourself." This is the kind of thing Mr Ayckbourn does least well (like the last act of Absurd Person Singular), but for most of the evening he is at his best.

His admirers seem split between those who prefer him to cram five plays into one evening, and those who like him to spread one play over three evenings. I am of the former party, especially since his fourth piece here offers a series of mechanical gags - I mean gags involving machines - unequalled outside Feydeau, or maybe even inside. As his characters fell victim to the ravages of berserk technology, I laughed as heartily as at the bun-fight in Funny Peculiar. In another piece, John Alderton, a travelling salesman, proceeds with great speed and smoothness from affability to desperation in his efforts to seduce Pauline Collins and Sheila Gish, two travelling salesgirls. This is Mr Ayckbourn's best dark piece to date; all three characters are naturals for the turns.

A restaurant episode includes some virtuoso timing and miming of simultaneous conversations, and a final sidelong glance at husbandly complaisance that Wycherley might have approved. This leaves piece number one, which is based on an over-extended joke but which is still funny a lot of the time and can be forgotten by the end anyway. The actors (James Cossins and Derek Fowlds are the others) are all immaculate; the Alderton-Collins duo is developing as richly as could be wished.

  

Andre Obey's Noah has been a favourite school play for 40 years and so it looks at Chichester; especially with Gordon Jackson, a good and gentle actor, but no patriarch. Occasionally the play explores the nastier aspects of being the beneficiary of a holocaust, but generally it sticks to the dramatic lode (nostalgically Biblical but scrupulously irreligious) that Godspell was to mine so profitably. The Bear (Carl Oatley) is, I will say, endearing.

If Chichester is childish, Hampstead is horrible; the production of Moliere's Dom Juan is fitted out with tricks apparently designed to draw attention to its director, who would be better advised to cower in a corner. Tom Conti can encompass some of Juan's charm and a fraction of his demonism, but - in this eighteenth-century translation - hardly any of his language.
1976-05-30-farewell-to-that-old-acid-dre:
Farewell to that old acid dream

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

AT ONE point in David Hare's Teeth 'n' Smiles (now transferred from the Royal Court to Wyndham's) the following words occur: "It's not worth saying--nothing's worth saying--it's all so obvious." I know the feeling; nobody wants to be caught being obvious, that's obvious.

The situation--a rock group playing at a Cambridge May Ball in the last year of the sixties--automatically suggests a theme: the confrontation of two cultures. Mr Hare defuses our expectations on this score by more or less eliminating one side. Cambridge is represented on stage by one porter and one harmless medical student with ambitions of becoming a drop-out (after he's passed his exams).

If he is the opposition, then the battle is already won, the enemy within the gates. Only they are in no state to fight. The group is on the verge of breaking-up, their lead singer--self-cast in the self-destructive mould of Garland or Joplin--falling apart from drink. Our student asks her whether she believes that pop is any challenge to the established order; she obviously regards it as a silly question. So, I guess, does the author. But I have to guess because he is chary of making statements, even about not making statements.

A strange self-mockery permeates the evening. Sometimes it seems like irony; often, like the hedging of bets. A songwriter who escaped from the old values (he quit this same college) and is still attached to them (he lounges around singing Cole Porter) proclaims that "the acid dream is over," then undercuts himself by adding "it said so in the Daily Express," finally caps it all by telling the singer "but you and I still want to say something." What they want to say, he doesn't say, and she certainly isn't telling.

Mr Hare has perceived that the acid dream was never any use, but this perception is difficult to make into a play, at least into a play with this setting, so sometimes he forgets it and settles for the shadow of a conflict instead. He lets his characters jeer at themselves for paying so much attention to their exhibitionist star, who will survive, while forgetting their stoned bass guitarist, who won't. But after all, the author is the one who gave them the concern, pushed the lady into the centre of the play, and--since he is his own director--engaged Helen Mirren for the role, gave her the limelight, the billing and our attention. He then keeps telling us how boring she is (the character, not Miss Mirren, who is furiously good) as if by way of atonement. He also pads the evening out by engaging her in a romantic triangle which--despite sympathetic playing from Martin Shaw and Gay Hamilton as its other sides--never begins to take hold.

I suspect, too, that he became fascinated in researching the play by the life-style of the band, and threw in more detail than his story required. This, however, is his salvation; much of his dialogue is brilliant and its last-gasp cynicism has its own momentum and its own mood. These keep the play alive most of the time.

The production seems both less comfortable and more uncompromising in the West End than at its cosy old home in Sloane Square. (Its relation to its audience rather resembles that of its characters to Cambridge. I even heard shocked gasps; I only wish the shock had been caused by something more disturbing than the odd four-letter word.) The band's first number now sounds, as it should, really bad: a difficult effect to achieve in a straight play, where any outburst of music is generally welcome. They act contrastingly well, but the two most successful characters are Antony Sher's student, who significantly never finishes a sentence, because its ludicrousness always strikes him en route, and Dave King's manager, smilingly jaundiced about absolutely everything. If the play has a heart, he, effortlessly delivering all the best lines, is it.

  

Athol Fugard has also directed a play of his own which came to London last week: Dimetos (Comedy), of which I saw half, but heard much less, in Edinburgh last year. This time I stayed till the end: you do not walk out on Paul Scofield, who is awe-inspiringly audible and whose acting is inclined to suggest that he has a hotline to the Almighty. On this occasion he gives a great display, craggy and troubled, rather than a great performance, Mr Fugard having provided him with a situation rather than a character. Derived from an obscure passage in Camus, it presents a man paralysed by guilt over the suicide of his niece, after whom he lusted. He did not assault her; he merely upset her by playing the voyeur.

The second part of the play, which is Dimetos's agony and redemption, is considerably the better, but it sinks under the delusion that a writer may create a myth simply by taking thought. Camus may have achieved it in a casual paragraph, but Mr Fugard, excluding domestic detail in favour of conscientious metaphor, denies his play a chance of life.
1976-06-02-voices-off:
Voices off

Edward Albee, writing his first radio play (broadcast last Sunday on Radio 3), took to the restrictions of the medium with wary eagerness. Listening was the title, putting the audience on the spot from the moment they read the billing. On another page of the Radio Times could be found the baleful news, imparted by the author himself, that the play was "just another of those things about people's failure to communicate". His characters were less casual about it; there were three of them, and the least comprehensible of the three repeatedly complained that the others did not listen. Then, having made the charge several times, she refined it: "pay attention is what you don't do". Mr Albee's regard for language is as scrupulous as ever.

It is the only thing for which he does show any solicitude. His stage plays since Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? have been increasingly hard on their spectators; All Over, his latest play to be seen in London, was as difficult to sit through as any piece of the last decade. Listening to Listening was easier, by the difference between an Aldwych stall and one's own armchair. One could fidget in comfort. And the banality behind the lines was less oppressive. One resents a play like All Over that fools around with death; fooling around with non-communication is permissible--everybody does it.

The protesting character was called The Girl; she seemed disturbed, and possibly in care. She and The Woman bitched at each other with varying degrees of elegance. The Man stood by, defensive and appalled. An American actor, James Ray (the play was recorded in New York), played him in a style of fruity bewilderment dispiritingly observable among radio performers in this country. Irene Worth, having proclaimed herself a more disciplined actress on the air than on the boards, justified the assertion with a reading of precise and silvery inhumanity. The author, though billed as The Voice, was not heard from.

There were two moments of solidity. In the first, Miss Worth told the story of her grandfather who had vanished; to judge from the conflicting reports of those who had seen him depart "he'd gone off in several directions at the same time ... he had, in effect, dispersed". Since present relationships were so tenuous, it was nice to have this bit of past to cling to. The second came when The Girl jumped into a fountain: no audible splash (this is modern radio, very pure) but at least we got our bearings for a moment.
1976-06-06-vague-views:
Vague views

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

LAST WEEK I got my first glimpse of the St Georges Theatre in Islington, dedicated to putting Shakespeare back where he belongs. The externals are plain: quaint music, doublet and hose, and an apron stage. This, of course, is the easy part; it brings us no nearer to an understanding of how the Elizabethans thought. If we are to find out, we will have to give the matter a lot more investigation than George Murcell, the director of the theatre and of its new Romeo and Juliet, can reasonably be expected to have had time for.

When he declares that Shakespeare's characters were 'bounded by certain attitudes and beliefs relative to his time and not by modern political, ethical and psychological factors', he is talking obvious sense, though there may be more overlap between the two sensibilities than he allows. But he then goes on to tilt at productions which make 'Hamlet an Oedipus complex melancholic and Julius Caesar a fascist dictator in the Hitler mode.' But those are not today's distortions; they belong to the thirties, when the second was tried out by Orson Welles and the first by Tyrone Guthrie -- whom, funnily enough, Mr Murcell names as one of his mentors.

His views on modern Shakespeare production seem, in short, a bit vague. The chronology of Mr Murcell's own career and his invocation of Guthrie and Michael Benthall suggest to me that they really boil down to a feeling that Shakespeare was getting on very nicely in the 1950s until Peter Hall and the Royal Shakespeare Company came along and spoiled everything. This is quite a widespread attitude within the profession and among theatregoers; having myself received my theatrical education at the Old Vic in the fifties, I may still unconsciously regard that style as the norm, and everything else as a mutation. But when I think clearly, I can see that it was no more 'authentic' or 'Elizabethan' than what has displaced it.

There have, God knows, been absurdities perpetrated in the name of 'making Shakespeare relevant.' (Actually I don't believe that you can make a play relevant; either it is or it isn't. I doubt if you can even 'bring out' its relevance, though probably you can, accidentally or on purpose, obscure it.) But basically Mr Murcell is bugged less by modern directors' treatment of Shakespeare than by their treatment of actors. The dominance of the major companies has led to the disenfranchisement, in the name of some rather academic conceptions of theatrical taste, of a whole parade of players. Some, like Mr Murcell himself, have gone rapidly through these companies and come out the other side. Others have never got in; in these terms, Mr Murcell has a lot going for him.

However sympathetic many of us may be to the RSC ethic (which is what we read about), we have become increasingly resistant to the RSC mannerisms (which are what we actually see). Here Mr Murcell's 'Romeo' scores heavily over this year's production at Stratford. It is refreshing to find that double-entendres can hit their mark without laborious underlining; that a clown (Ronnie Stevens) can be a clown and not an angry underdog; and that the young men of Verona do not have to be irredeemably vicious. David Collings's Mercutio is even quite likeable; his Queen Mab speech, in the displaced lyrical tradition, for once makes atmospheric sense.

Peter McEnery's Romeo is interestingly tough; he does not actually duel with Tybalt and Paris, just goes up to them and stabs them. Sarah Badel's Juliet is tough, too, though this is more an inbuilt facet of her personality than of her interpretation. The two are at war, but it is a thrilling battle and since all Miss Badel's skill and intelligence are exercised in Juliet's cause, not her own, she has some ecstatic moments; her stillness after her one night with Romeo is very moving. She is hampered by a miscast Nurse (Rosemary Leach) who comes on like her older sister; altogether too bright and personable to sort with the text.

C. Walter Hodges's permanent set may have the prescribed number of balconies and alcoves, but is garishly coloured and looks strangely insubstantial. Mr Murcell directs for the open stage by stringing his actors across it, even in conversational scenes. Extras, reacting, look lost; routine naturalism is occasionally disturbed for the sake of a picturesque but improbable grouping. There is not, in short, much style, but there is plainness and energy, and for 'Romeo,' a narrative play, this works better than the more rarefied treatments we are used to.

I can see that it would have done less well for Twelfth Night, a mood piece, though I doubt if the St Georges production of the play (which I missed) was worse than the one that opened last week at Chichester. Keith Michell, like Mr Murcell an artistic director at large on his own stage for the first time, opts for regulation Chichester gaiety: lots of romping but no actual comedy. High life is pallid, low life denatured: Barbara Windsor's Maria even looks flat-chested. Gordon Jackson's Malvolio proves, for the second time this season, that this actor is no soloist.

In its last stages the production lurches surprisingly towards melancholy, allowing Tony Robinson to suggest that his Feste might have been quite interesting. Bill Fraser, Michele Dotrice and Charles Keating also have moments. Mr Michell places important scenes in corners of the stage, leaving the centre to attendants in whose reactions, with no ill will towards them, I was not much interested. There being so much Shakespeare, I defer Stratford's new Winter's Tale until next week.

After the achievements of Mike Leigh and Hull Truck there is an onus on improvised drama to prove that it can do things written drama cannot; Gin Trap (Bush) had me yearning for a playwright to bring the characters together, stop their conversation wandering (non-communication is no longer news) and focus a few themes. About to type, through force of habit, that the acting was good though, I realise that will not do for this kind of play and that the failure of Cecily Hobbs's tight-lipped baby-basher to make her lines convincing must be laid at her door as well as that of her directors (Sarah Anderson and Sheila Kelly). Other characters are competently observed and the ending is quiet but immensely forceful.
1976-06-13-musgraves-dancing:
I saw Sybil Thorndike only once on the stage: as the Nurse in the famous Chichester 'Uncle Vanya,' in which she was magnificent. I never met her. All the same, I feel this week as though I have suffered a personal loss.

The Family Dance (Criterion), by a new dramatist, Felicity Browne, is about a celebration-hop in the Berkshire home of a stockbroker called Ben Musgrave. Musgraves and dancing seem to go together in the theatre, though I doubt if John Arden's stony serjeant would relish the idea of a stockbroker for a descendant. At that, Ben is the only one of the new Musgraves to do any work at all. His brother, his sister, and their respective spouses live off his earnings in what he describes as 'a family commune.'

There are also, of course, children; it is they and their friends who are actually having the ball, though they are at it offstage; we are in the kitchen (a large one, of course) watching their elders collapse from underwork. It takes them in different ways: sister Diana has become the kind of hearty tyrant who, if our playwrights are to be trusted, may be found beneath every roof in the Home Counties, brother Toby has taken spinelessly to drink, and Ben's wife Sophie marks the evening's half-way point by gulping down an overdose of sleeping-pills.

Before taking this step, Sophie has asked Ben for a divorce, only to receive the reply--a witty one, I thought--that having been married for 17 years she might as well stick it out to the end. Miss Browne displays a great talent for the stylish display of selfishness; it is obvious that Ben has assumed the role of universal breadwinner largely in order to put the family in his debt. In Alec McCowen's bravura performance he careers around the stage looking for grievances, upbraiding his brother for a weakling, and his wife for a bad boiler of eggs and an even worse lay.

These bad manners are diverting, but they are not remotely believable. Or rather, they are only remotely believable: fine in long-shot, but not in close-up. Regarded as a verbal ballet of family discord, the play is very entertaining. Miss Browne has an eye as well as an ear and by putting Sophie, played waifishly by Annette Crosbie, into a biscuit-coloured dress ('the same colour as the rest of you,' says her sister-in-law, possibly meaning well) she isolates her effectively.

But she cannot get inside Sophie's character; cannot explain why she has stuck with Ben so long, or why, having done so, she should want to leave now. Indeed, despite the efforts of Miss Crosbie, Michael Bryant and Judy Parfitt (whose main contribution to the proceedings is to look handsome in green), the more downtrodden members of the menage never come to life.

The monsters, so glitteringly played by Mr McCowen and Helen Lindsay, overpower them. If their performances sometimes seem a bit relentless, the writing gives them little option. Nobody should accuse Miss Browne of glamourising family life or even Berkshire; when sentimentality breaks in, it is the character's, not the author's. But once we have agreed with her that the situation she presents is indeed unpleasant, there is little left for us to do. It is a watchable play, but not an energising one.

  

Anyway, there is hope for Miss Browne, as once there was, I suppose, for John Mortimer. However, Mr Mortimer is now one of the strangest phenomena in the English theatre: a brand-name dramatist for nearly 20 years, with only one play to his credit ('A Voyage Round My Father') that was even half-way good. There have also been some tolerable sketches: one of them is the second half of the double-bill Heaven and Hell (Greenwich). 'Hell's funny,' as we used to say in the sixties; heaven though, as tenuously dramatised in the curtain-raiser, is a drag and, as usual, difficult to believe in. The evening does offer Denholm Elliott, Peter Woodthorpe and Eleanor Bron; and, of course, many evenings offer less.

  

The Winter's Tale (Stratford) seemed promising, directed by John Barton 'with Trevor Nunn.' Mr Nunn staged this play excellently a few years ago and this season's 'Much Ado About Nothing' showed Mr Barton at the top of his form. But with the permanent Elizabethan set (of which the RSC seem already to have repented) masked in with furs and hieroglyphs, and the actors furry as well, this is dehydrated Shakespeare, the earnest tanning of a monster play.
