Talking of monsters, this is the play in which a character exits, 'pursued by a bear'; at Stratford he merely finds himself confronted by what looks like a walking totem-pole, which escorts him offstage with the apparent intention of taking his name and address. Not surprisingly a subsequent speech describing his dismemberment by the bear is neither credible nor funny. (Funniness may be assumed to have been among the author's intentions, since he entrusted the speech to a character called the Clown. Another RSC director, Terry Hands, has recently declared in print that Shakespeare never means what he says. This is as simplistic as claiming that he always does.)

Throughout the evening the cast seemed engaged in ritual games which they probably understand, but which leave the audience in the cold. There are good performances, of course: Barbara Leigh-Hunt a formidably nannyish Paulina, David Waller's warming first moments as the Shepherd, Marilyn Taylerson as statuesque a Hermione as could be imagined, and even Florizel and Perdita no worse than usual. Above all, Ian McKellen's Leontes is splendid; the actor's technical control (which in Shakespeare has never been more evident) throws into relief the character's disarray. As Leontes's lucidity goes, Mr McKellen's increases, the course of each shaft of jealousy precisely plotted. Particularly revealing is his clinging to his son, counterbalancing his revulsion from his wife.

  

Robert Stephens in Othello (Regent's Park) is similarly exact, though his jealous transports are messier. I always forget just how powerful an actor Mr Stephens is, but there are speeches here whose weight he cannot shift. But I should like to see him try again, under a roof (since my Elizabethanism is by no means fanatical) and with an Iago who has a finer sense of rhythm than Edward Fox.

  

Liza of Lambeth (Shaftesbury) is the latest overweight British musical based on an Edwardian novel: Maugham this time. It has one good idea (the substitution of short comic monologues for full-blown songs) and seems to despise its own insistence on Cockney jollity (big number: 'Going Down to Chingford on a Chara.'); it compensates with overpowering slum sets, and must be the dingiest musical ever. The authors offer us no reason to be interested in their heroine, and Angela Richards, poor girl, cannot make the deficiency good.

  

The rock 'n' roll musical Leave Him to Heaven (New London) is also divided; its starting-point is a Stan Freberg musical parody, but while Freberg hated rock, the authors here do not. How much was intended as a mockery and how much as straight nostalgia I cannot guess, but there is no doubt that nostalgia wins. Even a song as awful as the necrophile 'Tell Laura I Love Her' has grown charm with the decades. Brian Protheroe has awesome energy as the teenage idol and his rendition of 'Chantilly Lace,' the era's very best song, is irresistible.
1976-06-20-troilus-in-the-cut:
The National Theatre, playing at the Young Vic pending the completion of their own studio auditorium, have set Troilus and Cressida in what looks like half a bull-ring. Presently the actors enter; their costumes have traces of the classical drag usually adopt for this play but basically they are Elizabethan. Presumably, then, the arena really is a cock-pit; the author being Shakespeare and the subject war, it seems very plausible. The Greek warriors, Achilles and Ajax especially, are indeed so many fighting-cocks, and they spend much of the play crowing and preening themselves. In the battle-scenes at the end they are turned loose while Philip Stone’s Thersites, a malcontent battleman, sits on the enclosure-rail, cheering (and jeering) them on.

If the set takes some time to come into its own, the costumes help almost from the start. The Greek hierarchs- headed by Roland Culver, a wrinkled Agamemnon with a soul just visible beneath his pomposity - are encased, hemmed in by ruffs (Nestor’s appears to be mildewing). Ajax begins the play in silks and a string vest. Gulled into believing himself a champion, he joins the sartorial club. He even sports a laurel-wreath. He has a moustachioed air that is Caroline rather than Elizabethan; Gawn Grainger, who captures all the characters’s vanity, surliness and unexpected good nature, looks very much like Porthos, the nicest and thickest of the the three musketeers. Real viciousness is the prerogative of Achilles, a golden-robed prizefighter as played by Mark McManus, but a bantamweight rather than the expected heavy: a curious piece of satirical casting with which nothing else in the production- even the subtly disorientating costumes- really agrees.

The plainest-dressed of all is Philip Locke’s Ulysses, a free intellect who stands impatiently to the side while his colleagues windily dispute, then passionately calls them to order; or rather, his philosophy being what it is, to Order. The passion denotes as much respect for his own intellect- for intellect itself- as for his own immediate strategy. I have never seen this character’s status in the Greek camp - tolerated, needed, but not really liked, ignored on social occasions and more genuinely at home with his adversaries the Trojans- more fully realised.

The director, Elijah Moshinsky, has been nearly as successful with the Trojan councils as the Greek. Denis Quilley’s Hector, mature and sensible with fatal aberrations, embodies the chivalry whose death the play commemorates. Glyn Grain’s Paris, dashingly mean, is at least a temporary survivor; and Polly Adams makes a touchingly brittle Helen, another chivalric emblem in decay.

Between them stands Simon Ward’s Troilus, lucidly pleading the cause of a tarnished honour. There are areas, though, where lucidity is not enough and Mr Ward cannot make us feel the dangerous erotic power of Troilus’s false simplicity. So the love scenes suffer; as they also do from Robert Eddison’s Pandarus, accomplished but with hardly a trace of corruption, Chaucer’s Pandar rather than Shakespeare’s, and from Diana Quick’s Cressida, who departs from the recent tradition by not seeming a tart from the start, but fails to show us where the change comes. So the production’s success is partial, but it is usually engrossing, sometimes exhilarating, and with even the smallest parts vividly played, is palpable proof that, for the first time since Peter Hall’s accession, the National has a company.
1976-06-20-east-of-broadway:
East of Broadway

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a New York original.

DESPITE all pressures the New York commercial theatre remains more interesting than its counterpart in London. The pressures are certainly still there, and mounting; Broadway claims to have been enjoying a boom in the past couple of years, but however well the successful shows are doing, an uncomfortable number of theatres remain empty.

Nor would I assert that much of what goes on is very good; hardly ever, though, is it as unambitiously bad as much of what now occupies the West End. I have yet to discover the American equivalent of 'Murder at the Vicarage' or 'No Sex Please, We're British.' Most crucially, Broadway benefits from New York's lack of institutionalised theatre on the scale of the National Theatre or the RSC. (I am not claiming that this is a desirable situation or even, for very much longer, an economically feasible one.) For the moment, the best theatrical talent is still on Broadway, since it has nowhere else to go.

Occasionally, therefore, Broadway mounts an original work of a size and quality the West End has long forgotten--not that it always gets much thanks for it. The latest Harold Prince-Stephen Sondheim musical, Pacific Overtures, is about to close after a six-month run, never having recovered from its tepid reception at the hands of the local reviewers. It is unlikely to be seen in London, which is doubly sad, as all the English people I know who have seen the show or heard the score have loved it. I saw it twice within a week and thought it staggeringly good. Its setting is Japan, its subject the opening-up of that country in the mid-nineteenth century to trade with the West, America having taken the initiative in the matter by standing four battleships off the Nipponese coast. The commander of this expedition described his duties as the making of 'pacific overtures,' a euphemism which escalates the title of the show into, by my count, a five-way pun. Wit permeates the entire show. All the characters, Westerners included, are played by Oriental actors (many of them admittedly born in America) and it makes free and eclectic use of Japanese--mainly Kabuki--stage conventions: a narrator with accompanying musicians, an entry-ramp, men playing women. Screens are the basis of Boris Aronson's sets: maybe the finest that even he has designed. They make the show a bountiful gift of air and space.

The wedding of Kabuki techniques to Broadway skills produces of course a bastard form. But this is perfectly appropriate, since the subject of the show is bastardisation. Its upshot is the assumption by the Japanese of Western manners and--in a final jump to the present--their phenomenal victory at the West's own commercial game. A closing number balances the account: for most of the evening Eastern rhythms have been adapted by an American director, choreographer and composer; finally we watch American rhythms sung and danced by an Oriental cast--an ending which vindicates the American theatre's right to meddle with this subject and these styles.

As it is told, this is the most moving of the Prince-Sondheim shows. (I don't know whether Mr Prince considers himself a Brechtian, but I take alienation to mean not that emotion should be denied, but that it should be rigorously inspected.) The central character--a minor samurai employed as an intermediary with the invaders--is played by an actor called Isao Sato, who has a most beguiling quality: wry, tender, and quizzically hopeful. One song, 'A Bowler Hat,' which details his capitulation over the years to Western ideas and Western dress, he performs with surpassing delicacy. Indeed, not the least of the skills this show proves the Japanese to have acquired is that of acting in musical comedy; the level of performance is very high.

A couple of Mr Sondheim's lyrics unconvincingly credit some Japanese ladies with a fluent Manhattan wit (a multiple pastiche number for predatory European ambassadors is another, and a hilarious, matter), but his music--full of sweet dissonances, and haunting, angular melodies, has never sounded more individual or more dramatically apt. One song entitled 'Someone in a Tree' concerns, if you please, the impossibility of knowing the truth about any historical event, and the fading of an old man's memory--all set to a surging, questing rhythm that had me on the edge of my seat with excitement. And there is one song of farewell called 'There is No Other Way,' accompanied by a dance of floating silk, which--in sight, sound and sense--is as beautiful as anything I remember in the musical theatre. It can be heard in London--though diminished without the visual element--in the Sondheim compilation at the Mermaid, as can another song--a sailor's trio--actually done better here than in New York.

By way of consolation, Pacific Overtures has just been filmed for television, Japanese television, of course.
1976-06-27-the-glisten-of-humour:
The Glisten of Humour

ROBERT CUSHMAN writes an appreciation of American songwriter and singer Johnny Mercer, who died on Friday, aged 66.

I FIRST became conscious of Johnny Mercer as a singer: a man who did duets with Bing Crosby.

When I started listening to the radio in the late forties a record which they must have cut a decade earlier was still current (it hasn't died yet). It was a reworking of the old vaudeville cross-talk number "Mr Gallagher and Mrs Shean," with the lyrics altered to a dictionary of the jargon of swing. Mercer did the rewriting of course and there are many of his peculiar qualities captured on that disc. The rhythm, the fascination with jazz and with language, the poker-faced wit. Harold Arlen, the composer with whom much of his best work was done, said that he only once saw Mercer crack a smile.

Both as writer and performer, his work glistens with humour, but it is so slyly delivered in a tart voice that it can almost slip by the listener. Singing with Crosby, and later with Bobby Darin, he loved to assume the role of a slightly bemused peasant, counterpointing the hip behaviour of the professional singer he was teamed with. In fact, he could outswing them all. Recently he made a couple of albums of his own songs, and one of the saddest things about his death is that there are so many hundreds more of which he had still to make the definitive recording.

He wrote lyrics with everybody: with Kern, Carmichael, Ellington, Schwartz down to Henry Mancini and André Previn, with whom he collaborated on the recent musical of Priestley's "The Good Companions." That was not his best work; he could not adapt to an English idiom, or indeed to a theatrical one.

He wrote individual songs, not revelations of situation or character: the greatest he ever created -- Jubilation T Cornpone -- was the subject of the song, not its singer. And of course he was an American subject: Mercer was the lyricist of Americana, in two modes rural-bucolic (as in the score for "Seven Brides for Seven Brothers," or his host of ornithological songs -- "Skylark" and the others) and urban-hip. "One for my Baby" is the archetypal saloon ballad, suggesting the smoke of cigarettes as much as of lovers' torches. And it is less a moaning than a shrugging song; like all the best lyricists, he knew how to be wry about heartbreak.

Others of his songs are filled with a kind of crazy, irreverent euphoria; they sound fun to write and fun to sing. An obscure piece (in fact I have only just discovered it) typically entitled "Hang on to your Lids, Kids," concludes:--

"Ben Franklin once said it all
Divided we've got to fall
United we'll have a ball
Here we go again."

He seems hardly ever to have stopped writing, and he turned out a great many routine numbers. But few lyricists (or composers, for he furnished Fred Astaire with the music as well as the words of the magnificent "Something's Got to Give") can have turned out so many great ones.
1976-06-27-waiting-for-hickey:
Waiting for Hickey

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on revivals of O'Neill, Chekhov, Coward and Feydeau.

O'NEILL'S The Iceman Cometh (Aldwych) is the fountainhead of postwar American drama, the archetype of all the plays in which characters sit in bars or cafés or roadside diners or junkies' pads, interact and wait. It also has a considerable number of relatives living abroad; Samuel Beckett's bums waiting for Godot are in much the same predicament as O'Neill's waiting for Hickey, the travelling salesman. Beckett, however, let his characters off lightly; Godot never arrives. Hickey does show up and his acolytes barely survive his coming. That finally they do survive it is the cruellest thing in the play.

Iceman represents the underside of pop Americana: of Damon Runyon and of Clap hands, here comes Charlie. See the smile on all those hungry faces. They can tell that he's a buyer from the wide and open spaces. The men in Harry Hope's saloon, New York 1912, have permanently thirsty faces and Harry himself is usually pickled enough for his clients to grab themselves all the booze they want. Hickey's arrival will save them the trouble of scrounging; besides, a fresh face is always welcome if you never go out of doors.

O'Neill, writing in 1939, was again recalling his own youth. The claim most frequently made for him is that having touched bottom himself he was able to portray his fellows without any touch of patronage. Exploitation, though, can take many forms, and however much O'Neill may have respected his characters he had few qualms about moving them abruptly from one convention to another. Having set them up as individuals he turns them in his last act into a chorus; suddenly they start talking in unison. Harry becomes the chorus leader and Norman Rodway, who has kept his nose infallibly to the ground in Howard Davies's production, suddenly starts to intone. Visually Mr Davies manages the transition well; the drained, battered faces - 15 in a row - look like a rotting tapestry. Aurally it grates, and for the first time O'Neill's notorious deficiencies as a writer (generally more noticeable on the page than the stage) begin to obtrude.

The jolt is nasty, but the play survives it. Partly it does so by virtue of its length; it plays for four and a quarter hours. O'Neill gives himself room to stumble and get up again; and while a bad long play is insupportable, a good one is, from the audience's point of view, addictive. And because they give the actors a chance to dig their heels in, extended group pieces like this are almost invariably well performed.

The massive structure gives O'Neill the space to grade his characters. All of them are victims of a single disease; unable to face reality, each protects himself with a pipe-dream. At the centre is Harry, believing that one day he will take a walk outside. Around him are his clients, part refugees, part spongers, each with a past that serves also as an imaginary future.

Regarding them with pity and contempt is Larry, whose lack of illusion is itself an illusion. He is generally taken for the play's commentator, but even he is overseen by the barman, Rocky, the play's nearest approach to a man of the world; after all, he has a job, he can leave when he's not working and if he runs a couple of whores, they are only a sideline. His illusions are the hardest to crack because hardest to pin down. As Rob Hoskins plays him, Rocky is almost the centre of the play; certainly he is its pacemaker.

To them comes Hickey in the guise of an evangelist; he has seen through his own pipe-dream and wishes to cure them of theirs. He persuades each of them to try to realise his dream; predictably they all come back to the saloon, sobbing. They and the world have no use for each other. But this is Hickey's plan; what he has come to spread is not happiness but misery. (He deceives himself about this of course: he has merely traded one pipe-dream for another. O'Neill's philosophy may have been schematic, but its application necessarily involved him in greater subtleties than he may have envisaged.) The ground keeps opening. He has killed his wife. For a moment he even faces the fact that he hated her; then he lies to deny it, and his denial sets the bums free. They can claim that he was mad, that they obeyed him only to humour him, and that everything is as it was. If you like happy endings, hurry to the Aldwych.

  

The last developments can be hard to follow; O'Neill seems to regard illusion and reality as solid wedges to be moved around like chessmen. What is more, all the characters seem to know the rules. There is a parallel action involving young Parritt, who has shopped his mother as Hickey has killed his wife, and who comes to confess to Larry as Hickey comes to confess to the bums.

This is the area least well handled in the writing and in this production. Kenneth Cranham, usually an attacking actor, seems ill-at-ease with Parritt's whimpering passivity and plight. Patrick Stewart easily holds the stage; he does not make Larry's mental processes any too interesting. The rest, in Chris Dyer's set, high and wide if not handsome, is splendour. Alan Tilvern's Hickey is a perfect messenger of death, with slicked-down hair, slicked-down voice, and features locked in the permanent sneer bequeathed by years of successful salesmanship. The others - especially John Warner, Gary Bond and Richard Simpson - make their lurchings between the bottle and the door horribly involving. In its detail, more than its theory, the play rubs a universal sore; and in its attitude to hope (it exists in the saloon as in the proprietor's name and it depends on deception) it satirises tragedy, making it the archetypal modern play.

  

Not the greatest though: that is Chekhov's Three Sisters, which at the Cambridge is accorded, in Jonathan Miller's production transferred from Guildford, by far its best performance in my experience. There is at least one transcendent sequence: Natasha's proprietorial stalk around the sisters' bedroom in the third act is satirically reprised by Irena. Olga and Masha fall about; the trio are a laughing unity and the harmony prompts Masha to tell, still laughing, of her love for Vershinin.

Janet Suzman is magnificent as Masha; her reactions throughout are pointed but never planted. The flow of her performance is virtually unbroken. Nigel Davenport, partnering her, helps her to make sense; he is fleshily attractive, opportunist, a bit shabby. He philosophises because that is the thing to do, and he covertly laughs at those (like the doomed Trozonbach) who do it seriously.

The play takes shape, too, as an outsiders' revenge; Natasha and Solyony, both snubbed in the first act, naturally cause havoc later. June Ritchie's Natasha, in particular, is excellently rounded. Angela Down's Irena is refreshingly hard; she does not languish for Moscow, she merely wants it to hurry up. Mr Miller sacrifices intermediate climaxes (one or two, to be honest, I rather missed) for the sake of the last outburst, which comes hard and fast. Susan Engel puts more despair into Olga's last speech than I have ever heard before. Sebastian Shaw's doctor and Antony Brown's schoolmaster are particularly distinguished.

  

Blithe Spirit (Lyttelton) turns out more ghostly than might have been intended. Harold Pinter's production firmly outlines the marital discomfort at the base of the play, but he has little opportunity to build on it; and both Coward's prose and his artistic snobbery, the central character is a novelist with little good to say of anyone who isn't, seem petty and, what is worse, routine. A great Madame Arcati might save the day, as she saved the film, but Elizabeth Spriggs is no Margaret Rutherford. She has played too many eccentrics to conquer: the part from without, not enough to take it from within.

Maria Aitken has the right style - compounded of a witty drawl and a long, long back - for Elvira; Rowena Cooper deals professionally with Ruth's good lines, but cannot salvage the bad, which predominate; and Richard Johnson is dull. I think the production should be faster, but I imagine Mr Pinter trusts the text more than I do.

  

Nobody involved in Signed and Sealed (Comedy) seems to trust it at all, which is understandable. It is the least inventive farce ever to reach our stage under the name of Feydeau. If I had a line or two left, I could even summarise its plot.
1976-07-03-good-time-music:
3 JULY 1976, Page 25 - Arts Section

Good-time music

Robert Cushman

The first act of the evening at the London Palladium usually has my sympathy. Very often that is all it has; certainly it can boast very little in the way of an audience. The patrons trickle slowly and noisily in, knowing that whoever is holding stage it is not the performer they have come, to see. (The management seem similarly unconcerned, content to raise the curtain while half the punters are still in the bars. Of course the Palladium does have unusually capacious and attractive bars.) On the night of Monday, 21 June, it was different. Bing Crosby was beginning a series of concerts, and a rumour passed round the house that he was going to be on unbelievably, at the top.

It was true, too, or almost. He was actually preceded by a Movietone clip of his last appearance in London: during the war, at the Stage-door Canteen. He had more hair, then, but it was already beginning to go, and his outstretched ears made it look rather odd. The toupee to which he now frankly resorts—capped, if you will pardon the expression, by the declaration 'this time I brought my hair'—is a definite improvement.

Herbert Kretzmer observed in the Daily Express that jokes about his baldness are an index of what separates Crosby from Frank Sinatra. The only infirmities Sinatra parades are psychological; they colour his lovesongs (even now there is no bleaker sound than that of Sinatra in tune with a masochistic ballad) but, finally, they are there to be overcome—while with Judy Garland, they were there to overcome her. Garland's anthem was 'Over the Rainbow', a desperate retreat into childhood; Sinatra's is 'My Way' (a regrettable song but accurate enough), which uses the defeats of the past to highlight a victorious present. It is one of the few examples I can think of, of a singer attaching a song to himself by main force; 'Over the Rainbow' merely happened to Garland as part of a film score.

Crosby now closes his act with a thing called 'That's What Life is All About' which he admits to be his answer to 'My Way'. The admission is typical; he is the only man I have ever seen manage to be insouciant and apologetic at the same time. It is a better song than 'My Way', less bombastic ; it even scans. All the same, one or two lines—Tve had success, some mild acclaim'—strain belief; the man may well be that modest, but he could never be that naive. And precisely because of the song's unpretentiousness I doubt if it will ever have much impact as a credo; unassumingness, after all, is not something you can proclaim. There is a thrill to Sinatra's arrogance; at least there was until it declined, with his comeback and his political turnabout, into bumptiousness.

Sinatra's concerts are planned as acts of worship; supporting singers and comics spend the first half of the show preparing the way of the lord, and the wait can be tiresome. Crosby, ambling on (no other word suits). and compering his own show, earned our goodwill from the start ; it was the shrewdest, as well as the pleasantest and most characteristic thing he could have done.

Some of his performance was forgettable. He paraded his family, who were pleasant as an entity but no impression as individuals, and ventured out of navigable waters in singing 'Send in the Clowns'. (He set it up well, though, despite his inexplicable statement that this song, inescapable for the past year, had failed to be a hit.) Both the tune and the words seemed to elude him; more important, so did the emotion. And this, in view of his amazing track-record, is the most surprising thing about him : he has never managed to communicate pain. He has sung torch songs, as he has sung everything, but the words have never seemed to matter.

My first memories are of the late 'forties; about the first thing I took notice of Was the radio, on which he was omnipresent. He dominated all the record programmes, and there were regular spots entirely devoted to him, called 'Bing Sings'. I was taken to his movies (my mother was a fan) and these, particularly the Road pictures with Bob Hope, made a greater impact on me than the records. I retained my respect for him as a light comedian when I temporarily lost interest in his singing. The vocalists I came to adore were Sinatra, Ella Fitzgerald and Peggy Lee. Compared with their filigree voices, Crosby sounded cloudy (not the enunciation, just the tone); and his repertoire, to one elated at discovering Cole Porter and Rodgers and Hart, pedestrian. There was no sexuality in his voice, and that he should over two decades have been a romantic idol seemed to me puzzling and a little funny.

Slowly I came to realise that it struck him that way too. Part of his greatness has been that he started mocking his own status almost as soon as he achieved it. The comedy of the films carried over into the records, making him among other things the best duet-singer of our time; his meetings with Louis Armstrong, Fred ,Astaire, Johnny Mercer (he above all) are among the nicest things on record, wry, urbane, impeccably timed. They are marvellous good-time music, as also of course are his excursions into Dixieland. Excursions is really the wrong word ; they are more like homecomings, welcome relief after a hard day's doleful crooning.

And now, in his and the century's seventies, he is a hugely satisfying performer. For the swing and the humour, the good-time music, are what remain, along with a memory of the crooning more satisfying than the thing itself. The voice itself is better than ever; its deep notes were always its best and they have been not eroded but enriched by time. He takes a while to get going; but the closing sequence of his act—a medley of thirty-two old favourites—is spell-binding. The length of the thing is part of the magic; you lose track of time. You begin by liking him, and you end up knowing you were right. These songs, in total and so cunningly sung, will do for his testament ; that's what life is all about.

Mel Torme, who opened the same night at the Talk of the Town, has no theme song; he always sings 'Mountain Greenery' (the arrangement changing with the years) and we are always glad to hear it, but only because it is such a good song; too good for us to associate with one singer, however gifted. Torme ranks second only to Sinatra among the male singers who reached their peak in the 'fifties and stayed there through most of the 'sixties; with him, indeed, there is still no trace of decline. One of my greatest musical pleasures has been to follow his light, firm voice insinuating itself among the best songs, and some of the best orchestrations, of our time. There is a candid, almost boyish quality to the voice which offsets its owner's intricate musicianship. Not a soulful singer, he can nevertheless move you simply by letting good material speak, with crystal clarity, for itself. Ella Fitzgerald does much the same, though with her the process is instinctive; with Torme all is planned. The most complex improvisations (and he does some dazzling scat-singing in his current act) sound rehearsed; I doubt if his phrasing varies much from show to show. I shared a table with Henry Pleasants, the American music critic and author of a book on popular singers, who remarked that Torme, though he has terrific drive, does not swing (the reverse being true of Crosby). I agree; the tone, however nimbly he leaps in and out of keys, is surprisingly even and uninflected. I love him for his wit, his accomplishment and his ambition (the act, though too short, was surprisingly uncompromising for the Talk of the Town); he is, in many ways, the most exhilarating singer I have ever heard.

Conscientious too; guiding us through a Hollywood medley, he even got the names and dates of the movies right. He makes good jokes, but some of his patter is overornate and over-anxious; this is-one area where Crosby still reigns supreme. Maybe it is an attribute of his generation: the only other American entertainer I have heard speak with similar ease and unpretentiousness is Fred Astaire:
1976-07-04-better-black-than-white:
PETER SHAFFER'S Black Comedy, revived at the Shaw, is the theatrical equivalent of the Marx Brothers' stateroom scene in A Night at the Opera: a single mechanical joke indefinitely prolonged and becoming more irresistible every second. Mr Shaffer is a conscientious builder and both his blueprint and his construction are, on this occasion, immaculate. Black Comedy is probably the only classic farce written in England since the war.

To the initial premise - pitch darkness to the characters is brilliant light to the audience, and vice versa, and all stations in between - is added farce's essential staple: the hero to whom all this could not have happened at a worse moment.

Young Brindsley is faced with a power cut, a roomful of sculpture waiting to be viewed and hopefully bought by a deaf millionaire, the debbiest of fiancees to be kept sweet, her military martinet father to be impressed, expensive furniture borrowed to this end from the flat across the passage without the knowledge of its fanatically possessive possessor, the sudden return of said owner necessitating the return of the furniture before the darkness ends and he finds out, and the irruption of Brindsley's ex-bird, to whom most of this, especially the fiancee part, comes as a surprise. Mr Shaffer's deployment of these varied forces is masterly.

Paul Giovanni's production, which is more notable for spurts of energy than for overall rhythm, will not altogether satisfy those who remember John Dexter's original; though it is of course doubtful whether anyone who saw that production will ever be really pleased by anything else ever again. Celia Bannerman as Clea is a bit too self-conscious about her charming candour to lay the ghost of Maggie Smith, though Gemma Craven's deb is daintily determined enough to take on the shade of Louise Purnell, whose delighted trill of "Sexipegs!" still echoes down the years. Peter Machin as Brin keeps the engine running, but his chirpy demeanour has more to do with the manner thought proper to a light comedian of the sixties than with the reactions of this person in this play. But nobody is actually bad; and both the play and its characters emerge as the most credible and engaging Mr Shaffer has created.

Apart from Black Comedy, which is only half an evening, this has been the direst theatrical week my fairly young remembrance can furnish. The rot started early with Mr Shaffer's curtain-raiser, White Liars, professedly re-written since its first London appearance. The most interesting addition, in view of the long line of male attachments in Mr Shaffer's plays, is the explicit acknowledgment that this one really is homosexual. The most valuable subtraction is the disembodied voice with which the fortune-telling Baroness, who governs the play, was wont to hold interminable conversations.

The theme remains the same. All three characters are living protective lies: the Baroness is no Baroness, the Northern prole pop-singer is middle class and southern, the manager who claims to have created him is an emotional parasite. The play was planned to complement Black Comedy (which contains a helpful line - helpful since otherwise we wouldn't have noticed - about a darkened room acting as a lie-detector) and it also of course resembles The Iceman Cometh. Mr Shaffer seems more optimistic than O'Neill about man's capacity to survive the death of his illusions, which is cheering, but perhaps a dramatist needs to treat this theme at four hours' length if he is to quell our desire to know what else might be new. The play suffers, like many of Mr Shaffer's, from its failure to find a believable idiom, especially for its young: Timothy Dalton as the singer is wet, but he is not helped by his author or by Mr Giovanni, who lowers the lights on him and leaves him to soliloquise.

  

Rainer Werner Fassbinder's reputation is doubtless exaggerated, like all reputations, but I was enough affected by it to expect more from The Bitter Tears of Petra von Kant (Theatre at New End) than a boudoir weepie. Petra is a rich fashion designer spurned by her lover, who happens to be a girl; diligently I searched for irony, but found only stifling indulgence. (It was a stifling night and the New End is not air-conditioned; the heat-wave may asphyxiate the fringe.) I suppose the acting may have been intended ironically; Delphine Seyrig's English is very clear, but she gets the inflections wrong - as, with even deadlier effect, does everybody else in the cast except for Angela Pleasence, who is smoulderingly silent and for whom bully; seeing as those who speak have to say "certainly I can well understand your bitterness" or even, unanswerably I suppose, "he stank of man as only men can stink." The production by Robert Walker is not good.

  

The only fitting phrase for Hanratty In Hell was coined many years ago, at the opposite climatic extreme, by W. C. Fields: "Tain't a fit night out for man nor beast." It is Charles Marowitz's last production at the Open Space, before moving on to other premises and to a programme that will abandon a policy of plays in favour of unspecified company work. This is a promise that Mr Marowitz keeps making, but maybe this time he means it; his treatment of texts is, in general, poundingly inept, but Brian Carr's piece deserves the worst he can do to it and may be meant as a valediction.

Mr Carr assumes Hanratty to have been wrongly convicted of the A6 murder and begins with some laboured joking about his status as an innocent in hell. We then shift, unexplained, back to earth and back in time for a reconstruction of the police investigation, with the coppers humorously renamed Kray, with methods to match. I am prepared to believe the worst of anyone, but I want more than just assertion; so apparently do Ronald Lewis as the super and Ken Parry as Lord Longford (another gas), since they experienced great difficulty in getting Mr Carr's words out of their mouths. Valerie Storie is also portrayed; jumping out of her wheelchair with joy when she gets the wrong man sent down. Whatever else may be in dispute, nobody has ever questioned that Miss Storie was raped and was crippled; this does not make her a saint, but it makes one reluctant to laugh at her just for kicks. The play's choice of culprit is Peter Alphon, who repeatedly confessed and withdrew his confession. It ends up telling us where he now lives, presumably so that the lynch-mobs will know where to go.
1976-07-11-the-trouble-with-thrillers:
THE climax of Alan Drury's Sparrowfall (Hampstead) is the death of a comparatively innocent man. Just what special providence has decreed the fall of this particular sparrow is difficult to determine; though the motives of Mr Drury's characters - greed and self-protection - would seem to be conventional enough, it is difficult to come at them while the play is in progress. The form interposes. The play is a thriller, but not the kind that is usually found in the theatre.

If Time Out magazine is to be trusted (though its preview article laid so much stress on the play's extremely incidental music that I arrived at Hampstead half expecting a rock-musical), the influences were Alfred Hitchcock, Howard Hawks and (some inconsistency here) B-movies. But Hampstead has a small stage, and so one is more inclined, watching the play, to think of the small screen. Mr Drury gives us a business setting - his main character is something big and nasty in investments - and the effect is rather as if The Brothers had grown brains and sex organs.

Mr Drury's dialogue is studiously light and steely, and John Chapman's production matches it scrupulously. Nobody is allowed to betray any emotion except fear. As for the performances, they are well-tailored and well-groomed; collectively the cast displays the finest head of hair to be found on the London stage. The designer, Tanya McCallin, has divided her stage into a series of battleship-grey compartments, allowing the action to progress from flat to office to aerodrome with no immediate signs of strain.

There is strain, though; the play, production and design are faultlessly in style, but their success is self-defeating. Even in the hands of Hawks and Hitchcock the thriller is a pretty empty form, telling us things about human corruptibility which we knew already. The writers may supply smart dialogue - so does Mr Drury, at least some of the time - but nobody goes primarily to listen to it. Our object is to watch, and both cinema and television give us more to look at than the theatre ever can; even when the scene is stationary, the camera moves. Watching a single multiple set, however elegant and ingenious, is comparatively poor fun; all the action has to take place in corners and one aches to see the action take possession of the stage.

This play is the successor of the comic-strip pieces which a decade ago were going to save our theatre from bourgeois naturalism; they never get beyond the one-act lunchtime circuit because, by definition, they lacked staying-power. The form saves the playwright the trouble of exploring his characters; though Mr Drury's The Man Himself, which has been turning up at six o'clock performances in the National's Young Vic season, shows that he has the desire and the ability. In The Man Himself he exercises them in the simplest available form - the monologue - but he gives promise of becoming a public writer who can depict people as they are rather than as he would like them to be.

  

Emigres by the Polish writer Slawomir Mrozek, who has been absent from our stages for several years. He has been away from his homeland even longer, and this piece eventually supplies some piquant thoughts on the predicament of the expatriate. I say eventually since, at least in Kevin Billington's production, the play takes an unconscionable time to get going. Jim Norton, who is sort of intellectual, and Brian Cox, who is sort of thick, share a room in some city foreign to both of them; unfortunately both they and their environment seem very British, which saps the base of the play.

They might be in any old two-hander, and from time to time I was driven to think of them as two halves of the same character: a notoriously desperate critical gambit which proved as unhelpful here as it usually does. However, when Mrozek gets more specific about them - when each is forced to consider the possibility of the other being an informer, when Mr Norton forces Mr Cox to realise the unreality of his dreams of returning home and when Mr Cox half-heartedly and amusingly attempts suicide to Mr Norton's considerable impatience - both text and performance sharpen up.

  

Alan Badel is the leader of the lost generation of English classicists who give the St George's Playhouse its main reason for being. Appropriately, he is now appearing as Richard III. His Richard is less a devil than a driven imp, rolling downstage to deliver his first speech as a deadpan joke on the audience, and winning his way to the throne more by cheek than imposture. (This is reasonable: Richard, unlike Iago, is trusted by almost nobody.) His eyes are his tensest feature; they are hypnotically fixed as he waits to see how his victims will respond to his poison; always there is the chance of failure.

Richard's disabilities allow Mr Badel to act, fascinatingly, at an incline; even when he has reached the throne he hugs its side. As an ironist Mr Badel is in the Olivier class; though the St George's acoustics are cruel to his throwaways; he can never secure a full-throated laugh. This is the more unfortunate because he falls short of Olivier in passion and in vocal, as opposed to physical, command; there seem to be no heights or depths to his voice, no bark, no ring. He is best in the prolonged cat-and-mouse game he plays with Richard Gale's Buckingham, or in the briefer contest with Lynn Farleigh's Anne, who ends up actually flirting with him; weakest in the frenzy of the end, by which time he seemed to be acting by rote. Most of Richard is there, but you have to dig for some of it.

Douglas Campbell's production is a very enjoyable piece of storytelling in the Guthrie tradition; sometimes for worse (there is a spectacularly but pointlessly doddering Archbishop), but often for better. Richard's court is presented as a vast comfortless ante-chamber, the courtiers going on cold continuous progresses around the enthroned protagonist. The same idea works less well for the Bosworth ghosts, ceaselessly wandering at one and a half times normal speed (the approved theatrical rate for spectres). The cluttered facade of former productions has gone (and with it some of the Elizabethan theorising in the programme), leaving only the church's gothic pillars. These and the platform stage enable the production to look good even when its sound is muffled. Rosemary Leach's Elizabeth is the most commanding performance; and much of the personal interplay is on the road to being interesting.

  

The Pleasure of His Company (Phoenix) is, I suppose, well-named; it exists to introduce us to Douglas Fairbanks Jr, who is dapper if not exciting. But there is hardly scope for excitement in Samuel Taylor's comedy which, though written in the fifties, has now been set in the thirties, so that its anodyne unreality may pass for period charm - prompting the thought that if Mr Fairbanks had brought over a genuine antique of the period (Philip Barry or S. N. Behrman) the lines could have been wittier, the sets just as plush; the fans would not notice the difference, and the rest of us would have a little more to keep us awake. As it is Peter Dews's production is the slowest thing imaginable; Mr Fairbanks reduces its pace to a stroll, Dinah Sheridan (though hers is the most conscientious performance) takes it down to a crawl, and Wilfrid Hyde White finally stops it in its tracks. The pungent satisfaction with which he surveys its corpse - as if he had drowned it in dry Martini - is the most amusing thing in the evening. Mr Hyde White refers to himself as inhabiting an ivory tower and addresses his grand-daughter as "person." It is that kind of play; at least it would like to be.
1976-07-18-lessons-of-a-crisp-factory:
Lessons of a crisp factory

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

JOSEF FRANK, as I learned last week, was one of those hanged in Prague in 1952 after the Slansky show-trials. In his new play, Weapons of Happiness (Lyttelton) Howard Brenton imagines Frank, surviving, somehow, coming to England and working, now in a potato-crisp factory, in South London. It will be seen that, historically speaking, Mr Brenton's Frank is a ghost; dramatically, too. "I don't sleep," he tells us at curtain-rise. "I walk about London."

The crisp business is in turmoil. The factory is small, family owned and running down. Its work-force seems to consist entirely of kids and old men. Prominent among the kids is Janice, whose political education began early with a book called "The Evil That Was Lenin." ("Think it was meant to put me off. 'Stead it put me on.") Discovering that the management has plans to sell out she organises a workers' occupation. She does not organise it very well; and her forces have to decamp through the sewers. Anyway her own politicisation, though fervent, has never seemed very secure ("Couldn't understand a word. But I believed in it") and she has not managed to communicate much in the way of ideology to her followers, who are driven by gut-discontent, gut-hatred, and--at the decisive moment--alcohol. Besides this they have neither the finance nor the contacts to take over the machines and make crisps themselves.

It is Frank who points this out to them; but it needs no ghost to come from the grave to tell us that this attempt at revolt was foredoomed. Mr Brenton's full-length plays are characteristically organised around two disparate blocks of experience; in Magnificence his worlds collide with immense force, in The Churchill Play they remain obstinately apart. In Weapons of Happiness they are brought together but there is no impact. Frank, both in the writing and in Frank Finlay's performance, is carefully opaque. We are shown his past as well as his present; there are flashbacks to his days as a Czech Minister negotiating with Mikoyan and socialising with Stalin; monologues about his torture and interrogation. These of course are harrowing, but ever since Darkness at Noon, never mind The Gulag Archipelago, they have been within the grasp of any competent writer who cared to use them. And Mr Brenton does not use them to any new effect; he leaves us feeling (a) that in the light of experiences like these, English ideas of revolution look childish and (b) that the idea of socialist revolution has anyway been irredeemably tarnished. These conclusions might be reached by any liberal, and I doubt if they are what Mr Brenton had in mind.

When Janice, in the last line of the play, recalls Frank, she merely says of him, "He was a Communist." And that line, coming as and when it does, sounds like a declaration both of love and honour; but it can hardly counter-balance what has gone before. There is more swimming about in the play than has been resolved or made clear. Half of the evening works, though, as a furious lampoon on a decaying corner of capitalism. It is like Mr Brenton to choose a crisp-factory for his area of conflict, and to make the owner the victim of his own ingenuity ("It was the pork chop flavour that finally did for me") in the fight against "the monoliths of the crunch world." Michael Medwin has the best of Mr Brenton's dialogue (brisk, grotesque and concrete as ever) and does well by it; he is pitiable and amusing. Julie Covington, too, is excellent as Janice; compact and composed, frank, exact and enigmatic, she proves herself here (as she promised a couple of years ago in The Pleasure Principle) the most distinctive contemporary young actress we have.

There are some excess characters: a deaf-and-dumb boy who is not used for cheap effect but is not used for much else either, and Mr Medwin's unsatisfied spouse. (If industrialists could make love to their wives, would that solve everything?) But Mr Brenton still takes as much delight in stage images, and his director David Hare takes as much care over them, as in their Portable Theatre days. Operating now at the other extreme, using all of the National Theatre that works, they convey the same cool pleasure in stretching and challenging the available resources. Not every play can offer both a scene in the London Planetarium and the spectacle of cartons of crisps hurled on to the stage to vomit forth their contents.

  

A redoubtable company of underactors, guided by a television director, fall predictably foul of Webster's The White Devil (Old Vic). The setting would be nondescript were it not for a brace of swing-doors downstage which inescapably suggest the lobby of an hotel with delusions of grandeur; the costumes have the same seediness, the same unspecified modernity. Everything and everybody is undercut, which is part of the effect Webster presumably aimed for, but by no means all of it. He was obviously fascinated by his luxurious assembly of homicides, and the moral judgments he delivered were considerably more complex and evasive than the puritanical disapproval, compromised by prurience, conveyed by this production almost before it has started. The amount of mumbling and gabbling indulged in is phenomenal.

Michael Lindsay-Hogg's production does actually manage some things unexpectedly well; one is a contest in melancholia between a couple of the play's numerous villains which dissolves when one of them receives good news and explodes with laughter; another is the portrayal of the boy-prince Giovanni. Glenda Jackson gives a small but accurate account of the title role, but she cannot hold the play together; neither can Jack Shepherd, who as Flamineo has the most chance. He establishes a properly confidential relationship with the audience but none with anybody else; he seems to comment on his own villainy without ever executing it. So the most varied and rewarding role in English drama fades into nothing. James Villiers does better as Bracciano, whom he just manages to keep believable as a sulky, possessive head prefect. Frances de la Tour is properly ambiguous as the seeming-virtuous Isabella, and Jonathan Pryce hovers to some effect as the cut-throat Lodovico. The end of the play is left confused; one character even escapes, most apocryphally, with her life.

  

The following night another TV director, Jack Gold, succeeded triumphantly in making another diabolical (if considerably more tractable) play command the stage. Indeed Tom Conti, leaning handsomely and languorously against the door on first entrance, looks more like The Devil's Disciple (Aldwych) than anybody reading the lines Shaw provided for his conventional romantic ne'er-do-well might imagine possible. Mr Conti and Mr Gold have been as assiduous with the play's wit as with its avowed melodrama; and the RSC have cast the play up to, indeed some way above, the hilt. The deployment of John Wood as General Burgoyne, whose every line is an infallible wisecrack, is definitely luxury casting and is of course pure delight; Mr Wood, like Mr Conti, announces his intention with his first movement, which is to lie full-length upon a table and gaze upward with lazy, insolent defiance. Even the emotions of the besotted Mrs Anderson get scrupulous attention from Estelle Kohler. T. P. McKenna has a roaring time as her transfigured mate, and I must mention Patrick Godfrey's perfect butt of a major, if only because I always mean to mention Mr Godfrey when dealing with this company and nearly always have to squeeze him out. I should remind you that the play is set in the American War of Independence and that this seems to be topical: military bands play patriotic airs on fifes.

  

At the Mermaid Hugh Leonard has adapted a Labiche farce under the title Some of My Best Friends Are Husbands, and may well have interfered with it. I suspect, though, that he is less the culprit than the director, James Grout, who permits his stars, Patrick Cargill and Moira Redmond, to give performances that have everything to do with actors' panic and nothing with that of the characters. Hugh Paddick nearly redeems the occasion as a masochistic, hypochondriac and possibly fetishistic cuckold; he fills the character to the brim but never over. The same tact and good sense is evidenced in smaller roles by Granville Saxton and Peter Bourke. It is also exercised by absolutely everybody in Donkey's Years (Globe), an unmitigatedly glorious farce by Michael Frayn to which I must return next week.
1976-07-25-hallelujah-chorus:
SIX years ago, in his choreography for Company, Michael Bennett devised a new convention for chorus numbers in a musical. He did it by dispensing with a chorus; when massed song and dance were called for, he used the principals, a dozen actors whom we had already got to know as individual characters. It was a lot more fun than the multiple anonymity that is generally to be found treading vigorously just outside the star's spotlight.

In A Chorus Line (Drury Lane), Mr Bennett, now director and presiding genius as well as choreographer, has worked the same trick in reverse. Instead of making a chorus out of individuals, he has made individuals out of a chorus. The framework of the show is an audition session for an unspecified musical; we begin in the most electric opening sequence I have ever seen, by watching the applicants going through their paces in tap and ballet. Some of them are sent home, 17 remain.

The director says that he needs eight of them, and that they will have to do more than dance. They will have lines, so he wants to find out what kind of people they are. The audition turns into a trial by inquisition, a contest at which we have nobody in particular to root for; we can only love the 17 for themselves and by the end we love them all.

But the main reason we love them is not because they are cute or because they had difficult childhoods, though it transpires that they all had; it is because they are so exhilaratingly good at their jobs. And here the line between performer and role really ceases to matter; these are fine actor-singer-dancers playing fine actor-singer-dancers, American specials.

Good though they are, it does not follow that they would all be equally suited to the roles they are auditioning for. In effectively pretending that they would be, Mr Bennett cheats a bit. Seeing the show for the third time, I sagged slightly after the first number, when the dancing stopped and the confessional began. Part of the appeal of that beginning is its documentary quality; we are seduced into thinking that we are witnessing a dance-audition as it really is. What follows seems artificial.

The slump, though, is momentary, since we are soon given a bright succession of songs about professional hazards: about a girl who can dance but not sing, about another who stayed out of work until she got her breasts siliconised (the refrain of this song is "Tits and Ass," though the programme politely refers to it as "Dance: Ten; Looks: Three"), about a third who suffered appallingly from an actor-teacher who ridiculed her earnest attempts to impersonate an ice-cream. This one, called "Nothing," is the show's best song, but Edward Kleban's lyrics for all three are funny and sympathetic.

Marvin Hamlisch's music is serviceable, though too much of the score is pure Radio Two middle-of-the-road; not really theatrical, not really pop. The show's official climax is an appallingly vague ballad called "What I Did For Love," a detachable hit. It is supposed to be about performing, but takes care never to say so.

By this time we are far, but not very deep, into the characters' hang-ups, though these are usually dealt with in speech rather than song. Talking about why they are in the business, they never mention Applause. I capitalise that word since it was the title, a few years back, of a much inferior musical which, however, latched onto a point which A Chorus Line neglects. At least it neglects it explicitly; in style and performance, of course, it is a hugely effective machine for pleasing audiences.

As an epilogue, after the story is done and the winning eight selected, we get a unison number called "One," the cast of 19 (the director and his assistant thrown in) high-kicking in gold suits and glorious unison while the practice-mirrors revolve to turn a stark set into a sumptuous one. (Many of the most exciting things in the theatre are done with mirrors.) This finale also serves as a curtain-call; and it sends us wild. There are hints in the dialogue earlier that Mr Bennett despises this kind of Hello Dolly extravagance, and that he hates the idea of the chorus as an exploited centipede. I do not believe though that any audience in the world is going to leave the theatre seeing in that number what he wants us to see. It is simply too enjoyable. And, as in Company, we enjoy it the more for having got to know the performers beforehand.

Leonard Bernstein recently deplored the "phony vitality" of musicals. The achievement of A Chorus Line is to make the vitality genuine again. Obviously the performers believe in the material. A montage called "Hello Twelve, Hello Thirteen, Hello Love" (puberty recollected in rhythm) is the show's epitome: commonplace in substance, but conqueringly alight in delivery. Mr Bennett's choreography, as distinct from his direction, can be surprisingly uninspired; a solitary number not only compromises what the show is supposed to be saying, but fails in itself, being only a series of angular turns. I carp since it is difficult not to snipe at a myth, and in the best and worst senses that is what A Chorus Line is: not the best musical ever, not even the best of the last few years, but an insight into the essence of musical, the biggest theatrical high since the RSC's one-day marathon of The Wars of the Roses.

  

Chichester came back to scratch last week with a revival of Maugham's The Circle, which Peter Dews's production showed to be the kind of searching laugh at conventional society that only a conservative writer could bring off. (A radical wouldn't bother.) Bill Fraser and Googie Withers find the silliness and the pain in a raddled pair of elderly lovers. Actually Miss Withers scants a bit on the silliness, but she more than compensates with her virtuoso delicacy when counselling her daughter-in-law against repeating her own mistakes and eloping to the FMS (Federated Malay States).

Coincidentally, the FMS may actually be glimpsed, not looking at all pleasant, in Ben Travers's Banana Ridge (Savoy), just pre-war, spiced with Mr Travers's eccentric verbal wit, but never really sparking. Robert Morley and George Cole are a disappointing duo as members of a sort of paternity syndicate, blackmailed into supporting the offspring of a Miss Sue Long, from whom many must have departed to the strains of "Sue Long, It's Been Good to See You." The play blows its top too soon, leaving the last scene an anti-climax.

This could not be said of Michael Frayn's Donkeys' Years (Globe) which, having got all possible comic mileage out of a group of Cambridge graduates (now employed from the Ministry of Education downwards) returned for a college reunion, very sensibly turns itself into farce, among the most inventive, hilarious and scrupulously motivated to be found in London, even in this new heyday of the genre. Common to both the play's moods is the double theme of the turning worm and the jangled university belle; a brilliant pair of performances by Andrew Robertson and Penelope Keith. Her recoil from him is particularly memorable. Michael Rudman's production is blessed by an excellent cast, and you leave the theatre liking the author: not the highest dramatic gift but a rare and good one.
1976-08-01-trucking-in-from-hull:
Trucking in from Hull

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

ONE member of the Hull Truck Company claims in his programme biography to have been thrown out of LAMDA; another made a similar exit from Manchester Polytechnic School of Theatre. It is tempting to call Hull Truck a dropouts' group; that phrase belongs of course to the last decade, but it is no less appropriate on that account. The Truckers' most engaging quality is their independence of fashion. They are not themselves anachronistic; the characters they present may be nostalgic for the 1960s, but then that is one of the distinguishing marks of the 1970s.

So, at least, our playwrights keep telling us; Stephen Poliakoff's disc-jockey in City Sugar blamed his present cynicism on the wreck of his past dreams. Mr Poliakoff's Leicester looked like hell; Mike Bradwell's Hull (it is Mr Bradwell who drives the Truck) is more companionable. It tastes of keg beer and instant coffee, and it is unquestionably a university town; whatever their actual status, whatever their age, its inhabitants are leading a student life. They talk, since Hull Truck's plays are improvised, a great deal.

Their last show, Oh What, derived its unity from its characters' enslavement to past enthusiasms. Something of the same theme persists in their latest, Bridget's House, seen last week at the Young Vic, but here it seems peripheral, almost a mannerism. There is a difference - the characters are aware of passing time, they are consciously nostalgic - and there is pleasure to be derived from hearing pop-fans scrupulously distinguishing between the trends of the sixties and the early sixties. There is a pleasant song on the subject, too. (Hull Truck's use of music as commentary between scenes might one day lead us to a real native musical.) But it seems a long-winded, conventional way of establishing the two participants as, in Bridget's words, "emotional cripples."

Bridget is their landlady, as she is to most of the cast, and her estimate of them all is the same. It is the play's business to make us see that the words apply just as strongly to her. The trouble is that we can see this from the start. Bridget is an embittered divorcee, who has collected three properties by way of alimony. A psychology lecturer pursues her; she rejects him and takes a musician to bed, to the fury of his girlfriend.

Sexual situations are even more vulnerable than political ones to dramatists' distortion; the group improvisation method is a good way of preserving balance: We can see everybody behaving badly, weakly, embarrassingly, and no favourites are played. The dialogue is extraordinarily tight (theoretically it may vary in performance, but on the first night it seemed to have cast-iron consistency) and, most unusually in an improvised play, the actors know when to shut up.

Quite often the wit is sharp enough to make you wonder if Hull Truck are harbouring a playwright on the premises. The construction, though, cures you of that idea; Bridget's House, unlike Oh What, tells a story, and cannot raise interest in its outcome. It also differs from its predecessor in concentrating on middle-class characters and it has difficulty getting on terms with them, though David Hatton's lecturer is a clever study in ratty frustration. Rachel Bell's Bridget is clever, too, and as far as possible from her adenoidal tripper in Oh What. Here she shatters egos in a voice coated with iodine, stretches a leg across the lap of her intended with the brazen timing of a Maggie Smith.

This kind of acting (and I state it with no prejudice; in fact with all the approval of enjoyment) is, in the strictest sense, artificial, and needs a text to support it. If Hull Truck are going literary, Miss Bell, their most distinctive player, is going to get there first. The show is due at the Bush in November and the smaller space (though the Young Vic is hardly the Palladium) may suit it better. If the script of Bridget's House were written down, it would undoubtedly make a better read than that of The Canning Town Cowboy (Half Moon). This has an author, Shane Connaughton, and he brings off a few bright gags, but the play really consists of a single, rather arbitrary, conceit extended over a stretch of conventional community-theatre material. A ball of string is being unwound and it might be cut off at virtually any point. The hero is an East Ender who wants to be, and dresses like, a Wild Westerner; his non-conformity is the vehicle for some mild satire on bank clerks, policemen and such that might just as well exist without him. The acting is brash and genial, though it totters whenever the performers try to get a grip on surfaces too thin to allow them a foothold. Jill Richards, urgent and disdainful as the hero's girl, stands firmer than anyone else, though John Joyce, in various guises, grapples well.

  

The Only Way Out (Theatre Upstairs) is by George Thatcher, serving a life-sentence on a murder charge, having originally been condemned to death. It deals with a man in the early stages of the same situation: in the condemned cell, awaiting his appeal, protesting that he was framed, prophesying that the law, though it will spare his life, will be far too careful of its own ever to declare him innocent. Some of the action - notably the defiance of a bullying screw - comes over as wish-fulfilment, but most of it, in a well-controlled production by David Halliwell, is starkly convincing.

The inevitable bond between the prisoner and his unvarying attendants is traced without sentimentality or overt bitterness. Only his outline of his defence rings false: not the matter, but the manner. This may be how Mr Thatcher thinks now, but not how he, or anyone, would have spoken then; the pat phrases sink the actor, Brian Croucher, though earlier he is excellent, his accustomed casualness hardened into last-ditch defiance. I don't know if Mr Thatcher has another play in him, but it might be worth the while of a subsidised theatre to find out.

  

A few words of tribute to Side by Side by Sondheim (now at Wyndham's; I was away when it first opened at the Mermaid). Stephen Sondheim's best songs are built on fine gradations of tone and meaning, and the singers here are often more scrupulously aware of them than were the original interpreters. The duets - David Kernan and Millicent Martin in You Must Meet My Wife from A Little Night Music, or Mr Kernan and Julia McKenzie in Barcelona, the marvellous song of sleepy seduction from Company - become, as they should be, musicalised conversations. The emphasis is maybe too exclusively on sour urban wit (there are occasional cheerful songs in the Sondheim oeuvre), but Miss McKenzie, sad and hopeful, mines deep into Broadway Baby, the song of an unemployed showgirl, so that it passes pastiche and says, more movingly and economically, everything that is in A Chorus Line.
1976-08-08-mr-harrison-takes-a-train:
Mr. Harrison takes a train

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

The day after seeing M Perrichon's Travels (Chichester) I snatched a copy of The Selective Ego and was rewarded by the discovery that James Agate had been presented with a copy of this very play when about to board a train for Southampton, en route for New York. He did not, apparently, say much in the way of thank you, being mindful of M. Perrichon's odious habit of making speeches on railway stations, something about which Mme Perrichon had to speak to him severely.

Fate having made me a present of this information, I thought it only fair to pass it on. Anyway, it raises two points of interest. One: the incident occurred in 1937 when Labiche's comedy, written in 1860, was apparently a quotable classic. It was not, however, given an English production until last Tuesday. Two: now that it has reached us, the railway station seems almost its main reason for existence.

The director, Patrick Garland, and his designer, Eileen Diss, have expended enormous effort on re-creating for us the Gare de Lyon, where M. Perrichon's travels begin. Upstage a facade is projected; downstage arches are erected; smoke voluminously billows at the moment of departure; and Bill Fraser, our theatre's prime representative of bilious uniformed officialdom, slowly and resentfully combines the roles of porter and ticket-salesman, thereby occasioning factotum jokes which Labiche never invented but should have.

Mr Fraser's presence, together with that of a brass band to play us in (was the Gare de Lyon really such a fun-palace?), recalls the National Theatre's version of that other picaresque comedy The Captain of Kopenick. Mr Garland's production suffers in the comparison, since the play belies its title; having made such a fuss over dispatching Perrichon from Paris it follows him to Switzerland (land of merry alpenhorns and gemutlich hoteliers) for one scene only, then gets him home and belatedly settles into situation farce.

There is a continuous plot-line, concerning the efforts of two fairly indistinguishable young men to win Perrichon's daughter, but it hardly matters. What does matter, and might unify the evening, is Perrichon himself, a successful coach-builder who, as one of his employees cantankerously remarks, can ride in his own coach, to such a pass has French society now come. Perrichon, in other words, is a type of the emergent bourgeois, and at Chichester he is played by Rex Harrison, an actor who represents the bourgeoisie after a comfortable century in the saddle.

When buying his ticket for Switzerland, Mr Harrison tells us that he has never travelled before; this is an obvious lie, and Labiche's text compels him to go on fibbing for most of the evening. Perrichon is continually beset by hazards that scare the life out of him, but that Mr Harrison could shrug his way through; as a result the actor goes through the evening looking thoroughly ill-at-ease, but not the right kind of ill-at-ease.

In other roles, Mr Harrison has presented an ironist's complacency; Perrichon's complacency, however, is that of the buffoon, leading him into the solemn verbosity that alerted Agate. If it is his vice, it is also his armour, and it is linked to a meanness that gives the play some distinction as satire. Misadventuring on the Matterhorn, he is rescued from a crevasse by one of his daughter's suitors; a moment later he himself performs a similar service for the other. He much prefers the man he saved to the man who saved him; in gratitude, as in all else, he would rather be a creditor than a debtor.

Maybe this joke could sustain a whole play, but since neither Mr Garland (whose invention runs dangerously low as the evening proceeds) nor Mr Harrison gives it an honest try it is impossible to say. Mr Harrison does have a very touching few moments at the end, when Perrichon is told the truth about himself. Clive Francis, who was good in The Circle a couple of weeks ago, and Andrew Sachs do spirited work as the rivals; and Tony Robinson, suggesting Bob Cratchit gone mouldy a few years after Scrooge's reclamation, is fine as the captious clerk.

  

Little birds are bathing
Crocodiles in cream
Like a happy dream.
Like, but not so lasting:
Crocodiles when fasting
Are not all they seem.

That squib of Lewis Carroll's gives a tone as well as a title to Crocodiles In Cream (Mermaid), a one-man show devised by David Horlock, who directs it, and Michael Rothwell, who performs it. Carroll's verse and his fiction are subtly joined to his life and letters (I mean his correspondence) to reveal a man for whom existence was a perpetual jol, every Snark a Boojum.

Insufficient allowance is made, perhaps, for the success of his comic mask; when Mr Rothwell goes into extracts from Alice or recites 'Hiawatha's Photographing' ('From his shoulder Hiawatha/Took the camera of rosewood/Made of sliding, folding rosewood'), he eliminates the breeziness and concentrates on the melancholy. This makes him, of course, a magnificent Mock Turtle, a source of truly beautiful soup; and he holds the stage impressively throughout, with scarcely a moment's boredom.

Carroll cuts a more interesting figure than does the Roman satirist Juvenal in another solo turn, Juvenalia, which has just ended a run at the Bush, but may return; since the actor concerned is named Callow, the possibilities for punning seem limitless. Simon C. delivers the material in the style of a nightclub comic; in one of the dingier boites on the Appian Way, the kind you might drop into for compensation after a gladiatorial show with a low mortality rate. His flashing teeth and glasses, and his transfixingly chatty manner, suggest a Ronnie Corbett grown physically upwards and outwards and dyspeptically in all directions.

He comes out of it very well, better than his author. Juvenal's invective at the state of things in Rome (flattery, nymphomania and atrocious cooking) is pungent all right and if you want to think it topical you may; but it is very generalised. I never believed in the people to whom the satires were addressed (I always used to have difficulty with this particular convention when faced with Latin poetry at school) and I detected no specific concern. Juvenal is always compared with Swift, but his narcissistic vituperation runs the icy passion of the Modest Proposal a very poor second.
1976-08-15-the-gull-flies-again:
The gull flies again

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

Touching down in London for the first time in at least a fortnight, The Seagull (Duke of York's) can still spring the occasional surprise. Some of these are due to Mark Woolgar's unusually forthright adaptation; it may not signify much in London in 1976, but this is the first time in my experience that the language of Chekhov's heroines has caught up with that of Eliza Doolittle. One might be hearing much of the play for the first time; a compliment which Chekhov generally attracts and for which his various translators must take great credit.

Mr Woolgar's production, which has been brought in from Derby Playhouse, is as brisk and emphatic as his adaptation, which at least makes it a refreshing contrast to the curiously flat version which Lindsay Anderson directed earlier this year for the Lyric Theatre Company. (Whatever, by the way, happened to the Lyric Theatre Company?) True, there is no Helen Mirren in St Martin's Lane and I thought at first that Georgina Hale's Nina, curly and girlish, was going to be awful; she rattled off Konstantin's play as if it were meaningless (Nina may well have been defeated by it; but surely she put up a fight; at this point she wants to please Konstantin and impress his mother.)

Later on, Miss Hale begins to display real insight: she harps nervously and obsessively on the words 'fame' and 'glamour,' clasps her hands in adoring imitation of her idol Arkadina, directly anticipates -- with her fevered complaint that her head is spinning -- the dementia of the last act. This is played with a haunting self-mockery, if without the bedrock determination that allowed Miss Mirren to make final sense of the play.

Asked in the first act to recite something from Konstantin's play, Nina refuses to oblige; her cry of 'it's so boring' amounts almost to a long-range death-warrant for its author. Gabrielle Lloyd's Masha, who made the request in a solitary bright-eyed moment, sinks back into her usual bleariness, pushed a little further towards her hopeless marriage with Medviedenko, whose long-suffering futility is here given unusually sharp definition by Dennis Denny.

Their relationship, which foreshadows and inverts (since here it is the man who is baby-besotted), the ghastly union of Andrei and Natasha in Three Sisters, emerges more strongly in each new production of The Seagull.

Coarsening through the play, Miss Lloyd still preserves the thread of her feeling for Konstantin; it is she who pricks up her ears at his off-stage piano-playing, and she who knows immediately that he has shot himself.

Completing the play's sardonic picture of youth is Richard O'Callaghan's Konstantin, the best I have seen. He whines, he snivels, he hardly grows up, but there is passion and perception in him, however ludicrous, and he freshens the speeches about finding new theatrical forms without disguising their naivete.

He is also locked into his relation with his mother; when he quotes Hamlet at her he does so with real venom, the venom of absolute dependence. This Oedipal Konstantin might have fitted well into Jonathan Miller's production a couple of years ago. (When Seagulls come, they come not single spies.)

The elders fare less well; Mr Woolgar's emphasis on the primary colours in Chekhov makes them seem garish. Denis Holmes's Shamrayev shamelessly shouts (Mr Holmes was a notable quietist with the RSC, so maybe he is compensating now) and though Sheila Ballantine's Arkadina is a ruthless and witty study of a desperately dominating woman (whose main defence against time is her wig), this may be a part which really needs a star. This is especially so when a star is actually to hand in another role. Alan Bates's Trigorin is not a selfish performance, but it hardly fits; he is acting more elaborately than anyone else (perhaps more subtly, but in this context it is difficult to tell), gesturing and stammering more. The character never quite appears.

  

T. Zee (Royal Court), credited to Richard O'Brien and Richard Hartley, is the successor to Mr O'Brien's Rocky Horror Show, but completely lacks its lightness of touch. It also marks a partial return, after the skill and delicacy of Peter Gill's Small Change, to the hallowed Court tradition of high-minded bungling.

The stage is so destructively cluttered that the actors have no room to do anything but sing undistinguished songs into their hand-mikes, which gets monotonous. Even when the music stops, the lyrics seem to continue, since the script is written in doggerel couplets; anyone sensitive to rhyme will find himself in pain.

Mr O'Brien has written an awful part for himself as a knock-kneed anthropologist exploring the ruins of Los Angeles, and a better one for his lady companion, Belinda Sinclair, who can and does sing. Warren Clarke as Tarzan, into whose company they fall, also has an unexpectedly winning country-and-western way; most of what goodwill is going in Nicholas Wright's production accrues to him. The action takes place on a sort of giant pin-table in a libidinous inferno, peopled by the debris of Hollywood. But this time Mr O'Brien has forgotten satire and settled for celebratory camp. Nothing happens, fortissimo.

  

Four To One (Young Vic) is a first play by the excellent National Theatre actor Gawn Grainger which his colleagues seem to enjoy playing.
