Putting Daddy in the dock

by Robert Cushman

THE leading character of Denis Cannan's Dear Daddy (Ambassadors) is not always affectionately addressed as the title might suggest. Three of the cast are his children and they seem uneasy about what to call him. They seem uneasy about him altogether, and he knows it. His impulse is to blame it on them, or on youth generally. 'It's a sad generation that doesn't know what to call its parents' is his phrase for it.

He has a phrase for everything. His name is Bernard, and he is very verbal. In one of his aspects he bears out Howard Brenton's claim that the West End is the theatre of envy. I was certainly jealous of Bernard's collection of books; the towering shelves were enough to get me going. They dominate a set which bears witness to good things having come Bernard's way in the past.

Recently, though, they have stopped coming; and envy drops dead at the foot of the library steps. His brood, now in their twenties, have come to sign over to him money that was being kept in trust for them. Filial duty done, they spend the rest of the play remembering, in a long crescendo of bitterness, the details of life with father. Mother drops in to help them; she is Bernard's first wife, who was drying out at a nearby health-farm and just happened to be passing. (Mr Cannan is a bit cavalier about mustering his forces; the action presupposes an ever-open front door.)

All together they accuse him of surpassing, patronising selfishness; of subduing their personalities to his own, of always being ready to crush them with a quotation, of taking from them and never giving. Ex-wife claims that he laughed her out of her own career in children's publishing; present wife, who at first seems wholesomely inclined to avoid the battle, confirms that he has done the same to her talent for making clothes: 'It's known as "My sewing!"' As for the children, Charles, the youngest, a trainee teacher, is comparatively gentle but owes his survival to a girl-friend who is, by the family's standards, hopelessly unsophisticated; nothing exposes them more than their efforts to be friendly to her and Charles himself is shaping up to be as exploitative as his father. Brother Billy is a nondescript drop-out, Daddy's favourite butt; sister Gillian, who attracts and dispenses more venom than anyone else on stage, is an espouser of causes, and a ferocious victim, sexual and social, making more money as a typist than she ever could with her degree. (It could be the theme-song of a generation: women who are making it without men: divorcees, widows, unmarried mothers, etc.)

  

There is a poignant wedding of theatre to title: An' Me Wi' A Bad Leg Tae at the Theatre Upstairs. A Puerto Rican girl in A Chorus Line refused to change her name 'because I figured ethnic was in.' In response to Billy Connolly's first play, she figured wrong.

Mr Connolly is among the nakedest emperors to ride into London for some time. A soldier bound for Germany returns to the family hearth in Glasgow, and sets off some sub-O'Casey rowing, philosophising, boozing and raging, leading a clansman to a dead end, punctuated by spotlit monologues as a guarantee of seriousness. There is a rich and subtle portrait of a drunk by Bill Paterson, whose complexion sets you thinking of rubies or beetroot, and some good old jokes: 'I fought with Monty.' 'You could never get on with anyone.' There is even the one in which X says that he didn't come here to be insulted and Y replies as Y has immemorially replied. The innocent delight of most of the Press seems the innocentest thing on view.

  

Frank Dunlop's production of Antony and Cleopatra (Young Vic) is vigorous and fast. Delphine Seyrig's Cleopatra is vigorous and intelligent. Michael Graham Cox's Antony is vigorous. You will gather that all this, though welcome, is insufficient. Except in one scene, the soldiers' litany as Hercules, fares so well, the play is denied its wonder, hence its grandeur, hence its breadth, hence finally its point.

  

That a comedian as gifted as Ron Moody should have failed, for 15 years, to find himself a viable vehicle suggests a certain self-destructiveness. On the evidence of The Showman (Theatre Royal, Stratford) his fault may be excessive diffidence. In this musical of The Bells Mr Moody plays not the tormented villain Mathias, but the purely ancillary role of the hypnotist; his elaborate routines confuse the issue but cannot, unfortunately, stop the show. The score confirms that musical merit has nothing to do with memorability; though I fled at the interval two tunes pursued me pitilessly. Perhaps I should have stayed, but as Mr Moody said after a particularly strenuous exhibition of goodwill, Qu'est-ce que vous voulez, blood?
1976-10-31-national-disappointment:
National disappointment

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Goldoni at the Olivier Theatre.

THE Venetian Carlo Goldoni, Italy's most celebrated comic playwright, is high on the list of neglected writers whom critics like myself are constantly nagging the National Theatre to resurrect. This week, at the Olivier, they obliged us, in theory at least; in practice they annoyed us considerably. Il Campiello ('The Public Square') is as faint an evening's entertainment as this company can ever have offered.

Goldoni's career began in the mid-eighteenth century when Italian theatre was dominated by the stereotypes of the commedia dell'arte; his first success came in persuading its performers to act his texts instead of their own improvisations. Later he broke further out by discarding stock characters and plots and writing about his own society. Even by our own standards Il Campiello is unconventional, jettisoning narrative and character in favour of community and locale.

Dramatic interest is equally split among nine people who live on three sides of the square. (Who or what lies behind the fourth wall we never discover.) Three old widows and four youngsters play games, quarrel, rampage, enjoy themselves; at the end one boy and girl are married and another couple betrothed. A more sedate young lady and her bearish guardian make up the number; she considers herself a few notches above her neighbours, and he cannot stand any of them. He comes from Naples, and this seems to involve a class as well as a territorial difference, reinforced by the arrival of a Neapolitan count who seems remarkably well pleased by just about everyone.

Bill Bryden's production attempts a miniature re-enactment of Goldoni's own progress. There are puppet-shows in the foyer and a carnival procession through the stalls as the lights go down, corresponding to the commedia inheritance that Goldoni never thoroughly abandoned. Then flats are erected round the stage, representing the houses in the square and the play, more or less realistic, begins. The trouble is that both styles seem half-hearted; the cavorting in the audience is more noisy than vital, and there is more volume than energy about the main action as well. Everything is insubstantial; Hayden Griffin's set is probably true enough to the scenic modesty of the original staging, but we need more; we need to be given a solid awareness of a setting now so far removed from us, particularly if the setting is essentially the play.

Goldoni wrote more than 200 pieces, so it can hardly have mattered to his original audience if one of them was sketchy; it would be sustained by their experience of the others and--when he was in his realistic vein--by the life going on around. Of the two Goldoni plays that have taken some root in English, The Servant of Two Masters offers vaudeville pyrotechnics, and Mirandolina a captivating heroine. But in Il Campiello atmosphere is everything and this production muffs it.

The kisses and scuffles are routine; it is difficult to keep track of which daughter is jealous of whose son. The actors do little more than say the lines; the translation, which runs to such smart ripostes as 'the same to you with knobs on,' may sell the original text short, but not, I suspect, by much. Peggy Mount, flourishing a broom like a pantomime dame, puts in some ripe bitching with Beryl Reid, but it leads nowhere. Jeananne Crowley, fresh and baby-faced, adds to the excellent impression she has made in several small roles at the National. Patti Love, by contrast, always looks best in other companies; as the bride here she gives a clenched, raucous performance, leaping up and down to express proletarian joie-de-vivre.

She is unlucky in being burdened with what this production assumes to be the message of the play, defiantly asserting her celebratory rights against the noise abatement man from Naples, the square's square. The Neapolitans speak standard English, the Venetians mostly Scots; some are Irish and Miss Mount of course Cockney, so the pattern never quite establishes itself. It does enable Morag Hood to give a moderately delightful account of a young lady from primmest Edinburgh; though as the Count--the outsider and so the role that might focus the play--Michael Gough restricts himself to bland neutrality. The text at least hints that he might be an arrant fool or a fortune-hunter; but Goldoni is too carelessly sunny to pursue these possibilities and Mr Gough declines to take the initiative. That indeed is the note of the evening. Acoustically too it is unsettling, for ever perched on the edge of inaudibility.

  

An earlier National production, Peter Shaffer's Equus, seems set fair for infinity at the Albery: a cunning mixture of suspense, psychology and religion which is limited without being meretricious. Michael Jayston now plays the psychiatrist; conscientious and good-natured, he falls short of Alec McCowen's tortured pedantry and Colin Blakely's wild frustration, but far surpasses Richard Burton, who on Broadway offered boredom topped off with rhetoric. After so much exposure I was surprised to find the play still holding me; surprised, too, to find John Dexter's production now less remarkable for spectacle than for human detail.

Jane Wenham and Glyn Owen have discovered much in the bewildered parents though their social context is still baffling; why has their son never had any friends? David Dixon's performance, though the most accomplished I have seen, is too knowing to stifle doubts. The play shares the weakness of Howard Brenton's Weapons of Happiness: its elements (more particularly its characters) have not been welded together, craftily though they have been assembled. (Metaphors are dropped like clues in a thriller.) All the same, Mr Shaffer deserves defending on one point at least; he does not claim that the blinding of horses is a necessary part of Alan's vaunted 'worship' (it is a disastrous mutation that would not be repeated), nor does he suggest that what the boy needs is a nice lay. But Alan's equine passion is finally too specialised to be meaningful; the symbol rides off with the play.

  

A style of humour flowered at the beginning of the sixties, in the plays of Harold Pinter and the revue-sketches of Peter Cook: deadpan, London-accented, bleakly absurd and largely dependent on the blockish enunciation of unglamorous place-names. It has nourished the theatrical fringe for years: Henry Woolf, one of its best exponents as an actor, puts it to good use as a playwright in Underarm Bowling (New End).

Among his cast Robert Walker handles it particularly well, especially when deploring the ascendancy of his violent impulses over the pacific ideals that have led him to a Buddhist monastery. It is monastic politics with which the play is more seriously, but less happily, concerned; though Mr Woolf's wit is still sharp enough to evoke a rich American devotee, crazily game for anything and a terror when she finally knows she has been had, played to the life by Ellen Sheean.

  

Hull Truck is at the Bush this week with Bridget's House, which was intermittently good at the Young Vic and should be better now.

Caribbean cocktail

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

On a beach in Trinidad, Creator, a master calypsonian, and his apprentice, Bird, are trying to complete a song for the annual calypso competition. Creator is a three-time winner in this contest but his victories were years ago. That he is on the beach now is no accident. Every time a tourist passes (somewhere in the front stalls presumably) the two men leap to their feet and begin 'working for the Yankee dollar.'

That line is the refrain of the calypso that gives its name to Mustapha Matura's play: Rum An Coca-Cola (Royal Court). It forms half of their busking repertoire. The other half is 'Mary Anne' which Creator describes with justified scorn as the only calypso most tourists have ever heard of. For tourist, in Creator's vocabulary, read always mug; he hates them, he hates himself for his dependence on them, and his two standard songs, both obliquely concerned with prostitution, encapsulate the play.

For his current number Creator is trying out some broader double-entendres; it concerns a maid who finds her mistress in bed with the Minister of Works and Communications: 'the works were working and the communications were communicating.' Before they get that far, however, Bird and more particularly Creator go through agonies getting their first couplet right. They run through various adverbial possibilities for Ruby's execution of the housework: 'nicely,' 'tidily,' 'like a lady'; none of them sound to me like good rhymes for Ruby but then calypso is not my style.

In a few minutes, though, Mr Matura had me fascinated; this is the only play I have seen which successfully dramatises the writing process. 'You don't think "decide" is too big a word?' Bird asks at one point, and Creator replies authoritatively that it's a good word; 'decided' would be too big.

The minutiae of other people's lives are not always as fascinating as the Court would have us believe, but song-writers I could watch for hours. Mr Matura complements this scene with another in which we find the couple performing at a night-club. Creator sings a song by a successful rival and realises that it is beyond anything he could write. His relationship with Bird, always uneasy, deteriorates; Bird belongs to the younger generation who have either destroyed Creator's art or are indifferent to it, and he also lacks Creator's freebooting attitude towards vacationers -- more particularly towards women vacationers. He can take his position as a stud (a black musician, how can he lose?) both more seriously and more easily than Creator would wish him to. He takes up with a girl whom Creator eventually robs and murders.

This part of the play has met with cries of disbelief, but I see no reason to echo them. The character of Creator is of a piece, especially as played by Norman Beaton: spectrally smart, charming, cracked, and desperate. 'I'm gonna go on singing calypso' he cries with his arms outstretched; when he draws them in again, the glorious gesture contracts into a defeated shrug. Jocelyn Herbert's set makes beauty out of a couple of inclined planes; the director is Donald Howarth, himself a dramatist of proven wit, feeling and invention, the qualities that continue to distinguish Mr Matura's writing.

  

Susan Miller's Flux is the latest in a season of American plays at Square One. It concerns a college instructor trying to teach her class through love. If that sounds sticky I can only refer you to the saltiness of much of the writing, the literalness of the heroine's methods (she writes love-notes on her pupils' compositions when she approves them, and goes to bed with the beefiest 19-year-old, which certainly puts her a few jumps ahead of Jean Brodie) and her final realisation that passion, particularly across generations, is forever out of step.

Back home, waiting with increasing impatience, is a lesbian lover whom Jane Hallaren places in the great American tradition of joking bitterness. Robyn Goodman's heroine wavers more in detail, but has the right indomitable outline. Miss Miller takes technical risks whose success is difficult to judge in Annabel Leventon's hole-and-corner production; it is frequently difficult to tell what is going on. The straightforward bitching or teaching sessions work best; choric interludes and dream sequences worst. There is more snap in the dialogue than in its delivery.

  

For the second time in two weeks Goldoni goes down. The Artful Widow (Greenwich) is a slight improvement on the National's Il Campiello, mainly by virtue of one scene in which John Kane's Arlecchino furnishes instant interpretations of two misdelivered letters; here at last is the comic set-piece for which both evenings have been straining. Mr Kane's verve is helpful throughout; Greenwich indeed has a good cast or, not quite the same thing, a cast of good actors. Ursula Mohan's French maid is difficult to resist (though I tried) and Diane Cilento and Frank Barrie, in face of a determinedly uproarious production, are a cool pair of lovers whom one is glad to see finally united; believable Italians in everything except their gratuitous accents.

Venice, updated to what seems to be the 1920s, is full of funny voices; Miss Cilento's other suitors are a Frenchman, an Englishman and (substituted for Goldoni's Spaniard) an American, and the evening is a parade of tired nationalist jokes, applied without any apparent forethought; the American, for example, going a-wooing disguised inexplicably as Groucho Marx, gets a laugh for his make-up and nothing thereafter. It all makes nonsense of the play; if Miss Cilento's foreign lovers are obvious buffoons, she deserves no credit for seeing through them. The production, unconcerned with such things, relegates Goldoni to the gag-writer's position from which he spent his career escaping; judged on a purely statistical basis, it hits far less often than it misses.
1976-11-12-claudius-the-good:
Claudius the good

IN CHOOSING the Emperor Claudius as the protagonist of a pair of historical novels Robert Graves did something brilliantly perverse. The Roman historians have left little evidence of anything particularly interesting about Claudius. The chronicles make him out the least colourful of the Caesars; considering how lurid the others were this may be to Claudius's credit. It takes a novelist as clever as Graves to see the usefulness of a historical nonentity like Claudius--a blank sheet of paper on which the writer can scrawl whatever he likes. Graves's inscriptions have proved ineffaceable.

Doing Roman history at school I found myself glaring at the textbooks with exasperation, even resentment. How could they have got everything so wrong? If only they'd read I, Claudius they would have known what the people and events were really like. They would have realised that Claudius was no weakling but a canny and compassionate man, biding his time and trying to stay alive. And why should the professors worry about Claudius's contemporaries? It's all there in his memoirs, so meticulously ghosted by Graves.

The historical Claudius may have seemed recalcitrant material for a novel, but just try turning the fictional Claudius into drama. The film never got made. A West End theatre version raced aimlessly and incomprehensibly through random bits of the action. The television treatment takes its time and is enjoyable but it has not avoided the obvious stumbling-blocks. I doubt whether anyone--including the creators themselves--ever expected it to.

When they get to the second book, Claudius the God, the situation may be different, for that will show us Claudius as emperor, an actor as well as an observer. But as I write we are still on I, Claudius and there is no way--at least none has been found--of preventing that title from seeming a misnomer. For the action seems to concern everyone except Claudius himself. He claims the titular position not through his deeds but through his words, uttered many years after the events of which they speak.

This reminiscing Claudius is the only real character in the book; the others, including the narrator's younger self, are sketches. Their lives are narrated with earnest irony--and it is the irony far more than the lives (or, even, the deaths) that registers.

Television has settled for introducing each episode with a glimpse of old Claudius at work on his history (or at least wondering where he left the manuscript) and then more or less abandoning him--Claudius Interruptus. The bulk of the story is left to stand, not as a record of his impressions, but as history and drama in its own right. And here enormous difficulties arise, for Graves's novel provides, by design, a partial view of history and is almost indifferent to drama; though it is certainly full of events--battles, murders, conspiracies and sexual adventures ranging from simple adulteries to complex orgies--that could be described as dramatic.

Keeping the book's irreverence and informality

A reviewer on Radio 4's Kaleidoscope declared that Jack Pulman, the adaptor, could hardly have used Graves's dialogue since actors would have found it unspeakable. He proceeded to quote a line or two that should have given no ordinarily competent actor any trouble at all. The real problem with the novel's dialogue, from a dramatist's point of view, is merely that there is so little of it. The first half of the book contains only one conversation of any length: a philosophical discussion on the duties of the historian. When the characters are doing things--important things, even lurid things--they keep their mouths shut.

Mr Pulman has accordingly had to invent a great deal; sometimes--as in the episode of Piso's trial for the murder of Germanicus--extracting 50 minutes of screen time from two or three pages of narrative. In his invention he has obviously kept in mind the book's reputation for irreverence and informality, but his back-slapping joviality is an equivalent for the dry-biscuit wit of the novel. The actors have been faced with much the same problem; in reading we can accept Augustus described simply as "an overgrown boy". But, when Brian Blessed comes before us with the same interpretation, and we are asked actually to look, listen and accept him as the first Roman Emperor, the whole thing becomes a charade.

Siân Phillips as Livia: an artist in murder

That said, I found the Blessed Augustus endearing and at the approach of death (after which he became the Divine Augustus) honestly touching, like a puzzled teddy-bear. The performer who has done most to make the character her own (and it seems to me the actress's achievement rather than the adaptor's) is Siân Phillips as the imperial multiple murderess Livia. She is a creamier, wittier fiend than the book suggests, an artist in murder rather than a conscientious craftswoman; but Miss Phillips's handling of Mr Pulman's fairly shameless gags (one borrowed, presumably by augury, from Mae West) and her taunting of Derek Jacobi's stammering Clau-Clau-Claudius, made one disinclined to quibble. Jacobi has so far turned in two winning impersonations of the young and the old Claudius; it will be interesting to see them meet in the middle. And I liked the playing of the young Caligula as a malevolent Christopher Robin. But all Claudius's relations are becoming difficult to distinguish before they are assassinated. I wonder how those who haven't read the book are faring with the complexities of the family relationships.

Herbert Wise's direction has been excellent. The absence of film is a positive virtue. Its presence would suggest authenticity--and that would never do. The serial is fun but, unlike the books, it will never replace history.

Robert Cushman is drama critic of the Observer.
1976-11-14-garnett-in-his-glory:
Garnett in his glory

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

In The Thoughts of Chairman Alf (Criterion) Warren Mitchell as Alf Garnett comes in glory before, and very nearly among us. Though he stays up on the stage Mr Mitchell straddles, besieges and buttonholes his audience. He talks, sings, squeals and bellows directly to us, and most effectively; he was squandered on those other people, that family, on television, involving him in situations and even occasionally plots: a right waste of time.

Every so often Mr Mitchell, whose audience control is 95 per cent consummate, sings music-hall songs which--on the lips of a real character from a recognisable life--sound for once as good as has been claimed for them. They are, in truth, a bit genial and observant for near-sighted Alf, but only a quibbler will quibble. In Johnny Speight's script--a two-and-a-half-hour monologue--there are inevitable sags, but at its best it is extraordinarily resonant; it made me want to hear Mr Mitchell as one of the great Shakespearean or Shavian demagogues.

It even has a shape; after Alf has thoroughly aired his prejudices (alternately massaging and outraging ours) he compares his life unfavourably with that of an animal (and yearns to be a royal corgi or Princess Anne's horse) and finally subsides into silent despair, bald head quivering, piggy eyes sunk, moustache and glasses mute reproaches to an unheeding society. In so fully exhibiting and understanding a man whose views they detest, Messrs Mitchell and Speight have healed the bruised carcase of political theatre.

  

This was still aching from wounds inflicted three days earlier by A Seventh Man (Hampstead) adapted by Adrian Mitchell from John Berger's book on migrant workers. Confronted with characters (West German industrial doctors for example) of whom he disapproves, Mr Mitchell makes no attempt at understanding but he cannot bring himself to be honestly external either; so he throws in bits of discreditably "revealing" dialogue. The people he likes hardly do better: the script flounders between individual and group portraiture, and though the play declares that peasants should not be sentimentalised it seems unsure what else to do with them. The affecting moments are soberly factual; but most of the time the Foco Novo company provide sloppy dramatics. I was not convinced that any of the actors had ever met a migrant worker or that they had worked out any compensatory style. There are the obligatory songs; Mr Mitchell's lyrics carry the occasional charge defused by the uniformly dreary music. Some groups (7.84, Hull Truck) make effective use of music, others (Joint Stock) virtuously do without. Both ways are preferable.

  

Forty years ago Rodgers and Hart wrote a really meaningful song about a lady on a trapeze. In the main refrain she told us, in an appropriate metre, how she swung high and low, initially subject to falls but progressing to a state of perfect security. Extrapolating a general principle from her particular experience, she enjoined us to "stick to your trick and your trick will be art," adding that "artists are hard-working men." The subject of the song was Practice, long recognised as the only route to Carnegie Hall; its title was Over and Over Again.

There is no trapezienne among the characters of The Force of Habit (Lyttelton) but there is a tightrope-walker, sharing the arena with a clown, a lion-tamer, a juggler, and a ringmaster. They are not artists, they are artistes, and that extra undroppable "e" causes them great anguish. They are trying to better themselves, to double as musicians and play Schubert's Trout Quintet, and on the day they bring it off won't the paying customers get a surprise. That day, though, seems distant; they have yet to get through a rehearsal, let alone a rendition. Playing Schubert Over And Over Again is for them not Practice (noble) but merely Repetition (dull). The force of habit wearies even as it compels and the playwright, Thomas Bernhard (of Austria), pushes the point ruthlessly home.

He has constructed his play on the pattern of that very quintet, filling it with reiterated phrases. Today, like every day, will be the day that the circus left town; each player tells us, on many occasions, what he will do "in Augsburg tomorrow." This reiteration, most resourcefully engineered, is neither particularly haunting nor unduly significant, but it makes a bright running gag. At least it could. This being a National Theatre production we might expect acting to compare with a really sparkling professional recital of the Trout Quintet itself; here we get the equivalent of the show the circus five might put on if their great day ever arrived. Which is carrying Pirandellianism a bit far.

Philip Locke, a brilliant supporting actor, is monotonously querulous in the dominant role of the ringmaster, a musical man with a wooden leg and with a load of other grievances. Gawn Grainger, a character actor deprived of a character, settles for sneering camp. Warren Clarke works up a good head of drunken resentment and Oliver Cotton has a pleasant motley grin, but Brenda Blethyn, scornfully and almost silently pert, was the only one I credited.

Stripped of its surface entertainment value (you would never guess from Elijah Moshinsky's ponderous direction that the text is rhythmically composed) the play is forced to rely on its philosophical merits, which are small. In a key passage (a trade term for the bit reprinted in the programme) the ringmaster declares himself fed up with playing Schubert but condemned to go on trying; life, it is hinted, is one long process of failing to get through the Trout Quintet, a proposition that may be refuted by a visit to almost any reputable concert-hall. The participants don't seem to like their circus lives much either, but this theme is largely neglected in favour of the musical one and finally contributes little more than shades of Anthony Newley.

  

Simon Gray's Dog Days (an Oxford Playhouse production now on tour) was written before his Otherwise Engaged, and if it is not a trial run for that play the arm of coincidence must have stretched to extravagant lengths. Both plays concern publishers with teacher-wives, tired of their apparent indifference, and teacher-brothers, sucking up to their headmasters. The later version, in which the hero's icy smartness denoted bastardy all through, is preferable to this one in which it merely disguises pre- and extra-marital impotence. Not that this is a false conclusion; merely an uninteresting one.

The wit of the two plays is similar; which is to say that it consists of smug put-downs which I found very funny. Charles Kay dispenses them with address, though I was not convinced he had the right address. He may be one of those sharp mellifluous actors adrift outside the classics. Everyone else in Gordon McDougall's production (and especially Gayle Hunnicutt) looks not adrift but marooned.
1976-11-21-moli-re-caught-in-a-trap:
Molière caught in a trap

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

The Théâtre National Populaire from Lyons is visiting the currently unpopular National Theatre on the South Bank (ground floor, Lyttelton proscenium department). It began with Tartuffe, unexpectedly demonstrating that the French have the same worries over Molière as we do.

Once we used to ignore him, or treat him as rough rep. farce, freely adapted by Miles Malleson. The advent of acceptable translations in rhyming verse stepped up the number of productions (I have seen more productions of Tartuffe than of any play not by Shakespeare) and tore their style. Making sense of couplets, and making it quickly and gracefully, can easily become an end in itself.

It insulates the characters from recognisable psychological pressures; if you analyse the action of the play, you may see that in Tartuffe spirit and flesh are at war, that religion is being employed as a cloak for cruelty, that the duped Orgon under the spell of the sham-Puritan Tartuffe is unloosing all his worst passions on his own family, and that he passes from this moral danger into extreme physical peril; he is suspected of treason and may lose his life.

You may even see this when watching the play; it is very clear-cut. But it is, by virtue of that, very difficult to feel: no disfiguring emotion ever spills out. Complexities may be suggested, but they are not explored. Molière, too, peopled his plays with stock figures and put them through stock actions; this combination of style and substance is apt to leave you, at the end of a short evening, wondering "Is that all?" Something so fast, so basic, so simple--above all so soon over--is not what we expect of a masterpiece. We equate significance with the space between words, and in most Molière productions, English or French, there isn't any.

In Roger Planchon's production, however, there is almost an infinity of it; the running-time is three and a half hours, riddled with pauses. There is space in a more literal sense as well; Hubert Monloup's setting is immense. It is, to begin with, one of the highest I have ever seen; it stretches in fact to heaven, surmounted as it is by the life-size image of a suffering Christ. There is much scaffolding, suggesting that Orgon's family have either the builders or the bailiffs in. On the whole, they seem to be doing all right, living in a palace rather than a mere bourgeois mansion; and when Orgon himself appears, he looks like the Sun-King.

Each of the play's five acts is accorded a different background, each ready behind its predecessor, so that the play becomes a steady progress towards the back of the stage. Everything that involves a door or window is masterly, and André Diot's lighting is superlative. The production is a magnificent feat of stage engineering; its size, its length, its iconography, its music, the thunderclap with which it opens, are the trappings of a great theatrical experience. But it is the play itself that is trapped. It suggests the aesthetic which can sometimes be found--though on a necessarily smaller financial scale--in the work of the RSC, or indeed of the Glasgow Citizens': you testify to the stature of a play, and of your own thoughts about it, by encasing it.

But inside the case the same old text is unfolding, with much of its spirit denied. True, it is given great weight, and some of the family relations have great tension (quite possibly strengthened for us by the language-barrier; we expect a certain amount of boredom and the grandiose silences are more acceptable than they would be from a home team).

Planchon has been a great Brechtian, and he retains enough of his inheritance to give his actors household tasks; these always seem to me more immediately helpful to the actors than to the play, and they certainly add to the authority of Arlette Gilbert as the bossy maid. She even gets a few laughs. But consider: there is a passage at the end of the play in which Orgon's mother refuses to believe evil of Tartuffe. However graphic his descriptions of the man's attempts to seduce his wife, the old lady tells him he should have waited for further proofs. If that is not gag-writing I don't know what it is; and in this production I don't know what it is, except perhaps a testimony that those concerned are far too serious (again Stratford comes to mind) to bother with laughter. But Molière made serious jokes; anyone can preach serious sermons.

Planchon, like Jouvet, Barrault and Vilar before him, is his own leading man. France, whatever they may tell you, is the true home of the actor-manager, often to the detriment of the production. Though he goes through impressive motions (including, as far as I could see, the gnawing of a chair), he has not much presence.

The final entry of the king's officer becomes almost an invasion; soldiers fill the stage, the floor opens up, and the family find themselves in instant dungeons. The tables turned, Orgon practically assaults Tartuffe; and his brother-in-law's admonition not to waste words on the villain hardly meets the case. Louis XIV's intervention is deprived of its suspended wit, and made brutally corrupt. This, like most stage violence, is a cliché, an attempt to thrust significance upon a play by main force. Planchon keeps returning to Tartuffe, but he may now have loved it to death; as a compromise solution I would take John Dexter's Misanthrope in English, which showed that sparkling waters, too, can run deep.

  

A milder clap of thunder begins Arnold Ridley's The Ghost Train (Old Vic) and mild is the word throughout. This twenties thriller is pitilessly, not to say cravenly, guyed. Line after line is tossed to the audience, who are dared not to laugh; the first-nighters duly dissolved but less interested parties may not be so easily pleased. Boy and girl perch on a table as if about to render a duet from Very Good Eddie; the costumes are displayed; the thrills disappear. James Villiers slips commandingly into style, though I fear that prolonged immersion in it may damage his health; but it all seems pretty pointless.

  

So does Mr Laurel and Mr Hardy (Mayfair), which suggests, undramatically, that there was no tension between the team's on-screen and off-screen personalities: they merely played themselves throughout. John Shedden and Ian Ireland are thus compelled to do what others have done peerlessly before them, though Mr Shedden in particular comes wondrously near to Stan's agility and to his down-at-chin air of perky self-deprecation.

Tom McGrath's dialogue is Hollywood bio-pic, though derived less from the gossip columns than the cineaste's paperbacks; Stan discourses, with impersonal judiciousness, on the harm done to their style when the studio took them out of two-reelers and into features. But when they escape from words at the end they blossom; their final dance is one of the most enchanting things in town.
1976-11-26-looking-back-at-look-back-in-:
Play of the Month--Look Back in Anger, Sunday 8.45 BBC1

Twenty years ago, Look Back in Anger was first performed in London. It was only the third play ever produced by the English Stage Company at the Royal Court Theatre, and its author was an unknown playwright called John Osborne. But it became a pivotal point in British theatre. This week's special television production stars James Hazeldine as Jimmy Porter, Ciaran Madden as Alison and Neil Daglish as Cliff. Here Robert Cushman discusses the play's impact on contemporary British theatre and pictures take us from the first to the latest production.

Looking back at Look Back in Anger

IT IS a commonplace that the first night of John Osborne's Look Back in Anger 20 years ago at the Royal Court Theatre in London was a landmark. The stretch of theatrical history it opened up is the one in which we are still living.

It was the third production of the English Stage Company, a group set up at the Court with the intention of 'doing new plays': filling a hole that, nearly everyone was agreed, gaped wide. The question of what kind of new plays they should be was not much canvassed. The initial approaches made by the director, George Devine, were to novelists such as Angus Wilson and Nigel Dennis, who might be expected to come up with plays which--though certainly out of line with West End fashion--would be delicate, oblique, satiric in their approach; they would get reviews in which the adjective 'civilised' would feature rather strongly. This at least was true of Wilson's play The Mulberry Bush with which the new company went into business. It had already been done at the Bristol Old Vic, a 'civilised' theatre of the first order. So had the second Court offering, Arthur Miller's The Crucible. Miller, like Wilson, was a name, if not a commercial name.

But nobody had ever heard of John Osborne before 8 May 1956; the day on which the English Stage Company (not a name which ever caught on--from here on I'll call it the Court) staged Look Back in Anger as its third production. From that date, the Court was the theatre for New Dramatists, and the British theatre took its tone from the Court.

New dramatists were, and have remained, what it is all about; and critics gnash their teeth and point their fingers whenever some extravagantly long period of time--a fortnight, say--passes without one appearing. This has, one must admit, been hard on the old dramatists; I mean those still alive and producing. (Death pays all debts.) And of course even a new dramatist grows old, and may find himself unwelcome in his own parish. The Court has been faced with a tricky problem as the years have passed. Should it remain faithful to the authors it has nurtured, or should it cast them out?

For close on 15 years it took the first course; now it seems to have decided on the second. Of Osborne's last three London premières, two have been at Greenwich and one at the National Theatre. The dramatists who, within a couple of years of his debut, had most auspiciously followed him into Sloane Square--Arnold Wesker, John Arden--have likewise been absent. I have even heard it maintained that Edward Bond, whose debut came a full decade after Osborne's, has no right to a place at the Court. That opinion was advanced by one of Bond's greatest admirers, who still felt that the Court should be ashamed of itself harbouring someone so ancient. I honestly don't know why; the place has no particular obligation to youth. There's nothing about youth in its charter. I'm not even sure it has a charter.

Even so, ever since those brave days of '56, it has behaved as though it had: for better and for worse. Critics who objected when the worse predominated were apt to be met with aggrieved incredulity: 'Don't they know that we started a revolution? We've always been terribly brave, it says so in the books.' And, as far as those early days are concerned, the books are right. I doubt if the Court knew when they began rehearsing Look Back the extent to which, in our minds if not always on our stages, things were not to be the same again. I doubt if Osborne himself knew when he started writing.

He has since referred to the play as 'formal and old-fashioned'. But this was its greatest strength; there is nothing about its form which could puzzle its audiences or distract them from its content. It is a three-act naturalistic play which--unlike most examples then successful in London--took the form literally; it was written out of its author's experience, which had not been glamorous. In the West End, a shabby-genteel hotel (as in N. C. Hunter's Waters of the Moon or Terence Rattigan's Separate Tables) was about the limit of imaginable squalor. A serious work usually had a comparably serious setting; Wilson's The Mulberry Bush was set in a university, as was the novel most immediately associated with John Osborne's play, Kingsley Amis's Lucky Jim. Osborne's hero Jimmy Porter has a university background, but we owe this information to his wife; he never mentions it. He never harks back to it, and he never complains about his present poverty--though he complains about a lot of other things.

Kenneth Tynan, the play's most vociferous champion among the critics, says now that for the audiences this was the most disquieting thing about it. An aspiring proletarian hero they could have coped with and recognised. But Jimmy refuses to be patronised. He has no apparent desire to rise to the social level represented by his wife Alison, her Indian Army father and dragon mother; the action of the play consists of his effort to make Alison live and love on his terms. On the first night Tynan spoke to the American dramatist and novelist Irwin Shaw, who said that Jimmy's lack of any wider ambition would doom the play in America: 'Nobody in the States will ever stomach a play about a hero who doesn't want to be a success.'

Shaw was not the only luminary present; unheralded the play may have been, but plainly something was in the air and could be sniffed for miles around. Tynan remembers encountering Amis (who ordinarily never went to the theatre and whose main comment on Jimmy was that since the chap played jazz trumpet he couldn't be all bad). His comment on the play was 'bloody good on language, bit thin on plot'. 'Binkie' Beaumont, the most powerful of West End managers (and one who, like all his colleagues, had turned the play down before it came to rest chez Devine) was present, and had premonitions: 'We may as well,' he was heard to say in the bar, 'roll up the map of the West End.' It seems to have been a night for quotations; Tynan remembers a gross figure moodily and repeatedly proclaiming that 'the rough beast has finally slouched home'. He will now swear it was Evelyn Waugh.

Tynan himself meanwhile was basking in 'the self-righteous glow that comes when you encounter a play that speaks directly to your own temperament'. The following Sunday, in the Observer, he was able, with lasting effect, to communicate that glow to his readership.

He admitted that the play had faults (he mentioned its length and the 'painful whimsy' of its end), but he disposed of them in a sentence. The rest was rhapsody, but trenchant rhapsody; Tynan's contribution to the play's success was less that he liked it better than other critics (he did but not that much) but simply that he wrote about it better. If there was a key-line in his review, it was that the play 'presents post-war youth as it really is'. It is difficult to judge the precise validity of a claim like that, but I am sure that it became truer once he had written it. Post-war youth, having read the review and/or seen the play, set about living up to its image.

Tynan made no detailed political claims for the play; he merely referred to Jimmy's 'instinctive Leftishness' as one of the traits to which he responded. John Glenister, who is directing the play for the BBC, reminded me of one fact--often forgotten: it came just before Suez and Hungary. It reflected a vague discontent that crystallised almost immediately, and of which the Court became one of the intellectual centres, so that the 'instinctive Leftishness' became more programmatic. In successive years a Royal Court banner flourished on the road from Aldermaston--and Osborne marched beneath it.

In the late 50s and early 60s he did his share of snarling at governments, and indeed at oppositions. But then he seemed to snarl at nearly everything. Once he had achieved success he fell with ironically obliging ease into the 'angry young man' stereotype invented for him by the gossip columnists (and incidentally by the Royal Court publicity department). But his personal brand of rhetoric, which has grown increasingly clotted with the years--ever since he wrote Luther, whose constipated hero moved his lips as violently and painfully as his bowels--has never been suited to the articulation of a political viewpoint. It was, and is, impossible to tell just what his famous 1961 'Letter to my fellow countrymen' (with its 'damn you, England' refrain) is meant to be about.

Jimmy Porter's rhetoric, by contrast, is free-wheelingly muscular; it is difficult to see how anyone could have failed to surrender to it from the outset. It is, apart from anything else, so funny. (The most recent London revival, at the Young Vic, had its audience rolling.) The most generalised and, I suppose, most famous declaration in the play--about there being no good causes left--is actually noticeably tacked on to the rest; what seem integral are Jimmy's onslaughts on specific targets. You do not have to be an ideologue to lampoon Tory ladies and the English Sunday, but they are subjects which would raise at least a wry smile, if not a whoop of assent, from any lively and reasonably cynical mind in 1956 (or indeed 1976); Jimmy's style, and his creator's, are very telling that way. I certainly, at the time, recognised and sympathised with the spirit evoked in Tynan's review (at 12 I was into reading reviews rather than seeing plays) and apparently though more hesitantly confirmed in Harold Hobson's piece in the Sunday Times. (Amusing that a play which begins with a riotous put-down of the posh Sundays should so quickly and decisively be enshrined in them.)

Obviously what was going on was wittily iconoclastic, and even I knew that that was a good thing to be. Others felt the same way, including at least one future playwright; Trevor Griffiths, just gone into the army, was also a review-reader rather than a playgoer and he too was convinced by Tynan that something good was beginning to happen, something to which he would later contribute. Some who saw the play itself took quicker action. Arnold Wesker who encountered it in Wimbledon later in the year, went straight home to write Chicken Soup with Barley, itself to become a Court play in 1958. What inspired him was 'something to do with the energy of the characters, a kind of impatience which came through the way they spoke'. He recognised it as an impatience he had expressed in short stories (he too had written about those 'bloody Sunday bells'), and wondered if Osborne 'felt the same way I did'.

I doubt if he did, quite, but perhaps the great attraction of the play at its premiere was its ability to act as a mirror of disaffection for a generation in need of it: you could read your own discontents into it. Jimmy's rages--which are not all the play but which drive it along--certainly give the scope; Osborne himself says of him in a stage-direction that 'to be as vehement as he is is to be almost non-committal'. But events rapidly conspired to give the vehemence a new edge; and before you knew it we had a committed theatre. Twenty years, two subsidised companies, and innumerable fringe outlets later, we still have. Tynan, now ex-Observer and ex-National Theatre, remains the dominant critical influence, and most reviewers still expect a writer to show his political colours. Or else.

Else can be quite stimulating; she even seems to function as Osborne's muse. Reviewers now accuse him of a swing to the Right; they recall the suspicious sympathy accorded the Colonel in Look Back and murmur that they should have known all along. But there has been no betrayal, since there was no real compact in the first place.

One phrase in Tynan's article which most pleased Osborne at the time was 'the determination that no one who dies shall go unmourned'. It is Jimmy's grief for his father and for the old woman who befriended him that gives him distinction in his author's eyes; it is Alison's loss of her baby that, according to the play's logic, finally makes her worthy of him. Death, as in a Jacobean tragedy, is the fount of honour--but this time for the living as well. The idea of an aristocracy of feeling is constant throughout Osborne's plays right down to his latest, Watch It Come Down. If he shows his chosen characters disdaining the outside world for no well-stated reason, he is honest enough to show them savaging each other as well. If we look back to Look Back we can find this double level already there; Jimmy's tirades may be detached from their context to be relished or detested according to taste (though the detestation, I think, has largely died out), but they are also part of his pursuit of Alison. The wit refuses to date (actually it's pleasant to be reminded of jazz and milk-bars) and the personal relationships seem more convincing in each new production; even the ending, with Jimmy and Alison playing at bears and squirrels, seems truthful enough to me. John Glenister, who directs the television production, describes the play as a love story, and he is surely right.

1976-11-28-dazzling-dispute:
Dazzling Dispute

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a French production of Marivaux.

Theatre critics are a notoriously ungracious, not to say ungrateful, crowd: not only can you not take them anywhere, you can't bring them anything either, certainly not a nicely wrapped company from abroad. Last week, noisily grinding their serpents' teeth, they outdid themselves.

Of the productions--no huge number--that I have seen outside Britain in the last three and a half years, two stand out. One was Pacific Overtures, the American musical over which I rhapsodised earlier this year and which my countrymen now seem unlikely to witness in any form; nobody has the money to put it on the stage and a television version has been rejected by the BBC. The other was Patrice Chéreau's production of Marivaux's La Dispute, which, being the work of a subsidised company--the Théâtre National Populaire--reached us, at the Lyttelton, only to be rejected by everybody else.

What these two shows most noticeably have in common--apart from intelligence, imagination and achieved ambition--is visual splendour. La Dispute is literally a dazzler. Much of it, under the best stage moon I have ever seen, is chiaroscuro, but the shadows are relieved by extraordinary flashes of light, chiefly refracted from mirrors: hard, cruel and, as will appear, eminently suitable.

Marivaux wrote a short piece about a human experiment. Two boys and two girls are each one brought up in isolation, then, when adolescence strikes, turned loose (the production suggests a colossal game of blind-man's buff) to meet one another. The object of the trial is to discover, by recreating the conditions of Eden, which of the sexes was the first to be unfaithful in love.

Girl One meets Boy One; both fall. Girl Two meets Boy Two; ditto. Girl One meets Girl Two; each is jealous of the other. Boy One meets Boy Two; they make friends. Girl One meets Boy Two; both fall again, though neither has any intention of giving up the previous love. Each wants as much as he or she can get. So dishonours are even; it might be claimed that the boys are the more amiable, but they are also the more stupid. Even their initial chumminess is suspect, since each considers himself impregnably secure in the affection of the most beautiful creature in the world, and so can afford to be kind.

What really possesses each member of the quartet is narcissism. The girl Eglé, of whom we see the most, is enraptured at the start by her own reflection in a stream, then by her own portrait, finally by the looking glass. Love, in a state of nature, is defined as meeting someone who will take you at your own estimation; an easy matter until the opportunity for comparison arises, when it becomes impossible.

Chéreau has literally fleshed out the text; where Marivaux's lovers engage with their hands and lips, his actors encounter with their whole bodies. But this is an extension of the play, not a distortion, and invaluable in making almost imperceptible the border between love-play and violence. Laurence Bourdil's Eglé is a kitten who might grow into a tigress. The force and freedom of her performance and her companions' would be remarkable in any company; in a team of French classicists it is a marvel.

The children have two black guardians, one of them given, in this dispensation, to singing the blues voluptuously well. (Voluptuous is indeed the word for the whole production.) Controlling the action, for the benefit of an inquisitive girl friend, is an anonymous Prince. Their presence prompted one reviewer, though more appreciative than some, to castigate Chéreau for ignoring Marivaux's pre-revolutionary social criticism. This is odd: the eighteenth-century French establishment had much to answer for, but I doubt if it went in on any considerable scale for the kind of emotional vivisection the Prince performs on the four youngsters, and I don't believe that Marivaux intended us to think that it did. It seems rather frivolous for the French revolution.

Actually Chéreau has gone further than his author in criticising the Prince and his company, providing a prologue which convicts them of the same ruthless self-regard as permeates the main action. This too is done with mirrors and with fierce acting; we are then transferred across a smoky abyss to a poisoned paradise, which the direction, Richard Peduzzi's setting--half architectural, half arboreal--and André Diot's lighting make palpable to the eye, to the ear, almost to the palate.

  

There is varied and ingenious design at the Marlowe, Canterbury, provided by Terry Brown to meet the demand of John Spurling's new play, While Rome Burns. While dissociating themselves on an unlocated island from England and the world, a community of well-heeled game-players come to grief: all save one, and she, in a haunting ending, wishes that she had. The engineer of their destruction is called Edgar Allan; the action is obscurely traceable to his namesake Poe's Mask of the Red Death.

It is obscure in other respects as well; though David Carson's production is resourceful and often stylishly acted, older or more idiosyncratic players might imprint the large but faintly drawn cast more firmly on our minds. But there is much wit in the dialogue and surprise in the action and, come to think of it, vice-versa; though the framework (there are distinct suggestions of a Chinese box) has turned out less sophisticated than may have been intended. It still ranks high among the growing band of doom-watch plays, aware of just how many laughs make a shudder.
1976-12-05-updating-king-lear:
Updating King Lear

ROBERT CUSHMAN in Stratford and London.

In staging King Lear (the final production of the year at Stratford) the Royal Shakespeare Company has done three things that may at first glance appear perverse. First, it has divided the play between three directors; and if the play teaches anything, it is that to split a property three ways is to invite disaster. Second, it has set--and more noticeably clothed--the action in the nineteenth century. Third, it has given the title role to Donald Sinden, our best classical comedian junior to John Gielgud, but with no particular reputation in tragedy.

These decisions seemed interdependent. Trevor Nunn is given top billing among the directing triumvirate, but it is with one of his colleagues, John Barton (Barry Kyle is the other), that one associates Victorian Shakespeare; he has utilised the period to great effect in Othello and Much Ado About Nothing. Those are both plays to which naturalistic detail seems appropriate, but Lear has generally been considered above such things. It used to be set in the vicinity of Stonehenge; nowadays it is usually done on a bare stage, all very grand and vague and icy. To put Lear into a recognisable context is to take him down a peg, perhaps to accommodate Mr Sinden.

Those at least were the current suspicions; and most unworthy they have been proved. Mr Sinden's performance may gain some flavour and particularity from its setting, but he is plainly an actor big enough to play Lear in any environment. As for the updating, it does the play more good than harm--for as long, that is, as it can be maintained. Halfway through the evening the text bursts out of its new time-lock.

In part, perhaps, this is a consequence of the size of the play asserting itself. But it has more to do with the actual location of the action. The first half of Lear is domestic, set in the king's house, or his daughters', or Gloucester's. But the second half goes out of doors, and a stormy heath or a cliff looks much the same at one period as at another. A madman's rags are similarly indifferent to fashion. But the wrench in style dissipates much of the production's effect; this is the only Lear I have seen that begins better than it finishes.

It is very bracing to be reminded that Lear is at base about a family, and to be given insights into what that family might be like. Lear's renunciation is staged without fanfare; the king makes a brisk entrance, somewhere between a stride and a shamble; all epaulettes and medals, he might be Hindenburg or Franz Josef. While he lolls on his throne, his daughters face him in high-backed chairs; the declaration of their love is an ordeal they have expected, and dreaded, for years. Goneril (Barbara Leigh-Hunt) speaks weightily and carefully, determined to get it right and win a major prize. Regan (Judi Dench) stammers, so that her father has to force her back on to the rails; she is willing to flatter but self-conscious and afraid, and her fear will eventually make her the crueller and less balanced of the two. Cordelia (Marilyn Taylerson) has a similar difficulty governing her feelings; her virtue comes out colder than she might wish, but her temperament denies her the alternative.

One can see the extent (considerable but not complete) of the father's responsibility for his children; the play's morality is given a chance to prove itself rather than having the situation rigged in its favour from the off. (Here, as in much else, Mr Nunn quite rightly follows Peter Brook.) Lear is avid for every flattering word: he cannot believe it when Cordelia breaks out of the system he has created. "Better thou hadst not been born," he says, and the words are calm enough to be accompanied by a puff of his cigar. He behaves as an absolute monarch should: he does not rage, he merely expunges; he does not kill, he merely denies life.

There is a new gravity in him; when he talks at the outset of "our darker purpose," it sounds dizzyingly deep. His old urbanity only surfaces at the onset of insanity (the approach has been finely navigated); when he inquires of the naked Poor Tom, "didst thou give all to thy daughters," he sounds crisply witty rather than distraught, and this note--which lends an unexpected meaning to his subsequent claim "here's three on's are sophisticated"--recurs to mar his madness. Nor does he command the sexual disgust of the Dover scene.

But there are many other moments when Mr Sinden sounds tones that he has never commanded before, when the stage resounds with the joy of an actor discovering himself in discovering his role, when you look and there is Lear in front of you. It is in fact Lear's own discoveries that are most memorable; his redemption begins when he first expresses concern, marvellously broad and deep, for his storm-soaked Fool. Here, and in the wondering dawn of sympathy for his "poor naked wretches" of subjects, he is immensely moving.

He has a very fine Fool in Michael Williams, an old and uncomfortably honest Northern professional, the ancestor of one of Trevor Griffiths's comedians. Good, too, are Tony Church's Gloucester, Robin Ellis's Edmund (a Thackeray cad) and John Woodvine's Cornwall. The ending is poorly orchestrated; Shakespeare has the nerve to keep telling us how painful it is, but the commentators here are not enough involved with the tragedy to justify their own words. The production is obviously ripe for re-working, and Mr Nunn may well decide (as with his peerless Macbeth) to purify and prune it. I rather hope, for once, that he opts for greater elaboration, making the second half of a piece with the first, and as fascinating.

  

The good news is that this season's exceptional Stratford company may stay together next year; the bad, that Square One in Edgware Road will probably follow the New End and ICA theatres into oblivion. Most of its brief unsubsidised life has been spent in introducing us to American plays; the present one, In The Boom-Boom Room, reaches us a mere three years late and is the first play by David Rabe, the most prominent young American playwright, to be seen here. It bears a surprising resemblance to Sweet Charity, the screwy, vulnerable and generous-hearted dance-hall hostess being replaced by a go-go dancer of similar tendencies.

Mr Rabe is widely touted as America's brightest--a proposition which, on the strength of this and his latest, Streamers, I would be unhappy to believe. The present play parades its characters at uncritical length, and its heroine's narrow escape from cliché and from sentimentality does not take her anywhere else much. But Mr Rabe writes fine New York dialogue, crisp and plangent; so long as he's not the best, he's good. The present production is necessarily makeshift, but that only increases one's goodwill; Jane Hallaren, a terrific wisecracker when last seen, is now a terrific kook, so qualifying at two strokes for most of the American repertoire. She also makes this the sexiest play in London. Save Square One.

Tom Stoppard could not be called under-exposed. The Real Inspector Hound now has its third London production (Young Vic) and is still a perfect ornament. One of its two onstage critics is Roy Hudd, which is what I call competition. Mr Hudd (whom only the Young Vic seems to have recognised as an enchantingly dapper actor, funny too, of course) plays a bus-conductor whose wife has been spirited away to work as the GPO's speaking clock in the curtain-raiser If You're Glad I'll Be Frank. This was written for radio, a faster medium, so the script stands around waiting for the production to catch up with it.
1976-12-12-delicious-tripe:
Delicious tripe

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN ranges from the Fosdykes to Strindberg.

The subject of The Fosdyke Saga (Bush) is tripe. That, you may say, hardly distinguishes it from most of the entertainment currently available in London. But tripe here is not a metaphor; it is the thing itself. The Fosdykes, abstracted from Bill Tidy's Daily Mirror cartoon by their creator and Alan Plater, manufacture the stuff and have grown great upon it.

The game is Fosdykes v. the Rest of the World. Roger Sloman, Jane Wood, Malcolm Ranson, Kevin Elyot and Penelope Nice are the Fosdykes. Philip Jackson is the Rest of the World which, being so outnumbered, not unnaturally loses, though Mr Jackson puts up a very good fight. The family resources are impressive; Dad Fosdyke is mean and rowdy, Mum is comfortable and a punch-bag, daughter Vicky is nubile, son Albert, a slimmer version of his old man, unexpectedly turns into an air ace come the First World War, and other son Tom, though he deprecates any kind of violence, does surprisingly well out of his pacific principles.

Recruited into the same war as a non-combatant linguist Tom discovers that the very first German prisoner he is required to interrogate is something very big in sausages. A mutually profitable merger is immediately planned. Thus the Fosdykes become a multi-national corporation and can sing--indeed do sing, and expect us to join in--as follows: "Tripe it is grand/Tripe it is noble/In every land/Tripe it is global."

The Fosdyke Saga is instructive as well as poetic. It shows us, and I quote, "the working-classes-of Europe exploited by the massed forces of capitalism in an ongoing counter-productive war situation." You may find that claim a bit inflated, but then you may also not have sat through the shows that use similar language in all seriousness, and on which the present uproarious entertainment is gleefully bent on avenging itself. Mike Bradwell is the director and the production is a boisterous counterpart to the filigree elegance of his work with Hull Truck. Occasionally he indulges his actors, and rather more often they indulge themselves; the show was into its second week when I saw it; I suspect that on the first night it was a little more sober and less aggressive in its goodwill.

Any gentleman sitting in the front row may get a cuddle from Miss Nice, who certainly is, but may also be belaboured about the head by Miss Wood when she impersonates a particularly militant suffragette. Patrons of either sex are at risk from the free tripe-samples energetically dispensed by Mr Sloman, or from this saliva with which he is no less generous. But from a greater hazard--that of not being amused--they should be totally safe.

The Fosdyke clan is first seen, at the dawn of the century, in direst poverty. Dad is a miner, until he gets persecuted for scabbing ("they broke both the windows of the hovel"), so the family emigrates to Manchester ("industrial Lancashire, I'd know it anywhere"), where the first man they meet is old Ben Ditchley, the reigning tripe-king, who offers a job in his factory ("report to work at three in the morning--seeing it's your first day"). Father prospers, partly through his own abilities, partly through Vicky's; she attracts both Ditchley and his son--naturally, since they are the same actor--and the resultant friction ends with the first dead, the second disinherited, and the Fosdykes in command.

From here on there are both thrills and tears (tripe and onions) as young Ditchley (reverting to tripe) attempts to regain control while the Fosdykes prove themselves more homely and lovable and regional and downright nasty than he is. The performances all get the strip-cartoon note of wide-eyed cynicism, and as the evening spreads itself into all kinds of pastiche--with Miss Nice executing another kind of strip and Mr Jackson imitating Hitler ("that is Herr Schickelgruber, he is painting my house") and soldiers unable to write home from the trenches without mouth-organ accompaniment and Mr Sloman going into a wild Cossack routine at the mere mention of Russia--there seems no reason for it ever to end. Just as you've reached this conclusion it does end, thereby--on top of all its other virtues--sparing you the pain of disillusion.

  

The Pip Simmons group, rendering Dracula (Royal Court), are hell-bent. They have a powerful talent for grotesquerie--and the music composed and performed by Chris Jordan is the most sinister I know--but hardly any for narrative, and not much sympathy for period. So apart from making the story incomprehensible, they butcher it in two ways: they play every moment and every character sinister, and when this fails they fall back on showing what a giggle the Victorians, clean-living heroes and pure heroines and all that, must have been.

Every scientist is mad, as menacing as Dracula himself; and he looks from his first appearance like something, underwear and hand-mike included, out of The Rocky Horror Show--of which one is enough. His first victim, an estate agent, looks, perhaps because of Mr Simmons's house-style in actors, every bit as frightening. The company still bring off some surprising feats; the fly-eating Renfield sings a song while hanging upside down, bound hand and foot. (He might, I thought, have completed the Houdini effect by escaping at the same time.) The opening could hardly be more nerve-jangling, but you know what they say about starting high.

  

Counting the Ways (Olivier) is what you would expect of a 60-minute duologue written by Edward Albee, and performed by two characters called He and She: a smoothly uninvolved catalogue of understated marital discontents, sometimes witty (there is a very funny line about a buffet), often arch, and leaving you at the end as unacquainted with the characters as at the beginning. There is still a senior faculty tone about Mr Albee's pair, the man shedding an unaccustomed tear at the decline of civilisation.

Either the actors in Bill Bryden's production are making intermittent stabs at an American accent or the rhythms of the text are asserting themselves at odd moments. Their delivery is short on both worry and crackle. Michael Gough, who used to be a specialist in neurosis, is getting much too gracious; Beryl Reid comes into her own when the words "Identify Yourselves" go up in neon at the back and she steps out of character and tells a cunningly-timed story about herself.

  

There are better short plays in existence. At the Roundhouse Downstairs, a new company last week dug up Strindberg's The Pelican, in which embittered juniors, embittered as only Strindberg characters can be, turn on their widowed mother to give the lie to her stories of all she has done for them, and of what she had to suffer from their father. It sounds like (and knowing Strindberg's feelings about Ibsen probably was) a riposte to Ghosts. I often find his supposedly major works trying: he was not a stayer. But into a miniature like this he could pack a prodigious amount and even his recurrent tics. The production and performances, like the play, were a strange mixture of clumsiness and accomplishment.
1976-12-19-updating-tartuffe:
Updating Tartuffe

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

The Victorians may not always have practised what they preached, but the fact that they did preach, and expected to be listened to, makes the nineteenth century a useful and agreeable refuge for any director seeking to update a classic comedy. Moral issues become clear-cut; and the treatment works particularly well for Tartuffe. For a British cast the release from seventeenth-century wigs and gowns is a blessing; they look as if they are activating a play, rather than stumbling through a charade.

David Thompson's production of Tartuffe at Greenwich is the best I have seen, providing the players with a congenial context and letting them get on with it. His translation is notable for strength rather than glitter; couplets are kept for special clinching occasions such as Orgon's eulogy of Tartuffe: "And since I've given him his bed and board/The moral climate in this house has soared."

The play accordingly becomes both funnier and more serious than it seemed in the elaborate Roger Planchon TNP production, which we saw a few weeks ago at the National Theatre. I was admonished by one or two readers for assuming in my review of the Planchon version that these two qualities, in Molière as in all great comic writers, must necessarily go together. Tartuffe, I was told, is a play far above such considerations as laughter, though Molière doubtless threw in a few gags for the incurably frivolous. This reaction was anticipated in the play itself by the sternly puritanical Madame Pernelle, who crushingly remarks that some people will laugh at anything; indeed they will, and Molière, who could laugh at her and at Tartuffe, was one of them.

The characters for once make up a recognisable household (British actors in this play usually look equal and anonymous) with unusual prominence given to the forces of reason; Denys Hawthorne gets an excellent hearing for the rational Cléante, Freda Dowie's Dorine is promoted from maid to spinster governess and it is made plain that she represents the biggest threat to Orgon's complacency; "she's turning my world upside down," he complains.

Ewan Hooper's Orgon has been built up from the text's few references to his distinguished military record; he becomes a Bible-punching general (rather like Sir Henry Havelock) adrift in civilian life, a little afraid of his young family and an easy mark for Tartuffe. The end of the first half finds them on their knees together, a disturbing reminder of Othello and Iago at the end of their temptation scene.

Leonard Rossiter's Tartuffe, from his first command to his servant ("you may put away my hair-shirt"), is bland and unreachable, immovable even in defeat. Only in his attempted seduction of Elmire does emotion seep out, and even here lust wrapped in self-satisfaction preserves a kind of sobriety. He is partnered by Ursula Mohan, demurely anxious as she warns her husband that she may have to lead Tartuffe on a little, "perhaps quite a long way."

The officer who brings rescue at the end is now a Wilkie Collins policeman, just a bit too nudgingly reassuring, so that Dorine's exclamation "perhaps the world just sometimes does make sense" retains its proper irony. Mr Thompson has in fact furnished his version with a built-in commentary: unnecessary perhaps in a perfect world, but much appreciated in ours.

  

Harold Brighouse wrote other plays besides Hobson's Choice, though on the evidence of Zack (Royal Exchange, Manchester) which came a year later, not so very other. This is another play about a turning worm. Zack, like Willie Mossop, is an exploited young man made aware of his own talents by the attentions of a determined young woman. This, the starting-point of Hobson's Choice, is the whole action of Zack, since the girl is less sure of herself, and a slower operator, than Maggie Hobson: though from the moment half-way through that she removes his glasses (a beauty treatment Hollywood was to appropriate for mousy heroines rather than cart-horse heroes) the end is apparent.

What the play loses in narrative grip, it gains in character; Zack ("I'm not as frequent at the soap as I might be") is drawn in more detail than his predecessor, Willie Mossop, and Trevor Peacock, though he can hardly help being huggable, never sentimentalises him; his is a long, slow awakening. His restraint is matched by that of Patricia Routledge as his bullying mother (Zack being, seasonally enough, a male Cinderella) and Cheryl Kennedy ties the package prettily together as his rescuer. The problems of the Exchange's arena stage are still not fully solved, but Edwardian Manchester realism takes to it better than the more stylistically demanding plays with which it opened.

  

The least-known of the week's three revived comedies is the most simply delightful; I doubt if any audience has been more surprised by joy than that for Wild Oats (Aldwych). The author, John O'Keeffe--a prolific stalwart of the late eighteenth century--does not make a good initial impression. Two young seafaring gentlemen are entrusted with the unfolding of the plot and the very best endeavours of Norman Rodway and Joe Melia foundered on the timber-shivering dialogue.

But much choicer jargon is in store; for the hero, though he will eventually prove to be someone's long-lost heir, is at present an actor whose profession has likewise gone to his head. The writing of his part is a tour de force of shameless plagiarism; if a storm breaks, he falls into Lear. Alan Howard, putting some of his own more orotund performances into quotation-marks, makes a great thing of him (though he does unflatteringly suggest that Rover has in his time made Hamlet, Coriolanus, Edgar, Richard III and Peter Quince sound the same) and whips the play into life.

In continuing the age-old war between players and Puritans (see Tartuffe, supra), O'Keeffe placed his hero among Quakers. One of them remains his inveterate enemy; he is called Ephraim Smooth, and in Patrick Godfrey's performance he lives up to his name; more can hardly be said. His fury ("this mansion is now a Temple of Baal") is matched by the delight of his young and very rich patroness, Olivia, to his Malvolio, who is easily inveigled into appearing as Rosalind in a home-grown As You Like It. Lisa Harrow plays Judy Garland to Mr Howard's Gene Kelly with charm and witty economy. The same qualities characterise Clifford Williams's production all the way to a remarkably happy ending.

  

I Gotta Shoe (Criterion) is likewise full of quotations: the songs of the celebrated Trad (in his black American guise) fit surprisingly well into a cabaret-style retelling of the Cinderella story (again). Archness threatens, but is more or less kept at bay. It makes a nasty mess, though, of the first half of the evening, a self-styled revue in which four performers (the fifth, Elisabeth Welch, condemned by laryngitis on the first night to be a beneficent but mainly silent presence) offer new black showbiz clichés for old. Some classic songs (Gershwin and a Harold Arlen medley) briefly relieve some newer stuff with lyrics (by Caryl Brahms and Ned Sherrin) too precious for this world.
1977-01-09-blunt-point:
Blunt Point

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

A Christmas gift unwrapped on Twelfth Night is apt to seem a little frayed. We critics were compelled to miss The Point when it opened at the Mermaid because, it was intimated, the technical effects were not in working order. Well, they are operative now; smoke swirls and retreats on cue, projections appear and disappear, and are often pleasingly geometric, and Ron Pember's production is altogether a tidy affair.

But though the trappings may have been brought up to scratch, the story itself itches. It concerns a boy who lives in a land where everything is pointed, notably the tops of the citizens' heads.
