He himself, uniquely flat-surfaced, is persecuted and driven out. (Brecht, curiously enough, allegorised Nazi anti-Semitism in a piece called Round Heads and Pointed Heads.)

That is Act One, the better half. Act Two finds him in exile, in a place called the Pointless Forest, which fails to live up to its adjective, though the pronouncements of its inhabitants are none too easy to follow. Much of The Point, to use the only idiom of the kind the script neglects, is beside itself, but not, I hope, with pride. Anyway, our hero gets back home and declares that everything has a point, so his compatriots can stop giving themselves such airs and tolerance is proclaimed.

The show originated as a TV cartoon, and the lack of an equivalent visual style undoes it on stage. Even the most regular inhabitants of the Land of Point have barely noticeable sharp ends, and had I been king (an office here performed in kindly fashion by Bernard Miles) I should have banished them all, especially the one who, doubtless on her director's instructions, trills every third word. Wayne Sleep is energetic, though hardly taxed by his own choreography; Oscar James has and communicates a good time impersonating Louis Armstrong, in by far the best of Harry Nilsson's songs, the rest of which contribute largely to the general flavour of cracker-barrel mysticism, soft-rock Disney, though his fables were far more inventive and made more sense.

  

I attended the King's Head to hear Loaded Questions, presented by the Phantom Captain School of Thought. Every spoken line in this piece is interrogative, with one exception. "And the next question is, what are the Greek, Roman and Nordic myths?" is of course a statement. Anyway, the entertainment is surprisingly varied in tone if not, strictly speaking, in mood.

The School of Thought has three pupils whom the programme identifies as Joel Cutrara, Louise Jones and Peter Deman. When they enter, the first looks serene, the second disdainful, and the third surprised and a little appalled to see us. They begin by tossing off a few conversational commonplaces ("Can we offer you a lift?" "Are you prepared to meet us half-way?") proffered with a steely politeness that immediately makes us feel got at.

They then proceed to some party pieces: various areas of life are defined for us in terms of the questions they occasion. Childhood is particularly vulnerable: a long period of being asked "isn't it about time you grew up?" They make up dialogues entirely composed of questions; a sex encounter is particularly easy to enjoy, as the performers are disconcertingly aware. Turning on us again, they ask us if we found the presence of recognisable characters helpful. They have already inquired if our attention is wandering, and if so where to: barbed, I'd call that.

Every so often they get portentous ("Are you changing your mind? Is your mind changing you?") and when they attack the fabric of their own performance ("after a while, don't you get hungry to make a simple statement?") they sound not so much self-doubting as self-pitying. Nobody, after all, asked them.

They also, from time to time, sing; pondering whether it's true what they say about Dixie, or wondering who's kissing her now. That, I'm afraid, is another statement. They might try Cole Porter's At Long Last Love, the only song I know composed entirely of questions. "Is it an earthquake or simply a shock? Is it the good turtle soup or merely the mock?" Loaded Questions is on the whole the good turtle soup. (Which reminds me; the food at the King's Head has improved enormously.)

  

Uhlanga (Theatre Upstairs) is merely the mock. So, at least, it seems here. In Johannesburg, where it was planned, or Lagos, where it was premiered, this one-man show, apparently dedicated to evoking the whole of black experience, would have found an audience more able--for we were certainly willing--to piece that experience together for themselves, though I am not sure they would need to be reminded of it in what appear to be simple terms, muddily presented.

In one respect James Mthoba's act rebounds on itself. He satirises the black image (simple, fawning, anxious to please) adopted to appease the whites, but when he himself breaks through as a performer it is on identical terms. His biggest asset is his shy smile. Though bitterness is implicit in his material, there is none in his persona. The most powerful thing in the evening is to be found in the programme, where is printed Strange Fruit, the American poem about a lynching which became a song-hit for Billie Holiday.
1977-01-22-standards:
22 JANUARY 1977, Page 27

Jazz

Standards

Robert Cushman

England is better at appreciating popular singers and popular songwriters than at breeding them.

It is not perhaps to be wondered at ; the great tradition of twentieth-century songwriting is American (a Noel Coward song is fine until you hear Cole Porter), and its interpreters must be so as well. Even our most glittering native star, Cleo Laine, whose earlier work challenged comparison

with the best, has recently become a perverse illustration of the rule. Her sophistication has become so pronounced, so aggressively flaunted, that it defeats itself and returns to gaucherie. Most others of course have never escaped from gaucherie in the first place. I except Annie Ross but much of her grounding was American. All the same it is here that the great old men, Bing Crosby and Fred Astaire, have resumed their recording careers. It was an English producer who persuaded the late Johnny Mercer to record two indispensable albums of his own lyrics. And jazz singers of a later generation—Blossom Deane, Marian Montgomery, Mark Murphy— have all found havens here. Salena Jones who comes from Newport News, Virginia (a town well publicised on record sleeves since it also nourished Ella Fitzgerald and Pearl Bailey), really built her career in Britain—though now she has qualified for the international circuit. It was a glossy as well as a powerful Salena who recently played two weeks at Ronnie Scott's in Frith Street.

Technically she is one of the best ; not so much a showy as a snowy singer, deep and crisp and even; sleek too in the style which took the white nightclub adaptation of black singing (as exemplified, say, by Peggy Lee) and, in the wake of rock and rhythmand-blues, blackened or at least browned, it up again. The most successful of this school is probably Nancy Wilson, who at the outset of her career had an enchanting directness of appeal; lateishe became mannered and breathy, as if trying to emulate all three of the Supremes at the same time. Salena avoids the mannerisms without quite recapturing the simplicity. There are girl singers and there are woman singers, and she is one of the latter. (The former is the larger category, including even such physically unlikely candidates as Miss Fitzgerald.) But she has—like many singers who came up in the :sixties—a repertoire problem. I would guess that she saw herself originally as a singer of standard material, jazz or theatrical—what the trade used to call 'classy.' But when she began to make it, this material was believed to be commercial death and singers were expected to sing contemporary: Beatles or post. Something called 'middle of the road music' was invented to make the transition easier; everyone sang 'For Once in My Life,' some fast, some slow, and was reckoned to be very sincere and dramatic. Jim Webb, with a touch more delicacy, turned out portfolios of the stuff. Now standards, following a few odd hits, are beginning to be respectable again, and Salena's act is crammed with them—on the assumption, unfortunately, that any old song (any old song) will do: sharpen it up, belt it (Salena's accompanying trio are very skilled at suggesting a big band) and the customers will be satisfied. You want to include 'Moon River' but it's been done to death so you swing it, hoping that this will be exciting (it is, a bit) and sophisticated (no way). But if you are not prepared to go

with the winsome ingenuity of the lyric, better leave it alone; the tune, though professionally shaped, is not strong enough to withstand the battering. (And really there is no urgent need, right now, to sing it at all.) Salena's act was all like that : initially exhilarating, because so sure-footed, but in the end insubstantial, almost characterless.

Susannah McCorkle is singing at the Taverna Syrtaki, a Greek restaurant in South Molton Street, Tuesdays and Wednesdays; Saturdays in the new and rather perilous setting of Langan's Brasserie, Like Salena she is American but there the resemblance ends. Her programme is even more heavily weighted than Salena's towards old songs. Superficially she seems to have less to offer them and us; her technique is less assured, certainly less assertive. And yet one listens more attentively to her material, because she herself is obviously more interested by it. Salena establishes herself in her first number, and the rest is repetition. Susannah values every song for itself, so can go on surprising us.

She chooses them well, of course. The last few years in New York have seen a notable revival of interest in the classic song; old interpreters have returned and new ones have arrived. Susannah offers the nearest glimpse of this resurgence available in London. This city has a large minority population of song-buffs, deprived of a natural rendezvous but in some ways more fanatical than their Manhattan kindred. Susannah sings for them—I should say, for us. And she is the more appealing for possessing a kind of dual nationality. She only began singing after coming to Europe, so she combines an outsider's enthusiasm for the American repertoire with a native's ability actually to put it over.

Somewhere in her travels she has acquired an intriguing lisp but he is too witty ever to be coy. Her wit, like that of many of the best singers, is deadpan; she makes sure we catch her lyricists' jokes but she rarely underlines them.

She sings Cole Porter of course, Rodgers and Hart, a blessed amount of Frank (Guys and Dolls) Loesser. She has no need either to emphasise or to avoid hackneyed material, since in the ears of the world nearly all this stuff is now unfamiliar. In the terms of my earlier antithesis she is a girl rather than a woman singer, knowing but vulnerable. The most obvious, and acknowledged, influence' is Billie Holiday. This, since she is white, may sound like impiety but she gets away with it and augments it with a further heresy; she proves Holiday, one of jazz's vaunted tragediennes, to have been the greatest of the ingenues. Coat her familiar sound with a couple of layers of camp and you arrive at 'Marilyn Monroe, whom Susannah also celebrates, dusting off 'Diamonds are a Girl's Best Friend' for a rowdy office party at the Syrtaki. From Billie she retains the upward murmur (a velvet croak) at the end of a phrase in a rhythm song, the wounded downbeat in a ballad. And she sings a dirty blues (`They busted the joint, took everyone away but me') with a deliciously sozzled, eyelashfluttering insouciance; there have been gutsier blues singers, by far, but few more humorous. Here she crosses cultures to remind you of that dustily majestic gutterlily Lotte Lenya—to whom she has an ash-blonde resemblance.

She is blessed in her accompanist, Keith Ingham, whose piano is powerful and discreet, pungent and plangent. They have an LP, The Music of Harry Warren (World Record WRS 1001), which is worth hearing; Warren, in the 'thirties and 'forties, wrote all the movie songs.

To sum up; both ladies are talented, both are welcome. Salena plays the more prestigious dates, commands more immediately attentive audiences. But in the wider sense she is the prisoner of her environment ; Susannah builds her own.
1977-01-23-norfolk-la-russe:
Norfolk à la Russe

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN in Leeds, Manchester and London.

Years ago Arnold Wesker gave us Roots, in which a Norfolk farm working family prepared to feed and welcome a Jewish intellectual who at the last moment chickened out and remained offstage. This was prudent of him on the evidence of The Wedding Feast (Leeds Playhouse).

The parallel with Roots is not exact. The Jew here is a tycoon named Louis Litvinov, very big in shoes; and he is not an expected guest but a gatecrasher. Two workers in his factory - one his secretary's brother - are getting married and he decides to grace the celebration. He is an affectionate employer who claims, more than once, to understand his employees; after all, he started poor himself. He is accused inevitably of paternalism; his reply, "Give everything a name and dismiss it," though not conclusive, is worth a ponder. It rebukes the jargon that is everywhere flung about in place of argument. The language in this play is thoughtful, judicious and finely shaped.

Structurally, however, there are severe flaws. The first act, mainly devoted to filling us in on Louis, is a disaster area and may well have scared managements off. The play is based (how distantly I have no idea) on a Dostoevsky short story, and a narrator, carefully setting the scene à la Russe (the country cottage on the outskirts of Norwich in the county of Norfolk), pays homage to the source. He does most of the preliminary talking, putting such a fine ironic gloss on the conversation of Louis, his colleagues, and his political adversaries to Left and Right, that the arguments become impossible to follow and the attitudes to comprehend. Louis accordingly walks into the central situation a hollow man.

The mannerisms are dropped for the wedding party itself, which extends over Acts Two and Three and constitute a naturalistic tour de force unapproached (indeed, unattempted) by any other recent playwright. The Leeds production by John Harrison and Michael Attenborough stretches its actors across one of those panoramic subsidised stages in all the awkwardness, acrimony and erratic euphoria of actual family festivity, culminating in something called "the shoe game," where Louis's employees, after some understandable initial nervousness, take the opportunity of beating the hell out of him with his own product. This use of ritual is the most successful, believable and suggestive in any of Mr Wesker's plays.

The family, then, are thoroughly convincing (David Troughton is an outstandingly sheepish bridegroom), but Louis himself strains belief, and his secretary annihilates it. She has a lot of work to do - linking two worlds and, as a Marxist who condemns Louis's attempts at rapprochement because they make class hatred harder, representing a third - and no personality to do it on. David Swift plays Louis decently enough within the bounds of the text.

  

Across the Pennines, the Manchester Royal Exchange Theatre has two productions in repertory. Orton's What The Butler Saw is far better done than on either of its appearances in London and two of the performances may be definitive: Trevor Peacock's immovable policeman and Michael Feast's extremely movable page-boy, in and out of women's clothing (in every sense) at a second's notice.

Lee Montague as Dr Prentice radiates the professional psychiatric calm that is unnerving. The play, though, rests on his superior Dr Rance, Inspector of Madhouses, dedicated to the discovery and exploitation of mental and physical deviation. Alfred Burke has some joyous moments, sniffing out enormities like the devil in pin-stripes, but he has not the panache to blend the various obsessions - censorious and libidinous, homo and hetero - wished on him by his author.

The play drives against society by mocking orthodox cases of sexuality; intellectually and imaginatively, it is of a piece, but the methods of attack are inclined to be indiscriminate. Mrs Prentice is lustful or repressed, predatress or victim, as Orton's mood takes him. Rosalind Knight, a witty actress with the law of averages and her own carving-knife voice working for her, opts for attack. Braham Murray's direction, though lacking something in frenzy, is well spaced; and a seat above the arena stage affords a god-like view of the human, and particularly the English, race making a delectable fool of itself.

  

For The Skin of Our Teeth I sat below and since this allowed me to be chatted up by the no less delectable Marsha Hunt on one of her exits, I cannot complain. Miss Hunt, though, complains a lot; as Sabina, the maid whom everybody ought to have, she complains about her domestic circumstances; but in her own person she grumbles about playing a role which requires her to step out of character and grumble about playing a role.

Thornton Wilder's self-proclaimed "history of the world in comic strip" presents mankind as a plain old family from New Jersey, successively surviving the Ice Age, the Flood, and War. It thus asserts (a) that people never change and (b) that they always get by. Put like that it seems rather cosy and like that, much of the time, Wilder puts it. Only in the third act is there real tension as Mr Antrobus, alias Adam, the builder, confronts his son Henry, whom you may call Cain if you dare. Lee Montague, still powerfully quiet, meets Michael Feast, a riveting young actor whose warrior is as dangerous as his page was perky. But to enjoy this scene you have to survive, not only the deluge (here unaccountably provoked by some perfectly decorous sunbathing on the boardwalk at Atlantic City), but the author's jokiness, bred ostensibly of his desire to remind us that we are in the theatre.

There is a nineteen-fortyish Middle American folksiness here beyond that of the Antrobi. There are stabbing moments, mainly connected with Mr Feast's destructiveness, and the direction by Richard Negri and James Maxwell capitalises on all the opportunities for spectacle. The theatre continues to excite, and the company to charm, but I still hope for more muscle.

  

Terence Rattigan's Separate Tables (Apollo) was the last West End prestige hit before the Royal Court era; the second of its two component parts has always been thought superior to the first, but time has narrowed the gap. The sadomasochistic couple of the first have good Strindbergian stuff in them, though their story is told with surprising clumsiness. The repressed pair of the second have compassion and Rattigan's best technique on their side, but their problems now seem enviably cut and dried.

The casting of this revival is not ideal; John Mills, that perpetual cock-sparrow, has the spirit but not the strength for his first role. Into the military posing of his second he slips almost too easily, while Jill Bennett, his partner in frustration, having dispensed virginal mannerisms with excessive generosity for her first 15 minutes, forgets them thereafter - perhaps because her mother (Margaret Courtney) is too comic-opera a monster to furnish convincing opposition. The small-hotel ambiance is as infallibly beguiling as ever; the supporting roles are all what are known as "little gifts" to their interpreters, who receive them graciously but with an undeniable air of self-satisfaction as each little laugh goes down. Raymond Huntley's schoolmaster is the most discreet, and hence the most durable.
1977-01-30-tales-from-vienna:
Tales from Vienna

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

Shamefully few of us had heard, until very recently, of Odon von Horvath, and most of us must still be in some doubt how to pronounce him. After the triumphant opening of Tales from the Vienna Woods (Olivier, National Theatre) we should have plenty of opportunity to learn. I advise you to go down to the woods at the earliest opportunity (there may be crowds but persevere); you will, though, be sure of more than the regulation big surprise.

As a German play of the thirties it is part of a still-growing legend. Horvath was actually born in Hungary, and he died in exile in Paris (a tree fell on his head in the Champs Elysées: an ironically impersonal end for a playwright concerned, on this evidence, with strictly human weakness and malevolence). But his career was in Berlin, and he was driven out by the Nazis.

Hindsight makes this play (staged in 1931) look at moments like a prophecy of specific cataclysm. But hindsight can of course do that job far more thoroughly itself; there are the expected sinister nightclub scenes in Tales from the Vienna Woods, but as intimations of Fascism they hardly compare with those in Cabaret. And though suitably ominous headlines illustrating the rise of Hitler are projected on to a screen, they seem to have little direct connection with what is happening on stage.

It is significant that Horvath, writing for a Berlin audience, set his play at a discreet but hardly flattering distance, in Austria. The title reveals the strategy; Strauss waltzes are constantly in our ears and Maximilian Schell's production sets the actors and the stage itself whirling in sympathy. Stephen Rea as Alfred, our hero, is a particularly nifty mover, continually doubling back on himself, always akimbo.

Actually Alfred is distinctly shabby, a small-time horse-player and gigolo; he is in himself enough to give the lie to the schmalz of old Vienna. Maybe Horvath overworks the irony, but the Danube in this production is so delectably evoked (intending bathers hold their noses, jump into the orchestra pit, and are seen no more) that he is worth indulging. A picnic by the river, all balloons and amateur photography and horrible children, is a tour de force. It is here that Alfred falls, so to speak, in love with Marianne, who works in a toyshop, and she genuinely in love with him. They have a child; Alfred runs out. Marianne, too tender-hearted for a career on the streets, winds up as a nude cabaret dancer: another story of old Vienna. This one, however, being squalid rather than glamorous, is for real.

At every step Marianne is betrayed by the authority of age: by her father, who disowns her in an ecstasy of sentimental horror, by the Church, which refuses her absolution unless she surrenders her child, by the Baroness who runs the nightclub, most hideously, by Alfred's grandmother, who allows the baby to die (and on whom Alfred himself is financially dependent). The horrors of the past make possible those of the future; the crown of Kate Nelligan's Marianne is her silent assurance, beyond stoicism, that the worst is yet to come (a point sympathetically made in Christopher Hampton's preface to a translation which reads stiffly but acts a treat).

Miss Nelligan - in bewilderment, anger, desolation or defiance - is superb. She is also believably good. Warren Clarke matches her as her first fiancé, an unromantic butcher (with a pork-pie hat for special occasions), Grosz in outline but sedate in feeling, and at the last crushing her with forgiveness; "I once told you, Marianne, you wouldn't escape my love" is a truly terrifying line, clinching a finale that must be one of the high points of twentieth-century drama. There are a dozen other performances to mention (including the leathery insouciance of Elizabeth Spriggs as Alfred's protectress); for once, everybody on stage looks right.

  

Scarborough, many have said and I can now confirm, is the place to see an Alan Ayckbourn play; his new Theatre in the Round (comfortably made over from a secondary school) currently houses his new Ten Times Table, a comedy about the organisation of a small town festival: more accurately perhaps about the organisation of a small town festival committee. The central historical event to be commemorated is a premature peasants' revolt. The meeting splits between the progressives (a Marxist schoolteacher in the van) and reactionaries, the latter heavily hit by apathy, but rallied by the arrival of a dog-breeder with the instincts of a commando and limited reserves of self-control. A minute after saying hello he is liable to scream of the opposition, "they are scum" to somebody. Christopher Godwin makes this a golden moment.

Others belong to a frail old lady whose conversational contributions are erratic (since her hearing is sharper than might be thought, though duller than could be wished), but contain at least three of Mr Ayckbourn's choicest lunacies. I also enjoyed her son, a dedicated committee man with apologetic glasses but terribly eager teeth. The author directs with an impeccable feeling for nuance, as well he might; this may not be his best play (it's a little too easy-going); but the cast give it a solidity that I would not expect the West End to match. This, in Scarborough, is popular theatre (community theatre, if you remember that old thing); the National should add it to their list of regional imports.

  

Good wishes to the new regime at the Royal Court, and commiserations to the old who, considering their inheritance (and I don't mean money) have not done as badly as has been trumpeted; there have been many rockier years in Sloane Square than the last, and the recent spectacle of the Court's biggest pots and kettles begriming one another has not been edifying.

As a rule, these days, if you want to buy their wares, follow me and climb to the Theatre Upstairs, treading carefully for fear of Traps, Caryl Churchill's latest, which has wit and much good acting, six characters, several relationships and a stark rural setting, and kept losing me. It ends with each person in turn stripping off and getting into a tin bath; the last is reluctant (he wears a tie, carries a box of chocolates and is repressed generally), but gives in and, though the water is by now an unspeakable colour, is probably the better for it. I don't want to dismiss this play. Actually, I don't think I dare.
1977-02-06-back-to-the-chorus:
Back to the Chorus

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

When the American company of A Chorus Line opened at Drury Lane last year the audience applauded before it had seen any one of them move a muscle. The mere sight of them, when the lights went up, poised in auditioning formation and reflected in the practice-mirrors beyond, brought down the house. This was not just first-night generosity; it was common form in the New York production, all nights of the week. When the British cast took over on Tuesday, that native electricity, visible even when latent, had gone back where it belongs.

After the visual impact, the aural: the most exciting line in the show, really, had always been the whiplash cry - part goad, part encouragement - of Zach, the director: "five-six-seven-eight." It sparked the whole opening sequence, made it an experience for which the show could be forgiven any amount of equivocation later. Now the vital words have lost their edge, become a muffle of unfamiliar vowels. In view of British Equity's bewildering vacillations over the proposed secondment to the British company of Donna McKechnie from New York, what is a Frenchman doing in the role of Zach? A French actor, too (Jean Pierre Cassel), who barely holds his own in the dance numbers, where his predecessor, the magnetic Eivind Harum, was their guiding force.

Replacing Miss McKechnie as Cassie, who struggles to get back in the chorus after an ill-fated attempt to leave it and become a star, is Petra Siniawski, who did better than one had dared to hope. She does not, as Cassie should, compel attention from the beginning; she lacks Miss McKechnie's generous features, her red dress, and her established reputation. But she plays the lines better and her big solo dance of frustration, hurling herself against the mirrors, is more powerful than it was in New York, where one kept waiting in vain for Miss McKechnie to take off, as she had in Promises, Promises and Company.

Actually many of the numbers looked better to me than ever before, perhaps because I was seeing them for the first time from above. (Critics are usually hustled down to the front stalls for a worm's eye view. Why? Don't answer that.) The long piece of rhythmic group autobiography, "Hello Twelve Hello Thirteen Hello Love," was a revelation; just as impressive as the group-movement with its rapturous climax is the sudden quick walk along the white audition line of a frightened dancer awaiting his turn at confession.

Michael Bennett's use of performers as mobile visual statements, each with his own identity, still outclasses everything else in London (though Tales from the Vienna Woods is a contender). Some of the new team sing well, though those who don't lack the American ability to brazen the thing out; one of the funniest songs goes for little and another for nearly nothing. Four of the boys are brilliant dancers, and Michael Stanniforth's long self-pitying monologue is excellent.

  

A Chorus Line began its life off-Broadway. Few fringe productions take so well to enlargement; the problem of what is to be done with them when they are good remains pressing and apparently insoluble. Barrie Keeffe's Gimme Shelter (Soho Poly) is due for a provincial tour; and Robert Holman's German Skerries (Bush) will probably have an afterlife in rep studios, those keepers of the regional theatres' conscience. But both deserve more.

Mr Holman's play indicates the richness and concentration available in a miniature auditorium. In Chris Parr's production every solid object from a lady's bicycle (ridden by a man) to a jotting-pad has a stunning, almost poetic, impact; a bank of mucky grass might have been transplanted from the Green across the road. Theatres apparently hopelessly equipped for realism are actually its citadels.

Of course we would all like the theatre to go beyond realism, but it does no harm to get there first. This Mr Holman beautifully does; his central characters, realised in loving detail by Paul Copley and Caroline Hutchison, are a young married couple poised between happiness and discontent. The setting is Tees-side, and in the central speech (which broadens the play out amazingly) Mr Copley evokes "a mass of industry ... stretching for 30 miles." He pays it a curious kind of respect, seeing that it has provided him with a dead-end job, and that its side-effects may include the dispersal of a flock of cormorants to which he, as a bird-watcher, is devoted. The German Skerries are the rocks on which they gather; they also, I fancy, stand for the shipwreck which menaces most of the characters' dreams, and which causes one death in earnest. The play has a distinctive flavour: bracing, lyrical, rooted.

Mr Keeffe has a harsher way with no-hopers, in whose predicament he involves most of us. Gimme Shelter is a triptych; its central panel, called Gotcha, is imbued with tremendous force. A 16-year-old kid, about to leave a comprehensive with no prospects and a damning report, holds his headmaster and two others to ransom. He falls into the situation, and knows that it is ultimately hopeless, but hatred keeps him going; he threatens them with a great explosion in a confined space, a powerful weapon of which Philip Davis's performance, one part snivels to nine of desperation, is itself a living theatrical example; his outbursts are the most overwhelming since Deborah Norton's in Kennedy's Children. Mr Keeffe, by probing the weak spots of all four characters, ensures belief and brings off the most guilt-inducing social play in years.

On either side of it stand two pieces about Kev, an ex-grammar-school rebel, now working for an insurance firm, scratching to keep revolt alive, the dupe of his own rhetoric and increasingly of his own compromise. In the last play he meets the piratical kid of the second, just out of Borstal and effectively brain-washed, and hails him as a brother revolutionary; he meets, of course, with incomprehension.

Mr Keeffe underlines too much here; the simple confrontation says everything necessary, and besides, Kev never quite convinces. But there is one masterly stroke of continuity; one of the kid's main grievances against his hostages was that in five years they never learned his name. But when his case gets in the papers his youth ensures that his anonymity is preserved, and when Kev wants to salute him he can only say "Day'll come, they'll chant your name. ... Whatever it is."
1977-02-13-royal-progress:
Royal progress

ROBERT CUSHMAN introduces Radio 4's mammoth history cycle, starting tonight.

TEN years ago I began my working life as a script reader, and occasional producer, in BBC radio drama. Doing the same job in adjacent offices were two ex-actors, Gerry Jones and Martin Jenkins. Both are still working in Broadcasting House. They have bigger offices now and are real producers; which in radio denotes both artistic and administrative responsibility. There is a great deal of both involved in 'Vivat Rex,' the project on which Jones and Jenkins are currently engaged and which is described -- not only by them -- as the biggest in the history of the department.

It is a Radio 4 Sunday serialisation in 26 instalments of 'the history plays' -- not just the familiar Shakespearean octet, from 'Richard II' to 'Richard III,' but a cluster of other Elizabethan chronicle pieces as well. It begins tonight with Marlowe's 'Edward II' and ends with 'Henry VIII' by Shakespeare and (probably) Another. En route it takes in 'Edward III' (by Another and just possibly Shakespeare) and 'Perkin Warbeck,' written by John Ford, one of the last of the Jacobeans and drawn from the reign of Henry VII.

Also included, a rare treat, is an incident from the scrawny and anonymous 'Famous Victories of Henry V,' on which Shakespeare drew for his presentation of Prince Hal and Falstaff; the episode is the mythical one of Hal giving the Lord Chief Justice a thick ear -- one of those pranks by which, as those incomparable historians Sellar and Yeatman remarked, he won all English hearts.

Jones, a prizewinning playwright, once spent a season at the Old Vic, but this is his first essay in Shakespearean production; Jenkins is a classical veteran. He has done many of the plays on Radio 3, and was co-founder of the Liverpool Everyman Theatre, which in his day was a stronghold of the set text. As an actor he carried an assortment of spears in Peter Hall's Stratford production of 'The Wars of the Roses,' from which sprang his determination to ride a history cycle of his own one day. A few years ago he drew up a detailed scheme for a radio serial of the usual eight plays; those done on television in 1960 as 'An Age of Kings,' and by Hall at Stratford in 1964. The idea stayed on the shelf; its present resurrection and expansion has been partly due to the BBC's desire to present something for jubilee year. (The series ends with the birth of Elizabeth I; the punch-line of 'Vivat Rex' is 'Vivat Regina.')

As usual in such cases, the decision was taken late, and the directors have had six months to prepare an operation that might have taken three times as long. They are now recording the middle of the series, playing back the beginning, and still casting the end. This is a perennial radio headache; actors like the medium for its speed and freedom, but will rarely commit themselves to it far in advance, for fear something more lucrative may turn up. Returning to my old radio haunts I have found myself involved in impromptu casting sessions, firing off brilliant and invariably impractical suggestions. I did, though, get to write an explanatory booklet filling in the narrative background to the series: all you need to know about 'Vivat Rex,' available from the BBC -- I weep to type it -- free.

To date, the line-up of actors is fairly stunning: Richard Burton as narrator, Michael Redgrave, Peggy Ashcroft, Paul Scofield, Diana Rigg, Derek Jacobi ('Richard II'), John Hurt (a feline Edward II with definite Caligulan traces), Billie Whitelaw, June Whitfield (as Mistress Quickly, why not?), Robert Hardy and, as Falstaff, Anthony Quayle; a part he played in 1951 when, as director of the Stratford Memorial Theatre, he masterminded one of the first and most successful history seasons, contributing greatly to the plays' rehabilitation in theatre and study alike.

Quayle attributes their triumphant track-record to their accessibility: 'Hamlet and Lear are more difficult to reach, for actors and audiences. The people in the histories are built on our scale. But psychological naturalism is set in enormous sweep of space and time; the action of 'Vivat Rex' covers 230 years. The histories win both ways: a homely epic.'
1977-02-13-the-curse-on-thebes:
The curse on Thebes

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

TALKING of chorus lines, the shortest but by no means the least effective in town can be found at Greenwich and consists of Freda Dowie. Slight of build, stern of face, sharp and glancing of voice, Miss Dowie compels attention both as commentator and narrator. She can suggest both the anxieties and sympathies of ordinary humanity and the wrath of most of the gods.

You will gather that the work in hand is a Greek tragedy. It is a rare and late Euripides, named originally for its chorus The Phoenician Women. For us that title is uninformative and the disappearance during rehearsal of an intended partner for Miss Dowie would have made its plural form positively mendacious. The new label is The Sons of Oedipus, which at least lets us know which myth we are in; we have fallen among Thebes.

It does less than justice, though, to the play's scope. Euripides and his heirs (the play was touched up and extended after his death) offer an omnibus edition of the Theban story as rendered by Aeschylus and Sophocles. In this version Oedipus's exile and Jocasta's suicide are postponed until the tragedy of the next generation has been played out, and their sons Polyneices and Eteocles have destroyed each other. Jocasta's opening monologue reaches back to Oedipus's birth, to his killing of his father and his defeat of the Sphinx.

The end of the play anticipates both Oedipus's death at Colonus, and Antigone's defiant burial of her brother Polyneices' body; she, plucky girl, seems all set to perform her role in both dramas simultaneously. En route we have been treated to an incident encountered in no other play: the self-immolation, in obedience to an oracle, of Creon's young son Menoeceus. This enables the authors to bring on, as bearer of the fatal prophecy, old blind Teiresias, without whose threats and grumbles they must have felt any Theban tragedy would be incomplete.

Formally the play is hardly among Euripides's neatest; nor is it distinguished for the satiric bite with which he often rehandled his predecessors' themes. But his most distinctive quality is intact: his inquiring sense of what it might mean to be a real person embroiled in a mythic catastrophe. Few of his characters emerge with much credit (the opposing brothers are a pair of self-justifying warmongers), but they are never sneered at. And as disaster follows disaster, striking everyone on stage and a whole population just off it, one loses the urge to apportion blame.

The curse, so often invoked, on Thebes and on the royal family of Oedipus ceases to be a piece of antique machinery and comes to stand for the agony of existence, to be faced without hysteria and without illusion. This is the tragic sense, and we need it. It even justifies the preliminary screening of horror-paragraphs from current newspapers; not that they illuminate Euripides (how could they when he has a 2000 year start?), but the reverse: he helps us to face them and to grow up.

David Thompson's translation and direction are as clear and sensible as his Tartuffe last year: for Greek tragedy he is, with a good Medea and magnificent Bacchae to his credit, literally the only man. Why he has never directed one of them at the National or RSC, Olympus only knows. (I wrote that sentence 10 years ago, but the gods still keep their counsel.)

This production is disfigured by some fumbling bits of naturalism and more seriously by performances that stay on the level of intelligent recitation. When Frank Barrie arrives to fill the stage physically as well as vocally (this does not mean leaping about) with the news of a triple death we are in another world: we enter it briefly, too, when Ewan Hooper's Creon mourns his son, when Ursula Mohan's Antigone mourns her whole family, when Siobhan McKenna's Jocasta just mourns--though since she does this passim (her inclining, not the play's) the effect is rapidly blunted. Oedipus is held in reserve till the last, a build-up to make Tartuffe's two-act intro seem trifling; when he arrives, in the person of Denys Hawthorne, he is a polite anti-climax. But it is still the biggest play in London.

  

In beginning her direction of Theatre Workshop with O'Casey's The Silver Tassie Clare Venables faces several obstacles, chief among them the extreme badness of the play itself. Its main concern is the indifference of society to its cripples: true enough, but once you've said it you've said it. This theme is dressed up in anti-war uniform; a placard reading 'War is hell' would say as much as the drearily extended symbolism of the second act. Since those who reject the hero have no attitude towards the war, the play has no continuity; lacking consistency of style, character or purpose it falls to pieces wherever you touch it, and the comic interludes are more than usually shameless. It needs to be done boldly with every opportunity seized for stylisation; Miss Venables's direction is timid and her players accordingly desperate. Only Vince Brimble imposes himself; the rest stub their toes in a vacuum. It all looks amateurish.

  

The Last Meeting of the Knights of the White Magnolia (Hampstead) by Preston Jones, of Texas, is better performed (with one exception), but similarly redundant. We meet half-a-dozen rednecks whose fraternity, originally a splinter from the Ku Klux Klan, is clearly both ridiculous and doomed. The rest of the play is devoted to reiterating just how ridiculous and doomed their fraternity is. In making this point the author has the aid of many repeated situations and cliche characters; one of the latter looks just like the placards of Colonel Sanders and is indeed both a colonel and a paste-board figure himself. Other people's iconoclasm can be very tedious.

  

Hampstead's honour is saved by the transfer of Pam Gems's Dusa, Stas, Fish and Vi (Mayfair), which, in Nancy Meckler's production, is gorgeous entertainment, full of sharp and stylish corners. Its buoyancy, though, is at odds with its suicidal ending; it is ironic that this much-touted feminist play should restore that by no means unfamiliar and decidedly unliberated figure, the girl who kills herself because her man has done her wrong. Two propositions that Miss Gems may not fully endorse are none the less floating around in her play: (a) that only women suffer and (b) that all their suffering is due to men.

The proffered antidote of female solidarity lacks dramatic force because its realistic basis--the flat-sharing routine--is never established. The girls-together title looks in fact like a fashionable blind: Dusa is a contrivance; Stas and Vi are comic relief, and the author's favourite dish is obviously Fish. But she is a creation; as played by Alison Fiske, a magnificent one. A rich girl on the Left, she delivers a lecture on Rosa Luxemburg with inescapable condescension, her head cocked as she makes her points. A proud woman in a state of sexual dependence, she has to keep her own intelligence at arm's length, and the impossibility kills her.

As the play proceeds, she gets wittier and more driven; she can shrug with her lip. Her movements become more extreme; she prowls the stage with her back arched. Meanwhile her words pour out, until the news of her lover's final perfidy silences her: in a startlingly erotic moment her hand goes up between her legs. Miss Fiske is an actress critics regularly re-discover; after this seething, churning, glowing performance, it should never again be necessary.
1977-02-20-uncle-leo:
Uncle Leo

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Chekhov in Manchester and 'Spokesong.'

ON the subject of Uncle Vanya I make no claim to be trustworthy. The great production of 1963 -- the Olivier-Redgrave-Plowright- and everyone-else version -- is generally agreed to have been definitive, and it caught me at an age too impressionable for me to entertain the possibility of its ever being equalled. I am therefore predisposed to underrate any new production; but I am also liable to make considerable allowances. Having seen the play so intensely lived, I still carry some of its electricity with me, and plug in my memories whenever other interpreters' batteries are running low. I may be disappointed, but I am never likely to be bored.

Michael Elliott's production at the Royal Exchange, Manchester, runs true to form. Observant and intelligent but uninvolving, it never made me laugh and so could hardly expect to make me cry. But if it is not really funny, it is sometimes amusing, and if not moving, it is often, at any rate, touching -- largely due to Leo McKern's rendition of the title role.

The evening is particularly strong on silent suffering; this is a play in which characters continually and painfully blunder into the truth. They learn from the lips of sympathetically disposed third persons that life holds no consolation for them. Here their faces fall in time with their hopes, and with barometric precision. With all this clarity of detail the impact of the whole is surprisingly fuzzy.

The play emerges as a pattern of masculine self-pity and feminine endurance. Even Elena's beautiful indolence is a form of stoicism, a device for keeping at bay the embarrassment of human contact. And Eleanor Bron is unexpectedly successful at delineating this defensiveness without patronising it. Only her breakdown, when Vanya's shooting-spree forces her to take notice, fails to convince; she is not a good weeper. Joanna David is a suitably spartan Sonya, though the girls' brief reconciliation, like much else, is only half what it might be (here, more than anywhere else, my memories obtrude).

The elder ladies, Susan Richards and Peggy Thorpe-Bates, offer contrasting and instructive examples of the healing powers of routine.

While they take disappointment for granted, the men cry out against it: even Michael Feast's Waffles, whose moment of recognition (when he overhears himself described as a sponger) is among the most affecting in the play. The monstrous Professor is allowed by Alfred Burke a measure of pity; his plight as he grows old is recognisably a variant on that of Mr McKern's Vanya and Albert Finney's Astrov -- though three growling actors in one production is a lot.

If, however, Vanya and Astrov are brothers under the skin, it helps if the skins are recognisably of the same vintage and Mr Finney is handicapped by his partner's visible 15 years' start. There is great subtlety in this Astrov, particularly in his bushily disfiguring moustache and in the hands which clutch obstinately at the vodka bottle while Sonya lectures him on his drunkenness. There is remarkably little elasticity; his drunken outbursts are compelling but not his ecological passion, and most crucially he fails to plumb the depths of disillusion that should bind him to Vanya at the end.

Even Mr McKern reaches the limits of his range about here; he can present disappointment most poignantly, but he cannot, as Redgrave could, universalise failure. There is a toughness in him not finally to be gainsaid. But he draws a fine straight line between his discovery of Elena in Astrov's embrace, and his explosion when he learns that the professor is about to sell him down the Volga.

Desolation, nothing left to lose, builds into near farcical defiance, and in his stricken face you can see the fuse detonating (at least I could; I doubt if those sitting opposite got as much out of the back of his subtly heaving shoulders). It is good, too, to see a Vanya who has run not merely to seed but to fat, and fine to hear one who gives such value to the man's irony. Perhaps the best thing is the sheer pleasure of seeing him on the stage again. Now how about Falstaff?

  

And so to the latest play in the Ulster Cycle. When Stewart Parker's Spokesong opened at the King's Head last year, I read the rapturous reviews with interest, since I remembered it from the Dublin Festival as a play of rueful, agreeable moments, all of them in the first Act. The second had sunk under a story line at once complicated and inconclusive.

Now it has transferred to the Vaudeville, I still feel puzzled. The charm remains; Jimmy Kennedy's music and Mr Parker's lyrics are well-matched. The argument of the play is, to put it very crudely, that bicycles are the opposite of terror. If everybody in Belfast rode a bike, this being apparently Dunlop's own city, there would be no more war.

The author is honest enough to admit that this is not going to happen and that his hero's bike-shop will be blown up like everyone else's, but even the first proposition is excessively winsome. He weaves it in and out, though; the play is well conceived. But it is not well constructed, and the flashbacks across two generations to the Golden Age of Dunlop add weight only in the strictly arithmetical sense.

There are, to agree with everyone, two extremely winning performances. Annabel Leventon shines with common sense as Daisy Bell (the best song is not original). As her part-time mechanic and full-time wooer, Niall Buggy begins with disconcerting coyness, but the arrival of his kid brother, who is even smilier, seems to cure him of that and he rides in a straight commanding line thereafter. Thanks for the Buggy ride; I'll take a rain-check on the cycling.
1977-02-27-camp-and-clicket:
Camp and clicket

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Peter Nichols's new play at the Aldwych.

THE Royal Shakespeare Company is back in Singapore. Two years ago, in Charles Wood's Jingo, it showed us how the British in World War Two absent-mindedly succumbed to what one of their number called "the little yellow men." Peter Nichols's Privates on Parade (Aldwych) now takes us on to 1948, His Majesty's Forces determined not to get caught the same way twice.

Particularly determined is the CO, Major Flack, who grimly anticipates a Communist onslaught composed of little yellow cyclists, all going "ting-a-ling, velly solly, no more clicket now." The major is a bit hazy about speech patterns of other races, and indeed of other ranks. He means well, rather like Alan Bennett's earnest vicar in "Beyond the Fringe," acknowledging how often his flock must be tempted to say "Oh, stuff this for a lark." Home for the major is a seventeenth-century mill-house, which he cites as a symbol of the everyday British life for which they are fighting. Nigel Hawthorne's performance, sternly fatuous and decidedly likeable, could hardly be bettered.

As is usual in service comedies, the men are clowns and the officer an uncomprehending stooge. But this time the distinction is more than metaphorical; since we are concerned with an entertainments unit whose contribution to freedom is the production of--in every sense--camp concerts. Double-entendres are the Order of the Day, beginning with the title; though strictly speaking the lubricious reading is here the literal one, for nobody appears on stage below the rank of a corporal.

In charge of operations is a rampantly homosexual captain, doing his bit out East since back home "life under Clementina Attlee wasn't exactly the Roman Empire." Denis Quilley, tempering his usual robust enthusiasm with a certain primness, storms gaily through impersonations of Marlene Dietrich, Vera Lynn and Carmen Miranda before coming to rest as a surprisingly fleshly Noel Coward (actually he looks more like Donald Sinden) icily inquiring, "Could you please inform us how we came to lose the war/That we lost in 1945?" If you can mentally combine "There Are Bad Times Just Around the Corner" with "Could You Please Oblige Us with a Bren Gun" you will have the right idea.

Certainly the author and his composer (Denis King) have it, here and throughout; with so many of our playwrights attempting to turn themselves into lyricists, Mr Nichols is ahead of the field. He remains supreme, too, as a fashioner of one-liners, dead in character and dead funny.

The play is, however, very long and decidedly unwieldy. Mr Quilley, who is its particular glory, has hardly anything to do with the plot and so is often absent. The story comes in two interlocking sections. There is a love-element, played with a nice mixture of passion and bewilderment by Emma Williams as a half-caste (part Indian, part Welsh, imagine the accent) and Ian Gelder, who impersonated the youthful Mr Nichols in Forget-Me-Not-Lane and is here, I imagine, continuing the biography. There is also a sinister bit concerning a villainous sergeant-major, a source of bafflement to author, actor, director and me.

In theory, all these scenes are stylised--dramatic "numbers" in the concert-party to balance the musical ones--but the idea is scuppered by Mr Nichols's frequent recourse to passages of extended naturalism. The framework vanishes, if not from the stage, then certainly from the audience's consciousness. I doubt its necessity anyway; the device, for all its fun, represents a step backwards for Mr Nichols. There are some dead spots, too, in Michael Blakemore's production, though there is also the expected verve in theatrical effects and the accustomed precision in the ranks: note Simon Jones's pugnacious public school boy and the mannish lance-corporal of the invaluable Tim Wylton.

  

At the Royal Court there have been premieres upstairs and downstairs. (I shudder to think what is going on in my lady's chamber.) In the attic there is Tunde Ikoli's Short Sleeves in the Summer, a prolonged marital row. Black boy wants out of the factory, to the uncomprehending disgust of pregnant black girl. She begins every complaint with "Well, I'm sorry but..." which is so true to life that one starts to yearn for a little artifice. The play, however accurately observed, remains obstinately simple, its naivety emphasised by Michael Joyce's abrupt direction but belied occasionally by the alert performance of Gregory Munroe.

Down below is Devil's Island, a first stage play by Tony Bicat, brought in by Joint Stock. It is a tripartite view of the sinking British middle class: perturbed in 1937 (post-Spain), disintegrating in 1977 (post-Concho), half-bestial in 1997 (post-holocaust). The same six actors recur in all three sections, portraying roughly similar characters and retaining the same names. Thus in each period there is a man called Kutchevski, always a jump ahead of those less exotically known as Hugh or Bill or Betty, always some kind of agent-provocateur, always a man of the world, though whether of a desirable world is left discreetly in doubt.

Episode One is the best, perhaps because its setting is, in recent theatrical experience, the least familiar. The actors helped to plan, though not actually to write, the play and they seem vulnerable to stereotypes: the Present comes over as a hip Onedin Line, and the Future (in which the survivors eat dog-food if available and dog if not) is anyone's apocalypse, from the fringe of five years ago. Mr Bicat's dialogue, which starts out both elegant and electric, decays along with the rest of civilisation. In terms of performance, actors' involvement certainly pays off (Gillian Barge, Simon Callow and Jane Wood in particular); and David Hare's production, though occasionally mannered, is very clean and very good. A white sheet spread across the stage makes a dazzling tablecloth for a dinner-party scene; the diners, their debate and their reactions stand out in the sharpest relief. Mr Bicat's view of the British class system, though more overtly grim, is not perhaps far different from Mr Nichols's; his jokes, though, are less adroit.

  

Joint Stock productions tend to run a gamut from earnest worry to icy disdain; they have turned away from the stentorian commitment of The Sell-Out (Library Theatre, Manchester), whose authors, Roger Smith and Tom Kempinski, are so confident of their cause that they forget to plead it. In arraigning Ramsay MacDonald for betraying Labour by hanging out with the rich (who idle around, as is customary, having sex and things) they suggest, not that real socialist policies might have worked, but that MacDonald should have resigned and let the Tories do the dirty work necessitated by the slump. Baldwin's refusal to let his opponent put this plan into action occasions the only scene in the evening with any political bite; but the show is still a jolly one, and the many musical numbers are handled with unusual efficiency.

  

In Edith Piaf Je Vous Aime (King's Head) Libby Morris, producer and star, gives herself little opportunity to do what she does best, i.e., sing very funny very fast. Maureen Scott gets closer to Piaf's chirpy vulnerability, and a new lyric by the admirable Fran Landesman to "La Goulante de Pauvre Jean" should ensure future oblivion for the "Poor People of Paris" in whose name this song has previously been impaled on the honky-tonk pianos of the nation.
1977-03-06-the-first-sex-farce:
The first sex-farce

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

IF ALL the young acting talent working in this country were laid end to end, in A Thought in Three Parts (ICA) some of it is. It gets laid in many other positions as well. Wallace Shawn's play, as you would gather from its title, is divided into three; the second third, called The Youth Hostel, is, as far as action goes, mostly orgy, graphically staged and energetically performed.

After a short time you stop gaping at the array of pretty bodies, tempting spread, and begin to laugh. This, however, is a reaction that Mr Shawn has not merely anticipated but encouraged. Youth Hostel is a play about sex without involvement. Its characters behave like demented automata. It is, classically, a farce; maybe the first real sex-farce to reach the British stage.

Four young Americans are mainly involved. Bob, who is nervous and seems repressed, asks Helen to take her clothes off, just so that he can have a look. She, apparently for the sake of a quiet life, complies, and next moment he is on top of her. Meanwhile, in the room next door, aggressive Judy comes upon solid Dick ("I'm sorry about that") and absolutely wrecks the quiet afternoon he had planned for himself. Before long, all four are together, and ceaselessly at it.

"Tired's not the word," groans Dick, understandably, after much activity, and adds engagingly, "I need such a rest, lots of swimming." But all that actually lies in store for him is more of the same, varied by some strenuous competitive masturbation. Finally, all passion presumably spent (though "passion" here is not quite the right word), they disperse to their respective quarters, Helen is joined in hers by Tom who is apparently her husband, and who, after a crisp introduction ("smells like sperm in here, darling, have you had visitors?") proceeds to beat her up. That's love.

I doubt, whatever breakfast foods may have done for the stamina of young America, that Mr Shawn means his playlet to be taken absolutely literally. It is a fantasia on the idea of sex as a trek towards a constantly receding nirvana of orgasm, yielding some fun en route, but ultimately frustrating. He is in fact using the audacious means to point a traditional moral: turning permissiveness against itself, you might say, though if all that bouncing flesh begins to look comical, that is maybe less a comment on sex than on voyeurism.

The two enclosing plays, however, darken the vision. The closer, a monologue, presents the morning fantasies of a businessman and they do not seem satisfactory. At least, I didn't get much out of them; neither did the rest of the mystified audience, and the actor seemed a touch baffled as well. In the opener a holidaying couple -- probably married and, the most sinister thing, certifiably in love -- reveal their relationship to consist of complementary solitudes.

Mr Shawn performs the same trick here with words as he does in the second play with actions; he uses stylised rhythms to create a recognisable reality. Love-making at the end of the first piece leads naturally into the second; and beneath all three violence simmers. The author's cynicism may be self-willed (a line in the programme "for the past five years Shawn has lived happily on 16th St. in Manhattan with a Miss D.E." suggests that he is holding something back, and should in all charity share his secret with us), but he tells no outright lies and many truths. It is easy to see why his work attracted the attention of Joint Stock, an ascetic group whose previous work has shown a curt disregard for worldly pleasures. Max Stafford-Clark's production is in their best traditions, with particularly good work by Jack Klaff, Stephanie Fayerman and the versatile Robyn Goodman.

Mr Shawn's viewpoint received unexpected confirmation two nights later at the Mermaid. Terence Frisby's It's All Right If I Do It (emphasis on the "I") is concerned with the double standard. Husband and wife look back on their respective infidelities, compare totals, become explosively disgruntled, finally settle for disenchantment. I found Mr Frisby's play far more depressing than Mr Shawn's, partly because its hopelessness (as the pronouncement of experience rather than innocence) must be taken more seriously; but mainly because someone has been at pains to impose on it the veneer of West End comedy. A passage of recrimination at the beginning of the second act is authentically painful; otherwise, every time the play veers towards truthfulness, it is thrown off-course by a mechanical gag. Ayckbourn, Nichols, Stoppard, Mike Stott in Funny Peculiar, see the world comically (joyously or bitterly, it makes for the moment no odds). Mr Frisby simply applies jokes. (So does Joint Stock's Devil's Island; it is not simply a commercial disease.) Prunella Scales, a fine actress, is ferocious when she gets the chance, but her familiarity from TV domestic comedy makes her casting seem part of the strategy. John Stride, another disarmer, builds up a good thunderous roar at climactic moments.

  

To take a moral stand over Vaclav Havel, the imprisoned Czech writer, is so easy and so inevitable that the excellence of his short plays Audience and Private View (Orange Tree, Richmond) seems almost suspect. But it has to be said; he makes most, not all, of our political plays look shabby, not so much because our playwrights lack his advantages (e.g., jail) as for his ability to see a situation, humanely and ironically, in the round.

Thus, in the first play -- which is considerably the better -- the dissident writer sent to work in a brewery, though intolerably treated, is no mere martyr; he feels but cannot stop himself being patronising to the drunken Head Maltster, who offers him protection if he will -- a mere formality -- inform on himself. When the Maltster, having imbibed gallons of his own product, explodes with the accusation that even persecuted intellectuals do all right in the end, while he himself has no hope, the situation is very uncomfortable. Gordon Reid plays unwilling pin to Bill Wallis's overbearing balloon; and comedy lives.

  

For reasons I do not understand, but which probably have to do with the balance of payments, visual spectacle, condemned in native productions, is always applauded in visiting companies. Peter Stein's production of Summerfolk (brought to the Lyttelton by the Schaubuhne am Halleschen Ufer of West Berlin) looks magnificent: not just its expansively wrapped sets, its lighting, which gets the chill of sundown into your bones, but its sense of a life being lived.

A whole picnic takes place on one side of the stage while non-participants agonise and philosophise on the other. At the end of the scene the doomed bourgeoisie seem about to advance on the audience, but they are swallowed up in darkness first: a master-stroke. One actress, Edith Clever, cracks quietly and memorably up amid the throng.
1977-03-13-signals-from-outer-space:
Signals from outer space

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'Illuminatus!'

THE Cottesloe Theatre, a three-tiered black box with flexible seating arrangements -- and by that token flexible acting arrangements -- opened to the public on the Friday before last. It may be described as the National Theatre's experimental space, or perhaps as its studio, or anyway as considerably smaller than the Olivier or the Lyttelton.

It is not approached through the main National foyer, but through its own tradesman's entrance at the side of the building, on your left as you clamber out of the river. The reason for this segregation, it has been said, is to spare the purchasers of the cheap seats in the Cottesloe the sight of the buyers of expensive seats in the other houses. Or possibly vice versa. Whichever way the prejudice runs, the National really has no business to pander to it; but I appreciate that this is hardly the time to start arranging the concrete blocks all over again.

The Cottesloe can seat 400; today and for the next two week-ends, as for those just past, it probably will. At least it will at 2 p.m., which is when performances of the initial offering commence. By 11 or so, which is when they tend to finish, some gaps may have become apparent in the ranks: not many though. Having stayed the course myself, and gladly, I urge you to reject all reviewers who departed early.

The show is the product of the Science Fiction Theatre of Liverpool, a new group, and it is called Illuminatus!, that being the singular of Illuminati, an old group. The Illuminati date back, apparently, to the eighteenth century (I think; you will appreciate that in a nine-hour play many statements are made, and some of them conflict) and now they control everything, rather like the Mafia, except that the Mafia is part of what they control. They are responsible for wars and political assassinations and forbidding notices hung up in supermarkets. Their agents range from Texan red-neck sheriffs to festival-circuit rock-groups. They are under the control of, or influenced by, or at least going along with, some malevolent forces from outer space.

Opposed to them are a hard-working New York cop named Saul, a gangling radical journalist called George, and -- most formidably -- Hagbard Celine, described as Last of the Freebooters. He is served by numerous beautiful and provocatively clad girls, a singing dolphin, and a computer which, for the best of reasons, talks like John Gielgud; and they all live in a yellow submarine. Except the dolphin, of course; he lives outside.

Celine, a dedicated free-market man, is an unlikely hero to find on the fringe right now, but he certainly strikes a chord. The conflict between him and the Illuminati is that between individualism (motto: "We Discordians must stick apart") and regimentation. Thus far have we come from the simple conflict between good and evil in Lord of the Rings.

I make that comparison because Illuminatus!, too, started out as a triple-decker cult-novel, the work of two Playboy scribes, Robert Shea and Robert Anton Wilson. It comes equipped with off-putting credentials (like a recommendation from Timothy Leary) and it has been compared to the works of Kurt Vonnegut, which I find impassable; it is nevertheless an immensely engaging read -- or, in my case this week, skim. It is much funnier than it is portentous.

In their stage version Ken Campbell and Chris Langham weave in and out less than their source, keep individual strands of narrative moving for longer. They have regularised the structure, so that it seems to be moving towards a definite climax: the salvation of the world, or some such trifle. When that actually happens, and turns out not to be a climax at all, one feels a bit cheated.

The show is best when it takes the material as it comes (nearly all the dialogue is straight from source) and here its greatest asset is its sheer length. It proves most of the usual quibbles about turning novels into plays to be purely academic; all you need is time, so that you are not pressured into squeezing all the juice out of the original.

The production, on a modest end stage, pursues a simple course until interrupted by some startling or hilarious image; Mr Langham's totally engaging George wedged unaccountably into a bed one-fifth his own size; or a dying gangster, raving through a damning but incomprehensible confession in a bed perched on an alarming diagonal tilt. Or perhaps Howard the Dolphin will swim by, melodiously imparting some fragment of his race's wholly oral culture. As Hagbard says, "how could they handle pens with their fins, you know?"

Neil Cunningham is a beautifully deft and uncaring Hagbard, James Broadbent and Chris Taynton play excellently any number of roles, and David Rappaport, a midget, has a long and masterly monologue which perfectly exemplifies the fusion of English music-hall's earthy charm with the airy wisecracking flights of the Americans -- a blend that I take to be Mr Campbell's peculiar contribution. The day is well sprinkled with intervals -- so many that one loses track of the five plays into which the event is supposedly divided. You simply swallow it whole, joining towards the end in a rousing chorus which goes "Situation Normal -- All Fucked Up," as wise a comment on practically everything as the theatre currently has to offer.

  

In Back Street Romeo (Half Moon Theatre) Steve Gooch wrecks what might have been a lively, even penetrating study of factional strife in the East End (trade unionists versus petty thugs) by pinning it on to the familiar titular love-plot in which I doubt he has much real interest. The effort to keep the two elements together makes the second half of his story impossible to follow.
1977-03-20-fun-in-the-suburbs:
Fun in the suburbs

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

I MET an actor who was juggling offers; should he accept a role in Alan Ayckbourn's Bedroom Farce at the National Theatre or in the same author's 'Just Between Ourselves', shortly to open in the West End? I felt that I had been vouchsafed a glimpse of the theatre of the future.

He's taking over, all right. 'Bedroom Farce' at the Lyttelton introduces us to Mr Ayckbourn the director (credit shared with Peter Hall), hitherto unknown outside of Scarborough and a very sharp and welcome operator. This is one of the best balanced accounts of his plays to reach London. The eight characters come out equal, though I feel inclined myself to single out one group.

Joan Hickson has emerged over the past few years as one of our most valuable senior comediennes, the spirit of suburban disenchantment. Yoked here in marriage to Michael Gough (gently cadaverous with reserves of patience that he kids himself are about to run dry), she exudes a kind of narrow tolerance, something short of primness on the one side and of outright kindliness on the other.

She has perhaps some reason to be complacent; her marriage has lasted, which is more than seems likely for the three younger couples who complete the cast. One notices, though, that all of them are living more or less in accord with the advice Miss Hickson's Delia claims to have received from her own mother: 'If SEX ever rears its ugly head, close your eyes before you see the rest of it.' But though manners may not have changed, morals have, and so they feel either guilty or deprived.

Trust Mr Ayckbourn to give such a title to a play in which adultery is not only avoided, but barely contemplated. There are three bedrooms on stage, each occupied by a lawful pair trying to get some sleep. That they cannot is the fault of the fourth team, Trevor and Susannah, who are also married, but are the type rarely to be found at home in bed, or at home at all. They live, emotionally, off their friends, which is a very good way of making enemies. They impose themselves, apart from anything else, through sheer bulk.

Susannah is Maria Aitken, one of the tallest actresses in the land, very scared and continually reciting desperate mantras of reassurance ('I am not unattractive. I am attractive'). Trevor, alas, is her male equivalent, unable to reassure anybody, vague and accident-prone, and clad for much of the time (a fiendish ingenuity of Mr Ayckbourn's) in a coat some sizes too bulky for him. One of his achievements is to lean on a nondescript piece of furniture whose owner has Doomed Himself on this same endless night. It collapses, in beautiful slow motion, and Stephen Moore as Trevor somehow manages to convey that the sloth is his fault as much as the collapse; both indeed are a part of him.

Derek Newark is the home-handyman whose final fury is left to our boggling imagination, Susan Littler his patient spouse: patient at least with everyone but him. The ritziest room is occupied by the creamily witty Polly Adams, and by Michael Kitchen; not hitherto my idea of a light comedian, who plays a brilliant variation on his usual thrusting young executive, this one being laid up with a bad back. His misadventures (it hurts when he moves, and people keep disturbing him) raise the loudest laughs of the evening.

Otherwise it is not, in decibel terms, an enormously hilarious evening; the main pleasure at the time comes from seeing Mr Ayckbourn solve his latest puzzle, threading his story through the three rooms with only one lapse in credibility towards the end. In retrospect, though, one admires the psychological patterning as much as the technical. The relationships illuminate one another as they interlock; a stray barb fixes each one; Trevor and Susannah acting as twin catalysts. Unfortunately, though, they also need a scene together and here Mr Ayckbourn deserts allusiveness for head-on collision, composed, it seemed to me, of scraps from his previous plays. Once again, he has failed to do full justice to his own talent; but it is something to have the talent.

Mr Ayckbourn, though one forgets it, is not a metropolitan playwright: his plays belong to a town in which people know one another. This is not maybe what we think of as community theatre, but what we think of as community theatre is not generally engaging. There are acceptable variations and the very lively Duke's Playhouse in Lancaster has found one in Philip Martin's Sambo. This, based on a local legend, reveals to us that Lancaster's prosperity was based on the slave-trade: a local fact. It proceeds to rhyme the past with the prejudiced present. It is part historical reconstruction, part theatrical games-playing, part modern documentary. No part is wholly successful (the last is least) but the whole is intriguing. John Blackmore directs, imaginatively, one of the best teams in the regions.

A couple of years ago I used Snoo Wilson's Vampire as text or pretext for an attack on what I called 'the sins of the fringe'. He and I and the fringe itself have, I hope, all moved on a bit since then; so indeed has the play which, in its revival at the Bush, sports a completely new third act. It also boasts some smashing acting, particularly from Clive Merrison with high fanatical forehead, Patti Love jumping as if electrically programmed, and Neil Johnston reassuringly down-to-earth and a phenomenally spacious production by Dusty Hughes, demonstrating again the value to Mr Wilson's interpreters of a clear head and a sense of humour. (Especially the latter: on a strict laugh-count the play is funnier than 'Bedroom Farce'.)

There remains, however, a disconcerting brittleness about the play; it pursues across three generations a conceit--dead ideas sucking the blood of the living--to which it gives wit but not flesh. The characters (especially the Victorians of the first act) are patronised; and the play is pervaded by a mocking self-congratulatory toughness.

The dead authors most recently on view have admittedly gone some way towards proving Mr Wilson's thesis. James Bridie's Tobias and the Angel (Young Vic) demonstrates the surviving conviction that a Biblical subject is good for children and (witness 'Jesus Christ Superstar' and Chichester's gala in reviving Obey's 'Noah') for trade. The Tobias story, being Apocryphal, may not count, though its treatment here illustrates the linked belief that winsomeness is next to wholesomeness. The home-life of the travelling Tobias seems to have been blighted by a father of stupefying saintliness; once the show gets on the road it improves a bit. Bridie, though, must have done better than this.

Twelfth Night (Greenwich), pretty but torturingly slow, fails to transmute text into enchantment; though in Anna Carteret it has the complete Olivia, melting into life, and in Frank Barrie a subtly narcissistic Orsino. His picturesque poses in the first scene are so neatly satirised that it was a shock to find the sailors in the second step up in all seriousness to the same tricks. Gayle Hunnicutt smiles through Viola, Max Wall grimaces through Malvolio; neither to much effect.
1977-03-20-the-noble-roman:
The noble Roman

ROBERT CUSHMAN interviews John Gielgud, who plays Julius Caesar at the National Theatre this week.

"WHEN I was young," mused Sir John, recalling the Shakespeare plays that have recurred most frequently during his career, "Romeo and Juliet was my metronome. I was always playing Romeo or Paris or Mercutio or directing it. Then it was Richard II, then The Merchant of Venice; now it seems to be Julius Caesar. A most noble, noble play, so strict to its own shape."

John Gielgud plays Caesar in the production which opens at the Olivier on Thursday. It will be the second time he has played the role; the first was in the film of a few years back in which he co-starred with Charlton Heston. Not a great success, but then, as Gielgud says cheerfully enough, "hardly anyone saw it." Many people, however, saw and enthused over the previous film of the play, made in the fifties, in which he played Cassius, a role he had already done on stage at Stratford. And to complement these two Caesars and two Cassiuses his career also yields two Antonys: one at the Old Vic in the twenties, and the other at prep-school, where he played it, he says, with great elan.

There was also a plan once for him to play Brutus. This was in the fifties, under the aegis of Hugh Beaumont, of Tennent's, but West End economics proved hostile to a play with so many characters, each demanding his own toga. In those days Romans always wore togas. In contemporary productions they are less apt to, which is a pity, since Gielgud's acting seems permanently modern. His comic technique is always something to marvel at; and his austerity (he loves playing Prospero because he's "so remote") perfectly fits the time.

Gielgud speaks more freely than any of his critics of his own mannerisms. His gods (his own word) are the directors -- from Granville-Barker to Lindsay Anderson -- who are "not afraid to tell you when you're using old tricks." Of course one is fighting one's old admirers who don't want you to grow old and are scandalised if you say something indecent on the stage. Knowing, while not quite daring to believe, that he appeals both to the old and the young, Gielgud can contradict himself with quicksilver alacrity: at one moment musing "I've never quite achieved the hardness as an actor that I'd like," while at the next admitting a desire to stage The Merchant of Venice "as a charming fairy-tale" and lamenting the sentiment of the modern world that might torpedo the project. "It's awfully difficult now to know how to present the pretty parts of Shakespeare. Young actors aren't beautiful any more.
