Of course it's a great help for people who are wonderful actors if they haven't got to worry about their looks."

After Caesar he plays another medium-sized role in Volpone. Peter Hall assures me that it's awfully funny; a way of winding down after No Man's Land -- on stage for two hours, over two years, and on two continents. Caesar is a similar relaxation; it was his own suggestion that he should play it, lending the weight of his experience to a role that can use it. Caesar begins as a dictator and finishes a ghost; for an actor at once so commanding and so haunting (not to mention so aquiline) it seems ideal.
1977-03-27-merchant-of-folly:
Merchant of Folly

HERE we are with 'The Merchant of Venice' as a Mafia musical. 'Fire Angel' (Her Majesty's) is set in New York's Venice Bar, constructed, like so many locales in expensive British musicals, out of garish tinfoil. There is a balustrade for the Heroine to perch on, and stairs descending from it just in case (why, hello Dolly) anyone feels the urge to descend and sing a show-stopper or two.

As it turns out, the only performer to make much use of them is Gaye Brown, who plays a kind of mistress of ceremonies. Miss Brown is well known to be a trouper (she has survived 'Mardi Gras' and worse), but nobody should have to troup this much.

The show began, apparently, on the Edinburgh Festival fringe in 1974 and it is possible that, then and there, it was a pleasantly campy little frolic. It may even have been funny, though in its present form it is more humourless than most rock shows. Imagine.

Paul Bentley is credited with the book and lyrics, though where the book-writing came in I am unsure since virtually every word is sung. Mr Bentley has also written a programme-note in which he blames Ray Cooney, the impresario. He thinks, apparently, that he is thanking Mr Cooney, but his unconscious has betrayed him: It was, he makes clear, the Management -- the Mgt as they call it in 'Illuminatus!' -- which blew the show so hideously up, flattering, magnifying and (of course) amplifying its youthful self-importance to an unbearable degree.

It was the Mgt, even, who suggested updating the story, thereby opening a can of many worms. For though there is a certain logic to the Mafia setting (where else today could pounds of flesh be considered common currency?), it involves the authors in a world of which, quite plainly, they know nothing. It also involves the cast in pretending to be Americans which, in a musical, is cruel. And it compels Shylock to ask whether or not a Jew hath eyes right in the middle of New York, a city which reached a favourable consensus on the subject some time ago. (This being a moment of stress, Shakespeare's words are employed. Let us be fair; he even gets billing, probably for the first time in all his years of work on musicals.)

Shylock, here called Barach, expresses some guilt at having betrayed his brethren. This could explain why he appears at one point devoutly clad in a prayer-shawl, but minus a cap. C. T. Wilkinson brings some guts to the role and profits from the best moment in Roger Haines's score, a falsetto cry of 'I am a vulture.' There is little else of musical characterisation; the fatal flaw of all rock musicals. Shakespeare's Portia had wit and good manners; her equivalent here starts bawling soulfully at us ('My Body's Weary') before we have even been properly introduced. She was only a godfather's daughter, but she knew about mercy and rain.

Her lover, rather neatly, pawns his own body instead of a friend's to raise the million bucks necessary to enter the casket contest. At the end boy and girl go off wearing musical haloes; since he has been a gangster like any other this seems a bit sudden. The implications of the story and the milieu have not, if I may understate, been thought through. Lorenzo and Jessica are also present, beseeching the 'shining moon, bright madonna' to help us find the wonder-world of love. If they haven't found it already, why are they eloping? What kind of musical is this anyway?

The answer, unfortunately, is that it is typical: a meeting of musical amateurishness and commercial know-how that doesn't. It is woefully important, too, since Mr Cooney controls five London theatres, and since this folly will probably lose enough money to ruin the chances of future investment even in good musicals. Especially in good musicals.

  

This has not been Shakespeare's week. At the Olivier, John Schlesinger has directed a Julius Caesar full of bright ideas on unimportant matters. A mysterious couple of lines in the murder scene for a senator called Popilius Lena are definitively explained. The murder itself, however, is not. John Gielgud as Caesar has his moments of public grandiloquence and private petulance, but it is not enough to deposit an actor of his rank in a young company and hope the contrast will do its own work.

Caesar is more a director's problem than an actor's and this production gives no idea of what kind of ruler he was or might have become. So the conspiracy seems pointless and so, by logical process, do the conspirators. Bits of Brutus and Cassius can be seen floating by, with the actors, Brian Cox and Ronald Pickup, making frantic efforts to jump on board. One feels sorry for Mr Cox, who acts sympathetically and with more technical command than ever before, and enraged for Mr Pickup, who should have been ideal for Cassius and who has to begin the evening by wondering what to do while Caesar speaks in praise of fatness right to his famished face. (There is a theoretical defence even of this idea, but no practical vindication on the stage.)

Mark McManus as Antony does come through, a little surprisingly since he has a shrill and unprepossessing voice, which wrecks him in his private grief over Caesar's body. His public grief is another thing and he manages it by sheer cunning; the shifting emphases on 'honourable men' are very clever. It helps, too, that he is acting in a real amphitheatre. Otherwise there is a warped amusing Casca from Gawn Grainger; murky sets and costumes that may not be fatal but are certainly depressing, and an all-pervading lack of impetus.

  

The most respectable offering of the week was probably Hugh Whitemore's Stevie (Vaudeville), but I cannot get very enthusiastic about a play which only attains to real life when its heroine starts reciting her own poetry. Since she is Stevie Smith she has the right, but the bulk of the evening is heavy and monotonous going; it concerns Stevie's relationship with 'the lion aunt' (Mona Washbourne, most comfortable of actresses) with whom she spent most of her life. So that we will not think that we are watching just another box-set play, a corner of the stage is sawn off and left for the unfortunate Peter Eyre to stand in. He narrates, and recites such verse as the heroine herself cannot manage. From time to time he enters the action as a collective Friend; he has the best scene, complaining of the poetess's assumption that every car-owning acquaintance was ipso facto her private chauffeur. Glenda Jackson in the title role is steely and remarkably sustained.

On the whole I shall vote for the Actors' Company, though they have lost most of their identity and their chosen vehicle, Pinero's The Amazons (Wimbledon), is a nonsense, as may be gleaned from its sub-title 'A Romantic Farce.' Of course it ends up neither, and its subject--three girls brought up to be boys and regretting it when suitors arrive--had better not be considered seriously. But it gets a bright production from John David, charming acting from Cheryl Campbell, and from Simon Cadell, as an insecurely Anglicised Frenchman, rather a tour of force.
1977-04-03-archie-rice-returns:
Archie Rice returns

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the Actors' Company.

WITH half its Arts Council grant about to disappear, the Actors' Company is understandably in turmoil. It has, however, other things to worry about. Three years ago it was a vital, individual and, as seen from the audience, exceptionally likeable organisation. Aesthetically it never strayed far from the middle of the road, but it lent exceptional gaiety to the locale. It has shrunk in spirit, in numbers, and in repertoire. With five plays in a season, across-the-board casting can be fun for everybody. When the board contracts, it seems pointless. There are only two full-length plays in the current list, and that is not enough for us to get the sense of a company.

The truth is of course that the organisation of a company matters far less than its personnel; when the original bright sparks moved on all they had to bequeath was an unwieldy--though not necessarily impracticable--principle. A committee of actors is still a committee, and its failure to come up with any exciting new plays (which are usually the products of individual enthusiasm) is understandable. Even their old plays have mostly been drawn from stock.

In the company's London seasons it has laboured under a further handicap: the looming Wimbledon Theatre, which blighted the rather sprightly version of Pinero's odd romp The Amazons. In John Osborne's The Entertainer, however, it has lit on a play which benefits to some extent from performance in a half-empty barn. If we respond warmly to Archie Rice's routines--the incredibly awful songs and the credibly awful jokes--the point is gone. Ronald Lewis's Archie offers a strikingly stylised image of variety in its death-throes. He is multi-coloured (grey hat, gold jacket, white gloves, red pants) and yet pallid: a puppet pierrot. Nicholas Renton's production makes a fine thing of Archie's preparations for his last performance: a slow, solemn robing followed by the ritual bound on stage to appallingly perky music. The speech that follows may still, in its controlled ashen bitterness, be the best Mr Osborne has written.

But the composition hardly matches up to its coda. One speech for Archie's son (given a tight, explosive delivery by Allan Corduner) exhausts what the play has to say on its removed subject, England; on its immediate subject, the music-hall, it is unconvincing, repeatedly stating a case for the glory of Archie's veteran father without ever demonstrating it.

When his daughter-in-law loses patience with him, it is a supremely welcome moment; it is tied to an actual incident, almost the only one in a wasteland of talk. Phoebe is a good chance for the right actress; and Margery Mason, alternating comfort and hysteria, is on her home ground. These domestic scenes need all the realistic help they can get, but the dramatists' scheme and the wide Wimbledon stage both deny it.

  

William Douglas Home's In the Red (Whitehall) started at the Theatre Royal, Windsor, a theatre which--like Chichester--tends to be more West End than the capital. Here we have our own problems and the anguish of a horse-backing playwright (this is the plot, not the author's biography). Surprised in his £65,000 house by demands that he pay off his £11,000 overdraft is apt to defeat us.

Mr Home in similar plight would probably buckle down and write a few more plays; he has three due in town this year. His hero, though, resolves (a) to play on his bank manager's sympathy and (b) to blackmail him: two plans which seem to me to contradict each other but which he puts into practice simultaneously. The plotting is repetitive and desultory, but the dialogue has pace if nothing else. Gerald Harper is smooth, Dinah Sheridan is gallant. Norman Rossington, playing banker, wins sympathy, both as character and actor.

  

The productions which have looked best at the Lyttelton, other than Bedroom Farce, have been imports: from Lyons, from Berlin, and now from Leicester, whose offering turns out the most exotic of all. The Phoenix Company has brought us The Magic Drum, adapted and directed by Michael Bogdanov from an original by James Kirkup, about a Chinese boy with a talking drum that only he can play. (Anyone remember Sparky and his magic piano?) Summoned by the emperor--a music-fancying tyrant, apparently--he runs away and is drowned, but enjoys a posthumous triumph. Aimed at five- to 11-year-olds, the play will actually enchant anyone who looks and listens. Its use of oriental techniques is the most delightful yet encountered on our stage.

  

There is more to gaze at in the Cambridge Theatre Company's Dog's Dinner, a first play by Robert William, playing this week in Harlow, after a fortnight at the Cambridge Arts. It is set in a rotting many-storeyed house. Jonathan Lynn's production, crisply manoeuvred and acted throughout, gets off to a taking start when a voyeur, spying on his ex-wife next door, tumbles from attic to cellar, setting off laughter, gasps, and a terrific dust-storm. He finds that he has fallen among tramps and beseeches them to kill him. They agree, though he nearly goes back on the idea when he finds that they dispose of corpses by eating them. He ends up crucified and the dialogue goes lightly abusive to match. Edward Petherbridge plays him with grace, but his character is too lightly sketched for us to care about the ramifications.

  

In Manchester the Royal Exchange Company has an uproarious though imperfect time with Present Laughter, which begins as Noel Coward's best play and ends as, at any rate, his most likeable. The limitation of Coward's world to an inner circle of theatricals is here a conscious device rather than the unwitting product of a patronising myopia. The major premise--everybody idolises and/or battens on star actor Gary Essendine--is triumphantly sustained; the minor premise--the comfortable mutual devotion of Gary and his immediate cabal is of permanent value--is far more dubious, and the dodo plot unfortunately depends on it.

Coward was always apt to fall back on priggishly elegant professions of faith, which Albert Finney delivers as he does much of the role--raucously. Mr Finney comes on, always, as an ordinary chap: very well for Hamlet or Tamburlaine, but not for Gary. Your true blue Coward is effortlessly actorish; Mr Finney has to work at it. He clowns engagingly, at times superbly, and carries the audience, but he is more friend than idol.

Gary is essentially sexless, but he competes too strenuously with the grotesques who besiege him. They meanwhile are building up their own excessive heads of steam, except as usual Michael Feast as the apprentice playwright Roland Maule, flinging himself devoutly wherever the Essendine feet may be planted: he is ecstatic. Alone in this company--not counting, on second thoughts, John Quayle's coolly independent manservant--he exercises both boldness and control.
1977-04-10-back-to-the-motorway:
Back to the motorway

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

STEPHEN POLIAKOFF has a keener eye and nose than any other playwright for British rubbish, new-style. No scene of his has registered more strongly than the young couple in Hitting Town up-ending the inedible contents of a Wimpy Bar. His latest piece Strawberry Fields (Cottesloe) takes us on a guided tour of the new wastelands.

Three young people make their way by van up the motorway, which got its own theatrical come-uppance some years ago in Lay-By (of which Mr Poliakoff was one of the multiple authors) and does not seem to have improved its image since. We see them picnicking by slag-heaps and tucking painfully into Chicken Maryland, waited on by the cleaner in an all-night cafe whence all but she have fled. They conduct conversations on the plastic orange chairs of a bus-station sun-lounge, in a men's lavatory which the girl of the party proclaims to be the ugliest place she has ever seen, and in a condemned corner of Doncaster, whose principal features are a cinema, closed down, and a hot-dog stand, unmanned. Finally they arrive in the cleaner air of rural Northumberland, and give thanks for an unspoiled bit of old England. The idyll, though, is rendered decidedly ironic by the fact that they are now on the run. On the journey up they killed a man.

Two of the trio, Charlotte and Kevin, represent something called the English People's Party; the third, Nick, conventionally decent, is along for the ride and to argue with them. The EPP appear at first to be ecologists; it then becomes apparent that conservation has led them to conservatism and beyond. They are right-wing fanatics, though they dissociate themselves from the National Front, perhaps because their own prejudices are aesthetic; they regard immigrants as blots on the landscape. It is Charlotte who pulls the trigger in Doncaster, thereby reversing most of our expectations; we are used to plays about left-wing guerrillas.

Much of the play indeed seems an attempt to give the devil his due; to put the opposition into the glamorous fugitive position usually reserved for the author's own side. Kevin dreams that he and Charlotte will achieve Bonnie-and-Clyde immortality, and he gets a tremendous charge when the news of their crime takes over the air-waves on all available stations. He is going blind, once spent all his time in cinemas, and claims that his head is so full of movies that if pointed at a screen he could disgorge a full show.

Kevin might be an orthodox counter-culture hero-victim out of Heathcote Williams. But, while we are dropping names, David Edgar in Destiny and Alan Drury in The Man Himself have delved into the psychology of the new fascist far more persuasively than Mr Poliakoff does here. He relies on big speeches, but keeps us waiting for them a long time; when they arrive so much rides on them that they can hardly help sounding forced.

His feeling for detritus remains as acute as ever and he can make you taste in your own mouth an endless motorway night, with no sleep and only sludge to eat. The odyssey of this play is a logical one for him to take, but his characters seem to have been press-ganged into it. Michael Apted's production is stronger on place (table and fruit machines dotted strategically) and on travel (headlamps raking the auditorium between stops) than on personality; nobody opens up much or even walks very far. You notice that the Cottesloe, though it may be the National Theatre's baby stage, is still a healthy size and not, on this showing, designed for chamber work. The principals--Jane Asher, Stephen Rea and Kenneth Cranham--are conscientious but subdued; though Miss Asher has both the hardness and the pale elegance for Charlotte, and it makes a change to hear Mr Cranham as the voice of reason. Maya Kemp's impromptu waitress is a gem; Mr Poliakoff has always been good at waitresses. This is not a disgraceful play for him to have written or for the National to have staged, but I hope for better.

  

For All Those Who Get Despondent (at the Theatre Upstairs last week) is not actually calculated to cheer anyone up. It is described as a cabaret, drawn from the works of Brecht and Wedekind--both performers in the vein themselves as well as writers, though much of the Brecht material dates from later, soberer years. The Wedekind words--and, at one point, the Wedekind music--are agreeably black and anarchic; the Brecht is preachier and the company seem disposed to ram it down our throats.

Myra Love, a smouldering singer, came among us looking not merely daggers but whole armouries; Anna Calder-Marshall, a powerful bleeding-heart actress in the right environment, drained all the slyness from such a question as 'where, the evening that the Great Wall of China was finished, did the masons go' and substituted black accusation. It was good to hear Hanns Eisler's Brecht-settings (particularly The Love Market), which balance harshness with subtlety; later chord-thumpers, take note. Peter Barnes's translations show, for one so steeped in the best of popular song, a surprising indifference to rhyme and metre.
1977-04-10-the-new-jenny:
The new Jenny

ROBERT CUSHMAN meets a Brechtian songstress.

IN A dance studio in Battersea, the familiar reed-laden orchestrations sounded more sinister than ever. This was the first and only orchestra rehearsal for the Oxford Playhouse production of 'The Threepenny Opera.' Gordon McDougall directs with, as he says, 'the same back-up team' who a year ago achieved a critical success with another Brecht-Weill show, 'Happy End.' They opened last week in Stirling. This week they are at the Cambridge Arts Theatre, then Torquay, and after that home to Oxford.

It's one way to see Britain, and the cast of virtual unknowns happens to be headed by a couple of visitors. Macheath is a Canadian, Cedric Smith; Jenny is a 32-year-old West German songstress, Eva Meier, whose sole previous appearance here was in a programme that played for one week at the Open Space just over a year ago. There she was seen by a BBC TV director planning an 'Omnibus' film on Brecht called 'Song of Mandalay'; he put her in it, singing a couple of numbers, and she made a considerable impression.

Brecht and his progenitor Wedekind--two writers who were linked in London last week in a 'cabaret' at the Theatre Upstairs--are the staples of Eva Meier's repertoire when at home. She admits, quite rightly, to being prettier than the average Brechtian: 'I'm not the type supposed to sing Brecht--you're supposed to look hard.' Singing the familiar Brecht-Weill songs in concert she broke with tradition, refusing to look 'sinister or whorelike or always in bar-rooms.' Instead she 'distanced' the material, which sounds a good Brechtian concept.

As for the later Brecht songs, the more overtly political ones with music by Hanns Eisler (whom she prefers to the more obviously appealing Weill), for them 'you can look as you look.' All that is necessary is to get the meaning over. As for the continuing importance of that meaning: 'I think the songs are still right in the big sense, but I don't think they can do very much, as theatre on the whole can't do very much. I think that's realistic.'

There is no shortage of Brecht singers in Germany; and German actors and actresses are bred on the songs. (In the same way, it struck me, British actors grow up with the songs of our own theatrical archetype, Noel Coward, and will sing them on any provocation.) Styles, however, have changed with the years. When she heard the original twenties recordings of 'The Threepenny Opera,' Eva Meier was surprised to hear how smooth it all sounded, with 'Lotte Lenya singing like a bird, very high. I thought it was very comical. It was only later that the style changed to being very harsh, and everybody did the political songs and forgot about Brecht having humour.' (A lapse of memory that persists to this day, certainly in Britain.)

Eva Meier started as 'a normal actress,' going the rounds of the German metropolitan theatres: Trier, Dusseldorf, Stuttgart, Munich. She got into singing almost by accident, when, disillusioned by the theatre (she had trouble with dictatorial directors), she approached Bavarian Broadcasting for work. A producer there asked her if she could sing, to which she replied that she had learned something about it at acting school. He decided she was right for a Wedekind programme he was mounting at the Piccolo Teatro in Milan. She spent six weeks practising, eight hours a day, and five days before the opening reckoned she was just about ready to get through the show.

That 'spectacular' debut (she laughs at the description) was followed by a Brecht-Eisler evening, and the realisation that this new career, in which she could do everything herself, was more enjoyable than the old. Brecht-singing being a crowded field in Germany, she has not been able to work at it full-time; she has filled the gaps studying jurisprudence. The Oxford production marks her first return to the theatre since the start of her concert career and, surprisingly, her first performance of this material. But then all Brechtian chanteuses do the Jenny songs, so she has kept off them. At least she hasn't had to unlearn the German before learning the English.
1977-05-01-after-the-fox:
After the fox

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

A CRITIC once described the late Donald Wolfit as 'the master of Renaissance excess.' It is not a mastery which anyone else in our theatre has visibly inherited. Two of the Elizabethan supermen whom Wolfit patented during his lifetime have now reappeared at the National Theatre in productions by Peter Hall; Jonson's 'Volpone' followed Marlowe's 'Tamburlaine' into the Olivier last Tuesday.

They are both outstandingly well-ordered productions. 'Tamburlaine' took full note of Marlowe's debt to medieval tradition, and 'Volpone' pays more of the same dues, along with a few more ancient. Jonson the classicist would certainly have appreciated the clarity of Mr Hall's production, both as narrative and morality. He does particularly well by the closing trial scenes, with their lightning series of reversals of fortune; I have never before seen these staged comprehensibly.

Earlier he lets us see exactly what is at stake in Volpone's attempted seduction of Celia. White innocence (well aware of its own merits in Morag Hood's delicious performance), is stalked by red luxuriance, a fittingly ambiguous term denoting both wealth and lechery. He woos her with a display of gold, and with an even more impressive display of learning, proposing that they re-enact together most of the erotic myths in Ovid. It is, until the last violent moment, aesthetic rape.

With Volpone the aesthete Paul Scofield is, as you would expect, thoroughly at home. The sonorous voice caresses the cadences, and there is enough heroic pride in him to make his final reckless self-exposure a believable (and thrilling) moment. He is the most bushily resplendent of foxes. But it is not enough. Critics are supposed to declare their prejudices, so here are mine. Memories of Wolfit's Volpone (which I saw only on television but that was enough) have conditioned my reading of the play: a greasier, dustier one than the Hall-Scofield combination provides.

Theirs is a world in which vices are emblematically displayed, verbally anatomised, but never solidly realised. Again, Jonson might approve (such restraint is perhaps the comic equivalent of keeping your tragic deaths offstage) and the production probably does full justice to his icy intent. It fails to account, though, for his less calculated qualities: for the gusto (not just the intellectual excitement) of his plotting, and for the excess spleen which turns his stereotypes into monsters. Thus Hugh Paddick's Corbaccio is a pretty neat sketch of senility but hardly virulent enough to justify the rhetorical abuse he evokes. Michael Medwin goes through the motions of Corvino's jealousy without ever probing its brutality. (The casting is as acquisitive as Volpone himself; just about everybody comes direct from a big success in something or other.)

Belief in Mr Scofield himself snaps when he attempts actually to ravish Celia; if that magniloquent figure were had up on a rape-charge he would not have to resort to Volpone's extremes to get off. He misses the earthiness of Volpone as Albert Finney missed the airy part of Tamburlaine; if these two might somehow be combined we could have a Wolfit-and-a-quarter, capable of versatility within a role.

Ben Kingsley makes a very nifty Mosca. John Gielgud gives a charming sketch of the English tourist Sir Politic (his fear that he may become 'a thing for tavern talk' is the evening's most memorable line, an improvement, as it happens, on Jonson's original) and Elizabeth Spriggs has no trouble with his spouse, tyrannically rouged and fearsomely loquacious.

  

Meanwhile at the Cottesloe we have had The Passion, derived from the York Mystery Cycle. There seems to be a belief, lurking somewhere at the National, that 'popular theatre' can be achieved simply by performing these plays in modern dress with reconstructed Pennine accents. Since the original performers were amateur and indigenous, where these are professional and from all over, the belief is ingenuous; there are actually many levels of artifice involved here, and the deployment of a folk-rock band, an artificial construct in itself, emphasises the point. Nothing is more calculated than an atmospheric pause for song.

The strength of the plays is altogether different; it arises when the authors almost lose sight of the Biblical story and write out of their own lives. Here too there is chronological confusion (are these torturers, British workmen who can't even get a crucifixion done on time, operating in the first or the fifteenth century AD?) but of a different order from that which the directors, Bill Bryden and Sebastian Graham-Jones, have introduced. Their concoction, though, is enjoyable, sometimes impressive, best seen from the balconies above, best experienced from ground-level where you mingle with the actors. The Albion Dance Band provide both joyous and chilling moments, and Brian Glover is a sensibly native addition to the company; he and Pitt Wilkinson make the priests the most convincing figures around. Richard Johnson's Pilate, a befuddled Lord Mayor, is a pleasing performance but unpersuasive; I don't believe that is how the authors actually saw him, though I appreciate that it would be nice to think so.

  

Oh, Mr. Porter (Mermaid) has the misfortune to be a double sequel; wittingly to 'Cole,' unwittingly to 'A Chorus Line.' Here the performers, duly employed, arrive for rehearsal to find themselves deserted. They break into a series of Cole Porter songs, 40 in all, and we could do with more as a relief from Benny Green's dialogue. This is mainly composed of random bitching, and even on that level it sounds inauthentic. It has nothing to do with the songs (compare Peter Bogdanovich's film 'At Long Last Love' which furnished characters fit to sing them) and seems intended as a parody of some form in Mr Green's head. Even his understanding of the music seems defective; the serenely triumphant 'I Concentrate on You' is introduced as 'an unrequited love song.'

The cast are required to spend a good deal of time looking indulgently at one another; none is better at this than Kenneth Nelson, who perches and lounges with a seraphic smile as if the others were things in his (happy) dream. He looks more like Porter now than when impersonating him in 'Cole,' and he phrases his share of the lyrics with becoming care; only Jeanette Ranger, of the rest, comes near him. Concerted numbers can be fun; having disinterred Porter's worst song ('Ladies in Waiting') from his worst score ('Les Girls') they perversely brought down the house with it. The show closes with more choruses of 'You're the Top' than I have ever heard at one sitting before; that may sound an arcane recommendation but enthusiasts will take the hint.
1977-05-08-home-with-sir-ralph:
Home with Sir Ralph

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

RALPH RICHARDSON plays every role as though he had written it himself. He does not actually give the impression of making it up as he goes along (he is far too deliberate for that), but he bestows upon his lines a weight which, however eccentric, registers always as unarguable, inimitable, right.

In The Kingfisher (Lyric) Sir Ralph as playwright is off form: or, to drop the pretence, William Douglas-Home's script is an unworthy choice. As in No Man's Land, Sir Ralph is a lonely literary lion -- in this case a literary laird -- reaching out for companionship while the effective prisoner of his own domestic staff (which this time numbers one). You do not have to be a Pinter fanatic to find yourself aching in this piece for a comparable wit or resonance. Sir Ralph, delivering his customary goods, keeps you aching. His words sound as ever like oracular utterances, if you can conceive of an oracle possessed of both humour and vulnerability. They ought to go beyond the commonplace, but they never make it.

Of course Sir Ralph is grouchily splendid, and of course Celia Johnson, as the lady of his past whom he hopes to make the lady of his future, is sweet and sensible, and of course Alan Webb as the jealous valet is superb. The triumphant narrowing of his eyes when he hears that his master's romance, once on, is now off, provides the most memorable moment of the evening, closely followed by Sir Ralph's defensive mockery of an unseen crippled neighbour.

  

Two breaks in the bland surface, though, are hardly enough; a third -- plainly intended to be the biggest of all -- misfires. Miss Johnson alleges that Mr Webb has been in love with Sir Ralph for 50 years. In a play of course you can allege anything; unless you can also demonstrate in action, though, your audience will refuse either to believe or to care. All that is really on offer here (stressed in Lindsay Anderson's direction and Alan Tagg's arboreal setting) is "atmosphere."

There are other atmospheres and one more invigorating may be breathed in Barrie Keeffe's A Mad World, My Masters (Young Vic). The title has been used before -- by Thomas Middleton in 1605 -- and though his play might repay revival, it is good to have the title to be going on with: an excellent one which sums up a whole genre. Middleton excelled in the Jacobean city comedy, which recognised corruption and obsession, shook its head, dried its eyes, shrugged its shoulders and laughed.

Many modern playwrights, feeling their own London to be every bit as steamy as their ancestors', have hankered after the form; few have plunged into it with as much spirit as Mr Keeffe. If some of his set-pieces of invective reinforce the suspicion that the English language now swings less easily than it did 350 years ago, what distinguishes Mr Keeffe is the ceaseless energy of his plotting; the play never stops moving. It has, what is more, a destination; everything converges on the Royal Mews where the Queen of England (this is a jubilee production) frostily announces that she is not in the habit of bestowing knighthoods on geese.

Middleton and company may have been Mr Keeffe's springboard, but other influences have come between; I was reminded of the Goons, of Theatre Workshop in its bustling heyday, and of the stage version of The Fosdyke Saga. Jane Wood, who was the scheming Mrs Fosdyke, is now the scheming Mrs Sprightly, deprived by a legal technicality of the insurance due on her son (who died when all he really wanted was, profitably, accident) and bent on revenge. Her prey is a tycoon, a fanatical monarchist whose main desires are under-age girls and a knighthood. His daughter careers through the play on a bicycle, dripping, in Cecily Hobbs's aptly dewy performance, with social conscience. A police inspector sizes up the opposing forces, decides that might could well be right, and goes into disguise as, roughly speaking, Margaret Thatcher: a role in which Simon Callow outdoes himself.

  

An Irish doctor feeds a whole housing development on tranquillisers and the occasional aphrodisiac. An out-of-sight (and out-of-mind) musician wanders through. Miss Wood doubles as the Queen. A younger Sprightly, persuaded of her resemblance (which is indeed considerable) to Angela Rippon, does a cunning and beautiful strip while reading the news; since the actress is Gillian Barge, previously noted in rather straitlaced roles, the effect is as great as if Angela herself had bared all. The Joint Stock company, directed by William Gaskill and Max Stafford-Clark, enjoys a marvellous holiday, and so do we.

Towards the end, Mr Keeffe introduces mayhem. I suspect that his principles were nagging him; the Jacobean Sprightlies would have been triumphant gull-catchers; Mr Keeffe has to remind himself that his are downtrodden. After an evening spent admiring their roguery, this seems like cheating. Still, I suppose he has the right to spoil his own play.

  

Peter Barnes's alteration of the ending of a genuine Jacobean comedy, Jonson's The Devil is an Ass (Lyttelton), is more questionable.

Jonson finished with some of his characters coming to their senses, and others behaving with positive decency. This seems to have disappointed Mr Barnes, who puts the whole cast literally at one another's throats and brings on Satan, who should know, to tell us how awful they are. Jonson wrote only one watertight malevolent morality, Volpone, set in Venice. His London plays are looser and, if only by default, more genial.

The refusal of Shakespeare's generation to be as cynical as we would like is a constant source of pain to our theatre. In The Devil's stablemate at the Lyttelton, Measure for Measure, the Duke is presented as an impish prankster concerned with nothing but enjoying his own manoeuvres. Nobody is going to believe this, but here goes: Measure for Measure is what it claims to be, a comedy. It has a happy ending. It is, what is more, a romantic comedy and the Duke is the juvenile lead. He gets the girl and deserves to. All that apart, these two Birmingham Rep productions, directed by Stuart Burge, are well worth their visitation and ours. Peter Vaughan's Fitzdottrel in The Devil has grown in stature; in foolishness, in vindictiveness, and in perverted geniality. The National's Volpone could use him. In Measure Anna Calder-Marshall and David Burke give great strength to the Angelo-Isabella relationship. Supporting playing in both is very solid.

  

King Lear (Aldwych), though a hell of a thing to encounter at the end of a long week, is another gift from the Midlands. Trevor Nunn's production is much tightened since Stratford; the Victorian costumes are unobtrusive and helpful. The wicked sisters (Barbara Leigh-Hunt and Meg Davies) develop plausibly from frigid propriety to sadism, and two performances (Bob Peck's Kent and Michael Pennington's Edgar) are much improved.

Hopkins must have been inspired by Lear when he wrote that "the mind, mind has mountains"; Donald Sinden frequently brings us, shivering, to their edge, lurching towards some terrible new thought. His recognition of Poor Tom, "the thing itself," is finely done; so is the robust tyranny of the beginning. All that is missing, in production and performance, is the concerted cataclysm of the end; this is not a great Lear, but it is a very good one.
1977-05-15-in-perfect-harmony:
In perfect harmony

THE lesson of A Midsummer Night's Dream may be that you never get out of the wood. Certainly that seems to be the upshot of John Barton's new production at Stratford. When we enter the theatre, mottled shadows, leaf-patterned, cover the back wall of the set. They fade to invisibility during the opening scene in the Athenian court, but once re-established they are a fixture. The final revels -- the marriages and the performance of 'Pyramus and Thisbe' -- take place in their shadow: almost it seems by their permission.

It makes perfect sense; we are explicitly told that the fairies who rule the wood also rule the world, and without their intervention the last act of the play would never happen. They make up its unseen audience; if Mr Barton has sacrificed some of the surprise of their final celebratory appearance he has made it seem perfectly logical. He has also made it an occasion of genuine joy; the choreographer Gillian Lynne is listed as his co-director, and the lyric accomplishment of this sequence, as of much else in the evening, must surely be credited to her.

It is something at Stratford in 1977 to see greenery that actually looks green; something, too, to find fairies who might have been taken from some sumptuously eclectic collection of children's picture-books. (There are even children present to play Peaseblossom, Cobweb, Moth and Mustardseed; with so much tradition about, I almost expected to hear Mendelssohn, but there are limits. Actually, by the Renaissance-Gothic standards that are established here, Mendelssohn would appear a strident modern.)

The politics of this fairyland are complicated; Titania has a copious train, but they all seem to be double agents working for Oberon. And though there is plenty of majesty in Marjory Bland's white-goddess performance, she cannot be said to stand much of a chance. OK or not, Oberon rules; you might guess as much from the casting. In a mainly young and untried company the experienced Patrick Stewart stands alone. Generally thought a dour plain actor, he has in fact (witness his Moor in Titus Andronicus), a considerable flair for the exotic. This Oberon, come from the farthest step of India, bronzed physically and vocally, is night to her day. When he threatens her the lights go down; when she defies him they go up again. But though sinister, Mr Stewart stops short of malevolence; his attitude to Puck ('I saw but thou couldst not') is patronising but protective. Leonard Preston is a cheery hobgoblin but capable, in his description of the lost-soul graveyard sprites, of real dread. Mr Barton, in fact, has thought out his fairy kingdom, even to the details of magic applied without anaesthetic: When Lysander receives the love-juice, he writhes violently; Titania, loving an ass, tries a few enthusiastic 'hee-haws' of her own and her revulsion when his true nature is revealed is not, for once, passed over.

The lovers run to type; there are not really too many ways of playing them. Marilyn Galsworthy adds to the treasurable list of funny languishing Helenas. Some of the mechanicals, too, are easily recognisable in outline, though transfigured by sheer intensity of performance; so Snug's declaration that he is 'slow of study' seems in Brian Coburn's performance as shattering a stroke of genius as anything in Shakespeare. (It is beautifully capped when Quince absently hands him the massive script intended for Pyramus.)

Richard Griffiths's Bottom, however, is a true original; not a shover, but a man quietly sure of his own talents, though still capable of modest musing when their full extent is revealed. He is gentle and a very good choice for Pyramus; he might also make a good Thisbe. (I would not myself cast him as the Lion.) The first entrance of this fellowship transforms the play, which gets off to a chilly start. By the end, all is harmony. It is ritual to say of a Stratford production that it will probably improve; this one is pretty good already.

  

David Edgar's Destiny (which has transferred to the Aldwych) has improved in most details, though not perhaps in overall impact. A play that seems to be bursting its bonds (as this one did at the Other Place last year) is obviously more exciting than one that seems snugly confined; in a big theatre some domestic scenes seem strained and the tendency of all concerned to speak in quotable quotes (a young Tory is described as 'all slim suits and unit trusts') jars rather.

David Edgar's characters convince most when addressing the audience (often in packed, witty verse) or when locked in ideological combat: an activity for which their author's scheme--to explore and document the advance of the far right in Britain--affords almost unlimited scope. Mr Edgar's strength is his refusal to recognise limits: to push every situation to the point where allegiances cross, friends divide, enemies unite.

The play begins with the breakup of the British Raj in India, whence four men return to England, home and disillusion. The device lends shape and meaning; British Fascism is traced to the imperial hangover. But there is never (except perhaps in an over-neat last scene) any simple finger-pointing; Michael Pennington's major calling for an 'iron dawn' has a moment of stomach-turning agony that is fully communicated, and Ian McDiarmid plays quite superbly the army sergeant turned dispossessed shopkeeper turned parliamentary candidate for Nation Forward. He charts magnificently the inroads of resentment, misfortune and fear: He has everybody's grievances and is everybody's dupe; his shell hardens then cracks before you.

John Nettles unerringly hits off his campaign manager, a media man misplaced, and Leonard Preston, cropping up again (though I suppose commuting presents few problems to a Puck), gives his youngest follower a fey, unnerving smile. The social types are immaculately hit off in Ron Daniels's production; and these, please note, are mainly the same actors who so richly inhabit 'King Lear' on other nights.

'Destiny' may be the best new play in London. William Douglas Home's Rolls Hyphen Royce (Shaftesbury) may be the worst. No, I suppose not, but the expensive chassis (cast of 30 and we thought the West End was starving) coats a mini-vehicle. Might this be true of the Rolls-Royce itself? All we learn is that Rolls (Peter Egan, good) was a young smoothie, Royce (Alfred Marks, better) an old roughneck and the hyphen was Wilfrid Hyde White who sat at the side of the stage amiably receiving and retailing information, and occasionally joined the action like one who wished he was elsewhere. The galleried set looks amazingly like a prison. The West End seems to have latched on to the documentary craze as once was, but at this date, and at these prices, who will care?

Once they gave us stoic plays about the middle class gritting its teeth at the loss of its privileges. (The other face of 'Destiny,' perhaps.) N. C. Hunter's Waters of the Moon is a perfectly decent example, worthily if stodgily revived at Chichester and pointing the necessary moral that for some people life is every bit as bad as it seems. Brian Spink, Mary Hignett, and Adam Bareham are among the noblest sufferers, with Wendy Hiller outstaring them all. Smiling in the opposite corner is Ingrid Bergman, every inch the guest-star, all wealth and charm, though perhaps more frivolous, less challenging, than the late author may have intended. There should, I fancy, be iron in her somewhere.
1977-05-15-profile-trevor-nunn:
PROFILE/Trevor Nunn

Ten years at Stratford

AT CAMBRIDGE Trevor Nunn racked up 32 productions for university drama societies. You can still see the persistence ("I overwork sometimes") nowadays when he is in his tenth year as director of the Royal Shakespeare Company.

In mid-rehearsal for Jonson's The Alchemist (opening on Monday week at Stratford's Other Place), dark and stocky in the inevitable denim, he looks ruffled, sounds urgent but contained. A short beard gives him a slightly Mephistophelian air. He is not smooth, however; earnest if anything, though an acquaintance says that Nunn and his wife, the actress Janet Suzman, make as witty a couple as he has ever met. They have no children; home life is split between Hampstead's Vale of Health and the director's house in Stratford ("nice but not extravagant" is the official description). He is the kind of leader whose charm derives from being almost one of the boys. It works with students, and it works with actors.

Still only 37, he was 28 when he succeeded Peter Hall at Stratford; Hall, in similar case, had been all of 29. Both were Suffolk-born as well as Cambridge-bred; Nunn's father was a cabinet-maker. Both are grammar-school products. Both are slowmen, intent on the texts they present. "Our goal," says Nunn, "is to do Shakespeare better than anyone else."

The main method of achieving it is self-criticism; his team of directors regularly flay and analyse one another's work. "One thing there's nothing of in this company is smugness," even though, he admits, "that may not be borne out by our public image." The RSC have always had a keen sense of public image; needing to be noticed in order to survive, they have reiterated their own achievements.

They have always needed to squeeze money out of the Arts Council (they pioneered the process) and curt references to "the Stratford begging-bowl" are not unknown among the sceptics. The grant for this year has been brought into line with inflation but, Nunn says darkly, no more than that. They will manage, he adds laconically, largely by their own efforts.

Nunn's public image is that of a man who doesn't want one. He speaks ruefully, but not guiltily, of his "failure to beat the drum as much as it should be beaten." There is another reason for his anonymity: his own identity has merged with his company's. He went to Stratford from Coventry's Belgrade Theatre as a very young Associate Director in 1965. After a first year of legendary disaster, directing a sequence of productions that failed to open or just failed, he found his feet quite spectacularly with The Revenger's Tragedy for which he more or less invented a style.

The following year The Taming of the Shrew and The Relapse confirmed his mastery, a controlled flamboyance rare in a generation of young scholastics. They were productions that looked fun to be in, and in fact Nunn's popularity with actors has rarely been in doubt. When his appointment as director was announced in 1968 the company is said to have clapped. At first there were complaints from actors who felt they were being rather coldly manipulated, not so much in plays as in the organisation. These grievances seem to have died away. His claims to have democratised the company are borne out by actors. "You get to see him," said one. "With Peter Hall you get to see his secretary."

Last year's successful season is regarded as his personal triumph. Not all the productions were good, but even the weak ones had a spirit about them. Not all the productions were his, but he was sole or joint director of five of them: a record in recent years. His achievements included a Macbeth at the Other Place crammed with imaginative energy: the completest realisation of a Shakespeare play -- and that one about the most difficult in the canon -- in a long time.

In the intervening years he has been a difficult director to pin down. One expected him to be intelligent, imaginative, thorough, and usually he was. But it is not easy, looking back, to differentiate his productions from those of his colleagues. He has kept the same team throughout: John Barton, Terry Hands, David Jones, Clifford Williams and hors concours Peter Brook. The continuity is, as he insists, remarkable (compare the mortality rate among directors at the National Theatre and the Royal Court).

Very few other directors have worked at Stratford during Nunn's tenure and I have often felt this to be damaging. He counters that working on that stage, for that organisation, is a daunting experience, that few young directors could cope with it, and that most are not interested in the classics anyway. He has often seemed to be interested in nothing else; in the past 10 years the only non-Shakespearian play he has staged was Hedda Gabler. He used to find most contemporary drama "pretty thin gruel" staged from a sense of duty, a sin of which the RSC -- at their London end, the Aldwych -- were themselves guilty. Now he wants to amend his neglect of modern work. The choice of new plays at the Other Place last year was all his own, and an important part of the RSC success. Another was the development of the Other Place itself as "a Midlands regional theatre. At Stratford for most of the year you play to a million passers-by. But our season now lasts into January and you don't get tourists then."

His schedule is punishing, though he has succumbed recently to nothing more than a two-day cold, caught when forgetting to put on an extra sweater after joining in one of the company's "crucifying" movement classes. Most of last year's repertory was taken for a five-week theatrical blitz on Newcastle on Tyne, the prelude, he hopes, to a permanent RSC base in the north. Now all the plays are coming to London.

He is far from exhausted or bored with it all, though he has other ambitions. "I'm covered with conventional embarrassment at saying so, but I want to spend some time writing. I'm not sure that when I finally leave here I would want to be a director of anything." The second half of that is the kind of thing people always say, and one is inclined to discount it. It will be a pity and a waste if we never have the chance to assess Trevor Nunn as a director outside the RSC. But it would leave him appropriately mysterious.

Robert Cushman
1977-05-22-further-thoughts-on-the-rsc-s:
Further thoughts on the RSC's fascists

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN returns to Destiny and discusses the first production at the new Open Space.

I WAS dismayed on opening last Sunday's OBSERVER to read a rather niggling review of David Edgar's Destiny; especially dismayed since I had written it. The only excuse I can offer for my guarded declaration that Destiny may be the best play in London is that it opened at the Aldwych on a Thursday, and my copy was due on Friday; hardly time to give the competition a thorough screening.

A week later (a week undisturbed by any theatrical experience remotely comparable) I am surer. There are of course much funnier plays in London, and one or two which probe deeper into private agonies. But only Bedroom Farce is, on its own enclosed territory, better organised; and there is nothing in town to touch Destiny for its excitement as a story.

It is, most importantly, the panoramic political play that writers of Mr Edgar's generation have been straining after for years. Often they have strained too hard; Howard Brenton (in the last major contender, Weapons of Happiness) was a poet trying to turn himself into a journalist. Mr Edgar has actually been a journalist and his play is, among other things, excellent reportage; dramatising a Midlands by-election he touches lightly but not superficially on the Tory and Labour campaigns before homing in on Nation Forward, the Fascist group who are his main concern.

By being so conscientious a journalist - by accumulating details - he actually achieves theatrical poetry, as he never did with the easy metaphors of his agit-prop plays. There is an uncommon charge here in the wry detached soliloquies through which his characters reveal themselves and their predicaments, and in the controlling myth of India.

It is of course an outrageous coincidence that four men, present together at the end of the British Raj, should all subsequently surface in the same suburb. But in a play as large as this some structural artifice is not only permissible but necessary, and as a metaphor for a play about the far Right in Britain today it is very pregnant. The National Front sprang in large part from the League of Empire Loyalists, and they did not choose their name lightly.

For once Marxism has inspired a playwright to generosity. Keeping his exploiters for the most part off-stage, Mr Edgar is able to see all his characters as victims: a limiting vision if he were writing tragedy, but liberating here. Sure of his own position, he can take time to understand everyone else's. Even the aspirant Hitler of Nation Forward has a biting speech (delivered with uncomfortable rasping power by Bob Peck) about the fears of an old man surrounded by immigrants. This rebounds ironically into the later scene - the best in the play - where Turner, the party's stooge-candidate (played by Ian McDiarmid with a marvellous blend of timorousness and jocularity), discovers that to be anticoloured is a breath away from being anti-Semitic.

Mr Edgar only cheats at the end when Major Rolfe, the officer funding the movement, is revealed as head of the concern which evicted Turner from his shop and destroyed his livelihood. Politically I can swallow this; dramatically the play breaks its own rules. No link is established between Rolfe the father grieving for his son killed by an Irish sniper, and Rolfe the grasper; he is simply kept out of sight which (at the Aldwych, far more than in the confined Other Place) means out of mind.

I should have commended last week the performances of Paul Moriarty, Greg Hicks, Cherie Lunghi and (also a King Lear) Paul Shelley; they all keep Mr Edgar's townscape alive and convincing. Mr Edgar's stance and his findings, incidentally, are similar to those of Martin Walker's book The National Front; we may hope that he overestimates the dangers, but we would be unwise to bank on it.

  

Moving not very far along: the key-line of Charles Marowitz's Variations on the Merchant of Venice (opening attraction at the new Open Space in Euston Road) is "If you wrong us shall we not revenge?," which Shylock utters on this occasion at the end of the trial scene, just before having his enemies mown down by heavily-armed allies from the Stern Gang. This is a moment of tremendous release; one has dreamed of seeing him get his pound of flesh, but here the stuff must run into hundredweights.

It is salutary to be reminded, while simmering down, that Zionist fanatics once blew up hotels and, like the PLO, thought themselves justified. In Robin Don's stoned and latticed set, the action unfolds, once you have accepted Venice as being a district of British-ruled Jerusalem, with a breadth and firmness unprecedented in Mr Marowitz's Shakespearean adventures.

But. There is still a great deal of The Merchant left over, and Mr Marowitz, though shuffling some lines and cutting others, retains it with no very clear purpose, other than the familiar one of making everybody seem as ludicrous and disreputable as possible. So Bassanio, leaving nothing to chance, plays all three of the casket scenes himself, the first two in disguise. (Had he struck lucky when done up as the Prince of Morocco, would he, I wonder, have been obliged to remain in black-face forever?)

But once we have giggled our way through the opening lines, these scenes are more boring than when played by actors under some obligation to find out what their author meant. Portia is a bored bitch, whose one racist line is pointed up by the presence of a black Nerissa. Mr Marowitz gives momentary pleasure by voicing all our subversive thoughts about the play, but this is not the same as illuminating it; and only with Shylock (well-mouthed by Vladek Sheybal) does he use the play - with an assist from Marlowe's more spectacularly machiavellian Jew, the one from Malta - to illuminate anything else: viz., the festering resentment of the persecuted.

  

A re-run of Four to One (Cottesloe), Gawn Grainger's tale of group violence over a backroom pool-table, underlines the punch and rhythm of the dialogue and the lack of a sustaining structure. The National's strong-arm boys are in great form; Mark McManus, in particular, has never seemed freer. The new victim is the formidable Warren Clarke, who puts up a great fight against the eponymous odds; his role has been re-written to advantage, though some of his thoughts on man's inhumanity seem, in the bloody circumstances, gratuitous.

Idi Amin, the leading character of Michael Hastings's For The West (Theatre Upstairs), keeps saying he likes Jews, and is rewarded by nervous laughter. The trouble with Amin (I mean the theatrical trouble; I'm aware that there are others) is that, for all our awful knowledge, we have been conditioned to think of him as a comic character with a script written jointly by himself and Alan Coren. Mr Hastings is not in this league; he is not trying to be, but he cannot escape its shadow either. Despite the remarkable simulacrum provided by Rudolph Walker (bullishness running to flab, heavily begonged), the character and the play are indeterminate, sliding by default into updated cloak-and-dagger.
1977-05-29-jonson-to-the-life:
TREVOR NUNN'S production of The Alchemist (Other Place, Stratford) is the funniest and most accomplished I have seen of this or any other Jonson. The Alchemist, being so well-erected on a basis of intrigue and trickery, presents the problem of playing its author in its purest form. The action seems to demand that the play be treated as farce, but if taken with that degree of velocity, the language -- that knotted, exuberant compound of music, pedantry and slang -- becomes an incomprehensible morass.

Most productions pause reverently for Sir Epicure Mammon's famous rhapsodies of covetousness, but otherwise devote themselves to knockabout, with tedious results. Others, operating with virtuous and scholarly restraint, have achieved a different kind of boredom. Nobody until now has bothered much with character. Mr Nunn's company reveal it to be the foundation of the play.

Each of the minor characters is given a sharp visual identity. Most striking of all is Nickolas Grace's Drugger, on whom the habit of nervous ingratiation has bestowed a permanent timid stoop, and whose complexion suggests either Chinese ancestry (unlikely, really) or a nasty case of jaundice. He takes some pride in his ill-health; his eyes almost pop out when he proclaims "I had another sickness worse than this", quite in the vein of Aguecheek recalling that he was adored once, too.

Alan Cody's Dapper, with the nose if not the brain of a sharper, Susan Drury's rampageous and catarrhal Doll (a very tart tart), Hilton McRae's rural quarreller and Bobbie Brown's outstandingly buxom widow, all fit neatly and assertively into place: a fine parade from the RSC's apparently endless reserves of new acting talent. Paul Brooke, though he might take his own injunction "be rich!" a little more to heart, wheezes and waddles quite acceptably along the paths of Mammon. Only the Puritans falter, surprisingly since they are usually infallible; the one line from the play that everyone remembers ("thou look'st like Antichrist in that lewd hat") goes for nothing, as -- more importantly -- does the greeting "peace to the household" at what should be the height of chaos. Mr Nunn still has some way to go in the orchestration of riot.

A subtler, more crucial orchestration really underpins his production. The play begins with a quarrel between the two cheaters-in-chief, Subtle and Face, issuing in forced reconciliation and a determination to see "who shall shark best" the rest of the day. Their relationship becomes part contest, part alliance; and its tensions are charted here by John Woodvine and Ian McKellen with wonderful concentration, each keeping obsessive score of the other's takings.

The tension is aggravated, and our evening made, by the succession of quick changes enjoined on them by their own and their author's plotting, transformations which Mr Nunn, with pardonable cruelty, has made as frequent and difficult as possible. The abiding image of the production is of the actors switching furniture and removing evidence with one hand, unbuttoning buttons and jerking-off jerkins with the other, while outside the door of Chris Dyer's ambuscaded set the customers pile up.

Each, besides, has a relish for disguise that goes way beneath the skin. Mr Woodvine when he plays the alchemical adept can be a self-flagellating fanatic or your gentle GP. Mr McKellen's Face lives up to his name; as himself he is nothing, but as patch-eyed highwayman, as fire-blower swathed and hooded almost to mummification, as primly subservient butler or -- in moments of great stress -- as bits of all three, he is everything. At the close his eyes, surveying his pile, have the gleam of the possessed: a striking finish if too insistently moral for my taste. The company has room to expand -- spiritually if not, in the Other Place, physically -- but it has the play under its belt and I left feeling that, at last, I have it under mine.

In comparison, the RSC's Man and Superman is a little tame, though certainly pleasant: exceedingly so if the circumstances -- reopening of the Malvern Festival and the weather and the Cotswolds -- are added in. Richard Pasco's Jack Tanner has exhilarating attack; his theories could hardly be better voiced. But the play hardly registers any more as one of ideas, and it is doubtful if it ever did.

Tanner the fine speaker is dramatically the mug; as he says himself, "the marked down victim, the destined prey" of Ann Whitefield. He realises it late, but we should be in on the joke almost from the start, enjoying her wiles and his helplessness. Susan Hampshire's Ann, sweet and sly, plays all that is in the text, but the role really needs a Maggie Smith to go beyond that and establish a conspiratorial rapport with the audience.

James Cossins and Nicky Henson are their expert selves in a production set, I imagine for economic reasons, in a void. At least I could discern no artistic motive for a drawing-room in which a solid flight of library steps leads only to invisible bookshelves. The play, robbed of stuffiness and prosperity, also forfeits its atmosphere.

At the Royal Exchange, Manchester, David Terence's dramatisation of The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn is mainly notable for the emergence in the title-role of Enn Reitel, all horse-sense and confusion; and for the proper establishment of the river, flowing serenely and invisibly through the middle of the auditorium, as the story's source of energy and of repose.

An earlier epic is given elaborate treatment by the Prospect company at the Old Vic; those bits of the Iliad dealing with the deaths of Patroclus and of Hector have been rechristened War Music, a title which seems, if taken literally, to signify percussion (courtesy of Gary Kettel, a virtuoso). While the beat goes on, the lights (Nick Chelton) turn blood-red, the set (Pamela Howard) looms wide, the ochred actors gyrate to William Louther's choreography. "Half-naked men hacked slowly at each other," says Christopher Logue's text, observantly.

Achilles's Myrmidons wear fearsome headgear, like black motor-bike helmets with teeth. It all looks like a Stratford production of Troilus and Cressida and it gets much the same kind of agitated acting; both sight and sound are more in place here, however. It is saved from being a celebration of war by Mr Logue's contribution, notable less for crude undercutting (which occurs -- e.g., "the Greeks are in a fix") than for an alternating command of momentary and sustained effects. The focus ("the daylight stiffens to translucent horn") is always sharp.

Mr Logue reclaims the blank-verse iambic as Tony Harrison the rhyming couplet. Most of its delivery is safely with Timothy West, a master both of rhetoric and the throw-away. Unlike Homer, however, the creators of War Music cannot make you care; the impressiveness of Toby Robertson's production is abstract.

The night after the fall of Troy, the Russian Revolution broke out. Robert Bolt's State of Revolution seems to me a pedestrian though not a boring chronicle, well produced and excellently acted. More of it next week.
1977-06-05-lenin-s-testament:
Lenin's Testament

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Robert Bolt's new play and Jacobi's Hamlet.

TOM STOPPARD has pulled the rug out from under any writer who attempts a play about Lenin. One's fond memories of Travesties are revived with unexpected sharpness in the very first speech of Robert Bolt's State of Revolution (Lyttelton), which happens to be delivered by Stephen Moore, a Stoppard actor par excellence. Addressing a Young Communist assembly in the role of Lunacharsky, Commissar for Education, he speaks of Capri, which "as some of you may know is a playground of the international bourgeoisie in its more light-hearted, less obviously offensive aspects." It looks as if we may be in for a merry evening of jargon exposed.

The opening scene puts paid to that. Set in Capri in a villa belonging to Gorky (not offensive, but not very light-hearted either), it lays out the play's battle-lines. It is for the moment Lenin versus the rest, Lunacharsky having produced a thesis which is acclaimed by most of his colleagues, but condemned by Lenin as "unashamed idealism."

Dzerzhinsky, goaded by Lenin, protests that "nobody here is afraid of action." Comes the revolution, he is to be held to that; he is put in charge of the Cheka, which he controls with merciless purity. Stalin, not present on Capri, is referred to as someone "who does what needs doing"; an opinion in which Mr Bolt's Lenin persists until he decides, too late, that what Stalin is doing is not needed after all, or at least that it is not what he himself wants. Having suffered a stroke he can afford to permit himself a few scruples.

Actually this Lenin has scruples all the way through. Mr Bolt's Lenin is, in his own terms, similar to Mr Stoppard's. The Stoppard Lenin was a man with the unusual ability to put ruthless theory into ruthless practice. He also liked music which symbolised the pull of conscience, or, if you prefer, of tender-mindedness. It was a schematic picture which Mr Stoppard's comic vision (summed up in Krupskaya's line "something went wrong . . . I forget what") could just about accommodate.

Mr Bolt's vision is, I suppose, tragic; at any rate it centres on a major figure falling into traps which he himself has set. The play was originally titled Lenin's Testament; perhaps it was felt that State of Revolution had more zing. But the first idea was the right one. Mr Bolt's glimpses of Russia at large are perfunctory. Infighting among the Bolshevik elite is handled with far more relish; the onset of the New Economic Policy sets off a finely orchestrated bitching-game for eight players.

Michael Kitchen's Trotsky emerges as the most gifted participant, running ironic rings round Terence Rigby's workhorse Stalin. Mr Rigby's performance is remarkable; he, more than anyone else on stage, settles into history before our eyes. At each appearance, it seems, his moustache acquires an extra bristle; painfully he learns to smile and each smile is less penetrable than the last. Every time he raises his hand to vote the gesture gets closer to a clenched-fist salute. He has, besides, a blockish manner of speech, a slow sealing of every word, that brings the conventional figure of the unimaginative tyrant to new life.

One is tempted to wish that Mr Bolt had put Stalin, Trotsky or both in the centre of the play, but he would probably have been less successful with them if he had. The biographical approach to history, for a playwright of less than genius, is a perilous one; the man in the middle always comes out unsatisfactory and Mr Bolt merely gives us the Stoppard Lenin at greater length. He spends the play being tugged: by Stalin in one direction, by his gentler colleagues - a conscientious collection with Gorky as visiting good uncle - in the other. Even while instigating action he remains a pawn. A pawn though of drama, not of history; Mr Bolt's characters spend much time debating whether man makes history or vice versa, and philosophically he probably has doubts. Theatrically he is a cult-of-personality subscriber with no dues outstanding.

Hence, perhaps, his choice of Lunacharsky, with his suspicious devotion to bourgeois artistic values, as raisonneur. To cast as Lenin so sympathetic an actor as Michael Bryant seems, whatever your politics, a bit soft, though it does guarantee an intelligent and technically flawless performance. Ralph Koltai's set of mobile slats frames a handsome production by Christopher Morahan, which does justice to the play's narrative virtues; it tells, after all, a very interesting story. The play has been given instant publication by Heinemann Educational Books; a format in which it seems perfectly at home. Mr Bolt's preface shows him to be one of the most intelligent men now writing plays; I wish his dialogue had a similar spark.

  

Toby Robertson's production of Hamlet (Old Vic) is the kind in which the players arrive for their Elsinore date whooping and tumbling and in which conversations come to guilty halts when soldiers cross the stage. But the Danish royal line comes over as remarkably intelligent.

Like most royals they say things you have heard before, but they make them sound fresh. Timothy West's Claudius is the best performance this super-competent actor has recently given: a narrow-eyed brute who has to force himself to be polite to Hamlet, gets giggles both at the Player-King and Ophelia's first couple of fits, and kneels to prayer with no belief whatever. His love for Barbara Jefford's Gertrude he has unfortunately to compress, owing to cuts, into an outstretched hand after the closet scene which she conscientiously rejects. She too seems often on the verge of losing her temper with her son: better for him, surely, than the indulgence he usually receives.

Derek Jacobi also suffers under the blue pencil; he has lost the "how all occasions" soliloquy, which only happens to be the turningpoint of his character and the play. I object less on Mr Jacobi's account than on my own; I liked listening to him. He is a prince who briefly attains the full passion of the Renaissance avenger ("now could I drink hot blood") and then stops, scared at himself. Earlier he tries to force himself into frenzy with the aid of the players' property sword. Abusing "this too, too solid flesh," he is furious, not mournful; "my father's spirit . . . all is not well" is reassurance. And so on; this is a superbly inflected, very likeable performance, courteous or embittered by turns: line by line surprising but, in the addition, a little short of startling.
1977-06-19-flying-the-flag:
Flying the flag

ROBERT CUSHMAN on two theatre festivals in Canada.

WHENEVER I see the stage of the Stratford, Ontario, Festival Theatre I want to pack it up and bring it home. It is the most exciting Shakespearean platform in the world: designed 25 years ago by Tyrone Guthrie and Tanya Moiseiwitsch, and still unmatched. (Chichester, in particular, looks like its deformed child.) Broad shallow steps approaching the stage, a pillared balcony at the back, the audience in an embracing arc, and a polished floor from which the plays rise up and hit you.

Stratford is now two theatres: the other is a refurbished proscenium house, the Avon. Together they will accommodate 10 plays this year, among them 'Richard III' and 'All's Well That Ends Well,' the two with which Guthrie commenced operations in 1953. (This is Stratford's means of celebrating its--what's the word--Jubilee.) Ever since Guthrie it has attracted--to an extent relied on--British talent. This year sees Robin Phillips in his third season as director and Brian Bedford, Maggie Smith and Margaret Tyzack heading his company.

Seven plays were unveiled in the opening week. Mr Phillips has flowered majestically at Stratford, and his production of 'Richard III' ranks with the finest Shakespeare I have seen. Richly spectacular (gorgeous Plantagenet costumes, caparisoned horses, flights of arrows in a battle fought not faked), it is never overblown. The text is taken literally, both as ritual--with Miss Tyzack a fearsomely crazed choric Margaret still roaming around in battledress as she mentally relives the Wars of the Roses--and as psychology.

Mr Bedford's opening soliloquy is full not of actorish glee, but, as the lines suggest, of corroding resentment. He enters through the audience and, with his hump to us, surveys the set: one man against the world. It is this solitariness--which rises to a dapper tense eroticism in the seductions of Anne and Elizabeth--that wins attention and even, though the production is unsparing and exact in its depiction of tyranny, respect. It seems fitting that he should impale himself on Richard's sword having whispered 'My kingdom for a horse?' in agonised wonder: all that for this.

Maybe this production had a concept, but I saw only the play. The idea of Mr Phillips's 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' was more obtrusive (though not necessarily comprehensible unless you read the programme): the play dreamed by Elizabeth I, who sees herself as Titania, Hippolyta and Helena. The first two roles are taken by Miss Smith; Miss Richardson having gone down with gastro-enteritis and taken 'Man and Superman' with him.

The patron was represented only by an atrocious production of 'Widowers' Houses.' The director of this (and of the festival), Paxton Whitehead, redeemed himself by playing the Ralph Lynn role in Ben Travers's 'Thark,' and striking an exquisite balance between the cad and the ass. This amazingly funny play was given by Michael Meacham a production to match: Britons all.

The remaining Shakespeare on the festival stage was 'All's Well That Ends Well,' given an intelligent if rather featureless production by the RSC's David Jones, with Miss Tyzack a lovely Countess and Miss Moiseiwitsch returned to clothe the play in the finest fashions of Charles I.

Shakespeare was also to be seen at the Avon: 'Romeo and Juliet,' again with a British director, David William, whose journey seemed hardly necessary, especially as his starting-point seemed to be the Old Vic of the fifties at its fussiest and most pedestrian. Canadian directors were confined to the Avon, where they served us smorgasbord: a forgettable 'Miss Julie' and a 'Ghosts' rendered memorable by the clinching demonstration of Miss Tyzack's tragic powers. Finally Mr Phillips directed Molnar's 'The Guardsman,' eagerly anticipated as a bonne bouche at the end of a hard week, but in the event unduly heavy.
1977-07-03-li-l-america:
Li'l America

ROBERT CUSHMAN reports on a visit to the New York theatre.

THEATRICALLY, America this year is for the Americans. There are far fewer imports than in recent seasons. There's even an American critic on the New York Times.

Not only were there more, and more highly-touted, native plays than usual; they all seemed deeply sunk in their own mythology. The season's prize musical (there have been few contenders) was greeted as Americana incarnate.

Annie, the show in question, is based on the "Little Orphan Annie" cartoon-strip, and has been diagnosed as a rallying-point for reactionaries. Actually it's nothing that positive. Its hero may be a golden-hearted billionaire (God knows how such an angel made all that loot), but it balances him with a social-conscious Depression chorus. The original cartoon was rabidly anti-Roosevelt; he is mocked here, but affectionately. True he can only think up the New Deal after he has heard 13-year-old Annie sing a hopeful ditty entitled "Tomorrow," but a policy thus inspired obviously carries the authors' seal of approval.

This general benevolence, and the lack of a firm story, get a bit cloying; you keep waiting for the show to justify its ancestry, turn into Li'l Abner, and satirise something. But caricature is left to Dorothy Loudon as the old maid in charge of the orphans and hating them ("Do I hear happiness, in here?" she snarls after one juvenile chorus), and since she ends up not only funny but touching hers is obviously the right course. But despite the blandness, and the performing moppets (plus a dog) and a score that exhausts itself after the first three numbers, the show survives through a mixture of tidiness and confidence. It looks well, moves well, and seems to believe in itself.

  

The opposition musical, I Love My Wife -- announced, like Annie, for London -- has much better songs which never succeed in taking the stage. They neither further the action nor comment on it: not that this fable of incipient wife-swapping in New Jersey would bear much comment. It is an economical show: four in the cast, four in the band, all performing engagingly, with the musicians lending an occasional hand with the acting and doing it with charm.

Thwarted sex in suburbia is a small American legend which has outlasted larger ones. Vietnam for example. David Rabe's Streamers, which recently closed, seemed, at its premiere last year, dated and -- at least to an outsider -- inaccessible. It was the last instalment of a Vietnam trilogy; the middle section Stick and Bones may be seen in Britain soon, and the first, The Basic Training of Pavlo Hummel, has been revived on Broadway with Al Pacino in the lead. (Returning movie-stars have contributed greatly to Broadway's unprecedented prosperity this season.)
