THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on de Filippo's Filumena

The initial situation of Eduardo de Filippo's Filumena (Lyric) is comic operatic. The Neapolitan prostitute Filumena Marturano, for 25 years the mistress of the rich Don Domenico Soriano, finally entraps him into marriage. Like Volpone or Gianni Schicchi, she takes to her bed. She seems to be dying and Domenico consents to make her happy in her last moments. The ceremony performed, Filumena jumps spryly from her couch.

This event is the most ravishingly theatrical, and also the least obviously credible, in the play. It happens offstage; not merely offstage, but before curtain-rise. What we first see is the volcanically quarrelling couple, flanked by their respective servants. De Filippo, with the craft of either great cunning or great simplicity, has had it all ways. We are given the measure of Filumena's determination, and the play acquires the flavour of classic comedy while remaining a realistic drama.

To see Filumena's stratagem in action would be to become involved in the sheer joy of deception, and thus to get the wrong idea about both the play and its heroine. For the lady differs from her ancestors in Italian comedy; in no way is she in the game for fun, any more than in her earlier years she was on it for fun. Born in the slums she has been prosaically dependent first on prostitution, and now on household trickery, to keep her head above water.

It turns out that she has been fooling Domenico for years. She has three grown sons whom she has brought up on his money and without his knowledge; without theirs, come to that. Her revelation of this fact turns the play into a prolonged family reunion: a joyous event with doubtful, bitter undertones.

One of the boys is Domenico's; she refuses to say which on the grounds that, at this stage, she wants no favouritism. By the end of the play their marriage is confirmed, as we always knew it would be, and Domenico has agreed to stop asking questions. But it is impossible to believe that he will be able to keep this promise; we are given a happy ending with the certainty of breakers ahead.

You have been out of the theatre for some time before this hits you. We actually end with Filumena, for the first time in her life, crying: a conclusion which, the adaptors, Keith Waterhouse and Willis Hall, and the director, Franco Zeffirelli, probably make more sentimental than it need be. A British audience, though, can hardly help abetting them. For us, these people are refreshingly exotic, and de Filippo sunnier than he probably seems to his compatriots.

For the most part, Zeffirelli works a refined version of the magic he exercised in Saturday, Sunday, Monday. This show is less of a carnival: like his author, Zeffirelli acknowledges farce, but does not exploit it; he gives us this time (in a verismo set by Raimonda Gaetani) something more believable and more moving. I almost wrote 'more restrained,' but in fact the production lacks nothing in explosiveness; and in Joan Plowright and Colin Blakely it has two of the most resourcefully passionate players on the British stage.

Mr Blakely starts on a high note of badgered belligerence; his rage at moments lifts him off the floor. And he has the measure of the play's greatest comic scene: Domenico quizzing his three putative heirs to find out which of them--as a singer, perhaps, or a womaniser--takes after him, and pulling up a chair to get a good look at the likeliest suspect.

The throb in Joan Plowright's voice makes it difficult to believe that she has never wept, but her banked-up furies are tremendous. She turns self-pity into honest, cleansing anger, and single-mindedness into generosity. Patricia Hayes as her confidante gives her fierce and funny encouragement, and Larry Noble is a philosophically downtrodden manservant whose every gesture reduces to a shrug. The three sons are fetching in their contrasts, and even more in their unanimity. London could hardly have found a better antidote to power cuts.

  

James Robson's The Factory Birds (Warehouse) is more or less defined by its title. We are shown men and women, mostly young but ageing fast, having their humanity blunted (they make machine parts for cleaning out battery hen-coops, and if that sounds gratuitously symbolic, reflect that somebody must be doing it) and, for the most part, acquiescing in it. In the last consideration lies the author's originality--he differentiates. I don't know his history, but it is hard not to identify him with the goaded, sensitive boy who in the end makes the break his loud-mouthed mates have always talked about. The loudest of them all is a self-proclaimed Casanova; the escaper is a virgin. The second act centres on an off-stage rape; and sexism, as the emblem and product of a shuttered life, is most on the author's mind.

None of this is controversial; but then none of it is deniable. The play's obvious weakness is monotony, but it is necessary and stops short of tedium. The play survives, in Bill Alexander's production, on its authenticity and its acting. Enforced companionship always brings out the best in actors, and there is of course the added kick that these are from the RSC, and so presumably used to higher things; Roger Rees is the most spectacular breaker of new and greasier ground, but there are no flies on any of the cast.

  

Nor are there any, once you accept a convention in which everyone talks like Valentine Dyall, in The Fall of the House of Usher, which last week was visible at the Cottesloe. Steven Berkoff's style of rigid fantastication actually suits Poe better than it did Kafka.

Alas, the flesh cannot be made to creep indefinitely, as Mr Berkoff seems to recognise, since he makes abrupt descents to the conversational for the odd camp laugh. But the music and movement are as accomplished as ever. Mr Berkoff arrestingly gives Roderick Usher the sound of a mechanical winch in the last stages of disrepair, and Shelley Lee, in her anguished groping from beyond the grave, is a quite transfixing Usherette.

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN in Paris and London.

THERE are those, and I fear they even include some theatre critics, who go to Paris to eat rather than to see plays. But happily we can do both.

As theatrical tourists we don't have to contend with first-night timetables and even if we did I suspect that the Parisian sense of priorities would make it easy for us to dine before. The rule in Paris theatre remains unaltered: everything starts late.

The centrepiece of this year's World Theatre Festival is Moscow's Taganka Theatre, whose arrival has occasioned a new brand of delaying tactic: the queue for simultaneous translation equipment. In Paris, of course, you don't queue; you mill. And money alone cannot hire you the gift of tongues; you hand over your identity card or, if you are foreign and easily intimidated by officialdom ahead of you and the shoving crowd behind, your passport. You have, of course, to get them back, under similar conditions, at the end.

Paris at the moment makes the Anglo-Saxon feel at home. Record-shop displays and Metro graffiti alike proclaim the supremacy of the Sex Pistols. And British playwrights rule (really one might be in New York). Bedroom Farce is there already, Equus approaches the home stretch after its customary lengthy gallop, and four chicks called Steffy, Pomme, Jane et Vivi are nobody but our own Dusa, Fish, Stas and Vi.

The stage-struck Briton, wondering why he left home, can anyway catch up with the generation of French actresses on whose names he grew up: Madeleine Renaud, Edwige Feuillère, Maria Casarès, Suzanne Flon are all on view. Mlle Flon's vehicle, shared with Dominique Blanchar (who is marvellous) and Françoise Lugagne, is Les Dames du Jeudi by Loleh Bellon, a striking example of boulevard theatre at its finest and one of the few new French plays of interest.

It is in a way the middle-aged equivalent of Dusa, Fish: three women, whose means stop just short of being comfortable, forgather every Thursday to bitch and reminisce over their sexual and political pasts. These are re-enacted without change of set or costume.

French companies visiting London, mainly in classics, have accustomed us to rhetorical virtuosity, but have given little hint of the naturalistic gifts, tender and fluent, on show here. Mlle Blanchar's role--a woman exploited by a wastrel son--recapitulates the theme of Marguerite Duras's Days in the Trees and makes it dramatic.

As for the classics: the Comédie Française had three Molières in the bill during my visit and apparently was doing very nicely with them. At all events, I couldn't get a ticket. Elsewhere there are three Ibsens; I would guess, without having seen it, that the Biothéâtre-Opéra's Master Builder is very good.

My evidence is a production by the same group (and the same young director, Pierre Sala) of a piece even crazier in its austerity, Claudel's La Jeune Fille Violaine, a fable of sin and miracle set, with some audacity, at the end of the last century, the author's own time. It has the rigour, if not the control, of Racine: and something of the same bemusing exhilaration--so out of step as to seem avant-garde. The company is, appropriately, a fiercely disciplined team of vocal gymnasts.

Before returning to the Muscovites, I should mention an American team playing cheek-by-jowl with the Paris Festival, though not a part of it. Guided by Elisabeth Swados (who was on Peter Brook's African trip, and provided the music for Andrei Serban's Greek tragedy productions), they offered Nightclub Cantata, full of the expected skills in song and full, too, of the portentous cuteness that passes for poetry off-Broadway.

If they were hung-up, the Russians were refreshingly simple. That, I suppose, is another cultural cliché, especially as applied to what is reputed to be Moscow's most adventurous company. But the Taganka (founded 1964) showed us, in its version of Gorki's The Mother, what could be done with a large stage (they performed in the huge Palais de Chaillot), great resources of money and manpower, and a tradition of strong, jovial, realistic acting.

The director, Iouri Lioubimov, goes in for stabbing lights, choreographic staging, and massed choral effects. There are times when his production sounds like Boris Godunov and looks like Fiddler on the Roof. It is everything that was once called arty; but it is done with great visual assurance and--thanks to the cast--with unlimited warmth. That may not have figured in the director's scheme; he is lucky to be able to take it for granted. It makes the strongest contrast with the Brechtian version of the same work which was so rapturously received in London a few years ago.

Does anyone remember the scene in which Brecht's Mother, pausing for a moment from her work of making the revolution apparently single-handed, told the mothers of her opponents that they had no right to grieve for their sons since they had fallen on the wrong side? Even that might have been supportable--it might have chimed with our masochistic notions of political toughness--in a play less concerned to wring every sentimental ounce out of the idea of motherhood.

There is nothing quite as bad in The Days of the Commune (Aldwych), but little good either. I found it difficult as the evening unfolded to apportion blame between author, director and actors, but by the end was too dispirited to care. I think, though, that Howard Davies has applied a disembodied idea of "Brechtianism" that works for almost any playwright but Brecht; certainly not for this late play that needs all the realistic help it can get.

It is set here in a kind of puritan limbo; no hint of Paris in 1871 or of anywhere else very much. (The set is this year's Shakespearean fixture. It worked for Ibsen, not for Brecht. Draw your own conclusions.) The play is slanted so heavily in favour of the Communards that my own sympathy with them quite disappeared. Most of the second act is devoted to the question of whether to preserve revolutionary purity and perish, or turn repressive and survive.

These are big questions but not, divorced from particular personalities, very subtle ones; or, after five minutes, very compelling. They are briefly enlivened by the cutting rhetoric of Ian McDiarmid, as the corresponding street-scenes about the gallant barricaders are fitfully rescued by the shy clowning of Mike Gwilym.

Dullards and dafties

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on plays at the Cottesloe, 'The Comedy of Errors' and a new farce.

CONSIDERED as the National's fringe studio or smaller-than-anything-else in the National complex, the Cottesloe suffers from having been purpose-built.

The most endearing theatres of this kind -- the Bush, King's Head, Other Place -- are conversion jobs. The closure of the Cottesloe, which has been threatened, would be a disaster: not because of its commitment to the fringe (which can survive without it), but because it alone stands between the National and gigantism.

Economies have already removed from the programme a couple of minor classics that should have been good company fodder; and the choice of new plays has so far seemed overly dutiful: self-conscious gestures towards current modes. Of the two latest offerings, Julian Mitchell's Half-Life bows low before the spirit of elegiac elegance, while John Mackendrick's Lavender Blue falls down and immerses itself in lyric squalor.

Half-Life, which would be an aptly dismal title for either play, actually refers to a method of measuring vast tracts of time, useful for archaeologists, that being the former vocation of the central character. He has not now much purpose of any kind, science having destroyed his favourite theory, viz., that Western culture is indivisibly Hellenic and Stonehenge merely an outcrop of Mycenae. Having established this at length, Mr Mitchell seemingly forgets it. His hero, Noel Cunliffe, passes on to general bitching.

Sir Noel, I should say, and ex-master of an Oxford college; though now residing in a luxurious country-house conveniently close to Salisbury Plain. We have another play about the English upper class being vile with style; and Waris Hussein's production reduces it, for much of the time, to its simplest form.

The voluble protagonist sits talking in his garden, his friends, pupils, hangers-on and (indispensable) lost love around him in a semi-circle. Outside the ring sits a contemptuous young female leftie, who says things like 'You people! You've no more idea of love than politics.'

We might almost be west of Suez, though Mr Mitchell's wit is far sharper than John Osborne's. Noel has an impressive armoury of curled, stinging one-liners; with which to discomfort his guests, among whom the ladies can give nearly as good as they get. The gentlemen are dullards, who reduce such actors as Hugh Paddick, Richard Pearson and even Paul Rogers (who is in golden form) to emblems of conspicuous waste; but the actresses are well displayed: Avril Elgar shrewish and Isabel Dean resplendent.

At the end of the first act, Mr Mitchell springs briefly and effectively into action, but mostly he talks. Relationships are assumed rather than dramatised; that between Noel and a young Australian protege (diggers both) in particular. Everyone talks as if it were the hub of the action but we can barely see it.

Noel has a fine set-to with the radical lady on the perfectibility of man, which he denies; and she asserts; socialism is, quite correctly, identified with religion. That could be the core of a play, but not of this one. They finish as friends: a tribute to Noel's charm which, with John Gielgud the actor, is immense. He handles the brief bitter flourishes with magnificent insouciance, but the real deep corrosion escapes him.

  

Social workers and their charges make up the cast of Lavender Blue. But in the printed version the author denies that he is concerned with social issues. 'It is, simply, about people.' This is unfortunate, since the issues are more interesting than the people.

There are at least two characters who have no bearing on the main action, but lend sociological colour. They are a retarded married couple, and they provide one of the play's two good moments when they protect themselves from a wife-beating drunk by pleading that they're 'dafties.' The other involves Susan Fleetwood as a child-care officer, carrying on a weary telephone flirtation with a policeman in order to get information. Her role in the play, like everyone else's, is to suffer and to talk about it; Miss Fleetwood deserves to smile a little.

The worst of the play is not its brutality but its winsomeness. It is not enough for the lead, another daftie, to rape a small girl, murder her, and walk around with her dress on; he also has to talk in nursery rhymes, which the author, and presumably others at the National, find interesting and even beautiful.

  

It's high time I gave Trevor Nunn a bad notice; and I approached The Comedy of Errors (Aldwych) with pleasingly low hopes, mindful that at Stratford I had found its good humour forced, the interpolated musical numbers pre-empting the text instead of complementing it. Alas, no joy, he's gone and improved it; or rather, unbounded joy, the comic pressure has been raised so high that song and dance are the only possible release. These chores are distributed among the principals with nice discrimination, the Ephesian twins being the top terpsichoreans (watch Nikolas Grace jump sideways on to tables) and the Syracusans the vocalists (hear Michael Williams's riotous patter on the subject of Time.)

I must have been partially blind at Stratford; Gillian Lynne's choreography, for heaven's sake, is the best in any British musical for decades. Her exorcism sequence tops everything, with John Woodvine's Pinch singing so fine you wonder why he wastes his time being a marvellous actor. The chase which follows -- whether due to Mr Nunn, Miss Lynne, or the shade of Mack Sennett -- is the best ever done on a stage. And that still leaves the final scene, with Mike Gwilym's Antipholus turned to a manic QC and Judi Dench as his wife hardly more patient, just two syllables behind the Duke as he kindly reminds her of the story of her life. Richard Griffiths, a pained and patient officer, promises to rival Arthur Lowe in his soft rotundity. One word more and I shall gibber.

  

Shut Your Eyes and Think of England (Apollo) is full of rubbishy jokes about Jews, Arabs and homosexuals (or accepted images thereof), but it is not rubbish. Like all farce, it upsets the status quo; uniquely in West End farce, it leaves it upset. In its modest way it is quite subversive (all right, so it's the fashion) and, though the plot-line goes thin, it never breaks. Donald Sinden begins with a pleasing sketch of a worm, then takes on real glitter as he revolves. Frank Thornton and Patsy Rowlands are the truest of his cohorts.

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on plays from Chicago and plays at the National

TITLE of the week, or rather the fortnight, was Sexual Perversity in Chicago (Regent). I mentioned this to a friend, pointing out that just about every play on my list seemed to concern sexual perversity (as opposed, note, to perversion) somewhere. The same goes, she said unimpressed, for most plays.

She's right of course, though there are exceptions: one of them being Duck Variations, the curtain-raiser on the same bill. It is another product of Chicago, Chicago, that toddling town, and of its - indeed America's - white hope playwright David Mamet. Two old men sit on a park-bench and talk, with considerably more humour than men on park-benches usually exhibit in plays, or indeed in parks. Part of the playwright's purpose may be to satirise all portentous dialogues. His characters gaze at a pond, situated somewhere in the front stalls, and discuss ducks.

Mr Mamet never claims, even implicitly, that ducks symbolise the human condition; he merely demonstrates the ease with which any line of conversation may be made to terminate in webbed feet. The forcible incarceration of barnyard ducks is given judicious consideration ("you can't put 'em on their honour"), and just occasionally someone springs an unanswerable ("I mean, what is worth living if not life?"). Albert Takazauckas's direction rightly cherishes Mr Mamet's words, which are spoken good by Bernard Spear and all right by Gordon Sterne.

There is a New York flavour about the production and it persists, with less justification, into Sexual Perversity, etc, which is less a comedy of language than of particularly thrusting urban manners. Chicago is carnivore city, and these actors are vegetarian. One of them, Stephen Hoye, is entitled; he plays the younger, rawer (and ironically more successful) of two questing males.

Courteously and rather shyly making a date with his lady after getting her to bed, he is gently hilarious. But as his friend and mentor, a self-proclaimed lecher condemned to continence, Kenneth Nelson gives a smooth account of a roughly assertive role, lacking the macho look of accustomed success; his rebuff by an unco-operative pick-up in a singles bar (one of the best of the play's array of short, sharp scenes) is accordingly less funny and furious than it should be.

The evening sizzles with promise. Sparkling set-pieces counterpoint the stabbing monosyllables of insecurity; partners work self-consciously to please and then to destroy each other, and friends do the same.

  

Do You Love Me? (Roundhouse) covers the same ground in dance and doggerel; the very title tells the same story, in more whimsical terms. This is the Actors' Company's second theatricalisation of R. D. Laing, and this time winsomeness, though inventively orchestrated by the director, Edward Petherbridge, takes all. Still, the company seem strong and, as they cycle, pirouette and banter around a white art-gallery in which they themselves are the exhibits, they can occasionally make us remember things in our own loves we'd like to forget.

So, even more fleetingly, can the characters in Terry James's Confession Fever (King's Head), a truth-game with some witty lines but too heavily contrived for the slender facts it reveals. Maureen O'Brien again proves herself one of our most stylish sufferers.

  

Sexual perversity on the grandest scale is the subject of Wycherley's The Country Wife (Olivier). It calls to mind a few of King Lear's pungent reflections on respectable womanhood: "Behold yon simpering dame. That minces virtue and does shake the head to hear of pleasure's name." The fitchew nor the soiled horse goes to't, with a more riotous appetite.

It may not greatly tax Elizabeth Spriggs to play another simpering dame, but as Lady Fidget, circumspectly salacious, she duly capsizes the house when rebuking a companion on whose tongue pleasure's name has trespassed: "for shame, sister; whither shall we ramble?" Others in place are Polly Adams as the virtuous and sensible Alithea (though this most charming of actresses might, as an experiment, deliver the odd line ungraced by a radiant smile), Robin Bailey most efficient as the masculine Fidget, and Susan Littler in the title role: an unmatched part for a classical debutante - and one in which Miss Littler distinguishes herself with her reeling delight after her first bouquet of extra-marital kisses.

One of the charms of this play is that all its characters get what they deserve. The country wife may be consigned to her tyrant husband, but she has learned to outsmart him. Her seducer Horner may, through his stratagem of pretended impotence, have gained access to all the women he desires; the joke on him is that he despises them too much to enjoy them. (The real prize is off to stale woods and pastures old.) He becomes, as his name implies, a cuckolding machine; what a passion goes he for. (In this production gowned and turbaned, he dresses the part.)

Albert Finney's Horner, having gained the audience's confidence, abuses it; for all his vigour he generalises, missing both Horner's misanthropy and his implicit discomfiture; he neither judges nor is judged. The sadistically possessive Pinchwife (who threatens to go for his wife's face with a penknife) is similarly reduced by Richard Johnson to mere bluffness; while Ben Kingsley makes a lisping, honking caricature of Sparkish. Peter Hall's production is a considered homage to Restoration theatre but with little feeling of Restoration, or any other, life. The actors talk more readily to the audience than to each other, brandishing a convention rather than honouring it.

  

The National has been firing all three of its guns. The Lyttelton houses a Christmas show, Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, based with remarkable fidelity on the old poem. Penguin Classic version, I would not have expected an uncompromising exposition of the medieval doctrine of chastity, tricked out with many acrobatics but no jokes, to hold an audience of six-to-twelves, but they seemed gripped. I thought it went on a bit, but I thought that of the original, too. And the symbolism of the Green Knight (nature, etc) seemed more convincing when standing a solid eight foot than ever it did in Middle English.

The Cottesloe's hospitality to touring groups, which reached a recent nadir with Babel's Tower, presented by Moving Being, perked up again with Paines Plough in two plays by David Pownall. One, Richard III Part Two, juxtaposes the maligned Crookback with a nervous George Orwell, wondering what the world will make of 1984: the two are linked, unnecessarily, by Betrayal, a board-game about Richard III, marketed in 1984.

Motocar is a far more powerful assessment of relative values; Rhodesia is finally on the brink of majority rule, and a black runs imaginatively amok in a white-run mental hospital, forcing the staff to participate in his own re-creation of oppression. The play, too, is overwrought: full of ingenious, even compelling images, but strangely lacking in urgency.

The Plough are not my favourite group, but they are thoughtful, stylish and unique; their imminent dispersal from lack of funds is to be regretted and, if possible, prevented. Though having said that I will add that were I keeper of contracts on the South Bank, until I had the signature of Joe Marcell, who gives sleek and mocking performances in both plays, firmly imprinted on a dotted line, I would not allow him to quit the building.
1977-12-18-enter-tripenstein:
Enter Tripenstein

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on three comedies

IT PROMISED to be a funny week; it threatened to be a glum one. Three comedies were billed; all of them classics. Hence the promise and hence the threat.

It may seem rather early to brand Fosdyke II (Bush) a classic, but the original Bill Tidy cartoon probably qualifies. While the success of the previous stage version, The Fosdyke Saga, has infected everybody's attitudes towards its successor, both audience and performers arrive feeling that a thundering good time is about to be given and taken. The notices have been good, the houses crammed, everyone laughed a lot and so did I. All the same it took me some time to get going and even when I did I had misgivings.

Assurance has, I think, edged over into complacency; the Fosdykes have become a cult, and cultists are not good audiences for comedy: their enthusiasm takes from the evening its edge of danger. More important, though, is the script that Mr Tidy and Alan Plater have provided. Part One had at any rate the tips of its toes just touching the ground; the Fosdykes were a gorgeous parody of all the gritty suffering families who ever got involved in trouble at t' mill. So their rise to brutal capitalist eminence as usurpers of the Ditchley world tripe empire had a touch of satire about it as well as fantasy. However, Part Two, which begins with them at the top and (I don't think I'm giving much away) ends with them there, is all fantasy. The Fosdykes have - you guessed it - lost touch with their roots.

A few weeks ago I suggested the Goons as an influence on Censored Scenes from King Kong. Their inky imperial prints are all over Fosdyke II as well, with Fosdyke missions despatched on hazardous missions to the African interior or the top of Everest. (Beaten to the latter by the Accrington Stanley expedition, tripe-eaters to a man.) A line like "men can be driven mad by his sinister oriental background music" could only have one fountain-head. In Mike Bradwell's production it is completely done, but I wondered if they weren't working on the wrong side of the street. Instead of pure Goons there is a large flavouring of music-hall and a dash of pantomime. The audience is bewitched, bullied and belaboured. (This, by the way, is enjoyable; nobody else had better try it, that's all. Except Barry Humphries.)

Only one episode, though, is really inspirational: involving the creation by a mad scientist of an artistic but threatening but vulnerable monster (called Tripenstein) and his encounter with the eternally nubile Victoria Fosdyke (Hazel Clyne), who wonderfully, but for this scene only, has regressed to childhood. Otherwise the Fosdykes as characters lose out to Jim Broadbent as their implacable opponent, gleefully self-described as "smelly old Roger Ditchley," disinherited, vengeful, and if not smarmy then certainly, in his ill-fitting shiny mohair and his ill-fitting shiny moustache, trying to be. Maybe he will sustain Fosdyke III which must come, for how otherwise will I be able to dub the finished epic not a trilogy but a Tripetych?

  

The Roundhouse, especially when two-thirds empty, is not an ideal setting for The Importance of Being Earnest, and the first act, through no particular fault of the players, was death. The lines were well enough spoken and the lines in that act are practically all, but most of us knew them by rote already and the house was not warm enough to rekindle our laughter. But Act Two is another matter; it is far more dependent on character and situation, greed and selfishness coming increasingly to the fore.

The tea-table duel of Gwendolen and Cecily is practically infallible and by the time Act Three rolled round we were conquered. The Actors' Company has been much strengthened by the return, as players and directors, of founder-members Tenniel Evans and Edward Petherbridge. Mr Evans, responsible for this one, also weighs in as both butlers, done in differing shades of depreciation, and Mr Petherbridge is Chasuble, walking delicately as Agag and continually shamed by his unruly tongue: since he cannot help licking his lips with it when in the presence of Prism. Ann Firbank is an impeccable Lady Bracknell; and though none of the juniors merit an adjective, they all seize vigorously on salient points. Thought has obviously been given as to which epigrams shall be rattled off and which shall be worked out in transit.

  

The strength of Trevor Nunn's production of The Alchemist, over which I raved at the Other Place this year, was always its steady build from solid foundations. At the Aldwych I feared for a time that it might be too steady; the opening quarrel, the first deceptions and disguises, were all deliberately done, but I wondered if they would ever cut loose. In one sense they never do; the text - a rare thing in Jonson - remains within their grasp, joyous and comprehensible. In another they certainly do: the craft of the cheaters, the hopes and then the furies of their victims rise like Wonderloaf and Hovis (Fosdyke II, song from) and beyond.

The most improved performance is Roger Rees's puritan Ananias; at any given moment he will mount a chair, preach and denounce, so that in the end people hide their furniture at his approach. It is a fine gag, but it would not work if Mr Rees had not the mortified fire and the airy comicality to set it off. John Woodvine's Subtle and Ian McKellen's Face have grown to virtuoso proportions; Mr McKellen, who has had a year, is as funny as, in his dedicated cupidity and his apparent sacrifice of identity in the cause of multiple illusion, he is frightening. Indeed this play in this production has it all: the dirt and detail of humanity, the broad sweep and cutting edge of moral poetry, the breathless dazzle of farce.

Mr Nunn's production finally accomplishes for Jacobean comedy what William Gaskill did in The Recruiting Officer et seq for the Restoration variety. To really pile it on: it is a match for Peter Brook's new Paris production of Ubu, which I shall write about shortly, and it exemplifies his comments on the paradoxical nature of textual fidelity: that you cannot release a play's anarchic spirit unless you strictly respect its letter.
1978-01-01-problem-of-plays-and-praisers:
Problem of Plays and Praisers

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the year's theatre--'except in one area, the worst in recent memory.'

EVERY year the theatre magazine Plays and Players takes a poll of the London critics, counts their votes, and bestows its annual awards accordingly. We electors then scan the published results, eager less to learn who has won than to watch our colleagues laying their preferences on the line.

Very rum they are too, especially for 1977. I speak, mind you, as one who this year failed to spot a single winner, but then who wants to run with the pack? Especially when you consider some of the things the pack is running after.

Actually I am worried less by their enthusiasms (which were not in most cases silly, merely wrong) than by their enthusiasm. A rumour is going round to the effect that 1977 was a good year in the theatre. Actually it was, except in one area, the worst in recent memory; and I can only surmise that the local scribes, having cried doom in excess of the facts for a couple of seasons, had worn themselves down into hoarseness and tolerance.

This was the year in which off-form plays by Alan Bennett (The Old Country), Peter Nichols (Privates on Parade), Tom Stoppard (the one-night LSO bash Every Good Boy Deserves Favour), Howard Brenton (Epsom Downs), Howard Barker (That Good Between Us), Ted Whitehead (Mecca), Robert Bolt (State of Revolution) and William Douglas Home (The Kingfisher) were both offered and lauded. (Stephen Poliakoff hit a bad patch too with Strawberry Fields, but he got clobbered.) Wills were taken for deeds on an unheard-of scale.

There were deeds as well of course. I counted six: Alan Ayckbourn's Bedroom Farce, David Edgar's Destiny, Terence Rattigan's Cause Célèbre, Arnold Wesker's The Wedding Feast, Ken Campbell's Illuminatus! and Barrie Keeffe's A Mad World My Masters--the last, incidentally, the only one to begin its life on a metropolitan stage.

The Ayckbourn case is particularly interesting. Bedroom Farce is probably his funniest play to date and by the end it has become his most disconcerting. Just Between Ourselves does prod and so disconcerts less, though the fact that it isn't very funny either (certainly not in its London production) was enough to get it some rave notices. An advance for Mr Ayckbourn--an advance presumably towards being as turgid as the other critical favourites. But I doubt if he'll oblige.

Cause Célèbre was a beautiful swan-song for its good (not great) and lamented author, and the only piece of the year to communicate deeply-felt emotion. That art may have gone with him. Some writers--John Byrne, Pam Gems, Mary O'Malley, Howard Schuman--promised to be good, and two or three others promised to be promising. Several of the acknowledged mastodons were silent, though John Osborne published a closet playlet (in the coloured pages of the Sunday Times) about reviewers: over-indulgent to both its subject and (the usual Osborne failing) its loquacious central character. The supports, though, were allowed to make some bitchily accurate points.

The West End maintained its accustomed state of suspended animation. Bubbling Brown Sugar had a troubling success: troubling since it confirmed British ignorance of popular music, and the consequent improbability of our producing a good musical of our own. The ravers, presumably, had never heard those old Harlem songs before: otherwise they would have noticed that they were being misinterpreted, and lamely at that.

Another successful musical, Something's Afoot, launched a new management, Backstage Productions, who subsequently introduced us to the American playwright David Mamet, and re-acquainted us with Eduardo de Filippo. Franco Zeffirelli's production of Filumena got performances of Latin intensity from all its actors and showed us Joan Plowright and Colin Blakely at their best.

Joy was otherwise this year almost the sole prerogative of the Royal Shakespeare Company. My columns have been so full of its good works that I feel obliged to offer a few provisos; the 1977 company, after all, arrived in London having run in its actors and several of its productions during 1976 at Stratford. But it built on these foundations superbly; by the end of the year we had been made acquainted with close on 50 actors.

The National Theatre, by contrast, had names: some famous, many still indistinguishable. This made its shows less fun: a factor particularly evident in its studio productions. The RSC's Bandits and That Good Between Us are not better plays than the National's Half Life and Strawberry Fields, but they had, in the circumstances, more personality. The National seems committed to juggernaut tactics even in the Cottesloe--where, incidentally, its two friendliest and most stimulating productions (The Passion and Bow Down) reached for their material far into the past.

This is a pointer; the National needs to do classics in a less demanding setting than the Olivier. The actors, brain-washed into contemporaneity, might complain, but it would be good for them and, more importantly, for us. We are not starved of new plays, and only a playwrights' pressure-group pretends that we are. A fully-stretched company could heat up the open spaces of the South Bank. Peter Hall created one at Stratford 17 years ago; now the finest thing we have, it still bears his mark. It's time he repeated himself.
1978-01-08-all-the-world-s-a-stage:
All the world's a stage

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

THE ORDER of the week, as ever, is role-playing. We have two plays set in the theatre, one of them apparently written in the conviction that actors are wittier and more fascinating than anybody else, the other that they represent, because of the conditions of their craft, all humanity.

Both these contentions are fallacious, and I do not know of any professionals who share them. (Have you noticed that when actors write plays, they are generally not about actors?) But it is difficult for the rest of us not to swallow them at moments; particularly perhaps if we are critics.

To prove the point, one of our number turns up as a character in Molnar's The Guardsman (Lyttelton) which, being devoted to the second or 'all the world's a stage' proposition, is the more pretentious play, but is also the more talented. It was written, and is set, in pre-1914 Hungary and our colleague's name is Bela.

Those were the days, it seems, when a critic was less of a drudge, more of a confidant. Bela never wastes his time going to plays; he pays social calls in opera-boxes, sits in sumptuous boudoirs (yes, those were the days) and advises his friends, the stars on how to run their private lives. Since these are extensions of their professional existence, having a critic on the premises may conceivably be helpful. Actually Bela spends most of his time saying 'I told you so,' so his private role is an extension of his public one. His clients are Nandor and Ilona, toasts of Budapest, married six months: just about time, on previous evidence, for Ilona to seek a new lover. To save her the trouble, and himself the pain, Nandor dresses up as a Guards officer and in this guise attempts to seduce her. Does she recognise him?

At the end of the play she says that she did, immediately; and in giving this away I reckon I am doing a service to all concerned. I saw the play in Stratford, Ontario, last year and I found that I relished the middle more for knowing the ending. (The beginning, which plods unmercifully, bored me on both occasions.) For Ilona may be lying; and it is the peculiar virtue of the play that every word of their central encounter will support either contingency. Scarcely less piquant is the dilemma of Nandor himself, not knowing whether success or failure in his project will harm his amatory ego the more. There is also the matter of his actor's ego; can he stand to have his deception detected?

But this is where the play, and the claims that have been made for it, become irritating. Acting has never been taken to mean persuading your beloved at point-blank range that you are somebody else; and it makes an extremely clumsy metaphor for the subtler deceptions of everybody's emotional life. Molnar's The Wolf, which we saw in London a few years ago, is a far more affecting study of marital distrust; not being concerned with actors it could not take short cuts to artifice or to glamour.

Nandor could of course be schizophrenic; Richard Johnson's jolly performance flirts with this idea. (If you really want to know, the situation was more wittily and penetratingly dramatised in Irma la Douce.) Peter Wood's production meanwhile goes very hard for theatre-as-image; we first see Nandor and Ilona from behind, taking curtain calls in Othello (what else?) and are later privileged to watch all the changes of Ralph Koltai's stridently artificial sets. None of this is necessary but reason not the need; it is very pleasurable. So is the fine balance between reality and artifice that Diana Rigg maintains as Ilona, and so is the performance of Brenda Blethyn as the maid, besotted and adenoidal.

Miss Blethyn, I feel, deserves a paragraph. She has been at the National three years, impressing immediately as the wife in Bloody Neighbours, a play hardly anyone saw. Since then she has mainly been employed in domestic service of some kind. She got a break, and took it, in The Force of Habit but that was such a flop that nobody noticed. She has also been a replacement for better-known actresses; she took over the heroine in Tales from the Vienna Woods, for which she wasn't suited, and is now more delightfully employed in Bedroom Farce. There, as in The Guardsman, she is quietly explosive.

  

The things actors get up to. In Spine Chiller (Duke of York's), they are assembled in a New York theatre to rehearse a play (called Spine Chiller) that 10 years earlier had been called off in the same theatre owing to the unexplained murder of three of the cast. Some of the survivors have actually turned up for the revival; remember that actors need to eat and producers love a gimmick.

Needless to say history repeats itself; the mock-deaths of the play within the play turn out for real. The story rapidly slid away from me (the killing at the end of Act One surprised me most since I had never registered the victim being alive) but the sheer cheek of author George Baxt is engaging. For once, though, a show suffers from not being camp enough; since the accents are wrong, the spirit is, too. 'Are you leaving your body to medical science?' 'No, to Paul Newman.' Some actresses could get away with that but not Sian Phillips who, for all her authority, has never struck me as the upstaging type.

  

Real people are no consolation: not in Laurence Dobie's Penny Whistle (Hampstead) which offers six of them, teenaged, unemployed or otherwise malcontent, drifting into an anonymously smart hotel for coffee, going in for confessionals and for some very rowdy games -- during which, surprisingly, they remain undisturbed. (Service sure is bad.) They are real, especially in their confusions, but unfortunately, in drama, as in life, they are going nowhere. Substance failing, we look for style; and find it in Nancy Meckler's direction, Grant Hicks's set, and the performance of Peter-Hugo Daly.
1978-01-08-swinging-back-to-words:
Swinging back to words

ROBERT CUSHMAN talks to Peter Brook about his latest Paris production.

AS usual the world is flocking to Peter Brook: not just to the Theatre des Bouffes-du-Nord in Paris, where he has just staged Alfred Jarry's Ubu, but to the man himself. He somehow manages to hold court even when sitting in the cafe next door to the theatre, dining off a glass of wine and a fried egg.

The Bouffes-du-Nord is a peeling dilapidated theatre (and jealously preserved as such) in an unfashionable part of town. Brook, though, has created his own kind of economy chic. At the end of the performance, director, actors and audience cluster together where the stage would be, if the Bouffes-du-Nord actually had a stage these days, and the admiration is as thick as it was in the cafe before the show. It's just as well the work is so good: the atmosphere otherwise would be unbearable.

One of the crowd is an Indian, who's arrived to work on the international group's long-term project, a dramatisation of the Mahabharata, which Brook describes as being to Indian culture "Dante, Homer and the Bible in one. Its themes and elements are relevant to everybody, but at the moment it's closed to us because its only theatre form is the Kathakali, which is too totally Indian for us to understand directly. Our aim is to become a bridge, to find a true non-Indian form for the quality of the work to come across. We've already been working on the basic script for a year."

Ubu is another step on the road, already marked by his Paris productions of Timon and The Ik and by his celebrated excursions to Persepolis (with the invented-language spectacle Orghast) and through the towns and villages of Nigeria; also by some less-publicised adventures: "doing incredibly crude improvisations on the streets of Brooklyn where gangs would throw stones at the group."

Brook still speaks of a synthesis between the two forms he marked out in his book The Empty Space -- the holy theatre (very serious, usually formal, but limited in appeal) and the rough theatre (popular but usually short on content). Like most people in this mind, he refers back to the Elizabethan achievement as the model of what he is after; and, in fact, he is about to have an Elizabethan, or rather Shakespearean year, returning to Stratford to direct Antony and Cleopatra with Glenda Jackson and an Actor Unknown, but before then, with his Paris International Brigade, doing Measure For Measure.

He once staged a reputedly definitive production of this play at Stratford, and it is unusual for him to challenge comparison so directly with his own past. For him it represents "the marriage of all the extremes. It has scenes of extremely bawdy comedy; it's political--it says all there is to say about justice and social order; and it's metaphysical--it deals with the relationship between the spiritual and temporal life. It's a story that can be told in the theatre to children, adolescents, old people simultaneously."

A few years ago Brook had the reputation of being an anti-word man. Probably the rumours were exaggerated; anyway, he's now swinging back the other way. "We've gone about as far as we could in direct off-the-cuff improvisation. We've done thrilling things, but they've only been for ourselves because they're swept away the moment the experience ends." So back to a text, in this case Jarry's piece from the 1890s, a schoolboy prank that set off an aesthetic revolution, what Brook calls "a masterpiece of non-official theatre, a classic anti-classic."

"The value of a text lies not in abstract literary merits but because it's life in concentration; it's a shrivelled essence that expands in performance. Jarry's very special because he provides the raw material for an anarchic explosion but he's also highly precise. There's an astonishing amount of unpredictable stuff in the play that could not be envisaged when you read it. But that doesn't mean that anything goes. You can only realise the new forms if you have a very precise respect for the forms themselves."

Brook's austerest pronouncements often boil down when you consider them to plain commonsense, and his best work often resembles what one has always believed to constitute good theatre anyway. So his Ubu is a classic piece of comedy. His actors have acquired a peculiar shared intensity which enables them to play in a vein of nightmare farce and make it seem the most natural thing in the world.

The young Jarry turned the hated schoolmaster into an archetype of ruthless mediocrity; Brook called Ubu "the eternal middle-class French concierge: narrow mean horizons fired with a passionate egocentricity." It is generally written that after Ubu's first word "Merde" the theatre was never the same again.

Recent productions have tried conscientiously to make it as explosive as possible. Brook, as so often, underplays: Ubu (the hulking Greek-American Andreas Katsulas) comes on at one door, his shrewish wife (Michele Collinson) at another, and they begin an ordinary day. Bad temper is not a means of shocking the audience but just their way of carrying on.

The play concerns Ubu's brief career as King of Poland -- brief, bloody, cowardly and spectacularly avaricious. (All his laws are tax-laws.) He is a cartoon blend of Tamburlaine and Macbeth and this production joyfully travesties all the Elizabethan battle-scenes you have ever seen. A giant wheel keeps appearing, cheerfully rolling over most of the cast and leaving a trail of limp bodies on the floor. Bricks recur as well; Mrs Ubu serves a banquet of them to Poland's rapacious nobility.

In the second half, Ubu Enchained (which was always less successful and still is), the focus changes; Ubu comes to France and decides that in the land of liberty and fraternity the only distinction, the only way to riches, lies in being a slave. Brook's view of this paradox ("he's terrifying but he challenges a society that has to be challenged") seems to me overblown but the production is still full of quiet splendours. When rain falls, seemingly from nowhere, into the Ubus' prison, it forms into the most convincing puddle in the history of world theatre.
1978-01-15-room-for-all-of-russia:
Room for all of Russia

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a Chekhov revival and new plays from Hull Truck and Barrie Keeffe.

THE whole of Russia is our orchard; and the set for The Cherry Orchard at Riverside Studios looks capable of accommodating the whole of Russia. Since the main auditorium of Hammersmith's new arts centre is a flexible space, the director, Peter Gill, must have consciously decided to give the Ranevsky family this infinity of lebensraum.

The width of the stage seems daunting when you enter the auditorium. Looking ahead, I thought I could see it working for the play's alfresco second act, but not for the interiors of the other three. I was wrong; the second act works the least well, perhaps because Mr Gill shows, understandably, fewer inhibitions about stringing it out across the entire area of William Dudley's spare, timbered, strictly non-representational scene. Indoors he concentrates his actors, usually centre-stage, and lets the surrounding vastness contract or expand more or less at will. (Ours rather than his.)

If you choose to look at the empty spaces, you may become aware, as never before, of the geographical isolation of the play. At the end Varya is off to keep house for people who are spoken of as if they were neighbours, and who live 70 miles away. The orchard itself exists not, as usual, in a spray of pink blossom glimpsed through windows at the back, but somewhere invisible behind our heads. As the characters line up at the edge of the stage to confront and describe it, it takes on more reality than I have ever known.

Mr Gill excels in deploying formal tactics in the service of untrammelled life. I have already said that he concentrates; and concentration, in another sense, is the strength and hallmark of this production. Shifts in relationships are denoted by slight but precise alterations in generally sedentary groupings. Thus Trofimov, at the beginning of the ball scene, moves along a row of empty chairs to sit next to Pishchik when he finds that this man whom he has despised has heard of Nietzsche.

Emotions among the minor characters (whatever people say, there are such animals in Chekhov) are played to the full, but never enlarged or prolonged. So the maid Dunyasha (Elizabeth Estensen) in the opening moments of the play goes into full-throated but momentary ecstasy at the false alarm of the family's return. Leigh Lawson as the flashy valet Yasha, usually the unregarded villain of the piece, sounds perfectly reasonable when he pleads to be allowed to return to Paris and escape provincial stagnation.

Eleanor Bron gives Charlotta a nervous protective hauteur (and is the best ventriloquist, though not the best conjurer, I have known in the part). Wensley Pithey is hugely good as Pishchik, George Howe's Firs is hardly a believable serf but his last moments are very affecting. Here the production's feeling for stress, pace and control is most evident. And the plot, of which there is a great deal in The Cherry Orchard, is clearly and rhythmically presented. We appreciate the full significance of the telegrams Ranevskaya receives from Paris, one each act, leading up to her departure in the last.

It is always possible to see what is driving Judy Parfitt's Ranevskaya; not so easy, though, to be moved by the results. This is a sharp, elegant and uncompromising portrayal of a character who compromises all the time, and the actress's steeliness has infected the character. Ranevskaya remains, stubbornly, a role for a star; since that is how she is regarded by everybody else in the play.

The playing in the upper echelons of this production (apart from Philip Locke's brilliant Gaev, whose billiards mannerism is plainly all that stops him from going to pieces) is just not volatile enough; Michael Elphick's Lopahin is well blocked in to begin with, but falls down (not literally, though that might work) in his drunk scene. All the same, welcome.

  

Hull Truck has its most complex show yet in A Bed of Roses (Bush). A vicar begins by announcing a Keep Our Churches Open campaign. ("KOCO," somebody christens it later.) He means psychologically as well as physically open; he and his wife are waif-and-stray collectors, and one of their acquisitions is a recidivist with a plate in his head and leanings towards the occult, living with a fierce girl who claims not to love him: an assertion which baffles the vicar's wife, though her own marriage is falling apart.

In another part of the forest we find a third doomed pair: a compulsive joker who can hardly speak without donning a funny voice, and a humourless Ulster girl out to lead him to the altar. Actionwise, they fall into line when they have a hilarious, prenuptial chat with the vicar, who lists as prime marriage-wreckers sex, money and "infuriating habits": with which last every character in the show is loaded. In the last scene he reads the banns, along with other bad news, straining and agonising farther along the booby-trapped road to Christian charity.

This struck me as the best deal religion has had on our stage in a long time; Robin Soans's performance, funny and anguished, is superb, as, in a simpler fashion, is Alan Williams's ferocious crook. The standards set by Mike Bradwell in his direction and improvised dramaturgy are now very high, and one may fault a couple of actresses for falling below them: one too theatrical to be real, another too real to be theatrical. But everybody joins with sparkling expertise in the songs, which are almost integrated enough to make a musical. Anyone on for studying the Rise of the Strolling Player as Musician?

  

Hull Truck is floating. Barrie Keeffe isn't drowning either, though in Frozen Assets (Warehouse) he splashes a bit wildly. He has returned to his old protagonist, the embittered young underdog, but he still has the more recent farcical style of A Mad World, My Masters clinging to him. The two do not blend. His hero, Buddy, is a borstal boy on the run, cheerful except that he has accidentally impaled a warder and has a raging toothache. The latter complaint is finally cured by an affluent dentist, described as the first kind person Buddy has met.

His memory is playing tricks; he has also been well treated by a priest (again), an MP and a Socialist peer who admittedly wants his body, but then who's perfect? Certainly not Buddy's brother-in-law, a house-breaker who shows him no sympathy whatever. The ambitions of the poor are shown to mimic those of the rich: a villa in the Canaries or an expense-account trip to the West Indies. Both sides too can deep-freeze their acquisitions: for further explanation of the title see the play. It will be worth your while, for though what Mr Keeffe conveys is different from what he means, his vigour, however diffused, remains unquenchable.

Barry Kyle's production does nothing much to tidy the play up, but Allen Hendrick as Buddy holds it together, and though David Waller comes on a bit strong for a screw in scene one, he doubles up finely at a later hour as the peer, who is as drunk as a lord.

  

I hardly warmed to the idea of a two-hander about the last days of Sarah Bernhardt, dictating her reminiscences to a male secretary who assists her in acting out scenes from her past. But John Murrell's Memoir (Ambassadors) is a very pleasant surprise, wittily and fastidiously written. Siobhan McKenna's Sarah is, as Beerbohm said of the lady's Hamlet, tres grande dame; Niall Buggy as her primly reluctant co-star is perfection.
1978-01-22-basho-and-the-tidal-wave:
Basho and the tidal wave

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Bond's 'The Bundle.'

MORE than likely Edward Bond's The Bundle will turn out to be the best play of 1978. It is certainly the best its author has written since Lear.

Like Lear, it has the force and the onward movement of a tidal wave. It communicates narrative joy; a complicated tale is to be told, spanning many years, and the playwright's craft in keeping us aware of our bearings is immaculate. Necessarily he writes many scenes, but he gives each one a shape and a dynamic. Where previous plays in the Warehouse season have reflected the staccato fragmentation of television, Mr Bond returns us to the weight and rhythm of epic theatre.

Talking of returns: The Bundle takes off from the same point as Mr Bond's 10-year-old Narrow Road to the Deep North. The seventeenth-century Japanese poet Basho sets out in search of enlightenment. He begins by crossing a river, bilking the ferryman ("I go to be reborn. Does the midwife charge the child?") and refusing to succour a baby left wrapped up on the bank by poverty-stricken parents. In Narrow Road the baby punished him by growing up and turning into a tyrant. In The Bundle the baby, for whom the play is named, does the same thing even more effectively by growing up and turning into a liberator.

Basho is in the grand time-serving tradition of Bondian poets: he becomes a judge and a ruthless servant of the established order, thus putting himself several strikes ahead of Mr Bond's Shakespeare in Bingo, who was merely a passive collaborator (and whose previous impersonator at the Warehouse, Patrick Stewart, now turns in a suitably flinty performance of Basho).

The territory is ruled by "the landowner" (unseen) and his main ally is the river; the iron fist of the one and the floods of the other keep the peasants in indigent subjection until Wang (the ex-bundle) teaches them how the landowner may be overthrown and the river tamed. His agents are a band of outlaws whom he has turned into guerrillas. Before this he has learned the enemy's ways by spending a period as Basho's servant: a post into which he was forced to sell himself to ensure the survival of his foster-parents, the ferryman and his wife.

The image of Wang shouting "Buy me, buy me" is a powerful one which somehow escapes self-consciousness; of all our current playwrights Mr Bond is the only one who can write large enough to bring this off. There is an even stronger moment later when the knives are out, and the ferryman has been killed by Basho's soldiers. His wife, half-senile, has been bound and gagged; she frees herself, but not to do or say anything: merely to scream. More than once Mr Bond seems to be learning from Brecht, and bettering the instruction.

Add to all this the bite and flavour of the language, a faithful production by Howard Davies and a performance of Wang by Mike Gwilym that releases all the strength, assurance and suppleness that have been welling up in this actor in the past few years, and we can get down to the play's flaw, which is one-sidedness.

One very discerning reviewer has claimed that the author maintains a measure of sympathy for Basho, but the drift of the play is against him. At the end Basho is still looking for enlightenment; and he is mocked, not honoured, for it. He is typed as the selfish aesthete (or holy man) seeking the good of his own soul at the expense of the general welfare. (He is pretentious too. All Mr Bond's characters speak with vigour and imagination of the river that rules their lives, but they see it only as a river. Basho alone goes on about it, in traditional literary fashion, as a source of spiritual regeneration.) And with him go all the humane scruples artists are accustomed to express if not to exemplify on the subject of means and ends.

"We have not," says Wang, "earned the right to be kind." He too has the chance of saving an abandoned child, but he throws it into the river. There is certainly irony here (where would he, or indeed the revolution, have been if Basho or the ferryman had done the same?), but it is not followed through. Wang's area of choice narrows from the moment he becomes a guerrilla. (His merry men, incidentally, speak in strange short phrases reminiscent of Mr Alfred Jingle or Big Chief Sitting Bull. Rather like the outlaws in The Two Gentlemen of Verona, they appear to choose Wang for their leader because he can talk grammar.) We are never made aware of the cost to Wang of revolution; or, except in the most general terms, of the cost to anyone else.

The violence in this play, compared to that in earlier Bond, is discreetly handled; but it is evident for all that. Evident, at least, when committed by the landowners; the process of Wang's revolt is unconvincingly bloodless, just as its outcome is unconvincingly idyllic. Unconvincing to me anyway; the fault may be in my temperament or conditioning but I believe it lies in the conditions of drama. We have spent years telling our radical playwrights that we know what they are against, but what are they for? Mr Bond shows us, and we must complain, ungratefully, of bathos. But it is more important that he has suppressed evidence and broken his own rules. In theory he endorses cruelty in a good cause; in practice he fails to present it.

The argument may be murky, but the style and the story are limpid. Most refreshing when you have to cope with the week's other offerings: both (to adopt a phrase I invented a couple of years ago and which inexplicably failed to catch on) transported Irish plays.

  

Ron Hutchinson's Says I, Says He (Theatre Upstairs) follows a couple of Ulstermen to the building-sites of London, and then back to Belfast, where they fall in, and then out, with the militant loyalists.

One reviewer has puzzlingly reported that they end up happy; actually they end up dead. What is more, they are foredoomed. Though the play has vigorous spurts of humour, boozy sexual or scatological (all fuelled by desperation and all excellently put over by the company, especially the swagger-bellied James Duggan), it is drenched in the most timelessly topical kind of Celtic gloom. It also mixes fact, fantasy, and flashback, which makes it difficult to follow.

It is simplicity itself, however, compared to the Caribbean-Irish musical comedy Kingdom Come! (King's Head), which recreates the Ulster situation on a tropical island, whose destiny is disputed by three rival groups, each consisting of one white person and one black. Power goes in the end to the people: quite distinct from their self-appointed representatives in the rest of the cast.

Kingdom Come! is a musical; much vital information, intended to be conveyed in the opening number, is lost in transit and never recovered. It is curious how prone the British musical is to return to its salad days, even when the basic subjects are as tough as this one, but Stewart Parker's lyrics are admirably turned if taken in isolation (I am in no position to judge their relevance to the action) and Shaun Davey's music, more Caribbean than Irish, is infectious, as are the performances. The costumes are good, too; though the lady responsible, whose name happens to be Maggie Smith, has been given what I could call unscrupulously large billing outside the theatre.
1978-01-29-not-so-funny:
PETER BARNES has all the right ideas. He wants theatre to matter, to change our thoughts, and if possible our lives.

He disapproves of cruelty, suffering, bigotry and privilege; also of routine theatrical naturalism. He believes in breaking down barriers by having his characters break into song, and for this material he goes to the best of modern musical comedy. He believes, I dare say, in the alienation-effect more wholeheartedly than Brecht himself ever did.

Mr Barnes often gives the impression of having read the shriller contemporary critics, and swallowed them whole. He then takes a further step--one the pundits themselves were too canny or too cowardly to take--and actually sets about writing and adapting plays. In the latter capacity at least, he has done us all some favours. I don't want, for the moment, to get involved in the rights and wrongs of his tamperings with the text of Ben Jonson (except to remark that his zeal to render the classics "relevant" is another example of his susceptibility to current dogma), but it is certain that without his enthusiasm we would never have seen The Devil is an Ass. Recently, too, he introduced us to a very funny Feydeau, The Purging, though it was typical that he should claim for his discovery that it shows "a Frenchman's main concern is not sex but money and the state of his bowels." The hero of The Purging is a manufacturer of chamber-pots; his professional preoccupations prove nothing at all about the rest of Parisian society.

Which brings us to Mr Barnes's latest, a double bill at the Royal Court: Part One, Ivan the Terrible; Part Two, Auschwitz; overall title Laughter!; purpose uncertain.

It may be to demonstrate that you can laugh at anything however horrible and feel better for it; or that you can laugh at anything however horrible and feel worse for it; or that some things are so horrible you can't laugh at all. The aim may be to challenge black comedy as a genre, or to show how people (as opposed to playwrights and audiences) can only contemplate atrocity by making jokes. Here Mr Barnes runs up against two handicaps: (a) he can't write people and (b) he can't write jokes.

He begins with an author-figure on the receiving-end of a custard-pie. No, he insists, it's not going to be that kind of show. "A sense of humour's no remedy for evil... It softens our hatred. We must root out comedy." The refrain "root it out, root it out" is taken up by the actors in the plays proper whenever they succeed in raising a chuckle. They are clutching, most of the time, at straws.

Tsar Ivan rages, repents, kills his heir and torments his courtiers while upstage sits one of his agonised victims, bloodily impaled. His presence has, no doubt of it, a dampening effect on one's sense of humour, but Ivan's jests would hardly raise the roof in any circumstances. "They don't," he says of the sufferer's screams, "write songs like that any more."

This is Mr Barnes's favourite, and draggy, anachronism joke. Most of the dialogue is in the mock-archaic style he used in The Bewitched, and it has a certain dusty effectiveness. At the close Ivan meets Death, who tells him that his random cruelties will soon be eclipsed by the computerised carnage of the twentieth century. This is our bridge to Part Two, which does indeed make us unexpectedly nostalgic for Part One, though not perhaps in the way intended.

We meet the civil servants who helped, from a distance, to run the death-camps, filing, typing memos, indulging in office squabbles, trying to get each other fired. Favourite weapon: trapping your colleagues into making jokes about the Fuhrer, which aligns with Mr Barnes's theme without illustrating it. Much of the piece is conventional home-front black-market comedy, and very feeble: ersatz seems the appropriate word. They are made, momentarily, to face the realities behind their work; they cry first that they couldn't help it, and second that it didn't happen anyhow. All accurate and unarguable, and in this lifeless context totally uninteresting.

At the end Mr Barnes does make a couple of points. He has his characters break into The Brotherhood of Man, a chorus from Frank Loesser's How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying; Loesser's amiable satire on office life suddenly becomes sabre-toothed. (A couple of gags have earlier been pillaged from the same score, which makes, I suppose, for consistency.) Then a pair of Jews do a cross-talk routine on their way to the gas-chambers. (Timothy West and Derek Francis are very good here; the only point in Charles Marowitz's production at which the actors seemed at ease.)

Some good lines have been appropriated, and we do laugh, and then we do feel sheepish: needlessly, since our revulsion at Auschwitz is not altered in the slightest--any more than Tom Stoppard's two plays last year made us feel indulgent towards the treatment of dissidents in Russia and Czechoslovakia. These plays, which were really funny, make the final case against Mr Barnes: that comedy of any complexion requires an unforgeable gaiety of spirit, and that wishing will not make it so.

  

Charles Wood's Dingo is a rerun of the war in the desert, designed to destroy our illusions about Montgomery, Churchill and glory generally. Ten years ago, when the play was first done, this was necessary and even exhilarating; now it suffers, in every sense, from overkill. But Mr Wood's disillusioned fascination with army and theatre language and his bizarre stagecraft still strike intermittent sparks; when he fractures forms he does it from personal necessity, not according to a programme. (So he gets attacked by critics; his last, Jingo, got a fearful unmerited lashing from Martin Esslin, who usually likes everything. Especially Peter Barnes.)

Barry Kyle's Warehouse production does everything for the play except cut it. Paul Shelley as the clean-nosed malcontent Dingo and Ian McDiarmid as the mountebank Monty give nifty performances, though they cannot disguise that their roles are respectively under- and over-written. The best on hand are Paul Moriarty and the extraordinary Richard Griffiths, gentle and immovable.
1978-01-29-the-authentic-thane:
The Authentic Thane

Profile of Ian McKellen by Robert Cushman

LAST YEAR -- in Newcastle and London -- we met Macbeth: met him, since this was a studio-sized production, face to face. We were in fact locked up with him, and felt it within ourselves to achieve success, to crave more of it, to kill for it, to live without hope and to smell damnation. We gazed on the face ('a book,' says Lady Macbeth, 'where men may read strange things') and heard the authentic voice, withered and curdling, of despair. Just occasionally we laughed, since the performance revealed a sardonic, courtly wit in Macbeth. And very often we smiled, from sheer joy at the skill and imagination of the actor; and above all -- making connections visible where none before had been apparent -- at the intelligence of Ian McKellen.

In my experience McKellen is the only actor -- almost the only person -- who admits to enjoying interviews. He comes on as a practical intellectual. He can argue with his directors on their own ground -- Trevor Nunn, welcoming the challenge, described the effect on him as 'rejuvenating' -- but having done this, he can get on with the job. 'He can be fantastically objective -- but then he can do it, he can deliver.' The words are Susan Fleetwood's, once Ophelia to McKellen's Hamlet and an adoptive sister ever since, and they differentiate McKellen from the majority of university-bred actors.

The fact that McKellen went to Cambridge already begins to set him apart from those other top stage actors of the past 30 years who have aroused general excitement, if not unanimous acclaim: Richard Burton, Paul Scofield, Albert Finney, Peter O'Toole, and Nicol Williamson, those who arouse the fiercest partisanship, for or against. Scofield excepted, they all have the name of being roughnecks. McKellen has been generally regarded as a sensitive plant; surprisingly, since he is one of the most solidly built actors around (all muscle, no fat) and even possesses the fashionable qualification of a north-country background. In fact he lays his first acting ambitions at the door of his primary school in Wigan. He was in the school reciting team, which 'used to go around to Nonconformist church socials.'

From here he progressed to Bolton School, a highly theatre-conscious establishment where 'we virtually did rep every term. I was forced into taking acting very seriously.' At the same time he was encouraged to follow his parents' example of going regularly to Bolton Rep, and began to enjoy working out for himself -- 'by surmise and reading the occasional book' -- how they got the plays on.

'What was amazing was that by the time I got to Cambridge and suddenly met, for the first time in my life, 20 other people who were as daft about the theatre as I was, I had more experience of acting than even Corin Redgrave. I knew more about upstaging and the techniques of acting at 14 than many of the people I now work with do. It was as if I'd been born in a trunk; which I wasn't -- my father was a borough engineer.' (Both his grandfathers, though, were preachers, a kind of histrionic lineage which can also be found in Laurence Olivier, Alec McCowen and Sybil Thorndike.)

He had been through the teenage stage of 'this is Ian, he's going to be an actor'; but (again a common condition) he had given up the idea by the end of his schooldays, and had decided to become a teacher. Continued success in university plays made professional acting seem possible and sensible. The turning-point seems to have been a Justice Shallow in his first year which, when Trevor Nunn came up to Cambridge a year later, was still being discussed.

That McKellen should have specialised in old men as an undergraduate is an index of his technical accomplishment. It also summed up the problem that faced him when he went professional. 'I was rather proud and pleased with myself that I knew how to do it; what I was hopeless at was stepping on the stage without any aids and just behaving in the style of the play as myself. It's only very recently that I've had the courage to forget the technical side of and think about the spiritual side. Not think about it, just let it happen.'

At this point in the conversation he pulls himself up and says proudly that he remains 'a very technical actor indeed. When I come to the performance, there's nothing I do that I'm not aware of.' Then he qualifies again: 'Most nights that I'm on stage I do something, consciously or unconsciously, that I've never done before.'

McKellen improvises, to bring the threads together, within a firm structure; and for the last two years it has been a structure on which he has collaborated with an extraordinary collection of other skilled masons. His half of the RSC (seen at Stratford last year and in London this) has been a compact yet various ensemble, who have restored belief in actors' democracy. There are pleasing ironies here; Nunn has remained the boss, his authority firmer and more popular than ever, and McKellen, once co-founder of the self-governing Actors' Company, is a brighter star than before. He has in fact played nothing but whopping leads; the chutzpah of attempting Romeo, Macbeth and Leontes ('The Winter's Tale') in the same season is what led him to Stratford; at the Aldwych he has added Bernick in Ibsen's 'Pillars of the Community' and Face in Jonson's 'The Alchemist'.

That's good casting for him, and not only because it allows him for once to be as amusing on stage as off. ('Not many laughs in Romeo; I make myself laugh as Macbeth.') Face is a virtuoso con-man; and McKellen plays him as a blank in repose, who comes instantly to life in each new disguise, and goes into a silent acquisitive frenzy at the end. The action and the frenzy are the distinguishing marks.

They do not necessarily imply frantic mobility. An actress who worked with him earlier in his career loved his stillness in rehearsal, though he lost it all before an audience. Susan Fleetwood, though, admired his Romeo for its repose: 'When he was still, he seemed so vulnerable and young.' There was none of this relaxation on the first night at Stratford; he fell back, presumably through nerves, on the idea of adolescence, looping himself round handy pillars. There was no comparison with the performance he had achieved when the play reached London a year later. His Stratford Romeo was (in the words most frequently used against him) a mannered performance; it obscured the part and the play. His London performance merely had a few mannerisms, which relate to his ordinary speech-patterns, are unassumed and unassuming: at best part of his appeal and at worst harmless.

He himself accounts Romeo a failure ('I came to it too late') but his comments on the role illuminate why the performance and Nunn's production gripped the audience as this play seldom does. 'Romeo's mad -- he's a suicide case -- he can't reconcile the enormity of love with the business of having breakfast and being nice to people.' McKellen commands the hollowest stare and the most drained and hopeless voice on the English stage. He can suggest blank black caverns in the mind.

Hence his extraordinary Macbeth, which owes something, to be sure, to the production and the other players and the intimacy of the studio auditorium (the way in which he wants, for the foreseeable future, to play Shakespeare), much to the intelligence of his characterisation but most of all to his physical and spiritual energy. For the first time the play in the theatre justifies the text-books; it releases a sense of evil. Though he bristles at talk of mannerisms, he recognises the complaint that 'Ian McKellen flogs his charm too much'; all the same, the performances of his new maturity have been marked as much as anything by their uncompromising ugliness.

Perhaps that's only possible for an actor who is sure of his charm to begin with; anyway it marked his thrusting arriviste Dr Faustus (a watershed for him in my book) and his grotesque Marquis of Keith (another con-man). It enables him to play the envy, the malevolence and the final nihilism of Macbeth and not to fuss about the 'nobility'; and yet to leave us with a sense of nobility, attained by forcing us to look at the truth. All actors talk, given half the chance, about the Truth; but it was Shakespeare's truth that reached us here.
