He brings his actors on in varying combinations, but the configurations seem arbitrary. There is, to put it at its most basic, nobody whom one is particularly glad to see. I don't mean they aren't credible or likeable; I mean they have no energy.

This is true even of the senior inquirer, invested by Fulton Mackay with his usual measure of frazzled Caledonian insistence. Mr Mackay is always a compelling actor but I liked him best in that other prison drama, Porridge, where the demands of TV comedy caused him to hurry on a bit. Left to himself he is apt to add 10 minutes to any play's running time. Nicholas Le Prevost elaborates on his particular speciality, the smart but nervous grammar-school boy fallen among bullies; while Nigel Terry, darkly mumbling, has another go at his. Gaye Brown, on the other hand, is cast rewardingly against type; the lady she plays could never be described as a good-time girl.

  

It would obviously be unfair to judge Ken Campbell's projected 10-part sci-fi epic The Warp (ICA) by the first night of its first instalment. At least I hope it would be unfair, since what I saw was mostly terrible. The acting, even by Mr Campbell's informal standards, was sloppy; I was relieved when a first-night cry of "Speak up for God's sake" turned out to have come from the maestro himself. (It worked too. Instant direction.)

Neil Oram's script, as so far revealed, plays like a pale copy of Illuminatus: conspiracy theories are adumbrated and the questing hero, a would-be poet, is passed on from one baffling guru to another; one grew to dread the announcement that someone had an interesting friend they wanted him to meet. There are also beddable girls for him to enjoy and policemen to stop him doing it (the number of arrests in this play must constitute an all-time record).

Only Jim Broadbent among the actors seemed to me to match Mr Campbell's exalted standards of frenzy. But the staging offers some promise of fun to come; the play is performed on a series of stages placed end-to-end around the walls of the hall. It chases you clockwise round the room; in fact I must confess to wondering what happens next. (Will I succumb? Watch this space.)

  

The heroine of Shaw's very late play The Millionairess (Haymarket) is required to be simultaneously bossy and enchanting. Penelope Keith can be bossy and hilarious (as in The Norman Conquests) or vulnerable and enchanting (as in Donkey's Years); the new combination is beyond her, though she manages both elements by turns and looks a treat; her giraffe height functions in the production almost as mobile sculpture.

Her colleagues mostly vary from grotesque to dull (Nigel Hawthorne performing needless prodigies of self-effacement), though Charles Kay has a pretty style as her chosen mate, the Egyptian doctor whom he plays, perhaps inevitably, as Peter Sellers' Indian. (Donald Pleasence once did so on television. And some movie producer saw him, and cast Mr Sellers in a film version, opposite Sophia Loren. Goodness gracious both of them.)

The play is a problem since its dialogue has sparkle far in excess of its weight. The piece races along, and the audience are left wondering what it is all for. At its heart, though, is a very powerful conceit; the heroine Epifania is sexy because rich: a lineal descendant of Portia in The Merchant of Venice and encumbered by much the same kind of paternal will. She is cold and challenging; so is the play.
1979-01-14-living-in-the-present:
Living in the present

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

NOW IT comes on the winter of 1979 and there is much snow on the ground, and also ice, and it is a miserable time for one and all, and many citizens and even theatres are compelled to do the best they can.

There is one theatre in East London called the Half Moon, which is formerly a synagogue in the days when there is a big call for such places in East London and what do they put on but a show which is entitled Guys and Dolls and which is well known to be a musical comedy whose plot is lifted from one of the short stories written by Damon Runyon. This Runyon writes many such tales back in the 1930s, and is such a guy, as hates and despises the use of the past tense. This tense is in fact employed more than somewhat in Guys and Dolls but I excuse it since the stage is well known to be a bastard art form, while the musical comedy stage has practically nothing legitimate about it whatsoever.

Personally I greet the arrival of this show with much enthusiasm for many citizens of my acquaintance regard it as the best musical they ever see, including many who never actually see it at all. The thing is, it is first staged in London in 1953 at an hour when many of my friends are tucked up in their beds, with their mammas maybe singing lullabies to them; and I myself do not see it at this date though afterwards I play the record maybe a hundred times, and also take two or three ganders at the movie. One way and another I feel pretty well acquainted with Guys and Dolls and I wish to say I never expect to see it performed in an ex-synagogue by a cast of seven. But the Half Moon is what is called an art theatre, with few potatoes to spare, and its patrons are very tolerant.

A guy named Shakespeare once says to make a virtue of necessity or some such; and Robert Walker, who directs this item, is very virtuous, in fact he is practically a saint. Many characters in this show are gamblers, and one or two are no better than common criminals, and it will be a dreadful thing if any honest guys or dolls in the audience admire them or find them romantic. But Mr Walker sets them all in a barroom which maybe once sees better days, though personally I will not like to bet on it; and he brings them all on very slow and sour, and sends them all off even slower and sourer, and one way and another he seems to think the show is what they call a black comedy though this is by no means the case.

Furthermore, he cuts out some of the best jokes from Abe Burrows's dialogue, though the book is still the funniest ever written, for Broadway at that. But Mr Walker knows what he is doing and is bigger than me, or at least broader, so I do not pursue it.

At first he seems to have 10 actors, only three of them turn out to be nothing but musicians; though one of this trio is liable to leave his piano and stand on a box to impersonate Big Jule who comes from Chicago and who many inhabitants of Manhattan wish will return there on account of his hasty temper. Also visiting town is Sky Masterson, the renowned sportsman, who falls in love with a Salvation Army doll, though neither of them, according to the song, is ever in love before; Barrie Houghton, who plays Sky, is as rat-faced a juvenile lead as ever I wish to see, but of course this is part of the intention, and he is slick and oily and also sings pretty good.

Maurice Colbourne, who shrugs in a very eloquent manner, plays Nathan Detroit, who runs a floating crap-game and on occasion that attracts much opprobrium from the coppers, and also from Miss Adelaide, who is Nathan's fiancee of 14 years' standing, though to hear her tell it standing is not her usual position. Adelaide gets to sing about her plight as a female who is "getting a kind of a name for herself and the name ain't his," which is maybe the most comical line any lyricist ever writes.

Adelaide is played by Maggie Steed, a long lady who honks very high-toned and has plenty of attack and makes me laugh ha-ha practically every time she opens her mouth. There is also a guy named Robin Hooper who plays seven roles, male and female, which means he is frequently on stage with himself and has to keep changing his hat. He sings a quiet ditty called "More I Cannot Wish You," which is such a touching ballad as you would not expect Frank Loesser to write, he being famous for such comedy numbers as "Take Back Your Mink," performed by Adelaide and the Hot Box Girls, only three, and "Sit Down, You're Rockin' the Boat." But such chorus numbers as "Luck Be a Lady" and "Sit Down, You're Rockin' the Boat" are done with great ingenuity, and also glee; and it is of course a great testimony to Guys and Dolls that it can lose so much weight and still live.

  

A month or so ago I am sitting in a restaurant on 72nd Street with David Edgar, the playwright, talking of his piece Mary Barnes which opens in Birmingham last year and is to transfer to the Royal Court where it arrives last week. "You are," he says to me, "the only critic who notices that the play is not only about alternative methods of psychotherapy but about the counter-culture generally. But," he says, "I see that you say this subject is skimpily treated and I rewrite the play accordingly."

I will not of course mention such a conversation, being a modest guy at all times, if this aspect does not strike me as being far more effectively handled this time round. But I am puzzled, for I do not notice any extra scenes or speeches; in fact I suspect Mr Edgar trims his play, reducing the social and historical background to scale and stepping up the ironies. Hugo, the Supershrink, who many spectators believe to be none other than R. D. Laing, is played by Donald Sumpter, who is teasing and testing and also cool. Simon Callow meanwhile is kind and furious as Eddie who guides and coaxes Mary Barnes through her ascent from schizophrenia; and Patti Love's Mary is so complete that I get a shock when she takes her curtain-call since by then I honestly forget she is an actress.

Up above Mary Barnes, in the Theatre Upstairs, there is Ron Hutchinson's Anchorman, which also comes from what is called the Midlands, namely from Coventry. Now Mary Barnes is such a play as turns pain into pleasure by illuminating it, but Anchorman keeps everything dark, including the audience. Four British soldiers, who will be considered very rough customers even in the army, are present at the end of the world, or at least of this society, though of course not being dramatic critics they have little experience of such cataclysms, and panic accordingly.

The production is on the dingy side, and is such an event as a scribe like Ambrose Hammer, who dearly loves to heave the old harpoon into actors, will enjoy reviewing; but I am kind-hearted and wish no part of such action, so I shut up.
1979-01-21-screaming-the-house-down:
Screaming the house down

Theatre

Robert Cushman on a Joe Orton revival

The programme for the revival of Joe Orton's The Erpingham Camp (King's Head) sports a paragraph by the author's biographer, John Lahr, claiming the piece as Orton's great transition farce, paving the way for What the Butler Saw and second to it in merit. This, I think, is a case of biographer's bias. The Erpingham Camp is an aggressive and exuberant work, but is also repetitious.

Erpingham is a holiday camp supremo, whose subjects rebel with bloody, and to him fatal, results. "You've struck a figure of authority," says a scandalised redcoat when his chief comes under fire, approximately, the tenth time the joke has been made with half the play still to go. That Orton should have been locked into it was perhaps unavoidable given the play's premise. The camp represents the connivance of the British in their own humiliation (patronised, ballooned and bingoed into grateful submission) and the image can hardly be quarrelled with.

Orton himself, though, seems just a little too delighted with it, and the self-satisfaction shows through, particularly in a small theatre where the audience gets to share it. There is not after all much overlap between the clientele of the King's Head and that of Butlin's. The play was written for commercial television when it must have seemed far more courageously subversive.

There is still much mileage to be had from the rebellious campers, who talk mainly in headline bromides. The rising comes about when an ambitious redcoat, newly in charge of entertainments, organises a screaming contest, into which one young woman enters so enthusiastically that he has to slap her to quieten her down. Her husband, dressed for other festive purposes as Tarzan of the Apes, takes this to heart; he had married her against the odds ("Our love was banned") and, what is far more, she is pregnant. He leads the mob "for the gratification of those in the family way everywhere"; Orton spins endless verbal variations on this theme and the satire - in a society and a theatre much oppressed by slogan - is extremely satisfying.

Said to derive from The Bacchae (but then, what doesn't?), the play asks for a larger production than Islington can offer; starved of accompanying spectacle, the glibness that Orton himself recognised as his own weakest spot is more noticeable. But there is still plenty of verve and intelligence in Stewart Trotter's staging, and a prime performance of Erpingham himself, domineering and grossly epicene, by Peter Vaughan.

  

Jennifer Phillips's Daughters of Men (Hampstead) was once a neat radio script. On stage it seems attenuated. There are large gaps in our acquaintance with the characters, while much of what we are shown is gratuitous - and, in Nancy Meckler's production, remarkably sluggish. The main conflict is between the estranged couple for possession of their daughter. The wife, an artist's agent, seems set to keep her; financially at least she is better equipped than her husband. The issue was left teasingly in doubt for most of the original; expanded for the stage - or rather with the same material gone over more slothfully - it merely drags.

The main story is framed by an interview between the wife and a social security official; stagecraft seems to amount to giving Frances de la Tour time to change her clothes while switching between past and present. Miss de la Tour has a couple of minutes of stylised verbal comedy on the subject of toothpaste; otherwise her gifts are wasted, indeed positively misplaced. With nothing to give her pouting angularity a charge, she just mopes through the evening. (I kept wishing she were playing the self-tormenting heroine of Bedroom Farce; she might bring it off like nobody else.) Two other prominent actresses, Anna Carteret and Annabel Leventon, are spectacularly wasted (Miss Leventon never even moves) and there are a couple of wretched performances further down.

  

Dick Vosburgh wrote the lyrics to a very funny song called "I love a film cliche," which has led a flourishing underground life for some years now. It crops up in the first half of his double-headed entertainment A Day in Hollywood, a Night in the Ukraine (New End) and it is the key to the entire enterprise. I quote: "I love the dialogue/like 'Please don't shoot my dog/Rusty couldn't have eaten those sheep'." That, in its mocking affection, is the spirit of film-buffery.

It hangs pretty limp in A Day in Hollywood, where the elements tend to cancel each other out. There are jokes about Nelson Eddy being dumb enough to turn down a Cole Porter song; the song itself, "In the Still of the Night," is then sung perfectly straight, to a beautiful accompaniment provided by Frank Lazarus. Mr Vosburgh's taste in movie music is impeccable, but he has gone to strange lengths to get in on the stage.

There are pleasures: Paddie O'Neil doing faultless imitations of Bette Davis and (especially) Ethel Merman, a performance of "Thanks for the Memory" that stakes a claim for Leo Robin as the most underrated lyricist in America, a Depression medley including a powerful "Remember my Forgotten Man" from Maureen Scott and a charmingly wistful "With Plenty of Money and You" from Mr Lazarus. But it all needs more shape and purpose, firmer direction and a choreographer. Also more stage space, since what there is at the New End is being held in reserve for A Night in the Ukraine.

This is much jollier, being Chekhov's The Bear as it might have been done by the Marx Brothers. There is, I must admit, something self-defeating about it; you can hardly parody the Marxes, you can only compete with them. Mr Vosburgh has hit off the style to perfection and many of his cracks are every bit as good as S. J. Perelman's: Chico of Margaret Dumont - "She's a-more than unhappy, she's a-house-broken"; Groucho of Chico - "I'm afraid this story has an unhappy ending, folks, he doesn't die"; Harpo of Groucho - any number of toots on a motor horn.

The song of self-introduction which Messrs Vosburgh and Lazarus have dreamed up for Groucho as Serge B. Samovar, the crooked lawyer, is quite perfect, and this unimpersonatable performer is actually brought off uncannily well by John Bay. Sheila Steafel's Harpo actually goes beyond imitation, having the delicacy and gusto of a genuine creation. And Mr Lazarus's Chico signals a welcome triple talent: as composer, pianist and Italian. There are two funny lovers as well. That it has all been done before is the evening's limitation, but also its glory.

  

The Grand Magic Circus are back in town, this time at the Shaftesbury which barn they almost succeed in humanising. I never tire of listening to their presiding genius, Jerome Savary, bidding us a mournful but obviously genuine welcome in his individually elongated English. ("Tonighter we are performing the entire show in Breetsher.") He looks and sounds like a mad undertaker, though for much of this show he is dressed as a Caliph, this show being 1001 Nights.

Scheherazade is explicitly disowned (things, we are given to understand, never work out as happily as that), but the GMC's technique of stopping and starting stories within the stories can get irritating. Chinese boxes full of shaggy dogs. The music and spectacle are well meant, as are the performances, but the really interesting objects are likely to be mechanical; a giant American eagle, for example, which comes down, I think, to illustrate a fable about capitalism. I would also like to mention a pantomime camel.
1979-01-28-rocking-the-future-theatre-ro:
Rocking the future

IN A week of bits and pieces the most substantial fragment made its appearance at the Bush. This was The Cockroach that Ate Cincinnati, presented by Hull Truck but differing greatly from that company's familiar group improvisations. This show has a script, and only one performer.

The performer is Alan Aldred, who in A Bed of Roses gave a memorable impersonation of a man with a plate in his head. He was glowering, unpredictable and rather frightening. Psychopathic hints similarly abound in his current vehicle, but they are softened by humour. Mr Aldred has formidable comic timing, but of course he owes something to his writer, Alan Williams. In fact Messrs Williams and Aldred are the same man and freely admit the fact, but their subterfuge does allow them a double entry in what would otherwise be an undercrowded programme.

The title may remind you of a notably unfunny comedy song of the last decade, The Eggplant that Ate Chicago. Such references are constant; our monologuist is a pop-fancier of the fifties and sixties who has found his faith destroyed in the seventies. He has had a vision, or at least he has heard voices. On record, untraceable in any catalogue, he has made out, between the grooves, what he describes as 'a prophecy of the future of rock from 1968 to 1983.' It includes, you may note with whatever response you feel appropriate, the death of Elton John.

Disillusion becomes retrospective; the reputations of the past come up for consideration and are rapidly and ruthlessly dismissed. I must admit that I have never understood why a whole generation -- my own, to add to the confusion -- should have supposed for a moment that rock could provide them with a moral and political programme, and should even furnish leaders to put its tenets into effect. No betrayal can ever have been more clearly foreseeable.

Mr Williams does not do much to explain such a state of mind, but at least he evokes it powerfully and wittily. It is worth going to the Bush to hear, delivered with curling relish, the definitive put-down of Bob Dylan and his worshippers. A poet who didn't know what he was writing down from one stanza to the next -- we were lucky to find him. Evocative name-dropping ('there wasn't really that much to Wayne Fontana and the Mindbenders') duly sets the nostalgia-glands working, as Mr Aldred recalls a youth spent playing his Woolworth Dansette record-player, clearly a gesture of rebellion in a household where Classics Illustrated were the only permitted comics.

Messrs Aldred and Williams lost me in their second half when a misty pretentiousness set in ('son of man -- Manson,' it went) suggesting that the Dylan influence had gone ineradicably deep. But the fun and the anger, while they last, are good value.

They will not however be available at the Bush until 5 February, for one week only; I was admitted to a press preview. Holding the stage until then is something called The Paranormal Review, which I cannot recommend too highly. In fact I am not sure that I can recommend it at all. It purports to be a meeting of the Charles Flynn Society, who collect rationally inexplicable phenomena. They present items from their collection in the form of dramatised sketches, most of which go wrong. The entertainment lies in their confusion when this occurs.

We are presented in fact with a pretty traditional form of backstage humour, to which the occult trimmings are strictly irrelevant. Indeed, since the Charles Flynn societaires are repeatedly shown up as incompetent fools the veriest sceptic (me, for instance) is likely to find all his prejudices confirmed. He will also laugh some if (again like me) he is a sucker for offhandedly delivered theatrical gags. Whether the odd bits that are funny justify the bits that aren't must be a matter of personal taste. There is not much polish in the performances, though Paul McDowell (what, Whispering Paul of the Temperance Seven?) makes a pleasantly wooden compere.

My reaction to The Putney Debates (Cottesloe: one more performance, on Wednesday), was anticipated more than a century ago by Lord Melbourne, who said of an amateur performance of a Ben Jonson play got up by Dickens that, though he knew it was going to be dull, he did not expect it to be 'quite as damnably dull as it was.'

This enterprise, a pendant to The World Turned Upside Down, involves 11 National Theatre actors in reading extracts from the deliberations of Cromwell's New Model Army shortly before their final defeat of Charles I. They were engaged in discussing just how revolutionary they were prepared to be, and notions of the necessity or immorality of property were freely tossed around. So you can't say that the ideas have lost all interest, and there is a sporting attempt to make Cromwell (quite the least radical man on hand) sound like the Prime Minister.

But the readings are appallingly slovenly and quite unco-ordinated. No actor establishes a relationship with the previous speaker; each in turn plunges in, splashes about for a couple of sentences hoping his personality will buoy him up, and then sinks. It is impossible for the audience to know what they're talking about, since they seem ignorant of it themselves. They wear civvies; though period costumes might at least make the proceedings look more appetising and would not, in the circumstances of the current repertory, cost anything.

I don't know if the Roundhouse Downstairs is the most morgue-like theatre in town, or whether successive offerings merely make it seem so. Latest occupants are a callow troupe who seem, to put it charitably, out of their depth with Pantagleize, a satirical fantasy from between the wars by the Belgian playwright Michel de Ghelderode. Centring on a simpleton who blunders into and through a revolution, it now seems unbearably arch.

The translation doesn't help, though, while the performance merely confirms that plays which are at once old, substantial and unfashionable are likeliest to be tackled by companies unequal to the job. A rotten week. Like the man said, I'm waiting for the weather to break so's I can get out of London and see some theatre.

  

Theatre round-up

THE CHANGELING (Aldwych): Steamily persuasive production of a Jacobean blood-and-lust masterpiece. Diana Quick excels herself as the fair murderess.

CLOUDS (Duke of York's): British Sunday paper journalists go junketing in Cuba and find that everything is in the eye of the beholder. Michael Frayn's best play yet.

THE DOUBLE DEALER (Olivier): The National Theatre regains its grip on Restoration comedy. Michael Bryant and Dorothy Tutin are going to be legends.

EGO JOO (Criterion): Michael Hastings's quick-witted farce on how to become a legal immigrant in one easy wedding.

MARY BARNES (Royal Court): Patti Love gives a stunning performance as a young nurse whose deliverance from schizophrenia (courtesy of R. D. Laing) has been dramatised by David Edgar with a judicious blend of irony and concern.

THE PHILANDERER (Lyttelton): Sparkling revival of Shaw's second play and one of his best; Dinsdale Landen plays, more or less, G.B.S. himself, the author being in a merrily self-scourging mood.

SARATOGA (Aldwych): Early American comedy that may never be revived again, but which Ronald Eyre and his company have made the occasion for a fine frolic that includes some of the best song and dance in town.

STRIFE (Olivier): A very pleasant surprise: Galsworthy's strike drama may lack something as a tract on industrial relations, but in Christopher Morahan's granite-hard production, it lives as a study of human obstinacy on the grand scale -- which is just how the author intended it.
1979-02-04-toss-of-the-coin:
Toss of the coin

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Alan Ayckbourn's new play(s).

ALAN AYCKBOURN'S Sisterly Feelings (Stephen Joseph Theatre in the Round, Scarborough) is at base a play in four scenes. However there are complications.

Mr Ayckbourn has written alternative versions of the second and third scenes, or rather he has written one alternative version of each. However, either variant of Scene Two is playable with either version of Scene Three. The play can be seen four times, with the spectator getting a different show on each occasion. I hope this is clear.

I went twice, which allowed me to collect the entire text while missing out on some of the juggling. I gather that the arrangements I saw are referred to among the Scarborough players as "the Abigail play" and "the Dorcas play." Abigail and Dorcas are the sisters with whose feelings we are concerned, and though Abigail is a housewife and Dorcas works in local radio (producer of two half-hour shows a week) they bear more than a passing resemblance to Goneril and Regan. They have a ga-ga dad, and a mother: in fact they are on their way back from her funeral when we first meet them. Above all there is a young man whom they both fancy, though unlike Shakespeare's Edmund he is in no sense a bastard. He is Simon, their brother's girl-friend's brother, a clean-limbed young man and also chivalrous.

At the end of Scene One there is some question as to with which of the two he will walk home. In the end the matter is decided by the toss of a coin (and that toss, which incidentally is left to chance in performance) decides the content of the second scene. For the walk home is the prelude to an affair.

Scene Two, whatever happens, is a picnic, and the feasters are the same either way, but their relationships obviously differ. The end of this scene provides another moment of choice that determines the nature of Scene Three; Simon may either be having it off with the same flame or with her rival. That Scene Four should be exactly the same, whatever has happened, is of course its own ironic comment. Abigail and Dorcas may pride themselves on their dissimilarities, but nobody else can notice any; to their despised future sister-in-law, for example, they are both "hopelessly neurotic and out of touch."

The one crucial difference between them is that Abigail is married; and since Mr Ayckbourn sees his people less in terms of character than in terms of domestic circumstance this is more than enough to justify his peculiar strategy. That the Abigail play works the better of the two is a tribute to the old-fashioned rules, both social and dramatic. Much depends, of course, on the quality of the cuckold. Here Abigail is in luck; her husband Patrick is an exemplary mixture of cynicism and complaisance. Professing complete tolerance of his wife's activities, he so contrives, with the utmost politeness, to make her life an embarrassment, while Simon, despite the obvious need for discretion, comes close to duffing him up. He is, besides, most incisively characterised as a man besotted with his job, his house and his car, particularly when they involve mechanical extras.

By contrast, Stafford, the gentleman whom Dorcas betrays ("Dorcas's thing," her father calls him), is a stereotype of the half-baked far Left intellectual already worked over (to rather better purpose) in Mr Ayckbourn's Ten Times Table. His jealousy takes far less inventive turns than Patrick's. Scene Three offers a choice of Abigail and Simon going tramping, or Dorcas offloading her cross-country race with Simon one of the favourites. Again Abigail offers the playgoer a better deal: acute situation comedy as opposed to overworked farce.

All scenes take place in a remote corner of Pendon Common. Pendon was also the scene of Ten Times Table and I suspect Mr Ayckbourn thinks of it as home. I wish Mr Ayckbourn had allowed his heroines one head-on collision, rather than confining them to polite fencing with undertones, but overall this related comedy is excellent value. As usual, the author's production offers resonances generally inaudible in London where, with rare exceptions, star casting has obscured his characters' unblinking ordinariness.

At Scarborough the audience take up where the play leaves off - and they are in no way patronised. After all, they get better new work on a regular basis, than can be found at any other regional theatre, in perfectly judged productions. Alison Skilbeck's Abigail, James Bate's Patrick and Robin Herford's Simon are splendidly recognisable.

  

The Glasgow Citizens, operating at the opposite aesthetic extreme, are offering Jean Cocteau's Orpheus - not the play, but a staged version of the film. Geoffrey Cauley, directing and designing, has set it among black cubes so highly polished that they act as mirrors, this being Cocteau's image (questionable but reasonably arresting) of the passage to death. Death is actually personified here as a lady in black; Orpheus falls in love with her, and she quite unconstitutionally with him.

Eurydice, though visually linked to her husband by the fact that they both wear red (nobody else dresses that warm), has no chance, which rather robs the evening of dramatic tension. It becomes an exercise in style: an envious choice for the Citizens, but rather an empty one. The acting is more dangerously underpowered than it has been there of late, with only Jack Elliott as Death's unwilling assistant impressing himself among a crowd of palely beautiful young creatures of both sexes. But then everyone is overshadowed by the open white Rolls, of Cocteau's own vintage, which is the underworld's gift to Orpheus and an irresistible bribe if ever I saw one.
1979-02-11-london-delights-in-the-artifi:
London Delights in the Artifice of an Early American Play

By ROBERT CUSHMAN

LONDON

Eight years ago the Royal Shakespeare Company, at London's Aldwych Theater, struck out in a new and -- as it proved -- profitable line. The RSC unearthed a forgotten comedy by the Victorian playwright Dion Boucicault entitled "London Assurance," and the title seemed an apt description of the style with which the company brought the play to the stage. The production ran the entire season at the Aldwych, played for a further year in the West End, and finally came to New York -- where it lasted a mere couple of weeks.

At home, though, "London Assurance" was regarded as a landmark for the RSC. Its success encouraged the company to cultivate what had previously been an underdeveloped sense of humor, and to indulge in further archaeological exploits. The RSC next resurrected the William Gillette version of Arthur Conan Doyle's "Sherlock Holmes," and this time had as great a triumph with it in America as at home. The RSC then went further back in time to "Wild Oats," a 1791 comedy of intrigue by an Irishman, John O'Keeffe. This was perhaps the biggest success of all. Opening at the Aldwych in 1976, "Wild Oats" ran in London for the next year and a half, and is about to be revived.

Now the RSC has revived another rarity, this time of American origin. "Saratoga" dates from 1870 and was the second play of Bronson Howard, who was later to earn the title of "Dean of the American Drama." Like its Aldwych predecessors it is a stock piece; the characters are types, and are blatantly proclaimed as such in the cast list. The hero, played by Dennis Waterman, is the traditional susceptible rake. Howard, with the 19th-century love of a pun (especially one with literary pretensions) describes him "One Who Loved Not Wisely But Four Well."

We meet three of the hero's four loves in the first act, which is set in a New York art gallery. They number one very short girl, one very tall one and a medium-sized widow. We learn that all three of these ladies, with their respective families, are off to take the waters at the newly fashionable Saratoga Springs. For the rest of the evening we join them at the spa, as does the hero, Robert, now on the trail of his fourth flame, a beautiful young lady chaperoned by a distinguished gentleman whom Robert takes to be her father but who is, in fact, her husband.

Halfway through the play, Robert's quadruple life catches up with him; each of his conquests learns of her competitors' existence and each calls on her menfolk to vindicate her honor. What with fathers, husbands, stepsons, and just plain swains, Robert finds himself the object of no fewer than seven challenges. (The play's subtitle is "Pistols for Seven.") Naturally he ends up more or less unscathed and in possession of his number-one girl, with consolation prizes provided for the others.

"Saratoga" is obviously an artificial piece, but its artifice is the key to the pleasure it provides. The RSC has never mocked its resurrected comedies -- it has always approached them too affectionately for that. Their style rests on a complicity between actors and audience. The RSC enjoys playing old tricks, and we enjoy watching them at it; each side of the footlights humors the other and each feels, atavistically, that in these routines resides the most basic kind of theatrical appeal.

This archaeological playfulness is at its most elaborate in Ronald Eyre's production of "Saratoga." Mr. Eyre was the director who started the whole cycle with his production of "London Assurance" -- a text on which he carried out extensive doctoring. He has not done this with "Saratoga"; rather, he has emphasized its period origin. Jocelyn Herbert's sets are an elegant series of cut-outs that provide an explicit, affectionate comment on the 19th-century stage itself. Mr. Eyre has also arranged a series of divertissements between the acts; the three black waiters who figure in the play are brought on, rather like the porters in "On the Twentieth Century," to sing and strut between the acts. Their best number, the misanthropic Bert Williams classic "Nobody" (in which they are joined by Mr. Waterman), brings down the house.

It is the undoubted highlight of the show, though there are passages of more than routine interest in the play itself. The first act in particular reflects Howard's own position as an American playwright wishing to strike out in a new and native direction but still in thrall to the European comedy of manners and intrigue.

Previous RSC revivals have been built around star performances: Donald Sinden and Judi Dench in "London Assurance," John Wood in "Sherlock Holmes," Alan Howard in "Wild Oats." "Saratoga" suffers by comparison, since Mr. Waterman's acting here is -- except in that one interlude of loose-limbed hoofing -- curiously tense. But there are enough high spirits and good humor all around to carry the evening.

Robert Cushman is theater critic of the London Observer.
1979-02-11-bad-temper:
Bad temper

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'A Fair Quarrel' at the National.

THE National Theatre continues its season of plays with turbulent titles. Strife, Betrayal, and The World Turned Upside Down are succeeded by A Fair Quarrel (Olivier). No doubt this bellicosity suits the times, but it reflects all previous ages as well. In the entire world repertoire the only beatifically named play that comes to mind is Aristophanes's Peace, a very long time ago.

Otherwise the world's drama is crammed with bad temper. There are three courses of it in A Fair Quarrel, which comes from Middleton and Rowley, the Jacobean firm who gave you The Changeling. Critics have pronounced that its separate plots are bound together by their concern with codes of behaviour under strain. It is difficult to imagine any story that wouldn't somewhere support that interpretation, but we may give the scholars two out of three.

Plot A, which is about duelling, is indeed parodied by Plot C, which deals with the 'roaring boys' who made a cult out of rowdiness and in one scene even give lessons in it. Plot B, though, leads a discrete, if not discreet, existence and is concerned with a girl courted against her will. All these juxtapositions involve the authors in some odd time-keeping; a heroine goes through the greater part of pregnancy, and is brought to bed, while a hero is strolling back from the field of honour. 'No wonder his mother worries.'

Her honour, I should explain, is itself in question. Young Captain Ager is called by his colonel a 'son of a whore' and, as was expected, challenges him immediately. Lady Ager, not wanting to see her boy carved up, blushingly (and quite falsely) admits to having slipped in her time, and the captain sets off prepared to apologise. His antagonist promptly calls him a coward, the captain's reflexes are reawakened and the fight is on again.

The Jacobeans, while regarding such behaviour as something of a joke and more of a public nuisance, would still have found it understandable. To us, unless we are properly instructed, it is only a joke; and the only time when a perplexed first-night audience felt the ground firm beneath its feet was when it could laugh at Nicky Henson's Captain striking noble attitudes.

William Gaskill's production is very clear; you can hear most of the words and the actors seem unusually convinced of what they mean. They also know what the issues are; to a man they jump whenever their reputations are called in question. But though clarity is an essential basis for a revival, it is not enough and this play -- no masterwork, but an entertaining genre-piece -- needs filling out. Some of the social detail that Mr Gaskill used to supply in Restoration comedy might be helpful, along with actions that explored and projected the characters' passions instead of just tastefully indicating them. The actors come mainly from Joint Stock (and are therefore, according to current doctrine, beyond criticism), but for this play, on this stage, they look under-powered.

The stage is part of the trouble -- this is another main house production with its heart in the studio. On this occasion, the back of the Olivier platform has been given over to the audience, which may cut down on the stage's intimidating vastness, but makes the house itself the biggest arena theatre east of Hollywood Bowl. The acting area is a timbered rectangle with a hole in its middle: a large trapdoor which the actors, thus democratically prevented from taking the centre of the stage, warily circumnavigate.

Those who make the strongest impression are those previously in residence: Mr Henson, and Dermot Crowley as a creepy physician. Among the insurgents, Fred Pearson has a good swagger as the Colonel and Marjorie Yates a nicely judged vulgarity as a bawd. I honestly believe plays like A Fair Quarrel should be revived, and I realise that I have not greatly assisted their chances this morning. But they can be done.

  

The staging of Tommy (Queen's) reopens some questions which one might have thought buried. It is boldly billed as a 'rock musical' and is one of the few of its kind to deserve the name. Hence of course its failure; rock cannot co-exist with drama, since the first depends on repetition and the second on variety. Whenever a supposed rock-score has been praised in the theatre it has been for its 'eclecticism': i.e., it has got away from rock as far and often as possible. (This has often been the case with pop music outside the theatre as well.)

But Tommy is sanctified as The Who's masterwork, a hit on records and filmed by Ken Russell (they deserved each other), so we get it now with its rhythms crushingly unvaried, its decibels ringing and Pete Townshend's atrocious lyrics generally inaudible -- which does nothing for the plot but something for the sensibilities. (Mr Townshend is not, as you might think, proudly indifferent to rhyme; when he can think up 'sorrow-tomorrow' couplets, however lame, he shoves it in.)

It is not altogether the authors' fault; Tommy, after all, wasn't written for the stage. To put it there is brutally (the right word) to expose its masochistic narcissism: here is the hero as deaf, dumb and blind boy, here he is as teenage idol, and here finally as crucified star. Filling in the visual details can't be easy; apart from some spectacular laser-work, this production settles for third-hand eroticism. If a couple of nurses have to appear they naturally flash their suspenders.

To show you how original it plans to be, the show begins by having its cast clamber down scaffolding in their leotards while clouds float across the back-projected sky. Things that on the record were just meretriciously menacing are here clumsily nasty; his relatives' sexual assaults on Tommy are played for laughs. (Bob Grant makes Uncle Ernie a perverted Bruce Forsyth.) Allan Love mimes quite touchingly in the opening scenes; but when his faculties are restored he has to grab a hand-mike just like everybody else. Character conflict in those constricted circumstances is hardly possible. Listen, people, nobody in America writes rock scores for the theatre any more, and they know far more about musicals than you.

  

It is a relief to turn to Talent (ICA), a cheeky title but something for the sensibilities. Victoria Wood, as author and performer, fully justifies. She is already the best songwriter we have, the best refreshing melodist to wry, funny, concrete lyrics, and she may have it in her to be our best female playwright (if we are to encourage such distinctions). Her present piece, though short, has perhaps too many personal memories pushed into it; but her dialogue lives and breathes, and though she can be sour -- she writes of northern working-girls with dead-end prospects -- she is resilient, and accompanies sexy, ambitious Julie, would-be singer, to a club talent contest.

As the night in the dismal dressing-room proceeds, Julie learns that she has nothing to hope for, while Maureen's prospects, briefly expanding, subside as quickly. Hazel Clyne, brittle and edgy, gets both Julie's selfishness and her vulnerability. The show is an object-lesson in making upbeat theatre out of downbeat material without ever falsifying it.

American cancer ward

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a Pulitzer Prize play.

THERE is a perpetual conspiracy in American drama to wring cosiness out of terror.

Soap opera is part of that story; but not all of it: soap of itself has always seemed to me a reasonably healthy phenomenon, since to simplify emotion is not necessarily to anaesthetise it. Soap knows its place. But Hollywood movies on 'important' or 'sensitive' subjects do not. And neither do the plays or novels from which they derive. Michael Cristofer's The Shadow Box was a Broadway success in 1977 and won the Pulitzer Prize. It has now been given its British premiere at the Arts Theatre, Cambridge.

It is about death. Three terminal cancer patients are living in some kind of medically supervised settlement, each in his or her own chalet. There is a restless-minded author, now living with a young male hustler and forced to cope with the sudden reappearance of his wife; There is a contrastingly uncomplicated working man whose wife has so far withheld the truth of his condition from their guitar-playing son. There is a rasping old woman, shunted round in a wheelchair by one daughter and anxious only for news of another. One faces the inevitable with resentment, another with resignation; and the third oscillates between.

Each has quite enough personal and family problems to be going on with, and these are duly aired. Where British drama generally avoids confrontation, American drama seeks it out (this will do as a generalisation about our private lives as well) so there is much hand-to-hand and heart-to-heart.

As domestic drama this is all conventional and innocuous if a bit dull (there being an overwrought gentility about much of the dialogue that recalls the suffering days of Bette Davis), but Mr Cristofer has of course the built-in gimmick of mortality. He has also -- and this is where my reservations harden into hostility -- a narrator. He introduces us to the sufferers; he is not, he insists, a doctor. Or rather: "We're not your doctors," he says, blandly and infuriatingly assuming the role of audience spokesman.

This device is given little scope -- the characters are informed of our presence, blink, and then retire behind their fourth wall -- but it is enough to bestow on the evening the aura of cutely earnest experimentation. Our fugleman sits there, wise and smiling and impotent, but we are back with the worst of Thornton Wilder -- as it might be, "The Skin of Our Town." "Joe," he says, summoning his first specimen, and you would not have thought a writer could sprinkle so much sugar on a monosyllable. At the end, the company, Jobs and comforters together, give up on action and address us on the wisdom and necessity of acceptance. After everything else, Mr Cristofer throws a tone poem at us.

The play has gained in one signal respect since I saw it in New York. The word "cancer" is now actually mentioned. It also has the benefit of a production by Jonathan Lynn which is -- until the closing stages -- livelier and less reverential than the original, and of a magnificently clean-cut performance by Madge Ryan as the senior patient (an easy role in which to be self-indulgent while still attracting good notices). Dick Wilson and Sheila Allen fill the family chalet with its proper measure of sympathy and bafflement.

The writer's menage is the most clumsily contrived and the fullest of reproaches. Anthony Bate is too restrained and trained for it and June Ritchie too emphatic; James Aubrey as the cuckoo in their nest begins splendidly, goes to pieces when the character does, but retrieves himself in time for the final curtain.

  

Tom Kempinski's Flashpoint (Mayfair) returns us to another traditional form: the enclosed army melodrama. Those with long enough memories will recall "The Long and the Short and the Tall," especially when confronted by the central character, the tough, foul-mouthed barrack buffoon who turns out to have the right moral instincts. The place is Ulster and the time "next year." Martial law has been imposed, a hutful of squaddies await the morning on which they are to shoot a convicted deserter. Some regard the prospect with indifference, one at least with positive pleasure, and one cracks up. He in effect hijacks the hut, turning the rifle on his mates and demanding the cancellation of the execution as the price of their lives.

Up to this point the play has dragged at comic-documentary level; now it jumps to life and -- despite some repetitious writing -- stays jumping, even treating us to a couple of prize twists at the end. Nothing much is said about the Northern Ireland situation, except that it is probably insoluble; nothing much about the British Army, except that it is as likely to be brutalised by war as any other. To go one further, and deduce a "troops out" message, requires a considerable talent for unassisted extrapolation. (A soldier after all might well baulk at shooting one of his own, whatever the ethics of the conflict.) The actors take full advantage of both the tensions and the humour, Tony Selby romping home in the plum role.

  

The Albany Empire is a community theatre in Deptford, which burned to the ground in July after presenting a cabaret show with an anti-racialist slant. "Controversy," say the company, "rages as to the cause." The theatre has now been rebuilt and I wish I could welcome the reopening production. But One Gun Salute, which purports to be a lament for the welfare state, is the dregs of agit-prop. Not that you could accuse it of unfairness to its opponents: it never keeps its eye on any object long enough to find any attitudes at all. Attempting to chronicle the disillusion of a social security official, it never lets you get a look at him, and its choice of surrounding incidents is arbitrary to the point of factitious non-existence. Messy acting, desperate music and a lamely allegorical structure complete the picture.

  

Michael Hastings's Full Frontal (Theatre Upstairs), a black African applies for membership of the National Front. His life is unhappy and he needs scapegoats, so his application does have a bizarre logic. He has no time for West Indians and is rather like Mr Hastings's Meadowlark Warner (from "Gloo Joo") in reverse.

But unlike Meadowlark he has no plot, and not very much wit, to keep him going; the piece is a monologue, Mr Hastings having kept the listening Front official off-stage. He has in fact forfeited the boldness of his conception, tacitly acknowledging that though it sounds a brightly provocative notion, it will not stand the test of actual dramatisation. All we get is another hard-luck story, though it's pleasant to hear it delivered by Winston Ntshona, who was once the plumper half of the "Sizwe Bansi" duo, but now seems pretty slim and twice as fluent.
1979-03-11-the-demon-barber:
The Demon Barber

Theatre

Robert Cushman on Sondheim's 'Sweeney Todd' in New York--and the Louisville festival.

I WROTE at the end of last year about a Broadway musical called 'A Broadway Musical' and wondered whether it would get past the New York critics.

It didn't; it died at birth. A pity, for though horribly confused, it was still appealing; it both dramatised and exemplified the lunacies of putting on a show in the face of murderous economics, artistic bewilderment and the theatrical withering of the popular song. It would have been pleasantly symbolic to have it around, welcoming subsequent arrivals with a deranged grin on its face.

For still they come. The blockbusters continue to bust blocks: 'Annie' and 'Ain't Misbehavin'' and grand-daddy 'Grease.' All in a row on 44th Street stand the choreographic musicals, 'Ballroom' and 'Dancin'' and 'A Chorus Line,' almost making a sentence. Then there is 'The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas,' a success and possibly the worst little musical in the world. It has country music and is stupid.

Of 1979's early comers, 'The Grand Tour' starring Joel Grey as a Jew on the run through occupied Europe, died young, possibly because its narrative techniques were old-fashioned, possibly because the world was not waiting for the musical-comedy version of 'Holocaust,' possibly because the authors (the 'Hello Dolly' team of Michael Stewart and Jerry Herman) hadn't realised that that was what they were getting into. 'They're Playing Our Song' looks like surviving, it being this season's Neil Simon two-hander embellished by smart production and negligible songs; its first half is bright, its second--in which the audience is invited to take an interest in a relationship it hardly knew existed--discouraging.

The palm would have to go to 'Whoopee,' a cheerful exhumation (the best of its kind I've seen) from 1928, were it not for the advent of a show differing in everything but expertise: the Stephen Sondheim-Harold Prince 'Sweeney Todd.'

This, too, might count as an exhumation (it is full of graveyard imagery and there are a couple of diggers on stage at the start to set the mood), since it brings to Broadway the fabled Demon Barber of Fleet Street. The source of the musical is a version by the English playwright Christopher Bond staged at Stratford East in 1973. Mr Bond took the central penny-gaff situation--the cut-throat artist practising above a pie-shop and supplying it with cheap and easy meat--and gave it with a beginning out of 'The Count of Monte-Cristo' and an end out of Elizabethan tragedy.

His Todd is an escaped convict, sentenced to transportation on a trumped-up charge so that the judge could have unimpeded access to Mrs Todd. Our barber returns years later to find his wife a suicide and his daughter, now adolescent, the judge's ward. He plans revenge.

The convict's return is a familiar Dickensian motif, and this 'Sweeney Todd' has more of the spirit of Dickens--the nightmare spirit of 'Oliver Twist'--than any show based on the novel. It presents Victorian London as a plague-spot. Eugene Lee's set, which just about takes over the vast and antiseptic Uris Theatre, is a combination of chapel (with organ), street and--overwhelmingly--factory; and a factory whistle sounds unnervingly at each curve of the plot.

The veneer of social criticism, though, is less important than the passion beneath. Len Cariou's death's-head Sweeney is a magnificent study of a monomaniac--and, in its bitter frantic clarity, the best rendition of a Sondheim score I have heard. It is a musical frenzy that carries Sweeney across the bridge from specific to general bloodlust, but the process is prefigured when he first appears, singing in a low, terse staccato: 'There's a place in the world like a great big pit/And the vermin of the world inhabit it/And it goes by the name of London.'

There is more to the score, and the show, than this: a laconic humour ('So what if none of their souls were saved/They went to their maker impeccably shaved') which expands to epic proportions with Angela Lansbury's pie-woman, looking with her hair piled high in unruly braids, like a monstrous tabby-cat. She and Todd make a marvellously complementary pair of villains: she jolly and practical, he the visionary and thwarted romantic. The tenderest strains of the evening sound around the barber's chair, as he regards his instruments ('my friends') or prepares to use them. This goes beyond grotesquerie or easy irony to a feeling for the criminal as outcast that is absolutely true to the underside of Victorian literature.

More conventional romance comes off less well: Todd's daughter and her sailor-lover are indeterminate figures. They can afford to be, in Bond's play (which reads as elegant, funny and gripping pastiche), but not amid the far greater density of this musical. I should add that Bond's plotting is excellent and the final retributive section of the show--in dialogue, song and Harold Prince's staging--stunning. There is no choreography, but there is consummate choral work. (The show is at least three-quarters sung.) I am sure there is a large, mainly young, audience for this show: the problem is getting them to Broadway. London must see it; it is as near as anyone has come to writing the great British musical.

It is a good season for Victorian misfits. The play of the moment is Bernard Pomerance's 'The Elephant Man' (seen last year at Hampstead) with its caustic use of a painfully intelligent freak as a moral measuring-rod for the society around him. A pellucid production is about to transfer from off-Broadway.

The other touted play is Arthur Kopit's 'Wings,' which begins as an interesting attempt to represent linguistically the dislocation caused by a stroke but falls apart when the author gets down to cases. (Just like Neil Simon.)

Recent American drama is a desert of promise; what is lacking is mature performance. Off-Broadway now has to compete for its white hopes with the increasingly prosperous regional theatre movement. In Louisville, Kentucky (home of Muhammad Ali and Colonel Sanders), the Actors Playhouse last week concluded its third festival of new plays. The theatre, housed in an old bank building, boasts two stages and, for the festival, a very good company. They have also found (and launched as far as New York) a local playwright, Marsha Norman, though her contribution this year was unimpressive: a play about a circus that just looked as though someone had sat down and doggedly written a play about a circus.

Slightly better were a double bill of musicals based on one-act Shaw plays (though performance style proved a problem here) and a programme of playlets entitled 'Holidays' contributed by 10 prominent dramatists, several of whom appeared to have dug out old scripts and written in a few lines about the Fourth of July or whatever.

A new playwright, Beth Henley, offered us 'Crimes of the Heart'; I never quite overcame my disappointment at finding that her piece, about three Mississippi sisters with problems, was not after all going to be a gothic comedy, since it started out that way. Miss Henley went some way towards reclaiming the domestic hearth (or, this being a kitchen play, stove) for respectable drama, but the antique associations proved overpowering.

The find of the festival was James McLure, whose two plays, 'Lone Star' and 'Pvt. Wars,' turned out to be exhilaratingly funny on old subjects, like growing up in Texas, and comparatively new ones, like looking back on war-service in Vietnam; this last hitherto a taboo subject, for laughter. Mr McLure writes cross-talk that builds; he could become a major comic writer, which would be fine, or relax into being a gag man, which wouldn't be so bad either.
1979-03-11-theatre:
Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN's round-up of the London stage:-

Betrayal (Lyttelton): Harold Pinter's straightforward (though played backwards) triangle drama. This critic was disappointed, but there have been enough intelligent demurs for it to be worth your attention.

A Chorus Line (Drury Lane): Mostly exhilarating (and, by the way, superbly lit) musical now approaching the final chorus.

A Day in Hollywood, A Night in the Ukraine (New End): After regaling us with movie songs and anecdotes, a talented cast--notably Sheila Steafel as Harpo--play at being the Marx Brothers playing Chekhov. Accurate and therefore funny. Last week.

Filumena (Lyric): Barbara Jefford has temporarily replaced Joan Plowright as the fiery Italian ex-whore and eternal mother, and should be ideal.

Flashpoint (Mayfair): Gripping if not over-profound military melodrama set in Northern Ireland.

Night and Day (Phoenix): Erroneously hailed as a new departure for Tom Stoppard, it actually follows logically from his previous works. It presents a clash of principles: the feminine, and that of Press freedom.

The Ordeal of Gilbert Pinfold (Roundhouse): Michael Hordern is far too nice to be an acceptable Evelyn Waugh surrogate, but he is always worth watching on his own account and the production marks the welcome arrival in London of Manchester's Royal Exchange company.
1979-03-18-tolstoy-at-the-national:
Tolstoy at the National

THE most surprising feature of Tolstoy's comedy The Fruits of Enlightenment (Olivier) is its mildness.

It was written late in its author's life at a time when he was denouncing all sexuality while wrestling unsuccessfully with his own; and while he bore the scars of battles with the peasants who had stubbornly refused to do what he thought was good for them.

Art, presumably, purifies. There is not a trace of sex-hatred in The Fruits of Enlightenment. Indeed, there is hardly any sex at all, only the conventionalised courtship of a maid and kitchen boy. As for the peasants, they seem to have been conceived in accordance with the beautiful visions in their author's head rather than with the reality on which he kept stumbling.

The play presents a trio of them, come to Moscow to buy land on credit from the master of the house, who would rather have cash. The plot turns on their efforts to get the bargain made on their own terms; the dramatic interest hangs on their bewildered sceptical reaction to the fashionable life of which they are the temporary spectators, and to the absurdities of that life itself.

The master believes in spiritualism, and the marriageable maidservant, by passing her boyfriend off as a medium, rigs a seance in the peasants' interests. The translator, Michael Frayn, has by his own account transferred the seance from the play's three-quarter mark to its end, thus keeping the story going, giving us the real climax, and sparing us a final act consisting mainly of comings and goings. It sounds reasonable, but I suspect that he has miscalculated; the comings and goings are the most enjoyable part of the play, while the story is thin and gains nothing from being protracted.

Mr Frayn's introduction to the published text (reprinted, with tactful abridgements, in the National Theatre programme) is engagingly frank about the play's defects. He acknowledges that the peasants are sentimentalised ("two of them are comic characters, one of them is sturdily outspoken"--I'm still not sure which is which) and that Tolstoy's jibes at the credulity of the educated classes weigh a little heavy at times too. He might have added that the whole menage--mother is a fussy hypochondriac, the son is a wastrel, the daughter is a blue stocking (or at any rate is outspoken and wears spectacles)--is hardly the occasion of trenchant satire, despite the amount of stage time that it takes up.

The Master is described by Tolstoy as "in the English sense a 'gentleman'"; and it is of course in the English manner of golden eccentricity--benevolent, slightly touched, and disregarding people even in the act of radiating good will at them--that Ralph Richardson plays. John Harding and Selina Cadell make him a bright pair of offspring, but everything in this area of the play seems forced; however hard and fast the actors talk, the play moves slowly.

There is, though, an intermediate layer to the play: that of the servants, who regard their employers with varying degrees of envy, amazement and, just occasionally, hatred. (The mutterings of an old cashiered cook, who has crept back to sleep on the kitchen stove, make one wish that Tolstoy had written a more splenetic play.) They also have a tremendous nostalgia for the land, sparked off by the arrival of the peasants. The lovers in particular can hardly wait to get back there and the fatherly valet wants a place kept warm for him.

As a displaced pastoral, the play has resonance if not exactly urgency; and there are good performances below stairs from Brenda Blethyn, Peter Copley, Peter Needham and Greg Hicks, whose Cossack dance is the best thing in the show. It may seem glib to blame Christopher Morahan's production for a general lack of Russian-ness (and I have no idea how he could have overcome the deficiency), but the play does seem to lack a necessary context. One notes yet again that the Olivier stage is a powerful devourer of detail.

  

Hoagy, Bix and Wolfgang Beethoven Bunkhaus (King's Head) is Adrian Mitchell's latest spasm of slightly dramatised hero worship. Hoagy is Carmichael of course, Bix is Beiderbecke, and Bunkhaus, we are given to understand, is their Indiana college pal William Monkhaus, a surrealist poet who re-christens Hoagy "Hogwash McCorkle" on sight. He talks that way all the time. An exasperatingly fey creation, he seems to be driving his actor (Murray Melvin) to distraction. Bix is fey in another fashion; white-faced and appealing, in Sylvester McCoy's performance, and naturally doomed. The play seems to be searching for somebody or something to blame for his dissolution, but not even Paul Whiteman (played, along with half a dozen other parts, very well by Roland Oliver) can quite make it as an exploiting villain.

I spent the evening waiting with increasing impatience for the music, which, of course, is lovely: most of Mr Carmichael's best songs are delivered with modest insouciance by John Vine, who actually bears a helpful facial resemblance to the patient young Hoagy, and with measured punch by Nicola McAuliffe, whose "Washboard Blues" is magnificent. The play, to use a suitable Dixieland word, rambles.

  

So, in effect if not in structure, does John Byrne's Normal Service (Hampstead), which is set in the design department of a Scottish commercial television company in the fifties. The author has a firmer controlling idea than is immediately apparent. He manages entrances and exits less mechanically than he did in The Slab Boys and he gets a sheaf of solid performances, notably from Garfield Morgan and Richard Wilson. But Mr Frayn's Alphabetic Order has rather spoiled the market for typical day-in-the-office plays, and Mr Byrne's dialogue is not funny enough (not consistently, anyway) nor his characters' passing troubles arresting enough, to make me sit through another one. I am rather sad, remembering the vaudeville of his Writers' Cramp, to see him buckling down to naturalism so soon.

  

Frederick Harrison's Subjects for Interrogation (Bush) is a double bill of cautionary parables about the breeding of torturers. The first is pre-packaged, an argument between a young terrorist and a gently mannered sensory depriver who have nothing to say to each other and at great length, and you may as well miss it. Be on time, though, for the second, in which an average unemployed man (most convincingly played by David Hargreaves) is put through the ordeal of putting someone else through one. Three characters--judge, tormentor and victim--make up a scale susceptible to gripping and cunning variations. The play also works, a lot of the time, as a parlour game, which is more than you can say for most plays.

Fats on the stage

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

A FRIEND of mine, a jazz pianist, walked out of the New York production of Ain't Misbehavin' (Her Majesty's). In doing so he missed out on a considerable quantity of fun, but his purist's response to this much-acclaimed Fats Waller compilation deserves some attention.

Waller's reputation, unshakable since the thirties (he died in 1943), is quadruple: he was pianist, composer, singer and clown. Of these four talents, the first was most obviously forfeit in the theatre. Luther Henderson, the piano man here, functions merely as a skilful and sympathetic accompanist: he is also the MD, and his men swing when they get the chance. A lyric in the show--a new and good one by the director, Richard Maltby Jr.--sports the wry line: "They like jazz but in small doses." Small doses are all that the theatre can assimilate; and my friend--who like most good jazzmen has in his time adapted dozens of show-tunes to his own purposes--should not logically have complained at the traffic being reversed.

It is more surprising that the show has ironed out Waller's verbal humour: the tolerant, disbelieving asides with which he sprinkled his vocals. The crazily elegant catch-phrases are reverently preserved, but instead of gently murmuring "Mercy!" or "One never knows, do one?" these performers declaim them. Trying to find a sizeable extrovert equivalent for Waller's intimate addresses, they assault the audience, especially during the first 15 minutes, with exaggerated coyness.

But the show takes its stand on Waller as singer and composer; every number we hear was written or recorded by him. (One of the surprises of Fats's career is how little overlap there was between these two categories.) He was not a great vocalist; and the two songs--"When Somebody Thinks You're Wonderful" and "My Very Good Friend the Milkman"--with which he came nearest to making a style out of rhythmic affability, are omitted here. So there is no question of imitation.

The cast are free to make the songs their own, their only impediment being the rather hollow soul-based seventies style to which the ladies in particular tend to resort in moments of stress and which can knock the individuality out of any voice or any vehicle.

They are a dazzling quintet, though, these performers. Andree de Shields is a devil-dancer whose voice drips feline disdain; his sinuous account of the reefer song ("If You're a Viper") raises the Harlem dandy to a new, and distinctly sinister, power; here the thirties and the seventies really do illuminate each other. Where he is all curves, his colleague Evan Bell is all bumps and angles: tall, broad and vulnerable, but still capable of turning "Your Feet's Too Big" into a bruised aria of insult.

Talking of insult, the two men also bring the house down with "Fat and Greasy" and pay acid tribute to "The Ladies Who Sing With the Band" by way of bringing on the girls. These are Annie Joe Edwards, a hugely cherishable mama; Charlaine Woodard, a baby tigress with a streak of self-mockery; and Jozella Reed, whose demure rendition of "Squeeze Me" is the first thing to set the evening alight.

That song proves one of the gems among Waller's own compositions, along with "I've Got a Feeling I'm Falling," "Keepin' Out of Mischief Now" (which amounts to a delicate reworking of the title tune) and, obviously, "Honeysuckle Rose." They make an appealingly and unaffectedly sexy bunch. But the show makes no musical point that could not as well have been gained by choosing at large among the songs of the period.

In the end, it is words rather than music that determine a programme; and Fats was not a lyricist. The songs tell us nothing much about him, and those lyrics that tell us about his environment or even his style of playing turn out to be Mr Maltby's own, fitted to Waller instrumentals. Even this much sense of period, allied to the snap and logic of the staging, is enough to leave Bubbling Brown Sugar struggling in the mud; and the show takes one risk that its predecessor would never have countenanced. The cast unite in an exquisite lament called "Black and Blue" that must have seemed charmingly ingenuous to its first white audience in 1929 and embarrassing to most people since. That black performers can sing it now--with passion but without apparent bitterness, placing it in its history without denying it--seems to me a sign of progress.

  

There's another Broadway hit across the street. The Crucifer of Blood (Haymarket) is another example of the American theatre's obsession with British Victoriana, most creatively exemplified in New York at the moment by Sweeney Todd; and The Elephant Man. The Crucifer belongs more at the Dracula end of things and is a new contribution to the Sherlock Holmes apocrypha.

Paul Giovanni, the author-director, makes affectionate fun of his hero without materially injuring him, though his plotting can be hurtful. Holmes has (a) to let a man be killed almost under his nose, (b) to deduce things we have already been told, which makes us unfairly impatient with him, and (c) I haven't the heart for (c) but the last five minutes are a real let-down. Up till then Mr Giovanni keeps his action and his hero moving inventively and spectacularly enough for us to be pleasured. Keith Michell's Holmes is sound, despite the falsest of noses and a nasty tendency to breathlessness in the throes of exposition, Denis Lill is a thoroughly worthy Watson, John Cater an admirable inspector, Susan Hampshire a provocatively demure heroine; while Edward Petherbridge takes us from a wasted youth in the Indian Mutiny through guilt-ridden old age in darkest Maidenhead to final peace in Limehouse's opium dens.

  

Willy Russell's One for the Road (Nottingham Playhouse) is about life on a housing estate and the difficulties of escaping from it. Early patronising laughter (at the mention of Beethoven Close and Mahler Crescent) freezes as a discontented young man quails before a professional harpy (his best friend's wife) and a keen amateur (his own), makes a bid for freedom and finds that his tormentors would be only too happy to join him.

Mr Russell switches moods rather too mechanically, but he knows where he is at any given moment. He has written a gentle account of a tough situation, nowhere more unnerving than in his hero's realisation of pleasures he is still permitted. They seem to boil down to adultery. Alun Armstrong gives a sweet performance in the lead.

  

Beowulf, a contribution to Puppet Theatre '79, was booked for the hospitality of the National Theatre, who had in the event to farm it out to St George's, Tufnell Park. Its creator, Christopher Leith, seems on the evidence to have been fired by the Japanese Bunraku theatre into attempting a puppet-play of comparable obscurity.

Finding a suitable theme in the Anglo-Saxon, he loaded it down with oriental music, while neglecting the Bunraku's sense of scale. He gave his puppets no environment, making them difficult to look at. His Fireworm had an elephant's trunk and wore a ballet-skirt, which was interesting in a giggly way. There were two readers, the lady more oppressively elocutionary than the gentleman. Boredom arrived early and stayed late.
1979-03-25-theatre:
Theatre

A CHORUS LINE (Drury Lane): And this week it's the final chorus--or, if you prefer, the end of the Line.

A FAIR QUARREL (Olivier): Ascetic revival of an interesting curio, shedding light on duelling, smoking, enforced marriage, and other Jacobean customs. Acting underpowered at the premiere, but hope springs.

FLASHPOINT (Mayfair): Lively barrack-room melodrama set during the Anglo-Irish war which, in case you're wondering, happened--like so much else in current drama--next year. Last week.

LARK RISE (Cottesloe): Coming up for the third time, a charming combination of epic and pastoral, set in Victorian Oxfordshire around (honest, it's in the book) Cottisloe Pond.

NORMAL SERVICE (Hampstead): Pleasant comedy set in the design-room of a Scottish TV company that will rank (let us hope) among coming playwright John Byrne's lesser works.

SUBJECTS FOR INTERROGATION (Bush): Twin plays by new writer Frederick Harrison on the rise of the British torturer; the first windy and worthless; the second ingenious and, to be disrespectfully candid, fun.
1979-04-01-that-old-sex-war:
That old sex war

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Caryl Churchill's 'Cloud Nine' and Bob Hope.

IT IS quite some time since the advanced wing of our theatre treated us to a mocking panorama of Victorian society with special emphasis on the hang-ups; and to that extent the first half of Joint Stock's new show, Cloud Nine (Royal Court), is pleasantly nostalgic.

The scene is Africa, the characters mostly British, and a lot of heavy irony about Empire is being energetically shouldered. "Come one and all for help," chants the cast in the course of a rhymed prologue, setting an airy and unimpassioned tone for the whole of the proceedings. However, this tone is difficult to sustain and, though Caryl Churchill's subsequent prose is very often witty, the play falters whenever the jokes run out.

The points being made are familiar, and no doubt truthful; they concern the warping of Victorian sexuality by the traditions of Victorian colonialism. Or it could be the other way about; author and company do not seem to have made up their minds. The trouble is that there is now an agreed code of laughter for dealing with such characters, a taboo in its way as pernicious as any of the Victorians' own, and one which this production does nothing to breach.

To the house of Clive, paterfamilias and famous explorer, Harry Bagley, and immediately the dovecote is a-flutter. The ladies of the household mostly fancy Harry; he himself is for the boys, whatever their complexion. He makes a particular impression on Clive's young son Edward, who is growing up confused: urged towards manly sports, while he would prefer to play with his sister.

A black servant, sniggering up a neighbouring lady's capacious skirts, is appalled when he learns of Harry's comradeship ("There's something dark in women that their men know nothing about"); so Harry must, for his own sake and the family's peace of mind, be married off to the family governess. We get the message--we in fact, within seconds, get all the messages about repression. They make occasional spectral reappearances in Part Two, which is set here and now, but since they were never really alive in the first place, it is difficult to attach much importance to their ghosts. They spoil what is otherwise a far more credible account of sex wars in this second half, which is almost the best thing to arrive on the London theatre this young and dismal year. Dealing with people they know and understand, the show's creators contrive to do them justice, to do themselves justice.

The play is still fragmentary. Act One has skits; Act Two has fragments. But the focus has shifted, and the second half's emotional meaning is as unmistakable as the first half's is over-emphatic. Here sexual role-playing is no longer an emblematic cartoon but something which changes as a personality expands.

The dialogue continues to ring and sparkle; it also, from time to time, probes. All that happens is that two young mothers shack up together and draw into their orbit a male homosexual whose former relationship has broken up. "Do you still," asks his ex-partner, "think of yourself as a woman?" "I'm not sure," is the reply, "what I think a woman's like." This bafflement is the limit of what most of us are prepared to admit in the way of affirmations about sex: one reason why the play's second half is so much more engaging than its patronising first.

Actually, if you did add the two bits together the result would not, I think, be much to the author's or performers' liking. The logic would seem to be that our great-grandfathers, trying to suppress or deny homosexuality, actually encouraged it and thanks to them here we all are in Sodom and Gomorrah and unhappy about it.

The acting is variable, but at best very fine. Julie Covington not only extends but refines her range as an elderly daughter of Empire confused among the vagaries of Britain today. She also plays the sailor-suited Edward in Part One, again with more than skill; but the sexual cross-casting, though maybe intended as its own political gesture, inevitably plays tricks with audience response. It matters more in Part Two, where Antony Sher gives a riotously accurate performance as a little girl; the laughs he gets, though, are bound to be at least those elicited by the performer as well as the character.

  

Bob Hope was back at the Palladium last week and more relaxed than ever; the highlight of his act came when he reclined on a chaise longue, slid his feet on to the floor and into a dance while the rest of him remained horizontal, and sang with feeling "Lazy." Jokes about his age blended quite naturally into the texture of his act; his pose has always been one of aggressive self-deprecation. Occasionally on the first night danger threatened; not all his gags worked, but he always managed to get to the next one in time. Occasionally he faltered at the start of a new joke, but he never mistimed the punch line; he may never have done so in his life.
