His is not the highest form of stand-up comedy (and I prefer him in films, where his persona expands into a character; a sneakily likeable one), but it is a good one. Unlike his late confrere Bing Crosby (to whom he paid the best kind of tribute in continuing to make jokes about him), Mr Hope did not come on at the Palladium until the second half. Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: the ears, too, since we listened in the interim to Leslie Uggams, a loud lady singer who brought with her something I have certainly never heard before, to wit a four-man rhythm section composed entirely of drummers.

  

Another soloist is at the Roundhouse Downstairs: Maxim Mazumdar, an Indian-born Canadian actor, whom I saw in Dance of Gods, a piece I hope is unrepresentative. He appeared before us as an ancient Greek actor-dancer, chatting mainly about his very good friend Euripides. Having just received the script of The Bacchae, he said right out, quoting without acknowledgment from the introduction to the standard modern translation, "It's that unmistakable thing, a masterpiece."

I object not to the plagiarism but to the assumption that expository prose can be made to work as dialogue. And I object beyond that to the whole idea of watching an actor spend an evening conducting imaginary conversations. We go (more or less reluctantly, most of us) to a one-man show in the hope that for once a performer will drop the humiliating pretence that we in the audience do not exist. If he still cannot bring himself to talk to us, then let him by all means talk to himself--but not, please, to invisible interlocutors in whom neither he nor we can believe.
1979-04-08-merry-stratford:
Merry Stratford

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on two new Shakespeare productions.

THE Stratford season opened last week with The Merry Wives of Windsor in a production full of quiet charm and local colour.

I can never think of this play as taking place in its advertised location: to me it's a play about Stratford, as I assume it must have been for the author. If he wrote it as quickly as tradition insists, he would hardly have had the time to go reconnoitring along the Thames. He must have reached back into his own boyhood. If you really want to read Shakespeare's autobiography in his plays, then avert your eyes from the mysteries of Hamlet and The Tempest; look instead at the brief scene in which a shuffling schoolboy (called William) is exposed to a Latin viva under the doting but doubting eye of his mother.

Schoolchildren, dressed up as fairies for the taunting of Falstaff, provide the finale of the play and Trevor Nunn's production gives them plenty of preliminary build-up: we see Elizabethan youth infesting the streets, playing conkers, haunting Peter Simple (here played as the village idiot, which may be in line with the robust Tudor idea of a joke, but is a bit of a damper now) and eventually--in the shape of Falstaff's page--providing a fat and thwarted knight with his only remaining companionship.

In all this, Mr Nunn's production is the heir of Terry Hands's previous RSC model, which it also resembles in the carefully assembled domesticity of its setting. The middle classes rise before our eyes; John Napier's beguiling set is timbered, thatched, cobbled, mullioned--in fact, it only needs a few tourists to make it seem an extension of the world just outside the theatre.

Howard Brenton once declared that there are only two kinds of play: plays set in rooms and plays not set in rooms. The Merry Wives is the only Shakespeare play to belong irretrievably in the first category. I suppose an abstract bare production is just about conceivable; most directors, however, give in to the temptations of realism, as presented by dialogue stuffed with law suits and laundry lists.

Mr Nunn's production gains on Mr Hands's in its careful treatment of the supporting bourgeoisie: particularly notable are David Threlfall's mooncalf Slender, Kate Nicholls's Anne Page and Geoffrey Hutchings's French doctor, a tidy volcano. (That long double take when he discovers Simple hiding in his closet, and reaches the front door before registering the fact--had I seen it before or was it merely a folk memory?) John McEnery makes sense of Pistol.

The central comedy, though, is less happy. The wives (Jane Downs and Susan Tracy) are not very merry and are frankly hard to tell apart. John Woodvine is a fine active comedian (cf The Alchemist and The Comedy of Errors), but Falstaff in this play is a perpetual victim, needing above all the massive dignity that demands deflation: the quality that Brewster Mason had in the role and that Mr Woodvine, whose voice does not match his padding, seems to lack.

However, the real originality of this farce lies in its provision of a second fall-guy; whatever hurts Falstaff goes double for Ford. Ben Kingsley makes him a deceiving bouncing blend of masochist and voyeur, his disguise a neat anticipation of bowler and dirty mac, his jealous soliloquies always starting a second earlier than you would think possible. He can, by such technical means, be funny, but he is too manic for comedy to flow easily from him.

  

In Stratford's Other Place, Ron Daniels has directed a necessarily plain version of Pericles, another play with a passive hero. To the ill-luck that dogs the protagonist in the shapes of lost wives and daughters, storms at sea, and encounters with incestuous despots, must be added the crushing blow of being removed from the play just when the writing is starting to improve. The first two acts either are not by Shakespeare at all or have suffered wholesale textual corruption; the relief to the ear when we finally arrive at verse that moves in paragraphs instead of single lame sentences is hardly to be described.

Only Griffith Jones's Gower, a gentle storyteller possessed by his story, escapes the monotony of the first half, despite staging visually ingenious and spiritually apt. When Gower mentions Antiochus, Antiochus simply appears, followed by a row of severed heads--a perfect image of fairyland tyranny. The long pantomime of Pericles's wooing is presented with a well stylised tournament (and less happy dance), but it drags; Peter McEnery is always sympathetic--and, when he returns for the reconciliation, moving--but he never achieves the Everyman status desirable in a hero almost uncannily innocent of personal attributes.

Studio Shakespeare can grab you more immediately than the full-stage variety, but it requires acting of unusual intensity and moment-to-moment suppleness to hold you throughout. Not all these actors come through; Marina (Julie Peasgood) makes it, but with nothing to spare. However, Peter Clough is economically good at the complexities of her seducer-turned-rescuer, and Emily Richard similarly adept as her unfortunate mum; while Jeffery Dench does a striking (and probably symbolic) double of King and Pandar. The brothel scenes in this play I would place second to the Windsor Latin-lesson as the obvious fruits of personal experience.

  

Tourneur's The Atheist's Tragedy, bravely and skilfully revived at the Belgrade, Coventry, gives us the Jacobean vision without the redemptive bits. It has its virtuous hero and heroine, but they are lay figures; though she was actually played (by Gay Wilde) with some spirit, he gained nothing by being acted as a fool. An avenger who refuses to avenge (and haunted by a ghost who tells him not to), he helps to differentiate this play from the other blood-and-lust pieces of the period.

The engaging traditional qualities are also present, of course, and are focused in the title figure, a thoughtful intellectual villain played with calm wit, if with some shortage of glow, by Jonathan Newth. He has a final haunting half-mad scene when his plans have misfired and he seeks the comforts of religion.

Ed Thomason's production established themes, types and motives with intelligence and got laughs where required and nowhere else. Maureen O'Brien played the stock lecherous lady with more than stock enthusiasm. The play incidentally provides an interesting back door portrait of contemporary vice (fornication, hair-dressing and other abominations) and is in its own terms outstandingly well made.

  

That brings us to Maugham's The Constant Wife which, as revived and reclaimed at the Cambridge Arts under the direction of Sheila Hancock, shattered its recent reputation as a museum piece for a museum star. Maugham's wife, winking at her husband's adultery until financial independence allows her to commit her own with a clear conscience, is a part for a young, clear-eyed and careful actress; in this case Susan Jameson whose sweetness gradually sharpened, but never curdled.

Most of the performances were comic triumphs, employing artifice without surrendering to it. Pamela Moiseiwitsch's ageing flapper was a prime example, the best lisped performance in ages; others were Trevor Baxter's immovably complacent philanderer and--showing that breeding always tells--the wise worldly mama of Margaretta Scott.
1979-04-08-hands-at-the-opera:
Hands at the opera

ROBERT CUSHMAN profiles the director of Covent Garden's new 'Parsifal,' which opens on Wednesday.

SURROUNDED by the massed choral heavies of the Royal Opera House, some of whom carried rubber swords while others were equipped with dustbin-lid shields, Terry Hands, slight in his black track-suit, looked distinctly vulnerable.

Directors of the Royal Shakespeare Company invariably look boyish; Peter Hall did in his time at Stratford, and so do Trevor Nunn who succeeded him, and Hands who last year was promoted in equal rank with Nunn. On leave from the RSC, he directs Parsifal at Covent Garden.

This is his second opera; the first was Otello, which he staged in Paris in 1976 with Placido Domingo singing the Moor. Georg Solti conducted and the association was a happy one. "I only accept one opera for every five I turn down," Hands says, but two years ago, when Solti telephoned him and asked whether he would by any chance be free for Parsifal in 1979, he agreed.

As might have been foreseen, he is not as free as all that. Apart from sharing the burden of RSC planning at a particularly tricky point in the company's history, he has to supervise the European tour of his highly successful production of Coriolanus, which played last year at the Aldwych and the year before at Stratford. In fact he will have to fly into the first night of Parsifal directly after seeing to Coriolanus's arrival in Vienna.

Of all the RSC's directors--apart, perhaps, from the special case of Peter Brook--Hands has been the most actively international. He has a production of As You Like It in the repertory of the Vienna Burgtheatre and he is a consultant director of the Comedie Francaise. It was at the Comedie that he had one of his greatest successes with a production of Richard III in 1972. Two years before he had come unstuck with the play at Stratford, but doing it in Paris turned out to be one of the key experiences of his career.

As his leading man, he had the most unconventional of French classical actors, the comedian Robert Hirsch, and he found that the French rhetorical acting tradition gave him a new insight into Shakespeare. He learned the value of "playing a line right through to the end" rather than breaking it up into anxiously-analysed sections; and this led the way to his most fruitful period of work at Stratford: the Henrys (IV, V and VI) and Coriolanus. These were all productions of a new muscularity and simplicity and, like the French Richard, they took much of their impact from the director's rapport with his leading actor, in this case Alan Howard. "Alan has no directing ambitions, he always speaks for the actor."

Opera, for all its fearsome logistics (all the problems of a play even before you start on the music), can be a comparative relaxation. Since the conductor is the boss, "if it doesn't work, you can only get half the blame. The problem with opera is that everyone is working in a different style; I feel sorry for opera-singers, subjected to one influence after another. The director is always hired after the singers have been approached."

Hands's father was a musician; he himself "learned the violin at eight, gave it up, took up the cello at 10, gave it up. I can read a piano score." He has, as it happens, a reputation as a somewhat operatic director of drama. The choreographer Gillian Lynne is assisting him on Parsifal and during the rehearsal I attended she congratulated him on the staging of Coriolanus, which she had caught up with the night before: "Very well choreographed."

The irony here is that Hands, by his own account, does not go in for strictly organised movement and certainly never works any out in advance. (In drama, that is; in opera, with a hundred-strong chorus to manoeuvre in short order, the situation is obviously different.) But it is certainly true that he has always leaned towards ceremonial, or anyway non-naturalistic drama. Naturalism he sees as an overrated passing phase that television has now thankfully taken over, much to the theatre's benefit.

Hands is 38. He grew up in Woking, Surrey, and as a teenager used to come into London by the early train to do the art galleries by day and the Old Vic by night. He went to Birmingham University and flourished there in the Guild Theatre Group "for purely social and ambitious reasons: I didn't have enough money for the Union, which was the only alternative." He wanted to do research, but his tutor John Russell Brown (now head of scripts at the National Theatre) doubted if he had the academic temperament. So he went to RADA and while there laid the plans for his first theatre.

In association with Peter James (a Birmingham contemporary, now director of the Sheffield Crucible) and Martin Jenkins (now with the BBC), he started the Liverpool Everyman Theatre. In their day it was a classical theatre; it has now changed its identity completely and is devoted to new and mainly local plays. After two years in Liverpool, Hands "ran out of everything I knew" and wrote two letters, "one to the National, one to the RSC." The second paid off: Peter Hall wanted someone to run the newly emergent touring group, Theatre Go Round. Hands was told to go away and make it work. "Within three months we had nine shows on the road. But I'd done all this kind of thing before, working with kids in Liverpool."

In 1967 he had his first solo flight at the Aldwych: a three-character Cuban play called The Criminals, done in a boldly extrovert style that confused the critics and had the audience booing and heckling--"most unusual, they usually just leave." Hall told Hands that the production was "very brilliant--I didn't follow the play for a moment," and Hands survived to direct a resoundingly successful Merry Wives of Windsor at Stratford the next year.

This supposedly intractable comedy became virtually his property for years (it was revived as late as 1975), though he says the only play about which he really feels proprietorial is Pericles, which he staged in 1969. These two plays, as it happens, have opened this year's Stratford season in other directors' production, so Hands is using his new authority magnanimously.

In some ways his post as Joint Artistic Director is a rationalisation of RSC policy over the past few years. He and Nunn have run alternate seasons at Stratford and the Aldwych, and each has developed his own team of actors. (Common opinion has it that Hands's bunch is the more roughneck of the two, and he doesn't deny it.)

The new season in some ways breaks the pattern; the company contains actors from both groups, and both Nunn and Hands are directing. Hands's play is Twelfth Night, which I said I thought unlikely for him; I don't associate him with comedy. He said nonsense, he's spent most of his life directing comedy. Are there any Shakespeares he yearns to direct in the future? "Yes, 22 of them. I've done 15. I want to do them all."
1979-04-15-disturbed-by-goldoni:
Disturbed by Goldoni

THE Glasgow Citizens' Theatre last week completed a typically even predictably adventurous season with a Goldoni piece called Country Life. The theatre will now be closed for repairs until September, though the company will be on view at the Edinburgh Festival in another Goldoni. Their refusal to repeat themselves is, I suppose, admirable, but it can also be frustrating; somebody should point a gun at them and demand a retrospective.

Country Life, for example, is far too substantial an achievement to vanish after a three-week run. It is, in fact, three plays, though crammed into one long evening, of which only the middle one has a rural setting, where one or two of the idle rich, plus several others who are idle but can only wish they were rich, fall languishingly or farcically in and out of love. Some end up mated against their wills; others achieve their desired partner, but seem set for no less disastrous matches.

The first play shows us these same characters wondering whether to spend their own hard-hoarded cash on the trip, or alternatively looking for someone who will give them the price of it; in the third they are all back in town, again trying to sort out the tangles--though Goldoni sternly refuses to give them all the help we might expect. I had thought him to be a strictly classical happy-ending man; these plays show him to have been altogether more untidy and more disturbing.

Robert David Macdonald, the translator-director, has advanced the play from Goldoni's eighteenth century to the beginning of our own. This is no help to the early scenes, which are thinly satirical; we are expected to laugh at a society which we are never permitted to see. But as the action grows lusher, the style begins to justify itself. Plangent operatic chords sound behind the scenes as self-destructive heroines surrender their lovers to rivals with a better legal or financial claim. Philip Prowse has set the entire action within a gigantic green conservatory, and the hot-house feeling suits the play's emotional climate.

Mr Prowse's sets are Glasgow's glories; this one is as striking as any, though less individual than most--one can imagine another designer coming up with it. His designs throw a strange light on the acting, which is always extravagantly young. Youthful companies generally cultivate the athletic and stentorian virtues; they come to notice with productions of, say, Shakespeare's histories. I generally begin in Glasgow by finding the playing hopelessly inadequate to the sophistication demanded of it, and then adjust as the evening proceeds and the production creates its own world. Comic performances, composed of immature and irritating mannerisms, turn out to be valuable counterweights in moments of stress; young actresses who seem hopelessly out of their depth in social comedy suddenly transfix you with their emotional candour. They also justify the peculiar style of Mr Macdonald's translation, in which academic archaism and flip modernity mingle with wedges of frank quotation, mostly Shakespearean. A more experienced and artful cast would point up the differences; this one sails blithely through them. You are never nudged into laughter. The Citizens' does not, despite some claims, represent the peak of British theatre, but it is invaluable and unique.

London critics, and London companies, are sometimes scornfully accused of never venturing north of Watford. That is a canard; it is travelling to Watford itself that we find a problem. But last week I finally made it to the Palace Theatre, for the British premiere of Lillian Hellman's 30-year-old play The Autumn Garden. I cannot say my intrepidity was rewarded. A shapeless and interminable round of domestic fidgets in a residential rooming-house on the Gulf of Mexico is given by Stephen Hollis a lackadaisical production almost in excess of its demerits. For three hours it is sleepy time down South. The drawl of course is a powerful brake on British actors; I sympathised with a couple who quietly forgot about it. The acting, some of it by well-known performers, runs a collector's gamut from the apathetic to the appalling.

  

A third regional theatre has brought its product to London: to the Cambridge, from Sheffield, comes Chicago. At this third remove the musical inevitably lacks both the spectacular inventiveness of Bob Fosse's Broadway staging and the refreshing spaciousness of Sheffield's open stage. Some performances, though, have ripened: Antonia Ellis now flashes a dazzlingly innocent smile as the murdering Roxie and Jenny Logan a trouper's weary grin as her cell-mate Velma, born to lose in the race for stardom.

The equation the show proposes is that crime and entertainment are one, and number after number makes this point with a relentless "Brechtian," or simply repetitious. The story, with both heroines in the same predicament and a chorus of other accused to back them up, already invites monotony; the treatment compounds it. Fred Ebb's lyrics and John Kander's music do not advance the story, they only comment on it--and it is always the same comment. Items billed as songs turn out to be exchanges of dialogue against a rhythmic background. Faced with a sequence that seems to call for sustained musicalisation--Roxie's trial, for instance--the authors back away.

This would be enough to make the show, despite the remnants of Mr Fosse's choreographic flair, a disappointment. What makes it detestable is epitomised in a number called "Razzle Dazzle." All the tricks of the showman's trade are presented for our applause--and the first night audience duly responded. Were they listening to the lyrics which mocked them for their acceptance? Well, a good joke on the audience you might think, but since razzle dazzle is in fact all the show has to offer (spiced with a cynicism as bland and automatic as the sentimentality of The Sound of Music when that was fashionable) the joke rebounds on the authors.

"Long as you keep 'em way off-balance / How can they know you got no talents," I wouldn't accuse Messrs Fosse, Kander and Ebb of being untalented (for the good and proven reason that they aren't), but all they are doing here is throwing their own self-indulgent misgivings about their craft in the audience's face, and despising them for not noticing. Throwing a few generalisations about crime and society, they have fooled the critics as well. There is not enough wit or substance in the writing to make the concert genuinely interesting. There is only flash, which the audience lapped up. Good flash, too, some of it--though one has to say, despite the pleasure of seeing an even competently staged musical arrive in London, that in this production it is not good enough. Not with all the pretensions it dangles from its spangles.

  

Last week, I committed a grave sin of omission in my review of the RSC's Pericles at the Other Place. I failed to mention Stephen Oliver's music, which not only contributes immensely to the atmosphere, and even to the plot, but is also historically notable as the first occasion on which a chamber Shakespeare production has come equipped with a full chamber score: part Oriental, part baroque.
1979-04-22-frightened-by-furies:
Frightened by Furies

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Stratford.

FEW directors these days write programme-notes, but for his production of The Family Reunion (Roundhouse) Michael Elliott--sensitive, articulate and embattled--has broken the rule.

He tells us that the only hope of realising the spiritual dimension of T. S. Eliot's 40-year-old play is to make its realistic ground-base as solid as possible. He hints that his playwright has not given him too much help here and that the passage of time has compounded the inadequacy, making us unwilling to take at all seriously the problems of guilt-racked, verse-spouting landed gentry or of their baffled, dependent relatives.

Even two years ago that latter objection might have held, but we are now just far enough away from the inhabitants of Eliot's Wishwood to re-extend them our sympathy; compared to the unholy abstractions more recent playwrights have expected us to believe in, they are flesh-and-blood itself. That nervous chorus of uncles and aunts was always well observed; perhaps too well--the author seems at times to be pinning them down under glass. One of the chief merits of Mr Elliott's production is that he adds warmth to accuracy, but author and audience are more on his side here than he admits.

His major contention passes unchallenged; nothing in the theatre can work symbolically or metaphorically unless it works concretely first. In this production that principle is carried to the extremest point. In picture-stage versions, the Eumenides--the Furies who according to classical precedent turn to "bright angels"--apparently lurked as embarrassing shadows outside the drawing-room window. Mr Elliott, working in the round, brings them on, to the accompaniment of nerve-wrenching music, as a circle of towering Klansmen. I was scared out of my life.

His direction is in fact superbly tuned throughout. Each area of the play is clearly demarcated, and varied within itself; thus the choral quartet includes virtuoso solos by Constance Chapman and Jeffry Wickham, matched by the kindly intrusion of Esmond Knight's doctor. Combining rigour and humanity, Mr Elliott makes you recognise how much sloppy approximation we are accustomed to accept in the theatre.

However, the play's central problem remains Harry the haunted hero. He believes for most of the play that he has murdered his wife, then comes to realise that he is bearing the burden of his late father who wanted to kill his mother. This uncannily subtle form of guilt (for somebody else's intention only) is difficult to express with dramatic precision; maybe an actor less craggy and more malleable than Edward Fox (who looks authentically racked and sounds like a young uptight Ralph Richardson) might bring it off, but there is no way of disguising the imbalance.

Harry turns out to be a vessel, rather than a figure, of tragedy; the real agony resides with his mother, who has hitherto been kept off-centre and is now dragged forward for a couple of climaxes (one her off-stage death) that only an actress of genius could manage so suddenly; Pauline Jameson supplies talent and a kind of willed hauteur.

But the whole play is dealt to us at one remove; mother and son are even denied a confrontation. Harry's prototype, Orestes, may have grown up in a disturbed household, but he had solid sins of his own to expiate; the Greek and Christian worlds, though equally harsh, do not mesh. Not ethically at any rate; the play does have an atmospheric unity, and this the production brilliantly captures, not just with its technical shocks, but with its careful attention to Eliot's equally careful imagery.

  

This may be mannered in its catalogues of bleak domestic horrors (can any poet ever have been so definite about his articles?), but even the mannerism is now effective. Thirties Gothic (the world of a myriad of ghostly black-and-white movies) is now a style. You emerge convinced that something has happened, even if you and the playwright failed to converge on the crucial moment. The play's most moving, as well as its most appealing, moment is Mr Wickham's declaration that he could almost grasp what was going on, if only someone would slow it down and explain.

This belongs with the immortal remark of Constable Dull in Love's Labour's Lost (Aldwych): charged with not having spoken a word, he replies, "nor understood none neither." That always gets the loudest laugh of the play, though in John Barton's production--which will do until perfection comes along--it has stiff competition.

This is as it should be; their predicament--ensnared by their own pretensions, the victims of desire and of mortality--is prototypically comic. If there is no sadder scene in Shakespeare than the message of death that wrecks the accumulated masque, there is none funnier than the lord's sequential realisation--piling farce on irony--that they are all in love and all forsworn.

Richard Griffiths's tubby King, agonisingly shy, is a glorious joke; though to appreciate it fully you may need to know how straight the role is usually played, and how much further down the social scale Mr Griffiths is usually cast. This is in no way to impugn its essential truth, matched by that of Carmen du Sautoy's Princess, whose final transformations--grief, disillusion, anger, charity--are triumphantly done. Tony Church now plays Armado--a shabbier, more mournful Don than he offered in David Jones's production last time round.

  

Meanwhile Mr Jones has staged Cymbeline (Stratford). The programme contains enough quotations about dreams for us to believe that this was his governing concept, the dreamer presumably being Griffith Jones's blind Soothsayer, alone on the stage at beginning and end and crumbling Jupiter's prophecy with a gesture I took to be contemptuous. There seems at least to be an acerbic edge to the production throughout. Jeffery Dench's Cymbeline is played as an ineffectual tyrant (married to a wife from North Finchley, judging by the sound of her) and the play's many references to the "gentry" are curtly underlined. (Mind you, the contrastingly noble savages do turn out to be princes in disguise.)

I wondered if Mr Jones had been reading Edward Bond, who sees the play as "an appalling slapstick rehash of King Lear," and whether a class-conscious version of a play obsessed with the differences between "court" and country might not work better in Jacobean dress than in the legendary-nondescript get-up affected here. Even Judi Dench plays Imogen's bad temper (she's always getting at people, often with some provocation) for all it's worth, leaving enchantment to take care of itself--as, with her around, it infallibly does.

Roger Rees digs deeper into Posthumus's jealousy than is customary and Bob Peck rather surprisingly essays the epicene as Cloten. He looks like the Jolly Green Giant and sounds retarded. The company is full of good actors (and, on this showing, at least one terrible one), but they have yet to draw together. Neither does Mr Jones's production really cohere, but I preferred it to Mr Barton's rather bland version, also last time round.

  

Talking of blandness, Etherege's She Would if She Could, the seminal Restoration comedy, is being walked through at Greenwich under the direction of Jonathan Miller. The play is full of troubling passions delicately drawn, but you would never guess it.

  

What price a really funny young playwright? Jonathan Gems is the man, and of his uproarious The Tax Exile (Bush) more next time.
1979-04-29-mr-brenton-s-original-nightma:
Mr Brenton's original nightmare

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'The Churchill Play.'

HOWARD BRENTON'S The Churchill Play (Warehouse) has finally come to London four years after its premiere in Nottingham; and seeing it again proves an instructive experience.

We have been heavily dosed with nightmare plays about Britain's totalitarian future, envisioned as transpiring any time from next decade to next week; this is the daddy of them all -- the first, the most ambitious and considerably the best written. It is set, you may recall, in 1984. There is a coalition government, predominantly Tory, and disaffected elements are placed in internment camps.

The play centres on a group of prisoners in one such place, mostly in, it seems, for minor offences such as being around picket lines when the police arrived. Few are consciously political; almost all are working class. (What has happened to the revolutionary playwrights, middle class almost to a man? Have they all been summarily shot?)

Under the sponsorship of the camp medical officer, who is a liberal (i.e. despised by everybody), the lags put on a play about Winston Churchill, and use the performance as the cover for an escape attempt; they must all have watched 'Colditz' in younger, happier days.

As it happens the puncturing of wartime legends is one of the things Mr Brenton is on about. The Churchill of his play-within-the-play rises from his catafalque and revisits former scenes, recalling his miserable boyhood, his lifelong fits of agonising depression and the heady times of his popularity, when the blitzed populace cheerily told him, "We can take it, guv, give it back to them."

Only his guide on this spectral trip informs him he got the second part wrong: the workers really said, "And one day we'll give it back to you." This is presumably what the prisoners are doing, or trying to do, when they stage their final break-out. Asked to justify himself, the mock Churchill grandiloquently says, "I won the war." He is informed that he didn't: "people won the war." Quite true: and on television last week Mr Brenton admitted that Churchill was one of the people in question. But there is no hint of it in the play.

That doesn't matter too much; the main snag remains that of linking the play's two myths. What is Churchill doing in a play about 1984? The most obvious answer is that the sentimental pull he exerts is central to modern Conservatism. I doubt it: I haven't heard many references to the Battle of Britain spirit in the election campaign; and if Mrs Thatcher gets in, her victory will not have much to do with the late Sir Winston. Besides, half the time Mr Brenton is asserting that the people never really fell for him anyhow; he can't bear to conceive of the Tory spell actually working. Or, rather, he can contemplate the result but not the process. (The truth is that the last generation did worship Churchill; this one doesn't.) So Churchill ends up in the play as just a symbol of upper-classness in a straight class-struggle; though even this is complicated by his scenes of intensive introspection accompanied by the "black dog" of melancholy.

That makes the play sound like a mess; and so, in some ways, it is. It is redeemed, though, by its narrative thrust, and by the power of its dialogue, second only to Edward Bond's; also by the fact that it has a direct line to current fears -- witness the number of plays that have cannibalised it since its first prophetic appearance.

Barry Kyle's production brings out most of its strengths, and though Raymond Westwell doesn't go much beyond impersonation as Churchill, he is excellent in his outer role as the prisoner who actually writes the play -- as are his colleagues: David Bradley bewildered, Bill Dean pawky and, especially, Hilton McRae ferocious. Their opponents are less well done; Mr Brenton's periodic attempts to get inside the heads of the officers running the camp are no more than dutiful and the roles are pallidly played. A brace of visiting politicians are straightforwardly -- and more efficiently -- caricatured.

Mr Brenton is more forthcoming than most of his successors have been in documenting his nightmare, but like them he can stop short at awkward junctures. Despairing of the escape attempt, one of his internees declares that there is nowhere to go: "They'll concrete over the whole world." A good image -- and one that almost sums up the succession of plays we have seen at the Warehouse -- but dramatically an odd moment to start getting rhetorical. They should have more practical things on their minds. One basic point of Mr Brenton's scenario is that Britain will become an extension of Ulster, and subject to similar military rule.

  

There has been a whole school of plays on this hypothesis and David Leland's Psy-Warriors (Theatre Upstairs) is the latest. It starts as a confrontation between a trio of suspected London terrorists and their military interrogators; we get an anthology of physical and psychological humiliation.

We have been here before and it seems that Mr Leland has nothing new to tell us; he hardly seems interested in probing the motives of either side. Then -- by a ploy which it would be dishonourable of me to reveal, but which resembles one already used in a play at the Bush -- he changes track, and the play becomes a debate on the ethics of counter terrorism. Or at least some of it does; there is still a story to be told and it gets in the way.

The arguments meanwhile are largely disembodied; and the actors, under the author's direction, tie themselves in knots trying to characterise them. They should probably settle for simple lucidity. It is not an enlivening evening and the scheme is over-complicated, but it does yield a few dogged insights.

  

But if you are really searching for metaphors-for-Britain, try Jonathan Gems's The Tax Exile (Bush), which sees the place as a high-rise flat, lavishly furnished but liable to systematic plundering. It is owned by an inventor who is having taxation trouble and should really flee the country, but somehow doesn't. He is estranged from his wife but becomes involved with her radical-feminist best friend, who finds that principles are not everything.

These characters are confused but likeable, and given performances to match by Richard Kane and Jennie Stoller. The young are represented by the inventor's hippie son (who, having been in prison, doesn't realise time has passed him by), his pregnant girlfriend and his blue-rinsed punk sister -- who may, amazingly enough, be the first of her kind to reach a London stage.

There is also a manic tax inspector acting, more or less, as diabolus ex machina. These are put through a farcical evening which sometimes runs out of steam but rarely of point, and has a rare ring of truth about it, dividing the characters into those who can't bear to leave home and those who can't wait to. Nancy Meckler's direction is lively; June Page's punkette is sensational.

  

We are more used to New York comedies of contemporary manners. James Kirkwood's PS Your Cat is Dead (Open Space) is actually cut to an old-fashioned pattern: uptight hero shown the way to a freer life by a kooky intruder. It always used to be a kooky girl, an actress perhaps: now, time having moved on, it's a boy burglar. It's the actor who has to burst out. There is not enough wit to go round, but what there is is pleasant, and is well dispatched by Christopher Gable and David Baxt.
1979-05-06-time-passes:
Time passes

SOMERSET MAUGHAM'S penultimate play begins with tea on the lawn and ends with tea in the drawing-room. During the first repast tennis is transpiring off stage; during the second madness is happening on it.

For Services Rendered (Lyttelton) is an unmasking play, in the grand tradition of English bourgeois comedy. The Ardsleys are a country solicitor's family who discover, during the autumn of 1932, that the world is slipping away from them. It is Mrs Ardsley who epitomises their plight; she finds she is dying. She doesn't seem to mind very much. "I'm not at home in this world of today. I'm pre-war."

All the characters are inclined to blame the war (now 14 years in the past) for their sufferings, and Maugham seems to agree with them. At all events he gives a key denunciatory speech to Sydney, the son of the house, blinded in action. A friend of the family, Collie, is an ex-officer trying and failing to make a civilian living as a garage owner; financial ruin leads him to suicide.

The Ardsleys have three daughters. Eva, the eldest, has been cast as nurse and martyr, looking after Sydney, and is sick of the role; she sees Collie (who gives her no encouragement) as her last chance of marriage and his death sends her round the bend. The second, Ethel, has made a miserable marriage to a drunken farmer who had the bad taste to do well out of the war and is now engaged in trying to seduce the youngest girl, Lois. He only succeeds in scaring her--temporarily at least--off an equally married but slightly less disreputable suitor whom she doesn't love. What he did in and since the great war is not made clear but--since he refuses to bale Collie out but can squander money on a necklace for Lois--it was presumably something shameful.

It is difficult to trace all the characters' troubles to the battlefield; where the three sisters are concerned you have to resort to that old standby, the shortage of available men. Maugham's polemical bursts are powerful enough, but they obscure the play's real perspective. Its villain is not war but time; the pivotal roles are the mother embracing death and Lois grabbing for life. (She fears the subtle burden of looking less than her age; nobody can believe that she has cause to worry.)

These shifts of focus create a jolting effect in the narrative which is curiously at odds with the lapidary ease of the style; but if Maugham can sometimes be confused over cause and effect, he has a lethal eye and ear for actual process. There is little communication between his characters and less consideration; they are a set of gleaming monsters.

The cankered comedy of manners is a genre at which the National Theatre has always excelled; and Michael Rudman's production is the most satisfying seen on the South Bank since The Madras House. Witty and moving, it is also rock-hard, its spirit enshrined in the dining-room of the play's central act which Carl Toms (aided by Gerry Jenkinson's ice-cold lighting) has rendered as a cross between barrack and counting-house.

Here, in Leslie Sands's iron-clad performance, Ardsley pere confronts the erring Collie and effectively condemns him. It is notable by the way that this paterfamilias hardly addresses his wife throughout the play and that she ignores him. Jean Anderson establishes a woman who finds her comfort in rigidity and cannot survive its passing as brilliantly as Elizabeth Romilly shows spontaneity and calculation at war in Lois. Robin Bailey reaffirms the pleasures of elegance; Harold Innocent, happily released from his usual joke-roles, is a piercingly mordant Sydney; and Peter Jeffrey and Phyllida Law make a funny, pathetic and dangerous pair of intruders.

The toughest role is Alison Fiske's as Eva; she is disconcertingly strident, presumably in preparation for her mad-scene which--it must be admitted--is crudely written stuff. Mr Ardsley's complaint-making, too, now raises horse-laughs rather than the intended shudders. It is in brisk meanness and casual lacerations that the play excels.

  

Bent (Royal Court)--a new play by an American author, Martin Sherman--is set only a couple of years later. We are in Germany in 1934; homosexuals, in the wake of the Night of the Long Knives, are being sent to concentration camps. The play centres on one who has a talent for surviving at the expense of friends and lovers. In Dachau he manages to exchange the homosexual's pink triangle for the yellow star of the Jew, which, in those early days, is slightly preferable. (There's a sick joke for you.) Also in Dachau he finds the love of his life and, true to form, is the indirect cause of his death. Finally donning his triangle he impales himself on the electric fence. This is the "coming out" play to end them all.

It's also a (strictly verbal) celebration of homosexual love; and I suppose there's a point in setting it in the extremest circumstances. With both fascism and sexual bigotry looming again, the play may even have value as a cautionary tale. But, inevitably, the setting overwhelms the play. Mr Sherman is reasonably sparing with the horrors, but he can of course unleash them at any time and produce a guaranteed (and therefore devalued) effect. And, by the opposite token, any play in which two camp inmates are left alone long enough to form a relationship, provokes incredulity: concentration-camp drama may be a contradiction in terms.

The second half consists almost entirely of a duologue while carrying stones, and Mr Sherman shows considerable skill in keeping it going. But in relation to what is supposed to be happening around, it seems mawkish--as, by any standards, does the end. If the hero had affirmed his identity, and gone on living, that would have been defiance. Ian McKellen sparkles in the character's early insolence and frightens in his rodent tenacity. His admirable partner, Tom Bell, I trust found the play less exploitative than Holocaust. I didn't.

  

The French Have A Song For It (Piccadilly) also takes on great events and falls short of them. In this compilation of chansons, the revolutionary section seems self-conscious; and Peter Reeves's singing of Let It Rock, Coco has lost the blazing ferocity of its simpler staging at the King's Head. But the evening is for the most part a joyful one. There are several funny songs delightfully hiccupped by Amanda Barrie; and above all there is the revelation of Helen Shapiro, who at 15 was the best pop singer this country has ever produced and is now nearly great. Her tone is as warm and deep as ever, her demeanour magnetically relaxed and her phrasing superb, whether singing a shrugging song of loneliness or, sable-clad, sending up My Man as rotten as it has long deserved. Most songs are sung in Mr Reeves's conscientious translations, but we also get to hear the Gallic original of My Way. It doesn't scan in French either.
1979-05-13-wiving-it-wealthily:
Wiving it wealthily

Theatre
by ROBERT CUSHMAN

I have deferred reviewing The Taming of the Shrew (Aldwych), partly out of sheer funk. I know I enjoyed the production but I am not sure how to interpret it. I judge from other reviewers that my confusion is shared. I fancy that the director, Michael Bogdanov, is none too clear himself.

The observable facts about the production are that it is uncommonly lively and inventive, that it is performed in modern dress, and that there is a shock effect at each end of it. For once it is more unfair to give away the beginning than the close. If I told you that the show opens with Jonathan Pryce, apparently drunk, clambering on to the stage and demolishing the set, before subsiding into a dream that consists of the rest of the play with himself in the role of Petruchio, you would never forgive me. But it is important to reveal that in the last scene Paola Dionisotti plays Katharina's famous (or infamous) speech of submission with such apparent sincerity that when she reaches the line about putting her hand beneath her husband's foot, and actually does so, he, with a guilty or embarrassed shudder, pushes it aside.

Note my equivocations: 'apparent sincerity', 'guilty or embarrassed.' The variant readings implied have all cropped up in reviews, and I hesitate to choose between them. However you take the moment, it remains an arresting one, that compels you to think about the play and what has gone before, and for that all praise to Mr Bogdanov. Much praise anyway.

Before I proceed, allow me to remark on a peculiarity of this comedy. Whenever it is presented the reviewers, who have appallingly short memories, congratulate the director concerned on having made it, for the first time in their experience, palatable and even enjoyable. I think it's time to give credit to the play itself. I have never seen a boring production of The Shrew. That makes it pretty unique in the canon, and suggests to me that it is a theatrical masterpiece.

Another point about it, much neglected by contemporary commentators: it's a romance. This in fact is why it always works. Petruchio and Katharina are funds of energy and therefore immensely attractive; whatever he does to her, or she to anybody else, it is impossible for an audience not to want to see them united.

At Stratford last year I thought Mr Bogdanov appreciated this point, and I applauded him. Now I am less sure. I don't really know what he's at. The relationship seems to proceed by disconnected stages. At first Kate, as usual, snarls at everybody (and is given the usual justification of a spoiled-brat younger sister). Then she meets Petruchio, fights with him, and--again as usual--rather likes him. Then we halt; the news that she is to be married out-of-hand, without any consultation, appals her and the relationship stops dead. Then come the familiar taming scenes, played by Mr Pryce with a touch more venom than is customary; Miss Dionisotti gives out howls of suffering but doesn't really look too famished. And so to the end: already described and ambiguous.

The production actually batters Miss Dionisotti worse than Petruchio does, and she cannot find a line to link her powerful individual moments. Mr Pryce, being steel and mercury, survives better, but Petruchio as the aggressor is the easier role; his reactions are hardly in question.

The production is at its strongest in establishing the play's monetary climate. Petruchio has come to wive it wealthily in Padua; Bianca's suitors make rival bids for her hand; and Baptista weighs up their respective offers on a pocket calculator. The final banquet is very much a feast of successful men: brandy and cigars at a green-baize table, which of course is a perfect setting for the concluding wagers on wifely obedience.

Michael Billington in the Guardian, while praising the presentation of this scene, has declared that it has not 'anything to do with the play that Shakespeare wrote.' Au contraire; it may not be the play he intended (we could argue about that for centuries) but, of the words he wrote and the actions they imply, it is an exact and acute rendition. So is most of Mr Bogdanov's mise en scène; it is the characterisation that is periodically wrenched out of true. That, too, at any given moment may be true to the text, or a defensible reading of it; that is always a matter of choice, but the choices here are not always compatible.

Mr Billington goes on to champion 'the right of any director to interpret a play according to the beliefs of himself or his age.' Well, if it's really a question of his own beliefs, fine; nice to meet a man who has some. But merely to adhere to 'the beliefs of one's age' is craven conformism.

'A scholar,' Mr Billington eloquently states, 'is free to propound his views on the printed page. Why should not a director have the same freedom on a wooden stage?' Actually a scholar's liberty is strictly limited; he has to base his case strictly on the facts (in this case, the text); otherwise, whatever he is engaged in is certainly not scholarship. Anyway, an essay on a play is at a tangent to it in a way that a production (unless it defames its terms very carefully) cannot be; it has to embody the play, not just comment on it. When author and director are visibly at war it's the audience that loses.

This is not to join with the cut-price Bardolaters who claim that Shakespeare's meaning is obvious; on the contrary, it takes hard work to discover it. That work is known in the theatre as rehearsal. To go to the trouble of finding meaning, and then to throw it away, is profligate; and few directors, to do them justice and however they may theorise, would in practice proceed that way. At his best Mr Bogdanov (like John Barton in his Merchant of Venice with its unsympathetic Shylock, now at the Warehouse) has dug out the play's situation and put it on the stage in front of us. We can then interpret it according to our beliefs, and if it shocks us--well, maybe Shakespeare isn't dead after all.

In Fifty Words (King's Head) some 'choice' Lenny Bruce routines are chopped up between three players. Wadya know, they're dramatic, it becomes difficult to understand how one performer could ever have handled them. They are also still pungent, though I think Bruce was funnier about Jews than about Catholics. (And he wasn't that liberal about sex, either; he never got beyond the inalienable right of the heterosexual male to get laid.) Deborah Norton is sometimes too heavy but her colleagues, Danny Brainin and Denis Lawson, are brilliant; and so, from time to time, is she.

At Riverside Studios Ekkehard Schall, star of the Berliner Ensemble, does--what else?--a Brecht recital. (Last performance tonight; rush.) He is probably a great actor, and is in terrific condition; a master of that peculiarly Brechtian gesture, the passionate shrug. He also moves like an athlete and sings like a snake. What you'd call an all-round entertainer.
1979-05-20-honest-trickery:
Honest trickery

Theatre
ROBERT CUSHMAN in London, Chichester and Salisbury

The reputation among us of Ferenc Molnar, the Budapest boulevardier, rose with 'The Wolf' and sank with 'The Guardsman.' The Greenwich production of The Play's the Thing, which appears to be his masterpiece, should more than reinstate him. It presents us with an evening of superbly honest trickery.

Audiences always like to see actors eating; remarks one of the characters over a breakfast consisting--in the best Central European dramatic and culinary tradition--of 'ham, eggs, cold chicken, smoked salmon, cold beef, bacon, butter, milk, honey, jam and rolls.' Right; but Molnar's charm is that he is not merely indulging us. He is indulging himself. Our luck is his good taste.

This is a play about playwrights: two playwrights and a composer. Also about an actor and actress. The three scribes have come to a castle on the Italian Riviera (they are successful writers, and the period is the 1920s) to recuperate after collaborating on their latest hit. The actress is engaged to the composer and she has the room next door. Arriving unannounced, they hear her apparently engaged in passionate dialogue with the actor.

It is likely to cross the mind of any audience that has entered a theatre before that dialogue is indeed all that they were exchanging; that they were merely rehearsing a scene, and that the heartbroken composer has in fact nothing to be jealous of. Such has been the resolution of many similar dramatic situations. Such, indeed, is the outcome of this one, but only because Sandor, the brains of the playwrighting team, knows that life needs a little help if it is to imitate art. He stays up all night writing a play that will incorporate such a scene, and then gently blackmails the culprits into performing it. He deserves that breakfast.

With charming impudence Molnar, with Sandor as his mouthpiece, teases play and audience along. Musing on how much easier and more pleasant drama would be without the customary rules of exposition he advances to the footlights and explains who, what and where he is, and has his fellows do the same--as if they were in a play. The 'as if' is kept going throughout, and Molnar only breaks his own rules once. At the end of Act Two Sandor asks for ideas as to what constitutes a good second-act curtain. Suggestions are proffered. And, at the climax of each, the curtain duly sweeps in, to be stopped in its tracks by Sandor, who always knows better. This, by making the convention manifest instead of leaving it suspended between stage and auditorium, tips the play into coyness.

But all is redeemed in the last act, where Sandor's play is itself performed and turns out to be full of sweet revenges at the expense of its blustering male protagonist. The effect, as immediate verbal comedy (much enhanced, I suspect, in this adaptation by P. G. Wodehouse), cascades through a situation of highly charged artifice, is altogether exhilarating. There is the requisite amount of bitterness in the happy ending (happiness, we are again reminded, is a state of being well deceived), but our main response--one of the primary legitimate theatrical pleasures--is of joy in the author's cleverness.

Alan Strachan's production might be speedier in its earlier stages, but it is knife-edged and splendidly cast. John Moffatt, a master of the languishing comic art of flicking off a line without ever losing it, may be giving the performance of his life as Sandor; and he has excellent, bumbling assistance from James Cossins. There are also contrasting displays of temperament from Julia McKenzie and Richard Coleman as the players; and a perfectly judged display of primness by Stephen Boswell as an impromptu prompter.

  

The Roundhouse, for all its renovations, is still a less-exciting arena than Manchester's Royal Exchange and it has had a particularly cramping effect on Laurie Dennett's marine set for The Lady from the Sea; we seem now to be in an aquarium rather than on a fjord. The sound effects, too, lack their former spacious stereophony. Enough survives, though, to make Michael Elliott's production the best theatrical vindication I have seen of George Steiner's paramount claim for Ibsen: that he 'invented his own mythology.' One wonders, in fact, why he should have invented it only to discard it; the call of the sea is so powerfully established that Ellida's decision to resist it and stay with her land-animal husband, Dr Wangel, seems to defy not the character's logic so much as the play's.

The development of minor relationships is delicately and humorously done by this company, setting off the serious Wangels' wrangles. It is much the husband's play as the wife's; perhaps more, since she can only make the crucial decision to stay after he has taken hers to let her go. Graham Crowden as the doctor is both enormously gentle and enormously assertive; the conflict within him is vein-bursting. Perhaps he permits himself too many symbolic lunges at the symbolic flagstaff. Mr Elliott's production is commendably unafraid of melodrama.

Vanessa Redgrave is believably, almost unnervingly, a creature of two worlds, equipped even with two modes of speech: drawly and precise when possessed, loose and fresh--sometimes even irritatedly commonsensical--when the demons lose their hold. Physically she is instinct, not just with gracefulness, but with grace.

  

The Chichester season began with a raucously efficient production of The Devils' Disciple, which occasionally sinks below mere competence--notably in a performance of the will-reading scene which tackles this theatre's sight-line problems by presenting everybody with a view consisting entirely of the backs of heads--but which rises above it in two performances.

Brian Blessed as Anthony Anderson, the turncoat minister, plays with conquering warmth and, when the military fit comes upon him, with startling violence. (Startling and funny, just as Shaw meant it to be.) He is also supple and sensitive in his scenes with Mel Martin, who plays his wife and matches him, balancing the reality of her emotions against a saving sense of the ridiculous. Ian Ogilvy, meanwhile, makes the title role a pleasantly swashbuckling blur: an approach it and the play can survive, but which diminishes them both. John Clements, who should have topped the whole thing effortlessly off as General Burgoyne, seemed on the first night well below par.

  

David Zane Mairowitz's Landscape of Exiles (Half Moon) traces the course of British Socialism from the death of Marx to the birth of the Labour Party. Its central characters are Marx's daughter Eleanor, her husband Edward Aveling and--pre-eminently--Engels. Interesting that an author presumably opposed to the great man theory of history should yet fall back on it as dramaturgy. Engels comes over as a negative great man sure enough--an almost Stoppardian figure, Marx's understudy--but everyone is hung up on what he will think.

The play is distinctly similar to Robert Bolt's State of Revolution, but dealing with British history rather than Russian it is considerably less picturesque. It is, however, well-written in a rather literary way, and an uneven cast is led with marked distinction by John Phillips.

  

In Miss Leasing Lady, the enterprising Salisbury Playhouse attempts at once to advance the cause of the British musical and of the rarer and later Restoration comedy (the source is Susannah Centlivre's decorous but efficient A Bold Stroke for a Wife). The two endeavours get fatally in each other's way.
1979-06-03-red-and-white-blues:
Red and White blues

Theatre
by ROBERT CUSHMAN

Mikhail Bulgakov's The White Guard (Aldwych) is celebrated as the play to which Stalin accorded his personal protection when the Soviet censors got at it. This may prove that Stalin was a subtler critic than might be expected, or merely that he was in certain moods an old sentimentalist.

The principal characters are recognisable human beings, and as such are by their rarity value alone to tap the tear-ducts of a post-revolutionary Russian audience. But they are also rarities in another sense. The White Guard are the military remnants of Tsarism, surviving in a Ukraine of which the Bolsheviks have yet to take possession when the play begins. Their survival depends however on the support of the German Army--who have set up a puppet regime. We see both Army and regime melt away, leaving the country to a triangular struggle.

Bulgakov's play is in three acts, and each party holds sway over the situation for one of them. Act I shows the Whites in their last days of command, Act II is a bloody interlude of victory for anarchic Ukrainian nationalists, and in Act III we hear, though we do not see, the arrival of the Reds.

If we assume for the moment that Bulgakov was writing official propaganda, then he was going about it in quite the most tactful and sensible way. He was keeping the approved side offstage, thus avoiding both caricature and hagiography.

Actually you can take the last scene any way you want, and this is for once a sign of strength rather than weakness. The struggle is obviously unresolved in the author's own mind, and you can feel the stresses at work in the action. Sympathy is tugged in all directions. It is notable, for example, that the last line of the play is one of regret for the old days, but notable too that the speaker is a Polish officer in a play where non-Russians are treated with suspicion. One Russian escapes to Berlin. He happens to be the husband of the play's heroine, and by that action he forfeits all rights to her. The only question is which of her native suitors she will take in his place. Yelena, the lady in question, seems to symbolise Russia itself. Patriotism is the play's moral absolute.

The domestic action only rarely takes on this kind of significance. For much of the time it is pursued for its own sake, and charmingly. But the Turbins are only the focus for the first and last sections of the play. If Bulgakov's aim was to dramatise the pressure of history through its effects on a family (as Chekhov did, without even mentioning specific historic events) then he failed; and in fact admitted as much by dramatising the German evacuation and brief nationalist triumph head on.

This results in one scene of cardboard chronicling, and one of arbitrary sensationalism. Barry Kyle's production finds no style for either of them. But the central flaw--that the play changes direction without any apparent awareness of the fact--is probably ineradicable.

The hearth-side scenes are well done in their own right, with Juliet Stevenson ending up as a vibrant Yelena after a shaky beginning in which her powers of responding to bad news seem overstretched. Patrick Stewart plays the Russian raisonneur, better, and more frequently, than any other British actor, and except when he shouts, his performance here is well up to standard. (To him falls the final task of welcoming the revolution, though since his aspect makes it difficult to forget Mr Stewart's television Lenin in The Fall of Eagles, the enemy seems within the gates from the start.) Richard Griffiths as a bumbling cousin confirms his status as this company's prime putter-in of feet and is still managing, somehow, to avoid stereotype. The other leading men are efficient, but there is a discernible gap between their native selves and their characters; and there is some awful acting further down the line. This is one of the RSC's middle-range productions: honourable but incomplete.

  

The theme of Brian Clark's Can You Hear Me at the Back? (Piccadilly) is presumably the gap between public speech and private action. There is a civic architect and his wife who is a doctor and their son who is taking his A-levels; and there are also a headmaster and his wife, a fashion designer. The latter lady is the only one who never gets to address an audience in the course of her work; and, lacking this outlet, she goes bananas.

At all events, she strips off in a middle-class home that is not her own. The immediate cause is that she is in love with the architect and that he is too good a talker to take her emotion, or anyone else's, seriously; he can always escape through words. Much the same accusation was levelled (by critics, chiefly) at the hero of Mr Clark's Whose Life Is It Anyway?; and he seems to have taken it to heart. At all events, glibness is here constantly berated, the result of course being more words. I think he should just have gone on giving his leading men good lines, and stayed unrepentant.

He remains an able writer, and one of his hero's set pieces--repenting of the monstrosities into which he has turned town centres in the name of progress--is not stuff, delivered with expected understated magnificence by Peter Barkworth. It does seem a cheat, though, to have put the Telford's Change ménage on stage in its entirety, with the relationships unchanged, impeccable though they all are at it: Mr Barkworth at conveying the doubts and assurances of a man wedded to his job but aware of its more dubious aspects, Hannah Gordon at being simultaneously loyal and impatient, and Michael Maloney--who comes off best--at bursting rebelliously out of his school uniform.

  

The Chichester production of The Eagle Has Two Heads has been attacked as too melodramatic; it is, in fact, not melodramatic enough. This is Cocteau once more in love with death, and to considerably more purpose than in Orpheus. A queen deprived of her consort on the marriage day finds his mirror image, years later, in a revolutionary poet who was attempting to assassinate her. They fall in love, and so can only be each other's death, as in fact they are.

Meanwhile there is some Ruritanian intrigue which can hold our attention only if it is pursued with gusto and if the protagonists are authentically doom-drenched. Jill Bennett suggests gnawing discontent but on too small a scale, while Christopher Neame scampers weightlessly through his lines. Heather Chasen and Michael Malnick make a sharp pair of lookers-on; Brian Blessed as the heavy is trying, I can only think, for shrill menace.

  

The American Repertory Theatre is composed of young transatlantic actors, and is situated on Tottenham Court Road, opposite Heal's. Their production of Archy and Mehitabel, based on the Don Marquis stories in which the cockroach plays Isherwood to an alley-cat's Sally Bowles, is enough to make me repent of any harsh things I have said of British attempts at American musicals. Truly, they ain't all born with it.
1979-06-10-a-sunny-outlook:
A sunny outlook

ROBERT CUSHMAN talks to Charles Strouse, whose new musical opens this week

CHARLES STROUSE, who was 51 last Thursday, claims to have "a very funny outlook," and I believe him. He talks cheerfully and temperately about both his failures and his successes as a Broadway composer. The successes include Bye Bye Birdie, Applause and the record-breaker Annie.

Right now he has a new show opening at the Queen's, not yet seen in New York, though already tried out in Canada: in Edmonton to be precise, at a theatre run--in the face of much chauvinistic discontent--by the British director Peter Coe. Coe also directs the musical, called Flowers for Algernon, in London where its early arrival is due largely to the availability and the enthusiasm of its star, Michael Crawford.

Flowers for Algernon is not the most obvious title for a musical (everyone immediately assumes it must be a version of The Importance of Being Earnest) but it apparently has considerable commercial appeal in America where the novel (by David Keyes) has long been a cult. When they filmed it in 1969 the name was changed to Charly but the show goes back to the original. It deals with a retarded man who undergoes brain surgery and becomes--temporarily--a genius.

It is, he admits, not merely a strange title but a strange idea for a musical. "But I've always liked the story; and anyway who can tell which the best ideas are going to be? I originally thought Annie might just about make a TV special. And I once wrote the music for what I thought was going to be a perfectly ordinary cops-and-robbers movie called Bonnie and Clyde."

Strouse's involvement in Flowers is due to a friend, David Rogers, whom he has known for 30 years ("I was at summer-camp with him") but with whom he has never worked before. "I saw the play on his shelf, read it and liked it." So the decision was taken to turn it into a musical, and necessarily a heavier one than Strouse has usually attempted.

And here we come to a paradox in him. His optimism seems to have its roots in a consciousness of pain. "My father was a very sick man, and I grew up hating and fearing illness desperately."

It has enabled him to write genuinely bright scores. "Bye Bye Birdie, his first major show and his first major success, must be one of the best escapist musicals ever written. Birdie is the kind of show that makes a composer not only rich but popular; everyone likes you because you're the smart kid at the party." Strouse has two favourites among his own shows, and neither of them are among his greatest hits. One, It's a Bird, It's a Plane, It's Superman, we have never seen over here, though to judge from the record it's a work of considerable charm and poker-faced wit. It may be his ultimate achievement as smart kid at the party. The other, Golden Boy, was staged here with Sammy Davis, as in New York, playing the title role: an updated black version of Clifford Odets's boxer-hero of the Depression.

Golden Boy was also one of the few musicals of the sixties (Cy Coleman's Sweet Charity was another) to make positive use of the pop-jazz idiom that was all around us at the time.

Strouse is aware that pretentiousness can kill a musical, if the talent involved is less than the aspiration. He often, to his bemusement, is asked to give college lectures on the form, causing him to wonder if the whole thing isn't getting out of hand. And yet, he says, "serious music--serial and electronic music--has totally alienated the middle-class concert audience, and intentionally so. So people turn instead to the musical theatre. We spent a good half-hour discussing the infuriating slippery boundary between musical and opera, and failed to define it. But he did say 'the musical differs from opera in acknowledging the third collaborator--the audience. I like people liking me. I like audiences.'

He has written a couple of operas himself, and he had a full musical training, studying with Aaron Copland and in Paris with Nadia Boulanger. "Boulanger was remarkably supple and supportive. She learns about you as a person through your music. She asked me to play her everything I'd written--I was 19 or 20 at the time--so I went through all the serious stuff. She said was there anything else? Well, when I was 12 there was a cute girl I'd wanted to impress and I wrote her this song full of local references called Moon Over 83rd Street." So I played this and Boulanger said very seriously--and she was the first person to say it to me--"you have a great talent for light music."

Trying to exercise this talent back in America, he met a journalist named Lee Adams with whom he collaborated first on songs for revues, then on Bye Bye Birdie and most of his subsequent shows down to A Broadway Musical, a likeable mess which flopped spectacularly last year and which I, as one of the few who saw it, would like to turn into a cult.

Annie and Flowers are among the few shows he has written with other lyricists. Adams, he says, likes to rest and enjoy life occasionally. "He has a healthier attitude than I do. I love the hustle and working all the time. Working with Lee is like a marriage; sometimes you like to have an affair." For the benefit of his wife, somewhere on the high seas en route to Thursday's first night: "Barbara, that is just a metaphor."
1979-06-10-playing-for-kicks:
Playing for kicks

Theatre
ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Manchester

The penultimate scene of Dispatches (Cottesloe) finds a war-reporter maimed in Vietnam, announcing that he has just received a major commission to write the conflict up. He is required, he says with a mixture of scorn and despair, to take the glamour out of war. 'You might as well,' he screeches, 'try to take the glamour out of sex. You might as well try to take the glamour out of the Rolling Stones.'

This production is here to prove him right, on all counts. It is based on Michael Herr's book, a self-proclaimed amalgam of novel and reportage; though really the only novelistic thing about it was the amount of dialogue it contained, and to that the new journalism should thoroughly have accustomed us. Bill Bryden and his company have added words of their own to the originals, but the joins are hard to see.

There is undeniably something odd about an attempt to put a documentary account of the Vietnam war on to a stage, and particularly on to a British stage. We in Britain have traditionally envied the Americans--envied them most when affecting to despise them; but it comes as a shock to realise that we envy them Vietnam. It was so traumatic, dramatic, cinematic a crisis (we also envy them Watergate); our own seem so squalid and unyielding by comparison.

Dispatches, apart from its obvious technical problems, is rather scrappy material for a play (it's rather scrappy for a book, come to that); but I knew it would infallibly find its way on to a stage. The lure of machismo is irresistible; every stage production is an assertion of power over the audience, and there are few more effective ways of reinforcing this dominance than by the liberal use of loud bangs.

Dispatches offers not only the clamour of modern armaments, but the clamour of modern music. One of the book's theses is that the war and hard rock were symptoms of the same disease ('actually, that's too specific: just say vaguely aspects of the same thing), and the Cottesloe weighs in with a live band.

I am not, by the way, suggesting that the motives of Mr Bryden and company are any more discreditable than are those of all of us (all of us) at work in the self-aggrandisement industry. But the circumstances of this production do make them stand out in unusually sharp relief. There is still a kick to be had from playing soldiers, and there is an additional Walter Mittyish kick for British actors in playing American rock-culture soldiers. In fact their enthusiasm does more than anything in the play itself--or even in the book--to justify the claim made on Mr Herr's dust-cover by Time magazine: that the author shows us that 'war thrives because enough men still love it.' This may just be true for the correspondents, but the soldiers cannot wait to get out; the play's substance is still unexceptionably pacifist.

Mr Bryden's production begins tentatively, but gains steadily in conviction, though the ending is theatrically as well as philosophically inconclusive. William Dudley's sandbagged set makes the scenes of actual conflict seem remarkably credible. (Can this cockpit hold the vasty fields? Yes, it can.) And the actors expand in their scenes of relaxation, generally stoned. Few individuals stand out, though the play tries to keep some character-lines going. The reporters are a notably more pallid crew than in the book (there seems to be no way of relaying the more interesting information about them), but Trevor Ray makes a marvellously solid photographer.

Among the soldiers, a trio of black actors (Oscar James, Don Warrington, Guy Gregory) exactly transmit varieties of resigned or angry desperation; and Oliver Cotton has a good comic solo as a marine panting to get home and avenge himself on an unfaithful wife. The narrator, Jack Shepherd, is beautifully watchful, but loses the flow and the vitality of the writing by trying to make it sound improvised.

  

Happy Days are here again; but Samuel Beckett's own production, at the Royal Court, does succeed in being different from anyone else's. There has been considerable rewriting, especially in the first act, most of it amusingly stressing Winnie's impatience with the world in general and her husband in particular. She has moments indeed when she suggests an immured Edna Everage, though this Antipodean connection may have been sparked off in my mind by Billie Whitelaw's delivery of the lady's opening line. Her 'another happy day' was surprisingly like the ironic greeting bestowed on the world by the transvestite hero of The Elocution of Benjamin Franklin: 'Hello, Sydney, I see you've got another lovely day planned for me.'

I am not sure whether Miss Whitelaw's interpretation works out more or less despairing than that of Peggy Ashcroft, who sounded as if she really did expect to have a good time. Miss Whitelaw shows no pleasure or affection until the very last moment, when Willie may or may not be going for her gun. Perhaps it matters little how an actress approaches the role; sooner or later Mr Beckett's strictures will get her; she will stand firmly rebuked for any optimism she may have allowed to escape her lips, and we along with her.

Miss Whitelaw patronises Winnie a little too much when she regards her husband's dirty postcard (Dame Edna again), but she is otherwise prodigiously varied and alive within a vocal range fined purposefully down. For once I did not feel the play's overwhelming statement on the way we compulsively and meaninglessly fill out our days to have been fully made within 10 minutes of curtain-rise. With Miss Whitelaw there is always more in the bag.

Probably no theatre other than the Royal Exchange, Manchester, would risk giving us Hofmannsthal's The Deep Man, a fascinating piece about an Austrian gentleman afflicted, in the dark and brassy days following the First World War, by a deadly realisation of how foolish any human word, any human action, can be. Exquisitely fastidious, he squirms each time any of his contemporaries starts speaking; they are always ready to strike attitudes and to make professions which they believe with all their souls, but which he knows to be ludicrous. He anticipates Christopher Hampton's philanthropist, and much of Simon Gray.

James Maxwell, an actor who sometimes errs on the side of beatitude, this time hits exactly the right note of embarrassed serenity, and Dilys Hamlett gives an enjoyably fussy account of the sister who is faute de mieux, his lifeline to the world. But that world is wretchedly portrayed: Clare Higgins shows promise, and Willoughby Gray and Michael Poole experience, but the rest seem to be vying in ineptitude. Let me for once name names: I thought Daniel Gerroll was awkward until John Somerville came on.

Jonathan Griffin's translation makes nothing easy (and why should it?), but it is composed of English sentences; however formal and convoluted, and the actors should be able to negotiate them sensibly even if they fail to penetrate the European mind beneath. Thanks to Mr Maxwell the idea that underpins the play comes through Casper Wrede's production; thanks to everyone else, the comic action that should expand and modify it is lifeless.

Alan Drury's An Empty Desk (Theatre Upstairs) is a modest but acute play about a local government clerk torn between his office routine, which wants to repress him, and his girl-friend who wants to set him free. (According to her own ideas, anyway; she too strikes attitudes.) Each environment has an act to itself and the upshot is the hero's breakdown.
