1979-06-17-life-s-hard:
Life's hard

Theatre
ROBERT CUSHMAN in Stratford and London

The only disco bit I have ever liked was Boney M's 'Rasputin,' and that mainly for its coda: a witty, admiring, exhausted cry, 'Oh, those Russians.'

As a reviewer, confronted by the repertory of the Royal Shakespeare Company, I know just how Boney M feel.

A Chekhov is promised, and a Gorky rumoured, for later this year; meanwhile The Suicide (Other Place, Stratford) continues our education in the theory and practice of Stalinist drama criticism, begun a couple of weeks ago by The White Guard. After a play that Stalin permitted, we have one that he obstructed: to such effect that though the author, Nikolai Erdman, lived apparently until 1970, he never wrote another play.

This one was written in 1928; hopes of staging it in Russia were finally abandoned in 1932. One can see Stalin's point of view; it is a wildly subversive piece, culminating in a shattering speech--superbly delivered here by Roger Rees--in which the protagonist, having decided that he doesn't think he'll kill himself today, expands his philosophy of life. 'Our achievements, our success, our reconstructed society, you can keep it. I want a quiet life and a living wage.' He goes on to demand the most inalienable of human rights, the right to grumble. 'Allow us at least to whisper life is hard . . . you won't even hear us.'

I suspect that any contemporary British writer who attempted to put so unrepentant an individualist on to the stage of, let us say, the Warehouse, would get rather short shrift. Erdman's hero dismisses society as 'a slogan factory,' and slogan factories are what our progressive playwrights, if we are to believe their declarations, would like to make of our theatres. And then consider the postman in Erdman's play who sees everything 'from the Marxist point of view' and only wants to read about postmen. Some Socialist companies have been looking for an audience like him for years.

These pleasures are not all that the play offers; if they were, it would only be a more attractive slogan-factory than most. Semyon, the would-be suicide, takes the entire length of the play to find his own voice. He begins, demoralised by long unemployment, nagging and terrorising his wife and mother-in-law. He is immensely impressionable; before he can entertain the idea of self-slaughter someone else has accidentally to put it into his head.

From then on, he is a universal prey; all sectors of Russian society converge, asking him to die for their cause. He may martyr himself for the discontented intelligentsia, for art or for the love of a woman. Death seems a flattering as well as a soothing fate; if only he could bring himself actually to pull the trigger. The play becomes 'to be or not to be,' acted out as farce. It is appropriate that one of the funniest sequences should turn on a misunderstood line from Hamlet, and that the end of the play--which brilliantly wrenches the action into a wider and bitterer focus--should parody that of Chekhov's Hamlet variant, The Seagull.

The play looks forward to the comedy of survival, as currently practised in Czechoslovakia, and back to that of Gogol (Semyon receiving his suitors like the Government Inspector), with whom it shares a certain prolixity. Ron Daniels's production is slow to get going and Mr Rees is probably more personable casting than the author envisaged for Semyon. The early routine grumblings do not sit well on him; only when he has a tangible object--a tuba, as it happens--and a solid comic situation on which to exercise his spleen does his performance spring into life. He is well supported by Lila Kaye as his ma-in-law and by Nigel Terry as chief tempter. Play and production could do with room to breathe; they should transfer to the Aldwych.

  

At the Stratford main house is a Twelfth Night that takes its title seriously. The first half is played against a bare and wintry treescape; at the height of the carousal scene Sir Andrew hangs up a paper-chain, which Malvolio, his puritanism outraged by such fripperies, promptly dislodges. We return from the interval, though, to find that spring has arrived; it seems to have taken the Illyrian tailors a couple of months to deliver Malvolio his yellow stockings.

Terry Hands's production trips itself up in other ways. Feste--acting presumably as a Lord of Misrule--oversees every scene; but why then should he, like everyone else, get the twins mixed up? And the lovesick absurdities of Orsino and Olivia are, not for the first time at Stratford, overplayed. Kate Nicholls's Olivia, emerging from behind a yashmak into unrestrained flapperhood, is a brave and intermittently delightful performance, but no actress should be required to giggle and gesticulate quite so often.

But there are virtues, and these become more apparent as the evening proceeds. One is Jane Downs's Maria, never quite sure of herself with Willoughby Goddard's heartless Sir Toby and most touchingly crushed when the news of their marriage is greeted with laughter by the juvenile leads--those who, according to the peculiar class-structure of comedy, think love their own prerogative. Another is Cherie Lunghi's Viola, no revelation but charming nonetheless. Above all there is John Woodbine's Malvolio, who makes more of the man's convictions than any I have seen.

His natural enmity with Feste (Geoffrey Hutchings) crackles with unusual force; so do his dreams of humiliating his kinsman Toby. Olivia's letter upsets his whole scheme of values; 'I will smile' is a grimly desperate statement of intent, whose achievement fully deserves its round of applause. The antic scene is, physically and mentally, the most daring in my experience; at the end, the Puritan again, he can utter his last line as a serious threat to everyone on stage: a threat which, as has been remarked before, history was to vindicate. This is a serious, foursquare and supremely funny performance.

  

Flowers for Algernon replaces Tommy at the Queen's, and has much in common with it. Instead of a deaf-and-dumb boy turned superstar, we have a retarded young man turned by brain-surgery to a genius. Where Tommy offered lasers, this has the play of coloured light on a vast steely maze lowered from the flies. (I name this style medical chic.) Flowers, unlike Tommy, is a work of decent professionalism, but if this story is not to be unbearably mawkish it has to be kept icy-pure, and musicalising it is no way to do that.

The numbers, quite naturally, beg for applause and everything turns cute. Besides, Michael Crawford in his retarded stage is indistinguishable from his usual backward hero. It is a pleasure to see him cope so well with the prodigy stage (I am doubtful whether a genius would sing these lyrics) and he is unsentimental when the experiment slips and the hero regresses. The hero, by the way, is not called Algernon. Algernon is a mouse. They do a song-and-dance together. It's a nice one (and Charles Strouse has supplied a couple of good ballads as well), but it demonstrates exactly what has gone wrong with the show.

Nothing much has gone wrong with the lavish revival of The King and I (Palladium), even though Virginia McKenna is an improbably demure, for a Victorian empire-building lady. Yul Brynner still makes an authoritative king; and his part is actually very well written. He's a real comic creation and, in his attempt to reconcile two cultures in his own head, a touching one as well.

The use of children may irritate you ('Annie' is a stringent comparison), but Jerome Robbins's choreography comes to the rescue, and the songs are still, mostly, lovely. Rodgers and Hammerstein at their best wrote well-made musicals the way Rattigan wrote well-made plays; we can't and shouldn't emulate them, but we can't deny that they still work infallibly.
1979-06-17-exchanges:
Exchanges

ROBERT CUSHMAN talks to Michael Elliott, whose production of The Family Reunion reopens this week in the West End.

Michael Elliott's production of his near-namesake T. S.'s Family Reunion has now been seen in three open-stage theatres: in the temporary structure that preceded Manchester's Royal Exchange playhouse, in the Exchange itself, and at the Roundhouse in London. This week it transfers to a West End theatre, the Vaudeville, and gets back again behind its proscenium arch.

It is a long-delayed return not only for the play but for the 48-year-old director. Probably no director in the British theatre commands more respect than Elliott, but he has reached his eminence on a surprisingly small body of work.

While The Family Reunion transfers, The Lady from the Sea runs on at the Roundhouse, completing a trio of Elliott productions that began with The Ordeal of Gilbert Pinfold. He insists, though, that the season was planned not as a showcase for his own work, but for that of the Royal Exchange theatre which has been open since 1976, though its prehistory stretches back to the early fifties.

It is the story of a group, one whose longevity and stability makes even the RSC directorate look tentative. It began in the post-war Old Vic School, run by Michel Saint-Denis, Glen Byam Shaw and George Devine. Among its graduates were a Finnish director, Casper Wrede, an Italian designer Richard Negri, and an anglicised American actor James Maxwell. Elliott himself ('half-English, half-Scots') met them in 1954, after being at Oxford. He and Wrede co-directed a number of plays for BBC Television. He also married (as did Wrede and Maxwell) an actress-member of the group, in his case Rosalind Knight.

The philosophy that held them all together ('through bitter and awful times') set them apart from the values that were already crystallising at the Royal Court and that have dominated the British theatre--including the National and the RSC--ever since. 'I've never believed,' says Elliott, 'that theatre was at its best when political, and I don't believe that social problems are its sole concern, though they are certainly a legitimate one. The prime concern of drama is to show that life has a larger dimension than that of ordinary reality.'

In 1959 a season of plays was staged at the Lyric Theatre, Hammersmith, by a group calling itself the 59 Theatre Company. Wrede was the director, Elliott his associate, and the actors included some of the best and solidest young talent in London. The (unsubsidised) repertoire was phenomenal. Wrede offered the first English production of Buchner's Danton's Death. Elliott, directing his first professional production, tackled Ibsen's supposedly unstageable Brand, and brought it triumphantly off, with Patrick McGoohan in the title role. At least two schoolboy members of the audience found the season indelibly influential. I was one; the other was Braham Murray, now the Royal Exchange's administrative head.

Elliott's next stage production was in 1961: the magical As You Like It that dominated Peter Hall's troubled second season at Stratford. The Rosalind was Vanessa Redgrave, still his leading lady at the Roundhouse and naming him unhesitatingly as her favourite director.

It was, though, the only production Elliott did for them. He left to run the Old Vic for what proved to be its last season before the National Theatre took over. He reassembled many of the 59 team and led off with a Peer Gynt to match his Brand. The logical sequence would have been for him to stay at the Vic as Olivier's lieutenant. This indeed was the plan and Elliott went along with it for four or five months. But I got more and more unhappy. 'I was only 31; I thought I should live more dangerously. So I went into a kind of exile, directing in television, and writing film scripts.'

It was a long exile; the curious thing is that though he had only six London productions behind him, nobody forgot him. He acquired a mythical reputation as a turner-down of key positions. Devine once wanted him to take over the Royal Court; there was a high-level offer from the BBC. 'I didn't turn them down out of Puritanism. They wouldn't have been the real thing for me.'

The real thing came along in 1967, when he directed Tom Courtenay in The Playboy of the Western World in Manchester. From this came the 69 Theatre Company, operating in a temporary home on the university campus, and from that the Royal Exchange. 'In Manchester we're free. We can be a community theatre with a loyal audience; an average 90 per cent of capacity. And we're far enough from London for actors only to come to us for the right reasons.'

My main criticism of the Exchange has been that, below the star line, there have been too many pallid performances. Elliott's defence is that 'one has a reaction against a certain kind of successful acting. We're going for essences, and maybe give that too much priority over technical skill.'

There is one other factor in the Elliott story: his health. In May of 1976, with the opening of the Royal Exchange four months away, he collapsed and was put on a kidney-machine. 'I was born with the condition though I hadn't known it.' He now spends three nights a week on the machine; but he emphasises he can still live 'an absolutely full life.' In fact the period since last autumn has been his fullest ever as a director of plays: 'I'll have had seven openings.'

All the same it's a mournful thing to have happened to him just as he was finally coming into his kingdom. It's ironic too in view of his continuing fascination with The Family Reunion. He identified with its theme of inheritance having had a successful preacher-father (known pre-war as 'the radio parson') to live down or live up to, and his copy of the play, acquired at Oxford, is now scored with the notes for five different productions.

'It's too difficult, its greatest fault is its obscurity, but that doesn't matter, because theatre is really emotional. It kicks you in the guts. It's a great play.'
1979-06-24-wenching-in-old-austria:
Wenching in old Austria

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Schnitzler at the National Theatre.

THE title of Undiscovered Country (Olivier) is a three-way pun: not altogether surprising when the translator is Tom Stoppard.

Arthur Schnitzler's play is certainly unknown terrain to us. Within the play itself the Shakespearean words are used to describe the depths of the human heart. But we are unlikely to forget that in their original context they refer to death. Death, in this piece, is a very fashionable concept; almost the latest thing. Sort of like love.

We are in Austria, in the years just before the First World War. The Romantic Agony has been assimilated, and reduced to an agreeably titillating ache. The leading character, Hofreiter, is a successful manufacturer of light-bulbs, though his professional activities in the play are largely limited to telling his wife that he has been detained at the factory. An indefatigable wencher, he passes more or less unimpeded from one friend's wife to another, and is finally brought up short by a friend's daughter. She, being young, makes emotional demands on him that he would like to fulfil but cannot; at the height of his ardour his sense of self-interest still keeps ticking away.

Self-interest is not the same as conscience. Hofreiter is contrasted with another successful man, a hotelier this time, who can still reproach himself with his conduct to his wife: 'I loved her so much and was still capable of deceiving her.' (Not that this stops him from stocking his establishment with nubile domestic help and taking full advantage of the supply--to, be it said, the dazzled admiration of all his friends.)

The precise emotional state of the Hofreiter marriage is murky. Socially it is a great success--they keep lavish open house--but both partners are uncertain as to the desirability of Frau Hofreiter's continued fidelity. During the play she causes the deaths of two men: one she has rejected, and one she has accepted. As a woman of feeling, she suffers. Her husband has a highly developed flair for cerebral self-torment, but he is definitely a survivor.

Schnitzler himself was a doctor by profession, and also an amorist. He seems to have split himself between two of the characters in this play. There is a family-friend and physician; and there is Hofreiter, who seems also to have absorbed something of Mr Stoppard. At least I doubt if in the original German Hofreiter spoke quite so lightly and knowingly of his son's English education with 'all that fagging and cricket.'

The familiar crackle in lines like these is enhanced by their turning up on the lips of John Wood, the Stoppardian actor par excellence. Messrs Stoppard and Wood between them have probably bestowed on this part, and therefore on the whole play, a lighter and more febrile texture than it had in the original. That, however, is no complaint: Mr Wood's corkscrew calisthenics have seldom been put to better use, his wit shines and his trapped disgust steadily deepens.

In the last act the man fights a duel, which seems improbable, but Mr Wood makes us believe not in any particular motive, but in a voluminous weariness that can take on anything. (His opponent is young, and Hofreiter--with a teenage affair on his hands--has some desperate, biting things to say about youth.) Dorothy Tutin matches him exquisitely as his wife and there are performances of ebullient assurance by Michael Bryant and of startling promise by Emma Piper.

Peter Wood's production, too, is a fine piece of showmanship, down to the changes of William Dudley's ravishing green sets. (This, following on his designs for Dispatches, is some double.) The emblem of the evening is John Harding as an engaging young bore who, alone in the play, seems to have no familial or carnal relations with anyone else but is wedded to his tennis-racket. Tennis, in various formations, becomes a metaphor for the whole play: summery, playful, combative and capable of inflicting ignominious defeats. It is the most substantial piece of theatre we have seen this year.

  

Sensualists receive a similar wry come-uppance in Fearless Frank (King's Head), a musical based on the dubious memoirs of Frank Harris. The glory here is Bill Stewart's performance as Harris himself, dictating his autobiography to a secretary just the vital bit less impressionable than he hopes, and realising as he does so that half his claims are lies and that half of the other half are disreputable.

Mr Stewart, at once seedy and crisp, turns the character into a self-puncturing, self-repairing mechanism, still gamely lusting (with a repeated murmur of 'legs, legs, legs') at the final curtain. It is too arhythmic a performance that takes to song and dance with noticeable awkwardness. Andrew Davies has written him a witty, if slightly repetitive, script; his lyrics, and Dave Brown's music, are good enough to make you wish they were better. One number, actually, is superb: a preening, lascivious account by Guy de Maupassant ('maitre de la conte') of his innumerable conquests, surrounded by crooning couples with umbrellas: Fred Peters's choreography is a dazzling piece of Parisian parody, and the other routines take fair advantage of Harris's peripatetic career.

We get London songs, New York songs, Wild West songs, all routine and performed with immaculate precision. Technically, this is probably the best of the burgeoning small musicals; credit to the director, Robert Gillespie, and to the cast, which includes in the rolling-voiced Nichola McAuliffe and the wicked-eyed Mandy More such at least two snow-white musical hopes.

  

A belated but commendatory word for Tom McGrath's The Innocent (Warehouse), which certainly rambles enough, but whose dialogue is mostly sweet and funny enough to compensate. It follows a group of Glaswegians from the jazz-cellar of 1960 to the hippie pads of London in the ensuing decade; the drugs getting harder all the time so that we finally find them back home in a mental hospital, trying to kick their various habits. Some succeed, some fail: it all seems arbitrary, and that may pass as being lifelike.

A more serious fault is that Mr McGrath can only characterise them at second hand; he has to have them describe each other as his only means of sailing them apart. The actors help here too, of course; my favourite was smiling Paul Moriarty, but there is stiff competition from Jan Chappell, David Bradley, David Lyon and Anthony Higgins, and from a ferocious Hilary McRae. Mr McRae does not get to go to London; he stays in Glasgow 'getting crazier' and it is borne upon us at the end that he is the real victim. His mates were just enjoying themselves, because they could afford to. That isn't a bad point, but it is made so late you wonder Mr McGrath didn't sit down and start the play over.

  

Charley's Aunt (Adelphi) is fairly amusing. I share the general feeling that it ought to be more, and that the way to make it so is to cast the leading role as a believable embarrassed hearty rather than as an accomplished, eccentric drag-queen. John Inman's performance is certainly expert, but he cannot disguise the miscasting. Helen Cherry and Allan Cuthbertson are stalwart, and the sets are handsome; commercial theatre's Oxford looks indeed as sumptuous as subsidised Vienna, and why not?
1979-07-01-plugging-the-gap:
Plugging the gap

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Pirandello's 'Six Characters'

WE ARE now at the half-way point of the year: a year so far distinguished by the absence of a single new play able to inspire real enthusiasm.

As usual, our theatres have partially concealed the vacuum by mounting a series of raids, often imaginative, on the past. Eliot, Maugham, Molnar and Schnitzler have been the top London playwrights of 1979. And now follows Pirandello, with a Greenwich revival of Six Characters in Search of an Author, a play apparently written to plug just such a gap. The Director, whom we find in rehearsal when we enter the theatre, complains that there is no good new stuff available and that he has had to fall back on reviving Pirandello's The Rules of the Game. (One of the author's little jokes, made even funnier by the fact that The Rules of the Game is a better play than Six Characters.) He is interrupted by the sextet of lost souls conceived and left unfinished by their unseen dramatist and now come to the playhouse in search of final realisation.

But here Greenwich's own director, Phil Young, has fallen foul of a difficult problem. The play was a bombshell at its first production in 1921, and a director naturally wishes to preserve as much of that explosiveness as possible. To that end he puts the play into modern dress and tries to pretend that the interrupted rehearsal is happening now.

But if he is going to get away with this, he needs to take more liberties than either Mr Young or his translator, John Linstrum, have permitted themselves. We now have obviously contemporary performers practising archaic rehearsal methods. They shrink from improvisation, blench at the thought of the heroine removing her dress, and never address one another by name. (The Director gives brusque instructions to stage management; they'd go on strike.)

It is a sad truth that nothing dates faster than experiment. A period production of Six Characters would allow us to pay our respects to it as a pioneering work, while acknowledging that its insights are now commonplace. (It would also ease the task of the actors playing actors, by making their roles characters as well. But would that make them more Pirandellian or less? No, that way madness, etc.)

When the drama closes in, the production improves considerably, though without ever stilling my recurrent doubts about the play. For, in the confrontation between the characters begging to be acted and the actors who try to oblige and immediately falsify everything, Pirandello, ingeniously but far from seamlessly, has jammed together three disparate notions. One is the inevitable gulf between the vision in an author's head and its expression by other minds and bodies on the stage. A second (adumbrated by Keats a century earlier) is the haunting stasis of art; its property of freezing a single word, gesture or moment forever. And linked to this is the despair of the man who finds himself judged for a single atypical action.

This is the plight of the Father, who entered a brothel as the unknowing client of his own Stepdaughter. For her, he will always be an exploiter and a seducer. And the emotional capital Pirandello makes of this has far more to do with their condition as people than as figures in an uncompleted play. The intensest moments, particularly well managed by Philip Stone as the Father despite some odd swooping movements, make the theatrical superstructure seem unnecessary and rather meretricious.

The Stepdaughter, forever striking vengeful or lascivious attitudes, is a tough assignment for a British actress, and Pauline Moran is liable to slide from brilliance to banality within a couple of lines. Hers is certainly a brave performance; more tactful direction might have stopped it seeming foolhardy.

  

Theatricality again runs amok in The Three Musketeers (Royal Exchange, Manchester), which aims at chaos and misses. The ambience of this theatre, and of Braham Murray's visually splendid production, is far too civilised to permit of the fun and games (actors stepping out of character and characters out of narrative) that Ken Hill used to bring engagingly off in the tattered days of Theatre Workshop.

However, there is one superb set-piece: a quick replay of the story so far, carried out half-way through Act One for the benefit of latecomers. Robert Lindsay is an engaging D'Artagnan; Derek Griffiths is in danger of forfeiting his status as the funniest clown in the land, and has also written some thoroughly undistinguished songs. I wish someone would realise that there is no need to send up Dumas; he was a very witty writer who furnished his musketeers with some of the best cross-talk in standard literature.

  

Barry Collins's Toads (Nottingham Playhouse) offers some amazing scenes: a couple of man-size copulating frogs, a lizard on a trapeze, some attractive nudes. These are intended to illustrate the life and thoughts of Paul Kammerer, Lamarckian biologist, and it is unfortunate that they are by far the liveliest things in the evening.

The text provides them with no fitting springboard. It consists of a long debate between Kammerer, who seems to believe in the benevolent operations of chance, and a police inspector who by contrast has the gift of pessimistic prophecy and has arrived to stop him committing suicide. They go on endlessly, two mouthpieces uncharacterised. The final blow in Geoffrey Reeves's production is dealt by the unchanging set, which looks like an old-fashioned Shakespearean arrangement of steps and rostra (mostly unexploited) hastily covered by a huge white dust-sheet.

  

There were two revelations for me in the Amnesty International gala, The Secret Policeman's Ball (Her Majesty's). One was Pete Townshend who, singing and playing solo guitar, made Pinball Wizard sound a better song than ever before; the other was Rowan Atkinson, whom I unwisely scorned at Hampstead last year, but whose bored sadistic schoolmaster was the most polished turn of the evening.

Peter Cook's E. L. Wisty, still the finest of post-war comic creations, wandered on to find his customary bench occupied by John Cleese; and a battle of equals commenced. Mr Cleese is the only comedian who, when baulked of his desires (cheese, in this case), can say to his adversary "I'm going to kill you" and mean it.
1979-07-08-four-courses-from-a-chinese-b:
Four courses from a Chinese banquet

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

DEMARCATION disputes have arisen over the arrival of the Peking Opera at the Coliseum. Nobody knows whether these productions are the province of dance or drama critics. (Nobody seems to regard them as the province of opera critics.) Alexander Bland, our dance critic, is also writing about them this week, so I shall confine myself to a few remarks on the programme of four short pieces I saw on Tuesday. On that evidence we have here a genre dazzling in form, but simple in content.

Two of the four were battle-pieces, and there were no exhausting moral issues to be faced. In each case one side was good, the other bad. Nor was there any worrying suspense over the outcome. The villains never stood a chance. Their adversaries were invariably fleeter, cleverer, more acrobatic as well as cleaner-living.

In The Phoenix of Fire the combatants are birds: white egrets and black vultures. All are lovely movers; the vultures at one point break into something that looks amazingly like a Cossack dance. Maybe Sino-Soviet tensions are being dramatised. At one point the egrets have a leading egret, but she has a secret weapon: her arms suddenly sprout streamers which she flourishes in their faces. There is one superb circus-routine in which the heroine deflects her enemies' knives faster than they can throw them.

In The Yandang Mountains we have two human armies. Though set in AD 589 this could be a post-revolutionary production. It certainly comes with a post-revolutionary programme note: "Meng Haigong, a hero of the people's uprising against the Aui dynasty, leads his insurgent troops against General Tienlong." Surmounting numerous difficulties and scaling the mountains, he destroys the enemy outposts. "Meng Haigong leads his men in a brave attack."

Actually both sides looked pretty brave to me, and I think the General deserves credit for fighting on when morally, if not physically, outnumbered. But again he just doesn't have his opponents' skills. These include leaping into the enemy stronghold in a ceaseless stream, like acrobatic lemmings, and then immediately rushing out again, victorious, through the front gate.

The bill also included At the Crossroads Inn, the piece that inspired Peter Shaffer's Black Comedy, by depicting, in bright light, actions supposedly undertaken in pitch darkness. The story is of the rescue of an imprisoned general (a good general, this time) by a couple of devoted servants, including an innkeeper who announces himself by turning an insouciant somersault.

Once again, you know who is going to win, but there is plenty of breakneck farce to delay the outcome, with the general's rival rescuers engaged in mortal combat at dead of night. Visually and athletically we have here a feast: a many-coursed Peking banquet.

  

Wild Oats has returned to the Aldwych with its good nature intact; enhanced if anything. Alan Howard's strolling player Rover, when not in thrall to what a friend calls his abominable habit of quotation, is not only kind, but humble, and his modulations from grandiloquence to homely quietude are the key to the complex playfulness of Clifford Williams's production.

Not only are the men and women merely players, but the player is the completest man among them, apt to regard his fellows as enthusiastic amateurs giving lively but one-dimensional accounts of their roles. Well done, old Abrawang, he calls out (that last nasal syllable is a gift to Mr Howard) as Norman Rodway's testy naval officer stomps about the stage like a man impersonating a testy naval officer. Apart from these two, Raymond Westwell's churlish farmer and Zoe Wanamaker's merrily impressionable maid are welcome survivors from the original cast; and among the newcomers Malcolm Storry soaks up every nuance of hurt pride from a valet who keeps his employer on a tight rein.

  

The rock Faust (Young Vic) is an updated version; indeed, since it envisions a Britain where the seduced Margaret can be condemned to death for killing her child, it seems to be jumping the gun.

Faced with damnation, this Faust declares that he has never believed in God, which presents a serious obstacle to the story and the character. It makes the pact with Mephistopheles considerably less momentous. The author, Jamie Reid, claims to have followed Goethe, but Goethe's Faust was a noticeably good man; hence the steepness of his possible fall. He was also redeemed at the end, which doesn't happen here.

Mr Reid uses Goethe's story, but his mood is much nearer Marlowe. Faustus begins as a terminally bored scholar, a Fellow of All Souls in fact, bemoaning his over-privileged surroundings in a monologue that the actor, Bill Wallis, does his best to endow with satirical edge. Power leads him to explore the underside of urban society (rotting precincts and plastic pubs) and tiring of that to become dictator, sacrificing human lives for dubious political ends.

Mr Reid has in fact written a reasonably well-observed standard modern play, to which the band occasionally add an authentic note of punk despair. There doesn't seem too much reason to drag Faust into it. Michael Bogdanov's production is efficient, but cannot supply any central vitality; James Carter endows Mephisto with the oily voice and leering demeanour of Leonard Rossiter in undertaker mood, and brings us closer to China by performing on a high-wire and a unicycle, though not simultaneously.

  

Two notable cabaret singers have arrived in London. At the Country Cousin, Morgana King deploys an unusual vocal range, but is often self-indulgent with the high notes and remorseless to the lyrics. Her interludes of straightforward swing (with superb guitarist Joe Puma) are the best. More importantly, the Playboy Club discotheque--an unlikely and discouraging setting--now houses Bobby Short, the dapper prince of New York singer-pianists. Mr Short is an enthusiastic performer whose pace and volume sometimes defeat themselves. But his repertoire is unbeatable and when he relaxes so is he.

He does a definitive version of I Can't Get Started, one of the great catalogue-songs, pouncing sardonically on every item in the lyric while affirming with his rapt, insistent keyboard work that it is also one of the great ballads.
1979-07-15-glenda-and-cleopatra:
Glenda and Cleopatra

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Peter Brook's production at the Aldwych.

IN THE last scene of Antony and Cleopatra (Aldwych) the heroine has a speech describing the dead Antony. "His delights were dolphin-like; they showed his back above the element they lived in."

It is magnificent writing, and Glenda Jackson delivers it beautifully. But, making full allowance for the fact that we never value anything properly until we have lost it, the words in this context do not make sense. They speak less of Cleopatra's love for her deceased Roman than of her admiration for him.

Love may take many forms, and the fact that Miss Jackson's reading hardly permits her to say a civil word to Alan Howard's Antony from one end of the play to the other may not preclude a real affection between them. She never seems, though, to have any kind of respect for him: she is the kind who would find it uncool to respect or admire anyone. So maybe, when she remembers Antony in those extravagant terms, she is just fooling herself. That, too, could be a defensible interpretation, though it impoverishes the play's last movement and does not seem to accord with what Miss Jackson does elsewhere in this scene, which is to present a woman finally stripped of illusions.

In fact she gets to that stage rather early. Trying to cheer Antony up after one of their military defeats, she cries, "Since my lord is Antony again I will be Cleopatra," and goes into a brief whirling dervish routine, presumably meant to represent the conventional idea of eastern promise. But after a couple of twirls, she gives it up; she really cannot play the Cleopatra game any more.

But Miss Jackson has never seemed a woman who would play that game anyway; she has other ways of keeping her man and they are cleverly counterpointed in this production against the more conventional seductiveness of her maids. I had better come clean and admit that I actually preferred the more conventional seductiveness. Everybody has his own idea of the kind of woman who remains irresistible despite behaving unforgivably, and Miss Jackson is not mine.

Which is not to deny her considerable qualities. She can jump instantly from one emotion to another, and though this may not quite equal the infinite variety needed to ensnare Antony, it enables her to do a thorough scare-job on the messenger who brings her news of his marriage. She gives us most of the strengths of Cleopatra but few of the weaknesses. She never looks likely to lose a kingdom.

Mr Howard, on the other hand, looks more than likely to lose an empire. It does not matter too much that he and Miss Jackson are playing, as the jargon unhelpfully has it, in different styles; they are after all playing different people. But except in the first scene (where Shakespeare more or less disposes of the love-interest and all the players have to do is go along with him) there is no rapprochement between them.

Hovering somewhere in the wings is an icy view of the play in which the protagonists only need each other to camouflage their personal and political weaknesses; but Mr Howard's is too swirling and choppy a performance (forceful, yes; there's always another bellow left in him) and never lets us get a steady look.

Peter Brook's production is frustratingly uneven. Scene after scene has been dredged for meaning which is then offered to us crisply and clearly. But overall that rhythm is lacking; Rome melts seamlessly into Egypt, with Cleopatra crying out for Charmian before Octavius and Lepidus have left the stage. Then all is spoiled by having everyone enter at a giggly run: a monumental Shakespearean cliche.

Jonathan Pryce's maturing Octavius retains its Stratford fascination, but has also acquired a London gabble. Two others stand out: Paola Dionisotti as Charmian and David Suchet, whose Pompey is the most fully Shakespearean performance of the evening -- which is to say that his is a solidly realistic portrait of a main-chancer dashed by his own impressionable weakness, who can also -- in his moments of contemplation or prevision -- capture the quality that makes the play leap out of time.

Leigh Jackson's Reggae Britannia (Royal Court) is an artless title that accurately reflects an unfortunate blatancy in the play itself. It should also serve as fair warning to the tender-eared. I find reggae unbearably monotonous, but as the numbers here ground each into its tenth minute I could recognise a force in the bellicose vocals and pounding guitar work that must appeal to those who like their music relentless. The question at issue in the play is how relentless?

The band in question, known as Pitch Black, is playing a school-gig, invited there by a Jamaican kid who hopes to find in the music a reflection of his own racial consciousness. This puts him slightly to the left of the group's leader, who wants reggae to have a cultural identity but doesn't mind proclaiming that identity to whites; who is himself more radical than the group's singer, who doesn't care much who hears her.

These positions are laid out on the line, but nothing much is done to flesh them out. Subsidiary white characters are strictly from stock. May be the blacks are more subtle, or written than I realised; it was difficult for me to tell from the performances on hand. It is a compliment to Mr Jackson, who is white, that he has written dialogue that slips so easily from the lips of these black performers but, though Debby Bishop is appealingly gritty and Ram John Holder artfully laid-back, they are pretty sloppy at communicating it to the audience.

Ten years ago, the Living Theatre of New York had the trend-followers of London crowding into the Roundhouse. Returning now with their Prometheus, they played on Thursday to rows of empty seats.

Well, their paranoia level has commendably in these aggrieving circumstances dropped considerably but then so has their level of presentation, which was hardly shattering before.

Imagery consists mainly of having a naked actor bound to a wheel, hands and feet splayed apart. The myth unfolds so confusingly that it has to be spelled out in the programme, which is scarcely more enlightening. What we used to call the underground has rarely considered that its audiences may be less deeply into its concerns than it is itself. As the actors wander round the hall spouting fragments, or just lie there and writhe, they end up with a very private form of theatre: what they, I think, would call elitist in others.

Anyway, Prometheus brings man the gift of fire, but man abuses it, or at least his rulers do, and Judith Malina, co-director of the troupe, complains that she is cold and cannot pay her gas-bills, and suggests, by an association of words if not ideas, the storming of the Winter Palace. Which means that Act Two is the Russian Revolution, though I didn't stay for it.

I don't know if Miss Malina is aware she is being disarming at such a moment or when, as the god-tormented Io in a Valkyrie's headpiece, she moans that she is unhappy and wants to go home, but disarming is what she is. It is difficult, now, to be angry with the Living Theatre. Their idolaters are, or were, another matter.
1979-07-29-mr-moony-s-music:
Mr Moony's music

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Songbook.

MOONY SHAPIRO, the hero of Songbook (Globe), is a famous songwriter who never existed. At least he never existed as a whole person; bits of him may be found dotted over the history of twentieth-century popular music.

Moony's career extends from Busby Berkeley to the Beatles; and his creators, Monty Norman and Julian More, have drawn freely on showbiz lore. He is reminiscent of Irving Berlin in his jackdaw adaptability, of Jule Styne in his unquenchable resilience, and of just about everybody when you set about examining his songs.

Mr Norman has furnished Moony's music, Mr More his lyrics, and the two of them have collaborated on the Songbook book. They have not been much heard from since the fifties, when they were variously involved in Expresso Bongo, Irma la Douce and Make Me an Offer; add those together and you have probably the most impressive track-record of any of those involved in the brief renaissance of the British musical.

Songbook reaffirms their craftsmanship. It is also an excellent advertisement for the Cambridge Theatre Company, which originated the show, and for its director, Jonathan Lynn. It is a pleasure to see wit, economy and commonsense again at work in the staging of a home-grown musical. It's been a long time. Taken all in all, Songbook is the pleasantest thing to have happened in the West End this year. All the same, there are nagging flaws.

It lacks a centre and, though it has plenty of incidental styles, an overall approach. Working on a combination of grapevine and guesswork I would say that it originated as a spoof on the anthology shows--Cole or Side by Side by Sondheim. But there is not much in those spare presentations that can be parodied, other than the songs themselves. Songbook has one basic turn-around idea; all previous anthologies have dealt, by definition, with successful writers, but Moony is depicted as a life-long failure.

We hear his contributions to the Broadway revue Feldman's Follies of 1926, to the Warner Brothers extravaganza Pretty Faces of 1934 (bad title--sounds more like stage than film), to the wartime weepie Bring Back Tomorrow (good title--sounds like Fox), to the folksy post-war stage musical Happy Hickory (Finian's Rainbow set in a tree) and to the ahead-of-its-time protest musical Red White and Black, which yields I Accuse, an Oriental duet pitched somewhere between Flower Drum Song and Pacific Overtures. In between these selections comes the odd number fashioned for Marlene Dietrich, Cicely Courtneidge and Adolf Hitler.

Oh yes, the plot. Though Moony began his days in Liverpool and ended them in Ireland, he lived mainly in America, where he was adopted by a Jewish couple named Shapiro; having adopted the name he nearly adopted the religion too, but stopped short. Success brought him an English, left-wing aristocratic wife, named Bella, and an English, right-wing aristocratic sister-in-law, named Charity. (No, prizes.) Charity introduced him to Hitler at the 1936 Olympics. His observation of the Fuehrer's fury at Negro athletic victories yielded the deathless number, You're a Nazi Party Pooper, Jesse Owens.

That very funny song is not a parody of anything; Messrs Norman and More have written it, so to speak, off their own bat. The same is true of much of the best material: a rather good torch-er that develops out of a running gag about a constantly rejected ballad and a savage--actually too savage for its context--complaint about Nostalgia; but the essays at actual pastiche tend to be vague or thumping. There are exceptions: the Depression chant Mister Destiny You Done Us Wrong is dead on the target and April in Wisconsin (rhymes with "dancin'" and "entrancin'") is beautifully orchestrated forties Sinatra.

The hawk-eyed may have noticed that I have referred to Moony both as a success and as a failure. If I equivocate it's because the show does. It exists number by number, joke by joke. Most of the jokes are good, but when they falter the script is apt to seem more knowing than knowledgeable.

Gillian Lynne's choreography is up to her usual spanking level and the performers are superb. Anton Rodgers is actually more, his frayed casualness as compere alternating with a series of knife-edge impersonations: an impeccably haughty chansonnier, a Ringo Starr drumming with hilariously unskilled abandon. Gemma Craven as Bella adds her own layer of satire by resembling Kate Nelligan at her most icily aggressive, and is also a charming and versatile singer. Diane Langton in ATS togs makes a commanding Courtneidge and Andrew C. Wadsworth is splendidly utilitarian. David Healy cannot bring Moony to full life, but is a pleasing personality on his own account.

  

The version of Euripides's Hippolytus at the Warehouse is described as "a realisation of the text by David Rudkin." This mysterious phrase turns out to mean that Mr Rudkin--who, if we confine our criteria strictly to the selection and arrangement of words, is the best dramatic writer we have--has rendered the play into stern, concrete English that rarely sounds like a substitute for anything and is never pushily colloquial; and that he has made the characters more explicitly aware of what is eating them than they are in the original (or rather, to be strictly truthful, in any other translation I have read).

So the hero's servant rebukes him for disregarding his sexuality and meets the stiff reply, "I acknowledge the erotic principle." This means that the opposing goddesses of love and the chase, being personifications of tragic forces anyway, have the easiest roles. Juliet Stevenson plays them both and her Aphrodite gets the play-off to a merciless, enticing start. Thereafter everything is valiant, but anticlimactic; a schoolroom aura descends as the actors battle to fill out the naked text.

Michael Pennington's Hippolytus comes off best; Natasha Parry makes a guarded Phaedra, while Patrick Stewart's rages as Theseus seem to come second-hand from Shakespeare.

The eternal chorus problem is tackled by cutting the ranks down to one, who naturally emerges, unprotected by convention, as the most inexplicably voluble character on stage. No particular fault of the actress, but one starts wondering, "Who is this woman?"

  

Regarding cricket-bores: as just that, I may be the wrong audience for Outside Edge (Hampstead), a quite promising farce by Richard Harris that takes us into the Ayckbourn territory of heedless husbands and neglected wives, obsessed by off-breaks and tea-breaks respectively. Mr Harris manages to keep four separate actions going, but he flogs them in the process.

There is a strong cast, though the men do little more than mark time. The ladies, being oppressed, have more rewarding tasks and Julia McKenzie delivers her best, straight performance to date as the most downtrodden. Maureen Lipman too is in good form as a tall tart with a short but sexy husband; this is the one joke in her role and she reiterates it with resource.
1979-08-05-springtime-in-arden:
Springtime in Arden

ROBERT CUSHMAN on As You Like It at the National.

JOHN DEXTER'S production of As You Like It (Olivier) is the best Shakespeare offered by the National Theatre since Peter Hall's initial version of The Tempest.

Like that production it is likely to be undervalued because it takes its material not only seriously, but literally. It is alive to all the values inherent in the text, many of them unfashionable. To take one small example: when the old servant Adam decides to follow his young master Orlando to the forest, he commits his welfare to 'he that doth the ravens feed.' This is the only production I have seen in which this profession of religious faith has been given any weight by the actor (in this case that marvellous National survivor Harry Lomax, repeating a role he played for this company at the Old Vic) and in which it has had any visible effect on the listening Orlando.

There are two dangers besetting any production that underlines its references as conscientiously as this one does, and neither is altogether avoided here. One is that an accumulation of detail will slow the pace; the show could profitably lose a quarter of an hour without cutting a line. The other is that ideas (and As You Like It is pre-eminently a play of ideas) may pass through the actors' mouths and, even through their minds, without entering the characters' blood-stream.

Nicholas Selby as the usurping duke makes an attempt -- unique in my remembrance -- to convey love for his daughter as well as hatred for his niece; he even changes gear in one of his tyrannical outbursts to get the point across. One felt, though, that a director's point had been made rather than that a character had been brought to life.

All right, this is a cerebral production; even when it attempts to turn itself into a fertility-rite it plaits its garlands (eventually to be hung around a phallic maypole of a sprouting shrub) with excessive determination. Similarly, in counterpointing the constriction of the court against the comparative freedom of the forest, it sacrifices some of the light and shade to be found in the former. Rosalind and Celia are attired in vast hooped skirts and look like effigies. Le Beau, who can be a pleasant enough time-server, becomes both the embodiment of corruption and the messenger of doom. But at least there is thoughtfulness here, and an awareness of the play's grand design.

There is, talking of design, a pleasing contrast between Peter J. Hall's gorgeous Elizabethan costumes ('the pompous court') and the bare timbers -- apparently taken over wholesale from this year's production of A Fair Quarrel -- that comprise Hayden Griffin's most satisfying scaffold of a set: another kind of Elizabethanism and one that makes an excellent springboard for the play in general and the 'all the world's a stage' speech in particular. As delivered by Michael Bryant, this has cheek as well as cankered wit. In the second half of the play springtime takes over, the stage blossoms, and so does the play.

No Rosalind can ever have looked more dashing than Sara Kestelman, and when she compares her love to the Bay of Portugal she manages some brilliantly searching modulations from passionate abandon to self-wounding wit and back again. All Rosalind is there in a dozen lines. In the central scenes of the mocking of Orlando the wit is there in plenty, but the undertow is missing.

Simon Callow as Orlando is caught in an interesting double-bind; he has both to establish himself as a romantic lead (not hitherto his accustomed metier) and then to undercut his new image, since this Orlando is played as unready and even naive. The play's two chief casualties are its commentators. John Normington's Touchstone has an authoritative moment when he discovers the virtues of 'if,' but most of the comic routines baffle him. He is the victim, too, of the evening's only arrant misdirection; since the play makes it clear that he marries Audrey as the only means of bedding her, it seems perverse to have her ready to drop her knickers for any male in Arden. It may be odd to nominate Mr Bryant's Jaques (looking like an unfrocked don) as a casualty, since his is outwardly the most accomplished performance on hand, but his cynicism is allowed too easy and unchallenged a path through the play.

I seem to have spent most of my space on fault-finding, but Mr Dexter's work is assured enough to make this a stimulating rather than a dispiriting occupation. His stagecraft, as expected, is excellent; the Olivier looks negotiable again.

  

Two years ago in New York, I walked out of D. L. Coburn's The Gin Game, depressed by the play and its public. Jessica Tandy and Hume Cronyn, Broadway's premier married couple were playing a couple of institutionalised unfortunates, living in retirement and on welfare, and the house could hardly get over its delight at how damn old the two of them were. He lost his temper and she was primly shockable; and she kept beating him at gin rummy, which was supposed to be his game. Wasn't that just the cutest thing?

The London audience, now that the play has arrived at the Globe, are blessedly slower to rise to the bait, and it is accordingly easier to appreciate the actors. Mr Cronyn still seems to me too calculatedly endearing, but Miss Tandy is admirably bleak; technically these are both performances of a most superior order. Staying the course, I was able this time to learn of the shocking revelations that Mr Coburn had in store concerning his characters' miserable pasts; I can't say that I was much surprised by them, and I wondered again at the persistence of the outmoded dramaturgy that conceals information it might just as well give away at the outset, thus clearing the ground for some real exploration. Still, thanks to the Cronyns, The Gin Game is now at least a painless occasion.

  

I spent last weekend at Spittal, in southern Austria, where the courtyard of the imposing Schloss Porcia, has for 19 summers been employed, under the direction of Herbert Wochinz, for a festival of classic comedy. The repertoire, even by continental standards, is enterprising.

I saw two plays done by a company that even included -- to my pleased surprise -- an Anglo-American actor, Gordon Sterne. The style was boisterous and for The Miser -- one of the few Moliere plays that can seem honestly funny -- disappointingly anonymous. But there was a prize in the shape of Jeppe of the Hill, a play by the eighteenth-century Dane, Ludvig Holberg -- Denmark got its national playwright a hundred years ahead of rival Scandinavians -- who has been likened to Moliere, but whose work, on this evidence, was far earthier, even anticipating some of Brecht.

The play treats the eternal theme -- familiar to us from The Taming of the Shrew -- of the drunken peasant fooled into believing himself a lord, and even pursues the jest to the gallows. He survives, of course, a tough victim. It is a rich, and possibly mordant, play that I recommend to the attention of some English company. Or better still -- since England rarely does well by rural plays, unless they're Arcadian -- to some Scottish company: and I don't for once mean the Glasgow Citizens.

1979-09-01-sir-alec-s-assignment:
Sir Alec's Assignment

THE MOMENT I walked into the lounge of the Connaught Hotel I spotted Alec Guinness. This is no great boast since I was supposed to be meeting him there for lunch anyway, but it was pleasant to prove to myself something I had always believed: first, that the invisible, anonymous Guinness of popular myth is indeed a myth. Even Kenneth Tynan has subscribed to it, declaring in his biography of Guinness that 'were he to commit a murder, I have no doubt that the number of false arrests following the circulation of his description would break all records'. This is possibly an unkind reflection on the capabilities of the police force, but it does little justice to the actor whose face is decently distinctive, whose voice has a totally individual sonority, and whose personality is unique.

The master-of-disguise legend may have started with his multiple appearance in the classic comedy film Kind Hearts and Coronets. However all the characters he played there were members of the same family. and it was the point of the joke that beneath their various beards, wrinkles and hairpieces they should all possess identical and immediately recognisable features. There was a time he says, when he used to hide behind false noses and spirit gum onstage, but this was in the 30s and 40s when all the rising young actors were doing it, chief among them Laurence Olivier and Ralph Richardson: (The apotheosis of nose-putty came of course with Olivier's Richard III.) Guinness is a quieter actor than either of them - perhaps that is how the legend grew.

Before taking on the role of George Smiley in Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy he had done very little television. There was some, he said, in America many years ago, 'in the days of black and white stuff'. Nearer to home, and nearer to now, he can recall only about four appearances. This is not due to any stand-offishness on his part. 'I don't,' he says, need to be wooed to do anything.' Later in our conversation he amplified this by saying that he has always ' been a snap-decision person. If I start to dilly-dally about something it usually means I shouldn't do it.' The trouble with accepting television work has been the companies' habit of phoning up and asking '"Can you do this in two weeks' time?

" In films and the theatre one's life has usually been arranged a bit previous to that.' He admits, though, that he had more fundamental doubts about television as compared to the two older media: 'I always had a slight feeling that it provided the worst of both worlds. But Tinker, has changed my mind This was partly because it was all done on film anyway ('no sets, studio work') and on 16-millimetre 'None of those huge 35mm cameras, or those cameras with cables trailing all over the place.' And the feeling of freedom was decisively reinforced by the director, John Irvin, to whom Guinness paid repeated tribute. The shooting, brought industrial as well as the usual technical and artistic problems, and Guinness thought Irvin's control magnificent throughout.

'I'm sure he's a superb technician. And he was very understanding of the actors. He'd alter set-ups to enable us to move more naturally. Often in films you find yourself making false moves purely for technical reasons.' He'd be perfectly happy to play Smiley again if he could have the same director. There is a strong possibility of such a repeat performance. Smiley, of course, figures in several of John le Carré's novels, 'It's all very well for novelists to describe their characters' mannerisms; actors actually have to do them' and is in fact the central figure of the latest of them, still unpublished, but already - with Tinker, Tailor a rumoured success - being discussed for future film treatment.

Smiley is the spy as super-professional: not a James Bond dare-devil, more a Sherlock Holmes of the files and dossiers. An infinitely conscientious civil servant, he devotes himself to his work as a defence »> against the ravages of life with a chronically unfaithful wife. Tinker, Tailor has him broughtout of retirement to trace an enemy infiltrator in the department of which he was once the prize employee. Thereisa story currentthat le Carré actually had Guinness in his mind's eye when he created Smiley. The actor discounts this; and, between accepting the role and beginning to shoot it, he got to know the author well. Le Carré has personal experience of the world John Timbers he depicts, and, when he lent the Guinnesses his house in Cornwall, they felt they were really getting into the world of espionage.

Not that there were mysterious faces the windows or unexpected cars parked outside the door; it was just that everything seemed so electronic: There was BBC 2 AUTUMN SEASON a battery of telecommunication things, all sorts of knobs to press - oh, and one door that was permanently locked. knew it led to his study but all the same. It is possible to rise from reading Tinker, Tailor impressed by Smiley's brain-power but with little sense of him as a physical presence. Something about the name George Smiley suggests to me a rotund untidiness (I always rather visualised Arthur Lowe in the role) and indeed Guinness put on a lot of weight to play the part, weight that he is now trying to lose.

He agrees that Smiley would be'untidy in his clothes but thinks that 'in the arrangement of things around him he would be very careful... meticulous. However it's all very well for novelists to describe their characters' mannerisms; There are three of them and Alleline. Sweat them, George. Tempt them, bully them - any damn thing' Toby Esterhase (Bernard Hepton), Bill Haydon (lan Richardson) Percy Alleline (Michael Aldridge) and Roy Bland (Terence Rigby)the all-powerful London Station. Once Smiley's colleagues and now the unknowing subjects of his scrutiny actors, when they actually have to do them, can find some things slightly inconsistent. The book endlessly gives descriptions of Smiley taking off his glasses and polishing them with the end of his silk tie.

But the story Guinness claims to have no favourites among his films, hardly to give them another thought once they're made takes place in wintertime, when ties are just not get-atable; there are pullovers in the way, or three-piece suits. I had to use a handkerchief instead, There is apparently one interior scene in which the silk tie routine is given its due before the cameras. We discussed Smilev over drinks (he had a Pimms) and Guinness over lunch (he had seafood crépes, followed6 raspberries and cream, some of which he generously transferred to me). More and more one is struck by the extraordinary qualities of that group of actors who came up in the classical theatre (mainly the Old Vie) of the 30s, and by the closeness of the links between them Guinnessis the youngest of them, and still talks admiringly of Gielgud as "the great enlightener' of Shakespearian verse. of acting with Olivier and Richardson in the legendary New Theatre seasons just after the war, of watching Michael Redgrave turn, at one crucial rehearsal of The Three Sisters, from a handsome leading man to a really fine actor and of the releasing effect of working for Tyrone Guthrie who "didn't know anything about acting as such but was a wonderful giver of the stage?

And of the 'great influence of-Edith Evans from the generation above, though in her heyday she was apparently very much the grande dame. Indeed, talking to him about his own career you continually find yourself discussing other actors. He claims to have no favourites among his films,hardly to give them another thought once they're made. I tried to +I want something new, although there are one or two classies P'd be amused to do? draw him out over Kind Hearts and Coronets, to my mind the best film ever made in Britain, but after paying tribute to its unusually literate script (whose wit, I may say, shone particularly through his own series of deliciously exact characterisations) he merely remarked that he had recently gone to see the grave in Sark of his co-star Dennis Price.

He is notoriously self-deprecatory, and aware of it;in fact, he is apt to be self-deprecatory about that, too. Recalling his legendary Fool to Olivier's Lear, he says. 'Even I couldn't pretend I wasn't successful-but that's mainly because I only played half the part. Larry was directing and he said "A lot of it's very boring, old dear," andcut it.' He's been an actor now for 45 years, and did the classics solidly for the first 15 of them. He's now virtually abandoned them. I want somethingnew. There are one or two classics I'd be amused to do.... but in a revival there's always a feeling that you're there to show off, you're saying now I'ul do this one...

Lear or Macbeth or whatever But I think Lear must be playedby youngish man,if onlyso he'll have enough strength to swing Cordelia around. Once you're 50 they're out. He admits to 68 or something'. I suspect that if Guinness seems to harp on what he can't do, it is because he is very sure within himself of what he can: a matter, as he says, of 'recognising one's own limitations and saying to hell with that'. Along with this goes a shrewd estimate of his own worth in the commercial market; his well-publicised two per cent of Star Wars has left him, he says, pretty flush' and free of any immediate necessity to work, but I doubt if he has really worried very much about that for years.

He has divided his career between screen and stage more carefúlly than 1 had suspected.a When I frst started taking an interest-in the-50s, I thought of him as an immovable pillar of the British film industry (along with Jack Hawkins) and hardly associated him with the theatre at all. In fact, he has never let a year go by without a stage appearance; and in the last few years, in plays by Sim on Gray and Alan Bennett and in adaptations of Swift and Ivy Compton-Burnett, he has been one of the few-regular ornaments of an increasingly. dispirited West End. He always projects a keenly amused moral intelligence. He has long since forsworn heavy disguise, only wearing a wig so that the lights don't beam too dazzlingly off his bald head.

He practises economy - 'I think the less I do the better'-though he characteristically adds, think maybe I've gone too far in paring things down? And then ne makes it more complicated Dilys Powell gave me a notice in a film, saying something like how nice to see him trying again. I thought, to hell with that, if you can see me trying, I'm not doing it well. You like it because I don't seem to be trying' He quotes T. S. Eliot, favourite writer, to the effeet that every new sentence is a struggle, you know you're not I I think one gets disillusioned with oneself. Irealise that I'm not as passtonate about aeting? going to get it quite right but you have to go ahead and try, and applies it to acting.

The inference is that you may occasionally surprise yourself by how well you have done it. Occasionally his quiet urbanity suggests a certain weariness but he denies that he's in any way disillusioned with acting. I think one gets disillusioned with oneself. I realise that I'm not as blinkered and passionate about it any more.' But the lure of the job remains. His Smiley should be fascinating.
1979-09-02-going-on-about-england:
Going on about England

YOU can empathise with a play for quite fortuitous reasons.

I have just returned from California, and was naturally delighted to find that Queenie, one of the four characters in Peter Nichols's Born in the Gardens (Theatre Royal, Bristol), had done so too. Admittedly she had spent far longer in the West Coast sun than I (years as opposed to one week), but our reactions on return seemed encouragingly similar. She, if I read her right, was rocked by the home country's tatty quaintness, and most dispirited by its attempts at modernity.

Asked about her life abroad, she replies among other things that she heard so much there about the wonderful English theatre she had almost begun to believe it. So, the previous night, before setting off for Bristol--which is the scene as well as the venue of Mr Nichols's play--she had gone to see a play in London. (I, of course, had had the same experience, though not for quite the same reasons.)

She doesn't seem to have enjoyed her evening out very much. At some point in every play, she says--generalising with remarkable accuracy from presumably limited experience--the characters will form a straight line and discuss the state of England, no matter how hard the dramatist tries to stop them. Mr Nichols is a formal kidder and he is on this occasion his own director. His actors at this moment are standing in the formation he describes, and talking just so.

ROBERT CUSHMAN on new plays in Bristol and London.

Years ago, in The National Health, Mr Nichols gave us the prototype national-microcosm play. Before that, in A Day in the Death of Joe Egg, he established himself as one of our best theatrical domestics. He has more or less alternated the two modes ever since. Born in the Gardens is an attempt to unite them, and if it succeeded it would be a tour de force. It isn't that, though the author's shining mastery of such neglected basics as character and dialogue make it the most entertaining native play to have crossed my path this year.

We are in Tudor Manor, a mullioned mansion (well up to the Bristol Old Vic's usual high standard of set-design) owned by a successful brush-manufacturer, recently deceased. His coffin lies on stage, Loot-like, throughout the first act. Gathered for the funeral are his widow Maud, a ga-ga lady with an overriding fear of insect infestation and a creative line in malapropisms; Mo, her 45-year-old son, who lives with her and for Dixieland jazz; Mo's twin, the aforementioned Queenie, who seems to fancy him something rotten; and their elder brother Hedley, a back-bench Labour MP who is determined to rearrange his family's life on sensible lines even if he can't do the same for the country. This means resettling Maud in a Primrose Hill duplex (or, as she fruitfully puts it, durex), while Queenie is more than willing to seduce Mo to her own chosen side of the Atlantic. Since both Mo and Maud have developed distressing characteristics--he talks to his cat and she to the silent TV screen--the audience have good reason to wish them shaken out of their respective ruts. It is obvious, though, that they are not going to be; the situation becomes frustratingly static, and the characters' individual comic routines overstrained.

The title refers to a gorilla, the pride of Bristol Zoo, born and raised there, and unknown to the outside world. His nearest human equivalent seems to be the cardiganed Mo, resigned to a life of captivity, knowing full well that he would be awfully disillusioned if he ever actually visited New Orleans. He has some smashing speeches on jazz and other things, but for the play to work he needs to be brought more ruthlessly to its forefront.

It is most enjoyably acted, though Jennie Linden bashes Queenie over a bit hard and Beryl Reid relishes Maud's material and her own perfect timing of it rather too obviously for credibility. It is left to Barry Foster to be both grotesque and believable (as well as personally unrecognisable) as Mo, and for Peter Bowles to make Hedley quite the most sympathetic of our stage's recent crop of joke Socialists.

His blinkered good intentions (and the mess that he, like Queenie, has made of his own emotional life--Mr Nichols holds the scales fairly) say a good deal about Labour in disarray. His mother's view of the party is also pretty close to the bone of popular prejudice. She blames them for post-war austerity: "After all we'd been through, they gave us another five years of it, without even the American soldiers to take our minds off it." For lines like that--burnished and rooted--I can forgive Mr Nichols a lot.

The state-of-the-nation speech in Howard Brenton's Sore Throats (Warehouse) is delivered by Sally, come to view a flat of which her privileged position as an Evening Standard telephonist has given her advance information. The speech has little to do with the rest of the play, which could be going on anywhere.

In the flat, which is desolate, Sally discovers Judy, the estranged wife of Jack, a policeman. Jack returns home to beat Judy up, so that she will hand him over half her money, enabling him to go to Canada with his new love and become a Mountie. He knocks her down, kicks her repeatedly in the guts, then invites her out to dinner. I can believe almost anything, but I want to know more about Jack's insensitivity and Judy's previous passivity before I can swallow that sequence.

Sally and Judy shack up together, devote themselves to sexual gratification; then Jack comes back again, still after money and delivering a searing speech about the birth of his child in the Canadian wilds. Mr Brenton is good, too, at startling images, like Judy tearing up bank notes, and shamefaced ripostes, as when Jack voices our guilty materialist thoughts by saying that if he sticks them together they will still be legal tender.

The play ends with Judy looking forward to a future of sexual, personal and financial freedom. Mr Brenton is not usually an ironist so one can only think, bully for you. Other reactions are stifled by the slenderness of his personal documentation. Paola Dionisotti gives some reality to both her suffering and her defiance; Malcolm Storry delivers his oration well, but is otherwise hard pressed to escape monotony. Jack's profession seems arbitrary: Mr Brenton can't believe that all coppers are wife-beaters, or vice versa. Ruby Wax does her bit, which mainly consists of taking some of the heat off Miss Dionisotti, ably. But if Mr Nichols's indecisiveness has led to dramatic obesity, Mr Brenton's single-mindedness has resulted in emaciation.
1979-09-09-dizzying-fantasy:
Dizzying fantasy

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a joyous revival by the RSC.

IT ASSUMED that Once in a Lifetime (Aldwych) would turn out the best thing of the year, but I wasn't prepared for it to be this good.

It is the play in which a movie executive upbraids a subordinate with the words, 'Do you know what you have done? You have made the wrong picture.' He then proceeds to announce a new studio rule: 'Every scenario we produce, somebody has got to read it.' I have quoted my two favourite lines - probably my two favourites in the whole of twentieth-century drama; there are plenty more where they came from.

America between the wars produced two great genre comedies - The Front Page and Once in a Lifetime - and both have now been given superlative British productions. The Front Page is much the grittier play of the two; its authors were writing, with as much cynicism as affection, out of their own experience in journalism. Once in a Lifetime approaches Hollywood at the onset of the talkies with awed disbelief.

Moss Hart, the original author, had never been anywhere near California. George S. Kaufman, who rewrote it with him, was wholly Broadway-bred. Of course they both knew the legends. So the play is a fantasy: an informed fantasy. This is its strength. It is not much good at sustained speeches. When the moment comes for a savage denunciation, all they can come up with is, 'I think Hollywood and this darling industry of yours is the most God-awful thing I've ever run into,' which is to the point, but hardly inspired.

It doesn't matter. There is a terrific energy about the play, as well as an enchanting buoyancy. Wisecracks are unstoppable, and so is the parade of characters. For the most part they are self-made monsters, the progeny of the silents, living by their own extravagant rules, which are only just beginning to be questioned by the talent necessarily imported from literature and the stage. Everybody who isn't actually in movies is either a fan, a parasite, or - most likely - an aspirant, filling in time as a bellboy or cigarette-girl. ('There's a call out for prostitutes... talking prostitutes.') Impromptu auditions - coming at him from the least expected quarters - are the hourly hazards of a producer's life.

The mogul we see most of is Herman Glogauer, who lives in fear anyway, since he is the man She once turned down sound. He is now inclined to say Yes to everything, and even to bargain with his arch-rivals, the Schlepkin Brothers, of whom there are 12, marching two abreast. (The last one, in this production, is black, which must have been a surprise to Mr Schlepkin Senior.) Out West come a washed-up vaudeville trio: ambitious Jerry, good-hearted May and George. George, though dapper and affectionate, is the complete chump. But it is he, achieving dizzying success through equally dizzying incompetence, who ends up running Hollywood. The Kaufman-Hart thesis seems to be that he still does, and always will. Could be.

Jerry is the least rewarding role of the three, though Peter McEnery, white-suited, pipe-smoking and sporting the most stylish of profiles, wittily hits off his attempt to play the Hollywood big-shot. But it is the other two who make the running; May will come up with a sardonic metaphor, George will take it literally, and that routine, repeated, accounts for much of the verbal humour.

The timing of Zoe Wanamaker and Richard Griffiths is quite unfaultable; and so are their characterisations. Miss Wanamaker, marvellously hard-boiled, also takes care in a properly brisk manner of the love-interest; and George is the crowning glory of Mr Griffiths's line of gentle buffoons. Indeed no jokes - which is to say no points - are missed in Trevor Nunn's joyous production. The supporting roles are all lovingly done, from David Suchet's glowering Glogauer and Paul Brooke's squeaky, paunchy genius-director (from Germany, natuerlich) to Carmen du Sautoy's angular, dismissive secretary and the horde of extras and electricians.

One of the delights of this generous show is that it actually takes us on set. John Napier's designs also run to a train, a Gold Room at the Hollywood Stilton, and - most dazzlingly - the reception room at Glogauer Studios, whose logo appears to be an elephant's head in glory, here flanked by two other tuskers, sitting up and begging. Even when the play ends, the show goes on, Gillian Lynne having choreographed the best closing number seen in London since A Chorus Line. This is the more remarkable when you consider (a) that Once in a Lifetime isn't a musical and (b) these are all straight actors.

  

But not every play can use such adornments and The Government Inspector (Old Vic) is merely impeded by having the local officials' dreams of St Petersburg periodically played out before our eyes. (This may derive from the Russian production of another Gogol play, Marriage, seen at last year's Edinburgh Festival.) It isn't even consistent since Klestakov, the supposed inspector, who fantasises just as much (hence the play's greatness), is allowed to do the job on his own: just as well, since Ian Richardson, after a slow start, plays a delicious cadenza of befuddled innocence.

There are also ripe Yorkshire performances by Hugh Sullivan and Barbara Jefford as the mayor and his wife; their colleagues gradually get in line behind them to present a believable homogenous picture of a comically corrupt society.

  

From the Gogol gang to The Gorky Brigade (Royal Court). These are the members of a youth colony in post-revolutionary Russia. Originally juvenile delinquents, they are converted to ideological solidarity (i.e. to replenishing the grain-store instead of depleting it) when it is pointed out to them that extorting tribute from rich peasants can be not only fun but politically admirable.

The lapse of a few years finds them in communal charge. Disillusion has set in; theirs is the only colony there is, they have no prospects outside it, and a visit from Gorky himself, on his return from the West (nobody asks him why he went), ends with him being belaboured by a college student whose professor is being prosecuted for reaching unauthorised scientific conclusions.
