An interesting enough story is efficiently enough told by Nicholas Wright, though for the most part in a false-naive style (I hope and believe it's false) that fills the air with self-righteousness. It gets a soft-edged production from William Gaskill; simple sentences (one actress's role seems to consist almost entirely of slogans) are not helped much by having emotion pumped into them, or by hopeful attempts to make them sound conversational. Philip Davis and, off and on, Elizabeth Estensen do best among the actors.

  

There is a considerably more bracing look at youth in Welcome Home Jacko (Riverside Studios), another good one from Mustapha Matura. Rastafarianism is helpfully expounded and caustically but understandingly pulled to bits. The writing and some of the performances (notably Trevor Laird's) are fine advertisements for the Black Theatre Co-operative. Mr Matura has written a taut and explosive final sequence, but here - on the smaller of the Riverside stages, which is still pretty big - it huddles in a corner.
1979-09-16-a-special-kind-of-culture-sho:
A special kind of culture-shock

Mexican notebook by ROBERT CUSHMAN, our theatre critic.

THE Jornadas Culturales Anglo-Mexicanas were, as you might very well guess, an artistic collaboration between Britain and Mexico. Not an exchange, since the traffic was all one-way. London dispatched to Mexico City a package containing the Royal Ballet, the London Symphony Orchestra, a Turner exhibition, a director and designer from the Royal Shakespeare Company, and me.

This is not to say that there was no native talent involved. A Mexican conductor, Eduardo Mata, presided flamboyantly over the LSO in a concert unfortunately shorn of its advertised visiting attraction, John Williams. (Mr Williams, like so many visitors to Mexico, was intestinally stricken.) The concert was held in the Palace of Fine Arts, a triple-tiered, concrete and marble edifice, in shape and dimensions a cross between the Albert Hall and Covent Garden, with a stained-glass dome for a ceiling.

The modern buildings of Mexico can be stunning. (It makes you realise with a start that everything we most prize in Britain is old.) The most celebrated, justly enough, is the Anthropological Museum, which seems to have been not so much built as sculpted: a series of long rooms, built around a fountain-dominated plaza.

The museum is set in parkland, some way from the centre of town. A short distance beyond it lies the Teatro del Bosque, the home of Mexico's National Theatre company. It's always refreshing to visit a theatre that stands in parkland; Broadway and the West End -- the crowded midways -- have their allure, but they cannot compare in attractiveness to a theatre that stands (as some do, even in the metropolises of Paris and Berlin) in its own grounds.

The play I saw -- the one which in fact accounted for my presence -- was Richard III, directed by Clifford Williams and designed by Farrah. The latter gave it leathery costumes and a deep open set, reminiscent of his Stratford Henry V and Coriolanus; the production, too, had a Stratfordian drive and lucidity -- and, what most astonished the audience, Stratfordian speed. (Acting is generally as leisurely as everything else in Mexico.)

For me it was a special kind of culture-shock: a recognisable RSC production, only spoken in Spanish. Vigorously spoken, too, especially by the women and by a Richard rather glamorously sardonic, and one who seemed to grow less deformed as the evening went on.

It was the first major production of Shakespeare by a Mexican company for about 15 years and likely to prove a landmark: this seemed at least to be the general opinion at a seminar conducted jointly by Williams, Farrah and myself, care of the British Council, on the two days following the first night. (Williams described this scarifying sequence of continuous activity as 'refusing to surrender to jet lag.')

Our audience were actors, expatriates and -- predominantly -- students and teachers of English. Clifford Williams talked about the difficulty and importance of finding a trustworthy text; I harangued them on contemporary Shakespearean production in Britain, which effectively meant that I talked about the RSC, appealing to Williams for memories and descriptions of his own productions just as sneakily and as often as I could.

I also lectured -- in Monterrey and Guadalajara, as well as in the capital -- on such generously fashioned topics as Shakespeare and Modern British Theatre; Mexicans in general speak of Monterrey with about as much enthusiasm as the British generally muster over Stockport, but I liked it; the traffic is less savage than in Mexico City -- where the density of the jams and the reckless competitiveness of the drivers reduces nervous newcomers to a steady ten miles an hour -- and you get a comforting view of the surrounding mountains.

Guadalajara, urbane and relaxed, was about the nearest I got to orthodox tourist's Mexico. All the same the talk I most enjoyed giving was in Mexico City, and to the National Theatre company. It nearly didn't happen; food and climate had caught up with me (after a week I had hubristically thought myself safe) and no official interpreter had materialised. I pressed into service a couple of English-speaking drama students, whose uncompromising dismissal of the National (they themselves, Grotowski-like, were 'into something more holy') had reminded me forcibly of home. Sternly flanking me on the platform, they translated the actors' questions and my answers. I felt like a foreign politician on a television newsreel, and looked apparently as if I were being guarded for my own safety.

August in Mexico City is the rainy season; in the good old days it rained at four every afternoon. You set your watch by it as you retreated indoors. Nowadays Mexico's weather is as capricious as everywhere else's and you can get caught. There is an uncompromising quality about Mexican rain: you feel you might drown in it. I felt entitled to seek some sun; and Acapulco being inaccessible (the natives, no fools, had every flight booked up) I retreated across the US border, fetching up in Los Angeles.
1979-09-16-who-cares-who-dunnit:
Who cares who dunnit?

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a murder mystery, and revivals of Brecht and Odets.

IN THE golden days of Beyond Our Ken and Round the Horne there used to be sketches which began with a genial narrator saying something like 'my name is immaterial: Sir John Immaterial' and proceeded to a 10-minute lampoon of the country-house murder mystery.

Tom Stoppard played the same joke at greater length in The Real Inspector Hound; but he diversified it with a chorus of critics and even so turned in less than a full-sized play. It has been left to Anthony Shaffer in The Case of the Oily Levantine (Her Majesty's) to spin the jest out over an entire evening.

The curtain rises then on the traditional panelled setting, and the actors arrive. At their head is Hywel Bennett as the eponymous (not to say oleaginous) Middle Easterner, come to spend a country weekend and to blackmail all his fellow guests, to wit: a crooked lawyer, a retired naval officer ('a bluff bugger' as somebody unaccountably forgets to put it), a she-dragon, a flapper and her go-getting fiance, and a prim lady archaeologist. Also the butler. All are deliberate stereotypes, and the cast grapple with them vigorously and even wittily. All the same, an hour of funny-voiced acting is rather more than flesh and blood can stand.

As it happens, the second act does induce a wholesale change of style. The reasons for this I may not, of course, reveal; but I am giving away hardly more than the programme does if I say that the oily Levantine is now the late Levantine, and that Mr Bennett has switched to playing the inspector come to ascertain which of the amply motivated survivors done him in. The inspector has fantasies of being a detective, and he conducts his investigation after the fashion of his favourite novels.

This is all very well for him, but it leaves the rest of the cast -- deprived first of reality and now even of artifice -- in a most unenviable position. You suddenly remember why Agatha Christie plays are always so badly acted: they offer nothing to act. But Miss Christie always kept her plot going, so that you got involved anyway. Mr Shaffer, intent on jokiness, keeps neglecting his, so that the cry of 'Who cares who kills Roger Ackroyd?' is all too easy to echo.

It may be a comment on Mr Shaffer's cunning, or merely on human nature, that when he remembers we do care, even while kicking ourselves. Some of the jokes are good (especially in some silky passages of narration), but many more are not; even if their ghastliness is intentional, it soon becomes wearingly predictable. Mr Bennett is supported in the second stage of his dashing double by Roger Hood's sergeant, a performance of welcome sobriety, while the others -- among them Adrienne Posta, Anna Quayle and Bernard Archard -- do their manic, and valorous, best.

  

The Private Life of the Third Reich (Open Space) is one of Brecht's least assuming plays, and also one of his most powerful. It is merely a sequence of episodes -- not all included in this production -- delineating the progress of 'fear and misery' (the original title) and most of all of universal mistrust in pre-war Hitler Germany. The scenes are offered to us as pieces of a parade, each representing a different section of society. The play is contemporary propaganda, but nobody is likely to quarrel with it on that score; it is in fact refreshing to encounter Brecht working journalistically rather than through some laboured parable.

There is one sense in which his political bias is a handicap; he is unable to face the idea of German workers actually being enthusiastic Nazis. They are all shown to us either as brave if unwary protesters or as terrorised into silence. He is sounder on the intelligentsia, showing us doctors refusing to ask dangerous questions when confronted by a victim of official brutality, or a teacher and his wife terrified that their young son might be informing on them -- a scene that is rather daringly tilted towards farce.

A Jewish wife preparing to leave her Gentile husband is movingly, and unsentimentally, detailed; and there are two sardonic masterpieces. One shows us two bakers meeting in prison, accused of breaking the food laws in precisely opposite ways. The other depicts a judge under conflicting pressures from the SA, the SS, popular opinion and (vestigially) his own conscience, and finishing by crying out, 'If the authorities won't tell us what they want, how can there be justice?'

Brecht was always good on the entwining paradoxes of the law, and this scene shows him at his best. It could do, I think, with a drier treatment than it gets here; Roger Kemp plays (believably enough) the confusion of the judge's situation rather than its irony. Mr Kemp and Susan Engel head a resourceful cast, in an equally resourceful staging by Nikolas Simmonds.

  

The Cambridge Theatre Company are on tour with Clifford Odets's fifties piece, Winter Journey. I saw them at the Ashcroft in Croydon; this week they are in Darlington and after that they return to base. The play is about the reclamation of an actor, brought out of drunken retirement by a young director who saw and worshipped him in his greatest days. But to get the performance he wants, the director has to battle with the wife on whom the actor is wholly dependent; so at least he thinks.

Formally the play is a melodrama; it is built on a technique of revelation and if you have seen the play before (or if, like me, you once caught the film, which adhered to the play's original title of The Country Girl), you may complicate your reactions by importing knowledge before the play is ready for it. This is a shame, for the story is tautly and amusingly built up, and the marriage at its centre is searchingly portrayed. The picture of the actor who has quarrelled with his wife for the hundredth time subsisting in his chair and sobbing for her -- his 'country girl' -- is unforgettable.

Joan Kemp-Welch's production suffers from lengthy scene-changes and, more crucially, from a pervasive restraint. These players are acting with their gloves on; the play's form, style and milieu call out for naked aggression. Laurence Payne manages the alcoholic jitters and the false bonhomie of the returned star very movingly, but he lacks the temperament that should underpin the whole. He plays the role, English, which immediately suggests a man who harbours his grudges, rather than one who ferociously displays them.

Eleanor Bron, though she is shrewdly and imaginatively cast and returns the compliment in her performance, could simply nag and domineer more if his accusations and the director's suspicions are to be in any way believable. Nick Tate is on the ball as the director. Smaller parts are undemonstratively well done.

  

The Yellow Dogs of Texas (ICA) is billed as a play about, and with, country-and-western music. The author, Alan Williams, did rather a good job on pop in The Cockroach That Ate Cincinnati, but what he's up to here eludes me. There are duologues between the put-upon owner of a vandalised C&W club, and an equally beleaguered lady. In the second act (and belatedly) the music starts, but raises the spirits only momentarily; it does enable Alan Aldred to give rather a stylish account of a fading singing star. I may have missed something (the proceedings are so low-key that attention easily wanders) but, in point of pointlessness, this seems to be the fringe's answer to The Oily Levantine.
1979-09-23-long-walk-to-downtown-la:
Long walk to downtown LA

ROBERT CUSHMAN, our theatre critic, reports on a recent visit to California.

THE popular idea of Los Angeles as an endless series of suburbs is not quite accurate. It does have a downtown, which is unlike any other metropolitan centre on earth. It's very peaceful, for the excellent reason that hardly anybody goes there. And it's equally far away from everything -- from everything, that is, except the theatre.

There is a civic arts complex in the heart of town. You may die of loneliness on the walk there, but it's impressive when you arrive. There is the immense Dorothy Chandler Pavilion, where the Civic Light Opera performs musicals (usually sharing them with San Francisco); it is one of the few theatrical organisations in the Western world to turn an infallible profit.

They were doing, when I was there, a pretty tepid production of Bells are Ringing. But better things were happening in the legitimate house, the Mark Taper Forum, which is a steeply raked and well proportioned thrust theatre. They were offering two linked plays by Lanford Wilson. Mr Wilson is a playwright who was known here in the sixties for a couple of one-acters that were among the earliest successes of the London fringe, but has since vanished from our sight. We should rediscover him.

The present plays concern an old Missouri family coming to terms with the outside world. In the first, Talley's Folly, set in 1944, the daughter of the house is wooed and won by a Jewish accountant. The scene is a boathouse: a set-up for atmospheric magic as the suitor, speaking for the author, brazenly admits. Self-conscious though it may be, the device works, and the mating-dance sparkles.

The Fifth of July, a more elaborate play, moves us on to 1977. The girl of the previous piece is now a widow, cherishing her husband's ashes, but preparing to part with them as the younger generation -- the Berkeley radicals and Vietnam casualties of the sixties -- try to find some use for the past in the present. The family wrangle is not my favourite kind of drama, but Wilson -- a playwright firmly in the American mainstream -- comes closer to revivifying it than any playwright I can think of. He has a winningly light touch, and his humour is always surprising. These plays, already successes at New York's admirable Circus Rep, surpass almost any of the American plays we have recently imported.

  

The end of the seventies has meant a reappraisal of the sixties. Topping all is Coppola's Apocalypse Now, playing in LA to five packed houses a day. The film is less about what America did to Vietnam, than what it did to its own youth. That was, if not a greater horror, a more immediately frightening one, and it was reflected in the protest movement. 'Hell, no, we won't go' was a more effective slogan than 'Ho, Ho, Ho Chi Minh.' At least that's how it sounds now.

At the Odyssey, a fringe theatre in Santa Monica, I saw The Chicago Conspiracy Trial, a reconstruction of those infallibly theatrical proceedings in which Black Panther Bobby Seale was gagged and bound to his chair, Yippie leader Abbie Hoffman drolly promised the court 'a very exciting cross-examination,' and over which Julius Hoffman (no relation, of course, but how beautiful the coincidence) presided as a judge Dickens might have written and Olivier acted. George Murdock's performance was actually on that scale; outrageously detailed in its pique and self-importance, tragic in the inevitability of its increasing tyranny once the first step was taken.

The trial was abridged with a careful eye to the juicy bits (I remember the brief apparition of Mayor Daley complacently regarding his fingernails while the judge commended him as an ideally co-operative witness), though with little regard for what the cases for prosecution and defence actually were. Two statements struck home. One, unexpectedly, was the prosecutor's allegation that the defendants undoubtedly had come to the Democratic Convention looking for trouble; against that was Abbie's avowal that he and the other supposed conspirators 'couldn't agree on lunch.' Only conclusion: the accused were guilty as charged, but they shouldn't have been charged.

The Chicago trial now seems at once supremely important and supremely ridiculous. This show, with a cast of 48 (thank Hollywood unemployment and fringe salaries), was breathlessly exciting, painfully nostalgic, and plain useful.
1979-09-23-triumph-of-a-salesman:
Triumph of a Salesman

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Arthur Miller at the National.

NO play written in English since the war has the emotional impact of Arthur Miller's Death of a Salesman (Lyttelton).

It may not quite be a universal work: I don't suppose it means much to orphans, but anyone else must respond to its scenes of family quarrel, with brief reconciliations giving way to fiercer misunderstandings.

It sounds obvious enough, and there have been plenty of critics to sneer at it on those grounds. But if it is so easy to make audiences cry by reminding them of their home lives, one can only wonder why more playwrights haven't brought it off.

The play's supporters have sometimes been as damaging as its detractors. It was hailed, after its premiere in 1949, as the apotheosis of American social drama, as the tragedy of capitalism. But Miller pointed out in his preface that the most sympathetic character in the play is Willy Loman's neighbour, Charley, whose values are in no way different from the salesman's own. Only he pursues them with far less tenacity.

As Charley himself says, "My salvation is that I never took any interest in anything." Willy takes a ferocious interest: in his career as a salesman, and in the future of his sons. Finding them to be good athletes, he thanks Heaven that they are built like Adonises, but there is no doubt that if they had brilliant academic records instead, he would have decided that their minds were all-important, just what was needed to get ahead in business.

Indeed Willy's downfall is that though he believes, he never knows from one moment to the next what his beliefs are. One moment he is telling his elder son Biff that nobody lends a kidder money, the next thing he is telling him to soften up a prospective benefactor with a few jokes. "We never told the truth for 10 minutes in this house," says Biff, but that's not because they prefer lying; it's just that they never know what the truth is.

"Mendacity" -- the Tennessee Williams word -- may be part of the Loman trouble; a greater part of it is credulity. Willy swallows things, and not just because he's a salesman. A revolution is unlikely to destroy the play's relevance; in a socialist society he would be just as gullible. He would still want to live again through his sons, and they would be just as unable to oblige him.

He would probably end up as before, rejected by the son who loves him but can hardly bear to look at him, while the shallower one prepares to emulate all his father's worst traits. (Nothing in the play is funnier or more telling than young Happy's repeated assurances -- quite sincere at the moment he makes them -- that he is about to get married: as if that would solve everything.) And Willy would still have a wife like Linda to bear with him, to try to save him from himself, and to storm at him, without realising that her fatal acquiescence has helped to make him what he is. Probably, if he took the chances he keeps talking about, they wouldn't have worked out, but she stops him even from trying.

While things go well, she believes what Willy tells her; when they disintegrate she sticks by him, knowing that he is trying to kill himself but unable, when it finally happens, to figure out why. I think that Miller keeps the precise degree of her knowledge unnecessarily foggy -- this is one point at which the play is open to the charge of sentimentality -- but the fuse leading to the suicide is immaculately laid.

Biff's last display of anger proves to Willy (quite rightly) that his son loves him; he commits suicide so that the boy will inherit the insurance money and make glorious use of it. That's not the only reason (Miller's aim of conveying an infinity of motives -- of writing clearly about something essentially confused -- is fully achieved), but it's the one that pushes him over the edge; just as it is the well-meaning Edgar who administers the final shove to the sanity of Lear.

To argue that it is Willy's nature, not his profession, that destroys him is not to deny that much of the play's value derives from its keen eye for the petty realities of salesmanship, and from its ear for the poetry. For when the younger, brighter Willy is reigning his sons with his triumphs on the road, he does seem momentarily to have, if not "a good dream," then an exciting one. He isn't necessarily lying all the time.

The language of the play has been grievously underrated. Line after line flashes out. If Willy's dream of his funeral -- "all the old-timers with the strange licence plates" -- obviously strains for poetry, it just as obviously achieves it. And even the supposed clinkers have their validity. Why shouldn't Linda tell us "attention must be paid to such a person"? Greek choruses make equally explicit appeals to our concern?

Michael Rudman's excellent production is graced by a superb Willy from Warren Mitchell, absolutely clued in to the man's essence, which is a fearful jauntiness; his mind hops, terrified or hopeful, from one subject to another. It is impossible to hold a coherent conversation with him. The scenes of semi-flashback (where Willy talks simultaneously to one character in the past and another in the present) are brilliantly done.

Almost equally good is Doreen Mantle's Linda, steadfast but rather bovine, and entirely free of false nobility. (The epilogue, though, is surprisingly unmoving; awkwardly directed against a new and superfluous backcloth. I also wish that John Gunter's set did not trundle so noisily -- or trundle at all -- whenever a time-slip occurs. They ought to take us by surprise.)

Stephen Greif, looking like a young Tony Bennett, and with some of the same ox-like sincerity, grows through the evening; his one calculated attempt to play his father's game and lie about a failed interview is thinly done. And David Baxt's Happy, especially when taking his ease in a restaurant, is a shiningly shabby heel.

The Mercury, Colchester, has made a speciality of reviving rare period comedies: currently, Hubert Henry Davies's The Mollusc, which has understandably been retitled Never Lift a Finger. All the same, the molluscs and even "molluscry" constantly assault the ear, less euphoniously than the author may have designed. The sea-creature is his metaphor for a special kind of idleness, one that consists of shuffling off all exertion on to others, while administering repeated doses of self-pity and self-deception. An Edwardian wife and governess are victimised by it, and her brother attempts to cure it. Languor can of course be sexy, though Davies never explicitly turns it on. All the same there are depths to be explored; direction chooses. David Buxton apparently doesn't, but still offers a pleasant evening with a pretty performance from Bronwyn Williams and a vigorous one from Philip Anthony.

Richard Crane's Gogol (Theatre Upstairs), only distantly indebted to the Russians, is a three-part saga progressing from repression to exultance to collapse. Both as writer and performer Mr Crane is immensely skilful: if I shuffled, blame it on my low tolerance-level for 50-minute monologues.

Finally an apology: my praise last week for the performance of the sergeant in The Case of the Oily Levantine was somewhat devalued by my calling the actor Roger Hood. He isn't a Hood; he's a Leach.
1979-09-30-tragedy-of-blood:
Tragedy of blood

ROBERT CUSHMAN in Nottingham and London.

JOHN MARSTON wrote a series of comedies with -- even for the seventeenth century -- a notably high scurrility content.

That is the side of Marston that we have known, insofar as we have known him at all. But now Nottingham Playhouse has given us the chance to see what he made of the tragedy of blood. Peter Barnes has clapped together Antonio and Mellida and its sequel, "Antonio's Revenge," and called the result Antonio. There are two rival dukes, Andrugio and Piero. Andrugio is good and Piero bad; or at least Piero's vicious qualities have greater scope, since he has defeated his enemy in battle and is now intent on killing both him and his son Antonio, currently disguised -- with an eye to safety and theatrical effect -- as an Amazon.

In the end father and son save their skins by appearing at court and shaming Piero into repentance. Antonio is even allowed to marry Piero's daughter Mellida, whom, naturally, he has loved all along. "Here," proclaims Antonio, "ends the comic crosses of true love."

He's right in a way. In Part Two tragedy -- or at any rate mayhem -- takes over. Piero begins by murdering the resident honest man (you can tell he's honest because he dresses badly and insults everybody), stringing up the corpse in his daughter's chamber, and accusing her of inconstancy. He then bumps off Andrugio, seduces his widow and forces Antonio into a second disguise: this time as a fool.

From this privileged position Antonio organises a conspiracy of more or less virtuous malcontents, who set on Piero at a banquet, extract his tongue and kill him. Along the way there have been minor murders and much girding at the rottenness of court life, as exemplified by a large supporting cast of gulls, degenerates, lechers and whores.

Marston was much mocked by his contemporaries for his rumbustious, neologistic style, but to us, coming to him from Shakespeare, he gives an impression of weightlessness. There is plenty of dirt in his writing, but no solid earth. The people are largely indistinguishable, all actions are liable to be undercut by a burst of sententious satire. You might take the piece to be a parody of Jacobean tragedy; certainly Antonio's situation echoes Hamlet's, but the great sanguinary writers, Webster and Tourneur, came after Marston. He is presenting us with instability for its own sake. This is a good bad-dream play.

Mr Barnes, in his adaptation and his production (co-directed with Geoffrey Reeves), serves his author wonderfully well. He has excellent technical back-up: designer Trevor Pitt supplies a simple, menacing set (a tilted golden disc overhung by a huge crown) and ornately bizarre costumes; choreographer Stuart Hopps sets the whole play moving like a masque; and composer Carl Davis fills it with music that -- in and out of ghost scenes -- truly haunts.

Mr Barnes has gone along with some of his author's strangest fancies -- letting Antonio and Mellida, for example, conduct their reconciliation scene entirely in Italian -- and they all seem to work. Though the overall tone is light, he plays less for laughs than I had expected; he cuts for example the assassins' dangerous declaration that, with their work now finished, they will retire to a monastery. The play remains enigmatic, but it seems to know its own mind, even if we don't.

The actors too, considering that they cannot play characters (since Marston didn't give them any and admits as much in his prologue) but can only play a style, are remarkably sure of themselves. The dominant performance comes from Christopher Ettridge as Piero, with his sickly usurper's smile. Alan Rickman, carefully patting his single Amazonian breast or swinging in on a rope and in motley, is a first-rate sardonic Antonio, and Derek Godfrey is manfully the butt finally metamorphosed (to his great relief, I suspect) into an avenger.

Just to straighten various records: this is (a) the best excursion into the Jacobean funeral parlour since the RSC's fabled "Revenger's Tragedy," (b) Nottingham's finest hour since "Comedians," (c) by far Mr Barnes's outstanding theatrical achievement to date, and (d) the most notable rep production in ages.

Marston's master -- indeed the model for the entire Elizabethan school of death -- was the Roman Seneca, from whose Thyestes he literally took a cue. "You cannot say you have avenged a crime/Unless you better it," says Atreus, the kingly villain of this piece, and Piero quotes him approvingly. Atreus avenges himself on his brother Thyestes by serving him up a pie of which the vital ingredients are his own sons.

  

Seneca may have lacked Marston's theatrical flair (and certainly his humour) in dealing with such an episode, but his rhetoric, even in translation, is superior. The problem is what to do while speaking the stuff, and the Company of Three (operating now at the Fountains Abbey pub in Paddington) fall back on the outmoded idea of turning every possible or impossible scene into an orgy: a small one, since there are only five in the cast. But the play takes hold; it has more to say to us than Marston about the ethics of tyranny. And it is frankly a relief to see the homicidal maniacs who people Greek mythology stripped of Attic dignity.

  

Ecstasy (Hampstead), Mike Leigh's latest improvised work, is as expected highly polished and -- as acted, or rather inhabited by, its cast of six -- flawlessly believable. At its centre is a woman alone in a London bedsitter with no prospects. She doesn't like the men she picks up, she says, and they don't like her; they just hit her.

The play is at its best in strong statements like that or in moments of silence. But it goes awry in a long sequence of joyless conviviality when three old friends descend on her for a grisly approximation of a night out. While it goes on, she is going to pieces. That much is powerfully conveyed, but it could be done more economically in a written play.

  

All the same, it can make a play like Men's Beano (Warehouse) seem obsolete. I am probably being unfair to the author, Nigel Baldwin, whose script is well observed and reasonably entertaining. But the territory he shows us here -- the desperate companionship of males in a dead-end world -- has been thoroughly explored before.

This saga of a trip to the seaside by minibus (how did they get it up the Warehouse's stairs?) is "Factory Birds" on wheels. The men pick up a female hitch-hiker and spend most of their time trying to make her. At the end she rebukes them for their sexism -- which would be fine if the author hadn't got most of his mileage earlier on from showing it off. The mixture is not too far from the pious sensationalism usually attributed to the News of the World. The best acting, with the best material, is Cheryl Hall's.

  

The revived Hello Dolly! (Drury Lane) is the loudest non-rock musical I have ever heard. The amplification strips the last vestige of humanity from the gravelly squawk that is the hallmark of Carol Channing's Dolly. She sells herself to the audience relentlessly; her performance is one long curtain-call. She is naturally irresistible in the title-number, which, however, puts paid to the rest of the show: after that gorgeous walk, about everything else is an anti-climax.

But there are pleasant numbers early on: the jolly "Put on Your Sunday Clothes" and "Dancing," which suddenly exposes the lyrical side of Gower Champion's choreography. Otherwise, this chocolate-box show is surprisingly short on romantic feeling, though Maureen Scott and Tudor Davies work attractively with what there is. Eddie Bracken's merchant of Yonkers is nobody's curmudgeon, but it is nice to have him back, even if it isn't quite where he belongs.
1979-10-07-the-sisters-of-stratford:
The Sisters of Stratford

ROBERT CUSHMAN on new productions of Chekhov, Shakespeare and Garrick.

MOST people in the RSC production of Three Sisters (Other Place, Stratford) lead lives of noisy desperation.

The play begins and ends, as it should, with the sisters in a tight group, as if waiting to be photographed. But on the second occasion they are broken. Suzanne Bertish's Masha has already shaken us with the bottled fervour of her farewell to Vershinin, and even more with the silent agony with which she sits through her husband's fumbling attempts to cheer her up.

Emily Richard's Irina takes over with the realisation that they will never escape, which hurts even more than usual since Miss Richard has carefully placed each of her previous cries of 'Moscow' at the apex of some scene of frustration, making them sound like the expression of a good and practicable idea. Finally Janet Dale's Olga, who up to now has been brisk and unobtrusive, delivers her message of hope and, without any obvious undercutting, makes it the cruellest threnody of all. The departure of meaningful life from the town has been made to seem inevitable, and the sisters' own survival almost unbearable.

There have been other tirades to match theirs. As Andrei, Timothy Spall, escaping from the mumbling schizophrenia in which he has specialised since Mary Barnes, talks loudly to the wall or to the deaf old porter as he sets his sights progressively lower--and Mr Spall, beginning tousled and clumsy but quite presentable, marks off every stage of his decline. Griffith Jones, though too gentle an actor to explore the drunken doctor's lowest depths, is nevertheless superb in his aria of self-disgust.

Sob for sob, this is the most moving production of Three Sisters I have seen. Its peaks glisten with the intensity that has become the distinguishing mark of Trevor Nunn's productions, comic or tragic. But comedy here is at a discount. It is true that it runs charmingly through Roger Rees's apologetic Tusenbach, and more subtly through Patrick Godfrey's conciliatory cuckold; it also flowers in such a group-moment as the sly descent of the entire company, playing gooseberry on Andrei's proposal to Natalya. But it is absent elsewhere, and some self-consciousness results.

The great virtue of Jonathan Miller's production a few years ago was that nobody seemed specially aware that they were playing Chekhov; a surprising proportion of the text made sense as ordinary conversation. But Miss Bertish tends to stridency even in repose, and Edward Petherbridge rather drifts through Vershinin. (It occurred to me that for all his well-publicised domestic problems this man suffers less than anyone in the play, but nothing is made of the point.) Bob Peck makes a powerful first statement as the murderous Soliony; if he then has to go on repeating it, that may be Chekhov's fault. But Susan Tracy's Natalya, after a fine first act as a nervous but determined man-catcher, develops into an equally nervous hysteric. She doesn't nag her sisters-in-law; she screams at them. This is interesting and unusual and gives her a good share of the production's strongest moments, but it finally impoverishes the play. It is far more frightening for Andrei and the girls to be up -- as they usually are -- against complacent insensitivity.

I should add that the smallest parts -- the junior officers, the silent maid, and Rose Hill's magnificent old nurse -- are better played than I have ever known.

  

Ralph Koltai's set for Richard III (Olivier) looks at first glance like a couple of sculptures purloined from elsewhere on the South Bank; further gazing reveals that one of them has the profile of an outsize executioner's block, and so indeed it proves. Richard's victims are decapitated on stage, although for Buckingham something nastier has been reserved.

If the sets are an unvaried grey, the costumes mainly ring the changes between grey and black (with the occasional extravagance like dressing Lady Anne's attendant mourners in plastic macs.) This has a cramping effect on the actors, who achieve almost uniform anonymity. I would have expected Basil Henson and Andrew Cruickshank to do wonders for Hastings and Derby, but they merely come on, say their lines fast, and go off again. Mel Martin has become mysteriously elocutionary as Lady Anne. Jeremy Kemp's Buckingham and John Normington's Clarence are good, Yvonne Bryceland's mad Margaret better and Anna Carteret's Elizabeth almost excellent, though both actresses are hampered by an apparent effort to play their scenes of incantatory grief (every son a goner, and all of them named Edward) naturalistically.

I also wondered what caused Margaret to make her first entrance in the middle of a court who had to pretend for ages that they couldn't see her, and why Christopher Morahan arranged his ghosts as a chorus instead of (as in the text) a series of solos. Massed supernatural exits are very hard to stage; this lot shuffled off as if someone in the underworld had just blown the whistle on them.

In the middle of it all John Wood gives his Richard, a performance in which for the first half I was quite unable to believe. Every hypocritical line was topped off by a sardonic glee that would have alerted the most unwary dupe. There is enough space in the soliloquies for Richard to enjoy himself, and these Mr Wood explored with suitable relish. But with the dialogue he seemed uneasy, determined to scale it all down to the cool mockery of his role in Travesties.

There is a limit to how far casualness can go in Shakespeare; I am used (though not resigned) to hearing actors preface each speech with 'well' or 'now'; Mr Wood comes up with 'I mean, cannot a plain man live and think no harm,' dealing a casual death-blow to metre and (using the word in its still valuable sense) decorum.

The second act, as the hunted king, gives more scope to his flair for logical dementia: the feeling of a mind running so fast that it will explode. (Mr Morahan in his treatment of Richard's henchmen comes up with some nice moments of what you might call police-state relevance.) I could accept that this Richard would play feverishly with toy soldiers, though toy drums and trumpets seemed a bit much. Besides there were no signs of incipient madness in what had gone before. Mr Wood seemed obvious casting for Richard, and that should have been a danger signal; he is settling into a mould.

  

The Old Vic is honouring Garrick's bicentenary with a double bill of rarities: an opera, The Padlock (music by Dibdin), which he once produced, and a farce, Miss in Her Teens, the better piece, which he wrote. Each has the same plot: a true lover wins his girl from obviously unsuitable suitors. The heroine of the second, though, has a welcome sense of mischief and -- on my visit the understudy, Vicki Luke, played her delightfully. Nickolas Grace has plum roles in both and his cavorting Negro slave should be seen before the Race Relations Board moves in; his timorous beau should be seen anyway. A strong cast surrounds him, including Benjamin Whitrow, Frank Windsor and Prunella Scales, who, as a prologue, informs us with relish that the second piece 'is a bastard.'

Peter Simpkin's Adam's Apple (New End) is an earnest treatment of the problems of the trans-sexual which falls sequentially into the traps of farce, melodrama and insecure realism. So do the acting and production. A brief post-coital dialogue, before the theme gets going, gives some promise of better things.
1979-10-14-case-for-subsidies:
Case for subsidies

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a worrying report.

NOTHING that happened on stage last week had quite the dramatic impact of the report in The Guardian that a dozen theatres, and four fringe companies, might have their Arts Council grants axed in the coming year.

It may be a false alarm. Here's hoping. But it's worth pointing out that the whole question of theatrical subsidy is at stake. It would be helpful if the Government could state clearly whether or not it regards the theatre as worth supporting. If it does, then it has to accept that the theatre is an entity, and indivisible. If sections of it can survive without public money, then hooray. But most cannot; and the theatres in question -- they include 10 reps and, in London, the Royal Court and Open Space -- would die without it.

If the theatre is to be subsidised, then the money cannot just go to a few centres of supposed excellence. In the first place, it isn't fair; in the second, excellence has a disconcerting habit of changing its abode every couple of seasons; and in the third, the best depends on the good--even sometimes on the bad. We need standards of comparison.

To make the argument less rarefied: a successful National Theatre or whatever needs to be able to draw on actors who are experienced on other stages and have not had their morale shattered and their skills blunted by almost total unemployment. None of the theatres reportedly threatened has an unblemished artistic record, but then who does? If the Government does not believe in supporting the theatre, then perhaps it should say so now, and put us all out of our misery.

  

Meanwhile (and I trust that nobody will take this as an argument for decreasing their subvention) I have to report two rather fidgety evenings with the Royal Shakespeare Company. Howard Brenton once illustrated his scorn of apolitical drama by pointing to the forgotten Russian playwrights of the years preceding the revolution. 'Fancy writing about drawing-room love in that situation,' he said. I doubt if Maxim Gorky was among the dramatists he had in mind. All the same, watching Gorky's 1905 play, Children of the Sun (Aldwych), I found myself recalling Mr Brenton's strictures, and unexpectedly endorsing them.

The play is not wholly about drawing-room love. There is a world elsewhere, a world full of cynically discontented peasants and servants. At their head is a drunken, wife-beating blacksmith. The gentry hate and fear him, but they need his services. Eventually he is quietly felled by the cool and competent yardman, the figure who seems most clearly designed to show the central characters up.

These characters are: an ivory-towered scientist, his wife who loves an artist, his sister who loves a vet, and the vet's sister who loves him. There is no way these relationships can balance out, especially as most of the characters, though terribly gentle and terribly polite, are blind egoists. So they thwart and stifle each other across four acts, at the end of which the most sensitive among them are either mad or dead.

In the meantime they have done much talking, for each is obsessed by an idea. The scientist, a benevolent Frankenstein, looks forward to the time when men will come into their inheritance as 'children of the sun.' His sister feverishly laments the cruelty and brutality of the world. The artist is understandably put out by all this vociferous idealism.

Chekhov's people talk and dream in much the same way, but with a firm structure to support them. Gorky's plays are peculiarly frustrating for an audience. Here is an obviously major writer, and he cannot hold your attention.

Terry Hands's production does not make concentration easy. The play at its best is a comedy of manners, so both text and actors could do with some realistic support from their surroundings. Here we get three hanging screens, with a fence (of both practical and symbolic utility) beyond; also a few very spartan chairs.

Carmen du Sautoy, Sinead Cusack and Natasha Parry all extend their range remarkably. Norman Rodway has a nice barking geniality, vocally in the Donald Sinden line, but he lacks the shameless Sinden bravura that might propel the play along. Alan Howard as the vet oozes distinction, but his performance is hard to get at, walled round as it is by an impenetrable Caledonian accent. John Shrapnel makes a cheerful vigorous job of the artist.

  

Anna Christie (Other Place, Stratford-upon-Avon) is well carpentered enough; the trouble is content. This is the most popular of O'Neill's early plays, largely because it provides a plum role for an actress: a prostitute who returns to her long-lost sea-faring father hating all men, but is eventually reconciled both to him and to her Irish stoker of a lover.

The final curtain finds them prepared to settle into a spectacularly ill-omened menage-a-trois, but for once in his career O'Neill seems to intend no irony. Anna's dad, old Chris, who has blamed their troubles on the malign influence of the ocean, now blesses it. The student may find some interest in the appearance of the symbols of fog and sea O'Neill put to richer use in his last work, and in the occasional unmistakable note of bedrock hopelessness, but for the most part there is only sentimentality and verbal and visual drabness.

Jonathan Lynn's production squeezes as much poetry from the text as may be, and Susan Tracy is generally excellent, foursquare and volatile, as Anna. When she faltered I was inclined to blame the text: O'Neill's notorious tin ear makes things difficult for a British player. You cannot just fall into the rhythms.

Fulton Mackay chuckles endearingly as old Chris (his constant invocations of 'dat ol' davil sea' are less trying to hear than to read, though no more relevant) and Lila Kaye livens up the opening wharfside scene as a precursor of Tugboat Annie.

  

Two new plays about police violence. The less successful, though the more ambitious, is Michael Picardie's Shades of Brown (King's Head), in which a South African cop comes to a coloured folk-psychiatrist and, after some preliminary intimidation, asks to be cured from the trauma that has haunted himself and his wife ever since she gave birth to a brown child.

This fanciful confrontation, and the lightness of much of the dialogue, do not really match the author's obvious underlying fury. Mr Picardie's witch-doctor is a charming performance; his patient is the brilliant Antony Sher, whose uncommonly keen nose for absurdity in dialogue or behaviour may have pitched the play further towards comedy than was intended. 'In my job,' he says, 'you need all the laughs you can get.' I know how he feels.

Barrie Keeffe's Sus (Theatre Upstairs) is a dour, economical and compelling piece about a black Briton pulled in, and similarly brutalised, on suspicion of having killed his pregnant wife. It is set on the night of the last election and his two interrogators look forward to the freedom from liberal restraints that they will enjoy under 'the Thatch.' Ann Mitchell's production is effectively low-keyed, though some of the acting may be more expressionless than was intended.

But there are even more frightening problems that Mr Keeffe, like most of his contemporaries, has yet to examine: the moods and attitudes in the British people, not just the police, that might explain why we now have a Conservative Government.
1979-10-21-prince-ss-of-denmark:
Prince(ss) of Denmark

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN at the new Half Moon.

THE new Half Moon Theatre, in the Mile End Road, promises to be as friendly a showplace as its predecessor - still operative - at Aldgate.

How can a critic feel hostile towards a playhouse which permits him to perch on its set half an hour before curtain rise, tucking into chicken sandwiches and cheesecake from the delicatessen down the road?

I should explain about that set. The opening production is Hamlet and it is mounted in what the National Theatre describes as promenade-fashion. That is, a series of rostra have been erected round the hall and on these the action takes place.

One construction represents the battlements, another the throne-room. The throne itself is a huge and fearsome piece of Meccano sculpture, with a skeletal 'royal' figure surmounting it. Vacant pieces of scenery are all the audience have to sit on: for the most part they mill around. Hamlet may seem rather a long play for this sort of caper, but the director, Robert Walker, has cut it severely; we begin with the second scene, and end with 'the rest is silence.'

Mr Walker perhaps underrates human laziness when he says that his scenic method offers the audience a choice of vantage-point for each scene; our view is as likely to depend as much on chance as choice. But the strangeness and the proximity - for the new Half Moon is a small, square room - make the play fresher than any amount of gimmicking up the text itself could achieve. The fundamental relation between actors and audience can never be altered as long as the latter pay for their tickets, but it is possible to play fruitful tricks with it.

Mr Walker's treatment of the play is actually rather conservative: in the attempts to saddle Hamlet with an Oedipus complex, positively old-fashioned. He concentrates on the corruption of the court (all white-faced, as is now the custom in productions of lesser Jacobean tragedies), and particularly on its propensity for eavesdropping - here shared, of course, by the audience. Polonius, in a clever stylised performance by Robin Hooper, becomes almost the leading figure of the first half, always peeping behind the nearest arras and eventually slain (with strict poetic justice) by an assailant who doesn't bother to look. Claudius is a neurotic, fear-ridden tyrant, and Gertrude a high-heeled, bare-bosomed belle, who can hardly forbear laughing at the idea that her precious son (much given to crawling up her skirts) might have fallen for so ordinary a girl as Ophelia.

The closet-scene accordingly takes on peculiar intensity; the intimacy achieved by Hamlet and Gertrude can only be described as sisterly. Which brings me to Frances de la Tour in the title-role. Mr Walker's decision to make this a walk-around Hamlet has deflected me from considering it as a female Hamlet. It works like that in performance, too; the vigour and intelligence applied to the play as a whole make consideration of the prince a secondary matter.

Much of the time he is a neutral figure, as were the women in the National's all-male As You Like It. But there neutrality was a deliberate convention; here, with all the other male roles played by men, it seems an accident. At one unguarded moment, bemused by both a scene-change and a cut, I found myself thinking of Miss de la Tour as Ophelia; I could never forget she was an actress. But on this occasion frailty's name is Hamlet. The actress has a biting wit, but her greatest successes are in the area of vulnerability: the 'rogue and peasant slave' speech is memorably trapped. But she only proves that there is a feminine principle and that it is far from being the whole of Hamlet.

Vivre la difference, I say, and roll on Miss de la Tour's Hedda Gabler (as opposed to, say, Tom Courtenay's). For, considered purely in terms of the actress's own development, this performance is a breakthrough, achieving a vocal and emotional range beyond anything she has shown us before. The evening makes anyway a rousing beginning for a new theatre; and when the cast applauded us, Continental-style, the gesture for once seemed genuine and even, may I say, merited.

  

Roger Hall's Middle Age Spread (Lyric) looks at first glance like a foray into Ayckbourn territory. Its main scene is a dinner party, interrupted by flashbacks showing us the previous relationships of the diners. But technical juggling is not the point, and where Mr Ayckbourn's tensions are largely unspoken, Mr Hall's are overt.

The play aligns more with the Peter Nichols school of menopausal comedy. Colin the protagonist, is a schoolmaster recently promoted to Head; finding his marriage intellectually and sexually stultifying, he has his first-ever affair with a rather idealised junior colleague, egged on by his cynically philandering best friend.

The three involved couples swap worried aphorisms (and if the audience applauded some of the more reactionary offerings, I am charitable enough to think that the laugh was on them) while waiting for the situation to explode. When it does, the size of the bang seems disproportionate to the length of the fuse; the play is not terribly shapely. But, moment to moment, it offers far more than most boulevard pieces; both its jokes and its misgivings are truthful.

Some of the performances are, like the piece, victims of a double standard. A man with the sharp-edged physical funniness and impeccable verbal timing of Richard Briers's Colin is wasted as a teacher; he should have been an actor. But in outbursts Mr Briers is quite unassailable, as is Paul Eddington in what amounts to a continuous acrid drunk-scene. There is also a splendidly needled piece of work from Sheila Grant, who deserves (but doesn't get) a flashback of her own.

  

Julia Kearsley's Wednesday (Bush) also strays into Nichols territory. It is the comedy of a widow with a retarded 15-year-old son, whom she both loves and resents, and a bitterly aggressive teenage daughter whom she mostly just resents. The man who comes to dinner this time is an old friend who once saved the boy's life at the expense of his own son's. Miss Kearsley puts her quartet through its paces with considerable skill - her dialogue has a rare conviction - though she has exhausted her possible permutations half an hour before closing-time. If Mr Nichols's Joe Egg suffered from abandoning its central theme, Miss Kearsley rubs our noses in hers.

Jean Boht's performance of the mother, bald beneath a glamorous wig, is a masterpiece of tact, playing on our feelings without lacerating them. David Bamber brings off the necessary tour de force as her son, Gil Brailey scratches with style, and David Hargreaves is a model of well-meaning Northern bemusement, like Michael Parkinson trapped in a documentary on approved schools. Grant Hicks supplies another of his stunningly believable sets; the kind that suggests somebody has gone homeless to provide it. In our smallest theatres, naturalism lives.
1979-10-28-adam-and-eve-and-ola:
THE HERO of David Lan's Sergeant Ola and his Followers (Royal Court) is a New Guinean NCO who fought for the British and Australians against the Japanese and returns home after the war to act as an intermediary between his own people and the white rulers.

The New Guineans, as Mr Lan presents them, are literalists. They believe everything the white man tells them and make no allowance for his propensity for metaphor. However, since those metaphors are now mostly cliches, the New Guineans who emerge as the more poetic; and it is his deployment of this poetry that gives Mr Lan's play its peculiar, and altogether delightful, flavour.

It is there particularly in the character of Ola himself. "That's not progress," he snaps on meeting a native with two wives. Linked to Ola's belief in progress is that of the Guineans in "cargo" -- the material goods that will arrive by boat, or maybe drop from the skies, as the British have promised. For the sake of cargo they abandon their own religion and turn to the white man's big, big ancestors, Adam and Eve. They have previously believed themselves to be descended from parrots, and when Ola stumbles across some fragments of Darwinian theory he realises the extent to which he has been tricked. The whites' real ancestors are monkeys; they have fobbed Adam and Eve off on his people in order to keep them in subjection. All right, he says, all right and okey-coke, and sets about the work of re-enlightenment.

I fear that I may have made the play sound insufferably quaint; it is actually extremely tough, but blessed by a pervasive lightness of touch: capable too of great poignance when dealing with the turmoil of Ola himself, or the desperation by her belief that "because of me cargo never come". In the second act, perhaps, one wishes that Mr Lan would bring on some heavier ammunition; tracing the first steps towards New Guinean independence, he hardly allows us to distinguish Ola's views from those of the more primitively inclined local leader, Takis. Weightlessness does have its limitations, but its attractions are excellently captured in Max Stafford-Clark's production, which boasts a major performance, quickfire but with rumbling depths, from Norman Beaton as Ola. There being, I imagine, a shortage of New Guinean actors in London, the play has been given a multi-national cast, among whom Bruce Alexander is particularly funny as Ola's Australian opposite number.

  

My Fair Lady is superlative: a fresh coat of paint for what I take to be the best romantic musical ever written. Surprise and enchantment set in from the moment the curtain rises, which it does much earlier than has been customary. What used to be the overture is now a prologue, in which Adrian Vaux's set (which remains as a glass-and-metal casing for the entire show) and Gillian Lynne's choreography bring Covent Garden market to pulsating life.

I have never seen a chorus act better, and Miss Lynne keeps them and the principals at it throughout. Wouldn't It Be Loverly is a touchingly funny slice of wish-fulfilment; dustman Doolittle's two numbers, crammed with comic detail, are great Cockney cadenzas radiating out from their central figure. But perhaps the most remarkable achievement is I Could Have Danced All Night, in which Eliza, tired beyond sleep, comes to emotional life. Liz Robertson (helped by a slowed-down final chorus I don't remember from the original) magically combines the academic mind at bay but fighting mad, emotionally childish but resilient.

There is a touch of archness about Tony Britton's Higgins and Peter Bayliss's Doolittle, but in the musical-comedy context that is reasonable enough. Mr Britton treasures his Shavian set-pieces and delivers his closing confession, I've Grown Accustomed to Her Face, with a finesse upon which Rex Harrison at his best (by the time I saw him his performance was a bit pitiful) could hardly have improved.

Shaw, you may remember, had Eliza marry the hopeless Freddy, rather than face a lifetime of fetching Higgins's slippers. (The ending of My Fair Lady, it must be confessed, makes The Taming of the Shrew look like a feminist tract.) Valentine, the philandering dentist, looks forward at the end of You Never Can Tell to similar subjection.

Peter Egan's performance of this role at Hammersmith is marvellously airy, and as much in command of the rhythm (letting it drag, then picking it up again in double time) as a first-rate jazz singer. The character men are out in force: Paul Rogers, who is expected perfection as the waiter, John Bryans in storming form as the Q.C. ex machina, Frank Middlemass as the solicitor and David Waller as the tetchy long-lost father. Mr Waller, though, makes Crampton rather lovable, and he wouldn't have lost his family in the first place if he'd been that. This softness, and accompanying sloth, in David Giles's production also spoils the antiphonal twins in whom speed and sharpness are all. But the last act is charming showing, with its harlequins and columbines and false noses, that Shaw knew both what he was about and where he got it from.

Ever vigorously Shaw may have protested his un-erotic intentions, his perversity was our profit; we have two pieces for the price of one, and Pygmalion leads a double life.

  

I am not sure what Brian Trueman, the author of Tishoo (Wyndham's), is about: it could be apocalypse, or the unacceptable face of trade union militancy, or the intellectual's supposed inability to love, or the place of disinterested science in a shabby materialist world. Most of these themes cohere in the central role, a researcher who has probably discovered a cure for the common cold, but finds the world doesn't want or can't afford it.

His defence of pure knowledge (above politics, above everything) yields a splendid scene in which he confronts his cynical vice-Chancellor: Geoffrey Palmer in the latter role is the embodiment of clipped pragmatism, while Alec McCowen repeats his matchless interpretation of the academic mind at bay but fighting mad, emotionally childish but resilient.

To watch this actor in top gear is always a pleasure. He also has interesting relationships with Penelope Wilton as his assistant (who, when asked if they're sleeping together, says "No, it's gone beyond that") and with his experimental rabbit, the most dramatically prominent of its kind since Harvey. Other elements are less satisfactory, and the play accordingly spends a lot of time running on the spot. But it's promising.
1979-11-04-amy-s-love-letters:
Amy's love letters

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on two plays by novelists.

BERNICE RUBENS'S masterly novel I Sent a Letter to My Love concerns a self-consciously ugly woman in a small Welsh seaside town, whose life is devoted to tending a crippled, and possibly dying, brother.

In her late fifties, she places a lonely-hearts ad, with a box-number, in the local paper. She receives one reply: from her brother. So she invents a persona, under which she conducts an increasingly passionate correspondence with him. By the end of it she is in love with him, while his passions have been so awakened that he becomes an easy mark for the spinster down the road, his sister's best and only friend. When their engagement is announced, our heroine's legs fail her; it is her turn to look forward to a life of being fussed over.

Miss Rubens has a dry way of telling this bizarre tale, one that keeps sentimentality, with the characters themselves, at arm's length. But in her dramatised version, now on view at Greenwich, she has changed her approach. Sister Amy, brother Stan, now tell their own story, and Amy is especially loquacious in a style that wavers between conventional soliloquy and unbuttoned direct address. By the second act Rosemary Leach as Amy has progressed far enough in intimacy to address the audience as 'my lovelies' - an unwarranted liberty, I thought.

When Miss Rubens invents a scene from outside the book - as when Stan confronts the actress whom Amy has hopefully, if improbably, hired to impersonate his unseen beloved - she comes up with something vigorously, if a bit crudely, farcical. It entertains, but it also jars.

The meat of the story, in whatever medium, is the correspondence of Stan and Amy, and in this version we are a long time both approaching and retreating from it. There is also the question of Miss Leach's looks, which are certainly not Amy's (not as described in the book, at any rate) and which makes her long shelf-life difficult to credit. I know this is what reviewers always say about leading actresses in plain roles, but then it's usually true. And make-up alone would not solve the problem.

As it happens, Miss Leach gives as warm, expressive, witty, tactful and malicious a performance as has sprouted in London this year. All this vitality is as much part of Miss Leach's attractiveness as physical beauty could be, and she would hardly command our attention - could hardly in fact be an outstanding actress, or even an actress at all - without it. The supporting cast are good, and if Miss Rubens has impaired and softened her original creation, she has not destroyed it. If there is still a place for matinee plays, this is the best in a long time.

  

Another lady novelist, Fay Weldon, has contributed a far more economical piece in Action Replay (Orange Tree), which traces the lives of three women from their student flat-sharing days in 1954 to their widowed and divorced flat-sharing days now. Also presented are the three men with whom they are severally, and sometimes collectively, involved: no doubt it is chauvinism that makes me ascribe the comparatively lustreless impression made by these males (whose only scene together is conducted by candlelight, a dispiriting fact in itself) partly to deficiencies in the writing and in Julia Pascal's direction - both of which, where the women are concerned, are admirably taut.

Anyway, it is the actresses - Katharine Schofield, Stephanie Turner, Janet Key - who make the running. Miss Turner has a rare directness, every resource in perfect order, as a self-proclaimed easy lay progressing to marriage by increasingly embittered stages, and Miss Key complements her pungency with a befuddled warmth that eventually evolves into its own mode of attack. But the play's principal interest is its construction. Though central events - marriages, divorces, births and deaths - remain constant, each step between is presented as a series of variants; the same opening gambit is developed in three or four different ways.

Enough lines are thrown around concerning the operation of chance or destiny on human lives for us to believe that Miss Weldon has a theme here. I think myself that she comes down in favour of destiny, considering how little is the effect of what her characters say or what they actually do. (Here, perhaps, is a belated reply to J. B. Priestley's Dangerous Corner, in which a chance remark was shown to have the direst effects.) But it is the device itself which tickles the fancy, and keeps play, cast and audience on their toes.

  

The Guise was the title of a lost play by John Webster, presumably concerned with that favourite demon-figure of the Elizabethan drama, the architect of the St Bartholomew massacre. One of David Mowat's contentions in his identically-named piece at the Theatre Upstairs seems to be that Webster's was a work well lost; his pastiche of it, though conscientiously bedecked with double-entendres and images of pond-life, hardly does the master credit ('for years now I, Guise, have chafed at this situation,' says the hero-villain, carefully identifying himself as if he were in a radio production); though the scenes of actual butchery do have a carnivorous relish that seems to derive from Marlowe's earlier play on the same subject, The Massacre at Paris.

Mr Mowat's play-without-the-play posits a revival of the Webster (formerly suppressed for fear of giving offence to royalty) immediately before the closing of the theatre by the Cromwellians. This occasions much devotional talk of 'theatre' by the endangered actors. Now the Elizabethans and their successors did not, to judge from their writings, talk in this way; they spoke of 'theatres' (good concrete things), perhaps even of 'the theatre,' but they steered off meaningless abstractions.

In making them talk as we unfortunately do, Mr Mowat has rendered his play 'relevant' in the unhappiest way. But beyond this, and leaving aside the comfortable feeling that theatres were coming under official threat both then and now, there is little to relate his play to us, or indeed Webster's supposed drama to his own. The production is heavy, the actors mostly speaking with a worried reasonableness that gets individual lines over, but obscures whatever larger pattern may lie behind. Only Adrian Vaux's timbered set for the Fortune Theatre (theirs, not ours) hits the right note of gorgeous simplicity, and makes incidentally a fine double with his work, at the opposite extreme of expenditure, on My Fair Lady.

  

Spoon River (Soho Poly) is an adaptation of a long poetic sequence by Edgar Lee Masters depicting life in an Illinois small town between the American Civil and First World Wars. The inhabitants rise from the churchyard and tell us their mostly macabre stories. This is Thornton Wilder without the cloying uplift, Our Town with the Grover's Corners knocked off. Spoon River seems to have contained an abnormal proportion of girls who went wrong in some picturesque way or other; Beth Porter, playing most of them, distinguishes them juicily and resourcefully, though she and her three adroit colleagues seem at unnecessary pains to disguise the fact that what they are speaking is verse.

With which I retreat for a month to the other side (to appear in an Ogden Nash revue at the King's Head, to be precise), bequeathing a four weeks' supply of bouquets and brickbats to Steve Grant.

(Apologies to Brian Thompson (author of 'Tishoo at Wyndham's'), who tossed Robert Cushman in last week's theatre column.)
1979-12-01-reviewing-the-70s:
Reviewing the '70s

BBC television drama entered the 70s with its eye firmly fixed on the past. I don't know if nostalgia can be prophetic but I'd like to believe that it was a charmed Entering this time. For New Year's Day universe 1970 brought us episode one of The Six Wives of Henry VIII, the series whose immense success pointed the way to custume drama at home and prestige sales (to American educational networks mostly) abroad. For those who have forgotten what outstanding they learned either at school exposi- or on BBC2, Henry's first was Catherine of Aragon, played by of Annette Crosbie. And just to show you how the wind was blowing, playing on BBC1 was a re-run of The Forsyte Saga Series were rampant: Z Cars and Softly Softly of course (I never could get used to the idea of them co-existing) and Doomwatch, the one about technology getting out of > 117 115 < «k hand and killing people.

Ian McKellen's twin kings - Shakespeare's Richard II and Marlowe's Edward II - were brought to the screen, after their phenomenal success in the theatre. But the new single play, whose supremacy had been taken for granted during the socially-conscious 60s, was already entering its fight-forsurvival stage. Tony Parker's Chariot of Fire tried to main- Radio Times Making War & Peace WAR AND PEACE SEPTEMBER 1972 tain the tradition, and Tom Clarke's Mad Jack (directed by Jack Gold) to extend it. But probably the most impressive dramatic achievement of the year was the serialisation of Sartre's The Roads to Freedom, with its fine performances from Michael Bryant, Daniel Massey and Georgia Brown. Television has never served a modern classic better.

After a re-run of Six Wives came Elizabeth R, chiefly memorable for establishing the bankability of Glenda Jackson. It was a Scandinavian period for ace director Alan Bridges first Bergman's The Lie (for which he won the STTA award) then in 1971 Ibsen's The Wild Duck with Denholm Elliott and Derek Godfrey. Bridges also directed Dennis Potter's Traitor; an untoppable partnership. Edna the Inebriate Woman won applause for its leading actress Patricia Hayes and its author Jeremy Sandford; it made his Cathy Come Home of the 60s seem like child's play. Dennis Potter aroused puritan wrath - and critical surpriseas writer of the serialised Casanova. It may have been the costume - and it launched Frank Finlay as a sex-symbolbut nobody called it escapist.

CHRISTMAS AND THE NEW YEAR 1972's modern classic serial was Man of Straw with Derek Jacobi whom RADIO TIMES tipped to become the next stage name to achieve television fame. There was a Merchant of Venice with Maggie Smith and Frank Finlay. There was no keeping the Tudors down - even the uncharismatic Henry VII was allowed his fling in Shadow of the Tower. And there was a production of Hedda Gabler with Janet Suzman in a role she would play more successfully in the theatre. Ian McKellen brought his greatly underrated Hamlet to the screen, Coral Browne flourished in Lady Windermere's Fan and, if any actress could play Shaw's Millionairess, it was Maggie Smith.

The BBC embarked on Tolstoy's War and Peace. Peter Terson's The Fishing Party inaugurated an affectionate cycle of plays about small masculine pleasures, and Alan Bridges directed Dennis Potter's pivotal Follow the Yellow Brick Road a play about death drawn from the author's own experiences in hospital. Peter Ustinov narrating and Galton and Simpson writing failed to make Clochemerle funny. Brecht's The Gangster Show: the Resistible Rise of Arturo Ui, directed by Jack Gold with Nicol Williamson playing Hitler-as-Capone took us into 1973 in high style - as television filmeraft it's still unsurpassed. Fine craftsperson Elaine Morgan dramatised the Bywaters-Thompson murder case in A Pin to See the Peepshow, and meanwhile Barlow and Watt had graduated (or been demoted) to investigating Jack the Ripper.

Kisses at Fifty was Colin Welland's best play and in the leading role Bill Maynard came in from the cold. While Colditz had caught on in 1972, 1974's The Pallisers didn't. Colin Welland wrote television's definitive strike drama in Leeds United!, given the semi-documentary film treatment by director Roy Battersby and producer Ken Trodd. The unlikeliest historical series of all was launched - Churchill's People, virtually a blank cheque for its writers. In Shaw's The Apple Cart, shown in 1975, Peter Barkworth played the Prime Minister; today he'd be the King. Our appetite for the well- / costumed past led to the Pre- Raphaelites being given their own series; they called it The Love School.

The admirable Miriam Mar golyes (self-described as fat and intellectually glamorous ) was one of Muriel Spark's The Girls of Slender Means. That had style. 1979-12-16-sandy-s-aladdin:
Sandy's 'Aladdin'

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Sandy Wilson's new Christmas show.

SANDY WILSON'S Aladdin is not a pantomime.

It might have been; when the new Lyric Theatre, Hammersmith, asked him to provide a Christmas show for them he dutifully looked up some panto scripts. But though he liked the traditional Victorian ones, he saw no point in competing with the Players' Theatre, which has made them an annual speciality, and the modern versions he found awful: 'Jokes about television interrupted by pop songs.' So he went back to the Arabian Nights.

Not having any children himself, he consulted relatives who did, and discovered what cannot have come as a great surprise, that children do not particularly like shows specially written for them. So the author-composer of The Boy Friend and Valmouth set about writing a musical like any other, but far more difficult than most. Difficult because 'everyone knows the story so well' and also because it requires a great number of numbers to tell it at all. 'Eighteen songs - the biggest score I've ever written - plus incidental music.'

Anyway, there it will be at Hammersmith (previews from Friday); an authoritative unpantomimed Aladdin, complete with Genies of Lamp and Ring, wicked Abanazar, simple hero, that least pronounceable of heroines, Princess Badroulbadour, and Aladdin's mother, known since pantomime immemorial as Widow Twankey, but now, as a concession to Chinese realism, christened Twankey-chung. She is played by a man, Joe Melia, an experienced song-and-dance artiste. There is also a wise woman named Fatima, who foretells what's going to happen to Aladdin. Wilson wrote her a number in the first act; then Elizabeth Welsh was cast in the part, so he wrote her one in the second as well.

Wilson was an obvious choice as creator of the first musical entertainment to be seen on the main stage of the new Lyric. His connections with the old Lyric go back a long way. In 1948, soon after coming down from Oxford (where he was part of the Tynan generation, an era copiously recalled in his autobiography, I Could Be Happy) he contributed numbers to a Lyric revue called Oranges and Lemons.

He supported himself as a revue-writer until the production in 1954 (at the Players') of The Boy Friend, the definitive spoof of the twenties musical. Indeed it is one case where a parody has superseded the original. Nobody thinks of reviving The Girl Friend, the Rodgers and Hart show from which Wilson borrowed a title and some elements of plot, or indeed any other of the indistinguishable shows about love in the playgrounds of the rich that were contemporary with it. But The Boy Friend seems always to be in production somewhere.

'It is astonishing that it continues to do so well,' says Wilson, who adds that it's marvellous that he can 'still live the way I like to live' (with comfort, but no particular extravagance) on its proceeds. For a time it also provided him with a second and much-relished career as a director. His own productions of the show extend from a version in Australia to a full-scale London revival in 1967 which proved the show to be still, in its own peculiar kind, a masterpiece.

Wilson's second show, The Buccaneer, was his only attempt at what was then a typical subject (the fifties rash of children's horror-comics) and is accordingly the only one of his shows to have dated. It is also one of his two previous musicals to have premiered in Hammersmith; the other was the much-remembered Valmouth, based on Firbank. It came along in 1958, and demands for its revival have gone on unceasingly since about 1959.

Wilson would like that himself - it's his own favourite among his shows - but he is realistic about the chances. It is, to begin with, an unusually difficult show to cast, requiring more than a dozen stylishly unlikely vocalising hags. Michael Codron cast it marvellously in 1958; Cleo Laine and Fenella Fielding were among the newish faces in the company, and the vivacious Big Best Shoes is still in the Laine repertoire.

More crucial is the question of expense. It is no longer economic to present Wilson's shows in the medium-sized theatres which housed them in the fifties. And in Drury Lane or Her Majesty's they - like all the better British musicals - would be lost.

Despite the discouragements, Wilson has gone on writing book, music and lyrics, a triple proficiency that puts him in the Noel Coward class. (To find an American equivalent you would have to go back to George M. Cohan in the early years of the century.) One show, Divorce Me Darling, which in the sixties took The Boy Friend characters forward to the thirties, was he feels 'a good show ahead of its time.' Then at the beginning of the seventies there was His Monkey Wife, successful at Hampstead and bought by a West End producer who could not, however, raise the money for it. (It makes you wonder when you see some of the things they do raise money for.) More recently there was The Clapham Wonder, a surprisingly sombre piece tried out at Canterbury. Next year there will probably be another show at another regional theatre.

Stirrings in small places suggest that, artistically if not economically, there may be a place again for a British musical that is not just a jaded showbiz juggernaut. This has not really seemed possible since the fifties. It was Wilson who gave us hope then, and it would be fitting if he - like his contemporaries Monty Norman and Julian More, successful with Songbook after a theatrical silence of nearly 20 years - were able again to join the parade.
1979-12-30-false-starts-big-moments:
