False starts--big moments

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Theatre in 1979--a year in which 'few talents have been at their best and some were absent altogether.'

The year 1979 was a bad one for new plays. I remarked on this at half-time and spent the balance waiting to be contradicted by events. Events did not oblige.

My initial outburst was questioned by one leading playwright, who wrote to me saying in effect that I hadn't seen everything, and therefore couldn't possibly know. He had a point (I missed out on the year's offerings from such notables as Snoo Wilson and Stephen Poliakoff), but my pessimism seems to have become contagious. The terribleness of the past year's work has become the current critical orthodoxy.

It has, in fact, been overdone. There have been interesting, even meritorious, plays around on various levels: David Lan's 'Sergeant Ola,' David Mercer's 'Then and Now,' Alan Drury's 'An Empty Desk,' Barrie Keeffe's 'Sus,' Peter Nichols's 'Born in the Gardens,' Roger Hall's 'Middle Age Spread,' Jonathan Gems's 'The Tax Exile.' But they have all been modest pieces, in scale as well as achievement, and it is not surprising that--despite Mr Lan's wit and imagination and Mr Gems's unusual funniness--the world in general remained unaware not only of their quality, but of their existence.

Only two plays actually impinged; and one can be grateful for their presence without feeling particularly enthusiastic about them. The two were Martin Sherman's 'Bent' and Peter Shaffer's 'Amadeus,' each distinguished by sensational subject-matter (a good thing, by the way) and a matching intensity of treatment, each disfigured and finally distorted by sentimentality and special pleading.

Mr Shaffer, after an infinity of false starts, began to develop a riveting case history of artistic jealousy which he proceeded to throw away in what must have seemed higher interests: offering us, instead of Salieri v. Mozart, Salieri v. God, God refusing to put in a personal appearance and thus breaking the back of the play's second act in which endless recitals of Salieri's grievances alternate with chronicle-play enactments of Mozart's last years, these being necessary to the story-line, but irrelevant to the theme.

However, the announcement of that theme at the half-way mark is as thrilling a long speech as has been heard in the theatre since 'Kennedy's Children'; so at least it seems on the lips of Paul Scofield, whose performance--camp comedy rising to gnarled grandeur--is his most entertaining in years, strongly recalling (like the play itself) John Wood's nostalgic tour-de-force in 'Travesties.' Felicity Kendal gives her earthiest and most delightful performance to date as Mrs Mozart, and Simon Callow copes well with the Shaffer-Salieri idea of Mozart as a foul-mouthed infant: an idea which I found perfectly credible (if that matters), but somewhat monotonous. The big moments apart, the most apposite and attractive thing about the play is its operatic structure, with which Peter Hall's production is perfectly at home.

The most encouraging thing about 'Bent' is that it secured a transfer to the West End and stayed there, attracting the young audience which is supposed to have abandoned the commercial theatre ages ago. It suggested that there may yet be a future for producers in putting on plays in which they might conceivably believe--or at least that they may as well go down fighting. With these two plays I should really bracket a third, and a more substantial, piece than either of them, David Edgar's 'Mary Barnes'; it belongs for me to 1978, when it opened in Birmingham. But its arrival in London brought us a stunning performance from Patti Love, ranking with that other Midland import, Jane Lapotaire's Piaf.

The Roundhouse did London a favour by exhibiting three productions from the Manchester Royal Exchange, the best of which ('The Family Reunion') proved another surprise tonic for the West End. The Half Moon, outstanding among fringe theatres, brought us some healthy blasts from the past. I have already mentioned Court; the revivals of three shows at the Royal ('Happy Days' and 'The London Cuckolds') were other credits. The record was patchier than in the preceding year, but since some Sloane Square heroes of the distant past seem to have a vested interest in disparaging the theatre's present, I had better re-state the plain truth, which is that the regime of Stuart Burge and Max Stafford-Clark is the most productive the place has known since the death of George Devine.

The National Theatre, having begun with a brace of disappointments, had a strike which acted, quite by coincidence, as a buffer: nearly everything that happened after it was a distinct improvement on what had gone before. If 'Richard III' was possibly the year's worst Shakespeare production, 'As You Like It' was probably the best. (Nothing at Stratford was as searching or as consistent.) 'Undiscovered Country' was rich.

Michael Rudman's double directorial debut brought fine ensemble work in 'For Services Rendered' (Maugham was actually the playwright of the year) and a flawless solo from Warren Mitchell in 'Death of a Salesman.' John Standing and Anna Massey did comparable work in Simon Gray's fairish 'Close of Play.' The Cottesloe did nothing historic, but nothing bad either, and kept a recognisable company together.

The RSC was weakest at the Warehouse, where the new plays merged into one another, and on the main stage at Stratford, where nothing (except John Woodvine's Malvolio, and maybe the 'Othello,' which I missed) caught fire. Still, the 1978 season hadn't looked too grand in its time, and those shows were mostly splendid when shunted down to the Aldwych, where they were rounded out by the joyous splurge of 'Once in a Lifetime.' The equation was balanced by an excellent year's work at Stratford's Other Place.

Here's a thing: it was a good year for musicals. And not only the old American behemoths, though 'My Fair Lady,' with magic enhanced, was an evening to rank among the thrills of the year (along with 'Lifetime' and 'Salesman'--the last the only one not choreographed by Gillian Lynne). 'Ain't Misbehavin'' was a pleasure; I hated 'Chicago,' but was glad to see it, and even to see it survive; even 'Flowers for Algernon' had its points; 'Hello Dolly' boomeranged on me; I wouldn't have thought that my description of Carol Channing's act as 'one long curtain-call' could have been taken as a compliment, but there it is outside the theatre.

The cheering occasions, though, were small and native: 'Songbook' and 'A Night in the Ukraine' and 'Fearless Frank' and 'Talent' from Victoria Wood, whose own extends in so many directions it's unfair.

Once you start cataloguing particular joys the landscape brightens. But don't be fooled. Few talents have been at their best, and some were absent altogether. That could be chance. But it makes this the gloomiest time imaginable at which to contemplate further financial cuts. These will not result in inferior work being squeezed out. Bad plays will continue to be written and--choosing being the rarest skill of all--to be staged. The good ones will continue to be flukes, nestling in the margin. If a margin still exists.
1980-01-06-richard-rodgers:
Richard Rodgers

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the great songwriter who died last week aged 77.

THE Richard Rodgers catalogue of standard songs extends from 1925 ('Manhattan') to 1951 ('Hello Young Lovers'). He wrote some songs before that period and many after, but that neat quarter-century encloses the work for which he will be remembered: the dazzling series of songs with lyricist Lorenz Hart, and four rock-solid collaborations with Oscar Hammerstein ('Oklahoma!', 'Carousel,' 'South Pacific,' 'The King and I').

Rodgers and Hart produced the best songs, Rodgers and Hammerstein the best shows. Hammerstein was librettist as well as lyricist, and an excellent architect; the added weight in Rodgers's music seemed to derive less from the lyrics than from the concept of the show: the integrated musical with all the songs dependent on the story (though in their last shows, notoriously in 'The Sound of Music' - their engagingly charitable outlook subsided into blandness).

In the Twenties, and especially in the Thirties, Rodgers and Hart turned Manhattan, as they had promised, into an isle of joy. Theirs was the style of the isle; hard-driving, witty, self-mocking, just occasionally passionate. Hart, who was engaged in drinking himself to death, was a very uneven writer, but his best work was superb and brought out the best in Rodgers. 'Thou Swell,' for example, is a joke song and a love song at once.

Rodgers, by contrast, was a survivor. Better than any of his great contemporaries (Kern, Berlin, Gershwin, Porter) he could write music with situation and character, though he had been in business for 25 years before his partnership with Hammerstein gave him the chance. Despite his major break in style, there was one mode at which Rodgers was always a master: he was America's greatest composer of waltzes. No theatrical writer of this century can have given more pleasure to more people.
1980-01-20-defending-a-good-man:
Defending a Good Man

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on plays by Howard Barker and Eugene O'Neill.

HOWARD BARKER'S The Love of a Good Man nipped into the Royal Court for a week, to be greeted with sniffy inquiries from the London reviewers as to just what their colleagues had found to admire in the play on its previous appearances in Sheffield and Oxford.

I happen to have been one of those erring provincials (I saw and praised the Sheffield production), so in defending the play now I am probably trying to justify myself. Bear that in mind. As it happens I share the growing dislike for the kind of play that The Love of a Good Man has generally been taken to be, the kind in which a playwright presents a received view of a Britain which he bothers less and less to check against the facts and which is dressed up in some suspect metaphor, bound to be described by someone as 'a powerful image.'

The Love of a Good Man does end (or at least should end - it goes on too long) with a powerful image: the selection, by a shivery and incontinent Prince of Wales, of an unknown soldier to lie in Westminster Abbey. The ceremony is performed on the field of Passchendaele, two years after the end of the First World War, and it has been rigged. The chosen corpse is German, as likely as not, though a visiting lady has been persuaded that it is not merely English but a particular Englishman: her son.

The undertaker employed to clear the field has fallen heavily for her patrician charms and has promised her to get the body back home. By hard graft and sharp practice he does so - or at least persuades her that he has. Meanwhile the Graves Commissioner has turned his own head into a cemetery; he knows the name of every fallen man, and can recite them alphabetically.

So we have a cult of death-worship, debased almost before it has begun: a campaign, not to make amends to the dead for the futility of their sacrifice, but to glorify it, and to get all the details wrong at that. (The one man who knows them is treated as a madman.) Brutality, nostalgia, snobbery and incompetence: a comprehensive indictment of the native myth, and it sticks. The distanced setting mercifully restrains Mr Barker from any pretence of ruthless realism.

His intrigue has a Jonsonian tang and is carried through with appropriate briskness. The dialogue is often pointedly funny: 'I think,' says Hacker, the sentimental mortician regarding the grief of his beloved, 'if someone made a picture of this, it would sell.' There is, on the other hand, a Lawrentian soldier who goes on about finding women with desire in their hips. But the girl he is leaving to pursue this quest knows he is talking embarrassing rubbish and says so. Mr Barker has the grace to loathe all his characters equally.

The only sympathy extended to them comes in the form of self-disgust, a state attained only by Hacker and the Prince. Ian McDiarmid plays Hacker full out, a jumping scream of anguished propriety; you expect to get tired of him after 10 minutes, but his energy and inventiveness never flag. There may be more to his inamorata than the brittleness discovered and exhibited by Diane Fletcher, but I have my doubts.

Nicolas Kent's production improves on its predecessor in most respects, but fails with royalty. The Prince is played for easy laughs (which are not always forthcoming); at Sheffield he was a pathetic, even poetic, oaf making sad but perfectly earnest attempts to reach his people. Here he patronises and is patronised. For all I know Mr Barker may prefer him played like this, but it robs his play of depth and dimension, and may partly explain why the critics have taken it for another easy attack on undefended targets.

This generation of playwrights has never been good on characterisation, which may partly explain why actors have felt compelled to take the matter into their own hands in improvised shows like Hull Truck's marvellous Ooh La La. That satisfies you as a schematic piece like this can never do. But in Mr Barker's own words, 'there are degrees of badness'; this is quite good as badness goes.

  

O'Neill, in his one-act plays of the sea, now revived as The Long Voyage Home (Cottesloe), worked in the opposite way; he was fiercely particular. He didn't exactly leave us to draw our own conclusions, but he didn't force a philosophy on us either. He showed us, and told us, that life for a merchant seaman at the beginning of the century was appalling. If we wanted to apply the point to life or society in general, that was up to us; though after watching a fresh-faced Swedish sailor shanghaied from a London waterfront pub to an even worst berth than the one he has just left, we may well consider that we have no option.

O'Neill himself was probably still on the way to engulfing pessimism, but this is recognisably the same world he was to show us in The Iceman Cometh (due later this season). Before that abduction - brilliantly handled as melodrama, so that we hope for a last-minute rescue even if we already know the outcome - we have seen meaningless celebration, lonely death and the brutal invasion of desperate secrecy. The episodes don't all add up to good plays, but the cumulative effect is very powerful.

The plays are, for the most part, excellently presented in a style that stops craftily short of naturalism. John Salthouse as the final victim makes touching use of those uniquely vulnerable Scandinavian vowels: a beamish boy snatched from the audience's arms.
1980-01-27-distant-laughter:
Distant laughter

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on new comedies by Ayckbourn, Frayn and Nichols, plus more O'Neill at the National.

THREE OF our four funniest playwrights had new plays on view in a week less riotously amusing than might have been expected.

Alan Ayckbourn won. His Stephen Joseph Theatre in the Round in Scarborough is one of the most important houses in the country, and his Suburban Strains is his most accomplished piece of staging to date. Two concentric revolves have been installed, the actors generally standing in the inner circle while necessary furnishings travel to them on the outer.

Suburban Strains is a musical, though one in which the songs are the least important part; Mr Ayckbourn's lyrics are well placed and technically sound, but they lack spring, while Paul Todd's music is rather tinkly. But the form itself has released something in the playwright. It takes any clinical curse off his accustomed games with time and space. And though his subject-matter remains much the same as before - loneliness and casual cruelty - the approach has opened up. He has tended before to show us relationships so far gone in decay that the participants are too tired to shift or too blind to notice. Here we see the rot starting, the characters struggling. There are even love-scenes.

The central figure is Caroline, a schoolteacher who flees from marriage with an actor, who messes up both her flat and her life, to an affair with a doctor who tries tyrannically to tidy them up. The treatment is generally chronological, but with leaps; moments from the first relationship are frequently recalled, to be juxtaposed with the second. On the outskirts are grimly cheerful dinner-parties and pep-talks from Caroline's appallingly optimistic newsagent dad, backed - in the happiest musical stroke of the evening - by a trio of OAP customers (including one who regularly thumbs through the girlie mags before settling for the Radio Times).

The story is too drawn out (and it was surely a mistake to have the doctor's estranged wife warn Caroline what he would do to her, rather than letting her and us discover for ourselves), but both the dialogue and the observation are unflagging. Lavinia Bertram is sweet and spirited as Caroline, and Alison Skilbeck - a regular Scarborough ornament - delivers, punctually, a varied quartet of Mr Ayckbourn's saddest sacks.

  

A government inspector arrives at the end of Michael Frayn's Liberty Hall (Greenwich), and the title may also put you in mind of She Stoops to Conquer, which is among other things a comedy of class-and-role-reversal. Liberty Hall ends with a positive riot of this, a Feast of Misrule: pure comedy. That's the theory, anyway.

The reversal that underlies all the others is based on an historical fancy; we are asked to assume that the 1917 Revolution happened not in Russia but in Britain. Twenty years on, Balmoral Castle is a holiday-home for State-approved writers. Four are in residence; their names are Warwick Deeping, Enid Blyton, Godfrey Winn and Hugh Walpole. Walpole, unpopular with the others for having grabbed the only warm room, expires and must be replaced so that he may be interviewed by a visiting representative of the Tsarist Press.

The entire Balmoral staff - consisting of a butler named McNab - is pressed into impersonating him. Rikki Fulton plays both Walpole and McNab, and the substitution, when as far as we can see the dead body is still on stage with its legs protruding from a cabin-trunk, is wondrously well managed in Alan Dosser's production. McNab, glazed, drunken, and blinking behind Walpole's thick glasses, proceeds to take full advantage of his new position; and Mr Fulton, with much assistance from his author, takes full advantage of McNab.

The conventions of stage disguise are wittily spoofed as the new Hugh relates just what he said to his butlering self at breakfast that morning. This middle section of the play is golden, but the sequel is forced and the preamble protracted. The mechanism hangs heavy; it is difficult to believe in science-fiction when it already hasn't happened.

Besides, the three supporting writers become positively irritating, so little is done with them; and it is far from clear why they participate in the charade, since they all dislike the Balmoral Warden, whose face they are being asked to save. He too is kept around with nothing much to do until the end; at which point George Cole does his considerable best with what is, by now, mechanical writing. Oliver Cotton has a stylish go at the Russian, and Jill Meager a bright one at his conscientious young escort from the Board of Trade.

  

Peter Nichols's Born in the Gardens (Globe) is, as its author wryly acknowledges en route, a state-of-England play. When done last year at the Bristol Old Vic it was also a state-of-Bristol play, and this was the aspect on which the local audience seized most enthusiastically and infectiously. For its London transfer the piece has understandably been trimmed of many of these references, but the unfortunate result has been to leave both play and audience in limbo.

This is the one in which brother Hedley, a Labour backbencher, and sister Queenie, now a Californian journalist, return to persuade other brother Mo and mother Maud out of their shared rut. Mo and Maud live in a Tudor mansion; she talks to the television and about the Michaelwave oven, he to his cat and about jazz. Their plight is compared to that of Alfred, Bristol Zoo's home-grown gorilla, who died happily in captivity.

I am less sure than everyone else seems to be that Mr Nichols approves of his characters' obstinate desire to be left to a similar fate; Hedley, the welfare statesman, facing similar defeats at home and at large ('offer them heaven on earth and they throw it back in your face') seems to me a character drawn with both sympathy and wit. But the conclusion is long foregone and this (certainly at a second viewing) weighs the play down; it has to subsist on Maud's eccentricities, which become mere running gags. Beryl Reid runs them.

  

For all they are worth, I thought her extravagant in Bristol, but I was probably wrong. Anyway she's perfect now. Barry Foster, in an unusual role for him, and Peter Bowles, in a usual one, are, as before, excellent.

The last time I saw The Iceman Cometh (which he doth again soon) I felt this was the underside of Runyon's underworld: bare bums. Hughie, the latest and briefest instalment in the Cottesloe's run-up to that marathon pub-crawl, brings the comparison more firmly home. Hughie is a deceased hotel night-clerk; Erie Smith - small-time gambler, small-time everything - pours out his heart to Hughie's taciturn successor, boasting not just about his past triumphs (illusory, we assume), but about his past boasts. He patronised Hughie, his one-time audience, but obviously was in piteous need of him: so much becomes rapidly, subtly clear.

This is a rich little piece, full of atmosphere, if lacking as always in verbal zing. ('When I say she was plain I'm giving her all the breaks,' the best O'Neill can do, places him pretty low in the ranks of New York humourists.) Stacy Keach's Erie cannot be faulted except for its carefulness; you expect a visiting American star to be a bigger spender. Hayden Griffin has designed a marvellously dispirited hotel lobby; Howard Goorney's mousy clerk looks like part of the furniture. He seems less at home when he opens his mouth, but that doesn't happen often.

More male camaraderie, much louder, in David Williamson's The Club (Hampstead), which is about backroom intrigues in Australian football. There is a funny but irrelevant pot-smoking scene. Ron Haddrick, as the unwary smoker, gives a performance of some distinction; the best you can say of the other bullies is that they're forceful.
1980-01-27-taking-up-the-baton:
Taking up the baton

ROBERT CUSHMAN talks to actor-manager Timothy West, who opens in London this week in Beecham.

TIMOTHY WEST believes that the cinema doesn't know what to do with him: 'My trouble is that I don't play the parts I look like.' What he looks like is teddy-bearish, most of the time anyway. At present he sports a goatee which makes him look like a minor Mephistopheles: a laughing devil.

It has been grown as a necessary adornment to his performance as Sir Thomas Beecham, opening officially at the Apollo Theatre on Tuesday. Written by Caryl Brahms and Ned Sherrin, it is not quite a play, not quite a one-man show; he shares the chat with a narrator. It is of course the latest in the West line of historical portraits, following his Churchill and Edward VII on television and his Oliver Cromwell on radio, not to mention a superb Oscar Wilde at the Open Space.

'People think you have a special talent for something because you've done it before.' He cites the case of Ian Richardson, approached to play Anthony Blunt after his success in Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy: 'They've decided he plays moles.'

There have obviously been peculiar problems involved with Beecham and Churchill, both well-remembered public figures; the actor - especially since the scripts are generally as much documentary as drama - has to have a touch of Mike Yarwood about him. West says himself that 'it's much more a graph-paper, and geometrical instrument kind of thing than ordinary acting. Beecham is actually not a terribly different problem from Churchill - they're both easily imitable men. Both, one might add, self-created enfants terribles, though the actor warms to Beecham, sympathises with him, more readily than with Churchill.

There have been only two major technical difficulties with Beecham. One is the voice: 'Beecham's delivery was so slow that you couldn't reproduce it accurately' without, presumably, lulling the audience to sleep. (West, as it happens, is a noticeably crisp, fast actor). The other is the conducting itself; sometimes it looked as if Beecham wasn't doing anything at all up there. But West doesn't think the audience would take that from an actor: 'They need to be assured that you know the rudiments of what you're doing, so I do more than Beecham did.'

Though happy with Edward VII in particular, West would admit that bio-drama is, at best, a sub-division of acting. That he should recently have done so much of it is a pointer to the peculiar position in which he has recently found himself. At 45, he is a TV star and a theatrical leader.

There are few actors who command more respect within the profession, both for his work and for his grasp of the theatre as a whole; art and business. But his recent theatrical roles have been modest: Claudius in Hamlet, the Doctor in A Month in the Country, Enobarbus in Antony and Cleopatra, Judge Brack in Hedda Gabler - all pivotal and rewarding parts, but none of them major challenges to an actor who eight years ago was an admired Lear.

Reviewing the Claudius - the most exciting of those performances, with a genuine sense of danger about it - I called him 'a supercompetent actor,' a description which I gather both amused and worried him. He admits that 'I'm somebody who demands quite a lot of good acting around me, and quite a lot of thoughtful direction. Left to myself, I have a facility for producing something that is serviceable.'

After his Lear, an actor told me that 'Timmy wants to go to Hollywood and be Rod Steiger.' That didn't happen; what did was a season as artistic director at the Forum Theatre, Billingham, acting in one play and directing three others. He discovered that he liked directing and enjoyed having some control of his own destiny.

Since then he has had a spell on the Arts Council Drama Panel and has been a co-director of the Prospect, now the Old Vic, Theatre Company. At the end of last year, on the resignation of Toby Robertson, he took over the direction of the company. He had in fact been asked to step in for a year's emergency rescue, but declined to take the job for less than two. Otherwise he would have no chance of implementing his own policies.

So for the last couple of months Old Vic plans have chased Beecham's scores and witticisms round his head. For the time being the Vic will be filled by visiting companies. (One aim is 'to revive, in some way, the World Theatre Season.') In September his first homegrown season begins with Macbeth, with Peter O'Toole ('very keen to be included: an artistic associate'), The Jew of Malta, directed by Jack Gold, West's own productions of Trelawny of the Wells and The Relapse.

West is the first man I have heard enunciate a feeling which many share but which he himself would have argued against three years ago, which is that he refuses to make a fetish of new writing. 'Nobody can tell us anything new; there are no icons left to be attacked. The writing is on the wall, in words of one syllable 10 feet high. In times like this the classics become especially precious.'

But they have to be presented properly, and he admits that 'a lot of our recent work has emerged looking a bit careless.' He will not, I think, be satisfied if after two years Prospect's reputation remains as obstinately behind that of the large companies as it has, to date. Because he is now, unarguably, an actor-manager running a company with a major touring commitment, he has been repeatedly compared to Donald Wolfit. But the comparison hardly holds. Wolfit always played the lead and never cared much about production standards or supporting playing.

Tim - I am tired of calling him West, which sounds quite unsuitably brusque - is a shrewd, sly judge of acting, who is likely not to play enough leads. He has had recent tucked-away attempts at Macbeth and Falstaff and found them discouraging. On the other hand he recognises that the public expect a certain amount of activity from their favoured players, and that this must include a few attempts on the peaks. His idol, unastonishingly, is Ralph Richardson, who has expressed himself in similar fashion on the perils of mountaineering, and whom he admires for attaining truth through eccentricity.

Tim is not an eccentric actor, though he can certainly play eccentrics. What distinguishes him is an odd combination of weight and roguishness. Other actors alternate between feet-on-ground and head-in-clouds; he can do both at once.

He has, on and off the stage, impeccable comic timing, an attribute shared with his wife, Prunella Scales, and indeed with his father, Lockwood West, who, in the juicy role of a crafty old malcontent, is the best reason for listening to Wagner's Walls.

Despite his theatrical parentage, Timothy West hesitated a few years, pretending he didn't want to be an actor. He was a recording engineer before taking the plunge. The delay didn't seem to do him any harm. To whatever he has done, he has always come well prepared.
1980-02-03-king-ramaz:
King Ramaz

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the Rustaveli Company, Brecht, 'Oklahoma!' and 'Beecham.'

THE Georgian Richard III, widely proclaimed as earth-shattering at last year's Edinburgh Festival, has arrived at the Roundhouse and has predictably proved to be merely very exciting.

The Rustaveli Company's most exotic adornment, to our eyes, is the bull-like force of its players combined, in the case of Ramaz Chkhikvadze's Richard, with a harsh wit. He is not a self-pitying Richard, though, since the production has his destroyer Richmond dogging his footsteps from the first, he might have some excuse for concern. He is not even particularly crippled, though he displays an impressively withered arm when the plot calls for it. He is a burly figure in a grey Napoleonic greatcoat and high black boots. His voice is mournful, with an ache in it. He seems driven neither by ambition nor villainy; he is a conscious agent of doom.

The second most spectacular actor is Avto Makharadze, a gash-mouthed player who supplies a joke-archbishop and a choric jester as appendages to a dying, suppurating Edward IV, a sick toad. There are interesting performances too among the courtiers: Buckingham is trim and gentlemanly, a chill time-server from the first. The council-scenes have the deadly, conscienceless efficiency for which British productions used to strive in the Sixties when Jan Kott was God.

But those productions were sleek and picturesque. The peculiar interest of these Georgian plottings is that they take place in an atmosphere of decay. Costumes are mixed modern, props are few and dilapidated. This too is a style familiar to us--more perhaps from other visitors than from native productions--but it is unusual to see it combined with political clarity. The pervasive mockery is as much aural as visual: a fiddler pops up to accompany the wooing of Lady Anne. There are occasional bursts of rock-music to accompany the more violent turns of action; other moments are underlined by a rottingly sweet Palm Court tune that seems always about to turn into the Pineapple Song from Cabaret.

Richard and Richmond fight their last duel with their heads popping out of a map of England; the kingdom is otherwise represented by a dirty Union Jack. Shakespeare is telescoped, so that Richard briefs the murderers as Clarence tells his dream; this kind of juxtaposition still seems to me the most fruitful form of Shakespearean distortion. But in fact very little damage is done to the values of the play, and its language of course was forfeit anyway.

Doubts occur when Robert Sturua's production fails to work in its own terms. Queen Margaret as an avenging chorus stage-managing the other characters is a logical extension of her role in the original; the idea falters because she is not very strikingly played. And of course the last third of the play is suffused in irony (hands up, incidentally, anyone who was not relieved at the despatch of the entire Bosworth sequence in 10 minutes), but the smirking clown who personifies fate and retribution is kitsch in any language.

Other arms reach out to me, other eyes smile tenderly, but Georgia remains on my mind.

  

The RSC production of The Caucasian Chalk Circle (Warehouse) fails to clear the play's notorious first hurdle: the actors playing peasants debating the proper fate of their valley seem dutiful, but unconvinced. Clive Merrison, as the presiding expert, sounds notably relieved when the play-within-the-play starts up and he inquires nervously as to its length; here at last is a subject he can identify with.

There were times when I shared his apprehension (Brecht liked his audiences to be physically comfortable, and there's small chance of that here), but a mostly excellent company proceed, under John Caird's direction, to give a good relaxed account of the play. Doubling becomes its own pleasure; one particularly looks forward to seeing Kenny Ireland's dim squaddie act or Charlotte Cornwell, flintily correct behind her mask, as the governor's wife. Kenneth Colley is a sharp narrator; Roger Sloman leads the soldiers whose barometrically shifting loyalties are possibly the richest stratum of the play: human nature seen face to ugly face.

Of the two leads Jane Carr's Grusha has a cockney directness that wins many laughs and even, at the end, the odd tear; it only seems out of place in the doggedly convoluted dialogue with which she confronts her lover. Alun Armstrong's Azdak by contrast is northern-urban: too lightweight to carry the philosopher side of the role (I remember Leo McKern on television becoming, orientally contemplative), but professionally adept in the clowning. The judicial topsy-turviness is a delight and he charts a remarkably clear course through the tugs of conscience that eventually determine Grusha's fate and his own. Stephen Oliver's melodious score adds considerably to a notably undogmatic evening.

  

It has been a musical week. Oklahoma! (Haymarket, Leicester) is in a sense beyond criticism. One would be hard put to judge the merits of these songs; they are a part of life. Still, at least one of Rodgers's tunes (the waltz, Out of My Dreams) is a masterpiece in or out of the theatre, and none is ineffective. Hammerstein's lyrics seem, to a late believer, perfect.

What gives the show theatrical body is the theme behind the love story. A cowboy is united with a farmhouse heiress, as the rivalry that breaks out in the square-dance brawl ("the farmer and the cowman should be friends") gives way to the irresistible affirmation of the title-song. Performance of this has become stereotyped; the waving wheat can sure smell sweet, but do all arms still have to sweep up every time it's mentioned?

There is still something tentative about the production (which begins its national tour this week at the New Theatre, Oxford): is Curly telling himself that it's a beautiful mornin', or Aunt Eller (good old Madge Ryan) who's on stage with him, or the audience? John Diedrich, though he ripens considerably later on, seems uncertain. Laurey, the heroine, is very English, the ballet-dancers' lumbering (though the bucolic numbers are fun) and though Alfred Molina acts, sings and dances well, he cannot explain, despite some Steigerish inflections, why Jud Fry is supposed to be so instantly dislikeable.

Not all the anecdotes assembled by Caryl Brahms and Ned Sherrin can fend off a growing suspicion that Beecham (Apollo) was a pill, appealing to the same English philistinism he professed to deride. I also doubt if his verbal timing was as good as Timothy West's; I sometimes wondered if anybody's ever was. This immaculate performance dusts Paul Scofield's Salieri as the best piece of stand-up comedy on the London stage. Two moments at the end are very touching: the conductor's statement at a children's concert that Mozart wrote the ensuing piece "when he was about your age, sir" (there is no catch in the voice, but suddenly gravity descends) and the sight of his hands fluttering professionally as the lights finally go down.
1980-02-10-war-murders-and-gods:
War, murders and gods

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'The Greeks.'

Despite the physical magnitude of the enterprise, John Barton's stated aims in his 10-play cycle, The Greeks (Aldwych), are modest: to retell the story of the Trojan war, as scattered across the surviving corpus of Greek drama, and to capture on a stage the spirit of Euripides, original author of seven of the 10 instalments.

He has succeeded magnificently in both. The story first: Part One, The War, begins with Euripides's 'Iphigenia in Aulis,' in which the Greek general Agamemnon sacrifices his daughter to the gods in exchange for a wind to blow his ships to Troy. Next comes 'Achilles,' Mr Barton's own adaptation of Homer, plugging the gaps that the playwrights left open; we see Agamemnon's quarrel with Achilles, the latter's consequent sulk, and his re-emergence to kill the Trojan champion Hector. Then the most familiar of all the plays, 'The Trojan Women.' Troy has been taken (destroyed, as in all RSC productions, by saturation attacks of dry ice) and its men killed. The women, led by Queen Hecuba, await their departure into slavery. We witness the killing of Hector's child, torn from the arms of his mother Andromache, to have his brains dashed out. This is the single most appalling act in the play, maybe in all drama; the other murders are acts of revenge, self-defence, perverted piety. This one is undertaken for cold reasons of state, and it can symbolise all the crimes that were ever committed in a national interest.

Part Two, The Murders, commences with 'Hecuba.' The queen has not been ennobled by suffering (it's difficult to think of anyone in these plays who is); she puts out the eyes of a Thracian king who killed her last surviving son. There follows Aeschylus's 'Agamemnon,' in which the returning hero is killed by his wife, Clytemnestra, partly in retaliation for the death of Iphigenia; and Sophocles's 'Electra,' showing Clytemnestra's death at the hands of her children Electra and Orestes.

In Part Three, The Gods, the jokers are dealt. In 'Helen,' the beautiful casus belli proves never to have been at Troy; an insubstantial look-alike took her place while she languished in Egypt, sunbathing on a sarcophagus, waiting to be rescued by her puzzled husband. (He duly arrives.) In 'Orestes,' Clytemnestra's assassins go berserk, killing Helen and threatening her daughter; chaos is averted by the descent of a smoothly double-talking Apollo, dealing out inconclusive happy endings. 'Andromache' reveals a bereaved heroine who has graduated beyond grief, and reunites a bewildering variety of characters. Finally 'Iphigenia in Tauris' pulls the rug from beneath the first calamity; Iphigenia was miraculously saved and is reunited with her brother, Orestes. The ending is qualified joy.

I must depend for my knowledge of Euripides on what translators tell me. Mr Barton and his literary collaborator, Kenneth Cavander, offer us a Euripides flip, angry, puzzled, enduring; never serene or piously accepting. This coincides with the view expressed by similarly enthusiastic scholars; and come to that with the baffled distaste of some others. I do not doubt that Mr Barton (quite apart from writing-in lengthy bits of his own) has gone beyond his author in some respects. Euripides seems to me to have written Helen as a housewife forced into the role of a siren; Mr Barton does her the other way round. It doesn't matter much. Either Mr Barton has reclaimed an extraordinary playwright, or he has invented one. Either way it's an achievement. And to have revealed so much of him within one piece of work; that really leaves you gasping.

The guest-shots by Aeschylus and Sophocles are the least successful (the famous scenes of pride and retribution are not lampooned, but there is little heart in them), so the resident writer is left unchallenged. Mr Barton has remorselessly ironed out narrative inconsistencies, but contradictions of tone and thought abound. The plays were written at various stages of a long career, and Euripides changed his mind.

But it is this quality of a sustained meditation that provides the power. There are shocking dislocations; finding Iphigenia alive at the end throws the whole experience into startling jeopardy; it is as if everything has happened, but nothing has. And seen in perspective the contrasts even out; the farcical mayhem of 'Orestes' and 'Andromache' (which are very advanced plays indeed) is no further from pure tragedy than the spectacle of the mad bitch Hecuba on all fours with her sightless quarry. And both follow logically from the reasoned killings of the first plays.

The progression of cause and effect is remorseless. 'Who is to blame?' ask the chorus in the very first line, and they're talking about the creation of the world. Different speakers blame different gods, and so it goes throughout. In fact when Apollo arrives and says to Orestes, 'What you did was right, and what Electra did was right,' he is, for all his infuriating silkiness, talking sense. There are no answers, and belief in the gods merely removes the uncertainty to another plane. To the familiar 'until he is dead call no man happy,' we might add, 'or miserable either.' Until they die people survive.

As adaptation 'The Greeks' is superior to (as well as more necessary than) Mr Barton's previous essay, 'The Wars of the Roses.' As production it is less accomplished -- which is forgiveable; there is no tradition to work from. The over-riding virtue is lucidity: The brandings and the clanking fetters of 'The Trojan Women' are the most memorable effects. The costumes begin classical and end modern; I found I could accept anachronism when it was comic (Helen's handbag and suntan oil for example), but not when it was designed to nudge me into noticing a perfectly obvious contemporary parallel (viz, Orestes and Electra as terrorists).

John Shrapnel excels himself as the vacillating Agamemnon and as Apollo, whose delivery suggests both a Python parody and Mr Shrapnel's own experience in the voice-over market. Janet Suzman's Helen (dismissing Aphrodite, purse-lipped, as 'sick and sexually obsessed') is brilliant, but her emoting as Clytemnestra, like Mike Gwilym's as Orestes and Billie Whitelaw's as Andromache, is routine. (I know that's hard, but so are the plays.) Eliza Ward's Hecuba bites as hard as she is bitten, Tony Church is a good fluffy Menelaus, and Peter Holmes as a messenger is a pleasant surprise. Lynn Dearth's uncompromising stridency is right for Electra, but it goes on.

In the long line of unfortunate princesses I also noted Deirdra Morris's Polyxena (in love with death, an interesting variant) and Avril Carson's flighty Hermione. The Chorus speak singly and, despite some atrocious individual readings, have never been so easy to listen to. The last play, done up in furs, is probably meant to remind us of that other enigmatic comedy of reconciliation, 'The Winter's Tale,' but the final dance that should tie it up is sadly below par.

I've left out too much. So has Mr Barton; there are at least three other plays he might have included. But we should both have time to make amends. This show should be around for years.
1980-02-17-lousy-sausages:
Lousy sausages

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN returns to Greek territory.

IN Steven Berkoff's Greek (Half Moon) a London couple are warned by a fairground gypsy that their son Eddie will grow up to kill his father and make love to his mother.

So, when he is a young man, Eddie is cast out from the room in which he has been accustomed to curl up with available girls or Stan Kenton records. Deciding against flying abroad he strays into a cafe, gets into a fight with the manager, kills him, and dutifully sets about consoling the widow.

From his new position of catering eminence he rises to great wealth, incidentally dispelling the plague which is ravaging the city, if not the country, at the time, and which he sums up as 'sloth, inertia, lousy sausages.' Later he kills a sphinx which seems to represent militant feminism. After this he rather belatedly invites Mum and Dad over. They reveal that he is not really their son; they found him. Their description of the finding leaves Eddie's lady in no doubt that he is actually her long-lost. Eddie declines to blind himself.

Some of this must sound familiar. The sharp-eyed, though, will have spotted at least one crucial, and destructive, departure from the Sophoclean source. It was Oedipus's real parents who heard the prophecy, and accordingly abandoned him. His adoptive ones would have had nothing to fear. The story no longer makes sense; the plague is no longer linked to royal guilt. In Mr Berkoff's scheme there is no guilt, and no king. The plague is just there; and it is unlikely that a restaurateur, however virile, could have such power over it.

And what is a sphinx doing in London, apart from providing a gloss on the values of the new version? Eddie's answer to her riddle again departs from tradition. Man goes on three legs in the evening not because he is old and needs a stick, but because he has an erection. That's potent enough to finish off any sphinx.

Mr Berkoff cleverly directs a cast of four who sit white-faced round a table and play everybody in Mr Berkoff's own style; Barry Philips as Eddie is a particularly trenchant surrogate. As author, Mr Berkoff (writing, as in East, in joky blank verse) has an equally firm control of sexual and scatological imagery and rarely--apart from an entertaining sequence about the difficulty of getting your coffee and cheesecake served at the same time--tries anything else.

Sometimes he decides it's time to write lyrically and at great length about love; Mr Philips then drops his Cockney and starts talking what used to be known as BBC, which is a dead giveaway. (It's strange--well no it isn't--how apt our supposedly revolutionary theatre workers are to come up with literary drama at its deadliest.) There are odd spurts of self-pity, but at least there is none of that compassion nonsense with which other writers are inclined to fill the occasional holes in their aggression.

Greek, being skilled, was, mind you, the brightest thing of the London week.

  

Before glancing at the surrounding debris I feel like expressing my bewilderment over the reception of the longer Athenian business at the Aldwych. John Barton, unlike Mr Berkoff, had me recanting my lifelong prophylactic against pretentiousness ('Beware of gifted directors bearing Greeks'), but others seem to have resisted, and for odd reasons.

In the New Statesman Benedict Nightingale described Helen as 'a superfluous anecdote' and blamed Mr Barton for including it. He might more straightforwardly have blamed Euripides for writing it. But he did write it; therefore it formed part of his vision of the Trojan War, the vision that this production is supposed to be presenting to us. Nor is it true that, as James Fenton said in the Sunday Times, 'the idea that the Helen of Troy was a wraith postdates most of the plays which we are shown and contradicts their spirit.' It was Euripides's Electra, written--according to textbooks to hand--a year earlier, makes explicit mention of it.

And why does Mr Fenton call Helen a satyr-play? Satyr-plays are quite easily recognisable; they have choruses of satyrs. We have one Euripidean example, the ripely farcical Cyclops, which also counts as part of the Trojan story and which Mr Barton might well include next time round. It would in no way spoil the painful emotion of, say, The Trojan Women; I fail to see how, once you have been moved, anything can take the experience away from you. To be able to sustain two emotions simultaneously is a sign of maturity; must we assume that the Greeks couldn't manage it?

  

Two more recent foreign classics have been dismally treated. Goldoni's Country Life (Lyric, Hammersmith) is the tripartite comedy about romantic entanglements turning bitter on vacation, which was patchily but powerfully done at the Glasgow Citizens' last year. This production uses the Glasgow translation (by Robert David Macdonald), which is a trap. It mingles standard archaisms with camp quotations, ranging from Polonius's 'wrung from me my slow leave' to Beatrice Lillie's 'two dozen double damask dinner napkins.' It requires either complete innocence on the part of its performers or total command.

David Giles's cast flounder somewhere between the two, with the exception of Ellen Pollock, who battles through as an Italian Lady Wishfort. Julia Foster also has one poignant moment of direct address to the audience. The pace is brisk but, through lack of underpinning, still gives the impression of sloth.

  

Paul Marcus's production of Hauptmann's The Weavers (Roundhouse) seems slow because it is: an apparently demoralised cast leave nervous pauses before every speech. The play deals--in terms which a brace of hectoring programme notes think is naturalistic, but they can't quite be sure--with a workers' uprising in Silesia in the 1840s. They're downtrodden all right; they live in pits sunk into the stage, which means the audience never get to see or hear them properly, and they are hardly livelier when they get to walk about. But the production is even-handed and allows the oppressors to be every bit as tedious.

  

There are some colourless performances in Marcel Achard's Rollo (Royal Exchange, Manchester), but with Leo McKern in the driving seat this 20-year-old comedy still puts on a good turn of speed. Mr McKern, bubbling over as a character and superbly controlled as an actor, plays a life-long failure whose survival depends on his envious contempt for a rich school-friend. He finds the friend to be his daughter's seducer: splendid, now he has the man at his mercy. But he cannot decide what to do with him once he is there; having your enemy on his knees soon palls.

The play spends a little too long running on the same sore spot, but it produces a good many nervous twinges along with the laughs, and Mr McKern, with Jack Hedley as his cool antagonist, floods every defeat and every triumph with comic energy.
1980-02-24-belfast-songsters:
Belfast songsters

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

STEWART PARKER'S Catchpenny Twist (King's Head) has the first mortar-opening number I have ever heard.

On this occasion the performers are three teachers in end-of-term drag, the headmaster, thanking them for their 'mirthful mouthfuls, their witty ditties,' refers to them as 'masters and mistress of terpsichore and rhyme,' and may be excused for having other things on his mind; his school is in Belfast.

He loses three of his staff straight off. The lady, Monagh, goes to Dublin to become a club singer; the two gents, Roy and Martin, try to make it in Belfast as songwriters. While waiting for the big break they knock out, on commission, a few commemorative verses on fallen Provisionals. This proves tricky for them, partly because the fallen have names like Quigley, which are difficult to rhyme, partly because they are doing similar hackwork for Protestants.

Reprisals are threatened, so they take off for Dublin, where they resume their partnership with Monagh. Like Crosby, Hope and (toujours) Lamour, they are soon on the road again, first to London, where they almost pick up a recording contract, and then to a Euro songfest, where their past picks them up. (Bob and Bing used to proclaim that 'Paramount will protect us 'cos we're signed for five more years.' No such luck here.)

Mr Parker writes with a smouldering joviality that is very attractive, and his storytelling skill has greatly increased. But his play is to an extent the victim of its own inevitability. His characters are so plainly foredoomed that what they do en route, or even who they are, seems immaterial. Their deaths cannot really be blamed on their being apolitical; we know the committed also cop it.

There are diversions along the way. We see our heroes creating, Martin knocking out the rhymes with a facility that might even arouse the envy of Sammy Cahn. We hear some of their songs, though they work in a watery ballad style too pallid to be parodied; Mr Parker and his composer, Shaun Davey, have much more fun with the German telesong entry, Zig Zag Zong (put over with delightful idiot relish by Tony Doyle). Roy and Monagh have an affair, and Monagh is said to be in love with a television producer emblematically named Playfair. (Trusted by both factions, he still goes to his grave.) But we never meet him and Monagh herself never mentions him; she shapes up dramatically as yet another self-destructive chanteuse.

There is some stiff supporting work, but the main trio are fine: Bryan Murray chipper, Tony Scannell tense and glowering, and Nichola McAuliffe vibrantly depressive. Robert Gillespie's production - monumentally lavish by King's Head standards - is quick and careful.

  

Frances de la Tour made some kind of fringe history the night I saw Duet for One (Bush) by getting around entrance applause, though who could be sure whether this was due to her television stardom, her theatrical cult status, or the fact that she entered in a wheelchair? Anyway, as things turned out, she deserved it. She plays a violinist stricken by multiple sclerosis, and dispatched to a psychiatrist by her glamorously talented musician husband. 'I can be sarcastic,' she warns the doctor unnecessarily; and much of the play, as the lady tries to sound practical and uncaring about her plight, finds Miss de la Tour at her most bright and waspish.

When her facade finally cracks, the effect is electric; and the author, Tom Kempinski, caps her tirade with another, in which the psychiatrist (played with unnerving accuracy by David de Keyser) begs her not to fall into the fight-for-life line. The play is biased towards him; we absorb his disease-wise charm, which occasionally he obliges, only by flying into jargon ('we're talking punk-rock') or syntactical impossibilities ('for your cynical information'). I also felt let down at the time by an equivocal end; in retrospect it seems fair.

  

The early Elizabethans were not good at women. (They were not, for the most part, good at men either, but they felt less compunction about stuffing them with Marlovian rhetoric.) So Marlowe's Zenocrate is a study in depth compared with the heroine of George Peele's David and Bethsabe (brought by the Riding Lights Theatre of York to the Upstream Theatre, opposite the Young Vic), which is unfortunate for the play when all King David's troubles (rebellious sons, etc.) are meant to spring from his guilty liaison. But Peele's textbook reputation as an undramatic lyricist is here belied; it is true he could hardly stop talking, but he could move a narrative along in bald strokes.

This production is done in modern dress, which lends a certain tickle to the battle scenes between Israel and Egypt. These are curiously staged (the opponents clap hands and dance tangos), but when the bits of production stop, the actors get on with it vigorously enough. I doubt if this heralds a full-scale Peele revival, but his strange folk-comedy The Old Wives' Tale - so naive as to seem furiously experimental - would be worth the attention of any company aiming to involve and bemuse its audience.
1980-03-02-our-old-friend-enoch:
Our old friend Enoch

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on new plays by Howard Barker, Nigel Williams and Philip Martin.

HOWARD BARKER'S new one, The Loud Boy's Life (Warehouse), takes us back six or seven years to the days when no fringe playlet was complete without an impersonation of Enoch Powell.

In this production the familiar turn is done by Hugh Fraser, who captures admirably the fateful braying tones and the pedantic periods, as of a thinking man's brimstone preacher. As it happens Mr Fraser is not the evening's Powell figure, but only a madman who thinks he is, having found the Napoleon beat to be overpopulated.

The man he imitates is Ezra Fricker, played by Clive Merrison, who nobly refrains from obtrusive mannerisms. He develops an anthropoid hunch of the shoulders and a thick, oily manner of speech, but nothing you could hang a writ on; if his performance remains uncharacteristically lifeless, it could be because he is attempting to play from the inside a role that has not been provided with any.

We first see Ezra as the guest of honour at a society of industrialists, lawyers, novelists and other reactionaries, who want him to take over the country on their behalf, he being "the loud boy," the only Tory with popular support. He refuses, largely it seems because it's past his bedtime.

Flashback to the war: Ezra is just out of college and into uniform, picnicking in Greenwich Park with a party of Fascist sympathisers, watching the docks burn and failing to be seduced by a friend's wife. The fighting done, he finds she no longer wants him and, what's more, has become a Communist. He vows vengeance, in the form of political success.

Flash-forward to his one chance of achieving it. The country is in crisis, the people shouting for Fricker. A top-secret, top-Cabinet meeting decides by a majority of three to two not to offer him the leadership. (A lady who resembles Mrs Thatcher is particularly anti.) He hears the news while opening a fete in the gardens of a mental hospital, and declines to go back to London and try force. Last scene of all: his ashes lie in state in St Paul's and people pay tribute, or not, according to their predilections.

Ezra's refusal of arbitrary power -- in the name of legality, parliamentary democracy and catching the last bus home -- seems to me entirely to his credit, but Mr Barker's tone, which is scornful, does not persuade me that this is the point of the play. The trouble is, he can't work up a dramatically justified hatred either.

Every reviewer in London has pointed out the gaping flaw, but even every reviewer in London can be right. To wit: The action rests on Ezra's supposed popularity, and we are never shown a reason for it. Mr Barker may retort that we already know, but the play lasts nearly three hours and that is a long time not to be told things. Mr Powell's appeal rested less on racism than on the belief that he had the guts to say unpalatable things. That belief may well have been mistaken, but it must have stemmed from something. Ezra, who speaks in meaningless generalities when he speaks at all, gives no clue. His wife hates him, by the way, and much is made, yet again, of the discovery that conservatives have sexual hang-ups.

The irritant is that the play contains some of Mr Barker's best writing. The play of wills, the icy contempt, of the secret caucus, is brilliant -- as is the indifference of the caretaker who lets them in and out. (There, for a moment, is political analysis dramatised.) The club dinner goes on and on, but it includes a glistening Donald Sumpter as an author squirming on the table, mimicking a housewife on heat. A female infiltrator points out the dreadful misogyny of all this; we are unlikely not to have noticed for ourselves, but at least her interruption, like the whole scene, is well orchestrated.

Ezra defying fate by aiming darts at the ace of spades is another strong moment. Howard Davies's production, though more than a bit portentous, makes the most of all of them. The various ladies are well chiselled by Jill Baker, Cheryl Hall and Mateylok Gibbs. Mr Barker, though, is throttling himself. Perhaps he was drawn to Ezra by their common inability to believe that an enemy could be worth understanding.

  

Nigel Williams's Trial Run (Young Vic) is also rather suicidal. Two Asians, victims of official mistreatment, hold two salesgirls, a student and a Securicor man prisoner in the basement of Woolworths. We are all guilty of looking the other way from, for example, the Southall disturbances, at which one captor was run in for assaulting a policeman; and the two intruders put the security guard, in himself a totally inoffensive teenager, on mock trial for our crimes.

There is enough generalised truth in this, and enough specific nonsense, to keep us interested; there is also, with guns being waved around and the police laying siege, built-in suspense. But the trial hardly ever gets going; one jailer is too furious and the other, mocking his own racial stereotyping ("oh golly gosh"), too fond of the sound of his own voice. His tirades get us resenting him, and then worrying about it. That's a complex effect, sure enough, but the writing is sketchy, and on this exposed stage weaknesses of text, acting and direction compound one another. One character is supposed to spend the play in terror of his life, but he never looks very bothered.

  

Bottom of the heap is Philip Martin's Thee and Me (Lyttelton). It is the year 2040, and natural disaster, maybe compounded by human recklessness, has reduced Britain to a dustbowl. It has also set the human race back, theatrically speaking, by a couple of centuries. A race of patriarchs walks the earth, guarding its water supply and its family, dispensing with its definite articles, and scheming to marry off its daughters to horse-traders called Jeremiah Stiggins. The characters live in giant disused water-pipes, which at least enables Sue Plummer to design a spectacular set, flanked by a heap of petrified motorcars.

A more recognisable civilisation, referred to as "state," flourishes to the north and representatives of both orders are felled in the end. The audience can hardly feel like choosing between them. Maybe there was an element of mockery in the original which attracted the director, Michael Rudman, but if so his production has failed to bring it out.

A bug kept me from Rose (Duke of York's), which from all accounts was my misfortune. It will be reviewed next week.
1980-03-16-two-of-the-best:
Two of the best

ROBERT CUSHMAN profiles a successful duo of American writers, whose latest musical, On the Twentieth Century, opens at Her Majesty's Theatre this week.

BY TRADITION the best American comic playwrights have travelled in pairs.

In the twenties and thirties there were Moss Hart and George Kaufman, Ben Hecht and Charles MacArthur. The latter couple wrote The Front Page and also the backstage saga Twentieth Century, which became a celebrated film with John Barrymore playing a megalomaniac actor-manager closely resembling John Barrymore.

Much later -- 1978 to be exact -- it became a Broadway musical, retitled On the Twentieth Century (this being not an era, or even a fox, but a train) and opening in London this week. Book and lyrics are by Betty Comden and Adolph Green, a writing duo who began working together during World War Two. Neither has ever written anything independently of the other.

They have carried over into the post-war years their predecessors' distinctive New York strain of madcap urbanity. The line of descent is quite direct; Kaufman and Hart's Once in a Lifetime must have influenced Comden and Green's own spoofing of the coming of sound to Hollywood in Singin' in the Rain, and that marvellous film has certainly bequeathed a few gags to the current London production of the play.

Two subjects, often overlapping, have preoccupied Comden and Green throughout their writing career: show business and New York. If Singin' in the Rain is the classic backstage, or in this instance offscreen, musical, their first stage show, On the Town, summed up wartime Manhattan. It's the one that begins with three sailors, on 24 hours' leave, singing 'New York, New York, a helluva town,' a chant that has become proverbial.

That was in 1944, when the authors themselves were still wide-eyed, as were their collaborators: a young composer called Leonard Bernstein and a choreographer, Jerome Robbins. Since then they have become part of the scene themselves. Both partners were born in 1915, and neither looks it. Green has a shock of white hair, an open face and a crinkly smile. Comden, a tall brunette, exemplifies the most sensible kind of Manhattan chic. I would guess that the fantasy in their work stems mainly from him, and the satire from her, but since they maintain that even their closest friends can never tell who wrote what, I would not press it.

They are not married; at least, not to each other. Green's wife is the actress Phyllis Newman, whom he met when she was Judy Holliday's stand-by in one of their most successful shows, Bells are Ringing; Comden was married for more than 30 years to art expert Steven Kyle, who died last October.

Actually they misled the world about their status when they wrote the film The Band Wagon, whose cast included Nanette Fabray and Oscar Levant as a husband-and-wife writing team who in other respects were clearly self-portraits.

Like their cinematic doppelgänger, Comden and Green are performers as well as writers. Indeed, like many others, they started writing because they couldn't afford to pay anyone else for material. They met when she was studying drama at New York University, and he was sort of unemployed. They teamed up with three other hopefuls, one of whom was Miss Holliday. They describe a perfectly true B-movie incident. Judy was caught in the rain in Greenwich Village and stumbled down some basement steps, and there was a man who turned out to be Max Gordon, who owned the Village Vanguard night-club and still does and looks exactly the same.

The new group were booked into the Vanguard under the name The Revuers, lampooning New York with particular reference to newspapers and theatres, and attracting distinguished and terrific audiences. S. J. Perelman, Robert Benchley and Lillian Hellman were fans, while Bernstein came to know their material better than they did themselves. He has been known to perform it from memory at parties.

The Revuers collaborated on words and music. 'Oh, we were both very musical. Betty,' says Green, waving at the piano in his partner's town house, 'plays four chords -- very well. Actually people still say "I love your music," and we have to disabuse them.'

After the Vanguard, the Revuers' career halted. They were out of work for almost a year, then made their way to Hollywood and break-up. 'The studios only wanted Judy. There was another B-movie scene; we had to talk her into deserting us.' A bedraggled duo returned to New York. Comden went first to join her husband, on a brief furlough from the Services. When Green followed, dejected, he was greeted on the station platform by his team-mate bearing a banner inscribed, 'Adolph Green Fan-Club.' ('I was a very gloomy fan club.') The incident was recycled in The Band Wagon; Fred Astaire, playing a washed-up version of himself, arrives at Grand Central to be greeted in similar fashion by, more or less, Comden and Green.

Their luck broke with On the Town. It was Bernstein's first musical and he, the city's favourite prodigy, insisted that they be commissioned to provide the words. They themselves insisted that they be included in the cast as Ozzie and Claire de Loon, sailor and anthropologist respectively. 'It wasn't so easy to sneak ourselves into the show. We had to audition for the director, George Abbott.' They haven't snuck themselves into any of their subsequent musicals, but they have appeared from time to time in a mélange of their own work called A Party.

On the Town was followed by Billion Dollar Baby, ruefully described as 'a succès d'estime.' 'It was a sardonic look at the 1920s and people weren't ready yet for a show with people jumping out of windows.' However, it planted in Hollywood's head the idea that they write about the Twenties, and they found themselves at MGM revamping the old chestnut, Good News. Then came the film of On the Town, and a trio of the studio's (and therefore Hollywood's) best musicals: The Band Wagon with Astaire, Singin' in the Rain and It's Always Fair Weather with Gene Kelly.

All three films took their tone from their funny, joyous, lemon-flavoured scripts. The duo fashioned theatrical satire that was neither inbred nor sentimental, but fastened a gleeful eye on cant or self-glorification. The pinnacle perhaps was the silent-movie queen (Jean Hagen) telling her adoring audience, 'If we have brought a little joy into your humdrum lives then it ain't all been in vain for nothin'.'

Back on Broadway they had one more triumph with Bernstein (Wonderful Town) and a string of shows with music by Jule Styne. On the Twentieth Century has united them with Cy Coleman, whose snazzy, jazzy style would seem to be a perfect match for theirs.

Unforeseeably, though, the collaborators have set this saga of battling egos as mock operetta. 'Cy played something and we said, let's hear that again. He said, you mean that bit of Rossini. We said that's it, and it became a song.' Having told me so much, they sang the song. Songwriters have hummed me the odd line on previous occasions, but this is the first time I have been treated to a full-throated duet.

They won't be at the London first night. They have been elected to New York's Songwriters' Hall of Fame -- an achievement if you are still alive and are generally thought of as theatre, rather than music people -- and they are staying in town for the ceremony. Coincidentally, Michael's Pub -- a jazz-spot that goes in for composer-tributes -- is running an evening of their songs.

If you are searching your memory for their hits, try 'Just in Time' or 'The Party's Over' from Bells are Ringing. But isolated songs, even isolated shows, are not the point. They represent some of the best of Broadway tradition, and some of the most essential.
1980-03-23-putting-paid-to-othello:
Putting paid to 'Othello'

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Scofield's Moor, a musical and Michael Frayn's latest play.

PETER HALL'S production of Othello, like his previous Shakespeares at the Olivier, is sternly devoid of anything you could call a concept.

This asceticism is apt to bear hard on those actors who have merely to stand around, especially if they are doing it on a stage this size. But Othello calls for fewer of these than any other tragedy; after all, the Venetian senate are likely to end up, however the play is staged, sitting in ranks and looking old. In this production quite a few of them are old, or at least mature. For once, too, the abundant talent and experience in the supporting cast is given the time and space to express itself.

Paul Scofield delivers the last three speeches of Othello himself -- especially the one that consists of the words "O fool, fool, fool" -- very simply and affectingly. Earlier he administers to Desdemona a crackling slap on the face. The rest of the time he is sonorously somnolent: no fires, no torment. Pride, of a quiet kind, there is; though what with his studied gestures -- which include the trying on for size of imaginary cuckold's horns -- it often seems more like self-approbation.

This suggests that Mr Scofield has adopted the Eliot-Leavis view of the Moor: an egotist who deserves even more than he gets. Why what amounts to a sustained jeer at the central character should be held to amount to a satisfying play I have never understood; but, such as it is, this interpretation needs to be followed through to the (literally) bitter end. Mr Scofield's end is sweet.

The first half of the play -- up to and including the brawl -- belongs to Iago, and Michael Bryant has no trouble with it, maintaining an even, sensible, humorous pace which enables him to switch effortlessly from manipulating his dupes to manipulating the audience. The chilled laughter he induces is just right. But he can make no contact with this Othello. The temptation scene is a slow fuse leading to a puff of smoke; it ends with no bond established between the two men, and that just about kills the play.

Felicity Kendal, who improves and improves, is a properly self-willed Desdemona, whose lies over the handkerchief are well marked. Yvonne Bryceland's Emilia has her usual unobtrusive firmness; Stephen Moore's kind and lazy Cassio, Michael Gambon's moon-faced, moon-minded Roderigo, and Penelope Wilton's Bianca, more housewife than hussy, all justify luxury casting. Mark Dignam even makes something of the sententious Duke.

  

As staged on Broadway, On the Twentieth Century (Her Majesty's) began with a theatre scene where a melodrama about Joan of Arc was interrupted by the absconding of the manager and the marooning of the cast who sang about it, feelingly and in operatic measures. "Screwed again," intoned a basso bishop, over heavy chords. This set up the style of the piece -- soaring tunes and ludicrous situations glorifying and undercutting one another -- as well as the vital relationship between the manager, Oscar Jaffe, and his two henchmen: business manager and press rep. It also delayed, and so made more effective, our first sight of the Twentieth Century itself, a glorious Art Deco beast, locomoting between Chicago and New York in the early Thirties.

This is a show about three monstre sacres: two people and a train. The train -- though it still gleams, shunts, jack-knifes and reverses with spirit -- is, perhaps through lack of space, less impressive than it was in New York: the people, though, are superior. As Lily Garland -- Oscar's one-time discovery, now lost to Hollywood and now his only chance of restoring his fortunes -- Julia McKenzie gives an authentic star-is-born performance, her top notes as triumphant as her snub-nosed comedy. (Often the two co-exist, which is the point of the show.)

Keith Michell is rather too low-keyed and likeable for the heartless flamboyance that book and score demand of Oscar; but there is enough chemistry between them -- and enough tact and timing in Peter Coe's direction -- for the romantic ending to seem crazily logical, where before it was inconsequential.

Betty Comden and Adolph Green wrote the book and lyrics from a play by Hecht and MacArthur; and the supply of one-liners is appropriate to the pedigree. Lily Garland, Miss McKenzie, shouts complainingly to the world, "has no life of her own." Equally absent-mindedly, she snarls of Oscar, "I wouldn't wipe my feet on this man if he was starving."

After the bludgeoning attempts at satire or nostalgia in recent musicals, this one's affable eye for the ridiculous may well come as a surprise. It is some time since a stuttering, and deliberately artificial, line -- like, but, but, but, but, but, but -- was given lyrical life. It's the verbal mainstay of a chase sequence, in which Robin Wagner's train really does its stuff; and which is followed by an even more stunning production number, a musical parody of a Somerset Maugham comedy, all silver-gilt and angular cigarette-holders.

Larry Fuller's witty, sometimes slapstick, choreography vitalises the longest numbers; and Cy Coleman's music, even at its lushest, retains his characteristic rhythmic pulse. This is actually his most theatrical score, appropriate to the characters and creating a style which the production (Harold Prince's originally and his touch still shows) takes up and polishes. I must mention David Healy and Fred Evans (one-time funny-faced dancer) as the sidekicks.

On the Twentieth Century is London's best musical since A Chorus Line.

  

You don't have to go back that far to find an exemplar for Michael Frayn's new play: Make and Break (Lyric, Hammersmith), but it ends an uncomfortably parched spell. It concerns the director of a British firm which makes walls, including doors, and is trying to sell them in German. He has erected his own psychological wall: an unshakeable absorption in his own work, maintained even while trying to seduce his secretary.

The seduction itself is undertaken because he thinks it's the thing to do: one way of taking an interest in his employees whom he questions unceasingly about their interests, as if seeking their technical specifications. Leonard Rossiter ferrets brilliantly; the role seems perfect for his particular form of withdrawn exhibitionism. A scene in which he thinks he may be dying of a heart-attack brings out unsuspected depths in both him and his author; it is not quite frightening, but it is certainly sobering.

Around him Mr Frayn builds a solid world, even though the construction is sometimes leisurely: the protagonist's entrance is too long deferred; and though Michael Blakemore's production handles a couple of dream-sequences (doors flying) with wit, he cannot quite make them fit. Pamela Salem as the secretary begins, so to speak, Sibylline, and steadily deepens, and there is a sensationally good (though quite unseasonal) performance from James Grout as second-in-command. The point boils down to "what's the point," but the question is seldom so carefully or sympathetically asked.

  

The new regime at the Theatre Royal, Stratford East, begins auspiciously with a revival of a Boucicault melodrama, The Streets of London; an exciting story and, in a burning-house scene, special effects to match.
1980-03-30-solving-the-problems-of-faust:
Solving the problems of Faustus

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London, Leicester and Sheffield.

IT is plain from the opening of Dr Faustus (transferred from the Lyric Studio, Hammersmith, to the Fortune) that the director, Christopher Fettes, has found a solution to the play.

A couple of soberly-clad young men sit studiously at a long table. A third enters, and delivers the prologue, coolly and a little insolently, with none of the thunderous rhetoric usually deemed appropriate for getting a Marlowe tragedy off the ground. Indeed, in generally accepted terms, this production never gets off the ground at all; it remains tethered to that table and to its attendant furniture: stools and a couple of forms.

When the two seated figures open their mouths they turn out to be, not Faustus's fellow scholars, but his Good and Bad Angel. Faced with the problem of bringing medieval iconography on stage the production merely sidesteps it, much as Jonathan Miller did years ago when presented with the supernatural extravagances of The Tempest. The effect--playing off what we get against what we expect--is very powerful. When spectacle is unavoidable--as in the show of the Seven Deadly Sins--it is dimly glimpsed behind a gauze.

Mr Fettes plays a pretty full text, including a generous selection of the prose scenes in which servants and ostlers try their own luck with Faustus's magic books. James Aubrey's Faustus is, in essence, the same kind of bemused simpleton, with the difference that he also happens to be an academic whizzkid. Mr Aubrey makes very believable the character's premature disillusion with conventional success, as well as the desperate shallowness that lets him convince himself--even when confronted by a spirit as palpably damned as Patrick Magee's sepulchral Mephistophilis--that there can be no hell.

Mr Magee is inspired casting; Mr Aubrey goes well beyond his previous range (mainly slim, disintegrating young men) to discover some authentic terror for the last scene. 'I'll leap up to my God' is an actual jump, horizontal across the table with an upward-stretching arm.
