But his vocal colouring is limited, and draws uncomfortable attention to the monotony of the play's middle. Whatever Faustus did with his 24 years of power would, in the end, seem inconsequential; but this fact is of little comfort to the audience while actually watching it.

Point by point, Mr Fettes has solved every one of the play's problems, but, though he expands for the scenes of Papal charade, all his answers have the same flavour; and though they may well have seemed inevitable in the original studio staging, on a proscenium stage--even one as small as this--they become mannered.

At the beginning one is continually startled by imaginative invention: by, for example, the presentation of Faustus's tutor Cornelius as a blind man in a wheelchair, whose 'the spirits tell me' is magnificently eerie. When Faustus calls for a wife he gets a husband-beating harridan, initiating a series of homosexual jokes on the ingenuous hero's ideas of pleasure.

There are no women in the cast of eight; and Helen, who finally damns Faustus, is a boy--a tribute less to Elizabethan stage convention than to what the production, probably correctly, takes to be the author's mocking, self-tormenting spirit. (We may want to believe that he dissociated himself from the orthodox judgment of the last lines, but there is no evidence for it.) Mr Fettes's production is the equal of John Barton's a few years ago, which means I do not expect to see it bettered; but it still disappointed me.

  

John Byrne's Threads (Hampstead) reintroduces us to the characters of The Slab Boys (nearly all played by the same actors, an impressive blow for continuity in these fractured times) and lets us accompany them to the works dance. The dialogue is as uncompromisingly, not to say impenetrably, Glaswegian as ever--especially in the first act, set in the ladies and gents cloakrooms, where, naturally, sexual segregation reigns. The linguistic barriers go down quite noticeably in the second, when the sexes mingle.

Either my ears were growing keener or Mr Byrne is making a point about the adoption of disguise (i.e. standard English) in social situations. Anyway the wit that I, encouraged by the spirit of the acting, had taken for granted in the first half, turned out really to exist in the second, as did a certain formality. Mr Byrne's characters soliloquise, none more poignantly than the girl-starved Hector, frustrated by the unaccountability of women: 'One minute I'm the bees' knees--next, I'm lower than a knat's ankle-socks.' He is actually the victim--as are the audience, to a certain extent--of the fact that each of Mr Byrne's people has a separate, and ruthless, strategy for survival.

The result is 10 separate lines of action. Pat Doyle's Hector vies for first claim on our sympathy with Robbie Coltrane's fat jokes, who has learned the ropes but still ties himself in knots, and with Claire Nielson's spinster, recalling a wartime meeting with Clark Gable in terms that reaffirm Mr Byrne's status as a punster: 'Rhett Butler in khaki, and me scarlet with embarrassment.'

  

Graham Greene's For Whom the Bell Chimes (Haymarket Studio, Leicester) is meant to unfold with the enchanting craziness of a Magritte tableau--as denoted both by the clinical set and by the painting of a snatch of sky that hangs crooked on one of its walls. There are even two characters who exchange a bowler hat; one a pearl-grey exquisite, the other a down-and-out ostensibly collecting for charity.

Some of the dialogue concerning the children whom he claims to represent (what an easy life they have, no responsibilities) is engagingly heartless. But the play winds down; the action becomes whimsically improvisational without (unlike Tom Stoppard's After Magritte or the best of Orton) any logical base to which to return.

The acting, too, is uneven, though Roy Macready's collector is fine, as is Derek Smith's fire-breathing colonel (resembling his brother-officer in Peter Shaffer's Black Comedy). Mr Smith is also seen to effect in Mr Greene's fairly engaging curtain-raiser, Yes and No, in which he impersonates a director instructing an actor in the difference between a Pinter pause and a Pinteresque pause. Privett being the author whom they are trying jointly to interpret.

  

Stephen Poliakoff's The Summer Party was done, by contrast, on the main stage of the Sheffield Crucible, a gamble rewarded by attendances if not by the play itself. It might actually have moved faster in a studio. As it is, a reasonably suggestive ending--hinging on the difference between the fake magic of an infant Uri Geller and the more respectable variety invoked by a chief constable to calm a rock-concert mob--took a wearying time to arrive.

Mr Poliakoff has assembled standard characters from the pop and law-and-order worlds, without giving them anything much to do. Only Dexter Fletcher, as the child, acted with a terrifying assurance that seemed in itself to justify the author's worst nightmares.
1980-04-06-on-the-razor-s-edge:
On the razor's edge

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Jonathan Pryce's Hamlet and The Shadow of a Gunman.

THE ovation which greeted Jonathan Pryce's Hamlet (Royal Court) announced that, for the first time since David Warner played the role 15 years ago, a generation has found and crowned its prince.

Mr Warner was acclaimed less as an actor than as an archetype; he was taken to be the essence of studenthood, 1965. The interest attaching to Mr Pryce is more strictly gladiatorial: that of seeing a prized young actor, not in himself particularly representative of anything, match his own talent to the role. Nobody expected heroic acting of Mr Warner; everybody expects it of Mr Pryce.

Heroic acting has nothing to do with nobility, or even with vocal resonance. It depends on authority, on variety, on the ability to play each moment to the full. More than anything, perhaps, it means the ability to remain attractive while behaving outrageously — in this play above all others.

It is odd, considering what they have to put up with from him, how much everyone in the play likes Hamlet. Nobody — except Claudius when lying and Laertes when duped — ever says a word against him. Mr Pryce's power and intelligence are amply backed up by sheer cheek — it may be his distinguishing mark as an actor — and few of Hamlet's attitudes give him visible trouble. No figure could be more palpably heartbroken than the one he presents in the first scene: with that cadaverous face, how could he wear anything but black? He seems totally open to grief; you see why Gertrude, Horatio and Ophelia all want to protect him.

When it comes to the great central encounters, nobody could balance more elegantly or provocatively on the razor's edge of pretended madness, whether baiting Rosencrantz and Guildenstern or tearfully abandoning Ophelia. (His quiet 'I did love you once,' when she produces his old letters, is inspired.) His technique is both formidable and individual: over a continuous ground-bass of hysteria, he executes the most telling and scrupulous individual cadenzas. Only in the graveyard struggle with Laertes — where rhetoric is for once undiluted by self-satire — do his guns fail him.

If you wish to see an actor wrestling vibrantly, wittily and honestly with a great role, then London offers nothing better. You will not, though, find an overall solution to the problems of the character. I wonder if Mr Pryce isn't a gentler actor than anyone (including himself) likes to believe; his description of the dead Polonius ('foolish, prating knave') comes out surprisingly affectionate, and though he seems to be aiming for a dark prince at the close he is frustrated by the text in which Hamlet acts with inescapable decency, never killing anyone unless seriously provoked.

Meanwhile Mr Pryce has presented us with a new interpretative conundrum, though it may have originated purely as the practical answer to a problem of production. The director Richard Eyre has decided against a visible Ghost, or even an independently audible one. The Ghost speaks through Hamlet, who struggles and retches as if in the grip of diabolic possession. This of course adds great point to the spirit that I have seen may be a devil, and to the later visitation in the closet-scene, but it seems to have little bearing on what the sane Mr Pryce does with the rest of the play. As it is, we admire his skill at switching between voices, but wonder whether the play doesn't present him with quite enough challenges as it is.

Mr Eyre's production has the same virtues and limitations as Mr Pryce's performance. It is thoroughly sensible and thoroughly alive, but offers no overall view. It does, however — much aided by William Dudley's burnished beehive of a set — offer atmosphere. This Elsinore, composed of an elegant series of adjoining timbered cubicles, is a paradise for eavesdroppers. It can be quickly, if noisily, rearranged while the air resounds with bangs and thumps, suggesting that the Danish royals are engaged in frenzied diplomatic activity or alternatively that they have the builders in. Ophelia's grave is not a trap, but a shelf in an upright mausoleum brimful of skulls. How the gravedigger can tell which is Yorick's is more of a mystery than ever.

Geoffrey Chater's brilliant Polonius is the scene made flesh: prying, self-satisfied, rabbiting both to and about his children, but showing no affection for them whatever. Michael Elphick's grossly practical Claudius is positively sympathetic by comparison, aptly conveying that he, like Hamlet, is in over his head, lumbered with a destiny he would far rather escape. Jill Bennett's Gertrude, like most others, is more impressive out of love with him than in; Harriet Walter's Ophelia, similarly, is a sweet blank at first, but improves with madness. Christopher Logue arrives as the First Player, bringing with him (for no very good reason) what I assume is his own rewriting of the Hecuba speech. A couple of small-part players I could cheerfully have strangled; otherwise it was a cheering and a cheered occasion.

  

Michael Pennington, who is to be the year's second Hamlet, is limbering up in the first of O'Casey's comedies of the Troubles, The Shadow of a Gunman (Other Place, Stratford-upon-Avon), as Donal Davoren, another poet posing as a killer. Mr Pennington has a particular talent for monitoring the movement and the meaning of any scene in which he is involved; sometimes this can be distracting, but the clarity with which he shows us Davoren's vanity, and his flirtations with the hero-worshipping Minnie, are immensely helpful. We get not a straight man and a clown, but two equally comic cowards, the other being the pedlar Seamus Shields, whom Norman Rodway — giving his best performance in ages — keeps rigorously clear of stage-Irish ingratiation.

I had always regarded the play as containing some good jokes, a burst of effective melodrama and a lot of winsome padding. Michael Bogdanov's production shows that, though the play is built like a vaudeville, there is muscle in every turn. All the intrusions build. Dearbhla Molloy is a merry, touching Minnie, and the play stands as one of the few in which the author can generalise about a country because he has been so particular about its inhabitants.

Another Irish actor, J. G. Devlin, can be seen at his best in the National Theatre's generally admirable production of The Iceman Cometh, which this week is visiting the Theatre Royal, Bath.
1980-04-13-bam-goes-shakespeare:
BAM is the pleasantly explosive shorthand used, on letterheads and occasionally in conversation, to denote the Brooklyn Academy of Music. This is actually an arts complex: easily accessible from Manhattan by subway, safely accessible by cab.

BAM is the current focus of one of the lesser-known American dreams: that of establishing a classical repertory company, in New York. Frank Dunlop, fresh from the Broadway triumph of Scapino, was put in charge of such an attempt a few years ago, but his reign was short-lived. BAM is now trying again under another British director, David Jones.

He has made a qualifiedly hopeful start. It was venturesome to begin with one of the trickiest of all Shakespeares, The Winter's Tale, and heartening that the audience seemed ready both to follow the story and to laugh at the jokes. They made the average British spectator seem blase. But as such a spectator myself, I was disappointed to find nothing -- except a lively and well-sung Autolycus from a black actor, Joe Morton -- that suggested a distinctively American approach to Shakespeare.

The production and design seemed merely pale replicas of standard Stratford practise; if one more RSC director introduces a rocking-horse into the early scenes at Leontes's court, people will begin to think that Shakespeare put it there. Expectedly, the two most authoritative performances came from the two players with the greatest Shakespeare experience: Marti Maraden (from Stratford, Ontario) as Hermione, and Sheila Allen, who injected some refreshing wit into Paulina's remonstrances, though I felt she erred in not wiping the smile off her face when "hastily married" at the end. The rest of the playing suggested that the actors chosen by Mr Jones from the resources offered by America's regional theatres needed more experience in the genre.

Hopes were raised by the company's second production. An American rep has to discover -- if necessary to invent -- American classics; and it has become clear that an endless series of O'Neill revivals is not enough. Vintage American farce (and, to a lesser extent, melodrama) is being explored; and BAM came up with a neglected example from the Forties, Johnny on the Spot, written by Charles MacArthur, for once without Ben Hecht.

Dealing with political chicanery in the South, the play lacks the forward drive of the Hecht-MacArthur Front Page, but is sustained by the same uplifting cynicism and by spurts of crazy invention. The state governor, a self-licensed autocrat presumably based on Huey Long of Louisiana, has died in a sporting-house on election day and his aides have to conceal the fact until the votes are in. (At one point they need the old boy's signature, and have to enlist the services of a champion forger, who has unfortunately got religion while in jail. Even the promise that he can sign his own pardon fails to move him from the paths of righteousness.) The production started slowly, but it was solid and by the end I liked it a great deal.

One of the attractions of the New York theatre, at least to a starry-eyed visitor, is its apparent homogeneity. The town seems aware of the theatre as London never does; there are recognisable theatrical restaurants. Even the uniformity of Playbill, the magazine programme sold at all Broadway theatres, is reassuring. There is a tourist audience, but it consists mainly of out-of-towners rather than foreigners (though there has been enough of a Japanese influx to prompt a revival of Oh! Calcutta!), so actors and playwrights still have some contact with the people to whom they are supposed to be talking.

Off-Broadway, at the Village Gate (a jazz-club, originally, now resembling a cavernous King's Head), I watched a revue called Scrambled Feet, devoted entirely to satirising the current theatre, and reflected that such a thing would now be impossible in London; you could never gather together enough people who would understand the jokes. This is our loss; a theatre needs to be able to laugh at itself. Scrambled Feet did so with great good humour; it was far less campy or inbred than I had feared, and had the grace to sympathise with the travails of audiences as well as actors.

One of its jokes was, perhaps temporarily, out of date; there is at the moment no British invasion of Broadway. The only British plays on view are Harold Pinter's Betrayal and Brian Clark's Whose Life Is It Anyway?, and both have American casts. Mr Clark's piece now has Mary Tyler Moore in the Tom Conti role. Night and Day and Filumena have both folded, though A Day in Hollywood, a Night in the Ukraine is about to open.

New York most resembles London in its paucity of new plays and musicals, and its dependence on revivals: often the same revivals. They have Oklahoma! and West Side Story, and are shortly to have My Fair Lady. A less expected treat is a musical version of Peter Pan, first staged 25 years ago. As a musical it is no particular shakes; even the choreography (originally by Jerome Robbins) is more energetic than inventive. But it benefits from the thoroughness and professionalism that New York expects in the genre, and which shames almost any children's entertainment (certainly any operating under this title) in London. The sets are smashing, the flying breathtaking (with an extra thrill saved for the curtain-call) and Sandy Duncan's gamin Peter, once you have got over her resemblance to Tom Sawyer, a joy.

The less acceptable face of nostalgia is represented by Sugar Babies, the hugely successful tribute to burlesque with Ann Miller and Mickey Rooney, which I visited in expectation of guilty uncritical enjoyment, but which doesn't even work in its own terms. There is a destructive imbalance in blowing up what was essentially a cheap and intimate form of entertainment to modern Broadway proportions at prices to match (and incidentally in amplifying the hell out of it). Near the end there's an animal act: a recalcitrant dog, with lugubrious master -- the only performers to make real contact with each other or the audience.

Animals are big at the moment, even small ones. The title-role in Scrambled Feet is taken by a black-tied duck, who shares the stage with an actress who warns her colleagues, in song, of the dangers of sharing a stage with such a creature. Strider, among the most esteemed new shows, is about horses' inhumanity to horse. It is an American version of a Russian play, based in its turn on a story by Tolstoy, and came to Broadway via the Chelsea Theatre Centre, one-time tenants of BAM. The beasts are mimed by actors, Taina Elg, as the mare of the unfortunate hero's dreams, is a really stylish high-stepper. The best and worst you can say for the enterprise is that it's cute.

I suspect that the most interesting play in New York is Lanford Wilson's two-hander, Talley's Folly, about the seduction of an impoverished daughter of an old American family by a self-satirising middle-aged Jewish accountant. London managements are reported to be queuing for it, and rightly.
1980-04-13-a-mad-world-in-arden:
A mad world in Arden

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in Stratford, Sheffield and London.

THE Stratford season has begun with As You Like It, very brightly. I have never known the first scenes to go at such a lick.

Any actor of Orlando, faced with the appallingly stiff, expository opening, is liable to devote his energies to persuading you that you have never heard it before; I assumed that this was what John Bowe was up to here, and applauded both the effort and the result. When Jonathan Hyde proceeded to give the full melodramatic works to his big bad brother Oliver, and when even the very minor servant Dennis shot off his two functional lines in a similar ecstasy of bad temper, I took it all merely for an extension of the same kindly process.

I was grateful, too, for a thrilling wrestling match in which Terry Wood's Charles looks so huge and fights so dirty that Sinead Cusack's Celia is provoked into assisting his opponent with some fierce maidenly pummelling. She comes indeed from a formidable family; Bruce Purchase as her usurping father quivers all over when banishing people (his favourite occupation), while Trevor Baxter as the rightful Duke lectures his followers on the virtues of the simple life with an oily self-righteousness that would be scary if it wasn't so entertaining.

By this point the story is more or less over, the real business of the comedy is beginning, and Terry Hands's production might be expected to let up somewhat. Not a bit of it: 'Love,' declares Rosalind, 'is merely a tame madness'; Mr Hands glosses over the adjective and goes straight for the noun. Silvius, for example, goes around with his shepherd's crook behind his neck, and holding on to it with both hands as if crucified.

Mr Hands's approach yields plenty of passing pleasures and some illumination. There is the moment, for example, when Derek Godfrey's Jaques, melancholy cloak outspread, advances on Rosalind in what others believe to be an attempt at rape (and who knows whether he thinks her a boy or girl?), but which I, in my innocence, took for an endeavour to convert her to his own philosophy by enfolding her in it. I liked, too, Joe Melia's professionally funny Touchstone and Raymond Westwell's Corin.

But in the end (and conceivably influenced by memories of gentler productions) I was unmoved. In particular, I found it difficult to get the measure of this Rosalind. Her work at the National established Susan Fleetwood as the most enchanting actress never to crack a smile, and I had looked forward to seeing her happy for once. In this production she can be merry all right, but she can seldom relax; the heart of both the character and the play is bypassed.

  

The RSC's Three Sisters (Warehouse) is a virtuoso production, but you are hardly aware of the fact until it is over. Trevor Nunn's direction is a feat of both emotional and spatial geometry; at any given moment three lines of feeling are criss-crossing one another on stage and you can see them all. I have never known a production that made so clearly one of the crucial Chekhovian points: that one person's suffering is another's oblivion.

The confined space helps, of course; putting us in the same room as the characters cuts down on comic amplitude, but makes tragedy horribly immediate. Pathos, though, is not indulged; every character save one is allowed a single moment of heart-break, or the memory of one; each is fully but sparely taken with no wallowing.

The one untouched figure is Susan Tracy's Natasha, harshly humiliated at the beginning and thereafter undemonstratively destructive; this is a much improved performance. Similarly Edward Petherbridge's Vershinin, which I liked the least at Stratford last year, is now almost the best, slipping in and out of relationships with a kind of glazed, well-meaning courtliness. 'Let's philosophise,' he says languidly; and Roger Rees's Tusenbach, infinitely trusting, takes him seriously.

Janet Dale's quietly defeated Olga and Emily Richard's Irina, progressively booby-trapped by existence, flank a Masha from Suzanne Bertish that is absorbing and, in its emphasis on predatory self-pity, strikingly unsentimental, but is sometimes--in its dropping of significant words into careful pauses--too obviously calculated. Bob Peck's Soliony, murderous in his vulnerability, broods over the play and is almost the key-figure. The production's aural elements have been as carefully calibrated as its austere visuals.

  

There was once a community drama company that stood outside Tesco's, haranguing housewives. 'Women of Britain, what do you want?' it asked. 'We want to get in to Tesco's,' they replied. I don't know what that anecdote does for you in print, but as delivered by Victoria Wood, who also wrote it, it creased me up. In her new sort-of-musical, Good Fun (Crucible, Sheffield), Miss Wood has consistently provided herself, in the time-honoured role of heroine's best friend, with the funniest lines recently heard on a British stage. Or is it the way she tells them? Either way, I laughed till I cried, Observer.

She also has, on this occasion, a theme. The five female characters in this piece all have pleasure, or the lack of it, on their minds; sometimes they advise one another on how or where it can be found, generally with disastrous results. Miss Wood is quite the most accomplished songwriter we have, and when her people use her nimble, observant lyrics to explain themselves or their situations, life is joyful. When she uses song to move her plot along, her muse clogs up, possibly because it isn't much of a plot to start with.

Annabel Leventon plays (very well) a community arts administrator with a talent for attracting the wrong men, if any. She is eternally hopeful until, at the end, she lets all her bitterness out. But she is not kept firmly enough in sight, and Miss Wood seems to be making up the supporting action as she goes along.

Men are allowed to appear, but not to sing, which in a musical is as sexist (and dramatically unsatisfying) as you can get. The production tries too hard, but the performances are good--or, in the case of Julie Walters's cosmetics saleslady, travelling with a heart-shaped box of samples, rather extraordinary.

  

On inspection, all the best songs of the rock 'n' roll era turn out to have been written by Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller. Apart from Randy Newman, they are the only rock writers whose work, with its tightly inventive rhythms and wryly detailed lyrics, sounds potentially theatrical. That in fact is the way they have gone in the past decade, and the highlight of Only in America (Roundhouse), Ned Sherrin's compilation of their work, is a song that was actually written for a show. It is called 'I Ain't Here' and is sung at an ironing-board by the magnificent Bertice Reading, as a black home-help taking a dreamy revenge on her white employer.

Others of the later, greater Leiber-Stoller songs come off less well; Val Pringle, a large resounding bass, sings a few lines of 'Feeling Too Good Today Blues' and is then silenced; the peerlessly sexy 'Some Cats Know' falls victim to its staging and also to the fact that, unless Miss Reading is singing (and she makes far more sense of 'Hound Dog' than Presley ever did), Mr Leiber's lyrics are only audible when the wind and the sound-system are blowing in the right direction.

The idea of the show--to create a tapestry of song untrammelled by dialogue--is fine, and most of the staging ideas are ingenious. They haven't, though, been very well executed, apart from one orgiastic sequence in the necking-section of a movie theatre. Being young in Brooklyn, 1959, is the theme, and as good as any; but few of the performers make much impact, and the designs are drab far beyond the call of nostalgia.

  

Andrei Serban's staging of The Umbrellas of Cherbourg (Phoenix), with the characters slinking round mobile perspex screens in sumptuous lighting by David Hersey, is extremely accomplished. That, however, doesn't save the evening. Michel Legrand's score runs to two pleasant tunes, the makings of a third, and an infinity of thin recitative. Sheldon Harnick's lyrics sound as ludicrous as would anyone's who tried to make dramatic points over so characterless an accompaniment.

The story is of boy losing girl and of both achieving a pained serenity; I might as well admit that their last meeting choked me up a bit. Heroine's mother runs an umbrella shop and goes bankrupt; since, in this Cherbourg, no one is ever seen without an umbrella, it is hard to see how.
1980-04-20-an-excellent-experience:
An excellent Experience

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Cymbeline, Twelfth Night, Private Lives and The Apple Tree.

IT IS reasonable to be wary of theatre companies who have names like the more sanctimonious kind of pop-group. But with Shared Experience, one's defences crumble; they live up to their title, pleasuring their audiences without ever patronising them.

The experience they share is a narrative one. They have already re-created for us the Arabian Nights and Bleak House; they specialise in tall, tangled tales. So it's appropriate that their first Shakespearean venture should be Cymbeline (now at the Lyric Studio, Hammersmith), whose complexities have defeated attempts at conventional large-scale production.

It is, to begin with, almost impossible to find a satisfactory visual style for a story that rambles between a Snow White fairyland, Druidical Britain, Renaissance Italy, and the Roman Empire of Augustus. Shared Experience, working without a set and with just five players in white shirts and slacks, make these odds all even. The inconsistencies and improbabilities are neither heightened nor abolished, but they are levelled down; no one style is more important than any other, and no glib overall solutions, technical or interpretative, are flourished in our faces.

We are not asked to believe, but alienation hardly comes into it since we are not asked to judge either. Indeed we're not really asked to do anything; certainly not, in the hectoring manner with which theoreticians love to bully audiences, to use our imaginations. This company doesn't make demands, which is not only polite but realistic of them. We, after all, are paying them. (Well, I'm not of course, but you are.) All we need to do is to pay attention and enjoy ourselves, not necessarily in that order.

The doubling involved is less hectic than might be expected; in this episodic piece characters tend, until the finale, to move around anyway in separate groups of two or three. Even at the end, their destinies are disposed of in batches, so a particular formation can dissolve and immediately realign as a collection of other identities. To help us through, the actors speak the opening stage-directions of each scene. This becomes an amusing running gag on its own account, but it avoids the coyness that once engulfed the RSC when they used the same device in the same play, apparently as a means of ducking a battle-scene. Shared Experience give us a battle, and a good one, with their own vocal cords as the chief weapons.

If the story works, so do the characters; there is some beautiful, unassertive acting. Raad Rawi's account of Cloten, the play's clownish (as opposed to comic) villain, is so complete that one hardly thinks of characterisation; leading with a thrusting chin and an indignant nose, he lets the princeling's baffled energies spring right out of him. Cloten defeats most actors by never quite settling into stock; he is a bully without being a coward. He manages, for example, an exaggerated but still quite stirring defiance of the Roman invasion, a scene which Mike Alfreds's direction handles with particular care, balancing Mr Rawi's eruptions against the more calculated bellicosity of Ruth Seglow's Queen and the pacific fumblings of John Dicks's Cymbeline.

Mr Dicks makes a sweet old king, though his treatment of Iachimo -- the play's afterthought on Iago -- betrays the feyness which can be this company's Achilles' heel; he isn't dangerous enough. All the same, he and Mr Rawi (who is the imperfect hero Posthumus as well as Cloten) get enough of the play's corroded male sexuality for Pam Ferris's Imogen -- ripe, sharp and appropriately housewifely -- to have something to transcend. Miss Ferris has one of the primal Shakespearean skills; she meets rage, joy or wonder, head-on. Indeed, despite some ill-advised gabbling, very little of the text is shirked by anyone; there are some subtleties the RSC might envy, while the celebratory ending is immaculate and irresistible. I have not seen all this company's work, and I have no intention of holding them up as a model for anyone. I don't believe in models, or -- since my bias has always been towards mainstream work and will probably stay that way -- in overnight conversions. Nor do I want to belabour the RSC, whose non-Shakespearean work has continued excellent.

  

Their Twelfth Night (Aldwych) is no atrocity, but -- apart from Cherie Lunghi's Viola, which fizzes with immediacy, and should go straight to the protective heart of every man in the audience -- it all seems jaded. Even John Woodvine's Malvolio has declined into a series of more or less expert gags; Terry Hands has staged the last scene suggestively, the stage gradually filling with seated, disillusioned figures: Andrew nursing his broken head, Toby subsiding beneath alcohol and marriage, Antonio lonely, the lovers apparently more oblivious by the minute. But it remains an idea, and not too interesting since the characters have rarely come to life in the first place.

I liked Willoughby Goddard's last, despondent moments as Toby, Geoffrey Hutchings's renditions of Feste's songs (especially "O mistress mine"), the funny duel, and Norman Tyrrell's Fabian, a role that can be done almost any way, and is here done old and rustic. (On a related note; in the Stratford As You Like It the performance of Corin I praised last week was given by the understudy, Tom Wilkinson.)

  

How, in these troubled days, do you ensure West End success? You revive Private Lives (Duchess) which has few characters, will always attract both stars and customers by symbolising the metropolitan entertainment tradition as few other pieces do, and is enough of a classic for aspiring suburban or regional theatres to feel justified in taking the initial plunge for you. It is a wonder the thing is not done more often -- and a blessing, since, good though it is (and possibly getting better -- Someday I'll Find You, for example, is now as much of a symbol for us as for the characters), you do need time to forget where the jokes come from.

As it happens, the best section of Alan Strachan's production (from Greenwich) is the last, in which the piece becomes four-handed. The minor couple, Victor and Sybil, have been strongly cast with Ian Collier engagingly boorish and Jenny Quayle coming shrilly and delightfully out of her shell to justify all her rival, Amanda, has said about her. It is always a relief in Coward when the butts turn out, as bad-mannered (and thus as privileged) as the wits. Maria Aitken swans through Amanda amusingly enough (by which I think I mean not quite amusingly enough); more of a surprise is Michael Jayston's Elyot. He manages to preserve Coward's rhythms (which are vital) without aping his tones, and his delivery of the notorious self-justifying lines about behaving like very small, quite idiotic children at a party is supremely tactful.

  

Those, understandably dismayed by Sheldon Harnick's lyrics for The Umbrellas of Cherbourg should rush to the Overground Theatre, Kingston, to hear what he achieved with his former collaborator Jerry Bock. Their 1966 musical The Apple Tree is, in fact, a trio of one-act pieces, derived from Mark Twain, Frank Stockton and Jules Feiffer. This production is happier with the first segment, an all-American Garden of Eden, than with the other two, which need more resources but could manage for the time being with more speed and a greater awareness of the score's beguiling line in self-mockery. Lesley Duff goes from Twain's Eve to the Turkish Delight Princess of Stockton's The Lady or the Tiger to Feiffer's Passionella, who herself goes from chimney-sweep to movie-star. Would you believe she prefers the second? She is dazzlingly assured as every one of them.
1980-04-27-juliet-and-the-wild-one:
Juliet and the Wild One

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in Stratford, Manchester and London.

THE Verona which Ralph Koltai has imagined for the latest Romeo and Juliet (Stratford-on-Avon) is an intimidatingly stylised urban jungle, composed of revolving slabs of wall, decorated by some civic-minded action painter. They have to be trundled around by half-lit supers, which seems to me to diminish their utility considerably, but when in position they make a fitting environment for roving teenage thugs.

'Punk,' one mutters when the lads first appear, but the analogy is imprecise. The young Montagues and Capulets are hardly underprivileged. The period of Ron Daniels's production is hard to locate, but Romeo's zippered leather takes us back 25 years to Marlon Brando and The Wild One. So does Stephen Oliver's music, the jazziest I have heard in a Shakespeare production; the Prince seems to like his fanfares blown on a cool blue trumpet. That sets one thinking -- and it's odd how little fashions change in juvenile delinquency -- of West Side Story. One way in which that show illuminated its source was in its emphasis on the escalation of gang warfare. Most productions lead us to believe that the two families have been slaughtering each other for decades; in fact the text makes it pretty clear that, up until the death of Mercutio, none of the participants could justifiably have been run in for anything worse than grievous bodily harm.

Mr Daniels is unusually scrupulous about this; his Mercutio and Tybalt begin by fighting a formalised duel with swordsticks, their friends egging them on with ritual grunts. When the blades come out, a new and scarifying stage has been reached; Mercutio's end marks a point of no return. But it's more or less accidental; it takes Romeo -- a self-confessed 'madman' -- to plunge his knife into Tybalt with conscious exultation.

Romeo is to be regarded as a sizeable but unrewarding cross to be chivalrously borne by some actor blessed or cursed with conventional good looks and a pleasing manner. Of late he has emerged as a rewarding character in his own right and the fulcrum of the play. Anton Lesser, physically small, makes him a clever, self-conscious, rather shallow youth with a violent sense of fun. He favours Benvolio with a friendly kick in the shin, and gives as good as he gets in verbal combat with Mercutio.

Juliet's love brings out the best and the worst in him. Mr Lesser, in line with current practice, gives full value to his screaming self-pity after banishment. This is a risky interpretation, only to be vindicated if the actor can at the end make Romeo grow up. Mr Lesser brings it off; his 'I defy you, stars,' rings round the theatre as Shakespearean syllables should and rarely do.

Jonathan Hyde offers a Mercutio high on blood and self-esteem. It fits, and Mr Hyde is an authoritative actor. But I have this old-fashioned idea that Shakespeare rather liked Mercutio, and meant us to. Actors and directors, though, are nowadays too highminded to let us. In fact, as Romeo has increased in prestige, Mercutio has declined; so, more surprisingly, has Juliet.

Judy Buxton's performance is at the moment an accurate but impersonal sketch. Her best moment is her first, gazing gravely at her own reflection before the plot descends on her. There is a determined Tybalt from Chris Hunter and a fine, unfussy Nurse from Brenda Bruce, who makes the advice to marry Paris sound the most logical thing in the world. Jimmy Gardner's Peter supports her from a world of his own, one adorned by some economical visual gags. The production grips both as a comment on the play and as a piece of story-telling.

  

A story perhaps more for our own time is Love on the Dole (Royal Exchange, Manchester), the Thirties success adapted by Ronald Gow from the Walter Greenwood novel. It has some of the marks of its origin; the action proceeds in chunks and set pieces, juicy scenes that the writers could not bring themselves to sacrifice. But they are juicy, and -- this is the rare thing -- remain so on stage.

A first-act seance, apart from drawing a ripe performance from Rosalind Knight as an amateur medium, works as an image of the desperate attempts at celebration necessary to keep afloat in Hanky Park, the slum that sucks down the unemployed. The heroine, Sally Hardcastle, has her moment with a young labour organiser. He is fired from his job, then (a too easy irony) killed while attempting to keep the peace at a demo. Sally takes the one escape route open to her, and becomes the mistress of a rich bookie.

Johanna Kirby is better at expressing Sally's bitterness than her moments of joy, but it is the bleakness that matters and she uses it electrically, attacking her family as they cling to a respectability that economics have rendered meaningless; Carmel McSharry as her mother, greying in spirit as she tries to balance conflicting loyalties; John Bardon as Dad veering between alcoholic joviality and righteous wrath as reaction to an intolerable situation; Alan Parnaby as young brother Harry, for whom love means a deeper descent into the poverty trap.

The play, compared to the dramatic preachings of our own time, is amazingly unsentimental. When Harry's pregnant girl laments in conventional terms that they cannot afford to get married, Sally coolly inquires the price of a licence and, with wet kindness, hands it over. Eric Thompson's production is one of the most firmly rooted I have seen in this theatre.

  

Applauding Ralph Richardson is one of the greatest pleasures of contemporary playgoing and there is ample opportunity for indulging it at the curtain call of Early Days (Cottesloe). We are afforded one of the longest looks so far at the Richardson eccentric, far gone in forgetfulness, but capable -- to paraphrase James Thurber -- of disconcerting spurts of lucidity. The author, David Storey, has supplied him with a political past and a fractious family in the present, but neither means much, either to him or us. He keeps harking back to a single miracle childhood memory -- it is rather like watching a print of Citizen Kane in which the Rosebud references have multiplied to the virtual exclusion of everything else.

There is some melody in the writing, and some wit -- though less than there was in Sir Ralph's speech at the Evening Standard drama awards. Supporting acting (except possibly from Barbara Flynn and Peter Machin as the youngest contributors) is stiff, possibly owing to Lindsay Anderson's directorial penchant for stoical groupings. Jocelyn Herbert's set and Alan Price's music are similarly economical, especially the latter. This, I fear, is what is known as Style. It would be interesting to see Mr Anderson at work on a good play, though my memories of his last two attempts in this line (The Seagull and What the Butler Saw) are not happy. But, if his celebrated intransigence is responsible for the Cottesloe seats being rearranged so that the stage is actually visible, he deserves our thanks.

  

It may be that Creditors (New End) is Strindberg's best play; at least its three characters -- a wilting artist, his vampire wife and her avenging ex -- are unusually well balanced. But it needs powerfully graduated acting to make it seem more than another exercise in bilious self-pity; this polite production, brought in from Leicester, seldom gets nearer passion than routine bluster.
1980-05-04-inside-pinter-s-hothouse:
Inside Pinter's Hothouse

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Manchester.

THE boss is having a drink in his office while talking to a subordinate. He loses his temper and empties the contents of his glass in the henchman's face. The response is unblinking: 'Shall I fill you up, sir?'

Harold Pinter's The Hothouse (Hampstead) was apparently his second full-length play, written between The Birthday Party and The Caretaker, but has only now been exposed to view. One sees why he has been so bashful about it: not that either its craft or its content are anything to be ashamed of, even now, but because it gives the Pinter game away. The combination of sudden impotent violence and unnervingly smooth obsequiousness has been repeated in most of his subsequent plays, but it has always been dressed up. The most effective disguise, paradoxically, has proved to be nakedness. Working on small canvasses, Mr Pinter, even when he has apparently filled in every detail, has still left us asking questions, even when (as in Betrayal) the question has been 'is that all there is?'

In The Hothouse there is, in terms of action and explanation, a great deal; there are seven characters -- Marlovian richness, by Mr Pinter's standards -- so the power games can be more extensively orchestrated than usual, the pecking yet more orderly.

At the end of The Birthday Party Goldberg and McCann dragged the catatonic Stanley away somewhere; the setting of The Hothouse could be where they dragged him. It is a mental institution, with a triple hierarchy: staff, understaff, and patients. The patients are referred to by numbers; the staff are called Roote, Gibbs, Lamb, Cutts, Lush and Tubb. Moral: never get yourself committed to the care of monosyllables.

Not one of them is what you would call compassionate, except perhaps for one underling who ends up with electrodes strapped to his head after undergoing what we used to think of as a typical Pinter interrogation. The play begins with one patient dying and another giving birth; by the end there has been generalised mayhem, which is ruefully surveyed by the man from the Ministry. The characters keep saying there's a Ministry and it turns out there is. So the play ends up making a statement: there is State-subsidised terror.

It isn't a particularly interesting statement, but the author is clearly more hooked on mechanics anyway. In The Birthday Party he left gaps in his story; in The Hothouse he takes us with him, but the results are less effective because more ponderous. This doesn't mean that mystification is more truthful, merely that you gain speed by cutting corners. The smooth brutality leads straight on to The Collection, The Homecoming and beyond, where the honing gets finer, and the people thinner.

What The Hothouse most clearly demonstrates is that The Caretaker, which followed it, was a glorious sidetrack. Mr Pinter has never matched its marvellous equipoise of character, language and feeling. And it's worth remembering that no subsequent playwright has come up with anything to match its critical and popular impact. The author has remained with us as a glory and an embarrassment: a major talent producing minor plays.

He has directed the current exhumation with great good humour, alternating between the avoidance and the exploitation of cliche. (It wasn't cliche then, but . . .) He benefits from the presence in the dominant role of Derek Newark, as forthright and unPinteresque an actor as you could find, who transmits a glorious bovine bewilderment. Others are more conventionally icy, the honours going to James Grant, suaviter in modo, and Angela Pleasence, a stunningly cool devil-woman.

  

Mr Pinter was once a small-part actor in Donald Wolfit's company; so, as the world is beginning to learn, was Ronald Harwood. The Dresser (Haymarket) is based on the strenuous provincial nights when Mr Harwood performed its titular function for Wolfit himself. There is little to say about it, except that it's very enjoyable. It sends a current of pleasure through the audience that is rare today, and was probably rare yesterday as well.

The theatre seldom attains or communicates this degree of affection when it is not dealing with itself, but there is little that is sentimental about Mr Harwood's play. His hero, known as Sir because he hasn't been knighted, is on his last legs, performing Lear during an air-raid, with his company depleted by the wartime call-up and himself uncertain whether he can bear the weight either of the role or of Cordelia.

Act One shows him in his dressing-room, being bullied and cajoled into going on (and discouraged from applying the Othello make-up by mistake); Act Two, set in the rest period between the hovel and Dover Cliff, shows him, bullying and flattering his troupe. The actor-managers used to dominate their plays to the exclusion of all others; Sir runs true to form. Every encounter tells us more about him -- his childlike courage and childish selfishness -- but his 'opponents' are so many ninepins.

This even applies to Norman the dresser -- queer (wrong era for gay); Northern, loyal and desperate -- who is excellent value, moment to moment, especially in Tom Courtenay's immensely skilful performance, but who counts at the end for less than his author imagines. It is the only real miscalculation in the play.

Freddie Jones as Sir, magically gaining in authority the second he has donned Lear's beard, is massively vulnerable, and we never tire of learning about him. The script and Michael Elliott's production are generous with professional jokes and practical detail. It is fitting that the best supporting performance should come from Lockwood West as an elderly Oswald suddenly promoted to Fool; his concerns are all professional and he is much the realest of the bunch.

  

This production comes from the Royal Exchange, Manchester, which is thriving. In repertoire with Love on the Dole is Gerard McLarnon's Blood Black and Gold, which uses religious imagery with the same abandon as Howard Barker, say, uses political, and seems to me worthy of at least as much respect. It has the same faults of over-ripeness (a trio of young crones, speaking antiphonally, is hard to stomach), but it makes scary capital out of the postulate of a personal God: if God became man, then man has a choice of becoming God or beast.

At the end a girl forced into the first choice lies dead; those who took the second are swathed together under the folds of a fairground monster. Mr McLarnon sends most of his characters around in groups, and individual psychology is hardly his concern, though Nick Stringer makes a striking figure, if not a person, of the master showman, and Dilys Hamlett (such a nice actress, I always thought) is in fine unrecognisable form as a banshee. Braham Murray's production copes imposingly with some terrifying scenic demands.

  

Constance Cummings is another nice actress, and an accomplished one, but she is hardly right for the inbred rudeness of Coward's Judith Bliss (who should have been a Dame as Sir should have been a Sir). The result is that Michael Blakemore's typically scrupulous production of Hay Fever (Lyric, Hammersmith) comes off a little flat, despite the deep, grizzled torpor of John Le Mesurier as father Bliss, the petrified politeness of Moray Watson, the pretty poison of Polly Adams, and Mary Griffiths as a dresser with little resemblance to Mr Harwood and less to Mr Courtenay.
1980-05-11-snobs-of-every-class:
Snobs of every class

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in Chichester and London.

I HAVE to confess to some affection for The Last of Mrs Cheyney, the Frederick Lonsdale comedy from 1925 that has opened the season at Chichester.

It is refreshing to encounter a playwright so completely cynical about all levels of society.

'The snobbishness of the upper classes,' says a butler to a footman, 'is only exceeded by the snobbishness of the lower and middle.' That, like most of Lonsdale's attempted epigrams, has the disadvantage of predictability; having heard the set-up, you can anticipate the pay-off. But it suggests that playwrights who have no idea of the social system giving way can afford to be far more scathing about its constituents than those consciously working to destroy it. Basking in a sense of security, false or otherwise, Lonsdale gives a lot away.

Not all his characters are snobs; some are crooks pretending to be snobs. Mrs Cheyney herself is a jewel-thief; her domestics are actually her accomplices. She invites the rich and titled to her home so that she may be invited back and have an opportunity to despoil them. (The story-line has much in common with Ben Travers's 'Plunder.')

A couple of young peers fall for her; one she despises, the other she fancies. The favoured lord finds her out, and then antagonises her by demanding her favours as the price of his silence: 'Five years in Holloway,' she declares, 'wouldn't be as long as one night with you.' She gives the alarm, and a brief nobility contest develops between them. The last act hinges on the discovery that her other suitor has written her a compromising letter; it suddenly becomes the interest of the assembled guests to buy Mrs Cheyney off rather than to prosecute her. This leads to some ringingly bitchy exchanges across the communal breakfast-table.

There are some remarkable technical gaffs. The fatal letter is never mentioned during the earlier scenes, so the whole last act has the air of a desperate if effective improvisation. The opening dialogue consists almost entirely of long hostile descriptions of those characters who have yet to enter; what grates is not the artificiality of this convention, but its impracticability; there is no way of retaining all this information, so when the nobs troop on we forget about individual characteristics and decide to regard them merely as a set of unpleasant dummies. It's enjoyable to watch Lonsdale playing Shavian games with the identical proclivities of the propertied and criminal classes, and to wonder how long he will be able to fend off the inevitable sentimental resolution. It gets him in the end, but he puts up an encouraging fight.

If the style is sub-Wilde (with the difference that it actually mentions sex) and the philosophy sub-Shaw, the plotting is frequently sub-Pinero. Reconciling these diverse styles would not be impossible but, although Patrick Lau's production is very well staged, his cast lacks gloss, or maybe simply cheek. Joan Collins is a suitably amused adventuress, but she shirks Mrs Cheyney's more melodramatic flourishes. So the play is less nonsensically entertaining than it might be. Simon Williams, though he has an air, ignores the frivolous suggestions of depth that are written into his role. Elspeth March times one line majestically, but the only actor really in control is Benjamin Whitrow, half-Raffles, half-Jeeves.

  

John Napier's timbered set for The Merry Wives of Windsor is snugger at the Aldwych than it was in Stratford and by that much more effective. The whole of this Trevor Nunn-John Caird production has gained in pleasantness; not that pleasantness is what it lacked in the first place. What is missing is drive.

At Stratford I was inclined to blame this on under-casting; in London, with everyone except the wives (one too young, the other too posh) much nearer to snuff, the fault seems, rather, that too many quietly good comic ideas--more of them verbal than visual--have been allowed to accumulate. This does very well for the opening, which is pure scene-setting and which establishes, for example, Patrick Godfrey's tetchily vivacious Shallow (far more efficient than his namesake in 'Henry IV') against Bob Peck's Page, the personification of solid bourgeois pipemanship.

Into this ambience John Woodvine's Falstaff waddles as another gentleman cracksman. His is a juicier performance than it was; there has been a similar ripening in Ben Kingsley's Ford, whose disguise as Master Brook consists mainly of the vocal quirks of Ian Richardson. But both fall in with the general ambling; even Lila Kaye's Mistress Quickly seems grossly misnamed. Geoffrey Hutchings's French doctor is the best and most economical work; the closing scene in Windsor Park has great charm, and may be regarded as a furtherance of Mr Nunn's claim to be regarded as our best director of musicals--a position he has reached, quite remarkably, without ever having done one.

  

The final section of Towards a Nuclear Future (ICA) is a staging success in Pip Simmons's best tradition: a vivid picture--achieved mainly by a lowering of lights and a deadly economy of voice and movement--of a desolate world. Whether this was meant to have been caused by the rejection of nuclear energy, or by a disaster in its functioning, I was unclear.

The evening is devoted to an unusually even marshalling of pros and cons. The subject could hardly be more pressing, but vital issues have a way of collapsing in the theatre. Certainly they will not just sustain themselves, a fact of which nobody is usually more aware than Mr Simmons. But his treatment here--some haranguing, some singing, some more haranguing--is strangely conventional.

My generation will trace the form back to Peter Brook's 'US'; others may even think of the living newspaper of the Thirties. There is some challenging of the audience, though by now both sides know this to be merely a ritual, and the actors don't even act aggrieved at getting no response. Why should we join in their games, when we have not practised and they have?

  

The Devil Himself, which has just completed two weeks at the Lyric Studio, is a Wedekind compendium by Peter Barnes, and a great improvement on his previous attempt at the Theatre Upstairs. The advertised topic is sex, but the evening proved most gripping when the range logically widened to include financial exploitation and social inhibition. These are most powerfully expressed in an interspersed series of hunted stoical monologues.

The main business of the evening is song and here we are at a double distance from the originals, served to us in new musical settings and in a number called 'Capitulation,' fitted out with a sweet-and-sour tune by Carl Davis; otherwise there are too many rhymes on the order of 'miseree' and 'chastitee' to keep me happy in my seat. The cast--Tina Marian, Charles Keating, Dilys Laye and Alan Rickman--was excellent; so was the setting--cabaret with a hint of prison--by Liz da Costa.
1980-05-18-return-of-the-crock:
Return of the Crock

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Rattigan double-bill at the National and `The Maid's Tragedy' at Stratford.

IF Terence Rattigan's The Browning Version (Lyttelton) were done in an ordinary West End house, it would probably seem a decent little play: a respectable exemplar of a dead tradition. On the sweeping width of the Lyttelton stage, facing a clinically challenging auditorium, it must expand or die.

In Michael Rudman's cool, passionate production it does the former. But there are no stretch-marks; the play, in one long act, remains a classically tight piece of work. It is, after all, patterned after the `Agamemnon'; and when Andrew Crocker-Harris, the unpopular Classics master forced into premature retirement, describes Aeschylus's play as the greatest ever written, you may be sure that Rattigan means it.

Mr Rudman uses his space like a battlefield. When he has Alec McCowen and Geraldine McEwan, as Andrew and his desperately embittered wife, sit at opposite sides of the stage, the air is dead between them. The marital poison is Strindbergian; so is the casual vitriol with which the Crocker-Harrises speak of their similarly afflicted acquaintances in between mounting more concentrated attacks on each other.

Millie's cruellest act is to destroy Andrew's belief in the present given him by his one receptive pupil: the `Browning version' of the Agamemnon. Miss McEwan lets you see exactly why she does it. `I would rather have had this present,' Andrew says, `than almost anything I can think of.' That presumably includes the pension of which he has been meanly deprived, to her quite justifiable fury. `Why,' as she says, `should he be allowed his comforting little illusions? I'm not.'

There is a kind of alliance between them, two failures against the world, and he has ratted on it. As he says, she is really quite as much to be pitied as he is. More, perhaps; he has his books, she has only a string of unloving lovers. In a later play Rattigan would probably have treated Millie's sexual dependency in more detail; here he lets Andrew tell us about it, rather than letting us see it for ourselves. Whatever his good intentions, however fine the work of Mr Rudman and Miss McEwan, it is the man's play, and it comes nearer to being a downbeat `Goodbye, Mr Chips' (Rattigan, with typical self-deprecating defensiveness, plants the reference) than might be comfortable.

When the play was first produced, making the protagonist so desiccated a figure must have seemed breathtakingly audacious. Now, when the Crock has passed into myth, we enter the theatre expecting to sympathise with him. Mr McCowen puts us brilliantly off the scent. There is no self-pity about him. His speech is brisk and level; he will remain the soulless, conscientious pedagogue to the end. Even the revelation of his unfortunate nickname hardly seems to disconcert him: `The Himmler of the Lower Fifth,' he muses, savouring the words like a lexicographer.

The piercing of the shell, so carefully built, is devastating--partly perhaps because it violates the actor's mask as well as the character's. (When did Mr McCowen last cry on stage?) But it is also momentary; what replaces it is a new bitterness, now willed and aggressive instead of a protective reflex, a schoolmaster's joke. His final muted defiance leaves the spectator torn between tears and cheers. It is a triumph for public-school understatement, a vein also skilfully and sympathetically mined by Nicky Henson as Millie's lover who doubles as the voice of decency--an awkward voice as might be expected in a world that deprecates explicit passion, even (or perhaps especially) in translation of the classics.

  

Mr Henson is the hero of Rattigan's afterpiece, Harlequinade, playing a harried stage manager on a subsidised tour of `Romeo and Juliet' (`I didn't know it was social purpose that brought us here--I thought it was the Arts Council'). Like Hildy Johnson in `The Front Page,' he is torn between a maniac milieu (Mr McCowen and Miss McEwan as a pair of empty-headed, fluffily forgetful stars) and the demands of a sensible fiancee.

As with Hildy, madness wins out; we leave him standing in for an absent actor in a brawl-scene, going devoutly through the one-two-three duelling motions, with an imaginary sword in one hand and a prompt-book in the other. It's a beguiling sight. Carl Toms's set delightfully recalls the days when Elizabethan plays were always set in a trim wilderness of steps and balustrades, wreathed in rosy-pink lights.

  

Today of course it's liable to be a sawn-off jungle--or else decadent within the decent limits of austerity. Judith Bland's set for The Maid's Tragedy (Other Place, Stratford-on-Avon) consists of a white pile carpet, dotted with garden furniture. It's a wickered world, and a dazzling one, the ladies of the cast strolling or languishing in primary colours.

Barry Kyle has engineered one of the most exciting of recent RSC productions. Beaumont and Fletcher's play takes as easily to scaling down as Rattigan's to blowing up. Concentration flowers for both actors and audience; every character is individualised, every line tells--especially the libidinous exchanges of a court mainly populated by panders.

A vaguely modern setting sharpens the all-pervading aroma of sado-masochism; with the king as its fountainhead. He is well enough played by John Carlisle as a disposable dictator; though this is hardly the ambience to inspire reverence for divine right. Unfortunately that is the governing force in the life of the hero, Amintor, married off to the royal mistress Evadne, but denied her bed; a more seasoned actor than Rob Edwards might reveal him as one of the more interesting Jacobean neurotics.

Tom Wilkinson gives a forceful account of his buddy Melantius, a war-hero turned terrorist--and, true to form, making a safe conduct his first demand; Raymond Westwell is his aged butt, drawn in considerable detail; Sinead Cusack is fittingly provocative as the bad girl who goes to the good by pinioning the king down (he just thinks she's into bondage) before stabbing him; and Domini Blythe makes something strong and disturbing of the suicidal virgin (who on paper looks wetter than Ophelia) for whom the play is named. Unless of course it's called after Amintor who, through royal caprice, goes virgin to his grave; those playwrights loved a joke.

  

Of the unsubsidised fringe groups trading in rare revivals, the best I have seen is the Cherub company, who infiltrate the Young Vic Studio with Barabbas by the Fleming, Michel de Ghelderode: not a likeable play (its Judas, certainly as played here, reeks of anti-Semitism), but a strong and original one, juggling familiar Passion Play characters into new baroque patterns with the released robber himself a bemused and furious thickhead. Andrew Vishnevski's production mostly avoids preciousness like the plague.

The week's one new play, Robert Holman's Estuary (Bush), has rather the look of a revival. What Mr Holman does well is as good as ever: natural, especially liquid, imagery, close male relationships, with Mark Eden especially good as a Tees-side Sunday fisherman, in collusion with his son and at odds with his wife. When the causes of conflict are revealed, they turn out to be as old as Aeschylus, and Mr Holman, though a quiet writer, will have none of Rattigan's pussyfooting. On this occasion, I think it might have helped.
1980-05-25-friends-romans-the-lot:
Friends, Romans, the lot

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

Peter Gill's production of Julius Caesar (Riverside Studios) has the best Shakespearian crowd scenes in recent memory. There is nothing apologetic about them; no pretence that three or four actors can -- if symbolically grouped, murkily lit and encouraged to stomp or chant in unison -- do the work of a dozen.

Mr Gill has about 20 actors to play with and he sends them on in swiftly varying formations: as soldiers -- standing, turning and even executing a balletic battle that is over before you have time to question it -- or as citizens. In the intervening scenes they play individual officers or conspirators, two or three apiece. But the doubling is never either obtrusive or confusing.

All the men are dressed in the same grey uniform: tunics, socks and long winter underwear. The effect is not prepossessing, but it is immensely useful -- an enshrouding anonymity from which each player can emerge and to which he can return. While on, he has to trust to the script and his own skills to establish him; and though the level of success is variable no-one actually fails. The play is kept taut.

The scenes of full orchestration are thrilling. Brutus and Antony make their orations from precarious plinths actually borne aloft by the mob they are addressing: a foot or a word wrong and they will slip and, presumably, be torn to pieces. Or be stoned to death: as happens, in the ensuing savagely staged scene, to Cinna the poet. As the lights go down on his remains, the first act ends with an off-stage shout of 'Caesar', a cry repeated at the close when the only figure visible, upright this time, is that of the glacial Octavius.

The effect -- cynically cyclic -- is the nearest Mr Gill comes to explicit political comment: kill a dictator and gain an emperor. Robert Flemyng's Caesar, though, lets you see why he was killed. Mr Flemyng must have a good 30 years on anyone else in the cast, but his career has not included much Shakespeare. So he is liable at first to appear both outmoded and unpractised: caged in mannerisms. But his isolation emphasises Caesar's own -- physically infirm, but inhumanly brave because afraid to admit to being anything else. Mr Gill has staged the murder superbly -- a series of sadistic lunges topped by the victim's suicidal advance on Brutus's sword, while the heavens belch red smoke -- and in dying with a Latin tag on his lips, Mr Flemyng strikes his finest attitude.

John Shrapnel's Brutus is another, even richer, study in egotism. He argues himself fascinatingly into killing Caesar for fear of what he might do, quizzically spelling out the arguments and then rushing, self-hypnotised, into a murderous conclusion. Brutus himself speaks of his state as 'a hideous dream' and this one never really wakes up.

Michael Byrne's Cassius, apart from a fine early spurt of venom, comes over as a solid Englishman out of Simon Gray; and John Price's Antony is little more than vigorous. The finest colouring in the production comes, unexpectedly, from Portia: a brief role into which Lindsay Duncan packs an infinity of poise, anguish and affection. Even in silence she rivets respect. Other performances are adequate if vocally limited. As stagecraft this is Riverside's finest offering to date.

  

It would be hypocritical to pretend that any critic approached Barnardo (Royalty) -- billed as a family musical -- expecting it to be anything but appalling. There must, what with Oliver and Annie, be a severe shortage of singing and dancing orphans by now; and the choice of theme and hero hardly seemed to promise astringency.

London's East End is the title of the first number. It seems a nice enough place, and not even the discovery of a few starving children can stop the chorus singing about it. But perhaps it's more menacing than it seems. One notices that none of the inhabitants dares to make a move on his own; and the exercise they do take, though certainly energetic, is severely limited: they rarely get beyond flinging their legs at the audience and their arms at one another.

This affliction strikes the population of the neighbourhood very young. Even when removed to the first Barnardo home -- and sleeping, incidentally, three in a bed -- they cannot refrain from sitting up in unison, folding their arms, rocking from side to side, putting their hands behind their heads and swaying. These are boys; the girls (they arrive in the second act, rather arbitrarily I thought, but maybe the Equal Opportunities Commission operates at unexpectedly low levels) are saucier; they turn repeatedly upstage and jut their behinds out. One even breaks ranks.

Their number is called 'Girls'; the boys' bedtime routine is entitled 'Snuggle Up.' I hate to think what effect these early experiences will have on their future development, let alone that of the British musical. One of the lads is Jewish and has a solo 'Oy Vey.' Lord Shaftesbury is needed for the story and, providentially, otherwise how would we work in 'The Midnight Waltz,' he is throwing a ball. (Not having a ball; only Victorian Cockneys use language like that.)

Barnardo wins a wife, with absolutely no trouble. In Act Two he loses her, because their son dies of pneumonia. She blames him for this, possibly because instead of putting him to bed (which might have occasioned a meaningful reprise of 'Snuggle Up'), he held the barefoot boy in his arms while singing at him, for what seemed like hours, a ballad ('My Son') about all the things he might have achieved had he grown up.

Ernest Maxin is credited as author, director and composer, and his work is certainly consistent. He has fashioned a collector's item, right down to the obligatory distinguished actor (John Arnatt) lifting voice and linking arms in praise of 'Lovely Hot Pies' (he's playing Shaftesbury, by the way) and the permanent crackle on the PA system. I wouldn't have missed it for the world.

  

Sam Shepard's Seduced (Theatre Upstairs) is, I suppose, a more distinguished piece of work, but it suffers from the same inability to do more with its central figure than just put him there. He is, more or less, Howard Hughes, discovered lying in a dentist's chair with fingernails a mile long (Image I). This is his Endgame, and he has a surly attendant to push the point. Two women arrive, and attempt to lure him back to life with many words and a striptease. (Image II.) The play ends with the stage bathed in the protagonist's blood. (Image III.) The Shepard plays I have enjoyed have been moved along as briskly as possible; this one sinks in the verbiage, despite striking performances all round.

  

Theatermanufaktur, a roving troupe from West Berlin, have brought to the Old Vic Murieta, which seems to be a free adaptation of a parable of Chilean revolution by Pablo Neruda. It was almost comforting to note that German actors seemed hardly more comfortable playing Latin peasants than our own, but the visual impact of Otto Zonschitz's production is considerable. The verbal was difficult to judge, owing to a faulty translation system (now apparently rectified). Even so, I wondered whether the liberal use of a narrator was not draining out the drama.
1980-06-01-shaw-s-bad-dreams:
Shaw's bad dreams

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on `John Bull's Other Island.'

NOBODY would ever describe Shaw as self-effacing, but it is only in recent years that we have begun to look in his plays for evidence of personal pain or personal guilt.

`The Philanderer' gained in interest a couple of years ago when we saw it as the confession of a womaniser for ever keeping fascinated tabs on himself. In John Bull's Other Island (Greenwich) the authorial figure is Larry Doyle, an Irishman who fled his native country after adolescence and made first for America and then for London, where he achieved success as a civil engineer in partnership with a hearty, sentimental and fearsomely energetic Englishman named Tom Broadbent. The play narrates Doyle's return to Ireland after an eighteen-year absence, as escort to Broadbent who wants effectively to buy up Larry's home village of Rosscullen. He succeeds; of course; and while he is at it, he also acquires Larry's former sweetheart.

If you want to interest an Irishman in Ireland, Larry complains, you've got to call the unfortunate island Kathleen ni Houlihan and pretend she's a little old woman. Shaw's method of interesting the English public in Ireland was to make her an attractive woman in her thirties and call her Nora Reilly. What Nora comes to feel for Broadbent is not so much love as incredulous fascination. Her compatriots have their own variation on her response. They adopt Broadbent as their parliamentary candidate. Larry, having declined the honour, though they find both his personality and his political views puzzling. The year is 1904, he is a Gladstonian Liberal, and the most vociferous Home Ruler among them.

What rivets the attention is Larry's anguished, sardonic impotence as his English friend (to whom he is devoted) comes into what should have been his own inheritance: one from which he is debarred from fighting by his own exiled nature. Larry is a man who sees through everything and so can do nothing; and he must have embodied some of Shaw's own worst dreams of himself. This was, after all, the only play in which he dared to confront himself as an Irishman.

The play has a curious, straggling construction: dropping either its romantic or political theme for an act at a time, but tying them together when we realise that Broadbent's pursuit of Nora and his attempt to bring progress--defined as a hotel with golf-links--to Rosscullen have in fact been identical. The last scene confronts the two engineers with Peter Keegan, the ex-priest who believes the world, since it is 'very clearly a place of torment and penance,' to be hell. His pessimism is a bracing tonic among the well-meaning fools who, here as elsewhere, people Shaw's universe; he is possibly the most persuasive of Shavian sages. (Captain Shotover of `Heartbreak House' seems a pretender beside him). His indictment of the 'efficient' methods that will ruin everyone except the projectors themselves sounds unanswerable. And what counters it is not argument, but Broadbent's approval. (`Too true, Mr Keegan, only too true. And most eloquently put') which reduces the whole matter to one of words, words, words.

That, if you like, was Shaw's vice; and in some plays the demonstration that one point of view is as convincing as another is only an infuriating, gentlemanly game. Here it is the base of a dramatic system, maybe even of a philosophic one. Keegan's final vision of heaven, `the dream of a madman,' is the kind of Shavian writing one is officially meant to find embarrassing; in fact it is haunting, and the more impressive in Alan Strachan's production for being delivered from an almost bare stage.

My main memory of Mr Strachan's previous production of the play at the Mermaid is of P. G. Stephens's quietly convinced exposition of those closing moments. He repeats the performance at Greenwich and the quality remains, though it was often obscured on the first night by uncertainties of phrasing and even of volume. Mr Strachan's current direction is uneven, at its best in the opening scene in London: a warmly exasperated duel between Christopher Benjamin's eternally boyish Broadbent and Tony Doyle's splendidly incisive Larry.

When the scene moves across the Channel, character acting, of varying quality, takes place, conspiring (with the author's connivance) to turn satire of stock comedy into the thing itself: honourable exceptions are Sorcha Cusack's Nora and Chris Gannon's Matt Haffigan, a small man in every sense, concerned that reform has gone quite far enough and had better stop lest other people have things easier than he did. Some of the electioneering scenes are impenetrably dated, but most confirm the impression that anything written about Ireland always sounds topical.

  

David Pownall's Livingstone and Sechele (Lyric Studio, Hammersmith) is latter-day Shavianising lacking the transforming features: witty without craziness, intelligent without communicated involvement. Livingstone, you know about; Sechele turns out to be his first convert among African chiefs; a conquest achieved only after years of endeavour, and then on dubious grounds. What Sechele really wants is (a) protection from the encroaching Boers and (b) rain. For this he is willing to embrace Christianity and give up most of his wives, one of whom is a constant--and, in Anni Domingo's performance, quite understandable--source of temptation.

Mr Pownall writes with arctic playfulness; his Sechele is a smooth-tongued sophisticate who addresses Livingstone with jewelled endearments--a vein of fun admirably mined in Joe Marcel's performance. Equally good are Peter Kelly's tetchy David and Jennifer Piercey as his understanding spouse. At one point, most decorously staged, both couples make love on opposite sides of the stage, all climaxing simultaneously and tempting reviewers into the forlorn hope of coming up with some new joke about the missionary position.

  

Theatermanufaktur Berlin completed their season at the Old Vic with Johannes Faustus, written by Brecht's musical collaborator Hanns Eisler, and finally sending its hero to perdition for devoting his magic powers to entertaining the nobility instead of assisting the peasants: following in fact in the footsteps of the proto-traitor Luther. To invoke eternal damnation as a penalty for being on the wrong side in the class war seems to me to conflate two irreconcilable myths; but Theatermanufaktur manage to draw on both traditions with gusto and imagination.

The preview of eternal torments to which Faustus is treated before the devils come for him is especially effective; a tattered banner is drawn aside, then replaced, while behind it the actors group themselves into some new tableau of torment. The unstressed joy they take in their own ability to frighten is typical of the production, which purports to be done by travelling players. So, come to think of it, it is.
1980-06-08-change-your-partner:
Change your partner

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Ayckbourn at the National.

PAY attention, and I will try to make clear the four-scene structure of Alan Ayckbourn's Sisterly Feelings (Olivier).

It all takes place on a green but muddy hill. Here long ago Ralph, a doctor, proposed to Amy, now deceased. After her funeral Ralph brings his family and their connections on a sentimental visit. Ralph has two grown-up daughters, Dorcas and Abigail. Owing to a shortage of cars one of them will have to walk home in the coveted company of a fancible young man named Simon.

Simon is (here we go) the girls' brother's fiancee's brother. Which lady he shall escort is settled for him (here we go again and deeper) by the toss of a coin. Its fall determines the content of the next scene, since it is taken for granted that the walk home will launch either Dorcas or Abigail on an affair with Simon.

The second scene accordingly consists of a family picnic (father's annual treat) in which Simon sports with Dorcas (or Abigail), jealously observed by Abigail (or Dorcas), and also by Dorcas's former boy-friend (or Abigail's husband), who wants her back (or wants her back).
