The end of this scene brings us to another junction-point; the sister in possession may either stay with Simon or abandon him to her rival. The decision is left to the actress concerned, and it determines the content of the third scene which may be either Simon participating in a cross-country race with Dorcas as a steward, or Abigail defying her business-executive husband by opting for one night of the simple life, spent with Simon in a tent. Either way the scene ends with Simon forsaken, and old ways resumed. The last scene never varies, and is cunningly constructed to make sense whatever has gone before. The upshot is that no decisions we make, or let chance make for us, have any effect on our ultimate fate. To register this point properly you have to see the play twice, taking in different versions of the middle scenes on each occasion.

Mr Ayckbourn offers us both a technique and a philosophy. The first works superbly. There are few theatrical excitements to compare with the suspense on Tuesday night when Penelope Wilton as Abigail, knowing she had the audience in the palm of her hand, lingered out her moment of choice at the end of the second scene. Our suspense had everything to do with the actress, nothing with the character; it is, after all, built into the scheme of the play that the character has no effective choice.

And here Mr Ayckbourn's comic determinism betrays him. 'We're really not at all alike,' says Abigail to Dorcas, and we are presumably meant to think that she is fooling herself. But from what we see they really don't seem to have much in common; and though Mr Ayckbourn gets a lot of acute fun out of their joint presentation, competing for their mutual flame or counting the odds on their father's decline into senility like a suburban Goneril and Regan, there is a damaging imbalance between them.

Dorcas, a local radio presenter and obsessive lame-duck collector, is considerably the nicer of the two and therefore, in an Ayckbourn play, decisively handicapped; Anna Carteret needs all her charm to fill the role out. Her lover Stafford, left-wing poet and layabout, is way off Mr Ayckbourn's beat, and his farcical attempts at re-conquest seem to have been written in the author's sleep; though Simon Callow (who, when on the fringe, was invariably cast as a pillar of the Establishment and is now in the reverse situation) plays him with compensating energy.

He responds ferociously to advertisements for four-figure bathtubs (if you follow me) in the Sunday supplements. Patrick, Abigail's husband, reads the same ads with (in every sense) consuming devotion. So they are really brothers under the skin; but Patrick, politely ruthless, is a far more tractable dramatic subject. Michael Gambon who plays him is a fascinating actor operating, behind a bland mask, on a scale that moves from fatuous benevolence to stark brutality and with a precise knowledge of how and when to adjust it.

Miss Wilton, spoiled and nasal, makes him the perfect attitudinising spouse, and their reunion is fore-ordained. Stephen Moore's vacuously athletic Simon jumps off hillocks or flies kites with a delicious air of modest self-satisfaction.

The play's underpinning is generous and secure; in its sequence of family reunions nearly every line tells, and very few cheat. It is typical that the sisters' crucial uniting drama is ticking away behind the amorous facade; they are determined that their brother shall not marry the girl, of his choice and here too fate overtakes them. Selina Cadell as the patronised fiancee is well worth cheering on.

The casting throughout is abnormally strong, though sometimes excessive; Andrew Cruickshank's fey plangency is too other-worldly for the decomposing paterfamilias and Michael Bryant's distinction emphasises rather than disguises the stock qualities of the policeman he plays, though it's something to hear him intone 'it's a free country' in accents of funereal regret. The author and Christopher Morahan manoeuvre the play impeccably across the treacherous undulations of Alan Tagg's set.

The reason, said Tom Lehrer in one of his few relevant remarks not quoted in Tomfoolery (Criterion), most folk-songs are so atrocious is that they were written by the people. He also (and this is quoted) paid sardonic tribute to the courage of the young poet-singers who pelted their audiences with admonitions with which they were fully in agreement anyway.

I am not sure that Mr Lehrer's position, singing anti-bomb and anti-religious songs to a liberal audience, was so very different; but with him there were the crucial differences of insight, flair and wit. By the Sixties I had lost touch with him; so his later songs seem much fresher to me. But I think anyway that he was developing from a sick joker to a satirist; these numbers have a broader base, and offer the performers more scope.

In Gillian Lynne's production The Vatican Rag and The Folk Song Army take imposingly to the stage. The evening even has a shape, with miniature reprises of previous numbers built into the final jolly nuclear chorus, We Will All Go Together When We Go, a song which, after some years' disuse, re-emerges as certainly apt but not at this moment very funny. To say that I admired Robin Ray's prowess as presenter, singer, dancer and momentary violinist is insufficient; I was jealous. A carp: audiences at Death of a Salesman are assumed to know what Linda means, so why Anglicise an all-American song like My Home Town?

Buchner the German prodigy of the 1830s who died at 23, may have discovered modern boredom, as eventually popularised by Samuel Beckett. In Danton's Death and in the strange comedy Leonce and Lena (now on view at the Gate Theatre in Notting Hill) his characters groan under the sheer weight of observed phenomena. It clogs their lives, and their conversation. Some of the tedium is transmitted all too efficiently, but more is bracing and amusing.

The Gate production is imaginatively designed, with Stuart Fox quite stylish as the hero, heir to the tiniest of principalities, who eventually blunders into a secret marriage with his own fiancee. Buchner's world, in the end, is surprisingly similar to Mr Ayckbourn's.
1980-06-15-travelling-nowhere:
Travelling nowhere

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London, York and Hornchurch.

IN HIS previous plays David Williamson has come before us as pretty hard-boiled. But of course hard shells are notorious harbingers of soft centres and in Travelling North (Lyric, Hammersmith) Mr Williamson exposes his.

His title is surely meant to possess more resonance than is actually summoned in the course of the play. Its surface meaning is strictly geographical: Frank, a widower in his seventies, and Frances, a widow 20 years younger, leave Melbourne and go to live on the coast of New South Wales. She has daughters who, selfishly, keep calling her back; Frank is afraid to let her go alone (afraid for himself, not her) and the distance, since he has a weak heart and an assortment of other ailments, nearly kills him. He too is selfish and Frances leaves him. But she comes back when, against all his humanist principles, he offers to marry her.

The wedding, or its aftermath, really does for him, and he expires on the front porch while listening to Mozart. Frances honours his last wishes by breaking open a magnum of champagne and, having fended off proposals from the local doctor and the man next door, decides to continue 'travelling north.' This, according to the map in the programme, would bring her to Brisbane; what else it would bring her to remains a mystery. You are presumably meant to think, approvingly, that she will keep on exploring life; if this were a musical, she would be singing an inspirational song about it. It is all very vague and, by that token, sentimental.

Mr Williamson does his best to be tough. He dwells on the awful snobbishness of Frances's family, and on Frank's crankiness, obstinacy and waning sexual powers. But he never writes a line that illuminates either character for us, and even his jokes are mechanical. ('Not another house in sight,' say the gratified couple arriving at their retreat. 'Anyone home?' inquires their neighbour, on the dot.)

There is nothing unbelievable about the play, and our attention is held, but at a moderate and unrewarding level. Frequent changes of scene elicit an unwontedly fidgety production from Michael Blakemore; and the supporting playing mostly lacks conviction. The two leading players, fortunately, have a grip; Peter Vaughan plays Frank's tetchy incredulity in considerable detail, and, as Frances, Rosemary Leach's shine is undimmed.

  

Travelling north myself, I came to York where the local cycle of Mystery Plays is again in session: a three-and-a-half-hour trip from the Creation to the Day of Judgment and, at that, considerably shorn. The medieval writers never had much time for the Old Testament--all they wanted was to see mankind getting itself thoroughly lost so that it could be redeemed in Part 2--and the present editors have less.

The plays are performed in the ruins of St Mary's Abbey, which helpfully arched pile shares the honours of the occasion with the arrival of darkness, an atmospheric blessing which falls, of course, on the just and unjust open-air productions alike.

Apart from Christopher Timothy's Christ, agreeable but not inspirational, the cast is composed entirely of local amateurs. They have been assembled in great numbers and the first stage-filling sight of them promises excitement. But it never materialises.

Patrick Garland's best production-touch comes at the Last Supper, where the disciples, having their feet washed, turn out to be ticklish. There is less of this detail in the writing than there is in the Wakefield Cycle, but more might have been imported. Mr Garland suddenly has his cast break out into Blake's 'Jerusalem,' which is contemporary neither with the plays themselves, the events they depict, nor the current production. The effect is half-hearted, and only flimsily related to the scene to which it is attached: the entry of Jesus into Jerusalem, on a real donkey. The shepherds also have genuine sheep, which may be seen grazing just off stage past a sign marked 'Actors Only.'

  

The Theatre Royal, York's Rep, has contributed to the Festival a Jacobean rarity, Webster's The Devil's Law-Case. The chief interest of this play lies in its central character, Romelio, who is the Websterian malcontent gone middle-class: not a poor scholar but a rich merchant, deeply contemptuous of the aristocracy and as capable as any of them of the behaviour expected of a good Renaissance Italian--debauching a nun, say; or persuading his sister to fake a pregnancy.

In The White Devil or The Duchess of Malfi, the most vital character is the commentator; here Webster turns him into the protagonist, but--in the interests of a kind of happy ending--cheats him of a tragic finish. This is frustrating; nothing but death should really stop Romelio; and the playwright has simply to fade him out. Elsewhere the comic format suits Webster's genius very well.

As important to the plot as Romelio himself is his mother: an elderly matron who falls for a young nobleman, she suspects her son of having killed him (he didn't, but not for lack of trying) and plans in revenge to disinherit him by declaring him illegitimate. This blackening of her own reputation suggests a reckless carnality which Webster obviously thought grotesque, and which Annette Kerr's discreet performance never communicates; however, since she too is dispatched to respectable happiness at the end, she may be right.

Damien Thomas gets a good measure of Romelio's cynicism, less of his bravado; I still wait to see this kind of role played with the right quicksilver touch. (No actor hung up on consistency is going to do justice to Webster.) The play, which incorporates much smoothly snarling satire on the venal lawyers, deserves attention at the highest level--a line touched here by Martin Johns's latticed chamber set.

  

Barrie Keeffe's She's So Modern (Queen's, Hornchurch) centres on a lady trying to cleanse television of everything save Come Dancing and the Eurovision Song contest. Mr Keeffe's reference point is not Mary Whitehouse (dismissed by his crusader as a sold-out softie), but Margaret Thatcher, and his real target, as suggested by the title and reinforced in song, is a state of mind and country that finds passionless toughness timeless and exciting.

Keeffe too is writing in a Jacobean comic vein, hindered I think by the fact that he doesn't really find his subject funny. It is not until the last 20 minutes of mayhem and straitjacketing that he comes near to making his point effectively. If he were really writing a satire on morality campaigning, his contention that the puritans are only randy hypocrites or plain crooks would be self-defeating; we know that their sincerity is what really frightens. After bigger game he is entitled to his angle, but he seldom makes it work for him.

It is as always a relief when Keeffe satirises his own side, in the shape of a chronically banned playwright. Otherwise his animus is liable to be self-defeating; one feels impelled to take sides against him. For the first time in my life--and aided by a straight-down-the-line performance from Charlotte Cornwell in stark contrast to some of the slap-happy approximations carrying on around her--I almost found the PM sympathetic.
1980-06-22-perils-of-eng-lit:
Perils of Eng. Lit?

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Educating Rita, A Quick Deco and Rutherford and Son.

TREADING eagerly in the upwardly mobile footsteps of Shaw's Eliza Doolittle and Arnold Wesker's Beatie Bryant comes the heroine of Willy Russell's Educating Rita (Warehouse), whose real name is Susan.

She calls herself Rita after the author, or is it the heroine, of a novel she has been impressed by: a circumstance which greatly irritates her English teacher. What turns him off is not her taste in literature, but the affectation of such an action and the suggestibility it implies. He is a weary don, supervising an Open University course to earn some extra gelt to get drunk on. She is a hairdresser's assistant in her mid-twenties, married without children, who left school soon bored and now doubts the existence of the working-class culture she keeps hearing about, and which seems to her to consist of endless drinking sessions and soulless mating sessions of the approved variety. Her enthusiasm for literature astounds her instructor (he doesn't come across much of that in his walk of life) and he tries to get rid of her. Stuck with her, he tries to teach her how to read books in the manner approved by examiners. He counsels her against answering questions according to the dictates of simple enthusiasm. 'Is your opinion worth the radio?' Give reasons, he tells her, and quote relevant authorities.

The play stays, ably and, on the principle of leaving the best till last, accurately with Rita. Miss Walters is unmatched among young actresses at suggesting a mind chafing against restraints, and she has been developing, in addition to her native canniness, a joyously exuberant comic style. (Her performance in Good Fun at Sheffield was a marvellous piece of tight-rope-walking.) In this play, with due help from her author, she gathers more laughs in an evening than have been heard in the entire previous history of the Warehouse. But she is also moving, and--again with Mr Russell's assistance--she brings alive, through narrative, the whole history of her disintegrating marriage to a resentful husband: something not necessarily to be regretted, but still painful to go through. She might develop in a lower register, though.

Her partner in this duet is another matter. The beginning of one scene catches him reading Jake's Thing and that probably places him. Once a poet, but all ambition and even interest long gone--and Mr Russell has added no new ingredients. Mark Kingston's performance is what I would call fluffy: pleasant, never actually wrong, but lacking in bite.

The play may lack the breadth of Roots, but in one respect it goes beyond it. It shows us the learning process, and makes us both anxious and involved. In Mr Wesker's play it had all happened, apart from the final traumatic piece of self-education, before the curtain went up. So Mr Russell burrows and questions. We were left in no doubt that Beatie Bryant was pursuing the right values; it was merely her mentor who let her down. Mr Russell doesn't fall for trendy philistinism; as a writer he values writing. But he assaults the ends for which it is taught; when Rita learns to give the right answers something of her individuality has been lost.

Actually I think the emphasis on exam-technique is exaggerated, but much of it is still alarmingly true. In literary criticism, Rita is informed, is an objective science, and she should not muddy it with such irrelevant considerations as whether or not she actually enjoys a book--all of which chills the blood considerably. Sent off to summer school, she returns able to make all the right noises about Blake, though she makes them, admittedly, with some dash.

Mr Russell hasn't shaped this material very decisively, but he has at least recognised that it exists. He has structured the play as a series of sketches with blackout endings: not very neatly handled in Mike Ockrent's production, which leaves scenes and actors hanging, but building up into a shaggy-teacher story, at the end. By prevailing standards, this is an exceptionally lively evening.

  

Of all the authors who most puzzles Rita is Forster; she has problems, as who wouldn't, with souls, and one admonitory lament begins, 'My son, I gave you the whole of myself jack'; it seemed to sum up the Genius of A Quick Deco (Chalk Farm). Chalk-striped suits and rimless glasses for the men, mandatory black dress for the lady, potted greenery for the set: that's the ambience. Nothing brassy; John Golder and John Harle, the two actor-musicians who devised it, are as discreet in song, speech and movement as a pair of Edwardian shadows.

When Duke Ellington's Mood Indigo, usually rendered as a lush lullaby, was rendered on a small set of flutes, with spare, court-romanticism, its despairing sweetness seemed to say--you could call the other side of it--Brecht and Weill. Later might be, Brecht and Eisler.

In fact this selection of the words and music of Noel Coward seldom strays far from fragmented revue form, is the perfect heir for actors who enjoy lecturing audiences. If I am to be bullied I think I would rather have it done by a live author.

  

Coward brings me to Mrs Worthington's Daughters about whom, on the evidence available at the Theatre Upstairs, he had the right idea. The touring ladies--and gentlemen--who make up the company travelling under that name will doubtless improve with age, but at present they are lamentably under-powered for Rutherford and Son, the harmless Edwardian drama of domestic exploitation (by Githa Sowerby, a woman; and so what?) they are supposed to be resuscitating. They sit around looking tired, and seldom raise their voices above a moan. The oppressed--on this showing as on many others--are not the kind of people you want to spend your time with. The oppressors aren't much fun either.
1980-06-29-novel-epic:
Novel epic

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'Nicholas Nickleby.'

David Threlfall as Smike (lower left) with a galaxy of the RSC's Dickensian characters.

THERE IS a lot to be said for length.

The Life and Adventures of Nicholas Nickleby (Aldwych) is the equivalent of two bumper plays, and has a total playing-time of eight and a half hours. The public instinct to queue for an epic is perfectly sound; quantity may not be a substitute for quality, but it is quality's most powerful ally. I came out of the theatre, going on midnight, wrung-out and grateful.

The critical reaction has astonished me: hours of pleasure, acknowledged as such, and people start wondering whether it should have been done. What comes through Nicholas Nickleby, as through The Greeks, earlier this year, is that those concerned were excited by the material and couldn't wait to get on the stage. That is not just a valid reason for putting on a show; it is the only reason.

Not every novelist inspires such feelings. Dickens, though, always has and always will. Nobody but Shakespeare created such insistent characters, such swingingly speakable dialogue, or so palpable a dramatic universe.

The theatre lost a great deal when the best men took to writing novels, and it seems sensible to try and regain some of the ground. Dickens communicates with an audience more fully, more theatrically, than most playwrights; the first-night cheers came from an audience rejoicing at their release from starvation rations. (Someone has to quote Squeers's "here's richness," so let it be me.)

I had better name the adaptor, David Edgar, and the directors, Trevor Nunn and John Caird, without trying to divide credit; the actors apparently worked from the book and it is Dickens's text, not a separate artefact, to which they must be held responsible. They have preserved all the strands of plot, sometimes in dazzling counterpoint, and nearly all the characters.

They have even tried to retain some of the narration, with varying results; Dickens wrote in sustained paragraphs and breaking these up, one line to an actor, destroys the impetus. The first 15 minutes had me very uneasy, but the later use of a doom-laden chorus to hunt Ralph Nickleby to death was very effective.

What has to go, irretrievably, is the insouciant asides ("two live Members of Parliament looking so pleasant that it seemed a perfect marvel how any man could have the heart to vote against them") that make Dickens so literally irresistible a satirist. The loss is compounded by a certain native earnestness in the RSC production. Any pamphleteer could make people shudder at Dotheboys Hall (and many did); it took Dickens to make them laugh, and to get the Yorkshire schools closed down. If these scenes at the Aldwych are not horrific enough, the basic reason is that they are not funny enough.

Squeers is a juicy character; Ben Kingsley, who plays him, is a dry actor. (He makes amends later as a drunken member of the Crummles troupe.) Then, what misplaced integrity caused John McEnery to play the imposter Mantalini, whose joke depends on exquisite affectation, as dead common? Melodrama is softened too.

Roger Rees as Nicholas and Susan Littler as sister Kate superbly avoid any suggestion of pasteboard heroics, and Mr Rees's native quality of slightly sheepish impetuosity could hardly be more winning or more useful. But they might have risked some of his higher flights (his description of the Hall, say, as a place where "infant misery stalks precocious"); they might have made his mother's absent-minded remonstrances more effective (Jane Downs seems too level-headed for the role) and also have given greater weight to his uncle's antagonism, which gets lost. Instead of a monster with a chink of kindness for his niece, John Woodvine sometimes seems to be playing an affectionate uncle driven into villainy.

But as the day progresses, into darker and less charted territory, most of these performances ripen; and there is a marvellous setpiece at half-time: a Crummles performance of Romeo and Juliet with a happy ending in execrable rhyming couplets. This is apocryphal Dickens as well as apocryphal Shakespeare, but at this point both cast and audience deserve to stretch out and relax.

Graham Crowden's actor-manager is rollingly definitive; and Lila Kaye makes a formidable wife both for him and the schoolmaster. In other parts of the forest Bob Peck doubles a cheer-worthy John Browdie with a baronet too deep for hisses, Timothy Kightley is a properly touchy rate-collector, and Suzanne Bertish plays an Italianate actress with an uncanny resemblance to Dorothy Tutin.

Edward Petherbridge's Newman Noggs, shuffling out of his skin with excitement as the plot thickens, just loses first place to David Threlfall's perfect Smike, which is dogged and occasionally humorous and so moving as to force a revaluation of Victorian death-bed scenes.

The adaptation infuses some doubt into the happy ending: justified in view of the distance we have travelled, but rather confusingly staged. Otherwise the book's morality, with every episode dependent on money, is allowed to strike home unforced.

  

Dickens distrusted all politicians. So, up to a point, do Howard Brenton and Tony Howard, authors of A Short Sharp Shock (Stratford East), but they waver, expressing a sentimental preference for the Left; and in this production it is sentimental, since the workers uniting against Thatcherism at the final curtain are written and played with the hollowness that invariably infects the favoured side in agitprop dramas.

However, the heart of the play lies in the Cabinet, and the two Howards have managed some vigorous and imaginative lampooning; having Howe, Joseph et al played by women adds an icy touch of style to the proceedings, though it seems to promise something more apocalyptic than is actually delivered. Nor does it quite jibe with Gwen Taylor's Thatcher impersonation, which is the equal of Janet Brown's on The News Huddlines: though I'm not sure that Miss Brown, speaking funnier lines to a larger audience, isn't doing more damage.

The ludicrous threat of censorship has caused mention of Fielding, whose political satires brought the Lord Chamberlain upon us 250 years ago. But Fielding was writing in a tradition that took personal attack for granted; we cannot do it without unconsciously congratulating ourselves on our daring. So political satire remains fixated at Private Eye level.

  

Nostalgia creeps fast upon us. Dusty Hughes's Commitments (Bush) takes us back to the early Seventies, and the end of the last Tory Government. The characters are assorted politicos, mostly engaged in luxury trades (writing, acting and so on) and wittily observed. (Notice how on the fringe industrial brand-names produce the same infallible laughter as place-names do in Shaftesbury Avenue.) The uncommitted character, with whom the audience is likeliest to identify, is the one of whom the author has selflessly declared he most disapproves. Alan Rickman, who plays him, has perfected a sardonic glide to match his deep deprecating voice; in a good cast Paola Dionisotti also stands out as his spiritual opposite.

  

But for political drama that comes anywhere near Dickens in trenchancy you have to go to the first half of The Arbor (Royal Court), whose author, Andrea Dunbar, puts an appalling life on stage without ever losing her cool or even her humour. It is the kind of artlessness only possible, or indeed tolerable, from a teenage writer depicting her own world. In the second half the lack of form begins to get to you; but before that the play has left its mark. Max Stafford-Clark's production is admirably acted, with Kathryn Pogson a memorable picture of hugged solitude as the twice-pregnant heroine, aged 15 and named Andrea Dunbar.
1980-07-06-the-demon-barber-strikes-agai:
The Demon Barber strikes again

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Stratford.

THIS week all our heroes have been mad: the Prince of Denmark, the Peasant Poet and the Demon Barber of Fleet Street.

Frenzy is the distinguishing mark of Stephen Sondheim's Sweeney Todd (Drury Lane), both as man and musical. A homicidal maniac in his original incarnation, Sweeney was equipped by Christopher Bond, in the dramatic version on which the current show is based, with a puritanical streak and an avenger's motive: both of them intensifying the blood-lust. The cast also includes an unquestionably demented beggar-woman and a heroine who, though sane, is something of a simpleton and is incarcerated for much of the second act in an asylum. A chorus of escaped lunatics helps speed the story to its climax.

Madness has cropped up in Broadway musicals before, with the afflicted generally represented as the coy repositories of a higher wisdom. Sweeney Todd is the first musical I know to take obsession for its subject and to depict it with a matching steely ferocity. It ends up as a moral show, but not by preaching, simply by the old approved method of showing passion spending itself.

This Sweeney is an escaped convict, who returns to Victorian London to claim the lives of the judge and beadle who had him transported so they could have easy access to his wife. Baulked in his first attempt at revenge, Sweeney, through a variety of motives--self-disgust, misanthropy and a praiseworthy desire to keep his hand in--turns to generalised mayhem.

The stunning number in which this bizarre transition is effected, `Epiphany', alternating fast crashing sequences of staccato determination with high-pitched yearnings for lost happiness and finally fusing them--almost closes the first half. But there is a further, cushioning, development.

Mrs Lovett, the `eminently practical' pie-lady, persuades Todd to put the corpses to use by joining her in business. The ensuing song, in which they jovially detail the contents of their individual meat-pies, is a compendium of sick jokes: some routine, but the best ingenious enough to be seductive. The tune is a robust waltz, and it is by now hardly a novel idea to set outrageous words to so reassuring a rhythm. What gives it distinction is an intervening theme, whose lilt is so insouciant as to be diabolical, and which provides an exhilarating but unsettling climax: it sweeps the characters beyond the pale and, momentarily at least, deposits us there with them. It serves also as an odd but potent love-duet.

Beauty, cankered but still attractive, hovers round the barber's chair; Todd has a habit of singing, and hauntingly too, as he slashes. This is an outstandingly melodious score; but the melodies come in short bursts, disappear and recur. About a dozen themes underpin, in variously ironic guises, a show which is three-quarters of the way to being through-composed. `The Ballad of Sweeney Todd', which flanks the score, is the prime example of power held in reserve; in a superlative orchestration by Jonathan Tunick, it begins as unnerving (a string figure seems to be echoing from the murkiest depths of the Thames) and ends--greatly enhanced by Harold Prince's staging--as shattering.

The music, and the headlong tensions of the melodrama, had me straining out of my seat. The narrative excitement is greater here than in New York. Scaling-down has helped; there is more pace, less fuss, despite some noisy trundling of scenic units wheeled into position so that actors may go up one side and down the other, like so many Dukes of York. Eugene Lee's iron-foundry set--presented in New York almost as an embodiment of the Industrial Revolution--is now just an impressive enclosure for the action; all to the good, since the supposed social comment always struck me as specious. Sweeney may live in a hierarchical society, but it seems more feudal than industrial.

The loss is in the central roles; in New York Len Cariou, satanically possessed, and Angela Lansbury, monumentally comic, were criticised for belonging to two different worlds, but that seemed to me the point; one had an insight into the coalition of deranged visionary and cheerfully amoral subordinate that can bring about mass murder. Here the show touched greatness, justifying its imagery of giant ovens and sulphurously smoking chimneys. There is certainly more contact--erotic contact even--between Denis Quilley and Sheila Hancock at the Lane; Mr Quilley grows steadily through the evening and Miss Hancock misses no syllable of Mr Sondheim's trickiest lyrics. They are admirable, but they are not archetypes. The supporting cast is uneven, but boasts a compelling beggar in Dilys Watling, a prepossessing young lover in Andrew C. Wadsworth and, in the van of a fine chorus, Oz Clarke, whose pointed singing of the first quatrain is the best of auguries.

  

A programme note to Hamlet (Stratford-on-Avon) clues us into a proliferation of theatrical references. In John Barton's production the first man on collects his helmet, cloak and spear before our eyes--gets into character, in fact--before embarking on sentry-go. The main acting-area is a raised quadrilateral: a stage upon a stage. Hamlet knows that all the men and women are merely etc., and is keen to get his own performance right. Michael Pennington delivers the pep-talk to the players without looking at them; he is really giving notes to himself. He is careful to get the proper costume for his mock-madness: imagine his surprise when, confronted by Ophelia, he finds himself overtaken by the real thing. His love for her was real as well; while she was tickled pink by his.

Carol Royle, immensely promising, adds an unwonted touch of pride to the girl and makes it plain that when she goes crazy she is imitating her lover. This is altogether the most civilised Elsinore I remember visiting; Tony Church's Polonius manifests unmistakable paternal affection; and Barbara Leigh-Hunt's Gertrude displays twinges of conscience even before the closet-scene (it is unusual for Gertrude to display anything so early in the evening).

Derek Godfrey's Claudius puts on so good a front I felt disinclined to credit all those stories his brother tells about him. The trouble is I liked his brother (Raymond Westwell) too; while there is a fine gentle Horatio from Tom Wilkinson, a man of many faces. (In The Maid's Tragedy he looked a double for Clive James. Here he looks vulnerable.) There is also a fine gentle Hamlet; Mr Pennington's intelligence blazes but never obtrusively (there being enough in Hamlet to occupy any actor's mind) and can crunch himself into and through soliloquy with absolute freshness. He almost gets a traditional exit: borne on four pairs of shoulders, head flung romantically back. But Fortinbras says, `Bear Hamlet to the stage,' and that, in accordance with Mr Barton's scheme, is as far as he gets. This production is simmering excitingly. I hope to be able to write about it again.

  

A second chance to see Edward Bond's The Fool (Other Place, Stratford) was certainly rewarding. I still cannot feel that the play's two acts absolutely balance out, but each is so crammed with invincible moments that it ceases to matter. Howard Davies's production is dour but reasonable; James Hazeldine, never pushing for sympathy, nevertheless makes John Clare's descent into the madhouse a thing of pity as well as terror.
1980-08-03-the-showman-and-the-ideologue:
The showman and the ideologue

ROBERT CUSHMAN assesses the achievement of his outstanding predecessor as theatre critic of The Observer

IT IS difficult to write theatre criticism in English without feeling, and maybe fearing, that Kenneth Tynan is hovering somewhere around the typewriter. If you write in THE OBSERVER it is probably impossible.

A great deal of theatre criticism in the Sixties and Seventies consists, more or less consciously, of imitations of Tynan. Three factors, beyond his actual writing, contributed. One, most practitioners had trodden the grammar-school and university trail that Tynan had so spectacularly blazed just after the war. Two, he himself had given the job up and retired to the National Theatre and points beyond, so sparing his juniors the harrowing trial of direct competition. Three, beginning in 1961, his criticism became readily available in stout but elegant anthologies: what a friend once referred to as `Ken Tynan's Bumper Review Books.'

It was all there to be consulted and to be rifled: Tynan jokes and Tynan theories have now been steadily--and often thoughtlessly--recycled for 20 years. It is quite possible that the jokes are more important than the theories. Occasionally they were decorative, generally they were structural, and precisely evocative. (Of Michael Redgrave's Shylock: `Mr Redgrave cringes and crumples every time Antonio opens his mouth--you would think he had never seen a Christian before.')

Once, considering an American polemic against criticism in general, he justified his own tribe with the words `what counts is not the opinion, but the art with which it is expressed.' This struck me when I first read it in 1956 (an earnest schoolboy, I was beginning to follow the master into the rigorous climate of committed criticism for a committed theatre) as evasive; and he contradicted it in later utterances (`If a man tells me something I believe to be an untruth, am I forbidden to do more than congratulate him on the brilliance of his lying?'). But he was right the first time; it is the art of his expression that made him a great critic.

This does not mean that he was a stylist in vacuo. The test of a critic is his ability to make you believe, while you are reading him, that his is the only possible view of the subject. (You are free to start disagreeing the moment you finish the last sentence.) Tynan achieved this more often than any theatre writer, and he managed it, of course, by virtue of the intensity of his reaction. You rarely feel that he willed an epigram into life: rather, that it was the inevitable reflection of the precision with which his mind had registered the performance he was describing.

I went through a period of thinking that his phrases were superb and his opinions absurd. Wrong: his judgments of particular plays and performances are, more often than not, unassailable. He was no great theorist; merely the great chronicler and evaluator of the passing moment. But the theatre is a collection of passing moments, and Tynan usually got them resoundingly right.

He was not, temperamentally or philosophically, much in sympathy with Beckett. But nobody in all the 25 years since the London premiere has got closer to the heart of `Waiting for Godot': `His two tramps pass the time of day just as we, the audience, are passing the time of night. Were we not in the theatre, we should like them be clowning and quarrelling . . . all, as one of them says, "to give us the impression that we exist."'

That review was written before he had fully discovered Brecht and before `Look Back in Anger' gave him the opportunity to become the journalistic spokesman for a new theatre movement. I do not believe that he, in any sense, created that movement (that would be beyond the power of any critic), or even that he procreated its audience, but he probably speeded up the process of recognition and codification. The latter, I think, he may have over-encouraged. Indiscriminate generalisation was his least endearing critical trait. His espousal of socialism came--as far as one can tell from his writing--comparatively late, and he displayed the proverbial zeal of the late convert.

Having decided on the kind of theatre he wanted, he sometimes distorted (with old plays) or rejected (with new ones) works that didn't fit into his scheme. Tynan, though, often left himself generous loopholes. What really attracted him to Brecht was the spectacular stagecraft and the breadth of the dramatic canvases; as much the director's craft as the writer's. He claimed that he began by believing in `drama about great men' and changed to believing in plays about society. In fact, what he always believed in, whatever his disclaimers, was showmanship. Or, to put it more bluntly, show-biz.

He was brought up, he once wrote, on the Birmingham Hippodrome, and the comedians he saw there may have been his greatest influences. He possessed the extremely rare gift of writing funnily--and illuminatingly--about great clowns, and he developed the gift in writing about great actors. Those he most adored--pre-eminently Olivier, of whom he wrote incomparably--had always something of the stand-up comic in them. (I think that by comparison he underrated Gielgud. I think he thought so too.)

When he moved on to become Olivier's Dramaturg at the National Theatre, it was the showman rather than the ideologue in him that was most influential. Puritans and academics chafed, the rest of us rejoiced in a subsidised company whose repertoire reflected, of all things, style and humour. Gestures towards social conscience were comparatively infrequent and not too successful. He described himself as a congenital enthusiast, and a look at the files reveals that he was less of a butcher than he was reputed to be.

I have cause to be grateful to him for personal help and encouragement, and most of all for the inspiration of his work. He did the job--word by word, sentence by sentence, week by week--supremely and intimidatingly well.
1980-08-10-pal-joey-s-back-in-town:
Pal Joey's back in town

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a Rodgers and Hart revival.

LAST YEAR, in their old quarters at Aldgate East, the Half Moon produced Guys and Dolls as if it were Pal Joey. They have now, logically and delightfully, presented Pal Joey on an approximation of its own terms.

The company are now in residence down the Mile End Road, and their standards in the mounting -- not to say the casting -- of musicals have risen meteorically. For a fringe company with a Germanic bias, Pal Joey may be the ideal American musical. The penultimate work of Rodgers and Hart, first staged in 1940, its originality for its time lies in its unremitting seediness.

It is set for the most part in a Chicago nightclub, some way down the minor league, and its hero is a song-and-dance man of similar status. He talks himself into a job as the club's m.c., and subsequently into the beds of most of the contiguous ladies. His biggest catch by far is Vera, nymphomaniac wife of a presumably purblind local millionaire who has made his bread out of bread. She sets him up in his own showspot (Chez Joey), but withdraws both her cash and her person when a blackmailer appears. Joey, if not quite down, is certainly out.

John O'Hara wrote the script from his own volume of short stories, which are Runyon-and-vinegar; he ran into trouble with his plot (his gangster is a compound of stock gags and stock menace), but he kept the show remarkably free from any trace of sentimentality. That includes the negative variety to be found in the current Chicago, slicker but bludgeoning show. Cynicism was nothing new in Thirties musicals, but it had generally been airy and flippant; O'Hara kept it tied to specific characters and events. Leaving the story in Chicago rather than moving it to Manhattan was in its way an act of integrity.

All this was new territory for Rodgers and Hart, who had previously written warm, high-spirited or melancholy songs with no particular regard for context. Those qualities are rather flattened out for Pal Joey; the score, despite its reputation, is far from their best work. But it is still enjoyable; and Rodgers, in particular, seized on the chance to write music that was smoky, brash or metallic.

Hart's contribution is more problematic. He was a specialist in bawdy (by the end of the Thirties he and Cole Porter had become competitors in innuendo); and in the jewel of the score, Bewitched -- particularly in its sardonic reprise -- he refined this vein to produce an erotic classic, sharply exultant. (The fact that we have grown up on a bowdlerised version of this song makes the original words all the more piquant. I wonder if the correspondent who recently quoted it to me as one of Hart's few touching ballads has ever heard them).

A lesser-known song, You Mustn't Kick It Around, does equal justice to Joey's cockily insensitive sexuality. The other standard, I Could Write a Book, is an example of what goes wrong in the show. Rodgers's tune is, for him, ordinary; and the lyric -- for two uncultivated people who have just met and are only superficially attracted -- becomes, with its dominating literary conceit, an expression of sophisticated romanticism: literal head-over-heels and Hart-over-head.

It is the lyricist himself talking -- which is the constant fascination of his work, but an intrusion here. O'Hara's dialogue set-up is, as is generally the case, clumsy.

And yet... the techniques of Pal Joey have been surpassed and finally superseded. Its style is one-of-a-kind. Robert Walker's mini-production, which cramped Guys and Dolls, releases all that is best in this show. Sian Phillips, in the maneating tradition of the late Hy Hazell, dominates as a Vera basking in financial and sexual security; all she gives to Joey, she knows she can get right back, herself most of all. (She's vocally secure, too: a pleasure to report.) Denis Lawson, appealing but not likeable, wisecracking on the edge of an abyss he senses but won't confront, has Joey sized up; his blank-faced clockwork hoofing is a treat.

So is most of Stuart Hopps's choreography, which picks off a series of tired floor-show routines with venomous enthusiasm. All his seven dancing girls can act, or maybe it's the other way round; anyway they're individuals, especially Susan Kyd's smart cookie and Jane Gurnett's dumb ox. Dodging in and out between episodes, they contribute much to the atmosphere -- mostly hard-boiled but sometimes a bit runny -- as do Jean Hart's lady journalist and Christopher Muncke's club-owner who shrugs through the show with the air of a man who could outperform the lot of them if only he had a number.

The textual history of Pal Joey is of Shakespearean complexity. Mr Walker has collated Good and Bad Quartos (plus his own interpolations), sensibly, barring some solecisms in the lyric-readings. (Details on request.) There is a six-piece band and good glitzy costumes.
1980-08-17-planetary-passions:
Planetary passions

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on `The Life of Galileo' and `Othello.'

IN an interview a couple of years ago Howard Brenton described himself as `an anti-Brechtian, a Left anti-Brechtian.' Now here he is as the translator of Brecht's Life of Galileo (Olivier): a play whose central event, fittingly enough, is a recantation.

There should be joy on the South Bank, if not actually in heaven, since Mr Brenton's version is mostly excellent. Its clarity is in line with the best aspects of the play and of John Dexter's production. This play, with a Renaissance European setting, has an Oriental delight in contemplation beyond anything to be found in Brecht's Eastern fables. Galileo, his disciples and his enemies are united by their passion for thought: by its shape as much as its substance.

I remember Mr Brenton, in his former mood, complaining that `The Caucasian Chalk Circle' didn't connect with the class struggle. I don't know; it features kindly exploited peasants and unpleasant masked landowners, and I'm not sure that `Galileo' gets much further. The play posits that the Inquisition's real objection to the physicist was not that his cosmology contradicted that of the Bible, but that in removing the earth from the centre of the universe it greatly diminished the prestige, celestial and terrestrial, of the princes of the church, and gave the masses ideas above their station.

Sometimes this is believable; a young monk, who almost against his will becomes Galileo's pupil, has a good speech about his parents, happy in their poverty, because they consider it part of a divine order. But once the scene is over you begin to wonder (in line with Brechtian theory but not with the thrust of the play) whether their faith would be much affected either way by the position of the planets. Tom Stoppard is not a playwright one would ordinarily compare with Brecht, but this play resembles `Jumpers' in overrating the influence of astronomy on personal conduct.

For the most part Brecht keeps the people offstage; when they do arrive they celebrate Galileo's ideas in a carnival scene which has rather more impact as spectacle (though it's oddly underdone in this production) than as argument. Mr Brenton suggests that Galileo's smuggled truths are a metaphor for Communism in our day. You can just as well equate them, if you start to think that way, with any other minority creed: with Christianity in Russia, for example. Actually, in the sharp early scene where Galileo debates with the orthodox thinkers, the traditionalists in their eloquent appeal to the beautiful symmetry of their received ideas sound more like Marxists than Galileo ever does.

Our hero is in fact transcendently selfish; that is what unifies his character and the play. In the last scene Brecht, disturbed by the atom bomb, gives him a social conscience: `I believe the only aim of science is to relieve the toil of human existence.' That's a noble aim, but it is as unlikely to inspire a great scientist as a great artist. It hardly squares with the Galileo whose opinion of other people is governed solely by whether they help or impede his work. Knowledge (as Brecht's own pupil Friedrich Durrenmatt was to point out in `The Physicists') is a neutral, therefore dangerous, force; Brecht wants to tame and moralise it. As usual he evades tragedy.

The play lives as a clean piece of story-telling, and as a celebration of genius. Mr Dexter's production, in which even Galileo's legs-akimbo stance at his wash-basin looks like a geometrical figure, does full justice to the first but little to the second. Michael Gambon, who plays the lead, is an actor of great skill and subtlety who excels in depicting the character's ageing process, and in elucidating his thoughts. But he has to try hard (in plain terms, to shout) in order to convey energy and the returns rapidly diminish. (I will muzzle the unworthy suspicion that Brecht protested so much about Galileo's sensuality because he couldn't actually dramatise it.)

Selina Cadell meticulously traces the development of Galileo's daughter from ingenue to jailer, but much of the acting is disappointing. On the principle of chastising the best-loved, let me pick on Simon Callow and Stephen Moore. Mr Callow plays the peasant monk as an urban mooncalf. Mr Moore negates his imaginative casting as an Inquisitor of Shavian gentleness by utilising his familiar spaced-out timing to get Ayckbournian laughs.

  

In Othello (Aldwych) Cassio's rhetorical wish that Jove might watch over the Moor is incongruously turned into a formal prayer. That is the only gaffe I could discover in Ronald Eyre's superbly lucid, detailed, eloquent and moving production. Relationships are tangible; the outbreaks of violence have the shock of inevitability; movements are always revealing. Othello, entering the Senate, makes straight for the military briefing table.

Some of the deepest obscenities of his degradation escape Donald Sinden, but he brilliantly captures the boyish innocence and uncorks a fine passion. Burnishing his voice, he reveals it as an instrument of unsuspected virtuosity; his clubman's warmth has given way to a suave authority that can turn `the goodness of the night upon you' into a genuine benison, disturbing in its confidence.

While his assurance cracks, that of Bob Peck's Iago hardens; he ends as a squatting statue of satisfied malevolence. The solidity of the character merges with that of the actor who discovers new conversational riches in every line without ever veering from his course. What tortures Othello most is Iago's conscientious matter-of-factness about Desdemona's infidelity; Mr Peck worries him into madness. These two performances, in opposed but complementary modes, are not only a magnificently interdependent Othello and Iago but golden examples of the strengths of contemporary verse-acting.

  

Writer's Cramp--which to these southern ears is John Byrne's most congenial play--has resurfaced at Hampstead, enriched all round. A prologue comments on the growing fame of F. S. McDade, Scots bookman and no-hoper, since this tribute was first unveiled three Edinburgh Festivals ago. Mr Byrne, with an eye as sharp as his ear for risible detail, has himself designed a McDade Memorial Corner, fit for the most painful of illustrated literary lecturettes. The cast of three has reassembled, with John Bett's narrator even more of a Muggeridge, discoursing in a silky wheeze that makes every word of praise come out as a disparagement.

Mr Bett doubles as McDade's flighty mother, sublimely. Alex Norton reads the poems, in tones of surprised disgust, and also plays a uniquely unnerving prison warder impinging on one of our hero's frequent darkest hours. F.S. himself, going from school to death-bed without so much as a change of blazer or moustache, is Bill Paterson, as a virtuoso blend of swaggerer and mendicant.

  

A full-stage revival of Elmer Rice's The Adding Machine, which in 1923 domesticated expressionism to the American marital front, would probably expose the play unkindly. The pocket production at the Gate, Notting Hill, allows us to take it as an elegant little joke, with enjoyable soliloquies for the nagging Mrs Zero and for her biddable spouse who turns murderer when automation pushes him off his counting-house stool. He goes to heaven, where he is revealed (and reviled) as the essence of wage-slave. He also meets another murderer, endearingly done by Mike Burnside, a plump and dignified comedian, like a louder Richard Griffiths.
1980-08-24-from-titus-to-virginia:
From Titus to Virginia

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN reports on a recent visit to the Stratford Festival, Ontario, whose company will be visiting London later this year.

I CAME to Canada, as I generally do, via New York, where the temperature was 10 intolerable degrees higher than it was in Stratford, Ontario. America, though, pursued me: the surrounding conversation suggested that the Stratford Shakespeare Festival gets much of its clientele from south of the border.

Brows were furrowed over Pelican editions of the coming evening's play, which happened to be 'Titus Andronicus.' 'Titus has cut his hand off. Can someone tell me why?' 'It's an act of atonement,' suggested someone not quite accurately. I wondered what they would make of the cannibal feast that closed the show. The conscientious continued to bone up, glancing enviously around as friends wandered away in search of ice cream.

The American connection does much for the alertness of Stratford's audience: also, of course, for its box office. In other ways, it saps Canada's theatre. The best Canadian talent gets lured to Broadway or Hollywood, even occasionally to London. (I don't know what can be done about this: natives can hardly be forbidden to leave the country. The alternative strategy, favoured by protectionists, of stopping other actors from coming in seems to me counter-productive.)

This is the Englishman Robin Phillips's sixth season as Stratford's director; the Festival Theatre's platform stage retains its magic, and he has unequalled ability to make it swirl. He has more bodies at his beck than any director could find in Britain, outside an opera house, and he pours them onto the stage. Maybe it was unfortunate that both his Shakespearean productions on offer during my stay were comedies, 'Twelfth Night' and 'Much Ado About Nothing' -- in which charm and movement, though certainly secured, seemed to have become ends in themselves. In 'Twelfth Night' the only moments of real resonance came when Stratford's doyen, William Hutt (who has been with the company since its inception in 1953), burst gravely into song as Feste, making -- as the finest theatre always does -- an eternal moment out of the evanescent.

In 'Much Ado' Mr Phillips has oddly done one of his crowd numbers on the church scene: a couple of dozen people seem to be in on the secret of Hero's 'death,' and it is inconceivable that not one of them would have blabbed. But in general this is a most solid production, blessed with foresight: even an initially unfunny Dogberry turns out to be holding himself in readiness for the revelation that he is an ass. The imported stars, as in previous seasons, are Brian Bedford and Maggie Smith; and they complement each other well. Mr Bedford's Benedick is firmly and stolidly a soldier (as his Malvolio is firmly and modestly a steward); he provides the anchorage and Miss Smith the pyrotechnics. Her Beatrice is a woman blessed with wit and passion and almost afraid of her own endowments -- in fact, a classic Maggie Smith performance. Stratford seems to have honed both her skills and her insecurities -- each perfectly timed riposte is prefaced by an unnecessary (and anachronistic) interjection: 'Well,' 'Do you know?', and 'I mean.' Maybe she doesn't know she is doing it: her talent is what makes her mannerisms so irritating. Her gift for self-deprecation -- dispatching her own wisecracks to the ground with a flick of the wrist -- permeates 'Virginia,' the festival's most-trumpeted new play. It happens to be dead wrong for the ineffable Virginia Woolf, who can never have seen a joke against herself in the whole of her life, but it saves Edna O'Brien's piece from complete inertia.

This is a play about sensitive literary people with sensitive literary problems acted out in sensitive literary writing against sensitive literary music. The three characters -- Virginia, husband Leonard and intrusive V. Sackville-West -- are grouped in Mr Phillips's production like ghosts from Harold Pinter's 'Old Times.' One expected better from this author and this director, if not, to be honest, from this subject.

Another three-hander, 'Bosoms and Neglect' (hot from failure in New York), is the work of America's most frustrating playwright, John Guare; frustrating because his wit and his perceptions hardly ever cohere. Here are an octogenarian woman, trying to deny that she has breast-cancer, her bookworm son, and his new-found lady-love, who, like him, is deeply into literature and deeper into analysis. Many of Mr Guare's sallies are funny, but as they pile up they group themselves into variants of the New York psychiatrist joke or -- with the old lady at the other end of play -- of the idea of salty old age, eccentric but indomitable. Each has been done to death, though the second at least gives the cue for a knock-down performance from Kate Reid.

So back to Shakespeare and to Mr Bedford's production of 'Titus,' simple but powerful, with everyone in the right place at the right time, and the play actually seeming to have something to do with Imperial Rome. Mr Hutt marks time during Titus's authoritarian phase, but in the onset and then the retreat of madness, with every line an ironic shaft, he is very fine. Other performances run the gamut -- too common at Stratford -- from vigorous-anonymous through serviceable-dutiful to ambitious-atrocious.

Mr Phillips's new production of 'King Lear,' with Peter Ustinov had yet to open when I left. It will, however, be seen later this year in London at the Haymarket. Next year at Stratford the power structure changes; Mr Phillips remains in command, but he will now have a phalanx of associate directors including Len Cariou, the Canadian actor who was Broadway's Sweeney Todd, and English-born Pam Brighton, who has recently scored a great success with her own conflated version of the 'Henry VI' plays.
1980-08-24-lucifer-on-a-fork-lift-truck:
Lucifer on a fork-lift truck

EDINBURGH FESTIVAL 1980

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the National Theatre's 'Passion' at the Assembly Hall.

THE pews have been removed from the Assembly Hall, and the ground-level is one great playing-space, where the audience, and even the actors, can disport themselves.

Ira Gershwin said it forty-odd years ago:

Each girl and boy alike,
Sharing joy alike,
Feels that Passion'll
Soon be National.

Here is the National Theatre production of The Passion, drawn from the York Mystery Cycle, and familiar from three years' appearances at the Cottesloe, now fitted out with a first part of equal length. This has been labelled Creation to Nativity, though, in the abrupt and rather frustrating manner of the Mysteries themselves, it gives up the Old Testament narrative halfway through Genesis and jumps straight on to the Annunciation.

Jesus's story takes up the last play-and-a-half, but in this version it has little contact with what has gone before. We are given a human drama issuing in a cry of despair. There is no resurrection, no judgment; only a curt statement of belief delivered by Brian Glover in a miner's helmet, whose beaming lamp provides the most original lighting effect in contemporary theatre.

But this moment hardly returns us to the beginnings of the first play, where Mr Glover is God: a businesslike deity as he goes about creating everything, glimpsed through a warming forest of lanterns somewhere up among the rafters of the Assembly Hall. In an even finer burst of visual inventiveness Lucifer (Jack Shepherd--the medieval guilds of glovers and shepherds would be proud to see their descendants carrying on their traditions in such surroundings) delivers his doomed challenge from a red plush armchair, perched halfway up a forklift truck. Perdition is a rapid descent into a smoke-filled tub, which is then whirled fiercely around the hall like an outsize dodgem car.

Such toys as these are the modern equivalent of the pageant-wagons on which the plays were originally performed (the medieval theatre was machine-mad, far closer in spirit to Drury Lane than to the Warehouse) and Bill Bryden's production resembles the RSC's The Greeks in being an all-purpose raid on whatever aspects of the ancient tradition may be made to serve a modern turn. It is unprincipled in all respects save the most important, that of telling the story. The means vary, even the promenading audience perform a different function in each half. In the first play they are employed as witnesses of the performance, in the second of the events themselves.

The new piece is in fact a patchwork, episodic where its sequel is centrifugal. Humanity only breaks in with Dave Hill's Joseph, honestly aghast at the news of his wife's pregnancy. It is maintained in the famous episode, interpolated from the Wakefield Cycle, of Mak the sheep-stealer. (Somebody should write a ballad of Mak the crook.) This astonishing playlet, with its story of a sheep hopefully passed off as a newborn child ("What the devil is this, he has a long snout") parodies the Nativity as a prelude to celebrating it.

Its equivalent in the second half is the scene of the grimly practical torturers at the Crucifixion, a triumph of unselfconscious sophistication. The Assembly Hall acoustics are not too kind to extended conversation-pieces like these, but actors with tirades--notably Mr Hill's John the Baptist and Mr Shepherd's Judas, registering resentment in alliteration--rise splendidly above them while the Albion Band contribute at least two smashing numbers.

Another smashing number begins the Canadian production, Billy Bishop Goes to War (Moray House Gymnasium): a quietly mocking lament, with simple but artful rhymes for the generation who went off to die in World War One. It is sung by the complete cast, which is to say Eric Peterson and John Gray; Mr Gray also plays the piano and wrote the show. He comes up subsequently with nothing as good. This story of Canada's most productive (or destructive) air-ace masters all the ironies about the simultaneous horror and exhilaration of combat and the patronising attitude of the British establishment towards its colonial cannon-fodder, but it does little more than lay them efficiently out. Mr Peterson plays all the parts well.

I might have enjoyed it more had I not visited the Traverse that afternoon to see Barry Collins's The Iceman, another monologue about a survivor of the same war with scars left this time by class rather than race, and seeking to erase them or himself by undertaking a solo ascent of Everest. Chris Ettridge, the actor here, does nothing wrong, and neither, in strict literary terms, does Mr Collins. But theatrically it is a deadening exercise. A one-character play with a subtext is, I suppose, possible, but in practice we have to believe what the character says. There is no undercutting, no conflict. We know the man has weaknesses all right, but only because he tells us.

I began to yearn, after these two shows, for the spectacle of a couple of actors talking to each other. The Tarnished Phoenix (St Cecilia's Hall) offered two actors, side by side reading--Ian McKellen as D. H. Lawrence and Sheila Allen as Frieda. Mr McKellen can give me enormous pleasure when immersed in a character or when he is simply being himself--as here in a few carefully artless sentences of welcome--but he was mostly betwixt and between: compelling admiration when turning the ending of "Snake" ("I have something to expiate: a pettiness") into a cadenza of disgust, but defusing Lawrence's intolerably censorious outbursts against people assuredly no worse than himself with a self-deprecation completely alien to them. Miss Allen got closer to the iron self-righteousness in "How beastly the bourgeois," though some of her other selections were, at the first performance, less assured (she was deputising at short notice for Janet Suzman).

The fringe are offering two Jacobean rarities, Massinger's A New Way to Pay Old Debts (the Priory Theatre Company) and Middleton and Dekker's The Roaring Girl (Cambridge University Mummers). The amateurs do far better than the professionals, and this only partly because they have the richer play. Massinger's piece, for centuries a stage and schoolroom classic, has fallen into disuse and it does emerge here as thinly as disconcerting to realise that the legendary extortioner-villain, Sir Giles Overreach, never stands a chance of grinding anyone's face in dust: they're all on to him from the start of Act One. The production is inspiringly stylised; because his name merely denotes his job: he's a watchman.

The Cambridge Players have correctly deduced that characters with allegorical monikers (as it might be, Dapper or Trapdoor) had better be played as real people. This they do, with assurance in a pleasing variety of styles: it is possible to make a book on which of these players is bound for the Half Moon, which for the Olivier, and which for the issue desk of the nearest public library.
1980-08-31-panache-from-poland:
Panache from Poland

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'official' and fringe theatre.

THE Polish painter-director Tadeusz Kantor has been back in Edinburgh, this time at the Moray House Gymnasium.

The approach to the audience is appropriately strenuous. There are no intervals, and a notice in the foyer proclaims that no late-comers will be admitted. This might be admirable if it were being done for the sake of the spectators. Actually the people being considered are the performers, so the edict counts as self-indulgence. More specifically it is an attempt to intimidate us into feeling privileged to be there.

Kantor's Wielopole Wielopole does in fact come off as something special. It is presented to us an evocation of the director's own childhood; and he himself is on stage throughout--the very picture of the Central European genius in shiny black suit and open-neck white shirt--to keep his memories in order. Mostly they revolve around the army and the church. Kantor's uncle is recalled as the priest of the village that gives the play its title, his father as one of a group of conscripts who for a long time merely stand and crouch ominously in a corner. They might be papier-mache: when they spring into life they are deeply alarming--and remain so for the rest of the action.

The priest seems to be blessing and encouraging the soldiers as they go to fight. When, later on, they turn on him and--all seven of them--bayonet him, this is something of a judgment and rather more of a moral and political truth. (They that live by the sword, etc.) We see uncle and father marching happily side by side, one with his weapons, the other with his Cross. The Cross, which is huge, later becomes a more oppressive burden. The priest staggers under it, like Christ en route to Calvary. But round and round with it he goes and it comes to dominate the play.

Crucifixion is certainly an apt enough image for twentieth-century Poland. All the same, the Catholic iconography had me confused, for I had always imagined Kantor to be Jewish: and confusion was compounded when one of the players (Kantor's wife in fact) appeared as a rabbi.

Had I understood the dialogue (one forgets that Kantor uses words, but he does), I might have been able to fit the pieces together. As it is I have to report a spectacle of undoubted panache and authority, but repetitive. The same pictures keep revolving through the evening at increasing speed. I don't know whether this is intended to illustrate the frenzied workings of memory or simply to pulverise the audience. Very loud music suggests the latter.

Of course if you really want to direct your actors while they are actually at it, you become a puppeteer. At the National Arts Centre in Ottawa they apparently specialise in marionette versions of nineteenth-century classics. The obvious candidate would be A Doll's House, but they have brought us Buchner's Woyzeck and Strindberg's A Dream Play.

The treatment of Woyzeck is elaborately structured to emphasise the elements of social and military exploitation. Soldiers enter and are barked at in German. When they have been thoroughly cowed, they are issued with puppets whom they have to control. Sitting above are a quartet of nobs (3m, 1f) who control them, announcing the scenes and reading the dialogue. Meanwhile the puppets oppress one another, with Woyzeck himself, a piteous sight with his bald lantern head and skeletal features, at the bottom of the heap.

Only the doll playing Marie seems miscast, making her a Hollywood vamp, and the execution is immaculate: the hero being a barber, there is plenty of opportunity for fancy handwork. But a drama which deals with the hounding of a man till he becomes a thing loses some of its impetus if he is a thing to start with.

In Le Songe (the Strindberg is done in French) all is sedate and beautifully modulated, and the piece loses its only interest--its phantasmagoria of changing scenes. It is also slow. But dreams are fast: ask Mr Kantor. The text is read by a series of actors, each in turn imitating the god Indra, whose daughter, on the main stage below, descends to earth to find that man is unhappy and has to do the washing-up. That, mercilessly reiterated, is Strindberg's message: one that can still find takers. Le Songe is ended, but la maladie lingers on.

After all this I looked forward to the flesh, bone and overflow of Henry IV, Parts 1 and 2 (Daniel Stewart's and Melville College). This RSC touring production, directed by Bill Alexander, captures a good measure of them. Alfred Marks's Falstaff gains in assurance all the way. The more complicated verbal architecture defeats him, but he is a wizard with one-liners, with impatient eye-rollings, with audience contact, and with comic situations: the ensemble scenes in Eastcheap build firmly outwards from him.

He has two striking female team-mates, though their styles hardly blend. Barbara Jefford's Quickly is an elaborate, textually observant assemblage of optimistically genteel vowels: Patti Love's Doll is jaggedly at odds with the rhythm, but her first drunken entrance is magnificent. Among the straights, Stuart Wilson's Hotspur (apart from looking and sounding like Richard III) has the same kind of problems as Mr Marks: Hotspur can hardly stop talking, and it sometimes seems that Mr Wilson can hardly start. But he develops great charm, especially in the scenes with Juliet Stevenson as his wife (this must have been how the marriage in The Taming of the Shrew turned out), and the baiting of Glendower can scarcely have been better done.

Mr Alexander seems, for an RSC cadet, uncommonly alive to comic nuance, and he lets the plays' two worlds (epitomised in a set composed of banners and barrels) unobtrusively illuminate each other. The thieves "make the commonwealth their boots" and so do the rebels, stomping all over a map of England. The Welsh foxiness of Bernard Lloyd's Henry recalls Emrys James's five years ago, but is less showy and allows the king nobility as well: David Rintoul's Hal is resonant but hollow. In general, company experience tells: as in John Burgess's politic Northumberland doubled with a properly actorish Pistol, and in David Shaw-Parker's string of roles, culminating in a Justice Silence who looks, in his modified balaclava, like a pantomime mole and blinks like one too.

One-man shows better be funny. Three on the fringe are: (1) Three Men in a Boat (at Buster Brown's). Jeremy Nicholas beautifully times the infallible jokes and also manages to place and accommodate the passages of fatuous moralising without patronising them. (2) The Third Nam (Heriot-Watt Theatre). In this play, credited to Bill Stair, Tony Robinson is a prodigy of naturalness as a company manager left to carry the show alone, and also conveys numerous misgivings about the spare-part section of humanity that he embodies. (3) Here's a Funny Thing (Viewforth Centre). John Bardon impersonates Max Miller to, apart from a slight lack of expansiveness, the life. The patter works and Mr Bardon stills the house with unmarked poignancy in the biographical section.

The Traverse, with money scarce, offers fewer plays than formerly and, as usual, quality slips with quantity. John Anderson's Snapshots is Forties-Fifties Americana, growing-up-in-New-York division, the hero too insubstantial to give it point. Song and dance erupt too late. There are some entertaining scenes and matching performances from Tucker McGuire and Ramsay Williams as crabbed age, Robin Pappas as youth, Janene Possell somewhere in between and Lou Hirsch all over.

Wielopole Wielopole can be seen at the Riverside Studios, Hammersmith, from 3-14 September.
1980-09-07-double-toil-and-trouble:
Double toil and trouble

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London, Sheffield, Glasgow and Edinburgh.

PETER O'TOOLE has not acted a major Shakespearean role for 17 years. Bryan Forbes has not directed in the theatre before. Macbeth (Old Vic) is a very difficult play. So much for excuses.

The designer is new as well, though his set looks decidedly old: standard-issue rostra approached by what you might call the general run of steps, the only playful variant being the daunting height of the bottom rung, on which somebody is going to come to grief before the end of the season. Surveying this structure, and noting too the grubby William the Conqueror costumes, I settled down nostalgically to a one-foot-up, one-foot-down evening. Expectations were dashed, however, as Mr Forbes's production began to take on a quite untraditional identity of its own.

He stretches, for starters, one of Shakespeare's briefest plays to more than three hours' playing time. Built up permanent sets are meant at least to permit of unbroken transitions from scene to scene. Here there are constant blackouts, filled with optimistically spooky music, and lifting to reveal a stage on which, puzzlingly, almost nothing has changed. Occasionally a few dead bodies will have disentangled themselves from the picturesque poses in which they have been cluttering up the place; and the prospect may be altered by the loss or gain of a stool.

A Cross is momentarily suspended, to show that someone has noticed the play's Christian imagery, though this perceptiveness does not extend to the English scene; Malcolm and Macduff conduct their heart-searchings beneath a fully-manned gibbet. This is the single most curious stroke of the evening, though the presentation of the witches as one of the sexier sister acts on the blasted-heath circuit runs it close.

A more defensible idea, made risible by the shaky tone of the production generally, is the voluminous bloodiness of Macbeth's hands, and subsequently of Banquo's ghost. Either sight would be enough to send the protagonist into a coma. Unfortunately Mr O'Toole has been in this state from the outset, so he has nowhere to go. Chances are he loves the play, but his performance suggests that he is taking some kind of personal revenge on it, methodically draining it of sense and variety. His last line comes out as 'And damned be him that first cries hold e-nough'; and though the pounding beat may suit Macbeth in extremis, he has given much the same emphasis to all the words he has encountered on the way.

Eccentric rhythms reminiscent of Ralph Richardson are relayed to us in the fretful tones of Malcolm Muggeridge, with a few intimations of the self-disgust found in the role by Ian McKellen. Mr O'Toole's conception seems to be that of a man somnambulant with guilt from the first, waking only to occasional extremes of laughing sadism or cringing terror. These are effective but they are very occasional. They are belied too by his physical glamour, which is unchanging.

Nobody else in the cast seems able to get through to him. They try various methods. Frances Tomelty's Lady Macbeth -- almost a Fourth Witch -- goes for sex, but elicits hardly a twitch in return. Brian Blessed's roaring Banquo slaps his noble partner's back a great deal. All, reacting to the rhetorical vacuum at the centre, try helplessly to be conversational; the only possible reply to poor Lennox's aggrieved 'Our chimneys were blown down' would be 'Well fancy that.'

Dudley Sutton's Macduff is a bit wild; when Macbeth's very convincing severed head was brought on at the end it looked so convincing one feared that, somewhere in the wings, Mr Sutton had lost control. Even as it was, Murphy's Law ran riot on the first night; lines were muffed and furniture bumped into. In the shambles John Tordoff's businesslike Third Murderer survived best.

  

The Macbeth set might almost have done for Alan Ayckbourn's Taking Steps (Lyric), which takes place on various levels of a decaying mansion. Here the ascents and descents are all mimed within Michael Rudman's production -- startling lack of finesse. This, like much else in the play, must have worked much better in-the-round, at Mr Ayckbourn's own unpretentious theatre in Scarborough. The play is a mixture of the light and dark Ayckbourn, the light farcically predominating until the end, when we are left, too abruptly, to consider how unhappy all the characters are.

One of them is, in his own words, 'a very successful man,' who accordingly wants to live 'in a very big house.' Dinsdale Landen plays him heavy handedly, though he gets drunk with some panache. His wife, whom he claims (probably correctly) to have saved from a deeply undistinguished career as a dancer, cannot decide whether or not to leave him. Nicola Pagett, in unaccustomed waters, begins very brightly, but the role gives out on her.

The supports have better chances: Paul Chapman a stylishly doleful chorus as a man born to be deserted, and Michael Maloney winning hearts as a solicitor who has difficulty finishing his sentences. He, with a girl of similar temperament, provides a fairly touching sub-plot, but the theme -- of manipulation and resistance thereto -- emerges unhelpfully late.

There is a good quota of laughs: as a writer of comic dialogue Mr Ayckbourn just keeps improving. But mechanically he is way off form: his developments are foreseeable without being inevitable. The play is dedicated to Ben Travers (and Mr Landen draws on his own performance in Plunder), but the Travers airiness has less and less in common with the cracking suburbia which Mr Ayckbourn's characters, waving and drowning, nowadays inhabit.

  

Pack Up All Your Cares And Woe (King's Head) is cabaret rather than theatre, and I'm not complaining.
