Farrah's design spans the aeons, via a majestically bronzed Trojan escarpment; wings swing up and down as they used to in the Wars of the Roses, and a pair of slatted frames lead us in and out of domestic scenes. We always know where we are, and--thanks to Mr Hands' extreme care with groupings and solo spotlights--who is who. This is the RSC's most lucid and exciting 'Troilus' since the famous 'sandpit' production.

Carol Royle's sportive Cressida establishes herself from the start as that most dangerous commodity, a knowing and flirtatious virgin. She convinces both in love and in betrayal; but she is also a victim. A moment in which she is posed alone against a united masculine front of Troilus and Pandarus reminds us how the cards are stacked against her. Nature cannot have intended Tony Church for camp comedy, but he still makes a fine, flexible Pandar. Two normally obscure warriors spring into life: Richard Cordery's blockish cuckold Menelaus and Pip Miller's Diomedes, seducer and cynical commentator. In the higher echelons, Bruce Purchase's Hector, Trevor Baxter's Agamemnon and Oliver Ford-Davies's Nestor all strike a proper balance between the sublime and the ridiculous.

Some of their gentler moments are achieved, it seemed to me, in the teeth of the production. Despite his proclaimed belief in Shakespearean plasticity, Mr Hands is apt--especially in comedy--to strike a single note very hard. Here he is out to rub the generals' faces in the mud; Nestor is particularly close to it, here, bent double under his shield. This is to remind us that Nestor is very old, a fact the text would hardly let us forget: any more than we would fail to notice, even without the face-paint, Hector vandalising everything not nailed down, that Ajax is dangerously vain. And when Pandarus turns to the audience to describe love as 'a generation of vipers' we ought really to yell back that we are quite capable of noticing that for ourselves, and would he kindly get on with his business.

More damagingly, John Carlisle shouts monotonously through the great speeches of Ulysses. Now it's perfectly true that Ulysses's 'policy,' like Troilus's love and Hector's chivalry, proves useless, but it should be given its due.

On which matter, Mr Hands has carried over from John Barton's 12-year-old production the conception of a preening berouged Achilles. The actor is David Suchet, who can cope with anything. But though this reactionary equation of homosexuality with decadence once thrilled the critics, it destroyed the company's credibility with everyone else for nearly a decade. It's hardly worth reviving now. Finally, James Hazeldine is a gruff, unmoving Troilus. The last battle, though, is superbly sustained; you come out feeling you have eaten a masterpiece.

  

'What made you act like this?' someone asks Krogstad, the blackmailer, in Ibsen's A Doll's House (Other Place, Stratford). The answer seems to be the director, Adrian Noble, who has drawn transforming performances from his entire cast. He has woken up Marjorie Bland, nervously alive as the confidante, Mrs Linde; quietened down Bernard Lloyd, whose Krogstad is an anxious schemer, not a gloater; and let us see, in John Franklyn Robbins's dying, frustrated Dr Rank, the lineaments of despair.

He has also drawn out to the utmost physical extent Nora's near-seduction of the doctor (tormenting him with the feel of her silk stockings), the shoulder-stroking uxoriousness of her husband Torvald invested by Stephen Moore with a passionate narrowness that never seeks easy laughs, and the Tarantella, in which Cheryl Campbell's whirling golden tresses almost consume the stage. This is a very sexy play; 'Hedda Gabler,' which it foreshadows in numberless details, is merely the de-gutted version.

Nora's revolt (known in New York 10 years ago as the 'right on' section) no longer seems detachable. It is the logical outcome of the battering she takes from the earlier intrigues; and Miss Campbell constructs a magnificent passion at bridge. Her determination visibly emerges from bewilderment which lifts only when she declares--realising it as she speaks--that she doesn't love her husband. It's a pole-axing moment, because we, like him, assume that in an eight-year marriage there must be something; there are amazingly few plays about the breakdown of a relationship, and this seems the greatest. We long for the final slamming of the door as a relief from what has become almost intolerable tension.

  

Of the four Jacobethan plays given this year by the RSC and National, three have already been done at the Mermaid, where the adventurousness of the repertoire is only matched by the carelessness of the presentation; the reopening production, Eastward Ho!, is typical. A barbed city comedy--by Jonson, Chapman and Marston--has been turned into a standard romp, interrupted by musical numbers.

The appropriate musical style would be super-Bart; Nick Bicat offers sub-Sondheim, with rock implications. This works just once--when the mock-repentant apprentice Quicksilver (a shaven, spectral Richard O'Brien) takes off into a born-again cantata. Howard Schuman's lyrics match the thrust of the dialogue, but not its style, and include the remarkable couplet, 'If you wed a man of rectitude/he'll grow to be a horse's neck to you.'

In War with the Newts (Riverside--appropriately) there is an actor called Andy Rashleigh, who can swim underwater and impersonate David Bellamy. These two ingredients--water and mimicry--are the chief attractions of this Ken Campbell production, based (distantly, I imagine) on a Capek novel. Three green-suited actors are kept continually afloat as salamanders, who threaten to take over the world. The threat is never really felt though, Mr Campbell being more concerned with fun than the story. Fun it is, though less than seems promised.
1981-07-19-bubbling:
Bubbling!

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Stratford.

AS AN occasional begetter of anthology musicals, I have enviously to salute One Mo' Time (Cambridge) as not only a treat but a milestone. Some shows have links; this one has a book.

Like the buoyant 'Ain't Misbehavin'' and the execrable 'Bubbling Brown Sugar,' One Mo' Time pays homage to black American entertainment between the wars. The show deposits us in a segregated New Orleans vaudeville house in 1926.

A depleted touring troupe, minus one coon comic (in those days even blacks had to black up) and one exotic dancer, try to make up the deficiencies by speedy doubling; otherwise they won't get paid: apparently a common occurrence on the TOBA (Tough on Black Asses) circuit. They have other problems; their constitution--one man, three women--is sexually combustible, and their star Big Bertha is both autocratic and unreliable, though forthright about it. ('If I ain't drunk,' she says arriving late, 'I've been cheated out of eight dollars.')

We watch them on stage going through roaring blues, rhythms, ballads and double-entendres: Sylvia 'Kuumba' Williams as Bertha has a wonderful hauteur intoning 'You've Got the Right Key But the Wrong Keyhole,' while Thais Clark, a rubber-faced comedienne who surprisingly gets the last solo spot (something that surely mama wouldn't allow), takes it to flood the house with 'Muddy Water.'

Between these and many other memorable things the cast bicker in their dressing-room; author-director Vernel Bagneris has provided them with dialogue which for wit and style (not to mention sociological interest) surpasses that of any supposedly proper play in London: not a rare thing in a musical, as witness also the funniest bits of 'Annie' and 'The Best Little Whorehouse.'

It is moreover delivered with consummate force and timing by a cast of whom Mr Bagneris himself also brings preternaturally long and flexible legs to a succession of apparently effortless dance routines.

I regret that the story-line is inconclusive; but otherwise there is only one respect in which the production has been misprised. It does not rescue black performers from the old-time stereotyping of 'Ain't Misbehavin''; any falsities in that show had to do with the forcing of Fats Waller's smokier material into a supposedly contemporary non-style, somewhere between Tamla Motown and Las Vegas.

The songs in One Mo' Time are less vulnerable to this treatment (though it strikes occasionally, as in the generally delightful Topsy Chapman's version of 'He's Funny That Way'), but anyone who objects to the spectacle of white audiences clapping along with black folks makin' rhythm should be warned that on the first night the house responded in exactly this way, even on such a condescending white-written song as 'Black Bottom' (the significance of whose title is topographic rather than anatomical, but still).

I can't see any way of stopping this, except by preventing blacks from performing jazz-based material or at least banning whites from watching them do it, which really would get us back to New Orleans 1926. By the way, the five-piece band in One Mo' Time is the best I have ever heard in a theatre, and its terrific trumpeter, Bill Dillard, also delivers, as trumpeters have a habit of doing, the finest vocals of the evening: serene and crackling, as from a small fire.

  

History-books suggest that the greatest twentieth-century production of A Midsummer Night's Dream was not Granville-Barker's or Peter Brook's, but Tyrone Guthrie's in the Thirties, with Victorian sets and costumes, Ninette de Valois ballets, and Mendelssohn music--everything, in fact, we have been taught to despise.

But, of course, extremes meet; Mr Brook's production, ostentatiously demystifying, only substituted one form of artifice for another, while Ron Daniels's new Stratford version, which returns to the full panoply of Victoriana, is actually playing very straight with us.

Maria Bjornson's lovely set is a nineteenth-century stage, a blown-up Pollock print; the production acknowledges that we still have a traditional view of fairyland and takes off from there. This is 'The Dream' in a special society and a special theatre, one whose devices are lovingly and knowingly employed, most consummately when painted flats descend for Puck's befogging of the lovers.

'Pyramus and Thisbe' becomes a Saturday-night melodrama, backed by yet more pastiche chords from Stephen Oliver (whose setting of 'ye spotted snakes' would, in a better world, make the charts).

Not everything works; the minor fairies as glove-puppets misfire, because we actually look at the manipulators, and the mechanicals are more winsome than hilarious, their tone set by John Rogan's dear old Irish Quince. (Mr Rogan is always playing a dear old Irish something). But the relationship of Geoffrey Hutchings's bantam Bottom and Juliet Stevenson's Titania is well sketched in.

Mike Gwilym doubles a courtly, caring Theseus with an Oberon who does the beautiful bits beautifully and whose deliciously deadpan "what hast thou done?" is worth the price of admission, which at Stratford these days is saying something. And the lovers are as good as I remember; better as regards the men, to whom Philip Franks and Simon Templeman give their full measure of rapture, folly and self-righteousness.

Meanwhile Jane Carr, while keeping all her comic expertise, at last succeeds in finding a classical rhythm (more successfully, to my surprise, than Harriet Walter's Helena); her stage-stomping cadenza on her rival's height, forsooth (the italics are hers, and heavy) is irresistible. Finally, Joseph Marcell makes Puck's farewell both a logical end and a teasing new beginning, which is the test of any `Dream.'

Pleasure and Repentance (Fortune), the RSC's answer to `One Mo' Time,' is an anthology of love stuff, light and varied, inclining to what one calls N. W. Twee. Casts vary, but on my night Michael Pennington was intelligently mellifluous, while Susan Fleetwood rejoiced far more than she repented, which is a good thing. The real star, though, was Tony Church.

The Merchant of Venice has come to the Aldwych, John Barton's production the best I have seen, with Sinead Cusack's painfully growing Portia now in full command; her appeal to Shylock `for charity' is the turning-point, and doom for both of them. David Suchet's Jew is fighting a private Middle East war with Antony Sher's Arab in `Goose Pimples' for the title of best performance in London. Is there an actor who can create complicated effects so simply? Every line tells, and then tells some more.
1981-07-26-impaled-on-a-rapier:
Impaled on a rapier

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

EDWARD BOND'S Restoration (Royal Court) is one of those triple-pun titles. Dug to its roots, it refers to a massive act of social justice, not seen to happen within the play, but implied and prophesied. It's also a varnishing job on a period of English history and one of its literary forms, the one generally known as Restoration comedy.

Late Restoration, I think. The play's most prominent character, who has the peculiar name of Lord Are, might have been written by Vanbrugh, with the difference that Mr Bond is concerned to show us the more distressing effects of a nobleman's glittering selfishness. Here is Lord Foppington matched not against a spirited younger brother well able to take care of himself, but against helpless servants. Here also Are, I mean is, Sir John Brute not just ill-treating his wife, but actually killing her.

Why does he so? She is a coal-merchant's daughter, wed for her money, and desirous of being taken to London (mainly, I think, so that she can go to first nights and be glamorously seduced; you know the kind of thing that goes on). To attain this end, she dresses up as a ghost and threatens her husband at the breakfast table. Not in the least disturbed, he carelessly impales her on his rapier. Discovering her identity, he is mildly surprised: 'I do not recall she mentioned a fancy-dress breakfast. . . Who can fathom the mind of one suddenly raised to the peerage?'

Mr Bond may have fasted in sackcloth and ashes after writing lines like those, but he obviously enjoyed them at the time. Simon Callow, who delivers them and who thrives on insouciant outrageousness, certainly does. ('Fore god I am taken with my style. Who'd have thought I'd unloose such a show of bravado?' Everyone, surely.) He proceeds to frame his footman with the murder, and gets away with it. I found myself wondering about the politics of a play which presents the aristocracy as wittily resourceful, and the workers as gullible bores.

I'm kidding of course. Lord Are actually condemns himself, very fully out of his own mouth, and it is Mr Bond's great gift as a comic moralist to make him do this without sacrificing a scintilla of wit. He takes the Restoration style (with particular emphasis on its contempt for all things rural or unmodish), enters it, and turns it against itself. But that still leaves the opposition, it being an unfortunate dramatic fact that the oppressed are not in themselves interesting: usually the reverse. Denied effective action within the play, they have regularly to leave it and deliver lyrics, which, though resourcefully set by Nick Bicat as rock Eisler, all say the same thing: the present is wretched, the future is ours. Worse, the murder scene is fun to watch, a nice conceit, but it is not realistically believable: certainly not as staged by Mr Bond, whose direction, especially after his conquest of the Olivier with The Woman, is remarkably clumsy. But in the second act one character -- the fall-guy's black wife -- takes it as her cue for an earnest protest-drama.

Mr Bond makes some painful points about optimism and gullibility, and even builds up some tension, but his structure gradually crumbles. Philip Davis does something to reconcile the play's two faces, singing powerfully and acting with rat-faced bewilderment, and there is an uproarious intrusion from Irene Handl, though she proves, in more senses than one, a hard act to follow. But mostly in the second half we just wait for Mr Callow to come on again and even his performance, as the material gives out on him, begins to look somewhat askew.

  

Dario Fo's Can't Pay? Won't Pay! (Criterion) is, I suppose, a farce. Anyway its characters spend most of the action rushing around trying to conceal things from their marriage-partners and the authorities. The things are foodstuffs looted by housewives from a Milan supermarket as a spontaneous protest after a 50 per cent price rise. But the ladies are afraid their stolid party-line husbands will disapprove: hence the secrecy, thence the chases.

So the play begins with a political statement and it ends with one, or at least with merrily sung slogans; the mayhem in between is motivated less by politics or even by domestic threat -- since the police are a laughing-stock and there is nothing at stake between spouses that couldn't be sorted out in a moment -- than by the author's talent. This seems -- at least in Robert Walker's version, which anglicises everything but the names -- to be less for the strict disciplines of farce than for random zaniness, including much involvement of the audience. (This contradicts one basic farcical rule: there is No Way Out.)

The result is sometimes uproarious, as in a spiralling sequence at the end of the first act involving a truly hysterical pregnancy. Sometimes it's just wearing, partly because though most of the cast have their moments only Alfred Molina has found himself an overriding style, fast but not fuzzy, furious but not strident. He gets the most acute laugh when he introduces his father: 'Dad, meet a West End audience,' a nervous tribute to the oddity (not wrongness) of the occasion: the Half Moon not in exile, but under glass.

  

The 'Goose Pimples' syndrome -- placing people through brand-names -- has reached the stage of acute dermatitis in Carol Bunyan's To Come Home To This (Theatre Upstairs). 'She told him she was having an affair with her yoga instructor, right in the middle of the Morecambe and Wise show.' 'I blame those new plastic dustbins.' 'No, I won't let them play with your model railway,' this last with special reference to the InterCity engine. Someone's children are called Branwell and Benedict and Nyree Dawn. The author tells us so much about the habitat, she hardly has time for the people.

This is a shame, since her principal ploy has some subtlety: depicting the breakdown of a marriage by examining its surrogate, the wife's ballroom-dancing partnership. But even a good scene in which this relationship is brutally broken has to be capped by having the scheming dance-instructress remark how handy it is to live near Tesco's. The heroine's drinking problem, supposed to be central, never comes into focus, and anyway sorts oddly with her other symptom, compulsive domestic orderliness.

  

At Stratford last year I thought Terry Hands's production of As You Like It wild and woolly: the white and furry first-act set looking to cost the hides of more sheep than you could find in Arden. If it seems less obtrusively frantic now, that is not I think because the staging has been toned down. What has happened is that the actors have ripened, giving Mr Hands his full measure of frenzy (some of it playfully melodramatic, the rest a full-throttle presentation of love's madness), while finding their own space within it. Susan Fleetwood, who is given two enchanting entrances, spills herself vocally and physically full length across Rosalind, and I could happily enthuse for a column over the rest of the cast. Everything comes together beautifully in the end; I have never enjoyed one of Mr Hands's productions more.
1981-08-23-rescuing-candide:
Rescuing Candide

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Festival theatre.

Twenty-five years ago Voltaire's Candide was turned into a musical by a legion of celebrities: Leonard Bernstein wrote the music, Lillian Hellman the book, and Tyrone Guthrie directed. The original lyricist, John Latouche, died on the job and was replaced, very wittily, by Richard Wilbur, with additional contributions from Mr Bernstein, Miss Hellman and Dorothy Parker.

It must, when the show failed, have been difficult to know whom to blame, but Mr Bernstein generally escaped censure. His music paid ironic, but innately tuneful, tribute to all the conventions of light opera; if it sounded pleased with itself, it had good reason. The cast album became a classic, and the show a retrospective cult.

Some 20 years on, Harold Prince examined it, and decided that it had all been too solemn. He engaged Hugh Wheeler to write a script that should be glancingly picaresque like Voltaire's, rather than stately and well-made like Miss Hellman's. This reordering of the book meant a reshuffling of the score, and a fifth lyricist was called in: Stephen Sondheim. (He did a workmanlike job, but no more.) Mr Prince dispensed with conventional staging. He directed the action on a series of islands dotted around the theatre floor, with the audience seated in the midst. It was fun.

Long awaited, this adaptation has been brought to Edinburgh's Assembly Hall by the Birmingham Rep. Peter Farago's production differs from Mr Prince's in confining itself to the platform stage, on which Poppy Mitchell has designed a heavily hilled and castellated set. I felt at first that an opportunity had been missed, especially since the National Theatre showed last year in their promenade 'Passion' how effectively space could be transformed. Compared with the New York production, Mr Farago's lacks inventiveness and pace; there are holes between episodes, orchestral tempi drag, and numbers which should bring down the house tail off to be greeted by polite applause.

But as the show progresses, Mr Farago succeeds where Mr Prince faltered; he maintains, and even increases, our interest in the story. Vocals are excellent: 'Glitter and Be Gay,' the variant Jewel Song, in which the much-ravished Princess Cunegonde decides that if rape is inevitable then rich is better, is a gift to an agile soprano; Mr Bernstein differs from other composers in his realisation that coloratura is intrinsically funny and Rosemary Ashe, with a fine air of impudent innocence, builds on that.

William Relton finds both melody and humour in the guileless hero, while Nichola McAuliffe's Old Lady is a tremendous comic presence, equally adroit at letting off one-liners, telling long hard-luck stories, or just singing. Binding all together is Nickolas Grace, who nonchalantly knocks off five roles including Voltaire as narrator and doddering cynic, and Dr Pangloss as pedant and irresponsible optimist. The folly of his position -- in a world that harbours cannibalism, earthquakes, warfare and the Spanish Inquisition -- is thoroughly, not to say repeatedly, rammed home.

For all the pleasures of script, score and performance, doubts remain. Maybe the original, necessarily one-dimensional, always resists dramatisation. I doubt if Mr Wheeler's book, entertaining though it is, really improves on Miss Hellman's; it loses in spreading the farcical miseries around, rather than concentrating them on Candide and Cunegonde, and the songs never quite fit; they were written, after all, for different situations, and in another, more grandiose, style. (In addition, their wit is static; there is nothing much to do with the songs beyond getting up and singing them.) It remains a distinguished musical rather than a great one, but it's a more festive event than is usually found at festivals and it should come to London. Why indeed should it not reopen the Old Vic?

  

Its Edinburgh stable-mate is As You Like It, performed on the same set gone green. Costumes are Regency-to-Watteau, the ladies' hats contriving to obscure large portions of the action. David Rintoul is a virile Orlando; Lynn Dearth as Rosalind begins and ends in ravishing solemnity, but jumps about inordinately between times. Mr Grace performs relentlessly as Touchstone, never allowing the clown a moment off duty, but since the production makes nonsense of his relation with Audrey (Miss McAuliffe amusing again) he may have had no choice. The senior gentlemen are uniformly reliable.

Shakespeare based this play on a novel, which brings it into line with 'Candide,' and with Richard Crane's Brothers Karamazov, played in a low-ceilinged eyrie at the top of the Freemasons Hall. Only the brothers -- four, including Smerdyakov, the bastard -- appear, though each has a go at playing Karamazov pere. Already a point is being made, and a strong one; indeed this production, in less than two hours' playing time, gives an amazing impression of having left nothing out.

There is, if anything, too much story; the inquiries as to Dmitry's whereabouts on the night of the crime become wearisome; and this passionate brother -- theoretically the easiest dramatic meat -- goes for least, though Bruce Alexander certainly acts him well. Ivan, on the other hand, all intellectualising, is excellent value: Alan Rickman, sardonically intelligent as usual, extracts terrific drama from the fable of the Grand Inquisitor and the visitation of the Devil; a devastating commentary on nihilism emerges as the joint creation of novelist and playwright. Stephen Boxer's Alyosha is a bit shadowy but, like his incidental music, haunting; Peter Kelly's Smerdyakov a fawning masterpiece.

  

Foreign companies have all been classically inclined. The Theatre de la Salamandre, from Lille, offered in the Moray House Gymnasium Racine's Britannicus. A programme note waggishly suggested that to a modern audience (one that has seen 'I Claudius' in its millions) Ancient Rome means nothing, so we got a Louis XIV Versailles setting, with tell-tale modern traces. A joke in fact on the company's own achievement, which is to give us Racine contemporary but whole: echoing his structural confinement by angling the set to allow the smallest possible acting area, and taking the unity of time literally, so that the first act is played before shuttered windows and the fifth in encroaching dusk. Subfusc staging can never have been so effective, setting off luminous, wonderfully spoken performances by Marief Guitier as a stifling Agrippina, Jacques Bonnaffe as a Nero with a strange air of innocence, and Marie Boitel as an ominous waiting woman.

  

Meanwhile at the Lyceum (and this week at the Roundhouse in London) the Amphitheatre of Athens offers Iphigenia in Lixourion, an eighteenth-century comic version of the legend of the sacrificial maiden, here presumed to be performed by locally rude mechanicals such as a candle-lighter (an even more specialised trade than bellows-mending).

The actress in the title-role is characterised as 'a harmless insane young girl'; Leda Tassopoulou plays her with a most expressive twitch of the cheek and a charming air of removing herself from the proceedings when they become too silly. She makes the first half engaging and sometimes touching; the second, straying far from the myth into traditional farce, probably works better if you understand the joke.
1981-08-30-life-with-george:
Life with George

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

The week brought four American plays to London, all full of marriage. It climaxed fittingly with the legendary George and Martha of Edward Albee's Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? (Lyttelton).

As marriages go in the modern theatre they have a good one. They share a sense of humour, which we are always being told is the essential thing. If it is destructive of course; they pass from tearing the skin off each other to flaying the younger couple who are their guests for an extended late-night early-morning drinking session. (As a temperance tract this piece ranks second only to 'The Iceman Cometh.')

George is a history professor promoted far short of his wildest dreams, Martha is the daughter of the university professor and never lets George forget his failure. But the play ends with him comforting her, and this finale, which was condemned as sentimental when the play first appeared, now seems perfectly logical. This is not a Strindbergian couple tied together by their hatred of each other. They hate themselves, but that's different.

The reality of this hatred gives the play more depth than you find in the average American wisecracking comedy; but it has all the vivacity proper to the genre. It used to be said that the play was great fun in its first two acts, and fell apart in its third, where we are told the truth about George and Martha's son, who serves as pretext and hostage in their verbal battles. We find they've made him up; a revelation to which the only response was, and ever will be, 'big deal.' So they're not buccaneering truth-tellers; they're abject -- and improbably consistent -- fantasists. This makes them more pitiable, but much less interesting. Now the play is a classic we know what's coming, and the anticlimax casts its shadow from way ahead.

It's not helped by the self-consciousness of the construction. George and Martha are constantly threatening that now they will really take the gloves off. But all that happens, melodramatics apart, is that the two jokers go on joking.

Development in this play really rests with their two victimised guests, and the realisation of this is one of the strengths of Nancy Meckler's production. Mary Maddox as Honey, the perpetual child-bride, draws a straight line from ingenuousness through shock to hysteria. David Schofield as her scientist husband charts a square-cut progress from shocked upholder of good manners to willing sexual prey of his hostess, goaded en route by George's rhetorical elaborations on the conflict between their two disciplines, one of his best little jokes. (If taken seriously, some of the decline-of-civilisation stuff is an ominous forecast of Mr Albee's subsequent plays, all much shorter, but seeming much longer.)

Meanwhile two of Britain's best, and most seemingly indigenous, players magnificently extend themselves. I last saw Margaret Tyzack on stage at Stratford, Ontario, in a range of roles that no actress could beat; but her most characteristic vein is that of a good sport and it makes, however distended, a fine base for Martha. She has found an American range of gesture: arms raised in mock horror, a swinging walk for raids on her husband or the drinks cabinet. Paul Eddington is, with the possible exception of Donald Sinden, our most polished high comedian (and there's still time for him to fulfill his destiny in 'The Importance of Being Earnest'); his George is a lethal teddybear, attacking silkily or volcanically from all quarters.

It's obvious that, whatever their friends may say, George and Martha will never split up.

Paul and Susan, in Mike Weller's Loose Ends (Hampstead), are the opposite, the golden pair with everything going for them. Naturally they don't last; though equally naturally they will never quite let go of each other, and will probably spend regular periods for the rest of their lives kicking themselves. We follow them through the 1970s (about time, after all those plays about the Sixties, an overrated period in which a lot of pop singers got rich).

They meet on the beach at Bali; ten years later they are both New York successes, he having switched from teaching to film-editing, she after a slow start having made it as a photographer.

Their marriage splinters because she doesn't want children; but without devaluing this quarrel the author only conveys that if it hadn't been this it would have been something else. A happy relationship is by definition precarious, easily taken for granted, easily wrecked. Paul and Susan know their luck and -- as one of their most perceptive friends points out -- can't stop worrying about it; and unloading their worries on other people.

  

Neil Simon's Chapter Two (Lyric, Hammersmith) is about second marriage; between a widower and a divorcee, seen very much from the former's point of view. He is played, with a great fund of unforced emotion, by Gary Waldhorn; a long speech on the guilt he still feels for missing his first wife is the only moment of sustained reality in the play's second half. By this time Mr Simon is writing sob-stuff, working his way to an improbable reunion that comes over as the impurest Broadway sunshine.

The first half, which is courtship, is much better; the jokes are good and are quite believable as defence mechanisms. Mr Simon doesn't make concessions to audiences; only to himself. Maureen Lipman is a delightful heroine, but she is kept short of material and ends up effortful. I had forgotten the sub-plot about the affair between the protagonists' two married confidantes and wasn't too happy to be reminded of it, but it at least occasions a very funny performance of outsized neurosis from Lynda Bellingham.

  

The play stands up better to a second look than Mark Medoff's Children of a Lesser God (Mermaid). This makes a worthy point about the need to regard the deaf (and by implication other disabled) as people with their own rights, even their own culture, but once made, it's made. In New York I enjoyed it as a love story. There are still some sparks, though there are fewer sexual sparks between Elizabeth Quinn and Trevor Eve than between their American counterparts.
1981-09-06-rough-not-holy:
THEATRE

Rough, not holy

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

A BLACKBOARD at the side of the Stratford stage announces The Two Gentlemen of Verona and Titus Andronicus but the two plays are given in the reverse order. So now we know why the RSC postponed the press night for this double bill; it took them two extra days to turn the thing around.

The present arrangement is surely the right one. Best to get the terrors of Titus over while you are still fresh, and to come back from your interval drinks to a divertissement. So it was at the Old Vic, in my extreme youth, when Titus was coupled with The Comedy of Errors in texts edited by John Barton, then still in his donnish days. Now, of course, he directs as well, inheriting from those long-gone productions the notion of having the two plays done as if by strolling players. When we arrive the company are hunting out props and trying on costumes; when the entertainment begins those not immediately involved sit around on hampers, looking duly horrified in the first play and amused in the second.

These responses are intended, I presume, to be contagious; and on the whole they are. There are, to borrow Peter Brook's terminology, two methods of staging Titus Andronicus: the holy and the rough. The first, by ceremonialising the murders and mutilations that comprise the bulk of the action, freezes any unseemly giggles on our lips; but may also stop us believing in the story. The second, which is Mr Barton's way here, is to play everything full-frontal. There are inevitably laughs when at the concluding banquet three characters fall dead in as many lines, or, more nervously, when Patrick Stewart as Titus chops off his own hand before our eyes. However, Mr Stewart is also capable of amputating audience reactions; from a fine show of mellow military authority, he passes into a cruelly gentle madness that repeatedly wipes the smile off our faces.

The moments of greatest risk afford the greatest rewards; Titus orders his daughter, Lavinia, raped and robbed of her hands and tongue, to bear his hand between her teeth; this is done quite realistically -- she has red stumps and a matching gash where her mouth should be -- and it is appallingly believable. Anyway the twentieth century has no right to patronise the sixteenth for its taste in atrocities -- except perhaps on the grounds of excessive tameness.

Sheila Hancock takes the Queen of the Goths seriously enough to play her with an appropriately Germanic accent (oddly not shared by her gangster sons who are played as a pair of engaging slobs kicked out of the very best schools) and once the initial shock is past -- for her, I suspect, as well as us -- she develops considerable power. In her black corner she has Hugh Quarshie, a very smooth Moor, and in her white, Bernard Lloyd, one of those silkily berserk Roman Emperors.

Capable and conscientious though it is, I doubt if this Titus is going to flower into anything definitive. The Two Gentlemen stands a better chance, being the fountainhead of the comedies of youthful folly that Mr Barton long ago annexed for his own. At the moment, it is rather faint and (sometimes actually inaudible), perhaps because in casting appropriately young, Mr Barton has wound up with actors unready to do more than go enthusiastically through the right attitudes. Peter Land's floppy, curly-topped Proteus is the best, especially commendable for doing his own serenading.

Otherwise the best performance is Mr Stewart's chivalrous old Sir Elgamour, who could be Titus fallen on good times. Miss Hancock appears as an aspiring Maid Marian with an unrequited crush on Robin Hood. Each of her fellow outlaws is doing his own comic bit but they have not been co-ordinated. It is pleasant, though, to see them all carrying their own chunks of forest as if getting in practice for Birnam Wood. The same idea is used non-comically in Titus; Aaron effects a scene change by bringing on a tree when talking of the woods, and it is very effective. There are also hobby horses in both; those in The Two Gentlemen are intentionally funny.

If not vintage RSC, this is still good exploratory stuff. How stands it in the world at large? Well, going from the ground up: perhaps the greatest change in Shakespearean production is that we now believe in flat stages. Twenty years ago the plays were always performed up and down staircases. There is a permanent reminder of those days in the platform stage at Stratford, Ontario, built to the specifications of the Fifties' maestro Tyrone Guthrie, with immovable steps at its extremities and a pillared rostrum at its centre. When full, this amphitheatre is the most thrilling house I know, with the audience sitting and responding in an unbroken homogeneous arc.

As for acting; if rawness is a recurring weakness here, anonymous competence is the curse of Canada. This was the case before Robin Phillips took over, it remained so during his tenure, and judging from what I saw there a couple of weeks ago, it has not changed with his stormy departure.

The new chief is John Hirsch, probably Canada's best director (the only man I know able to move with equal authority from Chekhov to A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum). But he was appointed too late to stage any shows himself. He has called on two veterans of the pre-Phillips era: Peter Dews, who contributed a fair Comedy of Errors, and the French-Canadian Jean Gascon, who did a first-rate version of Durrenmatt's The Visit, suggesting that the American theatre is closer to Europe, more at home with expressionism and its derivatives, than our own, which likes to humanise everything. Gascon also staged a clear, decorative Misanthrope with a lightweight but acute Alceste from Brian Bedford.

Mr Bedford, who was one of Mr Phillips's imported stars, has also blossomed as a director. Under the last regime he staged one of those ceremonial Tituses and this year a highly-praised Coriolanus. I found it disappointing; with the resources for a believable mob -- more actors than we these days ever dream of -- he failed to clarify their effect on the central political scenes, which are perfectly written and almost impossible to realise.

The main attraction was Len Cariou, who, though Canadian born, works mainly in the United States, where his Sweeney Todd had real, indeed frightening tragic stature. It may be, though, that playing in musicals has robbed his voice of the necessary jaggedness, for though he split movingly apart when Coriolanus yields, and had a tremendous defiance at the end, he missed the irony that runs through the part as well as the play. But he was a presence.

This hastily prepared season is turning out better than many people expected -- or, in some cases, hoped.

  

Attempts to put P. G. Wodehouse's novels on the stage are fatal; they evaporate. He must have known that himself, for Good Morning, Bill (Theatre Royal, Bristol), though set in the familiar world of useless aristocrats and barking uncles, has a decidedly unfamiliar backbone. There is the real love story; the serious-minded girl, from whom Bertie Wooster would have recoiled with our sympathy, is here given her due, is in fact the heroine. Sex is even mentioned, or is that an interpolation?

There is still plenty of puff-ball inconsequence, and though Eric Thompson (healing scars inflicted by the musical Jeeves) directs inventively, most of his cast weigh in over the limit. But it remains a delightful play, with the aplomb of Ben Travers and rather more finesse.
1981-09-13-in-stalin-s-labour-camp:
THEATRE

In Stalin's labour camp

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a play by Alexander Solzhenitsyn.

ERIC BENTLEY once wrote of Russian realism that "everything -- every single thing -- that we call either comic or romantic has to be there on stage." You could say the same of Shakespeare; no wonder the RSC does so many Russians.

Alexander Solzhenitsyn's The Love-Girl and the Innocent (Aldwych) is a panoramic picture of life in a Stalinist labour-camp. Our natural impulse is to soft-pedal the horror; and it happens that the play makes that process rather easy. It is concerned with survival rather than suffering; it is set just after the war, when the camp is said to be "a health resort" in comparison with previous conditions. And this camp ranks low on the current scale; one of the worst fears hanging over the prisoners is that of being sent on somewhere worse.

We don't see much overt brutality; the ruling forces are graft and bribery. The most powerful man in the camp appears to be the doctor, himself a prisoner. This is an enclosed society, obeying the same rules as any other. The audience leaves the theatre thinking that if that's a labour camp, it's really not so bad. That cannot have been the intention.

The most impressive aspects of Clifford Williams's production are mechanical. Ralph Koltai's set incorporates a foundry and a railroad track, whose purpose is to transport prisoners; a new consignment arrives at the end, scared and shivering. This is the first time in the evening anyone has looked cold.

Hunger and fatigue are elements mentioned in the text, but never dramatised; perhaps because Solzhenitsyn lacks theatrical skill, perhaps because he takes them for granted. But a production has to supply them somehow; without that centre, acting becomes a business merely of getting through the lines. As usual the more experienced players survive best; the younger, left to fend for themselves, die of exposure: an apt reflection of the play's world, perhaps, but not a helpful one. The play holds attention, but it jumps confusingly about from one character to another, and when it finally settles on the two in the title the result is bathos.

The love-girl lives by leasing her body; the innocent is an ex-officer who tries to bring some fairness and reason to the job of labour supervisor, only to be dislodged by someone with a talent for greasing up to the authorities. Together they are our old Hollywood friends, the well-bred young idealist and the girl from the wrong side of the tracks who ain't no good for him. They illumine nothing that the rest of the play does not make clear; here Solzhenitsyn himself falls short of the standards of Russian realism.

  

In C. P. Taylor's Good (Warehouse) another idealist walks through a concentration camp, this time as an official. A nice man who joins the Nazis will inevitably end up supervising gas-chambers; or, alternatively, even the men of Auschwitz must at some time have been conventionally decent people: it would be interesting to know from which end Mr Taylor started.

Alan Howard, when not playing trumpeting heroes, has a fine line in moony myopia; he plays an academic with problems: a slatternly wife, a blind and troublesome mother, an attractive girl-pupil, a Jewish best friend. He writes a novel which seems to advocate euthanasia; the Nazis spot him; he embarks on a steep self-justifying road: the burning of books, the night of broken glass, gassing of mental cases, gassing of Jews.

It sounds schematic, but Mr Taylor, aided by Mr Howard's nervous solitariness, keeps it fresh: juggling time-schemes, varying the hero's excuses, and equipping him with a marvellously useful neurosis. At the crises of his life he hears music, music he knows to be imaginary (at one point he is treated to Kurt Weill's September Song a full five years before its composition, though here of course it's the production that's having hallucinations); when he enters Auschwitz there is finally real music in his ears: the prisoners' orchestra. No recent play has had so macabrely elegant an ending.

Sometimes Mr Taylor's dialogue contorts itself for too long at a time; the hero's girl (Felicity Dean) says once too often that all they can do is love one another -- though her deterioration is nicely sketched too: Love indeed is what our man seeks, with fatal lonely promiscuity, from both his old Jewish friend and his new Nazi friend. These two roles are played by Joe Melia and Pip Miller; Domini Blythe is the wife; Howard Davies directed: congratulations to all, not least to Mr Taylor for somehow combining Holocaust with Pennies from Heaven.

  

A Waste of Time is a dramatisation of Proust; the cheek of both enterprise and title identifies it as the work of the Glasgow Citizens' crowd, whom it represents both at their best and worst. The worst resides in a streak of self-congratulatory cleverness, admittedly less evident in Robert David Macdonald's adaptations than in his original plays. This extends to casting middle-aged mondaines (this being the stratum to which the company is most attracted) with young actresses who proceed, in self-defence, to turn in impersonations of Hermione Gingold.

There is also a cavalier disregard for the audience's mental comfort; neither text nor programme offers much clue as to who is whom in the first act, as Marcel's memories go whizzing by. But even these faults have their virtues; the acting imposes itself, and you begin to respond, not to individuals, but to a collection of delicate monsters. Giles Havergal, the theatre's director, turns actor to deliver a choice piece of the highest camp: a towering falsetto Baron de Charlus, terrifying and terrified.

Steven Dartnall delivers a dry, precise Marcel; the second and best act concerns his relationship with Albertine, who is cast in double focus as girl and boy; we see both the heterosexual affair of the book, and the homosexual affair it masks. Finally there is the usual splendour of Philip Prowse's sets, lit by Gerry Jenkinson as a series of decaying old masters. Mr Prowse also directs; and his capacity for squeezing his actors, to maximum effect, into the interstices of his decor, is pretty extraordinary.

  

A literary week: Solzhenitsyn, Proust and Dusty Hughes, he standing in for Johnson and Boswell. He has brought their double-act to the stage in Heaven and Hell (Royal Court), which title may prefigure the distance between Edinburgh and London (a journey undertaken by both Boswell and the play), but probably has more to do with sexual pleasure, as embraced with regrets by Boswell and abandoned with regrets by Johnson.

Their struggles are brought delectably before us, in designs by John Byrne and in dialogue full of quotations; Mr Hughes's own linking bits don't really measure up. But he has given the material shape, especially in its first half (the second rambles), and has set up, in Richard Wilson's production, two fine performances. Jimmy Chisholm makes a prim bouncing Bozzy, the fashionable world his banana-skin, and Jonathan Adams is a vast growl and slouch of a Doctor.
1981-09-20-a-real-witch:
A real witch

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in Stratford and London.

Michael Pennington as Hamlet: "An unusually clear-footed production."

IF STRATFORD'S Other Place did not maintain the highest performance standards in the country, something would be seriously wrong. It has all the advantages. Here is the main-house company freed from the task of animating over-familiar masterpieces in a sprawling house for tourist audiences. For the fourth time this year the marvellously compact room down the road rings with the sound of rediscovery.

The Witch of Edmonton is the joint work of Dekker, Ford and Rowley, generally credited with homeliness, horror and humour respectively. It is late Elizabethan: in fact Jacobean, going on Caroline, a period in which drama had narrowed in both social and emotional scope. Tragedy meant either exotic trials of honour (as demonstrated to us last year in The Maid's Tragedy) or, as here, local woes hot from the press.

Elizabeth Sawyer was a real woman executed for sorcery. Dekker--it must have been Dekker--presents her with undeviating insight as a woman who was indeed a witch, but only because her neighbours drove her to it, abusing her as one long before the fact. (Dekker, who spent long periods in the debtors' gaol, was the most charitable of the Elizabethans. This has been his year, the National having already given us his Shoemaker's Holiday; it now remains to add that fine double Dekker, The Honest Whore Parts I and II, the closest English drama ever came to domesticated Breughel.)

Rowley gave the witch a comic antagonist--and incidentally wrote a fat part for himself--in Cuddy Banks, a gullible countryman, whose bigoted father is Mother Sawyer's chief persecutor. And Ford supplied much of the alternate line of action; a weak-willed young man, Frank Thorney, is duped into one marriage by the employer who has impregnated his sweetheart, then bullied into a second by his father as a means of retrieving the family fortunes. Both women love him; he murders the second to stay with the first, prompted to the act by Mother Sawyer's devil.

This familiar is the play's unifying spirit. He comes in the shape of a dog, and his emergence as a long creeping shape from a heap of sacking is the masterstroke of Barry Kyle's production. He frightens as a demon before he endears as a pet, and thus the play's main hurdle is surmounted. He beats out the cur in The Two Gentlemen of Verona as the best canine role ever written; this one talks and from his first ominous words ("ho, have I caught thee cursing") Miles Anderson's agile, grinning presence dominates the play.

Like any Elizabethan fiend he can assist a crime, but he cannot cause or commit it. He exercises a nice sense of proportion among his victims, pursuing Frank or Sawyer to damnation, but Cuddy to only a ducking. If he is one unifying factor, the other--brilliantly realised by Mr Kyle and his designer, Chris Dyer, who works with an economic sense of period--is Edmonton itself, a village with its own standards of kindliness and social responsibility, but bitter to outsiders; the production begins with the whole cast singing a Puritan hymn: all but the presumptive witch who is already isolated.

It is a weakness of the play that the authors plainly ran out of things for her to do, though they reverse normal dramatic practise in one scene where the law intervenes to save her from the town; instead of an imaginary witch hounded, a real one protected. This is the element Arthur Miller left out of The Crucible (women who indeed were witches or believed themselves to be); and Miriam Karlin explores both the suffering and the malice; her execution scene, sporting both, is especially fine.

The two wives are sympathetically played by Harriet Walter and Juliet Stevenson, both excellent at suggesting relationships with a glance. There is a similar alertness in Gerard Murphy's Frank, but since he gives all his words an equal hammering emphasis it becomes difficult to listen to him. There is much natural fun in Anthony O'Donnell's Cuddy, and warm work from George Raistrick, a stricken father who represents the community voice at its best.

  

At the beginning of Hamlet (Aldwych) the stage looks like a build-your-own-Elsinore kit; as the eye sweeps round, it encounters a table with tankards (for Rhenish-quaffing usurpers), candlesticks (for play-going usurpers), a crucifix (for repentant usurpers), swords, halberds, furled banners, benches, a throne: all grouped around a forward-thrusting platform, a stage upon a stage.

As the gravedigger says, "it argues an act"; this is John Barton's theatrical-metaphor production; and though the scheme might not be apparent to those blessed innocents who read neither programme-notes nor reviews, they could hardly fail to notice that something had clearly been thought by someone, that these thoughts had been communicated in rehearsal, and that what has resulted is an unusually clear-footed production.

Clear-voiced too; both Michael Pennington as Hamlet and Derek Godfrey as Claudius can whisper to excellent effect. Mr Pennington is to begin with an almost aggressively (i.e. defensively) traditional Hamlet; black suit, open-neck white shirt, sunk in grief, nonsardonic: in short, immensely refreshing. Humour comes in later; as does shock: "oh my prophetic soul, my uncle" is not ha-ha, but a realisation of a long-suppressed fear.

He proceeds to play the antic conscientiously and with enjoyment, with electric moments when--as in Ophelia's reminder that his father has been dead four months--his madness brings him up against the truth. He is best at argumentation, advice, badinage, despair, ratiocination and anything in soliloquy; defiance eludes him. (And if the Barton line is that Hamlet only plays at defiance, but can't bring it off, I don't believe it.)

I have known Hamlets who provided more incidental kicks, but none who drew a tauter, more elastic line through the play, which becomes a story of a conscientious, wayward young man in impossible circumstances, doing his best. The play has never made more sense, the acting motif helping it round corners and over stiles (and, indeed, styles). It also enables Bruce Purchase to provide an avuncular First Player showing the noble amateur how these things should really be done (modestly, with one climactic burst), and illuminates the Polonius household.

Carol Royle as Ophelia has also to go through a series of charades at her father's bidding, and the strain visibly breaks her. Nor is it surprising that she should so desperately miss Tony Church's loving, officious Polonius; anyone would. Derek Godfrey, who excels at playing jokey villains, is efficient but opaque as the tormented one of this play; Barbara Leigh-Hunt, however, finds volumes in Gertrude.

  

The Case of David Anderson Q.C. (Lyric Studio) offers the piquant spectacle of Corin Redgrave playing a defrocked Conservative MP; and playing him well, as a driven, honourable man. John Hale's documentary play is an argument for the reopening of Mr Anderson's case, he having been dropped from public life after allegations of importuning women; and a persuasive one. It is also an enthralling tale, marred only by a glut of undigested facts (undigested by me, anyway) and some melodrama--much curt turning on heels by subordinate characters--in the production.

  

Macready (Arts) is an instructive and entertaining one-man show prepared and performed by Frank Barrie; an account of one of the last century's two or three most lauded actors who hated doing it, except when he loved it.
1981-09-27-stoppard-on-the-razzle:
THEATRE

Stoppard on the Razzle

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Manchester.

PERHAPS the best place to start with On the Razzle (Lyttelton), Tom Stoppard's Viennese whirl, is towards the end, where somebody says indignantly of somebody else, "he's the real impostor." Or towards the beginning, where Dinsdale Landen, contemplating the immediate future, says, "one false move and we could have a farce on our hands." Or the middle, where we do.

But I think I'll begin by telling you a story. A year or so ago I was in Vienna and, conscientious creature that I am, asked to be taken to the Burgtheater. My host shook his head. "They're doing a Nestroy play tonight," he said. "You wouldn't understand it. It isn't in real German; it's in a strange Viennese dialect. Even we don't understand it. Have dinner instead." I decided to let the implied, and quite unmerited, tribute to my command of real German pass unchallenged, and took the dinner: which was excellent.

But in fact I probably could have made head, if not tail, of the play, since it was Einem Jux will er sich machen, on which Thornton Wilder based The Merchant of Yonkers, subsequently re-adapted as The Matchmaker, which I've seen, and musicalised as Hello Dolly, ditto. It would have been good to see the original, of which Mr Stoppard's piece is another free adaptation. Maybe the National should dig up the English farce A Day Well Spent by John Oxenford, on which Nestroy, some 140 years ago, did his own basing. Let's nail this thing, once and for all.

I am not suggesting that Oxenford's script would be as funny as Mr Stoppard's. Apart from Jumpers and The Importance of Being Earnest there may be no script in English funnier than On the Razzle. From political farce and philosophical farce Mr Stoppard has turned to writing farcical farce: both a raging example of the genre and a tribute to it. (The only comparable work I know is A Funny Thing Happened On the Way to the Forum.)

Once again two shop assistants abandon their groceries for a first and last night on the town. Once again they get involved with two ladies, one of whom is in hats, professionally speaking, and is also engaged to their employer. He is also engaged in trying to prevent his niece from marrying the man of her choice. Take the above, mix in several locations, bring to the boil in a restaurant scene and add, most vitally, Mr Stoppard's gift of language.

What makes On the Razzle unique is that every line in it is either a joke or part of one. There are half a dozen puns per page, and it is very rare indeed for anyone to say anything that cannot be misinterpreted, or that isn't. Mr Stoppard does not write wisecracks. His jokes, unlike, say, Neil Simon's, are not there to lighten or to accentuate the situation; they are the situation.

This is not as a rule how plays get written, though we might all be happier if it were. You will notice that I have referred to On the Razzle as a script; it recalls, alludes to, and cries out for the Marx Brothers, Morecambe and Wise, John Cleese and at one point (the "get it -- got it -- good" routine from The Court Jester) Danny Kaye. This obviously makes it rather hard on mere actors.

Mr Landen as the master-grocer and Michael Kitchen as his servant (whose catch-phrase, applied quite correctly in the circumstances to absolutely everything, is "classic") have the beginnings of a fine routine going, and in 30 years' time they will probably be wonderful. That's over-pessimistic; it took Mr Landen a few months to become his own man in Plunder, which presented similar problems. At the moment, though, his eyebrows work more expressively than his voice, which is too anxiously squeaky. Better and more relaxed are Ray Brooks and Felicity Kendal (en travesti) as the hellraisers for a night; Miss Kendal's mounting delight leaves a lovely taste.

Peter Wood's production struck me at first as too slow; that was simplistic of me, since some of the best comedy acts are deliberate. But the right pacing, whatever it is, has yet to arrive; some scenes are actually over-inventive. Carl Toms's sets, especially for the grocery emporium, are delectable; he fills scene-changes with projections of sheet-music, in witty tribute to Nestroy, who used actual songs.

Finally I have a confession to make; apart from a fine fantasia on the glories and uncertainties of the provisioner's trade ("we sit here flicking a duster over pyramids of uncertain dates"), Mr Stoppard has cut the play loose from the moorings it once had in Austrian social satire; and I doubt his wisdom. I found myself wondering what it was all for. This is an unaccustomed mood for me; and I would be very tart with anyone else who raised such puritanical objections. "It's hilarious," I would say. "Think yourself lucky."

  

Adrian Noble's production of Doctor Faustus (Royal Exchange, Manchester) is visually superb, both in set-pieces like the Pope's banquet and the show of the Seven Deadly Sins, and in such single moments as the first appearance of Mephostophilis, who shuffles on as an imp with a limp. Later he is metamorphosed into James Maxwell, saturnine in a cassock. The comedy scenes are kept nearly intact and, without raising any roofs, perform their literary function of showing up Faustus's own antics.

The point of the play has to be that any price paid for damnation is bound to look pretty silly; or, in secular terms, that power will bring out the schoolboy in any of us. This at least is how Ben Kingsley plays Faustus, getting a great bang out of disrupting the other kids' parties and developing a very persuasive self-intoxication. He only fails in the last speech, whose myriad gradations are ignored in favour of monotonous hysteria. Even a final coup-de-theatre, with the protagonist blown to Hell among withered leaves, cannot quite atone.

  

At the New Half Moon Instant Enlightenment Including VAT (sloppy title) examines the Est-like movements that bully their customers into what they take to be spiritual transformation. It is also rather a good advertisement for them; in Andrew Carr's production of his own script we are present at a series of seminars whose thrill and entertainment value seems extremely high; if one could attend without getting involved, it might almost be worth the money.

But would it be possible? You can't be sure; Mr Carr's resident sceptic ends up as cowed and accepting as any, but his turning-point is not actually shown. That's the trouble; the play has too many case-histories to get through. But it disturbs, not least because the unflaggingly abrasive guru (played with appropriate barking charisma by Robin Nedwell, whose throat will be a wreck by the end of the run) has some sense on his side. The charge that we are all ruled by neurotic patterns in our own minds sticks easily. What remains mercifully unproven is that he has anything better to offer.

  

The Orchestra (King's Head) of Jean Anouilh's play is an all-girl Palm Court aggregation, plus male pianist. Between and even during numbers they treat us to their complaints and fantasies, which would be much the same if they couldn't play a note. There is some bilious wit in both the substance and the superstructure, but they don't need each other. Nor does the author's harking back to the squabbles of the Occupation seem of much moment now. The play was written in 1957.
1981-09-27-the-hypnotic-miss-horne:
The hypnotic Miss Horne

ROBERT CUSHMAN reports on a recent visit to Broadway.

THE most beautiful woman in the world walks on to the stage, dazzling, in a white dress and gold necklace. The overture has been long--all her hits strung together--and we have had plenty of time to ponder and anticipate her entrance. An arm-waving march or a sinuous slink? In fact she just steps on from the side, downstage; it's so uncomplicated (not unassuming) it dazes you.

Lena Horne: The Lady and Her Music is the event of the Broadway season, a club act miraculously blown up to theatre size without bursting. It is, in fact, an extension of the routine Miss Horne has been doing for the last couple of years. She sings, dances a little and talks quite a lot. The chat now gets official status as "book"--for which she is given sole programme credit--so I suppose this counts as a musical.

At 63 she has a solid quantity of past to go over. Her characteristic gait is a rapid prowl, and her words have the same rhythm. They are delivered, often, in a tone of amused anger, especially when she comes to recall her wartime days as Hollywood's first black sex-symbol: not black enough, the bosses decided, so they devised a special make-up for her, afterwards passed on to Ava Gardner when she assumed the role Miss Horne should have played in Show Boat.

She gets away with much that I could not forgive in other performers: with telling the audience how wonderful and important they are and how excited and enthusiastic she is, with singing inspirational songs called "If You Believe" and "That's What Miracles Are All About," with gospel ornamentations of purely secular tunes. There is an uninterrupted flow of passion in her performance that carries all the mannerisms on its back. The prize is the way she can revivify a familiar song by striking directly at its heart: raw, full-throated anguish for "Stormy Weather," dreamy erotic lyricism for "The Surrey With the Fringe On Top," done with only a rhythm section though she was so rapt it took me ages to realise this.

She had noticed that this is really a song about hypnosis, and hypnotism--of herself too--is what she deals in. Between numbers she shakes her head sagely from side to side, with a burning glint in her eyes. It is as if we were not merely her subjects but her creations. That skin-tone MGM commissioned for her was called "light Egyptian," and Mr Factor may have had something of a point; who else could Cleopatra have looked or sounded like?

  

Increasingly on Broadway a show runs for a week or for ever. The latest candidate for eternity is Sophisticated Ladies, a nostalgia show like Sugar Babies or 42nd Street, but superior to either of them. It starts with the advantage of Duke Ellington's music; the show was planned as a biographical tribute, but the biography was jettisoned during a calamitous try-out tour. Michael Smuin, whose background is in ballet rather than musicals, was called in and saved the production by turning it into non-stop dance.

The routines would probably be just as exhilarating done to anyone else's tunes, though they reflect one side of Ellington--the raffish, Harlem dandy side--pretty well. The band (under the nominal direction of the Duke's son, Mercer) are irresistible from the first note, and the show strikes a pleasing blow against racism; that is, the white hoofers are as good as the black. The only problem is that, with no story and with every number clearly promising to be immaculate, the evening runs short on surprise.

  

It is still unusual for a show to open in the summer; though air-conditioning and tourism combine to sustain the existing hits. The only book (i.e. narrative) musical to achieve any success this past season is Woman of the Year, which has won a few awards and a fair amount of scorn. I can see why; but I had a better time at it than I had anticipated.

Based on a Tracy-Hepburn film, the show has been fashioned as a vehicle for Lauren Bacall, and aims apparently at keeping as close as possible to her previous hit, Applause. Again she is a successful woman who finds that love counts for more than career; or rather, this being 1981 after all, that love counts for just as much as career. Again there is a big number about how popular she is, with the chorus dancing round her, occasionally lifting her up and brandishing her to make it look as if she can dance too.

This time that idea misfires, accenting her limitations rather than concealing them. Her acting lacks range (every line comes out the same) and so, notoriously, does her singing, but this doesn't matter; she makes an attractive, casually sardonic noise, and she communicates an affable, unfazed enthusiasm, to which the house naturally rises. The show is machine-made, staged with expertise rather than inspiration, but it has a better than average score; one of its attractions is that John Kander and Fred Ebb (who also composed Chicago) do not spend the evening trying to prove how tough they are.

  

There are no new plays on Broadway (though Lanford Wilson's Fifth of July, which I saw and liked on the West Coast two years ago, has found itself a home) and the most praised piece off Broadway, a three-hander about love and cycling called Key Exchange, is only a nice trifle. Down on Theatre Row (a new development on the far side of the porno district in Forty-second Street) something stirs; something that was once called Four Jews in a Room Bitching is now named March of the Falsettos.

Thus it has two title-numbers; both are very niftily staged though hard to relate to the rest of the action. This concerns Marvin (intended, I think, to be an archetypal name), who leaves his wife and son for another man, but wants to hang on to all of them. Serene chess-playing child ("my father's a homo--my mother's not thrilled") is contrasted with nerve-baring adults.

The author, William Finn, writes effective lines rather than whole lyrics, motifs rather than melodies; but he is on the way to establishing characters and--especially--relationships through song; and in a theatre largely fixated on its insubstantial past that is a hopeful sign.
1981-10-04-not-just-a-capulet:
Not just a Capulet

ROBERT CUSHMAN talks to an actress who has achieved an unusual double.

"Why," Peter Hall once asked me very rhetorically, "should they have to be either Montagues or Capulets?" He was referring to actors who move from the National Theatre to the Royal Shakespeare Company or vice versa. This two-way traffic is more frequent than the image or publicity of either organisation would suggest. Not until now, though, has a player managed to work for both simultaneously.

That player is Brenda Bruce, appearing until November at the National as Margery Eyre in "The Shoemakers' Holiday," but also due to open this week at the Aldwych as the Nurse in "Romeo and Juliet" and shortly afterwards at the Warehouse as the Witch in David Rudkin's "Hansel and Gretel." If this display of ambidextrousness has gone largely unnoticed, that is of a piece with Miss Bruce's whole career. She has never lacked for appreciation, but she has only gradually crept up on us as the best undamed actress of her generation.

I have to declare a bias. In 1954, when I was taken on what was then the inevitable schoolboy trip to see "Peter Pan," she was playing Peter. I have a firm memory of her voice trembling as she thanked us for saving Tinker Bell.

She told me that she got the Peter Pan job very strangely. She was already an established West End player and, like many such, under contract to H. M. Tennent. They put her into a Henry James adaptation. "It was my chance to play the leading juvenile and it was the flop of all time. Kenneth Tynan wrote that I was foolishly and determinedly miscast as a radiant American of 18, considering that I'd made a name for myself as being incredibly plain."

This led to a bizarre competition in the Evening Standard, which ran her photograph over the ringing inquiry, "Is this the plainest face on the English stage?" Readers were invited to suggest their own nominees for the title, and they became known collectively as "the urchin girls." The Peter Pan management must have decided that any actress whose looks could inspire that kind of furore must at any rate be good for playing a boy.

Miss Bruce survived the Tynan review and the competition, having already surmounted a far more terrifying criticism from her mother, who "wanted me to wear frocks and look pretty," but pronounced, after seeing an early performance as Anne Bronte at Birmingham Rep, "it's a pity you look so ugly when you cry." "I think of it," she says, "every show I do." Her own word for her face is "perky" and it has led her to a great suspicion of perky characters: the kind for which directors think her obvious casting. She was resistant to the role of Maria in "Twelfth Night," and ended up playing her staid and stern.

She started very young. "Apparently I told my mother when I was three that I was going to be a fairy." She trained as a dancer, but gave it up at 12. ("I was hopeless.") A brisk, soubrettish air has clung to her ever since. At 13, though, she was a chorus-girl ("complete with chaperone") in a little revue, and in 1936, at the age of 14, she went to Birmingham ("Barry Jackson was very brave") and stayed there for three years.

She came to London during the war in Rattigan's "While the Sun Shines," and scored her first big success in 1947 at Hammersmith playing Eliza in "Pygmalion." The notices were excellent ("I found the Cockney all too easy," says Miss Bruce from Brixton) and a transfer was only prevented by a postcard from the author: "Don't know nuffin' of Brenda Bruce, don't want to know nuffin', am sick of 'Pygmalion'."

She stuck with Shaw, though, appearing in 1951 in the entire canon of his one-act plays. These were directed by her husband, Roy Rich, later head of Southern Television and of BBC Light Entertainment. During the Fifties they had their own television chat show, "Rich and Rich," presented in a studio replica of their Bloomsbury flat. "If we didn't already know the people we had on the show, we had them over for several meals. That's how I learned to cook and Roy had a heart attack. The two of us were news at the time. I was doing lots of West End plays, and I had a weekly column, mainly based on having two children: a very poor man's Katharine Whitehorn."

The children were adopted twin girls, and were later joined by a boy. Because of them she withdrew from the theatre and acted mainly on television. She was nominated TV Actress of the Year in 1962. In that year, however, she also appeared at the Royal Court as Winnie in the near-monologue of "Happy Days," and the career of an actress who had come to epitomise a very Fifties kind of sensible glamour began to shift.

In 1964, egged on by her husband, she went to the Aldwych for a single play which stretched into two, then into three. She has been with the RSC on and off ever since. "The Merry Wives of Windsor" was her first decisive success; she was the bubbly one, Elizabeth Spriggs the shy one. She had played very little Shakespeare before; she has since gone through the range of available parts, culminating in the Nurse.

Her Stratford years have been marked by professional success and private tragedy. Roy Rich had wanted to return to the theatre, but found it was too late: "People practically said 'Roy who?'" Despondent, he decided that they should live outside Stratford and run a "little pub" - one that turned out to have 11 rooms and room for 45 dinner-guests. But within a year he was dead of cancer. She faced "a nightmare year" with the business to run, the children still at school and - what turned out to be her salvation - a full season's work in the theatre.

Later she married RSC actor Clem McCallin, whom she had known since Birmingham days; soon after the marriage her young son, who had always suffered from asthma, died too. She also discovered that her new husband had leukaemia. In 1977 "he too" died, having worked almost literally up to the last minute. Within the last year she has lost both her parents. "One copes. I don't know what I'd have done if I were just a housewife."

"She's suffered enormously," says Ron Daniels, who directs both her current RSC plays, "and it gives her a tremendous vulnerability on-stage. She's extraordinary to work with, because she combines tremendous helplessness with an absolute sense of knowing what's right. She's very protective, very kind - and she stands up to the young ones with great finesse. I wanted a Nurse who wasn't the conventional type: one representing an active sexuality, a madam rather than a crone."

She says herself that she wanted to play "not a Back to Methuselah original ancient, but a substitute mother for Juliet. (She's played the real one in her time - a strong, embittered performance that dominated its production.) As for the Rudkin play: "You don't get to play a witch that often. It used to frighten us to death to do it. But the children adore it; it's the 30-year-old dads who pass out."
1981-10-04-trapped-in-a-tyranny:
Trapped in a tyranny

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Nottingham.

ONE scene in Mephisto (Roundhouse) depicts a rehearsal in a Hamburg theatre of a scene from Goethe's Faust. The year is 1930, and the mainly Leftish company are still reeling from the news of Hitler's first substantial election victories. One of the actors is a Nazi, and the theatre's star, who is both directing and playing Mephistopheles, makes life hell for him, finally demanding his dismissal.

This superb scene, confounding expectation and alive with political and emotional cross-currents, has several pay-offs. The young Nazi, when his party comes to power, revolts at the idea of becoming an informer, denounces the regime, and becomes the evening's first martyr. (This play is nothing if not magnanimous.) Meanwhile his former tormentor, Hendrick Hofgen, has become locked into the role of Mephisto, on and off stage, going to Berlin and accepting the status of honoured artist of the National Socialist theatre. He was the one who had yapped loudest, and his politics are now shown to be at the service of his career.

His comrades--more deeply committed, though all to different factions--had stood by embarrassed or openly offended during that rehearsal scene. They all now meet predictable ends. A Communist dies after 40 days' interrogation in Dachau. A Social Democrat refuses to divorce his Jewish wife; they throw themselves together off a railway bridge.

The play was adapted by the French director Ariane Mnouchkine from a novel by Klaus--son of Thomas--Mann. This English production was first seen last year at the Oxford Playhouse. Klaus Mann is presented as prologue and an occasional chorus. The play presents his world: his father and family appear in transparent disguise; as their society crumbles, they quote from memory the last section of The Cherry Orchard, first playfully, then elegiacally. It's a reasonable device for a play that questions the relationship of the theatre to politics, and comes up with bleak conclusions.

To Hendrick's self-serving must be added the spirited but ultimately useless agitprop cabarets with which he and his friends occupy their spare time, mocking Hitler not because they think he's dangerous, but because they think he's ludicrous. The play mordantly satirises, for example, the Communist reaction to the first Nazi victories: welcomed as a blow against the Social Democrats. Attitudinising is no good; all that can be done is to tell the truth, and this Mephisto does, re-charging our cherished images of Weimar decadence and evoking, like no other work I know, the sense of being trapped in engulfing tyranny.

It has the sprawling handicaps of most dramatised novels: too many characters are given too little time, resulting in baldly emotional speeches that need careful colouring, and a succession of short scenes that ask for careful orchestration plus a firm decision on such matters as the function of a blackout. Apart from lively handling of the cabaret scenes, Gordon McDougall's production muffs everything. I have rarely seen so many actors left with egg on their faces, or indeed so many who seemed to deserve it. Neil Phillips and Tim Hardy are exceptions; and Ian McDiarmid gives the devil his usual reptilian vivacity, though he is perhaps too obviously corruptible from the start.

But the material triumphs; I have not been so moved in the theatre for a very long time. The play ends with a display of the names of actual theatre workers killed by the Nazis. Among them is Klaus Mann himself, who committed suicide after the war with his novel still unpublished.
