He seems newly jowly, playing a police commander who combines a voracious sexual appetite with a public-school sense of propriety. He functions as both tempter and tempted, a combination that allows Mr Stephens a double ration of double-takes, all executed with consummate authority. He has always been good at bewilderment; now he has weight as well. Pam Brighton's production is very racy.

  

Beth Henley's The Miss Firecracker Contest (Bush) is, though never staged there, very Louisville Festival: that is, it takes a loving look at a stretch of the American hinterland which it has peopled with eccentrics. A mild word that. Miss Henley actually runs to screwballs, loonies and--let us not mince words--nutcases. But then her territory is Mississippi, and her style is southern Gothic.

In the small town of Brookhaven the event of the year is a beauty contest. The aspiring Miss Firecracker, first seen practising her tap routine (should she, she agonises, have chosen a recitation instead?), once known as Miss Hot Tamale, on account of her promiscuity, but she wants to live that down. Around her are her female cousin, herself an ex-beauty; her beloved male cousin who's had a chequered career and can do this trick where he wiggles his ears; the shy adoring girl next door who does her dresses; and the balloon salesman to whom she once gave the clap.

The dialogue is fine-spun but resilient; though the total effect--as of a soft-focus cartoon--does not engage as deeply as the author apparently wishes. She wants to touch as well as amuse; to her credit, she draws self-indulgent people without indulging them herself. Simon Stokes's production, sumptuously set and costumed, has especially good work from Sandra Dickinson as the contestant and David Beames as the beautifully off-the-wall dangerous relative.
1982-05-09-shaw-for-our-times:
Shaw For Our Times

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in Chichester and London.

IT rained heavily on the first night of the Chichester season. I have never known this happen before in all my experience as a critic. Truly the country is going to the dogs.

Or it's going On the Rocks. That is the title of a play by Shaw, written in 1933, which seemed topical when I read it 10 years ago, prescient when the Mermaid staged it a couple of years after that, and positively uncanny at Chichester now. It takes place in Downing Street, where Sir Arthur Chavender (Lib.) presides over a Coalition Government which is having trouble with unemployment. That is true in two senses: the governed haven't got jobs and the governors aren't doing too much work either.

Chavender is an amiable fellow, overwhelmed by it all and longing to get away for a spell of golf. Meanwhile he spends time dictating a flatulent speech on the sacredness of the family to be delivered to high-ranking churchmen. His own family does not live up to his prescriptions, his wife being at her Welsh sanatorium. During his stay there he gets through the complete works of Marx and comes back determined to push through a full Socialist policy. This turns out to have beneficent side-effects for the police, the Admiralty (hearty laugh when the Ruler of the Queen's Navee talks of sending warships to the Gulf), capitalists large and small, and the landed nobility, who see the abolition of death-duties as a lifeline.

The representative of each group pledges his support, delighting in his own perks and sure that everybody else's will prove chimerical. The only opposition comes from the resident Tory, whose threats include the raising of a private army in Union Jack shirts, and from the forces of Labour, threatened with the loss of the right to strike. This odd but quite plausible alliance scuttles Chavender; but in fact he has been ruined already by the factional selfishness of his own supporters.

At the end of the play, with the unemployed rioting in Downing Street and the mounted police charging them, and his secretary rushing out to aid the resisters, Chavender muses on what has to be done, adding, 'I shall hate the man who will carry it through for his cruelty and the desolation he will bring.' This is a jolt--almost the only point at which the play recognises the realities of dictatorship--and it carries a lot of weight.

By the end both children will have been taken in marriage--and I mean taken--by aggressive members of a deputation from somewhere called the Isle of Cats, who claim to speak for the working classes. One of them is a peer, the other a self-educated Shavian superwoman. This being late Shaw, he has christened her Aloysia Brollikins.

Sir Arthur is also visited by a lady in grey whom he takes to be a spirit, but who turns out to be a doctor offering him an extremely expensive rest-cure with awful persuasiveness of the failures of parliamentary democracy, and he has all the Shavian Cockney charm of Alfred Doolittle. The best book on Shaw I know ('The Shavian Playground' by Margery Morgan) describes Hipney as the Tempter, someone, presumably, to be resisted. But I defy any production to get that over. Certainly the present one (by Jack Emery and Patrick Garland) does not try.

It is a handsome affair, dominated by a long table that cries out for a full-scale conference scene. This does not arrive until the second half, but, when it does, it fulfils expectations. Both Shaw's characters and his jokes are thinner than in earlier plays, but he can still set up half-a-dozen opposed viewpoints and send them ricocheting round the room. This scene, naturally, brings out the company heavies: not before time in a production whose younger characters are poorly--in some cases wretchedly--played.

Keith Michell keeps the show going through the first act with appealing eloquence, though his conversion seems to make no change in him; he keeps vocalising, and mostly to the same tune. Paul Hardwick brings some good bluster to the diehard, Lockwood West a delightful ruddy benevolence to the Sea Lord, and Nigel Stock is ungainsayable as the Duke of Domesday. Arthur English deservedly stops the show as Hipney, but the most striking of all is Aubrey Woods's suave police chief, chilling the house with his memories of service in Ireland: 'Auxiliary forces . . . it means extermination; and when it comes to the point you can't go through with it.'

This is a particularly striking moment if you have read Shaw's preface, which uses the word 'extermination' with deliberate blitheness as a synonym for the painless weeding-out of social undesirables. This, remember, was in 1933. In that year Shaw could write, 'The extirpation of the Jew as such figured for a few mad moments in the programme of the Nazi party in Germany.' He was sharp enough to have noticed that, and stupid enough to dismiss it. He could write of the OGPU, not to qualify his enthusiasm for Stalin's Russia, but to reinforce it.

Somehow his dramatic instincts survived his polemical ones, and though On the Rocks is conclusive (the family metaphor is never properly pursued) it fizzes almost throughout. This production puts it effectively into modern dress (the substitution of 50p for 3s. 6d. is a comment in itself, if a wildly optimistic one), though it barks its shins a few times. Hipney claims that his father knew Karl Marx: in person? The show ends with an invasion by riot police: not what Shaw wrote, but a logical addition to it.

  

Proof that Shaw put the best of himself into his plays can be found in his letters: at least in those assembled by Jerome Kilty in Dear Liar (Mermaid), an epistolary account of his long and preposterously literary flirtation with Mrs Patrick Campbell. Robert Hardy and Sian Phillips, she especially, do their stuff with style as the correspondents (never, never co-respondents), but he comes across as a finger-wagging bully and she as a spoiled vamp. She was, by all accounts, a first-rate bitch. He, by all accounts, was very nice. Perhaps that is how he could afford to be so inhuman.
1982-05-23-in-the-trap:
In the trap

HERE they are again, Uncle Vanya and Auntie Hedda, trapped in their lives and their families, unlucky in love, mucking about with firearms, tramping round large rooms in impossible houses -- a point much stressed in both the new revivals.

Professor Serebryakov complains in the course of Uncle Vanya of the impossibility of finding anyone in a ramshackle establishment with 26 rooms. The National production makes it easy to sympathise with him. (An achievement, since he is not generally a sympathetic character.) Just as we may all have thought we were coming to terms with the size of the Lyttelton, here is a production that puts us back at the wrong end of the telescope. John Bury's sets extend to the edge of the proscenium and apparently beyond. Curtains doing duty for walls seem to extend into infinity.

Michael Bogdanov's production, maybe making a virtue out of necessity, is concerned to distance us, anyway. Like Mr Bury's designs, it is fine on its own terms, but unsatisfying. In the years since Tynan described Vanya himself as almost unplayable, a host of fine, occasionally great, performances have arisen to confute him. Michael Redgrave, Paul Scofield, Leo McKern, Nigel Hawthorne and Basil Henson's account of the gouty great-man himself is the best I have seen, the only one to make a case for the character.

The character has become a myth; the scene in which he talks feverishly of his wasted life and blighted ambitions, realises his foolishness, attempts to shoot the professor, bungles that too, and collapses in tragicomic fury, goes deeper than anything in modern drama. You have to be very smug not to recognise a piece of yourself in it. (And, as the Actors' Company once showed us, it carries some of the same charge even in the imperfect early version; The Wood Demon proof that Chekhov had struck gold even if at first he was unsure how to invest it.) But here it goes by with remarkably little disturbance.

From the moment he enters -- or, in this version, falls out of a swing -- Michael Bryant's Vanya is an outstandingly capable performance; too capable, perhaps, to have landed in Vanya's morass. As prescribed, he dresses well; but it seems less compensation than his natural mode. Self-hatred burns fiercer in Diaghilev; Langton's Astrov; there is unusual emphasis on the doctor's drunkenness and bitter sense of professional incapacity; he is, too, an active ladykiller.

One of Mr Bogdanov's happiest notions is the procession that follows the professor across the stage at the beginning. It establishes Cherie Lunghi's Yelena, indolent and inhibited, and Patti Love's Sonya, bustling to keep from crying, on lines from which they never deviate.

  

Hedda Gabler (Cambridge) inhabits an amphitheatre of a living-room, hung with draperies depicting spread-tailed peacocks. There is a French window for Judge Brack's regular entrance, a prominent bust of General Gabler and, stage-centre, a resplendent stove with a funnel so thick it might double as a Grecian column. This might be what inspired Hedda, who sees herself as a tragic heroine, to choose the house; one feels that, having chosen it, she deserves everything she gets.

This seems too to be the view of Susannah York, resplendently gowned twice over, and with as bronzed a voice as you could wish of a leading lady. She sails hatefully and uncompromisingly through the night. The play is one of which I must confess myself thoroughly tired, but Miss York's briskness does much to rescue it. It is far more satisfying, and fairer to women, than the new idea of Hedda as victim: whoever respected a victim of anything? It is not, for all its strengths, the most vapid, joyous performance in the world, and the same is true of its accomplices.

Tom Baker gives us a Brack whose every smile turns into a satyr's grin, but whom you can certainly imagine bullying witnesses. Ralph Bates is a nice old Tesman, even though young; Irene Handl a kind and even perspicacious Aunt Julie, who would certainly have driven Hedda to distraction (and who gets proper support in this line from Gretchen Franklin's maid); and Tom Bell a Lovborg with the proviso that Mr Wilson and Mr Firbank worlds collide; instead of running teasingly in parallel.

  

Valmouth

That at any rate is supposed to be the point, and I will accept it with the proviso that Mr Wilson Dexter, way off form, would have written jaunty melodies with surprising modulations anyway. His dialogue is cunning in its authenticity, but it is unfortunate that since 1958 camp has moved on, leaving Valmouth with the fatal sound of self-conscious, self-willed sophistication. All that now remains is the occasionally highly concentrated line, like Lady Parvula's about an unresponsive shepherd: 'Oh, I'd like to spank the white walls of his cottage.' That gives you dainty lust, quaint pastoralism, everything except religious satire.

Four members of the original cast remain and, since they are all playing freaks or degenerates, time has hardly impaired them: Fenella Fielding as Parvula, the role that established her and has haunted her ever since; Doris Hare as Grannie Tooke; Marcia Ashton as a singing nun; and Bertice Reading as Mrs Yajnavalkya, transformed from Oriental masseuse to Pearl Bailey jazz queen.

Robert Helpmann makes what amounts to a guest appearance as Cardinal Pirelli, but the best newcomers are Cheryl Kennedy as, most definitely, a wench, and Judy Campbell as the arch-religieuse, going through the action spectacularly dominoed, in search of a heretic, whether to burn or to convert remains uncertain. Indeed none of the various plot-lines amount to much, and they desperately need a proscenium arch to make their inconsequence charming. I suspect the production, rehearsed in tandem with Of Thee I Sing, opened unprepared: on the first night even Miss Reading lacked verve. The director is John Dexter, way off form.
1982-05-30-from-papp-to-pope:
From Papp to Pope

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'The Pirates,' 'The Jeweller's Shop' and 'Berenice.'

UNLIKE The Pirates of Penzance, who stymied themselves by practising fair play and kindness to orphans, Joseph Papp knows how to make money. Mr Papp runs the New York Shakespeare Festival in Central Park and the multiple Public Theatre in Greenwich Village. These operations have largely been financed by the profits from 'Hair' and 'A Chorus Line,' which originated at the Public, and the revival of 'The Pirates' was explicitly planned to carry on the good work. It started in the Park, where all who saw it seem agreed it was at its best, then moved to Broadway's looming Uris Theatre, where it still remains. It has now reproduced itself at Drury Lane; meanwhile the film-version waits.

'The Pirates' has claims to be considered one of the first American musicals; for copyright reasons, Gilbert, Sullivan and Richard D'Oyly Carte put it on in New York before bringing it to London. In lavishing on it the techniques of contemporary Broadway, Mr Papp's director, Wilford Leach, is merely returning a compliment. Actually, the compliment is still double-edged: G&S do as much for Broadway as Broadway does for them. It is a relief to see showmanship applied to a decently humorous text and score. For once all that leaping about seems justified. Well, most of it. The production has enough energy, invention and goodwill to pleasure any audience. Bear that in mind while I dissect it.

The music has been spicily orchestrated for, among other things, the merriest synthesizer you ever heard: all to the good. The performance style was set in New York by Kevin Kline, who, as the Pirate King, combined the looks, bravado and open-shirt sexiness of Flynn and Fairbanks with the cheeky self-mocking agility of the young Burt Lancaster (remember 'The Crimson Pirate'?) His pirate-technics infected the entire company, especially the choruses. There are, you may recall, three of these: Buccaneers, Bobbies and Beautiful Maidens.

In London the pirates retain most of their zest, dressed to the eight-and-a-halfs and carrying on to match. The police have lost a bit: conceived as wind-up Keystone Kops, they now fly through the air at less extraordinary angles than they did. General Stanley's daughters are presented as hysterical virgins, achieving by hard work effects that D'Oyly Carte ladies would have lumbered into by accident.

When Frederic, the virtuous pirate apprentice, sings and gyrates a pop aria at them, they practically wet themselves. Unfortunately the plot dictates that they reject him. The plot is of course nonsensical, but the players ought to believe in it. It is mock melodrama; and this show too often spoofs the spoof. It also treads on some perfectly good jokes.

The production is at its best when its extravagance accords with Gilbert's own: when the action suddenly stops dead for a full-stage Handelian ode to poetry, and above all when the pirates enter 'with cat-like tread,' which means with stamping feet and percussive accompaniment, singing at the tops of their voices, and about 27 abreast. This leads to a riotous chase-sequence.

Three performances outstrip their originals. George Cole, dressed for a tour of the pyramids, is a splendidly pointed Major-General. (Incidentally you don't have to be a besotted Gilbertian to suspect that the inept couplet, 'But still at getting off my daughters, eight or nine or 10 in all, I've shown myself the model of a modern major-general' was inserted into the finale by another hand, presumably piratical.) Annie Ross's Ruth is a bespectacled Scots gentlewoman, which does very well. Above all, Michael Praed sings Frederic into his rightful place at the centre of the opera; some gaucherie in his acting actually works to this priggish hero's advantage.

As Mabel, his beloved, Pamela Stephenson has inherited a mould--of a music-box shaped like a china doll--fashioned for the non-acting talents of Linda Ronstadt, but she makes it as funny as she can. Tim Curry's Pirate King is very acceptable if you've seen Mr Kline, and probably wonderful if you haven't.

  

From Papp to Pope. Karol Wojtyla's The Jeweller's Shop (Westminster) arrived in London three days before its author, giving theatregoers the chance of actually being a papal audience. There is a humane mind at work in this piece, but little instinct for drama; the author is probably better off in his other job. (He wrote this in 1960 when he was Bishop of Cracow.) What happens is that three couples parade outside a symbolic store; their wedding rings are only worth as much as the state of their marriage. Since we always seem to arrive after hours, this has to be explained to us, like much else, by a raisonneur called Adam. From the audience's point of view the main trouble with the relationships is that the participants never talk to each other. They only talk to Adam and--at length--to themselves.

Adam's line seems to be that they are in danger of substituting earthly love for divine love and so devaluing both; but he does not quite go uncontested. There is a brief and effective boost for human feeling, delivered by John Carson, but you wait a long time for it. Of the other players, Gwen Watford injects some feeling into a strictly externalised text. Robin Phillips's production, with pretty Perspex sets and wistful music, is reminiscent of 'The Umbrellas of Cherbourg,' which may not be so inappropriate at that.

  

A more respectable minimal action play is at the Lyric Studio: Racine's Berenice in fact, in which an Eastern queen, kept waiting for years by a prospective Roman emperor, realises that once in power, he will never marry her. Meanwhile a rival Oriental loves her, but decides he is not going to take what another has left. So we have a drama of triple abnegation, sadistically interlocked. The problem, crudely put, is how to pump some passion into it. Let us assume that French actors are helped by the text; they got rhythm. John Cairncross's translation is written in bloodless iambics. Like most English versions it is kinder to confidants who merely advise than to principals, who have to suffer.

The modern setting of Christopher Fettes's production is less offensively facile than the police-state ambience of his Britannicus. Indeed Kandis Cook's set, suggesting an antechamber to a Sartrean Hell, is excellent in its ominous politesse. But the suits and dresses are no help. Mr Fettes is very good at imposing concentration on both his actors and his audience, though the latter seemed to be responding with devotion rather than enjoyment.

Only at the end is there real illumination; Sheila Gish as Berenice, released from the shackles of hope, finds freedom in accepting despair; freedom expressed, as it should be in French tragedy, through restraint. The tension, in all senses, is tremendous.

Pam Gems's Queen Christina (Tricycle) is a superb play, though acted less rigorously than it demands. I hope to return to it next week.
1982-06-01-rodgers-and-hart-film-musical:
Sight & Sound (inc. Monthly Film Bulletin) Summer 1982
Robert Cushman

Writing about the Rodgers and Hart film musicals is probably, I realise as I sit down to it, an impossible task. Their names appear on the credits of more than twenty movies (most were shown in a recent season at the NFT) but there are only a few for which they can be held in any way responsible. On a few they obviously wrote the songs and then got out; on others their work was purchased without the writers getting any nearer to the scene of the crime than their lawyers' office. The output falls into three categories: the film originals, the adaptations from the stage, the biographies. The last consists of a film and a footnote. The footnote is the 1929 short Makers of Melody, in which they pretend to be interviewed about songwriting. Naturally they sound stilted. They reveal nothing except inadvertently-that Rodgers was a better actor than Hart. That is surprising. He is supposed to have been the straight man of the team, offsetting Hart's verbal cynicism with soaring melodies. "Laugh that off, Hart," he snaps at one point, and it's the sharpest timing in the picture. It is certainly unchallenged by the versions of "Manhattan", "The Girl Friend" and "The Blue Room" offered by singers apparently chosen for their vapidity, reinforcing all the worst rumours about the musical theatre of the 1920s. The full bio "Words and Music" (1948) bears a surprising resemblance to "Makers of Melody". Tom Drake has the Rodgers profile, and if Mickey Rooney overacts Hart, then so did Hart. I like Rooney's performance; its manic-depressive extremes tally with what is recorded of Hart's own behaviour; they seem melodramatic only because Hollywood could not mention Hart's homosexuality and had no intention of mentioning his drunkenness. The film has to rely on his self-consciousness about his height or lack of it; this is historical, he did wear elevator shoes, but it's unlikely that his final collapse occurred outside the shop where he generally bought them. The shopfront, incidentally, is part of one of the most uncomfortably stylised sets in movie history. But then the whole film is uncertain in its mix of conventions. When is Tom Drake himself and when is he Rodgers? (Brecht would have boggled at the alienation.) Why does Perry Como, who is supposed to be playing someone called Eddie, suddenly become himself at the end of the picture? Mel Torme, Judy Garland and Gene Kelly appear unambiguously as themselves, singing and dancing in what were then their contemporary styles. Since these styles were forged at least a decade after the material they were meant to be performing, it is no wonder that the picture is coy about chronology. From "Manhattan" (1925) on, all the songs are given the '48 sound. Perhaps MGM thought the public incapable of accepting anything else; perhaps they thought their own style unarguably superior. Probably both. Plus they didn't care.

One shouldn't tease an acknowledged bad film. (Actually I have some affection for it; it was my second introduction after Ella Fitzgerald's Songbook album to Rodgers and Hart, and it taught me some great songs.) But it does contain interesting pointers to the relationship between Rodgers and Hart on the one hand and Hollywood on the other. Though it contains a lengthy, mildly satirical sequence set in Hollywood, it includes none of the songs they actually wrote there; the score is drawn almost entirely from their Broadway output. The film respects this work, but is curiously shy of it. The script trades on the self-pity that Hart transmuted and universalised in his best lyrics; he mutters a few words of "Spring Is Here" ("maybe it's because nobody loves me") or the soundtrack orchestra offers a few bars of "My Funny Valentine"-obviously self dedicated. It's an affecting moment, if you know the lyric. (In the film as originally planned we would all have known it since Betty Garrett would have sung it in an earlier scene.) But these are teasers, unfulfilled in the musical portions. The great masochistic songs-"Spring Is Here", "Glad to Be Unhappy", "It Never Entered My Mind"-go unsung. (They still await respectable film performance.) Ann Sothern's "Where's That Rainbow" ("it is easy to see all right/everything's gonna be all right/be just dandy for everybody but me") is undercut by the arrival of a girls' chorus announcing that they have found that rainbow after all. So that's all right. Unfortunately, this is the only version of the song that most people, especially disc jockeys, have ever heard. "Words and Music" can just about cope with the jolly cynicism of "I Wish I Were in Love Again" or the flip tenderness which is basic Rodgers and Hart-of "Thou Swell", though they cut the first verse. But the shrugged-off pain-the most distinctive thing about the partnership-had to go. Their work was not treated much better when their shows were translated to the screen. Only one, Jumbo, was filmed in the era of respect for stage scores (in 1962, nearly thirty years after its Broadway premiere) and even that was adulterated by the addition of Roger Edens' "Sawdust, Spangles and Dreams". Pal Joey (1957) should have qualified; there was no question of adding additional songs for the movie companies to publish (standard practice before the war). Songs were added, but they were Rodgers and Hart classics from other shows; one can almost see Columbia's point since the score of Pal Joey is probably the most overrated in the history of Broadway. It tries very hard to be tough; and, interestingly enough, succeeds more often in its music than its lyrics. Rodgers was the real muscle of the operation, the survivor, even if his subsequent scores with Oscar Hammerstein veered towards sentimentality. But of course the changes in the Pal Joey film weren't made for aesthetic reasons. The original's special merit is its unity of tone, but since that tone was a dark one it had to be prettied up. Some misanthropy still hung around, and Sinatra's vocals are classics, but it was, like many of its time, a plastic movie.

Earlier R & H films had at any rate made no pretence of respecting the stage material. "Higher and Higher" (1940) was changed almost entirely into a vehicle for the younger Sinatra; "I Married an Angel" (1942) became Macdonald-Eddy fodder. "Babes in Arms" lost all but two of its songs, and "On Your Toes" lost them all: ironically since it had originally been planned as an Astaire-Rogers movie vehicle. (It offends one's sense of symmetry that Astaire, who sang scores by Youmans, Porter, Berlin, Gershwin, Kern, Arlen and Schwartz-all the other Broadway giants-never worked with Rodgers.) Too Many Girls (1940) was a happier event; it retained its Broadway director, George Abbott, and some of his cast; it also kept the collegiate atmosphere that adhered to Rodgers and Hart almost throughout their career: the sense of smart kids growing up by falling in love. Even some of Hart's bawdy managed to creep in. "The Boys from Syracuse" (1940) also got some respect, though "Falling in Love with Love" was dumbly treated as any old romantic song. Actually it's a frustration song. Rodgers offset a bitter-sweet lyric with a magnificent waltz melody. The producers merely heard the lilt and saw the word "love" in the title. Then there are the films that take us back to prehistory: the yacht-set comedies "Heads Up" and "Spring Is Here" (both 1930). These are faithful versions of 20s musical shows from which most of the songs happen to have been lopped off. "Heads Up" is very heavy but "Spring Is Here" is a joy, despite remarkably arbitrary camera set-ups that leave important characters half out of frame. There is a girl with two suitors and a genuinely funny father. There is a kid and sister and her suitor. (They sing "Spring Is Here In Person", not to be confused with.) There is very nearly extra-marital sex. Again the score is butchered (and oddly enough the main interpolation, Harry Warren's "Crying for the Carolines", is scampered through) but a crazy, frothy tone remains. Is it authentic Rodgers and Hart? One thing it lacks, that their best screen originals possessed in abundance, was class conflict. Their first effort, "The Hot Heiress" (1931), features Ben Lyon as an all-American artisan. "Nobody Loves a Riveter but his Mother" he proclaims, more or less in song, and it takes him time to be sure that rich girl Ona Munson is an exception. She proves one of the most persistent heroines in the history of Hollywood, continually changing apartments in the building he works on, so as to bring herself up to his level. This is fantasy at least tinged with reality; Lyon sings, so to speak, on the job. For its time it is, to wrest a line from "Once in a Lifetime," a welcome change from the avalanche of backstage musicals. It isn't coy about song. Maybe this was the studio's or the director's (Clarence Badger) idea, and Rodgers and Hart just went along with it. But they certainly were the moving spirits in their next step.

project: the great "Love Me Tonight" (1932). Their songs preceded the script and they set the tone-elegant, erotic, self-mocking-that is maintained in director Rouben Mamoulian's cascade of visual jokes. How we cheer when Jeanette Macdonald on horseback overtakes Maurice Chevalier on a train. Their rich-girl poor-boy romance is re-enacted, in more sombre tones, by A.J. Olson and Madge Evans in "Hallelujah I'm a Bum", justly famous as the performance, virtually his only film role, of George M. Cohan. I expected a barnstormer; but discovered an impeccably differentiated account of a dual role. Cohan plays a stuffy presidential candidate and his breezy double, a medicine-show man who supplants him in his election campaign, in the affections of Claudette Colbert and- a denouement you don't expect the film to risk-in the White House itself. As political satire it outclasses Gershwin's still-to-be-written "Of Thee I Sing". These three films, with "The Hot Heiress" and "Spring Is Here" as happy additions, are the Rodgers and Hart film masterpieces. All preceded the Hays Office clamp-down, and none would have been permitted after it. By that time the partners had returned to Broadway, writing a dazzling series of songs for mostly unrevivable shows. Their return visits to Hollywood were few and undistinguished but their earlier pictures are durable wholes; far more so than their stage pieces. The catch is that they contain few outstanding individual songs. The one ballad in "The Phantom President", "Give Her a Kiss", is mocked; birds sing it, Disney fashion, while Cohan fails to seduce Colbert. The big number is a convention scene in which Cohan's aide, Jimmy Durante, eggs on a mindless succession of delegations to vote for his boss: a virtuoso piece of shooting by Norman Taurog, the future director of "Words and Music". The score of "Love Me Tonight" is more expansive but equally subordinate to the picture as a whole; "Lover" and "Isn't It Romantic" became famous, but only with much altered lyrics. Only "You Are Too Beautiful" in "Hallelujah I'm a Bum" belongs in the great Rodgers and Hart tradition of serenades to the unattainable. It presents, in Hart's best manner, a closely argued case for suffering. This kind of ballad is what he was best at: his joke songs are often surprisingly clumsy, and the celebrated rhyming dialogue which he used gave the only musical to take serious note of the Depression. J. Olson leads a gang of hoboes living in Central Park, and when he sings "What Do You Want with Money" he seems to mean it. He acts better, with more warmth and more urgency, than in any other film, though you realise why he needed blackface; his natural features are unmemorable. Between these two pictures came "The Phantom President" (1932), the discovery of the NFT season. Its first revelation is in films as a lead-in to song has little more than curiosity value. Rodgers by contrast could write anything. He eventually progressed, with Hammerstein, to the integrated stage musical, a good ten years after pioneering with Hart the integrated film musical.
1982-06-06-judy-billie-co:
Judy, Billie & Co

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'A Star is Torn,' 'Queen Christina' and 'Talley's Folly'

ROBYN ARCHER does impressions. This is denied in the programme-note to her one-woman show, A Star is Torn (Theatre Royal, Stratford East), but the kindest word I can find for that is disingenuous. Miss Archer works hard and skilfully at recreating the sounds of Judy Garland and Billie Holiday. She does not generalise. She marks off the several stages of Garland's progression from the winning child to the driven woman with her voice in a state of terminal vibrato.

She gives us two periods of Holiday: the tragedy queen of the Fifties with her vinegar croak and the delicately barbed swinger, voice flavoured with alcohol but not yet coated, of the Thirties. Her interwoven medley of early Holiday standards is glorious, peaking in a 'Fine Romance' more pointed than the lady's own. (She, unlike Miss Archer, was no satirist.)

Other assumptions are less exact: Helen Morgan comes off too genteel, while Miss Archer loses the melody-line in trying to re-create the baroque edifices that Dinah Washington used to erect upon it. But for each of her ladies she creates a presence. She comes before us springy and white-faced (lighting as much as make-up) and immediately, with a gentle waddle and a pair of outstretched arms ending in upturned palms, she is Bessie Smith, black blues singer--though Miss Archer refreshingly emphasises the rampant bawdy vaudevillean.

She also does a good guttural Piaf. Indeed her mastery, if that's the right word, of differing styles is remarkable. You may guess her range from the fact that she is happiest in music-hall, where she does Marie Lloyd, and in rock, where she out-does Janis Joplin. You may also get the point, if the title hasn't given it away. These are all ladies untimely dead, victim figures, self-destructive. The latter would be the word generally used, but Miss Archer is out to lay the blame somewhere else or everywhere else: on the entertainment business, on audiences, on the male sex.

Marilyn Monroe, we are told, was destroyed by male chauvinism, which denied her talent its proper outlet. 'She could sing, she could dance.' Yes, but so could plenty of others, better. The charge in Monroe's personality and physique was precisely the element that appealed to male chauvinists. Without it she would have been nowhere: better off perhaps, but nowhere.

Miss Archer's thesis seems to be that what her heroines had to sell was vulnerability (wot, Marie Lloyd?) and that reality and fiction became confused, leaving them defenceless. Any kind of vulnerability will do, even vulnerability to traffic. When we were solemnly told, apropos the death in an air-crash of country singer Patsy Cline, about 'the physical reality of fast travel,' I temporarily lost patience with the show.

Wartime morale-builder Jane Froman is dragged in, because she was crippled in an accident, though as Miss Archer more or less admits, she was about as vulnerable a performer as Vera Lynn. I wish she had followed this up. She might have considered Ethel Waters, probably the most influential popular singer of the century, whose childhood exactly paralleled Billie Holiday's, but who survived--at a cost.

The contrast would have been instructive and Miss Archer could have had fun with the songs. (Waters sang everything.) It would have done more justice to her intelligence than handing out cliches about Holiday--'a visceral reality,' 'honey-and-molasses voice,' 'epitome of sex'--at a rate that would shame a sleeve-note, or retelling myths about the death of Bessie Smith (denied entrance to a white hospital) that doubtless should be true, but aren't.

Miss Archer's conspiracy-theories are possibly born out by the fact that the only male vocalist ever to trade on being lost was Frank Sinatra, and he snapped out of it. The doomed male vocalist had to wait for the rock age, though jazz was full of doomed instrumentalists: Parker, Beiderbecke, you name them. She has a case, but she spoils it when she talks--at least in her own voice.

She does a wonderful Joplin monologue ('it's not the having nothing, it's the wanting') that says everything about a performer who was really an artist in self-destruction, having learned from her predecessors who just fell into it. This even admits that Joplin, despite everything, had a better time than most. So did her other heroines; the satisfaction of applause may be transitory (what isn't?), but it is still very nice and they got a lot of it.

So does Miss Archer, deservedly; she is not very moving (you can't be when you sing heartbreak songs that the format forbids you to make your own), but she certainly excites. Her choice of material is admirably un-obvious; and a final medley in which she juggles her idols is sensational.

  

Pam Gems wrote a play about Piaf, and if her Queen Christina (Tricycle) had only sung she too would have made a great Archer subject. Raised as a boy, then placed on the throne of Sweden, she found plenty of reason to be contemptuous of both sexes. Miss Gems, with both logic and variety, shows her trapped but buoyant, bewildered but argumentative, brutal but agonised. She also endows her with wit, though in Chrissie Cotterill's performance this often emerges as bloody-mindedness.

Miss Gems writes heroic roles (in this, if in nothing else, she is John Osborne's successor) and Miss Cotterill, though chirpy and valiant, falls short. Apart from Peter Baldwin, smooth in a bunch of establishment roles, her colleagues amplify her faults. The prevalent note among younger British actors is unfocused sullenness: it distorts harmlessly neutral lines, while denying real anger. Pam Brighton's production is at any rate good-looking.

  

So is Talley's Folly (Lyric, Hammersmith) in Grant Hicks's boat-house set, moodily lit. Lanford Wilson's play is the story of a southern American girl wooed and won in wartime by a Jewish accountant; embodying the clash of cultures and union of personalities are Hayley Mills, strong and graceful, and Jonathan Pryce, fluent, versatile, funny, painful, alive. He starts the play with an ingratiating monologue explicitly designed to charm us. It succeeds. So does everything else.
1982-06-13-enter-the-barbican:
Enter the Barbican

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the RSC's first productions in its new home.

I HAVE nothing to add to other reports on the Barbican complex. It does combine the attractions of airport and subway station; you can get lost following the bright directional arrows. I only want to add that the main entrance reminded me of a Trust House Forte hotel and that so, unfortunately, did the catering in the Waterside Cafe.

The main theatre, though, is a triumph; in the fanned auditorium you are excitingly aware of being part of a large house in contact with both actors and fellow-spectators. I don't know how the stage will take, say, Chekhov; but a proof of its present success is that 10 minutes into the opening production of Henry IV I had forgotten the occasion and was following the play.

Or plays: we get both parts. I have an image of the opening of Part One, derived more from bad dreams than from any particular production. A king sits on a wooden throne, stage centre, flanked by three or four equally wooden courtiers. He looks out-front and talks vaguely about being tired and wanting to go on a crusade: then he looks left and interrogates his cousin Westmoreland about the doings of a host of unseen characters with even less inviting names. It all sounds very historical. A couple of scenes later, if we are lucky, the play begins.

Trevor Nunn's production actually capitalises on the divided nature of that first speech, refusing to slough it off as mere exposition. Patrick Stewart as Henry does the crusading half surrounded by clerics. He is clearly racked by remorse and by compensating religious fervour. Words relating to longed-for domestic peace get the works. Then the scene changes and the king is in the council-chamber, facing rebellion. And so, throughout both plays, it goes: minute exploration of the text and at least one detailed set-up for every scene. Between scenes, too, Mr Nunn is concerned to keep England before us: segments of the population regularly make pilgrimages across the stage, often wearing cowls. Half the country appears to be in orders.

Behind them is John Napier's set, a towering timbered maze. It recalls Nicholas Nickleby, as does much of the production. There are bursts of song; we end with a hymn; there is a manic chase-sequence; actors overpeer scenes in which they do not take part; Falstaff's Shrewsbury recruits look like graduates of Dotheboys Hall; the chorus of Rumour is divided among the company, a line apiece. These are details, but the aim seems to be to involve actors and audience together in the creation of a national panorama.

There is some wonderful small-part playing along the way; actors of the calibre of Bernard Lloyd and Griffith Jones are liable to turn up as sheriffs or carriers, and somebody unnamed makes a character of an ostler who in the text only says 'anon, anon;' and that offstage. Anything in the plays that can reasonably be called Dickensian--the daily life of tavern or stable--is fully realised. But Nickleby was a staged novel and needed our collusion; we had to feel that the actors were, in some sense, making it up as they went along and needed our help. We know who wrote Henry IV.

It is not so much that the detail swamps the plays. Mr Nunn has a firm grip on what Henry IV is about; and he presents with great clarity a struggle in Prince Hal to choose between two fathers, his own and Falstaff. Joss Ackland makes a really fine Sir John, vocally rich, adept at button-holing the audience (the Barbican stage seems fine for this), and increasingly unscrupulous: shocked by the ruthlessness of the age, as exemplified by the treacherous John of Lancaster, but still entering into it. To him belongs the show's one moment of greatness: a laugh after Hal's rejection speech, as if this were one more inexplicable practical joke.

Gerard Murphy's Hal, forever embracing the old man, clearly has a struggle to escape him; he plays the first reconciliation with the king as a partial, angry thing. This presumably is to explain why there has to be a repeat performance in Part II, but it implies a strangely linear view of human affairs; relationships in life double back on themselves and have to be repaired.

Mr Murphy eschews the usual lyrical approach to the 'golden care' speech about the crown; he hammers it, physically and vocally, with an emphasis I associate with players who know, somewhere, that they are doing it wrong. (The whole Bolingbroke clan are prone to hysteria, reaching psychotic levels in Prince John.) Hal's other main antagonism goes for too little, since Timothy Dalton makes an obstinately lightweight Hotspur with no chest-notes.

I am tempted to describe the event as an elaborate frame too sparely filled. But that would be to ignore a host of minor splendours: the cannon-shot that heralds the last fight of Hal and Hotspur; the entire battle, the first one worthy the name in years; the frantic irruptions of Mike Gwilym's pistol-packing Pistol and the insolence of Miles Anderson's Poins; the contrast in tavern scenes, the first rowdy and Hogarthian, the second beautifully contemplative; the revellers in Shallow's orchard all crowded on a single bench; Mr Lloyd's suave Glendower and the interplay of the Percy family; Falstaff's habit of playing to the crowd; three performances by David Lloyd Meredith. This is recognisably our best director working on the most capacious plays in the language. Only by the standards expected of such a collusion is it disappointing.

  

The Barbican's studio theatre, the Pit, is a spruce subterranean gymnasium, where things have commenced with Peter Flannery's Our Friends in the North. Actually the opening line of this is 'there is no beginning,' and certainly there seemed to be no end. This is less a comment on the play's considerable length than on Mr Flannery's purpose to convince us that political life--at local, national and international levels--is an untieable knot of corruption.

The past 15 years are his time-span, London, Newcastle and Rhodesia his foci. There are some character-links, but neither they nor his dialogue are strong enough to hold the strands together. The man probably meant as the protagonist has an unfortunate tendency to merge into the crowd. The actors who do best are George Raistrick as an atypically honourable cop and Jim Broadbent as a great ooze of a businessman.

You have to admire Mr Flannery's tenacity, and he is rarely glib, but his journalistic method (more short scenes than both Henries put together) is too thin to stop comparisons mounting. The publicity cites David Edgar's Destiny, but that play kept surprising itself, whereas you feel that Mr Flannery knew precisely where he was at before he sat down. And then the analogies become wilder. Episodes in Soho pornotopia recall Fings Ain't Wot They Used To Be; the northern featherbedding John Arden's long-ago Workhouse Donkey; police cover-ups the current W.C.P.C.; the conspiracy theories Illuminatus, all fantastic works, but all, in their insobriety, more convincing.
1982-06-20-a-midsummer-night-s-dream-at-:
Ron Daniels’s production of A Midsummer Night’s Dream has come to the Barbican, with all the delights of its Victorian-theatre setting preserved, indeed positively enhanced by the modernity surrounding it. They play begins downbeat, with Mike Gwilym’s Theseus remarkably low-spirited a the idea of his coming marriage. It takes the entire evening for him to cheer up; in the interim we have seen him, in his other persona as Oberon, transformed from jealous avenger to benevolent spirit.

The play’s final promise of peace has rarely carried more weight; nor has Titania’s revolution when released from her spell ever been more strongly conveyed than it is here by Juliet Stevenson. The lovers have relaxed into routine caterwaulings, but the mechanicals are more real than ever. Geoffrey Hutching’s Bottom is obviously a very reliable man to whom to take your weaving; and his frightened singing when Titania first lights on him is a joy. So too is Anthony O’Donnell’s Snug.

You remain in the same world when visiting Jean-Claude Grumberg’s Dreyfus (Hampstead). In a Polish village in 1930 an amateur group are rehearsing a play about France’s foulest hour of anti-Semitism under a writer-director (Tom Wilkinson) whose idealism suffers as many blows from his cast as did Peter Quince’s.

His senior actor (Gary Waldhorn) is a veritable Bottom for his omnivorous ambition, his Dreyfus (Alfred Molina) a Francis Flute for his bashfulness, hating both soldiers and the idea of playing one. Motel the tailor, (Jonathan Lynn) regards the occasion purely as an excuse for costume.

We see their identities changing as they rehearse; Dreyfus becomes military indeed when faced with an incipient pogrom. This struck me as wishful thinking, just as the characters’ wholesale emigration in Germany and ‘freedom’ struck me as easy irony. M. Grumberg, on the evidence of this play and The Workshop, is a slight though well intentioned playwright. But he has a gift for group-humour, splendidly realised in Nancy Meckler’s production by crack cast, among whom Ben Warriss makes a late but welcome dramatic debut as an ancient caretaker.
1982-06-20-peer-gynt-goes-roundabout:
Peer Gynt goes roundabout

ROBERT CUSHMAN in Stratford and London

IBSEN'S Peer Gynt (Other Place, Stratford) may be the supreme example in drama of a tragic theme treated comically. The play is about identity and vocation. Peer grows up as a Norwegian peasant, nourished on fairy-tales and projecting himself into them. After an imaginary fling at reindeer-riding and a real one at bride-rape, he falls among trolls, who are ruled by a ghastly gospel of self-sufficiency: "troll, to thyself be enough" run the traditional translations.

But Peer's own governing principle is never to commit himself to anything. He gets away from the trolls, physically if not mentally, and runs straight into something called the Great Boyg: something whose motto is "go roundabout" and who bequeaths Peer a lifelong habit of evasion.

Sometimes this comes in handy. It enables him, with the help of more yarn-spinning, to bestow on his mother one of the greatest death-scenes ever written. It also helps him get rich: as a slave-trader, typically salving his conscience by exporting missionaries as well.

All through his prosperous middle-age he prates of "being himself"; in Cairo, wandering into an asylum where the lunatics have truly taken over, he finds people who really are themselves suicidally self-obsessed.

In the last act he returns, an old man, to Norway for a brilliant replay of the events of his youth. Finally he faces death in the shape of a Button-Moulder offering neither salvation nor damnation -- Peer has been too half-hearted to deserve either -- but mere melting-down in a ladle. Peer protests that he demands better -- or worse -- but typically he excuses his sins even while proclaiming them. In fact there has only been one real thing in his life: his love for the pious girl Solveig. He once abandoned her through guilt (another case of "going roundabout"); now he returns, this time without excuses. He may yet escape the ladle.

The play is truly a comedy. There is a happy ending, even if provisional; Peer, albeit in peculiar circumstances, gets the girl. There is also unceasing humour. There may be the odd joke in Ibsen's later plays (and there are unceasing echoes of Peer, the fake idealist), but it is almost impossible to believe that the same man wrote them. This piece is buoyant, almost irresponsible, running to gags about a German echo with a Berlin accent and the unlikelihood of the hero's dying halfway through the last act. The ideal translation might be commissioned from Tom Stoppard as wit and Tony Harrison as poet.

The original is written not just in verse, but in rhyme, and I would guess that much of its impact derives from the tension between formal shape and colloquial content. David Rudkin's new version is in prose; so at least the director, Ron Daniels, informed me; there are many times when it sounds like verse.

Peer Gynt wasn't actually written to be performed, and a strange flatness sometimes betrays this. Ibsen claimed that Peer and his mother were fully-rounded characters, and so they are; their relationship is one of the richest ever dramatised. But the people never leap out at you as Shakespeare's or Chekhov's do; they obviously stand for something, even if you are not sure what. Ibsen's satire plays less exuberantly than it reads; it only comes to full theatrical life in the last act, which comes closest to morality play, but which raises the conventions to within sight of King Lear.

So at least it seems in this production, whose necessary starkness is perfectly attuned to Peer's last wanderings, but which makes his picaresque middle-age seem perfunctory. His youth is midway successful. The production is lively and intelligent and the love-scene between Peer and Solveig is breath-taking.

There are good physical reasons for the play's infrequency of production, but I have never understood why actors don't clamour to play a role that combines the attractions of Hamlet, Falstaff and Lear. The curve of Derek Jacobi's performance is that of the production: wily and beguiling at the beginning, rushed in the middle, moving and disturbing at the end.

A small supporting cast ceaselessly multiplies itself. Sinead Cusack has never been more unmistakably a star than in her doubling of Peer's major entanglements. John Carlisle does a majestic funeral orator, Derek Godfrey is an urbane messenger of death, and Robert O'Mahoney offers a delightful sketch of a sheepish bridegroom.

Meanwhile Mr Daniels's production of A Midsummer Night's Dream has come to the Barbican, with all the delights of its Victorian-theatre setting preserved, indeed positively enhanced by the modernity surrounding it. The play begins downbeat, with Mike Gwilym's Theseus remarkably low-spirited at the idea of his coming marriage. It takes the entire evening for him to cheer up; in the interim we have seen him, in his other persona as Oberon, transformed from jealous avenger to benevolent spirit.

The play's final promise of peace has rarely carried more weight; nor has Titania's revulsion when released from her spell ever been more strongly conveyed than it is here by Juliet Stevenson. The lovers have relaxed into routine, alternating caterwaulings, but the mechanicals are more real than ever. Geoffrey Hutchings's Bottom is obviously a very reliable man to whom to take your weaving, and his frightened singing when Titania first lights on him is a joy. So too is Anthony O'Donnell's Snug.

You remain in the same world when visiting Jean-Claude Grumberg's Dreyfus (Hampstead). In a Polish village in 1930 an amateur group are rehearsing a play about France's foulest hour of anti-Semitism, under a writer-director (Tom Wilkinson) whose idealism suffers as many blows from his cast as did Peter Quince's.

His senior actor (Gary Waldhorn) is a veritable Bottom for his conspicuous ambitions, his low cunning; his minor parts are Jewish as their non-professional conditions allow; given judicious editing and strong musical projection, it becomes a production with its own natural nobility.
1982-06-27-the-quixotic-mr-scofield:
The Quixotic Mr Scofield

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Cervantes at the National Theatre.

THE increasingly prevalent view of Paul Scofield is that he is clearly a great actor, but. The reservations have to do with monotony. No actor can so transfix you with his voice; it grows more weirdly sonorous with each new role, and it more or less dictates the content of each new role. Mr Scofield offers us a cracked nobility; only the volume of the cracks varies from play to play. Think of an ideal role for him, and you might well come up with Don Quixote.

So, at the Olivier, enter Don Q. on cue. He is riding a tricycle, a penny-farthing with two small back wheels instead of one. Affixed to the handlebars is the head of his horse, Rozinante; Sancho Panza's donkey, and the play's other steeds, are similarly represented though in appropriately smaller fashion. (The convention works surprisingly well.)

In the second half of Keith Dewhurst's adaptation Mr Scofield has a beautiful, even moving, vision of universal harmony. At other times he incorporates into his delivery a virtuosic number of wheezes which make him difficult to understand, but which do convey the impression of a dear, deluded old man.

Also, of course, a gentle one. It would be unbearable to see Mr Scofield roughed up, and Cervantes's cruelty is accordingly soft-pedalled. The fight with the windmills takes place off-stage; this may well be a technical necessity, but it sets the tone of the production. Even Tony Haygarth, more vulnerable as Sancho, escapes with one hurried tossing in a blanket.

The interplay between the two leads is much the most rewarding feature of the evening; it reminds us of Mr Scofield's skill in comic timing and it allows Mr Haygarth, too, to be gentle. In his brief regime as governor he dispenses justice with the paradoxical panache of Azdak, but with a grief all his own. In comforting his master he draws closer to him, comes to share his madness. Michael Redgrave once nominated Paul Rogers as the only actor who could play both Don Quixote and Sancho Panza. Mr Haygarth is a contender.

The benefits, of course, from the fact that Sancho develops; Mr Scofield suffers from the fact that Quixote doesn't. The play suffers too. Ken Campbell's Illuminatus, Shared Experience's Bleak House, the RSC's Nicholas Nickleby, have all shown us that novels can live on the stage if their plots are respected. They have of course to be respectable plots in the first place. Don Quixote, being a comic epic, hasn't got one, and I don't see how any adaptation could avoid turning into a repetition of one joke.

In the later stages Mr Dewhurst (maybe the only adaptor who ever got as far as Part II of the original) tries to inject modern allusions, but they merely confuse the issue while further slackening its pace. Meanwhile Bill Bryden's production, faced with repeated scenes of rural riot, falls back on bucolic cliche: when in doubt, thwack a chambermaid. He has brought his Cottesloe company with him, but after the considered richness of their work in The Passion and Lark Rise, they are here dismayingly hesitant.

We don't even get period prose clearly delivered; we get the prose, but not the delivery. We also get what used to be the Albion Band, now hispanicised, at least in their headgear, and initially, and excitingly, in their rhythms. But they too grow homogenised, dragging in echoes of protest-rock and what sounded like the theme from Rawhide. William Dudley's set is a flat plain, that sometimes raises a corner flap to suggest Andalusian foothills. I, who have never been to Spain, was convinced, but still wished that it would do something else occasionally.

  

Even less hospitable terrain is explored in Abe Polsky's Devoir the Snow (Bush), an American play based on the experiences of the notoriously unfortunate Donner party who attempted to cross the mountains to California in 1846, and who mostly froze or starved or both. Those who survived had to eat their dead companions, and Mr Polsky's play concerns the trial of one survivor, accused by his companions of having slaughtered his own meal, rather than waiting for it to drop. (Actually he sues them, for slander, but the play comes off as his trial.)

Mr Polsky seems to be asking whether a man in his last extremity is still human; he decides, of course, that he is, but merely having the man mutter "human . . . humano . . . humanum" with desperate conviction does not illuminate the matter much. Nor is the fact that he is German, while his opponents are Americans who may have killed their Indian guides, much more than that: a simple fact.

But it is the facts that make this play thunderously successful, arranged as they are into an infallible courtroom drama on the 1950s pattern of The Caine Mutiny Court Martial and The Andersonville Trial, spotlighting characters, issues and events. If you stop to roll Mr Polsky's dialogue around in your mind, you are liable to find it stilted, but most of the time you will be too involved to care. Simon Stokes's production is as well orchestrated as his previous and very different American venture, The Miss Firecracker Contest: a palpable sense of horrors re-lived hangs over it, not least during the hushed interrogation of a 10-year-old child (Joanna Dukes, quite remarkable). Two performances, in opposite modes, drive the play: Stuart Wilson as the German in whom spitting resentment wars with burning self-hatred, and David Hargreaves, an actor whose excellence only seems to be recognised by this theatre and who finds stirring drama in an upright judge.

  

And so to the Warehouse. No sooner has the RSC turned its back on its experimental pad than Ian Albery, its former landlord, does the place up with mirrors, pink wallpaper, a bar and even comfortable seats with leg-room. All very stylish. So too is Robert Walker's production of Aunt Mary, a play in which Pam Gems seems to be writing under the influence of her son Jonathan, a specialist in the presentation of bizarre life-styles.

Here we have three male transvestites, running a garage and a small theatre while functioning pseudonymously as, according to convention, the 10 leading authors in the country. For all this 'bizarre' may not be the right word; Miss Gems takes her characters as they are, subjecting them to nothing so exploitative as dramatic exploration.

This may be tolerable, but it is also dull; there is the occasional smart line, but the story--involving love, jealousy and marriage, just like any menage--is negligible. The cast seem to know what they are about; Alfred Marks makes a splendid first entrance in a blue frock, looking like the all-time bully of St Trinian's, but his gruffness wears a little thin.

Kings and Clowns

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the new Stratford Lear.

Antony Sher as the Fool: "Playing like Grock while singing like Formby."

AT Stratford there is a new production, dumbfoundingly exciting, of King Lear. It begins with a brief silent flash of Cordelia and the Fool, perched together on Lear's throne, their necks joined playfully by a halter. Or threateningly by a noose.

"And my poor fool is hanged": a vexing line since when it is uttered the Fool has long disappeared from the play and it is Cordelia who has been strangled. Maybe Lear confuses them. He has good reason, since the Fool, who had much pined away since Cordelia went into France, replaced her as his conscience. This relationship between monarch and jester dominates the production, down to the curtain-call and the photographs in the programme.

For much of the time Michael Gambon's Lear plays unruly straight man to Antony Sher's desperate pro. He has after all heard all the routines before and knows where to come in. Mr Sher is a red-nosed tatterdemalion amalgam of all the tramp clowns of the twentieth century. He has a violin which he plays like Grock while singing like Formby: a discordant premonition of the stringed magic that finally, under Cordelia's direction, restores Lear to sanity. His musical jabs enrage Lear, to the point where he has plaintively to remind him ("Whoop, Jug, I love thee") that this is all for his own good. He is literally the power behind the throne--that being his favourite crouching position--and he lets no knife go untwisted.

This performance drives Adrian Noble's production into superb comedy of the grotesque but also into Blakean grandeur. Smoke suffuses the heath while king and fool actually stand atop the storm. The entry of Poor Tom is literally shattering; he comes up from the ground, splitting the floorboards and in one moment hurling the king into madness; Lear's "Hast thou given all to thy daughters" has never sounded funnier or more terrible.

Jonathan Hyde, playing Edgar, is intelligent enough to turn his insanity up a notch when his father appears; and the mock trial in the hovel has unexampled intensity and crazy logic. I really believed that Lear believed that Goneril was a joint-stool.

This of course only gets us to half-time; and Mr Noble's heavy investment in the Fool may be excessive. Theoretically he should hand over to Cordelia, but Alice Krige's performance has insufficient moral and vocal strength. Then there is the small matter of Lear himself. Mr Gambon's performance is fuller of incipient violence than of actual authority, and lacking in any sense of mental adventure. (There is far more tangible progression in David Waller's Gloucester.)

Sometimes Mr Gambon thrills and surprises, as with the curse on Goneril which is that much quicker, more detailed and more vindictive than one expects. He comes near greatness almost at the end; "let's away to prison" is so quietly sensible as to be heart-rending.

I expected much of his death, and I think Mr Noble may have let him down. He has cut Edmund's repentance, thus depriving us of the momentary belief that Lear and Cordelia may survive. The rhythm--in possibly the most highly-wrought scene in English--is disturbed, and Lear seems to have come on too early. Presumably Mr Noble thinks he is making the play tougher.

Now you can play the ending as bleak as you like--he does it very well with a bunched bewildered group of survivors--but it is crass to snuff out the momentary lights of hope before the author does. Hence perhaps the downplaying of Cordelia (the scene describing her "better way" is drowned out by the sound of the French fleet landing), Edgar's dirty tactics in an admittedly rousing duel, and the behaviour of Cornwall's servants who shove the blinded Gloucester while pretending to pity him.

But what distinguishes the blinding from every other Jacobean horror scene is just this: somebody protests. This, perhaps, is why Edward Bond, whose own Lear is being done in tandem at the Other Place, says that Shakespeare was out of date even in his own time. He has also said that the protesting servant could never have happened in a feudal society. But feudalism was not quite totalitarianism (his own speciality); it involved a human bond.

The blinding itself should be as horrible as Mr Noble makes it, with Pete Postlethwaite's Cornwall visibly getting off on it: a fine contrast to David Bradley's gradual awakening from the role of scholarly nincompoop as Albany. Even the smallest roles are individualised, from the rival suitors France and Burgundy down to the very herald and up again to Chris Hunter's cocker-spaniel Oswald. There is a very strong Kent from Malcolm Storry, a white-hot Goneril from Sara Kestelman, and in Jenny Agutter a Regan who projects vindictive gentility.

The whole is encased in an ominous fortress set by Bob Crowley with time-warping costumes. The play makes direct audience contact in a supposedly impossible theatre.

  

Many of the same actors are present in the Bond piece. The Misses Kestelman and Agutter give, with no offence, versions of the same performances; Messrs Bradley and Postlethwaite make themselves very useful. Bob Peck thinks through Lear's journey--from tyrant to madman to pacifist--in far more detail than did Harry Andrews in the original production. All the same Mr Andrews had a stature that persuaded you of the play's own; when he tried at the end to tear down his own great wall it seemed a metaphor for the playwright's own dogged determination to turn Shakespeare to his own ends, conflating characters and incidents like one possessed.

In Barry Kyle's studio production, unfaultable on its own terms, one is aware only of verbal and narrative skill and ingenuity. It is good to have a sharp critique of Stalinism coming from the left; the play has been an important source for many since but it does not now seem, as I have thought it for 10 years, Mr Bond's best. I jib at its ghost character, here played irritatingly fey even when alive, and the whole thing has the tininess of parable; it says, forcefully, what it wants to say but I cannot imagine it occasioning a great performance.

  

At the Cottesloe, Richard Eyre succeeds with The Beggar's Opera by the simple method of playing it as written. Previous directors have thought, "What nice tunes, let's expand them" or "What a suggestive script, let's alter it." Mr Eyre gives us dialogue interrupted, constantly but briefly, by songs, the actors passing unfussed and unchanged from one to the other; it is a technique the modern musical might do well to rediscover.

The second half, when Gay ran out of plot, still seems perfunctory but the louring satire, in a menacing sort-of-Victorian set by John Gunter, is very powerful. More urbanity might have helped; some of the actors, from Harry Towb's Peachum on down, have difficulty with eighteenth-century dialogue. But a Glaswegian accent puts barbs on Paul Jones's acting as Macheath and the dishonour of the Lockit family is firmly upheld by David Ryall and Imelda Staunton, a tiny tornado, momentarily moving. The whole thing reeks of gin and bitterness.

  

Private Dick (Whitehall) is a Raymond Chandler spoof. There is cleverness in writing, production and acting (especially Lee Montague as a bullying cop) but it never comes to life.

Under false pretences

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a new play at the Royal Court

LONDON is suddenly full of impersonators pretending to be something else.

I'll try that again. Obviously all impersonators pretend to be something, or somebody, else. These are pretending that they are not pretending to be somebody else; or at least that they are not pretending to be the somebody else they seem to be pretending to be. Robyn Archer, in A Star is Torn (which is about to move into the West End), reproduces the vocal styles of Billie Holiday and Judy Garland, but says she isn't an impressionist. She could have fooled me. (And she does. Only she doesn't want to. Apparently. Is this clear?)

Now, at the Royal Court, there is a play called Insignificance by Terry Johnson. The scene is a New York hotel-room. I would like you to meet the cast.

First on is Ian McDiarmid as the Professor: small, impish, gentle, with pattering feet and a white moustache. He turns out to have been a refugee from Nazi Germany and to have discovered that e=mc2. If he doesn't look like Einstein, then he looks like the Einstein playing-card from Cluedo. To him enter William Hootkins as a Senator, fat, redneck, Southern, an emissary from HUAC. No dead ringer he, but since every word he utters reeks of McCarthyism, audiences can hardly be blamed for making the identification.

The one lady in the cast is Judy Davis, star of My Brilliant Career, playing another star who is blonde and very beautiful, has a soft dumb-sounding voice but reads Dostoyevsky, and is making a film in which the wind from a man-hole blows her skirt about her legs. (The Seven Year Itch was released in 1955. Mr Johnson says his play takes place in 1953. Maybe he's trying to hang loose. And then Marilyn Monroe was a notoriously unreliable performer whose movies probably took years to shoot.)

Finally there is Larry Lamb, playing a baseball star who claims that his picture has figured in 13 series of bubblegum cards. Since I didn't collect any of them, I have to rely on his being married to Marilyn to know that he is Joe DiMaggio.

Plot. Joe McC summons Albert to a committee hearing, promising roughness if Albert does not co-operate. Albert refuses. Marilyn, tired from a long night's skirt-blowing, takes refuge in Albert's room, and proves to him with the aid of flashlights and toy-trains that she understands the Specific (not the General) Theory of Relativity. She then invites Albert to bed with her. But Joe diM breaks in, angry, as he apparently usually is. Theirs is not a happy marriage, what with his boorishness and her instability. Next morning Joe McC returns and blackmails Albert into handing over his current researches on the shape of Space-Time.

That's all really. You will guess that, apart from an astral touch of the Snoo Wilsons, the play resembles two Tom Stoppards: Jumpers (the professor and the actress) and Travesties (comedy of famous persons). Mr Johnson says, "There are no impersonations in this play. The life of each character is based on a handful of facts . . . those facts are the only resemblance." Come, come now. Actually Mr Stoppard's frankly-named Joyce, Lenin and Tzara are more original creations than Mr Johnson's Professor, Senator, Actress and Ballplayer. Of course the story is fanciful, but its interest derives from the fame or notoriety of the people jumping through its hoops.

So I thought when reading it, after seeing it. But seeing it I had thought different. In performance the people do, by the end, cut loose from their prototypes. Les Waters's sharp production helps and the acting is excellent. Mr McDiarmid, no longer vulpine, has never been better and Miss Davis is very tasty. Besides, there is a theme. The Senator learns a new word every day; in Act One it's "solifluxion" (look it up); in Act Two "solipsism," the belief that only the believer exists. Only the Senator subscribes to this, but they all carry on as if they do, right down to the end, where Albert has a vision--approximately--of the end of the world, while Marilyn keeps right on learning her lines.

This happens to be Mr Stoppard's central theme (that's what I believe, though nobody, including Mr Stoppard, seems to agree with me), but I doubt if he would have been content with only two keywords; he would have used, and illustrated, dozens. Mr Johnson's wit is neither as sharp, as fecund, as integral nor as funny dammit, but it will serve.

  

For a play concerning disarmament (also incidentally the price of fame, but that's no big deal) Insignificance is appropriately disarming. All its characters are allowed a case, and three of them come up likeable; that may not be the sole true end of dramaturgy, but charm isn't exactly rampaging through our theatres at the moment, is it? Mr Johnson is very promising, and if we survive to the end of the year I shall probably vote for him.

I probably shan't vote for Alan Symons, whose first play, Maybe This Time (New End), is a real old-fashioned terrible: a cosy confection set in a marriage-bureau run by two youngish ladies, one divorced, the other with a husband who disapproves of her work and says so, at length and in bed. (Comedy of this order should never have been taught the facts of life; it was far happier as a virgin.) "You promise the world and you don't even deliver Iceland" is about as far as the wit and the indignation go, en route to a tantalising mention of "our friendly neighbourhood bank manager, dear Donald Ingram," which is no way to conduct a conversation or a play; I mean, if Donald is so fascinating, let's meet him. (And ask him to bring Marcia Taylor.)

Mr Symons also fails to write convincingly one end of a telephone conversation but then whoever has. Proof of the unfairness of life is that his play is better acted--at least by four-fifths of its cast--than the presumably more deserving works of Racine, Kleist and Ostrovsky available elsewhere. Judy Carne, the English girl who had everything socked to her on the Rowan and Martin Laugh-In, is very perky.

  

I recently attended the first international festival of Jewish theatre, held in Tel Aviv. I and an Israeli critic spoke on the Anglo-Jewish theatrical experience, undaunted by the fact that no such thing exists. Other seminars were concerned with ritual and tradition; there was little consideration of the work of current Israeli playwrights. They apparently don't have to be Jewish; at least, unlike those in the Diaspora, they are not expected to prove it.

International representation was patchy, partly in protest at the Lebanon war, though since the festival was organised by dissidents (headed by Danny Horovitz, one of the aforementioned playwrights) it seemed an odd target. Britain mainly sent bad fringe, though I was glad to catch up with Seamus Finnegan's James Joyce and the Israelites, a garrulous but enjoyable talk-piece (with Joyce as raisonneur getting rather lost) about the Jews and Irish as lost tribes.

Five years ago I nominated Susan Littler as best new actress for her stolidly distraught young wife in Bedroom Farce. She was a marvellously clear and versatile player, and her death is heartbreaking.
