Telling a tale of two cities

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'Danton's Death' and a new musical.

THERE are very few plays that capture the movement of history. Shakespeare's Coriolanus is one; Büchner's Danton's Death (Olivier) is another.

Büchner is the most notoriously youthful of playwrights; he died in 1837, at the age of 23, with three plays behind him, of which Danton's Death is the first. Its energy and its profligacy with scenes and characters mark it as a young man's play; but it also seems strangely apt as the work of a man two years away from his coffin. This chronicle of what Lady Bracknell called the worst excesses of the French Revolution is as much about death as it is about Danton.

He happened to be in mortal danger when he wrote it: a known subversive with the authorities on his trail. But his was a compressed life, and he had already gone through his agitational phase and come out the other side. Danton's Death is a play desperately critical of revolution, though it cannot be said to be against it. Robespierre's reign of terror, which kills Danton (once the initiator of the September massacres, now of all ironic things a moderate), is a phenomenon: something to be observed.

Büchner was also a medical student who won a doctorate through work on the nervous system of fishes. Organisms, processes, things fascinated him. Danton walks out into the street and scents lechery among the passers-by. "I can't see," he says in Howard Brenton's new adaptation, "why people don't just stand still in the street and laugh in each other's faces." Life brings him to a gaping standstill and, logically enough, he throws it away. Despite the urging of his friends, he doesn't fly or defend himself. He bellows when he comes to trial, but he doesn't expect to get away with it. He just enjoys it. It's his nature.

That is the key to Büchner's Danton. "Men," he says to Robespierre in an earlier translation that has stuck in my mind, "are epicures, coarse or fine. Christ was the finest." Robespierre, the virtuous exterminator, latches on to the same analogy: "He redeemed them with his blood, I redeem them with their own." They are like the tramps in Waiting for Godot, who all their lives compared themselves to Christ. This is the play in which, 100 years ahead of time, historical drama meets the theatre of the absurd.

The sense of teeming, vein-bursting life that the characters express is also present in the action itself, especially in the crowd-scenes, which derive bookishly from Shakespeare (Büchner gives us a clowning lynch-mob out of Julius Caesar), but have a fragmentary identity of their own. Meanwhile we get cameos of the politicians intriguing, orating, surviving.

Danton's Death is many kinds of play and Peter Gill, in his best production yet at the National, makes a fair bid to give us all of them. On a set by Alison Chitty of constantly reforming wooden slabs he transports us from brothel to courtroom to guillotine. Every character is allowed his say, and takes it lucidly; while no director is better than Mr Gill at the instant collection or dispersal of crowds. He gets fine central performances from Brian Cox's Danton, a bull who thinks, and John Normington's Robespierre, a machine who feels.

Below this line there is cause for complaint. Saint-Just and Camille Desmoulins are colourless young men, and Paul Moriarty as Lacroix imports vigour at the cost of treating every scene like a public meeting. Real life stirs in the reminiscences of Frances Viner as Danton's whore, whose philosophy of pleasure parallels his own, and in the suicide (another Caesarean section) of Elizabeth Bell as his wife. Their love is one of the mainsprings of the play. "I in love you," says Danton at the start, "like the grave."

From Paris to Chicago, the Windy City of the new musical at the Victoria Palace. This is based on The Front Page, greatest of American comedies, and is patently the work of men who love their material. For a British show it looks and sounds remarkably authentic. Dick Vosburgh, adapting, has got the flavour of Hecht and MacArthur into his own dialogue ("Duncah," dictates a telephoning reporter, "as in coffee and doughnuts") and I liked what I could hear of his lyrics, especially one called Perfect Casting.

This is sung at scheming editor Walter Burns and ace scribe Hildy Johnson by Hildy's fiancee (here redrawn as a scion of Hollywood nobility) and is about how they two are company and she's a crowd. ("Svengali and Trilby you'll still be, I know.") A number entitled Long Night Again Tonight draws together all the characters who have been scuttling over Carl Toms's magnificent rabbit-warren of a set. (It shifts elegantly from side to side, revealing reporters' room, prison cell, sheriff's office and assorted staircases, plus heavenly glimpses of Chicago's elevated railway.)

Tony Macaulay writes good ensemble-music, though his ballads have the anguished anonymity of current pop. There is one which might as well be billed as Diane Langton's Big Number. She sings it as Mollie Malloy, tart with heart, to Earl Williams, the convicted murderer who is her only friend (and vice versa).

This song is a puzzler. It sounds like love-interest; but, as per the play, none develops. So it merely gets in the way. And that is the show's problem. The Front Page cannot really be enhanced. It could perhaps be changed (as Pygmalion, with fewer alterations in dialogue, was radically changed--romanticised--to become My Fair Lady), but the authors of Windy City love it too much for that. We get the same wonderful blend of farce, melodrama, verismo and social comment, but diluted and slowed down. Pace is the one element that Peter Wood's generally admirable production does not supply.

Dennis Waterman's Hildy lacks daemonism and sings anachronistically, though he looks well. Anton Rodgers's Burns has a Groucho-air (in moustache, delivery, hairline, even walk) that suits Mr Vosburgh's writing (his last show was A Night in the Ukraine) down to the floorboards. Victor Spinetti is funny as the dainty poetaster Bensinger, here supplied with a rollicking pastiche of Hiawatha; and Robert Longden is inspired as Earl, being really and amiably mad. That at least is a creative addition. A larger one, the rewriting of Hildy as a woman, made the movie version His Girl Friday into one of the best films ever. That added romance without sacrificing speed. I wonder.

In Regent's Park, under the stars and the Jumbos, there is a Shaw double-bill, both halves chippings from Shakespeare. The Admirable Bashville is a very jolly blank-verse spoof about a boxer and a lady that might benefit from a firmer sense of parody in the performances. Oscar James, looking like a cannibal, has the manner best. In The Dark Lady of the Sonnets Shakespeare (as Shaw always spelled him) breaks into Queen Elizabeth's court and pleads for increased arts subsidies, a course I recommend to modern intruders. (Start with the Theatre Museum.) He also includes All's Well That Ends Well among his favourite plays. The Barbican production almost proves him right. I shall return to it--on the page, that is--next week.

A Tale that's too comic

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on three RSC productions.

THREE transfers from Stratford to the Barbican. The Winter's Tale got under my guard last year. The first half was plain but intelligible, the second pepped up by Stephen Oliver's tunes--classy Victorian pop. The assorted swains and wenches at the Bohemian sheep-shearing seemed to enjoy dancing to them, and certainly Geoffrey Hutchings's cockney Autolycus enjoyed singing them.

Last week at the Barbican Mr Hutchings was acting his socks off, but his heart seemed to have gone out of the job. It is not too easy to evoke bucolic revelry, or come to that bucolic melancholy, on the bare platform--alternately draped or polished--that is all this production has for a set.

Nor is it very kind to scenes of jealousy back in Sicilia. (Only a matter of time before someone tries a Mafia setting.) Patrick Stewart as Leontes goes through the motions well enough, but there is no sense of his behaviour having thrown his entire court into disarray; not much court, indeed, for him to throw. The actors look isolated, and any effects they bring off they have to manage on their own. Gemma Jones does it briefly in Hermione's trial-scene; Julia Hills as Perdita has some moments, notably her versified seed-catalogue, that suggest a lyrical actress in the making. For the rest, one hardly knows whether the performances are failing to catch fire because of the staging, or vice versa.

The director, Ronald Eyre, takes the play strictly as a comedy, a form dedicated to undermining dignity. At the height of Leontes's transports, his rejected baby cries, causing embarrassment all round; he has outraged nature, and this is nature's revenge. This kind of thing always seems to be happening to him. Antigonus (Robert Eddison, wry and resonant) is henpecked and knows it; his wife (Sheila Hancock) well known as the court scold. Her abrupt re-marriage at the end gets another laugh, but I can't see that the play needs it any more than it gains from having young lover Florizel played aggressively gauche. In a richer production, laughter enhances the pattern; here it makes the play seem shallow.

Trevor Nunn's Chekhovian production of All's Well That Ends Well, by contrast, is crammed with visual detail. No, not crammed; everything here is carefully measured, beautifully disposed. Last year I failed to mention the King of France's red smoking-jacket, the green lampshades that adorn the matching baize tables of his salon, the march-past of the Florentine army, who weave in a series of semi-circles as the spectators change position, the momentary impersonation by one of the Countess's three maids of her humpbacked clown. And who can forget the last waltz as Helena and Bertram enter upon their ill-omened marriage? 'All yet seems well,' says the King, choosing his inflection with care.

Hold on. Everyone knows that Helena and Bertram are ill-matched. That has been the ground of critical dissatisfaction with the play for centuries. Why spend five acts bringing them together? Mr Nunn leaves you wondering. To rationalise my lingering dissatisfaction I must resort to comparison. In 1967 there was an RSC production by John Barton adorned by a dozen fine and forthright performances, crowned by Ian Richardson's Bertram, a searching high-comic portrayal (by an actor slightly too old, which helped) of a desperately insecure young man needing to be saved from himself.

The salvation was, as comedy tends to be, a rough, loving process. But the purgation worked; at the end he and Helena had some chance, the play some point. The choric comments of Brewster Mason's Lafeu, disgusted ('I will buy a son-in-law at a fair') or reconciled ('mine eyes smell onions'), effortlessly brought the house down, teaching me more about classic comedy than any production I have witnessed. It's a hard discipline; Mr Nunn's melancholy (yes, I confess, magical, magical) is easy by comparison.

This has partly to do with lightweight acting: Harriet Walter's tearful, determined Helena (has an actress ever been so autumnal so young?) is fine for the first part of the play, under strength for the second; Philip Franks's Bertram intelligent but blank; Cheryl Campbell's Diana over-eager in her management of the last scene. Interest shifts from youth to age, where the characters are well-meaning but powerless. 'To be young again if we could' becomes the key-line, matchlessly delivered by Peggy Ashcroft's Countess. This is being widely described as Mr Nunn's best production. In terms of mise-en-scene maybe it is; of performance, hardly.

The Twin Rivals have come to the Pit. Mike Gwilym's Benjamin Wouldbe came into the world some 30 minutes' lag of a brother, and spends the piece trying to get even. Mr Gwilym has developed, while few were looking, into the most accomplished comedian in this company. There is usually, even in his Oberon, a malignant base to his humour, a grudge turned outwards. He hugs himself with contagious joy when his schemes go right; comes down to earth with endearing abruptness when they disintegrate. His timing of throwaway lines is a joy, setting the tone for a production that confirms Farquhar as the most approachable of Restoration writers.

Miles Anderson repeats his first-rate account of the virtuous twin, and is now matched by the uncommonly attractive Sarah Berger; a pair of spectacles. (Both, like all the best people, wear glasses.) Another newcomer, Roger Allam, is a very smooth and hypocritical villain. (Watch him: he also does a good bit in All's Well.) John Caird's production is a delight: playful in tone, serious in purpose. Observe the brisk passages of mime, the uproarious duels and the costumes that denote a London consumed by greed, drained of colour except for the kirtle of Miriam Karlin's bawd which is composed entirely of overlapping pockets.
1982-08-08-ghost-of-salonika:
Ghost of Salonika

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a striking new play and revivals of Chekhov and Coward.

DARE I announce a new genre? Meet the retrospective beach-drama. Earlier this year there was Edward Bond's Summer, in which wounds from the Second World War were reopened on an island. Now, strikingly, there is Louise Page's Salonika (Theatre Upstairs), in which the memories stretch to the war before that. They are embodied in a soldier who, before our astonished eyes, rises from beneath the sand.

Mr Bond has taught us not to be afraid of ghosts, and Miss Page handles her apparition with great tact. He may not be a presence at all, merely an embodiment of the thoughts and emotions of four contemporary Britons visiting Salonika 65 years on. (Miss Page breaks this convention only once, when she ill-advisedly has one character remark to another on the strange people you meet in these parts.) If he is a ghost, the other characters treat him with remarkable calm. Calm, with turbulence beneath, is the play's great virtue.

The four survivors are the dead man's wife, now 84; their daughter, a spinster in her sixties; the wife's septuagenarian suitor; and a young beach-bum, who is stretched out sun-bathing when the audience arrives. He might be dead; and images of death recur throughout the evening. It is a subject much on the characters' minds. Even the young man survives by keeping the roll of honour at the local cemetery, supplementing his income by selling his blood.

Mother and daughter have to think of mortality, and it is the mother who is the sprightlier. Daughter, who has had no fun, fears the final injustice of going first. Sheila Burrell, one of our best actresses, conspires with the author to create a fine picture of bottled-up innocence: a mind that at times snaps shut like a handbag, at others reaches out wanly for help.

The frustration issues in unconscious (and very good) jokes. Of the mother: 'We can't put her in a home, there's not enough wrong with her.' To the suitor: 'Stop calling her kitten. She's 84. You might at least call her cat.' The reversal of roles between the two women is a constant source of dramatic energy. Gwen Nelson gives the elder a thin crust of jollity, and Richard Butler hits a note of surface joviality as the man in her life.

The young men of the present and past are excellently played by Garry Cooper and Christopher Fulford; the entrances of the deceased punctuate the play, an image of what the other characters discuss. The remainder of his fate, the bitter comparisons of then and now, overhang the bickerings, jealousies, frustrations and occasional kindnesses that are the play's substance. It is a dark but thoroughly undepressing piece; the best to arrive in London in months. (Cruel, though, to young actors: one has to lie buried in sand, the other to lie still while his naked body is washed all over.)

Directors have tried hard to persuade us that Chekhov can be a laugh a minute, but they have never really succeeded, and it is something of a relief to find Christopher Fettes's production of Uncle Vanya (Haymarket) reverting to the old-fashioned way. There is comedy, rich but short-lived, in Bill Fraser's waffling Waffles (a snorting-heavy instead of the usual wisp) and in some of Donald Sinden's early tirades as Vanya, but this remains a play to weep over, its ending less compromised by optimism than any other Chekhov wrote. When Sonya says 'we shall rest,' she means 'we shall die.'

There are some very fine passages in Mr Fettes's production. The second-act storm, raging, modulating and spending itself beyond the windows. The reconciliation of the two young women, making a ritual out of drinking from the one glass. A protracted moment when Vanya thinks he really has killed the Professor. The end, with Frances de la Tour taking off unforced into Sonya's last speech of hard consolation. Add some of Harry Andrews's laments over his professorial gout, and a general lucidity that finds particular expression in Sheila Gish.

Her Yelena is rather chill and matronly, but she has a clear attitude to every other character and unsparingly shows the lady's helpless distaste in the face of emotion, her own or anybody else's. Mr Sinden, unfamiliarly round-shouldered, crumples at the end into a very moving heap, but is short of the nervous energy that lends meaning to his downfall. (He may never have lived, as he claims, but there should have been a spark of life in him.)

A really crippling defect is that there is no communion between this Vanya and Ronald Pickup's Astrov, the two cultivated men in the district; in the end the same kind of failure. Astrov is said to have 'a fine sensibility,' coarsened. Mr Pickup gets the sensibility, tries too hard for the coarseness, and so misses it. Unhelpful all round are John Murrell's contorted translation and Daphne Dare's set, which looks like an ingenious answer to the problems of doing the play on an open stage. In this proscenium theatre it merely shreds the action.

  

I like a Gershwin tune, and I was happy when Design for Living (Globe) kicked off with a Thirties recording of, appropriately, 'Beginners' Luck.' We then plunged into the relationship of painter Otto, playwright Leo, and late-flowering decorator Gilda, interrupted at, and during, intervals by selections from Cole Porter ('What is This Thing Called Love?' when Gilda left one for the other), Harry Warren ('We're in the Money' when Leo had a hit, 'You're Getting to Be a Habit with Me' when Gilda changed partners again), Billy Hill ('Glory of Love' could have been any time in the mad, mad whirl), Rodgers and Hart ('Manhattan' when the action moved there; a bit obvious if you ask me) and Harold Arlen ('As Long as I Live' when the threesome finally got stuck with one another).

Couldn't we have ended with Coward himself? World Weary to underline their beastliness to everybody else, or I'll Follow My Secret Heart to show their egotism, or I'll See You Again as they inevitably would? I'm showing off; but so do the characters, and so does the play. Even if we grant the stars to be as fascinating as Coward thought them, they are shown to us for at least one whole act too many. They are taken seriously here by Maria Aitken and her two cohorts. Alan Strachan's production doesn't play for laughs. At least I hope it doesn't; it didn't, on the first night, get many, though Miss Aitken fairly timed a very funny line about salmon.

  

At the Cottesloe you may catch a workshop production, previously toured, of The Caucasian Chalk Circle. It's followed by a discussion on the environment, but it isn't that bad. In fact it's very lively, its eight players rising spiritedly to the challenge of improvising their own props while playing multiple roles. Peter Needham is a reduced Azdak, but Patti Love's Grusche is a love.

James Hayes, smirking and dark-glassed as a gubernatorial prince, Greg Hicks as his overbred bureaucrat nephew and Roger Gartland as a stormtrooper are all hissable nasties. Only the music grates; a melange of oversweet pop-styles, including a spot of Country suggesting someone has the wrong Georgia on his mind.
1982-08-15-spectacular-tempest:
Spectacular Tempest

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in Stratford and London.

RON DANIELS'S production of The Tempest (Stratford) begins with a first-rate shipwreck. It is mechanically persuasive, and even allows us to tell the characters apart. They are all rushing about at the sharp end, which juts out at us. Then, with a lightning-flash, it is gone, to be replaced by Derek Jacobi's Prospero, a conductor lowering his baton on a taxing finale. Behind him lies the wreck of another ship; presumably the one on which he came to the island. It looks more impressive than you might guess from the paranoid tale he tells his daughter (the way he talks, it was nothing but a coracle), but, as designed by Maria Bjornson, it makes a splendid unifying setting for the rest of the play.

Like Peter Hall in his National production, Mr Daniels pays rewarding attention to music and spectacle. He too has a master showman at the centre; Mr Jacobi's is a gripping performance on several levels. It takes him as an actor beyond the skilled charm that got him through Benedict and Peer Gynt; there are deeper tones in his voice, more iron in his soul.

Technically commanding, he is psychologically very acute. His Prospero is a man moving from one loneliness to another. His magic powers give him a relationship with Ariel that inspires affection on both sides, but no contact; the desires to have freedom and to bestow it become ambiguous things. For the masque of Juno the bleached boat sports a traverse curtain, much in evidence thereafter and making the analogy of Prospero as magician with Shakespeare as the towering playwright more potent than I have known it.

He stops the show with a passion that encompasses vocational disillusion, and leads logically - i.e. bitterly - into "Our revels now are ended." Magic drains him, and it is a relief to give it up. A risk and a sacrifice as well: Mr Jacobi gives careful emphasis to Prospero's decision to choose "reason" over "fury" and foreswear revenge. "And they shall be themselves," he says of his enemies: for better, but probably for worse.

Mark Rylance's Ariel, as widely advertised, comes on with a quintet of lookalikes: actually a backing group, Ariel and his Full Fathom Five. They help out with music - the sea-dirge has been beautifully set by Stephen Oliver and is as beautifully sung - and with the tricks. They are notably effective manipulating the yapping skeletal dogs that torment the clowns, less so when cluttering the place up striking attitudes.

Bob Peck's Caliban is disappointingly average, though vouchsafed a last ominous appearance. The love scenes are a bit giggly, though Alice Krige is coming on as Miranda. The courtiers are livelier than usual, with the descent into madness of Alonso (Paul Webster) given something of its proper weight. They turn up for the final judging one lord short. Did he ever get off the island?

  

At Stratford's Other Place, Bulgakov, one of the contenders for RSC Top Ryssian (in place of Gorky, retired), is represented by a play called Moliere. This, according to a prologue and a programme note, dramatises the author's own relation with Stalin (his unpredictable fan) as that between Moliere and Louis XIV, who first protects, then abandons, him.

Moliere had a troubled, foreshortened run at the Moscow Arts in 1936, and scenes of the hero's colleagues pressured for information by a hooded inquisition could well be read with reference to the Cheka. Ralph Koltai's set, unusually splendiferous for this space, is dominated by a giant head-and-shoulders of the Sun King; it seems to get more serenely menacing by the moment.

The surroundings seem to demand an audacious central performance, and Anthony Sher, a dusty weakling who snaps his fingers at surprising moments, duly delivers. But there is nothing to him; all the play tells us about Moliere is that he was a thorough professional who, in all circumstances, judged people by how well they could act.

It is, for all the bustle, a shadowy piece; the scenes with Louis come off best, no actor being better at dangerous urbanity than Derek Godfrey. He is well served by Malcolm Storry, David Bradley and especially Albie Woodington as a cobbler kept on hand to arrest people. Joanna Foster is an alluring Mrs Moliere, Chris Hunter fitfully good as an informer who hides in harpsichords. Some other performances lack poise. But Bill Alexander's production is good at back-stage flurry and, if all else fails, plays with pretty costumes are preferable to plays without.

  

One of the Moscow Arts' greater hits, the Cherry Orchard, is at the Round House, en route for the Oxford Playhouse, which has a proscenium stage. That's a problem, since Mike Alfreds's production has to be plonked on a platform at an odd angle to the audience. If he were going to use a set, I think he should have had a proper one, instead of the present arrangement of mingy drapes and ugly furniture. It spoils the considerable if wilful production, which sees the play as a comedy of humours.

The most successful monomaniac is Pam Ferris's fierce German governess (with performing dog); she is helped - though I don't think the play is - by a reversion to the dialogue and scene-order of Chekhov's first draft, which gives her solitude greater prominence. Alison Fiske explodes Ranyevskaya, as Francesca Annis did Natalya in A Month in the Country, presenting, with great integrity, an habitual charmer who turns every situation into a scenario; a trait, inherited by her daughter, reacted against by Varya, who goes to an opposite but equally neurotic extreme. Miss Fiske's performance has a stunning end: she wants to feel for the loss of the orchard; she tries hard; but - unlike her brother, who is really cut up - she can't make it.

John Dicks has the right mixture of intelligence and absurdity for Trofimov, and if Roger Sloman's Lopakhin leaves out too much, what it puts in, in the way of a vulnerable vulgarity, should certainly be there.

  

William Gaskill has correctly said that there is nothing much you can do with She Stoops to Conquer (Lyric, Hammersmith), and similarly there is nothing much you can say about his production. Like a good inn, it is clean, warm, funny and hospitable. Anthony Sharp and Betty Marsden set up the Hardcastles to perfection in the exposition (what a nimble piece of writing, incidentally), and if they have nowhere much to go from there, they still mark time admirably; Miss Marsden does a great Gingoldian take when she hears that 50 is a fashionable age.

Tracy Ullman's Kate is an event; too many half-baked insecure classical performances have recently been extravagantly praised, but she is for real; a trifle milky in her best clothes, but solidly radiant. Karen Archer reflects her glow as Constance, and Hugh Fraser actually gets laughs as Hastings; who would have thought this subsidiary couple had so much blood in them? There have probably been more hilarious Lumpkins and Marlows than Ron Cook and Nigel Terry, but both are believable, Mr Cook's bantam rebellion in particular. The production never stoops; the play conquers.
1982-08-22-exit-mr-miller:
Exit Mr. Miller?

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'Hamlet' and 'Rocket to the Moon.'

JONATHAN MILLER may believe in quitting while he's ahead. That could explain his announcement that after 'Hamlet' at the Warehouse he will direct plays no more. But I'll believe that when I don't see it. We've been here before.

In the meantime this studio 'Hamlet' is a fine production in which all the characters are human beings. Iain Mitchell's Laertes, for example, comes on as a school bully, dragging his sister unceremoniously across the stage with what he must take to be affection. Indeed there is affection -- this Laertes is far from being a scoundrel -- but what he really enjoys is lecturing her.

Kathryn Pogson's Ophelia is just the right target for him, a long, slender, obedient girl with a nervous smile. She is apparently religious -- she wears a crucifix -- and she wants to please. She wants to please her family, though she is hurt and appalled when she has to stand by (a touching innovation) and hear Hamlet's letters to her read to the king and queen; nevertheless she figures daddy must know best.

She wants to please Hamlet, an endeavour that would drive anyone crazy. Most Ophelias turn in good mad-scenes, but Miss Pogson's -- with, I imagine, much clinical help from the director -- is one of the best. The bawdy songs are done with a giggly desire to shock, and all the antics seem native to the character we have seen; we have actually watched her crack in the nunnery scene. Most Hamlets, having read the footnotes, say 'nunnery' as if they meant 'brothel.' Anton Lesser's, who seems to have a highly developed moral sense, is telling her for her own good to get into a convent. He loves her, as one would love the girl in the next castle. Only when he scents eavesdroppers does he go in violently for double meanings, accompanied by physical molestation.

Mr Lesser's Hamlet has been slighted in the press, perhaps because, hewing so closely to the text, it leaves few gaps (known politely as 'interpretation') to be written about. He offers a small, intelligent and desperately young trouble-maker, who does much to re-activate the play as sheer stagecraft. Technically it is by far his best Shakespeare performance; he misfires in attempting to play the closet-scene as a continuous sob, but he is very acute, for example, in the 'rogue and peasant slave' soliloquy, trying to force himself into the postures of a theatrical avenger and giving up with an embarrassed shrug. What a Hamlet most needs is nervous energy judiciously disposed; and with this Mr Lesser is loaded.

One of his best foils is Philip Locke, doubling a quietly agonised Ghost with a long-suffering First Player, professionally pained both by Polonius's inattention and Hamlet's ill-timed notes. Then there is a honeyed politician of a king from John Shrapnel, charming everyone by phrasing blunt statements as tactful questions, moving into tragic gear not only at prayer, but when confronting Laertes's rebellion.

I tip my hat to Alan MacNaughtan's Polonius, Paul Curran's Glasgow gravedigger, Ian McNeice's omnipresent Osric and Susan Engel's Gertrude, who is not helped by a monstrously hooped gown, which makes her look as if she's sitting down even when moving about. (Kandis Cook's other subfusc costumes are admirable as is his subfusc set.)

There is unusual prominence for Ken Stott's Rosencrantz, a bungler, and David Firth's Guildenstern, a smoothie; someone should write a play about them. John Grillo rewardingly adopts the mature scholar approach to Horatio (pioneered by Mr Locke); he is notably polite to the Ghost, and impressively careful when he sums up the bloodshed at the end. Here my one doubt arises. When he speaks of 'accidental judgments, casual slaughters,' he seems to be referring to carnage on a grander scale than anything we have witnessed. Studio-production does, in the end, reduce the play. But it also spotlights it, and rarely more illuminatingly than here.

  

Rocket to the Moon (Hampstead) is an Odets play from the late Thirties: it is summer, it is New York, and it is the Depression; all aspects powerfully summoned in Robin Lefevre's production. A dentist appears to be the central character. David Burke, who plays him magnificently, is one of our best stolid actors: that is to say, as the play goes on, he turns out not to be stolid at all, but a mass of repressed nerves, all displayed without cracking the mould. Annabel Leventon plays his wife, who is tyrannically tolerant. These two performances leave behind them an impression of great weight; they are broad-beamed edifices around which the other characters can swirl.

This play, like so many of its time and place, has wonderfully generous dialogue; it is a treat for actors, and such plays tend to get well performed. This one, anyway, has been intelligently well cast. John Woodvine plays Miss Leventon's rich and unloved father, self-described as 'the American King Lear'; the play has Chekhovian aspirations, and Mr Woodvine, white-suited and manipulatively witty, might indeed have come from a dacha.

Then there is Harold Innocent as another dentist, going gaga from insolvency, and Martin Cochrane as a younger doctor; a cynic, and Peter Kelly as a predatory choreographer who looks and sounds like a gangster. (Costumes, again, excellent, likewise Eileen Diss's glass-panelled office set.)

All these people are trapped because after all this is New York, and the summer, and the Depression; but they don't make as much of a pattern as Odets hoped: God knows, most of it strikes home; this has so much more juice than Arthur Miller's 'The Price,' a late exploration of the same territory. Moment to moment, I loved it. But eventually it crumbles in the mind.

  

Patrick Magee, who died last week, had a provocative tongue. It was he who, on leaving the RSC, said, 'I don't mind being in a kindergarten, but a kindergarten run by the Mafia.'

Mind you, the family cast him in some of his best roles: in 'The Marat-Sade,' 'The Birthday Party' and, of course, 'Endgame.' I was discourteous about his last Beckett performance (in 'That Time' at the Royal Court) and he wrote to me about it. It was a very charming letter; I read it with apprehension, expecting vitriol in the last sentence; but none came. He was a gentleman.
1982-08-29-a-cumquat-from-tokyo:
A cumquat from Tokyo

EDINBURGH FESTIVAL

ROBERT CUSHMAN on companies from Japan, America and Italy.

FOR the first time in over 30 years there is no play at the Assembly Hall. The drama section of the Edinburgh Festival has contracted in size, and what remains is interesting and -- what should please the internationalists -- every last bit of it is foreign.

More foreign than Sankai Juku they do not come. People may carry on like this all the time in Tokyo, but the charge this Japanese dance group brought to Edinburgh was extraordinary. Aghast city fathers glimpsed them from their windows, falling to the ground upside down in very slow motion. At a new official venue in the Assembly Rooms (you lose a hall, you gain a room) they presented Kinkan Shonen, translated as 'The Cumquat Seed.'

I could make nothing of title or translation, but I was entranced -- literally -- by much of the performance, due at Sadler's Wells in London in October. The director-star, Ushio Amagatsu, began by executing a backward fall that looked very much like death; like most of the evening's movement, it supported the programme's claims for the unique subtleness of Japanese hips. The body fell on to a dust-strewn stage.

I thought, as Westerners are prone to do, of Hiroshima; and I thought of it again, much later, when a dwarf appeared: a smiling, bald, swaying midget in a smock. The feet were visible, but no hands and indeed no arms; they might only have been stumps hidden in the folds. The smile looked beneficent, but seemed menacing; the figure made a long progress towards the audience, who sat terrified at what might be revealed. There was bagpipe-music playing -- which I took as an ironic tribute to the host-city -- and the actor seemed to be sobbing. Then the figure retreated to a small ledge, which it tried, unavailingly, to scale; the performer was demonstrating horrifying agility. Then, at last, unbelievably, the figure straightened up and was our star again, full size.

If the programme was to be believed, I had got it all wrong; we were being offered 'the dream of a young boy wondering about the origin of life' and I can just about see how that fits. There is a supporting cast of four, whose heads are shaven and whose faces are often obscured by putty masks; they are much given to undulation. I found their effectiveness varied with the music. Sometimes it was pounding, characterless rock: the kind of music you can't listen to -- I can't anyway -- but which gets you focusing on the actors in sheer self-defence. When it changed to jazz, and to a recognisable tune (Miles Davis's 'All Blues') the spell was broken; one saluted an amazing versatility of limb, but we were in the self-regarding world of modern sculpture: very arty. The last theme was the 'Going Home' bit from the New World Symphony; whether the homewardness or the new-worldliness was the point, I couldn't tell; certainly the peace was shattering.

Co-starring is a peacock, which gets fondled as if about to be made love to or to get its neck broken. But it survives, and is granted its own pool of light, in which it bathes for a while before -- at my visit -- walking off. I have irreverent memories of an off-Broadway revue called 'Scrambled Feet,' whose title-number was about the inadvisability of ever sharing a stage with a duck. For the most part Kinkan Shonen is traumatising theatre; by far the finest performance art -- if that's what it is -- that I have seen.

  

From the Drama Centre at Harvard (headmaster, Robert Brustein) came the American Repertory Theatre in Sganarelle (Lyceum): a programme of four Moliere farces, originally staged at Yale when the director, Andrei Serban, took against Bulgakov's Moliere play, currently visible at Stratford.

Sganarelle was the name Moliere always bestowed on his leading clown-characters. They are not the same character, and were played here by four separate actors. The best was the first, a young harlequin with an air of cheeky innocence, named Thomas Darrah, who in 'The Flying Doctor' appeared as his own imaginary twin, delabouring himself like a one-man Punch and Judy. He was the centrepiece of a fast, airy production that raised spirits and hopes. Slowly they were dashed, as the same slapstick techniques were applied to dissimilar plays. In 'The Forced Marriage' a series of intellectual quacks were lamely parodied as American gurus of 15 years back. In 'The Imaginary Cuckold' the zippy couplets of Albert Bermel's translation were gulped into obscurity, while the actors rushed around disguising the plot. Charm returned with 'A Dumb Show' (based on 'The Doctor In Spite of Himself'), in which the actors spoke jibberish, whose meaning was revealed to us in sub-titles. This was cute; as, potentially, was much of the evening. Maybe I would have surrendered to it more easily if the programme had not described the show's use of traditional shtick as an 'attempt to rediscover the wellsprings of farce itself.' Maybe an academic theatre has to go on like this, but, as a professional company, the ART should just shut up and get on with it.

There was more manifesto theatre from the Cooperativa Teatromusica of Rome, which presented L'Olympiade (Lyceum), described as an opera without music. A 1733 libretto by Metastasio was performed without a note of music (there were, apparently, some 30 settings for the production to reject). We began with silence; this, presumably, was the overture. Then on came Irene Worth to tell us the story. A complicated tangle of lost children and courtly love, like 'Oedipus' crossed with 'The Two Gentlemen of Verona.' Even Italians find it hard to follow, said Miss Worth, who seemed to think the whole thing a bit of a giggle. The audience tended to agree (opera without music, just listen to those words) was, after all, a standby of intimate revue, and the rhythmic repetition of key-phrases is reliably risible. Sandro Sequi's production had some impressive painterly groupings, but it all made for a faint experience.

  

Critics are easily jaded by the Festival fringe; we forget how exciting an experience it is for everyone else. The multiplicity that defeats us turns them on. The most substantial show I saw was Men Should Weep (Moray House), a revival by the Scottish 7:84 Company of a Glasgow Unity Theatre play written just after the war, but set in the Thirties. It is directed by Giles Havergal, and is a fascinating application of the Glasgow Citizens' style to mainstream naturalism.

The set is done in grey sheets; supporting characters become a chorus; Ena Lamont Stewart's Gorbals drama becomes a tenement symphony. The treatment does some harm to the play's flow, but enormously enhances its peak moments, of which there are hundreds. The substance -- resilient suffering women, sexist men -- recalls Juno and the Paycock, and, though that play is funnier, this one is more emotionally truthful. Elizabeth MacLennan heads an enormously good cast.

A Traverse late-night show, Woza Albert!, begins with a really swinging band: trombone, trumpet, guitar and drums are prominent. But there are only two musicians, and they have no instruments. They are two black South African actors, Percy Mtwa and Mbongeni Ngema, who deploy a great range of vocal and physical effects with terrific energy and precision. Their main business is a parable. The Messiah arrives in South Africa and finds himself en route to a white supremacist Calvary. The performers exude all our sympathies, much of our horror, a lot of our admiration; but the script's exploration of its basic idea is dogged rather than inspired.
1982-09-05-churchill-at-the-court:
Churchill at the Court

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'Top Girls.'

Last week Caryl Churchill's Top Girls opened on the Royal Court's main stage, while Louise Page's 'Salonika' ended its run upstairs. For a short time the Court housed the two most interesting new plays of the year, both of them written by women. A chap has to take notice.

Miss Churchill's last play, 'Cloud Nine,' had a complicated time-scheme, simplicity itself compared to what happens in 'Top Girls.' In the first scene Marlene, who has just been made managing director of an employment agency, hosts a dinner-party at a London restaurant called 'La Prima Donna.' Her guests are various historical prima donnas: Isabella Bird, Scots Victorian lady traveller; Lady Nijo, thirteenth-century Japanese courtesan turned Buddhist nun, and also a traveller; Dull Gret, kitchenmaid in armour, centrepiece of a Bruegel painting depicting a female invasion of Hell; Pope Joan; Patient Griselda.

These are all ladies who have suffered. Joan, for example, may have been Pope, but she ended up stoned to death, having ill-advisedly given birth. On the other hand, they are all, in some sense, successes. Even Griselda, as Marlene points out, made it into three best-sellers through the terrible psychological battering she took from her husband.

They all profess devotion to the men in their lives: fathers, emperors, lovers actual or platonic, even husbands. This shocks Marlene; she wants them all as her patron saints, but she can't stomach Griselda, who typically arrives late and will only order cheese and biscuits. At first we share her irritation: after all, she's modern and they're archaic. Then our feelings slide.

Dull Gret doesn't say much. She's the real subversive. She -- if you except an even more silent waitress -- is the only person present not, by birth or adoption, upper class. She is played by Carole Hayman, who appears in the rest of the play as a modern girl similarly disinherited: someone who has dreams but no prospects.

This girl is presented to us as Marlene's niece. The bulk of the play is split between Marlene's London office and her East Anglian roots. The office is revealing, since not only is Marlene a success herself, but she is in the business of sniffing out success in other people, and of mercilessly weeding out failure. The play here goes down intriguing side-turnings, showing us two of Marlene's juniors, both self-consciously tough, and a variety of their clients.

One of them is nervous and middle-ageing, aware of having suppressed her sexuality to survive on men's terms in their world. She is played by Selina Cadell, who has already scored a booming success as Pope Joan. Another is differently androgynous, with salesman fantasies.

Meanwhile there is Marlene's sister, who stayed at home. (Isabella Bird's sister also stayed home, though I confess I failed to pick up this thread at the time.) She points out that Marlene's upward mobility has changed nothing for most women, or indeed most men. Marlene declares herself a Thatcherite, which we might have deduced for ourselves. Her sister's political stance comes as a surprise, and seems manufactured for the occasion.

But the play runs thin nowhere else. Thoroughly personal in tone and structure, it manages to be an amazingly full polygonal presentation of a feminist predicament: career-women behaving like career-men. The situation is (mostly) deplored, but sympathy is withheld from no-one. Miss Churchill also does for overlapping dialogue on stage what Robert Altman has done in the movies.

The seven actresses are terrific. Gwen Taylor, in her third play on socially sundered sisters (she's also played Mrs Thatcher), is Marlene; Lindsay Duncan is gorgeous as Lady Nijo, wrestling simultaneously with the ways of Western woman and her first zabaglione. Max Stafford-Clark directed; I congratulate him, and wonder how he felt at rehearsals.
1982-09-05-lulu-in-new-york:
Lulu in New York

FOR its second production at the Lyceum, the American Repertory Theatre offered Wedekind's Lulu, directed by Lee Breuer and set in New York.

One was less aware of time and place than of technology, though I suppose the production was trying to prove that they are the same thing. The stage was filled with cameras, lights, projections. Lulu danced in silhouette behind a screen. All lines were delivered through hand-mikes, as in an old-fashioned rock musical.

According to Mr Breuer (this paper, last week), this does away with artificial vocal projection. It sounded pretty artificial to me, having the whole play done in a sinister whisper. The actors seemed competent enough, but they were prevented from ever making contact. I liked the looks of Catherine Slade's Lulu, but can make no other comment. It looked to me like a stage version of the 20-year-old Julie Christie film Darling.

This, again, was Concept Theatre, much in vogue in serious America. You buy this concept--it usually boils down to relocation--and it's so dazzling you don't have to worry about character or dialogue or situation. If you don't believe me, read some American criticism. It results in a series of jokes--solemn jokes, what's worse--at the expense of the plays. And, of course, of the audience. There's only one way to build a classic theatre tradition, and that's through acting.

To be fair, Lulu is a concept play; this story of a sexy girl sounds more fun than it is. I left half-way through. In other circumstances I would probably have stayed, but there were hundreds of things to see on the fringe. Many of them are concentrated this year in the Assembly Rooms and the Circuit, both multiple spaces operating round the clock.

The Assembly Rooms offered Mr Breuer in better form with The Gospel at Colonus, Sophocles in black American church, preacher as protagonist, choir and congregation as chorus. This was powerful stuff that brought the play to life, though only in bits; the idea was deposited on stage rather than developed, the story so truncated it was hard to care.

Ben Halley Jr as Oedipus looked, as you would expect of a black man playing blind in dark glasses in a gospel setting, like Ray Charles; fortunately the resemblance was aural as well. He also made a smooth narrator in the companion piece, Sister Susie's Cinema, prettily inconsequential and described as an a capella doo-wop opera. The singing by 14 Karat Soul was much the same in both secular and spiritual settings, which may make a musicological point.

Also singing a capella, and not quite doo-wop, though related, were The Flying Pickets, who obviously want to be the Four Seasons, but are handicapped by being six. Never mind: their rock 'n' roll recreations are awesome, their occasional jokes barbed, and their appearance, especially their hats, superbly delinquent. Even better, slick and chic, were Raving Beauties (Anna Carteret, Barbara Rosenblatt, Sue Jones-Davies), whose In the Pink is a fast compilation of songs and poems, written for, or slanted for women.

Feminist cabaret trios (it's a tough city, even the traffic wardens go round in threes) are a feature this year, and the same songs criss-cross: one staple, "My Heart Belongs to Daddy" another. I heard Angela Holmes do both in Whores and Wars; she's very strong on Brecht, also on "Brother Can You Spare a Dime," which is every bit as good. More soberly, the Cherub Company presented John Spurling's chronicle of the various invasions of South America, Coming Ashore in Guadeloupe, respectable if cerebral. Mary Keegan is a promising actress.

On the Circuit: The Medieval Players, the best-educated company I have seen (they'd have to be, doing all their plays in Middle English) failing to make Gammer Gurton's Needle primarily hilarious, and not helping by doing it in masks. (Concept again.) The National Theatre of Brent, advertising Gotterdammerung but actually offering the entire Ring story with two actors, a pianist and help from the audience: fun except when they turn serious. A cabaret act, Bouncing Cheques, who play another cabaret act entertaining at a Hawaiian honeymoon hotel with hits of the Thirties, Forties and Fifties, spoof and musicality beautifully balanced. They were getting some lyrics wrong, but I put a stop to that.
1982-09-12-caught-in-a-trap:
Caught in a trap

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on plays by Pirandello and Lee Breuer.

THE JOY of Pirandello's The Rules of the Game (Haymarket) is its undeviatingness, its straight-aheadness. It shows one man setting a trap and another falling into it, with no hope of escape. Or one man falling over a trip-wire which another has drawn absolutely taut.

Italy in the Twenties. Wife takes lover. Husband, apparently complaisant, lives downstairs, popping up every now and then to see how they're getting on. Wife is fed up with both men, but husband's imperturbability at least interests her. She wants to smash it. A group of men about the piazza enter her flat, thinking it to be a brothel. Their leader is a famous swordsman. She demands husband challenge him to a duel. He does so; makes lover his second. At the last moment he steps aside, leaving lover to face music.

The fascination of the play is that the husband never seems to do anything. He is a devoted cook, but that is his only activity. The lover, Guido, tries to talk him out of the duel; then, exasperated, makes the conditions more stringent, thereby sealing his own doom. It is unfortunate for the actor that Guido's change of heart takes place offstage. On stage he is just a punching-bag for the married pair. Stephan Chase in this production gives him a dumb conventional decency (one way of explaining his acquiescence at the end), but cannot bring him to life.

Meanwhile Leonard Rossiter is giving a compelling, pained account of cuckolded Leone. He enters his wife's boudoir humble but curious. At the National some years ago Paul Scofield played this character as the all-time lounge-lizard, too lazy to seem dangerous. Mr Rossiter, though in a brown smoking-jacket, is more of an alligator. Obviously he can bite, so it's odd that nobody notices it; strange, too, that people are not alarmed by the permanent sneer in his voice. Mr Rossiter, bending obsequiously backwards, from the waist, lets you feel every moment of his humiliation, and he is in his element when the trap finally closes; but he narrows the play.

Much remains though; and Mel Martin, though running out of steam in the last act, is silkily excellent as the all-round-bored wife, stirred into excitement by the men who want her to dance naked in the square, repressing her feelings, taking them out on the more immediate menfolk. I suppose an Italian actress would be steamier; or maybe that's just a British fantasy.

I never saw the Italian production of this play that came to a World Theatre season in the Sixties, but those who did have apparently never got over it. We are always told that Pirandello is a more passionate playwright than he seems, and he would be a prime candidate for the old National Theatre practice of letting European directors loose on British actors. This play, though funny and ruthless, looks currently a bit prim.

Still, at least its symbolic elements--mainly to do with eggs--are ignorable. Pirandello poked fun at them himself in Six Characters in Search of an Author. (A much inferior play, incidentally, based on the idea that people have difficulty distinguishing between theatre and life; you have to be a playwright, or otherwise deranged, to find that interesting.) Leone, who says that he does his utmost to exist as little as possible, is an alluring figure and very believable: sure as eggs is eggs.

  

Lee Breuer's productions of The Gospel at Colonus and Sister Suzie Cinema, noticed at Edinburgh, are now at Riverside Studios along with a third Breuer opus, A Prelude to Death in Venice. This time Breuer's yeast ferments. The piece is set between two New York phone booths, simultaneously employed by the same character. His name is John and he is a dummy. Literally; his manipulator stands behind him, doing the voice, very occasionally cutting in his own. Obviously he has something to hide. He conducts frantic conversations with girls, family, his agent. He seems to be trying to set up a film or, presumably, Death in Venice. (I bet Visconti didn't have to make his deals on public phones.) The text is littered with jokey references to Aschenbach, and to Mann in general. At the end, John is doing deals with the Devil, reminding the erudite of Doctor Faustus.

This must all sound very pretentious. As a matter of fact it is. It is also elitist as hell, so kindly stop generalising about the fringe, which this, being from Off-Broadway, technically is. But the pretentiousness never gets to you, for the following reasons:

(1) The piece, though not without its seconds of boredom, has the grace to be very short. (2) It is off-the-wall funny and draws, in the way that Sam Shepard is supposed to but rarely does, on multiple facets of American mythology. (I apologise for that phrase.) John wants to address a message to "Mr and Mrs North and South America and all the ships at sea." That was how Walter Winchell used to begin his broadcasts. I felt very smart for getting that. (3) It is very well performed. (4) It is partly owing to (3)--very scary. Phones, especially dime-hungry public phones, have few rivals as images of urban desperation. They're probably frightening in the country as well.

  

Neil Innes (King's Head) is a comic who looks funny. He wears a baseball cap and kimono before the interval, and something else after. He plays four instruments, two of them guitars, and parodies popular songs. This is a stiff task, as ever since Bob Dylan, pop songs have parodied themselves, but he makes it. He does a very good Dylan, using the blind-bluesman-with-mouth-organ image, and intoning a song that contains as much stoned contemptuous self-centredness as the most besotted fan could desire. Sitting at the piano with the Elton John look, he gives out, with Godfrey Daniel, a lament for the death of the lyric:

If all the trees were candles
And who's to say they're not
The earth would be a birthday-cake
And we could eat the lot.

And who's to say they're not? is brill, the ultimate summation of an era. Not everything is as good, but he does a cracking Charles Aznavour impersonation.
1982-09-19-in-love-with-earnest:
In love with 'Earnest'

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN
in London and Exeter.

I always knew the National Theatre production of The Second Mrs Tanqueray would come in useful. Pinero's piece is the best walking example of late-Victorian society drama, the kind of play at which Wilde had three ill-fitting attempts before settling on The Importance of Being Earnest for burlesquing all its conventions.

Last year at the Lyttelton, Aubrey Tanqueray was brought by a long, hard road to recognise the immorality of there being one law for men and another for women. So it's all the more refreshing to find Jack Worthing, on the same stage, reclaiming those same sentiments to the woman he momentarily believes to have borne him.

Insufficient tribute has been paid to Mr Worthing's nobility at this moment; by so enthusiastically embracing a governess as his mother he surely denies himself any hope of gaining his Gwendolen, guarded as she is by the most snobbish of dragons.

The first-night audience often laughed, as one claps the opening bars of a favourite song, before a line. That is the trouble with the play. One falls in love with it, memorises it, and then can never respond spontaneously: except in certain scenes -- the girls' tea-party squabble, most notably -- where the humour is situational, rather than just verbal.

The construction is of course superb: that handbag, for example, which not only successfully satirises farce (an almost impossible achievement), but allows Lady Bracknell to reveal herself, and her class, in their truest colours. Wilde lets his characters condemn themselves out of their own mouths, and for 70 per cent of the time he does it brilliantly. The rest is mechanical inversion, with some scenes, such as the courtship of Algy and Cecily, where the satire runs irredeemably thin.

Peter Hall offers a straightforward production which wins more than it loses. Its prime attraction is Judi Dench's Lady Bracknell: a source at the premiere of quite remarkable tension. Everybody loves Miss Dench; nobody could quite see her in so unsympathetically formidable a role. We waited with bated breath for her solution, and our joy when she revealed it knew no bounds.

Physically, she makes no concessions to gorgondom; she is trim, and immaculately preserved. What terrifies is her vocal manner, which is hard and fast and dismissive. (She talks of Lord Bracknell like Edna Everage discussing her prostrated, prostated, Norm). Really, we were there to hear how she would say 'a handbag'; she does it quietly, as if morally outraged, thoughts on the French Revolution already fermenting. Only the suggestion of marital (i.e. financial) eligibility will soften her; sofas are patted, and room made for the lucky winner. Every laugh Miss Dench gets (and she misses only one, through mis-stressing the line about 'the social habits of Markby, Markby and Markby') enhances her portrayal of a blinkered, therefore all-powerful, woman.

This is probably the best acted Lady Bracknell there has ever been. (Edith Evans's was a Happening.) And somehow, through sheer technical prowess, this uncompromising portrayal floods the auditorium with more warmth than has been generated by any actress since Miss Dench played O'Casey's Juno. But then, we all wanted her to win.

Anna Massey's Prism is perfection, Paul Rogers's Chasuble, with his lolloping walk and eternal puzzled silences, scarcely less so. These (along with the Jeevesian Lane, well done by Brian Kent) are the sure-fire roles, bred from healthy stock and invariably cast with actors who have had time to master the manner. With the youngsters you take more of a chance. Martin Jarvis's Jack is the best here, a predestinate Ernest. He has to leave the sparkle to Algy; Nigel Havers, who promises but does not deliver. Zoe Wanamaker is a fierce Gwendolen, not just a chip but the whole old block, and her idea of passion is beautifully posed, but she sometimes punches too hard. Elizabeth Garvie as Cecily may not punch enough.

John Bury's sets move oddly from real to stylised to in-between; but his geometric arrangement of furniture in the last act allows Sir Peter some satisfyingly calculated grouping. The end is messy, though.

  

Some of what Wilde was lampooning survives in Coward's Bitter Sweet, long unseen but revived at the Northcott, Exeter, prior to a tour. This operetta is really the story of a song: a conceit (both senses) that Coward justified by coming up with 'I'll See You Again.' At the close the young man, to whom our heroine, Sari, has related her sad story of lost love and old cabaret turns, simply says 'what a tune' and rushes off to play it. Art has conquered life, leaving Sari with her memories and another reprise.

I am not sure that this moment compensates for what precedes; much of it flashback. Sari's tale is simple, and wilfully pathetic. Wit has been largely banished, erupting only in odd speciality numbers. The score includes 'Zigeuner' and 'If Love Were All' (the talent-to-amuse one), and many ensembles, the best of them an Act III set of regrets by the married women who were young gels in Act I. But the songs rarely forward the story; nor do they qualify, here, as events in their own right.

The two best performers depart too quickly: Richard Muenz as the hero and Jill Martin as Manon, the humble diseuse for whom life is very rough-and-tumble. Jan Hartley cannot cope with the acting demands of Sari; who is required to stand idly by while her husband virtually commits suicide in a duel and then to throw herself on the corpse sobbing, 'I'll always love you.' What stops you laughing is that Coward obviously believed it.

  

Whenever I am summoned to see dance, because 'it's really theatre,' I assume I am in for something violent. Not so with Pina Bausch's Tanztheater Wuppertal: not, at least, in 1980 (Sadler's Wells). This is described as a Proustian meditation on youth and age. Proustian, as understood in Glasgow: there is a verbal dinner-scene, very spread-out and seductive in the Citizens' manner. Youth and age; well, anything fits into that scheme, some bits more obviously than others.

We get, on the soundtrack, Judy Garland singing to her dog about the land over the rainbow, followed by the audience baying for her in Carnegie Hall 20 years after; certainly a chilling transmutation. But what, in this context, to make of the very funny beauty-contest sequence, with each lady in the multi-national troupe relating her background, or the related bit in which they free-associate on the word 'dinosaur'; or the hauntingly precise hand-jives which regularly accompany their descents into the auditorium to a Twenties dance tune and which I could have watched over and over, and did?

In the four-hour length my attention often wandered, but it did so in the comforting knowledge that it would have something worth contemplating when it returned. I didn't want to leave, least of all at the end. That's what long shows, when they're good, do for you; they give you an alternative world, cosier than the real one. The dancing, when it happens, is superb. The whole thing is like a cross between A Chorus Line and the People Show.

  

More Female Trouble (Drill Hall) is about three women in search of, oh, well, I don't know. They ended up identifying men with thinking and women with feeling. I don't approve of sexual stereotyping, but on their own showing they're 50 per cent right.
1982-09-19-in-love-with-the-national:
In love with the National

ROBERT CUSHMAN talks to Julia McKenzie, who stars in 'Schweyk in the Second World War,' opening at the Olivier this week.

NOBODY doubts that Julia McKenzie is something special. Without her the National Theatre production of 'Guys and Dolls,' in which she plays Miss Adelaide, would be an entirely different proposition.

The director, Richard Eyre, admits that he was at first reluctant to consider her for the role: "Sheer perversity on my part, resisting the idea of the most obvious person being the best." Once she had auditioned--at her own request--there were no more hesitations. Now Eyre directs her again, as Mrs Kopecka in Brecht's 'Schweyk in the Second World War.' He ranks her with Bill Paterson (who plays Schweyk) and Jonathan Pryce: actors who are not satisfied with what could already be a remarkable performance. She says nice things about Eyre too.

"I've only done one Brecht before, so I keep saying, 'What about Brecht's style?'" Richard says, "Forget about the style, just do it." It's a very plain part, not showy like Adelaide: a rather dour, hard-faced innkeeper, who epitomises the Czech people in an occupied situation. The joy's gone out of her, she's dried up, a widow. What gives an extra dimension to her is the music." The play has songs composed by Hanns Eisler.

It's a long musical road from Julia McKenzie's first job, in a touring production of 'Rose Marie' in 1961. She had originally trained for opera, but discovered that it wasn't her voice or her world. She went to the Guildhall School of Music and Drama, though she "had to push them" to let her do the drama.

"'Rose Marie' happened because she was sent to audition for second understudy to the leading lady. At Coventry she had to go on and play the part, with no rehearsal. ('That young, you have the confidence.') The director said afterwards, 'You're going to make a wonderful comedienne'; prophetic, but, at the time, a bit dashing. 'I didn't really wake up till I was 30.'

She did rep, and in the 1960s was in a lot of West End musicals. Some good parts, too: though not many people noticed, since they were usually taken over from other people in the course of the run. She took over from Georgia Brown, for example, in 'Maggie May'; and got to play the blowsy pick-up in 'Promises, Promises,' a small part, but a plum one, and still one of her favourites.

She was also Patricia Routledge's replacement in the first of the Mermaid songwriter revues. That's the way people used to see her: as 'upper-class jaded ladies.' So in 'Cole,' the successor to 'Cowardy Custard,' she got the witty, world-weary Porter songs when she wanted to do the torch-ballads. She puts it down to her tilted nose.

"My face has worked against me. Now I'm growing into it, but I never used to get partners at dances; they all thought I was upper-class. Actually I'm the most suburban person you ever met in your life." (She comes from Enfield in Middlesex.)

She got a chance to play the suburban quality in the cricketing comedy, 'Outside Edge.' She was offered a more glamorous role, but held out for the dedicated player's long-suffering wife, "a cleaning maniac--me, if I hadn't come into this business. Actually it was a great emotional thing in my life to have a cleaner for my own house at all."

I don't know if 'Outside Edge' was a turning-point in Julia McKenzie's career, but it certainly changed my estimate of her. I had decided, after seeing her in Alan Ayckbourn's 'Ten Times Table' (doing what she admits to be 'the Penelope Keith part'), that she wasn't a comedienne. 'Outside Edge' revealed that she was, but that she was an emotional comedienne, one with warmth.

That she could wring your heart had already been proved in her third Mermaid anthology, 'Side by Side by Sondheim.' That was a turning-point; and her slow, dazed, hopeful rendition of 'Broadway Baby' has completely erased the brassy old trouper of that song's original conception. Every girl who auditions for a musical now sings 'Broadway Baby,' and they nearly all sing it like Julia McKenzie.

'Side by Side' took her to Broadway ('I couldn't let myself believe I was singing American material there; getting expenses like Monopoly money'). Between here and there she did the show, for 18 months and was never bored. 'It took me all the time to be equal to the material. Every number was an acting exercise.'

It set her up for her only whacking great big leading part to date, in the glistening spoof operetta 'On the Twentieth Century.' One thing that is not suburban about Julia McKenzie is her voice. It may be the best ever sported by a British musical-comedy lady, and 'Twentieth Century' used all of it. She played a prima donna with the heart of a guttersnipe, and in blending these elements gave the show a warmth to match the style it was granted at birth. You laughed with her.

And so to Adelaide in 'Guys and Dolls,' singing in difficult keys for the proper squawking effect. 'Adelaide's my kind of part. She's suburban; that's why she worries so much what her mother thinks. I know lots of old-fashioned chorus-girls like her.'

It's easy to see why Julia McKenzie and the National love each other. She is the pro who could reassure the actors through a three-day technical ('I told them, "This always happens in a musical"'), while acting with as much honesty and skill as the most dedicated social realist. Eyre says she's a "terribly good touchstone of a production; she never does anything with conviction that she doesn't believe the right thing to do. And because she's so good, people listen to what she says and watch what she's doing."

As for her: "I love it here--I want to do it for the rest of my life. But I think I will have to leave. I get guilty. I think, this isn't acting if you're comfortable. You've got to be uncomfortable."
1982-09-26-the-little-man:
The little man

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Brecht and Kyd at the National.

AS I understand it, the character of the Good Soldier Schweyk is a kind of unholy fool. He doesn't defy authority; he is merely incapable of engaging with it. It can't get on his wavelength either, so for much of the time he eludes it.

I may have got it wrong. Certainly that is not the character who appears in Brecht's updated dramatic version, Schweyk in the Second World War; at least not as played by Bill Paterson at the Olivier. Mr Paterson is a very canny actor. He can knot his limbs into apparently impossible positions, but he can always untie them again, swiftly and gracefully. He treats words in much the same way.

One scene finds him in the Prague railway-yard. An SS man mounts guard over a waggonload of weapons destined for Stalingrad. Schweyk, professing to help him remember the waggon-number, reels off a dizzying assortment of mnemonics, blowing his mind. The weapons roll off back to Germany. Maybe Schweyk, idiotically good-natured, was genuinely trying to help. But Mr Paterson leaves you in no doubt that he is a conscious saboteur. He destroys by clowning.

He is the quickest-witted man in town, covering up for his friends at the Tankard tavern when they say something indiscreet. He may say things that sound treasonable, but he can always explain how innocent they are. Defending himself with proverbs and folk-stories, he runs rings round the enemy. 'I don't know why I listen to you,' says Harry Towb's dazed SS lieutenant, but he has to anyway. There is a golden moment when Schweyk offers to take him outside to explain something; Mr Towb takes a hypnotised step in that direction before controlling himself.

Mr Paterson's performance is the greatest piece of virtuoso comedy yet seen on the South Bank. (Well, maybe Dinsdale Landen in 'Plunder'.) The scene in which he wriggles on his belly, dangling a sausage, to catch the dog demanded of him by the lieutenant, is a classic. The dog rather steals the limelight, though.) It does create a problem, however. Schweyk doesn't deliver the dog; he turns it into a meal for his ever-hungry friend Baloun. He thus forfeits his only protection, and is sent to the front. It's impossible to believe that so expert a nose-cleaner would let this happen.

But Brecht was never much interested in (read, was never much good at) plot. He just wanted a way of moving the action to Russia, and didn't care how. The play has the saving grace of being funny, but it's a very lazy piece of work: far inferior to Jack Pulman's television classic, 'Private Schultz', which it probably influenced.

It starts out with Hitler displaying a surprising interest in 'the little man'; then introduces that man, in the unlikely person of Schweyk, and leaves him to get on with it until it's time to ring down the curtain on a rousing hymn of hope. Along the way, though, Brecht suggested some wonderful stage-pictures, and on these Richard Eyre's production joyously seizes.

William Dudley's set wraps the playing-area, and part of the auditorium, in a frieze of Low cartoons, depicting the war-leaders. Dead centre is Hitler, whose portrait lifts to reveal him in conference with his henchmen. They are outsize human puppets, except for Goebbels, who is minute. (Poor old Goebbels.)

This is all in the text, but it's not usually as well realised as here. Nor has any other production I have seen brought on an eight-foot Hitler to confront Schweyk at the end. Life-size, the encounter makes no sense; here it takes on great symbolic force, Hitlerism, rather than Hitler, lumbering in defeat and finally disappearing down a trap-door.

It is difficult to laugh much at Nazism, easy to be impatient with Brecht's cartooning of it, so Mr Eyre points up the violence. At other times the stage is bathed in pure fun; Schweyk's hat hangs in mid-air, awaiting his return. The sets indeed give as polished a comic display as the actors, which is saying something.

Brian Glover puts real feeling into Baloun's gastric cravings; Imelda Staunton and Kevin Williams are strong in the younger element; and Julia McKenzie deals magically with the Eisler music, even getting a hint of the blues into 'The Song of the Gentle Breeze.' 'I've only got to hear you sing,' says an admirer, 'and I've got to get a grip on myself.'

All the Czechs are played north-country; fascists come from London. Susan Davies's translation, which has Hitler promising 'more order than you would have thought humanly possible,' is excellent.

  

For a story, try next door. At the Cottesloe, Michael Bogdanov has revived Kyd's Spanish Tragedy, excitingly. This pre-Shakespearean bloodbath influenced Hamlet obviously, plus Macbeth, plus King Lear, plus -- you might assume from Mr Bogdanov's unflattering view of the Watch -- Much Ado About Nothing.

It is a multiple revenge-piece, framed by what might seem a dead mechanism. A ghostly nobleman comes on at intervals to plead for retribution on his murderers; he is attended by the spirit of Revenge, sent from hell. Mr Bogdanov's master-stroke is to keep them on stage throughout: the late Don Andrea mutely lamenting while his enemies temporarily prosper; Revenge (a very cool performance by Peter Needham, smoking a cigarillo, hell being a city much like Seville) languidly placing weapons or fatal letters where they are likely to do most harm.

It might not work for a greater play, but it fits Kyd's determinist universe (where death only heralds greater torment) perfectly. Mr Bogdanov even makes a gratuitous sub-plot seem relevant; revenge rules here, as well, and it also inaugurates a spectacular series of executions, requiring only a chair, a steel frame and actors unafraid of hanging upside down.

The main avenger is old Hieronimo, whose son is killed. He hesitates, goes mad, finally produces a play in which he kills four people. (One of them seems innocent; maybe Kyd thought he'd made him a villain: a pardonable lapse in the circumstances.) Michael Bryant is not a tearer of cats, and his insanity sounds more like sarcasm, but his wit, his determination and his stoicism are unchallengeable.

The rest include a spruce Machiavel from Greg Hicks, a sturdy double (General and Hangman) from James Hayes, and a king from Nicholas Selby as authoritative as the 17 or so other lordlings he has played for this company. Patti Love, confronted with some taxingly regular verse, sometimes sounds as if she is spelling the words rather than saying them, and there are some rough-edged performances further down the cast.

In a posh Olivier production they might be fatal, but here they do no serious harm. The cast and the audience are with the play; Mr Bogdanov's interpolated joke delights, and leaves the tension quite unimpaired.

  

Miss Margarida's Way (Hampstead), hailing from Brazil via New York, is a monologue for a teacher. It is obvious after 10 minutes that she is a crazy lady, but the author, Roberto Athayde, continues with his parable of authority none the less. If we are not bored it is because Estelle Parsons plays her with consummate timing and great attack (don't be late, or she'll make you regret it) and because, while her claim that 'everyone wants to be Miss Margarida' may not be true, everyone has had a teacher who resembled her.
1982-10-03-musical-cartoons:
Musical cartoons

MUSIC

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'Andy Capp,' 'The Paranormalist' and 'Mass Appeal.'

MOST British musicals of the past few years have been imitation Broadway. There are worse things to be. But there is a native tradition, and Andy Capp (Aldwych) revives it.

Everyone knows that the Andy of Reg Smythe's comic-strip is a drunken, pigeon-fancying, football-playing layabout who treats women abominably and whom his creator never even upbraids for his misdeeds.

Critics in what I would call the new Salad Days tradition ('oh look at me, oh look at me, oh look at me, I'm progressive') rushed last week to condemn him as atypical of the chivalrous, temperate, politically aware north-countrymen they presumably know at first hand. I hope they will be consistent about this, and never say a word in favour of Sir John Falstaff.

The behaviour of both derides the sober, responsible virtues to which we are all supposed to aspire. Falstaff charms and insults Mistress Quickly just as Andy does his Flo, though Andy, being married, does it more aggressively.

Mr Smythe's Andy always wore his cap right down over his eyes, while Tom Courtenay on stage wears his pulled right up. There are sound practical reasons for this: a musical-comedy hero has to see where he is going, or he might trip over the massed ensemble, and an audience that pays to see Mr Courtenay doesn't want vital bits obscured.

Besides being less blinkered than we might have expected, he is softer-centred. He has to cope with unprecedented problems: criticism and (though not quite on the Falstaffian scale) rejection. Flo leaves him, and he has to go for days without changing his socks or -- as far as we can tell -- eating. He does try cooking toast (in a saucepan), but it's beyond him.

All this is only symptomatic of the one great new factor in Andy's life: plot. When funnies turn into musicals the protagonists lose their mythic immobility. They have to act and be acted upon; they develop. Andy Capp delays this process as long as he decently can. The story doesn't start until the last line of the first act.

Before that we have been taken round Andy's milieu: home, pub, streets between. We have watched, in instructive counterpoint, the ladies (an admirably grim and un-uniform chorus line) at work in the factory and the gents getting changed for soccer. A lot of our time has been spent on, or with, Alan Price.

Mr Price is a problem, twice. He wrote the music, and collaborated on the lyrics with Trevor Peacock, who wrote the book. He also narrates and comments, mainly from the piano, though there are attempts -- vain and wasteful, since he isn't an actor -- to make him part of the action. These merely give the show more framework than it needs, like Amadeus.

Then there is the music. It's good to have Mr Price's own singing; he's the most talented musician in British pop, and has been for nearly 20 years. His composing is best here when it is least like itself: in a Formbyish item, 'I Ought to Be Ashamed of Myself,' for Andy to demonstrate how he gets everyone eating out of his hand while he drinks out of their pockets, or in a couple of extended nursery rhymes, one about rolling home at night plastered, the other about waking up next morning.
