But his production numbers, in jazz-tinged rock, get in the way of the words while supplying little impact of their own.

Andy has a neighbour who, under his wife's thumb, never says a word. He then acquires some money, finds his voice (he actually says 'bollocks to my wife,' which amuses the ladies in the audience no end), buys drinks all round and bursts into song. The actor, Robert Vahey, has pleased us so much that we want him to stop the show, but the material Mr Price gives him is so fussy he doesn't have a chance.

So, structurally and musically, the piece falters. But there is still plenty to enjoy. Mr Courtenay proves himself a consummate singing actor, never losing continuity as he passes from one mode to another and full of shy cunning. Val McLane as Flo heads the bold, beautiful and wholly convincing female brigade.

Michael Mueller is charmingly gormless as a young bridegroom who goes everywhere in a hesitant rush. There are some knockdown comic lines, not all of which can be Mr Smythe's. Braham Murray's staging, with Johanna Bryant's tabloid sets and Sue Lefton's jauntily utilitarian choreography, is the best he has done for a musical.

  

In the title-role of The Paranormalist (Greenwich) Denholm Elliott levitates, which is something the Living Theatre tried and failed for years to accomplish. Later on he performs an exorcism on his middle-aged daughter, who is played by Angela Thorne. She, and two admirers, then join in singing 'The Song is Ended,' though according to Miss Thorne's daughter, played by Catherine Hall, they're singing it wrong.

Thus corrected they try again, and the melody lingers on as the lights fade. It's an effective close, and stirring too; if a 1982 teenager can enlighten her elders on the harmonies of a 1927 Irving Berlin tune there is hope for the world. Compare the pessimism of Howard Barker's 'The Hang of the Gaol,' in which 'Moonlight Becomes You' was mis-titled and attributed to a non-existent composer.

For an exorcism you need devils; and Jonathan Gems fills his characters with them. Miss Thorne is a late-starting psychiatrist who keeps threatening to put Mr Elliott into an old-people's home. (For those of us who grew up on Mr Elliott as a juvenile this is very disturbing.) Her lovers are a television producer (Christopher Godwin) and an American academic (Stephen Creit). Her daughter is a tease who inveighs against education and society until she learns she's got her A-levels.

Mr Gems makes the erotic and professional torments credible (most erotic torments are) and all the actors are good, though Mr Elliott, being comparatively on the side of the angels, has less to work with than the others. He gets fine writing where the others get wit. Moment to moment Mr Gems seems in command -- he even writes good old-fashioned curtain-lines -- but this play, more elegant than his 'Naked Robots,' but less lively, has also to be written down as promising.

  

It's better on religion, though, than Bill C. Davis's Mass Appeal (Lyric, Hammersmith), which is the standard young rebel and nice old conformist play given Catholic trappings and an ameliorative ending (also standard). It shows that what Broadway takes for serious remains unchanged (though this piece, sadly, originated off-Broadway at the well-thought-of Manhattan Theatre Club), despite the fashionable focus having changed from disability to faith. Our unbelief is not helped by the casting of Gordon Jackson; though we keep telling ourselves there's no reason why a New York priest shouldn't be a Scots immigrant, he makes the colloquialisms seem very self-conscious.

The Tom Allen Centre (round the corner from the Theatre Royal, Stratford East) has commenced operations with Fuente Ovejuna, by Lope de Vega, a play much written of, but seldom seen. It depicts a Spanish village defeating a local tyrant by collective action and -- though the performance and Steve Gooch's demotic adaptation are a bit sheepish about this -- royal intervention. Otherwise both are very lively; I doubt, indeed, that Mr Gooch has ever written better. Last performance is tonight.
1982-10-17-faraway-places:
Faraway places

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a Pinter triple bill

The Cottesloe offers Other Places, an assortment of brief pieces by Harold Pinter. The first, already seen as a platform performance and heard on the radio, though not by me, is called Family Voices.

It is an exchange of letters, though we may doubt if they ever were exchanged. Ever reached the mailbox. A mother writes to, or of, her son who has left home and whom she misses. She becomes more and more distraught as the play proceeds, increasingly possessive. He tells of his experiences in a lodging-house whose proprietress, also possessive, is called Mrs Withers. (Note to scholars: in the decisive television production of Mr Pinter's The Birthday Party the smothering landlady was played by Margery Withers.)

Another resident is an older man who tries to seduce the son. Mother, coincidentally, fears--or says she fears--that he is being used as a male prostitute. Actually it is his burgeoning heterosexuality that seems to disturb her. Meanwhile his adopted household assert their claim over the boy by giving him a nickname. They call him Bobo. (The tyrant in Alan Ayckbourn's intriguing Way Upstream uses a similar tactic.)

On second thoughts, I believe the letters were sent, and that the correspondents merely carry on as if they hadn't received them.

There is a third voice, belonging to father. He is apparently dead. Mother says memorably that he died 'in lamentation and oath' and blames it on the boy. He says he's looking for his dad, and blames her for the disappearance. Anyway, from the grave or wherever he is, he speaks. A speaker at a theatre conference in Tel Aviv this year described Mr Pinter as a writer presenting Jewish themes (mainly to do with suffocating families) in Gentile settings. Family Voices can be read in this way.

Victoria Station, by contrast, takes him back to his roots, or at least to his revue sketches. A minicab controller tries to send a driver on a job, but the driver seems in a daze. Finally he vouchsafes that he has fallen in love with his current fare. The controller, at first bloodthirstily furious, succumbs to envious rapture. In my experience, conversation on cabbies' airwaves is rarely so expansive, being ritually punctuated by calls of 'roger' or just 'rog,' but Mr Pinter substitutes his own conventions.

The closer, A Kind of Alaska, is a departure for Mr Pinter as Footfalls was for Samuel Beckett. Once again we are presented with a character in a world of her own, but we are given medical evidence for her condition documented in the programme. She is a victim of sleeping sickness, rescued after 29 years by the invention of L-dopa. We watch her awakening. She displays unlikely fluency, pinpointing all the memories that the playwright needs in order to evoke her lost world, but he plays cunningly with the limits of her awareness. Her last words are 'I think I have the matter in proportion,' but she has actually misplaced one vital part of the information she has been given.

As interesting--more interesting, though kept on too tight a rein--are the reactions of her doctor and her sister: 'It is we who have suffered.' They are married. The sister calls herself a 'widow,' since the doctor has given his life to his patient. Isn't it unlikely that she would wax insistently metaphorical at such a time? Is it a metaphor? Isn't there enough in the play about the borderline of life and death already? And if it's mystification, who needs it?

The reality of the situation brings out unusual compassion in Mr Pinter. Judi Dench's performance, an adolescent's consciousness in a woman's body, is magnificent (and her first efforts to walk a brilliant pairing-down of clinical reality); she really is total theatre. Paul Rogers as the doctor is as fine, though his cab-commandant is too stolid to keep the second play alive. (It starts funny but when the laughs are withdrawn nothing replaces them.) Nigel Havers, Anna Massey and Martin Jarvis divide the other roles, expertly.

Peter Hall's direction is supremely tasteful, everything exact, nothing overdone and certainly nothing overlit. I resented it. The Hall-Pinter treatment puts the audience in a false position, awed by the intransigence of it all.

At the opposite extreme of expansiveness the Glasgow Citizens' Theatre has espoused weekly rep. (I thought critics were the only people left doing weekly rep.) O'Casey is playing now to be succeeded by de Sade, Goethe (you heard) and Brecht. They commenced with Massinger's The Roman Actor, a Jacobean piece about a decadent Roman emperor (a gift for them, and played with quivering effectiveness by Robert Gwilym) and his entourage of parasites, whores and players: the latter the only admirable people around and given, paradoxically but naturally, the least mannered performances; Ciaran Hinds made of the title role a very upright and well-spoken juvenile. The empress who tries to seduce him was flamingly done by Elsa O'Toole; one of the many witty touches in Philip Prowse's production is her treatment of despised former queens, put to work with mops. Supposedly virtuous senators were contemptuously treated, one with a speech impediment ('It is in vain to stwive against the towwent'). They died horribly, with power-drills twisted in their guts, drawing ketchup in vast quantities: an ingenious realisation of Massinger's do-your-own-thing stage direction which is 'they torment 'em.'
1982-10-24-play-it-again-bobby:
PLAY IT AGAIN, BOBBY...

ROBERT CUSHMAN calls for a revival of cabaret

AT THE moment London seems to have a jumping cabaret scene. I'm thinking especially about singers. They're raising their voices again in restaurants: at Langan's Brasserie, for example, where the emphasis has been on the more cute or flippant songs of the Thirties. Even the old tradition of the thé dansant has been revived; a lady will warble to you, with Palm Court backing, over scones and cream cakes in the Waldorf Hotel.

The leading jazz places, the Pizza Express in Dean Street and the still-new Canteen in Covent Garden, sometimes put on singers, even devoting special evenings to the work of particular lyricists or composers. And of course, for years now, London's premier jazz joint, Ronnie Scott's, has presented star vocalists from Ella Fitzgerald down.

All the same, for singers and those who want to hear them, it can still be an uphill struggle. After all, people go to jazz clubs primarily to hear instrumentalists, and to restaurants primarily to eat. In a huge and popular place like Langan's, the combined clamour of knives, forks and conversation could drown any soloist. For singers of Porter, Coward, Sondheim -- singers who want you to hear the words -- these are not the right places. What we need is what they have in New York: supper-clubs.

Every so often somebody tries to start one. Country Cousin's in farthest Chelsea made an attempt, but it failed to pay. Quaglino's, which had the tradition from before the war, also went dark after a period of grovelling to the coach-parties like a small-scale Talk of the Town (which has gone, too). The Playboy Club had a few tries. Mabel Mercer, the doyenne of city singers (English-born Paris-bred, New York-based), the lady who taught them all, including Frank Sinatra, played there in triumph, and was followed by Bricktop, the legendary Paris-American hostess who taught even her.

The singers were accommodated in a ground-floor room with a view of Hyde Park; too elongated for proper audience contact but still pleasant. But the Playboy then showed just how we go wrong by putting Bobby Short, the reigning male singer-pianist, into a deafening subterranean disco, to the mystification of its regular dancing public, and the frustration of his own fans.

Thankfully, amends have been made these past two weeks with a highly successful season of Mr Short, in the far more sympathetic ambiance of the Pizza on the Park, which has an elegant piano room in its basement. Short's stamping ground back in New York is the Carlyle Hotel -- and ideally hotels are the places, especially if they can steel themselves a) to provide an intimate room, b) to keep the catering simple and c) to admit listeners for the price of a drink.

This formula is currently being proved at the Algonquin Hotel in New York, a place much frequented by actors and Englishmen, where they have installed Steve Ross, a young man with a clear, high baritone, a whimsical face, and a standing repertoire of 200 songs, many of them little-known and often hilarious show numbers. (This kind of singer inhabits a rarefied but rewarding limbo between jazz and the theatre.)

Ross recently made his London debut, to much applause, at the Carlton Tower Hotel: a ritzy one-night stand. They are thinking of asking him back. If they don't, some other establishment should, arranging for others to follow him. The thing will never work on a one-off basis.

There are American artists we should see, and British ones we should encourage. The material is too vast, and too rich, to be neglected. And it has nothing to do with the present vogue for nostalgia. Nostalgia is about liking a song because it's old. In cabaret, you like it because it's good.
1982-11-01-art-is-a-meaningless-word:
Art Is a Meaningless Word

Most theatre reviewers, I imagine, have been browsing through Diana Rigg’s book No Turn Unstoned if only to find some extracts from their own work. We have to browse because the index lists only the victims of the worst reviews ever, not the perpetrators. That really is the actor’s revenge.

The reaction of most of us, I think, will be that we never knew we were so nice. Do these amiable squibs really represent the worst havoc we have wrought on the egos of the distinguished players who replied to Miss Rigg’s questionnaire? They’re jokes; taken as such, frequently written as such. Quite often they are neutral, if amused, comments on the fix in which some poor performer has been placed by his author or director. They do not strike at the core of anybody’s talent. They can be laughed at, laughed with, laughed off. They will not provoke angry letters. You only, in my experience, get those when you have told a central, unwelcome truth. It doesn’t happen often.

The art of the showpiece bad review—as practised by Shaw, Tynan or Walter Kerr—seems to be dead. Bernard Levin tried to revive it in his period on the Sunday Times but how much more spontaneously vitriolic he seemed on the Mail or Express of the fifties. But the scene was different then. The commercial theatre was still thriving, so its worst products could be attacked with a clear conscience. They stood for something. Now, who cares? I used to enjoy myself writing elaborate demolitions, generally of misbegotten musicals, in this magazine. God, I was funny then. But it would seem perverse to give Fire Angel or Barnardo the lion’s share of a 1200 word piece in The Observer when there are worthy products of the subsidised theatre to be examined. Of course worthiness in itself is only a minor virtue, and may cloak major vices. That’s in theory. In practice, the National and the RSC have drawn some of our stings. Their offerings have a nasty habit of being at least technically sound. As demolitionists we are out of practise. Peter O’Toole’s Macbeth was, by general consent, the most notable of recent debacles, but how much truly sparkling prose did it elicit? Rapiers are rusting. Bludgeons are clumsy. Is there anything worse than the critic who, to show how uncompromising he is, goes on making the same negative point in every sentence of his review? There are critics who like dancing on graves in hobnail boots. But it’s themselves they condemn.

I believe that I now write best about things I like. For me the acid test comes on Sunday when I see the column in print. It reveals—perhaps to my eyes only—the differences between what I’ve really enjoyed and what I only thought I enjoyed. Too late then of course to do anything about it. I can only make good resolutions for the coming weeks, resolutions I almost invariably break.

A certain amount of self-deception goes on. Years ago, before I was doing this kind of thing for a living, I wrote in these pages that though no critic would turn black into white (‘integrity feels so much nicer’) every critic must often have juggled with the various shades of grey at his disposal, so as to come up with a shaped coherent account of a play which may have inspired no strong feelings in him either way. (Critics who claim to be passionate about everything are phonies.) But, where it matters, critics are usually honest, not because they are knights-errant but because they cannot function any other way. The typewriter keys freeze beneath the fingers of a liar (not always, unfortunately, beneath those of a fool). As I say, we may deceive ourselves, but we are truthful with you. We do not perjure ourselves for the sake of a good joke, because good jokes are born of conviction. They have always been made by the best critics. I suppose bad jokes are indefensible but I would suspect a critic who did not at least try to be amusing. I would wonder why he was wasting his time on two such frivolous areas as journalism and the theatre.

Our absence from Miss Rigg’s index is probably symbolic. Individual friendships may flourish between the professions but really they don’t think we count. They think we’re too kind. A critic who takes an actress to the theatre is in for a humbling experience. She will be more withering about the pathetic efforts of the people up there then he would ever dream of being, discussing them with the kind of scorn he reserves for talking about other critics. She went to a drama school that taught her the importance of Truth; those clowns on stage had obviously never been told about it and wouldn’t have had the taste to profit by it if they had. Meanwhile playwrights roam the streets in gangs, ready to mug any reporter who says a word in favour of some other mob. They seem to want us to adopt them (and most ungrateful children they’d prove). The constant cry of the professional is ‘you don’t mean you liked that’. The Brecht industry shows this in its most rarefied form: not its purest, since it allows academics to join in. It’s all fascinating; and I have to admit to feeling pleased when I find the professional opinion tallies with my own. But that’s a weakness in me. Professional opinion is immaterial. Actors aren’t audience. Theatre for actors (or, as it is known in a few remaining outposts, lunchtime theatre) is a sterile exercise. We might all just as well stay home and play charades.

Those who’ve actually been involved in whatever show is under inspection are likely to find the review irrelevant: not wrong, irrelevant. My own professional theatre experience has been minuscule—half-a-dozen shows directed, mostly ages ago, two appeared in—but it’s greater than any other critic’s so I may as well sound off about it. What it’s taught me is that there can be no reconciliation between those who live with a show for weeks and those who live with it for a couple of hours. Moments that have been lovingly prepared or elaborately despaired of are likely to pass by the assessors quite unnoticed. They rarely like what you think they should like, and they are unperturbed by what you expect them to hate. Reading the reviews, even when they’re favourable, is like getting a bucket of water in the face. Suddenly you are looking at the show from an angle you never knew existed. And then the angles multiply; an actor I worked with told me he could read all the reviews of a show, find them contradicting each other, and understand and sympathise with the reactions expressed in all of them. That’s unusually philosophical but I have something of the experience when I read my colleagues. A good reviewer is one who persuades you while you’re reading him that his is the only possible view of a play. The ones I respect are those who make me momentarily doubt my own judgement. (The opposite of that is the critic you dread agreeing with.)

Now you would think that the public, who also are only with the play for a few hours, would be closer to the critics than they are to the practitioners but this may not be so. For the spectator, as for the participant, the show is a special event; it bulks larger for him than it does for the reviewer who goes to the theatre four times a week. (That’s my own average, and incidentally the answer to the question I am most frequently asked.) The spectator has also paid money: a sobering fact that critics should bear in mind more often than they do. He may well be more attentive than the reviewer who only needs to get enough of the play to furnish him with copy, he will be more demanding, and also more tolerant. One common critical fault—I’ve often committed it—is to point out weaknesses and inconsistencies that will have no effect whatever on anyone’s enjoyment of the show. (We strain over implausibilities in new plays that we would swallow whole in a classic.) Our job is not primarily to pass judgement on a text or even on a performance but to take the temperature of a theatrical event and try to account for it. Many events are simple: we arrive, they perform, we applaud, they bow, we leave. But there can be complicating factors: audience expectations or suspicions of a particular actor, play or subject, the laughter of discovery, the confirmation of boredom, the draughts or heatwaves, the unacknowledged conventions. (People always enjoy songs in plays, because they put a stop to that endless dialogue. They are critical of songs in musicals, because they are meant to be the point of the evening. Folk-songs mean moral uplift and are greeted with suspicion except by devotees.) These are what I most like writing about, and I should do it more often.

Art is a meaningless word, employed to give false authority to personal preferences. There are just shows, enjoyable or insufferable. That is the one critically useful thing that working in the theatre can teach you. The customer is always right. Since the theatre is a collaborative form, it’s also theoretically useful to know who does what, but even then you can’t always tell from out front. A really scrupulous critic would probably never even mention a director. Directors, for this reason, often get an easy ride from critics; so, most of the time, do actors. The ones who really suffer are playwrights. There is no known way of reviewing a play without referring to its author. There was once a critic who was invited to rehearsals, and came away impressed by how hard everybody worked and how arbitrary was the convention of the first night; but let us assume that whatever their faults most reviewers are ordinarily sensitive people who can work this out for themselves.

I now want to contradict myself and assert that critics are quite close to audiences after all. Ralph Richardson, quoted in Miss Rigg’s book, gives me the cue. He says that all spectators worth their ticket-stubs criticise the show when they get home. This reassured me since I was once dashed by what seemed an unanswerable criticism of critics by William Gaskill. He said that we always got the theatre wrong because we were concerned with judging it while the right thing to do was just to experience it. (‘What else can they do?’ he asked, sympathetically but unforgivingly. ‘They are critics.’) But I now believe, fortified by Sir Ralph, that this audience which experiences without evaluating is a sentimental myth. As soon as you have seen more than two shows you begin comparing. I bet Mr Gaskill himself judges unmercifully.

Another myth is that of the lost, scorned masterpiece. I doubt if a play has ever been produced that somebody didn’t champion. Look at the list of approved martyr-works. Saint’s Day? JC Trewin, not usually an avant-guardian, included it in his ‘Plays of the Year’. Serjeant Musgrave’s Dance? Philip Hope-Wallace loved it. Afore Night Come? Tynan called it a work of genius. The Birthday Party? Harold Hobson will never let us forget. Now of course these were all minority voices. But that’s fair enough. These plays were all, when they appeared, minority tastes. The mass of the public—even of regular theatregoers—would have been bored by them, and there’s no point whatever in boring people. The critical majority prevented this happening; the minority insured that the plays would stay around to be revived when tastes had changed. Meanwhile the reviews acted as a barometer of public reaction: a considerable sociological service. The strength of our pluralistic situation is that every shade of response to a given show is likely to be represented somewhere in the reviews. This has nothing to do with the competence of reviewers. It’s merely a vindication of the law of averages.

I’m not consistent about this. I snarl when other critics praise a show I despise or when audiences flock to it. I sulk when something I have praised bites the dust. But really I have no right. I have had the chance to state my own opinion. I should take it, as vigorously as possible, and then shut up. The play has to make its own way—as it inevitably will, acquiring in the public mind a ‘critical reputation’ that may have little to do with what the reviewers actually said. Our effect on the commercial fortunes of plays is infinitely variable. We do have power, and it’s good for our souls that we should be aware of it, but we never know how much, and that’s probably good for us too. We can inflict pain; the knowledge should not inhibit us but it should not be spared us either. And perhaps the best thing to be said for the critic-as-practitioner is not that he can learn something but that he can add a little to the universe’s stock of cosmic fairness by getting shot at himself.

Readers, by the way, treat critics as cavalierly as critics treat theatricals. I have been accused of favouring the fringe, of favouring the establishment; of always raving or damning, of always sitting on the fence; of being solemn, of being flip, of being American. I have been asked, regularly, whether my first responsibility is to the theatre or to my paper and have still not figured out where the conflict is supposed to come in. I have comforted myself, when told that critics know nothing about acting, with the reflection that most actors know even less about journalism.

All a critic really needs—and it cannot be manufactured—is a temperament. Without it he may, in Lionel Trilling’s valuable terminology, be sincere but he will not be authentic. His only real subject is himself. But he’d better forget that while he’s actually writing. Critics who keep telling you who they are don’t trust themselves to be anybody. We should be able to convey our enthusiasms by describing the shows: bold admonitions like ‘a triumph—rush for seats’ are a cop-out like appending ‘recommended’ or the reverse to a review Time Out fashion.

Critics should, preferably, be able to write. And they should, undoubtedly, have standards. I want the theatre to make me laugh, cry, tap my feet or hold my breath. I think that covers everything.
1982-11-07-a-case-of-nuts:
A case of Nuts

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Glasgow.

I CAN'T think of much to say about Nuts (Whitehall). It is an American court-room drama, obeying most of the American court-room dramatic rules, though with a few twists. The setting is the Bellevue mental hospital. A call girl has been accused of the manslaughter of one of her clients; everybody except she and her attorney is trying to prove that she is insane.

A psychiatrist, as is customary (cf. The Caine Mutiny novel, play or film), has his testimony rubbished by counsel for the defence, who is young, aggressive and Jewish. (Only bland Gentile lawyers are ever allowed to appear for the State. This looks like discrimination and somebody should investigate it.) Usually in such circumstances defence wants to prove its client mad; here of course it's the opposite.

Later the heroine's stepfather is forced to admit that he molested her somewhat in her youth. This helps to explain why she is disturbed, though I thought we were trying to prove that she wasn't. Anyway, the matter--and the feminist point--once established, both are dropped.

She herself takes the stand in Act II and demonstrates that, lucid or not, she is one hell of an actress. She has given indications of this earlier on with well-timed dismissive interjections about everyone present. Anne Twomey takes full advantage. I did not believe in her--she is too like the sardonic sufferer of a dozen social-conscience movies--but I enjoyed her.

On its own terms, Tom Topor's play succeeds. Its jokes made me laugh. The tension, when the judge decides whether or not the lady is fit to stand criminal trial, is effective. But the form is restrictive, and the content largely unexplored.

  

The Young Vic is engaged in a season of plays about Venice. They have omitted Volpone (and, come to that, The Gondoliers), but the two obvious Shakespeares are there, and there has been a brave, and surprisingly successful, resurrection of Byron's Marino Faliero. Promised for last is Otway's Venice Preserv'd and I look forward to it, hoping it will atone for the current production at the Almeida.

Otway's play, like Byron's, concerns a plot against a corrupt Senate, undertaken by conspirators whose noble motives are tarnished by social or sexual pique. Otway has far less sense of place than Byron, for whom the glamorous, already decaying, Venice outweighed everything else. But he sees far more incisively into character and has the advantage, writing in 1682, of a blank-verse tradition not yet demoralised by Shakespearean blackmail. Byron's, like all the plays of the Romantics, is a book of quotations. Otway's protagonists are heavily indebted to Brutus and Cassius, but his language is darkly and unselfconsciously his own.

At the Almeida most of it is moaned or mumbled. Plainly Tim Albery intended a neurotic, nihilistic, battened-down production; the set suggests a ruined ballroom with clouded mirrors on the wall, chandeliers on the floor and pillars that come in for a lot of heavy petting from the actors. Costumes are early twentieth-century; the general atmosphere is rise-of-Mussolini.

Two actors alternate the star turns of Jaffeir and Pierre at successive performances; two actresses deal similarly with the leading ladies, and also share the subsidiary male roles. There are, as you might expect, some suggestive quick changes, as when Helen Cooper (Wednesday's casting) switches from Antonio, the masochistic senator, to Belvidera, who also enjoys suffering. But there should be more to her than that; more even to Antonio. He pays to be ill-treated; but he can pay, so he can threaten as well. As written, the scenes are scurrilously funny; here they are monochrome.

If Mr Albery had cut the play down to an hour, his treatment might work. To give the full text with so little variety is to induce screaming boredom. Andrew Wilde's Jaffeir is a sickly public schoolboy, Jonathan Moore's Pierre a tone-deaf lout. Johanna Kirby gets some flavour into the courtesan Aquilina.

Jaffeir threatens his wife with a dagger in one hand, and the other up her skirt; but even this blend of cruelty and eroticism has no shock value in a production that is down on the characters from the start. An interpretation for our time, perhaps, but even our time doesn't have to be that ungenerous.

  

There are so many hints here of the Glasgow Citizens' style that I flew to the fountainhead with foreboding. Goethe's Torquato Tasso was the play; the tribute of one (by us) neglected poet to another even more so. The decor is again 1920s: 150 years after Goethe, 350 after Tasso.

We start with two ladies taking champagne on top of a giant haystack; beneath them is a flock of plainly artificial sheep. A flunky presses a switch and a loudspeaker emits equally artificial bleats. Later the rural crops get swathed in some of the Citizens' regulation dust-sheets. Michael Levine's set, richly and satirically decorative, is well up to Glasgow scratch.

As usual, the initial effect is relentlessly jokey; Robert David Macdonald's translation is fuller than ever of tags from other writers. As usual, the jokeyness gradually becomes transparent, a way of getting us into the play.

The subject is the tragic vanity of princes and poets. Tasso presents his masterpiece to his patron, the Prince of Ferrara; he senses slights everywhere and is also hopelessly in love with the prince's sister. If the hero recalls Moliere's Misanthrope, the technique--suffering endured with decorum, exacerbated by it, and finally shattering it--recalls Racine. But the play is more powerful than any Racine I have seen. Mr Macdonald gives the play an English form that is probably inexact, but allows you to apprehend the original, without ever denying its tantalising remoteness. Self-consciousness is the name of the game, but it is also what the play is about.

As director, he gets some of the best acting I have seen at this theatre: Dikran Tulaine, brittle and explosive as Tasso; Peter Rumney, stiff and benignly blinkered as the Prince; Ciaran Hinds, smooth and unswerving as the politician who is the poet's chosen enemy. The women, as generally happens here, are closer to caricature, but vigorous: Kate Ingram a suffering over-bred princess; Jill Spurrier a jealous go-between.

The original Tasso wrote accomplished pastorals, and Goethe here reactivated the genre. This production reminds us what a powerful and attractive form it can be.

The Bouncing Czecks (King's Head) remind us of the enduring comicality of some oldish songs, and some older jokes. They also do some funny original numbers. Their assumed personae--an overweening act at a dreadful Hawaiian holiday resort--break down into Sharon Campbell, pretty and ingratiating; Brian Bowles, in a zoot suit until briefly dragged up as a hapless Forces Favourite with a Rose Murphy falsetto; and Richard Lee, the prime mover, who implants Frankie Howerd grimaces on a countenance that is definitely Albert Finney.
1982-11-14-play-of-the-book:
Play of the book

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a successful adaptation of Evelyn Waugh.

I DON'T want all plays to be based on novels. I don't even want most plays to be based on novels. But such adaptations have provided some of the finest theatrical evenings of the last few years, the latest being Shared Experience's version of A Handful of Dust at the Lyric, Hammersmith. It has been depressing to find this production, a full two years after Nicholas Nickleby exploded at the Aldwych and with the television version now going full blast, greeted with the same old objections.

The original reviews of Nickleby were the most disgraceful I have ever read. Obviously they were not as vituperative as Clement Scott on Ghosts or the daily prints of 1958 on The Birthday Party. But for those writers there was much excuse; they were reflecting public distaste or bewilderment, and were actually helping the plays to become embattled legends. Where would minority art be without the philistines?

But what happened at Nickleby, not least on the first night, was public acceptance and public joy. The flow of feeling from stage to auditorium and back was as near to being an objective fact as anything in the theatre can be. By ignoring it, or wishing it away, or pettishly denying its right to exist because it carried the wrong identity card, theatre critics were committing the ultimate trahison des clercs. And they're still at it.

A Handful of Dust has not the same scale or intensity, Waugh being in every way a smaller writer than Dickens. But there is a moment at the end, when Tony Last realises he is trapped forever by Mr Todd, when the same kind of fusion takes place. The audience gasps, then smiles; gasps at the cruelty, smiles at the elegance both of the thing itself and of its congruence with all that has gone before.

Of course you can get this from reading the book, but that is hardly an argument against enjoying it in the theatre as well. And of course the comedy translates superbly from page to stage. Most of us, when we read something that makes us laugh, want to share the joke, and this is one of the basic instincts informing Shared Experience. It is overwhelmingly sound. (I assume you would rather laugh in company than alone. I mean, what are you, some kind of pervert?)

And the purists are terribly inconsistent. Nobody objects to novels being turned into films. Come to that, no theatre critics objected to Fanshen or The Ragged Trousered Philanthropists deriving from books. Presumably their political credentials got them through. And nobody has jumped on Brecht for adapting The Good Soldier Schweik or the authors of Guys and Dolls for resorting to Runyon. It must be who you know.

Shared Experience are their own kind of purists. They employ no adaptors, use no additional dialogue. Every word in their four-part Bleak House was by Dickens; who, neatly enough, supplies the only words in A Handful of Dust that are not Waugh's. (When Tony starts reading the complete works to Mr Todd, you half expect the company to begin acting them out.)

Ten actors, grey-suited or grey-gowned, appear before a panelled set, to Ilona Sekacz's haunting distillation of 1930s cocktail music. There is less instantaneous doubling than there was in Bleak House, and the characterisations are necessarily slenderer, but they are as precise and enjoyable as ever. Sam Dale, who has a small moustache, hardly impersonates the exasperating child John Andrew, but he so precisely captures his rhythm that it is a jolt to find him playing adults later on.

Alison Steadman has a high time with the self-dramatising Jenny Abdul Akbar, Philip Voss's unassuming Todd is doom itself, James Smith is fuzzily upstanding as Jock, whose conscientious inquisitiveness about pigs is a charming running gag, and Nick Dunning is all calculating precocity as Beaver, the extra man who becomes the other man. These and other cameos surround John Price's full-length portrait of Tony; aptly named Last, emerging innocent and constrained, from his Gothic pile to be hacked down by savages before he even reaches the jungle.

The actors speak narrative as well as dialogue; the third-person convention is worrying for two minutes, acceptable and enriching thereafter. The production may be too prodigal with group mime; we could listen happily to Mr Tendril's sermon without seeing his congregation. But such devices pay off in, for example, the staging of the hunt. An earlier school of adaptation would have left this offstage, which may be what brought adaptation into disrepute; we were merely offered chunks of conversation, often in paraphrase, which were called scenes.

The new theatrical form is fluent, inclusive, and contrapuntal. It is also faithful to its author's style. This version is fast, but never rushed. It represents another triumph for Mike Alfreds, who is known by most people in the theatre, and by a faithful audience, to be among our best directors, but whom few critics seem disposed to recognise.

  

Ducking Out (Greenwich) is a heavily punning title, referring both to avoidance tactics for dealing with life (you act nice like a Christian, bend your energies to constructing a crib, and, when it all gets too much, have a stroke) and for a Christmas bird favoured by those who don't like turkey. It has been furnished by Mike Stott for a comedy by Eduardo de Filippo, whose scene he has transferred to Lancashire.

The origins keep breaking through; the obsessive Catholicism or a family quarrel in which the antagonists pick knives from the table keep turning our thoughts back to Naples. In its own right, though, Mr Stott's adaptation is skilful and funny, and it never sentimentalises. Indeed, by coming closer to us, it hits harder as what looks like a charming, if barbed, family comedy turns steadily grimmer, its protagonist ending up bedridden, misunderstood and misunderstanding.

It is the kind of finale Alan Ayckbourn sometimes strives for, but brought off with less obvious effort. Warren Mitchell in the leading role has a northern accent far gentler and subtler than southerners generally attempt, and his whole characterisation flowers from it. In Mike Ockrent's production he is excellently supported by wife (Gillian Barge), daughter (Diane Bull) and a large, obstreperous contingent of family and friends.

  

It has been said that Kevin Elyot's Coming Clean (Bush), about the break-up of a homosexual marriage, would not have been produced had it been--as it could easily be--heterosexual. This may well be the case; but actually a hetero play on, or with, these lines would be quite acceptably entertaining until betrayed set in and the words turned weepy, and the same is true of this gay version.

There is a very good performance of an acerbic American writer-academic by Philip Donaghy, an aptly twitchy account of his spouse by Eamon Boland, and admirable work from C. J. Allen as a compulsive cruiser (the only camp one) and Ian McMurrach as The Threat, an unemployed actor written and played with obvious conviction.
1982-11-21-playtime:
Playtime

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

In style and subject Tom Stoppard's The Real Thing is distressingly like other people's plays. Its central character is a playwright called Henry. There is some neat juggling (including one well-contrived surprise) with the plays he writes and the play we are watching.

Henry bears a considerable resemblance to what we know or surmise--from statements, interviews and his previous plays--of Mr Stoppard himself. He even re-cycles some of his own past reviews; Henry's teenage daughter accuses him of getting good notices by writing the kind of plays his critics would write if only they could write. Somebody said that about Jumpers.

Henry has a big success with a play that seems the kind Mr Stoppard would be expected to write if he ever wrote about middle-class adultery. It's full of structural puns (the hero is an architect whose model tumbles when his marriage does, the play being called House of Cards) and cuckoldry is greeted with fluent, if embittered, wit.

The Real Thing is the play Mr Stoppard does write about middle-class adultery. The actor who has played Henry's protagonist loses his own wife--to Henry--and he behaves very differently. He doesn't joke; he breaks down and sobs. Later on Henry has to cope with infidelity from the same source, and he doesn't find it funny either. We have been with Henry now for about three hours and his despair is no more moving--less, in fact--than that of his predecessor whom we hardly know.

Henry combines a set of characteristically Stoppardian attitudes: a belief in love coupled with a diffidence about expressing it, a distaste for strident political attitudinising calling itself drama, a liking for unpretentious popular music. Specimens of the latter--from Rodgers and Hart's I Wish I Were in Love Again to the Righteous Brothers' You've Lost That Loving Feeling--link the scenes, with the implication that they say more about love than most playwrights.

I wouldn't quarrel with that. But it may not be the point. Henry seems meant to win through--to rise above jealousy--and in doing so to prove that his author can create real characters, although people (including, on occasion, himself) have said he can't. If he doesn't bring it off, well, that just proves that the heart's a mystery. It's double bluff.

Actually, he has shown himself perfectly capable of handling people and passions, when required. Why does he mess around with drawing-room naturalism, with its unnaturally and unsparingly fluent characters? Henry's daughter criticises her dad's long speeches, and then embarks on an indistinguishable tirade herself.

The best speech in the play is of a different order: Henry's defence (using a cricket bat--a public private joke--as analogy) of literary craftsmanship against raw polemic. His wife Annie puts up spirited counter-arguments, mainly in the cause of Brodie, an imprisoned demonstrator who has written a bad play out of his own experience.

She has an affair with the actor who plays Brodie's spokesman, having previously played opposite him in Ford's incest tragedy, 'Tis Pity She's a Whore, in Glasgow. We see bits of both plays. This unwieldy structure operates so that Henry may be jealous. The various themes are successively switched on and off; in vintage Stoppard they would be combined, explosively, in a joke.

The two best jokes here are purely decorative. Felicity Kendal does everything asked of Annie, but though she explains herself at some length, she is never believable. Roger Rees is more visibly at sea as Henry, worrying at lines that could probably stand some attack. Polly Adams and Jeremy Clyde are briefly, too briefly, helpful as their discarded partners. Peter Wood directs, in handsomely framed sets by Carl Toms.

I began making my own private jokes. Miss Kendal played another Annie in The Norman Conquests, and she actually played Ford's Annabella for the Actors' Company, though I can't see her doing it in Glasgow. Henry retreads some of the same aesthetic arguments advanced by his namesake in Travesties. It occurred to me that if he applied his professional standards to his favourite Neil Sedaka ("Oh, Carol, I am but a fool/darling, I love you, though you treat me cruel") he would be in trouble and I wondered why Annie, a classical music buff, didn't point this out. Feeling really elitist now, I mused if having Annie emphatically docket Ford as Elizabethan, not Jacobean, when he was actually Caroline, was an unreachably subtle dramatic point or just an astonishing lapse on the part of a literate playwright, a class cast, and an associate director of the National Theatre.

  

I share enough of Henry's tastes to feel fairly confident of his reaction to the week's other shows. He would not like either Peter Sheridan's Diary of a Hunger Strike (Roundhouse) or Caryl Phillips's Strange Fruit (Factory, Paddington). The former holds the attention as a documentary account of life and death in the Maze, though it skimps on clinical detail. It is fair enough to state most defiantly its own positions while leaving you in little doubt at its own. But it does so woodenly, and the actors act accordingly. It's a play for people who feel virtuous for sitting through something about Northern Ireland. Pam Brighton directs for Hull Truck, though the company has now only a subsidy and a touring-circuit in common with the one run by Mike Bradwell.

Strange Fruit likewise deals with real dilemmas, of black British allegiance; surrounding characters hint that the author may have some doubts about his mouthpiece, but he lets him go on talking regardless. The length is hardly justified by the writing, the direction, the acting, or the seating.

  

On the other hand I think Henry would enjoy Yakity Yak (Half Moon), despite its defiantly dispensable script. It's an anthology musical of the Fifties songs of Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller, previously collated by Ned Sherrin in Only in America. I preferred Mr Sherrin's selection to Robert Walker's, and Mr Walker hasn't a performer to match Bertice Reading, but his production is far superior in street-wisdom and bluesy energy, exactly the qualities which distinguish the songs themselves. They will survive when most of rock has crumbled. The show features a great honking sax, some encouragingly audible kids, older performers who sing better than they act and look better than they sing, and enjoyably tacky choreography.

The sets for Man and Superman (Haymarket) are also tacky; the components don't seem to meet, and at times they open arbitrarily up to admit Jack Tanner's car. This, directed by Patrick Dromgoole, is an applause-seeking production as may be judged from some foolish running gags and from Peter O'Toole's prima donna performance, yellow-haired, pale-faced, and strep-throated.

Still, Tanner is a prima donna character, and Mr O'Toole's timing at least is intact. The guts of the comedy are here, with Lisa Harrow a deceptively docile Ann, James Grout a robust Roebuck Ramsden (who flaps his fins to suggest emotion), sweet performances from Timothy Ackroyd and Joyce Carey, and Michael Byrne one of the best in a long line of infallible Enries.
1982-11-28-fairy-tale-time:
Fairy-tale time

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Shakespeare at the National and Camelot.

THE band strikes up 'If It Wasn't for the Houses In Between,' and we wonder what that has to do with a wood near Athens, or near anywhere else. It then segues into 'Lily of Laguna,' which is even more bemusing, and finally settles on 'Beautiful Dreamer,' which makes sense.

A Midsummer Night's Dream is, if anything is, the great English folk play. Its fairies are a compendium of Elizabethan lore on the homelier supernatural. I had expected Bill Bryden, whose productions at the Cottesloe are generally historically-minded, to explore the play's Elizabethan-ness. In fact, as may be gauged from that opening medley, he places us on the cusp of Victorian and Edwardian. The mechanicals might be the Lark Rise and Candleford Dramatic Society. The lovers are out of Jerome K. Jerome.

Theseus signals the onset of holiday by throwing his bonnet over the windmill, or at least his boater into the audience. Only the grey-green fairies transcend the period. They might come from a nineteenth-century picture-book, but they could equally come from a sixteenth-century one. They are free, and in control.

This production's great concern, and great excitement, is to bring the play's levels together, and yet keep them tantalisingly apart. The fairies are everywhere, overseeing the mortals from every level of stage and auditorium. They bring on the lights that mark out the mechanicals' acting area. Oberon and Titania come face to face with an unseeing Theseus and Hippolyta: a more powerful moment than can be produced by the now orthodox doubling of roles. When the fairies perform their dance of blessing at the end, the mortals return to do their own concentric routine.

The key line might be Puck's 'I'll be an auditor; an actor too perhaps.' When he and Oberon watch the lovers, when Theseus and Hippolyta watch the play, they sit with us. The audience, in a modified form of promenade staging, constitute the play's fourth estate; we too participate and we become part of the party at the finale when Puck's 'give me your hands' becomes the cue for handshakes all round.

Actually I suspect the line just means 'please applaud' and I also suspect that the 'general harmony' interpretation of the play is getting overdone. The different worlds brush, but they do not collide; only Bottom actually meets Titania (and cannot believe it afterwards), and while he and his friends are dismissed by the duke before the end. We are in danger of underrating the elusiveness of this play; I was longing for Puck to shake just one hand, and disappear. If we are to participate, this is as close as we should get.

Which is not to deny the delight of what Mr Bryden has actually achieved. It still lacks an overall rhythm, and there were moments on the first night when it came to an abrupt and puzzling halt, sometimes in the middle of a line. Paul Scofield as Oberon seemed occasionally overcome by the power of his own words; pardonably, since his grizzled, solicitous, sonorous and quietly self-mocking Oberon could raise some very potent spirits.

Susan Fleetwood's sensuous Titania matches him (their quarrel carries unusual weight) and Jack Shepherd knows exactly how to hush the theatre as Puck. Edna Dore, a dewdrop-bearing drudge, admirably rounds out the immortals. The clowns are led by Derek Newark's quietly self-confident Bottom and include a Snout by Tony Haygarth, who, as Wall, drops delightful bricks. The Bergomask is done, with superb devotion, as a four-man sand-dance: Wilson, Keppel, Betty and Friend.

The upper-class ladies--especially Marsha Hunt's Hippolyta and Bernadette Shortt's Hermia--are cowed by the verse; though Jennifer Hall as Helena has some nice vignettes of self-pity. The men are stronger, with Edward de Souza a jovially seignorial Theseus (who actually thinks his way through 'the lunatic, the lover and the poet'), David Rintoul a down-the-line juvenile Demetrius, and Karl Johnson's Lysander emerging, unprecedentedly, as the sharpest character in the piece: a priggishly ardent young man who gives lectures on the course of true love, and carefully arranges flowers for his pillow before sinking in a trance. At its multi-levelled best, this production makes Pirandello look a bit sick, as of course does the play. I preferred it, though of course I don't dare say so, to Peter Brook's.

  

I have always found the ending of Camelot very moving: on record, on film, and now at the Apollo Victoria. It has something to do with the continuity of tradition; the doomed Arthur, on the eve of his last battle, sending off the boy who is to grow into Sir Thomas Malory. (I know it sounds awful; I can't help it.)

It is also the moment when the title-song justifies itself. In the first scene it combines the worst aspects of jogtrot and jingle (and Camelot proves fatally easy to rhyme); in subsequent reprise it acquires wit; and, at the last, dignity. The one thread that keeps the story going is the birth and erosion of Arthur's idealism; he apparently invents democracy, and then watches it undermined. This is one of the very few male leads in a musical worth acting, and Richard Harris, happy or tormented, does it justice.

Elsewhere one's patience is, admittedly, tried. Alan Jay Lerner's source is not Malory, but T. H. White's Once and Future King, whose reverent jokiness turns to whimsy on the stage. Mr Lerner's lyrics are filled with cute abbreviations and patter-rhythms left over from My Fair Lady. The jousts are the Ascot Gavotte all over again. The best song, the ghostly 'Follow Me,' is hidden away, and others are given unwise prominence; in one attempt at celebration people bound on with flowered hoops and then sing a ditty that begins 'tra la.'

American Anglophilia runs riot; Pellinore, the funny man (well done by Robin Bailey), is an acceptable old stick, except that you suspect the authors of believing he really exists. Lancelot begins as an ineffable twit and in Robert Meadmore's performance stays one; Guenevere (Fiona Fullerton) is giggly. Frederick Loewe's best known tune, 'If Ever I Would Leave You,' does its work, but the resources for frustrated passion are otherwise lacking. The show is almost bound to look like pantomime and in Michael Rudman's production, with variable sets and awful dances, it does. But still.

  

Waiting (Lyric Studio, Hammersmith) is what people do when a simulacrum of the Yorkshire Ripper is at large. The men mock, fear or despise the women, so any one of them (or us) might have done it. The women fear or despise the men, but they're entitled, because they've been abused, though some women like their men, which just shows how they've been fooled. The story, designed to carry the thesis, limps, though the end has clout. Julia Kearsley writes well, but this play about oppressiveness is itself oppressive.
1982-12-05-life-and-times-of-the-slab-bo:
Life and times of the Slab Boys

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Still Life, Call Me Madam and Aladdin.

THE theme of John Byrne's Still Life, the last play in his Slab Boys trilogy which is now being given in its entirety and in repertory at the Royal Court, is that we all grow old, or at any rate older: "If"--as John Whiting, the late John Whiting, once put it--"we are lucky."

It is not a new theme, but maybe it is the only one that any writer is really capable of treating. Write anything that has a time-span attached, and there you are. Anyway, Mr Byrne gives it a very entertaining whirl, clinching it by writing two acts between which years elapse, but which both occur in the same spot, a graveyard, designed incidentally by Mr Byrne himself.

Of the three original Paisley slab boys only two remain, the always unfortunate Hector having met with his final accident. Over his grave meet Phil, with aspirations towards being an artist, and Spanky, now a scuffling pop musician, who may be about to get his big break with a fleeting appearance on Juke Box Jury. That dates us all.

They reminisce about the past years, and we may join in, especially if (as in my case) it is ages since we saw the previous plays. Mr Byrne is very good at jogging our memories through jogging theirs. They also fight, since boys will be boys, even when men, and especially when back in the company of those with whom they were boys. They run up against another despised old acquaintance, now in gents' outfitting, and they exchange a wife: Lucille, formerly sweetheart of the slab room.

In Act Two, Spanky has actually made it, and comes back a rock star. Underneath of course he hasn't changed, though whether this is as much to his credit as the fan press would have us believe is a matter for doubt. Phil has grown increasingly bitter, which is nothing for the audience to worry about, since it also means he has grown increasingly funny.

The play's greatest attraction, apart from its extreme believability, is its exploration of a shared, and persisting, joke-world. Black humour very often: Mr Byrne can be hilariously callous. He also covers a wide span of remembered pop-culture: from the days when George Elrick presented Housewives' Choice (wasn't he the one who used to sing along with the signature tune?) to the days when Spanky could meet and actually rap with Kris Kristofferson.

The only other influence I can detect is Samuel Beckett; Lucille's announcement of her pregnancy, following some farcical business with the late delivery of Phil's late mother's headstone, comes as near to a physicalisation of "they give birth astride of a grave" as most of us will care to get. The acting is very lively, with Billy McColl as Phil, Gerard Kelly as Spanky.

  

Rep revivals of large-scale musicals are chancy things, but Roger Redfarn has made a slick and sensible job of Call Me Madam at Birmingham. He has been much aided by Terry Parsons, whose sets for the two mythical countries of Lichtenburg and Truman America are lavishly practical, and by Tudor Davies for choreography conceived and executed without raggedness (though with one notable lift from Evita).

Mr Davies moves American politicians and socialites wittily about in the Washington Square Dance and gets his people dancing as if they had just popped out of clocks for The Ocarina, a manufactured folk-dance that sounds bearable when speeded up. Then, in Something to Dance About, he sails buoyantly through a medley of wartime-and-after styles, transforming the gentlemanly Jeremy Hawk into a flaming jitterbug, with upstretched wing and intoxicated smile.

Linking the two countries, as ambassadors, is party-giver Sally Adams, queen of all the madams, an Ethel Merman role probably unplayable as anything else. Miss Merman's strength, as we were reminded at this year's Royal Variety Performance, is uninhibitedness under complete control. She never overstates, but then she never has to. A Lichtenburger calls Sally "the most American American I have ever met," to which she replies, with her authors' obvious approval, "that's the nicest thing anybody ever told me."

It may not be Henry James's idea of Yankee innocence abroad, but it is American, 1950s American anyway, and when it is Miss Merman's the confidence cannot be begrudged. Noele Gordon's impersonation has nice moments of elephantine tenderness; she looks right, dumpy and determined, and eventually she sounds right, though the orchestra drowns out her first two numbers: Ethel would never be so unready. She has solid support from Basil Hoskins; William Relton and Veronica Page are tuneful and mobile in the juvenile element.

The script is thin (being post-Rodgers and Hammerstein, it is obliged to have a story, but would probably be happier as a string of gags), but there is an atavistic pleasure in hearing the thumping song-cues, especially when the resultant sound is something so effortlessly effervescent as It's a Lovely Day Today. This is reprised four times; by the last I felt we deserved It's a Lovely Day Tomorrow, which Irving Berlin, who had firm ideas about weather, had actually written earlier.

Other Berlin goodies in the score are The Best Thing For You, subtler than he is generally given credit for, and You're Just in Love, which is the one in which he complains that he smells blossom when there's no-one there, or something on those lines, and she tells him that he's okay, indeed enviable, and then they repeat it, contrapuntally, at increasing speed, and generally with encores. Miss Gordon, on the first night, was more than happy to oblige.

  

There could hardly be more contrasting composer-lyricists than the supremely popular Mr Berlin and Elizabeth Swados, who makes pronouncements like "some people don't want intensity, they want entertainment. That's not what I'm about." Her more ambitious scores are as unentertaining as she could possibly wish, but she has provided a propulsive backing of mainly African sounds for Aladdin (Commonwealth Institute), performed by an international cast, but stemming from New York's La Mama company. Visually, this is a ceaselessly inventive production. The language is invented, Peter Brook style, so it would be kind of the management to leave us enough light to read the three-page synopsis. I never met anyone who could memorise a synopsis.

One more week to see the American Dance Machine (Adelphi), who preserve old routines. Their selection has many gaps, but there is Gower Champion's funny shrine-number from Bye Bye Birdie, a beautiful intersection of black-and-white clad figures (like dancing dominoes) in a twenties party routine by Dan Siretta; a clog dance arranged with typical wit by Danny Daniels from Walking Happy, based on Hobson's Choice; and the presence of Zan Charisse, remembered here from Gypsy. Barry Preston does a wonderful fast walk in a routine from Half a Sixpence, but should realise that singing cockney doesn't mean dropping your t's.
1982-12-12-hoping-for-a-miracle:
Hoping for a miracle

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Messiah, Steafel Variations and Alcestis.

IN Bent, Martin Sherman wrote a celebration of homosexuality set in a Nazi concentration camp. In his new play, Messiah (Hampstead), he goes to similar extremes, using the pogroms of seventeenth-century Poland as the backdrop for a celebration of Jewishness.

Not of Judaism: the play's attitude towards religion is, at its most enthusiastic, a weary shrug. It is epitomised in the character of Rachel, an ugly young woman with a lively mind, who treats God as a confidant, someone to complain to. Reluctantly, she lets herself be married off to a rich middle-aged fruiterer. Then news comes, relayed by her new husband's scholarly nephew, of the advent of the long-awaited Messiah, alive and working miracles in the Middle East, under the name of Sabbatai Sevi, and prepared to go to Constantinople and take the Sultan's crown from him.

The news produces galvanic effects; the Messiah proves a focus for the community's hopes and fears. The fruiterer, hitherto a worldly man, gives away his possessions and persuades himself he can fly to Jerusalem. He throws himself off the roof, with disastrous results. (Clive Swift plays the role, and any saviour who would kill off Mr Swift halfway through a play has got to be suspect.) Rachel is sceptical, but nevertheless, as an almost merry widow, she accompanies the nephew and her old mother, traumatised into dumbness when the Cossacks killed her husband, on the boat-trip to Turkey. She does not enjoy the ride.

Asher, the nephew, says that under the rule of Sabbatai, all the scriptural prohibitions are abolished. He persuades Rachel to eat non-kosher meat. She persuades him into bed with her, and is delighted with the results. When disillusion strikes, Asher violently rejects her. Worse follows. It seems that the Old Testament God is revenging himself. Rachel tries to reject him, but finds she cannot; she goes on addressing him, even telling him he doesn't exist. She is saddled with the idea of God; which is why I call the play a celebration of Jewishness.

"God damn you, God," says Sarah at the moment of despair. That ought to be a neat and poignant paradox, but as dramatic English it is badly strained. Mr Sherman strongly resembles Peter Shaffer in his choice of themes and in his execution; his audacity and his stagecraft run considerably ahead of his actual writing. It is hard for any playwright to portray an orthodox Jewish character having chucklesome conversations with the deity without summoning up Fiddler on the Roof, and Mr Sherman does not escape the cosy shadow.

What he is saying is far from cosy: a rejection of salvation in human form (Rachel has some wry asides on what Jesus meant for the Jews), an acceptance of a capricious and implacable presence that exacts worship, but does not reward it. Rachel's mother, breaking silence, sees God as the demon who led the Cossacks to her husband. Sabbatai's wife (we meet her, but not him) has her own views, though they are not easy to follow.

Ronald Eyre's production, whose merits include a brilliant instantaneous evocation of a Turkish bazaar, cradles a conquering performance from Maureen Lipman, funny ("Of, do I have impure thoughts"), erotic and adventurous. (The play has a strong feminist strand.) Jack Klaff's Asher is a strong, cracked idealist and Shirin Taylor a sultry Sarah.

  

Sheila Steafel, flying solo in Steafel Variations (Apollo), has acquired a new opener, with which she closes, and a new closer, with which she opens. These are not original ideas, but she performs them so intently that they acquire shine. Also new is a fanatically rhymed song, written by Dick Vosburgh and Frank Lazarus and recalling Lorenz Hart on an over-ingenious day: clever in itself and funny as parody.

I was happy to meet again the chanteuse who smokily celebrates a certain Mère Brun (who must go sous la table), the lieder singer performing extracts from the Freierreise cycle and showing a marked impatience with her subject ("The Maiden and the Halibut"), a pubescent variety star called Popsy, whose breathing is hopelessly out of sync with her lyrics, and a pinched-voiced impressionist, whose act consists of a hopeful re-creation ("and look who's standing over here") of a Hollywood party. Small and quizzical, Miss Steafel preserves an ironic detachment not only from the people she does, but from her doing them. It has been suggested that she needs a smaller theatre; actually she just needs a larger audience.

  

Theatro Technis, a Cypriot company in Crowndale Road near Mornington Crescent, has revived Euripides's Alcestis. Alcestis was a queen who sacrificed her life for that of her husband Admetus, a deal sanctioned by the god Apollo, who owed Admetus a favour for hospitality received. Ted Craig has staged this perplexing tale in Edwardian country-house clothes (Heracles comes for the weekend bearing racquets) against red upholstery on red carpets, which is striking; and has pointed up the family background, which is apt. The chorus become, more or less, the waiter and the porter and the upstairs maid; Andreas Markos's old retainer is especially convincing. Admetus does not seem to have decided just how selfish he is meant to be (Euripides seems to think very), but Anthony Woodruffe is quite uncompromising as his horrible dad (doubled with Death, done as an undertaker) and Anna Savva is quiet and gentle and very beautiful as Alcestis, who is, of course, at the point of death. If she can play alive as well, she may be an important actress.

A few days before she died I received a commendatory note from Caryl Brahms concerning a review of a show with which she had no immediate connection. This was generous and possibly eccentric; Miss Brahms was well known to be both. She co-authored some extremely funny novels and was an enthusiastic and thoroughly individual critic. She was one of our few genuine characters, and since I cannot thank her in person, I do so here.
1982-12-19-renovated-relic:
Renovated relic

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on the RSC's Peter Pan

THE traditional dilapidated productions have left Peter Pan looking like a relic. Now the Barbican takes it over, in a careful and occasionally brilliant production by John Caird and Trevor Nunn, and it still looks like a relic: a fascinating one, but appealing more as a guide to the author's psyche than as a play or adventure story in its own right.

What we get is a voyage around Peter Pan, a tour conducted by Barrie himself in the person (about twice as high as the original) of Stephen Moore in several varieties of Edwardian gentleman's relaxing or travelling dress. Mr Moore, the only actor I know able to convey nervousness and urbanity at the same time, narrates impeccably, his material drawn from Barrie's discursive stage directions and his novelisation of his own play.

The latter takes the story further than we are used to. We glimpse the Lost Boys grown up (into dizzyingly varied professions) and we are told that Wendy continued to do Peter's spring-cleaning on an annual basis (when he remembered to call for her, that is) until her own daughter was of an age to take over, followed by her grand-daughter; "and thus," says Mr Moore, putting on the agony, putting on the style, "it will go on, so long as children are gay and innocent and heartless." Pan will endure "until we wake up."

Is that to be wished? The last line could be the author's savage (and quite justified) comment on his own infantilism, or it could be a desperate prayer for it to continue. Probably it is both. This RSC production, by bothering to act what others have skimped (i.e. nearly everything) makes us more than usually aware of the cloying awfulness of the Darling household (words it is difficult to type with teeth clenched), simultaneously loathed and desired by its creator. Wendy, in the finest of Jane Carr's little madam performances, becomes the central character, trying desperately to seduce Peter even as she meticulously mothers him. As a fearful, fascinated view of womankind it is practically definitive, besides being extremely funny. Sheila Hancock gets more charm and grief out of Mrs Darling than previous actresses can have thought possible.

But the middle episodes are diminished: the fact of the children's escaping to Neverland is more important than what happens to them there. John Napier's revolving design transforms the place, as stipulated, into a closely packed adventure playground, though the components are of unequal merit (pirate ship, yes; lagoon, no). The flying is thrillingly done, up to the full height of the monstrous stage; though if ever a play cried out to be turned into a musical it is this one at the moment of lift-off. All forms of animal life are enthusiastically and skilfully represented, but the humans are disappointing. One lost boy (Anthony O'Donnell's Tootles) and one pirate (George Raistrick's Smee) stand out but the others are anonymous. And the central duel of Pan and Hook turns out not to be central at all.

We have been told for years that having Peter played by a boy instead of a girl would be a revelation. Maybe it would, but Miles Anderson here demonstrates that there is not much in Peter for a grown-up male actor to act. What there is he does well and, at the end, hauntingly. There is something of the Restoration fop in Hook but Joss Ackland, black-curled and almost a Pirate Queen, plays it, excellently, to the exclusion of everything else. Doubled with Mr Darling he is presumably meant to represent the full horror of adult malehood, but here there is no menace in him however much he waves his implement. He is not helped by the direction, which makes the pirate scenes strangely cluttered, or by the writing which in effect castrates him, helpless against all-powerful Pan. Barrie goes on and on about his buccaneers but as a pirate story the play is not much cop.

Something else it signally lacks, compared to other fantasy classics, is laughter. Most children's favourites--Lewis Carroll, Kenneth Grahame, A. A. Milne--satirise the adult world; this one wants to exclude it. Instead of wit Barrie offers whimsy camouflaged by very defensive irony; match the lost boys' imaginary supper against the Mad Hatter's tea-party. Miss Carr, by the way, would make the perfect Alice.

This variorum Peter Pan is a better adult entertainment than most others on offer.

  

Peter Whelan's Clay, in the Pit (appropriate match), is an exhaustive study of the states of mind of two married couples, former friends reunited, for whom the magic has gone. Mr Whelan cares enough about them to stimulate some excellent acting: Fred Pearson and Janet Dale jauntily or placidly normal before disintegrating, Jim Broadbent effortlessly and Gemma Jones effortfully odd before their suffering humanity comes through, but they don't half go round in circles.

Their muddle is set, in time-honoured fashion, against the painful clarity of old age, represented by Sylvia Coleridge in remarkable form, and John McAndrew, struggling boyfully against his exclusion from most of the action. When he returns it is to remind us of the nuclear threat, potent even in this play's rural setting. This is hopefully (I use the word, of course, advisedly) meant to set the domestic anguish in a wider context. Pull the other one.

  

More bracingly Steven Davis's A View of Kabul (Bush), whose title refers to a brand of dope, is another nail in the much-studded coffin of 1960s idealism. It is actually set in 1972, getting on for aftermath time, and juxtaposes two fashionable figureheads, supposedly allies: the rock musician and the socialist. The ideals of the former are shown to be bogus and those of the latter unworkable; the latter therefore loses out to the former who steals both of his women. Mr Davis works in a consciously artificial mode--characters walking on when needed rather than when motivated--so knowingly and symmetrically handled as to be a pleasure in itself: likewise his dialogue, which runs to elaborate double-entendre. Talk of the vulnerable heart, following an emotional bust-up, turns out to mean something quite different. The director, Richard Wilson, keeps his author's cool, and the acting is not to be quarrelled with.

  

Me, Myself and I (Orange Tree) is a musical by Alan Ayckbourn and Paul Todd. A parody of teenage romance, Fifties style. Mr Ayckbourn, who has never written worse, is the slave of his rhymes; as he usually writes short lines, the rhymes come round very often. It might work for light-headed comedy but he is trying to make character points.

Three of the characters are aspects of the same woman, though there are hardly enough characteristics for two of them. Her, herself and she are interviewed, as mother of the year, by two reporters and finally return to their husband. There is little wrong with the performance. Go and see Why Upstream instead.

  

The New Vic company have been touring with The Night They Raided Minsky's, caught by me at the plushly refurbished Theatre Royal, Bath. The film took us in and around the flavoursome world of 1920s burlesque. The stage version eschews around, and seems hung up on its own skill in evoking the old routines.

The girls have the right shape and the right squeal and there are authentic-sounding songs by Charles Strouse and Lee Adams (whom I credit since the programme neglects to) but it goes on for ever, varied only by endless replays of the same piece of plot, denunciations of everything by a prurient Puritan. In the interval he assails drinking patrons and takes their names. He took mine: What has he done with it?
1983-01-16-first-the-bad-news:
First, the bad news

THE Broadway theatre is in bad shape: official. The news was broken in the New York Times on the first Monday of 1983. Statistics were flourished, among them the fact that 15 theatres were dark.

A commonly reiterated view is that admission is too costly for theatregoers to afford. A more rational one is that the prices merely make them selective, and that recently there has been precious little for them to select. Even so, two productions managed to play to audiences of more than 100 per cent, a feat accomplished by counting those standing up. Of these, one was the held-over 'Dreamgirls,' the other the season's only new hit, 'Cats.'

When 'Cats' opened in London, there was a thrill in discovering that English performers could dance. Of Americans though we expect it; the show uses some of the best dancers in New York, but leaves them looking underemployed, even if continuously active. Singing, though, is far better than in London; Betty Buckley gives a piercing account of 'Memory'; her Grizabella is a creature of emaciated sensuality, though her apotheosis seems more arbitrary than ever.

Where the production has been elaborated, the results are unfortunate; Mungojerrie and Rumpleteazer have been put into clown-costume and are not even allowed to sing their own song; in 'Skimbleshanks the Railway Cat' -- musically the best number -- the train is now made of objets trouves rather than of the performers themselves. This signalises the show's main loss: good fellowship. We can take a local pride in Trevor Nunn's showmanship, while hoping that he won't make a career out of it.

'Cats' was a sell-out in New York before it opened; they were selling mementoes last summer, long before there was anything to mement. Now in the lobbies they sell everything, even the book: 'Buy the poems,' cried the hucksters, 'by T. S. (a quick look down) Eliot.' Broadway programmes are institutionalised and Thomas Stearns Eliot (Poet and Lyricist) duly gets his biography, just ahead of Andrew Lloyd Webber (Composer and Co-orchestrator).

The New York theatre is raining dogs as well as cats. 'Snoopy' is the second small musical to be based on the 'Peanuts' strip; since the mutt was the de facto star of the first one, it seems reasonable to give him a show of his own.

A sturdier mini-musical, due in London soon, is 'The Little Shop of Horrors,' which is real trashy and means to be. Who could resist a man-eating plant that sings soul? Nobody, that's who. (We are told in a final recitative that 'the plant achieved its purpose, which was to eat Cleveland.') Its inventor, a Bowery Faust residing at the double unlucky number of 1313 Skid Row, christens it Audrey II after his girlfriend. Audrey I, a dumb blonde, is a tour-de-faiblesse for the actress Ellen Geer.

With these last two shows, we have wandered off Broadway. Back on, there is 'Nine,' which last season wrested most of the Tony awards from Michael Bennett's 'Dreamgirls.' 'Nine' is also the creation of a gifted choreographer who has apparently foresworn choreography; Tommy Tune's staging, stylishly set and elaborately costumed, ranks very high as mobile sculpture.

Dancing is kept to a minimum; a number called 'Folies Bergere,' which most directors would festoon with high kicks and ostrich feathers, is here restricted to a series of languorous arm movements by the seated ladies of the chorus who comprise most of the cast.
