The result is to make the scene dreamily effective if bewilderingly irrelevant. This, though, is a trouble that pervades most of the evening, and one which goes back to source.

The show is based on Fellini's '8 1/2': a much overrated movie, but at least it gives you the director's narcissism neat. Somebody else trying to tell his story is in trouble, mainly because he hasn't got one. 'Nine' gives us the conceit of the hero (an unappetising blank as played by Raul Julia) presiding like a conductor over the vast orchestra of women in his life. At the end he is reconciled with his wife: a happy ending (like that of 'Dreamgirls' and indeed of 'Cats') about which it is impossible to care.

Some of Maury Yeston's music is operettishly attractive (to my chagrin: I was looking forward to reporting that the only Good Tune was the director) and Mr Yeston also wrote the lyrics. The hit number ('Be Italian/you rapscallion') stays with you however much you wish it would leave.

A widely noted phenomenon is that Broadway, like the West End, prefers to get its dramas pre-tested. Currently this means buying British.

Sometimes, though, Broadway's liberal conscience will support a play that would not survive commercially in London. Athol Fugard's 'Master Harold . . . and the Boys' has had a good run. It is the liveliest of his plays, but still suffers from there being nothing Mr Fugard could say about South Africa that we would not all heartily agree with; he is not enough of a poet to make his particular case (in this case, a white youth who has grown up on intimate terms with black servants and is now pressurised into rejecting them) take on general significance. There was a performance of expected dignity from James Earl Jones, but the other acting was weak.

That often happens in New York. It afflicted Jonathan Reynolds's 'Geniuses,' an established off-Broadway success that, in the sage judgment of Variety, would have been a natural Broadway choice before economic panic set in. It certainly belongs to the favourite Broadway genre of showbiz satire, being set in the Philippines during the shooting of a megalomaniac movie which could hardly not be 'Apocalypse Now.'

It is really an extension of the scene in 'Once in a Lifetime' in which the captive East Coast playwright rails at Hollywood and all its works, and it hardly amounts to more than sporadically effective joking at arbitrarily assembled figures; not at least until the third act when Morgan Fairchild takes control.

Miss Fairchild is a soap-opera queen whose bio reads like a joke. (She has played 'paranoid murderess Jennifer Pace Phillips,' 'warped actress Dulcie Warwick' and 'spoiled bitch Constance Weldon Carlyle.') Playing a blonde starlet of limited mental horizons, but unlimited sexual ones, she is the realest person on stage, and the play takes wing when she is allowed, at remarkably inoffensive length, to beat up a macho set designer.

A more complicated revenge play is Christopher Durang's 'Sister Mary Ignatius Explains It All For You.' For most of the play Sister Mary gives a simple interpretation of Catholic dogma: a hilarious parody, but an easy target. Then some of her ex-pupils intrude, and the play rollercoasts. Nancy Marchand, a crisp, mannish actress, is fearsome and funny in the title role.

The nicest trend is late-night intimate revue, usually staged in or above restaurants. 'Forbidden Broadway' sends up the theatre by rewriting familiar songs to pillory successful shows, actors and (most often) actresses. Spotting the tunes and the victims affords low-level enjoyment.

The best joke (to the tune of 'Well, Did You Evah') is at the expense of the lyricist-director of 'Annie': 'Annie's closed and Charnin's blue/I hear he's copying some revue.' In fact Martin Charnin's copy, 'Upstairs at O'Neal's,' betters their original. For one thing, it has a wider range of subjects and writers; for another it has an insolent punkish style in staging and performance; for yet another it has Mr Charnin's own best lyrics, one of which, called 'Stools,' is addressed, devastatingly and ungainsayably, to the one prop without which no revue can do or be done.

What is enviable about these shows is that they assume, and attract, a knowing homogeneous audience. New York, unlike London, is still theatre city.
1983-01-30-biases-in-bombay:
Biases in Bombay

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on David Hare's 'A Map of the World.'

DAVID HARE'S A Map of the World (Lyttelton) is set, for the most part, at a UNESCO conference on poverty, held in Bombay in the mid-1970s. One of the participants is a novelist called Victor Mehta, born in India, but living in England, who has written satirically of Marxist regimes.

He thus attracts the hostility of Third World delegates, who demand that he preface his address with a disclaimer to the effect that since all fiction is a distortion, his audience need not believe a word he has ever written. It turns out that this has been drafted by a young British journalist, Stephen Andrews, who regards Mehta as reactionary and has already told him so. Mehta, meanwhile, has put Stephen down as a courier of received ideas. Mehta refuses to have Stephen's words put into his mouth, but consents to engage with him in a formal, private debate.

There's more to it. Mehta has been to bed with Peggy, an American also fancied by Stephen, and she offers herself as prize to the winner of the contest.

There's more yet. Mehta has turned his Bombay experience into a novel. This novel is made into a film. Intercut with the scenes in and around the conference are episodes on the movie-set. Shooting is interrupted by the arrival of the real Mehta and Peggy, who complain of falsification.

To take the three levels separately: the first, the polemical, is fine. Mehta speaks for the writer's duty of non-involvement, Stephen for his public obligations. (There is also a good number for an African delegate on the irrelevance of Mehta's ironies to the experience of a developing nation.) Mehta and Stephen know how to expose each other's weaknesses, and we can sense in both of them the moments at which prejudice or defensiveness take over from argument.

Indeed, with this sense of what the current Tom Stoppard play calls "the public configuration of private derangement" already so firmly expressed, it is doubtful if we need the second, sexual, level at all. However we have it, and it's calamitous. The characters have no existence outside their opinions. Peggy has to be hastily fitted up with a case for sexual freedom to justify her generous offer.

Her one scene with Mehta in the bedroom (not in bed) tells us nothing; the play indeed is continually stating relationships - as when Stephen says he's grown fond of Mehta - that it doesn't dramatise. And this exacerbates a feeling that the argument, if not actually rigged, is hanging on the wrong hinge. When Mehta is asked to proclaim something he doesn't believe, one is shocked, and nothing that can later be said for or against him erases that shock. What good would it do anybody for him to tell lies? (The conference can go on without him, and does.)

Finally, the form: the play-about-a-film-about-a-novel-about-real-life. I assume that the conference scenes depict what really happened rather than the movie distortion. (The production doesn't make it very clear, but there's a clue in the text. The real Peggy is an actress; the film turns her into that rarest of birds, a jazz violinist. If you hear references to Peggy acting, you'll know you're all right.) If this isn't the case, then the whole play is frivolous beyond redemption; but unless Mr Hare is offering us the longest takes in film history it can't be. The alternative, though, is only the lesser of two evils.

We get some entertaining backstage stuff, including a very funny scene in which the solving of a crossword puzzle sets off a political row conducted by people entirely locked into their own preconceptions. This is a pleasing comic comment on the main action, but it could have been worked in without the superstructure.

That structure itself of course echoes the play's concern with partis pris; here are all these characters seeing things from their own points of view, and here's the film adding its, and getting it wrong. Oddly enough, not even the director gives Mehta much of an argument on this and the actors all agree with him that the picture's rubbish. So all we have is another statement about all art and all thought being biased: the film, and Mehta's novel, and Peggy's reminiscence, and Mr Hare's play. It's true of course. It's true of every play ever written. Audiences (Dr Johnson pointed this out 200 years ago and he can't have been the first) take it for granted.

Roshan Seth has charm and assurance as Mehta, though he seems to be forcing himself up to the size of the theatre. Bill Nighy is a speedy, pugnacious Stephen and between takes he is the most convincing actor I have ever seen acted. Diana Quick as Peggy is defeated by an American accent and the amorphousness of the role. Sheila Scott-Wilkinson is forceful and refreshing, except in one scene where she is just forceful. There are witty cameos from Stefan Gryff as the director and Ronald Hines as a pugnacious performer. Nick Bicat's music is powerful. The best of Mr Hare's stage pictures as director is of four diplomats sitting in a row, listening intently to the main proceedings.

  

The Actors Touring Company have begun a season at the Warehouse with Alfred Jarry's Ubu, which they bill as Ubu the Vandalist. Ubu is the regicidal monster, egged on by his wife and with much else of Macbeth about him, in whom Jarry caricatured what he took to be the worst aspects of the French bourgeoisie, and he does indeed, after his career in a mythical Poland, take refuge in France.

Peter Brook, who must have suffered in Parisian lodgings, has described him as the archetypal concierge, but his own production was noticeably unvengeful: I remember it as good fast knockabout. John Retallack's for the ATC is a lot slower, and seems to be taking the piece very seriously.

The play was designed to make its audiences uncomfortable, an invitation few directors can resist. But it is now a classic, fit to be performed by a group whose repertory also includes Cervantes, Shakespeare and Vanbrugh; so the ATC are trying to scandalise, enlighten and entertain us all at the same time. (Scatological dialogue and frantic action are good for you, runs the message.) The production is inventive, in bursts, and the cast are neat in their timing and their miming.

Chris Barnes and Christine Bishop, masked and puffed up as Pere and Mere Ubu, have found a vocal style to match. It's a slow bellow and is cleverly, if wearingly, maintained. The not noticeably bad King Wenceslas is played by Russell Enoch, in whom I thought I recognised William Russell, television's Sir Lancelot of the Fifties.

  

Carol Williams's And All Things Nice (Old Red Lion, Islington) is about a 15-year-old black girl whose dad throws her out and who ends up double quick in a punk squat, on drugs and the game. Only linking narrative makes any attempt at sophistication. The jagged short-breathed scenes may reflect an inability to write anything else, but as the essence of the world it presents is a brief attention-span (life would be unliveable otherwise) it suits very well. Charlie Hanson's production uses the window of this upstairs pub-room, to breezy verite effect, as the window of an upstairs room.
1983-02-01-new-records:
New Records

Though I enjoyed Andy Capp in the theatre I had doubts as to how it would sound on record. But Key Records' cast album (KEY 4) is excellent. It shows off Alan Price to advantage, of course, and his opener "On My Street" comes off all the better as a prologue for our not being bothered by the show's rather desperate attempts to integrate him later. It's unfortunate that his incursion into the main action, duetting with Tom Courtenay on "The Trouble with People", is one of the weaker numbers. Its recurring punch-line 'you really bore me' is meant to carry more dramatic weight than it can bear, and it's also a tough one to rhyme.

Actually there's a fair amount of sloppy rhyming in these lyrics, but the musical forms are usually loose enough for them to be bearable. Mr Price wrote the music, Trevor Peacock the book, and they collaborated on the lyrics, or more likely alternated. At any rate it's Price I hear in the musing pop numbers, Peacock in the music-hall ones. Andy's credo 'I Ought to be Ashamed of Myself' is shades of Formby, and mostly delightful. I don't think I've ever liked Tom Courtenay as much. (Dees anyone remember Courtenay singing Mr Peacock's masterpiece Mrs Brown You've Got a Lovely Daughter' before Herman's Hermits got to it and ruined it?) The number for the women (Val McLane as Flo, Nicky Croydon as Raquel planning her marriage to Elvis) get the exact note of cartooned domestic bite.

The weakest numbers, as on stage, are the sentimental When You've Lived in Love with Someone' and the cluttered, supposedly celebratory 'Mr Scrimmett'. The best, as on stage, is 'Good Old Legs' sung by Andy and Chalkie (John Bardon) as they reel home from the pub. Its sodden euphoria, reflecting its performers' uncertain gait, is something new in musicals. There are two records of the RSC. First Poppy (WEA 250000-1), Peter Nichols's pantomime, Terry Hands's musical. (I only know what I'm told.) I can't see that much separates the two forms today; a Palladium panto and Annie have much the same production values, and either is available for imitation or subversion. If a pantomime storyline required an opium dream or an Anglo-Chinese battle I'm sure the result would look much the same as at the Barbican.

And it isn't as if all pantomimes were alike; Aladdin is not the same bag of goods as Dick Whittington. The claim that the revivalist number The Blessed Trinity, not in Nichols's original script, weakens the anti-imperialist message, can hardly be taken seriously. It positively blares it out. The real objection to this number is that it comes off as the RS's pale answer to the National's 'Sit Down You're Rockin' the Boat'. That the same man, David Toguri, should have choreographed both of them is almost incredible. The decisive objection to the show is that the pantomime convention is not a good way of telling the story. I don't know much about the Chinese opium wars but I do know they weren't fought by characters called Dick Whittington and Obadiah Upward and I got fatigued by the pretence that they were.

Maybe pantomime, in its Victorian heyday, summed up complacent British jingoism but it doesn't any more; as Hands's showbiz spectacle unwittingly proves. The show's attempts to drag the story back to its panto base becomes increasingly desperate. Robert Cushman On record, of course, it becomes a musical anyway, with a competent pastiche score by Monty Norman; though the title song gets as tedious as the Beatle Indian epics it is supposed to be parodying. Nichols's lyrics, though, fulfil the promise of Privates on Parade. The radio critic who called them 'the wittiest since Cole Porter' was going a bit far, but as he then added 'or John Lennon' he obviously didn't know what he was talking about.

In fact they show a feel for rhythm as well as rhyme that is extremely rare among lyricising playwrights, though they frequently try to dispense more historical information than they or the audience can cope with. The highlight is undoubtedly the chanson duet 'Nostalgie de la Boue'. The cast, notably Stephen Moore and Julia Hills, come over very well. As a record it is, surprisingly, a better buy than the National's Guys and Dolls. I, who taped all nine hours of the television version, can hardly object to souvenirs of Nicholas Nickleby. But the album (That's Entertainment TER 1029) is fairly pointless, It gives the main themes from Stephen Oliver's score, of which the first - billed here as 'Overture London' though I think of it as Main Title Theme - revives happy memories.

Others I don't remember at all, and something called "The Farewell Waltz' is interminable, The cast are heard in choruses whose words are a bit more distinguishable than they were in the theatre. Mr Oliver's words for the 'Patriotic Song' that concluded the Romeo and Juliet travesty are excellent pastiche, as his snippet of Rossiniesque opera, with John Weedvine doing what sounds like the heavy father. A few scenes, or bits thereof, might have made the album indispensable. But then I don't understand why people buy LPs of film background music Courtney Kenny is an Irish pianist and opera executive who also performs programmes of arcane popular songs. His album Let Me See You Smile (Erase EO697), recorded before a live but muted audience, presents 14 of these.

He is best with British material, notably a pair of charmers by his great-uncle Percy French, and a gem called "Rheingold" (from The Girls from Gottenburg, an Edwardian show of which I had never heard) by Lionel Monckton and Adrian Ross which sends up Wagner - lyrically rather than musically - very nicely. There is also an Auden-Britten collaboration "Tell Me the Truth About Love' which ranks as a curiosity but sounds like an etiolated imitation of Cole Porter. Sondheim's 'Losing My Mind' is not his meat but he is the only singer I have heard make 'Home Sweet Heaven' (a mechanical list song from the musical version of Coward's Blithe Spirit) sound tolerable and even witty - and that includes Coward himself who didn't write it.

Two real rarities are "The Ragtime Pipes of Pan', very early Porter and very bouncy, and the Gershwins' party song 'Mischa, Jascha, Toscha, Sascha' which is about Russian composers and has very odd lyrics. Pace the sleeve this has been recorded before, on an American collectors' label, by a singer whom that sleeve declares to be Bobby Short but who is actually Arthur Schwartz, another of Mr Kenny's heroes. He does both verses and all three choruses of 'I Guess I'll Have to Change My Plan, Mr Schwartz's first (1929) hit and just about my favourite song. Mr Kenny has taste.
1983-02-06-coward-up-ended:
Coward up-ended

EVERY generation has its own bright-young-thing play, and Doug Lucie's Hard Feelings (Bush) will do fine for this one. It actually both accepts and subverts that description; most of its characters are addled, but one delivers the minority opinion -- obviously endorsed by the author -- that 'people aren't kinds of things, they're people.'

It is Coward up-ended: 'Living for Design,' perhaps. In the spring of 1981, Viv, recent Oxford graduate in English, holds court on an island: more precisely, in a posh house in Brixton owned by her parents, currently living in California. Young plays are beginning to divide into those about the poor unemployed and the rich semi-employed; Mr Lucie offers a familiar enough accumulation.

There is one model, female; one rock musician, male, looking androgynous, but with a hearty heterosexual appetite; one floating entrepreneur, currently very big in frisbees. Also one law student, apt to make the others uncomfortable with her seriousness, not to mention her Jewishness, not to mention her heavy left-wing boy-friend prophesying the coming riots. He is boorish; and it is notable that Mr Lucie eventually makes him sympathetic, not by softening him or pleading his case, but by turning the screws on everybody else.

He gets his characters on stage with remarkable rapidity, four of them rushing in and out the door while the remaining two sleep, their curly tops just visible above the duvet. Subsequent development, as the people get established, is a little slack, but the action gradually crystallises around Viv, hugging her space. ('Hello, room, you're all mine,' she says pitifully, left alone at the end of a scene, after squabbling over lovers and electricity bills.)

In the second act the poster explodes as Viv turns relentlessly on Jane the lawyer, provoking her with a Hitler poster, telling her to leave and refusing explanations with a neurotic self-righteousness (the thin hysteria of style) that is beautifully observed, forbidding the household to talk to her. They acquiesce, with or without misgivings according to temperament. The end finds Viv frantically tidying up against her parents' return. You might call it reversion to type, except that she never really went away.

There is nothing very new here, but the writing and the organisation are first-rate. I even want to see it again. The acting, under Mike Bradwell's direction, is excellent all round the clock. Frances Barber is Viv; Diana Katis the model who echoes her at her worst; Jennifer Landor a troubled presence as Jane, and Stephen Tiller a disruptive one as her man. Ian Reddington does Rusty the rocker with a quivering mastery that suggests a great future in the more neurotic classics; Baz the businessman, in whom decency stirs and is squashed, is played by Chris Jury with a slow, queasy comic authority that suggests a past with Hull Truck. The programme confirms the suggestion, and also -- in describing the piece as 'a viciously funny play set in Brixton in 1981' -- writes its own (accurate) review.

  

Peter Tinniswood's You Should See Us Now (Greenwich) begins as a toothless suburban comedy in which the men behave like little boys (the hero makes model trains) and the women boss them. This turns out to be the point; the play states that we are forever trapped in our childhood states. This is probably true, but by that time the damage has been done; we have spent ages watching the cast exercising in Ayckbournian style without getting laughs, while incidentally standing around in situations when most people sit down.

Once the author's thesis has emerged, all he can do is restate it; and the device he chooses -- having his grown-up actors actually play children -- yields an embarrassment far out of proportion to its occasional acuteness. Christopher Cazenove goes valiantly through an endless routine of holding his nose, jumping round in circles, and hooting; Delia Lindsay plays a shy girl (which she does well) who grows up into a trainee Penelope Keith, with which she seems unhappy.

For old-style domestic naturalism -- mainly wives yelling at their shiftless husbands -- you have to go these days to black plays. But being an old style -- and a thoroughly artificial one -- it needs tremendous gloss if it is to be brought off; and neither the writing nor the acting of Bitter Milk (Drill Hall) supplies it. The play is described as 'written by David Clough with original plot and additional material by Alton Kumalo,' and rather a lot of the material sounds additional.

Mr Kumalo himself plays with some panache as an illegal immigrant (a musician, who, in Dave Frischberg's immortal words, is so hip he even calls his girl-friend man), caught between the woman he lives with and the white feminist with whom he tries to contract a marriage of convenience. There is some decent writing ('you need O-levels to clean the toilets here'), but the production is listless, causing the audience to clap before the end because they hope it is the end.

  

The same thing happened at Beau Monde (ICA; ends today), presented by Omnibus, of Montreal, who seem to be school of Pina Bausch. But where the Bausch group have a mysterious gaiety about them, this dance-mime troupe go very earnestly through some familiar motions about people being group-oriented, but self-obsessed. Their chosen period is the Fifties, and they parade in the crew-cuts, bouffant hair-dos, sports jackets and prom dresses, familiar now only from the sleeves of Frank Sinatra reissues. (Which reminds me; the music, billed as 'popular tunes of the 50s,' is invariably too early or too late.) What is interesting though is that their image of prosperity is similar to the one of recession in Hard Feelings.

  

Readers who don't take the Guardian may like to know that David Hare, responding in that paper to the reviews of his play A Map of the World, has let it be known (a) that critics who like his plays are good guys and those who don't aren't, and (b) -- with reference to a late scene in this play -- that aid to Third World countries is given with strings attached. I tell you, this man has insights.

On his main, philosophical, argument, I think Mr Hare has gone raving mad. He claims that the reviews, being biased, prove the point he was making in the play: that we all see issues and events partially, and from whatever angle suits us. You'd think he'd be grateful for the corroboration, though he doesn't seem to be. But if the distorting tendency is as universal as he seems to believe (and as I certainly do), then critics are not going to be exempt from it.

It is not even desirable that they should be. It is not the critic's job to paraphrase the play, even if he had the space to do so. It is his job to describe, and try to account for, its impact; and, unless there are violent scenes in the auditorium, this has to mean its impact on him. This will not usually, from the public's point of view, be very misleading. I reckon that the percentage of good reviews received by most plays is about equal to the percentage of the potential audience that will enjoy them.
1983-02-13-touch-of-the-bunters:
Touch of the Bunters

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on a revival of 'Charley's Aunt,'

THOUGH he is no more than stocky, something about Griff Rhys Jones's performance of Lord Fancourt Babberley in Charley's Aunt (Lyric, Hammersmith) suggests the classic fat boy. He has a real Billy Bunter entrance, sneaking in to snaffle the other fellows' tuck -- or, this being undergraduate Oxford of the gilded days, champagne.

What keeps him going in his transvestite masquerade is vanity; one flourish of his fan, and one falsetto trill, and he realises he is very good at it. Thereafter he may grumble -- and he complains very Bunterishly about the ingratitude of the fellows for whom he is so spectacularly putting himself out -- but he perseveres, through a maze of curiosity, exhilaration and embarrassment.

At moments the surrealism of it all overcomes him; having poured tea into a gentleman's topper, he adds milk and sugar and stirs vigorously. The basic business is traditional, the additions not specially inventive, but the whole is carried by Mr Jones's frantically logical conviction; he really wants to be hung for a sheep. He is also rather touching when explaining the depths of his lovesickness. (And, what's more, he's lost his appetite.) His friends are sceptical, believing him to be a fool and love to be their own prerogative, so the play becomes a kind of revenge comedy. I, who have seen Frankie Howerd play Fanny and Babs, can hardly proclaim Mr Jones the funniest ever, but he is undoubtedly a good chap.

The production, by Peter James and Peter Wilson, is unusually solid. You may learn much from it about the petty snobberies that infected Oxford in the 1890s, if that's what takes your fancy. College gents habitually borrow money from their servant in order to tip him; David Ross is brazenly long-suffering about this, and about his sudden transformation to somebody else's butler in the last act; a symptom of both social and theatrical economy.

Brandon Thomas, who wrote the thing, took little trouble with subsidiary roles; Charley's aunt's nephew must be the most thankless character ever to insinuate himself into a title. (I mean the play's title; he doesn't become a duke.) But Mark Payton makes Jack, the prime mover, into a spoiled young intriguer, kicking the armchair in amorous frustration while declaring, 'I'm regularly nonplussed.' Mr Payton is an alert young actor who makes something of every line and plays fine period duets with bluff, broke dad (Terence Longdon) and antiphonally agreeable sweetheart (Anita Dobson).

  

A few weeks ago I turned the corner of Tottenham Court Road to see a coffin being loaded into the back of a small van. Even the undertakers, I decided, had been hit by the slump; but when I came up with the vehicle, it turned out to belong to Paines Plough, the touring theatre group. On Tuesday I tracked the hearse down to the Old Town Hall, Hemel Hempstead, where it played a leading role in Tony Marchant's Welcome Home.

Inside it is said to be a British soldier, killed in the Falklands. We meet five of his mates -- a corporal and four privates -- deputed to be official pall-bearers. The corporal is a hard man who says things like, 'Remember why we are here -- commit it to memory.'

Intentionally, accidentally or by happenstance the line-up recalls Serjeant Musgrave's Dance, and I started waiting for Mr Marchant to turn the tables: to reveal his characters as militant pacifists. One of them does momentarily go that way, brandishing the flag and asking what for. But it's a passing climax only; the play's instant political content is slight. The focus is not on the Falklands (Mr Marchant must trust us to make up our own minds about that), but on what makes men soldiers and what soldiering makes of them. The answer, much of the time, is bullying, verbal and physical; plus a kind of masochistic camaraderie that occasionally flowers into actual protective friendship.

Mr Marchant brings a fair amount of it off. The current white-hope playwright, he is the strongest example of a drift back to character. Our old young playwrights were either uninterested in people or contemptuous of them; they sounded dogmatic even when they weren't. That mould began to break with Stephen Poliakoff; and his juniors have cracked it open. What were thrilling ideas to the children of prosperity are ugly realities to those of the recession; and they are interested in their victims. This can result in sentimentality, but at least it starts in the right place.

In this play the more convincing the basic observation, the less are the proclamations. These characters do proclaim, usually in the wrong vocal register. When the corporal says, with sinister intent, 'We could become the nation's nurse,' he is having words put into his mouth. Even more unbelievably knowing is the weakest soldier's explanation of why pop music means so much to him. And the physical symptoms of his breakdown seem to have come out of a play.

You begin to see why naturalism is so frustrating a medium, but also why we have to keep coming back to it. Maybe a stylistic compromise is possible, but this production, though potentially well acted, has yet to find it. Nor has the play's argument been properly aligned with its action. The show visits York and Lancaster this week, and arrives at the Theatre Upstairs in March.

  

Secret Gardens (ICA) is sort of trancey. Composed of dance, music, bits of speech and fractions of song, it begins hypnotic, and ends tedious. It is based on the Edwardian children's classic of almost the same title and on the life of Nancy Cunard, these being taken as feminine poles of security and danger. I only know this from having read previews; none of it is mentioned in the programme or, to me, apparent in the show. (I haven't read the book, but so what?)

I suspect the obscurity is due less to arrogance than to absent-mindedness; they never dreamed we'd never know. All I got were some pleasing visuals (the verbals were very banal), the pleasure coming partly from the dance, but chiefly from the art (credited, like the direction, to Tim Albery, Antony McDonald, Geraldine Pilgrim and Ian Spink), a deep louvred chamber in which anything would look good.

At Pentameters, in Hampstead, there is by contrast a very basic staging of a fascinating text: Red Magic by Ghelderode (1898-1962, of Belgium). Mixing in the traditional characters of miser, misanthrope and alchemist, it builds up a marvellous nexus of sex, money and death: a man so covetous he even preserves his wife's virginity as a prize before losing to it a cozener who says he wants to get to Muscovy. (Haven't I heard something like that before?) The play goes way beyond practical joking, though, into real cruelty and obsession. Jeremy Blake acts best, though his range seems limited to various kinds of scorn, but this is a playwright who should be rescued from the devout, preferably by the National Theatre.

  

Caryl Churchill's Top Girls, reviewed here last year, are back at the Royal Court after success in New York; and unless something unfathomable has happened to them en route, they are the best play in London.
1983-02-20-breaking-bonds:
Breaking bonds

CARYL CHURCHILL'S Fen (Almeida) is about broken links, chiefly family ones. It takes place on an East Anglian farm, whose owner regards it as a money-machine, but also, quite genuinely, as a heritage. He is obliged to sell out, becoming a highly-paid employee on what was his own land. As someone remarks, nobody knows who owns anything any more. Probably, to judge from a sprightly prologue, it's the Japanese.

The main drama unfolds among the farm's potato pickers, mostly female. One, Val, leaves her unseen husband for a tractor-driver who is not strong enough for her. She also leaves her two small daughters. She cannot, however, keep away from them, and the conflict finally kills her. Another, Angela, has a teenage step-daughter whom she torments. She can't stop herself, but she wants to be stopped. Two lines sum her up: 'I have to hurt you worse' and 'Why do you like me, I don't want you to like me.'

Perhaps I should have made it broken bonds. Topographically, this is Edward Bond country, and so it is dramatically as well, far more a rural Saved than another Afore Night Come. Like Mr Bond, Miss Churchill writes bluntly, but not coarsely, about passion. Like him, she can put cruelty on stage (she does it, in the Angela scenes, with remarkable tact), and a classical death scene, and ghosts; this last as a very straightforward way of reminding the farmer of the sins of his fathers. She also has a good line in elders who remember, but cannot necessarily be trusted.

Top Girls was, is, a hard act to follow, and this play is far less high-spirited. But it picks up some of its predecessor's themes. It is, again, about women having to make up the rules as they go along. Val opts for a kind of liberation and finds there are taboos she cannot escape. The traditional comforts are no good to her (a sadly amusing prayer-meeting scene makes that clear), but she can find no new ones. Anyway the community in which she lives is tradition-steeped and family-fixated; people never stop talking about their relatives or their ancestors.

Apart from a whimsical finale everything in this play fits, no matter how eccentrically shaped it may seem. Miss Churchill tells us all we need to know; not necessarily, though, all we would like to know. But that may be the fault of the production; or, rather, of the kind of production. It is from Joint Stock, whose actors, though they did not improvise the play, researched its background and, presumably, assembled its details. But despite the title, and despite Annie Smart's wondrously earthy set, the play is not finally about the land, but the people on it.

Six actors play 21 roles, which means restless doubling and no chance to get to know anyone, this last compounded by an ostentatious chastity of outline. The method actually works against a sense of community; there are simply never enough people around. Jennie Stoller is fine as Val -- a real tragic figure, bewildered but whole -- but she is helped by having to play no other part save that of the ghost, which can reasonably be done as a guest appearance. My frustration at a potentially superb evening was aggravated by the theatre itself, which was freezing.

  

Pinter and you have some idea of Peter Gill's Kick for Touch (Cottesloe): two men, buddies; a woman, married to one and desired by both; all three characters Welsh instead of just one; the dialogue allusive, but moving occasionally into direct emotional statement. This shift of gears Mr Gill handles very well; he can make realistic dialogue work for him (cf. last week's remarks on Tony Marchant, who can't quite).

The three characters don't move about much; they sit round a table, and even when one is presumed to have left the stage, that one remains. Scenes blend into one another, disregarding time and space; the relationships dissolve and reform (neither man is called Jules, but one is Jim); mates are revealed as brothers, and wives as eternal mothers. It is all too compressed and too generalised to make any impact, and though it starts surprisingly un-boring, it does not continue so.

There are three very good actors present, though only one is at the top of his form. This is James Hazeldine, toused and disruptive. Kenneth Cranham is subdued, but rises to a rumbling climax; Jane Lapotaire's only noticeable acting blemish, a tendency to sing-song, is compounded by Celtic. Three actors, however good, is not many; in general practice, more means merrier, and the National is in a better position than most to act on this observation.

If a three-hander is The Caretaker or American Buffalo or (upping the number slightly) Mr Bond's Summer, then all is forgiven; if not, not. Minimalism is being confused -- especially at the Cottesloe -- with poetry; puritanism with integrity. And who wants integrity anyway? Not that spectacle is everything. At the Sheffield Crucible there is Don Juan the Lover (to be distinguished, of course, from Don Juan the Marine Biologist). This is set in a bull-ring, which certainly looks good and could hardly be more Spanish. Just to reinforce the point, the Don and his servant go through numerous matador's passes, a peasant girl says 'Ole' as soon as entering, and a wedding is accompanied by keening music, though that sounded oddly Jewish.

In addition there is an onstage audience that applauds the Don every time he says or does anything especially typical of himself, and there are frequent references to the fact that he is a legend in a pre-ordained play: scripts are consulted. Michael Boyd, the adaptor-director, is inventive, but I don't like any of his inventions.

  

What he has adapted are Moliere's Don Juan and the first play on the subject, Tirso de Molina's The Trickster of Seville; the story is told in alternate scenes from each. However you treat it, Juan had a one-track career; and by depriving each playwright of his own rhythm for disguising the fact you merely compound the monotony. Anyway they don't match; Moliere's Juan never gets it on, and Tirso's never fails to.

At the end Mr Boyd abandons both, to leave the eternal woman-chaser on stage with the eternal woman of his Catholic upbringing: i.e. at the foot of a large statue of the Madonna. It's a point. And, yes, it's more enterprising than doing Agatha Christie. And Siobhan Redmond as seduced fishergirl looks, acts and sings luscious.

James Hayes, a National Theatre actor of excellent character, is out on parole for two weeks at the Gate, performing A Horde of Unemployed Ventriloquists. This recital is drawn from the works of Flann O'Brien, in his journalistic Myles na Gopaleen hat. Some -- several -- of his erudite japes are too convoluted to survive theatrically, but Mr Hayes's delivery of them is impeccable, his pleasure communicated. His enunciation, while disguised as a remarkably seedy Dubliner, of the words 'Horse d'oeuvre' is a rich entertainment in itself.
1983-02-27-gill-in-a-pint-pot:
Gill in a pint-pot

Theatre

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

FORGIVE me for flogging an ailing horse; but I continue to wonder why the term "literary theatre" is applied to teemingly theatrical events like Nicholas Nickleby and A Handful of Dust that happen to be based on novels, while denied to the skeletal mood-and-memory pieces that have returned to fashion. The pieces whose dialogue - or monologue - so often harks back to the Georgian poets, and whose staging is the last refinement of the stripped, mannered naturalism pioneered at the Royal Court. The kind whose sets, production, acting and lighting shriek sensitivity at you. The kind currently represented at the Cottesloe by Harold Pinter's Other Places, by Peter Gill's Kick for Touch, and now by Mr Gill's revived Small Change, first seen at the Court in 1976.

There is an unspoken, maybe unconscious, assumption in these presentations (Fen, as produced by Joint Stock, is another one) that the audience should consider itself pretty privileged to be there. Since the audience pays to get in (I can just about remember what that feels like), this seems to me unwarranted, and on the verge of insulting. (I know that there are playwrights who believe in insulting the audience, but I think they are in the wrong profession. I do not, incidentally, count Messrs Pinter and Gill among them.) As I have said before, I resent it.

But I confess that these productions do create a kind of tension, and that it gets to me as well. Sometimes I fall asleep in my seat, but more often I sit on the edge of it, straining to catch something. (That's what I really resent. You can't even dismiss them with a good conscience.) Kick for Touch, though too small even for the Cottesloe - a Gill poured into a pint-pot - still kept me listening, and Small Change actually offers something.

Chiefly this is the relationship between two Welshwomen, living in neighbouring back-to-backs, resentful or afraid of their unseen husbands, bearing with their growing sons. (We watch the growing.) They console each other, even breaking at one point into a charming impromptu song-and-dance. One endures, the other cracks. One lives in unacknowledged bonds of passion with her son, the other can make no contact with hers. Maggie Steed is affectingly gentle, June Watson affectingly rugged. We see them in short scenes, ranging forwards and backwards in time. The duration is exactly matched to the dimensions of the subject.

The boys - James Hazeldine and Phillip Joseph - we get at length. They engage in lyrical retrospectives; indeed Mr Hazeldine seems to be the play's voice, which only confirms that autobiographers are their own least satisfactory characters. At the end, grown, they are given a sustained scene to themselves, making emotive accusations of betrayal on evidence that has never been presented.

The construction goes lumpy, and the lines collapse. The English will accept a lot of verbiage from the Welsh, as from the Irish but such phrases as "the hysterical flash of the present" would be unbelievable from anybody. The play concludes with a reprise of significant lines from its beginning: pure kitsch.

I dunno. When I saw Small Change on its last night at the Court, I was bored to death, but thought that it might be me, and that I was missing something marvellous. This time I wasn't bored, but I didn't marvel either.

  

Berlin, Berlin (Actors Touring Company, Warehouse) is an adaptation of a novel, and it is literary, by which I mean that it never takes on dramatic life. You don't actually feel that life slipping away between the adaptor's fingers, as in the bad old days of filleted schoolroom classics, but you come to the end of the evening realising that nothing has happened, though much has occurred, and that you haven't actually met anybody.

John Retallack, directing his own version of Robert Musil's book, delivers an intelligent, good-looking production, subverted by its need to make a statement. The more it goes on about Berlin, the less I felt like believing it. We are shown a collection of alienated people living in, or visiting, the Western sector. There are also songs, redolent of Brecht/Weill or Dietrich.

These, of course, are the ultimate cliches about the city. I imagine the intention is ironic, but they play as if there for their own sake. Why have all that music anyway? Isn't there enough to get through without it? That's another mark of literary theatre: excessive theatricalism. What we learn about Berlin is that it has a red-light district, paranoia, and a lot of anxiety about the bomb. It could be anywhere.

  

On the evidence of The Two Ronnies (Palladium) the West End's idea of showbiz luxury is, or remains, a flight of gold-painted steps adorned with light-bulbs. Aslant this, a line of dancing-girls do high kicks. Later on, and on, the same girls do the same kicks (though, to be fair, the sets change), while a quartet of haughty, glaring chorus-boys swivel their hips. British show-dancers might be great, they might be terrible; British choreographers aren't going to give us a chance to find out. Also on the bill are some good acrobats (French and Polish) and Strutz Bear Cats, a vocal group who represent Britain's latest ingenuous answer to Manhattan Transfer.

And there are Ronnie Barker and Ronnie Corbett, doing an anthology of their television material. They have not made the best possible choice: I remember their early shows, before their humour came to depend entirely on the great British euphemism, i.e., longish words taken to refer to parts of women's bodies.

I don't much mind this being sexist, but I do object to the monotony. Also to the waste of talent, especially of Mr Barker, a superb character actor with a rare blend of precision and effervescence, plus a virtuoso line in double-talk, fortuitously but pleasantly teamed with Mr Corbett, a stand-up comedian who does his stuff sitting down.

So what would I actually spend money on, if forced? A handful of classics; a couple of old musicals, Guys and Dolls and Mr Cinders; an extravaganza, Top Girls; a mod comedy, Hard Feelings; maybe a traditional piece of West Endery, Another Country. And of course a farce.

  

A new team of actors, mainly from what I think of as the Rudman era at the National Theatre, have taken over in Michael Frayn's Noises Off (Savoy); and they are mostly splendid, especially Benjamin Whitrow's desiccated charmer of a director. They all of course have great parts to play: Mr Frayn sets his characters up before he brings them down; and his farce-within-a-farce promises to be first-rate. The third act is still incredible (plays don't go to pieces in that way), but nobody minds. Michael Blakemore's direction remains exemplary.

None of my approved shows is what is known as "demanding." It's not the function of the theatre to make demands; that's for the audience. Nor is its function to "make you think"; you already know how to do that, and the chances of a playwright telling you something you don't already know - except on a purely factual level - are remote. Make them entertain you.
1983-02-27-poet-on-a-hot-tin-roof:
Poet on a hot tin roof

ROBERT CUSHMAN,
our Theatre Critic,
looks back on the life
and work of Tennessee
Williams, who died in
New York last week.

Tennessee Williams died at the age of 71. You have to go steadily back in time to find his landmarks.

1961: The Night of the Iguana, his last generally successful play. 1955: Cat on a Hot Tin Roof, the last to be greeted as the work of a modern master. 1945: A Streetcar Named Desire, his most famous play. 1944: The Glass Menagerie, his first hit. These last two the ones on which his reputation currently rests, the ones that get revived.

So for nearly 40 years his career went downhill: for the last 25, pretty steeply. And yet his reputation never really faded. He might be forgotten for lengthy periods but when remembered he was never discounted. He was ritually ranked with Arthur Miller as one of America's two best living playwrights, the two of them, with O'Neill, as the three best ever. Of their juniors, only Edward Albee looked briefly like a contender, and that was very brief.

Veneration of Williams was not just a patriotic American custom. For the 10 years after the war he and Miller were the dominant dramatists in the English language, the inspiration of our own new wave in the Fifties. They coincided with a great period in American acting and direction. Stanley Kowalski in Streetcar was Marlon Brando's last and greatest stage role; Elia Kazan directed both that play and Cat. Kazan's contribution is evident in the published scripts; they are immensely atmospheric plays, delighting in the stagecraft that summons up the Deep Williams South. The pre-war American playwrights had been gaunt realists, as Miller was. Williams was sensuous, a post-austerity dramatist. That was part of his early appeal in Britain.

Everything about him was picturesque. Born in Columbus, Mississippi, he spent his early years in genteel poverty in St Louis. College was interrupted by a Dickensian period in a shoe factory, culminating in a breakdown. Before his first success, he was a waiter in New Orleans and New York. That success was the autobiographical Glass Menagerie, in which the narrator, Tom (Tennessee's real name was Tom) recalls his dreambound mother, his shy, crippled sister, and the stolid gentleman caller who raises and then crushes their romantic hopes. The young heroine's cherished glass animals were part of Williams's and his sister's own past. They stand for the bright, vulnerable creatures who go through all his plays, subjected to increasingly harsh pressures.

The belle of them all, of course, is Blanche DuBois, the heroine of Streetcar, who comes to her sister's New Orleans apartment, echoing to the sounds of jazz from the streets, weakly but valiantly upholding the flag of art, reeling from marriage to a homosexual, toying with the men who come her way until Stanley, her brother-in-law, ups and rapes her.

When Streetcar was revived in London in 1974, it seemed as full of quotations as Hamlet: "It's Della Robbia blue," "Sometimes there's God so quickly," "I have always depended on the kindness of strangers" -- the last a wonderfully moving plea as Blanche surrenders herself to the men from the mental hospital. Williams had a feeling for degradation which at this time was wholly compassionate. It may be that Streetcar drained him of what he had to say; though he arranged it more ambitiously, or at least more allegorically, in Camino Real, a flawed fantasy that preaches idealism while revelling in the gutter: a Spanish-American gutter (Williams was always a Hispanophile) that must be an irresistible lure to directors.

Streetcar was first presented in London in 1949 by a non-profit company exempt from entertainment tax; there was much fuss about the taxpayer's money being used (or at least rebated) for immoral purposes. Ludicrous as that now seems, Williams's later plays began to look like parodies of the sex-obsessed dramas he had been accused of writing.

Cat on a Hot Tin Roof, powerful in its day, now reeks of Southern Gothic and also of a homosexual writer's self-conscious attempts to grapple dramatically with heterosexual themes. These became increasingly strident, just as the titles -- Orpheus Descending, Sweet Bird of Youth, The Seven Descents of Myrtle -- became increasingly flowery. A sort of sadism crept in, the cruelty being piled on in direct ratio to the helplessness of the victims. It got more than Jacobean; there was cannibalism in Suddenly Last Summer, a poet dismembered by dogs in Orpheus.

Williams had always had talents for melodrama and farce; some of his later work became unconsciously farcical as the melodrama jumped out of control. But there were still surprising spurts of genuine humour. The Night of the Iguana was a notably benign work, and Vieux Carre, his last to be seen in London, revisited the scene of Streetcar in rambling autumnal mood.

In person Williams was an unpredictable but enthusiastic laugher; I once sat in front of him when he almost brought a performance at the Royal Court (of someone else's play) to a roaring standstill. He was also a fully paid-up paranoid. Kenneth Tynan has left an affectionate portrait of Williams preparing to meet Ernest Hemingway ("they tell me that Mr Hemingway usually kicks people like me in the crotch") and William Goldman wrote of him passing from the particular ("the reviewers don't like me") to the general ("I was not a well-liked kid"). Working, he said, was his escape, and he never let up.

The RSC wanted to do Sweet Bird last year, but say they were gazumped by Elizabeth Taylor. Either way we should see it soon. It was once dismissed as over-heated but our harsh climate is surprisingly favourable to hot-house art. We could be in for a Williams renaissance.
1983-03-06-living-in-the-dark:
Living in the dark

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Glasgow

THERE are two plays going on in Crystal Clear (Wyndhams), which in a short show is remarkable and - since they don't get in one another's way - very good value. One is an informative account of the experience of blindness. Of all the afflictions recently examined on the stage, this is probably the one most suited to exploration in the theatre; the one most easily related to what the audience itself experiences.

There are three characters: Thomasina, who is blind; Jane, who can see; and Richard, a diabetic who loses his sight in the course of the action. The most electric moment comes after a scene between Thomasina and Richard; he is now blind, so obviously the light is off. Enter Jane, who switches it on. The audience, who have also grown accustomed to the gloom but still find it frustrating, blink.

Earlier we have watched a one-eyed Richard, trying to seduce Thomasina, bring her back to his flat and show her round. That may be an odd choice of phrase, in the circumstances, but it's how he behaves; he even hides the underwear that, being a born slob, he has left lying about. "What are your first impressions?" he asks. "It feels," she says, "very spacious."

The piece was evolved by its three actors, under the direction of Phil Young. They have uncovered extraordinarily fruitful territory; the opportunities for heartrending comedy are almost limitless. With remarkable tact they pass on to other ground. Richard and Jane are at the fag-end of a relationship. She wants commitment from him: failing that, confrontation. He will do anything - including, it seems, go blind - to avoid confrontation. What Richard wants is to be dependent, on his own terms: a neurosis which, allied here to great joky charm, lifts the play partially clear of the current rut of disability drama.

Does that sound grudging? The play is thoroughly honest but obstinately small, and the two qualities are interdependent. A row, here, is just a row; so baldly that Jane (Diana Barrett), meant to be caring but tactless, comes out bloody-minded. Anthony Allen's Richard is finely balanced between the attractive and the unforgiveable, and Philomena McDonagh gives Thomasina an aspect of serenity that the play finally shatters.

The shattering, though, is where the production falls shortest: when the two blind lovers lose their defences, we get two actors shouting at each other. But the piece pulls itself together, ending, with universally applicable bleakness, as a picture of love trying to shut out the dark. Images like that seem impossible to avoid. The play vibrates with them. Jane says to Richard, "I'm fed up with a relationship where we never see each other." Intentionally or not, it rings.

  

I don't know why Michael Wilcox wrote Lent (Lyric Studio, Hammersmith), but I'm glad he did. He tells of a boy being 13 in 1956; as Mr Wilcox was himself, and as I was. Greedily I lapped up the references: Journey into Space, the Goons, The Cruel Sea (cadet edition), the Jennings books, Ainsworth's antiquated Old St Paul's borrowed from the school library and cherished for its horrific bits. Only the local cinema bothered me, showing The Crimson Pirate and Captain Horatio Hornblower; but maybe they were revivals, shrewdly programmed for school holidays.

Our orphaned hero spends these holidays at school; he has to, since his grandmother owns it, or at least holds it in trust for him. This is one of a series of puns supporting the temporal title. The boy starts by "borrowing" a starting pistol. "Don't be foolish, Paul," says his headmaster, temporarily misleading us as to the kind of play we're getting into, "hand over the gun."

The headmaster is a narrow man, but he is also a disappointed one, and Dennis Edwards makes him comprehensible and almost sympathetic: ditto Jean Anderson as his peremptory wife, who lets murder stories go to her head. Grandma, whom they simultaneously fear and despise, gives Patience Collier her best, and best taken, opportunity for years: dignified and probably wise. An assistant master, Paul's confidant, is given an enchantingly easygoing performance by Wensley Pithey: beset, like all the adults, by a long consciousness of failure, but transmuting it into autumnal avuncularity.

The play, indeed, has some of the shock-effect of 84 Charing Cross Road; everybody in it is decent. This even applies to Paul, played without embarrassment (high praise for a grown-up) by Jonathan Kent. I can't see that it is about anything more than the delayed consequences of having been born in 1943. I think that's a superb subject, but I'm biased.

  

The Custom of the Country (Citizens', Glasgow) written in 1619 by Fletcher and Massinger, is the most improbable play I have ever seen. The custom is a droit du seigneur; to escape it, two heroes and a heroine rush off to Lisbon, where they are separated, and meet with many strange and sexy adventures.

One fellow becomes the prey of a rich nymphomaniac; his ruttish brother is employed as a stud in a brothel for ladies. Both get exhausted. There are also duels and potions. After five acts have elapsed the play stops.

This kind of purely narrative, purely titillating drama stopped being written when the theatre ceased to be a mass medium. It passed, of course, to the cinema; accordingly Robert David Macdonald, directing, and Michael Levine, designing, have set it in Hollywood, or at least have peopled it with movie archetypes. After an outrageously drab prologue we pass to a land full of pink furniture, lit by studio lamps.

Guiomar (Jill Spurrier), a predatory matron, is Gloria Swanson in Sunset Boulevard; Duarte (Rupert Farley), her braggart son, is Mickey Mouse, complete with tail; Zabulon (Ron Donachie), the sinister Jew, is Sydney Greenstreet; and Hippolyta (Fidelis Morgan) sounds like Mae West, but looks like Jean Harlow; whichever, her entrance, acknowledging applause and clutching an Oscar, had me laughing very loud. The melodrama can be played full out, and the occasional genuine emotion can quite unexpectedly register.

The less lovable side of the Citizens' is also on show. Heavy cuts become, by the end, cavalier and confusing; and whatever became of the funniest line, a ruffian's declaration that he is always available for a murder, but he's out of practice at beating? More serious is a pervasive misogyny that delights in leaving all the women frustrated, and plays the plight of the knackered gigolo (Lorcan Cranitch) not for laughs against him, but for horror of the predatory female sex. Still, where else?

  

Clare Davidson's production of Miss Julie (Duke of York's) is much the most lucid I have seen, particularly in its marking off of the social and sexual components in the confrontation of lady and servant. Stephen Rea as Jean lets us see every calculation, every spasm of lust, every pang of fear. Cheryl Campbell, tresses flaming, is audacious to a fault, sounding as if she has wound herself up in the wings, and doesn't dare let go. Occasionally she touches ground and is great, but she is in danger of acting herself into a corner.
1983-03-13-half-cock-heartbreak:
Half-cock Heartbreak

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Shaw at the Haymarket.

IT would be nice if the classical programme at the Haymarket had managed to include one play that had not previously been done by the National Theatre. The management might have done themselves a service as well as us; unfortunate comparisons were bound to be made, never more than in the new production of Heartbreak House, which, with Captain Shotover at its helm and his nautical house as its setting, seems fair to describe as the flagship of the season.

John Schlesinger directed this play, to great admiration, in the National's last days at the Old Vic; and I feel, after all this time, like apologising to him. I stated then that, given a good enough cast (and this play always attracts stars), no director could go wrong with Heartbreak House; the luminaries, all having their moments, would automatically arrange themselves into an ensemble governed by the English sense of fair play, and Shaw's text, self-orchestrating, would do the rest. John Dexter's production is here to confute me. It is cast to the nines and it is no disaster, but it falls continually short.

His actors rarely connect with one another, and the play disperses into a series of random conversations, which themselves sometimes become collections of random remarks. I now see that for the whole thing to come together, and to make patterns in the mind, some kind of confidence trick has to be worked.

Shaw gives the hint by insisting on a thick and rambling setting, and by beginning romantic comedy; Jocelyn Herbert's ascetic design kills its atmosphere almost at first glance, besides denying the actors effective entrances. It improves in the second act when curtains are drawn, and even more in the third when the action moves outside, but by then the damage has been done.

It is compounded by Rex Harrison's performance as Shotover. He has some perfectly timed deflationary throwaways, and he rises to the prophetic moments, but in the middle ground of the role he offers only mildly eccentric geniality. There is no iron in him; and we disbelieve not only the captain's seafaring past, but his despairing present. Shotover talks of "the horror of an old man drinking," but we feel no horror here. It should represent Shaw's terror of his own decay; if that is absent, the play becomes very complacent.

Of course it is an attack on the governing and intellectual classes of the First World War, but that assault is less comprehensive than is often supposed, and unless the author is personally involved, it is of little interest. Anyone can satirise other people.

On the first night Mr Harrison was uncertain of his lines (he destroyed Shotover's first good joke and his last great cry) and slow on his cues; and the second fault was even more alarming than the first. It defused the tension of the air-raid, otherwise the best of the production, with Doris Hare's nurse turned to a harpy exulting over the dead.

En route there are other lightweight performances: note Rosemary Harris's Ariadne, professional but subdued, and Frank Middlemass's capitalist Mangan, pleasant enough, but too unassuming to be worth bringing down. Paul Curran, another actor afflicted with uncertainty, nevertheless brings great quizzical force to the gentle Mazzini; Simon Ward is a public schoolboy spoiled for life as Randall the rotter; Mel Martin, though too old for the virginal role, goes a fine disillusioned progress as Ellie.

The flamboyant Hector is done by Paxton Whitehead, an actor to whom extravagance comes natural; only his Act Two invocation, "fall and cease," is underdone. On which note, it is ingenious to have the personnel singing the blues for the incantation that ends the previous act, but the effect is to make the words sound as much like doggerel as they look.

There remains, thankfully, Diana Rigg's Hesione, which combines gypsyish beauty, moon-faced comic attack and an honest, unembarrassed audience rapport. Miss Rigg is a rarity - an apparently unselfish personality performer. But Shaw needs - and used almost automatically to get - star performances thoroughly fused. The recent National Major Barbara gave us the fusion without the stars; this offers the reverse. Neither is enough.

  

La Fianza Satisfecha is the play, conjecturally by Lope de Vega, which John Osborne once adapted as A Bond Honoured. As The Outrageous Saint, it now arrives at the Grove, Hammersmith, unadapted but not quite unashamed. In some ways the Stage Fright company's approach is more perverse than Mr Osborne's. He found a play he could not stomach and rewrote it, chiefly by denying repentance to the central character.

This is Leonido, a Sicilian blade who rapes his sister, blinds his father and is probably not above ringing the church bell when everybody is trying to sleep. Like Satan, Cain, Don Juan and Faust (there is, incidentally, a play called Don Juan and Faust by the German romantic Grabbe, and I want to see it), he gets a divine comeuppance, and ends crucified and repentant.

Mr Osborne kept the crucifixion, but not the development, which was odd; Gub Neal's production keeps both, but signals its disbelief in them, which is odder, especially since the play plainly has the courage of its convictions and communicates them powerfully. I see the problem, but I cannot officially approve of the solution, nor in any capacity of the musical interludes, even if it is fun to hear a Moorish maiden sing country-and-western.

However, staging and performance are far above the level we addicts usually endure when seeking neglected texts in neglected venues. John Lyne Pirkis acts Leonido as a baffled biker; the others, including several women playing men and playing them well, portray his opponents as deserving everything they get. His conventionally conventional servant is changed to a sceptical harlequin (or columbine), but what else would you expect? Some day - not necessarily tomorrow, since there are other Spanish plays to be attended to - I want to see this work done straight.

  

The Soho Poly last week harboured two plays advertised as about radio, and full of static. The first, Nature of Communication, was sketchy; the second, World Service, protracted. They're off now anyway.
1983-03-20-florentine-intrigues:
Florentine intrigues

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN in London and Oxford.

I GRUMBLED recently about the National Theatre's weakness for small-cast plays, but the British premiere of Lorenzaccio (Olivier) does a lot to balance the books. I counted 45 actors' names in the programme, and most of them are doubling. It is a gladsome spectacle and surprisingly easy to keep track of.

Alfred de Musset wrote this Renaissance extravaganza in 1832, and its prodigality has two traceable causes: (a) he and his compatriots had just found out about Shakespeare, and felt liberated; (b) precociously disillusioned with the theatre at the age of 23, Musset gave no thought to practicalities. His text has as many scenes as this production has players.

Lorenzaccio is a denigratory nickname bestowed on Lorenzo de Medici, young cousin of the equally young Duke of Florence. Tyrannicide is his mission in life, and he becomes the ruler's confidant and procurer, so as to get within sword's reach of him.

He gives Florence the chance to become a republic again, a chance Florence - through a combination of clerical intrigue, military intimidation and popular apathy - fails to take. In this, we are assured, Musset saw the reflection of his own society, the bourgeois monarchy of Louis Philippe.

He stakes everything on his protagonist, and wins. Lorenzo has been described as a modern Hamlet, but in fact he is never in doubt about whether to murder. He more resembles Hamlet's Jacobean successors, the cankered sensualists, critical appraisers of their own degradation.

Lining up a female relative for the ducal bed, he more or less re-enacts 'The Revenger's Tragedy.' He feels himself unworthy of his destiny because he has been corrupted, not by his revenge, but by its preparation. He has been the duke's accomplice, so, except as a kind of suicide, his deed is ethically meaningless. It turns out to be politically meaningless as well.

It is a fragile, skin-deep world we are presented with, alive to sensation, but to little else. Its hero, embodying it, gives unity to a sprawling canvas.

It is, in the best sense, a lightweight play, and one informed by a lazy whimsicality very much of its period. In the original - not, unfortunately, in John Fowles's adaptation - we hear of Lorenzo 'spitting into a well to make circles in the water: my greatest pleasure.' That may be camouflage, but it also sums up the play and the character.

One of Lorenzo's pranks is striking off the heads of statues; and one he seems to have decapitated - unknown to art historians - is Michelangelo's 'David.' At any rate, there it is when we enter the Olivier, its head on the ground, but still dominating John Gunter's set, and there it remains. I suppose it is possible that the National imported the original from Florence and dropped it, but it seems more likely that we are being offered a metaphor.

The statue sprouts scaffolding, and a stonemason - who appropriates the citizenry's most defiant lines - spends the evening on it, trying to put Humpty Dumpty together again. He never does succeed.

The stage is patrolled - Florence being a fief of the German empire - by guttural soldiers with gutterish manners. These devices are heavy-going but effective, and this is true of Michael Bogdanov's production in general. It has no special imagination, and the abrupt endings to the brief scenes often leave it with egg on its face; actors stomp off or stay to move the furniture. But it has plenty of guts and energy, and these are the immediate requirements.

Later productions may add in subtlety, but they are not likely to improve on the bloodbath Mr Bogdanov offers at the climax. His casting in the higher reaches is, shall we say, unsurprising: Michael Bryant as wronged honest man and grieved father, Basil Henson as smooth cardinal. Lower down there is a lot of backslapping, more verbal than physical; Mr Fowles's version may not be virtuoso prose, but it deserves finer tuning than it gets here. Frances Viner pummels her way through the moral qualms of the duke's mistress, and she is one of the better ones.

The duke himself is more a condition than a person and Clive Arrindell leaves him that way. Everything rests on Greg Hicks as Lorenzo and he, if lacking in mischief, gives a very clear picture of a disgusted spirit. The play makes sense, grips attention, and smells of immortality.

  

Second billing in Marilyn! (Adelphi) goes to a character called the Era, who sings at the close: 'Write your books and write your plays and try to capture her in your songs/I'm the one to whom the girl belongs.' This, preceded by a brilliantly engineered montage of Monroe clips, decisively trumps the show itself: they say one cannot capture Marilyn Monroe on the stage, and we believe them.

To do it, they upstage their own star, Stephanie Lawrence, which is unfair. She acts well, dances splendidly, sings superbly: the last without the self-congratulatory air generally assumed by British musical starlets when they hold a high note. She cannot capture the original's sexuality, but it is a condition of the myth on which the show trades that nobody could.

As an actress Miss Lawrence is at her best before the fall, growing up in an orphanage, marrying teenage, switching off the radio which is only announcing something about Pearl Harbour. As Tom Stoppard might have phrased it, she wasn't Marilyn then; the script is happier with Norma Jean. Once in Hollywood it accelerates through the familiar biography, leaving by default the impression that Marilyn consciously created her own image. If she was that much in control, why did she go to pieces?

Meanwhile one ticks off the echoes, some of them probably accidental: 'West Side Story,' bopping at the prom; 'Annie,' an orphanage and two dogs; 'Sweeney Todd,' a crazy mother; 'Fiddler on the Roof,' a Jewish wedding, courtesy of Arthur Miller; above all 'Evita': distant but omnipresent narrator, media heroine and the experience of being told nothing you did not already know.

Also the form, pop eclecticism with the bits joined together to make a kind of opera. As such, it is a smoother job than 'Evita'; the music may not be distinguished, and the lyrics less than, but they do link up persuasively, sped on their way by Larry Fuller's very tidy staging, which incorporates a couple of fine ensemble numbers, including a dance by adoring males gazing at the famous nude calendar: the one time the show makes a real musical-comedy statement. Bill Byers's orchestrations resound with nervous energy, though the music may be what they are nervous about.

  

The Oedipus Plays (Oxford Playhouse) should really be called the Creon plays; he is the one character common to 'Oedipus the King,' 'Oedipus at Colonus' and 'Antigone,' the Sophoclean trio (not trilogy) here combined by Stephen Spender. Arthur Cox plays him as a pot-bellied politician who never dared hope for kingship and is over-assertive when he gets it. Having made his fatal mistakes, he exits moaning 'blind, blind,' thus linking up of course with Oedipus, who puts out his own eyes (and starts the proceedings by announcing that he has come 'to see'), and Tiresias, the sightless prophet.

If this strikes you as facile, I would not argue with you. All three plays are done as bold political melodrama, the last right, the first tight but bafflingly cheapened, and the middle one incomprehensible. Richard Durden as Oedipus maintains his actor's dignity whatever may have been done to his character; Moira Redmond is a smooth and powerful Jocasta; and the choruses seem out of place.

  

Vanbrugh's The Provoked Wife (Warehouse) is the best of the three ATC productions I have seen: a sane, bitter view of sex, marriage and divorce. Lady Fancyfull, a spoiled beauty, is serenely played as a frump, but Christine Braddell's Lady Brute is a treasure, an actress more provoking (never mind provoked) drawing her clothes on than many are taking them off.
1983-03-27-bits-of-bradshaw:
Bits of Bradshaw

Theatre

ROBERT CUSHMAN on Howard Barker's new play at the Royal Court.

There is a current form of play that proceeds by seizing a small historical moment, and imagining around it. An example is Howard Barker's Victory (Royal Court), which begins with the exhumation of John Bradshaw.

Bradshaw was president of the judges who condemned Charles I to death; at the restoration of Charles II he was one of those whose corpse was dug up, gibbeted and exhibited. Bradshaw's wife, or widow, is the central character of this play. Described in text and programme simply as Bradshaw--either for feminist reasons or because Mr Barker did not want to remind us of the Mrs Bradshaw who featured so prominently in early soap-powder commercials--she goes through the play searching for the remains of her severed spouse.

By the end she has assembled all the bits, including the head: a collectors' piece, since the current monarch has been using it as a mascot. Bradshaw's quest thus serves dramatically as a means of bringing disparate characters together. This is Mr Barker's shapeliest play; his penultimate scene is as comprehensive a reunion as could be found outside a Shakespearean epiphany or a pantomime finale: less cheerful though.

Apart from Bradshaw and the monarch (Sellar and Yeatman laid it down that Charles II, being merry, was less a King than a Monarch, and Mr Barker's Charles likes it that way) those present include the founder of the Bank of England, a semi-discarded royal mistress, a court poet, a cashiered Cavalier bully who has spent the play in lubricious pursuit of Bradshaw, the atheistic Puritan who has accompanied her on her flight, and her long-lost son, a medic now specialising lucratively in venereology. They make up a ripe slice of post-revolutionary old England: a state-of-the-nation play in wigs.

Victory is Bondishly subtitled Choices in Reaction. Main title and sub are both, of course, loaded with puns. There is the royalist victory, which leads to acts of revenge on dead bodies and a reign of terror against the living carried out by pox-ridden old soldiers. There is Bradshaw's victory in coming through this landscape with herself, if not her husband, in one piece. There is her reaction to her situation, which is to keep her head down and her pockets, where possible, full; and there is that of her male companion, who blunders outspokenly into martyrdom, but happens to be consumed by guilt at having revealed the dead leveller's grave in the first place.

Bradshaw thinks this man is a fool, and she is probably right. Her own course is not heroic, but it is not despicable either, and any blame can be attached to the times rather than to her. Some of her actions may be reactionary; as are certainly those of the king, trying to hang on to his prerogative, and of the new financiers, trying to limit it. Reactionary of course meaning right-wing; by what romantic-semantic convention do we accept that the left never reacts to anything?

A primal banking conference is cartooned in Mr Barker's best brand of deadly knockabout, and he is very good on sex: from Charles's compulsive fumblings to Bradshaw's enforced composure after rape to her assailant's disappointment: 'I come off so miserable. I think love would be to come off and be happy.' That is the best moment in the play. On the other hand Charles's melancholia is over-extended, and his courtiers are grotesques assembled so that the author can tell us at length how grotesque they are.

The movement from one set piece to another tends to be clotted. But the dialogue can be off-handedly funny and is modern without obvious anachronism. Continual expletives do a lot to link the two periods, though I had an old-maidish sympathy with the odd character who wished they would stop from time to time. Bradshaw, in this Joint Stock production, provides a superb role for Julie Covington, who excels in commonsense and bewilderment, the last reserved for people--the majority--who do not see the world as clearly as she does. Also notable are Eleanor David as two strumpets and a maid, David Lyon and Kenny Ireland. Nearly everyone in fact.

Clegg, Mr Barker's poet, says that he has written a tragedy and been promised production 'for what a promise is worth, not a lot in the theatre.' That little in-joke gets us to Michael Rudman's Short List (Hampstead), which is about the deliberations of a committee judging a playwriting award apparently modelled on that given annually in memory of George Devine. At least, the Harry whom this one commemorates, and whom the characters obsessively remember, was a producer much given to encouraging new talent.

His heirs are a shifty but engaging bunch: rather frightening emblems of the radical impulse gone prosperous, and furious at the idea of rebellion going on without them, and clutching a young writer yearly to their collective breast as a prophylactic. A young male playwright who turns up and insults them (they interview candidates as well as reading their plays, which seems a daft idea) is obviously one of their sort; a shy, resentful female playwright is obviously not. Morally, if in no other way, she has the last laugh.

I got a great deal of pleasure merely out of trying to identify the characters. Three I was certain of; and even if I am wrong, it's too late now, I've had my fun. Mr Rudman's prowess at keeping a stageful of characters verbally active and alive should not be underestimated, even if at times he coasts on bitching. He did not direct the play; Mike Ockrent did, with a wonderful cast.
