Spacious and resplendent, the redone Old Vic is once again an exciting place to visit. Ed Mirvish has done a good deed, giving the place not only a new coat of paint, but a new sense of purpose.

His first subscription season kicks off with Blondel, which is fun if nothing else. Its hero is the medieval minstrel who notoriously hung around outside every prison window in Europe, humming and strumming, before finally locating his incarcerated monarch Richard Coeur-de-Lion.

In this version he unhistorically, or at least unlegendarily, arranges his master's escape, though since he is but a singing fool he needs help. He gets it from his determined girlfriend; she may be a serf (though an uncommonly well-dressed one), but she is never the weaker vassal. Also of assistance is an assassin; hired by Prince John to kill the king, he would prefer to murder the minstrel (he knows his own limitations), but he actually and accidentally bumps off Richard's gaoler, the proto-Nazi Archduke of Austria.

Blondel ("he was overdue to write a million-selling rondel") is presented as an aspiring pop-star whose previous near-misses include Groats from Heaven and Send in the Jesters and who travels with a trio of back-up vocalists called the Blondettes. Doesn't that tell you all you need to know? Welcome to 1189 and all that.

Narrative links are chanted by a quartet of monks; these are played by Cantabile, who sound like the King's Singers, only -- since their plainsong McGonagall is meant to sound funny -- a lot less irritating. They explain that the Lion Heart's subjects would never have thought of him as Richard I, since they were ignorant of any future royal Dicks.

Tim Rice's lyrics take him back to Joseph and the Amazing Technicolour Dreamcoat, a good place for him to go. His jokes do not always sit comfortably on the music, but they are mostly good and they keep coming. Stephen Oliver's tunes have less theatrical size than Andrew Lloyd Webber's, but more wit and taste; and the main love-duet, The Least of My Troubles, is charming. It does not manage to make the love-interest interesting; and though Paul Nicholas does heavy duty as Blondel, the evening runs out on him.

It is probably impossible to be funny to music for a whole evening; and, like all the Rice and/or Webber shows, this one eschews dialogue almost entirely. If the most successful performances come from David Burt as John and Chris Langham as his hit-and-miss man, this is partly due to the allure of villainy, but also because they are occasionally allowed to talk.

Peter James's production makes the most of all opportunities, including those provided by Tim Goodchild's sets, which divide and conquer like richly coloured amoebae. The Falklands are momentarily a factor when our heroine derides the Third Crusade as "a war in some far-off place no one has ever heard of." (Jerusalem?) Blondel, outside the prison, does not sing "Open the door, Richard."

Blondel was by far the best of the week's three tuners. Many of its weaknesses -- a dull central romance, undeveloped characters, a tendency to wander musically into the middle of the road -- are shared by Dear Anyone (Cambridge), where they are far more damaging, since this show takes itself very seriously. Its heroine is the agony-aunt on a New York daily. She seems to reply to her correspondents directly rather than in print, but this odd practice at least brings together (through a mix-up in envelopes) a shy Manhattan cabby and a New England illiterate.

Their story is told in the best number of the evening; they are then dropped. So, for the most part, is the show's ostensible subject; we proceed to the familiar story of the career-woman, and the conflict between her work and her love-life. We are told nothing substantial about either, so the show keeps wrong-footing itself.

Don Black's lyrics are competent and consonant, but lack any individual spark. Geoff Stephens's music is mostly hollow, especially when it attempts to be dramatic. Jack Rosenthal wrote the book, which, coming from so able a workman, is a disgrace. However, since he had to fit his script around existing songs (this is one of those started-as-an-album projects), it may not be his fault that the story caves in. The uncertainty of focus was there from the start, and he has thrown in some good one-liners.

An abiding puzzle is why an all-British team set their tale in America. Have they doubts about its universality? Or are they merely trying to make us, and themselves, feel hip? Imitation Americana is all over the theatre at the moment; it is a trend to which I have probably contributed myself, but that doesn't mean I have to approve of it.

As a vehicle for Jane Lapotaire (authentically tender-tough) it halts. Better to have brought over Woman of the Year, a more efficiently mechanical show with the same plot. Or revived Bells are Ringing, which also has a scatty interfering heroine. Other influences, conscious or otherwise: Chicago, for one whole song; On the Town, for one whole dialogue routine. Not to mention Guys and Dolls; Stubby Kaye, the first man to sing "Sit Down You're Rockin' the Boat," obliges here with another gospel rouser, only this one doesn't rouse. Was it in his contract, or just last-minute desperation?

Mr Kaye, who is wasted, plays a mailman who gets to be features editor. I thought this was going to turn to a practical joke, but it's for real. (The other way round, I might believe it.) Ralph Koltai's three-decker set is equally cut off from journalistic reality; it also eats up most of the playing-area, confining choreography to a few automaton formations on the front strip of the stage. I liked Arlene Allan best, as Birdbrain of Boston. David Taylor's direction is diffuse.

  

The Duenna (Young Vic) is a ballad-opera by Sheridan to which Lance Mulcahy has affixed not only new music but additional dialogue and extra lyrics. You do not need a crib to identify these; whenever a clinch is imminent, Mr Mulcahy has one lover sing to another "Each time I wonder where you are/I turn round and there you are." This happens five times; no wonder we are gladdened.

Sheila Steafel looks deeply uncomfortable in the title-role, Trevor Peacock is a reliable heavy father; but the only performer to emerge with real credit is Amanda Redman, a very handsome heroine. Sheridan's comic Jew, who was not very offensive, has been changed into a comic Australian, who is. The setting is Seville, so Frank Dunlop's production has a lot of heel-clicking. I think I hate musicals.

  

Marivaux's masterpiece False Admissions has been brought to the Lyric Studio, Hammersmith, by Shared Experience. In this comedy every character is simultaneously gripped by sexual and economic passions, and in his determination to make all clear Mike Alfreds offers an over-disciplined but fascinating production. Another Marivaux is added this week, so we shall speak more of this.
1983-11-20-masterly-marivaux:
Masterly Marivaux

THEATRE
by ROBERT CUSHMAN

MARIVAUX, who wrote comedies in Paris in the first half of the eighteenth century, has a fair claim to be the classic playwright most unfairly neglected by the British theatre. Very few of his plays have ever been published in English; though I remember stumbling some 15 years ago on a clumsy translation of his 'Fausses confidences' and deciding, in its despite, that this was a masterpiece.

I have waited ever since for official confirmation, now finally supplied by Shared Experience at the Lyric Studio, Hammersmith. The play has been translated by Timberlake Wertenbaker under the title False Admissions; and is performed in repertoire with another Marivaux, here rendered as Successful Strategies. They come, in Mike Alfreds's productions, as a pair.

Paul Dart -- responsible for sets, costumes and lighting -- has supplied each with a unified colour-scheme. Successful Strategies is decked out in a dazzling array of whites and creams; False Admissions rings more changes on the colour black than might have been thought possible.

Both are plays of amatory intrigue, with several characters in common. Each cast, for example, includes an Arlequin, wearing the traditional suit of lozenges, bleached up in one play, mired down in the other. He comes, in False Admissions, disconcertingly close to the Watteau idea of a broken-hearted zany. I suspect that Marivaux meant Arlequin's comedy to be rather broader (he is a pushy, discontented domestic) than Mr Alfreds has allowed for. But these possible distortions are forgivable in productions that give each play so strong an identity.

'Amatory intrigue' may be a phrase that slips too easily off the typewriter. These are plays about lovers lying, without ever -- which is where Marivaux gets his peculiar tang -- ceasing to be in love. In False Admissions, Dorante, who is poor, gets a job as steward with his adored Araminte. On his behalf Dubois, his former servant, wages psychological warfare; he tells Araminte that Dorante is crazy about her, and waits to see propinquity, vanity and his master's personal charms do their inevitable work.

All good fun: the pain comes in with Marton, Araminte's paid companion, who is led to believe Dorante loves her and who gradually finds out her mistake. Maggie Wells does some memorable silent suffering in this role, while Holly Wilson is decorous and alluring as Araminte.

A scene between them reminded me of the two women quarrelling over the young tutor in A Month in the Country, or at least of how that was done in Peter Gill's National Theatre production, which placed Turgenev firmly if unexpectedly in the Marivaux tradition. Instead of a matchmaking doctor, we have here a matchmaking solicitor: a good enough fellow in Philip Voss's performance, but a thoroughly practical one who cannot see what business people have marrying for anything other than money. Araminte's mother would agree with him, except that she thinks in terms of rank rather than cash.

Apart from the chessboard manoeuvrings, the fascination lies in the degree to which emotional and monetary desires can coincide. The clarity and the subdued intensity of the acting matches that of the decor, though there are times when the banked-up feelings threaten to outgrow the studio.

If False Admissions sometimes becomes oppressive, Successful Strategies makes amends. Here everything sparkles, not least Miss Wertenbaker's text. This time we have a Comtesse who loves another Dorante, but jilts him in favour of a conceited Chevalier. Dorante makes common cause with the Chevalier's old flame; and their subterfuge carries them almost to the marriage-altar.

The same comedy is played out among their servants; Mr Voss's complacency as the Chevalier is matched by James Smith, superbly supercilious as his valet; while Sam Dale makes an aggrieved Arlequin, fearing forcible separation from his fiancee. Miss Wilson is again the cynosure; serene before, she is here manipulative and flirtatious without ever becoming dislikeable. Her caprice -- her greed, if you like -- and the jealousy she both suffers and inspires are, after all, thoroughly human.

These complex comedies make one wonder whether we have not been misdirecting our energies; we have persevered with Moliere, to be rewarded by powerful sermons on the inadvisability of being a miser, a hypochondriac or a possessive husband: sermons that have left us thinking yes indeed and what else is new.

The depth and ambiguity in Marivaux is far closer to our own tradition, even if the style takes some decoding. This task has been masterfully performed by Mr Alfreds, to whom a final bouquet: for his consistent adventurousness and for the relish with which he has shared his experiences with his excellent actors and they theirs with us.

  

Bob Fosse's Dancin' (Drury Lane) begins with a proclamation about how musicals have been destroyed by their sappy and portentous books. I have some sympathy with that position; I certainly think it a welcome confession from the creator of Pippin and Chicago. This show promises amends; no speech, just movement and music. Of course it breaks its own rule even by announcing it; and it goes on doing so.

It is a choreographic revue that feels compelled to explain everything. Mr Fosse is not for the most part at his best (the best of Sweet Charity or How to Succeed) and his American company is less than top-notch; all right in their dancin', but not in their singin' or their talkin'. Just one number burns up the stage: a homage to swing in which the performers are shot across the stage in groups of three (Mr Fosse's favourite formation) before combining for a marathon jitterbug.

The music is the Benny Goodman war-horse Sing, Sing, Sing, and it helps a lot. The insinuating I Want to Be a Dancing Man (by Warren and Mercer) similarly supports a mass tribute to Fred Astaire; you might think that the Fosse tension was at odds with the Astaire cool, but there is an area of nonchalance, the hat tipped rakishly over the brow, at which the extremes meet.

  

Michael Abbensetts's Outlaw (Arts) takes us nostalgically back to Rachmanism and the beginnings of Black Power. Another thing it takes is a long time; I was reminded of a favourite Goon Show in which, every two minutes, Peter Sellers would intone, 'this is where the story really starts.' That it never did was fun then, but not now.

Robert Gillespie's production does nothing to sharpen matters, either in staging or editing, but there are lively performances from Raul Newney as a would-be wide-boy turned politician and Joy Richardson in a witty double of his girl and his mother. Jacqueline Pearce, who once did the nude scene in Otherwise Engaged, has come on a lot since.
1983-11-27-hdg-t-c:
HDG
T/C

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

OUT OF the Barbican and into the Adelphi comes Poppy, in which Peter Nichols tells the story of the Chinese opium wars and of the very bad show put up in them by Queen Victoria's English chaps.

They were saying last year that Mr Nichols had written a pantomime, and that Terry Hands had directed a musical. I pass on that, chiefly because the two genres are hopelessly entangled. Doubtless things were different in Victoria's day, or even in Mr Nichols's childhood, but today, from the Palladium to your local Empire if any (and if any, then what a suitable site for this saga), Christmas entertainments have the same production values as a revival at the Apollo Victoria.

The gambolling maidens and grumbling swains who open 'Poppy' might have stepped out of a George Edwardes chorus at the old Gaiety, but so might the merry villagers of your average 'Dick Whittington.'

If I must, I will say, in the teeth of my colleagues, that this West End re-staging has moved away from pantomime and towards musical. The Fairy Queen and Demon King, alias Victoria and the Chinese Emperor, are now denied their traditional entrances at opposite sides of the stage; it is an earnest of the show's sympathies that he comes down on a heavenly cloud while she rises up from an infernal trap.

New choreography, by the American Onna White, smells of Broadway; also, in a naval battle fought under the command of our long-legged principal boy prancing about like Eleanor Powell, of Hollywood. Farrah has designed new sets, simpler than the old and more beautiful. The salient features are a dauntingly tilted floor, on which the lighting throws opalescent patterns, and a series of coloured projections.

Mr Nichols's chosen convention—Dame, Squire, Idle Jack, pantomime horse—remains perfectly clear; and so does his point of view. I doubt that any in the audience will fail to notice his disapproval of imperialism, capitalism, class distinction, and organised religion. Whether they will think this quite enough is another matter.

I can imagine the opium wars being dramatised in strict epic style, dispensing the maximum of information, or through a close focus on the people involved. I know little [about them], but I am positive that they were not called Lady Dodo, Jack Idle and Obadiah Upward, and I grew weary of the increasingly desperate [attempts] to pretend that they were.

The contention that pantomime is itself a jingoistic form, deserving to be up-ended, may have been true in the nineteenth century, but not now. Nor does Mr Nichols play very fair; he gets his Chinese characters giggling when they see women dressed as men and men as women; since they themselves are supposed to be part of the panto, why should they question its methods? And anyway what right have the Chinese—whose classical theatre is founded on transvestitism—to balk at a pantomime dame?

Monty Norman's music is catchy, rather like the common cold; both have simple and familiar germs. I liked best 'They All Look the Same To Us,' the Rodgers and Hammerstein parody, all shuffling feet and tinkling bells, with which the inscrutables greet the unspeakables. Line by line, Mr Nichols's lyrics are admirably turned, but the weight of information they have to carry frequently sinks them as songs. The format allows him to make some excellent jokes, but as the proclaimed swan-song of one of our best playwrights this is thin stuff.

Similarly, Mr Hands's direction, though smart, hardly caps his imposing triptych of 'Much Ado,' 'Arden' and 'Cyrano.' Geoffrey Hutchings repeats his forceful Dame, but the other leads (Alfred Marks, Antonia Ellis, David Firth, Janet Shaw) are muffled. The best newcomers are Ken Wynne as the Emperor and Nichola McAuliffe who, with a wicked grin and a noble voice, doubles as queen and missionary and is able to put over not only a number, but the thought behind it.

Athol Fugard's Master Harold and the Boys (Cottesloe) is about a white male, growing up in South Africa in 1950, and crumbling under family and social pressures. His mother runs a Port Elizabeth tea-room, his father is an invalid, his only friends are two black waiters. He ends up humiliating the more authoritative of them, Sam, whom he has previously treated as a substitute parent.

The play is an acknowledged piece of autobiography, and its remembered pain is indisputable, as is the author's desire and ability to see right round the situation. The action can easily be taken as a metaphor for the shocks that await anyone living in a prejudiced (not just a segregated) society. But its dialogue is too laborious, its images too calculated. The waiters are ballroom dancers, and dance is extensively discussed as a metaphor for life; its grace and its collisions.

You know that the lights will go down on a foxtrotting couple; the moment, when it arrives, is nice but no more. There is a sort of visual poetry in the readying of the shop for the next day's custom, but it relates to nothing more than itself. (You want trends? I'll give you trends. With this and 'Glengarry Glen Ross' the Cottesloe is mounting a season of restaurant plays.)

The play was given a better, or at least a better-cast, production (directed, like this one, by the author) in New York last year. There I saw the towering James Earl Jones play Sam. Here he is John Kani, the brilliant improviser of 'Sizwe Bansi is Dead,' but a flyweight actor not easily acceptable as anybody's father-figure. So the piece lacks a dimension.

Theatro Technis, in Mornington Crescent, is doing Aristophanes's The Frogs as a musical, which is much how Aristophanes himself must have done it. The score (John Gould music, David Dearlove lyrics) has a collegiate charm and joyfully points up the irrelevance of the famous froggy chorus ('brek-ek-ek-ek-ex, koax koax,' that one) to what the play is supposed to be about.

Aristophanes was never a great one for keeping his eye on the object. The god Dionysus, a drastic but conscientious theatre critic, descends to Hell to bring back a playwright; he has to choose between Aeschylus, whom Aristophanes worshipped, and Euripides, whom he didn't.

Ted Craig's production puts up a lively case for the play if not a conclusive one. Guy Siner's Dionysus is an amusingly discomfited cad, like a thin Simon Callow; Keith Varnier doubles a donnish Aeschylus with one of Hades' heavies; and David Shaughnessy as the comic slave combines a winning surliness with a singing voice that lifts him clear above 'The Frogs' and right up to 'The Birds.'
1983-12-04-the-girl-from-iowa:
The girl from Iowa

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN on 'Jean Seberg.'

AT the very least Jean Seberg makes an interesting bridge in the National Theatre's repertoire between Tales from Hollywood and Saint Joan. For those of us with a romantic streak it was pleasing to discover that the rumoured disaster at the Olivier was no such thing. It has in fact some striking merits.

Peter Hall has delivered a polished, logical production. John Bury's designs get us from Iowa to Hollywood to Paris through exquisite use of back projection. Barring a couple of lapses, Marvin Hamlisch's score is the best he has written for the theatre. (It is an indication of Broadway's decline in quality and quantity that we should already be talking of Mr Hamlisch, who has written only three shows, as if he were an old master.)

Two other New York professionals, orchestrator Bill Byers and vocal arranger Buster Davis, give the music the best possible chance. The Olivier is a marvellous theatre in which to see and hear a musical, and this is in many ways a slicker, sleeker presentation than Guys and Dolls.

It is nothing like as enjoyable; and that is not just because it has a serious subject. It traces Miss Seberg's career from small-town drugstore-counter girlhood, through her disastrous film debut as Joan and her subsequent success riding the nouvelle vague, to espousal of the Black Panthers, persecution by the FBI, and suicide.

That is a lot of ground to cover; music speeds us along, rather too fast. It also imposes some conventions of its own. Hopful Minds audition for Otto Preminger by singing a bit of text. This is bizarre; Saint Joan was not a musical. It also signals desperation: almost inevitable in a musical show about a non-musical performer.

Jean Seberg has to go looking for hooks on which to hang its song-and-dance. Some are all too obvious: the Panthers get a juiced-up number to which they caper belligerently while chanting Black Revolution. Some are crazily far-fetched: at one point Jean puts on view the body of her dead child, in order to prove that it was not black. A suitable song for such a moment is hard to envisage, but what we get is a homogenised lament about loneliness, shorn--like the egregious "What I Did For Love" in A Chorus Line--of any reference to the dramatic situation. When Mr Hamlisch's pop instincts come out, there's no holding them; I wish there were still a Tin Pan Alley so I might call him Hamlisch, Prince of Denmark Street.

Somewhere between these extremes comes a wisecracking female duet for two of Jean's Hollywood enemies. It is much in the manner of Bosom Buddies, from Mame, and is presumably trying to transcend it. But it ends, for lack of wit, not using the musical genre, but being used by it. Julian Barry's book has similar problems. It is one device after another.

Jean at the point of death watches and comments on the mistakes made by her younger self. Within this framework is another: Jean as Joan, on set and on trial, with J. Edgar Hoover doubling as Inquisitor. Gamely Mr Barry touches all the bases--puritan upbringing, father-fixation, early social conscience, black boyfriend, dreams of stardom--without exploring them.

In a musical that may be the job of the songs, but it places on Christopher Adler's lyrics a responsibility they cannot sustain. They are, on the whole, painless, but they never dig and they never glisten; they merely paraphrase the obvious. All we discover about the heroine is that she was a victim; and victims are not interesting.

Our pair of Jeans are an appealing Kelly Hunter and a stylishly ravaged Elizabeth Counsell. There is solid work from Joss Ackland (spending yet another evening getting sung at) as Romain Gary, and from Michael Bryant as Hoover. He doesn't sing, but Jean-Luc Godard does. So does Otto Preminger, a fabulous-monster role fully relished by John Savident.

At the end these distinguished British players relax into their native accents to deliver an epilogue. It is a dignified moment, and it takes some of the curse from the experience of being lectured, by a British company, on the failure of the American dream.

  

Our luck is holding with the Spanish Golden Age; Calderon's Life's a Dream works finely in Stratford's Other Place, staged by John Barton in an enclosure that looks like a corrida. (My stock reaction to Spanish sets.) Adrian Mitchell's translation swings, taking in enormous narratives and short jokes.

This is an amazing play, a tragedy in which only the clown dies. The tiresome platitude adumbrated in the title is brought to life through ceaseless twisting narrative energy; how lucky is a theatre that believes in romance. A Polish prince, kept confined since birth, is allowed a testing day as king and blows it by turning Caliguloid. Persuaded that it never really happened, he achieves maturity. In counterpoint, an enthusiastically wronged maiden learns to snap out of her own dream of revenge.

These roles are enterprisingly played by Miles Anderson and Barbara Kellermann, though Mr Anderson is too spryly earthbound to realise the play's full scope, and bright-eyed Miss Kellermann occasionally flags. They have fine support from Anthony O'Donnell, Charles Kay, and David Waller, who has now attained a state of grace that enables him to play wisdom.

The play, by some extra-continental coincidence, wakes echoes of half-a-dozen Shakespeares. On the first night a steed made a notable appearance underneath Mr Anderson, but cannot, it seems, be afforded in future. Obviously Equine Equity drives a hard bargain, but here is an opportunity for anyone wishing to put money on a horse.

  

Songs in Wedlock/Deadlock (King's Head) weakens an already ailing fabric. This is a concatenation, by Fidelis Morgan, of three eighteenth-century comedies, one called--the third time this year--The Custom of the Country. It plays as a collection of roistering Restoration jokes about marriage, camped up into a Caribbean musical. There are imaginative touches, though, in Miss Morgan's direction, and witty performances from Paola Dionisotti, Sian Thomas and Celia Imrie. All these ladies are former Glasgow Citizens. Their presence is missed back at the ranch, where a tragedy of similar vintage, Southerne's Oroonoko, suffers from lack of acting. It does not of course lack design; it is set in a West Indian slave-port, which Philip Prowse has envisaged as a ghostly shanty-town.
1983-12-11-fraynand-farce-go-hand-in-han:
FRAYNAND FARCE GO HAND IN HAND
Date: 1983-12-11
LONDON

Sometime in the middle of the 1960's, Michael Frayn wrote an article in the British Sunday newspaper The Observer entitled ''Business Worries.'' The business in question was show business, and the worries were those of the audience. Or rather they were those of the actors that communicated themselves to the audience. The key sentence in the essay is, ''All the time one is waiting aghast for some embarrassing disaster to occur.''
Among the disasters itemized by Mr. Frayn are the supposed corpse that can hardly avoid taking visible breaths after perishing in a strenuous sword fight, the pause that may turn out to be pregnant with a forgotten line, and the vital prop that gets lost. Mr. Frayn was not a playwright when he wrote that piece, but he is now. And in ''Business Worries'' may be discerned the promise of ''Noises Off,'' the backstage farce that is currently exhausting its third set of actors in London and that opens tonight on Broadway at the Brooks Atkinson.
Before being a playwright Mr. Frayn was a novelist and before being a novelist he was a journalist. Before being a journalist he was very young. Born in 1933, he was a student at Cambridge University in the mid- 1950's: a good time for aspiring writers and theater people. His Cambridge days were prefaced by what were then the statutory two years in the army. A linguist, he found himself assigned to a military Russian course, during which he appeared in a production of Gogol's ''The Inspector General.'' He recalls one night on which he attempted to make his prescribed exit: ''I pulled a door which I should have pushed, and stood there while stagehands on the other side fought with crowbars to open it. It broke my nerve.''
He has never appeared on a stage since. But in those moments were sown the earliest seeds of ''Noises Off,'' which is about a production of a play in which everything goes wrong. It concerns a group of actors on tour with a sex-farce called ''Nothing On.'' In Act One we watch a dress rehearsal, even more than usually fraught, of the opening scene. In Act Two we are backstage while the same scene is performed to a matinee audience; we watch the actors rush silently on and off (or off and on), and we glimpse them in silhouette going through the motions of what we have already seen. In Act Three the tour, the play and the actors are on their last legs; all is chaos. The usual theatrical hazards are reinforced by sexual jealousy, drunkenness and lost contact lenses among the cast, and friction between the director and the stage management.
Writing it was ''extremely hard work,'' Mr. Frayn said recently. ''I thought my brain would fall out. Long before I'd finished I thought I'd walk off a cliff.'' The director Michael Blakemore, one of the shrewdest craftsmen in the English theater, said frankly that when rehearsals began he didn't know whether it would work or not; it was pretty unprecedented to ask actors to spend a third of their time acting with their backs to the audience. '' 'Noises Off,' '' said Mr. Frayn, ''is about the necessity for keeping a performance going - which is what we all do, though not many people have recognized the play as having a general application.''
Since ''Noises Off'' is a play about people at work, rather than the neat artificial mechanism that usually constitutes farce, there has always been a problem about winding it up. Mr. Frayn says he has lost count of the number of endings he has written. (The original London cast finally rebelled and refused to try any more.) For the pre-Broadway tryout in Washington, and for the new cast in London, he wrote what he describes as ''a quite workable ending.''
Most British critics found the original ending unsatisfying but had laughed so much during the first two acts that they didn't care. Americans who have seen the play in London have had varied reactions. One lady stormed out after the first act, having mistaken a parody of British sex- farce for the thing itself. On the Washington evidence, though, Mr Frayn does not feel that British and American reactions have differed much. Indeed, he said, ''In Washington they laughed more, if possible, than in London. We've only changed one or two words, though we have just discovered that the title (which refers to offstage sound effects) is meaningless in America. They think it's a political slogan, like 'Tories out.''
The atmosphere of the play is so authentic that one would assume Mr. Frayn to have been soaked in the theater all his life. Actually, he came late to it. Traumatized by the Russian experience, he kept away from plays at Cambridge, though he did develop an interest in revues. ''The first thing I did at Cambridge,'' he recalled with a blush, ''was to buy a dinner jacket'' - dinner jackets being de rigueur for members of the university revue club, the Footlights. He wrote one of their annual shows single-handedly, but after that, he said, ''I turned my back on the theater, except for making fun of it.'' He did this to great effect in many of his columns as a professional journalist.
Journalism had been his main extracurricular pursuit as a student, though he had ''distant hopes of being a novelist.'' (As he wrote self-mockingly in another article, ''Is there any other honorable career for an arts graduate?'') In the meantime, he thought of himself as a reporter and got a six-month trial on The Guardian, the national daily newspaper based in the north of England. His six months in the north expanded to two years; The Guardian then moved him to London as a columnist. He had written what he calls ''funny leading articles''; comedy now became his profession. He pursued it thrice weekly on The Guardian from 1960 to 1962, and then, on The Observer, every Sunday from 1962 to 1968. The change was made partly in order to buy time to write books.
The Frayn columns have become classics. They were regularly collected into book form in the 60's, and a new retrospective selection has just been published, with an editorial introduction describing the author as ''the funniest journalist of our time'' and one from whom all his British successors have stolen. The essays stand in fact in a very recognizable tradition of English (and American) humor. They deal with social and domestic mishaps and embarrassments; from trying to help your wife cook from impenetrable recipes to pretending you have caught someone's name at a party. What Mr. Frayn added was a gift for characterization.
The 1960's were Britain's most fashion-conscious years, and he created the ultimate trendy couple, Christopher and Lavinia Crumble, childless themselves but always willing to pass on to the author the most advanced ideas on how to raise his own brood. The Crumbles, we are given to understand, live in streamlined comfort while the Frayns make do with companionable squalor. And beneath them are their other friends, Horace and Doris Morris, who live in uncompanionable squalor. Times have changed but the types remain recognizable. And Mr. Frayn fused them into a comic system. At Cambridge, he passed from studying languages to Moral Sciences, a subject known in most other places as philosophy.
His humor has a wide frame of intellectual reference, from the outlandish to the everyday. He considers the complications of abortion as exemplified by the unborn 16th-century genius Ivan Kudovbin (''He Kudovbin but he wasn't.''). He furnishes a guide to parent care for progressive children (''Parents are just large human beings. They aren't as fragile as they look.''). He writes a long poem, ''The Rime of the Wedding Guest'' (''My intention is that it should be recited, or murmured, simultaneously with the recitation of 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner,' as a sort of accompanying ostinato.''). The style is always gentle, always lethal.
Besides, farcical things happen to him. He bears a passing physical resemblance to another British playwright, Peter Nichols, and once sat at a dinner graciously accepting condolences on the closing of a play which Mr. Nichols had written. What made it worse was that his interlocutor was an official of the National Theater, which was staging one of Mr. Frayn's Chekhov translations at the time. I myself remember sitting with him in a noisy restaurant, and saying that my favorite among all his novels was ''Toward the End of the Morning.'' He said that he was interested to hear that, but he could not agree; his own favorite was ''Toward the End of the Morning.''
That novel, which we both enjoyed so much and on whch we were so signally unable to communicate, dealt - very much from Mr. Frayn's own experiences - with life on a quality newspaper. Its characters are a few effortless high-flyers and (in the majority) effortful trudgers, impatient with their wives and doomed never to appear on television. They are, mutatis mutandis, the same kind of people who appear in his journalism and his plays. He is not one of Britain's playwrights of social unhpeaval; he belongs with Alan Ayckbourn, Tom Stoppard and Mr. Nichols: the middle-class ironists.
His theatrical career got started in 1970. ''Having come to mock, I stayed to pray,'' he said. The Broadway producer Alexander H. Cohen was then operating in London, and commissioned a two-character sketch from him as part of a program to be called ''Mixed Doubles.'' The sketch was eventually turned down on grounds of taste; it required a baby's diaper to be changed on stage. Mr. Frayn was ''so riled that I determined to write three more short plays to go with it.'' All were duologues, and the four were staged under the title ''The Two of Us.'' The last was a miniature but fully plotted farce in which two actors play all the roles. Mr. Frayn noted that ''the hectic activity looked funnier from behind,'' and this too was stored up for ''Noises Off.''
''The Two of Us'' got terrible notices but ran nonetheless. Since then Mr. Frayn has had critical and popular success with ''Alphabetical Order'' (set on a local newspaper), ''Clouds'' (set in Cuba), and ''Make and Break'' (set at a sales conference). None of these plays, though, are about their settings. They are about people colliding, competing, seeing things differently: the stuff of philosophy - or of farce.
The hero of ''Make and Break,'' a manic worker, is, according to his author, ''an extreme version of someone who needs to consume the world around him - someone like myself. Not only inert material but human beings get consumed.'' But this is not a despairing vision, he insisted: ''It's not bad to be made use of. One of the strengths of life is to feel that one could be of use.'' Just as ''Make and Break'' is not a denunciation but an exploration,'' so ''Noises Off'' is not based, as some critics have suggested, on ''hatred of actors'' but, as Mr. Frayn puts it, on ''admiration for their courage.''
Many writers lose their comic sense as they grow older. Mr Frayn at 50, and in a menacing world, is as funny as ever. But then he has never sold comedy short. ''Comedy is about the grimness of the world,'' he said. ''It's one way of looking at pain and difficulty.''
Robert Cushman is theater critic of The Observer.
1983-12-11-adultery-adulteration:
Adultery, adulteration

THEATRE

by ROBERT CUSHMAN

DENNIS POTTER'S Sufficient Carbohydrate (Hampstead), his first theatrical original, starts, as so many other plays seem in memory to have done, with Dinsdale Landen being witty and hung-over. It is early morning; he is holidaying in a Greek villa. 'The sun is not up yet, so why,' he inquires of another character, 'are you?' Asked 'Is there any juice left?' he replies with a rueful sense of double-entendre. His virility is in question: a necessary condition, the play suggests, of being English. Now where have you heard that before?

Actually we are not in for yet another attack on an undefended home team; rather we are attending the xenophobic school of which John Osborne is the headmaster. Jack, Mr Landen's character, has many weaknesses, but just wait till you meet Eddie. Eddie is American, and both men are high up in a food-manufacturing business, a transatlantic conglomerate that has bought up Jack's smaller concern, while being obliged to keep him on the strength.

They are having this trip, along with their respective wives, on the firm. 'Have you ever wondered,' asks Eddie as the dialogue moves, a little ponderously, from atmospheres to exposition, 'why Greenace should pay for this jaunt?' The reason is that Greenace, as exemplified by Eddie, are heavily into additives and strange vegetable mutations, while Jack is a traditional whole-food man who is to be made to see the error of his ways. Also, Eddie is getting off with Jack's wife: adulteration on the one hand and adultery on the other.

A fifth sunbather is involved: Eddie's teenage boy by his first marriage, gazing with idealistic disgust at the antics of his elders while harbouring a secret passion for his young stepmother. He is a dead ringer for the student son in Smiles of a Summer Night (whom I of course think of as the student son in A Little Night Music). He scores fairly highly in the test that Mr Potter has devised for all the characters to take at the end of the play.

Jack, though smashed in more ways than one, can see a ship, a 'black freighter' -- a mystic sign of hope and continuity on the horizon. Those who can see it with him are saved. (Eddie of course is damned.) This seemed to me an image laboriously manufactured to prove a point that Mr Potter had had in mind before ever creating his characters. The development of the action is not altogether predictable -- Mr Landen has a mid-play outburst of violence that is a surprise at the time and a puzzle afterwards -- but you feel that the people have been programmed, even if only the author knows the code.

My problem was that I was less interested in the characters' souls than in their sex-lives, and more interested in their business problems than in either, while Mr Potter's priorities appeared to be the exact reverse. And though he probably tries to be fair, he really does seem to regard Americans as slimy things that have crawled out from under stones.

I found myself wondering if the food-juggling was a metaphor for what Hollywood had done to Pennies from Heaven; then remembered that Hollywood had actually improved it, and that Mr Potter himself had written the screenplay. Anyway, Eddie is a boor who can't tell Keats from Shakespeare; and is patronised passim.

Jack, a glamorous blend of sinner and seer, gets all the witty remarks, together with a crucial sermon which says that what people really like to eat is other people. He is also allowed to be the audience's point of reference while the other characters pose behind a glass partition. The narrative excuse is that they are taking refuge from the heat, but the dramatic effect is to make them look like insects.

Nancy Meckler's crisp production, perhaps wisely, makes no attempt to suggest the temperature of which the characters keep complaining. She may have erred, though, in casting Mr Landen. He does a spectacularly effective job, but he has now played so many despairing zanies and mid-life madcaps that we find ourselves thinking of Jack just as the Dinsdale Landen role: a disservice both to the play and to the actor who can (vide On the Razzle and Uncle Vanya) do other things.

Nicky Henson as Eddie has to work hard at the age, the insensitivity and the accent. Jill Baker and Jennifer Hilary do creditably with the underwritten ladies, while Rupert Graves glowers and suffers quite admirably as Youth, insufferable one moment, unanswerable the next. There are some really funny lines. Boring the play is not, but it is sanctimonious as heaven.

  

At Theatro Technis, Mornington Crescent, a musical version of Aristophanes's The Frogs closes tonight. Aristophanes was never a great one for keeping his eye on the object and the famous frogs' chorus ('brek-ek-ek-ek ko-ax ko-ax,' and if you believe that's what frogs do, even in Greece, you'll believe anything) is gleefully mined for its irrelevance to the main plot, which has to do with Dionysus travelling to Hades in order to bring back a dead playwright: an extreme example of practical criticism.

The candidates are a languid senior common-room Aeschylus and a redbrick Euripides. A comic slave is played by David Shaughnessy with a winning surliness, which he combines with a singing voice far too good for a frog; he should be ideal when they get round to The Birds.

  

Currently weighing down my desk are two volumes of financial scrutiny of the Royal Shakespeare Company, commissioned by the Minister for the Arts. It is an intimidatingly thorough document, full of interesting details of people's salaries and even running to a certain amount of dramatic criticism, some of it indulgently enthusiastic, some quite terrifyingly rigorous. There are productions that have got clean past me and my colleagues but which these accounting gentlemen take firmly to task.

Conclusions are that the RSC cannot continue on its present subsidy, that its only means of doing so would be to abandon the Barbican, and that this would be disastrous. Well, the report doesn't actually use the word 'disastrous,' but it does say that 'without a London base the Stratford theatre would lose its "national" company status.' In other words the report confirms what the rest of the world, or those of us enthusiastic about the theatre, or me and my mates, have always known.

The two stages in Stratford, the two in London, the season in Newcastle, the small-scale provincial tour, are all necessary and interdependent. They enable the good work done in a season of Shakespeare to reproduce and extend itself; without which opportunity, it could rapidly cease to be good. Besides, scale has its own attractions. Small may still be beautiful, but big is exciting; medium is tedium.
1983-12-18-in-acton-and-india:
In Acton
--and India

THEATRE
by ROBERT CUSHMAN

BRIAN THOMPSON last appeared on a London theatre programme as author of a National West End comedy called Tishoo. He now has a play at the Bush called Turning Over, and it is a beauty. The play is exotically set in India and Acton. Not that the Acton shown here is the Acton I remember, rather it is the new featureless could-be-anywhere Acton as colonised by the BBC.

In a Shepherd's Bush theatre, Mr Thompson's play must almost count as community drama. Half the stage represents a cutting-room, where editor, director and writer in that order of importance are toiling over a documentary that was shot on the other half, back to which we constantly flash. It is part of a misbegotten series entitled I Could Be Happy Here. The writer, a children's author new to television, decided that he could be happy in India. So they took him there.

Happiness, rather than India, is what the play is about. It is, as the bumper-stickers have always proclaimed, different things to different people. It is also, as the bumper-stickers forgot, unattainable, especially if you go looking for it. This is not a revolutionary idea, but ideas are less important in plays than the way in which they are fleshed out, and here Mr Thompson scores highly.

He distributes his theme right across his cast. The chippy editor in Acton, the lugubrious sound-man in India, mainly want to get their respective jobs done; they stand a chance. The director is pushier; he wants a finished film and a divorce and the opportunity to look down on the writer, who was brighter at school than he was.

The writer is the most muddled of all, increasingly conscious of his presumption in projecting his own dreams onto a society of which he knows nothing, and grabbing frantically at an illusory permanence with an expatriate married lady on the basis of -- if I counted rightly -- a two-night stand. Mr Thompson also throws in a P.A. girl, rushed out from England at short notice, and projecting her dreams on to a middle-aged Indian tour-guide with problems of his own.

The casual way in which Mr Thompson brings this young lady into the centre of a picture to which she had seemed peripheral, is quite masterly. Indeed all the parts are worth acting, and all in David Hayman's production are well played; especial mention for Gary Waldhorn's puzzled ache ("I have no influence; I write for children"), Charles Dance's sparky spikiness, and Geraldine James's placid radiance.

Mr Thompson stands with Stephen Fagan (The Hard Shoulder) among a new breed of acute social comedians, the heirs of Alan Ayckbourn and Peter Nichols. And though he has Scarborough training, it is Mr Nichols (who is earth to Mr Ayckbourn's air) that he more resembles. He also has television training, and much of his play's appeal comes from the hilarious accuracy of its ear for jargon and its eye for the boredom and indignity of filming. Note how those at home are always accurate when speculating on what may have happened sexually on location. And why has nobody thought before of acting out the way that sight and sound get distorted when a film is run backwards.

  

As it happens, they have thought of it again in Abbacadabra (Lyric, Hammersmith) which, in conception at least, is a super-pantomime, corralling characters from four or five different fairy-tales and turning them loose in a staged video-game, with three modern children to show them the works. The title, which you had better look at again, is occasioned by the musical interruptions: hits by Abba fitted out with new lyrics, which, since they don't belong, are even worse than the old. This is music that rots the teeth and stops the action, what there is of it.

The show's central conceit, pleasant and accurate, is that kids are far more at home with technology than are grown-ups, but they cope here so easily as to deprive David Wood's script of danger and finally of interest. Nor, apart from the odd mechanical wonder, is any supplied by Peter James's production; he seems to have used up his current stock of energy on his ace direction of Blondel.

The stage is occupied by actors given too little to do and non-actors given too much, though in the latter category B. A. Robertson comes through as an engaging Beast (as in Beauty and). Dexter Fletcher is a masterful schoolboy wizard and Elaine Paige as the wicked fairy tries hard, but fruitlessly, to send up her own Eva Peron. But she is unexpectedly convincing as a frumpy teacher in prologue and epilogue.

The mixture of myths, though, is a tempting economy offer, pre-empting both the West End's Aladdin and the National's Cinderella (Lyttelton), on whose first night a child in the audience stopped the show by shouting, as Buttons improvised a ball-dress for Cinders, "she hasn't got a belt." This was the best line of the evening, though it was closely followed by those which Tony Haygarth, a charmingly bashful Buttons, had to invent to save the situation.

Anyway, some contact with the target-audience was obviously achieved. (Of course you may doubt whether National Theatre children are real children. Give them another year and they'll be on the mailing-list.) To this particular Scrooge, however, the evening seemed supine. The script is "adapted by Bill Bryden, Trevor Ray and the company" from what sounded to me, with my limited experience of panto at the Players', like a remarkably sub-standard Victorian original.

The couplets, which are almost constant, are not gorgeously awful, but just execrably limp. They imprison the actors; you can feel Derek Newark, Robert Stephens, Jack Shepherd and the others pining to get out and be funny, but to no avail. The only escapers are Janet Dibley in one song as the heroine, and two guys who emerge from within the pantomime horse to perform a highly professional whitewash routine.

Susan Fleetwood's Prince, William Dudley's backcloths, and the transformation scene (with real ponies) are all worth gazing at; but the total experience makes you feel nostalgic for the commercial product. I may of course regret having said that before the week is out.

  

The School for Scandal (Duke of York's) was, at its final preview, in a semi-comatose state, certainly as far as the scandalous college itself was concerned. Things improved when the plot veered towards domesticity, with Nicola Pagett a Lady Teazle of great comedic skill, if hardly a country girl, and Donald Sinden a Sir Peter who made all his humorous and emotional points, even if he did deposit them too firmly in the audience's laps.

There is too a ripely fruity Sir Oliver from Michael Denison, a Joseph from Clive Francis of amusingly stylised primness, and in Julia Josephs a Maria who bounds on as if to announce that she knows this is a thankless part but is not going to be defeated by it, and, as it turns out, isn't. John Barton's actual staging, on Christopher Morley's silver-gilt sets, is often admirable; the screen scene, for once, almost lives up to its reputation.
1984-01-01-robert-cushman-s-1983-year-ro:
Robert Cushman's 1983 Year Roundup

Robert Cushman OBSERVER BEST NEW PLAY: Glengarry Glen Ross (David Mamet) BEST NEW MUSICAL: Little Shop of BEST PERFORMANCE (ACTOR): Michael Gambon (Tales from Hollywood) BEST PERFORMANCE (ACTRESS): Geraldine McEwan (The Rivals) BEST DIRECTOR: Terry Hands (Cyrano de Bergerac) BEST DESIGNER: John Gunter (The MOST PROMISING NEWCOMER: Alexandra Mathie (Daisy Pulls It Off) MOST PROMISING PLAYWRIGHT: Michael Rudman 1983 will be remembered as the year in which we lost Ralph Richardson, but also as the year in which he gave one of his finest performances. He came, with Derek Jacobi, at the top of my runner-up list. Several of my perennial favourites suggested themselves for other awards: Mike Alfreds finding a way - indeed two ways - to do Marivaux; Victoria Wood in the onlv show of the vear to make me helpless with laughter (but what category is there for her?); Stephen Sondheim, whose Merrily We Roll Along certainly had the best score of the year but which, since we only saw it in a student production, cannot qualify; Judi Dench, again.

I have voted for her on three occasions in the past, and she has won on two of them. I rather hope she does it again. I count her actress the most important thing to hap. pen in my ten years as a theatre critic. If I were forced into voting for British play I would probably choose Howard Barker's Victory (as much, I imagine, to his surprise as to mine) and follow it with Falkland Sound if it was a play, and Tales from Hollywood whose wit and good nature had me on its side from the start, though they proved insufficient to carry the evening. I have reluctantly to place it at the head of the Great Overrated, a bulging category that this year embraced plays, musicals, productions and performances.

I have never known so many marks to be given for good intentions: for the drama with the socially significant theme or the actor with the throbbingly sincere voice. A patchy year for the National Theatre, though, as my nominations indicate, when they delivered they delivered. Some of their less trumpeted shows remind me that this was also the year of the Great Underrated: Inner Voices (even without Richardson) and The Fawn were absorbing, unobtrusively ings; even The Trojan War might have worked. The Rivals set wins because it knocked me out from the moment I entered the auditorium, but there were plenty of contenders; Cyrano by the omnipresent Ralph Koltai, Hayden Griffin's Chinese restaurant in Glengarry, the light and shade of Paul Dart's French double for Shared Experience.

It was also a bumper year for new players: at the National, Fiona Shaw and Miranda Foster, and at Stratford the whey-faced Paul McGann. I wrote in P&P that I wanted the theatre to make me laugh, cry, tap my feet or hold my breath. Using those criteria let me put in words for Noises Off (new cast), The Hard Shoulder, Blondel, Volpone, Pack of Lies, Mr Cinders, Snoopy, Pericles, Susan Fleetwood, Sinead Cusack and Juliet Stevenson.
1984-01-01-the-musical-gets-respectable:
The Musical Gets Respectable

Musicals may decay but music proliferates. It is becoming harder than ever to decide exactly what a musical is; or, if you prefer, what is a musical. Songs are increasingly squeezed into plays; the audience welcomes them, irrespective of quality, since they break up all that endless talking. Incidental music in the classier Shakespeare productions is now omnipresent music; directors grab at any attempt to do a number. Since nostalgia is in — or, as I prefer to put it, since the classic popular songs are recognised to be just that — there is a rush on those plays of the 20s and 30s into which they can plausibly be slotted. The actual presented by the National Theatre (Guys and Dolls, The Beggar's Opera, Jean Seberg) and the Royal Shakespeare Company (Poppy)fall outside our time-scheme, but their presence has been pervasively felt.

They have given the form a new respectability. Forget about the clown wanting to play Hamlet; our Hamlets are lining up for tap-lessons. We are constantly being told that the main theatrical growth-area is cabaret, and especially alternative cabaret, and most alternative feminist cabaret. But little of this has worked its way through to the world outside its own circuits. The most notable example has been Cut and Thrust, presented at the Drill Hall with some technical aplomb and a lot of glitter. Devised and directed by the Australian Robyn Archer, in the wake of her one-woman success A Star is Torn, it turned out to be a radical rag-bag, tossing satirical or just plain abusive grenades at all the accepted targets.

As a celebration of left-wing togetherness it had some point, but it quickly became monotonous because nothing was being challenged and few jokes were being made. Miss Archer herself, who did not appear, contributed some good original material and there were raids on other sources from Brecht and Adrian Mitchell to Noël Coward, who might have been surprised to find himself in such company but whose 1951 masterpiece 'There Are Bad Times Just Around The Corner' remains perenially topical, and whose conservative sentiments can easily be turned themselves. Two neglected Broadway musicals, How Now Dow Jones (Elmer Bernstein and Carolyn Leigh) and Jamaica (Harold Arlen and EY Harburg) were plundered for numbers on, respectively, the stock market and the bomb; Leave The Atom Alone', sung by Australian dynamo, Noni Haslehurst, was the highlight of the show.

The same inbreeding afflicted a show at the other end of the cabaret spectrum. Liza Minnelli visited us, and seemed imprisonedby her own mannerisms andher own myth, though most of allby an atrocious sound-system. more fun in seeing Bertice Reading, last of the black-hot mamas, going into action again with her blues volce and her waddling personality. Her show, called Every Inch a Lady, began at the King's Head and moved to the Donmar Warehouse, once the RSC's studio home and now intended by its owner Ian Albery to be a small super-theatre. One can only wish him luck. London certainly needs such a place. Mr Albery also found himself the owner of a large super-theatre, having leased the Piccadilly THE MUSICAL GETS RESPECTABLE Observer critic Robert Cushman looks at the musical in London in a year when RSC and National Theatre involvement helped to make it a particularly respectable sector and now musicals Geraldine Gardner in the Peter Nichols/Monty especially Norman musical Poppy directed at the Barbicanby Terry Hands.

It transferred to Adelphi. Photo: Reg Wilson. for what was intended to be a lavish Folies Bergères style "show called i. Amid almot unprecendeted chaos, the show was abandoned in rehearsals. What eventually opened was a show called Y: an invitation to critics if ever there was one. Much of it was indeed terrible: pointless floor-show routines, deep-frozen glamour, characterless singers, performing waiters who danced and opened champagne. bottles equally ineptly. But stuck in it all was some real imagination: gorgeous costumes, some good choreography, and an interesting star. Arturo Brachetti had been hailed as some kind of genius; he hardly seemed that, but his strange combination of talents (magician and female impersonator) gave the show an odd, sinister flavour, a cut above what the coach-parties used to get at the Talk of the Town. against There were one or two anthology shows.

Noël and Gertie was the second such at the King's Head to be presided over by a critic; though one reviewer was heard to mutter of Sheridan Morley that he was no Robert Cushman. (Neither Mr Morley nor I would would want it any other another way). His compilation suffered fromthe fact that, famous though the Coward-Lawrence stage partnership may have been, it never added up to much; and of those on stage only Simon Cadell as Noël seemed to have much idea what he was up to. Giving the two leads a couple of singing alter egos with pear-shaped voices was a There was particularly maladroit move. 'Nostalgia' word tossed about too glibly in the theatre, as in the music business, but this production merited comic it; it traded almost exclusively on faded glories.

At the other extreme from this gentility was Yakety Yak, the second attempt at fashioning a show out of the 1950's hit of Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller, maybe the only team to take the craftsmanlike? values of American popular song into the raunchier precincts of rock-and-roll. Leiber's barbed lyrics and Stoller's holy-rolling music should be theatrical naturals; though their own attempts at writing shows have so far been abortive. Robert Walker's choice of songs in Yakety Yak was less enterprising than Ned Sherrin's a couple of years back in Only in America, but Mr Walker revealed a far shrewder grasp of what the songs are about; urban blues for teenagers. There was plenty of guts in the playing of the Darts and the singing of the McGann brothers (of whom one, Paul, has blossomed as an actor).

There was an appallingly scrappy script, but at the Half Moon, where the show originated, it hardly seemed to matter. I can imagine that when the production transferred to the Astoria, Charing Cross Road, its faults were far more noticeable. It must still have been able to give any number of points to a subsequent Astoria attraction, Jukebox. This merely strung together all manner of hits from the fifites on, and put projections behind them. The cast were energetic, Cliff Richard impersonation stopped the show, and if it all seemed silly, then so did the music it was celebrating. Only when it became apparent, with nods to yesterday's protest and today's feminism, was it unbearable.

There is a kind of almost-musical that one thinks of as a play-with-music. Maybe this is because they are written -book and lyrics - by real playwrights; and the only real playwright who has shown any signs of being a real lyricist is Peter Nichols (in Privates on Parade and Poppy). Alan Ayckbourn has tried often, with mixed results; the best were in Suburban Strains. The worst - that I have heard, at any rate were in Me, Myself and I, staged at the Orange Tree in Richmond, equipped by Paul Todd with short-breathed tunes that emphasised the plonking rhymes. This could be a way of writing comedy songs but Mr Ayckbourn was out to write character songs, about a woman treated unfeelingly by men.

Three actresses played our heroine simultaneously, hence the title; but there was hardly enough of her for one consciousness, let alone a trio. Mr Ayckbourn can rhyme; what mars his lyrics is a lack of fluency. They sit awkwardly on the music; the words have no zing to them. Willy Russell, who wrote book, music and lyrics for Blood Brothers, hardly bothers at all with rhyme. He doesn't take the logical - and perfectly permissible step - of dispensing with it altogether; he merely takes boss-shots at it. It didn't seem to bother many critics, or maybe many members ofthe audience; pop lyrics have obviously desensitised them. But it is worth protesting about; we are being denied an acute source of pleasure.

Bad rhymes tend to be accompanied by general fuzziness. Most of Mr Russell's music was folk-tinged is a rock. Rock is of limited theatre; it can be celebratory (as in The Wiz Oz and that is about it. Its monolithic qualities preclude the cut-andthrust of character and narrative. Blood Brothers comes from and is set in Liverpool. Most of its characters are working-class. Fine, but in the second act Mr Russell introduces a bureaucrat, whose function is to fire people; he represents a different world, and yet hesings in exactly the same idiom. The story is of twin boys, separated at birth, one to be brought up poor and the other posh. Of course they meet, and fate, or class-warfare | Jerry Bock's music are good, even if they could be better (and in other shows were).

Topol, far too young when he started, has grown into the role of Tevye. The show is far less sentimental than everyone thinks, and its closing number 'Anatevka' is an abiding image of dispersal. The end of Camelot is moving, too; Arthur finding a way out of despair by entrusting the telling of his story to the future Thomas Malory. Suddenly the show, and the jungle that is its titlesong, take on tragic dignity. The saving grace of Alan Jay Lerner's book is that somehow, through all the protracted love-interest and the whimsy of Mehemer's lyrics and Frederick Loewe's lightweight score, it keeps the theme of Arthur's puzzled idealism before us. ('What a magnificent dilemma' says Mordred, and he's right).

Mr Harris rose splendidly to one of the few great male roles in a musical. The production (which had toured America) was tired and pantomimic, the supporting cast scratch and below, as they also tended to be in Fiddler; but there was still something big here. The casting of these revivals meant that audiences were in some sense being offered the show of the film. This was more literally, and disturbingly, the case in two other productions: and shows that took a movie musical and attempted to put it on stage. One was Bugsy Malone, a epic cringing evening both on stage and in the auditorium: a gangster story acted out by a cast of kids who — because to see children killing and falling down dead would have been far too disturbing an experience - usedguns that sprayed cream-cakes instead of bullets.

It was the most sustained custard-pie joke in history; but it made nonsense of the dramatic conventions, ( while the cast's inability to speak made the whole thing meaningless anyway. The problem was not that one couldnot follow the story, but that one's will to do so was steadily sapped. Gillian Gregorydevised some neat' pastiche choreography, but a chorus-line of schoolgirl vamps recalled the worst of children's television (Hughie Green spotting kiddie talent) in the 1950s. To cap everything, the children were not allowed to do their own singing; this was handled by an unseen adult group in a side-box. So we got a whole evening of lip-synch How 'Bugsy Malone On Stage' (such was the billing) compared with its screen original I cannot say: I missed the movie, having no desire to see the gangster and musical genres purged of sex and violence in the interests of juvenile cuteness.

Singin' in the Rain, of course, I know by heart; and there was something hopelessly self-defeating (except, it seems, commercially) in Tommy Steele's attempt to put so well-loved a picture into another medium. He complained that the critics had misunderstood him, that what he was trying to do was not to stage Singin' in the Rain, but to create a new work out of the same material. In fact what appeared at the Palladium looked as if Steele had attempted a facsimile, only deviating from it when something proved technically impossible or when the rights to some of the material was not available. (The film score was nearly all by the same composers, Arthur Freed and Nacio Herb Brown, but it was handled by a variety of publishers).

So sometimes one applauded the cleverness of the imitation, but it was hardly possible-to get excited over it. Steele re-created Gene Kelly' routine in the title-number (and got heroically wet); Roy Castle re-produced Donald O'Conner's amazing pratfalls in. 'Make 'Em Laugh, though what he sang, a surreal experience for movie-buffs, was "Be A Clown', the Cole Porter song from which Freed and Brown had originally lifted their own. With all the money and enthusiasm in the world the show could never re-produce the speed and lightness of the film; those who had never seen the original actually found the Betty Comden-Adolph Green script (one of Hollywood's greatest and most unified comedies) toothless and overblown. The thinking behind the production was objectionable than the production itself.

Apparently producers believe that they can lure audiences into a theatre by taking some property the public already knows, and ruining it. Marilyn almost counts musical. The work of an American team it premiered in London in expectation (presumably dashed) of a Broadway transfer. Larry Fuller, Hal Prince's regular choreographer directed in his master's (especially a narrator) from Evita but doing a tidy enough job. The score was no worse than that of most current musicals. But it was another self-destroying mechanism that did for the show. Did you know Marilyn Monroe' they all chanted at curtain-rise, and proceeded to tell us that only the movie-camera really did. That seems to rule her out as a stage subject, and indeed they finally upstaged their own production with a brilliantlyedited montage of authentic Monroe film-clips.

This was very unfair to Stephanie Lawrence, who played Marilyn and revealed herself as that rarity, a British musical performer with style. She doesn't brandish a big number at you; she sings it. The nearest thing to a large, successful original musical was Windy City, and it was still a good way off. It was craftsmanlike, and it was authentic. Based on the classic American newspaper comedy The Front Page it maintained much of the flavour of its original. What it could not maintain was its pace; the songs stopped the story without stopping the show. It was in many respects too faithful; it never became its own View of Farrah's setting for Poppy at the Barbican. animal.

A musical adaptation of a good play has to alter the original decisively (and it can be done, as in My Fair Lady, with only a slight tilt) to justify itself. Dick Vosburgh's lyrics were though not up to his Macaulay's music competent, sometimes snazzy. Dennis Waterman's Hildy Johnson was fatally lacking in dynamism, but Anton Rogers had it as Machiavellian Walter Burns, and as the murderer Earl Williams, Longden did sometimes manage to move the show into a world of its own. That leaves us with three small treasures. One was a revival of a 1929 British hit Mr Cinders; British in setting and origin, though actually the work of five composers and lyricisits, from both sides of the Atlantic.

The joints didn't show; there was a carefree international style in musicals at this period. The major partner- still around to write a new title song - was Vivian Ellis. I have to confess an interest; when Dan Crawford, who runs the King's Head, first told me of his intention to revive this show, I said he was mad. I was founded. The show, a variant on the Cinderella story in which the exploited poor relation is a man, proved to be not only tuneful but funny; and intentionally so. It gained much from the casting of Denis Lawson in the central role; he gave the show a sardonic edge, and — when he sang the magical cheer-up song 'Spread a Little Happiness' — understated emotion.

He consummately; incorporating parody of the 'Dying Swan' at one point, and at another singing a polysyallabic nonsense song 'On the Amazon' with lunatic authority. The show transfered from the King's Head to the Fortune, and lost some magic en route; but it ran through the year. The other gems came from off-Broadway. One was Snoopy, the second musical to be based on the Peanuts strip, and taking the logical step of putting the dog in the centre of it. A situation outlined in the drawings took on effortless threedimensional life. Snoopy is ineffably superior to the mortals who surround him, but he is also dependent on them. This, together with the assorted one-upmanship the young humans with the beaming Charlie Brown eternally at the bottom of the heap, made an evening.

There was no story but the unity of tone and characters made it a musical rather than a revue. It was spunkily performed by a British cast, headed by Teddy Kempner as Snoopy; and was buoyed up by a score of America's best current craftsmen, Hal Hackady and Larry Grossman. Finally there was Little Shop of Horrors which proved my point about rock as celebration. Emotionally, rock songs are overblown; they are always louder and usually longer than the situation warrants. So, when put on stage, and theyare funny;the smartshows are those thay capitalise on the fact. Little Shop of Horrors reached back to the seedy 1950s, age of the Chiffons, the Ronettes, and the Shirelles.

A girl trio, called Chiffon, Ronette, and Shirelle, told the story. A sadist who had found his vocation as a dentist, came on like Presley. Having disarmed us, the show plumed into another shock, the junk horror movie, and took our breath away by playing it for real. A strange plant, reared in a Skid Row flower-shop, grew and began eating everything in range, including the hero and ominously over the stalls, it threatened to devour the world, beginning with Cleveland. It now had a raucous voice of its own, and it tempted the schlemiel who had tended itlike a Mephistopheles combining soul-snaring with soul-singing. Barry James was a perfect victim, and Ellen Greene came from New York to recreate her original role of Audrey, masochistic girl-friend of the dentist and self-sacrificing love of our hero; a dazzlingly stylised dumb blonde, she even walked with a lisp.

Howard Ashman directed niftily, and also authored the book and lyrics, to gleaming parody tunes by Alan Menken. Their work had rare insouciance; and they trusted nobody. When the florist, rather than lose the services of his green-fingered assistant, offered to adopt him and make him a partner, they came up with a tango harnessing exploited vulnerability ('come kiss me quick, I'll be your son') to calculating disgust ('don't make me sick, just be my son'). One had almost forgotten such snappiness was still possible, and it was a tonic.
1984-01-01-a-wider-view-of-music:
A Wider View of Music

"There is no such thing as 'serious music' and 'light music' - there is only good music and bad music." Where does this leave the musical? Robert Cushman is in no doubt.

The premise underlying Book Music and Lyrics is that the music of musicals is worth listening to. That may sound obvious; but when our first series was reviewed on Critics' Forum we were informed that such material might be just about acceptable in a late-night slot on Radio Two, but had no place on Radio Three, unless backed up by large slabs of sociological analysis.

This really puzzled me. Either music is worth hearing or it isn't; and if it isn't I don't see that its case can be improved by any number of spoken programme notes. A Richard Rodgers song needs no more apology than a Franz Schubert song. Knowledge cannot create enjoyment, though it can enhance it. That enhancement is part of what these programmes are about. Each individual edition has a theme, and most of them have an argument. But then these are a practical necessity anyway. The modern musical (which, in practice, means mainly the American musical) started gathering momentum around 1920, and since then it has accumulated a huge recorded literature. Choosing from it is a daunting task, and you need some manufactured support just to get through the undergrowth. With a theme I can mitigate the agonies of selection; if I leave out something I love, I can feel that it is, somehow, not my fault. Besides, finding what fits and what doesn't is a fascination to me, and, I hope, to listeners.

One criticism levelled at the first programmes was that I was making distinctions between different lyricists and composers that could only be appreciated by specialists. This is probably true; but then part of our aim is to turn listeners into specialists; to make them pleasurably aware of the differences between one talented and intelligent creator and another. This seems to me the kind of knowledge that is worth having: more so than historical background ("this song was written in the Depression; it is therefore about money") though I enjoy filling that in as well. If I had to defend the presence on Radio Three of a series about musicals I would do so by analogy with jazz. Both are forms with popular roots that still have some contact with everyday pop music. There are jazz standards and show songs that everyone knows, but there are many more that have passed into obscurity and that need explaining. Apart from anything else, the songs in musicals written since 1945 are tightly connected to the plots of the shows and need to have their dramatic context supplied. Even a song as familiar as People Will Say We're in Love gains in interest when you know that it is sung in Oklahoma! by a couple of Western lovers, too proud and shy to admit their feelings. It also helps if you realise that Oscar Hammerstein had spent his life trying to write conversational lyrics that fitted the characters singing them. This - since the work itself is excellent - is the kind of exegesis that belongs on a serious music station; and deserves, I self-interestedly think, as regular exposure as is granted to jazz. Charlie Parker was a fine artist, but there is no way that he was any more important than Irving Berlin (who, if radical chic appeals to you, started life every bit as poor and disadvantaged).

We have some self-imposed rules. We are not Songs from the Shows or Your Hundred Best Tunes; we steer off the best-known songs and we try, whenever possible, to use original cast recordings. These however have only been systematically issued since the 1940s; when dealing with shows written earlier we look either for individual records by original performers or for the completest possible version by an outsider. (This usually means records issued on small labels within the last 20 years.) From these sources we have attempted to create our own re-creations of little-known shows. It is surprising how solid an apparently flimsy number can sound when fitted into its context, even if that context is a frivolous one.

The first programme of the new series is entirely made up of cast recordings which give it, I think, an exciting theatrical flavour. The subject is Devils, Villains and Anti-Heroes. The thesis is that the musical theatre reached maturity partly through treating its rogues and scoundrels as more than plot mechanisms. Brecht and Weill's Macheath (The Threepenny Opera) was the long-distance inspiration; Rodgers and Hart's Pal Joey, Rodgers and Hammerstein's Jud Fry (Oklahoma!) were pioneering examples; Stephen Sondheim's Sweeney Todd, a mass murderer, is the ultimate. But Sweeney is also a figure we identify with; he is the anti-hero as, in a much lighter vein, was the agent con-man of the British show Expresso Bongo (a rare opportunity to hear Paul Scofield in song: Cockney song at that.) The devil-figures, the tempters, are something else, and wonderful insinuating musical subjects; their lineage stretches back to Gershwin's Sportin' Life (Porgy and Bess) and goes forward to the epicene M.C. of Cabaret whose "wilkommen, bienvenue, welcome" takes us back in its milieu and its orchestration to Brecht and Weill.

Programme Two is about Rodgers and Hart, the most fascinating in their checks and balances of all composer-lyricist teams. It concentrates on two periods of their work: the twenties, represented by the yacht-set comedy Heads Up, and the forties, which they inaugurated with Too Many Girls, one of the many musicals dealing with collegiate football. From it came one of the most charming of all love-songs, I Didn't Know What Time It Was. We don't always eschew the familiar, though the recording we have chosen is an unstandardised one, that does more justice than most to the development of Hart's thought-line. It's sung by an actor, Anthony Perkins.
1984-01-08-capturing-the-whale:
Capturing the whale

THEATRE

ROBERT CUSHMAN
In Manchester and London.

By all accounts including his own Michael Elliott has for years been as intent on bringing Moby Dick to the stage as was Captain Ahab on bringing him to the slaughter. A director can convince an audience with complex machinery or seduce it by extreme simplicity. Mr Elliott, at the Manchester Royal Exchange, does both.
