He makes super-subtle use of his theatre's unrivalled acoustics, and his towering arena is ideal for evoking first a port, then a ship, finally the sea itself. Laurie Dennett's setting, as one would have expected, fills the stage with rigging. Also as expected, the cast, in the cause of atmosphere, spend a lot of time and energy heaving at capstans while singing shanties.

And yet, when the hunt is on and the boats are out, we easily accept a new convention whereby groups of actors sit straining at invisible oars, before being tumbled into invisible waves. Finally, by a magnificently simple trick that it would be heartless to reveal, the naked stage becomes simultaneously the ocean and (Tynan's phrase when reviewing Orson Welles's adaptation) the supremely unstageable whale, unstageable no longer. For a moment, Mr Elliott captures him.

The whalers prove unexpectedly harder quarry. Mr Elliott keeps faith with the language Melville gave them, that flaming amalgam of Victorian badinage and Jacobean oratory. Ahab's 'I'd strike the sun if it insulted me' is one perfect iambic among many. His last harpooner's rhapsody ('What ho, Tashtego, let me hear thy hammer') is shirked, but we do get the second mate's request, when on the verge of becoming whalemeat, for one red cherry ere he dies: one of those lines that passes in a mere book, but shrivels when exposed in a theatre.

I usually think of Moby Dick as a novel I never finished, but under pressure my memory reveals that I did indeed get to the end, though only by skipping large portions of the middle. What stays with me is the beginning, and I recall in Ishmael's narrative a humour, and even wit, that is missing here; Mr Elliott would hardly have cast so truculent an actor as Nigel Terry had he wished to preserve them. Something of them survives in Terence Wilton's Queequeg; and there are worthy performances from John Cording, earnest as Starbuck, and Tim Healy, jovial as Stubb.

No other individuals come through, but maybe none needs to. Everything must depend on Ahab: a natural dramatic subject (the classic avenger), but conceived in a totally undramatic fashion. He cannot be acted, he can only be embodied; and whom would you cast? Brian Cox approaches him with devout intelligence, but he seems even saner than Gregory Peck. His eyes grow wild and his hair matted, but his voice refuses to follow suit. He seems a strict but amiable man with a sound Presbyterian upbringing and, it has to be admitted, an unaccountable thing about whales: not enough, you feel, to keep him from yielding to Starbuck's entreaties and sailing right back to Nantucket.

Failing to draw us into Ahab's obsession, the production cannot involve us with what it might actually mean. (Mr Elliott does some regrettable circling in his programme note: the whale must be meaningful because the novel is so great, and the novel must be great because the whale is so meaningful.) But if we are not caught up in the captain's quest, we are enthralled by the director's; by quiet things like the swaying of the crew even when the seas are calm, and by overwhelming ones like the vision of St Elmo's fire, which strikes black magic from the lighting grid.

  

Bernard Slade, the Broadway playwright who through taste or economic instinct specialises in two-handers, presents us in Special Occasions (Ambassadors) with the passage through the years of a divorced couple. Always each other's best friends and confidants, they remain so, whatever the breaks: an easy situation to swallow, but a difficult one to develop.

By the end of the second act Mr Slade's dramaturgy has degenerated into a prolonged tease over whether our hero and heroine are going finally to remarry. (The slob in you hopes they will, the pedant prays they won't; choose your weakness.) Some of the earlier writing connects with real pain, though the fatal flaws -- she drinks and he writes -- are never very believable.

Somebody has transferred the characters from there to here: a decision that involves them in uttering such typically English remarks as 'You resent the hell out of me' and in claiming to have got drunk on the flight from London to Manchester. (Try even getting a drink.) Jan Waters does handsomely, though John Alderton is hamstrung by the author's refusal to acknowledge what a bastard the fellow is. Mr Slade also directs, on somebody's misconception of a unit set.

  

Peter Pan (Barbican) impressively consolidates last year's uneven promise. With everyone sure of the special effects, events in the lagoon and on the pirate-ship are twice as lucid as before. Katy Behean, as Wendy, unemphatically brings out all the facets of the child-mother; and Mark Rylance, with his vigorously piping voice, gets both the boy Peter and the spirit Pan.

Edward Petherbridge is a winsomely confidential narrator, and though Stephen Moore hardly tries to make Hook frightening, he does make him very entertaining. There has been a definite rise in the quality of pirate and lost boy, and the wildlife remains endearing, especially the crocodile, the only character in world drama of whom it is reasonable to inquire what makes him tick. (Cap'n Ahab's life would have been transformed if Moby Dick had swallowed a clock.)

  

The revival of Oliver! (Aldwych) is glorified by the return of Ron Moody to the role of Fagin: capering in his juvenile thieves' kitchen with his tattered cloak outstretched in all directions, like an inspired animated cartoon of the Pied Piper of Hamelin. Sean Kenny's copious set, wonderfully lit in blues and ambers, shows its age with dignity.

Some of Lionel Bart's lyrics may be slipshod (not all) and some of his music cheap (again not all), but his fairy-tale version of Dickens's horror-story has its own integrity; like My Fair Lady, it corresponds to a romantic image which, however perversely, we have all carried away from the original.

  

Hello Dolly (Prince of Wales), by contrast, merely trims and decorates its source. Its historical importance is that it institutionalised the idea of the Broadway leading lady, forever descending staircases. Carol Channing, when she finally climbed down in London, was playing like a drag-queen; to cast Danny La Rue seems the logical next step. Unfortunately Mr La Rue's talents are not musical; to play Dolly you do not have to sing exactly, but you have to move the earth with your voice. Here we are asked to get our kicks from a parade of frocks.

The only performer I felt like applauding was Lionel Jeffries, a beleaguered walrus. 'Hello Dolly' depends on its original staging; in David Toguri's new choreography respectable shops are invaded by dancers who plainly have no business there. Several of Jerry Herman's tunes still appeal. When a musical is described as having a one-song score, the description is always false and the song that is meant will be far from the best. That is infallible wisdom. Goodbye.
1984-01-27-critics-cool-to-play-but-warm:
Critics cool to play but warm to star

Friday, January 27, 1984

ROBERT CUSHMAN

London ENGLAND -- BY ROBERT CUSHMAN LONDON THIS WEEK Larry Finebergs Eve was added to the list of Canadian plays which have opened in London to a frosty response from British critics. It may, however, stand a better chance with British audiences.

One thing that could recommend the play to them is that - unlike such previous imports as Balconville, Waiting for the Parade and Billy Bishop Goes to War - its drama is not dependent on either a Canadian setting or peculiarly Canadian characters. The play, which was first seen at Stratford, Ont., in 1976, happens to be set in Montreal (where Fineberg grew up) but its story would ring true anywhere. The title almost shrieks universality; the heroine's name is actually Eva, but there she is on the marquee simply as Eve.

Fineberg's Eve may not quite qualify as Everywoman but she is a lively lady in a painfully recognizable situation. In her sixties, she finds her marriage has worn out. She leaves her invalid husband and goes to live alone in a seedy rooming-house. Conventional society, represented by her lawyer son, assumes she will soon be back, but the end of the play finds her reasserting her precarious independence. The play almost becomes propaganda for the liberation of senior citizens, but the writing is real and rooted enough to transcend this.

That, at least, was my reaction. The London daily reviewers were generally less enthusiastic. The Daily Telegraph called it a slight, monochrome study of a lonely woman with "little but its quiet integrity to recommend it." The Financial Times said there was little fabric to Mr. Finebergs text and little weight - little wit, too, for that matter. The Times was heavily critical of the technique: "The play runs into the dramatic quicksands of solitude, and attempts to extricate itself with non-stop monologue - part free association, part explanatory narrative - plugging the silence with garrulous telegraphese." The Guardian was the most positive: "one or two shrewd points . . . accurate and optimistic." All were united, however, in their enthusiasm for the central performance. At Stratford the role was created by Jessica Tandy, a British actress who has spent most of her life in America. In London, neatly enough, it is a triumph for Constance Cummings, American-born but British- based. Her career reached a new plateau when she played opposite Laurence Olivier in Long Days Journey Into Night at the National Theatre. More recently she won a Tony as the stroke-victim heroine of Wings. Her forte is playing women in extreme states while keeping us constantly in touch with their normal selves.

Miss Cummings, who is herself a stunningly youthful 74, makes the audience feel the astonishing ease with which a middle-class woman can turn into a bag-lady rummaging in trash-cans. She is very fine in her scenes with a heavy-drinking Hungarian refugee who breaks into her room to throw up in the sink, and stays to help her rediscover her womanhood. She has an admirably light touch in a play whose preponderance of monologues could easily drag it down. Fineberg accounts her performance the best he has seen in the role.

Ronnie Letham, a Scots actor-director, has staged the piece in the studio space of the Lyric Theatre, Hammersmith, one of London's outlying theatres but also one of its most prestigious; it has originated several successful plays, including the current West End and Broadway smash Noises Off. The Hungarian is admirably played by Glyn Owen; Canadian actor Blain Fairman is the son.

Robert Cushman is drama critic for The London Observer.
1984-02-05-the-actor-as-team-player:
The actor as team player

Profile

ALBERT FINNEY was not, in 1956, the kind of name one had if one was an actor. Well, maybe it would pass for someone who specialised in playing wizened northern caretakers, the kind of pawky old actor who cannot be imagined as having ever been young.

At Birmingham Rep, where its bearer began his career, 'Albert' must have stood out at a terse, awkward angle in the programme among the expected Geoffreys and Michaels. Agents and producers in his early years begged him to change it but he refused.

He was right; and not just because his arrival coincided with the eruption of working-class (actually lower-middle class) plays that started with 'Look Back in Anger.' The name may have become fashionable but it has, oddly, remained unique. When anybody in the British theatre talks about Albert, there is only one Albert they can mean.

It is worth dwelling on the name because it has always suited him so perfectly. It has a stocky, humorous ring to it: it suggests common sense, athletic virility (his namesake, Tom Finney, was a star footballer) and, emphatically, the North of England. Finney has always been able to capitalise on his background. He is better than just northern; he is from Salford which, at the beginning of his career, had a brief moment as centre of the universe. Shelagh Delaney came from there, and told us all about it in 'A Taste of Honey.'

Even before his Birmingham debut Finney had been the subject of prophecy and speculation. Kenneth Tynan, in a prescient review that he was careful to preserve among his collected works, had called him a 'smouldering young Spencer Tracy.' This was for a performance he gave at RADA, where his generation was a famous one: Frank Finlay, Brian Bedford, John Stride, Peter O'Toole. He and O'Toole were linked together, groomed as rivals.

When Finney was at Birmingham, O'Toole was at the Bristol Old Vic; and those were the theatres that were expected to produce future classical stars. When he left Birmingham, at 21, Finney had already played Henry V and Macbeth, and people were getting ready to call him great. He went, as was expected of him, to Stratford to play juvenile leads, and had a fairly disastrous season. His best notices were for playing the First Citizen in 'Coriolanus,' and the same production gave him his biggest break of the year. He understudied Laurence Olivier in the title role, and had to go on for him.

There were no reviews but the echoes of his success reached London. Years later, on television, he was characteristically funny about it, saying that the audience knew what an impossible job he had, following Olivier in one of his greatest roles. Once they had swallowed their disappointment and puzzled over the slip in the programme ('Albert who?') they had to be on his side.

He broke through the following year, a long way from Shakespeare but close to his roots, in the stage version of 'Billy Liar.' He was due to appear a few months earlier in a similar flamboyant role in 'The Long and the Short and the Tall' but he got sick and the break went to O'Toole instead.

The two of them were now the official figureheads for the New Actors who were patently needed for reasons of both art and public relations, to complement the New Playwrights. It was a time, the late Fifties and early Sixties, when anything seemed possible; a renaissance in the British theatre was taken for granted, and there were even rumours of one in the British cinema.

Both actors were launched as film stars: Finney in 'Saturday Night and Sunday Morning,' O'Toole on a wider international stage in 'Lawrence of Arabia.' When Richard Harris made 'This Sporting Life' his name was added to theirs. They were touted as the hell-raisers of British acting, young men who would give truthful, searing, hilarious pictures of contemporary life and then go on to revitalise the classics. They were going to be the leaders of the profession.

It is a commonplace to say that they, like Richard Burton before them, have proved lost leaders. But Finney has been less lost than the others. His public image has always been milder, sometimes in the news for womanising (he has been twice married and divorced), but not for drinking. He has seemed disciplined, and he has emerged as a different kind of actor: not a doomed Celtic prophet but a solid comic pragmatist, with a puzzled awareness of pain.

He has organised his career in slabs, taking long absences from the theatre to make films, from the cinema to do plays, and from both in order to travel exotically. (A couple of years ago he and Diana Quick were briefly feared to have been lost up the Amazon.)

It was after one such absence, in 1965, that he entered the National Theatre, disdaining the offer of pre-arranged star parts with the memorable words 'I'll play as cast.' He stayed for 18 glorious months.

Controversial

It was the high noon of Olivier's regime and Finney was an integral part of it: if Olivier was to have a successor as actor-director of the National he would have been the only choice. He was the kingpin of Feydeau's 'A Flea in Her Ear' (still regarded by many people as the funniest show they have ever seen) and did a delightful camp cameo in Peter Shaffer's 'Black Comedy,' but his influence seemed to permeate even the plays he wasn't in. When he left, the company's fortunes took a long dip.

Ten years later he was back, to lead Peter Hall's actors into the new theatre on the South Bank. Between 1975 and 1978 he played one leading role after another, all of them under Hall's direction. His Hamlet was, to use the standard euphemism, controversial; it was tough and unkempt (as the text suggests) but excitingly conveyed the race of the hero's mind across conventional frontiers. He did all with the marathon role of Tamburlaine that one could reasonably expect but no more—which, paradoxically, means that he was slightly less than one had hoped for. He was a good Lopahin in 'The Cherry Orchard' but a terribly flat Macbeth. He had insisted on playing the role but one senses the relief when he turned to his one modern role at the National—a John Huston facsimile in the movie-making comedy, 'Has Washington Legs?'

During both his National stints Finney stood in for other actors in supporting roles. That kind of ensemble work he clearly enjoys and it makes him popular with colleagues and audiences. Hall's Diary is full of appreciations of Finney as a company man, a morale-builder, a star; but also hints that their relationship deteriorated after 'Macbeth.' Finney also had a spell as an associate director at the Royal Court, but he did few actual shows there, and though his commitment to a theatre can be intense it usually operates under a time limit.

Movie stars are proverbially restless, and he remains bankable: having fun as Hercule Poirot in 'Murder on the Orient Express,' or Daddy Warbucks in 'Annie,' an anguished success as the raging husband in 'Shoot the Moon,' tipped for an Oscar as the old actor in 'The Dresser.' (A sign of the times: Albert Finney at 47 playing old.) He has also had a fling as a singer-songwriter, and a more substantial stab at film-directing with 'Charlie Bubbles.' And for years, as founder and co-director of the Memorial Enterprises production company, he has been a quietly effective showbusinessman.

His latest venture draws many of his interests together. It is United British Artists, a co-operative mainly of performers (others include Diana Rigg and Maggie Smith) to get on plays, movies and video-tapes according to their own tastes and without benefit of subsidy. It reasserts Finney as an actor among actors, and it is typical of him—or of the Royal Court, New Actor side of him—that the first production, at Riverside Studios, should be a sober documentary on the Steve Biko inquest which he directs and in which he appears. Next comes the showier role of Sergeant Musgrave in a revival of the Arden play at the Old Vic. The part—a disciplinarian possessed by a cause—could be ideal for him. He has not betrayed his early promise but he has not yet fulfilled it either. To qualify as a great actor you have to set your seal on a great role—to make others afraid of following you in it—and that he has yet to do.
1984-04-01-in-celebration:
In Celebration

We are still living in the stretch of theatrical history that was inaugurated by the premiere of Look Back in Anger in 1956. That is a sentence I have been employing, more in conversation than in print, over the last ten years and it is one that has usually been greeted with corroborative nods. Last year, however, there was mutiny. Channel 4, in their Voices series of colloquies for the insomniac intelligentsia, mounted a discussion under the heading 'Is Jimmy Porter Dead?" Playwright David Edgar asserts that, as of 1980, he was. This was then debated by Richard Eyre of the National Theatre, Gavin Richards of Belt and Braces, and Michelene Wandor, writer and woman.

Mr Edgar posited that John Osborne had invented a drama that existed to slag off its audiences: a purpose inherited by every subsequent playwright worthy of the name but now displaced by what has been called "celebratory theatre', most prominently represented - as he admitted with a becoming twinkle - by his own adaptation of Nicholas Nickleby. He evinced mixed feelings about this 'sea-change' (he's a scrupulous man) but he found it worrying. The theatre, he said, now colluded with its audience instead of disturbing it. He quoted Hamlet on holding up mirrors, and on guilty creatures. Hamlet, when he made those references, was engaged in mounting a production for a very specialised purpose; and nobody can have heard that passage about showing scorn her own image without finding it, in its context, strangely reductive.

If that's what Shakespeare thought drama was about (Hamlet also recommends showing 'virtue her own feature', which suggests a blueprint for a particularly sanctimonious theatre of reassurance) then he didn't know his own strength. Macbeth, of course, is a pretty stern warning against regicide, but that cannot be what has kept us interested in it. Mr Edgar asserted that Look Back in Anger took up an adversary position, and that that position was primarily political. I doubt the last part. Mr Osborne's autobiography A Better Class of Person indicates that when he wrote the play he had a lot of bile to work off, but his grievances, in book and play, are strictly personal. They could of course be politically interpreted by critics, and Mr Osborne obviously believed his own publicity enough to go on and write the first metaphor-for-England plays in The Entertainer and The World of Paul Slickey, but after that he went back to the confessional.

Of the playwrights who followed him in the 50s and 60s some, like Arnold Wesker and John Arden, wrote on explicitly political subjects and some, like Harold Pinter, did not; but I can detect in none of their plays the confrontational aggro that Mr Edgar recommends. I can detect it in what was written about them, both the reviews and the in-house proclamations. Indeed I can remember, as a teenager, feeling it myself: the clenched-teeth adrenalin of liking something that other people would hate, of wanting to rub their noses in something they would prefer to ignore. Do you recall the last scene of Beyond the Fringe? Four prophets gather to await the end of the world, a rushing wind that will annihilate everything except the mountain on which they themselves are standing, from which they intend to watch the destruction and have a good giggle.

That is the best image I know for the theatre of shock. The people who advocate it always want it to shock someone else: the perpetual 'other' which for the last century or more we have stigmatised as the bourgeoisie. Shock tactics Jimmy Porter found lots of chums. Ken Tynan, in his myth-making Observer notice, said that all the youth of England would respond and many of them did. At 13 I loved the opening gambit about the two posh Sunday papers. I still love it; the main reason the play has survived is that it is funny, i.e. we recognise the references. The people who didn't share them stayed away, so in the theatre the promised confrontation never happened.

This did not stop it being discussed in what were not then known as the media, but that is another kind of happening. Oddly enough Mr Osborne did develop an adversary stance in his latter plays, and little thanks he got for it from those who are supposed to favour such things. Witness the revolted response to A Sense of Detachment, which ironically is partly about the extreme difficulty of shocking that damnably adaptable thing, an audience. The playwrights of the 70s - Mr Edgar's generation did behave as if they believed the propaganda; they tended, in his own words, 'towards cynicism, nihilism and arrogance.' At least that was part of it; Richard Eyre, who was involved, testified during the debate that they were also looking for an audience that agreed with them.

But, to do them justice, I think they felt uneasy when they found it; scorn was faced with her own image and reacted by getting even more scornful. The discussion, inevitably, rambled. Miss Wandor wandered to feminism, saying that Janey Porter (at least it wasn't Jemima) had hardly had a look in. She was interestingly sceptical about the new female audience; justifiably so, since women have always gone to the theatre more than men. Mr Richards attacked "these managers and people" ', though with no mention of his own long West End run in Accidental Death of an Anarchist. He also said that you should not work "for an audience that you actually despise." I found this cheering; in this situation you should either stop working or - preferably stop despising.

Serious fun How does the despising start? People go into the theatre, as they go into any other public activity - criticism, for example - for only one reason: exhibitionism. This is generally thought to be a discreditable motive, so others are adduced: like political commitment. Besides, a play has to be about something and politics will do as well as any other subject: better than most, probably. But we should not confuse the material of making theatre with the thing itself. There is nothing than can be said in a play that cannot be said in some other form. If this is the one we choose - well, we choose it largely because we believe it is where our talents lie but also, I hope, because we think it an attractive thing in itself.

Because, to put it briefly, we think it is fun. If we think that, we have every reason to do what Mr Richards wants which is to share it with the largest possible audience. It is difficult, though, to reconcile ourselves to so frivolous an endeavour, so we talk instead about reaching the working class with plays that are relevant to them. Mr Richards spoke of doing The Ballygombeen Bequest, which is set in Ireland, at the Bush; and of moving the Irish bar staff to tears. Fine. You can always reach people with subjects that are close to them. If you can do it skilfully you deserve applause; but not, I think, marks for virtue.

There is a myth about the ideal audience that you are not playing to. Last year I sat in the bleachers for another Channel 4 programme, Shakespeare Lives, and heard Michael Bogdanov talk about the untapped audience that was young and vibrant. I decided that youth was nothing special, that I had never met anyone who vibrated, and that Mr Bogdanov should energies to entertaining the audience he actually had. If that can be done - without lies and without condescension - it can be a cure for guilt, a salve for contempt, maybe even an antidote to theatrical megalomania. If that is what Mr Edgar's 'celebratory theatre' is about, I am all for it.
1984-05-26-the-art-of-the-actress:
The art of the actress

Journey into the Shadows, Sunday 9.10 BBC2

Anna Massey has recently discovered a new talent - that of painter. It's part of her preparation for her dramatic portrayal of the artist Gwen John, as she explains to Robert Cushman.

A year or so ago there appeared in The Sunday Times colour magazine a portrait of the painter Gwen John. Her face had reminded somebody of another face: superimposed on it was a photograph of actress Anna Massey.

If ever a hint were dropped to a casting department, that was it. When television director Anna Benson Gyles suggested a dramatised documentary on Gwen John, Anna Massey was the actress she wanted for the lead.

Anna Massey's favourite word for acting is "journey", and Elaine Morgan's script appealed to her as a more extensive trip than most. It follows Gwen's life from 1903 when, in her late 20s, she was part of the London menage of her more famous brother Augustus John, to 1926, the year of her first exhibition in London, with a glance forward to her lonely death in 1939 in Dieppe.

She spent most of her adult life in France, much of it in Paris, living in small, poor rooms. Paris was also the scene of the one great love affair of her life. She was the mistress - one of many - of the sculptor Auguste Rodin. Their affair lasted on and off for ten years, but after that she went on writing him letters. At the height of their relationship she was writing to him twice a day, and it was to these letters - nearly 2,000 of them, all preserved in the Rodin Museum - that Anna Massey turned to research her role.

"People are like shadows to me," wrote Gwen John, "and I am like a shadow." The letters demonstrate an extraordinary mixture of passion and reserve. "She was," says Miss Massey, "extraordinarily shy to people she didn't know. But I was once told by a friend that shyness is actually a selfish, attention-getting thing; you walk into a room and you expect that people will notice you. Gwen was renownedly shy; she became a sort of recluse. And yet she was, in her own way, assertive. She walked in a speedily determined way. You can see from her photo that she has a wonderful, upright stance. She was indomitably there."

Anna Massey could take for granted a physical and facial resemblance. The next thing was to get her own painting right; or at least the appearance of painting. "I couldn't paint a pin-person for love or money, but I hate plays where actors are supposed to be painting and they're obviously not doing it. So I said I've got to learn to paint."

She turned for help to Mary Taubman, a painter herself as well as an expert on Gwen John and one of the programme's accredited advisers (the others are Ben and Sara John, Augustus's grandchildren, and Michael Holroyd, probably the finest living biographer, whose books include one on Augustus John). "Mary was incredible. Every time on the set I picked up a paintbrush or a palette or an easel I knew, technically, what I was doing." She also worked with a painter friend. "We forged some wonderful Gwen Johns. One of them she now has on her wall."

It was, she says, riveting research. Gwen John revealed a lot of herself in the letters. She wrote with a childlike innocence, and in a childish hand. Rodin, it seems, was sexually the only man in her life. "She had a lot of passionate relationships with women; I've never been sure whether they were consummated or not. I think probably not. There's an obsessive quality in the Rodin letters; they're very flowery, very free. She had been obsessed with another man before she met him, but I think she was probably a virgin. There's a virgin quality in her writing; at the same time she makes the Rodin relationship seem very luscious, very free."

All this is quite apart from her relationship with her brother, complicated by her friendships with both his wife Ida and his mistress Dorelia McNeill (with whom Gwen set out to walk from London to Rome). Augustus emerges, in Miss Massey's words, as "quite monstrous, certainly in his later years". But she can see resemblances between him and his sister. "They both drew with incredible speed; I could see in their work that they were from the same world." All the same, as they grew older their styles, especially in portraiture, diverged. "She was more agonised in her work; he suffered pain, too, but he escaped from it in a tempestuous way. Augustus said of her work: 'The little pictures to me are almost painfully charged with feeling'."

The mixture of shyness and spirit in Gwen John is something that should suit Anna Massey very well. At 46, she is one of the most respected and versatile actresses in the country, with a range extending from the luckless spinster of Angela Huth's TV play Virginia Fly is Drowning to the imperiously witty Ariadne Utterword of Shaw's Heartbreak House. What remains constant in her work is a firm backbone (mental and physical) and a fastidiousness enabling her to rescue the dowdiest characters from dullness.

She too has a successful brother, Daniel Massey, in the same profession, though their careers have grown pretty much side by side. But she has, like Gwen John, in some sense had to break away from her family in order to find herself. The daughter of two famous actors, Raymond Massey and Adrianne Allen, she grew up in the atmosphere of the West End, and began her career - without drama-school - in the title role of an enormously successful boulevard comedy, William Douglas Home's The Reluctant Debutante. It was 1955, and she was 17. She was actually offered a smaller role in the play, and turned it down. The management said, "Well, would you mind coming and just rehearsing the lead for a week," and at the end of that time she had the part, almost literally for keeps.

She stayed with it for years ("It ran for so long I felt imprisoned"), in London and on Broadway. By the end of it she was a star, or at any rate a starlet, who was not taken quite seriously and, in her own words, "was using the West End as a repertory", since she had no other way of practising. Another fluffy comedy followed, and then a T. S. Eliot play in which she admits to being hopelessly out of her depth. The turnaround came in 1961 when she won ("after endless auditions - well, no, there were only two, but it seemed endless") the role of Annie Sullivan, the Irishwoman who turned Helen Keller from a vegetable to a person, in The Miracle Worker: a role that had already made Anne Bancroft a star in New York.

Anna's own life was fairly traumatic at the time - her marriage to actor Jeremy Brett was breaking up, and she was decorating her flat for the first time in her life - but the pressure may have helped. Certainly she delivered an unsparing performance that took her out of the debutante class for ever. She had, in fact, been in on the last stages of the West End's period as centre of the British theatre: since then her stage career has leaned increasingly towards the subsidised sector, especially the National Theatre and the Royal Court, together with an enormous amount of work on radio and television.

Two especial problems in playing Gwen John. One, minor, was nudity, since Gwen first earned her living in Paris as a model. That was how she met Rodin. "I thought," said Miss Massey, bemused at finding herself faced with this for the first time at this stage in her career, "that I'd faint; but I didn't." (She adds that the script of Alfred Hitchcock's 1972 film Frenzy called for her to walk naked across a bedroom in long-shot, and she was rather annoyed that Hitchcock didn't actually ask her to do it.)

The other, larger problem is the perennial one in playing the famous: people expect them to be more elevated than they really are. As Anna Massey says: "Even Michelangelo must, occasionally, have said 'Pass the salt'."
1984-07-01-little-me:
Little Me

Not too many musical comedies are actually funny. Guys and Dolls of course, but even there the romance is meant to be taken pretty much at face value; laughter is a strong but not a pervasive element. Otherwise there are three, all clustered together at the beginning of the 1960s: How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying, A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum, and Little Me. Forum, as an exemplar and a celebration of farce, is sui generis; a musical based on Plautus and set in ancient Rome would have to be. But the other two have much in common. They arrived in consecutive seasons, both produced by Feuer and Martin, both choreographed by Bob Fosse.

Both have fragmentary literary sources: suggested by rather than adapted from. Both are satires, dealing in a bland acceptance of the outrageous. Remember mediocricity is not a mortal sin sings Frank Loesseer's climbing tycoon, for the delectation of an audience largely composed of the mediocrities themselves. "So here's a good tiding, if men you are killing, a talent you're hiding, to be a performer' sings Carolyn Leigh's vaudeville booking agents to the innocent multiple murderess who is the heroine of Little Me, thereby saying in four lines what it took Chicago two laboriously cynical hours to establish. Both, How to Succeed and Little Me, are brilliant. Little Me is the story of Belle Poitrine, née Schlumpfert, a girl of extreme poverty and Four of the parts Russ Abbot plays in Little Me - top, Amos Pinchley, and Noble Eggleston.

Below: Fred Poitrine and Val du Val. ignorance, and of Noble Eggleston, a youth of extreme riches and accomplishment who is educated at Yale and Harvard, simultaneously, and in later years pursues a dual career as lawyer and surgeon, taking time out to be a World War One flying ace and to save the lives of all passengers and crew in a shipwreck of Titanic proportions. Noble's one disadvantage is his mother, who is unspeakable. She disapproves of Belle, especially of the way she smells, and keeps the two apart. To prove herself worthy, Belle, who has the kind of figure that used to be described as pneumatic, determines to acquire wealth, title and education.

She gets them through the good offices of a succession of mostly rich lovers (and even a couple of husbands), each of whom accidentally expires after giving Belle his all. The story is told to us as a showbiz autobiography, the mature Belle commenting from the sidelines on the adventures of her younger self. It is interesting to see this device again in the wake of its use in Jean Seberg and to realise that it could never be anything but funny, intentionally or otherwise. In its original (1962) incarnation, the story was told on the golf-course by a successful elder Belle to the ghost-writer of her memoirs. In the current version, deriving partly from an unsuccessful New York revival of a year or so ago, our narrator is on the skids, telling her tale as part of a seedy saloon act.

This means a new opening number, 'Don't Ask a Lady', to replace the original "The Truth' (which went, in part, 'as in a haze/I see a Doubledays/all shining in a window full of Arthur Miller plays'). The replacement is a better song but not as apt; and the show is robbed of some of its point if the sacred monster romanticising her past is nudged from her outrageous pinnacle. Indeed all the obvious structural alterations are questionable; instead of being a childhood admirer, Belle's gangster wooer now emerges from nowhere, does his big number and disappears until the ending, by which time we have forgotten him. The natty title song, an overlapping duet for old and young Belle, is confused by having their mother get into the act.

(For some reason, however loose a show's structure, reassigning numbers is always a mistake. Two more of the original songs have gone; one, 'Poor Little Hollywood Star', is unlamented, but deletion of the other, the aforequoted 'Be a Performer', not only robs us of a wonderful song dripping with callous insouciance ('unless you, God forbid/get hung for what you did/oh-ho you naughty kid') but leaves very cloudy Belle's crucial progression onto the boards. Having written a classic showbiz satire, Neil Simon has nearly taken the showbiz out of it. But a lot of great stuff remains. Some of Mr Simon's best work is in his books for musicals. Removed from its usual realistic confines, his imagination thrives; it expresses itself generally in jokes, and the audience is spared the discomfort of wondering whether any characters would converse so exclusively in one-liners.

These are not people; this is a cartoon with a laugh in every balloon. My admiration for the lyrics of the late superb Miss Leigh must now be manifest; her JULY 1984 rhymes are prodigious, her jokes as good as Mr Simon's and tougher. The score is actually a little more sophisticated than the book, but since this is not your integrated Rodgers-and- Hammerstein musical the discrepancies hardly matter. Miss Leigh and Cy Coleman were the premier song-writing combination of the postwar years, and superior pop songs witty, rhythmic and curvaceous - are what they offer here. The score takes in the jazz anthem of 'On the Other Side of the Tracks', the blatant, pounding slinkiness of T've Got Your Number', the hilarious Central European prance-lament of 'Goodbye' (subtitled "The Prince's Farewell'), the affecting waltz of Real Live Girl', and the tongue-in-cheek hoe-down morality of 'Deep Down Inside'.

Mr Fosse's reconstructed choreography makes the Western origins of this last one invigoratingly clear; the bums who dance it have been fitted out by Tony Walton in bucolic splendour, the gladdest of rags. His costumes and sets, especially the vast tilt of his sinking liner, are triumphs. The older Belle is well handled by Lynda Abbot as Eggleston with Sheila White as the heroine, Belle. Baron, and the younger is scintillatingly done by Sheila White. While two actresses share the female lead, the male star appropriates no less than eight individual roles. Traditionally this feat has been performed by a television comedian: Sid Caesar, Bruce Forsyth, and now Russ Abbot. Mr Abbot has not Mr Caesar's mastery (on the record anyway) of the wry aside, or the killer instinct of Mr Forsyth.

It is an index of his essential gentleness that his most successful assumption is that of Fred Poitrine, the appallingly vulnerable doughboy whom Belle marries in order to have a father for her child. As Mr Pinchley, a face-grinding landlord of 88 or as a Ruritanian monarch with a fatal case of National Debt, he lacks something in ferocity and in precision. But goodwill takes him a long way in his other roles, and each of his recurring appearances as Noble is more confident than the last. Little Me has never been a commercial success. Maybe musicals attract a sentimental public that resents being made to laugh. Maybe audience identification is thwarted by a split heroine and a subdivided star.

Maybe the show is imperfect; certainly this revival is. It is still the second most invigorating show in town....
1984-07-15-the-world-over:
The world over

ROBERT CUSHMAN

SALESMAN IN BEIJING
by Arthur Miller
Methuen £9.95

IT should by rights be eerie to carry a 35-year-old success around with you as if it were a case of samples. Arthur Miller hit his stride early with "Death of a Salesman." It remains his masterpiece, and he shows no signs of bitterness or embarrassment towards it. He not only loves it, he admires it: passionately but, it seems, objectively. He knows what it means, why it moves people, and every detail of how it works. He seems to be its ideal director.

Last year he directed it. In China. This book is the diary of his rehearsals at the People's Theatre of Beijing. Michael Rudman, who directed the most recent revivals in London and New York (the latter with Dustin Hoffman as a scrawnily brilliant Willy Loman), says that the main problem with the play is to keep the actors from playing their own families, since we've all been through similar rows and regrets, rather than the people Miller has drawn. The fact that we can all identify with it has always guaranteed the play a kind of success. Taking it to China -- where salesmen and Western drama are equally unknown -- was testing that guarantee to the limit.

It survived. "The audience," Miller notes at the end, "laugh in just about the same places as we do in the West, and I have seen many of them weeping for Willy." He found unexpected areas of recognition among the actors. Trying to explain Willy Loman's trick of ignoring obvious disasters, he is told "we're always doing that -- finding some hope where there really isn't any. It's our whole history." Apparently it's "as Chinese as hell." "I had always thought it Jewish. Obviously it's merely human." With Willy's overriding passion -- his love and ambition for his sons -- the Chinese had no trouble; they call it wanting their sons to be dragons.

The book is not especially surprising about China outside the theatre; rueful complaints about service and plumbing alternate with humane anger over the Cultural Revolution. What counts is Miller's remarks on the play. Like Willy, he lives partly in flashback, recalling Elia Kazan, Lee J. Cobb and the original production: the solving of problems that in China have to be faced all over again. Pondering the play for himself so that he can explain it to the cast he comes up with a definitive diagnosis:

"Willy is a lot of things but he is not particularly Good; it may even be that his faults and failings dominate him altogether. But at the same time the play obviously presents him sympathetically . . .

"Willy is indeed a social product while his autonomy as a person remains intact, and this can drive the dialecticians crazy."

It drives them crazy here too; academic critics, incensed that a play should succeed on Broadway and be taken seriously, have never ceased pointing out the protagonist's faults as if they somehow disposed of the play. (Try that line of reasoning on "Macbeth.") Actually it is purely a critic's problem; it has never bothered actors or audiences. A play that can make people laugh and cry for 35 years -- or one year, come to that -- is obviously a good one, though it may have to hit a century before it can be judged great.

It stands a chance; Willy's fate is shaped by the society he grew up in, but is in no way limited to it. In another culture he would have found another way of screwing up his life, and he would still have told himself that he was doing it for his boys. Miller always knew that; the Chinese confirmed it for him. "Death of a Salesman" may have kept him young.
1984-08-01-the-merchant-of-venice-chiche:
The Merchant of Venice — Chichester

Alec Guinness plays a very dignified Shylock, and a very quiet one. It is at the opposite extreme from his Fagin, which was overflowing with extravagant Jewishness. You might say that where Fagin was an old-style orthodox performance, this Shylock is strictly reform. The character's more obnoxious traits are played down. There is nothing of the passionate killjoy in his attacks on carnivals in general and music in particular; no grotesque oscillations between bloodlust and cupidity when Tubal goads him with the tale of Jessica's elopement. He is heartbroken at the loss of his wife's turquoise; and you wonder when the balance will come. Is Guinness declining to acknowledge that the man is actually a villain?

The moment arrives when he is told that Antonio is certainly undone; he murmurs 'that's very true' RevIeWs with adamantine reflectiveness. His revenge-scheme snaps into place. From then on, he is a man possessed. It has little effect on the tenor of his voice. He remains serene and businesslike, confident in the impregnability of his case. His addresses to the Venetian court sound as unanswerable as his early meditations on Antonio. He has one moment of triumphant diablerie, feeling for the beating of his enemy's heart so as to know just where to stick the knife; but even that is done as if it were the most natural thing in the world. Defeated, he tries to salvage what he can; as each line of defence is destroyed by Portia, he falls back unflinching on the next.

His exit must be the least obviously spectacular in the play's history. This Jew knows better than to put up a useless fight. My favourite subtlety, in a performance full of them, is the pain in his eyes as he tries to persuade himself that he is glad to see the back of Launcelot Gobbo. This should be the most sympathetic of Shylocks, just as David Suchet's, full of the virulent gusto that only a Jewish actor could permit himself in the role, should have been the least. And yet I remember that when Mr Suchet was order to convert to Christianity, the whole house went into shock. Up to then one had thought as usual, a Jewish villain, okay, I'm broadminded, I know about Elizabethan prejudice, I'll accept it for an evening.

It's a comedy; maybe Shylock deserves what he gets. Then comes that crucial humiliation, whose memory one had blotted out, and it is intolerable. But when Guinness got the order of the font, some people in the first-night audience, very Elizabethanly, laughed. Now this may be a reflection on the Chichester punkers who spent the evening applauding mostly dreadful acting (with particular warmth for the mirthless Gobbo and unspeakable Prince of Arragon) and who even sabotaged Guinness's first sly entrance; it took them a moment to spot him, but they tumbled eventually and clapped him anyway. But for that last laugh he was, in a sense, asking. This is not a Gentile Jew (it is racially perfect, however modest) but it is a Christian Shylock: the Jew seen as wronged, wronging, and wrong.

The values of the play are against him; and they are perfectly articulated in the trial. This scene has a tonic effect on Patrick Garland's production; everyone in the cast suddenly starts acting, something which up till then they have left to the star and to Leslee Udwin's Jessica. Joanna McCallum, a principalboy Portia before she goes into disguise, does the mercy speech as if she and the play really meant it; and she extends it into the series of lifelines she throws to Shylock (trying to save him as much as Antonio) and the matching series of body-blows with which she destroys him. The Venetians remain horrible, but the play's morality transcends them. No wonder Shylock goes quietly.

Whether this atones for the rest of the production is dubious. It all takes place on a remarkably lazy revolve, which bestirs itself only to shift a fountain from one side of the stage to the other. We learn that Venice is a place where they keep their water-supply stage right, and Belmont is where they keep it stage-left. Belmont is also a place where three large lace table-cloths drop from above, whenever someone wants to have a go at the caskets. Chichester remains a place where a large and lopsided theatre terrorises designers, directors, and performers. David Yelland gets the better of it in a thoughtful account of Bassanio's casket-speech but nowhere else. Miss Udwin commands from her first entrance to her last.

And Guinness, who moves as gravely and lightly as he speaks, is magic as only experience allied to inspiration can make an actor. In 25 years of haunting theatres I have never before seen him in a classic. My loss, and yours, and maybe even his.
1984-08-12-burton-s-last-role-a-supporti:
BURTON'S LAST ROLE: A SUPPORTIVE FATHER
Date: 1984-08-12
LONDON

Robert Cushman frequently reports on the London cultural scene.
When Richard Burton died suddenly last Sunday in Geneva, he had just finished filming scenes in London for what turns out to be his last role - a pivotal, though not a dominating part in ''Ellis Island,'' a CBS-TV mini- series that will be shown sometime next season and in which the actor appears with his 26-year-old daughter, Kate Burton. Earlier last month, Mr. Burton and his daughter had been interviewed about the experience of their working together.
Mr. Burton, displaying paternal pride, had confessed in his dressing- room trailer at the Shepperton Studio, ''On the first day of acting with Kate, I was so nervous I cracked up. When I looked at her face, it was so similar, the bone-work was so like mine, it was frightening. It took us half an hour to get over that. And then she just sailed through the scene, like a beautiful yacht.''
Miss Burton had observed that it was her belief she had inherited her father's ''sensibilities'' about acting, which she summarized, in a phrase he would undoubtedly have endorsed, as ''not taking it too seriously but still working very hard.''
In a phone conversation shortly after her father's death, Miss Burton said, ''He was incredibly supportive without being vocal. He let me do my own thing. He said, 'I think you're a wonderful actress on your own and you don't need any help from me.'' 
She did cite one instance when her father had cautioned against her tendency to overact toward the end of what had been a tiring day before the cameras. ''Don't be too theatrical,'' he had said, ''Use your fatigue.''
The actress also recalled how her father had summed up the characters they were each portraying in ''Ellis Island.'' ''You're playing a person with no humor and I'm playing a pompous ass,'' he had said, hoping that they might be cast more sympathetically ''next time, perhaps.''
Such irreverence was, of course, typical of Mr. Burton. ''I have never played a small part before,'' the actor had commented further. ''A day off bewilders me. What can they be doing without me?''
But although Mr. Burton's role is small, it is not simply one of those guest-star cameos; the character keeps turning up. ''I'm here, there and everywhere,'' he had stressed.
Ellis Island, of course, long served as the point of entry - or of dismissal - for would-be immigrants to America. The script for the seven-hour mini-series was adapted by Fred Mustard Stewart from his best-selling novel of the same name, which recounts the fortunes of four Europeans who arrive, steerage, in the New York of 1907. The sizable cast of the television dramatization also includes Faye Dunaway, Claire Bloom, Peter Riegert, Ann Jillian, Melba Moore, Milo O'Shea and Ben Vereen. Mr. Burton, however, had not been cast as one of the scenario's immigrants; he portrayed a rich and ruthless United States Senator who marries a successful actress, also not an immigrant (played by Miss Dunaway). The Senator has a daughter (Miss Burton); both fictional wife and daughter become romantically involved with an Italian immigrant, Marco Santorelli (Greg Martyn).
Mr. Burton and his daughter Kate (by his first wife, Sybil Williams) first acted together last year in ''Alice in Wonderland'' on American public television: she in the title role, he as the White Knight. It was a rare television appearance for him. This spring, Mr. Burton was in England, filming ''1984,'' in which he played the interrogator O'Brien, when Kate telephoned him about ''Ellis Island.''
''She said,'' the actor had recalled, ''she was playing a leading role in this TV thing and that they were going to ask me to play her dad.'' Miss Burton had, in fact, been the first performer to be cast for the project. When, three weeks later, CBS told her that ''we've cast your dad,'' her initial reaction was ''wary.'' Her next was that it would be great to work together - ''While we're both young.''
Many years ago, Mr. Burton did a John Osborne piece (''A Subject of Scandal and Concern'') for the BBC; in 1952, he made his American video debut as Mat Burke in a live presentation of Eugene O'Neill's ''Anna Christie.'' June Havoc played Anna; at one point, Miss Havoc missed an entrance cue. Left alone on camera, Mr. Burton decided to fill the time by smashing a chair. The staging called for him to do just that later in the play anyway, and the prop master had provided an especially smashable chair. At this junction, however, the actor picked up the wrong one, and viewers coast-to-coast were treated to the sight of an anguished Mr. Burton trying to cover by struggling with an unbreakable prop.
A different kind of trouble befell his more memorable television role as Winston Churchill in the 1974 dramatization of Churchill's war memoirs, ''The Gathering Storm.'' Prior to the airdate, Mr. Burton had written an article for the Arts and Leisure section of The New York Times on what the experience had taught him. ''I realized afresh,'' he wrote in part, ''that I hate Churchill and all his kind. . . . They have stalked down the corridors of endless power all through history.'' He accused Churchill of desiring the genocide through blitzkrieg of the German people and expressed special scorn for his writing: ''Churchill's use and misuse of the language he loved so much and his contortion of syntax were so acute that I thought I was going to go mad trying to figure out what the hell he meant.''
The article provoked a torrent of letters to the editor, some supportive but most bewildered or indignant. The protestors included some of the program's own production team. According to them, Mr. Burton had given every sign of liking the man he was playing.
It is possible that his depiction of Churchill may be eclipsed by another forthcoming television portrayal: that of the German composer Richard Wagner in the film of the same name, as yet seen by very few but already famous for its nine-hour length and its stellar cast, which also includes Laurence Olivier, John Gielgud and Ralph Richardson.
During the checkered course of its production, the film's projected destination kept switching from television to theatrical release and back again. Now it seems it is to have a bit of both. A condensed version - a mere five hours - has already been shown at the London Film Festival, to a mixed response; a marathon theatrical showing of the full version is scheduled for November in London, to be followed within the year with a television presentation in abbreviated form. There are also plans for a theatrical showing in New York in the coming season, probably in the nine- hour version, and negotiations are afoot for an American television sale, again at full length.
Mr. Burton's memory of the role was that he ''never stopped talking'' and that, after a certain amount of token but exhausting arm-waving, he realized ''why conductors live such a long time: It's a very healthy occupation.''
Miss Burton's career consists so far of Yale Drama School, a couple of productions on Broadway (the short- lived musical ''Doonesbury,'' ''Present Laughter,'' with George C. Scott, and ''Alice in Wonderland'') and a stab at Juliet in Riverside Park. Her father's career encompassed more than 40 films, nearly all of which he said he had enjoyed making, few of which came out as he had hoped they would when he read the scripts, and only seven of which he admitted to having seen - at command performances, from which he could not very well have absented himself.
Of those few, he had noted that the 1969 ''Staircase,'' in which he and Rex Harrison played a homosexual couple, to be the only one he liked watching (''I thought I was good for the first time''), though on second thought he had also cited ''Where Eagles Dare,'' which, somehow, he had seen twice: ''That was fun.'' He hadn't mentioned another war adventure, ''The Wild Geese,'' although he was about to embark on a sequel to it in the near future.
In addition to his numerous films, there were, surprisingly, 60 plays; surprisingly, since Mr. Burton had the reputation, especially in Britain, of being the theater's great lost actor. Still, he said, ''I am not as at home on film as on the stage.''
Throughout the interview last month, Mr. Burton had mentioned the name ''Elizabeth'' warmly and casually. His most recent professional reunion with Elizabeth Taylor had occurred last year in a revival of No"el Coward's ''Private Lives,'' which was greeted by unanimously dismissive reviews and invariably full houses. It was the latter to which Mr. Burton had first pointed when defending the production. He added that he did prove, to his own satisfaction as well as to his own surprise, that he could play Coward.
''I'd thought that lightness of touch alien to me,'' he said. ''I got laughs in the right places.'' Nonetheless, he admitted to ''doubletakes No"el would never have done.'' Of Miss Taylor, whose performance was the more critically abused of the two, he gallantly said, ''Elizabeth is a genuine clown.''
Earlier this week, when Miss Burton was queried as to whether she felt that her father had wasted his career, she said, ''He made a definite choice in the early 60's, when he married Elizabeth, to be a movie star. He made some bloody awful films, but some great ones, too.''
Asked if she thought he had of late been less in demand than before, she said, ''No, but perhaps people were nervous about asking him because they didn't quite know what he wanted to do at this stage in his career.''
Miss Burton added that she and her father had recently been looking over scripts they might perform in together in the future; among them was ''Painting Churches,'' Tina Howe's drama about a complex relationship between a daughter and her parents.
1984-08-12-burton-s-farewell:
Burton's Farewell

The last interview Richard Burton gave was to ROBERT CUSHMAN. He said: 'I can't keep away from the stage. I can't stop scratching the pimple.'

I met Richard Burton, three weeks before his death, at Shepperton Studios. He was filming an American TV series called Ellis Island. It was about immigrants in New York at the beginning of the century, so naturally it was being shot over here. The hook for the interview was the fact that his daughter Kate was co-starring with him; her role in fact was larger than his.

I went in trepidation, half-expecting to meet a wreck. I knew that drinking had once nearly killed him, and that a neck operation was said to have immobilised him. At all events it had put paid to his much-vaunted ambition of playing King Lear. (He said: 'I couldn't carry on Cordelia at the end.') In fact, the man I met was alert, relaxed and apparently unshadowed, his eyes and voice -- his prime acting assets, both hypnotic -- in fine working order. Kate Burton confirmed that, in recent years, she had never seen him look better.

There was, all the same, a tiredness about him: spiritual rather than physical. Shepperton had supplied him with a caravan ('comparatively glamorous -- at least we can have a fry-up') though it compared unfavourably to the 'super-glamorous' dressing-rooms he had known when stars were stars and film studios made films. Sitting hunched on a couch he pointed out of the window behind him at a housing estate where once, apparently, there had been a lawn.

'That's where we danced the pavane in Anne of the Thousand Days. Worst dancers I've ever seen. Brook was one of them, weren't you, Brook?' Brook Williams, son of Emlyn, smiled agreement, having graduated from acting to being a one-man Burton entourage, responsible for handling connections to the outside world. Next to Burton, and saying little, sat his fourth and last wife, Sally, English and young.

He spoke of the film career to which he had devoted most of his life as enjoyable but frustrating. 'You accept a part in good faith. The script seems all right. Then six or seven people re-adapt it and ruin it.' However, since he claimed to have seen only seven of his own pictures, he may not be their most reliable critic. He had made, he said, some 70 films, and done about 60 plays. The reference books suggest that he exaggerated on both counts, but his claim to be a workaholic was clearly justified. But -- more obviously even than most actors -- he was drifting where the work took him.

In Ellis Island he played an unscrupulous US senator. Watching a rehearsal did not convince me that it would rank among his greatest roles, but he went through it with grizzled cheerfulness. Kate said that acting was not the all-important thing in her life, and that this was a balanced attitude -- 'working very hard but not taking it too seriously' -- that she had inherited from her father. It may well be true of her. I was not sure about him. The man I met seemed kind, good-humoured, and a little desperate.

The self-destructive Celt is a stock figure in British mythology. Usually he is Irish, but two men, Burton and Dylan Thomas, have staked a solid -- or if you prefer, a liquid -- claim for the Welsh. Both were in part weighed down by the expectations placed upon them. Burton grew up as a figurehead for his family, his community, then his country, and eventually his profession.

He always retained a passion for the written word: the 'absolute passion' (his words) of someone who had once had to fight to master it. Home, in his last years, was officially either Switzerland or Haiti, but really it was 'where the books are,' which mostly meant a converted barn near Geneva. Here he had, among other things, all thousand volumes of the original Everyman's Library.

Perhaps because English was officially his second tongue (he still spoke Welsh every time he went home) he was audibly enraptured of it. His most enduring performance may well be his radio narration of Thomas's Under Milk Wood, with its imperious sense of wonder, its delight at what another Welshman had done with the language, and its whimsical pride in the village whose 'lazy, lecherous day' he was describing. His bookishness never hampered his performing.

The young Burton had the voice of a Gielgud, the virility of an Olivier, and an 'aura' (a favourite word of the time) all his own. His Stratford season in 1951 crystallised it.

Burton himself said to me, 'I'm not as at home in film as on the stage. I can't keep away from the stage. I can't stop scratching the pimple.' He started outlining plans for next year, which he said was still 'relatively free so far.' He talked of doing two plays in repertoire, one Shakespearean and one modern, and doing them on both sides of the Atlantic. He said that as a classical actor he was luckier than most, able to come to the plays absolutely fresh, 'rather than being pushed into the mannerisms that come with the sort of workload you get at the National Theatre or the RSC.'

This sounded to me like rationalisation on a large scale, and I did not feel much confidence that his theatre plans would actually materialise. Nor was I very sure that I wanted them to materialise. When an actor returns after a long absence, the expectant audience are on trial as much as he is; it's difficult to make an honest response. We have seen it with all the men who have, wholly or partially, followed the Burton trail, all the dynamos: Albert Finney, Peter O'Toole, Richard Harris, Nicol Williamson, Anthony Hopkins (something of a Burton clone), maybe Jonathan Pryce. The only heroic actors who have followed the Scofield line and stuck to the stage are Ian McKellen and Alan Howard.

Burton's most recent, and most notorious, stage venture was Private Lives, which he and Miss Taylor, professionally reunited after two divorces, played all over America. It broke, as he said, box-office records everywhere; although he admitted in the same breath that most of the audience were there for the wrong, voyeuristic, reasons. (You've read about the Burtons fighting; now see it on stage.)

But he also claimed to have discovered a comic finesse he didn't know he had. While Elizabeth, he said, 'is a natural clown.' He brought her name up, warmly, casually, and early in the conversation, knowing perhaps that I would have to if he didn't.

Another subject he brought up early was money. He was 'amazed at the money being so good in TV' but that 'truly didn't influence me at all.' In the same vein, he's never had any 'ego problems or bothers about billing; it's only agents who care . . . once I hit the jackpot as 'twere (a favourite phrase) no one ever had billing over me except Elizabeth.'

This can only have been amiable doublethink; he simultaneously wanted the money and prestige (and indeed the Dick-and-Liz notoriety) and felt he should despise them. But, given his early struggles, that was inevitable.

This kind of dichotomy ran through his life. The rolling sonority of his television Churchill, simultaneously weary and indomitable, was a perfect match for the massive folds of Churchill's rhetoric. But once it was shot he felt he owed it to himself to write an article in the New York Times attacking Churchill as a mad, sadistic warmonger.

I saw him a few years ago on Broadway playing the psychiatrist in Equus. He seemed to be sleep-walking through it. He only roused himself at the end, for a long speech riddled with self-disgust; there the actor and the orator in him caught fire, and it was thrilling. And from his films it is the guilty, tormented, disillusioned moments that one remembers best.

His drunken, eloquent (and tempestuously married) academic failure in Who's Afraid Of Virginia Woolf? must have tapped a large part of him. Few actors can have made the decline-of-civilisation aspect of the script so convincing; it must be one of the best bespectacled performances in movies.

Best of all perhaps was his double agent, used and abused by both sides, in The Spy Who Came In From the Cold; it is impossible to forget the ravaged deliberation with which, at the end, he exposed the rules of realpolitik to his idealistic girlfriend. (She was Claire Bloom, the actress -- with one obvious exception -- whose career has most frequently intersected with his; from their joint West End debut in The Lady's Not For Burning, right down to Ellis Island.)

And we have still, most of us, to see the nine-hour Wagner in which, by his own account, he 'never stops talking' -- and the new 1984 in which he plays the interrogator O'Brien. In the novel Orwell emphasises his intellect and his weariness; it should be ideal Burton material.

In The Sandpiper, the most fondly remembered abomination of the Burton-Taylor period, he played a lust-tormented priest. It was oddly appropriate; there has been an element of the defrocked saint in most of his best work. At Stratford a fellow actor described him as 'bringing his own cathedral on with him.' That is apt and impressive, and also a tribute to the transforming powers of art and of ambition. For Burton himself, of course, was strictly chapel.
1984-09-01-the-way-of-the-world-chichest:
The Way of the World — Chichester

Well,' said the gentleman ahead of me, tolerantly, as we left the theatre 'you can't win 'em all.' I saw what he meant. The Chichester audience had already been given a vapid The Merchant of Venice to clap and giggle their way through, and by comparison William Gaskill's production of The Way of the World was bound to strike them as discouragingly sober. It actually seemed to be taking the play seriously and, heinously, to be communicating that seriousness. It was also disconcertingly well acted on almost every level, and handsomely rather than prettily designed. Outdoors was economically distinguished from in, the governing and immovable factor of Hayden Griffin's set being a majestic doorway. From wherever you looked at it - and I changed sets at the interval - this arch refused to settle into a perfect central position.

This may conceivably have been a cunning concept, intended to suggest insecurity in a play that is riddled with it; but I have never seen a set that didn't look lopsided on that Chichester platform, which surely has at least one edge too many. (To appreciate what is wrong with it, you have to see the perfectly proportioned stage and auditorium at Stratford, Ontario; Chichester looks as if the Canadian plans were flown over the Atlantic, lost en route, and reconstructed from somebody's very fallible memory). It is no wonder, to be fair to them, that Chichester's regulars have developed such an overwhelming taste for superficiality; the sight-lines and the acoustics are cruel to anything else.

Mr Gaskill's intransigence, as viewed from the middle distance, often seemed to amount to a couple of gaunt profiles in fancy dress lost in a tall story. Most productions of this play that I have seen have strenuously sought, in acting and in programme-notes, to make the narrative clear; an ill-fated endeavour on the whole. Mr. Gaskill is comparatively insouciant about it and yet he captures what is important; the individual situations and their emotional strengths. At most given moments one knew who was double-crossing whom, even if one could not quite fathom how; and one also knew just how the predators and the victims felt about it. It was also clear that a predator could become a victim with lightning speed. Ian Hogg, first-rate when looking in my direction and inaudible when not, plays Fainall as a haggard plotter with a deep awareness of the unfairness of life.

An amused awareness too; his recurrent phrase, Tis but the way of the world', is accompanied each time by a hollower laugh. His bond with Mrs Marwood (which a National Theatre production once tried unhappily to convey by having the two of them start to undress at the first-act curtain) is here a strong but subtle mixture of lust and mutual protection. Sara Kestelman, with her decibels lowered since playing the equivalent role in The Double Dealer, commands the stage whenever she is on it. She may now be our best actresss of villainesses; she makes their case, not by whitewashing but by allowing them the dignity of their own passion. These two in showing what love, wit and marriage can so easily come to provide the right context for the hero and heroine.

Maggie Smith of course gets every laugh there is to be had from Millamant but, as in all her best work, the perfect timing has an edge of Above: Maggie Smith as Mrs Millament in Bill Gaskill's production at the Chichester Festival Theatre. Photo: Nobby Clark apprehension; she is fighting for survival. 'If Mirabell should not make a good husband, I am a lost thing'; she means it. Many critics have expressed surprise that Michael Jayston's Mirabell fails to match her in sparkle; surprising surprise since Mr Jayston has always been one of nature's straight men. He does at least suggest a decent disposition and a quizzical mind and is something for the wits, harmless or malicious, to bounce off.

Chief among the harmless is John Moffat's Witwoud; one of the production's chief charms is its eclectic choice of actors. The National, the RSC, the Court are all well represented; and Mr Moffatt points in a strong claim for the Tennent tradition at its best. He gets with total lack of fuss to the heart of every joke, and is well matched with James Villier's beamish Petulant (who does not live up to his name, but what actor in this role ever did?) Joan Plowright as Lady Wishfort made me Right: Joan Plowright as Lady Wishford and Sara Kestelman as Mrs Marwood. Bill Gaskill's production is designed by Hayden Griffin. Photo: Nobby Clark laugh a lot when deciding, after painful experiment, not to sit to receive a suitor.

At other times she laid the character's vulnerability on a bit thick. The lady is a comic monster and she is a tyrant; witness her fury when she turns against her maid. Miss Plowright as in The Cherry Orchard is inclined to sink into self-pity, and Mr. Gaskill, who does not approve of a caricature, is inclined to abet her. The same indulgence affects Geoffrey Hutchings' Sir Wilful; an ingratiating performance (heaven forefend we should mock a country bumpkin) but underpowered for the long drunk scene which no actor except John Woodvine has ever rescued from dullness in my presence. Jane Carr as Foible delivers a welltuned version of her customary performance, Sheila Allen is a gracious presence as Mrs Fainall, and there are even two new actors to round out the cast.

One, Tim Swinton, is presently out of his depth with Waitwell but Amanda Holmes as Mincing is pertness personified. It is 20 years since Mr Gaskill began his cycle of Restoration comedies and the evening's pervading pleasure is the sense that here, at last, is the masterpiece. It was actually the first time that I have felt able to give more than formal assent to the play's official status. Like his only (and very different) rival in the field, Peter Wood, Mr Gaskill is heavily dependent on casting; these plays with their stockcompany roots are the ultimate actors' pieces. This time his touch has been golden. I want to see these actors in this production at a real theatre.

It is the best thing at Chichester since - I am swallowing hard but I think I mean this — since Uncle Vanya.
1984-10-01-pump-boys-and-dinettes:
Pump Boys and Dinettes

I have a dream, same as most English people, of driving westwards across America, stopping off in small towns, sleeping in motels, eating in diners: plotting my course not so much from maps as from the music on the car radio which would grow more countrified and westernised with every mile. It is well known that, once past the Rockies, country and western takes over the airwaves. The snag is: I can't stand it. That's a generalisation. I really mean that I can't stand the lachrymose, whining type (was ever a singer better named than Tammy Wynette?). I used to like Johnny Cash being tough or funny or (preferably) both; and I acknowledge that recent country songs have done something to restore to pop music the traditons of narrative and of realistic, even sardonic portraiture.

The film Coal Miner's Daughter had me rooting for the life and music of Loretta Lynn, even though I would never give her records house-room. A flavoursome lyric can sometimes conquer a boring tune; and even the syrupy songs have some value as a demonstration of how America likes to think it feels. I still tend to turn off the car-radio when a country song threatens but that's because I do most of my driving in London, where who needs it. In the theatre it's another thing. There is actually a respectable tradition of Broadway composers (Irving Berlin, George Gershwin, Richard Rodgers, Cole Porter for a gag, Arthur Schwartz repeatedly - Mr. Schwartz, one of the greatest of modern melodists and an octogenerian of amazing youthfulness, died last month and we should mark his passing - Burton Lane and Cy Coleman) adapting rural styles to their own sophisticated ends; and some ten years ago, a show called The Robber Bridegroom began a superb score in the eighteenth-century backwoods fiddle.

More recently The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas confirmed that country, intelligently adapted, has a lot more to offer the theatre than rock. Its rhythms are relaxed enough for the words to come through, and it presupposes people and a way of life. So I approached Pump Boys and Dinettes with hope. I expected a rich slice of Americana. The stage of the Piccadilly, and a small portion of the auditorium, have been transformed into the stuff of any highway-riding dream. Stage left is a luncheon counter, staffed by Kiki Dee and Carlene Carter. stage right is what looks like a music store, but is apparently the inside room of a gas-station, whose employees just happen to have left a piano and assorted guitars lying about.

These workers are Paul Jones, Brian Protheroe, Gary Holton and Julian Littman. It seems that the restaurant and the garage are actually the same establishment, designed to feed car and driver at the same time. (A motorway service station OCTOBER 1984 is compartmentalised in comparison. A niftier title might be Cooking with Gas. Opening song is called Highway 57'. That tells us where we are. A snatch of dialogue is enough to tell us who the characters are. Mostly they just sing: about small loves and jealousies, about going fishing and falling in love with the girl on the sales counter at Woolworths. I felt very distant from it. but then I was sitting halfway back in the dress circle.

For the first half I told myself that if I were watching this at the King's Head or the Warehouse or even in the front stalls of the Piccadilly I would love it. In the second half I acknowledged that it would stupefy me wherever I met it. Such plot as there is was apparently added between off-Broadway and on; but it is so embarrassingly slight you wish they hadn't bothered. What we are offered is an evening of songs, a form to which I have absolutely no Reviews objection. (Well, I couldn't, could I?). But if songs are to work in a theatre they need wit and they need dramatic fibre, in themselves and in their relation to one another.

Those in Pump Boys and Dinettes have neither; and the music, despite some blues and rock injections, is soul-sappingly monotonous. All my prejudices reawoke; the rest of me was sent to sleep. Mr. Jones, who lent a whole new dangerous dimension to the National's Guys and Dolls when he took over as Sky Masterson, is here thrown back on charm, with which he is mercifully loaded. At one point he has to chat up a member of the audience; on my night he got an actual American tourist, which immediately set up two levels of stage reality. Mr. Jones commuted between them with more humour than was in the rest of the show put together.
