He plays the good boy of the outfit; the bad one is Mr. Protheroe, who has the best (or at least the raunchiest) numbers and growls them out well, on voice and piano. Nobody else reached me but then, as aforesaid, they had a long way to travel. And on American highways, as this show demonstrates, there are very severe speed-limits.
1984-11-01-from-sondheim-to-la-cage:
From Sondheim to La Cage

One can hardly complain of a shortage of musicals in London at the moment. All the same there is little sign of the latest Broadway crop getting to us. For the moment we have to be content with the records. Most interesting of them, I supbose predictably, is Stephen Sondheim's Sunday in the Park with George, available as an import on RCA HBC1-5042. This show began its life as a workshop at the off-Broadway Playwrights' Horizons in 1983; it is now playing, most unusually for a musical, at one of the smallest Broadway theatres. But if ever there was a chamber musical, this is it. Its subject and its techniques are almost aggressively rarefied. George is Georges Seurat, the French pointillist painter, at work on his masterpiece A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte.

That at least is the George of Act One. That of Act Two is Seurat's fictitious American great-grandson, an avant-garde artist of our own time. Seurat cailed himself a Chromo-Luminarist (something only revealed to me by the synopsis that accompanies the record); our George calls his creations Chromolumes. Old George created patterns of light on canvas; young George does it with lasers. Old George built up his pictures by connecting a myriad of brightly coloured specks for your George 'connecting means making contacts in the museum and foundation world, to finance his next Chromalume. Andrew Lloyd Webber, the only other composer I can imagine writing a musical about pointillism, would undoubtedly have called it Dots. Sondheim and his librettist-director James Lapine have actually provided Seurat with a mistress called Dot; she, having emigrated to America with another man, bears Seurat's daughter, present in the second act as George's 98-year old grandmother named Marie.

In both these guises she is, as Shaw put it in 'Man and Superman", the Mother Woman to George's Artist Man. Which brings us to the question: what is Sunday in the Park with George actually about? Obviously, it is about The Artist; but what, on the stage, can you do with that? The show manages, to a surprising extent, to dramatise the actual process of creation. Seurat's continual mouthing of abstractions - Design, Composition, Tension, Balance, G Light, Harmony - is too self-conscious to be credible; but it is another thing when he gets into a song called 'Colour and Light', with a compulsive bass-line reminiscent of 'Someone in a Tree' from 'Pacific Overtures' and a freeranging melodic line held in check by a taut, staccato rhythm; the song acts out the artist's balance of liberty and restraint, and almost provides an aural equivalent for the dabbing of paint.

On a larger scale the show's first half enacts the composition of the painting Grande Jatte' is a large group-portrait, of mainly middle-class Parisians at play. The figures from the canvas wander through the musical, leading fragments of their own lives. We watch Seurat observing them while ignoring 98 4 their preoccupations. Finally he breaks up the groups into which they have arranged themselves, and disposes them in accordance with his own plan. plots. And there they are, for ever Fine. But the Job of the Artist will not fill the whole evening, so we get the Plight of the Artist as well. His battle with the philistines, gently adumbrated in Act One, is given fuller treatment when our modern George is let loose among the vultures of the museum, criticising, flattering and, above all, patronising him.

"That is the state of the art, my dear' they croon, with unfortunate glibness. They strongly recall the party crowds of "Merrily We Roll Along" and they arouse the same kind of misgivings. They are crucifying the artist-hero but since he is part of their world just what makes our chromoluminary so superior? There is another aspect: the Artist as Human Being failing to relate to other human beings. Of the figures who fill his painting, the ones with whom Seurat seems to have the greatest rapport are a couple of dogs, for whom he improvises a sprightly dialogue. His apparent human indifference is what Dot, his model as well as his mistress, most objects to.

Not only does he keep her standing around for hours in uncomfortable positions, he refuses to take her out at nights, preferring to work on his picture. (Key song: Furbishing the Hat'). So she leaves him for Louis, a baker and as she insists, an artist in his own way, if not perhaps George's equal. As she puts it, with superb Sondheim economy; '... there are Louis's And there are Georges - Well, Louis's And George'. Sondheim has trodden some of this ground before, with Sweeney Todd and Mrs Lovett. Sweeney was surely an artist, in hair and in death; George, musing over his pallette, hums in the same accents as Sweeney instructing the sailor Anthony in the niceties of wigmaking.

George and Dot are pale by comparison, though their relationship progresses. Dot ends up grateful to George for having given her the most prominent position in the picture. Her act Two alter ego Marie gives affectionate advice to her George, and finally Dot herself makes a spectral re-appearance to reinforce her daughter's good work. Artists, it is suggested may not make good husbands but we should love and tolerate them because they give us immortality. As Keats told us, thereby turning the trick himself, they freeze time for us, on Grecian urns or French impressionist canvases. Seurat, not a noticeably good son, doing what his mother wanted him to do: preserve the Grande Jatte in its glory before progress takes over and ruins it.

In Act Two the island is in fact shown to be overrun with high-rise buildings. These themes are kept in tandem, tantalisingly but stimulatingly, in the first act. The second is more problematic, largely because it is difficult to take young George and his chromolumes as seriously as the show apparently wants us to. (There are satiric notes but they are not consistently sounded). Musicals have traditionally had second-act problems: difficulties in winding up their. "Sunday in the Park", having no plot, experiences corresponding difficulties in developing its ideas. When I saw it in preview in April its second half was definitely undernourished; when I returned in August two new numbers had been added. One of them, a threnody called "Children and Art", does much to pull the show together.

Marie sings it, invoking her mother Dot; as the title suggests it is about two kinds of continuity, the kinds provided by the two central figures of the first half and, perhaps, by their descendants. The "perhaps" is necessary for the song is full of gentle ironies. Dot, with only the painting to go on, blatantly sentimentalises the rather unpleasant characters it depicts. But, since they are dead and the picture lives, she may be right. The song, smilingly, allows us to make up our own minds A later number, 'Move ON', is the hard sell. It is, as the title suggests, Dot's advice to young George; 'Stop worrying if your vision Is new. Let others make that decision - They usually do.' That last bruised qualification is worth having but otherwise the song is uneasy Sondheim, a retreat to Rodgers and Hammerstein territory.

I have nothing against 'You'll Never Walk Alone'; when 'Carousel' was revived in Manchester this year its went straight to my tear-ducts. But there it came naturally; as affirmation has never done to Sondheim. The score picks itself up for a stirring hymn called 'Sunday' during which the Seurat painting reassembles only to vanish again leaving George with a blank sheet. His turn now. If the show doesn't quite add up, the score does. It is constructed (with the help of some piquant percussive building-blocks left over from 'Pacific Overtures') on internal echoes. It may be Sondheim's most tightly-knit composition. An initial impression of severity gives way, on third or fourth hearing, to one of spare, elegant melody.

"The Day Off", George's dog duet, is a song that first strikes the ear as odd and angular and then takes on a wholly satisfying logic. The lyrics, probably the unshowiest he has written, are also among the subtlest and most suggestive. (In his previous two scores I felt that their edge had been blunted). And their half-tones can never have been better conveved than in Bernadette Peters's performances of Dot and Marie. In sensitivity, vivacity, intelligence, sensual ache, and the suggestion of bottomless wit, she is just about the perfect leading lady: for musicals in general and Sondheim in particular, I warmed less to Mandy Patinkin's two Georges but maybe I was meant to; he certainly has extraordinary vocal abilities, with a diabolically haunting upper register that is almost part of the orchestration.

(By Michael Starobin this time, not Jonathan Tunick). Nobody else has much opportunity. I enjoyed the show more on record, you may guess, than in the theatre. Not only Sondheim borrows from Sondheim. The Rink, another of last season's still running Broadway successes, repeats themes and techniques from 'Follies'. That took place in a theatre on the eve of demolition; a haunted theatre whose former inhabitants were squabbling about their wasted lives. "The Rink' takes place in a skating-rink on the boardwalk of (presumably) Atlantic City. It, too, is about to be pulled down, at the instigation of the widow who owns it and in the teeth of her daughter, recently returned from a long spell of hippiedom.

(At least it started as hippiedom; it must, the sixties being long past, have turned into something else. We are made privy to of their rows and reconciliations past and present, additional roles in the past ones being assumed by the wrecking crew brought in to do the rink over. Why librettist Terrence McNally is telling us this story never becomes clear; the show keeps changing focus. It is a horrible mess, but a fascinating one: fascinating because some top practitioners are involved and because the musical is still so central an American form that any show makes, consciously or not, some kind of statement about America. This one resolves into a lament for the time of innocence, before muggers.

It is also full of left-over family melodrama (the characters are Italian) and rouses itself at the end to look at the lost-and-found generation of the sixties. That is to say, daughter recalls her own departure with a song called 'All the Children in a Row'. The song is embarrassing, not because it is technically incompetent (it isn't), but because its authors, Fred Ebb and John Kander, don't know what they are singing about. They are mainline showbiz, and the rock-era names they invoke (Joplin, Kesey, Steppenwolf) sound spurious. Mostly, the show takes itself very seriously; though it loosens up for a comedy duet between mother and daughter, The Apple Doesn't Fall because the roles are being played by two stars, Chita Rivera and Liza Minnelli, and the audience needs to see them at some point together and happy.

The song is modelled on Kander and Ebb's superb "The Grass is Always Greener' (from Woman of the Year') but it provides an enjoyable oasis on its own terms, catapulting the show into yet another convention, the barefaced star vehicle. Maybe it should have stayed there. Strangely, considering the names involved and the box-office success, the show was passed up by the major record companies. That's Entertainment moved in from London and recorded it, on TER 1091. My favourite number is the simplest, the title-song ('I wanna go round the rink, the rink/There's nothing to beat the rink, I think') sung by the wreckers. The same firm have recorded Baby (TER 1089), the most refreshing show on Broadway in some vears uniquely among post- Sondheim musicals it manages to be intelligently celebratory.

Indeed it does one of the things the musical is most basically for; it expresses a joy and wonder too basic and too intense to be From Sondheim to La Cage captured in words alone. The show's climax is childbirth, and it is very moving. The preceding action shows two expectant couples (one young, one middle-aged) and a third, who want are desperately to conceive but cannot: the same situation as in 'Ashes, with some of the same developments, but without self-pity and hence far more affecting. Nothing earth-shaking happens, but Sybille Pearson's book is so humorous and sympathetic that we are amused and involved. (With two of the pairs, anyway; the older ones remain rather wooden).

The score is by Richard Maltby Jr and David Shire, more adroit than any others at blending the traditionally effusive attitudes and concerns show music with contemporary words and sounds. Shire, the composing half, is especially good at rhythm numbers; to match his mixture of sweetness and sophistication you may have to go back to Harold Arlen. in Malthy takes us where no lyricist - on Broadway anyway - had travelled before. Picture a failing spermatozoan, Nor even knowin' where he is goin'. What's that ahead? diaphragm! Screw It! He knows he's dead - my God he slips through it. Nothing here is as good as the best in their anthology 'Starting Here Starting Now', but that after all represented the cream of 15 years' work.

Especial treats here are the title song, sung to the mother's belly, 'Fatherhood Blues', 'Romance' (a grimly determined tango for the deprived couple, regulating their sex-life to medical instruction), a soaring ballad "The Story Goes On, for the tenderness of its lyric, 'At Night She Comes Home to Me'. The show was not especially well reviewed; a particular pleasure of seing it was watching the audience, who had come with low expectations, surprised and, finally, lifted out of their seats. The audience for La Cage Aux Folles, by contrast, comes programmed to cheer. Its status as a pre-sold hit caused RCA (who, one imagines, took on the uncommercial Sunday in the Park out of loyalty to Sondheim and pressure from producer Thomas Z.

Shepard) to record La Cage before the Broadway opening: most unusual. I was present at the session, and enjoyed the atmosphere. Hearing George Hearn as the drag-queen singing 'Mascara', I felt sure I was in the presence of a smash. I still think it the best number in Jerry Herman's score, but neither in the theatre nor on the disc (where something seems to have happened to the dynamics) is the impact as great as in the studio. I have friends who consider the show to be the work of the Cavi Myself, I would not call it anything worse than mediocre. Its chief fault is that, taking over the farcical plot of the film, it reduces the characters to storming or mincing caricatures; the normality that makes farce possible has been sacrificed, and so has much of the structure Why has it been such a success?

It follows Torch Song Trilogy (by the same author Harvey Fierstein) in presenting a view of homosexuality just outrageous enough to make a Broadway (i.e. tourist) audience feel tickled and tolerant,; it has, and parades, what is known as 'heart'; and the Herman score is in what is still taken to be the show-music tradition: simple, plangent, hearty. A couple of numbers dire miscalculations, others are routine. But 'I Am What I Am' is better than such conventional affirmations of unconventionality have any right to be; "The Best of Times' effectively plunders the 'Milord' tradition; and the song that is meant to touch you, 'Look Over There', is actually touching. And of course La Cage has upstaged The Rink as a leading-lady show, èven if the lady is Mr Hearn I find the score has been implanted in my ear less by the original than by the venomous parody in the cabaret show Forbidden Broadway'; 'We could discuss the way they watered down the plot.

We could discuss the orchestrations, but let's not'.: that to the title tune. I doubt if the show will have quite the same success London, there being no exact equivalent for the middle American audience. The record is on RCA HBC1-4824. A Broadway hit of a few years ago has made a belated appearance on B'way Entertainment BE 8302-R. This though is Sugar Babies, a tribute to burlesque which, by shirking the full tawdriness of the original, becomes even tawdrier. My favourite item, a dog act, obviously finds no place on disc, and Mickey Rooney, who was short-changed in the show, is even more so here. I like Mr Rooney (notice how defensively everyone says that - everyone I know, anyway) and hope to see him in another vehicle.

The score here consists of some standard, and some amended, songs by Jimmy McHugh culminating ina spine-chilling flag-waver called 'You Can't Blame Your Uncle Sammy'. I have been playing through some back numbers in the That's Entertainment catalogue. Pride of place must go to two operettas in their recent Sadler's Wells productions: Lehar's The Count of Luxembourg (TER 1050) and, an especial melodic revelation to me, Kalman's Countess Maritza (TER 1051.) Besides filling gaps in my strictly non- Viennese education, these are excellent digital recordings. (The technology doesn't always pay off so well). Reissues continue as various as ever. They include the derivative tedium of Goodbye Mr Chips (TER 1025) with its watery cinematic score and Thomas and the King (TERS 1009); though I suffered through this in the theatre I had not realised just how dead a ringer it was for Camelot, right down to the prophetic ending.

John Williams, anyone is interested, wrote the music. More interestingly awful, perhaps, Treasure Island (TER 1008) which the Mermaid did as a musical one year, resumably because, to adapt Michael Flanders, they could not face doing it straight. Songs were accordingly thrust in regardless; the story starts at the Admiral Benbow so there is an opening number about what a great inn it is. Bernard Miles, still a good Long John when he talks, drones with young Hawkins through a duet about being 'Shipmates, Partners and Pals'. Two highpoints: a crazy song about cheese (all kinds) for Spike Milligan's Ben Gunn, with chorus of goats, and Cap'n Smollett's rhythmic insult to Silver: 'while we're on the subject, you're a rotten cook as well.

Neither I nor Stevenson had ever thought of that. More respectably, the RSC panto Swan Down Gloves (TER 1017) takes surprisingly well to record; Best Foot Forward', (with its odd refrain 'put your brains in your feet'), allowing us to imagine Alan Howard as a dancing dragon, is a meritorious show-stopper, and we can reminisce about a vintage RSC period: Pasco, Melia, Hyde, Cusack, Buxton (very nice), Hendrick, plus the irreplaceable Derek Godfrey (billed but unheard) and Terry Wood, the best Dame I ever saw but a bit subdued here. Two basic components in the British library: Salad Days (TER 1018) revival cast, hard to take today but necessary, and Valmouth, (TER 1019), the Chichester revival.

Comparing this to the 1958 original (once on Pye) is, as ever, swings and roundabouts. It is good to have Bertice Reading to set against Cleo Laine, and to be rid of the horrible electric organ of the first orchestrations. Lyric readings, were generally sharper first time even when the cast was the same. Fenella Fielding, however, remains unchanged to the syllable. Two oddities, Nightingale (TER 1031), Charles Strouse's Chinese fairytale, in its Hammersmith incarnation, sounds delectable. Underneath the Arches (TERX 1015), Roy Hudd's Crazy Gang collage, is like its stage original and its original, unreviewable.
1984-12-01-fool-for-love:
Fool for Love

Fool for Love is my Smirnoff play, until I saw it I thought that Sam Shepard's vociferous followers were so many sheep. My conversion came last year in New York, when I saw the play staged at the most consistently excellent of off-Broadway theatres, the Circle Rep. Their current production of Lanford Wilson's Balm in Gilead is one of the most exciting orchestrations of a large cast in a small space that I have ever seen. I relished it the more having witnessed the previous day, uptown at the Promenade, David Rabe's Hurly Burly, three hours of all-star tedium in what had become officially known as Mike Nichols's wonderful ensemble production: the kind of rave bestowed on any show in which a collection of well-known actors avoid actually stepping on each other's lines or bumping into the furniture.

Where was I? Balm in Gilead really was an ensemble production, order drawn out of engulfing chaos, and so, at the same address, was Fool for Love. Mr Shepard directed it himself, and created extraordinary tension. The air was full of the threat of violence. This was remarkable since the stage was full of actual violence, and the two are generally incompatible. But somehow Mr Shepard had succeeded in setting a play at what we were assured was one end of the civilised world - the edge of the Mojave Desert, the barest of motel rooms - and filling it with emotions to match. Here, from the comparative civilisation of Wyoming, comes Eddie, a cowboy seeking and finding his lady, May.

She ran off in disgust at his infidelities. He wants her back. Someone else wants him back. It seems (Mr Shepard offers no firm assurance) that his latest conquest, referred to by scornful May as 'the Countess' will stop at nothing to get him back. Outside the window, lights blaze and guns resound. When a harmless hick arrives to take May out to a movie, he walks onto a hotter stage than he can ever have expected. There is an explosive charge in the May-Eddie relationship anyway. They are half-brother and sister. When Eddie says that May can never get away from him or he from her, he is probably right. The violence of the play is its appeal: better face that.

The stuff that critics have fastened on, about Eddie the cowboy representing a doomed type of American manhood, an extinct American buffalo: that you can keep. It is the kind of windy pronouncement that echoes through and around Mr Shepard's worst and most static plays: The Tooth of Crime and whatever that thing about Howard Hughes was called. Fool for Love does have a sort of exotic geographic appeal, what with the 1950 country hit I'm the One Who Loves You' welling sardonically but quite sincerely up at the final curtain (somewhere the world of 'Pump Boys and Dinettes' is calling), but it is important less for what it tells about the American landscape than for what it tells about the American theatre and its continuing capacity to go to extremes.

These extremes pose (I hate to drag out a traditional phrase but I know no appropriate other) a severe challenge to an English production. I wonder if the National, who are rather hot on authors directing their own work, attempted to bring Mr Shepard over for this one. In the event, Peter Gill directs loyally. He seems to have followed the stage directions to the letter; the slam of the motel-room door - a constant motif - is as furiously loud as Mr Shepard demands, and rather more so than in his own production. But only half the play well, two thirds - is there in the acting. David Troughton provides fine shy comic relief and Julie Walters is superlative as May: majestic in her anger, her fears, and her whiplash putdown timing.

She seems able to do anything: the best actress to appear among us since Judi Dench. She gets not only the accent but the temper. Ian Charleson as Eddie is determined but ineradicably soft-grained, though he twirls a mean lasso (taught, the programme acknowledges, by the superbly named Rex Roper). I don't know what other British actor one would cast in the role, nor, short of resurrecting Wilfrid Lawson, can I think of one to supply the swaggering rye-whisky authority missing from Tom Watson's performance of the Old Man. This Old Man, he plays dead. He also plays dad, May's and Eddie's. He sits at the side of the stage, abrasively commenting and rosily reminiscing.

Mr Shepard suggests in his commentary that he exists only in his children's thoughts, that he is a thing in their dreams. But, as the play unfolds, they seem like things in his. He is the guv'nor, and unless he does govern, the play sags. Mr Gill's production ends curiously like his Venice Preserv'd: an uncompromising but unavailing attempt to capture an alien, extravagant style. Still, the Cottesloe has here the second-best contemporary play in London; and in Glengarry Glen Ross, of course, still the first best. Both, for our chauvinistic comfort, are indebted to Harold Pinter; but it is no wonder that, despite the success of sundry British plays on Broadway, Americans are losing their long-held sense of dramaturgical inferiority.

We could yet return to the post-war situation in which Arthur Miller and Tennessee Williams (with whom Messrs Mamet and Shepard have, respectively, obvious affinities) were the envy of the English-speaking theatre. Nobody, not even Tom Stoppard, writes dialogue as good as Mr Mamet's, and we have nobody who can do melodrama, and even incipient tragedy, as well as Mr Shepard. No other current playwrights create characters who stand this tall.
1984-12-09-cry-god-for-harold:
Cry God for Harold

ROBERT CUSHMAN on theatre books

HAROLD HOBSON still writes an elegant, teasing prose unmatched by any practising theatre critic. He can be roguishly apt. In Theatre in Britain: A Personal View (Phaidon £19.50), his new survey of the theatre since 1920, he observes that many social plays seem to have been written not out of liking for the human race, but out of a curious detestation of everyone who does not agree with them. 'Right, as we used to say, on.'

Hobson piles on the paradox, which can be provocative but also provoking. Faced with such bland, unremitting irony you begin to wonder if he actually means any of it. His gift to criticism is the principle of the still, small voice. Where others single out ringing lines and thunderous effects he dwells on quiet, hidden moments; murmured declarations of marital love are favourites. He is quite justified in picking these out, but whether he should cite them so remorselessly is another matter.

Taking his cue from Matthew Arnold's theory of poetic touchstones (itself a suspect monument to High Seriousness) he trots out the same instances again and again across the years; the focus has shifted from whatever value they may once have possessed to his own tenacity in remembering them. Here he recalls yet again the impression made on him in 1947 by five words spoken by a walk-on in a production of The White Devil: 'The message is "aren't I sensitive?"' and, latterly since the actor turned out to be Patrick Macnee, 'aren't I a good talent-spotter?' Hobson is an artist in self-congratulation; after their deaths he wrote startlingly uncharitable pieces about George Devine and Richard Burton saying what second-rate men they were and how they always made a point of asking for his advice.

One longs, in the face of Hobson's boast, to blow a few gaffs. To point out that, whatever he and Ken Tynan may have done for its fortunes in London, Waiting for Godot came here (as Tynan admitted) with a ready-made Continental reputation; and that Hobson's deservedly famous championing of The Birthday Party was done from a position of advantage. Alone among critics, he had already seen a Pinter play: The Room at the NUS festival. He knew what to look for.

He is not prepared to allow other crusaders much credit; he lets us know that he had to fight for Beckett and Pinter, while Brecht entered unopposed. This is rubbish; Brecht received a lot of flak -- some of it from Sir Harold -- and still does. These writers, along with Osborne, founded (he says) the modern drama: something he used to approve of but now has doubts about. The argument here gets curious but it seems that the progressive drama has been irredeemably tainted since Auden fled the country in 1938. Since Auden was barely a playwright at all, it is difficult to believe that anyone in the theatre cared much about his defection then or now. But it gives Sir Harold the chance to compare the overtly highbrows with the brave Entertainers who kept the wartime theatres open (presumably because people were actually going to see them).

The intellectuals, he says, despise entertainment and this has caused a 'ruinous rift in our theatre.' My own observation is that the intellectuals are dazzled by entertainment; witness their compulsion to turn everything into a musical. They pilloried Rattigan -- though not as pertinently as Sir Harold suggests -- not because he was entertaining, but because he was an unfashionable kind of serious.

Actually, it is not so much laughter that Sir Harold misses in recent drama, as religion. It sometimes seems that he will give a rave to any play that contains a Biblical quotation, though he does not always salute joy and compassion when they are set before him -- there is no mention here of Jumpers or Nicholas Nickleby. Another oddity is that he seems to think Bob Peck and Jonathan Pryce are the same actor. The danger for the Christian critic (a category into which Sir Harold fits somewhere between G. Wilson Knight and Malcolm Muggeridge) is that, being on the side of the angels, it makes him very cavalier to those below. Which explains why Sir Harold can be the most patronising, and on occasion the cruellest, of modern theatre critics.

From theatrical management, two autobiographies. In Empty Seats (Hamish Hamilton £9.50), Michael White, who progressed from novel-writing in a lighthouse to being our second most prominent independent producer, infectiously conveys the dandyish enthusiasm that he brought to A Chorus Line, The Rocky Horror Show, Joe Orton, Edna Everage, and an aborted disaster called I.T. Sometimes radical and usually chic, he has done more than anyone to keep alive the spirit of Carnaby Street; when he writes, as he often does, of 'a key Sixties figure' he means it as a compliment.

Kitty Black writes of the days when Tennents, under Binkie Beaumont, ruled the West End. That would be worth exploring in depth; but her Upper Circle (Methuen £10.95), occasionally evocative, is more often pointlessly anecdotal. Black and White presumably know more about their own lives than I do; but both books seemed to me full of mistakes. Some of them are grammatical (whatever happened to publishers' editors?) though both can give points to Michael Coveney, a full-time writer, whose Theatre Royal (Quartet £12.95), an otherwise conscientious history of the Theatre Royal, Stratford East, dangles enough participles to cause a hernia.
1985-01-01-of-mice-and-men:
Of Mice and Men

When I read the book Of Mice and Men I thought it had the most speakable dialogue of any novel I had ever encountered. I knew that it had been turned into a play, and I could imagine the words just falling off the page into the actors' mouths. A wiser man had apparently had the same reaction; George S. Kaufman (described, almost insultingly, in the Mermaid programme as "an eminent director and writer of the time" had said to Steinbeck "it drops almost naturally into play form." Perhaps the lack of sweat is what made Kaufman, that voracious collaborator, take no official credit for his work on this one. Steinbeck seems to have been a natural playwright.

It is not just the arranges itselt races a it a tibe plot dialogue that plays easily; the guidly, around the stage. I could spot only two flaws. First, the minor characters are developed at greater length in the first half of the play than can well be supported in the second. But that is almost a virtue; it makes every role richly playable, a point on which the present production gratefully seizes. The second is that the catastrophe - Lennie's accidental killing of Curley's wife - happens rather hurriedly. She dies before she has fully come alive: the penalty of being a woman is what is, in its heart, an all-male play. For those who don't know, Of Mice and Men is set in California in the late thirties.

George and Lennie are itinerant workers, George small and reasonably bright, Lennie huge and retarded. They love each other, and they are unique among the roaming farm-hands of the West in that they have each other. They also have a dream: of saving their money and buying their own place. (The point of this is that they will be able to take the day off if a circus or a ball-game is in town; they sound more than a little like Tom Sawyer and Huck Finn.) George keeps Lennie in line through threats, cajolements, and repeated stories that Lennie likes to hear, Lennie loves to pet anything small and soft - mice, rabbits, puppies and he invariably pets them to death.

He also likes to caress women's soft dresses, and this has got him in trouble; the two are on the run from their last job when we Lou Hirsch plays George, the exasperated companion to the dopey Lennie (Clive Mantle): another well received production from the Nuffield, Southampton, this time in the hands of Geoff Bullen meet them. At their next they fall foul of Curley, the boss's son, a vicious bantam who likes provoking fights and who picks on Lennie, the gentle and - usually unresisting giant. This is smoothed over but it leaves Curley's frustrated and seemingly flirtatious wife, of whom he is violently jealous, disgusted and ready to go. But she gets into conversation with Lennie and her proximity turns him, fatally, on.

All right. The title. There is not much about mice, as rodents, after the first scene, but there is a lot about best-laid plans ganging agley. George and Lennie have their vision, for the first time, within reach; a disabled farm-hand Candy, fearful of being put out to grass, offers to come in with them and donate his savings. (A third possible flaw: Candy does go on a bit.) Lennie's act snuffs out that dream as suddenly and irrevocably as it snuffs out Curley's wife. Callous, and even misogynist, it may be, but we feel the death of the dream more acutely than we feel the death of the woman. The play's achievement is to make us feel it, physically: to want, desperately, to turn the clock back.

All that is left for George is to kill Lennie before Curley's lynch mob gets him. And then back, this time in solitude and without hope, to the fearful life of a migrant worker in the Depression. Not perhaps as fearful in the play as in reality; the life has been tenderised (the language certainly has and Slim, the kindly foreman, is maybe too good to be true. But the back-breaking barleypicking, and the aimlessness, and the fear ('can't ever tell whether you're talking to a nice guy or the Boss') and the lure of the cat-house that leaves a guy as poor as when he started work, are all vividly there. And, like most plays depicting an enclosed life, this is a treat for actors.

Clive Mantle, being nearly seven foot, has apparently made something of a career out of playing Lennie, and has evolved a vocal and physical language that puts him, as he should be, in a world of his own, its boundaries derived by bafflement (turning dangerously to terror) and desire to please. Lou Hirsch as George is may too hyper, too emphatic, but he gets infuriated protectiveness very well liam Roberts, drawling and solid as Slim, and Christopher Ryan, spluttering and febrile as Curley, are positive and negative poles for the currents that flow through the bunkhouse; Francis Drake (fairly endearing as Candy), Peter Banks and Ian Tyler go with it; Barry J. Gordon has him a stylish moment or two as the Boss who may even be a nice guy; and Calvin Simpson is splendidly grouchy as the black stableman, an unsympathetic victim of discrimination.

Susan Penhali- Sean Cavanagh's evocative and watery setting suggested an element of Mark Twain Susan Penhaligon as the floosie whose death at the clumsy hands of Clive Mantle, the benevolent giant, is the undoing of Steinbeck's itinerant duo gon is, like her character, initially rather out of it playing against the grain as a walking smudge of lipstick; when the lady is allowed some feelings, she develops. Geoff Bullen directs firmly and unhurriedly (this play could quite easily slip out of control); Sean Cavanagh has designed a variegated set that trucks back and forth over a stretch of river that looks real and poisonous enough to have been pumped in from the Thames on the other side of the stage.

Of Mice and Men, we are told, won the 1938 Critics' Circle prize over the heads of Golden Boy and Our Town. It deserved to beat the Odets, ambitious and tormented though we have this year seen that to be. Steinbeck, working out of the mainstream, was writing better common-man drama than those striving to do it in New York. As for the Wilder, it would be nice to have a chance to do our own judging. I don't promise to like it but I promise to attend.
1985-01-01-waiting-for-cage-aux-folles:
Waiting for Cage Aux Folles

There were far fewer musicals produced in London in 1984 than we have been led to believe. I counted seven major shows, plus a couple of marginal entries (semi-musicals, almost-musicals, maybe-musicals) at the National. Considering the number of theatres still left alive in the West End, that is not a very great number. There were very few significant items on the fringe. Let me dispose of the marginals first, though that seems an unkind term for Animal Farm, the best evening to be had on the South Bank in 1984 (appropriately) and the best thing Peter Hall has done in years. It did no more than put Orwell clearly and skilfully on stage, but the obvious technical difficulties provided built-in suspense, and the voice was one we needed to hear.

The show-trial scenes were as chilling an enactment of police-state justice as I remember. The musical element - Richard Peaslee's tunes and Adrian Mitchell's lyrics - was probably the least impressive thing about it, but the songs were still a needed lubricant, raising the tempo and temperature of the novel to that of the stage. Only once did the score go glaringly wrong: in the provision of a big song for Barrie Rutter as Napoleon, the porcine Stalin. It tried to explain the character by referring back to the early biography of his role-model. But Orwell here is not interested in psychology, and the show was elsewhere faithful enough to him for this one departure to Jar.

Music and lyrics too, were among the weaker points of Tom Stoppard's Rough Crossing. What do I mean, weaker? Isn't the whole thing weak? (The world 'abysmal' has been used in my hearing). No, it isn't. I am a sucker for Stoppard jokes and for the spirit that keeps him making them. They are a lot more use to the theatre than anybody's sermon: more worthwhile, for example, than The Real Thing, and the first act of Rough Crossing, with John Standing exhibiting his impeccable lounglizardry as a Hungarian Coward and the underrated Niall Buggy fluttering in hypochondriac attendance and Michael Kitchen's uncannily assured delivery plonking his words down in marvellous counterpoint to his wavering sea-legs (in dry dock, yet), is as cheerful an offering as London offers.

In Molnar's original some tongue-in-cheek fun is had with the mechanics of exposition; Mr Stoppard expands and improves it immensely. The toast, in which Mr Kitchen obligingly unloads all the details of the plot, is a masterpiece of cheek, in both writing and acting. The performance style, indeed, is far surer throughout than in this show's predecessor, On the Razzle. I even enjoyed the running gag that enables Mr Kitchen to drink every glass of the Pernod that he is supposed to be serving to Mr Standing. I confess that I could feel the plot and the point of the original drifting away as the jokes accumulated, to be finally lost from sight in the second act.

Where this really founders, though, is on Mr Stoppard's attempt to burlesque the impossibly tangled plot of an inter-war musical. I am not convinced that this is a form he knows very much about; and anyway he falls foul of basic audience psychology. Given a story, any audience will try to follow it. If it cannot be followed they get frustrated. It is no help that their WAITING FOR CAGE AUX FOLLES Robert Cushman looks at the musical in London in 1984 frustration is meant to be the point. Mr Stoppard is usually kinder to his public; and his good nature is the main attraction of Rough Crossing. It even works musically in the first-half closer 'Where Do We Go From Here' (based, presumably, on the Gershwin' 'Things Are Looking Up').

The finale, though, looks like the nadir of the subsidised companies' attempts to cash in on the musical: a desperate attempt to send us out happy, presuming on a goodwill that has long since dissipated. Probably the most genuinely musical aspect of the entertainment is Carl Toms's ocean-liner set: it should be held in storage, against a National revival of Anything Goes. I suppose the polar opposite of Rough Crossing, which would do anything for a joke, was The Hired Man which disdained them (eschewed them, as Bette Midler used triumphantly to pronounce it) altogether. With the possible exception of Man of La Mancha it was the most humourless musical in memory; and I don't quite see what it had to be so miserable about.

(Poverty? Mining disasters? The First World War? A load of laughs. Everyone knows that.) Altogether to its credit was Howard Goodall's music. Rich and rousing, owing nothing to Broadway and little to pop, it affirmed that a genuinely British musical might after all be a possibility. But Mr Goodall's lyrics were banal in the love-passages and awkward throughout (an especial attraction of the choral numbers was that the music tended to drown out the words) and Melvyn Bragg's book, based on Melvyn Bragg's book, as chaotic as his script for Mardi Gras a few years back. Its opening number promised, at some length, the story of an agricultural labourer who then spent most of his time down the pit or in the trenches.

Its indeterminate love story had nothing to do with its social history, beyond the fact that they both happened to the same people. The war introduced for chronological rather than dramatic reasons; it happens because it happened. It seems, too, typical of the show's high-mindedness that the musically impressive war-number was faded out, giving a frustrated audience no chance to applaud. Nor was the constant use of a split-level set very happy; more than half the action (including all the best numbers) got pushed into the middle distance. What was most infuriating was the failure to individualise the characters: a matter partly of acting (only Julia Hill as the heroine really communicated) but mostly of writing.

The show obviously felt deeply for them, but it gave us no chance to share its emotion. Just what constitutes a revival in 1984 is difficult to estimate. New shows are steeped in nostalgia, and where exactly do you place 42nd Street? Perhaps this is why The Boy Friend fell flat; we do not, at this moment, need a meticulous pastiche of the 20s seen through the eyes of the 50s; it hardly makes a change. That, at any rate is my theory, even though Sandy Wilson's score remains indestructible. It needed to be, in this heavily camped production, one totally lacking in the essential innocence. To compound it all, Anna Quayle was off sick at the performance I saw.

This was frustrating; having often seen Miss Quayle salvage bad material I was eager to see how she would cope with good. On Your Toes was a more respectable enterprise but not a really satisfying one. Rodgers and Hart wrote it a great score, or a least a great collection of songs; most of them (even such a triumph of bittersweet as 'Glad to Be Unhappy') go for nothing theatrically because they are not keyed into the book, an insubstantial but also plodding affair that lacks even the fizzing silliness of an Oh Kay or Whoopee. (And why, I want to know, does the villain who plans a murder get off scot-free — even marrying the leading lady at the end, while the gangster he hires is dragged off to gaol?) What remains is the dancing, and - in London - the performance of Natalia Makarova and Tim Flavin.

The first balletspoof, 'The Princess Zenobia', is a damp squib; Slaughter on Tenth Avenue' still has impact. The title number - the real heart of the show and a knock-out on Broadway with its sustained friendly battle between ballet and tap - just refuses in London to take off. This may be because all the best dancers had been nabbed by 42nd Street. The tapping here really is exciting, and Clare Leach in the Ruby Keeler role - the aspirant showgirl - gives the piece a heart it never had in New York. This it needs, for this, unlike The Boy Friend that JANUARY 1985 Sandy Wilson actually wrote, is calculated camp: plundering the old conventions but showing no real affection of understanding for them.

I invite you to consider 'Lullaby of Broadway', here borrowed from Gold Diggers of 1935 (which doesn't matter) to provide the key number. To begin with, James Laurenson, snappily though he acts the role of the director, cannot really sing it (and the part exists for that song). After him, the whole cast arrive on the stage, begging Miss Leach to come back to the theatre and save the show. They've chosen an odd song to do it with. 'Lullaby of Broadway' is about New York night-life: the hookers, the sugar-daddies, the daffydills who entertain at Angelo's and Maxie's... the one aspect of Broadway it does not mention is the theatre. The show obviously believes (and, sadly, it may well be right) that nobody listens to lyrics; we are expected to hear, and respond to, the word 'Broadway' and forget about context.

Nor are we really meant to share the emotion; we are supposed to regard it as absurd: as so much generalised razz-ma-tazz that we cannot believe in but may still think adorably ridiculous. "Think' bellows the director of musical comedy, the two most beautiful words in the language'. Nobody who really cared about musicals (which entails keeping them in perspective) would ever say, think or believe such a thing. And you state the case for the musical by doing it, not by orating over it. You can sit at Drury Lane and sense the trouble that 42nd Street itself must have been in out of town. The film, within its conventions, is a rather realistic piece about the tensions of doing a show; all this has gone out the window in favour of more and more numbers.

Some of them, especially at the start, are stunning, but they end up as overkill; the title-number, the one we've all been waiting for, is a particular disappointment. And yet... there is more fun in 42nd Street than in most current shows, and Margaret Courtenay's performance, bulldozing laughs out of a recalcitrant script, is something Broadway never had. For me the two best revivals were Little Me - brilliant score, funny book, all right production - and West Side Story: a treat to see Jerome Robbins's dances back in stage convention and stage scale; the realism of film murdered them. Some of the book may be forced, some of the score overblown, but it still gets you by the throat.

A first-rate Tony and Maria, though Anita and Riff went for nothing very much. Which leaves Starlight Express. I was away when it opened, and if it were not for this article I would probably still not have caught up with it. I had somehow got the impression that cast-changes would be immaterial: that technology was all and personality nothing. I had been lied to. Jeff Shankley, Lon Satton, and Michael Stanniforth are all terrific, and the energy-level, nine months into the run, would not disgrace New York. As far as I can gather the show has been attacked as whimsical, sentimental, relying on spectacle at the expense of story and character - by critics who bypassed exactly the same flaws in Cats.

It does perhaps repeat the Cats structure too exactly for comfort, right up (or down) to the heavenly intervention in favour of the most despised member of the pack. It is also true that the warmth, the sheer likeableness, of Trevor Nunn's direction, (that reached its apogee in Nicholas Nickleby), may be softening into a formula, to be sprayed on like Showbiz Warmth. But the anthropomorphism is more successful here than in Cats. The real weakness there was in Eliot's verse. He hardly bothered to make his practical pussies feline; he drew human types, artitrarily fitted out with fur and whiskers, and there is something self-defeating about putting actors into cat-gear and catmovements to impersonate them.

At least the trains in Starlight Express are described as such, and put through a story that has something to do with locomotion. Richard Stilgoe's lyrics are neat, sometimes even funny; he is only defeated by Andrew Lloyd Webber's customary refusal to allow dialogue. It may make him feel operatic, but it inolves his lyricists in writing awful doggerel in the name of recitative. The music has plenty of drive and - especially in its blues and boogie moods — more conviction than any Webber score since you-name-it. The intended big ballad is as watery as ever but at least it has had the grace not to become a hit. The unequivocal failure is the racesequences; repetitive, difficult to follow, and has anybody known a theatrical production to make successful use of video screens?

It is a cop-out: simply not what you go to the theatre for. But the adventure playground aspect is fun, and John Napier's costumes an all-out triumph: gold not only in themselves but in the whirling contribution that they make, especially when deployed en masse, to Arlene Phillips's choreography. The predictability of the story - you know who will win and who will get whom from the outset - drags the show down rather. As a fulfilling experience it hardly ranks with Guys and Dolls or Gypsy or Carousel (bravely and movingly revived at the Royal Exchange) or, in better days, The Boy Friend. But there is juice in it: something to keep us warm while we ready ourselves for La Cage Aux Folles and wonder when or whether someone will take a chance on the better shows in the recent Broadway crop: Baby or Sunday in the Park with George or — most stylish of the nostalgia trips — My One and Only.

And God knows, if skating's your fancy it's better than The Rink.
1985-02-01-bloody-poetry:
Bloody Poetry

A few years ago Shelley was reclaimed for the revolution and made intellectually respectable. We discovered that the bits of him we had read at school were quite unrepresentative; he was the poet of fiery protest, not of nature rambles. From this newly received wisdom Howard Brenton takes off in Bloody Poetry, a play boldly and fully conceived but unevenly executed. I assume that he wrote the programme notes as well as the play. Anyway there, alone with a photograph that makes Mr Brenton look (appropriately in this new Eng Lit arena) more like Simon Gray than ever, is the assertion that 'with, for some, the exception of John Milton, he (Shelley) is the greatest poet in the language after Shakespeare.

That 'after' is presumably meant to be chronological; otherwise, what about Chaucer? And other some might put in a plea for Donne or Keats or (though I can hardly speak for them) Wordsworth. And there was Byron. Byron shares the limelight with Shelley in Bloody Poetry. They are seen with their women (Shelley's women, really, but one of them is shared) roaming the more picturesque parts of Europe in their last years. Byron is within sight of his Grecian death at the final curtain; Shelley has already drowned. Byron the cynical rake, with no apparent principles to flourish, gives his life for freedom; though of course the struggle may for him be merely an antidote to boredom.

Shelley, the conscious ideologue, far away from home at the time of the Peterloo massacre, gets as far as commemorating it in the biting, stirring lines of The Mask of Anarchy': recited in the play to great effect. But what is a poet supposed to do anyway? The question and its possible answers - in varying shades of praise and blame, guilt and exultation - chase each other round the stage as they must have done for years in Mr Brenton's own head. Lines cross. Bryon attacks the verse of Wordsworth (though he asks to do the job less vivaciously in this play than in his own Don Juan); Shelley, Wordsworth's sworn political enemy, defends the work because it sings'.

Unlike most so-called dialectical plays this one does not bank its argument in neatly parcelled cases for prosecution and defence. The issues here dart and glint like kingfishers: much helped by being posed, in Roland Rees's production, across the aquamarined screens of Poppy Mitchell's set whose dazzling starkness sets off the flowing line of Sheelagh Killeen's costumes. Felicitous tableaux are the playwright's as well as the designers'; much is made of these Romantics' disregard of their women and children; Shelley's wife Harriet, having gone prettily and melodiously mad at the beginning of the second act, corporeally haunts the rest of the action. It sounds a solemn touch but is actually a mischievous one. All the same, both play and production could use more wit.

The ideas are beginning to be exhausted in the second half, and the author has increasing recourse to straight-faced biography. But he has not established the characters firmly enough for this; he is more interested in what they can be made to stand for than in what they are. The play is closer to Travesties than to Total Eclipse, and it even boasts a Henry Carr figure: Polidori who follows the bloody poets around memoiring 1 185 Howard Brenton's Bloody Poetry at Hampstead with Jane Gurnett and Fiona Shaw directed by Roland Rees. them and relishing the reflected glory. To do this he has to be a fair masochist. Only a Stoppard - not that there is more than one — would make the impotent onlooker endearing: Mr Brenton, though not a cruel writer, is a hard one and Polidori is a humiliated character.

William Gaminara plays him admirably. Acting is generally good and, in one instance, outstanding. Fiona Shaw, having spent a year at the National breathing life into Julia in The Rivals (and doing, inexplicably, nothing else there), presents Mary Shelley as a warm, lofty bluestocking able to suffer, to laugh and to attack. Miss Shaw, with a Georgian plum in her voice, is sense and sensibility confined: actually the nearest our stage has come to an embodiment of the complete works of Jane Austen. Bloatedness is the note of James Aubrey's Byron (it does inevitably seem to be the Simon Callow role), tense piping high-mindedness that of Valentine Pelka's Shelley. Obviously Mr Brenton's favourite, Percy Bysshe is both judged more harshly and indulged more generously than George Gordon Noel, Lord.

Tastes differ. I went into the theatre believing Bryon to be the wittiest versifier in English, and Shelley a windy sentimentalist, endlessly parading the sensitivity of his own soul, and responsible for foisting the figure of the Poet on the world. I came out still believing it.
1985-02-01-the-winter-s-tale-the-crucibl:
The Winter's Tale / The Crucible

Promenade performances as we have known them, mainly at the National, have been of pieces specially adapted from non-dramatic sources, or - as with The Passion or the Exeter version of The Dynasts - of plays so extensive as to need drastic re-working anyway. Making them go walkabout was only the final emendation; and one that suited their essential sprawlingness. It was almost comforting that we had to trail around behind the performance, never quite catching all of it; it testified to the size of the endeavour. The RSC's Nicholas Nickleby, was sort of a promenade in reverse; it moved around among us. These two RSC productions, brought to a cold and echoing but undeniably imposing London church after the provincial tour for which they were conceived, are the first promenades I have seen (or I suppose the right word is experienced) of orthodox plays: the kind you think twice about cutting.

Promenade Shakespeare sounds a reasonable idea; Bill Bryden thought of trying it with A Midsummer Night's Dream (or so said the initial publicity) but settled in the end for a modicum of audience involvement. It has been left to Adrian Noble, with The Winter's Tale, to go the whole peripatetic. He did not, except in the most literal sense, take me with him. Some of the fault may well have been mine. I arrived late, to find Leontes into his first jealous soliloquy. Even in a conventional performance, latecoming is its own penance. It takes time to adjust, physically and psychologically. You miss more than you actually missed. Sometimes you never catch up. That was my case here. My fellow spectators were pretty well rapt; caught up in the fable, Shared Experience style.

(The production is played on Persian carpets that reminded me strongly of that company's Arabian Nights.) Some magic had been worked of the kind that this tall and beautiful story requires. But when I looked at Alun Armstrong's Leontes, with his genial nose, I could not believe in him. The production risked a lot in making his jealousy comic, but it was the wrong kind of comedy: a therapeutic demonstration of the savage silliness of an imaginary cuckold. It would in fact have done very well in Moliere, but Mr Armstrong as a king - even in this production's variegated modern dress - I could not credit. Lynn Farleigh was a good if not remarkable Hermione, Janet Dale a labouring Paulina; she pushed her way through the verse instead of riding it.

Ron Cook's Autolycus, a historically early exponent of Cockney rock, left me dispassionate for or against, but the clowns were fine (they actually dared to be funny) with Trevor Martin's Old Shepherd, solid lovely, the best performance of the evening. There were some coups of the calibre we expect of Mr Noble. A frightening bear was one, remarkable at these quarters. The whole conduct of the trial was another, with king and queen on rostra at opposing ends of the hall, the freezing judicial atmosphere reinforced by the use of microphones. Hermione's defence, with Miss Farleigh at her best, was at once distanced and brought closer: distant from her auditors (she was a woman in a cruelly impossible position), closer to us (the woman on the stand became part of our own experience.) The literal and forcible breaking-up of Apollo's oracle was really exciting.

A quieter detail was the establishing of the married state of Paulina and Antigonus: something on which Shakespeare presumes but which he does little to depict. If the Bohemian revels- done with effortfully phallic folk-dancing and the audience set on the sidelines at supposedly festive tables - failed to convince they were in good traditional company. Less expected was the failure - for me, at any rate - of the final resurrection; that moving statue usually brings on the gooseflesh even in the most dismal productions. was not dismal; I should probably acknowledge it as the best Nunn's sixties version. I do, with the proviso that it comes a long way atter. The Winter's Tale, a play that rambles famously in space and notoriously in time, would seem a better bet for promenade production than The Crucible, a traditionally well-made piece composed of four long and independently located scenes.

It is the portrait of a society, but mainly by implication. The Barry Kyle- Nick Hamm production attempted to open it up with some community hymnsinging and by showing us, before the scripted action began, actors engaged in seventeenth-century rural crafts. looked, for the most part, like RSC actors engaged in seventeenth-century rural crafts; one could see why they were doing it but it was the attempt and not the deed that registered. The first scene was en- livened by letting us see Reverend Hale from Beverley arrive at Reverend Parris's Salem front door in a covered wagon. (Mr Parris seemed to have lodged his sick daughter in a very exposed place.) After all this period detail it seemed strange to find the court-room,like the one in the modern dress Winter's Tale, equipped with a microphone.

Was it to affirm the twinship of the two productions? Or to remind us of the affinity between Judge Danforth - the man behind the mike and contemporary witch-hunters? If the latter, it was needless. I have never seen a production which so strongly affirmed Salem's links with McCarthyism and subsequent persecutions: not because it was trying hard to be relevant, but because the play itself is rooted in the parallels and they were doing very well by the play. In its essentials the production was superb, outclassing both its National Theatre predecessors: by Laurence Olivier's florid version and Mr Bryden's tight-lipped one. Melodrama was given full rein without ever getting out of control, and the trial was the most physically exciting piece of theatre I have seen in ages.

This had something to do with the mechanics of staging - we lined the walls of a long courtroom-but more with the quality of performance. The actors were the right weight for this play, as they were not for The Winter's Tale, and they drove the scene on to its culmination in the cry of Mr Cook as the disillusioned Hale: "I denounce these proceedings! I quit this court!" The stage was in uproar but he dominated it; I have seen no other actor dare to carry off this moment. Actually it was the only moment I liked in his entire performance, which was otherwise maddeningly studied. It seemed to have its basis in Arthur Miller's description of him as like a young doctor on a house-call rather than in the ebb and flow of his relations with the other characters.

He played a generalised idea of quiet fanaticism; Hale is more interesting and more ordinary than that: more interesting because more ordinary, the play's Everyman in whose crumbling beliefs the action is mirrored. But everyone else was wonderful. Mr Armstrong's bulldozing honesty surpassed even Colin Blakely's; for once the long final scene between Proctor and his wife -usually a grinding shift from the political to the personal - did not seem an anti-climax. Miss Farleigh's melting ice-maiden of an Elizabeth, moved and moving (a vast improvement on her National performance) set him off splendidly. Julian Curry made a suave, powerful judge: an emblem of civilised bigotry. The girls were young enough for history but strong enough for drama, and the elders (Mr Martin and Margery Mason) invincibly and invaluably human.

And, yes, in the end you did feel you had met a community because you had met, and been involved with, a number of its inhabitants. Which proves that the truth about promenade performance is the same as the truth about the theatre in general: acting is all.
1985-05-01-tom-and-viv-and-jumpers:
Tom and Viv and Jumpers

Robert Cushman at Tom and Viv and Jumpers / Royal Court/Aldwych

Two plays have recently returned to London in which Bertrand Russell plays a peripheral, unseen role. In each, he is the occasion of wit. In Tom and Viv he is T S Eliot’s early room-mate, ‘the most hated man in London’ who, despite his reputation as a seducer, signally fails to get anywhere with the first Mrs Eliot: a circumstance that fills all concerned with the gloomiest apprehensions for that lady’s future. In Jumpers he turns up in Professor George Moore’s speech on the possible existence and interdependence of God and morality as ‘my friend the late Lord Russell’, a phrase that George admits does not sound quite right, perhaps, as his wife Dotty drily points out, because Russell wasn’t his friend.

In short, we are among intellectuals. Tom and Viv is Michael Hastings’s treatment, unauthorised but far from unsympathetic, of Eliot’s wretched first marriage whose upshot, in Edith Sitwell’s phrase, was that ‘Tom went mad and promptly certified his wife’. Tom here does not go mad; he merely goes English and Anglican. Banker and publisher as well as poet, he wants his life to be tidy, and so there is no place in it for Viv. She dazzled him at first: an apparently free spirit with upper-class connections. In fact her family accept him rather more enthusiastically than they do her. Viv has menstrual problems which embarrass her family, her doctors, and herself; and which, ignorantly treated, drive her further and further into neurosis. Most of all do her illnesses, physical and mental, embarrass her husband. They have, it seems, no sex-life. Eliot hopes that Russell might actually seduce Viv, just to take the strain off him, and he is crushed and desperate when he learns the truth. The information passes between them in a gentlemanly exchange of letters. It is one of Mr Hastings’s best, most economical, strokes to have Viv discover this correspondence and read it to us.

I have no especial biographical interest in Eliot, and no more than a polite literary one, but the treatment of all parties seemed to me acute and sympathetic. Tom’s gradual withdrawal into English religion and society, his abandonment of his wife and his guilt over it, all seem likely enough. His growing rapprochement with Viv’s brother—an amateur Blimp whose stumbling good intentions, economic misadventures in Africa, and decline into shabby gentility make him seem like a figure from Anthony Powell—is especially well delineated. I believed it all. But it is not a very dynamic progress, and it is half the play. It weighs the evening down, and the second act in particular becomes dull.

The play seemed notably wittier when I read it afterwards than it had in performance. Max Stafford-Clark’s production is, after its own fashion, impeccable: elegant, icy and precise. But it is also insistently ascetic, ending scenes abruptly and changing them in full view of the audience. I know this is Royal Court style and has been for years, but I am beginning to suspect it. The assumption seems to be that the audience does not want illusion, and would be angry, even insulted, if it were offered. Or perhaps the idea is that we should take what’s good for us. The denial of illusion can overlap with the denial of pleasure. (This kind of staging bothered me particularly in the recent production of The Pope’s Wedding; it seemed a reflex, nothing to do with the rhythm of the play and actually harmful to it.)

I admired Edward Herrmann’s gradual suppression of his American accent as Tom sank into his chosen milieu. Julie Covington is one of my favourite actresses but her Viv, after all I had heard about it, (I missed the play on its first London outing) disappointed me. Everything is there—the 1920s brittleness, the defensive descents into mock-Cockney, the fraying nerves, the final desperate gallantry—but it adds up to the solution of a set of acting problems rather than to the creation of a person.

Another disturbed marriage is at the centre of Tom Stoppard’s Jumpers. How disturbed seems to vary from production to production. But troubled depends on which production you are watching. The three I have seen have all been directed by Peter Wood but they have varied considerably. The National Theatre original had Michael Hordern and Diana Rigg radiating in opposite directions; one wanted to believe that there was hope for them, because both are such likeable players, but there was little optimistic evidence. In the National revival Hordern and Miss Covington had some newly-scripted moments that hinted an underlying sympathy. Both were oral beings, in a newly amoral universe. The current version is the bleakest yet. Felicity Kendal’s Dotty is vivaciously vulnerable but, as far as her spouse is concerned, unreachable. Paul Eddington’s George radiates pain.

I am unsure how much the darkness is intentional, how much was due to the second-night performance I witnessed (which was very second-nightish) and how much, as some reviewers have claimed, can be blamed on the times. Certainly there was nothing like the effervescence of the original production. That came at a buoyant time, theatrically and even nationally. It was 1972, London was still vestigially swinging, and a rejuvenated National was specialising in luxury-pad plays; Jumpers, the modern-dress Misanthrope and Trevor Griffiths’s The Party were plays of ideas acted out in coolly luxurious settings. Mr Stoppard’s jokes were all wonderfully new, and newly wonderful. Hordern was playing his greatest role, Miss Rigg was beautiful, and the occasion oozed confidence. Even though the odds were stacked against Mr Stoppard’s well-meaning professor, even though one sympathised with him deeply when he stepped on his tortoise in the very act of mourning his slaughtered hare, the wit in his presentation (some of it his own, some of it at his expense) kept us buoyant. It seemed possible that some time, at some future date, George would invent God and win through.

Now we are less confident. England is gloomier, ruled by a government of a different complexion from Mr Stoppard’s Rad-Lib but equally convinced of its own rightness. The political acuteness of Jumpers, as of Travesties, has always seemed to be undervalued; it is not so much that it starts where orthodox political plays leave off as that it goes further back than they would dream of delving. Mr Stoppard asks why people go after power, what it is in themselves that they have to deny, and why the world makes it easy for them. George’s harried defeat is what Mr Eddington now captures; the fun of George’s monologue largely escapes him. He has not Hordern’s quintessential donnishness, nor his eagerness, nor his absurdity. To put it another way, the second act of his performance and hence of the production, is much better than the first, during much of which one sits lamenting lost chances.

Simon Cadell makes a smooth job of the omnicompetent Archie though he seems very young to have amassed so many credentials, even in a relativistic world. Andrew Sachs is an oddly manic choice for the plodding Inspector Bones, and it is very confusing when he turns up in the dream-coda as Archbishop Clegthorpe. ‘Will no-one rid me of this copper’s nark’ is the new link-line provided to carry off this identification; it seems, like most of the re-writes, unwise. The coda was much criticised at the time of the first production (epilogues nearly always are) but actually, it makes, on its own terms, perfect sense: an accurate tally of George’s bewilderments and of his failures. Tricked up as it is in this production, it merely confuses. The performance I liked best was that of Timothy Bateson as Crouch, the metaphysical caretaker (‘it’s just a hobby with me’): a gift role for the gentle mole-like character actor that Mr Bateson superbly is.

Need I add that the play still fizzes and that its ceaseless agility, its determination to leave no hole unstopped with laughter makes it the most delightful—or why not simply say the best—of post-war British plays? (Forget the stuff about its philosophic content flattering the audience’s self-esteem; you could say as much of the acclaimed political plays that seem intended to compensate critics and publics for the activist past they never had.) No playwright since Shaw has written comedy this sparkling, and Mr Stoppard is ahead of much of Shaw in clear-headedness and in honest good nature. You never feel that he is patting you on the head or that he thinks he has all the answers.

And you actually feel for George and Dotty: far more, speaking for myself, than for the central couple of The Real Thing where Mr Stoppard piles on the psychology without getting any nearer the truth. Better the pure fun of On the Razzle or Rough Crossing than a solemn Stoppard building a structure as complicated as that of Jumpers but without its aerating humour.

That The Real Thing should have been hailed as an advance for Mr Stoppard, or that Tom and Viv should have been taken more seriously than Mr Hastings’s hilarious Gloo Joo, is as sad a sign of the times as anything prophesied or adumbrated in Jumpers. We prize our playwrights, but not always for their best work. I could name other victims, laughing on their way to the bank while their audiences sit dutifully moping in the stalls.
1985-05-24-yip-hip-hooray:
Yip, hip hooray

Robert Cushman on the joys of an American lyricist

THE THING I have always loved most about the classic American lyricists is their mixture of casualness and formality -- a national characteristic, in writing and in conversation, that they carry to delicious extremes. "Anything goes," said Cole Porter, and he meant it as far as diction and subject matter were concerned.

But when it came to form, he and his peers were fanatical. Their rhymes were exact, even when outrageous; their scansion ensured that the stress always fell on the right conversational word. Anyone bred on them is likely to find most pop lyrics (and a lot of current British theatre lyrics) physically painful.

As a wartime baby, glued to the radio in the late forties and early fifties, I caught the bug young. When rock came along I found myself out of step with my generation. Bill Haley, the Beatles, Bob Dylan left me successively unmoved. I was now hooked on the theatre as well as on song, and I learned that Broadway (and, to a lesser extent, Hollywood) had originated most of my favourites; their verbal and melodic strengths were born of dramatic discipline.

I was learning to distinguish Kern's music from Gershwin's, and to tell the wordsmiths apart. I noted that Porter was a hothouse wit who needed exoticism to stir him into passion, and that Ira Gershwin was sly and easy-going, and that Lorenz Hart displayed a mixture of smartness and vulnerability ("the self-deception that believes the lie/I wish I were in love again") worth striving for as an ideal -- except that it was fatal to look as if you were striving.

I loved the way that Johnny Mercer, the only country boy in a predominantly urban Jewish profession and one of the few with strong links to jazz, came on as a mixture of hayseed and hipster. And when it came to getting high on words -- ransacking them, re-arranging them, up-ending them, and sometimes inventing them -- I learned to revere E. Y. (known universally as Yip) Harburg.

Harburg wrote at least two of the iconic songs of our century. Buddy Can You Spare a Dime and Over the Rainbow -- and they have more in common than you might think. Both are songs about hope deferred: one stark and accusing, the other brave and wistful. One stems obviously from the Depression, the other, less obviously, from the New Deal. When I came to consider doing a stage show about Harburg that would be a mixture of anthology and biography, I considered calling it Brother Can You Spare a Rainbow. I was persuaded that Look to the Rainbow would be catchier.

Look to the Rainbow is actually a song from his most successful show, Finian's Rainbow. The persistence of rainbows (and of moons and zippers) in Harburg's lyrics must, to an extent, be automatic writing. But much of it is conscious, and serious. There was no rainbow in The Wizard of Oz until his song put it there.

Harburg actually lived his lyrics -- he was a romantic who found fantasy an outlet for his wordplay and a vehicle for his satire. The son of turn-of-the-century immigrants, he enacted the classic American progress from ghetto to penthouse, felt guilty about it, became a prominent Hollywood radical, and fell inevitably foul of McCarthyism after the war.

Before that, in collaboration with some of the best composers -- Jerome Kern, Harold Arlen, Burton Lane, Vernon Duke -- he had run the popular-song gamut from yearning (April in Paris) to torchy (Happiness is a Thing Called Joe), and from brash (It's Only a Paper Moon) to hilarious. He wrote naturally for Durante, Bert Lahr, and Groucho Marx, for whom he created the immortal Tattooed Lady, Lydia ("that encyclopaedia"). His most characteristic song was written for a leprechaun; "When I'm not near the girl I love, I love the girl I'm near," proceeds from that opening gambit to half a dozen closely-woven conceits that tell an everyday story of helpless promiscuity.

Yip died in 1981, leaving a mound of first-person material, and it seemed more and more logical to have him tell his own story in his own voice. I screwed up my courage to ask the ideal actor, Jack Gilford, Broadway veteran, comedian and musical star, a friend of Yip's with the same background, many of the same experiences (including the blacklist), and something of the same puckish personality. To my delight he accepted, and had to face the unaccustomed rigours of a London fringe theatre before moving into the West End.

I hate to see these songs classified as "nostalgia." I could no more be nostalgic about Harburg or Porter than about Beethoven, and I hope that their current revival is a matter of musical appreciation, not of fashion. The musical director, and most of the cast of Look to the Rainbow are ten or more years younger than I am, but they are more at home with the idiom than most of my contemporaries. I may have been a freak in my own generation, but I feel vindicated by the next.

Look to the Rainbow is playing at the Apollo Theatre, Shaftesbury Avenue.
1985-12-01-a-chorus-line:
Sight & Sound (inc. Monthly Film Bulletin) Winter 1985 - 86
Robert Cushman

Broadway's longest runner
A Chorus Line

How do you film a stage-bound musical?

The question is nearly as old as the movies themselves, but A Chorus Line raises it in an especially acute form.

Here is a show that, in New York at any rate, is not just a hit but a legend. The longest-running musical in Broadway history, it is, and deserves to be, part of the fabric of the city. It is not the greatest musical ever, but it is the greatest tribute ever paid to the people who make the musical.

In a town fixated on show business, A Chorus Line rates as an icon. It is, as everybody must know, about auditions. There are eight chorus roles to be assigned in a Broadway show, and we witness the final countdown. Zach, the director-choreographer, has twice as many on his short list as he can use.

The show A Chorus Line is stagebound in a very special sense. It is not a backstage musical; it is an onstage musical. The candidates audition on the stage; Zach watches them and harangues them from, as far as we can tell, the back of the auditorium. The audience is caught between them, eavesdropping; perhaps the greatest thrill of the evening is the element of verite.

The opening number, with the cast being put collectively through their paces under whiplash instruction from the assistant choreographer, persuades you that this is what an audition is actually like. That number is there in Richard Attenborough's film too, but with only a fraction of the impact. It doesn't, as in the show, come at us out of nowhere.

The film (Rank) begins with a long, moody aerial tour of Manhattan; handsome of course, seeming to owe something to the beginning of the West Side Story film, and something perhaps to the Tony Awards show the year that Chorus Line swept the board. But unlike its predecessors, this opening conveys no sense of expectation. It feels explanatory; this is New York, this is where these characters come from, this is the theatre.

We are taken on a tour of last year's Broadway marquees, avoiding the Shubert where A Chorus Line is actually playing; we have to avoid it, of course, but it feels somehow like cheating.
