How can this be the real Broadway, if it's deprived of its major exhibit? But it isn't its own fictional world, either. It is a compromise, and so goes the rest of the picture.

Much of it faithfully follows the stage original. Zach, on the pretext that the chorus roles have to be acted as well as sung and danced, interrogates his candidates.

What kind of people are they? How were their childhoods and adolescences? (This seems to translate into: How uncomfortable was their discovery of sex?) Why did they get into dancing? In most cases the answer to that one is, as compensation.

They are all pretty screwed up, though no more so than most of us. So we identify with them and sympathise with their experience of being on trial for a desperately needed break.

We make an emotional investment in every one of them (we are told nothing about the parts they are trying out for, so can have no preferences on the grounds of suitability—cunning move that it is), and when the final selections and rejections are made we are guaranteed fifty per cent heartbreak and fifty per cent exhilaration.

With so potent a mixture the show's success is hardly surprising. The movie, though, lets us off the hook. There is no interval in the stage show; we, like the performers, are trapped in the shell of that stage and auditorium. There is no break in the film, either, but there is a change of scene. It is minor—we wander no further than the greenroom and the sidewalk outside the theatre—but fatal.

One of the applicants stands apart from the others: Cassie, an ex-almost-star and the director's former lover. She now comes to him desperate for a fresh start in the chorus. He refuses; he says it's because she's too good, but he may just think she's too old.

On stage the story of her past life was compressed into some embarrassingly overwrought exchanges. In the screenplay these have been ironed out, and she herself (affectingly played by Alyson Reed) is more fully realised. But that turns out to be the greater evil.

She becomes the central character (old Hollywood logic, perhaps, to give us a protagonist to identify with) and the collective strength of the material vanishes. The other auditionees become shadowy (not one has the immediacy I remember from stage companies in New York, London and Toronto) and Zach, a highly visible presence instead of a disembodied goading voice, is transformed from ambiguous father-confessor to unadulterated bullying bastard.

Actually, the star part in the picture is Larry (Terence Mann), the assistant who carries messages from Zach to Cassie and back again. His is a basic narrative function, and Attenborough seems happier with it and with Larry's flair, kindly embarrassment at going between, than he does with musical numbers.

Zach won't let Cassie on the stage, so she wanders around the theatre. We wander with her, and in doing so plunge into a routine kind of realism.

There is in fact a horrible clash of conventions. Even in the stage show there was a hiccup when the characters switched from singing and dancing as they believably might at an audition to singing and dancing as in a conventional musical—i.e., as a heightened substitute for conversation. The sheer assurance of Michael Bennett's staging overrode the problem.

But here you don't know where you are.

Zach interrogates his first victim: ordinary conversation. The victim replies with an autobiographical song-and-dance called "I Can Do That": stylisation but treated as if nobody knew the difference, prosaically and head-on. Then cut away to Cassie, pursuing her destiny; back to naturalism.

Then we are onstage again, the number is still in progress, and another auditionee, who has no narrative connection with it, is joining in.

Why? Sheer joie de vivre? We would have to get pretty high to believe that; and nothing in the shooting of the numbers does that for us.

Considering that the company spends all their time either dancing or talking about dancing, it is extraordinary how little sense of dance you carry away from it.

A Chorus Line might have been filmed entirely in its stage setting: at worst we would have had a record of the original, at best a picture that created tension from confinement. Or it could have been thoroughly restructured: perhaps letting us see the characters growing up in their hometowns before bringing them together to be judged.

I have no idea how, or even whether, either approach could have worked out, but it is significant that Bennett himself, who reportedly had first option on directing the film, passed it up. Perhaps he thought there was no way of making it work.

The most effective things in Attenborough's film come straight from the original: the vestigial strength of the central conceit, and the occasional telling detail ("Watch Larry," says Zach condescendingly, "He's got the right style—very 30s") that persuades you this is how the Broadway cattle-market really is.
1986-03-01-women-beware-women:
Women Beware Women

In The Irresistible Theatre, his inspired and inspiring history of English drama, W Bridges-Adams remarked of Middleton's Women Beware Women that 'it is a play that makes one sigh for the hardihood with which our forebears improved on Romeo and Juliet, for its principal theme fulfills its promise almost to the last'. Some 30 years after that sentence was published comes Howard Barker to grant the half-strangled wish and re-order Middleton's conclusion. Bridges-Adams was a gentleman of the old school, and it is unlikely that the ruderies of Mr Barker would have much appealed to him. What he objected to in the original play was its final scene: a colourful revel in which six characters meet violent and generally spectacular deaths.

(One is pierced by a flight of poisoned arrows; another falls through a trap-door onto a very nasty spike). This finale has also displeased Royal Court impresario Max Stafford-Clark who says in the current programme that he finds it 'unperformable and rather silly. The first charge is demonstrably untrue (the scene worked in Anthony Page's fine production at the Arts years ago) but the reaction is an understandable one. Mr Stafford-Clark talked to Mr Barker and then to William Gaskill. The present production is the upshot. One thing it does is to reprieve every character on Middleton's death-list. This is unlooked-for mercy in Mr Barker, and in another programme-note (no production in recent memory has arrived so bristling with defences) he admits as much.

I almost said he admits it wryly, but that would have been lazy of me. Wryness and Mr Barker are not frequent companions. He admits it aggressively. Middleton's play deals with Bianca, a 16-year-old, who elopes from Venice to marry Leantio, a Florentine clerk. She is raped and/or seduced by the Duke of Florence, and shortly moves to his palace. Her husband, whose poverty now disgusts her, is bought off with the captaincy of a fort. Meanwhile, this being of course a play with a sub-plot, a yo ing gentlewoman LONDON NOTICES Ine Mara called Isabella, who fancies and is fancied by her uncle Hippolito, is falsely persuaded that they are not related at all.

To disguise what would still appear an incestuous affair she marries a rich half-wit known as the Ward. The two plots are thus linked by sex and money; and — this being an unusually tidy tragedy they are further unified by the character of Livia, a court procuress who decoys Bianca to the Duke and invents the story that takes in Isabella. To round everything off she falls for, and wins, Leantio: going into business for herself, so to speak. It is at this point the beginning of Middleton's fourth act that Mr Barker takes over. He begins by letting Livia and Leantio celebrate their loves. Five days and nights they have been at it, and their dreamy rejoicings are like post-coital Donne with the four-letter words left in.

('We fuck the day to death' says Leantio by way of getting things rolling). This scene is brilliant and confirms my impression, first bred by Victory, that nobody in the British theatre writes better about sex - the thing itself, as distinct from what may be made of or deduced from it - than Mr Barker. But of course he does try to make something of it: a revolutionary force, in fact. Awakened by her now love - the love itself rather than the lover - Livia determines to topple the Florentine state. The quaint means she employs is to have Bianca, the duchess elect, raped a second time: this time by a virginal malcontent called Sordido.

What? Let Livia explain (and note how Mr Barker's prose, purposely or otherwise, apes the rhythms of Middleton's verse): 'By this catastrophe she'll grope for knowledge her ambition hides from her. And simultaneously, Sordido's crime will rock the state off its foundations, which is erected on such lies as ducal marriages. 'Where', asks Leantio, 'is the realism in all this?' 'Realism', Livia screams back at him, 'I hate the word'; and so of course does her author. But an attack on a society is pretty hollow if the author is allowed to invent that society as he goes along. The royal-marriage satire has its point, but philosophical rape is hard to credit after the real thing.

In Middleton men ravish and murder for good solid reasons like lust and ambition, and that is far more satisfying. LAMDA THE LONDON ACADEMY OF MUSIC AND DRAMATIC ART Tower House, 226 Cromwell Road, London SW5 OR 01-373 9883 His characters act; Mr Barker's attitudinise. This does not actually make them less Jacobean, but they have more to do with Chapman and Webster (both great spinners of words and postponers of action) than with Middleton who loved to get down to things; as witness the famous chess-game whose every move is a double- Bianca. entendre to accompany the entrapment of Mr Barker is of course under no obligation to complete the play on Middleton's terms; that, after all, has already been done by Middleton.

His avowed motive is to reclaim sex from seventeenth-century cynicism; even his lecherous Duke ends up a slightly better if broken man and he has so little quarrel with incest that the theme just disappears. His Sordido is a low-comedy servant transformed; and his Ward turns out to be no fool at all. (These two between them do a lot of talking). In the most hectoring of all the programme-notes the Marxist academic Jonathan Dollimore writes scornfully how else?) of 'those who want to fetishise the play as fixed and unalterable in its greatness. But revision-worship is no less of a fetish, and comparisons are unavoidable. In the original, the Duke is upbraided for adultery by his brother the Cardinal, and decides to reform.

His method is to have Leantio killed so that he may respectably marry Bianca; playing on the snobbery of Livia's brother he persuades him to murder the upstart. There you have social comment, religious satire, structural irony, personal pain, in a couple of acrid, economic strokes. Mr Barker — though he offers some off-thewall wit and a general rallying of forces at the end - cannot compete. The actors though are far happier with the modern half of the play than with the ancient. (I agree with Irving Wardle that the modern half seems more ancient, but never mind). At first I put this down to their inexperience with Jacobean verse, and that probably has something to do with it, but it became clear that William Gaskill's production was reining them in for the sake of consistency later.

Middleton's Livia is generally played (and was surely written) as a merry widow; Maggie Steed can give her only the graveyard shadow of wit, so that the well-fucked lady may have something to awaken from. She then takes control and quivers with life. Gary Oldman's Sordido is fairly arresting, but the character - or rather the style for there is nothing else — is a cliche of modern baroque. Simon Russell Beale who sang and clowned beautifully in Look to the Rainbow last year, is effectively giggly as Middleton's Ward and has immense innocent authority as Barker's; only Nigel Davenport as the Duke commands the stage as well. Joanne Whalley was a promising Bianca on the first night, and probably ripened later; her character, though, is squeezed for development: a metaphorical pawn in the first half, a dramatic pawn in the second.

Leantio goes for practically nothing; while Mr Barker's blows for revolution, Middleton's class consciousness breezes out the window.
1986-04-01-brighton-beach-memoirs:
Brighton Beach Memoirs

Brighton Beach Memoirs is, as far as I know, Neil Simon's best play. It is not his funniest, but that works to its advantage. When one breaks up at Mr Simon's wisecracks (as I nearly always do) some guilt usually goes along with the enjoyment. You have to ask yourself would people really come back as snappily as this?" Actually my own, possibly starry-eyed, belief is that in New York they would; sardonic attack, for those who can do it, is the best form of defence. It becomes less convincing, though, when the mannerism takes over the whole of the dialogue and becomes the author's defence rather than the characters'; as Pauline Kael once put it, 'it's not the one-liners that get you down, it's the two-liners.' The Sunshine Boys and The Prisoner of Second Avenue are depressing (at least in their film versions, which are the only way I know them not because their LONDON NOTICES flare Ins Atre 198C subject-matter is dark, but because the author never faces up to how dark it is, and tries to conceal it from himself with mechanical joyless brightness.

It is himself, I'm pretty sure, that he is trying to protect. He doesn't pander to audiences, he panders to himself. Little of this applies to Brighton Beach Memoirs. Most of the gags here are given to the central character, who represents Mr Simon's teenage self, and how else would a precocious gag-man speak? He tells us his story and the story of his family, scraping a living in New York as the depression ends and the war begins. His narrative is the autobiography he is writing; the convention only breaks down when he addresses us as if we were spectators rather than readers, (yes, I know we are, but I don't think he should; it makes him stickily ingratiating.

But it's only a minor irritant). Does he ever have problems. He is forced to eat liver and cabbage, his mother sends him on errands at ten-minute intervals, he has an unsatisfied curiosity about girls, and he worries about masturbating. His older brother, who gives him good but infrequent advice on the last two, is in danger of losing his job. His fatherless cousin wants to quit school and join a Broadway chorus. Her younger sister has asthma, and is a brat. Their mother has very bad eyes, worries at being a burden on the family, and is attrac ted to a drunken Irishman across the street. Her sister, our hero's mother, thinks she should stick to her own kind, or at least stay away from other kids.

("That's what they have gutters for.') That isn't all she worries about. As a matter of fact she worries about everything. Her husband, meanwhile, struggles to support this menage by working day and night: literally. When his night-time employer goes bust he turns to taxi-driving. It is not good for him. Each of these dramas rises to a confrontation, open or subdued; each subsides. The orchestration of all this is masterly, each character and incident in place at the right time, and Michael Rudman's production never misses a beat. Steven Mackintosh holds everything together as the young Simon, and Robert Glenister as the brother does some lovely modulations from fright to defiance. Harry Towb is an underplayed embodiment of paternal authority: authority unsought-for but conscientiously executed.

Mr Towb, by the way, must have played more cabbies than any other living actor, and he is, altogether, pretty obvious casting for this role. But one of Mr Rudman's great qualities is to take chances with actors he trusts; I remember how he extended Harold Innocent in For Services Rendered and Geraldine McEwan in The Browning Version. Here he casts Alison Fiske, usually a very English smoulderer, as an ex-beauty determined to be downtrodden, and is rewarded by a time biding performance that finally explodes. He also permits Frances de la Tour to break the mould of the lewish mother; it may be that she is too obviously intelligent for the role but in underpinning the nagging and the irrationality with nerves and intelligence she gives us a richer character and therefore — since the mother is of course the soul of the household - a richer play.

She has a moment of silent weeping on a staircase, the mask dropped when nobody can see her, that has haunted me for days. But she never betrays the play's comic mode: is actually happier in it — or at least made me happier _than in the heavy-breathing roles she has been playing recently. The big fight in the play is between the two sisters, a contest in self-abnegation simultaneously proclaimed and resented. It is patched up, like all the others, and we leave the already overstretched household preparing to take in any number of refugee relatives in Europe. They will cope. I don't know if this is sentimental, but it is probably true — and less of a jolt here than it was in the darker-toned New York production.

For all I know the real Simon family were more durably miserable than their stage surrogates here. But the fictional image is sturdy enough to survive in its own right; Brighton Beach Memoirs will probably work better for an audience that has never heard of Neil Simon than Long Day's Journey Into Night could ever hope to do for an audience that cared nothing about the real O'Neill. (Funny the chime of names: Neil, O'Neill. And the author's rep here is called Eugene.) The National were justified in presenting it; it has a better chance of survival on the South Bank than in the West End, and it is the most evenly satisfying play by a living author in their current repertoire.

That does not mean that they have to present the sequel Biloxi Blues, Mr Simon's military reminiscences and a play disfigured by self-consciously earnest writing. And the sequel to that, the yet-to-be-seen Broadway Bound, will have to meet sterner standards; the nearer we get to present reality, to Mr Simon the career playwright, the more uncompromisingly honest we will require him to be.

Anyway Weill knew what he was about right through this work; I doubt if Brecht did. Hence his heavy rationalisations afterwards. One trouble with writing a satirical version of The Beggar's Opera is that Gay had written one already. It may be difficult to get a modern audience to see through his highwaymen to the crooked politicians beneath, but there are at least a few explicit lines to make it easier, and there is a lightness of touch, an uncaringness in Gay, that Brecht found hard to emulate. People who acclaim his irony always quote lines like what is the crime of robbing a bank compared to the crime of founding a bank' which isn't ironic at all, just heavy.

There isn't much Brecht can do to Gay's purposefully preposterous ending but underline and expand it; though here at least he has Weill's assistance. Where The Threepenny Opera gains over The Beggar' Opera it is because Weill is a more resourceful composer than Trad. The plot-line of both plays is confused and perfunctory; the coup-de-grace always comes with the last scene between Polly and Lucy: a new development when we would all much rather go home. Scholars of the original work and its offshoots have no cause to complain of the recent programming at the National: Gay and Brecht/ Weill and A Chorus of Disapproval and some would even include Guys and Dolls. (Anyone on for Beggars' Holiday by Duke Ellington and John Latouche?

No, I thought not.) It is clearly an area of work that sets people fantasising. In The Neophiliacs Christopher Booker coined the word 'nyktomorph' to describe the fantasies of violent artistic gratification common in the fifties and sixties. The image of satirical cabaret, as practised in Weimar Berlin, was one he singled out, and certainly one that was much touted by Ken Tynan: something to please the righteous, something in which to rub the noses of the bourgeoisie. Low-life musicals were a new and appealingly subversive form in the 50s; to Mr Shulman (a firebrand critic in his time) The Threeperny Opera must have seemed a successor to Pal Joey. It must at least have seemed a welcome antidote to Salad Days.

And the nyktomorph persists. Critics still expect The Threepenny Opera, a 60-year-old musical, to do something to them. Or at least to do something to someone else, while they have a bit of a gloat. At times, too, Peter Wood's Olivier production seems to be trying. 'What Keeps a Man Alive', the big savage number, is given the works, all downtrodden actors with shaking fists. PROSPECTUS: The Academy Secretary, 30 Clareville Street, London SW7 SAP. (01-370 4154) MAY 1986 But it comes out of nowhere. No context has been created for it. It is at best dutiful, at worst embarrassing. And you may blame Mr Wood, and I do too, but I also blame Brecht.

Because what the text offers us is undigested moralising anger. It is a song about hunger coming out of a story in which nobody has starved. (Peachum's beggars are fakes.) I don't know whether Brecht had the talent for satire; he certainly had not the temperament. When he wants to make a point he makes it, directly. He tells us what to think. Mr Wood's production is another victim (after Saint Joan, The Trojan War Will Not Take Place, Mandragola and other small, interesting plays) of the Olivier stage. It is probably possible to make the show work in so large a space — one hears enticing tales of an expressionist production at New York's Vivian Beaumont, a white elephant of white elephants — but it has not been achieved here.

The thinking, I imagine, was that the Olivier needed to be filled with another hit musical, and here was one with cultural credentials. But it would have had to be made over into another animal, and this has not happened. Mr Wood's production is actually pretty faithful, with no obvious distortions or omissions. (I missed the line about the banks but that was probably my inattentiveness rather than the result of Citicorp sponsorship.) There is for example no softening of Macheath in Tim Curry's performance. Would that there had been. He tries to play Mackie nasty and heartless as required, and doesn't have it in him; so nothing comes over.
