But with this company, to judge from this show and Love for Love, he has been forgetful or unlucky or both. Only two actors have been delivering at full throttle. One is Michael Bryant, who after jigging and jogging through an opening funeral cortege to eye-catching scene-stealing effect, proceeds to establish a punch-drunk, cauliflowereared Crookfingered Take. (That was the role the Bob Peck character was first offered in A Chorus of Disapproval; Mr Bryant suggests that he might have been a happier man had he stuck with it.) The other is Sara Kestelman, whose Mrs Peachum is unfussed and acidulously phrased in speech and song. Stephen Moore as her spouse shouts his laugh-lines which with him is always a sign of desperation; still they do make, with Sally Dexter's Polly, a credibly shabby-genteel menage, and Miss Dexter, who has a lot of singing to do, does it well.

Eve Adam's Jenny in her red dress looks like Georgia Brown in Oliver! and has the twang if not the dynamism. Niall Buggy's fruity Tiger Brown may be inexcusable but I enjoyed it. Barry James probably sings the Moritat very well (I'd certainly expect him to) but the funny funeral cancels him out. The other praised visual set-piece, Macheath's flight over the rooftops, merely holds up the action, and seems borrowed from Mr Wood's production of The Provok'd Wife. Robert David Macdonald's translation is lively, and seems to have inherited whole phrases from Eric Bentley and Marc Blitzstein. Either coincidence or Mr Macdonald has done wisely here for Blitzstein's versions, the abomination of professional Brechtians, are the only singable ones anybody has come up with.

All they need is to be de-bowdlerised, and that task has been thoroughly accomplished here.
1986-08-01-goodbye-columbus:
Goodbye Columbus

Robert Cushman goes to the Ritz to meet a new master of the classic show tune, Michael Feinstein

"IF YOU'RE interested in show music you don't have much outlet in Columbus, Ohio," said Michael Feinstein, over tea in his suite at the Ritz.

This boy from Columbus is the latest in the line of propagandists for the classic show tune to play late-night cabaret in the Ritz dining-room. He wears a tuxedo, plays piano, and sings Porter, Coward and (his speciality) Gershwin. He is not a leathery survivor of the golden-age 1930s. He is 29, and has been a full-time entertainer for only four years. Before that he was an archivist; in a way he still is.

He will be at the Ritz until August 29 after a record-breaking season at the Algonquin Hotel in New York, a trail previously blazed by Julie Wilson and Steve Ross. They share a repertoire, and a standardised sartorial elegance, but their styles are different. Feinstein does not have Julie Wilson's ashen theatrical intensity or the Grande-dame slyness of the late Mabel Mercer or the fizz and drive of Bobby Short. He does share with Ross an appealing boyishness of voice and manner. Ross is the eternal Princeton man, a vocal Scott Fitzgerald. Feinstein suggests more the bright scholarship kid from the Bronx. He has yet to find his own style. In the meantime his strengths are enthusiasm, musicianship and knowledge.

Father sang as an amateur with local bands; mother had been a tap-dancer. When he was five they bought a piano. "I started playing it by ear -- to everyone's amazement. I played Do Re Mi from The Sound of Music. My mother said, 'When did your father teach you that?'; I said I'd taught myself, and got sent to my room for lying."

His contemporaries of course were listening to rock, and he grew up "a lonely, isolated child" which only pushed him further into show music. By the time he was 10 he knew who George Gershwin was, and what he'd written; the rest of the pantheon followed. He had to know who had written what, and for which musical. He still collects this information, and details it in performance. This sets him apart from most singers, who don't know anything.

He began his opening show at the Ritz with a statement of purpose: a song called Wanna Sing A Show Tune. I thought this self-conscious -- I'd rather he'd just gone ahead and done it -- but there is something to be said for a lyric that rhymes "stylish" with "Kurt Weillish." But then he was on to a totally forgotten antiquity called China (America's congratulations to the old country on becoming a democracy) that was captivating, and made me wish he would do more comedy songs.

His set was heavy on ballads, some of them throbbed too much, but on one, Oscar Levant's Blame It On My Youth, he was truly touching, finding the vulnerability the cabaret medium needs. There was a medley from Of Thee I Sing, full of verve, and a lot of other Gershwin, including famous songs with unfamiliar lines. I never knew before that "'S Wonderful" contained the couplet, "Say, what's all this dizziness/I thought that I came here on bus-i-ness," or that How Long Has This Been Going On climaxed with the declaration, "Heads may roll but bless my soul." In both cases I was delighted.

Feinstein has access to this classified information because he spent his early twenties working for Ira Gershwin, George's lyricist and elder brother, at his home in Hollywood. First he was engaged to catalogue Ira's record collection; then, as his employer realised the scope of his knowledge of the Gershwin oeuvre, he became his full-time archivist, friend and "the son he never had."

And of course through the Gershwins he encountered other musical greats. ("I always seemed to meet them a few days before they died.") He also met Liza Minnelli, a Gershwin god-daughter and his second great patron. She threw parties for him, opened doors. On his first night at the Ritz she sent him a gargantuan first-night bouquet that now dominates his room.

Ira Gershwin, Feinstein says, "had an endearing, whimsical quality." Like his songs? "Exactly." It's that innocently sophisticated delight in the choice of words that Feinstein communicates in his singing of Gershwin songs.

He's chosen his moment well. Next year is the fiftieth anniversary of George's death, and already the record albums are pouring out. Porgy and Bess is thrilling Glyndebourne audiences with the forbidden aroma of show music. Feinstein himself is planning a book setting down Gershwin anecdotes hitherto unpublished. Goodbye Columbus; hello world.
1987-06-04-casting-a-critical-eye-over-a:
Jonathan Miller, announcing a brave new season of plays for his first year at the Old Vic, took the opportunity to inveigh against the rest of the British theatre. "Bureaucratised" was his word for the subsidised wing. The West End, where four plays closed only last week, was a wasteland, governed by the untutored whims of "Attila the tourist". Actually the situation is even bleaker than he describes. I am not at all sure, though, that any individual, even Attila, is to blame.

Nobody could accuse Dr Miller of pandering to the Philistines. Planners looking for untried classics to fill up their seasons, or even fans wondering what theatrical cadavers they would most like to see resurrected, are apt to throw up their hands and fall back on the same old Chekhovs, Ibsens, and Shaws. Dr Miller has come up with seven titles of which only one could possibly be called familiar. And that one, being The Tempest, hardly counts. Shakespeare is allowed to break everybody's rules.

For the rest, we have a musical, Candide, which I have seen in New York and Edinburgh, but never in London; and plays by Racine, Ostrovsky, Lenz, Chapman and N. F. Simpson, that I have never seen at all. And I've been around.

It's a cheering catalogue, made more so by Dr Miller's assertion that the season only needs to play to a modest sounding 60 per cent of capacity to break even. "There is," he said, "no way we can make ourselves millionaires out of this theatre." But then his backer, Ed Mirvish, already is a millionaire. He rescued the Royal Alexandra, which is Toronto's most beautiful theatre, and is doing the same for the Vic, which is ours. A few years ago he saved its body. Now he's working on its soul. Dr Miller's tribute to his "pragmatic philanthropy" is, if anything, an understatement.

Some of Miller's pronouncements are more questionable. To declare in advance that none of your productions will transfer to the West End sounds to me like giving hostages to misfortune. True, a West End management is not that likely to bid for Bussy d'Ambois - not, at least, without Michael Caine in the leading role - but it is possible to imagine the Shaftesbury Avenue boys knocking on the door at Waterloo Road and asking if Candide can come out to play. If they do, and if they ask very nicely, will Dr Miller really say no? And if so, why?

One reason may be that he needs something to fight against. He has to construct a demonology. I imagine that he sees bureaucracy and commercialism as aspects of the same phenomenon and would point to the National Theatre and RSC's string of West End transfers as proof. Some years ago Lindsay Anderson started a classical repertory company actually in the West End and used the occasion to proclaim the virtues of the commercial theatre (against which he had been inveighing all his working life) and to deplore the feather-bedding of the subsidised theatre (which he had always supported). Funny how your view of other people's work is governed by the conditions under which you yourself happen to be operating at the time. As it happens, Mr Anderson's company speedily found itself playing a straight run of a Ben Travers's farce, and then expired, thereby confirming everybody's worst fears about the West End. A question-mark hangs over the more recent attempt to buck the system of another distinguished director, John Dexter.

On the other hand... the success of The House of Bernarda Alba, a play of which few West End punters could previously have heard, has been hailed as a sign that a play of quite menacing seriousness can survive in the West End. And so it can, if it has rapturous notices and Glenda Jackson. Miss Jackson can sell almost anything. Television stars, the West End has been discovering, lack the magic, maybe because on their own turf each of them is only half a star. Peter Bowles doesn't sell without Penelope Keith, or George Cole without Dennis Waterman, or Mel Smith without Griff Rhys-Jones. Les Liaisons Dangereuses, the remaining class contender, has no stars but it does have rapturous notices, plus sex. It was also, for more than a year, an acclaimed play in a small theatre that nobody could get into. One of the subsidised theatre's attractions for a commercial producer, greater even than the money it saves him, is the expectation it creates.

That leaves the mega-musicals about which there is nothing to be said except that they run because people enjoy them. This may sometimes be perplexing, but it is not sinister. I cannot see that anybody's pleasure in Les Liaisons can reasonably be damaged by the existence round the corner of Les Miserables.

It all means, though, that there are few categories of shows with any chance of West End success. Dr Miller blames it on the tourists ("the Huns of modern Europe"), but this is unfair. Tourists can only patronise the shows that producers offer them and most producers would be far happier to play to a more reliable indigenous audience. The problem is that it does not exist, or at least not in sufficient numbers.

Does it matter? Probably not, except to those of us hoping in one way or another to make a living out of it. The average theatre-goer does not care much about "the state of the theatre". He only wants there to be a few shows on that theme which he would like to see, and it cannot matter much to him whether they are located in Islington, Chelsea or the Strand.

Or, of course, on the South Bank or in the Barbican. The National Theatre's repertory is, all of a sudden, as varied and as well performed as anyone could expect. The RSC is known to be in desperate financial trouble, but this does not seem to affect the monotonously high standards it achieves on its smaller stages. The big ones are more problematic, apparently resistant to any play that is not either a set text or a vehicle for Jeremy Irons. The directorate has been publicly flagellating itself for its choice of non-Shakespeare plays at the Barbican, but they actually looked perfectly reasonable on paper. A few years ago there would have been a decent audience for them. The awful truth may be that there is now almost nothing that a large audience really wants to see. I do not like to think about this very much. Neither, I imagine, do most people in the theatre. But it must give us all the odd, unguarded sleepless night.

So Jonathan Miller's instinct - to retire to a promontory in the Waterloo Road and fortify it - may be the correct one. He will be putting on minority plays for short runs on, presumably, modest budgets. That may be the best that anyone can do. Unless they want to get rich.
1987-12-24-romancin-the-one-i-love: Indefinite run. Box office: (416) 872-5555.ROMANCIN' THE ONE I LOVEWinter Garden TheatreThere is something unwieldy about the title Romancin' the One I Love; its overlong and somewhat tautological. (I mean, who else are you gonna be romancin; unless of course you're two-timin'?)That makes it a good fit for the show itself, which is groaningly unwieldy -- a scene-for-scene enactment of The Taming of the Shrew, with a couple of dozen songs thrown in -- and is also a tautology in itself: Its a Shrew musical that acts as if it didnt know that there was -- indeed, still is -- a show called Kiss Me Kate, drawn from the same source. Quite often in Romancin', we seem to be hearing cues for songs that we already know, and it's frustrating when new ones turn up, especially when ... but Ill get to that.Mind you, I read recently that someone in the United States is writing a musical based on the stories of Damon Runyon, thereby going head to head with Guys and Dolls; by that yardstick, the hubris of John R. Briggs, creator of the present show, seems like modesty itself. Romancin takes both plots of The Shrew -- the subduing of Katharine the fierce by the upstart Petruchio, and the wooing of her younger sister by three competing suitors, most of them in disguise -- and sets it down in 1930s Miami Beach.The show starts with everybody silhouetted in Art Deco poses, prior to going into a welcoming company number that does something to set up the basic situation. One of the crowd turns out to be Kate herself (she likes to be called Katharine, but her creators put her in her place by calling her Kate in the program) but we hardly notice her; this must be the weakest first entrance ever inflicted on the leading lady of a musical comedy.Anyway, the whole sequence turns out to be superfluous, since the identical ground is immediately gone over again, courtesy of Shakespeare's own exposition. Or of some of it; here, as throughout, the harder Elizabethan words are replaced by modern slang, not all of it native to the Thirties. This is probably meant to be funny.If the dialogue aims at pastiche, the score, by Briggs and Dennis West, is outright nostalgia. The 1930s were the greatest decade of American popular music, and if you're going to use its styles now, you have to use them, comment on them in some way; otherwise youre simply competing with the incomparable.All this score conveys is a fervent desire to put the clock back: understandable but vain. The songs arent actually that bad; it's just that they all seem to have been written at least once before. The words are mostly after Cole Porter (Kate's Nobody Loves Me is a list-song uncomfortably close to Porters Nobodys Chasing Me), the music mostly after Gershwin (the title song has the impudence to quote directly from I Got Rhythm). Kate's big torch song, My Attitude, crammed with blue notes and low-down throbbings, is after everybody; it seems to have been written 17 times before. It's also dramatically destructive. She sings it while waiting at the church for her non-appearing bridegroom, and its all about how much she really and secretly loves him. Meanwhile the text, which suggests nothing of the kind, is still chugging incorrigibly along around her.This is a musical of The Taming of the Shrew thats plainly embarrassed by The Taming of the Shrew.Plenty of straight productions -- most straight productions -- manage to suggest an instant attraction between hero and heroine. The play's appeal is that it's about the coming together of a pair of outsiders too good for the society in which they find themselves. But they neither of them give in that easily. In this version, Petruchio overhears Kate moaning another love song, is touched, and gives up on the taming idea altogether. The final notorious wager on Kates obedience is played as a pre-arranged put-up job, thereby destroying any dramatic point it might have. It would be better to cut it altogether; this is, after all, an adaptation.The couple signal their love-at-first-sightedness by doing an energetic Fred-and-Ginger routine, dancing over sofas. But thats not enough to give them chemistry.Camilla Scott's Kate is less a characterization than a prolonged display of good sportsmanship, while Brad Aspel's slick bantamweight Petruchio is charmless to the point of being repulsive. Hes played as an out-of-work song-and-dance man, which makes it seem very strange that Kates mercenary father would accept him as an eligible suitor. It does mean, though, that he can take her home, not to his country seat, but to a New York rehearsal hall, where his troupe, though presumably unemployed, are still hard at work.We'll keep her awake," he says of his bride, "by rehearsing our closing number -- at which promise of yet another generic routine I, case-hardened though I am, heard myself whimpering Oh, no!"Sergio Trujillo's musical staging is a complete compendium of choreographic cliches, but he does not, in fairness, have much to go on. Supporting performances, mostly executed with an air of gamely desperate professionalism, are similarly stereotyped; Grumio (Lloyd Culbreath) is the heros black hoofing-and-gospelling sidekick; Hortensio (Larry Mannell) is the cheerful, brow-mopping, all- purpose second banana; Gremio (Gerry Salsberg) is a stock rich Jew, breaking into Hava Nagila when he thinks hes got the girl; and Tranio (Derek Marshall) is a tireless impressionist who -- after flying at Groucho, Cagney and Jerry Lewis -- settles for imitating Tony Curtis imitating Cary Grant in Some Like It Hot. Bianca (Melissa Thomson) is your standard cute minx.In one of the show's token gestures to feminism, all the women get behind Kate to sing a man-defying song called I Don't Have to Listen to You; but it goes nowhere, since Shakespeares Kate stands for no one, male or female. (And no one, which is their loss, will stand for her.)Kiss Me Kate, which has an elaborate play-within-a-play framework, is far more cavalier with its source (it actually makes it difficult to follow the Shakespearean plot) but, by virtue of being a good show with its own identity, ends up being more respectful of it.Its certainly no accident that makers of musicals keep returning to Shakespeare's comedies, and especially to his earliest comedies; between them, Shakespeare and Broadway-Hollywood are responsible for most of our modern conception of romance. This, with especial reference to Kenneth Branagh's new and (I think) unfairly maligned movie version of Loves Labours Lost, is a subject worthy of further exploration.IllustrationBlack & White Photo: David Hawe / Borrowing from everyone: Brad Aspel and Camilla Scott in Romancin' the One I Love. ;Word count: 1134
1988-04-26-demon-drive:
Demon drive

The star of Ziegfeld has the right training for his challenging part. Robert Cushman weighs him up

FOR ME, Len Cariou will always be a homicidal maniac. That is not a personal aspersion. It means I am haunted by his New York performance as Sweeney Todd in the Stephen Sondheim musical. Sondheim's demon barber is a man much wronged for whom revenge is the force that drives him to slit his customers' throats. Cariou's feeling on approaching the role was "Thank God I've done Lear."

He is about the only actor whose career alternates between leads in Broadway musicals and major classical roles, usually at repertory theatres in America or in his native Canada. Florenz Ziegfeld, the role that brings him to London for the first time, is not exactly in the King Lear or even the Sweeney Todd class. All the same, it is quite a weight to carry.

To begin with, the musical Ziegfeld has cost about £4 million to put on at the Palladium, and to be the centrepiece of something so expensive is a responsibility.

Cariou, in the role of Broadway's legendary impresario, is on stage almost throughout. The show purports to be Ziegfeld's autobiography, his story as he would have told it had it been one of his own shows, festooned with showgirls and sequins.

Of course nobody's life really resembles a spectacular revue, and in the end reality catches up with him. In Cariou's words, "He's told, 'OK, you've done all right, you've more or less stuck to the truth, but that's enough.' He's interwoven so intricately with the show, it's like reading your own obituary."

Ziegfeld was obsessive, getting through money and mistresses as relentlessly as Sweeney got through throats. It's the girls rather than the gelt that the show focuses on. We see Flo with two wives, two floozies and a secretary: a representative sample.

Along the way Cariou gets to sing a lot of standard songs: from A Pretty Girl Is Like a Melody, which historically has very strong Ziegfeld connections, to I'm Always Chasing Rainbows, which has no Ziegfeld connections whatsoever.

Singing is where it all began for Cariou: "I was born a singer. My mother was a singer. The Irish side of my family were all musically involved."

He started in the musical theatre but quickly went legitimate, somewhat aided by geography. He grew up in Winnipeg, where, in the late 1950s, a brilliant Hungarian-born director, John Hirsch, was starting Canada's first major regional playhouse -- the Manitoba Theatre Centre. Hirsch let him play his first Shakespeares, Petruchio and Caliban, but also advised him, "Don't ever give up musicals."

In the early Sixties Cariou did three seasons at Stratford, Ontario, but found himself "pretty low on the totem-pole", unlikely to get the leads he coveted. Stratford's then director, Michael Langham, whom Cariou now rates "far and away the best Shakespearean director alive", told him: "There's no way you can play Prince Hal."

But Stratford also had an operatic arm and Cariou was able to spend a pleasant season ("the first time in my career I had the leisure to play golf") appearing in Mahagonny.

From there followed an invitation to cross the border to act at the Guthrie Theatre in Minneapolis; he played Orestes in The Oresteia for Tyrone Guthrie himself. Since 1966 his career has been US-based.

He was at Stratford, Connecticut playing Henry V when the call came to audition for the musical Applause, a vehicle for Lauren Bacall. He had a conventional leading-man role and displayed not only personality but one of the most pleasant voices on Broadway. He left after 13 months to return to rep. "Betty Bacall couldn't understand it. She said, 'Why are you leaving this job?' "

Hal Prince, after seeing Applause, told Cariou: "You're the best leading man I've ever seen." That was in 1969. In 1973 Prince got round to honouring that opinion and cast him in the male lead in Sondheim's A Little Night Music. From that followed Sweeney Todd. "Hal told me it was written with me in mind. I don't know if Stephen would agree."

Whatever the case, Cariou sang and acted it with a fierce lucidity that allowed the passion and fury and sour wit of the score to shine as if through clear glass. I thought it was a great tragic performance.

He has since returned to Stratford, Ontario as a star, playing a Coriolanus stronger on blunt anger than patrician pride. He also directed his old home theatre in Winnipeg for a season, but found his energies diverted from administration into a couple of whacking leading roles.

He wants to go on directing occasionally, but running theatres for the time being is out. "I'm an acting animal."

Ziegfeld opens at the London Palladium tonight.
1988-05-02-ziegfeld-would-have-loved-thi:
Ziegfeld would have loved this Ziegfeld Len Cariou moves on

Monday, May 02, 1988

ROBERT CUSHMAN

London ENGLAND -- BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail LONDON Len Cariou is playing another obsessive. The actor from Manitoba, whose career has included Coriolanus at Stratford and Sweeney Todd on Broadway, made his West End of London debut last week at the world-famous Palladium in the title role of Ziegfeld, a musical biography of the United States most celebrated showman.

Florenz Ziegfeld was known for the opulence of his decor and the quality and quantity of his chorus girls, and London producer Harold Fielding has spent $8-million in an attempt to emulate him.

To get back this kind of money, a show has to appeal to the coach-and- tourist trade. No one would claim Ziegfeld is attempting to compete with Shakespeare or even with Sondheim. So, for a leading actor who has triumphed in both, what was the attraction?

"Ziegfeld was a very interesting character. The way we're doing it, he tries to tell the story of his life as if it were one of his own shows. And for most of the evening he gets away with it," Cariou said between rehearsals. However, nobody's life really resembles a spectacular Broadway revue from the palmy decades before the Depression, so in the end reality catches up with him. In Carious words, Hes told, okay, you've done all right, you've more or less stuck to the truth, but thats enough.

The show keeps Carious Ziegfeld on stage almost throughout. "He's interwoven so intricately with the show, the role's about as long as Sweeney Todd. Its also like reading your own obituary."

The historical Ziegfeld went through money and mistresses relentlessly, but the show passes lightly over the financial problems, concentrating on the women - a course that Ziegfeld, whose self-proclaimed mission was Glorifying the American Girl, would probably have approved.

He also did a certain amount to glorify the American songwriter. Jerome Kern, Irving Berlin and George Gershwin were among those whose services he commanded, although he was somewhat cavalier in the way he treated them. (One Broadway historian said: He must have had a taste for good writing, just no interest in it.) The show Ziegfeld draws eclectically on the music of the period. It allows Cariou to exercise his lyric baritone on numbers ranging from A Pretty Girl is Like a Melody - the theme song of the Ziegfeld Follies - to Im Always Chasing Rainbows, which has no Ziegfeld connection whatsoever. Of course, the real Ziggy is unlikely ever to have sung a note, but there is such a thing as poetic licence.

There were rumors that the almost operatic demands of Sweeney Todd had destroyed Cariou's voice, and they certainly took a toll. "The only way to rest your vocal cords is to rest them - completely - and there's no way I could do that."

He was heard to croak in his subsequent Broadway musical, the short- lived Dance a Little Closer, but he has recuperated. The rumors of my voices death, he says, choosing his words with dry deliberation, "have been greatly over-produced."

This is just as well, since there are many who would agree with Hal Princes estimate that Cariou is the best leading man I've ever seen as far as musicals are concerned. Certainly he ranks with Alfred Drake and the late Robert Preston. Prince, Broadway's leading producer-director, paid Cariou that compliment in person after witnessing a run-through of Applause, the show in which Cariou made his Broadway debut opposite Lauren Bacall.

Cariou was gratified, of course, but as Prince hadnt introduced himself it was some time before the importance of the accolade came home to him. "Somebody said, That was Hal,' and I said, 'Hal who? " That was in 1969. Cariou heard nothing more from Prince until 1973, when he was asked to audition for a subsidiary role in Princes production of Stephen Sondheim's A Little Night Music: So he's a man of his word anyway, even if he does take his time. He was then offered the male lead, a 50-year-old lawyer. When he protested that he was too young for the part, Prince said crisply, "Youre an actor, arent you?"

I get tightened up like a corkscrew at auditions, Cariou says, who these days refuses to do them. Having become, as he puts it, "an international twinkle-twinkle," he no longer has to. These days, if somebody wants to know if I can sing, I say, 'Send them an album.'  His role in the Prince-Sondheim Sweeney Todd was, he believes, written with him in mind. "Hal told me it was. Stephen has never said."

The legendary barber of Londons Fleet Street became in Sondheims version a figure of tragedy rather than melodrama: a wronged man whose justified grievances against society turn him into a creature of homicidal madness. Cariou's feeling on approaching the role was, Thank God I've done Lear.

That of course is the other side of Carious career. Americans regard him as a musical star who regularly takes inexplicable salary cuts to play the dramatic classics in regional repertory theatres. (When he left Applause after 13 months, he says, "Betty Bacall couldnt understand it. She said, 'Why are you leaving this job?' ") Canadians, though, think of him as a classical actor who makes occasional lucrative forays into song and dance.

Historically, the Americans may be nearer the truth. Cariou began as a singer. I was born a singer. My mother was a singer. All the Irish side of my family were musically involved. I started in the musical theatre, but I quickly went into legit. I discovered the classical theatre.

Winnipeg, where he grew up, was a good place to discover it. "In the late fifties," Cariou recalls, there were not an awful lot of professional actors there. But John Hirsch wanted to make a professional theatre there, and he founded the Manitoba Theatre Centre. Cariou "got the bug, and jumped in. But Hirsch, who was my mentor, also told me, Dont ever give up doing musicals. You have a natural bent for it.' " Under Hirsch's influence, he progressed in the early sixties to Stratford, Ont., where he joined the companys operatic arm and spent a pleasant, relaxed season in a single show. It was, he remembers, "the first time in my career I had the leisure to play golf."

Since 1966, his career has been U.S.-based. Douglas Campbell was running the Guthrie Theatre in Minneapolis in the sixties. He had seen Carious work at Stratford, and asked him to join. Cariou muses on how easy it was for actors to cross the border in those days, and how hard it would be now for an actor who was less than an international star.

His last role was Teddy Roosevelt in the musical Teddy and Alice, which opened and closed in very short order earlier this year. His own notices, though, were excellent, and the invitation to play Ziegeld followed immediately.

It means a chance to work with Joe Layton, the top director and choreographer whose successes include two previous showman bios, George M. and Barnum. Layton believes in giving the old razzle-dazzle and Ziegfeld is very much his show. For Cariou, it's a high-kicking step into the West End.
1988-05-07-crawford-is-one-fantastic-pha:
NEW YORK - Michael Crawford gets to his Broadway dressing-room at four every afternoon, 3 1/2 hours before curtain time. The 46-year- old actor is known for his devotion to his craft, but in this case, his daily vigil has little to do with easing himself spiritually or psychologically into the character. Playing the title-role in the wildly successful The Phantom Of The Opera, he needs all that time to have his make-up applied.

Compared with some other parts he has played - Barnum, for example, which turned him into a singing acrobat - the Phantom is not physically demanding. The character emerges occasionally from the recesses of the Paris Opera to terrify a recalcitrant producer, abduct a diva, sing an aria or two on his own; and his face is obscured by his elaborate disfigurement. Crawford has to do a lot of his acting with a single visible eye. The vocal demands are another thing; this, in keeping with its setting, is Andrew Lloyd Webber's lushest score. Surprisingly, though, Crawford does not regard the music as the role's principal challenge.

"The main challenge is the emotional involvement," he said, between blows from the powder puff. "It isn't necessary but it's the way I like to play it."

Phenomenal success

Some of this may be actor talk, but it does connect with the phenomenal success of the show, in London and New York. Despite its menacing title and reputation as a horror movie, Phantom makes its great appeal as a romantic musical. Some people have complained that it isn't especially scary, and Crawford agrees with them.

"It doesn't frighten me, either. I found Lon Chaney in the movie very frightening, but not very romantic. I couldn't copy his appearance; you can't pad your mouth out and sing." What goes for the character goes also for the special effects: notable the chandelier the Phantom sends crashing from the real theatre ceiling to intimidate those who dare to thwart him. As Crawford admits, it does not and cannot fall fast enough to be really terrifying: "there are safety regulations."

In the main, though, audiences at Phantom are not there to feel threatened, but to feel moved, especially by Crawford when his monster loses the girl he adores to the inevitable handsome young aristocrat. "By the end, the audience have forgiven him everything, and they all cry at the end when he just says, I love you. We've all felt like that, because we've all lost somebody at some time. We recognize that cry of anguish."

Crawford first heard about the show four years ago when he met Webber at the last London preview of the composer's previous musical Starlight Express. "He said to me, 'We must do The Phantom Of The Opera together.' I said, wonderful. Then I didn't see him again for a year and a half."

Quasi-operatic singing

As always with Webber, songs were released on record long before the show reached the stage, and Crawford noted that on disc the role of the Phantom was sung by rock singer Steve Harley. "I thought, well, he must have got my name wrong." However, Webber tends not to get things wrong and Crawford got the part.

An actor's life, especially in rehearsal, tends to reflect that of the character he's playing, and Crawford's existence became rather solitary. "I used to rehearse all by myself in the theatre boiler-room. I didn't meet anyone." He settled down to learn how to make an impact in a star role that actually occupies only 30 minutes playing-time, and how to do most of his acting with his cloak and, of course, do the most wih his voice.

He needed a more legitimate voice. "Every time Andrew heard I could do something, he wrote something else more difficult." It took Crawford months to learn, but he ended up singing in a quasi- operatic manner six evenings a week and two matinees.

His Phantom vocalizing has taken him back to the beginnings of his career. Shades of Benjamin Britten hover over the end of Webber's score, and it was Britten with his children's work Let's Make An Opera, who gave schoolboy Crawford his first experience of performing. "I got a taste for it. I liked being rewarded with people laughing when they were meant to - instead of being beaten, as I was during the day." School, acting and singing apart, was not a happy experience: the only place where Crawford has felt no inclination to work hard.

Big break

He made his escape, ironically, into schools broadcasting for BBC radio; starting at age 15, he did about 500 of these educational stints, gaining most of his own education in the process. He did another Britten opera (Noye's Fludde), professionally this time, and worked with the composer's English Opera Group. But he was also moving away from opera - into repertory theatres and TV soaps. His big acting break came in the London production of Neil Simon's Come Blow Your Horn, as an awkward young man trying to leave his Jewish- American home.

The role established a Crawford persona: shy, youthful, gangling. This was perpetuated in the mid-'60s in two Richard Lester movies: The Knack and A Funny Thing Happened On The Way To The Forum. In the latter, his first musical, he was officially the romantic lead, but in Forum the lovers are there to look ridiculous, which in ancient Roman costume, isn't too hard. The movie turns up on TV quite often, causing Crawford to writhe a lot. "If only I didn't have to look at my legs in that toga. It's so humiliating, those legs."

Barnum, which he played for four years in two separate London runs, was a landmark for Crawford. Playing the master showman and con man - "the prince of humbug" - was a decisive break from the line of gawky young men that had remained more or less unbroken since Come Blow Your Horn.

"Gormless" they call them in England and Crawford had become the paragon of gormlessness: a latter-day Harold Lloyd, his misadventures growing more outlandishly acrobatic with every role and culminating in 1974 in his first stage musical, Billy, based on Billy Liar.

Aggressively versatile

American musicals are famously dependent on dymamic leading ladies, from Ethel Merman on. Britain has always favored leading men, and in the last few years - the commercial glory years for British musicals - those men have been Tommy Steele, Jim Dale and Michael Crawford. They are, in a terrible but unavoidable showbiz phrase "all round entertainers," aggressively versatile. They are singers, hoofers, comedians, actors; their collective background runs from pop music to classical drama.

Of the three Steele is the most effervescent, the eternal Cockney kid, and Dale the most raffish; he created the role of Barnum on Broadway. His Barnum was far tougher than Crawford's and therefore more credible, but Crawford was more popular with audiences.

He is unquenchably motherable; and now, with sympathy pulsating through his vocal chords, he makes you weep for the Phantom Of The Opera. But nobody gets to the top through being a jellyfish. On stage, Crawford is appealing, off it he is courteous and thoughtful. But in neither environment is there any doubt of the iron - or the terrifying single-mindedness - beneath.
1988-07-25-night-of-passion:
Night of passion

Robert Cushman reports from Ontario on the Shakespearefest

THE BEST Canadian theatre, rather to my surprise, happens in small venues and is off-the-wall comic. But prestige and expectation still reside, as they must, in the two classical festivals: the flagship Shakespearefest at Stratford, Ontario, and the more gemütlich affair at Niagara-on-the-Lake, where the patron saint is Bernard Shaw.

Stratford's current director is John Neville, the Old Vic's golden juvenile of the 1950s and a buccaneering director of regional theatres -- first in England, then in Canada -- for the last two decades. This is his penultimate season.

Official secrecy surrounds the choice of his successor, but most local money is on the return of Robin Phillips, who ran the place dynamically if unevenly for most of the seventies.

Whether or not Phillips returns, Neville's regime has had an inescapable feeling of interregnum.

He has restored the theatre's financial fortunes and recaptured some of its departed talents. One of them is Phillips himself, who has been running a training battalion, known as the Young Company. This is housed in the Third Stage, smallest of Stratford's trio of theatres.

Its inaugural production this year is Twelfth Night, staged with the emphasis on romantic self-deception -- but treated sympathetically rather than satirically for once. True, Orsino (Kevin Gulahi) begins the play on a masseur's table but this may suggest virility as well as languor, and he balances these qualities beautifully.

Olivia is a similarly full-blooded conception; at the height of her passion for Viola/Cesario, this lady lies down and offers herself to him/her. This is startling, but we do need to be reminded that there is actual sex behind this play's formality.

The contrast is accentuated by Phillips's choice of an 18th century setting: a mixture of the mellow and the sedate, with Malvolio played as a majordomo imported from Japan. Oriental impassivity unfortunately spills over into uninflected dullness. There is, though, a sardonically vigorous Toby Belch and a very funny duel scene: an episode scorned by a recent generation of puritan directors.

It is heartening that a director who might have overdosed on Shakespearian comedies still has things to say about them.

This Twelfth Night is ahead of recent RSC attempts but behind Cheek by Jowl's.

  

The two plays with which Tyrone Guthrie inaugurated the theatre in 1953 have been revived this year, in unluckily tame productions.

Richard III is a stolidly archaeological affair, incongruously framing a super-cool Crookback by the current white hope, a slim and dapper actor called Colm Feore. He has too little weight, the production too much.

It keeps tumbling into hearty conventionality, ending with the victorious faction shouting, uncanonically: "Long live Richmond, King of England" -- a solecism on any number of levels.

All's Well That Ends Well, directed by Peter Moss on the proscenium Avon stage, is given (as in Guthrie's and Trevor Nunn's productions) an American Civil War setting, though it was not until Confederate uniforms started swaggering through the Tuscan wars that I got the reference. The stepped classical facade that dominated the stage was meant to be the Tara of Scarlett O'Hara; I had taken it for the British Museum. I had also taken Helena (Lucy Peacock) for a Charlotte Brontë governess.

Bertram's apparent seduction of Diana was played in her bedroom: fine -- we appreciated the psychological reality that underpins the Elizabethan bed-trick.

But the scene was prolonged so that we saw Helena creep in to take Diana's place. Fatal: theatrical convention cannot bear that much reality (and besides, it's supposed to take place in pitch darkness).

There was a time -- Guthrie's time -- when fluidity was the watchword of Shakespearian production. These days we pause to change scene as frequently as did the Victorians. The Stratford first-night audience is very occasion-conscious and it loves to applaud. So it clapped at the end of each scene.

That, when the show is going less than wonderfully, can begin to seem ghoulish. Fortunately, the remaining Shakespeare opening gave cause for applause.

  

Richard Monette, a noted Canadian actor, made an auspicious directing debut on the festival stage with The Taming of the Shrew. He peopled the stage with irresistible bravura, pitching his tent in the Italy of the 1950s. This was evoked with a mixture of Zeffirelli carnival, Bogdanov brutalism, and the kind of ice-cream extravagance that I recall from Frank Dunlop's production of Scapino: a super-jape under Martini parasols. Some comment on machismo is plainly intended but the main business is pleasure.

It doesn't quite fit, however, with the director's unusually lyrical view of the two central characters. Colm Feore's Petruchio, though a dab hand at beating up servants, is an introspective sex-warrior genuinely uncertain of the best way to tame a shrew, and in love to boot. Goldie Semple's Kate does a brisk about-turn half-way through the play, so as to match him in warmth; earlier on, however, she has been a strident virago. Hints in the text that Kate's home-life fully justified her tantrums are inflated literally beyond beliefs. Bianca, the spoiled and subtly exploitative younger sister, is here a vulgar dumb blonde who would not fool the most credulous parent or suitor. But the show does buzz.

  

Stratford's non-Shakespeare repertory has always seemed pretty arbitrary. This year they celebrate the T. S. Eliot centenary with Murder In The Cathedral, given an appropriately elocutionary production by David William. Everything is lucid. Nicholas Pennell's Becket fights a good and even gripping fight with his Tempters; the four disinterested knights are engaging as they discuss how much against the grain it goes to kill an archbishop. This is a Brechtian scene before the fact; the murderers attempt to implicate us in their crime and we are supposed to consider their arguments and reject them.

Actually, the play's spiritual snobbery -- its unqualified endorsement of its hero's martyrdom -- becomes so oppressive that we're likely to defy the author, do the knights' bidding, and endorse their verdict of "suicide while of unsound mind".

In the early stages the production tries unwisely to individualise the Women of Canterbury, which is not convincing, over the hieratic rhythms, which are.

But they come together at the end and so, consequently, does the play.

Murder is doing brilliantly at the box-office so, predictably, is My Fair Lady. Stratford's big money-maker last year was Cabaret; in Canada as in Britain classical companies turn avidly to musicals. This one, with the orchestra sounding as if it were being piped in from the next province, is an actors' show. Nobody can quite make the songs work -- make them, that is, the dramatic forces of the evening.
1988-07-30-the-impossible-william-shakes:
WILLIAM SHAKESPEARE: A TEXTUAL COMPANION BY STANLEY WELLS AND GARY TAYLOR WITH JOHN JOWETT AND WILLIAM MONTGOMERY Oxford, 1,250 pages, $137.50

The impossible William Shakespeare

WILLIAM SHAKESPEARE: A TEXTUAL COMPANION BY STANLEY WELLS AND GARY TAYLOR WITH JOHN JOWETT AND WILLIAM MONTGOMERY Oxford, 1,250 pages, $137.50

Saturday, July 30, 1988

ROBERT CUSHMAN

REVIEW BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Shakespeare's first editors were actors. Chances are, they were not very good actors. Certainly they fell on hard times and were obliged to support themselves by putting together texts of Shakespeare's plays - the so- called "Bad Quartos" - based on their memories of appearing in them. This meant that their own characters' speeches were reproduced with intermittent fidelity, while everybody else's came out as wild paraphrase.

It sounds a hell of a way to make a living, but as the editors of the Oxford Textual Companion remark, "Mere impossibility has seldom deterred human need, greed and ingenuity." They themselves, at the opposite extreme of scholarship and assiduity from the Elizabethan textual pirates, are still their heirs. They too, attempting to assemble a definitive edition of a writer 400 years dead and unconcerned with the publication of his work even when alive, are attempting the impossible.

In Shakespeare's own day the Bad Quartos were followed by authorized "Good Quartos," issued in self-defence by the theatres that owned the plays. The availability of plays in print was generally believed to harm the box office (today, play texts are marketed in the lobbies alongside the T-shirts and the original cast album), but the managers obviously figured that if anybody was going to make a profit on this kind of deal, they might as well do it themselves. Finally - well, no, not finally, far from it, but eventually - in 1623, seven years after Shakespeare's death, two of his fellow actors redeemed the honor of their profession by seeing through the press a one-volume collected edition of 36 plays, the First Folio. And that should have been that.

Unfortunately the Good Quartos and the First Folio, each with a claim to authenticity, repeatedly contradict one another. Besides, seventeenth- century printing was messy, primitive and prone to error. Spelling and punctuation have changed. The twin tasks of deciding what Shakespeare actually wrote and presenting it in readable form have entertained centuries of subsequent editors.

The actors left the game early. Shakespearean editing became the hobby of gentleman amateurs or, more frequently, a sideline for professional literary men of the stature of Alexander Pope or Dr. Johnson. They in turn have been supplanted by the new academic industry. Over the past 100 years, top-level Shakespearean editing has been an Oxford-and-Cambridge sport, like the boat race.

Cambridge University Press pulled strongly ahead in 1863 with an edition in nine volumes, subsequently reprinted in one. This is still in some sense the "official" edition; most scholarly works refer to it, if only to keep the line-numbers straight.

Nevertheless, by the 1920s it was felt to be outmoded, and Cambridge embarked on a new one-play-at-a-time series called The New Shakespeare. It was essentially the work of a single editor, the redoubtable John Dover Wilson, and not surprisingly it took him 40 years - half his lifetime, during which his status changed from iconoclastic firebrand to lovable doyen. The New Shakespeare didn't remain very long and Cambridge is now replacing it, again play by play, though with an individual editor for each the obvious plan is to get the job done more quickly this time.

But Cambridge is being overshadowed by Oxford, making up for a false start early in the century when the designated editor, R. B. McKerow, proved so conscientious (he was the founder of modern textual scholarship) that he died while still at work on his preliminary researches. Such quixotry belongs to another age, for Oxford now comes forth, simultaneously and confusingly, with three editions. There are individually issued plays to rival or eclipse the Cambridge versions, each the work of a different scholar under the over-all editorship of Stanley Wells and Gary Taylor.

Meanwhile, Wells and Taylor, with a couple of helpers, have edited two separate omnibus volumes: one in old spelling for the purists and one modernized for the rest of us. And since these new folios, stout though they are, have no space for anything besides the plays and poems themselves, we have this equally bulky Textual Companion to accommodate notes and commentary on each work and battery of introductions to the canon in general.

Stanley Wells, as critic, teacher, journalist and broadcaster, is probably the most visible of current Shakespeare scholars in England. I think of him as providing the project with its solid bottom, and Gary Taylor, a young academic from the United States, as supplying the gunpowder. Most of the introductory writing is Taylor's, and it races. He can even generate interest in the working habits of individual scribes and compositors in the Elizabethan play text business. (It's wonderful what they can reconstruct these days.) Anxious to return as closely as possible to the Shakespearean manuscripts, not one of which survives, the editors enjoy being ruthless toward our inherited textual illusions. They demonstrate (and a current production at the National Theatre in London accepts their findings) that Imogen, the beloved heroine of Cymbeline, is a chimera. Somebody misread "m" for "nn" and the lady's name is really Innogen. The Imogens named down the years in honor of Shakespeare's princess owe their chistenings to a Jacobean printer's howler. The revelation saddens me, but I will bear it like a man.

On the other hand, I rebel against Taylor's decision to re-allot most of the Dauphin's role in Henry V to a faceless French nobleman. I don't care what the scholarly evidence is; a French prince who goes right through the play, from tennis-balls to Agincourt, as a cocksure poltroon provides a dramatic counterweight to the English king, whose saving grace is his insecurity. If that wasn't Shakespeare's intention, it should have been, and some playhouse or printing-house reviser did him a favor.

This Oxford Shakespeare may come to be known as the Oldcastle edition. It is well known that the fat knight of Henry IV Part One was originally named Sir John Oldcastle. Only when contemporary members of the Oldcastle family objected was he renamed Falstaff. The Oxford editors put him back as Oldcastle. ("Sweet Jack Oldcastle, kind Jack Oldcastle, valiant Jack Oldcastle, and therefore more valiant being as he is, old Jack Oldcastle.") This is very odd, and not just for sentimental reasons. The editors are very hot on authorial revision; they approve of it, and of incorporating it where it can be detected. Changing Oldcastle to Falstaff was a Shakespearean decision, even if made under duress; when he got to Henry IV Part Two, he wrote the character as Falstaff without it seeming to cramp his style at all. His second thoughts should be respected. (A minor point: in Part One Prince Hal calls Jack "My old lad of the castle." If the charcter's name is Oldcastle, that's a weak pun. If it used to be Oldcastle but had to be changed, then it's a nice in-joke. You don't have to believe me.) The editors' decision here seems to me a piece of bravado: nobody else has dared to do it, but by God, we'll show 'em.

Or it may be known as the twin-Lear edition. So concerned are the editors by the differences between the Good Quarto and First Folio Lears that they print both: The History Of King Lear and The Tragedy Of King Lear, amounting, they inform us, to two totally different plays. Where the differences occur - whether they make any major difference to the esthetic experience of the play - they do not tell us; the companion eschews critical interpretaton.

Wells and Taylor accuse the First Folio editors Heminge and Condell of inventing the Shakesepare history play by lumping together in chronological order plays that had been written at various times and in various modes. Shakespeare probably thought of Richard II and Richard III as tragedies, and he never wrote a play called Henry VIII. That was a title slapped, for reasons of uniformity, on a piece that had hitherto been known as All Is True. I am sure the Oxford boys are right, but Heminge and Condell knew what was commercial; I cannot see any future producer ditching the title Henry VIII, which means something to an audience, for All Is True, which doesn't.

All Is True is forthrightly credited here to Shakespeare and John Fletcher. In the most fascinating of the introductory chapters, The Canon And Chronology Of Shakespeare's Plays, Wells and Taylor are often inclined to admit collaborators. That takes us back. Editors in the nineteenth century used to fall over themselves to assign to other writers the parts of Shakespeare's plays of which they personally disapproved. In reaction, twentieth-century scholars have made a fetish of "integrity" - if we can't believe that gentle William perpetrated the horrors of Titus Andronicus, that's our problem. Now the tide is turning again, and it seems like common sense. We know that all Shakespeare's contemporaries collaborated with one another. Why should he have been exempt?

The companion's editors, printing the plays in what they take to have been the order of composition, finish with another Shakespeare-Fletcher tandem, The Two Noble Kinsmen, the first play to be reputably admitted into the canon since 1664, when the Third Folio squeezed in Pericles. But it is not just late and early plays in which they detect other hands. They attribute much of the middle-period Timon Of Athens to Thomas Middleton. I had never thought of this, but now that I have, I believe it. In fact, it's a great weight off my mind.

"We do not know what Shakespeare wrote," says Gary Taylor (answering the presumptive question, "Why bother?"); "someone has to decide . . . on the basis of the evidence available at a particular time." And this evidence changes - multiplies, rather - as time progresses. But whether it makes any essential difference to the way we read, stage or interpret a play, I doubt it. The main lines of story, character and language remain the same. Look at a facsimile of an early quarto or folio and it seems, for a moment, passing strange. But when you start reading the words, you automatically begin translating them into the patterns of your own mind: modern patterns, of course, of which a modern edition is a symptom, not a cause.

With all its dash and finery, the new Oxford Shakespeare, including its Textual Companion, is a luxury object, like all its contemporaries and most of its predecessors. It is also inevitable, since it is a contribution to knowledge; and knowledge, especially on so fascinating a subject, must always tempt us. And it is a beautiful job. Robert Cushman is former theatre critic of The Spectator of London. His study of contemporary British theatre will be published next year. Robert Cushman, who reviewed William Shakespeare: A Textual Companion in the book pages of July 30, is former drama critic of The Observer of London. Incorrect information appeared at the end of the review. (Saturday, August 6, 1988, Page A2)
1988-11-05-children-s-books-treasured-st:
Children's books Treasured stories

Saturday, November 05, 1988

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN They don't all live happily ever after. Most childrens stories, of course, pretend that they do, but there are some bleak exceptions. Darkest of all is Peter Pan In Kensington Gardens, J. M. Barries trial run for his full-length play and novel about the boy who refused to grow up. Peter, having at one week old abandoned his mother for childhood everlasting in a London park, passes up the chance to return to the nest. It will not come again: "There is no second chance, not for most of us. When we reach the window it is Lock-out Time. The iron bars are up for life."

Which sobering words round off The Victorian Fairy Tale Book(Random House, 386 pages, $27.95), an exhaustive anthology of what the blurb reasonably calls the Golden Era of the fairy tale. Barrie was providing a mirror-image of his own misery; he felt as trapped in adulthood as Peter was in youth. Hence the peculiar tone - alternately gloating and coaxing, whimsical and ironic, queasy and compelling - in which he addresses his readers; he is the nice old gentleman bearing poisoned sweets.

But, this book has us asking, weren't they all? Robert Browning's The Pied Piper Of Hamelin with its ingeniously execrable rhymes (So, Willy, let you and me be wipers Of scores out with all men, especially pipers") offers a mass drowning of rats, told from the rodent point of view, as prelude to the abduction of a townful of children. This is a horror story for parents; since one crippled child is left behind to lament his loneliness, its a nightmare for children as well. And the kids never return; there is no second chance, not for Hamelin.

John Ruskins The King Of The Golden River, the first story in the collection, finishes off two skinflint brothers by turning them into rocks. Now there's a forever punishment. Their virtuous younger sibling is a chronic sharer of his last crusts with the elderly and indigent, and it's never suggested that he has read enough stories himself to know that in fairyland such behavior is bound to pay off. He is just naturally good, and he ends up making a fortune.

But it is the villains geological transformation that claims both the tales final sentence and the readers' shuddering imagination. As Oscar Wilde might have observed: "The good end insipidly and the bad unforgettably; that is what Legend means. Wilde's own The Selfish Giant, by the way, is the sickliest thing in the book, an exercise in Christian masochism.

But the book, with its scholarly introduction and exquisite but limited original line-drawings, seems primarily intended for nostalgic adults. My own most delightful discoveries were Ford Madox Fords The Brown Owl, very funny; George Macdonalds The Golden Key, a wonderful quest-story on the borderland of faery and science-fiction whose hero and heroine age decades in a sentence; and The Magic Fish-Bone, an unfamiliar bit of Dickens. In this one, a shabby-genteel London family is playfully given royal labels (there are about 20 princes and princesses" in the overstretched household) so as to qualify for magical relief from direst poverty. Only magic can do it. Outside the bounds of fairy-tale, as Dickens is mercilessly aware, the iron bars are up for life.

The Canadian Children's Treasury (Key Porter, 294 pages, $22.95) is weakest when closest to fairy tale. Eva Martin's Goldenhair, for example, is a painfully uninventive pendent to the European tradition (a gardener turns out to be a knight, and marries a princess. So what else is new?). Indian or Eskimo legends, authentic or fabricated, about the discovery of fire or of story-telling, are the kind of thing that gets Canadiana a bad name, solemnly banal.

Realism and contemporary fantasy are the strong points. The first category yields a masterpiece, Morley Callaghans The Shining Red Apple, a study of adult bitterness operating at a childs expense. It is a story written about rather than for children, but many juvenile classics started out that way. So this anthology takes in The Cremation Of Sam McGee (too macabre for kids? Only a grown-up would think so) and a chunk of Stephen Leacock which, like all the Leacock I have ever read, left me feeling that the really funny stuff must be going on somewhere else.

The production is child-oriented with large print, attractive if unexceptional color illustrations and a chattily informal introduction by Janet Lunn. Lunn claims that Canadian writing is distinguished by humor, darkness, common-sense and - carefully covering all bases - versatility. With criteria that loose you could prove anything. But an excerpt from Lunn's The Root Cellar whets the appetite for the whole book. Indeed, all the bits of longer stories are keenly - even cruelly - calculated to leave the reader screaming for more. They range from the arrival of Anne Of Green Gables, letting you see exactly why Matthew must have wanted to strangle Anne and why he didn't, to visions by Suzanne Martel and Monica Hughes of the world after apocalypse. The assumptions here are more nakedly brutal than anything in Dickens or Barrie: a contrast not in continents but in centuries.

Stephane Poulin's Could You Stop Josephine (Tundra, unpaginated, $12.95) is the third instalment in the continuing chase-story of a boy and his cat. This time they go to a farm, which gives Josephine unlimited scope for running and hiding. It also gives Poulin, as his own illustrator, the cue for dazzling aerial views of grass and wheat fields, as sharp and magical as the paintings of the Douanier Rousseau. With these come beguilingly unsentimemntalized close-ups of the shock-headed pug- faced Daniel. Words, with this writer, come a definite second. But there is great pace to the story, and a nice shape. For 3-year-olds and up.

The test of an alphabet is what it does with X and Z. Jan Thornhill's The Wildlife ABC (Greey de Pencier, unpaginated, $16.95) cheats with X- ray (of a dinosaur) and Zoo. H, more inventively, is for Housefly, "inspecting your fridge with a skewed, creepy-crawly illustration of him at it. My 2-year-olds (I have triplets) enjoyed the pictures, which are bold and, where water is concerned, enticing, but had no interest in the text. This may be just as well; exposure to rhyme and scansion on the order of K is for Killer Whale In the deep blue sea" L is for Loon Who swims excellently" might stunt their growth.
1988-11-12-early-radical-chic-and-attrac:
THE POLITICS OF PARADISE: A VINDICATION OF BYRON BY MICHAEL FOOT Collins, 424 pages, $34.95

Early radical chic and attractive wit

THE POLITICS OF PARADISE: A VINDICATION OF BYRON BY MICHAEL FOOT Collins, 424 pages, $34.95

Saturday, November 12, 1988

ROBERT CUSHMAN

REVIEW BY ROBERT CUSHMAN This, I have been informed with awe, could never happen here. A retiring Canadian political party leader might try to turn a quick buck with a volume of scabrous memoirs (his own), but would never squander his newfound leisure on composing a scholarly essay in literary biography.

I hate to admit it, but it doesnt often happen in Britain either. Michael Foot, former leader of the British Labor Party and still a liltingly powerful voice on the back benches, is no commonplace politician. He was generally reckoned to be too civilized, too intellectual, too vague, too nice to succeed as a leader of the opposition, and so in fact it proved. But he always had a second career going as a journalist and man of letters, and the boot in this study of the life, works and opinions of George Gordon Noel , Lord Byron is firmly on that other Foot.

If the phrase man of letters sounds old-fashioned, it was meant to. Foot is that good old left-wing thing, a self-trained scholar. His nearest equivalents on the British right are Paul Johnson, a self-educated pundit, and Bernard Levin, a self-made mandarin. They have the advantage of him in wit and stylistic grace; he beats them on enthusiasn. By modern LitCrit standards he is an amateur: certainly no computerized academic.

Consider Foot's footnotes: not curt acknowledgements of sources, but effusive tributes to all authors who have taught him anything about Byron, which seems to mean just about everyone who has ever written about him. They also give him a chance to vent some spleen held politely in check in the text itself. A description of Byron's ill-suited wife ("high moral earnestness in belligerent abundance, absolute assurance that she knew all the . . . answers . . . evangelical zeal to subdue others") reminds our author irresistibly of Margaret Thatcher. Or so he mischievously says.

This Byronic education, so conscientiously detailed, seems to be a fairly recent event. It has left him convinced that the poet, dismissed in the text books as an aristocratic cub high on charm, low on convictions and zero on morals, was actually a misunderstood and golden-hearted radical: an early nineteenth-century Michael Foot, in fact, but sexier.

The Politics Of Paradise is a celebration of this Byron rather than the vindication announced in the subtitle. The need for vindication arises in Foots mind because of William Hazlitt. Hazlitt, essayist andd critic, is a longer-established hero in Foots pantheon, his paradigm of the radical journalist. He was Byron's contemporary and should have been his ally. It seems, though, that Hazlitt disliked Byron and disapproved of him: the time-honored reaction of the ink-stained activist to the apparently careless dandy. Foot is grieved by this disobliging lapse in Hazlitt and sets out to explain it.

So his book has an odd shape. Its first chapter - a book in itself, really - is a detachable essay on Hazlitt that would be worth having if only for Foot's skill in quotation. The purpose of poetry, said Hazlitt, is to relieve the aching sense of pleasure by expressing it in the boldest manner. "Aching sense of pleasure" is wonderful, as applicable to the flesh as to the spirit, and without Foot I might never have known about it. We find Hazlitt attacking Shelley as a revolutionary without principle (He strives to overturn all established creeds and systems; but this is in him an effect of constitution), and going for Byron on much the same grounds: "He exists not by sympathy, but by antipathy. He scorns all things, even himself."

I have never been able to take Shelley seriously, perhaps because he was so solemn about himself that any gravity on my part seemed superfluous. But what Hazlitt objected to in Byron is dazzlingly attractive. Mockery, rather than scorn, directed at himself and at the world, a world that, as always, deserved it. Don Juan, his longest and greatest work, is an extraordinary feat of sustained humor, the funniest poem in the English language. Funny is not a word you are supposed to use about major poets (I was ticked off at school for applying it admiringly to Dryden), but Foot, operating outside the industry, comes near to calling Byron funny. And it is on Byrons funniness - his wit, if you prefer the respectable term - that Foots case really rests.

"I am like Adam," said Byron in a letter, "the first convict sentenced to transportation." Implicit in that throwaway line is a compassionate attack on orthodox religion and, beyond that, on the orthodox society that took the first opportunity of expelling him. It is sentimental to pretend that all humor is subversive (though reactionary jokes are funniest when there is not a reactionary governmennt), but the satirist, committed in the first place to attacking pomposity, usually finds himself attacking other complacent evils as well. Byron in the Prologue to Don Juan was hilarious about Wordsworth and the other lake poets not just because they wrote stodgy landscape verse, but because they had bounced from starry- eyed enthusiasm for the French Revolution to sycophantic distrust of any kind of change.

Byron himself was never starry-eyed. In his maiden speech in the House of Lords, he spoke on industrial riots, not so much defending the rioters as attacking their exploiters, while admitting that he himself as a nobleman had everything to lose from an overturn of society. This thread ran right through his life, culminating in his death in Greece, a practical fighter in a practical cause. There may of course have been an element of pose in this. So there is in most activities, especially writers' activities. The question is which pose you choose to adopt, and what the results are.

Foot skimps on the Greek Byron. The book is not a full biography, and he probably thinks - wrongly - that the end of the story is too well known to need retelling. On the other hand, he luxuriates in Byron's response to Italy, especially Venice, partly because it suits his political purpose but more because he enjoys it. This is not a very rigorous book, and Foot turns out not to need Hazlitt as a stalking-horse after all. Having set him up, Foot finds little use for him.

It is just possible that had Foot been their contemporary, he would have been as impatient with Byron as was Hazlitt. Radical chic backed up by aristocratic cool can be unbearble at close quarters. A century and more on, it can be irresistible. Foot obviously finds it so, and his enthusiasm has fed my own. Robert Cushman is former drama critic of the Observer.

BOOK REVIEW But what about the music, Mel?

Thursday, December 29, 1988

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail MEL TORME is on his fourth marriage and his umpteenth recording contract. His life has been successful but, as you would guess from those statistics, checkered. His autobiography tells more about his marriages than about his music, which is a mistake.

Maybe that's how he wanted to write it. Maybe that's how he believes books are sold. Maybe that's what his publisher told him - in which case he has been manipulated by the book trade much as he claims to have been by the record business. Virtually the only recording executive for whom he has a good word is Carl Jefferson, who runs the modest and tasteful label known as Concord Jazz and who also happens to be Torme's current employer. Similarly, Torme's only good wife, by his account, is his present one.

IT WASN'T ALL VELVET

BY MEL TORME , Viking, 400 pages, $24.95 I'm being unfair. He dismisses his first two marriages (to a starlet and a fan) as immature mistakes, but shoulders much of the blame himself. His third venture was with British actress Janette Scott, a lightning love-match that ended for him in tears, scars and a losing battle for custody of their two children. That is his side of the story, and he tells it at length. Presumably Scott has her own version, and it would have rounded things out if Torme could have brought himself to summarize it. Maybe he really is the worst wronged husband in the civilized world, but he sure protests a lot.

Why? As he himself says, if you want showbiz scandals, there are far juicier ones available. His rationale is that he is a popular singer, pop songs are mainly about love, and so his feelings and experiences are relevant to his work. That might hold, if he told us more about his work: not just where he has done it and how much he has earned from it, but how he approaches it: what songs he sings, and how, and why.

To begin with, he does. He writes about growing up in Depression Chicago with his ears glued to the radio, so fixated on the big bands that by the age of 4 he could sing with one of them. Thus established as a prodigy he progressed to child acting on the air, and to singing and songwriting in high school. He almost went on the road with Harry James, and finally made it - as singer, composer and vocal arranger - with a band ostensibly fronted by Chico Marx but actually run by swing drummer Ben Pollack. (Which is appropriate, because Torme himself is a nifty drummer and only an average pianist.) Here he lost his professional and - about which he is quite funny - personal virginity. Going solo, he had a couple of years of postwar Hit Parade successes as a singer of moonstruck ballads, rendered with fanatical delicacy and sureness of pitch. He was all-American boyish in looks and voice, an image he maintained through half a dozen mostly forgotten films. Movie stardom eluded him, but he survived; he devotes an angry, compassionate couple of pages - in some ways, the best in the book - to those who did not: the Hollywood kids who became teen-age stars and were then unceremoniously beached.

He himself progressed by outgrowing the bobby sox and turning - or returning - to jazz. And this is where the story really starts; or should. In fact, it's where the music stops and the life and loves (not to mention the gun and car collections) take over. Some of the best vocal albums ever made are dispatched in a sentence or ignored altogether.

This is howlingly frustrating, not just because Torme can write (though he has an unfortunate addiction to the reconstructed conversations, outrageously fake and jaunty, that are the curse of U.S. biography) or even because he is intelligent; as he says, a large number of singers are. Many of them keep it under wraps, but with Torme, intelligence is what he has to sell as a performer; you can hear his brow furrowing in keen appreciation of the wit or the emotion he is transmitting. Musically he is an endless explorer, a consummate enthusiast. As an incorrigible singer- along-with-records I have found his instant key-changes and on-the-note gymnastics a bracing challenge.

He has lasted better than almost any singer of a generation that was reared on jazz and Broadway standards and dethroned by rock. He has cut his small share of sell-out albums (covers of pop numbers better done by others) and he rails now at the record bosses who forced him into it: the CBS rep, for example, who looked forward to a Mel Torme album you didn't have to listen to, an Andy Williams or Johnny Mathis sort of album.

Norman Granz of Verve may, as he says, be no gentleman, but he still presided over two of Torme's consummate collaborations with arranger- conductor Marty Paich, who brought the cool, spare Gerry Mulligan sound to vocal accompaniment and rejuvenated the genre. The Torme-Paich partnership has just been renewed, after 25 needlessly dormant years, with a reunion album on Concord, and it exhilarates. Joy and precision spill off the record, the singer unmistakably back where he belongs.

I want to know more about Torme and Paich and the nuts and bolts of how they operated. I want to know more of Torme's sense of his own position in musical and showbiz history, subjects of which he plainly has an excellent grasp. I want to know how Torme feels about his peers and predecessors, who influenced him and how. He says he gave up criticizing other singers after getting a murder threat from an Elvis Presley fan, but he is obviously bursting with opinions. I want to know about Mountain Greenery, a song he has featured since having a surprise British hit with it in 1956. He has now recorded it four times, all live, all different. That must mean something. I want, in short, another book. Maybe he'll write it.

INSIDE THE SLEEVE Classical singers visit Broadway Show Boat The Sound of Music

Tuesday, February 21, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Telarc DG 10162 Of Thee I Sing" Let 'Em Eat Cake CBS F2M 42522 ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail For some years now, opera has been trying to do musical comedy a favor. Record companies have signed up divas, symphony orchestras and assorted Placido Flamingos and unleashed them on the Broadway repertoire. For obvious reasons, they have concentrated on the graver or more pompous musicals, and the results have been grisly. We have had a West Side Story with Kiri Te Kanawa that unerringly emphasized everything most unbearably overbearing in the score; a South Pacific in which the same dame sang as though English were her third or fourth language; and a My Fair Lady on which I cannot comment. Te Kanawa singing Cockney, in a show that is actually about authentic accents, was more than I could face.

For some reason, classical singers in complete shows sound more grotesque than when they record solo albums of pop standards, which at least give them the chance to stretch out and impose a personality. The disciplines of a score throw them back on technique, and it's usually the wrong technique. But there are always exceptions; and the box-set three- record complete Show Boat is a glory.

Frederica von Stade plays the heroine Magnolia, and Jerry Hadley her gambler lover (and later husband) Gaylord Ravenal. The crucial point is that they have been engaged as the servants of the show, rather than the show being recorded as a vehicle for them. The presiding genius is conductor John McGlinn, who has made it his scholarly mission to restore classic musicals to their original form. Broadway's habits are chaotic, and McGlinn has had to cut through the detritus of revivals, adaptations, cuts and rewrites. The results are revelatory, right from the start; Jerome Kern's overture, generally replaced by a medley of the show's half- dozen hits, turns out to be a murkily ominous Mississippi tone-poem. The first sung line, "Niggers all work on the Mississippi," jolts as it was meant to. Lyricist-librettist Oscar Hammerstein was telling a serious story about race relations in the old South and he knew what he was about. The restoration later on of a prophetic chorale, Mis'ry's Comin' Aroun', raises the score to Porgy and Bess level.

In fact, McGlinn gives us every note of music: songs full-blown and fragmentary, dance-interludes, even underscoring - which means we get sizeable chunks of dialogue as well. These suggest that Show Boat, if not precisely a tragedy (its story develops but its characters don't), is still a drama. It was first staged in 1927, and not for decades did Broadway attempt anything comparable. McGlinn also throws in an appendix, of songs deleted from the first production or added for subsequent versions, including the 1936 film. This is a Variorum Show Boat.

Hadley is sound and round, if stolid. (But Gaylords always are; their glamor has to be taken on trust.) Von Stade is delightful, without a hint of condescension, though some of the later jazzier numbers tax her a bit. I'm prepared to believe that she has rhythm in her soul, but she cannot always get it through her lips. McGlinn claims that pop singers have swung and"or torched these songs out of recognition, but they were responding to something that is really there, whether Kern himself knew it or not.
