(And whether he liked it or not.) The real cross-cultural dynamo here is Teresa Stratas as the doomed mulatto Julie. She acts with the sad worldliness of a Kurt Weill heroine, and sings with a purity and ease that transcend categories. She leads an ensemble rendition of Can't Help Lovin' Dat Man that is the most joyous thing I have heard in ages. (It's a happy song, whatever nightclub tragediennes may have done to it.) You yearn for a full-scale stage revival, harnessing talents from opera, drama and musical comedy; the show deserves them. Recording quality is crystalline. Neatly balancing Hammerstein's first major show is his last: if The Sound of Music could ever be described as major. This is another musically complete version (every chirrup of birdsong and every clang of the church bell), but this time with von Stade as unchallenged star. She is an expectedly pristine Maria, though she has surprising trouble with breath- control; her Favorite Things are interspersed with audible pants. The entire show has been cast operatically, which is a mistake. The show contains two bracingly cynical numbers (it's always a shock to realize that this, of all Rodgers and Hammerstein scores, contains anything cynical, and certainly the film had no truck with them), but they are ruined here by a stodgy buffo and a vapid mature soubrette. Accompaniment is by Erich Kunzel and the Cincinnati Pops, who are appropriate. The treat is the presence of Eileen Farrell, America's Schwarzkopf and the greatest of all cross-over artists, as the Abbess. She was always able to cope with both classical and popular material by having, as she says herself, two voices; and her Climb Ev'ry Mountain, supremely relaxed, is the most tolerable I have heard. More in the Show Boat line, for authenticity and importance, is the double-headed recording of George and Ira Gershwin's two political comic operas. Of Thee I Sing, a whimsically disrespectful spoof of the U.S. presidency, was a prize-winning, record-breaking hit in 1931; Let 'Em Eat Cake, its dyspeptic successor, was a quick flop in the more defensive atmosphere of 1933.

There is plenty of good wisecracking though, both in book and lyrics. Union Square, with its refrain, "Down with everything that's up," anticipates and deflates the all-purpose protest song. The Gershwins are audibly flexing their muscles, George especially, though the constant references to Gilbert and Sullivan become a crutch rather than a satiric device. On the other hand, when a Southern belle strikes up a lament, the music is limbering up for Porgy. (She's lamenting because the President, having promised to marry her as part of his election platform, has turned her down for a girl who can bake corn muffins. You get the picture.) The score, despite brisk conducting from Michael Tilson Thomas, is tamer than it might be because as the opportunist hero Larry Kert, the original Tony of West side Story, still sounds like a blameless juvenile lead. However, Maureen McGovern is an unexpected pleasure, soaring sweetly like a pop Barbara Cook; there is smart comedy singing from David Garrison and Paige O'Hara (both heard to less advantage in Show Boat); and there is the gentle presence of Jack Gilford as the perpetually overlooked Vice- President Throttlebottom, gracefully resigning his one chance of glory with the words, "You can be President and I'll go back to Vice."
1989-03-11-g-k-chesterton-in-the-age-of-:
GILBERT: THE MAN WHO WAS G. K. CHESTERTON BY MICHAEL COREN Random House, 270 pages, $29.95

G. K. Chesterton in the age of chumminess

GILBERT: THE MAN WHO WAS G. K. CHESTERTON BY MICHAEL COREN Random House, 270 pages, $29.95

Saturday, March 11, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

REVIEW BY ROBERT CUSHMAN An age of chumminess is upon us. Michael Coren, a British journalist now living in Canada, is far too young ever to have known G. K. Chesterton. But here he is, in his title and throughout his text, positively on first- name terms with the chap. This is impudent and grating, and sometimes confusing. Corens very first paragraph contains a reference to a more familiar Gilbert, the one who wrote with Sullivan. You would think he might have noticed.

After a few pages of Coren's slipshod prose you realize that he wouldn't. Pondering his heros sexuality - it is possible, though Coren judges it unlikely, that Chestertons long and happy marriage was unconsummated - he announces: "In the early 1900s, the pre-permissive decades, faithfulness within the marriage bed, even if that bed was used only for sleeping upon, was considered standard." If that sentence is unravelled, it seems to mean that Edwardian husbands never brought their mistresses home, for fear of waking up their wives. That is what it seemsto mean. What it probablymeans is that Edwardian husbands rarely took mistresses at all. Which is not true.

It is mystifying that a man can write so clumsily after immersing himself in prose as felicitous as Chesterton's; sad, too, since Coren is intelligent and has a respectable supply of insights. By his account, Chesterton had not at all a bad life. At his death in 1936 he was one of London's pre-eminent literary journalists, and a respected biographer, essayist and versifier. As for his fiction, he had written some striking satirical fantasies (The Napoleon Of Notting Hill, The Man Who Was Thursday) and had created Father Brown, the Catholic priest as detective, or, as I like to think of him, the Bloodhound of Heaven.

Chesterton was probably the most famous British Catholic writer of the twentieth century, at least until the advent (is that the word?) of Graham Greene. The contrast between the two is instructive, a matter not just of temperament but of era. Greenes religion, at any rate as it appears in his fiction, is an instrument of torture. For Chesterton, a late but predestined convert, it was an emanation of well-being; one would call it a source of consolation, except that there didnt seem to be much he needed to be consoled about.

In his youth he was exploited - overworked and underpaid - by publishers and editors, but he liked working and was unconcerned about money. When, later, he needed it, he made it. There was not even much trauma in his childhood. His father was a rationalist who nevertheless sent his children to nonconformist chapel, thereby giving his son two things to rebel against but apparently nothing much to resent. At school, an outsize shambling figure, Chesterton became, says Coren, a mascot, accepted as the archetypal eccentric and tolerated as such. He made good there as part of a self-created elite, helping to found a magazine and a debating society, two entities that, in one form or another, followed him through his life. He needed not just friendship but fellowship, companions to write, talk, eat and drink with.

That eating and drinking, as was more or less said of Sir Toby Belch, nearly undid him. He was obese by 30, and at 40 almost succumbed to a combination of gout and heart trouble, though he rallied and lived another 20 years. He was also very tall. In the dust-jacket photograph he looms at you, a rumpled, squinting figure in an untidily curling collar and layers of coat. He looks a slightly Frenchified (which would have pleased him) Victorian sage, just out of his time.

Like those Victorians, he invariably knew he was right, or wrote as if he did. In this he greatly resembles his contemporary and sparring partner, Bernard Shaw. Philosophically they had nothing in common, spiritually they had everything. ("I am the only person who understands him," wrote GKC of GBS, and I do not agree with him.) Chesterton's prose reeks of the saloon bar and Shaw's of the health farm, but essentially both are saying the same thing: "How simple life would be if people would only listen to me."

The paradox, Chestertons famous weapon, was Shaws as well. Both were masters of the verbal rapier, but used it so remorselessly that it might as well have been a bludgeon.

Chesterton could toss off an aside as enchanting as this on Prohibition: Well-to-do Americans were only too delighted to discuss it over the nuts and wine. They were even willing, if necessary, to dispense with the nuts. He could also write verse as unbearably back-slapping as his address to F. E. Smith, a politician who had had the temerity to express an opinion on religion: "Talk about the pews and steeples and the cash that goes therewith! But the souls of Christian peoples . . . Chuck it, Smith!"

This cocksureness also led Chesterton to espouse the cause of Distributism - or every man his own smallholding - as an alternative to what he saw as the doomed creeds of capitalism and communism. Coren, a little severely, sees this as a mild forerunner of fascism. He never engages, though, with the criticism George Orwell made of Chesterton: that though a true friend of democracy according to his lights, during his last 20 years he "suppressed his sensibility and intellectual honesty in the service of Roman Catholic propaganda." Indeed, Coren never mentions Orwell at all.

He writes at length, however, of the greatest stain on Chesterton's reputation: his alleged anti-Semitism. He acquits him of any vicious prejudice; some of his best friends truly wereJews. Unfortunately some of his best friends were anything but; they included his brother Cecil and - notoriously - Hilaire Belloc. Belloc wrote a jolly poem that ended: Now and then we persecute these curly-headed men. It is unlikely that Chesterton would ever have made jokes about persecution, but over a glass of beer he might well have laughed agreeably at Belloc's. Chesterton, says Coren, "gave in to the meagre temptations of a vile fashion."

Oddly enough, he had himself been the victim of a bizarre form of anti- Semitism; an editor had turned down one of his early articles because he thought the handwriting too Jewish. When he came to write on the Jewish question - it is significant that he thought there was one - his attitude was paternalistic. He was prepared to judge tolerantly, but he reserved the right to judge. But it is doubtful that he did much harm, and more important that, long before it became fashionable, he was an unflinching anti-Nazi. "I am quite ready to believe now that Belloc and I will die defending the last Jew in Europe."

He may even have been right about Belloc. After all, Ezra Pound was sobered by the revelations of the death camps. Chesterton died too early for that experience. It would doubtless have made him very tactful - for a time. A permanently tactful Chesterton would be difficult to imagine, and impossible to enjoy.

In accordance with the canons of pop biography, Coren has written his book as a flashback, devoting his first chapter to his subjects death and funeral. It is difficult to produce tears over the fate of a man to whom your readers have not yet been properly introduced, but Coren does his best. "Around 10:15 on the morning of 14th June, 1936, Gilberts soul passed gently from this earth." There's pathos for you. Chuck it, Mike. Robert Cushman is former drama critic of The Observer of London.
1989-04-13-shakespeare-as-anti-semite-th:
Shakespeare as anti-Semite The racism in The Merchant of Venice is a sign of the Bard's biased times

Thursday, April 13, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Mr. Cushman was theatre critic of The Observer in London for 11 years. He now lives in Toronto and writes regularly on theatre for Saturday Night magazine. THAT OLD RACIST William Shakespeare is catching it again. The Stratford Festival has announced it will present what is, in Canada, his most notorious play this year, and the news is causing the customary concern.

Coming from Britain, where there seems to be a major production of The Merchant of Venice every other season, I was surprised (and a little envious) to learn that this Merchant will be only the fifth in Stratford's 37-year existence. Presumably the play's rarity is not due to its being a financial or artistic risk. But it has a history of causing trouble.

Shylock - customarily the star role and technically the villain - is a Jew. Whenever the play is revived, it provokes at the least unease and, at most, accusations of downright anti-Semitism followed by demands that it be removed from the repertoire.

This happens all over North America, but hardly ever in Britain. This is partly because the Jewish community there is less sensitive - or less vociferous - but it is also due to Shakespeare's being part of the national bloodstream. He is simply there, like the weather, and it would be both unsophisticated and unproductive to call for the abolition of either. All they can do is adapt - adapt themselves to the climate or, since he is rather more malleable, adapt Shakespeare to themselves.

That Shakespeare and Canada are also being acclimatized to one another is proved by the low-key, sensible character of this year's controversy. No, says the Canadian Jewish Congress, we wouldn't dream of asking for censorship; we merely ask that children be kept away from the play until they are old enough to appreciate its implications. That seems fair, though it is more a matter for the schools than for the theatre, which can hardly be expected to turn away customers, young or old, singly or in groups.

The CJC asks that teachers, when confronted by the play, put it in context, which for us, if not for Shakespeare, must include the history of anti-Semitism. Again unarguable: teachers of literature should always put works in context. It's their job.

As it happens, the Merchant was the first Shakespeare play I studied in school. I was 13 and the only Jew in the class, and I was not aware of any ill feeling toward Shylock spilling over on to me. (Come to think of it, I wasn't aware of any ill feeling toward Shylock at all; kids, even more than adults, love a good villain.) But I may have been lucky; I went to a big-city school.

The CJC seems more concerned about children growing up in rural areas: "Shylock represents their first encounter with a Jew . . . Then, every Jewish child they encounter is a Shylock." This is a bit puzzling; if they've never met any Jews prior to seeing the play, why are they going to start meeting them now? But the risk of Jewish children, or any children, being made to suffer is not worth taking; there are 36 other Shakespeare plays for young students to cut their teeth on.

For Stratford, literary adviser and assistant director Elliott Hayes has countered - as I imagine I would in his place - that, although the play contains anti-Semitic lines, Shylock is no stereotype and Shakespeare himself was no bigot. I wonder how he knows: about Shakespeare, I mean. There is a distinction to be drawn between the man and the playwright.

Shakespeare the playwright distributes his emotional sympathies with Sphinx-like impartiality; even Iago and Richard III, far more comprehensive rogues than Shylock, are allowed voices and feelings of their own. But in the end the forces of conventional society tell us exactly what we are meant to think of them. The moral standpoint is not very exciting or subversive, but it's probably Shakespeare's own.

On the evidence of the Merchant, Shakespeare was anti-Semitic. Not viciously and maybe not consciously: it was simply part of the air he breathed. Officially there were no Jews in Elizabethan England, so his Shylock was a fantasy figure drawing on the legend of the Jew as Christ- killer (which isn't much dwelt on in the play) and as usurer (which is dwelt on a great deal).

Shakespeare is capable, in this play and others, of using the word ''Jew'' as an automatic, casual insult. But the toughest thing for a modern Jew is not that Shylock is a comic miser who loses his daughter and his wealth, or that he is a would-be murderer itching for a pound of his arch-enemy's flesh. What hurts is that he is finally forced to convert to Christianity and that this is meant to constitute a happy ending.

The Elizabethans presumably took it, according to temperament, as a thundering good laugh on Shylock or as a charitable contribution toward the saving of his soul, a practical demonstration of the quality of mercy not being strained. Liberty of conscience was not one of that age's priorities.

But it is a moment that I blot out from my memory of the play until I encounter it in performance, when it hits me like a blow in the face. I don't think that this is what Shakespeare intended. But then I don't think that it's my job as a spectator to respond to his intentions; he has had his say as a playwright and I am entitled to my reaction. Besides, his intentions may be at variance with his execution.

There is one other famous Jew in Elizabethan drama, Barabas in Christopher Marlowe's The Jew of Malta. He is far more of a monster than Shylock ("Sometimes," he remarks with engaging off-handedness, "I go about and poison wells"), and Marlowe has no sympathy for him. But then he has no sympathy for anybody; he creates a vicious cartoon world and, as a natural rebel, clearly enjoys using his villainous outsider to expose official (which is to say Christian) hypocrisy.

Paradoxically, Shylock is a more anti-Semitic creation than Barabas just because he is more human. You have to take him seriously. His opponents in the play are pretty colorless, so you can argue that Shakespeare, too, was making a point about hypocrisy. But it's just as likely that he meant his Christians to be positively likeable and didn't do a very good job of it.

Shylock has the vitality of villainy, which I perversely feel is a greater compliment to a Jew from a Christian writer than any amount of virtuous martyrdom. When he so famously inquires, "Hath not a Jew eyes?" he is not cringing or pleading or making a case for tolerance. He is leading up to the further question, "If you wrong us, shall we not revenge?" with the attached threat, "the villainy you teach me I will execute and it will go hard but I shall better the instruction."

Morally this may not be admirable, and it does not have much to do with Judaic law. But it is dramatically exciting and for Jews, after centuries of subservience, it is an emotional release. We identify with Shylock as instinctively as we identify with the state of Israel; and the two causes torture our consciences in similar ways. Shakespeare may not have liked Shylock, but he must have ended up respecting him, and that is a lesson worth teaching to any age.

The theatrical appeal crosses racial and religious barriers. Actors, Jewish and Gentile, dream of playing Shylock, but few line up to play Antonio, his noble if intolerant prey. Jewish actors are actually less likely to compromise over Shylock than are Gentiles, who tend to arrive full of compassion and understanding.

In the British theatre there have been two great Shylocks in the past decade. One was a Jew, David Suchet, whose Shylock was a compulsive joker who had adopted a mask of self-mockery as camouflage in an alien society and found it had stuck to him. He was not noble but he was unpredictable, flesh-and-blood real. On the whole you felt he got what he deserved - until the final humiliation, which sent the house into a palpable state of shock.

At the other extreme there was the notably Christian Alec Guinness, whose Shylock was all subtlety and dignity, a walking dossier on the corroding effects of persecution. You sympathized with, and lamented for him - but, ironically, when he received the order of the font, the audience reverted to Elizabethan type and laughed.

Admittedly, he was playing at the Chichester Festival Theatre, which has an unusual clientele drawn from England's conservative stockbroker belt and probably more in need of consciousness-raising than any Canadian school children, however rural.

Probably the most famous of postwar Shylocks was Laurence Olivier in the 1970s, playing with quicksilver attack, protruding teeth and a Rothschild accent. It was his "I can be Jewish" performance, to match his "I can be black" Othello (a more substantial achievement) of the previous decade. Next month London will see Dustin Hoffman, who can presumably take the Jewishness for granted. Maybe he'll give an "I may be a movie star but I can speak Shakespeare" performance.

Stratford's Shylock is Brian Bedford, an actor whose natural habitat is the borderland between comedy and tragedy. This is precisely where Shylock lives, stretched between Elizabethan popular prejudice and Shakespeare's instinctive commitment to complicated humanity.
1989-06-14-a-whiff-of-anti-semitism-on-t:
Shakespeare in Britain is like the weather. One does not complain about either, since both are inescapable. The Merchant of Venice is produced at least every other year, and nobody gets too exercised over Shylock as a figure of anti-Semitism.

If anybody does, there are two ready answers: Shakespeare was an Elizabethan and could hardly be expected to transcend the prejudices of his time; and the play is actually subversive, with Shylock its most sympathetic character. As a British Jew, product of two pragmatic cultures, I enjoy reconciling these two contradictory positions.

In Britain, Shakespeare is simply there. In North America he's often nowhere, so when he does appear he gets a reaction. Joe Papp, the impresario most responsible for keeping him on display in Manhattan, was recently informed in the correspondence columns of New York magazine that, having once produced The Merchant, he had forfeited his right to take any moral stand whatever on questions of racial prejudice.

American Jews are perhaps more sensitive, certainly more vocal, than British (also, of course, more numerous) and many of them, when they come across The Merchant, cannot believe their ears. Even the Canadian Shakespeare Festival at Stratford, Ontario, has fought shy of the play. In 37 years this British byword for theatrical popularity has surfaced there only five times. When the festival first attempted it, in 1955, the Canadian Jewish News denounced the play as "pure, unadulterated anti-Semitism" with "no place in modern society".

Since then Shakespeare has become enough of an institution in Canada for outrage to have modulated into polite concern. When the play was announced for this year's season, the Canadian Jewish Congress expressed the reasonable hope that visiting school parties would be confined to children old enough to understand the play and its implications, and that their teachers would tell them all about its historical context. (They certainly should; that's their job.)

For a modern audience the play's main stumbling block is Shylock's enforced conversion, as a condition of his pardon, to Christianity. This is a happy ending? Michael Langham, the director at the Canadian festival, then surprised everybody by announcing that he was going to cut it. He believed in the play's final harmony, the victory of mercy over justice, and he did not want it compromised by what a modern audience would take as an act of gratuitous cruelty.

This decision, undoubtedly well meant, pleased nobody. The Jewish community said it certainly was not being done at their instigation. Censorship is as live an issue in conservative Canada as it is in Britain, and teachers and libraries were aghast to see Stratford apparently censoring itself.

Newspaper editorials, calling for the sacking of just about the entire festival, defended the play's integrity as shrilly as if it had once been attacked. Real anti-Semites strutted out of the woodwork proclaiming, usually on the telephone, that Jews ought to be forcibly converted, or that it was too good for them, or both.

At the theatre, Brian Bedford, a brilliantly contained actor, delivered the speech "hath not a Jew eyes" with furious effect into the face of a small boy who had been taunting him a second earlier. I thought it a wonderful image of the persecuted turning on his tormentors, but a Jewish professor of English condemned it in a Montreal newspaper as a stereotype of the Jew as bogeyman. Both of us, I suppose, saw what we looked for. Art may have the power to change our opinions, but it is far likelier to confirm them, whatever they are.

No critic noticed, but it was not only Jewish sensibilities that were spared in this production; Portia's parting shot to the Prince of Morocco ("let all of his complexion choose me so") went as well. But the better Langham's production got - and it got very good indeed - the more one regretted its compromises. He was obviously capable of giving us the play in its full complexity.

I wondered what would happen if he went to the logical extreme and cut all references to Jewishness. You would be left with the comedy of a villainous usurer who lost his daughter and his ducats, and deserved to. Maybe that's all that Shakespeare, who probably never met a Jew, really intended. But one clings to the belief that he intended and what he wrote were two different things.

Peter Hall, interviewed about his London production with Dustin Hoffman, was quoted as saying that The Merchant is "the most pro-Semitic play ever written". I'd like to know how he works that one out.

The play's superficial assumptions are certainly anti-Semitic; the Jew is assumed to be a villain, and proves one. But it's also his villainy - his flesh-and-blood unwhining villainy, more interesting than any sanctity - that saves him and saves the play.

If it were deeply anti-Semitic then its vileness would, in some form or other, infect all its author's other works and we should expunge them from the centre of our culture. But if some remain they all must: including those, like The Merchant and The Taming of the Shrew and Henry V, that offend against fashion. A theatre explicitly devoted to Shakespeare - in Stratford, Canada or Stratford, England - has to keep showing us all the play in all their facets.
1989-07-01-the-devourable-bernard-levin:
ALL THINGS CONSIDERED BY BERNARD LEVIN Random House, 305 pages, $29.95

The devourable Bernard Levin

ALL THINGS CONSIDERED BY BERNARD LEVIN Random House, 305 pages, $29.95

Saturday, July 01, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

REVIEW BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Here is a collection - the fifth - of articles written for the Times (of London) by Bernard Levin in his role as Personality Columnist. Levin is the most celebrated columnist - maybe the most celebrated journalist - in the British press, and quite deservedly so. He is opinionated, unquenchable and writes elegant English, which seems colloquial even when it isn't. (Nobody could talk that well that fast, though in his TV appearances Levin often gives the impression that he might; oh yes, he is also very fond of parentheses and has seduced many into the erroneous belief that they can get away with it as well as he does.) His long, cascading sentences appear to pour on to the page of their own volition, though they must really be the result of immense and painful effort. At least I hope they are.

Most of all he is extremely funny. He once supplied the Times with a hilarious fantasy on the social life of the lobster, though he weakened its impact by serving it up in other guises on subsequent occasions. He seems to have given up now on writing set-piece funnies, but his sense of humor, which is fundamentally a sense of paradox, still informs nearly everything he writes. In this, as in much else, he has learned from Shaw.

Levin started out as a political commentator, and politics is still very much his beat. He has moved over the years from centre Left to centre Right. I might have said extreme Right were it not that the preface to this volume reveals that he is finally having doubts about Thatcherism; he still seems impervious to its essential meanness, but at least he worries about its threats to free speech.

As well as getting conservatism he also got religion, though of no recognized brand. Or if it is, he isnt letting on. A born but non- practicing Jew, he is now a fascinated observer of Christianity. "I would like," he says of Christ to be written down a fan. He might also, I think, be written down a mystical moralist. Theres nothing cloudy about the morality, but its source remains myterious.

The central piece here is called The Evil That Men Do. It deals with the Cambodian nightmare, or rather with a book about it, or - rather still - with a review of that book by Salman Rushdie. Rushdie refers to atrocities performed, and boasted about, by a certain Comrade Tek, and says, "How can men become like Comrade Tek? . . . The terrible lesson of our century is that it isn't difficult. I could be Comrade Tek. And so could you."

In jumps Levin to say, with no desire to exculpate the century, that no, we couldn't. We - he and Rushdie and their readers - have all doubtless done shameful things in our time and under pressure might do far worse, but still there is a gulf. Comrade Tek and a handful more are beyond it, writes Levin; the rest of us would never go to the Tekian extreme of tearing out the liver of captured prisoners and then demonstrating the process on live monkeys.

I hope hes right. I cant help thinking, though, that Nazi Germany was able to staff a great number of concentration camps with men who proved capable of sustained inhumanity. They cannot all have been monsters from the outset. Some of them must initially have been responding to pressure - propagandist pressure, peer pressure, fear pressure.

What interests me, though, is Levin's next point. "Some people are evil; are evil, not are made evil." Don't blame heredity or environment because some people have a propensity to criminal behavior by reason of what they wish to be, not of what has been done to them. Why do they wish it? Because, like Comrade Tek, given the choice between good and evil, they choose evil. But this simply moves the question back a stage. Why do they choose evil? A "propensity" (Levins word) is something youre born with. And something you're born with, like something you're born into, is not your fault.

Now, according to Levin, the cry its not our fault is the sickness, and may prove the destruction, of our age. But what his argument really seems to point to is that nothing is really anybodys fault. And, though it makes me nervous to say so, I have to say that it's a conclusion I find inescapable. Nobody is fundamentally to blame for anything. Of course we cannot live our lives on that basis; we have to judge, and if Comrade Tek were in my power I should have no compunction about consigning him to any punishment that was available. But perhaps we should think of justice merely as one of society's modes of self-preservation, and stop being hypocritical about it. Nothing is more nauseating (and here I suspect that Levin would agree) than the judge who, having passed sentence, complacently lectures his victim.

If, as is probable, Levin is thinking of a morality that transcends human judiciaries, he still raises intractable problems: questions that 700 years ago came near to fazing Dante. Having depicted the damned in his Inferno, he could not avoid asking how anybody could deserve such unending torment, not merely permitted but decreed by a beneficent God. He could only still his own questionings by invoking a doctrine of predestination that even in the Middle Ages required a supreme act of faith to accept. Most of us today find it hideous, but we have yet to come up with an alternative.

Levin and I were colleagues for a time; at least we were both theatre critics for leading Sunday newspapers. We didn't fraternize much, coming from different generations and different traditions, but I do have pleasant memories of being goosed in the National Theatre and turning to find a beaming Bernard chortling, "Aha! The opposition!"

I enjoyed reading him when he was flaying something pretentious, but I found the Higher Levin difficult to take. Any play that could be construed, however fancifully, as having reference to God or art seemed assured of a rave; actually, for Levin, God and art were identical, and before Peter Shaffer's Amadeus, which invoked both, he practically prostrated himself. To judge from his tribute in the current book to a short-lived West End piece called J. J. Farr (about a rationalist who sees the error of his ways), he is still at it.

But prostrate prose does not become him. He is insufferable on music where soprano-and-conductor worship has supplanted any pretence at analysis or even description, better on books than on plays and on things than on books. I can take or leave his reviews, but my first action on picking up a copy of The Times is to see if there is a Levin column. If there is, I devour it immediately. So, I imagine, does everybody else. Robert Cushman is former theatre critic of The Observer.
1989-07-04-jazz-reviews-jazz-divas-serve:
JAZZ REVIEWS Jazz divas serve up musical feast

Tuesday, July 04, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Due mainly but not entirely to the du Maurier Jazz festival, last week in Toronto was a continuous feast of singing.

At either end of the week in Roy Thomson Hall were the accredited jazz divas Sarah Vaughan and Cleo Laine. In between, delighting a smaller group for one night at Harbourfront was the cult vocalist of them all, Sheila Jordan. And just next door, independent of the festival, Harbourfront kicked off its summer season of offbeat stars with a week of recitals by Barbara Cook, Broadway ingenue turned cabaret madonna.

All of these ladies, now in their sixties, are formidable technicians. A lot of notes got polished, a lot of octaves spanned.

They share a basic repertoire of jazz standards and show tunes, though none of them drives through the centre of it in the manner of a Sinatra, Bennett or Fitzgerald. Rather, they chip away at its edges.

I missed Sarah Vaughans concert but what I read about it suggested that she is still, as always, subordinating sense to sound. Like Ella Fitzgerald, she can move you if the arc of her musicianship happens to coincide with that of the lyric, but this is likely to be more chance than design.

Ella, whom I find more congenial because less overwhelming (she could never sing opera as Vaughan conceivably could), seems a more sensitive interpreter because she ornaments less; you could trust her with a joke. Vaughan may be a riot in private life but her singing rarely betrays a hint of a sense of humour.

Ella is really two singers: unbridled scat-artist and simple balladeer. Sarah is always herself, compulsively (or helplessly) inventive, which may be why diehard jazz fans prefer her. Of course, the grandeur of her tone can be overwhelming; there are at least two oft-thumbed ballads, The Man I Love and My Old Flame, on which I have never heard her surpassed.

Cleo Laine is all kinds of singer. In forty years, almost, as Britain's top vocalist she has done dance bands, musicals, poetic song-cycles, a spot of lieder and a lot of pop. On Saturday night, though, accompanied by husband John Dankworth and his quartet, she was back to her roots, beginning with a salvo of Gershwin and ending with a medley of Ellington.

Her Gershwin arrangements must go back 20 years, and she seems to be singing them note-for-note the same; she is not an improviser. Rather than exploring a song she decorates it with frilly preludes and codas apparently designed to prove that she is more than just another vocalist riding a familiar war-horse.

Her spouse's penchant for chamber jazz, sturdy but polite, seems to have rubbed off on her. She can sound affected, which is odd since in the important things she is unaffected. She can handle comedy; as it happens, her repertoire on this date didnt give her humour much scope but at least her links between songs were delightfully down-to-earth. It is another shared Dankworth trait, and, I chauvinistically believe, a British one. And she can handle passion; for so studied a performer, she delivers a majestic blues. She irradiates Ellingtons Sophisticated Lady with stabbing single notes of pain and anger. She selects her dark tones with the care of an actress.

That sonority, like Sarah Vaughan's, is the source of widespread popularity. Sheila Jordan, another singer of phenomenal range and control, is never going to challenge them in the lullaby stakes. She sings unyielding bop lines, and her preferred accompaniment is a solitary bass, generally manned by a virtuoso named Harvie Swartz. These spartan tastes make her records easier to respect than enjoy, but in person she proved a surprisingly warm performer. She was apt to bend in low towards the bass, as if about to lock horns with it, and she carried on a genially flirtatious relationship with Mr Swartz.

Sometimes she seemed unnecessarily stark, prefacing a Billie Holiday selection with impromptu blues about the Lady's persecution by the New York cops. Its her job to move us with the song, not the legend. But then she proved she could, and overall she showed that she was into songs, not just sounds. Her high and hauntinng Baltimore Oriole was memorable, and she made Oscar Brown Jr.s Dat Dere a persuasive ode to her own daughter.

Barbara Cook is not jazz, and probably doesn't intend to be, though her buoyant rendition of Sooner or Later (a rhythm ballad rescued from Song of the South, Disney's cartoon of the Uncle Remus stories, which was withdrawn from circulation through racial sensitivity) made you wonder how she would fare with backing less formal than she gets from Wally Harper, a fine man in the Broadway-pit and supper-club mold. Their showboating Sweet Georgia Brown, replete with a few needless bars of scat, does everything but swing.

What Cook does best is to distill the essence of musical theatre: that is, to be musical and theatrical at the same time. She can do this with an isolated standard (Arthur Schwartz's I See Your Face Before Me was lovely) but her strongest suits are drawn from her own Broadway wardrobe: Dear Friend, a complicated song from She Loves Me that she makes crystal clear, and the enchanting Mister Snow from Carousel.

Harry Connick Jr. is a ringer in this company, being young, male, and mostly a pianist. At the Diamond last Monday night he played an intoxicating couple of sets, in every keyboard style from Bourbon Street to Birdland, with a lot of stomping boogie-woogie on the way. (He also brought on Branford Marsalis in the kind of last-minute surprise that makes a festival festive.) From time to time he sang. He mooned Satchmodically through I've Got the World on a String; he orated Come Fly with Me, with only a bass and his own snapping fingers, which seemed fated not to work bbut took off through sheer ebullient insistence; and he hunched over the keys to croon There But For You Go I, an elusive song from Brigadoon in a subfusc rendition that lingers as potently as any of the full-throated singing that filled the rest of the week.
1989-07-05-book-review-prince-of-the-gre:
HAROLD PRINCE AND THE AMERICAN MUSICAL THEATRE BY FOSTER HIRSCH Cambridge University Press 187 pages, $29.95

BOOK REVIEW Prince of the Great White Way: a stagestruck showmans story

HAROLD PRINCE AND THE AMERICAN MUSICAL THEATRE BY FOSTER HIRSCH Cambridge University Press 187 pages, $29.95

Wednesday, July 05, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

REVIEW BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Cambridge University Press kicked off its Directors In Perspective series a few years ago with studies of Adolphe Appia, Gordon Craig, Meyerhold and Peter Stein. Appia and Craig were basically design theorists, and Stein, though greatly talented, has an unfortunate effect on the theatre academics who write this kind of book: they use him as a stick to beat the Anglo-American theatre, its audiences and its reviewers, who have been known to treat the visiting giants work with less than the obligatory reverence.

There were no English names on the list except Peter Brook, whose volume has yet to appear, and who commends himself by working mainly in Paris and having ideas. Gordon Craig doesn't count, for he hardly directed a thing in his life. Why, I asked, with what I hoped was a disarming blend of philistinism and xenophobia, could we not have books on the directors who actually did the work - Trevor Nunn, say, or Hal Prince?

There is no sign of a book on Nunn, but Prince has now got his and it's excellent. Cole Porter and Rodgers and Hart scores, than Prince himself would be, who dismisses them as antiques that are only revivable as curios." Hirsch is more temperate: "If it no longer speaks out of a current sensibility, a well-performed Rodgers and Hart book can still entertain . . . the frothy book has the courage of its unimportance. Hes dead right.

The musicals that Prince has direced - stretching from A Family Affair (1962) to Roza (1987), with some rather more famous and successful names en route, have by contrast the courage of their importance. More exactly, they have the intelligence of their ambitions - which, in the case of Cabaret and Evita and the six shows with music and lyrics by Stephen Sondheim, are considerable. They are not pretentious, and they are not self-consciously experimental. They all give the impression that their creators, having unusual stories to tell, simply lit on the most appropriate theatrical means. The Sondheim-Prince Pacific Overtures, to take the furthest-out example, blends the forms of Japanese Kabuki and the American musical because its subject is the rape of the old culture by the new.

Most people who write about musicals are silly; others are human computers who know the date of everything and the value of nothing. Hirsch is one of the few who never denies either his brain or his appetite for fun. He sees that musicals are to be judged by different standards from plays or operas but not by lower ones. This makes him the ideal commentator on Prince, who is a mixture of explorer (not visionary) and showman. Abbott, who today is an active centenarian, was Broadways grand master of farce and melodrama as well as of musicals; Prince, who began his career in Abbott's office, learned from him pace, discipline and clarity.

When Prince turned producer, with The Pajama Game in 1954 (he was 26), he became his master's employer, and Abbott worked for him too on such other super-formula shows as Damn Yankees and Fiorello! Abbott also directed A Funny Thing Happened On The Way To The Forum, but had to call in the greatest of the choreographers (and another Abbott disciple), Jerome Robbins. It was Robbins who directed the two most ambitious of Princes early productions, West Side Story and Fiddler On The Roof, both of them fluid, impressionistic social canvases. Princes greatest achievements as a director, from Cabaret to The Phantom Of The Opera, combine Abbott's stagecraft with Robbins' scope.

With Cabaret and Phantom, Hirsch classes Princes direction of Follies, Pacific Overtures, Evita and Sweeney Todd. He excludes A Little Night Music for its linear conventionality and, though hes not quite forthright about this, Company, for its brittle script. He had doubts about Sweeney Todd, too; he seems to doubt that Prince's overlay of social combat on the industrial age was really relevant to the show's Grand Guignol story (hes right) and he questions the universality of Sondheims stated theme of revenge (he's wrong). The musical does not quite add up. Maybe it has worked better in its later chamber stagings. And yet, in memory, it seems an extraordinarily big, bold achievement.

There is also a chapter on Prince's recent acknowledged failures: Hirsch pays encouraging tribute to the underrated Larry Grossman, who composed two of them. (He was also the musical director of The Muppet Show, which makes him a hero in my house.) And, rounding out his general study of the musicals to include the post-Prince generations, Hirsch is fair to the Lloyd Webber shows that Prince didnt direct: Cats and Starlight Express are entertaining high-tech vaudeville."

Any book about Prince must in part be a book about Sondheim, and Hirsch, in limited space, offers the shrewdest Sondheim criticism yet to appear in book form. He also holds out a tantalizing promise of a renewed collaboration, after a lapse of eight years. This is how he sums the partners up: "Both are stagestruck showmen weaned on a romance of the Broadway big time that they have never outgrown and that helps to explain their drive for continued achievement, and for critical as well as popular acceptance. In terms of their record they qualify as theatrical elder statesmen, but both cloak their hefty egos in an appealing modesty.

One of Hals favorite words in rehearsal," Sondheim once said, "is energy - by which he doesn't just mean energeticness." Prince's energy - and his energeticness - pervade this book. Robert Cushman is former drama critic of the Observer, London.
1989-07-12-sir-laurence-olivier-on-stage:
Sir Laurence Olivier On stage, he seemed indestructible

Wednesday, July 12, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail A few years ago Laurence Olivier played King Lear on television and made me cry. This should not, on the face of it, have been surprising. Here was the official great English actor of his generation, maybe of the century, in the greatest tragedy in the language. But among all the qualities attributed to Olivier that of being moving had never ranked very high. Exciting, witty, hypnotic, athletic, protean: these were adjectives nobody ever denied him. He was, from the 1930s to the 1970s, the master of the British stage. But the Lear, a decade after his last appearance in the theatre, was something else.

Physically shrunken, he seemed to have a new moral authority, a new simplicity, an amazing lack of self-consciousness. Part of the effect was in the implicit homage paid him by the other actors in the cast. Leo McKern, a major actor of the generation immediately junior to Olivier's, played Gloucester; and scuttled to his masters side with the duty a fine actor might pay to a great one. Players like Dorothy Tutin, Diana Rigg, John Hurt and the late Colin Blakely, added to the tributary effect; and the faithful, loving Cordelia was played by Anna Calder-Marshall, an actress who almost personifies goodness. Her tears sparked everybody elses. Like Lear, Olivier had lost his kingdom and discovered love. That may seem sentimental, but the parallel was close enough to be affecting. And for those of us who grew up on his name, and admired him without ever being able quite to surrender to him, it was a cathartic release.

There is a story about Olivier, rehearsing for a charity matinee at London's Royal Court Theatre. He was due to re-create one of the Court's, and his own, greatest triumphs: Archie Rice, the leering, self-hating music-hall comic in John Osbornes The Entertainer. He suddenly appeared in the stalls in full costume and makeup and muttered to the director, "this is really me, isnt it?" He identified, apparently, with the hollow mountebank in Archie; and the identification allowed the performance to go beyond the obvious thrill of seeing a classical actor impersonate a low comedian. When the film version resurfaced on TV recently, I reflected that I had never had less trouble believing in an Olivier performance. All the glittering technique was on display but it never obstructed the truth. In fact, it was part of the truth.

Some of this may, at this moment, sound ungracious. It isn't meant to be. But I have to acknowledge a difficulty in dealing with Olivier: one that I think may be characteristic of my generation. The classical performances that placed him on his pedestal, at the Old Vic just after the war - Oedipus, Hotspur, Richard III - were before my time; though when the Richard appeared on film I was ready for it and was duly devastated. I wasn't moved; but then I wasnt asked to be. I was hypnotized into aghast complicity with this lank-haired monster with the iron-filing voice. Above all, I was amused. His soliloquies, delivered straight at the camera in defiance of convention, were a cinematic breakthrough. On reflection, they were a breakthrough period. I have rarely known an actor to achieve such audience rapport, even in the theatre.

The makeup, the cleverness, the impersonation - this was acting. His contemporaries, John Gielgud and Ralph Richardson, by contrast seemed distant, mannered, always themselves. As time went on, this unchanging humanity is precisely what I came to treasure in them. When Richardson died, I felt a sense of personal loss. I found Oliviers centre harder to locate. This is, of course, precisely what some of his greatest admirers - most notably Ken Tynan, who should have written his biography - most valued. One problem is that Olivier was largely absent from the London stage during the 1950s. I didn't get a good sustained look at him until he took up residence as first director of the National Theatre in 1963. And by then he was a living legend: a myth that dared you not to believe, and in doing so made belief harder. You sat there silently saying, Prove it.

He must have felt this burden himself. Certainly he never ducked a challenge. The burden of running the National for 10 years he shouldered magnificently, establishing a genuine classic repertoire and bringing on new generations of actors, playwrights and even directors. There were rocky periods but some of it seemed like a golden age, and in retrospect it all does. There has never been such a glittering muscular acting ensemble in Britain, and nobody else would have had the technique and the application to bring it off. He directed few plays himself, but one of them - Chekhov's Uncle Vanya in the first season - was the greatest production I have ever seen. He himself played Astrov and his duets with Michael Redgraves Vanya were, among much else, a superb display of mutual respect at the highest level.

His classic performance at the National, though, was his Othello. This was a triumph of vocal and physical control, as well as being a white mans consummate appropriation of negritude. It turned off as many people as it turned on. I felt, and still feel, hopelessly equivocal about it. The performance wanted to impress, and it did. It wanted to overwhelm, and sometimes it did. I assume it wanted to move, and it didn't. But I realize, 25 years on, that I have never seen an Othello to match it. Actually, I have seen few Othellos at all; the Olivier dust has yet to settle. The role needs the size that he gave it; the words shrivel in anybody else's rendition. And perhaps everything else is unimportant.

His other major roles at the National - Shylock, James Tyrone, the Captain in Strindbergs The Dance of Death - evoked the same mixed feelings. I resisted what were plainly intended as their emotional peaks, while acknowledging that nobody else could even have built the scaffolding. He played some gleeful cameos in Restoration and other comedy; again it was difficult to judge if they were more or less funny for having his name attached. He went out, predictably unpredictable, as a working-class ideologue in Trevor Griffiths highly political play The Party. Officially, it was a supporting role and Griffiths spoke to me endearingly of this "ambulant black hole" entering the rehearsal room and effortlessly sucking all energy toward it while making elaborate attempts to be inconspicuous.

Actors who worked with Olivier, even younger ones theoretically distrustful of him, invariably ended up worshipping him. (Directors tended to be warier.) My only personal encounter with him concerned a TV documentary for which he vetoed the idea of filming National rehearsals because "it always makes the director look clever and the actor a fool." He was always protective of actors, and they, as the Lear showed, returned the compliment. He ran the National from an actor's point of view which, in these days of director-power, was a valuable gesture, maybe an invaluable precedent. His last years, as everybody knows, were wretchedly shadowed by illness, but he seemed triumphantly to overcome one setback after another. He seemed, in fact, indestructible. As with his life so with his death: I am not sure whether I am moved by it, but I feel an immeasurable sense of shock. Robert Cushman was theatre critic of The Observer in London from 1973 to 1984.
1989-07-13-music-review-show-tunes-ideal:
MUSIC REVIEW Show tunes ideal for summer night

Thursday, July 13, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail AND NOW, said John McGlinn, raising his conductors baton over the Toronto Symphony at the Ontario Place Forum, "we'll give the folks over the hill a run for their money." McGlinn was presiding over a concert largely devoted to the Broadway songs of Rodgers and Hart, and rock music had been wafting competitively through the mountain greenery.

Admission may be free, but in other ways you pay heavily for the balmy atmosphere down by the lake. A huge circular amphitheatre is not the best environment for an evening of sophisticated song, especially with soloist and orchestra being whirled slowly and inexorably on the rotating platform to give every spectator a fair fragment of the action. McGlinn promised that his singer Kim Criswell would treat us to the pungent, full original lyrics of Bewitched and so she did, with perfect clarity; but our isolated chuckles could hardly jell into a homogenous response.

There is on the other hand a perpetual joyous youthfulness about the R& H catalogue that sits very well on a summer night. It infects even the sadder, more mature songs, such as the bittersweet masterpiece It Never Entered My Mind, which was taken at an unexpectedly brisk tempo, Criswell singing with a most effective toughness enhanced by some piquant interjections in the accompaniment.

What we were hearing, here and throughout, were the original Broadway orchestrations, long thought lost and now being reinstated by McGlinn with missionary zeal. Symphony orchestras give him a bigger string section than was ever penned in a Broadway pit; these gentlemen seemed to be having fun, and we got the essential keyboard duo who provided a fascinating contrast in visual styles, one intent and the other laid-back. McGlinn has already worked similar restorative magic on the music of Kern and Gershwin; he conducted the complete recorded Show Boat over which I rhapsodised some months ago, and this Rodgers and Hart programme is the warm-up for a forthcoming album of the songs with his Show Boat leading lady Frederica von Stade. Wasn't this, I inquired when I met him next morning, a little hard on the deputising Criswell?

Kim, he said, "is doing all right." She has recorded two Cole Porter shows for him: Kiss Me Kate (not due out for a year) on which she sings Bianca and, coming in October, Anything Goes on which she has the Ethel Merman role.

McGlinn is a plumply dapper thirtysomething New Yorker, still delightedly surprised at being able to make a good living fulfilling a personal dream. Criswell, who substitutes a trained mezzo belt for the instinctive Merman bray, has the air as well as the voice of a modern soubrette; from the perplexing angles at Ontario Place she looks a bit like Bette Midler. And she is alleged to hate Love Never Went to College, a song McGlinn says he loves. I'm with him; in its cheeky precocity it's the essence of Rodgers and Hart. But on The Lady Is a Tramp, the number with which McGlinn threw down his gauntlet to the acoustic disturbances, everything came together - words, music, voice and players - for four gloriously confident choruses. This repertoire, given interpreters who both know and care what they are doing, just refuses to lie down.
1989-07-22-two-stout-giants-of-the-scree:
ZERO MOSTEL: A BIOGRAPHY BY JARED BROWN Collier-Macmillan, 334 pages, $31.50

Two stout giants of the screen

ZERO MOSTEL: A BIOGRAPHY BY JARED BROWN Collier-Macmillan, 334 pages, $31.50

Saturday, July 22, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

CITIZEN WELLES: A BIOGRAPHY OF ORSON WELLES BY FRANK BRADY Collier-Macmillan, 655 pages, $34.95 REVIEW BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Two fat volumes about two fat actors: one man who played Falstaff and another who should have. The Zero Mostel biography, to be truthful, is no more than becomingly stout; the Orson Welles is positively obese.

Both actors possessed deep, rolling voices that were among the most distinctive of the century. Welles, marinated in oil and honey, courted us from his early radio triumphs down (in every sense) to his efficacious TV commercials for sherry. He remains the only major movie director who can claim the recital of his closing credits as part of his legend. His habitual sign-off since radio days ("Obediently yours, Orson Welles") could only be matched for bland, patrician irony by Duke Ellington's repeated declarations that he did indeed love us madly.

Mostel's irony was more of the harsh, blistering kind. He was a teddy- bear with teeth. His biographer claims that the impact of his clowning was primarily physical while admitting that it was an impact too overpowering for film. On the evidence of The Producers, Mostels one totemic movie, he is right; Mostel is funny, yes, but leeringly, disconcertingly grotesque. From the one time I saw him on stage - as Leopold Bloom in an overblown Broadway revival of Ulysses In Nighttown, the Joyce adaptation that had established him off-Broadway in the fifties - I recall his inspired mime of martyred disgust when required to enact the line Bloom kissed the oozing, suppurating wounds of the veterans.

Otherwise my Mostel memories are vocal ones. I recall the introductory voice on the Broadway cast album of A Funny Thing Happened On The Way To The Forum, promising us Comedy Tonight: "We shall employ every device we know in our efforts to divert you." The promise held more than a hint of threat: we were to be steamrollered into hilarity and would very possibly die laughing. He struck the same note in Fiddler On The Roof when he told his wife, to whom he was about to relate a bad dream, Dont get frightened - it could bring on a heart attack, such solicitude. He spoke slowly, massively, in capital letters, as befitted his bulk; he sounded like the archetypal wise fool but genuinely wise, magisterially soothing. His Tevye the dairyman was plainly a great performance.

But he didn't give it for very long, at least not in its pristine form. There is debate about this, but the concensus seems clear: Mostel, blooded as a nightclub comic, quickly got bored in a stage show and began improvising lines and business, to the frequent delight of the audience and the consternation of his authors and colleagues. Jack Gilford, his co- star on stage and screen, once feelingly described to me how he suffered from Mostel's more aggressive antics: "I used to think, hes doing this to me and Im his friend; what would he do if I were an enemy?" (I suggested that if he had been an enemy, Mostel would probably have left him alone. Gilford seemed to think there was something in this.) Gilford, way back when, recommended Mostel for his first club engagement. Much later Mostel reciprocated by backing Gilford for his role in Forum. Besides being life-long friends both men were victims of the Hollywood blacklist. It skewered Mostel's career, probably accounting for much of his insecurity, though he sometimes claimed that it was a blessing in disguise; it allowed him to get on with what he really cared about, which was painting. It is also something of a boon to his biographer; it gives him something to get his teeth into, and Jared Brown (himself the son of a blacklisted actor - one who did not bounce back) duly supplies two incisive chapters.

Many of the Commie-hunting congressmen were plainly concerned with their own advancement, but the corruption of the proceedings is actually less disturbing than the absurdity. As Mostel himself inquired, What sabotage could actors be accused of - giving acting secrets to the enemy? And then the writers - they were accused of peppering their scripts with subliminal subversion that escaped the studio bosses but could somehow influence the great American public. Just what was going on in the mind of Laurence Johnson, the Syracuse supermarket king who blackmailed the TV sponsors? In Harris' words, he "would remove their products from the shelves of his supermarkets unless they agreed to fire the artists he named."

Even more terrifying than Johnsons blacklist was his whitelist, the roll of actors he approved of. No one worked without Laurence Johnsons consent. It must have done wonders for his ego, but plainly more than vainglory was at stake. He, and the thousands who thought like him, were simultaneously fuelled by a blind hatred of "Communism" - the word, rather than the thing - and a prurient, very American obsession with show business. Everyone wants to be a casting director.

Mostel managed to reconstruct his career but played it cautiously, lambasting the world for its philistinism but sticking himself to commercial products. There is no need to lament his involvement with musicals (both Forum and Fiddler are classics), but Brown plainly wishes that he had risked some of the classics he kept talking about; they might have bolstered a career that seems now to boil down to five shows and two movies. Falstaff he might or might not have encompassed, but he would surely have been superb in Moliere, as a comic obsessive, and defintive as Azdak, the holy vulgarian of The Caucasian Chalk Circle.

He and his wife fought constantly but were totally interdependent. On stage and off he felt compelled to be the centre of attention. Brown makes you love him and hate him on alternate pages. In the end, though, with Mostel dying on the brink of a probable artistic breakthrough as Shylock in Arnold Wesker's The Merchant (typical Wesker luck, by the way), you give in and are moved.

Mostel's career intersected once with that of Orson Welles, who was to have directed him opposite Laurence Olivier in the London production of Eugene Ionescos Rhinoceros. An awful accident - he almost lost a leg to a rampaging bus - kept Mostel out of it, but he triumphed in the play in New York, transforming himself from man to rhino in full fascinated view. Brown judiciously criticizes the play - its allegory is too pat - while Frank Brady, Welles new Boswell, tosses off the word "masterpiece."

Brady is not to be trusted on plays; at one extreme he thinks King Lear's howl, howl, howl, howl comes in the storm scene, and at the other he doesn't know what a curtain call is. He teaches film at an American university but hes no fount of enlightenment on that medium either; he lists Howard Hawks as a producer rather than a director, and discusses The Magnificent Ambersons with what seems like mild distaste. He may love it, though; with a style like his, its difficult to be sure. My favorite sentence among many: "Welles had long been interested in Bertolt Brecht's brilliant but thus-yet-to-be-produced The Life Of Galileo, upon which the latter had collaborated with Charles Laughton." That Galileo, he couldn't do a thing for himself.

That a man who writes so badly should be teaching anything anywhere is depressing. I suppose, though, that he has to be congratulated on pulling Welles overlapping projects into some kind of order, though in a career that defies chronology, more dates would have been helpful. And toward the end he gets us not only sad but angry at the moneys refusal to bankroll Welles for projects that could hardly have lost more than the commercial dodos that they finance all the time. He reveals that at the memorial ceremony Welles' long-time Polish mistress succeeded in making a few sycophantic skinflints thoroughly ashamed of themselves.

Welles escaped the blacklist, though his progressive views and his involvement with Roosevelt's Federal Theatre Project would certainly have qualified him for it. Perhaps it was felt that he had already blacklisted himself, or that the Hearst press, incensed by Citizen Kane, had done it for him. Louella Parsons, who worked for Hearst, and Hedda Hopper, who didnt but liked to be helpful, were McCarthyists before the fact (and during and after it as well). They couldnt get Kane banned, but they virtually ensured its box-office failure, thereby dooming Welles in Hollywood. Studios expected him to lose money, and made certain that he did. So they stopped employing him altogether.

He connived a bit at his own downfall but only on one film (It's All True) does he seem to have been truly irresponsible. Otherwise his cinematic career appears to me blameless, quite apart from the fact that it encompasses three masterpieces - Kane, Ambersons and the Falstaff picture Chimes At Midnight - plus the immensely enjoyable Touch Of Evil and his acting contribution to The Third Man. Nor can I condemn him for his nomadic, epicurean lifestyle; when he could not enliven the world with his work, he did so with his personality. Brady, obviously a very nice man himself, makes his hero appear curiously innocent; and he probably was.

It's difficult to see, though, why he didnt return more often to the theatre, which would surely have been glad to have him. His Mercury Theatre productions in the thirties sound mouth-watering, though Brady hardly conveys the excitement of his British Moby Dick in 1955, which Kenneth Tynan said dwarfs everything London has seen since, perhaps, the Great Fire. Tynan, a founding Welles cultist, is curiously ignored in this book which dismisses him as "the caustic and stuttering young drama critic." We do, in compensation, get the gorgeous prose of Welles first theatrical employer, Irish actor Michael Mac Liammoir, who wrote of his protege: He was precisely what he himself would have chosen to be had God consulted him on the subject.

This youthful self-confidence suggests nobody so much as Charles Foster Kane ("I think it would be fun to run a newspaper"); and it is amazing, considering his choice of title, how little Brady makes of the connection. Citizen Kane is of course as much Welles as Hearst, some of him prophetically so; that accounts for some of the film's power and much of its gaiety.

There are a few people with whom all the world is on first-name terms. Blossom Dearie used to sing, courtesy of the late Johnny Mercer, "When I mention Orson, I refer to Bean and not Welles." But she was kidding. Orson Bean must fend for himself; the name is bespoke. And how many other Zeroes are there? The answer is in the question. Robert Cushman is former drama critic of The Observer.
1989-08-01-broadway-star-brings-impressi:
Broadway star brings impressive repertoire to Toronto The songs of Bernadette

Tuesday, August 01, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Bernadette Peters may be the last of Broadways great leading ladies. She is about to play Toronto as half of a two-star package at Roy Thomson Hall, opposite Peter Allen. Opposite may not be quite the right word. "We wanted," she says, to work really together. So they start off the evening with some joint numbers; she does some stuff, then he does; and the last segment reunites them.

Following which, presumably, they live happily ever after.

The Allen section includes some songs from Legs Diamond, last season's superflop musical which he both wrote and starred in. Musicals flop easily on Broadway these days, so it is quite possible that out of context these numbers will have much to say for themselves. But show-fanciers may be more intrigued by the Peters repertoire. They should certainly be impressed by the Peters track record. I estimate that in the last five years, six successful new musicals have opened on Broadway. She has been in three of them. They were Stephen Sondheim's Sunday in the Park with George, Andrew Lloyd Webbers Song and Dance, and Sondheims Into the Woods. For each of the first two she won the Tony Award as best actress in a musical, surprising nobody. Actually her performance in Sunday in the Park ranks with Angela Lansbury's in Gypsy: simply the best I have seen in any musical.

Peters' Broadway career is actually on its second lap. Born in 1948, she started performing informally at the age of five ("I sang in front of the TV set"), joined the actors union at nine (I was in a play directed by Otto Preminger - it closed out of town) and went on the road at 13.

She started studying acting at 17 and decided, "Hey, this is cool, this is for me." Cooler still was her appearance, shortly thereafter, at an off-off-Broadway coffee house called the Cafe Cino in a spoof of the thirties Busby Berkeley movie musicals entitled Dames at Sea; she was Ruby Keeler.

From there she went into summer stock, and then into a disastrous musical with Bea Arthur called A Mothers Kisses from which she was fired just as the show was hitting the road. For this, she had turned down the off-Broadway transfer of Dames. When she called the Dames producers to say that she was now available, they told her politely that they had hired somebody else. Oh, she said. "That's great." And she meant it. (I was 17. I had such ethics.) The somebody else was Sandy Duncan, who promptly landed a role in a bigger show - one that ran, this time - and Peters found herself back at the centre of a sizeable cult hit. "People would say, 'Youre the hottest thing in town, and I would say, 'I am?' But I certainly knew more people all of a sudden."

She finally made it to Broadway playing the lead in a musical version of La Strada; it ran for one night. "Suddenly I wasnt so hot any more," she says. She stayed warm, though. The highlight of a string of near- misses was Mack and Mabel, a musical with a terrific score, a problem book, and a great posthumous reputation. It cemented Bernadette Peters performing image as that of a resilient waif: a potential legend waiting for the right setting.

The memory lingered during a 10-year absence from the theatre, spent mainly in California. On television, she did comedies, dramas and game shows. She made movies: she was superb in Pennies from Heaven, and wasted in the film version of Annie. She was playing the Fairmont Hotel in San Francisco when the offer came from writer-director James Lapine to take part in the workshop of Sunday in the Park.

Her specialty in her early roles had been wide-eyed appeal. She patented it as the imaginary movie queen in Dames at Sea, and developed it in Mack and Mabel, playing a real-life movie star who came to a bad end. (The bad end was one of the show's problems.) The innocence began to be edged with toughness, and the kind of worldly wisdom that is bred by necessity, out of self-defence. This appeared most poignantly in Pennies from Heaven; in her recent shows the image has matured and deepened.

In Sunday in the Park she was Dot, mistress and model of the pointillist painter Georges Seurat, by whom she was bewitched, bothered and explosively bewildered. Frizzy-haired above a square-cut gamine face, she was impossibly attractive, with a personality that lit rockets. She had a song called Everybody Loves Louis which she sang on leaving her artist for a less demanding baker; the mood was bravado with severe misgivings. Words and music bristled with quickfire jokes and tell-tale changes of mood. She made every point with coruscating precision, but the song never fragmented. It remained a shimmering, immaculate whole, and so did she. She embodied, in a new mould for the 1980s, a fundamental truth about the musical: wit, especially when combined with vulnerability, is very sexy.

The attack is that of a traditional Broadway soubrette, but the sound is new: modern, bruised, post-rock. It also adapts well to a Cockney accent. At least it did in Song and Dance, whose song component was virtually a one-woman show for her: the saga of an accident-prone English girl at large in the United States. She switched from nervously reassuring letters home (very funny) to stabbing fury at errant lovers to yearning arias of regret like Tell Me on a Sunday. Sunday seems to be her day.

The partnership with Peter Allen stems from the 1982 Oscar show when they both appeared in an Irving Berlin medley.
1989-08-28-academics-and-theatre-people-:
Academics and theatre people come to praise (or blame) Shaw

Monday, August 28, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail "This," said one delegate to the Guelph University talk-in on Bernard Shaw , "is the nicest conference I have ever attended." He was an academic, and they know about junkets. Part of his point, though, was that university people were sharing the occasion with theatre professionals and theatre journalists, and all three groups were rubbing along famously.

Guelph split the sponsorship of the event with the Shaw Festival . Last Wednesday and Thursday were spent on campus; the caravan - actually a large bus - then moved on, to mingle with the tourists for two days at Niagara-on-the-Lake. (There may also be native Niagarans, but nobody ever actually sees them.) By this time, everybody was literally unbuttoned. Jackets were discarded, and with them went neckties, name tags and long pants. Scholars and directors stalked the streets, bare-kneed and anonymous. You may put it down to the heat. I think it was the encroaching camaraderie. Some people blamed Shaw.

Well, no, they praised him. They praised his friendliness, ebullience and unquenchable optimism. There were demurrers, most of them British. Irving Wardle of the London Times, delivering a paper on recent English stagings of Shaw, disclosed that there had been embarrassingly few of them and diffidently suggested that his unfashionable upbeatness was the cause. London's last Shavian sighting was a West End revival of You Never Can Tell and Toby Robertson, who directed it, was on hand to confess himself as being, in this context, an amiable fraud, or at any rate a skeptic. He had actually directed very little Shaw, and had got tired of hearing the professional Shavians tossing around such words as genius. Actually not words like genius: the word itself. Shaw was all very well but comparisons (Shaw's own especially) with Shakespeare and Mozart were impossibly inflated. If Shakespeare was Mozart then Shaw was Salieri. There were audible intakes of breath at this analogy; Robertson had Gone Too Far.

Professor Dan H. Laurence, editor of the Shavian corpus (official) and custodian of the Shavian repu tation (unofficial but floridly energetic), arose to do battle. If the British theatre despaired of doing Shaw, then that was the British theatre's fault; from what he himself had seen, it had forgotten how. Here in Canada Shaw had his own theatre and the tradition was safe: preserved by the old actors and diligently imbibed by the young. Belligerent though he was, he had a point or two. I would count myself a Shavian - largely because Shaw makes me laugh, and his prose rhythms are compulsive - but a couple of years ago I attended a Royal Shakespeare Company production of Misalliance that was like travelling the Road to Damascus in reverse. Suddenly I knew exactly how the doubters and the haters felt; the man just would not shut up. I dreaded the mention on stage of any new topic, because I knew that somebody would infallibly and interminably start sounding off on it. But the fact was that the actors had forgotten how to orate. They have the same problem with Shakespeare. It can only, given the instinctive distaste for rhetoric of the modern TV- bred performer, be conquered by practice, which is born of continuity. Hence the ironic advantage of Niagara and Stratford, Ontario, over comparable theatres in Britain, where long-term casting is a nightmare.

The Shaw Festival is, when you think about it, a pretty funny idea. Or a pretty Wilde idea: to dedicate one national theatre to a foreigner may be accounted generous, but to do it twice looks like desperation. But it has worked out, largely because the patron saint's annual contribution has been severely rationed. Christopher Newton, the festival director, said in his inaugural address to the conference that Shaw is harder to do than Shakespeare, which surprised me: I have always believed (I still do) that nothing is harder than Shakespeare. Shaw, being nearer to us and almost maddeningly explicit, should be a doddle. But a later Irish playwright, Hugh Leonard, said that Shaw must be a dream to speak and the devil to act; and this, I think, is part of what Newton was getting at. He spoke of constriction, of Shaw limiting the space around characters: "in Shaw you have to fight for the right to pause" and the plots - meaning how the characters progress beneath the dazzling surface of their dialogue - are difficult to enact. (He instanced the Don Juan in Hell segment of Man and Superman which, being pure debate, is extreme but crucial.) Newton has the knack of sounding self-critical, and fallible, and totally sure of himself. Even when he says he has got something wrong, you feel sure he will get it right next time.

Since the theatre's mandate is not just Shaw but plays written in his lifetime, Newton has the opportunity to preserve a century of drama: plays written for a tradition of acting that was, until recently, second nature to the English-speaking theatre and that Niagara may be able to prevent from slipping away, down the lake and over the falls: a tradition of eloquence and high comedy. It's a pity that Shaw's one successor in wit and confidence falls outside the time-frame. I mean Tom Stoppard, who has added to the glitter a modern vein of self-doubt. But that may be there in Shaw as well, an inner conflict obscured by the dazzle. Even if it isn't, we might do worse than pretend that it is, a hidden play within the apparent one. The gaiety will still remain to infect productions, audiences and future Shaw conferences.
1989-10-02-royal-shakespeare-company-adv:
Royal Shakespeare Company advertising for help

Monday, October 02, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

London ENGLAND -- BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail LONDON And what, inquired one of Britains more prominent theatre directors, "is the word on the street about the Royal Shakespeare?"

He was asking me? Still, I ran down the list of rumored candidates for the most prestigious arts vacancy in the United Kingdom.

Terry Hands, current artistic-director of the Royal Shakespeare Company and associated with the RSC for as long as anyone can remember, is stepping down as of 1991; and his job is being advertised in the national press. Qualifications are vague (a distinguished artist is called for) and salary unspecified, though, as one actor acidly remarked, it will be large.

This public advertising is itself an unheard-of phenomenon; company power has previously been transmitted by a form of apostolic succession. However, the RSC is generally perceived to be in a state of artistic and financial disarray, and there is no inescapable heir-apparent within its bulging ranks of youngish associate directors.

There are fashions in these things. At the moment the company's successes are being used against it, cited not as encouraging signs of breakthrough but as sad reminders of past glories.

An outstanding success is Othello, directed by Trevor Nunn at the Other Place, the legendary shed that for more than a decade has been the company's Stratford-on-Avon studio space. It is about to be pulled down, supposedly to make way for a custom-built replica operative in two years time.
