It has certainly gone out in style. Nunn once directed a terrifying stripped-down Macbeth in this room; for Othello, scenting a different kind of writing, he has gone to the opposite stylistic extreme, setting the play firmly and with abundant physical detail in the nineteenth century.

Ian McKellen, who was his Macbeth, is now his Iago; where once he involved us in his surrender to evil, he now keeps us at a mesmerized distance from a man wholly immersed in it. Charming when he needs to be, lucid in dialogue and in soliloquy, he is still scarily opaque, giving no more away than Shakespeare himself did.

If there is a clue, it appears to be a corroded bisexuality; he can fascinate his wife Emilia without loving her, and he is himself dazzled by Othello. When he tempts the Moor with "beware, my lord of jealousy" the irony is that Othello is as yet free of that passion, while he himself is enslaved to it.

Iagos tend to come in two varieties, Machiavellian enchanter and bluff NCO; McKellen combines them. He recently played Hitler on TV, and has kept not only the malignancy but hints of the mustache. His power is that of the consummate parade-ground sadist: equally adept at bullying and coaxing.

Othello is Willard White, the Jamaican-born opera singer who played Gershwins Porgy in Nunn's memorable production at Glyndebourne. This is not merely his Shakespearean but his straight acting debut, and though his tone never gives out, his phrasing sometimes does. But the essentials - pride, assurance, bull-like bewilderment, and the essential counterpoint of crudity and nobility - are all there, and the production, ruthlessly well cast, is craftily designed to cushion him. His Desdemona, Imogen Stubbs, seems at times excessively flirtatiously girlish but when she engages with Othello, pleading for the discarded Cassio with exquisite tactlessness, you feel exactly the qualities that have enraptured the Moor and will now destroy him.

Zoe Wanamaker as Emilia is a wonderful embodiment of rough-tongued loyalty; when she turns on Othello at the end - saying, as Granville- Barker once put it, all the things we have been longing to - she brings the audience's emotions to boiling point and a little over.

She is actually more moving than Othello himself. But maybe that is as it should be. The characters who get to us in Shakespeare are not the enthroned protagonists but the lesser figures who suffer with and for them. In which connection Clive Swift, an RSC stalwart from the 1960s, makes more of Desdemonas bereaved father Brabantio than any actor I have seen.

He is probably the only actor ever to make anything at all of her ineffectual uncle Gratiano. This doubling means that he has the rare privilege of announcing his own death: a minor heartbreak but one more element in the masterly orchestration of the last scene.

The production moves from its short season in Stratford to another at the comparably intimate Young Vic in London. All tickets are sold, but returns would be worth lining up for. Failing that, and for the world in general, it is due to be filmed, and will undoubtedly turn up on television.

There must be many who dream of Nunns permanent return to the company he led triumphantly through the 1970s. It seems unlikely; most of his recent career has been devoted to giant musicals - Les Miserables, Chess, and assorted Andrew Lloyd Webbers - of which he has now three running on Broadway and four in the West End.

The latest is Webber's Aspects of Love, which has been given a sleek, cavernous production that sits oddly on what was surely meant as a chamber musical. Based on a novel by one of the Bloomsbury group, it is a daisy- chain of achieved couplings and frustrated yearnings. The crowning romance is between two people who, as far as the audience is concerned, have barely impinged upon one another. Once again, the new British musical demonstrates its indifference to dramatic design - and also its prefabricated idea of emotion: if you're in love, you sing loud.

The theme tune, Love Changes Everything, turns up in every situation, suggesting one of those old-time song titles with its second half in brackets: Love Changes Everything (But Nothing Changes Love). In the second half, though, Webber does manage one pleasing song in Rodgers and Hammerstein style that had me - for the first time at one of his shows - nodding my head and murmuring "nice.".

In this context, Nunns Othello, like his Porgy, is not only a triumph but a considerable personal relief. (And his next project, the resuscitation of The Bakers Wife, a U.S. musical that died on the road, is awaited with real interest.) For the RSC, if not Nunn, then who? Bookies' favorite is Adrian Noble, for some years the company's boy wonder, whose stock must have risen dramatically last week when his production of Ibsens The Master Builder opened to almost unanimous raves.

Before that, he had given us The Plantagenets, latest in an honored line of Shakespeare marathons, being three plays carved out of the Henry VI trilogy and its sequel Richard III.

The pattern was set 25 years ago by The Wars of the Roses, drawn from the same sources, and some things remain unchanged across the decades: doughty barons, weeping queens, smoke-filled battles and identical- sounding fanfares. Plus the presence of a diminutive magnetic actor - Ian Holm then, Anton Lesser now - as crookbacked Richard, and Lesser succeeds, where his predecessor faltered, in making his play a true climax to the cycle.

Nobles staging, always inventive, reached virtuoso levels here. What was missing was personality, and even skill, in those around him; most of the same actors seemed a lot happier to me in Kaufman and Hart's 1940 romp, The Man Who Came to Dinner. British classic companies have a touching faith in the appeal of vintage U.S. comedy, not alwaysshared by British critics; this one was generally panned as dated and patronizing. It is indeed both those things, and I loved it.

These shows were at the operation's London end, in the unloved and unlovely Barbican. Meanwhile, the Stratford company, outside of the elite Othello corps, was being damned for incompetence. From what I saw, their main vice was simply inexperience; a lot of them, given the chance, are going to be good. In the enchanting Swan theatre, dedicated to the plays of Shakespeares contemporaries, they kept me happy with Marlowes perennially perplexing Dr. Faustus and Ben Jonson's Epicoene or The Silent Woman, bilious, hilarious, rare, and welcome.

One actor, David Bradley, an untrumpeted mainstay of the company for years, made Marlowe's devil and Jonsons misogynist quite the nicest characters around. You couldnt help warming to him because he was so good at what he did.

Whoever takes over, the RSC needs to be preserved. It is a national - at times, an international - resource that will not come again. It needs to regain its confidence in Shakespeare, whose plays are its identity as well as its trademark. And it needs to get out of the Barbican into a more welcoming London home. Almost any theatre would fit that description, but the ideal, in ambience and tradition, would surely be the Old Vic. Are you listening, Ed and David?

The RSC's founder, Peter Hall, has recently moved into the West End and set up a line from there to New York, His initial production of Tennessee Williams's Orpheus Descending, with an endearing bravura performance from Vanessa Redgrave, is now a Broadway success, and The Merchant of Venice follows shortly.

American Equity has finally agreed to let Dustin Hoffmans Shylock be supported by the British cast that supported him in London. New York will, I think, be proud of its favorite son. His is a quietly authoritative performance (not small-scale, as all the London critics had it), only overstretched by the rhetoric of the trial scene.

An initially listless production - with picture-book sets that can only be Halls concession to the tourists, since they have nothing to do with his established Shakespeare style - snaps suddenly into life when Antonio, at their first encounter, spits in Shylock's face. It's like activating an electric field. Our sympathies go to Shylock (certainly no one else has much claim on them) and remain there.

To that extent it's a soft-centred production, but Hoffman himself never sentimentalizes. He suffers in piercing moments, but he hates at length - and I can report that in London both emotions carried cleanly and clearly to the back of the dress circle. His Willy Loman a few Broadway seasons ago was a virtuoso job: the performance of an actor with technique to burn. In his Shylock, everything is concentrated on the job in hand.
1989-10-04-pop-review-dome-can-t-daunt-e:
POP REVIEW Dome can't daunt electric pair

Wednesday, October 04, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail They were two tiny, strutting dots on a small platform, somewhere at the bottom of a huge, tiered canyon. You had to watch them on the big video that unfolded above their heads, and that is not what you go to a live concert for. The sound system was muggy, though mysteriously sharper for him than for her. All the same, Frank Sinatra and Liza Minnelli , performing at Torontos SkyDome Monday night, were magnificent.

In his solo set, Sinatra padded over the stage as if he owned it. Apologies for the staleness of that image, but he is a proprietorial performer. He owns the members of the orchestra; he more or less conducts them with his singing and surveys them during the instrumental breaks with confident paternal pride. (Appropriately: Frank Jr. is now his musical director.) He adopts the audience, with an ease that in any other singer would be insufferable, and of course he takes possession of the songs.

Some very good singers can persuade you that they have written every word they give voice to. Sinatras authority is different. The song is a pre-existent entity, and he displays and explores it. He can find beauty in the strangest places; someone should make a study of the way he sings the word "and, coming down very hard on the final consonant. The chat in his act is kept to a blessed minimum - he seems to be saving himself for the important business of singing - but he did at one point refer to our great library of American songs" and he seems, after some years of floundering with repertoire, to have found himself as its curator.

He meticulously credits composers. Before embarking on For Once in My Life, he announced it as the work of Orlando Murden and Ronald Miller "whoever the hell they are. (They are the guys who wrote For Once in My Life. They have no other identity.) But mostly the names are Rodgers, with both Hart and Hammerstein, Arlen and Mercer, Cole Porter. There are nostalgic lapses from this standard, but he lightly mocks Strangers in the Night (doesn't even say who wrote it) and tells us that when he first heard My Way he didn't like it. I always knew he had taste. The song is, and always has been, atrocious, but the way he sings it now, shorn of bombast, it is hard to resist.

The voice, variable in recent years, was excellent Monday, compensating for the missing high notes with gravelly low ones. He no longer sings the songs of old age in which he specialized when he was merely approaching it, and he takes extraordinary chances. He managed, for example, the entire Soliloquy from Carousel, with every mood in place and strength in reserve for the climax. And there were other songs that he has recorded superbly but which I never expected to hear him do live: Come Rain or Come Shine, and Cy Colemans wonderfully taut and carefree The Best Is Yet To Come. These performances find him at his most commanding and exuberant, riding and cresting exhilarating orchestrations by Don Costa and Quincy Jones. He credits arrangers as well as writers, but he establishes a different stage relationship with them. He seems to be calling the orchestral figures into existence as he goes. It is a truism that Sinatra has perfected the art of singing directly to and for the listener. But he does it less by direct address than by telepathy. He imagines the song inside his head, and it reaches you. How many thousands of times has he sung One for My Baby? It still comes alive.

If Sinatra has drawn back to jazz, Minnelli, the compulsive extrovert, has found herself on Broadway. She can act, and is at her best when doing so with uncomplicated panache (Some People, from Gypsy) or daffy wit (Sara Lee - yes, about cakes). She also offered a disco version of Losing My Mind that suited the songs nightmare quality surprisingly well, especially as she kept the lyrics crisp against the beat. She still can be tempted into the maudlin or the melodramatic - two stark Charles Aznavour laments sounded melodically identical, but then French songs do - but these tendencies are held far more likably in check than they used to be.

When, by way of overture, the band struck up a few bars of New York, New York, I fell to wondering whether Sinatra or Minnelli would sing it. In the end, they both did, as the climax of a strange closing set: one that was probably rather hastily stitched together after the hospitalization of co-star Sammy Davis Jr. A Guys and Dolls medley threatened to become a recital of the entire score in a rather peculiar order, and when they came to alternating their trademark songs, it was apparent that he had a lot more of them to draw on than she.

Sinatra is not one of nature's duetists, nor is he of an age to compete with Minnelli's compulsive trouping. As she cavorted, he uncomfortably stood, and for the first time in the evening he blew lyrics.

I always knew these were good for something," said Minnelli, winning all hearts by removing her eyelashes. "They're for catching bugs." Ground level at the Dome was an insects' paradise; this, plus the acoustics and the distance and the fact that the orchestra sounded like it was playing on an adjacent planet, drove some people to ask for refunds. This, to understate matters, was a shame. I want these performers to come back, some place where I can see them better. Or just where I can see them.
1989-10-05-in-person-the-flagship-of-new:
IN PERSON 'The flagship of new writing in Britain' hits Toronto

Thursday, October 05, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail TONIGHT, THE Canadian Stage Company presents the English Stage Company. It all happens at the Bluma Appel Theatre in the St. Lawrence Centre; Toronto theatre has become very confusing.

As for the English Stage Company, nobody in Canada has ever heard of it. Thats forgivable; neither has anybody in England. But if mention were made of the Royal Court Theatre, where the ESC has hung out since its inception in 1956, then there would be recognition. For some reason the name of the company has never taken, but the theatre always has.

Max Stafford-Clark is not shy about his theatres importance. "We are the flagship of new writing in Britain," he says. I call it his theatre, since he has been its director since 1979. He also directs the two linked plays that the Court is presenting in Toronto. One is a Restoration comedy, George Farquhar's The Recruiting Officer. The other is a new play, Our Country's Good, by Timberlake Wertenbaker, which upheld the best Court traditions by winning all the major awards for best new British play of 1978.

The new play is actually about the old one. Based on The Playmaker, a novel by the Australian Thomas Kenneally, Our Countrys Good deals with the first play ever to be presented in Australia, which just happens to have been The Recruiting Officer. It was acted in 1789 by a group of transported convicts. It was undertaken as a form of prison therapy, and some of the tension in Our Countrys Good comes from the conflict between those officials who foster and approve the experiment, and those who regard it as the dangerous mollycoddling of proven criminals.

The sympathies of Wertenbaker, Stafford-Clark and company are hardly in doubt and the play ends as an affirmation of, in the director's words, the power and enduring worth of theatre. The Recruiting Officer is a good play to be affirmative about. Stafford- Clark's synoptic view of English drama is "if Shakespeare takes the gold medal, Farquhar is well in there for the silver." This may sound extravagant; Farquhar died at 29, having written a handful of comedies. But they are among the most likeable and actable in the language, and his maturity might have been staggering.

He does have the Shakespearean quality of humanity; he paints a broader social canvas than his contemporaries, he is concerned with sex as more than boudoir-hopping, and his dialogue can make you laugh even in reading. Actors seem to love playing him. Stafford-Clark has become not merely his fan but, in a strange way, his friend. During rehearsals he kept a journal in the form of an imaginary correspondence with his deceased author, which has been published under the title Letters to George.

Its a great play, George, writes a relieved director after the first run-through.

Affirmation is needed at the Royal Court these days. "In the last few years," Stafford-Clark says, weve dropped from seventh to sixteenth place in the national subsidy league. This is alarming for what is generally regarded as Britain's third national theatre, the contemporary counterpart to the classic orientation of the National Theatre itself and the Royal Shakespeare Company. The Court has been caught in the crossfire between local and national subsidy, each refusing to give more money until the other makes a move.

The Court used to present up to a dozen productions a year; now it's down to four. Is there a danger of its closing altogether? Stafford-Clark says no, though he admits that Napoleon would have said as much about the likelihood of a retreat from Moscow.

Thirty-three years ago, two months after its inception, the Court presented Look Back in Anger, and as far as popular mythology is concerned its still John Osbornes theatre. It has been patron and protector to a long line of subsequent writers: Arnold Wesker, John Arden, David Storey, Edward Bond, Christopher Hampton, Caryl Churchill. Not all of them still write for the Court, and its record is marked by bitter feuding as well as by fruitful collaboration.

Stafford-Clark, who is in his late 40s and has been in the driver's seat for 10 years, is still regarded by some of the old guard as an intrusive juvenile. Educated in Dublin, he made his reputation in the sixties as director of an experimental theatre in Edinburgh. Many of the plays of the seventies and eighties that I most enjoyed were Stafford- Clark productions: Howard Brenton's Magnificence, Snoo Wilsons The Glad Hand and, the most widely known and exposed, Caryl Churchills Top Girls. He also forged a valuable exchange link with Joseph Papp's Public Theatre in New York.

He is unusual in having made a front-rank reputation purely as a director of new plays. The Recruiting Officer was a new experience for him, the first time in 10 years he had worked without a living playwright at his elbow. (Hence, in compensation, the charming and informative Letters to George.) But doing occasional classics is a Court tradition, inspired by "the importance of measuring the standards of new writing against the past," (his phrase) and by box-office necessity.

In this case the economic imperative was twofold; doing The Recruiting Officer in tandem with Our Country's Good enabled him to engage a comparatively large cast for both. We have 10 actors. Its a knife edge. You couldnt do The Recruiting Officer with 9, and we couldn't afford 11. Even so, there is a bit of doubling, some of it across the gender line. You might say that Our Country's Good was created in workshop except that the director has come to distrust the term. "Its become a new verb - to workshop - being a way in which limping plays are eased into existence."

Joint Stocks best work transcended that, and so does Our Country's Good. It's the accredited work of a rising playwright. Wertenbaker, incidentally, is of Basque-Canadian extraction; and the plays designer, Peter Hartwell, rated by Stafford-Clark as brilliant but too self-effacing to be fashionable, is wholly Canadian.

Research is a directors prerogative as well as an author's. Stafford- Clark's imaginative involvement with Farquhar has led him to research eighteenth-century theatre, and to realize that the classic comedies were written for a theatre at least as intimate as his own. When the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, was rebuilt it became a forcing-house for spectacle, and dramatic writing went into a long decline. We're still suffering, he says, from the building complex that has made the major new theatres in London and elsewhere into arenas that can be filled only by star turns, whether from actors or designers.

The Royal Court is a 400-seater inhabiting a part of Chelsea in southwest London that was fashionable in the days when London supposedly swung, but is off the beaten show-biz track these days. The productions will have to be blown up a bit for St. Lawrence Centre. But if they live up to the promise inherent in their authors, director and cast, they should be treats.
1989-10-21-the-shavian-mask:
BERNARD SHAW VOLUME II: 1898-1918 THE PURSUIT OF POWER BY MICHAEL HOLROYD Random House, 422 pages, $36

The Shavian mask

BERNARD SHAW VOLUME II: 1898-1918 THE PURSUIT OF POWER BY MICHAEL HOLROYD Random House, 422 pages, $36

Saturday, October 21, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

REVIEW BY ROBERT CUSHMAN The first panel of Michael Holroyds official Shavian triptych was subtitled The Search For Love, and brought its subject as far as marriage. The last instalment, due in two years, has already been tagged The Lure Of Fantasy, and here we have The Pursuit Of Power. The divisions, though necessary, are arbitrary. The three goals were constant and indivisible.

Shaw, believing himself unloved in his childhood and achingly unforgiving about it, was astonished to discover in his late twenties that he had power over women, and was never thereafter able to relinquish it. The mastery he sought was mental rather than physical, but it was certainly sexual. His marriage, contracted when he was 40, was unconsummated, and he drew the line at adultery, so fantasy increasingly ruled. The biggest fantasy of all was his pose of being above emotion. He described vehement sexual passion as "an experience which it is much better, like the vast majority of us, never to have passed through, than to allow it to play more than a recreative holiday part in our lives." That's a neat trick, if you can manage it; Shaw, despite his public protestations, never could.

With his erotic life on hold and his playwriting career still to take wing, Shaw immersed himself in politics. He had done time in London local government, but he increasingly devoted himself to the Fabian Society, the intellectual pressure group that saw itself as the responsible vanguard of socialism in Britain.

Fabianism - pressing its advice on any politician, regardless of party, whom it deemed worthy of it - was presided over by the mole-like Sidney Webb, buried deep in bluebooks and pamphlets, and his censorious wife Beatrice. The most respectable of revolutionaries, they seem in retrospect a slightly risible pair, and must have done at the time. They especially disapproved of H. G. Wells, Shaw's junior rival as a popular prophet, whose public image was as lascivious as Shaws was puritanical. Shaw, who regarded Wells as his protege, was torn between admiration and disapproval.

Wells was perfectly capable of quoting Shavian scripture for his own diabolic purpose: You have it from Mr. Bernard Shaw, he told the Fabians, "that poverty is a crime, and if so, then by the evidence of your balance-sheet ours is a criminal organization." Orthodox Fabianism was for Wells the politics of fantasy; and Shaw was more than half-inclined to agree with him. With his customary self-destructive love of paradox, he campaigned for the removal from the Fabian executive of the Old Gang, himself included. In the end, he went, but the Webbs stayed.

Frustration upon frustration. But love, power and fantasy were all aspects of the one compulsion, which was fame. And in this quest, on the face of it, Shaw was triumphantly successful: spectacularly so within the confines of this volume. Over 20 years he went from aging young coterie playwright to unquestioned contemporary champ. The period yielded Man And Superman, his first success; Fannys First Play, his biggest initial success; and Pygmalion, his most durable success. There were also such key works as Major Barbara, John Bull's Other Island, and Androcles And The Lion. Shaw found a use for the mask he had been constructing all his adult life: G.B.S. the philosophic joker, illusionless, ruthless, heartless.

Unfortunately for him, he wasn't heartless. Two things in particular breached his defences. One was the First World War. He opposed this from the start. He might have got away with that, but he ridiculed it as well. Even those who sympathized intellectually thought his tone misguided. (They included his fellow playwrights, who had similarly deserted him over the smaller matter of theatrical censorship.) Once again the Shavian myth took over, so much so that when peace came he had to issue a book called What I Really Wrote About The War. By this time public opinion had caught up with him. And what he really felt about the war is summed up in a letter he wrote to a bereaved mother: Oh, damn, damn, damn, damn, damn, damn, damn, DAMN DAMN! And oh, dear, dear, dear, dear, dear, dearest!

The recipient was Mrs. Patrick Campbell, the original Eliza Doolittle and Shaws other nemesis. A monster by most accounts, she emerges here as a victim who extricated herself just in time: when Shaws intentions, after a long teasing (and largely epistolary) pursuit became avowedly carnal. She was a straightforward egotist; he played it hypocritically and self-defeatingly cool.

When he gets in Volume III to discussing The Apple Cart, Michael Holroyd will doubtless have much to say about the way that play reflects this affair. King Magnus there is one of the more transparent Shavian masks, with his tempestuous (and platonic) mistress Orinthia, whose letters he shows to his motherly queen Jemima. "I believe," says the royal secretary, that they make me as sick as they do her. Shaw played the same unlovable trick on Mrs. Pat and his wife Charlotte, who emerges as something less than the all-wise and all-forgiving protectress of earlier biographies and of Shaw's wishful thoughts. The union in fact seems pretty miserable. Neither woman lived up to Shaw's exalted standards of civilized behavior; nor did he.

Holroyd makes few value judgments on Shaws writings (it is barely possible that he dislikes them all), but he is scrupulous in referring them to the life and thought. The test case here is Man And Superman, in which the Artist Man falls prey to the Mother Woman. The terms are Shaws own, though they only become clear in the long and detachable dream sequence Don Juan In Hell. This introduces us to the Life Force, Shaw's synonym for God, and ends with the heroine rushing off crying, "A father, a father for the superman." In waking life, though, she remains unconscious of her biological destiny (it isn't even her dream), and simply wants to get her man. So Shaw has it both ways; but the messianic view of human reproduction comes oddly from a man who had just contracted a marriage plainly destined to avoid it.

It used to be claimed - and Shaw often made the joke against himself - that the characters in his plays were merely mouthpieces for his ideas. Now we see that they are indeed Shavian masks, but emotional rather than intellectual. They body forth his own conflicts. He was a tormentedly autobiographical playwright, closer to Strindberg than to Shakespeare - except, a very large reservation, in his unquenchable sense of fun. The ecstasy keeps the plays alive, but the agony helps.

George Orwell held unarguably that any life seen from the inside is a series of defeats. Holroyd helps us to see that Shaw, despite his posing, was no exception to the rule. Which is not to denigrate the man - with defeats like his, who needs victories? I sometimes missed in Holroyds massively scrupulous account the gossipy involvement that you get from St. John Ervines less responsible life of 30 years ago, but I have only one real complaint. At the end of Holroyd's first volume, and intended to serve for this one as well, is a long list of acknowledgements that includes the name of almost every extant theatre critic. Among this is one John Cushman. I am in a position to assure you that this person is a mistake. That's all right - just don't let it happen again. Robert Cushman writes on theatre for Saturday Night magazine.
1989-10-28-spectacle-it-is-but-thrilling:
Spectacle it is, but thrilling it's not SkyDome's Aida: opera of a phantom

Saturday, October 28, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail YOU ENTER the SkyDome for Aida to find yourself confronted by a Sphinx: a large Sphinx, sure - did you ever see a small one? - but cuddly-looking, with a blandly optimistic expression on its face, and great welcoming paws. Any prima donna would find it a comforting perch from which to agonize and, as the night wears on, several of them do.

When Frank Sinatra and Liza Minnelli played the Dome, the place seemed huge but that literally wasn't the half of it. For Aida the whole arena is in play: the biggest chocolate-box since the Colosseum, housing one of the world's most renowned confectionery entertainments, a luxuriant tale of pageantry and pointless suffering.

This production, with its well-publicized cast of hundreds, may be leaden but it is not inappropriate. What did Verdi expect to hap pen during that endless processional music? The problem is that the rest of the opera is not built to the same scale. Half of it is Racine, and the other half Barnum and Bailey. A production as heedless of expense as this one should probably transport the audience, by a fleet of private helicopters, to some more intimate space - the O'Keefe Centre, say - for the scenes of in-fighting and self-immolation. They could always fly us back again for the curtain-calls.

But then the Dome people have not yet figured out how to deal with the cultural mafia. They supplied the critics with press kits (these are files of waste-paper stuffed with statistics) instead of programs, and seated us in a balcony which gave a panoramic view of the whole enclosure but was several hundred miles away from the action. It is probably a great angle for reporting ball games, but it is no way to respond to live performance. The best that can be said of this perspective on Aida is that those hundreds of ant-sized extras did give some feeling of the kind of society that must have built the pyramids.

Oh yes, there were pyramids on stage, three of them, as well as the Sphinx. They were not as impressive, though. As a back-drop for the old vaudeville cross-talk act of Mr. Gallagher and Mr. Shean, they would have been swell; for a tale of dynastic passion in old Egypt they seemed a bit weedy, a bit camp. There is some attraction in the arguments of the produc tion's conductor and presiding spirit, Maestro Giuseppe Raffa (though none at all in his compulsive use of that title), that opera needs visual allure, though I doubt the wisdom of his statement that if it fails in this regard it will go the way of the Pharaohs. The Pharaohs, on this production's own showing, were very much into spectacle; and where are they now? Where, in particular, is the one whose name was Ozymandias, king of kings? Look on his works, ye mighty, and despair. Or if that doesn't get you, look at the myriad empty seats at the SkyDome Thursday.

Look at the myriad full ones, too - in the SkyDome's house are many myriads - all their occupants glued, as usual, to the video screen, the only way of seeing the singers. Film critic Pauline Kael once noted that one of the few rules in movies is that all pictures set in ancient Egypt are ridiculous. Aida as seen here is one of those pictures. Viewed in close-up, the show seems to be trying for some kind of archeological fidelity, sabotaged by the grandiosity of the music which is unmistakably nineteenth-century European and by the visible discomfort of the extras, cast for costume-size rather than acting ability.

Weight of numbers does not in itself amount to thrilling spectacle, not even with the addition of dangerous animals. (There are fleeting glimpses of a lion in a cage-on-poles and a python draped round somebody's shoulder.) Any decent opera-house gives you more to look at, qualitatively, than this. Half-way through, the Sphinx cracks apart, and the applause this raised was slightly more justifiable than the equivalent raptures at Les Miserables when two bits of scenery slot together. But compared to the witty and sophisticated visuals of The Phantom of the Opera this Aida is a joke: the opera of a phantom.

And how does it sound, through its million-dollar system? Not bad. The orchestra is tinny in the martial passages, which may be Maestro Raffa's fault or even Verdi's, but individual ardors and agonies inspire considerable sweep. One winces, superstitiously perhaps, at the idea of miked opera voices, but Grace Bumbry has enchantingly rapt moments, and the video camera catches her at becoming angles. It doesn't do the same for Amneris or Radames, but all concerned sing on with their professionalism admirably unruffled.

There are also dancers, whose efforts are indecipherable on stage but are revealed on screen as balletic yoga. The screen also gives us surtitles which are admirable. It is good to know from moment to moment what is being sung. Otherwise, subversive thoughts arise concerning the frivolity of a form that employs words while rendering them incomprehensible. The same screen is used during the 30-minute interval to credit the production's sponsors. The show's official dry-cleaners called to ask for a mention. We refused, of course, very much on our dignity, but that call gives the flavor of the event as well as anything could. Actually, as it turned out, their work looked spotless.
1989-11-04-cabaret-communion-its-priests:
Cabaret communion Its priests, parishioners get together to discuss and celebrate the charms of supper club entertainment

Saturday, November 04, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

New York NY -- BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail NEW YORK SOMEWHERE at home I have a boxed set of records entitled Songs of New York. It contains three LPs, so its trawl of Manhattan melodies is extensive. But it is far from exhaustive. Everybody knows that New York is a great place to write songs about.

It has also, traditionally, been a great place to listen to songs. The arrangement used to be that the Broadway stage furnished material, which then turned into popular song. This transmutation happened on records, in jazz clubs, and in diverse establishments where singers and pianists held sway. These joints were variously known as supper clubs, boites, upholstered sewers (a presumably affectionate description current among performers) and cabarets. The last of course suggests Brecht-and-Weill and Juliette Greco to cultural snobs and Liza Minnelli being divinely decadent to everyone else. It is a strange label to stick on the U.S. performance of U.S. songs. But stuck it has, and last month New York beheld its first Cabaret Convention.

Three lunchtimes of panel discussions at New York's Town Hall gave way to three evening concerts with a fourth gala concert lying in wait at the weekend. The convention was convened by the Mabel Mercer Foundation, named in memory of New York's figurehead cabaret singer. Born in Britain at the turn of the century, Mercer arrived in the United States during the Second World War and exemplified the conversational delivery of colloquial lyrics. (That, as far as I can define it, is the genius of the classic U.S. popular song: text and performance.) She had an excellent voice - her records of the fifties, when she was in her prime, are unfussily thrilling - but her style and authority survived its passing. To the end of her life, she could talk in tune. Among her early disciples were Frank Sinatra and Billie Holiday, and her influence has passed into jazz and pop singing. There are even a few rock singers who are Mercerites unawares.

So much for legend. Present reality is that, though there are plenty of fly-by-night rooms where apprentice singers (and experienced ones) can flex their vocal cords, few of them stay around and fewer still pay a living wage. The economics of the game are self-contradictory. When, exceptionally, a performer gets famous - as happened recently with Michael Feinstein - he moves into bigger spaces, Broadway theatres and even stadiums. Feinstein still sings the same repertoire, rooted in Gershwin and Berlin, and he can still, thanks to microphones, sing intimately. But his audience cannot respond intimately, which is half the equation and maybe the more important half. Occasionally - not often - cabaret has had me weeping with laughter and delight, or so touched that I closed my eyes to shut out everything but the voice and my memories. The theatre at its best can hardly do more.

I was in a small room with a drink in my hand. Fellow delegates to the convention deprecated my insistence on this last factor, but I was strengthened in it by the best new cabaret singer to appear in ages, a lady called Andrea Marcovicci. "The drink" she told me "is very important."

Marcovicci sang at the convention, but she also had her own act going in the Oak Room of the Algonquin Hotel, now the flagship venue of New York cabaret. Uncomfortably long and narrow, it still wins on history and ambience. I approached her with some mistrust, engendered by a rather doomy album and by a public image that suggested a thinking man's Madonna. Even her name seemed to promise an overpoweringly throbby romanticism: a veneer that can easily be applied to U.S. love songs but is at odds with their magical informality.

"We are going," she warned us at the start of her Algonquin program, "to wallow." An actress as well as a singer, she had just finished playing Saint Joan; being burned at the stake every night had given her, she said, a new insight into the meaning of the phrase "torch singer." She offered a madcap, self-mocking commentary - the wittiest I have heard in cabaret - between committed cameos of lost, longed-for or unrequited love. It was a Dorothy Parker mixture, and she is the only singer to render Parker's routine pop lyric to I Wished on the Moon, and make it sound as if Parker had actually written it. She never quite moved me, but she surprised, involved and delighted me.

This healthy blast of the new romanticism was balanced by a delightful whiff of the old. Elisabeth Welch is a singer whose New York career goes back a long way: to be precise, to Blackbirds of 1928, the show that gave us I Can't Give You Anything but Love. Shortly after that, she left for Europe, and since about 1933 she has been a much-loved fixture of the entertainment scene in Britain. Only in the last few years have her compatriots rediscovered her. So her career has followed the opposite trajectory to Mabel Mercer's. So has her image: Mercer was housewifeliness overlaid with glamor, Welch is the reverse. As a performer she is supremely likeable (as opposed to the suspect "loveable") and of course she has no need to re-interpret the old masters. Singing Porter, Gershwin or Berlin, she is authenticity personified. Having reached the age where any act must be autobiography, she simply talks to you, in song or anecdote. As well as lighting up the convention concerts, she had her own show at the Weill Recital Room in Carnegie Hall, a room whose elegant simplicity matches her own. The audience reacted to both with a huge collective smile.

Not all the convention performers were as warming as Welch or as bracing as Marcovicci. The curse of cabaret - one that it shares, though it would be horrified to admit as much, with pop and country music - is that it sees itself as the Last Bastion of Love. This can result in emotive stridency, in hard-sell vocal buccaneering masquerading as swing, and in displays of what I can only describe as aggressive vulnerability. All of these were well in evidence at Town Hall. But there were also glories. Jackie and Roy, a jazz duo of venerable youthfulness, pursued a sparkling musical courtship barely dimmed in 40 years. Julie Wilson, the reigning cabaret diva whom I often find too studied in dramatic songs, sang funny ones with regally eccentric force. Sylvia Syms, another veteran whose public persona has all the acerbity of a vat of chicken soup, becomes another person when she sings: toughly sensitive, sharply pointed, subtly rhythmic. (Both jazz and cabaret people love her, which is rare.) Barbara Lea, who started in the fifties and is now a consummate singer of popular songs - she acts from within and swings without sweat - stilled the house with a hushed, architecturally shaped Begin the Beguine (of all stereotyped familiar things). She plays Toronto next March. Weslia Whitfield, a younger, jazz-inflected lady from San Francisco, tried a little too hard but is plainly going to be exceptional. Barbara Carroll, a great unsung jazz pianist, proved also to be a good unsung singer. Two other musicians - Anne Hampton Calloway and Daryl Sherman - upheld the treasured image of the smart, funny woman sitting at the piano. An even funnier female named Julie Kurnitz sang newly minted sagas of misfortune and disgust. She also paid her respects to the classics. "Kurt Weill," she told us, "is one of the great popular composers of all time." She wasn't going to sing one of his songs. She just thought we should know. She was the discovery of the week, and manna from heaven.

It was ironic, of course, that all this cabaret talent could only be accommodated in a concert format that, by definition, is not cabaret. But it was close enough to proclaim the form, and to validate it as the best showcase for a repertoire that is still alive, and still being added to. It has two hang-ups. One is the conviction of the audience that the word "cabaret" signifies something too expensively rarefied for them, or too cheaply sleazy, or even both. The other is the reluctance of practitioners and promoters to accept that they are no longer in the mainstream of show business, with a clear shot at the really big money. There are enthusiastic claims about breakthroughs and changing tastes whenever a young face is spotted in the audience. There is a young audience for cabaret - there has to be, since there is a ceaseless stream of young aspirants to perform it - but it is a minority audience. That does not in itself spell cultural or financial disaster, but it can be hard to adjust to. (Black singers, once the backbone of the craft, are now conspicuously absent.) Mabel Mercer never made millions. But she survived. She still does.
1989-11-28-theatre-review-the-half-of-it:
THEATRE REVIEW THE HALF OF IT

Tuesday, November 28, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written by John Krizanc Directed by Richard Rose Starring Nicky Guadagni and Gordon Pinsent The Half Of It has full slate of problems BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail John Krizanc's The Half Of It is billed as "almost a comedy," and the archness of that should be fair warning. It also counts as unconscionable conceit. Krizanc is messing here with the destruction of the environment and the glamor of greed: topics reasonably likely to wipe the smile off any audience's face. To pull off that trick, however, you have to put the smile there in the first place. Krizanc can turn the occasional neat line, but in the production of his play by the Necessary Angel Theatre Company and the Canadian Stage Company that opened in Toronto last week, he leaves his spectators with little more warming than an embarrassed grin.

Krizanc wrote Tamara, a successful play that nobody has ever actually seen. All anybody remembers about it is the experience of tracking the actors from room to room of a large house and, speaking for myself, the high quality of the gateau they served in the interval. (The cookies at the Stage Downstairs at 26 Berkeley St. cannot compete.) Emerging from it with only a hazy idea of what was supposed to be going on, you decided charitably that the scenes you missed must have been the ones with the story and the characters. Richard Rose, who directed Tamara, must have learned the useful lesson that it's harder to hit a moving target. His Newhouse last year tried to disguise its portentous banality by keeping the audience trekking round the hall and playing everything simultaneously on stage and video. There was no life but there was the illusion of liveliness. Reunited with Krizanc for The Half Of It, Rose has rashly confined himself to a single conventional stage. He tries to disguise the fact with a few nervous gimmicks.

It starts well enough. A young science teacher named Jillson lectures her pampered private-school charges on the progressive degradation of our view of nature: from the primitive tribe who wouldn't lop a branch without asking the tree's permission to the modern acceptance of the principle of Dog Eat Dog. (Nobody, she points out, has ever seen a dog eating a dog, but we go on believing it anyway.) This is all good stuff, pointedly written, and it gains from being acted in front of the curtain, before we get a look at the set.

Soon we are into plot. Our heroine, Jillson (Nicky Guadagni), has been dismissed from her job, her advanced views having disturbed her pupils and their rich mamas. Jillson herself has a rich mama who fears, in the wake of her husband's death, that she may be down to her last million. Jillson's sister inhabits a similar rarefied atmosphere, being a successful real-estate agent. She sort of approves, though, of Jillson's boy friend, whom she describes as "an environmentalist with ambition - perfect combination." He is corrupted when he falls into the orbit of Freddy Boise (Gordon Pinsent), a stock-market entrepreneur with limitless assets and no scruples. Freddy thinks he may be Jillson's father, and his fixation on her unreachable idealism is his Achilles' heel. He also has an amputated arm, which sends him through the play looking successively like Dr Strangelove and Captain Hook.

Jillson and her family own a lot of timber, which they call Birnam Wood, though by the way they react to the idea of anyone chopping it down you would think it was a cherry orchard. Freddy, who by the end of the play has gone slightly off his trolley, is last heard of trying to fell it with his bare hands. (By the way, did you notice that his surname more or less means "wood" in French? There's richness.) All of which, plus the ecology theme, may account for the stage floor being covered with grass even though much of the action takes place indoors. Backing everything are three panels of blue-sky-with-fluffy-clouds, which look remarkably tacky, even before characters start making dramatic entrances by busting holes in them.

Dotted about the acting area are a desk, a bed and some garden chairs, because this is one of those plays that just can't stand still. It hops from one short scene to another, with actors who are naturalistically in one location frequently operating from another. This is all meant to be very fluid and sophisticated and subversive of the space-time continuum, but it just looks messy. The players hang onto handy bits of furniture for dear life. Right downstage and very pleased with itself is a real pool. People keep emerging from underwater.

Now, the pre-publicity has suggested that Jillson is not meant to have things all her own way and that the play presents the attractions of capitalism as well as its deformities. But that is not the way it plays: not with the boy friend asking rhetorically, "How did we get so ugly" (parody? who can tell?), and ol' Freddy bugging everything that moves. True, Jillson is rather a pain, but idealisic heroines always are. Nicky Guadagni does her opening number with a tremulous kind of authority that subsequently gives way to an unguarded and indiscriminate intensity. She pumps her arms up and down at emotional moments. She does have a lot to put up with; at various times she gets pelted with leaves, squirted with water and amorously debagged. To cap it all, she makes a naked, dripping entrance followed by a hasty retreat to the wings. I don't want to sound prurient, but this is cheating. If you are going to make a statement using the human body, you should try not to look ashamed of it. But Rose's production lacks all sense of rhythm. It keeps springing trick effects without knowing how to time them.

Gordon Pinsent as Freddy skims across the play's surface with tactful accomplishment. Sheila Moore and Lisa Bunting play the rich-bitch roles with appropriate creamy smoothness, and Janet Land deals energetically with a young aspirant to the same status. Greg Ellwand and John Bourgeois are stolidly competent as the men in our little girl's life.

She ends the play much as she began it, only making unfortunate references to a drowned-girl motif that the audience has spent much of the evening trying to ignore. Krizanc certainly piles it on, and without the effortful zaniness, the play might pass as an ambitious attempt at serious themes that has no idea when to stop. At least the environmental theme is serious; the rest, unless you actually believe that greed is an invention of the 1980s, is merely trendy. But, as presented by the Necessary Angel and Canadian Stage companies, that isn't The Half Of It.
1989-12-04-theatre-review-the-philadelph:
THEATRE REVIEW THE PHILADELPHIA STORY

Monday, December 04, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

LONDON, Ont. -- Written by Philip Barry Directed by Robin Phillips Starring Nancy Palk and Joseph Ziegler Phillips tells an elegant probing Story BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail LONDON, Ont.

The audience at the Grand Theatre clapped when the curtain rose on The Philadelphia Story, and for once the applause was justified. Elis Y. Lam has designed a drawing room that is a symphony in pearl-grey. With its mirrors, windows and double doors, the whole thing is a touch larger than life but not so as to be overwhelming. Abstract enough to be esthetically respectable, it is still a solid machine for acting in.

The visual pleasures extend to the staging. Nothing in Robin Phillips's production is obviously spectacular, but it is a tonic to see a show in which everybody seems to be in the right place at the right time without having to resort to violence to get there.

As expected from Phillips, the craft supports a probing, elegant view of a play that, if only by default, ranks as an American classic. The Philadelphia Story is Philip Barry's best-known portrait of what one jaundiced outsider describes as the privileged class enjoying their privileges. A Broadway success in 1939 with Katharine Hepburn in the lead, it has reached millions in the film version that teamed Hepburn with Cary Grant and millions more when musicalized in 1956 as High Society. That title, by the way, denotes a certain democratic unease. The accompanying slogan, as I remember it, was "the low-down on high life," suggesting that the rich were there to be goggled at. Barry, born to the money himself, had taken them on their own terms.

Or nearly. One of his lowlier characters, a reporter, does put the surly question: "What right has somebody like Tracy Lord to exist?" thereby raising all kinds of awkward considerations. The immediate answer is that if she didn't, the play couldn't. Tracy is our heroine and the play is her fable: the thawing, in the play's reiterated imagery, of an ice-maiden. A young lady with exalted standards, she disapproves of her father for philandering, and of her first husband for reasons unclear, but she seems to find him lightweight.

We encounter Tracy about to take on a replacement: a foursquare, not to say stuffy, young man who has worked his way up from nowhere to be something big in coal mining. Of course, he is quite wrong for her, and the play's objective is to reunite her with C. K. Dexter-Haven, her number one spouse and social equal. However, before reaching the desired Haven, Tracy has to go through the mud. She (a) gets drunk and (b) imagines that, while under the influence, she has gone to bed with the reporter. This humanizes her.

There is a dispensable major character and a confusing subplot involving blackmail, but your attention is captured from the outset and never released. The dialogue is beguilingly smooth, part of a confident Broadway tradition. At least it seems confident; there are tell-tale glitches. Tracy calls her father "Father," which is reasonable, but he calls her "Daughter," which suggests a straining after style. This, all too obviously, is comedy with heart. It puts up a sophisticated front, but it goes to bed early.

Then there is all the chat about class, issuing in the comfortable conclusion that there is good and bad at every level. A true comedy of manners would ignore the issue entirely or would bore from within, no moralizing. Barry exemplifies the embarrassment of being earnest.

This solemnity can trip Phillips's production up. At times he digs amazingly deep. Nancy Palk as Tracy makes it clear that her frigidity is more than a matter of style; her sexuality frightens her, and the revelation of that fear disturbs her even more. Hers is a good, serious performance with the appropriate rangy looks. But it lacks fizz. Barry, bastardizing the American screwball tradition, assumes a sparkle if he doesn't actually write it, but this Tracy gets drunk without a trace of madness. And this uncertainty bedevils the entire show. Give this cast a line that's actually funny and they will hit it good and clean, but tripping blithely through the barren bits between is beyond them. It may be a lost art.

The most surprising performance is Joseph Ziegler's Dexter. He seems so young: a dark-glassed drifter in a style 20 years junior to the play, and hardly in a position to lecture Tracy on life or love or anything else. But, through sheer wit and panache, he imposes himself, indeed, makes excellent sense. This is a Dexter who resembles a reed but proves a rock. As opposed to George, the intended, whom Peter James Haworth presents as a splendidly complacent hunk, a man who gravitates naturally to platforms. The drawing room has a dais, and he lives on it.

Peter Donaldson's journalist is another reappraisal, not a James Stewart charmer but a roughneck intellectual who looks like Andre Previn redrawn as a prizefighter. Dixie Seatle as his camera-toting partner is thoroughly traditional and a thorough joy, the infallible hard-boiled gal with a heart of silver. Lewis Gordon and William Webster are reliable elders, respectably raffish and responsible. At the other extreme, Tracy's kid sister, played by Marguerite Pigott, seems old enough to be her twin, which has an unfortunate effect on some passages of text that have staked their all on being bewitchingly precocious.

I regretted, too, that economy has dictated the omission of Mac, the nightwatchman, "a prince among men," whose absence severely damages the second-act curtain. All the act-endings, as it happens, are staged with surprising tentativeness. And bringing on balloons and confetti at the curtain-call is no compensation; neither play nor production has been that kind of festive. Besides, on the first night, Friday, some of the decorations descended three whole acts ahead of their cue, which disconcerted everybody. I suspect that the whole show is going to gain in confidence.
1989-12-27-beckett-was-a-born-playwright:
Beckett was a born playwright First time out, he produced a masterpiece

Wednesday, December 27, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Not all authors come to resemble their work, but Samuel Beckett , living on rice and giving no interviews, nearly brought it off. He approached the end of his life as ascetic and unreachable as one of his own plays. Only death itself - last Friday in Paris - has by a typically black Beckettian paradox, spoiled the likeness, imposing a finality that the work itself could never achieve. Beckett's characters court insensibility but never achieve it. He rages, not against the dying of the light, but against its stubborn refusal to go out altogether. He liked low-key lighting effects, but he steered clear of blackouts.

The flaw in Beckett's despair was pointed out long ago. His work appears to emanate from a depression whose logical outcome would be catatonia. But, of course, if you're catatonic you can't write; and if you could, you wouldn't produce anything as elaborately controlled as Watt, his most challenging novel, or Waiting for Godot, his most famous play. Plainly, Beckett used his writing to escape his demons as much as to express them; and the outward shape of his career bears witness to this. He moved from the hermetic form of the novel - hermetic at least as he practiced it - to the inescapably sociable mode of drama. Nor did he cloister himself from the process of production. He attended rehearsals, worked closely with actors, and wound up directing his own plays. The thought of Beckett supervising a technical is a piquant one.

He seems to have been a born playwright. First time out, he produced a masterpiece. What is more, it - Waiting for Godot - was an entirely theatrical masterpiece. It was called anti-theatrical, but only because at the time (the early fifties) that was a fashionable term. There was no plot machinery in Godot, and the characters had no visible means of support. Indeed, their pants kept threatening to fall down. But there we are; they were clowns, and Beckett wrote them two acts of cross-talk, interspersed with slapstick. It is difficult to think of anything more theatrical - anything less calculated to work in any other medium - than that.

Because Vladimir and Estragon await the mysterious and perpetually unpunctual Mr. Godot by the side of a dusty road, it is customary to present them as tramps. Beckett's text, though, makes no mention of this. They might be agricultural laborers. They might be novelists or playwrights; the worst insult in their vocabulary is "crrritic," and they converse with an oddball erudition that Beckett must have encountered, or even practiced, in Dublin pubs and Paris cafs. (In at least one respect he was the last of a line: that of Bohemian expatriates.) Anyway, they are among the few great characters of postwar drama: those who have entered the mythology of actors and audiences. Owing something, surely, to Laurel and Hardy they have in turn influenced such later masters as Tom Stoppard (Rosencrantz and Guildenstern) and Jim Henson (Bert and Ernie). Stoppard has insistently proclaimed his own debt: the reassurance Beckett gave to playwrights lacking in conventional narrative and psychological skills that they could keep a stage alive, largely through making jokes.

Stoppard's jokes are profligate and sunny, Beckett's measured and funereal - which doesn't stop them being funny. But he makes it clear that the joking and the waiting are strategies of escape. Beckett's bums talk to keep from thinking; or perhaps they think to keep from feeling. "That passed the time." "It would have passed in any case." "Yes, but not so quickly." Life is small-talk, improvised to camouflage a void. We will do anything to keep from confronting it, even write plays. The only victory is suicide, which the characters contemplate but never perform. It would, they decide, be a shame to miss out on Godot, who may, like love, be just around the corner.

This terrifying but curiously consol ing view of life is not really capable of development, but it can be refined and explored. Beckett went on prodding it in progressively shorter plays as well as in prose vignettes, such as the pungently dismissive (and very Irish) First Love, that have become favorite party-pieces for his favorite actors. Of the plays, Endgame projects the Godot vision into science-fiction; it seems to take place one week after the end of the world. In reducing human relations to those of master and slave it suggests that Beckett is not as apolitical a writer as some would have us believe.

Subsequent plays are more realistic. True, Happy Days shows us a lady buried first up to her waist and then to her neck in sand, which is not a situation one encounters every day, but the immersion plainly symbolizes an entombment in routine ("Winnie, begin your day") that is all too recognizable. Winnie is even more scared and evasive than the tramps, and a long way further from salvation; even cross-talk has contracted into monologue. The piece called Play scrambles the elements of a sexual triangle into a series of intercut fragmentary confessions from three figures encased in funerary urns. The piece gives us a clear, cruel view of their relationship while also functioning as a study in the psychology of interrogation; each jabbers frantically in response to a harsh beam of light. Not I refines this still further: one breathless outpouring from a disembodied Mouth, addressed to a silent, barely visible Auditor. Footfalls is the most recognizable of all: a self-sacrificing daughter paces to and fro while her mother upbraids her. This is Beckett writing domestic drama while providing us, for the first time in years with, literally, a full-length character. And not only did she have legs, she used them. She seemed pretty miserable doing it, and this may have been the author's joke on his critics. There, he says, that is what movement gets you; don't ask me for it again.

Philosophically, Beckett's plays have had little influence. Or rather, what they say seems so unanswerable that there has been nothing for subsequent writers to do but move on to other areas. Technically, his influence has been immense. He cleared away a lot of debris, and even writers who have backslid into naturalism have economized somewhat on the clutter. In the writing of charged dramatic English, only Harold Pinter and David Mamet have approached him. This is not to deny that his plays can be trying. Their constriction may be wholly justified on their own terms but it can easily be monotonous. Still, even when Beckett is boring, there is something creative about the boredom, nothing soulless or mediocre. And narrow though his range of effects may have been, he employed them with consummate assurance: the greater the economy, the bigger the punch. "Mr. Beckett," I once wrote, "is a gentleman and a showman." I expected some pious demurs to that, but all I got was a warm, approving letter from the late Patrick Magee, who with his creaking gate- hinge of a voice and louring sepulchral presence may have been the quintessential Beckett actor, just as the warm and loving Billie Whitelaw has - because she trusted him - become, in another paradox, the definitive Beckett actress. Let the final farewell be Stoppard's, paying homage at the end of his supremely effervescent Jumpers to his melancholy master: Wham, bam, thank you Sam.
1990-01-18-theatre-review-drinking:
THEATRE REVIEW DRINKING

Thursday, January 18, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Directed by Daniel Brooks Written by and starring the Augusta Company A high-speed merry-go-round for sorry players in a social circus BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail DRINKING, the Augusta Company's new group-authored play at Toronto's Poor Alex Theatre, is a quick and lighthearted look at human misery. The social and marital kinds are especially favored.

It begins forbiddingly. The Poor Alex is, to be frank, a rather dingy theatre, as befits its name, and on Tuesday night the house lights were still dimmed when the audience was admitted. Back in the dear old experimental days of the sixties, this kind of ritual humiliation of the spectator was common form. It was regarded either as well-intentioned therapy or as a suitable punishment for doing anything so bourgeois as going to the theatre in the first place.

Eventually the lights went up, leaving the impression that the whole thing had been a mistake and allowing the audience to read their programs. There was an evangelical tone to the cast bios, which tended to be light on theatre but heavily into health.

Dimly visible at the edge of the stage are seven filled wine glasses, all in a row. Presently the acting area brightens and, one at a time, the actors wander on: four men, three women. Some look bemused and some belligerent. None seems happy. One makes his way to a microphone and suggests getting proceedings under way with a drink. Like alcoholic vultures, the company descends on the glasses and disposes of their contents.

The man at the mike periodically returns to it and gives further orders. This is his party, and the guests are to be regimented into enjoyment. At his bidding, they sing, dance, tell stories: all the things we do to convince ourselves we are having a good time.

No characters are named, either on stage or in the program, but some identities begin to emerge. One lady requests her husband not to drink too much this time, and he sarcastically thanks her for drawing attention to his problem in public. Dancing becomes frenetic, seduction violent, some people fiercely disrupt other people's enjoyment, and in general a good time is had by few.

Oh, what a circus. When the merriment is at its depth, the ringmaster loses patience and tells everybody to start again "and to get it right this time." What ensues is a double-speed replay of the preceding action, foregrounded by a monologue from the host. He, too, has problems. We have already seen a shy young woman commanded to sing, and obliging with an ancient show-tune called Nice Baby. A surprising choice for 1990, but gratifying for musical-comedy buffs. (Early Gershwin? I'm not certain.) But more is involved than nostalgic titillation. The singer is the compere's wife, and the song a commentary on their relationship. She wanted children and couldn't have them. So she infantilizes him instead, and he is not happy about it. In fact, he is cracking up. Such is the state of their marriage. Such, or worse, is the state of all marriages. The show never actually says this, but its whole stance implies it. We drink to forget but all we do is bitterly remember.

Actually the title, despite the elegant introductory image, is a mistake. It suggests a mislaid intention. The show, as we receive it, is not about drinking. That is merely one component in a pretty generalized view of behavior. Still, we get the message; and, were there an interval, bar-takings during this performance might well reach an all-time low. Were there a bar.

There is something of Beckett here, recalling the peremptory stage- direction in Play ("repeat play exactly") and the classic synopsis of Waiting for Godot: "Nothing happens, twice." There is something of the Australian playwright Peter Handke: the opaque revels of The Ride Across Lake Constance. And there is a lot of Mike Leigh. Leigh i s the highly skilled British director of improvised plays and films (High Hopes) who throws people together in unfortunate social situations and watches them comically suffer. His worst fault is a tendency to patronize his characters. Drinking resembles choreographed Leigh; and the choreography (by Claudia Moore) helps to keep portentousness at bay. In a longer show it might have the opposite effect, but Drinking only lasts an hour. By paring down dialogue, Daniel Brooks' direction keeps a neat and clinical distance from any suggestion of real suffering. The show's notions of human conduct are shallow and conventional but the execution is so fleet and twice-over-lightly that you don't have time to resent it.

The actors are loyal and in step. They are Don McKellar, Tracy Wright, James Tait, Claudia Moore, Valerie Campbell, Chris Gerrard-Parker, and David Ramsden, who is sweatily effective as a fat and frightened guy with a guitar.
1990-01-20-theatre-review-best-friends-a:
THEATRE REVIEW BEST FRIENDS AND OTHERS

Saturday, January 20, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Directed by Scott Burke Written by Edie Pistolesi Starring the Harbinger Theatre company In the centre of a dispiriting tradition BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail THE HARBINGER Theatre is a new company, and what it is harbinging is an era of new Canadian drama, building on the best traditions of the past three decades. That, at least, is the substance of its opening manifesto, though the ringing phrases tail off into a few lines of special pleading on behalf of Harbinger's first show, which happens to be written by an American.

Edie Pistolesi's Best Friends and Others is not, truthfully, a script worth breaking one's inaugural vows for. It is a collection of seven vignettes, some of them too slight too qualify even as one-act plays, all standing smack in the centre of a dispiriting tradition. Call it the cult of good-hearted domesticity. However dark it gets, it excludes the larger world. One does not want playwrights to spend their time self-consciously addressing issues - that it is the kind of thing that has been stifling British drama - but one would like to see people on stage with some believable connection to a society that penalizes its poor, lays waste its cities, and finds the damndest ways of exporting democracy. David Mamet and Sam Shepard, neither of them political dramatists in the glib sense, show us such people. Nobody else does.

Certainly Edie Pistolesi doesn't. She is a young playwright, showing some evidence of humor and observation, and may be capable of devloping them. She cites Harold Pinter as an inspiration but leaves out his cruelty, substituting a vague melancholia. Two of her pieces are female monolgues. One woman compulsively devours M & Ms; the other's life revolves around her ironing-board. Well, what's it matter as long as they're happy? And it would be perfectly possible to take the two playlets as defiant assertions of a person's rights to her own simple pleasures. But Pistolesi herself declares that she thrives on subtext. (It is probably unfair to use an author's extra-dramatic statements against her but, given the opportunity, who can resist?). If the text says somebody's happy, the only subtext can be that she isn't. Maybe it's the way we've been programmed, but the message all these plays seem to be booming out is: Oh, look at all the lonely people.

In the neatest sketch, Waiting, a young woman professes herself to be waiting, not unhopefully, for just about everything but especially for Mr. Right. But when he, or an approximation of him, arrives, his timing is off. This is amusingly revealed to us in a blacked-out bedroom scene; climax for him is frustration for her. (This must be a breakthrough; premature ejaculation is usually portrayed, if at all, as the man's problem.) "Damn it," she cries, "why couldn't you wait for me?" That's funny.

Two other segments, like Mr. Right, promise more than they can perform. In one, a waitress is goaded to desperation by a regular customer who takes no interest in the day's special, the salad dressing, her undressing, or anything except the book he is reading. The build is excellent, but then the man turns out to be crazy. (How, exactly, must not be revealed.) But since there is no attempt at exploring him - in this show women are subjects, men are objects - it is a cheap random pay-off.

In the other, a wife and mistress find that their experiences of their common mate are very similar. This is amusing if not very startling, but then it turns out that mistaken identity has been committed, leaving us to infer not just that one man is alike but that they all are. And then farcical melodrama takes over, or tries to.

That leaves us with two unre deemed clinkers. In Spitting Image, a woman, searching endlessly for the son she abandoned at his birth 20-odd years ago, meets a young man searching endlessly for the mother who, and I refuse to complete this sentence.

Supermarket is the title and setting of the finale piece, and the only one to deploy the acting company at its full five-fold strength. A man and woman fall in love over still-frozen chiffon cake, consummate in the car- park and marry in the aisles. Meanwhile, two women compare shopping-lists, the honors going to one whose purchases are dictated by the spirit of Elvis Presley. At the end, these two fantasies coalesce. But we know that supermarkets are not churches, and that their managers are not empowered to conduct weddings, and it would take more wit and imaginative power than this writer can muster to persuade us otherwise. What comes through is that these poor people, symbolizing millions of others, are just shoppers drugged by the mart. It may be meant as a celebration but it plays as a whimsical sneer.

Carol Sinclair, as a manic frump who shops by the alphabet, could get laughs with a jab of her elbow and a gleeful push of her trolley. And since, in Scott Burke's production, this section is largely staged as an angular ballet, she does. Earlier, she plays the importunate waitress, escalating from wounded goodwill to erotic frenzy, and the progessively disillusioned mistress; and she conveys the pain of both without ever losing her comic balance. Strangely, she makes least impact in what should be her tour-de-force as the soliloquizing ironist (i.e. one who irons) but she has an invaluable gift for aerating dubious lines by gently deflecting them.

Nora Sheehan is more inclined to bash them over but she has her moments. Kate Johnston, the one non-Equity player, lacks defintion. Michael Howell, playing the older men, has little to do except beam with varying degrees of self-satisfaction, and Doug Curtis, playing the younger, has less.

If Harbinger needs the excuse, there is nothing here that need seem alien to Canada. The condition of soap-opera, after all, is that everybody can identify with it. Condescension masquerading as compassion is an infallible formula. The clinical description is sentimentality.
1990-01-29-theatre-reviews-unidentified-:
THEATRE REVIEWS UNIDENTIFIED HUMAN REMAINS AND THE TRUE NATURE OF LOVE

Monday, January 29, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written by Brad Fraser Directed by Jim Millan Starring Brent Carver and Lenore Zann Crow's Remains glows with confidence BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Crow's is flying. Correction: Crows are flying. That doesnt look right either. Anyway, the theatre group known as Crow's and based at Toronto's Poor Alex swoops brilliantly into the nineties with Unidentified Human Remains and the True Nature of Love. As titles go, thats a beakful.

It provides a good overview of Brad Frasers play, which is half horror story and half romance. Interestingly, and all too credibly, Fraser's characters are self-conscious about their love affairs, to the point of emotional suicide, while taking the horror pretty much in their stride. They are not monsters. They are, for the most part, well-intentioned people genuinely shocked by what is going on around them. Shocked, but not surprised.

The play is set in Edmonton, Fraser's home town. By the time he is through with it, it has taken on the aura of Dostoevskis St Petersburg. Both are cities made up of back streets. The inhabitants, spiritually isolated, still cling together in unexpectedly close-knit communities. People know one another. In Dostoevskis The Devils, an escaped convict terrorizes the town. In Fraser's play, a psychotic is on the loose, killing and dismembering women.

David (Brent Carver) is a local boy made bad. After fleeing success as an actor in Toronto, he is back and working as a waiter. Or, as he puts it on entering his apartment, Hello, I'm homo. That is cheekily effective exposition, or sexposition. It is the plays first conversational line, and its first big laugh. Later on somebody asks David if he can stop playing the professional faggot. It turns out that he can, which is probably wonderful for his personal growth. But while the act lasts, it gives the audience a lot of fun. David is terrific at it.

His sex life is a series of anonymous, dangerous encounters, given an extra spice by the unremitting threat of AIDS: cruising plus condoms. Scared of commitment, he consistently attracts it. Two theoretically straight men are spooked by him. The 18-year old Kane (Duncan Ollerenshaw) , busboy at Davids restaurant, is dazzled by him, and plays out an agonized, puppyish scenario of advance and withdrawal. Bernie (Daniel Kash), David's long-time buddy, is more ominously fixated. Married and a self-proclaimed womanizer, he turns regularly and bloodily up at his old friend's door, asking for shelter from jealous wife or jealous husbands.

Nor are women immune. Benita (Kristina Nicoll), a chains-and-leather hooker, has at least a sisterly affection for David. Besides being his confidante she is the plays chorus; sex and violence are her hobby as well as her livelihood and she has a telling collection of atmospheric anecdotes.

Candy (Lenore Zann) is Davids flat-mate, and may have been his one heterosexual entanglement. At one admittedly pressured moment she cites him as the love of her life. But she is his female counterpart, besieged by the two remaining characters - an adoring lesbian (Arlene Mazerolle) whom she hurts, and a bartending pick-up (Joe-Norman Shaw), who winds up hurting her.

So far we have a landscape with figures, the most impressive theatrical descent into the urban inferno since David Mamet's Chicago nightmare Edmond. (Recent Canadian shockers have been of documentary interest at most.) But this picture is really animated. It grips as a thriller. Brian de Palma might relish the scene in which Candy finds herself locked in with the fiend of Edmonton. (There are Elizabethan plays, set in what is now a North London suburb, called The Merry Devil of Edmonton and The Witch of Edmonton . Fraser could have used both titles.) It scintillates as a comedy of manners, almost invariably bad, and at times as a bedroom farce, the funnier for being underpinned with real embarrassment and real pain.

Its more conventional bedroom scenes actually have the surprise and abandon of real sex about them. And all these levels are there to support a single theme: the search for love in all the wrong places. If the statement of this theme is more persuasive than its hopeful resolution, that may be the nature of the beast. Or of three related beasts - modern drama, modern audiences, modern life. All take naturally to cynicism and reject uplift.

Jim Millan's production is a feat of verbal and visual orchestration. One bed and one futon - referred to by Robert the bartender as a tofu - do unembarrassing duty for all. Brent Carvers David levitates the play with a wit and insouciance that he never relinquishes. Asked to leave when both Candys lovers turn up at once, he replies, "are you crazy?" and settles in to enjoy the scene.

But as the play peels layers from the character so does he, and he seems to grow older by the second.
