Lenore Zann partners him with comparable crackle, nerves more obviously frayed but the instincts, however she may kid herself, of a survivor. And the others are unfaultable, from the disparate earnestness of Mazerolle and Ollerenshaw, through the doom-laden relish of Kristina Nicoll and the emotional and social clumsiness of Joe-Norman Shaw to the true desperation of Daniel Kash.

There is some glibness in the writing, some portentousness in the direction, but the overall effect is one of triumphant fluency. The show glows with confidence, and it's justified. Today Toronto; tomorrow Edmonton, where the playwright with some audacity will direct it himself. The day after tomorrow, maybe the world.
1990-02-05-theatre-review-echo:
THEATRE REVIEW ECHO

Monday, February 05, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written and directed by Robert Lepage Starring members of Thatre 1774 God takes a wife and He sings in Lepage's dynamic play Echoes of enthusiastic atheism BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail In Echo, God sings. It seems to have been a lifetime's ambition. He stands erect at the mike and, with the falsetto fervor of a paid-up Mills Brother or Inkspot, gives out with a couple of choruses of You Always Hurt the One You Love. A suitable number for Him. If He does love us, what other excuse could He have?

Echo is Robert Lepage's adaptation, apparently a very free one, of Ann Diamond's prose fiction A Nun's Diary. It has been brought to Toronto's Theatre Passe Muraille by the Montreal group Thatre 1774. Like the novels of Joyce or the films of Bunuel, it comes across as a work of enthusiastic atheism, the kind that blooms by reaction in a Catholic culture.

Take another example. Take another song. (The only other song. Nobody would describe Echo as a musical.) Disinterred, like the previous exhibit, from among the lachrymose laments of World War Two is We Three, subtitled My Echo, My Shadow and Me. This has all kinds of resonances. One is historical; if the show has any time-frame it is that of the war. It refers us back to - well, it echoes - the show's title, which might otherwise seem a bit capricious. Which still does seem a bit capricious. It reminds us of Lepage's own directorial virtuosity with light and sound. Nobody uses echoes or shadows more expressively than he does. But really it's the show's mocking acknowledgement, disaffected but still affectionate, of the Trinity. God is a character in the play. This is how He introduces Themselves.

Lepage's set, impeccable as expected and predominantly white, is a high, narrow box within which nestles a bed, on which nestles a married couple. A preliminary voice-over has informed us of their condition and made it sound desolate. They bear this out by indulging in the most loveless love-making yet simulated on a stage. Or he indulges; she endures. For better or worse, it's soon over. What happens next is a dream. This is only revealed at the end. Normally I hate giving things away, but in this case I think you're better off having the information beforehand.

War has broken out, and he dreams of falling in with the German army. The ensuing brutality is tactfully depicted, but still predictably disturbing. The planks of the bed are pulled up, and prove capable of instantaneous transformation from splinters of the cross to splinters of machine-gun and back again. It is all beautifully dexterous but finally not too interesting. The soul of the show is in what happens to her.

She dreams of becoming a nun, in a medieval French convent, she afterward says, but it could just as easily be a modern one. After all, habits die hard. At first she finds the routine mortifyingly congenial, or congenially mortifying, but later she rebels. The Mother Superior, who has literary aspirations, is a particular pain.

This is where God comes in. He is not dead, He has merely got Him to this nunnery. Old and bearded, of course, but still hale and very hearty, He wants a wife. And though nobody explicitly points this out, He has come to the right place. Everybody on the premises is theoretically His bride. So at the show's climax He and the heroine are married, maybe in the convent chapel. And then, as the groom enthusiastically strips and begins vigorously to enjoy the bride, a kind of sinister soot descends from the ceiling, engulfing everyone.

Alerted by the publicity to expect Holocaust imagery, I took it that we were now transported to the gas chambers. The final solution is surely the ultimate question that anyone would wish to put to the Deity. Nothing else here qualifies. If "holocaust imagery" means merely corpses and green uniforms, then terms are being thrown around with culpable looseness.

God has the last, echoing words, peering over the rim of the box at the human cauldron: "I just wanted to see how they were made." Hence His interest in sex: the summation of an attitude to humanity that can most charitably be described as detached curiosity. War, sex and religion make in this piece an unholy trinity. When the male and female dreams intersect, a nun is raped. During the initial coupling on the marital bed (surveyed, of course, by a crucifix), the wife's rosary beads fall one by one to the floor, a recurring note in Lepage's sound-score. The themes are not new, and only Catholics, present or lapsed, are likely to find them shocking, or even particularly provocative.

For the rest of us the fascination lies in Lepage's stagecraft, in the measured, unfaltering accumulation of images, and the inexorable (and truly dream-like) merging of each with the next. Not in the same league as the mammoth, exuberant Tectonic Plates, this is still the minor work of a master. Nobody else in Canada is doing this kind of world-class work. (And nobody in the United States or Britain either. A few in those places are doing other kinds of world-class work but not this kind.) What distinguishes him from the self-appointed prophets of Performance Art is his interest in acting, and his ability to help it happen. Opportunities here are more spectral than in his other works, but they are mostly well taken by a mixed anglophone and francophone cast working in English, some of them doubling across the gender line as nun and Hun. God is good.
1990-02-27-a-slick-and-sleek-dose-of-llo:
A slick and sleek dose of Lloyd Webber

Tuesday, February 27, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail The Music of Andrew Lloyd Webber in Concert, now at Pantages Theatre in Toronto, is slick and sleek. Fourteen formally clad singers sit or stand in a straight line, before 50 musicians of symphonic bent. The vocalists do not get about much, but when they do they move with point. They exert themselves most in the songs from the two earliest Webber musicals, Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat, and Jesus Christ Superstar.

Probably the concert format makes the songs seem more static than they really are, but we do seem to spend a lot of time listening to grandiose, slow-moving ballads. These, of course, are what make the hits.

Webber was famously turned on as a boy by the musicals of Richard Rodgers, and the one that seems to have influenced him most was South Pacific. Webbers love songs all seem to be struggling toward Some Enchanted Evening, conceivably Rodgers's worst song, certainly his most inflated. It has little to do with the actual experience of love, either the fun or the pain, but a lot with how people like to fantasize about it. Passion, tenderness, vulnerability are excluded in favor of a pre- fabricated vision of Romance: Love as the fabled Many-Splendored Thing.

Memory, the Webber variant on the theme, has rather a poignant middle section, but what sold it was its thumping, unrelenting opening, not so much an affair of the heart as a heart attack.

Amplification helps, of course. Webber may have left rock 'n roll behind him but he can still use rock triplets to pump up an emotion. The concert extracts from Joseph and Jesus remind us that once there was hope for the rock musical as a vehicle of theatrical playfulness.

Webbers music bounces, and Tim Rice's lyrics are delightful. You have to forgive the rhyming of "biscuit" with district, a venial sin by most contemporary standards but hurtful coming from a writer who knows how sharp words can be. Joseph's most celebrated couplet on the subject of Pharaohs Dream ("all those things you saw in your pajamas"were a long- range forecast for your farmers) is absent from this selection, but what remains demonstrates both the supreme value of insouciance to the musical theatre and how much it is missed.

There were still glimmers of it in Evita, but you wouldnt know it from this concert, whose mind is on higher things. There is an overture, with Latin touches that do not so much invoke Edmundo Ros and Xavier Cugat as succumb to them. And there is, of course, Don't Cry for Me Argentina, a boring song that has great ironic point in its dramatic context when you know Eva is lying, but which went over big with record-buyers who neither knew nor cared. What we do not hear is the tune's bustling reprise as Oh What a Circus, with its line about Peronism being good for the country in a roundabout way." That kind of mordant offhandedness is what makes a serious musical. Pretentious earnestness, though, is generally better box- office.

In subsequent Riceless shows Webber has had to work harder for his fun. There is some of it in Cats, though Eliots light verse was never really funny. Webber himself has said that the rhythms of the poems more or less dictate the musical settings, which may explain why the music sounds competent rather than inspired. True to form, the concert includes the one really portentous tune in the piece, The Addressing of Cats.

Starlight Express, a more entertaining show than is usually acknowledged, is similarly slighted. Instead of One Rock n' Roll Too Many or the C&W spoof Uncoupled, we are regaled with the reverential title song. This wasn't even a hit.

The second half of the concert is largely devoted to plugging The Phantom of the Opera. The ensemble number Masquerade, bereft of the Hal Prince staging and the Maria Bjornson designs, just dies; being able to hear the lyrics is no compensation at all. But the ballad All I Ask of You actually gains from being set adrift. Heard on its own, divorced from the two uninteresting characters who sing it on stage, it soars. It is not opera, whatever claims may have been made for it, but it is very good operetta.

That is more than can be said for Love Changes Everything, the lung- bursting hit from his latest show, Aspects of Love, which serves as an encore. It is back to Webber's impersonal style, which has given rise to impersonal singing.

The lady singers in this concert work firmly and selflessly in the tradition. Among the gentlemen, Sandy Winsby stands out as a helpful, tactful compere.

It is a good-taste occasion. And that, along with the obvious entrepreneurial genius, is a Webber attribute. (He put this show together, apparently.) At his most poundingly effortful, he never writes anything as desperately bad as The Impossible Dream or whatever you care to name from Les Miserables. Whatever the Broadway chauvinists may claim, this intrusive Englishman has not destroyed the American musical theatre. They did that themselves.
1990-03-09-theatre-review-young-cast-str:
THEATRE REVIEW Young cast struggles to develop Album's snapshots of the sixties Album

Friday, March 09, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written by David Rimmer Directed by Bernadette Jones Starring Laura Partland, Kirk Dunn, Shelley Owens and Bryan Elliot At the Tarragon Extra Space BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail THE PRESS release says: "Modern Times of Theatreworks Productions seeks to reach out to young adults in an effort to reflect their needs and to give young artists a unique opportunity to work in a professional and challenging setting."

These are noble aims, and only a curmudgeon would fault them. But they do entail pitfalls, and into those pits MT of TP has fallen. The cast it has assembled for David Rimmer's play, Album, at the Tarragon Extra Space, is only just professional, and the setting may be a little too challenging.

Also, I am unsure who the young adults are whose needs are being reflected. According to the PR, the magic age range is from 15 to 25, and Album does indeed deal with four kids growing together, apart, and together again from 14 to 18. But the years in which they do it are the mid-l960s, and the play's heavy reliance on the sounds and icons of that era may make it of greatest appeal to today's young middle-aged.

Peggy and Trish and Billy and Boo - it sounds like a pop song already - transfer their adulation from the Beach Boys to the Beatles and from the Beatles to Bob Dylan. Progressive degeneration, I'd call it, but then I just missed being a baby boomer. Anyway, the songs, quoted in the dialogue and heard between the scenes, exemplify my personal definition of nostalgia: music one thought negligible at the time but that casts an irresistible spell years later. What today's young make of it, only they know.

Still, let us assume that youth is always youth and that one generation's rites of passage will seem poignant and funny to another. Album starts with an abortive game of strip poker, the girls running for cover and the boys stomping about in self-consciously masculine frustration. Cutting across the gender lines are one confident pair, Peggy and Billy; Trish and Boo are separately despondent over whether they will ever make out. It is reassuring, considering that they are only 14 and this is only 1963, to discover that for them "making out" means at most heavy petting. Of course, it turns out that Peggy and Billy have their problems, too, and that Trish and Boo have less to worry about than they might think. At least Trish does; Boo seems well on the way to being a fully paid-up weirdo. He worships Dylan, despite Billy's impeccably mathematical put-down: "How can he be greater than the Beatles? They're four guys." Boo's discourse becomes a full-time Dylan impression: the snarl, the whine and the more aggressive sections of the lyrics. One of the problems with Bernadette Jones' production is that, though Kirk Dunn does a very good Dylan, he cannot place the impersonation within the characterization of Boo. He is too belligerent to be good company, but the audience has to spend a lot of time with him.

This is just an extreme example of a general malaise. The actors may be slightly older than the characters but they are still too young, or too raw, for the play. The U.S. theatre turns out such pubescent memoirs in large quantities, and they need speed and flash and wit and charm. They need to be framed, not by production tricks but by the actors' own skills. You cannot act vulnerability just by being vulnerable. The characters' tentativeness here is often indistinguishable from the actors'. Missing the pain, they also miss the joy. The play is meant to end in a precarious afterglow, the foursome - fresh out of high school and finally into sex - joyfully hurling appropriate song titles at one another. It is plainly intended to be a great scene. Here, it is just dogged.

The set, even given the constrictions of the space, is baldly unevocative. A scene meant to be done in near-darkness is staged in a half-hearted murk. The play seems truthful but dull.

Bryan Elliott is the most advanced actor, too slight for Billy but with the right dubious swagger. Shelley Owens as Peggy - "the girl most likely to be the girl most likely" - is a great provocative gum-chewer. Laura Partland as sensitive Trish is, well, sensitive. They have their individual moments of rightness, but they never fizz together.

According to his program bio, Album was David Rimmer's "first Broadway hit." Come on; Album was staged in 1980 at the delightful but diminutive Cherry Lane, a prototypical off-Broadway house, and it lasted there four months. As to what his subsequent Broadway hits may have been, the program is oddly coy. On this evidence, we have still to mark him down as a promising playwright, in need of more than promising performance.
1990-03-10-sesame-street-s-charm-lost-on:
Sesame Street's charm lost on stage Sesame Street Live

Saturday, March 10, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written by Jon Stone and Joseph A. Bailey Directed by Marilyn Magness Starring Jim Henson's Sesame Street Muppets At the O'Keefe Centre, Toronto BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail ONE of the perks of parenthood is being allowed to watch Sesame Street. Clearly, it is the best children's TV show in the world. It is also one of the very few U.S. television products that are suitable for adults. Significantly, it comes out of New York, not Hollywood. The version shown on TVOntario is fatally slowed by cumbersome Canadian content, but on Channel 17 (PBS Buffalo) you get the wittiest, most imaginative, most musical, most literate program on U.S. television.

Also one of the most self-indulgent. At least half the jokes, and most of the musical pastiches, come across as though they are being perpetrated for grown-ups. The hippest pre-schooler is unlikely to appreciate waiter Grover's injunction to the kitchen to "break out the good stuff" when his lunch-break rolls round, or the accuracy of the show's loving homages to every popular music style from vo-de-o to video. I don't think, though, that the show's creators do this just to curry favor with people like me. They do it to amuse themselves, and to keep themselves on their toes, in the honorable tradition of Lewis Carroll, A.A. Milne, Huckleberry Hound and Muffin the Mule. Not talking down to children means working to your own best standards, and giving yourself the occasional break.

To be honest, my own kids are no more addicted to Sesame Street than they are to the Care Bears or Polka Dot Door: the easy, patronizing stuff. But they are no less addicted, and at low moments I tell myself that regular exposure to brilliant entertainment will have an educational effect far more important than Sesame Street's declared purpose of teaching them their numbers and letters. They will learn to enjoy and expect the best.

Anyway, they clamored to be taken to Sesame Street Live at O'Keefe Centre. And my trio of critics were very nice about it. Anthony leaned forward in his seat, entranced by the experience of being in a theatre; Mitchell, who is very laid-back, coolly appraised the bright lights and ticked off the characters; and Chloe, whenever the music started, threw herself into choreography more inventive than anything on stage.

The show, in fact, is miserably unimaginative. The cast consists of actor-size replicas of the original puppets, miming to a pre-recorded track of dialogue and music. The voices are either those of the original performers or extraordinarily good mimics, but this is depressing in itself. The sound, and therefore the whole experience, is dead and distant; Jim Henson, Frank Oz et al have no business lending themselves to such a travesty of their own work. The story is How Sesame Street Came To Be On TV. Big Bird conceives the idea of a kids' show that will Also Teach Things. He is as earnest about this as the fund-raisers - my brood calls them "the Money Ladies" - who periodically solicit our alms on public TV: the ones whose devotion to "culture" is so schoolmarmish that you pledge yourself to watch nothing but game shows and commercials from here on in. This may be a necessary pitch for the foundations, but it should be kept from the kids. They should be watching for the stories, the fun and the characters. A dozen are on view here, but they have nothing individual to do or say, beyond the odd catch phrase.

Bert looks better than Ernie, whose large head does him in when blown up to stage-size. There is no Kermit; you could hardly blow him up without forfeiting his frogginess (and he demands good material). There is no Snuffy; he, I suppose, would have to be blown down. And, crucially, there are no human characters - making you realize just how much the TV show owes to its adult actors and continuing situations. They give it reality and, incidentally, femininity. (The puppet characters are overwhelmingly male.) Without them, the TV show would be, at best, cute. Apart from the occasional intervention from Oscar the Grouch ("hope you hated the show," he says encouragingly), the stage version isn't even that. It may have the official imprimatur, but it's still a ripoff. It even sinks to interpolating songs from other sources: a frantic, meaningless version of Kids, from Bye Bye Birdie, for instance. That is the stuff of cheap English pantomime: a mixture of instant recognition and total opportunism.

Infant middle-class Toronto was out in force, and it clapped and joined in at all the prescribed moments. But I think it felt cheated, and I hope it will grow up to know why.
1990-03-17-yarns-and-slow-burns:
BROADWAY ANECDOTES BY PETER HAY Oxford, 395 pages, $24.95

Yarns and slow Burns

BROADWAY ANECDOTES BY PETER HAY Oxford, 395 pages, $24.95

Saturday, March 17, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

ALL MY BEST FRIENDS BY GEORGE BURNS with David Fisher Putnam, 320 pages, $23.50 REVIEW BY ROBERT CUSHMAN A book of anecdotes, like a dictionary of quotations, is not something to be read. It is to be consulted, dipped into, rifled. A browsers delight, it is guaranteed to put a reviewer in a foul temper. He has to plow through it, thinking about all the real books in which anecdotes have been welcome diversions from the serious business of narrative and analysis. He knew he'd have to pay for them some day. Here is that day, and if he doesn't watch his language hell find himself dragging out the old image of an indigestible meal entirely composed of hors doeuvres.

There, I warned you.

Peter Hay's collection of Broadway Anecdotes is committed to myth- making. No matter how sharp the practices or inflated the egos revealed by his stories, everything contributes to the greater glory of the American showcase. As Hay points out, the alternatives to Broadway - the regional theatre, the road, off-Broadway, off-off-Broadway - define themselves by their distance from the Main Stem, and so pay inadvertent tribute to it. Broadway may not create much any more, but it remains the great theatrical market-place.

Like New York itself, Broadway glories in its own impossibility. New Yorkers deplore their city's violence, but they secretly pride themselves on their own ability to live with it and survive. Hays last tale is of a rehearsal fight between playwright Clifford Odets and director Harold Clurman. As these two luminaries swore, screamed and, in Clurmans case, rolled raving on the carpet, actor Sanford Meisner smiled and said, I wouldn't be in any other business.

Broadway's survival depends on making everybody believe that. And we do, easily. The slightest exposure to the disease and you catch it, even as a member of the audience. Hence Broadways devotion to its own legend. Hence the succession of backstage musicals. Some people even believe the Tony Awards.

And thus, apparently, it has ever been. This book takes us back to 1713, when New England Puritans, bridling at the rumor that a play was being planned, exclaimed, "Let not Christian Boston go beyond heathen Rome in the practice of shameful vanities." It seems that American censorship pre-dates American drama. It took some time for sinful vanities to get off the ground, but they finally succeeded, with encouragement at the highest level. We all know of Abraham Lincolns enthusiasm for the stage, and how it turned out; it seems that George Washington was an addict as well.

Hay reprints interminable and pointless accounts of the hucksterism of Phineas T. Barnum, who really does seem to have been the most flamboyantly boring showman in history. Moving on, we meet P.T.'s nephew, Herbert Barnum Seeley, who tried to make himself notorious by sponsoring scenes of debauchery, and not just on stage. He once threw a bachelor party with Little Egypt, the hoochy-koochy dancer, providing the cabaret.

There is a chapter on critics, reprinting famously rude reviews. They seem terribly mild; we could all do much nastier than that. A lot of them are just laborious. George Jean Nathan, revered for being not only smart but clever, could sink to this: I always said that I'd like John! Barrymores acting till the cows came home. Well, ladies and gentlemen, last night the cows came home. Faced with a play called Tonight Or Never, Nathan came up with: "Very well, then: I say, Never." Its not just on the Broadway stage that a reputation for wit can be lightly won. Really wonderful, though, is somebody's response - I always thought it was Dorothy Parker, but Hay leaves it unattributed - to I Am A Camera: No Leica. But he errs in describing the piece itself as a bad play; it would rank as a minor classic if Cabaret hadn't come along and disinherited it. Only Pygmalion has been able to beat the odds and lead a double life as play and musical.

But I am digressing. Anecdotage is contagious.

I am sure Hay misattributes the career-destroying review perpetrated on an actor called Guido Nadzo: "Guido Nadzo nadzo guido." He says it was Brooks Atkinson, long of The New York Times, who would have been too sober to think of it and too kind to use it. (Actually its not that great. How are you supposed to pronounce it?) All authorities agree in crediting it to George S. Kaufman, critic, playwright, director, oracle and general embodiment of the inter-war years when glamor was glamor, Broadway was the theatre, and most of this book was born. Everyone was witty and wore a tuxedo or a backless gown. Dont argue; I've seen the movies.

My favorite criticism here comes from a non-professional - critic, I mean - Noel Coward. I cannot imagine how I have managed to live until now ignorant of his response to The Seagull: I hate plays that have a stuffed bird sitting on the bookcase screaming 'Im the title, Im the title, I'm the title!' I am grateful too for Kaufmans question to a drapery salesman ("Do you have any good second-act curtains?"), and his terrified instruction to a chauffeur who was speeding toward George Washington Bridge (Dont cross that bridge till we come to it). On the same page, "a now forgotten playwright" called Edward Peple tells a universal story that begins, "It may sound incredulous." It doesn't. But I was.

Then I loved the Drama Bookshop's list of strange titles requested by customers. I Cant Bear You When The Waters Running loses narrowly to She Stops The Concorde. Canada, by Shaw, is another good one, and should definitely be revived by Christopher Newton. There is a treasurable quote from Louis Jouvet: The one thing constant in a changing world is the avant-garde.

I like anecdotes that have punch-lines. I'd be perfectly content if they had nothing but punch-lines.

Now, if you want a good anecdote, listen to George Burns on Al Jolson: "After his first few movies, Jolie wasn't a big draw, and gradually his career seemed to be over. Id see him sitting in a corner all by himself at the Hillcrest Country Club and Id go over to talk to him. Jolie was always very nice to me. In those days there was a law against bringing sturgeon into California, because it was only caught off the East Coast and it was so expensive to keep it refrigerated while shipping it west that it was usually spoiled by the time it got there. But Jolson had it shipped into California and kept his own supply in the Hillcrest kitchen. Then he'd sit alone in his corner eating it. I'd go and sit with him and compliment him, and every time I did hed offer me a piece of his sturgeon. Believe me, I liked sturgeon almost as much as I liked Jolson."

Then came The Jolson Story: Larry Parks impersonation of Jolson was so good that Jolson actually stole the picture without even being in it. Everybody wanted to sign him to do something. This was the greatest comeback in show business history. So one day I walked into Hillcrest and saw him sitting in the corner with his packet of sturgeon. I went over and said, 'That's the best picture I ever saw, and waited for my sturgeon. Nothing. So I tried again, That's the best soundtrack album I ever heard.' Finally, Jolie looked at me and said, Forget it, Natty. Im hot again. Get your own sturgeon.' The story is good enough in its own right, but if you imagine him speaking it, it's hilarious. In his 90s, Burns has entered into a state of comic grace. That wizened, apparently uninflected voice, with the snap- pause at the end of each line as the cigar re-enters the mouth, doesnt so much dare you to laugh as forbid you not to. It isnt a matter of bullying. It's a modest awareness of perfection. The timing isn't especially fast or slow. Its unhurried. The book capitalizes on this. Its set out as a routine. There are self-conscious references ("Thank you. You've been a wonderful reader"), but more important is the rhythm. How much of the credit for this should go to Burns's co-author, David Fisher, cannot be known, but I imagine its considerable. As Burns himself reminds us, once he and his colleagues got out of vaudeville and into radio, they depended on writers who played to their strengths.

This book is about those colleagues. Jolson, George Jessel, Eddie Cantor, Milton Berle, Jimmy Durante, Groucho and Harpo Marx and, above all, Jack Benny are the recurring figures in the tapestry. We hear of Jolsons egomania, Jessel's erotomania and Cantor's sheer mania, each motif recurring like a well-loved catch-phrase in a comedy series. There is little directly about Burns himself (stray bits of George-and-Gracie have to be cherished as they fly past) but then, This book is a little different than anything Ive ever done before. And believe me, at my age its difficult to find anything I haven't done before. And even harder to do it.

It's an important book. As Burns says, his group invented much of show business, and he tells us how they did it and where. "In retrospect, small-time vaudeville was fun - but as Groucho might say, everyplace else it was very tough." This book is a definitive portait of a theatrical form, one so voracious and with so many outlets that anybody could get work, but only the best could get anywhere else.

I think, Burns says, "I loved being in vaudeville more than any other part of my career." Later on, he says exactly the same about radio, movies and television (but he probably means it about vaudeville). The references are so widely spaced, though, that it takes you time to realize it. The running gag creeps up on you. That's his technique. Slow Burns.

In a book full of funny people being funny, the best line comes from a civilian. A coat-check girl refuses a handsome tip from Burns' closest friend. Please, Mr. Benny she says wistfully, "let me keep my illusions." Robert Cushman is Toronto writer.
1990-03-22-theatre-review-a-tasteful-tri:
THEATRE REVIEW A tasteful trip into Never Never Land Peter Pan

Thursday, March 22, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

A musical production of the play by James M. Barrie Directed by Fran Soeder Starring Cathy Rigby, Stepehn Hanan and Cindy Robinson At O'Keefe Centre in Toronto BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail PETER PAN may not be one of the great U.S. musicals, but it is one of the most efficient and effective. It was done on Broadway in 1954, and conceived as a vehicle for Mary Martin, whose spirit - puckish rather than pannish - still hovers over it. It certainly does in the first-rate touring revival that opened Tuesday night at O'Keefe Centre in Toronto. The star, Cathy Rigby, as befits an ex-athlete on wires, does a pretty terrific hover herself.

The musical hews closely to the J. M. Barrie play. All the dialogue seems to come from source; there is no separate credit for a librettist. The songs, about 10 of them, are thriftily slotted in to accentuate the high points of the drama and they do this very well. I first saw the show some 10 years ago in a Broadway revival with Sandy Duncan as Peter. Soon afterward the Royal Shakespeare Company in London mounted a sumptuous revival of the original play that left me, in comparison, strangely unsatisfied. It seemed to cry out for music and for musical staging, especially at those moments when the story literally takes flight.

The musical also irons out some of the originals psychological creases. It doesnt stint on the bloodthirstiness: Captain Hook still terrorizes his crew by flourishing his implement, plots infanticide on a grand scale (he even speaks chillingly of a holocaust of children) and, in the lagoon scene, puts in peremptory orders for his favorite cocktail - drowned-Indian-maiden-on-the-rocks.

Pan, equally murderous in intent and more so in achievement, blithely disposes of a couple of pirates before insouciantly tossing their skipper into the jaws of his nemesis, the clock-eating crocodile. Death in this story is never far off, even for fairies. The show, like the kids watching it, takes all this in its stride. Barrie's bleak ending, where a grownup Wendy cedes to her own daughter her place in Peter's affections, is defused by a reprise of the song Never Never Land. This is the point where the show comes closest to Disney - heavenly choirs over the final credits - with the crucial difference that the song, a long-limbed waltzing charmer, is sweet without being sugary.

What we have here is not a re-invention of the original (like My Fair Lady) but a showmanlike and surprisingly tasteful distillation of it, with a strong emphasis on story. Harmonious as it all now seems, the original production, masterminded by Jerome Robbins, must have been a bloodbath. The neophyte songwriters, Carolyn Leigh and Moose Charlap, had half their original score thrown out; Peters anthem I Gotta Crow and the simple but rushingly appropriate Im Flying are theirs. Reinforcements were supplied by the more seasoned team of Jule Styne, Betty Comden and Adolph Green; Never Never Land, Distant Melody, and Hook's musical soliloquies are theirs. Hook, a baroque comic monster, is a very Comden-and-Green conception.

Apart from a tiny, tinny orchestra, the O'Keefe version, directed by Fran Soeder, has all the elements to honor its ancestry. Lost Boys and Indians do some splendidly infectious hoofing when pledging blood- brotherhood; the architecture of this number is authentic Robbins, comedy and drama built from simple steps.

Sets, climaxing in a luridly purple sky over the pirate ship, and colorful costumes abound in their own adventure playground, with the Darling family nursery the most mysterious locale of all.

Cathy Rigby, a spunky and surprisingly tuneful Peter, not only woos but wins the audience, and Cindy Robinson is an authentically bossy Wendy. Stephen Hanans Hook, intentionally or not, comes over as a spoof of Laurence Olivier in his Restoration fop roles. Its done effectively, with a kind of cringing panache, and indeed "Brimstone and gall, what cozenage is here?" is a fairly typical example.

It might, though, be funnier and more frightening to play against this, and make him a businesslike villain. He suffers dramatically from the fact that none of his schemes works, but we ought to believe that they might. My own children's favorite character was the crocodile. This may reflect on their upbringing, but he is an endearing specimen, a bit undersized, but then an exclusive diet of pirate (when you can get it) and timepieces is probably not very nourishing. Maybe, too, the reptile's simplicity attracted them. The croc with the clock is, after all, the least complicated figure in the piece. We know exactly what makes him tick.
1990-04-04-current-crop-of-musicals-prov:
Current crop of musicals proves lights still bright on Broadway

Wednesday, April 04, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

New York NY -- BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail NEW YORK RECENTLY, COMPLETING a report on Andrew Lloyd Webber in concert, I remarked that the American musical had done itself in. This was a bit sweeping, and the current Broadway season has seen a possible resurgence. There is still the question of whether the economics can be bucked, but at least there is talent on show, both among the young and the ageing, and a satisfying number of bodies turning out to bear witness.

The surprise hit is City of Angels, which opened with a minimal advance but was turned around by a rave review in the New York Times. The Times hailed it as the funniest musical in years, which it may be. (There has hardly been much competition.) The script is by Larry Gelbart, who co- authored A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum, back when there really was such a thing as musical comedy, and was more recently responsible for the TV version of MASH.

His subject here is Hollywood: the myth and, if there is such a thing, the reality. Its the late forties, and a writer called Stine sits in L.A. working on a screenplay about a private eye called Stone, who also sits in L.A. Stine sees Stone as a lonely holdout for integrity in a corrupt world, rather like Philip Marlowe. Raymond Chandler's Marlowe, that is, not Dennis Potter's. The show might quite reasonably be called The Singing Detective, though, as it resembles the TV serial quite a lot, what with its film noir pastiches, its appearance-reality games and its pair of attendant goons threatening to beat up Stone. Come to think of it, both the games and the goons were also forecast in Kiss Me Kate.

Chandleresque narration has always been a fertile ground for parody, and Gelbart mines it richly. His wisecracking style serves him well when Stine gets into his own integrity battles. His opponents are movie moguls, after all, and we expect them to be cartoons. But when we are asked to take a serious interest in Stines love life, the writing cannot take the strain.

The entire supporting cast doubles in parallel roles, though Stone and Stine are played by separate actors. They have a duet, of course, called Youre Nothing Without Me, rather than - as might be feared - Don't Alter My Ego.

Surprisingly, this show has a British director with no track record in musicals. For once, this does not spell disaster. Michael Blakemore was probably hired for his immaculate work on Michael Frayn's equally convoluted backstage piece, Noises Off. Beyond that, he has a real flair for hard-nosed Broadway comedy (his National Theatre production of The Front Page is legendary) and an apparently equal relish for text, acting and theatrical mechanics. His work here is witty and level-headed, involving the best use I have ever seen of a live performer against mobile projections. Robin Wagners sets build up a shadowy, sinister film city before colorfully blowing their top in a climactic studio scene.

What the production has been unable to do is to integrate the script with the score. The musical parts of the story were hard to follow since David Zippels lyrics were drowned out by Billy Byers' joyful big-band orchestrations. Cy Coleman is almost my favorite Broadway composer, and I shall probably love the album, but his tunes here inhabit a world of their own, short on menace and late in date. They hail from the fifties rather than the forties, and one song might have been scored by Nelson Riddle for Frank Sinatra: a gorgeous sound but as self-contained and resistant to drama as anything in rock. Performances are disappointing as well - only James Naughton's stylish Stine has much impact. I applaud the elements if not the totality, and am glad the Times loved it, otherwise it would not have survived and I could not have seen it.

There is at least a healthy low-down Americanness about the show. The seasons other big contender, Grand Hotel, also invokes Hollywood - being a musical adaptation of a novel that everybody remembers as a movie - but is also one of Broadways recurring obeisances to the old world. Staged by Tommy Tune, in an opulent setting by Tony Walton (two tiers of old gold), it looks stunning. But you grow tired of being stunned and, in terms of narrative, nothing much happens. Or quite a lot happens but none of it seems to matter.

A couple of nice songs by the old Kismet team of Robert Wright and George Forrest prevent me from saying that the show has only one good Tune. Tommy Tune may be the last great director-choreographer on Broadway, with Bob Fosse, Michael Bennett and Gower Champion dead and Jerome Robbins retired from the fray.

City of Angels eschews dance, as do the recent Sondheim shows and the various successes of the Lloyd Webber school, Cats excepted. Story and song are back, in various combinations. Even the compilation Jerome Robbins' Broadway (now in its second year) reminds us in fractured form what a superb storyteller he was. This season has brought a full-blown revival of one of his triumphs, and one of the most dramatic musicals ever. Gypsy, directed by librettist Arthur Laurents, reinstates Robbins' choreography which boasts, in the young hoofers All I Need is the Girl, my favorite of all musical numbers: half brash, half shy. Tyne Daly, in the linchpin role of Mama Rose, lacks the bizarre grandeur of Angela Lansbury in the last revival, and she has an uphill battle with some of the songs. But her gritty determination pays off; she is a very believable theatrical mother. When Lansburys Rose said of her own performing ambitions, "If I could have been I would have been, and that's show business," it was with a resigned, healing acceptance. Daly says it with bitterness, still fighting. The end of the show, when she allows herself to be led off by the daughter who is now Gypsy Rose Lee, is not only moving but disturbing.

When at the outset I mentioned young writing talent, I spoke comparatively. The team of Richard Maltby Jr. and David Shire has been at it since the early sixties, but only a few seasons ago did they make it to Broadway together with Baby, a refreshingly humane musical about parenthood. A few off-cuts from that show, together with a raft of new songs, make up Closer Than Ever, an off-Broadway four-performer revue about life and love among the early middle-aged. They have a distinctive sound of their own, soaring and percussive, recognizable through a variety of musical styles. Maltby's lyrics are inquisitive and genuinely observant; Shires best melodies re-invent the Broadway show tune, maintaining the lift and the drive and purging the banality.

Another composer of new grown-up songs is Craig Carnelia, who, like Maltby and Shire, is a post-angst writer. (As the maestro would probably not put it, theyve been through Stephen Sondheim and they're here.) His music and lyrics were the best things in two unsuccessful Broadway shows, Working and Is There Life After High School. His songs generally sound like pieces of his own or someone else's autobiography, and this retrospective mode may limit him, but within it he demonstrates a rare combination of delicacy and strength. He showed his wares, under the title Pictures in the Hall, at a Greenwich Village cabaret called Eighty Eight's in company with his wife, an actress-singer named Maureen Silliman. She made one of his confessionals, Just a Housewife, an eye-piercing mixture of pride and heartbreak. Carnelia's taste - as lyricist, composer and husband - is impeccable. Remember his name.
1990-05-18-sammy-davis-jr-s-early-career:
Sammy Davis Jr.'s early career will be remembered with affection A black performer who succeeded on white terms

Friday, May 18, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail FOR THE first 30 years or so of his career - and remember he started right out of the cradle - Sammy Davis Jr. was strictly a North American phenomenon. Davis, who died Wednesday, was a Broadway star in 1956 in Mr. Wonderful, but the show, though a hit, was ephemeral, best remembered for a hit recording of its title song by Peggy Lee. Over the years, she probably did better out of it than he did. Anyway the show was essentially a blow-up of Davis's night club act, and American club acts have never really been big anywhere outside America. The informed bought his Decca record albums, but to most people he was another U.S. singer, covering the same standard repertoire as everybody else. Some said he did impressions.

He went world - I think it was in 1959 - at a Royal Variety Performance in London. The bill was crammed with American performers - Nat King Cole and Eartha Kitt, both much better known, were on it - but Davis was given the top spot. He looked disconcerting, with his diminutive frame and crooked face: "like a gnome" somebody said. He also, to British ears, talked funny. ("This song was one of our first hits, and therefore will always be a great favorite of ours." Royalty was surely meant to be in the audience, not on the stage.) Limited to an eight-minute spot, he sang, danced, clowned and impersonated in dizzying quick succession. He was overwhelming.

Later we found that he could stretch out as well. He did a couple of BBC television specials, just him and a band. It was his Civil Rights period, and we were all with him. "Back of the bus, indeed," he muttered, and we were delighted; in those days middle-of-the-road performers, black or white, didn't say such things. We warmed to him, even more, when he suddenly added gunslinging to his repertoire. After a few quick draws and rapid fires he favored us with a broad ingenuous grin. "Gosh," he said, "I wouldn't do it unless I was good at it." That was his compact with us. What we wanted from him was energy, versatility and personal communication. "Look," he said, delaying the next scheduled program for five minutes while he did his encore, "Perry Mason you know about, he wins every case. I'm only here tonight." Doubtless it was all scripted and rehearsed, but we loved it.

The early sixties were really Davis's years. The Beatles had yet to turn show business upside down, and Las Vegas still seemed like the entertainment centre of the world. Frank Sinatra started his own record label, and Davis and Dean Martin signed with it. In the antics of The Clan, which seemed fresh and amusing in those days, Davis was our representative. Sinatra was too unreachably talented and Martin too impenetrably laid-back for us to identify with, but Davis was the feisty little guy, setting off firecrackers, asking questions, and always doing more than any of the others.

As Sportin' Life, a role he had always longed for and was probably born to play, he periodically electrified the moribund movie of Porgy and Bess. Nobody else could have led on those Catfish Row picnickers with such loose-limbed enticing abandon. It was at this time, too, that he did his best singing. Not a jazz singer, he could still swing with ingratiating hipness in the right company. He learned as much from Mel Torme and Buddy Greco as from Sinatra. All his influences seemed to be white: Fred Astaire, Buddy Rich - and Mickey Rooney, with whom he shared a theatrical energy and intelligence in the reading of lyrics.

Being black, though, he had a more personal stake in Kennedy liberalism than any of his colleagues; and the second Kennedy assassination ended an era for him. He was in London again when it happened, opening a revised and improved version of his second Broadway hit, Golden Boy. The killing and the premiere coincided and for several nights he claimed to be unable to go on. This may have been self-indulgent and professionally dubious. But I was lucky enough to have tickets for the night of his return, and it was unforgettable. The show was an expert, and surprisingly tough, musical updating of Clifford Odets' thirties play about a young Italian - now of course a young Black - struggling out of poverty and into disillusion through the boxing ring. Odets' hero was granted a sentimental death: Davis, having killed an opponent, turned on us and sang "what became of me? and what became of you?" These seemed apposite questions, and Davis, if a limited and unsubtle actor, was a powerful one. And here, by the way, at the heart of commercial theatre, was a show that for once genuinely upset and disturbed its audience. The people who had booked to see Sammy Davis in Golden Boy were not expecting this.

It was quite a decline to his next and last stage show: a revival of Stop the World - I Want To Get Off. He had been singing its songs for years, and seemed to have persuaded himself that Anthony Newley and Leslie Bricusse were the contemporary Rodgers and Hart. This though was a symptom of the musical confusion that plagued all but the best singers of his generation when their citadel crumbled. He was after all an old vaudevillian; and when he stopped performing standards he lost much of his identity. If Sweet Gingerbread Man was ingenious and catchy, Mr. Bojangles was maudlin. He lost his political identity, too (as he more or less confessed when his second autobiography was published last year) and the basics of his act began to age; how late in the twentieth century could a man go on doing James Cagney? It was good, though, to see him on film and TV going back to his roots and upholding the dignity of tap.

As a kid in the army Davis had lived out his own version of Golden Boy; having grown up in an all-black world, he had to fight his way to acceptance and even survival. This part of his life story reads like something out of The Young Lions or From Here to Eternity.

In later years, he sang with feeling Stand Up and Fight, Carmen Jones answer to the Toreador Song. That he succeeded as a black performer on white terms is undeniable: also, as far as I can see, admirable, good for the world if not altogether for him. On Entertainment Tonight he was seen regretting that he had reduced admirable sentiments like "peace and love" to glib showbiz slogans, and it would have been good to see a real interviewer probe further into his reality and his image. That the image, in later years, turned many people off is undeniable and understandable. But those of us who were around for Davis's first impactcould never lose our affection for him.
1990-05-25-theatre-review-misalliance:
THEATRE REVIEW MISALLIANCE

Friday, May 25, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE, Ont. -- Written by George Bernard Shaw Directed by Christopher Newton Starring Sharry Flett, Barry MacGregor, Jennifer Phipps and Helen Taylor At the Festival Theatre in Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont. Shaw Festival opens with a triumph of the comic spirit BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE, Ont. "READ Whatsisname," says John Tarleton, absent-mindedly seeking a reference for the idea of the Superman. Tarleton, self-taught intellectual and self-made millionaire (very big in underwear), is a walking library catalogue. "Read Tennyson." "Read Darwin." It's a running gag. Whatsisname, of course, is George Bernard Shaw, whose lifelong habit of flattering himself by deprecating himself reached its apogee in 1909 when he wrote Misalliance, a production of which opened the Shaw Festival Wednesday night.

"Democracy," says another character in the same vein, "reads well but it doesn't act well, like some people's plays." Misalliance can act agonizingly badly, like an anti-Shavian's nightmare come true: a formless debate that never stops, so that you feel like screaming every time a new subject appears on the horizon, knowing that it and you are about to be worried to death.

For the same reasons it can, if taken with lightness and decision, be a delight: thought made manifest, transformed into shimmering, self-mocking and terribly serious farce. So it is here. Christopher Newton's production is a triumph of the comic spirit.

Its main weapon is a ferocious insistence on form. Shaw set the play in the greenhouse of Tarleton's capacious garden in the Home Counties. Newton and his designer, Leslie Frankish, have elaborated this into a spectacular jungle of a conservatory, full of overgrown undergrowth. One of the main strands of the play's action - it has plenty of action, despite its author's playful pretenses to the contrary - is the pursuit of Tarleton's daughter Hypatia by various admirers and her pursuit of them. As they chase one another through the trailing ferns the comedy takes on the aspect of A Midsummer Night's Dream.

And why not? "Read Shakespeare," advises Tarleton, "he has a word for every occasion." When these rich, bored characters express their chronic wish for something exciting to happen, strange sounds reverberate in the air.

Excitement does descend from on high,in the shape of a crash-landing airplane. This is the cue for cascades of smoke. Through it all looms the goggled figure of the aviator, obviously charged with some oracular pronouncement. What he actually says is, "I'm really very sorry," to which Tarleton has the only appropriate English reaction: "Not a bit. Come in and have some tea."

Accompanying the flier is a Polish lady acrobat, an extravagantly free spirit who arouses the libido of every male on the premises. Even this luscious apparition is eclipsed by the play's subsequent intruder, an underfed clerk. Long ago Tarleton seduced this young man's mother and he is intent on revenge. Gunner, the name bestowed on him by his intended victim in honor of the weapon he ineffectually brandishes, is a sure-fire comic creation. Every word he says in defiance of capitalist exploitation is justified, and every word is joyously undercut by his novelettish posturing.

Newton does not quite trust his author here, allowing Gunner a couple of speeches' worth of unnecessary (and inconsistent) dignity. The actor, Simon Bradbury, takes some time to hit his grotesque stride, and when he does he gets his effects as much through a mock Socialist salute, a political nervous tic, as through his lines. But his first-night ovation was understandable, as was that bestowed on his opposite Pole, Sharry Flett, for whom the accent does wonders and who marshals her anti-romantic rhetoric very tidily. The production sets her up for exit applause and she gets it. Neither performance is quite as good as the audience took it for, but both are more than all right.

The evening's foundations, though, are laid by the solid older characters: by Richard Farrell, plangently disillusioned as an ex-colonial governor; by Jennifer Phipps as Tarleton's imperturbable wife; and above all by Barry MacGregor, whose Tarleton is the bluff Yorkshire businessman turned inside-out, making every point both for and against himself, and never lingering over any of them. A self-indulgent Tarleton can ruin the piece.

The younger actors have more trouble, as is customary. Newton sees Tarleton's son, Johnny, as the villain of the piece, complacently preening on the edge of national and global catastrophe. So Mark Burgess plays the role as a nasty, thin-lipped Philistine, though it is surely written as a beefy good-hearted Philistine. Like father, like son. Helen Taylor is a forthright Hypatia, maybe too much so; too little the young lady for people to be scandalized when she fails to behave like one. Peter Krantz gives her chosen prey a damn decent profile and demeanor, which may be all that can be done with a role stronger on build-up than on substance.

Two minor quibbles. The show's joyous momentum is halted by one interval too many. The play's final burst of self-parody - Tarleton admits that there is nothing more to be said, and Hypatia exclaims, "Thank goodness" - is muted in the interest of a pastoral dying fall, effective on its own terms. But the total is exhilarating: a moody, sparkling reclamation that affirms what the Shaw Festival should be about. It does credit to actors, production team and Whatsisname.
1990-05-26-theatre-review-the-waltz-of-t:
THEATRE REVIEW THE WALTZ OF THE TOREADORS

Saturday, May 26, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Niagara-on-the-Lake ONT -- Written by Jean Anouilh Directed by David Giles Starring William Hutt Missteps break this Waltz's rhythm BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE INTHE LAST year of his life, Bernard Shaw wrote to his old friend and impresario Barry Jackson who was about to present a play by Jean Anouilh: "I never heard of the unspellable and unpronounceable M. Anhouilh. Is he available in English? Are you translating?"

Since then, Anouilh has come into fashion and gone violently out again. His tragedies seem soft-centred and many of his comedies merely whimsical. Probably the most durable plays are his black satires on marriage, age and disillusion: Ardele (the play Jackson was gearing up for) and its sequel, The Waltz of the Toreadors, which opened at the Shaw Festival Thursday night.

As a festival choice, The Waltz barely scrapes under the wire. Shaw died in 1950 and this play was written, according to the program, in 1950- 1 and first produced in 1952. Along with this information comes a note by the director David Giles, correctly pointing out that a play once thought savage now seems "almost tender" and identifying one of the major keys in its constantly shifting score as being "sheer farce." His production does quite well by the tenderness, muffs most of the farce, and misses out almost entirely on the horror that underlies them both.

Everything hinges on the play's central character. As in the previous night's production, Misalliance, we are in the run-up to the First World War, this time of course in France. General St. Pe, veteran of several military campaigns and rather more amatory ones, sits dictating his memoirs and seducing chambermaids. Lechery is a habit with him, mechanically indulged to help him forget his jealous ex-opera-singer wife, lying apparently bedridden in the room next door, and to escape the tormenting fantasies of the man he could have been and the young man he once was. Seventeen years ago, a dashing major at a military ball, he met the love of his life, danced the eponymous waltz with her, but never bedded her.

Now she returns, still faithful and with evidence that his wife isn't. Divorce and happiness are within his reach. But, of course, they elude him. Too much time has passed. A pair of ungainly daughters bear witness to that. So, in another way, does the presence of his 20-year-old secretary, a personable male virgin. Even his besotted beloved begins to feel and resent the pressure of the years. And besides he cannot leave his wife, however she may bore and torment him. He lacks the courage to be cruel. That is the diagnosis of his friend, a doctor as kind and cynical as doctors always are, at any rate in plays, at any rate in this kind of play.

The General is a buffoon who suffers, and we cannot get at the suffering except through the buffoonery. William Hutt is too old for the role and would not have been right even when younger. He is a gallant actor - in both senses: brave and courteous - and he won all hearts at the curtain call. His technique, despite some fumbling with words on a heavily jinxed first night, remains impeccable: give him an ironic aside and he will time and dispatch it with perfect finesse. But most of the time, his distinction works against him. Vulgarity and bluster are not in him; his balloon arrives on stage already punctured. There was once a movie version with Peter Sellers who probably played it as Major Denis Bloodnok. (You don't remembr Major Bloodnok? Suffer.) That, however overdone, would have been nearer the mark.

The core of the play is the General's confrontation with his spouse, who stands up in bed to denounce him: a grotesque effect that Anouilh planned with exquisite care and is severely impaired if, as here, she has to hold onto a bed-post to do it. Marion Gilsenan lends this harridan far too much glamor but is otherwise efficient. The scene, though, is chaotically directed; it has no rhythm and therefore no impact. You get more domestic horror in the average episode of Fawlty Towers.

There is nothing much to say about other performances. Allan Gray's surprisingly Caledonian doctor finds his form in some scenes of worldly philosophizing, that also find Hutt at his mellow best. Diana Leblanc as the aging female ingenue and Blair Williams as the young male one are mechanically moonstruck: on the right lines but not very far along them. A maid and a priest are grotesquely overplayed, perhaps to compensate for the lack of comic energy elsewhere.

Kenneth Mellor's set has spacious suggestions of the General's past campaigns in North Africa. The audience applauded it before it became fully visible, which is typical. As with Misalliance, two intervals wreck the flow. There is, of course, less flow here to wreck, but that is not the play's fault. Anouilh uses a superb variety of styles to get at an anguish we can all recognize. This could be one of the funniest plays of the twentieth century. Its time will come again.
1990-05-28-night-must-fall:
NIGHT MUST FALL

Monday, May 28, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE, Ont. -- By Emlyn Williams Directed by Randy Maertz Starring Peter Krantz, Sharry Flett and Jennifer Phipps Murder a natural theatrical thrill BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE, Ont. Heralded by a rather alarming advertising campaign (the irresistible charm of the smiling psychopath - where else but the Shaw Festival?) Emlyn Williams's Night Must Fall duly descended on Niagaras Royal George Theatre Friday afternoon.

Director Randy Maertzs program note asks questions too: "What is the morbid fascination we have with murderers?" Well, part of the attraction for Williams the playwright back in 1934 was the chance of writing a smashing part for Williams the actor. As for the rest of us, the answer is obvious: murder is the extreme act. It affects us that way, just as citizens. As playgoers, the theatre being above all the place for extremes, it positively attracts us. We don't condone it, but we want to understand it. Some of the best playwrights have catered to our prurience. Shakespeare's most compelling psychological study is Macbeth.

Williamss protagonist, a Welsh boy called Danny, is the runner-up among English dramas Celtic killers. A page boy in a hotel near London, he has before the play begins disposed of most of an importunate lady guest at the bottom of someone's garden, reserving only her head, which he keeps in a hat box. This is not to give anything away; it is obvious by the end of the first act that Danny is guilty. The suspense lies not in discovering who done it, but in anticipating who is going to get done next.

As a sideline, our boy has impregnated a parlormaid and he now insinuates himself into the household and the affections of the girl's employer, a cantankerous and hypochondriacal widow. As everybody else sees through her, she naturally warms to Dan, who plies her with sympathy and chocolates. The one person he apparently cannot charm is the old ladys niece and companion; and she, it turns out, is the most deeply affected of all. She suspects him from the outset and is hostile. When suspicion turns to certainty she is captivated.

A police inspector drily remarks that this is only the beginning; when Danny stands trial he will be deluged with proposals of marriage. This seems to please the lad no end. The point Williams insistently makes is that murderers crave the attention we so freely bestow on them. Its a mutual contract. This may not hold true for all cases, but for a psychopath like Danny it seems plausible. Certainly it carries dramatic conviction. The sexual bond comes out very clearly in this production, with an uncompromising Sharry Flett who finally melts with alarming abandon.

One presumably unintentional symptom of stress is that she loses her English accent - rather a rare fault at the Shaw Festival - and while Peter Krantz never forfeits the Welsh lilt that Williams, for reasons of theatrical charm as well as native convenience, wished on Danny, he does sometimes seem oppressed by it, as if the voice were playing him. He still gets across all the salient points: orphaned resentment, spiralling fantasies of omnipotence, the total confidence of the charismatic dissolving into black terror when things misfire, and by the way, the perfect nannying tactics to disarm his victims.

The relationship takes time to come into focus and until it does, the production has the fidgets. Excellently made though it is, the play is cast in yesterday's mold, the hardest of all to bring to life today. It is a three-act one-set job and the tiny Royal George stage is unkind to it; even by 1930s' standards "the sitting room of Forest Corner" seems hideously cramped and cluttered. Characters stare fixedly at what is presumably meant to be the fourth wall, and sometimes press their noses up against it. Or they stand in straight lines, reacting by numbers.

They also make a lot of noise. Jennifer Phippss chair-bound tyrant is exaggeratedly coarse-grained and the rest of the household must take her tone or perish. She does noticeably improve when Dan has softened her up.

The other characters are stock, vigorously dispensed. Lorna Wilsons Cockney cook leads the field, but Ian D. Clark's stolidly beamish suitor and Helen Taylor's permanently gawping mother-to-be bring up a creditable rear. The play grips. And if it falters you can beguile the time calculating which of the two leading ladies sports the more revoltingly improbable wig.
1990-05-28-theatre-reviews-trelawny-of-t:
THEATRE REVIEWS TRELAWNY OF THE 'WELLS'

Monday, May 28, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE, Ont. -- By Arthur Wing Pinero Directed by Christopher Newton Starring William Hutt, Barry MacGregor Julie Stewart and William Vickers Time turns Trelawny of the 'Wells' into Pinero's best play BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE, Ont. George Bernard Shaw, who had little time for the plays of his honored colleague Arthur Wing Pinero, made an exception of Trelawny of the 'Wells'. Pinero the problem playwright, the Pinero of The Second Mrs. Tanqueray, was in Shaw's view a fake, writing reactionary melodramas and trying to pass them off as challenging pictures of modern life. Pinero, thought Shaw, derived his views of modern life from the work of other playwrights as blinkered as himself. But Trelawny is a period piece - written in 1897, set some 35 years earlier - and Shaw was happy to applaud and endorse its nostalgia.

Time has agreed with him. Trelawny now looks like its author's best play, and 25 years ago (more nostalgia) there was a production at Britain's National Theatre that made it seem like a masterpiece. It gave the very rare and stirring sensation of history - theatrical history, in this case - on the move. Some of this was sleight-of-hand, taking place between the acts. Scenes were changed in full view, while a generation of actors melted into the wings to be replaced by a new vintage. This gave extraordinary resonance to what are anyway the key lines of the piece.

James Telfer, an old leading man fallen on hard times, complains that "this new-fangled stuff, and these dandified people are to push us, and such as us, from our stools!" To which his wife replies, "Yes, James, just as some other new fashion will, in course of time, push them from their stools."

The catalyst for the anti-Telfer revolution is Tom Wrench, once a despised walk-on in the same company at the Banigge-Wells theatre (a transparent disguise for the shabby but historic Sadler's Wells in North London), now emerging as a successful and revolutionary playwright.

His innovation is to put real people onto sets that incorporate real doors and real windows. Of course, the realism of one generation is the escapism of the next, and Pinero gives us a perspective on this. His model for Tom Wrench was the Victorian actor-playwright Tom Robertson, whose works are now charming Dickensian curios.

The Trelawny of the title is Rose Trelawny, an actress who leaves her precarious profession to marry a swell, but who finds her period of enforced probation with his family - an old judge and his spinster sister - too constricting to be borne. She returns to the boards, but her experiences have sobered her so that she no longer believes in the overblown texts she is required to inhabit. (Shaw would have seen a lesson for Pinero himself in that.) Wrench sees, however, that she is just the actress he requires. The fact that he has always been in love with her doesn't hurt - at least, it hurts him, but he rises above it to play Cupid for Rose and her intended. More melodrama: but we gladly give in to it.

Christopher Newton's production that opened on Friday is pictorially splendid but humanly hollow. No play has ever given a more detailed, loving account of the actor's life: the warmth and camaraderie, the jealousy and insecurity. Like Shaw, we are made to feel nostalgia for a world in which every player had his sharply-defined rung on the ladder, from the heights of Leading Man to the depths of General Utiliity: a world in which the most crushing condemnation of an aspiring actor was that he "lacked vigor."

Well, none of the Wells company in this version lacks vigor; they are falling over themselves and one another with it. What they lack is credibility, or any communicated belief in their own dignity. The old Telfers are caricatures, even in their downfall, which accordingly lacks all pathos. Sure, Pinero dictated that Colpoys, the low comedian, is "unable to forget" that he is one; but Simon Bradbury's antics in the role are pasted-on and very wearing. Nor is this a long-term strategy designed to highlight the "real world" outside. The landlady and grocer who attend the actors, the straight-laced toffs who are Roses's prospective in-laws, the new wave of players who arrive in the last scene: all are equally artificial. The play's lesson is surely that all are equally real.

It is not a matter of eschewing extravagance. There are a couple of cameos - Peter Hutt's overbred officer, Robert Haley's excitable Irish prompter - that work because they are affectionately judged.

Barbara Worthy's comedienne has some warm moments. And the parts that have to be taken seriously repay the effort. William Hutt's old authoritarian is beautiful: frail of body, stern of tongue, generous of spirit. Julie Stewart's Rose is poised and vivacious; so, more surprisingly, is Duncan Ollerenshaw as her shy cipher of a lover, though the suggestion that he may be a future Edmund Kean has to be ranked among the more improbable moments in world drama. (The same actor - Ollerenshaw, not Kean - was squeezed out of my notice of Misalliance, in which he throws several impressive tantrums.) William Vickers, after an embarrassingly overdone first act, recovers himself to make an affecting Tom Wrench, with the steel of achievement in him. These players dominate the last section; thanks to them and the author, we leave reaonably happy.

P.S. Two intervals are still one too many.
1990-05-29-theatre-review-when-we-are-ma:
THEATRE REVIEW When We Are Married

Tuesday, May 29, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE, Ont. -- y J. B. Priestley Directed by Tony van Bridge Starring George Dawson, Irene Hogan, Jack Medley and Tony van Bridge At the Shaw Festival With Priestley, the meek inherit the mirth BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE, Ont. Putting down the mighty while exalting the humble and meek is a venerable tradition: admirable in theory and a neat if extremely uncommon trick in practice. It also makes very good theatre, and has done at least since the Middle Ages, when it was given ritual form. They called it the Feast of Fools then, and it was the occasion for the lord of the manor to step down from his seat and minister to his meanest dependents. Mind you, it was only allowed to happen once a year.

In subsequent centuries, it developed into a classic formula: the Comedy of the Turning Worm. J. B. Priestley stumbled on it in 1938, when he wrote When We Are Married, and in so doing created his most enduring play. Its appearance at the Royal George Theatre on Saturday brought the Shaw Festivals opening week to a fittingly festive finish.

The play is literally festive. Set in West Yorkshire in the prosperous days of 1908, it depicts the silver wedding celebration of three prominent couples, who have grown up together and were all married at the same ceremony.

The men, in particular, are much on their dignity and well aware of hierarchy: Alderman Joseph Helliwell, Councillor Albert Parker, Mr. Herbert Soppitt. They are now informed that there has been a terrible 25- year-old mistake, and that they were never legally spliced at all.

This doesn't half put the cat among the pigeons. Or rather, it temporarily de-claws the cats while arousing the pigeons to the possibilities of independent flight. Among the six parties affected, two are pompous, two are rather sweet and two are downright horrible. The sweeties, of course, have been matrimonially shackled to the horrors. Aroused by alcohol and freedom, they begin to assert themselves.

In Britain, the play has always been a favorite: at worst an amiable repertory romp, at best a rich, sly human comedy. Tony van Bridge's production, which clocks in somewhere between these extremes, is most dignified by his own performance. Van Bridge plays Henry Ormonroyd, a photographer from the Yorkshire Argus, an old man so resigned to his own habitual drunkenness that when somebody falsely tells him he has come to the wrong house, he turns unprotesting on his way as if it were just what he had expected. He acts as raisonneur, lecturing the estranged couples on the pitfalls and consolations of marriage, and also as deus ex machina; it is he who resolves their problems by the kind of outrageous coincidence that we accept as being not only necessary but uplifting. Van Bridge shares some cherishable scenes with an uncannily pert teen-age domestic played by Sherry Smith. She lacks his seasoned timing but, with her mob- cap permanently over her eyes, she too conveys the sense of a life going its own unalterable way.

Other performances vary from the proficient to the rowdily amateur. After all, the discovery that three couples are not actually married is in itself pretty tame, as is the further discovery that they actually are. What counts is how they wriggle in between, and to do this to maximum effect they have to be rounded and real. In this production, they are superficial: not caricatures, but types. Irene Hogans uncompromising harridan does best in this vein, with Jack Medleys spongy alderman a fair likeness of your average complacently sensual man. Graham Harley's councillor is a hand-wringing Dickensian hypocrite, effective enough until his partner (Barbara Worthy) tells him what he is. There is more craft and humanity in this scene than either player shows us. George Dawson takes the Waking Up of Herbert Soppitt in one great gulp; it might be more delightful as a series of exploratory sips.

To vary the marital pattern Priestley brings on a mature good-time girl, adorned here with the largest, most extravagantly ribboned and pom- pommed hat to appear on a stage since the last chorus girl paraded out of the Gay Nineties. Mary Haney, underneath it, sounds uncertain which end of England she has wandered in from.

The set makes the stage look as easy and comfortable as in Night Must Fall it seemed crabbed and constricting; perplexingly the same man, John Dinning, designed both.

The title song that the actors warble in improbable unison as the play ends cheapens the evening; the endless recorded reprise that chases us out of the theatre nearly ruins it. The crazy thing is that Priestley took his title from an actual parlor ballad of the period; if they had to sing, they could have sung that. Anyway the real music is in the play's dialogue, which, like its cunning construction, seems artless while coming closer to real theatrical poetry than its author ever achieved when obviously trying.
1990-05-31-anything-goes:
ANYTHING GOES

Thursday, May 31, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Music by Cole Porter Directed by Jerry Zaks Starring Mitzi Gaynor At O'Keefe Centre, Toronto Time-tripping on a musical luxury liner BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail ANYTHING Goes, which opened at Toronto's OKeefe Centre on Tuesday, is the quintessential thirties musical. The Cole Porter score, studded with standards, has a lot to do with this, but the shows main attraction may be its setting. It mostly happens on a luxury liner making the transatlantic run. Here are the rich and frivolous, Porter's people, in their natural habitat and with very little chance of getting out of it. Something about the holiday mode makes the transition from speech to song seem very natural. Besides, Art Deco nautical can be a very attractive style.

This production is a travelling spin-off of the quick and confident version, directed by Jerry Zaks, that played successfully at New York's Lincoln Centre two seasons ago. Tony Waltons set is a symphony in whites, blues and creams against which his costumes, with flashes of scarlet on the passenger list cutting across the resplendent white ducks of the crew, fairly dazzle. This is the most painless revival of a pre-war musical that I have seen.

Anything Goes - written by Guy Bolton and P.G. Wodehouse, revised by Howard Lindsay and Russel Crouse, re-revised by Timothy Crouse and John Weidman - has the reputation of being a "silly" musical. Actually, it is a very good farce, far worthier of serious attention than many intended heavyweights. The set incorporates a line of ceaselessly swinging doors, and there is always a perfectly timed surprise waiting behind them.

The story centres on Billy Crocker, a dashing young Wall Street broker who defies his employer to stow away in pursuit of his beloved who is destined for marriage with a silly-ass Englishman (the Wodehouse-Bolton touch) who is turn pursued by Reno Sweeney, a nightclub evangelist (you heard) who also has a soft spot for Billy as does a bumbling gangster who is pursued by just about everybody. As is Billy.

Are we all clear, so far?

The high point comes when Billy is himself mistaken for a prominent mobster - Public Enemy Number One - and feted by his celebrity-crazed fellow travellers. As he says, if he had just been a stowaway, they would have put him in irons. Pertinent satire in the 1930s, this still strikes a chord in a world less loveably confused than the one whose topsy-turviness Porter mocked and celebrated in his title song.

Apart from that hymn to amorality, the score includes I Get a Kick Out of You, the greatest of hard-boiled love-songs, and Youre the Top, the nonpareil of list-songs, plus such minor classics as the yearning ballad, All Through the Night (which, typically Porter, depicts frustration rather than loss) and Reno's rouser Blow, Gabriel, Blow. To these five we may now add Easy to Love, which fits very well, perhaps because it was written for the show in the first place. It was cut because the 1934 Billy found it too taxing. Other interpolations pad the evening out excessively but at least the selectors have had the grace to draw them only from scores that Porter wrote, as he did this one, for Ethel Merman.

Here looms a problem. There are, apparently, no more Mermans. In olden days an actress oughta Know just how to sing Cole Porter But now, God knows, Anything goes. Old ingenues may do it sweeter Than divas who sang Evita Right through their nose - Anything goes.
