At Lincoln Centre, Patti LuPone's Reno played a sour Brechtian toughie rather than a Broadway broad, honking the lyrics - in this of all shows - into inaudible oblivion. Mitzi Gaynor, starring in very large lettering and a long solo curtain-call, has far better diction but the tone defeats her; she cannot sustain the brass for more than a couple of phrases at a time and lapses into metallic harshness. Merman spent her career doing what came naturally; her successors have to work at it. Gaynors natural mode is apple-cheeked healthiness - essentially, she is still playing Nellie Forbush in South Pacific - and when she tries for Renos straightforward sexuality, she becomes aggressively coy. She still has great legs, though whenever Tom Mahoney's crisp choreography really hots up, she makes a tactful exit through one of the doors and leaves the chorus boys to get on with it. At the number's climax, she returns in an outfit cut even more arrestingly away than before and carries on, not altogether inappropriately, like a manic Tammy Faye Bakker.

Billy is even more of a problem, a mixture of collegiate charming and Broadway brash. Scott Stevensen doesnt exactly torture Easy to Love, but he sounds as if its torturing him. In fact, nobody sings very well but there are plenty of good comic roles, and lines, to compensate. Robert Nichols as musical comedy's eternal crumpled crook (Public Enemy No. 13) heads a valuable echelon of revitalized types. Most important, the music and the comedy reinforce one another. The evening begins with Porter's own brittle rendition of the title song fading into the orchestras modern tribute to him, and the double focus is maintained throughout. This is us looking, with delighted but irreverent respect, at them. So though its not a great revival Still anything this alive'll Make quite a show - Everyone - go.
1990-06-04-theatre-review-lion-in-the-st:
THEATRE REVIEW LION IN THE STREETS

Monday, June 04, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written and directed by Judith Thompson Starring Tracy Wright, Jane Spidell and Ann Holloway At the du Maurier Theatre Centre in Toronto Exploring a limitless domain of human misery By ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Judith Thompsons Lion in the Streets, which kicked off the World Stage season at Harbourfront, is a daisy-chain drama. This is an uncommon species in which an opening scene between A and B is followed by one between B and C, and so on, as far down the alphabet as the author cares to go. It is a point of honor with most practitioners to come back to A for the final eposode.

Actually the only other practitioner who comes to mind is Arthur Schnitzler whose La Ronde goes on a progress through the bedrooms of old Vienna, beginning and ending with a prostitute. This single-minded concern with copulation gives unity to a form that can use it, having denied itself such conventional crutches as character and narrative.

Thompson also concentrates on a city; her play belongs in a thriving line, being the latest vision of Toronto-as-urban-inferno.

Thompson's subject is human misery, a limitless domain that she has to fence in a bit. So she varies the pattern by keeping her initial character on stage throughout, a generally silent witness to everybody else's suffering. This all-seeing person is Isobel (Tracy Wright), a Portuguese girl who begins the play being taunted by neighborhood kids and then turning on them with scary ferocity.

She is rescued by a do-good middle-class mother, subsequently seen being tauntingly abandoned by her husband in the presence of a roomful of their friends.

One of these friends then takes the stage at a meeting of concerned parents, denouncing a nursery teacher for dosing her charges with sugar. The teacher, feeling distinctly battered, meets in a restaurant with a friend who turns out to have bone cancer. The waiter from the restaurant drops in at a cathedral for confession (this is a very Catholic play) and encounters a piece of his past - and so it goes.

Isobel shadows all these people, hoping, she says, that each will provide her with a home, and being progressively disillusioned.

In Act Two her function changes. She no longer mopes, she warns. She tells some well-heeled Torontonians who are watching their off-stage offspring cavorting in the park there is a lion at large. Cant they hear it roaring? (We can, but they dont have our privileged access to the theatre soundtrack.) The lion, it becomes clear, represents the destructive qualities in everybody. Up till now violence in the play, though ubiquitous, has been purely psychological.

From here on in, respectable people take to beating up on one another, not always convincingly. It all culminates in a cemetery where a child- murderer confesses to his adopted mother. He then has a vision of his victim, who turns out to be Isobel. A verbal reconstruction of the crime brings, in some mysterious way, peace. Some kind of atonement has been made. Isobel, having taken the sins of the city - if not of the world - on her shoulders, ends the play standing aloft, arms outstretched, looking crucified.

This rhymes with the first-act finale, which has found the entire cast boogeying on down, around the cathedral altar. But Isobel's redemptive powers do not extend to her own function in the action. As a device she is kitsch, and as a dramatic presence she is very irritating. Whatever the theory, in practise her antics come between us and the other people, cueing us in to be moved, amused or horrified by them.

This underlines the extreme inequality in the writing. On the whole, the starker it is, the better it is. The mother-and-son confrontation in the graveyard is calmly horrific with a murderous pulse beating in the dialogue. The sugar meeting (program description) gets sympathetic comedy out of the caregiver's defence and patronising comedy out of the parents prosecution. It is too easy to make a middle-class audience laugh at itself - there is a comedy of guilt in the auditorium as well - especially when parenthood or marriage are involved.

A husband who had found a younger woman might very well leave his wife as callously and abusively as the one in this play, but it stretches credibility to have him do it so publicly. Stylising the guests embarrassment recognizes the problem without solving it.

The author is also the director and reportedly has firm ideas about the way in which her lines should be delivered. So the wife's metronomic response - "I-can't-believe-I-am-hearing-these-words" - is presumably her idea of irony.

More perplexing is the bad radio acting, full of significant pauses before emotive words, that disfigures much of the evening and yet co- exists with playing as subtle and flowing as Stephen Ouimettes. He is entrusted with three varieties of gay guilt.

First, and amusingly, he is the waiter, once an altar-boy, whose past impulsively reasserts itself to get us into the cathedral. Then he is a journalists researcher forever haunted by a homosexual incident in his youth; the actor's command of first-person reminiscence is seamless. Finally he is the killer, convincing in his aggression and harrowing when he recalls its origin - continual sexual abuse by his stepfather.

In the economic and unsentimental evocation of childhood helplessness actor and author are at their best. Other performers - Maggie Huculak, Ann Holloway, Jane Spidell - can be on the ball in one scene and off it, exaggerated or inaudible, in another. Staging similarly varies from taut to drab. The set mainly consists of a rotating raised disc on the floor, and a stationary flat one on the wall.
1990-06-08-theatre-review-the-house-of-h:
THEATRE REVIEW THE HOUSE OF HORROR

Friday, June 08, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written, directed and performed by Paul Zaloom At the du Maurier World Stage in Toronto A comic-strip view of the human race destroying itself BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail PAUL ZALOOM is a name with possibilities. You can imagine it - the Zaloom part, anyway - spattered across a strip-cartoon panel, as one of the sounds of mayhem. It goes well with his form of theatre, which is a comic- strip view of the human race destroying itself.

Zaloom functions as actor, puppeteer and stand-up comedian. There can be no question of his energy. Nor is there any doubt about his moral credentials: He opposes nothing of which anyone in his audience would conceivably be in favor. According to his publicity, he was against pollution long before most people sensed that there was anything funny in the air. Now that they know, he can hardly help seeming a bit conventional.

The show he has brought from New York to Toronto's Harbourfront (where it opened Wednesday as part of the du Maurier World Stage) is in three parts, of which the second is by far the best. It is also much the shortest. Let us save it till last, so as to end on an up beat.

First, anyway, comes the title-piece. The House of Horror turns out to be a doll house: necessarily, since it is inhabited by puppets. They are glove-puppets, manipulated by a fully visible Zaloom. He enters in protective clothing: a mask and what look like yellow oilskins but are likely something far more chemically sinister. He needs his armor, because the house is a deathtrap.

A Mr. and Mrs. Smith are being shown over it by a Bermuda-shirted real- estate salesman. They take it on an afternoons trial, and proceed to do incautious things like breathing and sitting on the furniture. Mrs. Smiths hair falls out, her already horrible twins - they look like two of the three little pigs - develop rashes (identical, as they disgustedly note), the baby disappears, and grandma sprouts a split personality. This last symptom is niftily represented by having her turned upside-down and inside-out, to reveal a totally different face, dress and manner.

There is a peculiar rushed tempo that afflicts puppeteers and ventriloquists when they change voices. It is as if they can hardly trust themselves to get plausibly from one characterization to another, and hope that the quickness of the tongue may deceive the ear. (Impressionists have the same problem.) This is bearable when conversation is just something that happens between one man and his dummy. But when the jerky rhythm is imposed on an entire sitcom it becomes intolerably scrappy.

Zaloom likes to draw attention to his own shortcomings. Calls himself a puppeteer, complains one of his creations. "You can see his lips move when I talk." (You bet.) This kind of self-deprecation is funny, but not really disarming, maybe because it's all that is funny. At one point the doorbell plays O Canada and Zaloom says: Canadian content. It's the law. This got the loudest laugh of the evening. Its nice of him to try to make us feel at home, especially when hes the visitor, but even ingratiation has its limits. Meanwhile, his satire suffers; usually a puppeteer's characters take on independent life, but these remain puppets.

The last segment, entitled Yikes! is in a form that Zaloom seems to have invented: the Theatre of the Found Object. He mounts three little parables - on Peace, Justice and Religion in America - and peoples them with things. An egg carton packed full of eggs represents a progressively intimidated jury. The President of the United States, knuckling under to the military, is a shrub. These are neat visual puns, but neither they nor the stories they fill out are bold enough to justify the complacent aren't-we-being-irreverent vibes that shuttle between stage and auditorium.

Only in the religious section do things perk up. The situation is an ecumenical conference with the Archbishop of Canterbury played by a feather, a Cardinal by a piggybank, and a homburg giving a richly ethnic performance as a rabbi. This has some good jokes, and is fast as opposed to frenetic.

The brief, effective middle piece is called Phood, and is announced as a world premiere. Here Zaloom takes the stage as the glad-handing host at a manufacturers convention for the promotion of what he calls "food-like substances." His foils here are blow-ups of genuine promo literature, and hilariously horrendous they are. (How do you fancy Its Not Lobster, cooked in Not Butter?) Zaloom discovered, assembled and now underlines them. This is an accomplishment, as well as a public service, but the essential comic work has, of course, been done for him by his targets.

The late Jim Henson was apparently a great admirer of Zaloom's, so there must be more in him than I can see. But Sesame Streeters will know what I mean when I say that though this may indeed be Theatre of Trash, it hardly merits an Oscar. Zaloom!
1990-06-09-theatre-review-sheila-s-day:
THEATRE REVIEW SHEILAS DAY

Saturday, June 09, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Conceived and written by Duma Ndlovu and Mbongeni Ngema Directed by Mbongeni Ngema Produced by Crossroads Theatre Co. at Harbourfronts Premiere Dance Theatre Sheila's Day depicts black struggle in a beautifully sculpted production BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail THERE have been plays about apartheid in South Africa and there have been plays, though fewer of them, about the civil-rights struggle in the United States. Sheila's Day takes on both: an original idea and a brilliant one, and - like all the best notions - perfectly obvious, once somebody else has thought of it.

The show is in fact an African-American collaboration: one that started life at the Crossroads Theatre in New Brunswick, N.J. It opened here as part of the Harbourfront World Stage season on Thursday.

Sheilas Day is the day off given to black female domestics in South Africa by white employers who, confused by their names, called them all Sheila. It is also a day for strongly musicalized prayer meetings: for celebrating, mourning and remembering.

An opening sequence of irresistibly rhythmic chanting and hand-clapping puts us unshakably in the shows corner. The leaps from one story, one continent, one time frame to another can be shockingly abrupt but they are technically seamless. The director, Mbongeni Ngema, first came to international notice with Woza Albert, a two-hander about the black South African experience that I found worthy but interminable. But then it didn't have music. Ngema has since staged Sarafina, a musical that was a surprise success on Broadway and is due later this year at the Royal Alex.

Music oils the wheels of Sheila's Day: music exultant and magisterial, performed a capella by the 11 women who make up the cast. (The unaccompanied music matches the unadorned stage; everything is focussed on the performers.) "The same folks who were partying all Saturday were the first ones to arrive in church Sunday morning. Those words, spoken in the show by an Alabama waitress, obviously point up the unity of sacred and profane, blues and gospel. They also suggest a global unity in black culture: one that the show enacts in form and content.

The evening builds toward two murders: a black African thrown in front of a moving train by two white policemen and his American equivalent beaten to death by a segregationist mob. Both men died trying to protect women; and the shows protest and its affirmation are as much sexual as racial. In each case the murder is described to us by a female witness whose individual story we have previously been following. One has struggled painfully, sometimes illegally, toward a position as a teacher in Johannesburg. The other is the Alabama waitress, whose name is Ruby.

One performer, Ebony Jo-Ann, gets a special credit for creating, writing and acting this character (the others are listed with no identification) and she has also been issued with an individual dramatic licence. Ruby is on a bus when a black woman is arrested for refusing to give up her seat to a white; she is serving at a lunch counter that becomes the scene of a sit-in; she is back on the bus when freedom riders get on board. Being present at these historical flashpoints gives her no pleasure. She is a little annoyed and a lot frightened, and she transmits these feelings to us with an accumulation of why-me-ness that derives from a whole tradition of black comediennes but that she still makes her own.

As a theatrical device, this is both resourceful and appealing. We can sense Ruby getting reluctantly radicalized, but our blushes are spared; there is no scene of flaming conversion as in Brechts atrocious The Mother. The last words we hear are Ruby's account of the killing of her friend Jimmie; and for the first time she isn't funny. Then we may think back to the beginning of the show, and to her first words at the meeting: I cannot forget Jimmie Lee Jackson."

Qedusizi, her Zulu counterpart, also falls foul of history, caught up in an anti-passbook demonstration, and imprisoned in consequence. There is comedy in her story too, though it resides less with her than with the Afrikaner woman in whose house she works for seven years. The few white characters are all bracingly played - trenchantly outlined but not cartooned - and none is more devastatingly hit off than this young chatelaine, benevolent without kindness, cruel without malice. (Ruby too has a spell of domestic service; admonished by a remarkably similar employer to use plenty of elbow grease she spends her first morning looking for it.) The show has been criticized by some U.S. reviewers as being fragmentary. So it is; but that is the point. A full-scale epic, paradoxically, would have to concentrate on one conflict or the other. We are being offered glimpses of a world-wide whole: one that can be extrapolated beyond the black experience. The show is buoyed up by the knowledge that, however painful the cost, the struggles it depicts are going to be won. Imagine a similarly-structured drama that paralleled Nazi Germany and Khmer Rouge Cambodia. It could be done. You wouldn't want to sit through it.

In a sense Sheila's Day has it easy. It drives straight at our consciences and our sympathies, and it does so through joy. But this is a show that depicts oppression without indulging in it, and that takes a religious ground without sermonizing. It is a beautifully sculpted production. It has earned its keep.
1990-06-11-theatre-review-the-servant:
THEATRE REVIEW THE SERVANT

Monday, June 11, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written by Robin Maugham Directed by Allan Davis Starring Keir Dullea and David Ferry At the Bayview Playhouse Stage version of Servant better than the 1960s film BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail The Servant is best known as a movie: a typical early 60s piece of swinging Gothic, directed by Joseph Losey from a script by Harold Pinter. Before that, however, it was a novella by Robin Maugham, Somerset's nephew. He subsequently turned it into a play, which on Friday became the first offering at the re-opened Bayview Playhouse.

Pinter or no Pinter, the play is more satisfying than the film, which was high on atmosphere and low on story. The present staging is generally lacklustre, sometimes inept, redeemed by a couple of good performances, one of them mercifully in the star role. Nevertheless, its grip on the audience is hammerlock.

Tony is a young Englishman, back home after several uncomfortable years in Africa and possessed of "a moderate sum" of money. This seems an understatement; everything's relative, of course, but Tony's modest fortune enables him to buy and maintain a large house in one of the most expensive parts of London and to engage a full-time manservant to maintain it and him. The man in question is Barrett, an opaquely obsequious Midlander (actually from D.H. Lawrence country) with a Jeevesian degree of domestic competence. He also cooks like Antoine, the fabled Frenchman who cosseted and tyrannised Bertie Wooster's Aunt Dahlia. This puts him ahead of Jeeves whose culinary talents may have been limited to the preparation of hangover cures - admittedly a service which Tony stands, or reels, in increasing need of as the action proceeds.

The play might be called The Secret Life of Jeeves and Wooster. It shows the man's manipulative skills employed to subjugate and humiliate the master, with the latter's increasingly enthusiastic co-operation.

It seems that Barrett can give him everything, including sex. There is an implicit homosexual bond between them, and an explicit heterosexual one; Barrett instals in succession two of his own girl-friends, each with instructions to minister to the young master while remaining in thrall to the servant. Submissive by profession, he gets his kicks from dominance.

Territorial struggle, sado-masochism, the idle rich: no wonder the material attracted Pinter (and was baroqued asleep by Losey.) Maugham's own treatment is straightforward and economical, the erotic games outlined but never demonstrated. So a production needs to be stylishly suggestive. Allan Davis's hovers between blatancy and embarrassment.

The program gives the setting as "Chelsea, London, England, Today" and we get "floppy disks" in the dialogue, current pop on the speakers (with actors writhing zombie-like to their Walkmans), and remote control for the onstage television. But the play is a period piece, immutably ensconced in the innocent decadence of post-Profumo Britain. It precedes the boom that preceded the slump. Tony is extinct, replaced by young men equally callow but of tougher fibre, who made their own fortunes and probably have no souls to lose. Even more antediluvian are his bovine long-suffering fiancee and old school chum, forever turning up to receive confidences and - in this production - perching on the arm or back of the sofa for the purpose. Yes, people do that in real life but not very often and not in other people's homes. It is meant to denote casual ease but actually suggests a director at his wit's end to vary the blocking.

However, there is Keir Dullea. He is best known for his leading non- role as one of the astronauts in 2001, and second-best known for having elicited from Noel Coward the salutation "Keir Dullea, gone tomorrow." But, no, he is still here, and an excellent actor.

As Barrett he is socially and geographically exact (lone distinctions in this cast), with an exact balance in his early scenes between courtesy and insolence. Initially he seems ageless and maybe sexless but still a threat; anyone this confident has to be. Above stairs he is content to hover and shimmer and, in an extremity, apologise. His moment comes when Tony takes the fatal step of invading his kitchen. This is a hostile kingdom and Barrett, who has spoken in humble sentences, unlooses a tirade. Dullea takes it thrillingly. Then he subsides, without ever relinquishing his authority. "Mister Tony" who was once "Sir" becomes "Tony": not even an equal, an inferior. It is finely noted in the text, firmly nailed in the acting.

The only performance of comparable command is Erin McMurtry's as Second Bimbo. Unfortunately her role is brief and her appearance long delayed. Her predecessor, Sally Cahill, flounces and bounces - which is an improvement on Eric McCormack's earnestness and Jayne Lewis's plain immobility as the two upper-class stooges.

Which leaves us with the lad himself. If you remember the movie and James Fox's elongated Tony, David Ferry's stumpy, uneasy equivalent will confound you, being devoid of social graces in a play that largely hinges on them. However as Tony descends his personal slope, he comes within the actor's reach; his coarseness becomes convincing, and piteously naked. He is a lost boy. You resent and feel sorrow for him at once, which is as it should be.
1990-06-15-theatre-review-the-cezanne-sy:
THEATRE REVIEW THE CEZANNE SYNDROME

Friday, June 15, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written by Normand Canac-Marquis Translated by Louison Danis Directed by Jim Millan Starring John Jarvis, Martha Burns and George Merner At the Brigantine Room, Toronto Onstage car repairs notwithstanding, some things are just plain mystifying Now, is that Cezanne or Suzanne? BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail THE Cezanne Syndrome opened at the World Stage festival at Torontos Harborfront on Wednesday, three years after receiving its world premiere in Montreal. In the meantime, it has been seen in Ottawa, Chicago, Vancouver and New York. In each city, it received reviews that the Toronto producers have been happy to flourish in their handouts. It is a horrible thought, but maybe there should be a theatrical Meech Lake, charged to expedite the progress of important Canadian plays to the city that fancies itself Canada's theatrical capital.

I make that point out of a sense of duty, since personally I could have lived without The Cezanne Syndrome for another three years if not for ever. It reaches us as a piece of fancy cultural bullying. At an early point, a police officer wanders on - at least, that's what he is for most of the evening, but at this moment hes moonlighting as an art critic - to tell us that Cezanne in his painting ignored realism in the interests of a deeper reality. Due warning is also given by the program, which tells us, more or less, that we are to see a series of disjointed flashbacks in the mind of the central character.

This suggests the need for a highly theatrical symbol-crashing production, such as the play apparently received at earlier points in its odyssey. However, Jim Millans talent, at least as demonstrated in Unidentified Human Remains and the True Nature of Love, is for lucid storytelling lubricated by wit. Normand Canac-Marquis's text has few pretentions as narrative, and is not, one hopes, trying to be funny, though some of its shortcomings here may be attributed to Louison Danis's stilted translation. Millan accordingly comes up with doggedness tempered by oddity. Everything seems to be going on in a stodgy, interminable present tense.

There are, admittedly, strange things. The hero, Gilbert, is a motor mechanic and he appears to be fixing a car in his bedroom; at least, he and his live-in lady make love on top of it. Other times they quarrel, and the author has a keen eye, if not ear, for the architecture of domestic warfare. This, though, is something for which most people hardly need to go to the theatre, and if they do they generally have several plays a season from which to choose.

The woman, identified in the cast list as Her, conducts a tape-recorded correspondence with an idealized friend who apparently has everything she herself lacks. The name of this friend is Suzanne, so the title is a highly significant joke. As if that wasnt enough, it turns out at the end that Suzanne is really Hers own name. This is not a satisfying discovery. Indeed, it reeks of old-fashioned mystification.

Now, Gilbert's love in fact left him; she drove off, taking their child with her, and both of them perished in a grisly crash. So Gilbert has plenty of reason for feeling disoriented, and for taking a blowtorch to the car, literally, and to his memories, figuratively. In retrospect I sympathize with him. At the time I was exasperated; I couldn't tell what was going on, and had little interest in finding out. The play's doughy quality enervated me.

It was greatly assisted in this by the lifelessly literary performance of Martha Burns, which must have got stuck during rehearsal, just after the line-learning stage. By comparison, John Jarvis as Gilbert quivers with humanity, perhaps too tremulously; most patrons will wish that they could entrust their own auto repairs to so sensitive a soul. George Merner completes the cast as the cop whose name is given to us as Thomas Wancicovski, which certainly puts him ahead of Gilbert and Her in the identity stakes. He has a lot less to say, but contributes generously to the pervasive portentousness.

And those of us who, what with Robert Lepage and Denys Arcand, have been inclined to prostrate ourselves before the dramatic talents of French Canada have learned a chastening but probably useful lesson.
1990-06-16-wisecracks-to-poetry:
SOME FREAKS BY DAVID MAMET Viking, 180 pages, $24.95

Wisecracks to poetry

SOME FREAKS BY DAVID MAMET Viking, 180 pages, $24.95

Saturday, June 16, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

REVIEW BY ROBERT CUSHMAN ONCE, greatly depressed, and in New Haven (but I repeat myself). . .  That is playwright David Mamet writing, the same David Mamet who in the play American Buffalo had one of his semi-criminal characters advise another to arm himself on a break-in in case, God forbid, something inevitable should happen." The first line is a lovely wisecrack; the second is comic poetry.

Mamet is the most distinctive stylist to appear in the English-speaking theatre since Harold Pinter. They have plenty in common. Both were actors and have since become screenwriters and directors. Mamet has done especially well at this, with two Hollywood directing credits under his belt. Both write enclosed plays for small casts. Both are verbal experts with the knife and the needle; their texts always seem to carry the threat of physical violence, and sometimes unleash it. Mamets plays have a more direct line to the outside world than most of Pinter's. They are set in specified, recognizable locales. His latest, Speed-the-Plow, takes place in a movie executive's office; he, like Pinter, is going up in the world, maybe not with the happiest results, though God knows Speed-the-Plow is funny.

Pinters masterpiece remains The Caretaker, a tour-de-force of scruff. Mamets twin peaks are American Buffalo, which happens in a junk shop, and Glengarry Glen Ross, from the suspicious end of the real-estate trade. They are the best plays of the last 10 years.

Also, both Pinter and Mamet are Jewish, though neither has made an issue of it. Pinter did write (and has even played) the virtuoso role of Goldberg in The Birthday Party. Mamet's ethnic coloring has always seemed Italian. He grew up in Chicago, and his work is usually set there. In the film The Untouchables, which he wrote, it's Capone Chicago. In Things Change, which he co-wrote and directed, its present-day mobsville (with a side-trip to Nevada). And in Buffalo and Glengarry, the hoods may be just around the corner. The characters, small-timers all, act like they have connections, though if those connections were actually to connect, our guys would probably drop dead from fright.

So I have always believed that Mamet was Italian Catholic, and it has taken Some Freaks, his new collection of essays and occasional items, to disabuse me. He has, of course, the right to write about whomever and wherever he pleases. The thing is, in Some Freaks he has a couple of pieces about American Jewry being ashamed of its own identity, ready to champion every minority cause except its own, proud and envious of the Jew who succeeds without obvious Jewishness, the Jew who "passes. In his plays Mamet is passing: passing, I should say, with honors. The two essays are perceptive, though they are essentially the same piece. So let me splice together a few sentences from them: The lesson of my Reform Temple was that metaphysics is just superstition - that there is no God. And every Sunday we celebrated our escape from Judaism. . . . For my generation, Jewish culture consisted of Jewish food and Jewish jokes, neither of which, probably, were very good for us. . . . Yes, I know that its funny. It is the funniest humor in the world, it's how I have made my living all my life, and it is self-deprecating."

It is funny even, as Mamet has proved, in the mouths of ostensibly gentile characters. He uses it better than Neil Simon, maybe better than Woody Allen. Unlike Simon's and Allens, Mamets are context jokes, not readily quotable, something I find admirable in general if awkward at this moment.

Mamet compartmentalizes in this book too. There is no mention of Jewishness in other contexts. Much of it is insistently all-American. Mamet celebrates the small-town Vermont community in which he now lives, and such manly pleasures as cards, guns and hanging around with the boys, but I get a disarming sense of a shy guy watching himself playing tough.

On his own turf Mamet is thoroughly assured. He writes engagingly on schools of acting, pointing out why Stanislavsky and the Method were exciting and necessary, and why they have ossified. His conclusion - that the theory has lost touch with the life it is meant to reflect and the plays that reflect it - is not new, but it is elegantly and authoritatively stated. He tells us, fascinatingly, how he planned and bluffed his way through the direction of his first movie, House Of Games. ("I found Eisenstein's theories particularly refreshing, as they didn't seem to call for any visual talent.) He writes about women, apparently because a magazine asked him to, though he said that he didnt know anything about the subject. His wife agreed with him about this. Women are notoriously absent from most of his plays. He does know about his own perception of women. Basically, its that they're nicer than men, certainly stronger, and - especially as film and theatre producers with power over playwrights - ruthless. (Speed-the- Plow does have a female, an idealistic bimbo who might develop into a manipulator if not checked as, by a couple of shabby males, she is.) I have seen women do things that the worst man would never entertain the thought of - I do not imply that he would be stopped by conscience, but he would be stopped by the fear of censure." Even if that's wrong about women, its all too right about men - each of whom, as Mamet has repeatedly shown us, yearns to remain one of the boys.

"Over the years, I have come to rely completely on my wifes judgment of character; and am coming to rely on my daughter's ability to assess a situation completely, because she cried when he accidentally stood on her foot. I don't want to be chauvinistic, but a boy might be trusted to do that too. But I like the sentence anyway. And I love this one: As long as Im coming out, I might as well add that I think Mozart couldnt adjust Bach's shoe buckles - an opinion which can be of interest to no one, and which I include solely because I have been trying to work it into cocktail conversation for many years and I have recently stopped drinking."

The book is called Some Freaks because Mamet started by thinking that artists were privileged oddities, and then came to realize that all people are. Robert Cushman is a Toronto writer.
1990-06-18-theatre-review-that-ll-be-the:
THEATRE REVIEW"That'll be the day when this paeon to a rock icon adds up to something theatrical BUDDY

Monday, June 18, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written by Alan Janes Directed by Rob Bettinson Starring Paul Hipp Royal Alexandra Theatre, Toronto Buddy more concert than musical BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail THE program includes a couple of articles on Buddy Holly, the man and the myth, that are well worth a look. In fact they are essential reading, since the show itself has virtually nothing to tell us on either subject. Buddy is a fairly rousing pop concert, thinly if laboriously disguised as a musical.

I don't deny that it got to my feet and my nostalgia-glands. I'm fairly sure I never cried when I read about his widowed bride - truthfully, I don't remember his death in the l959 airplane crash registering at all - but in the years that followed Holly loomed larger in my life than Elvis ever did. His twangy, unthreatening music was the soundtrack to every teen-age party I ever attended, at least until supplanted by early Beatles. Those were innocent years. Holly, in the nicest sense, was kid's stuff.

And he was nice. Geoff Pevere and Peter Goddard tell us so in the program and the show backs them up. That is to put it a bit too positively; let us just say that it never contradicts them. It has little truck with characterization, and not much with narrative. But then there isn't much to narrate. "All that happens in the play" say its creators "is based on fact, even those events which seem beyond belief." But what they show us is that Buddy and the Crickets started out playing country-and- western in their native Texas, graduated to rock'n'roll, encountered early resistance, but soon became very successful. That's Act One. After the interval Buddy gets married, splits from his record producer and his sidemen, and accidentally dies. Only the most fearful skeptic could have trouble with any of that.

They do try and pad it out. There is a running gag, repeated roughly 18 times, about Buddy's mother phoning him to make sure he's eating right. The hero is given heroic lines ("I don't want to play country-and-western, I wanna play my music") and there are awfully knowing ironies; he is told that he has about as much chance of recording in Nashville "as that fella Ray Charles has of playing in the White House." There is suspense. When the group is booked into the Harlem Apollo, they are told - endlessly - that the black audience will eat them alive. But we know all along that they are going to be a smash.

Actually if you are looking for improbabilities, it seems odd that at a time when Buddy and the Crickets have had two number-one hits, nobody at the Apollo knows enough about them to realize they are white. Going a bit further back I was surprised to see the three guys making out with three local girls under the local stars (I don't mean that the girls are under the stars - well, maybe I do) when they are already successful enough to afford motel rooms. And further back still, the arrival, unheralded and unexplained, of a fourth Cricket halfway through the first recording session could do with some fleshing out. But strange things happen in studios; when trying desperately to explain themselves to the good ol' boys at Nashville Decca, the trio go into an impromptu rendition of That'll Be the Day, exactly as it sounds on the record.

The story swiftly becomes a matter of success and more success, linked by the triumphant pronouncements of disc-jockeys (though the one in Philadelphia sounds really mean) perched in eyries all over the colorfully ugly set, which is meant to be redolent of the Fifties and is. The sequence with most theatrical potential is the build-up to the fatal flight after a snowbound concert in Iowa. History has laid on the ironies thick. Holly was actually scheduled to go by bus, and only flew on a whim; his co-star and fellow-victim Ritchie Valens had to plead and wheedle to get on the plane. (As played here, like a gyrating Liberace, he was no great loss.) The script gives us the facts but doesn't know how to dramatize them.

Even musically Holly begins to seem an odd subject for a show. The numbers that tear the place up have nothing to do with him. A female trio at the Apollo sing an R&B number, indistinguishable from hundreds of others, but enough to put paid to the already dubious claim that Holly had a black sound. (The rednecks think him uncommercial because of it; this at a time when Presley had already broken.) The Big Bopper, his other doomed fellow-passenger, precedes him in Iowa with a number that anyone would have trouble following: Chantilly Lace, the best song of its era, performed here by David Mucci panting and lolloping all over the stage with a grin full of certifiable fangs. And for Buddy's closing number (a last-minute panic measure to judge from the song-listing in the program) the producers abandon Holly's own catalogue and have him do Chuck Berry's incendiary Johnny B. Goode.

Paul Hipp's Buddy is gawkily good-natured as prescribed, and his re- creation of the songs is note-and-letter perfect. Amazing that a mere ten songs and horn-rims should make a legend, but so it is; and you don't tamper with a legend. It means that the performer has no chance to personalize the material; the audience would hardly stand for that. It has more to do with necrophilia than with theatre, but it is a burgeoning genre; and this is one of the better examples. It comes to us from London, where it is a big success. So what do I know?
1990-06-25-jazz-festival-gets-under-way-:
JAZZ"Festival gets under way for its 10-day summer run Downtown Jazz hits the streets

Monday, June 25, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail JOE Williams is famous for singing blues, and he also sings ballads. According to critical legend he has an artistically split personality. In fact he is a seamless stylist with a large repertoire. Drawing on two main sources, he splits the difference between them, bringing urbanity to the blues and soul to standards. The proportions may vary from gig to gig, but the recipe remains constant.

Opening the du Maurier Ltd. Downtown Jazz festival at Roy Thomson Hall on Friday, he naturally had his Count Basie side uppermost. Rob McConnell's Boss Brass, which has its own Basie aspect - an overhanging sense of power held pleasantly in reserve, waiting to spring - seemed more than happy to co-operate. Williams was a mellow singer even when young, and in his enduring prime (old seems quite the wrong word for him, even if he has turned 70) he radiates sensual assurance. Grey-haired and white- suited he is a smiling jazz aristocrat: positively Ducal.

The voice rasps a little more than it used to, and the falsetto is a bit less thrilling. But the instrument still rings at both ends of the register; there is a tautness about it that stops it from being cavernous (like Billy Eckstine) or overly smooth (Nat King Cole). A couple of years ago I heard him still a New York club with a wonderfully modulated and, it seemed, deeply-felt How Deep Is the Ocean. It's on his latest record. That night it took everybody by surprise, maybe including him.

There was nothing like that on Friday. Maybe the occasion and the hall forbade it. His program was relentlessly up; even the contemplative moments had a Vegas tinge. Alec Wilder's A Child Is Born, which craves simplicity, was pumped up with two wedges of recitation. He opened and closed with one of those philosophical autobiographical numbers by which all mature singers get visited sooner or later - without exemption. Sure enough, he did it his way.

There were no classics and only one warhorse: a welcome retread of Alright O.K. You Win. There were also homages to his Basie predecessor Jimmy Rushing: I Want a Little Girl, the most satisfying number in the set. It was all expert and enjoyable, a master in repose. But one waited in vain for lightning to strike.

Williams has probably the least bruised voice of any accredited blues singer. He saves his vulnerability for his ballads, when he sings them, but his blues are rhythmically jovial assertions of male supremacy. Operating at the other end of the system - in gender, attitude, age and, on this occasion, place on the bill - is the evening's opening act: Holly Cole , dynamiting the American popular song.

Cole is a cunning subversive;, she dresses like a nightclub siren, with the off-the-shoulder air of a hipster's Madonna, and she has the traditional musical virtues as well. She swings mightily, phrases with point, and has a powerful way with dynamics. She began with that most standard of standards, The Man I Love , and served notice of her agenda from the second line which came out as "he won't be big and strong." This might have been a sad acceptance of unavodiable reality but it sounded more like a statement of principle. According to Ira Gershwin "he'll build a little home" a mere meliorist might change "he'll" to "we'll" but Cole went all the way to "I'll." I want to hear her sing Ol' Man River, toting dat barge, lifting dat bale, getting more than a little drunk, and landing, at a defiant up tempo, in jail.

This kind of vocal deconstruction is stimulating for a couple of numbers but self-defeating in the long stretch. Love for Sale doesn't need an extra coating of savage irony; it's already there in what Cole Porter wrote. The contrastingly regretful irony of Johnny Mercer's Talk to Me, Baby ("tell me lies") needs a filigree touch.

Her centrepiece - and the title-cut of her first CD - is Girl Talk, a mid-tempo mid-60s ambler about women chattering among themslves. It was composed by Basie's ace arranger Neal Hefti; and Joe Williams might have sung it to paternalist perfection. Cole tried valiantly to turn it against itself, but it kept asserting its own identity. Maybe it should have been left to die of disuse.

Cole's voice filled the hall more effectively than her presentation. She allows her two sidemen plenty of musical space, and rightly; pianist Aaron Davis is an especial wizard, conjuring a whole melody through a few driving fragments. But she has to do either more or less while they're playing; she can't just stand there and undulate.

In between the voices the Boss Brass, crammed with Toronto's best, had a joyous reunion that went from a restfully rocking Smoke Gets in Your Eyes to McConnell's own Traditional Piece, a solid piece of three-story masonry. Its name notwithstanding, the heart of this band is in its rhythm: Don Thompson thoughtful on piano, Ed Bickert incomparably relaxed on guitar, and Jerry Fuller suspending the whole mighty operation securely between his drumsticks from first beat to last.
1990-06-27-jazz-review-wynton-marsalis-g:
JAZZ REVIEW Wynton Marsalis guides his bright crew with a sure hand Magnificent Seven on a musical ride

Wednesday, June 27, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail THE group that played Torontos Roy Thomson Hall on Monday night should really be billed as the Wynton Marsalis Septet. The trumpeting prodigy, still a safe distance from 30, stands alone on the posters and programs, but not on the stage. He is fronting a band of musical equals even if he is its unquestioned leader.

The leadership is theatrical as well as musical. Conservative lookers though they are, these musicians are unusually satisfying to watch as each in turn weaves in and out of the solo spotlight. Sometimes the four horns will parade discreetly to the back of the platform while the marvelous rhythm section gets on with it. Spare though it is, it looks choreographed - a sort of post-modern homage to the showmanship of the big bands - and one detects the elegant guidance of Marsalis. His own announcements, though sometimes modestly witty (or wittily modest), lean too far toward minimalism. I mean, they're quite hard to hear.

I am fairly sure, though I had to strain to catch it, that the opening number was called Uptown Ruler. It was announced as a five-song suite, four-fifths written by Marsalis with the balance by tenorist Todd Williams, detailing the trials and triumphs of a young man in the big city. It did recognizably move from the exploratory to the exultant, with some plangent lamentation in the middle; but as usual with program music, jazz or other, the plot-line rapidly got lost. One responded to magisterial moods: to the way a questioning Marsalis solo emerged from a richly growling, almost Ellingtonian, ensemble.

A later and longer suite, Sugar Cane and Sweetie Pie, was introduced as a tale of boy chasing girl. It lasted more than half an hour, and the shape of the pursuit was difficult to discern, though it gave everybody ample blowing space. Hypnotic for most of its length, it finally outstayed its welcome, only to recover with a solo from Williams of liquid beauty and a brief extraordinary cadenza from the bassist, Reginald Veal.

Among the more brief numbers, Embraceable You was a jewel. Marsalis plays a lot of standards like this on his latest CD, which I think of as Wynton Plays Pretty For The People. He sticks to the melodies and his pianist father supplies the spice. But this was different: an object lesson in when to adhere to the Gershwin line (since some of it is unimprovable) and when to spin out a tribute to it. It was impossible to listen without feeling a beatific smile engulfing your face.

The Cat in the Hat is Back, another Williams tune, was as nimbly joyful as its name: a bright group workout to conclude the first half. The second officially ended with Marsalis's own much-bruited Majesty of the Blues, very heavy on mutes, which seemed to me lacking in blues and majesty alike. Both were abundant, though, in the encore, Jelly Roll Mortons Jungle Blues. Marsaliss style and stance for most of the evening had harked back to Miles Davis in his glory days with Gil Evans: the haunted, dignified tone, the economy, the general sense of a confident navigator on a deceptively glassy sea. His crew were pretty much in the same boat, except for the trombonist (his name escaped me) who kept waking discreet echoes of New Orleans. For the Morton number, everybody joined him there. It is, after all, Marsalis's hometown and he is a supremely accomplished eclectic, the heir to just about everybody. The result was not exactly traditional jazz, but it was a powerful, moving distillation of a great ancestral spirit. It rightly brought the house down.

If septet is too hard a word, they could always call themselves Wynton's Magnificent Seven.
1990-07-01-in-the-languages-of-star-cros:
For the last 30 years, consciously or not, most productions of Romeo and Juliet have been competing with West Side Story. They may emphasise sex, like Franco Zeffirelli's Renaissance epics of lust and dust on stage and screen, or violence, as in Michael Bogdanov's spirited RSC attempt to pin the blame on Verona's capitalist system. Here is one Shakespeare play - about teenagers, for God's sake - that should be able to realise the fantasy of every populist director and hit the kids where they live.

If where they live is Canada, there are other possibilities. This is a riven country, maybe on the verge of splitting apart. So a homespun company called Shakespeare on the Saskatchewan has pitched tent - literally - at Harbourfront, which is where Toronto holds its annual international theatre festival, with a bilingual production. Anglophone Montagues spit their hatred, in the original text, at Francophone Capulets who retaliate in translation. When they want to get really nasty, either side is liable to adopt the other's speech. Appropriately, there are two directors: Saskatchewan's Gordon McCall and the Quebecois Robert Lepage, whose massive original creations are too dynamic to be called performance art, and who is one of the world's best directors.

Characters enter by car or, more commonly, truck. We are in a car-town, and the lovers meet at the Capulet barn dance. Some oddities cannot be overcome. The man reverently referred to as the Prince is more like the local cop. Gee, Officer Krupke, fancy meeting you here.

At first the concept seems to have got stuck in the traffic. It is impressive to see just how many vehicles can force themselves into a space, and exciting to watch them and their occupants bashing one another. The opening brawl is as mean as it should be ("Do you bite your thumb at us, sir?" is the first line in clear English). Juliet's balcony is the top of a pickup truck: no deterrent to Romeo who is on top of her - literally - before they have exchanged so much as a sigh. This is presumably meant to be fantasy, but the heavy-handed staging has no magic. The first half is brutalist Shakespeare at its most reductive. After the interval all is superbly changed. A tiresomely coarse Mercutio becomes witty just in time for death. The traffic thins; the lovers wheel a bed on for their farewell scene, with a rope attached. When they part, Juliet pays the rope out and Romeo crawls along it. Somehow we are convinced this horizontal flight is a vertical one. This means Lepage is in charge. Every moment seems right, and most of them reverberate. When Juliet takes the potion we share her fearful vision of the corpse-strewn family tomb; this time we are not confused, and we do believe.

Unlike most directors praised for command of imagery or the ability to create events, Lepage is sensitive to text and acting. From the start the two leads show unusual promise: Romeo sturdy rather than moonstruck and Juliet's accent enchanting enough to justify the language experiment on its own. They grow remarkably; and the other characters give them a belated but illuminating context. (A young, coldly frightened Lady Capulet explains a lot about her daughter). The last speech, done by the whole cast, with alternate lines in French and English, returns us impressively to the concept. But anyone can have a concept: Lepage has peopled his.

The importance of basics has been further demonstrated by Kenneth Branagh's Renaissance Theatre Company which wound up its six-month world tour in Toronto prior to a British tour leading to the Edinburgh Festival. Branagh's King Lear and A Midsummer Night's Dream are disfigured by a unit set that looks dingy under lights and too many performances of matching shabbiness. But they survive as fine pieces of story-telling. Richard Briers's Lear has unexpected authority, somewhat at the expense of his own actor's identity; but his madness has a lucidity and immediacy I have never known bettered. The Dream has lively lovers and brilliant mechanicals, among whom Branagh's Quince is a real original: a smug village intellectual, resentful of Briers's buoyant Bottom. Clearly, if you are going both to act and direct in the Dream, Quince is the role to choose. In Lear Branagh plays Edgar, another character who tries to control peoples' lives. It must work off all kinds of tensions.
1990-07-05-theatre-review-oklahoma:
THEATRE REVIEW OKLAHOMA!

Thursday, July 05, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written by Richard Rodgers and Oscar Hammerstein Directed by John Davidson Starring John Davidson and Kim Crosby The latest version of Oklahoma! to hit Toronto should introduce some emotional delicacy in its treatment of characters Makeshift revival needs reworking ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail IT has often been pointed out that an old-fashioned show about Oklahoma (you think Oklahoma! is an old-fashioned show? You don't know from old- fashioned) would have started with that song. Wise after the event, we can all see that it would not have had a tenth of the impact that it has at the musical's climax. This is not just because of the architectural advantage of a slow build. It is because, at the beginning of the show there is no Oklahoma, so the song would make no sense: not that that would deter some producers, then or now. When the show starts the characters are living in an unnamed area of the American West (I believe it was called Indian Territory but the show ain't lettin' on); when it ends, statehood is looming. A mere three weeks have elapsed, but that of course is an eternity in politics.

Oscar Hammerstein, who wrote the book and lyrics for Oklahoma! in 1943, had done the same for Show Boat 16 years earlier, so he presumably knew a big subject when he found one. Show Boat knew all along that it was an epic; Ol' Man River winds through the action to prove it. But in the years between Hammerstein had had flop after flop so perhaps he felt cautious. He keeps Oklahoma! domestic all through the first act. Then, without warning, he takes up the second act curtain on a hoedown number called The Farmer and the Cowman, all about how territory folks should stick together, not to mention what will happen when this territory joins the union just like all the others. The show's perspective deepens, and stays deep. The hero, Curly, is a cowboy, and the heroine, Laurey, owns her own ranch. So their eventual union mirrors the bigger one. That is what the title song is about. But it is very abrupt, and I wish that a few hints could have been dropped earlier.

Similarly with the love story itself. Everybody says how audacious it was (the less charitable say, how childish) to build an entire long first act on nothing more momentous than the question of who is to take Laurey to the box social. This is rubbish. A subject is important to an audience if it is important to the characters, and everyone on stage knows that Laurey's choice of escort is vitally connected to her eventual choice of a husband. Which is something that she and everyone else in her close-knit community might be excused for finding of absorbing interest.

The problem is that while Laurey's pattern of advance and retreat from Curly is well documented, her attraction towards his rival, the unsavory hired hand, Jud Fry, is never explored.

Jud himself is a terrifically powerful figure; he makes Curly so jealous that the cowboy tries to tempt him to suicide. The resultant song, Pore Jud Is Daid, is brilliant black comedy, the kind of thing the wholesome Hammerstein is supposed to have been incapable of writing. He was obviously so disturbed by Jud that he felt compelled to reject him, falling back on a boy-scout great-outdoors morality that only the unfailing lilt and vigor of Richard Rodgers's music can make palatable. Jud is a creature of dark corners, meditating revenge and gloating over pornographic photos; Hammerstein cannot really have believed that the emerging United States would render him obsolete.

A misfit dramatically as well as psychologically, Jud adds immeasurably to the strength and range of Oklahoma! and there is no point in tidying him up. But a first-rate revival, which the show needs and deserves, might well amplify the libretto a little. It should certainly re-think the ballet. And it should balance an overall spaciousness with a comic and emotional delicacy in its treatment of characters who spend their time hiding from themselves and one another.

I offer these thoughts to get myself off the hook of considering in detail the makeshift revival at O'Keefe. John Davidson directs and plays a smily Curly; he means well but the attitudes he strikes are singer, not cowboy: more country than western. Kim Crosby's Laurey fought, on Tuesday night, a losing battle with her personal amplification system, which had arranged for her to sing all her songs to buzzsaw accompaniment.

Natural sound might also make the orchestra screech less horrendously. The tunes are admittedly indestructible, (12 songs, 11 famous) though one does not so much listen to them as pleasantly register their re- appearance. I enjoyed the eccentric male dancing in the Kansas City number, led by Christopher Wells as Will Parker, and the horseplay generally. The comedy of the subplot - another case of a girl and two suitors - may have whiskers but they are very presentably combed, and Andrew Boyer as Ali Hakim the skirt-chasing marriage-fleeing peddler is neat. ) Darrell Sandeen's Jud hulks, skulks, and dominates, an old Beast forever denied his Beauty.
1990-07-12-theatre-review-out-there-toni:
THEATRE REVIEW OUT THERE TONIGHT

Thursday, July 12, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Directed by Alan Johnson Starring Shirley MacLaine O'Keefe Centre Shirley MacLaine's zig-zag smile and precision movement are just two of the attratcions her charming show Shirley goes beyond the confines of fame ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail HERE are two unbroken hours of Shirley MacLaine: no interval, no supporting acts, no false exits. We arrive to find the curtain already up on a set that looks, in an Art Deco hue, somewhere between white and grey, like a bandstand. This it turns out is exactly what it is, though complicated by an arrangement of stairs and railings that might have fallen off the back of an ocean liner. Maybe they were left behind by Anything Goes, when everything went.

Presently the show starts. Musicians wander on and, with purposeful casualness, start tuning up. Then technicians, or guys pretending to be, appear and execute sound and lighting checks. Ah, the thrill of rehearsals. If only it could be captured in performance; but it never is. You start fretting at the artful artlessness of it all, and nerve yourself to applaud the stars inevitable grand entrance. Then suddenly, just when and where you would least expect it, she is discovered. Grudgingly, you admit that this production may know what it is doing.

The first thing the lady does is sing the title song, which is devoted to second-guessing all the things the audience might be thinking about her. It is rather accurate, in a self-confidently self-deprecating way, and the lyric is neatly turned. (The program contains the novel credit: "Writing by Buz Kohan.") When MacLaine did her first one-woman show, 16 years ago, it was all about how amazing it was to find someone we all knew as a movie star appearing on stage at all, let alone singing and dancing and doing it well. In another 16 years she may, I fear, be doing a show about how amazing it is to be doing a show at her age. This time round, she has a running gag about her well-known spiritual preoccupations, and how weird she knows everybody must find them. She also delves into her performing past to do what she calls her hooker-victim medley, composed - or so it struck me - of songs she almost did in the movies: somebody elses big number from Sweet Charity and a ballad she would have sung in Irma la Douce if Irma la Douce on film had stayed a musical.

I like Shirley MacLaine, which I assume puts me in the majority. I think she is entitled to her opinions, however bizarre, and I would back her to defend them against any talk-show host in the hemisphere. I also find her, still, desperately attractive as only a funny girl can be, and I can have little serious quarrel with a show that exhibits her in a black lame leotard. She may not be the world's most spectacular dancer but she moves with zest and precision, no slacking, while her zig-zag smile, piquant nose, mocking eyes and cropped red hair are practically choreographic features in themselves.

Some of her self-satire is very effective. She tells a solemn story about a trip to the Andes, and just as we are becoming bored and embarrassed it turns into a tribute to Jimmy Durante. For a moment she really had us fooled, as she gleefully claims. Indeed I found that she was second-guessing me all evening. "I bet you thought I was Mitzi Gaynor" she said, as if the set raised for her the same associations it did for me. Then, just as I was wondering why she didn't play a role in a real musical - Mama Rose in Gypsy, for example - she went into what amounted to an impromptu audition for it. As it turned out we were both off-beam; maybe Roses Turn could never work out of context but I suspect MacLaines vulnerability is too near the surface for Rose, a woman who only discovers that she has feelings belatedly and by accident. But I would like to see her as Adelaide in Guys and Dolls or Desiree in A Little Night Music or maybe Ella, the Judy Holliday role, in Bells Are Ringing. If she loves the stage as much as she claims I don't see why she has to limit herself to evenings of snippets.

But since she has: The snippets I liked best included a song about the supermarket tabloids and, incredibly but truthfully, the ritual thanks to her musicians and back-up dancers, done as a number and a rousing one. There is also a prolonged tribute to Broadway choreography which starts, spiffily and instructively, with a pastiche of the late Bob Fosse, but then founders on the fact that no other maestro has as recognizable a style and disintegrates in an MTV parody that is generalized and fundamentally (and forgivably) bored. Otherwise Alan Johnson's staging is unostentatiously shrewd, while the music has been composed and arranged by industrial heavyweights: Larry Grossman, Peter Matz, Billy Byers.

The show as a whole swings between exhilaration and queasiness. She is Shirley MacLaine, and the audience knows she is, and thats why both parties are there, and maybe its honest of them to admit it, and especially her. Post-modern critical theory holds that all art is self- referential, which is true, but then goes on to assume that that's the most interesting thing about it, which isn't. Shirley MacLaine is famous for being famous, but she does not have to settle - even in the 1990s - for being famous for being famous for being famous.
1990-07-19-theatre-review-starlight-expr:
THEATRE REVIEW STARLIGHT EXPRESS

Thursday, July 19, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written by Andrew Lloyd Webber and Richard Stilgoe Directed by Arlene Phillips At O'Keefe Centre, Toronto The trouble with Starlight Express is that this musical on wheels is, at times, not spectacular enough Exciting, sometimes beautiful, but not always on the right track ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail STARLIGHT Express is one of those shows that nobody likes except the public. It is everlasting in London, ran respectably in New York, and is doing well on the road, if that is the right expression for a show ostensibly about the lives and loves of a set of trains. But critics everywhere have despised it, and the O'Keefe's pre-publicity material was confined to a single word, repeated over and over. The word was "spectacular" and all the critics had used it because they had to. It isn't a value judgment; it's a statement of fact.

One is supposed to have extreme reactions to Andrew Lloyd Webber. But I have never been able to regard him either as the messiah of the musical theatre or as the devil incarnate; and I have a soft spot for Starlight. When I saw it in London I could not comprehend its savage dismissal by the same journalists who had creamed over Cats, for the two shows have the same strengths and weaknesses. Both are environmental entertainments of a particular childlike kind: adventure playgrounds. Both are ensemble shows, and a lot of the good feeling they generate is company feeling. Neither is strong on individual character; and both are at their worst when trying to gouge sympathy for a protagonist, whether Grizabella the Glamor Cat or Rusty the Steam Engine.

I doubt if anyone unbriefed by the publicity or by what they could make out of the lyrics would realize that the 37 brightly-clothed roller-skated actors at the O'Keefe are actually meant to be trucks and engines. A train that stands up on its hind legs is a train in very bad trouble. In fact, Starlight is in large part an abstract entertainment in which color and movement are ends in themselves. Or rather an end in itself, since at the best moments the two fuse. When Arlene Phillips' choreography sends John Napier's stunning costume creations whizzing up the ramps and down the runways of the same designer's girdered set, the upshot is excitement and sometimes beauty.

What it is not, is narrative interest. Starlight Express is presented to us as a child's bedtime fantasy. There is an offstage narrator who calls himself Control and sounds like Christopher Robin gone beyond bears. He dreams up a Trans-America train race that attracts the locomotives of the world. In the end, the competition narrows down to three emblematic natives: the diesel Greaseball, the electric Electra, and Rusty. Steam is the underdog, and therefore the hero. Each engine, male, draws a single coach. Most are female, so we get a romantic subplot.

Rusty's precarious confidence is bolstered by his blues-singing Dad, and by some mysterious choo-choo deity called the Starlight Express which eventually materializes as a fierce drifting cloudscape framed by green lasers. It tells Rusty to believe in himself. It has probably seen too many musicals. Its wisdom is the wisdom of the ages, at least those between Carousel and Sunday in the Park with George.

The story, such as it is, is easier to follow in the North American production than in the London one, where the human trains went racing all over the auditorium, with the action monitored on video screens for those spectators who might have their backs to any of it. Here it all happens on a large but conventional stage, except for the races themselves which are on film. This last device is horrendous. First, it is an admission of failure: it is telling us that the climax of this stage musical cannot be staged. Second, nobody goes to the theatre to look at a screen. Third, while we may accept that these actor"dancers on stage are trains, film ineluctably reveals they are just people in warpaint being silly. Fourth, the sequences probably cost thousands to shoot but they still look cheap, grainy and unimaginative.

In fact, the trouble with Starlight Express is not that it is spectacular, but that it isn't, at key moments, spectacular enough. Theatre has every right to be visually extravagant; other things being equal it has a duty to be. (That a play like Love Letters gets praised for not having crowd scenes and falling chandeliers, as if this were a positive virtue, shows how confused our values have become.) Starlight Express is planned as a story musical but can't quite tell its story. Cats was a vaudeville that at desperate moments fell back on a fable at least as maudlin and sententious but mostly kept it out of sight. Which is preferable I don't know. But, though I am shouting with the minority, I prefer the music of Starlight. Webber has written a pop score, and an entertaining one: from the chugging and churning opening number Rolling Stock to the generic but rousing gospel closer Light at the End of the Tunnel, by way most notably of One Rock and Roll Too Many, the repentant lament of the losing locos. There are, admittedly, no hit ballads of the calibre of Memory. Thank God.

The touring production is crackerjack, with Jimmy Lockett's sonorous Poppa and Todd Lester's capering Red Caboose earning special credits in a troupe that brims with energy and, come to think of it, courage. The electronics are impeccable: as, of course, they have to be. That a show so dependent on high-tech should be so Luddite in its sympathies is a paradox. Though no more so than that a creative team from Britain, which still has a railway system worth the name, should have set a train musical in the United States, which hasn't. There is a sickness here somewhere. I think it's called nostalgia.
1990-08-09-theatre-review-jesus-christ-s:
THEATRE REVIEW JESUS CHRIST SUPERSTAR

Thursday, August 09, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

By Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice Directed by Tony Stevens Starring Stephen Lehew At O'Keefe Centre Jesus Christ Superstar is an up-to-date Sunday school treat with an impressive score and lyrics that are fresh and intelligent The Passion story as rock oratorio BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail THIS is the way it goes. A lot of street-life is happening in old Jerusalem, a territory with a hitherto unsuspected incidence of dry ice and late sixties tribal bopping. A token military presence, composed of young men in tunics and gleaming ironmongery, polices the quarter in the desultory fashion referred to in the training manuals as crossing from stage right to stage left and exiting; but as soon as this manoeuvre has been accomplished the locals return to their customary avocations. The righteous among them go looking for prostitutes to insult; the free- thinkers spring to the ladies defence; and there is a violent outbreak of Choreography. Then a long-haired young man in off-white Biblical togs appears atop the flight of steps that is the places principal architectural feature, and everything and everybody goes very quiet.

And the age-old question arises: is He or isn't he?

I may be the only theatregoer on the planet to whom, on Tuesday evening, all this was news. Until then I had never seen Jesus Christ Superstar.) Of course I had heard lots of it, and heard lots about it, and I approached it with certain prejudices. Many of these were positive; I wanted confirmation of my suspicion that Andrew Lloyd Webber's best shows were those he wrote with Tim Rice. On the other hand I distrusted rock musicals (remember rock musicals? nobody writes them now but they were quite a thing in the seventies) and though this may be because I distrust rock music anyway, I like to think that there are purely pragmamatic, theatrical reasons connected with lack of flexibility, and inaudibility of lyrics.

I remain as helplessly agnostic as the show itself. It is the Passion story, told as a set of reactions. The most famous of these is Mary Magdalenes chirpy professional response, cast as the prototypical early Webber ballad: the one that goes I Dont Know How To Cry For His Memory, Argentina. The others express various shades of skeptical bewilderment and human unworthiness. The Roman governor does his conscience-stricken hand- washing act: automatic Pilate. The High Priests are cardboard villains. Except in the taut Last-Supper-and-Gethsemane sequence, nobody interacts. At its inception, the show was tagged as rock opera but in its stasis it is more like rock oratorio.

Two characters, though, stand out. The authors, like many before them, reckon that Judas had a lousy deal: damned for carrying out a preordained divine plan. They give him a cogent case: disillusion with his leader's increasing intimations of immortality. He comes back for an 11 o'clock number - the original Superstar song - to ask Jesus a number of jivily sardonic modern questions. Does he believe in himself? Wouldnt his message have stood a better chance in an age of mass communication?

The second question history has answered. The final tableau - stars descending on the Crucifixion, like a Hollywood logo - graphically demonstrates the endurance of Jesuss legend. The audience cheered, partly out of nostalgia for the musical styles of 20 years ago but also out of a more deeply-rooted atavism. Ours may be a godless society but it has taken a lot of religious trappings on board. There is always a market for Biblical epics. Jesus Christ Superstar is an up-to-date Sunday school treat.

It doesn't have to be that way - Monty Python's Life of Brian proved that - but it is hard to avoid. Rice and Webber failed to avoid it perhaps because they had no fundamental interest in the subject. They pick it up, shake it about a bit with some smart points and exciting noises, and put it back precisely where it was.

On their own terms, though, they wrote an impressive score. Webbers ballads may be bathetic but his more barbaric noises - most notably the sardonic Hosanna chorus - are more than literally electric, and are offset by a recurrent haunting use of Mexican guitar. Only the pounding title phrase, like its pattering successor in The Phantom of the Opera, sounds risibly reductive. Rices words are often themselves reduced to doggerel by the insistent rhythms, but their concepts if not their execution are fresh and intelligent.

The Jesus of Stephen Lehew and the Judas of Milton Craig Nealy are powerfully sung, with tireless and rabble-rousing falsettos. Performers in this kind of show don't play the character, they play the style. That may be rock's legacy to the musical theatre.
1990-08-18-the-confidant-to-whom-garbo-o:
The confidant to whom Garbo opened her soul GARBO Her Story

Saturday, August 18, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ANTONI GRONOWICZ General, 476 pages, $34.95 REVIEW BY ROBERT CUSHMAN HERE is something new in as-told-to autobiographies, though I am unsure about the exact nature of the frontier it crosses. It might be a triumph of imaginative ventriloquism or it might be the nadir of exploitative chic. Or cheek.

Antoni Gronowicz was an expatriate Polish writer who, in 1938, was invited to Switzerland as the house-guest of his musical countryman, Ignace Paderewski. One day the host took himself off, promising in a strangely English manner to be back in time for tea. He really wanted to give Gronowicz a fair crack at another guest, who happened to be Greta Garbo.

Gronowicz and Garbo got on famously. They walked through the woods, and engaged in profound conversation: She: The sun is shining the same way on flowers and on mud. . . . A man gets married because he is in love.

He: "But a woman?"

She: A woman pushes herself into love because she wants to get married.

He: "Let's say openly what were thinking about instead of playing with abstractions."

Of course, Gronowicz wasnt taking notes, and probably remembered the conversation as more stilted than it actually was. Maybe he'd seen too many Garbo movies. Anyway, it seems to have worked for him, because very soon (by page 20, to be exact) he and the Swedish Sphinx are in bed together. This is good for a few paragraphs of light-breathing prose (Although she didn't show a special ecstasy, I felt that she gradually began to like my lovemaking, which lasted minutes or hours). But Gronowicz was not just after her body. He wanted her memoirs.

Over the years they talked and she reminisced, on the conditions that he take no notes and that nothing appear in print until after her death. In fact, he died first. Still, she finally fulfilled her part of the contract, and out the book has come.

On the copyright page the publishers advise that "the author wrote much of this book using the first-person literary device to emulate the voice of Greta Garbo. The words are those of the author, based on his recollection." But, leaving aside the self-aggrandizing prologue, why did he not maintain this literary device throughout? There are sections dealing with Garbos youthful emergence from embittered poverty in Stockholm which are written in the third person, but which seem no less reliant on the subjects own memories. If Gronowicz went to Sweden and conducted additional interviews, he makes no acknowledgements. Maybe he grew tired of his own "literary device." Maybe he just wanted to move the story on a bit.

There is actually no discernible stylistic difference between Gronowicz-as-Garbo and Gronowicz-as-Gronowicz. Both rely heavily on reported speech. This is not of the crassly informational variety usual in showbiz sagas (Judy, do you remember those fun-filled days back in 1932, when we turned out eight two-reelers at RKO and moonlighted on a couple of features at Paramount, one of them directed by Eddie Frankovich?). The Gronowicz style is more loftily unspeakable. "Here we are locked in a cage which races through states and which does not allow us to do anything but eat and sleep." That, supposedly, is Garbo talking to Mauritz Stiller as they cross America by train.

Stiller shares much of the limelight in this book. He was an apparently brilliant director, and expert con-artist, who discovered the teen-age Greta, changed her name from Gustafsson to Garbo (It's the Polish word for the process of making leather, he tells her, after she has spent several years wondering), and brought her to Hollywood anticpating fame and fortune for them both. He started as her Svengali and ended as her Norman Maine. She made it, he didn't. He even - like Maine, the outclassed husband of A Star Is Born -tried to end it all by walking into the sea. He survived (unlike Maine), returned to Europe and died young: the Only Man She Ever Loved.

Far less, however, than she loved herself: that is made very clear. "From the very beginning of my career I believed that with my talent and my capacity for work I could play any role better than anyone else." I despise people. . . . My legend is everything to me now. "Ambition and egoism drove me to achieve fame and money."

Her honesty does her credit, but how do we know for sure that it is her honesty? By his own account, Gronowicz wrote up their conversations from memory. Nobody talks like Gronowicz says Garbo talks. He could have misreported her as well. One ends the book disliking its subject intensely, not for being egotistical but for being boring. Then one remebers to transfer ones dislike to the author. An actor, after all, is under no obligation to have something to say. But a writer is, especially a writer with pretensions.
