Nobody asked him to write Garbos biography: least of all, one gathers, Garbo herself. But then, it was notoriously difficult to get a striaght answer out of her about anything.

As movie history, the book is useless; the transition from silents to talkies, crucial in Garbo's career as in everyone else's, barely registers. All we learn about the films she made for MGM - her only studio -is that she thought nearly all of them unworthy of her. The numbness induced by this reiterated information is an accurate reflection of the torpor with which one greets the prospect of watching any of her pictures now.

If you think that is harsh, you should read the afterword affixed to this volume by Richard Schickel, movie critic for Time magazine. He thinks that her only bearable picture is Ninotchka. His trenchancy is a welcome antidote to what precedes it, but even I think he is unfair. Trapped into seeing Grand Hotel or Camille, I can goggle at the one and be moved by the other, smothered though they are in the upholstery that was MGM's idea of style.

Schickel points out that she could have jumped ship; there were other studios in Hollywood far more attuned to the pulse of American life. But she stayed, and trusted to her legend to sustain her: I chose as a weapon complete silence. You can use this weapon very successfully if you have enough money to maintain absolute privacy.

Her career ended after the failure of Two-Faced Woman in 1941: "My 24th film in America. And I have no regrets that it was the last film of my life." Whether she meant it to be at the time remains ambiguous. But she was locked into her self-created role. A legend can hardly ask for work, least of all a silent legend. Ahead lay 50 years of emptiness.

The book shows her fiercely asserting her own greatness while deploring its misuse, taking some blame but dishing out a lot more. It is an unattractive posture. But the woman Gronowicz presents must be partly his own literary creation. Maybe he had a phenomenal memory and the words really are all her own. But if she was self-serving, he was still more so. Robert Cushman is a Toronto writer and critic.
1990-08-21-appreciation-the-extraordinar:
APPRECIATION"The extraordinary voice crooned, throbbed, stomped, shouted. It could soothe and it could lament Pearl Bailey never lost her rhythm or her humor

Tuesday, August 21, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail AN agency report on Pearl Bailey, who died Friday at age 72, announced that Pearlie Mae was best-known for her rendition of Hello Dolly! This must have been news to many of her fans. Pearl - she liked to speak of herself like that in the third person - did indeed play Dolly during the original Broadway run; she was something like eighth in line for the role and represented a desperate attempt by producer David Merrick to revive interest in his long-running meal-ticket by turning it into a black musical. Desperate and yet highly successful: Pearl, uniquely among take-over artists, was permitted to record a new cast album on the score and her singing of the title song, on stage or on record, probably raised the regulation number of goose-bumps. But identified with it? Oh, honey.

Anyway, Pearl Bailey didn't have hits: not Hit Parade hits. Turntable hits - songs played year after year on radio - she did have. There was Tired ("darlin', Pearl is exhausted") and Takes Two to Tango: mildly salacious double-entendre numbers. If we're talking Broadway, there was St. Louis Woman and House of Flowers, both legendary flop shows with golden scores by Harold Arlen, Pearl's favorite composer. She played a good-time girl in the first, and a madam in the second: both good-hearted, of course, and both more than a little skeptical about their work. That was the Bailey style: lazy, sensual, funny.

She was born in the same year (1918) and the same town (Newport News, Virginia) as Ella Fitzgerald, with whom she also shared a superb voice and an ineradicable sense of swing. But where Ella was pure singer, Pearl was half vaudevillian. She came out of the Harlem tradition of bawdy, bastardized blues exemplified in the twenties and thirties by the great actress-singer Ethel Waters. Ethel, before she turned respectable, could double any entendre in the book.

Pearl and Lena Horne were the two star performers who extended this line into the post-war golden age of jazz-tinged standard singing. Lena was the unattainable exotic temptress, preserving her image even while mocking it. Pearl was earthy and available. Lena brought out the sex in the ostensibly chaste mainstream catalogue of Broadway and Hollywood. Pearl cut albums with titles like For Adults Only and Come On Let's Play with Pearlie Mae, drawing on contemporary revue and nightclub material and on songs that, as she acridly reminded us, were older than she was: Row, Row, Row or - obviously a family standby - Bill Bailey, Won't You Please Come Home. Nobody ever sang them so well, and her explorations of the more sophisticated Porter-Gershwin-Arlen repertoire are among the best on record. Alone among her generation she remained unshakably loyal to the songs and styles that had nourished her. Even in the philistine 1970s she persisted in recording standard songs with big-band backings.

Typically she would sing a straight but buoyant first chorus and then embark upon a second in which the written words were interspersed or elaborated with wryly relevant asides; the end of the song would often wander off into free-associating mumbles. But her embroideries never destroyed the musical line; her sense of time was absolute. She was also one of the very few who could tamper with a lyric without destroying it. Hers was a rare example of a cabaret style transferring successfully onto records. She could even break up the archival solemnity of an Original Cast Recording; on one song in House of Flowers she instructs the back-up trio that has been raucously protesting its devotion to her to "stop yelling in my ear, I've got a terrible headache" before serenely returning to the canonical text, not a beat out of place.

In her later years, as UN goodwill ambassador and compulsive autobiographer, the world learned, not always to its fascination, that she had got religion. But musically she had always had it. Like most black singers she was raised on gospel. Her recording of the Arlen-Mercer mock- spiritual Ac-cen-tchu-ate the Positive is majestic; she delivers the verse as an a cappella sermon worthy of Mahalia Jackson and then moves pulsatingly through the chorus. She was often described as a great jazz singer sidetracked into comedy, as though the two modes were incompatible; in fact, it was rhythm that made her humor so effective, and she never lost it.

The voice was extraordinary; it crooned, throbbed, stomped, shouted. It could soothe and it could lament. There is at least one song, the tragic I Had Myself a True Love, on which it can be heard doing all these things. She brightened up several films, as actress as well as singer. And she could sing opera; at least she was one of the few undubbed performers in the movie versions of Carmen Jones and Porgy and Bess. Her solo in Carmen might have become her anthem if she had chosen to exploit it. It was Beat Out Dat Rhythm on a Drum, Bizet's gypsy celebration effortlessly transposed into swing, incorporating a guttural quotation from Stormy Weather, a dry interjection ("maybe I do") halfway through the line "I don't need nothin' more to start me off" and a final mood of controlled frenzy. One would like to think that the eponymous drum solo was played by Louis Bellson, one of the best in the trade as well as being her fifth and lasting husband. He was one of her two mentors; the other was Don Redman, one of the architects of black thirties swing and her musical director on her choicest LPs. Through him and then through her a tradition lived. The great ones are dying, one by one. Pearl was one of the best and most deservedly loved.
1990-08-24-cross-current-miss-saigon-con:
CROSS CURRENT Miss Saigon controversy illustrates hypocrisy in racial casting

Friday, August 24, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN THE Heat Is On In Saigon. That is the title, and the pounding refrain, of the opening song in Miss Saigon, a musical that's very big on pounding refrains. For the moment, as far as this show is concerned, the heat is off in New York. Or rather, it is on hold.

The show, a huge hit in London, was scheduled to open next April on Broadway. It was stopped in its tracks when American Equity objected to the importation of British actor Jonathan Pryce to play the pivotal role of the Engineer, a Eurasian pimp. Pryce created the role in London and has played it for a year, to great applause. Cameron Mackintosh, the show's producer, threatened to pull the plug on the Broadway version if Equity persisted; they did persist and he duly pulled it.

This was a shock. The cancellation of a guaranteed money-maker, which had already raked up a record advance sale, felt like a breach in nature. Hits travel, especially to Broadway; it's a rule. Perhaps in recognition of this Equity retreated, acknowledging that Pryce's star status (he won a Tony some 15 years ago for his performance in Comedians) was an automatic passport to Broadway. Somewhat surprisingly Mackintosh refused this olive- branch. In a statement, Mckintosh said in effect that instead of grudging assent, he wanted enthusiastic co-operation from the union, especially from its Asian members.

My first thought was that he was being unreasonable, even petulant; that he should quit, or rather restart, while he was ahead. Re-reading his statement, I changed my mind. The show, if and when it opens, is bound to attract some flak. But attacks from fringe elements are one thing; official union-endorsed hostility is another. It would make the position of the show and its cast untenable.

In fact, I am not sure Mackintosh goes far enough. Before Pryce was cast for Broadway, there was the regulation search for an American - and preferably an Asian-American - actor to play the part instead. This should not have to happen. A successful production should be able to transfer from one part of the world to another with its original cast intact. If the producer or director want to tamper with it, that's their prerogative, but it is only theirs.

In practical terms, we are talking about transfers from London to New York, and vice versa. If we have to appease the protectionists, who are rampant in both places, we can point out that over the years the proportion of success in both centres evens out. Further, a hit show now runs for years and needs many re-castings. If only for convenience' sake, there will mostly be locally recruited.

Miss Saigon is a retelling of the Madam Butterfly story, updated to the Vietnam war and its aftermath. Some characters are American, mainly GI's; most are Vietnamese, and in London they have been cast ethnically, or approximately so. (The leading lady is actually from the Philippines.) Mackintosh and his colleagues claim that the Pryce role, being a half- caste, is a special case: mother French, father Asian. He would, a spokesman told me, be played by anyone - white, black, Asian, Hispanic - providing he were good enough.

This, I think, is disingenuous. If the show had originated on Broadway 25 years ago the role would probably have been played by Joel Grey. But I am sure that, if it were starting on Broadway today the role, if only for the sake of a quiet life, would go to an Asian. However it started in London, and the part went to Pryce, and he is now identified with it. The audience - the forgotten factor in all these calculations - want to see him do it. And his star status, as I think he himself would admit, is irrelevant.

An enormous amount of hypocrisy and inconsistency surrounds the question of racial casting. Directors who expect you to respond to every visual nuance in their productions also expect you to go color blind when they cast a black actor in what was plainly written as a white role, without stylizing anything else to match. "If you notice an actor's color," says Joe Papp of his multi-cultural Shakespeare shows, "you're not seeing Shakespeare." And as a Jew, should I object or rejoice if Shylock is played by a Gentile? It's very perplexing. If blacks or Asians can freely be cast as Caucasians, then the reverse must apply. And in either case - I think I'm brave enough to type this - they should try to look the part. That's a component of acting. The only yardstick can be talent, and that is not objectively measurable, certainly not by a committee. The only people who can make casting decisions are the people putting on the show. If I had to (and I know I won't) I would defend Mackintosh's right to cast non-Asian actors in every Vietnamese role in Miss Saigon, and to bring over Brits to play the Americans. If he got it wrong the critics and - far more importantly - the public would soon let him know. Give my regards to Broadway. The heat is on.
1990-09-28-the-new-season-performing-art:
THE NEW SEASON PERFORMING ARTS THE SON KING David Mirvishs theatre empire, stretching from Toronto across the continent and to London, is based on the principle of talk softly and carry a big hit

Friday, September 28, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

By ROBERT CUSHMAN There is a theatrical producer in New York of whom it has been said thateverybody hates him at first sight, because it saves time. David Mirvish has theopposite problem. Everybody likes this gentle, soft-spoken man as soon as theymeet him; I have yet to encounter anyone who has had cause to change thisopinion. Nor does it help his credibility as Canada's major theatrical powerfigure that as his hairline recedes he gets to look increasingly like his evenquieter father the self-made, self-satirizing tycoon, Honest Ed. Still, there must be iron in there somewhere as well as a lot of disposableincome. Both will be needed this fall, as, after more than a year of housing thehit musical Les Miserables, Mirvish and his venue, The Royal Alexandra Theatre,have returned to limited runs and subscription audiences. Meanwhile the worldaround them has, at least superficially, changed. Toronto now has a commercial theatre sector.

Anyway it has commercial theatres.There, sharing the same block on Yonge between Dundas and Queen, are GarthDrabinsky at the Pantages and Marlene Smith with the upstairs-downstairscombination of The Elgin and Winter Garden. Toronto may not be the hub of worldtheatre but it can certainly claim to be the world capital of theatrerenovation. Even The Alex's plush comforts pale beside the gleam of the Pantagesand the magnificence of The Elgin and Winter Garden. Never mind the product.Feel the foyers. In fact, Toronto still lacks a commercial theatre as the term is understood inLondon and New York. There it means putting a show on, and hoping it will runforever. That is the scene that The Royal Alex got into with its long fit of theMiserables; its how Drabinsky opened the Pantages with The Phantom of theOpera, whose cast has been signed up for a second years contract. But inToronto these megamusicals, which invariably begin their existence somewhereelse, are the only products with that kind of life expectancy. No ordinarymusical will do the trick, and no play either. This fact is what marks Torontoas a provincial theatre city. There's something depressing about the inevitability of the behemothproductions. Granted, they are enormous risks at source but once successfullylaunched, they hardly have to prove themselves. The one-to-one relationship ofan audience to a show, the true lifeblood of the theatre, disappears, andworldwide marketing takes over. They say of these musicals that the show is thestar" it would be more realistic to say that the hype is. David Mirvish doesnot have the Canadian rights to Miss Saigon, the new musical from the creatorsof Les Mis. However, he was able, when I met him, to offer me coffee in a MissSaigon cup a memento of the London production. That said a lot. Garth Drabinsky does have the rights to the most recent Andrew Lloyd Webbermusical, Aspects of Love, but, as he is not about to close The Phantom, no houseof his own to put it in. Since he wanted the province to lease him The Elgin andWinter Garden in the first place, he would have to be a saint not to be castingcovetous eyes down the block. It is, after all, a law of nature that no LloydWebber show shall go homeless; Drabinsky will solve his problem somehow.Meanwhile The Elgin and Winter Garden, under Marlene Smith, steer a middlecourse, lacking either sure- fire marathon attractions or a year's worth of thekind of guaranteed mixed bill that makes up a subscription season. Living handto mouth is perilous, and Smith sometimes finds herself wondering whetherToronto has a big enough audience to sustain all the theatre that is currentlybeing thrown at it. So, back into this competitive local arena comes David Mirvish, who for thepast few years has been in charge of an international theatre operation: Ed hasgradually bowed out. "I ask my fathers opinion but I make the decisions. Ithink people go into this business to be pretty independent. This September hisindependent organization, Mirvish Productions, has six separate shows on theboards or in rehearsal in Toronto, London and at various stops on the NorthAmerican road. That includes both coproductions and plays specially mounted byMirvish himself for his own faithful Toronto audience. One hopes it is faithful, not only for Mirvishs sake but for Toronto's. It isimportant that at the heart of the city there should be an established theatrewith a changing and varied bill. The Royal Alex matters, even to those theatreworkers and theatre fans who would never go to it. It defines the middlebrowground. Changes," says David Mirvish, "come out of the times, and even anaudience that's behind the times is affected by them. His father firmly advocated the subscription system; when he bought LondonsOld Vic, he claimed it would be that theatres salvation. But Londoners with 50shows to choose from on a given night declined to commit themselves to onetheatre months in advance. Subscription presupposes an audience attracted bybrand names and security, and the idea may be outmoded. Now, even in Toronto, Edis having doubts. David says, My father sometimes envisions a theatre withoutsubscribers: a theatre with open-ended runs." But for this season David is sticking to the package deal. An engaging mixtureof idealism and caution, he sounds shy but certain. "I was one of the audience,and I wanted to be better entertained. I see the theatre as something thatexists for a brief period of time, and while it lasts I want to be absorbed byit." But this prophet of evanescence and nostalgia is well aware of the need fora show to stay around if it is to pay for itself and for others lessfortunate. For weeks now there has been a large glossy photo of Albert Finney outside TheAlex. Finney, coming to this theatre near you in his latest London vehicle,Another Time, is the one marquee name The Alex's season can boast, and naturallyhe is being plugged. (Subscription audiences have not quite cottoned to the ideaof the play being the star. They think the star is the star.) At the other endof the scale, and the tail end of the season, is Dry Lips Oughta Move toKapuskasing, the Native play that scooped the 1989 Dora Awards. Putting thisplay on his bill has earned Mirvish unprecedentedly warm words from the leadersof Toronto's nonprofit theatres, who dont go around being as nice aboutDrabinsky or Smith. Thats unfair: Both moguls have in their time promoted plays from the fringefor commercial runs, as is common practice in London and New York. ButDrabinsky's transfer of George F. Walker's Love and Anger to the Bluma AppelTheatre met only limited success; perhaps the ideas time has not yet come inToronto. For The Phantom, Drabinsky draws in audiences from hundreds of miles,in all directions; its difficult to imagine the tourists flocking to Walker. For now, Toronto has two different theatre worlds The Phantom audience isnot being siphoned off from Theatre Passe Muraille. But these worlds do have tocoexist, and people do move from one to another. Bill Glassco, until the end ofSeptember the interim artistic direetor of the Canadian Stage Company, directsat The Royal Alex this season a Broadway hit, The Heidi Chronicles, whichMirvish is coproducing with the nonprofit Manitoba Theatre Centre. Meanwhile,Mirvish sends Les Mis on tour (in Montreal it will be retranslated into French such is the cultural unity of show biz) and brings it back for a limited seasonin 1991. The Royal Alex is the Toronto theatre scene's nearest approach to abroad church. It might, in an odd way, be regarded as our national theatre. Itcannot do everything but it can do more than most. Dry Lips oughta move to KingStreet. It could become a habit.

CROSS CURRENT An exhilarating ride on the shifting tides of the music business

Friday, October 05, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

ROBERT CUSHMAN IBLAME Ella Fitzgerald. She marked me for life. My first clear pop-record memory, I have to admit, is of Music, Music, Music, with Teresa Brewer beseeching everybody within earshot to put another nickel in, in the nickelodeon, because all she wanted was loving us and the title phrase. But then nostalgia can exact blushes from us all. The reference books tell me that song came out in 1950; I would have been 6. The radio was constantly on in my home, but it was Teresa who first made me aware of the shifting tides of the music business. For a few weeks her hit number was inescapable and then gradually it disappeared, to be replaced by something else that followed the same course. I accepted this as a system, benevolently ordained. I was right about the system part.

For some years after this it seemed that every song I heard was a bouncy shanty about girls who wore red feathers with hulie-hulie skirts (I blush again but that's how they pronounced it) or were called - clap, clap - pretty little black-eyed Susie. Everything seemed to have a Naval angle. I didn't know it at the time but I was listening to Korean war pop. All the songs were sung by the same man, so omnipresent that it would have seemed sacrilegious to inquire his name. (He did have one. It was Guy Mitchell.) This was the fag-end of the Tin Pan Alley tradition that had been dominant since 1900; my generation was being softened up for rock and roll.

I escaped. My mother, like everybody's, was a Crosby fan. Bing was singing novelties too, but they were wittier than other people's; Busy Doing Nothing struck my playmates and me as admirable philosophy, and Sunshine Cake at least sounded edible. I like to think, too, that his musicianship got to me although it still puzzles me that so avuncular a figure could ever have been a sex symbol.

I was also taken to movies. Even before my Brewer experience I saw Easter Parade. Fred Astaire and Judy Garland doing A Couple of Swells introduced me to show business at its most delightful. I didn't know that Irving Berlin had written it or that such a person existed, but in retrospect I see that it was typical of him. He had spent most of the century doing the right thing at the right time. Called upon now for a show-stopper, or movie-capper, he simply and unostentatiously provided it. I was lucky. A generation later I might have had to make do with Hello Dolly! It could have stunted my growth.

I got hooked on the theatre. Guys and Dolls and My Fair Lady became part of my mythology. The airwaves were still filled with songs from the shows, and I learned some names, Gershwin, Cole Porter, Rodgers and Hammerstein. In 1960 I bought Ella Fitzgerald Sings the Cole Porter Song Book Volume One and sealed my fate as a song-freak.

Ella was working her way methodically through the Broadway repertoire and I followed her, generally a record or three in arrears. Her Rodgers and Hart set especially got to me: vulnerable as well as sophisticated, intoxicatingly witty and melodic, and the essence, I was sure, of being young, broke and in love. (Hart's characters neaerly always sound like perpetual students.) The albums were also my gateway to jazz. I know now that there were emotional depths in the songs she never sounded; Sinatra taught me that. I also know that there were many songs she didn't get around to; the Manhattan cabaret specialists, Mabel Mercer and Bobby Short, taught me that, beginning with my first trip to New York in 1967, just before a new Dark Age removed their records from circulation.

Whitney Balliett, The New Yorker's jazz critic and champion list-maker, once spent two pages cataloguing the great American singers of great American songs, and he still left plenty out. It's an accommodating repertoire that has thrived on cross-fertilization; theatre, movies, jazz and pop have continually swapped idioms, in writing and performance, and even some classicists and rockers have contributed. Much of the foundation was laid by blacks and immigrant Jews, running creatively riot among European harmonies and English words. They fused them into an American language; even the debased stuff, kiddie-pop for adults, that I was exposed to in the early fifties, preserved some of its disciplined slanginess. It exhilarated me then, and it still does.

Robert Cushman's new radio series, Songbook, exploring the American popular song, begins transmission on CBC-FM this Sunday at 5 p.m.
1990-10-05-theatre-review-the-northern-q:
THEATRE REVIEW THE NORTHERN QUARTER

Friday, October 05, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written and directed by Alex van Warmerdam Presented by The Mexican Hound At the MacMillan Theatre in Toronto Alex van Warmerdam's staging of The Northern Quarter is thoroughly painterly, in a minimalist way Interminable father-son battle soon becomes monotonous BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail IT can be tough trying to escape from your father, especially when he is the kind of man who refuses to let you out of the house on your own, even when you are 43. This is not a situation too often encountered in everyday life, but nothing is impossible, especially when all concerned take a deep breath and agree to call it metaphor.

In The Northern Quarter, a Dutch production that opened Wednesday at the MacMillan Theatre in Toronto, the metaphor is pursued even in the casting. The play, which will close tomorrow, is presented by a long- established group whimsically called The Mexican Hound, whose guiding spirit is Alex van Warmerdam, writer, designer, director and actor. He appears here as the father, dominant even when dead. For when his oppressed son understandably takes a shotgun to him, he is still on hand to lecture the boy in the same tone of maddeningly silken sweet reasonableness he has adopted throughout. It's worse if anything, since as a ghost he now appears on film, eternally preserved and eternally re- runnable. His son is still a live actor, subject to all the ills and uncertainties performing flesh is heir to.

The son, whose name is Faas, wishes in the play to be a painter. But, in real life, van Warmerdam is himself a painter so the situation is even more oppressive; when, in his stage role, he offers patronizing comments on Faas's work, he can do so with real conviction. And though Jack Vecht, the actor playing Faas, is not himself related to van Warmerdam (at least, not that I know) he is surrounded by people who plainly are. Credited with general management and production, and also taking a subsidiary acting role, is Marc van Warmerdam. At times the show aspires to the condition of rock opera: more convincingly, as regards both halves of that equation, than most claimants to the title. In control of the music is Vincent van Warmerdam. Vecht's performance is most charmingly and persuasively harried, and it is easy to cheer him on in his doomed struggle for independence. But obviously, when he chafes against family bonds and family pressures, he knows whereof he speaks.

The staging by the founding van Warmerdam is thoroughly painterly, in a minimalist way. It unfolds in tableaux, and each character is nattily and consistently decked out in a single color: grey, green, red. There is some wit in the varieties of parental torture on display. Mother, a subtler tyrant than father, declines to make her son his favorite fish-paste sandwiches on the ground that adding to their happiness would risk spoiling it.

Faas is informed that children, no matter their age, never go anywhere without their parents, unless of course those parents are dead. This comes under the heading of putting ideas into people's heads, and father's final fate shows where that leads. On the whole, ideas are things with which the family has no truck, and books are banned for that reason. Faas's parents do make him a present of a dictionary, but with the dangerous words (the vast majority) scored out.

In a play written, say, two years ago, by Vaclav Havel, that last detail might count as a neat piece of subversive satire. And apparently, when The Northern Quarter was first seen in Holland, it was taken by some critics as a blast against the enforced conformism and designer drabness of, say, East Germany. Even then that interpretation must have seemed smug; now it looks impossibly dated. Either way, the reaction has to be that of the criticized African ruler in Beyond the Fringe: "Take the mote out of your own eye before you start messing around with our beam." But if author-director van Warmerdam is going in for de-moting, his methods are of limited use.

Most adults are, to a degree, stunted children, so we can all identify with Faas. But as it becomes clear that he is never going to win, not no way, the show becomes monotonous. And even designer-director van Warmerdam's trompe l'oeil visualization of the urban desert begins to resemble that horribly patronizing Pete Seeger song about the people who live in little boxes and all look just the same. Yes, it's sort of true and, yes, the show is fluent visually and - performed for our benefit in English, with no apparent strain - aurally. But (a) enough already and (b) what else is new?
1990-11-02-theatre-reviews-the-london-pr:
THEATRE REVIEWS"The London production of Miss Saigon is loud and manipulative and the score makes one nostalgic for Andrew Lloyd Webber. But the West End boasts some other choice pickings A hit that's actually a big miss

Friday, November 02, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail WHAT'S entertainment? In the old movie The Band Wagon Fred Astaire and friends proclaimed, joyously and irresistibly, that anything could be. "The lights on the lady in tights . . . the scene where the villain is mean . . . the plight of the children in flight. . . ."

The last one is my own invention, based on a much-applauded number - the second-half opener in fact - in Miss Saigon. The musical, just into its second year at London's Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, is now set for an April opening in New York, complete with Jonathan Pryce as the Eurasian pimp the Engineer. This is what I hoped, expected and argued for in an article recently in The Globe and Mail. Having done my bit as a cultural reporter and running dog of Western imperialism, I would like to revert to theatre criticism, and explain why I hated the show.

Miss Saigon doesn't flinch from showing us the fall of its eponymous city at the end of the Vietnam war. Great gates swing back and forth, evacuating Americans and desperate inhabitants mill back and forth on either side of them, and finally the famous helicopter takes off, brutally separating Miss Saigon, an updated Madam Butterfly, from her Pinkerton. It is all expert, exciting and perfectly legitimate. But though the show trusts itself to portray violence theatrically, it loses its nerve when it comes to pathos. Miss Saigon has a child and flees with him to Bangkok. At this point we are shown film of Vietnamese children in Thai refugee camps. It hardly rates as atrocity footage by today's competitive standards, but these are still real children in distress, being used in the service of a fictitious story. The esthetic gaffe is nothing to the ethical offence. I kept averting my eyes. I doubt if I would have flinched from the same material on the TV news or in the interstices of a Live Aid concert: which does not mean that the suffering would have affected me less. Here it is used as illustration to a song, so of course it gets applause. It's a number.

Not all of the show is on that manipulative level, but much of it is. Claude-Michel Schonberg, whose music might have been designed to make us repent any uncharitable thoughts we may have had about Andrew Lloyd Webber, has a reflex reaction when emotion seems called for - up the volume, up the key - but his garish idiom is at least more appropriate to the Coca-Cola ethos of the Americanized East than it was to the streets of nineteenth-century Paris in Les Miserables. Alain Boublil's libretto is also more specific about historical cause and effect than the previous show.

Despite the frantic toughness of the treatment, the Butterfly story remains as droopy as it always was. And yet this version does offer one unforgettable image. Across the seemingly vast expanse of a hotel room, Miss Saigon confronts her lover's new American wife, who thinks for a moment that she must be the maid. Characters and audience look simultaneously into an abyss of shattered hopes. The authors then spoil it all with a long song, but silence has said more than all the noise they can generate.

Nicholas Hytner's direction and John Gunter's designs are as remarkable for their poise as far as their fluency; this is the best- staged of all the giant British musicals. The embattled Pryce is commanding, tireless, sly and very likeable: maybe too much so. The character he plays is meant to be a creep, using the heroine and her boy to hitch a ride to the place where he knows he belongs, the corrupt United States of his dreams. Pryce is a heroic actor and too big for the Engineer's sneakers. He is, in fact, miscast, and not for ethnic reasons. But he was irresistible in London, and will be so in New York. A Welshman, he has been replaced at Drury Lane by a Scot (and another classically based actor), Hilton McRae. Occidents will happen.

Meanwhile, the London dramatic stage has got religion. If the local press is to be believed, the value of a play is in direct ratio to the number of clergymen it has in its cast. Simon Gray's Hidden Laughter is currently the biggest dramatic hit in the West End, thanks partly to the participation of Felicity Kendal and Peter Barkworth, both fine stage actors who are also popular TV stars. Barkworth plays a country vicar who becomes the friend and confidant of a weekending family from London. Devoid of faith themselves, they expect him to have it for them: a professional duty he finds onerous since he has barely enough for himself. The play somewhat resembles the same author's Quartermaine's Terms, whose central character was the selflessly ineffectual centre of a mean and striving world. Here the divisions are less clear-cut, with the emphasis equally on the crumbling marriage of his charming neighbors and on their horrible children. As the author digs deeper, both the charm and the horror wear off, which is a relief; Gray is almost too good at depicting the casual cruelty of what are currently known in Britain as the chattering classes, and the first half of the play seems in consequence a bit glib. What comes over in the second part is pain and honest bafflement. Kendal plays a woman who belatedly discovers herself as a writer, Kevin McNally her literary-agent husband: obviously a doomed match. McNally ends the evening surveying the wreckage of his home and family and asking what went wrong: a commonplace ending but maybe inescapable.

Religion seems to stand in this play for something that people crave but cannot trust. In David Hare's Racing Demon, at the National Theatre, it is whatever the characters would like it to be. Some 20 years ago, a British bishop created a furor with an un-doctrinal book called The God I Want. Each of the characters in this play is granted a short soliloquy addressing a deity created not so much in their own image as in their own physical and spiritual environment. The rector of a poor London district, with little trust in ritual or in anything except his own limited capacity to do something practical for his parishioners, is crushed between his right-thinking bishop and his evangelical curate. Conservative and radical join forces to defeat the lonely liberal: a traditional, and still potent, British theme.
