THEATRE REVIEWS"Among London's many offerings are the flawless ensemble productions of David Hare's Racing Demon and Arthur Miller's After the Fall, featuring a brilliant performance by black actress Josette Simon as Marilyn Monroe National Theatre struts its stuff

Saturday, November 03, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail ARTHUR Miller's 25-year-old play After the Fall has finally been given its London premiere at the National Theatre. This, whatever the author's protestations, is autobiographical, self-justifying drama, and its protagonist-narrator hardly seems to stop talking. James Laurenson, who plays him, probably deserves a medal for remembering his lines, let alone making them lucid and urgent.

But within this exasperating framework are scenes of startling immediacy, reflecting their author's continuing obsessions. One is betrayal, as exemplified in the McCarthy era, here dealt with directly instead of by historical refraction as in The Crucible. Another, more crucial, is family relationships: not, for once, between father and son but husband and wife. Miller's first two marriages are laid remorselessly, but not cruelly, bare. The second of course was with Marilyn Monroe: the reason for the play's notoriety but also for its fascination. Miller tried to distance himself by writing her as a singer rather than an actress; this production goes further by making her black. She is played, brilliantly and mercurially, by Josette Simon. The autobiographical interest remains (sometimes we seem to be watching a play about what would have happened if Arthur Miller had married Billie Holiday) but the endless cycles of elation, guilt and recrimination ring universally true. The exquisitely detailed direction is by Michael Blakemore, than whom there is no better in Britain.

Indeed, both After the Fall and David Hare's Racing Demon are pretty well flawless ensemble productions: a credit to the National Theatre. There was riveting acting in everything I saw there: even in a generally scorned production of Racine's Berenice, a noble play of pent-up passion, culminating here in a long whispered speech of renunciation by Lindsay Duncan in the title role which had a skeptical house spellbound.

Berenice was the only example around of something called Designer Theatre, which is supposed to be killing or saving the drama according to taste; on this occasion, it looked as if somebody had delivered all the elements of a stunning set and then assembled them in the wrong order. The costumes, too, mixed periods pointlessly, whereas the National's King Lear mixed them pointedly. Here again, though, the main consideration was the acting - and the assembly (miraculous, in the context of recent British theatre) of a company that could do justice to every role save one in the most taxing ensemble drama ever written. Deborah Warner, the director, has emerged in the last couple of years as a director who never cuts a line and gets her actors burrowing into every one of them. The breakthrough moment came in the Dover scene where the blind Gloucester (Peter Jeffrey) breaks down in tears at the sound of his mad master's voice. The text prescribes this but I had never really registered it before. It put my own tear-ducts on alert for the rest of the play, and they duly erupted during Lear's reconciliation with Cordelia and his passion at her death. Brian Cox, a craggily honest actor with a streak of Celtic craziness, was the player responsible. He is now one of the two prime classic actors in Britain. The other is Ian McKellen who was playing Kent.

The following night, the compliment was reversed, with Cox playing Buckingham to McKellen's Richard III. This is state-of-the-art British Shakespeare (as opposed to the makeshift offered by the Renaissance Theatre Company) and though we don't have to fall down and worship it we could use it as a measuring rod. Richard III is a bravura modern-dress production, directed by Richard Eyre, the National's supremo, also responsible for Racing Demon and clearly back on form after a period of treading water. McKellen's Richard is a warped British Royal with a blistering contempt for anybody to whom he is not related and a consuming hatred of anyone to whom he is. He is Edward VIII reborn as Hitler: not an exhaustive interpretation of the role and rather short on humor, but savagely convincing as the begetter of a police-state. Here the production backs him up with imaginative relish; one scene shows us one of the Princes-not-yet-in-the-Tower playing with a toy train. After his exit, it whirrs all alone across the wide empty stage. We know what the boy's fate will be; this makes us feel it.

These productions bring the National Theatre as close as it has ever come in its 27-year history to doing its duty by the national playwright. Generally, it has consigned that responsibility to the Royal Shakespeare Company, which in London is in one of its periodic troughs, financially buffeted (to the point of closing its Barbican Theatre for the winter) and artistically under par.

There is no point in assessing the RSC at present. For one thing the current Stratford-on-Avon season, the basis for next year in London, is reportedly excellent. For another, a new artistic director is about to take over, with a new executive structure. The director in question, Adrian Noble, is currently represented in London by a production of Three Sisters which inaugurates a new but obviously limited trend: dynasty Chekhov. A trio of Redgraves will be performing this same play in the West End in December. In the meantime, imported from Dublin to the Royal Court Theatre, we have a quartet of Cusacks: the sisters Sorcha, Sinead and Niamh as the sisters and, as the drunken doctor, their father Cyril. Cusack pere is the patriarch, not just of this family but of the English-speaking theatre; his capacity for just existing on a stage, unruffled and mesmeric, is the ultimate in relaxation. Beside him, all other actors look hypertense. The production takes its tone from him; it is unhurried almost to a fault, but within its unfolding length is an immense amount of felt life. The older one gets, the more painful this play seems, and the actual familial bonds on view here make the snapping seem all the uglier.

I feel fairly amazed at the things I didn't see. A new Alan Ayckbourn play. A trio of star actors in well-received productions of modern classics: Glenda Jackson as Mother Courage, Richard Harris as Pirandello's Henry IV, Derek Jacobi as Sartre's Kean. An epic nine-hour staging of Malory's Morte d'Arthur in a West London suburb. The first ever London revival of the Elizabethan history play, Sir Thomas More, with one scene reputedly by Shakespeare. (I'm really chagrined at missing that one.) I was too late to catch the London production of Sondheim's Sunday in the Park with George and too early for his Into the Woods, produced by David Mirvish. It almost makes me credit the theatrical tourist view of London as the centre of the world, and it increases my fury and frustration at the financial jeopardy most of it is in. I even begin to wonder why I was so crabby when I was a London reviewer.
1990-11-12-cross-current-sure-bernstein-:
CROSS CURRENT Sure, Bernstein was gifted, but was he any better than Gershwin, Kern . . . ?

Monday, November 12, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

ROBERT CUSHMAN THE late Leonard Bernstein was a gifted composer, in several genres. His five Broadway shows are a distinguished bunch: On the Town, Wonderful Town, Candide, West Side Story and the one everyone forgets, 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue. That's one dud, one cult classic, two orthodox hits and a landmark: statistically stunning.

The exhilarating impact of New York, New York, at the start of On the Town, is a typical Bernstein opening. Arresting openings are de rigueur for a successful musical, but the first rumble in West Side Story and the Candide overture are exciting in a manner peculiar to Bernstein. There is a density of musical texture, a richness of allusion, beyond what we expect on Broadway, and that has to be traced to Bernstein's involvement with - to use a term I hate but can find no substitute for - classical music.

The musical establishment has various strategies for dealing with those of its members who stray across the lines. Gershwin, patronized during his lifetime, was posthumously deified; since he wrote Por gy and Bess and the concert pieces, his popular songs were accorded a sort of grace-by-association, respected by people who would consider Richard Rodgers intolerably middle-brow and may never have heard of Harold Arlen. Kurt Weill, when he wrote for Broadway, was accused of selling out. Nobody ever levelled that charge at Bernstein. He was cheered on, in the cause of reclaiming popular art for real art.

Bernstein's four big shows fall between the years 1944 and 1957. That is to say, they are part of the Rodgers and Hammerstein era; they rode Broadway's most self-confident wave. They were a vital part of that wave; it would have been poorer without them. But it is a jump from acknowledging that to assuming, as did one British obituary tribute, that they were the best Broadway had to offer. Globe and Mail music critic Robert Everett-Green declared that "as a writer of popular music, he was unbeatable, and a truly original artist." Well, he owed a lot to the example of Gershwin and Rodgers, but that's no crime. Still, "unbeatable"? Consider the above-named, plus Kern, Berlin, Porter, Loesser, Sondheim. Not all as well-trained as Bernstein, but all capable of writing music that stands up at least as well as his, both in and out of its theatrical context; all of them (and I don't except Sondheim) his superiors as melodists.

Everett-Green is right that Bernstein would have found post-1960 Broadway a less congenial place. I doubt, though, if he would have found it impenetrable. Sondheim, whose shows are more experimental than any of Bernstein's, Candide excepted, still gets them on. And is it true (Everett-Green again) that Bernstein's shows "changed the nature of the genre?" Wonderful Town is a celebration of New York, not much different in form or spirit from Guys and Dolls, which preceded it, or Bells Are Ringing, which followed it. On the Town showed how much of a story could be told in dance, but Oklahoma! had pointed the way. Candide, a comic opera, was one of a kind: brilliant, but it has had no successors.

There's a delicious moment in Wonderful Town at which an innocuous tune reveals itself as an Irish jig and dances - the music, not just the choreography - all over the stage. The entire score of that show is scintillating 1930s pop pastiche, as Candide is wonderful operatic pastiche. But the fun is always about how wittily Bernstein can imitate other composers; it rarely, as it does in Sondheim, serves a dramatic purpose beyond itself.

That leaves West Side Story; and it is this show, maybe with side- glances at Candide, that people have in mind when they speak of Bernstein as a Broadway trailblazer. Its "serious" subject matter was no great departure; South Pacific, which anticipated it in killing off its juvenile lead, was thought just as contemporary and hard-hitting in its time. (Today's realism is tomorrow's escape.) Like On the Town, it crossed choreographic frontiers and achieved a new, and certainly influential, fluidity of staging. But that, again, was Jerome Robbins; he could have done it with any composer. No, that's not fair; Bernstein's fierce, jagged dance music is vital to the effect.

However, West Side Story is supposed to be a musical, not just a ballet. When its love songs were plugged for the movie (though not before), they became hits. But they are terribly syrupy. The most famous one, Maria, is finally not about the boy's love for the girl but about the tenor's ability to hit a climactic high note. Maybe that's what is meant by raising musicals to the dignity of opera; and Bernstein's heir may not be Sondheim but Andrew Lloyd Webber. West Side Story may have reached its apogee in the "operatic" recording, conducted by the composer, which unerringly emphasized everything that is worst about it. The Pavarottis and Domingos have gone for the score, but the best popular singers - Sinatra, Fitzgerald, Mel Torme, Peggy Lee - steered clear of it. That may not be conclusive but it's significant.

It points to a lack of jazz in Bernstein: a lack that once led me to propose Andre Previn as a superior example of the popular composer with classical credentials. That was foolish of me; Previn may have been a more relaxed songwriter than Bernstein but even his best tunes are slight and, theatrically, he barely exists. There's a wistful masterpiece of a song in On the Town - We'll catch up - Some Other Time. I'm not sure Bernstein ever did, not in that area. But we are the richer for the chase.
1990-11-16-theatre-review-the-crackwalke:
THEATRE REVIEW THE CRACKWALKER

Friday, November 16, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

By Judith Thompson Directed by Urjo Kareda and Andy McKim At the Tarragon Theatre in Toronto The Crackwalker tells the bleak story of four people who dont have much going for them, but manages not to be depressing. A harrowing walk with the urban underclass BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail JUDITH Thompson is being doubly feted - practically festivalized - at Toronto's Tarragon Theatre. Her latest play, Lion in the Streets, is the current main-stage attraction, while the Extra Space has a revival of the piece with which she began her career 10 years ago.

The Crackwalker now seems a good play but a bad argument for progress. Life for the urban underclass, in whose Kingston, Ont., sector the play is set, has hardly improved since 1980; Thompson's four major characters have very little going for them, but none is actually homeless. A fifth figure seems more prophetic: an insensible, bloodsoaked silent messenger of doom, he crouches menacingly at the edge of the stage while the others get on with the action. His lurching and vomiting are unflinchingly realistic but his placement (Is he the Crackwalker? If not, who is?) is disconcertingly Symbolic.

But The Crackwalkers principals - the Kingston trio plus one - are mesmerizingly real. All are young. Theresa, plump and retarded, lives chiefly on doughnuts, and sells and gives sex fairly indiscriminately. (In this production, she sounds Irish.) Sandy, the friend on whose sofa she regularly crashes, is the most together of the bunch, except for her dependence on Joe, who abuses her and may have raped Theresa. Joe feels permanently trapped and is first seen stripping a stolen motorbike. Alan is Joes sidekick, helplessly anxious to please.

Alan takes on Theresa. He marries her and, against all expert advice, they have a baby. Both the marriage and the child are doomed and, on our awareness of this, Thompson builds a fearful arc of tension. I don't know that the gods of the drama require such a propitiatory sacrifice, but Thompson is the second modern playwright - Edward Bond with Saved was the first - to build a major debut play around an infanticide. (And both have gone on to write even starker, more ambitious and less convincing things.) The baby-killing scene in Saved was sickening. The one in The Crackwalker is even more painful, since we care for the parents, and believe that they care for the child and one another.

The Tarragon production, directed by Urjo Kareda and Andy McKim, is unsensational and unfussy. It finds room, like the writing, for a surprising amount of warmth and humor. The humor, actually, is almost of the Ben Jonson variety: set up a collection of monomanias and watch them collide. Sandy, being the most balanced, is the toughest assignment and Cheryl Swarts's performance does exude, in her hands-on-hips declarations of independence, the faint taint of slumming. She is a lot better when pitiable, in her scene of silent erotic surrender to Joe, or pitying, in a toughly compassionate monologue that ends the play. Each character has one of these soliloquies. They could be dangerous authorial intrusions, but they actually seem to come from within their speakers skins.

Joe is played straightforwardly by Ron White as an angry uncomprehending stud. His paranoia infects the admiring Alan who takes it, in Randy Hughsons performance, to awesomely grotesque extremes. Alan is haunted by his father's death from lung cancer and makes it a pretext for a virtuoso tirade against Sandy's taste for cigarettes. The same experience makes him distrustful of doctors and, since a social worker has told him that he is a good father, he takes it on himself to throw out the babys medicine. The childs fate is sealed by a volcanic outburst when Theresa, fearing another pregnancy, denies him sex. Alan grows credibly from a shambling incompetent to a death-dealing obsessive; to conceive this progression, and feed it into a coherent dramatic structure, is quite an achievement.

Alan may be crazy but he is not irresponsible. Theresa, lacking the power to connect, can step through life moment by moment, suffering sorely but never long. She bridles at being called a whore, but she is in fact a mental nymphomaniac: always ready for the next experience, which needn't be sexual (motherhood will do) but generally is. She even fantasizes herself as "the Madonna lady" - a phrase that of course has rather a different ring to it 10 years on. She is multifariously single- minded; you might even call her oxymoronic. These sudden dislocations make her funny, and Debra Kirshenbaum's performance, blowsy and befuddled, is richly comic - but never patronizing.

These people live with you. The play is harrowing without being depressing. And that is high achievement.
1990-11-24-theatre-review-the-playboy-of:
THEATRE REVIEW THE PLAYBOY OF THE WESTERN WORLD

Saturday, November 24, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

By J. M. Synge Directed by Vincent Dowling Starring Roma Downey Macdara O Fatharta At the Elgin Theatre, Toronto VIOLENCE EMPHASIZED"Caustic comment on a culture that venerates violence, gets a sexual charge out of it, lives on fantasy and alcohol, and is governed by counsel of unseen priests Playboy a scathing comment on the soul of Ireland BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail SURE, and it must have been a glorious thing to be alive in Dublin in 1907, when the Abbey Theatre was giving The Playboy of the Western World its world premiere, the way the people would be takin' to the streets and riotin' and they red-faced and slaverin' mad over the defamation of Irish womanhood and the utterin' of filthy words.

Today's realism is tomorrow's escape, and the problem with The Playboy -maybe inside Ireland and certainly outside - is how to recapture that delicious feeling of shock. Synge's characters live in what one assumes to be direst poverty in the remotest part of the country, and they seem to have little on their minds besides sex, drink and violence, but you have to analyze long and hard before these facts come into relief.

The piece plays, stubbornly, like a charming fantasy; it may be hard work for the heroine to get up early in the morning to fetch goat's milk for the hero's breakfast, but to us it seems kind of cute. We expect her to meet a leprechaun on the way.

The same young lady gets to speak the word that struck the original audience as the ultimate obscenity. The word is "shift." As well as discussing her undergarments so frankly this girl, Pegeen Mike, bridles at being left alone for twleve hours while her dad goes off and gets stinking at a wake, and demands a man on the premises. This forwardness shocks her intended, a shy one called Shawn, and he rushes off to church for counsel. (The apparent concensus of priest, betrothed, and original spectators is that it would be preferable for her to be murdered in her bed.) Meanwhile Pegeen finds her protector in Christy Mahon, who wanders in from nowhere claiming to have murdered his father. This impresses the men, and dazzles the women. Pegeen, known throughout Mayo for her scoldin' tongue but actually a deep romantic, sees in him the warrior of her dreams. The local widow, and a quartet of young girls, are more starightforwardly predatory.

All this does wonders for Christy's confidence, which is dashed to the ground when his dad arises from it.

A second, more delibetare, attempt at bumping the old man off proves disastrous; the villagers - witnessing the deed instead of just hearing about it - are horrified, and Pegeen most of all. So we have a caustic comment on a culture that venerates violence, actually gets a sexual charge out of it, lives on fantasy and alcohol, and is governed by the counsel of an unseen priest.

If they got beneath their surface outrage the rioters should have seen a scathing comment on the soul of Ireland. Very likely they did.

But it doesn't play that way. Sean O'Casey's Abbey plays (among which The Shadow of a Gunman is alsmost an urban rewrite of The Playboy) say much the same thing, and say it less eloquently, but they carry a greater theatrical charge, simply because they are set amidst actual historical carnage that is still with us, even if its address has changed from Dublin to Belfast.

Synge has bequeathed us a wry fable - tart but charming.

The new Abbey production, on tour in North America, is a conscientious attempt to preserve the flavor while capitalizing on the charm. The cottage-cum-pub in which the play is set - the Pegeen shebeen - is sparely furnished but seductively lit. Some of its outside walls are down, so we get a glimpse of countryside and of characters approaching through it: ingratiating in itself. Characters, especially female ones, flounce around musical-comedy style but the violence is carefully emphasized. It culminates in Pegeen applying a firebrand to the leg of the bound and helpless Christy. This is a savage moment, but its impact quickly passes.

This is odd because it seems to be happening in slow motion. The action is preceded, accompanied and followed by acres of chat. That is the way in this play. All the characters talk, talk, talk; or - with acknowledgements both to Benny Goodman and the play's celebrasted folk- poetic quality - they Synge, Synge, Synge.

It is not so much the dialogue that is difficult to animate - it is lyrical, pungent and sometimes very funny, if incurably hung up on its own metaphors - as the reactions to it. Anyone not talking in this play is on his own. That at least is the impression derived from Vincent Dowling's production which is mosytly good at driving a straight dramatic line through the speeches while relishhing their style, but leaves those listening to them much to their own devices. There is a lot of standing around, registering by numbers.

Some of the most enjoyable performances are the most ancestrally shameless: John Cowley waddling and slithering as Pegeen's pa, drinking himself asleep at a wake, or Peadar Lambe, a real Abbey veteran, as one of his two choric cronies: the one with the better lines, or at least the more accommodating timing. (You know when he is pausing for a laugh, but one reason is that you are actually laughing.) Frank McCusker is a febrile, wire-drawn Christy, definitely a person if not quite a prototype. (The play does have religious overtones beyond the obvious satiric ones; it teems with scourgings and resurrections, and its protagonist is not Chrysty-an for nothing.) Roma Downey's Pegeen, physically and temperamentally, is pretty rather than handsome, nothing for anyone to be afraid of, which diminishes Christy's conquest. There is a buxom widow - would there be any other kind? - and among the four girls, whose names I can never get straight, there is a very striking ringleader.

People are always adapting this play. How about a slicked-up homogenised version called The Penthouse of the Western World?
1990-12-09-national-s-continental-drifte:
AFTER Robert Lepage's show Polygraph, at the Almeida Theatre in 1989, Richard Eyre called it "the most exciting piece of theatre I have seen all year". Now Eyre has managed to lure Lepage to the National with Tectonic Plates (see review), an epic play about continental drift which also contains some very funny scenes set in restaurants.

Still in his early 30s, Lepage is one of two Canadians in the performing arts attracting worldwide attention; the other is the film director Denys Arcand (in whose Jesus of Montreal Lepage was an actor). Both are French-Canadians; both, that is, are part of a culture and society that seems in the process of cutting its links with the rest of Canada.

Quebec theatre attracted attention some years ago with the aggressive plays of Michael Tremblay (Lepage calls it "Tremblay's outburst"), and subsidy began to pour into the province's theatre, most of it going into lavish productions of Broadway-style musicals.

"We thought," says Lepage diplomatically, "that that was wrong." He looked towards other influences: "Dance theatre... visual theatre... it helped Francophone theatre to express itself without language."

In practice Lepage himself has never spurned language, on or off stage. (Some of the more intimate scenes that I saw in the Quebec Tectonic Plates might have been directed by Mike Leigh.) Lepage warily accepts the definition of his work as "performance art" - "though not," he qualifies, "in the Laurie Anderson sense" - but it has few of the more forbidding aspects of that genre. It welcomes the audience in.

Eyre wants Lepage to direct a play - "a European classic" - for the National. On the basis of what I have heard of Lepage's productions of Galileo and A Midsummer Night's Dream and what I have seen myself, it sounds a great idea. This year, working in conjunction with a Shakespeare troupe from Saskatoon, he directed a literally bi-lingual production of Romeo and Juliet set in a town - the Capulets spoke French and the Montagues English - that begged a few questions, but was both poignant and thrilling.

Two months ago he staged Durrenmatt's The Visit, exploiting the play's bizarre imagery to the limit. The two castrati, who are the playthings of the vengeful Old Lady, were discovered trussed up in a giant suitcase; the unemployed citizenry sat around the railway station glued to the kind of tiny TV monitors you see in airports; about as potent an image of depression, spiritual and economic, as could be imagined. The play's glib parable was sharpened but not distorted, its human action moving as well as frightening.

This was Lepage's first production at his new home base, the National Arts Centre in Ottawa, where he heads a Francophone drama unit. It seems a good place for him, since, apart from being Canada's capital, Ottawa is on the cusp of the country's two major cultures. It is a kind of no man's land, and ironically Lepage feels he may be more necessary there than in his native province.

"As Quebec gets more independent culturally, they don't need me." He begins to see himself more as a world citizen. Certainly he is in international demand. He ranks with the hottest: "Interviewers used to compare me with Peter Brook. Now they say I remind them of David Lynch."

He manages to be bold without pretension, playful without facetiousness. The movement of oceans and land masses in Tectonic Plates corresponds to "separation, meeting and drifting of people - or society or a culture."

It is evidence of his charm and authority that he can persuasively make a claim like that within moments of describing himself as "an actor, a group guy, a trouper: more a coach than a director". In fact, he is suspicious of conventionally scripted plays (and hopes gradually to wean his new Ottawa audience away from them) because, he says, they force him into the traditional theatrical hierarchy: below the author, above the cast.

It's all been said before: and nobody really believes that Lepage, even if he lets his actors write most of his experimental pieces themselves, really functions as no more than a catalyst. The Group ethic can be oversold. But whatever it is he does, it has rarely been done so winningly.
1990-12-22-double-double-toil-and-troubl:
ROBERT Lepage's production of Macbeth, recently performed by the Graduate Centre for the Study of Drama at the University of Toronto, begins tremendously with the three witches hanging upside-down; talk about the suspension of disbelief. Then Macbeth and Banquo appear, riding. They are not actually on horseback, but they are performing a detailed and energetic equestrian mime, which they accompany with much syncopated stomping of feet. They are joined by a couple of message-bearing thanes who are executing the same routine. In the received text this is the play's third scene; the first two have been cut.

So might this one be, for all the information we get from it. The Weird Sisters, immune to vertigo, have no trouble communicating the sense and the feeling of their lines, which, being venomous doggerel, are not that challenging. The mortals are handed complex blank verse, not easy for student actors to get across and downright impossible if their voices and their bodies are beating out rhythms that are at cross-purposes with one another. A dozen dramatic signals go unregistered, all sacrificed to one gratuitous effect. The important things that happen to Macbeth and company in this scene could equally well happen to them on foot. And they look pretty silly doing it.

One thing that sets Lepage apart from most conceptual or gestural or performance-oriented or anti-textual directors (choose your label; none of them quite fits) is his obvious trust and belief in actors. However graphic his effects, the people in his shows have carried the weight. But here he has either lost faith in his cast or, more likely, he has overestimated them. Either way, he has staged a puppet show.

It even looks like one. The stage can expand or contract, vertically. Sometimes it has its full height; at others it's a letterbox. Since there are definite Japanese traces in staging, costume and hair styles, the actors often resemble Bunraku marionettes; you expect to see human manipulators alongside them. At crucial moments in Macbeth's descent you do see the witches silently crouching beneath the main action as if controlling it. When it isn't a puppet-play it's a shadow-play. Giant silhouettes are cast on the back wall with majestic spookiness.

They are impressive, but so they would be in any context. Devices like this can help intensify the terror in Macbeth but they cannot generate it. That can be done only by the players.

They actually look weaker here than they might in a less overpowering presentation. The traditional amateur virtues - intelligence and vigour - are neutralized. And the production's principal device fails to register except as an irritant. The men are played by women and the women by men. This may be a commendable blow for Equal Opportunity, but an audience can hardly be expected to get off on that. Since nobody is acting with much conviction anyway it hardly matters which gender they are.

Lady Macbeth (Patrick Garrow) dutifully switches on some extra voltage for the "unsex me here" speech but switches it off immediately after. When Macbeth (Anna Migliarisi) comes home, the two of them go into an elaborate clinch. But conventionally cast couples can do that too. (And do; every production of Macbeth thinks that it's the first to discover sex.) The splitting of the bond between them is more powerful than its sealing; Lady M's slumped acceptance of her husband's independent criminal career after the banquet leads logically to her somnambulistic breakdown. The minor character of Lennox became, in one ironic monologue, the most fully realized person on stage. Whether the portrayal of Duncan as an especially vexing English nanny was accident or design I cannot say; it certainly made a new and persuasive case for regicide.

There is cross-casting, too, in the Equity Showcase Macbeth, but it is less pervasive. Three male roles - Duncan, Banquo, Old Siward - are played by actresses; and only at the end had I worked out the rationale for this. These are all fathers whose children are either killed or threatened by Macbeth and they presumably seem more bereaved if they in effect double as mothers. Macduff loses his children too, of course, but as the text provides him with a wife he is allowed to keep his manhood. He is played by a Polish actor; I don't know whether we are meant to register this as more non-traditional casting, or simply to accept the actor (Vieslav A. Krystyan) on his own considerable merits. His collapse at the news of his family's massacre is done with uncompromising power.

So is the massacre itself; so is the attempted killing of Banquo's son Fleance. The production presents the Macbeths' career as a revenge of the childless on the fertile. It is so stated in the program, and it is intermittently noticeable on the stage. Macbeth, having dispatched Young Siward in the final scene, gives his dismissive epitaph - "thou wast born of woman" - a peculiarly malignant sting; though, just to make sure we get the point, the victim, who is fighting in a full-scale professional battle, is played as a 10-year-old. Which is not believable. "Macbeth," says the program, "does not murder people; he attacks families." So, if you think about it, does any murderer who does not restrict himself to killing childless orphans. Resentment at his lack of an heir helps to corrode Macbeth, but it is not what first motivates him. He makes no attempt to kill Duncan's sons along with the father, though doubtless he would get round to them in time. Like many partial interpretations, this one is more impressive as a disembodied bright idea than as part of a story told by actors.

The old chestnut "how many children had Lady Macbeth?" - once a sure laugh-getter in academic circles - has come round again with renewed seriousness. When the lady talks about having given suck, a Macbeth brooding on his childlessness should surely take some interest; this one just stands there, arms akimbo. Indeed, the actor, David Schurmann, is singularly impassive in the earlier part, strolling through temptation, murder and kingship with scarcely a flicker. Only when his world begins to crumble and viciousness sets in does he come to snarling, desperate life. He reverses his wife's diagnosis; he is quite without ambition but a wiz at the illness that attends it. His partner, Kate Lynch, lights a fire under him regardless, and her desolate cry in the sleepwalking scene sounds, as it should, like a soul at the end of its tether.

Alex Fallis's staging has at least one brilliant moment - the sudden dissolution of the witches to a heap of rags on the ground - and the general acting level is alert and alive. With all its eccentricities, this showcase has something to show.
1990-12-22-recordings-performances-of-co:
RECORDINGS"Performances of Cole Porter's work are going in opposing directions: a search for authenticity and attempts at new interpretations. Both schools are represented among these albums A stocking full of Cole

Saturday, December 22, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

RED, HOT AND BLUE, Chrysalis VKS 41799 DIONNE WARWICK SINGS COLE PORTER ARISTA AL 8573 JULIE WILSON SINGS THE COLE PORTER SONGBOOK DRG CDSL 5208 JOAN MORRIS, NIGHT AND DAY, THE COLE PORTER ALBUM OMEGA OCD 3002 THE COLE PORTER SONGBOOK VOLUME ONE ELLA FITZGERALD Verve 821 989-2 BY ROBERT CUSHMAN The Globe and Mail COLE Porter used to fire off telegrams to the likes of Bing Crosby and Frank Sinatra, tetchily inquiring why they botherd to sing his songs when, as written, they obviously didn't like them.

An aging songwriter is generally delighted to hear his songs sung by anybody and Porter changed, so to speak, his tune. But his earlier intransigence is a reminder that what most of us regard as the right and obvious way to arrange and perform a Porter song - the fifties' way of Crosby and Sinatra and, pre-eminently, Ella Fitzgerald - is as much an interpretation as anything that has come later.

Performances of Porter, and of the other standard American composers, have recently gone in two opposing directions. One is the search for authenticity, assisted by the rediscovery of original thirties orchestrations and their use in recordings of complete scores. The other is represented by Red, Hot and Blue: 20 current pop acts charitably doing it for AIDS relief and research.

Red, Hot and Blue annotator-producer John Carlin tells us that Porter's "music presents love as a personal, almost subversive, force, that enables us to transcend life's hardships" and that Porter was rebelling against a "repressive" Victorian hangover that feared and distrusted love. Actually the Victorians were all in favour of love, an opiate second only to religion: read their novels. What they distrusted, some of them, was sex.

Carlin draws a disingenuous parallel between Porter's Let's Do It and John Lennon's All You Need Is Love. Now when Lennon's song first came out in the late sixties I took it to be a satire on the sentimentalities of flower-power. There seemed no kinder way of accounting for its banality. Subsequent history suggests that Lennon was in earnest, and that when he said love, he meant love. Porter meant copulation. Birds do it. Bees do it. Sweet guinea-pigs do it. Buy a couple and wait.

"Use your mentality, wake up to reality." Those words, plus the title, are all that remain of the original lyric in Neneh Cherry's rap version of I've Got You Under My Skin, the album's opening cut. But Porter was no preacher, and he undercut that exhortation in his very next line: "but each time I do, just the thought of you makes me stop before I begin" which in this context would translate as "I'm far too excited to put on a condom." I am not decrying safe sex; I merely question the efficacy of pop rhythms, from Porter's time or ours, in pleading its case. The medium and the message are in flagrant contradiction.

The point is not that these tracks don't honor Porter's originals but that they don't make sense in themselves. And they are in close enough proximity to the originals for their verbal sloppiness to be doubly painful. Frank Loesser, spoofing calypso in the forties, was prophetic: "We put the accent upon the wrong syllable, and we Sing a Tropical Song." Or, here, a Topical Song.

Rock has systematically devalued the word (never more so than when its lyricists have been touted as poets) and it may be too late for recovery. These triumphantly conversational songs are mostly delivered in a series of bleached monotones.

Debbie Harry's Well Did You Evah suggests that she is about to be sick, which may be a legitimate extension of Porter's jaundiced insider's view of the high life but is a lot less pleasant. I Love Paris is deservedly (but is it intentionally?) parodied by Les Negresses Vertes, droning accordion to the fore. On the other hand, Aztec Camera's Do I Love You is haunting, even moving, and k. d. lang's So in Love is triumphant, plumbing the song's masochistic depths like no other singer I have heard. Lang has been threatening for some time now to move into jazz, which I take to mean that she intends to sing some decent songs. Here she serves notice that, when she does, the competition will have to look out.

She even makes the song seem relevant to AIDS, simply by singing it with so much conviction that we are are forced to consider its sentiments in the context of our own lives. Annie Lennox's Ev'ry Time We Say Goodbye also benefits from the fortuitous but shocking impact of its key phrases - "I die a little . . . I wonder why a litle". Which, by the way, is all that the updating of any performed work, from Shakespeare down, can hope to achieve.

Red, Hot and Blue is a more stimulating item than the competition, Dionne Warwick Sings Cole Porter. Here is a once distinctive if limited singer, trapped within her packaging. The album jacket promises within not merely a disc but rave reviews of it from Sinatra and Quincy Jones. Advertising the advertising may represent a new frontier in hype. The arrangements are lush disco, down to the extended fades in which a single boring riff is endlessly repeated. The vocals, including a bowdlerized I Get a Kick (1990 is a little late to deny the existence of cocaine) are clear but distant. Porter was worldly; Warwick is other- worldly. Only on a post-Charleston Anything Goes are there signs of life, and even here the production effort is out of all proportion to the result. A closing "jazz version" of Night and Day is a joke; a squad of fusionists noodle innocuously while Warwick delivers a vocal identical to her opening "straight version."

Those wishing to celebrate Porter's approaching centenary more traditionally already have a fair choice. Julie Wilson, the reigning diva of New York cabaret, growls through an adventurous choice of songs. She sometimes underlines the jokes, but she does appreciate them; and so will you. Joan Morris, whose roots are in art-song, vaudeville and operetta, is also good at comedy, though less so on heavy Porter drama. Her sparkling My Heart Belongs to Daddy is a lot better than her earnest Night and Day.

Ella's 1956 set, blessedly available on CD, shows why fifties style remains the benchmark. Its best practitioners had an assurance, and a reservoir of repertoire, unmatched by any pop singers before or since. Though some degrees away from Porter's theatrical manner they were in touch with it; had in fact grown up with it. Ella's songbooks (19 of which this was the first) are a bother to jazz and Broadway purists but a delight to the rest of us. True, she doesn't improvise much, but with that gentle voice caressing the melodies, and that gutsy voice attacking the rhythms, who needs it? Nor is she an actress, but she lays out the text so firmly that you can build a theatre in your head. These are not definitive interpretations, but they are essential education. Cole, unless he were having an extremely bad day, would surely have agreed.
1991-01-14-in-person-the-turning-point-i:
IN PERSON " The turning point in Derek Jacobi's career came in I, Claudius, which made him the most recognizable classically trained British actor of his generation A survivor who knows exactly where he's going

Monday, January 14, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail WHEN Derek Jacobi was winning all hearts with his TV starring role in I, Claudius, somebody - my mother actually - asked me if he was really as nice off screen as he seemed to be on. With heavy heart I had to tell her the truth. Yes, he is.

Edmund Kean, the great English actor of the early 19th century, was, by historians' consent, not nice. On and off stage he was one of your hell-raising self-destructive actors. Jacobi, by his own estimate, is temperamentally light years away from Kean, certainly as a human being. Still, Jacobi recently scored a great success playing Kean at Londons Old Vic in a production that is now playing at the Royal Alexandra Theatre in Toronto.

Kean is not one of those biographical one-man shows. Its a proper play, of mixed ancestry: a translation by the British director Frank Hauser of a drama by Jean-Paul Sartre, itself based on an old play by Alexandre Dumas. The attraction of the material to Dumas, France's grand master of romantic swashbuckle, is obvious. Sartre should have been a much tougher nut, but of course he, like both Dumas and Kean, was a great womanizer; and is anybody really surprised that the existentialist's facade should have masked a susceptible bourgeois heart? Besides, any play about an actor is automatically concerned with appearance and reality and if that isnt philosophically respectable I would like to know what is.

One of jealous, passionate Keans greatest roles was jealous, passionate Othello; we get to see him playing that part and then, under pressure, stepping outside it. He talks directly to the audience, at which point, says Jacobi, there comes a further twist. "He starts talking as the actor playing Kean. It's that amount of passion. Total reality."

The play had been done in London some 20 years previously, with the late Alan Badel in the leading role. Jacobi remembered that production and especially recalled one line. Kean, having auditioned an aspiring actress, says to her: You were worse than very bad. You were quite good. That withering dismissal of mere adequacy has, he says, "a terrifying resonance for actors." Last year, when having a what-would- you-like-to-do-now conversation with London producer Duncan Weldon, Jacobi mentioned Kean; the upshot was this production.

So, on this occasion at least, Jacobi belied his assessment of himself as not a mover and shaker. What he is, he says, is "a survivor," and he has survived at a very high level. He was born during the Second World War into an East-end-of-London family with no theatrical connections. As a schoolboy, he was a star, both in school and with the fledgling National Youth Theatre, and played more leading roles in the competitive hothouse of Cambridge University. When he turned professional, he went straight to the prestigious Birmingham Repertory Theatre. In 1963 he became a founder-member of the National Theatre, under the direction of Laurence Olivier. Olivier's National is remembered now, a little rosily, as a glittering ensemble that commanded the loyalties of some of Britains best actors for astonishing lengths of time. Jacobi was one of the longest-serving of all. He stayed eight years.

In retrospect his career there was less than meteoric. He had good roles from the start - he was Laertes to Peter OToole's Hamlet in the inaugural production - but only at the end of his stay did he get an unequivocal lead: the saintly Prince Myshkin in a dramatization of Dostoevski's The Idiot. The production was generally (and somewhat unfairly) judged a disaster, but Jacobi came out of it well. He was believably Slavic and he had genuine authority; his holy fool did justice to both the noun and the adjective.

It was a suitable, if muted, climax to his National years. Everybody except himself had expected him to become a matinee idol, but instead he turned into an unusually attractive character actor. His contract with his audience was based on affection rather than hysterical devotion. He showed unsuspected strength; in the problematic role of Cassio, he held his own with Oliviers legendary Othello. And, to his own surprise, he became a comedian. Cast as the clown Touchstone in As You Like It (I read it and panicked - there wasnt a laugh in it), he borrowed some aghast mannerisms from National colleague Maggie Smith and somehow made them his own. They have been on call, when needed, ever since.

After the National he freelanced, on stage and TV. And then came the turning point.

I, Claudius was one of television's most successful prestige entertainments. Episode 9 - recalled by Jacobi as "the gory one, with John Hurt running amok" - is about to be rerun on PBS as part of Masterpiece Theatre's 20th-anniversary celebrations. I was, he says, tucking appropriately into a plate of Caesar salad, "far from the first person they thought of." I asked idly who was, and got the astounding answer, Charlton Heston. Astounding because Heston is no comic and it was the comedy, in the script and the playing, that made the series take off. But of course Heston was considered bankable by the American co- producers, and it was a long time before the BBC could persuade them to take a chance on Jacobi.

It was, he says, a big challenge, though apparently more technical than temperamental. It was shot in sequence but began with a flashback, so having established Claudius as old at the outset, they had to hold the image in their minds and return to it weeks later, a problem for the director, the makeup people and the actor. There were still six instalments to shoot when they began transmission. "The critics were lukewarm when it started," Jacobi says. But gradually it took over and became a cult. It got an instant repeat at home, and abroad it made Jacobi the most recognizable classically trained British actor of his generation, a position only to be challenged when Jeremy Irons achieved a similar TV success in Brideshead Revisited.

Jacobi returned to the classic theatre, this time in a position of strength. In one season with the Royal Shakespeare Company, he played three whopping roles. His skilled charm carried him through Benedick in Much Ado About Nothing, and even through Peer Gynt; and sounded newer and deeper notes, vocally and psychologically, as Prospero in The Tempest. The following year he added Cyrano de Bergerac.

This was another makeup challenge, and a temperamental one as well. "On the face of it," he says, not referring to the celebrated Bergerac nose, Cyrano wasnt me. His director, Terry Hands, told him cheerfully that if he failed in this one, his previous successes wouldnt mean a thing. With these encouraging words ringing in his ears, Jacobi set to work. Everybody knew that he would bring off the pathos of Cyrano, and his death scene duly had the audience weeping buckets. The flamboyance was more in question, but he brought it off through sheer energy and attack. The show was a sell-out success in London and New York.

Being ugly and sensitive, Cyrano looked backward to Claudius. Being demonic, he looked forward to Kean, and Jacobi acknowledges that the two roles presented him with similar problems of self-transcendence. "Kean says that you want to be what you can't be; you get fed up with what you are." The line reminded him of his own approach to Cyrano.

Jacobi has made his biggest cinematic splash to date as Arthur Clennam, the repressed Victorian hero of the two-part Little Dorrit. He has just completed another film called The Fool, based on the sociological writings of Henry Mayhew, chronicler of the London poor. I play two characters who are really halves of the same personality, Jacobi says. "One rich and powerful, one poor and downtrodden. It's basically a story about money. Very contemporary." Next, Pierre, the massively self-doubting hero in a two-part stage version of War and Peace. Sometime, I imagine, he will play a definitive Jekyll and Hyde. Offstage he gives the impression that he lets his career happen to him. Onstage he knows exactly where he is going.
1991-02-26-sinners:
THEATRE REVIEW" SINNERS

Tuesday, February 26, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY NORM FOSTER Directed by Michael Ayoub Starring David Nairn, Araby Lockhart and Ted Follows At the Bayview Playhouse in Toronto In this part farce, part thriller, it's curtains for the clergyman Energetic Sinners hard to forgive BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto THE first sinner on stage is Monica. She is spread out on a bed, languorous in her lingerie, awaiting the arrival of a man not her husband while doing mild calisthenics. Obviously a loose woman.

Just how loose I cannot tell you without delving into details of plot. This is generally regarded as unsporting when a play is either a farce or a thriller. Sinners is trying to be both, so giving away its secrets would be murder. But there I go.

It is fair, though, to examine the drama's moral outlook, which is that a woman with a hearty sexual appetite is capable of anything and deserves all she gets, as long as it's not what she wants.

Monica is married to a clergyman who returns unexpectedly (the sainted Kenneth Tynan once remarked that nobody in farce ever returns expectedly, but a good farceur is supposed to provide some rationale for the apparently irrational, a point by which playwright Norm Foster seems sublimely unbothered) and finds her with her lover. There is an embarrassing apology for a blackout; some actors get up and lie down visibly and risibly, and when it seems decent to look at the stage again, we find that there is a dead reverend on it.

Monica is prepared to rise above this. Her boyfriend, a furniture dealer named Peter, is not. We spend the rest of the evening watching him squirm. And when he looks out front, as he does with amazing frequency in Michael Ayoub's production, he can watch us doing the same.

I hate to admit it, but Sinners is not absolutely terrible. The author may care little for rhythm and nothing at all for plausibility, but he does provide some narrative energy and a certain amount of cheek; if his two-hour piece were boiled down to 30 minutes, it might make a bearable black sitcom, supposing that there were a network that would countenance such a thing.

The smoothest and the blackest twists arrive simultaneously; a police chief, who for reasons of his own wants a quiet life, connives at - no, engineers - the suppression of a criminal investigation. But there is no use pretending that Norm Foster is Canada's answer to Joe Orton. He may blunder into subversion for a giggle, but there is no answering sparkle in his dialogue. "Whenever I kill a minister, I get a little cranky" is as funny as it gets.

The acting gets a lot cranky. Ted Fellows' old cop, leading a life of quiet desperation, is an oasis of professional calm. Araby Lockhart, as his meddlesome wife, probably knows her business equally well, but her role is such a grinning caricature of censorious repression that I began to resent her for going about it so enthusiastically. (She is burdened with the final witless gag: one that perfectly encapsulates the nudge-wink tabloid mentality of the whole thing.) An oddity of both promotion and construction is that these two players, who don't appear until the second half, are billed as "starring," a tribute to their longevity and, I assume, popularity, but below the title.

The only actor above it is David Nairn, who plays Peter: Fair enough, he has to do most of the work. His performance, given the play's divided nature, is loyal to the point of schizophrenia. He acts at two speeds, careering through the farcical parts in high grimace, which he freezes every so often into a mask of horror, as if he had suddenly been informed of the reality of his situation.

It's a valiant and ingenious endeavour, but to bring it off, you maybe need to be Bob Hope at his cowardly comic peak, and preferably with access to Hope's team of writers.

There remain two actresses afflicted by their author's mindless misogyny. Michelle Hart, as the lewd Monica, gives in without a murmur but with plenty of noise. Glynis Davies, cast as a stock spinster despite the technicality of being married, puts up a spirited but unavailing fight.

Set and lighting design are credited to Rod Hillier; the set, looking like no home ever lived in by anyone, has walls that quiver under pressure, and the lighting goes on and off with startling abruptness or, to put it crudely, crudity.

The press kit informed me that this is an early Foster work and that he has moved on to "more sophisticated comedies of manners." They are probably masterpieces, but right now my pulse does not race. The same kit promises us "two hours' respite from wartime worries." The implication is that ordinarily you wouldn't bother with it, but there's a war on that makes the world safe for Sinners. That's the most terrifying explanation I've heard yet.
1991-03-14-theatre-review-pinocchio:
THEATRE REVIEW PINOCCHIO

Thursday, March 14, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY JEROME COOPERSMITH, MARY RODGERS AND SHELDON HARNICK Directed by Carl Harms Starring Bil Baird's Marionettes At the Bayview Playhouse, Toronto His nose still grows when he lies and contracts when he tells the truth, but in this marionette version at Toronto's Bayview Playhouse, Pinocchio breaks convention by having no aspirations toward humanity Updated classic loses relevance BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail AFTER years of Muppet-gazing, it is rather a shock to be confronted by dolls which are visibly wired. But Bil Bairds Marionettes are pedigree puppets. Baird himself died in 1987 after more than 50 years of string-pulling; his son Peter S. Baird has been minding the store since then. The troupes version of Pinocchio has been in the repertoire since 1973.

I don't recall whether self-referential is a term we were tossing about much 18 years ago; if we weren't, this show was ahead of its time. For Pinocchio himself, of course, is a puppet, and even though he started in a book and hit the big time in a Disney cartoon, it was left to the Bairds to present him in his existential state. We actually see him transformed, at his own clamorous insistence, from a block of wood that might be raw material for a rolling pin into a toy boy, the immediate apple of his creators eye. That creator, the carver Gepetto, is played logically by a full-sized actor, decked out in a commedia mask in presumed homage to the storys Italian origins.

Other grown-up characters are played by other grown-up actors. I assumed that it was always the same grown-up actor, until two of them ganged up on my theory by appearing simultaneously. Gepetto is reduced to puppethood after being swallowed by a dolphin, and Pinocchio, on joining him in the interior, takes a corresponding reduction in size. This is sporting of Pinocchio and ingenious of the Bairds, but I still felt cheated. A basic convention had been broken: all the more basic in that, in this version, Pinocchio has no aspirations toward humanity. Each species is allowed its own pride. Block is beautiful.

Unfairly perhaps, one takes the best things for granted. Ten unseen hands bring the accoutrements of the carpenter's shop to quivering life. Pinocchio takes gradual shape before our eyes. There are comic interludes involving collapsing puppets felled by their master's sneeze, and a school of conversational fish. Pinocchios nose lengthens when he lies, and contracts when he tells the truth, and we dont give the mechanics a thought.

But we do notice - at least I did - that this crucial element is introduced rather late, and with no prior warning. The storytelling, in fact, is scrappy. Here television probably has done us in. We expect fluidity, and get small pauses between each tableau, pauses which the narrative is not strong enough to override. It is, after all, a reworking of the Everyman story, just one temptation after another, and hence very prone to monotony. Nor do the Baird bunch seem to have total faith in it. They don't wholeheartedly spoof it, as might be done on Sesame Street. They intermittently update it, like their Greenwich Village neighbour Joe Papp, knocking himself out to make Shakespeare relevant to the inner city.

Pinocchio, strictly for Toronto's benefit, is on his way to school on Eglinton Avenue. Waylaid by a streetwise Fox and Cat, he is busted by the cops and befriended by a social worker, standing in for the originals Blue Fairy. All these inventions have their funny moments, but their combined effect is anything but relevant. Its digressive. The least-guyed element - the relationship of father and son - is by far the most effective. Especially marginal is Pinocchio's conscience, a Hispanified cricket, who never stands a chance of influencing anyone.

He's the best singer though. The mini-score is the product of two hot Broadway talents, hot at least in 1973: Sheldon Harnick (Fiddler on the Roof and Fiorello!) and Mary Rodgers (Once Upon a Mattress, and daughter of Richard). They preserve the disciplines of the old school while flirting daintily with the rhythms of the new. The prerecorded vocals (also 1973?) make a bright but jarring contrast with the acting, which is altogether more homespun. The virtuoso puppet stuff comes in a post-story variety show which includes one of those dazzling abstract montages on a black background in which Central Europe meets Off-Broadway: no words, no strings. My own brood, having loved the Young People's Theatre's live- action Christmas Carol, which made far fewer concessions, were fitfully enchanted.
1991-03-15-theatre-review-tabu:
THEATRE REVIEW TABU

Friday, March 15, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- Created by The Canadian Stage Hour Company Starring David Findlay, Alisa Palmer, Shaun Phillips and Dawn Roach At The Stage Upstairs, 26 Berkeley St., Toronto The show Tabu, which is a lot more didactic and less exploratory than it would like to think, moves quickly and skillfully but in no direction Of Flowers and sexual stigma BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto THE Hour Company's Tabu is billed as "a celebration of sexuality." It is a collective product, and one thing the collaborators discovered in their research was that in 1832 a Canadian infantryman was hanged for making love with another man. The victim's rank was private, and his name was Flowers. Private Flowers. The words fairly pulsate with imagistic possibilities.

The Flowers story is intercut with an invented modern one. Two young women are surprised in one another's arms. One of them, called Garten, has abuse hurled at her by her brother and is more gently intimidated by her boyfriend. When they call her a lesbian, she bridles, on one of three possible grounds: (a) the term is accurate but the straight world has made it sound derogatory; (b) she is actually bisexual; (c) her sexuality is her own business, and to slap any kind of label on it is to diminish her as an individual.

The evidence points to the third option. Private Flowers proclaimed on the gallows that his body was his own to do with as he liked, and the memory of his defiance in the extreme gives Garten the strength to proclaim her own. That seems to be the idea. Whether it is given concrete embodiment is another question. The show moves quickly and skillfully, but in no direction. Garten's words ("I'm not a lesbian") are the same at the end as at the beginning. Ritual repetition in the theatre generally does more for the actors than for the audience. We have not a character's journey of discovery but a parable proving that she was right all along. The show is a lot more didactic and less exploratory than it would like to think.

There are four actors - David Findlay, Alisa Palmer, Shaun Phillips, Dawn Roach - and two musicians, and the standards of acting, singing and miming are high. The use of a row of bunks to evoke the army life will win no prizes for originality, but it is done with great efficiency and dispatch. In fact, not just the acting but the writing of the historical sections is excellent. There is no individual author's credit, but whoever invented the words has done an impressive job. We are informed that authentic records of the Flowers case are non-existent. The gap is filled with period dialogue that rings true without pedagogy, and is executed with chilling economy. As was Private Flowers himself, who never had a trial.

The Hour Company will have it that he was hanged to save the skin of his partner, who was also his officer. I doubt if there is any direct evidence of this, but it plays plausibly. It does, however, make the peer-group pressures faced by the play's contemporary gays look mild in comparison; and they are the only pressures we are shown. I know we are meant to extrapolate and start thinking in terms of society and other evils, but on the theatrical evidence, why should we? The past gets careful writing and performance; the present gets slogans.

It gets a pretty good song as well: soft rock, with a nifty lyric, including the memorable couplet "when I'm in a crowded room" surrounded by the baby boom." We also hear, by way of warm-up, the old Eartha Kitt record, I Wanna Be Evil, arch but still amusing. At the end of the show proper, the company, in accordance with what are apparently their immemorial principles, hold an audience discussion, not even pausing for a moment to allow those who prefer the base role of consumer to make a discreet exit. It was then that I recalled the darkest step on Eartha's downward path: "And in the theatre I want to change my seat" just so I can step on everybody's feet." None of us, though, had the guts. Shaw had the right phrase for it: intimidated, that's what we were, by middle-class morality.

THEATRE REVIEW A GAME OF INCHES

Saturday, March 16, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

WRITTEN BY AND STARRING LINDA GRIFFITHS Directed by Sandra Balcovske At Theatre Passe Muraille Mainspace, in Toronto In her latest solo turn, actress and writer Linda Griffiths presents a concoction thats too elaborate to be a comedy and too sketchy to cut it as a play A Game of Inches comes up short BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail IHAVE only seen one previous Linda Griffiths show, the embarrassingly amateurish Maggie and Pierre. I know it's considered a landmark in Canadian theatre, but so much the worse for Canadian theatre. I recall a smug endless monologue that was tickled pink by its own daring at lampooning the First Couple, and laid itself in the aisles at the audacity of having both of them done by the same actor. Since that actor's sole idea of characterization was to portray everyone as Barbra Streisand joke-Jewish, jabbing nasally at anything that resembled a comic point, the notion palled rather quickly.

I am pleased to report that, since then, the Griffiths timing has improved no end. The character she assumes in her new solo turn, A Game of Inches, is loaded with pent-up angst, but Griffithss delivery verges on the laid-back. The effect, as of someone teetering high-heeled on the edge of desperation, is rather piquant.

She no longer honks. She does squawk. Indeed I wondered for a time whether she had any lower register at all. It turned out she does - it comes out when her character briefly impersonates other characters, mostly male - but she sure is economical with it. Mostly, whether by accident or design, her range is cramped, like certain kinds of Oriental music. She plays on a single note of haughty hysteria. But there is something appropriately stylish about that; Pamela, the lady she plays, has dallied with some Eastern philosophy, not happily.

She hasnt dallied with men at all; not till recently. Alone in her 40s, surrounded by books, she decides with many misgivings that it's about time and invites into her spare room a man named John. One day he utters the fateful words, "Mind if I watch the game?" and from then on they are both glued to the television. Baseball invades her dreams; the Blue Jays become her fantasy-life. But on an earthly plane nothing happens and eventually John moves out, leaving Pamela to lament an ice- box stuffed and chances missed. It's very sad and very funny, no?

No. Its quite sad and a little funny. Pamela confronts the world with a mixture of rage and resignation. (Well, thats what they do, isn't it, she keeps saying of the men about whose filthy habits she has heard and imagined so much.) Griffiths brings her to a shadow of eccentric life, but in the end Pamela is just an excuse for a performance: one that gets only skeletal support from its script. The writing gestures hopefully toward black humour; Pamela leads off by telling us that she is suffering from "terror and horror and loss and panic . . . and terror and horror and loss and panic." (The audience laughs dutifully at the repetition; it can take a hint.) Sometimes she settles for getting laughs by dropping familiar Toronto names; sometimes this blossoms into a full routine. Even I, who could not care less about baseball in general or the Blue Jays in particular, could appreciate that her instant impressions of particular players were sharply observed and executed. They turn Pamela into a stand-up comedienne, working out of her own desperation - a role in which she seems more credible than at any other time. But A Game of Inches is too elaborate for a comedy act, too sketchy to be a play.

It is the third hour-length piece I have seen this week. I begin to yearn for a really elaborate play, one full of themes and characters, maybe with an intermission or two. I shall regret having said that.

IN PERSON"In a generation of writers stridently clear about what they are against if about nothing else, Christopher Hampton stands out as one of nature's liberals. His latest play, which deals with his own childhood, paints a portrait of a vulnerable survivor Hampton gets personal

Tuesday, March 19, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

London ENGLAND -- BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail London CHRISTOPHER Hampton's biggest success as a playwright has been the stage version of Les Liaisons Dangereuses, which, being based on somebody else's novel, is of necessity a rather impersonal work. His subsequent and latest play, however, makes full amends. White Chameleon, just opened at the National Theatre in London, deals quite explicitly with its author's childhood.

That childhood was spent in various parts of the globe. Hampton's father was an engineer working for the British company Cable and Wireless, which moved its employees around as if they were minor diplomats. The Hampton family's most fateful posting was to Alexandria, which is where the 10-year-old Christopher found himself at the time of the 1956 Suez crisis. He had a front-row seat for the death of the British Empire.

These two themes - the beginning of a life, the end of an era - are superimposed, one upon the other, in Hampton's play, and they make a neat fit. Only in scenes devoted to the onset of the protagonist's playwriting instincts does another drama seem to be flailing about inside. This is, of course, a constant danger in autobiographical drama - things happen because they happened - compounded when the subject is also the narrator. In White Chameleon an excellent actor, David Birkin, plays Christopher as a child while an even better actor, Tom Wilkinson, plays his reminiscing older self and doubles as the father reminisced about.

A caveat in the program warns us against taking the self-portrait too literally, but Hampton confirms that all the incidents in the play are true, although some have been enhanced and reshuffled.

Central are experiences of being bullied on two continents: reviled by Egyptian schoolmates as "filthy English" and, after repatriation, by British schoolmates as "wog-lover." The incidents balance, like most elements of the play, and they leave their victim essentially unscathed and unembittered. This, too, seems to be true to life; in person he appears the most equable of dramatists. In his stage persona, he muses that "these symmetrical assaults made a valuable contribution to my political education," and adds, "I've been wary of every known brand of confident certainty ever since." A playwright contemporary advised Hampton to cut this line, on the grounds that there is far too much of that kind of pronouncement going around these days. But he protested that he was not following a weak-kneed fashion of the 1990s. He had always felt that way.

In fact, in a generation of writers stridently clear about what they are against if about nothing else, Hampton stands out as one of nature's liberals. But talk of generations can be misleading. As he put it during an interview in London, "it all depends when you started."

He began very young. In White Chameleon, the elder Hampton, hearing of his son's literary ambitions, advises him to waste no time, citing in support writers obviously dredged up from his own boyhood: Arthur Conan Doyle, H. Rider Haggard, Robert Louis Stevenson. None of them, apparently, wasted any time. This is true to life: Despite the fact that "there was never a book in the house," Hampton's father was very encouraging. He died in 1965, a year before his son, still an undergraduate at Oxford, saw his first play performed at London's Royal Court Theatre. Subsequently, Hampton joined the Court as resident writer.

The theatre produced four more of his plays, including Total Eclipse, about Rimbaud and Verlaine, and The Philanthropist, a modern comedy of academic manners that shows the benefit of Hampton's own scholarship. He majored in modern languages, and The Philanthropist is a systematic inversion of Moliere's The Misanthrope, beginning with the title. Its hero defines himself with the memorably Hamptonian line, "I'm a man of no convictions; at least, I think I am."

The Court, the theatre that pioneered the right to fail, was a prickly environment for the perennially successful Hampton. He tells of the directorate watching the previews of The Philanthropist in mounting dismay, finally deciding that it had to be faced, the trouble was the play. It opened, and fulfilled their worst fears. It was a success, transferring to the West End for a marathon run that prefigured that of Les Liaisons (which ran for years in London, did very well in New York and is now playing in Toronto at The Elgin). Hampton said he left the Court with a definite feeling that he had let down the school. Again.

Hampton believes in the importance of "choosing the right moment to sit down and write a play." Maybe it is letting the moment choose you. He acknowledges that "the theatre is more subject to fashion than other literary forms," and quotes Stephen Frears, who directed Dangerous Liaisons, the film version of Choderlos de Laclos's novel, as thinking that the play "hit its moment. It spoke to the selfishness of the 1980s. It would have failed in the seventies."

Hampton has fallen foul of fashion in his time. "There was a woolly moment for me at the end of the seventies. It was a period when the most interesting work took up a forceful position about social issues." He liked some of these "drift-toward-fascism plays," and their authors were more or less his own age - Howard Barker, Howard Brenton, David Edgar, David Hare. But their sensibility - and it's a matter of sensibility rather than opinion - was more radical than his. He turned to writing film scripts, mostly unproduced, and "kept in touch with the theatre through translation."

He did versions of Ibsen, Moliere and, most significantly, Odon von Horvath, a prewar Austrian dramatist rediscovered by a new generation of German writers as an antidote to the ideological certainties of Brecht. Hampton eventually put him on stage in his own right in Tales from Hollywood. In this, Hampton's favourite among his own plays, Horvath is reprieved from his historical death and brought to California among the movieland population of European emigres. He serves a useful structural purpose in linking characters - Brecht and the brothers Thomas and Heinrich Mann - who were rarely on speaking terms. But so warmly does Hampton identify with his weary scepticism that Horvath takes over the play, making it Hampton's most obviously personal prior to White Chameleon. In general, the fugitive Austrian, who was killed when a tree fell on him in the Champs Elysees, emerges as a very English kind of loser.

So does the Christopher of White Chameleon, against all the odds of his real-life success (and he has a fine house with a spectacular view of the Thames to prove it). All right, not a loser. The Christopher of the play, who speaks of his own "optimistic temperament," is more a vulnerable survivor.

It's an attractive stand, and not unlike Tom Stoppard's. The difference is that Stoppard's plays, however serious, are always farces, while Hampton's are essentially drawing-room comedies. (No disparagement is intended in either case. Both are perfectly valid genres.) This gives Hampton's a slighter flavour; even Liaisons is less metallically stylish than it would probably like to be. But they are intricately, elegantly patterned; and they wear well.
