THEATRE REVIEW"The publicity for The Noam Chomsky Lectures at Theatre Passe Muraille may be high-flown, but it is a good 70 per cent accurate as well Critics hit with tactical, strategic attacks THE NOAM CHOMSKY LECTURES

Friday, March 22, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- Written and performed by Daniel Brooks and Guillermo Verdecchia At Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace in Toronto BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto THE press handout for The Noam Chomsky Lectures describes the show as a meta-theatrical onslaught . . . unrelenting and sometimes rabid, adding that it "reaffirms the theatre as a place of dissent" and will radically alter your understanding of the theatre, the mainstream media, yourself and the world you live in. But I went anyway.

Just because the publicity is pretentious garbage, I told myself, it does not follow that the play will be. But I admit it, I was wrong. Not about the play, which isnt, just as I expected it wouldn't be, but about the publicity, which isn't either. It is high-flown, yes, but it isnt pretentious; and, fairly far from being garbage, it is a good 70 per cent accurate.

Ill get back to that, as writer-performers Daniel Brooks and Guillermo Verdecchia would say, and do. (I mean do say, not would do, although that would work too.) What really lured me to Passe Muraille was the prospect, well publicized in the press though not in the official handout, of hearing some of my fellow critics roasted.

Brooks and Verdecchia deliver. They read out, and also project onto a screen, extracts from reviews written by The Globe and Mail's Ray Conlogue and the Star's departed Robert Crew and current Geoff Chapman, extracts they plainly believe display the authors as priggish and"or reactionary buffoons. I didnt say a word, thank you very much, and why should I defend them, theyre big boys. As for me, I knew that I was far too young and inoffensive to draw any flak myself. If you must know, halfway through, one of them said, in reference to some passing flippancy I emitted last week: "Yes, Mr. Cushman, this is an intermission. Honestly, I was enjoying myself too much to want an intermission, and The Noam Chomsky Lectures is not the kind of piece that needs one.

The attacks on the critics are tactical, designed to secure the audience's complicity in the baiting of a common enemy; and strategic, setting up the creators' main theme, which is the manipulative power of the press. They have little to say about television, despite the generalized references to the media." Maybe they dislike that word as much as I do. Or maybe its because there is hardly any theatre criticism on TV to give them a handle.

The show consists of two fellows at a table haranguing us, and sometimes one another, with arguments, facts and jokes. They are confessedly performers and we are voluntarily an audience, so the event is theatre, but its distance from what usually passes under that name gives it the latitude to question its own identity and, in so doing, to reaffirm it. This is, as per the blurb, meta-theatre. It is also known as double- bluff. And what you are reading is its literary equivalent, which we might call para-journalism, designed to evoke the theatrical experience by simultaneously miming and mocking it - without malice, since I really liked it, but without ever allowing the show to distract attention from my main preoccupation, which is, as Brooks and Verdecchia will be the first to recognize, myself.

(What I agonized most about in constructing this review was where to insert my reference to the shows reference to me. I contemplated leading off with it, and I also considered inserting it in an arch parenthesis like this one.) I don't think I would describe the show as "rabid - I didn't catch Verdecchia foaming at the mouth more than once or twice - but it is unrelenting. The polemics never let up. At one point the actors instruct us in their understanding of the word terrorism" - which is different from the newspapers - by shouting at us while simultaneously assailing us with lights and noise. It hardly compares with the average rock concert, but it did reduce an infant in the audience to tears. (My respect for the actors was somewhat lessened by their failure to take account of this.) What they are banging on about mainly is U.S. foreign policy and Canadian complicity in it. I guess this "reaffirms the theatre as a place of dissent, though doing so may not be that novel. And here I call Geoff Chapman to witness. Brooks and Verdecchia wouldnt be having such a go at him if he hadn't been having a go at plays whose attitudes they approve of. And, by the way, I don't think the laugh-count mentality they attribute to Geoff - yucks for bucks" - is such an outrageous criterion for judging most plays. They subscribe to it themselves, as they admit, and then satirize themselves for admitting it, which is all the funnier, and puts us in the mood for absorbing their anger, and I imagine youve got the idea by now.

Both the anger and the humour ring true. And when they attack their own hypocrisy (i.e. their greed and professional ambition), that rings true too. It does seem to justify their attacks on larger hypocrisies. They are more enraged by governments sanctimonious excuses for inhumanities than by the inhumanities themselves. Or maybe I'm projecting my own feelings onto them.

Brooks does a virtuoso job in outlining the ties that bind print and finance in Toronto. This is done with the aid of a chart, on whose showing I have been working for some of the fattest cats on two continents. So how come I ain't rich? If the guys want conspiracy theories, have they noticed that all four of the theatre critics they mention have the same last initial? This may mean that arts editors have a suspicious regard for the ghost of Nathan Cohen, or just that they interview candidates alphabetically and get bored early on. Or is that too rational? I knew before I went near the theatre that I would end up describing the show as a cross between My Dinner with Andre and Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead, and now I have. I think that both Brooks and Verdecchia, especially Brooks, have prosperous careers ahead of them as licenced gadflies. No, it wasn't Chomsky who coined the phrase "repressive tolerance," but I have to get him in somewhere. The boys do quote him, constantly, but I gather that he had his doubts.

BY MARTIN GOTTFRIED Bantam, 483 pages, $29.95

Backstage with the music men INVENTING CHAMPAGNE:The Worlds of Lerner and Loewe ALL HIS JAZZ: The Life and Death of Bob Fosse

BY MARTIN GOTTFRIED Bantam, 483 pages, $29.95

Saturday, March 23, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

REVIEW BY ROBERT CUSHMAN "THE writing of a book begins long before the writing of a book begins," says Martin Gottfried at the beginning of All His Jazz, unbearably arch before we have even got started on the acknowledgements. But he pulls himself together and offers a riveting account of a life that might have been lived for the benefit of a biographer. Bob Fosse began his career at age 10 as a child hoofer, calling himself Bobby Ritz. At an impressionable age he was exposed to Depression burlesque houses and strippers' dressing-rooms. Life was a cabaret, old chum, and a seedy one. Gottfried makes much - maybe too much - of the unfulfilled performer striving to assert himself in the feted choreographer, but history does keep playing into his hands. Back in 1955, choreographing Damn Yankees, Fosse worked out an aborted routine for a compere-figure in a gorilla suit. In 1972 Fosse was able to take over the gorilla in Cabaret and embrace it like an old friend.

It wasn't all he took over. Fosse radically altered the structure of the show Cabaret for his film, but he kept its style and tone. Having discovered sleaze-as-metaphor he stayed with it, using it to fuel a gnawing self-hatred. In Pippin, Chicago, and All That Jazz, he brilliantly exploited all the theatrical tricks while reviling the audience for accepting them. This always seemed to me pretty self- indulgent (if you feel like that, Bob, why go on?) but now that I know its personal springs I feel more tolerant. All That Jazz proved prophetic of Fosse's own fatal heart attack, which argues a kind of terminal integrity, although his old rival Gower Champion stole some of his thunder by actually dying on his own last first night.

I still prefer the earlier Fosse: the choreographer whose tight neurotic formations - the terpsichorean equivalent of close harmony - so hilariously impaled the corporate life in How To Succeed In Business Without Really Trying, the director whose mobile image of New York in Sweet Charity (sleaze-as-fun) provided the perfect frame for his wife Gwen Verdon, the ultimate soubrette. Part of Gottfried's story is how, long after their separation, Verdon remained Fosse's professional aid, coaching all the substitute Charities and finally emerging as the official widow. The relationship is part touching, part chilling, like nearly everything about Fosse.

He was the best at his game, more stylish than Jerome Robbins, more individual than Champion or Michael Bennett. Only Mamoulian, Welles and Kazan moved between stage and film with comparable mastery. Gottfried knew the man and can evaluate all his work.

In 1971 there was a musical film called The Little Prince. Alan Jay Lerner wrote the screenplay and lyrics, Frederick Loewe the music, and Bob Fosse played the Snake. It was Lerner and Loewe's last collaboration, and the only time either of them worked with Fosse.

The three men had differing attitudes toward work and - as three of the musical theatre's minority of male heterosexuals - toward women. Loewe was a hedonist, businesslike but relaxed. Having known poverty in early adult life, he relished success and retired on it, leaving both his career and his one marriage for the sunbelt life of an elderly playboy.

Lerner went on without him; he had to work, though he was very undisciplined about it. The same might be said of his personal life; he was married eight times, one of his divorces being spectacularly messy. Fosse, similarly driven professionally, acquired only three wives but an uncountable number of girlfriends. Gene Lees thinks Lerner's masterpiece, My Fair Lady, is the greatest of American musicals: I hope he's wrong, since the show, except in the quality of its craftsmanship, is so very un-American. It lacks the Broadway tempo and the Broadway brass. Its genius lies in extracting from its Shavian source the romance that everyone but Shaw himself had always known was there; really it's the last great European operetta. Loewe was Vienna-bred, and though Lerner was native New York, he was happiest writing about un-American activities.

My Fair Lady and Gigi stand apart from Lerner's other shows in having solid literary foundations. The other musicals - Brigadoon, Camelot, On a Clear Day and lots of lesser work - are mystical or preachy or both.

Not that they lack qualities. Camelot is one of the very few musicals that approaches tragedy. The ending - King Arthur clinging to the hope that some tattered fragment of his achievement may survive in the world's imagination - is extraordinarily moving. Lees, though, is too busy clocking up the show's anachronisms to notice; but since Camelot is based on a 20th-century reworking of a medieval epic about a warrior from the Dark Ages, such pedantry seems triply ludicrous. But there's no stopping Lees, once he starts making lists. He can and does name half a dozen figures in the arts who anticipated Loewe in taking early retirement, and he attacks the myth of the Broadway songwriter born into poverty by supplying the backgrounds of 17 who weren't.

He is a resistible writer when he starts laying down the law, but he has a brain. Not until the book is over do you notice that he apparently never met either Lerner or Loewe. (At least, he never says he did, and he is not generally bashful about such things.) Also, he never quotes a line of Lerner's lyrics; the rights were presumably unavailable or prohibitively expensive. So he cannot analyze them, which one wants him to do since he is a craftsmanlike if excessively solemn lyricist himself. There are two or three factual howlers and the book is an ugly object, its chapter headings surrounded by spots that are possibly meant to suggest stardust but look like measles.

"I couldn't write My Fair Lady now," said Lerner, "because I don't feel My Fair Lady now." But he couldn't write what he did feel. Fosse fitted better into the sixties and seventies but he may have died at the right time; his last show, Big Deal, was the only Broadway flop he ever had. Fosse's kind of theatre, a machine that danced, ousted Lerner's, a toy that sang.Now we have a video game that counts: in all currencies. Robert Cushman writes and hosts Songbook on CBC radio and stereo.

THEATRE REVIEW ANNE OF GREEN GABLES

Saturday, March 23, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- Written by Donald Harron and Norman Campbell Directed by Alan Lund Starring Barbara Hamilton and Gordon Pinsent At the Elgin Theatre in Toronto Most childrens classics from the last century and the early years of this one have in common a certain tartness that most modern adaptations are sworn to eliminate. This production of Anne of Green Gables follows that vapid tradition A musical monument to innocuousness BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto THE show starts with the entire company discovered behind a scrim singing "Anne of Green Gables, never change" and a few other profundities. They get a round of applause for being so outstandingly good at turning up in the same place at the same time. They then disappear, as pointlessly as they came, and after a brief musical pause the action begins.

That prologue, of course, is stale Broadway, and it is at least an honest forecast of coming events. There are worse musicals than Anne of Green Gables, some of them American, but it is depressing to find that the most popular show in the history of the Canadian theatre, based on a book that's a national classic, is actually a catalogue of cliches from south of the border.

Most of the children's books that have survived from the last century and the early years of this one, have in common a certain tartness, but that is the one element that most modern adaptations are sworn to eliminate. (cf. the collected works of Walt Disney.) The show at the Elgin is in the tradition, a monument to innocuousness.

Lucy Maud Montgomerys book is rooted in a specific rural community in Prince Edward Island. Here it is Main Street, Anywhere, with fields attached. Nobody looks or sounds much pressed for money or anything else, though they occasionally say they are. The mainspring of the story, come to think of it, is that Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert adopt young Anne because they desperately need some cheap help on the farm. They wanted a boy but an inefficient orphanage misplaced their order.

Everybody looks effortlessly scrubbed and spruce; the general ambience is that of a day spent cruising the fudge stores at Niagara-on-the-Lake. The biddies of the town start the show proper by singing about their charitable pursuits; these have little to do with the subsequent action, or even the subsequent atmosphere, but everybody knows you have to set the scene with a chorus.

Things get even more generalized when Anne goes to school. The kids, especially the boys, never walk anywhere; they cartwheel or leapfrog, sometimes for minutes on end. When Anne arrives, she is 11 or 12; by the end she has won a scholarship to college while one of her contemporaries is hilariously pregnant. (Her teacher, in the shows one ill-judged concession to ruthless realism, has spent much of the first act energetically groping her. I think this is meant to be funny.) But there is no sense whatever of the passage of time; they told Anne never to change and she didn't. At the end they tell her again; perhaps they are anticipating sequels. Somewhere, somehow - offstage perhaps and between the acts - she has become terribly popular; it's as if everybody suddenly woke up to the fact that she has the title role. A boy called Gilbert has put in a lot of time pining for her and being rejected. How long has this been going on?

As if Annes scorn wasnt enough to live with, Gilbert is saddled with a ballad of generic banality, the kind of song that has nothing to do with being a person in a situation but everything with being a character in a musical. This kind of thing happens, I hasten to add, in far more pretentious circumstances; Les Miserables is lousy with it.

It can also happen up-tempo. In act two, Anne and company get a new unstuffy, female schoolteacher, a cross between Jean Brodie and Auntie Mame. Naturally, she gets to sing a song about opening windows. To be fair, this number may originally have been ahead of its time (Anne of Green Gables is an older musical than Mame), but the brassy orchestration, with its hapless genuflections toward swing, could hardly have less to do with P.E.I. c. 1906. Author Donald Harron and composer Norman Campbell, perhaps without even thinking about it, were imitating the imitators of Rodgers and Hammerstein; the present production, touted as the most elaborate the show has ever had, compounds the offence. It cannot get by on homespun charm.

One song works: Anne's melodramatic apology to a neighbour she has offended. Her inflated self-abasement ("I have sinned, Mrs. Lind") has a mock solemn identity of its own that is right for her, and hence for the show. It is also the only occasion on which Harron's skill at rhyme catches up with his enthusiasm for it. As a librettist, he strings anecdotes together, marking time till the final curtain. He remembers the second half of the title at the very last minute; Anne gets passionate about the fate of her adoptive home when the audience never knew she cared.

The point about Anne is that she has derived her imagination and her vocabulary from years of solitary romantic reading. Her exaggerations seem natural to her, which is why people come to love her. Jessica Wilson plays her cute, as a conscious put-on artist. Solace comes from Barbara Hamiltons crusty Marilla and Gordon Pinsents twinkling codger Matthew, though they are more like man and wife than brother and sister. In musical-comedy terms, they derive (are you listening, Garth Drabinsky, Hal Prince?) from Cap'n Andy and Parthy in Show Boat. Pinsent, in particular, seems far removed from the helplessly shy old bachelor of the book, but you feel that he could play the real man if his authors would let him and that, in the meantime, no one could possibly do this sweet substitute better.
1991-03-25-theatre-review-the-duke-of-no:
THEATRE REVIEW THE DUKE OF NOTHING

Monday, March 25, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

WRITTEN AND DIRECTED BY ALAN WILLIAMS Starring John Jarvis, John Dolan Clare Coulter and Patty Jamieson At Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto Theatre emerges as just another weapon in the inter-cultural war between the two main characters here - one English, the other Canadian Firing cultural salvos in a war of egos BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail ALAN Williams first came to Canada 10 years ago with the improvisational English theatre company Hull Truck and he's still here. My abiding image of a Hull Truck show is of a roomful of people, making like students though clearly well past the age, sitting around drinking, quarrelling, making hopeful"hopeless sexual passes, and generally wondering where all the fire went.

The room always looked like a bedsit, but never was; the characters could afford a full-sized flat, but were reluctant to advertize the fact. Their heads had been shaped in the '60s, and the increasing brutalization of society affronted them, especially when they were doing well out of it.

In his new play The Duke of Nothing, Williams has updated and transplanted all this to Toronto. It is now the '70s that the characters are lamenting - the time when they had some chance to put their ideals into practice. Those ideals are mainly theatrical.

Reg is the artistic director of a small Toronto theatre. Kim is a young actress he lives with. Robertson is a social worker and first-time playwright, whose first-time play Reg is producing. Mary came over from England and is now teaching other first-timers how to write plays, having admitted that she can't do it herself. Also English is Andre, director and all-round loud mouth.

Theatre, says Andre, dictatorially, is a way of saying the unpalatable and making it palatable. Williams's play is very palatable, though I doubt if what he has to say would be all that hard to stomach even if his style were less ingratiating than it is. This is, in fact, the most hilarious play I have heard in ages. It is less strong on structure, in fact it comes off lopsided. They keep talking about theatre, but that never focuses as the real subject; it seems more a play about guys scoring off one another while women wait angrily or resignedly to pick up the pieces.

The play begins and ends with Reg, but Andre steals much of the limelight and most of the thunder. This is not because he is more likeable. Reg may be weak - he has a history of failing to defend his own corner - but Andre is an unlovely mixture of abrasion, conceit and self- pity. He is only just off the plane but, at an hour when any decently sensitive chap would be paralyzed with jet-lag, here he is knocking back the local beer, slagging off the local men and chatting up the local women.

Andre has an infinite capacity for aggression. He can switch targets in a moment from his own country ("I wish I could tell you how much I hate it") to somebody else's ("Like a lot of English people when they arrive in Toronto, I thought, Wow, it's great to be near America.") Introduced to Robertson, who is an Indian (a term he prefers - "people have dreams about Indians"), Andre is lecturing him within two minutes on how he should be writing about "the whole situation." He also takes it as a personal insult when Robertson, an alcoholic, refuses a drink.

"Indians" says Robertson, immortally, "hate to see it when white guys don't like Canada. We think, Gee, another dissatisfied customer." Williams, after ten years here, has a lot to say about both places, much of it scintillating, and he orchestrates his jokes into a war of egos. Neither Reg nor Andre can resist a jab at their own expense, or at anyone else's; conversation becomes a matter of keeping one's cynicism in perfect equilibrium. When the war winds down, so does the play.

Theatre emerges as just another weapon in the inter-cultural war. Often it's a good one; there's an irresistible moment when Andre, surveying the Toronto listings notices that The Mousetrap, eternal in London, has also been running for 12 years here. "I expect," he says "it's performed with much bitter post-colonial irony."

John Jarvis's Reg goes beyond self-effacement into amorphousness. John Dolan as Andre starts with high energy and ascends into one continuous shout. As moral judgments on the characters, these readings may well be perfectly valid; as performances to sit through they quickly become monotonous.

The real strength in the show (and, I suspect, the real sympathy in the writing) comes from Clare Coulter as Mary, a permanently displaced person, witheringly aware of her own deficiencies and everyone else's. She and Kim (Patty Jamieson) sit silent through one prolonged scene between the men, and the silence says a lot. Clayton Odjig's Robertson is, by any orthodox standards, an unskilled performance, but it unquestionably has presence.

So does the play. "Generally," says Reg in one of his best aggressive- defensive moments, "our shores have been untroubled by talented British people - present company excepted, of course." Of course.
1991-03-29-that-scatterbrain-booky:
THEATRE REVIEW" THAT SCATTERBRAIN BOOKY

Friday, March 29, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

WRITTEN BY JOEY MILLER Directed by Peter Moss Starring Trish Lindstrom, Mary Ann MacDonald Young People's Theatre, Toronto A fine collection of 1930s songs and some nifty choreography are not enough to make this trip to Depression-era Toronto work Weak story line hurts nostalgic tale BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail That Scatterbrain Booky is a nostalgic trip back to the Toronto of the 1930s when things were really bad, though naturally the politicians tried to deny it. "Prime Minister Bennett," goes one ironic line, "says it's only a recession." Hollow laughter in the house, much of which, I fancy, will never have heard of former prime minister R. B. Bennett.

If the target audience of the YPT will have no memory of these events, neither will their parents. In fact "nostalgic" is quite the wrong word, and I was seduced into using it by Joey Miller's songs, which it would be churlish to describe as pastiche. They are, with a couple of folksy exceptions, as good and musicianly a bunch of songs of the thirties as anyone is likely to write in the nineties. Sprucely orchestrated and played by a band (musical director, Boko Suzuki) that sounds much bigger than it is, it also sets off some nifty choreography. For his first trick William Orlowski fashions a tap routine out of hopscotch - not such a stretch, perhaps, but still done with rousing precision - and if he never quite tops that, he still keeps the show, and his mainly juvenile cast, hopping. This is a kids' show - one that may teach its audiences a lot, both historically and emotionally - but it also demands to be judged as a full-grown musical.

Here it runs into trouble. Miller has written the book as well as the score, and his script does not have a central dynamic. The title refers to a 12-year-old girl, the third child of a poverty-stricken family. (A fourth is on the way as the show starts.) Father is unemployed but is too proud to tolerate his wife or children looking for work. Mother is a beleaguered rock. Elder sister has a Jewish sweetheart, whose range of interests - "books and boxing" - are oddly reminiscent of the Golden Boy of Clifford Odets. The bailiff is constantly battering at the door. Eventually they are evicted. They relocate, just managing to avoid the lowest depths. ("Cabbagetown - that's where the real down-and-outs end up.") So a fair amount happens. But none of it counts for very much. A lot of the blame probably lies with the source material. The show is based on a trilogy of books by Bernice Thurman Hunter, about her own childhood. Booky is her. At one point in the show she tangles with the school authorities, but she does little else to earn the adjective bestowed on her in the title. In fact she shows no positive qualities of any kind. She is not a person who makes things happen, which is the best qualification for being the centre of a show. She is not even the one they happen to, which is the second-best, though perilous. She is the one who watches things happen, and describes it all for us. In fact she is that great scourge of autobiographical drama: She Is A Camera.

To make it worse, she is a mini-camera. What I am about to say may constitute cruelty to children, but there is no help for it. Trish Lindstrom, the 11-year-old who plays Booky, cannot carry the weight. Her singing - of which she has to do a lot - is not clear or true enough; her timing and delivery are muddy. We rely on her to tell us what is going on, and what is going on is often obscure.

Even when we see or hear it for ourselves there is a curious lack of urgency about it. Family rows, fuelled by desperation and at one point ascending to violence, keep going off half-cocked. Neil Foster's Irish dad is a resolutely soft-grained underpowered performance. The staging, in Peter Moss's production, may not help. Leslie Frankish's set - a collection of front-stoops - is impeccably evocative of time and space but it is less helpful to action. Booky's clan seem to be taking all their meals alfresco, in a small square in the middle of the stage. It isn't spacious, but it isn't helpfully constricted either. It merely looks cramped and uncomfortable and so does the acting.

Mary Ann McDonald as Mother does get a chance to take off when she sings The Palais Royale, a glowing number about the dancehalls of her youth. But it's wrong. For one thing, she's singing about 1922 and the music remains resolutely 1930s; for another the song comes at the end of the first half after we have been conditioned to think of singing as something that is done by childhood. That seems a very useful convention - it sets them off in a world of their own - and breaking it is fatal.

There is a Halloween sequence which is well staged and designed without quite shaking off memories of Meet Me in St. Louis. The domestic tensions and the adolescent rites of passage never stop recalling Neil Simon's Brighton Beach Memoirs, dramatic memories of the same period which had the great advantage of not being based on a book. Writing music Joey Miller seems at home in the past but still his own man. Between songs he is thrashing about, looking for a story.
1991-04-09-theatre-review-flesh-and-bloo:
THEATRE REVIEW" FLESH AND BLOOD

Tuesday, April 09, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY COLIN THOMAS Directed by JoAnn McIntyre Starring Mark Saunders, David Orth, Rob Osborne and Amanda Stepto At The Stage Downstairs, Toronto Passive suffering is not very interesting dramatically, and a call to action merely leads us outside the theatre Morality not simple in moral Theatre Direct play ufbyBY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto FLESH and Blood is a good play trying to pass itself off as a social tract. It is being presented by Theatre Direct, which tours plays to schools. With the play comes a glossy informative brochure about AIDS and how to avoid it. Flesh and Blood, though, is not about AIDS but - it is not a very subtle difference - about people living with or dying from it. Its subjects are the eternal ones: sex, friendship, family and death.

Acquired immune deficiency syndrome, let us pray, is not an eternal subject though it is disturbing enough to be mistaken for one. The first wave of AIDS plays made that mistake, putting the disease on stage and saying, in effect, "Isn't this terrible? Something must be done." Both utterances were undeniable, but passive suffering is not very interesting dramatically, and a call to action outside the theatre merely leads us outside the theatre.

Colin Thomas, a Vancouver playwright, starts by introducing us to two brothers, one straight, one gay, both the victims of a guilt-dispensing offstage mother with a virtuoso line in intimidation. (She laments that she lives in Saskatchewan where abortion is illegal; otherwise, she might have spared herself all the pain of parenthood.) She has discovered Allan, her youngest, more or less in flagrante with his girlfriend, Sherri, and he has left home in consequence. He now moves in with big brother, Jim, and Jim's lover, Ralph, at Jim's insistence, moves out.

Jim has AIDS, but not until halfway through the play does Allan find out. Jim has always seen himself as the protector in their relationship, and he is not about to have the roles reversed. Nor, protest though he may, does Allan find the strains and responsibilities easy.

Both brothers are self-destructive. Allan drinks; Jim invited his condition. Having been cautious since the epidemic broke, he succumbed one night to unsafe sex. Allan, similarly insisting on one night of unprotected passion, provokes the breakup of his own affair with Sherri. Indeed, the playwright manages to make the humble condom a potent (you should pardon the expression) dramatic symbol. Allan's mother retrieved the one he used at home and waited, vengefully, to confront him with it. No wonder he left.

The play's later developments are controlled, as all plays involving AIDS tend to be, by Jim's deterioration. The details are helpfully and economically filled in by his increasingly frail testimonies at an encounter group, but the progress toward the hospital bed is inevitable in more ways than one.

Here, Flesh and Blood does become "an AIDS play." For all its compassion, it leaves you wanting to blame someone. Drama works either toward anger or acceptance. There is no point in being angry with a medical phenomenon; you end up railing at life itself.

But acceptance seems inhuman. It could be that the only satisfactory play about AIDS could be written from a standpoint that none of us could tolerate: a fundamentalist one, like that of the mother in this play, that sees death as the wages of sin. Given the scale on which those wages are being paid, it could be our equivalent of a Greek curse.

Flesh and Blood comes to a liberal accommodation with tragedy. Jim (Allan, too) is not punished for sin but for carelessness or, from another point of view, for love. Passion breaks the rules. The play is moral all right, but its morality is not simple, JoAnn McIntyre's production spreads the action across a wide space, and in doing so loses visual and aural focus. (The theatre has an awkward echoing acoustic.) But she gets good performances from Mark Saunders, grey with pent-up suffering as Jim, and David Orth, wild and flailing as Allan. Rob Osborne's Ralph is a neutral performance, perhaps because the script seems unwilling to characterize him as a camp queen, but is unable to come up with an alternative. His role in the structure is to keep returning loyally to the vortex of sickness, while Sherri has to get away from it. Amanda Stepto starts her as a pert caricature and gets steadily deeper.
1991-04-09-theatre-review-triptych:
THEATRE REVIEW" TRIPTYCH

Tuesday, April 09, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- Presented by Crow's Theatre At the Poor Alex Theatre, Toronto Half a dozen actors gather together to play all the roles in three short plays which, unfortunately, run far too long Childishness portrayed in three too many stages BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto THIS is indeed a cryptic Triptych. Crow's Theatre has assembled three short pieces - each runs just under an hour - and handed them over to the same half-dozen actors to play back-to-back-to-back. No common theme is declared, though one that suggests itself is childishness.

We lead off with "6": six the title, six the number of actors, six the age they play at being. The six characters have found eight authors, who have pooled their memories, their observations, and their inventiveness in order to re-create the world of first-grade. First, as adults, they reminisce about that age of innocence, or at any rate of unselfconsciousness: the days when, as one of them memorably says, "I never broke eye-contact." Then, having fought their way out from underneath a large tarpaulin, they start in on impersonation, and on a lightning series of group vignettes. It is reasonably well done, but it never progresses beyond agreeable cuteness. It arouses impatience, but not hostility.

Having rampaged around as children, the actors move on in the second piece to playing grown-ups. This they do with far less conviction. There is not a moment of weight, style, or even simple skill in the entire performance: doubly unfortunate since they are supposed to be playing a tankful of media barracudas. We may be dealing here with an ensemble of total deadheads, but that is always unlikely (and their work in the surrounding playlets does not, on the whole, suggest it.) Maybe it is the fault of the director Blake Brooker, who fails to create anything in the way of atmosphere or tension, and who constantly leaves his actors hanging around in unhappy poses. Nor are they much helped by the set, a wall of silver foil inset with television screens.

Then there is the play. It is called Prince, and Jim Millan, Crow's Artistic Director, wrote it. He posits a young TV magnate appointed by a reactionary senator to the chairmanship of the CBC with explicit instructions to destroy it. The author can hardly have foreseen the elevation of Professor Crispo but events could hardly have conspired to make his theme more pertinent. In fact he neglects it completely. Prince, the whizz-kid mogul, sits ensconced in his office playing mind-games (and occasional body-games) with everyone who strays within his orbit. Here we are again with the memoirs of a maleficent megalomaniac, being told nothing that we have not heard a hundred times before.

Anything to praise? A sequence in which Prince is interviewed by the National shows a fair command of obsequious telespeak; and Tom Nardi, who plays him, has the interesting look of a young slicked-down Dustin Hoffman. I could call the thing half-baked, but I'm in no mood for compliments.

In the last segment, Brownie From Hell, Millan reverts to directing and does a respectable if ultimately aimless job. This piece, like both the others, starts with a possibly bright idea that it fails to develop. The baking Brownie is of the Girl Scout variety, and met an early death on a guided tour of a hot dog factory. Now she sits and ponders what might have happened to her had she been allowed to grow up. From what she can see, a woman's life is still not much, the whole sex having been conditioned by their childhood reading to settle for domesticity and dependence. Both in books and (therefore) out of them, boys have all the fun.

She is very likely right, though personally I would back Jane Eyre to beat up Oliver Twist any day. I cite these books since they are among the few she doesn't. Some selectivity might not hurt. Nor is there any particular reason for the case to be made by a brownie - though, to return to where we came in, it helps the cuteness-quotient.

Carol Sinclair, who wrote the piece, also plays the lead and she is good at being wickedly gleeful. Her acting colleagues climb out of various holes to offer support. Either they are heckling demons or illustrative figments from stories, movies or TV series. The latter catagories are there to bring the cultural argument up to date; though if you are going to make What Ever Happened to Baby Jane a prime exhibit, it might help to draft an actress who can impersonate Bette Davis. The woods must be full of them.

Not a very fulfiling evening. As Cockney cabdrivers used to say when they strayed into Hollywood movies, Cor, lumme guv'nor, stone the flippin' Crows.
1991-04-12-music-review-acting-ability-s:
MUSIC REVIEW"Acting ability shines through during her elegant satirizing of sex Talented Wilson proves real trouper

Friday, April 12, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto JULIE Wilson, the regent of Manhattan cabaret, began her opening-night set Tuesday at the Top O' the Senator with Most Gentlemen Don't Like Love, a Cole Porter song that Sophie Tucker introduced on Broadway back in 1938. Not unnaturally, she employed Tucker's haughty, staccato tones for the purpose. These tones persisted, however, on songs that Tucker never had anything to do with. Wilson has borrowed creatively from her predecessor to develop her own style.

Like Tucker, Wilson is largely in the business of satirizing sex. She does it, though, from a very different standpoint, and from within a very different body. Tucker was dumpy and gemutlich; Wilson, now in her 60s, is tall, lissome and a lady, a slightly swacked lady, incredulous at some of the scandalous things she finds herself singing, but elegant forever. She is also an actress.

She is maybe more an actress than a singer. Cabaret singers traditionally lack voice, but most of them cultivate an easy going naturalism, gliding informally between the notes. They also tend to hide behind pianos as their own accompanists. Wilson commands the stage, and adorns it, in a diva's red dress, a white gardenia, and alternating boas of black and rose-pink. Her delivery is conversational - she is a mistress of phrasing - but not informal. She has slightly more voice than the late Soph - who by the end of her career was just talking to music - but like her she orates her songs.

Wilson's program was mostly Porter, as a centennial homage. Porter also satirized sex, when he wasn't celebrating it. Sometimes he did both at once, and Wilson included a generous number of these ambiguous comic classics, songs like Let's Not Talk About Love, or But in the Morning, No! an epically libidinous celebration of erotic hangover that, if Wilson's patter is to be believed, even succeeded in shocking Ethel Merman, who first sang it. Another Merman number, Down in the Depths (on the 90th Floor), was a Wilson triumph, luxurious heartache simultaneously mourned and mocked; her navigation of the treacherously simple Miss Otis Regrets was all but impeccable.

Sometimes her theatricality undoes her; in ballads she can dwell on her emotions instead of simply letting the song move us. All the same, she managed to freshen that most venerable of standard warhorses, Night and Day. She strayed occasionally from Cole to Coleman, Cy Coleman, that is, whose Don't Ask a Lady (from Little Me), raucous erotica to contrast with Porter's brittle, tore the place up. It showed her in a new light; a warm woman at a refreshing angle to the cool of most of her material. She is a trouper. She must come back and show us her Arlen, Weill and Sondheim programs. Her accompanist, William Roy, occasionally lifts his voice with hers: modest but true, and surprisingly legato. They match wits beautifully.
1991-04-15-theatre-review-dry-lips-ought:
THEATRE REVIEW DRY LIPS OUGHTA MOVE TO KAPUSKASING

Monday, April 15, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY TOMSON HIGHWAY Directed by Larry Lewis Starring Gary Farmer, Graham Greene and Billy Merasty At the Royal Alexandra Theatre, Toronto Tomson Highway's play is about what people do to themselves under pressure, though the pressures may be externally imposed. It is especially about what men do to women From ideal to painfully real BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto DRY Lips Oughta Move to Kapuskasing, which opened Saturday at the Royal Alexandra Theatre in Toronto, begins with magic. At the side of a great, bare, tilted platform, white with a black surround, stands a figure, recognizably and traditionally Indian. The figure gestures, and snow falls.

After this descent another, more prosaic. A sofa is lowered from the flies. Visible upon it is a naked male body. A female in black underpants detaches herself from it, and begins to dress. Actually she dons, slowly, a monstrous pair of false breasts. Music sounds: The Stripper, played plaintively and incongruously on a mouth organ. Not a word spoken and already we have been moved - beautifully, comically and with enormous theatricality - from the ideal to the painfully real and on again to the satirical-grotesque.

Larry Lewiss direction keeps this imaginative energy throughout. Everything is precise, everything is beautifully played. The set continues to come down in sections; a common enough device, but here it becomes a style. And no matter how many elements are added, or how sordid the action, John Fergusons design retains an unshakable elegance, and also wit.

Playwright Tomson Highway's characters live, for the most part, like poor whites; they have adopted rock-bottom American values. This is not a play about racial prejudice; it couldn't be since there are no non-Indian characters. It is about what people do to themselves under pressure, though the pressures may be externally imposed. Especially it is about what men do to women.

This is the most powerful play I have seen about misogyny, and it is fitting that it should be the work of a man. The cast contains one woman, in a multiple role, but eight men; for the most part, their view of women is accurately summed up in the opening dumbshow. The extreme case is Big Joey (Ben Cardinal), whose wife is the one with the falsies; he is virtually prostituting her as part of a blackmail scam. His ambitions to run a radio station conflict with those of his pudgy victim Zachary (Gary Farmer) to get money to open a bakery. Big Joey cannot stand the sight of female blood, and his phobia led to culpable negligence at the birth of his son (in a barroom, by the light of a juke box). Seventeen years on, he watches while the boy commits an especially brutal rape.

The scene in which Joey explains himself is one of the plays weakest, matched by one in which the baker takes on the Christian God, defying Him to justify the misery in which the community is living. These both sound like the playwright being painfully explicit. He also spreads himself so that his play, though actually tightly plotted, seems to sprawl. But the weaknesses are those of talent and ambition. At times he writes with horrific power; more often he deploys a barbed, juicy laughter that exploits and explodes masculine obsession and masculine bluster. Sometimes he suggests a grown-up Sean OCasey. Urban-sharp this Highway may be, but he belongs in the line of ethnic comedy that periodically rejuvenates the Anglo-American theatre. When this line breaks through, as Indian writing now has, it does us a double service; it introduces us to new scenes and puts us in touch with old ones. At moments we seem to be reaching back to the roots of the theatre.

A crisis finds Pierre St. Pierre (Graham Greene, at the furthest remove from his wisdom-incarnate role in Dances With Wolves) posed at a window, pulling a nightcap on and off as he wrestles between the demands of sleep and conscience. The sequence is prolonged past the limits of farce, and becomes agonizingly tense. We desperately want him to do the right thing, and know how easily we ourselves would do the wrong one.

Greene also has a protracted clowning triumph as a hockey referee, slithering around on invisible ice, in abject fear of the game and the unseen players. These players are the women on the reserve and it is these sporting ambitions that put the fear of whatever it is into most of the males. The men literally fall backward with astonishment when they first hear about it. But they recover.

The women in the play, even more than the men, have a rich variety of names and labels: from Gazelle Nataways to "that awful dictionary woman" to the eponymous Dry Lips. The men end up hooting the dismissive title line, Big Joey once more in the lead.

Cardinal's Joey, balefully unrelenting, makes a strong negative pole in a group otherwise composed of weaklings, misfits and the odd doomed idealist. They have all - Tom Jackson, Gary Farmer, Billy Merasty, Dwayne Manitowabi, Kennetch Charlette, Doris Linklater - appeared in the play before, at Theatre Passe Muraille in Toronto or in Manitoba, and they are an ensemble.

The arrival of this show at the Royal Alex is an event. One hopes that a general audience, subscribers or otherwise, will fill a large theatre for a major new play. This is a matter of economics, but also of morale and of ultimate value. If the Canadian theatre is to mean anything, it cannot skulk forever in holes and corners.
1991-04-23-theatre-reviews-masada:
THEATRE REVIEWS MASADA

Tuesday, April 23, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY ARTHUR MILNER Directed by Simon Malbogat Starring Gary Reineke At the Theatre Centre, Toronto GOD AND THE BIG BLUE CHAIR WRITTEN BY RAYMOND STOREY, EDWARD ROY AND THE COMPANY Directed by Edward Roy At the Passe Muraille Backspace, Toronto Gary Reinekes refreshing one-man show about Israeli history is neither academic nor didactic, though it is informative Giving the devil his due BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto MASADA, a Mixed Company production at the Theatre Centre in Toronto, is a breezy, biting conspectus of Jewish and Israeli history from Abraham to Shamir. The title refers to the Zealots' last stand; it was at Masada that fanatical Judean rebels chose suicide rather than surrender to legions of the Roman Empire.

Masada is also a one-man show. It takes the form of a lecture, supposedly delivered by a visiting Israeli historian to a Jewish audience somewhere in Canada, a young audience that has to be reminded that Moshe Dayan was the one with the patch. It is not, however, either academic or didactic, though it is informative.

Solo performances are often remorselessly dreary, but when they work they can be refreshing. It is a relief not to have to struggle through furlongs of exposition, or listen to actors trying to make conversation out of some playwright's tin-eared meanderings. A man speaking directly to us or himself can talk as he likes. And if he wants to make us laugh he can set about it directly, without involving third parties. As does Gary Reineke, the actor here, when he dryly remarks that if God had asked him to pick out a promised land he would have chosen France.

However, Moses plumped for what was then called Canaan, and by that ancestral choice our speaker stands. Or, perhaps more accurately, flies; he is a far-out hawk. The message he has come to deliver is: "Sure the Palestinians deserve a state. If they can get it." What Israel has it holds, not just the occupied territories but eventually - and here the actors eyes perceptibly glitter - Jordan as well.

And here, of course, if not before, shudders run down our liberal spines, as we sit with hackles ascendant. These are not opinions that can be expected to go unchallenged in an alternative theatre. And if there is nobody else on stage to challenge them, as of course there isnt, then it's up to the audience. Indeed, if there were no tension between the speaker and the house, there would not be a play here at all, merely a weird vanity showcase. But plainly playwright Arthur Milner has not gone to the expense of hiring an actor in order to spout his own beliefs. We are expected to ponder the title, and to reflect that unrestrained zealotry can be the path to self-destruction.

Our lecturer is in fact an anti-mouthpiece, not so much the devil's advocate as the devil himself. So you will be pleased to learn, especially if you dig proverbs, that he is given his due. He is rather convincing, which may be to Milners disadvantage as a polemicist, but does him credit as a playwright. It is actually refreshing to hear a Zionist argument that makes minimal reference to the Holocaust, one that sees the Jewish state as the reward of struggle rather than the worlds pat on the back for sufferings rendered. The speaker doesn't flinch from endorsing Irgun terrorism, and he doesn't whine about the PLO employing the same tactics. This is the world we live in, and here at least there is no politicians hypocrisy about it. Reinekes performance, balancing the demands of narrative with those of character, the pedagogue with the fanatic, is excellent.

Where is God in all this? Nowhere much, except in a mood-setting reference to Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son. But a character in Topological Theatre's God and the Big Blue Chair does see God sitting on, indeed, a big blue chair, and dozens of similar furnishings hang from the ceiling over the acting area at Passe Muraille, perhaps to encourage others who would like to be similarly privileged. As the lights go up we see a selection of them, apparently fighting over a chair. That is, each of them is gripping onto it with one hand, while keeping the other arm balletically outstretched. It looks like the kind of thing that gives religious drama, and group-improvised drama, and drama itself, a bad name.

And so it proves. Half-a-dozen stories of people seeking faith are intercut and occasionally interwoven, though with five actors in multiple roles it is difficult to keep track. There are some passages of anecdotal, or even anthropological, interest: a mother-goddess priestess draws thoughtful parallels between her own cult and that of the Virgin Mary. Some, including a scene depicting a young woman searching for her hospitalized grandfather, are pointlessly feeble. And even the better bits suggest a mechanical searching of received scenarios to pad out a prearranged theme. Here is another gay couple blighted by AIDS. Here is another yuppie hitting the skids among hookers and winos.

Debra Kirshenbaum rises above her material as an Alabama housewife, pregnant in middle age, who goes looking for herself on the road and mysteriously winds up in Canada. This at least allows her to meet the rest of the cast, who have been striving and suffering here all along. Toward the end, moments of exaltation abound, though probably not for the audience. Some performances are anonymously competent; some others aren't.
1991-05-14-theatre-review-andromache:
THEATRE REVIEW" ANDROMACHE

Tuesday, May 14, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY JEAN RACINE Translated by Richard Wilbur Directed by Ian Prinsloo Presented by Orange Dog Theatre at the Glen Morris Studio Theatre, Shoestring production in a small space manages to project the essence of a masterpiece A powerful, witty Andromache Toronto BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto THE director of this production of Andromache thinks that it is a play about war, best served by being togged out in the high fashions of the early 1920s while interlarded with projected stills showing the carnage of 1914-18. He is wrong on all these counts but still manages, powerfully and wittily, to project the essence of a masterpiece.

Andromache was the wife of Hector of Troy, whose death, as narrated by Homer, is the first tragedy in Western literature. She is one of the principals in Euripides unrivalled denunciation of post-war reprisals, The Trojan Women. A captive after the fall of Troy, she has to endure the killing of her infant son Astyanax. This judicial murder - offstage, of course - is probably the most searing event in world drama: a meeting- point of ancient tragedy and modern realpolitik.

Racine takes the traditional figures and rearranges them in a scheme of his own devising. His Andromache is a captive at the court of the Greek king Pyrrhus, the son of Achilles, who killed Andromaches husband. Her child still lives, but is again under threat; the other Greeks are demanding that Pyrrhus give him up. He refuses. This may be because he is a reformed character, with a genuine distaste for further atrocities. But he has an ulterior motive. He is in love with Andromache. He is also, of course, in a perfect position to blackmail her into marrying him.

The Greek emissary is the fury-driven Orestes, best-known for having killed his mother. His current problem is that he loves Hermione, daughter of Helen, while she is in love with Pyrrhus, and hence murderously resentful of Andromache. It all makes a perfect pattern: love and hate, politics and justice, cancelling one another out. It is resolved when all give way to their worst impulses. Jealous Orestes, at the prompting of jealous Hermione, assassinates Pyrrhus, thereby unwittingly creating a power vacuum. Andromache, who has spent the play feeling suicidal, ends it, irony of ironies, as proclaimed queen.

None of this would have happened if there had not been a Trojan war. But it is a leap from that to assuming, as Ian Prinsloo's production does, that the brute realities of warfare lie behind every chiselled, courtly line. The fate of one child does, and it is the genius of Racine to show us how the characters react to this. Orestes treats it as a diplomatic counter, Hermione couldn't care less, Pyrrhus remembers it when it suits him, and even Andromache wavers between the roles of protective mother and sacrificial victim.

Pyrrhus risks another war, but Racine, 17th-century snob that he was, was indifferent to the plight of the ordinary soldier. Pictures of gas- masked Tommies and bodies hanging on wires can make no headway against a text that has other things on its mind. The best that can be said is that the reflections make intriguing shapes on the stage-floor.

When the memory of war does erupt in the dialogue, it obliterates the visuals and everything else. This is when Andromache describes in detail Pyrrhuss record at the fall of Troy to explain why she can never forgive him. Jani Lauzon, who has moped her way uneasily through most of the role, rises magnificently to this, in a white-hot fusion of agony and anger. It must be the most powerful moment in current Toronto theatre.

It is the women who make the action in Racine, and Hermione rather than Andromache who does so here. Jealousy on the grand scale is hard to sustain, and Alyson Green, dressed up as a white-beaded flapper, substitutes pique, which is arresting to begin with but palls before the end. The trouble with deflating tragic characters is that once you have made your comic point, there they still are, orating. Orestes (Alex Poch-Goldin) comes over as a tremulous dupe and catspaw and though one feels there should be more to him, it would be hard to say what.

Richard Wilburs translation is, like the original, in rhyming couplets, to English ears an instinctively comic medium. The most complete performance here, and the only actor who firmly controls the verse, is Michael Healey as Pyrrhus, a neatly bearded monarch in knickerbockers who receives Orestes' embassy while stylishly dismembering a boiled egg. Only his grizzled confidant (Peter J. McConnell) has a comparable assurance. The other principals might be better off talking to themselves.

Racine in English is traditionally a no-go area; last year's Phedre at the Stratford Festival was, at best, worthy. Andromache is more accommodating: a psychological drama but devoid of modern sentimentality. This is a shoestring production in a small space with an unpaid cast. I expected little of it. I was bowled over.

THEATRE REVIEW THE 10,000 YEAR-OLD WOMAN

Friday, May 31, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN AND PERFORMED BY CHERYL CASHMAN At the Theatre Centre, Toronto Cheryl Cashman's one-woman show has half a dozen clowns, one gifted and ebullient comic sketch, and plenty of self-indulgence Sincerity is no excuse for embarrassing the audience BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto ACTUALLY, Cheryl Cashman confides at the beginning of her one-woman show, she isn't 10,000 years old at all. She's only 580 but the management bumped her age up so that they might more easily take our money. (This isn't quite as funny as the show gets, but for a long time it seems uncomfortably likely that it will be.) In terms of arithmetic, I suppose Cashman has a right to detain us five times as long as Mel Brooks's 2,000-year-old stripling, but I question her tact in doing so. Besides, Brooks had a first-rate foil in Carl Reiner, while Cashman has only half a dozen painfully grimacing red-nosed acolytes who minister to her needs when she is on stage and move things aimlessly about during the few moments when she isn't.

They are billed, low down the program, as "clowns," and the show adheres to the fashionable belief that this gives it and them a special claim upon us. A clown, by this reckoning, is no mere entertainer but a licenced holy fool. Cashman herself is the arch-clown and we are privileged to have her attention for three hours.

She adopts seven personae in this time, and one of them I liked. This is Sonya, a self-proclaimed cheerleader from the Yukon (I think she said Yukon; she sounds more like the Ukraine) recruiting for the emotional Olympics, mainly from among the audience. We are urged to converse entirely in vowels; consonants, she convincingly explains, are inhibiting. She all but blames them for the state of the nation.

Sonya is the only one of her creations whom Cashman doesn't patronize. The others are winsome or downtrodden or both, but Sonya shows her to be a gifted, ebullient standup comic with a firm command of the house. She even managed a perfectly timed put-down of some jerk in the congregation who had muttered an obscenity at her 10 minutes earlier when she approached him in one of her previous incarnations.

I was the guilty man, and I fear that if I had my time over I would do it all again. The lady was impersonating a sweetly smiling male half-wit at the time. Before this she had given us her frustrated housewife (is there, in this kind of comedy, any other kind of housewife?) and, some kind of summit in pointlessness, a failed performer ("I played the streetcar in Streetcar Named Desire") who adopted a second career as a vampire.

There is also the recurring title figure, who speaks in a bad-tempered wheeze and wears a moldering wedding dress like Miss Havisham. Everything else about her is borrowed from the fatuously enduring heroine of Beckett's Happy Days, including her name, Winnie.

She has not, however, inherited Beckett's wit or his poetry. Cashman the performer is done in by Cashman the writer, who is mercilessly self- indulgent. (There is no director and it shows.) It made me angry; and that was just the first act.

In the second, she comes before us in her own person and talks about her life, as if she were bestowing some kind of gift. If she wants to give an inspirational discourse on how she beat cancer, that I guess is her privilege. It made me queasy, but that could be my hangup. But she also talks about her friends: about the playwright George Ryga, with whom she apparently had a relationship and who died on her, and about others, teachers or colleagues, who committed suicide or died of AIDS. At one point - Happy Days is here again - she arraigns God, whom she imagines saying, "Let's get the artists; let's invent AIDS" as if nobody who was not an artist had died of it and as if even artists do not, eventually and invariably, die of something.

She sings, very well, some excruciating songs of her own composition; and she reads, beautifully, some intimate poems written to her by Ryga. She uses all her skills. The effect is way beyond embarrassing.

It is also very instructive. In shows that there are, after all, some barriers between life and art that must not be breached. She is asking to be applauded for her grief. She is unquestionably sincere, and almost inconceivably cheap.

The import of Porter MUSIC"Cole Porter, who was born 100 years ago tomorrow, was an impeccable craftsman in words and music, an elegant, priviledged patrician who made sophistication commercial. But there was more to him than that

Saturday, June 08, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail THERE is a bouncing, but little-known, Cole Porter song called It Ain't Etiquette, hidden away in the score for his 1939 musical DuBarry Was a Lady and written as a vehicle for that show's star comedian, Bert Lahr. It begins: "Missus Emily Post Who they tell me is most Reliable For a helluva sum Wrote a book that's become My Biable."

It goes on to counsel us: "And if only you'll look In that etiquette book Of dear Emily's You can co-habitate With America's great Femilies."

That's still pretty funny, especially if you imagine Lahr gnong- gnonging out the trick rhymes in the Cowardly Lion voice that he had patented to immortality the same year.

What is impressive, though, is the way in which the rhymes reinforce the jokes; and what is really impressive is the way in which, without any apparent forcing, the jokes connect, so that an attitude and a thought- line go through the whole passage.

Porter is famous for list-songs like You're the Top, spectacular accumulations of one-liners, but what really distinguishes him from all other U.S. lyricists is his ability to write in paragraphs. Begin the Beguine, the longest popular song ever written, became a hit through its throbbing exoticism, but it would fall apart if Porter had not managed, through 108 virtuoso bars, to tell a coherent story.

It was a story that the public wanted to hear, of love found and lost in a tropical paradise. That was a standard theme in tin-pan alley.

But Porter, Broadway's favourite rich boy, gave it a flavour of his own. He made it a sophisticated traveller's tale, which was fair enough since he was known to be a sophisticated traveller. People expected him to entertain lavishly and to go on world cruises, though many of them would have been perturbed had they known what some of Porter's cruising entailed.

He was a life-long homosexual, sheltered from scrutiny by wealth, both inherited and earned, and by a happily platonic marriage that incidentally brought him a third fortune.

Of all the American Golden Age songwriters (and they are an extraordinary parade; just when you think you have them all down, you realize that you have forgotten Kurt Weill or Duke Ellington) only two had high public profiles, personalities that the public saw reflected in their work. There was George Gershwin, buoyant and aggressive, the archetypal poor boy made good; and there was Porter, the Yale man, elegant and patrician and all-around WASPish.

Gershwin must have been easy to identify with; Porter's popularity - at its height during the Depression - is less expected. People should have resented him, but in fact they cheered him on. They didn't feel part of his world, but they didn't feel excluded from it either. They were let in, so to speak, on the ground floor.

Porter made sophistication commercial. There is a universal masochistic appetite for songs of lost love, but he put a new spin on it.

"So goodbye, dear, and amen Here's hoping we meet now and then It was great fun But it was Just One Of Those Things."

Wouldn't we all like, in romantic extremis, to be capable of that wit and that courtliness? Porter makes it seem like everybody's birthright.

Indeed, he perfected the art of the gracious farewell. During the Second World War, when relationships faced challenges far deadlier than erotic caprice, he wrote what is arguably his finest song, Ev'ry Time We Say Goodbye, in which parting is seen as an inescapable event, one that recurs if you're lucky. The serene logic of its melody is so convincing that the song's most famous moment of cleverness - when the words speak of "the change from major to minor" and the music follows suit - registers as an unself-conscious emotional peak. The feeling is universal, but it's still conveyed in Porter's own fastidious language, complete with reference to "the gods above me, who must be in the know."

The gods often came in handy for Porter. In the early I Loved Him (But He Didn't Love Me), "they sit in crowds on exclusive clouds and laugh at our love affairs."

That was the brittle jazz-baby Porter, known mainly to the small fraction of his total audience that attended his Broadway shows. They heard the famous ballads in a different context, surrounded by comedy songs satirically depicting a heterosexual world in which every woman seems to be a nymphomaniac and every man either a stud or a dud.

Or there were songs in which Porter seemed to be amusing himself and his friends, actual or vicarious, with patter that catalogued the Manhattan party-givers among whom his own life was lived. These songs were as much celebration as lampoon.

He reserved his bile, expressed with acidic restraint, for social unfortunates: for Mrs. Lowsborough-Goodby, too gauche to know how to organize a weekend, or for Mister and Missus Fitch, the nouveaux riches, strongly reminiscent of the Veneerings in Dickens' Our Mutual Friend, who were taken up by society, and then promptly disowned when they lost all in the Crash.

The middle America that took Porter to its heart might have expelled him, had it heard some of these songs.

In fact, for all his privilege, he was doubly an outsider: not just for his gayness, but also because, in his heavily Jewish professional milieu, he was not Jewish. He told Richard Rodgers that he had discovered that the secret of songwriting success was "to write Jewish," by which he meant he would specialize in minor-key laments. (The Slavonic melancholy of I Love Paris prompted Alec Wilder to dub it I Love Russia.) Similarly, his boy-girl love songs were riper and more urgent - sometimes, in their mixture of the taut and the torrid, exaggeratedly so - than anyone else's.

It's tempting to see him as a Joe Orton figure, playing a prolonged joke on the straight world by providing the soundtrack for its mating rituals, starting with his first big hit Let's Do It, Let's Fall in Love, which, when you boil it down, amounts to a chilling catalogue of animal compulsion. ("Moths in your rugs do it"What's the use of moth-balls?") But if it is a joke, it's one that most of us will happily go along with.

Nobody, even in this centenary year, has called Porter a warm man or even a very nice one. Socially gracious, yes, and unquestionably brave: in 1937, a horse threw him and crushed both his legs. His doctors wanted to amputate, his wife and mother forbade it, and the resultant agony was ended only by his death in 1964.

But he rarely complained and went on producing good work, including his most acclaimed score, Kiss Me Kate. His stylistic range was wide and his craftsmanship in words and music almost always impeccable, but there was more to him than that. He had a sensibility, an individual view of the world, that was implicit in every word and note. If the word had not become so suspect where songwriting is concerned, I would call him a poet.

Robert Cushman is the host of Songbook, broadcast every Sunday at 3 p.m. on CBC Radio and 5 p.m. on CBC Stereo.
1991-06-09-a-kick-out-of-cole:
Today is Cole Porter's 100th birthday, and what a swell party this is. Porter knew all about swell parties, and his public image - he really was a legend in his own lifetime - was that he was always either giving or attending one. The legend survives, and so does the work. The celebratory CDs have been coming out, compilations of old performances, and collections of new ones. He has even, on one of the latter, acquired a new identity as a crusader against Aids.

This would have surprised him. Porter was never regarded in his lifetime as socially conscious. Society-conscious, yes: he was born rich, and married richer, to Linda Lee Thomas, a bruised divorcee who was content to provide gracious cover for her husband's voracious homosexuality. Song-writing made him a third fortune. He was not just rich and famous; he was famous for being rich. Though not a native New Yorker - he was a back-country boy from Peru, Indiana - he and his work came to typify smart Manhattan society. Icy-smart he often seemed, and so did his work, at least the verbal part of it. The music, though, could be tropically torrid: making for a highly personal mixture - half refrigerator, half hothouse - that had huge appeal. Porter, as an admiring contemporary remarked, made sophistication popular.

He still does. In fact, the composer-lyricist who in Kiss Me Kate advised us to Brush Up Our Shakespeare ("and they'll all kow-tow") has himself been undergoing a Bardic canonisation. Like Shakespeare, he attracts two types of devotee. There is the purist, represented by last year's EMI recording of "Anything Goes", which might have been sub-titled "Everything Stays". Every word and note of text, score and orchestration was recreated from the 1934 originals.

Then there are the modernists, the proponents of Porter our Contemporary. This has been going on since the Twenties when, after a long apprenticeship devoted largely to amusing himself and his friends in Paris and other backwaters, he arrived on Broadway (and subsequently in London) as the composer of scabrously romantic propositions like "Let's Do It" and lush philosophical inquiries like "What Is this Thing Called Love?"; and was acclaimed as the playboy of the West End world, the spirit of the age. Then came the Crash, and Porter couldn't have cared less. All through the Thirties he wrote successful stage musicals that were purely escapist. The only changes he noticed were of style, not substance:

In olden days a glimpse of stocking
Was looked on as something shocking
But now God knows
Anything goes.

For this he was not merely forgiven but feted, as if he had grasped some fundamental American truth.

In the staid Fifties, his raffishness was forgotten and his yearning love-songs enshrined in the respectable fabric of middle America. Frank Sinatra and Ella Fitzgerald recorded them superbly, for many definitively, but they worked from edited texts. To the vast pop-song public that never went to the theatre, Cole's bawdier comedy numbers were unknown. In 1965, the year after Porter died, an American revue that emphasised his naughtier songs ("Do you use the breast-stroke, dear" / Yes, I use the breast-stroke, dear / But in the morning, No!") claimed him as a liberated and liberating harbinger of the permissive society. That was pretty desperate opportunism; Cole, despite the splendour of his buttonholes, was nobody's flower-child.

This year, the charity record Red Hot and Blue - known as "The Cole Porter Aids Album" - inadvertently proved the point. The performers, all current pop acts, show what 35 years of rock have done to the ability to inflect a lyric. Or, apparently, to understand one. A rap reduction of "I've Got You Under My Skin" tells us repeatedly to "Use your mentality, wake up to reality", that being all that is left of the original lyric, apart from the medically suggestive title. To wake up to reality apparently means to use a condom. Porter would probably endorse that if he were alive. But it's not what his song says. In fact, it's the opposite. The lyric tells us that the singer is beyond using her mentality. The music agrees, even more insistently. So do Porter's other trademark love calls, a variant of the torch song that we might describe as a scorch song. "Night and Day", "Begin the Beguine" are about being too consumed by passion to want to take precautions. For a pop song to convey that amount of emotion without making itself ridiculous is very rare.

"Begin the Beguine" is actually about remembering that kind of passion rather than experiencing it, which is just as well, since its exotic throbbing would be pretty hard to take neat. It has an ironic thread running through it, a thread superbly sustained through an extra-long lyric. This is one of Porter's special strengths. His rivals could throw off brilliant one-liners, but Porter had a unique ability to construct in paragraphs.

He never tells us much about his love-objects. "You're The Top" is wonderful fun, but no beloved is actually like the Louvre Museum. What is really celebrated is the ingenuity, skill and effervescence of the admirer. Even an apparently tender ballad like "Easy to Love" ends up focusing on the gently woebegone suitor who sings it: without asking, however, for more than token sympathy. Others could admit to vulnerability and indulge in self-pity. Porter never stooped to either.

"Let's Do It" (1928) was his first classic and in some ways the archetypal Porter song. It is a biological catalogue whose arch subtitle "Let's Fall in Love" allows it to pass itself off as a ballad, risque, of course, but probably sincere. (It actually replaced a more direct and therefore less acceptable invitation, "Let's Misbehave".) The world accepts it as a celebration; the initiated note its jaunty and slightly chilling reductiveness:

Old sloths who hang down from twigs do it,
Though the effort is great,
Sweet guinea-pigs do it,
Buy a couple and wait.

As assured as he was, Porter was an outsider in his professional life. In the procession of lyricists and composers he was the only patrician, the only Yale man, practically the only Gentile. His competitors were mainly lower-middle-class Jewish boys with their ways to make. He ended up composing more minor-key laments than any of them. He wrote riper, more urgent boy-girl songs - sometimes exaggeratedly so - than the heterosexual lyricists.

The comic counterparts of his famous ballads are the countless speciality numbers, many introduced in the Thirties by Ethel Merman, in which every woman is a nymphomaniac and every man either a stud or a dud. He amused himself and his audiences with patter songs that catalogued the Manhattan party-givers and world-cruisers among whom his life was lived. The songs are as much celebration as satire. Porter reserved his bile, expressed with acidic restraint, for social unfortunates: for Miss Otis who allowed herself to stay down in Lovers Lane and was lynched by a vengeful mob; for Mrs Lowsborough-Goodby, too gauche to know how to organise a weekend.

In the quintessential Porter song, love is "a trip to the moon on gossamer wings" (breathtaking invention so precisely matched to its music that we take it for granted) to be dismissed with delicious panache as "just one of those things". We would all love to say goodbye like that. Unless there's a war on, in which case, Ev'ry Time We Say Goodbye, we would like a tug as romantic as the one depicted in 1944:

Why the gods above me
Who must be in the know
Think so little of me
They allow you to go.

At the famous climax, when the lyric talks of the strange change from major to minor which the music proceeds to enact, we react to the emotion rather than to the cleverness. We smile but we are also moved. The serenely beautiful music gives us little choice. It may be his best song.

His tastiest opening couplet is the one that begins "At Long Last Love":

Is it an earthquake or simply a shock?
Is it the good turtle soup or merely the mock?

Porter claimed to have written that song, in 1937, as he lay trapped beneath a horse which had thrown him and crushed both his legs. It inaugurated 20 years of agony, endured with stoic courage, and marked the beginnings of a slow artistic decline - arrested by the creation of Kiss Me Kate, possibly his masterpiece, certainly his greatest success. Porter would attend it with friends and murmur artlessly, "Good, isn't it?"

'Robert Cushman's Songbook,' exploring the American popular song, starts on Radio 2, Saturday 29 June at 2pm.
