THEATRE REVIEW THE WILL ROGERS FOLLIES The American satirist said his life story would never work as a Ziegfeld spectacular, but this award-winning Broadway musical takes the plunge, synchronized high-kicks and all An act of folly? Will was right, as usual

Friday, July 12, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

New York NY -- WRITTEN BY PETER STONE, BETTY COMDEN, ADOLPH GREEN and CY COLEMAN Directed and choreographed by Tommy Tune Starring Keith Carradine and Dee Hoty At the Palace Theatre, New York BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail New York IENTERED the theatre knowing little about Will Rogers, but well disposed toward him and mildly curious, and I left in much the same state. Rogers was a homespun American satirist who in the early decades of the century told the people the truths they wanted to hear. He wrote newspaper columns and he appeared on the stage, notably as a continuing star of The Ziegfeld Follies, providing interludes of comic sanity while all around him were getting on with the job of Glorifying The American Girl. The Will Rogers Follies, this years Tony Award-winning musical on Broadway, presents Rogers' own life story in the terms of a Ziegfeld spectacular.

There is a problem here, and Will himself, played with all-conquering charm by Keith Carradine, is allowed to state it in the show with his customary candour. He says that he told Ziegfeld his biography would never make a Follies but Ziegfeld wouldn't listen. Will was right, as usual, but the creators of The Will Rogers Follies, having put those words in their heros mouth, have gone ahead and done it anyway.

Tommy Tune, New Yorks reigning director-choreographer, has given the show a lavish staging, one that provides more dancing-girl employment than any New York show has done in years. The dancers cavort with tireless precision up and down a flight of steps worthy of Grand Central Station, but then synchronized high-kicks are the least you expect on Broadway and after a time you yearn to see some dancing on a flat surface.

From all the staging, one moment lingers. The Wall Street Crash brings an especially spendthrift routine to an abrupt close; chorines who a moment before were strutting their stuff in exotic plumage huddle shivering in grey blankets. The Follies has self-destructed before our eyes.

This, obviously, is what it was meant to do all along. Next thing we see, Rogers, at the behest of President Hoover, broadcasting to the nation about his bewilderment at what has happened and the shameful contrasts of riches and poverty that it has revealed. The text is authentic, and the house-lights are brought up (as apparently they were for Rogers' stage routines in his own day) so the exposed audience may ponder the relevance of his words now.

The double focus is integral to the show. It is understood that we are watching a 1991 Follies - an item that the show seems to think is a contradiction in terms but kinda fun anyway. Ziegfeld is long since dead, though he is still likely to boom down instructions from wherever. His prerecorded voice actually belongs to Gregory Peck, suggesting that the Great Glorifier has become a lot more benign since going to glory himself.

Will, though thoroughly and enchantingly present, is also dead. He was killed in a plane crash, a pleasure jaunt over Alaska, and the pilot he went with (a great flier, says Will, "except for that one time") is on hand in a side-box, looking darkly sinister and periodically luring him to his doom in an ominous monotone. (The part is played by Carradine's understudy. Ive heard of motivation but this is ridiculous.) The show begins with a squealing song-and-dance about the joys of aviation, but as we have yet to meet Will or learn anything about him the ironic point is rather muffled. Frankly, it was done with more finesse in Buddy.

This number is followed by another flag-waver called Will-a-mania, which is not an easy word to sing. Who, one wonders, is this Wilhemina? It gets the evening off on the wrong daintily tapping feet, since it is ages before we get to see Carradine, who in every sense is what the show is about. The real Rogers was probably slyer but this one can spin ropes, jokes and homely wisdom with an open-faced gaucherie that conceals enormous professional skill. He can even sing, which is more than his prototype could, or anyway did.

The problem of what he should sing, though, has hardly been addressed, and his numbers melt into the parade. So does his relationship with his loyal and loving wife, played with almost equal appeal by Dee Hoty. Their courtship is rendered as an intentionally bad Follies skit, which is an example of a concept eating itself. It leaves us nothing, either style or substance, to believe in.

And yet the shows total gesture is not meant to be cynical. Unlikely though it seems, the best number is an expansion of Rogers' famous catch- phrase, I Never Met a Man I Didn't Like, a closing chorale stirringly set by Cy Coleman to believably benevolent lyrics by Betty Comden and Adolph Green. (Elsewhere their distinctive talents - his for personalizing traditional forms, theirs for satirizing or celebrating show-biz monsters - are muted.) Finally, it seems, we are meant to take heart in our own troubles, spurred by the example of an Oklahoma boy who made good and did good and whose jokes are still genuinely funny. In which case, debunking the Follies seems a red herring. Tune's staging seems uncertain, whether it is supporting Peter Stone's script or compensating for it, veering between the styles of Gypsy, Barnum and Chicago and finally settling - right down to a scene-stealing dog act - for Sugar Babies. In fact, the ground was burned up 20 years ago by the Hal Prince"Stephen Sondheim Follies, which deconstructed the form before most of us had even heard of deconstruction.

BY LESLIE GOURSE McClelland & Stewart, 309 pages, $29.95

Nat King Cole, the smooth old soul UNFORGETTABLE: The Life and Mystique of Nat King Cole

BY LESLIE GOURSE McClelland & Stewart, 309 pages, $29.95

Saturday, July 13, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Review by ROBERT CUSHMAN LESLIE Gourse starts her biography with an "Overview" that commends Nat Cole's "subtle swing" as a pianist, of which his singing style was initially just an extension. Of his ballad singing she remarks, justly and evocatively, "there was a humming quality to his sound that suggested the murmur of a bee flitting around a rose garden," adding that listeners were "touched by the kindness, tenderness and patience in his voice," while his friends and entourage found the same qualities in him as a man. She alludes to the "frightening racial clash in Alabama" when white racists jumped the stage and pummelled him to the ground. Gourse also points to the crucial influence on his career of his second wife Maria, "an unabashed snob" but "renowned for her shrewdness . . . and for her stylishness and taste." She was his unofficial manager, though his official one, Carlos Gastel, was important too; he "had a magic touch."

All this is fine, but I am not sure that any but diehard fans need to read the rest of the book, except perhaps for the indigestibly informative chapter-headings, the like of which I have never seen. They run from "Nat Begins Family Feuds with the Jazz Critics and His Own Jazz Trio" to "The Coles Adopt a Son, as Nat Searches for a Way to the Broadway Stage," with "A Chops-Breaking Ground-Breaking on Television" thrown in for light relief. I found the book hard going, in the way that Easy Listening can be hard going.

Cole's career certainly has significance even apart from his talent. He was the son of a preacher - from Alabama, ironically enough - who disapproved of the profane music that attracted Nat and his three brothers. Born, probably, in 1916, Cole became a full-time pianist in 1935. He scuffled in Chicago and Los Angeles, eventually formed a successful trio with a piano-bass-guitar format that has haunted cocktail lounges ever since. His singing career famously started when an insistent customer demanded a vocal on Sweet Lorraine. By 1950 he was an institution, and remained so up to and following his death from cancer in 1965.

He still suffered all his life from racial discrimination. The Alabama outrage was only the least subtle expression of it. He had his own TV series, but it was pulled for lack of sponsors. He was a very black black; and at one point - not mentioned in this book - they tried to lighten him up. They reckoned without his slanted eyes; he now looked sinister and, for some weird reason, it made his singing sound mannered.

Cole ran into serious tax problems; they were cleared up, but not before, Gourse says, "he had gone through the tortures of the damned." That is what she says; it is not what she makes us feel. She even fails to move us with her account of his death. She gets more caught up in his funeral, doubtless because it's better documented. She piles on the facts, but however much she tells us, she cannot get us interested in the man, maybe because she herself shows no great interest in the music. She characterizes herself as a jazz fan who has tried to take a "mellow" attitude to her subject's involvement with pop, but mellow, once past the overview, turns out to mean non-committal. Even the song that gives the book its title goes unremarked. So, more importantly, do some of Cole's best records, from his wackily exuberant Orange-Coloured Sky to his silken, definitive Stardust. During the 1950s, Cole's smoothness was a reassuring contrast to Sinatra's edge; in that sense he took over from Bing Crosby, who was ceasing to be a major recording presence at the time when Cole became one.

Sammy Davis, Oscar Peterson, Carmen McRae, Mark Murphy, Johnny Mathis and now daughter Natalie have all recorded tributes to the man and his repertoire. There have been few similar testimonials to Crosby and I doubt that there will ever be many to Sinatra. There is a recognizable, manageable body of Cole songs. Bing's portfolio is almost too vast to encompass, while Sinatra, who has had surprisingly few hit singles, is a National Theatre of song, doing the same numbers as everybody else, only better.

The Cole cult is also partly the result of his having died young; we feel robbed. Author Gene Lees thinks his life may have been shortened by suppressed anger. In The Singers and the Song he tells a story of Cole calling his record company, being greeted by the bright announcement "Capitol Records, home of the Beatles," and slamming the phone down in fury. None of that ever got into his music, which may be the poorer for it. The bosses and the public preferred him bland and so, it sometimes seemed, did he. Gourse, belying her prickly name, goes with the flow.

Robert Cushman writes and hosts Songbook on CBC Radio and Stereo.
1991-07-28-five-go-up-down-and-round-the:
There is real grass on the stage of the Bush, and a real play on top of it. Catherine Johnson's Dead Sheep is about five variously troubled people who set out to climb a Brecon Beacon, represented on Geoff Rose's set by a large boulder that rises and falls with majestic ease according to whether the characters are huddled at its foot or perched on its peak. They do have their ups and downs.

This is hardly surprising. Three of them are ex-addicts. Middle-aged Eve was an alcoholic whose children were taken into care. Zoe and Holly were both junkies. All three are inmates of a rehab centre presided over by Philip, a nannyish religious fanatic who, like many evangelists, identifies God's will with his own. He has brought his flock on this adventure weekend as a treat. Jon, their hired guide, is ex-SAS. A self-made macho man, he could well be more disturbed than any of his charges.

All have their decent moments, but there is too much envy, frustration, resentment simmering inside each of them for the party to go by without disaster. The petty strains of five people in two tents are nearly enough to get the outing cancelled. The play chronicles them in hilarious detail and Mike Bradwell's production revels in it. Bradwell, who founded the Hull Truck company, has over the years perfected a farcical style that goes effortlessly into higher gears, and this play is ideal for him, becoming progressively bleak without ever losing its salty comic texture.

One subject he has always been good on is religion: both its pain and its absurdity. Philip, always ready with a prayer or with a fulsome word of rebuke or encouragement, is seen by the other characters as an embarrassment. Partly this is because he is a dwarf; both his enthusiasms and his malevolence seem out of scale. He embarrasses the audience too, but that doesn't mean that the author dismisses him. By the end he has lost one of his flock (see title) and is ranting uncontrollably, addressing his principal antagonist as Satan, desperately denying facts that he cannot face. But he has at least - strikingly so in Jon Key's performance - the dignity of his own fury.

What does him in is the women. Ex-pop singer Zoe (Kate Hardie) is supposedly his success, having forsaken dope, chosen Jesus and decided to set up as a carer in her own right. Holly (Katrin Cartlidge) is at the other extreme, practically catatonic. In her few lucid moments she sounds like the most intelligent person around and Jon (Gary Love) brings her right out of herself, by what you might call the traditional route: direct but, as it turns out, extremely dangerous. The other girls are both curious and furious, and Gwen Taylor's Eve - the most strikingly fake of a quintet of fine performances - especially takes fire. One moment she is raucously asking Holly how it felt since in her own case it's been so long; the next she is an avenging angel. She exemplifies the most imposing thing about the evening; its seamless mastery of tone. I have not seen Catherine Johnson's previous plays but on this evidence she is a treasurable talent.

Johnson creates stage-size characters, something notably lacking in The Manchurian Candidate. This may be because it is based on a novel, though one best known as a film. Here too the personnel go through all kinds of hoops, and though some have the excuse of having been brainwashed, others do not.

Richard Condon's original fable concerned a US marine sergeant in the Korean War, turned by communist manipulation into a killing machine and used, in a sublime game of double-bluff, as a weapon to advance the cause of McCarthyism. You want to destroy America, was the caustic message, what difference if you do it from the left or from the right? John Lahr's new version advances the story to 1996; the rabble-rousing senator now takes for his theme not the number of commies in the administration but the proportion of America owned by the Japanese. Lahr may be prescient; this could be the theme of US stump politics in elections to come. But the new wrinkle does not provide the frisson of the Cold War original which lampooned a very recognisable demagogue.

Lahr is an adept adaptor, with some nifty lines and a competent way of unfolding a complicated story. The production only shudders to an embarrassing halt when the cast sing a xenophobic anthem obviously intended to chill our blood and discourage anyone who might be considering voting Republican. But the more techniques the show uses, the harder work it all seems; and the occasional use of video only reminds us of how much more we would like to see in close-up. These people need to be brought close for us to believe in them or to be gripped by the story they serve. Gerard Murphy, even from the middle distance, has the right sickly grin for the homicidal hero; Sian Phillips is the monster's suitably monstrous mother; and Manning Redwood is a boyish senator to the podium born. Clive Carter, as the officer who drags the truth to light, looks craggily and appropriately like a junior George C Scott; and Connie Booth lends him a sympathetic ear, which is all that is asked of her. A fella needs a girl if he's in a novel or movie, but in a play, with time at a premium, he should be able to do without.

Tovarich is a 1930s success by Jacques Deval disturbed from its long slumber to provide a vehicle for Natalia Makarova. When it wakes up, which takes time, it allows her to exude a ravishing hauteur while twirling about in a maid's uniform and to fill the theatre with romantic longings for a White Russian past. She and her Grand Duke husband (Robert Powell) are forced into domestic service with the bourgeoisie through poverty and loyalty, and some of their encounters with their dazzling Parisien employers are very funny. The evening then starts leaning on sentiment and charm, but the two stars supply both.

Alan Ayckbourn's Scarborough Theatre has moved into its restaurant to accommodate the American Tom Dulack's Breaking Legs, which is set in one: a New England Italian establishment whose proprietor (Jeffrey Chiswick, all olive oil and unction) ropes in two business associates (Glyn Grain, a master of slow-burning comic menace, and Robert Austin, a credible hulk) as backers for a play written by a nervous but increasingly confident academic (Peter Bourke, priceless) who happens to be loved by his daughter (Susan Denaker, making energetically like Angelica Houston). Ayckbourn wonderfully orchestrates a stagefull of flawless cartoon performances. The production outshines the play which is a collection of mild gangster and showbiz jokes, though one speech does begin "I can only speak for myself but I know I speak for all of us." Now that's eloquence.
1991-08-04-lady-of-the-deep-gets-stuck-i:
Lady of the deep gets stuck in the shallows

THEATRE
ROBERT CUSHMAN

LET no one say that Ibsen's later plays are invariably dark and obscure. The Lady from the Sea has a happy ending that can be seen coming a nautical mile off. A minute into the show a painter, working on a picture of a mermaid, says that "the lady who lives here inspired me to paint it". Enter Ellida, the lady of the painting and of the title. She has been for a dip ("she swims every morning, whatever the weather") and surfaces in this production cropped and shiny in a green towel. She looks healthy but asked if she feels refreshed she replies: "I don't; I never do."

She is pining for the open sea beside which she grew up and which she associates with a sailor to whom she once plighted her troth and who then disappeared on suspicion of murder. Now he arrives to reclaim her from her husband, an amiable if incurably land-locked doctor who would be many women's ideal son-in-law. A dab hand at a diagnosis he picks up immediately on his wife's complaint that if she stays with him it will be "not of my own free will". He gives her her freedom - you half-expect him to write a prescription for it - and she exercises it by electing to stay with him. That is what the play has promised to show, that is what it does show, and there is not a note of irony to be heard.

Heidi Thomas's adaptation, from which I have been quoting, is brisk and generally colloquial and it enables director Jules Wright to deliver the play in what may be record time. There are no significant pauses, and few insignificant ones. The principal emotion transmitted is a terror of being thought pretentious.

In the last major British production, Vanessa Redgrave gave a visual and verbal resonance to Ellida's marine compulsion that transcended polemics. The one before that, also with Redgrave though in a different role, found its texture in the life of the household, this being one of the few Ibsen plays to have one. Ellida attracts men as ineluctably as a Chekhov chatelaine, and they sublimate their feelings by hovering around her two stepdaughters. The elder of these is courted by her ex-tutor who wants to take her away and show her the world, which is fine with her, but also wants to marry her, which isn't. She looks like repeating her stepmother's mistake with a far less sympathetic partner. Or maybe they'll be all right.

But in either case we have here two people at a crisis of their lives, and it passes belief that they would get through it at an even pace, in unvarying profile, without once taking a moment to sit and think. But that is how this production goes. People face one another and deliver their lines, as conversationally as possible. When passion seems unavoidable they stomp about a bit and switch to a tone of petulant self-pity.

Kathryn Pogson as Ellida has a still, troubled presence that persuades you something is going on beneath, but it never breaks surface. "I can't see him any more" - referring, at the height of her disarray, to the husband she cares for - is not a line that can plausibly be muttered. And with the central performance so battened-down, the others sink automatically lower; for a man in imminent danger of losing the wife he loves Hugh Fraser's doctor is amazingly unruffled. Alister Cameron as the local jack-of-all-trades is nice, but his is the smallest role. We learn that mature Ibsen played purely at dialogue level seems impossibly glib.

After The Lady from the Sea, The Boys from Syracuse. (Next week The Girl from Nantucket, The Man from U.N.C.L.E., and The Creature from the Black Lagoon.) This is the 1938 Broadway musical based, with considerable resource and fidelity, on The Comedy of Errors. The opening number, "I Had Twins", handles the cumbrous exposition a lot more adroitly than did Shakespeare. Otherwise Lorenz Hart's lyrical wit shines less in the obvious comedy songs than in the bitter-sweet spin he puts on the love ballads. In fact the best-known lines are the best: "falling in love with love is falling for make believe", "this can't be love because I feel so well" - the latter sung by the visiting Antipholus to (I think I've got this right) his brother's sister-in-law. Meanwhile the prodigal grace of Richard Rodgers' music extends to what, for any other composer, would be throw-away numbers; mark the tripping verse to "What Can You Do with a Man?"

Grace is what George Abbott's book rather lacks, but it keeps the jokes coming, and some of them are funny, and Judi Dench's good-natured production enjoys them all. It reaffirms that, barring the occasional Anything Goes, musicals of this vintage are more fun when done on a modest scale, and it plays wittily with its own pastoral setting.

The action revolves around a parkland bandstand, and James Merrifield's bold, gorgeous costumes make the ladies look like animated bell-tents. Accents are emphatically American, with Jenny Galloway's frustrated wench a Brooklynese triumph. Louise Gold, one of our best soubrettes, makes a valiant prima donna. Gillian Bevan sings beautifully. Musical direction is excellent.

As long as wars leave human debris Euripides' Women of Troy will be the world's most topical play: so pertinent as almost to defy revival. The women awaiting deportation and enslavement are eternal. The murder of the boy-child Astyanax, slaughtered for policy, is the greatest atrocity in world drama, a breach in nature. Millennia later, Edward Bond in The Woman presented it as the way of the world. By so much have we fallen.

The temptation to cheapen the play with facile parallels must be enormous, but Katie Mitchell's production never succumbs. Nothing is vague; every line means something, either as fierce lament or - where the gods or Helen are involved - bitter comedy. The style, which involves a lot of perfectly controlled chanting and dancing by a large ensemble, is extraordinarily strong.

I didn't like all the choices (Kathryn Hunter's crazy Cassandra, a Jewish-American rather than a Greek princess, I found especially hard to take) but the point is that they are choices, intelligently made and uncompromisingly carried through. Paola Dionisotti's flinty Hecuba is too young to suggest the mother of them all, Barbara Flynn's bereaved Andromache almost too selflessly stoical to be moving, but they are fine performances and great figureheads.

The Lady from the Sea, Riverside Studios (081-748 3354); The Boys from Syracuse, Open Air, Regent's Park (071-486-2431); Women of Troy, Gate (071-229 0706).

Irving Wardle is on holiday.
1991-09-29-sir-john-replays-his-greatest:
Sir John replays his greatest hits

SHAKESPEARE: HIT OR MISS?
by John Gielgud with John Miller
Sidgwick £17.50

JOHN GIELGUD and Shakespeare have not kept company much in recent years. Although a compulsive theatre-goer since the late 1950s, I have seen Gielgud in only three Shakespeare roles. Two of them, Wolsey and Julius Caesar, he was essaying for the first time and neither ranks among his greatest hits. The third was Prospero, which he had already played twice and which I saw him do twice more. He also had behind him multiple assaults on Lear and Hamlet, and was reckoned supreme in both parts - as he was in Richard II, Angelo, Benedick, Cassius and Leontes.

All of which suggests that Shakespeare is a young man's game. (Or, increasingly these days, a young woman's game: we breed far more Rosalinds than Hamlets.) Sir John, in this book of reminiscence, seems inclined to agree, constantly protesting how out of touch he must seem, how long ago his triumphs were, and how seldom he goes to the theatre.

Actually this most effortlessly modern of actors seems to have kept up with all the best things, from Peter Brook's Dream to Richard Briers's Malvolio, and he is discerningly enthusiastic about them. Even at his most apparently reactionary he talks sense, as when he doubts that young audiences are much beguiled by seeing the plays done out of period.

This is a light, anecdotal book, pleasing because you can hear the Gielgud voice in it but frustrating because he says so little about the characters he has played. He checks them all off, unchronologically, but almost the only specific comment he makes is that Richard II "has no humour". This is startling, given the actor's own comic genius, but it does reveal what the subsequent line of waspishly witty Richards have been reacting against. His editor/collaborator should have pressured him for more.

Far more instructive, and almost justifying the graceless title, is his constant emphasis on the theatre's fallibility: on the things that work one night and not another, and on the actor's quixotic insecurities ("I was afraid," he says of an early success, "of becoming a bit too pleased with myself"). He combines specific modesty with an overriding assurance of his own place in history. "Audiences," he says "often credit you with far more intelligence than you actually possess."

Critics, I am sure, will often take a hint from a performance and proceed to father on the actor their own fantasies about the play; several set-pieces of criticism are reproduced here. There are also some invaluable notes on Lear from Granville-Barker, who once directed Gielgud in the role, and whom he reveres as he does Brook. This book could use a director.
1992-01-16-the-fever:
THEATRE REVIEW THE FEVER

Thursday, January 16, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY WALLACE SHAWN Directed by Andy McKim Starring Clare Coulter At Tarragon Extra Space Rating: The Fever's naivete is its strength BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto WALLACE Shawn, who wrote The Fever, says that he "loves" Clare Coulter, who is performing it; says even that he had her in mind when he wrote it. I admire her myself, and I certainly applauded her tension and variety in this monologue. It lasted nearly two hours and seemed much less.

All the same, I kept seeing past her and what I saw was the author himself. Shawn is a droll button of a man, a solemn twinkler, familiar on the edges of Woody Allen movies and as author and co-star of the play and film My Dinner with Andre, in which he played himself. This, plus the fact that I know him slightly, is my excuse for getting personal. With most plays it would not matter, but The Fever, which Shawn himself has performed in London and New York, is as confessional as anything gets.

It is a guilt trip: the result of several more literal trips that Shawn has taken to various parts of Latin America. There he discovered repression, torture, murder. He had always known they existed, of course, and had deplored them. But this was the first time he had seen the scars, met survivors, talked to witnesses. As a U.S. citizen, he had to accept that his own government had kept the oppressors in power. But The Fever doesn't dwell much on this, and it impales citizens of all other Western democracies just as firmly on its hook. Insofar as the two can be separated, it is less concerned with politics than with economics. It charges, to split a few more hairs, not that things are evil but that they are unfair.

The speaker summons a moment at which he lay vomiting in a foreign hotel bathroom, consumed by the knowledge that at the same moment, in the same city, a man was being executed. From there, he spirals back to his own daily life, to the friends and the shows and the restaurants, to the parents who loved and schooled and pampered him. Themes dissolve and recur, there are whorls within whorls, but writing and performance are firmly controlled and we generally know where we are.

The script is devoid of place or gender so Coulter can play it without changing a word. But its details fit perfectly into everything I know or surmise about Shawn's life as a reasonably successful playwright and actor in New York. When the script spoke regretfully of its subject's liberal upbringing, I thought of Shawn senior, for years the gentle editor of The New Yorker, that bastion of stylish decency.

The play is about stylish decency not being enough: actually about its being irrelevant. It pushes toward the realization that "the life I lead is irredeemably corrupt . . . (nothing) justifies what the beggar has and what I have."

Right, for all of us. So what is he going to do about it? He raises a couple of options. He could give all he has to the poor, or he could become an active revolutionary. He has not, as far as I know, done either of those things, and I cannot say I want him to. It's not just that I have rational doubts about the efficacy of either course. I don't want to be shown up.

He has, of course, done one thing. He has written this play. But this is just compounding the problem. (He says: "Artists who create works of art that inspire sympathy and good values do not change the life of the poor.") However, I don't think there is anything shameful about that. Unless, and it's a plausible position, concerned drama is more shameful than escapist drama because it pretends to help, and doesn't. But if political theatre is valid, then this is a refreshingly honest example of it: one that accepts guilt rather than shrilly apportioning it.

The Fever lacks the nightmarish brilliance that its mode and its title seem to demand. It spells everything out. It talks flatly of "the poor" instead of using euphemisms like "the workers." It laboriously discovers things that, at some level, we have always known. But its naivete is its strength. The author wryly admits to discovering Marxism just when everybody else had discarded it. But if the Marxist answers are discredited, the questions still remain. And this time, I like the guy who's asking them.
1992-01-18-knights-of-the-endless-day:
THEATRE REVIEW KNIGHTS OF THE ENDLESS DAY

Saturday, January 18, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY ROBERT PRIEST Directed by Jennifer Stein Starring Cliff Saunders At Young People's Theatre Rating: YPT's enlightened tale is a knightly quest for a plot High dudgeon and dragons BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto GOOD intentions are running amok at YPT where they ride out to slay the unenlightened dragons of medievalism under the sacred banners of childcare, health food, environmental concern and a classless society.

There actually are dragons on view in Knights of the Endless Day -a big one and its brood - and very impressive they look, curled and many-faceted and taking up every available space on the multi-crannied stage. It turns out, though, that they are more afraid of that predator Man than he is of them so the threat turns out to be a swindle.

And so it goes. All of it.

The five-year-old next to me was still asking at the end what the title meant, and I found it hard to enlighten him. Casting my mind back, I could recall an early scene in which a bright yellow disc hung a few feet above the stage and people sang about it. The music was fidgety and the words indistinct, but the general impression was that this was a sun that never set. The matter is never alluded to again. But we do learn that author Robert Priest is not the man to let mere theatricality stand between him and an easy pun.

All the early scenes (and songs) are choppily unhelpful, but eventually a situation emerges. There is a king who proclaims his intention to dub three new knights, humble birth no object. From an impenetrably staged series of tests three candidates emerge - two toffs and a commoner called Ogo - and, as in all folklore, the lowliest comes out on top. Untraditionally, he faces judgment in the middle of the sequence rather than at the end of it. Imagine Cinderella trying on the slipper with one Ugly Sister still to go, or the leaden casket opened before the silver one.

All three are allotted Quests, which occupy the second act and are non- events. The most uppity adventurer endures a humorous humiliation which might be fun to watch if it didn't happen entirely off stage. The second, who thought he was facing monsters, has a pain-free journey in search of garlic. Our hero, who must transport the royal infant across the kingdom to his mother, gets the giants and dragons, only it turns out they aren't really dangerous. Ogo doesn't draw his sword because that might endanger the baby, and, besides, his mother has counselled him in non-violence. Of course, the giant survives to eat more people, but nobody said pacifism was easy.

Not even this play says it. Ogo has an inner battle to fight, against his own warlike instincts. But he wins it every time in two seconds flat, so it's not much of a conflict. The YPT production is most charitably described as inconclusive, though the baby noises are stylishly done and Cliff Saunders' Ogo is the triumph of likeability over winsomeness. His carol on changing diapers has a perky tune but gives away its joke in the first stanza, and the rest of the score is mired in the innocuous banalities of folk-rock. The finale may be the most perfunctory on record. "Happy earthday - it's your birthday." The royal babe is one year old. Kids - of any age - deserve better. Knights of the Endless Day continues at Young People's Theatre until Feb. 9.
1992-03-06-theatre-review-field:
THEATRE REVIEW FIELD

Friday, March 06, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- CREATED AND PRESENTED BY POW POW UNBOUND Directed by Darren O'Donnell At Buddies in Bad Times Theatre Rating: Dexterity of speech is not what you expect from this kind of spectacle, but the words here, such as they are, are delivered with stinging expertise A fighting-fit mix of vocal and physical skills BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto FIELD is an extremely efficient production that begins by having its seven actors chant, each in turn, "welcome to the show - the show Field" after which they take their bows. Having thus provided us with an unassailable beginning and end, they proceed to the middle which is a lot less easy to describe.

The troupe - that seems the right word to do justice to their fighting- fit combination of vocal and physical skills - springs about in red track suits, all but one menacing woman who is in black and resides mainly in a large box of the same colour which is usually centre-stage but can be moved. From here she spits out the story of Kathy, who moved from one part of Canada to another, and was exploited by men every step of the way.

Not too much is made of this; it seems, the show implies, to be just what you'd expect. And Kathy's story is only intermittently part of the proceedings which are otherwise rather abstract. Or to put it another way, I didn't understand them. Which isn't to say that they don't evoke a kinetic response. Early on, an elaborate syncopated counterpoint is created of screams, grunts, and the hypnotic movement of an actor on a swing. It is prolonged to a head-splitting point, but anger is defused by admiration. There is inventiveness here, and there is also precision. Dexterity of speech is not what you expect from this kind of spectacle, but the words here, such as they are, are delivered with stinging expertise. The performance level is the highest I have encountered on the Toronto stage in some time.

You would be safe in assuming that it is all about sex. A recipe for nipple cupcakes (in which the ingredient "homo milk" is afforded gleeful reptilian emphasis) is nipped in the bud, so to speak, when one performer claims to have lost her nipples, which is even worse than it sounds because she cannot experience orgasm without them. Another actor then mimes, hilariously, to a 1950s-sounding novelty record about how to look for something you have mislaid. I don't think they ever turn up, but I may have missed something.

There is also a grisly sequence - meant, presumably, to conjure up memories of childhood intimidation - in which masturbation is satirically discouraged because it can call up monsters. (The word used to be "monsterbation.") There are horrific nursery rhymes, some passing theatrical satire in which a tyrannical director is used as a metaphor for cruelty in general, and a lot of screaming putdowns, some of them funny. Some actors have roses protruding from their crotches; toward the close they remove them and strew them elegiacally on top of the now-deserted black box. The mood is enhanced when somebody runs back and forth across the stage spinning wires across it as he goes. It's magic.

The show projects a mood of embattled disdain. It is not my preferred way to spend an evening, but they do it awfully well. Field continues at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, 142 George St., 863-9455, through March 16.
1992-03-20-theatre-review-brother-andre-:
THEATRE REVIEW BROTHER ANDRE'S HEART

Friday, March 20, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY LINDA GRIFFITHS Directed by Jim Millan with Linda Griffiths Starring Arsinee Khanjian At the Poor Alex Rating: 0 Linda Griffith's new play suggests a riotous black comedy but . . . Brother Andres Heart flatlines BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto THERE are many ways of hiding from life, and being a compulsive watcher of Star Trek is one of them. That is the uncontroversial premise of Linda Griffithss new play, which introduces us to a couple of guys in Montreal who once had film-making ambitions but have given up on them, and on just about everything else. Scared by the state of the city, the country and the world, they rarely leave their apartment, and live only for their daily dose of sci-fi. You've heard of being spaced out. These boys are spaced in.

A lady friend, marginally more together than they are though much oppressed by memories of a Catholic girlhood, talks them into accompanying her to a local Oratory, where reside the remains of Brother Andre, a Jesuit and a possible candidate for sainthood. Her idea is that such a demonstration of piety will comfort her grandmother, who is old and near death. They go more than once, but these errands of mercy always take longer than they expect and when they return home the best they get from their TV set is a merciless rolling of the final credits. (What they really need of course is a VCR but obviously they can't afford it. Besides if they had one there would be no play, though that might not be such a great loss).

Driven to desperation they make off with the oratorys prize exhibit, Brother Andres formaldehyde-soaked heart. They spend the second half of the play wondering what to do with it and scared of being caught. The situation suggests riotous black comedy on the order of Joe Orton's Loot (which has a faintly similar set-up) but not much is made of it. Not much is made of anything. No mileage is extracted from the characters being failed filmmakers rather than failed anything elses, though their Trekkie fixation is exploited. It allows them to keep addressing one another as "Captain and Number One" and this keeps the script going for pages.

Grandma herself turns up, much healthier than we are led to expect. In fact she is crammed fit-to-bust with the life force. She talks to the others about her own past and their futures and turns them into better people. The meaning may be that we must work our own miracles, or that a holy relic is what you make it. At one point the audience is invited to get up on stage and inspect the heart for themselves. This is even more embarrassing than most audience participation, since it represents a total break in convention.

To give the author her due, she has handed one of the actors, Andrew Miller, a couple of off-handedly funny lines which he delivers very well. The rest of the time he is just fey, while his partner, Shawn Williams, is a hole on the stage. Debra Kirshenbaum has energy, more than the play can use. Arsinee Khanjian, as granny, has some stage presence but not enough. To get her inner youthfulness to really impress us, she would first have to seem convincingly old. Her arrival is meant to be the play's big surprise and it's certainly a jolt. There she is in the doorway, and as we catch our breath the lights go down for the intermission. But on the first night Jim Millan's production, by botching the blackout, gave us a large anti-climax.
1992-03-21-theatre-review-to-grandmother:
THEATRE REVIEW TO GRANDMOTHER'S HOUSE WE GO

Saturday, March 21, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY JOANNA M. GLASS Directed by John Wood Starring Rita Howell, Marion Gilsenan and Joyce Campion At the Bluma Appel Theatre Rating: This old-style family play, and a very accomplished one, contains just one surprise, whose detonation is superbly timed Grandma, what big ideas you have BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto ON Wednesday we had Brother Andre's Heart, in which a grandmother pays a call on the young folks. On Thursday it was Joanna Glasss play, which gives us, as promised in the title, the same situation in reverse. Who says the Toronto theatre lacks variety?

The grand-matriarch of the Glass menagerie is an 81-year-old New Englander. Her house is large, handsome, and a brute to manage. She lives in it with a slightly younger brother who is a whimsical ex-academic, a widowed daughter who paints, and a supernally devoted Irish servant, everybodys nanny. The daughter's own children, one male and two female, are now in their 30s. Each has had a failed marriage, and each is limping through the resultant wreckage. The family home is their haven, often deserted, always taken for granted. When we meet them they have returned in force for Thanksgiving. All have plans to stay longer, and to fill the house with their own children. Grandie, as they call her, quails at the sacrifices that are still expected of her. But, in good patrician fashion, she grits her teeth and agrees to accommodate yet another generation.

Grandie is no saintly pushover. She is an impoverished chatelaine, caustically outspoken about modern manners, and none too forbearing with her contemporaries. Her polar opposite in the play is her grandson's new girlfriend, vigorously up-to-date about everything from finance to food. (Her habit of chewing her bread without first breaking it drives Grandie to distraction.) The play extracts comedy from the prejudices of both age groups. In general, though, we laugh with the old woman and at the young one. Glass, who apparently married into just such a family herself, writes as an outsider but as one who has been taken over.

This is as much a matter of technique as of substance. This is an old- style family play, and a very accomplished one. Its narrative contains just one surprise, whose detonation is superbly timed. The presentation matches the text. Patrick Clarks set, which lays out the all-important battleground, is enough to make you purr with pleasure: so detailed and so beautifully proportioned in its clutter, an infinitely desirable residence, fraying at the edges. John Munros lighting is exquisite, especially when streaming through the windows of a morning. John Wood's direction balances the scenic and human elements with immaculate skill.

The play neither sentimentalizes nor caricatures. There are no epiphanies or sudden reconciliations. The juniors may be more blinkered and objectionable in their selfishness, but they have no monopoly on it. Even the faithful domestic turns out to have her own agenda, while to the widowed daughter, whose efforts at the easel are either patronized or ignored, goes the best speech in the play, one in which she flatly and finally refuses to adapt herself to anyone else's convenience. This is a worm-turning moment to inspire any actress; and Marion Gilsenan, an admirably amorphous mass in her earlier scenes, chisels herself into dignity and independence before our eyes. You can feel the audience reflecting with mingled guilt and admiration on how it has treated its own mother.

She deserved her exit applause. All the same, I wished that the scene had not been so obviously structured for her to achieve it, just as I resented the similar response exacted by Grandies anticipation of the behaviour of her great-grandchildren, who will fill her house with videos "full of extra-terrestrials who explode at the end. That speech, too, explodes at the end, and people do not talk like that: not even, I would hazard, in Connecticut. I have no quarrel with Rita Howells performance of the old lady, but does the character have to make such an emphatic claim on adjectives like feisty" and "indomitable"? And does the nanny have to be Irish? And do the grandchildren have to fall into high-pitched speech rhythms that have less to do with life than with the actors' recollection of similar performances in other plays? The well-made drama, of which this is a rare late example, always seems to demand belief and almost always frustrates it. Similarly with the well-made comedy; I recognized that I was in a climate of wit, but I laughed only once because only one comic moment caught me off guard. We are dealing with an articicial genre that never acknowledges its own artificiality. But it has its pleasures, and this time they are worth collecting. To Grandmother's House We Go continues at the Bluma Appel Theatre, 27 Front St. E., until April 11.
1992-03-27-theatre-review-let-us-talk-ca:
THEATRE REVIEW LET US TALK CARIBBEAN

Friday, March 27, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

WRITTEN AND PERFORMED BY MARVIN L. ISHMAEL Directed by Damir Andrei At Canadian Stage, Berkeley Street Rating: Storyteller Marvin Ishmael tries to keep his audience hopping with too many vignettes; compasses keep needing resetting with nothing much to steer by Caribbean journey, a strain BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto MARVIN Ishmael stands before us, casual and collected in a floral shirt that might give even Joseph some amazing technicolor nightmares. As well as standing before us, he runs around quite a bit. The movement amounts, according to the program, to a Caribbean storytelling journey, but I would settle for describing it as a series of vignettes. Or just as a good old-fashioned one-man show.

During a warm-up thoughtfully designed to sensitize us to his speech rhythms, he tells us that he is addressing us in mid-Caribbean. Midway, that is, between Trinidad and Jamaica: a dialect that must be spoken mainly by fish. Ishmael himself is Trinidadian, and has no need to worry about being understood. He has invented an alter ego called Trini who is accident-prone but a survivor. "Trini wanted to be single - independent - have his own apartment." In pursuit of this ambition, he goes to Canada, under strict instructions from his relatives to tell Harry Belafonte to stop singing Yellow Bird. (A forlorn hope, of course, but one thanks them for the thought.) Trini's mistakes and misadventures when faced with his first airline seat belt or his first North American breakfast are not record-breakingly droll, but Ishmael, by serving his hero up in alternating layers of wide- eyed innocence and smouldering indignation, keeps them appealing. Every so often, too, he whips up a really big laugh. I would have been happy to stay with Trini for the duration (about 90 minutes) but Ishmael keeps changing tack, spiriting us back to Trinidad for a ghost story, or sashaying into Jamaica to be ambushed by indigent Rastas. An appeal to their sense of brotherhood gets a stony response, something along the lines of "Okay, man, your money is mine and my poverty is yours."

Keeping your scene and your audience hopping is, on the face of it, a reasonable way of warding off the monotony that always threatens a solo performance. In fact, though, it imposes a strain; we have to keep resetting our compasses with nothing much to steer by. The subject changes but the mood remains the same, since Ishmael is no quick-change virtuoso, physically or psychologically. In this sense, perhaps, his billing is accurate and he is a storyteller rather than an actor, in which case it would be more pleasant to stay immersed in one story. When we do return to Trini for a final Christmas story, he has turned all mawkish and Miracle on 34th Street. The total is sometimes charming, ocassionally very funny, and a bit monotonous. Let Us Talk Caribbean continues until April 12.
1992-03-31-theatre-reviews-macbeth:
THEATRE REVIEWS MACBETH

Tuesday, March 31, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- BY WILLIAM SHAKESPEARE Directed by Robert Lepage At Hart House Theatre MACBETH BY WILLIAM SHAKESPEARE Directed by Alex Fallis Starring David Schurmann and Kate Lynch At Equity Showcase Theatre Rating: The traditional amateur virtues - intelligence and vigour - are neutralized in a production of Macbeth by Robert Lepage Double, double, toil and trouble BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto ROBERT Lepage's production of Macbeth, recently performed by the Graduate Centre for the Study of Drama at the University of Toronto, begins tremendously with the three witches hanging upside-down; talk about the suspension of disbelief. Then Macbeth and Banquo appear, riding. They are not actually on horseback, but they are performing a detailed and energetic equestrian mime, which they accompany with much syncopated stomping of feet. They are joined by a couple of message-bearing thanes who are executing the same routine. In the received text this is the play's third scene; the first two have been cut.

So might this one be, for all the information we get from it. The Weird Sisters, immune to vertigo, have no trouble communicating the sense and the feeling of their lines, which, being venomous doggerel, are not that challenging. The mortals are handed complex blank verse, not easy for student actors to get across and downright impossible if their voices and their bodies are beating out rhythms that are at cross-purposes with one another. A dozen dramatic signals go unregistered, all sacrificed to one gratuitous effect. The important things that happen to Macbeth and company in this scene could equally well happen to them on foot. And they look pretty silly doing it.

One thing that sets Lepage apart from most conceptual or gestural or performance-oriented or anti-textual directors (choose your label; none of them quite fits) is his obvious trust and belief in actors. However graphic his effects, the people in his shows have carried the weight. But here he has either lost faith in his cast or, more likely, he has overestimated them. Either way, he has staged a puppet show.

It even looks like one. The stage can expand or contract, vertically. Sometimes it has its full height; at others it's a letterbox. Since there are definite Japanese traces in staging, costume and hair styles, the actors often resemble Bunraku marionettes; you expect to see human manipulators alongside them. At crucial moments in Macbeth's descent you do see the witches silently crouching beneath the main action as if controlling it. When it isn't a puppet-play it's a shadow-play. Giant silhouettes are cast on the back wall with majestic spookiness. They are impressive, but so they would be in any context. Devices like this can help intensify the terror in Macbeth but they cannot generate it. That can be done only by the players.

They actually look weaker here than they might in a less overpowering presentation. The traditional amateur virtues - intelligence and vigour - are neutralized. And the production's principal device fails to register except as an irritant. The men are played by women and the women by men. This may be a commendable blow for Equal Opportunity, but an audience can hardly be expected to get off on that. Since nobody is acting with much conviction anyway it hardly matters which gender they are.

Lady Macbeth (Patrick Garrow) dutifully switches on some extra voltage for the "unsex me here" speech but switches it off immediately after. When Macbeth (Anna Migliarisi) comes home, the two of them go into an elaborate clinch. But conventionally cast couples can do that too. (And do; every production of Macbeth thinks that it's the first to discover sex.) The splitting of the bond between them is more powerful than its sealing; Lady M's slumped acceptance of her husband's independent criminal career after the banquet leads logically to her somnambulistic breakdown. The minor character of Lennox became, in one ironic monologue, the most fully realized person on stage. Whether the portrayal of Duncan as an especially vexing English nanny was accident or design I cannot say; it certainly made a new and persuasive case for regicide.

There is cross-casting, too, in the Equity Showcase Macbeth, but it is less pervasive. Three male roles - Duncan, Banquo, Old Siward - are played by actresses; and only at the end had I worked out the rationale for this. These are all fathers whose children are either killed or threatened by Macbeth and they presumably seem more bereaved if they in effect double as mothers. Macduff loses his children too, of course, but as the text provides him with a wife he is allowed to keep his manhood. He is played by a Polish actor; I don't know whether we are meant to register this as more non-traditional casting, or simply to accept the actor (Vieslav A. Krystyan) on his own considerable merits. His collapse at the news of his family's massacre is done with uncompromising power.

So is the massacre itself; so is the attempted killing of Banquo's son Fleance. The production presents the Macbeths' career as a revenge of the childless on the fertile. It is so stated in the program, and it is intermittently noticeable on the stage. Macbeth, having dispatched Young Siward in the final scene, gives his dismissive epitaph - "thou wast born of woman" - a peculiarly malignant sting; though, just to make sure we get the point, the victim, who is fighting in a full-scale professional battle, is played as a 10-year-old. Which is not believable.

"Macbeth," says the program, "does not murder people; he attacks families." So, if you think about it, does any murderer who does not restrict himself to killing childless orphans. Resentment at his lack of an heir helps to corrode Macbeth, but it is not what first motivates him. He makes no attempt to kill Duncan's sons along with the father, though doubtless he would get round to them in time. Like many partial interpretations, this one is more impressive as a disembodied bright idea than as part of a story told by actors.

The old chestnut "how many children had Lady Macbeth?" - once a sure laugh-getter in academic circles - has come round again with renewed seriousness. When the lady talks about having given suck, a Macbeth brooding on his childlessness should surely take some interest; this one just stands there, arms akimbo. Indeed, the actor, David Schurmann, is singularly impassive in the earlier part, strolling through temptation, murder and kingship with scarcely a flicker. Only when his world begins to crumble and viciousness sets in does he come to snarling, desperate life. He reverses his wife's diagnosis; he is quite without ambition but a wiz at the illness that attends it. His partner, Kate Lynch, lights a fire under him regardless, and her desolate cry in the sleepwalking scene sounds, as it should, like a soul at the end of its tether.

Alex Fallis's staging has at least one brilliant moment - the sudden dissolution of the witches to a heap of rags on the ground - and the general acting level is alert and alive. With all its eccentricities, this showcase has something to show. The Equity Showcase production of Macbeth continues until Saturday.
1992-04-09-theatre-review-the-cost-of-li:
THEATRE REVIEW THE COST OF LIVING

Thursday, April 09, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY MORRIS PANYCH Starring Tim Battle At Young People's Theatre Rating: AIDS message is in the medium Morris Panych's, The Cost of Living is a brilliant and cleverly disguised lecture on AIDS using banks of video monitors to reach its teen audience BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto THE Cost of Living is a brilliant play about growing up - brilliant in both writing and performance - disguised as a lecture on AIDS awareness. Or maybe it's the other way round.

Produced by Vancouver's Green Thumb Theatre, Morris Panych's wittily- written script plays with its audience's dread of the moment when the message will be delivered. The piece is a monologue: an multi-media presentation by a teen-ager identified solely as Our Guy (played by Tim Battle) who is telling his classmates about himself and the assistant librarian he is in love with. She has promised him a birthday treat, which he assumes means she will go to bed with him. In fact she takes him to see an ex-lover of hers, now hospitalized with AIDS. Depressed and embarrassed he expects an awful warning. He gets one. It's something to do with the inadvisability of the shirt and tie he is wearing.

Great comic release though it is, this doesn't quite let Our Guy off the hook. A message is duly forthcoming, about placing a value on life, your own and everybody else's. If this is a let-down, it is because it seems terribly vague. What - in concrete terms and especially with reference to Angel (that's his girl-friend's name) - is Our Guy going to do about it?

One asks, because up to that point the play has been exhilaratingly specific. For a start it conquered my prejudice against using video in the theatre. (It's like sex and violence; we can get all that at home.) Here it's an economic way of bringing in other characters, notably the hero's parents whose attitudes to his sexuality vary between embarrassing tolerance and embarrassing embarrassment.

Adolescence was always a minefield. It's now more booby-trapped than ever before. Battle's performance, wonderfully fluent and engaging, a Catcher in the Rye for the 1990s, builds a bridge between the problems of now and the problems of always. For those of us who grew up in the 60s the return of the condom, with multiplied trauma, is one of life's more sourly ironic jokes. Not that the play is meant for us, but it's a tribute to the play that it can take us in along with its target audience: who, when I saw it, seemed enthralled.

This is the first AIDS play I have seen that has not degenerated into hospital-ward drama; and the first that has not presented it as an exclusively gay issue. It is also legitimately entertaining. Being on the side of life is easy. Bringing that life to life is an achievement. The Cost of Living will continue until April 12 at YPT; St. Catherines, April 21-24; Ottawa, April 27 to May 1 and London, Ont., from May 4 to 16.

CORRECTIONS & CLARIFICATIONS

The Cost of Living, now playing at Young People's Theatre in Toronto, will run through April 16. Incorrect information appeared in yesterday's editions. (Friday, April 10, 1992, Page A2)
1992-05-29-theatre-review-bye-bye-birdie:
THEATRE REVIEW BYE BYE BIRDIE

Friday, May 29, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY MICHAEL STEWART, CHARLES STROUSE AND LEE ADAMS Directed by Gene Saks Starring Tommy Tune At OKeefe Centre Rating: Back in 1960, Bye Bye Birdie had a lot going for it, but time and a less than rigorous revival have stolen some of its charm Musical feeling its age BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto HEY says Tommy Tune, favouring the audience with a winning smile that must have been honed by a year of touring, "its 1959." He was responding to a barrage of hisses, occasioned when the guy he plays, a turning worm, starts screaming at his girlfriend that a woman's role is to obey. The barracking was as idiotic as such displays usually are. For one thing, the character at this point is plainly seen to be ridiculous, and, for another, the show is full of sexist assumptions which the same house had swallowed with gurgles of enjoyment. Subtlety was wasted on them; so, apparently, was cartoon blatancy. Tune's reminder that the musical - first seen in 1960 - is a period piece, was apposite and charming. It also raised a lot of questions.

Bye Bye Birdie has two story lines. One concerns Conrad Birdie, a rock n roll idol who, Elvis-like, is about to be drafted. Teen-aged girls react to him as adoringly and hysterically as you would expect. But though the show is named after Conrad, more stage-time is given to his manager Albert, the Tune role here, and to Rose his secretaryfiancee who is far more competent than he is but nevertheless hangs around devotedly, carries his bags (a running gag), and waits patiently for him to marry her. Which, at the happy fade-out, he does.

Obviously the scenarios converge. To secure maximum hype from Conrad's exit (and therefore more money for Albert to marry her on) Rose dreams up a gimmick: have Birdie bestow One Last Kiss, duly publicized, on a random fan. The lot falls on Kim McAfee, a bobbysoxer from Sweet Apple, Ohio (pop. minuscule) and to Sweet Apple from the big apple the show goes. There, just enough complications ensue to keep things ticking over till curtain call.

Back in 1960 the show had much going for it, of which some still remains. But a lot has departed, some of it chargeable to time and some to this revival. Michael Stewart's book is slick, and sometimes funny, but nobody could call it rigorous. Developments are arbitrary, climaxes do not satisfy, and even within the separate plots characters wander off and do their own thing. Rose is especially good at this. I saw the original production when it came to London; and my memory is of two distinct entertainments. There was the show, and there was Chita Rivera, gloriously and repeatedly stopping it. Maybe in New York, where Rivera was co-starred with Dick Van Dyke, the balance was better. This time round it has tilted the other way.

This Birdie is being promoted as Tunes show, and he is certainly its most luminous presence: acting fair, singing excellent, hoofing unrivalled. But his role does not give him much scope, and he is wrong for some of what it does give. Albert is a comic neurotic, too nervous even to take a pill, and oppressed by a stock Jewish mother raised to a higher power. Marilyn Cooper plays her as the ultimate in doleful emotional blackmail (composite sample line: dont bother to drive me to my funeral, I'll walk") and, though any actress would play her that way, Cooper does it especially well. Tune's enormous height might theoretically make him gangling and unsure; but moving as confidently as he does, in a wardrobe that looks to have eaten half the budget, it actually makes him seem impregnable. Lenora Nemetzs Rose is all-round competent (and vocally a dead ringer for Rivera) but, whether vamping or vulnerable, she poses no threat.

Conrad himself is curiously underwritten; this was Broadways first encounter with a pop music it thought would go away, and there is nobody inside the sexy-sullen mask. Marc Kudisch wears it well, though. Susan Egan as Kim and Steve Zahn as her unsteady steady do equally good by the youth of Sweet Apple. Their elders are more of a problem, given sit-com sensibilities that Gene Saks's production seems unsure whether to milk or mock. Here, admittedly, it reflects the script, too much of the 50s to get a satirical bead on it. But that is what Bye Bye Birdie now needs: a stylish sense of period. (Hey, it's 1959). It could also do with a brighter tone and a less sluggish pace, from the overture on.

And, reaching back 30 years, I miss Gower Champions champion staging. The shriners ballet, involving Rose and a stageful of bashfully predatory men in fezzes, is much as I remember it though it means less without a teasing presence at its centre. The terrific opening number An English Teacher - that's what Rose thinks Albert should be - and its successor The Telephone Hour have both been truncated, depriving them of shape, sense and impact. Put on a Happy Face no longer has Albert going head to head with a pair of defiantly mournful moppets: a pity since partnering someone a fraction his size is one of the things that Tune (cf. My One and Only and the film of Hello Dolly) has always done best.

I don't drop those song titles idly. Anyone who knows them (plus Kids, A Lot of Livin to Do, Rosie and others) will recognize that what remains undimmed about the show is Charles Strouses music. It is one of the best- humoured scores I know, full of sweetness and juice. Lee Adams's lyrics are perky, too, though they fall apart when they go for sustained satire. Two new numbers, inserted to let Tune and Cooper strut their respective stuff, strike me as inferior; but they would, wouldn't they? Bye Bye Birdie plays until Sunday.
1992-05-30-theatre-review-the-goodbye-pe:
THEATRE REVIEW THE GOODBYE PEOPLE

Saturday, May 30, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY HERB GARDNER Directed by Douglas Campbell Starring Al Kozlik At St. Lawrence Centre Rating: A dogged portrayal of how you gotta have a dream' BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto THE Goodbye People is one of those pieces, regularly turned out by U.S. playwrights, about how you gotta have a dream. They go back, I suppose, to William Saroyan (The Time of Your Life) who thought delusions were necessary and desirable, and Eugene O'Neill (The Iceman Cometh) who thought they were necessary and destructive, though not quite as destructive as the truth.

Some of the appeal of the Saroyan and ONeill plays lies in their archetypal bar-room settings, and in the generous size of the clientele that inhabits them. Its always entertaining to watch the ball being passed among 20 actors. The orchestration counts for as much as the theme. Herb Gardner's works are more sparsely populated, which may be due to deteriorating economics but probably reflects his own taste as well. He writes chamber-pieces for appealing derelicts, Samuel Beckett sunny-side- up. And he sets them out-of-doors.

His most recent and successful slice of down-and-out whimsy was I'm Not Rappapport, two old men in a park, which I enjoyed though Ive forgotten most of it. It had the occasional barbed line and, when I saw it, it was performed with flair. The Goodbye People, which is about 20 years older (the St. Lawrence programme is coy about dates) is being done with doggedness. It takes place on Coney Island out of season, here represented by a bit of pasteboard design that will have no nonsense about finding beauty in ugliness or style in sleaze. It may be truthful, but its oppressive.

It is not as if the play were offering searing insights into the human condition. Gardner's attitude toward the dreams we're alive for is cautiously approving. His prime mover is Max, an old Russian immigrant who once owned a hot-dog stand - Maxs Hawaiian Ecstasies - on this stretch of beach. It went quickly bust, but he has always wanted to try again. All he needs is a partner"investor with $10,000. He finds one: a young man who has been trying for years to quit his job with a Christmas-toy company and realize his ambitions as an artist. Hes been coming to the beach every morning to see the sun come up, and missing it; the opening moments find him phoning the New York Times and giving it hell for printing inaccurate sunrise information. He can only express his feelings over the phone.

However, meeting Max's daughter brings him out of all that. Though, needless to say, she has her own hangups.

The project, despite repeated warnings from members of the uptight outside world, goes ahead. The excitement kills Max, courtesy of an onstage heart attack. So reality wins out. But wait: the younger people, the man especially, have caught the bug, and as the curtain falls it looks as if they will persevere with both the business and their relationship.

There is some sense in this. At least, there is some emotional satisfaction. I was quite happy to see the end of Max, and the thought of Hawaiian frankfurters makes me ill. But the others have much of their life before them and might as well try spending it together. That's my rationalization.

Some of it is due to the acting. The role of Max has Shameless Virtuoso Performance written all over it - written so large, in fact, as to leave little space for characterization - and Al Kozlik is, at best, okay. He functions all right in dialogue, but in the long solo riffs he stagnates. The author has not made it easier by decreeing that the more excited he gets the thicker his accent becomes; the actor is not magnetic enough for us to make the effort to understand him, or to love him without understanding him. The character becomes unbearable, with his endearing refusals to recognize his daughter because shes had a nose-job or his son because hes a lawyer. He even dies with cuteness on his lips. Other characters make a case against him - Gardner is a conscientious playwright - but the play is doomed if we agree with them. I agreed even before they'd begun.

I believed, though, in Peter Binsley as the artist. Not at first, when I thought him too insistently strident, but I came to value the detail with which he built up his picture of a salvageable neurotic, and the rare ease of his silences when he watched the others. I did not believe in Brenda Robins as the daughter (who, as is customary in this kind of play, sees through her dad but not far enough) but I did enjoy her, with her swagger and her crackle.

Besides, what do I know? Al Kozlik got exit applause after his first big tirade, and so did Sandy Webster for a grimly unconvincing performance as his former partner, who arrives late to do a number about the advantages of accepting old age. They were being clapped for playing old men who make long speeches. So, clearly, the play has succeeded. The audience has bought into its values. The Goodbye People plays until June 20.
1992-06-06-finally-a-confident-declarati:
BY RUSSELL FRASER

Finally, a confident declaration: This was a man SHAKESPEARE: The Later Year

BY RUSSELL FRASER

Saturday, June 06, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Columbia University Press, 380 pages, Review by ROBERT CUSHMAN THIS is a fine, unfashionable book, the second half of a two-part life and works of Shakespeare. Actually, it takes in most of the Works. Russell Fraser's Young Shakespeare got his man to London, and tracked his beginnings as actor, playwright and poet. Plague had closed the theatres, and driven our hero to narrative verse. (London, says Fraser, "was a pesthouse.") Then, in 1594, the playhouse had re-opened and Shakespeare, 30 years old, supplies them with Romeo and Juliet and A Midsummer Night's Dream: a tragedy and a comedy on identical themes.

What kind of man wrings laughter and tears from the trials of young love, on alternate afternoons? A wise man, and a cold one. Frasers Shakespeare is both, though for cold we should read guarded rather than heartless. You dont imagine Shakespeare going to the stake or the block and we might add that martyrdom wasn't his job. There are other ways of bearing witness to the truth. As Fraser puts it, "the prudent man was disinterested: a virtue rarer than heroism."

Shakespeare was probably a Catholic like his father, but he kept it under wraps. Religion was of only superficial importance to him anyway; it colours the plays but it doesn't govern them. (Like Fraser, I am inferring the man from the work. What else is there to do?) His fathers failure in life weighed heavily on him, and he himself valued success. He bought himself a coat of arms, plus the second-best house in Stratford, and generally invested wisely. He was probably the only Elizabethan dramatist to make money out of the theatre. Most of his fellows died broke. That includes Ben Jonson, whom Fraser describes, wonderfully, as Shakespeares self-appointed conscience. There is embodied a whole relationship, personal and professional, between the playwright who always told you what to think, and the one who never did.

Of course Fraser cannot know for certain how Jonson regarded Shakespeare; and though an academic himself (English faculty, University of Michigan), he disdains to shield his hunches with the usual apparatus of footnotes and perhapses. Anyone accustomed to the idea that we know nothing about Shakespeare is going to be shocked by Fraser's confidence. Actually we know quite a lot, but much of it is in legal documents and parish records and I wish myself that Fraser had been more forthcoming about his sources. But his boldness stems from his overwhelming virtue: he believes that somebody, at a succession of moments in time, sat down and wrote the plays.

That sounds embarrassingly obvious, but it is a notion that critics have always had trouble with. Old Bardolaters thought it disrespectful to the mystery of creation, and post-modernists view the whole matter of authorship with distaste, preferring the idea of discrete texts that derive any meaning they may have from a convergence of formal and historical pressures. (Logically, this would make Shakespeare's plays indistinguishable from those of his contemporaries but, strangely, it is Shakespeare rather than Dekker or Heywood whom they continue to write about. Perhaps theres more promotion in it.) Fraser looks for the life in the work and vice versa. He does not assume a one-to-one correspondence. Sometimes he goes by what the plays leave out. Hamnet, Shakespeares son, died at 11; but "the greater life's impact on Shakespeare, the less the plays announce it." Fraser finds it reflected indirectly in Much Ado About Nothing, "where a bereaved father, railing out of control, intimates the playwright's involvement." The child he mourns is a girl and she isnt really dead and he knows it; though Shakespeare may, at that moment, have forgotten. Both his own girls survived and nobody, looking at King Lear or The Tempest, could doubt that daughters were much on his mind. I might add, since its one of the few connections Fraser overlooks, that in The Winter's Tale the jealous king Leontes, after 16 years' penance, gets his lost daughter back but never his son. Maybe that was Hamnets epitaph. Or maybe it was the tragedy that Shakespeare steeled himself to write about a hero with almost the same name. (He could hardly have failed to notice.) Fraser sees Hamlet as Shakespeares self-portrait: a man whose mind never stops working.

He also never stops criticizing himself. Shakespeare, stockholder and landlord, was very hard on money-grubbers in the plays. In Coriolanus, inspired by Jacobean riots against property-owners like himself, he is almost infuriatingly even-handed. Edward Bond's play Bingo has Shakespeare committing suicide, disgusted by his own connivance at oppression. This is to underrate the human talent for compromise and self-deception. Besides his plays had already given him all the escape-valves he needed. Fraser is inclined to credit the old story that he died after a drinking-bout with Jonson. He could have done worse.

Tracing a story through the plays Fraser brings them alive as no other critic has done in years. What he offers us, with cool and elliptical stylishness, is the old, familiar, skeptical, all-encompassing humanist Shakespeare. I believe every word of it. Robert Cushman is former drama critic of the Observer.
