THEATRE REVIEW A MIDSUMMER NIGHT'S DREAM

Friday, June 19, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- BY WILLIAM SHAKESPEARE Directed by Alex Darie Presented by Teatrul de comedie At the Premiere Dance Theatre, Toronto Rating: Serban Ionescu takes on three roles in this brilliant Romanian Dream A triple tour de force BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto ICAN get very Blimpish about the doubling of characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream, inclined to point out that the play got on perfectly well for centuries before certain young fellers - and Peter Brook, contrary to popular belief, was not the first - decided that Theseus and Oberon, the plays two authority figures, were actually the same person.

These days its nearly always done, and perhaps the strongest argument in its favour is that it can be. In a play that depends on the intermingling of worlds, the Duke of Athens and the fairy king never appear on stage at the same time. Nor do their respective consorts, Hippolyta and Titania. The strongest argument against it is that the actors concerned invariably end up giving the same performance in both their roles.

In this visiting Romanian production, part of the du Maurier Ltd. World Stage festival - and which, before I forget, is brilliant, shouldn't be missed, and all that jazz - the pros and cons are multiplied since the leading actor, Serban Ionescu, doesn't just double, he triples. (Or should I say he trebles? Actually, he baritones.) The ruler he portrays swings unpredictably between benevolence and spite, and might fit very nicely into The Tempest. He is also an actor, and he seems to be dreaming the whole thing; we find him at the outset, before the received text gets going, enduring a fitful sleep in a tatty circus tent.

Not satisfied with his aristocratic and supernatural fiefdoms, Ionescu takes on the working class as well. His third role is that of Peter Quince, the carpenter, who masterminds the Athenian amateurs one-night stand of Pyramus and Thisbe. When they finally get to do their show, the text dictates that Quince must revert to being Theseus. This means that not only are Bottom and his friends at the mercy of their own stage-fright and the ill-bred comments of their well-bred audience, they have also been abandoned by their director who is right out there, leading the jeers. But they rise above it, asserting their own dignity and that of the art they have adopted. Brooks production tried for the same effect, but it seemed pasted on. This is far more organic and far more moving.

My other comments are best arranged under the following heads: 1) Eroticism. Every production of the Dream thinks it has invented sex and this one contains the regulation amount of pawing. However, it has been integrated with the characters and the action. The fondling that goes on between Oberon and Titania during their quarrel not only freshens a familiar scene. it gives an added charge to his subsequent jealousy. It also links with his attitude toward the human lovers, which is usually a matter of an actor passing from one compartment of the play to another. The love-juiced squabbling of the four kids, which often seems to go on for ever, is here sharp and funny and ends with the four of them trapped beneath a huge red stage-cloth, thrown over them by Oberon and his minion Puck (a stockier and world-wearier sprite than usual).

2) Reality. I have never seen a more believable crew of mechanicals. They even, especially Starveling the tailor in his rimless glasses and Snug the burly joiner, look as though they might be good at their jobs. Bottom (Serban Cellea) quite shook me up with his passionate demonstration of how he would play a tyrant. The same actor plays Egeus, the heavy father of the first scene, which I once bitterly decided was the least rewarding small part in Shakespeare. Here he comes in sick on a litter, looking like a cross between Gianni Schicchi and Red Riding Hood's granny. It somehow makes his tantrums mean more.

Helena is the very ecstasy of self-torturing adolescence, while Lysander, when he falls for her, goes to hilarious extremes of machismo. He and Demetrius are great ones for kicking sand in each other's faces. Naturally there is sand in this circus-ring. There is also, less naturally, a pool. Daries production gets a lot out of it; or, more accurately, throws a lot into it.

3) Terror. In Oberons entourage are four squat individuals whose trench-coats and trilbies proclaim that, in Brendan Behan's immortal phrase, they are secret policemen and don't care who knows it. By the end, they have disappeared. I dont know what this proves. Maybe that Ceausescu was long but art is a bitch.

4) Rhythm. Once you have accepted its terms, everything here looks right and inevitable. Sounds it, too. Of course any show in a language you dont understand takes on an air of ritual. Observing this, English- speaking directors and critics sometimes go into furies of self- flagellation. They needn't. Shakespeare in English and Shakespeare in translation are two different animals. Unshackled by the original rhythms (which, when you have them, can no more be ignored than the written notes in Mozart), they are freer than we are. But we, on the rare occasions when we can harness that energy and make it our own, are luckier.
1992-06-21-top-hat-white-tie-and-tails:
Top hat, white tie and tails

Robert Cushman

JAZZ SINGING
America's Great Voices from Bessie Smith to Bebop and Beyond
by Will Friedwald
Quartet £22.50

ONE of my favourite neglected vocalists, an intelligent lady named Barbara Lea, once wrote that she believed in jazz and in singing but not necessarily in jazz singing. She counts as a jazz singer none the less. Her work is ignored in Will Friedwald's book -- one of the few things I have against it -- but he takes a wide view of the territory.

He includes Fred Astaire. In 1952 Astaire, with Oscar Peterson as his accompanist, recorded a three-LP set of his signature songs: the most delightful vocal album I know. I was waiting in suspense to see whether Friedwald would include him, and on page 364 he came through with a passage that left me, as any good description of Astaire should, smiling. 'Astaire doesn't try to scat . . . or "sing like a horn" or any of the other things that hack reviewers think "jazz singers" are supposed to do.' He 'sensitively interpret[s] great songs through a dancer's sense of rhythmic style'.

Except that they didn't get their sense of rhythm from being dancers, the same holds good for most of the other figures in this chronicle. Innumerable lyricists have named Astaire as their favourite mouthpiece, and at the outset Friedwald notes that far from being note-bending for its own sake, vocal jazz 'operates as a key to lyric interpretation'. Manipulating the beat entails balancing the words, which calls for words and melodies worth interpreting. Here again Astaire provides a key.

The jazz-singer's repertoire, like the art itself, expands as you look at it, but in practice it has drawn most heavily on the songs that Gershwin, Berlin and their peers furnished for Broadway, Hollywood, and Tin Pan Alley. In one of the century's happier coincidences, jazz and musical theatre grew up together with the technology needed to preserve them and to inspire new practitioners.

Pursue these lines of repertoire and interpretation to their logical conclusion and you arrive at Frank Sinatra. Arriving after Bing Crosby, Louis Armstrong and others, Sinatra can hardly be judged America's first great singer, but Friedwald makes a convincing case for him as the first to be great on purpose. And if he isn't a jazz singer, then so much the worse for jazz.

Perhaps anticipating some purist grunts, Friedwald sometimes falls back on a parallel category that he calls 'adult pop', figureheaded by Sinatra and Peggy Lee, and best represented now -- in my judgement -- by Rosemary Clooney, who has found an easy route, comparable to Billie Holiday's, except that where Holiday's was bruised, hers is bruised-and-healed. It is rare to find Lee and Clooney taken with the seriousness they deserve, and unprecedented to find it accorded the male post-Sinatras, generally dismissed as faded showbiz. Friedwald, by distinguishing among them, rehabilitates them. At last I can take my Bobby Darin and Sammy Davis records out of hiding.

His technique is to start with an aphorism -- 'Billie Holiday's art is the kind that takes you deeper inside yourself and ultimately out again; Ella Fitzgerald's is the kind that takes you outside yourself and ultimately in again' -- and then dig in to what his favourites do and how they do it. He hangs this on a lively narrative thread that runs from Al Jolson, at whom he declines to scoff, to Bobby McFerrin who abandons conventional song but exhilarates anyway. He does all this with an authority unpardonable in one who turned 30 last year. But his youth may be an advantage. So much of this happened before he was born that he surveys an even field. It makes his dismissal of rock'n'roll particularly invigorating.

He has his deaf spots, principally comic or cerebral singers: Blossom Dearie scanted, the wonderfully brainy Jeri Southern buried in a list of 'cool singers', Pearl Bailey ignored though her clowning depended on her jazz-derived sense of time. And to dismiss Judy Garland as 'the stuff of anti-swing' is evasive; this 'square at the fair' interpreted pop songs better than most of the hip.

I wish too that some of the book were better written and much of it better edited. He sneaks his boldest assertion into a parenthesis; Bing Crosby 'gave American music the wherewithal at last to compete with (and, in my ears at least, surpass) opera and the European art-song tradition.' I agree. I would not make an equivalent claim for instrumental jazz, much as I love it. Jazz that disdains singing doesn't know its own strength.

CROSS CURRENT THEATRE Robert Cushman sees Kiss of the Spider Woman as a rare serious musical

Wednesday, June 24, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

ROBERT CUSHMAN The musical Kiss of the Spider Woman ends with a posthumous triumph for its leading character. He (for those who have not read the book, seen the movie, rented the video, or attended the show) is Molina, a window dresser imprisoned by a despotic South American regime for homosexual activity and forced to share a cell with a revolutionary activist named Valentin. The two move from mutual distrust - actual repugnance on Valentins part - to love. When Molina is released he carries a message to Valentin's girlfriend. The prison warden, who has planned it all, has him rearrested, tortured and killed. Cue for song.

Molina is a film buff, and this closing number is called Only in the Movies. For me, though, its hook was in its first words, which are Optimistic Ending. They made me very nervous. Up to that point I had been thrilled, gripped and moved. Now it seemed that the show's honesty was in jeopardy, about to be sacrificed to a musical-comedy finale. The composers, John Kander and Fred Ebb, and the director, Harold Prince, were too bright and too experienced not to know what they were doing, and they presumably intended irony. That did not mean they could bring it off. Could there be such a thing as a serious musical?

The answer, to put you out of your misery, is yes. The number keeps its balance: between the form of song-and-dance, which entails celebration, and the facts of the situation, which are appalling. Love does not conquer all. Molina keeps getting up, but he is still dead.

To see how rare this is, look at history. A Chorus Line, masterfully staged, ended with exhilarating glitz. It was intended to expose the pitiful plight of hard-working hoofers condemned to prance mechanically behind a star, but who cared? At the other extreme, Kander and Ebbs Chicago turned the form against itself, apparently to accommodate the disillusionment of its director, Bob Fosse. Dismissing its own accomplishments as "razzle-dazzle", it ended up blaming show business for the state of the world.

Between those two shows esthetically, before them historically, came Cabaret, the first Kander-Ebb-Prince musical, which put the birth of Nazi Germany stealthily and scarily on stage, and did it in musical terms. But it too faltered at the end, sending its characters scurrying around the stage mouthing significant reprises of earlier lines. One of the mouthers was a Jew, and my awareness of what was in store for him left me uneasy at the curtain call, when they tried to send us away happy. There is an unwritten rule that you dont applaud plays about genocide.

At its best Cabaret was history on the move: a rare achievement in the theatre, and one that Prince repeated in Pacific Overtures. That, and his other collaborations with Stephen Sondheim, showed musicals could connect intelligently with the real world: a challenge variously flunked by Aspects of Love (underwritten), Miss Saigon (tasteless) and Les Miserables (mindless).

Kiss is the best prison musical since Fidelio, and I'm not kidding. Are musicals escapist? Well, this one is about escape, physical and psychological. It doesn't transcend the medium; it uses it. So Chita Riveras Spider Woman - a diva playing a diva - is a chanting, swaying symbol of fate and of freedom. When the prisoners lust for her its like South Pacific's "There's nothing like a dame" once more with desperation.

Brutality doesnt sing; and the Wardens one number is a mistake. So is the explicit protest song; the love story is its own protest (it makes amends for the silencing of the gay theme in Cabaret) and the jail shows what there is to protest against. It falls short of the real horror - but then I once saw a Solzhenitsyn play that made the gulag look bearable. What it does show - men crammed inhumanly into a cage, for example - is done with the quick fluidity of musical staging. That is putting the form and its technology to serious use; just as the same director, with equal brilliance, put them to decorative use in The Phantom of the Opera. Love them or hate them, shows of this complexity don't get onto the stage on their own.

Above all, Brent Carver's Molina, though real enough for any play, belongs in a musical; there is rhythm in everything he does. Prince once described Guys and Dolls as one of the few mindless musicals he loved; he was wrong - not to love it but to call it mindless. It respected its source by transmuting it and by respecting itself; My Fair Lady and Cabaret did the same, and Kiss of the Spider Woman is their descendant. Robert Cushman writes and hosts Songbook, Sunday afternoons on CBC Stereo.
1992-07-01-musicals-american-tragedy-rob:
MUSICALS / American tragedy: Robert Cushman on Kiss of the Spider

Robert Cushman Wednesday 01 July 1992 00:02 BST

I HAVE been saying for years that there are only three American musicals of tragic dimensions: Porgy and Bess, Camelot and Sweeney Todd. Now make that four. Kiss of the Spider Woman, with music by John Kander, lyrics by Fred Ebb and directed by Harold Prince, got off to a false start in a New York workshop two years ago. Revived and revised at Toronto's St Lawrence Centre, it looks and sounds stunning. Manuel Puig's novel- turned-play-turned-film has been intensified, but it has not been distorted.

The story is of two cell-mates in a South American gaol: Molina, a gay window- dresser and movie-buff, and Valentin, a dour Marxist agitator, who move from mutual suspicion to love. The most obvious way of musicalising it is to make exotic production numbers out of the kitsch movies that Molina describes to Valentin. That apparently was tried before and failed. In this version the numbers have been directed inward. Aurora, Molina's favourite star, appears - in the eminently suitable person of Chita Rivera - to soothe and tease his dreams.

The threatening Spider Woman is the one role of Aurora's for which Molina never much cared; she represents an ineluctable fate that he half-knowingly embraces when he and Valentin make love. It turns him, against his will, political. Their relationship has been engineered by the prison warden who, having failed to break Valentin, hopes Molina will betray him. Molina dies instead; and the show's achievement is to make us believe it.

The mark of a good Hal Prince production is showmanship guided by brains. The descent of the Spider Woman, her web superimposed on the prison bars, is a visual coup to challenge any in his portfolio. The designer, Jerome Sirlin, comes from photography; working within a frame that expands and contracts with flabbergasting ease, he makes projection seem a new device.

In general, Terrence McNally's book carries the narrative brusquely and involvingly, while the songs depict the dreams (Kander and Ebb, best known for dark or flippant shows, have done soaring work here). When these lines of demarcation are breached the show falters: the warden, a character whom neither art nor nature can ever have intended to sing, turns into a melodramatic heavy and Valentin becomes a cardboard hero out of - to coin a genre - agitproperetta.

But Molina is written well and played superbly. Brent Carver makes him quiver with life. This is an authentically heroic performance, complete with apotheosis. Molina must always have wanted to be in a musical; the show plays with this idea by giving him a posthumous old-movie triumph. At the end of it, however, he remains unalterably dead. If most musicals are escapist, this one is a fantasia on escape. Characters yearn for it, clutch at it, and in the end achieve it: inescapably.

Tribute exudes a certain sweetness MUSIC THEATRE"Jackie Richardson's salute to Manhattan cabaret singer Mabel Mercer at Top O' The Senator does credit to both ladies. Their qualities don't match, but they do touch

Saturday, July 11, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail IN the mid-1970s Mabel Mercer, the doyenne of Manhattan cabaret singers, played an extended season at the Playboy Club in London. Though born and raised in England, she had not set foot there in decades, but she refused to play the sentimental homecomer. I interviewed her for a BBC-TV special called Miss Mercer in Mayfair, and at one point suggested, with possibly exaggerated tact, that during the sixties she had gone into semi- retirement. "Nonsense," she said with a dismissive guffaw, "I was out of work."

Mercer's earthiness was one of her essential qualities, a counterweight to the image of the supersensitive interpreter of hothouse love lyrics, singing of heartbreak at daybreak. She came out of the music hall.

Jackie Richardson, who plays Mercer in Mabel!, a tribute directed by Richard Ouzounian at the Top O' The Senator, has her own earthiness, but it comes out of jazz and gospel.

Mercer had great rhythm but she didn't swing. Local hacks have been describing her as a jazz singer (even, God help us, a blues singer), but Richardson knows better and, being a good actress, subdues her own style to that of the lady she is impersonating. But here lies the nagging problem with a very pleasant show, as with all others of its kind: Is she impersonating Mabel or isn't she?

The answer, as usual, is that sometimes she does, sometimes she doesn't. The show is nominally set in the seventies, by which time Mercer, also in her 70s, was largely talking her songs. Sometimes Richardson does this too: "Jenny Rebecca, five days old," she exclaims in a wondering parlando that exactly matches Mercer's own. At others, having more voice and a different background, she strikes out on her own. But she cannot simply offer her own interpretations of songs that somebody else just happens to have sung before. For one thing, the show's format is modestly biographical, and for another Mercer's repertoire was very specialized. Drop in on her nearest male equivalent, Bobby Short, and you will hear a representative cross-section of the great American songbook. Mercer, however, chose only songs that reflected her own sedate, maternal, worldly-wise persona: a performing persona that related to but did not duplicate her off-stage self. In Funny Girl, Barbra Streisand created a fictitious character and called her Fanny Brice; but then she didn't sing any of Brice's songs. Richardson doesn't have that option.

The first half shows Mabel rehearsing, running through songs and reminiscing about her life to her accompanist Jimmy Lyon. Norman Amadio, who plays both the man and the piano, is nothing like the dapper Lyon but is very nice anyway, gravelly and self-effacing. Sometimes the patter is ingenious, sometimes it's painful as if taken from a book. ("It reminded me of Wales where I had spent my summers as a child." Nobody talks like that.) The relation of songs to life is most effective when most oblique. Being Green works surprisingly well as a song about being black, and Send in the Clowns unexpectedly illuminates Mabel's reunion with a neglectful mother. But The Last Time I Saw Paris is an obvious choice that's merely obvious, as is If Love Were All, Noel Coward's threnody about having a talent to amuse. I once asked Mercer if she identified with that song, and she pooh-poohed the idea, saying it was her job to sing to the audience's emotions, not her own. She always said that. She says it in this show. But the show doesn't believe her.

Act II is Mercer in performance. Richardson sits in a straight-backed chair, as Mabel did, and raises her hands eloquently to Heaven, as Mabel did. She also indulges in coy banter with the audience, which Mabel never did. And she sings, increasingly her own woman. She does a sublime Lazy Afternoon, a song Mercer featured but didn't own; Amadio, shedding cabaret conventions, supports her with some beautifully spare chording. On Isn't He Adorable, a Mercer specialty, she outshines the original. Occasionally, though, she sounds provincial rather than urbane; and Alec Wilder's enigmatic Did You Ever Cross Over to Sneeden's, Mercer's high-point as a tragedienne, eludes her.

Anyone approaching the show without my niggling preconceptions will find good songs well sung. More than that, the evening exudes a certain sweetness, which does credit to both ladies. Their qualities don't match, but they do touch.
1992-08-08-theatre-review-the-rise-of-ed:
THEATRE REVIEW THE RISE OF EDWARD 04

Saturday, August 08, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- BY WILLIAM SHAKESPEARE Directed by Bob Baker and Peter Hinton At the Dream in High Park Compressing Shakespeare requires more than simply speeding up the old order Edward fails to rise to the occasion BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto SHAKESPEARE of course never wrote a play called The Rise of Edward IV, let alone Edward 04. Why the Canadian Stage Company should be so scared of Roman numerals is a puzzle. Maybe it's their contribution to universal ignorance.

Shakespeare did write a three-part play entitled Henry VI. Early work, with a high quota of verbal and physical violence, it shows rival dynasties of robber-barons double-crossing and decimating one another in the Wars of the Roses. Scorned for centuries, it has recently been rehabilitated. The Royal Shakespeare Company has mounted three major revivals, the latest a two-part reduction called The Plantagenets. This is the version - Edward 04 is its second half - that the CSC has brought in.

It is not too satisfactory. Whatever their crudities, each of the original Henry VI plays has a shape and temper of its own, and if this is to be denied we have to get something in exchange, not just the old order denatured and speeded up. The main impulse here is simply to cram three nights action into two.

Henry VI Part Two, as written, is a wonderful portrait of courtly in- fighting. For three acts there is nominal peace; the fourth erupts in a stage-managed popular uprising. Edward 04 starts with this peasants revolt, Jack Cade's rebellion, which plays like a comic interlude cut off from its moorings. The local yokels assemble for a country dance. Then they stand around, holding scythes and billhooks but looking harmless, though they are supposed to have professional soldiers running scared.

By the end of the evening the beginning has been forgotten - which is both the blessing and the curse of episodic theatre - and things have perked up. War has broken out, and it occupies the whole of Henry VI Part Three, which is given pretty much intact except that one battle has been superimposed on another.

None of the stylized fighting works, and little of it is necessary, but the action really lies in individual atrocities. The Duke of York's young son is killed, and he himself subjected to a prolonged humiliation, presided over by the gloating Queen Margaret. Hours later, she witnesses the killing of her own boy. On one estimate, both she and York deserve all they get, but the play allows them their suffering and we feel for the situation if not for the people.

The agony is ritualized when the pious Henry sits on a battlefield wishing he were a shepherd, while behind him appear two representative victims: a son who has killed his father and vice versa. This already stylized scene is given a staging twist that nearly ruins it but not quite. Henry meets his own end at the hands of his polar opposite, the future Richard III. And in Hardee Linehan's performance the Crookback's emergence becomes the main excitement of the play.

A salty brutal joker, he carries his destiny with him; even at the beginning of his career, when his hands are no bloodier than theirs, people address him as if he were a mass murderer. The production marks him out from the start, giving him a compartment of his own in a multi- levelled set, and pointed entrances down long flights of steps. Tanja Jacobs as Margaret catches the lightning in her most sadistic moments, and Juan Chioran is a sprightly Edward who, the tides of war being what they are, shares the crown with Henry on a 50-50 basis.

Nearly everybody wears red, making it impossible to tell York from Lancaster or rank from file. Armies line up to defy one another at opposite edges of the stage, leaving us interesting stretches of totally empty space to gaze at. The actors yell with gusto but the production lumbers. The Rise of Edward 04 continues until Aug. 23.
1992-08-11-theatre-review-point-valaine:
THEATRE REVIEW POINT VALAINE

Tuesday, August 11, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont. -- WRITTEN BY NOEL COWARD Directed by Christopher Newton Starring Fiona Reid, David Schurmann and Simon Bradbury At the Court House Theatre Rating: Point Valaine's secret weapon is its location, and director Christopher Newton spendidly exploits it Chewing on Coward's Point BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont. MORTIMER Quinn, "a crabbed, embittered old writer" (his description) vacationing at an outpost-of-the-Empire hotel in Trinidad, consents to be interviewed by a local journalist. He deals with the situation by asking her all the questions. She has, to nobody's surprise, written a play. Comedy or drama, he inquires? She says, in effect, that it's drama but with a few laughs.

This is Noel Coward winking at himself. Point Valaine, the 1935 piece that accommodates this brief encounter, is drama with a few laughs; Coward could hardly have refused to supply them, nor would he have wanted to. "We get some pretty bad gnats in Horsham," says one resident, showing proper respect for the unfailing comic potential of minor English place-names. Mortimer Quinn himself is very Coward (although apparently modelled on Somerset Maugham): comic not so much in what he says as in the world-weary shadow he casts. His presence suggests what he himself, when finally pushed to it, explicitly states: that nothing is as tragic as we would like to think it, and that that is the bitterest thing of all.

"I must see about engaging a new headwaiter," says Linda Valaine, hotelier and protagonist, at the end of the play: a tour-de-force of stoicism since the previous incumbent, who was her lover, has just been eaten by sharks. A moody and muscular Russian he was, name of Stefan: her sexual outlet for seven years, driven furious when she finds romance with a clean young English flier. This boy has Mortimer to put his battered ideals in perspective. Stefan, a permanent exile among temporary expatriates, is less fortunate.

As University of Toronto drama professor Ronald Bryden remarks in a program note, the balance should have been more explicitly colonial and Stefan should have been black. In other respects, though, Coward is remarkably explicit. Linda is a capable and sympathetic woman shipwrecked by her own needs; make her more helplessly exotic and you are in Tennessee Williams country, more helplessly domestic and you get Terence Rattigan. A couple of gay young men, Mortimer's anti-chorus, are kept under only the thinnest of wraps.

However genuine the emotions may be, they are still expressed in the primly hysterical language - with little as the ultimate pejorative - that 1930s playwrights in general, and Coward in particular, thought proper for passion. Even the master's comedies can be undone by his own echoing speech-rhythms. But Point Valaine's secret weapon is its location, splendidly exploited in Christopher Newton's production. Down come the rains; and down, at every edge of the three-sided stage, come the tropical blinds. The veranda setting (designer, Yvonne Sauriol) is stereoscopically real, but distanced. Stefan's jealousy and Linda's despair are played out under gauze, and it filters out the mannerisms.

Fiona Reid's Linda may not need even this camouflage. She has recreated the role in depth: an angular Anglo with ease in her walk and sex in her nerve-endings. Stefan must have been a star role when created by Alfred Lunt, surprising casting for a vulnerable brute with only one big scene. Robert Persichini's Stefan is relegated in the Shaw Festival's rigid pecking order to supporting status, but imposes himself nonetheless; the worse he behaves, the more we sympathize. David Schurmann's Mortimer is amorphous but sufficient. Snob that I am, I thought some of the others half a class too low in the social scale, but Tony Van Bridge's brief appearance as a departing guest speaks splendidly for the old regime.

Point Valaine continues until Sept. 26.
1992-09-02-cross-current-theatre-a-1931-:
CROSS CURRENT THEATRE A 1931 political satire now seems prophetic, Robert Cushman finds

Wednesday, September 02, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

ROBERT CUSHMAN EVERY four years, come U.S. Presidential election time, I fall to wondering why nobody revives Of Thee I Sing. There may well be very cogent reasons why they don't, but for the moment please allow me my fantasy.

Of Thee I Sing, staged on Broadway in 1931, was the first musical comedy ever to win a Pulitzer Prize. It had music by George Gershwin, lyrics by his brother Ira, and a book by George S. Kaufman and Morrie Ryskind. Kaufman famously - too famously, since it's one of the most over- quoted of all apothegms, and here I go with it again - defined satire as "that which closes on Saturday night." But he disproved his own dictum since Of Thee I Sing wound up the longest-running musical of the thirties. And it was a satire on presidential politics: the story of John P. Wintergreen, his road to the White House, and what he found there.

I used to think the satire of Of Thee I Sing pleasant but toothless. Now it begins to seem prophetic. The show begins with the ultimate in campaign songs: unambiguous in its message (Wintergreen for President) and vigorously ecumenical in its supporting statement ("Hes the man the people choose"Loves the Irish and the Jews.) The torchlit marchers who sing it carry banners inscribed in a similar spirit: A Vote for Wintergreen Is a Vote for Wintergreen" and, my own favourite, "Vote for Prosperity and See What You Get. There is also Turn the Reformers Out," pungent but a little odd, seeing as Wintergreens party are actually the incumbents. Maybe, though, they were having trouble with a gridlocked Congress; the spirit behind the slogan is unmistakable, and I recommend it to President Bush.

Behind all this public confidence lies, as so often, private panic. The party doesn't have a program, and its credibility with the people suffered a grievous blow when it sold Rhode Island. In search of a platform, the party bosses ask their hotel chambermaid what she most cares about. "Money, she says, an unhelpful answer given the economic circumstances; the show is set, of course, during the Great Depression. (Maybe I should clarify that and say that is set in the last Great Depression.) Allowed a second try, she shrugs and suggests love." And there they have it. An issue. "Something that everybody is interested in, and that doesn't matter a damn.

Love" as an issue has the same weight, and fulfills the same evasive purpose, as "family values today. And it seems to carry the same connotations, right down to the cookie connection. Wintergreen pledges to marry the winner of a national beauty contest, and to make their courtship his platform. But he reneges and marries Mary Turner, whose main attraction is that she can bake corn muffins. A taste of these muffins is enough to put the moulders of opinion on his side. And when he has been installed, and impeachment threatens over his earlier breach of promise, Mary has merely to get pregnant to win the country over. She then clinches the matter by bearing twins. And when a White House pretender arises, Mary can squash him by pointing to his suspiciously unmarried state: A selfish old bachelor he!" (The style can get very Gilbert and Sullivan.) Im ahead of myself. This last wrinkle does not come from Of Thee I Sing. It belongs to the sequel, Let Em Eat Cake, which appeared in 1933 and was a failure. Wintergreen, despite banners that read, "The Same Promises as Last Time," loses the next election to a President Tweedledee, and can only oust him by staging a military coup and becoming dictator. Dislodged himself by extremist supporters he survives by turning counter- revolutionary. Mary, as ever, shows him the way.

One or two numbers from these two shows achieved independent popularity as love songs. In context, though, they are shamelessly self-serving: displays of emotion for public consumption. The only character with any thought beyond self-interest is a comic butt: Vice-President Alexander Throttlebottom, accident-prone and incurably low-profile. (Well, half of that could be Dan Quayle.) For everybody else, politics is a matter of diverting attention from what is actually going on and from their own inability to deal with it. They are so frank about this as to be almost lovable. After all, nobody, in any era or any country, expects politicians to know what to do about the economy. We don't really mind this. What we object to is their pretending that they do have the answers.

Now admittedly the shiftiness of today's leaders outdoes anything that these 1930s humourists dared imagine. We have watched a U.S. president get through a whole convention without mentioning the most important event to have occurred in his own back yard all year, the L.A. riots, while simultaneously taking credit for happening to be in the White House as societies crumbled on the other side of the globe. John P. Wintergreen, challenging the League of Nations to a baseball game for the amount of their war-debts, double or quits, seems a visionary idealist by comparison. But his creators undoubtedly had the right idea.

Fashions in satire grow fiercer, though not necessarily more accurate. Of Thee I Sing, thought in its time to be acute good fun, now seems a little quaint, while Let 'Em Eat Cake, once thought to be unconscionably virulent, now seems like acute good fun. I would like to see them cut down and combined into a single show. If we start now we should have them ready for 1996. Nothing much should change in the interim. Not even if Clinton wins the victory that his opponents have worked so hard to make him deserve. Robert Cushman is host of Songbook on CBC Stereo.
1992-09-25-theatre-review-power-play-or-:
THEATRE REVIEW POWER PLAY or RACE TO OBLIVION

Friday, September 25, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY MARTIN HUNTER Directed by Richard Monette Starring Peter Boretski, Albert Millaire and Goldie Semple At the Tarragon Theatre Rating: Intended as an excoriating satire on devious government, Power Play is presented by something calling itself Mulroney Productions. The title of course is a pun, the power both political and nuclear, the play both drama and game Flying blind to Rio BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto TO begin with a detail: a Cabinet Minister glowers at his aide and asks, Whats this cable from our ambassador in Rio supposed to mean? Since the fellow has just handed him the wire, he hardly needs to be told who sent it. The information is included purely for our benefit, and it seems ungrateful to complain. Ungrateful but necessary: as conversation that line is unbelievable and hence unplayable.

Still, exposition is a problem that can baffle the best. It may be fairer to judge Martin Hunter's style by something less nakedly functional. A fey aging gentleman announces himself to a pair of eager youths as "the alcohol in the civilized drink they call modern society." You can tell the kind of decadent wag he is. If that isn't wit enough for you, step outside the play proper for a moment and observe that the piece, which is intended as an excoriating satire on devious government, is presented by something calling itself Mulroney Productions. The title of course is a pun, the power both political and nuclear, the play both drama and game. Lest we forget how deadly that game can be, the author throws in a but-seriously sub-title; though even here - and we are now on an altogether superior level of wordplay - oblivion may signify either annihilation or forgetfulness.

It is 10 years ago, bar an epilogue, and Canada is peddling reactors to Brazil. The minister doing the deal is Jean-Pierre Maclean, a name for all bases. He is consistently needled by a phenomenally belligerent TV reporter who runs a show called Dateline Ottawa; "that" she says, signing off with a sneer, "was the Honourable Jean-Pierre Maclean." We dont see too many interviewers like her on mainstream news, and were lucky. More soul-shaking flak comes from the minister's son, a God-haunted adolescent who switches from doing relief work in Rio de Janeiro to blowing up a statue of Christ just outside it: a form of protest incomprehensible to most of the other characters and at least one member of the audience. Everyone not already there goes flying down to Rio, and the plot manically thickens.

There is a widespread feeling in Canadian theatre that plays should be about Issues: the same issues you can read about in any newspaper or hear about on any newscast. This of course is bloody rubbish, and Hunter has got a bit beyond it; he makes his position on nuclear energy clear at the start (he's against it) and then writes a play. But he seems to think that black farce, his chosen form, permits an uptight seminarian to turn, with no seams showing, into a comic-opera Latin revolutionary, and a victim of police torture to groan one second and grin the next. It may be cranky to complain of inconsistency in characters who were never alive to begin with, but two wrongs dont make a right in art any more than in life. Not that the author is above wringing our withers in deadly earnest. Quite near the end of the play, a character reveals that he has cancer, and I bet that wiped the smile off your face. Having thus staked his claim to human depth, he drops the subject.

There is, as you might expect, carnival in Rio, and Richard Monettes production works in the odd swirl. He also moves locations fast, much helped by the most attractive feature of the evening, Martha Mann's cream panelled set. But he cannot take the curse off the scenes themselves, and at one maladroit moment, when somebody literally ducks out of a conversation, he actually intensifies it. The cast all seem to be playing the idea of being in a hard-hitting play. Peter Boretski has it easiest; as the alcohol in the civilized thingummy he at least gets a chance to be sly. Goldie Semple, as the media person, has it toughest; she bulldozes remorselessly, even when teetering in high heels and a wildly improbable backless dress. Albert Millaire as Jean-Pierre seems unwilling to commit himself to any positive quality whatever; this, given the dance his author leads him, is understandable but it is not satisfying. Power Play continues at the Tarragon until Oct. 10.
1992-10-03-theatre-now-for-one-cell-of-a:
THEATRE / Now for one cell of a musical

Robert Cushman Saturday 03 October 1992 19:02 EDT

WHAT could be jollier than a musical about a revolutionary and a homosexual facing torture and death while sharing a prison cell in South America?

The show is Kiss of the Spider Woman, already familiar as a novel, play and film, and due soon at the Shaftesbury Theatre after a try-out in Toronto. Fred Ebb, the lyricist, had the idea for the show after seeing the film. His rationale was simple: 'It's a romantic piece.' Ebb and his composing collaborator, John Kander, both in their early sixties, are leaders of what seems fated to be the last great generation of Broadway songwriters. If Kiss goes to New York it will be their 10th show there. Their words-and-music partnership, stretching back to 1965, is the longest in Broadway history. Their personalities, as well as their skills, are complementary. Liza Minnelli, who has sung more of their songs than anyone ('Cabaret', 'New York, New York'), once summed them up with: 'Fred can make you laugh . . . John can make you smile.'

Harold Prince directs Kiss, reunited with Kander and Ebb for the first time since the Sixties when, in their words, 'he invented us', putting them together for Flora the Red Menace, which flopped, and Cabaret, which did not. Prince compares them more elaborately: 'Freddy's quiet, reflective, a little acid; John is bouncier, takes a lot of pleasure in serious music. Every Friday, whatever happens, he's off to his place in the country. Fred is much more showbiz, much more New York.'

In conversation, Ebb jabs and Kander flows. While his friend is wired up for a television interview, Ebb clowns affectionately: 'I'm thinking of getting rid of him . . . I hear Cy Coleman wants me.' The joke works because separation is so unlikely. What they like about working together is, simply, working together. When directors nervously ask them for last-minute rewrites, they could not be more delighted. They leave the rehearsal room, in their own description, 'like schoolboys skipping down the hall'.

Ebb prefers writing comedy, Kander likes love songs. In their most successful shows, Cabaret and Chicago, it is the gritty, sardonic Ebb style that has dominated. Kiss of the Spider Woman seems a natural for the same treatment, and has, in fact, turned out to be one of their most melodic and emotional scores.

It centres on Molina, former windowdresser and eternal movie-buff, who lives on memories of his favourite films and relays them to Valentin, his Marxist cell- mate. The two move from mutual distrust - or, on Valentin's part, revulsion - to love. (This is never going to be the favourite musical of the Republican right.) The upshot is tragic, but there is also, to quote the closing number, 'an optimistic ending'. And though there is irony, it is irony without cynicism.

Ebb sold Kander the idea, and they both sold it to Hal Prince. 'Hal's always the first director we think of if you're stretching the form - if he'd turned us down we'd really have been discouraged.' They first tried it out two years ago on a New York campus: it seemed a lot more realistic and a lot less real. Sets were heavy, the staging laborious and there were (Prince winces at the memory) 'graphic torture scenes'. The key to making the show speedier and more allusive was getting the designer Jerome Sirlin, a projection wizard who turned the Toronto stage into living photo-montage.

Kander and Ebb, meanwhile, revised the score. 'We thought we were being very clever by not allowing Molina and Valentin to sing to each other. We were patting ourselves on the back for our sophistication. But nobody noticed.' One crucial new number was prompted by the original author, the Argentinian Manuel Puig. He loved having his story turned into a musical (according to Ebb, Puig really was Molina) but he insisted that, when the two men made love, their motives should be seen to be ambiguous. 'They're using one another,' he said. 'You've got to take the risk.' Kander was 'worried', Ebb was 'passionately for it'.

Then there is the Spider Woman herself: Molina's favourite movie star doubling as a symbol of death. In the first version her numbers were satirical, 'feeble take-offs' of actual Hollywood archetypes. Now they are 'dead serious' - part of the narrative and a commentary on it. Chita Rivera, with her smoky, shimmering bravura, helps. Playwright Terrence McNally, author of Frankie and Johnny at the Clair de Lune, who wrote the libretto, thought of her for this 'mythical goddess role' and Ebb, who has worked with her twice before, 'can't think of another person in the American theatre who communicates like her'. Balancing this diva playing a diva is the cast's one Canadian. Brent Carver, best known as a classical actor, plays Molina and is, by general consent, sensational.

For Kander and Ebb, the show, with its multiple threads of plot, theme and style, is 'the biggest juggling act we've ever attempted. It would be dead wrong to make it a Brecht-Weill score. These are two people of rather pure feeling; we would not want to mock them. It is not just the love story that makes this a passionate piece; their view of the world - politics, movies - is romantic. And death - the Kiss of the Spider Woman - is compassionate'.

'Kiss of the Spider Woman' previews at the Shaftesbury Theatre (071-379 5399) from Thurs and opens on 20 Oct.
1992-11-05-theatre-review-lost-in-yonker:
THEATRE REVIEW LOST IN YONKERS

Thursday, November 05, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY NEIL SIMON Directed by Gene Saks Starring Mercedes McCambridge and Susan Giosa At the Royal Alexandra Theatre Rating: The New York setting and the presence of two brothers recall the charming fairy tale of Brighton Beach Memoirs Lost again in Simon's past BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto LOST in Yonkers is Neil Simon being autobiographical at one remove. That, at least, is how I interpret its New York hinterland Second World War setting, and the presence at its core of two brothers, aged 13 and 15. These elements recall the charming fairy tale of Brighton Beach Memoirs, the first and by far the best of Simon's trio of self-confessed confessionals.

You can't be in two suburbs at once, and there is no way of reconciling Lost in Yonkers with the Simon chronology we already know. Put it that if the two boys of the earlier piece had lost their mother, been temporarily abandoned by their father, and been billeted on a belligerently reluctant grandma, Lost in Yonkers would be their story. They are, if anything, more convincingly drawn here than in the earlier play. Taro Alexander and Phillip Reese give remarkably unself-conscious kid performances, nourished by writing that is just precocious enough. Competitive but supportive, growing up uncomfortably fast, they make sharp, defensive jokes: the only jokes, though not the only laughs, in the play.

The kids have plenty to be defensive about. Dad has gone dangerously into debt to pay his late wife's hospital bills, and to make up the cash he must spend a year in the South, peddling scrap iron. His own mother's Yonkers apartment, above the family candy store, is the only place he can leave his sons. She is German, a refugee from pre-Nazi persecution whose life has been a personal crusade against sentiment, family or otherwise. She doesn't want them; they are terrified of her. Nevertheless, in grandmother's house they stay.

Two more of her grown-up children share the place. Uncle Louis, a smalltime hood, is one of nature's transients, but Aunt Bella is doomed to permanence. Strappingly in her 30s, she is mentally "a child. Not crazy. Not stupid. A child." Another sister has a bizarre vocal tic; Eddie, the boys' father, is weak but tries hard. Their upbringing ran to blows from their mother's cane, poisonously-tasting medicinal soups, threats of commitment to an asylum, actual confinement in closets, and some more ingenious refinements of blackmail masquerading as discipline. Their present deficiencies give the old lady more to blame them for. In her defence, Louis claims she made them tough, but Louis lies about a lot of things.

Simon sets all this up with breathtaking efficiency, and with great conviction. It feels lived. He is also pretty skillful at keeping it going. (Eddie's letters home keep hinting at a dodgy heart, a useful sword of Damocles to keep suspended over the characters' heads and ours.) Resolving it is another matter. Grandma is a splendidly imposing monster, secure in her own system and, when pushed, fiercely articulate in her defence. Mercedes McCambridge, seated most of the time, which she makes a position of power, embodies her to granite perfection. What is to be done with her? A comeuppance seems in order, especially from a playwright so committed to family values: maybe the belated revelation of a heart of gold.

This, of course, would be terribly sentimental, and Simon can be seen struggling with the problem rather like the critics who veer between reviling him as a jumped-up hack and acclaiming him for making money and art together. (Lost in Yonkers comes bearing Pulitzers, not generally a good omen.) Eventually, he compromises; not, I think, with his public - he never has - but with himself. He offers a feel-good ending; not quite a happy one but close.

This involves much speechifying. A lot of worms turn in this play - they have to, given the situation - and the spectacle is, as usual, heartening. It is not always convincing. Susan Giosa's Bella, a specialty turn that holds up surprisingly well, has a climactic outburst that is part affirmation, part cry for help. As she delivers it, it is moving. It has a great future as an audition piece. But its hectoring syntax, its throbbing delivery, its unheralded eloquence, are Hollywood sincere.

Bella also has psychic powers. She can casually turn on a radio, and catch the exact beginning of a song. It figures. This is a very neat show.

Lost in Yonkers continues until Dec. 19.
1992-11-09-theatre-review-the-queens:
THEATRE REVIEW THE QUEENS

Monday, November 09, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY NORMAND CHAURETTE "DIRECTED BY PETER HINTON At the Canadian Stage Theatre at Berkeley Street Norman Chaurette's play brings together the female survivors from Shakespeare's Richard III for an airing of royal grievances The Queens merely chatter ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to the Globe and Mail Toronto I am reviewing this show against the expressed preferences of the Canadian Stage Company. The production inaugurates a scheme of Advanced Workshopping: audiences will be canvassed for their opinions so that authors, directors and performers may learn from them. To keep these reactions free and uncontaminated, critics are being discouraged until late in the run. There is much sense in this. Spectators can be conditioned by reading reviews, though the logic of CSC's position would be to ban critics altogether. There is a lot to be said for this, though less than there is to be said against it.

Normand Chaurette's The Queens is an odd candidate for trial-by- perpetual-preview, having already been done in Montreal. (It is played here in an English translation by Linda Gaboriau.) The production is extremely assured; and Friday night's audience obviously felt it to be in no need of fixing. They laughed in what I imagine were the right places, and they cheered and stamped at the end.

I don't want to spoil anybody's fun, but I thought it was terrible. The Queens is an extension of the scene in Shakespeare's Richard III in which the female survivors gather to lament their fallen husbands, sons and grandsons, nearly all of whom seem to have been called Edward.

The play brings together six women intimately involved with the soon- to-be-crowned Richard: Anne Warwick, the Crookback's own consort; Elizabeth, wife of his brother, Edward IV, and mother of the princes in the Tower; his mother, the Duchess of York, ancient mother-in-law of both the above ladies; Isabel, sister of Anne and wife of his brother Clarence, the one who drowned in a butt of malmsey; Anne Dexter, his (and everybody's) silent sister, who mutely patrols the stage looking sorry for everybody including herself and - from the other side of the rose garden - Margaret, widow of Henry VI and last spark of the House of Lancaster.

They are corralled together in a tower in London (maybe even the Tower of London) on a snowy day on which Edward IV may or may not be dying; time is compressed here and whole lives are meant to be passing before us. But what lives? For much of the time Chaurette's women behave just like their Shakespearean namesakes: that is, they complain and they insult one another.

In the original Margaret does nearly all the bitching but here she takes refuge in zaniness. Instead of talking about going home to France she sets out for China but soon comes back. And despite the play's calculated unreality, I have to ask: what is she doing here anyway, sharing a house with her sworn enemies?

This is a literary-historical fantasia that ignores the rules. When the source-material runs out, the author draws on his own store of black whimsy: We are told that Clarence has not spoken in years, and Richard's Anne is ambitious rather than resigned. Well, why not? But, more importantly, why? None of these inventions establishes itself as dramatic fact. They are merely talked about; everything happens off-stage or in the past. Recrimination is these characters' game, and - adrift between history and Shakespeare's distortion of it and Chaurette's distortion of the distortion - they can say whatever they like. Since it's all arbitrary, none of it matters.

Yes, they talk well; or at least they make long speeches with images in them. I can see the attraction for a director, even without Peter Hinton's printed assertion that he loves the play. And if it were as good as his production thinks it is, it would be a masterpiece.

Naked firelight gilds the walls, which are done up in a rich golden shade of perspex-baronial; a soughing wind yields musical punctuation, and real musicians do the same.

The actresses revel. Marion Gilsenan has the best and most authoritative time as a tyrant Duchess of York with a face like a bleached skull and a presence to match. Margot Dionne is an imposing Queen Elizabeth - she looks about seven feet tall - and Tanja Jacobs' Queen Margaret, sounding more Scots than French, is the tartest vinegar.

At the end they all go very reverential, suggesting sisterhood. But, beside the charity of Shakespeare's Duchess, it pales. Think too of his Margaret scattering men with her curses, and his Elizabeth blithely double-crossing Richard when he wants to marry her daughter.

Those women did things. Chaurette's regal victims merely chatter. Instead of griefs they have grievances. Politically I sympathize. Theatrically I am bored to tears.

The Queens runs until November 21.
1992-11-13-theatre-review-whale-riding-w:
THEATRE REVIEW WHALE RIDING WEATHER

Friday, November 13, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY BRYDEN MacDONALD Directed by Annie Kidder At the Factory Theatre Rating: Bryden MacDonald's Whale Riding Weather is dedicated to the propositions that all we have is one another and that love will conquer all Whale Riding delivers maximum voltage BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto ALLAN Gray is the first actor I have seen who can act with the whites of his eyes. Or maybe, since Im terribly unobservant, he is just the first actor I have noticed doing it. In Whale Riding Weather, performed now by the same cast that originated it last year, there is a moment in which Gray looks at a lover - by this time an ex-lover - with pupils that are absolutely dead. That may be expected. What surprises and alarms is that the sockets encasing them look so blank, weary, hopeless: whiter than white.

The more dead beat the characters the livelier Bryden MacDonalds writing gets. Gray plays Lyle whom we find in a cluttered, decrepit apartment that he has not left in years, lying on a couch from which he has probably not risen in days, and wearing underpants on which I prefer not to speculate. His mind and his tongue, though, remain in brisk working order. They are exercised on various subjects: his past (in another life he had a wife and son), his current life. Remember, he says, unarguably and with relish, "mediocrity rises."

He is addressing his younger companion Auto who sits near-catatonic at a table covered with pills and booze, and whom Lyle once, in every sense of the word, took in. Auto turns out to be capable of speech, and even of going outside to do the shopping. This time he returns with more than cat- food. This time he brings home a man, name of Jude. (Patron saint of lost causes, sneers Lyle: you've come to the right place.) A pick-up is something Lyle has satirically been urging on Auto, but he is of course disagreeably surprised when it actually happens. He can see how things will go.

So can we. Jude, first off, is predatory, and alarmed by Auto's desperate physical and emotional state: his walking zero-ness. He then becomes moved by it, involved with it, which of course is medicine in itself, and the two go off together. But predictable is not necessarily bad; when its good we call it inevitable. Inevitability is implicit in every mocking suffering glance, or witty suffering word, that Lyle directs at the newly happy couple, and it sustains the play. Also there is an exploratory excitement about the love scenes themselves; or about the mere fact of encountering love-scenes, of any gender, in the theatre today.

As long as the play remains in the present, it is riveting. It loses its grip when it ventures into the past, and I do not mean flashbacks. The confrontational scenes in which, with a great show of indignation, characters tell one another things they already know or, even more alarmingly, things they unaccountably dont. As always these scenes, because of their inherent improbability, are stuffed with Fine Writing, here of the lyrical great-outdoors type. This is where the whale-riding comes in. It derives from Lyle's Maritime past. What it signifies, I leave you to discover for yourselves. And when you have found out, please tell me.

I am praising and blaming this play. That is reasonable. Despite its sexual orientation, despite its Pinteresque triangular warfare over a tattered piece of ground (The Caretaker, the classic of the genre) this is a mainstream work, dedicated to the propositions that all we have is one another and that love will conquer all. Auto is an original creation, who in Randy Hughson's performance never loses his mystery, but Jude, far from obscure, is a standard stud, though Patrick Galligans performance individualizes him. Lyle we have often met before, though generally with his clothes on; ageing (i.e. older than other characters) homosexuals in plays can usually be relied on to greet visitors, and delight audiences, with quizzical put-downs. Of course theyre in pain underneath it all; here gay pride and straight morality find common satisfaction. Still it is remarkable how much resigned anguish, and how little self-pity, Gray's Lyle can inject into a line like "for an instant you thought I was beautiful," spoken very quiet and quick.

In fact, any reservations I have about the text are effectively quashed by Annie Kidder's direction. An electric current flowing from stage to auditorium and back again, growing stronger with each transaction defines successful theatre. Here it is at maximum voltage. Whale Riding Weather continues until Nov. 29.
1992-11-16-theatre-review-fallen-angels:
THEATRE REVIEW FALLEN ANGELS

Monday, November 16, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY NOEL COWARD Directed by Marti Maraden Starring Rosemary Dunsmore and Fiona Reid At the Bluma Appel Theatre Toronto Rating: Delightfully decadent in its day, Noel Coward's Fallen Angels is played today for the comic effect that has always existed in the text New production revives discarded Coward BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto WHERE I come from, revivals of Noel Coward comedies are a feature of the landscape or, for a critic, an occupational hazard. The danger part is that the West End of London long ago decided that its favourite son, the boy-genius who persuades them that nothing has changed and supper is still being served at the Savoy Grill after the show, wrote only four plays worth bothering with: Hay Fever, Private Lives, Blithe Spirit and Present Laughter. Others of course are tried from time to time, but they are generally found wanting and replaced with a shudder. In my day, one of these discards was Fallen Angels; some distinguished players performed it conscientiously, but conscience cannot make Cowards of us all.

So Marti Maraden's sharp and funny production is a bit of a revelation, hauling the play right up into the pantheon. In its day, which was 1925, Fallen Angels was a shocker: ironic considering its author's crusty attitude toward the playwrights of the 1950s and 1960s, but that kind of mutation is one of time's favourite tricks. Fallen Angels presents two society ladies who (a) had sex with the same man before marrying two other men; (b) are eager to do it again when the old flame flickers back into their lives, seven years on; and (c) while awaiting his arrival, get very very drunk and very very jealous.

The CSC program prattles about this being "delightfully decadent" but grown-ups in the audience are unlikely to be so easily thrilled. All that can tickle us now is the contrast between the heroines' unctuous primness before temptation and their lubricious abandon after it. This production plays both moods to their respective hilts; even more important, it keeps them in constant tension. Every line and every moment is mined for comic effect but hardly anything is imposed. It was all there in the text, just waiting.

The play begins, most reassuringly, with breakfast: the kind you hardly get any more, on stage or off. Fiona Reid's Julia, addressing her stodgy spouse across the marmalade, remarks that "Muriel Fenwick is divorcing her husband." Her acerbic delivery, light and inventive, is offset whenever she smiles by a display of eager, nervous teeth. When she says of her lover, "it's probably all an elfin joke - he always was being elfin," she reaffirms Coward's skill with an adjective, mainly by not stressing it. Describing passion as "a base, uncouth thing lurking within us," she makes it sound hilariously obscene, while also suggesting a woman rebuking an embarrassingly unruly poodle. Apart from her intoning a phrase from Blues in the Night, 15 years before its time, I cannot fault her.

The play's middle section finds Julia and Jane, her friend and rival, indulging (definitely the right word) in a champagne-and-oyster supper while awaiting their fate. The things that Julia does with a telephone receiver will surprise you; they might even have surprised Coward.

Rosemary Dunsmore's Jane provides fingertip counterpoint in their scenes together, though on her own she's all thumbs. The husbands are wretched roles; and Richard Binsley, an elfin joke in his own right, is horribly miscast as one of them. There is naturally a maid, whose name is Jasmine but who is addressed as Saunders because her employer can never remember the name Myfanwy, if you follow me. Hazel Desbarats plays her with awesome assurance, that being what the character is about.

The fallen angels expect a lot of their nemesis. I didn't; but Nicu Branzea makes him a very suave dieu hors de la machine. (For an English matron temptation has to come in French.) At the end he helps them hoodwink their husbands. The traditional lesson of comedy - that happiness consists of being well deceived - has seldom been so conclusively taught.

Fallen Angels runs until Dec. 5.
