Obituary: The man who defined Sinatra - twice: Sammy Cahn died on

Robert Cushman Sunday 17 January 1993 00:02 GMT

SAMMY CAHN used to begin his stage act by singing one of his most successful later songs, 'Call Me Irresponsible'. He would then draw it to our attention that this was a lyric based on a five-syllable word, adding that this was remarkable as he came from a two-syllable neighbourhood.

He belonged to a tradition of New York Jewish songwriters who emerged out of actual or comparative poverty to do triumphant battle with the English language. Compared to an Ira Gershwin or Yip Harburg, Cahn kept his sophistication under wraps. He didn't flaunt his rhymes, though he was as fanatical as any of his peers about getting them exact and matching speech rhythms to musical rhythms. His words always fell naturally, which is how they seem to have come to him; and he poured them on to a typewriter, unheard-of in a pencil-chewing profession. He was one of the fastest writers in the business.

'Rhythm is our Business' was actually the prophetic title of his first successful song, and it became the theme tune of the Jimmie Lunceford Band. That was in 1935; Cahn arrived just in time for the swing era, and he was always a pop writer at base. Like Johnny Mercer - his only superior as the master of the one-shot song - he thought in terms of songs rather than scores; in a 50-year career he wrote only five Broadway shows, one of them a success (High Button Shoes, in 1947). Jule Styne, his collaborator on that and on much else, thought Cahn's facility undid him as a theatre writer; he didn't have the patience or the in clination to dig into character.

He did create two characters, though. One was his own; he made it to Broadway and the West End in the 1970s as a performer, in retrospectives of his own material that evoked the glory days of Hollywood and Tin Pan Alley. ('Shows you how long ago that was', he would say every time some once-famous name of the Thirties, Forties or Fifties surfaced in his reminiscence.) He was a natural clown, capitalising on his unglamorous appearance; 'most of us,' he said of songwriters in general, 'look like dentists.' If he couldn't really sing, he could certainly phrase. He punched out syllables with punctilious urgency, as if determined that none of his words should escape our notice. He sang as he talked, with a quiet voice and a loud personality. The show was the natural climax of his career as a hustler of his own wares. 'Can you imagine,' asked the pianist Marian McPartland, 'meeting Sammy Cahn without him pulling out a song he wants you to hear?'

His ego was immense, but he seemed secure within it and happy to give colleagues their due. I once stopped by his office in New York's Faberge building on my way to see the stage version of 42nd Street. 'I envy you the fun you're going to have,' he said, with scratch-voiced fervour, and repeated the line, as he often did to make a point. Maybe that was a lyricist's instinct.

His other creation was Frank Sinatra; anyway he helped. From the Forties on - first with Styne as composer, then with Jimmy Van Heusen - he wrote most of Sinatra's film songs and special material, defining him first as the devoted, bashful romantic ('Time After Time', 'I Fall in Love Too Easily'), then as the high-loving playboy ('Come Fly with Me', 'Come Blow Your Horn') prone to peaceful or lacerating introspection ('Only the Lonely', 'All My Tomorrows', 'September of My Years').

Moods were what Cahn, like any good pop writer, was about. He could be euphoric, and he could strike a nerve. In a world full of songs about first love, 'The Second Time Around' was an inspiration. He was perfectly capable of being clever; in 'Thoroughly Modern Millie', a Twenties spoof, he wrote 'Men say it's criminal/What women'll/Do', adding wide-eyed 'what they've forgotten is this is 1922'. He was also the industry's favourite parodist, happily burlesquing his own lyrics or other people's ('you made me love you, you woke me up to do it').

His most famous mot was his answer to the question of which comes first, the words or the music: 'first comes the phone call.' He would have relished the thought of his obituarists responding to the summons yesterday morning to give him instant commemoration. He would have been - he liked punning on his own name - cahncerned but cahntented. He enjoyed cutting a figure. Call him irrepressible.
1993-02-06-the-cd-collector-show-tunes-u:
THE CD COLLECTOR Show tunes underscored BROADWAY MUSICALS

Saturday, February 06, 1993

Robert Cushman

Robert Cushman IN a haphazard way, Broadway cast albums have figured among CD reissues since the beginning. There were predictable releases of the most famous titles; there were also surprise appearances of the most obscure. (Would you believe Whoop-Up?) Now, however, the companies are becoming more organized: Capitol, Decca and RCA - or their corporate descendants - are all inaugurating systematic show-album policies.

Leading the field, as is only fitting, is Sony, inheritors of Columbia which, from the late forties to the seventies, recorded more musicals, better, than any other label. The expected My Fair Lady, West Side Story et al are now being supplemented by a marvellously conscientious series called Sony Broadway which has restored and remastered - impeccably - many scores that had been unavailable for years. Each comes with a booklet providing synopsis (in four languages) and background material from one of three writers: Ken Mandelbaum who is formidably sensible and informed, Marc Kirkeby who is witty, and the producer of the series, Didier C. Deutsch, who is at any rate enthusiastic.

The first 18 sets cover shows from 1949 to 1978. Most momentous is The Most Happy Fella (S2K 48010), which on two discs gives virtually the complete show, Frank Loesser's score being of operatic breadth if not depth. I have never seen it on stage and the excerpts I had heard made me nervous; it sounded stickily mock-Italian, being set among immigrant wine- growers in California. Heard in extenso, though, the story of a shy elderly man and his young mail-order bride is touching, except when it tries too hard as in the attempted aria, My Heart Is So Full of You. The melodrama is gripping, and there are refreshing injections of Loessers own city smarts. Take the wonderful opening in which Susan Johnson, a peerless soubrette, sings Ooh My Feet, the plaint of a weary waitress and originally earmarked, if thats the word, for a similarly afflicted cop in Guys and Dolls.

From possible opera to (intentionally) risible operetta. On The Twentieth Century (SK 30589) found librettist-lyricists Betty Comden and Adolph Green on home ground, affectionately satirizing the sacred monsters of Broadway and Hollywood. Cy Coleman's smilingly ornate melodies and rhythms combine with the faux-naif lyrics and overripe performances to put the Arch into Archetypes. It is all of a piece, and a favourite of mine, right down to its Art Deco poster, reproduced in time-honoured cast-album fashion on the CD logo. Madeline Kahn apparently found the prima donna role too taxing to sustain on stage, but she gives her all on the record whose sound has been not merely remastered but revitalized. A few restored cuts help too; the conductor on the 20th Century Express who suddenly bursts into song with the announcement that he has written a play (as has everybody else the actor-manager-hero encounters) is a mere snippet but sets the tone of the whole show.

Gentlemen Prefer Blondes (SK 48013) is formulaic but pleasing. Carol Channing's innocent-vamp act on Diamonds Are a Girls Best Friend is still the best monument to her peculiarly metallic charms; other numbers in Jule Stynes score vary from breezy to routine.

Irma La Douce (SK 48018) is a French musical - an almost unheard-of commodity in the 1950s - that became a major West End hit in an adaptation by Julian More, David Henker and Monty Norman (who separately or together wrote many of the most successful British shows of the time) and a production by Peter Brook who wasn't always the ascetic experimenter he is now. A gently cynical story of prostitution and petty crime in Montmartre, it fitted right in with a contemporary British vogue for low-life musicals: social significance without tears. It then went to New York with its three British stars, Elizabeth Seal, Keith Michell and Clive Revill, and had a more modest success. The Broadway album, though proficient, has far less atmosphere and punch than its London predecessor. It does though have the signal advantage of being available.

The same goes for Wonderful Town (SK 48021). This 1953 Broadway smash was given a cast recording by Decca that has yet to make it to CD. Sony's version features a TV cast that was largely identical, and above all had Rosalind Russell repeating the only stage musical role she ever needed to play. The score sparkles; the 1930s' New York setting inspired Leonard Bernstein to create some of his most buoyant musical pastiches, and the lyrics show Comden and Green at their comic peak. The first time around Russell dispatched them with a matchless economy and panache; in this reprise she tends to spread herself - a familiar phenomenon most notoriously exemplified in Rex Harrison's steady decline through the successive versions of My Fair Lady. Wonderful Town used to be truly wonderful; here it is merely terrific.

There is much more. Tune in next week.
1993-02-13-the-cd-collector-there-s-more:
THE CD COLLECTOR There's more of the golden oldies to come BROADWAY MUSICALS

Saturday, February 13, 1993

Robert Cushman

Robert Cushman Robert Cushman continues his survey of the Sony Broadway series of reissued cast albums. I LOOKED forward to hearing The Rothschilds (Sony SK 30337), but this Jerry Bock-Sheldon Harnick score - inevitably tagged as the rich man's Fiddler on the Roof -is an attempted epic that comes off as inflated- domestic. By contrast the normally grandiose team of John Kander and Fred Ebb attempted their smallest subject in 70, GIRLS, 70 (SK 30589) and emerged with their most charming score. It flopped but is deservedly a cult. The renowned character actress Mildred Natwick as the leader of a gang of senior-citizen fur-thieves sounds radiantly sensible, and The Elephant Song, her cheerful homily on death, is one of the great neglected numbers. The score contains too many coy songs about old age, but it also boasts one of Broadways few palatable anthems of affirmation, unabashedly entitled Yes.

The disc of Over Here (SK 32961) was a guilty pleasure for me. The first musical I ever saw on Broadway for reviewing purposes, it showed the two surviving Andrews Sisters building morale on the Second World War home-front: just like real life, in fact, though broaching a few subjects that were left untouched in the forties. Who then could have imagined that Patty Andrews, the dynamo of the group, would one day be entertaining the troops with something called the VD Polka. The show was dimly lit, had an impenetrable story, and was generally ridiculous, but it is periodically ignited with a big number. If the dancing is missing on disc, the big-band sounds are still there, and the songs (by the Sherman brothers, Disneys men of choice in the Mary Poppins era) are as good or bad as the real thing.

Mr. President (SK 48212) was Irving Berlin's last show and the only tame score he ever wrote: the blandest of Valentines to the White House, though today, that might give it curiosity value. 1776 (SK 48215) digs rather deeper into constitutional history, being a straight-faced resume of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. Pop songwriter Sherman Edwards, whose cherished project this was, wrote a rather stirring score, compromised by the lamest lyrics this side of Blood Brothers.

1776 might have been called All American (SK 48216) if that title had not been pre-empted by an early sixties campus frolic that differed from previous college musicals in focusing on faculty rather than students. No wonder people worried about the musical becoming a middle-aged form. Mel Brooks wrote the book for this one, and it was apparently a worthy precursor of Springtime for Hitler. The score, though, by Charles Strouse and Lee Adams has been maligned; it's tuneful and even funny. Ray Bolger is said to have been miscast but actually comes across very well; as does Eileen Herlie, a noted English tragedienne who found an incongruous second career on Broadway with a voice that sounds wavery but hits the notes anyway.

Hallelujah Baby! (SK 48218) was an ambitious 1967 attempt to musicalize the history of black Americans; its one of those shows in which time marches on but the characters, representative figures, stay the same age. Its good intentions were overtaken by actual events; like The Rothschilds it suffered from the convention - not overturned until the next decade - that every musical had to be a love story. The recording conveys little sense of dramatic unity but there are individually effective songs (by Betty Comden, Adolph Green and Jule Styne), most of them put over by Leslie Uggams, who became a star in a role originally meant for Lena Horne.

The Broadway ethos takes a heavier toll on Dear World (SK 48220). Jerry Herman followed his huge successes with Hello Dolly and Mame by turning Jean Giraudouxs Madwoman of Chaillot (which Arthur Miller once called the most subversive play he knew) into yet another thoroughly conventional ode to non-conformity: a sequence of up-tunes and lukewarm ballads with an accordion written into the orchestration to prove that we're in Paris. He was obviously trying for something more, and Angela Lansbury, cast in the lead, could probably have given it to him. Anyway, she's in great voice.

In Out of This World (SK 48223), another composer-lyricist also offered the mixture as before, but since he was Cole Porter its worth savouring. The setting is ancient-and-modern Greek: the Amphitryon legend turned into standard U.S. sex-farce. The score, Porters first after the triumph of Kiss Me Kate, was inevitably underrated at the time and has been just as inevitably overrated since. But it does offer the king of the gods' complaisant self-introduction I Jupiter I Rex ("am positively teeming with sex"), the delectable duel of compliments Cherry Pies Ought To Be You, and for Charlotte Greenwood as Juno the indignantly rueful Nobody's Chasing Me (nobody wants to own me and I objectnobody wants to phone me, even collect.") Completing the list: A Tree Grows in Brooklyn (SK 48014) with wonderful songs by Arthur Schwartz and Dorothy Fields and a honey of a performance by the late Shirley Booth; Miss Liberty (SK 48015), middling Irving Berlin and the earliest show in the batch; Candide (SK 48017), the first and best reading of Bernstein's greatest score; Dames at Sea (SK 48214); a spot-on spoof of the Busby Berkeley era that introduced Bernadette Peters; and Goldilocks (SK 48222), another Hollywood lampoon, partly written by critic Walter Kerr and offering Elaine Stritch some good material ravenously accepted.

And there is already much more where they came from.
1993-02-20-rodgers-and-hammerstein-fresh:
RODGERS AND HAMMERSTEIN BY ETHAN MORDDEN Abrams, 224 pages, $57

Rodgers and Hammerstein: fresher than springtime

RODGERS AND HAMMERSTEIN BY ETHAN MORDDEN Abrams, 224 pages, $57

Saturday, February 20, 1993

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Review by ROBERT CUSHMAN RICHARD Rodgers and Oscar Hammerstein are 50 this year. Their first show, Oklahoma!, opened in New York in 1943, changing the American musical. First past the post in the anniversary stakes is this luscious and intelligent coffee-table book.

To many people Rodgers and Hammerstein have always seemed to be 50. Coming between the giddy irresponsible musical farces of the twenties and thirties and the fleet-footed theme-and-variation shows of today, they look like Broadway's middle-age: sober and moral and carefully plotted. For most of us they have always been there, if not on stage then on screen: lengthy square-cut roadshow movies, devoutly respectful of their originals.

Ethan Mordden persuades us this pair of stodgy uncles were actually daredevil innovators, not revolutionaries but evolutionaries. This was certainly true of Hammerstein. In his youth he wrote the words for the most durable American operettas: Rose Marie and The Desert Song, shows with strong if ridiculous stories. From this followed Show Boat, with a strong story that was quite sensible. After that came 15 years of failure; but when Rodgers was asked to put music to a Western play originally called Green Grow the Lilacs it was Hammerstein to whom he turned for lyrics and libretto.

For Hammerstein this meant picking up where he had left off. For Rodgers it was an about-face, since with his previous partner Lorenz Hart he had typified Manhattan smarts. Rodgers and Hart did not write rural shows, and Hart refused to do this one, thereby signing his own death- warrant. (He was already far-gone in alcohol and despair; the success of Oklahoma! seems to have pushed him over the edge.) Apparently overnight, Rodgers turned off his nervous energy and tapped a new motherlode of bucolic charm. By the end of his career this style had curdled - nearly every song sounded like a jog-trot nursery rhyme - but for a good 10years it was theatrical magic. After all these years the score of Oklahoma! still sounds miraculously healthy.

As Mordden points out it is the score, rather than individual songs, that became the hit, and though Oklahoma! was not the first show to have a full cast recording ("an idea made of lightning") it might as well have been. "Oklahoma!'s score arrested the ear because, from one end to the other, a story was being processed, characters came forth, ideas were told." The story may not have been complex but it was strong, the characters were unsophisticated ("not one of them has a brain in his head" said Hammerstein cheerfully) but they were winning and the overarching idea - the birth of a state - is extremely powerful. Oklahoma!, more than any of its predecessors, was all of a piece; in Rodgers' words "the orchestrations sound the way the costumes look." And it is something unique: a lightweight epic.

Some wag once quipped that R&H did not so much bring the musical to life as bring it to death. In Oklahoma! they kill off the villain, an authentic psychopath. In their later, more ambitious entertainments the victims are more central: the anti-hero in Carousel, the male juvenile in South Pacific, finally in The King and I the hero himself. (Women, in these shows, are survivors.) Two of these are very moving. We cry buckets at The King and I because the leads have never told their love, even to themselves; we however have seen it graphically demonstrated in their Shall We Dance duet. As for Carousel, where the protagonist comes back from the grave to witness his daughter's graduation and to find grace in a small-town sermon: well, it sounds gooey (and in the film it looks it) but Mordden puts up a persuasive case for it as a dark masterpiece. ("Still, the guy is dead.") Reports from London suggest that a new and uncompromising production at the National Theatre has proved him right.

He also writes temptingly of the team's three lesser-known shows, the ones that never got filmed or toured or revived. Finally he faces up to The Sound of Music where the old themes come back softened and nobody dies: where nice nuns balance nasty Nazis. After saying some pleasant things about it he convicts it of hypocrisy - its happy ending comes too easy - and concludes, what is surely true, that its sugar and its success have made people think that all of R&H is like that.

Actually Mordden's last two pages are confusing. "Listen. European art is honest. . . . American art is dishonest." (Take that, Mark Twain. Wipe that grin off your face, Eugene O'Neill.) Hence the musical. But R&H "brought it close not to what life is like but what life is about." Does that make them uniquely honest, or forgivably dishonest, or is there some level of irony here that I don't get? In fact - Mordden is thoroughly convincing on this - they told what they believed to be the truth and if they never dwelt on the ugliness they seldom denied it either. Which sounds honest to me.

A sprightly writer with a gift for distilling slang into elegance, Mordden is oddly suspicious of other people's light-heartedness; it would, I fear, be hard to convince him that America's greatest musical is actually Guys and Dolls. He also, in this instance, goes light on the biography; Rodgers' more curmudgeonly traits are underplayed. But he is great at dramatizing main issues, and as an omnivorous buff he also explores any number of byways. Omnivorous but not omniscient - and I cannot resist pointing out a couple of gaffes. Howard Dietz did not write the words for the TV musical of High Tor; Maxwell Anderson did. (I bet you're glad to know that.) More alarmingly, he describes Rodgers and Hart's Love Me Tonight as an Ernst Lubitsch film. It was actually the work of Rouben Mamoulian, who a decade later directed Oklahoma! and Carousel on stage: a vital connection. I don't know if Mordden selected the pictures himself (233; 58 in colour) but whoever did, they're wonderful.

Robert Cushman will perform "This Funny World: A Celebration of Richard Rodgers & Lorenz Hart" on Feb. 28 at 8 p.m. at the Top O' The Senator in Toronto.
1993-02-28-book-review-not-the-very-mode:
BOOK REVIEW / Not the very model of a major life in general: Gilbert

Robert Cushman Sunday 28 February 1993 00:02 GMT

W S GILBERT'S original libretto for Iolanthe included a song about crime. The hero, born to power and riches (father Lord Chancellor, mother a fairy), considers the 'watchful thief' and asks:

What is he but I

Robbed of all my chances

Picking pockets by

Force of circumstances?

In the finished production, this powerful rhetorical question went unasked, a tactful precaution in a critical climate that thought anger 'a passion altogether out of place in a fairy opera'. So much I have learned from Michael Ffinch's book on Gilbert and Sullivan, the men and the operas; and it makes me question the author's introductory statement that Gilbert's satire had 'nothing of waspishness about it'.

In that same Iolanthe, the sentry's famous song about every British child being either a little Liberal or a little Conservative is the kind of avuncular chuckle at political conformity that G & S are famous for. But the implications are more disturbing, and the style less roguishly sedate, in the Chancellor's song about his early career at the bar. His vow of good conduct - no hoodwinking of judge or jury, no bullying of witnesses - is seen as an extraordinary aberration. Gilbert had been a barrister himself, and an unhappy one; for him, as earlier for Dickens, the law became a symbol of everything he detested in his society. His Bleak House is the brilliant jeu d'esprit of Trial by Jury: an outrageously cynical courtroom burlesque from which sentiment and pomposity are cheerfully, and ruthlessly, excluded.

'I don't think much of our profession,' says the Pirate King (of Penzance), 'but compared to respectability it is comparatively honest.' Brecht couldn't have put it better; indeed, his celebrated line about robbing a bank being less criminal than founding one sounds like a clumsy imitation.

Still, however trenchantly the scripts may read, in the theatre their bite is muffled and their style antimacassared. Gilbert, less a committed satirist than an ad hoc ironist, saw or invented the absurdity in everything. When invention failed he could be coy or long-winded. Sullivan's music sweetens and softens the text, and the heavily jocular performing style embalms it. This seems to be the case whoever is doing the performing.

There is also the problem of the dyed-in-the-wool G & S fan, to whom this book is the perfect monument. It begins, some 30 years too late, by prophesying and deploring 'weird interpretations' now that the D'Oyly Carte monopoly on the operas has lapsed. The ensuing loose-jointed biography is mainly about Gilbert; he gets the most space and, when the rows come, the most sympathy. The partnership's massive impact on the British and American theatre is barely discussed. Instead there is synopsis: outlines of the 14 operas that manage to be both slipshod and laborious. Plot twists and paradoxes are brought to our attention with exclamation marks, as in a really bad stage production. Lyrics are quoted, with frequent misprints, but the idea of literary or musical analysis seems not to have entered the author's head.

The publishers' blurb claims that no major study of G & S has appeared for 40 years. Ain't that the truth - still.
1993-05-28-theatre-review-saint-joan:
THEATRE REVIEW SAINT JOAN

Friday, May 28, 1993

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont. -- WRITTEN BY GEORGE BERNARD SHAW Directed by Neil Munro Starring Mary Haney, Michael Ball, George Dawson, Richard Farrell, Peter Hutt and Simon Bradbury At the Festival theatre Rating: Neil Munro's production powerfully makes the play's final point, that the world will always reject its saints, but he seems impatient with its more temporal messages Shaw's out-of-context Saint Joan BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont. FIRST comes a bit of production. On a ravaged landscape, people - peasants, probably - are methodically and mercilessly gunned down. Ethnic cleansing, we are programmed to assume.

From here we progress to the first scene of Shaw's Saint Joan, in which there is still a war on: the First World War, by the look of it. Robert de Baudricourt, Joan's feudal lord and first convert, communicates by field- telephone whenever possible, and the stage is dominated by a gigantic uprooted cross, now horizontal, around and beneath which the actors dutifully scurry. At her first entrance Mary Haney's Maid is invisible from the waist up.

"All dress is fancy dress is it not, except our natural skins," says Dunois, the easy-going Bastard of Orleans, in Shaw's epilogue; and, though there are no nude scenes, Neil Munro's production seems to have taken this remark as its text. The epilogue, in fact, is the only scene done in medieval costume. There is a practical reason for this - Shaw brings on a gentleman in 1920s clothing and we need the contrast - but there is also a prankish one. The scene as written is a dream, out of time, so Munro shoves it back into history.

There is a perverse consistency here, since the avowedly historical scenes have all been shoved forward. Sometimes, as noted, the time-scheme is 1914-18; if the Baudricourt episode looks like the Expressionist war canvas from O'Casey's The Silver Tassie, the Earl of Warwick's tent is a dugout from Journey's End. (The references to other plays may or not be intended, but post-modernism is a game critics can play as well. Indeed, it was designed for critics to play. And since Shaw was defiantly pre- modernist, or at least the modernists thought he was, some occult justice is being dispensed. Where was I?) However, when we reach the trial-scene, we advance to now, what with the house-lights being up and Joan's judges confronting her from behind a row of microphones. She, facing them, has her back to us, but if we want to look at her we have a dozen TV monitors to choose from.

As it happens, the last thing I want to do in a theatre is look at a TV screen; and the video aids, like the ubiquitous phones and intercoms, looked to me like director's toys. But the fragmentation, right from that obscured first entrance, is plainly intentional. We never get a good look at Joan; and Haney's performance is teasingly disjointed. To begin with she is a cartoon visionary, autistically stammering when she speaks of her voices, whispering an unheard message of inspiration in the Dauphin's ear, throwing a possible epileptic fit when given command of the army. In her subsequent scenes, all these symptoms disappear. Then at the trial, despite the sparky dialogue she is given, she is broken from the beginning. Moon-faced and moon-voiced she is predictably haunting; bit by bit, she does everything well. In the epilogue, as a ghost, she is most like a person; and there, infuriatingly but inspringly, she is very moving.

In fact Munro's production makes the play's final point, that the world will always reject its saints, more powerfully than any other I have seen. With its more temporal messages he seems impatient, and he signals his contempt by periodically drowning out the debates with sound-efects or mocking them with visual gags. It might be more honest to cut them altogether but the Shaw Festival's mandate might not permit that.

Shaw, unlike Shakespeare, was too much the pedant and too little the poet to write timeless history; and it is irritating rather than stimulating to hear people talking about horses while travelling in jeeps. It also patronizes the audience, who might be able to make their own connections. But, as often happens, modern dress does jump-start the acting. Michael Ball's Cauchon and Barry MacGregor's Inquisitor would probably be as good and judicious as they are, whatever the frocks, but the Dauphin's courtiers, generally ciphers, are here individuals: Neil Barclay's Bluebeard a frivolous viper, Tony van Bridge's La Tremouille bluff, ignorant and finally villainous. The character who benefits most from updating is Richard Farrell's de Stogumber, an invincibly chauvinistic English army chaplain. But then that is how Shaw conceived him, as a blind blimp of his own time - which, I don't need telling, is the time that much of Munro's production is concerned to evoke. Disregard the rating at the head of this notice: my head dictates two stars , but my heart would offer three. (Or maybe the other way round.)
1993-05-31-theatre-review-and-then-there:
THEATRE REVIEW AND THEN THERE WERE NONE

Monday, May 31, 1993

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont. -- BY AGATHA CHRISTIE Directed by Jim Mezon Starring Michael Ball, Norman Browning, Peter Hutt and William Vickers At the Shaw Festival, Royal George Theatre Rating: Jim Mezon gives this Agatha Christie chestnut a stylish roasting A compelling process of elimination BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont. THE story is told of a London cab-driver who picked up some uncouth Americans on their way to see The Mousetrap. Aggrieved by their loudness, rudeness and refusal to tip, he shouted after them as they entered the theatre, "The detective did it."

It's just as well that there was nobody I disliked in the audience for And Then There Were None, because I saw the play in England years ago, so many years that it still bore its original title of Ten Little Niggers. In America, that had already been changed to Ten Little Indians. And then there was what we have now, another label for the same old Agatha Christie story.

It's the one about 10 assorted people summoned to a deserted house on a deserted island off the coast of Devon, on various pretences, by a host they have never met. When they are all assembled, a disembodied voice accuses each of them of having committed murder; and it turns out that in each of their pasts there has indeed been a death of which they are legally innocent but may have been morally guilty. Then one of them drops dead and, as the action progresses, more of them do: each in accordance with a stanza of the familiar rhyme about the 10 members of a visible minority. It dawns on the survivors that the killer is not merely among them but is one of them.

I, of course, knew which one. But though I knew who had done it, I had forgotten whom he had done, or at least how and in what order. So there was still suspense for me, not much affected by my superior knowledge. In fact, though I expected to have a mildly enjoyable time, I had a thoroughly good one. Jim Mezon's production makes it impossible for anyone, actor or spectator, to condescend to the material.

He gives it just as much style as it will take. Much of it derives from film: chilling music rising to a screech every time somebody hits the carpet, a sunset for the last character to walk into. It doesn't swamp or mock the play, and it allows the actors to play the characters for as much as they are worth, or - if we are being mean about it - considerably more.

Those assembled include a hanging judge, a boorish ex-copper, a dashingly sardonic young army officer, a nervous nerve-specialist formerly a surgeon (one of a long line of stage doctors who have bungled operations while drunk), a rigid frigid spinster with zero tolerance for "nudity and gramophone records" . . . shall I go on? It is tempting to describe them as a cross section of English society c. 1940. (Well, they start out cross. They end up hysterical.) But, of course, they are merely a selection of crime-fiction dummies, apprentice corpses. Their saving grace is that not even their author believes them to be anything else. She may just hint that it's a bad idea to drink or drive irresponsibly or for anyone to be judgmental, especially judges; but she doesn't push it, and neither would I. The play is totally without pretension. It's just good at its job.

Michael Ball has an endearingly sepulchral voice as his honour, coupled with what the text identifies as a typically judicial forward roll of the head. Norman Browning is all thug, Peter Hutt curls his lip romantically, and Roger Rowland is a retired general out of any British film you care to mention. (Playing Christie, it occurs to me, must be a lot like playing Brecht. In both, social role is all.) Wendy Thatcher may try too hard as the maiden lady - she pumps passion into what is by definition passionless - but it's a venial sin. What a good show. And how depressing if it turns out to the best thing in the Festival.
1993-05-31-theatre-review-gentlemen-pref:
THEATRE REVIEW GENTLEMEN PREFER BLONDES

Monday, May 31, 1993

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Niagara-on-the-Lake ONT -- WRITTEN BY JULE STYNE, LEO ROBIN, ANITA LOOS and JOSEPH FIELDS Directed by Susan Cox Starring Rosemary Doyle, Lee MacDougall, Paul McQuillan, Ian Simpson, Jan A. Smith and Karen Skidmore At the Shaw Festival, Royal George Theatre, Rating: A big show in its own day, Gentlemen Prefer Blondes is an inconsequential one in ours; and the Shaw Festival's miniature musical revivals are instantly disarming affairs that never pretend to offer us the greatest show on earth Playing fast and Loos BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Niagara-on-the-Lake SUSAN Cox has directed Gentlemen Prefer Blondes, quite niftily, as though it were a 1920s musical. In a way, it is. It is set in that decade and based on one of its classic texts: Anita Loos's study of the theory and practice of gold-digging, the beddable in full pursuit of the bankable. But Loos did not turn her novel into a show until 1949, by which time musicals were standing heavier in the scales. This one spends its first half on a transatlantic liner and its second in Paris, both locations being theatrical shorthand for frothy hedonism. Even so, it lacks the dizzy salacity of its forebears, and its music, written in the aftermath of swing, is beefier. A song called Homesick is so concerned to evoke the New York of the twenties, so crammed with nostalgic detail, that it could only have been written later.

There is much to be said for sweating some of the weight off. A big show in its own day, Blondes is an inconsequential one in ours; and the Shaw's miniature musical revivals are instantly disarming affairs that never pretend to offer us the greatest show on earth. We take what we can get, which often turns out to be considerable. Dialogue is invariably fast and frequently funny; unfamiliar songs can take us by delightful surprise, and so, when we hear them in context, can familiar ones.

Blondes is the story of Lorelei Lee and some others, the others being established with a song or a scene each, then left to languish for the rest of the evening, and abruptly picked up when needed. It gets increasingly hard to remember which swain is the prey of which floozy, which dragonish mother owns which emotionally stunted son.

Sensibly and economically, these scattered principals are here gathered up and made to do duty as a chorus. This often involves them in voicing sentiments that are clearly not their own, but nobody minds. Nor does it matter that the dancers, even the good ones, are constantly flashing nervous smiles at one another ("how are we doing?") or triumphant ones at the audience ("hey, we made it"). It's all fun.

But there are limits, and Rosemary Doyle's non-performance of Lorelei is way beyond them. It has to be dwelt on, because Lorelei is the show's reason for being. She is the quintessential predatress, fanatical in her determination to turn her temporary physical assets into permanent financial ones, genuinely appalled that anyone - especially her best friend Dorothy who starts with the same advantages - should fail to understand. She says outrageously cynical things with an innocent's conviction; Carol Channing on stage, Marilyn Monroe on film, patented a style of playing her for which nobody has ever found a better word than "wide-eyed." (And who knows in either case how much was luck and how much was judgment?) If there is another way of doing it, it has not been discovered here. Lorelei's unconscious epigrams slide tonelessly, witlessly by; you have to create your own entertainment by replaying them in your mind with appropriate inflections. In song, she is a little better; the house rose to her Diamonds Are A Girl's Best Friend (and how can you resist a lyric that rhymes "pear-shape" with "their shape" and "stiff knees" with "Tiff'nys"), but it is my opinion that they didn't know what they were applauding about.

Jan Alexandra Smith almost compensates as Dorothy, a role that starts out ace with a did-she-really-say-that song I Love What I'm Doing (When I'm Doing it For Love) -i.e. giving it away for free - but declines into romantic second banana thereafter. (But she too winds up with a millionaire. Discuss.) Paul McQuillan has presence and drive as Gus Esmond Jr., heir to a button empire, whose position as Lorelei's sugar-daddy is seriously threatened by the advent of the zipper. Choreography sometimes seems uncertain whether or not it is trying to be funny, but in these reduced circumstances Cassel Miles's hoofing almost justifies the script's trying to pass him off as the late, great Charles Honi Coles.

The real thing, though, is Jule Styne's score which ripples with energy and invention. It boasts Bye Bye Baby and Just A Little Girl From Little Rock (Dorothy helping Lorelei out so enthusiastically that it almost becomes Two Little Girls, as in the movie) and It's Delightful Down In Chile, a self-parodying tango. (Is there any other kind?) Leo Robin, the most overlooked of Golden Age lyricists, springs some surprises; a song called I'm A Tingle, I'm A Glow, turns out to be a hymn to laxatives. Christopher Donison's musical direction is fine, and I liked the reference to Look for the Silver Lining that creeps into the arrangement for Homesick. The sets, attractively featuring a blue sky and hatboxes, were designed by William Schmuck. Such names they have at Shaw. One of the actors is called Geoffrey Whynot, and whynot? Just think, if the original producers had brought in Howard Fast to help Anita Loos with her libretto, what headlines we might have had.
1993-06-01-theatre-review-the-silver-kin:
THEATRE REVIEW THE SILVER KING

Tuesday, June 01, 1993

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Niagara-on-the-Lake ONT -- WRITTEN BY HENRY ARTHUR JONES Directed by Christopher Newton Starring Stuart Hughes, Neil Barclay, Sharry Flett, Barry MacGregor, Jack Medley and Robert Benson At the Shaw Festival, Festival Theatre Rating: The Shaw Festival's The Silver King is a big, fat, teeming melodrama; and it does seem at times to hold the whole of late Victorian England in its hands. This, though, is more a matter of breadth of canvas than depth of theme Facing a Dickens of a dilemma BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Niagara-on-the-Lake THEY applaud easily at the Shaw Festival, and they erupted when the lights went up to reveal scaffolding, three tiers no less, with lots of actors standing on it. The lights then went up a little more, and we beheld machinery. A massive wheel was there, and it turned, and somebody was crushed beneath it. It recalled the Hal Prince production of Sweeney Todd, and it too seemed to be signifying the fate of man in a newly industrialized society, and to be impressive, and somewhat tangential to the piece in hand.

Only somewhat tangential. The Silver King is a big, fat, teeming melodrama; and it does seem at times to hold the whole of late Victorian England in its hands. This, though, is more a matter of breadth of canvas than depth of theme. Like many of its breed it plays a game of cops-and- robbers. The hero is Wilfred Denver, who has many good qualities plus a wife and children, but who gambles and drinks too much, and is framed for a murder he did not commit but would have quite liked to. In fact he thinks himself guilty, and only escapes the law by what he takes to be a miracle. A train in which he is believed to have been travelling crashes, causing many passengers to lose their lives and Wilfred to thank his "Merciful Father" for a second chance. God moves in mysterious ways but, as Peer Gynt once said, nobody could call him economical.

Wilfred takes himself to the silver fields of Nevada and returns a millionaire: hence the title. He rescues his loved ones from direst poverty, punishes the guilty and, by dint of some virtuoso skulking and disguising, establishes his own innocence. His opposite number is Captain Herbert Skinner, alias The Spider, a villainous toff who robs, kills, and evicts widows and orphans. Between them stands the regulation implacable detective, keeping tabs on both.

The only Victorian play with which I can make comparisons is Tom Taylor's The Ticket-of-Leave Man, an earlier piece about an innocent who slips through society's net: cruder in many ways, but at least its victim does go to jail and is truly at odds with his world. Henry Arthur Jones, who wrote The Silver King, went on to compose Ibsenite problem-plays, and he was obviously trying for some sophistication. He, unlike Taylor, gave his hero flaws. But they are superficial. Wilfred's line "Oh God, put back thy universe and give me yesterday" is supposed to strike deep chords, but they are undercut by our knowledge that it's all a mistake; he never done it. The Count of Monte Cristo, who knew all along that he was wronged, was a more impressive avenger, and Dickens's Magwitch (Great Expectations) who knew his own guilt, a far more impressive benefactor. Dickens of course is behind all these panoramic plays, and especially behind their portrayals of crime; The Silver King features a patriarchal fence called Eliah Coombe who is nicknamed Father Christmas but who sounds - in this production anyway - like Fagin. Dickens really hated the social order. For Jones, there are no corrupt or cruel judges, and the police are really quite nice. Once the upstart Spider's stolen jewels are returned to their rightful aristocratic owners, all's right with the world.

But it's an exciting resurrection, and an exhilarating show. If asked what makes it superior to the Agatha Christie down the road, I can only say helplessly "its size." I like plays with lots of scenes and characters, and so does Christopher Newton, judging from the relish with which he moves this one: from town pub to country inn, from railway terminus to dockside wharf, from criminal hang-out to stately home (not to mention chez Spider, which doubles as both.) Each locale taps a new vein of humanity, and this prodigality of minor figures is a virtue in itself.

Among the majors, Barry MacGregor is a handsome Spider, not subtle exactly but relaxed, making the most of the qualms - esthetic rather than moral - that link him to his refined wife (Jan Alexandra Smith, good) and distance him from his emphatically unrefined colleagues (Robert Benson, Simon Bradbury, excellent.) But you expect villains to be enjoyable. More remarkable is Jack Medley as the old retainer who stands by the Denvers in all weathers, advancing them his savings and taking any reference to wages as an impertinence. He's impossibly, even unhealthily, virtuous, but written and acted with such gusto as to be the success of the evening. The comedy, played to the limit, doesn't overwhelm the pathos; it preserves it. The enduring Mrs. Denver has less variety in her suffering, and Sharry Flett nags at her a bit, but she has strength when called for. Wilfred himself is required less to act than to radiate: to stand there and project conscience, or endurance, or triumphant serenity. Stuart Hughes lacks the full romantic glow but manages an effectively intense gleam. The production ends abruptly. It needs a celebratory finale to balance its implacable start.
1993-06-05-theatre-review-guys-and-dolls:
THEATRE REVIEW GUYS AND DOLLS

Saturday, June 05, 1993

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY FRANK LOESSER, JO SWERLING AND ABE BURROWS Directed by Jerry Zaks Starring Lorna Luft, Lewis J. Stadlen, Richard Muenz and Patricia Ben Peterson At the Royal Alexandra Theatre Rating: Damon Runyon it aint. But Guys and Dolls is worth a look, especially if you never see the show before Sit down, sit down, sit down... BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto THERE are many citizens who believe that Guys and Dolls is the best musical comedy that is ever written, and personally I do not disagree. In fact, I hold this opinion since long before I ever see the show, as I grow up listening to the original cast recording, and in fact I play this disc so often that I wear it out and have to buy a replacement, although such extravagance is by no means my custom.

It is common knowledge that the guys and dolls in question are first dreamed up in the 1920s and 1930s by Damon Runyon, who is such a scribe as hates and despises the use of the past tense. This Runyon is in his day the second highest paid reporter in the United States of America, while his short stories are widely held to be the essence of Broadway. Indeed it is a wonder that they are not turned into a musical until 1950, as they are already the source of many movies. On the other hand this procrastination is maybe a blessing, as if the show is done sooner it may be done by guys other than those who actually do it, and the chances of them doing it anything like as well are very slim indeed.

The book of Guys and Dolls is credited to Jo Swerling, who does not actually write a word of it but has a good lawyer, and to Abe Burrows who is called in at the last minute and winds up writing a masterpiece. He tells two love stories. One concerns Sky Masterson, who is known across the country as a most intrepid gambler, and Miss Sarah Brown, who is a sergeant in what is plainly the Salvation Army but is here called the Save-A-Soul Mission.

The other is between Nathan Detroit, who operates a floating crap game - which is to say a game that changes its location every night so as to baffle the gendarmes - and Miss Adelaide, a nightclub chanteuse who is Nathan's fiancee of many years' standing, although to hear her tell it standing is by no means her usual position. She gets to sing a song about this situation, in the course of which she says that she is getting a kind of a name for herself and the name aint his, which is maybe the funniest line that any lyricist ever dreams up for a musical.

Anyway, to make a long story short - which of course is the precise opposite of what the musical does, though this is by no means meant as a criticism - the whole action turns on the result of a crap game, and the construction is nothing less than classical. It is also very hilarious in its dialogue, and though there are many who attribute this to Runyon, it is really down to Burrows who here does nothing less than create his own style.

What he does take from Runyon is an atmosphere and characters, and especially their names. The guys of Guys and Dolls are called things like Benny Southstreet and Liver Lips Louie and Society Max and Honest Ed, though the last-named is not on the stage but in the auditorium. Ed makes a fortune in the retail dodge and subsequently in the restaurant business, and he is a well-loved figure and a cultural force, and on the first night his pin-striped suit and natty demeanour will certainly earn him a part in the show in the unlikely event that he should want one.

The revival he brings in originates two years ago in New York where it wins every award, except for one or two that are left over to prevent the competition from killing themselves. It is a colourful affair, to say the least, and the red decor that Tony Walton dreams up for the nightclub - which is called the Hot Box - is as deep as Hell or maybe deeper. Nor will you ever see a more spectacular sewer. It is possible, though, that the emphatic style amounts to overkill, and that the striking stripes affected by the chorus might look better in a zoo. Lieutenant Brannigan of the local police force wears a yellow raincoat like Dick Tracy, but he is meant to be an overworked cop, not a dashing private eye. Some guy in the audience is heard muttering about a production mounted by the National Theatre in London, Europe, that he much prefers, and though he himself is nothing but an Englishman he may have a point. As regards dancing and orchestrations the limey version cannot compare, but it radiates love of the material, and also trust, and every character in it is truly and thoroughly acted.

In this one, many lines are overstressed or mistimed, others are murdered by having the actors laugh themselves, which is unforgivable, and the minor people tend to be either caricatures or nonentities. Nicely- Nicely Johnson, for example, is deprived of his greed and his girth and other endearing qualities, so when he comes to sing Sit Down Youre Rockin' the Boat, he has no special claim on our affections; and the number, which usually raises the roof, will leave Honest Ed with not a cent to pay in ceiling repairs.

Nathan Detroit is played by Lewis J. Stadlen, who spends much of his previous career impersonating Groucho Marx, which turns out to be a useful accomplishment. He sings Sue Me better than I ever hear it done before. Miss Lorna Luft, his Adelaide, is willing but loud. I like the best Patricia Ben Peterson's Sarah, who acts as good as she looks, and sings even more so.

I prefer Jerry Zakss direction of Anything Goes to his work here, but I do not expect anyone to agree with me. Nor would I dissuade anyone from buying tickets, especially if they never see the show before. After all, the score is intact, with Frank Loessers comedy lyrics the best anyone ever writes, while to hear his music travel from the wistful romance of I'll Know or More I Cannot Wish You to the stage-grabbing panache of the title-song or Luck Be a Lady is to experience a perfect marriage of style and substance. It is certainly true that they do not write them like that any more. It is also true that except in this one instance - and for the verb that I am about to employ may Damon Runyon forgive me - they never did.

Guys and Dolls continues at the Royal Alexandra Theatre until July 17.
1993-07-10-theatre-candida:
THEATRE CANDIDA

Saturday, July 10, 1993

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont. -- BY BERNARD SHAW Directed by Christopher Newton Starring Seana McKenna, Jim Mezon and Duncan Ollerenshaw At the Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake Rating: The Candida conundrum In this naturalistic play, in which nothing really happens, there is little space for Shaw the intellectual comedian or Shaw the crazy clown ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont. OF all Shaw's plays, Candida is the least like a public meeting. That sounds like a compliment but isnt. Generally the fun in Shaw comes from seeing ideas hurled through the air from one player to another, and returned at unexpected angles. Shaw the intellectual comedian is entertaining in himself; his doppelganger, the crazy clown, is even better value. The partners are inseparable, and they bring out the best in one another.

There is little space for either of them in Candida, a perfectly conventional (by Shavian standards, anyway), naturalistic piece in which nothing happens. I know that last clause is the standard complaint about Shaw, but it isnt generally true. His debating plays may be short on what is officially known as plot, but they are crowded with incident, much of it riotous. Candida has a plot: a married woman has to choose between her husband and a feverish young admirer. That is all. It is a shapely enough action, one that would keep many craftsman playwrights thoroughly occupied for an evening; and advocates of the well-made play, Edwardian style, used to seize on it with relief. Its having only one set and half-a-dozen characters didn't hurt its commercial chances either. To us it has to seem emaciated.

The one set is a drawing-room in unglamorous North East London, 1894. It belongs to the Rev. James Mavor Morell, Socialist parson, and it doubles as his office. Morell's doctrines, largely Shaws own as far as explicit politics goes, are sincerely espoused but they matter less for their own sake than for what he gets out of them: mountainous self- satisfaction at the sound of his own voice and the sensation of his own energy. Again, he seems much like his creator, but Shaw has put another part of himself into Eugene Marchbanks, an agonizingly shy and sincere young poet (post-pre-Raphaelite, it seems) whose revulsion at the sordid realities of life - i.e. poverty - is as heartfelt as Morells. What affronts him, though, is not the injustice but the ugliness. The focus for his esthetic transports is Mrs. Morell: Candida.

Not having seen the play in decades, I was struck by how little the title character is given to say, and how much of what she does say is bad- tempered. She certainly has her reasons; for years, she has made her husband's career possible by running his house and family, and she gets no thanks: only generalized worship. Now she has to put up with a teenage poet's unworldly rhapsodies as well.

Most actresses - mindful that they are the leading lady, dammit, and two men are supposed to be head-over-heels with them - cover the facts of the case with a generalized veil of charm. It may be to Seana McKennas credit that she refuses to do this, but the play suffers for her integrity. I make it a rule never to question the likelihood of anyone, in fact or in fiction, falling in love with anyone else, but here goes: Marchbanks is looking for a muse, and I cannot see what he sees in this one.

It is certainly a tingling moment when this Candida turns on the two men bidding for her affections and says, tightly, I am up for auction, it seems. The words leap off the stage. But then they leap back again, because they connect to nothing else in the text. Candida turns out to be an up-market version of Nancy ("as long as he needs me") in Oliver!; and a program-note denying that this is a feminist play (whatever that might be) seems perfectly justified.

A traditional problem with Candida is her father, a successful sweat- shop merchant, who is one of Shaws comic Cockneys: all vulgar bounce and fluent self-interest. Father and daughter usually seem miles apart. This production brings them closer together, Candida being aggressively self- made and Sandy Webster as her dad a touch wistful and crushable. Even their vowels have some points of contact. It ought to work but it drains the juice of both characters. Maybe Candida should have been staged in the main Festival house; it needs to be brought out of itself, not turned in on itself. I cannot decide whether Jim Mezon is giving a bad performance of Shaw's Morell or a good one of somebody else but the self-confidence he offers seems so ascetically hollow from the start that there is no point or poignancy in seeing it crumble.

Christopher Newton's production does, however, boast two excellent performances. It is easy to make us feel for Marchbanks; less easy, as Duncan Ollerenshaw does, to make us feel with him, even while laughing at him. Elizabeth Brown performs a similar balancing-act with Prossy, Morell's adoring typist: an economic and emotional victim but not defined by that. The scene in which they discuss the impossibility of expressing love - he intolerably extravagant in his sensibility but inarguably right, she goaded out of her prim professional shell into a desperate avowal - breaks the play's complacent surface as nothing else does.
1993-07-11-the-astaire-way-to-heaven:
The Astaire way to heaven

LIVES OF THE GREAT SONGS
THE WAY YOU LOOK TONIGHT

There are a million songs about falling in love, but few that capture the moment like the Kern-Fields classic. For the third in our weekly series, Robert Cushman tells its story

POPULAR songs freeze the moment. That is what they're best at. Some of the finest - the Gershwins' "How Long Has This Been Going On", or Rodgers and Hart's "I Didn't Know What Time It Was" - celebrate the moment of falling in love, and are bemused rather than euphoric. The joy is tempered with a wistful incredulity. How could this have taken so long to happen? How can it possibly last? My favourite song, "The Way You Look Tonight", music by Jerome Kern, lyric by Dorothy Fields, does all this and more. It evokes the moment of discovery, dramatises it, and - the last and most brilliant refinement - discusses it. It is, in the least pretentious way, about itself.

Like many songs of its era, it leads a double life. If you hear it as an independent pop song it seems to be about a first, rapturous meeting or - perhaps more likely - about the start of a date. Man greets woman, who is looking especially radiant, and compliments her. You can, within limits, construct your own scenario; and it helps if you have someone in your mind to attach it to. But it was written for a specific situation in a still-current film: Fred Astaire sings it to Ginger Rogers in their 1936 film Swing Time.

The extra-musical portions of Swing Time are, for me, the hardest to sit through of any in the Astaire-Rogers canon. This is largely because Astaire's usual comic foil, the heavyweight bumbler Edward Everett Horton, has been replaced by Victor Moore whose clowning is so gentle as to be practically invisible. Alas, the film's planned opening number was cut, so there is an interminable wait before any singing or dancing gets done. When it does, and for as long as it does, the film is a masterpiece. Song by song, it may have the best score of the series; certainly the numbers are the best integrated with one another and with the plot. In fact, the songs are the plot.

"The Way You Look Tonight" has a modest set-up. There isn't even any dancing. Fred sits at a piano while Ginger is showering in the next room. As he plays and sings she appears with her hair all suds and enchantedly drinks in the praise. It's absurd that this should be the way he is vowing to remember her: absurd and, of course, totally endearing. His singing is straightforward, with a hint of melancholy; the tone, in the fashion of the time, is surprisingly formal, though the phrasing isn't. The song, interestingly, jumps straight into sadness: "Someday when I'm awfully low / And the world is cold . . ." Having admitted the odds the song makes its first and most important statement with a slight but definite lift in the melody: "I will feel a glow / Just thinking of you / And the way you look tonight."

Then comes the masterstroke: "Oh, but you're lovely . . ." That "oh, but", deftly fitted by Fields to Kern's pick-up notes, forestalls any chance of the second eight bars being mere repetition. Disarmingly conversational, it also suggests uncertainty, inability to find words, a sense of how-could-you-be-so-lovely, and of "lovely", though conventional (and more or less patented by Kern's contemporary Irving Berlin), being the only possible word. The song then proceeds to specific compliment: "Your cheek so soft . . . your smile so warm . . . with each word your tenderness grows tearing my fears apart." The qualities praised are gentleness, wit and compassion; and the song exemplifies them even as it cites them. Kern's middle eight, trim but expansive, is remarkable even for him (by this point, it seems, an orchestra has crept into the room); and Fields's climactic bouquet - "that laugh that wrinkles your nose touches my foolish heart" - clinches both the romance and the reality. A person is being sung to, whether it's Ginger or another. And that "foolish heart" phrase has been plundered by other lyricists ever since.

The last section begins by repeating and savouring the word "lovely" - this time without the hesitation. The song and the singer have moved on to a new plane of confidence. "Never, never change / Keep that breathless charm / Won't you please arrange it . . ." Obviously she can't - nobody can - and in making the request the song acknowledges its impossibility. Nobody but Astaire could be so urbane and so diffident at the same time. But, of course, he and his writers have worked the trick anyway. As long as the song lives, so will the beauty it commemorates. Shakespeare and Keats had observed this phenomenon for their respective centuries. Kern and Fields have done it for ours.

As usual Astaire made a commercial recording of the song, done in suave dance-band fashion. It's more insistently rhythmic than the film version, more obviously sung, but also more acted. "Your cheek so soft" is gently emphasised; "Never, never change" is quietly pushed home; "breathless charm" has a tremble to it. Astaire's great singing years, though, were the Fifties when the voice was lighter, more intimate, and, if I may, de-theatricalised. His film vocals of this time were a marvel, and a three-LP set on which he reprised his classics with a jazz quartet led by Oscar Peterson must be the most charming vocal record ever made. He murmurs a lot here, moving at a conversational rubato through the opening section, caressing the first "tonight", then picking up a moderate tempo, kicking the beat with an amiable desperation on "There is no-thing for me but to love you". That "for me", by the way, is a hidden rhyme with the "warm" in the previous line; it keeps other lyricists goggling.

Though nearly everybody you would expect has recorded the song since, only Astaire has come close to owning it. Billie Holiday, who spent most of the Thirties singing inferior songs, never seemed to realise her luck when, as here, she got a great one. Her version is jaunty, no more. (Her records of the Fifties tell a different story, but this song is not part of it.) Like nearly everybody, including Astaire, she neglected the song's coda; a series of precisely notated hums that balance the stammers of the beginning. (Once we couldn't find the words; now we don't need them.) Most singers leave these sighs to their accompanists; a happy exception is Peggy Lee, who recorded the song with Benny Goodman in 1942. Cool and tingling, it's one of the few mementoes of her band-singing days that forecast greatness.

My two favourite instrumental versions date from the early Fifties, and both emphasise joy, not regret. A buoyantly rhapsodic interpretation by Coleman Hawkins (with Miles Davis in support) does especial justice to the coda. Sonny Rollins's work-out with Thelonious Monk ("The Way You Blow Tonight") is an amiable hurricane. Its vocal counterpart is Mel Tormé, paying tribute to Astaire in 1956, and sailing exhilaratingly through and around a fast West Coast arrangement. He starts with a coda: "Lovely . . . never, never change." There seems no chance that she will. There is no uncertainty in Tormé's version, no psychological progression; the drama comes from his exploration of Kern's harmonic possibilities and from the insouciant accuracy of everything he does. Dick Haymes, a magnificent balladeer, took the opposite tack. He starts sombre: "Awfully low . . . the world is cold." He is wonderstruck, and gets half way through the song before he can believe his good fortune. His final "I love you" is triumphant (it helps that he can hit the note so ringingly) but the possibility of loss still hovers.

Neither Ella Fitzgerald nor Frank Sinatra got to the song till the early Sixties: a little late, I think. Both used arrangements by Nelson Riddle. Ella's is a lullaby version: sweet, of course, but too slow to flow. And since she isn't a dramatic singer, the pauses don't mean anything. Sinatra merely crosses the song off his list: a swinging lovers' treatment, without the commitment. Neither he nor Ella explores the song as they could. They should have exchanged tempos. More recently and eccentrically Peter Skellern offers one of his passionately sedate, oddly touching Astaire homages; Kiri Te Kanawa, though less overbearing than often in this territory, glides through the song without leaving a mark.

The song itself glides. That is the mark of an Astaire number, even one that excludes dance. But I can imagine it being sung out of tempo all the way through: thoughtfully, musingly, ecstatically. With each word its tenderness grows; and the encounter might as easily be sexual as social. The voice I hear in my head is that of Rosemary Clooney, who today sings classic pop more warmly and expressively than anyone, and has never recorded this song - she might do it definitively.

Recently too, "The Way You Look Tonight" has gone back to the movies. It is a grace-note in Kenneth Branagh's film Peter's Friends - a quiet moment in the otherwise stormy reunion of half a dozen college friends. Hugh Laurie sits down at the piano and dreamily plunks it out; Imelda Staunton, the singer of the bunch, begins it sweetly; the others - Branagh, Alphonsia Emmanuel, Emma Thompson, Stephen Fry - drift over and join in. Whether the writers chose the song purposefully or whether anything equally "squishy" (their word) would have done as well, remains uncertain. But the song brings the friends together as almost nothing else does (the hangers-on they have brought remain pointedly outside the circle). It's a hedge against the world for them, the poignantly miserable, just as it was for Fred and Ginger, the poignantly happy. The song, concerned with preserving the present, began by projecting itself into a chilly future which it proceeds to redeem. It seems to have got it right.

Robert Cushman's series "Book, Music and Lyrics" returns to Radio 3 on Monday 26 July.
