THEATRE REVIEW THE MAN OF DESTINY

Monday, July 12, 1993

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY GEORGE BERNARD SHAW Directed by Miles Potter Starring Stuart Hughes and Deborah Lambie At the Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the Lake Rating: 0 An incoherent Man of Destiny BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail SHAW'S earliest one-act play, this year's lunchtime show at Niagara, is also his first stab at history. He presents the young Napoleon, billeted at a wayside inn while campaigning in Italy and on the verge of decisive military success. Like other Shavian powerhouses, he talks a good game and prides himself on his freedom fron cant and illusion. Also like them, he is outmanoeuvred by a woman,one who acts instinctively on the principles - or lack of them - that he has had to work out intellectually.

Not much is at stake. The lady in the case is an Austrian spy who has defrauded Bonaparte of dispatches that he can live without anyway and secreted them, as he immediately guesses, in her bosom. (In which movie did Groucho Marx say: There must be a way of getting at that letter without upsetting the censor?) Among them is a piece of mail that could compromise Mrs. Bonaparte ("tonight, Josephine") but the play - a self- confessed trifle that is more trifling than its author may have acknowledged - cannot make this matter either, to the characters or to us. The plotting is irritatingly weak, but the dialogue is reasonably cheerful and the play should pass a painless hour.

The director, Miles Potter, muses in the program on Shaw's fascination with "great men" (and women) and sadly connects it to his infatuation, some 40 years later, with Stalin: "I like to think that if Shaw had lived to know the 'destiny' of Stalin as he did that of Napoleon or Saint Joan, he would have abandoned the character." What character? Shaw never wrote a play about Stalin. And it was a little late for him to tear up his earlier chronicle plays. Anyway, the truth about Stalin - as about Hitler, on whom Shaw was embarrassingly equivocal - was amply available during Shaw's lifetime, for those who cared to know it. And as far as it goes, his early view of Napoleon seems tenable enough. It's one of cynical admiration, and the play's title - slapped on to a virtual burlesque - is coolly ironic.

A director may be forgiven an incoherent program note, but not an incoherent production: certainly not of a play as slight as this one, which depends entirely on poised flamboyance. Shaw called it a "display of my knowledge of stage tricks," as opposed to its immediate predecessor Candida, of which he said - I'm plundering the program again - that when he read it to people "they can be heard sobbing three streets off." Which reminds me, I'm afraid, of his comments on a French troupe that came to London with productions of Ibsen that were said to have made their authour cry; "That's nothing; I've seen performances by English companies that would have driven him to suicide." I don't suggest that a bad production of The Man of Destiny would have impaired Shaw's own life-force, but he might have felt inclined - his words again - to rush upon the stage and rend the actors limb from limb.

Robert Benson, who plays the innkeeper, would probably have got off with a mild dislocation; he is not sufficiently ripe or olive-oily but he can time his lines. Peter Wilds as a blustering blockhead of a sub- lieutenant substitutes his own unreadiness for the character's and keeps his hat on in the presence of his general, which is not only insubordinate but untidy. It is also in flat contradiction of Shaw's own stage directions, which are not sacrosanct, but will do until something better comes along. The play needs a clean line, and this is not achieved by having the actors perch with attempted nonchalance on all available bits of furniture. Deborah Lambie's Strange Lady, substituting simpers for wit, is intolerable (and most unbecomingly costumed). Napoloeon, whom Shaw specified as having "no revolutionary untidiness about his dress or person" is loaded with it in Stuart Hughes's performance, which reeks, physically and vocally, of the post-hippy 1970s. He pulls himself together, though, to deliver a next-to-closing set-piece about the invulnerably hypocritical English. Shamelessly unmotivated, this speech plays triumphantly to a stereotype that Shaw himself did much to create. With England in tatters and the Empire a joke, it should now seem hopelessly dated, but some kind of race-memory sees it through.
1993-07-12-theatre-review-the-unmentiona:
THEATRE REVIEW THE UNMENTIONABLES

Monday, July 12, 1993

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY CARL STERNHEIM Translated and adapted by Paul Lampert and Kate Sullivan Directed by Paul Lampert Starring Norman Browning, Tracey Ferencz and Wendy Thatcher At the Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the Lake Rating: A German comedy about underwear transplanted to the Shaw Festival offers fun, social comment and large helpings of nostalgia for the 1950s Consumerism exposed in translation BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail THE title chosen by the Shaw Festival for a German comedy previously billed in English as The Underpants or The Knickers, is The Unmentionables . ("Truly," remarked Eric Bentley, an earlier translator, "an inexhaustible subject.") Anyway, whatever they are, they are inadvertently dropped - offstage, I hasten to add - by a young married woman in a public place. And that is where the story really starts.

It was told originally in 1911 by Carl Sternheim, a satirical playwright who devoted much of his oeuvre to anatomizing the rising middle class of his own time and place. At the Shaw, these have been transposed to the United States of the Eisenhower years. Theodor Maske, minor civil servant and husband in the original play, becomes Ted Mask, ditto, in the adaptation. His fury at his wife Louise's bloomer, or bloomers, begins the play. What will the neighbours think? What might the government think? What were the bystanders' thoughts?

The last question is quickly answered: unclean, unclean. Two male spectators follow the Masks to their suburban bungalow (Flushing, N.Y.), hoping for more. They rent rooms, to Ted's avaricious satisfaction. One is a preening Frenchman, who enters through the window and spouts philosophy. The other is an extremely nervous barber. Louise, who feels both oppressed and neglected by her husband, prepares after a short preliminary stage of virtuous indignation to succumb to the more romantic of the two. She is much encouraged in this by a female neighbour who has resigned herself to living vicariously, and who sets about embroidering her friend some new and frillier underwear.

I guess you could call Sternheim's original a play about fetishism. (The word I heard bandied about on the Niagara streets was "risque." The implication was that the metropolitan sophisticates who run the Shaw, and we decadents who write about it, have lost touch with the people.) The current adapters, Paul Lampert and Kate Sullivan, give us, by fairly logical extension, a play about consumerism. Between scenes, and even during them, the relentlessly cheerful sound of 1950s TV commercials fills the blacked-out air, providing fun and broad social comment and some hefty helpings of nostalgia.

Ted, the play's monster-in-chief, is Mr. Materialist, pleased with his place in the world and terrified of any threat to it. The set, designed by Yvonne Sauriol and representing the kitchen-and-living-room plus a few doors, is a luscious nightmare of pinks and yellows; and Louise is dressed to match.

The German bourgeoisie of Sternheim's plan were possibly more given to conceptual thought than their North American successors. "What," asks Ted, contemplating a newspaper report of a fabulous creature discovered in the Indian Ocean, "do I have in common with this sea-serpent?" The choice of words, and even of thoughts, sounds strangely formal. But mostly the transfer works amazingly well. It even fills a gap. As greed, lust, hypocrisy and prejudice continue their spiral, this becomes the hard U.S. comedy about the 1950s that nobody would have thought to write at the time or have bothered to write since. It even avoids being patronizing. Sternheim's original generic title was From the Heroic Life of the Middle Class and he was only half joking.

Certainly there are some heroic performances here, in stature if not in ethics. Norman Browning's Ted is a mentality come to life: chunky, crew- cut, blue-suited. Only his red tie seems odd, considering he's a zealous McCarthyite, but his gleaming tie-pin - when did you last see one of those? - makes amends; it's positively artifactual. He is not inhuman; he even acquires a stolid, blinkered dignity when he defends the instincts of the little guy against the Nietzschean posturing of his Gallic lodger. William Vickers as the barber, a short and manic hypochondriac with a passionate reverence for Rodgers and Hammerstein, seems to cover all the native bases his landlord leaves untouched. Wendy Thatcher is the heroine's dowdy best friend from any sitcom with all her defences down. In this menagerie, Tracy Ferencz as Louise manages a few moments of vulnerability without insisting on them; though - I may as well rise to this bait - it seemed to me unlikely that someone capable of singing Que Sera Sera right through would need to be informed that South Pacific is a love story.
1993-07-13-theatre-review-blithe-spirit:
THEATRE REVIEW BLITHE SPIRIT

Tuesday, July 13, 1993

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont. -- WRITTEN BY NOEL COWARD Directed by Susan Cox Starring Jennifer Phipps, Diane d'Aquila, Sarah Orenstein and David Schurmann At the Festival Theatre Rating: True to the spirit of Noel Coward The Shaw Festival production is one of the most familiar Cowards, with a plot best recounted in shorthand and adding up to seances and bickering, but it is a combination that fills out an evening of substantial length with no fatigue BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont. PROBABLY the salvation of the Canadian theatre will not lie in accomplished revivals of Noel Coward. Nevertheless, here is another one.

The play is one of the most familiar Cowards, with a plot best recounted in shorthand. Successful novelist consults medium for research purposes, and finds himself haunted by ghost of first wife. Second wife is chagrined, and scenes of three-sided jealousy ensue. That is all there is: seances and bickering. It is a measure of Coward's mature skill that the combination fills out an evening of substantial length with no fatigue.

Part of the secret is that the witching gets equal time with the bitching. This makes a change from the theatrical inbreeding of most Coward comedies. Madame Arcati, the medium, is probably the best role Coward ever wrote for anyone other than himself. Jennifer Phipps, who plays her here, is the first actress I have seen to, if you like, lay the ghost of Margaret Rutherford: a substantial ghost since the original performance is still available on film. The key to the character's magnitude is her professionalism: her pride in her work and her total commitment to it. Rutherford's aura was that of an enthusiastic sports- mistress: thoroughly at home in her own milieu and quite unfazed by the dry-martini sophistication of her hosts, but inevitably a little dotty when seen through their eyes. (And a standing rebuke to them because of it.) Phipps is a suaver sort, a clubwoman with good contacts in this world as well as the next, sublimely matter-of-fact. "My reply" she says when confronted with skepticism, "is fiddle-de-dee." Rutherford made that sound like a gleeful incantation. Phipps makes it an unanswerable debating point.

Elvira, the disembodied wife, is usually reckoned a pretty good part too, coming back from the beyond to wreak mischief and sow temptation; Sarah Orenstein plays her quite effectively without getting beyond the standard model of husky minx. Ruth, the embodied one, is usually deemed a pill: both to her spouse and to the actress saddled with playing her. But one of the greatest strengths of Susan Cox's production is that it makes Ruth the comic fulcrum of the play. Unlike her husband she cannot see Elvira, only be jealously aware of the havoc she's creating. Trying to be patient, she points her remonstrances, logically enough, at the spot where she imagines her rival to be sitting. This of course is a losing game; and Diane d'Aquila's gyrations as she strives to keep up with an invisible opponent have been honed to a fine farcical edge. When she finally explodes, goaded too far, it is a virtuoso job: a hairpin bend, driven at speed.

Charles, the disputed husband, is accorded no such release; and inbuilt frustration may explain why Coward himself never bothered to play him. He has to stand around being alternately pained and polished and you have to be Rex Harrison to make much of that. David Schurmann once played an interesting Macbeth (another character oppressed by ghosts and wives, though not simultaneously), but in lounge comedy, it seems, he merely lounges. He sounds fretful, bland, and finally smug.

Assisting at the seance (do they need a quorum?) are a local doctor and his wife. Mary Haney, who I imagine is the only actress ever to play Mrs. Bradman and Saint Joan in the same season, dispenses the special joy with which an actress who has proved herself in a major role can fill out a minor one. She is the quintessential physician's helpmeet, English county style, with a keen, friendly disposition and a snort for a laugh, while Richard Farrell as her elderly husband is a walking piece of history, an inch away from petrifaction. They add to one of the great strengths of play and production: their sense of place. You feel a social round, of drinks and dinners and trips to the cinema, going on at a comfortable distance from town. You also, though it's never mentioned, feel the engulfing presence of war. (The play was written in 1941.) We get amusing glimpses of the maid (Deborah Lambie) who's been told not to rush, alternately sprinting and moonwalking across the back of the stage. There is a world here to be disrupted; and Charles's house, which is its centre, makes a better battleground for looking so seductive when at peace. What is billed as the living room seems to double as an exceptionally desirable library. The audience plainly wanted to live there; and so did I. Leslie Frankish is the designer, and at the end his set does a terrific turn of its own.
1993-08-16-theatre-the-marrying-of-ann-l:
THEATRE THE MARRYING OF ANN LEETE

Monday, August 16, 1993

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Niagara-on-the-Lake ONT -- WRITTEN BY HARLEY GRANVILLE BARKER Directed by Neil Munro Starring Ann Baggley, Seana McKenna, Jim Mezon and Christopher Newton At the Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake Rating: The Marrying of Ann Leete is so precisley styled - as opposed to stylized - that it presents great challenges to its audience and its interpreters. Haunting play never quite comes into the light BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Niagara-on-the-Lake THIS is a fascinating play that begins in darkness and never quite comes into the light. It starts shortly before sunrise in an English country garden. On a bet, an aristocratic house-guest surprises and kisses the daughter of the house. Whether this is a joke, a serious affront, or a sign of actual feeling, nobody seems quite sure, least of all perhaps the assailant himself. Halfway through the play he is engaged to the girl, though not before he has fought a duel with her father. At the final curtain the young lady, Ann Leete, is indeed married: to her father's gardener.

As actor, director, playwright, theorist and critic, Harley Granville Barker has a good claim to be considered the father of the modern English theatre. He wrote The Marrying of Ann Leete, his first play, in 1899, and set it 100 years earlier; every character in it is, in some way, reeling from the impact of the revolutionary events across the Channel. "France!" cries the conservative Mr. Leete at one moment of reminiscent anguish. But it's an isolated cry: isolated from the dialogue immediately surrounding it, and from the ostensible concerns of everyone on stage. What is most crucial goes unmentioned, and that is typical of the play: startling when it was new, and fairly surprising even now.

Barker's dialogue is hauntingly, searchingly precise. It also - a huge achievement - manages to keep faith with its own time and the one it's writing about; nothing is anachronistic, nothing is archaic. There are quotable lines too good - too humanly and dramatically truthful - to be epigrams: "When you consider it, no one lives in the polite world" "Why did you desert the army for politics? - Better fighting." And, as dawn breaks on the opening episode, "The sun has risen to show us to ourselves."

What it reveals, as the brighter among them are aware, is not preposessing. Ann's father is a member of Parliament who has quit his party and is being wooed back: hence the presence in his house of the noble lord, Ann's suitor. The engagement is a front for political reconciliation, and Leete Senior's ambiguous attitude to it reflects the self-disgust that has become his ruling passion. Some of it is diverted toward his son ("the begetting you, sir, was a waste of time" - it sounds like something out of Restoration comedy but is meant in deadly earnest) who professes Republican principles but is ashamed of having married beneath him. An older daughter, on the brink of divorce, looks sardonically forward to an enforced rural seclusion, well supplied with "milk, butter and eggs." As a breed, the Leetes are intelligent, but Ann is the only one in whom it hasn't curdled.

I love the play. But I have to admit that a piece so precisley styled - as opposed to stylized - presents great challenges both to its audience (maybe one should always be seeing it for the second time) and to its interpreters. Neil Munro's production is lucid, but its first half looks and sounds surprisingly tentative. Eighteen years ago the Royal Shakespeare Company inspirationally cast Mia Farrow as Ann, but for any other actress the precise blend of innocence and toughness must be difficult to find. Ann Baggley is frequently too knowing, actually too modern. Christopher Newton has all the urbanity for her father, but the corroding pain, though present, is subdued. Seana McKenna as the incipient divorcee bites the hardest; and her interview with her husband's emissary (Sandy Webster, painfully discreet) is the best-acted scene in the show.

The last act is Ann's marriage party. Her relatives are on hand to patronize the new son-in-law: a ceremony that Leete himself savagely orchestrates. Affronted servants look on, their snobbery even more thoroughly inflamed than their employers'. The scene plainly is meant to be a rout, out of a cartoon by Hogarth or Gillray; Barker wrote it on those lines, though he maybe threw in too much too quickly, and Munro takes him up on it. Silent at the back, stands the gardener-groom himself, not too subtly named Abud; as Roger Honeywell plays him, he has loomed through the action with increasing authority, and you can see why Ann chose him. At the end, the focus narrows to the two of them in their cottage; it's a chill, unromantic scene, but vestigially hopeful. Ann Baggley, at her best here, is still, painfully, but obdurately, learning.
1993-09-01-show-boat-s-cool-hand:
Harold Prince is known for making musicals that, within the narrow world of the theatre, make history. He also makes musicals that are made of history. I first became aware of this in 1968 when I saw the London production of Cabaret, the show that Prince himself rates as the real beginning of his style as a director. Probably everyone who saw the show remembers the opening: the uneasy silence in which the audience gazed at its own slightly distorted reflection in a huge on - stage mirror, then the roll of drums as the master of ceremonies proceeded to welcome us - in three languages - to the nightclubs of 1930s Berlin and topromise us a temporary escape from our troubles. "In here everything is beautiful... the girls are beautiful... even the orchestra is beautiful." The beauty was grotesquely rouged, the music was a sweet cacophony, but it was undeniably alluring: alluring and menacing.

As the evening progressed, the menace began to outweigh the allure. In the world outside the club, Hitler was coming closer to power, and an engagement scene in the second act -- a Jewish man, an Aryan woman -- was disrupted by a brick hurled through the window; I reflected at the time that, with pogroms the current in - subject for musicals, that single stone was scarier than all the carefully choreographed furniture - smashing in Fiddler on the Roof. The scene was followed by one of the shows periodic returns to the nightclub, where the routines had been getting progressively seedier. The number at this point was the famous one in which Joel Greys epicene MC danced romantically with a large, sad - faced lady gorilla and sang of how people misunderstood their relationship, building sweetly to the punch line: If you could see her through my eyes, she wouldn't look Jewish at all.

I was blown away. Nazi anti - Semitism had crept up on the audience, as insidiously as it must have done in the Germany the show depicted. It is rare enough for a straight play to capture the movement of history. It was, as far as I knew, unprecedented in a musical (though with its battery of production devices -- above all its in - built talent for self - parody - the musical starts with every advantage). And though many people -- librettist, composers, choreographer, designer -- had contributed to the effect, it was obvious that the show's trajectory had been plotted and piloted by one man. If programme credits meant anything, that man was the director, Hal Prince. (As Harold he seems to exist only in programmes. In every other context, including the title page of his autobiography, he is Hal. It must be the most constantly and affectionately employed diminutive in all of show business.) "If its a Hal Prince show he is the Muscle," wrote William Goldman in a show - by - show analysis of Broadway, The Season, and if you like Cabaret, praise him, but if you dont, blame him. I liked it.

After seeing the show -- it was the second night of the London run -- I ate with friends, and poured out my enthusiasm. When I got to "she wouldn't look Jewish at all," a frost descended. There was a young American lady in the party, and she had found the line gratuitously offensive. (Of course I'm Jewish myself, she said, smiling defensively and pugnaciously at the same time. "So am I," I said, probably looking much the same.) The song, she told me, had ended differently in New York, and she strongly implied that its present state must be a sop to English anti - Semitism.

Actually, I discovered, the show had previewed on Broadway with the incendiary line in place, but had changed it after objections from Jewish pressure groups deaf to arguments about dramatic context. Prince, producer then as well as director, regards his capitulation as a professional defeat -- one he emerged determined not to suffer again. (Fred Ebb, lyricist of Cabaret, said sorrowfully at the time, Ive never known you to pander before.) The affair of course prefigures the storm over Princes Toronto production of Show Boat, a point not lost on Prince himself. "Here," he said, we go again.

Prince says of Show Boat that, despite a "transcendent score," I've never seen it work entirely. Which might seem to give comfort to the show's detractors until you realize that hes talking not of the musicals racial attitudes but of its structure. Based on a sprawling novel, Oscar Hammerstein's script loses focus in its second half, largely deserting the showboat itself and leapfrogging all over the States, something Prince blames partly on the demands of the show's original 1927 producer, Florenz Ziegfeld. Prince has never directed a full - dress musical revival before, unless you count Cabaret, to which he returned twenty years after his original production, and Candide, a wholesale re - inventing, with a heavily adapted score and an entirely new text, of a show that had flopped first time round. He has directed operas, though, specializing in Puccini: "Id never seen a Butterfly or Fanciulla that I liked, so I did them; Ive seen any number of wonderful Bobemes so why compete? I want to see if I can make Show Boat work for me."

If the show's size is a problem, it's also an attraction. It has a time span of forty years -- the 1880s to the 1920s -- and Princes design - scheme is based on the passage of time -- from gaslight to automobile -- in line with his belief that "the most effective social commentary is to illuminate one period through another." Cabaret -- in its creators minds, if not in those of audiences -- was as much concerned with the 1960s and civil rights as with the thirties and Nazi Germany; and the passage of time has been a Prince preoccupation in such later, and diverse, works as Follies and Pacific Overtures. Apparently, though, historical does not, in this instance, mean "political"; and on this matter Prince sounds exasperated. This isn't a political musical. It's an absolutely romantic, beautiful story about naive, good - hearted mummers on a show - boat. Still, that boat is being designed not by Maria Bjornson, who did Princes visually ravishing Pbantom of the Opera, but by Eugene Lee, his collaborator on the overwhelmingly threatening Sweeney Todd; to judge from the set - model, this is not going to be a prettified Mississippi.

There is an imbalance in the show as written, though not one that any of the protesters have pointed out. The theme of racial oppression is subordinate to the main love story, but theatrically it bulks very large, inspiring some of the most powerful writing: "Ol Man River" - - not explicitly a protest song but certainly a song about suffering and the one part of the show that everybody knows -- and the miscegenation episode in which Julie, the mulatto actress, is thrown off the showboat for the crime of being married to a white man. This, despite Prince's insistence that Show Boat is "not a musical of 'Strange Fruit [the celebrated Billie Holiday song about a lynching]," has to be taken seriously.

Of course Im taking it seriously. I have respect for these characters; I had respect before people started making any noise. What does Joe [the stevedore who sings Ol' Man River] actually do? No previous production has made it clear what his job is; I'm going to. Theres a difference between history and stereotyping. Butif they say that you cant use a sepia photograph of a black man carrying a bale on his back, then that's denying history. Nobody is going to question my integrity." (The italics are his, if it's possible to talk in italics.)

All the same, the controversy exists, and it hasnt gone away. Is it going to weigh on him in rehearsal?

Not one whit. The show will offend no - one. That Im darned sure of. People misunderstand. They misunderstood Cabaret. But they got over it quite quickly."

Nor was Cabaret even the first time. The New York Board of Rabbis, Prince says, "harassed me over Fiddler on the Roof." This sounds improbable, but apparently they objected to the rabbi in the show being depicted as a marginally comic character. Like Cabaret, and indeed like Show Boat, Fiddler is a show that plays off the epic against the domestic. Prince produced but did not direct it; although his directing career was under way when the show was conceived, he was always insistent that nobody except Jerome Robbins should stage it. There's a paradox here: Robbins -- an icy, dictatorial figure who withdrew from musicals in favour of ballet where he could have even more complete control -- nevertheless came up with warm, moving shows: Fiddler or West Side Story (and a string of totally light - hearted musicals before them). Prince -- confident, courteous, and gregarious -- has the reputation of doing cool shows: a label that he acknowledges and ascribes to his own sense of what excites him in the theatre: "theatrics... tension... conflict."

These are not the qualities traditionally associated with musicals though there is no reason why they shouldn't be. But Princes position in musicals is an anomalous one. He has now produced twenty of them and directed twenty (that doesnt make forty shows; there is a considerable overlap), and he has won more awards than anyone else in the field. To many people, he personifies the musical. But he says it's a form that he slipped into and that he "didn't like musicals as a kid." He was born in 1928 into a New York middle - class family, and grew up in the thirties and forties seeing a lot of plays. His idols were such as Orson Welles and Eva Le Gallienne who worked in classical theatre, and its easy to see how Welless scope and ambition have affected his own work. prince did see musicals as well in those days; he seems to have seen everything. He still talks excitedly about having caught the first major revival of Porgy and Bess in 1942; but a more typical show of the period was Rodgers and Hart's Too Many Girls (1939), about a football - mad college where the girl students wore beanies for as long as they remained virgins, and the principal narrative interest was in seeing which were still wearing them by the end of the evening. Those silly old shows with the swell songs are, for Prince, dead beyond recall, and he seems mystified that so many people should regard them with affection and even want to revive them. But then he has also confessed that "there are pitfalls in my preferences, and they tend to take the fun out of an evening." He seems on firm ground, though, in his bewilderment at silly new shows that don't even have swell songs.

Still, it was through the world of Too Many Girls that Prince came to work in musicals. That show, like many more of its era, was directed by the legendary George Abbott, and it was to Abbotts office that Prince, an ambitious theatre - struck twenty - year - old, naturally gravitated. Abbott hired him for his brightness and enthusiasm; Prince worked as a stage manager on Abbott musicals and came to admire the complex craft involved. From Abbott and later from Robbins, he found that "I could use the form to do what I wanted" -- which wasnt necessarily what they had wanted. And gradually he was seduced: I've done straight plays, but without music I feel like I'm only doing half a show. Or: a rehearsal room without a piano in it has to be kidding.

In 1953 Prince and an older colleague, Robert Griffith, were stage - managing Abbotts production of a Leonard Bernstein musical, Wonderful Town. They were looking for a property to produce, and they found it in a novel, Seven and a Half Cents, by Richard Bissell. Their employer became their employee, Abbott co - writing and directing the musical version that they called The Pajama Game. He also helped them raise the money, though this apolitical showmans typically blunt announcement that "this is a musical about a strike in a pajama factory" scared away more backers than it attracted. It was Prince, the socially conscious, who charmed the investors by describing it as Romeo and Juliet in the Midwest. The show was a hit and Prince became famous as, in Goldman's words, "the last of the boy wonder producers."

So he can claim, I've been doing political musicals since 1954 -- a claim that seems a little excessive until you look up a standard history of the musical that describes this harmlessly enjoyable show as "noisy, coarse - grained and leftish," three traits apparently equally objectionable. It makes you realize how much Prince has been up against when he has tried to buck the Broadway mentality -- or, more precisely, the Broadway - fanciers mentality.

Do you, I asked him recently, ever feel out of place doing musicals?"

No. Why should I?"

Well, to be blunt, you and your work often seem a lot more intelligent than most of whats around.

Yeah. That's certainly blunt. I suppose I do feel like a fish out of water sometimes. I feel out of place when a jolly, mindless musical is overly welcomed. Unless it's stylish. I loved Me and My Girl. And Ill take Guys and Dolls and How To Succeed every time.

To this list of stylish comedy musicals I imagine he would add A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum, which he produced but didnt direct, and On the Twentieth Century, an updated comic opera about sublimely selfish theatricals, which he directed but didn't produce. Somewhere in the same category -- though it's romantic rather than comic escapism -- I would place The Phantom of the Opera, far and away his greatest commercial success. (Prince likes success; when we spoke he delighted in pointing out that Phantom was still the highest - grossing show on Broadway.) Surprisingly weak on story, Phantom is a gorgeous feat of visual orchestration. A sneering review in The Globe and Mail loftily declared that spectacle can be bought in. Of course it can; so can good actors. But, once bought, they have to be used. (Princes name, amazingly, was omitted from the Globe reviews of both Phantom and Kiss of the Spider Woman. Nobody is obliged to like either show, but to ignore the director of two productions to which the director was so obviously crucial is professionally irresponsible. If you hate them, blame him.)

The Harold S. Prince of early days -- the middle initial presumably there to balance that of his partner, Robert E. Griffith -- appears in photographs as an eager, glossy - haired young executive, fairly recently out of college. Robert Morse once played him that way in a musical roman a clef called Say, Darling. Prince, unamused at the time, later acknowledged that it was a funny portrayal, adding that Morse -- who now, decades later, is his Capn Andy in Show Boat -- "still looks like me. It is I who don't." And indeed young Harold Prince -- the S. was dropped when Griffith died in the early 1960s -- is almost unrecognizable in the Hal Prince of today: white - bearded, spectacles permanently elevated on his shining dome (he must sometimes wear them on his nose, but nobody can remember seeing them there), an appealing mixture of handyman and sage. His energy is proverbial and, though much of his artistic frame of reference is European, his enthusiasm is engagingly all - American: nobody else can get away as he does with describing something as swell or addressing any gathering of two or more people as "gang." Searching for something to say against him, I can come up half - heartedly with a story I once heard of his storming out of a rehearsal of one of his less - successful productions exclaiming, I don't care what you do, only make it better; and even that might be taken as a demonstration of faith in his assistants. An English actor who loves working with him confirms his impatience at rehearsals -- "He has the lowest boredom threshold of anyone I know" -- and it seems generally agreed that detailed work with actors is not his strongest suit.

I prefer sweeping, dramatic grand theatre. Small, delicate character studies are not my forte. I dont think my experience with musicals has fitted me to direct Ibsen and Chekhov. I do think its fitted me to direct Shakespeare. [He never has, though.] I don't talk for two weeks about motivation; I wouldn't know how to spend two weeks that way. I point the actors at the end result and lead them to it; the more experienced and inventive they are, the less I have to do, the more I serve as editor.

On his first major directing assignment, an atypical musical (it might even qualify as small and delicate") called She Loves Me (1963), the actors asked a lot of awkward questions. Nowadays its easier, as he acknowledges: "I bring a whole lot of experience and reputation with me. Theyre not going to argue with me.

From She Loves Me (Bock and Harnick) to last year's Kiss of the Spider Woman (Kander and Ebb) Prince has worked with nearly all of the last great generation of Broadway composers, all like him now in their sixties: not the last talented generation but the last whom economics permitted to make a fulfilling career in the theatre. From 1970 to 1981 he worked consistently with the best known of them all.

When Steve Sondheim and I were working together, people thought we were taking the fun out of musicals. Sure we were -- for anyone who wants a steady diet of Hello, Dolly! and Mame. The six - show collaboration of Sondheim, composer - lyricist, and Prince, producer - director, is unique in theatrical history. They had known one another since 1949 -- they met at the opening night of South Pacific, one having come with Rodgers and the other with Hammerstein -- but it is unlikely that when they finally embarked on their first full collaboration they envisaged a decade's worth of joint ventures. But their talents turned out to be complementary: Sondheim digging into human character -- and especially human frailty -- in a manner unprecedented in musicals, Prince conjuring up the broad social context. (Sondheim once summed up Princes talent as the "ability to handle unconventional material in terms of truly popular theatre.") Even when their preoccupations might seem to conflict, they managed to coexist. Sondheim, the prime mover in this case, conceived the musical of Sweeney Todd (1979) as a serial - killing melodrama expanded into a tragedy of obsession; Prince -- who says I cant afford to be interested in revenge -- saw it as a parable of social alienation in the industrial age and set the whole thing in a giant factory. In strictest terms the production was too big for the play; and yet -- with archetypal performances from Len Cariou and Angela Lansbury that got the best of both worlds -- the human passions survived, and the combination looms in memory as an enormous thing. (The National Theatre in London has just staged a fine, smaller production, but it doesn't have the same impact.) Prince and Sondheim always knew how to end a show, and the closing moment of this one -- a contemptuous slam of a great door by the two leading characters, both locked in their own disgust -- was blackly witty and brilliantly powerful.

And so, in a different key, was the augustly sorrowful narrator who bade us "welcome to Japan" while a Broadway chorus, made up of Asian - Americans, raved on behind him. This was the close of their previous show, PacificOvertures (1976), which presented the forcible opening - up of Japan to European and American interests in the nineteenth century as a No or Kabuki play gradually infiltrated by the tones and techniques of the American musical. Only Prince would have wanted to turn that subject into a musical, and probably only he would have come up with that theatrical metaphor. Sondheim, who "couldn't have been less interested in politics," had to be talked into the project and then fell in love with it; Prince said, He may not come in political but he goes out political. Obviously he relished the opportunity to cauterize political opportunism, East and West (the show is remarkably even - handed); he also explored the human consequences, so that a musical chronicle with little conventional characterization was nevertheless suffused with emotion.

The production, not surprisingly, lost its entire investment; and Prince himself had to put up the money to bring it into New York. It virtually ended his career as an independent producer, though I suspect that he often regards this as a blessing in disguise. Ambitious as it was, the show was never pretentious. It seemed the logical way to tell the story. And this has been the great strength of Prince and Sondheim; they go where their intelligence leads them. Or, as Prince puts it, "I put on the stage what I would like to see myself."

This includes a lot of machinery. I sat with Prince at a technical rehearsal for the New York opening of Kiss of the Spider Woman and marvelled at his apparent command of every element of sound, setting, lighting, music, and performance; also at his good humour under pressure. He kept reverting, as he invariably does these days, to the impoverishment of Broadway; to the lack of opportunities for experiment or for developing new talent; to the prohibitive sky - high economics; to the lack of community spirit in a threatened and diminishing theatrical population; to the impossibility, in short, of a career such as his ever getting started today. He pointed to a rehearsal pianist talented enough, he said, to be the next Gershwin or Sondheim, but who would give him the break?

Well, I said, maybe you could."

The gleam in his eye suggested that he very well might.

Hey," he said sharply, turning back to the stage, "look at that." One of his favourite numbers was in progress; he has turned into an ideal father - figure, but he still seemed boyishly happy in his work.

There is more to Kiss than computerized cues. Part of the thrill of it is the expertise with which it has been manoeuvred; part is the skill in storytelling; part is the moral passion, which feels genuine; a larger part still is the music, which has real romantic appeal; and the largest part is the human element. Brent Carver's performance is about as good as I have seen in a musical. Though all three of the stars won Tonys, and the show itself was voted best musical, Prince lost out as best director. He has won as many prizes as anybody needs so one hardly needs to cry for him (yes, he directed Evita as well), but it was odd. He drove the show. And it was a swell ride.

BY JOAN PEYSER Simon and Schuster, 319 pages, $33.95

Rhapsody in black and blue THE MEMORY OF ALL THAT: The Life of George Gershwin

BY JOAN PEYSER Simon and Schuster, 319 pages, $33.95

Saturday, September 11, 1993

ROBERT CUSHMAN

GERSHWIN REMEMBERED BY EDWARD JABLONSKI Amadeus Press, 181 pages, $17.95 Review by ROBERT CUSHMAN LOOK here upon this picture and on this. Joan Peyser directs our attention to two portraits of George Gershwin. One is a Hirschfeld drawing of a composer smart and self-confident, chin and cigar rampant, addressing the piano with one set of fingers elegantly curled and the other aggressively outstretched. The second picture, painted by Gershwin himself is, says the biographer, "melancholy, thoughtful." The world is still deceived with ornament, and it has accepted the picture of an extrovert Gershwin and ignored the pain within.

You could have fooled me. Does anyone believe that Porgy and Bess -or, come to that, such popular songs as The Man I Love, But Not For Me, They Can't Take That Away From Me, Love Is Here To Stay -could have been written by a man who was not at least "thoughtful" and probably, from time to time, "melancholy" as well? Even the most superficial, pot-boiling accounts stress a dark side. His film biography, Rhapsody in Blue, presents his life as a guilt-ridden struggle; he can never enjoy his commercial success because he keeps remembering the old music-teacher who wanted him to starve in the cause of art. It has also been soberly suggested that his death in Hollywood was due not to a brain tumour but to a broken heart, brought on by the studios' refusal to treat his music with the respect it deserved. That, of course, is ludicrously sentimental, but it does suggest that the Gershwin legend has never depicted an uncomplicated golden boy.

Joan Peyser needs to believe that it has, so as to bestow on her own shadowed portrait the grace of novelty. Her book is not precisely a hatchet-job. The Gershwin it presents is less villain than victim: mainly of his own inhibitions. It seems that back in 1917 the teenaged Gershwin missed some cues while accompanying a vaudeville comedian who responded by shouting abuse at him right in front of the audience. The humiliated prodigy later recalled that "I could have lifted the piano and hurled it at him." Naturally, though, he didn't. "Such internalization of hostility and aggression," says Peyser solemnly "is not good for one's health." At that rate, 90 per cent of us must be headed for brain tumours.

When not swallowing his pride or silently smarting over bad reviews, Peyser's Gershwin, like everybody else's, is the life of the party, monopolizing the piano to spin out countless variations on his own tunes: the Gershwin who prompted Oscar Levant to ask, "George, if you had to do it all over again, would you still fall in love with yourself?" Can it be news to anyone that a man who showed off like this must have had plenty of self-doubt to assuage? Come to that, has there ever been anyone in any of the arts who was not a bundle of insecurities?

Gershwin had plenty of affairs, but steered away from any real commitment. This too is well known, but Peyser does supply more names than we are used to. She also tells a story of Gershwin going to a Paris brothel with a couple of friends who spy on him there and are astonished both by his ineptitude and by his subsequent boasts about his prowess. Curiously, she seems to think it is Gershwin rather than his companions on whom this anecdote reflects badly.

The book's real punch, however, lies in its allegation that Gershwin had an illegitimate son named Alan, who is still living, and whose chorus- girl mother left him to be brought up in poverty by relatives. Gershwin continued to see him, but furtively and infrequently. Again a picture is crucial: the book includes a photograph of the grown Alan that certainly bears a resemblance to George, though hardly a clinching one. Peyser threads Alan's tale through the book, which is good human interest but bad advocacy. She never gathers the threads together to make a really convincing case.

There are two monsters in Peyser's story. One is Gershwin's mother Rose, who contributed to her son's problems by constantly decrying his music, while enjoying the money it brought in, and by a terrifying coldness. The other is Leonore, wife of George's lyricist brother Ira. "The most striking similarity," says Peyser, "between Rose and Leonore - apart from an imperious, demanding manner - was an obsession with diamonds."

Leonore's husband, on the other hand, has always enjoyed the reputation of a saintly teddy-bear, and here Peyser does break new ground. To begin with, Ira's talent is downgraded. There is no mention of the immense contribution made by his lyrics to the charm and quiddity of the brothers' songs; George apparently took him on in order to keep the royalties in the family. The author sets our pulses racing with the suggestion that Ira's lyrics constitute a coded biography of his brother, but in fact she produces few examples, none of them very illuminating. Meanwhile Ira and money become her idee fixe. References in Ira's letters to his earnings, harmless enough to the casual eye, are continually held against him. "When George began to immerse himself in Porgy and Bess, Ira, to keep money coming in, increased his collaboration with others." I suppose that's one way of putting it.

Indeed, Peyser's approach to biography seems to be to take the worst possible view of practically everybody, a task made easier by her apparent lack of a sense of humour. The Gershwins' father, known to musical anecdotalists for his pronunciation of Fascinating Rhythm as "Fashion on the River", was asked at one of their first nights how he liked the show, he replied 'What you mean how I like it? I HAVE to like it.' Peyser: "While many writers report it as another example of Morris Gershwin's wit, it is a hostile response by an uninformed and jealous man." Well, it's possible. But how does she know?

Peyser's own comments on Gershwin's music, though sparse, are sound and sympathetic. And in further fairness to her, it is true that a hagiographic Gershwin cult has always surrounded both the brothers. Biographer and musicologist Edward Jablonski has written several books about them that are invaluable resources but leave you longing to hear that the Gershwins wrote just one imperfect song, or behaved with less than impeccable propriety. Jablonski's latest offering, Gershwin Remembered, is a flavoursome collage drawn from the immediate reactions and later reminiscences of those who were there. No mention, needless to say, of Alan Gershwin or any other unacknowledged progeny; plenty of evidence, though, pace Peyser, of unhappiness and "internal conflicts." One figure whom both authors agree on demonizing is Gregory Zilboorg, a psychoanalyst who bullied his patients and failed to notice George's developing tumour. Peyser says that Gershwin's seeking this man out was part of his self-destructiveness. Jablonski, in a frosty footnote, says that he "was merely curious about psychoanalysis and himself, not a neurotic with a mother complex, as has been suggested." So you see how it goes. Robert Cushman is a writer and broadcaster, who hosts Songbook on CBC radio.
1993-10-02-theatre-review-five-guys-name:
THEATRE REVIEW FIVE GUYS NAMED MOE

Saturday, October 02, 1993

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY CLARKE PETERS Directed by Charles Augins Starring Kevin Brackett, Doug Ekew, Milton Craig Nealy, Jeffrey Polk, Kirk Taylor and Kevin Thorne At the Royal Alexandra Theatre Rating: One guy named Louis Jolly, but lacking the true wit and musicality of the master BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto LOUIS Jordan, the 1940s king of rhythm and blues, is commonly held to be the missing link between jazz and rock 'n' roll. Actually, the more you listen to his records the jazzier he sounds. None of the fifties rockers, with the possible exception of Chuck Berry, could come anywhere near him in wit or musicality.

Five Guys Named Moe, which comes from London via New York, is an anthology of songs he sang and, in a few cases, wrote. (He got co-author credit on many of the numbers in his repertoire but the selection here is stacked against them.) The title derives from one of his earliest hits, about a fictitious jumping band whose members were all namesakes: crazy but it makes as much sense as singing sister acts. Here the five Moes emerge from a radio - in a puff of smoke, natch - to offer comfort and advice to Nomax, a young man whose girl-friend has left him: apparently with some reason though the details are left vague. By the end of the evening his visitors have taught him the error of his ways and he is all set to be a better lover and a better man. This is an interesting switch on the actual Jordan, whose only recorded advice to his listeners was that they should Let the Good Times Roll and who, when he sang What's the Use of Getting Sober (When You're Gonna Get Drunk Again), sounded as though he meant it.

Actually, the show is engagingly frank about its own inconsistencies. Most of its second half is devoted to a nightclub sequence in which the Moes drop all educational pretences and just do numbers. Then, with surprising effectiveness, it wrenches itself back to base for a medley of lovelorn ballads, including Jordan's classic Is You Is or Is You Ain't My Baby and the preternaturally haunting Don't Let the Sun Catch You Crying. The vocal style is Broadway-souls: usually the ghastly mating of two kinds of musical excess but here pared down to something spare and affecting.

None of this has much to do with Jordan's own style. For one thing, as a soloist, he never had to bother much with vocal harmonies. For another, most of his numbers - including the original Is You Is -were, in some way or other, comic. Here the show has a problem. It doesn't really have a sense of humour. It has a sense of good humour; it practically assaults the audience with jollity. But what wit there is comes between songs; the comedy in the lyrics is never released. Somewhere in the show's promotional literature is the claim that Jordan didn't shy away from addressing problems of black life in his music. That's probably true, but you wouldn't know it from what happens on stage. The show wouldn't dream of taxing its audience with anything as demanding as historical context.

In fact, a lot of the music is homogenized. Jordan could even make Calypso hip, but the show makes it an excuse for an excruciatingly extended sequence of audience participation: one of several. This kind of thing used to be confined to kiddie-shows, and its spread prompts two thoughts: 1) if spectators are going to be roped in to provide the entertainment they should start a union; 2) I have never seen a show that was so professional in its execution and so amateurish in its tone.

As for the executors: Kirk Taylor's downbeat defensiveness as Nomax makes him an increasingly sympathetic foil to the aggressive exuberance of everybody else. He even gets specific with his songs, as does Milton Craig Nealy (Four Eyed Moe), who not only dominates as performer but gradually and irresistibly takes over as host: a role initially filled by hulkingly genial Doug Eskew (Big Moe). Kevyn Brackett (Eat Moe) has a lustrous sequence of flash acrobatic tap. Charles Augins's choreography is first rate throughout, always moving, never forced. The sets are stylized-dingy, but the costumes are a symphony of coloured shirts and suspenders.

Side by side by Glynis Johns

Sondheim wrote it; just about everybody has sung it. Robert Cushman, re-starting our series, tells its story

LIVES OF THE GREAT SONGS
SEND IN THE CLOWNS

VICTORIA WOOD once wrote a musical called Good Fun whose heroine, at a point of emotional catastrophe, sang out approximately as follows: "This isn't going to be a song about clowns; I hate bloody clowns." I know how she felt. However, the song to which she was implicitly referring isn't about clowns either.

The story goes that Harold Prince, directing A Little Night Music on Broadway, summoned Stephen Sondheim, author of the music and lyrics, to rehearsals to watch how Glynis Johns, the leading lady, was playing a particular scene. The show is based on Ingmar Bergman's Smiles of a Summer Night; Johns played an actress who tries to lure her ex-lover, a lawyer, away from his unresponsive young wife. He feels the tug but cannot break free. Johns was bringing such intensity to the scene that a song seemed called for, an expression of her pent-up feelings. And so, impromptu, a song was born: not Sondheim's best song, not even his best ballad (I prefer "Not a Day Goes By", a real heartbreaker from Merrily We Roll Along), but easily his best-known.

The tale has always puzzled me. "Send in the Clowns" is Johns's only song in the musical's second act, and her only solo anywhere. Weren't they intending to give her one? The show would certainly have been unsatisfying without; in a musical songs are how we get to know people, and she is the heroine. In the event, "Send in the Clowns" not only evened the balance; it centred the show.

I found this out in stages. Night Music opened in 1973; I first saw it the following year in Toronto: the road-company version with Jean Simmons playing Desiree, the actress. I admired its elegance and I liked the music, but I was unmoved. The next week in New York I was persuaded to see it again. To begin with, the show and I kept our accustomed distance from one another. But Glynis Johns's husky humanity warmed me from her first entrance, and when she got to the song she transformed the evening. Night Music is a parade of lovers, most of them poignantly or hilariously mismatched; the pattern was clear but not very involving. Johns's song - about the acceptance of heartbreak - not only brought her own situation to life; it illuminated the complications and resolutions that were to follow and - in some not quite explicable way - made sense of what had gone before. It was as if a frieze had come to life.

The entire Night Music score is composed in waltz time, though the lilt is often disguised. "Clowns" is a sober, cold-light-of-dawn variation on the theme. It begins with a chaste woodwind statement of the melody, taken up - still soberly - by the strings. Then the voice comes in: "Isn't it rich, are we a pair . . ." The lines are short, and they could conceivably be bitter, but the tone is maturely ironic: if there is any anger she's directing it at herself and saving it up for later. This man has been chasing her and now, when she's ready to give herself, he's unavailable: "Me here at last on the ground, You in mid-air . . ." The images are economically exact if you know the story, tantalising if you don't. Sondheim habitually deals in half-truths and unconscious self-betrayals, but here Desiree is singing exactly what she feels. The greatest irony is that her partner isn't listening.

Since she is an actress, her vocabulary is theatrical. "Send in the clowns" - the phrase that, with variations, ends every section of the main strain - is the traditional command when something goes embarrassingly wrong in a circus or vaudeville and the audience has to be distracted: a kind of desperate shrug. Towards the end Desiree ruefully recognises the image's reference to herself - "Don't bother, they're here" - but she isn't indulging in Pagliacci self-pity.

The song is divided into the pop song's traditional four sections, AABA; and one of the loveliest things about it is the ease with which the A section, the main strain, flows into the B. This bridge begins in very similar vein - same rhythm, same sawn-off lines - "Just when I'd stopped / Opening doors" - and then stretches itself, gets more open and voluble - "Finally knowing the one that I wanted was yours / Making my entrance again with my usual flair" - before returning to cryptic defeat - "Sure of my lines / No one is there". We are back in the mood and meter of the main melody, so the second transition is as tight and logical as the first. At the end, when her lover has gone, Desiree sings an extra A section: an instant reprise. The short phrases were written to accommodate Johns's limited voice, which also accounts for the song's truncated range. It's meant to be acted. But it's also meant to be sung, and it's notable that Johns sang nearly every note. The glory of Sondheim's lyrics is their conversational quality, but this point is lost when people start speaking them. After all, anyone can talk conversationally.

Matter-of-fact, gently sardonic, temperamental but vulnerable, Johns's performance - of the song and the role - remains definitive. How much so was revealed in London when Jean Simmons resumed the part, and was beautiful but bland. (Elizabeth Taylor in the film was blank.) However, by the time of the West End opening, Night Music was able to advertise itself as "the 'Send in the Clowns' musical". The song had become a hit.

This was odd. Plenty of good theatre songs, including Sondheim's own, have been ignored by the pop world; and, out of its context, this one is hard to understand. But paradoxically that may have helped it. The Seventies were the time of the singer-songwriter, when the favoured style was the sensitive-obscure. "Clowns" must have seemed to fit right in with Joni Mitchell; certainly it did in Judy Collins's best-selling and totally uninflected performance. Listeners could make of it what they wished; and I swear that most of them thought it was a Pagliacci song. So did some performers. I remember a Manhattan club singer furiously embellishing the lyric: "Where are the clowns? You promised me clowns." It didn't work.

Other singers were more thoughtful. Cleo Laine, one of the first to adopt it, appreciated the drama; she was actively sad, bristlingly ironic, sometimes coming close to milking pathos but stopping in time. Some tried to explain it. Bing Crosby provided an outline of the plot, adding that he was surprised more singers hadn't taken the song up. (Where had he been? It was inescapable.) Late Bing made any song a pleasure to hear, but his mellow style hardly suited this one.

Frank Sinatra was another story. Most unusually, he provided a spoken introduction on record as well as in person: an edited but acceptable version of the facts. "This is about a couple of adult people . . . it's a break-up." His voice is at its gravest and most gravelly, and so it is in the song itself. He starts with world-weariness - the opening is slightly dismissive - then opens up, emotionally and technically, with virtuoso extended vowels - "you in mid-a-a-air, one who can't mo-o-ove" - to activate the rhythm. The accompaniment is solo piano, and there are seconds of troubled silence. "Just when I'd stopped opening doors" is harsh and abrupt, "making my entrance again with my usual flair" speeds up lightly for self-mockery, "sure of my lines . . . - no one is there" gets one of those haunted pauses. It's one of his finest, most compassionate performances; the fastidious separation of consonants on "don't you love farce" is trademark Sinatra - though this time Glynis Johns got there before him - the insistent definition giving both performances a signal authority.

The song also brought out the best in Barbra Streisand, who tackles it on her The Broadway Album without a trace of histrionics and with an orchestration closely resembling the original. She claimed never to have understood the lyric, and Sondheim obliged with a second B section that spells everything out: "What a surprise! / Who could foresee / I'd come to feel about you / What you feel about me?" I doubt that it improves the song, but it gives it a more orthodox shape.

The song has undergone other kinds of expansion from singers who feel that the one Broadway standard of the last 20 years deserves the grand manner, or can be knocked about a bit, or both. From the first it was a fixture in New York supper clubs. Mabel Mercer, the Queen Mother of cabaret, was in her 70s when it came out, and she sang it on a rising arc of passionate regret. Her successive readings of the recurring title-phrase - beginning nonchalant, ending up fierce - epitomised her fastidious fanaticism about lyrics. (I once heard her get the pronouns in the opening lines the wrong way round. She stopped, briskly apologised, and started again.) She also insisted, more firmly than any other performer, on the song's identity as a waltz. Mel Tormé made it an explosive jazz waltz, with a Stan Kenton-ish big band and a roguish introduction to the effect that he hoped the composer never got to hear about it; the lyric comes out neutral, but an all-out sarcastic whiplash approach at this tempo might be very effective.

In 1977 the song went disco, courtesy of Grace Jones, with a calliope-carousel intro to show that nobody was afraid of the obvious. Jones sings the words clearly, but they could be any words; though "making my entrance again with my usual flair" is an idea she seems to relish. This is her Broadway medley; the song segues into "What I Did for Love" and thence into "Tomorrow" - with both of which she seems to have more empathy and in both of which the beat makes more sense.

Perhaps the furthest stretch from the song's original economy was Sarah Vaughan's use of it as a showpiece encore, doubling the number of octaves the author first thought of and making all the drama strictly technical; "she holds the word my," wrote the American jazz critic Gary Giddins, "longer than you can hold your breath and then plummets into career." Whatever she was losing, it wasn't her timing.

The song, or its title, has also long served as a headline for any story involving comedians; and I once appropriated it myself to deplore some lacklustre comedy in a Shakespeare production at Stratford. "Where are the clowns? There ought to be clowns. Well, maybe next year." Unfortunately, my editor lopped off the last phrase, and I've waited all these years to reinstate it. Capers like these, added to the song by just about everybody (Ella Fitzgerald may be the only one holding out), have made it over-familiar; but it keeps coming back to life. It did in the show. At the final curtain, happy ending secured, it surges up full-bodied in the strings to feed the starved romantic in all of us. It's just as well he went to that rehearsal.
1993-12-05-jazz-ain-t-misbehavin-just-la:
JAZZ / Ain't misbehavin', just laughing at life: Robert Cushman

Robert Cushman Sunday 05 December 1993 00:02 GMT

THOMAS Fats Waller did not compose either 'My Very Good Friend the Milkman' or 'When Somebody Thinks You're Wonderful'. This may explain why neither was included in Ain't Misbehavin', the theatrical celebration of Fats that took New York by storm in the 1970s. It may have contributed to the show's failure in Britain where Waller's recordings of both numbers - one spry, the other lolloping - have always been treasured.

They were perennial favourites on Housewives' Choice in the Fifties, but I doubt if many of the choosers were hardcore jazz fans; Waller was probably more successful than anyone at translating jazz into pop. I suspect that he appealed to a wider audience even than Louis Armstrong. Armstrong's humour sometimes puzzled or unsettled people, but Waller's was an intrinsic part of the act. His singing, too, was more accessible. The voice - a high baritone - may not have been conventionally beautiful but it was clear, and uncluttered, and always in tune. It was gravelly only when its owner wanted it to be, and it always sang recognisable words; no scatting. And of course Waller the pianist had one signal advantage over Armstrong the trumpeter. He could sing and play simultaneously. His piano sparkled, and if Fats's music could hardly match Louis's for intensity that may not have hurt it with the customers. People knew Waller wanted them to be happy.

'When Somebody Thinks You're Wonderful' radiates insouciance; it's a suave foot-tapper. The 'Milkman' song is another long-line melody but one that bounces rather than glides. It's one of Waller's gentler comic turns; he doesn't have to inject humour because it's there already. The lyric is by Johnny Burke, a master of discreetly balanced whimsy, and the song tells how the singer is being willingly badgered by the local tradesmen into proposing marriage. Like many songs of the 1910s it takes pride in spinning lightly witty variations on a romantic theme. It says that being in love is a serious matter worth being funny about. Waller's gleeful performance says the same about the business of singing and playing a love-song.

The point is worth making since the standard line is that Waller despised the songs he was forced to perform and showed it by exaggerating the lyrics in his singing and deflating them with his patter, all the while reshaping the music far beyond its intrinsic worth. This is a neat combination of tricks if you can manage it, and doubtless he did from time to time. But one can't generalise. One of Waller's most virulent performances is of a sodden number called 'How Can You Face Me'. 'WOMAN,' he thunders, 'have you no conscience?' He seems to have been remarkably even-handed; the song he is mocking is one he wrote himself. Maybe he just got carried away. One of his most sardonic comments - 'I wonder what the poor people are doing tonight', with its wry sequel, 'wish I was doing it with them' - crops up in his performance (instrumental only) of a song he certainly respected: the spiritual 'Sometimes I Feel Like a Motherless Child'.

The biographers tell us that for most of his life Fats did feel like a motherless child. Born in 1904, he adored his mother, who spoilt him and whom he lost at an early age. He had an uneasy relationship with his father, a Harlem preacher who distrusted secular entertainment but none the less had a musical influence on his son; some of Waller's profoundest playing was done on the organ. He was a successful musician and composer by the end of the 1920s and a recording and radio star from the mid-1930s. He made big money (and spent it), and did time in jail for non-payment of alimony. Playing the American South, he commented bitterly on the audiences who applauded him and then barred him from their hotels. He said that many black musicians 'went South by Greyhound and returned by bloodhound'.

It's conceivable that he wasn't even too thrilled by his weight. He had a good-time image in work and in life, but he was warned that his eating and more especially his drinking might kill him, and eventually they did. He died, 50 years ago next week, on a train from Los Angeles to New York; of pneumonia, but it would not have got him if his system had not been so thoroughly abused. The familiar pictures of Fats, all derby hat and roguish grin, suggest a man laughing compulsively and therefore defensively, not at music but at life.

Which doesn't mean the laughter wasn't genuine. On his recording of 'Until the Real Thing Comes Along', a middling-good song, he interrupts the musical flow of protestations about what he'll do for love with a quickfire 'You want me to rob a bank, well I won't'. It bubbles up out of nowhere, and he gets back to singing without a break in rhythm. His biggest hit, 'I'm Gonna Sit Right Down and Write Myself a Letter', goes by without an interpolation. Maybe he sensed that the song was its own little joke, needing no embroidery. His opening instrumental chorus harks back to the Harlem pianists' roots in ragtime: not in its metre but in its delicate, contemplative tone. He then takes a plaintive, understated vocal - no kidding, and with a clarinet obbligato reinforcing the mood - and a rejected song turns into a standard before our ears. It's undergone some strange mutations since, including a feverish performance from Lena Horne that so muddles the pronouns you want to sit her right down and ask her just who she thinks is writing what to whom.

I get the same feeling from Waller's most celebrated comedy turn, 'Your Feet's Too Big'. Nobody could resist a song with such a title, and you can hear Waller taking off on it, pounding out the rhythm, inflating the title into 'your pedal extremities are colossal'. But I still don't know whose feet are being arraigned: his own or a male or female friend's. It's very frustrating.

Most of Waller's own songs were written before stardom struck, and he only returned on disc to the best-known of them: to 'Honeysuckle Rose', or 'Ain't Misbehavin' ', which may have the best title of any song ever, so casually, wickedly disarming in its double negative. Very Fats. One of his last recordings was a slow version of it with wonderful piano runs that make a square-cut staccato tune sound languorous.

In his last year Waller returned to composing, becoming the first black composer to write a non- black Broadway show, a carnal romp called Early to Bed. The show is forgotten and so, undeservedly, are the songs. They include the best ballad he wrote, 'There's a Man in My Life', and a first-rate comedy production number, 'The Ladies Who Sing with the Band', which suggest that, had he lived, he might have become a major theatre composer. The tag-line for a talent so bountiful, so agreeable, and so self-destructive, is inescapable. One never knows. Do one?

'Ain't Misbehavin' ', a CD EP containing six of Waller's hits, is released on 13 Dec (BMG/RCA). 'Lives of the Great Songs' returns next week.
