SPECTATOR The art of corruption, where British TV is king

Saturday, February 12, 1994

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to the Globe and Mail FOR some months now my most compulsive TV date has been with the British drama series Inside the Line, about crooked cops. Over the last four weeks, though, it has had to share my favours with the British drama series To Play the King, about one spectacularly crooked politician.

A lot of the attraction of both shows has lain in the acting - not just its quality but its familiarity. These are the actors I grew up on. I watched Ian Richardson, the lizardly Francis Urquhart of To Play the King, over some 16 years of work with the Royal Shakespeare Company, working his way up from fops and minor villains to tragic monarchs, high comic lovers and major villains. (Most of that experience must have come in useful for Urquhart: a ruler, a killer, a sexual magnet and a fastidiously natty dresser.) Richardson, maybe the last major British actor in the ringingly precise John Gielgud tradition, became a Shakespearean virtuoso, exhilarating to watch and listen to because he was in such total control of his means. He still is. Nobody else's voice flashes such effortless steel, while to find a precedent for his chillingly cozy conspiratorial asides to camera you have to go back to Olivier's Richard III. On TV the only precedent for such convention-shattering intimacy is George Burns in the halcyon days of the Burns and Allen show.

Soliloquy ought to be a natural for television, but it's hardly ever tried. Its appearance on To Play the King and its predecessor House of Cards derives, like so much in British television, from the theatre. Actually the best British TV surpasses - in wit, trenchancy and narrative skills - most of what's being offered on the English stage. But, in terms of tradition, the theatre contributes hugely: The writers and directors are theatre-influenced, the actors are - overwhelmingly - theatre-trained.

The writing and performance of To Play the King, with its obsessive references to the archetypal usurpers Richard and Macbeth, are obviously joke-classical, and the joke is all the richer for being played by people who could do it straight. Inside the Line, like other cop series before it, comes out of the tradition of naturalistic protest associated for nearly 40 years with London's Royal Court Theatre - though there is no rigid divide between classic and modern and the same people move between the two sectors to the benefit of both. Nearly every instalment of Inside the Line features some old sweat from the National Theatre as a senior policeman who before the hour is out will have been revealed accepting bribes, beating up suspects or suppressing evidence. All these guys are actors of weight; some have been my favourites for so long - one or two of them are friends - that I find myself instinctively rooting for them, but it seems the more respectable your lineage the guiltier you inevitably are. Neil Pearson, playing the younger officer from Complaints Division whose job it is to expose them, is so right in this role that I find it hard to imagine him in any other. His Superintendent Clark is an abrasive, philandering cynic whose saving grace is that he is dedicated to his job and does it honestly and compared to most of what's going on around him - humanely.

If British TV drama comes out of theatre, American comes, naturally, out of cinema. But the results look inevitably like cut-rate movies, than which nothing is more deadening. The background music ends up doing most of the acting, and does it garishly, sucking out the life. American TV has never been much on live actors; its best shows are Sesame Street and The Simpsons. NYPD Blue, the U.S. equivalent of Inside the Line, is incorrigibly glossy, however hard it tries to be gritty.

The bent coppers of Inside the Line, protected by official apathy or official complicity, get away with it more often than not. This is in step with the despair that has understandably infected political theatre in Britain since Thatcherism came in, and that has trickled down to films and TV. Still, Clark and his team survive to fight another week so the conventions of the genre are not altogether breached. The Francis Urquhart saga has ditched them completely. This was not so evident in House of Cards, where F. U. was the outsider intriguing for the premiership and as such had our imaginative sympathy if not our approval. But in To Play the King he has been the man in power; we have been shown the tyrant triumphant. This is unprecedented: even Marlowe's invincible Tamburlaine had finally to give in to Death. Upping the ante, To Play the King gave us not only the victory of the villain but the defeat of the hero, Hamlet going down without Claudius.

House of Cards didn't have a hero, only dupes and victims. It didn't really have politics either; Urquhart's foils were wets and softies so we assumed he was a hard-liner, but little was made of it. In the sequel he stood revealed as an authoritarian inching toward fascism, and the only man apparently capable of stopping him was the monarch. Michael Kitchen's puzzled, caring king transcended the obvious (and delicious) impersonation of Prince Charles to become a genuine serio-comic creation; he got and deserved equal billing with Richardson. Why royalists objected I cannot imagine; this was the best publicity the throne has had in years. All our hopes were pinned on him; up to the last moment the plot and all our expectations of poetic justice pointed to his victory; and then he lost. It was, unquestionably, more like real life than most drama; and it was very hard to take.

Andrew Davies, who wrote the screenplay, is about as good a playwright as Britain has, in any medium. His double series A Very Peculiar Practice surpassed anything by the acknowledged TV masters, Dennis Potter or Alan Bleasdale, and his adaptations - the bulk of his work - are the best there are. He has a version of Middlemarch that's currently a hit on the BBC, and is presumably en route for Masterpiece Theatre. I worry though whether, as is rumoured, he could go a third round with F. U. If Urquhart remains victorious he could become as predictable as Perry Mason in reverse, but to bring him down now might seem like cheating. (Will the icy Mrs. U. anticipate her inevitable elevation to Lady U. by taking up sleep- walking? I can't see it.) But, if and when it happens, I'll be there. Meanwhile I shall have to get my fix from the cops. What a dull world it would be without corruption.
1994-02-26-the-life-and-songs-of-a-scand:
ELLA FIZGERALD BY STUART NICHOLSON Gollancz, 286 pages, $30

The life and songs of a scandal-free first lady

ELLA FIZGERALD BY STUART NICHOLSON Gollancz, 286 pages, $30

Saturday, February 26, 1994

ROBERT CUSHMAN

THE COMPLETE ELLA FITZGERALD SONG BOOKS Verve 314 519 832-2, 16 CDs Review by ROBERT CUSHMAN FEW singers get good biographies, but Stuart Nicholson's Ella Fitzgerald, timed to the singer's 75th birthday year (she was born on April 25, 1918), will more than do. Famously shy and reclusive, notoriously straight, Fitzgerald is a tough item for a chronicler. She has been successful since she was a teen-ager, her life has been devoid of scandal and everybody loves her, though few really know her.

Nicholson endearingly quotes a press agent's description of Fitzgerald as "sweet and charming as can be" until asked to do an interview, at which point "her face will fall and she'll stamp her foot and say, "Gosh, darn it, Virginia, I can't do it - I have to go SHOPPING]'" Her petulance here sounds little-girlish, as befits a singer who had her first (and biggest) hit at age 21, with A-Tisket A-Tasket.

She had already been dubbed the First Lady of Song, a nickname that has stuck ever since. Youthful prodigies rarely endure so well, so her life might seem to have been the plainest of sailing. In fact her early life was tough - tougher, on Nicholson's showing, than has previously been suspected. Childhood (Yonkers, New York, in the 1920s) wasn't bad; it was poor, and her parents split up, but she was good in class and apparently happy. When she was 15, though, her mother died, and soon after, Fitzgerald dropped out of school. In 1934, when she entered an amateur- night contest at the Harlem Apollo, she was living on the streets. What happened then is legend. She was going to dance, but nervousness made her switch to singing at the last moment. She faltered, recovered herself and won.

Professional work was slow to follow, largely because she wasn't presentable. A friend says: "She hadn't had a bath and smelt like it could have been a year . . . . She lived with people she talked to, and she ate with them, she slept wherever she could." Eventually, though, she was taken on by drummer and band leader Chick Webb, who groomed her and spotlit her (though he didn't, contrary to legend, adopt her), and, in an age when singers other than Bing Crosby were still second-class citizens, made her a star. After Webb's premature death, Fitzgerald fronted his band for a couple of years, then became one of the first band singers to go solo.

Musicians, it seems, were awed by her range, her tonal warmth and her innate swing, but they weren't too fond of her personally. They found her snippy. As the years pass the quotes change, and adoration takes over; insecurities that are forbidding in a newcomer become endearing in a celebrity. Fitzgerald - though hardly prey to the demons that destroyed Billie Holiday or Judy Garland - has obviously had her share. She has inevitably faced racial prejudice; as a girl she felt gawky and as a woman overweight. She has had two brief marriages, and a series of shadowy affairs. But her prime relationship has been with her audiences, and unlike some other love affairs between performer and public it has been creative rather than morbid.

Nicholson tells of a celebratory evening for Fitzgerald in 1955 at which she told the audience: "I guess what everyone wants is to be loved. And to know that you can love me for my singing is too much for me. . . . Maybe I can sing it and you'll understand." I'm especially fond of that quote since I originally encountered it on the back of the first Fitzgerald album (and one of the first records of any kind) that I bought: Ella Fitzgerald Sings the Cole Porter Songbook, Volume One. It was the first of a series recorded between 1956 and 1964: 19 LPs devoted to the songs of 10 major U.S. songwriters. They have been constantly reissued, and here they finally are in a single package: 16 CDs in a cute red box.

The songbooks were the brainchild of Norman Granz. Granz had presented Fitzgerald in his Jazz at the Philharmonic concerts since 1949, he became her manager in 1953, and in '56, after serpentine negotiations with Decca, who owned her disc, he began recording for his own new label, Verve. Their association endures to this day. Granz had discerned in Fitzgerald virtually two distinct vocalists. One was the rhythmic and harmonic virtuoso, out of swing and into bop, who could scat and improvise with endless bravura and invention. The other was a ballad singer whose range, ease and beauty of tone - a comfortable, unthreatening beauty rather than an awesomely operatic one like Sarah Vaughan's - could make any song a pleasant experience.

As well as being a jazz buff, Granz was a song freak. He assembled generous quantities of the best songs of the best composers, sat Fitzgerald down in front of them, and let the tape roll. The results, as John McDonough says in his new liner notes, "change the way we hear our music." A canon was established of the American popular song. For myself, and I imagine I am one of many, the songbooks were a major part of my education.

There have always been objections to the songbooks, from two schools of purists. Jazz fans with no interest in songs point out that the albums' heavy orchestral settings preclude improvisation. Theatre fanatics, mindful that most of these songs come from shows, cite Fitzgerald's limitations as an actress. Both object to the singer's lack of "personal involvement." Actually the absence of heavy drama is often a blessing. One of the rarest treats of the cycle is Irving Berlin's You Can Have Him, in which a woman feigns gladness to be rid of her man by listing the mundane domestic things she wanted to do for him. The few other divas who have tackled it (Nancy Wilson, Nina Simone) have slowed it to a self-pitying dirge; trying to bring out the irony, they have squelched it. Fitzgerald's voice is gentle, her pace brisk, her manner matter-of-fact, and her effect extremely touching. This may be luck or it may be judgment - hers or Granz's or arranger Paul Weston's; what matters is that it happens. And that in a song crammed with detail, every word tells, simply because you can hear and understand it.

Her perfect (though totally unaffected) diction lights up the list- songs that typify this era: most spectacularly, Porter's You're the Top. Even if she didn't get all the references, we do. Actually I think that Fitzgerald's deficiencies as a lyric interpreter have been grossly exaggerated, certainly in comedy songs. She does have a comic personality: a wryly innocent, self-mocking wickedness, a husk in the throat that's the vocal equivalent of a raising of the eyebrows or a hopeless throwing-up of hands, whether she's assassinating a succession of husbands (To Keep My Love Alive, Rodgers and Hart) or contemplating life with just one creep ( Boy! What Love Has Done to Me, Gershwin). And on the Kern songbook, she makes I'll Be Hard to Handle, which has an atrociously clumsy lyric by somebody's nephew, a lot funnier than anyone else is ever likely to.

If the songbook series has two hidden heroes, they are Fitzgerald's long-time accompanist Paul Smith, who plays sensitive and inspiring piano on every record though not on every track, and Alvin Stroller, whose drumming sparks every disc except the last one. The 32 Porter songs are a reasonable, if bowdlerized, cross-section of his output - but jaded was never Fitzgerald's style.

She is far happier with the bittersweet of Rodgers and Hart, and here Buddy Bregman's functional arrangements are less of a handicap; the songs are the thing, and their wit and tenderness are dazzling, eternally youthful material for an externally youthful singer. This was the songbook that opened most windows for me. Still, it's a relief to hear Fitzgerald in the next installment with the Duke Ellington band, in one of its best incarnations. A ringer in the series, since Ellington's were not show songs, it holds up very well. The sound is rich, Fitzgerald gets to stretch out (hear her joy on Drop Me Off in Harlem), Johnny Hodges has a honey-dripping solo on I Got it Bad, and there are some lovely small-group sides on the numbers the Duke's band didn't want to play.

The Berlin set has the series' most imaginative selection of songs, and from Paul Weston, working in the fifties cool style, the most distinctive arrangements so far. They are eclipsed, though, by the next batch. Granz brought over Nelson Riddle for a recklessly expensive five-LP set of George and Ira Gershwin. The 53 songs had perforce to be "ground out" in the studio, but as Paul Smith comments in Nicholson's book, it somehow never sounds that way. Nearly every song comes complete with verse, each given as much thought as the chorus that follows. Riddle's orchestrations are suave and endlessly inventive, and Fitzgerald's easy swing is an exact translation of George's own; while Ira's lyrics, love songs that keep an amused and beguiling distance from their subject, are perfect for her.

Some prefer the succeeding Harold Arlen volumes, with muscular arrangements by Billy May that give the musicians (notably Benny Carter) an unaccustomed main chance. The choice of songs, though, is almost unrelentingly mainstream. Arlen's earthy style is at the opposite extreme from Porter's refined one, but it reveals Fitzgerald's limitations in much the same way. She is best in the middle ground.

The two remaining songbooks are addenda, tributes to Jerome Kern and Johnny Mercer, given a scant one volume apiece; either money or enthusiasm was running out.

No straight or theatre singer could hold your attention for so long; no jazz or personality singer could cover so many bases, though some have dealt more memorably with individual songs. Fitzgerald's mixture of self- assertion and self-effacement, her strengths as little girl and first lady - or Granz's selection among her strengths - are exactly right for the project, and the project itself is a major service to humanity. It does not exhaust the repertoire but for three decades it has pointed the way to further discovery.

A word about the packaging. This is a Chinese box set. The outer case contains two smaller cases to house the multi-disc Gershwin and Ellington sets, plus a mini-sleeve for each of the less ambitious compilations. Each disc also has its own inner sleeve. The compacting of everything means that we get all the original liner notes, the Gershwin ones amounting to a doll's house book; they come in print too small to read without a magnifying glass but it's comforting to know they're there. The producers would, I thought, be caught out by the original Gershwin sleeves; Granz, at his most prodigal, had commissioned a Bernard Buffet lithograph on each of the five LPs, and these could hardly fit onto three CDs. Not to worry; they come anyway, in a separate envelope. Who could ask for anything more? Robert Cushman is a writer and broadcaster who hosts Songbook on CBC radio.

HAROLD PINTER and Peter Brook have gone beyond being legends in their own lifetimes. They are myths.

There hardly seems to have been a time when Pinter was merely a successful playwright. One moment - 1958, actually - The Birthday Party, his first full-length play, was a three-performance flop savaged by nearly every critic. The next - well, almost the next, 1960 - his second full-length play, The Caretaker, was an instant classic, and incontestably The Play To See In London.

No subsequent British play has quite achieved that status, and no subsequent British playwright has been accorded the same cultural authority. We talk occasionally of something being Stoppardian or Ayckbournian, but never with the same confidence, the same certainty of being understood, as when we dub an action, a line, a moment - in life or art - Pinterish or Pinteresque. The man is a fact of English literature.

This can make meeting him in the flesh daunting. When he first spoke to me - I don't think I would have had the nerve to speak first to him - it was a little like being accosted by T. S. Eliot. There was this thing abroad, this body of work called Pinter, and you didn't expect to encounter it in a suit. You certainly didn't expect it to start quizzing you about your own work, which is what he did to me, asking me to clarify something I had said in a column the previous week. He really seemed to want to know. I felt elated.

When it comes to talking about his own work, Pinter has been famously unforthcoming. His own reticence has fused in the general imagination with the celebrated opacity of his plays; their refusal to supply what others would regard as essential information.

This was what most infuriated critics about The Birthday Party and, it seemed, what most impressed them about The Caretaker. The turnaround was lightning-fast; it was eased by a TV production of The Birthday Party that played up the sinister ballooning cross-talk of the dialogue to the point of gimmickry, but was totally riveting.

The concept of Pinterism was born, I suspect, in that production, which prepared a large audience for the subtler virtuosity of The Caretaker whose star role - the lying, scheming, pitiable tramp Davies - may be the last great character creation in British drama ("You were in the colonies, weren't you?" "I was over there, I was one of the first over there"). He takes on independent life through his author's mastery of language: his ability to take familiar speech rhythms and make them sing, to build up long tirades and crown them with catchphrases.

This mastery of tone remained when Pinter - perhaps reflecting his own material success - moved into glossier stage surroundings; the speeches of Spooner, the poetaster of No Man's Land, are quirky and elegant at once, and frostily witty. No other current playwright writes as well; he established his authority by insisting, almost to the point of perversity, that his plays speak for themselves and by giving them a triumphant voice to do it in.

Pinter, however the academics may celebrate or condemn him, is an exceptionally adroit nuts-and-bolts playwright, who works through comedy and suspense. Peter Brook, who ranks among theatre directors as the guru's guru, has a similar command of showbiz values. In his youth, he directed musicals, drawing-room comedies, and pictorial Shakespeares, and even the most ascetic or exotic of his more recent works are designed to have maximum impact as shows.

The Ik, his study of a starving and predatory African tribe, was as casually stark as he could make it. Ubu Roi, the foundation stone of the Theatre of the Absurd, was as anarchically funny as he could make it. Both displayed a very light touch. These latter-day Brook productions originated from his International Centre for Theatre Research, a multi-ethnic troupe based at the Theatre des Bouffes-du-Nord in Paris. There is a sense of Brook holding court, either in the theatre or the cafe opposite; he enjoys being a sage.

The Bouffes-du-Nord is an old suburban theatre with much of its interior torn out. It looks at once the essence of all theatres and the negation of one: the paradox is obviously intentional and very Brookish. He seems sometimes to want to get away from the idea of theatre altogether, and once took his actors on a tour of African villages, playing to people who had never seen anything approaching the European idea of drama.

The trip was much publicised, and widely attacked as a piece of fake primitivism. But Brook has never claimed that what he was doing was superior to playing to bourgeois audiences, in orchestra stalls, just that it was different and might shed some light on the irreducible essence that keeps audiences looking at actors in the first place.

Brook started the tradition of the brilliant post-war just-graduated director, a line over which he still presides. He still seems like a prodigy, having been the premier director in the British theatre probably since 1946 when, at 21, he directed a ravishing Love's Labour's Lost at Stratford.

His austere Measure for Measure and horror-comic Titus Andronicus were the leading Stratford productions of the Fifties; and, in the Sixties, he moved into the reconstituted Royal Shakespeare Company with a monumental King Lear - you could practically smell greatness on it - and with The Marat-Sade, a historical-philosophical piece which he staged like a musical.

In 1970, came the legendary Midsummer Night's Dream which Brook described as his return, after a spate of fearsome Vietnam-era productions, to the light.

It was also virtually his farewell to Britain. But, despite two decades of apparent exile, everybody thinks of him still as part of the British theatre. He never went away, just as Pinter, despite writing little more than playlets in the Eighties, was never seriously thought to have dried up. They still set the standard.

A revival of Pinter's The Birthday Party opens at The National Theatre on Thursday (071-928 2252). Peter Brook's The Man Who begins a national tour at the Contact Theatre, Manchester on Wednesday (061-242 2555).
1994-04-02-theatre-review-once-on-this-i:
THEATRE REVIEW ONCE ON THIS ISLAND

Saturday, April 02, 1994

ROBERT CUSHMAN

LYRICS by LYNN AHRENS MUSIC by STEPHEN FLAHERTY Directed by Bob Baker Canadian Stage Company Rating: The Toronto production of Once On This Island may be lacking in natural hoofers, but there are impressive lyrics and some good musical numbers in an adult show that has some of the virtues of good children's theatre Musical love story ends up in tropical foliage BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail BRIEFLY: girl gets boy, girl loses boy, girl turns into tree. That is a tidier and more engaging story than most musicals have these days, and what is most impressive about Once On This Island is its single-minded dedication to telling it.

First seen in New York four years ago, the show is The Little Mermaid dried out and transposed to the Caribbean. Somewhere in the French Antilles poor Ti Moune falls for rich Daniel. She nurses him back to life after a car-crash, but neither he nor his family has any intention of letting this liaison be permanent. Daniel marries his childhood sweetheart; Ti Moune is cast out and dies.

No fairy story, this still has a supernatural superstructure. Ti Moune has attracted the attentions of four suitably jealous gods, three of them more or less benevolent but the fourth, Papa Ge, is the Demon of Death. A sinuously cavorting devil with patent Broadway connections (call him Sportin' Death), he makes a deal with Ti Moune: Daniel's life for her soul. Later on he reverses the offer: her soul for his death. It is one of the strengths of the show that Ti Moune really is mad enough to take a knife to her beloved; it is a further and greater strength that when one of the nicer deities intervenes we still believe that her final decision is her own. All the gods can do is transform her into foliage in which guise, says the synopsis in the program (and if they can give it away, why can't I?) "she sheltered peasants and grands hommes alike." Whether this has had any permanent effect on the island's class structure we are not told.

Oh, yes, I'm glad you asked. The grands hommes are the Beauxhommes, Daniel's mob, and they are not your ordinary sneering aristocrats. They are a special kind of sneering aristocrat, descendants of a French lord and a native girl. In other words, half the cast are half-caste: barred from France for being black, despised on the island for not being black enough. The Beauxhommes carry a burden of self-hatred that the show might probe more deeply than it does. But there are some stabbing moments. "I am Daniel's mistress," cries Ti Moune as the gates slam on her. She is also in love with him, but this he has never noticed. It's left to his washed- out fiancee to point it out - without prejudice to their marriage. Daniel's own attitude is expressed and exposed in a beautifully crafted song - light in its ironies, tight in its rhymes - called Some Girls. As in some you marry, some you love. Whose feelings is he trying to spare?

Lynn Ahrens's lyrics are impressive throughout. After a diet of Tim Rice and his lesser successors - the kind of lyrics that make one good joke and then lean back exhausted - it's a blessing to encounter a writer whose words, though short on obvious flash, always land in the right place. She also wrote the book, which is skeletal but firm. Again, it's a relief to find a show that has one; dialogue really is better than doggerel. Stephen Flaherty's music is more problematic; calypso and reggae, the obvious modes here, have severe dramatic limits, and when the score tries to step outside them it falls too often into the mode I think of as Euro-Broadway: the kind that tries to soar without first establishing a base. The big ballads are the weakest songs. But a musical scena called Rain is exciting and, as staged, a worthy addition to the long line of umbrella numbers.

I remember the New York production, staged by Graciela Daniele, as one long exhilarating dance. Few of the Toronto cast look like natural hoofers, and this version (directed by Bob Baker, choreographed by Mabel Robinson) is comparatively flat-footed. But it tells the story at least as well, and - most importantly - communicates a joy in doing so. This is an adult show with some of the virtues of good children's theatre. Leslie Frankish's set is routine cardboard cut-out in its basics, but some beguiling things pop out of it. The strongest singer in the cast, Salome Bey, is also the strongest presence; I only wish that as Ti Moune's mother she had more to do. Strength seems to run in the family with Ti Moune's dad (Jeff Jones) a haggard rock, and Cee-Cee Harshaw, the girl herself, assertive as well as sweet.
1994-04-06-reaching-for-the-king-s-crown:
GOODBYE, Renaissance Theatre Company. Or, at the very least, au revoir. The announcement of the company's closure stresses that there will be no more Renaissance films but says that the theatrical end of the operation will retain a nominal existence "in case we want to resurrect it". So there could be a renaissance of Renaissance. But I doubt if anyone is betting on it.

The obvious thought is that the company has been the victim of its own success. Or, more precisely, of Kenneth Branagh's success. The company's moving spirit is currently directing Robert De Niro in Frankenstein. When you are in demand for that grade of movie project, running a theatre company must be difficult to fit in. The wonder may be that he has managed to keep it going at all for seven years.

Some more obvious heavyweights have done less well. When the young Orson Welles went out to Hollywood he took his Mercury Theatre actors from New York with him. The Mercury label was attached to his first two movies, Citizen Kane and The Magnificent Ambersons, but neither the name nor the acting ensemble were heard from subsequently. Albert Finney, despite associations with the National Theatre, the Royal Court, and an outfit of his own, has never found a long-term theatrical niche. Ian McKellen originated from the Actors' Company in the 1970s and devoted himself to it for three years. Despite its co-operative ideals, it was never the same after he left.

Renaissance started with some of the same professed aims as the Actors' Company. It was to be an expression of actors, rather than of directors and administrators. It was to present an alternative - though without that word's political overtones - to the established classical companies. It never claimed to be egalitarian.

Branagh has directed and/or starred in all the productions and he even wrote the first play. It has been not so much his showcase as his springboard. It has propelled him into areas of success that he might have reached in any case, but never as quickly. The big leap, of course, was Henry V. To direct and star in the film soon after acting the role on stage was to court inevitable comparisons with Laurence Olivier. And however British critics debate the differences between the two, on a global scale that courtship has succeeded.

I live in Canada, where it is taken for granted, even by people who have never seen him, that Branagh is the world's leading Shakespearean actor. And, like Olivier, he owes that position to his films. He has made only two Shakespeare movies to Olivier's four, but that is two more than most actors can claim. And he has gone beyond Olivier in one respect: Olivier filmed two histories and two tragedies, all with himself in the title-role, all of them - as Shakespeare plays go - natural movie subjects; Branagh went on to do Much Ado About Nothing, riskier because a comedy (dependent on atmosphere, full of obscure jokes) and an ensemble piece. His own laughing-boy performance of Benedick was actually one of the weaker elements. But the film worked.

Olivier once said that directing movies was the most exciting thing he ever did. But he came late to it and only directed one mainstream (that is, non-Shakespearean) picture: the undistinguished The Prince and the Showgirl. Branagh, starting young, has moved insouciantly on to Hollywood's own turf, directing thriller spoofs and horror pictures. He seems to be, as Olivier never was, a career film director.

But Branagh is not, as Olivier was, a career film actor. Here it is worth looking at the two actors' early careers and at what they tell us about British theatre now and between the wars.

Olivier staked his claim as a classical actor at the Old Vic in 1937 and 1938, beginning with Hamlet. He was 30, already known in the West End as a juvenile lead and with a solid grounding at Birmingham Rep.

Branagh, like most of the meteors of his generation, bypassed rep (which barely exists now, in the permanent-company sense); although, with his chipper solidity, he is one of the few who can be imagined doing time there. He made his mark, straight out of drama school, in the West End play Another Country, and was next heard of at Stratford playing Henry V. He was 21, and brought to the role a heaven-sent mixture of beamish youth and iron-clad confidence. After that he founded Renaissance, which has kept him, despite the filmic excursions, constantly in the theatre: in London, Stratford, Chichester, and on national and international tours.

The young Olivier was more fickle. After the Old Vic he went to Hollywood, only returning to the stage towards the end of the war, again at the Old Vic, which he and Ralph Richardson (co-stars and co-directors) took to unprecedented heights. After that it was movies again; plays, too, of course, but never for long runs. In fact it was not until he became director of the National Theatre in 1963 that you could be sure, theatrically, where to find him. From 1974, when he left the National, until the end of his life he was wholly a movie man.

It's a smaller world now, certainly for British actors. Paradoxically, while American actors have to choose between the East Coast and the West, stage and screen, Britons seem able to hop continents with relative freedom. The end of Renaissance may signal Branagh's intention to devote himself to films, but it doesn't have to - and if it does, it is more likely to be as a director.

One obvious difference between the two films of Henry V is that Olivier's was made as wartime propaganda while Branagh's came out of the more customary 20th-century mood of military disillusion. But that is not the only reason why Olivier trumpeted his speeches, while Branagh talked them. They were playing in their personal styles, Olivier's the more exciting and memorable, Branagh's the more congenial and credible.

For a star actor, Branagh is uncannily unmanicured, which may mean that he is not actually a star. Or, more exactly, not a movie star, which Olivier certainly was. Although the cinema is supposed to reject rhetoric and rejoice in naturalism, it has never been too keen on ordinary chappiness. (Dustin Hoffman is not ordinary, and neither, even when young, was Marlon Brando.) Live audiences, however, like to be talked to in their own language, especially when it's done with flair and cheek.

Branagh is a terrific comic: something the movies have so far failed to capture. I loved his performance as Peter Quince in his own production of A Midsummer Night's Dream: a village savant who, when it came to rehearsing his rude mechanicals, suddenly mutated into Erich von Stroheim, complete with megaphone. Critics protested at the inconsistency, apparently not realising it was precisely the image this Quince, who had undoubtedly read too many books about directing, would think appropriate. It was also a nice joke on his own position as actor-manager. Renaissance established no individual style or ethic, and it did disappointingly little to bring on young actors, but it did do something equally important: it recharged the batteries of older ones, encouraging Judi Dench and Geraldine McEwan to try their hands at directing and establishing Richard Briers as a major classical performer.

Olivier's record as a commercial manager was far less distinguished; people forget that he even had one. Branagh must be sick of the comparison, but he must be aware that if an actor is ever again to run the National, he - with the exception of McKellen - is the only one to have staked a claim.

THEATRE / It's only a part of love: The word is that 'Passion'

Robert Cushman Saturday 21 May 1994 19:02 EDT

STEPHEN SONDHEIM has frequently been criticised for not writing songs that say 'I love you' straight out. This seems to me more of a virtue than a vice, especially when you consider the recent musicals that have fallen over themselves to say it, usually in the most bloated, generalised and pseudo-poetic terms. In treating the subject urbanely, circuitously, or obliquely, Sondheim has been following an older and nobler Broadway tradition.

Anyway he has written plenty of touching romantic songs, though admittedly they have tended to do with love misprized, misplaced, or simply missed. His new show Passion, which has just opened on Broadway, is, as both its title and advance publicity suggested, the nearest he has got to a direct take on love reciprocated and attained. If taken as a definitive statement on the subject it's frightening, and more than a little suspect. Passion and love may overlap, but they are not the same thing. As a study of a special case it's convincing and compelling.

The case in question is Fosca, a 19th-century Italian woman who is sickly - dying, in fact - and ugly. She is also intelligent, shameless, infuriating, a moral and emotional blackmailer. Her prey is Giorgio, a handsome young army officer whom we first meet in bed with his equally presentable married mistress, assuring one another that nobody in the world has ever loved as they do, or words and notes to that effect. By the end this affair has proved too conventional to stand up under pressure, most of it applied by Fosca. At curtain-fall Giorgio is singing a different love-song: Sondheim at his most fastidiously stark. Fosca's obsessive-possessive devotion has, finally and painfully, awakened a corresponding devotion in him.

Passion is based on a film by the Italian director Ettore Scola, itself derived from a novel. One can see why it attracted Sondheim. Obsession is one of his themes. Think of Mama Rose in Gypsy, Seurat in Sunday in the Park with George, Sweeney Todd, the entire cast of Assassins - most of them, come to think of it, sexy and capable of inspiring love though not too good at returning it. Mostly, they turn their lovers off. Fosca turns hers on by turning him off; in the show's most brilliant number she dictates to Giorgio, from her sickbed, the love- letter she would like him to write and he, torn between pity and embarrassment, complies.

That sounds horribly funny. So does the idea of Giorgio, bouncing between his two flames and getting increasingly scorched. So does Giorgio embracing the love of his life, while knowing she is under effective sentence of death. But that is all in the story, not in the treatment. Apart from some perfunctory writing for Giorgio's brother officers, there is less humour here than in any other Sondheim score.

I regret that, but I think I can see the reason. I have to do some guessing here, not having seen the movie, but people who have describe it as a black farce, with Fosca an outright grotesque. The adaptor-writer James Lapine (Sondheim's collaborator on Sunday in the Park and Into the Woods) has softened and humanised it. Donna Murphy, the stunning young actress-singer who plays Fosca, is something new in Broadway divas: she makes her most powerful points quietly. Her voice encompasses dark cello notes that alternately soothe and disturb; her presence is a standing, or reclining, rebuke to the comparatively happy or healthy people around her. She is plain and severe, but she is not hideous; if she were a female Phantom of the Opera or Hunchback of Notre-Dame it would actually be easier.

We could feel sorry and dismiss her, as if she were a fairy-tale. The show allows us to resent her manipulations, but it asks us to believe in her and respect her. And, while the music is playing, we do.

Giorgio has more work but less opportunity; the show is actually his journey but in Jere Shea's performance he emerges as little more than a hard-pressed juvenile lead with a good voice. Lapine's staging, minimalist by current Broadway standards but lavish by most others, uses spare suggestive sets that only hit trouble towards the end when they have to run rather hard to keep up with the story; his dialogue, of which there is a good deal, is admirably functional. The show is a favourite to win the Tony Awards for new musical (the only real competition is the Disney stage version of Beauty and the Beast, which has some thematic similarities), so Broadway audiences, and London audiences later, should have some time to respond to its demands. These are not unprecedentedly harsh but they are unusual; girl, in a manner of speaking, gets boy, and we are challenged to feel good about it. I would hate to think that Sondheim and Lapine feel that this is all there is to say about love, but it makes a stimulating interim report.

Plymouth Theater, 236 W 45 St, New York (0101 212 239 6200): Mon-Sat 8pm, mats Wed & Sat 2pm.

THEATRE REVIEW DEATH AND THE MAIDEN

Monday, May 23, 1994

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY ARIEL DORFMAN Directed by Jonas Jurasas Starring Robert Haley, Fiona Reid and R. H. Thomson The Canadian Stage Company Rating: This production of a worthy, gripping story banishes an essential doubt Death and the Maiden revisited BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto THE story-line of Ariel Dorfman's Death and the Maiden must by now be fairly well-known. Fifteen years ago, a woman named Paulina was tortured and raped by the secret police of a South American country, probably the author's own Chile. She is married to Gerardo, a lawyer about to head an inquiry into the judicial crimes of what is now, mercifully, the former regime. Into their beach house comes Roberto, whom Paulina recognizes - by his voice, since she was blindfolded through her ordeal - as the doctor who officiated at her interrogation. She proceeds to interrogate him -with a gun at his head and with her husband's reluctant co-operation.

Paulina doesn't just want revenge. She wants exorcism. She wants, among other things, to be able to listen once more to a piece of music that she once loved - music that was destroyed for her when it was played as background during her ordeal. The piece is the Schubert quartet that gives the play its name. It's a somewhat laborious device, but it does provide an image of concord, fragile but precious, needing desperately to be restored.

The play has two overlapping themes. One is the horror of torture, including the anguish that remains with the victims long after the event. The other is the agony of a country trying in a still-compromised present to come to terms with its past, the danger of imitating your persecutors while trying to bring them to justice. The physical pain inflicted on Roberto is nothing to what Paulina went through, but the psychological pressures are alarmingly similar. The doctor gives in and signs a confession. Afterward, he protests that it was all a lie; he did it only to save his life. The play leaves us almost convinced of his guilt, but not quite; and that nagging doubt is essential to the effect. Without it, the piece becomes a tract: worthy of course, and gripping, because the issues are vital and the story good, but obvious in its attack on an evil we would all condemn anyway.

Here I have to confess a bias. I saw the play four years ago in London in a rigorous and unsentimental production, distinguished above all by the performance of Juliet Stevenson as Paulina. She had two great qualities, strength and speed; she was possessed and her motor ran dangerously fast, but she was terrifyingly sane. Fiona Reid's Pauline is bird-like and brittle: not just damaged but unhinged, even before her tormentor appears. There is little warmth between her and her husband, and we are robbed of one of the play's most striking qualities: its assertion that even the worst of traumas can be absorbed into the cycle of blame and forgiveness that constitutes the average marriage. R. H. Thomson's Geraldo offers her bluff tolerance shading into exasperation, but not much sympathy. The one person who must surely believe in Roberto's innocence is the actor who plays him, but Robert Haley with his oily smile, short-back-and-sides haircut, and gleaming Gestapo glasses is the Inquisition personified. His final broken recantation shifts the balance, but too late. All three performances are alive, but only as people in a play.

Jonas Jurasas's direction is tricksy. The shanty-like set by Sue LePage has no solid walls, but finds space for a moored boat into which people retreat at improbable moments. Paulina trails a tape of the Schubert; periodically she pulls it taut and notes emerge. When she tells her story, the houselights go up and she wanders among us. When Roberto tells his, he remains onstage, his face bathed in a demonic glow. In fact, the production plays its own power games. If these are the author's instructions, the British production did him a favour by disregarding them.

And then there is the epilogue. Gerardo's official inquiry is over. Roberto is at large. The three characters meet again at a performance of guess which string quartet. In London this was a brief and simple scene, a chilling question mark. In Toronto we are ushered onstage for a proper performance by four live musicians. While they play, Roberto acts smooth and sinister, Paulina distressed and Gerardo concerned. All doubts about the doctor's guilt are banished. Then, having had its fun, the production stops being environmental, and the actors climb onto the podium to take their bows. We have heard some great music beautifully played. Everything else is 100-per-cent phony.
1994-06-04-passion-flowers-theatre-revie: Passion flowers THEATRE REVIEW / Stephen Sondheim has his humour on a very tight rein in his latest musical, a comparison of different kinds of loveSaturday, June 04, 1994ROBERT CUSHMANNew York NY -- BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail New York STEPHEN Sondheims new musical Passion (Plymouth Theatre) has no separate musical numbers listed in the program. That might suggest that he has succumbed to the fashionable lure of Broadway opera, but this is not a through-sung work; the book, by James Lapine, has a lot of dialogue. All the same, the songs it separates do coalesce in memory into one continuous threnody, and there is something about it that might loosely be called operatic. The setting is 19th-century Italian, and the music is taut, plangent, yearning. Passion (which has been nominated for 10 Tony awards) is a love story, or a comparison of different kinds of love. Sometimes, describing a relationship that is over-confident and probably shallow, music and lyrics relax their grip and become suspiciously sweet. At other times, they grow spartan; the music tightens, the lyrics avoid easy images like the plague. What we get, in fact, is passion.It's a peculiar kind of passion, and I would like to think that the show is sympathetically examining rather than whole-heartedly recommending it. The pivotal character is Fosca, a tolerated resident in the quarters of her cousin, an army colonel. She is wasting away from a fatal disease, and is physically ill-favoured as well: crushing disadvantages in the culture she inhabits. (Or, to be honest, in almost any culture.) Into her environment comes a young and handsome captain, who is polite to her and respects her considerable intelligence. She flings herself at him, relentlessly, with no inhibitions about embarrassing him or humiliating herself; in one virtuoso number she dictates from her sickbed the letter she would like him to write her, and he helplessly complies. In the end, her devotion gets through to him. It compares favourably to the more conventional affair he has been enjoying with a beautiful married woman who, when the crunch comes, refuses to leave her husband.The show is based on a film (by Ettore Scola) which I have never seen but have heard described as black comedy. A spirit of irony hovers about the show as well - most explicitly in the choral comments of the captain's uncomprehending brother officers - but it never takes over. The mood is claustrophobic: in Lapines elegant but unspectacular staging, and in the construction of the score. There is much use of letters whose contents may be sung by the sender, the recipient, or the ensemble; everyone, knowingly or not, is caught up in the same emotions. Sondheim has habitually made his most serious points through wit, but in this show he has his humour on a very tight rein. There is less to savour joyfully in these lyrics than in any he has written. But there is also nothing that sounds unskillful or false; which suggests that, as usual, the words are doing their job.There is a tremendous performance by Donna Murphy, who quietly (a rare word to use in connection with Broadway musicals) imposes herself as both suffering martyr and relentless fury. Her voice, especially in its lowest reaches, is almost an additional instrument in Jonathan Tunicks dark, string-laden orchestrations. The hero (Jere Shea) is mellifluous but rather bland: unfortunate since this is at least as much his story as hers. He is the one in the centre of the relationships: the one to whom things happen. (She is the one who makes them happen, which is far more rewarding.) I am skeptical of claims that the piece marks an emotional breakthrough for Sondheim; he has written soaring love songs before, and only in a very special sense could it be claimed that this show allows its lovers a happy ending. Not that it matters. There are quite enough affirmative ballads in the world, and most of them are awful. Arthur Miller, now aged 80, has a new play on Broadway: cause for congratulation, especially as it's quite a good one and another Tony candidate. The title of Broken Glass (Booth Theatre) summons the German Kristallnacht of 1938: in retrospect, the real beginning of the Holocaust. The play revolves around a New York Jewish woman of the time, who seems alone in recognizing the horror of the situation, as depicted in newspaper photographs. Especially oblivious is her husband, a specialist in Jewish anti-Semitism; he votes Republican, and takes a nervous pride in being the only Jew employed in a Gentile firm, a position from which, in the course of the action and after mishandling a real-estate deal, he is fired. (At long last, you might say, Willy Loman has come out.) Either because of her unsatisfactory sexless marriage or her historical intuitions or both, his wife has suffered a hysterical paralysis. The sympathetic family doctor, also Jewish, never quite decides; but then his feelings toward her are not entirely professional.Only one of these themes is resolved, and powerfully; the husband has a heart attack and his wife walks. That sounds crude, but in context it's powerful and credible. Nothing else quite coheres (what, for example, are we meant to make of the doctors own marriage, to a Gentile?) and the plays most resonant point begins to count against it. As the wife senses, the really important and frightening things are happening in Berlin, but the play goes on happening in Manhattan. John Tillinger's production is not ideal. Though individually effective, each of the three leads - Ron Rifkin, Amy Irving, David Dukes - seems cocooned from the others; she in particular is warmly persuasive until she hits the line "I'm a Jewish woman" at which she goes into sing-song and never gets out. The WASP boss (George N. Martin) seems more ostentatiously callous than is absolutely necessary. And there must be a smoother way to handle the constant scene- changes than the trundling revolve in evidence here, even if I don't know what it would be. One line pleased me immensely: "So you have a sense of humour after all." It sounded like a wry self-tribute. Miller is not now and never has been Neil Simon, but he can be as funny as he wants when he wants. This is his most entertaining play since The Price.Word count: 1083
