THEATRE REVIEW SCENES FROM AN EXECUTION

Saturday, June 04, 1994

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY HOWARD BARKER Directed by Rodger Barton Presented by Equity Showcase Theatre At Harbourfront until June 11 Rating: Portrait of an artist This plain, lucid play shows a painter pitted against authority, and it can be applied to any number of contemporary issues BY ROBERT CUSHMAN The Globe and Mail Toronto WHAT gets executed in these scenes is not a person but a painting: an outsize depiction of the Battle of Lepanto, 1571, and defeat of the Turkish navy by a Christian coalition. The Doge of Venice commissions a commemorative canvas from his citys greatest artist, who happens to be a woman. This defiance of gender barriers is historically unlikely, but Howard Barker has never been a playwright to be inhibited by petty facts of life. Indeed he ignores them on principle. Scenes from an Execution is phantasmagoria, and a brilliant one.

Of the politically-minded - or bloody-minded - English playwrights who came to prominence in the 1970s, Barker is the intransigent lone wolf: the only one never to have collaborated on a play with any of the others when it was the fashion. Prolific though he is, he has never had a play presented on a large subsidized stage, but he has been a studio favourite and some actors rate him highly. There is even a company in Britain dedicated to performing his work and calling itself the Wrestling School.

The plays themselves are correspondingly strenuous, though less so than the polemical articles in which he and his disciples describe them. The literature surrounding this Toronto production proclaims the author's commitment to complexity and contradiction, and his loathing of easy options. You may have noticed," writes Barker in a tone befitting his name, "that we live in a laughing society . . . a theatre that takes itself seriously cannot any longer afford to be comic.

This is rubbish; and anyway Barker doesn't believe it himself. The alternative to what he calls diseased comedy" is healthy comedy, and Scenes from an Execution has the audience laughing almost from beginning to end. This may explain why director Rodger Barton has described it in an interview as the authors "most timid and accessible play. (Is he apologizing or what?) That may explain why I like it so much. The historical setting also helps. It puts us immediately in a free imaginative zone. The play shows the artist against authority, and we can appply its story to any number of contemporary issues.

Its like this. Galactia, the lady-genius, paints a horror-picture, and her patrons want a valour-picture. She herself calls it a noisy" painting; and, indeed, in the real world and a few centuries later, the same battle elicited from G. K. Chesterton an uncommonly noisy poem, the one in which Don John of Austria goes repeatedly clip-clopping to the war. The Venetian admiral, confronted by Galactia's depiction of him, proclaims that she has got him wrong, giving him the hands and face of a monster while he knows himself to be exceptionally nice. (Playwright and painter combine a witty and magisterial command of detail). Galactia - having offended church, state, and the military critical establishments - is sent to a dungeon, but her talent proves embarrassing. She is released and her work exhibited, as a demonstration of offical tolerance and commitment to art. Since Galactia is fiercely loyal to her own vision, but has no ideological beliefs beyond that, she seems half-willing to compromise with her enemies.

I can't quite see what is meant to be so complex about all this. Its a familar, even predictable story, right down to the ambivalent ending. What makes it live is the vigour with which Barker infuses Galactia herself - even her prison meditations rise above the stock modern vein of mock- Jacobean - and the urbane cartooning of her opponents, with all their scruples and cruelties firmly in place. "Your anger, says the Doge to Galactia is as much an act as my self-denigration, and more difficult to keep up." You can hear Barker, who plainly identifies with his heroine, saying a rueful amen to that.

There is a sexual story cutting across the political one. Barker writes extremely well about desire, and Galactia has a disabling weakness for a male married painter whose work (one Biblical subject endlessly recycled) she despises. He gets the job of replacing her, but isnt up to it. Having betrayed her, he falls more deeply in love with her. This gives the play added flavour, but no more than that.

The production, plain and lucid, does very right by the play. Wenna Shaw's Galactia is sometimes merely bossy where she should be arrogant, but she has no trouble driving the show. I also liked Michael Anderson's Doge, a picture of elegantly modulated pragmatism; Robert Dodds, who, as Galactias model as well as her lover, spends a lot of time naked; and Barrie Baldaro as her real inspiration, a damaged veteran with an arrow sticking out of his head. All these actors grow with the play, and all have first-rate timing. There are some weak performances but you can usually see what theyre getting at. "An honoured audience, says Barker, lecturing us on what's good for us, will quarrel with what it has seen, it will go home in a state of anger." I went home pleased and unquarrelsome. Incorrigible creature that I am I shall have, like Galactia, to live with dishonour.
1994-07-12-theatre-review-twelfth-night:
THEATRE REVIEW TWELFTH NIGHT

Tuesday, July 12, 1994

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- BY WILLIAM SHAKESPEARE Directed by Jeannette Lambermont Starring Lynne Cormack, Patrick Galligan and Ellen-Ray Hennessy At the outdoor ampitheatre in High Park, Tuesdays through Sundays until Aug. 14 Rating: Shakespeare, through the looking-glass There's nothing wrong with tampering with Shakespeare, but there is with doing it inefficiently, leaving loose ends from the original lying about for the cast and audience to trip over BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto THERE are some lively things in Jeannette Lambermont's production of Twelfth Night. One is the life-sized portrait of Countess Olivia that hangs in the chamber of her admirer, Duke Orsino. It actually consists of the actress playing Olivia standing motionless behind a large frame. It has a double effect, since it also looks from the audience as if Olivia herself is gazing into a mirror for extended periods.

Since narcissism is a major concern of the play - what with Olivia indulging herself in an extended period of mourning for a dead brother, Orsino indulging himself in his hopeless infatuation with Olivia, and the steward Malvolio explicitly diagnosed as being "sick of self-love" - this seems very neat and very apt. I'm not at all sure, though, that it is intentional. The show has other things on its mind.

The production starts with a lot of prologue. The storm that lands the twins, Viola and Sebastian, on the coast of Illyria, is energetically mimed. Before we get even that far there are songs welcoming the audience to "our fairy tale," songs actually drawn from the introductory verses to Lewis Carroll's Alice books. When the play itself gets going, it seems to be partially set in Wonderland, filled as it is with outsized props such as Alice might have beheld after sampling one of the cakes marked "Eat Me." Olivia's portrait is one of them. A monstrous green bottle that follows Sir Toby Belch around looks capacious enough to quench even his thirst. The ring that Malvolio delivers to Viola is the size of a tambourine. Most entrancing, and most Wonderlandish, of all are the huge pink flowers that shelter the plotters who spy on Malvolio while he reads the letter that ensnares him; Maria, the scheme's prime mover, has a similar bloom growing out of her hat. Danny Lyne's set and costume designs are gorgeously sophisticated by the standards of most open-air productions, and admirable by any standards whatever.

The program contains a heap more Alice quotes - of the "you're mad, we're all mad" persuasion - and a synopsis that tells us that "Viola, with the help of Feste the conjurer, disguises herself as a young man." Here the synopsis, if its writer has read the play, is lying. In the play's text, Viola's helpmate is an anonymous sea captain, and that is how she addresses him - even in this production, where his lines have indeed been taken over by Feste. Textually, she doesn't encounter Feste - who is actually a jester, not a magician - until several scenes later. When she does, it seems odd, in view of their intense earlier relationship, that she doesn't recognize him; especially since this clown, with his white death's-head face, shaven skull, magnetic presence and haunting singing voice, is not easily forgettable. It's strange too that Feste, who hovers over every scene in this staging, still gets the twins confused like everybody else.

I probably sound hopelessly pedantic. My objection is not to tampering with Shakespeare, but to doing it inefficiently, leaving loose ends from the original lying around and then tripping over them. Twelfth Night is not The Comedy of Errors; its use of the mistaken-identity motif is sparing and carefully motivated. Nobody in it is mad; a couple of people are falsely suspected of madness, but the point of that is lost if you subscribe to half-baked ideas about everybody being crazy. And it is not a fairy tale. It is part romantic comedy, with passion and skepticism in perfect balance, and part social comedy, tart and class-conscious. Over it all hang the matters that fairy tales exclude: time and mortality. It is probably a tribute to the director's better instincts that by the end of the play her initial concept has evaporated.

That does leave us, though, dependent on individual moments, individual performances. Fortunately, there are several to cling to. Alex Fallis's Feste, described above, is one of them; Ellen-Ray Hennessy's Viola, a good sport with an engaging sense of wonder about her, is another. She too sings well (and Phyllis Cohen's music is exquisite). Lynne Cormack is an interestingly skittish Olivia; Patrick Galligan makes a devastating exhibition of Orsino's self-pity. Below stairs is dominated by Michael Hanrahan's Malvolio, the actor as relaxed as the character is uptight. Benedict Campbell's Sir Toby is conceived as an effete habitue of one of the less-particular London clubs: valid enough in theory, but not very resourceful in practice. Since he is playing in the same register as his dupe Sir Andrew (Steve Cumyn), their scenes together quickly grow monotonous.

There are also two varieties of cross-gender casting. The sea-dog Antonio is played by a woman as a man; and you would have to go to Penzance to find a less convincing pirate. The possibility of Antonio's devotion to Sebastian being homosexual is effectively neutralized; thus does one kind of liberation drive out another. More defensibly, the servant Fabian, a notoriously indeterminate character, is played by a woman as a woman; you do wonder, though, why Maria, grimly hanging on to her position as Toby's intended, isn't jealous of his new confidante; it's another example of the production not looking where it's going. Still, for pastoral Shakespeare, this is well above average, beguiling even before darkness falls to work a magic far more infallible than any conjuror's.
1994-07-24-theatre-same-old-south-hot-ne:
THEATRE / Same old South, hot new play

Robert Cushman Sunday 24 July 1994 00:02 BST

THE ONLY problem with 900 Oneonta is its title: hard to remember, understand or pronounce. It turns out - late in the evening - to be an address: the street-number of a posh mansion in Louisiana whose doors and windows hang at crazy, sloping angles, as do most of the inhabitants. They have names like Dandy, Tiger, Persia and Burning Jewel and they are rotten.

Dandy is the patriarch, oil-rich, feisty and outspoken. That is, he insults everybody, especially his family who are absolutely dependent on him. 'There's going,' he taunts, 'to be some bizarre stipulations in my will.' Everything points to a confrontation between Dandy and Tiger, his favourite grandson: a re-run of the star scene in Cat on a Hot Tin Roof with the difference that this Big Daddy knows he is dying and is baiting his relatives on that hook. Tiger is crisply characterised as 'a dope addict living with a nigger whore'. It turns out that he was sexually abused by his mother, which seems fair enough as she was sexually abused by her father. Neither revelation is much of a surprise. Along with the lusts of Tennessee Williams and the racial tensions of William Faulkner goes the greed of Lillian Hellman's Little Foxes. It's the same old South.

There's also a transplanted touch of O'Neill's New England, what with daughter Persia emerging in her nightgown to mope around on morphine, and to be greeted by her children with the kind of exasperated contempt that the boys of Long Day's Journey never quite summoned up.

David Beaird (and how do you pronounce him?) has claimed that his play is partly autobiographical, but he should have little difficulty facing his dear ones in the future. It never feels like a slice of his or anyone else's real life. It seems instead like a spoof of every overheated family drama in the American repertoire. On this level, it starts funny and gets funnier. Even more to its credit, once accepted as comic it can be taken with increasing seriousness. It even, except when the author explicitly insists on it, stands up as an image of America, complacent about its past achievements and ripe for takeover.

Beaird, who directs his own script, is a superlative technician in both hats. Having lured his audience in on a promise of mint-julep languor, he accelerates tempo, tightens screws, and lands surprise after surprise, none of them resistible and most of them sprung them like perfect traps. He has tremendous cheek. Tiger arrives just in time to give the old man an unsuccessful kiss of life: an action which immediately places him on a higher moral, and even practical, plane than anyone else on stage. Dandy's demise, which could be a terrific miscalculation, is actually a kiss of life on its own account. Leland Crooke's Dandy, excellent when not shouting, shouts 70 per cent of the time. The play runs more smoothly without him.

Ben Daniels gives Tiger a lot more style and conviction than doomed golden studs usually get, and there is strong work from Susan Tracy, Angela Bruce and Paul Chapman. The driving force though is second grandson Gitlo, a 'normal Joe' in a family of monsters, and the character for whom the author has the least respect. (The one for whom he has the most is the local minister.) He is mocked by his grandpa, threatened by his brother ('I'm going to put you out of my misery'), and demolished by the family's black maid ('I changed your diapers, so it must be partly my fault that you turned out like you did'). In Jon Cryer's delirious performance he starts out understandably twitchy, and progresses into an ecstatic dance of self-abasement; he will submit to anything in order to safeguard his inheritance. With him in its sights the play transcends its immediate forebears and joins hands with such classic ballets of cupidity as Volpone. It has no truck with compassion but it never succumbs to contempt.

Imogen Stubbs makes an attractive, tomboyish and ultimately moving Saint Joan. That sounds simplistic but the performance does not offer a huge variety of mood. Neither, though, does the role, and the only fault I can hesitantly find with Stubbs is that in the trial she goes for downtrodden-in- shackles, at the expense of what her judges call her 'pert answers'. Shaw's play remains not as overwhelming as one would like, but not dismissible either. Twice it touches greatness: in Rheims Cathedral, when Joan's allies severally desert her for respectable-sounding reasons, and (against received opinion) in the Epilogue where they do it all over again. Stubbs's Joan is at her finest here, triumphant in rejection; and she makes a good stab too at the booby-trapped recantation speech, scuppered when heavenly music creeps in to underline the ecstatic bits. This is a rare gaffe in Gale Edwards' clear, cool and handsome production; it takes the play on its merits as a debating-piece but also manages to squeeze in some moments of spectacle, generally glimpsed going unobtrusively by somewhere at the back of the stage. Prize supporting performances are Ken Bones's smooth and brainy Warwick, Peter Jeffrey's chillingly kind Inquisitor, and Jasper Britton's uninhibited grotesque of a Dauphin; special mention for David Daker's de Stogumber, the bigot who awakes too late and whose private tragedy is the inevitable counterpart to Joan's public one.

An alternative title for Shaw's play might be The Miracle Worker, appropriated some decades later by the American William Gibson for his account of the young deaf- and-blind Helen Keller and her rough but charitable awakening at the hands (and I do mean the hands) of novice teacher and orphanage graduate Annie Sullivan. In this revival, both teacher and pupil got cheers at the curtain. Without wishing to denigrate either Jenny Seagrove's Annie or Catherine Holman's ferocious Helen, I found this suspect.

The audience was basking in the reflected glory of an unambiguously happy ending that actually happened. Whether it happened quite as neatly and theatrically as it does in the play is another matter; even as the lump rose obediently in my throat I questioned my own response. The early scenes, sketching in Helen's blinkered Southern family, are a chore by any reckoning, the actors trudging through the dialogue as if they had never encountered it before (which does not mean they sound spontaneous). I dreamt of having them worked over by David Beaird. Things improve considerably when words give way to gestures and grunts: to Helen's violence and Annie's responses in kind; the first time the governess thumped her charge, a houseful of frustrated parents erupted in approval.

Comic juggling is an honourable tradition; a few years ago one of its practitioners kicked Sugar Babies briefly into the land of the living. As an inflexible rule, the better the juggling the better the clowning; only the four Flying Karamazov Brothers, however, have made an evening out of it. In Juggle and Hyde they erupt onto a stage full of cardboard boxes, in some of which they hide and some of which they juggle. They also toss about traditional clubs, Japanese fans, and xylophone mallets, the last while actually playing the xylophone; somehow the sticks always land on the notes. On the first night their repertoire extended to a dead fish, a pizza on a plate, and a very wobbly jelly. Their final eight- handed routine, constantly shifting positions and rhythms, is breathtakingly beautiful. Their delivery of lines is rather lightweight. I do not suggest that either they or you should worry about this.
1994-07-31-theatre-the-little-goose-grow:
THEATRE / The little goose grows up

Robert Cushman Sunday 31 July 1994 00:02 BST

THIS WEEK, authors who have been dead for an inexcusable number of years have sent their actors prancing about in thrall to moral and social codes of ludicrous antiquity. Luckily, we don't have to believe what the characters believe. We only need to believe that they do.

By this test, and by most others, Philip Prowse's production of Oscar Wilde's Lady Windermere's Fan is a triumph. As designer, he has made a domestic cathedral of the Windermere drawing-room, a great semi- circle in sky-blues and salmon-pinks, stretching up to embrace an invisible dome and an extremely visible chandelier. This vast feminine shrine is contrasted with young Lord Darlington's bachelor pad, all squared off with screens apparently done up by Aubrey Beardsley.

The ladies chez Windermere dress to match the sofa cushions, which suggests a truly alarming sense of style. Most terrifying is Jennifer Hilary, a Duchess of Berwick who snaps out epigrams, commands and good advice with iron-clad confidence. She leads around a smugly subservient daughter whom she marries off to a rich young Australian; he will then be kept firmly in his place which, whatever he may think, is not Australia. We are in the 1890s, the age of Victoria approaching its terminus, and the play, like Wilde's other social comedies, brings centre stage the world of snobbery and duplicity to which people keep making off-handed allusions in The Importance of Being Earnest.

Like Wilde's other plays, too, Lady Windermere has the lineaments of melodrama; but here lines that are impossibly purple on the page come out in credible black and white. Lady Windermere, young and sheltered, is incensed to see her husband paying court to Mrs Erlynne, an older woman with a mysterious but indisputable Past. Of course there are reasons, of course the demon turns out to be an angel of mercy, but there is plenty of suspense in finding out the details.

Amanda Elwes transforms the innocent little goose into a troubled, thoughtful woman - a woman who truly believes in the standards to which the others pay lip-service. Francesca Annis's Mrs Erlynne matches her in seriousness, if not quite in her passion, after swanning enjoyably around in scarlet-woman mode. Only Rupert Frazer's Lord Windermere remains an unconscionable stick; and since the production leaves him in pointed isolation at the end, this could be intentional.

This is not the Wilde play with the line about sincerity being like an iron girder in a house of cards. But we get the girders and we get the cards, a whole pack of them, led by David Foxxe as a fat frog-faced dandy with a green carnation ('the reason for the Nineties being gay', according to Noel Coward, though the phrase is not - infuriatingly - from his musical of this play). He might be Wilde; and he conveys, as does the whole play, the sense of relishing and fearing his society simultaneously. Frank Middlemass huffs and puffs endearingly as a resolute old suitor and Simon Dutton cuts a figure as a resolute young one, Lady Windermere's greatest fan. Walk through this play with standard West End elegance and it falls to bits; what it needs, and gets, is a rich environment with people inside.

The Lady from the Sea offers a spare environment with people inside, and that's all right, too. The set features a lot of rocks arranged on a grid, which rises from the stage floor as the play starts and overlooks the action thereafter. Well, the play is partly about getting one's rocks off. What actually happens is landlocked domestic drama that Lindsay Posner directs with great finesse. Josette Simon plays Ellida, the self-styled mermaid who equates freedom with escape from her doctor husband, and she makes a beautiful centrepiece. She does not supply much depth but I doubt if the character has any; she is more of a predicament than a person.

Her old man compensates, though; in his frock-coat and whiskers Pip Donaghy seems at first a caricature of a buttoned-up Ibsenite physician, but a heart beats beneath. He is formal, then puzzled, then wounded, then enormously, tactfully caring; it is no wonder that, granted her liberty, Ellida uses it to stay with him. Liam de Staic, as the Stranger who claims her, is just real enough to make it a fair contest.

Ellida's two stepdaughters play out their own variants on her drama of choice. Emily Watson makes the younger one more stridently viperish than necessary but Paul Higgins is deliciously vain as the young doomed sculptor who vaguely woos her. The play offers masculine extremes of love and self-absorption with Sean Baker charting a careful course between them as the tutor who wins the elder daughter by default; she, as Matilde Ziegler makes achingly clear, accepts him because she has nowhere else to go. Peter Kelly wraps the play up most satisfactorily as the local jack-of-all- trades who has difficulty pronouncing the word 'acclimatise' but finally manages to say it when Ellida finally manages to do it. A hard word well said, a hard play well done. Hardest of all must be Corneille's Le Cid, the play that in 1637 ushered in French classical tragedy. The Wilde and Ibsen productions achieve their success in part by scaling down the rhetoric. You cannot do this with Corneille, and though the director, Jonathan Kent, finds some room for wit he stakes most on passion. Sometimes this amounts to fervent groping, amorous or murderous: wrong, either way. Duncan Bell plays the title role with his sword drawn and his shirt undone; he is usually on his way to or from some duel or battle, and he always wins. He loses the play, though, to the two women who love him. Peter J Davison's set is dominated by a pair of great gold frames, one of which functions as a two-way mirror. While one heroine orates in front of it the other is seen behind, suffering in silence.

The more active is Ximena, who loves the Cid until he kills her father, by way of avenging an insult to his own. She then becomes a fury, never admitting to mixed feelings though obviously possessed by them; Susan Lynch hurls herself at the role, and though she does not always connect with it she is thrilling when she does. Meanwhile the king's daughter, too far above the hero to marry him, is a prey to alternating varieties of despair; Samantha Bond suffers with terrific poise. The last word, though, is with urbanity, represented by Bernard Lloyd as the king. Ranjit Bolt's rhymed translation sounds especially good coming out of him. You begin sceptical of the play's greatness, and end convinced of it. It's a world.

Noel Coward was a less resourceful lyricist than Cole Porter, and a far less accomplished composer, but in the joint tribute Let's Do It, he comes out on top since, having a playwright's instincts, he wrote songs of greater theatrical presence. Performing pianist Peter Greenwell gets all the juice out of 'Mrs Worthington' and all the sorrow out of 'If Love Were All' without over-stating either of them. Returning veteran Pat Kirkwood makes another good case for simplicity. But the twin subjects go essentially uncontrasted.
1994-09-24-appreciation-jule-styne-an-in: APPRECIATION / Jule Styne An infectious delight in songSaturday, September 24, 1994ROBERT CUSHMANBY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail IN 1974, a memorable production of Gypsy, starring Angela Lansbury, was passing through Toronto, en route from London to New York. So, perhaps less memorably, was I. I saw a performance, applauded my hands off, and afterwards went backstage. Apparently there had been trouble over tempo, and the composer had been summoned from Manhattan. He was a five-foot- tall, copper-haired man, middle-aged by the look of him and incredibly energetic, physically and vocally. He was exploding all over the star's dressing-room, pounding out - without benefit of a piano - the rhythms that the conductor should have been keeping. It was an awesome display, my first personal sighting of Jule Styne.In New York the following week I described the scene to a friend of Styne's, expressing both my admiration and my concern for the composer's health. If he kept up that level of nervous tension, he was surely going to have a heart attack. I was reassured that Styne was not, as I had assumed, in his late 50s. He was 70, and that high-pressure manner was habitual. He thrived on it.Four years later he wrote the score for a London musical, Bar Mitzvah Boy, his 20th show. I reviewed it, not too enthusiastically. But he didn't seem to hold that against me. "We're going," he said, "to be friends."That never really happened, but we did have dinner in New York. He talked quietly but propulsively, always about his own work, in which he took infectious, childlike delight. There was nothing offensive about this; he seemed to have boundless ego without conceit. (Besides, it was what I wanted to hear about, and it certainly made conversation easy.) He painted glowing word-pictures of future projects, and spoke of rehabilitating work that had failed in the past. A few days later I met E.Y. (Over the Rainbow) Harburg, who had written the lyrics for one of those flop shows, and mentioned that Styne was talking about reviving it. "Of course," I said, as tactfully as I could, "Jule is a great optimist." "You are," said Harburg, "a master of understatement."Styne's buoyant spirit got him through two virtually separate composing careers - one in Hollywood, one on Broadway. Having ideas was never a problem for him; impatience was. Stephen Sondheim and other lyricists have testified that Styne would always rather write a completely new tune than tinker with an existing one. His impulsiveness on the job, and his habit of discussing three or four matters at one time, found expression in a personal language that his faithful collaborators, Betty Comden and Adolph Green, labeled "Stynese," and of which they once supplied the following example: "What we in the theatre call 'dynamics' is - well - fast . . . but not - you can't do that - a slower tempo would - together - that's not how, well, if two - not right away - but - Dorothy, let's go have a cup of coffee."Dorothy was Dorothy Dicker, Styne's long-serving assistant, whose overriding task was to bring some order into his life. This involved keeping an eye on his finances, and keeping at bay both the IRS and the bookies. Styne was a compulsive gambler whose habit kept him on the verge of bankruptcy when he should have been making several fortunes.His best work did not always bring him the best rewards. He won an Oscar for Three Coins in the Fountain, a really turgid film title-song, rather than for such genuinely distinguished movie ballads as Time after Time or I Fall in Love Too Easily, both of them fashioned, as indeed was Three Coins, for Frank Sinatra in his gentle period. (In the forties Styne and lyricist Sammy Cahn were virtually Sinatra's private songwriters.) He got his only Best Musical Tony for Hallelujah Baby, a show he himself knew to be inferior. Shows of his that had been passed over in previous years included Gentlemen Prefer Blondes, Bells Are Ringing, Gypsy and Funny Girl. "There comes a time when you say, 'We ought to be fair and give it to him this year,' " he said at the award ceremony: marks for honesty.The whole score of Blondes came up delightfully fresh at last year's Shaw Festival. Bells Are Ringing, apart from the standards Just in Time and The Party's Over, includes character songs like Judy Holliday's It's a Perfect Relationship that are actually musical. Gypsy is one of the half- dozen best musicals, and seems infinitely revivable; having given Ethel Merman her best role, it has worked for Lansbury, Tyne Daly and Bette Midler. Funny Girl, structurally something of a rerun of Gypsy, may have even better individual tunes: not the irritatingly homiletic People (a hit that has long since faded), but the jazzy Cornet Man, the driving Don't Rain on My Parade, and the sweeping torch-song The Music That Makes Me Dance, Styne's second-best individual melody. The very best was Time after Time, which he claimed was improvised at a party as a pastiche of Jerome Kern. As a melodist he did not generally have the originality of Kern, or of Rodgers, Arlen or Sondheim. Their best songs transcend a given genre; Styne's sound more like competent examples of it. But he knew how to bring a theatre alive. Only four years younger than Rodgers, he came to the theatre 20 years later, but he went on to dominate his generation. "Jule," somebody once said, "thinks of himself as a doyen." But he had earned the right.I last saw him two years ago, ostensibly to talk about Comden and Green but really to listen to him talking about himself. At 86, he was obviously flagging, and his conversation wandered more than ever, but his concentration wonderfully improved when he focused on an imminent revue of his work at the Rainbow Room, or on a musical he was planning of The Red Shoes which was going - of course - to be his biggest hit in years. He hadn't had a show in New York since 1980, and I didn't expect this one to materialize, but it did. It was a disaster, but I am somehow glad that in his last year he still managed to get a show on. I doubt if any other composer his age has managed it. I hardly knew him, but I am going to miss him. Robert Cushman writes and broadcasts on theatre music in Canada and the U.K.Word count: 1118
1994-09-25-time-after-time-jule-styne-19:
Time after time: Jule Styne, 1905-94: an appreciation

Robert Cushman Sunday 25 September 1994 00:02 BST

JULE STYNE, who has died at 88, had a new show on Broadway only last year. The show, The Red Shoes, was a disaster but to have got it on at all at his age is an achievement, unequalled by any other composer. In that sense it was a fitting finale. Styne, only four years younger than Richard Rodgers, got to Broadway 20 years later; but made up for lost time by writing music for 22 staged shows. Before that he had written songs for countless movies, but even in Hollywood he had been a late starter, coming to the job after working as a pianist, bandleader and vocal coach.

Like Rodgers - though as bubbling and enthusiastic as Rodgers was reserved - he proved to be an all-round, besotted theatrical, producing as well as composing. He had a sense for drama. With some roots in swing, he mostly wrote shows with Broadway tempi, Broadway sentiments and Broadway guts: the greatest of them Gypsy, with its searing strip-motif overture. His lyricists included, in rough order of frequency, Sammy Cahn (mainly in Hollywood and often for Sinatra), Betty Comden and Adolph Green, Bob Merrill, Leo Robin, Frank Loesser, Stephen Sondheim, and E Y Harburg (who, when I described Styne to him as 'optimistic', looked at me and said, 'you are a master of understatement').

He was, if I may split hairs, a strong composer rather than a fine one. His Forties hits, such as 'Five Minutes More' and 'It's Been a Long, Long Time', are more nostalgia-objects than standards. Discerning singers are likelier to feature the more distilled love-songs of Jimmy Van Heusen. Van Heusen, though, lacked the muscle that enabled Styne to compose Ethel Merman's scarifyingly exuberant numbers in Gypsy or to furnish 'It's a Perfect Relationship', Judy Holliday's expository song in Bells Are Ringing, with a beguiling tune that far transcended strict dramatic function. One of his proudest boasts was that he always knew how, and what, to write for stars; this included writing tunes that smile. His ballads, for the most part, lack this transcendence; numbers such as 'The Party's Over' or 'Guess I'll Hang My Tears Out to Dry' seem to have sights set on being a particular kind of tune - sophisticated lament or wistful torch-song - and to fit comfortably into the required mould. But there are exceptions. 'Time After Time', from the 1947 film It Happened in Brooklyn, is an ardent masterpiece, inevitable without being predictable. Much later 'The Music that Makes Me Dance', from Funny Girl, takes the torch-song, on a continuous melodic line, back to the blues. And in Peter Pan - his most durable show after Gypsy - 'Never Never Land' is a long- lined beauty.

As a man Styne had his share of demons, including a gambling habit that nearly destroyed him. He also had an ear that drove musicians mad; they could never get away with anything. As a worker and a conversationalist, he was galvanic: a small, bespectacled, copper-haired man, juggling projects and talking about them ceaselessly. He had boundless ego, but not, I think, conceit; he was generous and genuine, and in some ways childlike. Even I, who hardly knew him, will miss him.
1994-10-09-lives-of-the-great-songs-thes:
Lives of the great songs: These Foolish Things: The classiest

Robert Cushman Sunday 09 October 1994 00:02 BST

SOME list songs are sad songs, guaranteed to strike a chord in anyone who has enjoyed nursing a broken heart while pretending to ignore it. The main strain compiles the list; the middle - variously known in the trade as the bridge, channel or release - extrapolates, generalises, draws conclusions. The pattern occurs in 'Thanks for the Memory' (where the bridge summarises 'many's the time that we feasted, and many's the time that we fasted') and it seems endemic to songs of regret. The paradigm is 'These Foolish Things', music by Jack

Strachey and Barry Link, lyric by Holt Marvell.

Those are not household names, and one of them isn't a name at all. Holt Marvell was a nom de plume for Eric Maschwitz, who in the 1930s was a scriptwriter for the BBC. In urgent need of a song for a radio revue, he ground out the words one Sunday morning and read them over the phone to Strachey. (As for the mysterious third name on the credits, the missing Link: Harry Link was an American whose name also crops up as co-composer of Fats Waller's 'I've Got a Feeling I'm Falling'. Presumably he had something to do with sprucing up 'These Foolish Things' for the US market, though it's hard to tell what. Maybe he was just good at royalties.)

Perhaps it's hindsight, or hindhearing, but the tune sounds as if it were dictated by the words in more than the literal sense. It's a compelling melody but repetitious: compelling because repetitious. The principal task is to provide a long, wistful line to accompany each of the foolish things and - what Strachey does best - to build to a climax, philosophic or despairing as the singer chooses, on the final 'oh, how the ghost of you clings'. Strachey never wrote another tune as resonant but Maschwitz, who went on to great success as a BBC executive, has some claim to be considered the leading

British lyricist of his era. Two of his songs - this one and the contrastingly happy 'A Nightingale Sang in Berkeley Square' - have become nostalgic shorthand for old Mayfair.

'These Foolish Things' attracted little attention on its radio debut, and not much more when it was sung in a 1936 West End revue called Spread It Abroad. Still unpublished, it was discovered - as a manuscript on a piano, according to Maschwitz - by the singer-pianist Leslie A Hutchinson, alias Hutch.

Hutch, born in Grenada, professionally blooded in New York and Paris, was English society's pet exotic, exposed to a wider audience by records, radio and the last gasps of the music-hall. Right into the 1950s he remained the living definition of a certain idea of sophistication. There is a controlled ardour about his performances that is rather intimidating. Hutch served his public by reflecting, as in a shiny chafing dish, their own grandest conceptions of wit and high romance. Mostly he used American material - he was London's most reliable conduit for the songs of Cole Porter - but in 'These Foolish Things' (HMV 1936, reissued on Hutch at the Piano, World Records) he found a native work that suited him to perfection. The words with which Maschwitz unfolds his roster of regrets may not be greatly witty, but they are evocative. The first image is enough to create a feeling and a world: 'A cigarette that bears a lipstick's traces.'

So it's a shock to find that that line doesn't figure on Hutch's classic recording. Maybe it was written in later, after the song took off; maybe Hutch simply preferred other bits of the lyric. He had plenty to choose from; the song, copious as a list song should be, boasts three choruses, of which he sings two.

He also sings a verse: one that begins, after a brief snatch of muted trumpet, with the blunt inquiry 'Oh, will you never let me be?'. It goes on to set up the song with a reference to 'those little things . . . that bring me happiness and pain'. Most singers have tipped that balance in one direction or the other. Hutch keeps it exquisitely poised; he suggests that he has the heart for grief but would never dream of wallowing in it. His voice, famously, throbs; but it throbs with dignity. He is

suffering greatly, but he knows how to live with it. His cut-glass diction, with its outlandishly elegant vowels, actually contributes to his haunted sound: the upper crust of soul. He must have sensed that in this still obscure song he had found a perfect showcase. He sings it as if it were already a standard.

In place of the opening cigarette, he offers us a more rarefied commodity: 'gardenia perfume lingering on a pillow'. Maybe the explicit sexuality of that image alarmed the publishers; subsequent singers, if they have used the line at all, have pushed it way down the song. It goes with 'wild strawb'ries only seven francs a kilo', a rhyme that Hutch's accent makes more plausible than most have managed. This, we are being told, is a lusciously cosmopolitan affair, the kind we would all like to be regretting. Another key memory is 'the Ile de France with all the gulls around it', again somewhat dubiously rhymed with 'the park at midnight when the bell has sounded'. Maschwitz was not always scrupulous in the way he combined his images, but he was a whiz at picking them.

The sights and scents are well enough, but what have always struck home are the sounds. For happiness, 'the tinkling piano in the next apartment'; for pain, the universal ache of 'a telephone that rings, but who's to answer?' - a brilliant blow below the belt, real chanson noire. Hutch serves them all up polished and gleaming, at a pace noticeably faster than later generations would think proper for a ballad.

In New York in 1936 pianist Teddy Wilson, in a model of understated swing, set an even jauntier tempo to usher in a single chorus from the 21-year-old Billie Holiday. She brings a new note to the song: disappointment verging on anger. Hutch sang of loss; Holiday sings of betrayal (Brunswick 1936, reissued on The Quintessential Billie Holiday, Vol 2, CBS). When she refers to 'those stumbling words that told you what my heart meant' she isn't congratulating herself on her own bashfulness, she's asking how she could have been such a fool. Indeed, on her lips the title sounds less affectionate and more bitter than on any others. She injects acid into the regrets, and erotic pain as well, gilding 'a fairground's painted swings' - one of the more hackneyed items on the agenda - by italicising 'swings' with a vocal shiver.

Most striking is what she does with the bridge. 'You came, you saw, you conquered me . . . ' Hutch sang that melodramatic observation from the heart, which in his case seems to have been the site of conquest; Holiday is unmistakably

physical. The song's middle interrupts the catalogue to offer a comment. Musically, too, it makes a break; Strachey abruptly offers a new, if foreshortened, musical idea.

In 1961 the song turned up on the Frank Sinatra LP Point of No Return, the last of the six great ballad albums he recorded for Capitol. Each of them had its own distinctive mood; this one, following on the sustained angst of Only the Lonely and the bleak hopelessness of No One Cares, settles on a plateau of acceptance, lost love recollected in something

approaching tranquillity. 'An airline ticket to romantic places' is the line most savoured; the ghost of you still clings, but it

imparts a glow rather than a chill. Forsaking the deep cello timbre of his previous laments, Sinatra sings here with a light, burnt-out quality and with an unexpected casualness of

tone. When he is not on his best behaviour vocally, when the vowels get broad and the consonants sibilant, he can sound surprisingly like the late Sid James.

I suppose the best-known of recent versions is Bryan Ferry's (on his solo debut, These Foolish Things, Island 1973). It's also textually the fullest. Ferry, who seems to have his mike turned way down low at his entrance and only becomes fully audible at the end of the first line, is a broken man. He sings out of tempo, in traditional verse manner, but he's backed by a piercing trumpet and exaggeratedly docile piano: a Brecht-and-Weill combination. The jazz critic Francis Davis describes the record, approvingly, as 'fiendishly syncopated'; to my ears, certainly on first hearings, the reggae beat to which Ferry

submits the bulk of the song is remarkably foursquare, flattening out melodic shape and verbal nuance. But coming back to it, I can hear more.

There is a point in each of the song's long lines where the tune turns a corner; Ferry pounces on and isolates each of these moments, almost regardless of what the lyric might be doing at the time. We get 'the winds of March that make my - heart a dancer' and even 'first daffodils and long ex-cited cables'. The equivalent pause in 'but - who's to answer' makes obvious dramatic sense, though, and nobody could accuse Ferry of swallowing the words. They all come out clear if somewhat odd; the park at evening becomes 'the park atevening', reminding me of Ken Tynan's comment on an especially eccentric performance by Ralph Richardson: 'a mode of speech that democratically regards all syllables as equal'. My very favourite item - 'the sigh of midnight trains in empty stations' - seems to appeal to Ferry too: he is momentarily gleeful, while 'the smile of Garbo' makes him come over all knowing.

All the elements of the song are laid out - the elegance, the nonchalance, the driven misery - but dislocated and jumbled, so that Ferry seems simultaneously to be commenting on traditional pop style and re-enacting it. In this he was a harbinger. Davis calls him 'the British postmodern crooner', and he seems to enjoy tipping his hat to Bing. (That's on the line 'the song that Crosby sings', which, if you'll follow me into the hall of mirrors for a moment, 'These Foolish Things' had actually become. He recorded it in 1955, though without the self-reference. The Groaner reserved his postmodernism for jokey duets.) The most disconcerting thing about Ferry's performance is its persistent refusal to honour the final resolution of Strachey's melody; the foolish things sound as if they are going to be around for a while yet, all three choruses of them.

Ferry's sweet-sour version might be the one I would play on my Platonic ideal of a radio programme. But if I were simply going for the best post-war recordings, I would have to choose between a pair of chartered cabaret singers, one old, one young. Mabel Mercer, the doyenne, sang 'These Foolish Things' in concert at New York's Town Hall in 1969 (Mabel Mercer and Bobby Short Second Town Hall Concert, Atlantic 1969). She was 70 and had a cold; her delivery was husky and very conversational. But she still had power in reserve, and it is fascinating to hear when she decides to unloose it. There is a definite sense as she proceeds of the song taking her over.

She sings two choruses, both rubato, easing in on the 'cigarette' line before the inevitable applause of recognition. At the mention of 'romantic places', her voice begins a steady climb up to the first climax of 'still my heart has WINGS'. Mercer, renowned for her treasuring of a song's lyrics, had one especially cunning method of illuminating them. She rarely stressed an adjective; she knew that they would do their own work. So she sings 'THESE foolish things and 'those stumbling WORDS'; treating the descriptive words as functional, she makes them all the more striking. It isn't an inflexible rule; she lingers irresistibly on 'LONG excited cables', though it's still the noun that brings out the wonder in her. And there's yearning in there, reaching a tantalising peak unscaled by other singers in the hushed rapture of 'silk stockings THROWN ASIDE'. At the close her voice breaks, and it hardly matters whether that's an emotional effect or a technical defect; it's moving anyway. Mercer enjoys some of the memories, cherishes all of them, but finally arrives at a grief as wrenching as Billie Holiday's and rather nobler. Hers is the most balanced account of the song since Hutch's, and a lot more approachable.

A more extreme treatment is Andrea Marcovicci's. Marcovicci is an actress turned singer, and when she sang this (it was released in 1990, on What is Love?, DRG, but I think recorded earlier) her voice was flawed. But she overrides her imperfections in an insistently on-the-beat treatment that rarely isolates a phrase (though she does highlight 'the waiters whistling as the last bar closes', a late and especially magical item that less patient singers never reach) and drives through on a controlled arc of intensity.

When she has finished, her accompanists take the tune out: piano, sax and violin in a shrill chamber-music frenzy. This echoes a possibility already raised by Marcovicci's escalating stress on the thrice-repeated 'oh, how the ghost of you clings'. She may be coming to terms not with an unfaithful lover but with a dead one. No previous singer has made me take the words that literally. I doubt if the writers did. But after all these years of harmlessly foolish things it makes startlingly good sense.

REVIEW IN BRIEF THEATRE / More Divine

Saturday, October 15, 1994

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written and directed by Sky Gilbert. At Buddies in Bad Times Theatre until until Oct. 30. Rating: -1/2 No plot but lots of poetry BY ROBERT CUSHMAN 'IT is advisable, if a play has neither plot nor characters that it have poetry." That is a line from Sky Gilbert's latest. The self-reference is blatant, and as charming as it is obviously intended to be. More Divine has no plot, and at most one character, but it does have poetry.

Some of this poetry is visual. The show begins in Paris, done as a black-and-white etching from a stage-size comic book. A bevy of schoolboys - in berets, short pants, satchels and umbrellas - coyly burlesque every Parisian rain-dance that ever cluttered up a movie musical. They also arouse the attentions of the late critics and philosophers Roland Barthes and Michel Foucault. Barthes is first seen, in a room the size of a phone- booth, actually waiting in stoical agony for the phone to ring. Foucault is first seen aggressively masturbating. They are rivals for the same boy and, naturally, macho Michel wins him from reclusive Roland.

Barthes, however, is soon off on the road to Morocco which differs from Paris --most effectively - in being a bare wide stage with a Sky-blue backdrop. Here he finds happiness, or anyway three available youths. But he is tracked down by Foucault who tells him a) that he should come out; b) that he is exploiting his young Arabs; and c) that AIDS will not only unite but exalt gays everywhere. That's about it for dialectical conflict, though Foucault seems to score a posthumous victory when Barthes, back in Paris, is lured out to a fancy-dress disco peopled by the guests from Buddies in Bad Times' own reopening party; everybody parties while the play gracefully self-destructs.

Earlier the two gurus visit a plush Parisian theatre (another minor coup for designer Steve Lucas) to see a revival of a society melodrama which they have chosen over a possible Pinter on the wildly improbable grounds that it's shorter. What they see is a strident burlesque, in which the promiscuous heroine is really a man. It's mostly feeble, a parody of a non-existent form, but occasionally inspiration descends. An actor detaches himself to lament his plight as a heterosexual forced to comply with the (artistic) whims of his - I quote from memory - "camp fag drag- queen director." The is-he-or-isn't-he questions that this sends buzzing round the audience, and then reflects back on to them, knock Pirandello out of the ballpark.

Gilbert probably couldn't tell a story or conduct an argument for nuts, but at his best he writes with real wit and real rhythm, and as a director he communicates these qualities to his actors. Randall Lanthier's unassuming balding Barthes is far more winning than anybody would guess from reading his logic-chopping prose, and though this Foucault is a caricature intellectual (thin-rimmed glasses and a thin-rimmed mouth) Mark Christmann animates the skeleton to perfection. Everybody else is very good. So is the new theatre: Buddies in Bad Times, they've seen it all and, my dear, they're still here.
1994-11-09-the-queens-merely-chatter:
I am reviewing this show against the expressed preferences of the Canadian Stage Company. The production inaugurates a scheme of Advanced Workshopping: audiences will be canvassed for their opinions so that authors, directors and performers may learn from them. To keep these reactions free and uncontaminated, critics are being discouraged until late in the run. There is much sense in this. Spectators can be conditioned by reading reviews, though the logic of CSC's position would be to ban critics altogether. There is a lot to be said for this, though less than there is to be said against it.

Normand Chaurette's The Queens is an odd candidate for trial-by- perpetual-preview, having already been done in Montreal. (It is played here in an English translation by Linda Gaboriau.) The production is extremely assured; and Friday night's audience obviously felt it to be in no need of fixing. They laughed in what I imagine were the right places, and they cheered and stamped at the end.

I don't want to spoil anybody's fun, but I thought it was terrible. The Queens is an extension of the scene in Shakespeare's Richard III in which the female survivors gather to lament their fallen husbands, sons and grandsons, nearly all of whom seem to have been called Edward.

The play brings together six women intimately involved with the soon- to-be-crowned Richard: Anne Warwick, the Crookback's own consort; Elizabeth, wife of his brother, Edward IV, and mother of the princes in the Tower; his mother, the Duchess of York, ancient mother-in-law of both the above ladies; Isabel, sister of Anne and wife of his brother Clarence, the one who drowned in a butt of malmsey; Anne Dexter, his (and everybody's) silent sister, who mutely patrols the stage looking sorry for everybody including herself and - from the other side of the rose garden - Margaret, widow of Henry VI and last spark of the House of Lancaster.

They are corralled together in a tower in London (maybe even the Tower of London) on a snowy day on which Edward IV may or may not be dying; time is compressed here and whole lives are meant to be passing before us. But what lives? For much of the time Chaurette's women behave just like their Shakespearean namesakes: that is, they complain and they insult one another.

In the original Margaret does nearly all the bitching but here she takes refuge in zaniness. Instead of talking about going home to France she sets out for China but soon comes back. And despite the play's calculated unreality, I have to ask: what is she doing here anyway, sharing a house with her sworn enemies?

This is a literary-historical fantasia that ignores the rules. When the source-material runs out, the author draws on his own store of black whimsy: We are told that Clarence has not spoken in years, and Richard's Anne is ambitious rather than resigned. Well, why not? But, more importantly, why? None of these inventions establishes itself as dramatic fact. They are merely talked about; everything happens off-stage or in the past. Recrimination is these characters' game, and - adrift between history and Shakespeare's distortion of it and Chaurette's distortion of the distortion - they can say whatever they like. Since it's all arbitrary, none of it matters.

Yes, they talk well; or at least they make long speeches with images in them. I can see the attraction for a director, even without Peter Hinton's printed assertion that he loves the play. And if it were as good as his production thinks it is, it would be a masterpiece.

Naked firelight gilds the walls, which are done up in a rich golden shade of perspex-baronial; a soughing wind yields musical punctuation, and real musicians do the same.

The actresses revel. Marion Gilsenan has the best and most authoritative time as a tyrant Duchess of York with a face like a bleached skull and a presence to match. Margot Dionne is an imposing Queen Elizabeth - she looks about seven feet tall - and Tanja Jacobs' Queen Margaret, sounding more Scots than French, is the tartest vinegar.

At the end they all go very reverential, suggesting sisterhood. But, beside the charity of Shakespeare's Duchess, it pales. Think too of his Margaret scattering men with her curses, and his Elizabeth blithely double- crossing Richard when he wants to marry her daughter.

Those women did things. Chaurette's regal victims merely chatter. Instead of griefs they have grievances. Politically I sympathize. Theatrically I am bored to tears.
1994-12-05-theatre-review-still-alive:
THEATRE REVIEW STILL ALIVE

Monday, December 05, 1994

ROBERT CUSHMAN

WRITTEN AND PERFORMED BY ANDY JONES Directed by Jackie Maxwell At the Factory Theatre until Dec. 31 Rating: One-man show is built around an insight found on a crowded bus Mid-life crisis clocked for laughs BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail A FEW seconds into Andy Joness solo show, his glasses fall off. He never replaces them, which may be a statement in itself. We are easily thrown off course, and once this has happened, struggle as we may, we may never get back on again.

Sort of tubby and with a hairline situated somewhere in the middle distance, the despectacled Jones looks a little less like Jason Alexander in Seinfeld, but not much. He certainly has the same demeanour, that of a man who earned his right to a mid-life crisis long before reaching middle age but is really going to collect on it now. Perkily despairing, he tells us "I'm 46 years old and I know nothing."

Jones, once of Codco, makes a fair number of Newfie jokes, mixing local pride with mild hostility. His religious education seems to rile him more. As one of his three rules of life he offers the Catholic Church should completely close down. He goes into some detail about his reasons for this, but not much.

What he is after now is insight. He had one once, and he wants to recapture it, and if possible share it with us. He was on a crowded bus and it came to him: "We're all in the same boat." You might not want to give him a responsible job in transport, but you can sympathize. In fact, I reckon that, given reported world levels of existential angst, he could count on 100 per cent audience agreement. However, Jones is anxious about his own anxiety, and he hands out a questionnaire, with a space for patrons to describe their sexual fantasies. (Its strictly confidential. Well, he does read some of them out at subsequent performances, but you dont give your name.) Meanwhile, an erotic toy is passed around the house. We behave, naturally, like embarrassed good sports.

Jones also refers to philosophers (Martin Heidegger and his brother Jerry) and to his own goal of the pure or Ontological Truth. Trying to pass this off as Irish ("the O'Truth") struck me as one of his more desperate expedients, but then he also says that "the critic is an impediment to the truth" (and that the better you know said critic personally, the more likely you are to realize this) and he is probably right. When really at wits' end, he does a routine that he calls dancing his life, expressive of frustration.

The show has a shape but Jones, like most stand-up comics, spends the evening interrupting himself. He is an expert at this, but not quite a virtuoso. I wanted most of his riffs to be more sustained, more imaginative, funnier than they were. His most inspired idea is to have a stage manager come on stage to clock our laughs. Watching her keeping meticulous score, we cant stop ourselves laughing and pushing the count still higher. Jones also has great extrovert-victim charm and he gets a standing ovation. I dont join in but I don't begrudge it.

BY HAROLD BLOOM Harcourt Brace, 578 pages, $39.95

Canons to the left and right of him THE WESTERN CANON: The Books and School of the Ages

BY HAROLD BLOOM Harcourt Brace, 578 pages, $39.95

Saturday, December 24, 1994

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Review by ROBERT CUSHMAN WHY do we read great books? Quite often because we have to; we are taking or teaching a course, or we feel some kind of cultural compulsion, or we are just driven readers.

Harold Bloom is one of those. A voluminous critic, 40 years on the English faculty at Yale, he seems to have read everything. The Western Canon -an intimidating, uneven, repetitive and magnificent book - is his attempt to order and to crystallize the tradition of European and American literature. Bloom does not deny that there are other canons, but what concerns him is the nature and the probable fate of this one.

Shakespeare - whom he places, uncontroversially, at the very centre of the canon - is also his main exception: the only one exempt from what Bloom calls "the anxiety of influence," which is his pet theory. As I understand it, which is probably imperfectly, major writers are affected by previous major writers, and do battle with the influence in their own works. (But are they conscious of this? That's what bugs me.) How good a fight (an "agon") they put up determines whether they themselves become canonical. Shakespeare influences everyone, but himself owes nothing to anyone except Chaucer; the Wife of Bath, in a splendidly gender-free gesture, begat Falstaff.

So authors rather than readers or critics, in Bloom's view, do the selecting; and the canon is self-perpetuating and elitist beyond the wildest nightmares of conspiracy theorists. It's a pleasing idea, but not entirely buyable; laypersons do have a vote, if only at the sifting stage. Bloom leans heavily upon his theory to shape his story; so Endgame, rather than the more obvious Waiting for Godot, becomes Samuel Beckett's canonical work, on account of its Shakespearean connections. Beckett is the latest author to whom Bloom gives detailed treatment; the earliest, since he doesn't deal with the Greeks, is Dante. More momentously he spotlights Bleak House, which may indeed be Dickens's masterpiece, while omitting Pickwick Papers, an equally great work in its own way and an obvious descendant of Don Quixote which has earlier inspired one of his best chapters. On the other hand, Bleak House does look forward to Kafka. . . you see how the game goes.

There are 26 authors on Bloom's short list, ranging from Tolstoy to Emily Dickinson, Dr. Johnson (the most human of critics and rightly Bloom's own favourite) to Freud, who gets in as a lousy theorist but a great essayist. There is a yawning gap where Dostoevsky should be, and I would love to read Bloom on Jean Jacques Rousseau; but obviously omissions are unavoidable.

A greater problem is that his theories cannot unify those he does include; the book is a collection of discrete essays, dotted with idees fixes. One is his insistence on the "uncanniness" of canonical works, "their ability to make you feel strange at home" - a description I find too Blooming flowery to be helpful. Then there are Bloom's beefs: his running battle with the enemies of the canon, and with its false friends.

The latter are the conservative moralists, the do-gooders of criticism whom Bloom has fought, he tells us, all his career and who profess to find in classic texts a validation of their own beliefs. I would call them the status-quoters. On the other side, but equally sanctimonious, are the assorted Marxists, feminists, deconstructionists and multiculturalists who denounce the canon for its exclusivity and whom Bloom dubs the School of Resentment. (A provocative label: what many of them seem to resent is that others can write and they can't.) Against both factions Bloom proclaims that books have no moral and little political value; they must be enjoyed for themselves. I'm with that, but I cannot help remarking that the Resenters are not always as resentful or as monolithically silly as he makes out, and that even sensitive readers make moral judgments (as Bloom's own commentaries bear witness), even when both the text and its author seem to be nasty pieces of work.

Bloom offers his canon as a labour-saving device, to stop us wasting our limited time on the wrong books, but he also writes as though his own choice were (except by Resenters) unassailable. It isn't. Milton's reputation has been up and down and over and out as often as Frank Sinatra in That's Life. Both Bloom and I know that Ibsen's Peer Gynt is the greatest play since Shakespeare, and one of the funniest, but a surprising number of people disagree. Walter Scott was once ranked ahead of all other novelists. I expect to go to my grave with The Faerie Queen and Finnegans Wake still unconquered, and probably unattempted.

As crotchety as he is defiant, Bloom constantly prophesies a new Dark Age with serious readers an endangered species even - or especially - in the universities, where Literature will become as small and specialized a faculty as Classics. This may not, he implies, be all bad; it will get rid of the fashionable charlatans. English as an academic subject is a recent growth anyway, regarded by the older disciplines as an intolerably soft option. (That generations of undergraduates have thought the same may be its best chance for survival.) If it goes as quickly as it came, novels and poems will still, for those who fancy them, remain.

Plays are a special case, and a fortunate one. "The theatre," Bloom remarks, "has its own traditions and its own continuity" or, to put it another way, it needs product. Hamlet gets staged a lot more often than War and Peace gets read, and it has to stand up and justify itself on each occasion. So do its interpreters; they have to co-exist with their subject, which makes even the most wayward actor and director more responsible than most critics. Bloom says that Shakespeare's supremacy "has little to do with drama as such" (in other words, he's a different animal from Ibsen or Moliere) but the physical persistence of the plays is the best possible argument for the canon.

A further case is presented in Bloom's appendix: a compendious list of the great and the good from the ancients until now. Up until the last century the list obviously aims to be definitive, and there is only one omission I would question: Dumas pere. (The Musketeer novels aren't canonical? D'Artagnan isn't a great soliloquist? Even Shaw knew better than that.) The modern section is confessedly more speculative, racing tips rather than classified results. I'm fairly aghast that the Thomas Mann canon doesn't include Buddenbrooks, and I wonder what Bloom has against the post-war English novel, with no bets placed on Anthony Powell, Angus Wilson, Kingsley Amis or Salman Rushdie. He also omits his own country's line of New York humourists, from Thurber to Catch-22, though he seems a funny man himself. I imagine him played by Zero Mostel. He writes fat. Robert Cushman is still trying to catch up on his reading.
1994-12-30-a-saving-spice-of-self-mocker: A saving spice of self-mockery APPRECIATION / Despite his long list of plays, plus four adaptations, a film script, and two volumes of autobiography, John Osborne remained the man who wrote Look Back in AngerFriday, December 30, 1994ROBERT CUSHMANBY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail JOHN Osborne had a peculiar relationship with history. He made some, and was made by it. He was its beneficiary and, inevitably, its victim. In 1956 he was the playwright who transformed the English (and, by extension, the English-speaking) theatre. He had to spend the rest of his days living up to that initial achievement. Impossible expectations were followed by implacable disappointment.Impressively, he never let up. His publishers list 26 of his plays, plus four adaptations, a film script, and two volumes of autobiography, A Better Class of Person (1981) and Almost a Gentleman (1991). But he remained, as his obituaries earlier this week bear witness, the man who wrote Look Back in Anger. He himself came to accept that, however much he may have resented it. His last play brought back the two leading male characters of Look Back, 35 years on, pairing them with two younger women bearing the same names as their predecessors in the earlier piece. It was part sequel, part (large part) self-parody, and part autobiographical fantasia. It was called Dejavu.What the admirers of Look Back said at the time remains true. It put contemporary life on the stage, and thus brought the stage back into contemporary life. Doubtless somebody else would have done it if Osborne hadn't, but his method of doing it was bracingly direct. He set his play in the kind of dowdy one-room flat familiar everywhere except in the theatre, and put in the middle of it a young man volubly at odds with everything in his world.As social realism it was sketchy but its feeling was contagious. It was a game that everybody - under a certain age, anyway, and even that barrier could be breached - wanted to join in. As an incipiently stage-struck 13- year old, I felt it myself. I didnt, of course, see the stage production, but I did catch a TV relay of the first act: a broadcast, incidentally, that made the plays fortune, since even Kenneth Tynan's landmark rave review had so far failed to fill the house. From the opening moment when Jimmy Porter, the check-shirted protagonist, flung the smart Sunday paper to the floor I was hooked. When he said I've just been reading three columns on the English novel - half of its in French, I was entranced.The last revival I saw confirmed my impression that the play worked largely because it was very funny. When the author felt obliged to wheel on a plot things began to fall apart but a lot of it was just Jimmy talking, doing a routine. It was exhilarating free-form theatre. Osborne had been an actor, at a now inconceivable time when there was theatre, however tacky, all over the country. He had a sense (shared in different ways by his peers and successors Harold Pinter and Peter Nichols) of what worked.His next play, The Entertainer, took this point to extremes. There was the failed comedian Archie Rice doing his routines, wonderful in their awfulness. THere were the naturalistic scenes in Archies family, which were deadly. It became conventional critical wisdom that Osborne wrote great star roles - a point proved by Laurence Olivier in The Entertainer, Albert Finney in Luther, and most of all by Nicol Williamson in what is probably his best play, Inadmissible Evidence -but lousy ensembles. As the 1960s wore on even the protagonists began to fade; the presence of Paul Scofield in Hotel in Amsterdam and Ralph Richardson in West of Suez ensured respectful notices, but the evenings were pretty boring.Osborne himself was in a bind. People had wondered whether Jimmy Porter was based on his creator. It seemed likelier that Osborne came to base himself on Jimmy Porter. He was expected to find new targets to lash out at, and inevitably passion gave way to bewildered tetchiness. One of the few good jokes ever published in the satirical magazine Private Eye depicted a successful playwright called John "Osbore" complaining there must be something wrong with a society that can produce me. Look Back had been one of the first plays presented at the Royal Court, a London theatre dedicated to new playwrighting; the writer and the theatre established one another, inaugurating a stretch of theatrical history that still just about continues. For 40 years the Court has remained identifiably left- wing, but Osborne certainly didn't. After doing his share of anti-nuclear protesting (and feeling, to his credit, pretty silly on a demo) he became increasingly, if idiosyncratically, Blimpish. He seemed incensed that anyone should have the cheek to be younger than he was. His plays invoked, but did not dramatize, things called "love" (an emotion apparently felt only by his favoured protagonists) and England.Of his later plays I liked best A Sense of Detachment, a much-vilified piece that was free-form with a vengeance: a debate on the awfulness of everything and the impossibility of shocking anyone. In a rather similar way, the autobiographies are irresistible; they put nearly everybody down but disarmingly, and are surprisingly free of self-pity. If Osborne's real talent was for monologue, these were the best he ever wrote. (A wonderful line about Beckett: "Uncle Sam had the monstrous good fortune of actually looking like one of his own plays.") Unhappily the autobiographies only get as far as 1966, though a notorious passage in the second flashes forward for the sole purpose of vilifying the suicidal actress Jill Bennett, last but one of his five wives ("this whole rotting body of lies and invention which was her crabbed little life"). Admittedly she had become one of the actresses one most dreaded seeing, but this was largely because during the nine years of their marriage she seemed always to be playing smug complaining roles in his plays.I have no idea how much of his work will survive. Look Back, presumably, as an unusually lively historical artifact. Inadmissible, probably, though so far it's proved unworkable without Williamson. But the life and the work together make an achievement, carried off with style and chronicled with a saving spice of self-mockery. Lines from the autobiography keep turning up in Dejavu, as if he were wryly admitting that for practical purposes Porter had become Osborne. It might have been calculated as his last play; he had become, as he himself said of Noel Coward, his own contribution to the century. It was not the most comfortable of gifts; its ultimate value remains to be seen.Word count: 1144
1995-01-05-last-respects:
THEATRE REVIEW LAST RESPECTS

Thursday, January 05, 1995

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- BY DEBORAH KIMMETT Directed by Sandra Balcovske Starring Martti Arkko, Clare Coulter and Maria Lamont At Tarragon Theatre Rating: Sometimes we wonder what Last Respects would be like without Clare Coulter as the quietly witty Sarah. Other times, all too many of them, we find out Once upon an evening dreary BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto CLARE Coulter, for whom thank God, spends most of Last Respects slumped in a chair. This is because she is dead. Obviously actors of her eminence are not engaged just to play corpses, and I am giving nothing away by revealing that the play frequently flashes back to a time when she was alive.

She plays Sarah, an old English lady now living - or, given the play's structure, now and then living - on Queen's Quay. Coulter is, if I may be parochial, better at British accents than any other Canadian actor I know. The one she adopts here is pinched, parched, quiet, relaxed and devastating: The voice of the London intelligentsia in reduced circumstances. "I have never," she says early on, "found much spiritual awareness in laundry." Well, who has? But she manages to make the admission sound like a masterpiece of wit.

She does the same for most of her lines, and without sounding as if she is bucking for some kind of one-liner award. (That would be an Epigrammy.) She never breaks faith with her character, a compassionate realist who has seen it all. Even just sitting, she looks understanding in a grumpy sort of way. A Buddhist, and a veteran of two marriages, Sarah has a fair idea of what to expect from life, both within and without. Hence her disclaimer about the laundry.

Sometimes we wonder what the evening would be like without her. Other times, all too many of them, we find out. When Clare Coulter is offstage. . . . I'll start that again, she's never offstage. When she is present but deceased, we are thrown back on two of her neighbours, young people who have been touched by her during their own messy and frustrated lives. One of them is Angie, a would-be model with an over-eating problem. Confronted by a man who's come to take her picture she simpers, "You're going to light me, that is so, like, hot." At this point, when she is comparatively carefree, she is probably meant to sound silly. But she isn't any more enlivening when she shacks up with the cameraman and starts in suffering on a steady basis.

One thing that afflicts her, and us, is the strange semi-literary dialogue in which Deborah Kimmett's play, like far too many other plays, is written. When it's not being oracular it tries for what might be called incremental comedy. Angie doesn't just protest that she's thin; she insists that "complete strangers come up to me and say, 'My God, you have small wrists.' " This is formula writing, but an expert comic might make it work. The central thread of the play is Angie's monologue, so she could use some sparkle. (So what if it were out of character? We would forgive.) Maria Lamont plays her doggedly, and without much range. If you take the humour of complaint, but hold the humour, you end up with whining. That is what happens here, and I honestly don't know whether writing or performance is most to blame, any more than I can tell how much credit the author deserves for the laughs Clare Coulter notches up.

Martti Arkko plays the man, who at one point renders the theme from Love Story on an accordion, a combination of atrocities to which it would take a Lady Bracknell to do justice. He drinks too much, and is Finnish; one of Sarah's former partners was Norwegian, a combination that occasions a line about Scandinavian gloom being caused by the sepulchral climate up there: offered, with no visible irony, as a totally new insight.

Audiences tend to suspect three-character plays about other people's domestic problems of being intolerably dreary, and Last Respects does little to disarm the prejudice. On the other hand, if you hang in there, you do get to hear Coulter's Sarah reflecting, with lemony stoicism, on her late husband's continuing inability to locate her clitoris, and that could make it worthwhile.
1995-01-07-theatre-review-the-monument:
THEATRE REVIEW THE MONUMENT

Saturday, January 07, 1995

ROBERT CUSHMAN

WRITTEN BY COLLEEN WAGNER Directed by Richard Rose Starring Rosemary Dunsmore and Tom Barnett At the Canadian Stage Co. Berkeley Street Rating: Treating the horror of war and violence against women as synonymous robs The Monument of its potential power Compelling play not very interesting BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to the Globe and Mail WHEN the lights go up, not that they go up very far, it looks like a scene from a Shakespeare history, brutalist style. A sombrely-clad man harangues us in the gloom from what might be a throne. Slowly we discern that it's actually an electric chair, and that he is strapped to it; the pointy thing on top of his head is not some kind of exotic crown. In the moments before execution he is making confession, though he does not seem very penitent. He is a contemporary soldier recalling the 13 women he has raped and then killed. There is one who especially attracted him and of whose fate he leaves us uncertain. He also speaks of the pressure from his peers that set him off on his career as a war criminal, of his increasing sexual difficulties, and of his own still-virgin girlfriend. What he really regrets, though, is having been caught. It is, as you may well imagine, a powerful speech.

Spotlit beside him, a woman appears. She offers him his life, if he will follow and obey her. We now get to see the entire stage, and a very bleak lunar landscape it provides. She chains him up, beats him unmercifully, forces him to drop a heavy stone on his own foot, chains him to a plow and has him work the barren field on which she apparently lives.
