Finally she takes him to the mass grave of his victims, and makes him dig up their bodies. One of them is her own daughter. These corpses will be a monument, a testimony against war. She wants him to speak to the women who come to view it, but he can't find the words.

The piece is compelling, but not very interesting. If Colleen Wagner were to write an article on the all-too-compendious subject of Atrocities Today, I would probably agree with every word (though I might enter a reservation about a world-view that apparently divides the population into Soldiers and Women, ignoring the fact that modern warfare takes in plenty of male civilian casualties.) But a play is, or should be, something more. Wagner's Soldier may well need the lesson she teaches him, but it's far from clear that the audience does. Though she claims in a program note that the media have neglected the horrors she depicts, and their psychological implications, news reports on the first trial of a Serbian war-criminal took me at least as far inside his head as her play does.

I have been calling the characters the Soldier and the Woman, but she gives them names: Stetko and Mejra. (We're never told it's taking place in Central Europe, but we're bound to think so.) The play is just far enough from being a simple parable to get us asking awkward questions. By what authority does Mejra strike her deal with Stetko? (You can't just walk out of a condemned cell.) Are there really supposed to be women gathered at the end just offstage, or is this a dress rehearsal in her mind?

If we take the play realistically, we spend a lot of it sympathizing with Stetko, whom she humorously addreses as Stinko. To begin with, I thought Tom Barnett's performance too hardened - he is supposed to be a kid scared into becoming a monster - but his choices turn out to be the right ones; the play supplies his vulnerability for him. Whatever he may have done before it starts, what we actually see is him being victimized. That he deserves it, makes little emotional difference. I was surprised that the author hadn't realized this would happen. On reflection I think that she did, and that she wanted to unsettle our preconceptions; at the end Mejra, too, is meant to learn something, presumably about forgiveness. But this isn't clearly presented, and it comes too late to save Rosemary Dunsmore's performance from its single note of strident implacability. She spends the whole evening being right. Richard Rose's production, which stakes everything on starkness, never allows her to play against her lines.

The play treats war, and violence against women, as if they were synonymous, rather than two overlapping horrors. At times it echoes Euripides' Trojan Women, at others Death and the Maiden, but mostly it summons the simplistic self-righteousness of Buffy Sainte-Marie's The Universal Soldier, one of my least favourite songs. Colleen Wagner deserves better, not least from herself.
1995-01-11-spectator-subsidized-or-not-s:
SPECTATOR Subsidized or not subsidized, artists want to please

Wednesday, January 11, 1995

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN THE cultural free market, or what likes to think of itself as such, has been running riot in The Globe and Mail the past two Saturdays. First Andrew Coyne, then William Thorsell.

It was, I confess, cheering to find Coyne, in his suave diatribe against subsidy, insisting on the importance of the audience to the various transactions that we lump together under the heading of art. As Coyne says, in most discussions about art the audience gets left out. Artists lured into public debate talk usually about themselves, occasionally about the few other artists of whom they approve, frequently and with understandable hostility about the critics who are a kind of audience but hardly a representative one. Coyne queries "where the relationship between the artist and his audience begins." It's a good question. But I don't get much out of his answers because, when he talks about the audience, I don't know who or what he means.

Does he think of the audience as one, undifferentiated mass whose taste can easily be gauged in advance? Does he think of it as somehow reducible to a single person? That suggests very tough times indeed, though it's the only context in which his suggestion that "the willing paying audience is present at the creation" makes any kind of sense. A painter might conceivably find room in the studio for a solitary spectator, and they might have some intense conversations about the brushwork; but it doesn't seem a very comfortable arrangement, even given the most cultivated of onlookers. Up the numbers and it becomes self-evidently absurd.

With performed art, there is an important sense in which a play or a piece of music only comes into existence in the presence of an audience. But many of the irrevocable decisions have already been taken before that happens. The show has been rehearsed, and an audience (whose function is to be an outside factor) has no place at rehearsals. Maybe Coyne sees the consulting process as taking place even earlier, with the artist or artists approaching prospective customers and saying, "Look, we have this idea for a comedy or a sculpture or a nude mime of a black mass, does it sound like something you'd be willing to pay money to see?" This does admittedly bear some resemblance to the way in which a commercial production solicits investors, but that has nothing to do with asking the audience what they want. It's asking other people what they think the audience will want.

When we see the finished product, we may hate it. In which case it is our right and maybe our duty to leave, and vow never to spend time or money on any such entertainment again, and advise our friends to go, or rather not go, and do likewise. (Of course their tastes may differ from ours, but subtleties like these don't seem to be Coyne's concern.) It's called voting with our feet; it's a good old custom, and at the more rational points of his article Coyne seems in favour of it; Thorsell too. But they have got it into their heads that this is an audience prerogative that arts subsidy has eliminated. Coyne sees "unconditional granting agencies" indulging the whims of a bunch of pampered esthetes, oblivious of what the public may actually turn out to enjoy. Thorsell - well, if I read him rightly, he believes that country music is a brand-new popular form, called into existence by the Republican majority in the U.S. Congress.

I don't know what world they're living in, but I've never been there. Arts councils are actually cash-strapped committees agonizing between rival claimants; and no subsidized organization gets enough. Do you think the Stratford Festival would have announced such a miserably diminished season for 1995 if they could afford to be independent of the box office? (I'm sorry, but the theatre is the form of which I have most experience, so my terms and examples tend to come from there.) But even if they could, even if they were granted so much money that they could play with impunity to totally empty houses, no company would want to; and not only because their paymasters would get nervous. Artists hate being ignored. A work of art, any work of art, is a statement begging for a response; there is nothing more frustrating than the sound of no hands clapping.

Artists - like industrialists, politicians and journalists, especially columnists - are driven largely by vanity. It comes with the territory. So why do we indulge them in their self-importance? Because they make us feel important, too. They don't do it for all of us, and it's perfectly possible to lead a good, useful and intelligent life without being interested in any of the arts. But most of us have some kind of pleasurable response to some kind of music, drama, literature or visual representation.

Well, all right, but why should the government get involved? Coyne muddies his own waters by referring back to the golden eras of patronage, when Renaissance princes commissioned what masterpieces they wanted and took the consequences. So they did, but the resultant works were then available to all sorts of people who had not placed an order and who should therefore, by Coyne's logic, have been debarred from taking any meaningful pleasure in them. (And the descendants of these peasants actually have the gall to go and gawk at the stuff in galleries, some of it which until recently didn't even have the grace to charge admission.) He also tells us that such things as opera "began as popular art forms." Again true, but tastes have changed and costs have risen.

Few contemporary opera lovers could afford the prices that an unsubsidized opera house would have to charge. That is what subsidy is for: to help audiences, present and future. If it keeps artists from starving that's a benevolent side-effect, but it's not the main point. Why should those who don't like opera help pay for the fun of those who do? Well, why shouldn't they? We all pay taxes for some things we don't use or even like. (Pace Thorsell, it's not only cultural spending that would be questioned if our tax-dollars were itemized.) At this point in the argument it's traditional to invoke a comparison with schools or hospitals, but chances are that Coyne, who makes most Globe editorial writers seem like bleeding-heart liberals, doesn't approve of spending public money on them either. So how about public parks? Not everybody walks in them, but most people would admit their desirability.

Like Coyne I'm embarrassed by some of the claims that are made for subsidized, or indeed non-subsidized, art. I don't think that art has, or should have, much to do with "establishing a national identity" - except in the very important sense that the availability of enjoyable art, from any source, makes a country a nicer place to live in. Like Thorsell, I have my doubts about "Canadian cultural nationalism," though I can't see what this has to do with the attempts of the commercial monopolies who supply cable television to squeeze as much money as possible out of their subscribers. He seems to be using the admirable public revolt against this as a convoluted way of mounting yet another attack on the CBC.

As it happens, I grew up with British television, where subsidized and commercial networks had a virtually equal share of the action. It's obvious that the superiority of British to U.S. television is due to the British commercial companies having had the BBC to compete with and to emulate. Unlike Thorsell I wouldn't call that an elitist situation (isn't it fascinating the way that left and right have joined hands over the use of that word), but if it is, then the trouble with CBC-TV is that it's not elitist enough.

I also went a lot to the theatre, subsidized and other. I was the same person, with the same potential relation to what happened on stage, whether subsidized or wholly commercial. Many in the audience were probably unaware of which sector they were attending. Writers, actors and directors went with equal alacrity from one system to the other, and were as hard-working and as eager to please in either situation.

I don't know precisely what Thorsell's artistic tastes are, but I suspect that if he had to rely entirely on the free market to satisfy them, he might end up frustrated. Coyne disclaims any "neo-conservative ideology," but his theories are so wildly at variance with the facts that it's difficult to see what else could be driving him.
1995-01-14-theatre-review-six-degrees-of:
THEATRE REVIEW SIX DEGREES OF SEPARATION

Saturday, January 14, 1995

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- DIRECTED BY MARTI MARADEN Written by John Guare Starring Fiona Reid, Jim Mezon and Nigel Shawn Williams, At St Lawrence Centre through Feb. 4 Rating: In some important respects Marti Maraden's production measures up to the Fred Schepsi movie which playwright John Guare also scripted and which was terrific Retelling a great story BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to the Globe and Mail Toronto SOMETHING in me wishes that the plot of Six Degrees of Separation were the playwrights own invention. The most extraordinary thing about John Guares play is its narrative, a tall story that grabs the mind and the attention, and radiates in all sorts of directions. Guare - the most promising playwright in the U.S. for an uncomfortable number of years, and also author of the wonderful screenplay for Atlantic City -seized on a newspaper report that had lodged in his mind for years and turned it, in 1991, into his own masterpiece: the best American play since David Mamet's Glengarry Glen Ross (1984). As Shakespeare knew, the next best thing to telling a great story is retelling one.

There are Flan Kittredge, a very rich New York art-dealer, and his wife Ouisa. (Short for Flannery and Louisa - the diminutives tell you a lot about their style.) They narrate the story, and they also act it out. Into their apartment, on the night they are trying to stitch up a million- dollar-or-so transaction, there, literally, stumbles a black teen-ager called Paul. He is bleeding, and claims to have been mugged in Central Park. He also claims to be a college friend of his hosts' children, and the unacknowledged son of Sidney Poitier. Paul charms the Kittredges with his manners, his cooking, his unstoppable flow of casually erudite conversation, and, above all, with his promise of extras roles for them in his fathers forthcoming film of (wait for it) Cats. They take him in for the night. Next morning, they decide that it's they who have been taken in, when they discover Paul in bed with a boy of no social graces at all. They might, they scream, have been murdered or at least robbed. In fact, nothing is missing; though, God knows, they have a lot worth taking.

Later they discover that friends of theirs have been similarly stung. It turns out, thanks to the resentful detective work of the Kittredges' extremely sulky kids, that a former high-school nerd has given Paul the goods on them. He has also, in exchange for sex, taught him how to speak and conduct himself, and how to express gratitude for hospitality: with a basket of flowers in which nestles a small pot of expensive jam. Paul, meanwhile, has moved on to other prey: a young pair of would-be actors whom he fleeces, with tragic results. All the same, when he says that money is not his principal object, we believe him.

On one level, the play is an extremely funny satire on wealth-and- celebrity worship. If Paul wants in with the Kittredges, so do they with his supposed dad. The world may have room for just one more expose of radical chic, and Ouisa meditating on a possible visit to South Africa (she wouldnt want to see people who were just comparatively downtrodden," shed want the real thing) hilariously supplies it. It is also, rather portentously, about the ambiguity of people and things; Fran's most cherished possession is a two-sided painting by Kandinsky. Vitally, it is about loneliness, and personal and family failure.

The junior Kittredges are monsters; the boy, on first hearing about Paul, only breaks silence to scream, "You mean you gave him my pink shirt? " But it is pretty clear who has made them that way: clear too that Ouisa, even when she learns the truth about him, regards Paul as her second chance.

Their last telephone conversation is extraordinarily charged. Silly and snobbish as Ouisa seems, she can be awakened; and the play makes the process very moving. Its great triumph is that it slides from brittle to profound without any grinding change of gear. The title, like the play itself, derives from something someone once read; Ouisa has heard that everybody in the world is separated from everyone else by only six acquaintances. By my count, there are only four degress of separation between her and Paul but, as she says, it makes you think. It certainly makes you listen.

The play arrives in Toronto on the heels of the Fred Schepsi movie which Guare also scripted and which, apart from a new, sentimental coda, was terrific. It brilliantly expanded the play's narrative device, and it took us to places - the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, for one - that the play can only describe or suggest. It was also perfectly cast. In some important respects, though, Marti Maradens production matches up. Phillip Silvers sets and lighting create a shimmering background in acryllic, and Christina Poddubiuk's costumes are stunning; Ouisa ends the evening in a black off-the-shoulder number for which Stephen Caras gets a special credit, and for which it is truly to die.

To put it another way, it is worthy of Fiona Reid's performance, which duplicates the plays own balancing-trick; always incipiently but never actually absurd, she looks sharp and weights nearly every line of Ouisas to perfection. Nobody else is really good enough, except perhaps Clive Cholerton in a wistful cameo as Paul's last victim. Jim Mezon's Flan, though capable, fades too easily into the woodwork; Michael Ball doubles without special distinction either way; and all the rest push too hard for a script that demands a perfect Manhattan balance of energy and poise. This is most evident with Paul himself: Nigel Shawn Williams has the hungry power of the predator but, finally, lacks the assurance of the consummate con man.
1995-02-24-book-review-cats-of-any-color:
By Gene Lees Oxford University Press, 246 pages, $34.95

BOOK REVIEW CATS OF ANY COLOR: Jazz Black and White

By Gene Lees Oxford University Press, 246 pages, $34.95

Friday, February 24, 1995

Robert Cushman

Essays that explore race and riffs Reviewed by Robert Cushman IN a feature on racism in the current issue of Jazz Times, Gene Lees is quoted as saying, "If I was a black, I would hate white people, no question in my mind about that." Lees himself is a Canadian who grew up during the Second World War with a pantheon of black American heroes. ("Fifty years ago," he recalls, "it appeared that Canadians had never accomplished anything.") He has spent his adult life in the United States writing about and around jazz. The essays that make up this book provide plenty of grim evidence as to why blacks might hate whites, but are also full of heartening testimony from those who refuse to.

Louis Armstrong supplies the epigraph: "It's no crime for cats of any colour to get together and blow." Clark Terry tells a horrific story about being forced, as a young man, to hide under the mud of a building site after his friend had accidentally jostled a white woman in a Southern store. He then tells of how, decades later, his attempt to start a street- kids' band in Harlem was sabotaged when he brought in a white teacher. "Man," he was told, "we don't want Whitey teaching us about our music." A disgusted Terry insists that a note doesn't care who plays it, as long as it's done well. A third and much younger trumpeter echoes him: "Music is music."

That's Wynton Marsalis, discussing his own determination to prove that a black jazzman could also play classical. For Marsalis, though, this traffic seems to be on a one-way street. Such, at least, is Lees' contention in his last and most spirited chapter. He excoriates Marsalis, as director of the jazz program at Lincoln Centre, for excluding white composers and musicians. His real target, though, seems to be Marsalis's mentor, the critic Stanley Crouch, whom he accuses of rewriting history to marginalize white musicians such as Bill Evans and to downgrade blacks - including Miles Davis - who played with them.

Wars between jazz critics are bloody affairs, and it's possible that some old scores are being paid off here. But Lees documents his charges, sometimes to devastating effect. Having quoted Marsalis as claiming that improvisation was "invented" in New Orleans, he responds with a quick catalogue of improvisational European music, going back centuries before jazz. In more detail, he demonstrates that black swing bands were as eager to hire white arrangers as white bands were to "exploit" black ones. None of this cancels out the brutal discrimination suffered by black Americans in and out of the music business. But Lees' conclusion is unassailable. Either jazz is the protest-vehicle of a single race, or it's a major musical form and, as such, bound to be explored by anyone interested.

The rest of the book is made up of easy-going profiles: Of bop pianist Horace Silver, who says fairly and decently that if their talent were equal he would hire a black musician over a white one but does not believe that you can rectify an old injustice by inflicting a new one; of trumpeter and scam artist Red Rodney and masterful expatriate bassist Red Michell; and of Dave Brubeck, whose part-Indian descent allows Lees to highlight a racial component of jazz that has really been marginalized. His subjects all come out sounding the same - an occupational hazard familiar to all writers-up of interviews - though Lees reserves the really awkward lines for himself. " 'When and where does the black participation begin in America in what we imprecisely call classical music?' I asked." Did he really?

He is also keen to tell us how he used to hang out with Miles or to throw in a reference to "my friend Oscar Peterson" in a context to which their friendship is totally irrelevant. The dedication to Dizzy Gillespie is vintage Lees, shifting the spotlight firmly from the subject to the author: "I miss you Birks./ I thought you would be there forever / like the Matterhorn, and the Aurora Borealis / and Polaris." The comparisons sound like rejects from one of his lyrics. He has written many, including the tenderly awestruck words to Evans' Waltz for Debbie and Jobim's Someone to Light Up My Life, but their uniform solemnity keeps them out of the front rank. (He also performs them well; if you can imagine a critic who sings.) Much the same is true of his prose; if his last chapter here is the best, it's partly because in the excitement of polemic he almost forgets to be self-admiring. Robert Cushman is a Toronto critic who sings.
1995-03-17-torme-reads-well-on-stage-and:
Torme reads well on stage and page MUSIC REVIEW / In his Sing Sing Sing concert appearance this week, the singers joyous flow of musical ideas came through pristine and uncluttered. In his new book, My Singing Teachers, his specific comments are sensible and enlightening, but there aren't enough of them BOOK REVIEW MY SINGING TEACHERS

Friday, March 17, 1995

ROBERT CUSHMAN

By Mel Torme Oxford University Press, 228 pages, $27.95 BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail MEL Torme says in interviews that he sings better in his 70th year than he did at 35. I would dispute that - the records he made in the early 1960s seem to me unsurpassable - but I certainly think he sings better at 69 than he did at 67 or 68. On his last two appearances in Toronto his voice sounded cloudy and nasal, as if the Velvet Fog of his youth had resettled, and in a thicker formation. But on Wednesday at the George Weston Recital Hall, it had lifted, and his joyous flow of musical ideas came through pristine and uncluttered. He was magnificent.

The concert was named after Benny Goodman's old warhorse Sing, Sing, Sing -and a tune, ironically, that no one ever sings; Torme himself took to the drums for the duration. It was the climax of a substantial Goodman tribute, Torme and his musicians forming, as he said, a new Goodman sextet. (He has, in Ken Peplowski, an urbanely excellent clarinetist for the job, but his vibes player has some way to go before matching Lionel Hampton.) But it was only part of a set that otherwise had no particular theme except Tormes relish for, and knowledge of, jazz-flavoured popular song.

The knowledge is important, since Torme is a commentator as well as a performer: in the way he sings, in what he says between the songs, and - increasingly - in print. Reviewing his autobiography in these pages a few years ago, I hoped for a subsequent volume that would tell us less about his wives and more about his music. His new book My Singing Teachers is, I guess, the answer to my request: a quick trot through the singers, composers, instrumentalists and arrangers whom he most admires and who have most influenced him. There are a lot of them; he deals with so many vocalists, from Ella Fitzgerald on down, that one starts speculating on the few he has left out. His specific comments are sensible and enlightening, but there arent enough of them. One wishes he had chosen fewer subjects, dug deeper into them, and made more detailed connections between their work and his own. He is often most instructive - maybe because they're not direct competition - on people who stand outside the pop-singing mainstream: on Fred Astaire, who seems to bring out the best in everybody; on Woody Herman, the beloved singing bandleader; on minor Broadway figures like Stubby Kaye, the original Nicely-Nicely of Guys and Dolls who "held that company together like Krazy Glue."

This all-encompassing joy in the different show-business traditions is the glue that binds his own act. It enables him to start out Pick Yourself Up as a straightforward Astaire-Rogers tribute, funny and rhythmic, and then with no break in the performing logic to turn it into a scat showcase. With flawless pitch he negotiates every twist and leap in the alarming melodic line of Stardust and also - something I've never known before - manages to act out the lyric. Ballads bring out the best in him; his version of My Foolish Heart (another vocal back-breaker) with superbly sensitive piano backing from John Colianni, is spell-binding. He also tells you what film it came from and when he saw it; and you can believe him. Such factual reliability - in both his patter and his book - is almost unheard of.

He prides himself on his lyric-readings, which are always intelligent, always alive. But though his phrasing is impeccably conversational, his tone isn't - which may explain why he has never quite achieved the recognition afforded Sinatra, Tony Bennett, or Nat Cole who, with their more fallible instruments, always seem to be talking directly to you. A certain architectural remoteness is the price he pays for that beautiful voice; you can hear him taking a song and consciously threading it through his pipes, his arrangements. In the late sixties he recorded Beatles songs, but he seems now to have given up any strained attempts at modernity. This tubby, wizened septuagenarian is not nostalgia, he is living history: making and recording it. He seems undeniably pleased with himself but he deserves to be; and he turns that pleasure outward.
1995-04-22-spectator-following-rapunzel-:
Spectator Following Rapunzel and the gang into the enchanted Woods

Saturday, April 22, 1995

Robert Cushman

BY Robert Cushman THIS is not meant to be a riposte to theatre critic Kate Taylor's review of Into the Woods (When wishes come true, April 8), but I must answer her query about why the Canadian Stage Company should be doing this musical. They should be doing it because its a masterpiece. And its Canadian premiere is long overdue.

I love Into the Woods, and so do my children. (My wife does too.) This family agreement is especially pleasing, since the Stephen Sondheim-James Lapine show is partly about connections - sometimes made, more often missed - between the generations. It juxtaposes three familiar fairy-tales - Cinderella, Little Red Riding Hood and Jack and the Beanstalk - with a subsidiary role for Rapunzel and last-minute cameo appearances by Snow White and the Sleeping Beauty. Binding them all together in Lapines script is a newly invented fable: the story of the Baker and his Wife, and the Witch next door. The couple want a child, and the Witch promises them one, if certain quests are achieved. So into the woods they go, as do Jack, Cinders and Ms. Hood in pursuit of their own legendary goals. And their stories criss-cross, with the Baker slaying the Wolf with his bread- knife, and his wife helping Cinderella off with her shoe, and the witch revealed as Rapunzel's adoptive mother.

What I can only call the sheer story-ness of the show is the most captivating thing about it: the delight of never knowing who will come around the next corner, or lurk behind the next tree; the satisfaction of seeing how neatly the pieces interlock and how powerfully the separate tales flow into one in the show's darker second half, which is about what happens after happily ever after. It is, of course, this joy in narrative that unites children and adults (and, in my own case, has persisted through the multiple viewings of the Broadway-cast video that my own brood have wished upon me). Lapines book is one of the most satisfying ever written for a musical. Without denying us the pleasures of dialogue (as happens in the Lloyd Webberish pop operas), it merges seamlessly with Sondheims score. There are no jolts when one ends and the other begins, and in a musical that is the rarest kind of success.

It's partly because of the timeless world that the show inherits from its sources and then makes its own. Fairy-tale characters can burst into song with no questions asked. Also there's no question that in creating a classic it helps to start with another classic; or, as here, with a fistful of them. Myths reverberate; its their job. The Baker shares with his own estranged father a song of desperation called No More, in which he pleads, vainly, for escape from the world: "No more giants waging war/Cant we just pursue our lives/With our children and our wives . . .." I saw the show in London the night the Gulf War broke out, and the resonance was almost unbearable.

Then too the pastoral setting makes a perfect launching-pad. Anything, as the Prince Charming sings when he gets around to seducing the Baker's Wife, "can happen in the woods." Describing the appeal of his previous show Sunday in the Park with George (based on the Seurat painting A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte), Sondheim said, You just wanted to live in that park forever and ever. Personally I didn't, but I was very happy to stay in the woods; greenery, potent and deceptively soothing, can be the richest of dramatic environments. (The greatest play in the English language is A Midsummer Nights Dream; the most delightful is Loves Labour's Lost.) Canadian Stage has taken a puritanical attitude, cutting the trees down to projections on screens. They are lovely, and they go interestingly haywire when the action lurches out of control in Act Two, but they are overpowered by a surrounding array of steps, like something out of a 1950s Macbeth. This defoliation is one of my few cavils with the Toronto production.

Here I had better declare an interest. I auditioned - unsuccessfully - for the role of the Narrator in this production. (I'm not sure in which direction this biases me.) It was an interesting experience, not least because having to sing a section of No More heightened my already mountainous regard for Sondheims powers of musical and verbal characterization, in this case for the depiction, with piercing economy, of a mind that has gone to the end of its tether and back again.

I like most of his shows, some of them extravagantly, but none as much as this. I thought it was a near-masterpiece (Im a cautious soul) back in 1988 when I saw a preview of the Broadway production, which had an almost unbeatable cast. It was patronized by the New York critics who seemed to feel that a composite fairy-story was a letdown after the self-evidently Important Theme (The Plight of the Artist) of Sunday in the Park. It got far better reviews in London, where classic comedy and ensemble performance - every part in this show is worth performing - are part of the culture. The score, like the book, is a spider's web with ribs of steel: a cat's cradle of cunningly interwoven motifs, brief shafts of melody and lyric that grow richer at each repetition. For a taste, listen to the Bakers Wife as her princely fantasy develops through her scenes with her husband and Cinderella before erupting into a brief unsettling reality, with a truly shocking sequel. The tired old accusation that Sondheims music lacks emotion actually means that he offers crystalline intensity while most others today settle for deafening bloat.

"Children should listen," shrieks the Witch at the refractory Rapunzel. (An admonitory song while combing her daughter's hair had two mothers of my acquaintance asking the same question: How does he know?) "Children won't listen," she grieves after she has lost the girl for good. At the finale theres a final modulation as the company tell us that Children will listen. Its more a warning than a reassurance. "Careful the things you say . . .," your kids will pick up on them, not always as you would like. The music is healing, and the show over all is as compassionate as it's astringent, but the first time I saw it I wept. Admittedly, I was a soft touch. I had come through, just about, my own first year of fatherhood; and the show seemed to play out some of my fondest dreams and some of my worst nightmares. It still gets me.

It also makes me laugh a lot, never more than in the competing duet, Agony, of Cinderella's and Rapunzels royal swains, reprised with compound comic interest when they fall for a couple of other maidens. I must have her to wife, which is the ending first time round, mutates into "ah well, back to my wife." Their joint attitudinizing, like a couple of old theatrical prints of old theatrical princes, is deliciously handled at CSC: credit, I imagine, to the choreographer, Denise Clarke.

No family or romantic unit remains intact in this show, but the community just about survives. It might be a meditation on two essential texts: Philip Larkins imperishable they fuck you up, your mum and dad and Donne's "no man is an island."

I've left an awful lot out. Sondheims ability to penetrate and project the thoughts and emotions of his characters while retaining a recognizable personal voice, his range of subject matter and complete absorption in each new project, his wit and irony, his balancing of a faultless ear for human speech against the formal demands of verse and music, have long prompted the highest comparison: one at which Ive already hinted. Not all his shows could sustain it - but Into the Woods, showering sensual and intellectual delights while its themes and implications expand as effortlessly and implacably as Jack's beanstalk, is the most Shakespearean work of contemporary theatre that I know.

Robert Cushman is a freelance theatre critic based in Toronto. Into the Woods plays at Toronto's St. Lawrence Centre through May 20.
1995-06-01-the-boy-friend:
THEATRE REVIEW THE BOY FRIEND

Thursday, June 01, 1995

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Stratford, Ont. -- Written by Sandy Wilson Directed by Brian Macdonald Starring Patty Jamieson, Danny Austin, Eric Donkin, Karen K. Edissi and Cara Hunter At the Stratford Festival until Oct. 28 Rating: The Boy Friend a limited masterpiece Reviewed BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to the Globe and Mail Stratford, Ont. ACKNOWLEDGED masterpiece of the British musical though it is, The Boy Friend has yet to be seen at Britain's National Theatre. This may be because the current director of that institution, the estimable Richard Eyre (whose own acting career virtually ended with a role in the show) has a block about it. He has dismissed it as insipid nostalgia fodder for remote outposts of the Empire. He may not, of course, have had the Stratford Festival directly in mind.

I can call The Boy Friend a masterpiece without blushing, but I have to admit that it is a masterpiece of a peculiarly limited kind. In the mid- 1950s, Sandy Wilson came up with book, music and lyrics for what he called "a new musical comedy of the 1920s." He faithfully observed every convention. He set his story on the French Riviera, where rich, sweet young ladies at finishing school pretend to be typists in order to romance handsome young delivery boys who turn out to be aristocrats in disguise. Meanwhile, more madcap flappers disport themselves with young American millionaires, not in disguise. The action regularly stops for wistfully virginal ballads or exuberant dances, cued in with breathtaking (and frankly delicious) artlessness.

Compared with actual musicals of the twenties, The Boy Friend is a very gentle show, with no set-piece comedy routines and the merest wisp of a mistaken-identity plot. Wilson's songs are stylistically spot-on; his rhymes have just the right fanatical ease ("psychic/I kick") and the music, however derivative in theory, sparkles in its own right: the love- duets, I Could Be Happy with You and A Room in Bloomsbury, are at least as good as the Vincent Youmans and Noel Coward numbers that inspired them, and the title number is a worthy partner for Rodgers and Hart's Girl Friend.

The show, and especially its score, has tremendous conviction; as if Wilson truly believed that this was the only way to write musicals. (None of his later shows, in different styles, achieved anything like the same success, though he wrote an interestingly pungent thirties sequel to The Boy Friend called Divorce Me, Darling. Some enterprising theatre - hey, what about the Stratford Festival? - should revive them in tandem.) The Boy Friend isn't nostalgia, though most productions of it are. It isn't parody; it may not even be pastiche. It's a distillation, that separates out one of its mythical period's salient qualities: its innocence. What makes the show more durable than its role models is that, with all its silliness, it makes you care about heroine Polly Browne and her all too suitable suitor. Even if you smile at the style, you should believe in the people.

The balance, of course, is devilishly difficult to strike. Brian Macdonald's production cannot resist letting everybody pout, posture and preen too much; while it practically signals its willingness to do anything for a laugh by having one of its women played (not very well) by a man. More damagingly, it has a Polly (Patty Jamieson) whose talents are more soubretish than ingenuous, matched with a boy friend (Ian Simpson) who is the height of nondescript. Eric Donkin and Douglas Chamberlain do reliable senior-comic work; Donkin, the most restrained person on stage, looks woefully hilarious when kitted-out as a reluctant sultan at a fancy- dress ball, and Chamberlain shakes a mean elderly leg when paired with a flapper called Dulcie (inspired name) in the show's most infallible number, It's Never Too Late To Fall In Love (boop-a-doop, boop-a-doop, boop-a-doop). Choreographic verve carries the show through; Macdonald is a whiz at sneaking extra characters on stage so that a small ensemble becomes a big one without you noticing; and in a first-act Charleston and a thoroughly abandoned finale, the stage explodes.
1995-06-03-theatre-review-the-gondoliers:
THEATRE REVIEW THE GONDOLIERS

Saturday, June 03, 1995

Robert Cushman

Written by W. S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan Directed by Brian Macdonald Starring Curis Sullivan, Craig Ashton, Pamela Gerrand and Eric Donkin At the Avon Theatre, in Stratford, Ont., until Oct. 28 Rating: A spoonfed audience, an irresistible show Reviewed by Robert Cushman THE Stratford Festival should commission David Mayerovitch to write a satirical contemporary musical. The updated lyrics he has supplied for some of the songs in The Gondoliers are technically immaculate and sometimes very funny. They are also inexcusable. Mayerovitch's claim that he has merely supplied new equivalents for Gilbert's own faded topicalities is, to put it kindly, disingenuous.

In the original, Giuseppe, one of two republican-minded Venetian gondoliers unexpectedly promoted to the imaginary throne of Barataria, sings about being a neurotically conscientious king at the beck and call of his subjects. Here he does a number about our very own deficit. It's not as if the revisions were part of some thoroughgoing new production concept. Most of the time we're trundling through the old familiar script; then we're in contemporary Canada for the duration of one number; then it's back to Venice or Barataria as if nothing had happened. Yes, Gilbert set his show in an anachronistic never-never land, but he stuck by his own rules; crazy logic is one of the things he's famous for. And he didn't believe in pandering to his public. This Stratford version is spoonfeeding an audience that already gets indulged far more than is good for it.

The author's humour takes a lot of tumbles. The male members of the company display an interesting range of techniques for defusing the dialogue. The young ones - cast, presumably, for their singing voices - sail blandly through it, quite in the manner of the old D'Oyly Carte. At the more accomplished end, Eric Donkin as the Duke finishes off each of his lines with a self-deprecating cough, letting you know that he doesn't find this stuff any funnier than you do. Then there is Lee MacDougall's virtuoso turn as the Grand Inquisitor, giggling, hysterical, in fact Pythonesque: the kind of Spanish Inquisition nobody ever expects.

This is an extremist production; the bad things are painful, the good ones brilliant. (MacDougall's performance is both.) First among the virtues is Susan Benson's design, beginning with the vista of white steps against sheer black space that knocks our eyes out when we enter the theatre. It includes the dream in gold that is the Baratarian throne room. Then there is the surprising vein of melancholy that runs through the show; its emblems are carnival zanies and fast-fading roses, and it crests in Allison Grant's beautifully relaxed singing of "when a merry maiden marries." She and Aggie Cekuta Elliot, as the brides of the gondoliers, are the production's performing jewels, warm and witty. But the other ladies are good too: Glynis Ranney's uppity princess; Douglas Chamberlain's Duchess, who, like the best pantomime dames, is rugged as well as regal; and Karen K. Edissi, spitting fire as the beldame Inez. Her appearance - on a portable rack - is one of the two great coups of Brian Macdonald's staging. The other is the second-act Spanish dance: an ensemble number that starts as vigorous but conventional, mainly notable for the swirl of the costumes. Then one dancer, then another, then all, pick up dummies as partners and proceed to swing them in a manner that might appall the most intrepid of adagio artistes. It builds and builds, to become the wildest, funniest, most intoxicating production number I have seen in years. From then on, there can be no looking back; and the show is irresistible.
1995-07-13-music-review-barbara-cook-coo:
MUSIC REVIEW BARBARA COOK Cook delights fans with Broadway hits

Thursday, July 13, 1995

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto ONE of Barbara Cook's favourite lines, referring to her tenure as Broadway's favourite ingenue of the fifties and sixties, is that she never knew at the time that she was part of some Golden Age of musical comedy. She is not a nostalgia-monger, but her cabaret and concert act is based on our awareness of who she was and what she stood for. Performer and audience unite in contemplating where she's come from, and where she thinks she's going.

She rations her greatest hits severely. One pleasant chorus of 'Till There Was You (from The Music Man) is buttressed by the two longest- serving crowd-pleasers in her repertoire. One is Losing My Mind, the breakdown song that she sang in the celebrated concert revival of Follies. The other, Cook's tour de force, is Ice Cream, the ecstatic monologue of romantic discovery (finding her mind, perhaps) that she introduced in She Loves Me. Cook is now a voluminous woman with shimmering gowns, but when she sings this piece she creates a witty and precisely distanced cameo of rushing girlish excitement, culminating in a celebrated and intoxicating high B. It would bring down the hardest-hearted house.

That's it for history. There are none of her jewels from Flahooley, The Gay Life, The Grass Harp or even Candide, though she does tell a long anecdote about auditioning for Leonard Bernstein, and terrifying him with the top notes in Madam Butterfly. Turning to now, she does a couple of countrified plaints by Amanda McBroom that she rates more highly than I do, though I grant them the occasional piercing line.

After a roguish reference to Duke Ellington and the boys, she sashays into I'm Beginning to See the Light, to my complete disbelief. Her rhythm is perfectly fine, an exemplary Broadway lilt, but she is not a jazz singer and her paraphrases, extensions and elisions sound as if they have been written down and learned by rote. This is not to say that Ellington should be off limits to her, merely that she should find her own way into him, rather than trying to turn herself into a finger-snapper. I also, in the face of roomsful of cheering devotees, am appalled by her slow, show- boating one-long-climax version of Carolina in the Morning: because it has nothing to do with the song. Cook is an actress; to be true to herself, she has to find the truth in her material.

So Ice Cream works wonderfully and so does Arthur Schwartz's Make the Man Love Me, a lovely song simply sung, and another instance of innocence reached through experience. Losing My Mind fails (this is another minority report) because, emote though she may, she remains a very together lady. She cannot move me to sorrow, though she frequently moves me to delight. She does so in The Surrey with the Fringe on Top - it's the best thing in the show - where, though clearly not the cowboy envisioned by Rodgers and Hammerstein, she creates a new person with a delightful ironic kinship to the original. The voice is still a wonder, and the showmanship is impeccable.
1995-09-19-theatre-review-dionysus:
THEATRE REVIEW DIONYSUS

Tuesday, September 19, 1995

Robert Cushman

Based on The Bacchae by Euripides Directed by Tadashi Suzuki Starring the Suzuki Company of Toga At Harbourfront Centre in Toronto until Thursday Rating: Drearily predictable world-view mangles Euripides play Reviewed by Robert Cushman I HAD some trouble understanding this Japanese adaptation of The Bacchae, and not just because I don't speak Japanese. Euripides's tragedy, perhaps the starkest ever written, stages the conflict between Dionysus, god of wine and the raging unconscious, and Pentheus, the young and uptight King of Thebes. Dionysus's cult has invaded Thebes, and Pentheus wants to stamp it out. He imprisons its prophet: actually the god himself in disguise. The prophet escapes. He then persuades Pentheus to dress in drag to spy on the female Dionysiacs cavorting in the hills. The women discover and dismember him. Their leader is Pentheus's own mother.

There is nothing just about this; Dionysus may represent impulses in humanity that it represses at its own peril but he is also avenging a slight against his family. The Bacchae, like all Greek tragedies, only more so, is about the unfairness of life, raised to a cosmic level. There may be a suggestion that wisdom lies in some psychic compromise between the sensualist and the censor, but the play gives little indication that such a safety-zone actually exists.

The most obvious departure in Tadashi Suzuki's Dionysus is that it leaves out Dionysus. He makes no personal appearance, and his lines have been appropriated by the chorus: six sacerdotal gentlemen in pointed hats that made them look like bishops and to a friend in the audience like Venetian Doges. She shouldn't have said that: "Git along, little Doges", I found myself muttering as the sextet closed in for the kill, conceivably intoning the Japanese for "that'll learn ya."

Suzuki's view of the legend, as expounded in his program notes, is that "Dionysus never existed as such; rather (there was) a group with a communal need for unity and the will to spiritually influence the masses." Instead of the Euripidean conflict between a god and a man who between them speak for all of us (and who forge an eerily sympathetic bond), we get a struggle between two axiomatically corrupt political establishments. Suzuki says he has used Euripides "to stage my world view." That is his right but his world-view seems, especially when compared with the original, drearily predictable.

He has added another layer: a second chorus of moaning men in wheelchairs, like emissaries from the world of Samuel Beckett. Their leader is attended by a shambling figure with lank flaxen hair, an undead ringer for Lucky from Waiting for Godot. They are identified in the program as "believers of the Farewell Cult" though what that cult might be, we are not told. But their chief does speak (in English) of the desirability and the impossibilty of escaping history. They are not part of the story; they are an awful comment on its awfulness.

The execution is better than the conception. On a stage furnished only with seven uncomfortable-looking yellow chairs the actors move and speak with iron control. A trio of Maenads appear in red-and-white robes that trail enticingly along the floor. It's what a Westerner expects experimental Japanese theatre to look and sound like: savage, disciplined and sardonic. (By the same token I expect a well-drilled kick-line in a Broadway musical.) But only one scene stirred me, and it may be a comment on me that it was the only scene in the main action to be done in English. Agave, Pentheus's mother, discovers what she has done to her son, and banishes herself from the city. It is the most extreme of situations, appallingly difficult to act. The actress, Ellen Lauren, is Australian but she sounds like a Japanese speaking impeccable English rhetoric. Her words burn with implacable fire, as if sculpted out of sulphur. The chorus reply to her in their own language but at the same temperature. They meet the scene at its own daunting level. They made me wish Suzuki had staged The Bacchae. Dionysus is being presented as part of Harbourfront Centre's Today's Japan, an exposition of contemporary culture.
1995-09-23-theatre-review-the-escape:
THEATRE REVIEW THE ESCAPE

Saturday, September 23, 1995

Robert Cushman

Written and performed by Abel and Gordon At the Tarragon Theatre until October 8 Rating: -1/2 The Escape suffocated by winsomeness Reviewed by Robert Cushman ABEL and Gordon are very good at what they do. Dominique Abel is a sweet-faced Belgian harlequin who, when he perches on imaginary ledges 13 imaginary storeys up, can make you share his vertigo. He can pull the oldest trick in the book of mime - feeling his way along an invisible wall and convincing you it's solid - and render it new. Fiona Gordon, who has the absentmindedly sultry air of an elongated Carol Burnett, boasts a body that bends in all the recognized places plus a few on which the patent may still be pending. She is superb at jumping into bed. That may not sound like much, but her bed is fixed at a steep diagonal to the floor and is some five feet tall at its highest point.

It's what they do with what they do that's unspeakable. That may not be quite the right word, since they use their voices as well as their limbs. In fact, it's their dialogue, much reinforced by cute addresses to the audience, that does most to create the show's overall effect, which is one of suffocating winsomeness. (A new esthetic theory: The only thing more unbearable than mime is mime that talks.) Abel plays Modiste the Ripper, who accidentally stuck a fork into somebody's head in a restaurant and is now doing time. However, he escapes, by unravelling the bars of his prison window in a fashion known only to pantomime artistes, and is soon being chased through the streets by his co-star who is playing a Keystone Kop with a ginger mustache. (Naturally, the chase is in slow motion, but at least we're spared strobe lights.) Our hero then invades the apartment of a lanky female insomniac who is briefly alarmed but soon recognizes him for the harmless paragon he is. When the police interrupt their idyll, Modiste takes refuge in the fridge. When his beloved opens it he has disappeared. He subsequently explains that he was hiding in a can of sardines; and if that doesn't sum up The Escape for you nothing will.

Logic - the essence of nonsense - is sacrificed for whatever piece of whimsy comes into the performers' heads, as is suspense; why should we be concerned for someone who can do the impossible? The show's publicity blasphemously invokes Buster Keaton, who did admittedly specialize in chase-sagas shared with ditzy heroines. But Keaton always played, hair- raisingly and implacably, by the rules, and he never begged for our love; that was the great virtue of his famous stone face. Abel's bids for sympathy make Charlie Chaplin, Harpo Marx and even the super-masochistic Marcel Marceau look as misanthropic as W. C. Fields. At one point he reads the instructions on a bottle of sleeping pills, and pronounces them unfit for children, adults, cats, dogs and giraffles (I swear.) Gordon does look a bit like a giraffle, and she manages to appear coy while wearing a dress that starts off-the-shoulder and then plunges, which is quite a trick.

Two other recommendations: The audience bravoed, and it's all over in an hour-and-a-quarter.
1995-09-28-theatre-review-ph:
THEATRE REVIEW pH

Thursday, September 28, 1995

Robert Cushman

Created and performed by Dumb Type At the Du Maurier Theatre Centre, Harbourfront, until Saturday Rating: Glazed eyes ride an infernal machine Reviewed by Robert Cushman DUMB Type, a performance group from Kyoto, is among us as part of the Today's Japan at Harbourfront. According to its moving spirit, Teiji Furuhashi, the name "dumb type" refers to "a society that is overstuffed with information but cognizant of nothing." He obviously doesn't believe that he and his colleagues are cognizant of nothing; at the very least, they know that nobody else knows anything.

The show pH is concerned, says the director in the same interview, "with the relationship between technology and human beings. My inspiration for that set was the idea of performers being trapped in a copy machine." The set actually occupies what would usually be the auditorium. The audience sits in the theatre balconies and looks down on a long room empty but for a couple of lighting gantries. These stretch from wall to wall, one fixed high and one low, one with its lamps on and the other dark; and they sweep the stage, back and forth, ceaselessly, from before the show starts to just before it ends. There are five actors present, and they are very well drilled. This, according to another program note, is because they are portraying "automatons, robots, persons devoid of will and initiative." There could also be a more prosaic reason: If they didn't know exactly when to duck, they'd be decapitated.

One of the infernal arms projects crisp images on the stage floor: giant dollar bills and such. But it takes some time to realize that we are in the presence of a giant photocopier. (Some time for me anyway; I'm bad at these things.) Other symbols of alienation put in appearances, some on a screen and some in person. Actors push supermarket trolleys which threaten to take over their lives. At the end, the stage is invaded by little pink mechanical pigs. Piggy-banks, I thought, but I was wrong again; they actually represent the ascendancy of the Japanese toy industry. Still, the overall pitch is not exactly unfamiliar. If the Unabomber were to demand access to a theatre space he might come up with something like pH -if, that is, he had the flair.

The constant motion of Furuhashi's infernal machine is a genuinely original spectacle. It's also hypnotic; the show has rhythm. If it's monotonous, and if the technical content far outclasses the human, that presumably comes with the territory. The title refers to a chemical formula, used to denote the proportion in a substance of acid to alkali.

Other polarities ("question-answer, image-word" and 11 others) are said to underly each of the show's sections, but I wouldn't have known. To me it all looked much the same, and I have quoted so liberally from the official propaganda because it obviously knows far more about the show than I do. There are three white-clad young ladies who spend their time scurrying around looking oppressed, and a man who faintly croons a lyric about the benefits of modern civilization to the tune of Time on My Hands.

I was generally baffled and mostly bored, but not in the soul- destroying way that's induced by stupidity or incompetence. The show is probably about boredom: a Te Deum to tedium.
1995-10-01-all-the-rural-s-a-stage:
To see first-rate classical theatre in Canada you have to leave town. Perhaps only a pampered and insular metropolitan would put it quite like that; still, it's remarkable that Toronto, which preens itself on being the third(or is it the I second?) theatrical centre in North America, has an I overpowering commercial sector, a seething if permanently impoverished underground, and virtually nothing in between. In other cities the picture is similar, if smaller.

In the theatre, as everywhere else, to be cut off from the past is to be diminished. It limits everybody: actors, directors, audiences. (It's especially bad for critics; judgments made in a vacuum are apt to be vacuous.) It's an open if embarrassing secret that old plays are often more refreshing than new ones. Partly it's because they have to be fairly good to survive; but it's also because they allow us the pleasure of double vision. They cater to our conviction that human nature never changes (this is affirmed every time we laugh at an old joke) and to our more skeptical belief that everything else does. Past and present illuminate one another. Mercifully, the slack gets taken up each summer: at least for those prepared to travel. You may go to Stratford or to Niagara-on-the-Lake or, as of this year, to Wolfville, Nova Scotia, where a new classical festival has got off to a fine, invigorating start.

Wolfville, a charming town even by the standards of the Annapolis Valley, is the home of Acadia University and, now, of the Atlantic Theatre Festival. The theatre is housed in what was once the university hockey rink. Michael Bawtree, head of the university drama department, is the artistic director; he is also a former associate director at Stratford. His own associate at Wolfville is Michael Langham, who ran Stratford during its formative years of the 1950s and 1960s; at seventy-six he must rank as the elder statesman of Shakespeare production.

Wolfville has a thrust stage, strikingly similar to Stratford's, though more modest. At Stratford the player-spectator relationship is confrontational; the stage makes a public statement, almost irrespective of what you put on it, and the wraparound auditorium responds by clenching the play and the actors in its fist. At Wolfville the audience is more gently fanned out. A play needs to have a certain size, physical or emotional, to fill that space but it does not have to be epic. The three plays of Wolfville's opening season were The Tempest, Shakespeare's most reclusive work; Chekhov's The Cherry Orchard implicitly concerning the whole of pre-revolutionary Russian gentry fourteen years before the revolution but technically continued to a single house and grounds; and Feydeau's A Flea in Her Ear, the paradigm of a French bedroom farce. All three worked;

Langham's production of The Tempest was a model of lucidity. It shone a harsh light on the inner struggle of the exiled Prospero, torn between revenge and forgiveness and here supported by an unusually grim and recalcitrant collection of spirits. It also painted an exciting set of pictures. The opening storm took full and realistic possession of a stage in full sail. (So it should in the Maritimes. Actually, open stages invariably make very good ships.) The , shipwrecked nobles beat invisible bushes with their swords as they roamed distracted around Prospero's island. Phantom banquets appeared and vanished with bewitched and bewitching speed. ("Cool," breathed the nine-year-old next to me, who had been having trouble with the blank verse.) The wedding masque of goddesses was a stylized show -- half Greek, half kabuki that seemed for once to have some relevance to the betrothed couple watching it.

Langham co-directed Cherry Orchard with his actress-wife, Helen Bums, and this too was a good story. Anyone seeing this play for the first time should be agog to know whether the orchard will be sold and, if so, to whom. Interwoven with this central thread are half a dozen others that the author may seem to let drop but that it's the business of the production to keep in sight. The pivotal role of Madame Ranevskaya came over as shallow (whether intentionally or not was hard to say), but Taham's mastery of grouping and an overall quality of elegiac tartness -- we knew they were doomed, they didn't -- kept the piece flowing. Especially striking was the interlocking drama of the servants, each fighting for some kind of survival; I've never before seen it suggested that Dunyasha, the maid, not only gets seduced in the course of the action but also gets pregnant.

The twin enclosures of drawing room and bordello are not obvious candidates for the open staging demanded by a thrust stage, and characters in Michael Bawtree's production of a Flea in Her Ear sometimes took longer to get from point A to point B than is customary in farce. But this enforced deliberation paid off. It lent an air of solidity, even of reflection, that was rather helpful. For Feydeau's flirts, roues, and cuckolds are real people who occasionally stop to think, if seldom very edifyingly. This piece of Paris from the 1830s is not just social history but dispassionate social comment. It is also the most fun you can have in a theatre while still remaining cultural.

Two pieces from the dead centre of the established repertoire and one from the frivolous fringe may seem a safe selection. Actually, the better known a play, the more daunting the comparisons, and the greater the danger of slipping into routine. The Atlantic Festival is in the same position that Stratford faced at its inception: trying to build an acting tradition from local talent, fortified by some expert outsiders.

Three outstanding players have centred this year's company: a returning star, a stalwart from the Canadian classical establishment, and a local boy making surpassingly good. The star is Peter Donat, born just down the road from Wolfville and an old boy of Acadia, but long settled in California. He is now an edgy, quirky actor, slightly to the left of your conventional leading man. His Prospero is hoarse but compelling, a little overawed by his own magic. I preferred him, though, as Gayev, the fussy, helpless aristocrat of The Cherry Orchard, who goes through the play eating chocolates, radiating helpless goodwill, and reciting billiard gambits. Donat, uniquely in my experience, relates this last tic to Gayev's feelings and situation at each given moment, and the gain to the coherence of both play and character is immense.

Leon Pownall, a pillar of Stratford for many years, is vibrant as well as reliable here. Funny and warm in the Chekhov, flamboyantly hilarious as a homicidally jealous Spaniard in Feydeau, he is best of all as the faithful Gonzalo in The Tempest, usually an amiable bore but here a forceful and even radiant spokesman for good Pownall is the kind of actor no company should be without. Finally -- and apparently a revelation not only to me but to his local fans there is Bill Carr, well known in the Maritimes as a comedian and after-dinner speaker. A Flea in Her Ear is really his show. He plays twin roles: a solid-citizen husband and a downtrodden hotel porter whom he endows with a comic strength, alternately sweet and rough, that suggests music hall raised to a higher power. The same qualities, ground still finer, inform his Lopakhin, the peasant turned millionaire of The Cherry Orchard able to buy and sell any of the gentry but unable to shake off his emotional dependence on them. This is one of the great roles of the world, a historical moment made flesh; it's also one of the trickiest. I have never believed so completely in Lopakhin's compulsive need to work

I had expected good things, especially from Langham, but my expectations were surpassed. A winning choice of actors and plays was enhanced by the appeal of the town itself and by the pioneering excitement, shared by participants and spectators, of launching a new venture. There is a palpable local pride about, which I hope will weather what are bound to be difficult years ahead. Actors wander off, theatres grow into institutions, and towns turn into tourist-traps.

Stratford has been trapping tourists for a long time now, while Niagara-on-the-Lake a town that always seems to me to have been carved out of fudge -- was a holiday resort long before the Shaw Festival set up shop there. Both Ontario festivals do some pandering to undiscriminating audiences. The Shaw Festival, under artistic director Christopher Newton, deals with the mass-appeal problem by hiving it off. They do thoroughly respectable productions of vintage murder-mysteries (this year it was Ladies in Retirement, with the admirable Jennifer Phipps), taking them quite seriously on their own terms, and everybody is happy.

The Shaw's peculiar mandate -- plays written in the lifetime of its patron saint takes in Ibsen, Strindberg, Chekhov, Pirandello, Brecht, O'Neill: all of whom it has virtually ignored. But it also takes in quantities of minor plays that can still speak to us, largely because they have never stopped Every play written since the 1920s is familiar to us on film; if we have not seen it, we have seen one just like it, and so have the actors. This year John van Druten's The Voice of the Turtle charmingly reminded us of the amazing amount of booze that innocent young women used to get through in the 1940s. Robert Sherwood's The Petrified Forest is a windy play but its large cast and Depression dust bowl setting offer, immense opportunities for atmosphere, magnificently taken (and expanded) in Neil Munro's production. Jim Moon gives a superbly growly performance as a fatalistic gangster, kept largely in shadow to avoid damaging comparisons with Humphrey Bogart.

More obviously spectacular was Noel Coward's Cavalcade, directed by Newton and Duncan McIntosh with a cast of dozens. It was logistically flawless, visually stunning, and humanly empty, since this chronicle of the century's first thirty years has space for only one character (well done by Fiona Reid with wit and nerves plus an accelerating bitterness). It also has a great song, "Twentieth Century Blues," summing up a historical action that has been one bloody disaster after another. For all that, : the play has an upbeat aura that the production, savagely though it tried, could never quite dispel. The only emotion possible was awe at the spectacle.

Shaw himself was well served this year. Newron's production of You Never Can Tell, a seaside fantasia that blossoms into a harlequinade, is a pleasure to watch. It also has a perfect performance from Jack Medley as the omniscient old waiter. The Philanderer, a revealing piece of self-satire -- the artist as heartless womanizer -- was fitted out at some performances with an additional act. This begins with an anatomy of a dead marriage that for cold horror is unmatched in its authors work.'S wonderful. No wonder he suppressed it. Both these comedies are sex-war pieces, and when lines turn up that are critical or satirical of women, the actors tie themselves in fascinating knots to demonstrate their disapproval of what they are saying.

Not that the Shaw audience itself is beyond reproach. It seems to have terrible taste in acting. Exit applause at Niagara means that something horrendous has just happened: Nora McLellan steamrollering the epigrams of Oscar Wilde's An Ideal Husband or Simon Bradbury doing everything but turning cartwheels in The Philanderer. But the festival, guided by Newton's blend of scholarship and showmanship, still looks serious, and its uniquely specialized repertoire gives it an identity that's invaluable.

Stratford, in theory, can do anything. In practice, this is less enviable than it sounds. Stratford, for all its prestige and its three stages, is a summer festival. It is not a fully furnished, fully financed national theatre: the kind of year-round place whose absence I lamented at the beginning of this article. It can do only a few plays a year: in this financially oppressed year, fewer than usual. With the whole of world drama to choose from, where do you start? Something has to centre the repertoire, and there are practical as well as pious reasons for assigning this responsibility to Shakespeare. But if a season's Shakespeares fail to catch fire, as happened this year, then the whole bill starts to look arbitrary. This was Richard Monette's second season as artistic director. His first was a bravura success. This year he had to cut down to nine shows, two of them revivals.

No-one could begrudge a second showing to Diana Leblanc's world-class production of Long Day's Journey into Night; and time has welded these actors into an unchangeable family. William Hutt gets the peasant roots, peasant simplicity, and peasant meanness of old Tyrone, and he breaks your heart (which is more than Olivier ever did) when the old actor sobs over the ruin of his talent. Peter Donaldson drills with bloated accuracy into the depths of son Jamie's alcoholic self-hatred, and Tom McCamus, presumably Stratford's next Hamlet, makes Edmund, O'Neill's self-indulgent self-portrait, a thriving neurotic in his own right. It's the play's greatest irony that these squabbling men finally attain a dram (the right word, since it's whisky-induced) of mutual understanding while the wife and mother they all love slips away from them into a drug-addict's stupor. Some of the steps on Martha Henry's descent are uncomfortably actressy, but her best moments, especially the last, are uncanny.

Also outstanding was Werley's The Country Wife. Douglas Campbell's production went a little easy on the characters' I misogyny and cruelty; nevertheless this is the best staging of this great Restoration comedy that I have seen, and incomparably the funniest. Tom McCamus, Stephen Ouimette, and Scott Wentworth as lecher, fop, and cuckold seized on their roles and situations with deadly accuracy, and offered them up with infectious relish.

When actors can command the stage like that, the Festival Theatre becomes the most exhilarating space there is. It happened in this year's Macbeth: not, unfortunately, in the protagonist's soul searchings but in Bernard Hopkins's brief interlude as the Porter. Otherwise the play slid, as it so often does, inexorably into mediocrity. The only other Shakespeares were the most lightweight in the canon. I missed The Comedy of Errors. Monette's production of The Merry Wives of Winsdor (co-directed by Antoni Cimolino) had some hilarious moments, but it wasn't enough.

And then there were the musicals, done all too obviously to pay the bills. The Boy Friend was energetic but heartless. The Gondoliers had scenic and choreographic delights, nullified by a contemptuous attitude to the script. The show's basic comic point was scupperd along with some perfectly visible character jokes, in favour of new lyrics about contemporary Canada. The audience lapped them up, but they made no sense in the context of the original, which otherwise trundled along undisturbed A visiting American was heard marveling what a great show they had made out of a nothing source. You don't have to be a Gilbert and Sullivan fanatic to feel that something is wrong. I doubt that G & S would be treated so cavalierly if they were done at Niagara -- into whose time-frame they would of course fit perfectly. The only way of making an audience believe in a play is to believe in it yourself.

So standards at Shaw, and especially at Stratford, are uneven; and the consistency of Wolfville was achieved in the special circumstances of a first season which, in the nature of things, was likely to be either a triumph or a disaster. But all theatres are uneven, and the best work done at these three will stand comparison with any in the English-speaking world. Wolfville hopes to build an ongoing ensemble. Stratford and Shaw have more continuity in casting than the British classical companies have managed in years. Experience tells; and you can now hear Shakespeare and Shaw spoken at least as well -- as intelligently and dynamically in Canada as in Britain. Probably the festival set-up helps; actors will commit themselves for a summer more easily, and more repeatedly, than for a full year. I shall continue to regret our lack of urban repertory companies, but it's more important that we hold on to the classical theatres we do have and hold them to their best selves.
1995-10-07-the-glorious-12th:
THEATRE REVIEW THE GLORIOUS 12TH

Saturday, October 07, 1995

Robert Cushman

Written by Raymond Storey Directed by Bob Baker Presented by The Canadian Stage Company At the St. Lawrence Centre in Toronto until Nov. 4 Rating: 1/2 Play promises vicarious thrills Raymond Storey's two-tiered structure doesn't sustain this work about bigotry Reviewed by Robert Cushman BIGOTRY is a perennially fascinating subject, affording readers or spectators any number of vicarious thrills. If we don't share the prejudices on display, we can enjoy being shocked by them. Raymond Storey's play The Glorious 12th offers a double helping, being concerned with the interaction of the Orange Lodge and the Ku Klux Klan.

To take the first first: When the Protestant William of Orange - William III of England - defeated the Roman Catholic James II at the Battle of the Boyne in 1690, a new era of sectarian vindictiveness was loosed upon the world and has stayed loosed. Ireland has been the area most obviously infected, but the fever also took root in Scotland and, we are now reminded, in Canada. It is 1927, and the members of a small-town family are preparing for the Orange Day Parade, their annual gesture toward keeping the Pope out of Ontario. Head of the house is Dad, a scythe-wielding patriarch (Father Time, perhaps) who doesn't believe in patronizing Jewish stores. His son, Dalziel, is a war-hero whose principal peacetime activity seems to be keeping his wife pregnant; she is overworked, under-understood, and generally distraught. There is also a 14-year-old grandson who is being groomed for membership of the Lodge and whom we hear taking his initiatory oaths: a blood-chilling litany of curses against Catholics.

Still, there are degrees of hate, as the Orangepersons discover when Dad's doctor son-in-law introduces a white-suited visitor from Indiana who is part snake-oil salesman and part snake. He plans, in effect, to assimilate the Lodge to the Klan; he wants the Canadians' membership and he especially wants their money. He and the lady he travels with - a manic Bible-spouter - also engage in furious amorous wrestling whenever their hosts' backs are turned. It is hard to accuse a writer of vilifying the KKK, but, by making its representative a fraud even by his own dubious lights, Storey seriously weakens the conflict and the play. Nor is that the only problem.

The play has been planned as a two-Storey building, with a personal level and a public one. Dad has two daughters. One is the doctor's disaffected wife; the other is a singing-teacher whom the family regard as slightly crazy. This turns out to be a cover for their disgust at her having had a relationship with an Indian: a friendship brutally destroyed by brother Dalziel. One can see that the two levels were meant to reinforce each other, but in practice they amount to two plays delivered in alternating sections. There seems no connection between the cruel Dalziel of one scene and the comparatively tolerant Dalziel of another, nor between that one and the Dalziel who comes out for the Klan at the end of the play. Dad, meanwhile, takes a stand against the intruders, but whether it is his sense of decency that has been wounded or just his amour propre is never disclosed; the part is cruelly underwritten. In another sense the entire play is overwritten. "Everything about you falls so squarely, so completely into place," says the doctor's wife, brandishing adverbs as if they were hatchets. "You can't" runs a climactic and excessively detailed admonition "carry hate around - it's like acid, it'll eat the inside of the container." The play manages to titillate us with reminders of prejudices past, and it implicitly reminds us of their connection to prejudices present, but that's all it does.

Bob Baker's production looks splendid, beautifully lit by Kevin Lamotte and spaciously set by Sue LePage who starts things off nicely with the silhouette of what, in another locale, would be a perfect little house on the prairie. But the acting goes in fits and starts, especially fits. It seemed unconvinced and unconvincing. Mary Ann McDonald and Nancy Palk do best as the sisters, granted a determinedly lyrical and virtually free- standing scene of mutual confidence. John Bourgeois is flounderingly underweight as the Klansman; Brenda Robins's oratorical excursions as the evangelical Southern belle are best described as valiant. Ron Hastings as Dad grabs what opportunities he is given, but his hair and eyebrows look very false. Marjorie Campbell as the unwilling Earth-mother plays in a comic convention unbroached by anyone else on stage and got exit-applause after delivering a turning-worm tirade: a sign, as it nearly always is, that the actor has dragged the audience out of the play.
1995-11-05-the-standard-bearer:
Frank Sinatra will be 80 next month. He's the 20th century's greatest popular singer, with a career that stretches back over more than 50 years. But what is it about this '18-carat manic depressive' that has kept him at the top, from teen idol to grand old man?

Robert Cushman Sunday 05 November 1995 00:02 GMT

SIX YEARS ago I saw Frank Sinatra, aged 74, in concert at the Toronto Skydome. It may be stretching the truth to say that I saw him; the Skydome is a baseball stadium, supposedly the biggest in the world, and though its press box affords a fine panoramic view when the Toronto Blue Jays are playing at home, it reduces stage performers to distant, cavorting dots. There was a huge video screen, if you wished to survey the star in close-up, but you can get TV specials at home, where they come with interesting camera-angles. So one listened to the music, which was loud and clear, and concentrated hard on the fact that it was emanating from the intense, tuxedoed, pacing figure hundreds of feet below.

As critic and lyricist Gene Lees once pointed out, Sinatra can hire people to do everything for him - except sing. The thing that has set him apart and made a corporation of him also makes him a working animal like the rest of us. Strictly speaking, then, only the vocal part of the entertainment was coming out of him. But he makes it seem like more. In the 55 years of his performing career - a phenomenal span for a pop singer, with most of it spent at the top - he has consistently sung the best arrangements of (somewhat less consistently) the best songs around.
