A hit, a very palpable hit!

THEATRE Michael Pennington, one of our finest actors, has appeared in 'Hamlet' five times. Now he's written a book about it. Robert Cushman applauds

Robert Cushman Sunday 04 February 1996 00:02 GMT

MICHAEL PENNINGTON has played Hamlet five times and Hamlet twice. In other words he's been in five productions of the play, in three of which he has appeared successively as Fortinbras, as Laertes, and as Claudius- doubled-with-the-Ghost. But he started at the top, playing the prince in a Cambridge student production in 1964, and he returned to the part with the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1980.

With all that to go on, he has written a book: Hamlet: A User's Guide (Nick Hern Books, pounds 18.99). He describes it as "a kind of owner's manual. I'm offering no views on whether you should have left- or right-hand drive or what colour the model should be, but I know the push-bang-suck of the engine by now and how the distributor works - perhaps also which passages call for pure brake-horsepower and which deft cornering."

I suppose I have read, or pretended to read, car manuals that were as knowledgeable as Pennington's, but I have never come across one that was remotely as witty, or as charming. He goes through the play, scene by scene, analysing action, pouncing on character detail, outlining (though, as a matter of policy, never resolving) ambiguities, in fact rehearsing the play on the page. Occasionally he offers modest suggestions about staging. He makes selective but illuminating use of theatre history. Acknowledging that it sounds "hubristic", he places the book in the line of Harley Granville Barker's famous Prefaces to Shakespeare. He might also have referred back to a slightly earlier and even more celebrated critic, the Victorian A C Bradley, who said that his method of dealing with a Shakespeare play was to approach it as if he were an actor studying all the parts. That's what he said. Pennington seems actually to have done it. He's as illuminating on Gertrude, Polonius or Ophelia as on the parts he's actually played.

Unexpectedly perhaps, the book doesn't go in much for autobiography. What there is occurs in his introduction and footnotes, which are among the best things in the book. ("Some kindly people in Stratford have told me that [when I was rehearsing Hamlet] they would see me wandering around the town and be afraid that I would absent-mindedly step into the path of a bus.")

I'm not sure whether Pennington's five on-stage encounters with Hamlet constitute a record, but I would like to stake a small associated claim of my own. I have for reasons educational, recreational or vocational seen every one of them. As an undergraduate two years his junior, I saw his student Hamlet. I even reviewed it, for a short-lived university rag. I don't remember much of what I wrote (and, to my chagrin, he hasn't got it locked in his memory either) but I'm sure it was mostly favourable. I remember it as a lively, sympathetic and - I'm sure I used this word - conscientious performance, one that made sense of every line: not a quality to be taken for granted among amateurs or professionals. I know I called it "the most intellectually exciting performance" I had seen at Cambridge, a description that aroused howls of outrage from the arbiters of theatrical opinion. Excitement was supposed to be a visceral thing, and intellect, if not actually shameful, was quite beside the point. Pennington had quite a lot to live down, since he turned out to be the rare university actor who actually got a good degree. (He attributes this to a certain fluency in exam-speak.)

These days he also directs. At least he directs one play. He did Twelfth Night for the English Shakespeare Company, the maverick touring company he ran with Michael Bogdanov, and he then did it again in Tokyo. Now he's directing it at a small but thriving Shakespeare theatre in Chicago - one of the best Shakespeare companies on a continent that's dotted with them. Its director, Barbara Gaines, who raved to me about Pennington, is determined to have him back to direct Hamlet, which really seems sort of inevitable. Or as he says, it's putting his money where his mouth is. And, of course, he's now well qualified to write a user's guide to Twelfth Night.

So with all this activity, surely he must be an intellectual actor? In fact the idea makes him shudder. "I hate it. I never function intellectually as an actor. I'm not an analyst in rehearsal." Nor, I suspect, would he care to think of himself as a romantic actor, an Establishment actor, or an English-gentleman actor ("I'm a Celt. My mother was a Scots girl, my father was Welsh") though his fair hair and gentle, melodious voice have often typed him that way. Some canny directors have reversed or tilted the image. Peter Hall had him play Fortinbras, to David Warner's Hamlet, as a blond Fascist beast. His Laertes, with Nicol Williamson, was directed by Tony Richardson to have an incestuous passion for Marianne Faithfull's Ophelia. ("Just grab his cock, Marianne.") Whether for that reason or another, his grief at her grave was unusually convincing.

After all the unkempt Williamsons and Warners, Pennington was cast by John Barton at Stratford to restore some traditional princely glamour to the title role. He did not altogether oblige. "I thumped Ophelia to the ground in the Nunnery Scene." That's in the book. In conversation he expands on this theme with relish: "I think Hamlet's an intolerable man. It's no wonder the Romantics adored him. He has all the flabby idealism of the Romantic sensibility. I encouraged hostility from the audience when playing Hamlet."

I can't say that he actually got it. Like most Hamlets, rough or refined, he wound up with the audience's sympathy. It's built into the play, for aesthetic rather than moral reasons; as Pennington says himself, "Hamlet has your inner ear." Actually, one of the best things about the book is the balance it keeps between the intolerable in Hamlet and the irresistible. And the larger contrast it draws between the apparent faults of the play itself ("it seems impossible for a production to make the play frame the man and the man belong in the play") and its overwhelming virtues ("galvanic force in the theatre, an ability to heal, and an effect on an audience unlike any other I know").

He actually wrote it while playing Claudius, keeping himself busy while touring (Leatherhead to Brighton via Athens) in last year's Peter Hall production with Stephen Dillane as the Prince. "Now," he says with the authority and the tolerance of middle-age, "I find Claudius more interesting than Hamlet." Also perhaps more sympathetic. "There is no evidence that there's anything wrong with the status quo in Denmark." Claudius is "the perfect apple with the worm inside". He is also "very playable as long as you keep in all the plotting".

The Hall production did keep in all the plotting, and Pennington's Claudius emerged as the best I've ever seen: also possibly the best performance of his career. He started with an impeccable facade (some of its details seemed to have been borrowed from the public persona of Sir Peter himself) which eroded, slowly but remorselessly, from the first stab of acknowledged guilt. As his desperation grew, so also did his borrowed majesty. It was a perfect demonstration of the area where, in the actor's own words, "sympathy collides with moral shock".

Pennington's introduction to the classics was classic. At the age of 10 he was "dragged very unwillingly" to see Macbeth at the Old Vic and was hooked. It wasn't, he admits, quite as neatly revelatory as all that; he already "loved reading Shakespeare in class" and the Macbeth was "striking a bell that was already there". The Vic was working its way through the entire canon, and he had seen nearly all the plays long before he left school. It's the stuff that educational fantasies are made of, though it may be statistically likelier to produce critics than actors. It perhaps contributed to the traditionalist image that has dogged his career. People were surprised when he teamed up with the iconoclast Bogdanov to form the ESC, and even more so when he played a markedly unsentimental Henry V in the cycle of history plays that defined the company's style. It might have been called eclectic-brutalist, though the eclecticism embraced some conservative aesthetics as well.

Pennington recalls that "it was very cheeky what we did", challenging the National and RSC on their own repertoire and beating them hands down at the touring game, home and abroad. "They couldn't fault us on the verse- speaking or the editing. But we weren't regarded generously by the theatre Establishment." The ESC cast new actors in leading roles but, though they won high praise, it didn't seem to lead to much success elsewhere. "My regret is that we didn't change more careers." He doesn't regret having packed it in after eight or nine years, proud though he is of what they achieved. As an actor-manager he found that he ran into "the same crises every year - and always at the same time every year. And I didn't enjoy chasing money. I became very physically tired. I won't do it again."

Towards the end of his book Pennington refers to actors playing Hamlet as "part of the logic of that almost outmoded thing, a 'classical' career". His own Stratford Hamlet happened that way, even his Cambridge Hamlet may have been a conscious first step on the road, but as he says, "to decide now at 21 to be a Shakespearian actor would be regarded as eccentric".

He does have a new Shakespeare part coming up: Shakespeare himself, in a radio play by Don Taylor. And he still has ambitions for Timon, Lear and Prospero. But what he most wants to do now are new plays. (He's actually done more of them than he lets on: Shaffer, Stoppard, Pinter, Brenton, Harwood, David Edgar.) He also has a one-man show on Chekhov. And though all actors these days write books, his is exceptional.
1996-02-07-theatre-review-bedtimes-and-b:
THEATRE REVIEW BEDTIMES AND BULLIES

Wednesday, February 07, 1996

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written by Volker Ludwig Adapted by Dennis Foon Directed by Sally Han Starring Derwin Jordan, Paul Braunstein, Kim Renders, Patricia Vanstone. At the Young People's Theatre in Toronto through Sunday Rating: Production adds insult to perceived injury YPT presents a dull and innocuous show that the board of education blames for not being innocuous enough. They deserve each other. BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail COLOUR-BLIND casting is a fine idea, but it has occasioned more hypocrisy and muddled thinking than any other issue in the theatre. Audiences can no more fail to notice whether actors are black or white than whether they are tall, short, fat, thin, bald or hairy. How much it matters in a given play is a thing infinitely variable, and the variables include the nature of the material and the skill and style of the production. The latest disagreement on this comes to you courtesy of the Toronto Board of Education and the Young People's Theatre.

The YPT, doing a play for and about children called Bedtime and Bullies , has cast a black actor as principal bully - though if that is really what he is, he must be the most amiable, unthreatening bully ever put on a stage. The board has accused the theatre, pardon my jargon, of reinforcing negative racial stereotypes. The YPT has mounted a dull and innocuous show that the board has blamed for not being innocuous enough. They deserve each other.

On the way out I heard a little girl asking, "Mommy, which was the bully?" Her confusion was understandable but it was not the fault of the actor. Derwin Jordan gives a quick-witted, vulnerable performance that is much the best thing in the production. He plays Peter, a boy who is habitually spanked by his father and reacts by scaring two other kids: a brother and sister. In the play's German original (by Volker Ludwig) these siblings were called Max and Millie, as was the play. Alliteration still lives in Dennis Foon's Canadian version, which has renamed the characters Kevin and Kelly, while bestowing a new and portentious title on the piece itself. That title fits right in with the current YPT house style, which, from what I have seen (and I haven't seen everything) is mushy, preachy and desperately unimaginative.

Peter allegedly terrorizes Kevin and Kelly. But what we actually see is Peter flourishing an obviously toy gun, which arouses Kevin's envy rather than his fear. (It also arouses the shocked disapproval of Kevin's mother, a single parent of weary but unshakable high-mindedness. In Patricia Vanstone's amazingly unmodulated performance she is rather like the Young People's Theatre rolled into one.) Peter swaps his gun for Kevin's bike. This is a smart move on Peter's part, and one that he seems surprised to get away with, but it does not constitute extortion. Kelly puts it down to her brother's being easily frightened but there is no sign that he's frightened of Peter. It could of course be going on between the lines, except that in Sally Han's production there is nothing going on between the lines.

It does, to give it its due, have a bright and reasonably versatile set, and it tries to forestall the question of Peter's colour by abandoning naturalism. The actor is black but the character isn't, or doesn't have to be. To emphasize this, a white actor plays Peter's father while Kevin, Kelly and Peter himself are played not by real children but by young adults. This approach, however, demands high style, in acting and direction. Paul Braunstein as Kevin has a fair stab at it, though he's overly winsome; Kim Renders, in the trickier role of his kid sister, limits herself to squawking and bouncing. But the production, bar a couple of seconds of attractive clowning, gives them nothing to do except horse vacuously around.

Some exceptionally ghastly songs stop action and tension in their tracks, though sometimes this is managed without musical assistance. The play's moral climax comes after Peter has been reformed by his new friendship with the two Ks. (A celebratory sleepover puts everything to rights; the feel-good factor is working overtime.) Peter's dad, seeing the light, offers to let his son spank him, and Peter declines. There is no pacing here, no weight; the moment doesn't seem to matter to either of them. Intended as a tribute to the imagination of childhood, the show comes off as an insult to it.

If they had cast real kids they might have run into all kinds of problems, but the play might also have been something. We could have believed in Kevin's fears; there's a well-written scene in which he torments his mom with his refusal to go to sleep. We could even have believed in Peter's bullying. As it is, with the production giving us nothing else to think about and despite all the actor does for him, he is a stereotype - not the threatening one deplored by the board, but its depressing opposite: he's a victim. But the way to defeat stereotyping is not arbitrarily to ban one group of actors from playing one kind of role. It's to think, write, act, and direct in terms of individuals, not of statistics: in other words to do it well, and to trust your audience to respond in kind. Theatrical freedom has to include the freedom to play villains. (They're often the juiciest parts anyway; I doubt that Derwyn Jordan had to be bullied into playing Peter.) Whoever started this rubbish about the theatre providing "positive role models?" Can anyone name a good play that does that?

The management have inserted a slip in the program, solemnly informing us that parental abuse is wrong and that momentary repentance solves nothing. Either they think their audiences too dumb to work this out for themselves or they are bowing to pressure from officials who think that everything in a play must be spelled out. If our bureaucrats want to get into theatre criticism, and I'd rather they didn't, perhaps they should learn how drama works. The YPT, who presumably know already, should brush up.
1996-02-19-the-baker-s-wife:
THEATRE REVIEW THE BAKER'S WIFE

Monday, February 19, 1996

ROBERT CUSHMAN

WRITTEN BY JOSEPH STEIN AND STEPHEN SCHWARTZ Directed by Todd Stewart At the Studio Theatre, Harbourfront, until Feb. 24 Rating: Musical slight but roles charming BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail THERE is a category of Broadway show that devotes much of its energy to presenting cross-sections of some kind of enclosed community, real or fantastic. I think of it as the Merry Villagers Musical. It's an unruly category whose denizens, either sentimental or satirical, include Brigadoon, Plain and Fancy, Anyone Can Whistle, Lil Abner and The Most Happy Fella. The masterpiece of the genre, if you dont count Porgy and Bess, is Fiddler on the Roof, which owes much of its power to the staging of Jerome Robbins and, as is less often noted, to the supremely skillful libretto furnished by Joseph Stein.

In the 1970s, some 10 years after Fiddler, Stein wrote the book for The Baker's Wife, based on the celebrated 1938 movie with a script by Marcel Pagnol, the writer who for 20th-century popular purposes invented Provence. It's another village show, set in the 1930s. It echoes Fiddler (and quite a few other musicals) by starting with a company number thats three parts exposition, one part homespun philosophy. It describes the community and introduces its members, with particular emphasis on those, a majority, who are quarrelling with one another. These are people with hearty appetites: for liking and disliking, for drinking and especially for eating.

For some time they have lacked a local baker and their lives, it seems, have been desolate. Now, however, a new one is on the way. When he arrives he turns out to be an ungainly middle-aged man with a beautiful young wife. One of the local young men seduces and runs off with her. After a short period, during which the quality of the village bread supply declines precipitately, she returns. Her wounded but devoted husband still loves her, she really loves him. Thats all. It's touching, but it's throughly predictable and extremely slight.

When the musical was first conceived, it was planned that Zero Mostel would play the Baker. Mostel created the role of Tevye in Fiddler and as it turned out, it was another celebrated Tevye, the Israeli actor Topol, who actually got to play the Baker in the production that was aimed at Broadway. When the show was in trouble on the road, the producers brandished the ultimate out-of-town weapon: They called in Robbins. Presumably they wanted him to firm up the shows sense of place, to give it more of the strength of Fiddler. Despite his ministrations, the show never made it to New York; and structurally it must have been a hopeless case.

There is no way of expanding the central story, and the more you do with the supporting cast the more unbalanced the show seems. However hard you try, the ensemble of earthy Innkeeper, raffish Aristocrat, cynical Teacher, pious Priest, spinsterish Housekeeper remain exactly what those labels suggest: a collection of types. The more you try to flesh them out, the more insistently superficial they become. They can only come to life if they have a strong central drama to react to. Fiddler gives it to them in spades, personal and political; The Bakers Wife leaves them gasping.

Despite this, the show has acquired a cult reputation. It has the courage of its own innocence, which gives it charm, and it has the best score that Stephen Schwartz (Godspell, Pippin) ever wrote. His lyrics, though never painful, remain earthbound, as opposed to genuinely earthy which is what they are trying for, but his music has size and occasional sweetness; on the Broadway-to-contemporary scale it clocks in somewhere between John Kander and Andrew Lloyd Webber. One song, Meadowlark, sung by the heroine at the moment of temptation, has become an underground cabaret classic; I find it rather studied, but it does take the stage and enables the actress to do the same. Unfortunately, having sung it she sinks back into anonymity; her role is drastically underwritten.

Equity Showcase's necessarily miniature production at Harbourfront might seem the ideal solution, defusing false expectations. There are some nice performances and the rare treat of unamplified voices. But the piece seems barer than ever. It was written big, in intention at least, and it needs the help of size. It needs strings in the ballads instead of just piano and, to prove we're in France, accordion. It needs evocative sets and choreography thats more than standard-order jolly. It needs faces and voices that are older, stronger and more weatherbeaten than those on offer here. Nobody is really at fault, but its a no-win situation.

Not, however, a wholly unrewarding one. I was glad to see the show, and especially pleased with the performance of George Pothitos as the Baker. The character is a sensitive cuckold, a type that goes back at least to Moliere, but here transcends type; he is self-conscious about his love for his wife but absolutely strong in it, and in his reaction to the villagers' clumsy (and self-interested) attempts to help and comfort him, he becomes a hero, dignified and delicate, arousing sympathy without ever begging for it. Carol McCartney cannot bring his spouse to similar life, but she looks good and sings agreeably as, to a lesser degree, does Ian Simpson as her remarkably unlikable lover. And the show does take a firm hold on one of the primal passions; it is difficult, after all, to resist the aroma of good French bread.
1996-02-20-theatre-review-dr-jekyll-and-:
THEATRE REVIEW DR. JEKYLL AND MR. HYDE - A LOVE STORY

Tuesday, February 20, 1996

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- Written by James W. Nichol Directed by Neil Munro Starring Les Carlson and David Storch At St. Lawrence Centre until March 16 Rating: Jekyll plus Hyde is one too many One character with two personalities calls for one actor. With two on stage, the essence of a classic duality is lost. BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto RIGHT from the start, a horrible thought assailed me. Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde are the most famous double act in fiction. You may talk of Don Quixote and Sancho Panza, Holmes and Watson, Jeeves and Wooster, even Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, but you have to be modestly literate to do so. None of them trip as persistently and proverbially off the common tongue as do the doctor and his double. They did not, of course, reach this exalted state by being buddies; one is an unholy emanation of the other's worst instincts. Robert Louis Stevenson's brilliant fantasy dramatized a psychological phenomenon of which the world was uneasily aware, but for which it lacked a name. He gave us a double-barrelled one.

Being one guy, Jekyll and Hyde has long been reckoned an actor's treat. In most of its adaptations, play or movie, the story has been more or less an excuse for a transformation scene. The Canadian Stage Company, however, has cast two separate performers. That was what bugged me as the lights went down. It could only mean that Jekyll and Hyde were going to have scenes together. When one part of your psyche meets another part of your psyche they will obviously have much to talk about, but the encounter may, like an overheated family drama, leave outsiders firmly outside.

Funnily enough, in Neil Munro's staging the couple's first encounter shapes up as if it is going to be a transformation scene. It happens some 20 minutes in. We have met Dr. Jekyll, upright Victorian scientist coming apart at the seams. We have seen him scandalize his respectable friends with his free thinking, and seek consolation in the arms of a brothel keeper who believes in sharing her employees' workload. (This is a proclivity at which Stevenson barely hinted.) We have watched him embrace his teen-aged daughter with more than fatherly affection. (The doctor of the book is a childless bachelor.) So, after a hard day of tentative sinning, he comes home, locks himself in his lab, mixes a potion, swallows it, and starts writhing on the floor. He begins to crawl round the sofa, like a man who has something to hide: presumably himself. But no, he remains in sight, and when his alter ego flashes into view, they begin the first of many discussions. These amount to Jekyll saying "I summoned you," Hyde saying "you summoned me," and both of them saying "it's your fault."

Hyde seems somewhat of a lost child, and he, like the young Miss Jekyll, addresses their common progenitor as "pappy." To me this sounds more like Mark Twain than R. L. Stevenson, and such lapses in tone are a recurrent feature of James W. Nichol's script. They are, however, the least of its problems.

Les Carlson's Jekyll is grey, worried and uncommunicative. In a bizarre way this testifies to the truth of the legend; it's no fun being Jekyll if you don't get a crack at being Hyde. What's more surprising is that it works in reverse; David Storch's Hyde is even duller, being more of a victim than a fiend. He isn't even ugly. Eventually Jekyll uses him to act out his incestuous impulses; since Hyde is Jekyll's creation, this may count as a double case of child abuse. This, the fashionable issue, is the charge that sticks; presumably it occasions the play's ironic subtitle. Or maybe it's approving, and the play is wildly subversive. Or maybe the love story is between Dr. J and Mr. H themselves, which is why we need two of them. Along the way they do get up to a few other tricks. They hit an old gentleman in the stomach. (He and his friends take it with amazing sang- froid.) They cut up a prostitute. They murder.

They do all these things in different locations, and the production huffs and puffs to keep up with them, as do Cameron Porteous's sets, whose one graceful feature is a gorgeously receding set of street lamps. In one scene a character gets needlessly into a railway carriage and chugs away while his bags remain mysteriously on the platform; Munro, whose haunting production of The Petrified Forest was the Shaw Festival's best show in years, seems similarly stranded. The acting unfailingly heads for the nearest cliche, and which akimbo arms and wagging chins are due to incapacity and which to desperation is impossible to say. I have seldom sat among an audience so palpably disaffected; as the evening's shocking climax petered out, they felt - I felt - baffled, bored and finally beached.

But not, strangely, angry. There is some kind of ambition here, and I have seen or can imagine worse. Going round the United States at the moment is a musical on this subject with a score by Leslie Bricusse, which is made up, to judge from an advance CD, of generic ballads that could come from anything. Compared with Jekyll and Hyde - The Musical, or with my nightmares of it, Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde - A Love Story is merely a bad dream.
1996-04-13-writer-looks-too-lightly-at-l:
By Edward Jablonski Henry Holt, 345 pages, $49

Writer looks too lightly at Lerner's life BIOGRAPHY / The lyricist's complexities require more exploration than this ALAN JAY LERNER: A Biography

By Edward Jablonski Henry Holt, 345 pages, $49

Saturday, April 13, 1996

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Review by ROBERT CUSHMAN 'I COULDN'T write My Fair Lady now" said Alan Jay Lerner some time in the 1970s, "because I don't feel My Fair Lady now." Along with the rest of the world he had grown sadder, if not necessarily wiser. The trouble was that writing My Fair Lady (1956) was what he did best. He never equalled its success.

Neither, admittedly, did anybody else. Some musicals, in these inflationary times, have run longer and made more money and a few have enjoyed comparable critical esteem, but none - not even A Chorus Line - have done both. No subsequent musical has acquired the same cultural prestige or been so unarguably the show of its time, the one you simply had to see. It was the capstone of Broadway's great age of confidence - the era of the well-made narrative musical that was ushered in by Rodgers and Hammerstein's Oklahoma] in 1943.

Alan Lerner came in with that era. He was born into a comfortable if troubled household; his father was the masterful, philandering founder of a department store. He grew up in New York, seeing all the shows; went to Harvard; drifted into advertising and radio writing; joined the Lambs Club, a hangout for theatricals, where he literally bumped into Frederick Loewe, a composer looking for a lyricist. Their first show together, What's Up, opened the same year as Oklahoma] and was a thorough flop. Two years later they came up with The Day Before Spring, a success d'estime ("a success that runs out of steam") and two years after that with Brigadoon, a major hit and a charter member of the golden-age repertoire. After that there was Paint Your Wagon, which wasn't really a great success but has somehow maintained the aura of one, and then came My Fair Lady. That had a virtual, and triumphant, cinematic spinoff in Gigi, and Lerner and Loewe ended their stage collaboration with Camelot, a troubled show but an enduring one. It sounds like velvet.

It wasn't, of course. Lerner's private life was a romantic shambles. It's difficult to see how else you describe the existence of a man who married eight times. One of his seven divorces, from a predatory-sounding French lady, was quite spectacularly messy, gossip-page fodder for months. His biographer, Edward Jablonski, tries hard to be urbane about it but the cracks show. Jablonski is an experienced and knowledgable historian of musical theatre, who has written meticulously and respectfully on the Gershwins and Harold Arlen. He finds it hard to say a word against any of his subjects, so his books tend to be informative but bland. I am not suggesting that Lerner deserves a hatchet-job, but his complexities require more exploration than Jablonski can supply.

Actually, he has already had a hatchet-job. Gene Lees's Inventing Champagne, a joint biography of Lerner and Loewe published a few years ago, professed admiration for its subject but offered precious little of it. I never thought I would miss that book, but I have to admit that Lees is a better - or at least a more detailed - guide to Lerner's problems with debts, drugs, and women than the more circumspect Jablonski. Still, at least Jablonski, unlike Lees, does appear to have seen and studied all the shows. He doesn't go into them in much depth but he does tell us something, especially about the flops.

There were plenty of these. After Camelot, Loewe, an older and less driven man, took early retirement but Lerner persevered. He had already taken time out to work with Kurt Weill on Love Life (another success d'estime) and with the fine composer Burton Lane on the Fred Astaire movie Royal Wedding: a negligible film with a fine score. In 1965 he reunited with Lane for One a Clear Day You Can See Forever, which didn't really work; and that was as good as it got. Lolita My Love (1976), a foolhardy attempt to musicalize the Nabokov novel, closed out of town. Dance a Little Closer (1983) made it to New York but only for one night. Both had excellent lyrics.

Lerner, with the clout of his earlier shows, was the prime mover in most of his later ones. He was intellectually ambitious, highly intelligent, politically aware. (He was also, in my experience of him, shy, modest and courteous; and his last marriage, to the charming English actress Liz Robertson, looked happy.) He wanted to tackle new and uncomortable subjects, but his heart and the nature of his craftsmanship were with the older idioms; he was marooned between the worlds of Oscar Hammerstein and Stephen Sondheim. Like Hammerstein he was a librettist as well as a lyricist; like Sondheim he rarely had a pop hit.

Jablonski quotes a remark of Ira Gershwin's: "Alan, you don't understand trick rhymes." It's a shame he doesn't pursue this, because Lerner certainly tried for trick rhymes, rather in the whimsical word- inventing style of Gershwin's friend and contemporary E. Y. Harburg, another who mixed fantasy and social consciousness. The difference may just be a matter of generations: Wordplay came more easily to the writers of the thirties than to those of the fifties. Harburg took an almost messianic attitude towards romance; so did Lerner. In Brigadoon, love conquers literally everything. This is a sticky message to get across, and it works best in My Fair Lady, where the musical pits the cynicism of Shaw's original play against the rich operetta tones of Loewe's music. Shaw denied that Professor Higgins married Eliza Doolittle; audiences have always known better and My Fair Lady makes our fantasy flesh. I suspect that Lerner went on feeling My Fair Lady longer than he admitted. It was his good fortune, and ours, that in 1956 everybody else, on both sides of the proscenium, felt it too. Robert Cushman will be singing show songs - none of them by Lerner - at the du Maurier World Stage cabaret at the Rivoli cafe on Queen Street West in Toronto on Thursday, April 18.

NOTA BENE

From Alan Jay Lerner: At six-thirty the next morning, (Lerner) was in his chair again, pad before him and the aroma of coffee suffusing the room; again nothing. This continued for a week. By the second week he was panicky, and the third was no better. What especially alarmed him was the fact that he knew what he wanted to say but could not find the words to say it. By the fourth week he had lost eight pounds and 'become a basket case.' Distraught, almost frantic, he realized he needed help and sought out the analyst who had helped him through his first divorce, Dr. Bela Mittelmann. . . .

Enouched, Lerner tried to describe his anxieties, with scant enlightenment as to the cause of his mental inertia. The doctor observed, 'You write as if your life depended on every line.' 'It does.' "
1996-04-19-theatre-review-road-movie:
THEATRE REVIEW ROAD MOVIE

Friday, April 19, 1996

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written by Godfrey Hamilton Directed by Lorenzo Mele Starring Mark Pinkosh At the Studio Theatre, York Quay, until April 22 Rating: -1/2 A trip through bereavement Haunting portraits save play from the flaw at its centre. BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail ROAD Movie is a one-man show whose protagonist/narrator remarks on two occasions that there is a song about everything. I second that, and offer an example.

Theres a Wes Montgomery tune called West Coast Blues whose lyrics begin "I got a baby on the East Coast, I got a gig going on the West Coast . . ." and then proceeds to tell how the singer is tired of all this separation and intends to pack his bags and join his lover on the other side of the United States. Road Movie is a gay variation on this theme with the locations reversed.

Joel, our hero, has a gig going on the East Coast: an uptight and presumably corporate position in New York. Once upon a flashback he met Scott, who was leading a comparatively untrammelled life houseboat-sitting in Sausalito. It was only a one-night something-or-other but it promised more and now Joel is doing what Scott prophesied he would. Tired of bestowing and receiving insincere injunctions to have a nice day (they don't do that in California?) he sets off on the freeway to re-encounter the love of his life. Wherever he goes, though the tone of the play is comic, he meets distressed people. I was reminded of an old Peggy Lee LP called Blues Cross Country. (There is also an album title about everything.) What he really keeps encountering is bereavement. There is a woman in Texas whose daughter committed suicide with a drug overdose. There is another in Georgia whose son died of AIDS and who commemorates him by passing out the plastic: handing out condoms to other gay men. There is a girl in California who wears an earring for each of her dead friends; her ears are festooned. There is Scott's own obsession with a memorial to the American dead of Vietnam. Why, he wonders, was there not a similar shrine to the victims of AIDS? They too, he says, died for their country.

They didnt, at least no more than the victims of any other disease. A majority of people, homosexuals included, die of causes other than AIDS, and their passing inflicts just as much grief to the survivors. The plays insistence on its unsustainable analogy with Vietnam seriously weakens it, and might destroy it altogether if it were in a more conventional form. But a monologue, though it has its own inherent limitations, also has its own freedoms. "I want my friends back" says Joel repeatedly. As a general statement of loss, that's fine and touching. We can't respond to it very deeply because we havent met any of his friends; we only know Scott as the subject of one of Joels impersonations. As a fully realized character in a real play he could be far more moving. But of course if he were a badly realized character the whole thing would collapse. You pay your money.

Road Movie comes to us from Starving Artists, a California-based company of two. There are Godfrey Hamilton, author, and Mark Pinkosh, performer. Hamilton seems to be a competent craftsman with a good sense of structure and a weakness for easy effects. He tells his story economically and builds to the best kind of surprise ending: one that in restrospect seems inevitable. But he also permits himself spurious lyrical outbursts, one of them an opening sequence that gets reprised at the end, and one coincidence - Joel unknowingly stops off at Scott's birthplace - that is meant to be affecting but is actually sheer kitsch.

He also balances some stabbingly hilarious lines with standard bitch- comedy bits about Judy Garland and Liza Minelli. Enough already. Admittedly Pinkosh dispenses these very well. He does almost everything very well. He starts with a spiky, shaven presence: maybe too abrasive for the smooth Manhattanite Joel seems meant to be but a launching-pad for the rest of the show. He is a high-energy, high-precision performer who passes at lightning speed from one voice to another and back again. This is standard practice among monologists, as among ventriloquists, and it has little to do with the rhythms of real life, but it certainly moves the show along, while adding an air of desperation that is both relevant and useful. He can also relax it. His parade of sad and funny women goes beyond female impersonation and into acting. In each case, he starts with an accent and then works inwards. What emerges are tartly charitable portraits that haunt and linger. World Stage continues tonight with Line in the Sand at the Tarragon Theatre; Hysterica Passio at the Brigantine Room; Que-Cir-Que at Ann Tindal Park; The Waste Land at the Gooderham and Worts historic district; Riot at the Factory Theatre.
1996-04-22-shades-of-hamlet:
WE know it will be brilliant, but why do it? That was the feeling in the house assembled to watch Robert Lepage conduct his one-man, two-hour assault on Hamlet, retitled Elsinore. It was also, with an appropriate adjustment of tenses, the feeling after he had been and gone and done it.

Lepage tells us in a program note that he is doing it because he wants to; in fact, that he couldn't stop himself. That is the best reason for doing anything, but it seems that he also sees Elsinore as a way station toward a full-scale production of Hamlet: one, I guess (or hope), with a full complement of other actors. In the meantime, there is this tour de force with its obvious built-in excitements and limitations. "You cannot," writes Lepage, signing off with engagingly arrogant self-deprecation, "make a Hamlet without breaking eggs." (Is that the message one should send a Hamlet on his first night - break an egg?) Not the least dazzling aspect of Lepage's technique is his ability to crack a yolk, I mean a joke, as good as that in his second language. His production of A Midsummer Night's Dream at Britain's National Theatre was by most accounts ghastly, if admittedly with the ghastliness of genius; most harshly criticized was his actors' mangling of the text. Here, of course, he does all the speaking himself, and it's pretty good for rhythm, excellent for sense. There were times when he lost it (I've never heard an actor flub words on "to be or not to be" before) and I imagine the whole thing was more fluent when he did it in French in Montreal, but considering everything else he must have had on his mind, his vocal achievement was stunning. Apart from the Frenchified courtier Osric, he plays all the characters with perfect English accents. Not Canadian English: English English.

By "all the characters," I mean Claudius, Polonius, Laertes, Ophelia, Gertrude, the Ghost and, of course, Hamlet himself. This obviously necessitates much quick changing: of position rather than costume, though Lepage can do a lot by donning or discarding a cloak. He has the help of a mute double; still, we were all delightedly fooled when Hamlet was teasing Polonius, and the young man instantly appeared where we thought the old one still stood. (Eat your heart out, Heath Lamberts.) Hamlet in this scene reads a book; Lepage stages it most appositely in a library, glimpsed mostly through a window cut in a huge, hinged central flat. At other times this aperture becomes a huge playing card, which, through the miracle of back projection, can instantly change its suit to frame the appearances of Claudius (King of Spades), Gertrude (Queen of Hearts), Polonius (Joker), and Laertes (Knave). Even Lepage has to make some compromises, and the women at this Danish court unavoidably sport the same beard and mustache as the men, but if you want to watch two hours of legerdemain you have them here at a virtuoso pitch.

Personally, I tired of it. Even the final sequence of duel and massacre, a real piece de resistance, cheered me largely because it meant the end was near. The real problem is that Elsinore unwittingly gives us a new gloss on the old gag about Hamlet without the Prince. Despite considerable cutting, some of it rather arbitrary, and a bit of reordering, this is still the same old play telling the same old story, and therefore demanding the same old magnetic protagonist. And though the hero here is everyone and everywhere, he is also no one and nowhere. Hamlet says so much about so many things that he needs a generous leavening of the actor's own personality to make him cohere.

Lepage has simply spread himself too thin. He sketches in the minor roles quite nicely, but all he told me about Hamlet himself was that he had a mind for metaphysics, lying on his back and contemplating the heavens while considering suicide, and that he could be nasty about sex; he gets very graphic when quizzing Ophelia on "country matters." He is also, thanks in part to a menacing physical production and crushing musique concrete, the gloomiest Dane I have ever seen. He is bucking a trend, since the fashion now is for mordantly witty Hamlets, but I think the fashion is right.

Maybe Lepage is simply just too lightweight an actor to play the role, though, remembering his solo magnificence in Needles and Opium, I would like to think not. On the other hand, remembering the generally fine acting in Tectonic Plates and especially The Seven Streams of the River Ota, it could be that the way ahead for him would be to direct someone else in Hamlet. (Working on equal terms with a star might put an interesting new spin on his work.) There is still much to marvel at here. Nobody makes more stunning use of space, as when Hamlet gazes down through a trap at an invisible Player and wonders at the psychological gulf between them. The play scene itself is ingenious. And he ends one section by sending a table and carpet spinning into infinity while placed on a gravity-defying diagonal. I don't know that it signifies much beyond itself, but it takes the breath.
1996-05-01-much-musicals:
So what, other than an exceptionally ugly word, is a megamusical?

Garth Drabinsky claims that there is no such animal; and, since his Live Entertainment Inc. have brought The Phantom of the Opera and Sunset Boulevard to Canada, he should know. According to Drabinsky, "Hal Prince will go to his grave" denying that there is anything especially grandiose about Phantom. As Prince directed the show, which most people would regard as the very model of a modern megamusical, the whole existence of the phenomenon seems in doubt.

But it does exist, if only in the popular consciousness. Journalists slap the megamusical label on any show that has a pronounced technical gleam and that obviously cost a ton of money to mount: on the Livent revival of Show Boat, a classic American musical in the book-music-lyrics tradition; on Crazy for You, a free adaptation of another classic American musical, the Gershwins' Girl Crazy; and on Kiss of the Spider Woman, which in my judgment is a new classic American musical. But a purist definition of the megamusical would exclude all these. The megamusical is the Euromusical.

That means Cats, Starlight Express, Les Miserables, Chess, Phantom, Miss Saigon, Aspects of Love, Sunset Boulevard: i.e. any musical involving composer Andrew Lloyd Webber, director Trevor Nunn, producer Cameron Mackintosh, or some combination thereof. Let us call these works the hard-core canon. Among them they have set new standards for commercial success and international marketing -- standards that have inevitably affected the way in which the more traditional shows (Crazy for You, in particular) have been staged, sold, and received. They have also inspired emulation from other sources: notably The Who's Tommy and Beauty and the Beast.

Large-scale musicals have come to dominate the commercial theatre throughout the world. In Canada they are the commercial theatre, which was reinvented when the Toronto production of Cats proved that a show could settle down in one place for a considerable time: a lesson reinforced by the phenomenal run of Phantom. The failure of subsequent shows to duplicate this longevity has been taken to mean that the public has tired of the megamusical. But it takes a journalist or a pollster to believe that an audience buys or rejects a genre. People go to specific shows of which they like the sound. Hype can help, hugely, but it cannot create.

The hard-core canon is the work of a very small group of people, whose productivity was bound to slow down. But megamusicals have taken up a lot of space, and the phenomenon isn't going away. It's worth examining the salient features.

1. Provenance. As many an American practitioner has bitterly noted, the megamusical is a British invention. Webber, Nunn, and Mackintosh are all British, and it was Britain's Royal Shakespeare Company that developed Les Miserables, after its French creators, Alain Boublil and Claude-Michel Schonberg, had done it oratorio-fashion in Paris. Boublil and Schonberg's subsequent work, Miss Saigon, was launched in London -- as will be their next, Martin Guerre, the only pedigreed megamusical on the immediate horizon.

This Anglocentricity is hardly reflected in the shows' style or subject matter. America is the ancestral home of the modern musical, and even these authors who have supposedly supplanted the, American product like to strut in its feathers: to prove themselves American by association, with Miss Saigon and Sunset Boulevard. Though the musical idiom of the megashows isn't American, nor is it identifiably British or French. It's Europop: the toothless international style that turned middle-of-the-road into middle-of-the-ocean It was typified by the Swedish supergroup Abba, two of whose members duly composed their own megashow, the supremely rootless Chess. The one megaballad to have achieved the eloquence for which they all so laboriously strive is Lloyd Webber's "All I Ask of You," from Phantom.

2. Dialogue, Lack of. The oldest play we have are musicals. Ancient Greek tragedy and ancient Greek comedys told their stories through a mixture of speech, song, and dance. It's the purely sung or purely spoken drama that's an aberration.

Pop opera, the form to which the megamusicals aspire, wants you to hear the words but makes you wish that you couldn't. One achievement of the Boublil-Schonberg duo has been to reduce Herbert Kretzmer, a competent lyricist, and Richard Maltby, Jr., a brilliant lyricist, to writing doggerel (for Les Mis and Miss Saigon respectively). They use song to dispense information that could be conveyed with far more ease and elegance in dialogue. In Sunset Boulevard the supposedly sharp Hollywooders, chanting exposition at one another over endlessly repeated vamps, sound like earnest half-wits. Don Black, another experienced lyricist, and Christopher Hampton, an intelligent playwright, are the authors; possibly they blush on their way to the bank.

Audiences today are too sophisticated, the theory goes, to accept transitions from speech to song and back again. It's a weird idea of sophistication, and there's absolutely no evidence for it. The throughsung technique only works in Webber's early Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat, a short and breezy show whose narrative links are funny. Which brings us to

4. Humour, Also Lack of. Stephen Sondheim has described his latest musical, Passion (not mega, by any definition), as "the world's first humourless musical." He was being wry, possibly defensive, and probably disingenuous. He may have meant the first intentionally humourless musical. Most shows try at some point to be funny. Many fail.

There was wit in all the shows Webber wrote with Tim Rice, in Jesus Christ Superstar and Evita as well as Joseph. Rice's later work, though, has been as pompous as any in the genre. (There's a yawning gap between the flatulent additional lyrics he contributed to the film Aladdin and the stage version of Beauty and the Beast, and the sprightly words of his predecessor, the late Howard Ashman. It affects the music too There is one entertaining song in Les Mis and one that tries hard in Miss Saigon. Nothing resembling a good joke is allowed to profane the solemn portals of Phantom, Aspects, or Sunset. It weighs especially hard on the last, whose source, otherwise faithfully followed, was in large part a black comedy. Crazy as it sounds, there is probably a commercial logic to this. A lot of people suspect humour, especially the irreverent humour that was the hallmark of the Broadway musical in its prime. Consider this early (1917) lyric by P.G. Wodehouse, working with Jerome Kern:

Napoleon was a little guy, they used to call him Shorty,

He only stood about so high, and his chest was under forty

But they, couldn't faze Napoleon, when he started in to slap;

He was five foot high, but one tough guy, and I take after Nap.

There are similarly profane songs about Josephine, by Noel Coward and Cole Porter. Napoleon was also a comic character when he turned up in the title role of Canada's home-brewed megawannabe of a couple of years back: an idealistic loser whose fatal mistake at Waterloo was to dream about his discarded wife on the eve of battle. (Not tonight, Josephine.) Unfortunately, the authors didn't know they were being funny. A sense of humour is vital in musicals as in most other things. It teaches you how and when to be serious.

4. Performance. A peculiarity of the megashows is that nobody knows or cares who's in them. Michael Crawford's truly haunting performance of the Phantom, in London and New York, was a bonus but not a necessity. The only exceptions are Evita and Sunset Boulevard, two shows about stars, aspiring or actual, that require to be cast accordingly and have kept columnists happy for years. Or, in the former case, decades. That the movie role of Evita should finally have been won by Madonna, not so much a star as a parody of stardom, is true poetic justice: probably good casting as well. On film, Sunset Boulevard was an acrid examination of the star phenomenon; on stage it's a traditional showbiz hymn. Whoever the leading lady may be, the audience is required to worship her. It's why she spends so much time coming down staircases.

5. Sources. Most megamusicals are based on something else. That is not a crime. So are most old-style musicals. So are most operas and movies. So, at one time, were most plays. (Look at Shakespeare.) All the successful shows tell time-proven stories, except for Cats, which makes a point of not having one. If the story is bad (Tommy), confusing (Aspects), or just unmanageable (Napoleon), there is trouble: artistic and even commercial. And if the natural progression, from page to stage to film to television, is violated the results are almost invariably grisly. Turning a film musical into a stage musical is self-evidently pointless, even if the show's a hit.

The terrifying case of Beauty and the Beast finds people who may go to the theatre only once a year, putting down money, lots of it, for an inferior replica of something they have already seen -- and can continue to see -- on a screen. On the stage, Beauty is the spin-off of spin-offs, a long, slothful reminder of how good the movie was. Not one Toronto critic commented on this production's amateurishness, its merry villagers grouped around its trilling heroine in immobile clumps like extras in a provincial English pantomime. (And if you say that a live show cannot hope to rival the invention and agility of a cartoon, then that's a very good reason not to try.) The Toronto version has one thing going for it: a remarkably sensitive and flexible performance by Chuck Wagner as the male lead. Of course he loses appeal when he sheds his fur and whiskers at the end, but that's the nature of the Beast.

6 (and inevitably). Spectacle. I suggest a moratorium on dismissive sentences about chandeliers and helicopters. It's a lazy journalistic shorthand, supposed to signify mindless extravagance and in no way supported by the facts. I loathed Miss Saigon, but the helicopter wasn't what I loathed it for; it was a graphic element in the fall of the city, itself a vital part of the story. The descending chandelier in Phantom is an amusing and momentarily scary trompe l'oeil that contributes to narrative and atmosphere.

People confuse spectacle with mere lavishness. Spectacle (check out Aristotle) is an aesthetic quality; it's the way a stage looks, and the better it looks the better. Phantom, with its candlelit voyage to the protagonist's lair and its explosion of colour in the "Masquerade" number, is spectacular; so was the brilliant alternation of spare and cluttered staging in Nicholas Hytner's production of Miss Saigon; so, despite lousy material, was Des McAnuff's high-tech vision of Tommy. Sunset Boulevard is lavish; Trevor Nunn is the best director of plays -- certainly of classic plays -- in the English theatre, but his work on this show is stodgy, however much the set goes up and down. Beauty and the Beast is the dumping on the stage of expensive materials by people who have no idea what to do with them.

The hard-core megashows have their merits, and if they entertain people I'm glad, but they are a limited form -- more limited than the musical theatre need be, and historically has been. (You want to know what I love most about musicals] Smart lyrics. I've yet to hear one in a megamusical.) So, if Mirvish Productions have left the field, closing Tommy and renting their new theatre to Disney, I don't repine; to have first-class plays reinstated at Toronto's Royal Alex is a blessing. Livent remain committed to musicals and to developing their own. On their stocks are a version of E. L. Doctorow's Ragtime, with a score by the richly promising Broadway team of Stephen Flaherty and Lynn Ahrens; The Sweet Smell of Success, with music by veteran Cy Coleman; new productions of Candide and Pal Joey: all, intriguingly and encouragingly, in the American rather than the European mould.

There was a delightful moment in Crazy for You, when one tradition met the other, and tweaked it: a moment of what hip literary critics call intertextuality. The show's Ziegfeld figure surveys a stage piled high with furniture and declares that it looks like the French Revolution. He alludes of course to the barricade scene in Les Miserables. The joke is even better than the authors may realize, since Victor Hugo's novel deals with the Revolution of July, which took place some forty years after the 1789 affair. The audiences for Les Mis think they're getting a history lesson, and Les Mis wouldn't dream of disabusing them. Musicals will continue to dominate the commercial theatre in Canada. Let there be some intelligent ones.
