THEATRE REVIEW TRUDEAU AND THE FLQ

Monday, May 06, 1996

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written and directed by Michael Hollingsworth Starring John Dolan and Henry Tarvainen At Theatre Centre West until May 21 Rating: Hollingsworth take on FLQ crisis long on detail, short on depth BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail THE art of the cartoon is to reduce characters to the sum of their obsessions. Usually it's a very simple sum: one driving force per person. Even when the passion might seem to be an honourable one - a thirst for peace or justice or equality - by the time the cartoonist is through with it, it will look like just another lowest common denominator.

This is fine with most of us; we are habitually cynical about public figures of all periods and all persuasions. We lend a willing eye and ear to the Royal Canadian Air Farce and This Hour Has 22 Minutes and (on a far higher level of vitriolic inventiveness) the British series Spitting Image . And we are benevolently curious when Michael Hollingsworth tries to make this short-bite TV technique work for the duration of a 2-1/2-hour stage play.

Or a cycle of stage plays. Or two cycles. Having taken on most of early Canada in The History of the Village of the Small Huts, Hollingsworth is creeping up on the way we live now in a new collection called The Global Village. Trudeau and the FLQ is this second serial's second instalment. It deals, as you would expect, with the attempts of some Quebeckers to get in on the international protest-and-terrorism scene in the late sixties and with the reaction of that other favoured Quebecker who happened to be in charge at the time.

As author, and especially as director, Hollingsworth does his thing superbly. He calls his outfit VideoCabaret, and he comes as close to television as you can while working on a stage with actors who are patently and exhilaratingly live. This may seem a pointless exercise but the paradox turns out to be its own justification. The stage is a black box crammed with bold colour: the joint achievement of set and lighting designer Jim Plaxton, costume designer Astrid Janson, and prop designers Shadowland. (I've never encountered this last credit before, but they've certainly earned it.) The performing style, which never wavers, is similarly witty and similarly emphatic. Although the action covers eight years no character ever gets a change of clothes, though the individual actors, playing six or seven roles apiece, change a great deal. There are more than 100 scenes; and not the least impressive aspect of the evening is the ability of everybody and everything to be in the right place at the right time. The ambience is summed up in the presentation of the FLQ's letter-bomb campaign. A postal worker does a merry little dance to the recording of the Beatles' Please, Mr. Postman. He approaches his box. Bang. Blackout. The show is not selling compassion.

The revolutionaries, dressed in identical shabby, plaid jackets, are led by a squat malcontent called Maurice (played with salivating bravura by Henry Tarvainen), whose credo is that he wants to "kill all the bourgeoisie" he defines the bourgeoisie as "anyone with more money than me." After being locked up, he orchestrates the kidnap campaign as a bargaining counter for his own release. A female comrade called Suzanne is delegated to represent various stages of the sexual revolution: from "read the Kama Sutra or get lost" to "I'm not a woman, I'm a dyke."

Their escalation is counterpointed with that of Trudeau: coming man in Act One, Prime Minister in Act Two. At the very end, though mercifully not before, he meets Maggie, a voluminous flower child: watch, presumably, this space. He is given a superbly languid performance by John Dolan, who does not so much turn a caricature into a human being as persuade you that a caricature is more interesting.

There are, predictably, problems. Though the script is on its own terms well organized, the endless succession of minuscule scenes becomes exhausting. You begin to crave depth. I'm split on this; I think it's quite likely that the FLQ actually were the egotistical goons presented here, but it might make for more interesting drama if we pretended they weren't. At least, it might flatter my humanistic literary prejudices.

Despite all the blood and guts, the evening is short on conflict. The title is a pointer. Sure enough Trudeau takes up some of the stage time and the FLQ much of the rest. Unfortunately history dictates that they never meet. Nor do they have any subtler impact on one another. Though Trudeau keeps protesting his horror of nationalist fanatics, this has nothing to do with the strong measures he eventually takes; any head of state would have done the same. Still, if Hollingsworth merely means us to have a good sustained giggle at the recent past, he has triumphantly succeeded.
1996-05-11-the-diary-of-anne-frank:
THEATRE REVIEW THE DIARY OF ANNE FRANK

Saturday, May 11, 1996

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written by Frances Goodrich and Albert Hackett Directed by Leah Cherniak Starring Waneta Storms At Young People's Theatre in Toronto until May 26 Rating: Flawless acting unlocks Diary BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail EIGHT Jews hiding from the Nazis in an attic in Amsterdam, remaining there just over two years, finally betrayed and captured, herded off to concentration camps, only one of them surviving. Those seven deaths are the tiniest fraction of six million but the truism remains true: The only way to get some emotional purchase on the Holocaust is to remember that each statistic represents an individual agony, the tragedy of one innocent, terrified, defenceless person.

Add in the romance of the young girl's journal, miraculously preserved until after the war, and it's no wonder that The Diary of Anne Frank has become a classic. The dramatization by Frances Goodrich and Albert Hackett - two otherwise undistinguished Broadway and Hollywood writers - was first staged in New York in 1955, and it bears some marks of its time and place. It compresses its narrative into half-a-dozen shapely scenes, where later writers would probably have gone for something starker, more episodic, and a lot harder to sit through. But the new ways are not necessarily better; and Goodrich and Hackett, probably writing the only way they knew how, have given us an all-American family drama gone frighteningly askew.

I see nothing wrong with making soap opera out of the Holocaust, so long as it's honest soap opera. I don't want distinguished writers pirouetting over this subject, telling me how sensitive they are. We can all identify with these characters - partly from life, partly from convention - and that is what the play is for. That's the reason for putting it on a stage and making a shared experience of it. In Berlin in the fifties it was a nightmare of collective guilt; audience members couldn't look at one another or, in some cases, at the stage. For us, it's an imaginative opportunity to remember history or to learn it.

I have never seen the play before, but Leah Cherniak's production at Young People's Theatre must be as good as it can get. (And after my recent strictures on YPT it's a pleasure to say that.) She opens the play up a little, framing the stage with blown-up photos; and the final arrival of the Nazis, unseen but very heard, is a more elaborate aural nightmare than I imagine the Broadway of the fifties would have tolerated. Essentially, though, she gives us the characters, in flawless performances, flawlessly merged.

In most dramatizations of this subject the interesting characters are the persecutors and the onlookers, because they alone have some freedom of choice. Here, though, we can concentrate on the victims, because, however stressed, they refuse to act like victims. The point of the play is that, for as long as it's allowed to, life goes on; and it's a messy and occasionally joyful business. Anne herself (Waneta Storms) is adolescence in a pressure cooker, exasperating and occasionally charming her elders, nearly as much as she charms and exasperates herself. Her father (Jerry Franken), the only character who seems somewhat idealized, is still credible as a decent businessman and natural leader. Her quiet, bewildered mother (Robin Craig) finally erupts when her own unwritten rules are transgressed. Sister Margot (Marjorie Campbell) is unwaveringly, almost unbearably, sympathetic.

The more colourful family with whom they share their refuge are the Van Daans: father (Jim Warren) a powerful-looking man who is jelly within; mother (Tanja Jacobs - the showiest performance, and that is not a putdown) flirtatious, possessive and desperately clinging; their son (Derek Metz) a wonderful picture of hunched, calf-like, growing boyhood. A solitary late arrival (John Jarvis) is a petulant permanent outsider. Then there are the benefactors: the factory owner (Jarvis), as worried as he is kind; the secretary Miep (Missy Christensen), the link with the outside world, who is not above tingeing her devotion with silent exasperation when her charges' demands become extreme. (Her real-life original appeared at this year's Oscars, where she was justifiably acclaimed as "a real heroine.") Charlotte Dean's set is a fine picture of enforced neatness overlaid with rebellious clutter. There is very little sentimentality here; these are, or were, real people. As were all the others. And so, as this most hideous of centuries trundles to its conclusion, do they continue to be.
1996-05-12-necessarily-so:
NECESSARILY SO

Ira Gershwin, whose 100th birthday is celebrated this year, wrote many of Broadway's most memorable lyrics, and made his brother's tunes sing.

Robert Cushman Sunday 12 May 1996 00:02 BST

Ira Gershwin was the elder of the two famous brothers, and the gentler. He used to say that he would never have got anywhere if George hadn't pushed him. George had drive enough for three; you can tell just from hearing his surviving piano rolls, which may convince you that there never was a pianist with so much energy. When he first displayed musical talent his parents were not so much delighted as relieved. They'd thought he was going to be a delinquent.

We're talking here of a Russian Jewish family that had settled in New York towards the end of the last century. Ira, the first of four children, was born on 6 December 1896. Perhaps because of his quietness, he was pegged as the family scholar and then, by a kind of natural psychological progression, as the family musician. You read books, you read music; that must have been the theory. In 1910, when Ira was 14, the Gershwins acquired a piano. According to a famous story it had to be hoisted up through the window of their second-floor apartment; once in, it was immediately commandeered by the apparently feckless George, who, it turned out, had been learning from a friend to play by ear. The piano became his as of right, and no more was heard of Ira learning to play it. He must have been greatly relieved. He always shunned the limelight (here, too, he was his brother's polar opposite) - and, besides, piano-lessons must have seemed too much like hard work.

The author of "The Man I Love", "Love is Here to Stay", "I Can't Get Started", "I Got Rhythm" and countless others always claimed to be prodigiously lazy. In fact he was capable of great and sustained effort in one or two chosen areas, but for the most part he liked to take life easy and to laugh at himself for doing so: "I'm Bidin' My Time / 'Cause that's the kinda guy I'm. / While other folks grow dizzy / I keep busy / Bidin' My Time."

That song from Girl Crazy (1930) sounds like the authentic Ira, not least for the eye-rolling, I-bet-you-never-thought-I-could-get-away-with-that- ness of the initial rhyme. But he sweated over his lyrics, sometimes taking weeks to complete a single song, and "Bidin' My Time", a celebration of inertia, probably took as much out of him as any other.

His favourite activity seems always to have been reading. His bookishness made him not just a lyricist but a particular kind of lyricist; it also, in earlier years, carried him through the New York school system. He got a place at Townsend Harris, a high school for the more gifted kids of the Lower East Side. From there he proceeded to the City College of New York. (George meanwhile had dropped out of school, and was pounding pianos for the city's music publishers. It was the dirt road towards composing his own songs, at which he became very successful, very young.) At high school and college Ira wrote light verse, contributed to school papers, and started his own. What undid him was mathematics. Hearing, in his second year at CCNY, that "calculus was in the offing", he decided, he said, "to call it an education".

That phrase is very Ira: in its neatness, in its laconic self-deprecation, and in the allusive spin that it puts on a familiar piece of slang. It's typical of his prose style, which itself is closely related to his lyric- writing. There are very few lyricists of whom one can make this claim, because there are very few who have left us any prose to speak of. P G Wodehouse did of course, but his lyrics now count as the merest appendix to his fiction; both oeuvres, though, are recognisably rooted in the same meticulous, bizarrely innocent consciousness.

Ira never, strictly speaking, wrote a book. What he did - in 1959, when his songwriting career was virtually over - was collect and annotate a generous cross-section of his own creations, under the title Lyrics on Several Occasions. These annotations are gems. On Ethel Merman: "a no-nonsense voice that could reach not only standees but ticket-takers in the lobby." On filmstar Victor Mature's appearance in the show Lady in the Dark: "When handsome 'hunk of man' Mature sang, his heart and the correct key weren't in it." On the highly characteristic peculiarity of one of his best-known love-songs: " 'Embraceable You' is rather unusual as a more or less sentimental ballad in that some of its rhymes are four-syllable ones." On the prevalence of female names in show-titles: "The lone marqueed male I've worked for is Porgy and he had to share billing fifty-fifty with Bess." The songs are grouped in whimsically labelled categories. Dance songs, fashioned for Fred Astaire and others, are "Turns for Terpsichore". A bunch of "male-wanted" numbers, ranging from "The Man I Love" to a predatory Manhattan matron's "My Son-in-Law", are corralled together under the heading "The Not Impossible He". The same cheerful arbitrariness leads him to follow the lyric of "That Certain Feeling" with a paragraph headed "That Certain Question". (It refers to the ubiquitous 'Which comes first, the words or the music?' And, like most songwriters, Ira isn't telling.) It all adds up to a relaxed urbanity in the great tradition of light Manhattan letters. And it was Ira Gershwin, more than any other lyricist, who translated that spirit into song.

He and George wrote their first song together in 1918. Their first full Broadway score, also their first hit, was Lady Be Good in 1924. From then until George's shockingly untimely death in 1937, they were virtually inseparable, professionally and even personally. For a long time they continued to live with their parents - though it might be truer, as their success increased, to say that their parents lived with them. In 1926 Ira married Leonore Strunsky, who it has often been claimed was really in love with George but settled for his brother as her best chance of becoming a Gershwin. (George never married, and dreaded commitment.) She got her wish; George and Ira's menages remained intertwined.

The standard line on the great Gershwin songs is that George's music, with its roots in both jazz and Stravinskian modernism, furnished the hard edge while sweet, gentle Ira supplied the sentiment. A perfect mix. There's something in this, as far as their individual textures are concerned, except that Ira was never much interested in sentiment. An American scholar, Philip Furia, has perceptively suggested that Ira wrote love songs because it was expected of him - or because he had to write about something. But what really interested him was words. It was the streetwise George who anchored Ira's words in accessible emotions; Ira's verbal flights had to move with George's jagged syncopations.

Then again, Ira was lucky to come into his prime in the 1920s. Though hardly a Bright Young Thing he found the lingo of the flappers both useful and congenial. He loved their arch contractions. An early song (without George), "Sunny Disposish", is built on them: "It really doesn't pay / To be a gloomy Pill - / It's absolutely most ridic', / Positively sil'." (Elsewhere in the same song he goes to the opposite orotund extreme, rhyming "platitudinous" with "attitude in us".) "Be yourself, don't be sil' " was a Twenties catchphrase (and the same year, 1926, Ira used it in full in one of his biggest hits with George, Oh, Kay!) but Ira turned a fashionable mannerism into a style. He was still using it in 1940 when the heroine of Lady in the Dark, finding herself with "One Life to Live", announced for the sake of a rhyme that "gloom can jump in the riv' ".

Some people find this irritating. It's also possible to object to Ira's convoluted way with word-order. The generally wonderful "Nice Work If You Can Get It" includes the couplet: "The only work that really brings enjoyment / Is the kind that is for girl and boy meant."

And yet these weaknesses even out into their own kind of strength. Ira will twist language for a rhyme or just for a cute verbal idea - but that, done with sufficient consistency and ingenuity, is its own style. Many of his peers could do things he couldn't. Cole Porter could paint a hot-house society, alternately illuminated by frigid wit and torrid passion. Lorenz Hart could use flip humour to underscore personal pain. The still-underrated Irving Berlin could sound unforcedly right in every word he wrote. E Y Harburg, Ira's friend from high school on (this year is his centenary as well), could pun even more outrageously but with greater control; he also believed far more fervently in romantic love and social progress. (In 1934 Ira and Harburg collaborated with composer Harold Arlen on a revue, Life Begins at 8.40, that took Broadway sophistication in words and music to its zenith.) All these writers had a world-view; Ira had a word-view.

Ira was the writer whose literacy so impressed the moguls that they let him use a word as far-out as "picayune" - in a movie-song, yet. (The film was The Shocking Miss Pilgrim, 1947; the song was called "Changing My Tune".) He has a personal voice: a quizzical persona that can't quite believe it's writing love songs but creeps up on them slowly to make sure. "How Long Has This Been Going On" (1927), one of his very best, is about the moment of falling in love. The narrator tells an impossibly elaborate story about how "as a tot, when I trotted in little velvet panties" he was kissed by female relatives and loathed it. His first adult kiss has changed his mind and the main part of the song is given over to exploring, at succulent length, his new, delighted state of mind and body.

Two songs from the Astaire-Rogers picture, Shall We Dance (1937), explore the ramifications of the sinister word "they" meaning The Others, the enemies of romance. "They All Laughed" - a love song, as Ira pointed out, that never mentions love - exults in their outright defeat: "ho, ho, ho, who's got the last laugh now". "They Can't Take That Away From Me" acknowledges Their power in the physical world but defies Them from within. The memories that are the emotional weapons build from the delightfully trivial ("the way you wear your hat") to the downright superb ("the way you've changed my life") and the steady, passionate escalation makes the song a singer's delight.

Strictly speaking, "They Can't Take That Away From Me" is a lost-love song but nobody ever thinks of it that way. Ira hardly ever wrote a torch- song; God knows how he evaded them since the shows and films he wrote for must have included the regulation quota of boy-losing-girl. Faced with the situation in Girl Crazy, he came up with the superbly self-mocking "But Not For Me", full of wry literary jokes and ending with a twist: "The climax of a plot / Should be the marriage knot / But there's no knot for me."

Not till 1954 did Ira write an indisputable torcher, Judy Garland's last hurrah "The Man That Got Away", filled with curt, aggressive consonants. ("The night is bitter, the stars have lost their glitter.") It's magnificent, but it still has the feel of an exercise. It's Ira, proving he can do it. On only a few occasions did he actually project himself inside the skin of another character. One surprising example is "Someone To Watch Over Me" (1926), generally believed to be the ugly-duckling brother's rueful self-portrait ("although he may not be the man some / girls think of as handsome") but still perfectly matched to the girl who sings it. And in a class of their own are his contributions to George's opera Porgy and Bess. Ira was brought in to write some of the profaner numbers, in particular the songs for the dope peddler Sportin' Life ("It Ain't Necessarily So", "There's a Boat That's Leavin' Soon for New York"). Perhaps it was the Southern dialect that inspired him, perhaps it was the intensity of the work, but these songs are unlike anything else he wrote. Skin-tight to character, worlds away from standard Broadway cynicism, they give us diabolism itself: sleek, hard and irresistible.

After George's death - from a rogue brain-tumour - Ira was prostrated; he felt guilty, as if he should have been taken in place of his worshipped brother. Some say that he never recovered, that the rest of his life was a slow suicide. Still, he rallied enough to do some of his best work with other composers and to establish himself as official keeper of the Gershwin flame. The Fifties seem to have been golden times; he and Leonore kept the most hospitable house in Beverly Hills. But he progressively lost interest in work, in life and even in movement; he seems to have willed himself into becoming bedridden, biding his time till there was no more time left. The marriage, with no children, turned Strindbergian. The best memoir of Ira's last years is Michael Feinstein's Nice Work If You Can Get It. Before his success as a singer Feinstein worked as a cataloguer of Ira's musical archive, and became very close to him. Feinstein adored Ira, the writer and the man, but could still see his failings. He leaves no doubt that the wit and kindness, however compromised by self-pity and hypochondria, remained till the end. Ira died on 17 August 1983, aged 86: 46 years after his younger brother. The songs (this is not an original observation) are here to stay. !
1996-05-21-theatre-review-night-light:
THEATRE REVIEW NIGHT LIGHT

Tuesday, May 21, 1996

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- Written by John Lazarus Directed by Robert Metcalfe Presented by Green Thumb Theatre for Young People in Toronto THE CASHORE MARIONETTES Presented by Joseph Cashore A CHILD'S PORTRAIT OF SHAKESPEARE AND MACBETH Written and Directed by Lois Burdett Performed by Grade 2 students from Stratford's Hamlet Elementary School Young drama goes beyond child's play Performances geared to the younger set prove enchanting for adults, too. THE MILK FESTIVAL At Harbourfront on Saturday and Sunday BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto AMONG the formative influences of my youth was a book called Down with Skool. It was supposedly the work of an English schoolboy of about 12, named Nigel Molesworth, a.k.a. The Curse of St. Custard's.

Among Nigel's observations were the following on the hazards of encountering gangs of older boys. (Spelling regularized.) "There is always a big one called Ern. Ern is a bully. People always say stand up to bullies, they will run away, BUT DON'T YOU BELIEVE IT."

This refreshing wisdom is partially echoed in Night Light, brought to the Milk Festival at Toronto's Harbourfront by the Green Thumb Theatre of Vancouver. Victor, a nice kid, good at lessons, is regularly set upon by Farley, who forces Victor to do his math homework for him.

Victor reads a book on how to deal with childhood fears but finds its pat recommendations no help at all; after a moment of surprise, Farley simply laughs at him.

Digging deeper, Victor identifies Farley's weak spot: his terror of having his poor grades detected by his "genius" father. Even this one-to- one correlation between a bully's bullying and his insecurities seems suspiciously neat; problems in real life are not so easily solved. But it works in the play.

This is due, in part, to a shrewd stroke of construction by the playwright John Lazarus; we are introduced to Farley and his worries before we see him terrorizing Victor. For a crucial moment, the victimizer seems like the victim.

The writing in general is economic and unsentimental, as is the performance. Matthew Smith as Victor is especially fine, an adult actor clearly conveying a growing child's blend of innocence and experience.

Less successful is a parallel plot involving Victor's younger sister and her equivalent trauma over their father's hospitalization. The younger you play, the harder it gets; and the stylization, which involves a live floppy monster creeping out of a closet, doesn't belong to the same world as the rest of the play.

The nine-going-on-10-year-olds who accompanied me to these junkets thought it a little beneath them. That at least is what they said afterward. During the performance, they were thoroughly held.

They were similarly enraptured by the Cashore Marionettes, although younger kids were not. It probably was irresponsible of the organizers to announce this show as suitable for ages five and up. Joseph Cashore, a superlative puppeteer from Pennsylvania, does not tell stories; he composes visual tone-poems. On the end of his strings, a venerable European violinist fervently attacks a Vaughan Williams piece, bowing perfectly synchronized. An amateur trapeze artist, terrified but determined, manages to get through a professional routine, to his own amazement and the audience's delight. A homeless scavenger seems to find some hope at the black-clad leg of his manipulator; gazing upward, though, he encounters only the devastating shake of his master's head: God saying no. A perkier puppet is luckier; he manages to climb all the way up Mount Cashore to perch cheekily on its shoulder.

Technically, these performances are a marvel. Having the operator in full view only adds to the wonder of it: so many strings controlling so much detail. Each doll is perfectly costumed and characterized, their faces so detailed you could swear that you see them change expression.

The spirit of the performance is benign but stern. Cumulatively, it is rather frightening. Out in the world, puppetry is a metaphor for mental cruelty, and that is what emerges here. The more domestic items (a mother trying to quiet her baby, a girl avoiding her homework) are the least interesting. You remember instead the images of humanity in a bleak landscape, at the mercy of a capricious controlling fate. Cashore's art may be accessible to children, but it isn't kids' stuff.

Cashore is American, and the Green Thumb troupe stopped off in Toronto as a diversion from a U.S. tour. The Grade 2 kids of the Hamlet Public School in Stratford, Ont., are due to visit Utah later this year but their appearance at Harbourfront counts as a wholly Canadian achievement. It has, though, world-wide implications.

Teacher Lois Burdett insists, rightly, that her creations, which are being marketed under the rubric "Shakespeare Can Be Fun]," are not primarily designed to introduce her pupils to Shakespeare.

Rather, she uses Shakespeare - the stories of the plays and a little bit of the language - to introduce the children to themselves: to their own imaginations and their own inventiveness.

That they get, in the process, astonishingly close to the heart of the plays reflects great credit on all parties, Shakespeare included.

Of course, once you place these classroom projects in front of an audience, you add new, and conceivably distorting, dimensions.

What was a self-sufficient exercise becomes a show, inviting judgment. Children, if my companions are any guide, react with admiration and envy: Why can't they have so much fun in school? The answer seems to be that Burdett is an exceptional teacher, therefore unduplicatable. Still, this kind of stimulation ought to be generally available, even if it can't take this precise form.

I had already seen A Child's Portrait of Shakespeare performed at Stratford for a conference of theatre professionals, who reacted with predictable self-flagellating enthusiasm. I was as charmed by the kids as they were, and as awed by their clarity and assurance, but I had some doubts that were reinforced on a second viewing.

We are offered a dramatized biography of Shakespeare, researched by the children and cast into rhyming couplets by Burdett herself. It is acted out with several kids sharing the central role. It is charming and cute, but the presence of a grown-up audience ups the cuteness quotient automatically and dangerously.

Even as a child's portrait, it is dubiously sentimental: Shakespeare is unlikely to have slipped back from London to Stratford to spend weekends with Anne Hathaway; it would have been logistically impossible, and all the evidence suggests that he couldn't wait to get away from her. The burning of the Globe Theatre didn't break his heart and end his career; he was already in retirement. About the plays themselves we are told nothing. But without them, Shakespeare's life, what we know of it, is not very interesting.

The proof is in the school's version of Macbeth, which is riveting. The basic staging is the same; the performers sit in two rows, detaching themselves when their cue for action comes. Within this convention, the staging is very inventive; most professional productions gloss over the procession of Banquo's royal heirs, for example, but here we had a full implacable lineup with crowns. There is some very selective quotation ("bubble, bubble, toil and trouble" is in; "tomorrow and tomorrow and tomorrow" is out) but the basic medium, once again, is Burdett's couplets.

These are far less jingly and predictable than in the Portrait, probably because they are rooted in response to an actual strong story rather than to biographical wishful thinking.

There are also some outstanding individual performances. If Macbeth's self-torture is a little underdone, his wife's mixture of scorn and ambition is very compelling, and there is a strong avenging (and female) Macduff. (There are far more girls in the cast than boys. Are Grade 2 boys less interested?) As education and as entertainment, this is triumphant. Or as Nigel Molesworth might for once have put it, Up with Skool.
1996-06-01-noel-coward-is-revealed-as-hi:
LIVES / A new biography of Noel Coward comes the closest to understanding the genius of one of Britain's most famous playwrights and tax exiles. NOEL COWARD: A Biography

Noel Coward is revealed as his own disciple

LIVES / A new biography of Noel Coward comes the closest to understanding the genius of one of Britain's most famous playwrights and tax exiles. NOEL COWARD: A Biography

Saturday, June 1, 1996

By Philip Hoare

Sinclair-Stevenson, 605 pages, $50

WAS anyone ever as completely a creature of the theatre as Noel Coward? Moliere perhaps; but Moliere, as far as I know, never had much of a career as a songwriter or cabaret performer. Coward was actor, playwright, director, lyricist, composer, sort-of-singer -- and he also turned out novels, filmscripts, short stories, light verse and amateur but respectable paintings. How did he decide which of his talents to utilize on any given day? And how does a biographer, conscientiously following his tracks, keep from dropping in them?

Philip Hoare's account is the most comprehensive so far, and probably the best. Some of the story is familiar. Coward found his metier early, beginning as a child actor, spurred on by an adoring and ambitious mother. Before he was out of his teens, he had also discovered that he would write. A postcard, prophesying great things for him as long as he avoided the influence of Bernard Shaw, was sent to him -- by Shaw. (Now in Canada Coward's plays are a mainstay of Shaw's festival. It isn't only what goes around that comes around.)

The 1920s, which coincided handily with Coward's own twenties, established him as a cult figure: icon or iconoclast, depending on where you stood or how old you were. He wrote songs, and then whole scores, for hit revues. He established himself as a master of high comedy with Hay Fever, in which some innocent civilians (i.e. non-theatricals) go through a weekend of hell in the household of a famous actress. The American star Laurette Taylor was supposedly the inspiration for Coward's grande dame but she afterwards protested that the play did her and her family an injustice; they, unlike Coward's feckless individualists, were rude to people on purpose.

The solemn twin to this celebration of stylish bad manners was The Vortex, whose heroine was a married woman with a young lover and whose hero, played by the authyor at his most clenched and high-strung, was her drug-taking son. In those days, and for all of Coward's career, Britain had a theatrical censor, the Lord Chamberlain, and he was shocked. "This picture of a frivolous and degenerate set of people gives a wholly false impression of Society life". In other words, addiction and adultery were all very well, but not in evening dress; it might give the lower orders subversive ideas. The Chamberlain's deputy was more tolerant; he reported that the characters were "frivolous people who . . . attempt wit with rather poor results" (the Chamberlain's men, paid to protect the morals of the nation, seem to have been remarkably free with gratuitous literary criticism) but he also judged that "there are certainly people like Florence Lancaster (the mother) whom it would do good to see how they look to an observer." Since The Vortex borrows rather freely from the mother-son relationship in Hamlet, all this mirror-up-to-nature stuff was rather apposite; and the reporter had a fair sense of what Coward was up to. He may have enjoyed rubbing a smart audience's noses in some selected facts of life, and his young admirers and epigones may have got an even greater thrill out of it, but at heart he was a finger-wagging moralist. The same double message isn't this deliciously decadent and see what it gets you) is musically delivered in his two Jazz Age admonitions, Dance Little Lady and Poor Little Rich Girl, basically the same song written twice; they can easily be sung in counterpoint.

In two slightly later spectacular productions he made his peace with the prudes. The operetta Bitter Sweet showed him as a lush sentimentalist; the pageant-drama unquestioning patriot. In fact his patriotism, though genuine and essential to him, was complex and critical. (He wrote some bitter plays at this time, but he kept them under wraps.) By the time the war broke out, Coward was empowered to speak for England; he was successively employed in the secret serv ice, in entertaining at the front, and in making propaganda films. None of this work brought him official recognition, and he became increasingly estranged from his homeland. Since success first struck, he had always preferred America anyway. His dismissive views on the emerging Welfare State were expressed in There Are Bad Times Just Around the Corner, a song so trenchant in its cheerful misanthropy that it crosses all party lines; when the Tories are in power, it sounds like a protest from the Left. He became a tax-exile, with residences in Switzerland and Jamaica. Though he always maintained a large nostalgic constituency, he became an emblem of the unwanted and the out-of-date. I remember my father complaining about people who were great patriots while the war was on, and great expatriates when it was over.

In 1960 Coward attacked what was then the New Wave in the British theatre. Contemplating the Osborne-Wesker-Pinter generation he seemed appalled, more than anything else, by the squalor of their settings, just as they were offended by the unremitting gentility of his. (Ironic that they should find common ground with the Lord Chamberlain of 40 years before.) Coward had come on the scene when plays, earnest or frivolous, were automatically set in drawing-rooms, and it had hardly occurred to him to rock that particular boat. He had no social or political agenda. His rebellion, such as it was, had been the product of youth, ambition, and an instinct for the limelight.

Also of his homosexuality, on which Hoare is far more forthcoming than any previous biographer. Coward once publicly listed, among his components of the good life, "sexual intercourse in moderation" he did not of course specify the kind of intercourse, and the idea of moderation seems to have been a blind as well, designed to bolster his image as a paragon of cool. (He may have been trying to fool himself as well as others.) He had a long list of lovers, some of whom were also professional associates; these included John C. Wilson, Coward's long-time New York representative until Wilson's drunkenness and financial shadiness put an end to both aspects of the partnership, and Graham Payn, a South African-born actor and singer whom Coward tried vainly to turn into a star, casting him in nearly all his post-war shows. This relationship at least endured, as a live-in friendship; Payn now administers the Coward estate with, according to Hoare, surprising efficiency. There were also briefer flings with more notable actors: with Michael Redgrave and with the brilliant English character player Alan Webb. And he got his heart broken by a succession of shadowy young men; in this respect, "moderation" was hardly in it. Coward, the first to condemn emotional self-indulgence in his colleagues -- he thought it "unprofessional", the most damning word in his vocabulary -- was actually as vulnerable to it as anyone else.

It was, for obvious reasons of self-preservation, a subject he hardly ever wrote about, though of course it's possible to read it into some of his ostensibly heterosexual plays, notably the menage a trois piece Design for Living. There was an early long-suppressed piece called Semi-Monde; and in his last play A Song at Twilight -- produced in 1966, seven years before his death -- he came close to coming out. It was the only time I ever saw him on stage and -- insofar as one can judge a living legend -- I thought him excellent, his clipped hauteur a perfect mask for inner pain. He played a novelist confronted by the cover-up that had been his life.

The ostensible model was Somerset Maugham, but it was obviously Coward's own story as well. His sexuality, illegal for most of his life, had forced him into the role of an outsider: double ironic in one who so desperately wanted in. To most of the world he WAS the Establishment but the Establishment itself knew better, denying him a knighthood until 1970. He also, according to Hoare, had a complex about his origins. He liked to present himself as a boy from nowhere who made spectacularly good; in fact he came from a well-connected family fallen on hard times, and was driven by the desire to regain former status. This puts him in a respectable line of actor-playwrights; Shakespeare seems to have been consumed by the desire to erase the memory of his father's bankruptcy and prove himself a gentleman. His professional sympathies, though, were wider. Coward's portrayals of the working-class range from the icily snobbish to the embarrassingly patronizing. His nadir, I think, is an interminable Cockney number in his last musical The Girl Who Came to Supper, called London Is a Little Bit of All Right: the work of a man who had long lost touch with popular feeling and indeed with London.

Neither Shakespeare nor Moliere wrote much about the theatre. Coward seemed unable to get away from it. Even his non-professional heroes and heroines seem to be actors under the skin; the poor civilians are aliens, to be gazed atm, joked about, and touched with tongs. The same sensibility pervades his songs, whether punctiliously witty or ripely (sometimes overripely) emotional but, being much shorter, they are often easier to take. Unlike the plays, even the best of which languished until the Coward renaissance of the 60s and after, they never went out of fashion. Hoare, who does a masterly job of keeping track of the plays, gets rather overwhelmed by the songs; too many of them slip past him, though I was pleased to find him acknowledging Nine (from Argentina) as "sublime." (It rhymes "besought her too", "taught her too", and "Cole Porter too" it also tells a very funny story.) On the other hand he mis-identifies the song in Private Lives as I'll See You Again when it's actually Someday I'll Find You. Strange how potent cheap music is; it can even fog the minds of biographers.

In one respect Hoare's book is seriously disillusioning. I knew that Coward's was up-and-down, that his critical and political views were increasingly cranky, and that he could be excessively pleased with himself, but I had always understood that his behaviour to frÑiends and strangers was kind and honourable. It now turns out that he could be a petty tyrant to his tight and devoted entourage, sometimes downright cruel; and that his quip "I can take any amount of criticism as long as it's unqualified praise" was all too true. He preferred sycophancy to honest dissent, and his later work suffered because of it. On the other hand he faced life and death with consistent gallantry, his energy and efficiency were prodigious, and the style he worked so hard to perfect was authentic. He rarely wrote a graceless sentence and if his view of the world was narrow it was genuine and, within its limits, penetrating. "A camp classic, a nostalgic turn, or a lasting genius?" asks Hoare. The answers are yes, and yes, and yes.

Robert Cushman is a contributing editor of Saturday Night.

ELLA FITZGERALD

FACTS & ARGUMENTS LIVES LIVED

ELLA FITZGERALD

Friday, June 21, 1996

THIS is meant to be about Ella Fitzgerald's life, not mine, but I cannot escape the feeling that the two are intertwined. Not that I ever impinged on her life -- she had never heard of me -- but she changed mine.

I must have been 18 when I bought Ella Fitzgerald Sings the Cole Porter Songbook, Vol. 1. I was aware, through movies and the radio, of many of the great songs of Broadway and Hollywood. I knew the names of the major composers, and even had some rudimentary idea of who had written what. But it took the Songbook series -- 19 LPs recorded between 1956 and 1965, and continuously available ever since -- to codify the repertoire for me and to change a mild interest into an obsession. I devoted the next few years of my life to collecting the discs (I was in time to catch the last couple as they came out), listening to them, singing along with them, memorizing the music and lyrics. I must have been one of thousands.

When she recorded that first Porter album, Ella was in her 30s and had already been singing 20 years. A Harlem orphan who wanted to dance but got nervous at a talent contest and sang instead, she was rescued from poverty (she was actually sleeping in the streets) by a job with the fine Chick Webb band. She became their biggest attraction, adored for her sweet, husky voice and innate, invincible sense of swing. Most band-singers were hired for their looks; Ella was hardly a sex symbol, but the combination of personal shyness with professional accomplishment proved immensely attractive, and it remained constant throughout her life.

The voice itself was the best-loved of the century. Her range turned out to be the equal of any opera singer's but her actual tone was warm, honeyed and unthreatening. She could sound like a little girl, but one who sang her own lullabies. No matter what she was singing, she made the loveliest noise in popular music: maybe in all of music. She could have rested there. Wonderfully, she didn't. Many of the best popular singers triumph over their vocal limitations. Ella triumphed over her lack of them.

Eventually, her voice did give in to time. An Ella with imperfect pitch was an Ella inconceivable; nevertheless, it happened and the reality of it could be painful. But she was still worth listening to, for the joy she took in music and the further joy she took in communicating that joy. And that is the best answer to those who claim that Ella Fitzgerald was incapable of communicating emotion.

The sunny side of the street

JAZZ: She was the First Lady of Song - but, more than that, she brought happiness to millions. Robert Cushman pays tribute to Ella Fitzgerald, who died last week

Robert CushmanSunday 23 June 1996 00:02 BST

In New York last weekend you could not get into a cab without hearing the voice of Ella Fitzgerald on the radio. Record stores kept her discs playing continuously. It would be an exaggeration to say that the whole city was plunged into mourning, but there was a definite sense of shared loss. It was the same kind of bittersweet reaction that was in-spired by the deaths of Louis Armstrong and Fred Astaire. They were all artists who dealt primarily in joy and their passing makes you personally sad, but when you think of them, even at such a moment, you smile.

The first Ella record that I heard last Saturday was "Organ Grinder's Swing", a piece of 1930s trivia that she had sung as a teenager and revived much later on a date with the Count Basie band. It is not the kind of standard - in either the general or the specialised music-biz sense - that the world most associates with Ella. But she sang it as if it were, with the same infectious note-and-rhythm-perfect enthusiasm that she brought to the Porter or Gershwin songbooks, though with more bravura freedom. Even though she stuck to lyrics and didn't scat it was an obviously "jazzy" performance; and Fitzgerald, even at her most staid, would be inconceivable without jazz. But the secret of her popularity lay outside it. She had, simply, the warmest, loveliest, most appealing voice in all of popular music; in fact, you can probably cross out the word "popular". (She seems, incidentally, to have been most classicists' favourite pop singer.) It was an approachable, unassuming beauty - you could not imagine her, as you could Sarah Vaughan, singing opera - but it stretched across a preternatural vocal range. She might have been born to sing lullabies - her version of "Over the Rainbow" is, though in a wholly different way, as affecting as Judy Garland's - but she could also encompass grand laments. The little girl and the great lady seem always to have co-existed. Her first and biggest hit came with a nursery rhyme ("A-Tisket A-Tasket"). She was 21 then, and had already been dubbed the First Lady of Song.

Fame seems to have been good for her on every level. When she started (to judge from Stuart Nicholson's admirable biography), musicians, though awed by her technical qualities, found her snippy. But insecurities that are forbidding in a newcomer are endearing in a celebrity, and she became generally adored. She had a tough early life, living virtually on the streets for a time; she inevitably faced racial prejudice; as a girl she felt gawky and as a woman overweight; she had two brief marriages and a series of shadowy affairs. But her prime relationship was with her audiences, and unlike some other love affairs between public and performer, it was creative rather than morbid.

Really the most important man in her life was Norman Granz, who from the 1950s on was her manager, her record producer, and possibly her Svengali. Granz, both a jazz-buff and a song-freak, discerned in Ella virtually two distinct vocalists. One was the harmonic virtuoso, who came out of swing and into bop and could improvise with un-bounded inventiveness, and whom he promoted round the globe in an endless and exhilarating series of concerts.

The other Ella - the Ella of the studios - was a ballad-singer who could make any song a pleasant experience, and so might make a great song a great experience. Granz put this hypothesis to the test by assembling generous quantities of the best songs of the best Broadway composers, putting Ella in front of them, and letting the tape roll. The results were the Songbook series: 19 LPs, recorded over nine years, that codified the American repertoire.

Though immensely popular, and never out of the catalogues, the Songbooks have come in for heavy criticism from two sets of purists: jazz (not enough freedom) and theatrical (too much freedom). Both sides impugn the singer's lack of "personal involvement". Actually the absence of heavy drama is often a blessing. On Cole Porter's "Love for Sale", Rodgers and Hart's "Spring is Here", Irving Berlin's "You Can Have Him", Harold Arlen's "The Man That Got Away", the voice is gentle, the manner matter-of-fact, and the effect extremely touching. As generations of radio listeners know, she sums up all of brave young courtship in "Manhattan", all the pain of temporary separation in "Ev'ry Time We Say Goodbye". As a vocal comedienne, she was much under-rated. She could use her high notes for wonderful effects of exasperation, and she could also project a wryly innocent self-mocking wickedness. In songs where every word tells, you can hear and relish all of them.

The Rolls-Royce among the Songbooks was the Gershwin set, 53 songs on five records, with deluxe arrangements by Nelson Riddle. Ella's swing and drive match George Gershwin's own, while Ira's twinkling, bemused lyrics are perfect for her. I imagine I speak for thousands when I say that listening to the Songbooks (not to mention singing along with them) was a major part of my education. In more recent years I may have taken them for granted, but I cannot imagine being without them. One may prefer other versions of individual songs, but Ella's extraordinary oeuvre is always there to fall back on.

Always reliable, never dull, always beloved; that voice and the shy but expansive personality behind it were world possessions. She went on singing, against some heavy physical odds, until within sight of the end, and if anything her work increased in depth. But Ella with faltering pitch was no longer quite Ella; she did pay a price for her earlier perfection. What is wonderful is that she never coasted on that perfection. Many of the best popular singers triumph over their limitations. Ella triumphed over her lack of them.
1996-07-08-theatre-review-a-midsummer-ni:
A MIDSUMMER NIGHT'S DREAM

THEATRE REVIEW

A MIDSUMMER NIGHT'S DREAM

Monday, July 8, 1996

Toronto --

This lively summer Dream suffers from double trouble

Having the same actors play the fairy

royalty as well as the earthly rulers makes for staging

problems in this Shakespearean revival.

Special to The Globe and Mail

ABOUT halfway through A Midsummer Nights Dream in High Park, darkness descends, as its naturally bound to do, and enchantment comes with it. There is a new stillness in the air. Scampering actors, energetically trying to bash their words across while maintaining some kind of line on their characters, suddenly take on weight and definition. Silly, squabbling lovers turn into funny, touching emblems of the folly of youth down the centuries. Types turn into archetypes.

This, of course, is a blessing that descends on all open-air shows. Tom Wood's production, revived and improved from last year, is lively enough to deserve a blessing. It does not come bearing revelations; it is, in fact, rather cheerfully old-fashioned. You almost expect to hear the Mendelssohn music. The costumes worn by the more aristocratic humans actually suggest the old Athens in which the play is notionally set. The fairies stake their claim to supernaturalism by rushing around the parkland in their underwear, pausing occasionally to break into full-throated (and fully amplified) song.

Puck (Barna Moricz) demonstrates that he is a very bad boy by dressing up as shrubbery and jumping out at people. A relentless gymnast, he also has a habit of popping in and out of trap doors, with which this forest comes fully equipped. Less traditionally, he rounds off his first scene by attempting to have sexual relations (consensual or not, I was too far from the stage to tell) with one of Titania's gang. However, his master Oberon puts a quick stop to this and calls him back to the plot.

The king and queen of the fairies are doubled with the earthly rulers Theseus and Hippolyta. This is an idea sanctified, though not actually invented, by Peter Brooks legendary production of 1970, since when it too has become almost traditional. Of course it comes in handy for economy, but it does create problems. The two couples never have to appear simultaneously, but there is a point at which one is supposed to enter on the others departing heels. Brook's actors stayed on stage and simply donned new cloaks: a moment that was magical in itself, and suggested a shared identity for mortals and spirits. Wood's performers rush behind the bushes for a quick change; to cover it, the awakening speech of Bottom the weaver, newly deprived of his asss head, is moved up from its official position at the end of the scene. What should be a marvellously unexpected comic epiphany becomes a passing interlude. The cost to the play is not worth paying.

Nor do we actually get much for it. There is no suggestion here that Theseus/Oberon and Hippolyta/Titania are doubles in any but the logistical sense. (Im not at all sure that they should be, but if you cast them that way you inevitably raise expectations.) There are no premarital tensions at court that need to be smoothed out or sublimated in fairyland. The actors have trouble fleshing out one role apiece, let alone two.

John Ralston, in both his incarnations, is thoroughly competent and thoroughly bland. Alison Sealy-Smith has more temperament though she sounds happier lavishing insults on Oberon than endearments on Bottom. The production at this point, as at others, is trying hard for eroticism (Bottom hopefully pricks up his ass's ears when Titania speaks of having him "to bed and to arise "), but it seems pretty forced, as it very often does in productions of this play.

Most of the actors are half-way toward making the text work for them. They have found the meaning but not the flow. The young lovers' scenes, in particular, work in fits and starts. Clive Cholerton (Lysander) is the most in control; Philippa Domvilles properly self-pitying Helena would be twice as effective with half the gesticulation. Sarah Evanss Hermia is at her best when awakening in the wood, abandoned by her fiancé and clearly terrified.

This is one of the strengths of Wood's production. It does communicate a sense of alarm. Bottom and company arrive for their midnight rehearsal, feeling their way and carrying lanterns: obvious enough, but I've never seen it before. And when they come to perform their interlude of Pyramus and Thisbe, they are real enough characters for their disasters to be doubly hilarious. Snug the joiner (Jeffrey Smith), timid and bashful, terrifies himself into tears when playing the Lion: a remote ancestor, perhaps, of the one Bert Lahr played in The Wizard of Oz . Flute (Steve Ross) moves from indignation at playing a woman into stage-stealing triumph at having a death scene to emote.

And as Bottom, the ever-reliable Brian Tree is the top. He's a thoughtful egomaniac, quietly sure of his own prowess and on easy terms with everyone he meets, regardless of social or spiritual status. He has a crisp, solid Cockney delivery that reminded me of Cheerful Charlie Chester, a British comedian who was a formative influence on my youth and I suspect on his as well. As Pyramus he enters on a hobby-horse and nearly kills himself trying to keep up with the galloping sound-effects provided by his colleagues.

Ideas like these may have originated with actor or director or both, but I mean it in the nicest way when I say that the performer transcends the production and makes each moment his own. Or that you can't see the Wood for the Tree.
1996-07-27-spectator-from-what-complex-w:
From what complex well does Shylock's vitality spring?

Spectator

From what complex well does Shylock's vitality spring?

Saturday, July 27, 1996

A FEW years ago the Stratford Festival revived The Merchant of Venice , and set off a storm of protest. No, thats an exaggeration, but a comedy whose villain is a Jew -- a villain, apparently, because hes a Jew -- is bound to generate a certain amount of contemporary fallout. I wrote an article in this paper saying that the play was anti-Semitic, but only superficially; that its prejudices were less Shakespeare's own than those of his period; and that the character of Shylock was so complex, so compelling, and so attractive to actors that it would override anybody's attitudes.

The play is back at the festival this season, and last Sunday Professor Harold Bloom came to Stratford to lecture on it. Bloom is one of the finest critics alive, a teacher at Yale and Harvard, and author of the majestic book The Western Canon . He is currently writing a book on Shakespeares characters, a magnificently unfashionable enterprise in an academic climate that distrusts character nearly as much as it distrusts Shakespeare. For the rest of us, of course, hes right in the mainstream. Most real people watch plays and read novels in order to meet other real people, who just happen to be fictitious.

Bloom's own favourite Shakespearean character is Falstaff, whom he has re-imagined as a kind of secular saint, and he looks and sounds Falstaffian himself: witty, grandiloquent, silver-haired and, well, weighty. He holds to the good old romantic notion that Shylock is a character who got away from his author (as he phrased it, the wrong Jew in the right play), but he also believes that the play is "profoundly anti-Semitic." He thinks Shylock is a comic villain . . . a hallucinatory bogyman, conjured by an author who may never have met a Jew for an equally unknowing audience. He admits, though, that he is never played that way.

Certainly both the recent and the current Stratford stagings bear him out. The earlier one, by Michael Langham, worked hard and skillfully to present the play as a humane romantic comedy. Troubling moments were cut, most notably Shylock's forced conversion to Christianity as punishment for having plotted the death of the merchant Antonio. This year Marti Maraden has gone to the opposite but equally accommodating extreme, setting the play in immediately pre-Fascist Italy. Compelling and beautifully designed, her production is most notable for the quiet, contained Shylock of Douglas Rain. Looking like a walking photograph of the period, he presents a detailed portrait of a half-accepted moneyman, treading warily on the edges of his society. His patience is impeccable, his vengeance implacable. Cutting off a pound of your opponents flesh in the hope hell bleed to death is not a nice thing to do, any way you, so to speak, slice it. But the mocking, encroaching blackshirts make it clear that this Shylock is a victim of history, in the worst way.

Shylock, as Bloom trenchantly observed, has been the most influential Jewish character in world literature. His lines even sound Jewish: proof, I guess, of Shakespeare's controlling influence on the rhythms of English speech. His immediacy is astonishing; it may even have astonished Shakespeare. Did he realize what he had done when he wrote the tirade that begins "hath not a Jew eyes?" Bloom, ferociously on his guard against sentimentalizing Shylock, professed himself unmoved by this speech. Well, it isn't there to make us cry. But it should make us think, and feel.

Part of Shylocks greatness, as Bloom rightly claims, is the way he celebrates compulsiveness for its own sake. He wont explain why he hates Antonio; he just does. But there are two kinds of Shakespearean villain. There are the solitaries, who acknowledge no human ties: Richard III ("I am myself alone"), Iago, Edmund in King Lear , the bastard Don John in Much Ado About Nothing . Then, far more vulnerable, there are those with affections: Macbeth,the King in Hamlet who murders partly for love, and -- pre-eminently -- Shylock. He has a daughter, whose desertion torments him. He had a wife, whom he mourns. He even suffers a pang when a servant gives notice. Shakespeare piles it on. Why?

Bloom has an all-encompassing theory of literary creation. He calls it the Anxiety of Influence. Roughly, a writer reacts against some great predecessor. (This might not account for Homer who can have had few influences to be anxious about.) So Shylock was Shakespeare's attempt to outdo and exorcise Barabas, the gleefully unscrupulous hero-villain of Christopher Marlowe's The Jew of Malta . He must have been played, as Barabas assuredly was, as a red-wigged, hook-nosed caricature.

Unfortunately for this theory, Shylocks extremely vocal opponents in the play make no disparaging references to his personal appearance. They do seem to regard him as a human being, however unlikable. Even the forced conversion might be seen as a benevolent attempt to save his soul. It hurts to say this, but in the play the conversion is not presented as any big deal. It is not the climax of Shylocks punishments, and he himself says nothing about it. (The most disturbing Shylock I have seen, though not the best, was Patrick Stewart; he went smilingly down on his knees at this point, and cringed.) We of course can hardly pass over it so easily. It is Portia with her legal tricks who has brought Shylock to this pass (and after all that stuff about the quality of mercy). At Stratford, Susan Coyne's rather opaque Portia goes in at this point for some silent oh-God-what-I-have-done? acting. At least, I think that's what shes getting at.

Fiend or martyr, Shylock by this point has gone way beyond Marlowes Barabas in sheer humanity. Bloom would have it that Shakespeare's "pride in getting Marlowe out of his system increased his investment in Shylock." He can hardly have been unaware of Marlowe's Jew in creating his own, but I cant see that this kind of literary Oedipus complex accounts for the characters vitality. I can't wait to read Bloom's book, but Ill stick to the hoariest but most convincing explanation of Shakespeares greatness: his ability -- rather, his compulsion -- to think and feel himself into another person's skin. If that person is a Jew, then the play in which he has a key role is not going to be "profoundly anti-Semitic." And Stratford can go on programming The Merchant of Venice without making too many excuses.

Robert Cushman recently won the Nathan Cohen award for outstanding drama criticism in Canada.
1996-08-10-theatre-review-a-doll-s-house:
A DOLL'S HOUSE

THEATRE REVIEW

A DOLL'S HOUSE

Saturday, August 10, 1996

By Henrik Ibsen

Wolfville, N.S. -- Directed by Helen Burns

and Michael Langham

Starring Megan Follows and Jerry Etienne

At the Atlantic Theatre Festival

Wolfville, N.S.

Rating: 

Doll's House flawed but compelling

Special to The Globe and Mail

WHEN he wrote A Doll's House ,Ibsen created the most most potent metaphor and the most celebrated sound-effect in modern drama. The metaphor -- the one in the title -- stands for the life that Torvald Helmer, lawyer turned bank president, built for his wife Nora. He pets her, spoils her, tosses her spending-money, and implicitly denies her any moral or intellectual life of her own. The play shows Nora moving, in the course of a day and a night, from acquiescing in this existence to walking out on it. When she goes, she slams the door behind her -- a noise that invariably echoes round the theatre as, ever since the play's premiere in 1879, it has echoed round the world.

The Helmers have two small children, and the Atlantic Festival breaks new ground by giving them an actual doll's house to play with. It stands in spotlit isolation as the play begins. Then the other lights go up to reveal Nora reading her daughter a happy-ever-after fairy story whose words the little girl rapturously echoes as she leaves the stage in the custody of her nursemaid. This prologue is the production's own invention; as is its staging of the married couple's last confrontation. This is moved from the comparatively neutral territory of the drawing-room to the charged atmosphere of the bedroom. Sex is the last hold -- as it must have been the first -- that they have over one another. It's never explicitly mentioned, which may have been Ibsen's concession to his 19th-century audience. But as it plays now, Nora's refusal even to acknowledge a physical relationship is what finally crushes her husband.

At both ends of the play, this production by Helen Burns and Michael Langham both explores and enriches the text. It plays with prosaic immediacy, and also with poetic power: exactly the kind of double resonance that Ibsen's plays should possess. What goes between is more problematic; disappointingly so considering the depths and delights that the same team uncovered last year to Chekhov's The Cherry Orchard .

By historical accident, and in defiance of the author's stated intentions, A Doll's House ranks as the most powerful of feminist tracts. But it wouldn't have that power if its heroine's situation weren't so complex. Nora is deeply implicated in her own subjection; which is what makes her breakout so impressive. She plays along with Helmer's patronizing -- with his pampering and his baby-talk -- but she is secretly resourceful beyond his wildest nightmares. Years before the play begins, she has saved his overworked life by raising the money for a long holiday. She did this by borrowing, on forged security. Now her creditor, whose own shady past is catching up with him, returns to blackmail her; and Nora is horrified to discover that feminine charm and good intentions may not be enough to sway the courts. Consciously or not, she has lived her life by manipulating men; she carries on a shamelessly flirtatious, if largely unacknowledged, relationship with a family friend, a doctor who happens to be desperately ill. Trading on his adoration is her last chance to maintain the status quo; her transformation begins when she lets it go by. So the suppressed eroticism in the last scene is as logical as it's effective.

At any given moment Megan Follows as Nora commands the stage. She is charmingly capricious, with the tunnel vision of undeviating self-absorption, in the first three-quarters of the play, and after her thunderclap conversion she rebuilds herself with an inquisitive honesty, taking nothing on trust. (Nora's strength is not so much that she sees through her husband as that she has seen through herself.) What is missing is the progression from one stage to the other. There is not much desperation; when she dances what the other characters describe as a wild tarantella, it actually seems rather tame and tentative. Nor, except when absolutely unavoidable, are there many moments of self-doubt. She acts, most of the time, at dialogue surface.

So, and more crudely, do most of her colleagues. Helmer is a prig, a scold, a moral coward complacent in his own self-righteousness; and that is what Jerry Etienne plays. But it's all he plays; and if there is no passion in Torvald -- if he does not at least believe in his own values and his own love -- the play loses much of its emotional power. The money-lending Krogstad could be a subtle compound of bitter pride and calculating self-abasement; Julian Richings plays him as Uriah Heep, with a Cockney whine that would be a cliché in a British production and is mystifyingly irrelevant here. It's hard to tell what Nora's friend Mrs. Linde (rendered by Shelley Thompson with more noise than feeling) could possibly see in him.

Only Peter Donat, as the doomed Doctor Rank, has the subtlety and authority to pass by the high standards that Wolfville, in only its second season, has already set itself. The town, the festival, the theatre are enchanting; the stage (fetchingly decked out for this show by Neil Peter Jampolis in differing shades of green) is a miniature Stratford, even more sharply focused than its progenitor. Plays leap out from it, and this comparatively early Ibsen remains ruthlessly compelling. Shuffle the relationships a bit, rob Nora of her courage and make her suicidal, and you have Hedda Gabler . That's a much later Ibsen play, and the textbooks call it greater. But they're wrong.

Tripping through Anne country

Spectator

Tripping through Anne country

Friday, August 30, 1996

A WEEK or so ago, I was in Charlottetown, where the summers cultural attractions include a dinner-theatre show wholly devoted to spoofing Anne of Green Gables . It's called Annekenstein but, despite that, I wish I'd seen it. (Its dates and mine didnt match.) Certainly, its publicity hits the right note. "Know the book?" it asks. Seen the musical? Read the license-plate? That catches the mood of the place exactly: not just the town but the whole province. If Prince Edward Island is most famous for two things -- Lucy Maud Montgomery and the potato -- there can be no doubt that, in the battle for the spotlight and the tourist dollar, no one is putting money on the spud.

A gift shop on the island advertises itself as "celebrating the life and times of Anne of Green Gables." There cant be many fictional characters with lives and times. Usually these are reserved for their authors. The various Stratfords are devoted to Shakespeare, not to Hamlet. If you visit the village of Haworth in Yorkshire, you may take in a Brontë museum and nibble Brontë cakes, but even if you go for a walk on the Brontë moors you are unlikely to bump into Jane Eyre or Heathcliff. (Just as well in the case of the latter.) Anne is different. Anne manifests herself.

Like Santa Claus, she can subdivide. You may glimpse her on the streets of Charlottetown, decked out in the approved uniform -- green smock, white apron, Red Riding Hood basket, pigtails and a barrelful of freckles -- pointing out the sights to visitors and handing out leaflets for the local restaurants. But at the very same moment she may be in Cavendish, strolling with her friend Diana and delivering carefully scheduled impromptu performances, derived from the book and making generous use of the children in the audience. In defiance of the authorized pecking-order, it was Diana who emerged as the leader. She was the one with the merrier laugh. She was the one you could hear.

Cavendish is the heart, or the main cash terminal, of Anne country; here fact and fiction mate. You can stay at the Anne Shirley Motel and gaze across the street to the graveyard where Lucy Maud Montgomery lies buried, a circumstance emphatically announced on the cemetery gate. She actually died, as she had for many years lived, in Ontario; but she did grow up in Cavendish, which was the acknowledged model for Avonlea. Piety may have dictated the choice of resting-place, but commerce has certainly made the most of it. There are the Lucy-lived-here sites, there are the Anne-would-have-lived-here-if-she'd-existed sites, there are the beaches (once celebrated by Montgomery herself and as gloriously silky now as then), and there are the strip malls and theme parks.

There is also, and this I was in time for, the Lucy Maud Montgomery Festival, which included culinary events based on famous incidents from the books. There was an Old-Fashioned Ice Cream Social: not as old-fashioned as all that, since the ice cream was the island's dominant commercial brand selling more expensively than at the convenience store down the road. More agreeably, there were Old-Fashioned Games With Raspberry Cordial, which tasted delicious. Anne and Diana dropped by both events, though they didnt seem to eat or drink much. (Perhaps they were being careful. In the book, Diana gets famously drunk on cordial: a scene, if I may anticipate, thats particularly badly done in the musical.) Best of all, there was a barn dance, with a country string band that rocked the car park. The Avonlea connection seemed minimal, but the strain of Maritime culture that was being tapped into was arguably richer.

Was Montgomery a good enough writer to sustain a whole provincial economy? Probably not, if you're talking poetic rather than commercial justice. On the other hand, her tartness and narrative zest make her too good to deserve all the things that are done in her name. (And whatever Calvin Trillin may have said in The New Yorker, it isn't all being kept going just for the Japanese.) The Charlottetown Festival has of course survived on Anne of Green Gables -- The Musical for the 32 years of its existence. This year, notoriously, the main festival stage has been reduced to doing Anne and nothing else. The current production is enjoyable if coarse-grained. Its idea of comedy is shrieking caricature, and the heroines chums are a wearisomely energetic bunch of ballet-school dropouts. On the other hand its well sung, especially by Giulio Kukurugya as the painfully shy old Matthew. It's nice to have him sing that which he cannot say; it's desperately wrong to put him through cute little dance routines, just because hes in a musical. The show is at its worst when it clings to a 30-year-old idea of imitation Broadway, as in the obligatory anonymous love ballad. Its at its best when it remains its own native animal: as when Tracy Michailidis, a piercingly effective Anne, makes her enforced apology to the pompous Mrs. Lynde, rhyming her name with excruciating earnestness at the end of every overwrought line.

Which reminds me. There are an awful lot of words that rhyme with nation: for youthful patriotic euphoria you have generation, information, dedication and celebration. As a prophet of doom, you intone words like inflation, humiliation, damnation and colonization. I quote, all too literally, from Spirit of a Nation , which is being offered lunchtimes, free, by the Festival's Young Company. In a show that looks and sounds like a slightly dramatized aerobics class, they tell us what a great country this. They extend a compassionate welcome to the persecuted people of other lands. They demonstrate their multicultural diversity by doing folk dances. (This bit isn't bad.) And they warn us of the dangers of global warming, national disunity, credit-card overspending, and all-out nuclear war. For a happy ending they tell us, throbbingly, that they "want to be Canadian" though we thought they already were.

National pride can take some nasty knocks in Charlottetown. Outside the provincial parliament building, people dress up in frock coats and re-enact the deliberations of the Fathers of Confederation: an earlier and more consequential case of wanting to be Canadian. An initially respectful audience drifts inexorably away.

Ironic, and more than sad, because if ever a place were naturally calculated to be a source of pride, its Prince Edward Island, especially with the sterner scenic glories of Nova Scotia just across the water. It deserves better than its giving. And it's not all base tourism. If cooking's an art, then its being practiced with great invention, country-house richness, and impeccably local ingredients at the Inn at Bay Fortune, at the eastern end of the island. Here -- its probably true of the western end as well -- you can feel the imposed local mythology gradually slipping away. As you drive you see fewer and fewer Marilla's Antique Stores, Matthew's Ice Creameries, or Green Gables Anythings. I suspect that Lucy Maud would like it that way.
