ARTS: PLAYING PINTER

A new Harold Pinter play opens in London this week. And nearly 40 years after his breakthrough, that's still an event

Robert Cushman Sunday 15 September 1996 00:02 BST

A bunch of us had been to see Harold Pinter's play The Collection, done by the Royal Shakespeare Company at the Aldwych Theatre. As we descended the Holborn escalator a friend asked me, with memorable formality: "And what did you think of it? Both as a play and as a Pinter epic?"

The Collection was actually a 60-minute piece with four characters: numbers which must be around the mean average for Pinter plays over the years. But we used the word "epic" pretty promiscuously in those days. Those days. It was 1962, and Pinter was already a cultural fact: had been for two years. Thirty-four years on, he still is. Among playwrights, you have to go back to Shaw to find anything comparable. On the way you might pause, briefly, at Noel Coward, whose prowess as an all-round theatrical animal was even greater than Pinter's but who never had the same intellectual clout.

David Leveaux, who was in his cradle when The Collection opened, has in the last few years directed three acclaimed Pinter productions: revivals of Betrayal and No Man's Land, the latter with Pinter himself in the cast, and the premiere of Moonlight, which was his first play of substantial length in 14 years. Leveaux calls Pinter "the key living dramatist; he has converted the English language into a way of expressing English history. He makes us hear English: vulgar, austere, direct, beautiful."

In the late Sixties the American screenwriter William Goldman said the same thing rather more racily. He described Pinter as "an English stylist, talented as hell", an accolade with a sting of dismissal in its tail. He went on to account for Pinter's fashionable prestige by calling him "appropriately obscure ... he allows intellectuals to theorise".

Goldman was writing in the wake of The Birthday Party, Pinter's first full-length play, which had opened on Broadway 10 years after its legendarily disastrous 1958 premiere in London. Over the course of that decade derision had given place to respectful bafflement. These days we deride the derision, and claim to find the bafflement baffling. We claim, simultaneously, that the play isn't obscure and that its obscurities are part of its power.

Well, let's see. The Birthday Party depicts the abduction from a seaside boarding-house of a fearful, reclusive young man by a pair of thugs, one an Irishman, the other a Jew. Only we are never actually told who has sent Goldberg and McCann, or why; or what their victim Stanley is hiding from. Pinter leaves holes that most playwrights - playwrights not necessarily committed to a glib belief in the transparency of human motivation - would fill in: holes of plot, not character. It's no wonder that audiences, to this day, feel thwarted; though they've learned to believe that it's good for them. If we knew more, goes the argument, we would be less scared; as it is, for Stanley's nameless fears we can substitute our own. (The standard interpretation - that the intruders represent the forces of society come to impound a hapless nonconformist - has never seemed very exciting.)

The play has always tantalised, precisely because it works so well at ground level: as a macabre thriller (it has more overt action than all Pinter's subsequent plays put together), as a set-piece study of interrogation, and as expertly timed black comedy. It amounted to a wonderful theatrical calling-card, an exhilarating display of skills. And even the initial failure - one week's run at the Lyric Hammersmith and terrible notices - served to highlight the later success. It is hard to think of another playwright who has gone so quickly and so decisively from outright rejection to bank-breaking esteem.

Pinter was 27 when The Birthday Party opened, an actor who had already written a one-act play and much (unpublished) poetry. The son of a tailor he had grown up in the East End of London, suffered the traumas of evacuation during the Blitz and been a star student at Hackney grammar school. As a Jew he had also encountered the lingering spirit of street-level fascism; the verbal encounters of himself and his friends with local gangs are widely held to have fostered his later genius for barbed crosstalk. His acting career - touring Shakespeare and lots of rep - was unglamorous but helped nourish an unerring instinct for what sounds well and works well on a stage.

I don't believe in decades but it's hard here not to make an exception. If The Birthday Party was ahead of its time, it was only so by two years. The Pinter legend took flight in 1960 with his next major play, The Caretaker. The Fifties had belonged to John Osborne and the earnest realists of the Royal Court. Pinter's plays, despite their run-down settings, had a Sixties gloss and confidence. They also had an early-Sixties comic swagger. People talk of his debt to Kafka and Samuel Beckett, but if I had to choose his affinities I would go for the finest of British sitcom writers, Alan Simpson and Ray Galton. The world of their Cockney rag-and-bone men, Steptoe and Son, was the world that Pinter mined, explored and expanded in The Caretaker, The Dumb Waiter and The Homecoming. His view is far darker than theirs but the language - London slang that became the patois of a generation - is the same. Before Steptoe, Galton and Simpson had written for - had largely created - the great Tony Hancock, whose seedy, inconsequential grandiloquence was remarkably Pinteresque - or would have been if it hadn't got there first.

"The best modern British playwrights," says David Leveaux, with excellent reason, "have all been comic, and Harold is very good with the gags." It was fitting that his breakthrough, even before The Caretaker, should have come with a TV production of The Birthday Party that devastatingly combined horror and humour. They were most smoothly blended by Lee Montague's Goldberg, which must have been the most influential Pinter performance ever; God knows why it never gets into the history books or why he never repeated it on stage. (His "well over the fast", a Jewish greeting inserted into the proceedings with sublime unexpectedness, had my parents rolling and me with them.) The viewing consensus was that it was absolutely mystifying, and you couldn't take your eyes off it. When The Caretaker came along, Pinter had a constituency.

The Caretaker had a cultural impact unequalled by any subsequent British play - it was incontestably the show you had to see. It also offered what may be the last great (as opposed to big or showy) role created by an English dramatist. Davies the venomously pitiable tramp, originally played by Donald Pleasence, is a magnificent verbal and psychological construct. The Collection, which followed, is a neglected piece but crucial. The tension in Pinter's earlier plays had largely derived from men needling one another. Here there is a woman to fight over and fight with. It is a play about love and cruelty, and it suggests that the first automatically gives scope to the second; this has been one of Pinter's constant themes. It is the first play in which the characters are obviously keeping secrets from one another rather than from the audience. It is the first play with a middle-class setting, perhaps reflecting its author's new success. As a Pinter epic - belatedly answering my friend's question - I rate it very high.

It was also the first of Pinter's plays to be directed by Peter Hall, who was to become his regular interpreter - first at the RSC, then at the National Theatre. The partnership took in The Homecoming, the one- act plays Landscape and Silence, the matched triangles Old Times and

Betrayal (the first generally lauded, the second panned, though history might reverse that verdict), No Man's Land with the glorious high-comic partnership of John Gielgud and Ralph Richardson, and as a pendent A Kind of Alaska, a lyrical-clinical study of sleeping sickness, based on Oliver Sacks and featuring an extraordinary performance by Judi Dench, one that found a natural rhythm for unearthly experience.

These were all high-style, high-definition, high-precision productions, treating language and movement with scrupulous care. They were also high-cultural - theatre as chamber-music - and as the 1970s wore on, that ideal began to seem remote. And even at the beginning - with The Homecoming, the flagship production of the series - there was a sense of heavy significance, a return to mystification. I remember the woman in the piece, played by Vivien Merchant, sending her departing husband on his way with the line "don't become a stranger". It sounded so oracular; the words seemed to relate to some symbolic structure previously unnoticed. But all she probably meant was "keep in touch".

And then, for a long time, there was silence. Actually, it wasn't silence. Pinter continued his career as one of the most proficient and productive of screenwriters. He directed plays, notably those of his friends Simon Gray and Ronald Harwood. And he wrote a series of playlets on, for the first time, obviously public themes: brief fables of tyranny and torture. Strangely, all this peripheral activity was taken to be greater evidence of decline than if he had shut up altogether.

In a thorough and revealing new book, The Life and Times of Harold Pinter (Faber & Faber, pounds 20, out 4 Nov), Michael Billington claims that there has been no great change, that Pinter has always been a political playwright. He has always written about power and intimidation. It depends what you mean by "political". I would prefer to say that the skills he used and sharpened on his domestic plays were lying ready to be re-applied. In the scarifying 10-minute piece The New World Order (1991), Goldberg and McCann ride again, exchanging sinister pleasantries before getting to work on a bound-and-gagged new victim. This time they do let us in on their motivation: it's to make the world safe for democracy. Maybe Pinter can write this kind of cross-talk in his sleep but it's still good, and it's still right for the subject. ("Pinteresque" has entered the language like "Kafkaesque" and "Orwellian". Strange how all three relate to terror.) That Pinter came out politically late in life - because he was outraged by specific inhumanities - is to his credit. I trust him more than I would a writer who chose a cause in youth as he might choose a football team and went on supporting it just as automatically.

His briefest pieces reaffirm the central fact: nobody else puts words on a stage so fastidiously, so powerfully, so well. It's a quality that survives in translation. Richard Eyre, director of the National Theatre, testifies that the best production he has seen of The Birthday Party was in Czechoslovakia in 1969; it was "absolutely terrifying". Eyre, who has a revival of The Homecoming scheduled, calls Pinter simply "the best: his plays still have a resonance after 30 years and will have in another 30". And it occurs to me that they are the first plays since Shaw's to have proved indefinitely reviveable in their author's lifetime.

He's our most talented playwright, whether or not he writes our best plays. And though there is this thing in the public consciousness - this cryptic, aloof, uncommunicative thing called "Pinter" - it seems to have little to do with the man himself or the way he works. Those who know him describe him as "loyal", "funny" and "resolutely generous". One also hears that his "Churchillian" voice reverts to East End Jewish when he gets drunk, that he's "very proud of every award he's ever won", that "he can be quite thuggish", especially when dressing-room visitors are insufficiently effusive. In rehearsal, says Leveaux, his chief concern "is to remove from the audience any fear that they're watching something cerebral. He's consumed by what works in the present tense. Good actors are."

And Pinter, we have been learning, is a very good actor. Sharp, fleeting appearances in films have gleamed with the same piercing wit as his best writing. Gawn Grainger, who played with him in No Man's Land, is emphatic that "Harold could have made a living as an actor if he'd never written a word". He also, like everybody who has worked with Pinter, emphasises the scrupulous manner in which he distinguishes between his various hats: actor, director, dramatist. Staging one of his own plays Pinter famously announced to the cast "of course, we can't be sure of what the author intended here". He has directed some of his own short plays, and revivals of the longer ones, but his new piece, Ashes to Ashes, will be the first major, brand-new Pinter to be staged by its author.

In No Man's Land Pinter played Ralph Richardson's old role of Hirst, the lordly alcoholic author: "a great writer," says Grainger, "playing a great writer. There was something lyrical about Richardson. Harold was much more brutal." He has indeed specialised in the more aggressive roles in his own plays; in earlier years he appeared as Goldberg, as Mick the tearaway brother in The Caretaker, and as Lenny the pimp in The Homecoming. Last year his revived acting career reached its peak when he played the lead in a revival of The Hothouse, an early play that he suppressed after the failure of The Birthday Party, to which it is a kind of sequel. It takes place in a sadistically run mental hospital, the kind of establishment to which Stanley's captors might well have been dragging him. Pinter played the man in charge.

It's a surprisingly explicit play, with no nonsense about it, hard and fast and funny, and Pinter's performance matched it exactly. "Brutal" was again the word that came to mind: brutal and pitiful. He stormed, and drank, and grew increasingly bemused and bewildered, and came back to bully again. He was hilarious, frightening, uncompromising - in total command of himself and his audience. It exposed a cruel and violent character with great relish but without ever denying his humanity. It was an object lesson in how to play Pinter.

! 'Ashes to Ashes' opens at the Royal Court Theatre Upstairs at West St, WC2 (0171 730 1745) on Thurs.

You would have to be made of stone not to be moved by at least one of the books in Lit Hum,' said one of critic David Denby's youthful classmates. GREAT BOOKS: My Adventures with Homer, Rousseau, Woolf and Other Indestructible Writers of the Western World

Canon to the left, canon to the right

You would have to be made of stone not to be moved by at least one of the books in Lit Hum, said one of critic David Denby's youthful classmates. GREAT BOOKS: My Adventures with Homer, Rousseau, Woolf and Other Indestructible Writers of the Western World

Saturday, October 12, 1996

By David Denby

Simon & Schuster, 492 pages, $40

DAVID Denby is the film critic for New York magazine. His stuff there comes off as mimicry of the great Pauline Kael, of The New Yorker fame. However, when Denby himself writes in The New Yorker, as a general cultural commentator, he is his own man: an easy stylist with a concerned and generous temperament serviced by a quizzical, burrowing intelligence. These qualities come to brilliant flower in his new book, the story of a middle-aged quest.

Around 1990, Denby grew dissatisfied with his milieu: not bored, exactly, but hemmed in. "A member of the media, he says, I was also tired of the media . . . like many others, I was jaded yet still hungry." His hunger took him back to college, to the same university, Columbia, at which he had been an undergraduate 30 years earlier. In 1991 he re-enrolled in two "core curriculum courses that had been mandatory for all Columbia students in his day and still are. One was Literature Humanities (or Lit Hum), a survey of imaginative literature from Homer to, this time around, Virginia Woolf.

The other was Contemporary Civilization (or C.C.), encompassing major works of political philosophy, Plato to Simone de Beauvoir. They are familiarly known as Great Books courses. Denby wanted to see what the books could do for him now, and also to observe what they could do for the freshman students with whom he read and discussed them.

He tells three interwoven stories. One concerns his own encounters with the texts: the pleasure they gave or failed to give him, the reflections and the memories they stirred. King Lear -- this may sound crass but isn't -- reminds him of his own powerful mother and the guilt and confusion he felt during her last years. Hobbes on human greed and aggression and Hegel on the confrontation of opposites call up the morning he was mugged in Times Square. He retreats defeated before Dante and Goethe, revels in the cheerful sexuality of Boccaccio and the bracing political realism of Machiavelli, and is swept away by the greatness of Virginia Woolf, an author he had once thought dismissible. (With most of these experiences, I empathize.)

Foolhardily, he takes an exam (being examined is one of the things you become an adult to avoid") and has a violent reaction. ("Gee, I said to myself, after all these years its nice to find out what a nervous breakdown is.) He tries to teach a class himself and discovers, in a lovely comic build-up, how hard it is to make end-of-the-century American adolescents share his passion for Jane Austen.

These students are the books second story. Sometimes they remind Denby of his own youth, other times they seem like an alien species. Grappling with, or buffeted by, these demanding, unfamiliar texts, they move him -- and the reader -- to affection, exasperation and, ultimately, pride.

There are of course people who doubt the wisdom of putting them through it at all. Lit Hum and C.C. are embattled courses, the idea of great books" under constant fire. This, the book's third theme, is also its sexiest, and although Denby calls the chapters he devotes to it "interludes, they are obviously central. Harold Bloom, having expressed in The Western Canon his contemptuous indifference to the School of Resentment (his name for the anti-canonical critics), proceeded to yap at their heels on almost every page. Denby, who seems preternaturally decent and fair-minded, takes them steadily on.

Is the choice of texts arbitrary? Yes, but so is every syllabus; it has to be. Is too much being asked of students who have been under-educated in high school and don't know the contexts? Perhaps, but when the books were first written, people just read them. The notion of context is . . . academic."

This is a bit disingenuous (the original readers were the context), but essentially true; if the term "great book means anything, it means a work that continues to have an impact irrespective of specialized knowledge. Anybody who has taught will have seen this happening and been moved by it. As Denby says, the opposing logic seems to be, [The students] havent been educated properly; therefore lets not educate them properly."

As for the prescribed authors (Dead White European Males, plus a few propitiatory females) being "unrepresentative, the students don't seem to mind. A black undergraduate says, You would have to be made of stone not to be moved by at least one of the books in Lit Hum." Nor do the books make up a solid wall of repressive thinking; they constantly contradict one another. Many of them are still subversive. As Denby discovers, Marxism may be dead but Marx ("stern, logical, inexorable, implacably moral) lives. And even if you consider European civilization the enemy, getting to know it seems only common sense.

Denby's touchstone, carried over from his day job, is pleasure," the more complex the better. His bitterest quarrel with the "academic left is that they deny pleasure. I dont quite agree; in my experience, theyre eager to proclaim their enjoyment of movies and rock music, supposedly democratic forms that are actually the most commercialized on Earth. But when it comes to the art on which they make their living, Denby is right: They do not love literature." You can tell from the way they write about it. They read books, if at all, with distaste, to dredge up further evidence for opinions they already hold.

Denby is equally repelled by the conservatives' appropriation of famous authors as "bulwarks of democracy. Could such classic works actually be as boring as the right -- or as wicked as the left -- was making them sound?" He set himself to find out, and he makes his discoveries joyously real. In defending the humanities, he asserts his own humanity. This is a magnificent book.

When he reviewed The Western Canon, Toronto critic Robert Cushman was trying to catch up on his reading. He still is.

Related Reading:

Mimesis: The Representation of Reality in Western Literature (1953),by Eric Auerback.

The Western Canon: The Books and the School of the Ages (1986),by Harold Bloom.

Plus anything on the Lit Hum and C.C. reading lists, and a very great deal that isn't.

A CHORUS LINE

THEATRE REVIEW

A CHORUS LINE

Thursday, October 31, 1996

Directed by Baayork Lee

Written by James Kirkwood and Nicholas Dante

Lyrics by Edward Kleban

Music by Marvin Hamlisch

Rating: 

Chorus Line gets another kick at the cancan

The Broadway musical still has an impact,

21 years after its first opening night.

Special to the Globe and Mail

THE only song in A Chorus Line that I dislike is its solitary big ballad, What I Did for Love ,sung by most of the company. The title ostensibly refers to the characters' shared vocation as Broadway dancers, but there are no specific references to any of the glories or humiliations of the trade. The lyrics have been kept remorselessly anonymous so that they can be sung out of context as a heavy romantic number, a defiant lament, which it was during its rather brief career as a pop standard.

The song would be annoying enough in any musical, but in one that makes a fetish of its own integrity, and for the most part justifies the claim, it is infuriating. The number is, in the strict sense of the word, egregious; it stands out in the wrong way. And yet, out of the lyrical fog and the musical soup, there emerges the show's most chilling moment.

A Chorus Line is,after all, the definitive musical on the subjects of insecurity and unemployment. We meet the characters at an audition, 17 of them trying out for a show that has chorus roles for eight. They are both colleagues and competitors. The song has brought them together in shared affirmation. When it is over each freezes: lonely, frightened, awaiting the director's godlike decision on their individual fates.

A Chorus Line still has tremendous impact. It returns 21 years after its off-Broadway opening and six years after its Broadway closing. In 1983, an extraordinary gala performance marked the show's arrival as longest-running Broadway musical ever, a position since usurped by Cats .

The new edition of the spoof revue Forbidden Broadway commemorates this event showing a furry and disgruntled group of Chorus Liners reduced to auditioning for the Andrew Lloyd Webber show ("step, kick, meow, purr. . .") and intoning "Oh, God I hate this show. . ."

Broadway chauvinism apart, their chagrin is understandable. A Chorus Line should have run forever, if only as a talisman. It is not the greatest of all musicals, but it may be the essential musical. It celebrates its own craft and enshrines its own people. The original production -- directed, choreographed, and masterminded by Michael Bennett -- was showmanship raised to its highest power, every moment perfectly keyed, each passing pleasure part of an overarching design.

Bennett is dead -- as are all the show's begetters, with the exception of composer Marvin Hamlisch -- and the revival is directed by Baayork Lee. She knows the piece intimately (she created the part of Connie Wong) and, as far as I can tell, she has reproduced Bennett's steps and his mise en scène with minute fidelity. Robin Wagner's sets and Theoni V. Aldredge's costumes look the same, starkly emphasizing the leotards and mirrors of the rehearsal room before exploding into the shimmering golden glitz of the finale. The number itself, One , is still exciting. Edward Kleban wrote most ingenious lyrics: A star celebration, in the Mame vein, that also works as a triumphant metaphor for the chorus itself, the treasured individuals merged into "one singular sensation". Hamlisch's music, with its wrenching key-changes abetted by a killer orchestration, pushes up the temperature to fever-point. But it's not as exhilarating as it was in the original musical. There's a telltale pause before it gets underway, so it seems less like a culmination and more like a run-of-the-mill encore. And that is symptomatic of the production as a whole. Occasionally it sags; the line is not drawn quite tight enough. And -- something I don't remember in any of the Bennett companies I saw -- there is distinct unevenness in the cast.

There are three stand-outs. Cindy Marchionda takes over the stage as the Puerto Rican who tells about the crass acting teacher who railed at her when she couldn't imitate an ice-cream; her song Nothing is the best in the score, and the best-sung. Luis Villabon is touching as the former drag-artist whose confessional speech still seems a bridgehead for the treatment of homosexuality in a mainstream musical. Jill Slyter, arresting in a red dress, has the required almost-star presence for Cassie, trying desperately to get back in the chorus after failing as a solo act. She dances out her frustration in The Music and the Mirror , a frustrating experience for the audience, too, since the routine never takes off -- I have never been sure whether this is intentional. The character may not be able to act but the actress can. It's her former partner, the director Zach (Mark Martino), who comes off woodenly. Their relationship is the show's trickiest area. We are told less about it than we need to know, so we'd rather not know anything. Zach meanwhile interrogates those auditioning so that we can discover what we need to know about them, but he doesn't have to do it as aggressively and unsympathetically as he does here.

They tell their stories in tearful or funny monologues (the line about suicide in Buffalo being redundant still gets the biggest laugh from a Toronto audience), alternated with sizzling group dances. And there are practice numbers that have almost documentary authority; you believe that an audition is really like this. Probably these are the best scenes in the show. But its greatest appeal, as the focus shifts from group to individual and back again, is the sense that the performers have wholly identified with the show and are offering it to the audience. That is true of all the best theatre, but here they are making us a gift of their own lives, and their art is such that we can accept it without embarrassment.

At the O'Keefe Centre until Nov. 3.

William Hutt gives performance fit for a king

Spectator

William Hutt gives performance fit for a king

Tuesday, November 12, 1996

IT was Saturday, Nov. 2, the second last night of this year's Stratford Festival and the final performance of King Lear ,with William Hutt in the leading role. It was Hutt's fourth Lear, and presumably his last, though of course you never know. Anyway, it was a momentous confrontation, on two levels. Canada's pre-eminent Shakespearean actor says a putative farewell to the greatest of tragic roles, and a 76-year-old performer stars in the most harrowing play ever written about old age.

During the interval I asked director Richard Monette if Hutt's performance that night differed at all from those earlier in the run. "He's never done heart attacks before," Monette replied.

The immaculately rendered incipient seizures with which Hutt punctuated his performance made it seem as if Lear's rages were pushing him physically as well as mentally over the edge. I would have assumed they were integral parts of the characterization, carefully plotted by actor and director throughout rehearsals. But it seems they were brilliant improvisation, though they fitted perfectly into the rhythm of the performance. This is the kind of inventive thing good actors do, though it takes special nerve and special inspiration to bring it off on this scale.

Lear is 80, one of the few Shakespearean characters whose age is known, so Hutt is a few years too young for the part. In another sense, he's remarkably old for it. Laurence Olivier played Lear on television when he was in his 70s, and John Gielgud celebrated his 90th birthday by doing it on the radio, but most stage Lears are actors in their 40s. The reasons are obvious. The part takes stamina. Lear, whether asserting his authority or suffering from the loss of it, is in a constant state of anger or insanity or both. Any credible Lear has to be capable of sustained shouting.

So, here was Lear being played by a genuinely old actor. I thought I knew what to expect. There would be a forgivable lack of voltage, but Lear's sufferings at the hands of his ungrateful daughters and his reconciliation with their all-loving and all-forgiving sister would break my heart.

I was wrong, on both counts. There was no special vulnerability about this king, and I have never known the reunion with Cordelia to be less moving. (Olivier, who hardly ever got to me emotionally, made me cry in this scene.) The imperious Lear, however, was present in force. If Hutt passed up a few outbursts, it was to save himself for others more powerful. In the first scene the fury with which he banished Cordelia and the equally faithful Kent was frightening, largely because it seemed to well up from nowhere. Up to that point he had seemed rather benign.

His initial entrance had been breathtakingly playful. Monette's production, in a 19th-century setting, made excellent use of significant furnishings, and there was a Christmas tree on stage when the play began. Abdicating, dividing the kingdom and extorting declarations of affection were this year's party games in the Lear household.

Hutt strolled onto the stage with mischief in his eye and his walk: a man confident in his own outrageousness. And it was here, rather than in any authentic depiction of senility, that Hutt's own age came into play. This was a man who had been king for a very long time, far too long to take on a new career as a subject. While he still had the power, he greeted any challenge to it with incredulous fury.

After resigning it, he really tried. He still entered any house as if he owned it but he made elaborate attempts to understand his daughters' behaviour: so elaborate that they were liable to collapse into violent sarcasm. When he called down the curse of sterility on his eldest daughter -- "hear, Nature, hear, dear goddess, hear" -- he did it with terrifyingly calm assurance; he and Nature seemed to be on excellent terms. But he was being drained, and he knew it. "Oh let me not be mad," and "oh, fool, I shall go mad:" some of the most famous lines were so freshly timed that they took you by surprise. They also seemed inevitable, and those impromptu heart attacks were their physical equivalent.

Hutt is one of three actors in the 1996 Stratford troupe who were in the first company in 1953; the others are Douglas Rain, this season's excellent Shylock, and the splendidly reliable William Needles. Forty-three years is not that long ago (ah yes, I remember it well: the Coronation and Mount Everest), but such continuity in the modern theatre is still extraordinary. It certainly beats anything you'll find in Britain and the United States.

Hutt has been the exemplary Stratford actor, rising through the ranks with what you might call spectacular steadiness. He began in 1954, when he glorified the minute role of Master Froth in Measure for Measure , giving the character an invincible cheerfulness that clouded for a split second when his dead father was mentioned. (I trust the description of Robertson Davies who, in addition to his more trumpeted talents, was Canada's finest theatre critic.) Hutt is an actor of distinction, and I mean that rather specifically; he has always been a patrician player, in his bearing and especially in his sharply melancholy voice.

Whether he is a great actor, I don't know; What I have often found lacking in him, as in much Canadian acting, is temperament, volatility, urgency. And having written that, I remember two performances that confound me. One, years ago, was his Feste in Twelfth Night , a figure of wintry musical wisdom that governed the play. The other, only last year, was his amazingly honest and uncompromising account of James Tyrone in Long Day's Journey Into Night , a role in which he moved me as Olivier never did. Like Lear, Tyrone was a role he repeatedly returned to: a continual testing process that should be a normal part of a healthy theatre but today is very rare.

Was this last Lear in the same league? Not altogether. What it obviously had was the quality that the faithful Earl of Kent salutes in the old king: authority. I mean an actor's authority: the sense that he knew this play inside out and that we could trust him in it, whatever he did. It was the fruit of a life spent playing Shakespeare, of his previous encounters with King Lear, and of his detour playing the Fool to Peter Ustinov's Lear.

His relationship with his own Fool (the promising young Jordan Pettle) was rich; the two seemed to be moving in and out of one another's heads. Hutt's Lear was very funny in spots, and boldly macabre as well; when he came to the line "let them anatomize Regan, see what breeds about her heart," he mimed, with shocking force, the extraction of that organ from his daughter's body.

All this should have set him up for a probing examination of Lear's madness, of his denunciation of the injustices to which he had once acquiesced and of his sexual disgust. Certainly these themes were being well set up in the surrounding action. The lust-and-ambition triangle of the play's three villains was better done than I have ever seen it, with Goneril and Regan (Diane d'Aquila and Martha Burns) competitively slavering over Geordie Johnson's Edmund, who was outwardly demure as a candidate for the priesthood and doubly provocative because of it. (There are three women inthe play, and two of them fall for him; that's not a bad average.)

The meeting of mad Lear and blind Gloucester is probably the most stupendous scene in the world of drama, and Hutt laid out its revolutionary insights tidily enough. But there was no sense that Lear was actually discovering them and reinventing himself as we listened; they came prepackaged. And Lear's penultimate scene with Cordelia ("come, let's away to prison") was played at face value as a sentimental idyll.

Still, it turned out the best was yet to come in Lear's final confrontation with the worst. Cordelia, on the brink of rescue, has been hanged; Lear is faced with the fact that she will never be restored -- those five "nevers" that make up the bleakest line of blank verse ever written. The selective literalness of Monette's staging helped again; Cordelia's corpse actually looked as if it had just been cut down from the gallows. We don't all have to confront tragedy in such a brutal way, but the basic fact of loss is always the same and Hutt's Lear met it for us. The actor's vocal powers were at their fullest stretch when Lear lamented his daughter's death, and his technique was like quicksilver as the king's mind wandered again, sure of nothing but that dead body. Watching the scene, watching him, you despaired of humanity, and you marvelled at it.

The curtain call was its own event. In an age of meaningless standing ovations we rose -- more or less spontaneously -- to offer one that was deserved. Monette strode down the centre aisle bearing a bouquet; then mounted the stage and presented the flowers to his star, blew a kiss to the rest of the cast and made a graceful, showman's exit. Hutt stood holding the roses and smiled. He seemed pleased, and justly so. We saluted a memorable performance and, I think, a tradition, its guardians, and hopefully its heirs.

Robert Cushman won the Nathan Cohen award for drama criticism this year.

SONGS FROM RAGTIME THE MUSICAL

POP

SONGS FROM RAGTIME THE MUSICAL

Thursday, November 21, 1996

BMG

½

Powerful songs superbly sung

A LOT will obviously depend on the book and the staging, but the songs on this advance CD make Ragtime sound like the most exciting big musical in nearly a decade. Lyricist Lynn Ahrens and composer Stephen Flaherty -- who wrote Once on This Island , My Favourite Year , and the very funny Lucky Stiff -- have spread their wings dramatically here. There seem to be two layers of inspiration. One is E. L. Doctorows novel, with its interlocking chain of personal dramas set against the panorama of American life at the beginning of the century. The other, more fundamental, is that society itself, and its music. Or, rather, its musics.

In the novel, ragtime is a metaphor for the black presence -- and by extension other new presences -- in urban America: an extremely beautiful new rhythm that can be soothing or disturbing. The score honours it with a stirring Joplinesque title tune that's also exemplary theatre music and with a breathtaking song called New Music that both states and justifies that music's emotional effect.

But ragtime was hardly the only sound around, and the score also takes in waltzing parlour ballads, pepped-up marches, vaudeville specialties, spirituals and political anthems. It taps into the whole tradition of American song (though surprisingly, considering the storys immigrant themes, theres nothing that sounds very Jewish) and the effect is liberating: after all the crabbed Europop scores of recent years, it's a tonic. Some pieces of the mosaic are more convincing than others, but there are no songs that are just pastiche; they all make a point or tell a story. The authors' evident commitment to the subject, their passion and exuberance, carry all before them.

The aim seems to be to get behind Doctorows dry and laconic narrative style to expose the thoughts and feelings the novel lets us guess at. Most of it rings true, and little is sentimental. Even a protest song is kept very specific to the situation. The score has its own modes of irony. There are five first-rate comedy numbers on the CD (The Crime of the Century , Henry Ford , What a Game! , Buffalo Nickel Photoplay Inc. , The Show Biz ) and four of them are double-edged. Another very powerful song, He Wanted To Say , is actually about subtext. The performers, most of whom are in the Toronto cast, are immaculate. The marketing term "concept album" is a misnomer. (Whats the concept, other than doing songs from the show?) It's a work-in-progress; and, for once, progress seems to be moving in the right direction.

Songs from Ragtime the Musical is available in stores. The official original cast recording is expected to be released late next year. Ragtime: The Musical has its world premiere at the Ford Centre for the Performing Arts, North York, Ont., on Dec. 8.

ROBIN HOODThief of Nottingham steals heartsPANTOMIME / The villain as comic lead is a new idea in panto, and a glorious one. Ross Petty plays the part with elan. ROBIN HOODFriday, December 13, 1996Directed by Trudy MoffattStarring Karen Kain,  Ross Petty and Frank Augustyn  RATING:   and many, many moreSpecial to The Globe and Mail    THE first pantomime I ever saw -- actually the first show of any kind -- had Robin Hood for its hero, though he had to cede the title billing to his kid sister Red Riding. So Im glad to see that he now has his very own panto, though he doesn't exactly come off as its main character. He is played by Dan R. Chameroy, who was lately the vainglorious Gaston of Beauty and the Beast and who carries on here, especially in song, as if he still were. He may not, of course, be doing it on purpose.He should really be a girl. Pantomime is an old English form of seasonal entertainment, not much used in the colonies and directed chiefly at children with a few off-colour scraps thrown to their parents. It takes some folk or fairy tale, and cheerfully travesties it. I mean travesty partly in the traditional sense of cross-dressing; the hero is traditionally played by a lady (or what we used to call a strapping lass) while the principal comedian -- a far more important role -- is customarily a man dressed as an extremely plain woman: the Pantomime Dame.Here at least tradition has not been tampered with, and we have David Walden, playing Maid Marian's elderly Nurse Tickle. Dame is a tricky convention to animate unless the performer is exceptionally skillful, charming or delicate (delicacy and broad comedy are perfectly compatible), and Walden makes heavy weather of it. The running gags about Dame Tickles inability to get a man and consuming desire to do so become offensive: not because theyre sexist but because they're mechanical. But then, the anonymous scriptwriter hasn't given him any of the best lines.This may be because producer-star Ross Petty (who may well be the anonymous scriptwriter) has walked off with them. Or maybe its the way he tells them. Petty plays the Sheriff of Nottingham. The villain as comic lead is a new idea in panto, and a glorious one. Petty plays it with elan, éclat, and eh-look-out-hes-coming-up-behind-you. He's especially good at rebuking the house for booing him with insufficient enthusiasm.Pantomime, while rigorously observing its own rules, is very free with everybody else's; topical gags, ad libs, and general stepping out of character. The script allows Petty to levy GST (Grasping Sheriffs Tax) and he allows himself to rebuke the sound-man for messing with his miking: an opportunity which many performers in more prestigious musical productions must envy him. Mind you, he should worry; I thought I detected a pecking-order: the bigger the billing, the better the sound.The show has a good plot, as these things go. (They generally go as far as youll let them.) The Sheriff wants to marry Robin's Maid (June Crowley, who was Marian the Librarian in The Music Man at Stratford, and is getting name-cast) for the sake of her inheritance. He's foiled, partly by the Merry Men, but mainly by Karen Kain.She is the Spirit of the Forest and speaks in rhyming couplets. (Ive heard that they seize fairies in these parts/And turn them into tarts -- I havent remembered that quite right, but I promise you that was the rhyme and I haven't murdered the meter; it was like that when I got there.) There is a dream sequence in which every man in the cast gets to act out the fantasy of dancing with Karen Kain. She also performs more elaborate routines with Frank Augustyn. So this is what ballerinas do on their holidays.She is a delight, a real presence, with twinkle and timing: not just a pair of pretty legs and not just a classical star being a good sport. I started wondering what shows Mr. and Mrs. Petty might do together after the lady has hung up her shoes. If only she could sing . . . Hey, what about Peter Pan?I never thought to hear a pantomime score with 1½ Sondheim songs. (The half is from Gypsy, on which he collaborated with Jule Styne.) The boss is clearly a closet sophisticate. But he doesn't let it run away with him.The choreography when it isnt raising Kain (and sometimes when it is) might be described as primitive; at least it might if you were feeling charitable. The decor is far more attractively tacky, running to real old-fashioned borders, and real old-fashioned woodland cutouts. Its the kind of toy-theatre set you want to get up and play with. Speaking of which: Simon Bradbury magisterially presides over the audience-participation song-sheet sequence, which is mandatory. (It always comes just when you think you can go home.)Before this he plays the Sheriff's henchman, showing us what classical actors do on their holidays (his employer addresses him as "you Shaw Festival has-been"), and exhibiting total mastery of gormless North of England comedy. Master and man make a great double act. (I crave an audience. "You can have this one.")I promised my son that I'd give him a review if he got up on stage for the singalong. Well, he did; and he was terrribly good.    At the Elgin Theatre until Jan. 5  Word count: 1006

BELTING IT OUT / Toronto's two new blockbusters explore different traditions in musical theatre. Where Ragtime has spoken dialogue, Jane Eyre -- unfortunately -- is sung from beginning to end.

Megamusicals cannot live by song alone

BELTING IT OUT / Toronto's two new blockbusters explore different traditions in musical theatre. Where Ragtime has spoken dialogue, Jane Eyre -- unfortunately -- is sung from beginning to end.

Saturday, December 14, 1996

Toronto -- IN 1971, when Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice unveiled their Jesus Christ Superstar on Broadway, they were putting a hit record album on stage. Speech doesn't sit well on pop records, so Webbber and Rice did without it on stage, and found that they had invented the through-sung musical. Their subsequent shows, together or apart, institutionalized it.

I've always been suspicious of the genre, and I'm pleased to note that Webber's new show Whistle Down the Wind (which began its try-out in Washington this week) is a book show, that being the trade name for a musical with talking in it. This may be a happy portent. Of the two big new shows in Toronto, Ragtime is certainly a book musical, though its book is properly and most effectively economical. It's crammed with song, but each number is allowed to make its own statement. Jane Eyre isn't a book show, but probably should be.

The rationale for the through-sung musical has always been that contemporary audiences, in their infinite sophistication, would find ludicrous any transition from speech to song and back again. There may have been some sense in this in the days when Webber and others wrote rock musicals. The noise and hypertension of rock might leave the spoken word echoing forlornly in a void. But rock, unable to communicate much on stage beyond its own energy, has long since given place in the theatre to nondescript-contemporary: a sound of which a whole uninterrupted evening is a great deal too much.

The through-sung musical likes to fancy itself pop opera, and it probably thinks of the expository bits between the set-piece numbers as recitative -- the semi-chanted sections which in formal opera carry the plot and fill in the gaps between arias. I used to amuse myself by saying that the only reason people stood for recitative in opera houses was that they couldn't understand the words, but the implied comparison isn't really fair. Aspects of Love, Sunset Boulevard and now Jane Eyre don't use the semi-chant of recitative. They just insert small songs between the big ones. Small in scale, not necessarily in length; some of them seem to go on for ever. After all, they have a lot of story to tell.

A good song can certainly handle quite complicated exposition. Stephen Sondheim's A Weekend in the Country (in his 1973 A Little Night Music ) is a virtuoso example. It takes over from dialogue, and is more entertaining than dialogue, but we still need the book scenes -- if only to underline how much fun the songs are. There is no such safety-net in through-sung musicals. The characters are stuck with singing short-breathed lines whose rhymes come round with numbingly predictable regularity. They make themselves and their authors sound silly.

Paul Gordon, who wrote the score of Jane Eyre, does this doggerel stuff more resourcefully than most, with few real clinkers. But he is short-changing himself as a lyricist, and even as a composer. I would like to hear him writing in a more relaxed manner and on a contemporary subject. I suspect that his music, to adapt the old joke about Wagner, is better than it sounds. Wall-to-wall song becomes wallpaper song. There are some affecting tunes in Jane Eyre , especially the proposal duet for Jane and Rochester, but they sink in the surrounding sludge. The whole show is nearly all in the same nerveless style: one that needs to have drama pumped into it by vocal and orchestral hysterics. (One song that gets bellowed -- twice -- has the incongruously intimate title of Secret Soul. ) What it isn't is sexy, which the Charlotte Bronte love story certainly is. I don't know quite how you would find a musical signature for Bronte's novel, with its tragic undertones and religious overtones. Maybe by using folk-song styles, as was done in Broadway's The Secret Garden in 1991, another period tale from the Yorkshire moors. The gypsy song in Jane Eyre does something in this line; it breaks the monotony, is refreshingly rhythmic, and even has some wit. But a single song does not a complex novel make.

I can think of only three successful musicals based on classic novels: Oliver! , Man of La Mancha and Les Misérables. (The last two are among my least favourite shows but I can hardly deny that they work for huge numbers of people) The curse of adapting most novels for the stage, musical or otherwise, is that you end up filleting them. While E. L. Doctorow's Ragtime hasn't yet had time to become a classic, it's a very special case. It has a complex narrative structure but Doctorow's ironic and (his own term) "reportorial" style means that the task -- a far more congenial one -- is to put flesh on the bones. The book has a pattern of ideas and characters that needs to be respected -- otherwise it ceases to be Ragtime -- but its form, its ambience, and of course its title are inherently musical -- and theatrically musical. I noted when reviewing the CD that "ragtime" here is a shorthand for a variety of styles that flourished at the beginning of the century; we are in at the birth of American popular song, on the forked road that led to jazz and to the American musical. The tradition has been neglected and abused but it is inherently very strong, waiting to be re-activated. Unlike Jane Eyre, which uses a fraying musical convention with no particular relation to its subject, Ragtime naturally comes on singing.

The last musical to use pastiche on so grand a scale was Sondheim's 1971 Follies ,which implicitly criticized the old forms even as it celebrated them. Ragtime is less ambiguous, more open-hearted. Its composer, Stephen Flaherty, may not be a great original melodist but his music dances joyously to familiar rhythms, without great wit but with much authentic passion.

It also fuses perfectly with Lynn Ahrens' lyrics. Lyricists don't get no respect unless they're either Sondheim or dead, but Ahrens is an excellent technician. If you want to hear how cleanly, pointedly and exuberantly rhyme can be used, listen to the hard, clinching monosyllables in Henry Ford and Buffalo Nickel Photoplay, Inc. Ahrens is also a dramatist. She doesn't expose her characters as ruthlessly as Sondheim but she digs into them deeply and sympathetically. Celebrating the allure of the ragtime pianist's "new music," or expressing different shades of baffled social anger, some songs moved me to tears. Others made me laugh. Like ragtime itself, and unlike the screeching melodramas of recent years, the score -- and therefore the show -- has real dignity, real sparkle, real pathos.

Ragtime isn't the definitive American musical that it plainly aspires to be and, by right of pedigree and performance, should be. But it's already a once-in-a-lifetime subject, rapturously grasped.

It isn't the first show to attempt such a subject, but the line of musical epics that capture the movement of history is short. Ragtime 's only major predecessors are Show Boat and Follies, with Fiddler on the Roof as a sort of immigrants' prelude to the American experience and Sondheim's Pacific Overtures and Assassins as something different but allied: what an American critic has called "epics distilled." All these shows have used old musical forms, but with freshness and purpose. (Used otherwise they yield only nostalgia trips, which can range from Hello Dolly to Tommy. ) I don't think it makes them much of a pointer for future musicals -- they are rarities, almost by definition -- and anyway I distrust those critics who are already offering Ragtime up as a musical for the ages: a) they can't know how it will age and b) what matters is how well it works now.

Evolving a form of popular song that can carry stories and illuminate character is one of the great American achievements (and it's unspeakably depressing that they should have surrendered that inheritance to the soulless English and Europeans) but I don't think it can accomplish anything very substantial without the support of the spoken word. Weill and Gershwin accomplished it in their Broadway operas, but only by using a different weight of music -- and they did know about recitative. Speech, song and dance make up a magical trinity; why sacrifice any of them?

Knowing things that perhaps we ought not know FORBIDDEN KNOWLEDGE: From Prometheus to Pornography

Paradox of knowing is at heart of bold critical journey

Knowing things that perhaps we ought not know FORBIDDEN KNOWLEDGE: From Prometheus to Pornography

Saturday, December 14, 1996

By Roger Shattuck

St. Martin's Press, 370 pages, $35.99

'ARE there things we should not know?" asks the very first sentence of this book. To which the only answer can be another question: How do we know until we know them? By which time, of course, it's too late.

I waited with some impatience to see whether Roger Shattuck would acknowledge this paradox at the heart of his grand undertaking. Eventually, on page 301, he does. Reaching back past that opening sentence to his title, he says, "If we are familiar enough with any entity or domain to call the result 'knowledge,' then we already know too much about it to apply the adjective forbidden ." But he still finds the phrase useful, in many ways, and it's certainly suggestive.

As is indicated in his subtitle, From Prometheus to Pornography , Shattuck casts a very wide net. He's a respected literary critic and a professor of modern languages, with interests and experience far beyond his specialties. At one revealing point in this book he compares his feelings on reading the Marquis de Sade to his reactions on first witnessing surgery, and to the sensation of going into combat in the Second World War. So he himself has acquired a great deal of knowledge that is painful if not actually forbidden.

The operating-theatre experience he presumably went in search of, as an amateur scientist. He writes with ease and authority about astronomy and about research into recombinant DNA. The theatre of war -- again I'm presuming -- was wished on him. He was a pilot in the Pacific and believes it probable that his life was saved by the dropping of the atom bomb on Hiroshima. Later on, of course, he began to have qualms. The bomb and its successors are perhaps the classic example of knowledge-we'd-be-better-off-without, with J. Robert Oppenheimer, the physicist who later claimed to have "known sin" and to have blood on his hands, the central character in a tragic drama of Faustian dimensions. Except that the evil here is not in the knowledge but in its application.

I don't think I'm quibbling. "Knowledge," in Shattuck's book, turns out to be an extremely slippery concept, sometimes just a synonym for "experience." We begin, as advertised, with Prometheus, who in Greek myth stole fire from heaven and presented it to mankind. Zeus was furious and chained him to a rock, there to have his liver perpetually devoured by a visiting vulture. As further revenge, Zeus gave Prometheus a sister-in-law, Pandora, to release upon the world all the evils that our flesh and spirit are heir to. (Plus Hope, to keep us coming back for more; Shattuck leaves this last redeeming detail out.)

From there it's a skip across to the equivalent Judaic, and subsequently Christian, legend of the Garden of Eden, definitively fusing, as Shattuck says, "the themes of knowledge, curiosity, sexuality, the origin of evil, and immortality." Pandora and Eve, with their fatal proclivities for opening boxes and picking fruit, stand revealed as the first exemplars of what Shattuck calls "the Wife of Bath effect," after the Chaucerian character who declared, "Forbede us thyng, and that desiren we . . ."

The biblical creation story may have licenced millennia of misogyny, but that "we," at least as Shattuck uses it, means all of us; we all desire forbidden things. It's basic human nature, therefore presumably God-implanted, so it seems unfair that Adam and Eve should have been punished for it.

SHATTUCK writes that upon tasting the apple "straightaway, their innocent love changes into the dalliance of guilty lust." Does that mean they'd had sex before eating the apple but now it was somehow different? It's difficult not to feel that the Eden story has a lot to answer for. The Greeks, for whom the gods simply represented the way things are (i.e. unjust), were grateful to Prometheus for saving the human race from extinction and sorry for him afterwards. The Jews, as Shattuck points out, forgot the Eden story as soon as they'd written it; it is never alluded to in the rest of the Old Testament. For the Christians, though, it was central: The fortunate Fall, to be deplored but also praised for having made possible the rest of human history including the Redemption; indeed, it is precisely what was to be redeemed.

The double bind persisted. The Christian Middle Ages deplored too much curiosity, but could hardly help glorifying it at the same time. Dante's Divine Comedy is a huge apologia for orthodox thinking, and one of the lost souls of his Inferno is Ulysses, damned for voyaging in search of forbidden lands. But there is terrific grandeur in this portrayal of a man sailing over the edge of the world.

In the Renaissance, Montaigne, a tireless self-deprecator, kept proclaiming the limitations of the human mind but couldn't stop his own from working overtime. He virtually invented a new subject: human psychology. The self-proclaimed Age of Reason thought it had things in perspective. Alexander Pope in his Essay on Man (1734) famously proclaimed that heavenly speculation was futile and "the proper study of mankind is man," but that's not as safe as it sounds. Man was uncharted territory, and exploring it could get you into trouble.

Studying human biology certainly could, as Darwin discovered a century later. The Darwinian T. H. Huxley said that though he had evidence for his scientific beliefs, he had none for any religious views, and therefore was not prepared to declare any; he did the English language a major service by inventing a new word to describe his position. The word was "agnostic," and as Shattuck says, it's difficult to believe how long we got along without it. (At least I think it is; I don't really know.) As he also says, it's a shame that a term originally coined to denote honest ignorance has shifted to mean an aggressive rationalism. Faith in reason: That's an Inferno of a paradox.

GOETHE'S Faust , written across 50 years, shows what happens when the intellectual centre shifts. It's a dramatization by a man who didn't believe in damnation of a legend that depends on it. It's a brilliant mess; however shabby much of Faust's behaviour in pursuit of personal freedom, Goethe couldn't bring himself to condemn a fellow scientist and ends by letting him off the hook. Another Romantic, Mary Shelley, married one of those questing spirits. She wrote Frankenstein , the classic warning. Women, despite Eve and the Wife of Bath, often figure in Shattuck's account as restraining agents. There is Mme de La Fayette, whose novel La Princesse de Cleves (1678) glorifies the avoidance of passion, or at least of its gratification; not on prudish grounds, but rather to avoid hurt and disillusion. Emily embraces renunciation in her poety and in her life.

Shattuck as a critic is at his best on Dickinson; I found him revelatory. He seems deeply drawn to the ascetic esthetic. When he turns to science he applauds biologists who voluntarily imposed a moratorium on certain forms of DNA research. But vastly different kinds of "knowledge" are involved here, so different that the word begins to seem inadequate and ineffectual. Dickinson's denial was private and individual; the scientists' was public, collective and professional. It was also unique and, I would say, purely symbolic. If you can look far enough along a road to foresee its dangers, you have in essence travelled that road already. It isn't just that what is thought can never be unthought -- so that we would be living with the bomb even if every nuclear device on earth were dismantled -- it's that every step inevitably entails its successor.

Finally, Shattuck comes to pornography. He examines de Sade and finds him, rightly, appalling. No, he does not believe he himself was harmed by the encounter. Nor can he quite make up his mind that the sex criminals who read de Sade -- the Moors murderers in Britain, Ted Bundy in America -- were decisively influenced by him; at most, he may have suggested specific techniques. I doubt myself if de Sade's being "a classic author" had much to do with his appeal in this area, but Shattuck is right to be angrily ironic about the literary critics who, in the sacred cause of shocking the bourgeoisie, have bestowed that status on him. Answering a question once posed by Simone de Beauvoir -- "must we burn Sade?" -- he answers no. He thinks we should probably do something (moral health warnings, like on cigarette packets? Counter-productive, I'd say). But burning -- or banning -- would be ineffective and wrong, since "we should not deliberately destroy any human life or accomplishment." I find this conclusion disconcertingly flabby, the more so as I share it myself.

The book is graced with great lucidity and occasional wit. (He writes of Don Juan that "he seems to elude our grasp by dodging in and out among the several masterpieces that have brought him to life.") Half the time he is talking not about knowledge, but about action, and the book is crazily ambitious -- which means that the author is, in a way, the subject.

"The time has come" he says at close, "to think as intently about limits as about liberation." I take it he means intellectual limits. If he means limits we may impose on ourselves, then we have always had that right and sometimes perhaps that duty. If he means limits imposed by others, he's wrong; there's nobody we can trust.

Robert Cushman is a Toronto writer, critic and broadcaster.

Spectator

Diana Vreeland -- unzipped

Spectator

Tuesday, January 14, 1997

MY ideal Sunday kicks into gear around noon, with eggs Benedict and continues with a matinee. This only works if Im in New York. Toronto has both brunch and Sunday theatre, but not on the same scale or with the same feeling. London has never taken to the idea of Sunday theatre; the place's weekend rhythm is too sluggish without being -- as New York manages once a week -- relaxed.

The relaxation part is important, and to preserve it I go, ideally, to an off-Broadway show. Broadway is too frenetic, too big a deal, for a Sunday afternoon. It needs to be a night out; or, failing that, it should be taken in at a weekday matinee, where the routine unfolds with clockwork regularity. West 44th and 45th Streets, between 1:30 and 1:45 on a Wednesday or Saturday afternoon, are scenes of well-orchestrated frenzy as tourists and suburbanites crowd out of restaurants and into lobbies.

The 3 p.m. start is far more relaxing, a chance to be invited into somebody's world, rather than drummed into it as I was last Sunday at Full Gallop at the Westside theatre. Full Gallop is a one-woman show that invites you, rather imperiously, into the world of Diana Vreeland, first into her apartment and then into her head. Vreeland, as an editor at Harpers Bazaar and then as the editor at Vogue, presided over New York fashion from 1937 until being summarily fired in 1971. This is not in itself an achievement that interests me very much, and the snobbery that goes with the territory was as likely to repel as to intrigue me. On the other hand, I do like sacred monsters, at least from a distance. An unusual number of people had assured me that I would enjoy the show and I believed them. But I was curious as to how Mary Louise Wilson, performer and co-author, was going to bring it about.

She has done it, first of all, by looking outrageous. Her cheeks are rouged. In fact most of her face is rouged, all the way up to the hair line. (It actually looks like a wig line, but it could just be that her black locks have been spectacularly lacquered.) She matches her room, which contains one tiny expanse of white but is otherwise -- wall, ceiling, chairs, carpet and pillars -- all red. This is called practicing what you preach, since Vreeland was the Apostle of Red. (She was the inspiration for the fashion editor played by Kay Thompson in the Fred Astaire movie Funny Face . Thompsons big number in the film was called Think Pink , which seems appropriate since, for all her zing, her character was a pale reflection of the authentic Diana.) Early on in the play our hostess -- speaking in what I can best describe as a passionate drawl -- instructs us in her preferences and their attendant paradoxes: "I hate red with orange in it -- but I love orange with red in it." It's fascinating.

It's vital that a solo performer have someone to talk to. Otherwise you get stuck with watching them stumble around their homes, inexplicably talking to themselves or making marathon expository phone calls.

Vreeland talks to us because shes a compulsive chatterer, and well do. We have somehow to believe that we are simultaneously in a theatre and in her living room, but -- as always in the theatre -- that's all right with us if it is with her. Wilson and her collaborator, Mark Hampton, have plundered their subject's memoirs for bon mots, which she delivers with the swacked authority, the decisive delivery and abrupt changes of tack that constitute an American female comic tradition in themselves. It is, of course, the screwball style. Try to imagine a less fastidious Katharine Hepburn. Hepburn, even in the craziness of Bringing Up Baby , always sounded tinglingly sane. Wilson as Vreeland suspects that she might be what the world calls crazy, but doesnt care. Both are totally convinced of their own rightness.

Full Gallop , though it seems random, is rather cunningly shaped, filling us in alternately on her protagonists past and present. We actually meet her when she should be at the end of her rope, in the aftermath of being sacked. She is planning for a dinner party, despite having nothing in the house, a refractory staff, and the dimmest idea of where the kitchen might be. (She goes in search of it during the intermission, and returns from her expedition, shocked and blinking at its unconscionable whiteness.) A bill arrives, and is stuffed into an overflowing box of other bills. We sense -- she does make some phone calls -- that she is losing her social as well as her professional position. She ought to be falling to pieces, and after one call to her family in London, she does break down. Then we discover that she's crying not for herself but for her grandson: not that he's dead or anything, hes become a Buddhist and shaved his head. No one she cries "had hair like that," and its obviously heart-felt agony: a truth to her own principles more moving than any self-pity could be. That's what I liked best about the play; it could have been a tear-jerker and wasn't. And in fact Vreeland picks herself up at the end and accepts a job in the costume department of the Metropolitan Museum: a job that she has earlier scorned (who wants to work in the past?), but of which she apparently made a great success.

Vreelands mental, and certainly political, horizons were limited. One could wish that she had found something more to say about Hitler than that his mustache was unbelievable -- it was just wrong . On the other hand, given her delivery, it does sound like the last word in damnation. And when she says that "the best thing about life in London was Paris" or recalls New York frothing at the mouth at its first Balenciaga show, or declares that the twenties were "the whole beginning of the 20th century" (equalled, apparently, by the sixties), or proudly recalls that her husband ironed his shoelaces until the day he died you wouldnt dream of arguing with her. Actually you wouldn't dare, but more to the point is that you wouldn't want to. She can even take somebody elses line, acknowledge it as such, and still make it work for her. "As Joan Crawford said, if you want the girl next door, go next door." That got the kind of laugh that ripples round the auditorium, then starts all over again, louder.

One usually ends a piece like this saying how grateful one was to have been ushered into the presence of a rare spirit. I didnt feel that. I felt I had seen a woman who may have been entertaining brought to life by one who unquestionably was. I had recently made Wilson's acquaintance on, so to speak, the other side of the barricades, in an old Broadway musical called Flora, the Red Menace -- or, to be exact, on its original cast recording which I was reviewing for a book. She played a Communist agitator with a heavy schedule, and she brought the same fervour to that as she is doing now to Manhattan's queen of the transient but opulent. She makes you laugh with the woman, and, therefore, accept her. It's perfect for a Sunday afternoon.

Era of intelligent musical gaiety, gone but not forgotten

Spectator

Era of intelligent musical gaiety, gone but not forgotten

Saturday, February 8, 1997

LAST November I was in New York preparing a radio special for the BBC. (I felt terribly cosmopolitan.) The subject was the Cabaret Convention, an annual week-long songfest in which singers show off their wares while celebrating the American theatre and supper-club repertoire. One of the highlights was a concert devoted to the lyrics of E. Y. (generally known as Yip) Harburg, 1996 being the 100th anniversary of his birth. Among those billed to appear was the composer Burton Lane, Yip's collaborator on Finian's Rainbow and other pleasing, if less famous, things. Lane was a good pianist and a fair singer, and we expected to hear him give out with Old Devil Moon or How Are Things in Glocca Morra ?

In the event, Lane, who was then 85, didn't appear, at least not on stage. He was noticeable in the auditorium, looking frail though not alarmingly so, and smiling: The evening had after all been full of his tunes and they had stood up beautifully. Then, on January 5, came the news of his death which, coming just after the Harburg centenary, seemed to set the seal on an era.

As a team, Lane and Harburg never had the public visibility or the durability of Rodgers and Hammerstein or Lerner and Loewe. They could both be difficult men, and after Finian in 1947 they collaborated infrequently. But they were a good match. Each exemplified to a high degree the Broadway tradition that crystallized in the 1930s: intelligent gaiety against the odds. They wrote the kind of love songs -- flippant or heartfelt or both at once -- that sounded good on stage or screen, as vehicles for solo singers or swing bands. Harburg, who wrote Brother Can You Spare a Dime and the songs for The Wizard of Oz ,was the master equally of fantasy and of social comment; indeed, he regarded the first as a vehicle for the second. (A fervent Roosevelt supporter, he always maintained that If I Only Had a Brain and its subsequent stanzas -- "if I only had a heart . . . if I only had the noive" -- were a coded comment on the Depression and the New Deal. Eventually, and traumatically, he was blacklisted.)

He was also the grand master of lyrical wordplay; it suited his taste for whimsical satire and could also be a delightful end in itself. Harburg could call a song I Like the Likes of You or reel out such a string of compliments as "you are so lovable, so livable, your beauty is just unforgivable."

Once Harburg had bestowed Over the Rainbow on Judy Garland, therainbow -- an image he had previously used as automatically as any other lyricist might -- became his conscious symbol for hope and romance. Hence the governing motif of Finian. The score contains an admonitory song called Look to the Rainbow ; and 10 years ago, when I wrote and directed a Harburg anthology show in London, that seemed the perfect title-number. It's a sweet tune -- part optimistic, part homesick -- with an intentionally Irish lilt; speeded up it goes very naturally into a jig. All the characters in Finian are Irish wanderers, Southern sharecroppers or rednecks; to accommodate these specialized parameters Lane wrote swinging folk or gospel tunes as well as a couple of classic ballads. He set Harburg's virtuoso conceits ("when I can't fondle the hand that I'm fond of, I fondle the hand at hand") to an intoxicating waltz.

If Burton Lane was the last of the thirties songwriters it's partly because he began so early. When his first song was published, in 1927, he was 15. He was 18 when his first songs were interpolated on Broadway; 21 when he broke into the movies with Everything I Have Is Yours . In Hollywood he wrote with Frank (Guys and Dolls ) Loesser who, in those days was strictly a words man and just about the funniest, even when he wasn't writing outright comedy songs. The Loesser-Lane songs have a special kind of unbuttoned joyousness; I especially cherish How'dja Like to Love Me , a guarded preview of domestic bliss ("would you rise in wrath if I beat you to the bath each day?") that they wrote for Bob Hope and Martha Raye. Even greater fun musically was How About You (as in "I like New York in June, how about you?") on which Lane's partner was the fairly obscure Ralph Freed. The bubbling profusion of notes in the middle, when the lyric goes "I like potato chips, moonlight and motor trips," is the kind of logical surprise that makes a song's fortune.

In the 1950s, Lane teamed with Alan Jay Lerner, Harburg's heir as commentator (liberal rather than radical), compulsive word-juggler (he never got this bit quite right) and doctrinaire romantic (what else do you call a man who married eight times?). Together they wrote Royal Wedding ,a deeply unmemorable movie that nevertheless contains one song, Too Late Now ,that is as sublime as a pop ballad gets. In 1965 they reunited for the stage show On a Clear Day You Can See Forever :a consistently elegant work. The title song was an instant classic. I never liked it; but musicians kept telling me how great it was and finally, hearing Lane's tune away from Lerner's mystically preachy lyric, I heard what they meant. The melody soars on one continuous sweeping arc.

Lane's last Broadway musical, again with Lerner, was in 1979: Carmelina ,which flopped but contained some lovely songs. He wasn't finished even then. A few years ago there was a complete recording of Strike Up the Band ,a 1927 musical by George and Ira Gershwin. As is usually the case, the original materials were widely scattered. One song, Meadow Serenade ,had a full lyric by Ira but of George's music only the chorus survived; Lane supplied a new setting for the verse, and it's as beautiful as anything in the original score.

In 1990, Michael Feinstein released a recording of Lane tunes with the composer at the piano. One song, I Can Hardly Wait ,had been written only that year and it, too, is a beauty; though its lyricists, the compulsive Oscar-winners Alan and Marilyn Begman, clearly belong to a later and more solemn era than Lane's own.

Of course, eras don't so much end as merge and overlap. The work of Lane and Harburg is still abundantly alive, and the book is hardly closed on the generation that preceded them. I see that we have just lost Gerald Marks, who wrote the music for All of Me ,and before that Irving Caesar who, as is the way of songwriters named Irving, had lived to be 101. His last decades were comparatively unproductive, but in his youth he wrote the lyrics for Swanee , Tea for Two and Crazy Rhythm : none of them deathless verse but all apparently indestructible. Caesar and Marks collaborated on Is It True What They Say About Dixie? a question that has always seemed to me to beg for a disrespectful answer. Yip Harburg, preferably with a Burton Lane accompaniment, would have been the perfect man to give it.
1997-02-09-the-best-director-we-never-ha:
The best director we never had

THEATRE: He's one of Britain's finest directors, yet he works almost exclusively in Canada. Robert Cushman asks Michael Langham why he left us

Sunday 09 February 1997 00:02 GMT

The most satisfying productions of Shakespeare give you both text and texture. The play has been dug to its roots, so that every line resonates with hidden meanings while still sounding like the natural utterance of complex, flesh-and-blood characters. You get this in Trevor Nunn's best work and in Deborah Warner's. And you get it in the work of a man who has been at work much longer than either of them. His name is Michael Langham.

Langham is a British director who for decades has worked mainly in New York or at the Canadian Shakespeare Festival in Stratford, Ontario - not to be confused with Stratford-upon-Avon, where he has also worked. Langham was born in Somerset in 1919, became hooked on theatre as a young PoW in Germany - getting up play-readings every Monday night for a literally captive audience - and worked steadily during the Fifties at the Old Vic and Stratford-upon-Avon. In 1956 he directed a bare-stage Hamlet at Stratford, with the late Alan Badel in the lead. It was cruelly treated by the critics, but had a force and freshness that excited many less jaded spectators. Among the drama students who saw it was Brian Bedford, a future leading actor of the Albert Finney/Peter O'Toole generation who, after scoring a West End success in Peter Shaffer's Five Finger Exercise, crossed the Atlantic and became a star in the States and Canada. He recalls: "When Rosencrantz and Guildenstern came on, they were carrying suitcases. That doesn't sound like much now, but in those days it was a revelation. Langham made Shakespeare surprisingly real: something to do with your own life."

A few years on, in 1960, Peter Hall started the Royal Shakespeare Company. Langham was one of the directors Hall called on for his first season, and chose to do The Merchant of Venice, with the young Peter O'Toole as Shylock. The production got the best notices of the year, is still remembered for its balance, humour and excitement, and seems in retrospect the apex of O'Toole's stage career.

And now? "I think," said Hall, when I told him last year how much I had admired Langham's recent work in Ontario, "that Michael's doing wonderfully." Hall himself had just qualified for his bus-pass, and so presumably responded all the more warmly to a director who is thriving in his seventies. (In Europe old directors become sages; in Britain and America we expect them to quietly fade away.) Langham himself wryly attributes what he sees as a late flowering to having been "slow to grow up: my greatest growth has been in the last 20 years". (His wife, even more wryly, amends that to "the last five".)
