One important influence was becoming head of New York's prestigious Juilliard drama school in 1979: a job for which Hall recommended him and which he held for 12 years. "I now understand actors better, I understand myself better, so I'm a better director."

Before the Juilliard, he spent most of the Seventies in Minneapolis, running a theatre created by Tyrone Guthrie, the great British director who had long been Langham's mentor. At the start of his career, Langham had been an earnest idealist. "I was a romantic socialist, I wanted to do plays that would make the world better. I was on a serious crusade." But Guthrie, who believed in "the importance of not being earnest", brought out the showman in Langham; while still based in Britain he gave him work at the Old Vic and was eventually responsible for the decisive move of his protégé's working life.

In 1953 Guthrie had been invited out to Canada to start the Stratford Shakespeare Festival; housed, for economic reasons, in a tent, it was performed, for artistic reasons, on a platform stage, a sophisticated modern distillation of Elizabethan basics. Open staging was Guthrie's personal passion; he had come to believe that the plays could never work properly within the confines of a proscenium. Langham arrived to do a guest production in 1955, and found himself being groomed for the job of artistic director. He took the job a year later and stayed for over a decade.

This was far longer than Langham had intended, but there always seemed more to do. He oversaw the transformation of the theatre's outer shell from canvas to concrete, built up a muscular acting ensemble in a country with very little classical tradition, and gained complete mastery of a thrilling but demanding space.

To begin with, seasons were short, and Langham was able to make frequent working visits home. (One of my earliest theatrical memories is of a Two Gentlemen of Verona which he directed at the Vic; it was done in Byronic costume, and still seems like one of the most unforcedly funny Shakespeares I've ever seen.) His early RSC work fell into this period too; for one play he brought over his new Canadian star, Christopher Plummer. Then, in 1969, he directed a lacklustre Way of the World at the National. He hasn't worked in the English theatre ever since, though he and his wife still live in London.

His wife is Helen Burns, a London-bred actress with a European background. He is tall and reserved, she is short and voluble. They've been married 45 years, off and on. (On, then off, then on again. "One is," says Burns, "better-behaved in later years.") He first clapped eyes on her in 1949: "I saw her in a play called The New Morality and was very struck by her" - so audibly struck that Dame Wendy Hiller, who happened to be sitting in the row in front of Langham and was a friend of Burns's, rushed backstage after the show to tell the actress about her voluble admirer in the audience.

Before they met, Burns had an early success as Nora in Ibsen's A Doll's House, a play that has haunted the pair. "We didn't know till years later," says Langham, "that our honeymoon hotel in Amalfi was where Ibsen stayed. Our son Christopher was conceived there." (He's Chris Langham, the actor and comedian, now appearing in London in Les Miserables and the award-winning R4 comedy People Like Us.) Yet despite such intimate connections it wasn't until last year that Langham worked on an Ibsen play, when he and his wife co-directed, perhaps inevitably, A Doll's House. It was a finely conceived and staged, if unevenly acted production, that did justice to the play's roots in reality and its status as myth. The pair did it in Wolfville, an uncannily beautiful town in Nova Scotia and home of the new Atlantic Theatre Festival. This has a Stratford-shaped stage in a converted hockey-rink, and has got off to a tearing start to which Langham's skill and prestige have been crucial. The idea is to use local acting talent as much as possible, so he is once again involved in building a young company. Langham is billed as artistic associate, and has directed or co-directed four out of six plays in the first two seasons. Before A Doll's House he and his wife collaborated on an astringent and ultimately very moving Cherry Orchard. On his own he has done a very lucid Tempest and a mellow, melancholic Twelfth Night, that was in no way revolutionary but whose great distinction was that every moment in it seemed freshly-thought-out, every line rang true, and every actor seemed in the right place at the right time - a rarer occurrence than it might seem.

Twelfth Night was also the first play Langham directed professionally - at Coventry in 1946 - and it is the greatest tribute to him that he can take a play so familiar to himself and everyone else and still make it so unforcedly fresh. Three decades after his RSC triumph, he similarly rediscovered The Merchant of Venice; without shirking the darkness in it he made it work as romantic comedy. His Shylock this time - less the Hebraic prophet than O'Toole had been, but funnier and equally obsessed - was the same Brian Bedford who had so admired Langham's Hamlet. They have now made up for their delay in collaborating by doing nine plays together in as many years: all of them in Ontario with a couple of transfers to Broadway. Of their working relationship, Bedford says: "Michael usually makes a very good show. You feel very secure within that. He's one of a handful of directors who can make plays come vibrantly alive. He's totally obsessive and committed to what he does. When he's working I don't think he thinks about anything else."

Helen Burns defines her husband's talent by saying that he's "brilliant at moving people in rhythm with the play. He makes stage pictures that illuminate what's going on underneath." As for me, I don't know whether the current British theatre has a place for Langham's experience, his craftsmanship and his humane vision. But I think it would be worth the while of the National or the RSC to find out.
1997-02-19-theatre-review-the-cradle-wil:
THE CRADLE WILL ROCK

THEATRE REVIEW

THE CRADLE WILL ROCK

Wednesday, February 19, 1997

Directed by David Oiye

Rating: ½

Cartoon characters swarm cradle

Uneven performances detract from historic

musical of wit, passion and beauty.

Special to The Globe and Mail

THE mystique of The Cradle Will Rock has outdistanced the show itself. A political musical, allegorical in style and radical in content, its 1937 premiere passed into legend when its sponsors, the Federal Theatre Project, got nervous and cancelled the first night. Abetted by the performing unions, they locked the production out of its New York theatre. The performers, escorted by an ever-increasing audience, then marched through town to another house where the show went on: the author-composer Marc Blitzstein playing his score from the stage and the actors, officially forbidden to join him there, getting up and speaking or singing their lines from the auditorium. It didn't hurt the legend any that the director was a young prodigy named Orson Welles.

A decade ago Welles's assistant John Houseman was enlisted to tell the story as prologue to a notable revival in New York and London. Lacking Mr. Houseman's services, Equity Showcase preface their production with a brisk re-enactment of the events, or at least the discussions preceeding them; the really exciting bit -- the march -- is not readily stageable. The actor playing Orson (Steve Ross) manages a convincing look of the chubby boy-genius; the show's MD (Alan Moon) sits at the piano and announces the scenes just as Biltzstein did; and the first character, a moll called Moll, duly announces herself from the house. She plays her opening scene, with a predatory john and an even more predatory cop, at the front of the stalls. This episode is itself a kind of prologue; when the main action starts, the company gets up on the stage and -- as in Olivier's Henry V -- some kind of magical, seamless change in convention is deemed to have taken place.

But the preliminaries are either too much or not enough. Their main practical effect is to start the show 10 minutes later than advertised. There were great ironies attending the birth of Cradle ; a ferociously anticapitalist, pro-union show was nearly aborted by unions and a government agency, caving in to right-wing pressure: exactly the kind of spinelessness for which the piece itself arraigns the petit bourgeoisie. To explore all this might require the kind of wholesale rewriting favoured by Blitzstein's idol, Brecht. Equity Showcase, once past the starting gate, play the text straight.

It can stand the exposure. Frankly dated and frankly agitprop, it remains a work of wit, passion and beauty. (Besides, it's all true.) We are in Steeltown, fief of the all-powerful mill owner Mister Mister. Helping him run the place are toadying respresentatives of the church, the press, the arts, the universities and medecine; all of them co-opted on to Mister Mister's Liberty Committee, formed to opose the increasingly strident demands of organized labour. The latter are represented by the charming and incorruptible union organizer Larry Foreman. A series of vignettes shows how each of the sycophants have sold out, while the more innnocent prostitute Moll watches in amazement. If the show's view of union power now seems starry-eyed ( Larry, with his folksy wisdom and constant invocations of his off-stage Aunt Jessie, is very hard to take) it still looks better than the alternative.

David Oiye's production is smartly and inventively staged, stylishly constumed and unevenly performed. A large ensemble (only very rich or very poor theatres can afford to do this piece) is paraded in telling formations. Blitzstein had a gift for musical pastiche, and his Croon Spoon and Honolulu for Mister Mister's awful spoiled children are spot-on parodies of thirties pop archetypes. Jan Johanson's choreography accentuates the fun, laying on a swaying Hawaiin chorus of indetermninate gender. Similarly entertaining is the bitching duet of Dauber the painter and Yashua the violinist, a matched pair of parasites, biting the hand that feeds them for as long as they're safely begind its back, if you follow me. ("Oh, there's something so damned low about the rich . . . What can they do? Support you!") Blitzstein reserved his most withering fire for his own kind, and you could not accuse the show of preaching to the converted. Its original audience would have been the Liberty Committee and their friends: Mrs. Mister is a great, if simpering, patron of the arts.

Jay Turvey cuts a slick figure as Editor Daily, the one lackey to be allowed a modicum of professional integrity, and Robert Clarke finds the light and shade in Dr. Specialist, the only one with scruples. The others are cartoons, executed with insufficient force. The glaring lack is in Mister Mister himself (Andrew Scorer) who has no power and no presence. Gleamingly bald-headed, he resembles that even more trenchantly named tycoon Daddy Warbucks, and seems, unfortunately, even less of a threat. Among the goodies: Stefanie Roth carefully rescues Moll from the status of downtrodden symbol; her wistfully tough lament Nickel Under the Foot is touching, but not as piercing as it might be; he same goes for the threatening title song, an assault on complacency which, as delivered by Andrew Pifko's pugnacious punk Larry, sounds more like a pious hope than a prophecy. Nor does the angriest song in the score, Joe Worker Gets Gypped , realize its full devastating potential.

They still work, though; Blitzstein spent the rest of his career writing haunting scores for commercial projects that turned out to be uncommercial, but his music grows on you. His lyrics can be clumsy -- some of his scansion sets the teeth on edge -- but his ideas come through, sometimes to scorching effect. Amusingly, he was to achieve his greatest success solely as a lyricist, translating The Threepenny Opera ; his are the English words of Mack the Knife we've been singing since the fifties. It's fitting, because Cradle had actually been more Brechtian than anything Brecht and Weill themselves ever turned out. The first expressionist musical, its abstraction is what makes it live today; the techniques accentuate the show's period feel, but also cut through it. The Cradle still rocks.

At Harbourfront's Studio Theatre, York Quay, until Feb. 22.
1997-03-01-theatre-review-high-life:
HIGH LIFE

THEATRE REVIEW

HIGH LIFE

Saturday, March 1, 1997

Directed by Jim Millan

Written by Lee MacDougall

Starring Brent Carver, Clive Cholerton,

Randy Hughson and Ron White

Rating: 

A metaphor for a circular existence

In High Life, four free-floating characters

are forced into a tight scenario and a big part of the

attraction for the audience is getting the chance to watch them wriggle.

Special to The Globe and Mail

ASSURANCE is always attractive in the theatre, and High Life has bags of it. Some of this stems from its knockout success at last years World Stage Festival, but a lot seems built in. The play now returns to Harbourfront with its original cast and production. It looks, in its second coming, like something less than The Second Coming, but it is possible to see what its original enthusiasts were going on about.

Lee MacDougall, an actor writing his first play, has an enviable flair for spinning dialogue and the rarer ability for harnessing it to a plot. There is remarkably little fat on the play, even though it only lasts an hour-and-a-half. Its four characters are all morphine addicts. Addicts are by definition monomaniacs (though to be fair these guys smoke and drink a lot as well) and our quartets chosen path to the next hit is robbing banks.

They have a bright new scam hinging on the use of stolen bank cards and requiring seamless and unselfish teamwork: the one thing that these characters, if not these actors, are least equipped to deliver. They are constantly, and often literally, at one another's throats. Only one of the four seems to have any qualms about constantly shooting up and his, if you'll forgive the expression, are skin deep. The play derives its comedy from the fact that none of them has, or can afford to have, any convictions, other than strictly criminal ones; three of them have done time, plenty of it, and they look with considerable suspicion upon the one who hasnt.

The plays great attraction is that it gives four gifted actors the chance to fill their own space. Jim Millan's production boasts what one would call, if mixing metaphors were not as dangerous as mixing drugs, a crack cast. The junkie-ensemble play and the bank-heist play (although up to now there has generally been only the bank-heist movie) are two established genres that go surprisingly well together. It's a mixture of opposites: free-floating characters are forced into a tight scenario, and we watch them wriggle.

Brent Carver is a virtuoso wriggler. He plays Donnie, a laughing boy with a mean streak of self-pity, disturbed by what his habit has done to his body (hes down to his last kidney) but not enough to kick it. The play, for all its humorous veneer, is short on wit -- the lines are nimble rather than resonant -- but Carver is loaded with it. Donnies mind moves slowly -- he greets each new development wih a broad smile and a blithe, "Oh, yeah" -- but his body compensates. He nods his head repeatedly to take in bad news while his weaving hands seem to be pushing it away. Pervading the whole performance is a fey innocence. You wonder initially if a creation so bizarre, so obviously built by the actor, could exist outside the theatre; after five minutes you give in and enjoy.

His polar opposite, immediately credible, is Randy Hughson's Bug, a hoarse hulk in whom violence and the bottle serve as a nervous system. Clive Cholerton pays Billy, the smooth, new boy with a scarcely-concealed ambition to be top kid on the block; he's the most dangerous of all, not least to himself. And the kingpin is Dick, who hatches the scheme and tries to keep everyone in line. He has the shell of authority but not, being as hooked as any of them, the substance. This makes him an acting problem, and one that Ron White, though perfectly watchable, fails to solve. The writing traps him; he has lines that sound like failed Damon Runyon and, unlike the others, is given no real chance to implode.

The staging moves easily from Dicks room, where the four plan their caper, to the car from which they execute it. This last scene is a paradox; its absorbing but almost totally lacking in suspense. We relish the actors, and we appreciate the situation, but we couldn't care less what happens to the characters. Their own insensibility seems to have seeped into the writing. By the end, two of them have taken a dive while the others are back exactly where we found them; it's undeniably elegant, an apt metaphor for a circular existence, but no more than that. There seems to be nothing beneath the plays surface that really matters to the writer -- which, in a first play, is a considerable surprise. Its a diploma piece. It can hardly be called promising, because it's not fulfilled. And it offers no clues whatever to its author's future.

The Crow's Theatre production of High Life is playing at Harbourfront Centre in Toronto.
1997-03-08-theatre-review-the-attic-the-:
THE ATTIC, THE PEARLS AND 3 FINE GIRLS

THEATRE REVIEW

THE ATTIC, THE PEARLS AND 3 FINE GIRLS

Saturday, March 8, 1997

Created by Jennifer Brewin,

Leah Cherniak, Ann-Marie

MacDonald, Alisa Palmer

and Martha Ross

Directed by Alisa Palmer

Starring Leah Cherniak,

Ann-Marie MacDonald

and Martha Ross

Rating: 

Sisters wrestle skeletons in attic

AS a title, The Attic, The Pearls and 3 Fine Girls has an attractive lilt, not to mention a cute internal rhyme. It also boasts a pun. The piece that lurks beneath concerns a trio of sisters who are indisputably Fine by name and, more debatable, by nature. When they apply the adjective to themselves (and nobody else gets the chance, since they are the only characters) they do it with a certain irony. They have, in short, their hangups. But then who hasn't?

Theres Jo-Jo, an academic with uncertain career prospects ("If I were a lesbian, Id have tenure"); Jayne, who is a corporate raider and has the cellphone to prove it (she is a lesbian, but seems uptight about it); and Jelly, who is some kind of artist and has a floppy kind of personality (she, to her sisters' mild surprise, is pregnant). Their father has just died, and they have reunited in the family home for the most chaotic wake since Finnegans. In between the festivities, which are off-stage, they indulge in recrimination and remembrance, which are very much on stage.

To do this they retreat to the attic, suggested with brilliant economy in Dany Lyne's design by opening a trap in the stage floor and tilting two flanking sets of window frames to a smart and threatening diagonal. This upper room was also the site of the most intense scenes of their girlhood, one or two of which are recreated. As for the pearls in the title, they belonged to their late mother and are much coveted and much mentioned, although they never take on any compelling dramatic reality. Neither do the deceased parents, or the family friends and connections (including one ex-husband) hovering below. And, most damaging, despite their continuous visibility, neither do the Fine girls themselves.

The actresses playing them do. The show, moderately witty and physically very accomplished, has the feel of an acting exercise. The three performers are also three-fifths of the credited creative team; the others are Alisa Palmer, who directed, and Jennifer Brewin, whose job description is contributing artist. Leah Cherniak as Jelly and Martha Ross as Jo-Jo devote a lot of energy to being competitively flaky. Jayne is set apart because she belongs to what the business pages call "the real world." This doesnt make her any less desperate -- more, if anything -- but it does enforce a trim exterior to set off the inside churnings, and Ann-Marie MacDonald has the style, the poise and the technique to bring it off. She gets some of her best effects in off-hand sotto voce (theyve given me mergers and acquisitions, she mutters proudly),and when she and her siblings take us back to the wild days of their youth, it's she who can take fullest advantage of the contrast. The sight of two women twisting to an old record of Roaming in the Gloaming is striking enough; when one of them is MacDonald in a tartan beret, black bra, skirt and leopard-skin coat, it stakes a claim to the history books.

One scene does have autonomous life. It's a flashback in which Jelly, the youngest, is terrorized by her siblings when they tell her their parents will not be returning from an evening out. "Are they angels yet?" she asks. Its a brief, imaginative sequence that says much about childhood fears and cruelties, and also hints at why Jelly has wobbled so much in later life. Nothing else has that concentration. Its a foregone conclusion that, after all the jokes and the angst, the evening will end in some kind of sisterly affirmation. But if it's a self-indulgent occasion, the actors themselves have probably earned the right.

The Attic, The Pearls and 3 Fine Girls is at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre on Alexander Street through March 30.
1997-03-14-musical-review-damn-yankees:
DAMN YANKEES

MUSICAL REVIEW

DAMN YANKEES

Friday, March 14, 1997

Written by George Abbott,

Douglass Wallop, Richard Adler

and Jerry Ross

Directed by Jack O'Brien

Starring Jerry Lewis

Rating: 

Jerry Lewis in a devil of a role

Special to The Globe and Mail

A VETERAN comedian in full command of his means can take authority and relaxation to supernatural heights. In his last years George Burns, you will remember, took to playing God. Jerry Lewis has gone the other way.

In Damn Yankees he portrays Mr. Applegate, a.k.a. Satan, who purchases the soul of a middle-aged Washington baseball fan or, more precisely, takes it on consignment. Paunchy Joe Boyd is diabolically transformed into svelte Joe Hardy, the star hitter who will take the hitherto despised Washington Senators to victory over their hated foes, the New York Yankees. Hence the shows title, which has always seemed to me to come -- there is no other way to put it -- out of left field; the damnation is certainly pertinent, but the Yankees only function in the story as an offstage threat.

Like Christopher Marlowes Mephistopheles in Dr. Faustus , Applegate doesn't have to be conjured; he comes when he scents a likely customer. He arrives in a puff of smoke (the show is full of incendiary gags) but once there he just stands, Jerry Lewis immaculate in yachting blazer and glossy black hair, and waits sardonically. The script allows the devil no weak moments, and neither does the performer. It's an astonishingly economical and unsentimental performance, to rank with Lewiss egomaniacal talk-show host in King of Comedy .

He does make a few concessions, moments -- seconds, usually -- when he turns on his hysterical baby voice. He is also likely to seal a joke or a plot twist by turning to the audience with his trademark slack-jawed grin: a look that simultaneously signals complicity and denial. Having delivered what he must assume is expected of him (and the audience response suggested that his assumption is correct), he clicks back to business. He hasnt yet attained the Burns state of grace, which makes every line sound funny, and he doesn't exert himself too much in the matter of inventive line readings, but his timing is expectedly perfect. He has bite to match his bark. (All the actors in this show bark. So does the orchestra. It must be the amplification.)

In the second act he interrupts his one solo song to don a hat and jacket of appropriately infernal red, catch or artfully drop a series of canes hurled at him from the wings, and tell a string of jokes preserved in aspic from the palmy days of burlesque. They're rude and, at least as he does them, hilarious. Even as written, the second act of this musical tends to splinter into a series of specialty numbers, so this extra-special one cant hurt. Besides, if there is a devil he might very well be playing Vegas, and as most of the monologue involves sex, religion or both, it could even be defended as having character relevance. The great thing about this performance is that, though you have to admire Jerry Lewis in order to enjoy it, you dont have to find him endearing. That could even be a handicap.

The song itself (Those Were the Good Old Days ) is a barely serviceable comedy soft-shoe; this devil does not have the best tunes. Most of those go to his assistant, a vamp called Lola. Joe's contract has an escape clause, and Lola ("a little brains, a little talent") is enlisted to keep him off the straight and narrow. She does this mainly by gyrating. The role, which back in 1955 made Gwen Verdon a star, requires a performer who can project sex and satirize it at the same time. April Nixon is stuck at the first fence (all right, first base); whatever Lola wants, Lola gets, but this one's horizons seem unduly limited.

Still, she dances well, and in that respect shes in terribly good company. My memories of the movie, closely based on the 1950s stage original, are dim, so I cannot say how much Rob Marshalls choreography owes to Bob Fosse's; in the case of the spectacular mambo Who's Got the Pain I suspect its a lot. But that number, and a graphically funny losers ballet for the maladroit Senators -- with their famous morale-building Heart routine -- and the country cut-up Shoeless Joe from Hannibal Mo (dynamically led by Ellen Grosso as an intrepid sports reporter), are legitimate show-stoppers.

The ballads in the score by Richard Adler and Jerry Ross are far less effective (and the whole was a step back from their previous hit, The Pajama Game ). There has been much rewriting of the original book, and the tension between Lola and Joe has gone. Their duet Two Lost Souls has been reassigned to Lola and her master, who doesn't need it. This Lola never really tempts Joe, never goes soft on him, and the discomfiting moment in the film when the vengeful Applegate turned her back into an old crone has been cravenly eliminated. This makes young Joe (John-Michael Flate) into an innocent sap hardly worth playing. He spends a lot of time hanging round his old house and his wife, who seems surprisingly unperturbed by his disappearance; what emotion there is comes from Dennis Kelly's crinkly performance as his older self. Douglas W. Schmidts sets, including a kitchen in a bilious shade of salmon pink, do a neat and not unfriendly job on 1950s domesticity, but the script and the direction stick at automatic caricature; the suburbanites overact hysterically, except for those who underact hysterically.

These sins are serious but, in context, venial. There is a star performance, a smart staging, and a supercharged ensemble. (Did I mention Joseph R. Sicaris crackling coach? Well, I have now.) Star and production could probably exist independently of one another, but it's nice that they don't. This show is in far better shape than most of the roadshows that check in at the O'Keefe (sorry, at Hummingbird; old habits die hard). And now please can they bring in Carousel ?

At Hummingbird Centre for the Performing Arts through Sunday.
1997-03-17-theatre-review-my-mother-s-co:
MY MOTHER'S COURAGE

THEATRE REVIEW

MY MOTHER'S COURAGE

Monday, March 17, 1997

Written by George Tabori

Directed by Jennifer H. Capraru

Starring Elizabeth Shepherd,

Richard Partington, Bruce Alexander Pitkin,

Margaret Lamarre and Tom Barnett

Rating: ½

Jennifer Capraru's direction of George Tabori's play,

about the playwright's mother who must face the enemy,

is spare and superb.

Special to The Globe and Mail

ELIZABETH Shepherd's performance in the title role of My Mother's Courage is magnificent, possibly the finest piece of acting I have seen in Canada. Before exploring it I had better sketch in the background.

In his more than 80 years of life, the playwright George Tabori has lived and worked in half a dozen countries. The first was Hungary from which he escaped when Nazism loomed. His father was arrested and gassed; his mother too was taken but survived. My Mother's Courage is Tabori's dramatization of her miraculous escape. She had extraordinary luck, but the miracle was within her.

A modestly elegant, self-effacing Jewish lady, Elsa Tabori is picked up one morning in a Budapest street (by, in this telling, a couple of superannuated Keystone Kops), taken to a railway terminal crammed with human fear, misery and bewilderment, and herded into a cattle car. At the border they are to be transferred from a Hungarian train to a German one. At the checkpoint, Elsa finds herself propelled (almost literally) into the presence of the supervising German officer. Through her terror, she senses a discord between him and his Magyar subordinate and insinuates herself within it. She tells a story that the German chooses to believe. He sends her back home. The evening finds her in the apartment of her sister and brother-in-law, which is where she had been going that morning when she was arrested. She has been through the entire Holocaust experience, or a good part of it, in a single day, and come out the other side.

In his voluminous writings on the camps, George Steiner, the cultural critic, has repeatedly emphasized one of their salient horrors: that they existed in the same time frame as what we call normal life and that a victim could slip in a moment from one world to the other. This play makes it real. Mother Tabori acts out her account on stage (presumably as she told it to son George), and he, also on stage, introduces, narrates and comments on it. Does he ever. The play is partly about their relationship as mother and son, and even more as author and subject. It's also, I suppose, about the impossibility of dramatizing the events it depicts. This last point the play comes uncomfortably close to proving. The Mother complains that George, clever as he is, distorts things by embellishing them; and one often wants to throw something at him, to make him shut up.

At Theatre Passe Muraille the problem is compounded. On the first night, Richard Partington, who plays the son and apparently came into the production late, was not on top of his lines; there are so many of them, and they are so literary. Even without his obvious insecurity, the bland geniality of his performance might have seemed overdone: too much for the space, too much for the play. For the familiar lesser horrors of the beginning, such as the yellow star and the neighbourly insults, the script employs a tiresome cartoon style, to which the narrator liberally contributes. As the grip tightens, though, we are increasingly able to tune him out. We take in the facts and discard the mannerisms.

Jennifer H. Capraru's direction is otherwise spare and superb, visually and emotionally. Bruce Alexander Pitkin and Margaret Lamarre between them play a variety of victims and persecutors with wit and precision. Tom Barnett gives a troubled and troubling sympathy to the merciful Nazi who will balk at eating meat, speak sorrowfully of anti-Semitic incidents in his home town, and spare one woman (and order her a hot meal) while dispatching thousands of others in squalor to be slaughtered.

In the play's great speech, the Mother reflects on her mingled love and hate for this man. She had caught his attention, established herself in his mind as an individual, by fixing him with her still-beautiful blue eyes, but now she says, "beware of looking the enemy in the eye, my darling, or you might stop hating him and thus betray the dead." (She too can only hate people in the mass.)

One of the glories of Elizabeth Shepherd's performance is that she can play this passage for anger, with no hint of weakness and no drive for sympathy, and still move you with it: to tears in my case. This is authentic passion, experience distilled. Technically, the performance is immaculate; within its first two minutes she is required to sigh fatalistically in half a dozen keys, and she keeps each modulation distinct, appropriate, and, given the circumstances, hilarious. Physically she is perfect: a comfortable, golden-haired woman with more bloom, outside and in, than she might suspect. (Her journey includes a furtive and bizarre sexual encounter.) She affects no heavy accent, but her voice still resonates with what we take to be Middle European wisdom.

The play's title is, of course, a joke on Bertolt Brecht; and Tabori has been a leading Brechtian in his time. He is still using some of the techniques; and the play proves, what I have long suspected, that "alienation" is not a means of denying emotion but of questioning, channelling, and finally strengthening it. Some of the tricks are irritating, but the story transcends them. What Tabori is finally saying about his mother is that he never knew she had it in her; and she, whatever their differences, would agree.

Here, we have an added dimension; I have always respected Shepherd's acting, though I would never before have called her great. But, as with the character, the situation has called something forth. Our first sight is of her carrying a candle, presumably for remembrance, with grave, silent authority. The image returns at the end, and it's a consummation.

My Mother's Courage is on at Theatre Passe Muraille's Backspace, through March 30.
1997-03-21-theatre-review-come-good-rain:
COME GOOD RAIN

THEATRE REVIEW

COME GOOD RAIN

Friday, March 21, 1997

Written, directed, performed

by George Seremba

Rating: ½

Out of the heart of darkness

When Ugandan actor and activist takes centre stage,

his role requires him to be as theatrically

true as he is factually believable.

Special to The Globe and Mail

GEORGE Seremba survived torture and attempted execution in his native Uganda, and this one-man show is his story. He is also a professional actor and writer. His writing, on this evidence, is lively and evocative, at its best when swift and humorous. It can also be elaborately, and unconvincingly, literary. His acting has a sympathetic openness that carries him a long way, but rhythmically he is monotonous. Blessings and curses, memories and forebodings, all go to the same tune. And already I feel guilty.

He is at his best when at his most observant. He offers a humorous memoir of schooldays in the early days of Ugandan independence. He was asked to inform on fellow students heard speaking in African dialects; on one level this is a wry hangover from colonialism, on another a chilling forecast of the pervasive espionage of future years. He goes on to evoke the whispered barroom conversations on deaths and disappearances ("Did you hear about so and so?" "Yes, how sad indeed.") that characterized the successive terrors of Milton Obote and Idi Amin. He remembers cheering the first appearance of Amin as a reassuring father-figure ("the gentle giant") and remembers a choice malapropism in the General's professed wish to "undress the queen" on Ugandan soil. Seremba himself survived Amin, though he had to take refuge in Kenya. On his return, though, he was arrested by the security forces of the reinstated Obote. They beat him, humiliated him, took him to a forest -- a notorious killing site under two regimes -- shot him and left him for dead. The rain helped to stanch his multitude of wounds; friendly hands rescued him and smuggled him out of the country. Some of the helpers were his relatives. In one of the play's more resonant lines, he thanks God "for the African extended family."

His words ring less effective when he recreates his thought processes on the way to and from the place of execution. These thoughts were amazingly magnanimous (to use his own bitingly satirical word about Amin, just prior to his expulsion of Uganda's Asians); Seremba seems to have been as much concerned with the fate of his friends and his country as with his own. I don't doubt him, and I honour him, but I do find it hard to believe that the words in his head were as eloquently organized as the ones that come out on the stage.

This is a story that should be told. The theatre -- the most immediate of all narrative forms -- is an excellent place to tell it; and Seremba, perhaps uniquely among victims, has the skills to do it in his own person. But those skills impose their own standards. A non-actor getting up on stage and recounting his experiences would be a different matter; an actor impersonating Seremba would be yet another. Because he's playing himself -- something actors, with very good reason, rarely do, however much they may draw on their own personalities -- the demands on his credibility are extreme. He has to be not just factually believable (no problems there), but theatrically true. And, however much I might tell myself that I, who had never been through anything remotely comparable, had no right to judge, he lost me.

He also leaves a lot out. He seems to have been a fairly apolitical drama student at Makerere University. Suddenly he's an activist and a refugee; what were the stages between? The things he tells us about the world around him are fascinating; and one wants more facts, less lyricism. There is an obvious comparison with George Tabori's My Mother's Courage ,that other survivor's story about which I raved earlier this week. If anything the Tabori play has too many devices but in the end, by distancing its subject, it brings us closer to it. Both plays, by the way, begin with the protagonist entering, bearing a candle. Seremba gets excellent support from the drumming, alternately healing and threatening, of Emman Mutema.

Come Good Rain is at Factory Theatre Studio Space until April 6.
1997-03-22-i-d-love-to-win-but-i-m-reali:
IN PERSON / Oscar nominee Brenda Blethyn isn't a a marquee type, but she does have stellar talent, says a critic who spotted her potential early on.

'I'd love to win, ... but I'm realistic about it.'

IN PERSON / Oscar nominee Brenda Blethyn isn't a a marquee type, but she does have stellar talent, says a critic who spotted her potential early on.

Saturday, March 22, 1997

Special to The Globe and Mail

FOR several weeks now my local movie theatre has been showing Secrets and Lies ,"nominated" as the marquee proudly proclaims, "for five Oscars." That, of course, is a recent announcement. Before it came along the sign said, "Winner -- Golden Globes -- Best Actress."

It didn't say who the victorious performer actually was. You can see the theatre's point. Brenda Blethyn took home a best actress award from Cannes before collaring a Golden Globe, and she has a chance at an Oscar. But she is not a marquee name. Perhaps, more significant, she isn't a marquee type. She is, as far as a 51-year-old never-out-of-work actress can be, the girl next door. Not American small-town -- which has always signalled an acceptably glamorous kind of ordinariness -- but British big-city.

British actors picking up showbiz prizes have an endearing knack of enjoying the hype without surrendering to it. Watching Blethyn pick up her Golden Globe was a treat. When she said that she'd been thrilled to get into the building, let alone win a prize, you believed her. She said it with the same kind of high-pitched breathlessness that Cynthia, her character in Secrets and Lies ,uses to greet extremes of good and bad news. You believe her , too.

As Blethyn said herself, in an interview from an L.A. hotel room, "You don't expect to see someone like Cynthia" -- a scatty, guilelessly earnest factory worker and single parent -- "at the Academy Awards." Secrets and Lies ,like all the films and plays directed by Mike Leigh, was created using an improvisational style, so the presence of Cynthia's creator at the luncheon for nominees seemed to have caused confusion.

"I was introduced to one woman who slapped her husband and said, 'I told you you should have voted for her,' " said Blethyn. The husband's excuse was that he'd thought the movie's performers were all playing themselves and, therefore, it didn't count as acting. Others have been even less sophisticated. One admirer, congratulating her on her newfound stardom, asked her, "But won't you miss all your friends at the factory?"

In fact, Blethyn said, "One rule of working with Mike is that you don't become the character. After every improvisation, you have to stand back and discuss the person very objectively."

And the people Leigh works with are certainly not inspired amateurs; he habitually casts the best and most experienced actors in the British theatre. Secrets and Lies was only Blethyn's third movie, but she has worked consistently on stage and television for 20 years.

The foundations of her career were laid at the National Theatre, which she joined in 1976 and where she stayed for nearly a decade. She didn't become famous, but she did get respect. In the star-oriented regime of director Peter Hall, she was the only actor to work her way up steadily from walk-ons to leads.

Initially she shone in contemporary comedy, especially the kind of sharp, class-conscious plays associated with Britain's most prolific playwright, Alan Ayckbourn; she was indelibly sad and perky as a put-upon young wife in his funniest play, Bedroom Farce .

Initially nervous of the classics, she became an expert in Restoration comedy. Comedy has been her lifeline; she has the intensity to convey the self-absorption that underlies half the great characters in comedy, and the vulnerability for the self-doubt that plagues the other half. (Cynthia has both.)

Maybe the defining point was a play called Steaming ,set in a Turkish bath, which she did just after leaving the National and in which she had to spend the entire evening being both naked and eccentric. Recently she has found a home at one of Britain's finest regional theatres, the Royal Exchange in Manchester. She is "most proud" of playing Nora in Ibsen's A Doll's House there.

She has also done a lot of TV sitcoms. The one she's proudest of is Outside Edge , which has gone into three series in Britain, winning awards for her and for the writer.

Bourgeois British comedy also led to her first brush with Hollywood, in Robert Redford's A River Runs Through It . "I was in a play in New York, Ayckbourn's Absent Friends . A friend of Redford's came to see it and said, 'You should cast the English girl.' "

She had worked with Leigh once before, on a BBC film called Grownups , which had left her with "a wonderful sense of achievement. You get to use your brain with Mike. When he called me for Secrets and Lies -- I hadn't spoken to him for a couple of years -- he just said, 'Well, are you going to be in my film or not?' When I signed on, I was told nothing. He said that he might like to do a film about adoption, but it might change.

"Mike is in charge of the circumstances in which we find ourselves; he has the map. But every line that I speak has come from me. The words come easy. Some things that Cynthia says are deeply tragic. And funny. Like when she says to her daughter, 'You want to get yourself a coil fitted -- that's how I got saddled with you.' " She's especially proud of the companion line, "I've got a Dutch cap floatin' about somewhere upstairs," spoken with earnest concern.

Having given his actors their heads, Leigh is a ruthless, rigorous editor. The meeting between Cynthia and Hortense, the child she had given away for adoption now grown to a woman, is an extraordinary 12-minute single take in the film; when first improvised it ran four to five hours.

"I thought the film would be well appreciated: I didn't expect it to reach these dizzy heights. It struck a chord. The number of people who've approached me saying they were adopted. . . . The records have been closed in the States, you can't trace who your birth-parents are. Some cinemas have been picketed by a group called Bastard America who want to get the law changed. And people like the optimism in it."

When not promoting Secrets and Lies , she's been making a domestic comedy called Music from Another Room in Pasadena, Calif., and after the Oscars she flies home to start on "a buddy-movie with Julie Walters," called Girls' Night. Since the nomination, she is being sent many more scripts.

"People say, of course you won't be doing any more theatre. Not 'arf I won't be. I'm not going to give up theatre. Have I changed? Certainly not. People's attitudes to me have changed. And they'll probably change again when I don't win.

"I'd love to win, I'd love to, but I'm realistic about it. My head may be in the clouds, but my feet are firmly on the ground." And she hasn't prepared an acceptance speech.

I have to get personal. When Brenda Blethyn had been at the National Theatre for about two years I reviewed her in a play called The Guardsman . She had already done a lot of good work, but to the world at large, her name seemed to mean as little on a theatre program as it would now on my local movie marquee. This time she played the maid, and was hysterical. "Miss Blethyn," I wrote, "deserves a paragraph" and proceeded to give her one. Shortly afterward we were introduced and she told me that her colleagues had taken to calling her Miss Paragraph. Anyway I did notice -- and she has confirmed -- that from that point onward, her profile in the company markedly improved. So for once a critic did good. I feel not only implicated but -- to use her favourite superlative -- proud. I shall be rooting for her.
1997-03-22-circus-gothic:
CIRCUS GOTHIC

THEATRE REVIEW

CIRCUS GOTHIC

Saturday, March 22, 1997

Kudelka's many faces spin heads

Special to The Globe and Mail

JAN Kudelka is a lavishly accomplished actress who ran away to join a circus. She interrupted a promising career in conventional theatre to enroll in a classical clowning class, on the intelligent theory that learning to be a clown would make her a better actress.

Some weeks into the class, the teacher informed his students that they would be hitting the road and the sawdust. They were joining an American big-top troupe on a trek through the Maritimes. This show is her solo re-creation of the experience: A tale, theoretically at least, of three worlds colliding -- the circus professionals, the earnest novices and the audience.

Kudelka, it seems, can do anything. She can stand on a stage and be a still centre of energy. She can tell jokes, with minimum effort and maximum point. She can sing, melodiously and expressively. She can do tricks; at one point, out of nowhere, her face suddenly sprouts a red nose.

She can suggest any number of characters and switch instantaneously from one to another. Her own speaking voice is warm and dark, and physically she is somewhere between plump and compact. When she's playing herself, her tousled enthusiasm with a tart topping sometimes recalls Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Seinfeld 's Elaine.

There are, of course, different kinds of clowning. Kudelka's teacher, the late Richard Kosinko, used masks to release the inner clown, and hence the inner self. The circus types, not surprisingly, found this very high-flown and irrelevant and shocked their new apprentices by demanding slapstick.

It's an interesting battle (one in which my money is firmly on the Philistines), but it's never really pursued. For most of the show, the circus is on parade: the most unforgettable characters the author ever met, all briefly remembered. We learn of the tensions between performers and roustabouts, who, when young love tries to cross the lines, might just as well be Montagues and Capulets. We encounter stony-faced New Brunswickers trying to make the circus leave town, or their drunken partners taunting the acts from the sidelines. We spend a lot of time with Elly the elephant, one of Kudelka's most sympathetic assumptions, swaying gently from side to side as she bemoans the lack of water in her life: "Rain is no good -- you don't get soaked, you just get moist."

This is the second monodrama I have encountered in two days. Kudelka avoids some of the autobiographical pitfalls that beset George Seremba in Come Sweet Rain . For one, she isn't much of a presence in her own story, and when she wants to talk about herself she goes into standup comedy, a separate discipline in which she seems thoroughly accomplished.

Her story, though, is not as moving and compelling as Seremba's. In fact, I'm not sure it exists. She's a more resourceful performer, but she falls victim to her own facility. As she switches nimbly from one role to another, variety imposes its own monotony. We never feel we've met any of these people; they're snapshots in an album or butterflies daintily impaled behind glass. I wanted to get some actors in, cast them, and see if we might have a play.

She doesn't have a point of view, only the idea of one: something about "the rhythm of the circus is disaster." Mayhem does strike in the end, and it's quite powerfully conveyed, at least on a technical level. (Like Seremba, Kudelka gets invaluable support from her musician, Cameron Shook, who plays xylophone, guitar, musical glasses, drum and a variety of pipes.) But underneath it's just the dreaded spirit of Pagliacci descending again. It seems a waste: Jan Kudelka is too clever to be messing around with brokenhearted clowns.

Circus Gothic is running at Artword Theatre in Toronto until March 30.
1997-03-25-theatre-review-mrs-warren-s-p:
MRS. WARREN'S PROFESSION

THEATRE REVIEW

MRS. WARREN'S PROFESSION

Tuesday, March 25, 1997

Directed by Sarah Stanley

Written by Bernard Shaw

Starring Colleen Williams

and Deborah Lambie

Rating: 

Mrs. Warren needs some work

For a woman who made it rich as a prostitute and madam, Kitty

is rather downtrodden and her daughter Vivie is rather smug.

Special to The Globe and Mail

B

ERNARD Shaw called his first batch of plays "Plays Unpleasant," but they are among the most palatable things he ever wrote. He had yet to construct his own myth or believe fully in his own publicity; his trick of stating hard truths or outrageous paradoxes with a sweet smile had not hardened into mannerism; and his concentration on specific social abuses kept his wit barbed and focused.

Mrs. Warren's Profession , the third and last in the group (it was written in 1894), is about prostitution and society's complicity in it. As a girl, Kitty Warren turned from a life of near-starvation as a domestic or barmaid to a successful career as a prostitute, then to a madam. With a chain of brothels all over Europe, she has put her daughter, Vivie, through college on the proceeds. (Vivie, like her mother, is brilliant at figures.)

Mother and daughter have seen very little of each another, but now, over a couple of days at an English country cottage, Vivie learns the truth about her mother's past (which she doesn't criticize) and about her highly profitable present. Vivie rejects her mother's support, peremptorily ends a romance with the son of the local clergyman and takes off to London to become a partner in a friend's actuarial business.

The first half of Sarah Stanley's production looks Edwardian, as much as it looks anything. In the second half, things begin to slip a bit. Some costumes look modern; a character reads Time Out, the London listings weekly; and Vivie's office desk sports a laptop computer. The nudging is gratuitous -- you would have to cast this play with inaudible actors to stop it from ringing loud contemporary bells -- and it's far too fragmentary and unimaginative to constitute a style.

This play about the sex trade hardly mentions sex; the furthest even Mrs. Warren herself goes is to refer to her "turn for pleasing men." (The reticence may have been Shaw's as much as his characters'; he could flout the censor's taboos while leaving his own intact.) To compensate, the director has young Frank, Vivie's intended, push his hand up her skirt after receiving an exaggerated, unmaternal kiss from Mrs. Warren.

Despite that, the main erotic energies are homosexual. Mrs. Warren has an artist friend called Praed who's meant to represent the sentimental assumptions of the average audience; here he's a dear old queen (or, in Greg Kramer's performance, a mincing caricature of one) who appears to have an understanding with Vivie's young man. Vivie herself practically turns a double somersault when freed from her entanglement, and is plainly about to settle for domesticity with her business partner, Honoria, who is this production's off-stage heroine. (The producers call themselves The Honoria Project.)

Well, it's a point of view. It might even, if consistently and skillfully carried out, enrich the play. What makes this production so monumentally crass is not what is put in but what is left out. It lurches from one painfully bright idea to another. The director thinks she has a melodrama on her hands and self-consciously spoofs a moment of coincidence that is not, in fact, especially far-fetched. Actually, the play is what used to be called a "strong" society drama, in which one painful revelation inexorably gives way to another; as such, it is gripping, morally and dramatically.

But this director seems unable to orchestrate action or dialogue. The two women have two great scenes: one in which Mrs. Warren tells all (well, some), the other in which Vivie casts her off. These, by any reckoning, are traumatic encounters, but the actresses never make contact with their own emotions or with one another. They never seem purposefully to avoid it, either; they just wander gracelessly around the stage awaiting the next cue.

For a woman who got rich on her charm and guts, and who her daughter calls "the strongest woman in England," Colleen Williams is amazingly dowdy and downtrodden, likelier to be cleaning the house than running it. It also doesn't help that she's much shorter than her daughter. Deborah Lambie as Vivie is livelier, but much of her spirit comes out as spite, and her self-confidence as sheer smugness. Despite what they keep telling us, they don't seem to be going through anything.

John Blackwood plays Sir George Crofts, a tweedy club man who has profitably invested in what he likes to call the Warren hotel business. He's too lightweight, probably too young, not nearly coarse-grained enough, and, in general, comes over as a pantomime villain rather than a repulsive fact of economic life. Given all that, he isn't bad.

The performer who comes nearest to making the show work is Jim Jones as Frank. Initially, he seems to have decided that a feckless young gentleman who spouts period slang must, by definition, be a ninny out of P. G. Wodehouse, but he develops some brains and a dandyish sense of irony. His wit is fussier than Shaw's and takes up a lot more time, but it does have presence.

Whereas presence, for the first three-quarters of the evening, is totally lacking in Wendy White's sets, which are barren. Turns out they were being saved for the last office scene, which has a cunning sense of elevation. For the most part, however, this is amateur night.

Mrs. Warren's Profession runs at the Tarragon Extra Space until April 5.
1997-03-29-theatre-review-the-soldier-dr:
THE SOLDIER DREAMS

THEATRE REVIEW

THE SOLDIER DREAMS

Saturday, March 29, 1997

Written by Daniel MacIvor

Directed by Daniel Brooks and Daniel MacIvor

Rating: ½

Soldier comes off vague and arid

Special to The Globe and Mail

TWO Daniels have come to judgment. The Soldier Dreams was written by Daniel MacIvor, adapted for the stage by Daniel Brooks, and directed by the two of them together. The refining process has been going on through three years of trial runs and the final accomplishment is decidedly mixed. The form is often brilliant, the content banal to non-existent.

It's about death: doing it and watching it. A performance piece rather than a play, it has an exquisite score (by Richard Feren) and wonderful lighting (uncredited). Right at the start the two combine in a remarkably powerful theatrical statement: total darkness, daringly prolonged, over wrenchingly beautiful music. When at last the lights go up, they reveal a rectangular slab of stage, set well back and harshly illuminated against a wall-and-floor surround of implacable beige. Within this compartment are a sick bed and its attendants. Some of the images in this show are worthy of Robert Lepage, though he would have given us more of them. Lepage's motor runs extravagantly fast; Brooks and MacIvor are more economic.

Dying in the bed is David; around him, bickering, are his two sisters, his brother-in-law, and his boyfriend. In turn, they step to the front of the stage and deliver valedictory statements on David, who is now deceased. Whether they are speaking to us or an imaginary audience at some kind of memorial is uncertain; either way, we get the point that they are far more concerned with themselves than they are with David. David himself also gets to talk. The body remains on the bed but a second actor, MacIvor himself, strolls down to utter the dying man's thoughts and to re-enact a remembered scene from his past: a one-night stand in Ottawa with a German medical student.

Verbally as well as visually, the piece is quite cunningly patterned. Somebody tells a funny story that Richard, David's lover, reckons to be homophobic. Later on we discover how the joke came into the family in the first place, and it casts a whole new light. Like citizen Kane mumbling about Rosebud, the dying man mutters a phrase that sets everybody guessing. In his case it's "the German doctor." With the benefit of flashback, we know what he's talking about, but the other characters are baffled. Richard's professions of ignorance are especially emphatic, so he may be covering up. We don't know or, speaking for myself, care. The encounter itself is written and acted -- by MacIvor and especially by Volker Burger as the German -- with considerable humorous delicacy, but it's an oasis. The main action is arid.

The idea is apparently that we will see these people appropriating David's memory to their own ends, but his memory, even in distorted form, hardly gets a look in. We merely listen to unexceptionally selfish people being unexceptionally selfish; that is no great revelation. Jim Allodi gets some interest out of the gangling brother-in-law and Blair Williams gets rather more out of the prickly Richard, whose role seems more vigorously and specifically written than the others. The women are unhelpfully stiff. There have been deathbed-vigil plays before. This one is less agonizingly portentous than Edward Albee's All Over ,less sentimentally uplifting than the musical Falsettoland ,but it doesn't have a compensating identity of its own.

We're never told that David is dying of AIDS, but audiences are bound to think so and wonder whether he caught it from the German. To the play's credit, it never tries to make aggrieved moral capital out of this, or anyway not much; it's the fact of death that's important here, not the cause. Given that, it might have been helpful to tell us and get it out of the way. The characters would know; why shouldn't the audience? Mystification is an element to be used with caution, and with the utmost rigour.

The general mood is despairing, in an unpushy sort of way. "Life," we are told, "is a war; even when the soldier dreams, the war goes on." David's time in Ottawa was apparently a brief time out of war, but death, we later learn, is the only real peace. Seems logical, if bleak, but the characterization is too vague to be truly tragic. David, everybody tells us, loved dancing, and it's no surprise when, in the play's last moments, he goes into a dance: a frantic, desperate one. Maybe he's raging against the dying of the light; maybe he's frantically embracing it.

The Soldier Dreams runs at Canadian Stage until April 12.
1997-04-03-theatre-review-arrhythmia-and:
ARRHYTHMIA AND BLUES

THEATRE REVIEW

ARRHYTHMIA AND BLUES

Thursday, April 3, 1997

Directed by Jim Warren

Written by Howie Wiseman

Starring Andrew Massingham, Rena Polley,

Catherine Hayos and Steven Morel

Rating: ½

Arrhythmia could leave you blue

Trying to get laughs from this source material

would give anyone a heart attack.

Special to The Globe and Mail

THE title, a forced and feeble pun, gives almost too much warning. You expect the worst. Arrhythmia and Blues is not quite that. But it is pretty bad.

There is a screenwriter called Leah (Rena Polley) who is now scripting her first TV sitcom. Her modest concept is an updating of the Book of Job, with Job recast as a woman, and God -- to judge from the brief excerpts vouchsafed us over the theatre sound-system -- as a Jewish mother. (Satan remains male. Wouldnt you know.) Trying to get laughs from this source material would be enough to give anyone a heart attack, and that is what happens to Leah. She checks into the emergency ward of a Winnipeg hospital. For the rest of the action she stays there.

Sharing the space with her are Mel (Andrew Massingham), a hypochondriac of awesome proportions with a special fixation on his bladder and bowels, and two members of staff. These are Dr. Margolis (Catherine Hayos) and Robert (Steven Morel), a nurse, both harassed and overworked, both -- as far as we can tell -- efficient and conscientious but humanly imperfect.

What is supposed to bind the quartet together is hard to make out. True, they're all under pressure, but who isn't? Leahs impending deadline and impatient employers push her further into trauma; at one point she tries to discharge herself, aided -- for inscrutable reasons -- by the omnipresent Mel. Presumably we are meant to see Leah as the female Job she is trying to write about. The story of Job depends for its effectiveness on two things. He was unusually happy and prosperous before his downfall, and he fervently believed in the God who tested and tormented him. Leahs precariously lucky break in television-land doesn't compare with Job's accumulation of family and livestock, her personal life consists of an ex-fiancé of whom we know nothing, and her thoughts and beliefs are a blank. When her boss fires her immediately after sending her chocolates its a sobering moment -- the only one in the show -- but it does not rank as a biblical catastrophe. It doesnt rank as anything.

The program describes the piece as written by Howie Wiseman. This "written by" credit -- as opposed to the simple traditional by -- is one I have learned to distrust; it suggests a plea of diminished responsibility. Certainly the writing here is weightless; loose ends trail, relationships fail to relate. Dr. Margolis may have been responsible for a patient's brain death. The patient is still on the ward, playing percussion. I thought for a while that this was just an atmospheric effect, but no, we actually get some hurried glimpses of him, beating out that rhythm on a drum. This is not, to put it naively, credible. And what's a chronic patient doing on an emergency ward?

The doctor is also pregnant; why? (No smart answers, please.) The actress doubles as the voice of God in Leahs sitcom, so maybe shes the Old Testament deity about to give birth to the New. And Mel plays the voice of Satan, so perhaps that's why he tempts Leah to leave the hospital, thereby courting certain death. On the other hand, most of the time, Mel is a victim, and I wish I hadn't started trying to make sense of all this.

Jim Warrens direction is pretty slick in the matter of moving beds and screens around, but it doesnt impose much coherence on the play's story or even, as things get increasingly frantic, on its geography. Stiletto Theatre Company, who present the show, have won praise in the past for their visual skills, and the actors here all look their parts to perfection, but they don't seem good with words. Each exists in his or her own bubble, with none of the pace or flexibility with which people, on stage or in life, actually talk to one another. Andrew Massingham, doing Mel as a gentle comedy turn, comes nearest to turning this liability into an asset, but even he gets wearing. Both the women are thoroughly wooden. Admittedly the dialogue doesnt give them much help but since they, along with the writer, are credited with "creating" the show, its difficult to feel too sorry for them.

One more thing. The hospital is closing down. The piece was apparently conceived before the official assault on Ontario's health-care system turned murderous, but there are obviously lines that now resonate unbearably (and I imagine a few have been added). The show is on the side of the angels, but that isn't enough. In fact, it gets to seem like unearned income. The giggly pretentiousness in the title makes for an uncommon combination, but in this case it's all too appropriate.
1997-04-07-theatre-review-fool-s-paradis:
FOOL'S PARADISE

THEATRE REVIEW

FOOL'S PARADISE

Monday, April 7, 1997

Fool's Paradise not the soul of wit

Special to The Globe and Mail

THIS is a comedy show. Two actors, got up like academics, introduce a third who says he's William Shakespeare, come from the grave to tell us about himself. The three shoot off a quick-fire volley of familiar phrases: "my salad days," "brevity is the soul of wit," "it was Greek to me," and dozens more. They say that every time we repeat one of them, we're quoting Shakespeare.

They're right, of course, though maybe not 100 per cent. Look at their title. They blame it on Romeo and Juliet . The Nurse in that play tells Romeo that if he should lead Juliet "into a fool's paradise, as they say, it were a very gross kind of behaviour." That "as they say" suggests that the phrase was already proverbial and that Shakespeare on this occasion was quoting someone else. For all that, the title is a good one, with far-reaching reverberations. It sums up the show, which exudes witless self-satisfaction.

That hardly makes it unique in the current Toronto theatre, and I confess that I am about to break a butterfly on a wheel. (I'm not quoting Shakespeare.) Fool's Paradise is only a lunch-time production, lasting less than an hour, playing twice daily on a tiny stage in Scotia Plaza to an audience that, at the second house last Friday, numbered about a dozen. Its three performers seem to know what they're doing, though not necessarily why. Mark Ellis, the trim and bearded fellow who plays Shakespeare, also does a very sharp impression of Sean Connery as he might be in Macbeth . His two colleagues -- Gerry Butts, a genial heavy, and Adrian Hough, a querulous zany -- are less good at this routine, and why it should take all three of them is a question. The answer seems to be that Ned Vukovic, the production's director and guiding light, doesn't know when to stop. (This is apart from the times when he shouldn't even start.) You take the famous Scottish play and the famous Scottish actor, put 'em together and what have you got? If you're smart and lucky, a 30-second gag. If you're here, a one-joke comic-strip reduction of the entire play, with all three actors mugging through their burrs, or burring through their mugs.

Well, at least it's not pretentious. Actually, it is, but without the courage of its conceit. It seems to want to say things about Shakespeare, or at least about the way Shakespeare gets done. "Shak" -- that's what they call him in the program though mercifully not on the stage -- gets to tell off Hollywood for adapting his old plays rather than doing originals (which is rich coming from him, the plagiarist's plagiarist) and then rounds on Kenneth Branagh for taking four whole hours over Hamlet . Ellis has a touch of Branagh himself in his voice and bearing, though it isn't exploited. By way of rebuke, he and his guys offer us their four-minute version.

When I was at school we used to do this kind of number in end-of-term revues, and we had the integrity to employ only lines from the original. Once you start paraphrasing ("I was screwed," says the Ghost), you lose the entire point. Lay coarse acting over a coarse script and you get something that seems, no kidding, much longer than the Branagh.

We are then promised some really bad acting. That sounds interesting. Bad acting has been known to happen in Canada, and even to raise cheers from audiences and raves from critics; it would be good to see it skewered. Bad Shakespearean acting, in any country, is an especially juicy target; but the satire here bears no relation to anything. It couldn't, because they're not playing Shakespeare, they're playing the history-play skit from the British revue Beyond the Fringe . (A great, great show, but that was never its finest five minutes.)

Later someone recites the lyric to A Hard Day's Night with the voice and gait of Laurence Olivier's Richard III. This is an old Peter Sellers turn, and even he could only make it funny for a moment. At the other side of the stage someone else does Richard's opening speech in the accents of John Lennon, which I suppose is more original. When he got to the line about the "wanton, ambling nymph," he added brightly "Yoko!" At which dismal moment I realized that the show would do anything for a laugh. In retrospect, I sympathize. By the time it was over I would have done anything for a laugh myself.

Fool's Paradise runs through May 2 at Solar Stage.
1997-05-01-theatre-review-candide:
CANDIDE

Theatre Review

CANDIDE

Thursday, May 1, 1997

Directed by Harold Prince

New York City -- Written by Leonard Bernstein, Hugh Wheeler and Richard Wilbur

Starring Jim Dale, Andrea Martin, Harolyn Blackwell and Jason Daniely

Rating: ½

Plenty of cause for gratitude

THEATRE REVIEW / Inspired by Voltaires satire,

Leonard Bernstein first created this Broadway comic opera

in 1956. More than 40 years later, Harold Prince's revision

balances spectacle, humour and music.

Special to The Globe and Mail

LEONARD Bernstein composed Candide as a Broadway comic opera, and ever since the piece's premiere in 1956 the constituent parts of that definition have been slugging it out. No production is ever likely to get the balance of music, laughter and spectacle completely right, but Harold Princes new staging comes closer than any I have seen or heard of. It looks and sounds wonderful.

The shows source is of course the 18th-century satiric novella by Voltaire, the story of the high-born innocents Candide and Cunegonde who are told by their beloved tutor, Dr. Pangloss, that all is for the best in this best of all possible worlds and who go on believing him through earthquakes, wars, inquisitions, multitudinous ravishments and endless chicanery. Finally, experience gets the better of them and they settle for the more practical and limited philosophy that Voltaire summed up as cultivating one's own garden and that Bernstein hymns in the soaring finale anthem Make Our Garden Grow . The cast's massed voices, largely unaccompanied, ring gloriously here; and the stage looks like a sunburst.

Radiance is a feature of Clarke Durhams sets throughout, much enhanced by Ken Billingtons lighting and matched by Judith Dolan's richly frolicsome costumes. The designs -- which, having enveloped the stage as far as the orchestra pit, extend their arms to fondle part of the auditorium as well -- are a rich old storybook come to life, revelling in rococo, occasionally going for baroque. The dazzle persists through some of the story's darkest episodes, but it can also abruptly darken. An auto-da-fé sequence that starts as black knockabout comedy suddenly goes quietly and authentically grim.

The production -- the first Livent production to start life in the United States rather than in Canada -- is both an expansion and a refinement of one that Prince first staged on Broadway in 1973 and has been revising in opera houses ever since. The 1973 treatment turned Candide from a classic flop destime into a commercial hit. It jettisoned Lillian Hellmans script -- which hewed as far as possible to the structure of the mid-century American well-made play -- and commissioned a new book from Hugh Wheeler far closer in form to the picaresque original. It stressed informality and fun, seating the spectators amid the action in an audience-friendly staging of which traces still remain. It also shredded the score, leaving out whole numbers and drastically reducing the sumptuously witty orchestrations. Since then, Prince and his colleagues have been putting back the music, and now in New York we have virtually the original score, though not in the original order.

Wheeler's revision has itself been revised (by uncredited hands -- Wheeler himself is dead); but it is perhaps a judgment on the show that it can be so readily rearranged. "Picaresque" on the stage has a way of translating into episodic and the most common criticism of the piece has always been that it goes on making the same point in different locations. Prince's light-handed direction certainly reins in the didacticism but in doing so it goes to the opposite extreme. We frequently lose the moral compass altogether. In this tale of innocents abroad we get plenty of abroad -- as the story ranges from Germany to Lisbon to Buenos Aires to the Amazon jungle to Venice -- but not much innocence. Its missing in Candide, and in Cunegonde.

Well, not so much in Candide. Jason Danielys performance is the first I have seen to justify the show's title. He sings like an especially agreeable bird, plays charmingly with the audience, and is a picture of tousle-haired integrity. But the script increasingly takes his idealism for granted, and his conversion doesn't mean much because there is -- a really crucial lack in this text -- no intervening period of disillusion. Harolyn Blackwell as Cunegonde sings even more spectacularly, especially in Glitter and Be Gay , a spoof of the Jewel Song from Faust with an amazing cascade of trills. (Youve heard of coloratura, but this is ridiculous.) The number is, as it should be, a tour-de-force; but theres something wrong with it. It's supposed to be about the battle in Cunegonde, the self-consciously wronged heroine, between outraged virtue and gratified greed. Each side gets half the song, in strict alternation, but she keeps anticipating the transitions; finally she stops playing them altogether. Blackwell doesn't act as well as she sings but the script and direction dont help her; this Cunegonde isnt allowed to be virginal even when she's a virgin. The character's basic joke has gone.

Still, there is that voice; and if the shows horticultural moral can be paraphrased as "take what you can and be grateful," this show gives plenty of cause for gratitude. It is funny and, perhaps more important, consistently and contagiously good-humoured.

Jim Dale, narrating as Voltaire and playing Pangloss and numerous others, is a splendidly laid-back compère, with the art that conceals energy. Andrea Martin rampages effusively as Cunegondes abused but resilient duenna . She shares the ingratiatingly hilarious tango I Am Easily Assimilated (Bernstein's own lyrics) with a troupe of superannuated caballeros , who keep falling down before her charms and then inconsiderately getting up again. Patricia Birch has choreographed them delightfully, as she has done the whole show; there always seems to be something surprising going on. The score, one of the great achievements of American music, is buoyantly conducted by Eric Stern.

The original 1956 lyrics, pointed and urbane, were the work of the poet Richard Wilbur. They were supplemented in 1973 by Stephen Sondheim who has supplied extra material this time round. (Perhaps it's as well that we dont know which lyricist to hold responsible for rhyming hopeful with "Constantinople.") So the show marks the Broadway reunion, after 15 years, of Prince and Sondheim, one of the theatres great teams. For Prince, it's a golden production; the stage goes through a whole palette of tones -- when the actors arrive in a cart, drawn by pantomime horses, to start things off, it seems at once rowdy and autumnal but it's that final sunburst that seems emblematic. No other director of musicals marshals actors and design so richly; no other uses colour so well. In some ways this Candide is like the Masquerade number in The Phantom of the Opera ,expanded to the dimensions of a carnival -- and what's more, an intelligent carnival. This is Broadway's greatest showman at his zenith.
1997-05-03-theatre-review-titanic:
TITANIC

THEATRE REVIEW

TITANIC

Saturday, May 3, 1997

Titanic awkward but moving

ALL jokes about the musical Titantic were made when the project was first announced; my own favourite was Linwood Barclay's prediction in the Toronto Star that it would be like "Show Boat but with greater depth." There were technical problems during previews; one audience had to be sent home with a happy ending since the damn ship just wouldn't sink . Anyway, the show opened; and despite its promise and some intemperate reviews, it is not such a spectacular disaster. In fact -- and this is the trouble -- it is hardly spectacular at all.

It is a decent-spirited, hard-working show, defeated by the magnitude of its subject, and by lapses in its execution: lapses of imagination, finesse and possibly finance. It starts all right with the doomed liner's architect singing proudly about his "floating city" being the early 20th-century's equivalent of the Parthenon and the Pyramids, an artistic and technological achievement that represents the era at its best. Then we're at Southampton, and passengers and crew are embarking on the Titanic's maiden and only voyage. We meet a representative selection, and are furnished with names and salient characteristics to be filed away for future reference. Finally everyone enters in a long line from the wings, and mounts the gangplank. It's a stirring moment; it brings home to us just how many and how varied lives are involved, thousands of them. The line should stretch out till the crack of doom, or at least to the end of the scene. But they run out of people, and can't find any way of disguising it.

It's moving, since we know that most of them are going to die. It's also predictable, since we know that most of them are going to die. That double bind works throughout the evening. It would take rare incompetence to make this story ineffective. It would take even rarer genius to bring it off completely. We get something between. Much is made of the segregation of classes that operated snobbishly during the voyage and fatally in the selection for the lifeboats. (Though we're never shown in detail how this happened; one thing the show seriously runs out of is time.)

People are always telling us, as if it were a new discovery, that class had a lot to do with the tragedy of the Titanic, which is seen as the symbolic ending of 19th-century privilege. This show, with a politically conscious stoker as one of its heroes, is no exception. We meet the captain, ironically relishing this as his last voyage before retirement, and the head of the shipping-line, a melodramatic villain all round, who is constantly urging increases in speed so that his product will have the edge in future advertising. (It's his fault there aren't enough boats; he wanted the deck-space in order to provide additional first-class luxuries.) In Richard Jones's production, Stewart Laing's sets go elaborately but not very excitingly up and down to reveal different cross-sections of the ship and its population.
