His costumes fall someway short of elegance, the seams metaphorically showing. When the ship finally hits its iceberg, the convention totally changes, the set disappears, and we watch a model ship cheerily steaming toward its doom. As a way of rendering the climactic moment, this is insufferably cute.

Maury Yeston's copious score includes a couple of neat ragtime-era pastiches but otherwise goes in for elaborate and extended underpinning of the action. It works well in the first half for premonition; in the second act, it starts to get in the way. Music, we are always told, can speed things up. But it can also slow them down, especially when words are sung that could just as well be said. Yeston's lyrics, much inferior to his music, are plodding and prosaic; once the crisis is under way, they can be maddening. Song titles such as Wake up, Wake up! and Dressed in Your Pyjamas in the Grand Salon , as the stewards rouse the passengers, should give you the idea. As the boats are lowered, those who are leaving and those who are staying find time to salute each other with an inspirational chant called We'll Meet Tomorrow . This is Broadway striking with a vengeance; and it strikes again when a Jewish couple who have elected to stay and drown together toast one another in a last bottle of vintage champagne, the man concluding their duet by smashing the glass beneath his feet as in a wedding ceremony. Doubtless Titanic had to be a musical to reach the Broadway stage at all. It didn't have to be that kind of musical.

Peter Stone's book carries the story with dignity and economy, and allows a stageful of good performances from an ensemble cast. (Alphabetical billing and all that jazz.) To particularize; John Cunningham keeps his beard wagging bravely as the captain, Michael Cerveris's architect is all neurotic sympathy, ending his life scribbling plans for a new craft free of all social barriers, as around him furniture slides along the tilting floor. Jennifer Piech rivets eye and ear as a sparky young Irishwoman, off to America in steerage to find a father for her unborn baby. In second class -- whose occupants seem livelier on the whole than either their betters or their inferiors -- Judith Blazor and Don Stephenson gleam with fun and mischief as an eloping couple. Everybody sings well. I laughed occasionally, cried quite often, but never held my breath.

Titanic is at the Lunt-Fontanne Theatre, New York, for an indefinite run .
1997-05-08-the-life:
THE LIFE

Thursday, May 8, 1997

Directed by Michael Blakemore

New York -- Written by Cy Coleman, Ira Gasman and David Newman

Starring Pamela Isaacs, Lillias White,

Sam Harris and Vernel Bagneris

Rating: 

Life's hard to love, but worth respect

Special to The Globe and Mail

NOBODY could accuse The Life of being a glitzy musical. It is, by Broadway standards, a small musical in a small theatre. The life in question is that of prostitution; the play also finds generous space for the life of pimping, and some for those of drug-dealing and addiction. They are all, of course, intertwined.

After a brief introduction sardonically lamenting the cleaning up of midtown Manhattan, it gets down to the business of business. We are whisked back to 1980 or thereabouts, when vice around Times Square was at its peak. It is celebrated, but it is not glamorized.

Sam Harris, a lithe and accomplished actor-singer-mover with bundles of CDs to his credit, plays Jo-Jo, a small-time procurer and yes-man on his way to the top, or at least to survival. Jo-Jo is our guide and, tirelessly ingratiating though he is, he may be the least endearing front man a musical has ever had -- Pal Joey with the lovable bits left out, or better yet, Sportin' Life from Porgy and Bess , after the boat that was leavin' soon for New York had finally got there; a white Sportin' Life, although most of the other characters in The Life are black.

By contrast, the warmest character is Sonja, 10 years on the streets and past her prime at 26. Lillias White plays her, and when she sings a bitingly uproarious song called The Oldest Profession ,she brings down the house, not only with her gospel trills -- which theatre audiences always rise to, regardless of context -- but with her intelligence. (It's implied that the character is an early victim of AIDS.) Then there's Vernel Bagneris, the rubber-legged hoofer from the show One Mo' Time and the film Pennies from Heaven , easing up as a bartender with memories of show-business glory.

The Life features a compact and compelling corps of characters going through flavourful routines about being busted on the street and charged at the station; numbers with blunt titles such as My Body or Why Don't They Leave Us Alone , which Joey McKneely, the show's choreographer, has mounted with aggressive insouciance. Everyone on stage seems at ease with sleaze.

Michael Blakemore, an ace among British directors, has staged these scenes for maximum character value against Robin Wagner's bleakly unforgiving set.

So far, so impressive -- an aware, updated Guys and Dolls . There is also a plot, which remains subordinate in the first half of the show but gets dangerously assertive in the second. To be exact, there are two plots. One concerns Mary (Bellamy Young) an apparently virginal new arrival from the sticks whom one of the guys picks up to prove to another that any chick can be turned to profitable account.

She turns out to be a lot more knowledgeable than they reckoned: an example of the show getting its cynical wires crossed. It seems to be trying to prove simultaneously that there is no innocence and that innocence can be corrupted. Mary ends up with a promising future in porno movies, singing an uncomfortable duet with her producer called People Magazine . We know the scene is meant to be ironic, but it doesn't play that way, maybe because the authors are completely inside their musical idiom rather than at a sarcastic distance from it.

Then there's the more momentous story of Fleetwood and Queen. Queen -- played with a warm heart, a sharp tongue and an invigorating larynx by Pamela Isaacs -- loves and works for Fleetwood (Kevin Ramsey), a Vietnam vet with a damaged psyche and a coke habit. Memphis, the top man on the block -- toweringly embodied and toweringly sung by Chuck Cooper -- wants Queen as part of his own stable. This triangle gets pounded through scenes alternately brutal and maudlin, taking up a lot of time and trailing a lot of loose ends.

The power of the show is Cy Coleman. He co-produced it, wrote the book (in collaboration with David Newman and lyricist Ira Gasman), collaborated on the dance and vocal arrangements, and composed the music. He is one of Broadway's best composers, about the only one who still writes what we used to call songs, that is, shapely, autonomous melodies that please on first encounter, sound as if they would bear rehearing and attract pungent and bouncy lyrics -- songs, that is, that you do not despise yourself for liking.

There are plenty of them here, in those sections of the show that are strictly street-life; they are maybe the hottest, jazziest things Coleman has written since Sweet Charity in the mid-sixties. The Life is in some ways the coming-out version of that show: It doesn't call its hookers "hostesses," and it offers one song, Someday Is for Suckers , that might be the hard-driving answer to Charity's There's Gotta Be Something Better Than This .

However, when the melodramatic story takes over, Coleman starts writing the same kind of hollow, overblown dirges that everyone else turns out these days when emotion seems called for, and putting an overlay of soul on it doesn't make it sound any better. When Queen sings a fond song about her lover called He's No Good , it's like the hundredth retread of My Man . When she recalls We Had a Dream ,you start reflecting about what a happier musical theatre it would be if the word "dream', noun or verb, were banished from every lyricist's vocabulary.

When she and Sonja salute each other with My Friend ,it's time to leave the theatre; the show's running late anyway. But it's worth returning for the finale, which strikes the same bracingly sour note as the beginning, although, after all we've been through, more powerfully.

The Life is not an easy show to love, but a surprising amount of it is worthy of respect.

The Life is at the Ethel Barrymore Theatre, New York, for an indefinite run .
1997-05-10-musical-review-jekyll-hyde:
JEKYLL & HYDE

MUSICAL REVIEW

JEKYLL & HYDE

Saturday, May 10, 1997

Directed by Robin Phillips

Written by Leslie Bricusse, Frank Wildhorn

Starring Robert Cuccioli, Linda Eder

Rating: 

Jekyll lyrics plod through pop-cliche litany

IF it werent for the songs, the musical Jekyll & Hyde might not be too bad. Robin Phillips took over as director fairly late in the show's progress toward New York -- it has been on the road in America for ages -- and he has staged it as intelligently and adroitly as anyone could. He points up the drama and throws himself into the more risible passages with gusto. For the most lurid sequences, he bathes the stage in satanic red.

Phillips designed the sets, in collaboration with James Noone, and they give us rich pictures within a spare frame. We are taken on a neatly packaged tour of late-Victorian London as traditionally perceived by the musical theatre. As usual, the place is polarized between a comfortable, uncaring upper-class club land and a resentful, gin-sodden underworld that is populated almost exclusively by prostitutes, procurers and louche music-hall artistes. Dr. Jekyll's laboratory is an especial visual treat: a fairyland of bottles, flames and bubbling retorts.

Elsewhere, bubbling retorts are in rather short supply, Leslie Bricusses book being decidedly short on wit. But it adapts the Robert Louis Stevenson novella with perfect competence, drawing out themes for its own purposes. This Jekyll is a determined young idealist, bright-eyed and pony-tailed (no, honestly), who initially wants to explore mankinds divided consciousness by experimenting on inmates of a London mental hospital. The hospital board members, bishops, generals, society dragons and other uptight types, refuse permission. And when gentle Jekyll, having swallowed his own medicine, turns into horrible Mr. Hyde, he takes a grisly series of revenges on them, as part of a general war on what he calls "hypocrisy" in a society that's clearly rotten with it. (Shades, and they aren't the only ones, of Sweeney Todd .)

The show, faced with the problem of importing romantic interest into an original that doesnt have any, takes the same course as most previous adaptations and furnishes Jekyll with two contrasting female companions. There is Emma, the doctors adoring high-born fiancée, who spends the entire evening faithfully waiting for him in beautiful dresses and drawing rooms; and there is Lucy. Lucy is a loose woman -- you can tell, because she goes around in an off-the-shoulder shawl -- but pure and loving at heart. She works at a cabaret-cum-brothel known as The Red Rat, where we find her performing a number titled Good 'N' Evil . This might be a bit metaphysical for most of the Rats clientele, but it impresses the doctor, who is out slumming and naturally has these abstractions much on his mind. Befriended by Jekyll, Lucy is subsequently, and logically, brutalized by Hyde.

Bricusse as librettist can interest us in his tormented heros grapplings with the monster within, but Bricusse as lyricist thoroughly blows it. You might think that being English -- indeed, a Cambridge graduate -- he would find intelligent, stylish words that would suit the time, the place and the emotions. But he has been part of the mid-Atlantic showbiz circuit for more than 30 years now and obviously thinks and feels in its terms: Jekyll & Hyde adds the fatal extra ingredient of a Grand Subject. When Jekyll, after half a show's worth of preparation, is about to take his first draft of the fatal potion, he sings a big, big song called This Is the Moment . Need I go on? The lyric, perfectly matched by Frank Wildhorn's music, plods remorselessly through every once-in-a-lifetime, climb-every-mountain cliché in the pop litany, scrupulously avoiding any reference to the actual dramatic situation, since that might limit its chances outside.

(Songs like this may no longer make the pop charts, but they can still appeal to the less fastidious middle-of-the-road performers, or to any one of the Three Tenors. Or is that the same thing?)

I knew that it was not really the worst song I had ever heard in a musical. There are dozens like it, and when I switched on the radio that night I Dreamed a Dream from Les Misérables blared forth to confirm this. But that was no comfort at the time.

Other song titles include Once Upon a Dream (Emma remembering her courtship), Someone Like You (Lucy falling for her kind gentleman), and In His Eyes (the two of them independently expressing devotion toward the same man). Its a consistent score, all right. The collectors item is Murder, Murder , a weird piece of staging in which Hyde serially bumps off most of his enemies while the chorus stand a few inches away, fail to lift a finger and then have the nerve to complain about the killer's elusiveness.

As Hyde, Robert Cuccioli gets to do little more than cackle, but his Jekyll is a sympathetically tortured figure. He also has a powerful pair of lungs, though he is outclassed in this department by Linda Eder's Lucy, who cant be all amplification. Eder manages to make the stock musical character of a Cockney drab sympathetic, although in a musical so beholden to other musicals, it is difficult to banish the suspicion, when she turns up in the doctors posh rooms, that she has come to ask him for elocution lessons so that she can be a lady in a flower-shop. If her character is stock, the others are even stocker. Barrie Ingham, a British actor of excellent pedigree, is wasted as Jekyll's father-in-law-to-be, while George Merritt, described in his bio as "one of America's finest operatic baritones," acts stiffly but barely sings a note.

Jekyll & Hyde is at the Plymouth Theatre, New York, for an indefinite run.
1997-05-25-bullets-over-broadway:
BULLETS OVER BROADWAY

Just as war breaks out between blockbusters in Hollywood, so the home of American theatre is in the grip of a competitiveness previously unknown. Robert Cushman reports from New York

Sunday 25 May 1997 00:02 BST

Within the last month no fewer than six new musicals have opened on Broadway. Two of them have titles firmly tied to their sources and subject-matter: Jekyll & Hyde and - a subject that raised a lot of eyebrows and many giggles when it was first announced - Titanic. The other names - Steel Pier, The Life, Dream, Play On - give less away, though on inspection all is revealed: Steel Pier is about a 1930s dance marathon in Atlantic City, The Life refers to prostitution and allied trades, and Dream and Play On are animated song-recitals. Another new show, Juan Darien, opened and closed earlier in the season. As a total, that hardly compares to the glory days of the 1920s or even the 1960s, but it's certainly an advance on three seasons ago, when Sunset Boulevard won all the Tony awards for which it was eligible because there was, literally, no competition.

The Tonys - Broadway's equivalent of the Oscars - are a vital factor here. Titanic, the subject also of the ill-omened Hollywood blockbuster of the same name, cost between 10 and 14 million dollars to mount. (Figures vary, but in these circumstances it's usually safe to believe the biggest one). Steel Pier cost seven million. The Life, a relatively small show, came in at around five or six. Revivals of older musicals are a vital part of the Broadway economy these days, and there have been four of them: Chicago (the season's biggest hit), Annie, Once Upon a Mattress, and - the most recent arrival - a lavish production of Leonard Bernstein's Candide, which at $4m looks a comparative bargain. Sums like these are not easily recouped, and producers understandably seek insurance; in the words of Variety, "a Tony win has traditionally translated into a surge at the box office". Besides which, the telecasting of the awards offers all the nominated shows, winners or losers, an unequalled shop window.

Over the years, despite a few eccentric or spiteful decisions, the recipient of the best musical prize has generally been easy to predict. It can have been no surprise to anyone when Guys and Dolls, My Fair Lady, Fiddler on the Roof and A Chorus Line swept the board in their respective years. Those of course were the (moderately) good old days when openings were decently spaced out over the season, critical and popular opinion had time to crystallise, and the Tony merely figured as official confirmation that you had a hit. (This is still the case with straight plays, where both costs and possible profits are lower.) But as budgets have inflated, producers, anxious to waste as little time and money as possible, have pushed their openings closer and closer to the wire. This year five musicals opened within a week of the deadline. It seemed the curtain had hardly fallen on the last first night before the nominations were out. The contestants - there seems no other word - now sit back and try to look benign until the awards ceremony next Sunday. No sane theatre should be dependent on prizes to this extent, and this year's race represents a desperate attempt to rationalise an irrational situation.

There are, except in times of severe drought, four nominations in each category. The Best Musical contenders this year are Steel Pier, Titanic, The Life and the departed Juan Darien, which may be there because the nominators couldn't bear the thought of honouring Jekyll & Hyde. Billed as a "carnival mass", Darien was a dance-and-puppet piece with lyrics in Latin. It's just possible, though, that its being so out of sync with Broadway conventions may net it the award: it could serve as a rebuke to the more orthodox shows which, even when competent, have not been great. No new shows have caught the limelight as the rock musical Rent or the aggressive tap show Bring in Da Noise, Bring in Da Funk did in 1996.

The bookies' favourite is The Life, which has received more nominations - in performance, design and other categories - than any other show. And, taken all round, it is probably the best. It has a score by Cy Coleman, who for 35 years now has written the catchiest and jazziest music to be heard on Broadway and who gets down to the New York street-world of the 1980s, before the city's much-vaunted clean-up. The line of hookers here recalls the parade of dance-hall hostesses in Coleman's earlier show Sweet Charity - the ones who sang "Big Spender" - but with the pretences dropped. One of them, Lillias White, brings the house down with a sardonically aimed tribute called "The Oldest Profession" (lyric by Ira Gasman). White, who is black, ornaments the song with the soulful vocal fills that always titillate theatre audiences and that usually bore the hell out of me, but she never lets them obscure the words or the thoughts. Michael Blakemore, who directed Coleman's City of Angels, does this one too; a gentlemanly British director may seem an odd choice for such a show, but Blakemore has always been attuned to American sleaze (remember The Front Page at the National Theatre in 1972) and though his work here is physically unobtrusive he is admirable at keeping the actors focused. The genre pictures are good, acrid fun; it's when the story takes over - a convoluted affair involving one street walker's efforts to get her man off drugs and herself off the streets, while evading the clutches of the meanest pimp on the block - that melodrama strikes, even infecting Coleman's music. The good numbers predominate, though. The Life seems a good bet for best score and supporting performance, a reasonable one for best direction.

Its raunchiness, and periodic dives into a sour sentimentality, may work against it, though, and stir support for Steel Pier, which is sordid but wholesomely so. It even has a leading man who has returned from the dead to redeem the heroine, though this is so coyly stated that I was dumb enough not to get it until the last moment. Corrupt dance contests, extending false hope to victims of the Depression, sound like a wonderful subject for a musical, with built-in period style and instant choreography, but this one plays like a poor man's They Shoot Horses, Don't They? The result seems alternately predictable and arbitrary, with a below-par score by John Kander and Fred Ebb (Cabaret, Chicago, Kiss of the Spider Woman) and leading players who vary from competent-but-unappealing to terminally bland. Still, two of them have Tony nominations. Debra Monk, who plays a smaller role, is wonderful. She has two numbers - one blowsy, one wistful - and sings each to its limits; she probes beyond those limits to show the thoughts and feelings underneath - which is what musical-theatre acting should be about. If there were no Lillias White, Monk would be a cinch for best supporting actress.

Most ambitious of all the shows is Titanic and there are times when its reach matches its grasp. Its problem - with audiences, with critics, and I confess with me - is that it has never shaken off the aura of ludicrousness which has surrounded it ever since it was first announced. Most musicals are disasters, so what can you expect of a musical about a disaster? Music can speed a story along, but can also slow it down; why are the passengers lining up and singing when they should be fighting their way into the lifeboats? Prosaic questions like these are forced upon us by Maury Yeston's lyrics, the painstakingly literal kind that generally attach themselves to music by Andrew Lloyd Webber or Claude-Michel Schonberg. Here the music is by Yeston himself: sometimes schmaltzy, but complex in texture and interestingly dotted with recurring motifs. The script does a decent job of following a cross-section of passengers and crew from cheerful embarkation to icy doom, dutifully pointing up the class-distinctions inherent in the story. Richard Jones, another British director, fights oddly shy of either full-hearted spectacle or suggestive spareness, and ends up being half-heartedly literal. A look-out is dangled over the auditorium in a crow's nest (and he sings about "sailing on", which is strange considering he's on a steamer) but the moment at which he actually spots the iceberg goes strangely unmarked. Steward Laing's set, stolidly rising and falling between decks, has its moments, but we never see it sink, though all the logic of a big musical makes us want to. The cast is good - no stars, no nominations - and the show is sometimes (but how could it not be?) very moving.

The best thing about the spurned Jekyll & Hyde is that, though it has the deafening air of a pop opera, it isn't through-sung. This means that we get some relief from Frank Wildhorn's turgid music and Leslie Bricusse's mail-order lyrics ("This is the moment," screams Jekyll, to ecstatic Pavlovian applause, when about to take the potion - or, in this timidly trendy version, the needle) and that Bricusse as librettist can do a reasonable job of unfolding the plot. He gives us a Jekyll who, when he turns into Hyde, conducts an avenging campaign against Victorian hypocrisy, rather like Stephen Sondheim's version of Sweeney Todd. Robert Cuccioli, who plays the dual role, gets to do one song together, so to speak: as Jekyll he stands up straight and sings at the ceiling while as Hyde he crouches and sings at the floor. Presumably he can't stand to look at himself. There is an equally peculiar sequence called "Murder! Murder!" in which Hyde enacts most of his career as a serial killer while the chorus look on and then start wondering who done it. Love-interest consists of the regulation pure-and-patient fiancee and an equally standard doomed harlot, the latter roof-shakingly sung by Linda Eder. This is a score in which the sensitivity of Las Vegas mates with the creativity of Europop. It also has a story everybody knows. Second-hand though it is in every department, it may turn out to have more audience appeal - which, after the first couple of months, has to mean tourist appeal - than any of its nobler competitors.

Of the two songfests: Play On takes its title from the first line of Twelfth Night, and updates that play to a mythical 1940s Harlem by appropriating a bunch of standard Duke Ellington songs. This shouldn't work but somehow does. The show has an amateur air, but that may actually help. Malvolio (now called The Rev) becomes thoroughly sympathetic; an uptight club manager tricked into posing as a hepcat. He even gets Olivia. Tonya Pinkins, who plays the lady, is on the Tony list: largely, I suspect, through her ability to distend her body and the notes of a song simultaneously. I much preferred the cute (and unnominated) Viola of Cheryl Freeman. Andree de Sheilds, one of the original stars of Ain't Misbehavin', has aged into a shamelessly crowd-pleasing Feste; I loved him. He is up for a best supporting Tony, and though nobody takes the show seriously enough for him to win, I'd like him to. Dream tries to make an evening out of the wonderful but undramatic oeuvre of Johnny Mercer, greatest of all pop lyricists. It's an impossible endeavour, but it still comes out worse than necessary.

There's nothing wrong with honouring America's musical past. I wouldn't claim that this is the motive for Broadway's stream of revivals, but it's a pleasant by-product. Of this season's quartet, all duly nominated for best musical revival, the return of Annie attracted the least notice, perhaps because nobody realised it had ever gone away. Once Upon a Mattress, a delightful comedy musical from the 1960s, has been generally scorned, largely because its leading lady, Sarah Jessica Parker, though personally delightful, is no clown.

Candide, too, has been underappreciated. It's a revival of a revival. A satirical comic opera, based on Voltaire, it flopped at its premiere in 1956. In 1973 it was successfully re-imagined by director Harold Prince as a post-hippie, audience-involving pocket extravaganza. His new staging expands on his old, puts it back behind the proscenium arch in resplendent mock-baroque sets and costumes, and restores the style and substance of the music, much of which has gone missing in his first attempt. Some problems remain insoluble, chiefly that of getting a book to match Bernstein's munificent score. The present version (originally by the late Hugh Wheeler but much revised since his death) is exaggeratedly inconsequential. But Prince, in his most genial mood, keeps the stage endearing and alive, and the singing is superb. Leading comics Jim Dale and Andrea Martin are up for Tonys but the show has been generally damned as over-the-top. It's actually the best-staged musical of the season.

Chicago is the guaranteed winner for best revival, and the only show, new or old, with the assured aura of a hit. This is partly because it avoided the Gadarene rush at the end of the season; it opened early and has had time to establish itself. It started as a concert performance and was moved to Broadway pretty much unchanged, except of course that the actors learned their lines. There has been an exaggerated reaction on Broadway against "spectacle" (pointless, too, since not even cheap shows come cheap), leading to the understaging of Titanic and the under-rating of Candide. Chicago, with the orchestra taking up most of the stage, has been judged "brilliantly minimalist"; actually it looks cramped. But the performers are terrific, except for one who is magnificent: this is Bebe Neuwirth, a singer-dancer-comedienne with an endlessly eloquent body. In Chita Rivera's old role of a 1920s murderess aching to parlay her notoriety into a stage career, she renders "I Just Can't Do It Alone" with the devastating assurance of one who knows she can. One hopes that her co-star Ann Reinking, who has to sit and watch her do it eight times a week, is a generous person.

Reinking plays another murderess (Gwen Verdon's old role), and is also the choreographer, borrowing liberally and with acknowledgement from the work of her former lover and the show's original begetter, the late Bob Fosse. Fosse's original 1976 production was largely about his love-hate affair with his own talent for "Razzle Dazzle" (title of one of the best songs); with that element gone, the show - despite many pious pronouncements about its relevance in the wake of the O J Simpson trial and the new cynical mood of the 1990s - is both less exciting and more palatable. It's another musical about the delicious fun of sleaze. Like everything else, Chicago lost to A Chorus Line in '76, but the Kander and Ebb score still sounds fine, and it's perfectly possible that the goodwill it's earned them may win sympathy votes for their new show, Steel Pier. Let no one say that Broadway forgets.
1997-05-26-musical-review-steel-pier:
STEEL PIER

MUSICAL REVIEW

STEEL PIER

Monday, May 26, 1997

Written by David Thompson,

John Kander and Fred Ebb

Directed by Scott Ellis

Starring Gregory Harrison, Karen Ziemba and Daniel McDonald

Rating: 

Dance marathon takes a few missteps

THE ritual of 1930s dance marathons will be familiar to anyone who knows They Shoot Horses, Don't They ? -- the novel or the brutally exciting film. The Broadway musical Steel Pier is not directly adapted from either of them, but it has, unavoidably, many of the same features. Here are the children of the Depression, dancing till they drop in a seedy, glittering ballroom for the sake of free food and lodging, and a big cash prize for the couple who endure the longest. Here are the grinning radio sponsors, the vocal trio chirping out encouraging jingles, and the gradations of despair and ambition among the contestants.

Here also are a very similar trio of leading characters: the world-weary female veteran cranking herself up one more time, the idealistic young man who partners and loves her, the glibly corrupt master of ceremonies. This time the heroine and the emcee are secretly married, and working a scam at the expense of the other players. The hero, an aerial stunt man, also has a secret that is not fully revealed until the very end, at which point it torpedoes whatever credibility the show may still possess.

This, as it happens, is not much. Though the musical is professionally mounted and everyone in it moves very smartly, it has almost no energy. The show takes its name and its setting from a dance hall in Atlantic City, N.J., and Tony Walton's set lowers effectively through the spurious glamour; the evening's predominant visual impression is of black occasionally pierced with gold. Scott Ellis's direction is efficient but stolid. A dance marathon is a wonderful subject for a musical and one rather expects dance to drive the show, the way the late Michael Bennett once did with far less promising subject matter in a show called Ballroom . Susan Stroman's choreography is a persuasive synthesis of late-twenties and early-thirties steps, with emphasis on the sexier ones, and there is an extended first-act routine that really shakes the place up. There is also an unhappy attempt to do a dream ballet on old-fashioned airplane wings, in the manner of Flying Down to Rio , and there are moments in the staging (when the leading lady detaches herself from the ensemble for a personal showdown) that strike thunderous echoes of equivalent moments in A Chorus Line . Good or bad, original or derivative, the dances are kept strictly subservient to the book.

Unfortunately the book (by David Thompson) has no life. The characters go through standard permutations of yearning and betrayal, and the principal performers do little to vitalize them. The men -- Daniel McDonald as the nice boy, Gregory Harrison as the crook -- are two shades of bland. Karen Ziemba is livelier but charmless, and though she works hard at her big breakdown number, it just seems like hard work. The song itself, Running in Place ,suggests desperation on the creators' part as well as the character's. In all, this sounds like the weakest score that veterans John Kander and Fred Ebb have written since The Rink , another show that tried for bleak and ended up with dank. In fairness, I like that score considerably more now than I did then, and the hero and heroine in Steel Pier have one song, a playful poolside duet called Wet , that I expect to grow on me.

The two best songs, though, go to a supporting character. Debra Monk plays an aging good-hearted gal, and brings warmth, depth and bite to everything she does. First, to win pennies and applause from the dance-hall crowd during a break, she sings a song called Everybody's Girl that is so blatant it hardly qualifies as double-entendre. She makes it funny; she also conveys the woman's pride in getting the number across and her humiliation at having to do it at all. In the second half, she has a song in character, asking a younger man to take her away with him. This time the power comes not from denying the words of the song, but from conveying that she means them more urgently than she can bring herself to acknowledge.

Others stand out in a smaller way; Alison Bevan as a distressed gentlewoman among the marathoners and Ronn Carroll as a contest factotum, jollying up the dancers, counting them out when they fall, and strictly monitoring their styles for excess eroticism ("you can bunny-hug but you can't grizzly-bear"). We seem to have met them before, too. A musical of They Shoot Horses has been mooted for years; maybe the rights were unavailable, but its ghost hangs heavy over this show, sucking its blood. They shoot remakes, don't they?

Steel Pier is at the Richard Rodgers Theatre, New York, for an indefinite run .
1997-05-30-theatre-review-insomnia:
INSOMNIA

THEATRE REVIEW

INSOMNIA

Friday, May 30, 1997

Written by Daniel Brooks

Directed by Guillermo Verdecchia

Starring Daniel Brooks, Tamsin Kelsey,

Guillermo Verdecchia and Fiona Highet

Rating: 

High-gloss rant sure to keep you awake

ABOUT two-thirds of the way through Insomnia , Daniel Brooks, reaching a new plateau as a performer, stands at a microphone and delivers an extraordinary long speech. Perhaps I should call it a routine. Anyway, it's a rant, fast but measured, on all the things in modern life that displease or disturb him.

He arraigns the usual suspects: big business, politicians, technology, pollution, both mental and environmental. How, he asks, do we know what invisible substances may be poisoning us in this very room? And he outlines a series of new rules to live by -- he calls then protocols -- rules which, if followed, would transform or even eliminate civilization as we know it: no cars, for a start. He claims that he has summoned this meeting in order to raise the devil.

At this point I should make clear that, although Brooks is the writer of Insomnia as well as its star, he is not, as far as I know, playing himself. He is playing a character called John F, and John F is very likely mad: so much of what he says is persuasive -- and hugely enjoyable -- but you do begin to doubt his motivation. He lives with a woman called Gwen, and they have a child whom they seem to love. Nevertheless the ménage is breaking down, sexually and psychologically. John is part dreamer, part joker, part bully: easy to like but difficult to live with. Gwen is opaque, but thats probably her method of defence: She retreats inside herself. Their deteriorating relationship is shown to us in a series of chill, stylish snippets; the actors communicate their lack of communication quite perfectly. Tamsin Kelsey is very fine and Brooks is superb. As John F, his monologue is wonderful standup comedy -- impeccable in pace, timing and repose -- but the man inside it is plainly going bananas.

John F has a brother, William F, played by Guillermo Verdecchia, who also directs. His direction is terrific, making commanding use of lighting and sound, dividing the stage into new and intriguing shapes, using the space right up to the exit door in the back wall. His performance is less satisfying, or at least, his character is. William is richer than John and more at home in the world but he too has conjugal problems, which arent quite brought to life: No reflection on his acting, or on that of Fiona Highet (who plays his partner, Kate), but when they take the stage the temperature perceptibly drops. Gwen and Kate go off together, at which point the play takes shape as a classic piece of male paranoia, rather like Harold Pinter's Old Times .

As for the title: John can't sleep, and its either a cause or a symptom of his malaise. It may also stand for societys ever-deepening sickness, in which case the full title Insomnia: a Work in Progress may be a philosophical diagnosis rather than a technical description of the work itself, which has the high gloss of a work completed. But if they are still refining it, I'd like them not to worry about the performance-art side, which can take care of itself, but to concentrate instead on the relationships, which at the moment vary from sketchy to compelling. There were moments when I suspected that John and William were meant to be two halves of one personality, but these were blessedly few. In another respect the show earns its forbidding title: It keeps you awake.

Insomnia continues at The Theatre Centre until June 1.
1997-05-31-sorting-out-broadway-s-traffi:
Spectator

Sorting out Broadway's traffic jam

Spectator

Saturday, May 31, 1997

I

RECENTLY spent a week in New York City collecting Broadway musicals: eight in six days. Seven of them had crammed their premieres into the same two-week period at the end of April.

This Gadarene rush was no coincidence. It was an attempt to rationalize an irrational, and very unhealthy, situation. Broadway -- musical Broadway, anyway -- has convinced itself of its dependence on the annual Tony awards. All the shows were opening as close as possible to the cutoff date for Tony nominations. The awards are presented tomorrow night. On Monday, if they abide by their own logic, the producers of these multimillion-dollar extravaganzas (not all of which look so extravagant) will decide whether to run with their prizes or cut their losses and take early retirement.

I have reported on five of the new openings: Titanic , The Life , Steel Pier , Jekyll and Hyde and the Livent revival of Candide . The remaining two, both small-scale, were devoted to settling old scores: That is, they served up old songs in new settings. The first, Play On ,inserted classic (and a few obscure) Duke Ellington numbers into an updated Twelfth Night ,set in a mythical Harlem. There was no good reason for this to work, but in a naive and casually entertaining way it did. Andrée de Shields, a monstrously relaxed eccentric hoofer, has received a Tony nomination as best supporting actor in a musical. He deserves to win; however, as the show, sadly, has already thrown in the towel, he probably won't.

Dream ,the other new oldie, still hangs on, but this parade of the songs of Johnny Mercer is one dumb show. Mercer was an unrivalled pop lyricist but not very theatrical, and the production misses whatever comic or dramatic clues the songs do provide. His more obscure material, for example, is dispatched by lining up the cast and having them chant the titles, phrases such as "Liquapep" and "He Didn't Have the Know-How, No How" I've often wondered what those songs were like and I'm still wondering. If there was ever a concept to Dream ,it died somewhere on the road.

So hand me the crystal ball. I haven't seen many of this year's Broadway plays, but I note with pleasure that the four contestants for best dramatic actor (Brian Bedford, Michael Gambon, Christopher Plummer, Antony Sher) are all graduates of the British and/or Canadian classical theatre. Up for best new musical are The Life , Steel Pier , Titanic and an oddball, Juan Darien ,billed as a "carnival mass," with lyrics in Latin, that came and went earlier in the season. It might just win (all right, in my dreams) as a rebuke to the more conventional shows, because although none of them have been embarrassing, none have been inspiring either. Sometimes -- often ,actually -- one show pulls away from the pack, and even if you don't much like it, even if it's Hello Dolly ,you still can see why. Whatever wins this year will do so by default.

The smart money is on The Life ,which is street-smart and has the best score (or at least the best collection of songs) and, in Lillias White's jaded hooker, an unbeatable entry for best supporting actress. (Debra Monk in Steel Pier is as good but doesn't get to light as many fireworks.) Of everything I saw, I think I had the best time at it. But I don't know, in retrospect, that it's better than Titanic ,which has the loftiest ambitions and, surprisingly often, comes close to realizing them.

However, it would have had to be a masterpiece to overcome its image problems. A musical about a sinking ship is -- how can I put this? -- a downer. It also sounds, as a stage subject, inherently ludicrous, and the awards that tend to reflect popular sentiment -- this is their importance, however distasteful -- probably will reflect this one as well. Steel Pier is dreary, but some people are rooting for it. And having a score by John Kander and Fred Ebb may net it a sympathy vote.

That's not as rude as it sounds. Twenty years ago, Kander and Ebb wrote the score for Chicago . It lost to A Chorus Line ,as did everything, but its revival has been the unconditional hit of this season. (It's had time to establish itself as such; it opened well ahead of the rush.) Much as I enjoyed Candide ,I have no doubt that Chicago will win best revival and every other Tony for which it's eligible: some that it throughly deserves (best actress -- Bebe Neuwirth is sensational) and some (best direction) that it possibly doesn't. Chicago has won all kinds of dubious plaudits: for being refreshingly minimalist (it's a slightly blown-up concert version), for having been ahead of its time (actually, A Chorus Line would win now as it did then) and for being prophetic (though celebrity murder-trials are nothing new in the United States and Chicago's much-vaunted parallels to the Simpson trial are virtually non-existent). The truth is that, with the death of creator Bob Fosse, the show shed its load of self-hating obsession. It is now less brilliant but more palatable: another fun musical about corruption.

It will look great on the awards show. That's another producer's prayer: Even if you don't win, you have a terrific shop window. A few years ago, Maury Yeston's Grand Hotel lost to Cy Coleman's City of Angels ,but Grand Hotel staged such a great number that everybody turned off his or her TV set thinking it had won. Both composers are represented this year -- Coleman with The Life ,Yeston with Titanic -- and I'm sure they have not forgotten. I wonder if they'll show anything from Jekyll and Hyde , directed by Robin Phillips.It was snubbed for best musical, but rules can be bent. Did I ever tell you about the duet that Robert Cuccioli, in the leading roles, sings with himself? As Jekyll, he stands up straight and sings at the ceiling; as Hyde, he crouches and sings at the floor; he just can't look himself in the eye. Don't laugh too hard; I wouldn't be surprised if Jekyll and Hyde were the only one of this year's new bunch still open when next year's awards come round. It's in a pop-opera style that people seem to like, and it has a title with which they connect. (So does Titanic ,but in the wrong way.) It's all about image.

It's a sad truth: from Kiss Me Kate to Rent , shows that take the prize don't really need it. Shows that really need it aren't saved by it, even if they get it.

The 51st annual Tony Awards, with talk-show star Rosie O'Donnell as host, are presented Sunday evening, with the televised program starting at 9 p.m. (ET) on CBS and selected Canadian channels.
1997-06-17-theatre-review-hobson-s-choic:
HOBSON'S CHOICE

THEATRE REVIEW

HOBSON'S CHOICE

Tuesday, June 17, 1997

Impeccably constructed tale bubbles with comic spirit

THESE are the principal characters of Hobson's Choice , currently onstage at the Shaw Festival and one of the few genuinely infallible pieces in the English-speaking repertoire:

Henry Horatio Hobson, abusive, alcoholic proprietor of a 19th-century shoe store, a tyrant to his employees, a monster to his family, and a monument of stinginess to all; Maggie, his eldest daughter, dauntingly capable and businesslike, riding roughshod over everybody's wishes in the successful pursuit of her own; Willie Mossop, her father's best workman (whom she stampedes into marrying her), a genius at bootmaking but a repressed worm in all other respects, blossoming under her tutelage into the most unbridled egotist on a stage that groans with them.

Taken one by one, they are a remarkably unlovely trio. Thrown together in the presence of an audience they magically generate warmth.

First seen in 1915, Hobson's Choice looks back thirty years to the thrift and promise of late-Victorian Lancashire. Even in its own day it had period charm, a burnished quality that never denies hardship but carefully distances it. It's one of the Manchester school of plays -- hard-headed but warm-hearted -- that gave birth to the regional repertory movement, itself the foundation of British theatre for the next half-century. There are other plays in the group that deserve an outing, but this is the only one to be regularly revived -- and the only work by which its prolific author, Harold Brighouse, is generally remembered. He keyed into legend here, invoking elements of King Lear and Cinderella and every Victorian manual on self-improvement. Maggie rescues Willie from her father's domain and they set up in business together, successfully draining trade away from the old firm which is left fruitless and -- almost literally -- bootless. Old man Hobson spends all his time in the pub; his two younger daughters are greedy, ineffectual snobs waiting for eligible young men to carry them off. The difference between their selfishness and Maggie's is that hers is constructive and -- beneath it all -- loving. When father's liver gives way, the only ones who will return to look after him are Maggie and her Will . . . at a price.

More of a tale than a closely knit intrigue -- built, that is, more like a novel than a play -- the piece is still in its own terms impeccably constructed. Every line tells, for character, action, ambience or all three, and though there are no quotably funny lines the text bubbles with comic spirit: a frank relish of human frailty and human resource.

Christopher Newton's staging is keen and unobtrusive with one or two humane and individual touches. Traditionally, the play's wedding scene has ended with Maggie dragging Willie by his ear into the bridal chamber. In this production he goes, after some initial hesitation, of his own accord. This fits the arc of Simon Bradbury's performance, which is of steadily increasing assurance. Even at the beginning he is nobody's fool; by the end, taking steely measure of his father-in-law's property, he is progressive capitalism on the march. This makes the character less endearing than usual but more credible. Michael Ball's Hobson, by contrast, is altogether too endearing: a fuzzy, teddy-bearish figure and something of a hole in the play. Instead of flourishing his vices as weapons against the world, he hugs them to himself like the minor foibles of a black-sheep uncle. He presents no threat, and his fall is no surprise.

Still, he times his laughs well, and he has one virtuoso sequence: a long, agonized toying with his tea cup before his final capitulation. Corrine Koslo's Maggie is a short, chunky dynamo whose determination is bred of past endurance -- she has winced under the title of "old maid" -- and tempered by a virtuous desire to inflict no more suffering than is absolutely necessary. (The play is, among other things, a hymn to the English Noncomformist conscience.) At the performance I saw Koslo was overpaced and underenergized -- a cycling accident had nearly put her out of action -- but she was still, as she should be, the heart of the play.

As a good repertory playwright, Brighouse hands opportunities to everyone, and the supporting cast take them, for the most part, ably if not spectacularly. Barry MacGregor has the gift role of the Scots doctor who terrorizes Hobson into abstinence and he gobbles it up, more voraciously than he might with a more assertive antagonist. The production adds a character, a clog-dancing delivery boy, dropped in presumably for local colour. It isn't necessary; the play breathes its origin in every line, and William Schmuck's designs -- a series of chintzy or stony interiors backed by a vista of mill-country smoke stacks -- positively belches it forth.

At the Shaw Festival Theatre until June 28 .

A FEW years ago the Stratford Festival revived The Merchant of Venice , and set off a storm of protest. No, that's an exaggeration, but a comedy whose villain is a Jew -- a villain, apparently, because he's a Jew -- is bound to generate a certain amount of contemporary fallout. I wrote an article in this paper saying that the play was anti-Semitic, but only superficially; that its prejudices were less Shakespeare's own than those of his period; and that the character of Shylock was so complex, so compelling, and so attractive to actors that it would override anybody's attitudes.

The play is back at the festival this season, and last Sunday Professor Harold Bloom came to Stratford to lecture on it. Bloom is one of the finest critics alive, a teacher at Yale and Harvard, and author of the majestic book The Western Canon. He is currently writing a book on Shakespeare's characters, a magnificently unfashionable enterprise in an academic climate that distrusts character nearly as much as it distrusts Shakespeare. For the rest of us, of course, he's right in the mainstream. Most real people watch plays and read novels in order to meet other real people, who just happen to be fictitious.

Bloom's own favourite Shakespearean character is Falstaff, whom he has re-imagined as a kind of secular saint, and he looks and sounds Falstaffian himself: witty, grandiloquent, silver-haired and, well, weighty. He holds to the good old romantic notion that Shylock is a character who got away from his author (as he phrased it, "the wrong Jew in the right play"), but he also believes that the play is "profoundly anti-Semitic." He thinks Shylock is "a comic villain . . . a hallucinatory bogyman," conjured by an author who may never have met a Jew for an equally unknowing audience. He admits, though, that he is never played that way.

Certainly both the recent and the current Stratford stagings bear him out. The earlier one, by Michael Langham, worked hard and skillfully to present the play as a humane romantic comedy. Troubling moments were cut, most notably Shylock's forced conversion to Christianity as punishment for having plotted the death of the merchant Antonio. This year Marti Maraden has gone to the opposite but equally accommodating extreme, setting the play in immediately pre-Fascist Italy. Compelling and beautifully designed, her production is most notable for the quiet, contained Shylock of Douglas Rain. Looking like a walking photograph of the period, he presents a detailed portrait of a half-accepted moneyman, treading warily on the edges of his society. His patience is impeccable, his vengeance implacable. Cutting off a pound of your opponent's flesh in the hope he'll bleed to death is not a nice thing to do, any way you, so to speak, slice it. But the mocking, encroaching blackshirts make it clear that this Shylock is a victim of history, in the worst way.

Shylock, as Bloom trenchantly observed, has been the most influential Jewish character in world literature. His lines even sound Jewish: proof, I guess, of Shakespeare's controlling influence on the rhythms of English speech. His immediacy is astonishing; it may even have astonished Shakespeare. Did he realize what he had done when he wrote the tirade that begins "hath not a Jew eyes?" Bloom, ferociously on his guard against sentimentalizing Shylock, professed himself unmoved by this speech. Well, it isn't there to make us cry. But it should make us think, and feel.

Part of Shylock's greatness, as Bloom rightly claims, is the way he "celebrates compulsiveness for its own sake." He won't explain why he hates Antonio; he just does. But there are two kinds of Shakespearean villain. There are the solitaries, who acknowledge no human ties: Richard III ("I am myself alone"), Iago, Edmund in King Lear , the bastard Don John in Much Ado About Nothing. Then, far more vulnerable, there are those with affections: Macbeth, the King in Hamlet who murders partly for love, and -- pre-eminently -- Shylock. He has a daughter, whose desertion torments him. He had a wife, whom he mourns. He even suffers a pang when a servant gives notice. Shakespeare piles it on. Why?

Bloom has an all-encompassing theory of literary creation. He calls it the Anxiety of Influence. Roughly, a writer reacts against some great predecessor. (This might not account for Homer who can have had few influences to be anxious about.) So Shylock was Shakespeare's attempt to outdo and exorcise Barabas, the gleefully unscrupulous hero-villain of Christopher Marlowe's The Jew of Malta. He must have been played, as Barabas assuredly was, as a red-wigged, hook-nosed caricature.

Unfortunately for this theory, Shylock's extremely vocal opponents in the play make no disparaging references to his personal appearance. They do seem to regard him as a human being, however unlikable. Even the forced conversion might be seen as a benevolent attempt to save his soul. It hurts to say this, but in the play the conversion is not presented as any big deal. It is not the climax of Shylock's punishments, and he himself says nothing about it. (The most disturbing Shylock I have seen, though not the best, was Patrick Stewart; he went smilingly down on his knees at this point, and cringed.) We of course can hardly pass over it so easily. It is Portia with her legal tricks who has brought Shylock to this pass (and after all that stuff about the quality of mercy). At Stratford, Susan Coyne's rather opaque Portia goes in at this point for some silent "oh-God-what-I-have-done?" acting. At least, I think that's what she's getting at.

Fiend or martyr, Shylock by this point has gone way beyond Marlowe's Barabas in sheer humanity. Bloom would have it that Shakespeare's "pride in getting Marlowe out of his system increased his investment in Shylock." He can hardly have been unaware of Marlowe's Jew in creating his own, but I can't see that this kind of literary Oedipus complex accounts for the character's vitality. I can't wait to read Bloom's book, but I'll stick to the hoariest but most convincing explanation of Shakespeare's greatness: his ability -- rather, his compulsion -- to think and feel himself into another person's skin. If that person is a Jew, then the play in which he has a key role is not going to be "profoundly anti-Semitic." And Stratford can go on programming The Merchant of Venice without making too many excuses.
1997-07-01-between-the-lines-at-some-poi:
Between the lines

At some point in her post -- King of Kensington career, Fiona Reid decided good acting was more important than stardom. The money's not so hot, but who's complaining? By Robert Cushman

I HAVE THIS indelible memory of Fiona Reid in Noel Coward's Fallen Angels. It was in 1992, for the Canadian Stage Company at the St. Lawrence Centre. She played a fashionable 1920s wife awaiting the arrival of an ex - lover through a mist composed of equal parts lust, fear and alcohol. She created a character of wild gentility, pixieish in a cloche hat and flashing a smile crammed with eager, nervous teeth. In an outrageous piece of physical comedy, Reid's character, infuriated by a constantly ringing phone, stuffed the offending instrument up her dress and then tried to act unconcerned when surprised by the maid.

Fiona Reid, by her own admission, is associated with Coward heroines, and with what she describes as "witty, British, sardonic" things in general. She told me this over lunch at the Four Seasons, while gearing up to move with her family for a summer at Niagara - on - the - Lake. She's appearing there at this year's Shaw Festival, playing Madame Arkadina, the self - made theatrical grande dame who is the queen - pin of Chekhov's The Seagull. To balance that play, she will also appear in one almost totally unknown, The Secret Life, by the genius of the English Edwardian theatre, Harley Granville Barker. After that, she's back in Toronto to play in Edward Albee's A Delicate Balance, a Canadian Stage coproduction that will open here in January and then move on to Edmonton. This regular alternation between Niagara and the St. Lawrence Centre -- with the occasional television movie of the week -- has been the shape of her career for several years now, and it has brought her a stream of posh parts in high - gloss plays. But the financial rewards are slightly less glossy. "I must," she muses, "be the only person to have earned around $30,000 last year [an unusually bad one] and have a serious number of points at Holt Renfrew. I like to be generous, I like to enjoy life. If you have some notoriety, you have to act as if you have money. I spend lots."

There's a paradox here, in a career that's rife with them, and it says a lot about the Canadian theatre. Reid, now forty - five, has for years been one of Canada's leading actresses, and she seems to be getting better all the time. But her greatest period in terms of notoriety and earning power was twenty years ago when she landed the female lead, opposite Al Waxman, in the most successful of all Canadian sitcoms, King of Kensington. Influenced by the hit American series All in the Family (itself a clone of the British Till Death Us Do Part), King of Kensington was still innovative for Canada as a sympathetic comedy with a blue - collar setting. Reid played Kathy, the thirty - seven - year - old wife with a tender social conscience. (The age bit was a portent of her acting future: "I've usually played characters older than myself -- pressing into the next hormonal stage.") Rather sniffy about the show while she was doing it (she thought it "kitschy"), she now wishes that she'd been more appreciative of its groundbreaking qualities: "When I meet people who are first - or second - generation immigrants, who were teenagers at the time, I discover it spoke to them as no other show did."

She had already done TV comedy with John Candy and Dan Aykroyd, and though back then she may have looked and sounded like a dizzy debutante, those professional jokers weren't fooled. They ribbed her about her intensity. "Oh, Fi," Candy used to say when they were doing a show called Coming Up Rosie, "you wanna do a bit of Chekhov?" As it happened, she did, and during TV's seasonal layoffs she would play classics -- including Chekhov -- in regional theatres. After three years of King of Kensington, she got out, turning down a proposed series tailored strictly to her to be called simply Fiona.

She still retains the look, the style, the achievement and -- at least among the cognoscenti -- the reputation of a star. "I'm not," says Reid, "at all what I appear. I appear to have some degree of class, but it's a huge joke."

In fact, one of the things she's best at on stage is pointing up the absurdities, the insecurities, and through them the dignity, of people who might appear to have it made. She's been called a patrician actress, but it might be more accurate to say that she gets cast as middle - class characters with variously moneyed lifestyles. They could of course be British, but they could also be American, like the heroines of Terrence McNally's Lips Together, Teeth Apart and John Guare's brilliant Six Degrees of Separation, both of whom she has played for Canadian Stage. The Guare character -- a rich, vulnerable and exquisitely dressed woman, half - wise, half - foolish -- elicited one of her finest performances and won her her second Dora. Claire, her role in the forthcoming A Delicate Balance, is the prize member of a family of blue - chip Yankee neurotics.

She's good with words; or, as she puts it herself, "I've always had a sense of the music." Her first Dora had been for Fallen Angels, in which she had a line about passion -- "a base uncouth thing lurking within us" -- making it sound hilariously obscene, while also suggesting a woman rebuking an embarrassingly unruly poodle. Later, she remarked of her old flame's behaviour: "It's probably an elfin joke. He was always being elfin." Many actresses, faced with the delectable adjective "elfin," would have stressed it in the first sentence. Reid, by contrast, set it off by placing the weight on the noun "joke." This meant that "elfin" still had some life left in it when it came round again; it also established the speaker as a woman who would say such a thing without thinking about it. "You can't," she says, expressing her own distaste for acting that signals the audience when to laugh, "give away what reaction you might want." You can still of course get the reaction: the phone business earned "the longest, loudest laughter I have ever received."

Christopher Newton, director of the Shaw Festival and one of Reid's closest friends and colleagues, says, "I think the thing that happened to her was that she decided good acting was more important than stardom. It happened here at Shaw in the mid - eighties. That and having two kids." He also says that for the plays they do at Shaw, "it's quite useful if someone has an English mother and father. Fiona's parents are very nice British, middle - class people."

HER FATHER, Grainger Reid, is Scots, a doctor and a former officer in the Royal Army Medical Corps, which he quit with the rank of colonel. He worked for many years for the Ontario Ministry of Health and, his daughter says, "was viewed, and indeed carried on, as the ex - colonel." In fact, he grew up in very modest circumstances, "and to imagine how he got to the University of Edinburgh at age seventeen by dint of his brains puts a different light on the image I and my friends always had of him."

He married Becky Sharpe, an army nurse whose own childhood, according to her daughter, "always seemed charmed. Born in Tokyo, educated in Switzerland, she is the daughter of a Church of England missionary." The couple met just after the Normandy invasion, and their relationship developed during the liberation of Europe. Their medical duties involved them in the most traumatic episodes of that campaign. They were among the troops who saw the notorious concentration camp of Bergen - Belsen (it was the first camp that the British army entered, so all its horrors were fresh), and they conducted their courtship there. Her father never talked about it, though he was obviously deeply affected by it. Her mother used to speak in awed tones of the suffering they witnessed and especially of the extraordinary graciousness of the victims. "She said it taught her how lucky one was to be alive. After the war she had a bout of polio; she was in an iron lung, and was supposed to die, but said she couldn't because of her kids. She never complained." Fiona's parents followed the army to India at the time of partition; they married in Calcutta (while the riots were in progress) and honeymooned in Darjeeling.

Fiona was their third and last child, and her upbringing was even more geographically varied than her mother's. She was born in Britain and lived there between the ages of five and nine. "When I go back, I try to pretend I'm British; it works for about three weeks. You're British, so I slip into it when I talk to you, but if you were Canadian, I'd have an irreproachable Canadian accent." Other parts of her early childhood were spent in Germany, Africa and the United States. She wasn't terribly happy in the U.S. ("I wasn't friendly enough, my teeth weren't white enough, I came from a British girls' boarding school, wearing National Health Service glasses"). The family came to Canada in 1964 when she was thirteen, and she began to thrive, though not, initially, as an actress. She went to Lawrence Park Collegiate and couldn't get cast in a school play. Still, she went on to study drama at McGill, where she was ambitious but "not sure what I was ambitious about."

She seems to have been carrying a heavy load of paternal ambition. "I was the one he deemed to be intelligent -- he wanted me to be a doctor." In the post - Kensington years, she spent a couple of not too happy seasons at Stratford. This is another period of her life that she wishes she had enjoyed more; it was, after all, the kind of work she left television to pursue. "I didn't know how to play the game. I wasn't a very likable person then. I felt really exposed because of the TV success. I must have come over as a terribly insecure snob." She pauses. "What a dreadful combination."

One of the plays she appeared in at Stratford was The Comedy of Errors. The morning after it opened, her father called to ask how it had gone. When she said it had been all right, he responded, rattling his newspaper, "It says here you were awful." Having absorbed his high standards, she says, "I never enjoyed my success in my twenties; I never thought it was good enough."

Two years ago, her father had a stroke, and he has become increasingly immobile. Reid has begun to spend time putting his recollections on tape. "I had the feeling one had to get a complete document of his life. I never had the feeling my parents were normal -- I used to brag about that. We fought a great deal and there was a lot of humour in that. He swore, so I did. I'd stalk out of the room and he'd follow me. There was much shouting. But in middle age I'm coming to know who my parents really are. There's something heroic about both of them. My mother was never given much credit for being intelligent, but she is; her true personality was obscured over the years by the 'dutiful wife and mother' aspect. She sounds proper, so she gets misunderstood, but she's very funny. What makes her amusing? It's that she doesn't know she is."

Her mother's legacy can filter through into her performances in various and subtle ways. In 1995, in a Shaw Festival production of Coward's Cavalcade, she played Jane Marryot, the nearest thing to a full - length character in what is less a play than a huge pageant. On victory night, like a good patriotic English lady, Jane is out in the crowded streets of London, waving a flag. But she has lost a son in the war, so while everybody else is going crazy with joy, she's going crazy with grief. It's a wordless scene that Coward, always the showman, knew would be desperately affecting with the right actress. Reid made it the most human moment in the show.

Christopher Newton directed her in Cavalcade. He will also be appearing with her this year in The Secret Life. Their collaboration started back in 1984, when they played the lovers, Elyot and Amanda, in Coward's Private Lives, and led to what Reid calls "a very special relationship. It probably comes from being thrown into that play, kissing together on the sofa while not knowing each other. We still fight. One night I started telling him how to run his theatre. He looked at me coldly and said, 'Back right off.' Nobody had ever said that to me before. It made me realize I ought to be less confrontational. I spent the earlier part of my career vacillating between a ridiculous amount of confrontation and blind obedience.

I'm constantly discovering, contrary to what people may say about me, that acting is more about generosity than anything else." Newton points to her "increasing generosity of spirit" and adds that "she's very willing to have a go at strange stuff."

It doesn't always work. In 1994 she appeared for Canadian Stage in a much - feted South American play, Death and the Maiden, portraying a torture victim avenging herself on her chief persecutor. It should have been a fine part for her -- a cultivated woman in extremis -- but this time her brittleness went into overdrive, and the character, intended to be fanatical, came across as plain crazy. There is a kind of acting sometimes described by fans, critics and performers themselves as "terribly brave" and by skeptics as "over the top and unconvincing," and this looked like an example of it. (It turns out she didn't like it much, either. She and the director did not get on.)

THE MAIN stabilizing influence in her life has been her husband. She met MacCowan Thomas, now proprietor of a Toronto scenic workshop, in 1973 when they were both working at a summer theatre in Muskoka, and they married in 1977. "My husband has a terrific sense of calm; I instantly glommed onto that. He always loved working with wood, which represents everything I couldn't do, something methodical and painstaking." What do they have in common? "We both have a very good sense of humour, we both have champagne tastes with beer incomes, and we're terrific parents. Well, anyway, he is." They have an eleven - year - old son, Alec ("A bit like I was when I was young, he's easily impressed by fame -- he dreams of being in the NBA"), and a nine - year - old daughter, Julia ("She just reads and lives theatre, she dances and plays the violin").

This at least sets her apart from the lady she plays in The Seagull; Madame Arkadina was clearly an awful parent, and has the mixed - up, suicidal son to prove it. All the same, Newton says cryptically that "Arkadina's a bit Fi - like; Fiona knows what it means to be a leading actress who's gone out to the provinces. It seems to sum up where she's got to. Now is a good time in her life to play Arkadina."

Reid also acknowledges the fragility of early ambitions: "I used to think, if you're good, you'll always make movies; now I have a good laugh at myself. TV and film auditions are a modelling contest anyway. A lot about getting that work is acting as if you don't care; I'm getting better at that." What about balancing acting and motherhood? "Well, I never had to say, 'Will I work full time or not at all?' You're relentlessly part - time in the theatre whether you like it or not. It's been pretty hand - to - mouth for the last twenty years."

After which she pulls herself up. "I hope I don't sound like I'm complaining all the time. Perhaps you could add, 'She then gives a perky laugh.'"

She then gives a perky laugh.
