Close encounters with genius

The young Steven Spielberg could always persuade his friends and his three sisters to take part in his home-made movies, which from the start evidenced extraordinary sophistication and invention. STEVEN SPIELBERG: A Biography

Saturday, July 5, 1997

By Joseph McBride

Simon & Schuster, 528 pages, $39.50

THERE was a boy, born a year after the end of the Second World War, who spent his earliest days in an intensely Jewish suburb of Cincinnati. His mother was loving and chaotic, his father affectionate but strict and consumed by work. He was doing well in the new computer industry and hoped -- vainly -- that his son would inherit his passion for electrical engineering.

In pursuit of father's career the family kept moving: first to New Jersey, then to Phoenix, Ariz. In Phoenix the boy -- who from an early age heard Holocaust stories from relatives -- had what he later claimed to be traumatic encounters with anti-Semitism.

The boy was a loner (the word nerd crops up in the reminiscences of relatives and acquaintances) and was driven further into himself when his parents divorced. In one area, however, he showed great powers of leadership. He could always persuade his friends, and his three sisters, to take part in his home-made movies, which from the start evidenced extraordinary sophistication and invention. (He was inspired less by theatrical films than by television, whose U.S. golden age coincided with his childhood.)

The family moved again, to California, and he went to college there; the department of radio and television at Long Beach State, the chairman of which recalls that the student "knew more about cameras than anybody in the department . . . he could teach the department." He began hanging out at Universal Studios, making friends and contacts, learning by watching. Soon he was directing for television. At 24, he made a wildly exciting TV film, Duel , a chase picture in which the antagonists were a man and a monster truck. That took him straight into real movies, beginning with a more elaborate and psychologically layered chase picture, The Sugarland Express . Though thoroughly gripping, it was not a commercial success; people werent sure who to root for. It did not, however, interrupt the momentum of its directors career. For the next thing was Jaws .

According to Spielberg for the first 12 weeks of Jaws , people were thrilled by it. Six months later they were saying that no film that made that amount of money could be that good. This has been, as abundantly documented in Joseph McBride's excellent biography, the story of the rest of his life.

Actually, Spielberg understated the case. People were saying that no film that made that amount of money could be any good. And as for the man who made the film, and of course a good percentage of the money . . .

And that was only the beginning. I was surprised, reading this book, by the extent to which I had forgotten Jaws ; not as a movie but as an event in its director's career. There have been so many blockbusters since: Close Encounters of the Third Kind , E. T., the Indiana Jones trilogy, Jurassic Park , even Schindlers List earned substantial profits.

It also earned its director reviews that spoke not merely of professional and artistic advance, but of the justification of a life. David Denby wrote in New York magazine: "Its as if he understood for the first time why God gave him such extraordinary skills." Janet Maslin proclaimed in The New York Times: Mr. Spielberg has made sure that neither he nor the Holocaust will ever be thought of in the same way again. The italics are mine, to point up a judgment, and a juxtaposition, that I find embarrassing -- as I imagine Spielberg himself would. It is, however, preferable to some of the negative comment that McBride exhumes. He says that he was prompted to write the book by "the disdain of the self-styled intellectual elite for this great popular artist," and some of the reaction to Schindler's List amply justifies him.

Spielberg has suffered from an especially odious kind of the ad hominem reviewing rampant in North America. Its characteristic tone is patronizing; its underlying message is that all artistic practitioners are charlatans who must be slapped down in case they get above themselves and put something over on us. Spielberg, it was ludicrously asserted, had made a feel-good movie about the Holocaust; although Thomas Keneally told the identical tale in his highly praised novel, whose visceral impact -- it's a real page-turner -- is much like that of the movie.

McBride makes a lot, as has Spielberg himself, of the film returning him to his Jewish roots. (He had already denied that E. T. was a Christian parable: What would my mom say? She has a kosher restaurant on Pico and Doheny in Los Angeles.) Doubtless theres truth in it, but I think they both protest too much. McBride also emphasizes, but not strongly enough, that the film was not a conversion for Spielberg but a progression. He was a fine narrative director faced with a tremendous story; it should not be surprising that he told it so well. As for his humanity, that had already been demonstrated in Close Encounters and E. T. , science-fiction though they were.

McBride seems more sensible than most movie critics, but he still falls prey to director-worship, praising Spielberg for "penetrating the twisted psyche of Goethe" and quoting lines of dialogue to prove it. But those lines are in the script. Why should Spielberg get the credit? The director himself seems to have bought into the fallacious artist-entertainer dichotomy: Hes quoted as saying, I want to go back and forth from entertainment to socially conscious movies, though there is no reason why a "socially conscious" movie (note the Hollywood jargon) shouldn't be entertaining. Anyway, since this book went to press, Spielberg has broken his box-office records with The Lost World , which is admittedly as socially unconscious as a film can get, unless you're a dinosaur. One is supposed to deplore this, but I see no reason to.

There have been dark passages in Spielbergs career, mostly connected with his proliferating role as producer of other directors films. He distanced himself when two children were killed on the set of the Twilight Zone movie he produced, and his quoted pronouncement (it's made me grow up a little more) hardly seems adequate. He squeezed out the nominal director of Poltergeist ; one wag who visited the set remarked, "Well, now I know what the executive producer does. I've always wondered. He sets up the camera, tells the actors what to do, stands back, and lets the director say, Action! " Penitent, he gave subsequent directors a far freer hand.

The infantilization of Hollywood, for which Spielberg has so often been blamed, is in part the result of his presiding over pictures that have tried to be fun without the benefit of his wit, flair and intelligence. (I was pleased to find confirmation of my hunch that the brilliant casting of Sean Connery as Harrison Ford's dad in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade was his acknowledgement of the link between the action heroes of two generations.)

Spielberg's best films are all adventure stories, Schindler included, and there are other kinds of films. But he is the best presiding genius Hollywood is likely to get, and it obviously couldn't have happened to a nicer guy. There are nicer guys, but it couldn't have happened to them.

Robert Cushman is a Toronto writer, broadcaster and critic.
1997-08-28-new-recordings:
New Recordings

Thursday, August 28, 1997

POP

The Simpsons: Songs in the Key of Springfield

Rhino

Rating:

A few years ago there was a pointless CD called The Simpsons Sing the Blues in which the familiar characters were let loose on pre-existing songs; Homer, for example, got to moan Born Under a Bad Sign . This, by contrast, is the disc the world has been waiting for: a selection of musical highlights from the soundtrack of the TV show itself. There are more versions here of the Itchy and Scratchy theme and the final credits music than even devotees should require, and non-fans (I'm told they exist) may be confused by the rapid sequence of short songs, instrumentals, and dialogue snippets, but theyre unlikely to be listening anyway. The regular performers remain awe-inspiringly perfect, the writing fanatically and insouciantly inventive (this show has more and better jokes than the rest of American TV comedy put together) and the musical satire matches the social; sometimes we get both together as in The Amendment Song , introduced in disgusted tones by Krusty the Clown as a cartoon that tries to make learning fun. Its a spoof on condescending educational TV as it might be hi-jacked by the political Right, ("there's a lot of flag-burners who have got too much freedom/I'd like to make it legal for policemen to beat em") and featuring singing trumpeter Jack Sheldon. Other guests include Tony Bennett and Robert Goulet, though Goulet nearly fails to make it, a mischance to which Mr. Burns responds with the spectrally assured command very well, begin the thawing of Jim Nabors. And there is the Masonic triumphalism of The Stonecutters Song ("who rigs every Oscar night? we do!"), Apu rhetorically inquiring Who Needs the Kwik-e-Mart? (leading Homer to comment He lied to us through song. I hate when people do that), the muscial version of Planet of the Apes ("I hate every ape I see/from Chimpan A to Chimpan Zee") with its echoes of Annie , and the even more inspired Oh, Streetcar! Not only does this come to us complete with Jon Lovitz's unforgettable vocal portrait of a self-intoxicated director (perhaps we are all a little mad, we who don the cap and bells and tread beneath the proscenium arch), it also convinces us that a Broadway-influenced community musical of A Streetcar Named Desire would be exactly like this, from the melodramatic scene-setting ("a city that the damned called New Orleans") to the hell-kicking finale You Can Always Depend on the Kindness of Strangers, Marge as Blanche DuBois chirping "a stranger's just a friend you havent met" as the men in white cart her off to the asylum. The disk mysteriously omits everybodys most treasured Streetcar couplet (You're a girl and I'm a fella/"Stanley, stop or I'll tell Stella"). I also demand an explanation for the non-appearance of the Song of the Mediocre Presidents. Otherwise: a fine record of one of the peaks of Western civilisation.

THEATRE REVIEW / As Wolfville's third season of classical drama comes to a close, its three plays confirm a reputation for simple sophistication.

Classics buoy Atlantic festival

THEATRE REVIEW / As Wolfville's third season of classical drama comes to a close, its three plays confirm a reputation for simple sophistication.

Saturday, September 6, 1997

Special to The Globe and Mail

Wolfville, N.S. -- THE Atlantic Theatre Festival is in an enviable position. Wolfville is a charming location, and the new theatre has perceptibly energized it. The Maritimes have never before had a stage dedicated to the classics, and this too is an advantage. It means that the festival can present a standard repertoire and still feel fresh and adventurous. Here are the famous plays, and a receptive, unjaded audience. That combination, for any theatre, is a privilege -- and a responsibility.

It is also a danger. It means, for example, that standing ovations can come too easy. (Though that's hardly peculiar to Wolfville.) Getting these complex texts off the ground requires strong, flexible and experienced performers, and there are not enough of them to go around: not in Canada, not anywhere. At Wolfville, which tries to include a high percentage of native Maritime talent, the situation is even more acute than at the richer and more prestigious Stratford and Shaw festivals. But for all that, the theatre has maintained a fair degree of company continuity, and it has made a few striking discoveries. It also has top-of-the-line direction. Michael Bawtree, the Atlantic Festival's founder and chief, is an ex-Stratford director and dramaturge, and as a consultant he has Michael Langham, the doyen of Canadian classical theatre, who has staged a series of distinguished shows here, either alone or in tandem with his wife, the actress Helen Burns.

In the season that wraps up next weekend, the company is running Molière's Tartuffe, Oscar Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest and Chekhov's Uncle Vanya : all in some sense comedies (like all the plays in the two previous seasons) and all making stiff formal and technical demands. That's especially the case on Wolfville's son-of-Stratford thrust stage, that pushes the actors forward right into the audience. Such a stage can sometimes put proscenium-arch plays into sharp and rewarding relief: the best production of Uncle Vanya (or of anything else) that I have ever seen was presented on the British open stage at Chichester. But the wide open spaces can also leave plays and actors exposed, and encourage a kind of all-purpose animation. Michael Bawtree's production of Tartuffe, for instance, begins with an offstage burst of laughter -- a strange overture for a play whose characters first appear locked in a vicious family row. Madame Pernelle, mother of the Parisian bourgeois Monsieur Orgon, is lecturing her son's family on the virtues of Tartuffe, the puritanical evangelist whom Orgon has taken beneath their roof. The scene swings in Ranjit Bolt's new translation, in racy rhyming couplets (Molière's own medium, though it's taken English translators 300 years to come to terms with the fact.) But much of the wit is flattened out by actors desperate to stress every word.

The show begins to grip when Orgon comes on. Leon Pownall -- a reliable actor transformed through three seasons at Wolfville into an inspired one -- plays a calm, bearish paterfamilias who performs tyrannical acts quite peacefully in the name of humility. And of course when he finds that his idolized Tartuffe has been duping him -- that the holy man has in fact been intent on seducing Orgon's young wife -- the dam furiously and farcically bursts.

Molière, no shrinking violet, wrote the part of Orgon for himself -- Tartuffe does not appear until nearly halfway through. He is played by Bill Carr, the festival's most impressive local recruit: a fine Lopahin in the Cherry Orchard of the festival's inaugural season, and, in last year's She Stoops to Conquer , the only really funny Tony Lumpkin I have ever seen. But his Tartuffe is disappointing: a simple con-man, and tight-lipped at that, rather than a complex hypocrite who half-believes his own rhetoric. He only comes to full, vicious life when he turns on his protector; here the stage temperature rises and the play becomes, and remains, serious business.

Tartuffe ends far stronger than it begins, showing how a great play can gradually take charge of a theatre when both cast and audience pay it the basic compliment of trust. The same is true of The Importance of Being Earnest , whose epigrammatic prose is even more challenging than the couplets of Tartuffe -- which at least impose their own rhythm.

"I don't play accurately," says Algernon Moncrieff after taking an erratic turn upon the piano in the play's opening moments, and adds disparagingly "anyone can play accurately." No way: accuracy takes practice. Jonathan Watton, who plays Algy here, was very promising in gauche comedy roles two years ago. He has an interesting conception of the part -- a very young dandy, exquisitely groomed, prolonging his adolescence by throwing around words and attitudes -- but he has terrible trouble phrasing it. The other young persons have more technique but less originality, except for Kate Hennig's strident Gwendolen, which has neither. We know that Gwendolen will grow up like her Gorgon mother Lady Bracknell, but she shouldn't have got there yet . As it happens the veteran Jane Casson-Redlyon makes mama a rather restrained battle axe, scoring her points through incisiveness rather than volume. This pays off in the last act where she becomes an unchallengeably chilling Voice of Society, calling the errant Miss Prism to account -- "Prism! Where's that baby?" -- with the aspect of an avenging Fury.

It helps that she's dressed in red, while everyone and everything else on stage is in cream or off-white. Setting in this last scene is reduced to a door and two chairs, the culmination of a progressively (and stylishly) Spartan staging by young English director Dominic Cooke.

Paring the scene down is one effective way of using the thrust stage. Another is to build it up, which happens in Uncle Vanya , directed by Helen Burns and Michael Langham, the only one of the three plays with a script that might be called naturalistic, as well as the most elaborate production of the three and the most accomplished. You feel the rambling beehive of a Russian house where no-one is truly comfortable. The staging is crammed with revealing detail: Leon Pownall's Vanya, the smitten farm-manager, offers the beautiful visitor Yelena a drink, but his timing is off and she doesn't notice; Later, he all but makes love to her dropped scarf.

Pownall is not the best-defined of Vanyas, and his attempted shooting of the Professor, whom he blames for his misfortunes -- the great tragi-comic moment in modern drama -- achieves only half its effect. We laugh but we don't cry. Ideally we should do both at once -- Vanya, who dreams of all he might have achieved and then curses himself for his foolishness, is a mirror for all but the securest of us. Maybe the production, in driving for unsentimental comedy, is reacting against those mythical mopey productions of Chekhov which everybody castigates but few have actually seen.

The company's layers of strength are most apparent in this production. Megan Follows, whose work at Wolfville has confirmed her as a star, makes a supremely moving Sonya, Vanya's companion in misfortune, equally exploited, equally unloved. Peter Donat, a Canadian star of an older vintage manages an intriguing double focus as the Professor, presenting him as a monster of selfishness who still has legitimate grievances.

These three plays, for all their occasional faults, have a simplicity that at its best can encompass considerable sophistication. This suggests that the festival, after only three years in existence, already has an identity -- one that suits the territory. Wolfville is a tiny town with a high level of style. Building a major theatre there seems alternately a crazy idea and the most logical thing in the world.

Tartuffe runs until Sept. 11. The Importance Of Being Earnest and Uncle Vanya both close Sept . 13. 1-800-337-6661 for information.
