When Robertson Davies's diaries are finally published, we will have a stylish, invaluable history of the Canadian stage. But for now, Happy Alchemy is a blend of the inspired, the urbane, the pedantic and the querulous. HAPPY ALCHEMY: Writings on the Theatre and Other Lively Arts

Davies our best theatre critic, too

When Robertson Davies's diaries are finally published, we will have a stylish, invaluable history of the Canadian stage. But for now, Happy Alchemy is a blend of the inspired, the urbane, the pedantic and the querulous. HAPPY ALCHEMY: Writings on the Theatre and Other Lively Arts

Saturday, November 22, 1997

By Robertson Davies

Edited by Jennifer Surridge and Brenda Davies

McClelland & Stewart, 384 pages, $32.50

ROBERTSON Davies was an actor when young and wrote plays and opera libretti when older. He also wrote prolifically about the theatre, most notably in a trilogy of books chronicling the first years of the Stratford Festival, from 1953 to 1955: Renown at Stratford ,followed by Twice Have the Trumpets Sounded and, a little desperately, Thrice the Brinded Cat Hath Mewed .He and his publishers then called a halt, perhaps because they were unable to find a Shakespearean line about something happening four times.

It's also possible that as the festival grew and became established, Davies felt that it was time for celebration to give way to criticism. "If you can't spray the acid around," he wrote, "you are no use as a critic" that was a task which -- at least in public -- he felt unable to perform. A bad review from Davies would have been especially hard to stomach, because he so obviously knew what he was talking about.

In fact, the three Stratford books, especially the second, are enough to establish Davies as the finest of Canadian theatre critics. He was able to seize a national moment and place it in an international context. He conducted acute and probing meditations on the plays themselves. (He called The Taming of the Shrew a great play; this is demonstrably true -- the play always works -- but it was a statement as critically eccentric 40 years ago as it would be politically incendiary today.) He could describe and evaluate production and performance, and could estimate the contribution of each to the overall experience.

I associate some of his achievement with his having been involved himself. I don't mean that he knew in detail how actors and technicians go about their work; he may have done, but that kind of specialized expertise has little bearing on the broad task of writing a review. (Though since theatre is a collaborative art, it does help to have some idea of who does what before handing round the praise and blame. I have noticed, for example, that literary-minded critics have an exaggerated belief in the power of the director.) What I have in mind is not so much experience as temperament: The flair for recreating a performance on the page is likely to co-exist with the urge to join in. It hardly matters how well or badly; Davies never claimed to have been an especially good actor, though he said that he had his moments. But the power of evoking the event, of matching its rhythms with his own, was one that Davies possessed in spades.

In later life he did it in a kind of shorthand. From 1957 to 1995, he set down notes on every production he saw. These are nearly as illuminating as his full-length pieces, and often more trenchant. (On Barry MacGregor as a pox-ridden pimp in Pericles :"Despite all this elaborate decay he continued to look like a hero trying to be a wreck.") With no immediate readership in mind, he was able to spray the acid around, and with deadly aim. Of the four actors who have played Richard III at Stratford, "Colm Feore is the dismal forty-fourth" the whole production proves that the festival (this was in 1988) "needs shaking up from top to bottom" "Sheila Nadler as Mrs. Quickly [in Verdi's Falstaff ]has a fine voice and presence but is too pleased with herself as a comic." I never saw the performance, but I get exactly what he means, just as I can when he assesses Christopher Plummer's long-ago Cyrano: "Plummer's style is dry and ironic and he cannot suggest adoration . . .but in all that was grotesque, humorous and daring he was admirable." My admiration remains when I read him on shows I have seen myself. There is one recent Stratford production to which he seems to me absurdly indulgent, but on individual performances -- a whole raft of them, for example, in the Shaw Festival production of The Silver King --he is almost unchallengeable.

Happy Alchemy -- a phrase adopted by Davies to denote the transmutation of good theatre into great -- is a collection of essays and speeches to which a few extracts from the theatre diaries have been affixed as headnotes. In time we should have the diaries in full, but that time, in deference to the late author's wishes, is not yet. When they are published we will have a stylish history of the Canadian stage, or at least the classical and operatic end of it, over a period of 40 years. It should be invaluable.

So much for the wonderful book we don't have. The one we do have is uneven: a blend of the inspired, the urbane, the pedantic and the querulous. Davies is capable of writing a zestful, measured panegyric on the classical Athenians, fastidiously distinguishing their notions of democracy from ours: "The Greeks would have found the trust we place in elected persons utterly naive; they assumed, not quite that all men are crooks, but that all men are the better for watching." He then cheapens the whole thing, or his editors do it for him, by tacking on a schoolmasterly playlet about the Oedipus family, in which the wit gives way to smug jokiness.

The speeches are written with jaunty affability that can slide into condescension: It's one thing to buttonhole your audience; it's another to pat them on their darling little heads. "I am sure that some of you are from the United States, and perhaps you are wondering: Surely we too are a witty people? Of course you are." It may have been charming in person, but it grates on the page, and the manner infects the essays as well, nagging at their innate elegance. The editors have exacerbated it by retaining repetition from one piece to another. We don't need, though in their preface they protest that we do, to be told three times that Donizetti's Lucia di Lammermoor is a travesty of Walter Scott's novel, or twice that Vaughan Williams, being English, made a better job of musicalizing The Merry Wives of Windsor than Verdi, who couldn't help turning it into an Italian sex farce. (I don't dispute either opinion, by the way).

I have especially in mind a curious essay entitled Opera and Humour. It's curious because most of it is given over to a historical analysis of the things that make us laugh, a survey that, in typical Davies fashion, manages to be both concise and expansive. The section on opera arrives late and never confronts a basic point: Music, except at the level of rude noises, can only be funny if it is supporting funny words or parodying other music.

Davies's view of culture might be called maverick-aristocratic. He manages, in lamenting the decay in Canada of humane learning, to play the pieties of right and left alike. Sometimes, though, he betrays himself. He refers in passing to a Stratford production of Love's Labour's Lost ,and quotes a speech in which the curate Sir Nathaniel excoriates the ignorance of Costard the clown. "Sir," the speech begins, "he hath never fed of the dainties that are bred in a book. He hath not eat paper, as it were; he hath not drunk ink." Right on, says Davies, and please tell our philistine legislators.

Unfortunately, it isn't that simple. In the play, the words -- a series of amusingly strained metaphors -- are delivered by a sycophantic pedant to a pompous pedant. The clown, described by Davies as "a stupid oaf," proves, like so many Shakespearean fools, to be smarter than either of them. The play is actually about the triumph of experience over book-learning. It exalts, though not in terms any politician would be likely to understand, the virtues of common sense. If Davies had been responding to the play rather than simply using it, he would have enjoyed proclaiming this fact, especially if an actor worth celebrating were playing Costard.

Celebration is the key. Defining himself as a passionate playgoer rather than a critic, he says, "Critics often do not like the theatre; I have liked nothing better." This is unfair polemic -- most theatre critics do like the theatre whatever you might suspect from their writing -- but unimpeachable autobiography. Discussing Bernard Shaw's criticism, Davies writes of "a high-spirited enthusiasm which is always rare and which we seek with an unappeasable hunger." He might have been describing himself. He probably was.

Robert Cushman is a cultural and theatre critic.
1997-12-02-modernize-the-bard-no-way:
Modernize the Bard? No way!

Tuesday, December 2, 1997

DO you remember "Wipe the Blood off My Toga," the Wayne and Shuster spoof of Julius Caesar ? It was first aired in the 1950s and still looks good in reruns. Not only good but startling: It assumes its prime-time audience had a nodding acquaintance with Shakespeare, and it even throws in jokes about Latin. (Wayne orders a martinus . You mean martini, says the bartender. "If I want two," snaps Wayne, Ill ask for them.)

Even today, a theatre show like The Compleat Works of Wllm Shkspr (Abridged) , currently playing in Toronto,can be a tidy hit. Nobody goes to see it as a substitute for the original plays; the joke only works if you know them already. Universal dumbing down may be further off than we had feared.

Or maybe not: not if we believe a recent letter to The Globe and Mail from Brian Mossop, who declared the plays as obscure as Beowulf (which is in Anglo-Saxon, a language almost completely distinct from modern English) and The Canterbury Tales (which isn't and can still be enjoyed with the same application). He deplored "the veneration of Shakespeare as a quasi-religious figure" and called for an annual international contest inviting poets to submit English translations.

Mossop makes one very valid point: In non-English speaking countries, audiences don't have to grapple with all those hard old words. They see the plays in crisp, wrinkle-free new versions tailored to their own specifications.

Language, of course, isnt everything. A great play can work in translation. Britains second favourite playwright is Chekhov. The English may be getting him wrong, but they have certainly been getting something , and it's unlikely that responses sustained over so long a period could be wholly mistaken.

I remember this whenever I encounter estimates of Shakespeare based entirely on what sentimentalists used to call "the verbal music." I'll go further. Even for an anglophone -- perhaps especially for an anglophone -- Shakespeare translated can be a revelation. Actors, untroubled by memories of how their predecessors have spoken the familiar lines, can find their own way into the characters. Audiences, similarly unencumbered, can do the same. A Japanese Macbeth , an Italian Henry IV anda Romanian Midsummer Nights Dream have all afforded me insights into the plays that British or North American productions would find impossible to equal.

However, I dont understand Japanese, Italian or Romanian, so I'm responding to broad strokes of staging and the odd arresting gesture, backed up by my knowledge of the original text. (I recall at Umabatha: The Zulu Macbeth , which played Toronto recently,picking up the simultaneous translation system to check out the hero's state of mind and finding him wondering if that was an assagai he saw before him, which I must say was pretty much whatId suspected.) This suggests that audiences can follow and enjoy a play even if they dont literally understand every word of it, and therefore that we should all be able to cope with the odd archaic phrase.

Productions in translation are not better, merely different. Such freedom entails its own limitations. A translation is a lesser play that may cast light on a greater one. A good translation, especially of poetry, is its own animal and imposes its own rhythms. The rhythms of the original -- rhythms of speech, rhythms of action -- are what anchor an English production, or should. When what the actors are saying is at odds with what they are doing, the play no longer makes sense.

The same thing, only worse, would happen if someone tried modernizing the text while keeping it in English. A translator into French, Portuguese or Urdu has to change every one of the words. A modernizer would only change some of them, and the results could be extremely disconcerting: Friends, Romans, -- all right so far -- compatriots . . ."Countrymen" could mean people living in a rural area. Fellow countrymen would ruin the metre. ". . . please listen to me . . ." The confusion inherent in lend me your ears hardly needs emphasizing. Just one pentameter, and already we have a malformed, unactable bastard.

Maybe it's unfair to choose so famous a line, but then Shakespeare is full of them. They're famous because theyre memorable. They carry and enrich the meaning; they create the characters and tell the stories; theyre why we want to act and watch the plays in the first place. Any modernizer would have to face up to them.

"If it were done when 'tis done," says Macbeth, meaning if only committing the murder would mean that it would be over and completed without repercussions, and you see how long it's taken me to paraphrase a simple pun. "Tomorrow and tomorrow and tomorrow/Creeps in this petty pace from day to day . . ." The first line could hardly be clearer, the second involves a reversal of syntax and a couple of words whose meaning has changed, but who would want to tamper with the spitting alliteration or with the doggedly despairing movement of the verse? This, of course, is the fallacy in the poetry-contest suggestion. No French poets, however much they might enjoy recasting Shakespeare in their own tongue, would lay their hands on Racine. No reputable English poet would dream of competing with Shakespeare.

Actually, one has. In 1965, the British National Theatre, two years old and full of missionary zeal, commissioned Robert Graves to revise the more obscure lines in Much Ado About Nothing . Graves accepted with the stipulation that he would only touch passages in prose. The production, by Franco Zeffirelli, had its charms, but it proved no more funny, touching or comprehensible than others have done. The National never hired a rewrite man again.

Shakespeare, by the consent of centuries, used the English language with more imagination, resource and nervous energy than anyone else, ever. If that avowal sounds quasi-religious, Ill live with it. Actually, I think its Mossop who's being mystical: He seems to think that a prefabricated adaptation will have value -- will even be living entertainment -- because somewhere, at some remove, it had contact with Shakespeare. If the original texts are on the way to oblivion, all the more reason to enjoy them while we still can.
1998-01-10-what-is-this-thing-called-sin:
Four recent books about the famed singer are plagued by errors, inconsistencies and misapprehensions. Only one of them gets it almost right. ALL THE WAY: A Biography of Frank Sinatra

What is this thing called Sinatra?

Four recent books about the famed singer are plagued by errors, inconsistencies and misapprehensions. Only one of them gets it almost right. ALL THE WAY: A Biography of Frank Sinatra

Saturday, January 10, 1998

By Michael Freedland

Weidenfeld & Nicholson, 438 pages, $35

SINATRA: The Artist and the Man

By John Lahr

Random House, 168 pages, $45

THE WAY YOU WEAR YOUR HAT: Frank Sinatra and the Lost Art of Livin'

By Bill Zehme

HarperCollins, 246 pages, $32.50

ALL OR NOTHING AT ALL: A Life of Frank Sinatra

By Donald Clarke

Macmillan, 324 pages, $32.95

IF they asked him, he could write a book. The result -- to judge by the few pieces of prose, genuine or ghosted, that have appeared under his byline -- would be somewhat awkwardly phrased, over-earnest with occasional shafts of brash frivolity, but it would be compulsively interesting. They must, of course, have asked him countless times, and even though he could, he wouldnt.

Frank Sinatra has consistently refused either to author or to authorize his own biography. So others rush in. The present batch (not exhaustive) is ostensibly timed to coincide with his 82nd birthday. Now theres a nice round number for a celebration. It can't have escaped the publishers' notice that Sinatras health is precarious, though it may be less so than the doomwatching tabloids would have us believe; so, at least, I was told by someone who knows someone.

Michael Freedland describes Sinatra as conducting the orchestra with his voice. He is referring to the impact the young singer made on musicians at the start of his first solo recording contract -- with Columbia in the early 1940s -- but its a nice phrase that also evokes the authority Sinatra has always seemed to exercise over his material and his accompanists, live or on television as well as in the studio. It's about the only shaft of light in a murky and practically worthless volume.

Three of the four books on the table are named after Sinatra songs -- two after titles, one after a first line -- but Freedland's All the Way takes its label to heart and raids the canon for chapter headings as well. The young singers formative periods with the Harry James and Tommy Dorsey bands are Nice Work if You Can Get It ;Mia Farrow, his third wife, is The Girl Next Door .(Some neighbourhood.) Two chapters, not very far apart, are called Dont Worry 'Bout Me ,a duplication that suggests amazing carelessness on the author's part and quite astounding indifference on his publishers. Actually, it appears the first time, inaccurately, as Dont Worry About Me ;maybe Freedland thinks they're two different songs with only an apostrophe between them. Song titles give him trouble throughout; he invents songs called Those Little White Lies , That Old Devil Moon and If It's the Last Thing I Do. He thinks that Its All Right With Me ,a Cole Porter classic, is called Its the Wrong Time .Give him his due: When he quotes a politician who referred to the appalling My Way as I Did it My Way ,he appends a "sic."Chutzpah.

Freedland, an English journalist, is a prolific writer of showbiz biographies. Maybe he is cranking them out too fast. He commends Sinatra's recordings with the Dorsey band of What Is This Thing Called Love , South of the Border , Mandy Make Up Your Mind and Little White Lies , though Sinatra recorded none of these songs with Dorsey and never recorded the last two at all. He tells us that Lorenz Hart disliked the way Sinatra tampered with his lyrics to The Lady is a Tramp ,which he first sang in 1957, 14 years after Hart's death. Its doubtful that Hart ever heard Sinatra sing any of his songs which, considering the unrivalled way Sinatra was to draw out the gentle pain of Glad To Be Unhappy or the laconic wit of I Wish I Were in Love Again ,may be considered one of Harts greatest misfortunes.

Discussing Sinatra's first major film, Higher and Higher ,Freedland writes of a legal action involving the singer Jimmy McHugh, who apparently claimed that a number in the movie, The Music Stopped , plagiarized a song of his own. In fact, McHugh was not a singer but a composer, and he wrote and was credited with the entire original score of the picture, including the song The Music Stopped ;if there were any plagiarism suit he would have been on the receiving end of it. Freedland seems to have glanced at his sources a little hastily. Is all this just song-buff's trivia? Not really. McHugh was one of the most successful songwriters of his day, and an author who doesnt know who he was or what he wrote is unlikely to have anything valuable to tell us about Sinatra. And so it proves. He gets the content and chronology of the albums hopelessly confused; his approving comments on the fine September of My Years LP are vitiated by his citing three songs that werent actually on it.

It was also news to me that in 1962 Sinatra was burned in effigy by the Ku Klux Klan with a note attached, reading "Death to Nigger Lover Number One." That is one story I would like to believe. Otherwise, Freedland seems happier chronicling his subject's more boorish behaviour, which he does with the morose relish of a tired columnist. Presumably he has listened to the records and he tells us he has seen the concerts, but enthusiasm eludes him.

He wants to please his mother audience, was Shirley MacLaine's diagnosis of her famous friends overpowering ambition. At once spoiled and neglected by his real mother -- a backstreet abortionist and backstairs politician who ruled her patch of New Jersey with a rod of iron -- Sinatra grew up insecure, arrogant, lonely and gregarious. It was a winning combination for a pop singer, allowing him to touch all the genres important emotional bases with a depth and authority previously unattempted and still unmatched.

John Lahr quotes MacLaine (from her autobiography) in his monograph, originallya New Yorker profile -- he's their theatre critic -- with a lavish pictorial appendix. The photographs make an elegant mosaic, and so does the text. In contrast to Freedland, who is bursting with proudly proclaimed exclusives, Lahr never specifically claims to have interviewed anyone himself (he never says he hasn't, either), but he orchestrates a variety of voices to build up a sketch of the career and an impression of the talent.

His book, though incomparably better written (and incomparably briefer) than Freedlands, still ends up with an odd resemblance to it; it even sports a few howlers. Lahr deplores what everybody else has deplored, praises what everybody else has praised. He notes how "we preppy white boys" identified with the Sinatra who brought grace and sexuality into the pop music of the 1950s, but thats about it. This does not come across as one of his more personal projects.

Bill Zehme's book also derives from a magazine assignment, and a bizarre one. Totally unconcerned with the music, except as a source of myth, Zehme sent Sinatra a questionnaire about his philosophy and lifestyle and, surprisingly, got a reply. This became a profile in Esquire magazine:a tribute to the lost art of livin'  (the dropped "g" says it all), which seems to reduce to boozin, wenchin and stayin' up 'til 4, not letting any of your companions leave the bar before you do. (As one of them says in Lahrs book, Its Sinatra's world, we just live in it.)

In fact, the book is a nostalgic tribute to the Las Vegas '60s, the days -- and more specifically the nights -- of the Clan. As usual, Dean Martin emerges as the funniest of the bunch and Sammy Davis Jr. as the most interestingly articulate. There was also Peter Lawford, whose greatest achievement was to marry into the Kennedys, and whom Sinatra apparently used to call "Brother-in-Lawford," one of the few good jokes with which he is credited. The leader comes off as the straight man, even as strait-laced. (His behaviour around women is described as prudish, which is strangely credible.)

There is no logical reason why a great singer should exert Sinatras kind of personal power, but the charisma obviously carried over from professional into personal life, and the process, once started, must have been impossible to stop. You treat a man like a demigod, thats how he'll behave, his own beneficiary and his own victim. The book is written in the long, tense sentences that used to be regarded as the essence of hip. It is -- however queasy it makes you feel -- more fun than a biography.

Still, Zehme leaves out too much, good and bad, and one falls back on Donald Clarke's book, the best of the bunch. Clarke is an American who lives in England, and writes about U.S. pop culture with British breadth. A musical fanatic, he edited the Penguin Encyclopedia of Popular Music ,the best book of its kind, written in a brisk kind of synoptic shorthand. (The competing tomes are either academically stodgy or poisoned by rock snobbery.) He seems less assured here, writing proper sentences; his prose rambles, although not so much when writing about the music, especially the early stuff. He knows jazz, he knows pop, he knows the big bands, and he knows how they all intersected in Sinatras singing. His analyses are less lovingly detailed than those in Will Friedwalds book The Song is You .He doesn't share Friedwald's compulsion to find nearly every record a masterpiece, and he can be unjustly dismissive, but when he loves something he lets you know why.

He grapples with the dark side, too, especially in a long chapter called The American Aristocracy. This examines Sinatras gangster connections -- never legally proved but impossible to dismiss -- and the bullying that led Sammy Davis to declare "there are many things [Sinatra] does that there is no excuse for." (He had to grovel before being re-accepted into the Clan.) Clarkes conclusion, reached after much circling and repetition, is that Sinatra's life can be seen as a paradigm of the American experiment his "emotionally deprived childhood" parallels the continuous stumblings of a nation that has had to make up its own rules as it goes along. It craves style, it worships toughness, and it gets confused.

If you admire someone's work, you cannot help wanting to like them personally; performers, whom we have the illusion of having met, get to us with particular power. There is, after all, plenty to admire about Sinatra even outside the music. He used to have decent politics. (Its difficult to imagine Bing Crosby or Elvis Presley, the two idols who flank him chronologically, having any convictions at all.) His fabled generosity, to causes and individuals, may have had all kinds of dark psychological motives, but what doesnt? The important thing about good deeds is that they get done. Accepting a humanitarian award, he paid tribute to all the caring people who don't get prizes because they weren't famous to begin with, and this streak of self-deprecation may be the most endearing thing about him.

Sinatra knew he was in a false position (Ive been over-rewarded in my life, and thats the truth) and he resisted it when he wasn't exploiting it. He summed it all up in a phrase that's quoted by everyone whos ever written about him: Whatever else had been said about him, "when I sing, I believe Im honest." Some people put a comma after "believe,"turning it from a steady hope to a ringing affirmation, but it's better without.

Robert Cushman's new radio series, Sweet and Swinging: A Festival of Jazz Singing, begins on Friday, Jan. 16 at 9 p.m. on CBC Radio Two.
1998-01-31-song-titles:
Song titles

Saturday, January 31, 1998

Toronto -- Reviewing a batch of books on Frank Sinatra (Jan. 10), I strongly criticized Michael Freedland's All the Way for its inaccuracies. Among other things, I accused Freedland of "inventing a song called If It's The Last Thing I Do ." In fact, that is the correct title of the Sammy Cahn-Saul Chaplin song. Freedland called it If It's The Last Thing You Do ;I, typing too hastily, inadvertently replaced his wrong title with the right one. So, if it's the last thing I do, I would like to set the record straight.
1998-04-26-the-prince-of-broadway:
The Prince of Broadway

'The Pajama Game', 'Cabaret', 'The Phantom of the Opera': since the 1950s, Hal Prince has been the great musicals director of our time. Now, he's bringing 'Show Boat' to London. Robert Cushman met him in New York

HAL PRINCE - Harold Prince on official credits, but Hal everywhere else - turned around a photograph on his office desk so that I could get a good look at it. It was of his first grandchild; a second is on the way. "My shows," he said, "are a reflection of what I'm thinking about. Show Boat is about family."

Show Boat, first staged in 1927, is thought by many to be the greatest American musical. It was the first Broadway show to concentrate all the resources of the musical on telling a complex and coherent story. A headily innovative book was matched to an equally adventurous score. Oscar Hammerstein wrote the lyrics to Jerome Kern's music, and an extraordinary number of their songs have gone on to lead independent lives - "Ol' Man River", "Bill", "Can't Help Lovin' Dat Man", "Make Believe", "Why Do I Love You", "Life Upon the Wicked Stage".

But they all fit perfectly into their dramatic context: a considerable breakthrough for 1927, and one not to be rivalled for a decade or more. The narrative spans 40 years of American life - a hugely ambitious dramatic canvas. The "show boat" of the title is the Cotton Blossom, which ploughs the Mississippi River, bringing melodrama to the masses. The principal characters are its owners, actors and crew. They come in pairs: Cap'n Andy, the show boat's stage-struck skipper, and his wife Parthy, who rules it and him with a rod of iron; their daughter Magnolia, who proves herself as an actress, and Gaylord Ravenal, the feckless gambler she loves and improvidently marries; Julie La Verne and her husband Steve, a mixed-race couple who fall foul of the vicious Mississippi race laws; actor Frank and comedienne Ellie, the musical's standard light-relief couple; Joe the black deck hand and his wife Queenie, the cook.

It is Joe who sings the show's anthem, "Ol' Man River", described by Hammerstein as "an implicit protest song", and a magnificently economical depiction of human suffering and endurance ("I'm tired of livin' / And feared of dyin' ..."). The show's engagement with race may seem tentative by later standards, but it was unprecedented in its time, and can still strike sparks even today. The premiere of Prince's production - in Toronto in 1996 - was heralded by allegations that the musical was "racist" and "hate literature", the latter an especially strange accusation to hurl at a show that is demonstrably full of the milk of human kindness - full even to overflowing. It became clear that few of the protesters had seen the show, and once the production had opened, little more was heard of them.

Much revised during the lifetimes of Kern and Hammerstein, incessantly recorded and three times filmed, Show Boat has since rolled on as implacably and unpredictably as the river itself. Each version has been different from its predecessor. The text that Prince has adapted and directed draws on all available variants, including the Edna Ferber novel on which the musical was based. The year after the Toronto premiere, the show opened in New York, and has since toured all over America; indeed, it's still doing so. It has just opened in Australia. And this week, it has its premiere in London.

HAL PRINCE turned 70 in January this year. He started as a producer and is now a director. For a long and fruitful time he was both: nobody else has made that transition so successfully, and few have attempted it at all. The walls of his office in Rockefeller Plaza, New York, are crowded, as you would expect, with posters of his shows: the record stretches back now over 44 years. His first production, The Pajama Game, opened on Broadway in 1954. It was a big success, and established the 26-year-old Prince as, in the words of screenwriter and commentator William Goldman, "the last of the boy-wonder producers".

The "boy wonder" flashes a precocious grin from one of the photographs that have squeezed their way in between the posters. It depicts Prince and his producing partner of those days, Robert E Griffith, in the wake of that first success. Griffith is middle-aged and modestly managerial; Prince, spruce and glossy-haired, looks like an engaging and impossibly confident mixture of salesman and graduate student. He and Griffith had worked together as stage managers for the legendary producer/director George Abbott, and when they mounted The Pajama Game, they hired their former employer to direct. They themselves, producing on a shoestring, stage-managed their show; Prince has said that six months passed before he got to see his hit musical from out front.

PRINCE HAS never, to put it discreetly, had to go back to stage-management since. After The Pajama Game, Griffith and Prince went on to produce such notable things as Damn Yankees, Fiorello! (a little-known title in Britain, but one of the few musicals to win the Pulitzer Prize) and, most august of all, West Side Story. Then, after Griffith's death, Prince went solo and produced A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum, Fiddler on the Roof and Cabaret. Out of his office came in fact a staggering proportion of the best American musicals of the 1950s and 1960s. Cabaret (1966) was an especial watershed. To begin with, Prince himself directed it. He brought off something very rare in the theatre, musical or otherwise; he caught the movement of history. In a show set in Weimar Berlin, he let the onset of Nazism creep up on us scene by scene, number by number. Cabaret also began a movement away from linear narrative and towards fragmentation, montage and musical comment: a style that matured, along with a preference for unconventional subject-matter, in the musicals for which Stephen Sondheim wrote music and lyrics and which Prince both produced and directed, shows that - artistically if not commercially - ruled the 1970s: Company, Follies, A Little Night Music, Pacific Overtures, Sweeney Todd.

Then came the flop that ended the collaboration, Merrily We Roll Along. More flops followed with other writers: in the first half of the 1980s it seemed that Prince could do nothing right, and his producing career virtually ended. Salvation, for the man who once said that he had to direct his own shows because nobody else would hire him, came in working for other people. He had already, during the Sondheim period, taken time off to direct Andrew Lloyd Webber's Evita (1978); now he scored the greatest commercial success of his career with Lloyd Webber's Phantom of the Opera (1986).

The Phantom of the Opera, in Prince's luscious staging, has now gone around the world. One of the most enduring satellite productions has been in Toronto, initiating another fruitful association between Prince and the Canadian-based producing company Livent Inc. It led to Livent's producing Kiss of the Spider Woman, one of the most visually compelling and thematically adventurous of all Prince's shows. After this Garth Drabinsky, the company's presiding impresario, suggested a revival of Show Boat. (I have here to declare an interest: I work for Livent. However, my association with the company began only last year.)

Though Prince had generally avoided revivals, this was the one old show he had long wanted to do. Part of the attraction was in the show's scale, and how that connected with his own previous work. Cabaret, Follies, Pacific Overtures might all be called epic musicals, exemplifying Prince's stated belief that "the most effective social commentary is to illuminate one period through another". And Show Boat is America's home-grown epic, depicting life on the Mississippi from the 1880s to the 1920s. The staging scheme evolved by Prince and his designer Eugene Lee emphasises the passage of time "from gaslight to automobile". It peaks in detailed, wonderfully lit genre pictures: a waterfront casino filled with intent gentleman-gamblers, immune to every passion but their own; the Cotton Blossom floating theatre with actors and audience packed in together, feelings running melodramatically high on both sides of the footlights; a Chicago music hall glimpsed in the busy aimlessness of daytime rehearsal and then in the frenzied jollity of New Year's Eve (bodies crowded into a confined space are a repeated motif of the production); the decks, constantly rising and falling, of the show boat itself. Years pass before our eyes in a choreographed montage that is the production's own invention, designed to filling some gaping holes in the original second act.

It's generally conceded that the second act is where Hammerstein's script begins to buckle under the sheer weight of narrative, and this is where Prince's surgery has been most aggressive. Hammerstein's first act, by contrast, is brilliant story-telling, and contains one episode - the "miscegenation scene" - that Prince describes, with obvious conviction, as "the best musical scene I've ever worked on".

"The scene," says Prince, "is rich in apparent drama, and in subtext." The apparent drama comes when Steve cuts Julie's arm and his own in order to mingle their bloods, thereby proving that he has "Negro blood in him" so that his mulatto wife has broken no race laws. The "subtext" belongs to the onlookers, who between them embody every polarity in the story: black and white, old and young, liberal and puritanical, comic and romantic. At the end Cap'n Andy has to find a new leading couple to replace the banished Julie and Steve. To the fury of his monumentally censorious wife, he lights on Magnolia and Gaylord Ravenal. The two share a stage kiss that rapidly develops into the real thing.

"And the scene has always ended," says Prince, "with the two of them kissing, and a spotlight on Parthy having the vapours. Show Boat was originally performed by star personalities who made the roles their own. Then when they all had gone, in revivals they'd take movie stars and put them in the slot, to do their own thing. The tradition with Parthy had been to have fluffy comic ladies: they had the vapours a lot. What I have her do at the end of the miscegenation scene is what any serious actress would do: she sits there stone-faced.

"George Grizzard and Carole Shelley [the London Andy and Parthy] are two serious actors who happen also to have done a lot of comedy in their time; they're approaching the roles with the same reality as John McMartin and Elaine Stritch [who played the roles in Toronto and on Broadway]. They belong together. At the end of the show Carole does something nobody else has done; at the end of the show she shows with her posture that osteoporosis has set in. There can be vastly different performances of Andy and Parthy: the beauty of the material is that there's so much there. The vaudevillians and the young lovers tend to be played the same way, though Ravenal can be more romantic or more seedy older or younger." The London Ravenal is among the young and romantic; he is Hugh Panaro, who recently did time as Raoul, the juvenile lead in Phantom. (The older, seedier Ravenals are often actors who have played the Phantom himself.)

Among the London leads, the only two remaining from the Toronto premiere are the black couple: Michel Bell, who sings Joe with the ringing bass associated with the role since Paul Robeson, and Grethe Boston, who plays Queenie with more edge and less flounce than has ever been customary. "You have," says Prince, "to be so careful not to do caricature." In 1927, the show began with a chorus of black dock-workers singing "Niggers all work on the Mississippi / Niggers all work while the white folks play." The line has been changed, as in previous revivals, to "coloured folks work on the Mississippi ..." Hammerstein meant it to shock, and Prince considered using it, but he now concedes, "I wouldn't ask anyone to utter that word on stage." "Ol' Man River" occasions the fiercest piece of staging in the show; in Prince's words, you watch the characters "tear down a whole back-breaking class system". (It would be unfair to reveal how, except to say that Prince instructed the cast, "if you don't all pull together on the word 'tote' - as in 'tote that barge, lift that bale' - it's all over.")

I SPOKE TO PRINCE in a brief lull between his return from launching the Sydney Show Boat and taking off to do the same thing in London. Weeks before, he had rehearsed one of the American touring companies in Tampa, Florida, knowing that the Australian commitment would prevent him from attending their opening in Fort Lauderdale two weeks later. Phantom has been playing in Hamburg for eight-and-a-half years now: "I try to catch them once a year if I can. I get back to the Vienna production more often. I have a responsibility to keep the shows up - a responsibility, I may say, that rarely occurred to the directors I hired when I was a producer." In fact, when he was a producer, he regularly hired only two directors, but they were two of the best: Jerome Robbins and George Abbott. Robbins apparently never revisited his shows; Abbott would stand in the wings occasionally, with his hand on the stage manager's shoulder, making sotto voce comments on the actors and saying "tell them that ..." And Prince of course would know; for a long time ago, he was that stage manager.

"EVERYTHING'S a long time ago now," Prince says, mindful of his evolution from prodigy to grand old man. I once described him - and I can't stop myself from repeating the description - as an appealing mixture of handyman and sage.

Asked about the future of the musical, he says that it's safe as a form because they can't duplicate it on films and TV, and because there's so much money being made from it. But he despairs that young talents are not being widely nurtured. He tends not to see other people's revivals of his previous shows, but finds himself being nice about them when he does: "Actually, I've not got much to be angry about; even I realise that."

His next musical, Parade, promises to be exceptionally hard-hitting - it's about the lynching of a Jewish man in the American Deep South, just before World War One, and he says it's about his own antecedents - it's where his family settled when they came to America in the first half of the last century. For now, though, he's basking in the softer family glow of Show Boat. (I quizzed him a couple of years ago about his continuing reputation as a director of dark musicals: "Oh no," he said, "These days I'm very benign.")

Show Boat ends with a grey-haired Magnolia pointing proudly to her daughter Kim, now a star in her own right. This is apparently the first Show Boat in which Magnolia and Kim have not been played by the same actress. "So, at the last moment, you had the star, back as Magnolia, saying 'Hey, look, there's Kim,' and pointing at some mute chorus-girl half-hidden in the wings. And that was the final curtain." Here we get three generations on stage at the same time, indissolubly connected but each mentally in their own world. And, like the river, it's troubling and benevolent and irreversible.

Prince Edward Theatre, W1 (0171 447 5400), now previewing, opens Tues.
1998-05-16-the-voice-that-made-us-swoon:
The voice that made us swoon

Saturday, May 16, 1998

Special to the Globe and Mail

FRANK Sinatra was the greatest popular singer of the 20th century. No other singer had a more attractive or more interesting voice; the flaws only added to the individuality. No singer was ever more of a musician; his interaction with his accompaniment was always extraordinary. No singer ever read lyrics more intelligently or with more feeling. And all these gifts were in the service of the song. Yes, he took liberties, but they were always purposeful. Yes, he had a huge ego, but he was able to channel it through whatever he was singing. Song and singer fused to produce something bigger than either.

He was, obviously, a great actor in song. He was also a pretty good actor in non-musical drama, though he was never much of a screen comedian. (In High Society ,the ever-insouciant Bing Crosby wiped the polished floor with him.) For years he was equally big in movies and on records, a feat otherwise managed by only Crosby, Doris Day and Barbra Streisand. Oddly, he never made a first-rate musical. His three best performances were in From Here to Eternity , The Man with the Golden Arm and The Manchurian Candidate ,in none of which did he sing a note. (Even Sammy Cahn, Sinatra's shamelessly resourceful regular lyricist, might have been hard pressed to come up with a title song for the last of them.)

Those three performances -- two underdogs and a sleuth -- were in-character roles. They had little to do with the self that Sinatra, at the same period, was creating in song. In the 1940s, first with The Tommy Dorsey Band and then as a phenomenally popular soloist on the Columbia label, he was a dedicated romantic with a voice of pure silk, bringing to pop music a new kind of hushed intensity. In the 1950s and '60s he fashioned a more complex version of the same persona. The sound became more sonorous, more lived-in, grainier. He sought out the bittersweet wit in sad songs and found a contemplative edge in happy ones.

It is interesting to go back to what may be his definitive up-tempo performance -- the daffily devotional You Make Me Feel So Young ,on Songs for Swingin' Lovers -- and discover that it is not actually all that fast. The first chorus is rather careful and subdued; the second breaks increasingly free. The song's sentiments are intentionally over the top. Sinatra, poker-faced, makes implicit acknowledgment of its absurdity without ever questioning its sincerity. We are charmed, touched and, finally, exhilarated. And it's only the first song on the album. It's a significant track in many ways. It's one of Sinatra's happiest collaborations with Nelson Riddle, who was to arranging what Sinatra was to singing. Both were musical architects. Together they built songs and whole albums, and built them to last. It heralds an LP that was to define a whole genre of singing. It reclaims a then 10-year-old movie song that had never been given its due.

Sinatra was, whether by design or intuitive taste, one of the major archivists of American popular song, perhaps the most important, since no other singer with a comparable repertoire reached so wide a public or was so searching an interpreter. He didn't sing all the major songs (try finding a Sinatra version of Smoke Gets in Your Eyes or Ev'ry Time We Say Goodbye )but he knew which ones were right for him, and discovered them, often in bulk, in the catalogue of every major composer. These Broadway-Hollywood-Tin Pan Alley guys may have spoken the same musical language, but they worked in widely varying dialects. The airy elegance of Cole Porter, the smart vulnerability of Rodgers and Hart, the metropolitan blues of Harold Arlen and Johnny Mercer. These are very different commodities, but Sinatra made them all into facets of himself without losing their individual essence. Not just the essence of each songwriter, but of each song.

He was a diction fanatic. That was an enormous help in imprinting each song so clearly on our consciousness. He had grown up in jazz, so knew how to play with melody and rhythm in the service of the lyric. (One of his ablest disciples, Julius la Rosa, observed that Sinatra sang like Fred Astaire danced.) He was historically lucky. Coming at the end of two eras, the big bands and classic Broadway, he was able to survey them both and preserve the best of each. He was part of them and yet apart from them, which is maybe the best summation of his art in general. He was magisterially present in each song, and yet detached. He played to his audience but rarely pandered to it. He sang not about himself but from himself.

He could be urbanely disenchanted while still the romantic (I Wish I Were In Love Again , I Guess I'll Have to Change My Plan ). He could have enormous fun with a song (Don'cha Go 'Way Mad , Pick Yourself Up ). And, of course, his ballads had a majestic, sculpted quality. It was here that his fastidiousness was most telling; he never simply sang another sad song. Last Night When We Were Young (on the magnificent Wee Small Hours album) was toweringly yearning, reaching a climax three-quarters of the way through on the word "clung." (I use the word "climax" advisedly; this Riddle arrangement, with its use of tension and release, is about the most sexual thing recorded.) One For My Baby (And One More for the Road) has taken on mythical status; it's uniquely lost . When he teamed with Antonio Carlos Jobim for a bossa novaalbum, he made the genre his own and, it seemed, more fully itself. Dindi ,my all-time favourite Sinatra track, is extraordinary, a hushed acknowledgment of unfamiliar beauty. After his faux retirement, he investigated and invigorated Send in the Clowns ,subtly shading every line. In 1982, he cut his last great ballad recital She Shot Me Down ,a set of very specific songs about wrecked relationships. One song, I Loved Her ,is a textbook example of how to colour a song dramatically by singing it, not talking it.

And he kept on doing it, almost to the end (though the two last albums of duets are best forgotten). When I started listening to him seriously, in the '60s, we were already looking back on the Capitol '50s and thinking "what a legacy." At the time it seemed unbeatable, but he at least equalled it. It will take a long time to get his measure.
1998-05-17-one-melancholy-ballad-and-the:
One melancholy ballad, and the whole of his art

Robert Cushman Sunday 17 May 1998 00:02 BST

IN concert Frank Sinatra used to introduce "One For My Baby", the most celebrated saloon ballad in his repertoire, with an extended passage of spoken scene-setting. Over the years his description of the lonely loser at the bar became exaggeratedly flip and hip ("his chick flew the coop ... took all the bread"), but when, finally, he broke into song ("It's quarter to three, there's no one in the place") he was instantly another man.

There are four recordings of this song by Sinatra, but the classic is the one made in 1958. His favourite arranger, Nelson Riddle, provided the discreetest of string-and-woodwind punctuation, but the burden of the accompaniment is born by Bill Miller, Sinatra's pianist. He plays undulating chords in the background with a peculiar mixture of empathy and detachment, a kind of eternal bar-room honky-tonk man. He also offers a comment on the song and the man who sings it; he's the man who's heard it all before, the hypnotic repetitiveness of his playing suggesting some vast uncaring ocean, in which the protagonist's tears can be swallowed up and forgotten. And, in his professional capacity, Miller is the economical accompanist, setting off his employer's vocal and Harold Arlen's melody to maximum effect.

There is the same duality in Sinatra's singing: a perfectly controlled performance of a man who's falling apart. Miraculously, though the technique is there for all to hear, it never obscures the emotion. Sinatra's torch- song sound was that of a man near the end of his rope, and he never sounded closer to it than here. It is the sound of defeat but not quite of despair. At the end of the song ("That long, long road") the singer pulls himself together, at least enough to get himself out of the bar. The album, Frank Sinatra Sings For Only The Lonely, might have been subtitled "Songs for Swinging Underdogs" but the composite hero who sings them always retains a residue of dignity.

Johnny Mercer wrote the lyric for a specific situation in a Fred Astaire movie, but it sounds better out of context and it helps that we don't know the story. Mercer may not have been great on dramatic character but he was wonderful on detail. And it's these details - the small hours, the solitude, the wistful bravado ("Set 'em up, Joe"), the jukebox hungry for nickels, the compulsive button-holing, the implicit awareness that his hearer can't and doesn't care ("Joe, I know, you're gettin' anxious to close") - on which Sinatra seizes. He turns the song into an archetype that's intensely specific. His voice at this time was at its richest but he paints here with a small palette. However, our awareness of the power in reserve gives the haunted vocal a resonant undertow.

"Won't you make the music easy and sad?" he pleads, and answers his own request. Actually, Mercer wrote "dreamy and sad", but I doubt if he minded the alteration. And Sinatra never has to emote to convey emotion. Sometimes, later, he blustered his way through up-tempo numbers but in ballads his touch and his taste were infallible.

To hear the same hushed intensity elsewhere, listen to his tender recording of Antonio Carlos Jobim's "Dindi" in which he conveys a dawning humility in the face of beauty: the beauty of the song and of the person to whom it is sung. For evidence that he could maintain his finesse, his delicacy, his feeling for the specifics of words, music and emotions, in a happy mood, try "You Make Me Feel So Young", a classic that swings without ever hitting you over the head with rhythm.
1998-09-26-music-the-man-who-got-rhythm:
Music: The man who got rhythm

George Gershwin wrote some of the most beautiful songs you've ever heard. He has been brilliantly interpreted by all the greats, from Ella to Miles Davis. He was born 100 years ago today.

Robert Cushman Saturday 26 September 1998 00:02 BST

George Gershwin remains the archetypal American composer. Born into a modest, though hardly poverty-stricken, immigrant family, he began his musical education on the streets of New York in the early years of the century. It was a good time to be out there listening. The ethnic cultures converging on the city had all brought their music with them. Two predominated, and both were available to him, by birth or by affinity; he became the first Jewish composer - the first white composer - to work comfortably with black idioms. Jazz was imposing itself, and he used it; an indigenous musical theatre was developing, and by the time he reached his mid-20s, he was close to taking it over.

From these popular bases, he moved into the concert-hall, and if his original audience couldn't always be physically there with him, they were cheering him on from outside. He was doing a very American thing - demonstrating, in the teeth of academic snobbery, the unity of popular and official culture - and they must have felt that he was doing it for them, taking their music into grander settings. The gifts of melody and rhythm that made his concert works, from Rhapsody in Blue onwards, so attractive, were essentially those that had made his fortune on Broadway. When wedded to a growing sense of form and character, they produced Porgy and Bess whose intoxicating quality is that it is a true opera made out of show music.

Rhythm and melody. Rhythm - the feeling of 1920s jazz, adapted to the theatre - was what people loved about Gershwin and what he, quite consciously, was offering them. It was, both parties knew, the tempo of the times. In 1930, when a Gershwin song proclaimed "I Got Rhythm", it was an archetypal statement: so much so that seven years later, George and his lyricist brother Ira were able to quote it directly in another song, "Nice Work If You Can Get It".

Energy and drive were the Gershwin trademarks: his contract with his public. But "Nice Work" itself proclaims that there was more: it's a happy- sounding song with a sad edge. Gershwin himself was a fun-loving, gregarious, lonely, driven man. And melancholy - derived from the blues or the Hebrew liturgy, or both - is always likely to shade a Gershwin tune, though never to suffocate it.

Ira wrote playful, urbane, rather distanced lyrics. As has often been noted, his gentleness complements his brother's attack. Together, they created a world: a gallant one that laughs and yearns but prefers not to weep. (Porgy, one of the few tragic works of the 20th century, is a grand exception.) George's cruelly early death set the seal on his legendary status; he lived the American dream, and he died it.

Here, with some cheating, are my top 10 Gershwin songs and performances. The list is chronological by composition, and inevitably somewhat arbitrary. You may disagree with my choices; but then tomorrow, so may I.

1"Under a One-Man Top"

An early song, without Ira - but Buddy de Sylva's lyric, hymning the unpretentious joys of motoring the open road as a couple, is perfectly charming, as are the melody and unforcedly jaunty rhythm. Not trademark Gershwin, but the essence of 1924, when precociousness was all. Barbara Cook and Anthony Perkins (yes, he sang) capture it to shy perfection on George Gershwin Revisited (Painted Smiles).

2"Sweet and Low Down"

A relaxed rhythm tune, one of Gershwin's best, evoking New York nightlife in the speakeasy era: "There's a cabaret in this city..." Try Lee Wiley's 1940 recording - from one of the first ever composer albums, now available on Lee Wiley Sings George Gershwin and Cole Porter (Audiophile) - exuding, like all her work, veiled and smoky sexuality.

3 "Someone to Watch Over Me"

This was written as a fast dance tune, and the sensed presence of a beat accentuates the sweet and hopeful lyric it eventually received. "Although he [or I]/ may not be the man some/ Girls think of as handsome" makes everyone feel vulnerable or protective - and, most importantly, included. It's an irresistibly tender song. Every female singer has recorded it (plus a few brave men, including Sinatra). The palm may go to Dawn Upshaw, the new queen of crossover, who steadfastly irradiates it - and the rest of the score - on a complete recording of the source show, Oh Kay! (Nonesuch).

4 "Funny Face"

You can't go wrong with Fred Astaire singing Gershwin (or anything else, actually) - from the 1924 show Lady Be Good to the 1937 film A Damsel in Distress, plus all the subsequent recreations. He performed "Funny Face" twice - in the 1927 stage musical, trading affectionate insults with sister Adele, and the 1957 film (soundtrack on Verve), in which his singing is supremely warm and winning. It may not be a great Gershwin song but it's a defining Gershwin moment, brimming with wry confidence. The face serenaded in the film is that of Audrey Hepburn, who sings a divine "How Long Has This Been Going On": you'll love her funny voice.

5"Let's Kiss and Make Up"

From the same score, stage and screen, this pulsating, vivacious song is best preserved on the Ella Fitzgerald multi-disc, Gershwin Songbook; she especially revels in the urgent, playful extended ending. This is a not-quite-random choice from an essential collection, the crown of a great series. Another might be "They All Laughed", where the line: "They all laughed when Edison recorded sound," inspires a trumpet to pipe up in exact imitation of the legendary obligato of Harry "Sweets" Edison in, of course, recorded sound. Nelson Riddle's arrangements are elegantly swinging and endlessly resourceful. You want The Complete Ella Fitzgerald Songbooks (Verve: 16 CDs, and very dapper for a box-set), so get it.

6"How Long Has This Been Going On"

A long-lined, teasingly sensual ballad that begs for a slow swing, and gets it from Ella (Like Someone in Love, Verve). She sings it on the Songbook too, but this is better, including two full choruses of Ira's admirable lyric and the better of his two verses, rhyming "panties", "aunties", and "an inferno worse than Dante's."

7 "Embraceable You"

This can be cute when sung brisk and serious-comic (as it probably was in Girl Crazy) but for general consumption it's simply Gershwin's loveliest ballad, silken and languorous. Nobody has sung it more sumptuously or inventively than Sarah Vaughan with a trio led by pianist Jimmy Jones on Sarah Vaughan or The George Gershwin Songbook Vol. 2, (EmArcy). Beautiful tune and beautiful voice are mutually enhancing; even Vaughan sceptics, wary of her pyrotechnic excesses, will succumb. (This is the testimony of a convert.)

8"It Ain't Necessarily So"

The first near-complete recording of the opera Porgy and Bess appeared in 1951, and it's still the best (it's about to be reissued by Sony). Goddard Lieberson's production is enormously atmospheric, and the cast includes veterans of the 1935 original cast and the first major (1942) revival. Among the latter, is Avon Long, a gleeful and serpentine Sportin' Life whose mocking inflections have never been equalled. For a slow and soulful reading of this non-credo, hunt up Bobby Darin's version, tucked away in his first album of standards (the one that included "Mack the Knife"); it's haunting with witty, verbal variants ("Jonah resided in a whale"). The great instrumental Porgy is, of course, the Miles Davis- Gil Evans jazz suite, a masterpiece drawn from a masterpiece. "I Loves You Porgy" has received moving, emotionally naked jazz-pop performances from Nina Simone and from Billie Holiday who, had she possessed the voice and the acting ability, would have been the perfect Bess.

9"They Can't Take That Away From Me"

Gershwin's greatest song - a yearning but forbearing farewell - was written for Astaire, and his courteous elegance is written all over it. There are two great hip versions by Sinatra, but my choice is Ira's long-time neighbour, on Rosemary Clooney Sings the Lyrics of Ira Gershwin (Concord Jazz). Her reading is brisk and unsentimental, the facade subtly cracking only at the last fence: "the way you've changed my life..."

10 "Hi-Ho"

Written for the same film (Shall We Dance) and unused, though its strolling tempo and sunny wordplay would have been classic Astaire. And you feel his presence through the performances of other people. Tony Bennett does it well, and Bobby Short even better on a treasure-trove of an album, Bobby Short Is K-raz-y for Gershwin (Atlantic), that goes from rarities like this to a stirring revivification of "Love Is Here To Stay". This, appropriately enough, is prime cafe-society Gershwin. "Hi Ho" is a long song, but you don't want it to end.
1998-12-07-a-better-play-than-we-get-to-:
One Flea Spare

Canadian Stage Theatre, Toronto

Half-hearted applause at intermission is always a bad sign. It suggests that audience members are uncertain whether the show is over but rather hope that it might be. Naomi Wallaces One Flea Spare is, almost certainly, a better play than it appears in the shapeless, nerveless production that Alisa Palmer has directed for Nightwood Theatre. The play has a sharp, original aroma, though it's not always clear or agreeable. The production reeks of sludge and good intentions.

Wallace, a youngish American playwright who lives in England, has written what may be the first play ever to address the Great Plague that devastated London in 1665 and 1666. It's a juicy subject, though the dramatists who lived through the event can hardly be blamed for passing it by; this was the Restoration period when drama meant either bustling sex-comedy, or heroic tragedy in rhyming couplets. Neither form would have lent itself to the depiction of ones friends and neighbours dropping dead behind bolted doors and being carted off to mass graves on the edge of town.

A house in which the pestilence was discovered was locked up for weeks. This play begins by playing a cruel joke on two of its characters. Mr. and Mrs. Snelgrave, a well-to-do couple about to emerge from quarantine, are plunged back into it again when their home is invaded by two strangers: a sailor and a 12-year old girl.

So four apparently ill-assorted people are condemned to interact, while a fifth -- a watchman, who might as well be a jailer -- prowls sardonically outside.

The Snelgraves may have stayed alive but their marriage is dead.

She was badly injured in a fire, years before, and he hasnt touched her since. It's left to Bunce, the sailor, to seek out the few patches on her skin that can still feel, and to awaken them. We are told two things. One is that in a world of suppurating flesh, the body can still be a vessel of salvation: a striking notion. The other is that sex is something indulged in mostly by the lower orders: a snobbish cliche of British political drama, and historically unsound. To judge from the literature, the toffs of the 1660s were at it like rabbits.

Satire, sex and heroics are still there but they've been chopped up and seasoned, in a determinedly lyrical style that is partly the authors own and partly a reflection of whats going around today.

Wallace has been highly praised by Tony Kushner, author of Angels in America, and like him she takes large historical themes and fillets them into scenes that are variously funny, pungent, and screamingly tiresome.

It's unfair that the tiresome parts are largely dumped on the young girl, whose name is Morse. The plague has taken both her parents but she rises above it. She spends some of her time scoring pert points off the men in the cast, and 13-year-old Natasha Greenblatt does this very well. But she also functions as a narrator and as the bearer of some kind of transcendental message. She is not yet able to give colour and form to such a torrent of text, and most of what she said lost me.

Her elders don't fare much better. Exchanges that look sharp on the page emerge drained of wit. Actors bear down on one another with what is presumably meant to be an air of menace but there is no danger, no combustion: merely a series of short walks around the stage. Set-pieces come off best.

David Fox as Snelgrave is sweetly self-satisfied when demonstrating to a barefoot and skeptical Bunce the historical inevitability of his own possession of a pair of good shoes. He is even better when inquiring about the horrors of a life at sea, and taking a keen vicarious pleasure in them. ("Scurvy, was there?") But as the symbol of an evil patriarchy finally overthrown by servants and women, he seems far too amiable and rather lightweight.

Woody Dalrymple and Brenda Robins play their erotic encounter with great tact, though earlier she seems more of an automaton than is strictly necessary. Sky Gilbert plays the watchman, who veers between sexual exploitation, democratic rumbling, and half-naked apocalyptic prophecy. He is a presence on stage, but technically limited. He does get to slip us scraps of historical background, and what he says in this line is so interesting that you want the author to can the fantasia and cut to the facts.
1998-12-17-stoppard-in-love-in-his-lates:
Both of Tom Stoppard's most recent works have "love" in the title. He has only a joint screenplay credit on the new film Shakespeare in Love, but the picture has his erudite and hilarious fingerprints all over it. Meanwhile, his latest play, The Invention of Love, is running in London's West End. It too is vintage Stoppard. It too portrays an actual writer -- in this case the late Victorian poet and classical scholar A.E. Housman -- in the grip of erotic passion. Stoppard is now the foremost romantic dramatist writing in English.

This is not what he's been famous for. He's been known, quite rightly, as an intellectual and a wit. This, mysteriously, has caused him to be labelled cold and frivolous. In the two new pieces, romantic love co-exists with the love of learning, or of art, or of show business, and is the richer for it.

Shakespeare in Love is partly Stoppard in love -- in love with the theatre, of all ages. The Elizabethan playhouse manager Philip Henslowe -- historically a notorious loan shark -- is softened into a tradesman who has gone into the business for profit and has been caught up in the economic irrationality of it all. (A Renaissance Ed Mirvish perhaps, though not as well dressed.) Shakespeare (Joseph Fiennes) is the Bankside's flavour of the month, assailing his friend and rival Christopher Marlowe with the deadliest of compliments: "I loved your early stuff." John Webster, future author of such horror comic tragedies as The Duchess of Malfi, is an unappetizing youth, playing with rats and relishing the more sadistic death scenes.

In Shakespeare's time female roles were played by boys. Like at least two novels and one play before it, the movie offers a stage- struck young woman disguising her gender in order to become the first (uncredited) English actress. In most versions she gets to play Juliet; the present treatment is more sophisticated, and Gwyneth Paltrow's Lady Viola spends a lot of time playing Romeo behind an endearingly false little beard. And, of course, she bequeaths Shakespeare the name of a heroine for Twelfth Night. And, of course, they fall wildly for each other, despite him having a wife back in Stratford, and her being betrothed. And we -- buoyed up on the film's mixture of anachronistic satire, learned fantasy and radiant goodwill -- believe in and root for them. The action of the movie plays a brilliant and very Stoppardian cat-and-mouse game with that of Romeo and Juliet itself. Romeo is the play that first brought love believably to the stage -- or so we are told by Queen Elizabeth herself, magisterially played by the great Judi Dench in a performance that leaves her Queen Victoria in the dust.

So the film might actually have been called The Invention of Love if the play hadn't got there first. According to its hero, Housman, (best known as the author of The Shropshire Lad) love was invented by the ancient Roman poets. Horace and Catullus, in writing the first formal love lyrics, gave the rest of us something to live up to.

Certainly Housman himself takes them to heart. However, his passion, given his time and temperament, can hardly be declared, let alone consummated. He loves Jackson, a good-natured and thoroughly heterosexual athlete whom he met when they were both undergraduates.

Jackson's realization ("it's terrible but it's not your fault") and Housman's suffering are conveyed with an agony and delicacy unprecedented in Stoppard.

"You're half my life," says Housman. The other half is textual criticism; he's just as passionate about that, and a lot more articulate. Stoppard takes as his subject the scholar's lust to establish an accurate classical text and he actually makes it register theatrically as passion. It's difficult to imagine another playwright doing that.

It's also impossible to think of another actor who could embody that passion as thrillingly as John Wood, for years a player of flawless technical and intellectual prowess. In 1974, Stoppard wrote the central role in Travesties for him; and that play -- a kaleidoscopic political-literary-intellectual vaudeville -- in many ways prefigured The Invention of Love. Its onstage characters included Lenin and James Joyce, but it was haunted by the offstage presence of Oscar Wilde; a large part of the dialogue was pastiche of The Importance of Being Earnest.

The new play is presented as Housman's deathbed dream. We first meet him, as befits a deceased classicist, being ferried across to Hades. ("I don't suppose I"ll have time to meet everybody," he says to Charon, the mythological boatman. "Yes, you will," says Charon.) Later, he gets to meet his younger self, encounters to which Wood brings a pathos and vulnerability that I have never seen in him before. This play too is haunted by Oscar Wilde, an offstage personality in everyone's lives, first as the Oxford aesthete, then as the homosexual martyr. Finally, Wilde makes a personal appearance, to confront Housman -- the peacock recklessness of the artist against the lifelong timidity of the scholar. As usual in Stoppard, everything dovetails.

In fact, he's been a romantic -- an intelligent romantic -- for most of his career. Not quite all: His first success, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are Dead, had no discernible love interest. It was an investigation of the off-stage life of two notoriously indistinguishable minor characters from Hamlet -- part metaphysical game, part literary joke, and hugely funny.

But in his next major play, Jumpers, he was already moving on.

Its hero is a professor of ethics, pondering the differences between good as in "a good man" and good as in "a good bacon sandwich."

Helplessly anachronistic, he believes in God. His opponents, very modern, believe mainly in success. His wife, a disoriented former musical comedy star, no longer believes in anything much. One endearing feature of the play is that husband and wife seem genuinely fond of one another, however incapable of doing anything constructive about it.

Personally, I cared more about them than about the couple whose relationship -- first adulterious, then marital -- was exhaustively examined in Stoppard's later play, The Real Thing. This was a naturalistic piece by his standards, and a considerable commercial success; but it seems to me the Stoppard play for people who don't like Stoppard. It had the trappings of seriousness. But with Stoppard, the lighter the touch, the deeper the feeling. Arcadia was a triumphant demonstration of this. It juggled historical periods.

It took in literature, landscape gardening, and chaos theory. It also took in sex. And it was outrageously persuasive about all of them.

Shakespeare in Love is full of in-jokes, but they're incidental; if you miss them you won't miss them. The Invention of Love is more demanding: allusive, not to say elusive, even by Stoppard's standards. But the film and the play, a light comedy and a dark, go well together.

There has always been a pervasive joyousness in the way Stoppard structures his plays. The delight he takes in his own craft and his own wit is contagious; it suggests that life might be worth living and people worth loving -- unusual ideas to encounter in the modern theatre. As in all the best comedy -- screwball or Shakespeare, even sometimes in life -- laughter sets you up for romance.

- Shakespeare in Love will be released, and reviewed, tomorrow.
