1998-12-21-livent-s-musical-brilliance-m:
Parade

Vivian Beaumont Theater,

Lincoln Center, New York

A show about racial prejudice so virulent that it leads to murder. A show about the American past whose score is steeped in Broadway tradition but not in nostalgia. A show directed by Harold Prince that ends with Brent Carver getting executed.

Parade, a Lincoln Center co-production that officially opened on Thursday in New York after a long run of previews, is unmistakably a Livent musical.

It belongs, that is, in the tradition of Kiss of the Spider Woman, Ragtime, and the revival of Show Boat. None of those shows possesses all of the characteristics I've listed, but each of them some of them. There is a definite family likeness. Fosse, Livent's fifth original -- already seen in Toronto and opening on Broadway next month -- stands to one side of the tradition, being a retrospective revue of the work of one choreographer; by definition it too is steeped in the history of the musical but in a more nakedly obvious sense.

The four major shows seem to me to constitute a very impressive track record. Or -- if the most funereal predictions about the company's future prove true -- an impressive legacy. Either way, I can't think of any commercial producer in North America in the last decade with a body of work to touch it. (How many producers have ever developed a house style?) I have always loved musicals -- which doesn't mean I like all of them, far from it -- and I especially love American musicals; so I admit to a bias in favour of Livent's shows, which adhere devoutly to the American book-musical tradition.

The company's parallel role as importer of the complete works of Andrew Lloyd Webber seems to have had no effect on its own creations.

I also have a more immediate interest: For eighteen months -- from the spring of 1997 until the bitter downsizing of three weeks ago -- I was, very happily, an employee of Livent. (The group of people assembled there were the best I have encountered in any organization. Their dispersal is tragic.) I was director of corporate communications. Apart from my responsibilities as an in- house writer, I attended workshops of the new shows --

Parade, Fosse -- and gave feedback. Kiss, Show Boat and Ragtime were all done deals long before I joined; in fact, as a critic, I'd reviewed them.

It's probably fortuitous, but there has been a progressive concentration of the historical focus in Livent's shows. Kiss paints a recognizable if unspecified landscape of oppression in modern South America. Show Boat follows an array of fictitious characters across half a century; both time and space are clearly denoted, and the inherent epic quality is accentuated in Hal Prince's production.

Ragtime, still epic, moves over fewer years and fewer miles, and it brings in a handful of historical figures as symbolic markers.

Parade zeroes in on a single factual incident: the railroading in 1915 of a Jewish factory supervisor in a small Georgia town, on a charge of murdering one of his workers, a 13-year-old girl.

If Parade is the most intimate of the four musicals, it is also the most challenging. This is not because it ends with the accused, Leo Frank, being lynched. The same actor got himself tortured and shot at the end of Kiss. And if you want to talk about dark finales, you can't beat Cabaret, which sent its audience home on the rise of Nazi Germany. What's disturbing about Frank is not his death but his life. He's cold, he's aloof, and he's awkward; if we are going to sympathize, it has to be with his predicament, not his personality.

(There's a curious parallel here with Prince himself: the work, not the man. Because they don't gladhand the audience, his shows have been called cold.)

Brent Carver's particular brilliance as a musical actor is to find the rhythm of a character and carry it through speech, song, and movement. As the gay window-dresser in Kiss he was lithe, warm, and hopeful. As Leo Frank he's dainty, prim, and -- for a musical hero -- amazingly quiet.

It's nice to beat the americans at their own game

It's not just that he acts spooky; he acts guilty. When the cops first come for him, he volubly protests his innocence before anyone has accused him. I don't suppose Prince or his book writer Alfred Uhry actually believe that Frank killed the girl, but they never get around to saying explicitly that he didn't. There's a teasing vein of ambiguity in the show, and beyond that a scary truth: He may be guilty, he's probably innocent, but from the town's point of view it doesn't matter. They've all made up their minds, from hatred or opportunism or both; just as, 80 years later, congressmen and columnists have lined up for or against Bill Clinton entirely according to their a priori political opinions.

Ironically, almost the only character who seems to doubt is Mrs.

Frank, played with wonderful poise by Carolee Carmello. She almost deserts Leo at his trial; then, after he's been found guilty, rallies to his defence, wins his pardon from a conscientious state governor whose career is thenceforth ruined, and rediscovers herself and her marriage in the process -- at which unbearable moment the lynch mob moves in.

When I first heard about Parade, I was told that it was basically a love story. That, I thought skeptically, is what they would say.

In fact, when I saw the workshop, I found that they were right and that it worked beautifully; all the same, it has been strengthened by a couple of new songs. More important, though, are new numbers that fill in what was once a patchy racial and political background: a sardonic black ensemble about being for once not the most downtrodden people in town, or a savage spiritual that unites all the haters. (By the way, despite all the glib remarks in the press about corporate theatre and focus groups, musicals were workshopped at Livent in exactly the same way as they are everywhere else.)

There are still some loose ends: some characters abruptly introduced or dropped , some connections left shadowy or unexplained. The lynchers are individuals and full of misgivings; but since, for the most part, we haven't gotten to know them, the scene can't capitalize on this, and it's strangely ineffective. The staging lacks the burnished glamour of Show Boat, the sweep of Ragtime, or the visual jazz of Kiss (still my favourite Livent musical).

But Parade has its own stark power, and a highly encouraging score from a young composer-lyricist, Jason Robert Brown. This affirms, as did Ragtime, the wit, variety, and dramatic power of American song after all the constricting theatrical years of europop. It benefits too from not being asked to do what dialogue can accomplish better. Alfred Uhry's book, like Terrence McNally's for Ragtime and Kiss, is exceptionally adroit and intelligent, but perhaps the basic function of any musical book -- we've learned this the hard way over the last 20 years -- is to stop the score from sounding silly.

The 1990s have not been good for musicals. Even admirers of the British and French non-stop music machines would have to admit that in this decade they have been dying on their feet. (Sunset Boulevard? Martin Guerre?) There have been a mere handful of substantial American shows: Rent, Titanic, Passion (my least favourite Sondheim, but Sondheim nonetheless). There is The Lion King, but there's something dispiriting about plonking a film musical down on the stage, even if it's done with bravado. And there has been nothing funny.

I can't claim that the Livent shows have solved all these problems -- they haven't even begun with the last -- but they have recognized how much potential still resides in the language of the Broadway musical, how exciting its best practitioners are, and how both the art and the artists can leap at the right subject. The American musical's historic function is to show America to itself; and it's a pleasing irony that it has taken a Canadian-based company to reaffirm this. It's nice to beat the Americans at their own game.

Our nationalists may have other words for it, but I see no evidence that big musicals have been taking up space, physical or psychological, that would otherwise be occupied by Canadian plays. I think it's exciting that fine Canadian actors -- Brent Carver, Steven Sutcliffe, and others -- have held their own with the best on Broadway, and I would hope that in time there might be more: writers and directors too.

Finally, after years of hard labour as critic and audience, I acknowledge the brute fact that good theatre is always to be welcomed, whatever colours it sails under. If Livent does disintegrate, somebody had better pull up the slack. And fast.

1999-01-04-mercer-without-tears-too-marv:
Johnny Mercer was the prince of America lyricists, and to celebrate him is to salute the whole mid-century era of popular music he wrote with nearly every major composer, from Kern to Mancini. He was sung by literally every singer, and he worked in every available setting -- jazz, Broadway, Hollywood, big bands, Tin Pan Alley, and radio.

He was also one of the great American vocalists, perhaps the only singer-songwriter to justify this hypen. He sang rhythm and comedy songs with whimsical finesse and in his later years he was a uniquely wistful balladeer, singing less about love than about evanescence.

His personal style, impish and melancholy, has little in common with the chunky, cheerful approach of Scott Walker, CBC radio host and singer. Walker can hit deep notes that Mercer could only have reached in his dreams, but his idea of swing is to increase the tempo and self-consciously shift a few accents. Mercer was a Southerner who even some black listeners thought was black; Walker is definitely white-bread, looking and sounding like the front-man for a Glenn Miller revival band.

Not sounding like Mercer is no disqualification for singing his songs. But in Too Marvelous for Words (the New Year's Eve attraction at the Limelight Dinner Theatre, with dates lined up elsewhere in Ontario), Walker is actually playing Mercer. The premise is that it's 1965, and he's running through his massive catalogue in order to cut a retrospective album for Capitol Records, the company that he had co-founded 20 years earlier. One of the many unexplored ironies left lying about is that by this date, Capitol was re- making itself as "home of the Beatles." The new owners wouldn't have given Mercer the time of day.

Much of the script derives from an autobiographical "Lyrics and Lyricists" evening that Mercer gave in New York in the early '70s. It's diversified, though, with ancedotes drawn from all over, not all about Mercer.

Indeed, given the huge bulk of available material, the show goes off at a surprising number of tangents. It includes one song, Baby It's Cold Outside, that Mercer recorded but didn't write; an agonizingly protracted sequence about Sadie Vimmerstedt, the Ohio housewife who sent him the opening lines for I Wanna Be Around; and appearances by a character called "the Kid", an unnamed Mercer protege who seems to be based on Margaret Whiting but who also sings songs associated with Connee Boswell and Billie Holiday. This last device seems to promise some kind of pay-off, but it never comes.

Susan Henley plays all the women -- including Johnny's wife, Ginger -- and the two duet with great charm and spirit on Mercer's first published song, Out of Breath and Scared to Death of You, full of cute '30s wordplay. There are some other enterprising selections; I was delighted by the inclusion of The Matrimonial Stomp from Li'l Abner, though it lost its funniest lines.

If most of the other songs are familiar they're still worth hearing, and Walker communicates his own enthusiasm for them; he does a touching skylark. The musicians -- pianist David Warrack and bassist Bob Price -- are excellent. The commentary makes some interesting points -- Mercer's lack of success on Broadway, his long association with Fred Astaire, another small-town boy made good who was also a great part-time singer -- but except on the most obvious level of "and them I wrote", it never connects the man to the work. And the show doesn't end; it stops.

Missing are Mercer's destructive passion for Judy Garland, his increasing pessimism about America and the music business, and his drinking. Plainly it wasn't meant to be that kind of show; it's a small, unpretentious entertainment with no thought of disturbing anyone.

And Mercer is a difficult theatrical subject since -- as he himself readily admitted -- he wasn't an obviously theatrical writer. He knew as much as anyone about capturing speech rhythms in song but he didn't create or illuminate characters. He spent a lifetime writing about romantic love but -- unlike Cole Porter or Lorenz Hart -- he had nothing individual to say on the subject; he merely rearranged the conventional symbols.

He did it, though, with endless verbal resource; and it is his delight in the magical, unexpected but wholly appropriate world that gives his work its extraordinary distinction. The most famous example -- the "huckleberry friend" of Moon River -- may also be the best, drenched as it is in yearning for an unreachable past. Mercer was the most lyrical of lyricists -- a rural writer in an urban world -- and the themes of childhood and loss are the most personal in his work, increasingly so as his own death drew nearer. I wonder if that's a coincidence.

A couple of seasons ago on Broadway there was a full-scale Mercer revue called Dream, which seemed dimly aware of this but rang away from its own insights; it presented Moon River as an eleven o'clock star solo rather than as the ultimate home-town song. (It also managed, with awe-inspiring consistency, to misread such dramatic clues as do exist in the lyrics.) Mercer still awaits a worthy stage tribute. So do many of his peers. For any of them, the limelight is a jewel of a cabaret space.

1999-01-08-it-simply-doesn-t-ring-true:
IT'S ALL TRUE

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

Jason Sherman's It's All True is a clever, occasionally brilliant, evening with a fast pulse. It is not, however, anything more than that, and at some crucial moments it's less.

It's a play about a play. It takes off from one of the most celebrated first nights in theatrical history, and is part tribute, part expose.

In 1937, a new political musical, The Cradle Will Rock, was about to open in New York, sponsored by Roosevelt's Federal Theatre Project. Just before the announced first night, the FTP, rattled by allegations of left-wing bias, put the production on ice -- cancelled it. More surprisingly -- since the show was practically a hymn to organized labour -- the actors' and musicians' unions reinforced the ban. There was a rivalry between the two unions, and the script happened to be on the wrong side of it.

The Cradle was written and composed by Marc Blitzstein and directed by Orson Welles. Blitzstein was a virtual unknown -- an adventurous musician and a committed Marxist, greatly influenced by the Berlin classics of Bertolt Brecht and Kurt Weill. Welles was Welles -- at 22 a major force in theatre and radio and a genius in everybody's eyes, not the least his own.

With their theatre padlocked, they and their colleagues took guerrilla action. They marched their company, plus a couple of thousand fascinated spectators, through the streets to another theatre, and hey, kids, they did the show right there. Denied sets and musicians, Blitzstein sat on stage at a piano, played the score, and announced the scenes. The actors, forbidden to appear on stage, sang their roles (Cradle is virtually through-composed) from the house. It was, of course, a howling success; subsequent productions have all been modelled on that thrilling impromptu premiere, rather than on the expressionist spectacle Welles had originally devised.

It's All True takes us from the announcement of the ban to the climactic moment at which a frightened actress gets up in the auditorium and delivers her first line. This being the theatre, the legend of quick-thinking artistic solidarity dissolves on examination into a viciously diverting war of egos. In addition to Welles and Blitzstein, there are John Houseman, Welles' pernickety patrician producer, and Howard da Silva, a belligerent leftist actor. Then there are the women in their lives -- a fitting phrase here since the men all treat them as appendages.

The casting drives this home. Four actors get to stretch out in a character apiece; meanwhile, two actresses divide half a dozen roles between them. Tamara Bernier and Melody Johnson are the ladies, and their quicksilver doubling is one of the great pleasures of Richard Rose's staging. (This is a co-production between Tarragon, the host theatre, and Rose's Necessary Angel company.) By a sharp modulation of voice or stance, either of them, with no change of wig or costume, can propel us into a whole different phase of the action.

The play doesn't confine itself to the crucial day; it delves, through interlocking flashbacks, into the writing, casting, and rehearsal processes, and into what lies behind them: the backbiting, the agonizing, the artistic and sexual seductions. Like the performance it commemorates, Rose's production roams all over the auditorium as well as the stage, but through all its ramblings in space and time it never loses its way.

Neither does Sherman's script -- at least not in terms of narrative coherence. The opening scene -- a three-way quarrel when the axe first falls -- is done with great zest, as a staccato battle of unfinished sentences, revelling in its own stylishness. The backstage revelations are fun. So is the history: Welles has just done Doctor Faustus, and a congressman has asked, "This Christopher Marlowe, was he a Communist?" The contemporary resonances -- subsidies remorselessly whittled away, artists divided if not conquered -- are very pertinent. But the centre of the play is hollow.

Richard Binsley's Houseman is an amusingly elegant cartoon; Martin Julien's da Silva a feisty if rather monotonous Brooklyn whippersnapper. But the main burden lies on Blitzstein and Welles. Both are haunted by women who died on them: Welles' mother, Blitzstein's wife. It seems very pat. Citizen Kane's Rosebud, twice warmed over.

We are told that Blitzstein's wife gave him a) a temporary refuge from his homosexuality and b) all his political ideas. Unsure of his own talent (like everybody) he worships Brecht but snipes at Weill, whom he calls a facile crowd-pleasing melodist. (It's certainly true that nobody could ever have levelled that accusation at Blitzstein.) Tom McCamus doesn't have much room to manoeuvre but he sounds impeccable and, in derby and neatly rumpled brown suit, looks it, too.

Victor Ertmanis' Welles, by contrast, looks and sounds entirely wrong: a flabby, grumbling bully. Welles may well have been a bastard, he was certainly a megalomaniac, but he was never charmless. Welles at 22 was the classic boy wonder, and you have only to look at the early scenes of Kane to get the message. (Ertmanis, oddly enough sounds more like the real, and oily, Howard da Silva.) "It's All True is not all true, says the author in the program, and fair enough, but this Welles convinces neither as documentary nor as an original creation with the same name.

And there is the little matter of The Cradle Will Rock itself. At one point, Welles and Houseman dismiss it as "sentimental agitprop." Well, they're right, it is. It's also a passionate and original work, with clumsy words but powerful music. But we never get to hear it. Maybe it was an artistic choice, maybe they couldn't get the rights, but the brief excerpts we hear aren't Blitzstein, but somebody's approximation of Blitzstein. (And talk about imitation Weill: the opening vamp sounds as if it's going to turn into Pirate Jenny.) So we never get to feel what the fuss has been about. Imagine if, at the climax of Shakespeare in Love, Tom Stoppard had decided to indulge a passion for blank-verse pastiche. Coupled with the author's apparent dislike of his characters, it makes for a chilly evening.

When Welles the theatrical conjurer appears at the end to murmur "magic," it may be meant as ironic self-deprecation. But the joke rebounds.

- It's All True runs until Feb. 7. Box office: (416) 531-1827.

1999-01-11-lessons-that-are-hard-to-forg:
How I Learned to Drive

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

A woman in her forties looks back on the older male relative who sexually abused her throughout her teens, and wonders about his own formative years. "What," she asks "did they do to you, Uncle Peck?" That is a stunningly generous way for her to put it -- and she is not a sentimental person.

I am not a Christian, and I don't imagine that Paula Vogel is either, but her play How I Learned to Drive does seem to me to exemplify what I believe to be one of the principles of Christian charity: Hate the sin, love the sinner. Or, if not love, then understand. Understand, but don't presume to explain.

How I Learned to Drive has been mounted by the Canadian Stage Company after a lengthy run off-Broadway and a heap of regional productions. It also won a Pulitzer Prize which, for once, seems well-deserved.

The narrator-heroine grew up in rural Maryland, in an oppressively close family that gave its members nicknames inspired by their genitalia; hers is Li'l Bit. (We never do learn her real name.)

Mocked for her academic ambitions and literary inclinations -- how, asks her grandfather, will Shakespeare help her to lie on her back in the dark? -- she turns to Uncle Peck, who is married to her mother's sister, and who is courteous and sympathetic and helps with the dishes. He gives her driving lessons, starting when she's 13, and he proves an excellent and conscientious instructor. She passes her test first time, and in later life driving through the countryside is her main pleasure.

The rest of Uncle Peck's legacy is less benevolent. He uses their time in the car to seduce her. He also photographs her, and teaches her to drink. Confused but not exactly innocent, she, in her own words, "draws a line."

As far as we can see, he crosses that line only twice -- on their first and last encounters -- but those are enough to traumatize her; and her trauma, really, is the play. From a chilly, detached middle age (she's going through life with the brake on) she recalls, in scrambled order, the crucial events of her youth.

The scrambling provides a pleasurable puzzle for the audience. It also allows us to track the ebb and flow of her memories, and the way in which each contributes to the final picture.

Fiona Reid plays Li'l Bit with a wary spirit and an open face: The perfect counterpoint for a dual role. On this basic distinction she builds a more complex layering; she distinguishes not only between the girl and the woman, but between the girl at 16 and at 17, a bit more brazen, a bit less happy.

Jim Mezon's soft-spoken Uncle Peck, by contrast, comes to us fully formed, or fully malformed: Desperation kept in check (he's a reformed alcoholic), always patient, always polite, always, somehow, pink.

It would be difficult, by the end, to say which of them is the greater victim; though, mercifully, neither of them acts the part. Only one scene reveals how calculating, and how indiscriminately predatory, Peck actually is: One in which he takes a young nephew angling in a Southern stream. The boy is unseen, but he might have grown up to figure in an even more disturbing play called How I Learned to Fish.

Those supporting characters who do appear are divided between three actors, referred to by the author -- with needless pretention - - as a Greek chorus. In fact they aren't commentators; they merely announce the scenes with spoken captions drawn from a driving manual: "Reverse gear" means a flashback.

They are cast without reference to age: A device that levels the playing-field for the chronological leaps required of the leading actress. It also keeps the tone light; as played by two youngsters, Kevin Bundy and Cara Pifko, the scenes with Li'l Bit's grandparents are neat rather than gross. (He is unwaveringly horny, she unwaveringly censorious, memorably announcing "if women would learn to keep their knickers on, maybe somebody in this family would finish high school.") They also play Li'l Bit's schoolmates: Female and jealous, male and geeky.

Susan Coyne doubles as the heroine's mother and aunt. The first is indeterminately written and played, existing mainly for a dissertation on a lady's rules for drinking that is all too obviously a set-piece. The second -- Uncle Peck's wife -- is also defined by a single speech: A defence of her husband that's a beautiful blend of anger and protectiveness.

Joseph Ziegler's production equals the New York version on acting, and beats it visually. The original was not so much sparse as impoverished. This one, in sets by Peter Hartwell, lets us in on back-road, cocktail bar, motel-room America: Rather like Lolita, which apparently inspired the author. (Though in her version it's Lolita, not Humbert, doing the telling -- and she who's the intellectual.)

A British director once offered the best diagnosis I know of the sickness of modern drama: Its failure to create characters that actors of the future might conceivably want to play. This play offers two of them, and this production has the performances to prove it.

- How I Learned to Drive is playing at the Bluma Appel Theatre until Feb. 6. For tickets, call (416) 368-3110.

1999-01-15-from-a-gang-of-thugs-to-a-bun:
Steel Kiss/Gulag is in repertory at Buddies until Jan. 13. Box office: (416) 975-8555.

STEEL KISS/GULAG

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, Toronto

Robin Fulford wrote Steel Kiss 12 years ago as a response to the murder by four drunk youths of a gay man in a Toronto park. The play depicts a similar event, and focuses on the perpetrators rather than the victim. Last year's crucifixion of Matthew Shepard in Wyoming gave the play a renewed topicality, which its author would probably have been happy to forgo.

Buddies in Bad Times has now revived it, in repertory with Gulag, a sequel written nine years later that follows the killers into prison and out on to parole. The advance word on Steel Kiss was about the authors courage in presenting four homophobic homicides as human beings rather than monsters.

I wonder how else you could write a play about them? Delivering on good intentions is, of course, another thing. Steel Kiss brings its characters into the light but doesnt bring them to life.

It uses a stage full of devices. The actors playing the boys also perform all the other roles. They appear as family members, yackety- yacking their kids from behind a set of freak masks. They are preachers, filling the air with righteous prejudice (the boys don't look much like church-goers but we get the point), and they are high- school teachers, boring their contemptuous charges to death.

They also play the man who will be killed and his new-found lover. At least I assume he's new-found; the chronology is murky. Anyway it doesnt matter. It may seem heartless to say, but this element is sentimental and irrelevant. The crime would be just as appalling, whatever the state of the victims love life.

The role-sharing has another function. It points up the kinship between the prey, who may just have discovered his sexual identity, and the predators, who seem unsure of theirs and are furiously compensating. Their bull sessions, which take up most of the play, include much mocking of gay stereotypes, and they play the roles with great enthusiasm.

Other times they are taunting one another, and tormenting themselves, about the girls they haven't had and the booze they can't get enough of. Between scenes the stage darkens, and they thrash about in vengeful frustration to the sounds of an especially ugly rock score. (The production seems to be suggesting a new legal strategy: Heavy metal made me do it.)

The crime would be just as appalling, whatever the state of the victims

love life

Its a matter of time before they find a scapegoat, and the threat of violence -- implicit from the first moment -- is all that keeps the play alive. The writing is base-level competent, and three of the actors -- Shaun Benson, Paul Dunn, Gil Garratt -- go vigorously through the motions. The fourth, Jamie Robinson, does the same, only with a higher degree of fluency, authority, and sometimes even wit. The play gets us from "what a gang of thugs" to "what a bunch of losers," but that isn't much of an advance.

Gulag starts better and ends worse. We meet the characters at the end of their jail term and note how the experience has destroyed their previous pecking order. The class bully is no longer in command, and though he makes regular attempts to reassert his authority, it's gone forever.

Out on the street, they try to reassemble their lives. They might be any young men with dead-end prospects, except they are occasionally haunted by their past. (Whether they are most affected by what they have done or by being caught is something the author sensibly leaves unresolved --the characters wouldnt know either.)

They try to mend fences, or build new ones, with the women in their lives: mothers, sisters, girlfriends. A new cast-member, Stephanie Jones, plays all these roles, and does fairly well, though theres something temporary about her performance. She seems preoccupied at the end of each vignette by the thought that she has to rush off and change into someone else. But all these scenes are scrappily written, acted, and staged; and the attempt to play them in a kind of hopeful counterpoint doesn't add much.

Eventually one of the guys gets engaged, and the four convene to celebrate. A long party-scene ensues. It is obviously crucial, and it may conceivably be wonderful. I couldn't say since the director, Sarah Stanley, has placed the whole thing in the corner of the stage farthest from where I happened to be sitting. Anyway, the old acting- gay games resurface, and this time they turn serious: blackout, followed by lights up on one of the quartet recalling a forgiving homosexual experience in prison.

Its the end of the play, and its plainly meant to be an epiphany. But it can't carry the weight. The audience is left stranded, wondering if it's time to applaud. (To be fair, the previous transitions from ensemble to solo have generally been the strongest parts of both productions.)

Talking of sloppiness, where does the author get off appropriating for his title the symbol of an oppressive system far worse than anything his characters are likely to experience? Aren't their problems real enough without this inflation? All his sentiments are correct, but they don't make a play. Let alone two.

Black & White Photo: David Hawe / Paul Dunn (in can), Shaun Benson (left), Gil Garratt, and Jamie Robinson: just being guys. ;
1999-01-18-laughter-the-best-therapy:
Wit's End

Winter Garden Theatre, Toronto

Sandra Shamas' shows are avowedly autobiographical, and this one's title is double-edged. Wit's End is a neat reference to her own state of desperation when her marriage ended just as she had decided to put her career on hold for a year. It's also, if she is to be believed, the name she gave to the remote country house that she took as part of the settlement, and where she still lives.

One of the responsibilities of art (a word I hate using but sometimes there's no alternative) is that you shut up about your own problems. You use them, of course, but disguised, and mixed in with other things, and your audience knows it. At least they used to. When an old-style comedian said "take my wife, please" nobody actually took him up on it. When one of his successors, usually female, says the same thing or its equivalent, there's a rustle of sympathy in the house, and we're out of the theatre and into therapy.

Of course, if the performance is funny, all is forgiven; successful comedy creates its own world. You know that there's some saving artifice because, however hilarious real life may be, it has to be worked on and re-ordered in order to get laughs on a stage. Most of the time, Shamas is very funny, and even when she isn't, she avoids self-pity; her references to her ex-husband, for example, are remarkably magnanimous.

But there are moments when she seems to be parading her suffering and expecting brownie-points for it. Even more uncomfortable is when she implicitly asks the audience's approval for having called her mother after a lapse of 20 years. Even if she isn't asking for it, she gets it. She plays to a very cosy house, ("my darling audience" she alarmingly calls them in the program): a pre-sold congregation that eliminates the sense of danger which has traditionally given stand-up comedy its distinction.

I musn't exaggerate. The sheer technical challenge of occupying a stage on her own for two-and-a-half hours means that hers is still a high-wire act. She offers a series of cartoon outlines on a slim but cohesive narrative thread. She has an impeccable sense of rhythm. Most of the time you take it for granted, as you should; in retrospect you realize how perfectly she has pitched every line, weighted every word.

The first half of the show is devoted to the break-up and its immediate aftermath, the second to her recuperation in the sticks. "I always feel," she says, "like an anthropologist around men," and it's true that in both settings she's a keen observer of the habits of the tribe. What she gets most acutely is her reaction to their reaction to her: a bracing double focus. She outlines the qualities of a neighbour. "He's sexist . . . and racist . . . and homophobic . . . and a white supremacist. And I like him very much. Because," (pause) "He has a snow plow."

That is comic poetry, or nearly, though for me the barriers really came down and the tears of laughter helplessly flowed, when she recounted a phone conversation with a female official who mispronounced her name and seemed very aggrieved when the mistake was pointed out to her. The note of possessive indignation is probably not recapturable in print, but, trust me, it was sublime.

She probably throws in too much detail in the second half, and you wonder how and when it can possibly end. But it does with satisfying suddenness; just as, at the opposite end of the evening, she has slid imperceptibly from introductory apologia into the meat of the occasion. I've come to her late but then Wit's End is probably a new beginning. Put me down, with reservations noted, as a convert.

- Playing Thursdays to Saturdays. Box office (416)-872-5555.

1999-01-19-why-these-clowns-won-t-be-app:
Theatre Review

Mump and Smoot in Something Else with Zug

Canadian Stage Theatre, Toronto

Mump and Smoot are a pair of aggressively clownish clowns. Mump wears tight shiny-blue pants and Smoot, a baggy red smock. Mump has a blue spike sticking out of his head while Smoot sports a pair of little red horns, so they're colour co-ordinated all over.

Mump is dictatorial and thin, Smoot is subservient, though with cheeky moments, and chubby. Their relationship is like Laurel and Hardy with the dimensions reversed.

They are Toronto favourites, accepting outside bookings as well, but I had never seen them before. Still, from what I have read about them, I gather that they have been much the same from show to show, as one would expect.

In Something Else, which is their first full-length show with an intermission, they are first seen edging their way along a catwalk in the side-wall of the theatre, while making conversation in words that sound like WONGA-WONGA. When they arrive on the stage proper, it turns out to be a lunar landscape dominated by three large cones and a small plinth. After a certain amount of puttering and muttering the middle cone explodes to reveal a third character, a sinister fellow named Zug with an echo-chamber in his throat.

He terrorizes them both, making a wimp out of Mump and reducing Smoot to jelly. He proceeds to take control of their destinies. Vladimir and Estragon have finally found Godot, and much good it does them.

My research tells me that Mump and Smoot have run up against Zug in previous shows, but clowns, like comic-strip characters, seem never to learn from experience. They just keep right on, battling the same old adversaries. Zug, however, is offstage most of the time, and I suspect that what Mump and Smoot get up to behind his back is little different from the way they would behave if he'd never joined the cast.

They go through a series of routines. One is a magic act. In a variant of sawing the lady in half, Mump shuts Smoot up in a box and, despite his protests, chops off all the bits of him that protrude: his arms, his legs, even his head. The severed sections, very red and raw, are displayed to the audience; this presumably is why the show is billed as unsuitable for children. When Smoot seems, understandably, to be dead, Mump is distraught. When he miraculously returns (Zug does seem to have something to do with this) Mump is relieved.

There is a restaurant sequence, in which a member of the audience is brought on stage to serve as customer (and, on the press night, gave as good as she got); and a war sequence in which Smoot dons fatigues while Mump wears a Napoleon hat and tunic, and they pelt one another (and us) with cannonballs; and an interplanetary sequence. This includes a truly magical passage in which the two, in white space-suits, float weightlessly through the air, limbs gently flailing. It also has the show's finest comic moment: Just before take-off our two astronauts fling themselves to the ground and give themselves over to terrified prayer.

The language they speak is called Ummonian (the programme says so) and it's gibberish that sometimes verges, to humorous effect, on comprehensible English. It's a joke they use a lot, and it generally works. Even funnier, though, are the times when they break down and ad-lib what is definitely English, usually goaded into it by some intransigent member of the public. During the miltary campaign, Smoot descended into the auditorium, and asked a punter to write something on a tablet. When he got it back on stage and Mump told him to read it he found, apparently, that the man had left it blank.

"It's not," Smoot spluttered "my fault he's a friggin' mime." Those of us who distrust mimes even more than we distrust clowns were cheered by this evidence of dissension in the ranks.

Michael Kennard plays Mump and John Turner, Smoot. They have strong personalities, and seem completely confident in what they are doing, and in one another.

Rick Kunst plays Zug. The director is Karen Hines. There are nice bits but I found it long.

- Runs until Feb. 14. For tickets call (416)368-3110.

1999-01-21-into-the-pc-thickets-with-atw:
Theatre Review

Good Bones

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

I have admired Clare Coulter in plays that were one-woman shows and in plays that, to judge from the performances of the other actors, would have been better as one-woman shows. Good Bones is not a play, and that's a drawback, but it is a formidably accomplished solo performance, one that takes a collection of literary texts, and gets a character out of them.

The texts are taken from two collections of prose vignettes by Margaret Atwood: Good Bones and Murder in the Dark. They are, as the title indicates, moderately chilling.

The sequence begins with a gleeful reminiscence of a childs experiments in mixing poison: something, we are told, thats dear to the hearts of all the young. By the end, the focus has widened into a genteel vision of apocalypse.

Coulter delivers the material quietly but with the utmost clarity. She is fastidious and bemused: somebody who might quizzically raise her eyebrows at the absurdities and cruelties of life but would never do anything so crude as to burst out laughing. She begins the evening perched on a long kitchen table, one leg over the edge, the other drawn up on the surface. You might say she was hugging herself, but she's too fine-drawn for that; it's more as if shes marshalling her forces. Later, though her movements are still contained, she begins to roam the stage, taking possession of her world.

Tone, stance, and setting are quintessentially middle-class: urban with memories of rural. Ken Garnhum has designed a cottage set with visual reverberations; its comfort is pierced when panels open up in the walls to reveal wilderness landscapes that the script seems to regard with a mixture of yearning and terror. Bonnie Beechers lighting makes a major contribution; it starts out magically dappled, and in its darker aspects it's downright frightening.

Coulter's collaborators, Urjo Kareda directing, have given her every support, and she triumphantly makes the words flesh. Or, if I may take a hint from the piece that gives the show its title and that concerns the eviscerating effects of age, she makes them bone.

It is, all the same, not a very invigorating evening. Part of the reason, for me, is that Atwoods style of genteel lyricism drives me up the wall. Another is that the material is stubbornly undramatic. Coulter has no overarching story to tell, as she did in Wallace Shawns The Fever, and she never seems to meet anyone, even in her imagination.We are stuck throughout with the same omniscient mandarin voice.

We seize with relief on a couple of passages that do involve dialogue and that allow us to laugh, perhaps more vigorously than the material really merits, but you know what audiences are. One -- part of a sequence on The Female Body -- is an argument between two parents on the advisability of buying their daughter a Barbie doll. (She's for. He's against.)

The other, taking us further into the thickets of political correctness, imagines Cinderellas author up against an implacably right-on editor. No, you cant say she was a poor girl, how could she be poor when she had a real fireplace to clear the ashes out of? (I leave you to imagine what they do with the word girl. Unhappily, the interrogation doesn't last long enough to take in the Fairy Godmother, let alone Prince Charming.)

It's not exactly a new joke, but Atwood and Coulter pursue it with engaging implacability. Indeed, they dig it to its roots. How dare the author begin her story with "once when all that's really important is now"?

Seen in this perspective, the evening's pervasive nostalgia takes on the air of a ferocious rearguard action. Its serenity is doggedness in disguise.

- Runs until Feb. 21. Box office, (416) 531-1827.

1999-01-22-bridging-the-distance-of-four:
MY MOTHER SAID I NEVER SHOULD

Alumnae Theatre, Toronto

According to the press release, Charlotte Keatley's My Mother Said I Never Should "is the most widely performed play by a female British playwright." It has taken 12 years to reach Canada, which is par for the course, though our theatres seem willing to import just about anything from America.

The play was worth waiting for. It began its life in Manchester and then moved to London, a progress that mirrors that of its characters. There are four of these, all women: four generations of the same family, all -- thanks to a string of early pregnancies -- alive and on stage at the same time.

Doris, who married in the 1920s and relinquished a teaching job at the behest of her husband, gives birth to Margaret, who comes of age at the end of the Second World War, becomes a G.I. bride, and goes south to start a long and efficient career as a secretary -- the kind, we gather, who does most of the work while her bosses take the credit.

Margaret's daughter, Jackie, has a moderately rebellious adolescence that culminates in her having a child by a married man; she agrees -- partly from fear, partly from pressure -- to let her mother adopt the baby.

Rosie, the fourth generation, grows into her mid-teens believing her grandmother is actually her mother and her mother is big sister Jackie who descends periodically from a glamourous career in the art- world to take her on treats.

The action, abetted by jump-cuts and flashbacks, spans the years from 1923 to 1987. It also includes some interludes in which the four actresses appear -- with varying degrees of comfort -- as little girls, tentatively exploring the sexual world through games and rhymes. Among the latter is the one that gives the play its title: "My mother said I never should/Play with the young boys in the wood . . . ."

They all disobey this rule of course, thus occasioning all the play's heartbreak, and all of its happiness.

The grown women talk about their husbands and lovers with some frequency but the male-female relationship remains a subsidiary theme, and an unfocused one.

By the end, the only marriage I felt I knew about was that of Doris: long and faithful and -- to hear her talk about it -- gnawingly unsatisfactory.

The last speech in the play is the earliest chronologically. A shy, happy Doris tells her (unseen) mother that she is engaged. This movingly extends the timeline back beyond the boundaries of the main action, just as the scenes with Doris' great-granddaughter have implicitly pushed it forward.

It has echoes of the mother's great last speech in Long Day's Journey into Night ("I married James Tyrone and was so happy for a time").

But where O'Neill's finale projected despair, Keatley's sends out beams of North-country stoicism.

Jennifer Phipps does it beautifully, as she does nearly everything else. (The childhood scenes tax her somewhat.) She is tough, and delicate, and humorous, and subtle: as she ages, and her daughter and granddaughter go off to the metropolis, her own accent gets increasingly Lancashire; parents can rebel against their children as well as vice versa.

She is also the one performer with enough style and authority to override lapses in Jordan Merkur's production. The others -- in order of seniority, Claire Crawford, Alison Smiley, Maryke Hendrikse -- are none of them bad, but they flash on and off.

The network of mother-daughter relationships is very powerful, and the play's central situation -- the secret of Rosie's parentage with its accumulated freight of agony and anger -- is highly combustible.

The actresses explode as called for, sometimes when not called for, but there are no lines of force, nothing going on between the cracks.

Conceivably they need more physical support; in the published script the author calls for a bare, abstract staging, but even a minimalist staging can be suggestive; few of the scenes here feel lived-in.

One of the recurring furnishings is a piano, and it gives rise to one of the best exchanges in the play.

"At school," says Rosie, "we've got a synth."

"Ah," says Doris, "I had a friend called Cynth."

It's a nice little pun that lights up the distance between the oldest and youngest characters, and also unites them.

The closing scenes finds the two of them together, and back in Manchester -- actually in Oldham, which is Manchester's down-market neighbour. They seem, for the moment, happy.

The class-and-location theme is one that the author tends to pick up and put down as it suits her, and it carries some sentimentality with it. But it also has strength.

- Runs until Jan. 31. Tickets: (416)-366-7723.

Black & White Photo: David Hawe, Eclectic Theatre / The first Canadian production of My Mother Said I Never Should convincingly portrays a powerful network of mother-daughter relationships. From left, Alison Smiley, Maryke Hendrikse, and Claire Crawford. ;
1999-01-25-there-s-no-play-like-this-pla:
Honest Ed -- The Bargain Musical

The Poor Alex, Toronto

Honest Ed may be short, but his show has legs.

Honest Ed -- The Bargain Musical is not Ed Mirvish's show in any legal sense. He has not produced it, and it is not -- not yet, anyway -- gracing the stage of his stately Royal Alexandra. You will find it at the shabby, independent Poor Alex, which, given the circumstances, is a pretty cool choice of venue.

Ed has given the show something far more important than money or a stage; Ed has given it his life. The shows creators have taken this life, torn it into flamboyant little strips, and danced joyously over the wreckage.

Surveying the career of Torontos one and only retail king turned theatre magnate, the musical comes to a momentous conclusion: Ed was in show business before he was in show business. This, given his addiction to neon and slogans, is not news, but the show takes the proposition to mythic lengths.

Ed Mirvish: man or myth? is a question that scholars will be debating for centuries. This production leaves no doubt where it stands on the matter. The first thing we are told about Ed is that he was circumcised by Al Jolson's father, who materializes, shears flashing. (As far as I know, this is the first musical ever to begin with a circumcision number. Did anyone tell them to cut it?)

Brock Simpson, co-author of the music and lyrics, plays the title role, and in flat cap and smock shirt he makes a very persuasive young Ed of the Toronto street markets.

Later, he graduates to a nattier hat and jacket, this being his sole concession to the passage of time, seventy-odd years of it. And in his performing style, which is perky but contained, he does suggest the paradox, the oxymoron, the paradoxymoron, that is Mirvish, the low-key extrovert.

Early numbers include Dundas, which blends description, defiance, and daredevil wordplay (on Dundas . . . there's no shopping on Sundas . . . well be the boy wondas") and Subtle Sells, in which Papa Mirvish advises young Ed on the detail of retail: personal service, lots of credit, and no vulgar display. Having thus spectacularly misread the future, the old man, who knows how a symbol should behave, drops obligingly dead.

Lisa Lambert, the co-composer, appears as Anne Mirvish, here a dizzy beanpole with zero resemblance to the real Mrs. M but lots of charm. On their first date, Ed takes her -- or maybe she takes him - - to the Royal Ontario Museum, a magical place whose initials inspire him to acrostic rhapsodies ("a River Of Music flies from my Round Open Mouth) that she reciprocates (Ill Reject Other Men, like Ramon Or Moishe"). Now that's a love song. Rely On Me.

By intermission the big store has opened, and the foundations of the empire have been firmly laid. Now, a sad rule about biographies, even biographies as cheerfully cavalier with mere facts as this one, is that the early struggles play more interestingly than the years of success. If Ed has had any great tragedies in his life, he has kept them hidden, and this show is not about to go to the trouble of inventing any.

And there's another thing. The first half of the production uses theatrical pastiche to spoof non-theatrical subjects; its good double-layered fun when Anne and two wartime customers at Honest Eds turn into the Andrews Sisters, or when director-choreographer Scott Morel spikes a celebration of Ed's discount emporium with a dash of Bob Fosse's Big Spender.

But the second half gets us to Eds own theatrical career, and here showbiz parody becomes an incestuous end in itself. Theres a long audition number that is less a take-off of A Chorus Line than a warped copy of it. There's an endless sequence about Andrew Lloyd Webber, on the grounds that he was once Ed's unsuccessful rival for the acquisition of the Old Vic. (Maybe its because Im a Londoner, but I thought the show lost all conviction when it crossed the pond, exchanging loving caricature for bloodless stereotype.)

The second act also boasts the only unsuccessful Jolson impersonation I have ever seen; the same actor, scoring something of a grand slam, also turns in an even less convincing Robert Goulet.

Even after the break there are good things: a twangy, down-home song called Wilderness Girl ("a friend of the fox and the red- tailed squirl"), and a glimpse of David Mirvish in what we are told were his beatnik days, when he apparently had a lot more hair than he has now.

The cast is a winning bunch of quick-change artists. The production, with no designer credited, lays out its wares in orange- boxes, just as Ed did when he was getting started, and just as inventively.

And besides, what, at the dismal end of the 20th century, do you say to a musical full of funny, inventive lyrics with hardly a bum rhyme, and wedded to music that's merry and supportive? I'll tell you what you say: Thank you.

- Until January 31. Box office, (416) 870-8000.

Black & White Photo: Gary Mulcahey / Ed Mirvish and Brock Simpson in Mirvishs bargain mecca in Toronto, Honest Eds. Simpson stars in and co-wrote Honest Ed -- The Bargain Musical, which traces Mirvish's life from his circumcision by Al Jolson's father to his battle with Andrew Lloyd Webber over London's Old Vic theatre. ;
1999-01-26-acrobats-and-crazies-on-bus-w:
The Number 14

Royal Alexandra Theatre, Toronto

Axis Theatre, a Vancouver company, has taken The Number 14 from its home base to Hong Kong and New York before getting off in Toronto. That's quite a bus trip.

The show is set on a bus; Pam Johnson, the designer, gives it to us as a cut-out, a cross-section in attractive shades of red and white. There are six actors in the cast, all of them virtuosi of the quick change, and they come and go at a furious rate. We are told that they play sixty characters between them and although nobodys counting, it seems credible.

Sometimes they wear masks; there may be a system governing when they do and when they dont, but it is never made clear.

Their physical and rhythmic skills are immense. This is obvious from the start, when they all play corporate commuters standing, sitting, crackling their newspapers, and flourishing their cellphones in perfect unison. It seems a bit patronizing, but it's fun. Later on, they transform themselves, almost before our eyes, from a party of grumbling seniors to a party of grumbling kids, presided over by a monstrous teacher on stilts. Her physical bulk is used as a facade behind which the others can work their transformation scenes. It's very clever.

One man -- dressed as a woman, Monty Python style -- does a spectacular acrobatic ballet, vaulting over seats, hanging from rails, in time, presumably, to the jerking of the bus.

The ensembles names are Peter Anderson, Darlene Brookes, Colin Heath, David Mackay, Wayne Specht, and Beatrice Zeilinger; there is no way of telling who does what. They also sing well, mostly a cappella.

Theyre less good at dialogue, both the speaking and the writing of it. (Most of the actors share a "conceived and written" credit with Roy Surette, who directed, and Melody Anderson, who designed the masks.) Great claims have been made for the show; the bus trip has been touted as a metaphorical journey through the heart of the modern city. In practice it seems hardly to have an idea in its head. The point of buses is that they have routes and destinations; this show seems happy just to make it to the next stop.

We gather that the bus goes to the end of its line, turns round, and then comes back again, but the place is a void and the people are cardboard.

Half the passengers are presented as crazies, so that they can bore, scare, or irritate the other half: This effect is repeated with grisly regularity.

Every so often the authors feel an obligation to say something about urban decay, so we get a rap number or a schoolgirl's song about all the things there are to be scared of in the world.

The latter item, which comes out of nowhere and goes right back there, is the show's serious low point. Its comic low point is a verbal and physical duel between a couple of unemployed Shakespearean actors. There is no reason for this routine to take place on a bus (theres no reason for it to take place anywhere, but thats another thing), and the same goes for far too much of the show. Its premise is nowhere near as strong as its creators would like to believe.

A surprising weakness in the mise en scene is that it never makes us aware of anyone on the bus except the characters we actually see, even when we're told that it's rush hour. The ability to people the stage with unseen presences is one traditional mimes talent that this group appears to lack.

Toward the end, they try their hands at a good old alienation effect. A derelict wanders through the auditorium and up on to the stage, notes disgustedly that only half a bus seems to be present, and tells us that the whole thing is an illusion. In the interests of destroying it, he even drags one of the stagehands into the light. (This is justice. Running this show must be a very demanding job, and those doing it deserve recognition. The stage manager is Darren Adam; the assistant stage manager is Annette Devick.)

Much of the show in fact has the coy, hectoring tone of bad childrens theatre. My own kids liked the first half a lot. After that they decided -- correctly, I think -- that the show was willing to throw in anything for the sake of a laugh, and they clammed up for the rest of the evening.

The creators -- or their publicists -- acknowledge a debt to Mr. Bean as well as to Python; they have kept their models' cute trappings, but have jettisoned their bite, their wit, and their sense of structure. Invoking such classics in this context is hitching a free ride.

- The Number 14 runs till Feb. 6. Box office, (416) 593-4142 or 1- 800-461-3333.

1999-01-28-north-america-as-seen-on-tele:
SPIRITS

Bathurst Street Theatre, Toronto

There are eight people on stage during Spirits, four of them actors, and four musicians. On the night of my visit, there were exactly the same number in the auditorium. Several of the performers were also involved in the writing and staging, and one's heart naturally went out to them in all capacities. Which is ironic, because our hearts don't seem to be what this piece is angling for. I reclaimed my own fairly early in the bleak, 90-minute proceedings.

The show is a through-composed mini-opera. A girl goes out on the town. She is beset in a bar by two guys -- one smooth, one awkward - - who ply her with booze, very much with her own connivance. She drinks too much, chokes on her own vomit, and dies. Her father finds out and kills her killers. End of story.

Spirits, announces Peter Reitzel -- author, director, designer, actor, and program-note writer -- "is a show about North America." He goes on to say that he isn't concerned with the real North America, but with the image of it that might be conceived by some outsider -- in Eastern Europe, say -- who had been steadily ingesting schlock Western television. It turns out, by a sort of sleight of mind, that this is the real North America after all. We produce and consume this stuff, and by our dreams we shall be known.

Everybody who has written about this show -- except, to be fair, its author -- has invoked the names of Bertolt Brecht and Kurt Weill, and I'd like to join the party while questioning its logic. The Brecht-Weill operas of the early '30s were typically set in a fantasy Chicago, or a fantasy London, that its authors had constructed from bits of old plays, current movies, and dime novels. Stuck in Berlin, they naturally presented a Berliner's view of Anglo- American culture.

It's rather different to sit in Toronto and imagine how somebody thousands of kilometres away might respond to your society, rather than responding to it yourself. I don't think there should be a law against it, but I do suggest that it adds more levels of artifice than anyone is likely to need.

Spirits is not big on dramatic coherence -- that much it has in common with Brecht and Weill, though not with schlock TV -- and it never tells us, for example, how the avenging father discovered the identities of the guilty men, or how he tracked them down.

It does find time, though, for the actor (who happens to be the author) to turn to the audience and say, in effect, "Wasn't that exciting? I bet you didn't recognize me under my disguise." In other words, we're being chastised for lapping up suspense and mayhem instead of concentrating on the ruined, empty lives and the burning moral issues that are implicit in what we have just seen -- for behaving, in fact, like any dumb TV audience.

Well, we weren't, and you know something? TV audiences don't either. Even the most crass crime series makes its audience aware of the society that encloses these events; even when it isn't brought sanctimoniously to our attention, as it often is, it's still built into the structure of the story.

Alienation -- the deliberate breaking down of dramatic illusion - - can be a titillating theatrical effect in its own right, but it's kicking at an open door; it presupposes that there is such a thing as realistic drama, which there isn't, and that audiences completely surrender to it, which they don't. (The moment you say how good or bad the acting is, you've shattered the illusion -- and it's the first thing people always say.)

It also licences bad performance. If the cast of Spirits don't sing well, if two of them can't even be heard above the band -- well, that just keeps us on our toes. The exception here is Dennis Frey, whose characterization of the lumpier lover is excellent. He's also the vocal arranger and, with Christopher Cumming, co-composer.

The tunes are agonizingly limited, though Sam Allison's sharp, shrill orchestrations give them some edge. The lyrics are marginally better: "tonight I'll score / with some young whore" is an effective couplet in its own way, but that's the best it gets. The constriction may be a comment on the media's contempt for people, or it may just be down to the author's: I don't see how an audience could tell the difference.

Visually, the show is very assured; the design capitalizes on the dilapidation of the theatre itself; a set done in stylish sackcloth falls away at the end to reveal a piercing black vision of the beyond.

The play proper is preceded by a long vaudeville section -- a comedian who gets the hook, a conjurer who gets some laughs -- all intentionally tacky, so that we will know the show itself is just a show. The author disavows any intention to preach, but he does nag.

- Spirits runs until Feb. 6. Box office, (416) 533-7710.

Black & White Photo: Flip Publicity / Dennis Frey, Julie Reitzel, and Michael Chipman hoop it up in Spirits. ;
1999-02-05-and-fighting-and-dealing-and-:
SHOPPING AND FUCKING

du Maurier Theatre Centre, Toronto

The play begins with a character vomiting, apparently from a mixture of junk food and heroin withdrawal. One of its last scenes centres on a brutal scene of homosexual rape, with the added twist that the act is enthusiastically welcomed by its victim. (Try getting away with that in a heterosexual play.) The victim, by the way, is 14 years old. My, he looks tall for his age; though, from the standpoint of the audience's sensibilities, this slight implausibility is maybe a blessing.

What happens in between is not especially graphic; even the language is surprisingly decorous by the standards of most contemporary drama, let alone contemporary life. Mark Ravenhills Shopping and Fucking comes to us with glowing credentials from London and New York; it isnt as original as its fans have been claiming, and its Toronto production is muffled to the point of incoherence, but it's a funny, bracing, and talented work.

It's also a morality, as you can tell from the title. It might, I suppose, have been more discreetly phrased: Sex and Supermarkets, perhaps -- or how about Laying Em in the Aisles? But they wouldnt have had the same aura about them: the flavour of brimstone preaching for an age of cool.

There are five characters in Ravenhill's play, and it's notable that though they all have names in the program, those names hardly ever crop up in the dialogue. This may not be meant to have a distancing or dehumanizing effect, but it does. It also means that I may be about to get the plot wrong.

Here goes: There are Lulu, Robbie, and Mark who live together in London until Mark moves out to kick his heroin habit. Lulu seeks employment from Brian, the one prosperous character in the piece. He is in commerce, to put it sweetly, and he sends Lulu out on a test drive: peddling Ecstasy in a club. She enlists Robbies help, but he ends up giving it away, which puts them in Brians debt and thus in his power. Mark, meanwhile, is out and cured, though he now believes himself capable only of depersonalized sex. He thinks -- wrongly, as it turns out -- that he has found it with young Gary, who was systematically abused by his stepfather, and now seems to be making a career of it. Gary has even made some money; and when Mark brings him home, the two stories come, elegantly and bloodily, together.

"Look," says Lulu, opening a box of multiethnic fast food. An empire under cellophane. It would be nice to avoid the phrase "consumer society," but it's plainly what Ravenhill is on about; he's describing a world in which everything, notably sex, has a credit rating, and in which people are increasingly shameless about it. This is true, but it isnt news. British drama in particular has been harping on it for the past 30 years, and its amusing that the armchair apocalyptics of the '70s should now be turning on the new generation of what have been dubbed the in-your-face playwrights, and accusing them of heartlessness.

The tone and the sawn-off techniques are very similar. What is different is that the previous lot, university graduates at a time when that meant something, were writing from a position of chilly superiority; Ravenhill's bunch seem personally involved. They may even have earned the right to act tough.

That doesnt mean that everything rings true. In the rape scene, the play seems to be simultaneously knitting its brow and licking its lips. (The audience, too. Theres a complicity: They act tougher than they are. We react cooler than we feel.) Brian, the boss-man, is a rampaging cliche: the sensitive gangster who talks tenderly and proudly of a son who's a prodigy violinist, before punching his listener in the stomach. He also informs us that "get the money" is the first law of life, and invokes Biblical authority. His real sacred text, though, seems to be The Lion King. He quotes the circle-of-life stuff repeatedly and with reverence; in a week where the arrival in Toronto of a Disney roadshow has been trumpeted as if it were the second coming, that scene comes pungently into its own.

The play is built on the dangerous London wit that was patented by Harold Pinter and has been common dramatic currency ever since. So it's vital that the actors do it right; they have to get the laughs and connect the feelings behind them. Jim Millans production succeeds occasionally with the first -- usually when its a set- piece that's too obvious to miss -- and fails absolutely with the second. Sometimes it's slow, sometimes its fast, but it never has pace.

The actors lunge at the rhythms as if dimly remembering the last British cop show they saw. (For all I know, some of them are British; they still sound like imitations.) They all play moments rather than scenes. Damien Atkins, whose overgrown child Gary is after all the most isolated character, has the best of them, with Matthew MacFadzean highlighting the resentful and the happy-go- lucky in Robbie without ever fusing them. Alex Poch-Goldins Mark has the shell of a disturbing character but never fills it out; ditto for Julian Richings, whose Brian is whiny when he should be scary.

Natalie Radford as Lulu is new to the theatre and frankly acts like it; her performance barely travels into the auditorium. This is especially damaging since she has speeches, about witnessing the robbery of a convenience store and her own confused reaction to it, that are potentially the most powerful in the play. Lulu, ironically, is a trained actress, and she quotes Chekov and Shakespeare, using Juliet to arouse a client during phone sex. For the most part, these characters are not hardened; they have compassion, but they don't know what to do with it -- which, the play powerfully suggests, is everybody's problem.

- Runs until Feb. 20. Tickets, call (416) 973-4000.

1999-02-08-still-a-killer:
Chicago

Princess of Wales Theatre, Toronto

Chita Rivera, still a killer, gives a gleaming performance of Roxie Hart, the -- for want of a better word -- heroine of Chicago. Roxie is the failed chorine of the roaring '20s who shoots her absconding lover and finds herself, to her great indignation, up on a murder charge, her loving husband having fumbled in his gallant attempt to take the rap.

"I'm older" says Roxie, surveying her wasted dreams of stardom, "than I ever intended to be." It's a great line in its own right, and it gets an extra muted laugh here, Rivera at 66 being some 40 years older than the woman she's playing. But then, Chicago is hardly a naturalistic piece. It's a gleefully malevolent cartoon, in which all the conventions of musical comedy are explored, exposed, and returned to their most libidinous roots.

The numbers are self-contained parodies, formally announced by the conductor. Its message is that if you've got it, you flaunt it; but only if you can do it without sweat. Rivera has it all -- vocally, physically, and temperamentally. This, after all, is her territory; in the original 1975 production she played Roxie's sidekick and rival homicide Velma Kelly, and she wasn't in her 20s then.

Velma is basic brass, and that is how Stephanie Pope plays her, with a growling delivery and spectacular legs that apparently see no reason to stop. They aren't quite a satisfying pair -- the two women, I mean -- since Pope doesn't have Rivera's aura and Rivera doesn't have Pope's phenomenal height. Their final number, the wonderfully sinuous Nowadays, lacks its proper symmetry.

This, I must emphasize, is quibbling at a very high level. This is a far better company of Chicago than played in Toronto last year, and the 1996 Broadway revival from which they both derive was a knock-out to begin with. It was given special velocity by the deadpan amoral Velma of Bebe Neuwirth, but it also fined down the dark and elaborate vision of Bob Fosse's original staging to something more palatable.

Ann Reinking's choreography is described as "in the style of" Fosse, and at this distance it's hard to tell the difference. Numbers such as the opening All That Jazz, the Cell Block Tango for the massed murderesses (count 'em, six), and the frantic We Both Reached for the Gun in which Roxie quacks out her story to the press as a dummy perched on her lawyer's knee, are vaudeville routines raised to the highest power. The score never adds anything personal to its pastiche but on its own terms it's superb: John Kander's music a resourceful series of period archetypes, Fred Ebb's lyrics crammed with neat, smart jokes. ("She'd ask me, what state's Chicago in? I'd say, ill.")

The show is a triumph of style rather than substance. It tells us over and over how rotten and/or gullible everybody is, and if it weren't done with consistent wit it would become self-righteously monotonous. (That's what happened back in '75, abetted by Fosse's compulsion, ever since the film of Cabaret, to blame show business for the state of the world.)

Marcia Lewis has come up to recreate her prison matron, though she has lost some of the awesome economy she had in New York. Michael Berresse is a very dapper lawyer, though not as stylish in song or dance as he is in dialogue. M. E. Spencer is the best sob- sister reporter I've seen, and Ernie Sabella as Roxie's old man brings off the neat trick of filling the stage with his self- effacement. And Jack Gaughan takes full advantage of the best part ever written for a conductor.

- Runs until Feb. 26. For tickets, call (416) 872-1212.
1999-02-08-sweet-home-chicago-for-chita-:
"I feel," says Chita Rivera, "like a kid, looking at a toy she had all those years ago." Actually, it's quite a grown-up toy -- Chicago, the most cynical of musicals -- and she's playing with it, or in it, after leaving it alone for nearly 25 years.

What she is doing is unusual, possibly unique. An actor may go from playing Hamlet in his youth to Hamlet's wicked uncle Claudius in his middle years, and then may age still further into Polonius. It's common form for a grande dame to revisit the Chekhov plays in which she once scored as an ingenue.

That's in plays. In musicals, an actor may sometimes spin out a career by continuing to exploit a single famous role (Yul Brynner in The King and I, Carol Channing in My Fair Lady), but few shows offer more than one star role per gender.

Chicago is an exception: the story of two ladies of the 1920s, each of whom has bumped off the unfaithful man in her life and is now in prison awaiting -- or avoiding -- punishment. You might call them First and Second Murderesses; and which ranks as first and which as second is apt to depend on who the performers are.

In an ideal world, the two would be equal. This actually happened in the original 1975 production, when Rivera played Velma Kelly, the more hardened of the pair, opposite Gwen Verdon as the debutante killer Roxie Hart. The two top singer-dancer-actresses of the American musical, with Jerry Orbach, one of its best leading men, thrown in as well: It was one of the best package deals Broadway has ever offered. Directed, choreographed, and masterminded by Bob Fosse, the show ran a respectable two years but was overshadowed by the giant success of A Chorus Line, which opened the same season.

In 1996, the show came back in a revival that started out as a concert performance and was promoted to Broadway with its scale kept purposefully small. It tore the place up, and is still running. It has sent out touring companies, one of which played in Toronto last year. Now we have another; and it brings back Rivera, this time in the other role, that of Roxie.

"Both," muses Rivera, asked about the difference between the two characters "are killers. They're both desperate. Roxie starts out desperate; then Velma becomes desperate because Roxie is taking over." Roxie is the new kid in the jail, stealing Velma's thunder; and since Velma is a vaudeville performer in formal life, she feels the loss of limelight keenly.

The criminal-as-star is one of the main things the show is about. Roxie has a monologue ("wonderful to do," says Rivera) about having always wanted to be famous, and about the deficiencies of her kind but unglamorous husband. She's more obviously an acting role than Velma, who is "more physical -- she has chairs to deal with." (She picks them up and uses them as dancing partners.) This perhaps makes Roxie a more amenable role than Velma for a mature performer, but this is not a line of questioning that gets an interviewer very far. "I don't" says the lady firmly "talk about that kind of thing."

Her privilege: though it's impossible not to recall that she was in the original production of West Side Story, 42 years ago, scoring a major success (the greatest in what was primarily an ensemble show) as Anita, an updated and far sexier version of Juliet's nurse. Like Chicago, the show was thought in its time to be shocking: "People stormed out. They hadn't heard such language before."

Half wisecracker, half firecracker, the role led to her starring assignment in Bye Bye Birdie, an endearing if lopsided show (half of it was Rivera, and half was the story, and the two rarely touched) that confirmed her as a musical-comedy treasure. She worked steadily in the diminishing Broadway of the next 30 years, and was often the best thing in some dubious shows. The quality of her work earned her regular Tony nominations; the shows sank her chance of actually winning. This happened five times. She finally won in 1984 for The Rink: an especially noteworthy achievement, since this was another of those rare two-star shows, and Rivera was playing Liza Minnelli's mother. (I don't, of course, mean Judy Garland.)

As best-actress-in-a-musical awards go, this was especially well deserved, since Rivera really did act, truthfully and uncompromisingly, through and between the numbers. Perhaps it's the West Side Story connection that has tagged her forever as primarily a dancer, but in fact she is -- like Verdon and Minnelli -- one of those rare triple threats. Fred Ebb, lyricist of Chicago, The Rink and Kiss of the Spider Woman -- the recent show that found her at the top of her game -- once described her as one of the best singers he knew, and the echo of her voice clings distinctively to every number she has ever done.

That's one thing she has in common with Verdon, another who danced so enticingly that her singing was underrated. (Their performing lives crossed before Chicago. In the national company of Sweet Charity, Rivera played the title role that Verdon had created on Broadway. Neither got the role in the film -- it went to Shirley MacLaine -- but Rivera was in it as heroine's best friend. She had some great scenes, and led the Big Spender number unforgettably.) Their styles and personalities were complementary: Verdon melting and Rivera rasping, Verdon the gamine and Rivera the soubrette.

With Verdon retired, Rivera is incontestably the American musical's First Trouper. It will be interesting to see her crossing into her old colleague's territory, and seeing how the actress and the role adapt to one another.

As Rivera says, as everyone has said, the show -- written in the '70s, set in the '20s -- is topical today ("People only have to open the newspapers, turn on the news; they live with this kind of celebrity") but she adds refreshingly that it always was: "I thought at the time -- oh, please, this is nothing new. Look at history."
