1999-02-12-classic-pinter-carrying-pain-:
ASHES TO ASHES

Gramercy Theater, New York

Forty years after his debut, Harold Pinter remains the best living English playwright. I don't mean that he necessarily writes the best plays -- canon for canon, I get more out of Tom Stoppard -- but he has the most natural talent. He is in perfect command of his skills. He can write words and he can write scenes: His sentences, silky and precise, resonate individually and they set up instant tensions between the people speaking them. He is famous for telling us less about his characters than we want to know, but even when the surroundings are obscure, the moment-to-moment relationships -- the balances of power -- are needle-sharp.

After a few years of silence, Pinter has recently returned to the theatre with a series of miniatures. The latest, Ashes to Ashes, clocking in at 48 minutes, has just opened off-Broadway two years after its premiere in London. It brings together many of his previous preoccupations. He started out as the pre-eminent playwright of bullying, depicting struggles between men intent on gaining control of their space. Later on, he added women to the mix, and began to concentrate on the dynamics of sex. Most recently he has dealt with political oppression, though with hindsight it seems obvious that this Jewish playwright, growing up in the East End of London during the Second World War, must have had this in mind all along.

Ashes to Ashes is set in a living room, reduced by its designer Tony Walton to the elegant essentials of two chairs, a picture window and a drinks trolley. The chairs are occupied by an academic and his wife. As is usually the case with Pinter, the woman, Rebecca, seems to have a richer interior life than the man, Devlin, and he is badgering her about it. She recalls a man with his hands around her throat; this could be love-play or an interrogation or both.

Later she conjures up a persistent nightmare image: women lined up on a railway platform, soldiers tearing their babies from their arms. She speaks about this from the viewpoint first of a spectator, then of a victim. But she herself is childless. On another level she talks about her sister, who does have a family, with a kind of chilly concern.

Rebecca seems to have internalized some of the worst traumas of the century, and used them to fill, to bursting, the cracks in her existence. Her husband, meanwhile, is jealously concerned with bullying her back into his own frame of reference. Pinter's ambiguities dont guarantee profundity, in fact they can be irritating, but here he has compressed a rich amount of feeling into a small space, echoing his previous plays but not slavishly recycling them. (For those in the know, this piece strikes me as Landscape meets The Lover, watched over by Old Times.) Karel Reisz, celebrated movie director now working mainly and very effectively in the theatre, keeps the text taut and the performers free.

Pinter himself started out as an actor and he has probably occasioned more great performances than any other current dramatist. To a list that stretches back to Donald Pleasence in The Caretaker, through Dorothy Tutin in Old Times, John Gielgud and Ralph Richardson in No Mans Land, and Judi Dench in A Kind of Alaska, we may now add Lindsay Duncan, the English actress best known here for her TV performances in The Rector's Wife and GBH.

A slim but commanding blond in a permanent state of beleaguered repose (in shorthand: bleached and beached), strategically crossing and uncrossing her legs in the immemorial style of the Pinter woman, she strikes calmly and unerringly at the centre of the role: She carries her pain with pride, and uses it as a weapon. Her partner is David Strathairn, an actor whose energies seem to go into creating the exterior of the English professor, smooth even to blandness. I would love to see the author play this role. These days he gives forceful and exhilarating performances that couldn't be further from what is known as "the Pinter style;" he barrelhouses through.

- Ashes to Ashes runs until May 9.

1999-02-16-a-comedy-where-no-hell-breaks:
Neil Simon's latest play has nine characters, all of them in love to some degree, and by its close it has arranged them into four couples. Simple arithmetic decrees that somebody must be left out; and even apart from that, Simon's Proposals come in for a few rebuffs. This, in intention at least, is a mellow comedy about time and attrition; about grabbing things while you're young and maybe -- though there's no guarantee -- recapturing them when you're old.

Its values are unchallengeably decent, but it plays as soap opera (of the literate Dawson's Creek variety) with a couple of funny scenes. It's the late 1940s, and we are in Pennsylvania woodland country where Burt Hines -- the central character, or at any rate the one played by Al Waxman -- has a summer home. Burt is a retail store magnate, forced into retirement by a weak heart. He lives here with his daughter Josie, and Clemma the black housekeeper.

Burt's divorced wife, Annie, now remarried, is paying a visit. So is Clemma's ex-husband, Lewis. So is Vinnie, an admirer of Josie's. Josie has two other young men in tow. One of them, Ken, is local; the other, Ray, used to be and is now returning with a new girlfriend, Sammii, who's a model. All these people turn up on the same day, and there is much jocular comment from Clemma about the strain their arrival will place on the local roads and on her catering arrangements. But that's just talk; in practice the logistics work with amazing smoothness. Which may be swell for the characters but is a let-down for the audience.

The framework is similar to that of Noel Coward's Hay Fever, another nine-hander in which all the members of a family simultaneously invite summer house-guests, but the tone could hardly be more different. In Coward's play all hell breaks loose over the arrangements, everyone changes partners, and the visitors depart battered and baffled while the hosts sail on, egotistically oblivious. Simon, beneath the surface crackle, is a Broadway softie who wants to redeem his characters and bring them together. He realizes that's not always possible; that, plus the country-house setting, give him something of a Chekhov flavour, but it's Chekhov drastically sentimentalized. A scene in which one character surprises two others kissing is like a replay of Uncle Vanya, minus most of the farce and all of the heartbreak.

This is also a memory play, narrated by Clemma: a device very popular in American plays of the '40s and '50s (The Glass Menagerie, Our Town, A View from the Bridge) and perhaps revived here as a homage to the period. There seems little other reason for it, except to add a gratuitous layer to a slight story. It does dispose of some technical matters; instead of dropping basic information tactfully into the dialogue, always a chore, the author has the maid ladle it out for him. (In the very old days, she would have done it in conversation with the butler; the retrenchments of the last 60 years have left playwrights with their own servant problem.)

When the play proper gets started, Burt reveals an obliging habit of overhearing everyone else's conversations from his window, thus cutting out pages more of exposition. In all, Simon's craftsmanship seems to have gone a bit lax. Characters wander on just as other characters have wandered off, with none of the messy overlap you get in real life. Clemma's announcement that Lewis is coming is met with "Lewis? Your ex-husband?" -- one of those everyday expressions that trip so naturally off the tongue.

There is one set-piece that reminds you how good Neil Simon can be. It's a verbal showdown between Kenny, the buttoned-up young lawyer grappling with being Josie's unsuccessful suitor, and Vinnie, whom he takes to be his rival and who looks, talks and dresses like a junior member of the Mafia. Vinnie gets words wrong, to Kenny's vengeful delight. It then turns out that -- some of the time at least -- Vinnie does his malapropping on purpose (to attract attention, he says) and Kenny is left hopping, though still compulsively punching. This is fine-layered comedy that builds.

Duncan Ollerenshaw's Ken is an entrancingly stiff-necked performance: not just class but class of its own. Nothing else in Steven Schipper's production matches it for humour or humanity, though Art Cohen's Vinnie works pretty well as caricature, and so in a small way does Lisa Ryder's dumb blonde turn as Sammii.

The Hines family too are stock types, with the unfortunate difference that the author wants us to take them seriously. Al Waxman's Burt -- Willy Loman plus success -- is low on energy, even for a man between heart attacks. The best to be said for him is that he goes at his own tempo, unlike his wife and daughter, who are imitation Broadway, all fake pauses and emotional semaphore. Jennifer Gould at least goes through her awakening-princess routine with spirit and even some glimmerings of intelligence; Maida Rogerson's mom is a wooden attempt at glitter. Alvin Sanders (Lewis) is unexceptionable, Graham Abbey (Ray) also unexceptionable but dull.

As for Clemma, who in all senses runs the show: Patricia Idlette is certainly a presence but if acting involves interacting, then she hardly does any; when she confronts her ex, she's so busy scoring points that she barely looks at him. She talks about the house as though it were the real subject of the play; it isn't, but, as designed by John Lee Beatty, it gets to show itself off handsomely from a variety of angles: dark wood slowly revolving in the greenwood. The same designer was responsible for the contrastingly stark but equally imposing set for Chicago just down the block, making him the scenic king of King Street.

- Proposals runs until March 20. Box office: (416) 872-1212 or 1- 800-461-3333.

1999-02-16-taking-historic-liberties:
This low-budget Shakespeare is presented by a company called Royals and Rebels that presumably came into being just for that purpose. It is possible, of course, that they chose the name first and then scoured the libraries looking for a play that suited it, but it seems unlikely. Henry IV, Part One is the one in which rebels, led by the fire-breathing Harry Hotspur, rise up against the English royal of the title whose son Prince Hal is simultaneously giving grief by hanging out in taverns with the disreputable likes of Sir John Falstaff. This production is set in the time of the First World War: a period when, as you must know, opposing generals routinely challenged one another to single combat and the principal military weapon was the sword.

And while we're talking ludicrous: This show breaks hilarious new ground in the cause of gender equity. When Falstaff and Co. do their highwayman thing, their victims are played as women. (One of them, in a rare piece of actual rewriting, is described as "a rich widow from America.") They do not despair and beg for mercy, like their masculine counterparts in the text; they turn on their attackers and knee them in their respective groins. Indeed, they put up such a good fight that I wondered how the director, Sten Erik, could possibly keep faith with the play's storyline. However, he proves equal to the emergency. One of the thieves, Gadshill, has also been turned into a woman, and with just a few casual flicks of her dagger she has the situation under control.

One of the rebel leaders, formerly known as Sir Richard Vernon, also undergoes a sex change, which doesn't prevent her boasting about the prowess she will display, in person, on the battlefield -- a situation even less believable in the early 20th century than in the late 15th. By altering a character's gender you change the whole dynamic of a scene, and you cannot then simply play the text as written and expect it to make sense.

After which it's pleasing, if perplexing, to report that there are some good things going on here. Chief among them -- and a rarity in this play -- is the performance of the title role. Henry is a manipulative though not heartless usurper, and David Clark plays him as a glassy-eyed politician in a frock-coat. (My own theory about modern-dress Shakespeare, if anyone wants to know, is that it helps audiences far less than it's supposed to; if anything it patronizes them. But it does help actors, allowing them to present someone with a recognizable social, and therefore personal, role, rather than an amorphous being in an off-the-peg frock.)

This king enjoys baiting and humiliating his opponents, and he's very good at it; he also has a tormenting conscience. When he confronts his son, he lectures him as mercilessly as he would anyone else, until something cracks and he finds himself crying real and wholly believable tears.

Stephen Bogaert presents an arrestingly caddish Hal, very much his father's calculating son, torn between self-indulgence and self- disgust. He doesn't have much of an antagonist since Jerry Getty's Hotspur is a good-natured fellow. He isn't exactly helped by the lunatic decision to have him deliver his first long and dynamic speech sitting down with his back to us; the whole point of Hostpur is that he can't keep still.

This, though, is the only performance that's technically inadequate to the demands of the lines, and by current standards that's a very good strike-rate. Most of these actors a) know what they're talking about and b) can get it across.

Dennis O'Connor is not the funniest Falstaff you will ever see (at least I hope not, for your sake) but he has loads of sly, skeptical intelligence. The production goes sentimental in trying to turn him into a pacifist, but in bringing on the ragged, hopeless soldiers he has press-ganged, makes a valid point. (And here, yes, the modern dress does help.) And there's the rare pleasure of meeting a new Shakespeare character; the minute role of the Chamberlain, the thieves' informer, is brought to greasy acquisitive life by a mature actor, Howard Davis. He later doubles as Francis, the tavern drawer, who is usually played young; this actor, with his eyes briefly flickering at the thought of a royal advancement, gives him a new, poignant dimension. The evening gets better as it goes; by the end I even felt I'd like to see how they might all get on in Part Two.

- Until Feb. 28. Box office: (416) 466-3045.
1999-02-19-seduced-by-the-bible:
THE SONG

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

Nestled demurely among the more thunderous books of the Old Testament is one of the greatest pieces of erotica ever written -- maybe the most beautiful of all if you get the right translation. The Song of Solomon is, among other things, a testimony to the inclusiveness of the Bible as a record of human experience. It isn't a story about sex, it is sex.

The Song -- which comes to us, roughly speaking, as the play of the book -- reflects its source: It isnt much on narrative, but its a sensuous feast. It gains its effects with rigorous economy from the first moment.

All of us, at some time or another, have struggled to put on a recalcitrant sweater. Alon Nashman, one of the show's two actors, takes this simple ordeal and makes a spectacular ritual of it.

Armholes appear where the head wants to go and vice versa; the garment, instead of draping itself snugly around the body, insists on emerging skewed, and its victim -- though he actually owns the thing, for God's sake -- has to start all over again.

This is several minutes of silent comedy denoting frustration that is also, through sheer skill in execution, beautiful. I should mention that the actor performs the entire routine while perched precariously on a narrow strip of platform that represents the only stretch of level ground on the stage. Between it and the audience stretches a steeply tilted floor, criss-crossed by a lattice of wooden slats. The whole design looks like an ingenious machine for inflicting cruelty on actors.

Nashman plays a character called Alan, and he is also the artistic director of Theaturtle, the company producing the show. It was written and directed, however, by Adam Nashman. (Concentrate.) Alan is an accountant cast into desolate confusion by the death of his wife, Rachel, two years earlier. The Song of Solomon is a catalogue of all the delights, spiritual as well as physical, of which he is now deprived.

Alan thinks and dreams of Solomon himself, and of Rabbi Akiva, the ancient talmudic scholar responsible for establishing the Song in the biblical canon. Akiva himself, it seems, had a wife named Rachel (the name game is compulsive, in and around this show) and had to endure long absences from her, while commuting between Judea and Rome.

We see him attracting the attention of the Roman governors wife, who first tries to seduce him then settles for Bible classes instead. All I see, she says of the Song, "is a sexy little poem." Akiva has a reply to this, but its less concise and harder to remember.

`All i see is a sexy little poem'

The play, apart from the actual quotations, which are extensive, is a lot less compelling verbally than it is visually, and the actors can't always kick it into life. It doesnt help that the story of Akiva, which is meant to be subsidiary, has more going for it dramatically than Alans psychological progress, which it's supposed to illuminate. The play's rather meagre present tense has Alan striving to address a number-crunchers conference in Banff, and finding it understandably hard going.

One scene has real fireworks: Alan on the line to a government office trying belatedly to track down some information about his dead wife. The acting Nashman performs is a double balancing-act, literally and metaphorically at the end of his tether. He is grappling with bureaucracy, generally a hopeless battle, and in every sense he is losing it.

He is also stretched up, down, and across the acting area, holding on to a phone with a very long lead while grasping for a glass of wine that, however he contorts himself, remains stubbornly beyond his reach.

Deborah Hay is the other half of the cast, playing Solomon, all the Rachels, and the governors wife, and is especially enticing in the latter role.

Both players, as they intrepidly climb the stage, slide merrily down it, hang upside down from it, or disport themselves at languorous diagonals, pay implicit tribute to the possibilities of the human body and the human imagination -- which presumably is their point even as it was Solomon's.

(There is a third presence: a mute male double to facilitate some quick changes from Alan to Akiva and back. Even allowing for his assistance, they are amazing.) By the end, Alan has progressed so far that he can take off his sweater in one graceful action. That's a climax; and I'm not kidding.

- Runs until March 7. Box office: (416) 504-7529.

1999-02-22-waiting-for-godot-in-snappy-h:
The Roar of the Greasepaint, the Smell of the Crowd

Jane Mallet Theatre,

St. Lawrence Centre, Toronto

Between 1961 and 1972, the team of Anthony Newley and Leslie Bricusse turned out three musicals with long titles and grandiose ambitions. The first, and the most successful, was Stop the World -- I Want to Get Off. The last, and the least, was The Good Old Bad Old Days. The Roar of the Greasepaint, the Smell of the Crowd came in between.

Reprise is a Toronto company dedicated to presenting "great musicals" (well, of course they're great; this is show business, baby) "in concert" (this means the actors carry scripts, but the technical and performing standards are high). Roar, which played over the weekend, is their second production, an enterprising choice since the show has hardly been seen since its Broadway run in the mid-1960s. I am grateful for the chance of collecting it, and they did it well. But it is a truly terrible show.

It's a musical morality. Its principal characters are Sir, who is fat, and Cocky, who is starving. Sir wears a top hat and Cocky a bowler. Cocky staggers about carrying Sir's suitcases. Sir doesn't actually drag Cocky around on a rope, but in all other respects they might be Pozzo and Lucky, limbering up for the musical of Waiting for Godot. (You mean you hadn't heard?) Sir even oppresses Cocky with bogus Latin tags.

They spend their days playing "the Game," a sort of snakes-and- ladders with humans for counters. This is actually a ritual devised by Sir for the humiliation of Cocky, who is systematically deprived of food, drink, cash, and -- despite the tormenting presence of a sizable female chorus -- sexual gratification.

However, since Sir can change the rules at will, and since he treats Cocky the same even when they're not playing, it is all crashingly monotonous. There is some variation in the second act, when a character billed as The Negro comes on and declines to be oppressed, giving Cocky the inspiration for a revolt of his own; it's surprisingly easy when you know how. But even when the tables are turned, it's the same two dummies on either side.

Newley and Bricusse are English but even in England, even thirty years ago, the class war was subtler than this. Newley always starred in his own shows (he directed them, too), and Cocky does occasionally exude his personal brand of scary underdog humour, but the efforts to harness it to satire are embarrassing. They were even worse in Stop the World, a loathsome show, but at least in that one the protagonist functioned as both villain and victim, so there was some complexity.

But, of the two shows, it's The Roar that has the score. Nine of the songs became popular (a stunning number for a musical by that time, especially a British musical) and a couple have remained so. The best-known is Who Can I Turn to?, which has a hauntingly dark tune but a lyric so generalized as to be virtually meaningless. It's a shock to discover that, despite the song's generous use of the word "you," it isn't actually sung to anybody; Bricusse -- insiders generally credit him with the words and Newley with the music -- was already on his way to his current Jekyll and Hyde status as author of Broadway's most vacuous lyrics. The songs have a theatre sound but a pop mentality, and in their day their generic quality helped them get around; A Wonderful Day Like Today was every Vegas singer's favourite opener for a season or so, and Look at that Face has charm. To be fair, both songs in context have sardonic second choruses.

The show's abstraction goes well in a concert setting, and Tom Diamond directed it smartly on a stage marked out in three adjacent circles. Marek Norman's four-piece band sounded like more. Michael Fletcher embellished Sir's complacent pronouncements with extensive hummings and hawings of his own. If he slowed the show, Mark Cassius, with an impassioned reading of the Negro's anthem Feeling Good, outright stopped it, which is a far, far better thing. Steven Sutcliffe, the magnetic Younger Brother of Ragtime, played Cocky with a vocal infection that impaired his dynamics, but not his dynamism. Raging or suffering, he was in complete control.

- Reprise will stage a production of Anything Goes, opening in May.
1999-02-23-caught-between-the-need-and-f:
THE STONE ANGEL

Bluma Appel Theatre

St. Lawrence Centre

Hagar, a 90-year-old woman, lives with her son and daughter-in- law and resents it. She seems to have spent most of her life resenting things. The Stone Angel, James W. Nichol's dramatization of the Margaret Laurence novel, takes us backward and forward through that life: a long, packed, and rewarding ride.

"I always swore I'd never be a burden" says Hagar with self- indulgent relish. The paradox -- a common one -- is that her independence can only be asserted at enormous cost to everybody else. The saving grace is that her greatest victim is always herself. She is consistently infuriating: When her family is falling spectacularly apart, her greatest concern seems to be what the neighbours may think. She probably doesn't mean that, but it's significant she even says it.

All the same, she has her attractions. One is that though she may rage and complain, she never whines. Another is that, underneath it all, she doesn't have a heart of gold, although one lives in constant fear that her authors may decide to give her one. In her last days, in hospital, she does reach out to a couple of patients, but this is partly mischievous rebellion against the authorities. Besides, the play has consistently shown her to be as eager for human contact as she is frightened by it.

We see her as a girl, growing up in rural Manitoba at the end of the last century, alternately petted and bullied by her father. When she marries, he virtually disowns her. (He was planning to go on exploiting her in his old age.) Her husband turns out to be a drunk, though it's a nice question how much further she pushes him into it. At first repelled by his lovemaking, she grows to enjoy it, though she can never bring herself to tell him so. Of her two sons, she spoils one, and he, too, turns drunkard on her; she neglects the other, and when she finally apologizes to him, he hardly knows how to take it. We are not asked to judge how many of her misfortunes are her fault: We take her whole and acknowledge that, while her survival is itself a victory, the tide will roll over her as remorselessly as over everybody else.

Nora McLellan plays Hagar with complete command, slipping effortlessly into every age group that's required of her, anchoring all of them in the consciousness of the old and increasingly desperate woman. The play has been criticized for presuming to dramatize an interior monologue, but that is its strength. It makes an instructive contrast with Nichol's very free adaptation of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, which did a calamitous number on its original. This time, he keeps a fine balance between the narrative voice and the exterior world.

Hagar may think the supporting actors are only things in her dream, but they still live. Brett Porter is too soft-grained for her mud-caked farmer of a spouse (he looks about to burst into something rousing from Seven Brides for Seven Brothers), but Robert Persichini plays the long-suffering son with admirable shambling bewilderment, and there are excellent multiple performances by Michael Spencer- Davis and Elizabeth Brown. Janet Wright's direction is scenically resourceful and, most importantly, never yields an inch to sentiment.
1999-02-26-a-mere-boy-among-women:
CHERI

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

Up until now, the closest I had come to the novels of Colette was seeing the movie musical of Gigi, a picture I have reason to believe softened and sentimentalized its original. Nobody would accuse Paul Bettis' Cheri of that -- not the softening part anyway.

The play is an adaptation of two novels (Cheri and The Last of Cheri) written in Paris in the 1920s and set, mais naturellement, in that city's and that decade's legendary demi-monde. At the centre of this more or less glittering hemisphere is Lea, an ageing courtesan, obviously very good at her job but now semi-retired. For the last few years, Lea has devoted herself to the care and schooling of Cheri, a young man whose mother, an old friend and colleague, had once ever-so-gently flung him at her.

Now, however, the time has come for Cheri to move on. Lea knows the rules -- she has lived by them, after all -- and briskly, if regretfully, she sends him on his way, which means into marriage to a girl his own age with a fortune to match. The girl, however, rapidly turns into a woman -- an efficient businesswoman at that. Cheri, who has spent his life in the hands of women more competent than himself, finds himself in a situation where even his youth is no defence. He begins to despair.

The relationship of Cheri and Lea -- in its pure state, so to speak -- is excellently presented. For its first scene, which finds the couple in and out of bed, this seems to be a smart, sexy play. You see and feel why they are together, what they see in one another, and what they have tacitly agreed to overlook.

Donna Goodhand's Lea is not what I would call a raving beauty, but she has charm and sensuality and a sensible, worldly kind of compassion. She may tell her boy-toy that there are plenty more where he came from, but it's plain that she doesn't believe it.

Her performance reaches its peak at the play's half-way mark: Cheri has bolted and come back to her -- and for a moment it seems as if this will work. Then she considers the practicalities and, for the second and last time, sends him home. After which she quietly and discreetly goes to pieces, and so, less quietly and discreetly, does the play.

One grows tired of following Cheri's disintegration because, absent from Lea, there is not much to him. He expects other people to do his living and feeling for him: "I know how you should behave," he tells Lea; or again, "I don't mind not being your first lover, but it would have been fitting to be your last." I'm not saying that isn't acute characterization, merely that there's a limit to how often you have to hear it.

Michael McMurtry's performance might be described as uncompromising; he presents a rat-like youth who seems always to be pouting -- not just with his mouth but with his eyes and nose. To be asked to feel sorry for him -- or to feel anything for him -- is a definite imposition.

Soo Garay does a properly competent job on his betrothed, and the rest of the cast consists of Barbara Gordon and Jackie Burroughs, playing an assortment of hags. Gordon gobbles up the part of Cheri's mama without properly digesting it; she is actually difficult to understand, a matter of phrasing rather than volume. Burroughs, improbably billed as the "Pal" and sporting an alarmingly frizzy wig, plays everybody's confidante, plus Lea's maid, who has a scene- stealing limp.

The play's comic touch is very unsure; there was sporadic laughter on the first night, but it was scattered and half-hearted. The production invokes the elements of elegance -- gauze curtains and piano music and potted plants -- and then tries to undercut a style that it hasn't created; it wants to move us, but gives us no reason to care. On that count, it's more sentimental than Gigi.

- Plays until March 21. Box office: 416-531-1827.

Black & White Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / Soo Garay and Michael McMurtry in Cheri, adapted by Paul Bettis. ;
1999-03-02-shakespeare-as-it-was-meant-t:
"The theatre," says Richard Monette, artistic director of the Stratford Festival, "is not very generous. There's a lot of envy. But I don't know of any actor who doesn't want to pass on what he knows, and teach other actors." The Stratford Festival Conservatory for Classical Theatre Training has begun operations this year, and it's founded on that idea. It also springs from a widespread feeling that the classical actor is an endangered species, and, in particular, that the standard of Shakespearean verse-speaking is not what it was.

Now, it's probable that verse-speaking has never been what it was. I am certain that in 1660, when the London theatres reopened after 18 years of enforced closure by the Puritans, there were senior play-goers lamenting that a glorious tradition had been irrevocably lost, and that, on the lips of these new actors, the good old plays were barely recognizable.

Actually, these play-goers would have had to be very senior to have seen the plays in their original glory. Shakespeare's own company, the King's Men, had stayed in business right up to the lowering of the boom in 1642, but he himself, his star actor, Richard Burbage, and most of their contemporaries were long gone. So even before the ban, phrases like "call that a Hamlet?" must have been echoing 'round the taverns. (And this, by the way, is the definitive answer to anyone who talks about doing the plays "as their author intended." Even if we reconstruct an Elizabethan platform stage, even if we cast boys in the women's parts, we still have the fact that roles were written for specific performers who are no longer available.)

On the other hand, the late Nicholas Pennell, a regular leading actor at the Stratford Festival, used to say that "there is a direct link between the person playing Hamlet now, and Burbage." The plays do make specific technical and intellectual demands, and any actor who can meet them may reasonably be reckoned part of a "tradition."

Monette, who passed the Pennell quote on to me, also elaborated on it, with special reference to William Hutt, the Stratford doyen who, two seasons ago, played his fourth King Lear, and this year takes on the farewell role of Prospero in The Tempest: "Young people were inspired by Bill's Lear -- just as he had been by seeing Olivier and Gielgud."

Hutt is in his mid-70s, but he still speaks directly to a far younger actor like Albert Schultz. Schultz first attracted attention in the 1980s as a member of Stratford's Young Company, the precursor of the Conservatory, and he is now one of the moving spirits of Soulpepper, Toronto's new classical co-operative, which has its own training program: "I'm a huge fan of Bill's," he says. "He makes the text remarkably accessible and immediate." Personal example is the best form of teaching, but it doesn't have to be left entirely to chance; which is why we have schools. The Stratford Conservatory, a cherished project for years before it came into existence, is post- graduate, intended for actors who are already professionals. (It actually pays them.) It operates for seven weeks before the season starts -- next year they hope to double it -- and its students then pass into the company proper. There are 12 of them, whittled down from an initial 1,800 applications, and from auditions held coast to coast. ("We do this right," says Monette, "though we never get credit for it.")

Five of these apostles have been in the company before; the others are new. The project has cost $6-million, half of it coming from personal and corporate donations, and the rest a matching grant from the Ontario Arts Council.

There are classes in dance, movement, and swordplay, but the focus is on the text: on its meaning and on its rhythm. The two go together; in Monette's words "the Shakespearean pulse follows the heartbeat; it's very natural."

But there are technical standards: When an actor gets the stress of a line wrong, some of us feel physically affronted -- partly from a frustration that nobody on the production appears to have noticed.

Verse-speaking, though, is not about abstract music. Michael Mawson, the principal of the Stratford conservatory, insists that his purpose is "mostly to investigate the ingredients that lie behind the text, so that it's not just `stand and deliver.' " But he sees only a limited application to Shakespeare of the idea of "subtext" (which roughly means that the real thoughts lie between the lines). Elizabethan drama is relentlessly articulate, and its characters mean what they say.

Of course, you have to be a particular character with a particular story to arrive at those lines, and it is this level of subtext -- what he defines as "why you're saying this" -- that Mawson finds essential. It may be that the use of words at all, rather than the difficulty of these particular words, is the stumbling block for moderns. "Perhaps," he theorizes, "society needs less and less language: Most of what we communicate today can be done by body language."

Perhaps. But there is plainly a hunger for those old words; those 1,800 Stratford applicants didn't come from outer space. Shakespeare, we are told on all sides, has never been more popular; he is -- the ultimate accolade -- very big in Hollywood. An English professor in California has announced that the acting in Shakespeare films is incomparably better to what it used to be. It would be interesting to know which badly-acted old movies he has in mind (the Olivier trio? Julius Caesar with Gielgud and Brando? Welles' Chimes at Midnight?), but trendy philistinism is, after all, what you would expect from a Californian academic.

"If you can play Shakespeare" says Monette, "you can play anything." Schultz would amend that to "if you can play Shakespeare well," but I think all parties would agree that that's implicit. Mawson muses that it's not only Shakespeare who may be slipping away from us. Young actors whose highest dream is of snagging a lucrative TV commercial may find it hard to play a dramatist as recent as Pinter. In a recent review, I listed the great Pinter performances I had seen, and they were all given by classicists; Gielgud's delivery of the long speeches in No Man's Land was a wonderful bridge between the old and the new.

And maybe building bridges is what it is about. Soulpepper is devoting itself to modern classics this year as a prelude to a Shakespeare season in 2000. The Shaw Festival has just announced the extension of its mandate from plays written during Shaw's lifetime to plays written about it. Not many existing texts leap to mind, but there are two by Tom Stoppard that do; Travesties, and the new The Invention of Love, and the people at Shaw are better equipped to perform them than anyone on the continent.

And as for Stratford: To act a 400-year-old play, in verse, on a thrust stage, in front of 800 people, is as daunting a technical challenge as a young actor is likely to encounter; and technique is only the start of it. There will always be people, not just critics, making comparisons. But when it works, it works like nothing else; and audiences, too, can join hands with tradition.
1999-03-02-emotional-roller-coaster-make:
THE DRAWER BOY

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

Michael Healey is an actor whose past writing credits include a collaboration and his own one-man show. The Drawer Boy is his first, full-scale play for other performers, and it's a stunning debut.

The set for the play represents an Ontario farmhouse -- a bit of the inside, a bit of the out -- and the action starts with Miles, the youngest character, wandering in from the auditorium and inspecting it as if it were the set for a play. This is because Miles is an actor and he looks at everything that way.

The farm is owned and worked by two middle-aged men called Morgan and Angus. Angus is an apparent simpleton whose activities seem confined to baking bread, which he invariably overcooks, and doing the accounts, at which he is brilliant. He does the figures in his head, though he is unable to retain any other information for more than a second. Morgan explains his friends memory loss as the result of an injury sustained 30 years earlier during the London blitz, when the two were soldiers.

Miles comes to the farm for research purposes: He is working on a collective project bearing a strong resemblance to The Farm Show, which was an iconic Canadian production of the 1970s. One of the actors in that show was indeed called Miles -- Miles Potter -- and he is now the director of The Drawer Boy. So this is partly hall-of- mirrors entertainment.

Morgan permits Miles to stick around on condition that he help out with the chores. He then proceeds to razz the city-boy mercilessly. Miles asks what it feels like to rear animals and then slaughter them, to plant crops in order to pull them up again; Miles, says Morgan, looking him steadily in the eye, "its an emotional roller coaster." He also has the kid get up at 3 a.m. to rotate the crops.

Back at rehearsal, Miles' new agricultural expertise gets rebuffed; even his efforts to impersonate, what he calls, "the essence of cow" are spurned by his colleagues who, he claims, want the same old bourgeois cow.

The play may be meant, in part, as an affectionate homage to The Farm Show, but it does suggest that, these days, we're better off hearing about the old classic than watching it.

The only thing Miles can get into the show is something he overhears; the story, repeated by Morgan to Angus every night, of Angus accident, and of his youthful talent as an artist (hence the plays mysterious title), and of the two Englishwomen, magically described as "the tall girl" and the taller girl, whom they romanced and brought back to Canada, and of how that idyll ended.

Miles invites his two new friends to a run-through (his innocent insensitivity does take some swallowing) and is amazed at the effect it has on them: Angus starts remembering things and Morgan is not pleased.

It's surely no coincidence that in Act Two, Miles tells Angus the story of Hamlet, another reckless exponent of drama as therapy. I can hardly bear to type the words "reality and illusion," but, for once, that grindingly obvious old theme gets redeemed, lightly, intelligently, humanely, and with an unfolding awareness of all the ambiguities.

On a narrative level, the play resembles Pinter's The Caretaker, that fountainhead of contemporary drama; its another play about two symbiotic residents and an intruder, the difference being that Healeys characters all have the best of intentions. He has a wonderful ear and a great mastery of tone. You laugh and you grieve; it's an emotional roller coaster.

He also manages to combine in-house satire with an original story, or rather stories. Narrative trap-doors keep opening, and the pressure only slackens at the final set of revelations; they are perfectly believable but they seem, as is the way of final revelations, somewhat pat. This, significantly, is the only point at which the performances fall into predictable rhythms. Otherwise, the acting is lovely, with Jerry Franken's Morgan as witty, abrasive, and concerned, and Tom Barnett's Miles as gauche, earnest, and, beneath it all, strong. Angus, with his trust and his whimsy, is a role in which any actor might break your heart; David Fox, striking the keynote of the whole show, gains your respect as well.

Stephan Droege's design, principally the kitchen, is, as it should be, a self-effacing archetype.

I cannot recall a new Canadian play I have liked as much.

- Runs until March 21.

Box office (416) 504-7529.

1999-03-03-dying-is-easy-drama-s-hard:
For thirteen years now, Alberta Theatre Projects, one of the two resident theatre companies based in the Calgary Centre for the Performing Arts, has presented a winter festival of new Canadian plays under the banner Pan Canadian PlayRites. The shows are presented in repertory at ATP's Martha Cohen Theatre, a golden, welcoming auditorium surrounding a modestly sized but insistent thrust stage. This year's acting ensemble was solid, if not spectacular; the overall ambience could hardly have been warmer.

It could be savoured full-strength at the concluding Blitz Weekend, offering visitors, as well as locals who had been saving themselves, a chance to be bombarded by the entire program: four full-length plays in two crowded days. It's probably the best way to see them; the event takes over and stops you brooding too obsessively on individual merits. On this year's evidence, that's just as well.

The most interesting, and by far the most intelligent, was Richard Sanger's Two Words for Snow. This gave centre stage to two historical figures last seen in the theatre playing walk-on roles in Ragtime: Admiral Robert Peary, who may or may not have been the first man to reach the North Pole in 1909; and his black assistant Matthew Henson, who may or may not have reached it with or without him.

The play raises these multiple doubts but not does resolve them. Though there are many flashbacks to the expedition, the play is anchored in 1936. Peary is dead, but his son pays a visit to the American Museum of Natural History where an aged Henson is now employed as a kind of living relic; he is also a research resource for German-Jewish anthropologist Franz Boas in his studies of the Inuit culture and language.

Henson is not the first Arctic veteran to be put on show here; forty years earlier, Peary had brought back half a dozen Inuit and placed them in this same Eskimo Room, and they had died in the New York cold. A hierarchy of racial exploitation is suggested, criss- crossed by tentative moments of contact, intellectual or erotic. Peary and Henson have clashed over an Inuit woman, whom Henson accuses Peary of stealing from him. The most piercing moment in the play comes when old Henson hears that she bore him a son: a black man growing up in the tundra, though a little less black than himself. The same note is more mordantly sounded when Henson is told "the North Pole's a pretty, white place, Matt; Peary's not taking you."

Despite such resonant moments and an attractive sensibility (Sanger is a poet), the play is short on excitement; professing to be a fantasia on historical themes, it comes off more as a meditation. Peary junior, who has a lot of stage time, never becomes more than a mechanism. In Bob White's production, Nigel Shawn Williams see-sawed affectingly between the bewildered fire of Henson's youth and the quietly smouldering embers of his age, and Christopher Hunt shone out with a mischievous cameo of Dr. Boas.

There was more surface liveliness in Conni Massing's The Aberhart Summer, but far less going on beneath. Based on a novel (by Bruce Allen Powe), it probably tried to get too much in; the narrative was clear, but the dramatic point went missing.

This play, too, was set largely in the '30s, and it was the only one of the four with an Albertan setting; William Webster, the veteran actor who had given a sinister gloss to Peary, now did the same for William Aberhart, the prophet of Social Credit. Despite having the title role, he was marginal to the play, and though the rise of his party got a lot of attention it, too, turned out dramatically to be a large red herring. (Perhaps not red considering its virulent anti- Communism, but a herring nonetheless.)

The main story concerned the mysterious hanging of a teenage boy; unfortunately, he was dead before we had properly registered that he was alive, and all the flashbacks in the world couldn't revive him. Nor could all the tributes paid to him by his surviving friend, the play's narrator and an unrealized figure on a much larger scale. A character of whom we had seen too little eventually revealed the guilt of another character of whom we had seen even less; neither of them had any connection with Social Credit. We had to settle for a genre picture of a town wriggling in the grip of the Depression.

Stephen Heatley's production was impressively drilled, and the cast doubled and trebled with aplomb, but this kind of local epic has developed its own cliches: Speaking in unison as a shorthand for community spirit ranks high among them. When detached from the chorus, several young actors -- Christopher Hunt, Kevin Kruchkywich, Brian Marler -- made agreeably sharp impressions.

The latter two were similarly helpful in Frank Moher's Weather, which, theoretically, brought us up to date, being set in "Vancouver, recently." This also had a narrator-protagonist, a homosexual manic-depressive with a schizophrenic son. "You're in for a number of surprises this evening," he warned us, sounding rather smug about it, but the only really surprising thing was that he expected us to be surprised. The play had a pedagogical flavour, as of something to be taken 'round the schools to instruct older children about an issue.

"Everybody is mad in this play" we were told, and those not clinically affected had their own obsessions about how to treat those who were. The title seemed a metaphor for their collective state of mind, or perhaps for that of society as a whole. The son had designed a machine for controlling the weather, and though both he and the play soon dropped this idea, he did seem more in control of life in general than anyone else on stage.

Characterization was sketchy in the extreme: a matter of outlining each social and/or medical role, and letting the actors add a few tics. D. Michael Dobbin, artistic director of the company, also directed this play.

Dying Is Easy, another play about now, had some tastier writing, but was even more of a mess. "Dying is easy -- comedy's hard" are famous last words attributed here to "some old Shakespearean actor, British; I can't remember his name." I've always believed it to be the valediction of some old American vaudevillean (I can't remember his name), but since the character quoting it is an obnoxious loudmouth, the author may have meant the mistake as a subtle comment on her.

I wouldn't bet on it, though. She's a TV editor, making life hell for a pair of writers who are trying to develop a sitcom; if they fail with comedy, dying may well be their best alternative, or so they frequently feel.

Paul Quarrington frankly admits that the play is his revenge for having had a series idea of his own rejected by the CBC. At the risk of sounding unkind, if that idea was anything like the one his two heroes have come up with -- an adult comedy about rampant infidelity as seen through the eyes of the family dog -- my sympathies are with the Corp. A parallel plot about the pair being stalked by a wronged and vengeful female they call the Wild Woman is unfunnily unbelievable, or unbelievably unfunny.

One of the guys is an agoraphobic, so the play doesn't travel much, and in Bill Glassco's production it seemed unduly exposed, both by the open stage and by the acting of two thirds of the cast.

Peter Smith, the remaining third, had one splendid moment of anger and was a pretty good counter-puncher, but his colleagues (Nigel Shawn Williams, Mieko Ouchi) gave him nothing to feed off. They also displayed an unerring knack for emphasizing the wrong word in a sentence. That would be most enervating in any play, but in gag- comedy -- which this is, or aspires to be -- it's disastrous.

Nobody expects four masterpieces in one season; it may have happened in ancient Athens, but never since then. But when one considers that each part of this quartet had already been workshopped somewhere else, it was distressing that they should all have arrived on the Calgary stage sporting such gaping holes.

Black & White Photo: Trudi Lee / The cast of The Aberhart Summer, one of a series of plays from this year's festival, which is run by Alberta Theatre Projects. ;
1999-03-06-tova-s-holocaust-piece-is-str:
STILL THE NIGHT

Factory Theatre, Toronto

Theresa Tova's Still the Night is the story of the author's mother, and of her ordeal in wartime Poland as a Jewish teenager in flight from the Nazis. It comes wearing the badge of authenticity, and this is its greatest -- or anyway its most obvious -- strength. It is also a musical, and this, though useful in some ways, is its greatest weakness.

There are actually two girls on the run, cousins: Bryna and Little Bryna. Mary Ellen Mahoney, last seen by me as the hero's man- eating fiancee in Crazy for You, now wades into radically deeper waters to play both Big Bryna and her daughter Tybele who is the author-surrogate. The show's framework depicts mother and daughter living in Calgary, the daughter teasing out the mother's memories, which are then enacted for us. This -- following How I Learned To Drive, Stone Angel and Alberta's Two Words for Snow -- is the fourth play I have seen this still-young year that requires its leading actor to alternate constantly and instantaneously between an older and a younger self. It is the first that also requires her to play two separate characters who have conversations together, and Mahoney -- switching positions and personalities like a ventriloquist switching voices -- does it niftily.

We get a leisurely look at the two Brynas in the Polish countryside before the nightmare starts. Big Bryna's father is a factory man and a prominent local Communist; Little Bryna's is a farmer and apolitical. Little Bryna is unsophisticated, goes to a Jewish school, and loves Yiddish-American movies starring Molly Picon; Big Bryna talks tough and smart, goes to a Christian school and prefers Ginger Rogers. All this is a frame within a frame, and the show devotes rather too long a time to setting up the normality of their lives before it is brutally shattered. But once it is -- once the Nazis have taken both girls' parents and they set off to join the Yiddish partisans in the forest, it is as gripping as you would expect.

Along the way they are raped (with a resultant childbirth), tortured, and almost hanged; their successive ordeals are played out in passages of jagged mime, backed by harsh percussive music from the band. But they win through, their friendship inevitably stretched but apparently unbroken. They are the only characters we see, but one of the show's achievements is that it never feels like a two-person show. Script and performance make us aware, without any awkwardness or strain, of the hostile forces all around.

At the end of the war, in comparative safety, they do break up. Little Bryna emigrates to Israel and is apparently contented. Big Bryna goes first to France, then to Canada, and grows up embittered, hugging her pain. The show finds plenty to admire in her wit and resourcefulness but it does not pretend that suffering necessarily ennobles. When the two heroines are reunited after 30 years, they have nothing to say to one another: one believes in forgiveness, the other in grudge. It is left to daughter Tybele to make her own pilgrimage to the kibbutz and achieve some kind of reconciliation with her aunt.

We see Big Bryna keeping a store in Calgary, fighting, haggling and wheedling as she learned to do in the war. We can look the other way, remember the girls sneaking into movies as children, and see it as a rehearsal for the deadlier games ahead. Liza Balkan as Little Bryna is pertly convincing when playing young, and even better -- weathered, stooped and grandmotherly -- when playing old.

But there are holes in the development. Mahoney, tall and rangy in red, looks and sounds good but still offers a display of technique rather than a character. The ventriloquial technique doesn't allow for any real confrontation between mother and daughter, though that's what the show seems to be heading toward. Tom Diamond has staged the show incisively, on a set by Mary Kerr dominated by a tall step-ladder and a huge hammer-and-sickle and reminiscent of the expressionist theatre of the `30s. But the dialogue scenes are sometimes out of focus.

The play was first seen (though not by me) in 1996 when it was acclaimed. There have been two major changes this time around, and I suspect that they are both damaging. Mahoney's role was originally played by Tova herself, and though I have no idea how their performances compare, the author's presence must have upped the emotional stakes considerably. Then more songs have been added. The score comes in three varieties; there are authentic Yiddish songs in translation, there is specially written material, and there are a couple of barely relevant American standards. The old songs never quite fit the context; they might work as Brechtian commentary, but they're sung in character. They may add some ethnic flavouring, but dramatically they get in the way. The new ones, collaborations between Tova and John Alcorn, are lightweight: off-Broadway music and lyrics whose images and sentiments are taken from stock. They simply aren't up to the subject, and no wonder: with the partial (and special-case) exception of Cabaret, no musical has touched the Holocaust without cheapening it.

Music is the most powerful of all stylistic devices, and its presence allows dramatists to take chances, narrative short-cuts, that might not otherwise be possible. It can also raise the temperature, but here the emotions come between the songs. The script is stranded somewhere between being a fully-realized play and a musical book. That doesn't destroy it; the show, which is touring the country, is well worth seeing. But don't expect a masterpiece.

1999-03-11-the-end-draws-near-for-a-long:
Ten years is a long time in the life of any theatre, and in the Toronto commercial theatre it's unprecedented.

The Phantom of the Opera has run even longer in London and New York than it has in Toronto, and it was a proven phenomenon in both places before it came here. So Garth Drabinsky's acumen in bidding for the Toronto rights is not especially remarkable; everybody must have been after them.

What is extraordinary, given that he was a virtual novice in live theatre at the time, is the ferocious pertinacity that it must have taken to drive the deal through. The show became of course the foundation stone of the Livent empire, the cash-cow that made it possible to raise money for other shows and other theatres.

With Livent's present existence cloudy and its future doubtful, it's salutary to remember that Phantom made possible a decade of theatre that was certainly uneven but whose peaks were like nothing the city had seen. There has been a lot of crowing in the press over Livent's misfortunes (and it seems to have been directed indiscriminately at both past and present regimes, depending on who provided the tastier target at a given moment) but I don't know anybody in the theatre who doesn't recognize that, with Livent's fall, a degree of flash and brilliance has gone out of Toronto and out of Canada.

When I worked for Livent, which was roughly during the era of Ragtime and Fosse and Parade, it was possible to forget for long periods that Phantom existed. This was ungrateful but human: There was other, and fresher, fish to fry. The media forgot it too, except when prodded into brief awareness by yet another anniversary.

But the public at large, I think, have always felt differently; for them Livent was in the business of megamusicals, and megamusicals primarily meant Phantom. And there is a good reason for this, though I may have to swallow hard before writing it: Phantom is a good show.

It's good musically: Music of the Night and -- especially -- All I Ask of You are the best tunes Andrew Lloyd Webber has written in his lush style; and if the rest is overblown it can be defended as operatic pastiche appropriate to the subject. It isn't good verbally -- the lyrics are characterless, in every sense, and there is virtually no book, but then people have never gone to operetta for the words. Dramatically, it isn't much either; it takes a good story (one assumes it's good, because it has been recycled so often) and hardly bothers to tell it. What it's really about is atmosphere -- lush, spooky, and melancholy. It's everybody's idea of a romantic musical, given spectacular flesh.

This is partly Webber's achievement, and very largely that of Hal Prince and his design team. As pure form, irrespective of content, it may be Mr. Prince's masterpiece of staging. I've never failed to gasp at the explosion of colour in the Masquerade number that opens the second act. (I once heard that song in concert -- just sung, no visuals -- and knew the meaning of disillusion.) It's a show devoted to raising goosebumps; the setting and music do much of the work, the heroine's threatened innocence provides a mild sexual charge, and the hero's self-pity does the rest: everybody loves an unhappy monster. With the possible exception of Les Miserables (it would have been interesting to see how that would have done in Toronto in an open-ended run; somehow I don't think it would have done as well) no other modern musical had tapped so deeply into the public's most sentimental impulses.

"Perhaps it was the chandeliers." That was Alan Jay Lerner, lyricist and librettist, musing whimsically on the success of his own earlier, similarly successful, and frankly much better romantic musical My Fair Lady. (Coincidental historical footnote: Mr. Webber originally wanted Mr. Lerner as his collaborator on Phantom. What a career-capper that would have been.) A lot of people, less whimsically, have attributed Phantom's success to its falling chandelier. I don't think so; it's a passing, though pleasing, moment.

The London producers were smart to choose the Phantom's mask, not the chandelier, for the show's logo. And if we have to choose among lighting fixtures, I'd go for the shimmering candles burning around the boat in the subterranean scenes. They really stand a second look.

So it became part of the landscape, backed up by shrewd and energetic marketing and educational campaigns -- which somehow never worked the same wonders for some of Livent's more ambitious and indeed more distinguished shows -- and by the best radio ads anyone had ever heard. It went some way towards brightening a dingy section of the downtown core, and must have perked up the local economy no end. (I wonder what will happen to the delicious Phantom dessert they've been serving over the road at the Senator for the last decade.)

And of course it wasn't just the show; it was the theatre. However Toronto ranks in the hierarchy of North American cities as regards theatre production, it is certainly the capital for theatre building and theatre restoration. The Pantages is a jewel restored, and the perfect setting for the show. (You could stage the Masquerade scene on the foyer staircase.) But one would still love to see other productions there.

Whatever happens -- or whoever happens -- to the Phantom and to Livent, the Pantages has to have a future. It would be tragic if the Pantages post-Phantom became just another ghost story.

1999-03-11-the-man-seduces:
Tony Bennett

Roy Thomson Hall, Toronto

Tony Bennett began his mara-thon 90-minute set on Tuesday night with The Best Is Yet to Come, the magnificent Cy Coleman-Carolyn Leigh song about the beginning of an affair -- a song he introduced 40 years ago but which, in my ear, has always belonged to Frank Sinatra. He proceeded to reclaim it, and in significantly different terms: When Sinatra sang it, with a big-band Count Basie backing, it was an assertion of prowess; Bennett, accompanied only by his long- time pianist Ralph Sharon, made it a tender, confident promise.

Bennett has long been known as the nicest guy in popular music, and there seems no serious reason to doubt the proposition. With Sinatra dead, Mel Torme sadly silenced by a stroke, and Bobby Short a minority taste, Bennett -- in his handsome, grey-haired 70s -- is now the official elder statesman of the American popular song.

He is also one of its most fervent disciples, and though a packed audience had obviously come to worship him, his own devotion seemed to be devoted outward, making him a fans fan. Other singers have built programs around individual composers; Bennett's recent CDs have been tributes to other vocalists -- to Sinatra, to Astaire, and to the great female singers, especially Billie Holiday.

Though his Toronto concert must have been meticulously planned (there were no last-minute conferences with the musicians about what they should do next), it seemed spontaneous -- a relaxed ramble through the songbook, using those other singers as markers. Classics and rarities rubbed shoulders on equal terms. In his Astaire segment, he moved from a buoyant You're All the World to Me (a little-known song from Royal Wedding) to the two big ones from Shall We Dance: They All Laughed, sung with sly, driving wit, and They Cant Take That Away from Me, done with a yearning warmth that caught the audience delightedly off guard.

He also took a few brief canters on his own warhorses. I have sometimes wondered why I Left My Heart in San Francisco, an ordinary song that had been lying around for years before he got to it, should have caught the public imagination above all the others he had sung in much the same way, (I sometimes wonder the same about Ray Charles and the considerably better Georgia on My Mind) but he gets through it now with a nice blend of seriousness and self- mockery.

He had fun rocking I Wanna Be Around to a climactic "oh, yeah" that sounded like a homage to somebody (Louis Armstrong?), but was a bit weird considering that its been Bennett's own song from birth. He revisited his first hit, Rags to Riches, with a gentle swing far more appealing than the earnest nasal throbbing he gave it in the '50s. And the same understatement enabled him to give the only palatable performance of People, the Barbra Streisand anthem, that I have ever heard.

It may be a matter of age, economics, or simple good taste, but simplicity becomes him. He introduced himself as a jazz entertainer rather than "a jazz singer." If I can follow him into that minefield, it seems to me that he gets closer to jazz -- to the truthful reshaping of a loved piece of material -- the less obviously "jazzy" his surroundings. Singing with a big band, he often sounds choppy; but with just a piano, he can be magic. He did his first four songs with Sharon alone and they were enchanting; the hall became a supper club. After that, he added guitar, bass, and drums, but the intimacy remained.

This is the time to hear Bennett. He still has most of his bravura high notes, and the grey at the edges of the throat only enhances them. Sinatra made every song an individual event; Bennett, by contrast, offers a constant wash of good music with the occasional surprising peak. Like all good pop singers, he talks to you in song; like all great ones, he does it in an unmistakable voice, in his case gravelly and urgent. His tone can be world- weary, but his spirit is profoundly hopeful.

He still has his faults: Conversational singing shouldnt mean talking the songs -- not when you can actually hit the notes -- and Bennetts shouts and whispers are often overdone. (Speak Low, despite its title, was a casualty; it's a great lyric, and he rightly loves it, but he didn't have to demonstrate it so insistently.) His dynamics often seemed governed less by interpretative intention than by how far from his face he happened to be holding the mike.

But you wouldn't want Tony Bennett to be slick. He told us at the end that he was doing a long show because he loved Toronto and didn't get here often. I bet he says that to all the cities. But I believed him.

1999-03-12-french-historical-play-has-a-:
Monsieur D'eon is a Woman

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, Toronto

History's most celebrated hermaphrodite gets a going-over in Monsieur D'Eon is a Woman, a moderately interesting chronicle play with recurring fits of the giggles.

The Chevalier d'Eon de Beaumont was an 18th-century French aristocrat who achieved some reputation as a soldier and diplomat under Louis XV and XVI. He also insisted that he was a woman. Nobody was certain until after his death; an autopsy established his masculinity.

Mark Brownell's play shows us d'Eon, at age seven, taking Joan of Arc for his role model, she being a woman who fought and dressed like a man. In other words, d'Eon is a woman trapped in a man's body, pretending to be a man trapped in a woman's. (Or, as Stephen Sondheim once put it, "wait, I think I meant that in reverse.") When the Chevalier grows up, he wins battles and is sent on missions to Russia and England; but his success arouses the jealousy of the older Louis, the hostility of the younger, and the resentful enmity of just about everyone at the French court. He moves to London after being released from the Bastille by the forces of the revolution. To survive, he takes to giving sword instruction in skirts.

D'Eon doesn't seem much bothered by his own sexuality, and neither really does anyone else; it's just another handle for his foes to use against him. So the various bits of the play don't hang together and it's difficult to see what, if anything, the author is trying to say. Sue Miner has staged it capably, and it's always a pleasure to see a large cast (11 good actors, furiously doubling) disporting itself in fancy dress on a wide-open stage. Brownell has a talent for aphoristic prose, and the brief scenes between d'Eon and his patron saint, whom he calls his "shiny lady," strike sparks.

Ron Kennell gives a light, dignified, technically excellent performance in the lead, keeping a gracious distance from the other characters and thus explaining why they all hate him. The author helps set the tone in his performance as George III, not yet mad, whom he plays as an animated pudding. This is history in the style of Blackadder or Monty Python but without the wit or content. I thought we had outgrown this kind of show, but they keep coming.
1999-03-16-sons-and-daughters-of-famous-:
THREE DAYS OF RAIN

Canadian Stage Theatre, Toronto

There have been plays before in which the same actors have played different generations of one family, and there have been plays in which the action has rolled backward from the present to the past. Richard Greenberg's Three Days of Rain, which comes to us from America modestly laurelled, may be the first play to combine these devices, and they set each other off rather well.

Act One finds us in 1995, in a grubby Manhattan apartment inhabited by Walker Janeway, son of a recently deceased and extremely eminent architect. Like many sons of famous fathers, Walker has gone into retreat, in his case quite literally; sometimes he vanishes for weeks on end. His married sister Nan comes looking for him so that they may attend the latest variant of that hallowed dramatic ritual known as the Reading of the Will.

Among their late father's creations was a splendiferous house on Long Island, built for his own parents, and he has bequeathed it, not to his children, but to Pip, the son of his late business partner, Theo.

Pip is an unremarkable but contentedly successful actor. ("I eat chocolate and never gain weight; life is good.") Nothing earth- shaking happens between these three, but in the course of some mildly entertaining ructions, three skeletons lurch out of their respective closets: from childhood, Pip has had to walk on eggshells so as not to upset the super-sensitive Walker; Pip believes that Walker was/is in love with him (no comment from Walker); and Pip and Nan were once lovers.

Like much upscale American playwriting these days, this section suggests an episode of Friends masquerading as drama: not quite serious, not quite funny, and not quite boring. It probably has more wit than is apparent, but in Rosemary Dunsmore's production the timing is off; often, you have to replay the lines in your mind to get the joke.

What does emerge is that the late Ned Janeway was a very chilly father and, probably, colleague. When Walker and Nan discover his journal, Walker, in one of his many fits of pique, destroys it. "Now we'll never know anything," moans Nan. Which leads us, with an anticipatory thump, into Act Two.

This, set in 1960, is another world, though it's the same room: at this date, the young Ned's living and working space. The actors who were previously the sons are now the fathers; the daughter turns into her own mother, by the name of Lina.

There are shocks. Ned, whom one had pictured as a monstrous authoritarian, a Yankee equivalent of Ibsen's tyrannical master builder, turns out to be a whole other kind of distant: gauche, shy, and with a stammer. Theo has more social graces but is haunted by doubts of his own abilities. Lina shifts sexual allegiance in a scene that has already been craftily pre-figured -- or, given the time scheme, post-echoed.

All the characters, in both age groups, are bursting with high or middlebrow cultural references, and in act one, Pip has described for us an archetypal Broadway matinee play of the Sunday in New York variety: The kind in which the girl comes out of the rain from the hero's apartment and gets into a robe and they "dance around one another." It turns out that Ned and Lina have performed this choreography in real life, and that their rapturous routine lasted for the three nights of the title, at the end of which Theo walked in.

So it's possible that it was guilt that prompted Ned to leave the house to Theo's son. One also notes that while Theo was crippled by the thought of being untalented, Pip can live with it easily.

By throwing away the journal Walker has, once again, walked away, this time from any chance of exchanging his chilly illusions about his parents for the somewhat warmer reality. The sins of the fathers are not visited upon the children; they're invented by them. The play has its share of glib ironies, but it winds up worthy of respect.

The acting, too, improves with age. As Walker, Michael McManus is your standard languid commentator, happier talking to the audience than to the other characters; as Ned, he blossoms, apparently liberated by his stutter and building a character out of it. Paul Eves, alternately wooden and amusing as Pip, puts on a good show of desperation as Theo.

Only Camilla Scott seems thoroughly out of her depth. As Nan, rebuked by her brother for her "suburban alacrity" (the adjective at least is right), she is drab and toneless; as Lina, she has rather more energy, but most of it goes into maintaining her accent, which is Southern and very deep-fried.

- Until April 3. Tickets, (416) 368-3110.
1999-03-17-hit-the-road-jacques:
JACQUES BREL IS ALIVE AND WELL AND LIVING IN PARIS

National Arts Centre, Ottawa

Fate, as the late and chronically glum Jacques Brel would surely have agreed, is a cruel goddess; she may take her time about it, but in the end she will sashay up to you and slug you in the chops. For thirty years, I had avoided seeing Jacques Brel is Alive and Well and Living in Paris. Last week, at the National Arts Centre in Ottawa, I finally caught up with this perennially popular compilation of the Belgian bard's words and music; or perhaps I should say it caught up with me. Either way, I emerged with my spirits low, my ears enraged, and my prejudices bleakly confirmed.

In a former life, I developed a deep suspicion of actors who, with a whole world of song at their disposal, would choose a number from this show as an audition piece. Two of their selections stand out in my memory. One was Amsterdam, the landlocked sea shanty about a sailor who, at various unrelated times, "swallows the moon" and "zips up his fly." The other was Jacquie, an even more disjointed lyric in which a guy -- apparently some kind of troubadour -- breathlessly reels off three separate ways in which he might have sold out and been "cute, cute, cute, in a stupid-arse way." (A good description, I've always thought, of this show's title, even in the days when it was factually accurate.)

In this latter song, the author seems to be congratulating himself on his own integrity. That was also the impression I received from those long-ago auditionees (catch them being frivolous and ingratiating and singing Cole Porter) and, in spades, from this brand new production. (It re-opens today in Vancouver, and comes to Toronto next month.) It throbs with self-righteous emotion.

Jacques Brel is an American show, and it's possible that the French lyrics are not as wordy and incoherent as the translations (by Eric Blau and Mort Shuman) make them seem. Brel himself may not always have grabbed for the nearest lurid image as a way of getting to the end of the next line, and he may have written phrases in which the number of syllables bore some singable relation to the number of notes.

But the music, of course, is the same, and though this production comes with new and colourful orchestrations (by Steve Margoshes), they cannot disguise the poverty of the material.

No song boasts more than a single melodic idea, which it proceeds to pound into the dust. Sometimes the tempo steadily increases, and this can be effective; the celebrated if hardly profound Carousel number ("we're on a carousel . . . and then we go around") works this way, or might if the performance were not so intense as to be funny. Often, the repeated phrase is yanked up a key to signify passion. Always a song will end with somebody shouting.

This, I must admit, does move some people. There were cheers at the final curtain in Ottawa. But then, as an English critic once observed, an audience that's been yelled at for an evening is naturally going to want to yell back.

The show taps into a certain kind of Anglo-American snobbery; one that believes that the French chanson is, by definition, raw and uncommercial and deeply sexual and incredibly honest. But, without going outside this tradition, a writer like Charles Aznavour leaves Brel gasping in terms of musical invention and lyrical detail.

Even Brel's smartest satirical ideas (such as Middle Class Men, in which a pair of nonconformists become what they used to deride) run out of things to say or ways to say them, and fade into an overall surly smugness. And at that, Brel's misanthropy is preferable to his sentimental side. His ballads are as turgid as they come, culminating in If We Only Had Love, a strenuous and sanctimonious anthem that ranks with My Way and I Dreamed a Dream as among the worst songs ever written, even in Paris.

What is appalling is how influential all this has been: not so much the show itself as the sensibility it represents. You can trace it in the deafening pomposities of the European megamusical, in the quieter but equally formless breast-beating of all the North American singer-songwriters who don't happen to be Randy Newman, even in what remains of the New York cabaret tradition, which has taken to screaming the virtues of Love as if it were a brand of soap flakes. Craft has gone, wit has gone, irony is everywhere proclaimed but nowhere present, and bellowing is taken to be a guarantee of feeling.

Elly Stone, a veteran of the show's first cast, directs this revival in appropriately sepulchral fashion, on a set whose principal feature is a monolith with a doorway cut in it. There are some odd jokes: One song is mysteriously performed in Salvation Army costume, its heroine mocked for using the same outspoken language (e.g., "her new fuck-you stand") on which the show prides itself for the rest of the time. A number about bullfights has the ensemble laboriously acting out everything the soloist is describing.

The cast are four of the Canadian musical's top-rated voices, but voices is pretty much what they remain. The women, Louise Pitre and Susan Henley, are avenging angels, distinguishable only by one being fair-haired and the other dark. Michael Burgess flourishes a beautiful lyric tenor that doesn't always connect with the acrid material; he is stolid in a way common among actors who have done extensive time in Les Miserables. Jeff Hyslop is more malleable, with an impish gargoyle touch and nimble feet.

The men share a song, Madeleine, about waiting at a movie for a non-arriving date, that is the jauntiest thing in the show. It has humour, a tune, and a developing situation. It is, in fact, the only moment of joy in the evening.

- Runs at the Vogue Theatre, Vancouver, March 17-27; and at the Winter Garden Theatre, Toronto, April 5-27. Tickets: Vancouver, (604) 280-4444; Toronto, (416) 872-5555.
