1999-03-19-the-pantheon-of-hard-luck:
PURPLE HEART

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, Toronto

Plays about solitude are getting so plentiful, you can't move for them.

Purple Heart is a one-character piece about a young woman named Constance who rarely leaves her Toronto apartment. When she does, to hear her tell it, bad things happen to her.

Once she ventured onto the subway and it broke down between stations, forcing her to descend to the track and walk terrified to safety, in the discouraging company of other passengers who seemed disconcertingly cheerful about it. So she took to cycling, and on one shopping excursion she met the love of her life. That sounds more hopeful, but, of course, every relationship comes with a price.

So she stays home, surrounded by fairy-lights, the pride and joy of her life. They trail along the floor, over the sofa, and, most spectacularly, in an arch that spans the stage, giving the effect of a false proscenium. (Our first sight of it is pretty amazing.)

She also munches her way through myriad boxes of Cracker Jack, and arranges the empty cartons to form what is by now a very high wall. She watches old movies on TV, obsessively it seems, her faves being Fred Astaire musicals and anything with Audrey Hepburn. Logically then, her ultimate picture would be Funny Face, which has Astaire and Hepburn, but I dont remember hearing it mentioned.

The top of her pantheon is Breakfast at Tiffanys, and her adoration of it has inspired her to write copious letters to the real Tiffany's with ideas for window displays. All her suggestions have been spurned, and the sight of the meagre jewelry store that actually faces her building is not much consolation. She is also very keen on The Little Mermaid whose heroine she compares to Hepburn's Holly Golightly. (Holly moved to New York; the Little Mermaid moved to Denmark; its the same, only Denmarks cleaner.)

I can't think what else to tell you. Purple Heart is the work of a visibly talented author, Gail Packwood, and actress, Kirsten Johnson, who have, like their protagonist, painted themselves into a corner. The title refers to Constance's belief that medals should be awarded not just for deeds of heroism, like killing people, but for long endurance -- for, if you like, constancy. She speaks of the pressure she feels "to be successful, to be happy, to be thin," and adds, I cant do it any more.

I doubt if she ever could, or would. We seem to be listening to a heavily decorated -- and perpetual -- hard-luck story. That doesnt make Constance's problems unworthy of our attention, but it does place a heavy responsibility on her interpreters to keep us interested. Johnson is very good at knitting her character's thoughts and emotions together but her range is pinched. Dismissive and defeated from the start, she has nowhere to go.

There is no point in calling Packwoods writing contrived (every play is a contrivance, unless its the work of an idiot savant) and she does build up her own pleasing Toronto mythology: a crazy woman blessing the traffic (one direction only), "that fancy Loblaws down in the Beaches."

Too often, though, listening to the play is like watching the shuffling of an over-familiar pack of cards. Now it's time for another letter to Tiffany's, now for a movie-reference, now for a joke about TVO.

Every so often Constance tells a story we would like to see, and hear, for ourselves: her subway misadventure (I can see there might be technical problems here), her crucial encounter with her lover.

Packwood can obviously write dialogue and it would be good to get it straight, rather than refracted. Solo shows have obvious economic advantages, and a fluent, competent writer can turn them out with comparative ease. But they ought to function only as a court of last appeal: a way of telling stories that can't be told any other way. This story as we see it probably couldn't be; the more interesting story-behind-the-story assuredly could.

- Runs until March 28. Box office: (416) 504-7529.

Black & White Photo: Kirsten Johnson, like the protagonist, Constance, paints herself into a corner. ;
1999-03-25-the-importance-of-being-true-:
The Importance of Being Earnest

Grand Theatre, London, Ont.

You know you're in trouble when, a few minutes after the rise of the curtain, the manservant perches confidentially on the arm of the sofa on which his employer happens to be sitting. The flunky in question is called Lane and he works for Algernon Moncrieff, one of the two young men-about-town who drive the action of Oscar Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest. For him to take such a liberty is not only unlikely in the social context of late-Victorian London, it is totally at odds with the way the scene is written. Algy, with no malice whatsoever, regards Lane -- and the working classes generally -- as a remote species, created to minister to his needs and to furnish material for philosophic speculation: "Really," he says, "if the lower orders don't set us a good example, what on Earth is the use of them?" This may not be democratically acceptable, but it is funny. It also sets up the whole world of the play -- a hermetically enclosed one, whose rules go unquestioned by all its inhabitants.

At this early stage, one suspects the director, Michael Shamata, of not knowing what he is doing. By the end of the first act -- in which he shows us master and man taking a glass together in even more flagrant contradiction of the text -- it is plain that he does know but that what he is doing is almost totally wrong-headed. His Algy, hob-nobbing with the help, is symptomatic of a desire to make all the characters -- with one important exception -- terribly nice. This -- I'm cheating by paraphrasing the program-notes -- is because they are in love: Algy loves Cecily, the niece and ward of his friend Jack Worthing, while Jack loves Algy's cousin Gwendolen. And the girls love them, but principally because each has got hold of the idea that her young man's name is Ernest, and the men are prepared to go to desperate lengths to maintain this illusion. In fact, each of the characters is a monster of egotism, and the fact of their being in love only intensifies each one's monomania. (This is psychologically very sound.) That doesn't make them unsympathetic; they are in love, and that in itself will have any audience rooting for them. We don't have to soften them as well.

The generic name for a play in which the characters' drives propel them into absurdity is farce. The Importance is the greatest English farce, but it's an unusual one in which the pratfalls are not physical but verbal. It is, in fact, a farce of manners -- a form that Wilde seems to have invented and in which only Shaw and Stoppard have to some extent followed him.

Let's forget about interpretation; the task of any production is to work out where the laughs are and then get them. In practical terms, this means wrapping your tongue around the sentences. There are great schemes afoot, on both sides of the Atlantic, for helping actors to speak verse. It strikes me that it may be just as urgent to teach them how to speak prose -- perhaps more urgent given that it's the medium in which most good plays have been written for the last 200 years.

In this production, a sentimental conception is compounded by inexpert execution. What are we to make of a Gwendolen (Lisa Waines) who, when she speaks of her own sweetness of manner and gentleness of disposition, seems to want us to take the description at face value? Cecily (Deborah Drakeford) is equally callow but, she being the youngest character, somewhat more acceptable.

Jack (John Ullyatt) has some of the determination proper to this country squire -- especially when it comes to his anguished complaint about Algy having "stayed to tea and devoured every single muffin" -- but none of the weight; he actually seems younger than his friend, which destroys both the logic of the plot and the balance of the dialogue. Patrick Galligan's Algy, a silvery aesthete, is by far the best of the quartet and the only one with a sense of pace, though it often goes to his head and turns into mere rush.

Fiona Reid's Lady Bracknell -- arch-gorgon of the British drawing- room, a "monster without being a myth" -- is, by contrast, impeccably phrased. In keeping with recent tradition, she is less battle-axe than sabre, though in her delivery of the play's most famous line she is the first I have seen to go toe to toe with the legendary Edith Evans; her "a handbag" is an anguished croak, crowning a long pause in which unthinkable things appear to assault her consciousness before being swept irrevocably away. This gets to the heart of the character -- a refusal to admit the existence of anything that might contradict her. She seems, though, to be acting in a vacuum, in terms of both values and vowel sounds. In fact, Lady Bracknell's values (the same, as has often been remarked, that were about to destroy Wilde himself) are shared by everyone else in the play; the only difference is that she's had them longer.

All of the other senior characters are disappointing. David Hughes' Canon Chasuble is competent but flavourless. Hazel Desbarats' Miss Prism stands up splendidly in her last scene but goes in for lachrymose, supposedly meaningful, pauses earlier on. (I'm all for subtext, but there's a time and place.) James Macdonald doubles as the play's two servants and, despite my opening strictures, earns excellent references in both.

John Pennoyer's sets have real disinction: a crowded bachelor- pad for Algernon, all Beardsley and bric-a-brac, and a luscious garden-come-conservatory backed by a giant projection of flowers. They outclass most of the acting, though this may be a matter of practice. Life may demonstrate the triumph of hope over experience; the theatre, especially the classic theatre, has a habit of proving the reverse.

- Plays until April 3. Box office: (403) 425-1820. At the Citadel Theatre, Edmonton, April 10-May 2. Box office: (519) 672-8800.
1999-03-26-this-loathing-for-mulroney-ca:
THE LIFE AND TIMES OF BRIAN MULRONEY

Factory Theatre, Toronto

Michael Hollingsworth's VideoCabaret is a company devoted to making theatre look and sound like television. This is more fun than you might expect; and technically, in terms of both performance and presentation, it can be enormously impressive.

The action unfolds within an oblong frame, as if behind an invisible screen. There is much use of projections; an actor playing, let us say, Brian Mulroney may be seen in three forms simultaneously -- front and back as a video-image and centre-stage in the flesh. Performers -- there are six in the current show, handling forty-five roles between them -- scamper tirelessly about while still maintaining absolute precision. Somehow every element, human or mechanical, arrives in the right place at the right time.

The Life and Times of Brian Mulroney is the twelfth and last instalment of VideoCabaret's comic-strip history of Canada. Its tone, like that of its predecessors, is remorselessly sarcastic; it's like an episode of The Royal Canadian Air Farce at four times the length, or -- less genially and more precisely -- like the British series Spitting Image, only with people instead of puppets.

The show presents Mulroney being groomed for the premiership, principally by Ronald Reagan and American Express, and then chronicles his terms of office. It also hints at the aftermath with a chilling little scene in which Prime Minster Jean Chretien promises the paymasters that he will stand by free trade and the goods and services tax despite anything that they might chance to hear him say during the election.

Meanwhile, the former PM has been portrayed as endlessly venal, selling out national liberties right and left, but especially left; and also as endlessly vengeful. (His response to any rumble of opposition is: "I'm gonna get that guy" -- or, as the roster of challengers begins to proliferate and he needs to distinguish between them, "I'm gonna get that guy.") He is eventually undone by his failure to secure a consensus over Quebec. Having initially seen Meech Lake as a golden opportunity to divide and conquer ("When I get through with Canada, it'll be 10 little dwarves in search of a master -- mark my words."), he finds himself faced by incompatible interests that not even he can smooth over. He finds himself haunted, in an especially vivid scene, by the spirits of Jean Chretien, Lucien Bouchard, and Preston Manning: an especially threatening trio of ghosts since, of course, they happen to be alive. His wife also takes to rubbing her hands a great deal.

These two cases aside, the Mulroneys are no Macbeths; no tragic grandeur is permitted here. When Brian goes down, he goes into financially cushioned oblivion.

I believed it. But believing something is not necessarily the same as enjoying it.

My one previous brush with VideoCabaret was Trudeau and the FLQ, two shows ago. This had the benefit of a good story about hostage- taking and a protagonist who was credibly something of a hero, something of a clown. Hollingsworth and company obviously had a sneaking admiration for Trudeau.

Mulroney they merely loathe. Although hatred might conceivably provide enough fuel for a full evening's theatre, loathing -- a far colder emotion -- runs out of gas. Despite Michael Copeman's best and sharpest efforts in the role, Mulroney does not emerge as either funny or interesting. There may, of course, be excellent reasons for this.

Ray Landry's Reagan -- a figure who seems to have existed principally in order to be impersonated -- is funny, and his John Turner is both funny and rather touching: ditto for Michael Carley's Joe Clark. Drama loves a loser -- which, the world being what it is - - is greatly to drama's credit.

As comedy the show suffers --certainly it did on the first night - - from the presence of a complicity captive audience, willing to lap up every line. This breeds complacency. The show improves the darker it gets, which is to say the second half is better than the first.

There is a subplot about the effects on three working Canadians of the New World Order (which, the Americans explain, they prefer to call free trade since everyone loves the word free). This starts out as a definite drag, but as its characters are thrown out of work and through the cracks, it does take on some power. And there are always the toys to marvel at.

The show runs until April 18.

1999-03-31-colonial-ladies-bring-a-few-g:
THE BUSH-LADIES

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

I can't remember the last time I saw so many bonnets on one stage. The Bush-Ladies is a splicing together of the memoirs of four Englishwomen who emigrated to Canada in the 1830s. Molly Thom, the adaptor-director, began to assemble this material 30 years ago and the show that has finally arrived at the Tarragon (which has something of a tradition of literary theatre) is transparently a labour of love. It is certainly an informative evening, and it is sometimes an amusing one. It is not what anyone would call thrilling.

Each of our heroines was responsible for one magnum opus. Anne Langton (played by Elva Mai Hoover), miniature-painter and musician, wrote A Gentlewoman in Upper Canada. Anna Jameson (Meg Hogarth), touted in the program as "an intellectual, a social critic, and an ardent feminist" married the Attorney General of Upper Canada, speedily left him, travelled through the wilds for a few months, and then went back home where she published Winter Studies and Summer Rambles.

Catherine Parr Traill (Wendy Springate), officers wife and botanist, wrote The Backwoods of Canada. Susanna Moodie (Mary Ann McDonald), Catherines sister and also an officer's wife, wrote about her experiences for magazines and called the collected result Roughing It in the Bush.

Set apart from her colleagues by this forthright choice of title (and also by the fact that her book has endured as something of a classic -- at least I've heard of it) Susanna emerges as the most individual, and as the one whose story is easiest to follow. She projects delicacy that gradually reveals its strength: The transformation from a sheltered existence to a life where shelter is the goal.

Its a shared trajectory, and the show alternates personal with communal experience. The observation that woman is a bit of a slave in this country -- an insight hardly won and somewhat reluctantly expressed -- takes shape as the outcome of backbreaking litany of chores. (These are rhythmically listed, and then made the foundation of a small dance routine, rather too redolent of Higher Amateur Dramatics. A burst of singing from McDonald, on the other hand, is delightful).

Admiring the characters abilities to put in such days, and then write at the end of them, you also reflect, somewhat ruefully, that this was an age in which literate people did write, and not just for publication. Intentionally or not, the show makes a very good case for Anglo-Christian gentility, presenting it as a tradition that expands under pressure but never breaks.

Much of the show is about homesickness, complicated by an increasing ambiguity about just what or where "home" is. The longer you remain in Canada, the less you will like it is what we hear at the outset; by the end, there has been a journey from enthusiasm for the new country to resentment to surprised acceptance: the universal immigrant experience, it seems.

All the deprecating lines about Canada, by the way, get laughs, as does a more localized observation about the remote possibility of bringing "a few grains of truth to Toronto." The ability to laugh at one's own culture -- or at least at one's own place-names -- is one of the things that British and Canadians have in common: an overlooked portion, perhaps, of the colonial legacy.

This is not a show that I could ever be wild about but it does what it wants to do, and the performance-level is unobtrusively high. Everybody resists temptation: Which is to say that nobody over- colours, and nobody recites.

- The Bush-Ladies runs until April 18. Box office: (416)-531- 1827
1999-04-01-cruel-lessons-from-a-sacred-m:
MASTER CLASS

The Royal Alexandra Theatre

There are two plays going on in Master Class. One of them can be very entertaining and the other is at least informative. They have the same central character, and they do, in a way, complement one another. But they do not add up to a satisfying whole.

In 1971, with her operatic career virtually over, Maria Callas agreed to give a series of public classes to aspiring singers at the Juilliard School in New York. These sessions provide the frame, and much of the detail, for Terrence McNally's script. It takes place in a bare, spacious cream-coloured room with imposing double doors in its back wall and a splendid cupola ceiling -- a great set (Michael McGarty is the designer) that, in its combined suggestion of gymnasium and church, pays appropriate tribute to the artists strenuous devotion to her art. This is certainly what the Callas of the play preaches, and it seems fair to assume that its what she has practised.

Elizabeth Ashley, playing the diva, enters -- but naturally -- through the double doors and proceeds to greet and harangue the assembly, played by us. The house lights are up, which is unsettling. (Are we meant to feel unsettled? If so, why? And are we meant to join in, to offer responses when the lady seems to be buttonholing us? Some people did. I rather wished they hadn't.) Callas finds it unsettling as well and complains, and after some humorous delay her complaints take effect. Everybody relaxes -- the audience, Callas, and the actress playing her, who up to this point has been noticeably edgy, seeking authority rather than embodying it.

Art, says McNally's Callas very wisely, is "making people think that for that precise moment in time there is only one way, one voice -- yours."

Unencumbered by any particular memories of the original, I could accept Ashleys Callas, for most of her moments, as the real thing. She is an imposing performer, with a sulphurous voice, a handsome presence, and an air of lived-in outrageousness. She speaks in the measured tones of someone who takes herself absolutely at her own valuation. Her timing, as opposed to her delivery, is very fast; and the meat of the show comes when she has a chance at cut-and-thrust.

Ashley has an air of lived-in outrageousness

Three victims, I mean students, present themselves for her evaluation -- one male, two female. The man gets a noticeably easier ride than the women. Each of the three delivers an aria; each is stopped after barely a note has been sung, interrogated, lectured, and criticized. It isnt their voices that's in question; it's their interpretation, their commitment, and even their appearance. A look, she says, is all-important: "If you dont have a look, get one, as soon as possible."

Sophie, the first contestant, has the wrong look. She is a plump girl in a pink flowered dress, and the divine one, perhaps remembering her own early weight problems, fairly dismembers her. Sophie, however, is possessed of a placid good humour and, though somewhat distressed, is not destroyed. In our eyes -- though not perhaps in Callas -- she certainly gives as good as she gets. And Frances Limoncelli's amused performance is absolutely perfect.

Tony (Alexander Kariotis) is a golden-voiced stud who wants to be Mario Lanza. Sharon (Melissa LaFrance), having perhaps taken to heart the earlier comments on a look, presents herself in a long, slinky number, purple and backless, that evokes an equally withering response. I would love to say that she also sings a long, slinky number, but she actually offers the letter aria from Verdi's Macbeth, which is neither. She proves Callas most formidable antagonist, being good but not in the way Callas would like. She, too, is very well played, by LaFrance.

Ashley apart, all the performers in Leonard Foglias production come from music rather than theatre, but their acting can hardly be faulted. In this respect, they're living up to Callas' own proclaimed standards. This even goes for the onstage pianist, whom Jeff Lewis endows with the courteous sufferance that has been the badge of the accompanist tribe since the beginning of musical time.

While Sophie sings, and while Sharon sings, the stage darkens and Callas thoughts go back to her own past -- to her early struggles, to her rejection and her triumphs, to her marriage, and in particular to her liaison with Aristotle Onassis -- to return in her mind from master class to mistress class. These monologues allow the star to stretch out (Ashleys earth-toned evocation of Onassis is terrific) and they provide some clues about the evolution of the sacred monster we have been observing. But they are an essentially crude device that lands the play in an indeterminate zone between full biography and licensed impressionism.

Back in the present tense, Sharon lashes out at Callas for trying to turn her students into carbon copies of herself. Callas responds with another statement, a little weary this time, of her own artistic beliefs: an avowal of the essential selflessness of egomania. Both are probably right. But by this point Ashley has run out of new notes to strike, and so has the play. It has held out against being just a solo turn, and against sentimentality about the sacred mission of the artist, but in the end it succumbs. You don't have to be a genius to portray a genius, unless genius happens as here to be your essential subject.

- Master Class plays at the Royal Alex until May 1. Box office: (416) 872-1212.

1999-04-06-thanks-for-the-condoms:
A COMMON MAN'S GUIDE TO LOVING WOMEN

Canadian Stage Theatre, Toronto

Glossy magazines remain full of articles for women on how to attract and hold onto men, though now, of course, they focus less on matters of dress and appearance than on sexual performance. Soberer organs, such as newspapers, are equally full of articles denouncing the assumption that keeping men happy should be a womans primary aim in life. It is seldom pointed out, though, that men are subject to much the same pressures and react in much the same way, thrashing about between dependence and whatever its opposite may be.

A Common Man s Guide to Loving Women presents the case -- or the conflicting cases -- for this neglected half of humanity. Andrew Moodie has written a conversation piece for four guys in their late 20s, all of whom seem to be doing rather well for themselves. One is a lawyer, another a corporate executive, a third works in television. But when something goes wrong in their relationships with women -- when a phone doesn't ring or a date fails to show -- their confidence evaporates, and they revert to confused little boys. And the other things they have in their lives, and even in their apartments -- video games, computers, basketball, strip- clubs, booze, and one another -- are apt to make them seem more boyish than ever.

All four are black, a fact that is sometimes of incidental importance and at others of no importance. Two of them are facing sexual and emotional problems of real magnitude. The lawyer is being dumped by his fiancee. The exec has been accused of rape and is liable to lose his job even before he comes to trial. To hear him tell it he is innocent. And even that is somewhat punctured by his lawyer friend, whose talk around this point has a decidedly journalistic air, redolent of the things people read and write rather than how they speak. Mostly, though, the dialogue is sparky and the issues compelling to sustain us through some rocky areas of narrative and characterization.

The characters are paper-thin, and the author jerks them around. One actor abruptly lets loose with a long speech about having been abused as a child. It's powerfully written and acted but once its over the speaker reverts to his previous status, that of a jokey commentator. We dont feel that hidden depths have been uncovered, merely that someone has been drafted to fill in a theme.

At other times, there is some tentative mixing of fact and fiction. We are told that the lawyer' s ex is an actress, and we hear that she has been seeing more than he would like of an actor called Randy Hughson. That happens to be the name of a real Toronto actor, so there were in-joke giggles on the first night. I thought the idea desperate rather than helpful, but I laughed as loud as anyone when our jilted guy consoled himself with the reflection that at least he wouldn't have to go to see any more of those damn plays. He should think himself lucky he hadnt been dating a critic.

Talking of art and life: After the premiere, there was the customary reception in the lobby and -- for the first time in my experience of these festivities -- there, laid out beside the regulation carrot-sticks and chicken wings, was a selection of brightly-coloured condoms, along with literature on how to use them. This was generous of someone, as well as being a praiseworthy reinforcement of the plays concern with safe sex. (Though the implied estimate of the amount of fun people have at first-night parties seemed to me wildly optimistic.)

The actors are lively (we're talking about the play again, now) though three of them -- Derwin Jordan, Andrew Jason Wade, and Conrad Coates -- are stronger on enthusiasm than on finesse. The author is the fourth player, and in strength, urbanity, and emotional grip he excels. His role is that of the only married man in the gang, though there's little sign that he spends much time at home. He talks about his wife in tones of propietorial affection but he never actually mentions her name.

- A Common Man's Guide to Loving Women runs until May 2. Box office: (416) 368-3110.
1999-04-09-restaging-a-slice-of-quebec-l:
LES BELLES SOEURS

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

Thirty years ago, Michel Tremblay's Les Belles Soeurs, a group picture of working-class French-Canadian women in a Montreal apartment block, took the Quebec theatre by storm. It subsequently repeated this feat across the country, and now it has been revived, in English, by Canadian Stage. It's possible, with some historical imagination, to appreciate the impact it must have had. Less easy is to accept it now as entertainment.

At the centre of the play is Germaine, who has won a million trading stamps in the lottery, and now enlists her relatives and neighbours to help her paste them into the appropriate little books.

Her helpers are jealous of her good fortune and -- in the intervals of bickering, complaining, and even the odd bout of shared cheerfulness -- they start pocketing the stamps themselves, some with more misgivings than others. Germaine stumbles onto what is happening and unleashes her fury on everyone, including the two or three who tried to put her wise.

The play reaches its climax in a maelstrom of rage, recrimination, and -- the evening's recurring note -- self- righteousness. Tremblay may, as has been asserted, love these women, but nobody would accuse him of sentimentalizing them.

But maybe we should. Rightly, he exposes the drudgery of their lives: an unending round of chores performed for ungrateful children and exploitative men. He also shows their narrowness: the way in which they suffer under stifling social and religious conventions, while turning savagely on any of their number -- an unmarried sister who has dared to set foot in a nightclub, the hostess-prostitute who hardly ever gets out of it, the younger generation in tow -- who threaten to escape.

But his principal method of doing this is to line them up and have them express their grievances in unison. You almost expect them to put on expressionist masks, as befits choral representatives of a social class. (It's alarming to find this supposed new dawn in Canadian drama parading techniques that the rest of the world had outgrown 30 years earlier.) The devices undoubtedly make their point but they do so at the cost of patronizing the characters. This applies in the jollier moments. A maiden lady tells a mildly salacious joke, and we are asked to laugh, not at the joke itself, but at the characters for being titillated by it.

The whole cast erupts into a well-drilled song and dance in tribute to the joys of bingo, whose effect is less celebration than deprecation. Or you may think of it as a detachable bit from an unwritten musical, noting that the cutest high-kicker is a demented 90-year old whose principal function elsewhere is to be repeatedly bopped on the head by an exasperated daughter-in-law.

Tremblay orchestrates his effects -- and an ensemble of 15 characters -- deftly: This was his first play and a considerable technical achievement. Nor is its subject matter all that dated; some things may have moved on but the cruelties and hypocrisies are still with us.

Germaine has two harridan sisters, and a third, named Pierette, routinely referred to as "that whore," who pays a visit (in full tart's gear - a surprise if she's looking for a welcome in this censorious quarter), befriends a tearful pregnant friend of Germaine's daughter, and steers her toward an abortion. Unfortunately, when Tremblay is not writing barbed group scenes, his characters expose their true suffering selves in sensitive soliloquies that force the actors into taking portentous pauses before significant words. (People baring their souls in real life never, ever, talk like that.)

There is, of course, a problem of language. The play was originally acclaimed for its innovative use of Quebecois slang, and the flavour naturally evaporates when it goes into standard English. On the simplest level, vive le Bingo has a zing that "long live bingo" undeniably lacks. I can't think of any solution to this, except perhaps to put the whole thing into Irish. (A couple of the cast did seem to be leaning in this direction.)

And the presentational devices that might have seemed so new, now need recharging. In fact, one would like to let a director as imaginative and as culturally compatible as Robert Lepage loose on this play. The present staging is by Denise Filiatrault, a veteran of the first production, and I would guess that her production is an echo of the original.

The actors go through the more stylized passages with routine devotion, but left to themselves they relax into unsteady naturalism. This means a lot of shouting. Janet Wright, as Germaine, goes through the first 10 minutes of the play on a single strident note, and though she is more palatable when she gets a chance to relax, this doesn't happen often. Most of the others get their turn, with varying degrees of authority. The only one who surprises us is Rose (Nicola Cavendish), the most monstrously unforgiving of the sisters.

After demonizing unwed mothers, and arraigning French films for being "too real" and "too exaggerated," she tells us about her life with the man to whom she said "yes," and who has been legally forcing himself on her ever since.

The imposing set, by Andre Barbe, takes an entire tenement facade and tilts it at a perilously fascinating angle.

- Les Belles Soeurs runs until May 1. Box office: (416) 368- 3110.
1999-04-13-morality-tale-plays-out-at-th:
BABES ON BAY STREET

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

The title suggests a movie that Judy Garland and Mickey Rooney wisely forgot to make.

But Babes on Bay Street is a surprise: a smartly amusing comedy about the business of business, written by someone who's been there. Lilia Csorgo's day jobs have been in financial consultancy of one kind or another and this is her first professionally-staged play.

That makes it the second consecutive debut on the Passe Muraille main stage; it isn't in the same league as its predecessor, The Drawer Boy, but they make a lovely couple.

This one presents a short period in the life, and especially the conscience, of a young woman called Jane. Jane works for a company that works for other companies, moving intangible assets to untaxable places. She is halfway up the building (unable, as she points out, to make it either to the street or the roof in case of fire) and her position inside the organization is somewhat similar. She worries about her success, or the lack of it; and about her social usefulness, or the lack of it.

She is flanked, as in a morality play, by two friends: Brenda, who is moderately idealistic, and Jake, who is moderately cynical. Brenda has left the race, having acquired a prosperous husband and twins, but then -- as Jake, who was once her boyfriend, loves to point out -- she can afford to. Jake is thoroughly happy in and with the system, and especially enjoys observing the femininity that passes down Bay Street; as he more or less puts it, we're talking serious babe here.

There have been theatrical satires on the money-market before -- it was an unsurprisingly hot subject in the 1980s -- but I like this one more. It is cooler in some ways, warmer in others; its characters may be types but they are not automata, and we see them manoeuvring in a world where cupidity is a negotiable norm, rather than an unprecedented aphrodisiac blast. (If Jane has a love-life, she keeps very quiet about it.)

The action runs on well-oiled wheels: literally so in Michael Waller's quick-witted production where characters sit in their office-rollers and propel themselves from corporate cubby to chromium cafe to thoroughly nondescript apartment on a functional if decidedly unlovely unit set. God is also in the details: in Brenda's habit of dispensing moral advice in the same cooing tone with which she addresses her babies; in the pre-recorded phone message which informs Jane that her place of employment has been massively re- structured; or, climactically, in Jake's reaction to the suggestion of a spot of insider trading. There is, he insists, a pale, and this is beyond it. The play itself, of course, written from experience, might count as insider trading in a peculiarly benevolent form.

As Jane, Elisa Moolecherry ends up striding towards an unspecified future that seems, from the staging, to reside somewhere up the centre aisle of the auditorium. She negotiates her way to this point with sparkling eyes, crackerjack timing, and a fine bewildered turn of speed. Maureen Kirkpatrick oozes comfortable sensitivity as Brenda, and Jim Jones is first-rate as Jake, shiny but not oily and resembling, with his eager beam and cockatoo quiff, a young political pundit with all of the answers and none of the questions. Bob Nasmith, in a dual role, can't get a handle on Jane's boss who needs to be simultaneously bland and scary, but is admirable as a friendly street-person whom she uses as an unconscious moral sounding-board and who is called Frank.

The choice of names is unspectacularly perfect; and I don't think it's fanciful to suggest that this is one mark of a natural playwright, especially a natural comic playwright.

The author is mining familiar territory here -- familiar to her and, only by hearsay, to us -- but she makes it seem fresh and quirky. As Jake might say if he understood irony, we're talking funny here, seriously funny.

- Babes on Bay Street runs until May 2. Box office: (416)-504- 7529.

1999-04-16-is-anything-worn-under-this-k:
THE KILT

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

You can bump, you can bump, you can bump, bump, bump

Until your privates wilt.

Me, I bump and I bump and I bump, bump, bump

But I do it in a kilt.

I offer the above, with apologies to the strippers number from Gypsy, as an anthem for Tom, a Toronto table-dancer of Scottish descent who is the hero of Jonathan Wilson's new play.

Tom uses his Scottishness as the gimmick every professional undresser, male or female, gotta have. His actual theme-song is Donald, Where's Your Troosers?

Before introducing him, however, the play transports us to the Second World War where we meet Mac, another young man in a kilt, serving as a private in the North Africa campaign and having a brief but happy homosexual affair with an equally young officer. At the end of this scene Mac performs a fierce and vivacious Highland dance, and by the end of that scene, the actor has turned into Tom, performing 50-odd years later for his Canadian clientele. After discarding the idea that he might be Dorian Gray, one realizes that Tom is Macs grandson. I thought for a while that he might be his son, but Im very dim about these things.

In fact, Tom's dad died when Tom was a child, and it was at this point that he and his mum, whose name is Esther, emigrated to Canada from Glasgow. Esther now teaches Scots dancing in Hamilton, and is pretty intense about it. She is gorgeously played by Maja Ardal as a miniature

dragon-lady with darting suspicious eyes and a mind to match. Although proudly tolerant of her son's sexuality (she chirpily informs him that a friend of his has "come out of the cupboard"), she doesnt know about his job and is livid when she finds out.

Old Mac has just died, so Esther and Tom return to Scotland to attend the funeral and see the family. This seems to consist of Esthers sister, Mary, and the two of them indulge in the lovingly prolonged recriminations that are customary on these occasions, especially in plays. (Deborah Lambie plays Mary and, spikily generous, she gives as good as she gets.)

Tom rushes out on to the street where he encounters David, an elderly man who turns out to be Mac's wartime love, also in town for the obsequies. David spots the family resemblance (not surprising in the circumstances) and a tender, funny and, let me add, chaste scene ensues. All then repair to the burial, which turns out to be a cremation, and is a hoot.

The only thing wrong with the play is its structure, which is a shame since the author has obviously worked very hard at it. In order to keep the relationship of Mac and David in our minds, he keeps wafting us back to Africa, distracting us from the engrossing present while having nothing new to say about the past.

Tom is a decorous stripper; his granddad may have served under Montgomery but he himself stops somewhere short of the full Monty. In fact -- despite kilt, gayness, and casting -- Mac and Tom do not illuminate one another much, although Paul Braunstein plays both of them well: openfaced and open-hearted as Mac, wryly smouldering as Tom. Even the Scottishness is not much of an issue. We meet Canadian Scots and Scottish Scots, but when they fight they fight like any other relatives, although more entertainingly than most.

Tom's sex life has resolved into encounters with customers, which have left him disillusioned, but the feeling is announced, rather than dramatized. Meanwhile, David, played with wistful courtesy by Gerard Parkes, has kept his love for Mac bright through the years; this is moving, but it isnt connected to anything.

Wilson seems to have a huge talent for making his characters live in the moment but not much as yet for digging beyond it. We are left with a vague feeling about the persistence of love -- family love, erotic love -- which is comforting but hardly profound. There is less beneath The Kilt than seems promised but whats on the surface should keep most people happy.

- Runs until May 16. Box office: (416)-531-1827.

1999-04-20-tell-us-a-story-and-spare-us-:
Theatre Reviews

Waiting for Lewis

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, Toronto

The Other Side of the Closet

Young People's Theatre, Toronto

A good old playwrights' rule states that if a play has a message, the characters had better not know what it is. The urge to do plays that are ostentatiously about issues afflicts all levels of Canadian theatre but it is especially rife among those companies who do shows for kids. These productions often give the impression that the creators have mistaken their vocation and would have been happier as social workers.

The company known as Theatre Direct Canada are, from what I have seen, an exception. Their show The General (which I saw when they brought it to my own children's elementary school) might be said to have been "about" community involvement, but it took shape as an individual story about an eccentric crossing-guard and two reasonably complicated kids who came to his assistance when he was abruptly fired.

Their new play Waiting for Lewis, playing for two weeks at Buddies in Bad Times, is a more complex piece designed for older teens; and the company's publicity, which doesn't always do their work justice, suggests that it is "about" careers. But that word never crossed my mind while I was watching it and -- more significantly -- it never passed the lips of the actors either. The play, written by Fabrizio Filippo, concerns two households in emotional chaos; it deals in people, not abstractions, and thereby makes a profounder connection with its audience.

The first scene, hilariously well-observed, shows a family moving from the city to the sticks. Dad, an architect, wants to rediscover his vocation. Mom wants to keep everybody happy. Son Ben is doing the driving, and writhes uncomfortably when told how well he is doing. Younger sister Carey is in a mood of foul-mouthed resentment at her enforced departure from civilization.

Once arrived, in a small town that seems to be its very own Bible belt, father lets his dreams slide while his wife turns into the complete nest-maker -- to nobody's gratitude. In truth, they rather fade out while the play focuses on their children's relationships with one another and with their new schoolmate Lewis. Lewis lives with an alcoholic and smotheringly possessive mother. He is the local high school's star student but a loner nonetheless. He has some charm and distinction (he wears a suit, for heaven's sake, which is so uncool it's cool) and he is wildly unhappy. He plays on Ben's insecurities. (They first meet in the school washroom where Ben is having a self-conscious smoke. Lewis inquires whether he is trying to quit to which Ben replies that he is trying to start.) Sexually fearful himself, he tells Ben that Carey is sleeping around -- an allegation that, when she hears it, sends her into free fall.

The play hinges -- less firmly, I think, than the author would like -- on the visit to town of its one famous son, a rock star; on the enthusiastic reception he gets from a community that disapproves of everything he represents; and on the rejection by Lewis, himself groomed for success, of the hypocrisy involved. It isn't that much of a progression -- Lewis has seemed like a nay-sayer from the start -- and the choice of a pop-idol as focus seems rather obvious. What counts is the play's texture, the ebb and flow of its dialogue as it charts the simultaneous yearning of adolescence for privacy and for contact. Most unusually among plays in this area, it dares to be elliptical. It is staged by Joanna McIntyre with both sense and sensitivity, and finely acted, especially by the juniors: Shaun Benson, Gil Garratt and Maryke Hendrikse. I have seen plenty of plays for adults that were less grown-up.

The other side of the coin is The Other Side of the Closet, a previous season's success now revived at the Young People's Theatre. This, as the title amply indicates, is an upfront play about coming out. As didactic drama goes, Edward Roy (who has also written and directed a couple of plays for Theatre Direct) has written a superior example of the species. But even its complexities are simplistic. It starts with three boys yelling "faggot" at someone unseen, and from there you can count off the minutes before one of them is revealed as a closeted gay himself and his buddies start persecuting him.

It's only slightly less predictable that the most vicious of his attackers should be revealed as over-compensating for his own insecurities. This is a comforting thesis, and it certainly happens in real life, but maybe not as uniformly as playwrights would have us believe.

Meanwhile, there are two girls present: one of them thoughtlessly prejudiced and the other shiningly enlightened. The author does his sporting best to give her some flaws, but there is no escaping that she has all the answers, apart from a few that the hero has to learn later from fellow-students in a gay school program.

He himself is decently characterized, his experiences an updated reflection of what the author himself went through in school. But even with this role, the impression remains that this is a play in which the author has decided on an issue and then devised people to fit it.

They all seem to know they're in a play about homophobia, and their and the author's awareness makes the teen language -- however accurate it may be line-by-line -- sound very self-conscious.

The YPT's slogan is "theatre for a better world" but good theatre, in itself, makes a better world. (And that is something kids should be taught.) Plays like this seem to exist less for their own sake than for that of the discussion afterwards. Bigotry of any kind is a dead subject for a play unless you're prepared to enter into the minds and hearts of the bigots. And for that, pamphleteering plays like this have neither the time nor, seemingly, the inclination.

The performances, under the author's direction, are mostly good; and the social and educational intentions admirable. We are always told that plays should ask questions.

But this kind of theatre has already decided what the answers are, and the audiences are expected merely to agree with their instructors. Don't they get enough of that at school?

- Waiting for Lewis runs until April 24. Box office: (416) 975- 8555. The Other Side of the Closet runs Fridays and Saturdays until May 8. Box office: (416) 862-2222.

1999-04-23-blackface-would-be-more-corre:
JOLSON

Princess of Wales Theatre, Toronto

I greatly enjoyed Jolson when it played in Toronto two years ago. A biographical fantasia, it was really just a cunning and elaborate excuse to revive a bunch of old songs, but it was done with exceptional sharpness and vivacity. I wasn't expecting a second visit to reveal any previously hidden depths, but I would have been happy to revel on the surface again. What we have now, though, turns out to be a different and much inferior show.

Most obviously we are denied any indication Al Jolson, the song- and-dance man still ritually described as "the world's greatest entertainer," spent almost his entire career performing in blackface. It's obviously a ticklish matter, and the original production found a witty and ingenious method of dealing with it. We saw a scene from a terrible musical of the 1920s or earlier, with Jolson playing a stereotypical funny servant scoring points off julep-sippin' white folks. At a certain point he stepped out of character, dismissed the other actors, and told the audience that rather than subject them to the rest of the plot he would just sing for the rest of the night. This is truly the kind of thing Jolson did, although he never took off the burnt-cork to do it. The show managed to elide his (real) desire for the solo spot with his (fictitious) discomfort at blacking-up, and by this sleight-of-hand honour was satisfied, history acknowledged, and blushes spared.

Even this seems to have been too much for the U.S. audiences at whom this touring version is aimed. (Political correctness now seems thoroughly reactionary, the politics of the apolitical: You can ignore real-life abuses as long as you act properly shocked by words and images on stage or page.)

We see Jolson in his dressing-room applying a touch of black and immediately wiping it off; we hear him complaining about playing "Gus the butler" without being given any idea of who Gus the butler was. This has ramifications. It means that Mike Burstyn, playing Jolson, has nothing to act. By the time we get to intermission Al has divorced one wife and married another woman, gone solo on Broadway and made the first talkie, but it still feels as though nothing has happened.

The show's authors (Francis Essex and Rob Bettinson) are English, and Jolson in its origins is a very English show. I mean that, for once, as a compliment. The British have a huge sentimental appetite for mainstream U.S. showbiz. The British approach can be bland and get the idioms wrong, but it cares and sometimes it works. It did with Jolson, first time round, thanks to a central performance by Brian Conley that transcended impersonation. It was cavalier with details but totally commanding: a star turn in its own right.

The most cunning device of the show as written is that, for most of its length, it is sparing with the famous songs and unleashes most only at the end, when we are supposedly present at Jolson's last one-man show. When Conley played it, I actually believed by this point that he was Jolson. I even found myself believing in his dresser, the most English of all the performances and charmingly camp, who hung around most of the evening singing snatches of The Spaniard Who Blighted My Life and was finally dragged on stage to perform it with the maestro. In this version, the character, the number, and the set-up all go for nothing.

The show's second act shows us Jolson during the war, when he exhausted himself performing for the troops, and, after it, when he became hot again after Hollywood filmed his life, using his voice and a younger actor's body. This does work up a certain amount of steam, although we do seem to keep watching the same scene -- one in which Jolie's comparatively estranged wife and his long-suffering manager try to talk sense into him. The wife, who is supposed to be Ruby Keeler, has the evening's most resonant line when she tells him that the movie will present his life "not as it was, but as you want it to be," which is a charming acknowledgement of the show's own strategy. Heather Mazur plays her as a mechanically efficient good- hearted belter, a falsification a lot less forgivable this time around that it did before.

Burstyn's Jolson, meanwhile, is far closer to the original's vocal mannerisms, and to his unglamorous looks, than Conley was, but in his hands the show becomes a nostalgia-package. A good actor, he works hard at the character's egomania, but we never feel it; he seems a nice guy who boasts. To be honest, this show needs blackface; if you're going to impersonate, go all the way. Down on one knee without it, he looks incomplete.

Harry A. Winter plays the agent wearily and well. The young Gershwin who turns up in Jolson's dressing-room to audition Swanee ("don't give up the day-job, George" advises Al) looks amazingly convincing. Bill Castellino's direction is otherwise unremarkable, and Broadway choreographer Joey McKneely is in mundane form. The sets (James Fouchard) remain glittery, and of course there are the songs. One -- Harry Warren's About a Quarter to Nine -- is superb, and the others corny, well-crafted, and infallible.

- Runs until May 2. Box office (416)- 872-1212

1999-04-28-tennessee-williams-for-two:
TALK TO ME LIKE THE RAIN AND LET ME LISTEN / THIS PROPERTY IS CONDEMNED

Solar Stage, Toronto

Here, performed twice daily at lunchtimes in the bowels of Scotia Plaza, is a pair of early sketches by Tennessee Williams on his perennial themes of fantasy and defeat. Each is a duet, and the same two actors appear in both.

Talk To Me Like the Rain and Let Me Listen unfolds in a seedy hotel room in (one assumes, since it's Williams) New Orleans. A young man lies on the bed and murmurs, I wonder if I cashed my unemployment, an admirably economic way of clueing us in both to his social and his mental state. He also has recent memories of waking up in a bath full of ice cubes.

While he seems pretty much content to go with the flow, his female partner projects a more active discontent, a forcible though probably doomed desire to escape. "Ive been passed around," she complains, like a dirty postcard among people in the city. She says it twice, which is once more than the image will take. As so often happens in Williams, the lyricism walks a fine line between the hypnotic and the absurd.

This Property is Condemned, a more substantial and better-known piece, presents a boy with a kite and a girl with a doll. Hes playing hookey from school, down by a deserted stretch of railroad track. She's playing hookey from life, teetering along the track in a tattered parody of elegance, saying things like "I'm glad I didnt wear my silk stockings," and Wheres my diamonds? The boy sagely doubts her possession of either.

She is spinning yarns about her family; about her sister, who seems to have been a popular attraction locally, and about her own very different existence. "I don't have time for inexperienced people . . . I'm going out with popular railroad men."

The boys buddies have told him different, but -- like the heroines of The Glass Menagerie and A Streetcar Named Desire -- she fights fiercely to maintain her shell. The doomed property of the title is her grand old family home (which may or may not have ever existed), or her own life, or the whole decaying edifice of genteel Southern society.

In both plays its the female who does most of the talking (like the rain, if that means persistently) and the male who listens -- or is, at least, sceptically there. In Martin Hunter's modestly atmospheric productions, Peter van Gestel fills his double subordinate role admirably. Marjorie Chan gets the lioness' share of the taut, lazy rhythms and seductively quotable lines, and does very well by the angry aimlessness of her first character; she doesn't find enough variety in the more obvious vulnerability of the second. But she gets the drawl right, thereby setting up the mood of gentle desperation on which these plays depend.

- Runs until Friday at 12:12 and 1:11 daily. Box office, (416) 368-8031.

1999-04-29-if-only-sexual-relations-were:
DEFENDING THE CAVEMAN

Elgin Theatre, Toronto

The first thing we hear is a disembodied female voice saying men are assholes. Then there's a brief video segment during which the camera pans in on a series of books whose titles suggest a gulf between the sexes that is a) unbridgeable and b) entirely mens fault. Knowing that we are here for a one-man show called Defending the Caveman, we brace ourselves for a biliously partisan male rebuttal. And on comes Rob Becker, author and performer, sporting an appropriately anthropoidal lope.

Becker is an American stand-up comic, but this show comes to us publicized as "the longest running solo play in Broadway history." Its claims to dramatic independence are reinforced by its having opened in London with another actor. I dont know what that performer made of it, but in its creator's hands it remains a comedy routine with elephantiasis.

The opening turns out to be a false trail. Becker is not taking on radical feminism and he is not peddling misogyny; the evening might be more fun if he was. He is out to build bridges. Despite his title, he does not advocate clubbing anyone. His caveman is an amiable fellow who, he says, has appeared to him in a vision to vouchsafe a piece of ancient wisdom: Men are hunters; women are gatherers. The business of the vision is, I think, the author's gesture toward a unifying dramatic structure, but it merely clutters the place up.

Clutching this philosophy, Becker surveys relations between the sexes and finds that everything slots in. Women like to shop; men dont. Women like to exchange confidences at great length; men prefer to commune in silence while fishing or watching TV. Men have, shall we say, a more narrowly concentrated attitude toward sexual pleasure than women. None of these insights, except perhaps the last, is going to be news to anyone who remembers the old-style comic monologues of, say, Alan King. Indeed, much of it, as far as it goes, is confirmable from real life.

Occasionally, Becker strikes some imaginative sparks from these age-old conceptual glitches. (She, bright-eyed: "Wouldnt that look good in our bedroom?" He, deeply perplexed: But it doesn't belong to us. No, I guess that doesn't look too funny. You had to be there.) All the same, even on shopping, which is an easy one, he manages nothing as authoritative, or as funny, as Germaine Greers summation in The Whole Woman: "Most exchanges between men and women shopping together are more or less bad-tempered."

But its a limited vision, and grossly unfair to men, who in reality are a more interestingly varied bunch of selfish bastards than this show lets on. There are heterosexual males -- I wouldn't be surprised if the numbers stretched into double figures -- who are bored by sports, not glued to the television, and enjoy the company even of women with whom they don't intend to get in bed. We arent all characters out of Home Improvement. Indeed, this show seems to be presenting the world view of Tim Allen through the stand-up techniques of Jerry Seinfeld.

Part of the appeal of Seinfeld, whom I think a superb comedian, is that he varies his subject matter and filters his aghast urbanity through silken virtuoso timing. He takes you by surprise.

Becker ploughs the same field for an hour-and-three-quarters -- the penalty, I suppose, of doing "a play" rather than an act -- and attacks all of it bullheaded. I dont mean he's aggressive -- though his miking makes him sound metallically inhuman -- merely that he's technically limited.

He ends by asking each of the sexes to enter the others imaginative space from time to time. That is an admirable prescription, and I dont think anyone would quarrel with it. I'm all for sweetness and light; I just don't want it running amok in our theatres and corrupting the middle-aged. I laughed about half a dozen times, never very loud. As grounds for defending Defending the Caveman, that is not enough.

- Runs until May 9. Box office: (416) 872-5555.

Black & White Photo: Joan Marcus / Writer and performer Rob Becker: like a one-trick Jerry Seinfeld, minus the virtuoso timing. ;

IN 1960 a song called Do You Mind? - as in "If I say I love you, do you mind?" - reached number one in the British pop charts. Lionel Bart wrote it, Anthony Newley sang it and it had a cheeky cockney twang, overlaid with imitation American. Some time later, Newley, who had turned to songwriting himself, said what a brilliant idea it had been of Bart's to base a song on such a sharp conversational phrase and how he wished he'd thought of it himself.

I hadn't thought about that song in years, but the deaths of Bart and Newley have got me humming it again. It may have been the only time their paths crossed professionally, but it wasn't all they had in common.

Both, for a start, owed a considerable debt to the same literary classic. Newley first came to notice, in 1948, playing the Artful Dodger in David Lean's film of Oliver Twist and his performance remains indelible: an urchin wise beyond his years, whose insolence had something mournful about it. Bart, of course, entered the big time in 1960 as author and composer of Oliver!, the most successful British musical of its era.

Now what era was that exactly? It's a lost period of popular English theatre, between the end of Noel Coward and the beginning of Andrew Lloyd Webber. It began with a roguish little bang in 1954, and had petered out by 1970. Bart and Newley were among its leading practitioners, but they took some time to emerge.

For the decade after the war the musical had been an American preserve. It was the period of Oklahoma!, Annie Get Your Gun, Carousel, Kiss Me Kate, South Pacific, Guys and Dolls, The King and I, and so on. Home-grown musicals were produced, but few were successful. The big shows (I'm speaking of scale, not quality) were either blown-up seaside entertainments, or imitation Broadway.

This changed with that curious masterpiece The Boy Friend, written by a young man called Sandy Wilson. I say curious because masterpieces are supposed to be original and Wilson's was an imitation - of the fluffy musical comedies, both British and American, of the Twenties. But the pastiche was so loving and skilful and sure of itself that it became its own creation. Promoted to the West End in 1954, after a club try-out in 1953, it ran for ever. It is, like Oliver!, always being done somewhere.

In its time it suggested that British musicals might best assert themselves against the Americans by staying small, maybe even quaint. (Note that this was also the time of the Ealing film comedies.) The idea was reinforced when Julian Slade's Salad Days came to London.

Unlike The Boy Friend it was set in what might just, in 1954, have been the present: a world of debs and perpetual students and harmlessly mad scientists and everybody transported by the sound of a magic piano: "Oh look at me, oh look at me, I'm dancing!" Clearly the real world could not be kept at bay for ever, and the small musical, with roots in the old intimate revue, seemed to call out for satire.

Wilson realised this and followed up The Boy Friend with The Buccaneer, which was rather like a parable on the state of the musical, in terms of children's comics; it set the wholesome English model against the brash American horror strips.

I have a fondness for it since it was the first musical I ever saw. I persuaded my parents to take me on the understanding that it would be, in the words of one its song titles, "good clean fun". It was. However, for the angry young Fifties it was altogether too middle-class. The musical needed a proletarian voice. Some years on, in the wake of Albert Finney and the Beatles, this might have been North Country, but the Fifties was a London decade. Musically, the period belonged to jazz and to Tommy Steele, our first rock 'n' roller.

The breakthrough musical was actually a satire on Steele's rise to fame, entitled Expresso Bongo. Set in the capital's musical and social underworld, it established the convention that a socially significant musical had to involve tarts and small-time crooks, and it inaugurated what I call the Soho musical.

Much of this was like Salad Days in reverse: "Oh look at me, I'm sophisticated!" There was The Crooked Mile and Irma la Douce. The latter, a French Soho musical, was put into English by Julian More, David Heneker and Monty Norman, three writers who had collaborated on Bongo and who combined and separated throughout this period.

Norman wrote music and lyrics for Make Me an Offer, which was about squabbling antique dealers in the Portobello Road and was the best show of the entire period. Heneker, the oldest and most persistent of the trio, had hits a little later on with Half a Sixpence (a cheery adaptation of H G Wells's Kipps) and the monstrous Charlie Girl.

These were both wholesome vehicles for cockney former pop stars (Tommy Steele, Joe Brown) and they served notice on the Soho school. Before doing so, however, it had thrown up Fings Ain't Wot They Used T'Be, the seamiest of them all, with a debut score by Lionel Bart.

Bart was a theatrical natural who had come up through pop (he wrote all Steele's hits) and had a wonderful ear. He had already written lyrics only for Lock Up Your Daughters, which, based on a play by Henry Fielding, was an 18th-century Soho musical, a bit of slap and a lot of tickle. Political correctness makes a revival unlikely. The source play is called Rape Upon Rape. Actually it's the word "rape", not the act itself, that the play and musical make fun of, but I wouldn't envy anybody who tried to make that case in detail.

What is remarkable is that Bart, who was probably not brought up on Restoration comedy, caught the style exactly. He was a lot less fastidious a year later when he set about musicalising Dickens, but the music-hall panache and narrative energy of Oliver! carried it, and continue to carry it. It was the apotheosis of the Soho musical (all the crooks and whores you could desire) and also its death knell. Social significance had given way, inexorably, to family entertainment.

Anthony Newley followed Bart into the arena in 1961 and pursued an opposite course. With his collaborator Leslie Bricusse (dyed-in-the-wool showbiz and still active) he took theatrical cliches - principally the broken-hearted clown - and tried to wring a moral out of them. As a performer, Newley had preserved a dark anarchic streak. He had done some adventurous if whimsical TV work and he had made some funny records. He had started out satirising pop singers and had briefly turned into the real thing.

So when he did his first musical, Stop the World - I Want to Get Off, we all wished him well, even though the show's idea of satire was to put stereotypes on stage and get angry about them. Its idea of emotion was to shed buckets of tears over those same stereotypes. They got away with it, at least commercially, at least once. The follow-up - The Roar of the Greasepaint, the Smell of the Crowd - was a statically self-important allegory that took its imagery wholesale from Waiting for Godot and never made it to London, though it did run on Broadway.

Both these shows, though, had several songs that were hits at the time and some of which - Once in a Lifetime, Who Can I Turn To? - are familiar even now. And this was significant. In the Fifties and early Sixties, before the rock takeover, you could always turn on the radio and hear American theatre songs. You never heard any English ones. Bart began to change this: As Long as He Needs Me, the big one from Oliver! (and a rotten song, but never mind) had a Shirley Bassey record that was number one for weeks. American heavyweights, notably Sammy Davis Jr, adopted Newley and Bricusse.

Both Bart and Newley went into steep personal declines, and neither had a second success to rival their first. Bart's career post-Oliver! was outright disastrous. But they had moved the British musical into the commercial mainstream, and paved the way for the mid-Atlantic musical, as personified by Lloyd Webber. They represented both the triumph of an era and its decadence. Those were interesting times, and bits of them still linger.
1999-05-05-we-are-so-beautiful:
HELLO . . . HELLO

Factory Theatre Studio Cafe, Toronto

At the mid-point of Hello . . . Hello, a husband comes home from work to find his wife pregnant and cradling a dead rabbit. There seems to be no causal relation between these two circumstances, but everyone -- meaning he, she, and two choral figures who play everybody else -- behaves as if there is. They break out into a celebratory song -- "there's a new life flowing when a rabbit dies" - - designed to make us tap our feet and then feel thoroughly ashamed of ourselves. The show manufactures a coincidence and tries to make emotional and, for want of a better word, intellectual capital out of it. This is known as taking a bad idea and running with it.

It all takes place in a brave new ecologically impaired world where the seven seas have been reduced to six, the seafood dishes served in restaurants are dripping with mercury, and cod has been off the menu for 27 years. Artists, though dimly remembered, have disappeared, and so apparently have the poor and the ugly. All who remain are beautiful and affluent -- or aspire to be -- and there is a thriving service industry catering to their dreams, operating out of breathtakingly translucent Bay Street skyscrapers. These are described, at great length, but not seen; the actual set is a barely functional array of steps and platforms.

Our heroine, Cassandra, works in a boutique called The Abyss, which presumably is a yawning Gap. She encounters Ben, our hero, in a graveyard where each has buried a former partner. Cassandra likes to hang out there; it suits her temperament. She is named, of course, for the Greek prophetess of doom. Ben's name is less resonant, but it may signify benevolence; he certainly means well, toward her and the world at large. He works high up in one of those agencies as head of creative; the show's very best moment comes when he tells Cassandra this and she looks quizzical, as if expecting more. Dear old-fashioned thing, she thinks creative is still an adjective.

Anyway, they get married and Ben buys her everything she could wish, including -- a real luxury item, this -- a hospital bed in which to give birth. The baby turns out to be beautiful but extremely undersized. It stays that way; there is, we are told, a lot of it going about. And that's about it for plot. The show's real concern is to be a lyrical fantasia of the shimmering disaster that is tomorrow.

For approximately the 75th time this year, I am left wondering why a production (Chris Earle's, in this case) should go to so much trouble to persuade me of things that I already believe. To be sure, Hello . . . Hello is not your standard hectoring sermon. It is a small musical that wants to be simultaneously bright-eyed and cloven- hoofed. It alternates between coyness and the ironic exploitation of coyness, and it's very hard to tell the two apart, or even summon the energy to try. Narrative speeches, delivered in sickly sweet tones, hint archly at what we should be feeling and then back off with a sinister giggle.

Karen Hines, the author, also plays Cassandra, and her performance epitomizes the play. She devotes considerable skill, and a touch of the uncanny, to presenting someone very irritating, someone who specializes in delivering bad news with a cute simper. "There is a devouring blackness that has a hold on my imagination," she says, about 90 minutes after we've noticed it for ourselves. Like her classical namesake, she is right about everything, and therefore intolerable to have around.

The other actors -- David Jansen as Ben, Steven Morel and Teresa Pavlinek as the etceteras -- play with energy and good intentions, though Morel and Pavlinek are affected -- by text, direction, or both -- with advanced smirkiness. The author's lyrics are sometimes neat, and the music (by her and Greg Morrison) harmlessly tuneful. Occasionally, the intended chastening vision comes through, bringing with it hints that the piece might have been awfully interesting. Most of the time, though, it's just interestingly awful.

- Runs until May 23. Box office: (416) 504-9971.
