1999-05-07-a-tragic-life-played-tragical:
THAT DOROTHY PARKER

Canadian Stage Theatre Upstairs, Toronto

Dorothy Parker wrote fewer funny poems and less funny prose than is generally believed, and her more earnest ventures in both forms can be dreadfully soggy. Her one-liners have become so familiar as to seem mechanical. But she maintains her hold on our imagination: as the most durable of the self-anointed New Yorker wits of the '20s and '30s, as the only woman among them, and as someone who suffered with style and made sure everybody knew about it.

Resume -- her eight-line masterpiece cataloguing the disadvantages of all available methods of suicide and concluding "you might as well live" -- ranks with Philip Larkin's "they fuck you up, your mum and dad." They may not be the greatest poems of the 20th century but they are surely the most unanswerable.

In her one-woman show about the lady, an evening that swings metronomically between mediocrity and atrocity, Carol Lempert rushes breathlessly through Parker's canon against self-slaughter while struggling into a pair of shoes. Naturally, the points get blunted. Some of the more lascivious Parkerisms -- "one drink more and I'll be under the host" or "if all the girls in Vassar were laid end to end, I shouldn't be in the least surprised" -- she delivers in a tone of self-conscious schoolgirl naughtiness, with matching smirk. She doesn't seem to have an ear, a failing bad enough if you're delivering formal poetry and absolutely fatal to light verse.

The neat little ode that ends "I'm due to fall in love again" is massacred by having the emphasis placed on "again," which is filler, instead of "in love," which is what it's about. She also speaks, in prose this time, of "the elevated eyebrow-school of journalism" instead of "the elevated eyebrow school of journalism." If you can't hear the difference I'm sorry for you, but there's nothng I can do.

Anyway, you're not up on stage reciting the stuff.

In addition, the show -- directed, to spread the blame around a bit, by Mark Wilson -- has structural problems. Its jumps in time and space are fidgety. It is supposedly anchored in Parker's old haunt, the Algonquin Hotel, on the day in the Second World War in which she learns of the death of critic and broadcaster Alexander Woollcott, her long-time friend and sparring-partner.

Their relationship is the pivot of the evening; she keeps reminiscing about it. I may be biased, since I once tried to get through a whole book of Woollcott's appallingly arch prose, but he seems to have been as intolerable a man as he was a writer, snobbish and witlessly rude. The attention he gets here, considering the show is meant to be about someone else, is wildly disproportionate.

Valiantly but awkwardly, Dorothy tries to fill us in on the other regulars at the Algonquin's famous Round Table. "Edna" she name- drops, then switches into the expositional-interrogative.

"Edna?" she repeats, her inflection insistently rising, "Edna Ferber? The author of Show Boat?" A few minutes later she's at it again, with "Mr. Benchley? Robert Charles Benchley?" Benchley -- a nicer man than Woollcott and a funnier, though at this distance almost equally perishable -- is invoked here as good uncle to Woollcott's bad, or second banana to his preening ego. He never comes to life, though. None of them do.

And, though I revere the New Yorker and love the Algonquin, I suspect that their joint legend does not stand up to close inspection. They were not, most of those guys at their wisecracking alcoholic lunches, all that good.

Parker herself seems to have suspected it. Her increasing disaffection is one of the more interesting things about her, and one of the better things about this show.

We hear about her championing of the framed anarchists Sacco and Vanzetti, of her journey to the front in the Spanish Civil War. There is a scene of her phoning her young husband, stationed abroad and obviously tiring of her, that begins touchingly but that the actress cannot sustain.

Missing, in whole or part, are Parker's two finest prose arias: one in which she waits distractedly for a lover's phone-call, raising brittle self-pity to something like art, and The Waltz, a hilarious stream-of-consciousness while dancing with the partner from hell.

They might be difficult to stage, especially the second, but not, I think, impossible. Done well, they might centre the evening. It needs it.

I learned one thing that seems all too appropriate to pass on: Harold Ross, editor of the New Yorker, arrived late at lunch, his excuse being that he had spent the morning writing obituaries. Woollcott rejoined that he, Parker, and Benchley were all theatre critics and had been doing exactly the same. It hurts me to say it, but I couldn't have put it better myself.

- That Dorothy Parker runs until May 22. Box office: (416)-368- 3110.
1999-05-08-all-this-aggression-is-a-dest:
BETTER LIVING

George F. Walker's Better Living is about a family, predominantly female, that has cast out a tyrannical and abusive father. Some years later he returns and, before you know it, he has taken over their lives again and even got them liking it, at least some of them, some of the time.

It could be an allegory for a society that, after living under a self-righteous and authoritarian regime, turns right around and elects it again. Indeed -- since this is not a new play but a revival of one first seen in 1986 -- you might go further and credit the author with prophetic gifts.

Or maybe he just knows the way the world goes.

The particular microcosm he holds up for us is a cluttered, chaotic, peeled-wallpaper house in what is obviously one of the less fashionable sections of Toronto.

Here lives Nora, with whichever of her three daughters happens to be passing through at the time. There is Elizabeth, who is now a lawyer but once supported the family through her earnings as a prostitute. There is Mary Ann, married and a mess, who has surrendered her own child to the custody of her husband. There is Gail, the youngest, enthusiastically making out with a blockhead boyfriend, with the firm approval of her mother who fancies having as many grandchildren as possible.

At the start of the play, Gail and her partner are surprised by Uncle Jack, a priest who seems to have lost his vocation but kept his job. Gail acknowledges apologetically, or as close to apologetically as anybody gets in this play, that Jack must disapprove "of sex outside the church." (It takes Jack a bemused moment to realize that this is Gail's idea of a metaphor.)

The memory of Tom, her ex-policeman husband, has so traumatized Nora that when he reappears she refuses to recognize him. She calls him Tim. (She does, after he has moved back in and made himself at home, acknowledge a resemblance.)

One may sympathize with Tom, having his identity denied, but that doesn't last. He wants the family to repair and restore the house -- something they have signally failed at hitherto -- but he also wants to turn it into a fortress against the incursions of people less fortunate than they are: a startling concept, but they agree that such people may exist. Nora is newly energized, and sad Mary Ann finds that licking envelopes gives her a new purpose in life.

Tom's dreams of a society built on selfishness have to be violently imposed; and here, it turns out, history is repeating itself. His earlier behaviour had been so horrifying that Nora and Jack had, on several occasions, tried to kill him. They had of course failed; which, as they nonchalantly remark, is not like them at all.

There are echoes of the American Sam Shepard (a Gothic skeleton in every closet), and the British Joe Orton (mayhem taken comically for granted), but there is no question that Walker has created his own dramatic world. It is characterized by a high level of violence, physical and verbal, but it is cartoon violence in which nobody seems to get hurt. That may not be the intention; even if Walker is not exactly in the compassion business, I think he wants us to feel for his characters. But though they have a strong collective impact, and though they wake some disturbing echoes of the cruel world outside, they have no dramatic life as individuals.

That at least is the impression in this slapdash production by the author himself. It is very fast and very loud. Speed is certainly preferable to sloth, but it has no intrinsic theatrical merit unless it is allied to precision. Here, everyone gabbles, so the play is garbled. It's worse because -- this being a play about a family -- everybody also shouts. (Walker isn't in the subtlety business either.) Information gets obscured, and feelings drowned.

For the actors, all this aggression serves as a crutch, but a destructive one. The first night was two-thirds over before Nancy Beatty had established any kind of hold on Nora.

I felt grateful when Fiona Highet's Elizabeth was quiet and lucid, or when Thea Gill's Mary Ann was quiet and distraught -- and let down when they joined everybody else on the rampage. The men are less pressured. David Fox as Tom, the really crazy one, is ironically required to stay in control, and he does so with an imperturbable presence surprisingly similar to that of the benign idiot savant he played in The Drawer Boy. Michael Healey, the author of that play, appears in this one as the mentally-defrocked Jack. He is not, on this showing, as interesting an actor as he is a writer, but he is the nearest thing around to a calming presence, and benefits from being -- literally and metaphorically -- the last person in the cast to yell.

Either he has the funniest lines, or he is the only one given the breathing space to time them.

Runs until June 6 at Factory Theatre. (416)-504-9971

1999-05-15-mr-newton-s-profession-as-art:
Profile of Christopher Newton.

Christopher Newton has now been director of the Shaw Festival at Niagara-on-the-Lake for 20 years, which is a long time to stay in any artistic job. Ive stuck with it," he says, steering clear of any high-sounding manifesto, "because I like actors. He expands on that somewhat: I like to see good things, and its wonderful when you can put together good actors, good directors, and good designers."

Good plays help, too. The Shaw Festival began in 1962 and it has a unique mandate -- though mandate may not be the right word, since no outside authority has ever instructed the festival to do anything. The festival has more of a self-limiting program, devised as a harmonious expansion of its original purpose, which was, of course, to produce the plays of George Bernard Shaw. Since 1965, these have been augmented with works by other playwrights who wrote during Shaw's lifetime. Shaw himself preached the virtues of longevity and lived up to his own prescription on a grand scale -- his lifespan stretched from 1856 to 1950 -- so that gives the festival practically a century of more-or-less modern drama to play with.

In conversation, and in his own productions, Newton is urbane, intelligent, genially earnest. He has lived in North America for 40 years but he still sounds very English, with an accent and delivery that's understated, gentlemanly, like a BBC announcer off duty. (I always imagine him wearing a blazer.) His opinions flow freely and firmly -- and they draw on a wide frame of reference: musical, literary, and historical, as well as theatrical -- but he never seems to be imposing them. One imagines that, in rehearsal or in a boardroom, he makes an excellent chairman; the kind of democrat who unobtrusively gets his own way. He has a broad, open face, and his silver hair doesnt make him look in the least old. In fact, he seems boyish.

Although he is well-suited to Shaws period, the peculiar qualities of the plays -- what you might roughly call the drawing- room tradition -- inhibit experiment to some extent. They don't offer the scope of Shakespeare, either physically or spiritually. "You can move a Shaw play a couple of degrees right or left, and that's all. Its difficult to change even the time its set in -- a staple device for making a Shakespearean play seem fresh, or at least different. On the other hand, the small changes that you can make in a Shaw play may count for a lot; by turning those few degrees, you may bring a whole new angle into the light.

Newton seems to have come to his long posting in Niagara through a series of happy accidents, the kind that, taken together, point toward the inevitable. He grew up in England in the 1940s and '50s vaguely interested in the theatre, playing with puppets, acting in school plays and so on. "I never thought I could make a career in it," he says. I was at Leeds University, and I wanted to go to the States. This was the late '50s and America was the land of dreams. I suffered from the British thing of wanting to get out of Britain -- that probably accounts for the Empire.

He took an MA in Indiana, "got bored with it, wrote round the universities, got an offer from Bucknell University -- tiny place in Pennsylvania -- to take over their theatre department, so I did it, keeping just a little ahead of the students in the textbook."

He came to Canada by accident. I read a review in Time magazine of A Midsummer Nights Dream, directed by Michael Langham, and thought that this was something I wanted to be part of. I went to Stratford, and auditioned, and Michael turned me down on the spot. He said, `We dont need any more Americans.' So I found myself in Toronto with $60 in my pocket. And the day before I turned up, the Canadian Players, who were about to tour Julius Caesar, had lost their Cassius.

So Newton made his professional debut ("I'm a lucky person") in one of the juicier Shakespearean roles, and came to see Canada by bus.

He remained an actor for several years. He did get to perform at the Stratford Festival (Richard Monette, now his Stratford counterpart, was a contemporary) and he made a precocious appearance at the Shaw in its third season. He moved into directing when a fateful, if ambiguously phrased, telegram arrived, inviting him to act with Theatre Calgary ("We cant get Tom Kneebone. Will you do it?"). He stayed on, becoming artistic director and turning what had previously been a semi-professional company, fully professional.

He was there for three years, and then ran Vancouver Playhouse for a further six. Success there led to an exploratory visit from a couple of the Shaws governors, and the eventual invitation to take over there. I've always suspected that the Canada Council told them to get me, he says. "I thought I'd stay here for three years, but then I dug my heels in."

Id heard that Newton had arrived at the Shaw Festival carrying one serious handicap: He didnt like Shaw. He confirmed that this had indeed been the case. I'd been in some questionable productions, and the ones I'd seen hadnt inspired me. I took the job because I liked Shaws contemporaries.

In his first season, however, he directed Misalliance, one of GBS's most notoriously loquacious plays, "and I realized I had been crazy. It was a revelation. The people were more interesting than I'd ever realized." The production seems to have been modestly experimental, and free of some of the traditional Shavian clutter. The set that Cameron [Porteous, the Shaws principal designer] had done was very airy. We got very bad reviews.

A few years later, he directed a second production of Misalliance, and this time the reviews were considerably better. At least one of them was; I know, because I wrote it. I was especially impressed by the productions command of imagery. The design this time was not at all airy, rather the reverse. The play is set in a conservatory, which the production rendered as a miniature jungle. "I've talked," Newton says, about there being a `surrealist' edge to Shaw, but really its just a theatrical quality.

Theatre," he continues, "is about putting a strong visual image together with honest talk. It sounds like common sense but there arent many directors who consistently bring off both halves of the equation. Newton has managed it both in and outside the Shavian canon. His productions of Noel Coward's Cavalcade and of the Victorian melodrama The Silver King were finely organized spectacles that also told lucid stories.

Coward's plays have been among the mainstays of the festival repertoire, one that often seems to concentrate on the fringes of its chosen century. Newton says hes interested in obscure corners in everything; as a tourist, Ill go to Romania rather than Italy." As an impresario, he has done Vitold Gombrowicz and Stanislaw Witkiewicz, Polish playwrights whose names are more often found in scholarly histories than on mainstream theatre programs. That's one side of the picture. The other is the frankly popular choices -- Agatha Christie thrillers, miniaturized American musicals -- that the festival generally mounts with as much care as it affords to its secular patron saint. What seems to go missing is the centre: Henrik Ibsen, Anton Chekhov, Johan August Strindberg, Bertolt Brecht, and Luigi Pirandello all wrote their greatest plays during Shaw's lifetime, but they havent been much in evidence at Niagara.

Much of this goes down, as it should be, to Newtons own taste: "You start with what you like and hope people will share your enthusiasm. I've never understood Irish theatre, so we haven't done much of it. Im not a great Ibsen fan. Stratford seemed at one time to have a stranglehold on [Oscar] Wilde and Chekhov, but now we have started doing them. We have done the more obscure Cowards and J. B. Priestleys, as well as the obvious ones. And one of our major achievements is our Barker series. This refers to Harley Granville- Barker, the Edwardian actor, producer, dramatist, and theatrical prophet, whose plays Newton and his colleagues have been systematically working their way through, with results ranging from strenuously interesting to absolutely riveting. They are plays of ideas, with thick textures and elusive surfaces, whose peculiar demanding quality Newton summarizes by saying that they absolutely cannot be done by amateurs." Two of them (The Marrying of Ann Leete and The Secret Life) have brought him on to the festival stages as an actor: an indulgence, if thats the word, that he permits himself once every two years.

When Newton took over at Niagara, the theatre, he says himself, was "on a down; and his achievement, over two turbulent decades, has been to establish and maintain an identity. Much of this stems from the existence of a regular company. It's quite practical. Actors here can earn a reasonable salary, and be proud of what they do. Film and TV aren't available to most Canadian actors so the stage is the centre of our work-face. We have an experienced ensemble; the younger actors get to watch people who can do it, and they take it in by osmosis. The best kind of company is where, out of 70 actors, you have 50 who were there the previous year, 10 returning after an absence, and 10 completely new." There are dangers ("you can become fond of people and give them parts theyre not capable of doing) but the advantages are huge and, in the fragmented entertainment business of North America, nearly unique. The secret of being a good artistic director is surrounding yourself with good people."

This year, Newton himself directs two plays: Rebecca, this seasons upmarket thriller; and one of those unfamiliar Cowards, Easy Virtue. He plans to stay on as director until 2002, and he will have a slightly altered mandate to hand on to his successor: The festival will now be allowed to include plays written since Shaw's death but set during his lifetime. (Tom Stoppard's Travesties and The Invention of Love immediately occurred to me, on grounds of style as well as substance. They occurred to Newton, too, but there are no immediate plans to do them.) Will this perhaps allow the Shaw Festival to be more cutting edge? I asked him this, wincing at the phrase."I'm in my 60s now, came the reply. Not very cutting edge. I tend toward the old codger myself."

1999-05-18-there-s-no-way-the-performers:
Anything Goes

Jane Mallett Theatre, Toronto

First-act curtain of a 1934 musical: The captain of an Atlantic liner arrests a young insurance broker under the impression that he is a gangster, Public Enemy Number One no less. He is not, however, about to put the lad in irons. He intends to honour him as the celebrity passenger the cruise so badly needs.

Later, when he discovers that his star criminal is a mere stowaway, he will be far less indulgent. Cue for Reno Sweeney, nightclub evangelist (you heard), to let loose with a blithely sardonic musical commentary on modern manners that also happens to be the shows title number Anything Goes.

A famous song out of context, it is even more pungently effective within it: exactly the right statement at the right moment, relevant to its own time and to ours. It suggests that Cole Porter, who wrote the music and lyrics, had a more specific dramatic sense than is generally acknowledged. The opposite impression has been fostered by Porter himself, who liked to react with debonair unconcern when a number was axed, and by his executors who permit revivalists to transfer songs wholesale from one score to another.

A case in point is the version of Anything Goes that was successfully mounted in New York some 10 years ago and was subsequently seen on tour in Toronto. It has now been revived by Reprise as one of their "Great Musicals in Concert. It has a streamlined and vastly rewritten book (by John Weidman and Timothy Crouse, son of one of the original authors) which for commercial purposes may well be -- no, definitely is -- superior to the 1934 text.

But Reprises purposes are not commercial, or shouldn't be. Its actors perform, with the scripts in their hands, for four nights only. It is playing to an audience that is pre-sold on the opportunity of seeing Cole Porter's Anything Goes, in any form, and might welcome the chance of experiencing the original. It couldnt hurt them.

What we get is the reduction of a reduction. The Broadway revival featured a full band, stylish Art Deco sets, a lot of zippy dancing, and crack comic timing. The Reprise production, though tidily drilled by its director Anne Wootten, can afford none of these except the last, which it only fitfully exhibits.

Striving for wit, it generally settles for roguishness. A line of dialogue prompts the pianist to strike up Night and Day, at which the actors yell wrong show." They then proceed to sing Friendship, which is also from the wrong show, though I found myself wondering if anyone at Reprise knew this. It has been interpolated from another Porter musical of the 30s, as have several other songs, and lacking either context or staging none of them make sense, not even the nonsensical sense this kind of show is meant to make.

Goodbye, Little Dream, Goodbye -- a little-known but totally beautiful lament -- means nothing when the character hasn't earned the right to sing it. The songs from the original -- they include I Get a Kick Out of You, You're the Top, and Blow, Gabriel, Blow -- all work handily. As those titles suggest, this is a great score. If they want to do the Cole Porter Songbook instead, then why bother with a script?

There are some good voices around, most notably those of Barbara Barsky as Reno and Brian Hill who has some lovely high notes as the impromptu convict (or, as you might say, neo-con). But neither of them exactly sets the stage alight; she shies away from her characters forthright sexuality (the role was written for the young Ethel Merman) and he tends to disappear even when present. By miles, the best performance comes from Scott Walker as a silly-ass Englishman; the role is a brazen caricature but he finds its centre and that allows him to be as funny and tuneful and even touching as he likes.

Lost Musicals -- the London enterprise from which all these revival groups derive -- won its reputation by reviving shows from all periods in scrupulously authentic versions; they have had particular success with 30s Porter. Reprise's next season derives entirely from the '50s and '60s. They have announced Guys and Dolls, the best of all musicals but hardly in need of a concert performance; I Do, I Do, a syrup-bath; and Promises Promises, the one excusable choice, a renowned but little-seen show with a good book and a terrific score.

Reprise's policy ought to be re-thunk. They should be offering us more than just dinner-theatre with unlearned lines.
1999-05-20-surprisingly-superb-soliloqui:
STAY

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, Toronto

First produced in 1990, David Demchuk's Stay is the third notable Canadian play to be revived in Toronto this year, following Michel Tremblays Les Belles Soeurs and George Walkers Better Living. It is the least celebrated of the three, and the most compelling.

It is also the starkest. It consists of three monologues, divided among two characters. The "stay" of the title is a stay of execution. Joey, who begins and finishes the evening, is a convicted child-killer who has spent years on death row, waiting his turn. Now, however, his lawyer has mounted a successful appeal. Joey is happy for the lawyer's sake rather than his own. He wants to die: not necessarily to atone, just to die. To give up.

The speech that tells us all this is Joey's letter to Roberta, a close friend of his childhood who has never once visited him during his imprisonment. We find her in a graveyard, delivering a long, ruminative soliloquy, the filling in this theatrical sandwich. She, too, is living with (if not actually under) a sentence of death; her husband is in hospital with liver cancer. It also transpires that she and Joey carry the joint burden of an earlier killing.

Joey and Roberta will have one more meeting whose details -- the play being in part a thriller, and an effective one -- it would be unfair to reveal. We learn something about it from Roberta, and more, thanks to some chronological scrambling, from Joey, to whom we return for some final, devastatingly ironic words. Irony these days usually means an inflated kind of sarcasm, but this is the real thing: simple words that carry a dramatic weight beyond the knowledge of the speaker.

I expect to be bored by monologues, unless theyre funny. Those in Stay are not funny (though they have their wry moments), but they held me almost without a lapse. Joey, a child-killer who was also once a child killer, may take us further inside a murderers head than any dramatic character since Macbeth. (I'm not making absurd claims, just offering a historical observation. There really isn't much competition: Woyzeck, perhaps.)

What we discover there is emptiness: hardly regret, but acceptance, a willingness to let go of life, his own or anyone elses. He is interested in comic books, but not much else; he wishes his mother, his lawyer, and his former girlfriend well, but no more than that; he doesnt like being targeted by the other prisoners, but he hardly protests. It may not be true of all killers, but Demchuk convinces us that it's true of this one. Mark Harapiak plays him with an appropriate deathly calm, amiable but passionless.

Caroline Gillis, though technically quite accomplished, is less convincing as Roberta, but she has a harder job. Joey, in writing to her, can direct his speeches at someone; she is talking into a void. He has a present to act; she has only a past to remember. Since she is more intelligent, her consciousness ranges further, and is harder to anchor.

The playwright's attempt to centre her thoughts around a consuming interest in the stars struck me as a contrivance, and makes both writing and performance sound literary (though her observation that Cancer, the crab, is absent from the heavens tonight is a bold stroke, bitterness masquerading as acceptance). As the survivor, she should be the more frightening of the two, but this never registers.

The speeches are interspersed with some bits of video footage that looked, from where I sat, impenetrably blurry. Anne Driscolls direction is otherwise fine; she and the designer, Steve Lucas, manage, in a confined space, to nail the play with a couple of visual images. Both are doors. One is that of Joeys cell. The other is the screen door of Roberta's house, confronting us at the very end like the implacable entrance of a Greek tragedy.

- Runs until June 6. Box office: (416) 504-7529.

Black & White Photo: Caroline Gillis, as Roberta, has the more demanding role in the two-character play Stay. ;
1999-05-27-oh-what-a-lovely-dream:
HEARTBREAK HOUSE

The Shaw Festival

Bernard Shaw's Heartbreak House begins with a young woman waking up. It is the midpoint of the First World War, and Ellie Dunn is visiting the strange, ship-like house of the octogenarian Captain Shotover, situated -- appropriately enough -- on the English seacoast. Waiting for someone to notice her, she has fallen asleep over a book.

Tadeusz Bradeckis production, which gets this years Shaw Festival off to an uncommonly beautiful start, is not the first to treat Ellie's abrupt awakening as if it were a descent into a deeper level of slumber; in effect, to present the whole play as her dream. But it goes further than any other that I have seen. Bradecki frames the action by showing us Ellie approaching the house at the beginning and departing it at the end.

There seem, as well, to be dreams within dreams. One character is sent into a hypnotic trance, and the experience sends him into jerky, marionettish staggers. Another spends the entire last act in his pyjamas. The captain himself, who combines the roles of absent- minded inventor and angry sage, slips constantly between levels of consciousness. All this is played to the hilt.

Intellectually, this cuts very little ice; it is hard to interpret the dreams of people whom you have never known to be awake. Atmospherically, it is very effective, culminating in a Zeppelin raid that the characters ecstatically welcome (up to now, none of them has even mentioned the war) and for which the sky turns apocalyptically red while thunderous strains of Mahler fill the air.

Peter Hartwell's set is less obviously ship-shape than most; it has a somewhat Japanese air, with screen-like walls and a floor marked out in alternating squares of black and white. It is the kind of geometrically satisfying design on which everything and everybody looks good.

I said the production was beautiful; I didnt say it was totally satisfying. It takes very good care of the play but loses some of its endearing untidiness. This, according to taste, is Shaws richest play or one of his most wayward. (I pass.)

Probably, it's two plays. One of them is a savage arraignment of a bunch of drifters, exploiters, and ne'er-do-wells who deserve the fate they seem so enthusiastically to accept. Shaw said that Heartbreak House was a metaphor for cultured, leisured Europe before the war, but he seems really to have had something narrower in mind, and closer to home. "Learn your business as an Englishman," rails the captain, "navigation . . . neglect it and be damned," and in England, lines like that seem perennially topical. Im not sure how well they travel. (Closing your eyes and thinking of Canada doesnt quite do it.)

At the same time we have an enchanting bunch of talkers who make excellent jokes, flirt incessantly but passionlessly, and seem to be doing no harm to anyone. As one of them says, they have no hearts to break. Shaw was incapable of disliking his characters (the converse is that he couldn't love them either), even when he disapproved of them.

There is a supposed villain here: Boss Mangan, a middle-aged capitalist who has ruined Ellie's harmless father and now wants to buy her in marriage. But he never stands a chance; he is victimized and talked down by everyone. We spend most of the time feeling sorry for him. By the time its revealed that his millions are illusory anyway, its just another Shavian paradox, at which we merely shake our spinning heads. Seen in this light, the play's finale is just Shaw's way out of a tight corner.

Bradeckis production keeps the play firmly within its judgmental frame, while losing some juice and some jokes. This bothered me less, though, as the evening progressed and, looking back the morning after, I wonder at my own ingratitude. Bradecki can orchestrate actors as well as effects. Individually, I have seen most of these roles better played (except perhaps for the housekeeper, brought to fire-breathing Irish life by Patricia Hamilton); collectively, they make a very impressive ensemble.

Douglas Rains Shotover is a partial problem: impeccably phrased, but in tenor rather than bass (Shaw, music critic, was precise about these things), and physically slight, both as farceur and prophet. Shotover is Shaw's Lear, complete with daughters. One, Hesione (Sarah Orenstein, eye-flashing, eye-catching and warmly easy on the ear) is a gypsyish enchantress, married to a moustachioed ladykiller (Gordon Rand) who is tired of the role, and who acts as mouthpiece for Shaw's erotic despair; he and Hesione claim to have children, but I dont believe it.

Daughter two is Ariadne (Kelli Fox, imperious) married to a colonial governor who -- perhaps because he is kept offstage -- is the one character for whom his authors loathing rings true. Ellie, though unrelated, counts dramatically as daughter three, and is played by Fiona Byrne with appropriate cool detachment; her dad (David Schurmann) is very nice, in all senses.

Jim Mezon does Mangan, and has a sporting try at being simultaneously ogre and dwarf. There is also a languid toff (Kevin Bundy), similarly mocked before he even opens his mouth; and a logic- chopping burglar (Barry MacGregor) who seems to have wandered in from some more run-of-the-mill Shavian play.

A tot of rum -- or better yet champagne -- to all hands. (But don't tell Shaw.)

- Box office: (905) 468-2172. In repertory until Oct. 31.

1999-05-28-singing-and-dancing-in-the-fo:
A FOGGY DAY

Royal George Theatre,

Niagara-on-the-Lake

One of my favourite lovesongs, by the Gershwin brothers or anyone else, is Nice Work If You Can Get It, a marvellous piece of upbeat bitter-sweet. George's jauntily pulsating music -- one of the last melodic outposts of the Jazz Age -- sets off a piercingly wry lyric by Ira: Love is the nice work, "and if you get it . . . wont you tell me how?"

The song was written for, and thrown away in, the 1937 Fred Astaire movie A Damsel in Distress, where it was done as a comic glee-club number. That film was based on a play, an English country- house farce on the P. G. Wodehouse model -- hardly surprising, since Wodehouse wrote it, in collaboration with Ian Hay.

A Foggy Day -- the Shaw Festivals hit miniature musical, revived from last season -- weds the script of the play to the score of the film, filling out the latter with Gershwin songs from other sources. In this version, Nice Work gets a bit more respect. It's the opening number and is performed by the population of London, or by that percentage of it that spends its time dancing up and down flights of steps that are conveniently located on all the city's streets (well, such streets as have a registry office on one side and a stage-door on the other).

Its not clear why theyre singing this particular song, but it's certainly interesting to hear Canadian actors putting on strenuously English accents to deliver an extremely American tune. The arrangement is more authentically Gershwinian -- more syncopated, more pianistic -- than anything in Crazy for You, Broadway's latest and far more lavish plundering of the family vault.

There is much to enjoy in A Foggy Day -- its music, its good humour, its intimacy -- but it is dead at the centre. The story concerns an American songwriter in pursuit of an English heiress, who initially loves another -- I mean another American -- and has to be brought to realize her mistake. We have to want the central couple to get together, and this production gives us no reason to. (Crazy for You had the same problem, but could offer us more to take our minds off it.)

This is partly a matter of writing, and partly of performance. Glynis Ranney makes a sweet and clear heroine, but Larry Herbert as the hero is murderously charmless. Wodehouse called him George, in homage to Gershwin; hes been renamed Steve, though the actor does have the Gershwin nose. The amount of dancing he does, it must have been tempting to call him Fred, and he gets through long and complicated tap routines without putting a foot wrong.

But there is no heart or spirit in his dancing, no bite or wit in his singing, and not much personality in his acting. In a tight corner at the end of the first act, he says, or sings, that hes dancing and he can't be bothered now; he then goes into an elaborate number that ends up infecting the entire cast. If you're Astaire, this might be a reasonable way of reacting to trouble. If youre merely mortal, it looks like a forced way of bringing down the curtain.

John Mueller, who collaborated on the script with Norm Foster, wrote maybe the best book on Astaire, and he must know that Freds dancing -- especially in the Fred-and-Ginger movies -- was never unmotivated, always had a context. He must also know that the way to establish an attraction between characters in a musical is to have them sing and dance together. This show is nearly over before its principals share a number.

In the meantime, our attention and our affection have been usurped by two subsidiary couples. Richard Farrell, an endearing old buffer in many plays at Shaw, is now an even more endearing, more- or-less-singing-and-dancing buffer; he plays the distressed damsel's dad who is gobbled up by a Canadian show-business broad, a role in which Nora McLellan turns in a first-rate Ethel Merman impersonation. They share two duets and two-thirds of a trio, all of them delightful.

Then there is Todd Waite as an endlessly lanky dimwit, tormented by shyness, and his bespectacled beloved (Patty Jamieson), who is similarly afflicted. They also have a charming duet, and he leads a galloping ensemble number -- the very Bertie Woosterish Stiff Upper Lip -- which would be wonderful if it were cut by a third; overkill sets in when they lower the Union Jack and start spouting couplets whose attempts at rhyme would make P. G. Wodehouse turn in Ira Gershwin's grave.

Also very active is Karen Wood as a scheming Cockney skivvy, largely responsible for steering the plot. This is a mistaken- identity thing that takes some time to get going but is fun when it does.

Some of the interpolated songs work in their new setting, some dont. The ones that do tend to be funny; the ones that dont tend to be famous, and they also tend to be songs that were written to be sung to or with someone, and are here delivered into empty air. This brings me back to the opening song, not an interpolation but still somewhat arbitrarily treated; it's nice work but they don't quite get it.

- In repertory until October. Box office: 1-800-511-7429.

Black & White Photo: David Cooper, Shaw Festival / Glynis Ranney as Lady Jessica and Larry Herbert as Steve Riker: a lot of dancing and singing, but not much heart and soul behind it. ;
1999-05-31-it-would-make-a-good-musical:
THEATRE REVIEW

Rebecca

Royal George Theatre,

Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

I approach Rebecca in a state of comparative innocence. I have never read the novel or seen the film. I did catch the first half of the recent TV adaptation, but missed the second. I assume, though, that everyone else knows more than I do, and merely needs to be reminded that this is the one about the young second wife who is brought by her husband to his ancestral Cornish seat, only to find that the memory of her predecessor has taken threatening possession of both house and spouse. The previous wife's name is Rebecca, and her end was watery.

The book came out in 1938. Two years later, its author, Daphne du Maurier, turned it into a play; and it is this play -- with, I gather, a few re-interpolations from the novel -- that the Shaw Festival has revived. As a kind of ghost story, as a study of the hazards of second marriage and as an updated Gothic romance, it variously recalls Jane Eyre, The Turn of the Screw and Noel Coward's Blithe Spirit.

It also bears a surprising resemblance to Ibsen's Rosmersholm, a drama that also involves a tradition-encrusted house, its high- minded master and a drowned wife. In that play, it's the wife's successor who's called Rebecca, and we gather that she pushed the old girl in. It is gradually made clear to her that this was not, on the whole, a nice thing to do. You might think that was fairly obvious, but Ibsen seems to have considered it a moral conundrum worth spending four acts over.

Rosmersholm is an undeniably serious play. Rebecca is not serious; it gets into some similarly deep ethical waters, but it allows its characters an arbitrary escape route. Christopher Newton, its current director, describes it in his program note as a boulevard piece.

The best bits of his production come when the story takes on a momentum of its own, and investigations and revelations start flying thick if not fast. This accounts for most of the evening's second half, and it is riveting. But it's a long and frequently awkward time getting there. Newton may in part be inhibited by an excess of good taste. Each of the play's half-dozen scenes comes equipped with a thumpingly melodramatic curtain-line, but none of them is exploited; the endings just hang there.

Nor is the acting much help. There are three central characters. One is Mrs. de Winter, the incoming bride, at whom Severn Thomson has a fair shot, suffering with spirit and rebelling with grace. But we don't feel or fear for her as we should; she seems well able to take care of herself. Maxim, her husband, is reticent, tormented and -- this is England -- damn decent: qualities that Peter Krantz translates into stiff and querulous. It must, admittedly, be hard to animate such a stick figure 50 years on and thousands of miles off.

Then there is Mrs. Danvers, the famous one, the housekeeper, making life hell for the new wife on account of her passionate feelings for the old. My chief memory of the TV version I half saw is of Diana Rigg, looking like the wrath of God and sounding as if she were introducing a particularly blood-bolstered segment of Mystery! on PBS.

This, I feel certain, is the way to go. Sharry Flett seems to be trying for something subtler, and is consequently at her best when pretending to be agreeable. But her final, demonic actions, apart from being half-heartedly staged, are just unbelievable, and her recurrent appearances on the ancestral staircase are so many missed opportunities. (It's amazing that nobody has turned Rebecca into a musical. It has Andrew Lloyd Webber written all over it. It even has a fancy-dress ball. I shall regret having written that.)

The supporting cast are there mainly to dispense or withhold information. Brigitte Robinson, as the hero's sister, gets some teeth into her share of the exposition, while the veteran Tony van Bridge, as the local chief constable, gets some delightful flesh and blood into his.

William Schmuck's set, seductively lit by Elizabeth Asseltine, is an appropriate essay in classic baronial; the stairs are timbered, the windows are mullioned, the portraits on the wall look to be by Lely or Kneller, all that's missing is a suit of armour. It occurred to me that, if hard pressed, the festival could combine this setting with the one for A Foggy Day, the other country-house piece, that plays on alternate nights. Both these shows derive in part from 1940s movies starring Joan Fontaine as a damsel in distress. There are worse ways to build a season.

- In repertory until Nov. 28. Box office: 1-800-511-7429.

Black & White Photo: Andree Lanthier, Shaw Festival / Thumpingly melodramatic: Severn Thomson and Peter Krantz as Mrs. and Mr. de Winter in Rebecca. ;
1999-06-01-no-farce-but-still-a-blast:
YOU CAN'T TAKE IT WITH YOU

Festival Theatre,

Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

Maybe You Can't Take It With You, but you can certainly bring it back.

This comedy by Moss Hart and George S. Kaufman was successfully revived at last years Shaw Festival. We now have a revival of the revival, and its wonderful.

I was surprised. Kaufman and Hart wrote a succession of hit comedies in the 1930s, of which Once in a Lifetime is the best and The Man Who Came to Dinner the best-known. Most of these pieces are knowing satrical extravaganzas with a show-business background. (Their greatest descendant is the Betty Comden-Adolph Green screenplay for Singin' in the Rain.)

This play is different. Neil Munro, its director here, accurately observes that its "energy threatens to explode into farce, but the inner warmth of the characters holds it back." Trouble is, I've always believed that farce, liberally spiked with wisecracks, is what K&H were good at, and that their inner warmth was fraudulently sticky. Left to myself, I still believe that. But for its duration this production had me hooked.

The play takes place in the home of the family Vanderhof, just around the corner from Columbia University, but dont go looking for it. I quote from the authors stage-directions, which are generally more quotable than the dialogue. Their tone, though, is much the same; they are funny, and endearing, and don't they know it. (They are also infectious.)

Grandpa Vanderhof, now 75, was once in business but sometime in his 30s he got tired and got out; he must have done all right though for he now lives in some comfort, if in considerable disorder. Certainly nobody else in the household is bringing home much bacon. Son Paul makes fireworks in the cellar, and daughter-in-law Penny has been writing unperformable and uncompletable plays for the past eight years, or ever since a typewriter got delivered to the house by accident.

Paul and Penny have two daughters. The elder, Essie, is a long- time and extremely unskillful student of the dance whose every move is a foredoomed pirouette and whose husband likes to print things, any things. The younger, Alice, is a link with the outside world; she is a secretary on Wall Street and is in requited love with her boss' son. There are also various unrelated residents and semi- residents; people who drop in chez Vanderhof tend to stick around.

Two sets of intruders appear in this Eden: one would call them snakes except that the family already keep snakes.

First is the IRS, demanding Grandpas unpaid taxes for the last 24 years. He replies that he doesnt think much of what they'd spend it on, and of course we cheer for him. (If we are liberals or worse we assuage our consciences with the thought that the U.S. circa 1936 was hardly a welfare state.)

Next come Mr. and Mrs. Kirby, Alice's prospective and very respectable in-laws, who are naturally upset by the Vanderhofs, especially when their visit leads to a night in jail for everyone present. All, I need hardly say, works out in the end.

A Marxist would describe all this as a cosy bourgeois rebellion, and a Marxist would be right.

The authors themselves were among the most successful Americans of their time, and the fact that they made their pile in showbiz hardly removed them from the rat race. They tailor their nonconformity pretty shrewdly to a middle American audience; meals in this play begin with Grandpa saying a home-made grace that begins "Well, Sir . . ." and could be called ecumenical, in that its two secular Jews idea of a Norman Rockwell Christianity. We might also note that, alternate nights on this very stage, the equally drop- out Shotover clan of Heartbreak House (to which this play owes a lot) are being arraigned as crypto-Fascists.

Heartbreak House plays like an improvisation. You Can't Take It with You starts that way, and then turns out to have joints of steel. Munro's direction honours this irresistible craftsmanship; he steadfastly refuses, true to his own diagnosis, to get frenetic and the rewards are huge. The scene in which the Kirbys meet the Vanderhofs, each side trying gallantly to accommodate the other, is a glorious passage of blissfully sustained high comedy. And when the explosions come, they explode.

The productions virtues are enshrined in Bernard Behrens Grandpa, less zany than his descendants, with shrewd eyes and biscuit-dry delivery: a treasury of underplaying. He is superbly complemented by Norman Browning as the dyspeptic Kirby, a mountain of repressions waiting to erupt. A definite bonus is that the young lovers (Ben Carlson and Catherine McGregor) are positive personalities rather than romantic stooges.

Actually everyone in the cast deserves mention, from Mary Haney's dishevelled determined Penny and Peter Millard's unobtrusively supportive Paul, through Camille James and D. Garnet Harding as the coloured help (somewhat loosely described by Penny as "like Porgy and Bess"), down to the one-scene wonders: George Dawsons vulpine taxman, Lynne Carlsons sublimely alcoholic actress, Jillian Cook's pinched and frustrated Mrs. Kirby, and -- a last-act epiphany -- Jennifer Phipps' exiled Grand Duchess reduced to dispensing pancakes at Child's, done with a shy glow as warming as any histrionic firework-display. (As it happens, the show has already set off some splendidly literal fireworks.)

Sue LePage has designed a massive rumpus-room of a set, in sub- marine hues with mysterious trailing bits. It seems the Vanderhofs have fronds like other people would like to have friends.

- Box office: 1-800-511-7429. In repertory until July 24.

Black & White Photo: Andree Lanthier, Shaw Festival / Creating theatrical fireworks: Mary Haney, left, and Jenny L. Wright in a production in which all the members of the cast deserve praise for their performance. ;
1999-06-01-no-marriage-no-sex-yet-sparks:
GETTING MARRIED

Court House Theatre,

Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

I would count myself a fan of Bernard Shaw, but I have my limits; and I have always drawn the line at Getting Married. This puts me in the same boat as many of the characters in the play; they draw the line at getting married, too. The play consists of them talking about it.

The Shaw Festival's new production just about converted me. There were still times when I could have echoed the cry of Eliza Doolittle (Alan Lerners, not Shaws): say one more word, and I'll scream. But none of the discussion here is tedious, and some of it is downright scintillating.

The play breaks down into a series of ensembles, trios and duets; and Jim Mezon, the director, has arranged them, both aurally and visually, to maximum effect. He has also, I think, made some crafty cuts. This could be part of the theatre's Y2K preparation, though for them the millennium is an occasion for celebration rather than crisis. For 2000 is the year in which Shaws copyrights run out. And then "wot larks," as the blacksmith said in Great Expectations.

Getting Married happens in 1908, in the house of the Bishop of Chelsea. (Chelsea is a suburb of London; it has never had a bishop.) His Graces sister-in-law is about to tie the knot, but both bride and groom cry off when they realize at the last moment just what they will be letting themselves in for.

He recoils at the prospect of being held responsible for his wife's debts. She has a far longer list of the rights and freedoms that she stands to lose. Ninety years on, her concerns resonate considerably louder than his.

Around them are grouped a selection of representative attitudes. There are the bishop and his wife, comfortable in their marriage. There is the wife's other sister, name of Lesbia, a self-described old maid, courted for years by a retired general who keeps repeating that each proposal is his last.

There is her other sister, who has just traded in her foursquare husband for a younger and prettier model, in effect exchanging a diet of roast beef for one of sole meuniere.

The bishop is a worldly cleric, but he has a celibate chaplain, Father Anthony, who decidedly isnt. He is deputed to draw up a new kind of marriage-contract which will satisfy everybody. The participants cannot even agree on a first clause. They decide to consult a different oracle: Mrs. George, the lady mayoress, known for her wisdom, her devotion to her coal-merchant husband, and her wide experience of other men. She arrives at half-time and takes over the play.

As usual with Shaw, the one subject not discussed is sex: at least not explicitly, and not with any kind of poetic suggestiveness either. Sometimes this reticence serves him well. He can deal, up to a point with flirtatiousness, and erotic fencing. He can deal with disgust; few things in the play are more effective than when Lesbia hints darkly at what repels her about union with a man. He cannot deal with consummation; he gives Mrs. George a trance-like aria, widely regarded as the most embarrassing thing he ever wrote, in which love is depicted as a one-way street, the woman giving pleasure and receiving none.

The play has been wittily set by David Boechler in a partially- curtained gazebo, backed by topiary hedges with large holes, through which we keep seeing the characters in new perspectives.

Acting in this kind of play is a matter of striking 12 at once; you dont sneak up on these characters, you reveal them -- and yourself -- the moment you open your mouth. The best performance comes, for the second time this week, from Sarah Orenstein who makes Lesbia's thoughts flash across the stage.

Second best is Barry MacGregor as the abandoned husband, half aggrieved and half complacent. Third best is Gordon Rand as his ostentatiously fastidious rival, who doubles as the latest conquest of Mrs. George. Fourth best, lively though somewhat untidy, is Severn Thomson as the bride who keeps everybody waiting at the church.

After them the deluge; they're an intelligent and personable deluge but they dont have the authority to see their roles through.

That doesnt include the two outsiders who deserve special attention. The constantly tempted (and inflexible) Anthony is a clever creation, a lawyer turned priest, and Simon Bradbury plays him cleverly, though with an uneasy edge of caricature. Sharry Flett moves from Mrs. Danvers to Mrs. George, an even more impossible role, and is frustrating i.e. exciting without being satisfying.

She gets triumphantly through the long speech, helped by discreet staging, and is fine as the seductive sybil. She is not convincing as the coal man's wife, as far beneath her admirer socially as she is beyond him sexually. I hate to sound like Professor Higgins (Shaw's and Lerner's), but she hasn't found the right accent.

- Box office 1-800-511-7429. In repertory until Sept. 26.
1999-06-02-thunder-of-applause-for-hutt-:
The Tempest

Festival Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

William Hutt talks Shakespeare like a native. He is pushing 80 and for what may possibly be his farewell performance he has the greatest of all valedictory roles, Prospero in The Tempest.

As the opening production of the Stratford season, it's delightfully ambiguous, hail as well as farewell. Or as Groucho put it, "Hello, I must be going."

Hutt is a superlative verse-speaker -- maybe the best there now is -- on at least four counts.

First, most obvious though least important, there is the actual timbre of his voice, a taut, flexible viola.

Second, there is his phrasing, a matter of timing and control. When Prospero's daughter Miranda asks him, "Sir, are not you my father?" the reply is "Thy mother was a piece of virtue and/She said thou wast my daughter"; Hutt takes this line-and-a-half of blank verse fast and light on a single breath, making it wonderfully witty and affectionate, the aural equivalent of a quizzically raised eyebrow.

Third is his prowess as an architect, shaping the phrases into speeches, each an ongoing wave of sense and sound.

Fourth, subsuming all the rest, is the creation through language of a whole character: in this case a troubled, benevolent and uniquely powerful, intelligence facing the limits of its own achievement.

In fact the highest moment of this vocal virtuoso performance is one of silence. Prospero, the exiled magician on his desert island, has at his mercy the shipwrecked politicians who once drove him from his dukedom; he is also engineering a love match between his own daughter and the son of one of his enemies.

If we think of Prospero as a dramatist, a possible surrogate for his author (the line taken by Harold Bloom in his inspiring and infuriating Shakespeare: The Invention of the Human) then he is trying to write two plays at once: a marriage comedy and a revenge tragedy.

Naturally, something has to give and the crunch comes when Ariel, his attendant spirit, suggests he take pity on his extremely bedraggled foes. Hutt now takes a pause of quite extraordinary length, while the theatre holds its breath. He finally bows to the inevitable, which for once means accepting the best, in one of the two great moments of forgiveness in Shakespeare (the other is in Measure for Measure), and the acceptance energizes him for the great speech in which he reviews his magical achievements and then renounces them: a speech in which Hutt is magnificent.

He balances the light and the dark in Prospero without quite fusing them; the same is true of Richard Monette's production, which meets the play's daunting technical demands proficiently enough, and otherwise is carefully built around its star.

The lovers (Claire Jullien and Graham Abbey) are unusually charming and adroit, if overly given to giggles; whatever you may think of Prospero's obsession with Miranda's chastity, I doubt if it was meant to raise the laughs it does here.

The first long expository scene between father and daughter, though, is beautifully done; she seeing herself both as the audience for a fairy tale and as its heroine, he tenderly proud of his achievements in home-schooling.

Ariel (Michael Therriault) is, apart from his one moment of rebellion, a conscientious and thoroughly cheerful servant -- which is absolutely true to the text -- and his songs are excellently sung.

Prospero's bitterness breaks through most strongly, as it should, on the breathtaking "our revels now are ended": a speech which, despite its sentimental reputation, is a despairing vision of universal dissolution. It heralds Prospero's encounter with his other attendant, the savage Caliban from whom he took the island, shown here as a hairy monster with protuberant, if passive, sex organs, and played by Peter Hutt as a comic villain, almost a comic drunk, whose suffering and whose menace are both muted. It makes internal sense but something disturbing has gone out of the play.

Caliban's co-conspirators are contrasting types of English regional clown: Trinculo (Tim MacDonald), north-country camp with feathers on his head looking like TV antennae; Stephano (the splendid Brian Tree), a cockney thug sounding, as this actor often does, like a popular British comic of the '50s known as Cheerful Charlie Chester.

The deadlier villains of the court party are rendered (by Robert Benson and Ian Deakin) with unusual force but as invariably happens they fade out as the play proceeds; the director tries hard to keep them in the picture in the last scene but it looks like a pious gesture. The virtuous Gonzalo (Bernard Hopkins) is allowed for once to be suspicious of them; when he talks about "the beasts of the island" he means two-legged ones.

Another unaccustomed is the delight of the Boatswain (Bradford Farwell) at being reunited with king and company: a neglected but vital part of the finale.

Which brings me to the Epilogue, unique in Elizabethan drama. As often, the leading actor begs the audience for applause, but this time he stays in character to do it, speaking still as Prospero.

But of course, with Hutt doing it now, there are other dimensions. This is an actor who has been at Stratford since the first festival in 1953, and who has come to symbolize all that is best about this theatre and its tradition. He confronts us now on a stage remodelled to its original state: a simple platform with only a slim, sturdy arrangement of steps and balcony for scenery.

When he speaks of quitting "this bare island" it's his kingdom in more senses than one. Of course he gets what he asks for, and more: a thunderous and authentic standing ovation.

We weren't just cheering for him, we were just cheering for history, and we felt, justifiably, part of it.

Of course, he doesn't have to retire.

- In repertory until Nov. 7. Box office: 1-800-567-1600

Black & White Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / William Hutt, centre, puts on a vocal virtuoso performance as Shakespeare's Prospero. Claire Jullien (Miranda) and Graham Abbey (Ferdinand) are charming, if overly given to giggles. ;
1999-06-07-blood-toil-tears-and-music:
Dracula

Avon Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

One of God's young Englishmen travels to Transylvania to meet a sinister nobleman. He imprudently reveals that he has a beautiful fiancee back home, and that his friend has another. His host metaphorically licks his lips, and takes off to meet the young ladies and suck their blood. He has his way with one, but she is posthumously rescued from his clutches by approved stake-driving methods. So he turns his attention to the other, whose fate is touch and go. (Will he touch? Will she go?) Clap your hands if you believe in vampires.

Its hard to tell the story of Dracula while keeping a straight face, and most recent dramatizations of the Bram Stoker novel have accordingly been campy frolics. The new Stratford musical however, written and directed by Richard Ouzounian, wants very much to be taken seriously. It gets its wish. The first-night audience was manifestly held, and though standing ovations on these occasions are de rigueur, this one seemed genuine.

My own response was that a high level of craftsmanship had been expended on a very thin story. For me, this is one horror-fantasy that doesnt resonate. We can all sympathize with Jekyll if not with Hyde, and with Frankenstein as well as with his monster. We know what a tough life the Phantom of the Opera has had. We don't have to believe in damnation in order to appreciate the dilemma of Faust.

Dracula, though, doesn't have a dilemma. Once bitten, he incessantly bites. The fact that he prefers to get his fangs into nubile young women gives his career a certain sexual charge, but for real erotic impact we would have to know something about the people (for want, in the Counts case, of a better word) who are involved.

We dont. Dracula, by the time we meet him, is mere malevolent menace, undeviating and uncomplicated. His victims, Mina and Lucy, are indistinguishable Victorian young ladies in white dresses, while their lovers and protectors are similarly cardboard honourable young men. The Unliving are pitted against the Undead.

Music is among the most effective of dramatic aids when it comes to keeping things creepy, and the narrative conventions of a musical help greatly in moving a story along. The unfolding of this one is measured but smooth.

There are other things that songs in a musical can do, but this show has to pass them up. Humour is outlawed, since its presence would undermine the entire enterprise. For exploration of character, see above. As for emotion: Well, it depends what you mean. I'm out of step with what passes for passion in most current musicals. The convention is that a character declares his or her devotion with lung-bursting fervour, ending on a sustained high note and with arms outstretched; the audience then falls down and renders homage. (Don't they expect singers to be able to sing?) Its noticeable that when the hero, at this shows crucial moment, proclaims his love for the heroine, he looks fixedly at us before sparing a glance for her.

Dracula is billed as a chamber musical, and it has only seven actors and five musicians. This enables the composer, Marek Norman, to provide his own spare and stylish orchestrations; the accompaniments, specializing in one-note figures that tantalize like water-drops on stone, are often more compelling than the actual melodies, which lack curves; they have the idea of romance but not its contours.

It's a politely lush sound, as if Andrew Lloyd Webber had stuck the score for Aspects of Love on to the story of The Phantom. It is the same story (except that this monster doesn't even offer his prey free singing lessons) and its much the same style, but the reduction in scale makes it seem less blatant.

Ouzounians lyrics have syllables that fit and rhymes that rhyme and they avoid obvious cliches. (Well, most of the time. Consider this quatrain: You and I are lovers / I've known it since we met / With so much to remember / And nothing to forget.) But after appreciating their negative virtues you begin looking for positive ones, and find only a pervasive literalness. The song-titles clue you in: I Will Shelter You, Let the Night Begin, The Blood Is the Life and that old suspenseful favourite Just One More Night.

"What," asked a friend afterward, do you call a number where half a dozen people sing different things at the same time?

"A first-act finale," I replied. Here, it's called The Last Light of the Sun. Theyre all Big Numbers for Big Moments, and its a relief when the authors try something more subtle and sidelong. This is a sinister faux folk-song called The Spider and the Fly, performed by a mental patient who, like a certain old lady, is eating the first as a chaser for the second. Benedict Campbell plays him, with cringing demonic effectiveness.

His is the only performance about which I can think of anything to say. The others are proficiently played, but you know, as in all such shows, they would come out the same whoever the actors were, as long as they could stand up straight and hit the notes. Juan Chioran is the lank-haired Count with the funny foreign voice, Michael Fletcher his learned and equally guttural nemesis, and Roger Honeywell, June Crowley, Amy Walsh and Shawn Wright the long- suffering lovers.

Visually, the production is a treat. Douglas Paraschuk's sets are framed by a glistening pair of mirrored walls, constantly parting and converging. The furnishings that spring up between them are spare but beautifully evocative; projections do the rest. Dracula is spectacular: not the kind of rhyme the show goes in for, but one that its staging at least deserves.

- Runs until Nov. 7. Box office: 1-800-567-1600.

A Midsummer Night's Dream

Festival Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

Richard Monette's production of A Midsummer Night's Dream is, in one respect, quite recklessly experimental. It takes a play that is officially set in and around ancient Athens and dresses the characters as Athenians. This is unheard of. In most Dreams, shields, tunics and breastplates are reserved for the concluding Pyramus and Thisby scene in which the Athenian Working Men's Amateur Dramatic Association unintentionally burlesque the romantic antics of the main action. Here, though, all the courtly characters rush around in diaphanous frocks, even the women.

Well, they have to wear something; and one character is positively helped by his air of having just stepped off an antique vase. This is Theseus, legendary hero, urbane Earthly ruler, conqueror and fiancee of the Amazon queen Hippolyta. Jonathan Goad, a promising if currently over-emphatic young actor, makes his skeptical observations on the habits of lunatics, lovers and poets sound reasonably fresh, and also gets the proceedings off to a swinging start by seeming genuinely eager to bed his betrothed.

She seems less keen, a now-standard interpretation that has no warrant whatever in the text, and as usual condemns the actress to misread her one speech of the opening scene and then to stand around looking grumpy. There is supposed to be a contrast between the festive Theseus and Hippolyta, and the quartet of squabbling mismatched young lovers who immediately break up the party. It registers here only at half strength.

The pressure further decreases when the four kids take to the woods. Here they spend most of their time falling down and bumping into trees. (The trees are graciously and uncomplainingly played by the pillars of the Festival stage's chaste and versatile permanent set.) This isn't funny, not because it's slapstick but because it's slapstick executed by characters we don't care about.

The boys are anonymous, which isn't new; so are the girls, which is. Michelle Giroux as the masochistic Helena, who likes to call herself her lover's spaniel, has a fetchingly literal habit of going down on all fours, but she is no more successful than her peers at bringing the lines to life.

The long quarrel scene, always a hazard, has no shape. There are a few gestures towards fashionable darkness, but the production wants mainly to be light, if not downright pretty. There are dancing fireflies, twinkling stars, a charmingly artificial crescent moon, and a sudden attack of dry ice moving in from an easterly direction to engulf the entire stage, but it all seems like the gratuitous decoration of a void.

There are also, in time-honoured Stratford tradition, a lot of actors. Puck, who prides himself on his prowess as a practical joker, cannot so much as mislead a mortal without enlisting the entire corps de ballet of fairyland to help him out. He then has the cheek to go to Oberon and take all the credit.

Juan Chioran brings some authority to the fairy boss-man, but having brought it he never lets go of it; he chants everything, as if it were a condition of high immortal rank never to be caught addressing a conversational word to anyone. Seana McKenna's Titania is far more flexible and far more agreeable, the only person on stage who seems consistently comfortable speaking verse.

Otherwise, the best people in this production talk prose. These, of course, are the play-acting mechanicals. They, too, are dressed Greek (and they do their final dance to kebab-house music) but underneath they are still plainly their author's neighbours.

Brian Bedford's Bottom, far more detailed than his last Stratford performance of the role, is for once the senior man of the troupe, a village oracle whose assurance will withstand any challenge, human or otherwise. He doesn't have to jockey for position, he simply and delightfully takes it. He also wears an ass' head with style.

Steven Sutcliffe's Peter Quince, by contrast, is young and earnest: a self-taught intellectual, perhaps, who interrupts rehearsals to demonstrate some highly professional acting exercises. (The gods know where he picked them up. Maybe he's been hanging out with Sophocles at Epidaurus.)

Their play scene is not as effective a travesty of the main action as I had hoped, but it is acceptably hilarious on its own account. Starveling has a comic stammer, which is a bad sign, but Snout (Keith Dinicol) is a truly sweet and lovely Wall, and proud of it.

Best of all is the spectacle of Bottom stepping out of character to explain to Theseus, in Bedford's friendliest Lancashire, some subtle points about the action that the Duke has missed. Here the actor's natural rhythms fuse with those of the character and the result is magic. But the whole play should be.

- In repertory until Nov. 5. Box office: 1-800-567-1600.
