Profile of Randy Newman Robert Cushman's radio series Sweet and Swinging: A Festival of Jazz Singing begins on Friday, June 11 at 10 p.m. on CBC Radio 2.

A recurring feature of Academy Awards night these past two decades has been the unspectacular spectacle of Randy Newman not getting the Oscar for Best New Song.

Year after year, Newman -- the only singer/songwriter some of us can take seriously -- has sat hunched over a piano, sweetly croaking out some nominated composition of his own. Usually it has been something gently optimistic from a movie either for or about kids: I Love to See You Smile, from Parenthood, or You've Got a Friend in Me from Toy Story. Invariably, it has been the best song on offer.

Newman has always been the prototypical guy with the glasses, brainy and anxious. Both his work and his conversation suggest a civilized man with a huge awareness of life's unfairness and absurdities, sometimes angry about it, but more often resigned.

At the Oscars, he has looked and sounded even more resigned than he usual. This year, when he was nominated for That'll Do (from Babe: Pig in the City), and had Peter Gabriel to do the singing for him, he still managed to project wry fatalism from the piano bench (maybe contagiously, since Gabriel at the mike seemed to be projecting it as well).

He always seems to know in advance that his deceptively simple words and music are going to lose out to whatever overblown over- the-titles anthem is being bellowed loudest. He is too smart not to know. Over the years, Newman has been nominated, for best song or best score, a round dozen times.

He comes from a dynasty of film composers (his uncles Alfred and Lionel were both giants in the trade) and Los Angeles is his hometown. He was born there in 1943, grew up and raised his own family there, and has spent his career, apart from his live gigs, in the film and record studios. By his own count, he has personally attended seven or eight Oscarfests, and he has appeared on stage in four.

He points out that there is an especially daunting quality about an audience largely composed of nominees: "Eighty percent of them are losers. . . . So they're not happy."

Newman was in Toronto to promote Bad Love, his first assemblage of self-performed new songs in eleven years.

He has a reputation, partly self-fostered, for being lazy, so the discipline of movie schedules has been good for him. Producers, friends and even wives have prodded him into writing individual songs. "I haven't" he admits "made enough records in the time I've had." His first solo album was in 1968; Bad Love is his tenth.

Newman's songs occupy a fluid territory between rock, folk and traditional pop. His tunes have body, melody and shape; they even, on occasion, swing. His words have that most precious of lyrical qualities, poise: They sit comfortably on the music, convey their surface meaning without strain, and hang reverberating in the air.

He is a superb ironist, one for whom irony is a positive comic and dramatic quality, rather than a vague apology for meaning. This sets him apart from the wild and woolly supposed poets of his 1960s generation. (And, yes, that does include Bob Dylan.)

Bad Love is his first album for DreamWorks/Universal. He left his former label, Warner/Reprise, after Lenny Waronker, his producer and boyhood friend, had moved on. Newman found the move difficult since, "I couldn't find anyone at Warner to resign to." (He ended up leaving his name with the receptionist, which of course is how most people try to get into an organization.)

Warner has released a four-CD retrospective, entitled Guilty: 30 Years of Randy Newman, and going all the way back to his first song, Golden Gridiron Boy: a song about high school, recorded when he was 19. The chorus goes: "I'm too small to make the team/I can only play in the ba-a-and/But I'm big enough to have a dream/That one day she'll understand."

It inaugurated a long line of skewed love songs in which she doesn't. The persona has always reminded me of Piggy, the outcast schoolboy of Lord of the Flies, ridiculed because he knows too much and wears glasses.

The first Newman song I became aware of was Simon Smith and the Amazing Dancing Bear. I loved the subtle rise in confidence from the hopeful "they'll love us, won't they?" to the proud "they feed us, don't they?"; and the concluding "who needs money/when you're funny?" which reeks of tattered defiance, and the festive stride- piano accompaniment.

In the same vein, but cutting deeper, is Davey the Fat Boy, with its seedy showman's cry of "isn't he round"; no other lyricist would have found it, or made it wake such disturbing echoes. Or there is the promise of the slave-trader to his prey in the horrendously soothing Sail Away, that they'll no longer have to "run through the jungle and scuff up your feet . . . it's great to be an American."

"The tragedy America has visited on black people," says Newman, "will never be rectified," then adds: "I've written about it too many times."

But Newman ("I'm a liberal, very much so, I'm for throwing money at people") has specialized in writing about persecution from the point of view of the persecutor -- who usually turns out to be an underdog himself. He admits that song writing is "a strange field to try humour in," his kind anyway, and pictures some guy picking up one of his songs on the car radio and going "Oh, you mean he doesn't mean what he says."

On Bad Love, the "I" of the songs seems closer to Newman himself than on his previous records. The opener, My Country, beginning "let's go back to yesterday . . . the television turned on for the night," sounds initially like another of his ambiguous odes to Middle America. It turns out to be a confessional, "the most autobiographical I've ever written." He grew up glued to the family TV, and has remained so; now his children are grown but they still come around to visit, slightly to his surprise since they have their own TVs at home. A line about "a television large as all outdoors" made me laugh out loud. He sings, as ever, in an affectingly tortured mumble that alternately squeaks and growls.

It took him twelve weeks to write the songs for the album (he didn't have any stockpiled). There's a ballad on there that maybe doesn't belong (it was written for -- but was not used by --Michael Jackson), but most fit comfortably enough under the admittedly generous umbrella title.

There is Shame, a blues for a wealthy ageing man in thrall to a 19-year-old girl ("I've sunk pretty low this time"); Newman is now on his second marriage, to a woman much younger than himself. The One You Love is about being afraid of what your partner wants from you. ("My wife and I," he has said by way of commentary, "had a pretty turbulent courtship, and she scared me half the time.")

Better Off Dead is pretty much what its title suggests (unrequited love "makes you feel all dirty, nerdy"), and I Miss You is even more painfully romantic ("I miss you -- I'm sorry but I do"), something of a tribute to his first wife, to whom he was married for 18 years and whom he credits for bringing order to his life. These two songs set dark lyrics to lush, yearning, string- laden tunes: Newman functioning like a one-man Rodgers and Hart.

I Want Everyone to Like Me ("I'm really modest once you get to me") is the perfect closer, an ineffable compound of mordancy, modesty and cheek.

There are also overtly political songs. Great Nations of Europe is a jolly march, a movie-theme Marseillaise, which recapitulates colonial history. ("Hide your wives and daughters/hide your groceries too/the great nations of Europe are coming through.") Karl Marx is a great idiosyncratic song about liberal angst; the narrator, surveying the world from "my mansion on the hill" bewails the sight of beautiful young women appropriated by old rich husbands, "froggish men, unpleasant to see -- men much like me."

Newman, more than any of his contemporaries, thinks dramatically; he has written a musical, Faust. It was staged a few years ago in La Jolla, Calif., with partial success; he thought that the score "got too much credit" and the book (which he also wrote "with Goethe's help") not enough. It spawned an all-star concept album on which he played the Devil -- with, of course, the best tunes.

He wants the show to go on, though his views on musical theatre are mixed. "It's the lowest form of music, I'm more likely to cringe on Broadway than on any other street, and yet I'd like to get there."

Still, he admires Stephen Sondheim, invokes Lorenz Hart and Cole Porter as model lyricists, and wishes that it were still possible to earn a living "doing what Frank Loesser did."

He's still earning his in the movies. "They used to call me for comedies. But it's very difficult, and there's no point. If a picture's funny, it's already funny. Now I'm getting all these animated things. I'm doing Toy Story II."

Recall what I said about poise: When he writes songs for these pictures, Newman -- the smart, mournful kid -- puts his irony not so much on hold, as in suspension; he may not be challenging our intelligence but he still respects it.

At 55, he is wary of becoming old fashioned, of losing touch with newer composers, or as he puts it, "I watch myself for old crockery."

In fact, he doesn't need to worry; he crosses all the song writing traditions, all the time-lines.

- Bad Love is released on the DreamWorks Records label

BRING IN 'DA NOISE,

Bring in 'Da Funk

Hummingbird Centre

There are a couple of young guys in Bring in 'Da Noise, Bring in 'Da Funk by the names of David Peter Chapman and Dennis J. Dove, and they play drums. That's a serious understatement.

In the first part of the show, they appear before us, decked out in an assortment of pots and pans on which they proceed to execute a dazzling, intricate series of rhythmic tattoos. It's an interactive duet: Each beats on the other's armour as well as his own. They juggle, too, sending their sticks whizzing through the air and landing them always on the right beat.

In the second act, they execute an almost equally exhilarating routine using half a dozen upturned garbage pails as their instruments. I have decided, after carefully inspecting my fantasies, that I would rather be a drummer than a tap dancer.

Maybe, though, I don't have to choose. The point of Noise/Funk seems to be that drumming is a form of tapping and tapping a form of drumming. The whole show is a tribute to, and demonstration of, percussive rhythm -- 'da Beat. It was conceived by Savion Glover, the young American prodigy tapper, and it was presented in New York largely as a showcase for his talents. However, the touring production now in Toronto shows that it works only slightly less -- which is to say awesomely -- well without him.

Glover choreographed the show, George C. Wolfe of New York's Public Theater directed it, and the show is little -- though not much -- more than a non-stop battery of visceral excitement. There is a bit of a story in there, though it keeps (this seems to be the right expression) wrong-footing itself. It appears to start out as a history of tap; we're told that the black slaves on the plantations were forbidden to play drums, and therefore took to communicating messages with their feet. It could be that the two kitchenmen (billed in the program as the Panhandlers) are another part of this; denied proper instruments, you use what you've got.

As things progress, tap dancing turns from message to medium -- a means of representing and interpreting black history onstage. The show has started with the slave ships. After emancipation, it turns to the first years of supposed freedom. A number called The Lynching Blues begins with a cheerful dance done to the sounds of a washboard and ends with the miming of a noose around the performer's neck. A narrator and some projected captions help to keep us in touch, as both the show and the characters move north, lured by the promise of plenty. The beat, visual and aural, is brilliantly used to depict life on the assembly line. We are in Chicago, scene of especially virulent race riots, and then in Harlem, for a sardonic look at the birth of black show business and of new opportunities for exploitation.

After the intermission, the show gets increasingly fragmentary. What we have been seeing is an underground tradition of tap -- hard, fast and frequently angry. The more familiar mainstream kind -- economical, graceful and ingratiating -- is exhibited only to be mocked, in a sequence about the most celebrated of black tappers, Bill Bojangles Robinson (played by Dominique Kelley), and his movie career as a sidekick for Shirley Temple, which was lucrative -- but not as lucrative as hers. (There was more to Robinson than this, and if he was giving the white folks what they wants then so, in an altered climate, are Wolfe and Glover. Once again, you use what you've got.) A sequence about a character called The Kid (Christopher A. Scott) trying to make it as a dancer in Hollywood and falling in with a sultry chanteuse plays like a blackface version of the Broadway Ballet from Singin' in the Rain.

There is an extraordinary sequence in which Jimmy Tate, playing the Glover role, recreates the styles of four seminal tappers of the past, each more intricate than the last. There is a scene called Taxi in which four performers dance out the different kinds of rage engendered by trying to hail a cab on the streets of four different cities -- mockingly restrained in Paris or Rome, flat out furious in New York. (It's uncertain whether this is being presented as purely a black experience or as part of the universal urban agony.) Increasingly, as the show progresses, tap meets rap, and they seem made for each other.

There is a chipper if not always helpful narrator (Thomas Silcott) and a singer (Debra Byrd) who is sonorous but inflexible. Monotony, indeed, is a liability of the show, except presumably for dance buffs; but it's a hypnotic, dazzling kind of monotony. It's pretty much guaranteed to bring you to your feet, in homage to theirs.

- Runs until June 13. Box office: (416) 872-2262.

1999-06-11-from-an-original-masterpiece-:
PRIDE AND PREJUDICE

Festival Theatre, Stratford

The first week of Stratford openings concluded, not with a whimper exactly, but with a genteel sigh. Christina Calvit's adaptation of Pride and Prejudice is an exhaustively -- and yes, exhaustingly -- complete account of the action of Jane Austens novel. It also attempts to capture the books ambience and its tone.

As staged by Jeanette Lambermont, it is a pretty affair in which massed scenes of small-town gaiety -- life for the gentry of Regency England seems to have been a ball, invariably followed by another ball -- alternate with rather more effective scenes of one-on-one confrontation, played across the full bare extent of the uniquely compelling Festival stage.

Time was when the first casualty of any stage version of a major novel was the author's narrative voice. This changed around 1980 when the Royal Shakespeare Company staged their unforgettable marathon dramatization of Dickens' Nicholas Nickleby. This introduced us to the idea of having members of the cast recite, in concert, some of the books passages of commentary and description.

Its proved a hard act to follow. Most shows don't have eight hours at their disposal, so the device doesn't have time to gather force; and besides, not every authors voice is as robust as Dickens. Jane Austen's irony is likely to come between the lines, and the choral routines in this Pride and Prejudice tend to expose not the writer's insight but the characters lack of it. Dressed in black and bearing umbrellas, they keep telling us in awkward unison how vital it is for the young women of impoverished families to make financially advantageous marriages. They also sneer heartily whenever one of these young women, or the mother of one of these young women, fails to bring this off.

In short, they are jealous snobs. It is necessary to our understanding of the situation that they should be, and that we should be made aware of it, but once the point has been made, its been made.

More prominent individuals are allowed to describe themselves in the third person, making areas of the play sound like Ragtime without the songs. What is sharp on the page can be arch on the stage, and only one character seems thoroughly at home with the device. This, thankfully, is Elizabeth Bennet, who is both the centre of the story and the nearest thing to an author's representative.

Lizzie, second of the five unmarried Bennet sisters, is justly reckoned among the wittiest and most attractive heroines in literature, and Lucy Peacock's performance is refreshingly up to this mark.

The other Bennet daughters, being so numerous, put nearly as much of a strain on the audiences concentration as they do on their fathers purse. None of them comes to theatrical life, nor do any other of the young ladies of the district, nor the variously eligible young men, be their intentions honourable (the wealthy Mr. Bingley) or the reverse (the penniless and rakish Mr. Wickham).

Most wooden of all is Geordie Johnson as Mr. Darcy, the proud and handsome landowner whose relationship with Lizzie -- his pride, her prejudice, mutual misunderstanding giving way to mutual love -- is supposed to be the heart of the story. Whatever his fascination in one medium, it proves untransferable to another; lacking any spark of wit, and too much of a gentleman to give way to passion, he is simply unworthy of his partner.

This leaves the comics, who come in two categories: dry and juicy. Driest of the dry is Mr. Bennet himself, whom Austen saw as a self-centred bookworm bored by his family and neglectful of their welfare but who, having the funniest and coolest lines, invariably comes off as the most sympathetic male character in any adaptation; thanks to Brian Tree's perfect world-weary timing, he strolls effortlessly off with this one.

Juiciest of the juicy, by far, is Steven Sutcliffe as Lizzie's unfortunate suitor, the Reverend Mr. Collins, tiptoeing about the stage in an ecstasy of self-satisfaction, at a loss to imagine why, with his prospects and his connections, anyone should find him less than irresistible. This is caricature so precise as to be truthful, in contrast to Lally Cadeaus scattershot attack on Mrs. Bennet, the lady whose tireless intriguing on behalf of her daughters propels much of the plot and whose fits of the vapours at those same intrigues and daughters should theoretically account for much of the humour.

Broad as she is, she is restraint itself compared to Patricia Collins Lady Catherine de Bourgh, a tyrannically complacent country chatelaine who here sounds like the current Queen of England as impersonated on late-night television.

The greatest evidence of Lizzie's wit and courage is supposed to be that she stands up to this woman; yet, faced with a figure so far divorced from any conceivable reality, her victory evaporates. So we lose out on the social conflict, and we lose out on the love.

It is hard enough to turn the tensions and values of a novel into those of a play without falsifying them at the outset. The show trades on the assumption that anything based on a masterpiece and bearing its name is automatically worthy of respect. It seems intended, consciously or not, for those who know the book by heart and enjoy singing along with it, and for those who have never read it and feel guilty.

- In repertoire until Nov. 6. Box office: 1-800-567-1000.

1999-06-17-our-actions-reverberate-throu:
THE AWAKENING

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

Julian Garner is a British playwright who has lived for 15 years in Scandinavia and apparently writes in both English and Norwegian. His play The Awakening comes to Toronto bearing the somewhat rarefied accolade of Best Norwegian Play of 1989; about 100 years ago, insular Anglophones were probably making similarly frivolous remarks about Ibsen.

The play is set in the 1930s on an island off the Norwegian coast and concerns the spiritual progress of a simple-minded child- murderer. Its Canadian production is encrusted by a thick film of worthiness, involving the singing of mournful and incomprehensible folksongs by an otherwise totally extraneous character.

The package could hardly be more remote or forbidding.The play turns out to be enthralling.

We meet Johannes, the protagonist, in solitary, obsessively reciting passages from the Bible and being beaten up by a guard. He is rescued by Captain Agnes, a formidable prison visitor from the Salvation Army ("I am not," she stresses, "your run-of-the-mill do- gooder,") who has turned him on to religion and now gets him a place working on a farm, part of a national scheme for the rehabilitation of loonies.

That last brisk term is the one favoured by the farmer, a young lady named Unn, who has been running the place single-handed for years. In fact, ever since Agnes, whom she had looked on as a mother, left the island to follow her vocation, or advance her career, or both.

Unn has felt bitter ever since, and initially she takes her bitterness out on Johannes. She thaws somewhat when he turns out to have a natural gift for gathering eggs and further still when, after a little coaching, he proves adept at splitting wood. (This is done on stage. So is the gutting of a fish. Actors these days need varied skills.) She completely melts when he reports in alarm that a fishing net is full of holes. She bursts out laughing; probably her first laugh in a very long time.

Johannes meanwhile has arrived in his Bible study at the ripe erotica of the Song of Solomon (its second appearance on a Toronto stage this year) and it turns him on no end. From there, it's a straight road to romance, and the start of the second act finds Unn happily carrying Johannes' child.

There are many rough edges in Sue Miner's production, but it gets this central relationship absolutely right. Joris Jarsky's Johannes is perfect: childlike, obsessive, devout, capable of deep hurt, deep affection, and deep anger. Anne Page's flaxen, angular Unn is also fine, at least in her scenes with him.

She is a lot less convincing, a lot less fresh, when she comes up against Randi Helmers' Capt. Agnes; the actress seems unable to find any kind of key to this character and so tries, as actors will, to batter it open. (The director is no help here; whenever Agnes appears, the staging goes awkward.) This is unfortunate since Agnes' revulsion at the idyll she has engendered should lead us to another level.

We have been led -- by perfectly honest dramatic methods -- into identifying with Johannes, and rooting for his happiness and that of his lover. They share the awakening of the title. But Johannes' initial crime, which he never denies or excuses, is that he raped and murdered an eight-year old girl. So there are complexities here and to expose them (they can't be resolved) the author resorts to desperate expedients. The vicious prison guard reappears and turns out to be the dead girl's avenging father.

(Peter Smith gives a strong performance in this role, but it is strength unharnessed to anything as practical as a characterization.)

First he confronts Agnes, raging at her religion as mere useless "words," then the couple, and at this point the story, or my comprehension of it, goes very cloudy.

Regardless, we end with Johannes back in jail, the pregnant Unn denied access to him, Agnes banished from the prison service, and the bereaved father looming in an unfocused way, as he has tended to do throughout: four broken lives, though maybe not irreparably so.

It's a bleak conclusion, although -- the play being a good one that has held us with its story and involved us in the thoughts and emotions of its characters -- not a depressing one.

I don't know what the author is finally saying. Maybe that we must all live with the consequences of our own actions and of other people's, which seems reasonable.

I mentioned Ibsen, and Garner, his adopted compatriot, seems to share his forebear's fascination with, and skepticism of, Christian ethics, which gives his play a bracing, unfashionable flavour.

It's performed against interlocking slabs of what I take to be (isn't it good?) Norwegian wood, which the actors move about, though it's never clear to what extent this is part of the plot.

That folk-singer mostly stays at the side, but occasionally wanders through the action as if she were part of it. Why don't they ask her to muck out the hen-coop?

- Runs until June 27. Box office: (416)-531-1827.

1999-06-18-maritime-voices-cry-out-for-a:
THE DOGPATCH

Factory Theatre Studio

There is an area of Halifax called Kline Heights that is also known, or used to be, as the Dogpatch. The nickname presumably derives from the mythical backwoods community depicted in the Al Capp comic strip. The cartoon made capital fun of drunkenness, illiteracy and all-American fecklessness; Li'l Abner, Moonbeam McSwine and company seem to have led carefree lives in their picturesque squalor. Their real-life urban Canadian cousins weren't, and aren't, as lucky.

Chaz Thorne is a young Nova Scotia actor and playwright whose mother once assembled an oral history of life on the Dogptach, derived in part from the memories of her own parents and grandparents. Thorne used his mother's researches as the launching pad for a play, written when he was 19. It's a promising piece of work, with dialogue that slides easily off the actors' tongues, and characters who are thoroughly believable.

There's a gulf, though, between being believable and being interesting, and this play doesn't always bridge it. Its first 20 minutes just lie there, the author setting up his characters while implicitly asserting: "These are my people -- look at them" -- a demand that always prompts the unspoken response, "Why should we?" The play only becomes gripping when it becomes violent, which it does with increasing frequency.

We are in the house of Reuben, a soldier back from the war, the 1939-45 one. He was a drunken, abusive husband and father before he went away and he is worse now, a spell in a POW camp having equipped him with a grievance. His battered wife, Liz, strives desperately to keep the family together. They have three sons of whom the eldest, Doug, hangs out with Wally, who has done time for stealing a truck. When Doug turns up for work bearing the marks of a beating from his father, he is fired, and all he wants is to get away. He and Wally team up to rob a cab, and the driver is killed. Wally will do anything to avoid returning to prison, and the action spirals into inevitable catastrophe.

There is a ring of truth about this, but not a ring of freshness. I suspect, too, that the author has given too much space to Doug (whom he plays himself) and not enough to his parents. Adolescent rebellion is a well-worn theme and, even in these extreme circumstances, it comes out onstage much as it usually does. Wife beating and family abuse are subjects we read a lot about in the papers but rarely see dramatized, and it would be interesting to see the dynamics fully explored. This play makes a start in the character of Reuben, who alternates between brutality and displays of maudlin affection. When he paws Liz and she resists, he asks her what's wrong with the neighbours seeing that she has a loving husband; later, she remarks that she played the loving wife because it was what she wanted. Reuben's self-pity is kept going to the very end, and it's both well-observed and well-illustrated. Liz, though, isn't allowed to get much beyond standard stoicism. There are times when the play resembles Sean O'Casey's Juno and the Paycock without the humour though also, and mercifully, without the rhetoric.

Brian Richmond has given the play a full-bodied unforced production, and the action moves fluently around the neighbourhood, cortesy of Kelly Wolf, who has designed a setting of netting.

The acting is uniformly good, right down to Griffin Benger and Joseph Weissgold who make Doug's two younger brothers a couple of piercingly ordinary kids, trying to find their way through an inferno. David Ferry has the most generous opportunities, doubling Reuben with the unlucky and very loquacious cabbie. Kyra Harper is Liz, whose face can become a screaming mask of pain; Adrian S. Churchill plays Wally who, like nearly everyone else in the play, can tell a good scary story; Frank McAnulty is his damaged dad, rather too firmly docketed as poignant comic relief; and Barbara Gordon is the local healer, physical and mental.

If the play lacks an individual voice, it does present a collective one, a pungent Maritime accent that Toronto doesn't often get to hear.

- Runs until June 20. Box office: (416)-504-9971.

1999-06-22-the-drawer-boy-gets-load-of-d:
The Dora Mavor Moore Awards, Torontos annual theatre prize- giving, are never going to compare with the Oscars or Tonys for sleekness. Nobody onstage or in the audience is going to attract the favourable attention of fashion writers, people on the platform drop things, and the visual presentation is decidedly tacky, which is endearing up to a point and exasperating beyond it.

Surely when Toronto theatre gathers to pay tribute to itself, it should do better justice to its own sense of design and production - - which after all is what several of the awards are for.

The Dora organizers, unlike those of other awards, recognize that people other than actors work in the theatre and allow them to present some of the awards, which is a good thing.

This year, Torontos favourite clowns, Mump and Smoot, whose stock-in-trade is sulphurous surprise at finding themselves wherever they are, were welcome presences as assistant presenters and emphatically outshone Allegra Fulton, the official emcee.

Certain things about the Doras puzzle me. The awards, now in their 20th year, are officially described as "celebrating excellence in Toronto's theatre and dance communities. That word communities" always sets my teeth on edge; it's become a fuzzy synonym for "people": people who are often, in fact, fiercely competitive.

That apart, if dance is something separate from theatre, then why doesnt opera get similar individual treatment? As things stand, it gets lumped in with all other shows that sing. This means that Irina Mishura in Il Trovatore won for Outstanding Female Performance in a Musical. The male equivalent, meanwhile, went to Colm Wilkinson in Les Miserables, reprising the part he created in London umpteen years ago. Its difficult to see how either of these performances could be judged against those of colleagues who were playing by totally different rules.

We all know that awards are, by their nature, unfair and unreasonable, and involve comparisons between the strictly incomparable, but in this case apples and oranges seem to have been tossed together with astounding abandon.

The theatre, as opposed to dance, awards fall into two categories: General (meaning large) Theatre and Independent (meaning small) Theatre. However, the nominations are announced onstage in batches comprising both categories, which is extremely confusing.

The Outstanding General New Play was, uncontroversially, Michael Healey's The Drawer Boy; it could hardly have been anything else. As with the Oscars and the Tonys, one major award tends to pull others with it. So there were prizes for The Drawer Boy's producers, Theatre Passe Muraille, for its director, Miles Potter (shared with Soheil Parsa for Aurash), and for one of its actors, David Fox. These are more troubling. Mr. Potters work on this delightfully approachable play was fine but -- comparing the incomparable again - - it wasnt as impressive as Robin Phillips' rigorous direction for the Soulpepper company of the forbiddingly unfamiliar Don Carlos, which, disgracefully, was not even nominated. Mr. Fox was brilliant (he has been excellent in many plays this season), but it would be hard to place him above Peter Donat's icy Philip II, also in Don Carlos.

Amazingly, Soulpepper -- the best thing to happen to Toronto theatre in a decade, a company that was formed to produce classics to the highest standard and managed to fill the house with them -- received nothing at all. One sensed some resentment in the air, as if the Toronto theatre community would rather go on being parochial.

Outstanding female performance in a play was Nancy Beatty in Risk Everything, who was charming and won all hearts by searching for her acceptance speech in her purse. (There are no women in The Drawer Boy.) Outstanding New Musical, beating out heavy-hitters such as Fosse and Needfire, was The Nutmeg Princess by Richardo Keens- Douglas. Outstanding production of a musical was the Canadian Opera Companys Norma; outstanding direction of a musical was Stephen Wadsworths Xerxes, so opera pretty much cleaned up. Outstanding Choreography (not a dance award) was, perhaps inevitably, Fosse, shared between Ann Reinking and the ghost of Bob Fosse himself. Since Mr. Fosse's work was by definition not new, one wonders if it was Ms. Reinking's contribution that made it eligible.

Among the independents, the nod for Outstanding New Play/Musical went to Easy Lenny Lazmon and the Great Western Association, produced by Moriah Productions, in association with Go Chicken Go, which also got outstanding production and direction. The two dance awards -- for new choreography and for performance -- both went to Learie McNicolls in Armour.

Theres a separate one-slot category of Theatre for Young Audiences; it was won by Roseneath Theatre for Dib and Dob and The Journey Home. It was probably wonderful (I didnt see it), but I wish there had been a prize for Theatre Direct's Waiting For Lewis, which was one of the year's best plays, even by grown-up standards.

The special Silver Ticket award, given for overall achievement, went to native playwright Tomson Highway.

1999-06-24-the-glenn-gould-variations:
GLENN

Tom Patterson Theatre

Stratford, Ontario

Four intrepid and talented actors make up the cast of Glenn, and they are all playing the title role.

David Young's play is a fragmented account of the life, ideas and personal torments of Glenn Gould, the Canadian culture hero who detested most of what is officially revered as culture. It chops its protagonist into quarters, slaps a label on each of the morsels and distributes them among the company.

There is the Prodigy: a monstrously gifted juvenile pianist, excitedly calling to his mother that he has just figured out the structure of the Goldberg Variations.

There is the Performer, who develops the Prodigy's insights and displays them from the concert platforms of the world.

These two personae tend to slide into one another, perhaps because what both actors chiefly project is youth. Paul Dunn, who plays the Prodigy, is a new young actor, and Duncan Ollerenshaw, who performs the Performer, has been a young actor for years.

Their older colleagues are more distinct. Richard McMillan is the Puritan, who has forsaken live performance for the recording studio and, increasingly, the piano for the podium. ("I have finally learned," he says in a resonant pun, "how to conduct myself.") This performance, lank-haired and loping, takes some time to come into its own, but once arrived it presents a moving and scarifying portrait of a man tortured by his own talent.

Finally, there is Rod Beattie as the Perfectionist who sums up all the others. Rasping and chunky, he is the Glenn Gould we know from his late public pronouncements, the misanthropic tease whose bite was considerably worse than his Bach and who once told us that he found comfort in the idea that behind every silver lining there was a cloud. He doesn't say that in the play, but he does delightfully remark, looking up from perusing a page of Kafka, that "this guy knows how to have fun."

I guess, though I don't know, that some of his lines are literal transcriptions of Gould's own words. You feel that if Gould hadn't existed Samuel Beckett would have invented him; and the play, given its hero's increasing obsession with recording as the one true medium of creation and of memory, comes to resemble Krapp's Last Tape rescored for quartet.

Our first sight in the play is of four capped, scarved and cloaked figures, looking like the chorus of some expressionist drama sent over from Poland, but Beattie is the only one who wears this uniform throughout. (Gould apparently informed a startled New York taxi-driver that this was how all Canadians dressed in June.)

The author, of course, is far too sophisticated to present these four personae sequentially; they overlap, as they would have done in real life.

Indeed, overlapping isn't the half of it; they interweave in a sort of dramatic fugue apparently modelled on the Goldberg Variations themselves. This way of having drama imitate music isn't altogether new (I once saw an Austrian play that patterned itself on the Trout Quintet, and it was deadly) but David Young mostly makes it work.

At its worst, the constant counterpoint keeps us on our toes; at its median, it makes familiar but still effective capital out of the juxtaposition of different stages of experience; at its best, it is dazzling. Throughout, it demands and receives superb ensemble performance interlaced with an abundance of striking solos.

Richard Rose, taking his second shot at a play he directed six years ago in Toronto, dots his platform stage with significant furnishings -- a chair, a keyboard, tape-decks and a mixing-desk -- as if mapping out the hero's biography simultaneously; his life and personality become a level playing-field and the actors stroll, sprint or hurdle across it. They also get to play other people; Beattie does especially well here, impersonating skeptical record producers, guttural sound engineers, and Herbert von Karajan.

Great play is made of Gould's dismissive and historically absurd denigration of live performance ("a bloodsport") and especially of live applause, but it's also hinted that this monumental hypochondriac may be just have been rationalizing his own neuroses.

Anyway, the actors faced their own audience's applause with every appearance of equanimity and even took a standing ovation without flinching.

The play manages to dispense with most of the musical information necessary to its own comprehension, but it takes too much factual knowledge for granted; however unorthodox its structure, it trades as shamelessly as any other biographical drama on its audience's built-in regard for a national icon.

It's still a brave and demanding choice for Stratford; and, on the whole, I liked it.

- Glenn is in repertoire until September 25. Box office: 1-800- 567-1600.

1999-06-25-neither-then-nor-now:
THE ALCHEMIST

Festival Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

There are few better plays in the English language than Ben Jonsons The Alchemist, and fewer still that are harder to perform. Its problem is that it moves at two different speeds simultaneously. Its action is that of a quick-witted farce of roguery and deception. Its dialogue is a heady concoction of street slang and pseudo- scientific jargon, dense enough in its day and rendered even more daunting by the passage of 400 years.

Most productions turn into exhausting romps or enervating poetry recitals. (The Alchemist, most unusually for an Elizabethan or Jacobean comedy, is written entirely in verse.) Douglas Campbells Stratford production has the melancholy distinction of falling into both traps, though it is more consistent in the second. It crawls through the text without illuminating it, occasionally throwing in an arbitrary gag. As a farce, it lacks urgency: as a picture of a society, it lacks any kind of reality.

Jonson wanted both. He set the play in his own London, malevolent and malodorous, teeming with trickery and plagued by plague. A citizen, fearful of infection, has quit town and left his house in the care of his butler, who promptly invites a con man and a prostitute onto the premises.

Alchemy is their game -- the promise to turn all metals into gold by means of the mythical Philosopher's Stone -- with a bit of fortune-telling and prostitution on the side. Over a couple of hours, stage time more or less mirroring real time, we watch them entertaining half a dozen different clients, adopting different personae to swindle each one, and therefore under considerable pressure to keep them from colliding. Finally, the master returns and the syndicate, always fragile, breaks up.

The play, teeming as it is with local colour, works best in the trappings of its own time. Failing that, it needs to be set in some other recognizable world. Campbell's production, designed by John Colm Leberg, recklessly mixes periods, presumably on the grounds that greed and gullibility are eternal. So they are; but in order to draw general conclusions we have to believe in specific examples.

From time to time, this show brings on a writhing chorus in bodysuits to provide a spooky atmosphere. Just who are they meant to be? They cant be on the alchemists payroll -- he's too cheap and too secretive to have one. So they're real spirits? But that would mean he does have magical powers, which means the play is rubbish. Or are they just there to give the tourists, supernaturally unsated by The Tempest and A Midsummer Nights Dream and even Dracula, more of their moneys worth? Either it's an incredibly dumb decision or an incredibly insulting one.

The production's one merit is that it brings out the rivalry of the conspirators. The play starts with a quarrel between Face, the butler, (Benedict Campbell) and Subtle, the mystagogue, (Keith Dinicol) that is here taken far too ponderously but that does prepare the ground for some increasingly nasty needling later on.

But there is no joy in the intrigues that make up the bulk of the play, and no suspense. The one successful production of this play I have seen was directed by Trevor Nunn, with Ian McKellen brilliant as Face. Nunns version worked by making life as difficult for the tricksters as possible; for each encounter they had to re-arrange the furniture and don new disguises, and they had to do it at breakneck speed, increasingly so as events threatened to spiral out of control.

Here, the actors slip unconcernedly into their various get-ups, and then proceed to let the costumes play them.

As Dol Common, the resident temptress (a famous but underwritten role), Diane DAquila has more presence than either of her gentlemen friends, and most of the dupes manage to strike a spark or two. James Blendick as Sir Epicure Mammon, the visionary voluptuary, has some grandiloquence if not comic grandeur; his skeptical friend Surly (Bradford Farwell) initially takes the stage with more authority than anyone else, but loses it when he goes into disguise as a Spanish grandee.

The two comic Puritans, wonderfully written satires on greasy fundamentalist hypocrisy, are unprecedentedly unfunny. Michael Therriault as Abel Drugger, the shy tobacconist, is pretty good, and Thom Benson as an aspiring tough boy from the country, reasonably equipped with a kilt and a burr, even better.

The returning householder is Bernard Hopkins who is saddled, so to speak, with an entrance on a pantomime horse but manages in his sterner moments to rise above it. We also get Keystone Kops and a transvestite priest.

It is to weep.

- In repertory until Oct. 30.

Black & White Photo: Michael Copper, the Stratford Festival / From The Alchemist: Diane D'Aquila as Dol Common, James Blendick as Epicure Mammon, and Benedict Campbell as Face. ;
1999-06-26-hey-there-you-with-the-lukewa:
THE PAJAMA GAME

Princess of Wales Theatre

Richard Adler and Jerry Ross, who composed The Pajama Game, are famous for bringing what in 1954 were contemporary pop rhythms into the theatre.

Theirs was a world hovering unknowingly on the verge of rock 'n' roll; their love songs were more relaxed and sinuous than the Rodgers-and-Hammerstein norm, the kind of things that the young Tony Bennett or Rosemary Clooney could have crooned or belted (and did).

The air was full of Latin-Americana, of eccentric comedy numbers (novelties in the trade), and of twangy, muscle-flexing cowboy songs. There Once Was a Man, the principals post-coital duet in Pajama Game, is an exhilarating elongation of the latter form; crack a whip under it and its Rawhide. The blue-collar ethos extends from the score to the book; this show and the team's follow-up, Damn Yankees, are among the few musicals with convincing scenes set in kitchens.

In its day the show was controversial; it concerns a labour dispute at a pyjama factory in the Middle West, and there were many who thought this gratuitously bleak for a musical. The heroine is a union militant, the hero a boss' man who sees the light, and the ending is a happy compromise. The politics seem pretty innocuous now; all the same, a recent history of the musical describes the piece as "strident and leftish" so the creators must have been doing something -- you should pardon the expression -- right. Anyway, it ran for years, and the score took over the English-speaking world. In 54 and 55 you couldn't turn on the radio without hearing Hey There, the show's best ballad; and I can testify that when the show came to London, a coffee bar immediately opened just down the road from my school calling itself Hernandos Hideaway, after the shows main mambo. That, for those days, was clout.

Simon Callow's new British production (on a detour to Toronto between dates in Birmingham and London) is in intention a tribute to, and crystallization of, the high spirits of those sedately brash mid-1950s; the show may be a cartoon but the production is a caricature. It's quite an interesting caricature. It boasts eye- popping designs by Frank Stella. The main factory set, an assembly line of sewing-machines, is a stark, witty symphony in black and white with everybody costumed to match. (One character does sport a tiny blue necktie; you can tell hes a cut-up.)

When the action goes outdoors for the workers picnic, the stage explodes in colour: glorious whirling cascades that match the Stella murals and ceiling of the theatre itself.

There's one drop-curtain that the Mirvishes might consider taking legal action to hang onto.

As with sight, so with sound: Rather than the blaring Broadway noise of the '50s, John Harles orchestrations suggest the cool, inventive jazz that made up the periods alternative soundtrack, as if Gil Evans had scored The Pajama Game rather than Porgy and Bess for a collaboration with Miles Davis. The treatment demands singers who can track the original tunes through a luxuriant jungle of accompaniment and the two leads here really deliver. Graham Bickley is the best straight-arrow leading-man to appear in years; he acts with authority, displays the occasional glint of humour, and sings like an especially resilient lark; his falsetto ending to Hey There is a wonder. As intended, Camilla Scott is more standard-issue musical comedy, but she has great vivacity and has improved immeasurably since Crazy for You.

But even some of the production's merits work against it. The designs upstage the performers, and the sophisticated arrangements may prevent the songs from landing as forcefully as they should.

Numbers that should, on the face of it, stop the show play to polite applause. Some of this is due to David Bintley's choreography; he stages the duets nicely but his ensemble numbers dont build. For the picnic number, Once a Year Day, he steps outside the shows spiritual boundaries and takes us into Grease territory with a lot of energetic but random jiving. Still, this is at least another aspect of the '50s.

When Hernando's becomes a leather-bar and the shows dancing soubrette (Alison Therese Limerick), a 70s soul-singer, the production is well outside even its own rules. It is admittedly tough to stage the Steam Heat number, which only exists for Bob Fosse's choreography, in a town that recently saw a re-creation of the original.

The Pajama Game by the way must be the only show to boast four superdirectors on its original creative team; apart from Fosse it had George Abbott as co-author and director, Jerome Robbins as choreographer's babysitter, and the infant Hal Prince as producer. Apparently it wasnt too many cooks.)

Apart from the two leads and a couple of old reliables (Anita Dobson as a secretary, Peter Edbrook as the heroines dad) nobody in this revival is believable. The boss (John Levitt) is a puffing, gyrating buffoon, his main antagonist (Jonathan D. Ellis) an exaggeratedly preening narcissist, so bang goes the conflict; even the labour hymn, Seven and a Half Cents, which is well staged, doesn't mean much. John Hegley, the main comic, is a hyperactive performer who apparently can make his face, voice and body do anything except be funny. However much you may love a show's style, you cannot do it justice by neglecting to play its substance. I suspect that Callow, a fine actor and uniquely astute theatrical commentator, would in other circumstances be the first to acknowledge this.

But no man ever sees his own work through the same eyes as he sees everyone elses; and none of us could survive if we did.

Runs until July 24. Box office: 416-872-1212.

1999-07-01-down-down-he-comes-glistening:
RICHARD II

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

The most celebrated speech that Shakespeare gave to his Richard II is the one in which this king of England embraces defeat. He has learned that, while he was off campaigning in Ireland, his cousin Henry Bolingbroke has returned from banishment and, backed by the most powerful nobles, seems all set to replace him on the throne -- which, as Henry IV, he duly does. Ostentatiously spurning his followers' attempts at consolation, Richard embarks on the famous aria about sitting upon the ground and telling sad stories of the death of kings.

It is a tribute to Geordie Johnson's performance and to the intelligence of Martha Henry's direction that they can make this well-worn anthology piece the living centre of the evening. When this Richard sits on the ground, the image radiates outward; horizontal contact with the Earth is a leitmotif of this production.

Earlier in the same scene, with disaster hovering but not yet present, we have seen him prostrating himself and embracing the soil of his kingdom -- a sacramental gesture that embarrasses his friends by being at once monstrously self-indulgent and painfully sincere.

Earlier still, in his glory days, we have seen him lolling on carpets, living out a gay story about the life of a king. I use the adjective advisedly; Shakespeare himself used it by happy historical accident, making repeated references to "gay apparel" that now ring with prophetic irony. In this production, a figure we initially took for Richard's queen turns out to be one of his male favourites in drag. More intriguingly, Richard seems physically fascinated by the cool, stolid cousin who eventually supplants him; both when sending Bolingbroke off into single combat at the play's beginning and when handing him the crown at its climax, he clasps him an embrace that lasts considerably longer than etiquette would demand.

The death-of-kings speech culminates in the now proverbial image of the hollow crown, its wearer constantly mocked by his own mortality. It sends Johnson's Richard into a kind of trance, one in which he remains until his death. The text calls for him to come down from the battlements of Flint Castle in order to confront his enemy; "down, down I come, like glistering Phaethon" is his own operatic response to this request. This production's simple platform of a set can only afford him a modest flight of steps, but he descends it, zig-zag fashion, as if enacting a personal ritual, briskly self-mocking and deadly serious.

Within his own dream he is perfectly lucid, perfectly in control. "Hath Bolingbroke deposed thine intellect?" asks his queen (the real one this time) at their last meeting. No, he emphatically hasn't; this Richard retains to the last the ability to talk and think rings around everyone else in the kingdom.

This means that when reality hits him, it hits hard. His turning- point is a simple and brilliantly realized single line: "Set on towards London" he says, as one accustomed to giving orders. Nobody moves. He turns to Bolingbroke, and asks pitifully for his endorsement: "Cousin, is it so?" And at that moment everybody knows who's won.

Vocally, Johnson is remarkably fluent, and his ability to take any number of lines on a single breath -- very useful for the baroquely loquacious Richard -- speeds the play excitingly along. He only seems able, though, to hit a limited variety of notes; anger escapes him, and so do the full depths of Richard's irony, especially when directed at the successor whom he should embarrass on to the throne.

Physically he is a fair-haired boy dressed, with presumably purposeful anachronism, in white singlet and shiny silver pants (everyone else is unobtrusively mediaeval) -- a pointed contrast to John Dolan's practical Bolingbroke, who is grey and balding and interestingly ambiguous about the extent of his own ambition. (He is still equivocating on the subject at his death, two history plays later.)

The real dirty work here falls to his aide Northumberland, played by Robert King as a mixture of flatterer, which he has to work at, and unscrupulous hit man, which he doesn't.

The production also offers a new and effective reading of Richard's queen, usually presented as his contemporary; historically, though, she was a child and she is played here as -- or at least by -- a 16-year-old, who playfully perches on her husband's throne while his back is turned. This makes very credible both the king's oddly distanced affection for her and his boyfriends' head-patting solicitude toward her while he is away.

Technically, the actress (Maggie Blake) is not up to the lines, but the price is worth paying: The scene in which she learns of her husband's downfall is better interpreted than I have ever known it, with the gardener (Richard McMillan) who breaks the news movingly convincing as both man and messenger. The episode begins with a lady- in-waiting offering to play at bowls; and the bowling ball becomes the symbolic focus of the scene.

The director makes equally resourceful use of the mirror that Richard, a mean man with an image, smashes at his abdication.

The production takes time to hit its stride; the first half is clogged by cliches: baronial stomping, offstage monastic chanting, and much anonymous emoting by actors who plainly know that they are angry about something but haven't figured out precisely what. After the interval, Richard comes into his own, even while losing it, and the play comes with him.

- In repertory until Sept. 25. Box office: 1-800-567-1600.

1999-07-02-second-city-provides-a-day-at:
NUDE BEACH WEAR: 100% OFF

The Second City, Toronto

It was some time during the Trudeau era, when I was a mere visitor to Toronto, that I first took in a Second City revue. I was impressed, to the point of hysteria. A couple of years later I returned, and the magic had flown; perhaps I had gone sour but I think it's likelier that they had gone off.

Revisiting the organization for their 46th show, I find that equilibrium has been restored. There are no signs of comic genius on show, but there is a good level of competence and invention. The six writer-performers are all agreeable, and seem to enjoy one anothers company: just as well, since there are very few solos. Kevin Dorffs direction shows them off with unobtrusive efficiency.

The title Nude Beach Wear: 100% Off (or, Hanlan's Don't Point) is fairly funny for a start (though the bit in brackets isnt). Its even relevant, since the closing song is actually about Toronto's nude beach. It's the only extended musical sequence in the show. Its also about the worst thing in it. Its hard of course to cut a title song and leave your show without a hook, but maybe they should go ahead and do it. Nobody would care; improvised revue -- Second City do not, alas, improvise in performance but presumably they still do in rehearsal -- has always thrived on inconsequentiality.

The first-half closer, on the other hand, is a high point: a Ms. Millennium competition played out between Miss America, who is brassy and supremely self-confident and refuses to let the compere finish his sentences, Miss Rest of the World, who has two invisible children at her breast and who builds onstage an equally invisible hut with accommodation for eight families, and Miss Canada, who lollops into view, is chronically self-deprecatory and waves her hand with supreme listlessness but who takes a vicious mile as soon as someone gives her a generous inch. (Now, is this display of worm- turning acute self-satire or just poignant wish-fulfillment?)

This sketch has the texture that comes from functioning effectively on two levels: as broad political satire (Miss C gives thanks to Petro Canada-- whoever thought that an oil company could regulate a whole government?) and as narrow entertainment lampoon, with the oleaginous host flanked by a pair of overflowingly celebratory show dancers billed as the Dancing Homosexuals: a coming- out that was long overdue.

Not much else in the show qualifies as political, though there is a token jab at the Harris government ("things will be hard -- then they'll just be difficult") and I guess you could count an episode in which each member of the cast murders another, all of them hoping to secure the reversion of the others' welfare cheques.

But then, as that scene reminds us, the personal is political and this show is plenty personal. Its very much into relationships. These can be marital. In the shows opening number, one of its best, a husband is dismayed to find that Carol, his wife's old friend from nursing college, is actually a man by that name, just back from a tour of duty in Somalia that seems to have been rewarding financially and in other ways (you give them their inoculations and their faces just light up).

They can be extra-marital, as in a masochistic blues that includes the memorable simile "love is like a sausage -- you don't want to see it being made." They can even be fraternal: In one scene, -- the best-written in the evening -- a teenager beseeches her gay, and somewhat shocked, older brother for helpful hints on how to administer fellatio. (Never blow, he advises urgently, "it's a misnomer.") Or they can be a matter of group dynamics; three couples go into ecstasies of competitiveness over a new parlour game.

The dominating presence in the cast is Lee Smart, who has a smooth, rotund demeanour and very emphatic teeth, which he flashes to particular effect as the Pope, communicating with his Canadian flock through minimalist and somewhat esoteric mime.

Balancing his expressive placidity, we have the equally expressive edginess of Melody Johnson, who excels at playing women (and one cat) who are either repressed or aggressive. (As Miss Canada, she gets to be both.) The other women are Tracy Dawson, who is usefully exuberant, and Mary Pat Farrell, who is usefully controlled. The other men are Gavin Crawford, who is economically wry, and Doug Morency, whose specialty is a homespun smirk.

Many of the numbers have trouble finding a punchline: a condition common in revues, and also in reviews.

TORONTO FRINGE FESTIVAL

It's a funny old world we live in, and it's been that way for quite some time. That seems to be the message of this year's Toronto Fringe Festival, though admittedly these conclusions are based on a sampling (three shows out of more than 90) that lacks something in scientific rigour.

Back in 1978, apparently, the whole town was talking about The Jones Boy, a play by Tom Walmsley that, in revival, looks as if it were written yesterday. That is not necessarily a compliment. It takes a stern effort of historical imagination to realize that in its day this was not just another despairing play about pimps and prostitutes caught in a spiral of violence and addiction; it was, perhaps, the first -- the first in Canada anyway.

Twenty years on, it might still pack a fair punch in a suitably claustrophobic setting. For now, though, it's been deposited on the stage of a movie theatre (the Bloor Cinema, 506 Bloor Street West), a space that amounts to a narrow strip of platform confronting a cavernous auditorium.

Of the two male leads, one (Adrian Churchill) hardly concerns himself with anything as mundane as projection; the other (Shaun Smyth) makes only a weaselly kind of impact. They play a pair of junkies -- one is a bully disguised as a weakling, the other vice versa -- living off their female partners. Both of them are foredoomed victims, and neither writing nor performance can escape the dreary determinism of it all. (It's certainly true to life, but that's no consolation.)

The girls have more individuality, not to mention jobs that get them out of the house, and, therefore, more interest. One (Deborah Hay) has the tough resilience that comes with a narrow focus; the other (Brooke Johnson) has a tremulous sensitivity suggesting the kind of hooked hooker that the young Judy Garland might have played, had MGM ever countenanced such a thing.

The estimable Tom McCamus makes what amounts to a guest-star appearance as a falling-down-drunk client. (At some performances, this role is played by the equally estimable David Fox). His sprawling resentment sets off a chain reaction that results in the death of one character and the terminal desolation of most of the others.

The violence is random, but in retrospect it seems inevitable; the author has shown it built into every facet of the characters' lives and relationships.

Structurally, the play is an achievement, but it remains a genre piece, even if it invented the genre. It's being touted as a Canadian classic, but in the Canadian theatre, classic status comes cheap. It's a title bestowed on any play that makes it into a second production.

By that criterion, Mysterium Tremendum (at the Poor Alex, 296 Brunswick Ave.) will probably be a classic by this time next year.

It's written by Anton Piatigorsky and directed by Chris Abraham, who took home sacks of Dora Awards for their previous collaboration, Easy Lenny.

The new one is a piece of apocalyptic whimsy that taps right into our current discontents and may even start a few of its own. A serial killer is at large in the city (Which city? Don't ask.) and he strikes sometimes with a gun, sometimes with a knife, which in this production is the size of a sword; this is not your naturalistic drama. His victims include a priest, a young man who eats excrement and his understandably disenchanted girlfriend, a couple of street people and the detectives who are on the case. They make frequent reappearances after their deaths, sometimes escorted by a creepy celestial pair known as the Bald Archangels, who eventually cart everyone off to heaven: everyone, that is, except the two homeless.

The killer, meanwhile, is a yuppie lawyer; nobody can say this play isn't loaded with social comment. It also takes a broader view: A photographer wanders through the action, reflecting on the atrocious scenes she has encountered all over the world and, indeed, all down the ages, as far back as the attack on Troy.

The more you consider the piece the more meretricious and derivative it seems; but it goes with an undeniable swing, propelled by snappy staging, a few genuinely funny lines, and a couple of excellent performances.

Michael Waller is very smooth as the murderer; Jim Jones is beautifully witty as a pained sensitive Jewish cop, the first one I recall since George Segal in No Way To Treat a Lady.

A yuppie and an artist come into further conflict in Hot August Night (at the Helen Gardiner Phelan Playhouse, 79A St. George St.) They are brother and sister, reunited at a morgue to identify their father's body. They express their mingled love and resentment of one another and of their parents, sometimes by means of flashbacks. These demonstrate that people with tedious presents are likely to have had equally tedious pasts.

The intended tone seems to be mordant banter concealing unspeakable pain but relieved by tenderness; the actors cruise through it with their autopilots unwaveringly set to "sensitive."

One of them is the play's author, Teresa Pavlinek, who has given herself an opening monologue that promises better than what follows. The other, Jonathan Wilson, is also an author, though not of this play; he wrote last season's promising Kilt. He is additionally credited with "additional wisdom," which seems to me to speak unintended volumes.

- The Toronto Fringe plays all over the Annex until July 11. Check listings and leaflets for performance times. Box office (416)- 862-2222.

THE MADRAS HOUSE

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

A 90-year-old play that flashes prophetically, The Madras House is about the flesh-and-fantasy market and its impact on both sexes. The Shaw Festival has been steadily working through the canon of Harley Granville Barker, the all-round theatrical genius of the Edwardian period, and this is his masterpiece.

Its plot concerns the takeover by a U.S. company, in the first decade of this century, of a British drapery firm, specializing in ladies' fashions. There is also a sub-plot, centring on one of the drapers' female employees who has scandalized her paternalistic bosses by being unmarried and pregnant and refusing to act ashamed of it. Neither of these tales, though, is exactly mined for suspense; the takeover is a foregone conclusion and the fallen- woman narrative is confined to the second of the play's four acts. Barker was always more interested in ideas and patterns than in story.

He also had a highly developed musical sense and this play is his triumph in the art of theme-and-variations. You feel that if it were possible, he would have turned it into a fugue, staging the scenes simultaneously, cross-cutting and highlighting motifs. As it stands, it's a kind of intellectual collage, and Neil Munro's production is a sophisticated essay in verbal and visual cross-reference.

The Madras House is the flagship store; its founder, Constantine Madras, has grown rich by feeding -- and breeding -- the sartorial dreams of prosperous women and, even more crucially, the erotic dreams of prosperous men. An intelligent sensualist, Constantine has long tired of his trade and is retiring to the Middle East, there to adopt Islam and polygamy, the latter pretty much a rationalization of his existing lifestyle.

His son, Philip, wants out of the business for opposite reasons: A puritan, he is revolted by the contrast between the beauty and the luxury of his own social world and the misery and poverty everywhere else. He, accordingly, proposes to stand for election to the London County Council. (A revolutionary he ain't.) The only character to appear in every one of the play's four milieux, he can function in all of them and is at home in none, even though the last is his own house.

First, we see him in the suburban villa of the Huxtables. Mr. Huxtable runs the more down-market of the Madras House's two branches. He has a domineering and partially disabled wife and six grown, unmarried daughters. He also accommodates Philip's mother, Constantine' s long-abandoned wife.

The air reeks of male bafflement and female frustration: the atmosphere of a society that sees no role for respectable women but marriage, and leaves them miserable, both within and without it.

Act two takes us to the Huxtable shop, whose workers live on the premises in a cross between a boarding school and a model prison. Miss Chancellor, who presides implacably over their physical and moral well-being, has caught the dishonoured Miss Yates in the embrace of a timorous male employee whose wife (another dragon lady, constantly on the verge of hysteria) has now come to demand an official admission that her husband cannot be the errant father. Philip tries, conscientiously, to sort all this out.

In act three, we are at the heart of the Madras empire -- a West End hot-house where models parade the latest creations (some of them, in this production, more revealing than the period warrants) as a divertissement from the central business of the sale. The combination of financial and sexual stimulation sends the Yankee tycoon into prophetic transports. He has seen the future and it sells; he might be a retail Ziegfeld (was Barker aware of this, his polar opposite among showmen?) preparing to glorify the American woman.

Finally, we reach the domestic Madras house. Philip's parents have one last meeting: bitter and clinging on her side, urbanely dismissive on his. Philip tries to come to an accommodation with Jessica, his beautiful and cultured wife, the incarnation of everything that both attracts and disturbs him. They agree "to meet halfway:" on the marriage bed, anxiously watched -- as in a hallucination -- by everyone else in the play. This is the director's idea, and a good one. The stage, in Peter Hartwell's design, is backed by a wall of glass, sometimes a mirror, sometimes a transparent screen. The women are likely to be seen behind it, as if they, too, even the elegant Jessica, were mannequins, preparing to parade.

In a related visual pun, the Huxtable daughters crouch and scamper about, like the veiled inhabitants of Constantine's unseen seraglio. One of them ends the first scene cradling a dead pet frog: the nearest she gets to love.

Munro habitually builds the action round a central seated figure. Sometimes, as with the bigoted, swivelling Mrs. Huxtable (Donna Belleville), he overplays his hand. He does so even more when he turns the American (Douglas E. Hughes) into a laughingstock by having him orate into a megaphone. (This sequence begs for applause and, at the preview I saw, got it -- a besetting sin of the Shaw Festival and its audience.) On the other hand, he brilliantly brings off a scene in which Philip and his best friend, the play's exemplar of what the American calls "the mean sensual man," go walkabout, circling one another in wary incomprehension.

Both these roles are excellently played, with Blair Williams' Philip a lucid focus for the play's pinwheel galaxy, and Ben Carlson giving full value to the conventional intelligence of his pal: an ex- officer now reduced to eunuch in the fashionable harem.

Mr. Huxtable, beginning conscientiously if painfully to explore the world outside of trade, is a role that the genial Michael Ball could probably play in his sleep: To his credit, he keeps himself and us fully awake. Constantine can be an exotic star role (Paul Scofield played it in a London revival); Peter Millard's performance is decidedly plain, even shabby, but this has its advantages. There is no danger of him walking off with the play.

The women are generally less happy in their roles (which may, of course, fit the play's thesis): Jillian Cook, pointedly marooned in a corner, conveys something but not everything of Mrs. Madras' wasted life, while Philippa Domville gives us Jessica's glamour but not her brain. Shauna Black, though, is electric as Miss Yates, calmly confronting single parenthood, and Laurie Paton equally assured as Miss Chancellor, the proud, elderly singleton.

The play is periodically frozen by the director's taped reading of the author's elaborate stage directions. This is one aid we don't need: The text may be diffused, but the staging has centred it.

- The Madras House in repertory until September 26. Box office: 1- 800-511-SHAW.

ROCK AND ROLL

The Dream in High Park, Toronto

John Gray's Rock and Roll is another of those Canadian theatre classics that make you wonder where the audiences of 20 years ago got their standards. The combined charms of an open-air setting and a cheerful and dedicated cast make this revival moderately entertaining. All the same . . .

The show depicts the 1980 reunion, in an archetypal small Nova Scotia town called Mushaboom, of a four-man band called the Monarchs who 20 years before had torn up the Maritimes. They were adolescents then; now they're confronting the frustrations of early middle-age. Manny (Paul Braunstein) has inherited a retail empire that owns half the town but his wealth, as he repeatedly explains, has not made him happy.

Chink (Randy Kempf) was, and has remained, a drifter. Brent (Jonathan Whitaker) has a career in insurance which bores him, and is married to Shirley (Mary Ellen Mahoney) who used to hang out with the group, hoping vainly to be given a chance to sing.

The fourth man, Parker, is the only one to have stayed in the music business where he now makes an unglamorous living as an all- purpose entertainer. Here life and art begin to converge. The Monarchs are based on an actual band called the Lincolns, one of whose members, Frank MacKay, created the role of Parker in Rock and Roll's original 1981 production. He plays it again now, giving us nostalgia in two dimensions.

The format of the show, as you would expect, is that the regrouped group reminisce about their former life and start acting it out before our eyes. It's made clear -- and indeed we can hear it for ourselves -- that until Parker joined them, the Monarchs were terrible. When he auditions with a song called The Fat Boy (everybody has a problem, and that's his) the temperature rises vertically. MacKay sings and cavorts with raucous attractiveness, and propels the group through the inevitable final sequence: the triumphant reunion concert itself.

Even this, though, doesn't exactly lift the audience out of its seats: and for a fairly obvious reason. We have seen plenty of shows recently in which a biography culminated in a final unmediated sequence of show-stopping songs. There was Jolson and, before that, Buddy. I recall a one-man opus about Hank Williams, and a long- running British show titled John, Paul, George, Ringo . . . and Bert, which structurally was like Rock and Roll but had the benefit of being about a rather more interesting group. All these, of course, had their audience's memories ready primed; they concerned real performers who sang songs that we knew before we came. John Gray has to create his own nostalgia as he goes along: a fearsome task and one that neither his words nor his music are up to fulfilling.

The book and score of a musical are supposed to be mutually enhancing; here they seem to be mutually accusing. Each expects the other to do the work. Parker, on the verge of leaving both the band and the town, sings a song about his parents: Two people whom we haven't met and of whom, up to this point, we haven't even heard. There is a long sequence showing how Brent and Shirley, like any other teenagers, used to make out in his car. Big deal. Shirley periodically reiterates her wish to perform; she sings songs about wanting to sing songs. (I don't know how they kept her out; she looks like she could eat them for breakfast.) There's nothing else to her. In fact, all the characters are static.

Then again, no sooner has the group achieved success by taking on Parker than it begins to fall apart; we hardly see the band in its glory so we have no real reason to root for them.

There is one other character: a role-model rock-and-roller called Screamin' John McGee (Michael Blake) who teaches the boys the rudiments of their craft, and hangs around afterwards, commenting at great length -- in arch rhyming couplets and worse prose -- on the travails of youth: first love, first hangover. Even his early death doesn't free us from him, since much of the second act takes place (shades of Our Town) in the local graveyard.

There are a couple of sweet tunes, and the occasional neat line of lyric or dialogue. The basic themes -- the persistence and the erosion of youthful dreams, the importance of music to people who have no particular aptitude for it -- remain both potent and poignant; though they were far more elegantly handled in the recent Two Pianos -- Four Hands.

Katherine Kaszas' direction is not, to put it kindly, over- inventive, but it does convey some affection for the material, and the actors seem happy to be there, all of which helps.

- Rock and Roll runs until Aug. 22.
