THE PLAYS THE THING

Soulpepper Theatre Company

Three cigarettes glow in the dark. Then the lights go up on a trio of dinner-jacketed men in what appears to be a drawing-room, one sparsely, but elegantly, furnished and dominated by a great gilt mirror. The men, who seem to be theatricals, speculate on the difficulties of getting a play started; if this were a play, how would they convey the situation to the audience?

By way of answering their own question, they embark on some bald- faced exposition from which we learn that the room is in a chateau and that its inhabitants are two middle-aged dramatists and a young composer who are collaborating on an operetta and are here to present its script to their leading lady, who also happens to be the composer's beloved.

It's a magnificently cheeky opening, though it may make you wonder whether the author can possibly keep it up. He can.

The Plays the Thing was written in the 1920s by the Hungarian grand boulevardier Ferenc Molnar; the English adaptation is by P.G. Wodehouse, whose dialogue here has all the buoyancy and wit of his best stories plus a sharper edge. (When Wodehouse, who was also a first-rate lyricist, opted for prose fiction, the theatre may have lost a great comic playwright.)

The chateau turns out to have this wall; our heroes can hear their star, in the next room coquetting with a former lover apparently unwilling to settle for being former. The adoring musician, vulnerable and idealistic, is prostrated; and his colleagues are alarmed. Not only is their friends happiness at stake; so, if he should do something desperate, are their careers.

Turai, the senior partner in the playwriting firm, has an idea: He will pretend that the overheard assignation was the rehearsal of a play. All he has to do is write the rest of the script, which he accomplishes in a couple of hours before breakfast, and blackmail the guilty pair into playing along, which he managers in a couple of minutes after it. The full rehearsal of his play pretty much constitutes the last act of our play, and it is dazzling: a consummate piece of figure skating that sounds the occasional deeper note as the characters' inner and outer roles intersect. The dog- eared (and much overrated) themes of art-and-life, reality-and- illusion, are here accorded precisely the amount of mocking seriousness they deserve.

This production is the Soulpepper company's third venture, following Don Carlos and Our Town, into the territory of famous plays we hardly ever get to see; and it is a triumphant as its predecessors.

The actors have engaged a Hungarian director, Laszlo Marton, and he has kept them on an exhilaratingly tight rein. The play presents an absurd action, executed with the utmost suavity, and it demands the same degree of pose from its players; the balance here is almost perfect.

The evenings predominant flavour is the dry sparkle of Diego Matamoros Turai. Contemplating disaster with one hand in his pocket and the other cradling his specs, he is the drawing-room playwright as god: a controlling presence who never raises his voice.

William Webster, playing pompous, and Mike Shara, playing naive, make two fine foils; while Michael Hanrahan as a Magyar major-domo (a transplanted Jeeves, perhaps) almost matches the maestro in imperturbability. Their scenes together are a contest in cool.

The only performer who falls short is Karen Robinson as the diva of Budapest, trying hard for an authority that must come effortlessly or not at all; in her presence, Matamoros is reduced to playing straight man to a non-existent fireworks display. (The lady's sincere moments are fetching, but there isn't much call for those.)

There is gorgeous compensation, though, from C. David Johnson as Almady, her overweening paramour, an ageing matinee idol forced mercilessly into acting out his own follies; his humiliation may seem a little protracted, but both the text and the actor keep uncovering new abysses, new reserves. They even provide a moral, if morality is your thing.

There is also a gem of a small performance from Jim Warren as Mell, the castle secretary, temporarily and very conscientiously in charge of props.

The production is masterfully staged, every visual and verbal joke precisely timed, on an economically splendiferous set by Julie Fox. I have said that Turai tosses off his impromptu masterpiece before breakfast; the meal is served on-stage and its a corker, lovingly itemized and confirming my long-cherished belief that the Central European drama is the only drama that knows how to eat. It figures; the play is a feast.

- In repertory at Premiere Dance Theatre until Aug. 28. Box office: (416) 973-4000.

1999-07-19-theatre-is-the-thing-in-small:
Toronto is, or so it keeps telling us, the third most important theatrical city in North America, but -- by some quirk of fate or the tourist industry -- Canada's two most prestigious theatres lie well outside the city. In 1953 it was decided that a town called Stratford -- one standing on a River Avon, no less -- just naturally had to have its own Shakespeare festival. So, from an initial short season of two plays, the current Stratford Festival has grown into a seven-month festival, spread over three theatres, and possessing the de facto status of a national theatre. Like all national theatres, it attracts reverence and revulsion in equal -- and, in all fairness, equally unmerited -- proportions.

Meanwhile, in another part of Ontario, the second greatest British dramatist has been allotted his own playground. There are no ties of name or fame linking Bernard Shaw to Niagara-on-the-Lake but, 30 years ago, an enthusiast decided to stage a couple of his plays there, and that idea, too, has developed into a full-scale triple-staged festival.

Neither theatre is exclusively committed to the canon of its patron saint. Niagara confines itself, by self-chosen mandate, to plays written during Shaw's lifetime. (Next year they're expanding to include plays set in that time-span, but written later.) Since Shaw, the prophet of longevity, lived for nearly one hundred years, from the mid-19th century to that of the 20th, they have a wide -- and still pretty accessible -- field to choose from. It's far narrower, though, than Stratford's; the whole world repertoire is, theoretically, their oyster; and it must be agonizing wondering where to start. Not unnaturally, a season at Niagara will always appear more homogeneous than a season at Stratford.

There are other reasons for this. Both theatres have a reliable core of actors who return there year after year, but the permanent Shaw ensemble is larger and more faithful. (I should add that the kind of continuity you find at both companies would be the envy of the institutional theatres in Britain, and is unheardof in the United States.) There is a pervasive note of intelligent urbanity at Shaw, stemming both from the personality and the philosophy of its director Christopher Newton. For a director primarily concerned with very loquacious plays, Newton has a rich, painterly visual sense, a quality shared by his most regular colleagues, Jim Mezon and Neil Munro. All three of them -- like Stratford's director, Richard Monette -- began their careers as actors, and they still appear occasionally or, in Mezon's case, frequently.

There are two Shaw plays in this season's repertoire, both discussion pieces, both imaginatively presented. Heartbreak House, in some respects Shaw's masterpiece, is this year's flagship production on the main Festival stage, given a somewhat expressionist production by a visiting Polish director, Tadeusz Bradecki. The play's subject, according to its author, is "cultured, leisured Europe before the [First World] War," oblivious of the coming cataclysm and represented, somewhat whimsically, by an eccentric English family, presided over by a prophetic, absent- minded and extremely ancient mariner, composed of flirts and dreamers and confronted by cheats and money-grubbers who prove to be almost equally ineffectual. After three acts of finely orchestrated verbal music, the play concludes in the cacophony of an air raid, summoned up with majestic force. Douglas Rain makes a lightweight job of Captain Shotover, Shaw's home-brewed King Lear, but Sarah Orenstein is both commanding and bewitching as his number one daughter.

The same actress also dominates Getting Married, potentially Shaw's most tiresome play, an unabashed gabfest that is dated in many of its details. Some of it, though, remains pertinent; and Jim Mezon, directing at the small Court House Theatre, has cunningly staged the whole thing as an extended verbal dance. Individual performances vary markedly but the ensemble effect is excellent.

For some years now the Festival has been exploring the plays of Shaw's friend and contemporary Harley Granville Barker. This year they have arrived at his most substantial piece, The Madras House. Like Getting Married, this is less a story than a series of dialogues on relations between the sexes; like all Barker's plays it is more demanding than Shaw's, less funny, more complex and elusive, in many ways more modern. Neil Munro has directed it, barring a few gaffes, with great sensitivity to its musical theme-and-variations quality, and he gets especially good performances from an old Shaw regular, Michael Ball, and a newer one, Blair Williams.

The same director is responsible for the Festival's most successful all-round production this year, the 1930s Broadway hit You Can't Take It With You, by Moss Hart and George S. Kaufman, in which a joyous cast revolves around a wonderfully understated central performance by Bernard Beh- rens: a rare case at Niagara of a leading role being entrusted to an actor completely new to the company. Another play about a crazy escapist family (it actually owes a lot to Heartbreak House though it takes a far more benevolent view of the phenomenon it depicts) it is the kind of sturdy middlebrow piece in which a crack company, nurtured on sterner stuff, can reveal unsuspected riches. It leaves the repertory this week, so hurry.

The Shaw Festival extends the same unpatronizing care to the thrillers and musicals that nestle at the edges of its repertoire: this year Rebecca, and A Foggy Day, the latter being a cheerful if somewhat haphazard collection of Gershwin songs gathered around the plot of an old Fred Astaire movie.

This show's director, Kelly Robinson, is also responsible for this season's major musical, West Side Story, and the contrast is instructive. Musicals at Niagara are modest crowd-pleasers (A Foggy Day is back for its second year); at Stratford they are cash-cows, produced on a large scale and performed mainly by specialists -- which means a splintering within the company.

This year that price is probably worth paying; West Side Story is an exceptionally exciting production, probably the best musical Stratford has done. A new and smaller show, Dracula -- a sort of mini megamusical -- has closer casting ties to the rest of the season, but has little else to recommend it.

This is magic year at Stratford: Macbeth, one of this season's heroes, speaks of "supernatural soliciting" and a firm of supernatural solicitors seems to have advised on the choice of repertoire.

Dracula is one example; another is Ben Jonson's The Alchemist, a very great and very difficult Jacobean comedy that here unfolds in an undisciplined sprawl across the main Festival stage; it might have done better in the more concentrated environment of the Tom Patterson, Stratford's third and smallest theatre. Three of this year's four Shakespeares are fairy stories.

A Midsummer Night's Dream, being both dauntingly delicate and wearisomely familiar, is the hardest of all plays to make fresh, and Richard Monette's production hasn't managed it. The Tempest has Canada's pre-eminent Shakespearean, William Hutt, as Prospero, a valedictory performance in the greatest of valedictory roles. It's stirring as an event and as an interpretation, and something at least of Hutt's virtuosity conveys itself to the rest of Monette's production. Diana Leblanc's small-scale production of Macbeth has attracted a mysterious amount of hostility, and it does have its oddities; but it is immensely exciting with many scenes of stunning immediacy, among them Martha Henry's account of Lady Macbeth's sleep- walking.

This actress also directs the year's remaining Shakespeare, an extremely intelligent Richard II with a king (Geordie Johnson) who has his limitations but is very effective within them.

That leaves two shows: a dramatization of Pride and Prejudice, which is pretty but pointless, and -- at the opposite extreme -- Glenn, a taxing but rewarding collage in which four actors split the life and personality of Glenn Gould between them, and the audience tries to put it together again.

Stratford is patchy where Shaw is smooth; a distinction that says something about the two festivals' given policies, something about their methods of implementing them, and something, too, about the qualities of Shakespeare and Shaw themselves, qualities that seem to communicate themselves to the other plays that come into their respective orbits. It interests me that the two finest productions I have seen at Stratford in recent years have been Diana Leblanc's versions of Eugene O'Neill's Long Day's Journey into Night and Anton Chekhov's The Cherry Orchard, two shows possessed of a depth and turbulence that I would be surprised to encounter in Niagara though both plays fall within that theatre's mandate. Anyway, we need both; we need heroic emotion and we need heroic wit, and we need them both on the continuing basis that only organizations on this scale can provide.

1999-07-20-next-stop-heartbreak-and-dest:
A STREETCAR NAMED DESIRE

du Maurier Theatre Centre, Toronto

Like Hamlet, A Streetcar Named Desire is full of quotations. Tennessee Williams' play contains, in fact, an unfair proportion of the most famous lines in mid-20th-century drama from Blanche du Bois sometimes theres God so quickly" as she melts in the arms of the first man in years who seems likely to respect her, to her final, miraculous "whoever you are -- I have always depended on the kindness of strangers. It's always a shock to hear those much- parodied words in context, and to realize that Blanche speaks them to the doctor who is about to cart her off to a madhouse.

It is an overwhelming finale: the inevitable denouement to a long, tough and compassionate play. In Diana Leblanc's new production for Soulpepper -- thanks to magnificently counterpointed work from everyone on stage, both the involved and the indifferent - - it draws tears. It is also, as tragedy should be, appallingly ironic: Blanche, the faded Southern belle adrift in the lurid squalor of New Orleans, is being incarcerated as a fantasist and a liar. She has, indeed, been both, but what dooms her now is that she has told a truth that nobody wants to believe: that Stanley Kowalski, her brother-in-law, has raped her.

Blanche, on her tram-ride to destruction, says some other memorable things. There is her exhortation to her sister Stella, Stanleys wife, to have some regard for civilization, for art and literature, and not to hang back with the brutes" -- meaning Stanley. There is her declaration to Mitch, her admirer who has requested to see her in the light, that she doesnt want realism, she wants magic, "and if that is a sin, then let me be damned for it." These passages, the second especially, are often taken to be Williams' credo as well as Blanche's; and actresses have accordingly given them the works.

This can be unfortunate since, when isolated, these speeches sound overripe and embarrassing: the progenitors of far worse things in Williams later plays and in American drama in general. One of the great qualities of Fiona Reids Blanche is the way she folds these arias into her characterization; she races them, she argues them, making them means rather than ends. Put another way: She says them, urgently, to the other characters, not to us.

Everything in this Blanche is implied from the moment she sets foot on stage: a primly, fussily elegant overdressed figure wandering into a crowded, noisy, jazz-haunted slum, organdy adrift in a world of blue jeans. This is a fastidious performance of a fastidious character -- or of one so deeply convinced of her own gentility that she can black out any evidence to the contrary. She lives on her nerves and on her very considerable wits: the child of a vanished ancestral home, the bruised survivor of marriage to an idolized husband who killed himself when she discovered his homosexuality, a teacher dismissed from her school for seducing a 17- year-old.

Not all the more lurid aspects of this Blanche's past seem credible at the moment we hear about them; but they fall into place at the end. (Besides, if life and drama teach us anything, it is not to make assumptions about other people's sexuality.) This is a performance alternately feisty and flirtatious, coy and aggressive, one that is sometimes very funny (when she puts on her glasses and lectures people, she takes on a bizarre resemblance to Dame Edna Everage) but is not very moving, not until the very last moment, when it is overwhelming.

The play is in large part a duel between Blanche and Stanley, who suspects and resents her pretentions from the moment she crosses his threshold. Stuart Hughes Stanley is hardly the graceful gorilla immortalized by Marlon Brando (in a performance that has cast a longer shadow than any other in a modern play except, perhaps, Laurence Oliviers in The Entertainer); he is more of a preening, malicious chimp, a relocated Dead End Kid.

The central antagonism is very credible; so are Stanley's outbursts of violence against both his and her sister. But the actor doesn't have the vocal reserves for his more extended scenes -- most crucially, for his relishing revelations of Blanches nymphomaniac reputation in her home town -- and it doesnt help the play's balance that he looks shorter than she does.

Kristen Thomson's Stella, though, is absolutely perfect: practical, sensual, alternately careless and caring -- torn between sympathy for Blanche, passion for Stanley, and loyalty to both. She pretty much sums up the play in her own person. (Hers are the choices her sister never made; she prefers realism to magic, and is saved by it.) Oliver Dennis, though decently shy and well-meaning, finds less in Mitch than his author has provided -- until the climax when his silent disgust makes a powerful contribution.

Invaluable throughout is Maria Vacratsis as the woman upstairs whose marriage parodies, if such a thing is possible, that of the Kowalskis. She is part of the atmosphere -- which in this production, and in Astrid Jansons blue-hued set, is overpowering: lyrical, and austerely compassionate.

I didnt see Leblanc's production of Death of a Salesman but this must be its twin: another sub-section of that mythical post-war America where a person has to dream because, to quote again, it comes with the territory. And, by the way, according to an off-the- cuff remark of Williams' own, Blanche charmed the doctors and was out of that hospital in three weeks flat.

- A Streetcar Named Desire runs until Aug. 28. Box office: (416)- 973-4000.

1999-07-20-shaw-festival-finds-cancon-in:
In repertory until Sept. 25.

S.S. TENACITY

COURT HOUSE THEATRE, Niagara-On-The-Lake

Nobody would accuse the Shaw Festival of being nationalist, but like all this country's cultural institutions, it must occasionally feel some obligation to go digging for Canadian content.

Given the festival's commitment to plays written between 1856 and 1950, this can be a tough prospect, but they have found it this year, most unexpectedly, in a French play from 1920. S.S. Tenacity isn't set in Canada, but it concerns two young men who want to get there. We meet them in a waterside cafe in Normandy, waiting to board the eponymous vessel that will take them across the Atlantic. Its departure has been delayed, and they while away the time drinking with the locals and getting to know the attractive young lady who waits on tables.

The play's author, Charles Vildrac, was -- according to the Festival program, which I take as gospel -- an early proponent of the Theatre of the Unspoken, a movement that arose in Paris after the First World War as a reaction to the rhetorical excesses of earlier generations. This school was to reach its apogee in the plays of Jean-Jacques Bernard in which the drama became so unspoken as to be, to my ears, practically inaudible; and it made something of a comeback in the '50s and after, in the agonizingly rarefied dramas of Marguerite Duras. Vildrac, being a pioneer, is a vulgar exhibitionist by comparison with these later quietists; we have learned to take subtext inour stride, and his storytelling no longer seems especially subtle.

From the moment that our heroes, Segard and Bastien, wartime buddies about to emigrate together from a still-stricken country, set eyes on the fair Therese, it is obvious that they have both fallen for her. When Segard, the shyer of the two, spends a whole scene with her not mentioning it, he might as well, from the audience's point of view, be shouting his passion from the rooftops.

There is an attenuated charm to the play, best captured here in Catherine McGregor's Therese, a sensible but vulnerable girl, swept off by an unexpected passion.

Her suitors receive (from Craig Erickson and Jason Chesworth) somewhat callow performances; there is some poignancy in the outcome, since she chooses the one the audience is less likely to have been rooting for, and rather more when the loser must decide whether to stay on in Normandy, return to Paris, or travel alone to what is continually referred to "as the wilds of Manitoba" -- a choice, we are made uncomfortably aware, between three bleaknesses. At this point the play passes into the keeping of a weather-beaten barfly named Hidoux, whose musings -- both here and earlier -- on the situation and on life in general transport us from the Theatre of the Unspoken to the Theatre of the Positively Garrulous. He tells us that some people get to choose their destinies, but most are just carried along and, if I followed him rightly, that the important thing is to cleave to your fate with conviction. In other words, the S.S. TENACITY is the ship of your life, whether it takes you to Canada or just stays put. And don't think that the winners in love are, over the long haul, necessarily luckier than the losers.

Dennis Garnhum's production is pleasantly atmospheric; he plays both the first and the last moments in French, which gives the evening a much-needed pinch of salt, an intriguingly exotic frame, and a sense of life going relentlessly on according to its own rules and its own rhythms. The cafe seems authentic; you can almost smell the Gauloises.

Al Kozlik enjoys himself rather fulsomely as the bibulous Hidoux but as the kindly, taciturn patronne, Jennifer Phipps is a rock of believability.
1999-07-21-noel-coward-s-woman-with-a-pa:
EASY VIRTUE

Festival Theatre,

Niagara-on-the-Lake

The title Easy Virtue is double-edged. The play, one of this year's mainstage productions at the Shaw Festival, is Noel Coward's 1920s tribute to that old staple of English turn-of-the-century drama, the woman with a past. (Prize exhibits: Arthur Pinero's The Second Mrs Tanqueray and Oscar Wilde's Lady Windermere's Fan.)

On the surface, the title refers to the married lady whose position in high society is destroyed when it is revealed that before her marriage she had sex with someone other than the man who is now her husband. She is more to be pitied than censured -- except, of course, by those born censurers who make up the bulk of her present acquaintance.

In its second sense, the title refers to the puritans and stone- throwers who have come by their sense of moral superiority without in any way earning it.

There are still plenty of them around, but the playing field has changed, and it was already much altered in Coward's own day. His heroine, Larita -- who has lived most of her life in France but has no trace of an accent -- has in her past a marriage, a couple of divorces (one of them her own), and an undisclosed number of lovers.

She has now gotten married for a second time, to a much younger and much less intelligent Englishmen, Johnny Whittaker, who brings her home to meet his very rich and very hidebound family. They live in the kind of gargantuan splendour customary among people whose domestic affairs have to occupy large stages. Even before they meet Larita they disapprove of her; once they have met her, they loathe her.

The difference between Larita and her fin-de-siecle predecessors is that she believes in herself.

Poor Paula Tanqueray in the Pinero play thought deep down that society had a right to ostracize her, and she committed suicide over it. Larita thinks it a lot more appropriate to ostracize society, having first told it what she thinks of it. She does this at considerable and rather enjoyable length in the second and strongest of the play's three acts, after one of her skeletons has fallen out of its closet and her in-laws have attempted to beat her over the head with it.

We cheer her on. We agree with every word she says. That's the problem; Larita is banging on a door that is now completely open and must have been at least ajar when the play was new. Even if these complacent, dance-giving, tennis-playing philistines were as bad as Coward says they are, they must have had something to say for themselves.

But Coward was never good at characters of whom he disapproved, and he never lets this bunch get beyond generalized expressions of shock and disapproval; it may well be true that the prejudiced can do little more than keep repeating their prejudices, but maybe a dramatist, for the sake of conflict, should pretend that they can.

Goldie Semple makes a warm and glamorous impression as Larita, but the lack of effective opposition continually betrays her into over-emphasis -- that and the fact that Coward, much as he loved laying down the law, was never very good at it; Larita's rhetoric keeps buckling under the weight that the actress wants to put on it.

Larita is extremely articulate. The Whittaker family are defined for us by what she says about them, rather than by anything they actually do. We learn that Mrs. Whittaker (Patricia Hamilton being as imperious as the traffic will allow) is blinkered and self- pitying. Her older daughter Marion (sportily played by Kelli Fox in a voice that wears tweeds even if the character doesn't) is a pious backslapper, revolted to find that her new relation reads Proust. Larita does a first-rate demolition job on her, pointing out how both her religion and her heartiness derive from repression -- such a shame this isn't dramatized. Younger daughter Hilda (Fiona Byrne) is a jealous sneak who, when she tries to make up with Larita, is sternly instructed not to be a little toad.

The play ends with a house party at which our heroine, who has been sent to her room in disgrace, makes a spectacular surprise entrance, dripping with jewels. The female Whittakers then stand about sulking, for all the world like Cinderella's stepmother and the Ugly Sisters at the ball. The head of the family, Colonel Whittaker (latest in David Schurmann's line of basically decent chaps), also bears a marked resemblance to Cinders' dad, standing up for her when he can, and absenting himself from the merrymaking in his own home.

John (Kevin Bundy) proves, however, to be no Prince Charming, or rather charming is all he does; stretched between loyalties, he breaks -- but this, too, is underwritten, discussed (with a sensible former sweetheart, attractively played by Glynis Ranney) rather than shown.

Christopher Newton's production, handsomely designed by William Schmuck, has both clarity and sweep. In the aural and visual orchestration of the last act, he is at his showmanly best, bringing the curtain down on a crowd of insanely Charlestoning feet. The message presumably is that Larita goes off and life goes on, not knowing what it's missed.

Frustrating as it is, the play is never boring, and as Coward here is against all the same things as the rest of us, we can at least share in his relish at demolishing them.

- In repertory until Nov. 14. Box office: 1-800-511-7429 Theatre
1999-07-22-delightful-lunchtime-wooing-f:
VILLAGE WOOING

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

The Shaw Festival traditionally tops up its season with a couple of lunchtime productions, one of them drawn from their patron's own considerable corpus of one-act plays. This year's Shavian choice is as good as it gets.

Village Wooing is a comparatively late (1933) Shaw play that recaps, in delightful miniature form, the preoccupations of his best- known full-length comedies. As in Man and Superman and in Pygmalion (at least in the romantic, happy-ending Pygmalion that everyone except Shaw himself is convinced he wrote) a man who considers himself invulnerably self-sufficient finds himself falling into marriage with an irresistibly vital woman. Presumably convinced by now of the universality of his theme, Shaw, this time round, simply called the man A and the woman Z.

A is a widower, a self-proclaimed poet who makes his living churning out travel books with a catchy brand-name; he is, as he confesses with a grimace, "the Marco Polo man." Z is unmarried and works in a village store and post office; she has won some money in a competition and is spending it on a world cruise. Which is how they find themselves sitting side by side on ship (economy class to judge from the deck chairs, which look like instruments of torture) while crossing the Red Sea which, to Z's indignant disappointment, is blue. Her perky, non-stop conversation is a torment to A, who is trying to compose his daily 2,000 words; nevertheless, he cannot stop himself replying.

A second scene finds Z back home minding the store, and A coincidentally dropping by for supplies in the midst of a hiking trip. He has no memory of their previous encounter, but she recalls every detail. By the end of their conversation, she has talked him into buying the business from its current owner and keeping her on as an employee. The third and last scene sees their relationship converted, to nobody's surprise (least of all A's, though he wriggles a bit) from strictly commercial to commercial plus personal; it ends with Z, whose responsibilities include operating the local switchboard, placing a call on her own account: to the church.

The main demands made by the dialogue, as it progresses from A to Z and back again, are for fluency, pace, lucidity and ebullience, with all of which both the players in Nikki Lundmark's production are loaded. Neil Barclay may be a trifle too pettish, but he admirably conveys the writer as philosopher, revelling in the acquisition of knowledge -- knowledge in all spheres and hemispheres, from the glory of Greece to the going price of tea. Camille James, just as inquisitive but less contemplative, gives us a woman possessed by a demon of practicality; once she has set her sights she can be hurt, but not deflected. She is also able to switch delightfully from an English West Country accent (not quite accurate for Wiltshire, where the domestic scenes are set, but never mind) to the bright, clipped BBC tones of a professional telephonist; this is partly a play about love across class barriers, and she is already living out that conflict every day of her working life. (She does not, however, seem oppressed by it; she seems to enjoy ringing the changes.) Both performers, she especially, have the essential trick of playing Shaw: that of hitting humorous climaxes that are also emotional ones. He may be wise, but she is clever; so they need one another.

There is actually a third, silent character: a deck steward (Duncan Stewart) who serves soup by the sea and sticks around to set up the furniture on land, doing both jobs impeccably. The store that he helps usher into existence -- designed by Barbara Gordon -- is a nostalgic delight in itself.

Shaw, socialist though he was, had a passion for commerce; in both writing and presentation, this rural establishment is a visual ode to the days, which may even have existed, when service was personal and unhurried, customers dropped by on bikes and food stood neatly on shelves, actually looking like food, smelling like food, and quite possibly tasting like food when you got it home.

- In repertory until Sept. 19. Box office: 1-800-511-7429
1999-07-24-sharp-shakespeare-among-the-t:
LOVE'S LABOUR'S LOST

Michael Shamata Production

- - -

I doubt if there is a more beautiful setting for drama, anywhere, than the outdoor theatre in Oakville's Coronation Park.

The stage itself is compact and tree-laden; behind it in the middle distance, clearly visible (and audible) is Lake Ontario. Pedestrians and cyclists, glimpsed in the space between, look like part of the action, given that the play itself is likely to be pastoral and the dress modern.

At most open-air shows you wait till half-time, when darkness falls, for magic to descend. In Oakville it's there from the start, though it's certainly augmented in the second act.

And when the play is Love's Labour's Lost, whose comic climax is the most bewitching ever fashioned by Shakespeare or anyone else, we're in velvet.

It's tempting to call it a tragi-comic climax. Four young men -- the King of Navarre and three of his friends -- have spent the bulk of the play wooing four young ladies -- the Princess of France and three of her attendants. There have been plenty of misunderstandings, but all seems set fair for a happy ending. Then news arrives that the princess' father has died, and the sequel is the most abrupt and astonishing gear-change in the whole of Shakespeare. Some of the local inhabitants have been amusing the courtiers with a farcical pageant of the Nine Worthies.

Berowne, most articulate of the King's buddies and the key character of the play, turns on them to underline the moment with audacious explicitness: "Worthies away, the scene begins to cloud." The women tell their suitors to put their passions on ice for 12 months; the men reluctantly agree, though, as Berowne pointedly observes, a year's delay is "too long for a play."

As usual, the women are far more sensible than the men. The king has begun the play by dedicating himself and his circle to three years of study, fasting and celibacy, a vow immediately threatened by the arrival of the princess on a diplomatic mission. Behind the initial folly lies a deeper one.

The play, one of Shakespeare's earliest, both derives from and depicts a society drunk with words; it joins in the verbal game, with great relish, and ends by rejecting it.

Even when they fall in love, the men can't stop playing; that is the women's chief quarrel with them. Berowne, the most clear- sighted of them all and also the jokiest, is condemned by his love, Rosaline, to spend his year's probation entertaining the incurably sick.

Michael Shamata's production, consistently intelligent and inventive, captures a generous proportion of the play's wit, extravagance and sudden sadness. John Jarvis is a masterful Berowne; he handles his great speech of aghast self-revelation ("and I, forsooth, in love") with a drive and control that suggests he might play the great swashbuckling roles (Hotspur, Mercutio, Edmund) that seem to reduce most contemporary actors to dismayed disgust.

He also has one of the archetypal comic scenes; concealed in a tree -- this setting delightfully affords him a real, solid willow - - he smugly surveys each of his associates betraying their vows ("Like a demigod, here sit I in the sky"), before taking the heaviest and most humiliating tumble himself; as a study of too- smart complacency betrayed by passion, he deliciously foreshadows Frasier Crane.

Patrick Galligan makes a charmingly earnest King; Ann Baggley's princess doesn't get much beyond gracious forbearance, but Gina Wilkinson is a striking Rosaline, though she sometimes acts like somebody who has just discovered irony and can't wait to tell you about it.

The other characters who stroll through the royal park of Navarre are Elizabethan types whom this production, without any twisting, makes remarkably recognizable. They, too, are verbally obsessed.

John Blackwood's Don Armado, emphatically Hispanic, is a threadbare adventurer with the nobility of Quixote and the facial hair of Salvador Dali; his page, Moth (Stephen Smith), has the precocious fluency that presumably characterized the child actors of Shakespeare's own day. The schoolmaster Holofernes is marvellously well done by Robert Persichini: riding a bike, sporting a striped cap, dispensing useless learning with an unhurried pomp that arouses the timid local curate (Philip Riccio) to endearing ecstasies of sycophantic admiration.

Some hair's breadth doubling allows two of the courtiers (Shaun Benson, Sandra Forsell) to appear also, and more happily, among rustics; she makes a delightfully blowsy wench. As the clown Costard, the play's natural man, Christopher Morris is vigorous if not especially funny. They all appear to great effect among the Worthies: a scene that's subtler than the parallel charade in A Midsummer Night's Dream because its long-suffering performers are given far more chance to fight back against the carping courtiers. They help take our minds off the mortality and mutability of which the play then so bracingly and movingly reminds us. There are seeds in this play of Shakespeare's later, better-known comedies, though on some things on which he never improved.

Runs until August 14. Box office: 905-815-2021

1999-07-27-rage-against-the-body-s-limit:
ENDGAME

Premiere Dance Theatre

Once upon a time, it was considered the height of theatrical daring for the curtain to be already up when the audience arrived. These days, of course, everybody does it; and, besides, most of our new makeshift playhouses don't even have curtains. To install one is a radical gesture: one that the Soulpepper company have performed for their production of Endgame. This is appropriate since, 42 years after its debut, Samuel Beckett's voyage into the void remains mental shorthand for the avant-garde, an act that nobody -- including its own author -- has ever successfully followed.

The curtain rises in slow, jerky increments, emitting hilarious creaks of protest: a fitting overture for a play that is a searing vision of decay and an elegant theatrical joke. We behold a grey, bare fortress of a room (another splendid design by Julie Fox) pierced by a couple of unreachably high windows. It looks like the end of the world, and may be just that. We seem, anyway, to be in at the aftermath of some kind of cataclysm, possibly nuclear. (Endgame was first staged at the height of the Cold War.) Here live Hamm, his servant Clov, and Hamm's parents, Nagg and Nell, whom he keeps, famously, in garbage cans.

Beckett is notorious for his parsimony with plot and character, but he gets enormous mileage out of what he does provide. He superimposes on his disaster scenario a study of the dynamics of power and of parenthood.

Hamm is blind, crippled and confined to his chair. He relies on Clov for everything and gets away with this because, presumably, he always has; his exercise of authority is unquestioning, if not quite unquestioned. Clov grumbles -- a lot -- and even threatens to leave; at the end, he figuratively has his hat and coat on, which Hamm seems to half resent, half welcome. It will increase his desolation, but he likes desolation. A monster of self-pity (and of other things), he starts the play by asking "Can there be misery loftier than mine?"

Hamm reserves his especial fury for his father ("old fornicator") who has committed the unforgivable sin of begetting him: a charge to which Nagg replies that, after all, he didn't know at the time who it was going to be. Saddled with his own existence, Hamm can at least make sure that the thing doesn't go any further, and whenever some new form of life rears its head he calls for its elimination.

On a third level (or is it a fourth? -- one loses count in Beckett's universe) the play is a cry of rage against the human body, or the humiliations to which it is exposed by age. And, beyond this -- and brilliantly realized in Daniel Brooks' pellucid and perfectly-controlled production -- it is, to use the most un- Beckettian of words, a celebration: of the theatre. Beckett's jokes, which are excellent if dark, all depend on our awareness that this is a play. ("Not an underplot?" says Hamm irritably, when Clov spots signs of life outside.)

The play's title, and its first and last lines, derive from chess: a metaphor that I don't find especially fruitful. The constant allusions to Shakespeare -- to King Lear and especially to The Tempest -- are, however, immensely enriching. Hamm is a grand parody of a Shakespearean monarch (or actor of same -- just dig the name) and Peter Donat, fine player though he is, cannot find the grandiloquence that is built into the role.

Clov is magnificently played by Diego Matamoros, body arched, legs bent, voice somewhat Irish, feet performing a constant and spectacular double-shuffle. In the clarity of its outline and the quicksilver wit of its detail, this is an exhilarating performance. Coming on the heels of his cameo in Our Town and his star turn in The Play's the Thing, it made me seriously wonder whether Matamoros might not be the best actor in Canada. Jim Warren and Karen Robinson play sweetly as the two bin-ends.

The play is an ineradicable image of a desparing vision that most of us share from time to time. Only the terminally depressed live with it always and -- as has often been noted -- Beckett cannot have been living it while writing it. Work as finely organized as this is an affirmation of life in itself; and honest bleakness is far less depressing than phoney uplift.

- In repertory until Aug. 26. Box office: (416) 973-4000.

1999-08-20-homer-s-got-that-swing:
AN EVENING'S ODYSSEY

Tom Patterson Theatre Stratford, Ont.

THEATRE REVIEW

Homer, being a bard who literally sang for his supper, was never a man to keep his audiences hanging about. He taught all subsequent literature (which, in the West, means all the literature there is) a vital lesson by cutting immediately to the chase, and then keeping it going. In The Odyssey, he sets both the hero and his plight indelibly before us within the first two lines.

In Robert Fagles' translation, Odysseus is "the man of twists and turns. Driven time and again of course": a brilliant association of images that link the protagonist's unceasing and unscrupulous ingenuity to his incessant storm-tossed wanderings.

Fagles' version is poetry that arrests; it's also poetry that swings. It is, as befits a rendering of an oral epic, insistently speakable. An Evening's Odyssey is a three-handed entertainment in which Fagles himself speaks with quiet confidence about the poem and its themes, intones some resonant passages (notably the opening invocation to the Muse) in the original Greek, and sets the stage for more full-throated readings of some of the key scenes -- in his translation of course -- by two professional actors. At Stratford, they are Brian Bedford and Kathryn Walker, a U.S. actress with an extensive track record in this kind of literary theatre.

One notable feature of the show is how many of the famous bits of The Odyssey it leaves out. The monsters and temptresses who punctuate Odysseus' travels are much depleted; we get no Crice, no Sirens, no Scoylla and Charybdis (the rock and whirlpool so handily conjoined for your further shipwrecking pleasure). We do get the Cyclops, the giant cannibal whose one eye Odysseus -- passing under the name of Nobody -- so gleefully removes. The other Cyclops are momentarily perturbed by the screaming but when the sufferer says that Nobody is hurting him they shrug their gigantic shoulders and pass on. This passage is the Oldest Recorded Joke, and Bedford, having told the grisly story with restrained relish, makes the most of it.

The focus, though, is not on Odysseus the warrior but Odysseus the returning husband; and this turns out to be a sound decision. Of the two Homeric masterpieces, The Iliad has always struck me as intensely dramatic: a tragedy just waiting for the theatre to be invented. The Odyssey, in its picaresque aspect, resists drama, being one damned if exciting thing after another. But as a tale of reunion, moving toward a definite climax, it has immense resonance.

It is this element that Fagles stresses in his commentary, and the actors, while refraining from heavy characterization or excessive emoting, bring it home. Walker is the more lyrical and mellifluous of the two, but she also stresses the practicality of Penelope, the beleaguered wife, as resourceful at home as her husband is abroad. Bedford is playing, for the most part, in his lower register; he sounds at times downright grumpy. But after 10 years at war and 10 at sea, his hero is entitled to some weariness; and when he comes to defy (and destroy) his consort's battery of suitors, his voice rings and his anger blazes.

Taut or reposed, Bedford makes, as usual, every inflection tell. In some ways his Odysseus is a counterpart to his magnificent Sir Peter Teazle in The School for Scandal; the two worlds could hardly be more different, but both characters journey toward a hard-won domestic peace. The Greek one is archetypal, and one ends up believing that this is indeed -- as all the professors, including Professor Fagles, have told us -- the greatest presentation of a marriage in all literature.

1999-08-23-rage-and-regret-narrowly-focu:
Anton Chekhov's Uncle Vanya may be the most frightening play ever written. True, nobody in it is killed or blinded or driven mad, and the title character's attempts at murder and suicide are fumbling, farcical failures. That is what makes it so harrowing. The dramas involved are not the huge ones that most people get to contemplate only from a distance but the small, encroaching agonies that eventually impale us all.

Each of Chekhov's major plays depicts this world of rage and regret. In Vanya, which has a smaller cast and a narrower canvas than the others, the focus is at its most intense. Living in a huge house in the vast and echoing Russian countryside, the characters are engulfed by space. Their chief enemy, though, and the play's principal villain, is time.

Uncle Vanya himself wakes up in his 40s to the realization that he has wasted his life. "I could," he cries out, "have been a Schopenhauer, a Dostoevsky." Obviously he couldn't (and it's typical of Chekhov that Vanya realizes the absurdity, as soon as the words are out of his mouth); still, it's true that there were opportunities in his past that he might have seized.

He might, for example, have proposed to the beautiful Yelena, who is now the second wife of Vanya's ancient brother-in-law the Professor, a selfish fraud to the management of whose estates Vanya and his niece Sonya have devoted their existence. Sonya, who is self- consciously plain, loves Astrov, the hard-working and hard-drinking local doctor. Astrov has a passion for forest preservation; apart from that he, like Vanya, only has eyes for the Professor's wife.

Jealousy and frustration drive Vanya to the attempted shooting of the Professor, whom he sees as having ruined his life. He misses, twice: a scene that, above any other in drama, is capable of provoking laughter and tears simultaneously.

It takes a great production to scale those tragi-comic heights, and the Shaw Festival's version -- directed by Ian Prinsloo, of Theatre Calgary -- is not that. It has, nevertheless, a respectable amount to offer. It employs a lucid translation, by John Murrell, that allows the characters to talk to one another as if they had some reasonable expectation of receiving an answer. It maintains a very even tone, with its characters, in the famous Thoreau phrase, all leading lives of quiet desperation.

An even tone, though, inevitably results in an uneven effect, since Chekhov's characters are in fact extremely volatile. This has nothing to do with their being Russian, despite the recurrent masochistic moans from English-speaking critics that our actors are incapable of interpreting the Slavic temperament. (I have seen the Moscow Arts Theatre, admittedly well past its glory days, playing Chekhov; and its productions were just the same as ours, only less good.) It has everything to do with their being human.

Michael Ball's Vanya may be the first opportunity this actor has had at the Shaw not to adopt an English accent. This frees him from his usual teddy-bear persona to present an acerbic, envious, liquorous uncle, deeper into his vodka that any other I have seen. At the end he subsides movingly into the realization that his life is every bit as awful as he had suspected it was.

But Vanya should be manic as well as depressive, and his break- out here is too measured to be credible. The production's deliberate sloth at this point infects everyone, even Bernard Behrens' generally admirable Professor, who seems to be running for his life in slow motion while screaming for assistance as if it were a second glass of tea.

Jim Mezon's Astrov had me likewise split between respect for the actor and disbelief in the character. He is very fine when he expounds his ecological ideals to Yelena, his burning enthusiasm progressively undercut by her obvious indifference. But he seems too soft-grained for the life he leads and the things he says; Astrov is as much a failure as Vanya, but one who has seen more of the world and in whom self-pity has been replaced by a corrosive cynicism.

Yelena, meanwhile, is afraid of emotion; that doesn't necessarily make her shallow but that is how Philippa Domville plays her. Shauna Black similarly takes Sonya too much at her own wallflower evaluation, though her final speech on the relentless future that lies before her has its usual searing effect.

The Professor, who has spent a comfortable existence "writing about things that intelligent people have known all along and the stupid ones aren't interested in anyway" (Chekhov's sobering verdict on critics), departs from the estate preaching the sobering virtues of work -- leaving behind those who really know what work is and are being both sustained and destroyed by it.

There are useful performances by Jillian Cook as Vanya's purblind mother and Blair Williams as an ineffectual neighbour, both of them playing convincingly above their own ages. Amanda Smith, however, as the even older nurse, can manage neither the age nor anything else about the character, which is unfortunate since the nanny's undeviating serenity is central to the atmosphere; part merciful, part cruel, like time itself.

The production's overall buttoned-down effect may partly be due to the production occupying the festival's smallest stage, though nothing can excuse the interpolation of three Tom Waits songs, whose appearance is largely inexplicable and wholly demeaning.

- Until Sept. 25. Tickets: 1-800-511-7429 or (905) 468-2172.

ALL MY SONS

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

Arthur Miller's All My Sons was his first Broadway success, staged just after the Second World War. It concerns Joe Keller, who made a lot of money in that war manufacturing airplane parts. He allowed some faulty components to be sent out, resulting in the deaths of some 20 American pilots. His own son Larry was killed in action, though Joe takes comfort in the thought that he wasnt flying one of the defective planes. By the end of the play, however, old man Keller has been brought to realize that there is more to life than profits and family. The dead boys were all my sons. After making this affirmation, he stumbles off to commit suicide.

Now compare that title/line to the equivalent one in Millers next and most celebrated play, Death of a Salesman. Willy Loman is rhapsodizing about the old man whose example inspired his own choice of career, and he remarks parenthetically that "when he died, he died the death of a salesman." That death turns out to be very unlike Willy's own. So we have a play with a title drenched in irony, and one in which it's a climactic proclamation, bearing the plays full moral weight on its shoulders.

The ironic approach is the subtler and the more complex and, over time, the more satisfying. We never quite know why Willy kills himself -- we are offered a bewildering choice of motives -- but we believe it when it happens. Joes reasons are pretty clear, but his action comes too pat to be convincing. The pleasures offered by All My Sons are the simpler ones of moral melodrama. The morality is heartfelt and the storytelling extremely well-contrived, so it makes for an exciting evening.

This is how it works: Joe's business partner and next-door neighbour -- a weak man, easily intimidated -- took the rap and is just coming to the end of his jail sentence. The partner's daughter was engaged to Joes dead son; now she is about to marry his surviving brother Chris. This arrangement seems to please everybody except Joes wife. She clings to the belief that Larry is still alive, because if she admitted he was dead she would have to admit that, morally at least, Joe killed him. And if she believed that, Joe would be brought to believe it too, and that would be fatal. It's a convoluted course of reasoning, but it makes sense at the time -- emotional sense, anyway.

Back into their lives comes the partner's son, now a lawyer and newly convinced of his fathers innocence and Joes guilt. He also manages to convince Chris, which is what the mother most fears. For Chris' own war service has left him with a highly developed moral and social conscience; he is known throughout the neighbouring backyards as the local crusader. (For a CEO's family waxed fat on the war, the Kellers seem to be living on a remarkably modest scale. Maybe thats why Miller decided to set his next play further down- market; he obviously felt more at home there.) Chris duly turns on his father and, with a little help from his fiancee, gets him to acknowledge his responsibility.

Neil Munros direction is, as usual, intelligent, well-crafted and densely atmospheric, though he takes the last characteristic almost to excess: Joe and Chris have their crucial confrontation alfresco, with the shades of night falling so fast that we can hardly see the combatants. This may be intended to lend distance and texture to some pretty bald arguments, though time has already accomplished that; we swallow things in a period play that we would gag on in a new one.

Leslie Frankish has designed a pleasingly mellow variant on the house-with-a-porch setting that's de rigueur for American family plays of a certain age.

Most of the actors were in Munro's production of You Cant Take It with You earlier this season, and its intriguing to see them switch from domestic comedy to domestic drama; some of them play parallel roles.

Norman Browning, the dyspeptic tycoon of the earlier show, is the suicidal tycoon of this one, and he gives the role the same solid, chunky front, the same slow, lip-smacking delivery. Surprisingly, what worked for a caricature works equally well for a character. Joe remains a hollow man, but with the degree of hollowness that might indeed lead him to self-slaughter. He wouldn't have the imagination to figure out another way.

Ben Carlson again plays his son; he is maybe too sunny for the role, insufficiently obsessive, but he still has the authority to turn a juvenile lead into a person.

Mary Haney, who was previously a pleasantly batty mama, is now what Tom Stoppard once called "stark raving sane," a blend of delusion and absolute clear-sightedness. Miller's perception of the split maternal consciousness that desperately holds a family together is maybe his greatest insight (it was further developed in Salesman) and it strikes far harder now than the play's concern for our broader spiritual welfare.

Laurie Paton is as tough and as sympathetic as the fiancee should be, and Peter Krantz appropriately louring as her avenging brother. The various neighbours are so many rough edges, but the play's craftsmanship shines through: the guileful dispensing of some extremely complicated exposition, the early flashes of humour (a quality for which Miller is much underrated) before the claws begin to bite. And when they do take hold, they grip fast.

Theatre Review

WILD ABANDON AND SEE BOB RUN

Factory Studio Theatre, Toronto

Few people really warm to the prospect of monologues in the theatre -- except, of course, those who write and/or perform them. For them the one-person show is a dream of a workout. These two plays, written in the late 1980s by Daniel MacIvor, are superior examples of the genre: studies of individual desperation (naturally) in contrasting styles (mercifully). There are longueurs but for the most part the audience gets to share in the dream.

The first play, Wild Abandon, presents a young man of 25 at the end of his tether: literally, since the stage's few furnishings include a chair and a noose, and he has to make up his mind whether or not to use them. Life, sex and religion (he's a lapsed Catholic) aren't doing much for him, and his childhood memories amount mainly to resentment that his parents wouldn't let him paint his room black. (Which of us, he asks rhetorically, didn't want a black room as a child? There I go, out of step again.)

He has another more specific youthful recollection; when he was 11, an unknown woman whom he decided was his real mother approached him and, as he stood there waiting for her embrace, stuck a fork into him. She was taken away but the experience has, understandably, scarred him.

The piece unfolds as a kind of scrambled lecture, a fantasia on interlocked themes whose titles ("Birth Mother," "L-O-V-E") are flashed on a screen at the back of the stage. They amount to a generalized account of contemporary angst, making the speaker a character with whom everyone can identify but in whom nobody can quite believe.

There is plenty of spring in the writing -- some arresting images, some funny jokes -- and the actor, Jason Cadieux, delivers with magnificently casual accuracy. The program discloses that his character is called Steve, though I don't recall the matter being raised in public.

The protagonist of the second piece is, by contrast, extremely insistent about her name. She is called Bob, short for Roberta, and she is a terrified teenager, hitching a series of rides across the country, making for what she refers to as "the water." The play is called See Bob Run.

Bob is running from the memory of paternal abuse and also, perversely, from the two people who seem actually to have loved her: her boyfriend and her mother. Some of this information is relayed to us, poignantly and economically, through a fable that she recounts to us in between bending the ears of her various lifts. In this story she is a princess, and this connects neatly with her real life; her lover is actually a singer, an artist currently known as Prince. (It may even be his real name.) She is also fleeing an especially bloody scene at home; its nature, and her gradual acknowledgment of it, are slowly revealed to us over the course of the play. It is about one story and one conversation too long, but it holds.

There are two kinds of solo play. The first, typified by Wild Abandon, is the one in which the character talks to an indeterminate someone who may be himself or the audience; its pleasures are those of freewheeeling phantasmagoria, its perils are born of the belief that anything goes.

See Bob Run belongs, most of the time, to the second brand, in which a character talks unstoppably to another, unseen and improbably silent, character. It is difficult to bring this off convincingly (just as no playwright has ever managed plausibly to represent one half of a telephone conversation) but MacIvor manages surprisingly well. You may occasionally wonder why none of Bob's couriers push her out of the car (one does but not just for talking too much), but the dialogue is surprisingly free of the standard repetitions of what the other character has supposedly just said. Bob is a compulsive, overriding talker, and we come to understand why.

Tara Rosling, perhaps because she is older than the character, drives too hard and eagerly at it to begin with, but she settles down as things get grimmer, and by the end she is haunting. She is able to reveal a more shy, ingratiating persona in a little animal story that the two actors recount together before the evening's main business gets underway. (It's a woolly-sheep story, meaning a shaggy- dog story that happens to be about sheep.)

They both do this charmingly; and it's a treat, to be savoured while possible, to see two whole people on a stage, interacting. Ed Gass Donnelly's direction is, as far as you can tell with monologues, perfect.

- Runs until Sept. 19. Box office: (416) 504-9971.

1999-09-09-a-great-modern-play-brilliant:
PLATONOV

du Maurier Theatre Centre, Toronto

Until September 17, (416) 973-4000

In and around Toronto, this has been a glorious theatrical summer. There has been an impressive average of enjoyable productions at Stratford (six out of ten), Niagara (six-and-a-half out of eleven), and Coronation Park, Oakville (one out of one). But the crown, beyond any question, goes to the still-new Soulpepper company, which, in five ambitious shows, has hardly put a foot wrong.

Soulpepper has had the stunningly simple idea of putting good actors in good plays and lacing both in the hands of good directors. It's that last component that separates it from some other well- intentioned actors' collectives; and its association this year with Hungarian director Laszlo Marton has proved inspirational. His production of The Play's the Thing was a beautifully sustained exercise in high comedy; his version of Chekhov's Platonov is that and much more.

Any staging of Platonov is a "version" since the original, written and discarded when its author was 20, would play uncut for about seven hours. It doesn't even have a canonical title; it has previously been billed in English as That Fellow Platonov, Don Juan (in the Russian Manner), and -- in a translation by Michael Frayn, heavy on the farce and amused by the sex -- Wild Honey. Some things of course remain constant. That Russian Don Juan fellow Platonov is a schoolmaster in his mid-30s passionately adored by all four of the principal women in the cast, one of them his own wife.

He reciprocates their devotion, at least up to a point; they are all more forceful than he is and there is a definite sense that he is going with a flow that he may once have started but is now unable to control.

He also drinks too much and berates himself for the loss of his former ideals --when, that is, he is not berating other people for losing theirs or, alternatively, for still having them. These bewildering philsophic swings recur in Chekhov's later plays but they are never so vividly concentrated in one character as they are here. He is described as "the hero of a great modern play that unfortunately hasn't been written yet"; that line sounds too good to be true, an adaptor's invention, but no, it's in the original. And it's true, except -- we learn -- that the play was written. Carrying an equal load of his author's sympathy and disapproval, he comes to a violent end.

He has already survived two attempts on his life, one of them his own. His wife meanwhile, though generally equable enough, has tried to throw herself under a train, onstage. (The original gives her a second suicide bid, cut here.) Another character gets lynched, an event greeted by the rest with a modicum of regret and a total lack of surprise. This is not one of those Chekhovian plays in which nothing happens. Actually none of his plays are, but this one is more not that than any other.

The adaptation here is by Marton himself and Susan Coyne; apparently, he chose and edited the scenes and she wrote the words, which are occasionally too self-consciously slangy but are full of life. About half the original has been cut, and what remains has been re-ordered; notably, all the older characters have gone. (There are moments when they seem to be kept forcibly offstage.)

The location of one scene is left frustratingly unclear, but otherwise everything is marvellously lucid: a tangled scenario made brilliantly clear. All the characters are absurd, and most of them know it; and their extravagance is rendered with absolute precision; Marton seems to have drawn his actors to their limits -- and they do seem to have been drawn, not pushed. The play takes place in summer, and you feel the heat, inside and out. The play is performed in timeless costumes on an accommodating brown-canvas set; only some very recognizable Toronto carrier-bags seemed gratuitously jarring.

All the actors stretch out, sometimes literally; there never was was such a play for characters lying full-length across the stage, exposing their souls and occasionally their bodies, being doused with water, covered with newspaper. Albert Schultz as Platonov starts with a charming, self-lacerating languor that stealthily expands until he takes on the status, not of a tragic hero but of something more winningly, if uncomfortably, recognizable: the nearest thing in drama to a modern Everyman.

His female nemeses include a chatelaine, who in the original is contending with the loss of her estate (not actually a cherry orchard but you get the idea). Deprived of this dimension Nancy Palk plays her as a rangy, glitter-eyed and impatient seductress. Susan Coyne, as a friend's wife whom our hero seduces, is a challengingly chill idealist-turned-avenging angel. Robyn Stevan is magnificently believable as Mrs. Platonov, simultaneously stolid and vulnerable. As a bookworm whom he teases with disastrous results, Liisa Repo- Martell is magic: eccentricity rendered with dazzling economy and absolute truth.

Among the men, Stuart Hughes is inalienably North American (Stanley Kowalski in a white suit) but he rises beautifully to his great scene as a farcically tearful cuckold. Chekhov, when he wrote the play, was an incipient doctor as well as an incipient author and he paints a prophetically bitter portrait of a physician who has to be sent almost at gun-point to a sickbed; he also gets to speak the play's valediction, which Diego Matamoros delivers with an extraordinary blend of anger, grotesquerie and pathos.

Mike Shara is stiff-backed and very funny as a priggish student, Platonov's most implacable enemy bar one. The exception is a murderous horse-thief, accurately played by Michael Hanrahan as the most moral and clear-sighted person on stage. There is also a quartet of servants, tiny roles faultlessly played.

It's moving to see each actor take a quick, discreet call at the end. I confess that up to a couple of years ago I would not have thought theatre of this quality existed in Canada. This is a show that can face the world.
1999-09-13-nearly-authentic-shakespeare:
Shakespeare's Cleopatra is a role in which notoriously few actresses have triumphed; Britain, Canada and the United States can furnish between them an illustrious list of recent casualties. This summer in London, however, the jinx was laid at least temporarily to rest, though not by an actress. The serpent of the old Nile was portrayed by a man: Mark Rylance, a prominent actor with an indvidual piping voice who is also the director of the restorationist open-air theatrical project known as Shakespeares Globe.

The extent of this theatres antiquarianism seems to vary from one production to another. Some plays are mounted in modern dress, others in doublet and hose. (Of course, in Shakespeare's time doublet and hose were modern dress, so either approach can be dubbed authentic.) Antony and Cleopatra was done Renaissance fashion with the odd classical accoutrement, which would certainly have been the Elizabethan way. The purism in these matters can go to extremes of fanaticism; Velcro, that heavenly gift to the quick-change artist, is outlawed at the Globe, leaving the actors, some of them in Antony playing half-a-dozen roles apiece, to wrestle with good, old- fashioned, unyielding buttons. Stage managers, on the other hand, are equipped with high-tech walkie-talkies, possibly on the theory that stage-management is a diabolical un-Elizabethan activity anyway, and that if you're going to sell your soul you may as well get a good price for it.

Most of the Globes productions have bowed further to modernity by having women played bywomen, and even this Antony was not wholly true to 17th-century convention since these roles were written to be played by boys, not men. But, man or boy, a male Cleopatra is able to side-step the problem that dogs any actress cast in the part: the implicit demand that she convince us that she is the sexiest woman in the world. (This in a play that, despite its erotic reputation, has virtually no love scenes.) With an actor, this expectation goes into abeyance; we simply take for granted that what we are told of her attractions is true. Rylance made a dangerously playfulCleopatra, whose flurries of temper could turn into tempests. The text dictates that when the queen is brought the news of Antonys marriage to her rival, Octavia, she turns all her fury on the helpless messenger, dragging him about the stage by his hair, finally all but knifing him. Rylance's mood-swings were at once horrific and hilarious; no other Cleopatra I have seen has dared to play these scenes so whole-heartedly; the beleagured messenger seemed genuinely terrified, and no wonder.

Some 20 years ago, the British National Theatre mounted an all- male (and modern dress) As You Like It, whose four female characters were played in as many different styles, from an aescetic, virtually genderless Rosalind to a very funny pantomime-dame account of the country wench Audrey, from a young Anthony Hopkins. The Globe girls spanned an equally wide range; Octavia was dull, Charmian (Cleopatra's senior maid) an amusingly sharp-tongued piece of camp female impersonation,and Iras (her junior) a performance so accurately delicate that only the program cued you in that the character was being played by a man. This was a level shared by Rylance himself in Cleopatras transcendent last scene, which he played quietly and simply in a frizzy scalp, as if the queen had cast off her wigs along with her earthly hopes.

Antony is a role that has wrecked even more reputations than Cleopatra, and the actor here (Paul Shelley) could do little more than go decently through the motions. But the play held, captivating an audience most of whom were standing for upward of three hours in an open courtyard, occasionally spattered by rain. (My 13-year old son was among them, and remarked that at the end he had no choice but to offer a standing ovation. His pampered elders, meanwhile, sat above and behind the stage in the gallery known as the lords room from which they were rewarded stunning views of the tops of the actors' heads.)

The Globe has been in operation now for three years, and has proved a magnet for locals and tourists alike. Some of this, I imagine, has to do with the success of Shakespeare in Love, which has not only made Shakespeare's plays hot but his playhouse as well. Some has to do with the revival of the area: The South Bank of the Thames, east of the National Theatre and the Royal Festival Hall, was for many years an impenetrable wasteland but has recently become a walkers delight, dotted with museums, restaurants (the Oxo Tower provides a splendid view of the river) and extending down to Greenwich, with its famous Observatory and new Millennium Dome, taking in the financial district -- including the Reichmans Canada Square -- en route.

The Globe fits in right here, a cunning mixture of historical reconstruction and modern salesmanship; not that the Elizabethans themselves were backward in the latter regard, and the Globe's bustling entry-yard honours both traditional and modern commerce, being the only theatre lobby in London where you can buy fresh fruit. Theoretically, you can fling this at the actors if the fancy takes you, and it is true that the Globe has largely succeeded with rumbustious comedies (by Shakespeare and his contempories) that encourage audience participation, vocal if not physical. Antony and Cleopatra offeredheartening evidence that a great tragedy, honestly presented and wittily and intelligently spoken (the director, Giles Block, is billed as "master of the verse") can be just as captivating.

I wouldn't claim that this is ensemble theatre in the greatest English tradition. But then, there hasnt been much of that around recently: certainly not in the classics. There is more continuity inCanada, where acting standards have actually risen; certainly there is far more personality in the average Stratford cast than there was 20 years ago, which is as far back as my memory extends.

The British National Theatre had, in the last decade, given up any idea of maintaining a permanent company, but under its new director, Trevor Nunn, this may change. Nunn has established a company within the company: an ensemble, with a sizable black contingent, to perform half-a-dozen plays within the year. Two of these, Troilus and Cressida and The Merchant of Venice, seem to have re-established Nunn as the best director of Shakespeare in, probably, the world;unfortunately, neither was playing during my visit. The two major shows I did see were directed by John Caird, Nunns collaborator on Nicholas Nickleby and Les Miserables and author-director of the Jane Eyre musical seen a few years ago at the Royal Alex in Toronto. Both were delights.

A revival of Money, an early Victorian social comedy by Edward Bulwer Lytton, struck a fine balance between satire and sentiment. (The play, dating from 1840, would be a natural for the Shaw Festival if only its author had postponed writing it for 14 years.) Especially impressive was the ability of the hero -- Simon Russell Beale, the superb Widmerpool of TV's A Dance to the Music of Time -- to drive behind his often stilted lines to the genuine passions they were meant to express. Beale, as gifted a singer as he is an actor, also played the narrator and Dr. Pangloss in the endlessly problematic Leonard Bernstein musical of Candide. Caird's version was the most exhaustive attempt yet to do justice to both Voltaires novel and Bernsteins score; they still didn't quite cohere, but both were so wonderful it hardly mattered. My pleasure in the company's versatility (and this is a lesson for Stratford, which segregates its plays and musicals) led me to their one new play, The Darker Face of the Earth, by U.S. poet, Rita Dove. This turned out to be a mistake: an attempt to graft the Oedipus myth on to a story about Deep South slavery -- though when the heros parentage was revealed I found myself thinking less of Greek tragedy than of the handbag scene in The Importance of Being Earnest.

The best new play in London remains Michael Frayns three-hander Copenhagen, a hit last year at the National and now transferred to the West End. It is also the British play that all the Canadian theatres are bidding for, though it seems that, as usual, we shall have to wait until after a Broadway run that may or may not be followed by a tour. Frayn told me that moves to take the original cast to New York were meeting with resistance from American Equity, who queried the necessity of importing British actors to play two Danes and a German. I hope that they will at least admit Matthew Marsh, the youngish actor who plays Werner Heisenberg, formulator of the Uncertainty Principle, and displays a tremendous ability to transform abstractions into towering arcs of passion. The play depicts a mysterious wartime meeting between Heisenberg, his former mentor theDanish physicist Niels Bohr, and Bohr's wife; and offers a series of alternative readings of what may have taken place. At stake is the development of the atom bomb, and the question of who, if anyone, should be allowed to have it. The writing is notable for its extreme fair-mindedness, and for the artfulness with which it keeps opening new moral and psychological chasms beneath its characters' feet.

And what, after all this sobriety, of that all-conquering show business phenomenon, the British musical? According to a recent article in Time, its day is over. There are no discernible successors to Cats, Les Miserables, The Phantom of the Opera and Miss Saigon; the last of that quartet is indeed about to end its long run at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane. Meanwhile, the West end is being subjugated by alien song-and-dance forces from across the Channel. (They should never have built that tunnel.) The big shows promised for next season are all -- in subject, authorship or both - - French.

Or so says Time. I cant help pointing out, though, that the invasion has already happened, since both Les Mis and Saigon are French anyway. Besides this, of the half-dozen Gallic shows that figure in the march of Time, two are actually Canadian. London is getting Notre Dame de Paris, the blockbuster from Quebec that, if it takes off as its promoters seem to expect, will give Victor Hugo something that Shakespeare, Dickens and Shaw have failed to achieve: a second megahit musical. Its also getting Napoleon, which admittedly failed to bust any blocks when it was seen in Toronto but whose authors have reportedly been re-working it non-stop ever since.

So, a year from now, we may be clebrating a Canadian conquest of the London theatre. Alternatively, we may be trying to pretend the whole thing never happened. One never knows.
