Giles Block's staging is the first in many years to cast a man in the role of Cleopatra. It opened on July 30 to sell-out houses. ;
1999-09-15-cabaret-still-breaking-the-mo:
The new production of Cabaret is the re-invention of a classic musical, staged and performed with enormous verve and authority. You should see it. Moment by moment, it is hypnotic. Add the moments up, and doubts intrude.

First, the history. This is the latest incarnation of Christopher Isherwood's endlessly fertile Berlin Stories, which were based on the author's actual experiences of the early '30s; he witnessed the rise of Nazism and befriended a young night-club singer and all- around sex object -- English like himself -- whom he called Sally Bowles. In the '50s, Chris and Sally became the centre of a play, I Am a Camera. In the '60s, Cabaret arrived: a ground-breaking musical, directed by Harold Prince, with Chris transformed -- presumably for audience-identification purposes -- into an aspiring American writer named Cliff, and the Kit Kat club, Sally's stamping- and-vamping ground, transformed into the show's metaphor and nerve- centre. Then -- running with this idea and making many changes -- came the movie, directed by Bob Fosse.

The current version started small in London, triumphed in New York, and is now on the road. Its director, the British wunderkind Sam Mendes (the man of the moment in Toronto, with his American Beauty a success at the film festival and his production of Oliver! due to open at the Royal Alex) has stated that his aim is to seduce his audience with the delicious degeneracy of pre-Nazi night life, and then appall them with the more savage degeneracy that followed. That, as it happens, is what the original Prince production did; having hooked us with an opening number of incomparable seedy panache, it proceeded to deliver a trio of knock-out blows, each one small in itself but cumulatively horrific. A soaring musical salute to the approaching dawn was transformed into a Fascist anthem. A single brick was lobbed through a Jewish greengrocer's window. A floorshow routine showed the club's Master of Ceremonies dancing lovingly with a (presumably) female gorilla, ending by confiding in us "if you could see her through my eyes/she wouldn't look Jewish at all."

All those moments remain in the new production, but they have lost their impact. It has in fact been pre-empted. The hymn Tomorrow Belongs to Me is ended first time round with a Hitler impersonation, so the reprise has no surprise. The gorilla number lacks all lyricism, so its coda is no longer a slap in the face. Grace, indeed, has been conscientiously eradicated throughout. The chorus- girls -- and boys -- are mean and poverty-stricken. Sexy suspenders have given way to run-filled stockings, sly androgyny to sullen bisexuality; the joy of sex here comes not from doing it but from flaunting it. This may well be true to the period and it is also, as everybody keeps assuring us, very '90s, but it is also monotonous; the emcee starts the evening by grabbing his crotch, and from there he can only proceed to grabbing everybody else's.

The choreographer, Rob Marshall, has had some neat ideas for individual numbers, and the cast are as skilled as they are dedicated; they're musicians as well as actor-dancer-singers, and there is an unforgettable entr'acte in which they huddle inside, or spill out of, a giant tilted picture-frame while playing a Dixieland version of the title number. But, politically and sexually, the show has to keep upping the ante. The emcee moons the audience, to reveal a swastika tattooed on his buttocks. Finally, as Cliff's train pulls out of Berlin, we find ourselves transplanted to another railway platform, where our Master of Ceremonies again sheds his costume, to reveal a striped concentration-camp uniform, adorned with a yellow star and a pink triangle. Good taste hardly being the issue here, I should like to point out that at the Princess of Wales this is a bit deja vu; we have already seen The Pajama Game.

The serious point is presumably that this is the fate of those who think they can dance with the devil; Berlin clubland giggled at Hitler, instead of fighting him, and this is where it ended up.

The truth is actually more complicated; the more immediate objection is that the show hijacks the worst images of the century to underline what is already implicit.

To be fair, no one has ever known how to end Cabaret. (It transgresses the unwritten rule that you don't applaud shows about the Holocaust.) And even in its earlier scenes, the show is famously schizophrenic. There are the commentative nightclub numbers and there are the narrative book-show bits. This production tries to bring them together by setting the whole thing in the cabaret. Even in a big conventional theatre, this looks good; and Mendes and Marshall have bled the scenes into one another very cleverly.

But the styles still break apart.The emcee hovers over the whole action: echoing it, mocking it, influencing it. It's his brick that goes through the window. (So at this point he actually does represent Nazism? Very confusing.) One comes to resent his presence; Norbert Leo Butz preens and leers as expertly as could be wished, but he may be the first performer of this role not to walk off with the show. Perhaps because he's on stage so much. How do you steal something you already own?

Meanwhile the realistic scenes are working amazingly well; it's no great surprise that the John Kander-Fred Ebb score stands up so magnificently, but one hardly expected Joe Masteroff's book to equal it. But it does, and -- this production's real if unheralded trump- card -- it is wonderfully acted.

Best of all -- breathtakingly, undeviatingly so -- is Alma Cuervo as Fraulein Schneider, the Gentile landlady pressured into breaking off her engagement with the Jewish grocer. She is straight and clear -- even when temporizing or perplexed -- and unfusssily warm, and deeply moving. She also sings superbly, and her two songs of survival, one jaunty and the other desperate, are the best in the show. Nobody, not even Lotte Lenya who created it, can have played this role better. Hal Robinson, Drew McVety and Jeanine Morick are admirable as the other representative Germans, and Rick Holmes makes far more of Cliff than is customary.

Joely Fisher has got Sally absolutely right: an upper-class English schoolgirl gone off the rails and living, with tremulous bravado, on her nerves. Her voice is smoky, and she quivers; she does drugs but only admits to alcohol. You can see why Berlin would find her exotically provocative, and the staging of her Don't Tell Mama number takes full advantage. Her torch-song rendition of Maybe This Time is both touching and ironic. Sally is indeed the only character who bridges the show's two worlds, and the production comes closest to unity when she is on. Only the title song eludes her; it's done here for desperation rather than triumph, and she has already sounded that note to its depths.

It strikes me that the traditional affirmative reading of this number -- as exemplified by Liza Minnelli, and by Judi Dench who was the best of all Sallys -- is not only more immediately rousing but, given the ghastly historical context, more mordant. But I gladly concede that Cabaret, the musical that broke the mould 33 years ago, is still doing it.

- Until Oct. 13, Box office (416) 872-1212

THE ROAD TO HELL

Tarragon Mainspace, Toronto

The imposing title of The Road to Hell turns out to conceal a pair of one-act, two-actor comedies, written and performed by Michael Healey and his offstage partner, Kate Lynch. Healey is the author of The Drawer Boy, which reopens tonight at Passe Muraille: Comparisons are best avoided, though I do wonder whether, without the success of that more substantial piece, Tarragon would have given this innocuous new offering pride of place at the head of its new season.

Cuteness is the main ingredient here: cuteness of writing, acting, and of basic idea. Each of the two playlets boasts a single comic notion; each runs it nearly, but not quite, into the ground. Both plays constantly skirt the edge of the unbearable but manage to pull back and disarm you with a joke that's funny or an observation that rings true.

Yodellers, the first half, concerns the relationship between a champion lady golfer and the male sports reporter who comes to interview her. He ends up spending the night in her hotel room, thus fulfilling the fantasy of every journalist ever sent on a star assignment. He does not, however, have sex with her; they spend the night talking about the game, and the conversation has a tonic effect on her performance the next day. (This is another hack's dream: that he who only writes about it -- change the genders as you wish -- will give instruction to she who actually does it, and she will listen and be grateful. I'm still waiting.)

Inevitably, he falls in love with her and she, after a fashion, with him, their passion impeded by him being married, which he brushes off, and her being gay, which she doesn't. But she takes him on the road with her (hiding him away so as not to draw the ire of the lesbian golfing mafia, whose power I had certainly never suspected) and they try to work out a compromise that will be platonic enough for her and physical enough for him.

Much of the humour stems, inevitably in the circumstances, from male erotic vulnerability; but by the end the scales are balanced with surprising evenness. The idea is stretched dangerously thin, but there is a shape. We also learn how easily golfing terms (the title is one of them) can become sexual double entendres. But then, what can't?

The second number, Kreskinned, is about a male antiquarian bookseller and a female dog-obedience trainer. Both of them wear duffle coats, a circumstance that has prompted a mutual friend to fix them up on a blind date.

They go to see a show by a hypnotist, who's billed as the Great Kreskin. (I have to confess that this last detail passed me by, so I found the title as mystifying as it is ungainly.) He pulls them up on stage and has her imitate a chicken and him a car; we see them at it, though (another confession) I thought at the time that he was doing a gorilla.

Anyway, it turns out that the hypnotist has neglected to un- hypnotize them, and at any given moment either partner can put the other into a trance. This, as their acquaintance progresses from restaurants to movies to bed to the verge of marriage, proves an invaluable tool for defusing or bypassing embarrassing moments.

A more blatant device than the one in the preceding play, it's also more theatrically resilient: a neat metaphor for the amount of blind-eye-turning needed to sustain any relationship. Certainly this couple can use it; he has trouble making commitments (the piece makes no claims to great psychological originality) and I'm not sure what her problem is but she seems very nervous. This play, too, has a neat ending, this time one that tilts the balance rather than maintaining it. But it still lies uncomfortably between revue- sketch and full-blown farce.

As performers, Healey and Lynch are adroit and agreeable, but limited. Both have excellent timing (as, by the way, does their director, Andy McKim); hers is quick-fire and his is slow-burn.

Lynch indeed pounces on every line as if it were a prize wisecrack, which tends to leave those that aren't, but would like to be, a trifle exposed. Healey shambles endearingly but sometimes to excess, especially as the slovenly lover of Kreskinned; I'm a slob myself, but I like to think that, for a first date, I would try to hunt out a sweater that didn't actually have a hole in it. In his earlier role, though, he looks and sounds ideal, somewhat pedantic but boyishly enthusiastic; if the Globe and Mail's actual golfing correspondent -- I assume they have one -- isn't like this, it's he who is miscast, not Healey.

To sum up: We all know what the road to hell is paved with; some of the good intentions on this one pay off, but not enough. Unless you are charitable, in which case you're on the other road anyway.

- Until Oct. 24. Box office: (416) 531-1827.

STREET OF BLOOD

Canadian Stage, Toronto

One night it's The Road to Hell, the next it's Street of Blood. They turn out to be very different thoroughfares. The Road to Hell is at best a charade. Street of Blood means business.

It's the creation of Ronnie Burkett, an immensely talented actor, writer, singer and puppeteer. The last may well be what he has on his passport, and is probably how he is best known. His current show involves some 40 marionettes, every one of them immaculately manipulated, with exquisite attention to detail. There is wit in how they walk and sit and in the tilt of their heads. They occupy three adjacent doll's house stages (no design credit, so Burkett is probably responsible for that too) with the master visibly controlling them from above. The technical accomplishment, however, is the least of what is on offer. Street of Blood is a play, and a very fine one.

It is set in the small prairie town of Turnip Corners, Alta. -- which is pretty much what it sounds like -- and its central character is called Edna Rural. Edna is a plain, plump, bespectacled widow, though she always refers to her husband in the present tense. A deeply, if conventionally, religious woman, she is knitting a quilt; she accidentally gets some blood on it, sees the face of Christ in one of the squares, and announces the creation of the Shroud of Turnip Corners.

She has a grown-up adopted son who is homosexual and gives karaoke performances in geriatric wards, under the professional name of Eden Urbane. He is also a terrorist agent-provocateur, setting off bombs in order to arouse gay anger of which he harbours a dangerous amount himself. Both mother and son, but especially son, are fans of a former movie star -- equally at home, it seeems, in musicals and melodramas -- called Esme Massengill. A home-town gal herself, Esme has returned to Turnip Corners to launch a new stage musical in which she plays the Virgin Mary.

Esme is also, or principally, a vampire, and an exceptionally nasty one. I should add that Edna's husband, Stanley, who was somewhat homophobic, has died of AIDS following a tainted blood transfusion, and that he managed -- in their final, unexpected conjugal encounter -- to pass it on to her. This last twist strikes me as dramatically excessive, and pushes the play at the end over the line from affirmation to sentimentality.

They say blood will have blood, and this show is obviously awash with it. I don't find it as effective a unifying device as the author obviously intended, possibly because I've never been able to take any serious interest in vampires, either as myth or metaphor. To me they're theatrical camp, which is certainly how Esme registers here.

On that level, she's entertaining but beyond it she's a trial. She's actually one of a trio of bloodsuckers here, another being her co-star -- her Joseph -- who is a Jewish actor seeking revenge for the Holocaust. This matter is confined to one scene, which is either too little or too much. The play does not, in fact, hang together very well.

And yet it feels like a masterpiece. Edna, in particular, must be one of the great characters of modern drama, a comfortably minded woman whom tragedy forces into hitherto unimagined territory: a latter-day Mrs. Alving from Ibsen's Ghosts.

She is realized, in all her strength and silliness, with extraordinary solidity and compassion, and my reflex reaction is to compliment the actress. But of course there isn't one; there's only Burkett, writing the lines, doing the voice, pulling the strings. This creates a remarkable sensation. Usually when a character takes on this kind of autonomous life, you think of her as having escaped from her author. This time, though you can actually forget him for long periods, the author is physically, inescapably there, and you marvel at his understanding.

He is, as it happens, a handsome and mellifluous performer (his crooning parodies are spot-on) and he has given himself a couple of acting roles. He plays God, type-casting for a puppeteer, or at least he plays Jesus: a smooth and smiling Saviour who is mocked, and questioned, and bitterly resented, and finally - if I followed it right -- accepted.

Anyway, the play's metaphysics are a lot more compelling than those of Angels in America, which is the nearest stringless drama I can recall. There is also a flashback in which the young Eden (who is as compelling a creation as Edna) is discovered by his father in an early attempt at cross-dressing; Burkett plays the father, towering over his hapless marionette son in the most terrifying embodiment of paternal oppression I have ever seen on a stage.

At moments like this one -- which both exploits the form and bursts it open -- emotion rocks the theatre. At others, less frequent, laughter does the same. You don't expect a puppet-play to be like this. You don't, unless you're very optimistic, expect much theatre of any kind to be like this.

- Until Oct. 23. Box office: (416)-368-3110.

THE DRAWER BOY

Theatre Passe Muraille

David Fox, playing Angus in Michael Healey's The Drawer Boy -- back in town with its original cast -- has a large, craggy face with a steep forehead and jug-handle ears. It's a lunar landscape, lit up by grins that come and go in constant succession. Innocent though it is, it's also a used face, suggesting that long ago its owner got into fights.

That's quite apart from what we learn actually happened to this Canadian architect-turned-farmer years ago in the London Blitz, when the fallout from an air raid took off part of his head, leaving a gap through which, as his comrade Morgan so vividly tells it, "his memory escaped." Angus cannot now hold a thought for more than a second at a time, making him, from an actor's point of view, both a gift and a trap; the role is the kind from which the performer (think of Dustin Hoffman in Rain Man) usually reaps more respect than the character.

Fox, however, never patronizes the man he's playing, never begs for sympathy; Angus lives in the moment and Fox fills out each moment with massive gentleness and with the kind of sharp, unhesitating candour that comes from having no defences. He maps out the limits of Angus' consciousness, and then -- as he responds to new and unexpected pressures -- shows them expanding to take in bewilderment and even anger.

Gentleness also underlies Jerry Franken's Morgan, though his surface is rasping, sardonic and watchful, worn down from years of running the farm and caring for the friend whom he both loves and resents, and for whom he feels, in two senses, responsible.

The story of these two men and their wartime girlfriends -- the tale that Morgan tells to Angus every night, of the drawer boy and the farmer and the tall girl and the taller girl -- has already become part of Canadian theatrical mythology. Healey has found words for it that both fit the moment and resonate beyond it. He is almost equally skilful at developing the relationship when events force it out of its accustomed groove, and the two have to find a new way of living together.

Their partnership, impressive as it is (and dramatically unique as far as I know), is only half the play. The other half comes from their involvement with Miles (Tom Barnett), the young actor who comes to research his role in a collective show about farming, and who appropriates their story as a means of padding out his own role. Seeing him rehearse it reopens the hole in Angus' brain and sets off the changes in him that give the play its second act.

The bringing together of these two worlds seems more contrived on a second viewing, but the benefits remain substantial. We get Miles' impersonation of Daisy the stressed-out cow, desperate to give milk in order to avoid being sent to the slaughter -- a performance, we learn, that leaves his friends back at the collective deeply unimpressed. (Hence his determination to secure his place in the troupe by rendering Morgan's nightly monologue; as he says, like Daisy, like the farmers themselves, he has to produce or die.)

We get Miles telling Angus, once the dam in Angus' mind has burst, the story of Hamlet with special reference to his own performance of the title role, and his hearer's fascinated reception of it; this scene is worked up with delightful slyness, though it strains credibility when Angus later goes around talking about his own "antic disposition."

We get Morgan's brisk and bitter lecture on the economics of farming with Angus, an idiot savant where figures are concerned, muttering instant statistics in the background. We get Morgan's merciless practical joking at the city-boy Miles' expense, and the way in which Miles neatly and subtly turns the tables at the end.

Performance apart, the play remains remarkable for the ease of its dialogue (a few literary awkwardnesses aside) and the craft of its construction. It also offers the attractions of a well- burnished theatrical mirror. The Farm Show, the 1970s project to which The Drawer Boy tips its hat, was the creation of the Theatre Passe Muraille, whose Toronto stage now houses the play. Fox was a member of that company; so was the present director, Miles (note the name) Potter.

The Farm Show was intended as an instrument of social change; The Drawer Boy, more modestly but no less ambitiously, depicts it as the accidental cue for an individual transformation. It does so by placing a tall story, which we believe when we hear it, inside a taller story, which by natural progression we also accept. (It's at least as likely as having your stepfather reveal himself as a murderer by sitting him down in front of an old play to which you've contributed additional dialogue.)

Theatre paying tribute to itself can be bloated and embarrassing. This example, with much else on its mind and in its heart, is intimate, funny and touching.

- Until Oct. 24. Box office: (416) 504-7529

CREDITORS
Artword Theatre

August Strindberg, as almost any of his writings will attest, was not an easy man to please. But he would, I think, have approved of the new Artword Theatre on Portland Street, which has opened with a production of his short, sharp three-person play Creditors. The Artword is that rare phenomenon in Toronto, a comfortable small theatre. It also has a concentrated, intimate, head-on relationship between stage and auditorium -- exactly what Strindberg demanded for his chamber-plays, of which the prize specimens are this one and the better-known Miss Julie. Whether he would have been happy with the shallow production offered by the Actors Repertory Company is another matter. (The ARC is another new troupe devoted to matching up experienced actors with classic, and preferably unfamiliar, texts.) The form of Creditors is a sequence of three duets with a brief cataclysmic finale. Its content is a concentrated study of a destructive marriage, though with Strindberg thats pretty much a tautology.

Actually it's about two destructive marriages, superimposed. Adolph, an artist, is married to Tekla, a novelist; they are tracked down at a Swedish holiday resort by Gustav, Teklas discarded former husband and, in his own self- immolating words, a teacher of dead languages."

Out for revenge, and also for some kind of personal vindication, he sets about undermining their relationship. He does it mainly by messing, Iago-like, with Adolphs mind -- though this is an Othello in which the author thinks Iago has a case.

One of Gustav's tactics is to get Adolph thoroughly confused about whether he should be a painter or a sculptor, though it seems that whatever the medium the finished product comes out looking like his wife. Anyway, the play begins with Adolph sculpting: actually at it, before our eyes, according to Strindberg's stage direction. John Neville, the director, may have thought this would look like a cliche; in any event, he gives us Adolph sitting at a table with Gustav, amiably chatting. And so their long scene together goes; by its end, the ex-husband has persuaded his supplanter that Tekla has sapped his virility, stolen his ideas, cuckolded him with various young men, and generally sucked his blood.

Through all this, Alan Jordans Adolph just sits there, taking it on the chin and smiling. Strindberg wrote the play while in the throes of his own divorce from actress Siri von Essen and, as the most obsessively autobiographical of playwrights, he must have split himself between the two husbands. He may well have seen Adolph as a martyr but not, surely, as a wimp.

He also insisted that the play was "naturalistic, which this production takes to be a synonym for quiet." Considering whats going on, all this restraint seems remarkably unnatural. Later on Jordan throws a spiffy epileptic fit but the pressures that produced it have simply not been presented to us. We watch not a character in action but a participant in a debate, underlining his points with an assortment of earnest hand gestures.

This, though, is merely an extreme symptom of the production's general malaise. Brenda Bazinet's Tekla is a one-and-a-half-note performance. The single note is the teasing, patronizing one that she adopts for her entire scene with Adolf. The half- note, more interesting, is the confident erotic complicity that she briefly establishes when confronted by her ex.

(The sexual frankness in the play is, for a 19th-century piece, startling.)

Chuck Shamatas Gustav is indeed the most successful performance, a slug-like agent provocateur whose function in the play permits of a certain sinister blandness.

He does, though, make his authors insistence that the play was "humane, good-humoured, with all three characters sympathetic" seem more like wishful thinking than ever.

In theory, Strindberg is literature's supreme misogynist; in practice, once his characters reach the stage and take on flesh, both sexes seem equally diabolical, equally racked.

When he turns on the compassion, it comes out self-pitying and sentimental and I find the plays hard to take precisely because of his presenting his own hangups as an objective view of the entire human race.

Still, he not only based the character of Tekla on his own Siri, he actually offered her the role in the opening production and she accepted it, gleefully.

This suggests that though he may have been a bit extreme in his view of men and women, he was dead-on about playwrights and actresses.

Until Nov. 6. Box office (416) 368-3110

THE BEAUTY QUEEN OF LEENANE

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

---

When he wrote The Beauty Queen of Leenane, Martin McDonagh was 23 and, according to all the publicity, had hardly seen a stage play in his life. His ignorance is our bliss. No one seems to have told him that in the contemporary theatre, character is kept strictly subordinate to ideas while narrative is at best ignored and at worst despised.

Before coming to Toronto, The Beauty Queen has conquered audiences in its native Ireland, in London and in New York; and it has done so primarily by telling a riveting story. This makes life hard for critics. Even on a second viewing the play radiates suspense, but its initial impact depends largely on narrative surprise, and it would be unfair to spoil that. It is also full of psychological shocks; people behave in ways that initially seem incredible but then, after the next revelation, make perfect sense.

It takes place in a cottage in present-day Galway, the remote county in which McDonagh's parents grew up, though he himself, a Londoner, knows it only as a visitor. Here, amid constant rain and perpetual poverty, live Mag, a 70-year-old widow, and Maureen, her 40-year-old unmarried daughter.

Mag is a tyrannical and very cunning hypochondriac, existing largely on a diet of tea, porridge, dietary supplements and boil-in- the-bag fish, all of which she depends on Maureen to prepare. Among her endearing habits is that of emptying her chamber pot in the kitchen sink.

Maureen, who on the face of it is considerably more intelligent, loathes her existence but has to put up with it; the reason why is the first of the traps that the play keeps opening beneath our feet. When not attending her mother, Maureen looks after the livestock that presumably helps support them. ("It's at the chickens she is," explains Mag to one of their rare visitors. A spoof of the play in a recent Forbidden Broadway has one actor yelling at the other "Stop reversin' your syntax, you old cow.")

McDonagh brilliantly captures the dynamics of a strained mother- daughter relationship, carried to the bitterest extreme. There is mental cruelty and there is physical cruelty, and the former seems far the worse; indeed one of the play's disturbing aspects is the way in which, as in a revenge tragedy, the audience finds itself cheering on acts of violence.

This may explain why people, including the author himself, keep comparing him to Quentin Tarantino, but there really isn't much resemblance. The violence in Pulp Fiction is presented as amoral, impersonal and cool; in The Beauty Queen it's the work of amateurs, the fruit of agonized frustration and white-hot hatred. Only one of the play's four characters could reasonably be described as nice, but each has a point of view and each is fully dramatized.

The nice one is Pato, who works on the building sites in London (where he's mocked and exploited) and whose appearance as a suitor on one of his regular trips home presents Maureen with her one chance of escape. He is only the third man in 20 years that she has as much as kissed, though her mother declares this to be too many; one of the overriding ironies is that, though Maureen seems far the more sexual of the two women, it is she who is the virgin, a fact that Mag is not about to let her forget. It is Pato's presence that turns their antagonism into a fully fledged duel.

Beyond the personal, the play acts as a deft and unforced metaphor for a depressed rural Ireland: its culture dulled by television (principally Australian); its young people forced off to England or the U.S.; and its weather, apparently, terrible.

It is also extremely funny, and not, despite the bleakness of the tale, in any sniggering black-humour way. McDonagh's dialogue is as rich as Irish talk is traditionally supposed to be, but it never -- unlike the language in Synge, O'Casey and even Brian Friel -- threatens to swamp the play. Everything here is economical, and McDonagh is a master at preparing his ground. Thoughts, people, objects -- from a poker to a package of biscuits -- are mined for long-range comic or dramatic effect: often for both.

Garry Hynes, who has directed the play with Irish actors from Galway to Broadway, does it again here with Canadians (a double coup for Canadian Stage) in a production equally rich in theatrical tension and human truth. Fiona Reid is a superb Maureen, a character whose trajectory is faintly similar to that of the actor's last role of Blanche DuBois. (What with Lady Bracknell and How I Learned to Drive, she has had quite a year.)

Blanche, though, was a performance in which you could see the wheels going round; her Maureen is complete and alive from the moment she steps on stage, a flaxen-haired countrywoman, and begins snapping at her ma. She snaps, indeed, in all kinds of ways, and an increasing edge of disturbance both colours the role and holds it together. This is a ruthless, pitiable account of a ruthless, pitiable woman.

Joan Orenstein's Mag, a less monumental termagant than Anna Manahan's original, is still commandingly sly and cantankerous. Oliver Becker plays Pato with a gentle dignity that flowers in a long monologue in which he writes and recites two letters: a scene that breaks the play's convention without injuring it. In fact it enlarges it. All their accents are convincing, at least to my ear.

The only actor who has trouble here is Matthew Edison, whose performance as Ray, Pato's brother and the play's tragi-comic messenger, is indistinct in both voice and personality. Still, his second-act scene with Mag, in which for her own purposes she tries to get rid of him by boring and frustrating him to distraction, remains a minor masterpiece of atmosphere and construction. That makes it an apt image of the play itself -- though, things being as they are, it may not prove to be all that minor.

A SHORT HISTORY OF NIGHT

Factory Theatre, Toronto

Johannes Kepler was the 17th-century astronomer who discovered how the planets move. Tycho Brahe was the older astronomer whose work, though less momentous and less durable than Kepler's, paved the way for him; he was jealous of the younger man but nevertheless gave him a place in his royally-funded observatory and thus allowed him to pursue his research.

I have derived this information from the program notes to John Mighton's A Short History of Night, where it is set out rather more clearly than in the play itself.

The play begins with the infant Johannes being inspected by his father, who playfully inserts a knife into the crib in the foredoomed hope that his boy will grow up to be a soldier like his dad. It ends with Kepler instructing his 16-year-old daughter to stop thinking analogically; the habit of comparing things to other things, rather than accepting them for themselves, and which has apparently been the root of human ills. I can see no connection, other than a random biographical one, between these two bookends. The play does not seem to be about the march of the generations.

The action has certainly been chock-full of human ills, among them the brutal interrogation of Kepler's wife on a charge of witchcraft; one minor character does keep asking her what the Devil is like, but this sounds like gossipy curiosity rather than the expression of a fixed intellectual habit.

The Keplers are Protestants, most of the other characters are Catholics, and the European religious wars are raging. But the conflict implicit in the first scene between the scientific and military lives is never pursued, and it isn't as though anyone ever tries to push the grown-up Kepler into uniform. The war is often mentioned, but its presence is never dramatically felt.

In fact, very little in the play is felt. The actors playing the rival scientists stand around dropping the names of their favourite theories -- one declares that "all movement is caused by suction," to which another opposes the virtues of "straight flying" -- but if they know what they're talking about they don't communicate it to the audience.

The play, in the fashion of modern historical drama, is written in a series of short and supposedly sharp scenes, full of edgy anachronistic jokes and casual horrors; the intention is to keep us off-balance between then and now but the effect is to drain conviction from both. A lot of important stuff seems to happen in the breaks; reading between the lines may be stimulating, reading between the scenes is just frustrating.

Brahe's observatory, where most of the story happens, is peopled by a collection of Gothic clowns (including the regulation dwarf) who behave like rude overgrown schoolboys, especially when Mrs. Kepler is around.

Presumably they feel her sexuality as a threat (her husband certainly seems to), and the end result of this is the Inquisition, represented here by a 19-year-old prodigy of a witch-hunter who ought to be chilling but comes off just silly. Maybe I just mention the sex theme because it's in the air, much as one assumes the play is about the Renaissance clash between science and superstition simply because so many other plays, starting with Brecht's Galileo, have been there already.

This play was first seen in 1991 when it won three major awards. Assuming that these were deserved (they aren't always) Ken Gass' present production has done the piece a disservice. It is lax and scrappy; a woman greets the news that she is about to be subjected to severe physical torture as if she had just been reminded of an imminent dental check-up.

Kepler (Alon Nashman) is a persnickety little fellow with a suitably earnest demeanour; but what he believed, or why it mattered to him, were matters that left me baffled and finally indifferent. What bluff old Brahe (Gary Reineke) thought about Kepler was even more opaque, as indeed was what bluff old Brahe thought about anything, other than the loss of his nose in an early and unusually acrimonious scientific dispute. (He seemed to get over it surprisingly quickly, though people in later scenes said that he was still touchy about it.)

Most of the others stand around being competent in short bursts, though a couple aren't that good. It's very drab.

- Until Oct. 31. Box office: (416)-504-9971.

1999-10-08-shake-rattle-and-rock-n-roll:
SHAKING THE FOUNDATIONS

Buddies in Bad Times, Toronto

I went in innocent and came out impressed. The heyday of Carole Pope and her band Rough Trade was in the 1970s, long before I came to Toronto, and I probably wouldn't have been very interested even if I had been here. The band is usually cited as a progenitor of Canadian punk rock, and my own experience of British punk was that it was essentially -- indeed aggressively -- anti-musical.

The first and most durable surprise of Shaking the Foundations -- a staged assortment of numbers written by Pope and her collaborator Kevan Staples -- is how very musical it is. The songs, as performed by five female singers and one female pianist, seem to come out of the best end of rock 'n' roll -- the rhythm and blues end -- and they lend themselves very easily to the richly chorded jazz treatment they're given here. The result is a show that's cool in look, sound and attitude.

Highschool Confidential, Rough Trade's biggest hit (or foremost of the Pope-Staples pop staples), emerges unsurprisingly as their most immediately effective. The music swings and the lyric is wittily specific. Blisteringly sung by Tanya Rich as the second-act opener, it's a song of lesbian lust for the most icily desirable girl in the class that could probably, in the most traditional pop fashion, work just as well as a song for a horny male. (Whether the world would have been ready then for a man singing a lyric about creaming his jeans, any more than they apparently were for a woman, is of course another matter.)

It is, though, one of the few numbers in the lineup that could ever be that ecumenical. Most of the show is strictly girl-on-girl, "strictly" being the operative adverb since there's a strong S&M component as well: sometimes satirized, sometimes exalted.

It does get monotonous, though this is more a matter of style than content. Despite the resourcefulness of Bryden Macdonald's direction, which distributes the performers all over the Buddies in Bad Times cabaret space, the songs, like all pop songs, are easier to make theatrical than to make dramatic.

They are all confessional monologues, even if they're fiercer and more self-consciously outspoken than most. Every one of them is a solo. Some of them are solos with accompanying vocal harmonies, some are solos in which the lines are split five ways, but there's never any interplay between characters. Indeed, there are never, for more than a song at a time, any definable characters. (There is plenty of personality.) Any overall shape, as often happens in staged songfests, is in the eye of the compiler. As usually happens, there's an outbreak of togetherness at the end of the show.

The lyrics can be agreeably conversational -- "but I digress," says one song, in a Sondheim moment -- but they can also be melodramatic and pretentious. "There's no escape from this modern Third Reich," complains somebody (have they any idea what the Third Reich was actually like?), compounding the felony by adding, "there's no escape from this endless night." I think that this, which adds ineptitude to overkill, is meant to be a rhyme. There's no law saying that lyrics have to rhyme. Why try if you can't do it?

There is also a lot of the protest writing, endemic ever since Dylan and the Beatles, in which you spray aggression without worrying about the relation between the people you're attacking and the things you're accusing them of, or, come to that, the relation between one line and the next.

Some things are good, though. A very funny song called Grade B Movie is the closest the show comes to acknowledging the existence of heterosexual relationships. (It takes a dim view of them.) It is put over, with hilariously lampooned ardour, by Paula Wolfson, a chunky and magnetic performer who startlingly resembles the young Annie Ross: in her wry, tart, pervasive good humour; in her rhythmic sense; in her range, which goes from pealing highs to rocking lows; in her colloquial phrasing; in her general sense of grown-upness; even -- in certain lights -- in her carrot-red hair.

She also looks great in black lingerie, as do the admirable rest of the troupe -- Jane Miller, Gwyneth Baillie, Astrid Van Wieren, Tanya Rich and, not least, pianist and musical director Holly Arsenault. She, apart from Wolfson, is the real star of the show; she is certainly its pulsating engine.

- Until Oct. 31. Box office (416) 975-8555.

1999-10-09-a-self-indulgent-look-at-self:
Theatre Review

ACT OF GOD

Theatre Passe Muraille

Just what I needed: another monologue.

Lights up on a dentist's chair, front and centre of an otherwise empty stage. Enter James OReilly, author and performer, with a loping gait and even a loping voice, to discourse on the terrible state of his teeth.

Apparently he hasnt been to the dentist since he was a kid, when his parents told him that he didn't need those expensive braces, whatever the man said; after all, why preserve your teeth at the cost of an arm and a leg? (Note these parents down for later.)

So here he is, for major mouth surgery. He wonders why your teeth can't just drop out suddenly instead of slowly decaying like, say, the man in your apartment building who just quietly keels over and dies. He embarks on a full-blown fantasia about this guy, taking his tone from the common belief that extended whimsy is the same thing as comedy: pile on the quizzical inflections and somebody will laugh.

That was the prologue, now comes the play. The anaesthetic unleashes -- as he knew it would, having had plenty of non-medical experience with drugs -- a whole kennelful of memories. (Is he having a general or what Duke Ellington called, appositely though in another context, a Happy-Go-Lucky Local?)

His mind wanders over his early years, spent variously in Cleveland, Vancouver and Toronto; over his father, gamely refusing serious pain-killers after extended intestinal surgery; over arguments with contemporaries on the demerits of heavy metal versus progressive rock; on being pushed onto the streets by his folks to sell boxes of greetings-cards before graduating to a proper paper- route.

Everybody whom he quotes addresses him as Jim or Jimmy and the authors names is James, so we assume that what he is telling us is genuinely autobiographical; certainly there is no sense of a distance being kept between performer and material. It all seems random, and of a lot more interest to him than it could possibly be to us.

Shamefully, I found my mind taking off on its own excursions, and even asking some barely related questions. (How many plays begin in a tooth-clinic? Shaws You Never Can Tell, obviously. There must be others.)

In retrospect there does seem to be a shape, though that's not much consolation while you're actually listening. The protagonist circles around, finally zeroes in on, a specific youthful memory: a friend was struck by lightning and died, while he himself survived. (They had been under a tree; Jim had selflessly insisted on his friend having the best spot.) He recalls the nightmare ride in the ambulance. He feels guilty.

The shows title, Act of God, neatly points up its major flaw. An accident, however sad, is of no dramatic value; nobody is at fault and its unfair to treat the audience as if it were your insurance company, or -- if you feel really badly about it -- your shrink. We have been watching a self-indulgent play about self-indulgence.

The most effective sequence, by far, reaches back to a time when both Jimmy and his younger brother were small. They had been fighting for hours in front of the TV and their mother lost it. They were ordered to pack their bags (I was eight says O'Reilly pointedly, "my brother was six") and their father took them on a long drive to, he said, an orphanage. This understandably traumatized them, perhaps for life. It is suggested that the experience was ultimately responsible for the lightning incident, which makes no sense, or conceivably for our hero's reaction to it.

Maybe all of life is a guilt-trip, an especially vengeful act of God. Ultimately, though, it all seems like an excuse for the performer to get up and riff.

As a performer, he is fairly accomplished; he is not, as far as I can see, an actor (i.e. someone who builds a character and fits it within a context composed of other characters) but then he isnt pretending to be. Another James, James Thomson, perches in a gallery at the side of the stage, and supplies musical punctuation, witty and pertinent; they make a primal jazz duet, voice and bass, and OReilly's delivery is somewhat reminiscent of Ken Nordine, the 1950s word-jazz man, who is having something of a revival. It is dry and twangy, alternating between screeches of protest and murmurs of self-deprecation, varying the beat to emphasize the points. There are plenty of these but the sum total still seems pointless. Susan Potvin is the director and, apparently, muse. (Her credit in the latter capacity reads "dramaturged by"; now there's an ugly verb.) I wish theatres, and even some journalists, would stop promoting solo plays as if they had access to some special realm of confessional purity, when their real attraction is that they're cheap.

- Act of God runs until Oct. 24 at the Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, 16 Ryerson St. Call 504-7529.

1999-10-15-when-it-don-t-mean-a-thing:
SWINGSTEP

Ford Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

The title of this musical is somewhat confusing. Swingstep looks like a single word for dancing, any dancing, done to the music of a swing band. In fact its more what Humpty Dumpty called a portmanteau word, yoking together two separate concepts. There is swing, as in the newly popular hot music of the 1940s with its attendant jitterbugging, and there is step-dancing, the old Scottish form of tap that still thrives, or so were told, among its originators' descendants in Cape Breton.

Once you've taken this on board you expect a show about a culture- clash. Not a bit of it, the two styles get along famously; as somebody remarks, when were still only at the start of Act Two, you can hardly tell them apart. This is not a show thats big on conflict. Still, the actual dancing -- swing or step or both together -- is excellent. It's the best part of the evening. It's the only good part of the evening.

Our hero, Sonny Stone, is a New York bandleader and swing revivalist whose grandmother, herself a famous wartime singer, originally hailed from Nova Scotia. After her death, Sonny goes on a pilgrimage to her hometown that he finds to be populated almost entirely by restless but wholesome teenagers kicking up a storm on the cobblestones. He decides to put them in his show, thereby falling foul of the one non-stepping youth in the neighbourhood; a hard-working no-nonsense sort of lad, he suspects Sonny of having designs on his girlfriend, who is the local star attraction. (She can dance and play the violin simultaneously: a fiddler on the hoof.)

Thus far the action -- city slicker brings showbiz to yokels, with jealousy sub-plot -- has a marked similarity to that of Crazy for You, which was a retread to begin with. It also recalls classic Broadway hootenannies like Brigadoon and Finians Rainbow. Brigadoon was mixing swing and Celtic 50 years ago, with a jealous suitor thrown in, and Finians had a dumb girl who communicated through choreography; this show has a dumb boy who does the same.

The inhabitants also include twin brothers who talk in unison, a mixed-up girl from the wrong side of the tracks (I quote, believe it or not) and an endearing old man who gives his granddaughter tender advice in song about sticking to your true love, like the Salvation Army geezer in Guys and Dolls.

Coming up to date a bit, the show also resembles Rent in that it devotes a sizable chunk of its second half to mourning the death of a character who was never dramatically alive in the first place. I'm not accusing anyone of conscious plagiarism, merely suggesting that this is a musical that dwells solely in the land of other musicals. It does not create its own imaginative world, nor --despite gestures to Canadian content with occasional murmurs about a mining disaster that has traumatized the town -- does it have any connection with the real one.

What it does have are flashbacks: lots and lots of flashbacks. It seems that old Al, the grandfather, was once in love with Sonny's granny and -- through possessiveness and pig-headedness -- let her get away. He is determined not to let the new generation repeat his past mistakes, which are acted out in some detail. This means that a story in which we cant take any interest is periodically interrupted by another that we cant remember. This plot-behind-the- plot builds to a surprise ending that I wouldn't dream of giving away, if only because its memory brings on incapacitating fits of the giggles; it also, to be fair, incorporates the only passage of half-way decent writing in the evening, when Al and his Mary meet for the last time in a New York night-club.

Their relationship carries whatever emotional weight there is, but it has nothing to do with the supposedly central dance theme, so the production seems pointless. I knew it would come back," says Al, an all-purpose guardian of tradition, about the swing music of his youth, and that's as close as this musical gets to acknowledging the really interesting question, which is why a recycled form of music should have hit so big as to be worth building a show around.

My opinion of the book (originally by Ted Swindley, "adapted by Ted Dykstra) must by now be fairly clear. The direction (Allen MacInnis) is limp and fatally unfocused; it takes ages to work out who, on a crowded stage, is meant to be singing the opening song.

The set (Jean Claude Olivier) is an unseemly arrangement of steps and balconies, with a blue sky occasionally thrown in for spectacle; the costumes (Mary Fulford-Winsor), which might have provided some style, are nondescript.

As for the score: Charles T. Cozens, music and lyrics, has provided a couple of accurate-sounding pastiche novelties and has fitted them out with persuasive orchestrations. He has also (with lyrical help from Stephen Mayoff) written the usual turgid, anonymous contemporary" numbers for the today scenes. Not only are these bad in themselves, but they invariably tell us things that we already know; you can see them coming a mile off. (You can hear them, too; I havent heard such heavy-handed orchestral intros in years.)

The new numbers are padded out with standards: vocal (Smile, Ill Never Smile Again, You Made Me Love You -- none of them my favourites, but certainly with more profile than any of the competition) and instrumental.

Among the latter is Benny Goodman's Sing, Sing, Sing: an extraordinary choice since it has already occasioned one of Bob Fosse's most spectacular dance-creations, and there are other big- band flag-wavers. Too many shows seem to be chasing too few songs; Fosse had to compete with Cabaret and Chicago, now Swingstep goes toe-to-toe with Fosse.

Given this daunting comparison, Sergio Trujillo has done pretty well; on the evidence of this show and the Stratford West Side Story he strikes me as more a first-rate dance captain than an original choreographer, but he gets his company hopping here with vitality, precision and a trademark display of vivaciously upstretched hands.

Few individuals emerge from the mix, but Paul McQuillan as Sonny is both a zoot-suited slitherer and a sympathetic leading man; Tamara Bernier makes grandma Mary the warmest of ghosts; and Douglas Chamberlain, a trouper, is Al to the half-life.

The shows "original concept" is credited to its producer, David A. Ballinger, once a member of an English pop group called the Barron-Knights, who had a couple of hits in the early 60s with some rock-bottom comedy numbers in which they imitated other groups; I think I can discern some artistic continuity here. The show does in fact have a strangely British air; it recalls the kind of hopeful musical muddles that used to stagger across London stages immediately before the ascent of Andrew Lloyd Webber. (There's a scary thought; what rough beast, its hour come at last, is at this moment negotiating in Bethlehem for a favourable corporate rate, in hopes of settling in for a 10-year run?)

It's the kind of thing I thought wed got beyond; certainly its appearance on one of Torontos prime stages -- one with its own distinguished, if brief, musical history -- is ridiculous.

- Tickets: 416-870-8000.

1999-10-16-parody-a-comedy-at-your-peril:
MACHOMER
Tim Sims Playhouse

I would like to see The Simpsons spoof Macbeth. At least, I would have liked to see them do it up to two years ago, which is when the smartest and funniest show on television turned self-destructive and became one of the dumbest. Seeing somebody else spoof The Simpsons spoofing Macbeth is quite another matter, and not, I think, a very good idea. Rick Miller, who seems a gifted comic actor in his own right, stands at a mike dressed in a shiny red tunic and a mini-kilt, signifying Shakespeare and Scotland respectively. He embarks on a one-man miniaturized version of the tragedy, in which each character is given the voice and mannerisms of a figure from the TV series. Behind him is a slide-show, a swiftly-changing series of projections (his own drawings), which between them depict just about every inhabitant of Springfield ever to attract the cartoonists pencil. This is so that we will know which he is playing at a given moment.

Actually, he doesn't need the help. Most of his impersonations are fine. He is especially good at Mr. Burns (complete with fussy, masterful hand gestures), who plays Duncan and is allowed a very Burnsian posthumous triumph; at Burns acolyte Smithers, now transformed into the heir-apparent Malcolm; and at Ned Flanders, Homers pious and much-hated neighbour, who here becomes Banquo, Macbeth's virtuous and much-envied military colleague. His murder is a major act of Homeric wish-fulfilment.

Homer, you will have gathered, plays Macbeth. This is not happy casting, either way.

Miller is not that great at sounding like Homer, and Homer is terrible at speaking verse. He gabbles it. (There is precedent for this. The great Dan Castellaneta himself was unable to bring off an episode in which Homer recited The Raven.)

Quite often the Miller Homer slips out of character, wondering, for example, if that might not be a pizza rather than a dagger that he sees before him. And here beginneth, as Reverend Lovejoy might say, the first confusion: Are we watching the story of Macbeth, done in an assortment of familiar funny voices, or an actual production of Macbeth done by the citizens of Springfield? Miller calls his Macbeth, MacHomer but lets all the others keep their Shakespearean names. He keeps switching the conventions, grabbing indsicriminately at whichever might provide the easiest laugh. The law of diminishing returns kicks in early.

There is, as it happens, an actual, and classic, Simpsons episode that shows exactly where he has gone wrong. Oh, Streetcar was the Springfield community musical version of A Streetcar Named Desire.

The fun of this is that apart from adding songs (You're a gal and Im a fella/Stanley, stop, or Ill tell Stella"), the Springfield actors take both their own characters and Tennesse Williams' absolutely seriously. (I know that speaking of ficititious caracters as if they were real people is critical heresy. When the fictitious characters are cartoons it's probably an excommunication matter. But the fact is, I find the Simpsons crowd more real than anyone else on television.) Miller, by contrast, is stretching a facile two-minute gag to last an hour.

The basic problem is this. You can parody a tragedy, and all credit and hilarity to you if you succeed. It is very hard to parody comedy, because your audience has no way of knowing where your subject leaves off and you begin. All you end up doing is taking somebody elses jokes and passing them off as your own, which is what happens here. It comes off as a curious blend of plagiarism and sycophancy. It might be fruitful to satirize the marriage of the Macbeths in terms of the mariage of Homer and Marge, or vice versa, but youd have to work at it.

Miller doesn't seem inclined.

There are some nice things. One is the casting of Krusty the Klown as the drunken Porter, one hack comic desperately grappling with the 400-year-old routine of another. Another, though it's funniest in the program, is the casting of Groundskeeper Willie, Springfields one resident Hibernian, as "Token Scot. As for the Witches, the show was pre-empted by a Halloween special in which Marge and her dreadful sisters gathered round the cauldron. (If it were left to you, the whole soup would be nothing but newt eye.") Miller's choice of Captain McCallister, surely the least inspired creation in the series, to play First Witch is no competition. It seems arbitrary, like much of the show.

Miller changes voices with the speed of a virtuoso ventriloquist, and with the same unnerving hectic rhythm. There is an entr'acte in which he does a lightning series of pop-singer parodies and this, being less spun out and fawningly affectionate, is more attractive than the main attraction.

- MacHomer runs at the Tim Sims Playhouse, 56 Blue Jays Way, until Oct. 24. Call 343-0011.

1999-10-20-clash-of-egos-still-fails-to-:
IT'S ALL TRUE

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre

Jason Sherman's It's All True, back for its second Toronto run this year, remains a sizeable and very tasty slice of theatre. There has been some rewriting and re-casting, and both text and performance have sharpened and deepened. The dialogue has great stage presence -- it is weighty without being heavy -- and the construction is both graceful and ingenious. The show is more worth seeing than almost anything else in town. It is still, however, cold at the core.

This is a play set in a theatre and it uses the whole space. Richard Rose's production, in a spare and evocative set by Charlotte Dean, sits even better at Buddies in Bad Times than it did at the Tarragon; it makes especially effective use of a catwalk on one side of the auditorium, backed by a corrugated wall. This is where characters gather in twos and threes to confer and complain and romance and reminisce.

The time is 1937. We are in the throes of Roosevelt's Federal Theatre Project. The Cradle Will Rock, a "labour opera" written and composed by the unknown Marc Blitzstein and directed by the already famous 22-year-old Orson Welles, is about to open in New York when the government slaps a ban on it. Unexpectedly the actors' and musicians' unions, with their own territories to defend, play along with the authorities. "This show," protests Blitzstein, "is for unions." "But your union," says his producer silkily, "is not."

What happened next is theatrical legend. With their own theatre padlocked, the company marched downtown to another. Forbidden to appear on stage, the actors sang their parts from the house; denied musicians, Blitzstein played the whole score at an onstage piano. Welles' elaborate production, of course, went by the board, and the historical consensus has been good riddance. Whenever the show is revived (it's done with surprising frequency; I've seen it in New York, London and Toronto) it's staged as an approximation of that original impromptu spartan performance. I confess to an unregenerate wish to see it done with all of Welles' planned spectacular trappings and with a full orchestra.

Sherman's play shows us Welles and Blitzstein snapping continually over what one's showmanship is doing either to or for the other's pure political intentions. It is set on the crisis day, with flashbacks to earlier moments of planning, rehearsal and personal and political intrigue. One especially clever sequence juxtaposes the rehearsal of a key scene with instant fragments of the participants' private lives, called to mind by individual words and phrases, but it is clever rather than revealing. The play no longer presents its protagonists so insistently as men haunted by dead women (Welles' mother, Blitzstein's wife), but it still doesn't get very far with the relationship between them. There is Welles sure enough, the insomniac egomaniac, and there is Blitzstein, the nervous idealist, and they are both insecure (but then who isn't?) and they can both compromise despite their protestations. But the mere fact that they collaborated on a traumatic project doesn't make them illuminate one another.

What now stands out in the sharpest relief is the affair between two of Cradle's actors. There is Howard da Silva, who played the show's proletarian hero and is himself a glibly passionate social activist; and there is Olive Stanton, a desperate mother of three plucked from obscurity to play a highly symbolic prostitute, whom Howard seduces and drops when Welles and Blitzstein persuade him that it will be good for her performance and hence for the show. Martin Julien plays Howard with scrupulous attention to his mixed motivations, and Melody Johnson's Olive is a brilliant mixture of the downtrodden and the determined, pinched and scared but nobody's pushover.

There are two newcomers in the cast: Joseph Ziegler, in the most fluently detailed performance in the show, brings Blitzstein to life as a man in a perpetual state of discomfort with himself and everybody else; Vickie Papavs doubles as Welles' embittered wife and his stage manager, Jean Rosenthal, holding the show together as firmly and unobtrusively as the original must have done.

Victor Ertmanis' Welles still strikes me as implausibly charmless and sneering, but he is certainly forceful; and as John Houseman -- his colleague, producer and whipping boy -- Richard Binsley has grown considerably, from a spruce cartoon to a figure of bruised dignity. At one point, Welles tells him that he hopes he never takes to acting -- an elegant moment since that is just what Houseman, at the end of his life, successfully did.

Last time round I sniped at the absence of Blitzstein's actual music; unfairly, since the rights had been taken by Tim Robbins' imminent (and eagerly awaited) Cradle Will Rock movie. It's still a loss, though, with serious repercussions. If you want to show a historical instance of life imitating art, you break the rules if you manufacture the art yourself; and it's too tempting to lay on ready-made ironies. The play cheats; it pretends that Cradle is largely about the relationship between the Howard and Olive characters, whereas in fact they barely collide. Sherman has Blitzstein shouting, almost literally, "what about the workers?" when Welles supposedly cuts them from the last scene. But in the score as we have it they are only a rumbling offstage presence, and more powerful for it. Massed crowd scenes would have been more Welles' style than Blitzstein's anyway. The play seems willing to throw anything at Orson.

This may explain why the last scene, though atmospheric, is surprisingly unmoving. Blitzstein strikes up his one-man band; Olive, who has backed out because she cannot afford to be fired, nevertheless stands up and sings her opening lines. We aren't told why she changed her mind. Presumably she just felt that the show had to go on. The same feeling presumably unites all these rampaging egos. Sentimentalist that I am, I would go along with that. I just don't believe the play does.

- Until Nov. 14. Tickets: (416) 975-8555

1999-10-22-fear-of-fagin-is-political-co:
I recently caught up with the Stratford production of The School for Scandal and found it an intriguing mixture of good and bad. The characters in the play, as in most respectable English comedies of the 18th century, also divide into good and bad, morally speaking. What was interesting at Stratford was that, contrary to the general belief that vice is more interesting than virtue, nearly all the best performances came from those playing the nicest people.

The play itself is split between being a waspish satire on the theory and practice of character assassination, and a warmly charitable comedy about marriage and family. In this version, warmth wins. The stand-out performance, his every line both piercingly funny and poignantly true, is Brian Bedford's Sir Peter Teazle, the old man yoked in love and law to a young wife. The redoubtable James Blendick and the very promising Donald Carrier give him firm support as the most charitable members of the Surface family. In fact the only one of the goodies who fails to register is Brian Tree as the helpful moneylender Moseley.

Scholars of the works of Richard Brinsley Sheridan may rub their eyes at this point, and protest that there is no such character. That indeed is the problem. Sheridan's moneylender is called Moses and he is, of course, Jewish. This fact doesn't actually set off a flood of ethnic jokes, but it does underlie everything he says and how he says it. Deprived of this source of energy, a usually excellent actor has nothing to act.

As a Jew, I have never felt uncomfortable with Moses in previous productions; and I do recall that the broadest and funniest I have seen was in a British production directed by another Jew, Jonathan Miller. (This is the same Dr. Miller who years ago, in Beyond the Fringe, made the best of all anti-anti-Semitic jokes: "I'm not a Jew, actually. Just Jewish. Not the whole hog.") The Stratford decision, by the way, must have been made quite late; the original name figured in all the advance publicity. I wonder if Richard Monette, director of both the play and the festival, was responding to actual pressure, or if he was maybe attempting some kind of pre- emptive conciliation pending the next Stratford production of The Merchant of Venice. Forcible baptism is a discredited procedure, and I do find it piquant that in christening Moses, Stratford has lighted on a name only one vowel removed from that of the most celebrated of English Fascists.

A more celebrated literary Jew is about to undergo a similar conversion. A new adaptation of Dickens' Oliver Twist is being shown on BBC Television, after which it will undoubtedly make the customary trek to our own screens. The adaptor is Alan Bleasdale, author of the memorable GBH, and his leading actor from that series, Robert Lindsay, is playing Fagin, apparently as "a Czech magician who is only incidentally a Jew." I owe this information to Steven Berkoff, the ferocious British -- and Jewish -- actor, director and playwright who greeted the news with an aghast article in The Independent headlined "Don't deprive us of our best villains."

It's a new sensation for me -- I suspect it would surprise him too -- but I agree with Berkoff. He has, admittedly, his own axe to grind here; not only is he himself a powerful player of villains, he has even done a one-man show about them, including, I am reliably informed, a Shylock of quite mesmerizing political incorrectness. He also, with acknowledgements to someone's unerring sense of poetic justice -- played the only convincing Hitler (in the miniseries War and Remembrance) that I have ever seen.

He bases his Independent argument on two grounds: that Fagin, like Shylock, is a realistic illustration of the criminal straits into which Jews were driven by a Christian society; and that Fagin, like Shylock, is the creation of a writer of genius and should not be tampered with.

Whatever you make of The Merchant of Venice, there's no way any actor can play Shylock as a gentile. Fagin is theoretically a different case. He is, after all, a character in a novel, bound to suffer some alteration when transferred to stage or screen. And Fagin's Jewishness, unlike Shylock's, has no direct bearing on the plot. Dickens habitually calls him "the Jew" in the narrative, but the matter is hardly ever mentioned in the dialogue. Indeed, a non- denominational Fagin has already been tried, right here. A few seasons ago that bastion of right-mindedness, the Toronto Young People's Theatre, presented him as an indeterminate figure who sounded -- if you'll pardon the racism -- somewhat Irish.

It didn't work. And as usual in these cases you felt that nothing beneficial was being done for society but that those responsible were making themselves and a few adherents feel good. Like Stratford's Moses, the YPT Fagin faded into the woodwork -- and far more damagingly since, as written, he's the most vital character in the book. And that vitality seems inextricably tied to the charming, wheedling, sinister language that Dickens gave him, and that he obviously thought was Jewish.

At the end of his story Fagin, like Shylock, is brought to trial and condemned. Replying to the Berkoff article, John Sutherland of London University has protested that this is intolerable, that Dickens executes Fagin out of sheer malice: "what villainy is he hanged for? The novel never tells us." Professor Sutherland is an accredited Dickens scholar but he's wrong. The novel tells us, quite explicitly, that Fagin is hanged as an accessory to murder; it was he who goaded on Bill Sikes to the horrific killing of Nancy (the episode with which Dickens used to make ladies faint at his public readings).

The professor also points out that in his last completed novel, Our Mutual Friend, Dickens tried to make amends for Fagin by presenting a Jewish paragon, Mr. Riah. What he neglects to add is that Riah comes to life just once, and that's when his author finally loses patience with him; off to render charity to a man who has atrociously wronged him, he is told by his Christian friend Jenny Wren that "if your people don't know better [than that] it's a shame they ever got out of Egypt." Fagin, you feel, would have agreed with her. And Fagin, the solitary old man in the dock implictly demanding of his accusers "what right have you to murder me?", makes a far stronger case against his society and its prejudices than any plaster-saint could, simply by virtue of being alive.

Maybe, if you can't bear the idea of Fagin as Jewish villain, you should get rid of his villainy rather than his Jewishness. That is what the late Lionel Bart did when he wrote Oliver! which is about to come among us again, at Toronto's Princess of Wales Theatre. Turning a horrific novel into a family musical, Bart was unable to save Nancy or to whitewash Bill Sikes; the plot wouldn't let him. But he was able to turn Fagin into a lovable old rogue, with the accent and the timing of a great music-hall comedian, and I fancy that he didn't even realize he was making much of a change. That is how he saw Fagin and how, despite everything, generations of readers have seen him. That's why the musical works so well; it's a response to something that's actually in the book. Fagin is energy. So, in a much smaller way, is Sheridan's Moses, who doesn't even have to be bad to be good. The deracinated Mr. Moseley, who stands in for him at Stratford, doesn't manage to be anything. Possibly Berkoff got his war-cry slightly wrong. He should have been trumpeting not just Leave Us Our Villains but Let My People Stay.

1999-10-22-mcculloch-shares-his-hang-ups:
SLIGHTLY BIGGER CITIES

du Maurier Theatre Centre

I hesitate to describe Bruce McCulloch, sometime Kid in the Hall, as a stand-up comedian. For one thing, he does a lot of his current stage act sitting down, in a low-lying red armchair that one can only hope has seen better days. For another, every solo comic that I have seen -- good, bad or indifferent -- has had a fluent command of natural speech rhythms and has addressed the audience accordingly. McCulloch, who writes his own stuff, sounds as if he's reciting it, with a limited range of inflection.

He comes from Calgary, found fame of a kind in Toronto and is now based in Los Angeles. According to the advertising, this progression underlies the shows title, though the phrase itself only occurs once, in a reference to young women serving at McDonalds who dream of doing the same work "in slightly bigger cities." A not-bad observation, it is clearly meant to resonate plangently in our memories, and McCulloch apparently sees himself as a lyric poet of the world inside and around him.

Some of his phrases do recur, such as Is there anything sadder than a pair of empty shoes after they've gone? This baffling inquiry (is it the shoes themselves who've departed or their owner? - - in either case the answer is yes, in the real world there are many things much sadder, and anyone who needs to ask should get out more) makes its first appearance at the very start of the evening. It sets a tone -- one of winsome complaint -- for much of what follows. Repeating and elaborating the question at a later point, though, does not automatically qualify as dramatic structure.

Some lines are good; one or two are even funny. Just before winding up, he intones a look-at-all-the-lonely-people litany that includes a heart-warming reference to the hapless guy whose nearest approach to his beloved will be to sniff her bed-linen when he helps her move.

Earlier he has told us that you really get to know people not by loving them but by breaking up with them. This is a dubious theory, but he illustrates it engagingly by talking about a past flame who left him, it seems, to get in touch with her inner pain, though she already had a good pain thing going, being the kind of woman who, when served with the wrong wine, would describe the situation as "Kafkaesque," this despite, or more likely because of, the fact that she had never read Kafka. (I think Ive met her: repeatedly.)

I would not, though, want to push McCulloch too enthusiastically as an oracle on inter-gender relationships: not after hearing him go on for what felt like ages about his erotic prowess in a manner that is plainly meant to be self-deprecatory in its self-glorification and to reflect on the whole male sex rather than just him but is embarrassing anyway. And though I concede that the experience of watching a porn film with your father might give rise to some really lacerating comedy, it hasnt done so yet.

Passing, as one so easily does, from sex to religion, the unsupported statement that the latter activity gives stupid people something to do besides scratching lottery tickets, which in a way is the same thing, merely suggests that our commentator is in over his head.

Some topics he attacks at greater length. There is a flippant fantasia about a bun-fight between "the Clinique Ladies and the Body Shop Girls," and a solemn fantasia about a vigil for the late Kurt Cobain, and it's hard to say which is the more ineffectual. Occasionally, when his feelings become too overpowering for words, McCulloch gets up to do a pounding dance, his arms flailing and his legs rubbery.

In repose he looks tousled and sounds petulant. He is riding a depressing wave of men getting up alone on stages to tell us about their hang-ups -- real, imaginary or projected -- and passing off the result as a) social commentary and b) theatre. (The soiloquiser generally shares the stage with a musician; in this case it's a rock guitarist, Brian Connelly.) I speak of this plague as it afflicts Toronto, but I imagine that it's also raging, maybe even more intensively, in slightly smaller cities.

- Till Oct. 31. Box office: (416) 973-4000.
