1999-10-23-puzzling-symbolism-just-one-o:
Ghosts runs to Nov. 6 at the Canadia dell'Arte studio theatre, 186 Munro St. Call 465-7393

GHOSTS

Canadia dell' Arte

---

Just over 100 years ago, when Ibsen's Ghosts made its first appearance in English, the press gave it a notoriously rough ride. It was described in the London papers as "an open drain ... a loathsome sore left unbandaged."

It isn't as much fun as that makes it sound but it remains a taut, mesmerising play about a small group of people trapped by the mistakes of the past and by the way in which society continues to sanction those mistakes.

At the play's end Oswald Alving, a young Norwegian artist, sits slumped, his brain softening from inherited syphilis, while his agonised mother wonders whether to give him the morphine pills that will put him out of his misery. This scene, which so shocked the Victorian critics, was also responsible for the piece's glib dismissal by some of their successors; who needs a play about syphilis now that we have penicillin?

In fact, if Ghosts is a drama about syphilis, it's a pretty bad one; the subject isn't even mentioned till halfway through the action, and even then never by name. AIDS and the euthanasia debate have sharpened the impact for us, but Ibsen isn't asking us to build hospices or to put more money into medical research. He's asking us to live honestly, which is harder.

Peter Reitzel's production, for his Canadia dell'Arte Theatre Troupe (a cute name that sets my teeth on edge), is interestingly self-destructive. It is for the most part conventional and thoughtfully acted, and it traces the play's ideas with unusual clarity, but it has been placed in a self-consciously experimental setting and it features one oustandingly weird performance.

The play unfolds in a single bleak day. ("The weather," says the program breezily "is lousy.")

Mrs Alving has dedicated an orphanage to the memory of her late husband, a man much respected in the neighbourhood but known by her to have been a lecherous drunk. She herself, though, had never been much help to him; that is one of the crucial things she comes to realise in the course of her own long day's journey into a particularly appalling night. This production puts the play into modern dress while keeping the Norwegian references, though why it should assume that contemporary Scandinavia is a century behind the times is beyond me. The wide playing space, divided into three compartments, is littered with miscellaneous junk, presumably symbolizing the accumulated detritus of the Alvings' history. The living-room is dominated by a carpenter's work-bench - perhaps because one character is a carpenter, though he doesn't live there - and by a piano, which defeats me. Key scenes are acted on obscure parts of the stage and many of the moves are very awkward.

There may be beautiful intentions behind all this but it is not nice to watch.

The opening scene promises great things. Randall Lathier as Engstrand the wood-worker, and Julie Reitzel as Regina, his supposed daughter and Mrs Alving's maid, dig deeply but easily beneath the text, exposing all their characters' tensions, all their selfishness, all their distrust. She, as the play progresses, proves especially good, giving the girl -- for the first time in my experience -- a solid viewpoint of her own. These however are the easiest roles, the play collapses when Father Christmas comes on.

He is actually Pastor Manders, God's local representative, carrying a large cross and wearing what looks like a white muffler but proves to be a detachable beard. He takes it off (and parks the cross) during his more informal moments. Nobody else is acting in this ludicrously stylized convention, and the results are terrible.

Manders is the voice of stifling propriety (he's stifled himself, too) and any production's first job is to humanize him. Otherwise, even if you close your eyes and think of Preston Manning, he and the play just seem silly. In or out of mufti, Dennis Frey's performance is inadequate: bleating, inexpressive, and given to cartooned displays of sexual insecurity. Mrs Alving, a passionate and intelligent woman, is supposed to have loved this man.

This is like bad amateur acting.

The Alvings, mere et fils, are like good amateur acting: That is, they are clear and intelligent, but lacking in range and command. Jody Cummins' Mrs. A is a trim hausfrau (contemporary costume doesn't help her status) who learns and communicates her lessons bitterly and well; but when she speaks of the ghosts of the past she sounds impatient rather than haunted, as if she would like to get on with the hoovering. Michael Chipman is too subdued for Oswald's vaunted "joy of life" but his descriptions of his sickness and his final descent are wrenchingly believable. The two of them play their last scene with unforced concentration and harrowing force. The director then ruins it by junking Ibsen's last lines and having the company sing a hymn instead. I cannot imagine what this is intended to convey -- Ghosts, despite having a blinkered cleric and a Dickensian hypocrite in its cast, is a fiercely secular play -- but it is, as you may have gathered, typical.
1999-10-30-solo-artist-is-too-intelligen:
THE MALE INTELLECT: AN OXYMORON?

New Yorker Theatre

It seems a long time ago now, but The Male Intellect begins with something funny. Robert Dubac, author and sole performer, holds up a succession of self-help books on male-female relationships and recites their titles. He has arranged them so that each contradicts its predecessor -- no great feat, perhaps -- and he uses them to project a mounting sense of baffled incredulity.

His timing here is excellent. His timing throughout his ensuing 90-minute monologue is also excellent. His saving grace is that he is better than his material. His downfall is the material itself.

The show's full title is The Male Intellect -- An Oxymoron?, and your response to that may be the best index of whether you will find the piece itself hilarious, or intellectually challenging, or both.

Like too many items recently it is an unhappy compromise between comedy routine and full-fledged play. As a critic once said of Waiting for Godot, it doesn't have a plot but it does have a situation, and maybe even some suspense.

Dubac, in the tradition of comics from Jack Benny to Jerry Seinfeld, plays a character who may or not be himself but who has the same name. This particular Bobby has been deserted by his girl- friend for refusing to allow her cat in bed with them, but she has promised, or threatened, to call exactly two weeks later.

We are there at the moment of countdown, he can't leave until the phone rings and neither can we. I read somewhere that audiences in the halcyon days of movie-going, when they grew tired of waiting for the heroine to give in to the inevitable final clinch, would set up a ritual cry of "say yes, so we can all go home." In the same way, I wanted Bobby's girl to call early and maybe give him and us something else to think about.

As it is, his mind is naturally running on the gulf that seems to separate men and women. He is, in the literal sense, quite graphic about this, dividing the stage into two sections corresponding to the male and female halves of the human brain. (I don't think I want to hear about these any more.)

The male side, which he presumably knows most about, is very cluttered, crammed with sports gear and with filing-cabinets that turn out to be full of booze. This is in a show that ends by exhorting us to escape from gender stereotypes, and that preaches the sensible if uncontroversial doctrine that the sexes are complementary but different. The predictability of it all undermines even the good moments.

Bobby tells us that women dance because they enjoy it, men dance in order to get sex.

Well, that sounds accurate; I laughed. Then I thought about men I have known who do like dancing, and women who regard it as a tiresome social ritual. Maybe there's a difference between types -- who can certainly be the stuff of effective comedy, though they need a good story to activate them -- and stereotypes, who just hang around being dead. Dubac's format doesn't allow him to make a few good sexist jokes and pass on to other subjects; he has to hang in there.

Once again I appreciate the merits and the versatility of Seinfeld, both as a solo observer and as the organizer of 30-minute comedies of manners. Also, he wasn't concerned to make us feel fuzzily good about ourselves or other people -- which may be why, in this decadent age, people are turning against him.

Dubac comes from the same school as his fellow-American Rob Becker, whose extremely similar Defending the Caveman played here earlier this year; with a true comedian's long face and questioning eyes, Dubac has twice Becker's style but half his jokes. (Two instead of four.)

He is also a good mimic. He says that he has learned about women only from other men (why?) and impersonates a number of his old and young mentors and buddies to prove it. They come with an expertly- done variety of accents and grimaces, but all are essentially preaching the same insensitive doctrine, especially the one who talks about senstitivity.

You get the impression that Dubac is too intelligent for the company he keeps, even if the company is his own.

- The Male Intellect: An Oxymoron? Runs to Nov. 21 at the New Yorker Theatre, 651 Yonge St. Call 872-1111.

1999-11-01-no-more-tomorrows-for-phantom:
Last night, in the lobbies of the Pantages Theatre, they were selling souvenir programs and other memorabilia like there was no tomorrow. Which, in a sense, there wasn't. After 10 years, and on Halloween appropriately enough, the Toronto production of Andrew Lloyd Webber's The Phantom of the Opera came to a close.

After the curtain came down, the world repaired to a masquerade ball and charitable silent auction at the Windsor Arms Hotel.

This was perfect. The show itself includes a stunning-looking masquerade, and it begins with an auction, though not a silent one. Some of the same artifacts were on sale at both the real auction and the staged one. What was being commemorated was the end of a theatrical, maybe even a civic, era.

"There was more life in it," said Garth Drabinsky, who produced the show in Toronto and kept a tight grip on it for as long as he remained at the head of the now- extinct Livent empire.

"My plans ... would have kept it running for at least another year. But with no resources to market it, you lose momentum."

It doesn't mean much to call Phantom's run record-breaking, because there were no records to break. Nobody had tried to run a big musical indefinitely before; the two shows that have rivalled its longevity in London and New York -- Cats and Les Miserables -- have appeared in Toronto as recurrent attractions rather than permanent ones.

The Lion King, the only more recent show that might seem to have the same commercial legs, opens here next year; Disney produced it, the Mirvishes -- who have always seemed averse to unlimited runs -- are housing it, and what their long-term plans are nobody knows.

Mr. Drabinsky initially thought that Phantom would last three years, but when he told that to Mr. Lloyd Webber and to the press, "they thought I was nuts."

From the start, the selling of the play was unprecedentedly aggressive.

"We did over 100 radio ads. In terms of print ads, we had 400 different looks," Mr. Drabinsky said.

The radio ads, all of them built around the menacingly inviting Phantom voice as recorded by the late Stratford Festival actor Graeme Campbell, became part of Toronto's culture.

And not just of Toronto's.

Research commissioned by Livent a year into the run resulted in the show being marketed in Detroit, Cleveland, Pittsburgh, Buffalo, Rochester. The results, according to Mr. Drabinsky, were "astonishing," and put Toronto on the map as a theatrical tourist centre.

The effect on the surrounding economy has been incalculable. People came here to see Phantom rather than going to New York. And they stayed to eat, sleep, shop and even see other shows.

Mr. Drabinsky believes Phantom would have picked up business from next year's wave of tourists coming to see The Lion King. It would have had to weather a traditionally bleak January and February to get there, but then it always has. And then, Mr. Drabinsky said, the "Disney factor" would have kicked in; Disney rereleases their classic movies every seven years because "every seven years there's a new generation of audiences." And that should hold true for live theatre as well -- if it can hold on long enough to become an institution in the first place.

None of which explains why Phantom has exerted such a hold. Mr. Drabinsky is certain that it isn't the chandelier that falls at the end of the first act. When he first saw the show, fell in love with it and vowed to acquire the Canadian rights, he was seated in the back stalls of Her Majesty's Theatre in London underneath an overhang, and couldn't see the chandelier properly.

I agree with him: Once you've seen that effect, you've seen it and you don't need to come back. And people have come back to Phantom -- some devotees have made the pilgrimage dozens, even hundreds of times.

They like the love story -- it's the only single-mindedly romantic musical of recent years, and audiences get caught up in the central trio of virginal soprano, ardent young aristocrat and transcendentally ugly genius. (Or, to quote Mr. Drabinsky, "the triangle is ineluctable.")

Beyond this, of course, is the lure of the Phantom himself. All of us on some level feel misunderstood and unloved -- and the Phantom is both, on a truly gigantic scale.

And, yes, there is the spectacle, by which I mean the feeling of haunted lushness created by Hal Prince's direction, Maria Bjornson's sets and Andrew Bridge's lighting, which transports us from the Paris Opera to the Phantom's lair via a candle-lit subterranean lake. Visual splendour -- imaginative visual splendour -- is the one thing the theatre is about.

And the music helps. David Rogers is an actor who has been with the show since it opened. Starting as an all-purpose understudy, he graduated to playing Raoul, the hero, and has most recently been standby for the Phantom himself.

In the last week, he reverted to playing Raoul, with one shot at the Phantom when Paul Stanley took off on Friday for a one-shot gig in Las Vegas. (Mr. Rogers' audience probably got the better deal; Mr. Stanley, with his raucous rock-star voice, was nobody's "angel of music.")

Mr. Rogers told me that he still shivered when he heard Raoul's big song, All I Ask of You, welling up in the pit.

The show also contains excerpts from three imaginary operas: Each of these begins with some expert pastiche but in the last -- supposedly the Phantom's own -- the composer goes into his own melodramatic model, prompting the reflection that if the best aria Phantom could come up with was The Point of No Return, then maybe composing was not the greatest of his many talents.

Undoubtedly, though, the overall sound binds the package together.

And the Toronto production had one extra weapon: the theatre itself. The Pantages is a gorgeous piece of restoration, and an ideal frame for the show; it looks like the Paris Opera, and you can easily imagine the Masquerade number being staged on its main staircase.

Sadder than the show's closure -- all shows have to close some time -- is that nobody knows what future, if any, the Pantages has. Sad for the theatre staff, with no jobs to go to.

Sad for all of us.

1999-11-02-like-cole-and-mccartney:
THE JOHN PIZZARELLI TRIO

George Weston Recital Hall, Toronto

John Pizzarelli, jazz singer-guitarist, is the son of the noted non-singing guitarist Bucky Pizzarelli, and when he began his career he was billed as John Pizzarelli, Jr.

It was a good time to be a junior, and young Pizzarelli's record company promoted him as their answer to Harry Connick. Both came to prominence performing standard songs in ways that reminded people of older singers; Connick was touted as the new Sinatra, Pizzarelli as a latter-day Nat Cole. The two Wunderkinder have since gone in diametrically opposed directions.

Connick still sounds somewhat like Sinatra, tonally at least, but he has changed his repertoire; and the more he sings his own plodding songs, the duller his records get. Pizzarelli has dug further into the Cole mine, and his act might be described as a homage, but it is not an imitation; the more of Nats songs he does, the more he sounds like himself.

Like Cole in the 40s, he appears in a piano-bass-guitar trio format. The difference, of course, is that the leader and focus of attention is now the guitarist instead of the pianist. Instead of a reproduction of the King Cole lineup, we get a stimulatingly skewed revision of it.

The equation comes out about the same; the sweet and rhythmic guitar of Oscar Moore was as important to the original Cole trio sound as the leader's piano so Pizzarelli, who's a formidable instrumentalist quite apart from his singing, is a more than plausible leader now. And if his pianist, Ray Kennedy, has a self- effacing manner he turns out to be a furious player, as arresting as Cole but far more extrovert; more in fact like his apparent idol Oscar Peterson. The trio commenced on Friday night with a Pizzarelli original called Oh How My Heart Beats for You; unusually long for an opener, it filled its space, with Kennedy taking three fleet and seamless choruses in succession. In the second half, the three players -- the bassist is Pizzarellis brother, Martin -- did a storming instrumental of Sweet Georgia Brown.

Pizzarelli himself is never likely, I think, to escape from behind his guitar as Cole did from behind his piano. His singing is charming but small; indeed its charm lies in its modesty. Within it he can be witty -- as in his self-mocking treatment of the line about being "a rowdy-dowdy" in When I Take My Sugar to Tea -- and he can be touching; his Im in the Mood for Love was bashfully romantic, as if it were going on inside his head. He also did a trio of Beatles tunes. One, Honey Pie, he converted into his own currency; it could easily have been a swing-era novelty. And I Love Her he left, sweetly, much as it was -- but then his nice hip young man persona is not that different from Paul McCartney's. The third, Can't Buy Me Love, was indeterminate; it could have swung harder, as on the old Ella Fitzgerald record, without doing anyone any harm.

As a raconteur, Pizzarelli proved both voluble and valuable. He was very much on, spinning out finely-woven routines about opening for Frank Sinatra and almost meeting him, or about the indignities associated with making a vestigial appearance in The Out of Towners and about that movie's rapid (and merited) demise. These did sound spontaneous, even if they weren't.

Mimicry, however, is not his strong point; as he proved with an over-extended routine on I Like Jersey Best, which left to itself would be rather a funny song. This though was his closer, and by the time it came round he had earned far too much goodwill for us to hold it against him.
1999-11-04-a-play-always-in-search-of-th:
Everyone who has written about Art has said that it isn't really about art, it's about friendship, and I shall undoubtedly say it myself when I review Canada's first production of the play in English, which opens tomorrow. It will hurt to be echoing everybody else, and it will hurt even more to be repeating myself, but there's no help for it. I want to deliver some prefatory ruminations about Art, and I see no way of starting on them without telling you that this play concerns the relationship between three male chums.

There is Serge, a Parisian who buys a very expensive abstract painting, and there is Marc, who pours violent scorn on it, and there is Yvan, who bounces between the other two, trying to be nice to both. I saw the play in London, where it has now been running for three years, and about halfway through it I had a vision. I felt I wanted to see it performed by the three guys from Seinfeld. It seemed to mirror their relationship exactly.

Jerry would bring the picture home, ostensibly proud of his purchase, but full of doubts underneath. Kramer, acting very man-of- the-world, would ask him just what on Earth he thought he had spent his money on and would lecture him loftily on his lack of taste; to be sure Kramer has never, as far as I know, set up as an art expert, but his self-confidence has always been boundless and there's a first time for everything. George, meanwhile, would rush around flashing his insecurities and would keep trying to bring the conversation round to his own problems, just like Yvan, who in the play is largely preoccupied with his forthcoming wedding and with his friends' opinions of his fiancee.

I still think they'd make a great cast for some future TV production of the play, though there is obviously no chance they would ever do it in theatre. Even if he were willing to commit the time, I can't imagine Jerry Seinfeld sustaining a stage performance in a play for a whole evening, and I have no idea whether Michael Richards, who as Kramer seemed to be a clown rather than an actor, could do it or not. Jason Alexander, though, gives me the impression that he could do anything, and he would be a magnificent Yvan, who always steals the play -- just as Alexander's George, who became painfully real, used to steal the TV show -- and who has that rarity in modern drama, a show-stopping speech.

It's a shame there's no part for Elaine, but, at least as it stands, Art is an all-male play, even though its author, Yamina Reza, is a woman. (Incidentally, Seinfeld was unique among sitcoms in boasting four absolutely first-rate characters. Even Fawlty Towers could only muster three.)

Somebody else's similar fantasy, though, did nearly come off. There were plans for the three male stars of Frasier to do the play in Los Angeles and perhaps subsequently in London or New York, but it never happened. Certainly the roles would fit them up to a point. Connoisseurship is very much in Frasier's line and philistinism is very much in Martin's, though Serge and Marc ought really to be contemporaries. Niles into Yvan could be hilarious, though I'm not sure that the junior shrink's punctilious elegance would be of much use here; the two characters are different kinds of losers. Then again, Kelsey Grammer, David Hyde Pierce and John Mahoney are all practising and accomplished stage actors, and they wouldn't have to repeat their TV personae. And the characters in Art are very malleable.

There have to date been 12 separate casts in the London production of Art. It started out in 1996, with Tom Courtenay as Serge and Albert Finney as Marc. These two actors, like John Gielgud and Ralph Richardson, have increasingly become a double act as they have achieved doyen status. It was, however, the lesser-known Ken Stott who stole both the notices and the audience's hearts as Yvan, and this has been the routine ever since.

When the play appeared on Broadway in 1998, the usually urbane Alan Alda revealed an unaccustomed mean streak as Serge, and Victor Garber -- Canadian-born but part of the New York landscape by now -- was Marc. But it was Brit Alfred Molina as Yvan who captured the lightning and the Tony nomination. (Art, by the way, having lost most of the subsidiary awards to The Beauty Queen of Leenane, surprised everyone at the end of the evening by winning the award for best play.)

The characters in the New York production remained French; nevertheless, Molina, presumably to fit in with his colleagues, played with an American accent. There is an appropriateness about this; there is no way that these characters, with their intense notions about art and friendship, could be English, but they could just possibly be New Yorkers. They might even be Torontonians, if you confine your gaze to the areas within easy reach of the Art Gallery of Ontario. We will see what the Canadian cast -- Richard Poe, Scott Hylands and Stephen Ouimette -- make of them.

Molina's appearance also signalled an unusual period of transatlantic entente as actors commuted between the London and New York productions. There were four Broadway casts; the second one featured two wonderful character men, Henry Goodman and David Haig, who had been in the play in London but in different roles, confirming that in this piece an actor's individual qualities matter less than how he balances those of his colleagues. The third man, new to the play, was Brian Cox, Britain's best recent King Lear, who played the Finney role and looks rather like him.

Meanwhile, London played host to American actors such as Stacy Keach, David Dukes and Judd Hirsch. The West End production these days is peopled, as long-running shows tend to be, by solid backbone- of-the-profession kind of actors, bolstered by the odd former TV star. The current London Yvan is comedian Chris Langham (son of the great Stratford Festival director, Michael Langham), and I should think he would be wonderfully put-upon.

The final New York cast was heavy on comedians: Buck Henry, George Segal and as Yvan -- bringing my Seinfeld dream as close to realization as it's likely to get -- Wayne Knight, alias Newman. (I confess I find that one hard to visualize, but what do I know?)

Knight, of course, is also the cop in Third Rock from the Sun, but a Third Rock cast doing Art -- or anything else -- is more the stuff of nightmare. If you want science-fiction casting, imagine the play turning up as the cabaret at an intergenerational Star Trek convention: William Shatner being hectored by Patrick Stewart, and both of them making life hell for Leonard Nimoy.

That, of course, would mean upping the ages a bit; if you want to lower them, we could have the angst-ridden Dawson's Creek version, with the script revised to include a bit more navel-gazing and a lot more polysyllables: Pacey clicking his tongue over Dawson's ideas of how to spend his discretionary income, and Jack going really berserk over his wedding plans because he knows he's still gay.

We could even, if we could secure the services of a good medium, have a Marx Brothers version: Groucho as Serge, Chico as Marc, Harpo as Yvan. This, of course, would mean losing a third of the dialogue so that the play, already short, would run about an hour; but audiences' attention spans are growing notoriously short.

We have yet to see women in Art (as opposed to Women in Art), possibly because of the author's insistence that she was concerned with male relationships, thank you very much, and if she'd wanted to write about her own sex she would have done. Still, she can hardly expect to buck the Zeitgeist indefinitely, and I await Art: The Talk Show, with Rosie O'Donnell, Oprah Winfrey and -- for charity's sake - - Joan Rivers.

There could be the Canadian Stage Company version: I want to see Fiona Reid purchasing the art, Clare Coulter aghast at it, and -- I know -- Sandra Shamas going spare over the arrangements for her wedding reception.

Further along yet: when Friends finally comes off the air, and its cast are in need of a buck, they could all take to the road in a nostalgic production with rotating casting, segregated or co-ed as the mood or the fashion takes them. They could even use their old theme tune.

And then some curmudgeon of a critic could come along and ask them where they got the idea that the play is about them, because titles don't lie and it's meant to be about Art.

- Art opens at the Royal Alexandra theatre, Toronto, tomorrow night. Tickets: (416) 872-1212.

THE BUNDLE

Equity Showcase Performing Space, Toronto

Edward Bond's The Bundle, first seen in London 20 years ago, was described at the time as having "the force and the onward movement of a tidal wave." That's a good phrase, if I do say it myself; and I did say it myself, when reviewing the first production. My words, quoted in the publicity for this new Toronto staging, have come back to haunt me.

I stand by half of them, the half about the movement. The Bundle is a fable play, whose narrative extends over many years and many episodes, and Bond paces himself brilliantly. Every scene is clear, every scene has weight; and Bond's carved, tempered prose -- always cool, sometimes startlingly witty -- is a perfect medium, often imitated, never equalled.

The story begins with Basho, Japanese poet of the 17th century and master of the haiku, leaving his village to seek "enlightenment." Refusing to pay his ferryman ("I go to be reborn. Does the midwife charge the child?"), he spies an actual baby lying on the riverbank, abandoned by its poverty-stricken parents, but refuses to rescue it and risk spoiling his quest. After a token display of reluctance, the ferryman -- who calls himself a bad man but is regarded by everybody else as a saint -- takes the child in, and he and his wife raise it as -- since it's male -- their own son. They call him Wang.

Later on, the boy -- desperately crying, "Buy me, buy me" -- sells himself into nine years' servitude in order to protect his parents. Most of this time he spends in the house of the poet, who's now a judge. Thus educated, Wang joins a band of outlaws whom he turns into guerrillas. Their purpose is to expel the local landowner and to reform the economy, this by taming the river whose capricious floodings have hitherto kept the population at the authorities' mercy. They succeed; and at the end of the play everybody -- except Basho, who is still moaning about enlightenment -- seems dreamily happy, everybody left alive, that is.

Yes, there is a price to be paid. Bond dramatizes it by having Wang, like Basho, abandon a baby by the river just before taking flight. Basho is to be blamed for his action because his motives are selfish; Wang is to be endorsed because he's off to start a revolution.

Bond, in his voluminous commentary on his own plays, says that his purpose "is to demystify the use of moral argument." In other words, he's saying that the end justifies the means, which is something we shouldn't have believed even 20 years ago; writers as unimpeachably anti-capitalist as George Orwell and Albert Camus had exposed it halfway through the century. Anyway, Bond doesn't have the theatrical courage of his convictions. That baby on the bank is no test for an audience; it truly is a bundle, a prop made out of rags.

There are flesh-and-blood people who get killed in the play -- Wang's parents and one of his comrades -- but that is all the fault of the establishment that is chillingly, and very convincingly, nasty. Wang's own revolutionary hands are left amazingly clean. The play cheats.

I had the same intellectual doubts about the play's force when I first saw it, but at least the force was theatrically there, projected in a first-rate production by the Royal Shakespeare Company in one of its golden ages. Equity Showcase can hardly compete. Their new acting space, in the bowels of a church, is wide and bare and acoustically tough. The director, Dean Gabourie, puts his actors in monkish cowls and has them lie down end-to-end to simulate the river, which is striking, and he has a mobile raft, which is useful. He also has a habit of staging long, important scenes at the furthest reaches of the stage, which is infuriating. The brigand scenes are a dead loss, performed in an incomprehensible mumble, though the fault here is partly the play's; my admiration for Bond's style goes into abeyance when he gives Wang's merry men pidgin English to speak.

The company is large and unpaid and mostly inexperienced, which might seem right but isn't. The characters, in the style of a Brechtian or indeed a mediaeval morality play, have one dimension apiece but that is not a licence for monotony; if the psychological canvas is limited it needs to be all the more vigorously coloured.

Jovanni Sy's Wang has some youthful appeal but little ability at communicating thought processes. Christopher Kelk as Basho and Ed Fielding as the ferryman establish their basic qualities securely enough -- smugness and innocence respectively -- but can't put them to much subsequent use. There are some lively performances in small parts: from Richard Alan Campbell, very fluent as a smooth merchant; from Adrian Griffin as a secret policeman who twirls a sinister fan, and from Quyen Lee as a sly and desperate water-peddler.

Bond's group scenes of fear and mendacity are excellent; he may seem fuzzy about what society should be but he is mercilessly accurate on how it is.

DRINKING ALONE

Ford Centre Studio Theatre

Kenneth Tynan, whose great qualities as a critic included a substantial fund of common sense, once defined serious theatre as that which presents a view of life "from which the pain is not left out."

Theatre does not have to be serious to be good; nobody wants pain in Guys and Dolls. Trouble comes when a play flirts with pain without carrying through. You get semi-serious theatre, of which Drinking Alone is an example.

It belongs to an endangered species, in this town anyway. Norm Foster, who wrote it, is one of Canada's most successful playwrights; his plays, though, are hardly ever seen in Toronto, which notoriusly lacks a middle ground between shows with pretentions and shows with songs. We hardly get to see play in which the tone is comic, the settings middle-class and the problems soluble. The people who write them don't believe in them in the way they used to. So they try, conscientiously, to extend the boundaries. One character in Drinking Alone has cancer; that would have been at least unmentionable in a domestic comedy 20 years ago. The form, though, won't accommodate the content

Drinking Alone is actually more worthwhile than some of the more self-important stuff on our more self-important stages. It isn't especially funny (I think I laughed once), but it isn't boring either. But it has not found its own comfort-level; even structurally it seems to be two plays. We are in the home of Joe, a bachelor in his early thirties, and the frustrated proprietor of a modest dry-cleaning business. His sister, Carrie, a successful TV newsreader, is unhappily married and an alcoholic. Their mother was also an alcoholic, and this caused their father, Ivan, successful owner of a chain of bookstores, to leave home and set up house with another woman, name of Phyllis. The two generations have lived bitterly apart for years, but today, Ivan's birthday, they all gather in Joe's living room and reciminate.

Thus far, we have a predictable family drama. Father will tell son that he hasn't made anything of himself; son will reply he never had the chance; sister, in between kitchen trips to grab another beer, will accuse everyone of ruining her life. Stepmother will try to keep the peace; and we can be sure that, by the end, some kind of reconciliation will have occurred. All this does in fact come to pass.

There is, however, a fifth character, Renee, hired by Joe from an escort agency to pose as his fiancee and thus impress his father. (Why remains obscure.) Renee is, to use a suitably antique expression, a kook; told to talk as little as possible, she starts quacking away to her putative in-laws about her two-year engagement. Nobody is more surprised by her volubility than she is; her self- discovery through role-playing takes some swallowing but is entertaining. It does not, though, mesh with the familial squabbles; plainly meant to be a catalyst, she is at most an irritant. She is also the love interest: a single mother new to escorting who wants to be a hairdresser.

A play advanced enough to involve drunkenness, single motherhood and quasi-prostitution is not going to end in an old-fashioned love scene but the intention is the same. Joe and Renee begin and end the play; unfortunately, though, their growing attraction is a blank for the rest of it. Joe seems to be the metephorical solitary drinker of the title (as his sister is the literal one) but the idea is never developed. Other characters aren't much more substantial. None has a believable job.

A more accomplished production might have papered over the cracks, which could have been amusing, or exposed them, which might have been powerful. This one, directed by Eli Lukawitz, is the initial offering by a company called Tribal Productions which has taken up residence in the Ford Not bad, but unsteady.

The performances all lunge in the general direction of emotion. Lisa Messinger strikes out ahead as Renee. None manages to keep patness or cuteness entirely at bay. Life, in the end, goes on but it generally extorts a higher cost than this play seems able or willing to pay.

- Drinking Alone runs to Nov. 21. Call 416-733-0545

ART

Royal Alexandra Theatre, Toronto

Maybe Art really is about art. As you may have heard, Yasmina Rezas play -- a hit in Paris, London and New York -- concerns Serge, a dermatologist who spends the French equivalent of $50,000 on a medium-sized all-white abstract painting. This arouses the violent scorn of his friend Marc, an engineer and self-proclaimed defender of traditional cultural values. There is a third party, Yvan, an insecure chap who used to work in textiles and is now in stationery and who likes to agree with both of the others, which on this occasion proves both agonizingly and hilariously difficult.

Everyone -- including, on a previous occasion, me -- has said that the painting is just an arbitrary pretext for exposing the latent tensions within this trio, and that any other would have done just as well. Now Im not so sure. Art, or taste in art (I don't just mean the visual arts), occupies a unique position in human discourse; it is something about which we are all supposed to feel passionately but on which we can also agree to differ. This creates a strain. Politics doesn't do it, or religion; they create insurmountable barriers or none at all. The same with personal relationships: Of the three men in this play, Serge has been married, Marc still is, and Yvan is about to be.

Eventually -- the arguments about the painting having damaged the amour-propre of each -- they get around to badmouthing one anothers past, present or future spouses. But they would never have begun that way; if they had, there would quickly have been no friendship to salvage. As things are they can climb down, blame their indiscretions on that damn picture, and carry on more or less as before.

Serge even offers to let Marc deface his precious, vulnerable canvas, and Marc takes him up on it. Serge has a hidden agenda here and he is going to have to keep it hidden, for life.

Friendship stands revealed as being very like art: something good and necessary, but neither as holy nor as honest as we might like to believe. Each may convey a truth; each is rooted in deception. Each involves self-interest; Yvan has a spot on his hand that he would like Serge to take a look at.

The painting itself is generic-modern: the kind of thing people have been attacking and defending for ages. Serge claims that he can discern white lines on the white background (a whiter shade of pale, perhaps); and maybe he can. Maybe the painting gives him pleasure, or maybe he bought it as an investment, or maybe he just wants to annoy the possessive Marc, who claims to be his mentor. (It could of course be all of the above.) If its the last, he certainly succeeds; Marc sees red.

He has some very good arguments, does Marc. Accused of being old- fashioned, he asks "what use is being representative of your era? and, even more pertinently, how can a man live in any time but his own?" In other words, anyone alive is as much part of the age as anyone else; it's good to hear the boot being put into those who claim special privilege for their own tastes and beliefs by calling them "contemporary (or, God help us, relevant"). But it's just as good to hear Serge lay into Marc for his reverential and equally elitist use of the term "the Artist, i.e. someone, preferably dead, who doesnt paint rectangular slabs of non-representational monochrome. Marc is the intellectuals anti-intellectual.

In North America he'd be subscribing to, maybe writing for, Commentary or The New Criterion.

Like a good playwright, Reza spreads herself around. She claims to have got the idea for the play when she saw an all-white painting on a friend's wall and laughed; she seems to identify intellectually with Marc, while temperamentally lining up with the debonair ironic Serge.

Her heart, though, is probably with Yvan who is at sea through most of the debate, since he doesnt have any tastes or beliefs worth speaking of, and who is anyway preoccupied with his approaching wedding and with keeping his buddies on board for it. He has a long, frenzied speech -- one that never fails to bring down the house -- in which he recites the agonies he is going through just trying to get his mother, fiancee and prospective in-laws to agree on the wording of the invitations.

He suspects that the other two despise him, him with his spinelessness and his lack of success; he can hardly compete, socially or culturally, with his rich friends rich friends. (We hear of a dentist who only likes conceptual art.") His fears are well-founded; but it's also true that they need him as much as he needs them. Yvan quotes some gnomic lines from his shrink about the perils of letting yourself be defined by other people; Serge and Marc scoff but it's the boat that theyre all in, one that gets thoroughly rocked but cannot be allowed to capsize. Their relationship, like the play itself, is less about characters than about checks and balances between characters.

This elegant and original piece is the first French play in decades to have made any impression outside France. Marc the classicist would approve, since Paris used to be the theatregoers Mecca. Christopher Hampton has given it a splendidly springy translation; William Joseph Barnes' production (previously seen in Winnipeg), hewing closely to the London original by Matthew Warchus, is sharp, tense and funny. Scott Hylands plays a silvery schoolmasterly Marc, increasingly outraged by the unassertive independence of Richard Poe's Serge. Passions flare beneath their subfusc exteriors, though not enough to make us hold our breath as we should when they finally go head to head.

Stephen Ouimettes Yvan meanwhile takes his time; his big aria has less pace and definition than it might (it still gets applause, though), but his later wide-eyed writhings are delicious torture.

Mark Thompsons set is certainly about art; it makes its own minimalist statement, with each character in turn inhabiting the same pale room that is differentiated only by lighting and, naturally, the picture on the wall. Casual black sweaters and MJQ- ish music take us comfortably back to the days when Modern was still modern; and the radio ads are by Sean Connery, the show's co- producer, putting his mouth where his money is.

OLIVER!

Princess of Wales Theatre, Toronto

The great thing about Oliver! is that it doesn't play like an adaptation. Unlike most stage versions of classic books, musical or otherwise, it has its own identity, its own shape and its own jaunty tempo. Things do get rushed toward the end when hundreds of pages of novel are crammed into about 20 minutes of playing time. But even here the choices made are both clear and clever. And though Lionel Bart described this show -- for which he wrote book, music and lyrics -- as being "freely adapted from Oliver Twist, he was in many ways remarkably true to Dickens.

Oliver Twist, like many great books, has always led a double life. Its a horrific expose of crime, poverty and institutional cruelty in Victorian England, especially in relation to children. Its also a terrific adventure story, a kids' classic, and I suspect that if you asked most people to summarize their memories of reading it, they would come up with something very similar to the musical.

They would remember the hungry boy in the workhouse asking for more, and his subsequent flight to the excitement of the big city. They might remember that he turns out to be somehow related to the toffs who eventually rescue him, but would forget the complicated details; in this version he's revealed to be his benefactors grandson and thats that.

They would recall Fagin as a lovable thief, a funny if shady old man who gives Oliver shelter; they would filter out his involvement in Bill Sikes' murder of Nancy and his own eventual execution. They would not filter out the murder itself, a brutal battering that is one of the huge melodramatic climaxes of 19th-century fiction.

Whether by instinct or cunning -- I suspect it was mainly the former -- Bart made all these choices, arranged them logically, and made the whole thing move to music. His songs vary in quality but they all advance the action, present a character or glorify a moment.

As an unschooled musical dramatist -- a pop-meister who conquered the theatre -- Bart was something of a British Irving Berlin, if with nothing like the same talent, taste or discipline. Each of them spoke showbiz like a native, though by 1960, when Oliver! premiered, it was a more debased lingo than it had been when Berlin started up. Bart could articulate popular sentiment because he shared it; like Berlin, and indeed like Dickens. When Bart has his Oliver Twist pipe up where-ere-ere-ere is love/does it fall from skies above?" he is being more authentically Dickensian than we might care to admit. (Dickens' Oliver doesnt talk like that but he has a friend who does, a saintly orphan named Little Dick, foredoomed to an early grave.)

Sam Mendes production, which started out in London in 1994, has been widely hailed for putting some of the original Dickensian darkness back into the show. That's a matter of opinion. There is a new silent prologue, showing Oliver's mother staggering into the workhouse in the snow to give birth.

There is also a new scene for Fagin and Bill Sikes -- new to the show; the dialogue is in the novel -- well ahead of Bills originally scheduled entrance at the top of the second act: Fagin chatters nervously while Sikes remains hulkingly, terrifyingly silent, and the relationship between them is immensely strengthened. (Bart, who died this year, worked on the revisions for this production.)

But there was always terror nibbling at the edges of this show, and in some ways this revival is more of a jolly English pantomime than its predecessor. Matthew Bournes staging of the Consider Yourself number is awash in knees-up-and-see-the-sights-of-London choreography, and it all comes round again in the double-time reprise of Who Will Buy, effectively killing what used to be the most pulsating moment in the score.

The city itself is spectacularly rendered in Anthony Ward's sets. They don't unify the show as effectively as Sean Kennys legendary revolving original, which literally and figuratively swept all before it, but they have their own wonders; two separate bridges rise and fall, characters cavort in front of daintily-rendered Nash terraces (probably inspired by the film), and St. Pauls Cathedral makes an imposing appearance at the back. Fagin's den, somewhere beneath the sewer-line, is especially impressive.

This production's first Fagin was Jonathan Pryce, a classically trained actor having fun in a musical. We get the opposite extreme in Russ Abbot, a television comedian going straight -- which is what Fagin himself does at the end of the show, in Barts biggest but most logical departure from his source.

Abbot, a towering figure in the traditional hat and tatters, is actually at his best when trying least hard to be funny. His comic routines are pasted on but his moments of fear -- of Sikes, old age or the rope -- are very powerful. His voice, though, doesnt have the music-hall strength for which his songs cry out, especially the Reviewing the Situation soliloquy ("So at my time of life I should start turning over new leaves?) that is Bart's comic peak.

Sonia Swaby's Nancy, busty and red-dressed, is a production-line tart-with-a-heart; she, too, seemed to be having voice problems at the preview I saw, skirting the big notes of her big numbers, which include some of the best songs in the show. She did, though, gather all her forces for As Long as He Needs Me and was rewarded with cheers; its a shameless showstopper and a truly terrible song.

Everybody else is competent without being transfixing, and the orchestral playing is fine. The kids are all locally recruited, with Mitchell Moffitt appealing in the title role; and since it is the title role, I wonder why he isnt accorded a better showing, either in the billing or at the curtain call. (Are we still exploiting our children?)

Musical fanatics might note that one song has been cut, though its orchestral reprise mysteriously remains, and that Bart added some new lyrics to others. He was never what you'd call fastidious about rhymes, and in one of these late additions he couples utterly" with "gluttony." So at his time of life he should start turning over new leaves?

FAUST, PART ONE

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

---

Daniel Brooks' production of Faust is amazing. Its very existence is a cause for wonder: Goethe's long dramatic poem is only dubiously a play for the stage, despite its author's lifelong association with the theatre, and even in Germany productions of it are special events; outside, they are practically unheard of. When it is done, it is unlikely to be performed by a company of five, which is the total strength mustered at the Tarragon. It is even more unlikely to be done this hypnotically well.

The hardest thing to get one's head around is that this Faust is never in any danger of what we usually think of as damnation. That's not just because we are only being offered Goethe's Part One, which by definition leaves the hero on his feet; even at the end of the more densely philosophic Part Two he gets off scot-free. It's what he's escaping from that remains mysterious.

In Christopher Marlowe's Doctor Faustus, the English play that predates Goethe's by more than 200 years, the protagonist boasts that he thinks hell's a fable, to which his Mephistopheles sombrely replies, "Ay, think so, till experience change thy mind." You know where you are with that version, and where you are involves both tormenting fires and the eternal absence of God. Goethe, who just about personified the Enlightenment, never mentions the first and is at best equivocal about the second. He offers us a Faust without theology; he is elaborating on a legend, while ignoring or debunking the beliefs in which it was rooted. This makes the conflict stimulatingly, but sometimes fatiguingly, abstract. It also produces a mocking, questioning comic tone that this production superbly captures.

Goethe's Faust, like all Fausts, begins in his study, bored with it all. He has learned everything, cured everyone, won all the prizes (though not apparently much cash) and is 80 years old. Weary of earthly wisdom, he turns to magic and seeks union with an Earth spirit (the spirit of creation, I think), which rebuffs him. He thinks of suicide and then of the Devil, who appears first as a dog and then as a man. Asked what he is, this Mephistopheles suavely identifies himself as the spirit of denial; in other words, a universal cynic.

Faust makes a deal: Mephisto will become his servant and feed him with pleasures; if ever Faust confesses to a moment of real satisfaction, his soul will be the Devil's. He embarks in effect on a lifetime of asking, "Am I having fun yet?"

One thing Faust has been missing is sex. Mephisto takes him to a witch whose potions knock 30 years off his age. He then has a vision of a young country virgin and literally says to his attendant, "You gotta get me that girl." That line is the first-half closer, and gets a big laugh -- legitimately, since it's a huge anticlimax. Getting and abandoning that girl, Gretchen, takes Faust the rest of the play, and I've always thought it weird that a vast questing drama should decline so abruptly into a commonplace seduction piece. (It's far worse in the Gounod opera, which sentimentalizes everything.)

I was, it seems, wrong. In this production, the play still breaks into two clear halves, but they balance one another. Both are triumphantly lucid -- the first intellectually, the second emotionally. Faust's ruin of Gretchen and his degrees of remorse over it are the test of his surrender to the Devil's spirit of negation.

Brooks' staging is bracingly severe and wonderfully imaginative. The set (designed by Julie Fox, Jan Komarek and the director; lit by Andrea Lundy) is a wooden platform; it can divide laterally, and for his opening monologue Faust, placed between the two sections, seems in the half-light to be standing in a trench. When the lights go fully up, the front half of the stage is revealed as a long refectory table, at which the professor can receive worshipful students or diabolic house guests.

The supernatural effects are handled with dazzling simplicity; the spirits can be disembodied heads in fish bowls or red lights on the drapes (the devil dog's eyes) or echoing voices, booming or whispering.

Brooks is only defeated by Walpurgisnacht, but probably anyone would be; his version is seriously underpopulated, but I'm not sure that more would mean better. With the original's crowd scenes drastically and even cheekily reduced, five actors -- three male, two female -- actually seem a reasonable complement; there are, after all, only half-a-dozen named characters.

The five have to work phenomenally hard. Randy Hughson as Faust threads his way through the long debates -- internal, external and not all, to be frank, immediately theatrical -- while creating a sharp-tongued image of the scholarly mind at the end of its tether. It's a relief, though -- for actor, character and audience -- when the witch's Viagra lets him shed his beard and spectacles and offer what is almost a second performance: a callous, amoral young traveller (never without his suitcase) with the brain and recurrent scruples of an old one.

Chris Earle, by contrast, is enchantingly smooth and slippery as the tempter of the early scenes, but tends to repeat himself as the sinister valet of the later ones; even cynicism, it seems, can become monotonous.

Both these actors are a good deal more than good; the two actresses are downright magnificent. Maggie Huculak plays Martha, the heroine's friend and neighbour, and makes a full, sad, warm- blooded woman out of a conventional neglected wife and unmerry widow.

Waneta Storms' Gretchen is unforgettably real: In her blunt amazement that the glamorous stranger could possibly want her, in her progressive surrender, in her terror when she becomes pregnant and the village turns on her and in her madness when she has murdered her child and awaits execution. She is still sane enough to be instinctively repelled by Mephistopheles; her values are, in fact, traditionally Christian, and the play, after all its earlier skepticism, ends up endorsing them. I confess to finding this confusing, but its embodiment is very moving.

Ross Manson admirably completes the troupe as the aspiring pedant Wagner and as Gretchen's brother, in whom religion becomes a self- righteous, and murderous, code of honour.

The translation used is by Randall Jarrell and it sounds terse or expansive as required.

There have been some fine productions in and around Toronto this year, but I think this may be the finest.

1999-11-15-bring-me-the-ghost-of-gwendol:
Dont Sylvia Plath me, says Linda Griffiths at the beginning of her theatrical summoning of Gwendolyn MacEwen, "and I won't Sylvia Plath you."

This was encouraging; it confronted the primal fears of any audience about to experience a solo performance based on the life, works and personality of a female poet with a self-destructive streak. In fact, Griffiths-as-MacEwen is quick to point out that she didn't commit suicide: I drank myself to death -- theres a difference.

Rather a subtle one, I think, and not enough to prevent the built- in conventions of such an enterprise from exacting their toll. By the end, despite all her best intentions and even a few of my own, I felt thoroughly Plathed.

Griffiths has said that she came to MacEwen through working on a TV show about her and through reading what she refers to in a program note as a "biography of her life." (Those do tend to be the best kind.) The piece itself arranges its biographical information in a series of free-floating, non-chronological chunks; if you go in, as I did, with no more than a vague idea of the subjects notoriety you will be only a little wiser by the time you come out.

We learn that she was a fashionable and prolific writer in the 1970s when it was great to be young, and went into a steeply spiralling decline in the '80s when it was hell to be middle-aged, especially if youth was what you had had to sell in the first place. The piece is confessedly less about the woman herself than about a subjective conflation of performer and performed: what-Gwendolyn- means-to-me.

Very little of MacEwen's actual verse is included. This may be a prudent decision; poetry recitals are usually tedious, especially for an audience that has gone expecting a play, but removing the evidence of the subjects talent means removing the spectators main incentive for being interested in her in the first place.

In their place we have, from time to time, what Griffiths describes in the program as her own theatre pieces: little jingles that feature a recurrent obsession with nouns, mainly medical, ending in "-osis." At one point she falls back, with a great show of self-deprecation, on noses, leaving you wondering why nobody informed her of the existence of the word "proboscis."

Non-comic solo plays of a literary bent are generally boring; and my attention certainly wandered during this one. We are stuck with one person and with no chance of an alternate perspective; and the more hard-luck the story, the more we need an opposing voice to lift the curse of self-pity.

MacEwen herself was probably not self-pitying; the play presents her surveying the wreckage of her life with an air of mordant jocularity directed equally at herself and the shrinking world around her. (I didn't mean to go over the top. It's just that the top is so low nowadays.)

But the frame that it erects around her is ineluctably self- regarding; the tone may not be reverential but the event is. As for the occasional other people in the picture -- alcoholic father, crazed and verbally abusive mother, pungently malodorous first husband, unhelpful bank manager -- they do come momentarily to life, but only, and inevitably, as things in her dream. Reducing them to that level reduces her as well.

The show has considerable visual appeal in an austere way. MacEwen spent her later years in a succession of basement apartments; Jan Komarek, designing both set and lighting, evokes them with three variously shaded brick walls and a high bare window, which also suggest a prison cell. There is some play with the idea of MacEwen as a magician; the image is made flesh by having her perform a series of conjuring tricks, smoothly inserted by director Simon Heath and niftily executed by Griffiths.

She herself is a compelling sight: dark-haired and draped in a flowing, diaphanous red-and-white number, the love goddess of the Toronto book scene. As a performer she has improved enormously since her acclaimed debut in Maggie and Pierre, an atrociously smug show that must rank, despite severe competition, as the most overrated in the history of the Canadian theatre. She no longer scampers around the stage while gabbling her lines like a berserk ventriloquist; she now has stillness and pace and timing and command. She also, though she sometimes seems dangerously hung up on her own adjectives, lets her text breathe.

Griffiths does not, though, make it or her character live: not, at least, in terms that I could recognize or that could make me care. (Others apparently could; there were the regulation cheers at the end.)

The play is subtitled "a visitation" but it seems more like a rarefied seance.

MURDER ON THE LIMELIGHT EXPRESS

Limelight Dinner Theatre, Toronto

Mysteriously Yours, Mystery Dinner Theatre has been operating in Toronto for upwards of a dozen years now, playing in odd taverns and working the corporate circuit, doing no harm to anyone. They have now put down roots at the Limelight Dinner Theatre with a show called Murder on the Limelight Express, which -- obviously with that title -- is a spoof tailored to the locale.

I'm not sure that it's reviewable, at least not by any normal criteria, but it is some fun. It's what you call an experience: You go in and you eat.

The Limelight is a large, split-level room that, like so many in the real world, would be a very pleasant restaurant if it weren't for the food. Still, if you drink enough, you should be able to get into an appropriately receptive mood. You may even believe that you are in the dining car of a good old-fashioned European train, hurtling across the country in nostalgic luxury.

Actors come among you to encourage you in this delusion, dressed as collectors and inspectors. They chat you up and maybe ask you what you do for a living.

It's difficult to isolate the beginning of the play proper. There is a teaser in which a shot rings out and someone slumps over his table. We are then harangued by an implausibly slim young man claiming to be Hercule Poirot, Agatha Christie's famously pudgy Belgian detective, here to solve the case. He is speedily put in his place by the real Poirot, who rebukes him for the feebleness of his imposture.

This new Hercule is played by Jean Daigle, a founding father of the troupe, and his efforts are, well, Herculean. He directed the show and shares an author credit (with "Brian Caws, Andrew Welch & the Cast"). He speaks his lines Poirot-fashion (i.e. he is crisp and bossy and always refers to himself in the third person) and he governs the plot, the audience and his fellow actors with impeccable aplomb.

The train stops, because a man lies dead on the track. He is the rich owner of the railway and, naturally, the express is crowded with people just bursting with motives for doing him in. There are discarded mistresses, disgruntled employees and disinherited offspring -- he's been dissing everybody. The characters of course are not just stock but caricatures of stock. This makes them better and funnier company than the usual denizens of a whodunnit, but it does make it difficult to take seriously the question of what it was they've done.

I'm appallingly dense at picking up clues at the best of times. On this occasion it didn't even dawn on me that I was meant to be doing so until halfway through. I got a considerable jolt when I realized that the audience was going to be polled on the identity of the murderer. Those who were right would be rewarded and those who were wrong would be held up to public ridicule. I should have been among the latter, since I fingered the detective himself; not that I had any evidence, it's just that I'd longed for years to see that Brussels know-it-all given a taste of his own medicine.

Others in the audience apparently shared my feelings and, as had been threatened, their names were named. I was spared; maybe the PR department had blown my cover. Anyway, the real solution seemed very ingenious, as far as I could follow it, and I congratulate those who got it right.

The actors make extensive use of the audience, many of whom are drafted to play small parts, some of them involving lines. The best of them were amazingly good and should be retained for the run. You want appearance and reality, life and art, you got it.

A PERFECT ANALYSIS GIVEN BY A PARROT

Solar Stage Lunchtime Theatre, Toronto

Two mature Southern ladies, of dubious but carefully-preserved gentility, sit in a St.Louis bar, nursing their beers and wondering where their youths have gone. They also wonder where their middle- aged guys have gone; they are supposedly here with a couple of good ol' boys from one of the lesser-known fraternities. The Memphis Sons of Mars are in town for their annual convention, and these two hopeful daughters of Venus are, in every sense, hanging on.

It sounds like the archetypal set-up for a Tennessee Williams play, and that in fact is what it is; except that this piece only lasts half-an-hour, so the set-up is the play, a one-act vignette that Williams gave the world in 1958. It harks back to one of his best earlier dramas The Rose Tattoo, whose minor characters included an eager pair of harpy-groupies, given, like these, to saluting their beaux with a rousing chorus of Mademoiselle from Armentieres. This plays Flora and Bessie are the same women given a little time to rest their feet, contemplate their troubles, and delicately needle one another.

"Complacency is one thing," says Flora, the trimmer of the two when her friend reflects on the attractiveness of her own spreading figure, optimism another.

Williams is in fine verbal form in this dialogue, beginning with the girls displeasure at the seediness of their surroundings: "Waiter," they say, commenting on the room's lack of the entertainment promised at the door, this place is just a tissue of lies.

With that settled, they fall to recalling the more glamourous conventions of 20 or 30 years earlier, to lamenting their late husbands (granted one line apiece), to extolling or denigrating the restorative effects of golf and hair-styles, and to discreet boasts or disclaimers concerning their respective sexual availability. "Nobody's got any pride where men are concerned," says Bessie, who claims to be the more obliging of the two. Thats how it is, so lets face it.

Flora tells of having her character read by a parrot; you pay its owner a dime, and the bird brings you a piece of paper in its beak. Flora's particular fortune cookie reads "you have a sensitive nature and are frequently misunderstood by your close companions" which is archetypal Williams, both in its quivering pain and in the robust way that it burlesques that pain. (Williams himself read the role of Flora, to Maureen Stapleton's Bessie, at the premiere 40 years ago, and the play seems as likely as any of his others to be a coded gay lament.) Bessie laughs at this, thereby proving its truth, and Flora does the same thing back.

There isnt much else to the play, but you end up with a very good sense of these womens past and present, and can shudder sympathetically at their likely future.

There is probably more bite and shape to it than appears in Bernadette Jones' production, which plonks two distinguished actresses down at a table and lets them get on with it. Heaven forbid that I should appear ungallant towards Southern womanhood, but Williams describes his characters as "in the late afternoon of their youth" and these ladies seem to have advanced well past the happy hour. This, strangely enough, makes the characters less rather than more disturbing; instead of a desperate clinging to something only just out of reach, we get a good-humoured remembrance of times thoroughly past. They are a ringing pair of Dixie belles, played without grotesquerie. Charmion King as Bessie could actually afford to be blowsier than she is. Barbara Chilcott as Flora wields a sharp and fancy verbal stiletto

By way of prologue we get a glimpse of the two missing Martians whooping it up in another hostelry. Williams didn't write this, and the dialogue isnt up to his level; but its sufficient, and the men, heartily embodied by A. Frank Ruffo and David Dunbar, spend most of the time singing and pounding the piano anyway. (Baby Face is their ballad of choice.) Then, at the very end of the play proper, they reappear, to sweep the girls off for a good time.

I assumed that this was a director's interpolation, and a bad one; Bessie and Flora seemed all set for a defiant prowl of the city's best and second-best hotels, perspiring beneath the paint. It turns out that it's in the script, but I think Williams meant the encounter to seem more menacing in its automatic gaiety than it does in the rushed finale we get here. The characters may think they have a happy ending, but the production doesn't have to indulge them.

HOWL

Tallulahs Cabaret, Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, Toronto

You learn something every day. I had always assumed that the Beat Generation were so called because of their affinity with jazz. It turns out that Jack Kerouac, who coined the phrase, was thinking of beat as in deadbeat, broke, freedom just another name for nothing left to lose. (I never thought Id want to quote that line.)

Kerouac also used beat as an abbreviation for beatific; he thought of himself and his friends as exemplifying, in the program's phrase, the secret holiness of the downtrodden. (I got this information from the program note to Howl, which, as often these days, is a lot more informative than the play.)

There are four beats in Howl: Kerouac, Neal Cassady, William Burroughs and Allen Ginsberg, after whose well-known poem the show is named. As the downtrodden go, they seem rather perky; and though the show does seem to regard them as holy, we gather this more from the devout light that it shines on them than from anything they do, say or write.

The text is drawn from their verse and prose, and it begins with Ginsberg's celebrated "I have seen the best minds of my generation destroyed by madness...". That is a sonorous line, but it is much too rhetorical to be specific (i.e., its undramatic), and it doesnt seem relevant to the characters; their minds were good but they weren't the best, and they weren't mad.

Nor were they destroyed, or no more than anybody else; they were actually, Ginsberg and Burroughs certainly, survivors. If the madness that destroyed them is meant to be societys (it probably is), then the point isnt theatrically proven.

The idea of the Beats turns out to be more fun than listening to their actual writings, which are windy. The most attractive style belongs to Cassady (Hume Baugh), the non-professional scribe who limits himself to writing letters. The show proper begins with an anecdote about meeting, and nearly making it with, his dream girl on a Greyhound bus. The others greet this tall-sounding story with an assortment of whoops and giggles, but they all seem to believe him; they're just the thinkers, but Cassady is their action man.

This is another literary evening masquerading as theatre, and proceeding on the questionable assumption that slabs of non- dramatic text, lifted from the page and delivered by one actor in the general direction of another actor, constitute dialogue.

The extracts were apparently chosen by the director, Mark Cassidy, in consultation with the actors, and they vary. Burroughs' stuff comes over as a total loss, and Patrick Conner in an undertakers suit makes him seem an exceptionally nasty piece of work, superciliously sadistic.

Jim Jones Kerouac, on the road of course, is engaging, partly because he seems to regard himself as something of a fraud, perhaps because he keys into everybody's favourite myths about America as a place to be endlessly travelled through. His love of jazz is another bonus, occasioning some of the liveliest descriptive writing in the show, prose that gets entertainingly lost as it attempts to mimic the music. (There is an attendant saxophonist, Jon Stewart, whose mournful, fevered sound does more to conjure up the '50s than anything else in the show.)

Alon Nashman makes the finest impact as Ginsberg: not the hearty bearded prophet of later years but a nervous, spectacled sophomore - - one of Natures Woody Allens, or even one of her young Arthur Millers -- who suffers eloquently and movingly when he falls in love. I dont know why we're supposed to care so much about the foursome's love lives, but Nashman is the only one who makes it seem worthwhile.

The fact that the Beats had sex with each other is surely not such a big deal but we seem to spend an awful lot of time watching them doing it. The end of one coupling is accompanied by a back- projection of a mushroom cloud: a strangely ambiguous use of an image that elsewhere is used as a symbol of everything the Beats were rebelling against, along with footage of phenomena such as Nixon.

These pictures constitute the shows only gestures toward historical context, and as such they are extraordinarily lazy. Movements, after all, can often be best defined through their enemies, and the Beats had some lulus; Howl sells its heroes short by taking them entirely on their own terms. A subject and a conflict have gone missing.

The shows last words, like its first, go to Ginsberg; the complete quartet gather on a staircase to declaim his most exalted, or at least most excited, thoughts. This is where the holiness comes in: In the eyes of the master, holy are -- among many other things, and in ascending order of dubiousness -- the body, the typewriter and the bomb. (I wasn't kidding about the ambiguity on this last item; it seems Ginsberg and co. didn't need Dr. Strangelove to stop them worrying.) This is the kind of guff whose time came round again with New Age (if you'll pardon the expression) thinking, which is probably why it's in the theatre now.

1999-11-20-deeper-than-neil-simon:
Alan Ayckbourn used to be called Britain's answer to Neil Simon, both of them being prolific comic playwrights hugely successful in their native markets but a hard sell outside.

The comparison doesnt hold; Ayckbourn ranks far below Simon as a wisecracker. In fact, he writes few quotable lines though he occasionally comes up with beauties. In Communicating Doors, a lady off-handedly remarks that no woman in her right mind wants to relive her honeymoon.

Theres a depth of casual misanthropy there that Simon would never aspire to. In fact what distinguishes Ayckbourn from Simon (or his Canadian step-cousin Norm Foster), is that he never balks at bad behaviour, never tells comfortable lies, personal or social.

He also plays far more complicated technical games. Simon wrote Plaza Suite, three disconnected episodes in the life of the same hotel room. In Communicating Doors, Ayckbourn takes Simon's conceit and crosses it with Hitchcock's Psycho, J. B. Priestleys time-warp plays and The Lion, The Witch and the Wardrobe.

We begin in the future. It is 2019, and Poopay, a young dominatrix, has been summoned to the hotel to minister to a rich old man called Reece. It turns out that he doesnt want discipline, or even sex. He wants her to witness his confession. He has been married twice, and connived at the deaths of both his wives, though the murders were actually committed by Julian, his sinister aide.

Learning what is afoot, Julian chases Poopay first into the bathroom (definitely a place of ill omen), and then into an adjacent store room, which she locks against him. She finds it not only a refuge but a time machine. She emerges to find that it is 20 years earlier (now, in fact) and occupied by Reece's second wife Ruella, whom she warns of her future fate.

Ruella is finally convinced and goes back a further 20 years, by the same route, to perform the same service for Jessica, the first wife, who proves harder to persuade. And so it goes, the doors constantly swinging, the time constantly changing, and the women charging through both in order to rewrite history and save their own and one another's lives.

Time-travel stories always make my head ache; if you could go back and change things, the ramifications would be endless. Youd need parallel universes. Ayckbourn cleverly builds these quibbles into his scheme, and the piece is a structural delight. Its also a thriller that thrills -- though this production seems uncertain how far to stylize the melodrama -- and a comedy that's funny, though less so here than it might be.

It is indeed one of a kind, even in its author's capacious canon (53 and counting). He has sometimes been gratuitously dark, as if saying "you didnt expect a boulevard playwright to pull this, did you?" He may be, apart from Aristophanes and Feydeau, the only comic dramatist never to write a love scene (as opposed to a sex scene). But he has his feelings, and they seep through the cracks. The title refers to more than one kind of communication. The play expresses an unforced concern over an increasingly uncaring and dehumanized world (in Ayckbourns future even video stores have given way to "virtuality shops"). It's also a female-solidarity play: one in which the dominatrix really learns control. And it ends with a touching, and utterly unexpected, epiphany.

Ayckbourn's flaw is that he doesnt create memorable characters. They do what is required of them, but only the old couple in Bedroom Farce (his best play, and a minor classic), escape their authors jurisdiction and insist on a life of their own. On their home ground, his plays benefit from top-of-the-line casting. This doesn't happen here; Janet Wright's production is long on pace but short on flavour.

The performances -- notably Aviva Armour-Ostroff's Poopay -- markedly improve when the action takes over and they can do rather than just be. Kate Trotter briskly controls the proceedings as Ruella. Bruce Hunter is the actor charged with putting together the errant Reece's pieces; the character is really three separate roles, and he falters in the first two but does the last beautifully. The most in style, though not quite there yet, is Robert Persichini as a sad-sack hotel detective; he is, embryonically, a joy.
