THE GLACE BAY MINERS MUSEUM

Factory Theatre, Toronto

The great thing about the central performance in The Glace Bay Miners Museum is that it has no truck with worthiness. This is a blight that attacks every other aspect of Wendy Lill's play. Set among the coal miners of Cape Breton during the appalling Depression, it's based on the novel by Sheldon Currie that was also the source of the film Margarets Museum.

The audience arrives to find the stage covered in furniture and the furniture covered in dust sheets. We are plainly in for a domestic reduction of an epic theme; and the heart sinks. It rises, though, when Irene Poole takes the stage to perform -- in quick succession and ascending order of ferocity -- a mournful-sounding song in Gaelic, a bawdy song in English, and an aggressive bit of tap that I can now, thanks to Swingstep, identify as step-dancing. Then she introduces herself.

She is Margaret, daughter of a dead miner, granddaughter of another miner who is alive but severely damaged, and sister of two more miners, one of whom is also dead. She herself is known locally as the slut with a runny nose. She speaks plainly and racingly; she is bursting with intelligence and personality, and is hence very attractive. She may also be a bit crazy.

A table and chairs are unwrapped, and we are transported to a bleak cafe for a nicely crafted scene in which Margaret, suspicious but susceptible, meets the love of her life. He is Neil, who spent one day down the mines and then fled, and is an evangelist for the Capes ancestral Scottish culture. He woos Margaret by playing the bagpipes, and it works.

Everyone to his taste: My own feeling is that the presence of bagpipes in a play should be the subject of a warning notice in the lobby, like the ones they have for cigarettes, strobe lights, sex and swearing. There are no strobes in this play.

Margaret takes Neil home and he more or less moves in. So do we, the table and chairs having re-grouped to create the family kitchen. Poverty, illness, and the threat of unemployment weigh heavy on everyone's spirits, and we hunker down for two acts of bickering and making up, meant to reflect the wider tensions in the world outside.

Through it all, Poole's Margaret gives as good as she gets, generally better. Youre like a perfectly tuned set of pipes," Neil tells her, "you always make the right sound -- it comes from deep inside you. Its the truth. Alone in the cast, she avoids both rhetoric and sentimentality. The play ends with Margaret's three remaining men all dead, and deciding to take a body part from each of them, pickle and preserve it, thus creating the museum of the title. All we have of other people, she says by way of epilogue, is our memories of them.

This presupposes that they are worth remembering. In the theatre, it means that they should have lived while they were alive. This, neither the play, the performances, nor Rosemary Dunsmore's direction, can make happen. The actors are all recognizably talented, but theyre painting by numbers.

Wendy Thatcher as Margarets hard-pressed mother spits nails as required, is intermittently tender as necessary -- but when she harangues her family about their desperate position, a harangue is what it remains, and her shrill efforts to personalize it make it worse. Oliver Becker's Neil starts off cute and ends up wet, perhaps because his character, though certainly voluble, is crucially underwritten. He eventually gives in and returns to the mines, but this traumatic decision seems to leave no mark.

There is a running duel between the apolitical Neil and his kid- brother-in-law (Peter van Gestel), a strong union man who also happens to be carrying on, offstage, with a boss's daughter. Their debate mirrors the bitter paradox of all mining disputes: attempts to keep working in a terrible job. Eventually there is a strike. This too, of course, happens offstage; we learn about it mainly from Margaret, in her periodic capacity as narrator-of-last-resort.

I havent read the book or seen the movie, but I imagine that they got out into the community more. The boxed-in treatment here is not only claustrophobic but counter-productive. It is possible to illuminate big conflicts through small ones. Ibsen did it, Chekhov did it, and the best contemporary plays seen in Toronto this year -- The Drawer Boy, The Beauty Queen of Leenane, Communicating Doors -- have also done it. They summoned history; but not through talking about specific but invisible factual events that were happening on the characters doorsteps.

Onstage symbolism is provided by grandfather (Les Carlson, chairbound) whose lungs have been destroyed in the pits; who has lost the ability, or maybe just the desire, to speak; and who has been denied compensation. The implications are horrific, and all too likely; the presentation is merely irritating. The play harks back to a supposed golden age of Canadian theatre in which telling our story" -- putting bits of it up on the stage and making your audience feel proud or ashamed -- was thought to be enough. It isn't.

CHEKHOVS SHORTS

Factory Studio Theatre, Toronto

Four actors in rhythmic succession bob up before us on a sparsely lit stage, each of them wearing a dark overcoat and carrying a suitcase. They look very Russian and -- how can I put this? -- very mime.

They are Theatre Smith-Gilmour, a clown troupe consisting on this occasion of founder-directors Dean Gilmour and Michele Smith, plus guest performers Patricia Marceau and Liisa Repo-Martell. The last- named was last seen being wonderful in the Soulpepper production of Platonov, and here she is Chekhovian again. Chekhovs Shorts is not, as you might hope, a saucy comic anecdote about the great Russian author and his underwear. It's a dramatization of four of his short stories, presented within the framework of a fifth, depicting a long journey on a crowded train. The overall tone is one of foreboding farce.

Creating modes of transport without recourse to scenery seems to be one of the basic mimetic skills, but this foursome are exceptionally good at it. Using their bags to form seats or partitions, wielding them as weapons of offence or defence, shutting one another off with them, they perfectly suggest the fellow- travellers' habitual blend of bonhomie and hostility. They can laugh mercilessly at one of their number who has boarded the wrong train but they can also settle down for a cozy game of cards.

They also narrate and enact a series of dovetailing tales, each of them concerned with fear and loneliness. One depicts a schoolmaster whose relation with his colleagues is one of mutual suspicion and derision and who loses his chance at love because of it. Another presents a sleep-deprived nurserymaid, tormented by a crying baby and ceaselessly harrassed by its unsympathetic parents.

We then have the surprisingly similar story of a stray dog who experiences both the glamour and the cruelty of the circus. Finally, there is a coffin-maker, tetchy and self-absorbed, who moonlights as violinist in a Jewish orchestra and who loses the wife he has always taken for granted. (When the doctors refuse to treat her, he puts it down to Russias two-tier medical system; If I were rich, youd bleed her.) He sinks into terminal misanthrophy, from which only his music can rescue him.

All these vignettes are acted out with great quick-change resourcefulness, with the jolting rhythm of the railway always going on behind them; the performers generally look better than they sound but they are all unflappably secure. The mixture of gentleness and ruthlessness is very true to Chekhov, though I'm not sure that the phantasmagoric quality, endemic to this kind of show, really suits him. His poetry was realist, not expressionist.

When it comes to source-material, Theatre Smith-Gilmour doesn't kid around; they have an ongoing Dante project (Hell down, Purgatory to come) and they have done the Bible. They have also had one previous go at their present author, in what sounds like a heavily stylized version of The Cherry Orchard; Chekov admittedly said that his full-length plays were "almost farces" but it's probably imprudent to believe him.

He did, though, write a clutch of one-act farces -- he called them vaudevilles -- which, on the face of it, would suit Theatre S- G perfectly. But maybe a choice that straightforward would cramp their style.

SPRING AWAKENING

Studio Theatre,

York Quay Centre, Harbourfront

Any child caught up in the German school system at the end of the last century was lucky to get out of it alive. That at least is what the writers tell us, from the moderately conservative Thomas Mann to the unquenchably radical Frank Wedekind. In Mann's great novel Buddenbrooks, a well- meaning, not-too-bright boy is crushed between family expectations and academic cruelty.

Spring Awakening, which is Wedekind's first and probably best play, shows us a whole stageful of broken, stunted or cancelled teenage lives.

Their teachers are self-satisfied sadists and their parents, even the best-intentioned, not much better. Still, most kids survive and the title is not ironic. Spring Awakening is a surprisingly cheerful and even charming play. Spring not only awakens, it ripens to a sticky, pastoral summer.It is also, even by our complacently enlightened standards, both amazingly outspoken and alarmingly close to home.

Here is the roll call: Melchior Gabor, prize student, is sent to a reformatory for knowing too much about sex. He has got a 14-year- old girl pregnant and has written a basic biological paper, later found among the effects of a suicidal friend who had requested the information and been unable to find it in the encyclopaedias.

The friend, Moritz Stiefel, has shot himself, his desperation engendered partly by pubescent angst but mainly by an insanely competitive exam regime. (His surname, by the way, is misprounced throughout this production, perhaps they were trying for a pun on "stifle.") The girl, Wendla Bergmann, dies at the hands of an abortionist, procured for her by a mother who would have preferred her to go on believing in the stork.

Minor characters include a girl whose parents regularly beat her for their own amusement and a boy who has a long lyrical speech consigning to the flames the latest in a long series of classical nudes that have been his sources of erotic stimulation.

You use whatever is at hand, so to speak.

The play is full of these introspective outbursts, like Dawson's Creek with a classical education. Other scenes, especially those involving the grown-ups, are contrastingly brief and brutish.

Ed Gass-Donnelly's production has its flaws, mainly arising from a compulsion to underline the obvious. But at its best it is excellent: the best Equity Showcase show in a long time.

It is especially successful with the two principal boys whose scenes together have a remarkably easy flow. Both are, in their different ways, somewhat knowing, somewhat naive, and the balance here is just right.

Moritz ends by emerging from the grave to extol the virtues of death. Life, he says in a striking phrase, "is a sin of omission".

Melchior, momentarily tempted, resists and strides off to glory.

Philip Riccio's Moritz has a touching air of foredoomed defeat, ruefully acknowledged. Aaron Poole's Melchior, a touch less accomplished (and, as written, a touch less interesting), nevertheless drives the play forcefully and intelligently along. Both deliver their taxing texts with exemplary lucidity, as does Dylan Trowbridge as the incendiary art-fancier.

The girls are less convincing: They are inescapably contemporary Canadian kids who, in this context, know too much. Holly Lewis works hard at Wendla's innocence, but she seems inappropriately tough.

The big dividing-line, though, is between the children and the adults. Colleen Williams as Wendla's blushing mother seems in her earlier scenes to share her daughter's reluctance to believe that these people could possibly be real. She is moving, though, when tragedy finally strikes.

The other elders vary from well-meaning ineffectiveness to an apparent ignorance of what they're supposed to be talking about.

Though his staging is economically effective, the director is also prone to bouts of fashionable self-indulgence: there are two explicit masturbation scenes, which is one more than necessary, while Melchior proceeds from kissing Wendla to penetrating her with unlikely speed. (The ecnounter is not supposed to be a rape, though the production seems to think it is.) Most grotesque is the lip- licking staging of Melchior's interrogation by his teachers.

The satire here is admittedly heavy-handed as written, but it's not improved by having the principal excite himself to orgasm at the prospect of expelling the boy or by equipping the staff with goose- steps and Hitler salutes. The director obviously disapproves of Fascism and of sexual repression, but doesn't everybody? Whatever happened to the good old theory of playing even monsters from their own point of view?

Still, these are lapses of judgment rather than of skill or imagination. The all-purpose Germanness, by the way, extends to the background music which is Brecht and Weill. We hear a song from Mahagonny, and are sent home to the strains of Brecht himself warbling Mack the Knife.

The implication, a true one, is that Wedekind paved the way for Brecht, though I'm not at all sure that Brecht ever wrote anything as good or as enduringly pertinent as Spring Awakening. And if you like your drama to be socially useful, then this is the best sex- education play ever written.

- Spring Awakening plays to Dec. 5 at the York Quay Centre. Call 416-533-6100.

THE DROWSY CHAPERONE

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

Just over a year ago a Toronto actor, Bob Martin, married a Toronto actress, Janet Van De Graaff. A group of their friends surprised them with a pre-nup cabaret, a spoof 1920s musical comedy whose plot revolved around the wedding of two characters named Robert Martin and Janet Van De Graaff. They called it The Drowsy Chaperone. It went down well, and was expanded and re-mounted: first at the 1999 fringe festival; now for a regular run at Passe Muraille.

The real-life happy couple, safely spliced, have advanced from members of the audience to members of the cast. Janet plays Janet, a role in which she seems oddly miscast. Bob is a narrator-figure, billed as Man in Chair, and he has much the best of the deal.

He plays a helplessly enthused musicals buff. He sits at the side of the stage, spinning original cast 78s of his favourite show, The Drowsy Chaperone, and drawing our attention to its salient points as it comes to life before our eyes. "So many rhymes for Graaff!" he exclaims, after an opening number built around the central characters' names.

The song serves to introduce all the other characters as well: a device whose self-consciousness brands it immediately as parody rather than the real thing.

Among the throng are a pair of self-described "nameless, generic gangsters" whose presence immediately sends one's mind -- well, they sent my mind -- hurtling forward to the 1940s and Cole Porter's Kiss Me Kate. Sure enough, the two mugs get to perform an old-time Bowery waltz modelled in music, lyric and choreography on that show's Brush Up Your Shakespeare. When it's over our host steps forward to acknowledge the resemblance, thereby infuriating any critics who might have been itching to point it out for themselves. (Guilty.)

At other times he fills us in on the unglamorous future lives of the show's original performers. Ruefully, he acknowledges the gulf between the world of musicals, where bursting into song gets you applause, and the real world, where it gets you committed.

Martin, who somewhat resembles Danny Kaye and has the same mad glint in his eye, is a touchingly fragile figure who communicates, both through what he says and what he is, some very apt comments on showbiz nostalgia.

His role, though, has the unfortunate side-effect of killing the rest of the show stone dead. It's a tenuous concept to begin with and it never gets a chance to stand on its own feet.

The nonpareil of this kind of pastiche entertainment is Sandy Wilson's The Boy Friend, which offered songs that could stand comparison with those they burlesqued and took its story and characters absolutely seriously; spoof though it was, it actually involved you. It was some high-wire act. This show exists solely for its jokes, only a few of which make the grade. (There's one involving a telephone directory that's a gem.)

There is another way to use musical satire, which is to comment not only on other musicals but on the world that engendered them; Kander and Ebb did it in Cabaret and Chicago and Stephen Sondheim in Follies.

Come to think of it, the authors of this show -- Lisa Lambert, lyricist; Greg Morrison, composer; Don McKellar, librettist -- did it earlier this year, quite delightfully, in Honest Ed -- The Bargain Musical. Their biography of Ed Mirvish was a fanciful lampoon, but it gave them something to write about. Here all they can do is make fun of a form that was tongue-in-cheek to begin with.

Technically, their work is unobjectionable. The lyrics are, as the man in the chair observes, pretty good with the rhymes. I especially relished the couplet "down with your dour puss/hey little sourpuss" whose raised-eyebrow wordplay is redolent of Ira Gershwin. Indeed, the Gershwins seem to be the show's main point of reference, and it got me pining for a revival of Lady Be Good.

A dance-tune called Cold Feets has a Gershwin-out-of-Harlem touch about it, as if Duke Ellington had taken to writing show-tunes; our narrator duly mentions this, though a reference to "Harold Arlen drinking bath-tub gin while appropriating black rhythms" is an affront both to Arlen's musical genius and to his fastidious personal tastes: Also to history, since Arlen didn't get started till the '30s and the tone of this show is definitely, to adapt a Cole Porter phrase, pre-Depresh.

The Porter phrase the authors really seem to have in mind, though, is Anything Goes; they don't scruple to bring in Carmen Miranda in her tutti-frutti hat, to provide a finale that's anachronistic by at least 10 years. If all you have to sell are style and period, you better get them right.

The supporting characters are the usual-suspect bunch of cartoons -- harried producer, dumb showgirl, gigolo (one of those Continental types who used to come between Fred and Ginger and who here looks like Hitler), maid and butler -- and the cast, who are almost uniformly unappealing, do little to put fresh wit into them.

The plot, such as it is and sluggishly directed, just lies there. The costumes, designed by Christopher Richards and executed on a shoestring, are really stylish.

LESLIE ARDEN AND FRIENDS

Canadian Stage Theatre, Toronto

I laughed twice during the opening number, which is a self- deprecating, audience-welcoming thing called Don't Expect Too Much. They werent belly laughs, more warmly appreciative chuckles, but two laughs of any kind are a lot for any song.

And Leslie Arden is not primarily a comic writer. She is the composer-lyricist whose uneven but impressive The House of Martin Guerre was staged in Toronto last year. Her current show, subtitled A Meeting of Minds, is a kind of modified anthology. Assisted by three singers and three musicians, she presents a cavalcade of songs from her works in progress. (Any musical is a work in progress until it gets staged, and frequently afterwards as well.) The concluding sequence is composed of Guerre songs, and they stand up very well. They end the show on a note of justified triumph.

The songs are arranged in groups, but there are no announcements, and only a few minimal passages of dialogue. We can tell from internal evidence that Ardens portfolio includes a musical about 18th-century Canadian pioneer women of Scottish extraction, and another based on the fairy tale about the peasant-girl who could weave straw into gold.

You can usually tell how the various sections fit together but you can't always work out when one has come to an end. I was still mentally caught up with the pioneer ladies when a wistful song called Robert Dreams came along; even with my special interest, it took me some time to realize that Robert was not one of their husbands, off in a world of his own, but somebody modern. I assume now that he belongs to the same project -- something, I guess, modestly satirical about Toronto yuppies -- as the three females who follow him onto the stage to sing The Ladies' List, which is about love and friendship and shopping.

Arden was a student in the musical-theatre course that Stephen Sondheim taught for a year at Oxford, and she seems to be drawn to similar subject matter. The listing ladies come over as gentler descendants of the ones who lunched in Company, a show whose central character was also called Robert. The fairy-tale bits, also including a Hansel and Gretel witch who sings a cheerful confessional called I Eat Children, wake obvious echoes of Into the Woods, though their affectionate jocularity is even more reminiscent of Mary Rodgers Once Upon a Mattress. The imagery of Demons Fly suggests a downright homage to a song in Sweeney Todd.

Arden lacks Sondheims all-pervasive irony, and she is more inclined to straightforward affirmation. When she has a man sing The World is Changing he means it positively and so does she. Sometimes her awareness and her idealism clash, as in Happy New Year,which is about counting our individual blessings despite massacres abroad and poverty at home; one knows what she means, but as a dramatic statement it doesn't really balance.

Her great lyrical strengths, though (other than the rare but basic knowledge of what to do with rhyme and metre), are that she can handle conversation in song and that, when she writes a solo, she charts the developing awareness of the character singing it. She rarely just takes an emotion and has it jump up and down on the spot.

There are Sondheim touches, too, in the nervous energy of her accompanying figures. (She does her own orchestrations, on top of everything else; in fact, she has five separate credits on the program's title page.) Her melodies, though, are two generations further on, which makes them two generations removed from the last period at which theatre music was pop music.

Unlike some of her American contemporaries, she hasnt gone art- song; she tends to fall back on folk and soft-rock rhythms, which sap her strength and make too many of her tunes, at least on first hearing, sound the same. Shes also capable, though, of writing a blues-drenched secular spiritual that galvanizes both the audience and the performers.

I'm not sure that her present format shows her wares off to best advantage. The individual mini-musicals tend to end just when you're getting involved in them, and though Allison Grant's staging has elegance, it lacks shape.

The singers -- Glynis Ranney, Jay Turvey and Julain Molnar -- are not natural revuers; they have fine voices but not especially winning personalities: not, at least, without consistent characters through which to filter them. Arden herself, safe behind her keyboard, sings comparatively little; but when she does give out, she does it with more warmth and colour than anyone else on stage.

Down in the forest of Arden, something stirs, something ambitious and intelligent and -- to a Canadian musical theatre whose aspirations have previously been defined by Anne of Green Gables and Billy Bishop Goes to War -- it may be the best thing to happen, ever.

Black & White Photo: Michael Mitchell, Canadian Stage / Friends all: Glynis Ranney, Leslie Arden, Jay Turvey and Julain Molnar ;

THE CONJUROR'S SUITE

Royal Ontario Museum

A couple of years ago David Ben presented a magic show which he called The Conjuror. He performed, in costume, a selection of feats originated by the great illusionists of the 19th century. The tricks were amazing but the presentation stiff. The mixture is pretty much the same in the sequel, The Conjuror's Suite.

The premise of the new show is that, rather than witnessing it in a public theatre we are assisting at a private display in a Victorian or Edwardian salon. Frankly, I didn't notice too much difference. Ben performs in a smaller room at the ROM than he did last time, on a set with some scrambled elements of the drawing- room, but the audience still sits in serried rows and it still feels like a theatre.

There is perhaps a subtle change in the way he talks to us. Before, he acted the Victorian magician. Now, he speaks more or less in his own person about what it was like to be or to see a Victorian magician. He refers back rather too often to the previous show and seems to be trying for a mixture of old and new, formality and chumminess. The strain tells.

He still dresses in period, sporting a frock-coat and cravat, and with a lock of his floppily abundant black hair dropping down over one eye. (By the end of the show it was two locks over two eyes.) When he speaks, his rhythms are halting. He is not an actor and he doesn't carry the vocal or temperamental weight of an old-time prestidigitator. He is not a comedian either, and his banter with the audience -- especially with those, children and adults, whose assistance he enlists -- is forced.

For me, the best magicians, like the best jugglers, are the funny ones.

There is, after all, a built-in montony to the form. You know in advance that they are going to bring off whatever they attempt, and humour is the best way of lubricating the process and involving the audience. It can also, of course, distract the audience, taking its mind off the mechanics -- and in that sense Ben, possibly to his credit, is working without a net.

Not that I could do what he does, or have the first idea how he does it. There are too many card-tricks, montonous for those of us seated farthest from the stage, who are forcibly reminded that we are not in a salon. But there are plenty of more-involving feats. He causes balls to move invisibly underneath a trio of cups: a familiar routine but still a baffling one. In tribute to Harry Houdini he swallows a needle and thread. He robs a lady of her wedding-ring and then presents it to her, mysteriously ensconced in a box within a box within a box. (This, it struck me, was a Houdini escape stunt turned inside out.) This is genuine -- i.e. triumphantly false -- sleight of hand, and the young magicians in my company pronounced it to be all much better than David Copperfield, whose array of smoke, mirrors and dancing-girls they dismissed as high-tech fakery. The only Ben trick that had them thoroughly flummoxed -- not even guessing what kind of process was nvolved, let alone how they worked -- was one in which he identifies a specific word in a specific line on a specific page of one of half-a-dozen volumes of poetry. As he says himself, in one of his happier pieces of patter, this is the kind of thing for which.you might once have been burned at the stake.

I was dazzled, but also rather bored. And pulling this off may be the conjuror's neatest trick of all.

Black & White Photo: Tannis Toohey, National Post / Magician David Ben slowly removes a long line of threaded needles from his mouth in The Conjuror's Suite. ;
1999-12-11-nothing-but-cinders:
I'm sorry to say it but Sears aint got no class. Sears presents Cinderella, the program says, all big, bold and italicized. They seem to have taken their participation as a licence to plug their wares.

Most shows at least have the grace to spread the commercials around a bit. Here the backers even have their logo emblazoned on the toy sleigh that descends from the flies bearing presents for the intrepid kids who have climbed on stage for the mandatory sing- along sequence. The company may think this makes them look like Santa Claus. I think it makes them look like Scrooge.

It is also stretching things to describe this Cinderella as a contribution to the arts. Its the latest of Ross Petty's attempts to mount an English-style pantomime in Canada, an endeavour that peaked a few years ago in the memorable Robin Hood and has been in steep decline ever since. Petty, previously the fruity villain of his own pieces, has this time remained off stage as adaptor (from what?), and director.

Much of his staging is not so much traditional as antiquarian -- not since the '60s can a panto have begun with half-a-dozen merry villagers doing what might be charitably described as a dance while favouring us with a hopeful chorus of A Wonderful Day Like Today.

The old story has been given a few new tweaks, too. Baron Hardup, Cinderellas dad, has not yet taken his second wife, he is merely engaged. We never do meet his intended, but her daughters, the Ugly Sisters, have come to stay with their future in-laws. Even by pantomime standards, this raises serious problems of credibility.

If the sisters have just arrived and have no legal status in the household, why does Cinderella put up with their bullying? Why doesnt she just appeal to her father, who seems to dislike them anyway?

He is a puzzling character altogether.

Though apparently eligible for an invitation to the ball he a) stays home; b) is pressed into service, along with the faithful Buttons, as one of his daughter's coachmen; c) turns up anyway in his own person and gets an official welcome. The baron is played by Ernie Coombs, the veteran children's entertainer (Dressup as Hardup), and he won a little of my heart by trying less frenetically to be funny than anyone else on stage.

Cinderella (Laura Bertram) is a Disney heroine with glimmerings of a conscience. She disapproves of blood sports and hangs out in the forest with her furry friends singing Talk to the Animals.

Prince Charming (Laird Mackintosh) is thoroughly repulsive, making his first appearance swinging across the stage and back on a trailing vine, and then announcing, "My name is Prince. I swing both ways."

The Ugly Sisters are played by a couple of refugees from our classic festivals, Stratfords Juan Chioran and Niagaras William Vickers. Chioran, very tall, has the more originality and authority, and Vickers, rather short, the more music-hall spirit.

The production, whatever Sears' investment, looks as cheap as it sounds. Even the palace staircase lets us down, being poky and twisting and destructive of grand entrances.

There are a few good moments, such as Vickers singing, comically but also sweetly, Round Midnight. This must be the first time Thelonious Monk has made it into a pantomime. On the whole, though, if you want a show for Christmas, go to Oliver!

CINDERELLA

Elgin Theatre

1999-12-13-why-did-he-do-it-you-may-well:
Carols and seasonal novelties are playing as the audience enters the theatre, and there is a tree in the centre of the playing area. A young man is making some desultory attempts at decorating it. James Harkness' Pills, a success on the Toronto fringe, has been brought to the Factory for Christmas, but nobody is likely to walk into it expecting a happy holiday show

The young man is sitting on a small trunk, for lack of anything more comfortable, and he is surrounded by whisky and cigarettes. He is a former mental patient who has decided to give up on his medication; hence the play's title, though of course it ramifies.

He is called Jason. (At least I think he is; the characters have been christened in the program but the dialogue doesn't know from names and, since the actors are listed alphabetically rather than in order of appearance, I may have got them mixed up.) He is soon joined by his boy-friend Bill, who is older and a car mechanic. Love is in the air, but is greatly outweighed by desperation. It's a familiar message: this may be the season of goodwill but it's a wilderness out there.

One way for the audience to track a path through the jungle is to regard the action as the chronicle of one man's efforts to get laid. Bill tries to get it on with every other member of the three-person cast in turn and is thwarted every time. He is about to have sex with Jason, when the latter spies a dead mouse in the corner of the room, poisoned apparently by the hated woman in the flat upstairs. He is distressed and the mood is broken.

Bill wanders out into the park where he encounters Ron, a middle- aged teacher. They seem to be happily picking one another up, when suddenly Ron turns on Bill and savagely beats him.

Lurking in the shadows is Marie, Ron's colleague and sexual companion ; she circles the two of them, looking on with great fascination, and you wonder whether she will offer Bill succour or further torment. As it turns out, she gives him both.

Bill staggers home, to find Jason even more bloodied than himself. The boy has gone berserk and turned murderous. He is also conscience-stricken; and he ends the play by doing what might, in the circumstances, be called the decent thing.

Why, he keeps demanding of nobody in particular, did I do it? It's a good question, one the audience might well ask about everybody in the play. We are interested enough to want to ask, but not enough to care what the answers might be. (And of course the author isn't giving any.) We can tell that at least three of the characters are to some degree disturbed, and we can see -- if only because a string of other plays have subjected us to almost Pavlovian conditioning -- that they are the signs and victims of an alienated economically driven society.

There is a sort of effectiveness in taking the contrast between poverty and platitude to extremes by setting it at Christmas; but it's not as if nobody had ever thought of it before.

It's an easy irony: factually accurate, and excellent material for charitable appeals, but needing to be thoroughly re-imagined if it's to be the basis of a play. Here it reduces to a few lines of text and the choice of music to usher the audience in and out with.

Harkness has a talent for lean dialogue, and for depicting the bonds between characters. As directed by John Palmer, they work better as pairs than as individuals.

This is especially true (perhaps because we spend less time with them) of the two pedagogues lurking in the park; this seems to be a regular rendezvous for them, though whether gay-bashing forms an invariable part of their agenda is one of the things left uncertain.

Anyway, they move entertainingly from glum shop-talk ("done your report-cards yet?") to erotic banter ("dirty old man!"; "dirty older woman!"). When their prose turns pompously purple ("maybe we'll continue to thrive on sugar and fat while the rest of the rest goes hungry" -- I trust I got the last word right, the actor's delivery went very muffled) we can hope that they are either satirizing themselves or being satirized.

The couple give great scope for ambiguity -- who knows if they are even, in any orthodox sense, lovers? -- and the two actors run or amble with it: Sky Gilbert displays a considerable gift for subdued looming menace, while Caroline Gillis suggestively bobs and weaves.

The play's politics seem surprisingly conservative: Teachers are monsters and Jason wouldn't have gone so completely off the rails if he'd kept taking the tablets. Gil Garratt brings him to full febrile life, while Tony Nappo carries off Bill's largely reactive role in a quiet vein of sympathetic smouldering. Jason's teasing of him -- "I'm your dirty little secret -- that's exciting") and his reaction to it are among the play's more successful hints at hidden depths. A comparatively happy Christmas to all of them.

PILLS

Factory Theatre Studio, Toronto

1999-12-17-dickens-returns-to-the-stage:
Until Dec. 24 (a great way to spend Christmas Eve). Tickets: (416) 504-PLAY.

A CHRISTMAS CAROL

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

John Huston -- not that John Huston, but another -- is a Saskatchewan actor and director much given to solo performance. His one-man version of Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol puts him in the line of the late Emlyn Williams, whose evenings of Dickensian recitation were among his greatest successes, and ultimately of Dickens himself, who in his later years gave hugely successful public readings from his works. Unfortunately, the nervous energy he expended on these shows -- he used to drain both himself and his audience with the murder of Nancy from Oliver Twist -- took so much out of him that it may have hastened his death.

Huston's performance is unlikely to get anyone's pulse racing to that fatal extent, but it is an accomplished recital that tightens its grip as the story proceeds. Huston presents us with a costumed approximation of one of Dickens' own personal appearances; we might well be in a draughty hall in the Toronto that he visited on one of his American tours. He faces us across a lectern, bearded, frock- coated, watch-chained and throwing himself enthusiastically into every character who crosses his path.

Slight of build and light of voice, Huston is not the force of nature that presumably was Dickens. He can be fussy in his accumulation of comic detail: sometimes, it seems, assuming as many as half a dozen different voices in the course of a single sentence.

Piling on the humour, he sometimes defuses it, missing out on both the irony and the absurdity. There is nothing especially striking in his characterisation of Scrooge himself; and though there may be no positive reasons against endowing the Spirit of Christmas Present with a strong northern English accent, I cannot see much in its favour either.

It may be, too, that we have had enough over the years of the Carol's more emphatically benevolent characters, its Fezziwigs and Cratchits. The Cratchits' highly calorific Christmas merry-making is actually less effective now than its attendant melodrama, centring on the figure of Tiny Tim. In this account, he is very tiny; Huston indicates his presence by lowering his hand to a couple of feet above the floor. You feel his father's attachment to him, and you understand exactly why Scrooge melts.

Huston doesn't aim for the euphoric heights scaled on film by the late Alastair Sim (who was wonderful at this point, if a somewhat unlikely miser earlier on) but he does very well. And God knows he has stamina.
1999-12-20-clooney-the-queen-of-american:
Two years ago I went to see Rosemary Clooney, performing what was until recently her annual New York cabaret season at Rainbow and Stars, on the top floor of Rockefeller Centre. (Its still there, but no longer a cabaret room.)

Her opening song in that show was a brisk, no-nonsense version of Get Me to the Church on Time. It was captivatingly joyous, and it brought a beaming smile to every face in the house. Everybody knew that Clooney, then aged 69, was about to get married to Dante DiPaolo, her companion of 20 years and the man largely responsible for steering her through the most gratifying comeback in popular music. At the end of the set she brought him on to sing, in Italian and very sweetly, Come Back to Sorrento.

It occurred to me, in my cheerfully tearful state, that I would not have sat still for this from any other performer. I wouldnt have felt especially interested in any other singers' marriage plans, and I certainly wouldn't have felt happy for them as I did for her.

But feeling happy for Clooney is a legitimate payback for pleasure received. She can make you laugh at a comedy song or sigh at a ballad, but so can other singers; her ability to move you with happiness is unique. It doesnt usually operate on so unabashedly personal a level; generally the joy she communicates is in the music itself. She is the best living interpreter of the great American songbook.

There are three factors in play at a Clooney performance: her musicianship, her presentation and her personal history.

Her professional life divides into three periods, all of them illuminated in her new autobiography, Girl Singer (Doubleday, $34.95), written -- very well -- with Joan Barthel. For most of the 1950s -- her own 20s -- she was Americas top female singer, her success sparked by Come On-a My House, a monster hit that she had to be forced to record. (I didn't," she says in the book, "have any appreciation for the song's slightly tongue-in-cheek, self-parodic edge. These days she introduces it as a folk-song, written by an Armenian, sung by a girl from Kentucky, so of course we did it Italian.")

In the 60s her career slipped and eventually crashed: The pressures included the ascendancy of rock n' roll, a traumatic marriage to Jose Ferrer, the assassination of Robert Kennedy, which she personally witnessed, and pills. "And so it came to pass that in the summer of 1968, Rosemary Clooney, girl singer, age 40, was locked up in the psychiatric unit of the hospital for which, not so long before, she'd smiled and broken ground.

Discharged, and broke with five children, she had to start over, rebuilding not only her career but, as it turned out, her entire vocal personality. The turning point came in 1977 when she recorded an album for a small Californian label, Concord Jazz; it proved to be the first in an annual series that is still continuing.

One of the songs on it was Hey There, from The Pajama Game, a big hit for her in the 50s. She had done it then as a straight, plaintive theatre ballad; now she swung it, with a wry edge.

It remains a constant in her act (so youll remember which one I was," she says when introducing it), but though she plays with nostalgia she doesn't play on it. When I heard that '77 LP I suspected within minutes that she was going to be my favourite singer, but sentiment had little to do with it; she was only a vaguely remembered voice from my childhood and I knew nothing of her breakdown. Unlike Judy Garland or Billie Holiday, she has not turned her scars into a style. Holiday sounded bruised; Clooney, with her deep and round and richly-contoured voice, sounds bruised and healed, which I heretically find more interesting.

Humour has a lot to do with it; she herself once identified it as a salient quality of her singing, but it comes between the songs as well. Her patter is the best I have ever heard; gossipy and anecdotal and apparently spontaneous. The last has to be an illusion; I have now heard three times the routine about the grandchild who provoked her wrath with an unflattering imitation of her act ("the kids out of the will!) but it cracks me up every time.

Shes even been known to play the critic, remarking that White Christmas (her best-known film) is not a movie you'd want to risk seeing at the wrong time of the year, or that I'll Be Seeing You has a weak verse but a strong chorus; I disagree with the latter assessment but Im impressed that she should bother to make it.

She sounds both shrewd and generous, quizzical and self-mocking, emotional but unsentimental, and it is these qualities that light up her singing, along with an expert and irresistible rhythmic sense. She denies that she is a jazz singer (she doesnt improvise) but if you accept the definition of The New Yorker's Whitney Balliett, that a jazz singer makes everything she sings swing, then Clooney -- the post-'74 Clooney -- sings quintessential jazz. She finds the pulse in anything that has one (leaving out the occasional folk or soft- rock number that couldnt swing if you hung it), urging even the most lachrymose ballad along, stripping it of self-pity, and making it more rather than less affecting in the process. On the latest of her 24 Concord CDs, at long last, she is teamed with the Count Basie orchestra, the liveliest of ghost-bands, and delivers a deliciously rueful Guess Ill Hang My Tears Out to Dry and a wonderfully poignant Willow Weep for Me.

In the first half of her Concord period, the material is organized by composer, anthologizing songs by Arlen, Mercer, Berlin and Clooney's Beverly Hills neighbour of many years, Ira Gershwin. She was accompanied, superbly, by small groups of mainly young musicians; the vocal-instrumental interplay was the finest since the heyday of Holiday.

More recently she has been backed by big bands, and gone punch for punch with them (the Basie set is the apogee of this), and chosen her songs according to loosely autobiographical themes: an approach that courts self-indulgence but has usually -- not invariably -- avoided it. Discs have been devoted to songs evoking New York, to capsule summaries of her career (including a hilariously uninhibited revisiting of her old hit, Mambo Italiano, in tribute to her husband, who is both Italian and a dancer) and to her professional and personal association with the master arranger, Nelson Riddle.

My own favourite, For the Duration, collects songs of the Second World War, and presents an aching, mature refraction of their original innocence; it includes a particularly fine account of These Foolish Things in which Clooney's voice gently smiles on the line about the song that Crosby sings," Bing having been her friend, mentor and duet-partner.

Once you start listing songs from these discs, there is no end. They function among other things as a living library of the standard repertoire, with the singer mining the songs that she grew up on for wit and meaning. I think of a transfixingly confidential One for My Baby, accompanied only by Canadian guitarist Ed Bickert and the sole version to challenge Sinatra; a tough I Dont Want to Walk Without You, Baby, full of decisive consonants; an understated Autumn in New York, the yearning shrugged off but still potent.

She does especially well by Cole Porter, sliding in and out of his trademarked iceberg elegance; her Miss Otis Regrets is a comic tour de force, very clipped and businesslike before becoming deliciously sanguinary, while her Dont Fence Me In takes a sophisticate's throwaway parody of a cowboy song and turns it into an expression of real feeling, while still relishing the fruity absurdity of a phrase like "straddle my old saddle.

Perhaps her finest quality, apart from her intelligence, is her economy, though the two of course go together; at 70 she may sometimes meet a note she doesn't like, but she never injures or inflates a word. She is the only singer, apart from their composer, who can handle the songs of Dave Frishberg, jazz's reigning melancholy clown. The others all embroider them to death; her wistful Do You Miss New York? and rollicking I Want to Be a Sideman are sublime.

The word everybody uses for her is warm"; after hearing her sing, or after reading her book, you feel that you have met a real woman and that you would like to meet her again.

PINATA FULL OF BEES

Second City, Toronto

The second Second City is paying an anniversary tribute to the first Second City. The Toronto comedy troupe, now in its 26th year, is performing a show originally created by the parent Chicago organization, which is 40. The piece itself is two years old, and by all the rules of topical humour it should already be thoroughly dated.

It isn't, largely because it is not in fact very topical. Its comedy of attitude rather than of event, and the attitude it presents is a hardy perennial, neatly embodied in its opening number. A member of the cast is planted in the audience and then dragged from it by his five colleagues, who are dressed as terrorists. They dump an Uncle Sam hat on his head and arraign him for all the sins committed by America against the world and against itself. He, however, is empowered by the hat, and proceeds to kick every one of their revolutionary asses.

The moral, which manages to be triumphal and guilt-ridden at the same time, is that one American bully is worth five from anywhere else. The flavour of the satire naturally changes somewhat on the journey north. Performed by Americans it would seem sportingly if somewhat toothlessly self-critical. Done by Canadians it becomes a stimulating mixture of disapproval and envy: Theyre awful and we're awed.

In the best revues, all the performers are magnetic and all the jokes are funny; I saw a couple of these when I was young and impressionable. Below this top tier come the shows in which all the performers are likeable and enough of the jokes are funny for us to forgive the ones that aren't. This is the category in which Pinata Full of Bees belongs. The title, by the way, refers to a nasty device employed at parties by an evil-minded childrens entertainer; tempting on the outside and stinging underneath, its plainly a metaphor for how the show would like to see itself.

It has a Monty Python kind of structure, unlike most revues, which have no structure at all. Its sketches are not autonomous things with punchlines; they go off on tangents and beget other sketches, only to return when least expected, like deadbeat dads with nagging consciences. The guy in the Yankee Doodle headgear keeps popping up, very pleased with himself. Some of these running gags grow up and become running storylines.

There's one that parodies the social and sexual mores of the 1950s, and there's another that almost qualifies as a narrative spine. It takes place in a grade-school classroom, presided over by a subversive substitute teacher whose name happens to be Noam Chomsky. The kids call him Mr. Noam and are appalled by the things he tells them -- about the destruction of the American Indian, about global exploitation ("and the story ends with Little Bo Peep being forced to work in a Nike factory") and about the need to question authority whenever it raises its head.

A climactic flash-forward shows how his teachings have borne fruit; theres one backward boy -- well, he sits at the back of the class -- in whom it takes time, but one day in early middle age he wakes up to the lies society has told him (about 2% milk, among other things) and breaks out. He leads a march on and through Chicago, eventually returning to confront the brooding horrors that tyrannize his home suburb: ersatz Italian restaurant chains and monopolistic video stores that chop bits out of movies. He persuades some of the audience -- were talking flesh-and-blood paying customers -- to throw their Blockbuster cards on stage, and makes them promise not to renew them. It's like the '60s, only more practical.

Lee Smart, a performer massively delicate and delicately massive, plays this instant insurrectionist, as well as many other characters of various degrees of derangement; he is squishy, bland and scarifying by turns, and also simultaneously. Lisa Brooke does the evenings only sustained improvisational turn and does it brilliantly. Mary Pat Farrell has a strong line in beauteous hysterics. Paul Bates, Pat Kelly and Doug Morency are the rest of the gang.

All of them tread this alien turf as if it were their own; to an extent it is -- theyve done some rewriting. There is, besides, a comic language here that's spoken across North America and beyond, a dialect of hip despair intelligible to all of us. The show knows that Mr. Noam is right and it also knows that he's silly; it sets up a boycott of Blockbuster as a ludicrous image of revolt, but it cant think of anything better. And, hey, it would be uncool to try. The upshot, despite the tough facade, is a surprisingly gentle show that keeps suggesting that savage satire is just around the corner but wouldnt know how to turn that corner and doesn't really want to. It's a pinata full of butterflies, with maybe the occasional spider.

Maybe in two years time well see the new Chicago Second City show. I love its title. It's called The Psychopath Not Taken.

2000-01-01-look-back-in-anger-not-a-chan:
Robert Cushman is the theatre critic for the National Post

Theatre is about occasion, and the greatest night of the year was a last night at Stratford: William Hutt's Prospero in The Tempest, a valedictory performance in the greatest of valedictory plays: a play whose climax is a magician bidding farewell to his art.

Hutt is not apparently giving up acting but he is unlikely to play any more Shakespearean leads, and his half-century of achievement was magisterially summed up here.

In Richard Monette's lucid production, Hutt played with delightful ease and blazing authority. We cried and we cheered; it was like joining hands with history.

There are signs that the tradition might be maintained. It's too early to judge the effect of Stratford's new training schemes, but the standard of supporting playing there is creeping up (witness this year's Macbeth and Richard II) and, back in Toronto, the Soulpepper company's succession of shows unfolded like one long, exhilarating first night.

Their five productions -- from the urbanity of The Play's the Thing to the starkness of Endgame -- accounted for an almost embarrassing 50% of the year's best, culminating in the overflowing achievement of Platonov, a heartening and heart-warming display of casting (and acting) in depth. Quantity does count.

At the other extreme, Daniel Brooks' Tarragon Theatre production of Goethe's Faust Part One put an epic on the table with only five actors and hardly missed a trick.

This, like Platonov, was a pulsating show that took an unwieldy and supposedly unplayable text and made it live. I'd like to see Brooks move on to the even more problematic Part Two, or direct Ibsen's Peer Gynt, preferably for Soulpepper with Albert Schultz as Peer.

The most pleasant suprise of the year was Michael Healey's The Drawer Boy; an audience that had arrived at the Factory expecting nothing in particular found a funny, moving new play in a production to match. Healey's subsequent appearance as co-author of the humdrum comedy The Road to Hell -- this time we were expecting a lot -- was, let us hope, merely an aberration.

Fabrizio Filippo's Waiting for Lewis (from Theatre Direct) was children's theatre that didn't feel like children's theatre, and Jason Sherman's It's All True was flashily enjoyable if ultimately pointless. Both The Drawer Boy and It's All True were in part homages to older shows, making this seem even more like a year of revivals.

This, by the way -- unless you're one of those indomitably optimistic souls who expects a half dozen new masterpieces a year -- is a good thing.

Honest Ed: The Bargain Musical was a discount delight. The theatre of bigger musicals felt the draught left by the end of Livent (Swingstep made North York's Ford Centre feel like a ghost ship) but Ed & Son at least offered us a fortuitous Kander-and-Ebb retrospective, with Chicago coming through for the second and much- improved time and Cabaret over-heated but still hot.

Off my official beat, but certainly a theatrical experience, was Diana Leblanc's production of The Rape of Lucretia for the Canadian Opera Company. Canadian Stage (ironically perhaps, but who cares?) brought us the best foreign plays: How I Learned To Drive, The Beauty Queen of Leenane and Alan Ayckbourn's Communicating Doors, mysteriously described as an English bedroom farce by critics who can't have seen much English bedroom farce.

The year's most sinister development was the proliferation, in both commercial and subsidized theatres, of navel-gazing, one- person shows. Transcending this category, and most others, was Ronnie Burkett's Street of Blood: One extraordinary man with 40 puppets, all in the service of a genuine play whose reach only slightly exceeded its irresistible grasp.

And here, finally, is my off-the-cuff list of the year's best performances: Brian Bedford (taken for granted, as usual) in The School for Scandal; Richard McMillan in Glenn; Soulpepper's Diego Matamoros in everything; Peter Donaldson in Our Town; Kristen Johnson in A Streetcar Named Desire; the entire ensemble in Platonov; ditto in You Can't Take It with You (the Shaw Festival's best show); Sarah Orenstein in Heartbreak House and Getting Married; Brent Carver in Parade (admittedly at the end of last year and only in New York, but if you caught his number on the Tony Awards you'll know why he has to be here); John Jarvis in Love's Labour Lost; Alma Cuervo in Cabaret; David Fox and Jerry Franken in The Drawer Boy; William Hutt and Ronnie Burkett as aforesaid; Waneta Storms and Maggie Huculak in Faust; and Fiona Reid, crowning a wild year, as The Beauty Queen of Leenane.

PATIENCE

Canadian Stage Company

At least Jason Shermans 20th century Job doesnt get boils. (I apologise for making the play, now revived by Canadian Stage, sound so dated, but it is all of two years old.) His physical health remains good throughout, but he takes other knocks that reflect those of his Biblical prototype.

He loses his job to corporate politics, his wife and children to divorce, and his brother to death. Not surprisingly, he spends a fair amount of time asking "why me?" The only answer he gets from the other characters, or from the play itself, is why not? Which is fair enough but, at the almost three-hour length at which we get to hear it, frustrating.

Reuben, the hero of Patience, is an executive working in, and often by, cellphones. He is shafted by his colleagues when he fails to push a new Korean deal through fast enough; he also seems to have diverted company funds to his own use. His wife throws him out when she discovers his 10-year-old love letters to another woman.

Around this fateful time he runs into his old flame's husband who is putting the rat race behind him and flying off to a new life as an independent movie-maker. The implication is that Reuben had better follow his own dream before it's too late. This subsequently turns out to have been a mystical encounter, since his friend has actually been dead for a year.

The Job parallel is neatly signalled in the plays title, but Im still not sure that I would have got the point if I hadn't read the publicity. However, since I have: one thing Reuben doesn't lose is his faith, because unlike Job he never had any. He does, late in the play, meet a rabbi who has an exhaustingly roguish sense of humour; asked the perennial question about the unfairness of things, he pretends to put in a call to the Almighty who of course isnt telling. (Theres been no mention of Reuben's Jewishness up to this point and there's very little after.) He is also the means of reuniting Reuben with his old love, demonstrating that life is governed by coincidence, though theyre not always the coincidences youd like.

This has been a sound theatrical principle ever since Oedipus struck a man to the ground without looking where he was going. In this play, though, it's linked not to an implacable divine plan but to a lot of talk about the uncertainty principle and chaos theory. Philosophically these are very plausible. They clash, though, with the structure of what is still, essentially, a morality play. Job knew whom to blame, even though his complaints got a dismissive answer. Reuben just flails around in a context in which anything can happen and does, over and over.

He is split dramatically between Mr Everyman and a specific businessman and husband. In the former incarnation he floats around between three women, a ruefully amusing embodiment of the masculine conviction that the grass is always greener.

He has a virtuoso speech in which he tries to describe his marriage and keeps tripping himself up, unwilling to sound either too negative or too positive.

In the latter he is drawn in the broadest and most unhelpful strokes. When his wife turns on him to list all his marital faults she could be right, she could be wrong. Since his marriage has never been dramatically there in the first place we have no way of telling.

We learn a little more of his professional life, mainly that he was a driven and ambitious bastard. We first see him playing squash with the man who will soon unseat him. Actually we don't quite see it; the actors are glimpsed in silhouette, on a screen. Its a nice fancy effect to start the show but it left me too busy trying to sort out who was who to pay any attention to what they might be saying. The hero, though, keeps referring back to it as a crucial scene, the one where everything started to go wrong.

Since the play is a long and ambitious essay on important- sounding themes, it is already being hailed as a masterwork. It does possess intelligence, and some wit.

Some of the jokes are irritating but others are funny, though the best, whose punch-line is craftily withheld for half an hour, seems to be traditional.

It also has some clever structural strokes, unexpected jumps between past and present. Joseph Zieglers production throws in a few self-conscious tricks -- one scene is played with cross-gender casting though if there was any point to this beyond a fashionable one I didn't get it. (It produces some very bad acting.) Otherwise it's a straightforward, somewhat laboured, naturalistic staging in unlovely sets.

A nice crack about Ikea is spoiled by furniture that looks nothing like.

Jim Mezon as Reuben starts out with a fine blend of innocence and brutality but then has to go on repeating it. The women are little more than male fantasies, played, in ascending order of conviction, by Brenda Robins, Brenda Bazinet and Nicole Libin. Victor Ertmanis doubles as Reubens nemesis and his surviving brother and hardly differentiates between them.

David Storch does three roles, with style. The play at least sends us away with something to hum: For All We Know (the 30s standard, not the '70s impostor) hauntingly summarizing that uncertain feeling: "For all we know we may never meet again -- tomorrow may never come, for all we know."

It confirms Dylan Thomas' opinion that all the wisdom of the world lies in the lyrics to popular songs. They do it much quicker too.

2000-01-10-this-is-a-lear-who-s-read-lea:
Hysterica: Canadian Stage Theatre, Toronto. To Jan. 29. Box office: (416) 368-3110.

When Shakespeare's King Lear is about to topple into madness, he cries out "hysterica passio," which means just what it appears to mean -- hysterical passion. By invoking a condition he is hoping, vainly, to ward it off. The show Hysterica, evolved by Richard Rose and his Necessary Angel company, is not so much an adaptation of Lear as a fantasia, a series of riffs on Shakespearean themes.

But in its choice of title it has sold itself somewhat short. It has passion, of a cerebral kind, as well as hysteria. The hysteria is in the characters' behaviour. The passion is in the presentation, which is pitched at a chilly level of perfectionism. There are things to admire, especially at the beginning, but there turns out to be little to enjoy and nothing to love.

The focus is constricted, and not just by comparison with the immense original. The Baby-Boom generation, confident as ever that its concerns are those of the entire world, has recently decided that King Lear is really about the problem of what to do with your old folks. Actually, Shakespeare's play gives its characters and its audiences other things to worry about -- like the fate of a kingdom or the nature of morality. In this gender-bent four-person version, however, everything comes down to mother, sons and daughter-in-law.

Mother is Leda, an industrial matriarch who has a company rather than a country to give away at her retirement and who awards her grown boys 45% of it apiece, keeping the last controlling 10th for herself. (This is a cannier move than that of her role model, who insisted on retaining 100 attendant knights but left himself with no bargaining power. Leda is a Lear who has read King Lear.)

Of the two sons one, Edward, is a transparently cynical go- getter, while the other, Iain, is a dreamy idealist, a sculptor who likes nothing better than to shut himself up in his studio.

Leda believes she can play one against the other. She doesn't realize that apparent gentleness can be every bit as destructive as honest malice. She also reckons without Iain's wife, Gwen, whom she despises, excludes and fatally underrates. Gwen is a narcissistic schemer whose resentment matches her mother-in-law's dislike.

This set-up plays some ingenious games with its source -- games of combination and compression. Looked at in one light, Edward and Iain are the ugly sisters, Goneril and Regan, between whom Lear divided his power. Taken another way, Edward is Goneril and Regan combined, while Iain is Cordelia, the honourable sibling who got left out.

Then again, the marriage of Edward and Gwen is a reversal of that between Goneril and her well-meaning husband, Albany, who stood around vainly protesting while his wife made her father's life hell.

Shakespeare also wrote a subplot in which another father dealt equally misguidedly with his two sons, good Edgar and bad Edmund. The resemblance between these two and Leda's offspring is accentuated when Gwen starts dallying with Edward just as both Goneril and Regan did with Edmund. Act II even gets going with a modified storm scene.

Leda is a Greek immigrant with as much of Medea as of Lear in her, and Maria Vacratsis plays her very powerfully, in all her pain and all her unreasonableness. For cries to the gods she substitutes memories of how things were done in the old country.

Like Lear, she billets herself on each of her children in turn and calls down curses on their heads when she fails to get the treatment she thinks she deserves. Being more of a realist than Lear, she presumably expected less, but she is just as bitter when they turn her out. Or, in this play's terms, put her into a home. This part of the show feels, as you would expect, recognizably uncomfortable, and the Shakespearean echoes do give it an added resonance. When Leda threatens Gwen with ungrateful children or none at all, her words hardly match up to Lear's "Hear, Nature, hear," but they don't fall embarrassingly short either.

The play has been improvised (in rehearsal, not performance) by the actors themselves, under Rose's editorial eye. This means that everybody gets plentiful time to agonize. They do so with great conversational fluency and to increasingly hermetic effect.

The fate of the characters matters little, and that of the business even less; however much they talk about it, it never seems to exist. The situation evaporates for lack of effective action -- all text, no context.

Shakespeare's play is often supposed to have much plot; this distillation unwittingly shows that opinion to be wrong. Hysterica, like Lear, is a play about sight and blindness, literal and metaphorical. Scenes in Iain's studio are played in total darkness - - tough on those members of the audience who are trying to stay awake.

One makes the effort partly out of respect for the actors -- for Maggie Huculak, whose Gwen is a metallic control freak even able to dominate her (unseen) psychiatrist, and for Duncan Ollerenshaw, whose Iain is another of his compelling studies in indecision.

Hamish McEwan's Edward doesn't have quite the authority of the others (he came late into the game) but he does well as a neurotically glamorous villain who turns out to be longer on neurosis than on glamour, or indeed on villainy. Modern times. The production, austerely manoeuvred on a snow-white set (designed by Teresa Przybylski), looks good but in a bullying kind of way.

2000-01-12-the-play-s-the-film-one-of-ci:
Every entertainment medium loves to tell stories about the others. The movie genre with the longest pedigree is the backstage drama, and the live theatre has been known to return the compliment, though not nearly as often.

Radio and television have been obsessively concerned with the older media, and with each other, ever since they came into being; while newspapers, of course, batten off the lot of them and are battened on in return. Whichever area we work in, we apparently feel that the real action is going on in the next yard, and we would dearly like to grab a piece of the glamour.

The theatre, being so much older than any of its rivals, was for centuries compelled to pay tribute to itself, as it still with some frequency does. But it also remains the favoured object of all its competitors; movie performers, movie makers, who would keel over at the idea of working in theatre conditions for theatre money, nevertheless act out public fantasy lives as just plain kids putting on shows. And here they join hands with their audiences; it is after all the possible dream, the one that most of us have come closest to realizing. The school play is still a more universal experience than the school movie.

The minute they had learned to make their own noises, films institutionalized this fantasy as the backstage musical. In Hollywood's heyday, this genre accounted for at least 90% of all the musical pictures made; there they were, singing and dancing on celluloid, while simultaneously affirming that the only place in which such things could rationally be done was on a stage.

This is, of course, the literal truth, and Hollywood has always been a slave to realism. But there is another reason.

The backstage musical comes with a built-in climax; we spend the story watching a show being prepared, vicariously experiencing all the attendant traumas, and finally we watch it explode in triumph, all difficulties overcome, with an audience on screen to bear witness to the experience while we in the stalls validate their validation.

The form still survives, however battered, and it's just taken a new turn. Most backstagers -- 42nd Street is the archetype -- have depicted the birth-pangs of one fictitious production, dreamed up for the occasion. Real shows, from the actual theatrical past, have only been dealt with in biographies of particular stars or composers -- an Al Jolson or a Cole Porter -- and they have arrived there in platoons, usually with total disregard for content or chronology. We now though have two films, each of which deals, unprecedentedly, with the creation of a single historic musical. Tim Robbins Cradle Will Rock shows how Marc Blitzsteins almost-eponymous labour opera evaded official muzzling to receive an electric impromptu premiere, with the composer playing on the stage and the actors delivering from the house. Mike Leigh's Topsy-Turvy -- which opens in Canada on Jan. 21 -- follows W. S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan from the opening of Princess Ida, a comparative failure, to that of The Mikado, their most unmitigated success.

Both films build to the traditional first-night blast, though it's indicative of the difference between them that Robbins ends with it while Leigh progresses to the inevitable let-down of the morning after. Hes made a film about the theatrical process itself, and that process is ongoing.

Robbins is concerned with The Cradle less for its own sake or those of its creators than as an emblematic skirmish in the sociopolitical battles of of New Deal America. The plots and sub- plots, as chronologically scrambled as any old-style biopic, get very confusing, but theres much that you wouldn't want to miss. There is, for example, the scene before the nascent House Un- American Activities Committee, one of whose members seems willing to arraign all playwrights -- not just that notorious Communist Christopher Marlowe -- as rancorous troublemakers; censors are rarely so frank or, from their own point of view, so logical. When the cradle finally rocks, it really rocks; the last sequence is such a sure-fire rouser that I wish Robbins had resisted the temptation to sweeten and sentimentalize what actually happened, since what actually happened was quite stirring enough.

He turns a brilliantly planned guerilla action into a spontaneous gesture by a bunch of warm-hearted thesps, reinforced -- most unhistorically -- by a couple of tootling musicians defying their union. But then a solo piano backing would be unthinkable backing for a Hollywood finale.

Topsy-Turvy, too, features warm-hearted thesps: A choral deputation who gallantly protest the last-minute cutting of the one solo number allotted to the Mikado himself and get it reinstated. Leigh typically doesn't show us what any other musical would: The audience rising to cheer what turned out to be one of Gilbert and Sullivans signature songs -- the one about letting the punishment fit the crime. He does, though, show us the two collaborators taking their first-night bows; they look as if they barely knew one another as, in essentials, they barely did.

This, Leigh being English and a theatre animal, is an actors picture, just like his contemporary movies: researched by the cast, with dialogue improvised by them and refined and rigorously edited by him. To me it sounded far more convincingly Victorian than the matey adaptations of Dickens or George Eliot that we've been getting recently.

Some things, on the other hand, never change; and where the business of putting on a show is concerned, actors are in a better position to know that than most. An American critic has complained that the rehearsal problems depicted in this film are no different to those that beset all musicals. Precisely.

I suppose it's ironic that the blistering Blitzstein should have occasioned a more obviously riotous celebration of theatre than the incurably frivolous G&S. You could argue though that The Cradle Will Rock, still powerful but a period piece, needs to be celebrated more than The Mikado, a still-living classic that can generate its own fun. Anyway, were not exactly starved for celebrations of theatre, even ones without tunes.

Shakespeare in Love implicated us in the premiere of Romeo and Juliet as enjoyably, and as shamelessly, as any songfest. And the mechanical media too can be celebrated, even by themselves.

There arent many musical films about musical films but one of them was Singin' in the Rain, the best movie musical of all. It's obviously harder to involve an audience in a process whose real culmination comes in the editing room rather than in public performance, but it can be done, with a little cheating.

Galaxy Quest -- the most purely enjoyable picture since Shakespeare in Love -- would be far less pleasurable without its coda, in which the intrepid actor-heroes take their places for their reinstated series, waving to the fans as if they were doing it live. From sci-fi they have come and to sci-fi they return; its very satisfying.

Its also satisfying, or at least titillating, that we know who they are: That Tim Allen is playing a TV star without a show and that the uprooted Briton doomed to wear the alien's hairpiece, apparently in perpetuity, is Alan Rickman, whose character signs autographs with unimaginable disdain and finally redeems himself by breathing new life into the mystical catchphrases that he's always hated. Thats acting: or at least acting of acting, and it somehow cancels out and becomes the real thing.

There are scenes in Topsy-Turvy that work in a related way, scenes set in performers dressing rooms as the first night approaches. We believe so strongly in the actors as actors that when the civilians -- Gilbert or Sullivan or Richard D'Oyly Carte -- look in we forget for the moment that they are actors, too. I wouldn't make profound claims for it, but I think it can be a lovely game, like relishing the studios deft iconic use of Astaire and Rogers, or of Garland and Kelly when they played performers, or applauding John Malkovichs sportsmanship in being himself. The presence of actors as actors, or of a play within a play, doesn't necessarily guarantee a searching study of appearance and reality; or if it does we should be consistently solemn and rank 42nd Street with Pirandello. (Somebody somewhere probably has.)

It's a lightweight theme anyway, and its best handled with the steely delicacy that we saw on stage last year in The Plays the Thing. Or better yet with the superlative grace of A Midsummer Night's Dream, the play in which the professional theatre, with no other target yet available, sets out to mock the amateurs -- us -- and ends up doing us homage. It was the first play about doing the play right here, the first show about putting on a show, and the mould has never been broken.
