PERFECT PIE

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

Nancy Palk is an actress whose lean rangy build and alert glittering eyes usually lead her to be cast as high-style women in high-style plays. She also carries with her, though, a relaxed earthiness of which we got a rewarding glimpse last year when she played one of the mothers in Our Town. Her role in Judith Thompson's new play, Perfect Pie, summons the same quality, only deepened and enriched. It may be the best performance she has given.

She plays Patsy, who owns and lives on a farm outside a small Ontario town. She inherited it from her parents and now runs it with her husband, and its doing well for them. (Theyve recently been offered a million for the land.) She also, as the title indicates, bakes very good pies -- the talent was bequeathed her along with the farm -- and she begins the play by sending one of them, along with a taped greeting, to a girlhood friend whom she hasn't seen in years. The friend, in fact, left town, apparently never to return, following a grievous accident that put Patsy into a coma lasting weeks.

The two had come from opposite sides of the tracks, a metaphor given striking life in Sue LePage's set, which is dominated by a railway line curving up and round the stage in steeply diminishing perspective. (The publicity department has also got in on this act, describing the girls relationship as derailed.)

Patsy had been a loved, comfortable girl with no more than the regulation quantity of teenage problems, and she has grown up accordingly. Her friend Marie had been dirty, dishevelled, somewhat abused and chronically unpopular. Now she has resurfaced in Patsys perception as a svelte, successful metropolitan actress with TV credits ranging from Hedda Gabler to commercials for flavoured coffee. Her manner has changed, and her hair-colouring, and her name.

Patsy invites her to visit, and one afternoon, en route to an engagement in Montreal, the former Marie -- now Francesca -- materializes in Patsy's kitchen. They catch up, reminisce and compare; and as they do their younger selves appear, re-enacting episodes from their shared past.

The play started life as a monologue, performed on television by the author, and in essence it may still be that. There are four characters (or, if you like, two characters each split two ways) and they all have a lot to say, but the whole thing may be going on in Patsy's head.

Her friendship with Marie was certainly real, and there presumably is an actress out there called Francesca, but Patsys identification of the one with the other may be an illusion, and their reunion may be an extended piece of wish-fulfillment. It enables her to match what she values in her own life -- her home, her husband, her three sons -- against what she has missed out on: travel, glamour, sexual adventure. Francesca has had three husbands and, presumably, numerous affairs, but is childless and currently alone.

Patsy, as Palk presents her, has a roguish, round-voiced quality: unprudish but shockable. She can say "eh?" with more point and humour than anyone this side of the Royal Canadian Air Farce, and the surprise on her face can expand into a grin of amazement or freeze into a mask of horror. Marie used to have fits; since her departure, Patsy has had them, too. It is, she wryly comments, the only instance on record of epilepsy as a communicable disease.

If Patsy is fantasizing, an otherwise predictable structure -- joyful meeting, re-enacted trauma, acceptance, dying fall -- begins to seem more inevitable, less glib. (The play suffers the problem afflicting any drama hingeing on the delayed revelation of events known to the characters but not the audience; however horrific the details, its always an anti-climax.) We can also worry less about Marie/Francesca's self-conscious agonizing about her two names and two identities, and about the total disjunction between them. This, making all allowances for the thoroughness of show business makeovers, is incredible; there is no continuity of appearance, thought or speech patterns.

Even at face value, though, the play has a lot to offer. It creates a world; maybe a world and a half. Its two timelines grip as they converge, and their mutual dependence is increasingly persuasive. There is a rhythm, too, to the individual scenes.

Some of Thompson's more lyrical flights are hard to take; or maybe its the careful way that the actors, under her direction, deposit them directly in the audiences laps. (Pausing for effect, after harmless conjunctions like and or "like" is, categorically, bad acting. People in real life, other than the grossest poseurs, never do it. Ever.)

Otherwise, the performances are very strong. Sonja Smits as Francesca is glossy without and craggy within. (She also bears a noticeable resemblance to Joanna Lumley, which, what the old-girls- together theme and one of them being called Patsy, makes the whole thing seem, on occasion, Absolutely Fabulous.)

Of the juniors, Tara Rosling as Marie provides a fiery variation on her disturbed hitchhiker from See Bob Run: in the former play she delivered a verdict on runaway youth; here she provides the evidence. Liisa Repo-Martell's young Patsy, all emphatic concern, is a tumultuous prelude to Palk's luminous account of her older self.

This is undoubtedly the best new play set on a farm and reaching back into the past since The Drawer Boy; it's also the best new play of any kind, and leaves you wondering why rural Canadian plays should at the moment be so much more accomplished and affecting than urban ones.

BUILDING JERUSALEM

Factory Theatre

There's a kind of play, increasingly popular over the past 25 years, that throws together a number of historical figures from roughly the same period and has them bounce off one another. The prototype is Tom Stoppard's Travesties, which corrals James Joyce, Tristan Tzara, and Lenin, all of whom were on the loose in Zurich during the First World War, and has them going to bat for their various revolutions.

There's another, more venerable kind of play whose strategy is to gather its characters in an inaccessible house, at the behest of some mysterious non-appearing host, and let them stew. Usually they are there to be murdered, as in the Agatha Christie artwork latterly known as And Then There Were None.

Building Jerusalem, from a company calling itself Volcano, has bits of both. Of its five characters four are historical; they are not famous, but they all make good ideological figureheads, and all were alive and of the same age and in Toronto on the cusp of the 19th and 20th centuries. None of them are about to let their swords sleep in their hands. They are assembled on New Year's Eve, 1899; they can't get out since they are bound by polite convention and the weather is what you'd call seasonal. Nobody wants to kill them, but some absent mastermind has decided to rub them together for the sake of the sparks. They pass the time playing party games and otherwise creating their own entertainment, because these are the old days and that's what people used to do in them. The production is described as a multi-disciplinary event, which seems to be a fancy handle for a show in which the performers talk, sing, and dance; in other words, it's what is known in the trade as a musical.

The four prisoners are: the Reverend Silas Rand, a Baptist minister with a mission to the Mi'kmaq; Karl Pearson, an English eugenicist popular in Germany, with schemes for breeding inferior races to serve the ones he likes; Adelaide Hoodless, who thinks women need instruction in domestic science more than they need the vote; and Augusta Stowe-Gullen, who disagrees. Stowe-Gullen is a doctor, the first woman to graduate from a Canadian medical school. She is much exercised with the threatened closure and last-minute reprieve of Toronto's Women's College Hospital -- this is a hundred years ago, right -- and if that doesn't put her on the side of the angels, one would like to know what could.

Pearson is bad, but as everybody else on stage is against him, he does acquire a certain dignity, and he sticks to his guns; at one appealing moment he appends to a spirited chorus of D'ye ken John Peel? a new stanza of his own about the hell of being locked up with people you hate. (Add Jean-Paul Sartre's Huis Clos to the list of possible influences.) Augusta is good, and she has a very powerful speech about the horrors of force-feeding currently being inflicted on a suffragette in England. She is, though, inclined to hector. Adelaide seems to have, by the play's lights, the wrong ideas but the right feelings. The Reverend Silas seems to suffer from a more complicated version of the same complaint; he is agonizingly sincere, but his efforts to interpret a Mi'kmaq legend in Biblical terms are generally mocked as patronising and misguided. (I'm not sure why. There are common elements in most mythologies. Why not use them?) All in all, the characters are treated even-handedly. There are some arch moments early on, when the Victorians are apparently being mocked for their foolishness in not being us, but the show soon outgrows these.

The fifth character is a young girl, who draws her elders out and orchestrates their conflicts. She is called Alice, though the apparent homage seems misplaced; Lewis Carroll's heroine surveyed her elders with a child's clear eye, but she didn't act superior to them and she didn't have -- as this one seems to -- magical powers. Her choice of parlour-games is admirably calculated to unsettle the guests and get them quarrelling. (For the overall structure, credit Ross Manson, the show's conceiver and director).

The songs are prettily sung and tellingly chosen. (Arranger and composer, Bill Brennan.) The dances are festive but disciplined knees-ups with an increasing touch of frenzy. (Choreographer, Claudia Moore.)

Finally, though, this is a play of ideas, dependent on text. (Writer, Michael Redhill.) The performers, chosen largely for other skills, often supply readings that are awkward or toneless or both. Martin Julien's Silas, with his horrified acceptance of a world in which "God will be dead," is an exception; so is Ross Manson as the happy pioneer of genocide, when Alice shows them all the coming century and he cries out, "That is not what I meant." Singing apart, the ladies -- Claudia Moore, Kim Renders, Sarah Chase -- look better than they sound. Teresa Przybylzski's set, a receding series of curtained wings, has an appropriate air of an old puppet-theatre, and is helpfully lit by J. P. Robichaud.

Good though it is, the show seems rather slight to have been in development for three-and-a-half years, but you can't legislate these things.

THE YOKO ONO PROJECT

Theatre Passe Muraille

THEATRE

Against all augury, The Yoko Ono Project turns out to be a terrific show. Few people can have looked forward with enthusiasm to a celebration of one of the most reviled figures of recent times, a woman widely believed to have taken the worlds most overrated songwriter and made him worse. (Well, it did coincide with their marriage.)

Nobody liked her own music much either, or her art, or her theories. She was generally thought to be posturing and untalented. Her greatest sin, though, was to be Asian; any Western woman who became the second Mrs Lennon would have been granted a far easier ride. That at least is the position taken by the creators of this entertainment -- a troupe with the engaging name of Loud Mouth Asian Babes -- and they make it stick. They proceed on the ancient principle that the best form of defence is attack, but rather than charging head-on they bob and weave. If their show were not so witty, poignant, deft and agile, you would say that it was uncomfortably persuasive. As it is, it just persuades.

For a start, it looks great. The set (designed by Vikki Anderson) features a dazzling black-and-white chequered floor, on which stand panels of frosted screens. Dotted around are a large shiny black box, a short white monolith and a couple of black pillars. (These last aren't strictly part of this show -- they hold the theatre's roof up. But they blend in very well.) These objects are mostly Ono artworks, or reproductions thereof, and they make a very good case for their creator. Regardless of how they might look in a gallery, they are fine occupants of a stage.

There is a cast of six and all of them -- the four women anyway - - are in a sense playing Yoko. The one doing it most directly, though, is a musician, Lee Pui Ming, and our first sight of her seems to confirm our worst fears. She rushes through the auditorium, arms outstretched and flashing an arent-you-glad-to-see-me smile. After that, though, she retires to a gallery to do her own thing, and the actresses take over. There is, surprisingly, a story. It concerns three Asian-Canadian girls, the brother of one of them, and the European boy-friend of another. We see them in and around an exhibition: the Yoko Ono Project. This overlaps with the Ono exhibit at which she first met John Lennon: an encounter thats re-enacted for us, with the actor, Bruce Beaton, doing a first-rate Liverpudlian.

Two issues are on these characters' minds: one amusing, one not. One is the supposed preference of Asian women for going out with European men: a propensity of which Yoko herself of course provided a spectacular example, and a tendency that drives the brother (Glenn Marc Silot) crazy. Mischievously, the ladies conduct a poll of the Asian women in the audience. (Results on the first night seemed to confirm the theory.)

The other matter is the abuse hurled at Asian women by men -- especially North American men -- who have decided they hate Ono and who can't tell the others apart. The anecdotal evidence here is apparently drawn from the personal experience of Jean Yoon, who wrote the show and who has staged it (brilliantly) with Marion de Vries. The performers, though, easily make the words their own. One of them, Keira Loughran, is going to be a star; she has an enchantingly light touch and a fast, warm rapport with her colleagues and with the audience. (When her lover asks her to move in with him because "youre small and you wont take up much room" she details all the physical and psychological space that she will occupy, concluding I'm small, but I'm not microscopic. Its not the deepest writing but it tells.) Balancing her sharp joyousness is the wary, heavy-set sadness of Denise Fujiwara (a dancer making her acting debut) as a woman who has suffered more than her share of insult and has hardened because of it. At one of the shows climaxes she retreats into Ono's magic box and emerges strengthened if not transformed. M. J. Kang has less definition than the other two but is unexpectedly moving towards the end.

By dramatising their own experience -- and doing it blithefully and forcefully without self-pity -- they gain our respect for their unseen patron. "Don't diss Yoko" they say at the end, with awkward (and unncessary) explictiness, but their point is made. It's plain that she's been vilified over the years in ways that were not merely offensive but irrelevant. That does not in itself make her a genius, even if the show would like to think so, but in fact the issue is sidestepped. They make a better case for her visual creations than for her music: a lot of it is played but mostly while other more interesting things are going on. Some prejudices remain intact. The production itself, though, has a future.

-

ARCHER

Theatre Centre, Toronto

Once there was a kind of play for which the stock critical adjective was "civilized." It especially flourished in France in the middle decades of the 20th century, and it was a mainstay of high- end British radio back in the days when broadcasting was broadcasting.

It was written in ornate, epigrammatic prose that aspired to the poetic and it drew its narrative inspiration from Greek mythology. Sometimes it left the stories in their original settings; sometimes it tried to update them with much feverish application of makeup compacts and philosophical smoking of Gauloises. Philip Shepherd's Archer is a late, Canadian entry in the same tradition.

Time-wise, it has things both ways. It tells the story of Odysseus ( Ulysses, if you're a Latinist), who functioned at the siege of Troy as the Greek army's one-man think-tank. It takes him from the last night of the 10-year war, crouching with his fellows inside his personally designed wooden horse prior to getting out and massacring everyone, to his return home after a further 10 years of wandering, just in time to pick up his mighty bow and save his wife Penelope from her obstreperous bunch of unwelcome suitors by shooting them full of arrows.

That's half the play. The other half, running in parallel with it, concerns Archie, who leaves his home on Toronto Island to retrieve his daughter's Barbie doll from the mainland home of his wife's sister. We, apparently, have Barbie like the Greeks had Helen; and it's unclear whether the purpose is to show how far we have fallen, or to cut the old myth down to size; to shed some borrowed glory on our own times, or merely to do a little light dumping on everything. Missing the boat home Archie takes refuge in a hotel; he, like Odysseus, runs into surprises and temptations before getting home, 23 hours later, to his wife whose name is Penny.

Shepherd is not the first writer to have tried cramming the events of Homer's Odyssey into a single modern day; James Joyce once had a go. But not even Joyce tried to tell both the new and the old stories simultaneously. The trouble with Shepherd's version is not so much that one tale undercuts the other as that the author doesn't seem aware of it. The story of Archie even undercuts itself. It is mainly told to us in the third person -- by Archie's wife, who acts like a harpy, and by his sister-in-law, who acts silly. It's ages before we meet Archie himself, and by the time we do it's too late for us to take him seriously, even though it now appears that the author wants us to.

Meanwhile we have had the Greek story, presented as a series of recitations. The actors -- there are three, plus a musician -- tread carefully through the language, which is all-enveloping. Occasionally they say something really interesting: as when the nymph Calypso, who entraps the hero for years on her idyllic island and can't understand why he wants to go home, confesses "I'm afraid of pain, all the gods are." But they discuss feelings rather than express them, and much of the writing simply washes over you; anyway, it washed over me.

The goddess Circe has a long speech about Odysseus' proposed descent into Hades ("the underworld is hunger itself and would scarf you down") that itself descends into high-pressure obscurity, and stays there a long time. The actress, Alison Lawrence, climaxes this aria with some light, rhythmic tapping on her throat: one of the more hypnotic visual moments of the evening.

The producing company calls itself Phyzikal Theatre; and the director, Steven Rumbelow, boasts in his bio the direction of 100 music videos and of "one of the world's foremost physical theatre companies, Triple Action Theatre." He gets his actors here to do a fair amount of arm-waving, but nothing really out of the ordinary.

The finest effect is the presentation of the Cyclops: a crouching figure swathed in a black cloak with a light-bulb in front representing the monster's single eye. The cloak is then thrown off, to reveal the maid at Archie's hotel, giving him a scare with some furiously noisy vacuuming.

Clever though this is, it sums up the show's essential misconception. The maid who wants to clean your room is not as menacing as the ogre who wants to eat you: nowhere near. Archie's uncomfortable night on the town is not in the same league as the travels and travails of Odysseus. The worst thing that happens to Archie is being trapped in an elevator wth a lady lounge-singer, also called Calypso. The sexiest thing is being invited to her room when they're released, an offer that he primly rejects.

Leanne Dixon plays the Cyclops and the various wives. The author plays the twin-protagonists. He has an appropriately taut bow- string of a voice that he seems to enjoy flexing; to cast yourself as a guy whose wife waits faithfully for 20 years while nymphs and goddesses across the Adriatic just throw themselves at you must be quite a trip.

The play has all the literary pretentions and ironic double- bluffing of the old school of classics revisited; the production adds in the more recent conceit that an old myth will fill the stage with dark primal energy, something that somehow never seems to hapen. Also in there is a quite sensible metaphor about humanity taking responsibility of its own fate and declining to be a target for the gods, or fate, or whatever. So it isn't all that bad; just sort of terrible.
2000-01-19-never-mind-diana-krall-what-a:
TONY BENNETT

Roy Thomson Hall, Toronto

Whenever Tony Bennett appeared on my family's TV screen in the 1960s, my father would invariably describe him as the least likely pop singer he had ever seen. He looked, according to my dad, like a cross between a tycoon and a prizefighter: both, come to think of it, useful accomplishments in the vocal game.

He looks much more like a singer now; or maybe, as a great survivor -- less emotionally involving than Sinatra or musically than Torme, but still the last of the giants -- he has redefined his milieu, so that we expect singers to look like him. He still moves with engaging awkwardness -- he ambles where others would strut -- but his high, broad frame and silver mane (surely one of the most persuasive hairpieces in the world) give him the look of an amiable lion.

His singing, too, is mostly lean and leonine, especially on his current tour, on which he's accompanied by an unequivocal jazz quartet, headed by his perpetual pianist, the venerable Ralph Sharon. Sharon really does seem to get better with age; he took a couple of delicate, beautifully economic solos, which sounded like Count Basie waxing lyrical, and his mere presence was a blessing. He and Bennett climaxed the night with a dreamy, gently rocking duet on S'Wonderful (not usually either a dreamy or a gentle piece) on which the singer seemed to be backing the instrumentalist.

Intimate settings bring out the best in Bennett. (I'm talking about music, not venues. Nobody could call Roy Thomson Hall intimate. One would love to hear him in a club.) Shouting with a big band, he can sometimes be exhilarating but is often messy. Small groups let him concentrate on what he does best, which is to swing in a whisper.

Others, like Peggy Lee and Blossom Dearie, have done that, of course, but they are miniaturists by nature; Bennett, warm where they are cool, offers the attraction of power kept voluntarily in check. He takes this to extremes with his now-statutory practice of singing one song unmiked. It used to be Fly Me to the Moon; this time, in commemoration of Martin Luther King, he moved to a different part of the heavens and sang Kurt Weill's Lost in the Stars. It wasn't the best way of exploring the lyric, but the suddenly frail voice in the huge hall was its own metaphor for a song about man adrift in the cosmos.

We expected, on the basis of numerous interviews, to hear a lot of material from his new Duke Ellington CD, but it seems that, like Bogart in Casablanca, we were misinformed. He did only three Ellington songs, of which one -- It Don't Mean a Thing -- was mainly a showcase for his drummer, Clayton Cameron: a spectacular musician who went from a masterful juggling routine with sticks and cymbals to a rapturous solo with brushes.

Bennett came into his own on a sumptuous Mood Indigo, for which he supplied the mood while the lighting boys poured on the indigo. An unexpected absentee was his eccentric re-casting of I Got It Bad, which he sings on disc as She Got It Bad, at some expense to the rhyme-scheme and -- in its assumption that only women get the blues - - to the principle of equal-opportunity suffering.

Otherwise, his program was remarkably similar to the one he gave us last year. It derived from his previous half-dozen albums, all of them, as he kept reminding us, Grammy winners. Winning the prize for Best Traditional Vocal, or whatever patronizing title they give it nowadays, has become a running boast for him, just as losing it has become a running gag for Rosemary Clooney.

Incidentally, though the Grammys could hardly matter less, can anyone explain, fashion apart, why neither Bennett nor Clooney has ever made the crossover to a nomination for best vocal per se, while Diana Krall has? The songs may have been the same but much of the singing was better.

Another Weill song, Speak Low, which I thought over-dramatized last year, was beautifully controlled this time; even the studied descents into hushed parlando seemed to work, as a literal fulfillment of the song's injunction. Similarly effective -- though he should have found a different way of doing it in the second chorus -- was his stabbing isolation of the word "need" in People; he is the only singer to make this song (abstracted from his Here's to the Ladies CD, where it honours Barbra Streisand) sound good: important instead of self-important.

The selections from his Fred Astaire disc were suitably rapturous; they included, on the slimmest of historical pretexts, a superbly sly Old Devil Moon, in which Bennett sat out the kicker- phrase about "razzle dazzle" and let the drummer supply an aural equivalent. (This time the stage went gold.)

He did a no-nonsense hour-and-40-minutes with no warm-up act, no intermission and a minimum of chat. Most of the songs were done in a dancing, casual 4/4, supplying maximum opportunity for overall good humour and flexibly conversational phrasing; the latter quality helped People a lot.

He stiffened up only for the inevitable San Francisco (give him credit, he still sings it like he means it) and for his closer, How Do You Keep the Music Playing, a better-than-usual lyric by the incorrigibly earnest Alan and Marilyn Bergman, in which the soft concern that fills the outer edges of his voice builds to the ringing affirmation that he likes to summon from its centre.

Black & White Photo: Peter Redman, National Post / More warm than cool: He stiffened up only for the inevitable San Francisco. ;

HEAVEN

Canadian Stage Company

Stumbling out of Heaven, as befits a critic, I ran into my old friend Phyllis Stein. I was surprised to see her there. George F. Walker's new play is presented at Canadian Stages down-market premises on Berkeley Street, and Phyllis, who is a regular theatregoer and a CSC subscriber, is generally believed to confine her attendance to glossier offerings at the St. Lawrence Centre.

Were you shocked?" I asked her.

"No she said, sounding shocked that I thought she might be. Should I have been?"

"Well, I explained weakly. The management expected you to walk out. Thereve been articles in the paper about it. Previews. This is a dark personal vision, and it's not for the likes of you. There's even a sign in the lobby. It says that at this performance of Heaven there will be gun shots, and four-letter words, and sex, and violence, and strobe-lights, and all that jazz. By the way," I added, spotting a tempting tangent to go off at. "What do they mean, at this performance? Does it mean that tomorrow night, theyll be doing a cleaned-up version, and all this stuff was just put in on the press night to titillate the likes of us? Well, the likes of me, anyway.

She requested me not to be flippant. I said Id try but I couldn't promise.

I saw that sign" she said. "I thought 'um, everything I like.

And did you?"

Phyllis pondered. "Not really. I mean, it was all there. Well, maybe not the sex. People talked about it but they didnt do it. In fact, they talked about not doing it. They shouted about not doing it. They shouted about everything. Maybe there should have been a sign in the lobby about that.

It bothered you?"

"Well, yes it did. There's this first scene, and there are these two guys. One's a cop, and hes mad because his partner has committed suicide, after being sent down for killing a suspect: a black suspect. And the other guy is a sort of civil-rights lawyer, and he was responsible for the dead cop being convicted. And theyre both very angry, and every other word is fuck.

Maybe," I suggested, "that's understandable in the circumstances.'

Yes" said Phyllis, thoughtfully. "I realize that. But then theres this next scene, and theres this teenage girl, and she's trying to learn to juggle, and she keeps dropping the balls, and every time she does, she says 'fuck too. Well, yes, she would; I mean, I would too if it were me. I know you think Ive led a sheltered life but you should come around some time. And it's just a word, just a collection of vowels and consonants. But it does get monotonous. Especially when they shout.

That," I explained, trying not to sound patronizing because she gets enough of that, "is the Walker style. Especially when he directs his own plays. They shout, and they go very fast. Critics complain about it; I've complained myself. Now Im not so sure. I found myself thinking, how else could they do those lines? But it does leave them looking exposed. Youve got actors here with good reputations, you've got Ron White as the lawyer, and Wayne Best as the cop, and they're one-dimensional. One of them just bellows, and the other one just snarls.

I know said Phyllis. "I watch cop series on TV, and I see Homicide, and Cracker, and the cops there are so believable. You forget theyre actors."

I know, I said, with a worrying feeling that I was losing my vocation like a character in a George Walker play. "And the writing's usually better than what we're asked to admire in the theatre. But, look, maybe Walker doesnt want you to believe, at least not naturalistically. I mean, these characters have hang-ups like you wouldnt believe. The lawyer's a Catholic who took to fighting racism because of childhood guilt, and he married a Jewish girl to prove how liberal he was, and both the job and the marriage have gone sour.

And the cop turns into a serial killer, and he keeps hitting on the juggling girl, who learns to do it on stilts and a unicycle, which I think is a message of hope, and he also victmizes a young black drug-dealer. And the wife is in love with her rabbi, who must be the least Jewish-looking rabbi on record, don't you agree" (Phyllis agreed), but maybe theyre trying not to stereotype. Anyway, hes not as irritating as the funny rabbi in Patience.

"Being less irritating than a character in a Jason Sherman play is no defence" said Phyllis.

She had me there.

Anyway, I said, "you could probably authenticate all these things individually from the newspapers, but put them together and it's urban hell. And then they get to heaven, and that's urban hell, too. The murderous cop is privileged and the black boy is put into slave-clothes. Its one mans idea of organized religion's idea of what the world should be like. Very quirky. And there's fantasy: a dead woman comes down from heaven on a wire, and the audience goes wild, just like the people they despise would do for the helicopter in Miss Saigon or the chandelier in Phantom. Theres even a full- length song-and-dance number.

"I know, said Phyllis. Cheek to Cheek -- heaven, Im in heaven." (We hummed together, for a blessed moment.). "Wasn't it tacky? But they loved it. Don't these people ever get out? You know, I have a theory. People enjoy song-and-dance in a play just because its in a play. It seems sort of camp. And it puts a stop to all that talking.

Its my job to have the theories," I said stiffly, "but I think I'll steal that one. Anyway, you must have liked Ron White's stand- up routine at the end: God thinks Im funny -- and I think the same about him. It had real timing. Especially coming just after a scene the audience had applauded as if they thought the play was over. Rhythm is not Mr Walker's strongest point. But he does good one- liners.

Oh yes," said Phyllis, "I laughed a few times. And I can see he means it. But is that enough?'

Not really.

"And people say he's our best playwright."

"You know, the terrible thing is, that may just be true."

2000-01-24-the-perfect-titus-for-our-tim:
Just for identification purposes: Titus Andronicus is the Shakespeare play in which two men rape the protagonists daughter, afterwards depriving her of her hands and her tongue to stop her telling tales It is also the play in which the father, who has found out anyway, avenges her and himself by cutting the assailants' throats, grinding their bones to powder and serving them up to their mother as filling in a pie. It has been strikingly filmed by Julie Taymor who has performed her own amputation on the title, reducing it to Titus. It is also on the bill for this year's Stratford Festival, which could create some confusion. People may come expecting a sequel -- the further adventures of Titus, in the company of some guy named Dronicus.

The attendant publicity has included some pretty wild statements. The play has been widely described as Shakespeares first, which we certainly dont know; it was undoubtedly his first tragedy but there are no firm grounds for dating it earlier than The Two Gentlemen of Verona or The Comedy of Errors or the Henry VI trilogy. Frankly, there is no extant Shakespeare play that feels like anybody's first; they are all too ambitious or too accomplished or both. It is also being routinely described as his worst, as if that too were an agreed fact. Actually that caravan has moved on; these days it's likelier to be that slight comedy The Two Gentlemen that gets the booby prize. Scholars have discovered all kinds of virtues in Titus over the last 50 years; and the theatre has, if anything, been ahead of them.

The stage history of Titus is manageably brief. A hit with the Elizabethans (or rather, a phenomenon:Ben Jonson, the cutting-edge playwright of the next generation, was cheerfully sneering at its popularity some 30 years later), it was abandoned by later generations as an unstageable catalogue of horrors. It didnt come into its own until 1955, when Peter Brook, at the English Stratford, directed, designed and composed the music for a production so menacingly atmospheric that people were fainting even before the first knife came out.

Kenneth Tynan, who thought Laurence Oliviers Titus established him as pound for pound, the greatest actor alive," brilliantly described the play as crude but essential tragedy, "the piling of agony on to a human head until it splits. He also borrowed from Wilde's Lady Bracknell to describe its atmosphere of casual slaughter: To lose one son may be accounted a misfortune; to lose 24, as Titus does, looks like carelessness." Most of these losses have taken place in war, before the play starts. Titus is a successful Roman general who seems more than willing to pay the price for victory.

Brook and Olivier were obviously a hard act to follow, but they opened the floodgates. The Royal Shakespeare Company has done the play three times since, the last (1987) in a spartan production by Deborah Warner that many, including me, would rank as the most completely realized Shakespeare of the last 20 years.

This year's production will be the Canadian Stratfords third; Ive seen more Tituses there than I have Hamlets, Lears or Othellos. I have favourable memories of Brian Bedford's production, with William Hutt, and no memory at all of the second version, directed by Jeanette Lambermont.

It's noticeable, though, that the play has proved a favourite with women directors. Jane Howell directed it for the BBCs Shakespeare series and the Julie Taymor film follows on her stage version in New York.

Taymor has described Titus in an interview as "the play of the millennium; its reassuring to discover that she means, not the best play of the last thousand years but the play that best reflects the violence that has characterized it. Other things have characterized it too, of course, but yes, it has been appallingly violent. So, as far as we can tell, have earlier millennia, notably the one that Titus is set in. The temptation is to gloat over it; to take a grisly play, and exult in your own power to rub audiences' faces in it, usually on the pretext that it's good for them.

Taymor has also claimed -- in an interview in this paper -- that Titus isnt actually all that violent, no more so than Richard III. (Maybe its a close call, but 14 characters are killed in Titus, 11 in Richard, all but two of them offstage and with no mutilations, at least none we get to hear about.)

She has also pushed the line that everyone but her has dismissed the play, and she has had especially hard words for Harold Bloom (Shakespeare: The Invention of the Human), who thinks the play is a joke. I think that Bloom is wrong, but he isn't stupidly wrong, and it's certainly untrue that he has no sense of theatre; his tastes may be a little old-fashioned, but thats no crime. All this, of course, is the kind of thing that directors always say; and if Taymor had just made a film of Macbeth, she would be proclaiming that that was the greatest, too.

One may harbour legitimate suspicions of a director who chooses this source for her first feature film. But the results lift her clean off the hook. This may be the best Shakespeare picture ever made.

One thing that nobody seems to have noticed is that it is very true to its text; it probably includes a greater proportion than any previous Shakespeare film (with the special-case exception of Kenneth Branaghs full-length Hamlet). This is especially notable because many speeches in Titus are stiff and rhetorical, the kind of thing you don't expect a modern audience to sit still for. They require a lot of breath, and Jessica Lange -- who plays Titus' arch- enemy Tamora, Queen of the Goths -- unfortunately doesnt have it. But Anthony Hopkins as Titus does; and I doubt that Taymor could have made the film without him. What counts is not that hes played Hannibal Lecter, but that he's played Macbeth, Lear, Antony and Othello, though none of those performances were as good as this. His conception, I would guess, is a somewhat cozier version of Olivier's: a world-weary, weather-beaten soldier deaf to any code but the military one. When Tamora pleads with him for the life of her eldest son, marked as a victory sacrifice, he seems genuinely puzzled; war is war, and religion is religion, and surely she knows the rules. An outlook as rigid as this can crack horribly, and when Tamora, unexpectedly raised to Empress of Rome, begins to take her revenge, Titus sanity collapses; even words begin to fail him and he retreats into laughter. His perceptiveness remains, though, even sharpens; this, as far as I know, is the only Elizabethan play in which one character sees through anothers disguise -- and he has to be mad to do it. He plays the recognition with enchanting tongue- clicking drollery.

This is not -- pace Roger Ebert's review in the National Post -- a matter of the actor, the director or the playwright sending themselves or their material up; there is humour throughout, but it doesn't undercut the situation, it sharpens it. There are, I think, a few unfortunate if inevitable laughs, inherent in the medium itself; Titus specialite de la maison, seen in close-up complete with beautiful latticed pastrywork, has a more immediate impact here than it does in the theatre. But the fluidity of the screen -- its capacity to pile image on image as poetry does, in this case to complement rather than compete with it -- is brilliantly used.

And Taymor isnt sensational. The actual rape of Titus' daughter Lavinia is kept offscreen; few directors would be that disciplined. We then see her discovered by her uncle Marcus (Colm Feore) with branches apparently growing where her hands used to be. Marcus' long and, on the face of it, impossibly literary speech (why doesnt he just send for a surgeon?) has often been heavily cut, though Deborah Warners production revealed it to be the moving heart of the play: an affirmation of pity over terror. Taymor's version doesn't have quite that impact, but its very powerful. From her own stage production she has brought Harry Lennix as Aaron the Moor, Tamoras lover and the play's gloriously unrepentant villain. His verse has a colloquial gusto unlike anything else in the play; so does his occasional prose. Thou hast undone our mother" screams one of her sons, when he fathers a black child on her; "villain he replies I have done thy mother."' His villainy is totally unrelated to his colour (though some of the white folks think differently) but his speeches concerning his child, whom he will do anything to preserve, are the first black-is-beautiful writing in English, while the sight of the baby in close-up is a wholly positive example of films ability to adjust a balance.

No, it doesnt prove Titus to be as great as King Lear, or even as disturbing; there's nothing in it as horrific as the blinding of Gloucester, which is inflicted on a character we know and feel for and which is protracted longer than any atrocity in Titus -- partly, and with a sort of bitter compassion, because somebody tries to intervene. Titus strikes less deeply into the roots of human evil, but it presents a formidably convincing picture of the fruits.

Or, as both play and film so graphically demonstrate, the proof of the pudding is in the eating.

NOTRE DAME DE PARIS

Pantages Theatre, Toronto

God help the Canadian theatre if we lose Quebec. It's not that the rest of us get to see very much Quebecois theatre as things stand.

Robert Lepage is a national culture-hero but he only brings his shows to Toronto as an afterthought when he has finished trucking them around Europe. As for Notre Dame de Paris, the most exciting Canadian musical since -- well ever, probably: It played a short Toronto season last year in the original French and is now back for another one, but if we in English Canada want to hear and judge it in our own language, then we have to get into line behind English Las Vegas and even English England.

Maybe we'd get better treatment if we became foreigners, too. We would, though, lose any right to think of the shows as our own, and the national mix would be far poorer for it.

Notre Dame de Paris is based, of course, on the novel by Victor Hugo who is, as they say, no stranger to musical theatre. One of the few things harder than having a first hit musical is having a second, and I couldn't prophesy whether this show will equal the success of Les Miserables; my hunch is that it will do well but not quite that well.

It is, though, an incalculably superior show. It has, to begin with, a far more engaging musical identity. Instead of the endless rootless bombast of Les Mis, Richard Cocciante gives us tunes: tunes that even bear some relation to the story's time and place.

There is a rock beat, and it gets more assertive as the evening goes on, but it is clear from the first number -- a solo scene- setter called Le Temps des Cathedrales -- that we are really listening to updated chanson, clear and refreshing.

It's conceivable that I will like them less when I hear them with English lyrics; like most anglophones I regard sung French as a euphonious noise on its own account but, come the translation, I shall have to worry about meaning, and even about dramatic sophistication.

There doesn't seem to be too much of the latter; most of the songs are solos or duets about how happy or confused or erotically driven the characters are, broken up by the occasional chorus of complaint or defiance from the local homeless. (Les Sans-Papier -- those without visas -- they are called, in an engagingly transparent attempt to bring Hugo's 19th-century treatment of a 14th-century subject right into our own arriere-cour.)

As usual in a rock-opera, the lyricist, in this case Luc Plamondon, also gets credited with the book; equally as usual, there isn't one. There isn't even the pretense of one; the show is blessedly free of the droning explanatory mini-songs that generally separate the big numbers and that their composers like to think of as recitative.

Narrative coherence depends heavily on the audience's folk- memory: our shared awareness that there is a bell-ringing hunchback called Quasimodo who hangs out in the big church, and a gypsy called Esmerelda who camps out in front of it and with whom nearly all the men in the cast are in lust. It's enough: though it does result in a pile-up of sweat-soaked ballads in the second act, making the show sound more like other shows at its end than at its beginning. I couldn't swear either that, in a dark radio-station, I would be able to distinguish Esmerelda's song called Ave Maria from all the other songs I've heard called Ave Maria.

I may have a few doubts about the score but I have none about Gilles Maheu's production. The time of the cathedrals turns out to be a great time to look at. Our Lady of Paris is represented by a huge back wall, divided into panels and studded with foot-holds. It is, in fact, a climbing-wall, plentifully adorned with gargoyles who hang down in perilous positions and turn out to be people.

The second act begins with a tune that sounded to me suspiciously like the old French hit Les Trois Cloches (known in English as The Jimmy Brown Song); maybe I imagined that, but it is a fact that immediately afterwards three huge bells descend from the ceiling, each with an actor suspended upside-down from its base and swinging, as the phrase goes, like the clappers.

The cast numbers, according to the program, 15 dancers and five acrobats, and all 20 of them are fearsomely intrepid. Martino Muller's choreography, thrillingly performed, is abstract and expressive, by Bob Fosse out of Martha Graham; the chorus are used to act out the characters' inner drives, reviving and transforming the old tradition of the dream-ballet.

Sometimes the sets get into the act; Frollo, the priest tormented by his desire, spends one number apparently in an attempt to prevent one ecclesiastical column from crashing into another, but really trying to prevent his vocation from crushing his libido, or maybe vice versa.

The male leads -- Mario Pelchat (a Quasimodo who, compared to Charles Laughton's super-masochistic hunchback, is a positive pin- up), Robert Marien (Frollo), Sylvain Cossette (Gringoire, the driving troubadour-narrator) and Charles Biddle (Clopin, master of the rebels) -- are all strong on lungs, personality and presence. Esmerelda (France d'Amour, I am not making that up) can't match them for voice, but she certainly has a sensual slink.

Indeed, in all departments, this show is a forcible reminder of just how sexless the Anglo-American musical has become, and it's a bracing antidote. Consciously or not, it's also French Canada's answer to Rent, with equivalent street-smarts. Somehow it splits the periods: The actors are visibly miked, rock-concert searchlights rake the stage, and the riot-gendarmes quell the mob with recognizably modern mobile barriers, but contact with the source is never quite broken.

The creators have kept the original title (no Hollywood hunchback to lure us in) and the original ending, with Esmerelda hanged, and her Prince Charming, the captain of the guard, turning out a real bastard. What they've done that's less admirable, and all too modern, is use pre-taped music; there were musicians picketing the theatre on the first night, protesting that they were protesting on behalf of the audience's rights rather than their own jobs.

This was disingenuous of them, but their cause was just; you can tell the difference, and it's bad. To the barricades: After all, they're there on the stage, just waiting.

Black & White Photo: Notre Dame de Paris: A superior show despite the pre-taped music. ;

QUE SERA

Artword Theatre, Toronto

This staged biography of Doris Day begins with the central character behind the mike and in front of the band. There's a medley going on, and the musicians -- they're just a trio -- seem to be playing cut-down versions of swing-era charts, the kind of things that first put Day on top in the 1940s. The songs, though, sound strangely unfamiliar, and it takes a moment to realize that they are actually the title tunes from Day's light-comedy films of the '60s - - Lover Come Back, Pillow Talk, Teacher's Pet -- given a new sound. Or, more precisely, an older sound that seems new. This collapsing of two periods of the subject's career, as in a dream, is an ingenious idea. It turns out to be the last idea of the evening.

Morgonn Ewen, who plays Doris, manages to look not unlike her, especially after donning a full blond wig later in the show. Her singing, though it lacks the original's secure swing and strong lower register, is most of the time a fair facsimile in tone and phrasing. A singer rather than an actress (she may be the first leading lady to earn additional billing as "assistant musical director"), she manages to inject a tremulous appeal into her spoken lines. And that exhausts the litany of permissible compliment for what is otherwise an appallingly inept show.

Written by Claudette Williams and directed by Rebecca Cann, it seems to fancy itself as hard-hitting. It seizes on the obvious contrast between the sunny songs its subject sang and the troubled life she actually led -- and hits us relentlessly over the head with it, without ever exploring either the myth or the reality. The opening sequence concludes with Doris going into a genuine oldie, Lullaby of Broadway, and breaking up on it. She is then berated by the five other members of the cast for screwing up the lyric (to my chagrin, I hadn't noticed) and for self-indulgent behaviour generally. Clearly they represent her demons, mental and corporeal; and they hang around for the rest of the night, commenting and doing impersonations.

We flash back to the subject's childhood; she overhears her father having adulterous sex and she suffers a car accident that puts an end to hopes of a dancing career. In ironic counterpoint to these and other early traumas, she and her colleagues partly sing, partly intone, the optimistically romantic lyrics of When I Fall in Love. She grows up and goes through three marriages (and three sarcastically mimed wedding ceremonies): Her first husband abuses her, causing the miscarriage of her second baby; her second neglects her; and her third, her manager after she achieves stardom, all but ruins her. At some point in this progression she pauses to sing It's Magic.

Meanwhile, she's having a career. Still bearing her baptismal name of Doris Kappelhoff, she auditions for Les Brown -- a top and extremely durable big-band leader, here portrayed as an amiable hick -- and with minimal effort wins a job. Her audition song is Day by Day; her new employers feel she should change her name, and we sit there patiently -- or not -- waiting for the penny to drop. Later she gets to Hollywood and meets director Michael Curtiz, who demonstrates a great gift for helpful exposition: "I want you to come by the studio tomorrow" he tells her "and do a screen test for my new picture, Romance on the High Seas." So then come the movie musicals, and then the non-musical comedies opposite Cary Grant and Rock Hudson, and a TV series, and a retirement devoted to running hotels for dogs.

There was a war on when Day was a band singer and it contributed to her success, especially with her big hit Sentimental Journey. The show, though, hasn't noticed. Nor does it seem at all concerned with either the period or the content of her films. "She just floated along with whatever came up," a musician once said about her, but the show goes further and presents her as a total zombie.

In her movies, though, she appears not only squeaky clean, for which she's notorious, but capable, and the paradox might at least be worth mentioning. We never learn then what her fans saw in her, or why she has since been revalued as an unlikely feminist heroine. (She was an excellent singer, but that of course is the last thing anybody cares about.)

The only whiff of history, or even of drama, comes when we reach the '60s; we are reminded that the Charles Manson gang intended to kill Day's son Terry, who had let his house to Sharon Tate. This information is relayed to us by a couple of recurring ladies who keep gossiping about "our Doris" and who read about the murders -- for the first time, apparently -- in the centre pages of a supermarket paper; seems the story couldn't even make the front of the tabloids.

The worst of Day's assembly-line musicals can never have been as baldly or badly written as this; indeed, her own stab at a biopic -- Love Me or Leave Me, based on the life of '30s torcher Ruth Etting - - is by comparison a masterpiece of atmosphere or accuracy. Its title song, as it happens, occasions Ewen's best singing here; her worst comes in a closing rendition of 'S Wonderful (yes, there's an upbeat ending), done in a twittering style that suggests some confusion with Day's lesser alliterative contemporaries, Patti Page or the terminally syrupy Joni James.

Nobody else in the cast seems able to sing, though they're all required to. Their acting is unhappy, too; they all, whether slamming it across with desperate bravado or mumbling it like a criminal confession, radiate intense distrust of their material. Since one of them is also the author, this is really serious. The physical production looks poverty-stricken: financially, which is of course forgivable, and imaginatively, which isn't.

SONGS FOR A NEW WORLD

The Church at Berkeley, 315 Queen St. E., Toronto

One of the merits of Parade, the short-lived New York show that was Livent's last book musical, was that it gave a platform to a new young composer-lyricist, Jason Robert Brown. Brown was known previously only for an even shorter-lived but well-noted off- Broadway piece, Songs for a New World.

A talented and enterprising new company called Color and Light gave it a 10-day showing in Toronto; it closed on Saturday but should be brought back. It was a promising work when new; there is now the added interest that its promise has been fulfilled.

Brown's writing was to take a great step forward in Parade, partly because that musical's fable of injustice in the Deep South gave him a solid narrative springboard. In Songs from a New World he has to create story, characters and social setting all by himself; and to do it afresh, 16 times over. The show is one of those staged song-cycles in which previously unperformed composers show off their existing wares and try to impose a theme on them.

The masters of this form are the team of Richard Maltby Jr. and David Shire, whose anthology-revues are major influences here. (Their best-known show, Starting Here Starting Now, actually includes a song called New World Coming.) The predominant tone of the genre is optimistic urban angst; characters bitch and kvetch and fall very self-consciously in and out of love, but they do so to bracing musical rhythms that at least suggest that life might be worth living, and at the end of the evening they come right out in a soaring chorale and admit it.

Brown's lyrics don't have the observant wit of Maltby's, and his music doesn't surge like the best of Shire, but he upholds that wryly intense Manhattan perspective. When a character sings, I'm Not Afraid of Anything you know that she is terrified of everything.

I suppose that musicals have always gone in for uplift, but once upon a time, when audiences were told to lift up their heads and shout because there was going to be a great day, people took the pronouncement for granted. It was just one of those things; anything went.

In recent decades solemnity has skyrocketed, even -- or especially -- in romantic songs. Love has become less an emotion than a cause. Rock, folk and country -- all simple, didactic forms - - have had their effect on the younger composers, and Brown certainly bears the marks. His best single number here is The River Won't Flow, a sort of anti-gospel song: a rant against failure that's more invigorating than most odes to success.

The new world he contemplates seems at times to be a brave psychic landscape that we might all inhabit if we thought positively; at other more sobering moments it's the actual United States. We start with a song about Columbus, desperately praying; and even after we've plunged into the present we're liable to return to the War of Independence, where a potential battle widow is desperately sewing flags.

Though I had enjoyed some of the songs on CD, I was unprepared for how well they worked in the theatre. There is movement here both within and between the characters, and Tim Fort's staging brought it subtly but forcefully home. Dancing was minimal but neat, singing excellent, vocal harmonies especially rich as, in this kind of small- band show, they need to be. The cast boasted one of the best actress- singers in Canada in Tracy Michailidis, a performer with genuine poise and presence of whom I certainly want to see more. She both began and ended the show by making a grave entrance carrying a presumably symbolic lantern, and it seemed fitting that she was the only one in the cast who got to hold a candle.

Sharron Matthews specialized in songs about materialistic ladies who come to bad ends. She stops the show with Surabaya Santa, Mrs. Claus bewailing her left-alone lot after the style of Brecht and Weill; the lyric isn't as witty as it should be but the idea and the performance carried it.

The men, Thom Allison and Jason Knight, were less distinctive, though Allison mustered a tingling falsetto. A final word for Brown's rhymes, which are unshowily good, and nail his points down. Here at least he's a traditionalist, and in the best way.

JOSEPH AND THE AMAZING TECHNICOLOR DREAMCOAT

Pantages Theatre

Musical theatre partnerships -- Gilbert and Sullivan, Rodgers and Hart -- have traditionally been made up of opposites, each of whom could supply the qualities the other lacked. The word on Tim Rice and Andrew Lloyd Webber used to be that they complemented one another perfectly, since Webber didn't have a sense of humour while Rice had nothing but.

How true this may be of them, I know little (and what I do know I'm not telling), but it seems to work for their work. You can see it operating on a sliding scale, with Webber taking increasing control as their shows get more ambitious and less entertaining. But Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat, their first musical -- a genesis based on Genesis -- is the one in which Rice is in charge.

The words in Joseph, though generally delightful, are not above criticism. In London last summer I witnessed civilization take another step backwards when a TV host, flourishing a cherished copy of the original 1970s LP, enthused about Rice's rhyming of "biscuit" with "district": "You won't," he cried, "find that in a rhyming dictionary!" (No, you won't; and for very good reason.)

I even have problems with the celebrated couplet in which Joseph offers his meteorological interpretation of Pharaoh's dreams: "All those things you saw in your pyjamas / Were a long-range forecast for your farmers." The idea is witty, and the images superb, but try singing "long-range forecast" so the syllables hit the beats.

All the same, there's a flavour to those lines -- one of amiable disrespect -- that typifies the whole piece. Joseph is a very English show (American performers don't always get it), and when Rice invokes P. G. Wodehouse to describe Pharaoh's butler ("the Jeeves of his time") he is acknowledging a cultural parent.

Like a Wodehouse novel or, indeed, a Wodehouse musical, Joseph tells its story straight while looking at it askance. Characters are cut off-handedly down to size, and anachronism is used not to patronize but to humanize. "I don't speak Egyptian very well" the hero sensibly laments, as he's dragged off into slavery in a foreign land. "No one comes to dinner now / We'd only eat them anyhow," sing his brothers in the throes of famine.

The score is enchantingly eclectic; basically rock 'n' roll, with Pharaoh a born-again Elvis (or maybe vice versa), it also takes in country, chanson and calypso, each accorded a full-length number whose insouciant irrelevance is its charm. Rice not only writes funny lyrics, he gets Webber writing funny music.

I guess it's facile to say that this first score is its composer's best, but if it hasn't all been downhill since, then it's certainly been a very strenuous road up. Strangely, though, Rice without Webber has proved even more turgid than Webber without Rice; the composer has seemed far happier abandoning his roots and writing mid-Atlantic than the lyricist, who maybe had more roots to lose.

The show famously started as a 40-minute school entertainment; it was subsequently presented at a London's leading youth theatre, the Young Vic, in a double bill with extracts from the mediaeval cycles of Biblical mystery plays, which, as it happens, also thrive on anchronism.

That was the best production of the show I've seen. The problem since has always been to make a brief but obvious hit last a whole evening. Numbers have been extended; having wrung every drop of juice from the parody songs, productions have tried to squeeze the pulp as well. There is an epilogue in the shape of a dance-mix finale that amounts to a miniature recap of the entire score. A show that used pop is being used by it.

This is the formula bequeathed us by the production that criss- crossed Canada and parts of the U.S. for years, usually with Donny Osmond as Joseph. It was outrageously glitzy, but it winked at its own outrageousness, and was imaginative with it. It was crammed with visual jokes that matched the verbal and musical ones. It was a great deal of fun.

The present version is an economy-size derivative of that one, with sets that are cut-down cut-outs. It's a fair amount of fun.

Some things are far too literal; doing the C&W song in cowboy gear kills the joke by underlining it. Patrick Cassidy (as Joseph) is conceivably a better actor than Osmond, and he does some ringing singing, but he, too, lacks wit.

Joseph's prophetic smugness, which used to be guilelessly amusing, is now simply smug. (He tells the royal baker whose death he's foretold not to worry, but "it's just that I was never wrong before." One thing missing from this staging is the subsequent sight of the baker's head brought to Pharaoh on a platter.)

Like his predecessors, Cassidy only gets to wear his dreamcoat on very special occasions, going through most of the evening bare- chested; I suppose somebody's already called the show The Loin King.

In ancient days, children, the part of the Narrator in Joseph was always played by a man, and I don't know that having it done by a woman is a good idea, at least not the way it actually works out. What happens is that a lady who was once a pop star (Deborah Gibson this time round) descends to Earth and sings with a determined smirk, as if instructing the kids in Biblical history was a career move undertaken on advice of the highest authority, whose wisdom she was beginning to doubt.

The kids, naturally, are locals and are worked very hard. The grown-up ensemble are billed as The Osmond Brothers Second Generation, though if you look at the small print, only two of them seem actually to be called Osmond; as in the source material, it's difficult to keep track of who begat whom. But they all dance energetically and seem to be enjoying it, which is what counts.

One credit to Dallet Norris' production; for the first time I can remember, I was touched when Joseph was reunited with his brothers. And as musical-theatre messages go, this one's casual benediction (Any Dream Will Do) is remarkably palatable.

JEKYLL

Canadia dell'Arte Studio, Toronto

Where once there was Dr. Henry Jekyll there is now Henrietta. Robert Louis Stevenson's patient and unresisting novella has been wheeled into the theatre for yet another operation. This time, a two- woman troupe calling themselves Les Vaches have taken the story and transgendered it.

Sex apart, Jekyll is still what he always was: a respected and successful physician in late 19th-century London, playing around in the laboratory with phials and potions that will release the beast in herself. Gabriel Utterson, the doctor's lawyer, friend and confidante, is a woman, too.

As for the doctor's fiendish alter ego: When the monster first escapes from the lab and begins stalking the streets and brutally assaulting people, it is initially assumed that Mr. Hyde is still Mr. Hyde, and Utterson -- who is our narrator-figure -- is shocked. But it turns out that Hyde, too, is a woman (no first name given, there being no handy equivalent to Edward), and Utterson is appalled. The audience -- which had initially expected a Ms. Hyde, given the rules of the show, and had then been surprised, and then surprised again -- is pleasantly titillated.

The adaptation actually sticks closer to the spine of the original than some other recent versions have done. No romantic sub- plot is introduced, as in the frighteningly long-running Broadway musical. Jekyll and Hyde do not get to appear onstage together and indulge in long conversations, as they did a few years ago at Canadian Stage.

There are some changes, of course: Hyde gets pregnant and leaves Jekyll holding the baby, which wasn't an option open to their predecessors. But the show's main strategy is to plant an explosive new device within a familiar framework.

It isn't as explosive as all that. Indeed what the production really seems to be telling us is that girls just want to have fun. As actresses, they want to have the fun of acting out a story usually reserved for men. They might of course have done this by straightforward male impersonation, like Sarah Bernhardt playing Hamlet.

In fact, the writer-performers here, Ruth Madoc-Jones and Erika Hennebury, do play men as well. They play a pair of prosperous club men, who talk and behave like exploitative males from period porn. (Their dialogue could be a direct transcription, though such sources don't figure in the impressive bibliography cited in the program.)

One of these chaps tries to have his way with the lady lawyer; the other is sexually commandeered by Hyde, prior to being killed by her. One man gets what the other deserves, and they are indeed virtually indistinguishable: amazingly so, considering that each is played by a different actress.

They are putting their serious energies, of course, into playing the women. Madoc-Jones gives us an eager graduate-student Jekyll and a genuinely scary Hyde, with a high-pitched laugh and a voice like a rusty door-hinge. Hennebury promotes Utterson from disinterested observer to co-protagonist, with hang-ups of her own; she gets off on reading the horror stories in the papers, and is ashamed of it.

Jekyll helps her to get over this, though how good an example Jekyll may be is open to question. The intellectual progress of the piece is somewhat cloudy, especially toward the end; but however you twist Stevenson's story, "if it feels good, do it" is not, on the evidence presented, an acceptable moral.

The production comes accompanied by the usual promotional guff about intensely physical performance that plumbs previously uncharted psychic and erotic depths. (Do these groups ever read one another's manifestoes? Don't they know they're all claiming to do the same things? Why do they think we'll be impressed?)

Necessary quick-changes apart, movement and gesture are no more striking here than in most other shows, and though the actors wear clown makeups, they do most of their acting at dialogue level, just as if they were in a drawing-room comedy. They do it intelligently, though a lack of skill or practice sometimes leads them into over- emphasis.

As for making a statement on gender roles: Well, the show hardly bothers to grapple with the statistical unlikelihood of its doctor and lawyer having got where they did when they did, or with what it must have cost them, so social realism is obviously out. We are left with a game of "what if?"; and that does work.

It's hard these days to accord more than lip-service to the power of Stevenson's fable of repression released. Making the Victorian men Victorian women -- giving them a double load of bonds to break - - helps reawaken the sleeping demons.

The show does more of its source and for its audience than recent versions of the Odyssey or the Book of Job have done for theirs. It's also, from time to time, a laugh.

JIM AND SHORTY

Factory Theatre

Alex Poch-Goldin, the author of Jim and Shorty, is an actor who writes admirably for other actors. I don't mean that he writes them great lines -- the dialogue of this play is actually its weakest component -- but he imagines them clearly, and brings them to strong physical life.

Jim and Shorty are a couple of homeless men who spend three scenes interacting, sometimes helped out by a third man called Tom. They occupy a largely blank stage space that stretches to the back wall of the theatre, and is dominated by a bench and a garbage can. It could be a dilapidated parkette behind an invisible bus-shelter. Layne Coleman, the director, and Sherri Hay, the designer, have done a fine job here, staging the play in the theatrical equivalent of deep focus.

Most productions concentrate on stringing their actors out across the width of a stage, and the perspective here is exhilarating. When the dramatist contrives an effect -- when one character enters unexpectedly on a motorized cart, or another is discovered huddled, shocked and freezing -- it stands out in the sharpest relief.

When we first meet them, Jim is in tatters and Shorty wears a suit, and the contrast defines them: how we see them, and especially how they see one another. Shorty is indignant that the welfare officials -- government employees, for Gods sake -- come to work these days in T-shirts, and he lectures Jim, who looks back on his schooldays with bewildered distaste, on the importance of an education.

History teaches him to be aware of the difference between yesterday and today. In a life like theirs, where one day threatens to melt indistinguishably into another, maintaining that awareness is crucial to preserving a sense of self. Math helps him count any money he may have. The cost of things -- of doughnuts, beer and bus fares -- is on their minds, especially on Jims, who keeps comparing them to what they used to be. (He has perhaps learned Shorty's lessons better than Shorty thinks.)

If neither man is strictly an alcoholic, drink is still their most pressing concern. They also discuss the merits of the different shelters available, and the best ways of squeezing cash out of the system. They gossip vaguely about mutual acquaintances.

They even mention politics. There is an election brewing and Tom, the third character -- who is Indian, or native, or First Nations, depending on the awareness of the speaker -- starts the play by loudly recommending a candidate who is going to change everything. He doesn't give a name, but it certainly isnt Mike Harris.

Jim and Shorty consider voting, but they dont seem to get around to it. Inevitably, we start thinking -- as in so many previous plays --of Beckett and early Pinter, who taught us in the starkest terms that passing the time is both the business of drama and its subject, and in whose stretch of theatrical history we are still living.

The thought would hold even if the author had never heard or read a word of them (which, for a working actor in his thirties, is admittedly unlikely.) There is, though, a built-in twist. We are conditioned to think such characters as lacking a coherent biography; but each has one. If they are living an absurdist drama, they are living it for real.

It turns out, too, to be a conventionally well-made absurdist drama. Its second half is a black (well, grey) comedy of role- reversal. Jim, thanks to the vagaries of bureaucracy, now has the upper hand, and he uses it: not viciously but meanly. He truly has learned to play the system, at least for now. This is undeniably effective, but also undeniably glib.

I suspect the author was in a bind. The play was first performed two years ago, without its current last scene. I didn't see it then, but I imagine I would have found it unsatisfying, a pointless vignette needing development. Now it has been developed and it still doesn't satisfy.

Increasingly, one wants the text to resonate more. It carries the suggestion of wit without its substance. This is as good as it gets: Contemplating a burned-out butchers store, Jim thinks of "all that meat -- cooked."

The writing is never actually tedious and it certainly gives the cast enough to bite on. They could hardly be bettered, with Earl Pastko especially distinctive as Shorty, reaching out but essentially in a world of his own. Ron Gabriels Jim is a more conventional sly hobo (Estragon to Shorty's Vladimir) and Lorne Cardinal is a loomingly sympathetic presence as Tom.

There is intermittent kindness in all these characters, and the cruelty is all in the circumstances. The play opened on a snowy night, with some at least of the banned squeegee kids still at work. It couldn't have been more suitable.

Alex and Shorty runs to Feb. 26 at the Factory Studio Theatre, 125 Bathurst St. $15 to $18. Call 416-504-9971.

MELLA MELLA

Young People's Theatre

Lusciously imaginative, Mella Mella had been promoted from the Young People's Theatre studio to the organization's main stage as a contribution to Black History Month.

Gail Nyoka's play is a dramatization of a Zimbabwean legend. Mella (Joanne Degand) is the daughter of a village king who lies sick and apparently incurable. Two bullying young guards (Martin David Peters and Gneon Douho) are already preparing to take power, ignoring the hereditary claims of the princess. She, however, is modest but resourceful. On the advice of a village wise woman (Layah Davis), she goes in search of an even wiser woman, the medicine lady, N'anga (Djolei Gogoua).

N'anga, in turn, points her in the direction of a powerful cave- dwelling serpent known as the Python Healer. This is something of a kill-or-cure proposition, since the snake has a fearsome reputation. Indeed, when Mella's two male rivals make the trek to the python's cavern, he has them running away screaming, and they have to tell lies about their adventures after they have made it back to the village.

Mella, however, being a good person to begin with and having received much valuable instruction both from N'anga and from her father's loyal counsellor, Gamyambadzi (Beche Ako), charms the snake and, indeed, returns home with it wreathed round her neck.

It restores her father, who settles down to a long and healthy reign with Mella in unopposed line for the succession. She has proved herself both a strong woman and a dutiful daughter.

Many points in this story are legendary favourites the world over. On their respective journeys to the python's lair, both Mella and the guards encounter a sick merchant begging for water. Mella, as befits a heroine, takes time out to fetch him some; the men -- as befits greedy, impatient, uncharitable louts -- do not.

In patriarchal European fairy tales, similar incidents function as an infallible means of telling the good brother from the bad. The suppliant usually turns out to be some sort of supernatural benefactor in disguise; and even here, though the Python never actually alludes to the incident, we can be fairly sure he knows about it.

The tale, however, despite vigorous acting all round, is less important here than the telling, which is magical. Pierre Tretault's production looks and sounds splendid from the outset. Drums beat out complex and compelling patterns as a visual pattern no less compelling, made up of silhouetted branches and a golden sun, unfold on the cyclorama. Shadows, it turns out, will tell much of the story: shadows of vegetation, of masks, of human and animal figures. The prize silhouette, naturally, is that of the python itself, which has a sinuous and challenging neck and a darting, quivering tongue.

Groupe Bassan and Glenn Davidson are responsible for the shadow puppet design. Davidson is also credited with the set and lighting, which keep a constant stream of arresting pictures before our eyes and also make it worth our while to glance down to a mosaic stage floor in yellow and black.

The robes are gorgeous; they include one especially striking creation for a thin and apparently headless actor who looks like a walking clothes closet; he or she presumably symbolizes the kingdom deprived of its ruler.

Costume designer is the same Djolei Gogoua who imperiously narrates the play in the role of N'anga and who also does the voice of the Python, for whom she supplies some suitably intimidating sibilants.

A remarkable team also includes Beche Ako, choreographer, and Gneon Douho, who as an actor is one of the bad guys, but as a composer is on the side of truth, good order and a commanding beat.

A treat for the children for whom it's intended, the show also rewards the attention of any passing adults.

Black & White Photo: Tom Sandler / A treat for children and parents alike: Mella Mella's Joanne Degand, left, Gneon Douho, Djolei Gogoua and Martin David Peters. ;
