BELLE

Factory Theatre

I have problems with the idea of Black History Month, since it suggests that the history comes to a stop for the rest of the year. Still, we take what we get, and this February has brought two first- rate pieces of theatre. For the kids, theres YPTs Mella Mella ; for the grown-ups there's Belle, Florence Gibson's dazzlingly- written new play about the aftermath of the American Civil War.

One of the few things most of us know about that period is that it was one of massive internal migration. With the Souths economy in ruins, huge numbers of ex-slaves moved north, there to discover a different kind of misery: the freedom to start poor and stay poor. So here we find Belle and Boleyn, a young married couple who come with their baby to the big city (I think I heard New York mentioned) to find work. She scrubs floors, he tries setting up as a cab driver, having spent eight back-breaking years in the fields saving up to buy a horse.

There also turns out, less expectedly, to be white refugees from the same region. There is Nance, who fled in disgust from her plantation-owning daddy but is still financially dependent on him. She now devotes herself to the fight for womens suffrage. Then we have Lackley, known universally and to his great indignation as Lackey, who is trying to ingratiate himself with the new Republican Party, mainly by drumming up votes. Each wants something from Belle and Boleyn: political support and -- at least in Nance's case -- moral support as well.

Nance first encounters Boleyn when she hires his cab. She is his first fare and his last; she is on her way to disrupt a convention, he is implicated and his horse is impounded. Calling round to apologize, Nance meets Belle and spies a prize: a woman who is vibrant and intelligent and also coloured: an all-round standard- bearer for the oppressed. Boleyn discovers a talent for oratory in his own cause; he also signs up with the Republicans who are promising voting rights for blacks - though only for black men.

A brief period of solidarity is followed by disillusion. Boleyn discovers that his new rights are hedged around with conditions that prevent him from exercising them; Nance, to placate her white constituency, drops black suffrage from her platform. She is remorseful where Lackey is cynical, but the practical results are just about equal. Meanwhile, with Boleyn both resentful and defensive that Belle is now the breadwinner, their marriage sags and eventually breaks.

The play begins with a speech in rhyme. It then moves into prose, but prose of a richness to which we are hardly accustomed. It is aglow with metaphor but it is also tense with conflict. Prose poetry in the theatre is usually an ornamental disaster: an invitation to the audience to forget the characters and admire the playwright. Here it's an actors weapon.

Gibson can on occasion be devastatingly funny. You should be President of the United States says Nance to Boleyn, whom shes just met; he is taken understandably aback. She can be brilliantly and paradoxically compact: when Nance rails against "those Southern bitches" in her own caucus, Belle quietly reminds her I'm from the South.

She can also make her images flesh: as in a scene where the two women, discussing the effects of colour on the way we think and the way we talk, paint one another's faces. She uses her four characters to teach us, without apparent strain, a remarkable amount of history. She can illuminate the present through the past, and politics through sex -- especially with Nance whose relations with the two men seem equally fed by resentment and desire.

There are certainly flaws. The action -- black-white, man-woman - - can hardly help being schematic, and this takes its toll on the later parts of the play, where the characters get stuck in repetitive grooves. Belle herself, standing as she does at the epicentre of oppression, becomes an emblem rather than a person: this despite a performance by Yanna McIntosh that manages to be both earthy and radiant.

There is a fifth character, Belles sister left behind in Georgia, whom Boleyn calls "mad" and who in childhood was used and impregnated by her master; she hovers wraith-like over the action, always slightly out of focus, and is none too convincing when she comes belatedly to life.

The play deserves a more imaginative staging than it gets from Ken Gass. The characters may be poverty-stricken but the show doesnt have to be. The set, composed of planks and sackcloth, is simultaneously skeletal and cumbersome. The play is composed in bold, even melodramatic scenes; one concerns an attempted rape that climaxes in a fire. Here the episodes melt awkwardly into one another; actors don't even get the chance to make clean exits.

Still, Gass and his actors are on top of the dialogue, whose rich currency they convert it into lines of force passing between the characters. Soo Garay's Nance reclaims the image of the Southern belle: a second title-figure in fact and maybe the one to whom the author has lost her heart.

Nigel Shawn Williams' Boleyn is his strongest performance to date; he can tremble -- with rage, guilt or embarrasingly -- as eloquently as any actor I have seen. Alex Poch-Goldin's Lackey is a wily emotional derelict, an underdog with a perpetual itch in his voice. Here it is at last: a play that sings.

Black & White Photo: Kevin Van Paassen, National Post / Nigel Shawn Williams and Yanna McIntosh star in the drama Belle. ;

THE EDDIE CANTOR STORY

Solar Stage Theatre, Toronto

Eddie Cantor, comic and song-and-dance man, was a high-pressure performer and apparently a very nice man. He might be described as the light side of Al Jolson.

I'm not referring to their respective exploits in blackface, though for Jolson it seems to have been the life-blood of performance while for Cantor it was merely one routine among many. The jazz critic Gary Giddins once asked the veteran Avon Long, a great Sportin' Life in Porgy and Bess, if he hadn't been offended by Cantor's antics in burnt-cork. "We black people are not stupid," said Long. "We too can appreciate genius."

That's one of my favourite Cantorial tales. Another, also recounted by Giddins, concerns a 1950 Carnegie Hall concert at which Cantor made his audience very nervous by referring to "Senator McCarthy and other evil things that want to destroy mankind." And a third goes back to the early years of the 20th century, and the actors' strike that accompanied the formation of American Equity. George M. Cohan, the presiding showman of the day, proclaimed that rather than join a union he would quit performing and be an elevator- man. "Somebody" said Cantor, who was already a star, "better tell Mr. Cohan that if he wants to run an elevator he'll have to join a union."

None of these turn up in The Eddie Cantor Story that is a neat little lunchtime biography with an appealingly skilful performance by Glenn Roy in the title role. It tactfully avoids the blackface issue (thereby passing up the chance of making a back-handed contribution to Black History Month) but it does pay its respects to its subject's social and political conscience. It's 1940, and the sponsors of his radio show are threatening to cancel, offended by his on-air comments on the situation in Europe. He stands his ground: "The Nazis," he tells his producer "are fascists." It's rather an odd choice of phrase -- either it's redundant or it suggests that Hitler's bunch are nearly as bad as those guys in Italy -- but it's certainly honourable.

Otherwise, Aviva Ravel's script is a traditional rags-to-riches story, Lower East Side division.

Eddie loses his parents as an infant, and grows up in direst poverty. He survives on the streets through his urchin charm, his quick-wittedness, and his capacity for making people laugh. He realizes that he can make a living as an entertainer -- this despite the misgivings of his doting immigrant grandmother and the combined threats and blandishments of his prospective father-in-law. ("Look, here's some dollars. Go open a clothes store.") The last part of his career goes by in a triumphant blur; most of our time has been spent on the beginnings that are judged, probably rightly, to be far more interesting.

Basically, of course, the show is an excuse to perform some of Cantor's signature numbers. It abides by the usual convention that songs from any part of a performer's career may be used to illustrate any other part of it. Thus we hear Eddie, singing for pennies at the turn of the century, giving out with tunes that plainly belong to the 1920s or later; one of them even bestows icon status on Rudy Vallee, who was 10 years younger than Cantor.

I suppose only freaks like me care about this kind of thing, but it does seem a shame to tamper with the ambience. It's downright ridiculous, given the limited time available, to throw in a Jolson song while leaving out such genuine Cantor gems as Hungry Women ("I feed 'em and weep") and You'd Be Surprised, an Irving Berlin tune perfectly matched to Eddie's brand of lascivious coyness.

Scott White plays the piano and all the supporting roles, in a variety of accents and wigs. He even -- unwisely, since he physically towers over the star -- enacts the women in Eddie's life: his one wife, and his granny for whom he assumes a stoop, a shawl, and the tone of a gently muttering martyr.

Women who made it from the shtetls to the tenements must have been made of sterner stuff; and personally, I couldn't wait to see the old girl keel over.

There are hints that Cantor let his career imperil his marriage, but otherwise his behaviour seems exemplary. So does his performing; Roy does Makin' Whoopee and If You Knew Susie with impeccable vocal, facial and physical modulation. They don't make 'em like Cantor anymore, not since the invention of the microphone, and Roy is a gentler, tidier presence -- a quizzical flower-child rather than the eye-popping goatish momma's boy that was Eddie.

But there are enough points of contact to make sense, and I was able to abandon my usual prejudices against so-called plays in which one singer runs through another singer's repertoire.

Cantor was an excellent singer -- jazzier than Jolson, and one of the best pointers of lyrics, especially comic lyrics, ever -- but he was primarily a stage animal, and his songs can be acted. (And it's not as if the CD racks are bulging with Cantor reissues.) I'd suggest giving similar, but deeper, treatment, to the life, songs and monologues of Bert Williams, Cantor's idol and his colleague in the Ziegfeld Follies, whom W. C. Fields once described as "the funniest man I've ever seen and the saddest man I've ever known."

He was the first black performer to make it in white show business but, being light-skinned, he too had to black up: a scary concept and one well worth exploring.

SUNDAY IN THE PARK WITH GEORGE

Equity Showcase Theatre, Toronto

I have sometimes speculated that if Andrew Lloyd Webber had written Sunday in the Park with George he would have called it Dots.

The Stephen Sondheim-James Lapine musical, a succes d'estime on Broadway 15 years ago, is very loosely based on the reclusive life and short career of Georges Seurat, the Parisian pointillist painter who worked in tiny specks of colour which, seen from a sufficient distance, coalesced into dazzling and elaborate canvasses.

We watch him circa 1885, both in his studio and on location, assembling his urban-pastoral masterwork Sunday Afternoon on the Island of the Grande Jatte. He interacts, fitfully and reluctantly, with the locals and tourists who pass through this pleasure-spot in the middle of the Seine and who are to enjoy an unsuspecting immortality as elements of his composition.

He has a slightly more elaborate relationship with his mistress and model, an unschooled but vivacious young lady who occasionally fantasizes about being in the Folies but more often dreams of really, truly, attracting her lovers attention. And her name -- emblematic of all the atoms that make up the finished painting -- is Dot.

Tiring of the relationship (Thats right, George, hide behind your painting -- "I'm not hiding behind my painting, I'm hiding in it.") Dot, at the end of Act One, ups and emigrates to America. She has married a local baker but is carrying Georges child.

Act Two moves us on to contemporary New York; the child is now a 95-year-old woman, and her grandson, also called George, is himself an artist, presenting mechanized light-shows called chromolumes. He himself, enjoying a precarious success on the cocktail-chatter circuit, might be called a chromoluminary; and he doesnt like it much.

His grandmother sings from her wheelchair a wry, meditative, gently passionate song called Children and Art, whose burden is that those two things are all any of us can hope to leave behind us. This debatable thesis (which seems unnecessarily hard on childless non- artists) ties together, by main force, the show's principal preoccupations; fortunately it's a very good song.

Its balanced by another, Lesson #8, in which George hesitantly seeks and finds meaning in the simple questions posed in his great- grandmothers teach-yourself-grammar book. He makes a pilgrimage to his namesake's old Parisian painting-ground and there encounters the ghost of Dot.

She sings at him an anthem called Move On that alternates Rodgers- and-Hammerstein uplift with shrewd observation. (Stop worrying if your vision/Is new/Let others make that decision/They usually do.)

The show, plainly, is more about art than is, say, the play Art. When it deals with the Plight of the Artist -- as in George the Second's sparring with the Manhattan culture-vultures -- it becomes brittle and self-pitying. When it concentrates on the process of creating art -- as in George the Firsts driven, resigned song about staying home and finishing the hat -- it is illuminating and exciting.

But its real theme, admittedly closely linked, is time, or its redemption: George Is mother laments the passing of the park she used to know even while her son is painting it, and by the time George II arrives it's almost gone. The painting is all we have to remind us, and that of course is one man's manipulative interpretation.

The first-act finale, echoed at the end, is a soaring chorale during which the artist shifts the other characters around to fit his vision. Its moving and fulfilling and also somewhat unsettling.

I have always found this one of the least approachable Sondheim shows. It contains some of his loveliest and (as befits the subject) most shimmering music, and some of his most eloquent lyrics.

Lapines book has some suggestive scenes and some sharp lines. (I especially relish the comment of George's technical assistant who is leaving the art-world to go back to NASA because "there's too much pressure in this line of work.") But the action is fragmentary and the characters, apart from George and Dot and their later reincarnations, are lay-figures; and though this may be inherent in the conception its still frustrating.

Seeing it, though, for the first time since the original production, I found it unexpectedly coherent. The Toronto production combines professionals from Equity Showcase and students from George Brown Theatre School, and the lead actors alternate; I saw a student George and a professional Dot.

There are obvious limitations; I missed the sumptuous, tantalizing greenery of the original staging. (It got a Tony for design though Seurat himself, a vital collaborator, wasnt cited.) There are also gains. Bernadette Peters' Broadway Dot will never be equalled, but maybe she unbalanced the show; one missed her cruelly when she was off and resented that nobody else was as lively as she was.

Mi-Anne Dionisio (who was Toronto's Miss Saigon and Maria in Stratfords West Side Story) doesnt have much sparkle but she is intelligent and sings beautifully. Ken McClure as George is far more sympathetic than Mandy Patinkin's prototype, though his singing- voice is very similar; he is heavy-set and believably insecure without being a nervous wreck, and he centres the show.

The supporting professionals -- Shawn Wright as a rival artist, Jayne Lewis as his wife, Mary Pitt as the mother -- all do well; and the student talents seem ideally suited to the cut-out roles they're required to play. They seize with especial glee on the museum parasites who are skewered (unfortunately without having first been created) in a song too-cleverly titled The State of the Art.

Sue Miner's production is excellent, especially in its intricate movement. The musicians, under John Tute, play tautly and splendidly though they sometimes -- in an unamplified and acoustically unfriendly house -- drown the singers. But the dots get connected.

Black & White Photo: Connecting the dots: Shawn Wright, Jayne Lewis, Andrea Tutt and Ken McClure ;

THE OVERCOAT

Canadian Stage Company

Breezing in wordlessly but not silently from Vancouver, The Overcoat is in a category of its own. It isn't classical mime, since it's done to a full musical score, and it isn't ballet, since it's moved rather than danced.

Whatever it is, it's magical.

It takes its title and its nourishing idea from the appropriately hard-wearing story by Nikolai Gogol, which it moves forward, by about a hundred years, and also westward.

We are now in the 1920s in some unspecified, probably Central European, city in which people move about en masse like demented insects. In fact we are in the landscape of Franz Kafka who, roughly speaking, was Gogol without the laughs. Gogol took aim at a specific Tsarist bureaucracy; Kafka had it in for the capitalists as well as for the bureaucrats of his own time, but he seemed to regard oppression as a fact of life, hard-wired into the human condition. The Overcoat, as staged here, is a graphic illustration of the proverb about clothes making the man, showing that they can unmake him as well.

Our protagonist is a poorly-dressed clerk, that eternal victim- figure of bourgeois culture. Every day he gets up from what looks like a very hard and unwelcoming bed, avoids his predatory landlady (who seems to be demanding either his body or his rent), and commutes to his work-station, over which hang a couple of huge downward-pointing pens. His colleagues mock him, throwing his shabby coat on the ground (repeatedly) and him with it. Superiors either ignore or encourage the persecution. Desirable female workers troop by, carrying bundles of papers and with their noses in the air.

As a Gogol hero, the worm turns. As a Kafka hero, he doesn't have a prayer.

Tired of living off the peg, he gets a new overcoat made to order: a gorgeous purple creation with a collar of bristling ginger fur. His life changes; everybody swoons. Even his boss -- distinguished by an ample watch-chain and a head that's mostly skull -- takes notice; so does his boss's sycophantic brown-jacketed aide; so, even, do the women. He steps out into high society. Eventually, and predictably, he falls among good-time girls, sailors, and he loses it: loses the coat, loses everything. Police are aggressively unhelpful. He ends up in a mental hospital where, eased into a strait-jacket, he emits a beatific smile; it's a perfect fit.

Directed by Morris Panych and Wendy Gorling with great imagination, unflagging speed and perfect precision, the show unfolds to music by Shostakovich: music whose first bars plant a happy grin on the audience's face that subsequent developmentrs freeze into a horrified stare. It takes time; the full brutality of both the musical and visual score only become apparent when the victim visits the cops. Before that, our pleasure in the physical grace displayed takes precedence over any horror at what it's actually depicting.

The magic coat is created by five men working maniacally away at five sewing-machines, while a great wheel turns behind them. Maybe they're in a symbolic sweat-shop, but if that's what it takes, that's what it takes. Ken MacDonald's set is a double tier of square compartments each of which, craftily lit by Alan Brodie, can open up to reveal a new vista, threatening or seductive or both. A flawless, inventive company of 22 (surely the biggest ever seen on any of Canadian Stage's stages, and though some of them are students you wouldn't know it, except perhaps by their dedication) is headed by Peter Anderson who is billed as "The Man" and is indeed somewhat anonymous, but who is superbly skilled and resists any temptation to play cute.

I am sufficiently non non-verbal to register a few objections. Some of the ideas and the imagery here are familiar. How often have we seen ballets of automaton commuters strap-hanging their way towards another day of anonymity? The workplace routines recall the Bob Fosse of How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying with added misanthropy. (On the other hand, this could be the great Canadian musical minus songs.) If Anderson sometimes resembles the Chaplin of Modern Times, he's a Chaplin without the saving grace of a Paulette Goddard. The scales are weighted against him from the start, and they never look like shifting. Like most expressionist nightmares, this one is too wrapped up in itself to resonate much outside. I think I felt more threatened by the somewhat similar episode of The Simpsons in which Homer got respect when he grew some hair and lost it when he lost it. But the captivating confidence of the whole thing is irresistible, and, with no language barriers to crash, there seems no reason for it not to conquer the world.

THE MOTHER'S SAINT

Edward Roy's new play is about the abuse of children in Catholic institutions in Quebec 60 years ago, and about the effects on those children's own children. The author's other works include The Other Side of the Closet, seen last year at the Toronto Young People's Theatre, which was about growing up gay in contemporary Canada.

This form of dramaturgy -- selecting an issue and then trying to find a story and characters to illustrate it -- may be a legitimate approach when writing for children, though I have my doubts; its appearance on the main stage of a supposedly adult house is a reminder of how much growing up our theatre still has to do.

The Mother's Saint is actually much inferior to The Other Side of the Closet,which was at least honestly didactic and clear in its objectives. It was also, of course, short. The new play is long, chronologically complicated and confusing.

It kicks off during the 1998 Montreal ice storm; a young Torontonian named Robert is discovered in an otherwise deserted house, unconscious and in the company of a dead body. Revived and taken into custody, he is questioned by a police inspector who has reason to believe that a drug-related murder has taken place.

It transpires that the suspect has come to town to seek information about his late mother, whose erratic behaviour as an adult can be traced to her nightmarish experiences as a child. She had been abandoned to an orphanage run by an order of nuns; their regime, already oppressive, was much worsened when the province, in order to secure increased federal funding, encouraged the orphanages to reconstitute themselves as mental hospitals.

Since Robert's mother had been seeing unauthorized visions of what she called "the Lady" -- hence the play's title -- she was a sitting duck. (She was one of the "Duplessis orphans," named for Maurice Duplessis, Quebec's premier at the time; there were thousands of them.)

As Robert is interrogated, the earlier stages of his quest are played out in flashback; it is hard to tell which of these episodes are part of his statement to the inspector and which are stopping- places for his own train of thought. Interspersed with these, but operating on an entirely different convention, is another set of flashbacks showing the mother as a child, with the sisters of no mercy.

The author, who is also the director, throws in a few other devices. There is an introductory film sequence showing Montreal iced up; though if there is meant to be anything symbolic about the weather, it doesn't register. It doesn't even contribute atmosphere; we just forget about it. There are also a couple of cabaret turns by an audience-baiting drag queen. One of these routines ends the play, with breathtaking feebleness.

The drag artist's relevance to the action is that he is the lover of the guy in whose house the protagonist is discovered. Robert's reason for being there in the first place -- he certainly hadn't been invited -- is what the play slowly reveals; he says near the beginning that he feels like he's in a jigsaw puzzle, and so do we. Most of the pieces do fit in the end: all, in fact, except the hero's recurring encounters with the child who would grow up to be his mother, which must be hallucinations but are staged with the same prosaic dullness as everything else.

With its long succession of short scenes, the play is yet another theatre piece to play like a hack TV script minus the hardware; the technical problems it presents are insoluble, or at any rate unsolved.

It's especially hard on the actor playing the cop, who is constantly left on the edge of the stage, staring fixedly at scenes that don't involve him and trying to look as if he belonged. It's also hard on the audience. Our theatres seem to think that we will actually enjoy watching an endless series of furniture-removals carried out in a dingy half-light. (At one especially hilarious moment a bath, which has done double duty in two separate locations, is found to be no longer necessary and is unceremoniously pushed through a trick wall by one of the nuns. Presumably this is a standard architectural feature in convents, installed in case of Protestant persecution.)

The performances vary in skill; 13-year-old Tess Benger comes out in first place, with Steve Cumyn as Robert and Terrence Bryant as his unwilling host tying for second. But none of them seems very convincing, or indeed very convinced. They can't even get up and walk round a room, or perch on the edge of a table, as if they believed in it. (Actually I don't think I've ever seen a play in which an actor did perch believably on the edge of a table; it's one of those supposedly casual actions that always looks contrived.)

All of them are imprisoned by colourless dialogue that is mainly exposition, and by characters who are cardboard; nor does it help that half of them are playing two roles apiece. There seems no reason for either the drag or the drugs, except that the latter is a laborious device for getting the hero into a situation where he will be forced to talk.

He is also granted a girlfriend. Both the gay and the straight romances in the play have their problems, the latter especially. It's all about lack of commitment, and that kind of thing; these are the kind of relationships that consist mainly of talking about the relationships.

The point, presumably, is that sins committed against the parents will be visited upon the children and probably beyond; but it isn't dramatized. (The play is apparently autobiographical, but so what?)

Meanwhile, the really interesting point goes missing. Just what happened all those years ago when the orphanages sold their souls to become the wrong kind of asylum? How did the people most involved react? The moment is passed over in a bald exchange between a comparatively nice young nun who has qualms and a nasty old one who doesn't. If you're going to deal with issues, deal.

THE MEMORY OF WATER

Winter Garden Theatre

Shelagh Stephenson's The Memory of Water comes bearing garlands. It was a success at Torontos Tarragon Theatre a couple of years ago and is now being restaged commercially with the same director and blue-chip cast. In its native England it has just won the Olivier Award for best comedy of last year. It was its authors first play (there has been another since and a third is pending) and it is a recognizably promising and intermittently accomplished piece of work. It holds attention throughout.

But after all the fanfare it appears overblown, not especially funny, and essentially false.

It's another play about three sisters, and they break down -- in order of seniority and in strict accordance with tradition -- into a frayed and responsible one, a bitter and sophisticated one, and a romantic and loopy one. Contemporary Britain being smaller and somewhat more travel-friendly than, say, Chekhov's Russia, the two younger siblings have the resources to get out of their native small town and go to Moscow, or in this case, of course, London.

Mary, the middle sister, has a successful life there as a doctor, and also a long relationship with a married male colleague. Catherine, the youngest, has gone further, cutting a wide and increasingly unsatisfying swath through the continent of Europe. Puzzled by the frequency with which she has been dumped she exclaims, to the accompaniment of a massed raising of eyebrows, that she must be able to relate to men because she has slept with 78 of them.

That leaves the oldest, Teresa, and being left is something about which Teresa frequently complains. She has stayed home to run a health-food business (or, as she vociferously insists, a dietary supplement business) and to look after their widowed mother, who was stricken with Alzheimers and who has just died when the play begins.

So everybody is home for the funeral, and for the consequent bouts of reminiscence and recrimination. We are in Alan Ayckbourn territory; literally, since the play takes place in Ayckbourns own rain-swept high-altitude corner of the north-east English coast. It also shares his pained but amused concern with the middle-aged middle class, urban but not metropolitan, financially all right but emotionally disconsolate. What it lacks is his instinct for the humour of character and situation -- a humour that lies beyond and beneath single lines -- and for a governing and illuminating technical device.

As free-standing characters, the members of the sisterhood are fully drawn, or certainly well enough to provide chewable roles for actresses. In Jackie Maxwell's production, Martha Burns stands out as Mary, the career woman who longs for a child (it doesn't play as cornily as it sounds) and can get neither that nor any other kind of commitment from her lover. The play takes place in the late mothers bedroom, and the sight of Burns sitting on that bed in the later scenes -- smart, cropped, and devastated -- is the evenings most abiding image.

Vegetarian Teresa, who lives what she sells, is a tightly reined pull-yourself-together-for-God's-sake kind of woman until she takes a drink and lets everything hang out, which she does at great length. Nancy Palk is finely angular when she's sober and rather forced when shes drunk, but then so is the writing.

Kristen Johnson, so good last year as the placid Stella of A Streetcar Named Desire, goes indulgently wild as Catherine, who waits in hysterical agony for a call from her flame in Spain, and whom she plays as an escapee from Absolutely Fabulous. (There are times when the play seems to need the added dimension of a laugh track.)

The play is written, naturally, from the womens point of view, but the two men on hand are shrewdly and not unsympathetically depicted; both have arrived cold, wet and weary, and both are inclined to keep as clear as possible of the emotional whirlpool.

Peter Cockett is blandly believable as the gentleman doctor, pointedly referred to by Mary's sisters as the married boyfriend. Randy Hughson, especially good, is Teresa's husband and business partner, Irish by the sound of him, and mortally sick -- as he tells her in the plays most resonant line -- of travelling abroad to sell stuff he doesnt believe in to people who don't want it.

There is a sixth character, the mother: Dead and not only not forgotten but manifesting herself, though only to Mary, which seems unfair to the others and frustrating to the audience. The whole play hinges on, or at least keeps referring to, the baleful and continuing influence of one generation on the next, but it's never suggested that it is any more important for Mary than for her sisters, nor does the idea get any further than a generalized restatement of a familiar theme about mothers and daughters.

It connects, just about, with an abrupt revelation about a traumatizing episode from Marys youth, but thats a melodramatic device that her character could do perfectly well without. The deceased is described as flighty and repressive, but that's only what we're told; when she materializes, Corrine Kozlo can't provide her with much more than a dead-on North country accent.

Her daughters dress unpersuasively up in her clothes for a costume parade at the end of Act One, and her coffin dominates the stage during much of Act Two, and these are plainly meant to be striking images, but they are just effortful. So the play ends up both structurally and psychologically unsound.

There is also the question of tone. That "best comedy" award is probably misleading; the barriers between comedy and drama fell down long ago, and best comedy is now usually a consolation prize for something that didn't get best play. This one is plainly not trying to be a laugh riot. We know at the end, as in much diluted Chekhov, that the characters are going to survive, and we also know that they are going to go on being unhappy.

But a lot of i is designed as barbed banter; someone is arbitrarily described as having "an ego the size of Asia Minor," and that kind of one-liner -- not specific enough to be witty, too calculated to be natural -- is typical. There is a lot of this going around, and I have certainly heard worse. But I expected better.

BOYS

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, Toronto

Theatre Direct, the young people's theatre company who last year gave us the excellent Waiting for Lewis, are now presenting Buncha' Young Artists Having Their Say: a rather self-conscious label for a short, rotating festival more soberly announced as "four plays by young writers speaking to young adults." If the first one is any guide, they will be speaking to others as well.

Boys is a one-person play for three voices, or a three-character play for one actor. Its author and performer is Paul Dunn, who was seen last season at Stratford as the youngest of the four faces of Glenn Gould. One of his aims here seems to be to explore the pressures exerted on males of his own generation as they try to discover what it is to be a man. Another is to provide himself with a whacking good acting vehicle. He succeeds on both counts.

There are three boys in Boys: Tambourine Boy, Ham and Cheese Boy and Army Slut Boy. Tambourine Boy, whose friends, if he had any, would call him Jeff, is a busker with a very individual shtick; he hops around while banging out rhythms on a tambourine, in time to a soundtrack of tunes playing in his own head. The tunes are all by Abba and he describes them, with approval, as the work of Satan: his bulwark against a universe that otherwise seems to have rejected him. He's even convinced that one member of the group is his mother. (We in the audience do get to hear snatches of the music. They confirmed me in my long-held detestation of Abba and all their works, though I think I would stop short of calling them Satanic. Further thoughts on this subject had better await the coming of Mamma Mia.)

Ham and Cheese Boy, whose given name is Mike, works on an assembly line slapping together the sandwiches that his title suggests. His girlfriend resents the dead-endedness of his job and ditches him; he occupies himself piecing together a large jigsaw puzzle and deeply resents it if any of his friends butt in. He would rather get it wrong without their help than right with it. Finally there is Army Slut Boy, a.k.a Andy, a student whose campus psychiatrist wants him first to acknowledge his homosexuality, and second to go out and get laid. He finds love at a school dance, an experience he memorably recalls as being "finally in on what the rest of the world has been doing": a description that crosses all sexual boundaries. The object of his affection is about to enlist, and while Andy maintains that it's the guy himself to whom he is attracted, his shrink is pretty sure that it's the dog-tags; Andy, she insists, has a military fetish. It turns out to be a bit of both.

The play is composed of alternating monologues, the author-actor stepping nimbly, under Rosemary Rowe's firm direction, from one character to another with a change of sweater, apron or spectacles. For Andy's consultations with his lady-doctor (a sort of prose rerun of Gee Officer Krupke) he effects instant changes of identity by sliding his glasses up and down his nose. The boys themselves collide occasionally. Ham and Cheese, irritated by Tambourine's routine, insults and is mildly assaulted by him. Army Slut, feeling euphoric, gives Tambourine a large tip, which he spends on one of Ham and Cheese's ex-sandwiches. (Mike has just been fired, and there's no filling.) Ham and Cheese and Army Slut both turn up, though for different reasons, at a military recruitment centre, this being the only point at which the parallel impersonations become momentarily confusing.

There is a dummy soldier overpeering the action, and we heard a recorded announcement recommending the army as the career-solution for the modern young man ("and," it says as a hasty afterthought, "woman"). This connects with what Mike and Jeff are going through but it doesn't seem to have much to do with Andy. Indeed the three characters don't cross-refer as illuminatingly as the author obviously hopes. Jeff, with his musical and maternal obsessions, is entertainingly established at the start, but can't do much more than repeat them afterwards. Mike and Andy have stronger stories to tell, though Andy's is developed in far more detail. In addition, the play seems unsure how and when to end. There's no great statement here about modern youth, but the script is bursting with sympathetic humour, with just enough mordant implications to keep us feeling intellectually respectable. Dunn acts it marvellously; he is unpatronizingly witty, vulnerable without being anybody's puppy dog, and all-round appealing. His technique and concentration are awesome; each of the myriad opportunities he has set up for himself is also a potential trap, but he doesn't put a foot or an inflection wrong. This is the best performance -- or conceivably three of the best performances -- currently on offer in Toronto. It is also that great rarity: a solo show that keeps its audience awake.

Black & White Photo: David Hawe / Paul Dunn, the author and solo performer in Boys. His script is bursting with sympathetic humour. ;

ENIGMA VARIATIONS

Royal Alexandra

A now deceased English character actor once remarked of an especially portentous play in which he had been inveigled into appearing that "it all took place in Scandinavia, and rightly." Enigma Variations is not portentous; though it has some weighty themes, it handles them with a very light touch. It was written by a Frenchman, Eric-Emmanuel Schmitt, but takes place in Scandinavia -- on a remote island, in fact, off the Norwegian coast -- and this seems to suit it.

It especially suits the more assertive of the two characters, a Nobel Prize-winning novelist whom the awards committee must have welcomed as one of their own. The role is played by Donald Sutherland who, returning to the stage after an absence of 20 years, looks as if he has never been away.

He also looks, as he often has in movies, impeccably Nordic: tall, gaunt, and disconcertingly genial. It's disconcerting because the geniality on this occasion is that of egomania. Sutherland's performance describes a great arc of self-absorption, one that begins in vociferous scorn for the idea of conventionally tender feelings and ends by hugging them to his own chest.

He is moving here, partly because he is playing someone who has denied the possibility of being moved.

The one quality that you don't necessarily expect of film stars, he possesses in abundance: he can shape and sustain long speeches. There are moments when he seems like credible casting for King Lear.

Sutherland's novelist, who bears the uncommon name of Abel Znorko, has written a long and successful series of chilly philosophical tales but has scored his greatest hit with a piece of outright romance: a book that consists of an exchange of letters between two lovers who choose to live apart rather than risk having their passion sullied by routine. Everyone wonders what has caused this change, whether the book is autobiographical, and if so who the woman might be.

Abel, whose imposing island retreat is both the reward of his fame and the self-chosen symbol of his aloofness, has refused all requests for interviews, but he does give in to one. It comes from Erik Larsen, who claims to feel a deep connection to Abel's work and wants to write him up for a small-town newspaper -- though it turns out that the place in question is not just any small town.

Erik is a physically small man, nervous but pertinacious and with his own agenda. John Rubinstein plays him almost to perfection; the flaws are a few self-indulgent moments when he lingers too calculatingly on some speeches about the pains, pleasures and rewards of everyday love.

Abel, apparently, can tell that Erik is married just by looking at him. Abel believes in love as sex, which doesn't last except in memory; Erik believes in love as friendship, which endures almost by definition. In real life, of course, the two conceptions are not that starkly opposed; most people get a bit of both. But this is a stripped-down kind of play, and the convention works perfectly well.

Abel scoffs at Erik's literal-minded interpretation of his novel, but it turns out that Erik is right and that the book is a transcript of Abel's own experience. (As, more than critical theory would like to admit, works of fiction very often are.) And that is about as much of the action as I feel comfortable disclosing, and maybe more than I should.

Part of the play's fascination is that each of the two participants is playing a cat-and-mouse game, though Abel, accustomed to domination, is the more relishingly upfront about it.

The story is told through a series of surprises; there are four major revelations, two of them coming so close together that they seem like one. The first, and the most crucial, can be seen coming a long way off and is the more satisfying and persuasive because of it; it feels inevitable. The last is thoroughly disorienting; it means rethinking everything that has happened so far, and at the time I resented it. Now I think it makes sense.

This isn't a play that one would necessarily want to see a second time (except perhaps for the pleasure of comparing performances), not so much because it proceeds by shock effects (including, come to think of it, Sutherland's shock of white hair) as because everything in it is very precisely laid out.

The characters know what they think and feel, and they tell us; and when they are forced to change their minds or their hearts, they are very lucid about that, too. So it's all on the surface, which is not the same as being, in any derogatory sense, superficial. It is, in the French tradition, very elegant and economical, and the structural pleasure it provides is acute. (Abel has a gun, and the author has taken to heart Chekhov's admonition that you don't bring one of those on stage unless you mean to use it; it's used here as recurring dramatic punctuation, and it means something different each time.)

The things it says about love -- and, to a lesser extent, creativity -- are not new, but they are intelligent and felt, and often wittily expressed; the translation, acknowledged in the program in surprisingly small print, is by Roeg Sutherland, the star's son.

The only thing I don't like about the play is its title. It refers to the Elgar composition (of which we hear occasional snatches) and is used as a fancy cultural metaphor for the many- faceted unknowability of a woman. This is a subject that the two men establish perfectly well when they talk about her.

Anthony Page's direction is both intense and relaxed, and the set, by the celebrated Ming Cho Lee, contributes a glorious sense of space and elevation. The production is bound for Broadway, where it should be an enormous success and -- what is not always the case -- a deserving one.

KARMA; POP SONG; VICIOUS LITTLE BOYZ IN THE RAIN

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, Toronto

Theatre Direct's Buncha Young Artists Having Their Say are continuing to have it, in varying formats and with varying results.

One play, Karma, by Ivana Shein, seems something of a makeweight. Its a duologue between a respectable managerial gentleman and the bike-courier with whom he claims to be in love. The play actually begins in the lobby with the two actors (Murray Farrow and Joris Jarsky) trying to pretend that they are members of the audience, the younger one not used to going to the theatre and the older one trying to reassure him. It doesn't work. Placed among us like that, they are very plainly actors, their voices too well projected, their sentences too well formed. Not even a graphic throwing-up sequence convinced us they were real.

Once in their natural habitat -- on stage, playing scenes -- they were far more convincing, but by then it was too late. Nor did their author give them, even then, anything very interesting to say or do; it was as if putting two people on a stage and having them spend a certain amount of time discussing an unestablished relationship was enough in itself. The school parties in the audience were not, as far as I could tell, buying it.

They reacted with warm recognition, though, to Pop Song, which immediately followed it.

Their elders, especially if they were parents, probably watched in frozen horror. Sean Reycraft's play is another duologue, far more solidly constructed and based on the well-publicized news story of a year or so back about the Toronto girl who gave birth at a school dance, disposed of the baby in the garbage, went back to the floor, and kept on rocking.

The play imagines a relationship that might have led up to this incident; it isnt brutal but it is, to anyone outside the culture, unnervingly casual. We follow the characters through a school year, from one half-hearted institutional hop to another. (Now we know whats wrong with the educational system. There are too many dances.) Each scene, as per the title, is played out to the accompaniment of a different song, and they probably have more thematic relevance than I was able to distinguish.

Between scenes, we hear each upcoming function announced, and the come-ons, as increasingly desperate organizers try to appeal to an increasingly apathetic student body, can be moderately hilarious. The main dialogue (apart from an unfortunate matched pair of flowery voice-overs) is blankly functional, but that presumably is the point. These are traditional teenage rituals -- the girl who wants to dance, the boy who would rather eat chips, the criss-crossing patterns of physical and emotional need -- played out in a new and more dangerous context; and it's the context that creates the effect. Kimwun Perehinec and Matthew MacFadzean make a very convincing couple; he in particular is so real that one wonders if he is just playing himself.

The remaining play, Vicious Little Boyz in the Rain, proves that he isn't; or at least that if he is, he can do very different things as well. He appears in this as a teenage gang-leader called Freak: a preening, swaggering, homoerotic and extremely articulate mixture of Peter Pan, Charles Manson, and the choirboy bully of Lord of the Flies.

The play begins with him and his three followers swarming and presumably killing a middle-aged man with a briefcase (Murray Farrow reprising his character from Karma in extreme straits). In Andrey Tarasiuks production, this comes over as the archetypal scene of urban menace. Tarasiuk runs Theatre Direct and has established standards of presentation as high as any in the city. This though is the first play I have seen that he has directed himself, and its a tour de force.

Marshalling five actors on a sand-strewn stage he confronts us with one bold image after another, while securing a flawless level of commitment from his cast. If they believe this strongly in Gil Garratt's play, then there must be something to it. So, as it turns out, there is; but it can be tough sledding getting there. Much of the writing is in a vein of heavily abstruse lyricism; you often yearn for a few declarative sentences that would explain just what is going on. (You do eventually get them, but rather late).

MacFadzean's Freak presides over a trio of Lost Boys -- there is an explicit reference to never wanting to grow up -- who are either riding a wave of destruction or, more probably, have unleashed it themselves; it is, on a frightening scale, the revenge of the neglected and abused. The gang are trying to fight their way to a magical city; one of their number, Buzz (played by Paul Dunn, whose solo play Boys -- yes, with an s, -- kicked off this season in high gear) was told about the place by his mother; he expects to find his lost dog and dead brother there.

When disillusion inevitably sets in, Stupid (Joris Jarsky) challenges Freak's leadership, with distressing results; either Stupid is living up to his name or he's transcending it. The remaining lost boy, Rain (Kimwun Perehinec), so named because of an affinity to wet weather of which there seems to be a lot, may actually be a Lost Girl; I blush to admit it but Im not sure whether we have here a female performer playing a male role or a female performer playing a female whos playing a male role, like the tomboyish Anybodys in West Side Story. (This is the second play in the season to recall that musical, especially its kaleidoscopic Officer Krupke number, and it does so more strongly than the first.) Rain is sent on a mission in which he/she finds either straight or lesbian love, which has to be abandoned on account of Freak's stern injunction: No Wendies. (I don't think its just that he prefers Big Macs.)

Anyway, when everything explodes, the threads come satisfyingly together, although Stupids repeated admonition -- "Look what we've become" -- seems, in the blood-soaked circumstances, somewhat obvious. The underlying truth seems to be that if you demonize people they may indeed become the demons you fear, but they won't necessarily be happy about it. The cast ride the lyric-heavy dialogue with impressive ease; MacFadzean who seems to be playing with a British accent, perhaps in homage to Barrie, exerts a scary command on eye and ear. Its a demanding play, and Im not sure that all its demands are justified, but like all Theatre Direct's work that I have seen, it displays a heartening trust in both itself and its audience.

THE WHIRLPOOL

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

The set is a raised disc, green under the lights, with a line of plastic bags filled with water hanging down below. An additional supply of pendent bags hangs from an array of scaffolding behind; a construction that also supports some of the stage lamps and at times the actors. Sounds of plashing water fill the air.

It isn't especially redolent of Niagara, which is where the action is set, but it certainly seems marine. A sign in the lobby warns that there will be fog, but like so many weather forecasts this turns out to be a false alarm. Unless it refers to the writing and presentation which, if not quite foggy, are certainly misty.

Brian Quirts play is based on a novel by Jane Urquhart that I havent read. It is 1889 and David, a historian with strong nationalist feelings, has come to town to lecture; his theme is how what were apparently Canadian military defeats can be seen as victories.

With him, or much of the time at a discreet distance from him, is his wife, Fleda, who likes to spend her time reading poetry. She has a taste for the romantic verse of Robert Browning, but her husband is trying to wean her on to the more moralistic offerings of Coventry Patmore. He has presented her with a copy of Patmore's chef- d'oeuvre The Angel in the House, and he has promised to build her a house so that she can settle down to being the angel in it.

Soon she gets to meet a real, live and personably young poet whose name is Patrick and who comes into their orbit when he attends one of Davids talks. He has a dangerous fascination with whirlpools, especially the one in the Niagara River. Fledas thing is forests. Her husband's is Laura Secord; he tells Patrick of a dream in which his wife appeared to him in Laura's costume, bidding him remember her. (As Patrick acutely puts it, he remembers being told to remember.)

Meanwhile, Maud, a lady in the local undertaking business, is fixated on the names, histories and personal effects of those unfortunates who have come to watery ends nearby. This leaves her little time for her five-year-old son (played by a large grown-up actor), who has trouble speaking, or at least in arranging words in any meaningful order. Some encounters with Patrick greatly improve his fluency, though his mother seems less delighted by this than you might expect.

Things happen, but that doesnt in itself make a dramatic action. The characters spend their time mentally stalking one another (physically too, on occasion) and to convey this, Quirt, who directs his own adaptation, has enlisted the help of a choreographer, Julia Sasso. She gets the actors weaving around one another, dodging and avoiding, looking but apparently not seeing.

Sometimes they do indeed seem like swimmers caught in a whirlpool. At others they are more like wound-up automata, dodgem cars turned loose on a chessboard. This happens especially when Fleda, Patrick and David play a game of cards, the unacknowledged passions of their relationship simmering beneath. As they play their hands, the two men aggressively advance or smoulderingly retreat, suggesting nothing so much as the battle of the Red and White Knights in Through the Looking Glass.

At least this seems to be intentionally funny; much of the time this modified ballet just seems mildly, and not very communicatively, grotesque. The actors simply dont have the grace or the skills, though they certainly go through the exercises with unfaltering dedication. The only one, though, who can make them work for him is Andrew Massingham, who, playing the five-year-old, is in a strange place to start with.

I am willing to believe that the original material is neither as attenuated nor as pretentious as it appears here. But on stage the narrative doesn't cohere and the themes don't cross-illuminate.

There are some good evocative monologues, infused with a downbeat wit; Tracey Ferencz as Fleda, a woman half-protestingly trapped, does especially well by hers. Outside them, she seems involved in a husband-wife-poet triangle out of Shaws Candida, which the fragmentary dialogue scenes both underwrite and overvalue.

Jordan Pettle plays Patrick, Christine Brubaker does the funerary lady, and David is Martin Julien, who came into the show at short notice and has mastered a complicated script and movement-score with, on the first night, no apparent signs of strain.

His characters patriotic preoccupations seem to have no effect on anyone else, other than to provide them with a source of irritated amusement. (He goes around asking people if they dream Canadian dreams.) It's not his fault, or those of his authors, that commercial interests have turned the name of Laura Secord into an automatic source of giggles, but the fact remains. The Canadian content, though, does serve to infuse the audience with a certain amount of guilt when it feels bored or baffled.

Quirt's previous play was seen at the Passe Muraille, and he is resident dramaturge at the Factory; now here he is writing and directing at the Tarragon. Good for him that he gets around, but Toronto's leading small theatres do seem, to put it politely, close- knit. Maybe this is why much of the time they all seem to be presenting the same play.

2000-03-06-you-can-teach-young-dogs-new-:
"Young actors," says Bill Glassco over lunch in a Montreal bistro, "generally become lazy and cynical very fast." He's talking about actors in the immediate post-graduate stage; those in the disillusioning years that generally follow their emergence from drama school.

He himself has taught for some years now at the National Drama School in Montreal, and like most teachers in such a position he has been impressed by the dedication and enthusiasm of his students. He has then, all too often, watched it fritter away. "I want," he says, "to harness that idealism while it's still there."

The result has been his formation of the Montreal Young Company, made up of 12 players with no more than five years of professional experience apiece, eight of them Glassco's former students. The company has just concluded its first season of two plays in repertoire, and the results have been more than promising. Both the plays presented were English: Shakespeare's Measure for Measure; and The Possibilities, by the contemporary British playwright Howard Barker.

All the actors in the company were anglophones, which in Montreal puts them in an artistically beleaguered position. In some ways it's fitting that Canada's top theatre school should be in Montreal; French-Canadian theatre is legendarily rich. But the NDS attracts students from all over the country, and half of them are likely to emerge from it feeling disenfranchised. Where, I asked Glassco, do English-speaking graduates -- including those who've grown up in the city -- go to work?

He shrugged, gently (he's a gentle man): "Most of them," he said, "end up going to Toronto." There is regular English theatre in Montreal: there's the Centaur, of which Glassco speaks with guarded respect, and there's the Saidye Bronfman Centre for the Arts, which is where the Young Company staged its first season. (Arriving at the Bronfman after a day spent mooching around the city, and being greeted at the box-office in English, was a considerable culture shock.) All the same, older English actors could probably use a lifeline as well, and I asked Glassco why, in light of this, he was keeping the accent so firmly on youth.

He gave some of the expected replies: "Young actors inspire me ... It's easier to gain their trust and you don't have a lot of bad habits to break down."

But he also has some other, longer-term considerations in mind: "If the young actors benefit from this work, they should be our leading actors when they're in their 40s." He cites the example of Soulpepper, most of whose leading spirits first came together as members of Robin Phillips' Young Company at Stratford some 15 years ago.

Glassco himself is a Quebec native, but one who has spent most of his career in Toronto, as a founder member of the city's small- theatre movement. He founded Tarragon, and was one of the architects of what is now the Canadian Stage Company. When he left the CSC he felt the time had come to return to Quebec; at the moment, he officially lives in Quebec City, though he's in the process of pulling up sticks and finding a home in Montreal.

At 64 he is obviously his young company's patriarch; the rest of his staff is as youthful as his actors. This includes his associate director, Chris Abraham, 25 and already a recognized name on the alternative theatre circuit. They directed a play apiece; appropriately Glassco took the old play and Abraham the new one.

The Possibilities isn't that new; Barker wrote it about a dozen years ago. He's a playwright about whom I have very mixed feelings, and The Possibilities did nothing to resolve them. Indeed, since it consists of 10 independent sketches it can accommodate some various reactions in itself. Each of the playlets has a background set somewhere on a scale between crisis and cataclysm. Only one of the 10 -- involving a London vendor of forbidden books -- evokes a time or place that is the author's own.

This is probably to the good since, although Barker's plays are typically scathing in their attitude to contemporary society, they are seldom very precise in their depiction of it. Asked for more believable detail, the playwright and his adherents (who tend to be vociferous) are apt to inquire contemptuously "What do you want? Realism?" To which the answer, I'm afraid, is yes; if I'm being asked to take seriously the playwright's view of the world around us, I want some approximation to the ways in which people in that world actually behave.

Most of the time here, though, we are in fable-land; a world of stark situations and starker dialogue. One scene involves a Czar Alexander (which of the several, we are not told) on the eve of what will plainly be a bloody battle. Like Henry V before Agincourt he talks to a common soldier about their common humanity; he even gets the soldier to undress him, to demonstrate what a pathetically ordinary being he is. He then, presumably to reassure himself that he is after all the emperor, has the man taken away and flogged.

Often we are in some nameless village, typically in one that is about to be invaded and destroyed and whose inhabitants are pleading or planning for some means of relief and escape. One play gives us a gloss on the Biblical story of Judith, the Hebrew heroine who gave herself to her own people's invader Holofernes and then slew him. In the aftermath of the event, she sets about demolishing all her compatriots' comfortably patriotic assumptions.

The events are stark and so is the writing; writing in the wake of Brecht and Edward Bond, Barker has completely mastered the style of bleak elliptic irony, both capitalizing on the simplicities of folklore and exploding them. You sometimes get the feeling that he could do it in his sleep; that having settled on a style and a world- view, he is tearing off variously sized strips of it, and closing himself off to any alternatives. It is a very self-satisfied style. All the characters are in extreme situations, and the plays implicitly ask us to decide what would we do in their place. But the tone makes us disinclined to reach it.

One possible moral to be taken from the whole is that killing is justified so long as the victim is himself a killer and the avenger (or, I think Barker would say, the instrument of justice) is a woman. Anyway, it happens, over and over again, and it does seem a possible response to much recorded history, especially that of the last century.

Abraham staged it excellently, a series of spotlit vignettes against a dark and smoky background, and he caught the caustic, implacable style to perfection. All the actors got it, though some naturally communicated it better than others.

Among the best was Salvatore Migliore as Barker's most striking creation, a silkily-spoken travelling torturer (it's not apparently a job in which it's wise to stay in one place too long, and there's always a demand) who outwits some clumsy attempts at retribution. Mariusz Sibiga made a fine grotesque of the book-vendor, too paranoid to sell anything to anyone. Graeme Somerville, imperially insecure, and Paul Fauteux, justifiably watchful and worried, were excellently matched as Czar and victim. The simple characterizations and complex issues enabled an obviously thoughtful young company to play to its strengths.

They were also surprisingly well matched to Measure for Measure. There is only one character in this perplexing moral comedy, the "ancient lord" Escalus, who absolutely has to be old, and another, the Provost of the prison, who probably should be; the players here, Shawn Campbell and Eric Davis, had no trouble finding the necessary weight -- an old rep company characteristic that it's good to see re- instated.

Of the play's central trio, Isabella, the novice who refuses to surrender her chastity in return for her brother's life, is young by definition. Angelo, her puritanical would-be seducer, has in recent years been played so, and it makes sense; both he and Isabella are in part victims of their own too-confident inexperience.

The Duke, whose voluntary exile makes the city of Vienna the victim of Angelo's enthusiastic clean-up campaign, denies having "the aims and ends of burning youth," but that means he probably is young and that he, too, is trying to pretend to be above it. Playing the part this way enabled Graeme Somerville to play a plausible self- questioner who was also a reasonable romantic lead. And this is what the Duke is; at the end he get the girl. His being so may offend modern sensibilities, him being such an authority-figure and all (Howard Barker must itch to rewrite this play, or maybe he already has) but there it is.

Isabella doesn't explicitly say yes, and most directors make her silently reject him. But she doesn't say no, either, and Glassco's production, one of the most intelligent of this play that I've seen, showed that the happy ending is the right one; you can only refuse it by doing injustice both to the text and the audience.

It could have used a bit more setting up; Shakespeare is too busy with the plot to give the actors much help, and Somerville's Duke (a long but paradoxically under-written role) was sometimes more concerned with explaining the text than embodying it.

The Isabella-Angelo duets -- the most prolonged scenes of sexual exploration in Shakespeare -- were transfixing. Robin Wilcock played Angelo as a spoiled golden boy, one of nature's self-flagellators, "most ignorant," as Isabella tells him, "of what he's most assured." She, similarly brainy and similarly innocent, was played most forcefully, and finally most sympathetically, by Sarah Mennell. The comic scenes -- set in and around brothels, jails and police courts - - were excellent, with Salvatore Migliore's Pompey a superbly knowing androgynous pimp and Paul Fauteux' Elbow a wonderful local constable, blinkered and blathering.

All that was wrong was the constant use of music to underline tensions that were being created anyway. It blunted the drama and sometimes came near to killing the comedy. But the actors, plainly and hearteningly, are there and there must be more where that came from (which means all of Canada, though they have to audition in Montreal).

Glassco doesn't want to get bigger; to mount more plays per year or run his own space. He does want now to build some bridges with the Francophone theatre. If he can make this, and the rest of his scheme, work in future years, he will be doing us all a very good turn.

WELDON RISING

Alumnae Theatre, Toronto

Phyllis Nagy is an American playwright based in Britain, and this play, her first, received considerable acclaim when it was mounted at the Royal Court Theatre eight years ago. Either time has robbed it of its sheen, or its first Canadian production hasn't done it justice, or it wasn't that good to begin with. Or probably all three.

The play revolves around a murder. Natty Weldon, the protagonist, is that theatrically familiar oxymoron, a sad gay. He lives with his lover, Jimmy, on East 12th Street in New York, right in the meat- packing district. It is Jimmy who is murdered, knifed by a prowling young homophobe who has been taunting Natty. Natty flees the scene, leaving Jimmy to bleed to death. The killing is also witnessed by Jaye and Tilly, a lesbian couple in an upstairs apartment; they call the police but they don't go down to help. And crouching on the street corner, trying desperately and uncharacteristically to avoid being noticed, is a transvestite hooker named Marcel. All these onlookers, obviously, are afraid; and the point being made is that what they are really afraid of is their own sexuality.

There seems to be a rather basic confusion here. We know to our cost that witnesses to violence don't want to get involved. We know, for example, that when Matty Baranovski was killed in a Toronto park, there were people driving by who heard the sounds and didn't stop, and we know their inaction was due to a mixture of indifference and physical cowardice. We also fear that in similar circumstances we would behave equally shamefully. But however well or badly we acted would not, I think, have much to do with our sexual orientation or with how comfortable or otherwise we were with it. The play takes an untenable idea and works itself into a frenzy over it.

It makes slightly more sense with Natty himself than with the other characters. After all, it's his lover who was killed, and he ran away. What's more, Jimmy died trying to protect him; it was Natty who kept asking to be left alone; and in trying to face up to the killer and to set his own partner a good example, Jimmy ran right into the knife. Now, in the aftermath of the crime, Natty sits around in his shorts -- we are in a heatwave of mythical proportions -- and agonizes about not being the man Jimmy wanted him to be. He has gone through life trying to keep his homosexuality as quiet as possible, and Jimmy wanted him to come out.

Meanwhile, the two women pursue an apparently destructive, alcohol-filled relationship, and Marcel works the street, though with very little to show for it. Marcel therefore has a lot of time to talk, largely about the contrast between his flamboyance and Natty's repression. Marcel always speaks of himself in the third person. Marcel becomes very tedious. The four witnesses offer startlingly inconsistent descriptions of the murderer, though when he is actually produced each of them is able to identify him on sight.

This wildly improbable sequence is apparently meant to prove how self-hating they all are: Each has imagined this gay-basher as someone to whom they might be attracted. Here again, the author wills an image into life, and then builds on it as if it were a proven dramatic fact. The killer then speaks his own piece about how incurably full of hate he is, and very trite it sounds.

At a certain point, when the temperature has soared to heights unmentioned in the Guinness Book of Records, the characters are presumed to have talked and sweated themselves into a state of grace. A golden car cruises along out of nowhere (and just off stage, alas), perhaps allowing Marcel to turn the trick of his dreams.

Jaye and Tilly, currently in possession of a shopping cart loaded down with beer, give up needling one another and take to expressing their love, tenderly and physically, on the street. Jimmy returns to Earth to lead Natty into the sunset. And Natty, proud at last, goes with him: Weldon rises. (This is some clumsy title.)

He has learned that life's not worth a damn till you can say, 'Hey world, I am what I am.' I quote from La Cage aux Folles, Broadway version, and I can't see that the play expresses those admirable but generalized sentiments any more subtly than the musical did.

Besides, maybe what Natty seems naturally to be is shy. And maybe that's an index of repression but it looks here like he's being asked to exchange one stereotype for another.

The play's first five minutes promise good things, and Nagy does appear capable of caustic or evocative dialogue, even if it falls dully from the lips of this cast.

The actors (with the possible exception of Brendan Wall in the necessarily brief role of Jimmy) seem to be explaining or displaying their roles rather than embodying them. Hume Baugh, as Matty, at least does this on a fairly high technical level; the others -- Tori Higginson, Melee Hutton, Scott McCord, Mehron Paul -- clock in at various stages between strident and tentative.

Jordan Merkur's direction, meanwhile, drifts aimlessly between styles. The women's room is placed in realistic relation to the view it's supposed to command, but everything else seems to be happening in limbo. Natty sells lighting fixtures for a living, and he appears to have moved the shop counter into the open street.

This has been touted as a comedy but there are few laughs here. The director has even compared it to Seinfeld, on the grounds that it's about self-absorption and is set in New York (though in a very different part of the forest).

A show as good as even the best TV sitcom is not much of an inducement for audiences to leave home, but the comparison is presumptuous.

Seinfeld is, or was, not only funnier but more perceptive, and infinitely better constructed. It had one episode that featured a character who, like Marcel, always referred to himself in the third person; there, though, it functioned not just as a tic but as a plot device, and one that revealed character. A plausible action is the sine qua non of any kind of drama. Without it, characters are puppets, and ideas merely notions.

IF COWS COULD FLY

Artworld Theatre, Toronto

It seems that being the young Allan Merovitz meant growing up in the 1950s at Smiths Falls in the Ottawa Valley as a member of the third generation in a family of Jewish immigrants. Jews were a small minority in town but this never bothered Allan until a squabble with a gentile schoolmate led to some name-calling that had him running home in angry tears to his mother.

The grown-up Merovitz, self-described as "actor, singer and storyteller" (among other things) uses this incident as a springboard for an evening of autobiographical reminiscence. The title, If Cows Could Fly, resembles the proverbial expression about the unlikelihood of pigs having wings; its the kosher version. The show is a friendly but rambling affair that could use some tight editing and a firm decision on what it's supposed to be about.

The best of it comes early on, when Merovitz tells of his grandparents and of their coming to Canada. His maternal grandfather fled Poland at the beginning of the 20th century, travelling by hay cart and railway, to escape conscription. He had a spell in the Antwerp jewellery district, an atmosphere he found stimulating but - - after his previous life as a shoemaker in his native village -- grimy and constricting.

He then fetched up in London where he met his future wife, a refugee from Latvia, already the mother of two daughters and on the run from a husband rendered abusive by fits of epilepsy. Together they embarked for Canada where they found themselves in a tiny, remote fishing village in Nova Scotia, the only Jews the place had ever seen.

This collision of two cultures, each of them about equally remote from a modern metropolitan perspective, provides the most fascinating part of the show; you can sniff the sea-air, and taste the omnipresent fish, cooked every which way. Grandfather Abraham ends up making greatly improved boots and shoes for most of the population. Eventually the family moved on to the wider horizons of Antigonish, and from there to Montreal. We are told that they found it a blessing to arrive in a place where everybody wasn't speaking English.

It was in Montreal that the Waxmans, one side of our narrators family, met the Merovitzes. We learn less about this paternal branch, who had escaped from Russia during the czarist pogroms, but we are told that they managed to remain both prosperous and charitable after the 29 crash, the reason being that grandmother was running a gambling den in her parlour.

Hereabouts, though, the story starts to run thin. We aren't told how Allan's parents got together, or why they moved from Montreal to Smiths Falls. We do hear about other people, as the show succumbs to the fallacy that anything will be dramatically relevant just as long as it happened to one of the authors relatives.

There is a long self-contained sequence about the experiences of Allans uncle as a saboteur working for the British army. This ends the first act, literally with a bang (he blows up a German dam) but dramatically with a whimper.

Act two thrusts us into Merovitz's own boyhood, and gets still more diffuse. There are occasional encounters, triumphant or bizarre, with residual anti-Semitism, but nothing you could hang a theme on. There is a moderately entertaining bit about one of the narrator's aunts, carrying on the family shoe store tradition and terrorizing customers foolish enough to ignore her recommendations.

There is information, fascinating but misplaced, about a band of Jewish soldiers who came up from South America to help defend Canada -- well, English Canada -- in the 18th century. There is a really boring segment about hockey and there is a lengthy and mysterious digression about a friend of the authors who operated a home-made radio station devoted to country music.

Its mysterious because this buddy usurps the hero's own position as centre of the action. He even gets to sing the final song: a self- penned composition, or so we are told. Checking in the program we discover that Merovitz wrote it himself, so maybe his pal is really his alter ego. But it's confusing and a strange way to end.

However the music, and Merovitzs performance of it, are the strongest parts of the show. Most of the singing is in Yiddish, and some of the tunes are traditional chants. Some are klezmer, that beguiling Hebraic anticipation of jazz. But some of the music is outright American; we hear celebratory Yiddish swing and even an angry burst of Yiddish rock n' roll. That's not counting the Nashville stuff.

Its all done with great energy and authority; both in speech and song Merovitz seems to have every Canadian and U.S. idiom down pat.

He has two attendant musicians (who also occasionally, and awkwardly, stray into speaking roles). One is Anne Lederman, a tower of strength on piano, fiddle and musical direction. The other, strumming guitar and mandolin, is Ronnie Weihs, who is also the plays too-indulgent director.
