THE CLAIRVOYANT

Studio Theatre

We are in what is described as a large coastal city in the year 2038, a time and place apparently characterized by broken-down social structures and terrible architecture. The stage is occupied by half a dozen surly obelisks which, over the course of the evening, are shuffled around by sad-looking extras to create the play's various scenes.

The first location is a seaside cafe through which there mysteriously wanders an alluring blond lady. At your first dazzled glance, she appears to be about seven feet tall, is cradling a glass of champagne and is largely naked. When she reappears later she is fully clothed and remains so for the rest of the evening, even -- according to some pattern of behaviour reversal that will doubtless prove characteristic of this new century -- while having sex.

She is still, in the person of the actress Thea Gill, the most beautiful woman I have seen on a stage in months. The management may quote me on that.

I cant offer them much else in the way of advertising help. The Clairvoyant is the first offering of something called the North American Drama Alliance. Its the work of a Canadian, Larry Fineberg, but it has already been staged at a small theatre in Los Angeles, where it won a prize. This is fair enough; the play's unholy mix of mysticism, spy fiction, and apocalyptic social comment is the kind of thing that might well pass for profundity in the hinterlands of Hollywood.

Its title character, called Timon presumably in homage to Shakespeare's misanthrope, once had a thriving career as a psychic but has been driven into near-destitution, along with most of the rest of the world, by what everybody knowingly calls the crash. A courturiere friend advises him to join a cut-price fortune-telling operation since, as she approximately puts it, the future is just a commodity like any other. She also gives him a room above her store. Timon has come to dislike his gift of what he calls "reading people." But he needs money, and he soon attracts the attention of some very highly-placed human tea-leaves.

One of them is Goddard Bernstein (an inspired choice of name, I confess), who heads a corporation: the biggest of about 10 that between them control the planet. Another attraction of this brave polluted new world is something called ocean cancer, which has people nostalgic for the days when there were just ordinary cancer and AIDS.

As prophecy, all this is by no means unlikely, but it doesnt in itself make a play. Fineberg tries to structure his around the moral contortions of his hero who has never come to life in the first place and is anyway at the mercy of an increasingly frenzied plot. Goddard seems to be making billions from an extremely sinister social-engineering scheme; he is your standard amoral mastermind, with occasional glimmerings of a better self.

He is also ageing unnaturally fast; and his ambitious second-in- command who is very slimy (I think thats the intention; it's certainly the effect) wants to find out how long he has left. He wants Timon to find out and tell him, which would be a major breach of the soothsayer's code.

Timon is further compromised when, in strict accordance with fictional convention, he falls in love with the villains girl; she, the gorgeous blonde aforesaid, also falls for him, in what looks like a major piece of wish-fulfillment.

I suppose theres something cute about setting a fortune- teller's story actually in the future. (I was reminded of a deathless exchange from A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum: You want a soothsayer? "How did you know that?" "I'd be a fine soothsayer if I didn't.") The play occasionally captures the atmosphere of big business at its craziest. Mostly, though, it has all the self-importance and technical awkwardness of our local theatres of good works, plus an unctuousness all its own.

The actors grab for the nearest stock characterization and hang on to it like grim death; Hugo Dann is a ruffled Timon whose best moment comes when he lets out with an unnervingly-timed scream. Brian Richmond's production is mostly the victim of its own scene- changes; he seems to be trying for abstraction but caves in whenever he needs a prop. So people sit on plinths and drink from real glasses, which makes them look doubly uncomfortable.

GODSPELL

Bathurst Street Theatre, Toronto

This isn't Sunday-school camp, says Jesus to his disciples, as they arrange themselves in giggling formation for a military drill number. Hes wrong for once.

There was always a strong whiff of Sunday school about Godspell, the musical that repackaged the New Testament in the peace-and-love accessories of the 1960s. (The show dates from 1971 which, by theatrical standards, made it pretty hot off the mark.) The camp ingredient is supplied by the present revival which, coming to Toronto from the Georgian Theatre Festival, has summer theatre written all over it. It overlays the original with the pop-culture references of its own time, and is cheerfully indiscriminate about how and when it uses them. A show that was always irritating has become unbearable.

It is not in its own terms badly done. Michael McGinns staging has a lot of energy and a respectable amount of precision. Godspell's original productions are famous for breeding stars: Victor Garber, Andrea Martin, Martin Short and Gilda Radner in Toronto, David Essex, Jeremy Irons and Julie Covington in London. I don't know that any of the present bunch will make it to that level, but they should all have futures.

There are nine in the cast, though only two have identifiable roles. Adam Brazier gives us Jesus as hip holy fool, a gangling combination of clown and juvenile lead with a mask of innocence, a deep reserve of funny voices and a well-camouflaged broken heart; watching him is like seeing the Bible story acted out by Jim Carrey, however that may grab you.

Duff MacDonald is equally resourceful as the sardonic raven- locked character-man of the group, who starts out as John the Baptist and at some unspecified moment morphs into Judas Iscariot. Everybody sings well.

The material has its merits, too. The script is by John-Michael Tebelak, out of the St. Matthew Gospel; it begins and ends with dramatized narrative, but devotes much of the time between to acting out parables.

Tebelak doesnt seem to have worked much since but presumably he hasnt needed to. The score is by Stephen Schwartz, who has subsequently had an up-and-down Broadway career but is a considerable talent. His lightly rocking tunes (Day by Day and the others) sound, if anything, more infectious now than they did then, and his lyrics are refreshingly neat. They can even be powerfully dramatic. When this Jesus is on the cross he sings, "Oh God, I'm dying" to which the chorus respond Oh, God, you're dying, a simple change of possessive that shifts a remarkable amount of weight. The only thing wrong with the songs is that there arent enough of them, or rather that theres too much of everything else.

The actors in this production wear face-mikes: Those ugly and aggressively contemporary contraptions that make them look from the middle of the auditorium as if they've all grown moustaches, and from the back as if they're smoking cheroots. But basically they are got up as performers in this show as they have always been: a bunch of red-nosed troubadours, light of brain and pure of heart.

They begin by riffling through the pronouncements of great thinkers from Socrates to Sartre; these sound bites go by too fast to be understood but the implication seems to be that all these well- meaning intellectuals were wasting their time, and that all we need is love. That, at any rate, is what the show proceeds to give us in large sugary helpings.

This is a very soft show based on a very tough source. The Biblical parables are terse moral paradoxes whose implications, if people in any number were actually to act on them, would be cataclysmic. In Godspell their meaning, though not actually falsified, is smothered under a blanket of ingratiation: goofy young showfolk acting out all the parts and making nice.

There may have been some naive and sentimental logic to this in the shows counter-cultural youth; people then were able to identify their own sentimental and very commercial sappiness with the texts astonishing blend of fierce anti-materialism and all-embracing compassion. (It makes the term "religious right" seem a bewildering oxymoron.) Now, of course, all this idealism is long gone, so there might be room for a tough production that was consciously against the grain.

This one, though, wears the original concept like a quaint but endearing set of old clothes that needs tarting up a bit. They sense that it's basically a revue, so they bring it narcissistically up to date by stuffing in references to currently recognizable movies, songs, catch-phrases and stars. This may be all right in principle but the practice is outrageously self-indulgent; they throw everything in, from Bill Clinton to Celine Dion. Revue of all forms needs discipline; this is more like an out-of-control English pantomime.

I don't remember the original show being this long -- just when I thought it had to be coming to an end, Jesus prophesied an intermission. This was kind of him, but it was less than the mercy I craved.

Till April 6. Box office (416) 531-1827.

SIBS

Tarragon Backspace, Toronto

Anyone who's an only child may feel left out, but for everybody else Sibs, short for siblings, is a feast of familial fun.

Written and performed by Diane Flacks and Richard Greenblatt, the show presents a grown-up brother and sister, now comprehensively orphaned. They are in their parents empty home, having just emerged from the Jewish period of ritual mourning for their father; their mother died some years previously. Now its time to take care of legal and financial business, but there are problems. She (they are given no names, except the occasional insulting sobriquet) lives in another city and is about to fly back there; he, with his own problems, thinks she's being unreasonable. So they squabble and blame, as they have done all their lives. The show takes us on a whistle-stop tour of these earlier skirmishes, eventually setting us down just a few moments later than the point at which we came in.

The first flashback is a montage of encounters from childhood, adolescence, and early adulthood, done with enchanting precision and panache. The physical choreography, in Alisa Palmer's production, is as immaculately timed and executed as the verbal. There is no time and no need for any change of costume or make-up, and as most of their time together was spent in this same house, Glenn Davidsons comfortable set serves admirably throughout.

She is the older of the two, and was greatly disappointed when the stork brought a boy instead of another girl; she compensates by introducing her baby brother to strangers as her baby sister. Flacks air of overweening sweetness is perfect here; so is Greenblatt's google-eyed expression, as of one who suspects that something is being put over on him but cannot quite master the concept. He retains this suspicious look right into their grown-up years, though the eye-rolling becomes increasingly tinged with anticipated martyrdom, as if nothing she could do would surprise him but he still can't quite believe her. She has her own version of the same attitude, though its rather more aggressive. She remains -- implacably and irreversibly -- older. Which may have as much to do with gender as with chronology.

The relationship isnt all antagonism of course. There are moments of sympathy or solidarity, mainly in the face of the adult world: an attitude that doesn't alter much when they become adults. After puberty hits, they discover at least one other piece of common ground: each distrusts the other's taste in women. There is also their inescapable Jewishness, and the way in which each wavers between accepting and resenting it. He turns his bar mitzvah speech into a youthful political credo; she makes her speech at his wedding her occasion for coming out as a lesbian. The play is largely structured around a series of Passover celebrations; once married with children, brother assumes the responsibility for these family feasts. Sister is often absent but there is generally a phone call, at least one of which ranks among the most hilarious bits in the show.

I wouldnt say that, when we return to square one, we arrive there with any greatly enriched understanding of the inhabitants. The past does not greatly illuminate the present; it merely confirms it. It will probably not tell you anything about the human condition that you dont already know, but then how many plays do? What this one offers, in spades, is the comedy of recognition.

And maybe I should withdraw my caveat about only children; the piece should ring true to anyone who has ever weathered any kind of enduring relationship. The jousting between the grown-up sibs (I speak as one who half-identifies, having a brother but no sister) is not that unlike the tensions between spouses or longtime lovers. From the opening words ("God, I'm so exhausted") and the sight of the two of them slumped in opposite armchairs, it is clear that this is a play about the long haul, however arrived at, and about being there for it.

Some of the exchanges between the Him and Her in their maturity (You are such a jerk -- "What's your problem?") really do suggest that nothing changes after childhood. The thrust and parry can of course become somewhat more sophisticated (Do you have any unresolved issues? "Not that I want to resolve.") Rick Sachs contributes a background musical score, much of it played on xylophone, which suggest the water-drops of time falling with exquisite cruelty on a couple of human skulls. The rhythm of the two participants is equally impeccable; it's almost impossible to separate one from the other or text from execution; all are great. The bond between them seems, as befits the subject, unbreakable. The ending is as perfectly happy-sad as could be imagined. The show lasts for 80 minutes, no intermission, and I loved every second.

Black & White Photo: Greg Tjepkema / Co-writers and performers Diane Flacks and Richard Greenblatt in Sibs. ;

BEAVER

Factory Studio Theatre, Toronto

There are now three plays in Toronto whose starting-points are a family and a funeral. This, the latest, arrives a few weeks after The Memory of Water and just one night after the joyous Sibs. It too is largely concerned with sibs, and, as in The Memory of Water, they are three grown-up sisters. This time, one of the sisterhood doubles as the corpse, but -- again as in The Memory -- the deceased makes spectral appearances in the action. The person she appears to is her daughter -- 12 at the beginning of the play, 17 at the end -- whose name is Beatrice, and whose nickname gives the play its title.

So the play is about her; that, at least, is what the author seems to be insisting, both in the title and in the text. But in fact there is no central character and no real unifying theme. Beaver, which lasts three hours with the special-occasion luxury of two intermissions, is a meandering mess.

The play, in its present form, has no business on a professional stage. Its author, however, has.

She is Claudia Dey, whose first full-length piece this is, and she has been entranced by the way people talk in the snow-clad fastness of Northern Ontario. I have to take her word for it that conversation up there is as luxuriant and as incisive as she makes it out to be, but I'm happy to do so: at least as happy as when listening to Sean O'Casey's Dubliners whose lyricism seems self- conscious by comparison. The trouble is that having come up with a style, she has not found a story or characters to hang it on.

Things do of course happen, and to people. The place is Timmins, the date of commencement 1988. Beaver's mother, Rose, committed suicide, perhaps out of frustration at unfulfilled dreams or from the pain of living with her alcoholic husband, Silo. Her two aunts are Nora, nervous and all-round inhibited, and Shira who, not inhibited at all, is a noted local prostitute specializing in domination.

The family circle is rounded off by their mother, Edna, a saltily foul-mouthed old lady who, like nearly everyone else on stage, drinks a lot. Their first, improbable, action is to lose Beaver in the graveyard and return home, in the depths of winter, oblivious. Nora has persuaded social services to place the girl in her care: this over the objections of her father -- who loves her, whatever else -- and the jealous disgust of Shira. Beaver isn't happy and makes the first of several attempts to leave town. Eventually, though, she gives in. These manoeuvrings, interspersed with much rambling reminiscence, take up the play's first two acts. There is then a five-year gap, at the end of which we find Beaver about to get married (in a motel) to someone we never meet for reasons that are barely explored. Her relatives are still striking the same attitudes, except that the once-puritanical Nora now seems willing to swear and swig with the best. The end is predictably unpredictable.

A few scenes have tension and rhythm, notably one in which Silo (the best-drawn character in the piece, and richly played by Glen Cairns) clings desperately to his daughter, trying to be cunning, while Nora waits with a kind of embarrassed implacability. There are two characters from outside the family: an anecdotalizing neighbour whose quirk is that she wants to set up as an independent sovereign state, and a drinking buddy of Silo's. The former is well-enough played (by Tracy Wright) and the latter excellently played (by Lorne Cardinal) but the play would be better off without them. They merely add to the volume of self-reflexive talk, and slow the proceedings down further. They're already dragging dangerously, partly because of the amount of alcohol that goes down; you may think that your mind is racing when you're drunk, but from an outside viewpoint you're at a crawl. Sarah Stanley's droopily-paced production doesn't help. The actors in the communal scenes strike no sparks off one another though individually -- Charmion King gritty and commanding as Edna, Jan Derbyshire quivering as Nora, Linda Prystawska pluming and bridling as Shira -- they do their prescribed thing efficiently. Waneta Storms is wasted as the late Rose about whom everybody talks reverentially, but who never, either as a memory or a ghost, displays a single positive characteristic.

The same lack of definition more crucially afflicts Beaver, whose development is meant to be the spine of the play. It simply isn't there. Simone Rosenberg does strikingly well as the young girl forging a precocious personal and sexual identity, but she can't bridge the gap to the mystery bride of the last act, though by now she's playing closer to her own age. There is some kind of message here about working out your own salvation, and it seems to embrace the other characters as well, but it remains fuzzy and sentimental. The play suffers from the conviction that if you talk around something enough, then it's happened.

It also carries the curse of the shifting location. Most of it occurs in tucked-away corners of the stage; the centre goes almost entirely uninhabited, which gets very frustrating. It represents the impassable outdoors, and is piled high with blankets, which seem to be awaiting a dramatization of The Princess and the Pea. The stage, in Troy Hansen's design, points out into the audience, whose seats have been arranged in a receptive inverted V-shape. This is an excellent focusing device, and in the last act, when the weather has broken and we gaze on an inviting waterscape, we do finally get something worth looking at. For the previous two hours, though, we have watched actors bunched together in poky rooms whose barrenness suggests not so much the poverty of the characters are the non- arrival of the scene-painters. Bleak can be bracing; drab is just depressing.

Black & White Photo: Nir Bareket / The actors fail to spark off each other. Left, Tracy Wright, Linda Prystawska, Simone Rosenberg, Jan Derbyshire and Charmion King. ;
2000-03-18-lake-ontario-makes-for-potent:
The Water Crawlers runs to Apr. 9. Tuesday to Saturday at 8 p.m., Sunday at 2:30 p.m. Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, 12 Alexander St. $15 to $18. Call 416-975-8555.

THE WATER CRAWLERS

Buddies in Bad Times

The best thing about The Water Crawlers is its visual poetry. It takes place on the edge of Lake Ontario, or of the tiny portion of it that lies just behind the Etobicoke motel strip.

The front part of the broad, sunken stage is filled with water, and though we are repeatedly told how poisonously filthy the lake is, how full of needles and condoms and human waste, it has a kind of magic.

Potent enough in the daytime, it's even more so at night, with the lights shining down more intensely and the reflections more acute.

Stephan Droege, who designed both the set and the lighting, has also supplied a properly dilapidated motel-sign (Tourist Court, it says), some nondescript frontage and, very importantly, a couple of swings.

Completing the picture -- burly, sorrowful and moonfaced -- is David Fox in the role of Billy Musgrave, 63 years old, former champion marathon swimmer, and now -- O time! O manners! -- owner of the Marathon Motel. Now he shivers at the side of the water, trying to muster the will and courage to go in again.

I wish that he and his three acting colleagues had more to do, or at least more varied things to do. Geoff Kavanagh, the author, has taken an admittedly appealing image and stretched it beyond its natural resonance.

Billy, for reasons of both pride and finance, wants to enter one more race, but is both physically and psychologically fearful. (And, rather naturally at his age, out of practice.)

His wife, herself a former Olympic athlete, alternately doubts and spurs him on. Their daughter, Marilyn, ambiguously proud of the two of them, sits and stews at the motel reservation-desk, since her parents cannot afford to hire a clerk.

Marilyn was named for a 16-year old girl who was the first to swim across Lake Ontario -- a feat that is her fathers Holy Grail - - and she even gives lecture-demonstrations about her namesake to visitors. (The play begins with one of these and it is, at the time and for some time after, confusing.)

Finally, there is Martin, whose lover has recently died of AIDS and has resigned himself to following.

Four beached characters, all needing to take the plunge.

Billy actually succeeds in persuading Martin to enter the water with him as his pacer and guide. (Billy was once known as Billy the Baptist -- "he brought thousands into the water.")

Even more surprisingly, Billy triumphs in a qualifying race, though nobody seems to notice. (A 63-year old man wins a swimming race says Mrs M, vainly turning the pages of her newspaper, and nobody even mentions it").

Somewhere in the background there seems to be a national metaphor; Lake Ontario is referred to as "the toilet of Canada."

The play takes place in 1989, and the implication is that what was bad then is worse now. It doesn't mean much. There is immediate gratification though in the sight of the two men actually swimming while the two women swing on the swings and cheer them on.

All the characters get wet at some point; we don't see many plays in which so many real people spend so much time in so much real water, and its a genuine attraction.

When theyre not splashing, though, they're talking, usually about the past, in dialogue that is neither as witty nor as trenchant as it needs to be. There's a nice, charitable feel to the play, and Dean Gabouries direction gives it visual definition, but its inert.

Fox, who excels at presenting men who beat out of time with their fellows, does very well here, exuding a dangerous cheeriness, but he can't help running out of steam. Elizabeth Shepherd has elected to play his wife with a north of England heartiness that is not, I think, her natural mode; but the technique and her intelligence are impeccable.

Catherine McNally plays Catherine, who flourishes the scars of a convent education, on alternating notes of enthusiasm and derision, which seems fair enough. And Greg Kramer very skillfully navigates Martin's dramatic problem, which is that he talks too much and too introspectively for his own good as a person or ours as an audience.

The play ends, for all parties, on the standard tragi-comic note of hope deferred. It's a pleasingly elegiac conclusion; the trouble is that the whole play has been elegiac.

Black & White Photo: Courtesy Acme Theatre Company / Elizabeth Shepherd and David Fox portray former Olympians who live by the water's edge in the Etobicoke motel strip. ;

Not in This Lifetime, Jean Harlow runs until April 2 at Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, 16 Ryerson Ave. For tickets, call (416)- 504-7529.

NOT IN THIS LIFETIME, JEAN HARLOW

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace

We have seen real-life husbands and wives acting on stage together, brothers and sisters and lovers of all persuasions. The two performers in Not in This Lifetime, Jean Harlow, however, break new ground in consanguinity. Michael Rawley, who both wrote and appears in the play, is a victim of kidney disease who, after three years on a dialysis machine, became the beneficiary of a transplant. His donor, a miraculous match, was Wendy Krekeler, an actress- friend who is also currently his co-star.

The play obliquely reflects their off-stage relationship, both in its subject matter and in the mere fact of its existence. It is not, however, directly about it.

In this piece, which also covers a three-year period, both characters are undergoing dialysis and are hooked up, for reasons of both bureaucratic and dramatic convenience, to adjacent machines.

Three times a week they clock in, for four hours of excruciating inactivity. We observe them trying, in diametrically opposite ways, to prevent the experience from defining their lives. He does it by fighting his condition. She does it by ignoring hers.

He, who goes by the uncommon name of Chaelan, is a fitness freak who rollerblades to treatment. He conscientiously obeys dietary restrictions though, as a gourmet, he finds them especially agonizing. (One of his speeches is a valedictory ode to the tomato.)

She, called a little more prosaically Erdra, would also hate to watch her food if she gave it the slightest thought, which she doesn't. She also smokes, drinks and is diabetic; lack of circulation is slowly destroying her feet. He is toned, and she is beefy. He counts the years to a possible transplant; she isn't even on the list. She has decided that, when the doctors decree amputation, she will simply take herself off her machine and call it quits.

In the meantime, as the clinic's oldest inhabitant, she lords it over the staff and other patients and makes life especial hell for her immediate neighbour. The two of them bicker and worry one another and eventually, predictably but plausibly, establish a sort of sympathy.

They are, after all, in different stations on the same boat.

Nobody could accuse Rawley of writing a sentimentally sympathetic part for his benefactor.

Erdra is self-destructive, which theatrically can be a compelling quality, and loud-mouthed, which generally isn't. Krekeler plays her, I suppose, uncompromisingly; her character certainly supplies the most gratingly repeated laugh I have ever heard on a stage.

But both the writing and the performance of the role are heavy- handed; a character who doesn't know when to back off maybe requires an actor who does. Rawley's own role, the model patient and health- activist, seems to be autobiographical (the basic situation obviously is) and he is able to point up what's absurd as well what is admirable in Chaelan's undeviating right-mindedness. But he too remains a diagram rather than a person.

(He looks like Tim Allen and he sounds, at least in this role, like Alan Rickman, so he seems to be mounting a one-man Galaxy Quest.)

The play manages to be gripping and boring, simultaneously. It grips because this is, after all, a life-and-death situation, one that most of us will contemplate with a sense of worried involvement, of there-but-for-the-grace-of-Godliness. We also get the chance to feel indignant about a health system controlled by management rather than medicine; and to rage, with accustomed impotence, against the idea that pain and sickness should exist at all. In Erdra's case, the play makes a strong implied case -- and I am not being either callous or ironic -- for euthanasia. (We are also affected, of course, by our extra-mural awareness of Rawley's endurance and Krekeler's generosity.)

It bores because it's banal. The dialogue never lifts. Erdra's favourite diversion, both in the treatment room and at home, is to watch vintage movies featuring her favourite feisty female stars: Jean Harlow (who died of kidney disease) and others. "See you in a while, me darlin' Bette Davises," she says before settling down for the day's draining. People don't talk like that, and it isn't even much fun pretending that they do.

Everything here is too explicit, too obviously designed to convey information or to set up another verbal tennis rally. Maybe the off- stage reality has overpowered the on-stage fiction. I don't mean the clinical reality. I mean that these characters carry on like actors.

She donated the organ to Rawley to help battle his kidney disease. ; Black & White Photo: Dreamworks Pictures / The character Chaelan sounds like Alan Rickman, star of Galaxy Quest, says our reviewer. ;
2000-03-23-so-much-to-wonder-about:
Until May 14. Box office: (416) 862-2222.

ALICE

Young People's Theatre

A few years ago, the Stratford Festival mounted a version of Alice Through the Looking-Glass that seemed to have taken its cue from the famous judicial instructions issued by the King of Hearts in the high court of Wonderland: "Begin at the beginning, go on until you reach the end, and then stop." The Young People's Theatre, by contrast, gives us a new-look Alice that hops, or hip-hops, around both the Lewis Carroll masterpieces, throwing in fragments of The Hunting of the Snark for good measure and topping it off with a few familiar motifs from the author's life. This phantasmagoria (another Carroll title; it's a very funny poem about a ghost) is preferable to Stratford's prosaic literalness.

The adaptation, by Maristella Roca, is at least energetic in the way it hurls the elements together, and the production, by Gyllian Raby, has touches of imagination. Alice's fall down the rabbit hole, a notorious theatrical hazard, is nicely managed by a judicious application of modern technology. The show is, all the same, very sloppy.

It's also, I would think, in a no-win situation with the kids at whom it's directed. If they know the originals, they will resent, and be confused by, the liberties taken. If they don't know the originals (such childhood deprivation is unpleasant to contemplate but it undoubtedly exists), they'll be confused in another way as the allusions, which seem to be the point of the enterprise, come thick and fast and rarely stick around to explain themselves. The characters, filched and altered from Carroll, never come to life in their own right. The target audiences seem to be children who have been told about the books in some detail but haven't actually read them (a depressingly plausible scenario) and grown-ups who have the stories firmly under their belts and can get a mild thrill from seeing them mucked about with.

Here, as far as I can reconstruct it, is what happens. We begin with a nicely composed stage picture depicting a Victorian Alice, chaperoned by three tea-sipping older sisters and having her photograph taken by the real-life Carroll's real-life alter ego, the Reverend Charles Lutwidge Dodgson. He, far from being the child charmer of whom one has always read, is a short-tempered old party who really loses it when Alice makes an unauthorized grab at a tart that he was saving up for tea. (Look, it's the edible kind of tart; or does that make it sound worse?)

She, in her turn, is robbed of the cookie by a jive-talkin' bunny (honey, he ain't no white rabbit) and naturally she pursues him in a vertically downward direction. When she gets to Wonderland, or wherever it is, she learns that he has an unsavoury reputation as a ladies' rabbit; he supplies the Duchess with tarts, and probably other things. (She is not ugly in this version; indeed, she prides herself on her beauty.)

Alice meets the Jabberwocky, who recaps most of the known poetic data about himself, and advises her on how to ensnare and even kill the rabbit with the aid of a vorpal blade, or in this case vorpal carrot. (It looks like something out of a cut-rate tour of Star Wars.)

By the end of the show, though, the helpful Jabberwock has become the bad guy and the rabbit the good one. I don't know why, though I can tell you that the rabbit's name is Louis, presumably in reference to the original author's nice liberated side.

In his repressed and (ugh) Victorian aspect, he reappears as the Dormouse, linked to Dodgson by alliteration if nothing else. We also at various stages meet Tweedledum and Tweedledee, and a surprisingly svelte Queen of Hearts, still screaming for universal decapitation but a devotee of baseball rather than of croquet. This, presumably, is to make a 2000 North American audience feel at home.

One thing in the show's favour: Unlike most classic adaptations at YPT, it doesn't preach. This is emphatically true to Carroll; the stories are, among other things, ferocious satires on the moralizing literature to which Victorian children were routinely subjected.

But that's only a negative recommendation. The most vulnerable element in any dramatization of Alice is also the most important -- the humour. Either it gets ignored, by solemn psychological or sociological interpreters with higher things on their minds, or it gets trampled by guys who just wanna have fun. This show suffers from a little of the former affliction and a lot of the latter. Not much of Carroll's wit remains, and what there is is murdered. Instead we get a series of sidelong references to it -- self- conscious and intolerably self-satisfied.

This leaves the actors very little to act, and all the perfomances suffer from a debilitating lack of urgency. This is particularly true of Keira Loughran's Alice; deprived of the real girl's enchantingly demure bossiness, she can only be moonishly snippy. Her sole characteristic is a vaguely expressed desire to go home, as if the adaptor had got her source material confused with The Wizard of Oz. And I cringed at her repeated references to "Reverend Dodgson." It should be "Mr. Dodgson," and any properly brought-up English girl of the period would know that. An illiterate Alice is a contradiction in terms.

And so is an illogical Alice. I don't mind them messing with the storyline; that's an adaptor's prerogative. I do mind them missing the point. The books are built on the contrast between the implacable school-room reasoning that she brings with her and the equally impregnable upside-down arguments of the people in her dreams. This version, as far as I could make out through a fog of garbled speaking and inaudible singing, couldn't care less.
2000-03-28-knows-what-she-s-got-joni-mit:
The liner notes to Both Sides Now (Reprise CDM 4720), Joni Mitchell's album of standards, proclaim that "Joni has achieved something quite extraordinary in that she has truly sung [these songs] as if, as Nietzsche would say, she had written them in her own blood.

Oh, come on now, it's not that bad. As a matter of fact, its rather good. Mitchell is not a starry-eyed nostalgist, in the manner of Carly Simon or Linda Ronstadt. Unlike most post-rock singers who venture into pre-rock songs, she has some idea of how to interpret them. She explores the lyrics, and -- perhaps even more important -- she is able to spread her findings intelligently and intelligibly across the music. Her previous experiments with jazz (including her Mingus album) may not have been too happy, but they have taught her how, in this repertoire, words and music support one another; in most contemporary songs, one illuminates the other. She doesnt swing, but she can play with rhythm.

She includes a couple of her own compositions, but most of the material comes from the '30s and '40s. They were most popular, though -- certainly most omnipresent -- in the 50s and early 60s, and it's that period that seems to have inspired this production. That isn't a new idea; Ronstadts albums, widely criticized for their anachronistic feel, also harked back to the 50s -- it just happened to be the wrong kind of '50s. (Critic Will Friedwald said that Ronstadt came out of the classic Eddie Fisher-Teresa Brewer- Johnny Mathis tradition of really bad singing." She reminds me more of Connie Francis, but the point is the same. Everybody in the '50s was singing these songs, but they werent all singing them well. Which is why the "lounge music vogue, which lumps them all together in some camp idea of style," is so pernicious.)

Mitchell takes another idea that the notes describe as "innovative -- though it was quite commonplace 40 years ago: arranging the songs to chronicle the rise and fall of a love affair. The built-in attraction of this concept is also its built-in flaw: The songs as written divide into rigid categories of happy and sad, and within those categories they are, in narrative terms, pretty much interchangeable. So albums like Mel Tormes Prelude to a Kiss or Bobby Darin's Love Swings boil down to half a dozen fast songs followed by half a dozen slow ones.

Mitchell, though, is slow all the way through. Her CD recalls the Frank Sinatra ballad albums, each of which takes a particular mood (and it's a subtly different shade of despair on each LP) and dissects it. She ends with what is still her own best-known song, the one that gives the CD its title, but it sounds very out of place; the evidence is that shes looked at love from one side now, and it has, from the very first track, been the downside. I think that if I were selecting a song to illustrate the dawn of love, I might fix on The Way You Look Tonight or How Long Has This Been Going On, something that had wit in it, enjoyment -- maybe even a touch of optimism.

Mitchell comes up with Youre My Thrill, which expresses a masochistic devotion (You do something to me ... Here's my heart on a silver platter") that seems to belong more to the obsessive middle of a relationship, and in any case is bound to end in tears. She sings it with a tremulous air of drugged surrender that sounds, in temper if not in tone, like late-period Billie Holiday. She lightens up a bit for At Last (a song that seems to me to be getting slightly more than its due these days), sounding as if she's singing with her eyes closed. But then its Comes Love, a very 30s list song that, as written, is a merrily fatalistic catalogue of romantic resignation; she does it as a witch's curse. And then comes You've Changed, only the fourth song out of 12, and disillusion has set irrevocably in.

After that its all downhill, with Rodgers and Harts I Wish I Were in Love Again turning up near the end as a sort of summation. I've often felt that this, the best of all anti-love songs, could stand a more mordant treatment than it usually gets, but in this context it seems superfluous. Why should someone who has got so little fun out of love be so eager to go through it again? Larry Hart's lyric is full of fun, however ironically expressed; Mitchell, unfortunately, comes from a school of song that thinks of irony as something misty and mopey rather than something hard and bright. (Its a mercy she doesnt include any Cole Porter.) And why should she think that Hart's great couplet "The pulled-out fur of cat and cur/The fine mismating of a him and her is improved by the pedestrian subsitution of flying fur" and "fine mismatching? Or was she just being careless?

The arrangements, by Vince Mendoza, are sensational. On one cut, Stormy Weather, he shares credit with the late Gordon Jenkins; this turns out to mean that the chart is heavily indebted to the windswept, string-laden treatment that Jenkins supplied for Sinatra's No One Cares album. Its a credit to Mitchell that her vocal, which includes an unexpected banshee wail on everything I had is gone," stands up in the context. (And pleasing rather than embarrassing that the record appears on the label that Sinatra founded.) Mendoza, too, harks back to the 50s but in a wide- ranging way. At times he echoes Sinatra and Nelson Riddle. While his arrangement of Comes Love is something cool, dark and plangent that Gil Evans might have conjured for Miles Davis; it incorporates a startling trumpet solo by Mark Isham. (Other star guests are Wayne Shorter and Herbie Hancock.)

Mitchell's vocal choices are similarly eclectic, and sometimes memories of other singers seem to be descending on her line by line rather than song by song. But she usually makes the material her own and uses the erosion in her voice to good, craggy effect; occasionally she seems to be singing Canadian mountain blues. The songs themselves vary more in quality than she probably believes: A couple are certifiable classics, a couple more might as well be, half a dozen are good, and one -- Answer Me, My Love -- is a piece of '50s slush that there was no need to excavate. Its her own songs, though, that really get shown up. The lyric to A Case of You reads well (better, Im tempted to say, than the lyric to a good song would) but gains nothing when it's heard. Both Sides Now itself she has simply outgrown, and her efforts to pump maturity into it are painful.

It's a good fault, though. Compare her to Judy Collins, who had the original hit with the song and whose equivalent new album, Classic Broadway (Platinum 37522), shows her to be as blandly uncomprehending now as she was then. Mitchell has reached a new plateau; the notes may suggest that she is doing the old songs a favour, but she must know that it's the other way round.

Color Photo: Kirk McKoy, Los Angeles Times / Mitchell knows how to interpret pre-rock songs, exploring the lyrics with both intelligence and intelligibility. ;

GRACE

Theatre Centre, Toronto

The first scene of Grace is set on a bus. Two male passengers sit side by side, in uncomfortable proximity.

One is a florid middle-aged businessman, suited and briefcased. The other is in his early twenties and has the spikiest of hairstyles. As you would expect in a play, one intimidates the other. As you might not expect, it's the apparently straight guy who puts on the pressure. Its the young punk whos quiet and embarrassed, and wants to be left alone. The term "straight" proves (and remains) ambiguous, since the older man tries to pick up the younger; he even seems to be having some success, but it doesn't work out.

The tension in this apparently self-contained episode is remarkable, and it goes way beyond the weary conventions of theatrical menace. When the scene ends we still know few facts about the participants, but their encounter has had extraordinary resonance. Later we will learn a lot more, and will be able to see just how much the actors have had to draw on. For the moment all we can tell is that these characters have roots, and that they go deep.

Written by Michael Lewis MacLennan and directed by Franco Boni, Grace is a superb feat of dramatic orchestration. It unfolds through a further series of duologues. There are half-a-dozen characters; and they turn up, over a dramatic time of 24 hours, in almost every possible combination. There is only one re-match, included because the action would be frustratingly incomplete without it; otherwise we can follow the fortunes of the offstage characters from glancing references that accumulate as the day wears on.

The play has already been seen in Victoria, Vancouver and Calgary (not to mention London) and MacLennan has apparently rewritten and re-located it for each gig. This sounds opportunistic, but in Toronto at least it's been subtly and effectively done.

With only one mention of a specific location, the play still reeks of this city, especially of the run-down sections a short streetcar ride from downtown: the park thats both a haven and a threat, the draughty and deserted churches, the bars and coffee- houses where aspiring poets audition their wares, the rooms where people die. (Seeing the play out on Queen West helps.)

Compare this to the previous nights opening, The Lady Smith, up to here with local references but remaining obstinately in limbo.

I don't want to put anybody off, but the publicity claims that the re-writing allows the play to focus on brand-name Toronto problems: homelessness, spousal abuse, mental health and gay- bashing.

Why anybody would want to market the play as an identity kit issue-piece is beyond me, especially as it isn't about any of these things. They do all crop up, and none of them feels dragged in; they are things that happen to these characters, but they dont define these characters.

What does define them is desperation, past or present or both, experienced with varying degrees of intensity on a scale whose apex is self-destruction. Of the two men on the bus, Hugh the businessman has just been fired (he says, repeatedly and probably truthfully, that public transit is a novelty for him) and is also divorced. Jared, the punk, mourns the death of a caring lover whom he fears he didnt help enough; in the course of the day he will try prostitution as a means of survival (and will flatten his hair). Subsequently we encounter Lonnie, a radio professional who has just now left her husband and is at a loss where to turn, either physically or emotionally; Thomas, young and mentally ill, who carries a snake around with him in a box and attends a day-centre where he distrusts all his fellow-inmates; Ruth, a widow who looks homeless but isn't; and Paula, an aspiring poet and fully paid-up fantasist.

At least one of the six is a candidate for suicide, and one plot strand involves somebody who has recently committed it. Altogether it's a hot topic; we hear about a woman who spent three hours talking a man out of throwing himself off a bridge; she is now a local celebrity, known as "Our Lady of the Bridge" and with her own Good Samaritan phone-in show. Most of the sextet are skeptical about her, but the play moves to show its people helping, even saving, one another, and in so doing saving themselves.

For the most part, they spare our blushes by doing it tentatively. They can also, though none of them is malevolent, hurt one another; a frightened Paula does it violently to Hugh, Lonnie does it more subtly to Paula.

The most active agent of salvation, therefore the trickiest role, is Ruth, whose solo addresses to her unlamented but unforgotten husband not only infringe the convention but constitute the only soggy writing in the piece. Anne Anglin plays her much of the time as a standard mumbling bag-lady, but she rallies at the end with unsentimental benevolence; when Thomas (an innocent in Anthony McLeans performance) complains of being labelled a retard, she says crisply "thats why you're there."

Ralph Small's Hugh has the weariness and the turbulence of a full- blown tragic hero; Caroline Gillis, a ubiquitous actress, does her best work yet as Lonnie, her tartness and her terror all of a piece; Marjory Chan is piercingly accurate as Paula; and as Jared, Dylan Trowbridge is, in both feeling and technique, the plays title made flesh.

The script is frequently funny, and so pliant and unforced that one soon gives it mental permission to go where it likes for as long as it likes. In fact, this indulgence turns out to be unnecessary; as the permutations unfold, the structure is revealed to be extremely tight, themes and motifs echoing from one encounter to another. We are watching a connected world, where coincidence becomes a symbol of community. (Its like Six Degrees of Separation, laid out as a map.)

Boni's production taps, lightly but firmly, all the strengths of both the writing and the performers. In a season typified, with a few shining exceptions, by clumsy direction of half-formed texts, Grace is a blessing.

THE OFFERING

Artword Theatre

What did Abraham and Isaac say to one another as they journeyed to the mountain on which the father had been divinely commanded to sacrifice his son?

The Bible, which doesn't go in much for small talk, is largely silent on the subject. The first act of Anton Piatigorsky's The Offering, which transfers the story to contemporary Canada, offers to fill in the gaps.

Its second and third acts pursue the relationship of father and son unto the second and third generation, by way of two more of the most familiar Old Testament stories.

We see Isaac, now old himself, defrauded by his neglected son Jacob of the patrimony he intended to bestow on his favoured son Esau. Finally we watch old Jacob coming to request famine relief from an official who is actually his own long-lost Joseph. Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph: A remarkable family in anyone's book, as Tim Rice remarked in a somewhat similar context.

He might have said in everyone's book, since the Bible casts an inescapable cultural shadow on all of us, believers or not. Like any classic -- perhaps more than any other classic -- it is ripe for plunder.

Still its stories, like all stories, come with certain ground rules, without which they cease to make narrative sense. One thing that the Abraham of Genesis famously does say, when his son asks why they have brought along no animal to kill, is that God will provide a sacrifice. The Abraham of this play never mentions God, never even hints that he is acting under orders.

So why does he take a knife to his son's throat? It seems to be because Abraham doesn't like him very much. You get the impression the kid has repeatedly refused to clean his room.

It is rather on that level. Abraham is jealous of the easy relationship that Isaac has with his mother. (Later, Isaac will feel the same about Jacob.) In addition, the son's whole manner seems to mock the father's achievement; Isaac -- who is older than one has usually imagined him -- lounges around and smokes and is a musician, while Dad is a self-made tycoon. You don't have to be an uncritical fan of the nuclear family to find Abraham's actions improbably extreme (or extremely improbable).

A third character, billed as Ram, combines the Biblical roles of the angel who stays Abraham's hand and the male sheep who gets it in the neck as designated substitute. He is a hirsute, capering figure, who could be man or beast but who most suggests the Greek god Pan, with little horns on his head and a set of musical pipes at his lips. He might, come to think of it, represent the Christian God, preaching mercy and killed on account of it.

But neither the writing nor most of the acting can bring the fable to life. The original story is unpleasant on a grand scale, though it can be interpreted as instruction-by-extreme-case. (Abraham, and through him the human race, had to be taught the hardest way about the futility of human sacrifice; after all, every victim is somebody's child. Just telling him wouldn't have cut it.) This version is nasty on a small scale; Isaac, dizzy with relief, plunges the knife into Ram on Abraham's orders. The knife becomes a family heirloom; instead of a cycle of violence being ended, one has started.

We next meet Isaac blind, immobile and enthroned, and asking which of his sons loves him most: like a cross between Shakespeare's King Lear and Samuel Beckett's Hamm (himself a Lear derivative) from Endgame. Sycophantic Esau takes the Shakespearean hint, dresses up Elizabethan and speaks in the clipped blank-verse accents of Olivier's Richard III.

This is a stunt that British actor-writer Steven Berkoff has been pulling for years, and that is here sustained at wearyingly unfunny length, but Isaac seems to like it (and Piatigorsky, unlike Berkoff, does know how many syllables make an iambic pentameter). Jacob secures his hated brother's portion by putting on his cloak and aping his rhythms. This means he gets the knife; Isaac takes it and ritually cuts off the end of his tongue with it. So Jacob goes through the rest of this act, and the whole of the next, with a lisp.

The last episode, by far the strongest, departs from its source by having Jacob himself plead with Joseph instead of sending his remaining sons to do the job. Here at last we have a dramatic situation that's arresting in itself and fruitful in its implications. Joseph, a cold fish acting as the agent of an all- powerful businessman, takes down the old man's details (Jacob seems to have led a life both selfish and feckless) and realizes, though he does not disclose, that this must be his father.

His employer, Farrow, a.k.a. Pharaoh, is another figure out of Beckett (who is certainly another source worth stealing from): a ragged mechanical apparition who moves like a robot, needs to be wound up by his assistant, and when he eventually speaks, does so in a voice coated with rust. He is about to pull the plug on all charity but consents to let Joseph help Jacob, at a price: Joseph must bind his descendants to Farrow's service. This recalls some of Jacob's own shadier Biblical dealings, and looks ominously forward to the next book. It also suggests that Farrow may be the capricious Old Testament God who has so far failed to manifest himself.

So, on one side we have, finally, love between father and son, achieved by their never having had to live together; on the other we have its cynical exploitation by an outside force.

There may be a grand design when you mull it over but in the theatre you merely get a trio of revue sketches: one overblown; one cheaply thin; and one successful. Chris Abraham's austere production might be an impressive frame for a richer text.

The three actors divide the roles according to age rather than continuing character; much the best is Mark Ellis, playing the sons. As young Isaac he is a sharp-edged junior malcontent, deflating Abraham's grandiose schemes for land development on the sacrificial mount with the weary exclamation "Father, it's a national park!"; as Jacob he projects a cynical disgust worthy of Rowan Atkinson's Blackadder; and as Joseph he keeps the veneer and probes beneath it without ever letting it crack.

Gary Reineke, doing the three fathers, is monotonously mournful, though he manages some prickly pathos at the end. Dean Gilmour (of Theatre Smith-Gilmour, the high-end clown troupe) seems to have been hired as a performer rather than an actor: As the ill-fated Ram, he prances and pontificates; I could hardly wait to see him slaughtered. As Esau, he is doomed to repeat a single verbal joke to which he seems technically and temperamentally unsuited. He appears to be coming into his own as the spectral Farrow, a fine figure of a wind-up doll. He makes a superb visual impression; then, alas, he has to open his mouth.

THE EMOTIONALISTS

The Music Gallery, Toronto

Sky Gilbert's excellent new play about Ayn Rand bears a surprising outward resemblance to the old urbane kind of drawing- room comedy.

As in a piece of vintage Noel Coward or Philip Barry, we watch a magnetic central figure in comfortable surroundings, reclining on a sofa and accepting homage. Being female, she has a solicitous husband on hand to greet callers and be generally understanding. Being a successful writer, she is obliged to grant audiences to worshipful fans; in this case, having hit the jackpot as a novelist and as an ideologue, she gets a double dose of adulation. And since she was born in Russia but now lives in New York, she reaps all the rewards of Americas fascination with European accents -- which, at least in women, are taken to be infinitely wise and infinitely sexy.

Gilbert himself tells us in a program note that he encountered Rands works in early adolescence and worshipped them. Today, he still loves the novels but hates the ideas. I can't comment on the former, since I haven't read them, and all I really know of the latter is what I have gleaned from newspaper articles, which made them seem loathsome.

Gilberts play has left my distaste intact, and was probably intended to, but he makes the woman herself enjoyable theatrical company: engagingly monstrous and, by the end, somewhat pitiable. Since pity seems to be the last thing she would have wanted (its certainly the last thing she was ever inclined to offer other people), there's a special kick in extending it to her.

We meet her in 1955, riding high on the success of her first novel, The Fountainhead. We gather she divides the human race into two categories. There are the Objectivists, those with the courage and intelligence to see life as it is, i.e. to agree with her about everything. And, in a vast and despised majority, there are the Emotionalists, weak-willed and weak-brained, who use filthy words like feeling and appear to believe they actually mean something.

Ayn refers to Frank, her husband of 26 years, as "my rock" and my highest value, the latter being not exactly a synonym for love but a pretext for it. Recently, though, she has discovered another, younger, highest value: a psychotherapist in training (and also apparently in practice) named Nathaniel Branden.

Ayn and Nat announce to their respective spouses that they are in love and would like to have time together, twice a week. Whether these meetings will involve sexual intimacy is a matter on which Ayn remains maddeningly ambiguous, perhaps because she doesn't really know herself. She preaches complete honesty but will lie, to herself and others, when it suits her.

She is, in fact, as much at the mercy of her emotions as any Emotionalist. This much is predictable at the start: indeed, its signalled in the plays title. Gilbert's achievement is to mine this essentially static situation for high ironic comedy, and to sustain the mood throughout.

We have already watched Ayn indulge another kind of emotion, the joy of bullying. She has quizzed Branden's wife, Barbara, on the merits of three pieces of music, and has mercilessly berated her for placing Beethoven and Shostakovich above Saint-Saens. Barbara suggests it may be a matter of personal taste, but taste, to Ayn, is a feeble-minded obscenity.

Barbara seems understandably ready to fall apart, and its suggested she let her husband treat her. (This would, of course, be a major breach of professional ethics, but the subject isnt mentioned and one appreciates that from an Objectivist viewpoint it's a trifle, beneath consideration.) Confronted with her husband's putative infidelity, Barbara reverts to conventional type, and seems the stronger for it.

The imperturbable Frank, meanwhile, finally gets perturbed -- not (he says) by jealousy, but by the possibility his wife is about to be exploited by the ambitious Branden.

From what we see of Branden this seems thoroughly likely. Hes an accomplished sexual and intellectual blackmailer who knows exactly how to push Ayns buttons.

There is a parallel plot. Marcel, a young devotee of Ayn's, comes to grovel and to seek advice. He says he was homosexually abused as a boy, and the experience has robbed him of the ability to connect with women. Ayn plainly regards him as beneath contempt, but she preaches courage to him, and off he goes determined to emulate the egomaniacal hero of The Fountainhead.

He invites his assailant out for the evening and they picnic on top of a hill. The older man brings cucumber sandwiches, which gets the conversation around to Oscar Wilde. Marcel, barely able to utter the word "homosexual," lets out his rage, in full confidence he is doing the right Randian thing.

This is the closest the play gets to a critique of Rand's social and political influence, and there is not a word about her virulent economic views (which, through her disciple Alan Greenspan, may have affected us all).

But what we have is plenty. Gilbert has written dialogue that is witty, easeful and revealing; he has shaped it to tell a couple of compelling stories; and he has directed his own play with delicacy and lucidity.

Ellen-Ray Hennessys Ayn is a fiercely disciplined portrait of an outrageous woman, who commits some of the worst outrages on herself. Its especially fascinating to see Hennessy, in the play's early stages, pause and draw herself up before inflicting another humiliation.

She is finely supported by Philip Shepherd, whose Frank is a study in pained, watchful quiescence; by Veronica Hurnik, a touching portrait of decent ordinariness trying conscientiously but vainly to be something else; and by Alex Poch-Goldin, whose Branden, the one character with whom the author cannot bring himself to sympathize, is at least a glistening creep. Gil Garratt is brilliant as Marcel, clinging to furniture in an effort to express inexpressible shame; Patrick Conner as his antagonist is good, and gets better the closer he comes to the edge.

The play is presented by The Cabaret Company, a new group Gilbert has founded for the production of his own plays. That is in fact, he says engagingly, its only purpose. He adds that "each different project will bring together artists that I have worked with before, artists that I have never worked with before, and artists that I have longed to work with."

That seems pretty thorough. I think it means he will cast each play as best he can -- like everybody else.

Black & White Photo: David Hawe, The Cabaret Company / Ellen-Ray Hennessy as Ayn Rand, with Gil Garratt as Marcel: A fiercely disciplined portrait. ;
2000-04-01-eric-bogosian-likes-to-start-:
SubUrbia runs tonight at 8 p.m. ($15) and tomorrow at 2 p.m. (Pay what you can) and again at 7 p.m. ($15) at the Poor Alex Theatre, 296 Brunswick Ave. Call 416-539-9350.

SUBURBIA

The Poor Alex Theatre

Eric Bogosian, best known as author and protagonist of Talk Radio, inspired elevated comparisons when his play SubUrbia was staged off-Broadway in 1995. The New York Times called it "Chekhov high on speed and Twinkies," and the description isn't quite as glib as it may sound. Like Chekhov's three sisters yearning for Moscow, Bogosian's characters are stuck in a faceless and stifling American town from which they dream of escaping to New York. Or L.A. Or probably anywhere.

They also, in their own fashion, philosophize and talk about art and wave guns around. They also drink and, as testified above, do drugs. Unlike Chekhov's people they are social underlings, even in their hometown, but their ranks do include three brothers, sort of - - three guys who grew up together, went through school together, and now, in their early 20s, hang out together.

There is Jeff, who has liberal ideas and vague ambitions of being a writer. There is Buff, who seems to be permanently zonked, or maybe just dumb, who has even vaguer ambitions of making videos, and no ideas at all, just fantasies and prejudices. And there is Tim, who was in the army for a time and has returned as a poisonous and surprisingly articulate racist, or maybe just an all-round hater.

There are also Suze, Jeff's increasingly disaffected girlfriend, who wants to be a performance artist, and Bee-Bee, who is going through detoxification and is dangerously out of things. This group spends most of its time outside the local 7 Eleven, to the great grief and occasional terror of the Pakistani brother and sister who own it.

The play's title is honest but disorienting, at least in terms of an audience's preconditioned responses. Mention "suburbia" and most of us think of families; of lives centred, however discordantly, around a dining-room table.

We think, at this post-Oscar moment, of American Beauty, a film that I enjoyed enough when I saw it to make me feel uncomfortable now about joining in the backlash. Still, I felt cheated even then when Kevin Spacey in his final voice-over started going on about the loneliness of it all; I couldn't see where, other than beyond the grave, he was coming from. Apparently we had been watching a feel- good movie all along, and Hollywood responded with prizes as Hollywood always does.

Meanwhile, in another, but related, realm, the far truer if ostensibly lighter-hearted Freaks and Geeks had its plug pulled. Maybe it was headed in too grisly a direction. SubUrbia is Freaks and Geeks -- the freaky part anyway -- a few years on and with the screws tightened. These ex-kids are all intelligent, or most of them are, but that just compounds the frustration.

Back into their lives comes one who got away: Pony, now a rock star (probably of lesser magnitude). He's been playing a concert at the local stadium; his former friends haven't got it together to attend but they are still excited about his arrival, and he seems unfeignedly and unselfconsciously glad to see them.

He tries gently to disillusion them about the supposed glamour of his new life but is very ready to offer them a ride in his limo. Buff is dazzled (though he proves a graceless guest); Suze, scenting an exit route, is interested; Jeff is puritanically, and jealously, disapproving; and Tim continues to spray venom. With Pony comes his publicist Erica, for whom two of the boys make a play, to which she responds with apparent enthusiasm.

The action proceeds through some savagely unexpected reversals to a physical and intellectual showdown between Jeff and Tim, residual but hopeless idealist against incurable nihilist. The male Pakistani, the same age as the rest but seeming older, upbraids the bunch of them for all the world like Doc in West Side Story telling the Jets and Sharks that they make the world dirty; or at least like one of the Sharks telling it to the Jets. In this world, though, there is no redemption.

The story holds, and so does the dialogue, if you accept Bogosian's habit of using the characters as mouthpieces for their ideas, or lack of them. He is almost too ready to start an argument. There seems to be no reason for the play not to seem more powerful than it does, except that we have met characters like these before and this production doesn't do much to give them new life.

Ed Gass-Donnelly's direction has pace and drive, but not much finesse. The actors can handle the more contemplative moments well enough, except when they're extended into prose arias, but for scenes of conflict (which means most of them) they go into automatic attack mode.

This means jerking out every line on an upward inflection without reference to its content or the person at whom it's directed.

Very likely, this comes down to experience and technique, or the lack of them; the penalty of casting a young play is raw acting (though the same director did much better with the same age group in Equity Showcase's Spring Awakening).

It's probably no accident that the most accomplished performance, by several miles, is given by the actor with the classiest resume. Matthew MacFadzean (Shaw Festival and Theatre Direct) gives the visiting Pony a sustained rhythm and a filled-out personality, as of a guy bending over backwards to be pleasant (which he is) and trying desperately to avoid being patronized (which he can't).

There is something glazed about him, but he never snaps. The other characters snap all the time, and the actors buckle under the strain, except perhaps for Noah Cappe as Buff, who goes through the piece in a grossed-out world of his own.

In the pivotal role of Jeff, Gregory Thomas is overtaxed, though he does give good voice to what seems to be the author's own dilemma: Jeff has all the right instincts and he can even put them into words, but even as he utters them he despairs of them ever doing any good.
2000-04-03-a-bad-taste-that-lingers:
Singapore runs until April 16. Box office: (416) 504-9971.

SINGAPORE

Factory Theatre, Toronto

I doubt that I could pronounce any verdict on Singapore more damning than the one the performers themselves seemed bent on handing down. On the first night they gabbled and mumbled and shouted and gesticulated and swallowed words and acted past one another; the bare-bones production doesn't have much furniture, but if it had they might well have completed the traditional litany of actors sins by bumping into it. They behaved, in short, as if they were deeply embarrassed to be there, and were taking all possible measures to prevent the word, as well as the words, from getting out.

Initially, their efforts are successful. For the first half-hour of John Palmers new comedy, directed by himself, it's impossible to work out what's going on. You can tell that everybody onstage is meant to be venal and lascivious, but what else is new? The fog then lifts somewhat for a couple of bearable, even enjoyable, scenes. In one of them, Sam, a withdrawn young man in his thirties, shares some moments with his father, Felix, an extrovert with Alzheimers, whose favoured apparel is shirt and underpants. They are sitting in Felixs basement, which is where he is kept confined by the woman who is about to become his second wife; and they are going through some decade-old phone bills on which Felix thinks he can get a refund. They also discuss Sam's unfulfilling love life, in which Felix takes a commendable fatherly interest, despite the fact that he's aggressively straight while his son is reclusively gay. This leads them to consult Felixs list of his old girlfriends, and even to plan an excursion to one of them; this plan, though, is nipped in the bud by the girlfriend upstairs, who rightly suspects Sam of trying to take his dad to a lawyer in order to frustrate her own plans to gain control of his property.

We then listen in while the fair schemer herself, whose name is Marjorie, conducts a rebarbative phone conversation with her mother, explaining what she hopes to gain from her approaching marriage, how fast she intends to get out of it, and why this doesnt make her a gold digger.

Tanja Jacobs as Marjorie plays the first part of this scene stretched out on top of a table, and the second crouched underneath it (I lied a little about the furniture); she is occasionally interrupted by her young lover, but most of the time she has the stage to herself, which, in a production so uncertainly timed and choreographed, is lucky for her. She works hard at being shamelessly funny, and succeeds; she is the nearest thing to a reason for seeing the play.

Neither Felix's old flames nor Marjorie's mother has any subsequent part in the action. The play tries to place self- contained comic routines within an accelerating farcical action, which is a tough act if youre not the Marx Brothers. Palmer seems to be attempting a black satiric comedy on the lines of the late Joe Orton, whose comic specialty was to have his characters say and do outrageous things with perfectly straight faces. He brought great verbal skills, and more erratic structural ones, to the elaboration of this basic joke, and made it the vehicle for a sustained comic vision: an outsiders view of a society built on lies.

Palmer may have the same vision, but he doesn't, on this showing, have the skills. Also Orton never dropped his guard, never suggested that, underneath it all, he had a heart. Palmer is apt to go sentimental on us, even bringing down his curtain on some additional bonding between father and son in the geriatric ward, with Felix dementedly recalling his own dad, whom he believes to be not dead but in Singapore (in case you were wondering about the title). Since the characters are Jewish, this seems like an abbreviated relay of a subject currently being treated at great length in The Offering. Orton was insouciant; you never caught him trying to shock. You catch Palmer at it all the time. He starts his play with Sam's elderly lover stepping naked into a bath and trying, ineffectually, to open a vein. This is to stop Sam from walking out on him. He fails, but spends the rest of the play in hot pursuit, lunging at any piece of male flesh within groping distance.

Theres probably a way of making this entertaining, but it doesnt happen here; you keep blotting out the character's existence and groaning when he reappears. Louis Negin plays the role with an enthusiastic grossness born, I sincerely hope, of desperation.

Also on hand is Felix's divorced first wife, who is by no means reconciled to her situation and says of her ex, "I cant forget him like I did the Armani sunglasses I lost on the train to Montreal."

You can tell the type she is. You can also tell what constitutes the scripts idea of biting epigram. If you have to start dropping brand-names to make satiric points, you've either lost it or you never had it to begin with. Dawn Greenhalgh rattles through this entire role as if she, too, had a train to catch, and I found her actions baffling. Aron Tager as Felix starts similarly flustered and befuddled, but quiets down and warms up. Sam, who spends most of the play wishing he were somewhere else, is played by Alon Nashman, who seems to know the feeling only too well.

Shaun Benson plays Marjorie's boyfriend, who is brought to realize the advantages of marketing his gigolo talents to both sexes, and the cast is completed by James Harkness as a biddable rabbi whom Marjorie imports to officiate at her wedding.

The set is most kindly described as functional; walls keep sliding apart to reveal a new scene, even more crabbed and anonymous than its predecessor. For the wedding, the grand farcical climax on which all the characters converge in pursuit of their goals, a staircase is added. That brightens things, though not for long; the staging of the physical comedy achieves prodigies of awkwardness seldom seen on a professional stage.

The trouble with plays that try to wow you with their bad taste is that, when they fail, all you're left with is the taste.

I MIGHT BE EDGAR ALLAN POE

Alumnae Theatre

One has read of performers so versatile and energetic that they do everything but hand out programs before the show and sell drinks during intermission. Christopher Morris, sole acting proprietor of I Might Be Edgar Allan Poe, goes one better and actually does these things, or approximations of them.

This play doesn't have an intermission, but before the action begins there he is, wandering around the set and sometimes off it, to take our tickets. (He doesn't have to wander far: The upstairs studio at the Alumnae, where the show happens, is a bare room without a platform.)

This is not, it turns out, just an economy measure. The play solves the problem that dogs every extended dramatic monologue -- just whom is the actor meant to be talking to? -- by casting the audience as things in his dream; naturally, he has to welcome us. Apparently we play our roles pretty well. He judges it a good dream, and we can agree with him, though its contents are nightmarish.

Morris plays Joseph, a young man confined to a mental hospital who believes himself to be the Gothic fantasist invoked in the title and who is capable of reciting at least one long poem (right at the beginning of the play) and one short story (near the end) straight through, without mistakes and with an impressive variety of accent and gesture. This talent, which should have got him at least a radio contract, instead gets him locked up.

There have been other problems. He has lived in a world of his own since childhood, and has had one especially traumatic past incident involving a fire. His doctors have kept pressuring him to tell them about it but he has resisted. Finally, though, he does tell us about it, and it turns out to be more frightening, because more soberly realistic, than anything in Poe.

Morris, who was an appealing clown in Love's Labour's Lost last summer, plays Joseph as a good-natured innocent lacking a skin, sure of himself but puzzled by everybody else. He seems to have been banished to an attic room, like the madwoman in Jane Eyre. One of its few amenities is an old wind-up gramophone on which, before the play proper begins, he plays a varied selection of 78s. They don't seem especially relevant to what follows, but they do have charm.

So does Joseph, and he makes, much of the time, a lot of sense. Naturally, he sees things differently from his doctors. He complains, contrary to what might be the general impression, that they see life in extremes, take it far too dramatically, while he just accepts.

When he was a child he had a pair of hamsters who ate their young. He wasn't bothered by this but his parents expected him to be, so he obliged. Now he uses the same methods with his psychiatrists: He tells them what they obviously want to hear, and it seems to work.

Sometimes, though, they disappoint him. One shrink has told him that appearing in the hospital talent show would be good therapy for him. He takes her advice but she doesn't turn up for the show. His hurt, though he doesn't dwell on it, is very believable. He says, very pertinently: "Doctors don't have my thoughts -- it's not like they cut me open," so how can they presume to interpret what's on his mind?

The Poe story Joseph performs includes a definition of madness as "overacuteness of the senses." One can see that this fits his own case, and that Poe's affinity with the macabre reflects Joseph's acceptance of it. (He's able to throw in some funny impersonations of academics coming to grips with his favourite author. In Morris' performance, Joseph has a definite gift for mimicry.)

But the central identification seems strained, the quotations overlong (since the play is presumably meant to be more than an excuse for a couple of party pieces) and the title rather cheap. At their best, the writing and acting escape the frame: Joseph is more interesting than Poe.

There may, though, be a tale of mystery (and even of imagination) to be told of Dawson Nichols, who is named as the play's author. The program tells us nothing about him, though it supplies biographies of the director (Daryl Cloran), producer, actor, designer and stage manager. I cannot shake the suspicion that the author is one of the above, working under a pseudonym. On the other hand, he might be Dawson Nichols.

- Until Sunday. Box office: (416) 532-5831.
