WHAT ABOUT LUV?

St. Michael's Theatre

So what about What About Luv?

It derives from a Broadway comedy by Murray Schisgal, called simply Luv, a title that sends both me and my spell-check into convulsions. The play, a cute-as-a button number about a trio of New Yorkers swapping partners and aphorisms, was a hit in the '60s and, in its own inbred terms, it worked fairly well It became a terribly constricted and frenetic film, and much later, in 1984, like every successful American play lighter in tone and lower in ambition than Long Day's Journey into Night, it became a musical. Which is what we have here.

Like the play, the musical has three characters and is set entirely on a bridge. (It's closed to traffic, so there are no intrusions by other people, which might be awkward and would certainly be expensive.) Harry Berlin, who might be a neurotic if he wasn't so crazy, comes to the bridge intending to throw himself off. He is prevented by the arrival of Milt Manville, an old college chum he hasn't seen in years.

In temperament and accomplishment Milt and Harry are poles apart; Harry seems to have no purpose in life while Milt is bursting with it. Milt is out to make money and, by his own account, is doing well at it. He also has a rich emotional life; "I'm more in love now" he says "than on the day I got married. Unfortunately my wife won't give me a divorce."

He has come to the bridge intending to throw his wife Ellen off. His encounter with Harry suggests a marginally less drastic expedient; he will introduce Harry to Ellen and the two will fall in- - well, you know.

Surprisingly -- at least it would be surprising if the script in any way resembled real life -- the plan works. Ellen comes to the bridge not, as far as we know, intending to throw anyone off, though she seems capable of it. She is delighted to find a man who can appreciate her powerful mind. Harry is delighted to find a woman who can appreciate him in any way whatever.

Act two dawns. A year has passed, to the day. The three characters reassemble on the bridge and, would you believe, they are not content. Milt's great romance has not worked out. The marriage of Ellen and Harry (this is a world of short divorces and shorter engagements) is a bust. Harry is only happy when hiding from the world with a paper bag over his head; this, and their total lack of any sex life, is driving Ellen crazy.

So Ellen and Milt, whose repertoire of dirty tricks seems somewhat limited, plan to throw Harry off the bridge so that they can be together again. The show's surface is wrinkled by Harry's disturbance at Ellen's leaving him, but there is no suggestion of real pain.

The Toronto production, judging from a single reference to the CN Tower, has attempted to make the show locally relevant, but essentially it still takes place in a nowhere zone of brittle feelings and glib talk that we have agreed to call New York. It isn't much like the real place, if only because its inhabitants seem able to maintain comfortable apartment existences with no visible means of support.

In the '60s, plays with actions this improbable and characters this thin were routinely described as Absurdist (cf. Edward Albee); now they just look silly, though they still persist in all media (cf. Friends). The musical respects and reflects the play's timelessness, and is probably indulging its own nostalgia for the brand of sweet-and sour, comic-romantic, off-Broadway musical epitomized by The Fantasticks.

Howard Marren's music (which probably sounded even more anchronistic in 1984 than it does now) tinkles competently, and has a taste for pastiche that it indulges whenever possible. Susan Birkenhead's lyrics are adroit, except when asked to shoulder too heavy a burden of exposition. The book, by Jeffrey Sweet, hangs together well; so well that one begins to wonder what could possibly have happened in the portions of text that have been cleared to make room for the songs.

Maybe they included some mordancy, or some needling wit. The show seems to think it's making some sort of statement about life and love and the purpose thereof, and its characters can say, do or contemplate cruel things. But since they're all bloodless, the result is just well-intentioned mush.

So at least it seems in this production, directed by Daryl Cloran, who is also currently responsible for the much superior I Might Be Edgar Allan Poe; his staging here is again competent but the level of performance is wretched. Julia Moore-Gammie's Ellen is devoid of personality, and her singing can't even fill the tiny hall. Christopher Wilson as Harry does have voice, and his lanky frame and lanky personality are right for the role, but his perpetual sickly grin is insufferable. Chaz Thorne's Milt is the tidiest of the three, but for a self-described go-getter he is singularly lacking in get-up-and-go.

The whole show in fact seems to be going through the motions of having energy.When Harry and Milt meet up, they go into an old school cheerleading song and they think, from the looks of them, that they're raising the roof, but not a rafter stirs.

THE ORESTEIA, PART ONE: THE HOME GUARD

Du Maurier Theatre, Toronto

The last du Maurier World Stage season -- but, please the gods, not the last World Stage season ever -- begins with a brave raid on the foundation-stone of Western drama. Britain's National Theatre has brought over its new production of Aeschylus' Oresteia: the only full-blown Greek tragic trilogy that we possess, given in a magnificent translation by the late Ted Hughes and spread over two evenings.

This turns out not to mean one-and-a-half plays a night. Part one is entirely given over to the artwork formerly known as Agamemnon, first and best-known instalment of the original serial.

It's here re-titled The Home Guard, and in Katie Mitchell's production it turns out to be a play about a quartet of veterans from some unspecified war of the 20th century.

They are still wearing their frayed and crumpled demob suits, with poppies in their lapels, and they are in wheelchairs. They seem powerless, but their rulers pay them a lot of attention, so they presumably represent public opinion.

They are, of course, our old acquaintances the Greek chorus, perpetual challenge and perpetual bane to anyone who would stage one of these tragedies and anyone who tries to respond to them.

The dramatists themselves seem to have wearied of the convention, and the choral role in the extant plays grows progressively less.

But in The Oresteia the chorus is still in full flood: filling us in on the story so far, commenting, philosophizing, responding to or interrogating the principals, and listening outside the royal palace to the horrific deeds being committed within.

The climax of this play is the murder of Agamemnon, king of Argos returned from the Trojan war, by his wife, Clytemnestra, in revenge for their daughter Iphigenia, ritually sacrificed by her father 10 years before so that the Greek fleet might set sail for Troy.

As the king and his Trojan concubine Cassandra are slain in the royal bath, members of the chorus debate what they should do, in the end doing nothing.

A.E. Housman once wrote a hilarious parody of Greek tragedy, and especially of the old translations of it, in which the chorus, on hearing a series of blood-curdling screams, observes, "I would not be reputed rash, but yet/ I doubt if all be well within the house."

There is none of that prim vagueness for Ted Hughes. His translation is bold, iron-hard, and colloquial.

It seems to be written north-country; certainly much of it is here spoken north-country, especially the choral parts. Between them, Hughes, Mitchell and the actors have taken the curse off the chorus.

A modern audience, confronted by the traditional line of imposingly masked figures talking in unison, naturally assumes that it's talking for the author, even when it's talking in platitudes (perhaps especially when it's talking in platitudes). Mitchell's approach, veering about as far toward naturalism as Greek tragedy possibly can, establishes them as just another character in the play: a collective character with its own biases and limitations.

If we want to know why they don't intervene at the end, their chairbound state provides the perfect illustration and the perfect excuse. (Since the four actors also play the four named male characters in the piece, there's a sly pleasure in seeing each of them wheel himself offstage -- when we're not supposed to be looking -- to assume his new identity.)

I've never listened to a Greek chorus with more attention or more enjoyment. But this clarity, welcome though it is, comes at a price. In their zeal to communicate, the actors practically button-hole us with each line, frequently prefacing it with a chatty "now" or "look."

Trying so hard to avoid sounding rhetorical, they end up with a new and equally emphatic kind of anti-rhetoric. The principals don't have this option; or at least, and thankfully, they don't exercise it.

But they have other problems. They, too, are modernized. Agamemnon, returning home telling of rape and plunder is, by inescapable inference, a Serbian warlord; Clytemnestra, constantly posing and orating at a microphone, seems to be Eva Peron. Psychologically, these parallels are limiting; mythologically, they're demeaning.

Helen Schlesinger's Clytemnestra has power, and a sense of festering grievance under a politician's politeness, but she runs out of resources.

The old approach to Greek tragedy believed in heroes; the new doesn't. But it seems -- and I readily confess that here I'm at the mercy of what translators tell me -- that the plays believed in them, not necessarily with admiration but with awe.

This play contains the textbook example of hubris: Agamemnon, daring comparison with the gods, is persuaded to tread a ceremonial red carpet into his home. With Michael Gould playing Agamemnon as a cynically weary opportunist, it has no resonance, though the production tries hard to pile it on. The carpet here is composed of his dead child's dresses; incredibly in this realistic context, he doesn't notice. Or if he does, he doesn't say anything.

The production is surprisingly short on visual ideas. There is the carpet and there are the wheelchairs.

There's the sight of Agamemnon and Cassandra dead in the blood- filled bath, as if Charlotte Corday had climbed into the tub with Marat.

There's also a lot of pointless fiddling with tape recorders and video screens. And there's also the figure of the slaughtered Iphigenia, wandering accusingly through the action with a gag on her mouth.

You get the point early on and resent the repetition, but it pays off when her father is killed, and takes her ghostly place. The chain of blood, with two plays still to go, stretches on.

It stretches back, too, in the endless perspective accorded by Greek mythology. At the play's end we meet Aegisthus, Agamemnon's cousin and Clytemnestra's lover and accomplice, who reveals a whole new set of motives, stretching back into the previous generation of the proverbially cursed House of Atreus.

This sudden shift is confusing to us, but the Greeks would have taken it in their stride, as another leaf from a shared book of legend that could be opened or closed at will: a story in which, roughly speaking, everybody is guilty. Similarly the play provides us with a surprisingly complete retrospective of the horrors at Troy, vividly conveyed here in the herald's (Robert Bowman) matter- of-fact account of the city's destruction, or by Lilo Baur's Cassandra in her last prophetic trance.

The play has its own kind of timelessness, conflating past, present and future into a vision, pitiless but humane, of human violence and human suffering. That's what's in it for us now, and it's a lot.

Black & White Photo: Chris Bolin, National Post / The Royal National Theatre production includes Lilo Baur as a nurse in The Home Guard, the first instalment in the trilogy, translated by the late Ted Hughes and being presented over two nights. ;

THE ORESTEIA PART TWO: THE DAUGHTERS OF DARKNESS

Du Maurier Theatre Centre, Toronto

In its 40-year existence, Britain's National Theatre has staged two separate productions of Aeschylus Oresteia. In the early 80s, Peter Hall directed a version that was aggressively stylized: everyone in masks, an all-male cast and a translation that sounded like Anglo-Saxon. It was impressive, in a numbing sort of way. Now - - at the opposite extreme and imported to Toronto for the World Stage festival -- comes Katie Mitchell's production, modern in dress and in technological trappings, and as close to psychological realism as any staging of a Greek tragedy is likely to get.

Mitchell's approach, which I find far the more congenial, comes most into its own in the trilogys central section -- the play that Aeschylus, or his English translators, called The Libation Bearers and is billed here as The Oresteia Part Two: The Daughters of Darkness.

This is the section with the most action, the one closest to the familiar tragedy of revenge. In Part One we saw, or at least heard, Queen Clytemnestra of Argos and her lover, Aegisthus, murdering Clytemnestras husband, Agamemnon. Now they are themselves dispatched by Orestes and Electra, Agamemnon and Clytemnestra's surviving children. Orestes has been living in exile; Electra has stayed home, nursing her hate. When Orestes returns, Electra spurs him on to vengeance -- not that he needs much spurring. He does have momentary qualms about killing his mother, but his sidekick, Pylades (who is otherwise entirely mute), reminds him that they are acting under orders from Apollo's oracle, and he goes ahead. No sooner is the deed done than Orestes begins to feel the consequences. He has a vision of the avenging Furies, who are to dominate the proceedings after the intermission.

I enthused yesterday over Ted Hughes translation, the finest and most speakable dramatic verse heard in English since the same poets adaptation of Seneca's Oedipus, which Peter Brook directed (also for the National) in 1968. His lines make up a superbly flinty armoury for actors -- a set of weapons to be hurled across the family dining table, which is where Mitchell sets the murders. First we see Orestes, arriving in disguise and getting past palace security to be admitted through a vast and clangorous metal door. He announces his own supposed death, to the delight of the tyrant Aegisthus (played by Sebastian Harcombe as a smooth-fingered piano strummer and tango dancer).

The delight proves short-lived, as does Aegisthus, leaving the siblings free to deal with their mother. While she pleads (with a half-accepting desperation, in Helen Schlesinger's performance) and Orestes hesitates, Electra sits in silent, hysterical expectation. The reason shes silent is that her author never actually wrote her into the scene. Its hard for us to accept, but Aeschylus -- unlike Sophocles, Euripides and dozens of moderns who've built plays and operas around her -- wasn't much interested in Electra; after shed served her turn by recognizing Orestes, he dropped her.

Theres quite enough in the lady's one scene for Lilo Baur to get her teeth into; she paints a powerful picture of a gnawing, obsessive daddy's girl to the last, and she has no trouble maintaining it through her subsequent silence. (Silent, that is, except for her scream when she hears her mother being killed offstage. This is surprising, and a bit sentimental. Wouldnt she have gloated?) But it does point up a problem. Its thrilling to hear scenes written 2,500 years ago responding so readily to the modern actors' touch. But though these characters live very vividly in the moment, they don't accommodate much digging. Paul Hiltons Orestes establishes himself from his first line as a quivering neurotic who commits matricide in order to acquire an identity; he then has to go on striking the same note, and the effect is grindingly monotonous. (This is perhaps the place to point out that, for all its daring and all its excitements, this ambassadorial production does not present English acting at anything like its current best.)

The chorus in this episode are subsidiary figures: Trojan slave girls, confederates of Electra, who assist in the conspiracy and can easily take a naturalistic treatment. The last instalment, though, is the chorus play. They are the Daughters of Darkness, though some of them seem to be sons. More familiarly, they are the Furies, who subsequently change into the Kindly Ones, a.k.a. the Eumenides (that being the title by which this final section of the trilogy is generally known). Mitchell's visual presentation of these vengeful wraiths, as a troop of menacing nannies, is the least ludicrous I have seen, but she cannot solve the problems of the play's narrative, of which the chief is that it doesnt have one. What happens is that Orestes stands trial in Athens, the Furies attack him, and Apollo defends him. The jury is deadlocked, but the goddess Athena has the casting vote and she acquits. She then offers the Furies a consolation prize: They can have a new life and a new identity in Athens, presiding over the transformation from a culture of bloodlust and vendetta to one of peace and mercy. One of my old textbooks called this "the apotheosis of patriotism," and its still possible to be stirred by it. Aeschylus, who had lived through his country's wars with Persia, cannot have been too starry-eyed about human justice. Hughes certainly wasn't, and Mitchell obviously isnt. But its an ideal to be striven toward, and it has never been more nobly stated. It's worth remembering, next time you hear someone sounding off about "Judeo-Christian values" as the be-all and end-all of Western civilization, just how much we owe to the Greeks.

The Furies' transformation was the one point at which Halls hieratic approach worked better than Mitchells. But what really lets her and us down, despite the dignified lucidity of Joy Richardson's Athena, is the legal buildup. The arguments advanced in Orestes' favour are specious, not to say misogynistic; and as counsel for the defence, Michael Goulds sneering Apollo (a corduroyed flying doctor) does his client very little credit. One is humanely glad that Orestes gets off from eternal torments, or whatever it is the underworld social workers have in mind for him, but its difficult to feel much joy. It's an honourable failure, though; and where it succeeds, the show is electric.

THE MILL ON THE FLOSS

Premier Dance Theatre

A celebrated critic once said that if a novel worked on stage, it was fairly safe to assume that it wasn't a first-rate novel to begin with. He said it at the end of the 1950s, and we have learned a few things since then: We've learned how to make dramatizations of novels into more than breathless enactments of the basic story- line. We have found ways of capturing a novel's narrative voice as well as its incidents, and we have learned to give the texts room to breathe; the Royal Shakespeare Company's eight-hour celebration of Dickens' Nicholas Nickleby remains the classic in both respects. At the very least we've discovered that, even when it doesn't entirely work, an adaptation of a great 19th-century novel (that's usually what we're talking about) can provide a richer experience than a simple bad play. It has a penumbra; it can at least hint at richness of character, of metaphor and of social background.

All this can be felt, somewhere, in The Mill on the Floss, Soulpepper's contribution to the World Stage season and a production that reunites this company with its first director, Robin Phillips. It gets, though, progressively harder to hold on to.

The main device of Helen Edmundson's version of the George Eliot book is to chop its heroine into thirds. Three actresses share the role of Maggie Tulliver, daughter of a rural English mill-owner and possessed -- like her author -- of more passion, intelligence and imagination than her society knows what to do with.

Maggie finds neither a personal nor professional outlet for her abilities. She has little luck with men. She is passionately attached to her father, and especially to her older brother Tom, but both in different ways let her down. Two men court her : Philip Wakem, the sensitive and musical hunchback son of a lawyer, and a drawing-room Lothario named Stephen Guest.

She is drawn to both, but social and personal pressures prevent a union with either. Her father goes bankrupt and loses the mill, though he's allowed, humiliatingly, to stay on as manager. Maggie and Tom are immersed in the struggle to regain their inheritance and -- to adopt the prevailing metaphor -- to keep their heads above water.

The three Maggies are not cast according to age. (We first meet the character as a nine-year old, but none of them is that young, nor tries to be.) Rather they are cast according to developing temperament. So, Torri Higginson is the headstrong Maggie, whom her family call "the gypsy"; Julia Arkos is the ascetic Maggie, who finds a creed in the teachings of Thomas a Kempis on self- abnegation; and Brenda Robins is the gauntly sexual Maggie, trying to come to terms with her own emotions.

All of these characteristics, of course, are at least latent throughout, so while each performer carries the burden of the action for a certain time, the other two are always on hand to argue, advise or observe. The device has its moments, and the first transformation is magic, but mostly it's just irritating. It prevents any of the actresses from having a real crack at the part, and it prevents the audience from bonding with the character. (They've got each other. Why do they need us?) But we need to have a stake in Maggie, if we are to follow her through a long, increasingly complicated evening.

For the first half, adaptor and director have the narrative pretty well in hand. Eliot's family comedy is of Shakespearean richness, and it travels well. Terence Kelly, if not the rugged patriarch I have always imagined, brings out the prickly pride that makes Mr. Tulliver buy his son a classical education (against his own natural doubts) and that eventually brings him to financial and physical ruin.

Roberta Maxwell is economically delightful, and a little frightening, as his wife, obsessed with the family linen. The same mature actress inexplicably doubles as Maggie's cousin Lucy, her rival for Stephen's love, and it is here that disaster sets in. The play, which hitherto has pretty much set its own tempo, begins to sink under the sheer pressure of the novel's events; while, with no sense of the girls being contemporaries, tension evaporates, and meaning, and even understanding.

Most of the men, too, are cast above their proper age, but they get away with it. (And if that sounds sexist, too bad.) Steven Sutcliffe is superbly sensitive as the long-suffering Philip; Tom McCamus is suitably Byronic as Stephen (and even better as a sarcastic school-teacher); and Stephen Ouimette, cast rewardingly against type, has the full measure of Tom, from self-centred but likeable cub to prematurely hardened young bear.

We do, though, lose track of the relationship between brother and sister, and this has devastating consequences for the finale. The novel's epigraph is "in their deaths, they were not divided," and the pair end up consumed by the river that flows beside their home.

Even in the book, this conclusion seems arbitrary; in the play it comes out of nowhere, though in theory it's been set up by Maggie's life-long obsession with the fate of medieval witches who were hanged if they were and drowned if they weren't. As a woman intellectually advanced but emotionally unsupported, Maggie's felt herself in a similar position. Up until now Phillips has staged the play with sober skill, on a rostrum with a couple of drop-in screens. His evocation of the flood, involving a full complement of actors waving umbrellas, is all right but hardly cataclysmic; and when it was over, the audience seemed surprised to find that the play was too. From any director, this concluding stumble in rhythm would be regrettable; from one of Phillips' stature it's dumbfounding.

FOR THE PLEASURE OF SEEING HER AGAIN

Bluma Appel Theatre

Michel Tremblay's new play, much his mellowest, is a loving tribute to his mother. She died, nearly 40 years ago, too soon to see her son's career take off. As he tells us here, she was fascinated by drama; she would get engrossed in TV plays, caught up not only in their stories but in their mechanics.

What, she used to wonder, was going through the actors' heads while they performed, or indeed after the performance was over? She never got to go to a first night, much less attend a rehearsal, and the play is her son's attempt to make it up to her.

We can guess that she inspired some of the mother-figures in his earlier work. Now here she is in her own right, at the centre of a play that makes no bones about being a play. It's funny, and it's touching, but not quite enough of either.

Mother and son -- called here Nana and Narrator -- are the only characters. The play begins with the narrator outlining for us all the kinds of heavy drama -- from the Greeks to Beckett -- that are not in store for us this evening. (Several of them, as it happens, are currently available in Toronto on other World Stage stages. This play -- a co-production with the Montreal Centaur Theatre, is the Canadian Stage Company's contribution to the international festival but will run beyond it.) This speech is a piece of blush-making self- consciousness that the explicit theatricality of what follows does not excuse.

We then watch a series of remembered dialogues, scenes during which the son's age rises from 10 to 20; the consequent shifts in attitude are subtly captured by all parties.

We witness the son's teasing dissection of his mother's favourite romantic novels, and her passionately indignant defence of them. We hear her, who has spent her married life in Montreal, yearning for the plains of Saskatchewan, where she grew up. We listen to her describing and deploring, at length, the faults and foibles of her brother-in-law, whose conversation seems limited to descriptions of Fernandel films, and of his wife, whom she likes even less.

She muses on the problem of aristocracy; of which families have blue blood, and by what divine dispensation it got that colour in the first place. She accepts without fuss both her son's probable choice of career and his homosexuality.

Finally, we see her succumbing to stomach cancer and worrying how her family will get on without her. She acts everything out, with a zest for impersonation and a natural gift for language. She also invents and embroiders, partly for her own enjoyment and partly because she senses that this is the stimulation her boy needs; though she complains that as he gets older she "doesn't know what to make up any more."

Linda Gaboriau has translated the script from the French, and I suspect that the play, and especially the character of Nana, have lost something on the journey. There is a peculiar quality in French- Canadian writing and performance -- a sort of gnarled sophistication -- that generally keeps sentimentality at bay.

Nicola Cavendish as Nana seems to be having too obviously good a time; when she turns on the character's extravagances, when she doubles up with glee at her own comic turns, she is less a force of nature than a wind-up doll. She's better in the quieter scenes. Dennis O'Connor makes an admirable narrator, keeping the child alive within the grown man without any attempts at explicit juvenile characterization; but he, too, can be overly ingratiating. (Though it's nice to know that Tremblay can twinkle.) Gordon McCall's direction is efficient but sweet-toothed.

The play ends with the son contriving a theatrical apotheosis for his mother, a natural theatre artist who never got to set foot on a stage. As a joint tribute to the woman who nurtured his talent and the medium that let him express it, this should charm us off our feet; but it works a little too hard at it.

Tremblay tells us in his title that he wrote about his mother "for the pleasure of seeing her again." We can share some of that pleasure -- it would be impossible not to -- but not as much as he or we would like.
2000-04-17-german-language-drama-does-a-:
FIRE IN THE HEAD

Imperial Oil Opera Theatre

If Fire in the Head were an English play, one would take the title to be a conflation of Shakespeare's fire in the blood and D. H. Lawrences "sex in the head." As it happens, the play is German, brought to Toronto last week by the Berlin Schaubuhne Theatre as the first foreign-language offering in the duMaurier World Stage season.

The allusions, though, still seem pertinent. Both those quoted phrases are disparaging: Shakespeares a puritanical warning against premature experience; Lawrence's a furiously distasteful summary of whatever he disapproved of. They both concern sex gone wrong. In Marius von Mayenberg's play sex never seems to stand a chance of going right.

A bourgeois family -- father, mother, elder daughter Olga, younger son Kurt -- is paraded before us; and you can tell from their fixed smiles, dads especially, that theyre living a lie, or maybe a pack of them. (German theatre, even more than most, is still fighting the battles of the '60s.)

Kurt is on the brink of adolescence; Olga is in its throes. Both feel an acute discomfort with the human body, especially those of their parents. In Thomas Ostermeier's production, the family home -- and by extension the family itself -- is laid out for us as if in a diagram. There, side by side on a wide and shallow white platform, are the dining room, denoted by a table constantly laid; the bedroom, reduced to one frame and one mattress; and the bathroom, represented by a wash basin.

Mother and father, who seem in theory to be engagingly permissive, give their children brief, embarrassed and somewhat contradictory talks on sex. Olga gives Kurt, who is watchful and withdrawn, a more practical initiation by reaching inside his pants and manipulating him. He seems to like it enough to become obsessed with her. She, however, has found herself a boyfriend, a contrastingly sporty type named Paul. Her family approves of him; father even treats him to a jovial drink and handshake after Paul has deflowered his daughter.

The tone of the plays early scenes is comic, if not really funny, and its performed with a delicacy and fullness of detail that puts most of our local product to shame. (Of course, German subsidized theatres have resources we can only dream of.) All the actors have mobile faces that are just as expressive when they shut down -- as Karl's, in particular, often does.

The mixture of shyness and boldness in the sex scenes is absolutely truthful; and the end of the first encounter between Olga and Paul has maybe the most creative use of audience participation I have encountered. Paul, shaking off his underpants, has tossed them into the front row; now he has to ask for them back -- very politely and in English -- and in doing so he involves us in his embarrassment without actually embarrassing us.

Judith Engle, Robert Beyer and Mark Waschke give remarkably free and full performances as the juniors, while Wolf Aniol and Gundi Ellert give them solid but flexible support as the increasingly strained elders.

The strain sets in when Karl, who has perched impassively on the wash basin, either seeing or imagining his sister and Paul making love, begins to act out the play's title and turns into a full- blown pyromaniac, setting fire first to himself and then to everything else. Olga becomes his enthusiastic accomplice.

What was an acridly sympathetic comedy of puberty turns into an update of the Jacobean incest tragedy Tis Pity Shes a Whore, brother and sister against the world -- and whore is precisely the word that Paul throws at Olga when he finds out Kurt is revolting against his family, against society, apparently against human biology. He reprises his opening lament about the degrading process of birth, and one wants to shout back "get over it," or perhaps -- since the proceedings are now becoming exceedingly drawn out -- "get it over."

The problem is not that the couples excesses are incredible; it's that the characters don't have enough life in them for us to care either way. They are puppets for their author to manipulate as he pleases, and any obsession on display seems his rather than theirs.

Staging and acting are as good as they ever were, but their virtues now begin to seem like vices. They are taking enormous care over a text that doesn't deserve it.

I have two questions to ask concerning the program. One: Why is it so very difficult to discover the name of the playwright? The author of the simultaneous translation, relayed over rented headphones, gets better billing. Two: Why, given that most of the audience will be reliant on that translation to understand the play at all, is there no synopsis?
2000-04-18-cheerfulness-will-keep-breaki:
Krapp's Last Tape/Footfalls and Otra Tempestad close tonight.

FOOTFALLS/KRAPP'S LAST TAPE

Harbourfront, Toronto

OTRA TEMPESTAD

Buddies in Bad Times, Toronto

Do you remember last Saturday? It was lovely inToronto. How long ago it seems.

It must have been on just such a day that somebody in Ireland remarked to Samuel Beckett on how fine the weather was. Beckett, we are told, agreed.

"It's the kind of day," his friend continued, pressing his advantage "that makes you glad to be alive."

"Oh," said Beckett, "I wouldn't go as far as that."

Two of Sam's short plays -- Footfalls and Krapp's Last Tape -- are being given at Harbourfront as part of the World Stage season, and I emerged from them into the Saturday-night balm, just in time to collide with other spectators who had been spending a day at The Oresteia in the house next door. There we all were, grave but resilient, joint witnesses to two-and-a-half millennia of human tragedy.

With Aeschylus as with Beckett, cheerfulness will keep breaking in.

The last part of The Oresteia, after all, dramatizes the birth of a humane legal system -- the moment at which trial-by-jury replaced the more primitive process of trial-by-Fury.

There is no guarantee, though, that humanity will not slip back into its old vengeful, warmongering ways -- not with those capricious and extremely provisional Greek gods in charge. Beckett, working on a far narrower canvas, similarly gives us brief glimpses of happiness before proceeding to stomp all over them.

Footfalls, which is late Beckett, has always appealed to me as the author's sour joke on his audience. It came after a succession of plays in which the characters -- immured in dustbins or sandpiles or funeral urns, or just crouched and immobile -- had been progressively denied the use, and even the sight, of their limbs. Audiences (and possibly actors) were getting restless. May, the one visible character here, is seen, however, at full length and -- my God! -- she even gets to move about. In fact she paces ceaselessly. She doesn't, though, seem to enjoy it much.

"And that," you can hear the author saying, "is what movement gets you. Don't ask me for it again."

May is pacing because she has to attend to her bedridden mother, whom we hear but do not see, and the routine has turned her into a resentful automaton. But then, it seems, she always was that way inclined. She also has a very Beckettian habit of regarding herself as a character in a literary text.

The bare-bones situation is similar to the one depicted in a more recent Irish play, The Beauty Queen of Linnane, with the difference that these characters don't hate one another.

May's mother, indeed (especially as delivered here, in the deep, silver tones of Jennifer Phipps), is enduring, and even solicitous. She worries about her daughter -- as well, given Elizabeth Shepherd's performance, she might. Shepherd's physical aspect as the one proud walker is magnificent: her face is a tragic mask, with enough grief packed into it to furnish an entire Greek chorus. She matches it, though, with a slow, unvarying, agonized delivery, as of a rusting gate. The look is authentic but the voice sounds painted on.

This portentous way of doing Beckett derives, I think, from the vocal mannerisms of the late Patrick Magee, the momentous Irish actor who was one of his favoured interpreters and who, among other things, was the first to perform the earlier Krapp's Last Tape.

This monologue is an unqualified masterpiece: a work that illuminates a human condition (if not the human condition) through a single, transfixing image that is also both whimsically and sardonically funny. It's surprising the play hasn't been done in Canada before, since one of its principal early exponents, on stage and records, was Donald Davis of this parish.

It is also, even more than Footfalls, a realistic piece. You want to know where Krapp is? He's in what passes for his study. You want to know what he is? He's a writer whose potential, both personal and professional, has been savagely unfulfilled. You want to know what he's doing? He's replaying one of a set of tape recordings he has made at yearly intervals, as an aural diary, reflecting on his past and present. Krapp at 70 listens to Krapp at 40 vowing to cut down on his unhealthy consumption of bananas (he hasn't) and lamenting the end of a love affair that, it seems, he destroyed because it was going too well. He makes a new tape, castigating his own past sentimentality, but the pain in his eyes shows he still feels it.

John Neville plays him superbly at both stages: walking with an arthritic trudge, taking his last-ditch pleasures -- of peeling his bananas and enunciating his favourite word, "spool" -- with sybaritic relish, and generally reminding us how fine a character- actor he can be when not giving hollow displays of the voice beautiful.

An even finer vocal instrument, that of the 80-year old William Hutt, was celebrated on Sunday afternoon at the Winter Garden. With Diane d'Aquila as compere, this occasion was more fluent and mostly less sticky than such tributes often are. Colleagues and admirers paid homage, told stories, even sang songs (Mad About the Boy, with an additional male lyric previously unheard.)

There were videos of Hutt himself, revisiting past homes and enjoying his present one. He finally took the stage himself, to respond to what had been said with a presumably imprompu wit that vaildated the anecdotes. Much was justifiably made of his appearance on a Canadian stamp, in his last great role of Prospero.

So it was appropriate to repair to Buddies in Bad Times for Otra Tempestad, presented by Teatro Buendia from Cuba, and probably the first production of The Tempest in which the first character named in the program is Hamlet. Macbeth and Shylock also appear; and so, apparently, in an earlier version, did Othello, though he seems to have been lost in transit.

They share the stage, and the Afro-Caribbean island, with a bearded dictatorial Prospero, a lusciously bare-breasted female Ariel (well acted, too, by Giselle Navaroli), and a Miranda who falls for Caliban though her father wants her to marry Macbeth.

It's Shylock who snitches on the lovers, and he's sneaky throughout. He also chants, wears a prayer shawl, and is generally more regrettable than his Venetian prototype. Fidel-Prospero has his faults but, as yet another Shakesperean character once put it, "I fear there will a worse come in his place." Macbeth, who deposes him, turns out to be a cannibal.

Throwing Shakespeare wide open can be a fruitful idea, and the local colour and local music make Flora Lauten's production fun, but there seems little point to doing it beyond doing it. There is invention but no true inventiveness; and the audience, primed by scene-by-scene projected synopses, merely waits for each episode to give way to the next.

Black & White Photo: Rachel Clare, Du Maurier World Stage / Teatro Buendia's unusual production of Otra Tempestad (Shakespeare's The Tempest) includes appearances by Hamlet, Macbeth and others. ;
2000-04-20-a-soldier-s-tale-fit-for-rejo:
Gaudeamus runs till April 22

GAUDEAMUS

Elgin Theatre, Toronto

Let us rejoice. Gaudeamus, the much-travelled and much-lauded production brought to World Stage by the Maly Theatre of St. Petersburg, begins as amazingly as any show I have ever seen. A man dances onto a snow-covered stage, whirls happily around, then suddenly falls through a trapdoor.

Others follow him on, in accelerating succession, each cavorting in is own style and each meeting the same fate, each through a different trap. The stage becomes a maelstrom of prancing and disappearing bodies, a ballet performed on a minefield.

The men then pop back up like so many jack-rabbits, and we notice each is now in military uniform. One of them begins to recite, "To be or not to be -- in English. (His words are solemnly reproduced on the surtitles above the stage, also in English, though it might be a pleasantly surreal touch if they were to be shown in Russian.)

Those trapdoors might be foxholes, or they might be latrines. In the course of the evening -- two-and-a-half hours, no intermission - - they represent both. Gaudeamus is about the army. It's a kaleidoscopic play, worked up in rehearsal through collective improvisation, and based on a novel by Sergei Kaledin that has the distinction of being the only book to have been banned under Gorbachev.

One can see why: at least assuming the play, in style or substance, faithfully reflects its source. Scatologically disrespectful references to Lenin in the first dialogue scene suggest the work was moving with the times but was slightly ahead of them. It was also, and unforgivably, attacking from below.

The director is Lev Dodin, who is a legend. He has a company of 17, every one of whom seems able to act, sing, dance and play a musical instrument. The characters -- the male ones, anyway -- are members of a Construction Battalion, a division of the army used as a dumping-ground for ex-cons, physical misfits, ethnic minorities, and other undesirables, exploited as cheap labour with a few gestures toward military training. The period is the declining days of the Afghan campaign, with morale at an all-time low.

After the prelude, the infernal descent of the conscripts, we see a rookie recruit being hazed by a couple of old men," squaddies with a year's service behind them. Life, we gather, is a matter of survival: surviving the unofficial and generally vicious pecking order, surviving the work, surviving drink and drugs, surviving corruption.

The battalion commander promises three of the men --among them a Gypsy and a Jew -- an early discharge as a reward for cleaning the toilets; it turns out he wants money as well. Pay day is preceded by long and insanely repetitive lectures about taking care of your comrade when hes drunk.

For some practical indoctrination on Soviet policy in the Middle East, the men are divided into two groups -- Jews and Arabs -- the latter group unfeelingly including the one actual Jew in the brigade. Near the end of the play, there is a murder.

The weekly excursion into town, with the chance of picking up women, is of course all the men live for. Some of these encounters are unfeeling, some are actively brutal, a few are enchantingly lyrical. A junior officer brings his wife an unglamorous coat, a gift shyly proffered and rapturously accepted. A soldier suggests to a lady librarian she is frigid, and receives enthusiastic proof to the contrary. Their tryst takes place on top of a grand piano (flown on stage at regular intervals) and ends with the two of them picking out a tune with their bare toes.

Though individual characters persist and recur, there is no real story; there are 19 discrete scenes, some more dreamlike than others.

Dodin acknowledges a debt to the Russian experimental theatre of the 1920s -- the critical, surrealist kind murdered by Stalin in the name of "Socialist Realism" -- but the actual acting is earthy and colloquial in a way I dont associate with that tradition, or indeed with any other kind of Russian theatre.

Most of the exports I've encountered have been, for obvious reasons, classics, mainly Chekhov, or new plays performed as if they were classics -- with flexibility, certainly, and sometimes with humour, but always in a dignified, basso profundo, kind of way. (The men have generally looked and sounded like Boris Godunov.)

The actors here are as light on their feet and in their speech as the performers in any Western service comedy. The style connects in its rude subversiveness with the Central European tradition of The Good Soldier Schweik.

But it's also bound to remind us of Catch-22, especially in the day-tripper sexual encounters and in the mad futility of the army routine. A scene in which a soldier digs up an old field-telephone and finds that orders from the past have to be executed in the present is especially Heller-ish. Theres also a strong taste of Oh What a Lovely War, in the use of music and clowning

But then, Western culture, especially pop culture, runs right through the show -- final proof that it is, for better or worse, international.

Some of it seems added for our benefit, changing from town to town: at least, I doubt if a reference to Margaret Atwood played as well in Glasgow or New York, let alone St Petersburg, as it does in Toronto.

Others are plainly integral: the old Beatles song Girl, for example, cropping up at different times to yearning or malicious effect.

The actual text is, to judge from the surtitles, less rich than the staging or the basic idea -- there aren't many good jokes -- and thus probably takes its toll on the acting.

But talented and devoted as these performers are (many of them, as in the Vancouver production of The Overcoat, were students when the show began) it's hard to have any continuing involvement with these characters; there are too many of them, going on and off like lightbulbs. The show becomes relentless -- which, admittedly, suits the subject.

When they finally sing the title number -- Gaudeamus Igitur, the old school song about the glory of youth -- the irony seems very heavy. It's also, though, happily double-edged. The people on the stage are young, and in this production they do have something to glory in.

Black & White Photo: Erin Riley, National Post / Gaudeamus, from the Maly Drama Theatre of St. Petersburg, is based on the only book to have been banned under Gorbochev. ;
2000-04-21-lepage-returns-to-dazzling-fo:
Far Side of the Moon runs till Sunday, but is fully sold out.

THE FAR SIDE OF THE MOON

Premiere Dance Theatre, Toronto

I had forgotten how immensely charming Robert Lepage can be. The Far Side of the Moon, his new show, is a solo performance as dazzling as his previous Needles and Opium and even more enjoyable. It is also longer, at least approaching the scope of such ensemble pieces as Tectonic Plates.

After his more recent productions -- the clever but pointless one- man Hamlet and the dismally ragged Geometry of Necessity (the Frank Lloyd Wright one) -- we were praying for Lepage's return to form. Our prayers have been answered, and then some.

The marvel of Lepage at his best is he can mount the highest of high-tech productions and still place humanity lovingly and touchingly at its centre. He can achieve this with a large company or, more often these days, with just himself.

As it happens, the relationship between humanity and technology is much of what this show is about. Lepage plays, principally, a former philosophy teacher (cultural philosophy, he says his game is) who finds speaking in public almost impossibly difficult. He has in fact done the opposite of talking himself out of a job. He is obsessed with man's conquest of outer space, and especially with his journeyings to the moon.

He draws a stern contrast between astronauts (in it for the glory, and usually American) and cosmonauts (in it for the wonder, and usually Russian). Most space travel, he says, is undertaken for reasons of narcissism. His ideal observation post would be mounted on the far side of the moon, the side from which the Earth is invisible.

Our guy, who lives in Quebec City and whose name is Philippe, spends his weeks in study and his weekends working as a tele- marketer, in which capacity he at one point finds himself poignantly addressing a long-lost, now-married girlfriend. (The play is full of telephone conversations, of which we hear only one side, and not the least of its accomplishments is that nearly all of them are thoroughly plausible. We never feel one speaker is repeating the other, just for our benefit.) He was diagnosed in boyhood with an eye defect that still necessitates regular brain scans. He is also coping with the recent death of his mother, and with the care of her pet goldfish. He wanders around his tiny apartment, and also around the surrounding countryside, discoursing on the state of both locales and of the world in general for the benefit, it seems, of an audience of unseen extra-terrestrials. In these musing, misanthropic monologues -- hilariously written and perfectly timed -- he comes over as part Woody Allen, part Glenn Gould.

In the end, Philippe, who has never even flown before, gets to go to Moscow to give a talk. It misfires, for reasons it would be cruel to reveal. The event prompts Philippe's younger brother to describe him, also on the phone, as "a loser, but a nice loser."

The brother is a winner, and seems for much of the time to be not nice; certainly Philippe resents him, though both he and we may learn better. He is a TV weatherman, who seems to regard the North American climate as a conspiracy against French Canada. ("Yes, they're sending us their bad weather again.")

Rich and successful, also gay, he advises Philippe to consult a "wallet-psychic" who apparently can tell from the state of your purse whether it's ever likely to attract any money. (He drops this idea after opening Philippe's closet and declaring "if I were money, I'd never come in here.") He does, though, display a more vulnerable side when trapped in an apartment-building elevator -- and this, we are presumably meant to reflect, in an age when men can reach the moon.

Lepage also appears as a Russian spaceman and part-time painter; as his homier American counterpart televised live from his capsule to answer awkward questions from kids; and -- magically but mysteriously -- as a green-clad woman who reaches into a washing machine and fishes out a space-child.

Washing machines bulk large in this production; one of them apparently figured in a traumatic incident in the youth of the two brothers. Early on, we find ourselves taken from outside the wash to inside, an optical effect I commend to future stagers of Alice Through the Looking-Glass.

The laundromat is the basic location of a set (Marie-Claude Pelletier is listed as assistant designer, but it's not clear whom she's assisting) that displaces that for The Overcoat as the most innovative and effective in recent Canadian memory. Basically a long grey sliding wall, it reveals, among other things, Philippe's apartment, a large and lonely hotel bar (spectacular), the inside of a plane and an accusingly bare lecture hall. Within it are a few simple props (the different things Lepage as director can do with an ironing board are enough in themselves to guarantee this show a place in theatrical history).

Around everything there is music, unobtrusively spooky, by Laurie Anderson, and much film footage of the history of space travel. I'm not sure that this counterpoints the main action as meaningfully as Lepage intended, but then I had doubts about the equation of lunar conquest and declining human morality in Tom Stoppard's somewhat similar play Jumpers (which also had a vulnerable goldfish in its cast, along with a more celebrated hare and tortoise). It was still the best comedy of the last 50 years. This show has the wittiest script in ages (by Lepage, with Adam Nashman), perfect performance (in, for good measure, the performer's second language), and sly and superlative staging. It's an incomparably joyous occasion.

Black & White Photo: Sophie Grenier, World Stage / ROBERT LEPAGE: A marvel. ;
2000-04-22-oval-office-anguish-the-night:
Nixon's Nixon closes today at the Jane Mallet Theatre with performances at 4 and 8:30 p.m., $35-$45. Call 416-366-7723.

NIXON'S NIXON

Jane Mallet Theatre

It wouldn't be easy, but perhaps the only thing left for a playwright to do with the character of Richard Nixon would be to make us feel sorry for him.

There is one moment in Nixon's Nixon that comes near to doing this. The president, with Watergate unravelled and impeachment beckoning, protests the most hurtful thing about the situation is what it will do to his daughter, Julie. He mentally flashes back to his celebrated Checkers speech, and to how his little girl had melted in his arms after she had seen the broadcast. "Daddy" she apparently said "you mentioned Checkers on television."

That TV appearance, of course, is the one moment at which Nixon successfully twisted the heartstrings of the American people. It's notorious; and in invoking it, playwright Russell Lees simultaneously discredits it. That is pretty much his approach to Nixon throughout. The man was in a tough place, but he deserved it. I agree; but I don't necessarily want to hear it re-stated for 90 minutes.

Nixon's antagonist in this two-character piece (an Anglo- American contribution to World Stage) is a tuxedoed Henry Kissinger who is paying a reluctant evening call on his fallen chief in what is presumably the Oval Office.

Whatever it is, it's nostalgically rendered in Charles Towers' production by an economic assemblage of lampshades, rotary phones and radiograms.

Each man has his own agenda. Nixon's is the more complicated, as he alternately craves vindication, consolation and someone to join in his memory-gams. Kissinger merely wants an assurance that the incoming Gerald Ford will keep him on as Secretary of State.

Only so, he insists, can Nixon's diplomatic legacy be preserved; and the doggedness with which he keeps repeating it can be mildly amusing. Of course it's also, in the circumstances, somewhat unfeeling, and the play's title may be double-edged. It may refer to the president, trying to rewrite history according to his own prescription; or it may refer to Kissinger, ratting on his boss as his boss ratted on the country.

One can believe that in his desperation Nixon would keep re- playing his triumphant encounters with other heads of state, and that he would get Kissinger to listen to him. It's harder to credit that they would, at the commander-in-chief's insistence, systematically act out all the roles. ("I'll be Brezhnev; you be me.")

At first embarrassed, Kissinger gradually gets into the spirit of the thing; and at what you might call the Julie moment he takes on that part too; which gives it some of its zing.

The play is moderately well-written. It builds through a mind- bending rationale about the bombing of Cambodia as a way of disengaging from Vietnam ("They'll think I'm really off my rocker.") to a final fantasy scenario about engineering a new global conflict as a way to distract the attention of the American voter. (Well, we may be meant to think, it worked for Clinton; though one doubts that he ever contemplated unleashing a Third World War.) It climaxes with Nixon, momentarily appalled, computing the number of deaths engineered by his administration, with Kissinger meticulously doing the numbers. But it never takes off, unless you consider a cross- talk between two actual politicians to be hysterically funny in itself.

The acting is good. Tim Donoghue gets the look of Kissinger uncannily right (probably it's the glasses, and perhaps the hair), and if he often sounds like Dr Strangelove, well, who in this role wouldn't? Only once, though -- when he remembers his boyhood as a refugee from the Nazis -- does he seem like a human being; otherwise he's an automaton, and though this may be the intention, the effect is still dull.

Keith Jochim's Nixon is less of a lookalike: Lacking the oily civil-servant air that contributed to his downfall, and in fact seeming somewhat open-faced and rugged; but he gets the bluster and the hollowness very well. (Did you see Fail Safe the other week? And did you find yourself wondering what recent U.S. president could have behaved with the dignity and compassion of the one played by Richard Dreyfuss?)

Both characters are naturally preoccupied with those damning audio recordings which, at the time of the action, have yet to be released. In the context of this World Stage season as a whole, and given Nixon's notoriously earthy vocabulary, the play might be regarded as the real-life version of Krapp's Last Tape.

Black & White Photo: World Stage / Keith Jochim captures Nixon's bluster and hollowness, while Tim Donoghue looks uncannily like Kissinger in Nixon's Nixon. ;
2000-04-22-tribute-to-shakespeare-a-birt:
Shakespearean Gala at the Winter Garden Theatre at 8 p.m., $50- $100. For tickets, call 416-872-5555.

Last spring Don Shipley, director of the du Maurier World Stage, was watching Simon Callow, the rolling-toned and rubicund British actor, giving a benefit performance at Harbourfront of his personal program of Shakespeare sonnets.

Listening to Callow's lucid account of these difficult poems gave him the idea of presenting a whole evening of Shakespearean verse, done by some of its best international practitioners. It also struck him that Shakespeare's birthday -- April 23 -- was going to fall smack in the middle of the 2000 World Stage season.

So tonight -- actually one night early, but the exact birthdate is in dispute anyway, though we know he died on the 23rd -- Shipley mounts his Shakespearean Gala at the Elgin. It's the apex of a weekend of Bardic celebrations, and, says Shipley, "a chance to look at Shakespeare for the first time as we usher in the new millennium."

Shipley may be over-pessimistic in his belief that the speaking of Shakespeare is "a lost art -- a dying art" (theatres across the English-speaking world have training schemes in operation to preserve it).

However, we can agree that at the highest level it's rare, or imperilled, or anyway a treat to hear done well.

As well as being a celebration of the man himself, Shipley sees the occasion as "a tribute to Shakespeare's actors. He was an actor, and he wrote for actors; and these are the thoroughbreds."

The actual line-up of thoroughbreds is governed, as always, by availability. A lot of people who hoped to be free weren't. Shipley's been trying to sign them up for nearly a year. It looked, for a long and exciting time, as if he might secure the ultimate prize and get Judi Dench, who among other things is probably the best speaker of Shakespeare active today, but a film finally got in the way.

Ian McKellen, perhaps the nearest thing to her male equivalent, expressed great eagerness to appear and was similarly prevented (he's in Australia, shooting Lord of the Rings) but he has filmed an opening tribute to his colleagues.

The colleagues make an impressive list. Claire Bloom will host the evening, and will also figure in a couple of appetizing duets. In the '50s, at the Old Vic in London, Bloom was the Juliet of her generation; now she'll be performing the Balcony Scene, opposite John Neville, who in 1956 was her Romeo in a North American tour that included the Royal Alex in Toronto. (Well, John Gielgud gave thrilling renditions of Hamlet's soliloquies when he was in his '70s.)

Neville, who long before he came to Canada was Britain's reigning Shakespearean juvenile, will reprise his chorus from Henry V, and will end the revels as Prospero.

Bloom will also play Kate from The Taming of the Shrew, opposite the Petruchio of Christopher Plummer: Not roles with which either of them are associated.

Plummer might be called the senior member of the evening's Stratford, Ontario contingent; his juniors include Colm Feore and Brent Carver, described by Shipley as the best classical actors of their generation ("It doesn't get better than those two"). Carver will actually be singing a setting of a Shakespeare lyric; Shipley wanted a balance of spoken verse and song, and his other vocalists range from Melanie Doane to the operatic soprano Measha Brueggergosman, performing one of Desdemona's arias from Verdi's Otello.

I rather wish Simon Russell Beale were doing a song, since he has the voice of a trained chorister. He's a youngish English actor who's little-known over here (unless you caught his brilliant Widmerpool in the TV serial of A Dance to the Music of Time) but has already had a remarkable classical career. It's remarkable in that he's the kind of stocky unglamorous actor who doesn't usually get cast in the heroic roles. (He says himself that, though he always wanted to be a star, he wasn't sure whether it was going to be as Gielgud or as Zero Mostel.)

But he has now played Richard III for the Royal Shakespeare Company, and Iago for the National Theatre, both to great acclaim, and later this year he'll be doing Hamlet, also for the National and with an out-of-town date at the castle of Elsinore itself.

At the Elgin he'll be giving bits of his Richard and Iago: "I'm well known for playing bastards -- if I'm well known for anything. I'm fascinated by characters who live in hell -- by Shakespeare's picture of people at the limits of their behaviour. Iago really is a psychopath: a case study for a modern audience. Richard III just wants to be king; he has motives -- I understand them even if I don't understand his methods."

And, most encouragingly in this context, he's "very optimistic" about the future of Shakespearean acting.

"There are different ways of doing it. There are no rules -- just as long as you make people understand the meaning. There's the language and the emotion -- and they're identical.

"But you start with the language."

Which is where we came in.

MOTEL HELENE (TARRAGON); SHAKESPEAREAN GALA (WINTER GARDEN)

Francois, the narrator of Serge Boucher's Motel Helene and one of its three characters, is a young Quebecois who reads a lot of books and has ambitions to write his own. In the meantime he works for his father, who owns a convenience store across from a small apartment. This is the home of Johanne, a seamstress, who has packed rather too much living into her 25-odd years. At 16 she gave birth to a son; two and a half years ago the boy vanished from outside the apartment, never to be seen again. Johanne still maintains a monogamous relationship with Mario, the child's father, who comes around regularly to have sex; you might call him her live-out husband.

Francois, who is virginally gay, becomes Johanne's confidante and, one supposes, her friend, though an oddly passive one. He seems, if such a thing is possible, compassionately dispassionate; he resembles the narrator-figure of a Tennessee Williams play or, perhaps more precisely, the Christopher Isherwood of I Am a Camera (a fine, neglected play, obliterated when it became the source of the musical Cabaret).

He, too, treats the lives around him as raw material for some future literary work; he, too, makes copious notes that are pressed into service as dramatic exposition -- though, since we live in a more theatrically complicated time, Francois' notes (actually they're diary entries) are less straightforward, more compromised in their effects, than Christopher's ever were. To put it another way, Francois isn't as nice a guy and this is not as nice a play. (That's a description, not a value judgment.)

As Chris with Sally Bowles, Francois is fascinated -- part amused, part appalled -- by Johanne's sexuality. Her body is what defines her for Mario and -- dangerously -- for herself. Whatever else may have been in their relationship has been destroyed by the loss of their son, an event that both have tried, and failed, to blot out; the memory keeps resurfacing in shouts and tears.

Johanne makes her own dresses, experiments with the colour of her hair and -- under protest -- the size of her breasts. (Mario now says they're too big, though one doubts he always thought so.)

The play takes place in suffocating heat, during Johanne's summer break, and it unfolds in a series of short, sharp scenes, separated by bursts of pounding rock. This gives it a clinical air, as if Francois' detachment had seeped into its bones.

The action is sexually explicit, and legitimately so; the sex is necessary information. The visual rawness also contrasts tellingly with Johanne's crucial and rapturous account of a night of passion, spent with a stranger at the notorious Motel Helene. The ending is stark, and also logical, but not altogether satisfying; there is a disjunction between what we are told and what we actually feel.

Nearly all the action takes place in Johanne's kitchen, which doubles as a living room and is indeed very lived in. The domestic detail in Jackie Maxwell's production is superb; everything is in place, down to a trio of books that Francois brings Johanne as holiday reading at the beginning of the play, and that lie there unopened for the duration.

The script, adapted (this may mean roughened up) by Judith Thompson from a literal translation by Morwyn Brebner, whizzes compellingly by, though it also goes in for literary flights that the actors have trouble integrating with the rest of their performances. Tony Nappo's physically convincing Mario has recurring attacks of deadness. Francois' narrative fluency (very 1950s American) defeats Brandon McGibbon, but his conversational reticence comes over very well.

Jane Spidell is similarly in and out of the central character of Johanne. When she's out, she's telling us about her emotions, without much nuance; when she's in, she's perfect. The core of the character is there, a battered pride, and the look is wonderfully right.

Climbing into the World Stage ring after the two French-Canadian heavyweights, Lepage and Tremblay, Boucher can hardly compete with the former but easily outpaces the latter, in the way that salt can generally conquer sugar.

HAPPY

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, Toronto

That Ronnie Burkett is a master puppeteer can by now be taken for granted.

The marionette work in Happy, his contribution to World Stage, is fully up to standard. Each of the dolls is a lovingly individualized creation, and they are worked -- sometimes as many as half-a-dozen of them at once -- with the usual fearsomely intricate skill. Burkett pulls all the strings, does all the voices; he also designed the set and costumes, and of course wrote the script. Hooray for him.

He also has dramatic ambitions far beyond those of your average Punch-and-Judy merchant. His previous show, Street of Blood, realized them triumphantly. This one doesn't, though it certainly tries hard.

Its title, which has big-time thematic significance, is also the name of its chief character and raisonneur. Happy, named without apparent irony, is a loquacious old man who lives in a small-town rooming house, most of whose other occupants are his contemporaries. The exceptions are a married couple, very young and very loving; their happiness is cut short when the husband suffers an aneurysm and abruptly expires, just as they are on the verge of making love.

The rest of the action is largely concerned with his widow's attempts to come to terms with her loss. The old people around her are mostly in similar states of mourning, many of them maintained for years. They all nourish fantasies, some of them concerning one another. One innocent old fellow, for example, has for years been infatuated with the now-housebound town vamp.

I have to quote from the press release, which says that the play explodes "the commonly held belief that life exists somewhere in the subtle shadings of grey."

I am at a loss here because this common belief is not one I have ever come across, at least not expressed in those terms, or anyway not outside the lyrics of pop songs.

The contrary belief, apparently, is that "life exists ... in a rainbow of colours and endless dimensions." And Happy, whose crackerbarrel philosophisings are interminable, actually tells us with a straight face that if you want the rainbow, you must have the rain.

To support this theory of colours, Burkett has supplied an oppressively unwieldy superstructure. At regular intervals the doll's-house set is trundled around to reveal a puppet stage upon the puppet stage. On it there cavorts a godlike and/or Satanic figure, who seems to be running some kind of baleful nightclub while luxuriating over what fools them mortals be. His exact power over them is difficult to gauge; maybe he's just a voyeur.

Anyway, he don't allow no colour in his kingdom; the performers on his bill sing songs that make Jacques Brel sound cheerful, and he gets very angry when his assistant actually appears with traces of red on his cheeks. He himself has nothing new to say, and keeps on saying it.

Life below is repetitive, too. Every so often the play says things, about love and loss, that I found both true and moving, but they never have any vital connection to the people saying them. To call the characters puppets may seem pointless in the circumstances, but the joy of Burkett's best work is that one takes the characters as real, more so than many whom we see portrayed in conventional plays by flesh-and-blood actors.

The bereaved young wife, though she has a nasty surprise to spring on us at the end, spends most of the time just moping, repeating a catch-phrase about jumping or being pushed that doggedly fails to resonate.

Happy himself has very few scenes with his less-fortunate compatriots, and this adds to the monotony. (It also seems to undercut the play's philosophy: If you believe in the clash of colours, why not bring them together?)

Near the end, we learn his optimism has not come easily, but at this point the revelations about the traumas in his past seem gratuitous. It's just putting on the agony, like the last-minute disclosure in Street of Blood that the housewife heroine had AIDS.

Burkett's acting skills, which I had previously thought inexhaustible, turn out to have limits. They do not extend to giving vocal life to a stageful of characters who are old or depressed or both; the overall tone is a drone -- a whimsical drone, at that.

There is, though, one notably succesful scene. In Street of Blood, Burkett's confessed obsession with the Holocaust seemed dragged-in, perhaps because there was quite enough going on in the play without it.

Here, though, with less competition, he makes good on it. Happy remembers one of his wartime buddies who took part in the liberation of a camp, and we see him desperately trying to comfort a survivor. It's a very simple scene, and a powerful one. I don't think it would work with actors.

Black & White Photo: Peter Redman, National Post / RONNIE BURKETT: His acting skills are not inexhaustible after all. ;

THE LION KING

Princess of Wales Theatre, Toronto

The beginning of The Lion King is, as everybody has said, wonderful. It shows animals assembling, African jungle animals. They come down the aisles; some of them appear in side-boxes. There is always a certain pleasure in seeing four-legged creatures impersonated by two-legged ones, but the ingenuity of Julie Taymors staging (not to mention her design of costumes, masks and puppets)is of a different order from any we have seen before.

Two humans jammed together to create one elephant is not perhaps so very surprising (not that it happens in many shows), but we aren't usually allowed to see the actors through the skin -- and the frank artifice makes the result even more persuasively elephantine. The big elephant has a baby elephant in tow; and this, of course, is entrancing.

Then there are giraffes, each heart-stoppingly represented by a single actor on stilts, and both the sight and the movement here really are extraordinary. All these creatures are rendered with a grace that one might normally compare to that of gazelles, especially, of course, the gazelles.

Grace (extending even to a rhino) and wonder and a touch of humour: Like all good things, it's over too soon, but it is, of course, reprised at the end. Taymor, who went on in Titus to show civilization as a jungle, here gives us the jungle as a paradigm of civility.

There is a song going on during this prelude, Circle of Life, but one hardly notices. (Were more aware of it at the end, when the circle is completed.) There is also a dramatic situation -- the animals are gathered to render homage to the newly born cub who is to grow into the title character -- but one hardly notices that either. As the evening proceeds, both the plot and the score of the show remain negligible but, unfortunately, less easy to ignore.

There have, however, been magical diversions en route. There has been a stampede of wildebeests, represented by puppets (plus a few masked mortals) of increasing size and menace, silhouetted against a doom-heavy sky. There have been journeys through the veldt, in which rapidly moving actresses with grass growing out of their heads play the scenery. There has been a drought, represented by a pool of blue cloth that shrivels to vanishing point. (Richard Hudsons set -- a very traditional bare arrangement of three parallel sets of wings -- is most notable for what is put inside it.)

There have been lionesses in mourning, a majestic sight, with white ribbons flowing from their eyes for tears. There has been some hypnotic dancing; Garth Fagan's choreography is at its best in a celebratory set-piece that kicks off the second act, and in which muscles ripple in time to the music.

There has been some authentic-sounding African music, hypnotically sung and chanted, and most of it composed by Lebo M. This part of the score, written for the show, sits oddly with the songs carried over from the Disney movie, which are the stalest white bread. An occasional flicker in Tim Rice's lyrics recalls his younger, funnier days, but they rapidly descend to the standard contemporary level of gush and uplift, in which abyss they find Elton Johns tunes all ready and waiting.

With them go the story, which concerns the assassination of Mufasa, king of the jungle, by his jealous brother Scar; Scars successful attempt to pin the blame on Mufasa's son, Simba, who flees into exile; and the return of Simba, grown into young adult lionhood, to reclaim his inheritance.

There is the ghost of a love story, between Simba and a decisive lioness called Nala (a paler version of the new-look heroine who started coming off the Disney assembly-line when the studio discovered feminism).

There is also comedy. Initially this is supplied by Zazu (Jeffrey Kuhn), a horn-billed bird who acts as the king's supercilious advisor, and seems to have slipped out of Gilbert and Sullivan. He fades out, to be displaced by a trio of hyenas, Scars henchmen, who are fairly engaging; and by Timon the meerkat (Jonathan Wilson) and Pumbaa the warthog (Mark Terene), who befriend Simba and arent engaging at all.

Timon and Pumbaa belong to an old cartoon tradition, and their routines -- one squeals, the other lumbers -- are of the kind that can work on the screen, even when the material is as terrible as it is here, because of the distancing effect; it's cute to hear animated drawings talking and singing like old-time vaudeville acts. Real live actors, even if they're dressed as animals -- especially if theyre dressed as animals -- dont have the same charm. (Much of the schtick seems like a retread of earlier, better Disney pictures, especially The Jungle Book. The cheer-up jingle Hakuna Matata is The Bare Necessities, much diluted.) The fact that Taymor has dressed these scenes with the same visual sophistication as the others -- these characters, too, are half puppet, half visible actor -- actually makes them worse.

The nearest thing to acting comes from Richard McMillan, who as Scar combines the elements of pantomime villain and neurotic Shakespearean usurper, topping the mixture with a pungent whiff of camp and enjoying a spectacular death-fall. He also manipulates his mask quite beautifully. Eugene Clark is a stolidly imposing monarch, Phinda Mitya an even more imposing and not at all stolid female- baboon-as-shaman.

The nominal leads -- Araya Mengesha and Steven Allerick as the young and older Simba, Georgina Johnson and Saskia Garel as the young and older Nala -- do what's required, though the kids seem as usual to be having more fun with it than the grown-ups.

For all the fanfares about the happy union of Taymor and Disney, they aren't really a match. The bad parts of the show don't merely detract from the good; they travesty them. I would gladly sit through the highlights again, though I think I would prefer to stand; at the back, so that I could slip out easily.
