SHOCK HEADED PETER

Elgin Theatre, Toronto

The set for this British contribution to World Stage looks like a Pollocks' Toy Theatre -- one of the miniature playhouses, with plush curtains, three sets of wings, a balcony and two flanking doors, that middle-class English children used to be given for Christmas (perhaps still are given, in some enclaves of tradition) as a reward for being good. Its dimensions make one expect a pupet show; and, what with Ronnie Burkett and The Lion King, we have been having a basketful of puppets.

There are, it turns out, some dolls involved in the proceedings, but most of the work is done by grown-up, more or less human performers. They have to adapt themselves to their confined circumstances, rather like the actors in the between-floors scenes in Being John Malkovich. The show is not that witty, but it carries on as if it thinks it is.

The production is based on Struwwelpeter, a fringe-classic volume of poems and drawings first published in 1844 and the work of a Victorian doctor named Heinrich Hoffmann. Searching for a book to give his own children, he found only thunderously moralizing versified sermons, and so set out to write his own parody of the genre -- a collection of cautionary horror stories involving boys and girls who were not good and who came to deservedly ghastly ends. Struwwelpeter himself, a.k.a. Shock Headed Peter, refused to cut either his hair or his nails, and so turned into a monster of tangles and talons. He certainly gave me bad dreams when I first encountered him, though they were probably inspired by the illustrations rather than the text.

Hoffmann's verses ("Any thing to me is sweeter/Than to see Shock- headed Peter") are not especially smooth or inventive; actually they're rather poor stuff to have come from the century that gave us Lewis Carroll (whose lampoons of moral examples for kids are far more suave and lethal) and Edward Lear. But he paved the way for other, more accomplished, sick comics: for Harry Graham, with his Ruthless Rhymes for Heartless Homes, and especially for Hilaire Belloc, whose Cautionary Tales include the hilarious fable of Jim, who ran away from his nanny while visiting London Zoo and was eaten by a lion .The reaction of Jim's elders is very Hoffmanesque: "When nurse informed his parents they/Were more concerned than I can say./ His mother as she dried her eyes/Said, 'Well, it gives me no surprise ...' "

The current show, directed by Phelim McDermott and Julian Crouch, builds up the matter of Peter into a study of his concerned parents. Having waited long for a child, they are delighted when the stork delivers one (I do not speak in metaphor) and appalled when their son proves so spectacularly unconcerned about his personal hygiene. They push him under the floorboards, from which he eventually bursts forth, though not before his mother and father have taken on some of his most alarming phsyical characteristics.

In the intervals of this anecdote's slow unfolding, we hear other tales of Hoffman, concerning such delinquents as Harriet who played with matches, Conrad who sucked his thumb and Fidgety Philip who could not be discouraged from handling the cutlery at table.

They are told through music, provided by the Tiger Lilies -- a piercing lineup of accordion, percussion and double bass. They play a kind of art pop, which is sometimes appropriately haunting (notably in the song of Fidgety Phil) and sometimes just screechy.

Every story goes the same way: Child misbehaves, child perishes horribly, parents take it in their stride -- so essentially we are hearing one joke again and again and again.

A certain suspense is provided by Martyn Jacques, the white- faced leader of the band, who sings in an impressively sustained falsetto that makes the words extremely hard to grasp. He also wrote the lyrics, which are "adapted" from Hoffmann and not, as far as I could tell, adapted for the better. The show is described as a junk opera. They got it half right.

I hated it, but every so often it got under my guard. The staging is very assured, with many monstrous props festively deployed. Julian Bleach, one of the show's five credited creators, also presides over it as an actor-manager in an advanced state of rundown. He enters through one door, informs us in sepulchral tones that he is the "the greatest actor in the history of the world," gives up, leaves the stage and re-enters through the other door with no better success. He goes on to play many parts, some of them human, with a battery of snarls and grimaces that are certainly energetic but also seem endearingly half-hearted. When he's really disarming, though, is when he abandons all attempts at the grand manner, drops into the vernacular and treats us to the comedy of anticlimax.

Finally, even this proves insufficient and he explodes -- at us. "All right, Toronto" he yells, "I'll have you know I was trained in London." (I wonder what he said in London.) "This is absolutely meaningless to you, isn't it?" he grumbles, conveying equal disgust with himself and us.

It isn't quite meaningless; it seems to be a satire on 19th- century theatre and parenthood. But as both are caricatured from the outset (it's always open season on the Victorians), it doesn't mean anything. Even worse is the show's attitude to its own source; it tries to parody material that was parody to begin with, and that could only be funny if it were delivered fast and economically, with a straight face. It's comedy at the expense of comedy -- a theatrical definition of futility. The first-night audience seemed genuinely to love it, so by all means go and make up your own minds. And always keep ahold of nurse for fear of finding something worse.

Black & White Photo: The monstrous imagery of Shock Headed Peter is certainly scarier than the lyrics. ;

THE SUIT

Wintergarden Theatre

The name Peter Brook sets off literally great expectations. The shows for which he is most famous have large themes, or at least a lot of actors: King Lear, A Midsummer Night's Dream, The Marat-Sade and the Indian epic The Mahabharata.

The Suit, the piece he has brought to the World Stage from his Parisian headquarters, the Theatre Bouffes-du-Nord, is by contrast a domestic drama with only four performers, though between them they play about a dozen roles.

It isnt, in fact, as great a departure as all that. Ever since he set up shop in Paris 30 years ago with an international group of actors, Brooks work has emphasized the charming and the intimate; it has been a blend - sometimes disarming, sometimes disturbing - of outward informality and inward discipline. That isn't a unique combination; it characterizes much good theatre. I don't know if The Suit could have been directed this effectively by anyone else; chances are it could. But as it stands its a beautiful piece of work.

Like much of his Parisian oeuvre, it comes out of Africa, in this case directly. Its based on a story by Can Themba, a black writer from Sophiatown. Sophiatown, a suburb of Johannesburg, was apparently a cultural (and multicultural) oasis in the desert of apartheid.

When the authorities destroyed it, they effectively destroyed Themba too; he died in exile, an alcoholic. (Sophiatown was replaced by Soweto, which says volumes.)

The Suit was adapted to the stage by Barney Simon, a pioneer South African director who founded the famous Market Theatre in Johannesburg, in collaboration with a playwright and journalist, Muthobi Mutloatse. (Both men, like Temba, are now dead.)

Simon's production was a success at home and abroad (it was much- praised when it visited London) and Brook has directed its text in a French translation by Marie Helene Estienne, which, to complete the circle, comes to Toronto equipped with English surtitles.

It's a story of jealousy. Philemon and Matilda have an apparently happy marriage, full of mutual solicitude. One day Philemon is tipped off by an older co-worker that Matilda is having an affair. He rushes home and more or less catches her in the act; the lover runs away but, not having the leisure to get fully dressed, he leaves his suit behind. Philemon takes what the Elizabethans (those specialists in jealousy) would have called a quaint revenge.

He insists that the suit become part of the family.

It takes meals with them, draped carefully over a chair; they take it for walks. Matilda, at first abashed, begins to find her own consolations in the game; when Philemon is out she flirts with the suit; arranges it languorously over her shoulder, strokes it, finally and dreamily dances with it. Its a lovely theatrical image: perhaps the fundamental reason that both Simon and Brook were drawn to the work.

Its matched by the modest but merciless physicality of the play's ending, when Philemon takes his strategy one fatal step too far; if one thinks of Othello (one of the many Shakespeare plays that Brook has never got round to directing) it's not because the jealous husband is black -- so are all the other characters -- but because he is faced at the end with a loss as bleakly irrevocable as Othellos of Desdemona. Its symbolized, like Othello's, by the sight of a woman on a bed.

Then there is the music. Sophiatown was known, among other things, for poetry and jazz, and jazz -- plaintive trumpets and joyful vocals -- fills the air here.

Matilda was once a singer, and dreams of being so again. (Or perhaps -- since she protests so much and so self-consciously about "show business" -- her career was another fantasy; certainly her affair seems like a compensation.)

There is no direct political comment, and very little that's indirect: Philemons pretext for returning home is that hes forgotten his pass (the virtual symbol of oppression) and one of his friends dreams of being able to buy liquor without restrictions. But it is possible to see the marriage and its destruction as an image of Sophiatown itself: a precarious strip of happiness in a rough world.

So a simple story has theatrical levels; and, as in all Brook's best work, the actors flesh it out to the limits. Princess Erika's supple and delicate performance as Matilda is matched by Bakary Sangares open-faced Philemon whose defining quality is his humour; it starts as good humour -- hes a playful, solicitous husband, and modulates into bad; his life becomes the playing of a practical joke, good intentions corroding within him.

Mamadou Fomba and Cyril Guei play narrators, friends and neighbours -- including, memorably, a couple of committee ladies whom Matilda encounters when she turns to social work as therapy. They also give lightning sketches of a rapid succession of guests when Philemon, in the last stages of screw-turning, throws a party.

This isn't one of Brook's extravagantly cross-cultural productions but it has the grace and lightness from which, over the years, he and his players have forged an international style. It breathes trust.

2000-05-01-the-worlds-most-discussed-dir:
Profile of Peter Brook.

Peter Brook has had -- is still having -- a unique career. He is now 75, and ever since he was 20 he has been the most-discussed, most-admired director, first in the English theatre, then in the English-speaking theatre, and now probably in the world. Last week, he was in Toronto with his production of The Suit, probably the most anticipated event of a World Stage festival crammed with brand-name international goodies. It lived up to expectation, in quality if not perhaps in quantity. It was a four-actor play that achieved a piercing emotional effect through charm, intimacy, and firm but gentle persuasion.

In this it resembled the man himself, five minutes of whose conversation are enough to turn anyone into an admiring disciple. Partly it's what he says and the affable firmness with which he says it -- as of a man who, even when he's questioning himself, is secure in the belief that questioning is the right thing to do. Partly, it's a shared unspoken awareness of his track record.

And to a large extent it's his eyes; never having had the opportunity to sit at close quarters with either Paul Newman or Frank Sinatra, I have to pronounce Brook's the clearest, most dazzling and most penetrating blue that I have ever beheld. They subdue and captivate interviewers; they must have been of immense persuasive assistance; and they constitute, I am sure, a vital part of his armoury in rehearsal.

The Suit, like nearly all his work since 1974, originated at the Theatre Bouffes-du-Nord, an old theatre in an unfashionable part of Paris that Brook and his colleagues converted from a state of genuine decay into one of cunningly simulated dilapidation. He's placed a bare, open stage within a traditional proscenium auditorium, so actors and audience share a space. Here he runs an international acting troupe: French, English, American, African, Japanese.

In a recent memoir, Threads of Time, he says that "for years, when asked the inevitable question 'Why did you move to Paris?' I would give the answer that seemed to suit the questioner, and the reporter would scribble it down in delight." One favourite answer, he told me last week in the lounge of the Sutton Place Hotel when I too asked the inevitable question, used to be "because of Margaret Thatcher." Here is some more of what I scribbled down:

"In 1968 Jean-Louis Barrault" -- the great French actor and director who at that time ran Paris' world stage season, the Theatre des Nations -- "asked me to do a Shakespeare workshop. I said I'd do The Tempest with an international group, and see what common elements there are between actors from different backgrounds working on the same text. It proved interesting and it led to putting together the international centre.

"So the work had started in Paris; and this wasn't entirely fortuitous. Paris has an entirely different artistic background. English work is always parochial -- meaning that we always use our own local themes. For example, Ted Hughes' poetry is always north- country." This certainly seemed to be the case in Hughes' translation of The Oresteia, which also came to World Stage from the British National Theatre; the lines and the rhythms drove the actors due north. "In Paris, the whole tradition is of a meeting of artistic currents from all over the world: Picasso, Modigliani."

He might also have mentioned innumerable American writers, painters (or would-be painters) and jazz musicians.

I suggested that he might have felt happier working with an international group in a city in which he himself was an expatriate - - it created a level playing field, so to speak -- but he didn't seem to think there was much in that; besides, Brook has always been a dedicated traveller and explorer -- one of nature's cosmopolitans - - and Paris had long been a second home.

In the three years before they founded the Bouffes-du-Nord, the actors were, in his words, "a nomad group" playing in Iran, in America and in Africa, where they would famously enter a village, unroll a carpet, and see how they could hold the attention of an audience by the acting-out of stories.

Some of this had its seeds in Brook's legendary English production of A Midsummer Night's Dream. This is famous for its stage magic -- its juggling, stilts and trapezes -- but Brook cites a single performance given in a Birmingham youth club where none of the trappings could be used. They had to re-invent the performance as they went along -- while using all the knowledge they had accumulated of the play itself -- and to trust one another and the audience. They found that in these circumstances an audience "can give you more."

It also got him out from under the proscenium arch: a magical frame in which he had been able to conjure anything he wished. He was a comparatively late convert to the doctrine of the open stage - - actors and audience "in one room" -- but now it governs his work. The Bouffes -- certainly when I used to visit it regularly in the '70s -- is a superb space, a crucible of energies. And always Brook himself seemed to be somewhere in evidence, dressed in a smock, like an unusually cultured concierge. He had gone discreetly native.

The troupe's membership is fluid; people come, go, and constantly return. As semi-permanent pillars, Brook cites a remarkable Japanese actor, Yoshi Oida, and Bruce Myers, a thoughtful and mischievous actor whom I once described, to his own delight, as "a Royal Shakespeare Company dropout."

Brook is skeptical about the idea of maintaining an absolutely permanent company. "In the '60s we all had this dream of 'making a family' and it always exploded in a short time; a self-declared family is an artificial one. We don't have to do our casting artificially, around a fixed group; people can leave us and go out into the ordinary show-business world: into an environment that's less comfortable than ours, but necessary."

Brook himself was once a vital part of that "ordinary show- business world," directing musicals and London farces as well as Shakespeare and opera, and arguably he remains so. His most successful Paris productions tend to re-appear across the world (often transmuted from French into English) and he remains a master showman and visual orchestrator, even when working on a tiny scale; in The Suit he created magically poignant images with a single orange sheet on a bed. And the commercial theatre on which he cut his teeth -- the enchantment-hungry theatre of a London still locked in postwar austerity -- was in many ways an exciting one.

"In England, they'd never heard of the idea of ensemble," he says. "And yet John Gielgud had essentially been working over and over with the same people -- he had 30 years of ensemble. I was happy to be in a milieu of highly talented people, where the watchword was quality at all costs -- even if it was at the cost of a certain kind of reality. I consciously went on from that; I could feel the changing winds."

His work now varies between free-flowing but meticulous explorations of classic plays (Shakespeare, Chekhov) and new works often built on old literary or mythological foundations; the most celebrated a nine-hour version (sometimes done as "a dusk-to-dawn mar-athon") of the Indian epic The Mahabharata. The Suit, being a new but pre-existing play, is an exception, though its African cast and setting obviously carry on from some of his earlier work.

He is appreciative of other people's epic accomplishments; a few years ago he visited Montreal with a production of Samuel Beckett's Happy Days, a virtual monologue featuring his actress-wife Natasha Parry. Here he broke a self-imposed rule by writing to the local papers, protesting against what he considered their churlish treatment of Robert Lepage's masterwork The Seven Streams of the River Ota. Lepage must have been delighted; it's difficult to think of a theatrical figure whose good opinion is better worth having.

WORLD STAGE WRAP-UP

Anything That Moves (Canadian Stage Theatre Upstairs); Dali (Tarragon Extra Space), Toronto

Watching and listening to Anything That Moves, I was all set to salute Ann-Marie MacDonald as that rare bird, a playwright who can write lyrics: This at a time when even most lyricists can't write lyrics.

Six songs into Act One, however, she shook my confidence severely by having one of her characters launch full-throated into the astounding declaration "Monogamy! Monotony! There's a reason why they rhyme!"

There are far better reasons why they don't rhyme: hard, factual reasons having to do with the sound of words and the stressing of syllables. "Monotony" could rhyme with "botany", and Irving Berlin once built a whole song by pairing it with "have you got any", accent on the "got."

A celebrated jingle rhymed "monogamy" with "made a hog o' me", and that's good too. I trust you can hear the difference. I think people who believe that "monotony" rhymes with "monogamy" are largely to blame for the state of the world.

So, as it turns out, does MacDonald herself, though for reasons more moral than aesthetic.

Her musical -- it does seem to be her musical, more than the composer's -- is a paean to monogamy, even if of the serial kind. Straight, gay, or some of each, its characters end up wanting commitment.

The central romance is between Jinny, "research scientist by day, party girl by night", who has just broken up with the latest in a long line of unsatisfactory boy-friends, and Joel, a florist, whom she likes but whom she thinks is gay. Or rather whom she likes because she thinks he's gay. He isn't, and he's also in love with her, and much of the action concerns his desperate attempts to find the right moment to enlighten her (Keeping the charade going involves the author in some desperate measures herself.)

As a further caution against sexual stereotyping we have Tyrone, Joel's friend, who proves that it is possible to be a male chauvinist pig, even when your lovers are of the same gender, but who has his good side, too. Then there is Alberta, a funeral director whose business ("the last Tim Horton's on the highway of life") dovetails with Joel's for obvious reasons, and who is a lesbian who wants a child, or at least wants her partner to have a child.

There is a passing transvestite called Auntie Fey; and there is Jinny's mother, a recovering alcoholic taking it one day at a time while maintaining the standard abrasive relationship with her daughter; and Joel's long-distant father, a kilted military historian with skeletons in his sporran; so, altogether, all human life is there.

This is the first full-blown Canadian musical in at least a decade that is neither a campy spoof nor a rock-brained epic, and some of it is elating. Lapses apart, MacDonald writes high-gear lyrics, fluent and funny and occasionally penetrating.

There's a number called The Wardrobe Crisis in which Jinny, preparing for a date, enumerates the hang-ups in both her closet (literally) and her mind; it goes by at just the right speed and is a new addition to the treasurable list of list-songs. Allen Cole's music is more problematic; there are a couple of adventurous ballads, but in a more cheerful mood it simply tinkles.

But then Alisa Palmer's direction, though technically slick, never seems quite sure of its style; at various times the show recalls She Loves Me, Company and even Little Shop of Horrors. Mostly, though, it seems to derive from the innocent British shows of the '50s.

Passers-by in the street join in the hero's happiness and twirl umbrellas; it's as if Salad Days had decided to come out. But it's impossible to tell whether the resemblance is intentional or has just happened. A lyric that asks "why can't a straight man be more like a gay?" harks back very obviously to My Fair Lady but to no particular effect. It doesn't seem to be part of a whole structure of pastiche; it's just a nudge in the ribs, and less effectively knowing than it might think.

All the characters are very nice people, but they have their problems, and the playwright in MacDonald orchestrates and resolves these very skilfully in a dinner-party scene that takes up most of the second act. The songwriter in her seems more at a loss, as if she sensed she was no longer needed.

A forced show-stopper called Menopausal Mama disrupts both the text and the texture. On the other hand, a bitter father-son duet, Do You Remember?, finds both lyricist and composer at their best. At moments like these, and in the snappy duet for Joel and Jinny that succeeds it, there seems to be real hope for the human race. (The finale lets us down, but best not to dwell on it.)

Dan Chameroy, escaping from his usual musclebound roles, has considerable charm as Joel, and Tamara Bernier has considerable bite as Jinny. The others -- Marc Richard, Sandra Caldwell, Judy Marshak, David Dunbar -- are all fine.

It was part of the World Stage Festival (which ended at the weekend) but continues beyond it. The same goes for Dali, the revival of a 15-year-old show -- written, directed and designed by Jim Millan -- that starts with its central figure proclaiming "I am surrealism-m-m" while apparently suspended in a bubble. This is a great image, and the show never manages to top it, but it does keep them coming. It presents the artist in the terms -- calculatedly arbitrary and sometimes entertaining -- of his own art: good for atmosphere, initially terrible for biographical information, though more rewarding in its second half, which makes concessions to clarity. Richard Clarkin, in the title role, balances brilliantly and ineffably on the line between cunning charlatan and inspired natural; whichever he is, you're with him all the way. The rest of the show is split pretty evenly between delight and tedium.

Each of these shows makes a perfectly acceptable evening at its own theatre. In the context of an international festival they looked somewhat shrivelled -- as, perhaps inevitably, did most of the Canadian offerings; they were new productions, selected on their creators' past records, but up against shows from elsewhere that had been run in, sometimes for years.

It's unusual, in fact, for such an event to include home-grown offerings, but it's a risk worth taking, and one show this year more than justified it. Robert Lepage's The Far Side of the Moon not only survived comparisons; it was the pinnacle of the festival.

Not everything from abroad was golden either, but The Suit, The Oresteia, and Gaudeamus made Toronto feel like a privileged place to be. It was, in fact, an extraordinary event; and it cannot now be allowed, even without the sponsorship of duMaurier, to go up in smoke.

IF YOU EVER LEAVE ME ... I'M GOING WITH YOU

Winter Garden Theatre, Toronto

The American comedian Kaye Ballard, who is of Italian extraction, once remarked of her upbringing: "You know what Italian families are like -- they're so Jewish." If You Ever Leave Me ... I'm Going with You! is an extended sermon on this text, expounded by the acting- and-writing husband-and-wife team of Renee Taylor and Joe Bologna.

She is Jewish, he is Italian, they are both New Yorkers and they have been living and writing together for upwards of 35 years. The show, then, is a celebration of competitive and collaborative volatility. It seems to be their anniversary present to themselves, and the obvious dangers of narcissistic cuteness are accurately demonstrated in the title, which would be terrible even without the three dots and the exclamation point.

It is not, however, all like that. The evening proves to be entertaining and embarrassing in about equal proportions; which, considering the possibilities, is not bad.

The duo begin by telling us who they are and welcoming us into their lives. Bologna, who is dark and seemingly casual, manages this with laid-back aplomb. Taylor, who is blond and busty and speaks at this point in a whispering gurgle, seems less suited to it, and indeed appears likely to burst out of just about everything.

Then, though, they go into a scene from one of their early plays; and we realize that the lady has been holding out on us. Once relieved from the burden of playing mistress of ceremonies, once given a character and a situation to explore, she is revealed as a superbly accomplished comic actor, with quirkily impeccable timing and an unfathomably eccentric personality.

She is actually playing an actress in this bit: One who turns up to audition for a role in a commercial, a mainstream glamour part for which she is entirely unsuited, but who arouses the friendly and amused attention of the director. The scene, they tell us, is somewhat autobiographical, but it stands in its own right.

So Bologna was a director when they first met and Taylor an actor: It figures. Even when he is shouting and she is listening (a frequent occurrence) he seems to be detached and she seems to be involved. She is deep in her own concerns, and is rock-like. He is a counterpuncher, like Burns to Allen or Sid Caesar to Imogene Coca; he actually looks like Caesar, minus some of the height and all of the lunacy, and in fact played him (or a version of him, called King Kaiser) in My Favourite Year.

The evening progresses as a history of their relationship, reflected in excerpts from their scripts for stage, screen and television. Some of these are quite well-known (It Had To Be You, Made for Each Other, Lovers and Other Strangers), others aren't (Bedrooms, Bermuda Avenue Triangle). The titles sort of blend into one another, and so -- on the evidence provided here -- do the plays. They all seem to be wry domestic comedies, about squabbling but unshakeably bonded couples. They all, if the current staging is to be trusted, consist mainly of duologues conducted from a pair of adjacent stools; even a scene in a restaurant finds the diners seated at their invisible table side by side rather than across.

If the audition scene remains the best it's because, besides having a touch of genuine theatrical madness, it depicts a professional situation as well as an emotional one. There is a similarly welcome whiff of the outside world in a sequence where the couple, now middle-aged, lecture an unseen son who is about to disgrace the family by getting divorced.

But even here what we learn of the relationships is strictly from sitcom. The impression is that, as the performers' skills have sharpened over the years, so the writers' have dulled. They are set, spiritually if not materially, in Miami or the Catskills, and that, along with maybe Las Vegas, seems to be their target audience.

Usually Taylor and Bologna play married or engaged, but sometimes she's a widow or divorcee whom he is trying to seduce. A final encounter, in which they're a couple of numbly amorous octogenarians, definitely hits below the Borscht Belt. But even the jolts seem calculated for maximum ingratiation.

It would be easier to take the best and forgive the rest, if it weren't for the framework. Bologna and Taylor, it seems, have always lived out their relationship in public; this show is a culmination, not a departure. They got married on TV, on The Merv Griffin Show. (This was in the '60s; they were ahead of their time.) The reason they say, is that their respective families, who would otherwise have boycotted the ceremony, could certainly not resist appearing on television. Nor did they; the production has the footage to prove it.

The couple have re-plighted their troth at regular intervals since, always in a ceremony from a different religion, and we get to see the videos of those, too. It's as if we're asked to congratulate them on the durability of their marriage; there's a place for that, but I don't think it's the theatre.

When solo comedians, male or female, get up and tell us about their relationships or lack of them, the performer-audience contract comes with what Chico Marx might have called a sanitary clause; they aren't necessarily talking about themselves, they could be making it all up. But when both partners are onstage they bring an actual relationship with them; and they could be lying about it, or they could be telling the truth, but it leaves you feeling queasy either way. (Well, it does me.)

No director is named -- though somebody must have arranged the furniture -- but there is a choreographer: Danny Daniels, who did the great routines for the movie of Dennis Potter's Pennies from Heaven and has here devised a very funny tango that Taylor performs bent over in a terrified state of slump, her whole body suggesting that if she straightens up something is going to fall off.

The Hats of Mr. Zenobe plays until May 14, $10-$24. Call 416-504- 9971.

THE HATS OF MR. ZENOBE

Factory Theatre

David Astle, writer and performer, has based his solo play, The Hats of Mr. Zenobe, on the life of Vahan Poladian, who in his 80 years on earth came up against some of the worst horrors of the 20th century.

Poladian was an Armenian whose family managed to flee the country during the Turkish massacres. He was refused entry to the U.S. but gained admission to France. He married another Armenian expatriate and they had a daughter, but they were separated when World War Two broke out and Poladian was conscripted. He was captured and sent to a German prisoner of war camp. When he was released and returned to France, his wife and child had disappeared. He spent his last 20 years in the Armenian Home in the French town of St. Raphael where he seems to have committed a slow form of suicide. During this time, though, he blossomed as a performance artist; allowed one franc a day, he accumulated a collection of old clothes, especially hats.

Thus costumed, he gave twice-daily shows on the streets of St. Raphael, designed to remind the spectators of their own past and of his.

Astle has renamed his protagonist Monsieur Zenobe, and seems to have lengthened his life somewhat. Near the beginning of the show we find him mentally cataloguing his stamp-collection.

He seems to specialize in countries that have been sites of atrocity: Armenia, Germany, Yugoslavia, Rwanda -- the last two only qualified some time after the real Poladian's death, which occurred in 1982. Astle makes Zenobe into a walking catalogue of modern inhumanity.

Astle, a teacher and performer based in Montreal and with a background in clowning and mime, seems to have been attracted by two aspects of the Poladian story. First, there is the mans tragic personal history. The most haunting sequence in the show has Zenobe wearing a miners hat, with its light the only illumination on a darkened stage, searching for his wife and daughter and repeatedly calling out their names, over and over.

This glancing approach to the biography, though, isn't always as effective; and might well be impossible to follow without the information supplied in the program.

Most of Astle's energies go into re-imagining his hero as a performer. This Zenobe is in the concluding stages of a hunger- strike, and he imagines himself escaping from the home, locking himself inside one more welcoming home (which, he doesnt fail to tell us, is where you hang your hat) and giving one last show, an omnibus retrospective.

Its a technique that's become familiar in stage biographies of celebrated actors and singers: cf. Barrymore and Hank Williams: The Show He Never Gave. Zenobe calls his genre the Theatre of Forgetting, though what it wants us to do is remember. He wears a patchwork quilt of a coat, and round his neck he wears an empty picture-frame: empty, that is, until he recalls his lost family, at which point their portrait appears within it. He warns against the authority-figures of the earth --queens and generals and especially popes -- and lampoons them in sequences that are well-meant but laboured.

He wants to equip us for the 21st century. Meanwhile he constantly invokes the 20th, though I doubt that anyone who had actually suffered through so much of it would talk about it so much in the abstract. But then, as I said, he keeps his actual experiences mostly at arm's length. Unfortunately, they shame his chosen style; he speaks largely in a vein of melancholy whimsy that comes close to being unbearable.

There are recurrent loud knocks at the door: the recurrent nightmare of the lifelong refugee Sometimes he ignores them; sometimes he opens it and speaks to his unseen visitors. One of them is the district nurse, whose title he playfully alters to dirty news; the particular dirty news is the threat of an injection ("theyll put chicken in my arm" ) if he doesnt eat. We in the audience keep hoping against hope that there will be someone there, and that the someone will appear on stage.

But no, this is remorselessly a one-man show, and an elaborate one, complete with intermission. (Even Joe Bologna and Renee Taylor, celebrating themselves at the Winter Garden, manage without one of those.) Astle is a clever if lightweight performer, but he hasn't written himself a script inventive enough to sustain his bundle of themes. Would it be unforgivably flip to suggest that the star is wearing too many hats?

DARK DIVAS

Ranee Lee (Justin Time, JUST 132/3-2)

I have trouble with the word "diva," or at least with its connotations. It even bothers me on its home ground of opera, where it suggests soprano-worshippers devoutly savouring the finer points of their favourites' delivery -- literally comparing notes -- while displaying minimal interest in the piece itself.

Now, of course, jazz, pop and musicals have their divas, too, though they paint in broader strokes. If your classical diva- fancier listens for arcane detail, his non-classical equivalent reserves his adoration for rampant histrionics.

In both worlds, diva-status is determined less by what the performers do than by what their audiences do. Attending a show becomes a matter of counting off the minutes before attempting a seemingly impossible physical feat, that of prostrating yourself in a standing ovation. Diva worship is fan worship raised to a higher masochistic (and narcissistic) power.

It also affects other vocalists, generally younger ones -- post- divas -- who naturally admire their predecessors. The urge to pay explicit homage -- and also perhaps the lure of alliteration -- has impelled Ranee Lee, a highly skilled and very versatile Montreal jazz chanteuse, to put together a double CD called Dark Divas on which she does songs associated with seven famous performers who happened to be both black and female: Josephine Baker, Billie Holiday, Lena Horne (the only one still living), Pearl Bailey, Dinah Washington, Sarah Vaughan and Ella Fitzgerald. (What, no Carmen McRae?)

It's a selection that defines its own territory: the mid-20th- century musical mainstream, where jazz interacted with pop, while receiving a few infusions from old vaudeville and current Broadway.

It stops short of the classic blues at one end (so, no Bessie Smith) and of soul and the avant-garde at the other (so, no Aretha Franklin or Betty Carter) and bypasses the more rarefied world of cabaret (so, no Mabel Mercer).

The real missing figure, though, is Ethel Waters, surely the mother of them all and the only one who could do jazz and theatre with equal authority.

Every subsequent singer, male or female, black or white, is in her debt. I would say she deserves a place here more than Josephine Baker, who was more of a dancer than a singer, and whose real importance is as a symbol: the beautiful black American who had to emigrate to Paris on order to get personal and artistic respect.

That seems to be why she's here. Lee's CD is the pilot for a stage show (a cast album before the fact) and the finished product will apparently include considerable biographical information about its heroines.

It certainly needs a context. On the disc, we get only a generalized snippet of description before each section. It's mostly hackneyed stuff, though it is refreshing to be told Billie Holiday was great "not because of the dreadful things that happened to her, but in spite of them."

Lee never presents these women as victims: a welcome change from the only comparable show I've seen -- A Star Is Torn, by the Australian singer Robyn Archer -- which presented them as nothing but.

There's always a problem when a good singer devotes a whole evening to pretending to be another singer -- what is she trying to prove? -- and it only multiplies when she presents a group of them. Is she trying to impersonate them? The usual answer is, no; the truthful answer would be, sometimes; or, where possible.

Tonally, Lee does a very accurate Dinah Washington and a fair Sarah Vaughan. (Considering Vaughan's scary range, that's an accomplishment.) Otherwise, she contents herself with reproducing her subjects' phrasing. I don't quite see the point of reproducing, note-for-note, Ella Fitzgerald's scat extravaganza on Lady Be Good, but Lee has certainly got it down pat.

There is also an issue with repertoire. A lot of the time, after all, these singers were singing the same songs, and Fitzgerald was the repertory singer par excellence. There seems no particular reason for Ill Wind to turn up under Holiday, or One for My Baby under Lena Horne. They never owned those songs, and Lee's versions don't sound much like either of them. (Baby, in fact, summons the immovable ghost of Sinatra, while her Mack the Knife is less like Ella's than like Bobby Darin's.)

What we get, in fact, a lot of the time, is just Ranee Lee singing standards. But isn't that what she'd be doing anyway?

Sometimes, the selections belie their introductions. She tells us Horne's club act reflected her independent spirit --which may have been true when she proclaimed The Lady Is a Tramp, but not surely when she torched Stormy Weather, her signature song. (Surprisingly, there is nothing here from her civil-rights repertoire, for instance The Eagle and Me.)

Lee herself is a performer of great authority and she rides every one of these songs with unshakable confidence, backed by an excellent small band that sometimes sounds big. Her recording career started with a live album that was showbiz jazz at its worst, but she has long outgrown it. Indeed, the vaudeville touches in her work are now positively enriching. So the best section here is the one devoted to Pearl Bailey, a somewhat neglected figure who I am delighted to see being canonized, and whose personal (and largely unfamiliar) repertoire allows Lee to swing and be funny at the same time, honouring the original but on her own terms.

Vaughan, though, and even more Fitzgerald, were never remotely dramatic or autobiographical singers and there's nothing Lee can tell us about them except they had lovely voices -- though I do honour her for including my favourite Vaughan song, If You Could See Me Now.

She ends with one of my unfavourite songs, Yesterday When I Was Young, sung -- or so I assume -- in her own person. This is a typically monotonous French tune with a typically melodramatic English lyric. It also doesn't make any sense. It's a song about self-absorption: the singer lacerates herself for being concerned with herself and "no one else at all."

But Lee has just spent an entire double album talking about other people, and if the lyric is meant to reflect on them then it's ungracious and, if on her own showing, untrue. The one characteristic that unites all the women she honours is emotional generosity, reflected in music.

I suspect she was influenced by one line about being "left alone on stage to end the play" and by the opportunity the thing gives her for passion-tearing. This she certainly takes: divadom descends with a vengeance.

The last song isn't worthy of her, and if any of her subjects ever sang it (none of them, mercifully, was a sobber) then they were slumming.

There's some very canned-sounding applause sprinkled throughout the discs, but she can probably count on the real thing when she does the material on stage.

Black & White Photo: Ranee Lee: A performer of great authority who rides every one of these songs with unshakable confidence. ;

Despite being housed on the Comedy Channel -- or conceivably because of being housed on the Comedy Channel -- Improv Heaven & Hell is promoted less as a source of laughter than as a bloodsport. Its presiding spirits, Andrew Currie and Albert Howell, gained their notoriety on Citytv's Speaker's Corner where they put on horns and dark glasses, insulted people, and called themselves the Devil's Advocates.

Now here they are, still in the gear, puffing on cigars while making their entrance through simulated flames and proceeding to a couple of neat little Satanic thrones. I'm surprised that the Devil permits a couple of mere mouthpieces to have thrones; but it seems that hierarchy, even in hell, is not what it was.

They look as if they're killing time in Seville while waiting to carry off Don Juan, and in the meantime are looking for some fun on the side. Actually, they're improvisational comedians (former Second City) who are being denied the chance to improvise themselves; which sounds pretty diabolical in itself.

In the meantime, they have four other comics whom they can make jump through hoops. They throw them themes, ideas, on which to make up scenes, and if ever the performers threaten to get too comfortable with the material, they change the rules on them.

The idea is, of course, similar to that of the British-born, American-adopted Whose Line Is It Anyway? Many of the routines are similar, and Colin Mochrie, a veteran of that show, is also a regular on this, and quite the best thing on it. (He's billed as a guest star, but he seems to be the kind of guest who never leaves.) The difference is that Improv H&H claims to be the dirtier, and therefore purer, version. Whose Line is heavily edited, and the viewers only get to see the sequences that the producers think work. Improv is also pre-taped, but it makes a point of leaving everything in.

There is an unsurprising rule about improvised comedy, and that is that very little of it is actually funny. Sometimes it can take off and be inspired, but not often. It may be corrupt and commercial but Whose Line is a lot more entertaining because of being selective. (It's also more overall talented, though it's a better thing in its British incarnation, with Clive Anderson in charge, than in its American, with Drew Carey.)

All comics with any life in them improvise to some extent, but improvisation is the tool rather than the product. I have had a couple of the most hilarious nights of my life at Second City (this was a long time ago) but the laughs from sketches which, even if they had never been written down, had been carefully honed. The genuinely improvised bits were thrown in at the end of the evening - - free of charge, really -- by which time the actors were really flying; even so, one admired their guts and good humour rather than their actual accomplishment.

Also, it helped to be there. Just watching it at home, you feel removed. Improv is not, I would guess, as unedited as all that; the transitions between items seem unnaturally swift. Maybe this shouldn't matter (who wants to see people just changing position?) but it does.

It makes the show a package, to be judged like any other. It proceeds on the dispiriting principle that nothing much is going to be funny, and that we can laugh at that. This makes the hosts into downmarket Lettermen. They are there to make their victims (their word) suffer.

Now of course this isn't a game show; the performers are pros, and you don't have to feel sorry for them. In this season's first two episodes, Mochrie is quizzically commanding, fat Jack Mosshammer and bald Paul O'Sullivan are amiable punchbags, and Teresa Pavlinek, though often seeming out of it, blossoms when she has to make up songs.

But the set-up is inescapable; they are programmed to fail. Currie and Howell, meanwhile, are programmed to sneer and either they're not very good at playing devils (as opposed to advocates) or they've given themselves bad material. As stars, they are singularly unappealing; you can't even love to hate them, you just sort of resent them.

To be fair, they have expressed some discomfort themselves about being kept on the sidelines. Just once in each show, they are allowed to show off. They riff on a given subject; in the first show, it was toothpaste, in the second bumblebees, (for whose lazy habits they expressed amusing disgust).

The thing is that they improvise in unison. They've worked together a long time, and they've presumably developed a telepathic rapport; they also probably have some practised routines that they can adapt as necessary.

All the same, it's quite a trick; and though one must take his cue from the other, it's impossible to tell, however closely you monitor their lips, which of them is leading. It's impressive, though it's only funny when it breaks down. But the humour of things is worked overtime in this show.

It wouldn't matter -- it's a modest production after all -- except that it does make implicit claims for itself: claims to be mean and hard-hitting; our two fiends keep telling us how nasty they are, rather than just being. The comedy never has a chance to be about anything. It's too busy just trying to exist.

There's better news on the comedy front. This just in: The Simpsons were funny last Sunday. Funnier than they've been in nearly three years. Not as funny as they still are in all those infinitely re-watchable reruns, but comparably, with some of the old richness of character, structural complexity, and insouciant toughness. Pray that it wasn't a fluke.

The Rediscovery of Sex runs to May 28 at Theatre Passe Muraille Mainspace, 16 Ryerson Ave., Tuesday to Saturday at 8 p.m. Pay what you can Sunday matinees at 2:30 p.m. $10 - $28. Call (416) 504- 7529.

Unless interactive drama is your thing, the only sexual activity that the theatre can satisfactorily present is voyeurism. It can, of course, talk about all the other activities, it can simulate or even literally reproduce them, but it still leaves the audience in the position of watching other people at it. This is what has undone all the ambitious sex-shows -- or revues on sexual themes -- from Oh! Calcutta! down to this week's Toronto opening, The Rediscovery of Sex. No matter how many bases they try to cover, they get monotonous.

Oh! Calcutta! was very much into making us feel happy and liberated. Really, it preached; it took, as you must have known I was going to say, a missionary position. It said that sex was good, and even fun. The approach taken by The Rediscovery is more anthropological. It probably also thinks, somewhere inside itself, that sex is fun, but -- depending on your viewpoint -- it's either too cool or too square to say so.

It's a long-delayed sequel to I Love You, Baby Blue, a pioneering work mounted 25 years ago by the same director, Paul Thompson, and a show that briefly led to its cast and crew being locked up. It took off, in its turn, from some erotic movies that were being shown at the time on Citytv. Hence, rather belatedly, the present show's opening number retells some urban history in Old Testament language: "In the beginning, God created Toronto ... there was Bloor and Yonge, and it was good" -- that kind of thing. Arch Biblical spoof is not exactly a new device, but it has a sort of purpose: It's designed to set up a gag about Moses, a media tycoon who, like his celebrated namesake, led his people to the promised land, but couldn't stick around to escort them inside.

The style also signals that the show recognizes its responsibility, as a revue, to be at least intermittently funny. It doesn't, as it turns out, do this very well (for some reason, people who compile shows about sex always seem to know fewer good jokes on the subject than anybody else), and really its heart isn't in it. The best numbers here are a few that are outright sombre, as opposed to the many others that are just skittishly cynical. Six young people, in rapidly changing states of dress and undress, take us through the streets, bedrooms and public playing areas of the city, and return with the news that anything can be said, most things can be done, but nothing is being enjoyed. Whether it really means to say this, or just can't find ways of saying anything else, is anyone's guess.

Early on we meet a trench-coated detective who has been down our streets and has found them mean. He harangues us for our prurient motives in attending such a performance, compares our civilization to Sodom and Gomorrah, and generally hankers for some good old repression, and lots of it. He's a figure of fun, but the odd thing is that, as it develops, the show seems to agree with him. There are one or two other recurring characters, but it's hard to keep track of them, and you find yourself wondering if you have met this person before or if the authors have merely run out of names.

There is some kind of progression. The show begins by concentrating on heterosexual relationships, mainly between desperately lonely men and disdainfully lonely women. It gets steadily gayer, but no happier. The mood, in fact, gets darker, or maybe it's just that the background music gets heavier. (There are no musical numbers, which in any revue that doesn't happen to be Beyond the Fringe is a mistake.) Along the way, there's a fairly amusing item about a primly virginal researcher doing a thesis on porn, driving her male co-worker crazy as they watch videos together, and taking umbrage when he resists her disinterested attempts to give him a hand job.

There's a reasonably accomplished sketch depicting swingers who displease or embarrass their regular others by their choice of irregular ones. I forget where it happens, but there's a surprisingly successful pun on that well-worn word "hard." There's much mockery of brittle, driven types who never disconnect their cellphones and who dine at North 44. (The show seems to have a fixation on this restaurant, though I doubt that there's a promotional tie-in.) It's strongly implied that the real trouble with sex today is that yuppies do it, or at least would like to do it, or at the very least think that they ought to want to do it. They are, of course, obvious targets, but then the revue form thrives on obvious targets. It doesn't have time for anything else. That's why it needs music and humour. They're necessary lubricants, and they can also -- music especially -- be passports to emotion, which is as absent from this show about sex as it would be from a government report.

Bouncing cartoon-like from one subject to another, a revue can hardly explore feeling, but this one hardly suggests it. Almost inevitably, it ends up presenting sex as a mirthlessly absurd activity. I remember hearing the word "love" just once in the evening, and it was spoken by a rejected husband. It isn't sentimental to remark that people having sex, even in Toronto, even in the year 2000, quite frequently say, "I love you." What's more, they often mean it, even if sometimes they're deceiving themselves and/or their partners and harbouring baser thoughts at the same time: That, in fact, is comic and dramatic in itself. Oh, and sex has been known to be the cause of children; that isn't mentioned either. The piece, in fact, leaves a lot out; and isn't too illuminating on what it leaves in. It isn't unbearable, though it's much too long; the production is smooth, and although the performances vary from very good to very bad, the actors are all at least personable. Everybody seeing the show is likely to be faintly aroused at some point, although it probably doesn't see itself as an aphrodisiac. If anything, it's despairingly puritanical, or perhaps hedonistically disillusioned. It takes the received wisdom that sex is being destroyed for us by stress and disease, and does nothing to challenge it. Nobody is going to get arrested this time, and it's good that the show can happen. That doesn't make the happening fun.

2000-05-15-comedy-of-manors:
THE GAME OF LOVE AND CHANCE

Artword Theatre, Toronto

There is a dramatic subsection that might be known as the Theatre of Geometry, or perhaps the Comedy of Intersecting Lines. One of its prize exhibits would be The Game of Love and Chance, an implacably symmetrical pavane of assumed identities, choreographed by Marivaux, the foremost playwright of 18th-century France. Actually, any one of his long line of sweet-and-sour courtship comedies might have been given the title he bestowed on this one, but this might be his diploma piece; only 90 minutes long, it presents the game in its most concentrated form. The ground rules are traditional, but they have been refined and complicated in the authors own rigorous, and occasionally cruel, imagination.

The principal players are Silvia and Dorante, two young aristocrats who have been betrothed to one another, sight unseen, and are about to meet for the first time.

Silvia, like any good comic heroine, is skeptical about men in general and this arranged match in particular; her attendant Lisette, like any good down-to-earth comic maid, can't understand what she's making such a fuss about. Silvia asks permission of her father, Monsieur Orgon, to let her change clothes with Lisette, so that she may size her fiance up before surrendering herself to him; her daddy protests that he has never heard of such a thing (he cant have been going to the theatre much) but, being no tyrant, agrees. He then learns, again to nobodys surprise but his own, that Dorante has had exactly the same idea and will arrive dressed as his own servant, Harlequin -- and vice, naturally, versa.

So the game is on: a set of mixed singles between master and mistress, valet and maid, each with a mistaken idea of who the other is, while father Orgon -- knowing everything and telling nothing -- plays the genial umpire.

It sounds simple, but the fact that each player is both trickster and tricked gives every scene -- indeed every line -- a double layer of irony; matching the characters' awareness against our own can become quite a taxing, if stimulating, exercise. Of course Silvia and Dorante fall for one another, as do Harlequin and Lisette, so each one of them is faced with the prospect of crossing a social gulf that doesn't in fact exist. The playwright then tosses in a couple of additional hurdles. Dorante, thinking himself in love with the maid, is challenged for her affections by Silvias brother (who of course doesnt love Lisette but is in on the game). Dorante also reveals his real identity to Silvia, who however maintains her own disguise, so for a time the play becomes a French equivalent of She Stoops to Conquer -- which is what Silvia had wanted it to be in the first place.

For the most part, though, this, like all Marivaux' plays, is a very un-English work. About the closest our language comes to this rarefied and single-minded concentration on the codes of passion is in some of Shakespeare's comedies (As You Like It, especially) and even in those the outside world keeps breaking in. By the 18th century English comedy had become very genteel, at least sexually, but it still got its hands dirtier than the Parisians ever did; it ate and drank and talked about money. One permutation that this comic kaleidoscope noticeably denies itself is any encounter between the true master and maid, or the true mistress and manservant. This isnt a revolutionary play like Beaumachais Marriage of Figaro, from the same country and period; its social attitudes seem to be those expressed in HMS Pinafore by the First Lord of the Admiralty when it was suggested that he might marry an able seaman's daughter: "Love levels all ranks, but it doesn't level them as much as all that.

On the other hand: There is an implicit bitterness in the situation of Lisette and Harlequin, their fates and their feelings taken to be automatically subordinate to those of their employers. How often it breaks surface depends largely on the actors. The more we believe in them as people, the stronger, as well as funnier, the play becomes. Thats certainly the case here with Colombe Demers Lisette, a wonderfully vivacious performance, technically contained but overflowing in both joy and pain. Her opposite number is a tougher proposition; the name Harlequin stylizes him immediately, as the kind of sad clown (a Frenchified Italian) who figures in the paintings of Watteau.

It's not a tradition to which we have much access, and Alex Poch- Goldin has some trouble fusing the style with the feeling.

If the maid outpaces the man she also (and again perhaps traditionally) betters her betters.

Graeme Somerville's Dorante is vigorous but neutral, Amy Price- Francis Silvia confident but over-eager. As Orgon, Oliver Dennis is avuncular rather than paternal, and does not look happy in his wig.

Nobody, though, looks or sounds lost, which may have something to do with the director, John van Burek, also being the translator. His text tries hard for accessibility and mostly succeeds, though some of his attempts at modernity (cutie-pie" turns up a lot) actually sound dated, like an academic American translation trying to be racy. Nobody wants old-fashioned, but maybe the best thing to go for would be timeless. Its not as if this is a modern-dress production; it comes in the usual frocks and hats on a standard cut-price- elegant set of three pairs of arches in diminishing perspective. The production is virtuous pioneering work, in a field we are still discovering; it's only in the last 20 years that the English- speaking theatre has even discovered that Marivaux exists. (Though he's moving fast; he even made it to Broadway three seasons ago, as the source of the musical Triumph of Love).

It's a discovery worth making; the plays have a distinctive quality of disillusioned benevolence, the very essence of tragi- comedy. The emotions he isolates and dissects are real, and the technique is a pleasure in itself.

DOUBT

Factory Studio Theatre, Toronto

There is a venerable comic-romantic tradition that's known in Hollywood as "meeting cute." It consists of throwing the principal couple together for the first time in some mildly ridiculous or potentially embarrassing situation that will get the audience rooting for the characters and for their future happiness. Think Grant and Hepburn, or Gable and Colbert. The phenomenon isn't confined to the movies; there are two more-or-less likeable couples among the five characters of Michael Redhill's play Doubt, and each of them meets, or has met, cute.

There is Henry, who is a writer, mainly a novelist with poetry somewhat shamefacedly on the side. He met his wife, Helena, when she was out by the lakeside gazing at the stars; he was bathing, and emerged naked to find that his clothes had been stolen. He shyly begged Helena to lend him a towel, and true love was born.

Now Henry is at work on a thriller, which is giving him trouble; in fact, he has all but given up on it, and when the-story-so-far takes shape before us we can understand why. It concerns Keith, who has stolen something and, with the cops on his tail, has taken refuge in a hospital elevator; here he meets Karen, who becomes, in quick succession, his hostage and his lover. "We're in this together," says Keith, "like peanut butter and jam." His opinion of the dialogue Harry has written him is not high, and he complains about it. It's one of those plays.

The fifth character is Melanie, who seems to be living with Henry now; in fact, though the domestic arrangements are left vague, she looks as if she might be his second wife.

It's impossible to imagine Melanie meeting cute with anybody; she hasn't the humour. She appears for most of the evening to be a bitch, and not even on wheels; she stomps through the play, ordering people about and trampling on their feelings. There turn out to be good if totally unexpected reasons for her behaviour, but that isn't much consolation while she's actually behaving, and it leaves the actor (Deborah Drakeford) giving the one charmless performance in a show that otherwise stakes everything on charm.

It's subtitled "a suspended comedy," a phrase that has any number of implications. One is that the play could be funny, constantly seems about to be funny, but never quite makes it; that is indeed the impression that it gives, and it's a more agreeable feeling than you might imagine. On a more literal level, Keith and Karen are of course suspended in their elevator and in their author's stalled imagination. And there is Henry himself, his life and talent -- at the very least -- in a state of suspended animation.

The play begins with Henry rising from his bed in the middle of the night to grapple again with that long neglected cops-and- robbers epic. Melanie, finding him at it, is not amused and drags him off to confront his ex. When they arrive, Melanie tells Helena, roughly speaking, that Henry is her problem and she had better solve him; she still, though, seems reluctant to relinquish him. Henry, meanwhile, stands around in his bathrobe, looking half-tickled, half- pained.

Odd though these carryings-on may seem, we accept them, perhaps more literally than we should. But then, on the other side of the stage, Keith and Karen are playing at love in a lift or are asking Henry for better material; so anything could happen.

This play about writer's block seems to have been created by a whole block of writers. It's described as "written by Michael Redhill, with inspiration from the company." At least three of the cast have authored or co-authored plays in their time, as has the director, so the sweet aroma of deeply-felt communal anguish wafts off the stage.

Henry, fittingly enough, is played by Michael Healey, who has the most distinguished literary track record of any of them; he may not have the widest range of any actor in Canada, but he is good at being the ineffectual intellectual, and he gives the play the understated centre it needs. Martha Ross' Helena is a tough waif, while Chris Earle and Waneta Storms are the two characters who, unlike Pirandello's celebrated sextet, actually find their author.

The fact that they do makes this a very different, and much lighter, play. The Pirandello bunch are real people (no metaphysical arguments, please) who have burst the bounds of fiction; Keith and Karen are stock characters who glory in their stockness. They even boast of the past novelists whose work they have adorned: Dostoevsky and Stendhal and two scribes they are pleased to call Tony Trollope and Larry Sterne.

The play's real affinity is with Tom Stoppard (though Stoppard's jokes are much better); the teasing Tom of The Real Inspector Hound, mixed in with the authorial agonizer of The Real Thing (whose maritally challenged hero is also called Henry). Keith the thief also shares a vital quality with the Players of Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead; he knows the value of a good exit, and beseeches Henry to give him one. In other words, he wants to die cute. (Not to mention fast; he's heard there may be a vacancy with that Milan Kundera.)

In granting his wish Henry ushers us into the presence of the play's underlying theme; which, since it is tied up with climactic plot and character revelations, I feel unable to discuss. Let me just say that the matter turns out to be one of life and death. All the pieces come satisfyingly together, jigsaw-puzzle-like.

Leah Cherniak's production is very smooth, though I wish the transitions could be faster (as, probably, does she); Glenn Davidson's sets are otherwise useful, and, as lit by Andrea Lundy, they shimmer. There are no great depths here, but the surface holds.

Black & White Photo: CUTE MEETS FICTION: Helena (Martha Ross) and Keith (Chris Earle). ;
2000-05-20-balancing-on-the-wing-of-an-i:
Wings runs until May 28 at the George Ignatieff Theatre, 27 Devonshire Place. Call (416) 504-7529.

The American playwright Arthur Kopit wrote Wings after his father suffered a stroke and was smitten with aphasia: the loss of the ability to communicate through words. Kopit met other victims with the same condition, one of them a woman who had been a stunt pilot and wing-walker; that is, she flew old-fashioned biplanes, and even performed gymnastic feats on their wings.

Wings presents a similar character, giving a spare account -- part personal, part clinical -- of her journey through an appalling physical and mental crisis. It also uses her previous accomplishments -- summed up in the recurring phrase I walked out on wings" -- to provide an image of her present free-floating agony. It is remarkably successful on both counts.

We begin with our elderly heroine, Emily Stilson, sitting quietly, reading a book. Suddenly a lamp goes off, then on; a clock stops, then starts. Life has ceased to make sense. Actors in white coats shift screens rapidly about the stage, signalling both the short-circuiting in Emilys brain and her physical removal to the hospital. We hear her talking, or perhaps thinking, and much of what she says makes perfect sense, though sometimes -- and with increasing frequency -- she seems to have hit on the wrong word. The doctors and nurses around her, though, dont seem to understand her, and when one of them asks her something, her answer, though it's certainly in English, seems to bear no relation to the question. The agony of a mind still lucid within itself but unable to convey that lucidity to anyone else is given about as powerful a dramatic expression as it is ever likely to receive.

Emily does make progress; the turning point comes when, after a false start, she picks up a toothbrush and demonstrates that she knows what it is and how to use it. She even seems to be cured.

In the meantime, she has devised her own secret theories to explain what is happening to her, and why everyone around her is behaving so strangely; this, she decides, is no hospital but a farmhouse in disguise, probably in Romania (Radio Bucharest, jamming her intercom, figures at one point in her memories of life as an aviatrix) and she is being subtly interrogated.

Emily is established as a character in her own right -- a sharp- tongued, sharp-minded and self-sufficient woman -- and this is what keeps the play from seeming sentimental or exploitative. We have all seen plays in which the author has had a character diagnosed with cancer or AIDS: to assume a spurious air of tragic importance, to tug at the audience's heartstrings or simply to tie up loose ends. (AIDS, with its built-in political agenda, has proved especially useful here, and, in most cases, especially meretricious.)

There is no way not to be affected by a play about terminal or incapacitating illness; truthfully, it hits us far harder than Hamlet, or King Lear, or even some highly persuasive piece about nuclear apocalypse is ever likely to do. Medical melodramas tap into our solitary fears. Most of them, though, are pointless; they seem to be pointing a finger at an audience that is in no position to do anything. (At best, the position seems to be "these people are suffering and you should be sorry" -- but most of us were, even before we went into the theatre.) Also, they rarely tell us anything about the condition. Wings, being both brisk and evocative, does accomplish this, or something of it.

One aspect of the situation, and perhaps the most intolerable, it cannot convey: the sheer unforgiving ongoingness of it. The play happens to be short; it started some 20 years ago as a radio piece, starring the fine Anglo-American actress Constance Cummings, and directed by John Madden; their subsequent stagings of it -- at Yale, on Broadway and in London -- proved the climax of Cummings career and set Madden on the theatrical and cinematic path that led to Shakespeare in Love. But even if it were of Eugene ONeill length, it would still let the audience off lightly. There are some things that the theatre, perhaps mercifully, cannot do.

Ken Albanese's production, a belated Canadian premiere, is lighter in tone than the original (which I remember as oppressively portentous) and the more effective for it; it takes its emotional colouring from its clinical crystalline set, designed by Joanne Thompson and Graeme S. Thomson. Nonnie Griffin is excellent in the virtuoso role of Emily, meticulously accurate in her charting of confusion, and fastidiously avoiding both the plaintive and the excessively crotchety. In the only other substantial role, that of an inspiringly practical doctor and therapist, Claire Crawford is finely sympathetic, and Brian Otto has a bright, troubling little scene as the loose cannon at a rehab group. At the end, the performance takes off on its own winged metaphor; transcending what might be a cruel conclusion, it also mufffles it. That, though, is in the writing; and in this context, I'm not sure that it's a fault.

Black & White Photo: John Hryniuk, Weekend Post / Claire Crawford, left, and Nonnie Griffin in a scene from Wings. ;
2000-05-22-a-song-in-their-hearts-tonigh:
In the season finale of Ally McBeal (tonight at 9) everybody sings. Well, nearly everybody. The cast, we are told, will burst into a dozen Randy Newman songs (one of them new), plus one from Madonna (Hanky Panky, yet) and a couple of more innocent tunes from The Music Man. All of it, apparently, ties in with the plot.

This isn't the first time a TV drama series has gone musical. A couple of years ago there was an all-singing, all-dancing Chicago Hope special, directed, as it happens, by the same man, Bill D'Elia, responsible for tonights Tin Pan Ally. This, according to one report, will be different: "[The Chicago Hope episode] was akin to a classic movie musical, in which a tune stops the action. Ally McBeal, however, treads ground broken by the British miniseries The Singing Detective. DElia himself is then quoted as saying, Characters sing what they were saying, and it moves the comedy or drama along as it would have been had they been speaking."

It's unclear whether it's DElia or the reporter whos responsible for the Singing Detective comparison, but it reads like typical ignorance. In the first place, the characters in The Singing Detective didn't sing what they were saying; in fact, they didn't sing at all -- they mimed, to old pop records that were playing in their heads and that in some way echoed their present state of mind. Far from forwarding the action, they halted it, often enjoyably, in its tracks. The same author, Dennis Potter, had used the same technique in his previous series, Pennies from Heaven, so if he did break any ground, that was where he broke it. Second and more importantly, telling the story through song is what stage, and to a lesser extent, film musicals have always done. What else, to take the most obvious example possible, is Gene Kelly doing when he starts singin in the rain?

The fact that Ally: The Musical is not a death-defying leap into the dramatic unknown need not, of course, prevent it from being fun. If Calista Flockhart has any previous track record as a song-and- dance queen its escaped my notice, but her colleagues include at least two performers who have in their time stopped shows on Broadway: Jane Krakowski (Grand Hotel) and James Naughton (City of Angels and much else). You can find the same kind of talent in almost any regular TV lineup, drama or comedy. American theatre breeds great all-rounders. Maybe not all American actors can sing, but a huge percentage seem to have a kind of musical know-how. Musical performers can generally act, and since a full-time career in musical theatre is now impossible to sustain, many of them gravitate to TV.

Chicago Hope's musical excursion was of course spurred by its having Mandy Patinkin, a bona fide musical star, even if many people find his singing unbearable. And if a singing surgeon seems even more risible than a singing detective, what do you make of a singing shrink? Kelsey Grammer, a closet musical star if ever there was one, can do more than warble stylishly over the closing credits; he's sung Sondheims Sweeney Todd. Bebe Neuwirth made her name if not her fortune in musicals; her Second Murderess in Chicago was the only full-throttle star-quality performance I have seen on Broadway in a decade, and you can hear echoes of it in her great recurring hatchet job on Frasier, playing Grammers former wife; the producers of his Macbeth surely missed a trick by not casting her as his Lady.

Elliott Gould, now a daddy in Friends, started out in musicals (and was once, I believe, married to an actress who did the same). Seinfeld had in Jason Alexander the most accomplished musical- comedy man of his generation, though it resisted the temptation to let him, or anyone else, sing a note.

Such asceticism, though, is heroically rare. Most TV comedies like to squeeze in a musical interlude when they can; and now, as we see, dramas are following suit. A friendly editor at the Post suggested to me that this may be a sign that musicals are coming back. I think it's likelier to be the reverse. I think it's a sign that theyve gone, maybe for good, and that people enjoy playing with the memories. I think its camp.

To say that musicals have died may seem perverse considering that in the theatre they're making more money and drawing bigger audiences than ever. But none of the recent crop of stage successes are truly new; they're all revivals or built round old songs, or -- most depressingly -- adaptations of brand-name movies. The last trend does have an ironic appropriateness. All the legendary stage shows owe their real fame to their presence on film, and there is a sizeable, though not inexhaustible, list of original movie musicals with similar or greater resonance: Top Hat, The Wizard of Oz, Singin in the Rain. The line, though, has long since died out; in the last 30 years there have only been two attempts to revive it: Peter Bogdanovichs At Long Last Love and Woody Allen's Everyone Says I Love You, both of which used great old songs and both of which demonstrated a) that the charms of non-singing singers have their limits and b) even if you can carry a tune, it won't carry you if you dont have a style or a story.

Television itself has no tradition of original musicals. There were a few in the 50s and 60s, usually by old Broadway hands. They were mostly forgettable though one, Rodgers and Hammersteins Cinderella,was a classic; it was ritually desecrated a couple of years ago in a routinely philistine network revival. On TV, as in movies, the only recent evidence of musical style has come in cartoons.

Color Photo: Fox / Ally McBeal's Calista Flockhart ;
