THE THREE-DEGREE CABARET

Tallulah's Cabaret, Buddies in Bad Times, Toronto

The word "cabaret," attractive enough to most of us, has long exercised near-hypnotic powers on earnestly minded theatre people. It starts visions of old Berlin dancing in their heads: fantasies of creating hard-hitting, highly sexed satire that will have the public enthralled and the authorities incensed. The Three-Degree Cabaret seems to be the work of people who want to do just such a show.

Unlike most cabaret, real or self-styled, it has a storyline, and this in turn seems to be about people who want to do just such a show -- which could be confusing, and is.

The entertainment begins with three figures, identifiable as gangsters by their trench coats and variously coloured snap-brim trilbies, paying a call on Jimmy J. Tee the Emcee. Jimmy is, loosely speaking, our hero. He owns, runs and fronts the show-within-the- show. Naturally, he owes these hoods money, and they are here to put the moves on him. The moves they put are gymnastic, acrobatic and very neatly executed. Indeed, all the footwork in this production is both excellent and original. The choreographer is Nicola Pantin, who also makes one of the cast of five. Six, if you count the musical help, which you probably should.

Back to business: Jimmy, who of course has a show to do, manages to fend off the Mob but they take all his theatre's props as security. Next comes a sequence in which Jimmy takes three threatening phone calls, on three phones, simultaneously: one from a creditor, one from the morality squad and one from his girlfriend. Sean Power, as Jimmy, does both the physical and the verbal juggling with winning dexterity. He plays the jaded charmer with great style throughout. Words slip like butter off his tongue, which is more than they do off anyone else's.

Dancers the other performers (Sarah Martyn, Beche Ako, Paul Sun- Hyung Lee) may be; actors they are not, or at least not when it comes to the nifty handling of the verbals.

It's not as if the verbals they are given are too hot to handle. They are, actually, clammy. Adam Nashman, who wrote and directed, has done interesting work in the past, but everything here is sloppy, in both style and structure. Hard-boiled turns out to mean ungrammatical. (Did I hear someone say "this phenomena"? Is that the character being illiterate or the author being careless? Does it matter? Yes.)

None of the ideas set up is followed through. The central situation --protagonist tries to keep his show running so he can pay off the crooks so he can keep his show running -- served well enough in Kiss Me Kate, but it never develops any urgency here.

The performers complain about the missing props, but it doesn't seem to inhibit them any. (One of them also complains about not having a parking space. Actors.) A lady dances on, around, and under a table -- it literally chases her round the stage. It's a spectacular routine, but I don't see how it could be improved by classier furniture.

The offstage girlfriend remains offstage. The morality squad does appear, in the person of a horny blackmailing nun. This scene is the only extended sequence in the piece, and its heavy-handed pointlessness is enough to make you glad of that fact. Sidelong references to homelessness and immigration appear during or between numbers, but to no effect. Anyone can be on the side of the angels.

The trick is to do it with wit. The show hardly reaches the fabled level of Brecht and Weill -- though neither, to be fair, did Brecht and Weill, at least not most of the time.

It's hinted Jimmy's persecutors are not from the underworld but from the social and political overworld. They're the Establishment, trying to prevent Jimmy being artistic and rebellious. It's also possible Jimmy himself is not only slippery but tainted by the very evils he opposes. He finally disposes of his opponents with unscrupulous ease. So easily in fact, you wonder why he was ever bothered. But neither the writing nor the performance takes this ambiguity very far. The most we get is a generalized air of world- weary seediness.

Very helpful, atmospherically and otherwise, is jazz musician John T. Davis, who pounds out restful, rolling blues on the electric organ, engages in occasional smoky banter with the protagonist and takes time out to hawk his new CD. He looks and sounds like he's seen everything.

Black & White Photo: Buddies in Bad Times / Sean Power manages both physical and verbal juggling with winning dexterity. ;

MAMMA MIA!

Royal Alexandra Theatre, Toronto

The signature sound on the first night of Mamma Mia! came not, as is usual in a musical, at the end of each number but at the beginning. The score is drawn from Abba hits of the Seventies, and the audience greeted each one with the thunderous clap of recognition. But they didn't only applaud; they laughed.

They seemed endlessly tickled at the cheeky way in which free- standing songs had been shoe-horned into a story that in no way concerned them.

Count me out, twice. Abba's tunes (lets not even get into the lyrics) have always seemed to me like music to rot the teeth, when it isnt setting them on edge; and though songs like Money Money Money and Thank You for the Music actually sound better divested of the original group's saccharine harmonies, they still have no dramatic life. The show itself seems divided as to whether it wants to them to have any; the songs generally seem intended to forward the action, or at least reflect it; the ironic approach may well be more in the minds of the audience than in the intentions of the creators. But it's there, if only by default, and very irritating.

Theres good precedent for musicals in which the songs are irrelevant to the plot; the theatre of the Twenties and Thirties was full of them, if you believe the history books. More recently, Crazy for You, whatever its flaws, was a decently entertaining attempt to revive the tradition; the difference is that its songs, being by the Gershwins, had stage presence, while its book was a self-confessed piece of fluff.

The script for Mamma Mia!, however, has pretentions and sometimes even comes close to realizing them. It raises issues about marriage and parenthood, and it is has a 20-year-old heroine -- an incipient bride, name of Sophie -- who claims at the end to have learned something, though its unclear what. It also has an older heroine, Donna, the younger one's contrastingly unmarried mother; she is suddenly confronted with three men who played rapidly consecutive roles in her past, and any one of whom may be her daughter's dad. She is naturally vexed by all this, convincingly enough for us to want to hear her emotions explored, either dramatically or through a suitable song. What we dont want is to hear two of her old girlfriends launch into a chirpy cheer-up number whose lyric just happens to include a reference to a wedding, and at the end of which the narrative is picked up exactly where it was let drop. The two pals, who share with Donna a disco-singing past (they were Donna and the Dynamos) seem, in their present swacked and sexually ravenous states, to have lurched out of an episode of Absolutely Fabulous; as, come to think of it, does the central relationship between hip mother and square daughter.

Catherine Johnson, who wrote the book, is a tough and talented British playwright. She is slumming here (profitably, the show is a huge success in London), with second-hand characters and an arbitrary happy ending. Still, once past some stilted exposition (shamelessly employing a couple of characters we never see again) she manages efficiently to craft a story around 30 pre-existing songs and throws in a couple of good jokes.

The problem is not that her work isnt good enough for its surroundings but that it isn't bad enough. It's in competition with the score, and since decibels beat dialogue (which is why someone, out of desperation, invented the rock-opera) it inevitably loses. But it puts up a good enough fight for us -- well, some of us -- to resent the intrusion of each new number; which is a fair definition of musical-theatre hell.

The story is propelled by Sophies learning of her mothers three old flames and inviting them to the wedding. Each becomes happily convinced that he is the father, though -- since nobody suggests anything as unromantic as a blood test -- the matter has to remain permanently in doubt. One of them, however, gets Donna: again and for keeps.

The action takes place on an Aegean island, where Donna runs a taverna, and the situation is somewhat mythic, though perhaps less Greek myth than Italian: Variants of its triple-threat who's-your- father situation have turned up in the play Filumena, the film Buona Sera Mrs. Campbell, and an earlier musical, Carmelina, a flop with some lovely songs.

Interestingly, none of these versions has rushed to acknowledge a debt to any of the others; they too seem to want sole paternity.

So this is a Canadian production of a British musical with a Swedish score, set in Greece and with an Italian title. The British flavour -- a sort of low-down heartiness -- prevails in Phyllida Lloyd's production, but otherwise its remarkably un-ethnic. But that may be inevitable with this music; you have to hand it to Benny Andersson and Bjorn Ulvaeus, a couple of Scandinavians churning out songs that are blandly and effortlessly mid-Atlantic. Well, perhaps not effortlessly; I mean, has there ever been a dance hit as deadly static in its rhythms as Dancing Queen?

Anthony Van Laasts choreography doesn't move things around to much effect; it's cute the first time the chorus poke their heads over a parapet to join in a number, but not the dozen times they repeat it. Mark Thompsons sets are disappointingly picture-book pretty.

The performances, however, are good. Louise Pitre, silver-haired and real, gives a storming account of Donna, incisive when she talks, electric when she sings. She cant, though, fuse the music and drama, because the score doesn't. The power-ballads she gets at moments of crisis would be terrible even if they were relevant: All she can do is freeze and belt, on the fashionable principle that emotion equals noise: "Seeing me so tense/ no self-confidence" as one song puts it with typical lyrical finesse.

Rangy Mary Ellen Mahoney, repeating her man-eating routine from Crazy for You, and plump Gabrielle Jones, amusingly encroaching on it, are fun as her chums.

Tina Maddigan is sweet as Sophie, and Adam Brazier as her intended shows early signs of rising above juvenile-lead stereotype, though they aren't fulfilled. And everyone else is everyone else.

At the end, after the lovers have walked into a 360-degree sunset such as they presumably have in Greece, the show prolongs itself for a lame-suited reprise of most of the numbers: a pop concert in fact. This seemed to me to be, on its own terms, the most enjoyable part of the evening, and certainly the most honest. It has of course nothing to do with musical theatre.

Black & White Photo: Sweet: Adam Brazier and Tina Maddigan in Mamma Mia! Too bad about the vehicle, though. ;
2000-05-27-a-wonderful-treatment-of-shaw:
The Doctor's Dilemma continues in repertory until Oct. 29 at the Festival Theatre in Niagara-on-the-Lake, $25 to $75. Call 1 (800) 511-7429.

The Doctor's Dilemma, written in 1906 and one of Bernard Shaw's most durable plays, offers a rare example of a Shavian character actually dying on stage. The victim, struck down by tuberculosis in his early 20s, is Louis Dubedat, a gifted painter and equally gifted sponger. Shaw called the play a tragedy, but this must have been one of his jokes. Dubedat's end is not moving, except in the general way that death always is, and he isn't the central character; he enters the play late and makes his decisive exit early. The play's focus is on those who may kill or cure him: half a dozen medical men who among them make up perhaps Shaw's most extensive and entertaining portrayal of an English professional caste, and, through them, of clubman society as a whole.

The doctor in the title has just become a doctor with a title; he is Colenso Ridgeon, a bachelor of 40, knighted for his contributions to research. He has recently discovered a cure for TB; as yet, though, he can only apply it in a limited way, and his clinic is full. Jennifer, Dubedat's beautiful wife, comes to beg him to take her husband on; and Ridgeon falls for her. His dilemma -- complicated later -- is whether to save Dubedat in order to please the wife or to refuse him in order to please himself.

Few doctors, probably, have faced such a stark mix of personal and professional choices (though I bet some have). Nevertheless, the situation, outrageous though it seems, reverberates. The play is, between its lines, as sharp an attack on private medicine as has ever been mounted, but no system -- public, private or mixed -- is going to do away with the need to make choices. Money is the least of it; there will never be enough time or enough compassion. We can rob doctors of their godlike attributes and transfer them to administrators, but that only shifts the problem.

Christopher Newton's production is a first-rate ensemble showcase, full of rich comic acting and strikingly done up. Between the scenes, uniformed domestics shift the furniture to music, while a sextet of characters in simian masks cavorts in the foreground. Their faces are skulls; they hold their stomachs out before us in pot-bellied self-satisfaction. You feel that behind their masks, they may be blushingly conscious of their own absurdity. They are, of course, the doctors.

The inspiration for these interludes is apparently the Mexican celebration of the Day of the Dead, (though I only know that from reading the program so it doesn't count). It in no way interferes with the direction or performance of the actual text, but it gives the players a launching pad, and the designer, too. Released from stodgy realism, Sue LePage supplies a series of spacious environments in which the gallery that houses Dubedat's posthumous exhibition looks like an extension of Ridgeon's consulting room, with the artist's paintings looking, in long shot, unnervingly like the doctor's microscope slides. Especially striking is the design for a riverside restaurant -- a pattern of black branches on a green screen, lit by a broad yellow moon and a thin golden lamp. Dubedat's attic studio, with Jennifer languorously posing, is sensual enough to arouse any number of respectable gentlemen, if only to jealousy or disapproval.

These are largely what motivate Ridgeon, who must be the coldest of dramatic protagonists. He is not only the messenger of death, he is essentially dead himself, for all his mid-life stirrings; and it is this, rather than the disparity in their ages, that ultimately causes Jennifer to reject him -- a fact that Blair Williams brings out, at the climax of a fine and uncompromising performance, as he walks away rigid and broken.

His colleagues are the play's chorus, each with his own idee fixe or favourite cure, a device that Shaw overplays at the beginning, but orchestrates skilfully thereafter. Two of them stand out -- a wise man and a fool -- and it is not at all clear that the wise man holds any more of the truth than the fool does. They are both superbly played here. Bernard Behrens is Sir Patrick Cullen, the venerable physician who has seen medical fads come and go, and regards all medicines and all men with equal skepticism; he never says a kind word or performs an unkind action. His opposite number is Sir Ralph Bloomfield Bonington, "B.B.," doctor to the Royal Family, whose bland and mellifluous voice can itself make people feel better. (Shaw must have designed this role, prophetically, for that other Sir Ralph, surnamed Richardson, who unkindly never played it.) It is to B.B.'s literally tender mercies that Ridgeon fatally consigns Dubedat. Jim Mezon, whom I have never seen better, plays him splendidly, prowling distractedly around the stage whenever his vanity is pricked, deeply moved by his patient's death and saluting it with a patchwork Shakespearean soliloquy, and reflecting very persuasively that most people would indeed be "better dead."

The others, all admirable, are the surgeon Cutler Walpole (Lorne Kennedy, almost too incisive even for a man of his profession), Schutzmacher (Neil Barclay), a rich Jewish GP whom Shaw finds fun as a mouthpiece but then abruptly drops, and Blenkinsop (Guy Bannerman), a very poor GP, decent but dull, whose own case of TB gives Ridgeon the perfect get-out.

The doctors run the play, and the Dubedats are seen largely from their point of view. This makes Louis himself limited but manageable: a brilliant talent who borrows money and sex with equal unconcern. He spends most of his stage time shocking people and enjoying it; Mike Shara does this with wit if not quite enough spirit. Jennifer is defined by her blind hero-worship of him, which enchants some men and drives others mad; it gives her strength, and it does the same for Severn Thompson, who plays her like a mermaid: graceful, taunting, loyal and mysterious. There are notable small performances by Catherine McGregor as a chambermaid whom the painter once loved and left, and by Jennifer Phipps who, as Ridgeon's managing housekeeper, is perfect as ever; with her around, he's a baby for life.

SHE LOVES ME

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

The setting of She Loves Me is a parfumerie -- a cosmetics shop - - in 1930s Budapest. One of the items on sale there is a musical candy box, touted by one of the salesclerks as being "attractive to the ear, attractive to the eye and functional." That is also, as the authors must have known, a perfect description of the show itself, one of the best American musicals of the 1960s and surely the most charming.

A mild success on its first outing, the show -- whose ultimate source is a Hungarian comedy of 1936 -- has since established itself as a small classic. The operative word is small; coming from Broadway's brazen age (it opened the same season as Hello Dolly, which has similar Central European roots, but grew away from them), it's a singularly un-brassy piece. But it isn't whimsical, which is the usual American alternative. It's sweet but real and it requires acting and singing to match.

This makes it ideal for the Shaw Festival, which can cast pretty much from strength and can put the show into an intimate house without amplification. It fits perfectly not just into this theatre, but into this town.

Niagara-on-the-Lake is one of the few places where can you can still find pharmacies that resemble, in neatness and elegance, the one designed here by Patrick Clark. Though not even in Niagara should you expect this kind of service; the help down the street are unlikely to line up as they do in the show, carolling to each departing customer their gratitude for purchases past and their anticipation of those to come.

The great attraction of She Loves Me is that it isn't just a love story. It's the story of a store, and we follow the fortunes of Maraczek's Parfumerie through the changing seasons, culminating in a choreographed Christmas rush that's as wittily written as staged. We get the feeling of people working together, liking or tolerating one another, rubbing up against each other or rubbing each other the wrong way. This last is the case with Georg, the senior salesman, and Amalia, the newest recruit; they dislike one another almost on sight.

Since they are both fairly young, fairly presentable and single, it's a foregone conclusion that they'll end up together, and they have, in fact, been unknowingly corresponding: sending one another lonely-hearts letters that are always headed "Dear Friend" and that seem based on their shared taste for classic 19th-century novels. (Make them technology-literate rather than literature-literate, and it's a very contemporary situation.)

Georg realizes the truth at half-time; Amalia suspects it shortly after, but it takes the rest of the evening for them to act on it. Everything here is taut but nothing is rushed. It's very satisfying.

"Will wonders never cease?" asks Amalia, in the course of a show- stopping song of dawning recognition titled Ice Cream. With no break for dialogue, Georg bounds on stage to put precisely the same question by way of lead-in to the title song.

This has one of Sheldon Harnick's most agreeable lyrics: "She loves me" it proclaims, conscientiously adding "True, she doesn't show it/How could she/When she doesn't know it?"

Georg is Ben Carlson, who established himself last year in All My Sons and You Can't Take It With You as that rarest of commodities, a juvenile lead with backbone. Now it turns out he can sing as well. As a nervously ordinary hero, stolid without and impetuous within, he's a joy.

So, too, is Glynis Ranney, who conveys both Amalia's pertness and her loneliness, while managing some if not all of the high notes that made Barbara Cook a Broadway legend. Carlson and Ranney are recognizably from different schools -- he's drama, she's musical comedy with her charm a little knowingly sprinkled on -- but they meet very happily in the middle.

There's a secondary couple. Cameron MacDuffee hasn't the bravura for Kodaly, a Lothario among clerks, but as Ilona, whom he loves and leaves, Patty Jamieson is irresistible. She's also comparatively subtle, playing this soubrette role not (according to custom) as a cheerful nymphomaniac with occasional misgivings, but as a fairly experienced woman emerging from a hurtful relationship and embarrassingly liable to be drawn back into it. Watch her grapple hilariously with her feelings as the two of them dance a bolero.

As an assistant who will do anything for a quiet life, Jay Turvey is fine. So too are Richard Farrell as Maraczek lui-meme and, at the other end of the age scale, Mark McGrinder as an ambitious delivery boy, though both could use more vigour. I don't know the official tempo marking for the young one's big number, but it sounded slow to me.

Patrick D. Brown has a showpiece interlude as a proud head waiter, trying against all odds to maintain "a romantic atmosphere." This scene is one of several in Roger Hodgman's production to improve on a recent New York production, in which it was sent intolerably over the top.

As for the show's own romantic atmosphere: The program hints that it's the richer for being so fragile, what with our awareness of the Depression and the coming war. I don't think this is proven.

Certainly the characters are glad to have jobs, but Georg walks out of his without a qualm, and the store, dispensing mainly luxury goods, seems to have no shortage of clientele.

If Joe Masteroff, the librettist, meant us to brood on the historical context, he should at some point have mentioned it as he did, in spades, in his subsequent book for Cabaret. What matters here is the way in which his script supports and blends with Harnick's lyrics and Jerry Bock's crisp, versatile music -- both possessed of a shy warmth that expands under pressure.

On record, the score sounds nice but a bit studied. On stage it's magic. This may be the best romantic musical since My Fair Lady and the best musical production I've seen at this festival.

Black & White Photo: Magic: Ben Carlson as Georg Nowack (in foreground), Jay Turvey as Ladislav Sipos and Mark McGrinder as Arpad Laszlo (in background) in She Loves Me. ;
2000-05-29-with-him-dies-an-era-of-theat:
It seems a rough image to use of so fastidious a performer, but if ever an actor died with his boots on it was John Gielgud. He was 96 and he was still taking bookings, on film if not on stage, having made his professional debut a full 79 years earlier. He was a star before the end of the 1920s. No other major actor can have bestridden a century so completely.

So what everybody said a week ago remains true: His death signifies the end of an era. That doesn't mean that a particular type of acting has irrevocably died out; things are never that neat, and Gielgud's style, suitably adapted, lives on in actors of at least three generations whom he directly or indirectly influenced. What's more important is that, in his own generation, he was one of seven actors (and the number is precise) who came to prominence in the '20s and '30s and from that point dominated English classical acting, therefore English acting, and cast a long shadow over North America as well.

The obituaries have all linked Gielgud to Laurence Olivier and Ralph Richardson, but there were also Michael Redgrave, who, as a heroic actor, was at one time rated ahead of Richardson; Donald Wolfit, a barnstormer who stood apart from the others (he and Gielgud detested one another) but was undoubtedly a great actor; and Alec Guinness, still with us but retired. They were all knighted, of course, and most subsequent theatrical knights have seemed like pretenders. There was one woman in the group, Peggy Ashcroft, and she was damed. We are not going to see a bunch like that again, partly because the system that bred them has split apart. It was a system that Gielgud dominated for many years. He made the classical popular, and at mid-century he symbolized the best in British theatre, as a director and producer as well as a performer. Every actor in that group of seven, even Wolfit, worked at some point under his banner, and Ashcroft was practically his permanent leading lady.

How you respond to them all must depend to some extent on where you came in. For me it was the 1950s, and at that point Olivier was the man, largely on account of his audaciously intimate Richard III on film. (Even stagestruck and living in London, I had few chances then to see these actors in the flesh.) Gielgud seemed to me, not old-fashioned exactly, but remote; I couldn't get past the musical voice (I favour the cello metaphor myself) and the very identifiable tunes it kept playing. I heard him play Hamlet on records and I could tell he was being very sensitive and very intelligent, but I couldn't hear the character. He seemed vacuum-sealed (and it probably didn't help that at this point he was older than most of the actors playing his elders). Years later I saw him at a special benefit take a breath and launch into the "rogue and peasant slave" soliloquy on a great wave of nervous energy -- and that was it; that was history, being remembered and being made.

I saw him play Prospero in 1957 and again in 1975; felt cool the first time and bowled over the second. I think the change was partly in him, more in me and most in the climate. He often said himself that his approach to Shakespeare's verse grew less indulgent as he grew older, and that second Prospero was very rigorous. His last Shakespeare was the radio King Lear with which he celebrated his 90th birthday and which is available on cassette. The familiar rhythms are still there, and the phrasing is wonderful; he isn't too convincing as the former tyrant, but the reconciliation and death are, of course, sublime.

By the 1970s he and his contemporaries weren't playing much Shakespeare; they'd already done it all. They'd switched to the moderns, and here Olivier, with his zest for disguise (he was the only one who could do accents), should have been ahead. It didn't work like that, though.

What happened was that Gielgud took his own patrician qualities and made us respect them, largely through laughter. He held them up to the light and let them shine with an irony that oddly reinforced their dignity. He said himself that Peter Brook's savagely stylized production of Oedipus (in which he functioned, nobly, as a sacrificial victim) freed him to confront the audience head-on, which he did as the headmaster of the satirically named Albion House in Alan Bennett's disrespectful pageant Forty Years On; he was both a stand-up comic and a figurehead of England's past, slightly askew.

Then there was Veterans, a play neglected in the obituaries but absolutely pivotal, because in it he played himself, a classical actor bemused but unfazed by the madness of making an epic movie; Charles Wood, dramatist and screenwriter, wrote it out of his experience of working with Gielgud on The Charge of the Light Brigade. His comic timing was outrageously perfect. (I mourn having missed him in the great classic comedies, even more than in the tragedies.)

Finally, there was Harold Pinter's No Man's Land, the crown of Gielgud's recurring double act with Richardson, another actor whom it took me time to appreciate but whose truth-in-eccentricity I now adored; like many critics I seemed to spend much of the 1970s writing love letters to the two of them. Gielgud and Pinter brought out the best in one another; he made the speeches sound great, but he could only have done that if they were great. The role, of a parasitic minor poet in a rumpled pinstriped suit, brought him perhaps closer to character acting than ever before.

Still, if a character actor impersonates, then Gielgud wasn't one -- not really. Olivier was, but once I'd grown up, I was hardly ever able to enjoy Olivier. I'm not denigrating him (I didn't like his Othello, but I've never seen one to touch it), but I sensed a paradox: Olivier was always selfishly trying to be someone else, while Gielgud and Richardson were unselfishly themselves, to the benefit of the characters they were playing. (In Canada, William Hutt seems to me to have split the Gielgud-Olivier difference very neatly.)

This worked marvellously in the film and TV work that occupied Gielgud's last years. Take the butler in Arthur: Probably other actors could have timed as exquisitely his immortal response to Dudley Moore's announcement that he was taking a bath ("I'll alert the media"), but nobody else could have got such a laugh, because nobody else was Gielgud. He justified his presence in the Holocaust miniseries War and Remembrance with a moment of pure and truthful comic gold, when it was suggested to him that he pose as a journalist and he recalled, with a mixture of pride and guile, that he had indeed once written an article for Life magazine.

I met him just once, in 1977, when he was rehearsing the title role in what turned out to be an unfortunate production of Julius Caesar. He probably sensed trouble ahead but he still poured out his enthusiasm for the play ("such a noble play," he said). He dropped, alas, none of his legendary bricks in my presence; but in all other respects he was the man I had expected, and I was thrilled. He talked very fast. With the same understated urgency that distinguished his acting, occasionally he hinted he might be becoming old-fashioned, but was obviously not about to lose sleep over it. Nor should he have. He was, and remained, timeless.

EASY VIRTUE

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

It's unusual these days for actors in a Noel Coward play to imitate the Masters voice; it would be thought just too, too painful. However, in the Shaw Festival revival of Easy Virtue, Goldie Semple (reprising and refining the role she originated last season) bucks the trend, making fascinating play with Cowards famous clipped drawl, taking it down an octave or so to accommodate her own range and her own intentions. If she sometimes seems to exaggerate, it's done with conscious wit; the character she plays is being aggressively defensive. She's Larita, a creature of Cowards own 1920s demi-monde, thrown into painful proximity with the most repressed and repressive stratum of English country life.

Larita is a divorcee in her thirties whose proudest boast is that she never had an affair with a man she didnt love. This doesn't sit well with the Whittakers, whose son John -- "a boy," Larita calls him -- she has just married. They mistrust her, and lecture her, and end up hating her. She gives as good as she gets (better, since she has her author on her side), but she is out of place and outnumbered, and ends up acknowledging her mistake and walking out, at the height of a lavishly terpsichorean house party.

The visual panache of Christopher Newton's direction (energetic Charlestons and a hugely handsome drawing room set) is now matched by verbal and emotional depth. The cut-and-thrust of Cowards dialogue is impeccably arranged; and there seems for once to be as much going on beneath the jokes as there is officially supposed to be. People give themselves away, and the moments are nailed down for us.

The scenes between Larita and her Johnny have especial resonance, sexual and social; she reads Proust while he plays tennis, and though they still love one another they are drifting inexorably apart. Ben Carlson has taken over as John, and his performance -- another of his intelligently spirited reclamations of potentially tedious young men -- clinches his position as the best jeune premier (traditional juvenile) in Canadian theatre. It also helps transform the production.

John is about the only character to make an ambiguous claim on our sympathies. Otherwise, there are those we and the author like and approve of, and those we dont.

In the first camp are Larita herself and her new father-in-law: An officer (retired), a gentleman, an oasis of tolerance in a morally thirsty land, an admirable fellow whom David Schurmann admirably plays. (One misses him in the last-act shindig, from which his absence is never explained: a surprisng lapse in dramatic craftsmanship, considering it's his house.)

In the other there are the female Whittakers, who show their colours early on by piously despatching a fallen servant-girl to a life of shame in the capital. They run a gamut of censorious narrow- mindedness: from implacable matriarchy (Patricia Hamilton, a caricature but a skilful one), through neurotic piety of the muscular-Christian variety (Kelli Fox, irresistibly hearty), to adolescent hysteria. It isn't that Coward doesnt understand them; he has Larita offer several lively and plausible analyses of their behaviour. He even tries to sympathize with them, or at least with their predicament. But he cant love them; so they remain cardboard, and the play, though richer than it seemed last year, stays one- sided.

That's not to say it isn't fun. Its always jolly to see hypocrisy exposed, especially if you feel yourself to be safely on the other side. The Whittakers particular prejudices may be outmoded, but the urge to condemn what you don't understand remains universal. You may even wonder whether Larita's own world is so very enlightened, or whether her virtue doesnt come as easily as that of her opponents. When she meets up with an old Riviera acquaintance, and they start swapping memories and dropping names, it all seems frightfully shallow, like the Marvellous Party of a later Coward song; except that here it isnt being lampooned. Maybe that's intended, though; whatever bed Larita is repairing too at the end, it won't necessarily be one of roses.

The play runs out of story in its last act, but the spectacle sees it through. And the high-octane precision of the central performance makes the experience invigoratingly Semple.

Black & White Photo: Mrs. Whittaker (Patricia Hamilton) warns Marion (Kelli Fox) about Larita. ;

TIME AND THE CONWAYS

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

J. B. Priestley's Time and the Conways is a strong and bitter family drama, on a familiar English model, with a few metaphysical musings attached. First staged in 1937, the play takes a middle- class family in the North of England (Priestley's perennial stamping ground) from the end of the First World War to the brink of the Second, and -- here's the twist -- back again.

Act One, 1919: the widowed Mrs Conway, her two sons, four daughters and assorted neighbours have a party. They are celebrating the 21st birthday of one of the young Miss Conways, and they all anticipate bright years ahead. Act Two, 1938: the same young lady's 40th. The bright years have not materialized. Marriages, investments and ideals have all soured, and there is much recrimination. Act Three, 1919 again. We pick up exactly where we first left off. The characters resume their hopeful attitudes, even more intensely than before. This time, though, we know what they don't. The prevailing sound is what a colleague once described as a right crash of old irony.

To be more specific: Mrs. Conway gives herself airs (she also sings them) and seems jealous of her daughters. When we first meet them, Kay, the birthday girl, wants to be a novelist; Madge is a visionary socialist; Hazel is fashion-conscious; and Carol is simply and enthusiastically young.

They have a bony friend called Joan, who is inarticulately loved by their shy brother, Alan, but is swept up by their very un-shy other brother, Robin, a returning airman who's his mother's favourite. In the first act, the women are organizing a game of charades, into which all the male characters are, with various degrees of unwilligness, dragooned. (The word they're acting out is "pussyfoot" which must have thematic significance, though I couldn't say what.)

At the Shaw, Neil Munro stages all this with a great sense of swirl, but not much else. By the end of Act One I still hadn't worked out who the characters were, and when one of them failed to turn up for Act Two, I didn't notice.

The atmosphere is Little Women crossed with Chekhov: Three Sisters, of course, but also -- and increasingly, as the action turns to financial ruin and threatened family property -- The Cherry Orchard. The middle act is a variant of that fine old standby, the Reading of the Will. The family solicitor gives the Conways a bleak assessment of their financial position, and all hell breaks loose.

The only man who could save them is an uppity little entrepreneur who has married Hazel and seems to be treating her appallingly, and he refuses. (It's another old theme: the revenge of the nouveau- riche on the snobbish petty-genteel.) Mrs C. slaps his face: A moment brilliantly staged here with the other characters, their backs to us, gathered round like ringside spectators. He says she'll be sorry.

The time games aren't just a matter of flashback and flash- forward. When sensitive Kay asks kindly Alan for comfort, he says that we shouldn't get hung up on chronology; that one moment of time is as important as any other.

This makes sense, especially in the theatre, where first scenes are rehearsed as carefully as last. (Generally more, schedules being what they are.) But the play itself contradicts the theory. The last act's only interest lies in our awareness of what is going to happen later, and our withers are shamelessly wrung; Priestley even has a girl who is going to die proclaim how intensely she is going to live.

The middle-act quarrelling, though, is the goods: a rivetingly constructed display of all-around meanness. It doesn't, however, reverberate much beyond the personal level. Nobody would accuse Priestley of lacking social consciousness, and he plainly meant the Conways to reflect all the national upheavals of the Twenties and Thirties. But in practice, we are hardly more conscious here of the depression and the coming war than we were in She Loves Me the night before.

The individual performances find it hard to recover from the hustle of the first act. They never put down roots. Nora McLellan as Mrs. Conway certainly cuts through more incisively than anyone else, and her scream at her ineffectual son ("don't be so forgiving!") is superb; but she plays up the woman's affectations and neuroses so insistently that you never get to see the character beneath.

Jenny L. Wright cannot get a grip on Kay, who is the nearest thing to a central figure; while the other women (Laurie Paton, Jan Alexandra Smith, Jane Perry) make up an anonymous mass of suffering and complaint, relieved by the occasional moment of genuine pain.

Simon Bradbury plays the thrusting northern upstart, as he must have done in 20 other plays, but it's still effective. Peter Krantz shuffles sympathetically as Alan; Bruce Davies walks through the caddishly hollow Robin with no conviction whatever. Brian Perchaluk's drawing-room set shrinks suggestively from an overstuffed past, fit to serve as the frontispiece of a Samuel French acting edition, to a melancholy, shell-like present.

HAMLET

Festival Theatre, Stratford

Paul Gross' Hamlet is a very nice young man. I am not being sarcastic; like you, I am weary of scruffy, snarling Hamlets attempting to pin their own neuroses and those of the modern world onto a Renaissance prince whom nearly everybody in the play seems to like. When Gross Hamlet appears before us, mourning his fathers death and his mother's re-marriage, he is not playing games. He seems every bit as sad as he claims to be: consumed by grief, to the exclusion of all other feelings.

He also seems innocent; he may be in love with Ophelia, but he plainly hasn't touched her. A virginal Hamlet makes a lot of sense; it explains as nothing else could the intolerable tone, at once prurient and priggish, that he takes toward his mother. Considering the bad ends that await both the prince and his beloved, the play might be interpreted as a stern warning against the dangers of premature sexual inexperience.

This is not a case of a television star venturing embarrassingly out of his depth. Gross makes literal sense of the text, and rhythmic sense as well. (So does everybody else in the cast. A rumour persists that Stratford actors have forgotten how to speak verse. Maybe they did forget once, but they seem to be well on the way to remembering.)

Whats missing is not technique but temperament. He remains a diffident Hamlet.

Sometimes this works. About a third of the way through the play, Gross brings off something really enlightening. He has been listening with admiration to the First Players recitation about the fall of Troy. (As well he might; Juan Chioran's Player is the best performance of the evening. Chioran also plays the Ghost and -- with unusual sardonic dignity -- the First Gravedigger, making a triptych of characters who in different ways offer signposts to Hamlet while putting the fear of God into the king.)

Then comes the "rogue and peasant slave" soliloquy, in which Hamlet expresses his jealousy of the actor's capacity for passion; he tries it on himself, tries a tentative shout of oh vengeance!, finds it doesnt suit him, and subsides into the rueful self- mockery of "why, what an ass am I."

This respect for what professional actors can do that amateur avengers cant carries through into his advice to the players about holding up the mirror to nature, which he invests with unusual urgency, as if telling them that they have a moral responsibility to act well.

In the middle of this sequence comes the to be or not to be speech, which Gross delivers as a reasoned summary of the pros and cons of suicide. What he doesn't sound is involved, as if Hamlet himself might have been tempted to self-slaughter. There are no depths to this Hamlet, or none that the actor seems capable of sounding.

He probably knows they're there; he literally twists the arms of Rosencrantz and Guildenstern while hes interrogating them, but the gesture has no connection with the innocuous way in which he plays the rest of the scene. He has no capacity for venom (a quality with which Hamlets lines are loaded), no recklessness and no abandon. When he grapples with Laertes at Ophelia's grave, you wonder what he's going on about; his admission of the virtual murder of R&G goes by without a ripple; and he dies without having once disturbed us.

Joseph Ziegler, who directed, is an excellent actor, and this is very much an actors production. That is to to say its efficiently staged, traditional in appearance, and stronger on co-ordination of performances than on interpretation.

The setting (by Christine Poddubiuk) is so old-fashioned as to seem avant-garde; the Festival Theatre's familiar steps lead up to platforms adorned with yet more steps and crowned with a series of graceful arches. The indoor style is romantic, with a profusion of blazing candelabra;outside, it's more Gothic, the battlement scenes awash in dry ice, with a light fall of snow. Costumes are Regency English; the queen makes her first appearance in a riding-habit, courtiers wear frock-coats, and when hats are finally donned (for Ophelias funeral) they are toppers.

The productions two most original ideas are also its silliest. One involves having half-a-dozen actors march on the spot in a distracting effort to look like the Norwegian army.

The other is breaking the action just after Hamlet, sword in hand, comes upon the king at prayer; in fact, just after the first line of his speech ("now might I do it pat"). Clearly we are meant to go out into the lobbies in a state of agonized suspense -- is the king about to be slaughtered in the intermission? (An even nastier fate than being stabbed through the arras.) I don't think I'm giving much away if I reveal that he isnt.

Much, though, is intelligent, including the appearance of the king right on top of Hamlets line about catching his conscience. Ziegler shows what he can do with a pair of responsive actors in his subtle, supple treatment of the scene in which Claudius (Benedict Campbell, otherwise bland) and Laertes (Graham Abbey, good throughout) plot Hamlet's murder. Jerry Franken is a standard-order civil-servant Polonius.

Of the women, Domini Blythe's Gertrude looks handsome and sounds concerned, but the role still seems like the most underwritten major character in Shakespeare. Marion Day, like most Ophelias, is blank when sane and effective when mad.

This is Stratfords first Hamlet in years. More worrying than their having parachuted in a star to play the lead is the lack of any obvious contenders for the role within the regular company, current or recent. (The only one I can think of is Tom McCamus, whos already played it in Toronto.) In the meantime, we have a Hamlet who would probably make a first-rate Horatio, and a director whom Stratford should encourage. Between them, they tell the story. That's more than some productions manage, but it isn't enough.

AS YOU LIKE IT

Avon Theatre, Stratford

STRATFORD - There's no clock in the forest. That is what Orlando, the hero of As You Like It, tells Rosalind, the heroine-disguised- as-a-boy, when they meet in the Forest of Arden and she asks him the time.

A moment later, she's reading him an elegant lecture on the nature of time.

It's like being back at the Shaw Festival with J. B. Priestley's Conway family, though of course the thoughts are subtler and the language richer.

In this play, time is suspended and a significant percentage of the cast live in a state of perpetual courtship.

It's difficult to find a theatrical image that will denote the absence of something. The best you can do is illustrate its presence somewhere else, which is what Jeanette Lambermont's Stratford production does.

The pre-forest scenes are dominated by a couple of dark revolving wheels, with interlocking cogs and with a pendulum swinging between them.

Occasionally a savage ringing assaults our ears; the Duke and his retainers are living in a huge alarm-clock. No wonder people keep taking off for the woods.

The play ends in a quadruple wedding, presided over by Hymen, god (or, in this production,goddess) of marriage.

In this staging, Hymen comes equipped with another clock as if to say that holiday is over and that real life is to begin again, though on more hopeful terms.

The legitimate Duke, Rosalind's father, is to resume his dukedom; the couples have to make their relationships work. This is all very stimulating, though not very attractive visually.

Even Hymen's wedding-present clock looks grubby; and though the central forest scenes don't have time pieces,they're still lumbered with the production's permanent set, whose main feature is a broad curving ramp, and whose gestures towards the outdoors consist of lowering some ropes for trees, and backing everything with a green screen.

It isn't naturalistically convincing or sparely suggestive;and it certainly isn't pretty. The best you can say for it is that it permits some interesting groupings.

Its brutalism is the more perplexing, because this isn't a brutalist production. It's a stringent, and its' both sensitive and inventive. It's especially good at cross-reference, pointing up not just the obvious contrast between court and country, but the unexpected variations within the forest itself.

Counterpoint and overlap abound. It's a bizarre place, Shakespeare's Arden. It's an all-purpose green world, part farmland and part jungle, switching at will between agricultural realism and literary convention. Lionesses prowl and sheep are herded; a latter- day gang of Robin Hoods hide out there, but there seems to be easy access to and from the next village. Lucy Peacock is not, except in the epilogue, one of those Rosalinds with whom the whole audience falls irresistibly in love.

But she is witty and accomplished and especially good in the wonderful central scenes where the disguised Rosalind gives Orlando merrily disillusioned instruction on the nature of love, so that the two of them may get closer to the real thing.

All these scenes, by the way, are in prose: probably the greatest prose in the English language. It's a medium that seems to suit both her and her Orlando, Donald Carrier; he's less happy with his few passages of verse, but then Orlando is meant to be a lousy poet, a fact with which this production has more fun than most.

Brian Tree, a spiky-haired Touchstone, is split between playing the professional zany, at which he is tiresome, and the common sense commentator, at which he is delightful.

(It's a matter of taste, I guess, as are the decorations that festoon his scenes. I couldn't take the toy boat that he sails on an imaginary stream, but I had no objection to the three actors in goat- masks who attend his wooing of Audrey.)

As Celia, Jacklyn Francis aims, I think, at pert, but mostly gets stuck at shrill.

Juan Chioran is striking as the melancholy Jaques. As far as I can see, the only thing preventing Chioran from being a major Shakespearean actor is that he doesn't seem to fit any of the major Shakespearean roles, except perhaps Iago.

The minor players here all have at least a moment each. I especially liked the villains: Robert Benson an implacable Frederick, and Jonathan Goad a more malleable malefactor as Orlando's bad-brother Oliver.

The goodies have an eloquent champion in Joseph Shaw's old Adam. Shakespeare himself is traditionally supposed to have played the part.

The songs are mainly delightful, beautifully sung (by Steve Ross) and beautifully set (by Keith Thomas); the only exceptions are A Lover and his Lass, which is inexplicably thrown away, and Hymen's wedding-chant, which is tacky, though not as tacky as the pas de deux that goes with it.

Students of the play might note that it has lost a character. Orlando's and Oliver's brother, "the second son of old Sir Rowland," no longer appears at the end to tie up the plot; that function is now performed by Charles, the wrestler from the first two scenes. (He's greeted by name; just as well since it's hours since we last saw him.)

There is a fitness here. At the play's opening Charles spoke wistfully of the golden world of Arden; now he arrives there, to summon the characters home. In other words, he re-starts the clock.

Black & White Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann, Stratford Festival / Juan Chioran as Jaques and Jerry Franken as Duke Senior in As You Like It. ;

A WOMAN OF NO IMPORTANCE

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE - A cracking first week at the Shaw Festival ended with the least-known of Oscar Wilde's society comedies. It proved a fascinating evening, and an improving one as well: a steady upward climb. I cannot recall a production, as one of its characters might have said in an off moment, that began so badly and ended so well.

Like the other Wilde plays that led up to The Importance of Being Earnest, A Woman of No Importance alternates scenes of studiedly flippant commentary with others of solemn, palpitating melodrama. Once upon a time in the West End, the latter was regarded as the price you paid for the former; the staid characters had their scenes cut to ribbons while the beribboned ones were dressed to the nines. Surely, producers said, a writer as sophisticated as Wilde could not have meant his more overripe and overwrought exchanges to be taken seriously.

We have since realized that he probably did, and that, even if he didn't, we would be well advised to play them as if he did; there are just too many of them to be sent up. Besides, they concern real situations and real emotions, and good actors can get at the truth that lies beneath the purple. That is the approach taken in Susan Ferley's production, and it works superbly.

What works less well are the jokes, which is a shame, since they seem to be among the best in Wilde. (Or maybe it's just that they haven't been overexposed.) They are delivered by an assortment of peers and peeresses, languidly passing the time over a country- house weekend. Some of the lines relate to the individuals who speak them; others, the author seems to have distributed around the cast with magnificent impartiality.

There is one epigram here that has made the dictionaries of quotations: a description of fox-hunting as "the unspeakable in full pursuit of the uneatable." There are many about marriage, usually seen from the woman's point of view; one especially world-weary lady describes her husband as "a sort of promissory note; I'm tired of meeting him."

The female ensemble here is ragged; the only actress in command of the text is Jennifer Phipps, as a fearsomely benevolent dragon. She often seems to be woolgathering (metaphorically and literally; she's very attached to her knitting), but just when you think she's drifted off, she drifts on again, bringing down the house with another perfectly pitched punchline.

Nobody else has her gift of phrasing. Sharry Flett, as the hostess, has an air, but the benevolent vagueness of her characterization seems also to have infected her technique. And in what would once have been the star role, the glittering kind in which English high comediennes used to swan around in dresses by Cecil Beaton, Brigitte Robinson practically fades into the wallpaper -- or would, if the small, open stage at Niagara's Court House had any walls.

Wilde's paradoxes, so compulsively spun, tend to cancel one another out; but this chorus of wives, dowagers and divorcees is presumably meant to provide a background, tempting but unsavoury, against which the play's good characters can shine all the purer. That doesn't sound much like Wilde the dandy and aesthete, but it does seem to be the play he wrote. As it unfolds, the chorus recedes and the plot takes over, which, in this production, is a good thing.

The story concerns Mrs. Arbuthnot, who was once seduced and abandoned by Lord Illingworth. She bore a son, Gerald, who has grown up and is now, to his mother's horror, about to accept a position as his father's secretary. Neither father nor son knows of their relationship; when Mrs. A. in desperation reveals it to Lord I., it merely makes him more anxious to forward the boy's future.

Gerald, meanwhile, is unshaken by the revelation that his father once ruined an unidentified young woman. (Wasn't it, he inquires, the girl's fault, too? -- a question to which his mother has no answer.) But he is revolted when he finds him making advances to a young American woman whom he himself admires. All three make common cause against Lord Illingworth, who retires from the field, defeated but unbowed.

Pleading for her son, Mrs. Arbuthnot says things like "leave me the little vineyard of my life ... the ewe-lamb God sent me, in pity or in wrath"; she describes herself as "a woman who drags a chain ... like a thing that is a leper." Mary Haney, in a magnificent performance, cuts beneath the rhetoric to the angry, agonized woman beneath. Some of the morality may seem alien to us, but Wilde's loathing of the double standard comes through with scorching clarity.

Not all her colleagues can make the material work so well. The American girl (Severn Thompson) is a Henry Jamesian innocent abroad whom the decadent English deride as a prig and a prude, and one cannot help agreeing with them.

The one character who speaks in both the play's voices is Lord Illingworth, by turns a cynical wit and a man who both inflicts and suffers pain. He loves his son, somewhat ambiguously (their first scene together, as employer and protege, plays like a homosexual seduction), fights to keep him, and loses. Jim Mezon, pudgy and soft- spoken, is not the most obvious casting for an Edwardian roue, but he excels at playing men divided, men with layers, and his scenes with Haney reach a very high level of tension and involvement.

His resemblance to his author is clearly intended: Wilde may condemn the things that Illingworth does, but he clearly enjoys and endorses much of what he says. In his next play, An Ideal Husband, he presents an almost identical character as the voice of charity and reason. He was dealing, of course, with a social class that he had reason both to fear and to envy. Only in his last play did he get them in perspective; in The Importance, which opens tomorrow at Stratford, all the characters are monsters, but nothing -- unless, of course, it involves muffins or cucumber sandwiches -- is a matter of life and death.

The Three Musketeers is in repertoire until Nov. 1 at the Festival Theatre in Stratford. Tickets $38.50 to $67.50. Call the box office at 1 (800) 567-1600.

DArtagnan, a brave and hot-headed young man from Gascony, comes to the Paris of Louis XIII, hoping for a place in the Kings Musketeers. He is befriended by three members of that crack regiment, known by the mysterious names of Athos, Porthos and Aramis. Together, they foil one of the major plots of the Machiavellian statesman Cardinal Richelieu, venturing to England to retrieve some diamonds that the French Queen has bestowed on her would-be lover, the Duke of Buckingham, an indiscretion by which the Cardinal had hoped to ruin her. They also fall afoul of Richelieu's beautiful and fiendishly unscrupulous agent, Milady de Winter, whom they eventually track to a lonely village and judicially execute.

That is the storyline -- it isn't really a plot -- of Alexandre Dumass The Three Musketeers, and you probably know it already, if not from the book, then from one of the innumerable film or TV adaptations. It is, of course, only the skeleton; the novel is an intoxicating essay in the swashbuckling-picaresque, with a huge supporting cast and any number of incidents. The amazing thing about Peter Rabys dramatization (first staged at Stratford in 1968 and now back in a new production) is how many of these it manages to get in; most versions use up most of their time on the diamond-studs episode, and then rush hurriedly to some kind of climax. Raby's script has to rush everything, though never, amazingly, at the expense of clarity. It's a whirlwind scenario, and Richard Monette has staged it accordingly, in a superbly drilled and mounted production that glories in its own superficiality. (I had better make it clear, that is not a put-down.) It seems to have a cast of thousands, though the program reveals 40 actors, rushing about in an infinity of hats and cloaks.

It plays like a musical, with duels instead of duets. There is a mass fight, by way of overture, and when the real action gets going, it involves more swordplay than any entertainment since Errol Flynn last hung up his scabbard. It hardly encourages subtle acting, but it rewards players who can make a hard, fast and preferably amusing statement. Graham Abbey comes out very well as DArtagnan, and does develop before our eyes from callow bumpkin through ardently predatory lover to military leader: less a matter of tracing a psychological arc than of taking each moment triumphantly as it comes. Two of the musketeers are shadowy, but Benedict Campbells Athos is excellent in its hard-bitten hauteur. Kate Trotter is a superbly uninhibited Milady, and Stephen Russell stalks the stage to great aquiline effect as Richelieu.

The Queen of France seems a touch parvenu, and the King is played (by Ian Deakin) as an outright ninny. Some of the Parisian bourgeoisie have French accents, but -- mysteriously -- not all; Robert King, as D'Artagnan's poltroon of a landlord, sounds like Jean Chretien, or, to be more exact, like Chretien as rendered on the Royal Canadian Air Farce. Anachronisms abound, some more blatant than others. Berthold Carrieres music signifies its Frenchness with snatches of the Marseillaise, though the action takes place more than 150 years before the Revolution. It also runs to what sounds like Son of Star Wars (or maybe of Indiana Jones -- I can never remember which theme is which). Milady turns, in her last extremity, into a leather-queen with whip; and a posse of nuns includes a refugee from The Sound of Music. At one point, Cyrano de Bergerac crosses the stage, nose in air; but thats a fair deal, since D'Artagnan is a cameo character in the actual Cyrano, another Stratford favourite that's like The Three Musketeers with a play thrown in.

Some of these japes I would categorize as high jinks, and others as low. The rationale for all of them seems to be that the book is being read by a modern young boy -- whom we see for a few seconds at the beginning of the show -- and that we are watching the story as it would unfold in his imagination. (You may, of course, believe that Monette would have thrown in all these gags, no matter what.)

I wonder, though, if that boy got anything out of Dumas book that we dont see. Because there is a lot missing, much of it witty. At one point, in Raby's version, the musketeers plan to hold a council of war, but are prevented by pressure of events. In the novel, they are always holding councils of war, and these are among the best things in the book. They're how we get to know the characters; theyre four bright, young men (well, Porthos isnt bright, but he's lovable) scoring off one another. We lose much of the flavour of the quartet as individuals -- some interpolated, coarse comedy for Porthos is the production's lowpoint -- and therefore the all-important sense of them as a group. One of the originals set pieces shows them planning their next moves, while simultaneously fending off an invading army.

It would be a great scene, but theres no time for it. The play is composed of short, humorous dialogues, the novel of long, humorous dialogues that cry out to be acted. They would, of course, make the play last about 10 hours, but that would be all right with me.

Dumas was a playwright before he was a novelist; and he remained, in all senses, a very theatrical writer. Only three of his stories seem to be available in English at the moment: this one, The Count of Monte Cristo, and The Man in the Iron Mask (popular for its title, though it's actually part of a much longer novel, and must be incomprehensible to most of its readers). There is an enormous amount of other stuff, worth reprinting and worth adapting. The Musketeer sequels, in particular, are very rich; D'Artagnan at 40 and 50, witty and wise, is a figure of Shakespearean dimension, with soliloquies that compare with Falstaffs. Meantime, this Musketeers is fun. Its the best production of the festival, so far, and that's fine; if it turns out to be the best of the whole year, there'll be trouble.

Color Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / The Three Musketeers -- a superbly drilled and mounted production that glories in its own superficiality. ;

DIARY OF ANNE FRANK AVON THEATRE, STRATFORD

The Stratford Festival production of The Diary of Anne Frank is, by any conventional standards, extremely well done. The question, to which I do not have an answer, is whether the dramatization of the most poignant and familiar of Holocaust documents is a case in which conventional standards should apply.

I am surprised to find myself harbouring these doubts. A few years ago I saw the play at the Toronto Young Peoples Theatre, in a production that was excellent but with no pretentions to greatness, and it effectively disposed of my qualms. If you were to put the Holocaust on stage at all, then this modest craftsman-like approach seemed the way to do it: far less offensive than turning it into a self-conscious piece of Art and asking to be congratulated on your sensitivity.

Al Waxmans Stratford production is not essentially different, but it has more of a gloss, the performances are generally more striking (though not necessarily better, and YPT certainly had a finer Anne) and, of course, since it's at Stratford, the stakes are higher. The show implicitly realizes this, and it tries very hard to be real. But that is, by definition, an impossible attempt.

Once on stage, the eight Jews hiding from the Nazis in an Amsterdam attic -- the four Franks, the three Van Daans, the solitary dentist Mr. Dussel, never leave it, not even during the intermission: Never, that is, until the end when they are betrayed and herded off to the death camps. We feel something of the tedium and frustration (the words seem inadequate, but that's part of my point) of being pent up for two years, unable to make a sound until night because men are working by day in the factory beneath, knowing all the time that the alternative is unimaginably worse.

A few years ago the familiar 1956 dramatization by Frances Goodrich and Albert Hackett was thoroughly overhauled by Wendy Kesselman. That version was staged in New York in 1997, and its the text used here. Goodrich and Hackett, an anonymously competent Broadway and Hollywood team, cast the material in the mould of an American well-made play; in effect, they wrote a Broadway domestic drama with a death sentence hanging over it. And the last thing they dwelt on -- in deference to the susceptibilities of audiences of both persuasions -- was the characters Jewishness.

Kesselman has roughened and loosened it up, going back to the originally published diary, and incorporating some material that has been revealed since. The characters are now less, shall we say, assimilated than they were; there is more racial and religious detail. There is also more sexual detail: more explicit emphasis on Anne Frank's pubescent yearnings.

Anne's constant friction with her mother -- excised for years by her father, the one survivor -- is now front and centre. All these tensions , of course, are what happen in any family; its just that here theyre happening in a pressure cooker.

The old Broadway mould is further broken by letting us hear symbolic sounds of the outside world: Hitler's speeches, the sound of the trains. (Neither are exactly original choices). The original naturalistic epilogue, in which Otto Frank was reunited with his Gentile protectors and told them what had happened to the others, is replaced by a monologue that he addresses against a projected background of barbed wire and crematoria.

Before that we have seen the SS actually arriving on stage to arrest the fugitives; in the old play, we only heard them arriving. The change is, I think, a mistake; it tries to show us the cruelty, but can't do it justice: Better to leave it to our imaginations. Some of the changes are clearly improvements, but the old version worked better because of its limitations. It was what it was.

The Stratford actors are excellent, though Maggie Blake cant lift Anne off the page (shes more convincing in her voice-over narration than in her live scenes) and her older sister Margot seems only to exist as her foil. But George A. Sperdakos has great quiet dignity as their father, and Diane D'Aquila gives a beautifully modulated account of his permanently anguished wife.

The more extrovert, perpetually squabbling Van Daans -- he ever- hungry, she ever-gushing -- are played to the hilt, though never over it by Robert King and Lally Cadeau with Nicholas Van Burek as their son Peter, a lanky, embarrassed presence between them. (Why, incidentally, were these characters' names changed? Historically they were called Van Pels. Was that name thought to be insufficiently catchy for Broadway in the Fifties? And if so, why hasnt this new more outspoken adaptation, restored their identity? It makes you wonder about the whole endeavour.)

The benefactors are good, too; one looks forward to their visits just as the prisoners do, with Deborah Hays servant girl an especially welcome presence. The performances mesh together admirably: a smooth cohesive ensemble, each picking up infallibly where the last one left off.

That's really good theatre. It isn't real life, where people stumble and overlap, and the timing is awkward. Maybe the whole thing should be improvised. Maybe a genius-director could incite his actors to the level of reality this subject seems to demand; maybe it isnt possible, or shouldnt even be attempted.

As it is, though, one of the most detailed and intelligent performances, that of the crotchety Dussel (real name, Pfeiffer) was the one I had most trouble believing, simply because the actor, Brian Tree, is one whose work I know (and like) especially well.

There is a danger with this play, in any version: one that it shares with pieces like The Miracle Worker. The audience, having shared vicariously in someone else's historical agony, leaves feeling drained, certainly, but also spuriously noble. Maybe only a historically traumatic production in Berlin in the Fifties managed to escape that. But if the Holocaust is not to be theatrically off- limits -- and I don't think it should be -- then probably this is the only way to approach it: Take a small number of individual tragedies and multiply by six million.

FIDDLER ON THE ROOF

Festival Theatre, Stratford

Brent Carver belongs in a select group of performers whose roots are firmly in the legitimate theatre but who have realized themselves most fully in musicals: Others on the list are Robert Preston, Angela Lansbury, Len Cariou, British actor Denis Lawson, and -- of course -- Rex Harrison. They all act in musicals as seriously as they would act in plays; and speech and song in their performances are of a piece. Few of them are great singers, but they all have the knack of projecting the essence of their characters through music. And it works both ways; the rhythm of their singing feeds back into the dialogue, giving their whole performances a lift.

Carver made this team with his superb work in Kiss of the Spider Woman, and consolidated his position in Parade. In both of these shows he was playing beleaguered men: victims, in fact. Tevye the dairyman in Fiddler on the Roof is also beleaguered -- he's a Jew living in a village in Czarist Russia on the eve of a pogrom -- but he is nobodys victim, and when Carver was announced for the role in the new revival at Stratford, there were widespread mutterings that he was wrong for it. As it turns out, he is wrong in some ways. There are other ways, though, in which he is quite wonderfully right, and they are more important.

To deal with the faults first: Tevye is traditionally associated with actors who are fat (Zero Mostel) or at least physically powerful (Topol), and who have deep, rolling voices to match. Susan H. Schulman, who directs this production, has said that since Tevye is a poor man with a wife and five daughters to support, he is likelier to be tall and stringy.

That sounds plausible; but the script never suggests that either Tevye or his family go hungry -- rather the reverse -- and he has a standing in the village that seems to transcend his social position. Hes the one Jew whom the town constable treats as a confidant. The timid tailor, Motel, who wants to marry Tevye's oldest daughter, professes to be terrified that his future father-in-law might shout at him.

Well, when Tevye actually does, Carver manages a very respectable bellow, but he never suggests a man of whom anyone would go in fear. Tevye himself is henpecked, but that isn't funny unless he seems imposing to everybody else.

In fact, a lot of the humour goes missing; Carver manages Tevyes pained or ironic asides beautifully, but he doesnt have the folk or vaudeville touch for the milkman's sustained crosstalk act with God; Tevye is an orthodox believer who nevertheless finds the deity's ways too inscrutable for comfort, but Carver isnt one of natures kvetches.

In the same way, he misses the roaring comic climax that's built in to his big song If I Were a Rich Man. Indeed, the songs, most unusually for this actor, generally go for little.

The recitatives, however, do not. You may not remember, from other performances, that Tevye has recitatives; but he has -- they're chants, really, of a moderately Hebraic character -- and they all concern his daughters. In the course of the show, he loses each of the three eldest to a progressively less eligible suitor.

The first is the poor tailor; he can cope with that. The second is a political radical, with secular leanings; he can just about accommodate that. The third is a gentile; and that both enrages Tevye and -- because he loves the girl so much -- breaks his heart. It breaks the audiences, too. Carver may be the best actor in the world at conveying vulnerability and emotional need.

Fiddler, though not nearly as sentimental a piece as its often thought to be, is a show at which crying comes easy; but it's never likely to be more moving than it is here. It's largely a show about the fortunes of a family, and in this respect, Carvers performance cuts right to its centre.

Because of his acting, and that of several others, this production seems a more integral part of the season than Stratford musicals generally do. As the story of a vanishing community -- it ends with their expulsion -- Fiddler has an epic scale that suits the Festival stage; the setting is a revolving mosaic floor backed by an evocative line of tumbledown houses.

Some regular company members of various vintages find comfortable homes here: Keith Dinicol as the rabbi; Jonathan Goad as the Russian Romeo; and, especially, Michael Therriault as Motel.

Of the imported specialists, the best are the three marriageable daughters. They give the evening a musical-comedy lift with their singing of Matchmaker (don't ask what a scintillating Broadway waltz is doing on the Steppes), and then separate out into individuals: Robin Hutton modestly determined; Tracy Michailidis increasingly strong, and matching her father for emotion when she leaves him to join her banished husband in Siberia; and Amy Walsh featherlight and enchanting.

Barbara Barsky overplays the nagging wife (no actress can make much of this role; it must be the writing), and Yente the matchmaker, a character almost guaranteed to bring out the worst in whoever plays her, is done by Theresa Tova strictly according to form. And a classical company should be able to find an actor who can bring more weight than Craig Ashton does here to the part of the implausibly humane Constable.

The ensemble feeling is fine, though, from the opening Tradition number (which Carver leads in fine style) to the final mass departure. Some clown claims in a program note that Fiddler isn't really a dance-musical, but this production suggests different. Everyone knows that one of the shows highlights is its wedding scene, with the gloriously solemn bottle dance, representing the old ways, and the first dancing of men with women, dramatizing the advance of the new. But the earlier To Life carries as much weight: as a celebration, it brings down the house; as a meeting between Jews and Cossacks, it shows both the possibilities and the limits of co-existence. Ive never known it to work so powerfully before.

Michael Lichtefeld's choreography preserves the outlines of Jerome Robbins' original staging, and supplies some new detail of its own. Joseph Steins book remains one of the best ever written for a musical, breathtaking in the way it keeps four plot lines running so they seem like one.

The production complements the Shaw Festivals She Loves Me, to give us a fortuitous festival of the shows of Jerry Bock and Sheldon Harnick. Song by song, this isn't my favourite of their scores -- Harnick's lyrics sometime seem to falter under the burden imposed by having to explain themselves to the gentiles as they go along -- but, as a whole and in context, its invincible. Some of Bocks tunes -- Anatevka and, especially, Sunrise Sunset -- have a similar power to You'll Never Walk Alone; they get to you, at a level far below your rational threshold.
