THE IMPORTANCE OF BEING EARNEST

Avon Theatre, Stratford

"I trust," says Lady Brancaster as the final revelations approach, that nothing surprising is about to happen: a forlorn hope, in the circumstances. You don't know Lady Brancaster, at least not by that name. You may well know her, though, under a different title: as Lady Bracknell, the gorgon of the handbag and the cucumber sandwiches, who traditionally dominates The Importance of Being Earnest.

Oscar Wilde wrote his last comedy in the four-act format he had used for its three predecessors. George Alexander, the actor- manager who gave it its premiere in 1895, insisted that it be cut to three, and the result was the play that we have known and loved ever since. You dont argue with success, but Wildes original text survives, in various manuscript forms, and, from time to time, enterprising theatres have given the long version a whirl. Richard Monette's Stratford production is its big-time Canadian premiere.

Earnest's predecessors attained their length by alternating comedy of manners -- what the Elizabethans would have called wit- combats -- with heavy-breathing melodrama. Its an uneasy if sometimes fascinating mixture (as seen in A Woman of No Importance, currently at Shaw), and Wilde finally resolved it, not by jettisoning the melodrama but by turning it on its head and making it farce. The original Earnest is four acts of beautiful nonsense; this is rather too much of a good thing, and Alexander was quite right to cut it. A hundred years on, though, the excised sections prove refreshing. They supply some welcome new jokes to a text that rather too many of us know by heart.

They do other things, as well. They change and elaborate the structure -- the long garden scene that was once Act Two is now bisected -- and they alter the balance of the characters. Lady Bracknell, appearing in two acts out of three, can still be the star part; Lady Brancaster, scoring only two out of four, doesnt have a chance.

The name makes a difference, too; Jack Worthing (his name hasn't changed) complains of Lady B that she's a monster without being a myth, and though there is much that is monstrous about Patricia Collins Lady B, there is indeed nothing that is mythical. She isnt competing with Edith Evans or any other predecessor; and it couldn't matter less how she says "A handbag!" (actually, she throws the line away) when confronted with the information that Jack, her would-be son-in-law, had been discovered in one when a baby.

Collins' matriarch is erect and imperious: a battering-ramrod. With undeviating efficiency she fulfills her social and dramatic function, which is to enforce and enunciate English upper-class prejudices as if they were the decrees of Providence -- as, in this context, they pretty much are.

There is a strain of radical discontent in this ur-text, which the Alexander technique seems to have been at great pains to eradicate. There is also, intentionally or not, a strain of theatrical self-satire; the characters comment on the play as it happens. Lady Brancasters forebodings about the coming denouement are a case in point.

This, of course, is all very post-modern, and some of it is positively cathartic. When Jack, stunned by the relentless stream of paradoxes emanating from his friend Algernon, asks him: Do you ever listen to what youre saying? he voices sentiments that some of us have wanted to scream at Wilde's characters for years.

In this version, the play becomes, as it was probably always intended to be, essentially about Jack and Algy: the two young men about town and country, each leading a double life, each in love with a girl who will only marry him if his name is Ernest.

They are distinctively played here. Donald Carrier's Jack is not, as Algy claims he is, the most earnest-looking person you ever saw in your life, not in that canary waistcoat and wide, permanent smile, but there is an edge beneath the smirk; he is in command, but he is also an outsider, as if the mark of the handbag were on him for life. Graham Abbey, who, as Algy, completes a hair-raising opening week that began with Laertes and DArtagnan, seems less happy fencing with epigrams than with rapiers; but he, too, has depths, suggesting that Algernon still has some growing up to do, and knows it. He also, as the play goes on, becomes increasingly charming.

Claire Jullien, as his beloved Cecily, is as sweetly implacable as she should be, a pink rose with a thorn. Jack fears that his Gwendolyn will "become like her mother in about 150 years time"; Michelle Giroux makes the probability rather too blatant, but there is piquancy in her excited habit of crooking one leg behind her while being kissed, and in the way that she tests the competing vibrations of the names Jack and Ernest as if with an invisible tuning fork.

The most substantial new scene concerns the arrival in the country of a solicitor named Gribsby (Brian Tree, drily obsequious) to arrest Algy for debts that were actually incurred by Jack, living it up at the Savoy Hotel. I am not going to be imprisoned in the suburbs protests Algernon, "for having dined in the West End," but of course it all comes of having two elegant but improvident young men both going around under the name of Ernest.

The scene is watched, with a mixture of pious horror and delighted satisfaction, by the play's very moral senior couple. "As a man sows, so shall he reap" says Miss Prism, the governess; she only says it once in the received text, but here it's a running gag with a payoff. Truthfully, its overdone; but Domini Blythes Prism (not as senior as all that) is an Edinburgh spinster so delectable that I would have been happy to hear her say anything. As her admirer Canon Chasuble puts it, I would hang upon her lips; and, unlike him, I'm not even sure that I would be speaking metaphorically. (His metaphor is drawn from bees.) Bernard Hopkins' desiccated Canon is less original, but agreeable.

The extension of the action means that more eating gets done, in a play that already -- like most comedies -- turns largely on greed; lobster and pate de foie gras sandwiches have now been added to the menu. The production has a fair amount of style and a lot of fun; and due partly, but by no means entirely, to the unfamiliar material, the play comes up fresher than it has a long time.

RENT

At the Pantages Theatre, Toronto

To adapt one of the more powerful songs from Rent: "When you're living in America, at the end of the millennium, youre slightly out of date.

Much of this hugely successful shows music still resounds, and this third time around, I found it easy to walk into the theatre, intoning the pounding theme tune, the one that goes: How we gonna pay, how we gonna pay, how we gonna pay, last year's rent?" -- which is a bit whiny, but which later mutates into the more determined "we ain't gonna pay ..., and so on.

Most of us can sympathize with those sentiments. Weve been there. Its a stretch, though, to elevate them into a moral credo. And you may find yourself wondering just why the two young men who sing it should find their landlord's demands so unreasonable, and why the landlord himself, each time he puts in appearance, should be dismissed as Yuppie scum," self-evidently unworthy of a hearing. He may be all they say he is, but his treatment isn't dramatic. And the whole story of evictions and protests and lock-outs, which supplies the title, is confusingly raised and dropped during the show, and finally fades out long before the end.

As everybody knows, Rent is La Boheme, transferred to New Yorks East Village. Mark, an aspiring filmmaker and the shows narrator- figure, shares a currently freezing loft apartment (it's Christmas when we start) with Roger, a long-unproductive rock musician who, in common with half the principals, has AIDS. Mark has lost his girlfriend, Maureen, a performance artist, to her lesbian manager, Joanne, who has a day job as a lawyer.

Roger gets involved with Mimi, a junkie who works at an S&M club and who is fitfully involved with Benny, the landlord. Then there is Collins, a computer genius, who hooks up with Angel, a drag queen. Between them they go through an assortment of creative or emotional triumphs and disasters. At the end, Mimi seemingly dies of AIDS, like her operatic namesake of TB, but then makes a surprise comeback, having apparently had a vision of Angel, who is dead.

Well, you could probably make the story of La Boheme itself sound silly with a snappy synopsis. (Personally, I think it is silly.) Rent has at least outlived one canard -- that it owes its success to the death, just before its New York opening, of its then-unknown author-composer, Jonathan Larson. I doubt if many of its current audiences know about Larson, and I myself came to the show too late to be moved by the thought of his death while I was actually watching it.

Writing about it is another thing. It is distressing that the word that keeps coming to the surface is "promising. Larson succeeded better than anyone else in making contemporary pop theatrical. His lyrics are mostly rock-opera generic -- too much declaration, not enough detail -- with the bright exception of Tango Maureen, in which Mark and Joanne pool the exasperation they feel over their mutual flame.

The music, though, is varied and vivid, from Santa Fe, which suggests what Kurt Weill might have made of a country-and-western song, to a couple of lung-bursting bodice rippers for Mimi. There are also La Vie Boheme, a dinner-table celebration of everything the characters (and presumably the author) approve of, and the famous Seasons of Love, a sweet tune with significant verbal handicaps.

Good musicals are often about individual people loving one another. They are not about Love -- or, as this song has it lo-o- ove" -- in the abstract. That's pop: the mindless sickliness that has lain beneath the tough veneer since the 1960s. A U.S. theatre magazine, discussing Mimis resurrection, exclaimed "Ah, the American theater ending!" and blamed it all on Rodgers and Hammerstein. That is a lie. In a traditional musical -- and very notably in R&H -- when people die, they stay dead.

Rent has a peppy, atmospheric first act, and an increasingly clammy second. Its dramatic dishonesty really surfaces at Angels funeral. Mimi steps forward to say Angel was one of her best friends, though we've never seen them exchange a word. Other characters chime in, claiming for the deceased all kinds of noble qualities that were never dramatized. And from then on the name of Angel becomes an emotional beacon for the survivors. It's as if being a drag queen and dying of AIDS are automatic qualifications for sanctity.

When it opened in New York, and when it first came to Toronto, Rent had three things going for it: its music, its gritty-casual look, and its energy. The music remains, and so do the lineaments of Michael Greifs staging, but the performers of this touring version are sleepwalking.

The performances -- apart from Horace V. Rogers as Collins -- are zeroes. A charmless Mark -- who should be our window on the action - - and a raucously unenticing Mimi are especially damaging. If we dont warm to the performers, we're going to start seeing the characters as mawkish and self-pitying.

Why are we supposed to agonize with Mark when he gets a lucrative TV offer? Why should we care about Roger and Mimi when all they ever do, thanks to the musical idiom, is shout at one another? The sung- through rock-musical had always had problems with story and character, which tend to fall through the cracks between the screams, and this cast are especially incomprehensible.

Infrequently but regularly, a musical comes along that both depicts and speaks to disaffected youth -- or at least to those who would like to feel disaffacted for two hours or so. West Side Story is 45 years old and still cool (ask the Gap). Hair fell out, long ago. Rent will probably rank between the two. Its now-ness, so frantically proclaimed in the lyrics, was real but already feels nostalgic. It was last millennium.

Black & White Photo: SYCON SENGBLOH AND CARY SHIELDS IN A SCENE FROM RENT: The music remains strong, but the performances lack energy. ;

The upshot of Boxhead seems to be that God is dead, and that, although this is on the whole a good thing, man is having difficulty shouldering the added responsibility. We begin with darkness, and a voice telling us about a certain Dr. Thoughtless Actions, a young geneticist who woke up one morning to find a box on his head. A light comes up on the boxed scientist, who seems uncomfortable in his situation, but disinclined to change it.

Anyway, he goes about his business, propounds theories and attends conferences (I suppose it's crassly literal to wonder how he manages to eat) and, at a certain stage, encounters another young geneticist in a similar condition, whose name is Dr. Wishful Thinking. The two men have an instant rapport, fall in love and even decide that they would like to have a child. This last ambition is thwarted, though, by the revelation that they are, in fact, the same person: Wishful thinking and thoughtless actions inevitably go together.

Both doctors are endowed with eager, squeaky cartoon voices, like speeded-up tapes. Their stories are told to us by two contrastingly deep and languid voices that claim to live inside the characters and to have other voices living inside them. They are omniscient narrators and -- by explicit analogy -- they are God. (If God, according to philosophers, died in the 18th century, the death of the narrator was postponed until the 20th, but this play capsizes time.)

The voices are tired of both roles, although they are not above engaging in competitive cross-talk routines about the extent of their power. At times, one gets the impression that they would be quite happy to cede all authority to the geneticists, who have presumably been singled out because of their own professional propensity to play God. Most of the time, though, the boxed pair are the objects of sadistic games played by both their on-stage and off- stage creators. You might say that each of the two teams has, for its own pyschological purposes, invented the other.

There is a lot of the play -- notably the doctors' chat about the cloning of time -- that I didnt understand. There is also a certain amount thats neat and funny. But 90 minutes is a long time to spend attending to mind games, especially when the characters don't have minds, only reflexes, and have silly names, and are wearing boxes. The author treats them with contempt, so the audience can't take much interest. He also, of course, places a great technical burden on his actors. However, the playwright, Darren ODonnell, cannot be accused of asking the performers to do anything he wouldnt do himself. He appears as one of the doctors. Paul Fauteux is the other; and they perform perfectly (actors in this kind of show are always perfect, or else they're dead) in a style that seems to owe an immediate debt to the Canadian clowns Mump and Smoot, and a more distant one to the Marx Brothers' mirror routine in Duck Soup. They also, through the wonders of technology and sound-mixing, play the narrators. The action, in Chris Abrahams sharp production, takes place behind a transparent curtain, with the narrators presence denoted by percussive sounds and flickering lights. This is, appropriately enough, black-box theatre.

There is also, as you'd expect in so self-conscious a piece, some explicit involvement of the audience, which is referred to as the people in the room." Humanity, we learn, can always be fooled if you divert it with some "stupid object of no intrinsic value; and the creators are far too smart not to intend an allusion to their own show. At one point, the gods divert Dr. Wishful by taking him to a disco (he accepts the invitation gratefully because Dr. Thoughtless has been neglecting their social life recently) and the music is Dancing Queen, which to a critic fresh from Mamma Mia! seemed like cruel and unusual punishment.

Sometimes, the show comes down from its metaphysical perch to engage in social comment of, considering its pretentions, a rather parochial kind. Somebody or some entity says that nowadays only lard-brained, golf-club swinging, f--k-headed morons" get to be leaders. Not least of things to be held against Mike Harris is the clodhopping level of satire that he inspires. n

Boxhead runs to June 18 at the Factory Studio Theatre, 125 Bathurst St. Tuesday to Thursday at 8 p.m., $15. Friday and Saturday at 8 p.m., $18. Sunday at 2:30 p.m., PWYC. Call (416) 504-9971.

THE CRIMSON VEIL

Factory Theatre, Toronto

For a musical -- or indeed for any kind of entertainment -- The Crimson Veil looks remarkably drab. Its essentially permanent set is dominated by a medium-sized slag heap, with some smaller slag heaps clustered around it. It seems that they are meant to be mountains, and the big one is identified for us, rather late on, as Mount Etna; the story unfolds in a timeless Sicily, a territory famous for folk tales.

The show is a fairy story.

There is of course no such thing as a new fairy story, and Allen Cole, composer and (with Glen Cairns) author of this one, has created his own variations on some familiar motifs. As Gilbert and Sullivan did in Iolanthe, Cole tells of a fairy who falls in love with a mortal, and of the price she pays for this violation of supernatural family values. Her name is Bellinda, and she has a mother; her beloved, who loves her right back, is an aspiring clarinettist named Bruno who lives wth his father in a cabin in the woods. Neither parent approves of the match, and they unwittingly collude in obstructing it. Bellinda is instructed by her mother to entertain her lover over three evenings, while wearing the crimson veil of the title, which Bruno is under strict orders not to remove. Bruno's father advises him not to stand for this, and to tear off the veil at the last encounter; he does so, and Bellinda not only loses her magic powers (a sacrifice that she, like the Little Mermaid, was prepared to make for love) but is carried off to a cave by a couple of very bad brother and sister fairies. A penitent Bruno rescues her by defeating the male fiend in hand-to-hand combat, and then by kissing Bellinda three times on the lips: a tougher quest than it may sound since she's been transformed into a poison-fanged monster. He breaks the spell, but she's still sore at his betrayal and sends him away.

End of Act One.

Bellinda repents during the intermission and subsequently sets off on her own quest. Bruno has gone into a trance, but has left a helpful note saying that he can only be awakened by someone who will first watch over him for a year a day, without sleeping. Bellinda goes for it, though she runs into last-minute trouble from the evil sister who, it is all of a sudden revealed, has her own designs on Bruno. What isn't revealed is how Bruno, who doesn't have supernatural status, was able to engineer this test. Or how Bellinda, who has lost hers, was able to pass it; black coffee can only do so much.

Fairy stories, even more than mortal stories, are supposed to lay out their ground rules at the start, and stick to them.

This one doesn't so much develop as lurch from one idea to another, and it seems very thin to fill a whole evening. You appreciate the wisdom of Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine in interweaving four separate plot-lines in their fairy-tale musical Into the Woods, and their inventiveness in keeping them going. (That's quite apart from how funny, moving and frightening they made them.) The new show has several features in common with the older one: a narrative that starts up again when it seems to be resolved, an emphasis on father-child relationships (which here, having taken up a lot of space in the first half, wither away in the second) and of course a forest setting. Cole's music also persistently echoes Sondheim's, not in whole songs but in dark lemon-flavoured chords and sharp melodic fragments, notably a recurring theme on flute. His tunes actually sound better in overture and entr'acte than when heard full-length in the action. They are sweet; but they don't have the dramatic weight to carry the action without benefit of dialogue. They are also hobbled by the composer's own lyrics, whose choice of detail often seems dictated by the necessity to make it to the next rhyme. ("Trust me, Bruno, I know of what I speak," sings his dad, when advocating forcible unveiling, "how will you ever see her cheek?") There are more elaborate trick-rhymes, even including some triples, which would be unlikely to impress Cole Porter but are certainly aiming high by more recent standards. Tim Rice has laid it down that the biggest musicals of the last 10 years (by now it's 20) would have been just as succesful had their lyrics been 10 times worse, or indeed 10 times better, than they actually are. (He should know.) In smaller theatres, though, words do count; and the wit with which Ann-Marie MacDonald fitted Cole's music in the recent Anything That Moves is here much missed.

The song that comes nearest to rousing the house is an increasingly frantic patter-number with which Bellinda takes us through her year-long vigil; it's wildly out of sync with the rest of the score, but that, in the circumstances, is a relief. (James Fagan Tait is credited with unspecified additional lyrics, so apportioning praise and blame is chancy ) This number also gives Naomi Emmerson, as Bellinda, the one solid opportunity afforded any of the performers, and she grabs it with both hands. She's also appealing in her earlier seductive scenes, sashaying in her yashmac.

Kevin Dennis, though, makes a ploddingly plaintive Bruno, while Julian Molnar and Michael McManus as the dysfunctional parents seem to be hanging around waiting for some motivation. The sinister siblings, who carry on like vampires but are never identified as such, are unmercifully camped up by Paul Braunstein and Kelly McIntosh in what reads like a desperate attempt to inject some life into the thing.

There is in fact no consistent tone. Jokiness and solemnity, in Leah Cherniak's production, flash on and off in alternating bursts, colliding in the weakest fight scene I have seen in years.

The staging in general is awkward; Cherniak needs a choreographer like Cole needs a lyricist. The cyclorama occasionally turns some striking colours, but that's not enough to lift a spectator's heart.

NOT FAUST

The Great Hall, 1087 Queen St. West, Toronto

Snappily subtitled "a play in purgatory," Not Faust is an adaptation by Jennifer Tarver, who also directs, of Doctor Faustus Lights the Lights, a short and characteristically teasing play written by Gertrude Stein, rather late in her life. It turns out not to be purgatorial at all. In fact it is, in its own way, heavenly.

It even manages, most of the time, to render Stein's syllable- chopping prose, or whatever it is, without giving the audience a headache.

Steins original play seems, as far as I can follow it, to be split in two. One half concerns a woman referred to as Marguerite Ida Helena Annabel, which mouthful incorporates the names of the two most important women in the life of Goethes Faust. She has scenes with a viper, who presumably is some kind of devil, and Stein's Faustus may wish to be damned in order to impress her. But her main importance in this adaptation lies in the ritual repetition of her name. The wittier, more dramatic, section of the evening shows Faustus as a man of the 19th century who has invented the electric lightbulb.

This seems to make him as much malefactor as benefactor, and, of course, a modern Prometheus as well as a Faust (but then, people have always gotten the two legends confused). As he himself puts it, after a little prodding, I am the only one who can turn night into day. Which, if you bring the theology of the Middle Ages into the science of the modern world, might well suggest a presumptuousness meriting damnation.

As a man enlightened as well as enlightening, this Faustus doesn't believe in hell. In this he resembles his Elizabethan namesake, Christopher Marlowes Doctor Faustus, who jovially proclaims, "I think, Hells a fable." To which Mephistopheles, his attendant devil, knowingly replies, Ay, think so, till experience change thy mind.

The Stein equivalent of this is to have Faustus ask, "What the hell did you want my soul for?" (the question could hardly be better phrased) and then to express serious doubts as to whether he has one. To which the devil replies -- soothingly, in this version -- Yes, dear Doctor Faustus, yes of course you have a soul. There seems to be professional pride involved.

Perhaps the greatest achievement of Tarver and her three actors is to take Stein's lines -- with their deliberately stunted vocabulary, their relentless repetition, their general air of prose pretending to pretend to be verse -- and to turn them into drama. Or, to be fairer, to release the drama that's lurking in them.

The story of Faust, especially when you put it into a modern setting, is a perpetual paradox, and the style here is a way of ambushing and exposing the absurdity without slighting the tragedy.

Marlowes Faustus feared and suffered damnation; Goethes escaped it; Stein's scoffs but ends up embracing it, intellectual to the end. (To qualify for the inferno, he commits murder, of a boy and a dog. But they, too, are figures of the devil. Go figure.)

James Kirchner plays him with momentous searching quietness, twisting and lucid at the same time. (At the beginning he wears a bowler hat, the perpetual mark of the modernist avant-garde going slumming in show business.)

The other two players split the role of the devil, Raul Tome being dangerously boyish and petulant and Michelle Polak intelligent and enticing, though not given the scope to be anything else. A scene in which these two very civilized fiends toast the ensnared doctor in what looks like champagne -- conceivably before toasting him by some other method altogether -- is especially vivid.

The playing space is a basement. in a long white room reached by a bleak flight of steps, illuminated -- to put you in the mood for a play about the risks and benefits of light -- by a couple of spare blue bulbs. The play itself is staged and lit with similar spareness, similar intensity and remarkable variety. Jan Komarek is the designer and also collaborated on the direction.

The play begins (of course) in darkness, our consciousness pierced only by what sounds like the working of a giant, rusty winch. For this, and for subsequent effects, Ben Grossman -- credited with "sound composition" -- deserves any awards that may be going in his department.

The pace is deliberate (Not Faust is not fast) and every word, noise, step and gesture, seems precisely calibrated, but nothing is tedious or mechanical.

This is my first encounter with Tarver's work. I knew she had a considerable underground reputation as a drama and opera director (this show was first seen in another form at last years Toronto fringe) and its good to report that the empress has excellent taste in clothes.

For rigour and imagination, this production -- at the moment the best show in Toronto -- bears comparison with last year's Tarragon production of Goethe's Faustian thing. The text of this one is hardly as rich, but in trimming and reordering it, Tarver shows it off to excellent advantage.

She gives us enough. And enough, in this context, is very nearly as good as a Faust.

2000-06-17-so-where-are-the-circles-play:
Circle of Love plays tonight at 8 p.m. ($12 to $15) and tomorrow at 2:30 p.m. (PWYC) at Theatre Passe Muraille, 16 Ryerson Ave. Call (416) 504-7529.

The problem with Circle of Love is one that besets many first plays; the author, writing on subjects close to his own heart and presumably to his own experience, is so caught up in them that he assumes an equal fascination on the part of his audience. It doesn't happen.

Al-Noor Peera's play is set among first- and second-generation Indian immigrants in Toronto. There is Ishwar, a businessman, liberal in his politics (he's an obsessive Trudeau fan) and repressive in his domestic dealings, and Nigar, his submissive homemaking wife. Then there's their son Jamil, who's a student, and who has a gay friend, Rafiq, and a girlfriend, Zuhra, whom he impregnates and, at least for a time, abandons.

It's difficult to know where to start or to finish in detailing the plot because the playwright never quite lets on where the beginning is, while even the end seems more like a comma than a full stop. He tells his story in jigsaw fashion, constantly leaping backwards and forwards in time, bleeding one scene into another. He does this skilfully, and the transitions are fluently handled in Layne Coleman's production. This, though, is about the only saving grace of either the writing or the presentation.

At first, we seem to be watching an intergenerational conflict drama, indistinguishable from a hundred others except by the flowing drapes at the rear of the stage and the sitar music in the background. A few specialized references ("biryani again?") provide a mildly exotic laugh for half the audience and, probably, a ruefully reassuring one for the other half. Things then narrow down a bit. Ishwar turns out to have strictly patriarchal views on the place of a wife, and even of a prospective daughter-in-law. When Jamil brings Zuhra home for an inspection, she declares her expectations that her husband will do his share of the housework, take her to the ballet and provide her with romantic holidays ("in Europe ... and Muskoka"). Nigar leaves the room in silent protest, although whether because she is really shocked or because that's what her husband expects of her remains unclear. This scene, or at least Zuhra's part of it, is the brightest of the evening, but it still seems overly emphatic. She is being tactless so that the author can make a point.

In fact, all the characters are puppets, and little of what they say carries any conviction. Jamil, who seems to be the central figure -- the only one who gets to interact at length with each of the other four -- is an especially loquacious blank. His problem, he tells us, is that he grew up in thrall to his mother, and so is unable to cope with adult relationships, but this isn't dramatized; the scenes he actually has with his mother don't suggest it in the least. (He's also visited, at moments of stress, by frighteningly acute stomach cramps.) He expresses envy of his gay pal Rafiq's promiscuity: a rather slender excuse for protracted conversations of doubtful relevance. The range of cultural reference is refreshingly wide -- from Andrew Marvell's To His Coy Mistress to The Price Is Right -- but the dialogue is clogged and awkward. Male characters, in particular, express their antagonisms by lobbing elaborate metaphors back and forth. It smothers conflict; it also strangles belief.

The production, meanwhile, is lamentable, the actors behaving, as usual in such circumstances, with a sort of reverential defensiveness. They are all Equity members, but they come off like amateurs. The performances are not only low-key -- that can sometimes be very effective as Not Faust is triumphantly demonstrating -- but low-energy, which is fatal. The men -- Ishwar Mooljee, Vijay Mehta, Anand Rajaram -- speak in various tones of apologetic mutter. The women have rather more life, with Misha Vellani as a downtrodden mother with some troubling moments and Goldy Notay conscientiously spunky as Zuhra, though somewhat weighed down by having to express all the right sentiments; she is an assertive victim -- a combination that can certainly exist in real life but needs a few more connections than are supplied here. The underlying pattern seems to be that two generations of straight men are, in some sense, killing their women; but it's all very amorphous.

The author claims in a program note that he "wanted to explore memory." But this would only work if we were clear who was doing the remembering. The actual experience of the play is not of watching people alternately releasing and repressing what's inside them; it's of listening to an author who has all the information but is gratuitously capricious about the order in which he lets it out. Give him his due: Corny though the situations seem, we do go on wanting to know. But then we all have a built-in desire to be told a story, and it takes a lot to discourage us.

2000-06-21-when-comedy-comes-second-to-n:
Eric Idle Exploits Monty Python continues for a second and final show at the Hummingbird Centre tonight, 8 p.m.

ERIC IDLE EXPLOITS MONTY PYTHON

Hummingbird Centre

Vikings were visible in the lobby before the show started -- or at least men in funny helmets with horns sticking out of them. They weren't performers; they were members of the audience. Once inside, though, they and a host of other kindred spirits -- some with knotted handkerchiefs on their heads, others dressed in the red robes of the Spanish Inquisition -- became part of the show, which would indeed have been impossible without them.

Eric Idle Exploits Monty Python is sing-along, talk-along and dress-along entertainment: the apotheosis of audience participation.

As a comic event, this makes it difficult to judge. Comedy, after all, is supposed to have an element of danger about it, and this tends to vanish when the audience is there, not to be surprised by laughter, but to indulge its nostalgia and pledge allegiance to a cult.

Still, if anyone has the right to preside over such a feast of indulgence, its Eric Idle, who is among us as sole theatrical proprietor of Monty Pythons Flying Circus. The Pythons were a hilarious, cleansing comic force in the '1960s, and their impact, on those of us who were there first time round -- and, as I can now testify, on our offspring -- remains profound.

As a performer, Idle always struck me as the second funniest Python (no prize for guessing the first) and he takes the stage here at the head of a freshly recruited crew of singers, dancers and impersonators of the original sextet. Hearing other people trying to say "Nobody expects the Spanish Inquisition" as if they meant it is admittedly somewhat taxing; it's as if the cast, too, were members of the audience, acting out their fantasies.

But the show isnt just an anthology of Python. Some of it comes from Idles post-Circus career and from his impressive talents as a comic songwriter. Every Sperm is Sacred comes over especially strong; so does A Man Called Brian, the movie theme song that should have ended them all but didn't. Not to mention the unforgettable song about the uniformly drunken habits of the world's greatest philosophers.

Idle himself doesnt so much alternate between self-deprecation and self-aggrandizement as overlap. He has matured into a stand-up comic in the classic English tradition; he does a devastating impression of a sadistically smarmy master of ceremonies, in gold- lame jacket and what looked like a tinfoil waistcoat (though occasionally he loses the balance and comes uncomfortably close to the real thing).

He goes through his blazered saloon-bar (nudge, nudge, wink, wink) routine with impressive devotion, if with an inevitable air of doing it because its expected of him. On the other hand, a lesser- known routine -- an unstoppable catalogue of the horrors of an English holidaymaker's package tour -- is a tour de force, as impressive on stage as on TV.

Idle excels at carrying certain aspects of the English character, meticulously observed, to the fantastic limits; with him it's the futility and genial bloody-mindedness of the lower middle class. Maybe you have to be English and of a certain age to get the full acrid flavour, but it certainly seems to travel in time and in space.

Which reminds me: Why, given that this is Python and this is Canada, did the audience not appear to contain a single Mountie?

ROMANCIN THE ONE I LOVE

Winter Garden Theatre

There is something unwieldy about the title Romancin the One I Love; it's overlong and somewhat tautological. (I mean, who else are you gonna be romancin'; unless of course youre two-timin?)

That makes it a good fit for the show itself, which is groaningly unwieldy -- a scene-for-scene enactment of The Taming of the Shrew, with a couple of dozen songs thrown in -- and is also a tautology in itself: It's a Shrew musical that acts as if it didn't know that there was -- indeed, still is -- a show called Kiss Me Kate, drawn from the same source. Quite often in Romancin, we seem to be hearing cues for songs that we already know, and its frustrating when new ones turn up, especially when ... but I'll get to that.

Mind you, I read recently that someone in the United States is writing a musical based on the stories of Damon Runyon, thereby going head to head with Guys and Dolls; by that yardstick, the hubris of John R. Briggs, creator of the present show, seems like modesty itself. Romancin' takes both plots of The Shrew -- the subduing of Katharine the fierce by the upstart Petruchio, and the wooing of her younger sister by three competing suitors, most of them in disguise -- and sets it down in 1930s Miami Beach.

The show starts with everybody silhouetted in Art Deco poses, prior to going into a welcoming company number that does something to set up the basic situation. One of the crowd turns out to be Kate herself (she likes to be called Katharine, but her creators put her in her place by calling her Kate in the program) but we hardly notice her; this must be the weakest first entrance ever inflicted on the leading lady of a musical comedy.

Anyway, the whole sequence turns out to be superfluous, since the identical ground is immediately gone over again, courtesy of Shakespeares own exposition. Or of some of it; here, as throughout, the harder Elizabethan words are replaced by modern slang, not all of it native to the Thirties. This is probably meant to be funny.

If the dialogue aims at pastiche, the score, by Briggs and Dennis West, is outright nostalgia. The 1930s were the greatest decade of American popular music, and if youre going to use its styles now, you have to use them, comment on them in some way; otherwise you're simply competing with the incomparable.

All this score conveys is a fervent desire to put the clock back: understandable but vain. The songs aren't actually that bad; its just that they all seem to have been written at least once before. The words are mostly after Cole Porter (Kates Nobody Loves Me is a list-song uncomfortably close to Porter's Nobody's Chasing Me), the music mostly after Gershwin (the title song has the impudence to quote directly from I Got Rhythm). Kates big torch song, My Attitude, crammed with blue notes and low-down throbbings, is after everybody; it seems to have been written 17 times before. Its also dramatically destructive. She sings it while waiting at the church for her non-appearing bridegroom, and it's all about how much she really and secretly loves him. Meanwhile the text, which suggests nothing of the kind, is still chugging incorrigibly along around her.

This is a musical of The Taming of the Shrew that's plainly embarrassed by The Taming of the Shrew.

Plenty of straight productions -- most straight productions -- manage to suggest an instant attraction between hero and heroine. The plays appeal is that its about the coming together of a pair of outsiders too good for the society in which they find themselves. But they neither of them give in that easily. In this version, Petruchio overhears Kate moaning another love song, is touched, and gives up on the taming idea altogether. The final notorious wager on Kate's obedience is played as a pre-arranged put-up job, thereby destroying any dramatic point it might have. It would be better to cut it altogether; this is, after all, an adaptation.

The couple signal their love-at-first-sightedness by doing an energetic Fred-and-Ginger routine, dancing over sofas. But that's not enough to give them chemistry.

Camilla Scotts Kate is less a characterization than a prolonged display of good sportsmanship, while Brad Aspels slick bantamweight Petruchio is charmless to the point of being repulsive. He's played as an out-of-work song-and-dance man, which makes it seem very strange that Kate's mercenary father would accept him as an eligible suitor. It does mean, though, that he can take her home, not to his country seat, but to a New York rehearsal hall, where his troupe, though presumably unemployed, are still hard at work.

"Well keep her awake," he says of his bride, by rehearsing our closing number -- at which promise of yet another generic routine I, case-hardened though I am, heard myself whimpering "Oh, no!"

Sergio Trujillos musical staging is a complete compendium of choreographic cliches, but he does not, in fairness, have much to go on. Supporting performances, mostly executed with an air of gamely desperate professionalism, are similarly stereotyped; Grumio (Lloyd Culbreath) is the hero's black hoofing-and-gospelling sidekick; Hortensio (Larry Mannell) is the cheerful, brow-mopping, all- purpose second banana; Gremio (Gerry Salsberg) is a stock rich Jew, breaking into Hava Nagila when he thinks he's got the girl; and Tranio (Derek Marshall) is a tireless impressionist who -- after flying at Groucho, Cagney and Jerry Lewis -- settles for imitating Tony Curtis imitating Cary Grant in Some Like It Hot. Bianca (Melissa Thomson) is your standard cute minx.

In one of the shows token gestures to feminism, all the women get behind Kate to sing a man-defying song called I Dont Have to Listen to You; but it goes nowhere, since Shakespeare's Kate stands for no one, male or female. (And no one, which is their loss, will stand for her.)

Kiss Me Kate, which has an elaborate play-within-a-play framework, is far more cavalier with its source (it actually makes it difficult to follow the Shakespearean plot) but, by virtue of being a good show with its own identity, ends up being more respectful of it.

It's certainly no accident that makers of musicals keep returning to Shakespeares comedies, and especially to his earliest comedies; between them, Shakespeare and Broadway-Hollywood are responsible for most of our modern conception of romance. This, with especial reference to Kenneth Branaghs new and (I think) unfairly maligned movie version of Love's Labour's Lost, is a subject worthy of further exploration.

2000-06-27-weird-doras-in-a-strange-seas:
(From the National Post, Thursday, June 29, 2000) Reporting on the Doras two days ago, I re-christened prize-winning director Daniel Brooks as Richard. Sorry. 

Last night, at the Pantages Theatre, Toronto's Dora Mavor Moore Awards came of age. Well, anyway, they celebrated their 21st birthday.

They are, like most awards, weird. They are administered by the Toronto Theatre Alliance, and it seems that, once upon a time, just about everybody in the business (or, as they insist on calling themselves, the Community) got to vote, rather like with the Oscars. This apparently led to abuses, and in the last few years, it has been changed.

The awards are divided into four categories: General Theatre (big and medium shows), Independent Theatre (small shows -- and independent of what, for God's sake?), Theatre for Young Audiences, and Dance. Each is appraised by a separate jury of 10, compromising both participants and onlookers. Juries even include some critics, though none whom I know personally. (I'm not suggesting that's necessarily a bad thing.)

These jurors nominate five people for each prize, and then at a later date they choose a winner from among them. Since it's the same people voting at each stage, it's hard to see why they don't cut straight to the chase instead of teasing everybody. But it presumably helps in the publicity build-up. The envelope please -- and try not to drop it. (People do drop things at the Doras. I suppose it's endearing.)

The 1999-2000 season in Toronto was a strange one. Most of it was dull, but there was a small embarrassment of riches at the top. The most starved category this year was New Play, General: There was no predestined winner on the order of last year's The Drawer Boy. Ronnie Burkett's Street of Blood (a puppet show) and Morris Panych's The Overcoat (a mime) would have been worthy contenders this year, but both were excluded, presumably on technical grounds. If it was on grounds of quality, we're really in trouble. The best conventionally written play, and an unusually rich text, was Florence Gibson's Belle. Thankfully, it was nominated; depressingly, it lost. The joint winners were Linda Griffiths' Alien Creature, the latest instalment in Toronto's ongoing romance with the vaguely literary one-person show, and For the Pleasure of Seeing Her Again, a sub-standard Michel Tremblay.

Both Griffiths and Tremblay are, of course, long-standing OK names in Canadian theatre. To be fair, the equally revered George F. Walker and Judith Thomson failed this year to make the cut -- though Thomson's Perfect Pie should probably have been there.

Outstanding New Musical (an even murkier category) was the Ann- Marie MacDonald/Allen Cole show Anything That Moves, as good a choice as any. Things improve, markedly, when we get to the area of production.

Last year, notoriously, the voters shut out the Soulpepper company. This year it did rather better, if not quite well enough. Any one of Soulpepper's five 1999 shows would have been a credible nominee, or indeed winner, for best direction, but the two that actually got on the list -- Richard Brooks' Endgame and Laszlo Marton's Platonov -- probably deserved it the most. In the event, both won: Endgame for best production and Platonov for best direction. How anyone who wasn't at rehearsals is supposed to tell the difference is beyond me, but it spreads the glory around a bit. The directors' category was in fact the most agonizing, since two non-Soulpepper nominations -- Brooks' Faust and Panych's The Overcoat -- were equally deserving. (The fifth directorial entrant, Sarah Stanley's Beaver, must have been either a joke or a gesture of sympathy for being saddled with an unworkable play -- though, considering what was excluded, it's not funny.)

Another crowded category was that for best lead female in a play. The odd thing here is that none of the best available performances (Fiona Reid in The Beauty Queen of Leenane, Kristin Thomson in A Streetcar Named Desire, Nancy Palk in Perfect Pie) was even nominated. Of those who got the nod, only Yanna McIntosh in Belle was in that league. The actual winner was Nora McLellan in Music for Contortionist, another one-woman show, though I suppose you couldn't call it literary.

The men fared better. Soulpepper's Diego Matamoros got, deservedly, to run against himself: He won for Endgame and lost for The Play's the Thing. (The wrong way around, I think, but congrats anyway.)

The other nominees -- Oliver Becker (Beauty Queen), Donald Sutherland (Enigma Variations) and Burkett -- were worthy competition, though no more than Albert Schultz (Platonov), Peter Donaldson (Our Town) or Randy Hughson (Faust) would have been.

The insane policy of lumping opera and musicals together resulted, this year, in the older form not getting a thing. (Not even an opera house). A surprise, though not necessarily a mistake, was the judges' ranking of Sam Mendes' Cabaret, an overheated account of a good show, above Julie Taymor's The Lion King, an inspired salvage job on a poor one. (Taymor did get the costume award. Denying her that could have caused riots in the streets.) Norbert Leo Butz's show-off turn as the emcee in Cabaret was a disappointingly obvious choice for best musical male. Graham Bickley's straight-arrow hero in The Pajama Game (somebody has to do it, and he did it well) was far better -- as indeed were both Joely Fisher and the magnificent Alma Cuervo among the Cabaret ladies. I've no qualms, though, about the actual winner of the musical female award, Paula Wolfson in Shaking the Foundations. She was a turn-on.

Outstanding Performance in a Featured Role, Play or Musical, Male or Female (how do you choose?) went to Jonathan Wilson, one of the comics in The Lion King. He was all right, but when you consider they might have given it to Robyn Stevan in Platonov or Waneta Storms for her lovely work in Faust ...

Down among the independents, there were uncontroversial prizes for Building Jerusalem and Chekhov's Shorts. And, at the opposite extreme of prosperity, there were deserved special awards for David Mirvish, the producer, and Joan Chalmers, the patroness extraordinaire.

Theatre Direct, consistently first-rate by any standards, took the Young Audiences Prize for its production of The General.

The most disgracefully neglected show (in any category): Sibs, a sparkling two-hander , which may have committed the crime of being too entertaining. The Toronto Theatre Alliance seems to be a solemn as well as a sentimental bunch.

In repertory till September 30. Box office: 1-800-567-1600.

TITUS ANDRONICUS

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

Shakespeare's Titus Andronicus -- there doesn't seem any good reason for denying it's Shakespeare's -- is best known as the play in which the father of a savagely raped daughter dismembers her two assailants and bakes them in a pie, which he then serves up to their mother, who has been their coach and accomplice. This exceptionally bloody private tragedy, its author's first, is neatly packaged within an exceptionally cynical public one.

It all begins with the title character, an aged Roman war hero, returning from a victorious campaign against the Goths, and being offered the Imperial crown. He declines it -- an abdication that proves at least as unwise as that of his spiritual descendant King Lear, who at least was able to enjoy his power before surrendering it.

Before the arrival of Titus, the two sons of the late emperor have been squabbling over the succession. Asked to choose between them, Titus favours the elder, Saturninus, a transparently nasty piece of work, over the younger, Bassianus, a comparatively nice one. He even throws in his daughter Lavinia as a coronation gift.

By the time the play's long first scene is over, Bassianus, who loves and is loved by Lavinia, will have abducted her, abetted by most of Titus' family. Titus himself, shocked and disgusted by this conduct, will have killed his own youngest son. (He has four when the play starts, having already lost 21 on the field. He seems to consider this a good batting average.) The new emperor, piously dissociating himself from such a family, takes to wife Tamora, the captive Gothic queen, who has her own beef against Titus, since he has celebrated his homecoming (I nearly said his Romecoming) by giving up her eldest son for ritual sacrifice.

Virtue in this play, as in many others, is a function less of what you do than of what is done to you. Tamora, pleading for the life of her firstborn, is a sympathetic figure, but she forfeits this status as soon as she becomes queen and sets about avenging herself.

Titus, meanwhile, settles down to a career of crazed victimhood and his sufferings and those of his relatives should be catalogued rather than related: 1) Lavinia is ravished by Tamora's surviving sons, who then cut off her hands and tongue to stop her informing against them; 2) Lavinia's husband is murdered, and two of Titus' sons are framed and executed; 3) this may be too petty to include, but Lucius, Titus' remaining son, is banished from Rome for trying to defend his brothers; 4) Titus allows his hand to be chopped off as ransom for his sons, but finds he has been tricked. The subsequent stage-direction: "Enter a Messenger, with two heads and a hand," tells all you need to know.

Tamora, once the action is launched, hardly mentions her initial grievance. Titus, by contrast, never stops mentioning his. And besides, there is the mute and mutilated figure of his daughter as a constant on-stage reminder.

By the time he takes on the role of specialty-chef, Titus is firmly established as the good guy and his revenge seems not only justified but cute. He stages it at a peace conference, called between the emperor and the banished Lucius, who has returned at the head of an army of Goths. (These don't seem to be the barbarians of the history books. They talk blank verse as smooth as any Roman, and one of them takes time off to survey the ruins of a nearby monastery. There's no suggestion he himself has ruined it.) The central scenes have featured much talk of "Rome," but as an abstraction rather than a place. Now, suddenly, it swings right back into focus.

Richard Rose's Stratford production, excellently staged and intelligently acted, is especially good at summoning this public world. He has chosen a between-world-wars Italian setting, in which frock-coated senators earnestly and ineffectually debate, while black-shirted storm troopers besiege the Capitol and generals in desert fatigues use the public-address system to address the public on what they consider good for it. To his credit, he doesn't force his parallels and for much of the play one simply forgets the trappings.

The personal drama is gripping, but not moving. James Blendick's Titus is an admirable performance in a context where admirability looks somewhat pale. Like all Tituses, presumably since Olivier, he presents a soldier who has lived by the book and is maddened when it fails him. He speaks in the round and resonant Old Stratfordian style of a Douglas Campbell or a William Hutt, and with a matter-of- fact authority distinctively his own. What he lacks is the terrible, logical insanity brought to the role by Brian Cox on stage or Anthony Hopkins on screen. At any given moment he is honest and believable: fine as far as he goes, but never going quite far enough.

Xuan Fraser plays Aaron the Moor in a similar though less accomplished vein -- with a jaunty lightweight relish that stops a long way short of the role's full, and enchanting, diabolism. Aaron, who goes to his death regretting any good deed he may absent- mindedly have committed, is the play's arch-villain, though it's probably an index of the author's immaturity that one can describe the plot without mentioning him. He counsels rather than performs. (Note that he and Titus have only one brief scene together.)

Diane D'Aquila's lascivious Tamora seems to be hovering on the brink of full achievement. Scott Wentworth's Saturninus, though, is there already -- he's Mussolini crossed with Nero, a cringing, sneering bridge between two millennia of Adriatic tyranny.

Peter Hutt gives a sympathetic account of Titus' brother and Evan Buliung a commanding one of his son. These are two characters who lead charmed lives: on their feet at the end and with a full complement of limbs and organs.

Marion Day, as the spectacularly ill-starred Lavinia, moves through the play like a dark accusing Fury after her despoilment; and before it, too. The final cascade of killings is handled with great variety and invention, with never an unwanted laugh. The play, as we are increasingly recognizing, is a good one, and blisteringly credible.

- Reporting on the Doras two days ago, I re-christened prize- winning director Daniel Brooks as Richard. Sorry.

Medea runs in repertoire at the Tom Patterson Theatre in Stratford until Oct. 1. Tickets are $60.50 to $67.50 and can be ordered by calling the box office at 1 (800) 567-1600.

The infinitely quotable American theatre critic Walter Kerr once devoted a column to bemoaning the prevalence in modern drama of genteel dinner-party scenes, comparing them to the more robust culinary conventions of earlier theatres. "The Greeks," he said, "when they ate at all, ate their children: a procedure with some dramatic point to it."

It's a habit, as we saw earlier this week in the Stratford production of Titus Andronicus, that the Greeks bequeathed to the Elizabethans, or at least to the Elizabethan idea of what went on in ancient Rome. There are, however, worse things than cannibalism.

The night after Titus, Stratford took us back to Greek tragedy itself: to Euripides' Medea, a play that cannot compete with Shakespeare's in sheer volume of horrors but far surpasses it in intensity. The child-eating mother in Titus is the victim of a trick; she hasn't actually slaughtered and dressed the meat herself. Medea doesn't eat her own young sons or cause anyone else to do so. She does, though, kill them: on purpose. She does it to get back at the husband who is deserting her for a younger woman. It seems very modern.

In Greek myth, Medea was the Asian sorceress whose arts helped the heroic Jason to win the famous Golden Fleece; her services to him included the drowning of her own brother who was pursuing their escaping ship, the Argo. Euripides, never a great one for heroes, shows us this couple 10 years on, back in Jason's home city of Corinth. Given the chance to marry the daughter of Creon, the Corinthian king, Jason jumps at it; and Creon, acting presumably on his new son-in-law's advice, orders Medea to leave town. The whole action of the play is Medea's revenge. First, she gives Jason's bride (whom we never meet) and her father (who does admittedly seem insufferable) betrothal gifts: magic robes that burn and flay when they touch the skin, condemning their wearers to an agonizing death. Then, fearful that she may have let her ex off too lightly, she sacrifices their boys -- having first ensured that she herself has an escape route to Athens.

The play is performed in a free, and 50-year-old, adaptation by the American poet Robinson Jeffers (who, incidentally, gets far bigger program billing than the original playwright). Adaptation here turns out to mean a certain amount of softening; Medea is allowed more elaborate maternal qualms than I remember from other versions. It also means outright trivialization; Euripides is known for taking his mythic characters down a few pegs, but I can't believe that Jason's response when granted a peek at the fatal bridal shower is adequately rendered by the words "Medea, you shouldn't ... it's too much."

Still, this is a play that can use some help, or perhaps more accurately, a play whose audiences can use some help. It's an immensely powerful myth, with a ring of contemporary truth to it; but its heroine is not, to put it banally, very likeable -- not just because of the monstrosity of her actions but because her entire role is a litany of grievances. This makes the play itself difficult to warm to; and if Jeffers' text works too obviously hard at making it accessible, the work is usually justified.

Miles Potter's production approaches the play's two levels very cunningly. We begin with the sound of an off-stage lament in (presumably) the original Greek, and a brief glimpse of the company in masks: a brief gesture to the traditional tragic plateau we are trying to reach. The lights go down, to come up on modern actors, still in ancient robes but using their own faces and their own voices. We are now, give or take a few smashing special effects, in their hands, and, above all, in those of the leading actress. Seana McKenna's Medea is, almost unwaveringly, superb.

She is sulphurous and coruscating; a believable sorceress and a believably wronged woman, who at once thrives on her wrongs and is lacerated by them. She also has a whiplash wit, which she perhaps employs too freely; but then the translation encourages her. One still doesn't warm to Medea (and her adoption as a feminist icon has never seemed to me to do the women's movement much credit), but her play held me as it never has before. The scene in which she swaps recriminations with Scott Wentworth's Jason, each endlessly resourceful at blaming the other for the fate of their marriage, is bruisingly recognizable. The actor cannot always match her on her own level (he is more apt than she to fall back on stock anger or stock irony) but most of the time he is very fine, and he is never afraid to act contemptible.

"I believed I was alone," says Medea early on, proceeding to complain that "nothing is ever private in a Greek city." This is a bit like complaining that you didn't expect the Spanish Inquisition; you're never alone in a Greek tragedy, because the Chorus has always got there before you: listening, commenting, shuddering at the way you go on. There are three chorines here, drawn from three generations of Stratford leading ladies: Patricia Collins, Kate Trotter (both powerful) and Michelle Giroux (who seems out of her depth). Two kings appear; Robert Benson's Corinthian resident intones like a man who thinks he's in a Greek tragedy, but John Dolan's Athenian visitor is pleasantly doddery. Rita Howell's nurse matures impressively from glum nanny to messenger of death. She ushers us into the play's last phase, haunted here by the authentic sense of implacable doom; the action is both itself, and more than itself.

There is seldom any hopeful restoration of order at the end of a Greek tragedy, as there is with the Elizabethans -- perhaps because, with all the violence offstage, nobody has to supervise the removal of the bodies. For a modern actor to find within himself the final desolation of the bereaved Jason must be almost impossible; Wentworth goes honourably through the motions, but the production rescues him. There is a thunderclap; the lights again go down and come up, to reveal him again with a mask clapped to his face. We return again to the conventions for which the play was written; past and present, ritual and reality, join hands. Kenneth Tynan, my other favourite 20th-century critic, once said that he rarely emerged from a production of Medea feeling that he knew several marriages exactly like that. I think this production might have changed his mind.

ELIZABETH REX

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

There is a quiet but pulsating energy in Elizabeth Rex. The web of tension that it weaves holds everyone in the cast and -- at least on the first night -- everyone in the audience. It's magic, of a potency rare at Stratford or anywhere else.

The title character is, unsurprisingly, Elizabeth I of England, Shakespeare's queen, who famously said that she had the heart of a king in the body of a woman. Shakespeare himself has a leading role, as do two invented figures, members of his company: an Irishman, sexually and politically aggressive, named Jack Edmund; and Ned Lowenscroft, a 30-year-old actor of female roles. These two, when we first meet them, have just come offstage from playing Benedick and Beatrice in a royal command performance of Much Ado About Nothing.

We meet several of their fellow-actors, too: supporting players both in Shakespeare's play and this one. They spend a lot of time sitting or lying at the edges of the Tom Patterson's narrow promontory stage, listening. They do this with a remarkable, relaxed intentness, as if knowing themselves to be an integral part of something special.

It certainly helps, though, that it is at Stratford, especially concluding a week of premieres at the Patterson that has gone from good to better to best. There's a special kick in seeing a current Shakespearean troupe impersonate their ancestors; that's over and above the usual enjoyment that actors get from playing actors, and audiences from watching them do it. In that sense, Timothy Findley's new play is an indulgence for all parties, but it is no sentimental "celebration of theatre."

It takes place on the Shrove Tuesday night and Ash Wednesday morning of 1601: the hours leading up to the execution of Elizabeth's former favourite and supposed lover, the Earl of Essex. To take her mind off things, she has called for a play; after it's over, the actors, confined by curfew, take refuge in the royal barn. Here the queen herself joins them, seeking further distraction. The play becomes a debate, on how far her royal role has impaired her womanhood, and even her humanity.

Her main antagonist is Ned, the man who spends his professional life as a woman, and who is dying of syphilis and mourning the lover who gave it to him: a soldier killed in the Irish wars. Elizabeth hides her love; Ned flaunts his. The culminating point of their duel comes when each forces the other to reveal the pet name bestowed on their respective lovers at the height of passion.

Shakespeare, too, is involved; the Earl of Southampton, his former patron and the possible inspiration of his sonnets, is Essex's fellow prisoner, though unlike Essex he has the chance of a reprieve. Meanwhile, he is at work on Antony and Cleopatra, with Ned to play the Egyptian queen (if he survives), but he cannot hope to see it staged until after the English queen is dead; the historical parallels would be all too obvious.

I don't believe any of this. I found it hard to credit that actors or anybody else -- even the reckless, death-marked Ned -- would speak as freely as these do to an absolute monarch of uncertain temper. I doubt that Elizabeth actually went to bed with Essex; it wasn't her style and she wouldn't have risked it.

The parallels between those two and Antony and Cleopatra don't strike me as overwhelming, and the Roman play's style is wrong for that moment of Shakespeare's career; as Findley himself has pointed out, he would actually at this point have been writing Hamlet; he had to get through the jagged tragedies before he could write the suave one.

Finally, I am unconvinced by the author's pet theory that men, rather than boys, would have played the more demanding women's parts in the Elizabethan theatre. There is no evidence for it, and the assumption that boys would be incapable of doing justice to these roles is rather patronizing. There were Elizabethan companies composed entirely of choirboys, playing all the roles, male and female, in complex texts by Ben Jonson and others. Audiences, as they always do, would have adjusted their expectations to the prevailing conventions.

Antony and Cleopatra itself offers further proof; the captive Cleopatra's fear of seeing "some squeaking Cleopatra boy my greatness" lose most of its point and all of its audacity if the line itself is not spoken by a boy. (That's not to say that a grown- up male actor couldn't play Cleopatra splendidly; Mark Rylance did just that at London's new Globe theatre last summer.)

So much for pedantry. Findley's play is a splendid piece of dramatic architecture. The action unfolds in two long, unbroken acts with a sweep and fluency that, in these days of short, pinched scenes, seems miraculous. Themes and characters, exits and entrances, interlock flawlessly, and the Shakespearean inserts -- from Much Ado or Antony or the Sonnets -- fit powerfully into place.

Visually, the piece is a treat, superbly directed by Martha Henry on a set by Allan Wilbee that manages to be both spare and cluttered, and with exquisite smoky lighting by Louise Guinand. There is much play with costume and other trappings, culminating in the queen's grim removal of her red wig to reveal the baldness beneath.

Ned has a tame bear (gallantly inhabited by Aaron Franks) whose heavy caperings punctuate the play, up to an extraordinary lurch of sympathy when the bells peal the news of Essex's death. All this is in the text; Findley was an actor before he was a novelist, and he writes actions as well as words.

He may even write actions better than words. "If you will teach me how to be a woman" says Elizabeth to Ned, "I will teach you how to be a man." The play's real flaw is the bloodlessness of its language, incorporating a portentous signposting of issues, and a literary manner that I associate with the weightier drama of the 1950s. Findley can juxtapose Shakespeare's words with his own without making us cringe. (Is Elizabeth quoting Shakespeare or inspiring him when she says, "Oh fool, I shall go mad"?) But you do notice the difference.

But he has certainly inspired his actors. Brent Carver as Ned adds a new strain of stricken anger to his customary amazing grace (if the amazing can be customary) and aching tenderness; any play that begins and ends with Carver singing "fear no more the heat o' the sun" both starts and finishes ahead. Diane D'Aquila has at the outset some trouble with Elizabeth's imperiousness, but grows into it, and especially into her loneliness. (Though her love for Essex, unlike Ned's for his captain, seems more of a debating position than an emotion.)

Peter Hutt as Shakespeare is hobbled at the start by a scene- setting retrospective monologue (writing soliloquies for Shakespeare seems a risky exercise) but is superb in the main action: a watchful, secretive man whom nobody quite likes. And Scott Wentworth completes a week's trio of fine performances as the sullen, blazing Irish Edmund.

There is especially fine lesser work from Paul Dunn as a boy player and from Florence MacGregor as a generally silent and generally frightened lady-in-waiting. But everybody counts; and the image of the company huddled in a doorway at the end of the platform is going to be a keeper.

The Mill on the Floss continues to July 27 at the Premiere Dance Theatre, Harbourfront Centre. Tickets are $25 to $46 and are available at the Harbourfront box office or by calling (416) 973- 4000.

It may seem like quibbling but I wish the Soulpepper company had worked up its own dramatization of The Mill on the Floss rather than buying one from England ready-made. As it is, the company isn't staging a novel by George Eliot but a play by Helen Edmundson. Eliot is a name worthy to stand on this year's Soulpepper bill alongside Shakespeare, Moliere, Chekhov and Pinter. Edmundson is not, and though her adaptation is technically ingenious, it is also misguided. The novel is not the joyless, pentecostal affair she seems to think it is.

The play was first presented by Shared Experience, a British company that goes back to the 1970s, at which time it presented extraordinary examples of pure actor-based theatre; it used literary texts (from Dickens to the Arabian Nights) but mined them directly, without the benefit of a playwright. Its more recent work is still accomplished, but is much less exciting. It's from the company's later, more conventional, period that this version of The Mill derives.

Robin Phillips's Soulpepper production has improved immeasurably since its flustered debut at this year's World Stage season. Staged on a low versatile platform dressed only by a couple of screens, it moves with a sober grace that can rise to a dreamlike magic, especially when boats are involved. The excellence of the direction, though, points out the weaknesses of the script. The climactic flood is far more impressive than it was, though it still leaves a feeling of, "is that all?" But then so, in a more exalted way, does the book.

The flooding of the river Floss is the author's method of disposing of her two central characters, Maggie Tulliver and her brother Tom. They are the children of the mill, or more prosaically of the miller. We have seen their father lose his property, through hot-tempered litigation, and his life, through hot temper. We have seen Tom subjected to a private education that bears no relation to his talents, and then wrenched from it and from his dreams of a comfortable life as a gentleman on horseback, to take on the backbreaking task of repaying the family debts. We have seen Maggie, far the more sensitive and imaginative of the two, denied the schooling she deserves -- because she's a girl -- and growing up lonely and vulnerable. The two of them love one another, resent one another, depend on one another.

The novel's genius lies in the many-sidedness of its characters, who can be mean or ridiculous one moment, noble or generous the next. The play takes this very literally in the case of Maggie, whose role gets divided among three actresses, according to the character's spiritual development, which roughly corresponds with her chronological age. Torri Higginson is shiny-eyed, the bookish, romantic Maggie, a bit like Alice in Wonderland, always ready to lecture her elders or tell them stories. Julia Arkos is the religious Maggie, the most irritating of the trio, who, when trouble strikes, reads Thomas a Kempis's The Imitation of Christ, and sets about imitating the imitation. (The novel makes clear, as the play doesn't, that she has got it wrong, using self-abnegation as a form of self-indulgence.) Finally and commandingly -- if with rather more glow than is credible in the circumstances -- there is Brenda Robins as the grown young woman, faced with new temptations in the form of two rival suitors: an introverted hunchback and a self-satisfied young man-about-the-country.

All three Maggies are on stage simultaneously -- though in practice their interaction breaks down into Maggie Three weighing the attractions of a new dress or a new man while Maggie One tells her to go for it and Maggie Two adjures her to repent. In Phillips's production, these episodes are perplexing: beautifully staged but ludicrous. The math is wrong: Three one-dimensional characters do not add up to one three-dimensional one.

The treatment both diminishes Maggie -- she becomes a victim -- and unfairly privileges her. The story as written is Tom's as well as hers, but his more prosaic struggles are kept largely offstage. Still, with no alter egoes around, Stephen Ouimette can at least fuse what complexities are left him into a powerful whole; from first to last he is the same cub -- self-centred, patronizing, hurtfully well-intentioned.

The minor figures, meanwhile, are diminished. Eliot's Mrs. Tulliver is a great, almost Dickensian, comic creation, cluckingly devoted to her linen, her china and her family, especially her son, then surprising us with her loyalty to her daughter. Roberta Maxwell plays her as a sour-lipped woman who goes through the evening resenting everybody, especially her husband; her remark that he likes his tea early is practically a plea for liberation. She then doubles as Maggie's flaxen-haired cousin Lucy, light to her dark, who here emerges as another mother-figure. Both these performances are fine in themselves; they're just wrong, and I persist in believing that if the actors had gone back to the text, they might have been right.

As it is, they seem to be acting out somebody's second-hand ideas about Victorian repression, rather than the far richer, more- involved critique provided by Eliot herself. An incompetent teacher becomes a cane-carrying sadist; a level-headed rector seems, for an alarming moment, to have lecherous designs on Maggie. This is of a piece with Edmundson's dramatization of War and Peace, in which the pious Princess Mary was presented as a hysteric; it's pointlessly cheap.

Stephen Guest, Maggie's more persistent seducer, also comes off shallower than he should (he does actually love her) but within those limits Tom McCamus's performance is excellent, as is Steven Sutcliffe's as his disadvantaged rival. Sutcliffe also doubles, this time round, as one of Tom and Maggie's aunts; at one point the exigencies of costume-change force him to put in an amusingly unexplained belated appearance at a family gathering. The real multiple triumph, however, is that of Jack Wetherall, who gives delicate life to at least five characters.

Few of these actors have worked for Soulpepper before, though some are slated to reappear later in the season. A couple of weeks ago, John Neville's Krapp's Last Tape magically became a Soulpepper production, though it was exactly the same show as had been seen earlier under another banner at World Stage. This year will be a crucial one; by the end of it we should have a better idea whether Soulpepper is to be an identifiable company or -- what may be just as valuable -- a general classical-theatre resource.
