PLATONOV

Du Maurier Theatre Centre, Toronto

When Soulpepper first mounted Platonov last year, it was as a glorified --and glorious -- workshop. The production now returns with virtually the same cast but with a more durable set and with costumes more eloquently suggestive of the late 19th century, which is where Chekhov's play, his first, was written and is set. Both help.

The period frocks counterbalance a translation that is aggressively and exuberantly here and now: We can welcome the actors as Canadian while still believing in the characters as Russian. The setting -- designed, like the clothes, by Victoria Wallace -- is a high, bare room done up in what appears to be hessian.

Sometimes it is dotted with benches, the title character being a schoolteacher. At other times, it is just a mess; it looks unliveable but it feels lived in. These are middle-class people who have humour and intelligence and even, in a couple of cases, money. They still exist in chaos, or squalor, or both. Their voices echo in this spare environment, shouts ring and whispers pierce the air. The opening moments -- in which Platonov himself is discovered, quite characteristically, asleep -- are done with an extraordinary overheard naturalness. They set a tone.

The volume level of director Laszlo Marton's production is to rise considerably. The play -- which would take seven hours uncut but has here been reduced by half -- becomes a switchback ride between farce and tragedy. The people behave exorbitantly, though they never seem surprised by much, and the more extreme they get, the more we accept them. It all seems --how you say? -- wildly probable.

The production has lost a little in edge (or maybe just in surprise), but gained in richness. Albert Schultz's Platonov has developed from an acute sketch to a painting. He is a drunken, lecherous, ineffectual, cynical, self-hating man who, at 35, is in a permanent state of mid-life crisis. He is, in short, someone with whom we can all sympathize. Admittedly, he gets luckier than any man has a right to (every woman in the cast falls for him), but he compensates for this by not enjoying it much, or at least by having terrible remorse, sometimes before the fact. His position is complicated by having nearly all his acquaintances, male and female, regard him as some kind of idol -- a feeling that, in a warped way, he shares. He is the first to chastise himself for failing his own ideals and of course he tries to use this as absolution; meanwhile, he spreads his guilt around on everyone else. He can yearn for a better life while in the act of seducing a friend's wife. Mostly the women come to him, but he makes an effort for this one, probably out of sheer perversity.

Schultz, untidily bearded and moving sartorially from dishevelment to decrepitude, plays him from a permanent bedrock of charm, from which spring serpentine rivers of deception, which can convince everyone but himself. He spends a lot of time lying down, the victim of alcohol or inertia or sheer physical and moral exhaustion, but he can never stop his mind working -- which is both his saving grace and his destruction.

He has a brother-in-law, a doctor who has gone even further than himself in vodka and futility (he has to be literally dragged to a sickbed) but can always pull back from the edge. Diego Matamoros maybe enjoys his antics too much in the earlier scenes but is magnificent when he has to pull himself together to deliver the final, bitter epitaph ("Who will I get drunk with at your funeral?")

Stuart Hughes' tearful cuckold in a cream-coloured suit has perhaps benefited more than anyone else from the show's enhanced sense of period. It gives him a handle on an indeterminate character, one whom his author seems to have made up as he went along.

Of the women, Nancy Palk is gorgeously commanding, and rather sensible, as a local landowner who spends a lot of time trying to arouse Platonov by lying on top of him. Only the occasional touch of self-conscious irony betrays her in these encounters, as if she can't quite believe a lady could behave like this.

Susan Coyne (who adapted the play, with the director) has some trouble connecting the widely spaced dots that make up the role of the debauched wife. She is best at extremes, at the moments of surrender and of revenge. Robyn Stevan remains perfect as Platonov's own wife, a seemingly placid figure who nevertheless throws herself (non-fatally) under a train because it seems the thing to do. Her scenes with Schultz, in which he flounderingly and compulsively tries to restore harmony in the home, are among the funniest and saddest in the play.

Liisa Repo-Martell is tremulously earnest as Platonov's last and least likely victim, a biology researcher. And Michael Hanrahan is strong and supple as the local brigand, with whom everyone seems on remarkably easy terms, but whose death they take thoroughly in their stride.

The student whose idealism (or priggishness) Platonov especially loathes, and who returns the compliment, is now played by Christian Lloyd, whose performance augurs well both for himself and for Soulpepper's Young Company, of which he is a member.

There is, as before, a fine quartet of servants, including William Webster as a major-domo who submits to humiliation with scalding decorum, and Patricia Fagan as a maid who delivers a message to the protagonist as if applying to be his latest flame. Marton's staging seems as fluent and unforced as life itself, but can still form indelible stage pictures, especially at the end.

In a righteous world, this production would be permanently available, or would at least return at regular intervals. In the world we have, grab it while you can.

Stan Rogers -- A Matter of Heart runs to Aug. 5 at the Jane Mallet Theatre at the St. Lawrence Centre, 27 Front St. E. Tickets are $29 to $49 and are available by calling the box office at (416) 386- 7723.

Stan Rogers songs tell stories. That is the reason a theatrical show has now been built around them. There is a difference, though, between telling a story and acting it, and this distinction is the rock on which Stan Rogers -- A Matter of Heart runs aground and founders. (There are a lot of songs here about shipwrecks, and the imagery is catching.)

The show is a moderately elaborate folk-pop concert. Half a dozen musicians play on an assortment of rostra, while four actors sing either on or in front of some shallow flights of steps. Behind everybody is a cyclorama that goes from red to blue and back again, and is pretty in either shade. The performers' choices seem similarly limited: They can sing their songs standing up, or they can sing them sitting down. The vast majority of the numbers are solos.

This is hardly surprising since Rogers, in his brief lifetime, wrote them to sing himself. I'm not a great fan of the kind of show in which one performer spends a whole evening pretending to be another performer, but that might be the best way to present this material in the theatre. It might forge a direct connection between the actor and the audience, as happened long ago in Hank Williams -- The Show He Never Gave, a piece that turned me for one night into a country-music fan (a not inconsiderable feat). This production never establishes Rogers as an individual voice. Its brief narrative passages tell us that he cared passionately about his own roots in the Maritimes, and about what recession had done to the people there. We are told that he gravitated toward characters who had been buffeted by fate but refused to give in to it, and that he chose his subjects -- contemporary or historic, public or private -- accordingly. We are also told, in the evenings one joke, that he wrote about all kinds of ships, including relationships.

As it happens, relationships, in both the emotional and the dramatic sense, are what is largely missing from this show. We can appreciate, listening to the songs here, that Rogers was a strong and honest writer, and that his melodies are more resourceful than those of most neo-folkies, though after a while they do start to sound the same. (This is accentuated by the shows habit of grouping the songs by subject; the first half of the first half seems to be one sea shanty after another.) And the songs are, indeed, about people. The trouble is that in each song a character reveals himself to us, finished and complete, usually in the form of a retrospective monologue; everything has happened before the song starts. We don't see anybody evolve, and we don't see any characters interact. Any of these songs might make an agreeable point of rest in a conventional musical, with a story; but you cant ask them to be the story. As soon as one song is done, we have to start all over again with another, and we lose the will to follow. To make matters worse, the sound is muddy.

Im not sure whether it's due to faults in diction, miking or overall balance, but the words can be very hard to hear, especially when the tempo quickens. This means that the vaunted stories never really get told. It also means that there aren't many laughs. Im sure that theres plenty of gnarled humour lurking in the lyrics and that, heard at close quarters in a pub or club, they'd be a riot. But they aren't fall-down funny in the theatre with a band drowning them out, and Jim Bettss direction seems desperate to compensate. Charlotte Moore, who is both the most centred of the actors and the most vibrant of the singers, has two potentially good numbers shot from under her by fussy staging.

Of her three male cohorts, Don Mackay comes on initially as the statutory juvenile, but manages to transcend the blandness that implies. Frank MacKay and Terry Hatty are eccentric stage presences, one louche and louring, the other beaming and canonical; neither has harnessed his personality very efficiently to the materials. In the angrier songs, they seem to be acting the idea of bitterness, rather than the thing itself; just as too many of the songs seem to be about drama, rather than dramatic.

The most effective number concerns a small-town hockey player of indeterminate age; its lyric contrasts young ambitions and old despair, love of the game and desire to use it as a passport from a dead-end existence, and here the contrasts truly work as conflicts. They also create a world; you can see what Rogers was on about (and hear it too -- most of the words are clear). Some other songs -- about Irish-Canadians scorn for their sectarian past or about the opposing desires for adventure and for security -- are stronger on conception than execution but are interesting enough to hold the attention. But the show goes on too long, and every one of its last five numbers sounds like it ought to be the closer. A recurring song, heard in fragments, is Fogarty's Cove, a location we are told that existed only in Rogers' mind but is none the less real for that. The test of the show, I guess, is whether it makes us believe in the reality. I couldn't, but, to judge from the first-night reception, others did.

The Apple Cart is in repertoire until Sept. 23 Still Life until Sept. 20 Lord of the Flies until Oct. 29. Box office: 1-800-511- SHAW.

THE APPLE CART, COURT HOUSE THEATRE;

STILL LIFE, ROYAL GEORGE THEATRE;

LORD OF THE FLIES, FESTIVAL THEATRE

Niagara-on-the-Lake

NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE - David Schurmann may be the quintessential Shaw Festival actor. Most of his roles require him to be immaculately turned out, but there is something about his voice -- a creased, rumpled quality -- that inescapably suggests tweed jackets with leather patches at the elbows. He is intelligent, rueful, what used to be called civilized. I don't know his actual origins but he seems, in a pleasantly old-fashioned way, very English -- in the parts he gets, he needs to be.

Cast in The Apple Cart as Magnus, King of England, he reaches some kind of apogee. This is one of the greatest roles Shaw ever wrote -- one of the longest, anyway -- and the actors qualities carry him a considerable way with it, though less than the full distance.

The play, written in 1929, inaugurated its authors long, last period. He subtitled it, as he was to do many others over his remaining two decades, "a political extravaganza." This is a self- invented genre in which increasingly wayward ideas predominate over action (which tends to be either arbitrary or non-existent), social setting and character. The Apple Cart, being the first of its kind, still maintains links with convention; it has, if not a plot, a governing situation, and Magnus, who is hardly ever off stage, is a dominating presence, if not quite a unifying one.

He is a constitutional monarch, at loggerheads with a cabinet composed of one astute manipulator, one thwarted idealist and half a dozen clowns. Cleverer than any of them, he has started alluding to the royal veto; i.e., the fact that the one political power of his own is that of preventing them, in a last resort, from exercising theirs.

The politicians want him to shut up, or else. (What else may entail remains vague, but they seem to mean it). Eventually, Magnus finds a way of calling their bluff, though other events conspire to rob his victory of most of its savour.

Shaw set the play 40 years into its own future; Richard Greenblatt's production compounds the math, and pushes it 40 years into ours, though if he had merely set it down in 2000 it would still seem eerily topical. The world it presents is caught in a spiral of cynicism: rich countries stay that way on the labour of poor ones; politicians are controlled by business interests (national, though, rather than global); England survives as a dispenser of luxury goods; and democracy is falling into disuse because few people bother to vote.

Perhaps the least familiar part of the landscape, from a Canadian as well as an English viewpoint, is the presence of a hereditary monarch, both willing and able to challenge the general complacency; about the nearest approach we've had in the last 80 years is the putative Charles III, to whom Greenblatts slightly adapted text makes cheeky reference.

Shaw takes the traditionally appealing theatrical figure of the threatened king and gives it a comic twist; the fate of this monarch is not to lose his title but to keep it. In the meantime, he fights: with charm, with irony and with passion. Schurmanns performance has all the charm and its own brand of irony, but the latter is of the self-defeated kind, conceding points even as it makes them, so the passion leaks away. He has a great prose aria that prompts one of his hearers to remark "you spoke that piece beautifully, sir"; we should want to echo that sentiment (while chuckling at the author's self-deflation), but here we can only say that he spoke it very lucidly.

Kelly Wolf's set gives us a big shiny mirror to see ourselves in (this is always an effective device, but its been used a lot and, honestly, weve got the point) while her costumes combine a Regency cut with garish colours that pessimists might describe as futuristic. They certainly attract attention, but the actors get lost inside them.

Supporting acting is weaker than one expects at the Shaw, and only three of the cabinet are much good. There is Corinne Koslo, ringingly committed as the energy secretary (Shaw called her the powermistress-general) driven to distraction by a conglomerate known, all too persuasively, as Breakages Limited. There is Michael Ball as the aggressively proletarian Bill Boanerges, though he should really be a roaring bull rather than this actor's familiar cuddly bear. Pre-eminently, there is Peter Millard's prime minister, again not quite what the dramatist ordered -- he should probably be a more docile-seeming politician whose smartness takes us by surprise -- but commandingly incisive. Though, given that the play is basically a duel between him and Magnus, it hurts that they are - - tonally and temperamentally -- very similar kinds of actor.

The king has other problems. There is Orinthia, his mistress, with whom he shares one of Shaws most infuriatingly sexless love scenes, and who is jealous and demanding in every way, it seems, except physically. Its hard to make this kind of poseuse sacree attractive, and it's possible that Pamela Rabe, who plays her with ferocious langour, isn't trying; she actually comes off not only less comfortable than the queen (Wendy Thatcher) but less alluring.A final tableau -- undreamed-of by the playwright but very effective - - really turns the screws on His Royal Loneliness.

Then there is America, which puts domestic problems into perspective by applying to rejoin the British Empire, thereby effectively annexing it. In 1929, the year of the crash, this must have seemed whimsically amusing; now its just logical. The production turns the U.S. ambassador into an ambassadress (Lynne Cormack). This works amazingly well; it is also much, much scarier.

OH, FOR A 10-PENCE GLASS OF BRANDY

The Shaws second-favourite playwright is Noel Coward, who this year has as many plays in the bill as GBS himself, though one (Easy Virtue, just closed) was a repeat from last year and the other is a lunchtime show. This is Still Life, the one-act piece that became the emblematic British movie Brief Encounter.

It is the archetypal story of thwarted adultery; a confluence of timetables causes two married people to collide once a week at a railway station, and encourages them to arrange further collisions elsewhere. Furtiveness and guilt (hers especially) put an end to the affair, and he, a doctor, does the gentlemanly thing by accepting a position a very long way away.

The play derives from 1936 (the film came 10 years later), and Dennis Garnhum's unemphatically atmospheric production gets us duly and wistfully nostalgic for the manners and fashions of before-the- war. Also for the prices: The entire play unfolds, over the course of a year, in the railway refreshment room, and the cost of tea, cakes and brandy (ten pence a glass) are meticulously noted.

Behind the central couple, the station staff play out their own more robust romances; Coward, a suburban boy himself, was probably trying hard to do good by his roots, but the lower-class characters are patronizingly written and, for the most part, patronizingly played.

The middle-class figures, too, have an uphill struggle. The actors have to contend not only with the stiff-upper-lipness that befits their station (and I don't mean Milford Junction, wherever that is) but with Cowards own style which, sad or funny, is heavily reliant on bloodless adjectives.

Beneath this double overlay there is an unquestioned truth, but its hard to reach. Simon Bradbury, pleasingly released from his line of flat-capped northern roles, often manages to cut through; Coward himself, who originated the role, was probably far less convincing.

Jan Alexandra Smith (in the Gertrude Lawrence part) is less fortunate. I felt so cheap, she says, when one of their assignations is interrupted; yes, that is how she would have felt and what she would have said, but she can't help sounding like one of the parody heroines whom this text has so prolifically inspired. Her emotions seem buried inside her coat, until a silent, desperate movement brings them tearingly to the surface.

The play may be less touching than anticipated, but it's still thoroughly gripping. The masters technique is at its most magisterial, the structure as clipped as the dialogue, with the unseen details of the relationship seeping through the silences. When he brings on a new and fateful character near the end, its such an agonizingly clever stroke that you could kill him.

THE CALL OF THE CONCH

The pent-up legacy of civilized English loquacity (Shaw) and civilized English reticence (Coward) was devastatingly exposed in William Golding's novel Lord of the Flies. This is one of the few modern novels that everybody knows, largely because, being about schoolboys, it has for decades been an educational set-text.

A group of young evacuees, aged 12 or thereabouts, find themselves alone on a desert island, and act out, in horrifyingly short order, the decline of civilization. Arriving in dramatic form on the main festival stage, it is, as it should be, very tense and very frightening.

Its first act -- there are three in all -- is brilliant. The rhythms, both of Nigel Williams' adaptation and Neil Munros production, seem exactly right. The boys cluster together for their first assembly, an attempt that keeps breaking down, disrupted by compulsive horseplay that becomes progressively less innocent.

Piggy, the asthmatic and myopic state-school kid, is robbed of his specs so that his public school (which, translated into North American, means private school) confreres may use them as a burning glass to light a fire: Not a bad idea, except that they seem to have no intention of returning them. Ralph, the conscientious boy elected leader, has to insist on fair play, an insistence that gets steadily harder to enforce. The boys are played by young actors in their twenties, but we accept them completely.

As the castaways begin to lose it, so, unfortunately, does the play. It remains exciting, but it does not stay convincing.

One difficulty is the set: basically three wide carpeted steps, in a shade that the fabric catalogue may have listed as Basic Beach. Its anonymous but it isn't unlocalized, because landmarks keep being planted on it -- a pig's head, a sacrificial altar -- that cant be removed. So when three separate groups of characters, supposedly in three different places, all start wandering about it at the same time, they look silly.

Another problem is that, as the action unfolds, it stumbles into the waiting arms of some well-worn theatrical cliches. Youll remember the story: Jack, a bullying head choirboy, turns his angel- voiced cohorts into a gang of hunters whose appetite for blood doesn't stop at the local pig population. A small boy claims to have seen a Beast in the bushes, and it becomes the object of a cult. Simon, an epileptic choirboy, discovers the prosaic truth about the Beast -- it's already, with unfortunate literalness, been revealed to the audience -- and is set upon and killed when he tries to break the news. Jack says -- repeatedly -- that he wants his adherents to hunt, and eat, and dance: So a lot of tired ritualistic prancing takes place.

Also ritualistic are the politics. Williams was one of the more heavy-handed of the 1970s generation of British playwrights, and he makes class warfare -- a subsidiary theme in the novel -- the mainspring of the action. Jack is a lot nastier, a lot sooner, to the proletarian Piggy than the source gives warrant. (When, by the way, is all this meant to be happening? Presumably the war the boys are escaping is the Second World one; anything later would put the script outside even the festivals new extended mandate of doing plays set during Shaws lifetime. If it's now, as a couple of lines and many of the idioms suggest, then the choir would be as likely to imitate Piggy's accent as to insult it.)

As Jack matures into a full-blown fascist, so the writing of his role grows increasingly self-conscious; and so, accordingly -- despite Mike Sharas best efforts, which are very good efforts indeed -- does its acting.

The attendant savages are similarly effortful and largely indistinguishable, even before they put on their war-paint, though Matthew MacFadzean develops a belated sinister glimmer as Jacks lieutenant who is even nastier than he is.

But it's the good boys who deserve favour: Craig Erickson's Ralph and Dylan Trowbridges visionary Simon are both excellent, while Pete Treadwell as the doggedly decent Piggy is perfect. His end, most ineffectually staged, is unlikely to satisfy anyone who recalls Ralphs lament in the book for "the fall through the air of the one true friend called Piggy."

It's unfortunate, too, that boypower shortage keeps offstage the smaller kids, the "little'uns," who are mentioned but must be presumed to be on another part of the island, acting out some other fable entirely.

We can still feel in our bones the abiding power of this one. Golding was on to something: Something that confirms our worst fears about ourselves and our children, and that insistently invites dramatization. Forget the Peter Brook film; the best version I ever encountered was on BBC radio, the best radio play that I ever heard, better in fact than the book, and more terrifying than any visual representation is likely to be.

This attempt falls uncomfortably between styles, and the big stage hinders rather than helps. But it's plucky. Another '70s English playwright once said that there are only two kinds of plays: plays set in rooms and plays not set in rooms. Most plays at Niagara are definitely set in rooms; this, which could hardly be less so, makes a change.

SHREW

The Dream in High Park

This year's High Park show is Shrew, based on Shakespeares The Taming of the Shrew, but not to be confused with it. It is quite confusing enough on its own account.

Shakespeares piece is a play within a play; the main action, comprising the Petruchio-Katharina shenanigans with assorted subplots, is presented before the drunken tinker Christopher Sly, who has been tricked by a passing aristocrat into believing that he is himself a nobleman enjoying a command performance by some strolling players.

Sarah Stanley's production retains this framework; some of the pre-opening puffs have even suggested that she's rescued it from long obscurity. Actually, I cant remember a production of The Taming of the Shrew that didnt include the Induction in some form, though in recent years it's been treated with increasing freedom; i.e., it's been subjected to wholesale cuts and rewrites.

The present version is conservative by comparison. In the original, Sly gets thrown out of a pub for non-payment; he and the Hostess trade insults, and then she trots off to call the law. That happens here, too, except that the pair now come to blows before she goes. He then passes out as usual, and everything else unfolds according to text. Except that when the play proper begins, Sly, who for obvious reasons has gender-relations on his mind, imagines himself as one of the central characters.

Now, Ive seen productions in which the whole business of putting on a play is simply scrapped, and Sly just dreams the main action with himself as the star of it. Ive seen others, plenty of them, in which he watches the play and keeps interrupting it, courtesy of some scenes from an old Elizabethan text that never made it into the First Folio.

I've never before seen a production in which he is a spectator and a dreamer simultaneously. But that's the idea here, and the result is a mess. And thats even without mentioning the shows raison d'etre, which is that this time 'round Sly doesnt imagine himself to be Petruchio; that role goes to the actress formerly known as the Hostess. Sly himself plays the Shrew.

The point of this gender-bending is fairly obvious; Sly, the unthinking misogynist, finds out what its like to be on the receiving end. By the time he gets to the long speech extolling the subjection of women, he's feeling traumatized and/or ashamed of himself; he keeps stammering on the word woman. The result, paradoxically, is that the speech, which is usually guaranteed to make every man in the audience cringe, slips painlessly by; the actor is doing our suffering for us.

This Kate, by the way, never looks like a woman; he can't afford to, as he has keep popping back into bed to double as Sly. (I know that in Shakespeares day Kate would have played by a boy -- or, if you believe Timothy Findley, by a young man -- but thats not the convention here.) My children assumed that Katherine was her father's son, and were puzzled by the lines that kept telling them otherwise.

I mention this because production ideas like this are always announced as making Shakespeare more accessible, when what they're actually doing is making him impenetrable. Their only appeal is as mild titillation for people who know the plays already. And isnt High Park, in particular, supposed to be catering to new audiences?

Sometimes the casting seems, even by the productions own lights, counter-productive. When this Petruchio turns up for his wedding, he's wearing a dress; think how much more discomfiting that would be, if he really were a man.

The two leads, Jordan Pettle and Yanna McIntosh, are pretty good, and would probably be very interesting if they reversed roles. As it is, they and their director find subtleties in their first scene together that escape most performances. After that they settle down to rough-and-tumble, which in this production becomes an equal- opportunity pasttime. (Your average Petruchio never lays a finger on his partner, for the very good reason that Shakespeare never tells him to. She does, however, hit him. She also hits other people. By the end of the play, she isn't doing this any more. So maybe her taming is for the best. So thinks Germaine Greer, at any rate when she wrote The Female Eunuch.)

The production displays what, in the wake of Beaver, I am coming to recognize as one of this directors trademarks: a fondness for playing important scenes in cramped, remote corners of the stage. The text is played at surprising, even pedantic, length, though theres some welcome streamlining towards the end.

Supporting male characters wear funny hats and funny voices, while sister Bianca, whom her admirers call "a modest maid," struts through the action in a pink halter and hot pants. Maybe she's a projection of Sly's male fantasy; I cant think of any other excuse. When her suitors make their rival bids for her hand, neon lights start chasing each other round some hanging rectangular panels; it looks like the scene has suddenly been transported to Honest Eds. Roy Lewis has some welcome authority as Baptista and the introductory Lord, and Louis Negin is momentarily and unusually touching as the bemused Vincentio.

A play that usually emerges on stage as one of the funniest and least boring in the canon failed on Sunday night to raise a single full-throated laugh. After Romancin' the One I Love and now this, even the loudest haters of The Taming of the Shrew must concede that it has suffered enough. Even if it hasn't, the audience has.

A ROOM OF ONES OWN

Court House Theatre, Niagara on the Lake, Shaw Festival

Pamela Rabe, a tall and deep-toned actress who was born in Canada but has spent most of her career in Australia, made her Shaw Festival debut last week as Orinthia, the king's mistress, in The Apple Cart. Orinthia fancies herself, or Shaw seems to have fancied her, as an enchantress; but she emerged here, for all the physical and vocal exertions that the actress lavished upon her -- or maybe because of them -- as energetically repellent. A couple of nights later the same actress appeared at the same festival, as the gaunt, intense Virginia Woolf, delivering a lecture to a long-ago audience of Cambridge undergraduates, played by us. And this time she was dazzling: dazzlingly attractive too.

A Room of One's Own is adapted (not, I suspect, a very arduous task) by the English director Patrick Garland from a celebrated address given by Woolf in 1928, and subsequently published as a book. Its the talk in which she lays it down that in order to succeed as a writer, or indeed as anything else beyond wife- and motherhood, a woman needs financial independence -- she reckons this as (ps)500 a year, 1920s money -- and a place in which to work. She adds to this famous demand, the equally powerful image of "Shakespeares sister, an imaginary figure as talented as her brother who, Woolf speculates, would have come to a very bad end, had she had the temerity to follow in his footsteps.

The talk was given at Girton, Cambridge's first grudging attempt to provide a college for women, separate from but not equal to the many that already existed for men. Mordantly and wittily, she expounds on the difference in the amenities offered to the two student genders, notably the food. (Prunes, even mitigated by custard, are an unforgiving vegetable"; then, as if anticipating our objections, she delivers a perfect put-down of a coda: "Fruit, they are NOT.) According to her, the official feeling was that, if women had to be given a higher education, then both the prospect and the experience should be made as forbidding for them as possible.

She was undoubtedly right; indeed, the same ethos persisted as late as the '60s, when I was an undergraduate. Not that the cuisine at the mens colleges was anything to write home about (well, not in that sense anyway) but at least we were in town. Girtons geographical position seemed to have been chosen expressly to discourage the girls from leaving the premises and to deter any visitors, especially male ones. You wouldn't believe how long it took to get there, even by bus. Woolf herself, en route to her lecture, seems to have walked it. (She was a hero.) Brilliantly, she defines the male position; it's not so much that men want women to feel inferior, as that they want to go on feeling superior themselves.

Ive seen it objected that A Room of Ones Own isn't a real play." This, I think, is to its credit. Real plays about famous writers are usually terrible. They make unjustified demands for sympathy, based on the assumption that the audience will have read the books (or will feel intimidated if they haven't). Some years ago Stratford mounted a real play about this very writer, a play called Virginia; and even though it starred Maggie Smith in what was generally reckoned one of her greatest performances, it bored me, though to indifference rather than to tears. It wanted tears, for the protagonists sufferings; the present show wants respect, for her mind, and it presents the evidence.

Admittedly, I hadnt read any Woolf when I saw Virginia; since then I've read quite a lot, and having been awed by her style, I'm far more inclined to take an interest. As it happens I prefer the essays to the novels, whose style is so concentratedly dazzling as to cause headaches. The non-fiction is tight and argumentative and graceful and wonderfully witty: qualities that Pamela Rabe not only captures but embodies. Her phrasing is almost flawless; long, Augustan sentences twist and turn elegantly before us, and arrive always with their tails poised and stinging. She uses the style to get at the ideas, and the ideas to get at the woman. (She was probably trying the same with Orinthia, who was full of ideas; none of them, unfortunately, much worth listening to.)

It helps, obviously, that she looks like Virginia, spare and long- boned; she has also designed a physical vocabulary for her. In Micheline Chevriers production she roams, not too restlessly, around the stage, suggesting that, when confronting an audience, her body is nervous but her mind is absolutely at ease. Im tempted to call this solo show the best ensemble performance of the Shaw season.

The ideas are dramatic and still challenging; Woolf can move from amused indignation at the barriers erected against her sex on university lawns and in university libraries, to a combination of lament and celebration for the lives and achievements of the great Victorian woman novelists, to deliver a stark challenge to her hearers: "You haven't written Shakespeare's plays. (You might feel like responding that not many men have either.) The woman speaking the ideas is real and embattled, and the result is drama; the term lecture theatre" seems absolutely apposite.

You dont have to know anything about Virginia Woolf when you go in; though its certain that you will want to know all about her by the time you come out.

Black & White Photo: Shaw Festival / Pamela Rabe wholly embodies Virginia Woolf in looks and personality in A Room of One's Own, currently playing at the Shaw Festival. ;
2000-07-22-much-ado-about-oakville-s-pas:
Much Ado About Nothing continues to Aug. 12 at Coronation Park in Oakville. Call (905)-815-2021.

There is a moment in Much Ado About Nothing in which one character invites another on a short journey toward the nearest willow tree. (Don't ask.) In the new production in Oakville, it's an unusually quick trip, since the Coronation Park stage provides, perhaps uniquely, an actual and imposingly elegiac willow, right there on site. It's the centrepiece of what seems to me every summer to be the loveliest open-air playing-space in, probably, the world. It's practical, too: a concentrated space backed by a vista that stretches, clearly and hauntingly, down to Lake Ontario. For the past few years, it's been the setting for a series of Shakespearean comedy productions that -- for intelligence, imagination and all- around sparkle -- can match any in Canada.

Some plays, though, make cozier pastorals than others. As it happens, the two most celebrated scenes in Much Ado are set quite specifically in a garden; I refer to the matched pair of episodes in which the two squabbling anti-romantics, Benedick and Beatrice, eavesdrop on carefully rehearsed conversations designed to persuade each of them that he or she is loved by the other. The upshot, of course, is the invented love becomes real, for both of them; they have been compulsively sparring out of a mixture of pride and habit, and are delighted to find release. At Oakville both the scenes, enlivened by characterful and inventive business involving wine glasses and an unruly lawn sprinkler, are delicious; indeed, it's a signal achievement of Michael Shamata's production that he makes the second episode, which is an instant replay of the first, almost equally funny.

Still, for the most part, Much Ado strikes me, more than any other of the comedies, as an indoor piece. Its dramatic climax takes place in a church, and its comic resolution in a police court, and the wit combats that make up most of its dialogue have a salon quality, giving the play the air of a continuous supper party. This production begins with a messenger arriving on a motorbike that he rides over most of the available terrain; but after that the play doesn't seem to have much use for wide-open spaces.

That doesn't stop it from being enjoyable, with occasional bolts of magic. The action has been updated to the Second World War or thereabouts, and the Spanish and Italian place names have been expunged. Don Pedro, formerly of Arragon, now arrives as the head of a small detachment of Canadian servicemen; Leonato, with whom he and his pals billet themselves, seems to be a prosperous British expatriate. There have also been some discreet textual alterations, ranging from the helpful to the bafflingly unnecessary.

Shamata's production is an explicit sequel to his Love's Labour's Lost last year; John Jarvis and Gina Wilkinson, his Benedick and Beatrice, appeared then as Berowne and Rosaline, the characters' prototypes. Jarvis last year made exhilarating work of Berowne's great verse arias; Benedick, who speaks mostly prose, doesn't give him that scope, but he is very good at depicting a basic decency trying to escape the tangles of its own cleverness. Wilkinson is almost too tempestuous to begin with, but her defences once dampened (by the garden hose, in this version), she melts beautifully. What's best about them is the way they work together. In terms of plot, the Benedick-Beatrice action is completed halfway through the play, but the relationship goes on developing as the couple, having declared their love, keep advancing and retreating, each fearful of letting the other have the last word or the last laugh. We end by hanging, delightedly, on their every word.

My favourite performance, though, is Graham Harley's remarkably unsentimental Leonato, a stiff-backed paterfamilias, crafty and snobbish: delighted when he thinks his daughter Hero is loved by a prince, ready to settle for the prince's friend Claudio as second best, equally ready to condemn Hero when her chastity is impugned, and finally displaying real feeling when he turns on her accusers. Claudio, whose first question about his intended is whether she's her father's heir and who humiliates her in public with self- righteous relish, may be the nastiest juvenile lead ever written; Brandon McGibbon makes the only possible case for him by stressing his youth and his callow adherence to a military code. Glyn Thomas as his role-model Don Pedro lacks authority but is good at conveying a submerged love for Beatrice. One of the production's admirable subtleties is that when Benedick, their companion-in-arms, finds his true self, he goes into civvies. Darren Hynes, meanwhile, as Don John the bastard, keeps switching in and out of uniform; his performance is gauche in some respects but reveals the character's cankered heart; he, too, seems doomed to permanent immaturity. Marion St-Jules' Hero is delightful, as is Chris Adams' musical Balthasar, singing Shakespeare's lyrics to good new tunes by Don Horsburgh. Keith Knight doesn't find many laughs as Dogberry, the comic policeman who gets his words wrong, but he plays honestly, and I wound up liking him.

ON AN AVERAGE DAY

Helen Gardner Phelan Playhouse

On an average day in an average American play, you might well expect to meet up with two long-separated, father-obsessed brothers, inspired by Arthur Miller while playing reverential homage to Eugene O'Neill. Their reunion could be staged in the kind of derelict shack that Sam Shepard might call home, and they would express their distrust of one another and of everybody else in paranoid exchanges of the kind patented by David Mamet.

All U.S. drama would be there, at least in its macho aspects; and though On an Average Day, which unites all these elements, finally manages to exorcise its ghosts and establish its own identity, it takes nearly as long about it as the brothers themselves. John Kolvenbach, who wrote and directed it, runs a company in New York called Rocking Chair Test, and he brought his play to this year's Toronto Fringe Festival, picking up a couple of Canadian actors on the way. The production is now enjoying an extended run on the University of Toronto campus.

The Kolvenbach siblings are called Robert and Jack. They were abandoned by their dad when Jack was 15 and Robert eight; they lived together, Jack taking care of his kid brother, until one day Jack followed his father's example and decamped in his own turn. (A lot of tunes are relayed over the sound system before the play starts, but Hit the Road, Jack is unaccountably not among them.)

Fifteen years later Jack returns, to find Robert in a state of slump, at a kitchen table on which stand several beer cans and a bottle of whisky. About the only other furnishing is a fridge, crammed apparently with additional cans, and emitting, as we are constantly assured, an overpowering fungoid stench. Robert's first words to the brother he hasn't seen in years are: "I didn't do it, Jack"; we discover that he is on trial for something closely resembling murder.

Jack is impassive and taciturn; Robert, understandably in the circumstances, is twitchy and unstoppably voluble. Gradually and twistingly, we learn the facts of his case; what he did and why he did it. We also learn his opinion of his lawyer, whose courtroom technique apparently makes great use of significant pauses. ("That's a pause for 'shall we clap?' " says Robert; "I hate that." It's at moments like these, charged with free-floating aggression, that the dialogue is at its most Mamet, though it doesn't have his wit.) We also learn that everybody is town is looking at Robert like they want him dead, which again is understandable.

Robert discovers that Jack has a gun, and immediately decides that his brother has come to kill him. The drama now jumps into higher, if not immediately plausible, gear, as Jack, threatened but seemingly unperturbed, starts telling his brother the truth about their past lives. In particular -- and this is where the play resembles the perennial Miller's tale -- he tries to demolish Robert's illusions about the father who once left them "on an average day" and who is assuredly not coming back. And why should Robert believe that he would? Because Jack used to tell him so, along with many other stories, as a way of getting him to sleep. Finally we discover Jack's own hang-ups; his fear that he may be re- enacting the sins of his father. In his quieter way, he is as desperate as his brother. And it is here that the play, skirting but avoiding sentimentality, at last becomes its own animal, resigned and reconciling.

Both the performances are decent, though the theatre's unfriendly acoustic tends to swallow up the high-register neurosis of Jonathan Higgins' Robert; John Robinson's Jack, laid-back even when agonizing, has a better time and provides one, too. Both play and production have the air of an exercise, skilfully carried out.

COLLECTED STORIES

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

STRATFORD - The lights go up on an elderly, grey-haired woman sitting at a desk in her apartment, scribbling and frowning. From a semi-visible kitchen, there comes the sound of a kettle whistling. Since the lady seems to be getting somewhere with her work, she resents the interruption. On the other hand, she does want her tea. (We discover presently that she doesn't drink coffee.) Not a word has been spoken, but every nuance of her inner conflict has come across, in a perfect moment of silent comedy. We have also met a character -- complete at the moment we see her, but still open to exploration and even to growth.

The play is Collected Stories by Donald Margulies, an American playwright who has achieved great success in his own country over the last 20 years but is still little known outside it. The actress, recreating a role that she originated in New York three years ago, is Uta Hagen, at 81 the doyenne of American acting. She plays Ruth Steiner, a much-honoured author of short stories, who also teaches creative writing at a New York university. The play concerns the relationship between Ruth and a young woman named Lisa Morrison who, at the start of the actions six-year span, is Ruths newest student. Later she becomes her assistant. Later still she becomes -- at least as Ruth sees it -- her rival and possible supplanter.

The first scene is a tutorial, fetchingly written, with Ruth a stern but appreciative taskmistress, and Lisa a bouncingly eager pupil. Ruth has to rein her in; she is especially critical of Lisa's habit, endemic to young American women, of ending each sentence on a rising inflection, as if it were a question. (Or, as if it were a question? And you thought that was just a Canadian disease.) Lisa also, you know, says like a lot; Ruth doesn't pull her up on that one, but its notable that both mannerisms have disappeared by the second scene, Lisa having now become an official part of Ruths life. The play settles down into a study of an adoptive mother- daughter relationship, thereby becoming more commonplace but still engrossing. It finally comes to rest on the subject of literary appropriation; having made her own mark with short stories, Lisa tries her hand at a novel, something that Ruth has always avoided. She bases it on intimate details of Ruth's past life. Ruth is livid; battle is joined, an irreconcilable combat in which, as Margulies very fairly shows us, both are right and both are wrong.

As an imported text of less than classic stature, Collected Stories might well sit better at CanStage or Tarragon than at Stratford; though it's a far better play than, say, The Gin Game, the atrocious Broadway hit that was once shoe-horned into the festival as a vehicle for Jessica Tandy and Hume Cronyn. Hagens performance, though, makes quibbling irrelevant; this is seamlessly great acting that we would be lucky to see anywhere. (And great acting, though it cant be guaranteed, is presumably part of what Stratford is for.) Everything about it is implicit in that opening silent sequence; it sets a rhythm that can be varied but is never broken. At one point she makes satirical mention of the U. S. Cavalry and puckers her lips to suggest a bugle; that was her only moment that struck me as in any way forced or excessive. Her delightfully ambiguous facial play at the start finds a darker reflection later on when she learns that Lisa has placed her first story without her mentor's help; pleasure and pain fight a visible battle on her countenance. Returning from a triumphant public appearance Ruth announces "I was just acting a part -- the feisty old lady who can get away with saying anything." It's a part that, despite her protestations, she believes in, and its sheer comic gusto carries the play along, and us with it. But beneath it lurk an increasing frailty, that she resents, and a capacity for meanness that visibly shocks her but that she cannot control. Hagen communicates great complexity by the simplest means; the line of her performance is extraordinary. Thirty-five years ago she was the legendary Martha of Whos Afraid of Virginia Woolf: another aggressively witty woman who turned out to be jelly within. I remember that performance -- the only previous one of hers Ive seen -- as trumpeting and swashbuckling. The years have obviously shrunk her -- vocally and, I think, physically -- and the present performance is pitched very quietly But there's great variety in her pianissimo -- it can accommodate anger and suffering as well as wit - - and unquestionable truth, and, I might prosaically add, total audibility.

Lorca Simons' Lisa stands up to her very well, as actress and as character. Lisa, too, has to find a part to act and the one she develops -- and that we can see her working at -- is that of the bright-eyed, well-meaning, debutante, talented but humble; she goes from being innocently gauche to purposefully gauche. The persona (which is quite sincere) blossoms in the one scene that takes place outside Ruths Greenwich Village pad: Lisa, in the populist- cultural precincts of the 92nd Street YMCA, offering a preview of her novel. (It sounds absolutely dreadful, by the way, though Im not sure that was the intention.) The final showdown is very honestly handled; we don't doubt that the two characters are essentially through, but we know that they will continue to meet on occasion, and that their unbreakable bonds will continue to chafe.

The vice of the play -- like that of most American drama below the John Guare-David Mamet level -- is that it's self-conscious, without being truly self-aware. These characters speak, even for writers, in implausibly complex sentences, loaded with subordinate clauses; and they draw our attention to things, like the implicit, mother-daughter relationship, that are already in plain view. But Lisas placing of herself and her mentor ("you had that rich, wonderful Jewish life to draw on -- Ive only got WASP culture") is dramatically justified, if only for the fierce riposte it gets from Ruth. Hagen really does seem to have walked out of the New York Jewish intelligentsia; and it adds to the texture that she herself is as celebrated a teacher as she is an actor. If that's cultural appropriation, I'm for it. Im far less comfortable with Margulies device of making Ruth the fictitious lover of an actual dead writer: the alcoholic poet and critic Delmore Schwartz; since he hasn't taken the creative risk of actually putting Schwartz on stage, this strikes me as glory-by-association, and verisimilitude at one remove. It also makes Hagen, by strict count, 10 years too old for her role. But there's no point in worrying about chronology; what we have here -- living, breathing and making us part of -- is history. She never appears to trade on it, but that is what the actress brings on stage with her: that and surpassing accomplishment, honed and shining. The play itself is not especially moving but I was still in tears at the end.

PATIENCE

Avon Theatre, Stratford

The Stratford Festival has revived Gilbert and Sullivan's Patience (or Bunthornes Bride) as part of its Oscar Wilde centenary celebration. The opera, first staged in 1881, is a satire on Wilde, who at that time had yet to come into his own as an author, but was already considered a social and artistic portent. As the figurehead of an Aesthetic Movement, dedicated to what Lewis Carroll called reeling, writhing, and fainting in coils, he was both mocked and celebrated. Patience does mockery.

The Stratford production is a concert performance; one of those semi-staged, book-in-hand affairs that have become popular in London and New York as cost-effective methods of acquainting us with risky or unfamiliar old musicals. (A similar outfit existed recently in Toronto but seems to have gone into abeyance.)

This Patience is an unusually elaborate example of the genre, with a full orchestra and a carefully worked-out staging. The conceit devised by the director, Brian Hill, is that we are some kind of Victorian garden party, whose host hands out bound scripts and scores to his guests and conjures them to get on with it. He also sits periodically at the piano (he may even, for all I could tell, play it); reads the stage directions, which are among the juiciest parts of the text; ushers the other actors on and off; and generally fusses.

There is much merriment when things go intentionally wrong, and some embarrassment when they do it by mistake. This, in fact, is a concert performance that makes fun of concert performances.

It works very nicely, though it strikes me as strictly a one-off solution. If Stratford is to persevere with this format (which seems a not-bad idea) it cant go on apologizing for it. Even during the season, it tempts the curse of built-in obsolescence. Most concert- performances are put on for two or three nights. This one is sticking around for three months; and I can't help fearing that by the end of that period most of the cast will know their lines. The words, try as they may to resist them, will have forced their way into the performers' skulls. And what will the concept do then, poor thing?

Musically, the performance, under the baton of Berthold Carriere, is well up to snuff. Sullivans score, which I had never heard before, jog-trots along for its first half hour or so, but takes off halfway through the first act with a couple of sweetly yearning ballads, reinforced in the second by some top-notch comedy tunes. (One of them -- Then Go to Him and Say to Him -- I seem to have been humming for years without knowing it, like Molieres bourgeois gentleman speaking prose.)

Dramatically, the show leaves more to be desired. And at this point you will please excuse me while I attempt to summarize the plot.

The opera's Wilde-man is called Reginald Bunthorne. Personally, he has no use for poetry ("What's the use of yearning for Elysian fields when you know you cant get em and would only let 'em out on building leases if you had 'em?") but he thrives on adoration and, aestheticism being the going thing, he gets plenty of it.

All the high-born young ladies in the neighbourhood pine for him, in chorus, but he fancies Patience, the local milkmaid, who has never known love and is not impressed by what shes heard about it. She is persuaded that she is missing out, but somehow gets the idea that since love is unselfish, she can only love someone she doesnt like. (She's a proto-modern heroine, Patience is.) On this basis, she agrees to marry Bunthorne.

There then appears Archibald Gros-venor, a rival and apparently dishier poet, to whom all the girls immediately transfer their affections. Meanwhile, a troop of dragoons, all experienced ladykillers, hover around aghast at no longer being flavours of the month.

At the end, everything is worked out and everyone is paired off, except that nobody is Bunthorne's bride. He seems rather happy with this arrangement. Maybe Gilbert knew something.

There is a gulf, though, between the neat wit and elegant construction of the script when read, and the fruitily emphatic manner in which it gets deposited on stage. This is a constant problem with G&S, and it probably has much to do with trained singers not being always the niftiest dispensers of spoken humour (or even, sometimes, of sung humour).

The ornateness of Gilberts Victorian style is deceptive; he was out to attack pomposity with its own weapons, but too many productions seem to be on the side of the enemy. The traditional G&S performing style comes between the audience and the jokes, and its compounded in Patience by the affectation that the show is supposed to be satirizing.

The dragoons here are especially butterfingered. (And for them the concert format is a snare and a delusion; it's probably a mistake to embark on a G&S patter song if you're not sure of the words.) The lovesick maidens are rather better; Barbara Barsky is languorously statuesque as the ring-leading Lady Angela, and Barbara Fulton is Lady Ella, who doesnt say much but is delectable to look at. Theresa Tova, though, as the formidable Lady Jane (not pretty she admits cheerfully, "massive") seems keen to laugh at her character before the audience gets a chance to.

Three performers carry the show. Bruce Dow, a silently chortling master of ceremonies, goes on to play Bunthorne himself, whom he impales like a sulky butterfly; talking or singing, he is consistently and economically funny. George Masswohl, as his rival, is heavier and less precise, but knows fundamentally what hes about. (The two are dressed in identical bottle-green smoking- jackets; I don't know if this was actually de rigueur for fashionable versifiers of the pre-pre-Raphaelite era, but it certainly makes a helpful uniform on stage.) Christina Gordon in the title role is ideal: disconcertingly innocent, even more disconcertingly practical, all-over pert, and singing like a dream.

The production at least attempts to meet the piece on its own terms; it's far preferable to the camped-up, haphazardly updated G&S revivals with which Stratford used to tempt the tourists.

COPACABANA

Hummingbird Centre

His name was Barry

He sang some pop songs

And though they made him very rich

He would turn to friends and bitch

I want a challenge;

I want the theatre;

Theres a song that once I wrote

(You'll recall each pounding note)

It told a torrid tale

About a jealous male;

And if I stretched it to fill an evening

It could hardly fail.

It was Copa, Copacabana,

A tune in my floridest manner

Copa, Copacabana,

Keep the song, keep the title

(The title is vital).

They'll break the doors down;

Theyll fall in love.

It was Toronto;

The OKeefe Centre

At least that used to be its name

And though they've changed it; just the same

It houses op'ra

And sometimes dancin;

While to please the common man

They book road-shows when they can.

Its not an easy ride;

The house is yawning wide

Any piece that relied on nuance

Would get lost inside

Of the Humming-

Hummingbird Centre

(Its soul is maroon or magenta)

Of the Humming, Hummingbird Centre.

The Centre and Barry

Were fated to marry.

Hang the flags out.

They fell in love.

And it is, I'm afraid, a perfect match: a hollow show booked into an echoing hall.

Barry Manilow once recorded a CD of other people's theatre songs thats more palatable than the efforts of somewhat more pretentious singers with the same material, and he has to his credit at least one haunting tune in the great tradition, When October Goes.

So I would like to think he has a musical in him. But the new songs with which he pads out the story told by his famous old one are generic beyond the call of pastiche. They also sound consistently too late or too early for the mid-1940s period to which they are supposed to belong.

The lyrics (by Bruce Sussman and Jack Feldman) have a few neat rhyme schemes but no other ideas, and the book (by all three gentlemen) is brainless almost beyond belief -- its wisecracks, its narrative, and its attempts at period detail all in stiff competition for the booby prize.

We start with Stephen, a contemporary composer, trying to write the title song; we are privy to the eureka moment at which he realizes that "fashion" rhymes with passion (rather like the resident songwriter on the childrens TV show trying to figure out the right way to get to Sesame Street).

The rest of the song is strung across the evening as the show stretches out the lyric's three-minute storyline. We meet Lola ("she was a showgirl"), played by Darcie Roberts, who has come to town from the Midwest. After unsuccessfully auditioning for Broadway (Hello Mr. Lerner, hello Mr. Loewe), she gets luckier at the Copa, where she struts her stuff in front and on top of a white piano the size of a stretch limo, encouragingly accompanied by the lovestruck Tony (Franc D'Ambrosio), who seems anachronistically to be playing Dick Powell to her Ruby Keeler, though, for a hero, he has a remarkably sleazy singing voice.

In defiance of the rules of fantasy, Lola remains hayseed even after finding work in the Big City. Rico (he wore a diamond"), a racketeer club owner (Philip Hernandez), arrives and dances a bolero with her, at the end of which they are apparently in Havana, the hottest spot south of the Copa. It makes Guys and Dolls, in which the equivalent characters make the same trip by plane, look like ruthless realism. Meanwhile, "special guest star" Gavin MacLeod hangs around as a tough but kindly manager.

Stephen, the composer, at one point ambitiously describes the style of all this as being like an MGM movie; the stage is in fact an empty space populated by significant set pieces (staircases are favoured), occasional famous figures (Veronica Lake appears in a judiciously dim light) and characters in primary-coloured costumes that are sometimes striking.

Wayne Cilentos choreography is as ordinary as choreography gets. The cast perform with the heroic desperation customary in such circumstances; Beth McVey as the obligatory hard-boiled cigarette girl has my special condolences.

His name was Barry

And to his credit

Though his songs were once the rage

When he tried a show on stage

He wrote some new ones

Hes not like Abba

Who's idea of a score

Is some old hits, then some more

But I confess it's true

To get this news to you

I left left before the final gunshot

And just who shot who (grammer!)

I fled the Copa, Copacabana

If youve got the works, its the spanner

Copa, Copacabana

No Broadway baby is Barry

But maybe

Maybe next time

(Or hasn't someone written that song already)

2000-08-05-numbingly-terrible:
Memphis runs to Aug. 13 at the Robert Gill Theatre, 214 College St., Tuesday to Sunday at 8 p.m., with 2:30 p.m. matinees on Saturday and Sunday. Tickets are $20 except for Friday and Saturday evenings ($25) and the Sunday matinee (pwyc). Call (416) 978-7986.

Toward the end of Memphis there is a scene in which Martin Luther King, on the eve of his assassination, is badgered by a trio of reporters, asking a long series of hard and intrusive questions. (They have probably been stitched together from a whole series of such confrontations that happened over the years.) King loses his temper and shouts. I treasure this moment since it is the only point in the evening at which King, an inspirational leader and orator, evinces any passion, or even raises his voice. It's nice to know that the actor, Dwayne Morgan, has it in him. The rest of the time he performs in a apologetic mumble.

Subtitled The Death of Martin Luther King, Memphis is numbingly terrible. It switches back and forth between King's last day and events from his earlier life on the apparent assumption that they will automatically illuminate one another. The dramatist, John P. Moore, explicitly acknowledges three sources: the memoirs of King's wife, Coretta, and of two of King's closest associates, all of them characters in the play. His script suggests that he has put the language of these and other books on stage, without bothering to turn it into conversation. There are a couple of especially awkward telephone sequences. In one King fills in Coretta, long-distance, on the appalling working conditions of the striking black garbage workers whom he has come to Tennessee to champion. It's interesting stuff but a) she would have known some of it already and b) people don't talk, especially to loved ones, in crisp unmediated sentences filled with helpful facts and figures.

The dialogue is -- almost literally -- unspeakable. I say "almost" because really skilled actors can make sense out of anything that connects, however distantly, with human truth. The half-dozen performers here are, according to their biographies, experienced at many things but professional acting does not seem to be among them. Courtney Cunningham has some bright moments as an admiring Memphis minister, inviting King to a mouth-watering dinner that he will not live to attend, and Tamla Matthews brings intelligence, though not much technical backup, to the role of Georgia Powers who, after making history as a black female senator, found herself working as a stenographer for the civil-rights movement, and was also King's occasional mistress. Most of the time, though, the players don't stand a chance.

When King makes his first pass at the senator, she can't believe her ears. "Can we run that scene again?" she says; and, would you believe it, they do. This is dramatic straw-clutching -- throw in a theatrical device to prove this is a play -- and there's a lot of it. It culminates in the choral repetition of the casual words exchanged by King and his friends just before the fatal shot. Our awareness of the death is used throughout as a way of exacting attention for everything else. We hear at the beginning of King as a child being alternately terrorized and comforted by his family but these presumably traumatic experiences are never referred to again. The effectiveness or otherwise of non-violent protest is mentioned but never explored. King's womanizing is given a lot of space (and his wife's acceptance of it is given a little), perhaps to stress his humanity, perhaps because sex is easier to dramatize than politics, especially if you're doing vignettes. The hero's friend, Ralph Abernathy, asks him -- in a line that probably doesn't come from a book but that doesn't sound colloquial either -- if he ever met a black woman he couldn't charm. King responds that his first love was white, and that he almost married her, but was prevented by the prejudices of both families. That makes for a mildly effective scene, but again it serves no discernible dramatic purpose; it happens because, apparently, it happened. This is school-pageant stuff. Certainly you come out admiring and respecting King, but no more than you presumably did when you went in. Colin Taylor's self- designed production looks drab and feels drastically under- rehearsed.

SPINNING INTO BUTTER, YOU CANT TAKE IT WITH YOU, THE REAL THING

The American tradition of social drama -- well made and well meaning -- has been asleep in recent years, but it has never actually perished. A late example called Spinning Into Butter was recently given an enthusiastic welcome at the Goodman, the prestigious Chicago theatre David Mamet, among others, calls home. It has now been re-mounted in New York at the Mitzi E. Newhouse, the smaller of the two dramatic stages at the Lincoln Centre.

The elusive title (elusive meaning hard to remember, though not as hard as Mitzi E. Newhouse) derives from the nursery tale of Little Black Sambo. This isnt a story that surfaces much these days in polite society, but let me jog your memory: Little Black Sambo went for a walk in the forest, and was progressively stripped of his clothes by a succession of tigers, who then chased one another round a tree for the right of full possession. They ran so furiously they all melted away into butter. Little Black Sambo picked up his clothes and the butter, went home, spread the butter on a heap of pancakes, and wolfed them down, a conclusion that made me feel queasy when I was a child, and still does.

In Rebecca Gilman's play, a black student at a mostly WASP Vermont college receives a barrage of racial hate mail. Faculty and students go into various kinds of shock. When the truth emerges (it's predictable but had better not be revealed), one of the senior deans invokes the Sambo story to describe the unseen student who, he says, has been watching his seniors run themselves ragged and relishing the spectacle. That, of course, is just his interpretation and we arent encouraged to trust him. His reaction to the crisis has been to call a series of student meetings, where he can parade his own tolerance at -- we gather -- embarrassing length.

The college seems to be run by this man, three other deans, an absentee president and a security guard. The protagonist is Sarah Daniels, who is the dean of students (i.e., shes the one who has to talk to them). She is white, but previously worked at a black Chicago college, and seems to have been hired on that basis.

When the crisis strikes, Sarah reacts more directly and humanely than anyone else. But she has a guilty secret, and under pressure she reveals it: Sarah, despite having started her career with the best radical intentions, is a racist.

She makes this confession in a 20-minute monologue that is both well written and (by Hope Davis, a much-touted young actress who can be both tart and touching, and can gauge the distance between neurosis and dementia) and well delivered. In Chicago, Sarah found that her dislike of her more belligerent students outweighed her affection for the more agreeable ones. She also found herself cowering away from the scruffier black passengers on her commuter train.

This speech apparently shook the play's Chicago audience to its core. New York, not having the same local stake in the matter, seems to have taken it in stride.

It certainly gives rise to a lot of questions. The colleague who hears it (he also happens to be Sarah's ex-lover, a relationship that takes up either too much dramatic space or not enough) first reacts with stereotyped shock, then later admits hes quite careful about where he sits on a train as well.

He doesnt point out that Sarah would feel just as uncomfortable in the presence of threatening white travellers, or that no teacher is obliged to like all her students equally. We seem to be listening to a vastly inflated display of liberal guilt -- and one, by the way, that has little direct bearing on the main action. There is race in both, but that's not enough for dramatic coherence.

If I had to point out the author's moral for her, I would say Sarah should lighten up. She is the only person on stage, students included, who tries to treat people as people, rather than as issues. They all seem pretty buttery, even before they start spinning. (I except the security man, who seems to have all the compassion of the traditional working stiff, plus most of the answers. Frustratingly, he never lets on what they are.)

The storytelling holds attention, though, and on that basis one would once have prophesied a big-time transfer and a movie deal. The play is the Tea and Sympathy of its day. Broadway, for better or worse, now craves stronger stimulants.

Also obviously courting a commercial transfer is the latest production of the Roundabout Theater which, in 20 years of existence, has become the most successful producing organization off- Broadway. The Roundabouters mostly devote themselves, as off- Broadway always used to do, to smart revivals. (Cabaret is one of theirs.)

They now have a new home, the Selwyn (an old theatre on 42nd Street reconstituted, at great expense, to look like an old theatre on 42nd Street), which they have opened with The Man Who Came to Dinner, the 1939 comedy about a monumentally cantankerous celebrity writer, transparently modelled on Alexander Woollcott, the famous Round Table critic and wit -- though in his case I have always thought both those nouns to be complimentary to the point of sycophancy.

Moss Hart and George S. Kaufman, both Woollcott buddies, also wrote You Cant Take It with You, which the Shaw Festival staged so enjoyably last year. This play is that one in reverse: Instead of a Bohemian family invaded by Wall Street conservatives, we have a solidly prosperous Midwestern household exhaustively disrupted by the eponymous Sheridan Whiteside, a visiting exotic who came unwillingly to dine and stayed even more reluctantly, having broken his leg while saying goodbye.

The play belongs to an age when authors could happily write parts for 30 grown-up actors, and throw in half a dozen choirboys at the end of Act Two. All this abundance produces energy, as does the authors contagious delight in their material. The play is an in- joke preposterously expanded; but somehow, even if you don't get the references, you still get the point. (It's also, for all its apparent free-wheelingness, devilishly well constructed.) It, too, would be a natural for the Shaw, except I dont see how they would cast the lead.

Its a problem in New York, too. Nathan Lane seems to enjoy being wicked in his wheelchair, but he holds back too much. Perhaps in an attempt to inject variety, he soft-pedals some of the insults, but the point about Whiteside is that -- apart from a few moments of sentimentality dictated by the plot -- he is unrelentingly, exorbitantly rude. Even when paying a compliment, he's rude.

Jean Smart, playing a predatory actress, is similarly timid. She tiptoes around her character's monstrosity rather than stepping inside and taking possession.

Jerry Zaks production, though, has a good supply of fizz, and it takes full advantage of a couple of characters who are still cultural icons. One is called Beverly Carlton, but is transparently, and consummately, Noel Coward. Its madly gay. Another is an uncontrolled zany named Banjo, who has two off-stage brothers named Wacko and Sloppo. He is actually based on Harpo Marx, a real-life chum of Woollcott's, but since he talks, most actors play him as Groucho. Lewis J. Stadlen, an experienced Marxist fellow-traveller, plays him as both (adding a dash of Chico, I shouldn't wonder) and tops the mixture off with a heavy sauce of Jimmy Durante, who took the part in the film. Its madly wonderful.

In my very first column for the Post, I disparaged The Real Thing as "the Tom Stoppard play for people who dont like Tom Stoppard." I have now been conclusively contradicted. A revival that started in London last year has come to New York (the Barrymore Theater) and more than lives up to its title. Better than real, it is the best Thing in town.

What has changed ? David Leveaux's production, which originated in a studio space, is more scenically fluid and more economic than the original staging, and above all more intimate, in both the theatrical and the sexual sense. All these qualities have survived the transition to a larger house.

The play concerns a playwright who -- after writing glibly about love, jealousy and adultery -- has to discover what, in his second major relationship, he really feels about these things. His partner is an actress. Both their previous spouses are actors, whom we see in Scene One performing a scene from one of the hero's plays. Only in Scene Two do we realize that what we were watching was art, not life.

Stephen Dillane and Jennifer Ehle are the leads (both won Tonys, as did the production) and one believes in them, separately and together. Dillane is especially magnetic, a tousled compulsive thinker, from whom the authors epigrams and tirades flow as an expression of feeling, rather than as some kind of tortured display of cleverness, jokey appendages on an otherwise conventional play.

With the characters in focus, the plays structural and intellectual conceits no longer seem like minor Stoppard. In fact, they are dazzling. The Pirandellian comedy of the second scene is not only hilarious in itself, but offers a series of windows into the speakers' souls.

Toward the end, the talk threatens to outdistance the amount of relationship we have actually been shown, but the threat is averted. The play runs till Aug. 13. It's worth a trip or, if you already have one planned, worth a siege of the box office.
