2000-08-08-a-great-talent-a-modest-man-h:
Obituary of Sir Alec Guinness.

Earlier this year I wrote that the death of John Gielgud meant that, of the great generation of 20th-century British actors, only one now remained. That survivor was Sir Alec Guinness, who has died aged 86. Masters of timing, Gielgud and Guinness might have synchronized their final exits to coincide with the turn of the millennium.

Alec Guinness was known as the chameleon of the group, the character-man who never played anyone remotely resembling himself, and maybe never had a self to play. This is a myth. He had a very strong though quiet personality, and a spiritual dignity that, especially in his later years, imprinted itself on every performance he gave; the Star Wars people knew what they were doing when they cast him as Obi-Wan Kenobi.

Sometimes, indeed, the personal quality was excessive. Peter Sellers once invented a distinguished English actor specializing in mystical roles whom he christened Sir Eric Goodness; and when Sir Alec assumed an Indian accent to play Professor Godbole in David Leans film of A Passage to India (1984), he did seem to be stepping unwisely into Sellerss territory. (The compliment was often returned; Sellers, whose acting really did depend on impersonation, was the bizarro Alec Guinness.)

I once had to meet Sir Alec in the lobby of his London hotel (he lived in the country) and made some weak remark about how relieved I felt that I had actually recognized him. He smiled and said the legend of his anonymity had been much exaggerated. This was in the early 1980s when he was about to conquer a new medium, playing George Smiley in the television adaptation of John Le Carre's Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy. Over a sumptuously good meal (he is the only actor I have ever interviewed who has taken me to lunch, and he was the most courteous of hosts), the subject of his supposed self-effacement came up again. I asked about the Fool that he played to Laurence Olivier's Old Vic King Lear in 1946, a performance widely regarded as definitive, and one of his passports to wider stardom. He attributed part of his success to the fact that Olivier, who also directed, had mercilessly cut the part and the play. But he also said, "I was very good in that -- even I had to admit it. He could be self-deprecating about being self-deprecating.

Alex Guinness has a special place in Canadian theatre history, as having led the company at the first ever Stratford Festival in 1953. Not just that: He was the first actor ever to appear or to speak on the Festival stage. He played the title role in Richard III, a marathon he balanced with the supporting part of the King of France in Alls Well That Ends Well. By now he was not only a stage star but a movie star, perhaps the best-known in British cinema; not every actor in his position would have devoted a summer to leading largely untried actors, all unknown to him, in a tent, which is all the Festival theatre then was. He is remembered as having been an inspirational and remarkably untemperamental leading man; at the end he personally provided the money to have two promising young Canadian actors taken to London for further training. (One of them was Timothy Findley.)

Born in London on April 2, 1914, he was almost a classic example of the lonely child who becomes an actor. Officially unrelated to the brewery Guinnesses," he was in fact illegitimate. The name on his birth certificate was Alec Guinness de Cuffe. His mother was entered as Miss Agnes Cuffe; his fathers name, he said in his autobiography, was left "an intriguing, speculative blank.

His mother married when he was five, though the marriage only lasted three years. He didn't get good parts in school plays (you're not the acting type," he was told) but still managed to stop the show as a messenger in Macbeth. Thus encouraged, he took acting lessons in 1933 from the distinguished actress Martita Hunt (who told him "youll never make an actor) and then went to a real acting school run by the equally distinguished Fay Compton. He left there after a year, but he had been spotted in a school show by Gielgud, who gave him some much-needed money on which to stay alive, and then cast him in the eye-catching small role of Osric in Hamlet (1934).

The young Alec, like other future stars, spent much of the 1930s oscillating between the two great British theatrical leaders of the era: the intense Gielgud and the flamboyant Tyrone Guthrie, who was responsible years later for inviting him to Stratford. Guthrie ran the Old Vic, where he cast Guinness in the lead in a memorable and innovative production of Hamlet in modern dress.

Guinness, to judge from photographs, played the role frail and vulnerable, and was either promising or deeply impressive, depending on which historian you read. It didnt make him a star, though; he was still playing supporting roles (like the Fool, and the Dauphin in Saint Joan, whom Peter Ustinov described as one of those walking pear-drops he does so well") when he rejoined the Vic after the war, though he did get a crack at Richard II. By now, there was no doubt that he was a major actor waiting to happen.

His movie career did not get started until 1946. He had played Herbert Pocket in his own stage adaptation of Dickens's Great Expectations, and this led to him getting the role -- and giving a delightfully wistful performance -- in David Lean's film of the novel. It was perhaps the best Dickens picture ever made, rivalled only by Leans Oliver Twist the following year, with Guinness a superb Fagin. It was probably this performance, with its huge quantities of beard, that did most to create the legend of Guinnesss facelessness. Guinness-in-disguise was also a selling point of the 1949 comedy Kind Hearts and Coronets, in which he played eight sequentially murdered members of the same aristocratic family. (One has heard of serial killers; he was a serial victim.) Such was the wit, teeming but never overflowing, that Guinness poured into each characterization, and so great the glee the audience derived from it, that even an oil painting that bore his likeness seemed hilarious. But in fact it was the recognizability of the actor, guaranteeing the family likeness, that was the joke. The film, a masterpiece of tongue-in-cheek, was the finest of the Ealing comedies of quirky English gentility with which Guinness now became inextricably identified. Its only possible rival is The Ladykillers (1955), in which the boot was on the other foot; Guinness now played the leader of a gang of crooks trying fruitlessly to rub out one harmless old lady. (Sellers was a junior member of the gang.)

Alec Guinness became a Catholic convert in 1956 and his faith seemed in large measure to underpin his work. He became both a friend and partisan of that great Anglo-Catholic, T. S. Eliot; he was one of the finest speakers of Eliot's poetry and created the role of the mysteriously omniscient psychiatrist in Eliot's 1949 play The Cocktail Party. (Some 20 years later, he reprised this role under his own direction; both performance and production were riveting.)

He could be a great stage comedian, as when he played the lead in the Feydeau farce Hotel Paradiso (1956), but he increasingly projected an aloof, untouchable authority, which served him well as Prince Feisal in Lawrence of Arabia (1962), and in Terence Rattigans Ross (1960). He seemed after that to have turned into the most boring great actor in the world, and some of his other stage performances in the 1970s were excessively civilized.

He seemed to have largely given up on Shakespeare; his second Hamlet (1951) and his Macbeth (1967) were both severely criticized, though its more than possible they were searching, unromantic performances ahead of their time.

But he came back in glory in 1984, playing a magnificently dignified Shylock, a walking casebook in the corroding effects of persecution: a performance that lit up an otherwise dim production of The Merchant of Venice.

His most acclaimed film performance was probably his Oscar- winning Colonel Nicholson in The Bridge on the River Kwai (1957), another Lean picture, acclaimed at the time as a new pinnacle in British filmmaking, but much scorned since. His performance of a wartime British officer, fanatically devoted to his own interpretation of the military code, remains indelible, immaculately poised between tragedy and comedy.

Star Wars (1977) established him for a new generation (though his avowal that he would have been a forgotten man without it is typically overstated modesty), and having a percentage of the gross set him up for life. He refused, however, to appear in subsequent instalments (other than as a hologram). His George Smiley, seedily sensitive, similarly established him for TV viewers.

He was married, in 1938, to Merula Salaman, a former actress, whom he had met when they were animals together in Gielgud's production of Noah; their marriage lasted their lifetimes and they had a son, Matthew, who is also a talented actor. He was knighted in 1959.

Alec Guinness was not a figurehead to be mourned as Gielgud was but he will be equally missed and was, in a less spectacular fashion, equally loved. He seems to have been respected by everyone who worked with or encountered him.

THE SCHOOL FOR WIVES

Premier Dance Theatre, Toronto

Moliere's The School for Wives concerns a man who lives in mortal fear of being cuckolded. To avoid this terrible fate, he adopts a young girl and brings her up in total seclusion. He intends to marry her when she is of age, and assumes she will never betray him because she wont know how.

Laszlo Martons Soulpepper production is maybe not the most hilarious Moliere ever seen on a stage, but it goes unusually deep and it makes a gripping and rewarding evening.

The set, designed by Julia Tribe, takes the metaphor of imprisonment seriously. When the play begins, the jealous Arnolphe has brought his sheltered ward from the country to Paris, attended by a couple of blockish servants. The house in which he immures her looks at first glance like a cage: It's palisaded like an ancient public park, and as Arnolphe's obsessive jealousy grows he encloses it still further, personally inserting barricades between the spikes.

This is a dark production, but not a morbid one. It neither giggles nor gloats, and thats refreshing. Marton is a humane, grown- up director and in bringing him over from Hungary on a regular basis (this is his third Soulpepper production), the company is performing one of its greatest services.

Of course, a young man catches Agness eye, and of course they fall in love. The twist is that the lover is an acquaintance of Arnolphe's and, not knowing him to be his beloved's captor, confides in him every step of the way. The scenes between the two of them are a wonderful balance of forces: Arnolphe wounded but still feeling himself to be in control; the boy, Horace, acting like a dope but still carrying a biological guarantee of victory.

The play is better built than most Moliere and its confusions mount with steady logic. The knot is cut at the end by the usual revelations about mistaken identities and long-lost children. Its a true epiphany, but a cruel one -- bitter for Arnolphe, happy for everyone else. This production, rather remarkably, does justice to both sides.

Moliere wrote the part of Arnolphe for himself (as he wrote most of his star roles) and that of Agnes for Armande Bejart, whom he had married when he was 40 and she was 20. She was doubly his pupil, a member of his company and the daughter of his former mistress. (Its something of a Woody Allen scenario.) Many of Moliere's plays concern jealousy of one kind or another, but it's in this one and The Misanthrope (given an overly facetious production by Soulpepper two years ago) that art mirrors the real couples life most uncomfortably.

Forty is hardly over the hill, even in the 17th century, and part of the power of Joseph Zieglers Arnolphe lies in his being, on the face of it, a perfectly presentable suitor. He isn't a senile pantaloon (though there's a tradition of playing him that way) and he isnt a fool. His best friend pays tribute to his "good intellect." But he has undone himself: As both his friend and -- most devastatingly -- Agnes herself point out, by denying her worldly knowledge, he has left her without any defences against the first pretty face that comes along. Worse than that, by taking the girls love for granted, he has forfeited any chance of gaining it.

Moliere, we assume, was a natural clown. Ziegler, an excellent actor, is not. There are quite legitimate fits and double-takes written into the part that he doesn't even try to bring off. But he is sharp in the ones he does attempt, and he captures the deeper double-takes, of a man brought up against his own nature, and that's more important. His great confrontation with his too-carefully tended intended is very fine, with Liisa Repo-Martell perfectly capturing Agness funny simplicity and her amorous readiness and her deep sense of deprivation and hurt.

Most admirable, too, is Robert Persichini, who seems to have a droll, slow timing all his own. He plays Arnolphes confidant, whom I would expect to be played (not that I've spent years in thinking about it) as a city cynic, but who is here a wise and corpulent countryman, taking deception to be the way of the world and no reflection on the deceived. (Arnolphe's main problem is that he has a very fragile ego.)

Matthew Edison is a goofily agreable Horace, while Kristen Thomson (rather wasted) and Raoul Bhaneja are serviceable servants. A bemused Jim Warren and a twinkling William Webster satisfyingly round out the ensemble.

The production is as strong on story-telling as on theme and character, piecing out the action with some helpful silent interludes. (A couple of bits with dolls are heavy-handed.) The translation is one of Richard Wilbur's rhyming-couplet versions: not his best, and with some padding that sometimes leaves the actors gasping for air, but better than any other. Moliere in English took a great step forward when practitioners finally accepted -- I think it was sometime in the '60s -- that this is the form in which he wrote, and that we had better learn to deal with it.

2000-08-12-a-monotonous-musical-memoir:
River Road and Other Stories runs tonight and Wednesday to Saturday at 8 p.m. at the Canadian Stage Theatre, 26 Berkeley St. Tickets are $20 and can be ordered at (416) 368-3110.

The two most haunting songs in Sylvia Tysons one-person show are Womans World and Driftwood. More precisely, they are the two that I thought while I was hearing them would be the likeliest to make me require the services of Ghostbusters. Not coincidentally, they are the two songs that open the evening's first and second halves. My reactions had not yet been contaminated by a succession of other songs that sounded very much the same. Torpor, in other words, had yet to set in.

I came fresh to all this material, and that should make me either the best or worst audience in the world. Probably, it made me the worst. River Road and Other Stories is a quasi-autobiographical entertainment that depends heavily on the spectators' nostalgic affection for the performer. I am just about aware of Ian and Sylvia, the married folk-singing couple of which Tyson was formerly half, but thats as far as I go. If there is such a thing as active apathy, that is the feeling that folk and country -- the two modes in which the lady specializes -- arouse in me. Both forms can work theatrically, if dramatically juiced up, but here we get them neat. Even when Tysons words sounded like they might be interesting, the monotony of the music generally destroyed them for me before the song was over.

She herself comes before us as a pleasant, sensible, middle-aged lady with a nice singing voice. Her presentation, though, is stiff, stranded awkwardly between formality and its opposite. She sometimes picks up a guitar or one of two accordions, but most of her accompaniment is piped in, and that immediately has a deadening effect; visible interaction between singer and musicians can sometimes be a way of giving a club act the semblance of theatre. A face-mike snakes round her cheekbones, and since this is neither a pop concert nor a production of Rent, it looks weird: a sinister adornment for a raconteuse, which is what part of the time she sets out to be.

Her reminiscent script is carefully written and as carefully delivered, but her speaking voice obstinately refuses to fly. She sounds as if she's delivering memoirs into the void on some late- night radio arts show; she hasn't yet learned to make the live audience her co-conspirator.

Sometimes, in a gesture towards staging, she wanders over to a kitchen table at the side of the stage, sits down and tells us things her mother told her back in her small-town childhood. Later on, the same location serves as the setting for a routine about the horrors of being madeup for an early-morning television appearance. She sits there, suffering and grimacing, while we hear her own prerecorded voice playing the role of the makeup artist, cheerily patronizing her. This routine comes out of nowhere -- it corresponds to nothing else in the show -- and it is not especially funny. And her remark that TV is really just about commercials is not the revelation she seems to think it is.

A pattern begins to emerge. She will tell us about some old friend or acquaintance; about Maggie, say, who first taught her about sex -- not that Maggie knew all that much about it personally but, being Catholic, she had access to all those racy confessions. (This bit is quite funny.) She will then tell us that she wrote a song for or about the person in question, and will sing it.

That leaves the songs themselves, which, as Ive said, I can leave, though I appreciate that many people will take them. I noticed one recurring device; the repetition at the end of a song of a line from an earlier stanza, in lieu of a punchline. Theres one song about feeling awkward writing a song -- it's over too soon or it goes on too long" -- which sounds curiously (though I suspect unintentionally) like Monty Python. There's a persuasive monologue on the thesis that "love makes you stupid," followed by a corroborative song that I liked very much. I wish there had been more like it. There was no program available on the first night, so I can't tell you its title, but it confirmed that Tyson is observant, and knows how and when to rhyme.

As in the concurrent Stan Rogers show, the down-home title song is used as a teaser at the beginning and performed in full at the end. In her curtain speech, the performer thanked us for turning out to support Canadian music. A worthy cause, doubtless, but I'm not sure that customers who have paid (not me, of course) to be entertained should be addressed as if they were subscribers to a charity.

TARTUFFE

Festival Theatre, Stratford

STRATFORD - At the end of Friday's premiere of Tartuffe, Richard Monette, director of the Stratford Festival and of this production, paid tribute to Alec Guinness, the festivals first-ever leading man. Last week, fortuitously, was Ontario Moliere Week -- this Tartuffe following on the heels of Soulpeppers The School for Wives -- and the coincidence had me thinking what a waste it had been that Guinness, one of the premier comedians of the 20th century, never got to appear in anything by the most celebrated of comic playwrights. Think of what the master delineator of the beleaguered bourgeois might have made of the jealous Arnolphe in School; or of how our greatest actor of holy men, true and false, might have flowered as the arch-hypocrite Tartuffe.

None of which is to impugn the current performances by Joseph Ziegler and Brian Bedford. Bedford indeed, returning to a part that he played triumphantly at Stratford 17 years ago, renders Tartuffe as I like to think Guinness might have done: as a consummate religious poseur who may actually believe his own protestations. This makes him virtually impregnable. He is the lowest of confidence- tricksters, insinuating himself into the house of the wealthy Monsieur Orgon and proceeding to take over the whole family.

He stands by, volubly protesting his own unworthiness, while Orgon plans to marry his daughter to Tartuffe and to disinherit his only son in his favour. All the while he is plotting the seduction of his benefactor's wife. Tartuffe's first line, in Richard Wilburs translation, is a casual hang up my hair-shirt; Bedford -- sad- faced, scrubby-bearded and penitentially gowned -- never drops his guard for a moment. He takes a theological stance -- "heaven is not averse to compromise" -- even when proposing adultery. Since he is the first to confess that he is a sinful man, nobody can shame him by accusing him of it.

When his victim finally learns the truth, Tartuffe, enraged, takes the moral high ground. When definitively unmasked and consigned to prison, Bedford spits contemptuously at his persecutors and strolls impenitently off -- not an unmasked villain but a man unshakeably conscious of his own superiority. He will be out again soon and will find other dupes. Bedford plays with his customary dazzling economy; he is the only actor, in either of these two new productions, who consistently makes Wilburs rhyming couplets dance. He makes them sound like a very sensible, as well as a very attractive, way of carrying on a conversation.

For all that, something is missing now that was present the last time: sexual tension. I remember the seduction scene in John Hirsch's production as one of the most transfixing I have ever seen on the festival stage; Bedford and Domini Blythe gave it a degree of contact and intimacy that on that sweeping platform is very rare indeed. Each character seemed to be drawing out unsuspected depths in the other. In Monette's production, its high-grade situation comedy. Lucy Peacock, carrying her head as delectably high as that of her plumed namesake, plays the besieged Elmire with unruffled confidence; shes afraid that her husband, hidden beneath the table, may not emerge from his hiding place in time to rescue her, but she never has any doubts about herself.

The play's comic set pieces are done, on the whole, very well. Seana McKenna, in the best maid's part ever written (I read that somewhere and it seems to be true), has a great scene in which, bidden by an enraged Orgon to hold her tongue, she sits emitting great waves of infuriating silence; she gets more out of this than any actress I have seen.

Earlier she has had a famous duet with her master -- one in which he returns home and is told whats happened in the family in his absence. Informed that his wife has been seriously ill, Orgon responds with just two reiterated phrases. One is Ah! And Tartuffe?; the other, when he is reassured that his protege has been sitting up and wolfing down all available nourishment, is "poor fellow!"

James Blendick hits the perfect bass notes for this repeated tune -- hes something of a barrel-Orgon -- and in general does as much for the role as bemused stolidity can.

This, however, may not be enough. Orgon's part is bigger than Tartuffe's (Moliere played it himself, which should be a clue) and it is he who goes through the familiar Moliere hoops: He is the fool whose folly is anatomized and flayed, the monomaniac who refuses all good advice. (Most of the latter comes from his invariably sensible brother-in-law -- Keith Diniciol does an amusing job here of being both intelligent and insufferable) Blendick conscientiously huffs, but by the last act, when Orgon is undeceived and furious, he is all out of puff; the scene in which a bailiff arrives to throw him out of his own house is here very limp all round. Even when this Orgon is in the grip of his obsession, his dependency is strangely untroubling. The play doesnt require the insistent darkness with which Lazslo Marton has paradoxically illuminated The School for Wives -- Tartuffe is a stronger play to begin with -- but it could be more painful; and if it were, it would be funnier.

The costumes here seem a hundred years later than the play, leaving you wondering just which French king is being celebrated in the denouement, when he emerges as rex ex machina. (Molieres Louis XIV reigned long but not that long; and neither of his successors had his sunny reputation.) The set, on the other hand, is timeless; carried over from the earlier production, it's the work of Tanya Moiseiwitsch, doyenne of designers, creator of this stage, and present in person to receive another first-night tribute and a magnificently merited standing ovation.

2000-08-16-an-iambic-pentameter-you-can-:
Tonight Soulpepper open their production of Twelfth Night: a crucial production since it represents the company's first attempt at Shakespeare. (Even more will be riding on it than was first envisaged, since the intended accompanying production of Romeo and Juliet has sadly been cancelled because Anthony McLean, who plays Romeo, was injured in a car accident.) Unless the director has radically altered the text, which I doubt, this Twelfth Night will contain a great many songs, most of them sung by John Neville in the role of Feste. Neville, in addition to his distinguished classical career, has made several forays into musicals; he didnt have to change his style much. Twelfth Night itself could well be a musical.

In fact, it has been. One of the first and most likeable rock musicals, in the 60s, was a sliced and updated Twelfth Night called Your Own Thing, that being a modern translation of the Shakespearean subtitle, What You Will. There have been others, less successful, including one by the composer of The Pajama Game. It was called Music Is, as a sort of answer to the question implied in the play's famous first line: If music be the food of love, play on." You might say that Shakespeare was asking for it. And he got it, again, a few years ago, with a Twelfth Night musical that was actually called Play On: a show that used existing Duke Ellington songs that often seemed to have been forced into the action, but once or twice proved startlingly apposite.

Among Shakespeare's mature comedies, Twelfth Night is the only one to have attracted this kind of attention. I dont know of any modern musicals based on Much Ado About Nothing or As You Like It, and those based on A Midsummer Nights Dream or The Merchant of Venice have been calamitous. The later, so-called "bitter comedies - - All's Well That Ends Well, Troilus, Cressida, and Measure for Measure -- seem to have escaped altogether; though the low-life scenes of Measure would seem to offer irresistible temptation, while the sexual and political disillusion of Troilus might offer a perfect challenge to Stephen Sondheim. The final, redemptive comedies have also been left alone, unless you count Return to the Forbidden Planet, a stage-spoof of a movie-spoof that has distant ties to The Tempest. Scholars used to refer to this last quartet as the romances" but they are not what we, conditioned by Hollywood, usually think of as romantic.

But, right at the beginning of Shakespeare's career, there are four comedies that musical-makers have found irresistible, perhaps because the plays themselves are thought to be apprentice-work, ripe for irreverent improvement. (I know of two Shakespeare musicals that got that way because the directors were appalled at the prospect of doing the plays straight.) The best-known of all Shakespeare musicals, currently enjoying a hit revival in New York, is Kiss Me Kate, based on The Taming of the Shrew, a play that inspired Romancin the One I Love, which had a deservedly brief run in Toronto this year. The second-best is The Boys from Syracuse, whose source, The Comedy of Errors, has inspired at least three subsequent musicals. (One of them, Oh Brother, has a company number that appropriately begins "We love an old story ...) A musical of The Two Gentlemen of Verona was a Tony winner in 1970. This year Kenneth Branagh filmed Loves Labour's Lost as a musical, with a score mainly drawn from Astaire-Rogers movies of the '30s. Eagerly awaited, it sank almost without trace, and in truth it doesnt work. But it has charm; Branagh was on to something.

What exactly?

Shakespearean comedy, and classic American musical comedy, are the two great celebrations of romantic love in the English language. Each is more like the other than either is like anything else, even within their own time. We tend to assume that Shakespeares comedies are like other Elizabethan comedies, only better. In fact, they're unique. Most of his contemporaries wrote earthy, realistic, satiric farces that reeked of their own contemporary London. Shakespeare's comedies seem, by contrast, to be set in some kind of fairyland, usually Italian (Even 400 years ago Shakespeare was probably being attacked by trendy intellectuals for irrelevance. Ben Jonson didnt have the word, but he had the concept). And yet they keep striking us as real, the more acutely because their surfaces are so artificial. They are courtship-plays, leading toward marriage, which is one of the commonest human experiences. Most comedies of course, end with some of the characters paired off but that isnt usually the point of the play. In Shakespeare it is: some plays -- As You Like It, Dream, Much Ado -- are outright wedding celebrations. Love's Labour's ends with marriage postponed, and the maverick nature of this conclusion is explicitly outlined. The Shrew, a really radical piece, marries off its central couple halfway through the play -- a unique occurrence, I think -- and then gets them to work out their relationship.

All this may seem unacceptably idyllic but along the way, doubts get raised. Were dealing with an emotion -- romantic love -- that is evanescent but on which people base their lives. As You Like It, which doesnt have much of a plot (so probably wouldn't make much of a musical), is practically a fantasia on these themes. And so are many musicals, especially the pre-war ones, of which the Astaire- Rogers films are the purest distillation. They do have plots, farcical ones, but their feelings come out in the dances -- which stand in for sex -- and in the songs, which are, like Shakespearean comedy, bittersweet. They rejoice in the moment --and they preserve it for us, the audience -- but they recognize that it is only a moment. Branagh's Loves Labours is dogged by the director-star's apparent compulsion to play out his own Astaire fantasy; when he and his buddies sing I Won't Dance, you cant help remarking that nobody has asked them to. But there are two uses of Astaire songs that work perfectly. Geraldine McEwan and her fellow-comics pass around The Way You Look Tonight with a perfectly-judged sense of their own absurdity that yet leaves the songs magic untouched. (It happens to be my personal favourite, and it must mean a lot to Branagh too; he also used it in Peter's Friends.) At the end, as the men resign themselves to their long-distance engagements, Branagh sings They Can't Take That Away From Me; he is hardly the greatest singer but it seems the perfect musical expression of what his character -- and Shakespeares --is feeling.

I suspect that he was influenced by a recent Royal Shakespeare Company production of Two Gentlemen that wasnt a musical, but that interspersed the scenes with Cole Porter and Irving Berlin songs, performed as commentary. Apparently this worked very well; the songs fitted the mood, even the action, but weren't required to fit the characters. This year's open-air production of Much Ado, set in the 1940s, managed at one point to interpolate Rodgers and Harts My Romance. It fitted; in fact it was magic. (Much Ado, with its sparring hero and heroine, foredoomed to marry, is the American musical incarnate: prototypical Fred-and-Ginger.) When Porter wrote his score for Kiss Me Kate, he honoured his predecessor by turning scraps of lyric in the original into full-blown numbers. He was taking the advice that he places in the mouths of the shows two gangsters: Brush up your Shakespeare, start quoting him now." The idea of play-within-a-play is implicit in all musicals and in most Shakespeare. In the Shrew, it's an introductory framework; in Kate, it's the whole action. The current Broadway production has its weaknesses, but its very good at bringing out the parallels between the actor-protagonists on-and-off-stage lives. In that sense it's more Shakespearean than Shakespeare, as it is in tilting the action toward romance. Alan Jay Lerner did the same when he turned Shaw's Pygmalion into My Fair Lady. When he stopped being Shavian, he became Shakespearean. "Falling in love with love, wrote Lorenz Hart in The Boys from Syracuse, is falling for make-believe." Thats a very Shakespearean sentiment, though perhaps more suited to the more pensive Twelfth Night than to The Comedy of Errors which its supposed to be musicalizing. (But then, both plays are about twins.) The character who sings it is already married. But if she wasn't, she'd go ahead and get hitched anyway. They all do it. (Or Cosi Fan Tutte, as they say in another musical.)

Twelfth Night runs to Oct. 7 at the du Maurier Theatre Centre. Tickets are $25 to $46 and can be ordered by calling the box office at (416) 973-4000.

Soulpepper's Twelfth Night is a double first. Its their first attempt at Shakespeare, and -- since one doesnt want to see a prized classical troupe falling at the crucial fence -- it's a pleasure to report that the production is both lively and lived-in.

It's also the first show to feature the Soulpepper Young Company, a group of eight twentysomethings attached to, and partially trained by, the main body. They havent been left entirely to their own devices; the idea here is that the young ones play the young ones -- which in Twelfth Night means the romantic leads -- and also do the walk-ons, while their elders handle the character parts -- which in this play means the comics. One cant help feeling that the grown- ups get the better deal. The play was to have been paired with Romeo and Juliet, a youth-opportunity project if ever there was one, but that production got cancelled following an accident to Romeo. This misfortune does leave Twelfth Night looking, stylistically and logistically, somewhat orphaned. Or rather -- like its heroine Viola after the shipwreck scene so graphically staged at the beginning -- it lacks a twin.

You may be surprised to learn that Twelfth Night has a shipwreck scene. As written, it doesn't; the play begins with the vessel already sunk and the survivors arrived on shore. Undeterred, Albert Schultz, the director, has thrown in the entire opening scene of The Tempest. I must say this strikes me as excessive; the lines introduce us to characters we are never going to meet again, and if you really want to start things off with a storm, then a couple of rattles of the thunder-sheet and a few brisk bolts of lightning would probably do the job as well. The skipper, who sits serenely at the side of the stage while his boat goes down with all hands, is doubled with Feste, the jester, the presiding spirit of Twelfth Night itself; and there seems to be an idea that the whole thing is his dream.

The show doesn't have much of a set, but there is rigging that can seem suggestively nautical, and a curtain that in certain lights is very much like a sail. Periodically throughout the evening we hear the sound of the sea.

Before delivering the plays official first lines (which we do eventually get to) Duke Orsino is discovered peering fixedly through a telescope, and a later scene finds him apparently taking a dip in the ocean -- or, since the play is set in Illyria, the Adriatic.

The production as a whole shares his marine fixation but, though there is plenty of warrant for it in the text, the staging cannot make it stick. The trouble with concepts is that you need external effects to reinforce them; and this production, obviously done on a shoestring, looks ostentatiously economical. Furniture consists of a few tables and rostra, endlessly shuffled about. (Romeo was presumably to be done the same way, on the justified assumption that one production makes a convention, two make a style.) The evocativeness of this arrangement depends largely on the acting going on inside it. The below-stairs scenes leave little to be desired. When it comes to the grand reconciliation at the end, all concerned bust a gut to achieve epiphany, but it eludes them.

Concepts, to put it mildly, are not everything. This is still a good production, full of inventive and sometimes hilarious detail, and shrewdly alert to the dynamics between characters, though necessarily uneven in realizing them. There are actually three levels of experience in the cast. There are the youngers, the regulars and John Neville, who came to Canada from Britain some 30 years ago and was a classical doyen even then. He now perches with engaging ease at the top of the pyramid, playing Feste, whom he projects as an old Cockney music-hall comedian with a capacious hat and a sense of professional and personal disillusion that has long since gone through bitterness and come out the other side. He bristles, discreetly but noticeably, when anyone patronizes him, and enjoys affecting a Welsh accent to impersonate a parson. He also, of course, plays the Sea Captain: a one-scene role to which has probably never been afforded such weight in the preceding 400 years.

If I may wax nostalgic over a slightly shorter period: Neville was in the first Twelfth Night I ever saw, in London, playing a delicate Sir Andrew Aguecheek that I have never seen equalled. I havent, though, seen anyone get closer than Steven Sutcliffe, whose Andrew is an enchanting gull, infinitely suggestible, easily deflated, and prone to foredoomed bouts of foot-stamping assertiveness. The relationship between him and Randy Hughson's alcoholically exploitative Toby Belch is the best thing in the evening, and it is further enhanced by Maria Vacratsis's scheming Maria, superbly self-assured. The deluded Malvolio is Oliver Dennis, who manages a fine and very funny balance between the pompous and the pitiable: a Soulpepper regular who has never before had a part so good or played one so well. Michael Hanrahan, himself a good Malvolio two years ago, is now a first-rate Antonio.

The best of the showcased juniors is Kristin Booths Olivia, vivaciously clutching at any excuse to escape from her self-imposed mourning; you can see it, even before she falls in love, in the self- conscious giggle she emits from behind her veil when the clown makes one of his better jokes. Richard Clarkin gets Orsinos love-struck narcissism full-strength, but he doesn't have the authority demanded even of Shakespeare's most dubious dukes, and he pushes his way heavily through the verse. So, much of the time, does Patricia Fagan whose Viola suggests interesting ideas that are still at the planning stage. She does, though, have an enchanting moment when, disguised as a man, shes manoeuvred into a duel with the equally terrified Andrew: shes stiff as a board, he's wobbly as jelly. Part of the greatness of the play is the fearlessly fluid manner in which its worlds overlap and intersect; one of the best things about Schultz's staging is its constant awareness of this. This is his directorial debut for the company he founded and heads, which makes it, to amend my opening, a triple first.

The Matchmaker in repertoire till November 11 Six Characters in Search of an Author till September 23. Box office: 1-800-511-SHAW

THE MATCHMAKER; SIX CHARACTERS IN SEARCH OF AN AUTHOR

Shaw Festival, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

The Shaw Festival rounds off its repertoire with two plays obsessed by other plays. For Thornton Wilder, writing The Matchmaker, the existence of a long line of theatrical predecessors was a stimulant and a delight. For Luigi Pirandello, at work on Six Characters in Search of an Author, the whole idea of drama and its physical representation on a stage, was a stimulant and a torment.

The Matchmaker's central scene takes place in a moderately fancy restaurant, and the play itself might punningly be described as exceptionally richly-sourced. Wilder wrote it in 1954, basing it on an earlier comedy of his own, The Merchant of Yonkers. This in turn was an Americanization of a 19th-century Viennese piece by Johann Nestroy, Einen Jux will es sich Machen, which means, sort of, He the Town Red Will Be Painting.

Nestroy wrote in an urban patois, supposedly impenetrable even to other Austrians. He pinched his basic idea from a brief English farce by one John Oxenford, titled A Day Well Spent. Thats as far back as its possible to spool, though it's a safe bet Oxenford, too, had his sources, if only in folklore. Fast-forward, though, and we find The Matchmaker itself turned into a musical: a little thing called Hello Dolly! whose success has turned the play -- any of the plays -- into an endangered species. (I spent several weeks in the 1960s convinced that the song Matchmaker, Matchmaker must logically belong to this show, and was much dashed to find that it comes from Fiddler on the Roof.)

Even that's not all: 20 years ago, Tom Stoppard, ignorant of Wilders version, made his own, exceptionally hilarious, adaptation from Nestroy and called it On the Razzle. A Day Well Spent has proved to be A Play Well Spent, even if its original author has never been in a position to collect royalties.

The notion that has proved so attractive is the eternal one of the country mouse on the loose in the city. Or the industrious apprentice who gets tired of being industrious, and grants himself just one day in London, or Vienna, or in this case, New York. In The Matchmaker, as in all its companion pieces, there are two of these lads; they live, this time around, in the 1880s and are called Cornelius Hackl and Barnaby Tucker. They slave for a tight-fisted hay and feed magnate named Horace Vandergelder, of Yonkers, N.Y. The play retains the lineaments of farce. So naturally, when the pair head for the bright lights, almost the first person they run into is their employer, who thinks theyre home, minding the store. They spend much of the play trying to elude him. Cornelius spends another important part of it falling in love with a charming widowed milliner named Mrs. Molloy. Mr. Vandergelder also has a niece, who may or not be eloping with a young artist of whom her uncle, it goes without saying, disapproves.

Wilder added one important element to those he inherited, and it's emblazoned in his title.

Vandergelder's wife died years ago, and he is now looking for a replacement.

So, to help him search, he calls in Dolly: Mrs. Dolly Gallagher Levi, who is poor and bossy and multi-talented and herself bereft of a spouse. (Of The Matchmakers four central characters, three start the play widowed, which may be a record.) Of course Dolly, slowly and artfully, manoeuvres Horace into marrying her. The play proceeds on the assumption that Mrs. Levi is controlling the entire action, but it never quite dramatizes this. So a lot depends on the actress taking us in. The Mrs. Levi of the play is not quite the Dolly of the musical, and its nice to see the character back where she belongs. Which is to say, scrabbling for a living rather than descending a staircase in a red dress, with waiters falling inexplicably prostrate before her. This Dolly is philosophic and philanthropic, but even unmusicalized she is a force of nature.

Goldie Semple does the reflective moments (Wilder's specialty) very well, but the active parts find her anxiously characterizing -- in an Irish accent, that seems to absorb much of her energy -- rather than simply being. Intended to be irresistible she is, at most, sly.

Michael Ball, as her prey, does an initially heroic job of being tyrannical, but soon relaxes into his accustomed mode, gruff-but- likeable. Vandergelder may have a soft underbelly (another Wilder specialty) but it shouldn't protrude. Both performances have their pleasures, but I felt at ease with neither of them. And I suspect that the lady, at least, shared my discomfort. The central battle never gets fought.

So the production has to fall back on charm, which the play already lays on pretty thick. Wilder was an omnivorous and affectionate student of old theatrical forms, and part of what he loved was their artifice, unashamed and unself-consious His own adaptation is equally unashamed, but it is very self-conscious, and he delights in having his characters step out of the frame to favour us with little homilies. ("There," you hear the author trimphantly chuckling, goes the fourth wall.)

These speeches are often surprisingly sensible and are generally witty (as is much of the dialogue) but there has to be some tough love in the background if the general benevolence is not to seem cloying. And its not the plays fault, but many of the lines now sound like cues for song. This may testify to the inherent musicality of Wilder's prose, but it is a problem. "Put on your Sunday clothes," says Cornelius to Barnaby. We'll be wearing ribbons down our back, says Mrs Molloy, predicting next seasonsfashion. "Hello, Dolly," says -- well, nobody says it, but you can sense that theyre all thinking it. The awareness hangs especially heavy during the scene breaks: Actors perform little character-dances across the stage while the sets are changed, and at one point the front of a train reverses itself and turns neatly into a clothes-closet.

Christopher Newton stages this kind of thing better than most directors, but he is not at his most inspired. And though William Schmuck's costumes, and his Yonkers store setting, are treats, his Harmonia Gardens restaurant is disappointingly table d'hote.

The play and production are both at their best where the story is at its most Nestroyan (unless the word is Nestructive), which is to say with the young or youngish characters. Corinne Koslo, who was superbly stern in The Apple Cart, is now wonderfully roguish as the melting Mrs. Molloy. Dylan Trowbridge, another recurringly impressive actor, is equally enchanting as the bashful Barnaby, and Kevin Bundy does fine as the maturer scamp, Cornelius. (Thirty- three, actually, and never been kissed: His is the desperation that every farce requires.)

Good minor work is done by Craig Erickson as a surprisingly forceful artist and Fiona Byrne as his tear-gushing fountain of a beloved; by George Dawson as a shady manservant who matches the matchmaker for versatility of employment; by Lisa Norton as an assistant milliner; and by Peter Millard, one of the Shaw ensembles cornerstone actors, exemplifying its overall strength by playing the minimal role of a barber.

The final act is presided over by an elderly aunt who was jilted in her youth, an experience that has turned her into a sort of Miss. Havisham in reverse, dispatching young people to wedded bliss, whether they want to go or not. Patricia Hamilton gives her authority, but not the lachrymose zaniness for which she entreats.

Pirandellos Six Characters in Search of an Author begins by showing us a company of actors rehearsing, with signal lack of enthusiasm, another play by the same dramatist. Suddenly, there materialize among them a sepulchral, haunted sextet claiming to be figures from an unfinished play.

So they are in limbo and, after the fashion of theatrical ghosts, they seek revenge, not this time on the man who killed them, but on the man who gave them life but refused its completion. They want the actors to accord them this closure by performing their play.

There are problems here. First, there is no script. Second, when the actors do have a go, their efforts inevitably strike the characters as agonizingly unreal. Third, the characters squabble among themselves as to whose story this really is and how it should be interpreted, though they seem agreed on the basic facts, as follows: The Father and the Mother have a Son. Years ago, the Father encouraged the Mother to take a lover, with whom she subsequently left town. The results of this union were the Stepdaughter, the Boy, and the Little Girl. The lover died, leaving his family destitute, and the Stepdaughter went to work in a brothel, where one of her clients turned out to be the Father. The Mother burst in, just in time, and the Father took the whole clan back to live -- in misery, recrimination, and ultimate tragedy -- with him and the Son.

This is a lot of information to get across, which may explain why the characters' author gave up on them. Pirandello himself, a notorious sluggard at exposition, is here able to solve the problem by having the characters simply relate it to the actors. It still takes some following.

Various overlapping things, about life and about the theatre, are being said. One is that fictitious characters have a special and more intense form of life, being forever frozen in the moment of time that consitutes their story: Keats said it earlier in Ode to a Grecian Urn, and Shakespeare in Shall I compare thee to a summer's day, and Dorothy Fields was to say it again in The Way You Look Tonight.

Another is that a real person can be similarly hung on one shameful moment in his life -- as happened to the almost-incestuous Father -- and that being defined like this is a kind of Hell.

A third is that a playwright never gets the performance he wants, since actors and directors have their own ideas and personalities, and that the characters, if they could see the show themselves, would share their creators pain. (Living subjects of TV and movie biographies presumably do.)

A fourth is that every one of us goes through life as the hero of his or her own melodrama, impatient of anyone elses interpretation.

Yet another is that characters get away from their writers, even from those who persevere to the final curtain. None of this is news, and Pirandello often seems the foremost pactitioner of what Basil Fawlty would recognize as the Sybilline School of Dramatic Revelation. ("We should put you on Mastermind, Sybil. Sybil Fawlty from Torquay: special subject, the Bleedin' Obvious.")

On the other hand, it's all true, and Pirandello found the ideal crucible for it, by confronting working professional players with a family drama thats as extreme and believable as the tabloids. Just occasionally, a staging comes along that releases the agony and the dynamism beneath the mannerisms and the long-windedness. Tadeusz Bardeckis is one of those rare productions: a superb crown on a good Shaw season

It has its oddities. The play was written in 1922; the production updates it, reasonably enough, to now and -- presumably -- here. Barry MacGregor gives us and himself a very good time as a British director presiding over a North American troupe -- at, as it might be, the Shaw Festival. (Though one may doubt the Shaw's Chris Newton is the jaded dictator this man seems to be.)

The actors -- with Ben Carlson an earnest, floral-shirted leading man and Jillian Cook a super-cool stage-manager -- do a terrific job of playing themselves or people they know, though it remains true that nothing on stage seems quite as artificial as actors acting actors acting. (I'm not sure whether this proves Pirandellos point or contradicts it.) The characters remain in their original period and locale, and its odd that the actors -- who think them interesting lunatics -- never comment on how funny they're dressed or ask how they got here from Italy. Nor am I clear how it is that, when the Stepdaughter breaks into a song from the ancient musical Chu Chin Chow, the entire company is able to join in and turn it into a first-rate production number. (The show was in their recent repertoire? Now, there's a coincidence.)

Domenico Pietropaolos translation has punched up the periphery of the play. He might have been similarly aggressive with its centre.

Not that Im complaining much. Bradecki's choreography, with or without music, is magnificent. The production is full of bold, casual, heart-stopping groupings. The actors, occupying the front row of the auditorium to watch the characters, seem to blend into us, the audience, which is beautifully unsettling. The use of the silent, doomed, perfectly played Little Girl (Zoe Roycroft) is downright inspired: She carries a pool of unease around with her. The Boy (Devon Tulloch), more actively troubled, is similarly silent and similarly magnetic. Joel Hechter is fine as the sullen Son who wants no part of the others, on or off stage, and as the Mother, Sharry Flett is a bodeful presence, though rather upscale for the illiterate woman she's supposed to represent.

The performers of the two principal Characters surpass themselves. Norman Browning is superbly pained and contained as the guilt-ridden philosophizing Father who, every time he excuses himself, accuses himself. Kelli Fox hits barely a false note as the sulphurously vengeful Stepdaughter: The only unembarrassing account of this role I have ever seen.

"Reality! Illusion! Who cares?" snaps the enraged Director, or words to that effect. Whichever it is, the characters apparently crude story ends up moving us -- which may be Pirandellos special joke. He thought up a drama too sensational to be taken seriously, and found a way of putting it over. It's Six Characters and an Author in Search of an Audience, and finding one. The title, actually, is a wonderful come-on. Children hearing it are attracted by the idea, though they would probably be baffled by its realization.

The play has become Pirandello's flagship. We hardly see any of his 42 others, though enthusiasts claim many of them are masterpieces. They're probably lying, but one would like to find out, especially if Bradecki were directing.

I would like, for a start, to cross Right You Are (If You Think So) off my list.

LITTLE SHOP OF HORRORS

Top of the Square

It's not much of a contest, but (bop-she-bop) Little Shop of Horrors is the best rock musical ever perpetrated. Based on a grade- B, or grade-Z, science-fiction movie directed by Roger Corman in a couple of weeks somewhere near the start of his career, it represents the triumphant mating of two species of junk. Howard Ashman wrote the book and lyrics, and Alan Menken the music, back in 1982, when they were young things looking for a break. They subsequently got one from the Disney organization, which swept them off to Hollywood; but nothing they wrote there, not even Beauty and the Beast, compares for wit and invention with this, their one successful stage-show. Ashman died tragically young; Menken teamed up with other lyricists -- Tim Rice, for example -- and progressed from mock-schlock to real schlock, which is not progress.

Little Shop of Horrors is set in New York: in a flower shop on a Skid Row sort of street, called Skid Row. This is no kind of address at which to run a floral business, which may explain why there isnt any: not at least until the store clerk Seymour brings in a strange- looking little green plant. At first resistant to its guardians tender ministrations ("I've given you sunshine/I've given you dirt/ Ive given you plant-food/Youve given me hurt!") the plant perks up remarkably when Seymour accidentally cuts his finger. Having once tasted blood, it demands more, and grows on this diet into a strange- looking big green plant, with insatiate jaws. It makes Seymour famous and the store prosperous; so prosperous that the owner, Mr. Mushnik, who took Seymour in as an orphan and has been exploiting him ever since, now adopts him rather than risk losing him. Seymour has a fervent crush on Audrey, his pneumatic co-worker, and he names the plant Audrey II in her honour.

For its musical inspiration, the show reaches back to the Brill Building sounds of the late '50s and early '60s. The opening number is called Downtown, but has nothing to do with Petula Clark; rather, it is a scene-setting reversal of Uptown, the 1962 song popularized by the Crystals. (Downtown, where the folks are broke/Downtown, where your lifes a joke.) It enables Seymour, the complete nebbish, to sing of his existential angst ("I keep asking God what Im for/And he says 'Gee, I'm not sure. ") The show comes with its own girl-group, one of whom is indeed called Crystal; the others are named Ronette and Chiffon. They sing narrative links while aggressively gyrating their bosoms, and they close the proceedings with a terrifying recitative: Eventually the plant achieved its purpose, which was to eat Cleveland.

Most rock musicals are intentionally solemn and unintentionally ludicrous, since the level of noise and hysteria onstage is invariably in excess of whatever is supposed to be happening in the story. Apart from The Rocky Horror Show, Little Shop is the only show I know to capitalize on this; it goes over the top with its tongue in its cheek. (Besides its subject, which is world- domination by omnivorous green things, surely justifies any amount of overwrought emotionalism.)

Audrey II finds a voice, a raucously powerful one, and uses it to sing "Feed me!" and other stomach-felt lyrics to the same effect. Forced to do its bidding, Seymour decides to eliminate Audrey Is singularly unsavoury boyfriend, whose career path was set when his mother noticed his penchant for torturing helpless animals: She said, son, be a de-entist, and he did. ("He's a dentist" echo the girls, and he'll never, never be any good.) "I know Seymours the greatest," confides Audrey, her affections torn, but Im dating a semi-sadist. She's kidding; there's nothing semi about him. Freed from his domination, not to mention the attendant medical bills, Audrey gratefully bestows her love on Seymour, who cant believe his luck. But its bootless: Things Have Gone Too Far.

Seen in the context of other musicals, the show, combining the attractions of cannibalism and retail trade, is a cross between She Loves Me and Sweeney Todd, with -- for those who like their cultural references cultural -- a strong whiff of Faust.

The current production is the inaugural venture of a new dinner theatre situated above the Hard Rock Cafe at Yonge and Dundas. The space has housed other eating-and-acting enterprises in the past, but last Thursday neither side of the operation had its act together. Both were especially short on speed of delivery; when Seymour yelled at the importunate Audrey II "don't expect dessert" he seemed to be speaking for the management.

The program is unusually quiet about the actors' previous experience, and I sometimes wondered whether they had any. Presumably they are professional, but they seem like amateurs. The crude distinction, which you take for granted until youre forcibly exposed to it, is one of pace. Professional actors, even bad ones, know how to pick up cues; amateurs dont, not with any consistency, and even the best tend to exist as islands on the stage.

The lack of give-and-take can be numbing, as it is here. The worst performance here is lamentably underdone, the next worst appallingly overdone. The best is given offstage, by Jamie Hofman as the soul-singing voice of Audrey II. (Am I allowed to say that when he came on stage for his curtain call I was surprised to find that he was white and looked harmless?) Michael Munrow's Seymour and Elizabeth Jones' Audrey I are somewhere in the middle, conscientious and well-sung -- she especially -- but short on cartooniness; if we start taking these characters seriously we're in trouble. The choreographer, Allison Plamondon, proves resourceful at manoeuvring her performers round a central pillar that is hell on sight-lines but is probably there to hold up the building. The conductor, Steve Lavoie, also designed the lighting. That's nothing: The producer, Mike Murley, also functions as director, designer and dentist. Sometimes versatility can be a curse.

2000-08-26-the-grande-dame-of-stratford:
The person who may be most responsible for giving the Stratford Festival its shape, its identity and even its success has returned this year. When the festival began, in a tent in 1953, both the plays in its repertoire had their sets and costumes designed by a 39- year-old English visitor named Tanya Moiseiwitsch. But she didnt just design for the plays; she designed the stage, a spare and graceful projecting platform, challenging and energizing, that was unique then and is unique now. Richard Monette, Stratford's current director, thinks the stage may be the most important single element in the theatre's history: the one that has kept it alive when so many other classical theatres in North America have foundered.

Moiseiwitsch is now in a wheelchair but ebullient and alert; talking to her, I found, was like talking to a well-loved aunt from North London. She has been back in Stratford this year as a visitor: Fiddler on the Roof, she says, took my breath away" and she loves the small, intimate Tom Patterson Theatre (where she herself has never worked), though, nice person that she is, she refuses "to see Titus Andronicus. Once was enough. Ugh!

She is also, however, a participant. She designed the set for Monettes production of Molieres Tartuffe. Perhaps that isn't strictly accurate. In fact, in a fit of celebratory economy, the new production re-employs the set that Moiseiwitsch designed 17 years ago for a memorable staging by the late John Hirsch of the same play on the same stage (and with the same leading actor, Brian Bedford). It's a tribute by the 48-year-old festival to its doyenne, and it works on all levels. Like all her sets, it looks thoroughly at home in that space.

Obviously she hadnt reckoned, 48 years ago, on becoming part of Canadian theatre history. Her first reaction on being asked to come to Stratford was, she says now, terror, followed by complete absorption, and then by delight."

Part of her delight came from getting to know and work with the theatres founder, Tom Patterson, and its architect, Robert Fairfield. Another large part came from forming a closer bond with a man who was already her colleague and mentor, Stratford's first director, Tyrone Guthrie. It was in large part Guthrie's vision that she was realizing -- and went on realizing on that stage: his quest for a Shakespearean playing space that, without slavishly mimicking the Elizabethan theatre, would escape the constrictions of proscenium arches and painted scenery.

She first encountered Guthrie in the 30s when he was director of Londons homely classical theatre the Old Vic ("my favourite-ever theatre, she says, until it got bombed") and she was a lowly painting student. "I would go to work at the dress rehearsal; I was literally painting the stage cloth under his feet. It was a very low- key relationship. It moved into higher gear during the war, when the Old Vic operation was evacuated to Liverpool. By then, Moiseiwitsch was working at a theatre in Oxford, but Guthrie winkled me out of there."

Among other things, they collaborated on a modern-dress production of Ben Jonson's The Alchemist ("it must have three doors, insisted Guthrie because it's a farce"), which started with an air-raid siren (to establish that people had left town to escape the blitz rather than, as in the original, the plague) and with the apparition of the prostitute Doll Common emerging in her underwear. The crucial production, though, for the two of them was a more ceremonial piece: Henry VIII, mounted in 1949 at the Shakespeare Memorial Theatre in Stratford-on-Avon.

Architecturally, this big, flat house represented everything Guthrie hated. "He told Anthony Quayle [the theatres director], that he should push it into the water and build a tin hut instead; Tony said diplomatically that he didnt think the governors would like that.

Moiseiwitsch managed to tame the space with a permanent set that brilliantly reordered the essential Elizabethan elements: the levels and the alcoves.

A couple of years later, she did the whole thing on a larger scale for a whole cycle of the history plays. These designs were heavier on steps and staircases than would be fashionable now but they still look, in photographs, both functional and beautiful. They were the foundations of modern Shakespeare design, and they pointed the way for the Canadian Stratford.

The great thing about Stratford," says Moiseiwitsch "is that Guthrie got his way. It hadn't happened to him in any other country, except Scotland. (At the Edinburgh Festival he'd transformed the Assembly Hall of the Church of Scotland into a viable, if drafty, playing space, and immediately thought, This is the way to do Shakespeare.") "At Stratford the stage came first, and the theatre was built around it. Literally, it was only after four years of playing in the tent that the permanent concrete shell was erected.

In those four years (1953 to 1956), Moiseiwitsch designed every play on the Stratford stage. Id thought in my innocence that Stratford would be a one-shot affair -- for me at least -- but they kept asking me back." Her association far outlasted Guthries own, though his influence remained permanent.

The first year of the new theatre, 1957, also marked Guthrie's swan song on the festival stage with a production of Twelfth Night, and the first year that another designer -- Desmond Heeley -- got to work there. He designed Hamlet for Guthrie's successor, Michael Langham. "Michael was, says Moiseiwitsch the ideal person to take over; he didnt have Guthries visual sense -- with him it was more hit-and-miss at the beginning. But he has his own ideas."

She is, in fact, a one-woman Stratford history. She's worked happily and memorably with Langham, with Hirsch, with the long-time Stratford actor and director Douglas Campbell ("a very big fact in my life, and a wonderful director) and with Jean Gascon who, she says, brought Moliere into Stratford's life," where he has remained down to the present season.

Though he staged Oedipus Rex in his second season, Guthrie was skeptical of the stages suitability for non-Elizabethan plays. "He said, You can't do Restoration comedy on that stage; the asides would go for nothing.' Michael Langham proved him wrong.

In fact, the two plays in the very first season showed the different ways Stratford can go. The opening Richard III was a banner-waving show of the kind that still defines most peoples image of Stratford. But its companion, an epochal modern-dress Alls Well That Ends Well, showed that you could be domestic, intimate and even decorative. You can put things on that stage. Tartuffe takes place in a room, with doors and windows. They've reconstructed it very well."

The one Stratford director she didn't work with was Robin Phillips: "I liked Robin a lot but I didnt fall into his way of thinking. At the beginning of Phillips regime the central identifying feature of the Moiseiwitsch set -- the pillared balcony - - was made mobile instead of permanent. The trouble when you move it, says Moiseiwitsch, is you then get a huge, empty space. It's not good for acoustics, and it's worse for the budget, because now youve got to fill it." With the balcony in place, the stage becomes itself again: cheerfully ascetic, like its designer. "Im always sorry, she says now, when they move the column. It's my own personal column."

LAUGHTER ON THE 23RD FLOOR

Leah Posluns Theatre, Toronto

TORONTO - Jaws drop and mouths water at the list of comedy writers who, in the early 1950s, stoked the fires of Your Show of Shows. This was the Saturday Night Live of its day, only funny: a network TV show that convulsed select portions of America on a weekly basis. Sid Caesar was the star, and his contracted scribes included Mel Brooks, Carl Reiner, Woody Allen, Larry Gelbart and Michael Stewart, the future librettist of Hello Dolly, no great jokester himself but good at collating those who were.

Also present, the junior member of a youthful team, was Neil Simon, who some 45 years later delved into his reminiscences of the time and turned them into a play. Laughter on the 23rd Floor -- named for the exalted level of the New York office building on which NBC deposited Caesar and his staff -- is therefore another of the autobiographical pieces that have recently taken up much of Simon's time.

It is by far the best of them. The constant stream of wisecracks that make up much of the dialogue seems less forced and grating than in the authors more usual domestic settings; this, its easy to believe, is how these characters would actually talk. (Comedians offstage are rarely funny; their writers have to be.) The attendant sentimentality is also easier to take: I was able to convince myself that it is not a sentimental play, merely an accurate depiction of a group of hard-shelled but soft-centred people.

This may be Simon's best play. It certainly shows him on his most appealing turf; and it seems to me the best excuse that the commercial theatre (or at least the non-musical commercial theatre) has offered for its existence in several years. So it's a shame that this, the plays Canadian premiere, is something less than a full- blooded commercial occasion. Zed Pitkins production is well intentioned but slow; and though his mostly non-Equity cast all seem to have the right ideas, they are not so good at putting them into practice.

The action, of which there is not a great deal, unfolds in the TV series' dying season. The network, sensing the emergence of a new demographic with little taste for the crazy or satiric humour favoured by this collection of mainly Jewish New Yorkers, is cutting both the show's budget and its running time.

The star comic in the play is called Max Prince, but he is recognisably Caesar in his pomp, his generosity, his alarming battery of neuroses and his awe-inspiring fits of fury. He is overwhelmingly, and overbearingly, childlike. Angelo Celeste, who plays him here, has a baby-faced look much like Caesars own, but is much shorter. This is unfortunate: Caesars height, most unusual in a comedian, contributed largely to the fear and adoration that he inspired in his employees, and Celeste, though he tries hard, doesn't have the force of personality to compensate.

Simon himself is clearly present as Lucas, the gangling young narrator (at least he gangles as Carter Siddall plays him). Of the identity of the others I am, despite my opening show of erudition, uncertain. I assume that Ira, the scarf-draped hypochondriac whose doctors' appointments make him two hours late for every meeting, is Woody Allen; he is excellently played by Craig Mason. The sweaty, belligerently philistine Milt (Lou Israel) could well be Mel Brooks; and Carl Reiner could conceivably be figured by the temporizing, level-headed Kenny (Ted Powers who, more than most of them, looks like he belongs).

But I am at a loss to identify Val (Austin Schatz, ripely appropriate) as the Russian-born-and-accented head writer; or the Irishman Brian (Shawn Devlin), the token Gentile; or Carole (Andrea McCulloch), the token woman. Of course, there doesnt have to be a one-to-one resemblance in every case; Simon is, after all, a dramatist.

Whatever, or whoever: Watching them interact to the intermission is bliss. In the second half one begins to wish that Simon would draw his themes a little tighter; would actually dramatize, rather than just allude to, the extent to which political repression (the blacklist) automatically selects comedy as a prime target. You actually want to witness Maxs fights with the top brass, rather than just hearing his wayward accounts of them. (He has a lovely way of recounting defeats as victories.)

You also wish that Simon hadn't, like most writers, flunked the main challenge of writing about creative people, which is showing them actually creating. The Caesarean writing sessions, at which half a dozen brilliant people battled one another with jokes, are part of show-business mythology. The nearest we get here is a read- through of a spoof on Julius Caesar (Simon's way of saying "Hail Caesar"?), which may or may not be authentic; either way, its likely to leave a Canadian audience reflecting how much better it was done by Wayne and Shuster.

The setting is surprisingly spacious and sanitary and free of smoke; we seem to be in a kitchen/dining-room left over from another play, conceivably Simons Brighton Beach Memoirs. But until the real thing comes along -- and there's no guarantee it will -- this version is, cautiously, recommended.

Black & White Photo: Angelo Celeste: Recognizably Sid Caesar, but a bit shorter. ;

OEDIPUS UNMASKED

CBC-TV, 7 p.m. tonight

For reasons presumably known to somebody, CBC is tonight airing a long promotional video for a Stratford Festival production that came and went two years ago.

Oedipus Unmasked is, of course, meant to be something more than a promo. It masquerades, if that's the metaphor they want, as an arts documentary; and the gods know it has a promising subject. In 1998, Douglas Campbell, who as actor and director has been associated with the Stratford theatre since its inception, directed Sophocles' Oedipus Rex with his son Benedict Campbell in the title role. The staging, featuring tragic masks and platform soles, was modelled on a much earlier one; the first (and for several years the only) non- Shakespearean production at Stratford, Tyrone Guthrie, the festival's originating genius, directed it in 1954.

Make a note of that date, because the TV show gets it wrong. It tells us that Guthrie brought Campbell over to Canada with his family in 1954, and cast him the following year as Oedipus. In fact, Campbell was one of four British actors whom Guthrie brought over in '53, the year the festival started, and he was the only one who stayed. He did indeed play Oedipus in '55, but that was in a revival. In '54, Campbell had played the supporting role of the messenger from Corinth; Oedipus was James Mason, of whom you may have heard. Whether these facts have been fudged through ignorance or design I would not presume to guess.

As everyone knows, Oedipus was a legendary king of Thebes who unwittingly killed his father and married his mother, and who blinded himself when he discovered what he had done.

Oedipus Unmasked has barely started to unwind before we hear the narrator, Paul Gross, intoning about the Oedipus complex. Unfortunately, Oedipus himself didn't have one, and the text gives the actor no room to pretend that he did; he's too busy dealing with other matters, like the plague that's ravaging his city when the action starts.

I once had a theatre history student who twitched his way through a reading of one of this play's scenes. When asked why, he replied that he was trying to demonstrate the Oedipus complex. I nearly threw something at him. This was wrong of me, but one thing the play does show is that we all do impetuous things under stress. Oedipus killed his father, whom he had never previously met, because the old man wouldn't move his chariot out of the way. He is the man who invented road rage.

The film's thesis seems to be that even if the play itself is not Oedipal in the popular sense, this latest production just had to be. A father was directing his son in a role the father had once played. This circumstance, we are told, offers "a unique opportunity to see how an actor's skills are passed from one to another against the Freudian backdrop."

This idea, however, is decisively scuttled at the outset by Campbell pere, who says that he's never had any Freudian feelings about Ben and that it's "a lot of nonsense anyway -- not what the play's about." (It's a shame that he doesn't say what it is about, but conceivably nobody bothered to ask him.)

Ben himself seems less sure: "I've had the blessing and the curse of being very like my father ... we've had an up-and-down relationship. All kids blame their parents -- 'I'm like this because of you.' I'll be getting it from my own kids." Very true, but irrelevant to the Sophoclean Oedipus, who never had a chance to forge any kind of filial relationship, and not especially Freudian, either.

From the very brief glimpses we get of rehearsal, the Campbells could be any director and any actor, except that the directing Campbell, padding robustly around the periphery in shorts, seems unfashionably ready to offer the acting Campbell (and all the other actors) line readings.

It's a shame, because there are things to be explored here. If you want to extend the father-son idea, you might look at Campbell Sr.'s relation to his mentor, Guthrie. You might look at Guthrie himself, who is always worth looking at and listening to (he combined the frown of a dictator with the voice of a choirmaster); we see footage of him rising to his feet to tell the first generation of Canadian Stratfordians, "I do wish that all of you would get rid of the idea that acting is some kind of ..."

Some kind of what, we never learn, since he is faded out in favour of a voice-over. I mean no disrespect, but I would have been more interested in hearing Guthrie's ideas about acting than the ideas anyone else here expresses about anything. His Oedipus, judged by all who saw it to be a towering achievement, was filmed, and we see a few clips, but nothing that lets us measure it against the new one, of which we see even less.

Nobody asks why Tanya Moiseiwitsch's original, awe-inspiring costumes and masks could not have been used again, rather than redesigned. Nobody considers the different approaches to staging Greek tragedy, or why the plays have suddenly become so prevalent; a contrastingly naturalistic Medea is the high point of the current Stratford season, while in Denver, Peter Hall and John Barton, who in London have pioneered directly opposing methods of staging the Greeks, are joining forces on a 12-hour cycle.

Apart from its psychological top-dressing, this could be any superficial film about any show, down to the sound-bites of emerging first-nighters telling us how wonderful it was. Why did CBC bother? And why did Stratford let them?
