BETRAYAL

Soulpepper Theatre Company, Premiere Dance Theatre

When Harold Pinter's Betrayal was first staged in London in 1978, the local critics received it disdainfully. (I know -- I was one of them).

Since then, words have been feverishly eaten, and the play has become one of its authors most-admired and most-revived. The new Soulpepper production takes it a step further along the road to canonization.

One reason the play was scorned at its premiere was that it concerns English middle-class adultery, and we had all had quite enough of that. Let me rephrase that: It was generally believed that, at one quite recent time, all British plays had been about the anguished bed-hopping of the bourgeoisie and nobody wanted to see those dark, constricted days return.

Pinter, besides, was felt to have forsaken his roots. The man who had made his name writing about psychotic tramps and seaside boarding houses was devoting himself in this play to the emotional entanglements of the urban literati, i.e. the world in which he himself now moved. (How dare he flaunt it, seemed to be the feeling.)

Worse yet, his characters werent even real writers, just prosperous hangers-on: the people in Betrayal are Jerry, a literary agent; Robert, his best friend and a publisher; and Emma, wife of the latter and mistress of the former.

Also, we were tired -- justifiably -- of what had become known as the Pinter style: the icy-smooth, deliberate manner that Peter Hall, for many years Pinter's regular director, seemed to employ as a form of elegant intimidation. Every word, every movement, came loaded with significance, even though nobody could be sure what they signified. This, though, was part of the deal; the plays themselves usually had narrative glitches that made them seem, in a rather antiquated way, experimental.

Betrayal, though, didn't even offer the consolations of obscurity. Its story happens to unfold in reverse chronological order, but apart from that, its development is straightforward. Or at least straightbackward. Things that may seem puzzling in one scene are invariably clarified in the next.

The plays first scene shows Jerry and Emma meeting for a drink, some years after the end of the affair. We gather that Jerry would quite like to rekindle the relationship, and that Emma wouldnt.

The last scene shows Jerry declaring his passion for the first time and Emma responding. The mood, which survives even the sudden appearance of the about-to-be-cuckolded Robert, is one of delicate tenderness.

In hindsight, the beginning of their romance seems like its high point. Once consummated, it seems to have declined very quickly into a routine of lying, logistics, and regular rendezvous in a rented flat in an unfashionable quarter of London. (Probably only an English actor could pronounce the name "Kilburn" with the curdled contempt it requires.)

Like all Pinter's plays, but more nakedly and subtly than most, the piece takes shape as a series of psychological power struggles. In any given scene, two of the characters will share some piece of knowledge of which the third is ignorant. So each of the trio is at once both victor and victim: It depends which way the light is shining.

From one viewpoint, Jerry seems to hold all the aces. He has the woman he desires, and none of the attendant responsibilities. (His own marriage and family are kept off stage.) But he still has to live with the fact that Robert has first claim on Emma, and he is in constant fear of losing her. Robert is the deceived husband, but he has been enjoying infidelities of his own. Besides, about halfway through the action, Emma tells him about her affair, thereby strengthening the bond between them and making Jerry even more the outsider in their marriage.

Emma, meanwhile, is pointedly -- even brutally -- excluded from the camaraderie of the two men, symbolized by their regular games of squash, though these seem to be more talked about than actually enjoyed. (As also, from what we gather, seems to be the case with sex.) Still, Emma has had both men, and has moved on to a third: The play has a fourth, unseen, character, a writer named Casey whom Jerry represents and Robert publishes. They live off him but he walks off with their woman. It is, perhaps, the author's revenge.

The relationships pulsate, unspoken words conveying invisible words. (The spoken words are, as usual, brilliant.) As in any good play, all the characters have areas of unknowability. Some, however, are more unknowable than others. And, as often with Pinter, the woman is little more than an indecipherable, much-coveted Sphinx.

Susan Coyne gives her an air of chilly practicality, but little else; maybe thats all there is. Albert Schultz is admirable as the bemused, trying-to-be-cool Jerry whom we first meet, but as the onion gets unpeeled the layers beneath seem identical. (In a recent London production, it was Jerrys passion that drove the play.)

It is Diego Matamoros' Robert who predominates, showing us Pinter at his most uncomfortable. Robert, who cheerfully admits to hitting his wife and who has grown to hate his job, is a virtuoso put-down artist. He responds to the news of Emma's adultery with the kind of elegantly wounded barbs that Tom Stoppard lampooned in The Real Thing. Its the way that betrayed husbands behave in "civilized" plays, but in this text and this performance it rings true. Matamoros makes the cruelty irresistibly entertaining; he also manages to suggest that the man inflicts pain because he suffers pain.

All three performances are technically immaculate and they mesh beautifully under Daniel Brooks production, which, on the simplest of sets, cuts to the bone.

Not the least of its virtues is its enthusiastic pace: You will wait in vain for the notorious Pinter pauses. There are moments of silence, of course, but no more than in any other play in which the characters are not impossibly glib. (The author himself has recently returned to acting. And, even in his own plays, he performs with an exhilaratingly coarse barrelhousing energy that couldn't have less to do with the Pinter style. So we've been had.)

There is a good sound score. We still wait for actor-musician Ted Dykstra to make his onstage debut with Soulpepper, but in the meantime he has furnished this play, as he did Twelfth Night, with haunting incidental music.

Black & White Photo: Guntar Kravis, Soulpepper Theatre Company / Susan Coyne as Emma and Diego Matamoros as Robert: All the characters have areas of unknowability. ;
2000-09-12-dey-was-robbed-i-tell-ya-the-:
My favourite moment in The Sopranos -- many other peoples too, I hear -- comes during Episode 5. Tony Soprano, the middling gang boss from New Jersey, turns on his pre-collegiate daughter, who has just plucked up the courage to ask him if he is in the Mafia. He doesnt merely deny it -- he explodes, in an ecstasy of defensiveness that deliriously mixes straight street talk and self-righteous mediaspeak: "That's total crap ... That's a stereotype, and its offensive. Im in the waste management business ... There is no Mafia."

Well, the last sentence is a conscious lie , though there may be a tiny portion of his brain that can believe it. The bit about waste- management is true, to the extent that that's the front Tony uses for his extortion activities. The rest he, in a way, believes; he doesn't want to think of himself as a gangster. Certainly not of the kind that fills the public imagination. He doesnt feel part of the world that he saw depicted in The Godfather and Goodfellas; apart from anything else, he knows its too glamorous. Besides, what else is a conscientious father supposed to tell his daughter? His buddies and henchmen have the same problem with inquisitive offspring. It's tough, one of them laments, "raising a kid in the information age."

Writers can generally be judged by the quality of their jokes, and those in The Sopranos are about the best to be heard in any shows currently on television, including the avowedly comic ones. To an extent, the style of the humour goes back to Damon Runyon -- tough guys who talk fancy -- but it rings true here, especially in the grainy Italian-American accent. It's comedy of character, epitomized by Tonys mother, resentfully confined to a nursing home and exclaiming, when she hears that her son is seeing a psychiatrist, Hes gone to complain about his mother.

The Sopranos is both the best crime drama and the best family drama to come out of American television since, well, possibly ever, and the Mafia is of course the perfect site on which to combine the two genres.

On the one hand, we have Tony and his wife, coping with their sullen teenage daughter and unreadable schoolboy son.("Anthony Junior, just because you're suspended, it doesn't mean you can stay in bed all day.") Facing up to a critical child psychiatrist, Mr. and Mrs. Soprano seem oddly like a more intelligent Homer and a hipper Marge, anxiously inquiring about Bart; they have their differences, but their kids come first -- though they dont, of course, have the Simpsons financial problems.

On the other, we have the businessman who savagely beats his debtors and personally garrottes a suspected informer; the clan chieftain who fears he can never measure up to his dead father, can barely control his ambitious nephew and has handed over a dangerous amount of power to the uncle who played ball with him when he was a kid; the benefactor who thoughtfully burns down a restaurant so that his friend the owner won't be embarrassed by having a murder committed there. It's no wonder that the contradictions send Tony to a shrink.

The scenes one longs for in every episode are the consultations in which James Gandolfinis wondrous Tony sits hunched and fidgeting while Lorraine Braccos Dr. Melfi, her chin cupped in her hands, surveys him with enormous sympathy and fathomless stupidity. When we see her outside her office, she looks completely different (and oddly less glamorous, even when dressed up for a date) but in her own domain she is supreme, and it's no wonder that Tony falls for her.

I would have liked to see her get an Emmy -- as Edie Falco, who plays Tony's wife, Carmela, did last year. This time, however, The Sopranos was shut out even more comprehensively than before. Gandolfini got his due, but there was nothing for David Chase, the shows writer, creator, executive producer and occasional director, or for anyone else.

It was The West Wing that cleaned up, and it was notable that its producer began his acceptance speech for best drama by paying tribute to The Sopranos. Its conventional for the winner to pay tribute to the losers in bulk, but to single one of them out like that is unheard of; one detected the sound of fences being mended. (Though sentiment was not enough to secure a deserved award for the late Nancy Marchand, who played Tony's monster mother, a superb character who reminded me, among other things, of a line of Kaye Ballard's: You know the thing about Italian families -- theyre so Jewish. When even death cant sway the voters, then the ranks have really closed.) The West Wing's triumph may have owed something to its being the new show on the block, but then so, last year, was The Sopranos.

I suspect that a show about the White House -- with everybody behaving comparatively decently -- seems somehow more literate, more civilized, more in line with what "quality TV" is supposed to be. More, come to think of it, British, which remains a yardstick for American TV when it wants to rake in prestige as well as money. The New York Times has published a celebratory book on The Sopranos, including an introductory essay in which their critic Stephen Holden goes looking for exalted transatlantic comparisons. Unfortunately, he goes looking in the direction of Masterpiece Theatre. He claims The Sopranos to be superior in its richly textured comic realism, its "complexity and truthfulness" to Upstairs Downstairs, Brideshead Revisited and I Claudius. Of course it is; those genially escapist shows aren't even in the running.

If you want British exemplars for The Sopranos, go to the borderline crime series: to Cracker, whose protagonist is Tony Sopranos only serious rival for richness and breadth; or to Between the Lines (Inside the Line over here), that superbly exciting account of cops investigating cops; or Alan Bleasdales insanely ambitious masterpiece GBH. They are the shows with the real comic and dramatic edge, the ones that look at society from the underside, which is generally the most illuminating way of looking at it. The Sopranos surpasses them visually (American TV being a film culture and British TV a theatrical one) and it also goes them one better in eliminating the good guys, even the most compromised ones. Cops in The Sopranos are conspicuous by their absence. Tony and his various families have to work out their own damnation.

The West Wing also had the electoral advantage of being a major network production. The Sopranos was confined to HBO in its home country and to The Movie Network here; now we get to see it on CTV, without commercials and in versions edited by the creators themselves -- edited, we are assured, for time, not morality. (There is less nudity in the series than you may have heard, but the profanity and the violence are as advertised.)

Watch it from the start, because the pilot, directed by Chase himself, is a minor classic; with superb economy, it sets up all the characters, all the conflicts.

Also all the authentic locations: The Sopranos is one American series that got shot without disrupting Canadian traffic. (I've shot in Toronto, said Chase, "it isn't New Jersey."). After that, you should be hooked; like the British cop shows Ive cited, The Sopranos presents episodes each of which stand in their own right but whose main fascination is the way in which they contribute to an over-arching story.

The first instalment, by the way, gives us Tony squaring up to Dr. Melfi (I had a semester and a half in college -- I know Freud) and lamenting the loss of old-style values as exemplified by mobsters who squeal rather than go to the pen ("Whatever happened to the old respect for the penal experience?")

Writing like that, delivered with Gandolfinis particular brand of shamefaced bravura, you don't too often get.

Black & White Photo: Few TV characters offer the complexity of Gandolfini's Tony Soprano. ;

THE CORONATION VOYAGE

The Playhouse, Vancouver

It is 1953, and an ocean liner is sailing from Montreal to England, carrying customers for the crowning of Elizabeth II. The passengers we meet, all first-class, represent a cross-section of the French-Canadian upper crust -- and most of them have much to be cross and crusty about.

There is the Chief, kingpin of the Montreal underworld, now in desperate need of a new life and a new identity; and there is the Diplomat, who is prepared to accommodate him, for a consideration. The Chief is travelling with his two sons, born to him by two different mistresses, one French and one Italian. The Diplomat's price for three fake passports is a night in bed with the younger of the two boys, the Italian one.

Then there is the Minister, a thin-blooded high-rise politician whose own three sons were sacrificed 10 years earlier on the beaches at Dieppe, and his wife, who will not forget, and their daughter.

Aboard as light relief -- they certainly carry less baggage, emotional and physical -- are three girls called Elisabeth, lottery winners who are there because they have the same name and birthday as the English queen though not quite -- note the subtly nationalist point -- the same spelling.

The opening scenes, in which the characters are introduced to us as they embark, are rather like the long first number of Titanic (the musical), minus the reassuring knowledge that most of them are going to drown. The piece as a whole belongs to a much longer tradition of plays about representative figures outward bound -- going for trips on symbolic ships.

The Coronation Voyage is a five-year-old work by prolific Quebec playwright Michel Marc Bouchard. It's getting around; it received its English-language premiere earlier this year in Calgary, while the current production is a joint venture by the Vancouver Playhouse and the National Arts Centre in Ottawa. The stiff, formal language of Linda Gaboriau's translation may well be an accurate reflection of the original, but the play probably sounds better in French -- not just because abstraction usually does, but because the author presents a specifically French-Canadian view of a historical moment and of its reverberations backward and forward. Stripped of its native accents and performed in other provinces, the flavour becomes diluted and the stance questionable.

It has a few excellent jokes and a sharp and powerful ending. It also, early on, has suspense; we want to know how the blackmailed Chief will cope with his dilemma. This story, though, hangs fire while the author explores other avenues and then runs them in parallel; the situation may seem like Tosca or Measure for Measure with a sex change, but the example the play quotes is that of Abraham and Isaac, with the intervening angel left out.

So we have the Minister's wife, lamenting her killed or crippled sons; and we have her daughter and the Chief's elder son, both of them talented pianists. The boy, indeed, was a prodigy until a couple of his dad's mobster rivals slammed the piano lid on his hands and ended his career. The wife is named Alice, the daughter Marguerite, and the youth Etienne; his young half-brother is called Sandro. On this voyage, in a radical extension of traditional shipwreck etiquette, only women and children have names.

There is one further masculine-type figure: the Biographer, who functions as a part-time narrator and whose presence seems -- even in a play as avowedly non-naturalistic as this -- wildly implausible. The excuse for his presence is that he's writing the Chief's highly sanitized memoirs; from this, we are supposed to extrapolate the distance between the clean history we read in books and the dirty history that gets lived. On a national level we gather that, even in the flag-waving year of '53, Canadians -- certainly French Canadians -- weren't as delirious about England and its monarchy as the official record would suggest. (I wouldn't know, but I can tell you one thing from the other side: When we English kids watched the coronation parade, the guys we really cheered for were the Mounties. We loved you, even if you despised us. We also booed Churchill; I can't remember why, but the news should please Bouchard, one of whose characters advances the interesting theory that Churchill fought the Second World War as a favour to Stalin. I always thought that Britain and the Commonwealth countries were fighting the Nazis long before Russia, and that this was something to be proud of, but maybe this, too, is just the kind of history you read in books.)

On a more immediate level, we get the characters' ignoble behaviour and the Biographer's glowing interpretations simultaneously. The juxtaposition is good for a few ironic chuckles, but it gets worked overtime. The Biographer doesn't seem to be much of a writer; he describes sacrifices made by the Chief "to the edification of his success." Maybe he means "edifice." The writing of this role is, in fact, unspeakable; certainly that's how it sounds here.

The kind of updated morality drama that rates characters by their functions -- what you might call the genre of the generic -- is not my favourite kind of show, but I accept that it has its place. It demands, though, stern and ruthless playing; it has -- or should have -- no room for sentiment. Marti Maraden's production is lucidly organized, on a setting by Pam Johnson that's as handsome as luxury liner sets invariably are.

Too often, though, it goes soggy. Elizabeth Shepherd as the Minister's wife delivers her account of the slaughter at Dieppe not with the anger it seems to call for but as some kind of tone poem. She is fine, however, in the character's other, comedic aspect: as a frustrated mondaine, somewhat resembling Angela Lansbury in regal mode. (We are told that, when she requested a seat at the captain's table, the captain gave her his.)

Leon Pownall, one of the best actors in Canada (Stratford needs him), is a powerfully impassive Chief, never asking for sympathy even when it seems within reach. With these two players, experience tells.

Its opposite can be quite nifty, as well. Eric Bojm, a 13-year- old, is wonderfully natural as the threatened Sandro; even when he sounds awkward, he sounds real -- real enough for his possible sacrifice to be truly disturbing.

Inexperience is less helpful when it gets old enough to be self- conscious; Kevin MacDonald, an actor fresh out of drama school, is overtaxed by the embittered Etienne, who unfortunately is the pivotal character -- or at least the only one who undergoes any kind of development.

The Diplomat (Allan Morgan), by contrast, is bisected as well as bisexual: half slimy seducer, half sensitive war veteran. There is no reason why these characteristics shouldn't co-exist, but the author does no more than pull an on-off switch.

Patti Allan is pretty funny as a protocol expert, who instructs the three tin Lizzies in the niceties of obeisance to royalty and is mightily peeved when a cargo of Indians refuse to appear in ceremonial headdresses that seem to have been hired from a touring company of Annie Get Your Gun.

All these pieces fit together; story and ideas are slickly conflated. Neither, though, is terribly interesting, because the people aren't. If plays are cakes, this one is well seasoned but half-baked.

OSCAR REMEMBERED

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

The story of Oscar Wilde -- his fame and his folly, his imprisonment, and his endurance while in durance -- has been told on many occasions, several of them forming part of the Wilde Celebration at this years Stratford Festival. The familiar material gets another going-over in Oscar Remembered, the twist being that we get to hear it through the mouth of Wildes beloved nemesis, Lord Alfred Douglas: Bosie to his intimates, and to posterity.

The late Canadian actor and playwright Maxim Mazumdar put this piece together, and he performed it at Stratford some 20 years ago. His problem is the same as that which afflicted the American writers who once had the bright idea of making the Dauphin the protagonist of a musical featuring Joan of Arc. The audience's attention keeps straying back to the story's real hero and -- in both cases -- martyr.

Its aggravated here by the fact that Mazumdar uses the characters original words, and those words are far likelier to be Wilde's than Douglas's; more of Wildes have been preserved -- whether as letters or repeated anecdotes or formal literary offerings -- and they are certainly more memorable. They are funnier and they are more passionate.

Michael Therriault, the young actor who does the show now, is required among other things to read the eloquently bitter letter that Wilde addressed to Douglas from Reading Gaol. He needs to convince us that he has just got it in the mail. So he has to deliver it tentatively, as if it were all new to him, while also signalling his own shock-horror reactions as recipient. This is on top of conveying to us the sense and feeling of the letter itself, which is written in Wildes most fluent oratorical manner. (There is pain in the substance, but enjoyment in the style.) This amounts to a double, if not a triple, acting problem, and it is no wonder that Therriault fails to solve it.

You may add to this that Bosie, even when allowed to state his own case, remains a stubbornly unlikeable apostle: Judas crossed with Peter in his denying phase, and with a vein of self-pity and self-dramatization all his own. Pretty much by his own admission, he used his relationship with Wilde as a means of getting back at his father, the monstrous Marquess of Queensberry, and he eventually sacrificed Wilde to this vendetta. You feel that even Queensberry, who at least had the courage of his own prejudices, deserved better than this son, sniggering at him from a distance, and eventually fleeing the country while his lover stood the trial into which Douglas himself had goaded him.

He also seems, on a smaller scale, to have thrown a nasty fit when Wilde dedicated a volume of Salome -- the overripe Biblical drama that he wrote in French and that Douglas translated -- to somebody else. (Strangely the play itself -- the partners' one joint effort -- is not quoted in Mazumdar's text.)

In Bosies defence: He had to stand around at parties and listen to Oscar getting all the laughs. This cant have been fun, however much he may have professed his admiration for his friend's wit. (Did he ever remark that he wished he'd said that, and did Wilde ever reply "You will, Bosie, you will?" Well, now Bosie does.) He apparently helped provoke that wit to its finest flowering by suggesting that Wilde knock off a comedy about cucumber sandwiches, thereby earning the gratitude of playgoers and tea drinkers everywhere. (Cucumber sandwiches are a recurring motif in this piece.) He visited his imprisoned idol in Holloway, under atrocious conditions, if not in Reading.

Perhaps most telling of all, when the ordeal was over (and the tale remains appalling, however often you hear it), Wilde resumed their relationship. This, I think, is less a tribute to the power of love than an acknowledgment of human frailty and need, but it was Wildes own choice, and it should be respected.

At this last stage, Douglas didnt let him down. The play's most poignant remark is to the effect that Wilde could no longer write because one cannot write about life; one can only live it, which is what he had now been forced to do, in spades. That may not be a universal truth, but it applies here. Unfortunately it is, again, Wilde's perception, not Douglass; Bosie seems fated to be the permanent understudy.

So here he is again, soaking up somebody elses limelight; so, at a further remove, is the author of this piece; and so, at yet a fourth, is whoever plays it now. At this point, however, things begin to even out. I have to confess my own prejudice here; I once saw Mazumdar, in another of his own shows, and I thought him a wholly derivative writer and a thinly narcissistic performer.

Therriault is a far more talented actor, one of Stratford's genuine discoveries; he is currently excellent in Fiddler on the Roof as -- all together now -- the tailor Motel Kamzoil; and last year he was an impressive Ariel to the Prospero of William Hutt, who coincidentally directs him here. (The year before that he was unbearable as Mordred in Camelot, but it's an unbearable role.)

As Bosie he seems to be talking partly to an invisible Wilde, represented by an empty armchair, with a green carnation on a side- table; partly to us; and principally to his mirror. The production isnt very rigorous about these distinctions, but theres probably no way it could be.

Therriault delivers intelligently, moment by moment, and cumulatively suggests an overbred puppy dog with a grievance, one whose bite is worse than his whimper. Almost the last thing he gives us is a rendition -- truncated but still substantial -- of Wilde's last work, The Ballad of Reading Gaol; he gets very actorish here, fastening in a self-accusing manner on the famous repeated lines about each man killing the thing he loves, and elsewhere painting on pathos while neglecting the verse form. (Or, in layman's terms, he keeps emphasizing the wrong words.)

This may be a subtle comment on Bosie's incorrigible insensitivity, but somehow I doubt it. It also shows the evening decisively up for what it is; an unsubtle pretext for regurgitating, yet again, Oscar Wilde's Greatest Hits.

Black & White Photo: Michael Rafelson, Stratford Festival / MICHAEL THERRIAULT AS ALFRED DOUGLAS: An unlikeable character, although he did have to stand by and watch Wilde get all the laughs at parties. ;

ST. NICHOLAS

Artword Theatre, Toronto

TORONTO - Conor McPherson is the young Irish dramatist whose play The Weir was seen in Toronto two WorldStage seasons ago, on which occasion it took the town by storm. That's criticspeak, meaning that quite a few of those who saw it liked it. I was one of them.

I also like the same author's St. Nicholas -- the play if not the present production -- which was written before The Weir and looks like a trial run for it. The Weir was a symphony of narratives; half a dozen people met in a pub and told one another stories, the last of which blew the mind of everyone who heard it, onstage or off. In St. Nicholas there is only one storyteller, talking directly to us. We never learn his name, but we discover most of the other salient facts about him. He lives in Dublin, where he works as a theatre critic, if you call that work. In the course of his story he takes another job as an assistant vampire, which the playwright, with the insolence typical of his trade, seems to regard as being a natural career progression.

Not until he got involved in the bloodsucking business, he tells us, did he know what real power was. As a critic he seems very hung up on power, he relishes it, unlike most of the reviewers I know, who don't think about it much and worry when they do. But then Ireland, and Dublin in particular, may be the last bastion of literary punditry -- a place where a critic can still cut a figure, even if an ungainly one, in pubs and clubs and coffee houses. Our hero is, he tells us, one of the five best-paid writers on his paper. (I've always liked the Irish.) He has got to this position by having opinions: not -- McPherson really goes for the jugular here - -by forming opinions, which would require serious thought, but simply by having them.

He drinks, as an Irish critic would; and he seems to consume beer and whisky indiscriminately and in stomach-churning quantities. He loves but neglects his wife and children. His endearing professional habits include writing reviews -- almost invariably hostile -- before seeing the play. On one crucial occasion he socializes with the cast, leading them to believe he liked the show so that their disappointment will be all the more exquisitely flavoured when they read him. Unfortunately he offers one of the younger actresses a lift home and on the journey finds himself seriously smitten.

I would say that McPherson has nailed some of the social and psychological quirks of our trade unnervingly well, but that his total picture is excessively dark. But then, as I said, things may be different in Ireland.

He has certainly created a character and evoked a milieu; and he does both without apparent sweat. The writing rolls captivatingly along, sharp in detail and rich in wit. The play that the protagonist has so impetuously slammed moves from Dublin to London - - for a shorter run than was originally planned, thanks to his review -- and he follows it there, intent on pressing his suit (which, from the rumpled look of him, could probably do with it). McPherson writes as potently of English seedy-bohemian life as of Irish. Eventually our critic tires of humiliating himself and accepts defeat. Subsequently he encounters a pale man named William who is always on the lookout for new blood and recruits our hero to procure it. William is no Dracula and his victims apparently don't become vampires themselves, and his new helper never partakes himself. (You can hear his mother objecting "they couldn't make you a real vampire?" Do Irish mothers say things like that?) Initially happy in his new position, he begins to revolt against it and eventually quits when -- inevitably -- one of his new recruits turns out to be his beloved. So he is saved -- giving up power in favour of unconsummated love -- though the details of the epiphany are vague. The play has a Christmassy title, so maybe he is like Dickens' Gabriel Grub or Ebenezer Scrooge, redeemed by contact with the supernatural. (Vampires, of course, are not good spirits, but William seems to wish he had a conscience, which -- as the narrator acutely observes -- is much the same as actually having one.) I found the second half of the saga less involving than the first, perhaps because I felt less personally implicated; I am not now nor have I ever been a vampire (I swear it) though I do know people who persist in writing musicals about them. But even if the latter part of the journey slackens, it's fun getting there.

The author is quoted in the program as saying that it's especial fun "when we have a well-known actor in front of us." In London and New York, the play was performed by Brian Cox, who is fairly famous and certifiably great: the best Titus Andronicus I've ever seen, one of the best Lears, and just a week ago, a disturbingly magnificent Hermann Goering on TV. He has massive presence. The Toronto performer is Adam Bramble, who isn't up to it. He looks right -- grey hair, pot belly, black shirt -- and he gets through his allotted 90 minutes fluently and comprehensibly. But he never sounds convincingly Irish, which immediately denatures the piece (I always though the rhythms automatically imposed an accent, but obviously I was wrong) and he seems to be having trouble with the idioms; he speaks of his first batch of a vampire victims as "a tidy half- dozen," emphasizing the adjective as if it were their appearance rather than their number that was in question. He is both emotionally and vocally limited.

Each of his lines seem to describe the same upward arc, and they all strike a pleading note that is both inappropriate and draining. What our theatre most needs: actors and directors who can put the iron into irony.

The director here, Dean Gabourie, provides occasional bits of production -- bringing the lights up for the hero to come among us, piping in crowd noises when he talks of entering a pub -- that are not helpful. If the play has a primary moral, it is that salvation lies in not being a vampire, and to that I would give instant agreement. Its secondary moral may be that salvation lies in not being a critic, and that I would like more time to think about.

GREASE

Elgin Theatre, Toronto

And here it is, the show of the film of the show, Canadian style. It is, as you would expect, the worst of all possible worlds. It also lends a new edge to the old saw about nostalgia not being what it used to be.

There are many nostalgias at work here. There is the fondness of the show Grease itself, first staged in 1972, for the musical and social styles of the post-Elvis 1950s: the days when high school really was high school and rock 'n roll ruled. This obviously tapped in to something, since the original Broadway production ran for a phenomenally long time. I saw it when it came to London (with an unknown Richard Gere in the cast) and I have fond, if misty, memories of it. It was tuneful, it was funny, and it was terrifically danced. One number, Born To Hand Jive, was a legitimate riot.

So thats my nostalgia -- for the show, rather than for the period it depicts, even though I lived through it. It's more fun to remember than it was to experience; the pastiche is better than the real thing.

I never got round to seeing the 1978 movie, but it did very well without me. It was, in fact, the last movie musical with live actors to make any money. Its impact, of course, dwarfed that of the show - - a fact not lost on the originators of the current production, which started out in Montreal.

It sets out to honour (i.e. cash in on) its audience's fond memories of the film. Indeed, if we take the background article in the program literally, and I dont see why we shouldnt, then the producers were unaware Grease had ever been a stage show in the first place. This kind of ignorance (as opposed to innocence, of which this production knows nothing) makes me want to tear its owners into small pieces and scatter the sections around the stage - - which in this case could hardly make it look more of a mess than it does at present.

In practical terms, staging the movie means shoving into the stage script the two hit songs that were added for the screen: Hopelessly Devoted to You and You're the One That I Want. These numbers, credited to J. Farrar, have stronger tunes -- or, anyway, stronger hooks -- than anything in the theatre score, but their lyrics barely exist. The second one, in particular, seems ludicrously thin to function as the climax of what is still -- barely -- a narrative musical, however much noise it makes. They are also out of period: Seventies disco rather than Fifties pop.

This built-in anachronism seems to have been taken by the director, Denis Bouchard, as licence for chaos. The show still takes place in and around Rydell High (named after Bobby?), but the school seems to have been relocated in Canada -- or at least in some milieu where people automatically fall about at the word "Winnipeg." (In the States, they'd simply say Canada and expect the same response.) The clothes and musical are still just about those of the Fifties but the manners have changed and definitely for the worse. Shy louts and virginal flirts have become sociopaths, incipient or actual. I must be a hypocrite: Here I am, eagerly lapping up the violence of The Sopranos every night, but jibbing at the sight, apparently meant to be funny, of a leathered youth shoving a blind man. Even when the blind man was allowed, a full act later, to shove him back, I still didnt find it hilarious, just mechanical. The characters include the school principal, who seems to constitute the entire teaching faculty, and a gangling nerd with the giveaway name of Eugene; both are there only to be mocked, and in the crudest possible way. (The show sometimes seems like the late lamented Freaks and Geeks, shorn of its truth and its humour and seen entirely from the viewpoint of the freaks.)

The conceit seems to be that we are at a reunion in the school gym, interrupted by the more unruly alumni of the Fifties, who proceed to whisk us back to a simpler time. (Or is it just that their ghosts descend? Either way.) The gym, with a couple of shallow steps and a false proscenium, remains our unit set. But there must have been productions of Grease that actually were staged in high- school gyms and looked better than this one.

The actors, meanwhile, all wear those determinedly brutalist face- mikes. This makes them look ugly -- and not only ugly but wrong -- and it does nothing for clarity. (The sound-quality is appalling; its all blare). It also destroys the show's most appealing ingredient: the wit of the songs. Even now, the score is the one thing that saves the evening from being absolute hell.

Jim Jacobs and Warren Casey, the uncelebrated author-composers (this was not only their one hit, but their one show) heightened what was already Fifties rock's most endearing characteristic, its awareness of its own absurdity -- something that disappeared when the Beatles arrived and spoiled everything.

So we get Beauty Queen Dropout, with a full-dress Teen Angel descending in a burger bar to counsel and console the singer, and the heart-rending Alone at a Drive-In Movie ("its no fun watching werewolves without you." ) We even get, or should get, a certain amount of character development. I remember being pleased when the soundtrack recording of Summer Days, Summer Nights, a song that hadnt made much impression in the show, went to No. 1. That, I felt atavistically, was how hit records ought to sound. More than that, though, I enjoyed the neat wit with which the song laid out two teenage perspectives on the same relationship: Danny the jock, Sandy the demure, having their own little Rashomon. Here, though, you can't make out the words: Bang goes your only chance of getting to know the protagonists, who proceed to go through the most unmotivated sequence of partings and reconciliations in the history of either musical theatre or teenage romance. The original script must have been pared to the bone: I remember it as simple but not stupid. Rick Miller, who plays Danny, is credited -- rather far down the list -- with "script adaptation," so maybe it's his fault.

As an actor, hes pleasant when he gets the chance, but when hes with his buddies -- which is most of the time -- he simply merges into the crowd. As Sandy, Ma-Anne Dionisio is rather more plaintive than she was as the doomed heroines of Miss Saigon and West Side Story: this despite her obvious resilience. (Her biography informs us that in London she played star roles in Miss Saigon and Martin Guerre at the same time. Quite a gal.) Her Oriental looks may or may not be supposed to connect with her family's apparent strictness: something else the production hasn't thought through.

In what should be the plum female role of Rizzo, the One Who Puts Out, Katie Emmie McInich displays a powerful set of lungs, even when just talking. She sings her big number There Are Worse Things I Could Do (a not unthoughtful song, when she thinks shes pregnant) straight into the audiences face, rather than that of the person she's supposedly addressing. This, yet again, is the musical theatre as wannabe rock concert. Why bother? The director seems to have imposed a unified acting style -- i.e., all the performances are alike. They go on and off like light switches. It's probably not their fault, but the entire cast comes off energetically rotten.

2000-09-30-why-are-they-singing:
When We Were Singing runs at Buddies in Bad Times, 12 Alexander St., until Oct. 15. For tickets, call the box office at (416) 975-8555.

Three of the characters in When We Were Singing are female, one is male. Two of them are gay, two are straight. Three are actors, one is a writer. The quartet (even I can do that much math) are friends, and enjoy the kind of exclusive, not to say incestuous, relationship that only exists in plays and television sitcoms. They meet regularly over drinks, alcoholic or caffeinated, to exchange confidences and consolation. When at home, they spend much of their time telephoning one another, bitching about the third or fourth party. They dont seem to know anybody else, at least not closely. They have sex with people outside the circle, but that doesnt count.

When We Were Singing is, not surprisingly with that title, a musical, the first one to be written by a promising composer- lyricist from Vancouver, Dorothy Dittrich. (She's also the musical director, and a good one.)

It's a talented but very unfulfilling show. It unfolds over a single weekend, probably in the authors hometown. It starts with Abby, an unemployed actress, lamenting the imminent (and, shortly, the actual) loss of her latest boyfriend. We then move on, cross- cutting as we go, to Jenny, a documentary director and screenwriter, lamenting the loss of her latest girlfriend; to Les, actor-in- waiting and also acting waiter, lamenting the more brutal loss of his lover, to AIDS; and to Belinda, who, despite a lucrative career in commercials, just laments. Abby, heretofore heterosexual, finds herself in bed with Jenny, to their mutual surprise, though not apparently to that of the two others. End of story, though not end of show. There is a whole act of regrets and readjustments still to come.

Satisfying plays have been made of less, though Im not sure that satisfying musicals have. If a show is all about feelings and relationships, then it needs to dig into the people who are having them, and though song can be an admirable method of doing this, it cannot easily do the job unsupported. When We Were Singing might more aptly be titled When Aren't We Singing?, because the characters never stop; Dittrich has written a sung-through musical, just at the moment when the Andrew Lloyd Webbers are giving it up. To her credit, she never descends to the Webber level of quasi-recitative; she writes songs, one after another, in a variety of styles: not varied enough, though, to ward off monotony.

We learn that the characters are discontented with their professional and personal lots, but that hardly makes them special. They are, in fact, commonplace, without being representative. Writing of urban angst among the rapidly ageing young, she inevitably recalls the Sondheim of Company (but that had a book, if not a wholly satisfactory one, and a larger and more varied cast) and the Maltby and Shire of Closer Than Ever (but that was a revue, every number a new beginning). I'm not saying that what shes after is impossible. Ive known it to work, once: in William Finn's Falsettoland, which has a strong plot and solidly realized characters. His earlier March of the Falsettos is structurally diffuse and textually fuzzy, problems that beset Dittrich's show as well.

It starts on a promising level of acerbic wit, which it doesnt sustain. It goes far too easy on its characters, and it doesnt tell us enough about them. Nor does it always make their feelings very clear; the lyrics can be vague, and the music of Dittrich's more languid ballads is not much of an incentive to concentrate. The four characters share a nostalgic yearning for a level of luxurious ease they are never likely to attain; they sing a concerted number about escaping to the seaside, a pretty song beautifully harmonized and also (by Jeff Logue) beautifully lit. But the same note is struck too often elsewhere, both before and after. After all, none of us in the audience are likely to attain La Dolce Vita either, so while we can briefly sympathize with their frustrations, it gets irritating when we're asked to take them seriously.

Dittrich also writes compelling blues (blues in the theatre are usually compelling) and neat patter numbers. She also supplies what I can only heartlessly describe as the obligatory AIDS anthem. (Its also the title song.) We are, surely, past the stage of being moved by the news that the disease exists. If we are to sympathize with the bereaved, we have to know specific things about the relationship and the show doesnt tell us. And that is symptomatic of what's wrong generally; merely being told, to music, that people are suffering-but-surviving is not enough to make us care. Not even their recurring bouts of self-mockery are enough to do the trick.

The show has been lucidly and sympathetically staged by David Oiye and the performers are excellent. They all sing like birds, and they act, too. Marc Richard transcends some fairly routine writing as Les, defusing self-pity by nailing every bit of humour that comes his way. Jennifer Rayner is fresh-faced and bewildered as Abby, and Alison Woolridge melts agreeably in what seems to be the central role of Jenny; I assume that she's central because she gets the biggest of the big ballads. Paula Wolfson is both plangent and pungent, though she has trouble supporting her role description, which is that of a self-hating unloved alcoholic; this, in stage terms, should make her more fun than the material allows her to be. (She also, if youll permit me a bit of gratuitous stereotyping, seems to be wrongly christened. Belinda is a cuddly name; the character strikes me as more of a Jackie. Im really not kidding; we need these things as footholds.)

Note, by the way, the past tense in the title: a reference to a past, perhaps illusory, time when the characters were happy. But if characters are now, metaphorically, past the time of singing, then writing a musical about them, especially an all-sung musical, has to be an uphill job; ditto responding to it. Here's to the author's next.

OUTRAGEOUS

Canadian Stage, Berkeley Street Theatre

Brad Fraser's musical Outrageous begins with an elaborate company number called Carnival Country. It covers a lot of ground, scenically and otherwise, and it goes on long enough for my feelings about it to have progressed through three separate stages.

Its a busy item, scenically and musically, designed to start the show with a bang while setting up story, atmosphere and characters. First off, I was seduced by its high-powered theatricality. After a while, my enthusiasm was dampened by the realization that Joey Millers music, though kicky, was basic imitation Broadway. And after a longer while I decided that this didn't matter, that it was good at what it did, and that it perfectly supported what was going on among the actors.

The show is loosely based (via a film whose cult I haven't joined) on the early career of Craig Russell, the late Canadian female impersonator, and this number introduces him and the drag- queen world in which hes going to move. It also introduces us to the other principal character, a schizophrenic young woman we see gaining her discharge from the mental ward. The speed and clarity with which the focus shifts from one narrative to the other, and the energy and lucidity with which both are infused, is exhilarating.

You feel that if they can keep this up, the show may turn into the great Canadian musical. They cant, and it doesn't, but it's still the most exciting attempt Ive seen.

The energy keeps going, pretty much non-stop, and so -- in strict plot-synopsis terms -- does the action. The things that go missing are character and conflict. Russell has here been renamed Robin: a hairdresser with, at the outset, unsuspected talents. Liza, the schizophrenic, arrives unexpectedly at his apartment and moves in with him. Before you know it they are friends, the closest, for life.

Supposedly, this is the shows central relationship, but it proves unexpectedly hard to dramatize. Fraser, as author and director, promises in a program note that his will be no ordinary musical. And -- after the usual patronizing (and irrelevant) guff about chandeliers and helicopters -- he proceeds to swear off easy endings and "simple answers."

I don't know who he thinks he's kidding -- himself, probably -- but he concludes his first act with a syrupy song in which Robin and Liza pledge eternal devotion and his second with another, more mistily philosophical, in which they do the same thing. In other words, he offers us standard musical-comedy sentiments, and it makes no difference that the people concerned arent actually lovers. The show presents plenty of graphically simulated sex (of all persuasions) and lots of language, but in essence -- compared to a recent serious musical such as Kiss of the Spider Woman or an older one such as Carousel -- its kids' stuff.

The demons that reportedly possessed the real Russell have here been exorcised. This Robin is a nice young man, understandably shy at first and a little unsure of his talent, but once it's released, theres no stopping him. (He does full impersonations, outpacing his early colleagues, who stick with lip-synchs.) He has in the course of the show to make two crucial decisions, and theyre both no- brainers. The first is whether to go to New York, where he's been offered a club booking. The second is whether to return to Toronto, given that work in the Big Apple has temporarily dried up, and that Liza needs him. She has a taste, indiscriminately indulged, for casual flings with taxi drivers, and has had a miscarriage.

Robin has also been crossed in love: His manager, a bisexual cowboy stud, has become involved with the girl-friend of a lesbian club owner. But the situation carries no weight, because the depth of the two men's relationship has never been established. (Maybe they should have a duet.)

Liza is constantly besieged by people -- friends, family, social workers -- who want her re-committed, theres more obvious drama in her life than there is in Robins, but there's less obvious music. Robin -- whose life is glitz, feeding on more glitz -- is always good for a number, and so are his friends. A number called Have a Nice Day points the contrast, rather too acutely.

A succession of drag queens invade Robin and Liza's apartment, and what they sing is neat, pointed and funny. Liza has some very straight visitors, and the attempt to musicalize their shocked-but- polite reactions is embarrassingly clunky. Im not here to give advice, but it strikes me the number would work much better if the showbiz people sang and the civilians simply talked. This isnt opera, and they don't have music in them.

Miller proves better at composing set songs, which are competent if not striking, than at putting conversation to music. Maybe the latter, despite appearances, is the harder job. He and Fraser are jointly credited with the lyrics (Miller's are additional) and they are indeed uneven. Sometimes theyre doggedly prosaic; others, they positively dance along, with only the occasional bum rhyme to remind us that civilization is dead. Everything comes to a head in the title song, which is complicated.

Robin is playing the lead in a musical about Joan of Arc seen as a drag queen. Its obviously a terrible show, but our show's spoof of it -- with hooded priests denouncing Joan as "outrageous" -- is wonderful.

But we also keep switching back to Liza, who is experiencing similar pressures in Toronto and for real, and these bits are terrible. And yet the good parts of the song couldn't exist without the bad, so we have to accept them and -- thanks in part to Sergio Trujillos whirlwind choreography -- we do.

The staging throughout is first-rate: fast and witty and scary. Fraser has always been able to write funny, and he has directed his cast with such style and point that every joke lands.

Thom Allison is a magnetic Robin, strong and supple and sympathetic. His impersonations, most of them cannily saved up till late in the show, are vocally variable (he does Carol Channing very well, but shes probably easy). In manner and style and appearance, though, they're impeccable, with his Judy Garland especially, even painfully, acute.

Lorretta Bailey's Liza may be even better: very economical, with an unnerving, and clinically accurate, directness of approach. Both performers are finely served by their designer: David Boechlers costumes, obviously all-important, do great things for Robin and for the atmosphere in general. His set, a symphony in string, provides a menacing environment for Lizas lurking mania. Hands reach out at her from within its webbed recesses, simulating the entrapping voices in her head. (There's supposed to be a parallel between these voices and those of the divas waiting to be released from inside Robin. Joan of Arc ties the idea up but, frankly, I wouldn't have known if I hadnt been told.)

The performances dont stop with the stars. There's a special joy in a show in which everyone gets a chance and takes it, while remaining loyally within the framework. It's called ensemble, and this is the best example Toronto has seen since Platonov.

Timothy Murphy and Ed Saheely are riots as Robin's early partners- in-drag and permanent friends; Sharron Matthews and Karen Leblanc electrically tough as the New Yorkers; Tim Sell a tower of ambiguous strength as the manager; and Tim Howar unshakably insistent as a fellow patient of Liza's whose presence threatens to send her back over the edge.

Tamara Bernier and Susan Henley do more than might be expected with the ordinary people, and everybody doubles and trebles with furious devotion.

The show is too long and too sentimental -- outrageously so, in fact -- but it grabs from the start, and never really lets go.

I promised myself not to compare The West Wing with The Sopranos, but the temptation -- after the stand-off at this year's Emmys -- is irresistible. The West Wing took nine awards to The Sopranos' one: a political putsch or a gangland massacre.

They were up against one another as TV drama series. Really, though, they are different animals. Remember the Sopranos episode in which Chris, Tony Sopranos nephew, tried his hand at writing a movie screenplay, and lamented that his life, unlike those in the handbooks hed consulted, didn't have "an arc? He was right; none of the characters on The Sopranos has an arc, except one. The show is centrifugal: Its subsidiary actions are only important for how they illuminate the life, and possible downfall, of Tony himself. The Sopranos, in fact, is not a series at all: It's a cohesive drama that, for reasons of length, unfolds over a period of weeks. Whether it can maintain this achievement over successive seasons is, of course, another question.

On The West Wing, everybody has an arc, which is the same as nobody having one. Each is there to play out his or her personal soap opera, and they could obviously go on forever, or at least until the next election. The president gets special billing -- hes played, according to the opening credits, by and Martin Sheen" -- and you might claim that hes the protagonist; the other regulars depend on him for their jobs, and what they do might theoretically affect his position. But he doesn't dominate dramatically, and he doesn't have enough at stake. He isnt subject to a code of kill-or- be-killed, and he isnt even in danger of a nervous breakdown.

He's also, despite occasional crotchets, very nice. He bears no resemblance to any recent U.S. leader, but he does fit into what seems to be an imperishable American fantasy, that of having the country governed by Henry Fonda.

Departing from Hollywood tradition, The West Wing is brave enough to tell us which party its president belongs to. (He's a Democrat). Otherwise, its antiseptic as only American television can be; it looks like a hospital series in which the doctors and adminsitrators have mutated into politicians and civil servants. Its opening sequence is positively reverential: a flag waves, music swells, the White House facade is faded in, and the principal actors smile for their identifying close-ups. Apart from that last detail it might be a commemorative documentary left over from the Bicentennial.

An early episode in the first series had a cute-as-hell subplot in which Charlie (Dule Hill), a bemused young black man who thought he was applying for a job as a messenger, gets appointed to the post of presidential aide. He finds himself, at segments end, in the very room where the president is addressing the nation on a crisis in the Middle East. "I've never felt anything like this before whispers the new recruit to the superior standing next to him: It doesn't go away" is the reply. The music swells again, as does everybodys bosom, with respect for the democratic process. Charlie wins the presidents respect by finding his lost glasses, and the president wins his by promising stricter gun controls. (Charlie's mother was a cop, killed on duty.)

The show is also in favour of imposing measured sanctions on rogue states rather than zapping them into oblivion (the president, who can be something of a hothead, has to be persuaded on this, but he sees the light), and though it feels the emotional pull toward imposing penalties for hate crimes, it thinks that the law should punish deeds rather than thoughts. It disapproves of intolerant fundamentalists, and of self-righteous investigators who persecute loyal presidential assistants for their alcoholic pasts.

It believes, endearingly, that there are measurable differences between Democrats and Republicans, and that the former are the good guys, though some of the others can be decent at heart. It is, in fact, embarrassingly liberal: embarrassing to me, at least, because I share most of its assumptions and still wish that it wouldn't keep trotting them out so virtuously.

One of the series five Emmys -- the writing one -- went to a Christmas episode, titled In Excelsis Deo. Here, as might be expected, the cuteness quotient went to danger levels. The president played uncle to visiting parties of quarrelling schoolchildren, and did it to the manner born; maybe hed been an actor. He also went present-shopping at an antiquarian bookstore, and refused to turn the trip into a photo-op. (The show, of course, turned it into one for him.)

Josh (Bradley Whitford), his deputy chief of staff, protested that he'd rather be dropped from the Washington Monument than go along. "This is Christmas, Josh, said the Chief, with a twinkle. There'll be time for both."

On this show, even the twinkles are solemn. Another storyline involved Toby (Richard Schiff), the communciations director, described in the publiicty material as "sleepless -- to be distinguished from C.J. (Allison Janney), the press secretary, who is merely tireless."

Toby discovers that a dead street person is actually a Korean War vet, and organizes a state funeral for him, in the process encountering the sweetest, least threatening bunch of homeless you ever saw. This prompts the presidents secretary to recall her own twin sons ("I dressed them different but they still did everything together) who were killed as medical officers in Vietnam. They were so young," she says, "its hard not to think that right then they needed their mother." The music got especially insistent at this point.

It's probably a reflection on the Emmys rather than on the series that this tear-jerker of a show was singled out for special notice. The succeeding instalment was far jollier, with Roger Rees (known to me from Nichlas Nickleby and to everybody else from Cheers) turning up as a dissipated English aristocrat to sort out a border-conflict between India and Pakistan; the Oriental restaurateur from a famous episode of Seinfeld promoted to the post of Chinese ambassador; and Whitford and Rob Lowe invigoratingly turning the screws on a puritanical sneak who seems to be the series' stand-in for Ken Starr. Indeed, as pretentious soaps go, The West Wing is decent entertainment. (Nearly everybody in it seems to be single, allowing increased scope for romantic entanglements.)

But theres no way it can be taken seriously; everybody in it is too nice and the language is far too clean. With what we know of the real White House, and what we can imagine of the pressures, can anyone credit this absence of profanity? As a theatre critic, I know only too well how boring four-letter words can become; but The Sopranos has shown us how creatively they can be used.(So indeed has The Larry Sanders Show, which in its own mode was a far more credible political drama; while as character creations The West Wing people have nothing like the depth of the brothers in Frasier.) I dont believe that the way ahead for TV drama is just to make more gangster series (though it's a safe bet that the networks now do) but The Sopranos has acustomed us to a thickness of texture that makes the competition seem thinly transparent. The mutterings and the overheard dialogue of Tony and his various families may sometimes be trying to the ear, but once you've heard them the polite WASP lucidity of the presidents men and women is, inescapably, yesterdays news.

Black & White Photo: Martin Sheen, Richard Schiff and Rob Lowe play ambitious but agreeable characters -- and they're all Democrats. (Color photo ran in Toronto/Late edition.) ;
2000-10-05-it-s-a-wonderful-life-singer-:
Rosemary Clooney and her band, Big Kahuna and the Copa Cat Pack, perform tonight at Roy Thomson Hall, 8 p.m. Call (416) 872-4255 for ticket information.

I have always wanted to hear Rosemary Clooney sing The Way You Look Tonight. She never has: Not on record, anyway.

But a week or so ago I got to interview her on the phone -- she was at home in Los Angeles, preparing for a tour that brings her tonight to Roy Thomson Hall -- and mentioned the song to her. She immediately started singing it, beautifully and with confidence.

Talking to Ms. Clooney, I discovered, is a little like attending one of her shows: In any setting, she exudes intelligent friendliness.

Her career began in Maysville, Ky., where she was born in 1928, and made her first singing appearance there at the age of three on the stage of the local movie theatre.

Somewhat later, she and her sister, Betty, began singing on local radio stations. Just after the Second World War they got themselves a job with the popular Tony Pastor band. Rosemary went single, had a colossal hit in 1951 with the novelty song Come on-a My House -- which she recorded pretty much under duress.

She stayed on top through the 1950s, but her career began to slide in the 1960s, when pop-music tastes changed radically and when her own life -- including her marriage to actor Jose Ferrer -- fell apart.

She had a breakdown, and was committed to a mental hospital. She now simply refers to this event as "my illness. When she got out, she embarked on two new and enduring relationships. One was with an old friend, a former dancer named Dante DiPaolo (a couple of years ago they finally got round to getting married). The other was with a small California-based record label, Concord Jazz, which in 1976 asked her to record an album with a small jazz group. The album was called Everything's Coming Up Rosie. Twenty-five years later, she is still recording for Concord, at the rate of one CD a year.

It is an amazing thing to be with one company for as long as I have," she says. "I can choose the material I want to do.

This material -- which she characteristically performs with humour, warmth, insistent rhythm, and a unique kind of triumphant bittersweetness -- centres on what has become known as the Great American Songbook," the standard repertoire drawn largely from the songs of such composers as Cole Porter, Richard Rodgers and Irving Berlin. She and Tony Bennett are considered the foremost modern interpreters of these compositions.

It isn't exactly the world she was born into, but its one she speedily became part of. Indeed, even her home in Los Angeles resonates with the ghosts of some of Americas most important pop artists.

"I'm sitting now in the same room where I last saw Billie Holiday, she told me. I'm sitting looking at the sunshine just as I did then. Only then the room was full of smoke. And Billie was drinking gin."

The house she was talking from -- the one shes lived in for decades -- once belonged to George Gershwin. For years, Georges lyricist brother Ira was her neighbour.

These days, Love Is Here To Stay, the last song George composed, is one of her two favourite closing numbers. (Her other choice is James Taylor's philosophical The Secret of Life.)

At 71, Clooney has become one of the singers people go to for wisdom. She's also one of the few who can dispense it palatably.

In her Toronto show, shell be doing some things from her new album, Brazil, but shell also be harking back to "things I did with [Count] Basie.

I'll probably do I Concentrate on You -- a Cole Porter song that's achieved honourary Latin status --"but I havent spoken to [pianist] John Oddo yet." (I stole him from Woody Herman.)

She obviously cant sing precisely as she used to do. "The breath- support began to go" when she was 55.

"I cope with the changes in my voice as I plan the show. I try not to change anything about the song itself; I want to sing it as it was written. That's what I've always felt most comfortable with."

Black & White Photo: Fred Prouser, Reuters / Singer Rosemary Clooney with her nephew, actor George Clooney. ;
