Till Oct. 29. Box office: (416)-531-1827.

LIQUOR GUNS KARATE

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

You have to wait until the end of Morwyn Brebner's new play -- a short evening that seems long -- to encounter the title. Apparently, signs offering Liquor, Guns, Karate can be found dotted among the drive-through emporia in the strip malls of Los Angeles. Since my own acquaintance with L.A. is very slight, I'll take the author's word for it. The play seems to subscribe to the belief -- usually more prevalent in U.S. drama than in Canadian -- that if you stick a phrase in your title and intone it at a crucial point of your text, it will be very meaningful.

Let's see: You can kill yourself with liquor, you can kill other people with karate, and you can do both with guns; and of the play's four characters at least two -- the male ones -- might be desperate enough to try one or the other. It seems, though, that it's the sheer arbitrariness of the menu that has taken the author's fancy. The play's last line is something about the folly of going through life on the assumption that one thing will link up with another.

The play itself may conceivably be about the arbitrariness of life. Philosophically it's valid enough, but it's difficult to dramatize. It makes a play seem, well, arbitrary.

We begin in a bar: something of a coup de theatre since, when we arrive and look Sue LePage's creamy set, it looks like it will represent the living room of somebody's ritzy house. So indeed it will, most of the time; but first off, when the lights go down and then up again, we discover that its back wall was a false one and that we have been transported to somewhere dull and smoky in another part of town. A young Canadian woman and a middle-aged American man are trying to get sufficiently crocked to pick one another up. They make barbed, flippant conversation that varies from the effortfully whimsical (she recalls going to bed with a man who couldn't pronounce his r's and wondering if she would catch "a sexually transmitted speech impediment") to the genuinely funny (he claims to be a failed writer; she says this town seems to be full of them, and vaguely adds "you can't swing a cat..." It's the way her voice trails off that's hilarious.) We pay attention because there is something recognizably at stake here: The scene appeals to the basic human desire to see if two people are going to get it on together. Much later in the play, the woman, whose name is Laurel, will tell us -- quite acutely, I think -- that what she really likes about sex is the moment at which she knows it's going to happen; and it seems to tie in. I have a quite separate, and probably unworthy, suspicion that the first scene was written in very late; it seems out of style with the rest of the play, in which neither the characters nor the story seems to have any drives whatever.

They talk as if they have. The plush house turns out to have been the abode of Laurel's just-deceased father. She has come down from Toronto to collect what she hopes will be a sizeable inheritance. With her comes her boyfriend, Chuck, a stockbroker who needs the break -- both kinds of break -- since back home he's about to be had up for malpractice. Irving, Laurel's bar-room encounter of the previous night and a man who has failed at many things besides writing, comes in quest of her, smitten And Irving's long-estranged daughter, whose name coincidentally is Lauren, comes in quest of him, bearing divorce papers from his equally long-estranged wife.

And round and round the four of them go. Things do happen -- a car crash, a suicide attempt, the reading of the will, some kind of seizure -- and if you could draw a graph of the play's action it might well come out as a straight line, but if feels circular. And there seems be no point at which the audience can break the circle and get involved. The characters keep making long speeches about their previous lives but we don't believe in them because we don't believe in the people. Indeed, the more we learn of them, the less we believe. Whatever spark of language or insight it takes to bring characters to life the moment they step on a stage, this play not has not been able to provide. Some sharp moments do rise above the morass. Chuck's doomed efforts to get himself a new life by selling a movie idea down the phone are painfully entertaining, though prolonged beyond the limits of credible masochism. Most of the time, though, one waits for it all to stop.

The actors, under Jackie Maxwell's direction, play at full throttle throughout, which is probably the only way to do it. Victor Ertmanis as Irving comes off best: He's a burly jelly, and the mere fact he's older than the others helps give him weight, and even texture. Laurel is Waneta Storms, best known for her skill at waifs (Faust, The Diary of Anne Frank); here she plays a waif with ribs of steel, and gives some life to a character who is really an intellectual construct (she's described as "a poster-girl for apathy"). Tom Barnett is agreeable as Chuck, a loser in winner's clothing. Ann Baggley as Lauren has the hardest job; the moment she comes on, she's required to orate, in the centre of what suddenly seems a very big and empty stage, and she goes on to make detailed accusations against a man she hardly knows. The near-duplication of the two women's names yields nothing usable except a joke about changing the last letter on a tattoo.

The play takes place in the wake of an atypical Los Angeles ice storm. At its close, Laurel and Chuck share a humorous fantasy about skating their way to the airport, past the malls and past the postings of the play's title phrase. It seems to be intended as comment on the aimless sterility of Californian or maybe just modern life: In other words, a received idea of monstrous proportions. If the play is meant to be about Los Angeles, iced-up or otherwise, then it hasn't worked at it hard enough. We seem to be in Sam Shepard's spiritual territory, which is not a territory I've ever much cared for. But at least with Shepard, you feel as if you're at the heart of the desert; here, you're stuck in a suburb.

Black & White Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / ANN BAGGLEY, TOM BARNETT: A play that seems circular. ;
2000-10-07-of-white-mice-and-men:
White Mice runs to Oct. 15. For ticket information, contact the Theatre Passe Muraille box office at (416) 504-7529.

Darren O'Donnell, who wrote and directed White Mice, is also half of its cast. He and his colleague, Bruce Hunter, play just what the title says they play, and they establish this through a highly effective piece of theatrical shorthand. Each appears in a snazzy ensemble of shirts and jeans, with the unexpected accessory of a long, twirlable tail. In O'Donnells previous piece, Boxhead, the actors spent the entire show with their heads encased in boxes. Actors with tails turn out to be more fun to watch than actors in boxes, and a lot easier to listen to. Besides, what they say is remarkably straightforward. The subject is racism. The play is about how white mice -- white Canadian mice -- treat black and brown mice. We have people acting like rodents who act like people.

It takes one minute to get the idea, and another 10 or 15 to stop resenting it. The actors are acting brilliantly, but in this kind of show we take that for granted. Hunter plays Douglas, a stay-at-home mouse, and ODonnell is his brother, Robert, who goes out into the world and keeps returning with ever-more-disturbing news. The dialogue is a sustained crosstalk act, full of fast patter and dialogue that almost overlaps, and the performers' phrasing and timing are impeccable. Oh, they're fur and whiskers, but theyre funny.

We havent had a sustained anthropomorphic satire in these parts for some time, not since a certain record-breaking English musical last made the rounds. While Cats is away, White Mice will play. The comparison is instructive, since a very irritating thing about Cats is its redundancy; if the cats were all meant to be human types anyway, why spend so much energy on dressing them up?

White Mice initially irritated me in the same way; if they want to attack racism in Canada, then why not do it head-on, instead of resorting to coy metaphor? But the strategy justifies itself. It isn't a matter of sparing our feelings. The show doesn't; its as didactic as any piece of theatre youre ever likely to see. It's a way of making the didactic theatrical, of having a style.

It's a very self-conscious style, the joke thoroughly shared with the audience. At one point, Robert says "white people" instead of white mice, and then begins frantically backtracking. Douglas wonders aloud why anyone would ever want to play to an audience of white mice, and then gets similarly flustered. (When the lights went up, I conducted a spot check; the Passe Muraille audience was composed predominantly of white mice, but not exclusively.) The duo begin by talking, fairly whimsically, about "cap-ap-ap-italistic prop-pop-aganda" (I hope I counted the syllables right) and about drinking cappuccino weenies (I can hardly bear to type that) on College Street. Bay Street and Rosedale are also good for automatic laughs, even at a time when the script is getting fairly sanguinary.

Increasingly, Robert confronts Douglas with discomfiting facts and figures about how the white mice in Toronto, in Canada, in North America, in the Western world, treat mice of other complexions. Douglas keeps protesting that it isnt that bad, but as the debate progresses he is left with fewer and fewer legs to stand on. (Two fewer than the average mouse, for a start.) Robert quotes Amnesty International and, less expectedly, Adolf Hitler. It seems that in Mein Kampf, Hitler claimed to have modelled his racial policies on the American settlers treatment of their indigenous population. Having advanced this thesis, Robert ratchets it up and challenges Douglas to deny that he is living in the realized embodiment of Hitler's dream. Douglas can't. Its as easy to pick holes in Roberts arguments as in a piece of cheese.

"Hitler's dream" consisted of ridding the world of Jews, something that in North America has noticeably not happened. Even if you want to play the game (a dangerously frivolous one) of equating one oppressed people with another, the fact remains that if Hitler had not been defeated in war he would have killed every Jew in Europe. The slaughter of the American Indians was ineradicably shameful, but it was not as thoroughgoing and it stopped. Exploitation is not the same as murder or as (another of Robert's buzzwords) slavery; slavery consists of employing people without paying them, and of literally buying and selling them. If "the white race" -- according to Robert, a cultural construct defined by its enslavement of other races -- only came into existence around 1800, how does he explain the existence of slavery, usually conducted on racial lines, for most of recorded history? Is symphonic music any less, or less worthy, an example of white culture than jazz is of black? (Assuming, as I dont, that a work of art has to be rated as an example of something.)

The play is not a balanced contest; Robert wins every round. Its true that he turns out to have his own agenda (it has to do with his love life) but this is less than the twist it promises to be. Douglas doesn't press him on it very hard and Douglas ends up converted, a liberal-turned-firebrand, and hysterically asks Robert what he should do. (Robert can't tell him.) We, who have identified with Douglas all the way, are left writhing with him. Because, even if the play overstates its points, it makes them, unanswerably; there may not be genocide or slavery out there, but there is the next worst thing. And it makes them by a legitimate manipulation of its own medium.

The play ends with the two mice settling down to the giant piece of cheese that has stood temptingly on their table throughout. They are like the protagonists of Wallace Shawns monologue, The Fever, who could find no moral justification for his own privileged existence but went on with it anyway. ODonnell, like Shawn, has stated the problem by writing a play, directing it, co-designing it (with Naomi Campbell) and, finally, by acting in it -- which, of course, is not quite the same thing as acting on it. Maybe it is; I wonder whether he thinks so. White Mice is a production of Mammalian Diving Reflex; the mouse tails are by Lori Hickling, and they are, like everything else about the presentation, excellent. -

Color Photo: David Kinsman / Mammalian Diving Reflex's production of White Mice with Darren O'Donnell as Robert, top, and Bruce Hunter as Douglas. ;

Tarragon Extra Space

---

In the immortal words of the late George Burns: "The secret of acting is sincerity. If you can fake that, you've got it made." The same principle applies to allied trades, such as commercial voice- overs.

Radio: 30, written and performed by Chris Earle, takes us inside the head of one of its practitioners.

His name is Ron; we meet him, alone in his recording booth, on a day when he's taping a tribute to a burger restaurant.

It's also -- this being a play -- the day on which things go crucially wrong. It's hardly his fault. He's a skilled and conscientious worker, known for the low-key urgency, the buttery persuasiveness with which he can infuse any sales pitch: what's known in the business as "giving it that Ron thing." Today -- as presumably on most days -- he is no sooner inside the studio than he begins running through his script, trying out different inflections and noting the best in the margin. He goes for a take, and the recording engineer -- whom we hear but never see -- can hardly contain his admiration; he calls Ron a machine and a one-take wonder.

However, the sponsors -- who of course are sitting out there in the control room, with powers of life-and-death over the session -- ask for one tiny adjustment: will Ron make one phrase sound slightly more "quirky"? ("A little bit wry?" Ron himself helpfully supplements, and notes it down.)

And then there's discovered to be a slight factual error in the copy, so they have to adjust for that, and -- gradually but inexorably -- the whole thing starts to unravel.

Part of the problem is that Ron, in the intervals between takes, has let his mind wander. He has started to think. He has thought about his previous career as an actor, which was much harder because "it's not just your voice -- you have to lie with your whole body."

He has pondered the paradox of advertising, in which everybody claims not to believe but for which the clients still go on paying. He has reminisced about his personal life, which was brilliant until, as he says, he slept with his best friend's wife.

The implied link between the public and private values of people in the advertising game may seem a bit glib. The convention by which Ron talks to us when not talking into the mic is awkward at first. But the show easily overrides these objections.

The script is very accomplished, the action moving tensely and steadily forward while the speech proves full of echoes and parallels and verbal trap doors that fall open to reveal more about the speaker than he would want anyone -- especially himself -- to know.

"This is good work for a shy person," says Ron, and "shy," in his case, could also mean "remote" or simply "cold." The privileged solitude of the booth, and the inhabitant's heightened relationship with his own voice, are captured with an ease that I, as a sometime practitioner, found eerily recognizable.

I hesitate to congratulate Earle's performance on its truthfulness, but it's 100% convincing. Ron, youngish but no longer quite young, comes off ingratiating and well-meaning and not quite as shallow as he might want to be. He is troubled; he knows that he is only as good as his last performance, and that the Ron thing may go out of style; he has seen it happen himself, to older voice-over talents. He lives always with the knowledge that the last polite "thank you -- that's it" may mean that they think he's wonderful, or it may mean that they've decided to pay him off and get someone else.

Crucial to the show, and superbly executed, is the off-stage characterization of Mike, the guy at the controls, by Robert Smith. Mike has worked many times with Ron and is a fervent admirer of his skills; he may even be a friend. Or he may be an enemy, plotting with the eternally paranoid sponsors. Or he may just be chillingly neutral.

Shari Hollett directed the show, and also worked on the script. And, as a collector of unorthodox credits, I also note the presence of Caroline Gillis, noted actress, as "Girl Friday." I don't know what she did but I'm sure, given the general level of proficiency, she did it well.

Black & White Photo: John Scully / Writer/performer Chris Earle. ;
2000-10-09-pinter-s-betrayal-becomes-a-m:
When Harold Pinters Betrayal was first staged in London in 1978, the critics received it disdainfully. Since then, words have been feverishly eaten, and the play has become one of its authors most- admired and most-revived.

The new Soulpepper Theatre Company production, which launches the National Arts Centre's Studio Stage Series tomorrow, takes it a step further along the road to canonization.

One reason the play was scorned at its premiere was that it concerns English middle-class adultery, and everyone had had quite enough of that. Besides, Pinter was felt to have forsaken his roots. The man who had made his name writing about psychotic tramps and seaside boarding houses was devoting himself in this play to the emotional entanglements of the urban literati -- in other words, the world in which he himself now moved.

Worse yet, his characters weren't even real writers, just prosperous hangers-on: the people in Betrayal are Jerry, a literary agent; Robert, his best friend and a publisher; and Emma, wife of the latter and mistress of the former.

Also, audiences were tired -- justifiably -- of what had become known as the Pinter style: the icy-smooth, deliberate manner that Peter Hall, for many years Pinters regular director, seemed to employ as a form of elegant intimidation. Every word, every movement, came loaded with significance, even though nobody could be sure what they signified.

Betrayal, though, didnt even offer the consolations of obscurity. Its story happens to unfold in reverse chronological order, but apart from that, its development is straightforward -- or , at least, straightbackward. Things that seem puzzling in one scene are invariably clarified in the next.

The play's first scene shows Jerry and Emma meeting for a drink, some years after the end of the affair. We gather that Jerry would quite like to rekindle the relationship, and that Emma wouldn't. The last scene shows Jerry declaring his passion for the first time and Emma responding. The mood, which survives even the sudden appearance of the about-to-be-cuckolded Robert, is one of delicate tenderness. In hindsight, the beginning of their romance seems like its high point. Once consummated, it seems to have declined very quickly into a routine of lying, logistics and rendezvous in a rented flat in an unfashionable part of London.

Like all Pinters plays, the piece takes shape as a series of psychological power struggles. In any given scene, two of the characters will share some piece of knowledge of which the third is ignorant. So each of the trio is at once both victor and victim: It depends which way the light is shining.

From one viewpoint, Jerry seems to hold all the aces. He has the woman he desires, and none of the attendant responsibilities. But he still has to live with the fact that Robert has first claim on Emma, and he is in constant fear of losing her. Robert is the deceived husband, but he has been enjoying his own infidelities. Besides, about halfway through the action, Emma tells him about her affair, thereby strengthening the bond between them and making Jerry even more the outsider.

Emma, meanwhile, is pointedly -- even brutally -- excluded from the camaraderie of the two men, symbolized by their regular games of squash, though these seem to be more talked about than enjoyed. (As also, from what we gather, seems to be the case with sex.) Still, Emma has had both men, and has moved on to a third: The play has a fourth, unseen, character, a writer, Casey, whom Jerry represents and Robert publishes. They live off him but he walks off with their woman -- the authors revenge.

The relationships pulsate, unspoken words conveying invisible words. (The spoken words are, as usual, brilliant.) As in any good play, all the characters have areas of unknowability. Some, however, are more unknowable than others. And, as often with Pinter, the woman is little more than an indecipherable, much-coveted Sphinx.

Harold Pinter's Betrayal is in the NAC Studio tomorrow through Oct. 21. Evening performances are at 8 p.m., Saturday matinees are at 2 p.m. on the 14th and 21st. Tickets, from $23 to $28, are available at the NAC box office or, with surcharges, through Ticketmaster, 755-1111. Tickets for a special 8 p.m. preview performance tonight are $15.

GEOMETRY IN VENICE

Factory Theatre, Toronto

I wish I had read more Henry James. That isn't a feeling I have very often. I find James -- as a novelist, short-story writer and essayist -- extremely resistible: socially narrow and esthetically prim.

From time to time, though, I am confronted by a decent dramatisation of one of his works. James -- who, despite repeated efforts, never wrote a successful play himself -- has nevertheless been the cause of good plays in others. And then I start wondering about the source, and about how closely it resembles the piece before me.

I wonder especially in the case of Michael Mackenzie's Geometry in Venice. This derives from a James novella entitled The Tutor and obviously has a complex relationship to it, one that extends to bringing James himself on stage as a character. The play was first staged 10 years ago. After its initial Toronto run, it was staged in French in Montreal, and ran there five years. It therefore ranks as a Canadian classic: a phrase that usually chills the blood, especially when it heralds an actual revival. A classic is a work that resonates beyond its own immediate time and place: Geometry in Venice is one of the few acclaimed Canadian plays that might conceivably do that. And Henry James, though I hate to admit it, must probably take part of the credit.

The action concerns a late 19th-century English family, upper- class and on their uppers -- i.e. broke. They have holed up in Venice, though in the course of the action they move to Paris, and their name is Moreen. (Only James would do a thing like that: You keep wondering why the lady of the house keeps calling her spouse Maureen, and why he, a peppery type, puts up with it.) Their source of income is uncertain but Mr. Moreen periodically sallies forth (his phrase) and sometimes, apparently, he returns with loot.

Mrs. Moreen is an apparently gracious lady with literary inclinations. They have a 23-year-old daughter, Amy, whom they are anxious to marry off, an anxiety Amy herself more than shares. They also have a pubescent son, Morgan, about whom they are deeply concerned. He was born with a heart-defect -- they call it "a flaw" - - and they worry about the effect on him either of over-exertion and overexcitement. Previously, his mother has attended to his education; now, they decide to hire a tutor, a young Canadian (the playwright's touch), also literary, and named Pemberton.

Teacher and pupil take to one another immediately once Pemberton recognizes Morgan to be exceptionally intelligent. That's putting it mildly: The boy seems to be a genius. Already conversationally fluent in Latin (though he knows, to Pemberton's dismay, nothing of grammar), he speedily masters Greek. From there he moves on to the sciences and especially to geometry, for which his tutor has a logician's passion.

The only snag is that the Moreens keep neglecting to pay Pemberton, and seem hurt when he raises the subject. Finally he presents them with an ultimatum, which Mrs. M. defuses by taking him into her bed. Here, I imagine, the play makes explicit what the story left decorously clouded. Certainly, when the Moreens' fortunes take a final tumble, the language unleashed is beyond anything any Victorian novelist, early or late, would have considered proper. It's convincing, though.

In its master-student relationship, not to mention its mistress- student relationship, in its sense of an ancien regime in decline, in its literary trappings, the play now seems strongly reminiscent of Tom Stoppard's Arcadia, though in fact it came first. (Did England's favourite playwriting son haunt the theatres of Ontario and Quebec a decade ago? Investigate.)

It, too, sets up an opposition between mathematical rigour and emotional chaos, though it's more talked about than felt. The play never fully justifies its title. It's not as elaborate a fireworks display as Arcadia, but it has its own wit and its own tension, each sharpening the other, and it rises to a poignantly ironic climax that seems both surprising and inevitable.

Ken Gass' production at the Factory divides, if you'll pardon the solecism, into two unequal halves. On the good side, illuminating everything and everyone it touches and leaving the audience most touched of all, there is Luke Kirby's remarkable performance as Morgan, a wonderful mixture of intellectual prodigy and emotional infant. Almost morbidly considerate of others, he clings desperately to his new friendship with his master; the homosexual overtones are finely shaded in. In these,

Graeme Somerville acts Pemberton with perfect sympathy and perfect tact. He is far less at ease, though, when he crosses over to the other part of the play to meet the Moreens, probably because they don't seem at home there themselves.

Graham Harley as Moreen repeats the oily robber-baron performance he gave this summer in Much Ado About Nothing. It was effective there, since it cast a new light on a character generally seen as benevolent, but here it plays like a cartoon. At least, though, it works on its own terms.

Nola Augustson as his wife tries hard for elegance but cannot reach it, and without that initial veneer, the cracks beneath go for nothing. Nor is pumping emotion into the lines the same thing as portraying intellectual passion. Juno Mills-Cockell's Amy (an underwritten role) has the same complaint on a smaller scale: There's no shock when she lets loose with four-letter words because there has been no composure to shatter.

Victoria Wallace provides a stark palazzo set, lit (by Rebecca Picherak) with excessive dankness, and demanding a more rigorous level of acting and staging than it gets.

I've left out James himself (Adrian Churchill). He appears as Amy's escort, of whom the family entertain vain hopes, then vanishes. Finally, he returns when all is ruined and is told by Mrs. Moreen (in one of the actress' finer moments) to get lost. As a person, he has aroused expectations he could not fulfil; as an author he has set in motion passions he could not control, and that his characters have had the gall to take more seriously than he ever could. That, at least, is how I read it, though maybe I'm projecting my own feelings about the novelist onto the playwright.

The eveming is dedicated the late and dearly missed Mira Friedlander. And, though imperfect, I think it would have pleased her.

2000-10-14-little-joy-in-this-musical:
Joy runs until tomorrow at the Joseph Workman Theatre, Queen Street West. Tickets are $15. Call the box office at (416) 583-4339.

Obviously there is irony intended, but the title Joy refers to a character rather than an emotion. The producers bill their show as "a musical about depression" and they use the word "depression" in the clinical sense. They are also, perhaps unintentionally, using the word "musical" in a clinical sense.

Joy is a production of the Workman Theatre Project, which operates out of the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health on Queen Street West, and which -- apart from operating theatrical training programs -- regularly mounts shows cast from a combination of its own members and Equity full-timers. The present show has a script by Maja Ardal, former director of the Toronto Young People's Theatre, and a score by the increasingly ubiquitous Joey Miller, already represented in town by Outrageous. As a social enterprise, it's admirable; as a theatre piece, it's worthy and well-performed, but flawed.

The eponymous Joy is a woman who apparently has everything to live for but cannot believe it; less and less can she believe it and the spiral seems unstoppable, except through chemical intervention, which brings its own problems. Inevitably, her story recalls the recent suicide of a Toronto woman who was a psychiatrist. This story is not quite as horrific -- there are, for one merciful thing, no children involved -- but the echoes, though involuntary (musicals don't get written and produced that quickly) are inescapable. They work to the show's advantage in sharpening our antennae, but they also raise our expectations. We want to be told things: There is information and there are insights that we accept we cannot have in real life, but that we instinctively demand in the theatre.

Ardal's script, unfortunately, stays on an anecdotal level. These things happen to Joy, and then these other things happen to Joy. There are hints that her marriage is sterile and unsympathetic, but the means chosen to demonstrate this are so predictable that we can't tell whether we're dealing with a failed relationship or simply uninspired writing.

Perhaps that's the job of the songs. But that's another problem. As staged by Patricia Vanstone -- in a plodding, opaque fashion -- Joy is only a musical because it has songs. (That's why I called the classification clinical.) Which raises another question: Why -- except that everything seems to be nowadays -- is this show a musical? Musicals don't have to be celebratory, but they have somehow to raise the emotional and imaginative stakes. It's hard enough to write a play about illness, mental or physical, and make it anything more than a display of symptoms. The only way music might help is to make the whole thing a kind of phantasmagoria; there are occasional hints of this in Joy but they're kept in check by everybody's honest desire to avoid the sensational. There are some nice things in Miller's score: an early ballad for the heroine that begins by sounding like Andrew Lloyd Webber's Unexpected Song (from Song & Dance), then strikes out on interesting paths of its own; a despairing cry from her largely uncomprehending mother. Much of the time, though, the songs are stuck with reiterating emotions we already know about or with delivering exposition, which is hard work.

Jayne Lewis in the title role does well; script and score between them give her something to bite on and bite she does. She acts astringently, sings immaculately, and is never for a moment self- pitying or sentimental. She runs the show. Mary Ann McDonald is similarly powerful as Joy's mother. Nine-year-old Adanya Dunn is precociously professional as a ghostly little girl; and Mike Lummis makes a delicate impact as a sympathetic fellow patient.

As a self-described product of "the mental health community," the piece tells us remarkably little about that community. I don't suggest, though, that such scenes should be musicalized. We need to re-think what musicals can and should do. The prevailing wisdom is that they make forbidding subjects "accessible." They may make them more superficially approachable, but they are likely to make the most important issues even harder to get at. -

HYSTERIA

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

An aged psychiatrist, who only happens to be Sigmund Freud, is bent over with his hand firmly stuck inside a wellington boot. Beside him, standing on one leg, is his doctor, who appears to be trying a female undergarment on for size. There are logical, even respectable, reasons for all of this, but a casual visitor coming upon the scene would have no way of knowing that.

Naturally, in strict accordance with the rules of farce, such a visitor promptly appears. He's Salvador Dali, easily identifiable by the most distinctive moustache south of Groucho Marx. Another man might be appalled by the tableau, but he is entranced. What Dali merely dreams, he exclaims, "you live!"

I have been describing a moment from Hysteria, by the British playwright Terry Johnson: An extreme moment, but not an unrepresentative one. It is also a moment with antecedents. Tom Stoppard built a one-act piece called After Magritte around just such a stage picture, and he works several of them into his metaphysical farce, Jumpers. This is the second time in five days Ive invoked Stoppard, but it cant be helped: Blame the zeitgeist. He also, in Travesties, established the genre of the confrontational extravaganza by bringing together -- on a slender historical pretext -- James Joyce, Vladimir Leni, and Tristan Tzara, whose Dadaism, by blessed coincidence, prepared the ground for Dali's Expressionism. Johnson, though certainly his own man, has been following in Stoppard's footsteps for years. His first notable play, Insignificance, corralled Albert Einstein with Marilyn Monroe, bringing on a couple of more average Joes -- McCarthy and diMaggio - - in supporting roles. A few years ago, he had a charming though maybe unexportable piece about the stars of the Carry On movies. Before that, he had built another play, Dead Funny, around the same rude tradition of British comedy, though in that one he kept the famous comics off stage. It has never been seen in Canada, though its central icon, Benny Hill, is surely enough of an international name for audiences here to get the point.

Dead Funny is his best play. Hysteria, however, is a brilliant one, and its been given a superb production by Morris Panych, though the two are not invariably in perfect sync. The action has some roots in historical fact: Freud and Dali did meet in England in 1938 when both were refugees from imminent war and -- in Freuds case -- more than imminent persecution. Dali visited Freud, now dying of cancer, as an act of homage toward his spiritual father -- the man who prided himself on painting the unconscious acknowledging the man who, crudely speaking, discovered it.

In fact, the play is a triple study of Freud and the idea of paternity. The old supershrink receives two other callers at his Hampstead home. One, a composite of two historical figures, is Yehuda, his physician. Like Freud, he's a Jew; unlike Freud, he's a believer, and he takes great exception to his distinguished patients last work, Moses and Monotheism, which would rob Judaism of its spiritual father by claiming that Moses was actually an Egyptian.

Hes prepared to do anything to stop these ideas being published at such a time, including destroying the manuscript. Finally, and crucially, there is Jessica, a young woman who crashes into Freud's study and demands that he analyze her -- or rather, that he re- enact with her his 40-year-old analysis of a woman in Vienna.

At first, he had attributed this woman's hysterical symptoms to her having been raped in childhood by her father. Then, noticing he seemed to be making this diagnosis with suspicious regularity, he changed his mind and said shed imagined this abuse, in fact desired it, and that her condition was in effect her own fault: another blanket diagnosis and no less suspect than its predecessor. (The phenomenon of false-memory syndrome suggests were still paying the price of both.)

Jessica has a strong personal stake in this case, and she is not about to let Freud off the hook. She accuses him -- surely unfairly - - of trimming his sails to the prevailing Viennese winds: He didn't want to antagonize his wealthy male patrons. More uncomfortably the point is Freud's realization that he himself both had, and was, a father.

One other historical, perhaps even hysterical, footnote demands mention: Apparently, shortly after arriving in London, Freud was taken to see Rookery Nook, a classic English farce. He tells Jessica it had made him laugh; she says he lacks taste. (She seems humourless enough to be a theatre critic.) Anyway, the experience seems to have affected him: His own life becomes farcical. Jessica sheds most of her clothes and hides in a closet. He cannot afford to let her be seen, because that would give Yehuda a blackmailing handle against him. So doors furiously open and close throughout. Dali, when he appears, is instantly aroused at the sight of Jessica, and joins happily in.

Johnson, unlike Stoppard, does not write farce. He uses farce, which is a trickier proposition. He doesnt tie up all his loose ends with Stoppards dazzling neatness (though he does pretty well) and he doesn't have the same sustained gaiety of tone. Stoppard, even at his gravest, writes happy plays, making him probably unique among modern playwrights. Johnson writes dark plays and they are likely to break up into comic slabs and serious ones. Jessica's concerns here push Dalis and Yehudas into the background. Not everything in this play is what it seems. Or rather, it is what it seems but you have to wait until near the end to discover just what that is. There are one or two hints on the way, through. The time seems to fluctuate between 1938 (Kristallnacht is in the papers) and '39 (there are air raids). And you may notice, when you return from the intermission, that Ken MacDonald's set has reversed its position.

This set, which has a family likeness to the one MacDonald designed for Panychs production of The Overcoat, is gorgeous: a spacious white chamber that goes golden under the lights and with which the costumes, Freuds especially, are colour co-ordinated. The wall is composed entirely of filing cabinets. It isn't quite what the author ordered -- he wanted to disarm us with naturalism and I know Hampstead well enough to assure you this isn't it -- but its a trade-off worth making.

Toward the end, the play unleashes a surrealist maelstrom that this production, in a veritable Panych-attack, magnificently realizes. The physical comedy, too, is deliciously done, though the verbal sometimes suffers. There is more snap in the lines, and there should be more pace, than appears here.

The visuals may have soaked up some of the actors energy. Eric Peterson's Freud has great intelligence and a fine, sharp outline, but he doesn't command the stage as he should. The plays coherence is that its his agony, in all its aspects, but here he seems just one among equals. Peter Donaldson's Yehuda is somewhat stiff and not noticeably Jewish, though that's what the character is there for. David Storch, though, is a delightful grown-up schoolboy of a Dali. One of the plays charms is that he, of all people, functions as the audiences representative, the nearest thing on stage to an average man. He also gets a memorable come-uppance when Freud dismisses his painting as a conscious representation of the unconscious, rather than the real thing.

Kristen Thomson's Jessica is absolutely the real thing, a performance to rank with her work in Oleanna and Streetcar. Funny and determined, capable of both bravado and bravura, she can switch in and out of farcical gear in a second. And when it comes to the traumatic re-enactment at the heart of the play, she is movingly inside it and lucidly outside simultaneously.

At the beginning of a new season, CanStage, with this and Outrageous, has the two best shows in town. And Hysteria is not only the more hysterical but also the more truly outrageous of the pair.

Black & White Photo: Michael Cooper, Canadian Stage Company / Eric Peterson as Freud, Kristen Thomson as Jessica: Delicious farce. ;
2000-10-18-greetings-my-little-mooses-an:
"I don't do stand-up," said the Dame. "I'm a sit-down sort of person. I'm sitting down now. Of course I'm standing up, so that you can see me. But really I'm sitting down."

Dame Edna Everage, whose interactive theatrical experience, Dame Edna: The Royal Tour, opens at the Pantages Theatre on Nov. 7, was addressing the Toronto media at, fittingly, the Royal York Hotel yesterday.

Cameramen crammed the front rows, which is why she had to remain erect to be visible to the rest of us. She was worth seeing, attired in a lipstick-red dress, slit to reveal an impressive length of elegant leg. Her hair was its accustomed shade of electric mauve (natural wisteria, she calls it) and she wore her trademark rhinestone-encrusted spectacles.

Conspicuously absent from Dame Edna's entourage was Barry Humphries, the man she refers to as her manager. Asked about his responsibilities, she replied that his principal one seemed to be "to take an extortionate percentage of what I earn."

It is a suspicious fact that the two of them have never once been seen together in public.

She believes her Commonwealth roots (she is Australian) have given her an instinctive sympathy with the Dominion of Canada ("I love that word Dominion -- I think I'm a Dominionatrix"). She even speaks with sympathy about Toronto's garbage problem: She thinks we should compress it, send it to the Middle East, and use it to build a wall between the Israelis and the Palestinians.

She also speaks kindly, and with the brisk and generous candour that has always distinguished her, of her Toronto producers Ed and David Mirvish. "They seem to be lovely people. Of course, I haven't seen much of them yet. They're probably ghastly when you get to know them."

She has already developed an enormous affection for her new Canadian fan base: or, as she prefers to call us, "my little mooses and beavers."

SHEROES

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace

It starts like a celebration. Three chicks are dancing and drugging at a New Year's party. The conversations difficult to follow, what with the music and the general haze, but for the moment they seem pleased with themselves and with the world in general. They proclaim themselves "sheroes." Then one of them gets violently sick and goes home. The other two move on to look for further fun without her.

The rest of Sarah Martyns play, her first on a central stage, shows us in alternate bursts what came next and what had gone before. The three women turn out to be roommates. Rachel, the one who left alone, is a PhD mathematics student described (by the others) as a Jewish princess. We find her, three days into the year, still awaiting the return of Ester, an unemployed actress who survives by scamming the system; i.e., drawing multiple welfare cheques.

Rachel and Ester are lovers, and when Ester finally returns, Rachel is furious, especially when she learns that Ester's three- day adventure included having sex with a male drug dealer.

That's nothing to the fury of the third party, who is called Cat. The street-smartest of the three, Cat is Asian, a former waitress turned lap dancer; she decided, or so she tells us in the plays best speech, that if she was going to be humiliated in a service industry, then she was going to make serious money at it. She reveals that Ester also stole a large quantity of the guys stock- in-trade, thereby putting all of their lives in danger.

So that's the central situation: They wait, terrified, and wonder what to do. There's moderate suspense; were not actually on edge to discover what happens next, but since were there anyway we would quite like to find out.

There is also moderate humour; they spend a lot of time insulting one another. All three seem sexually insecure; the fact or the idea of being with a man can be used as either a boast or an accusation.

But the characterization is generally thin, and the flashbacks don't help much. Indeed, they hinder; they are built on the assumption that we are interested enough to want to know how the characters got where they are, and we aren't.

We see Ester meeting Cat for the first time and inviting her to move in; but there is nothing to make us believe that Cat has ever occupied the same space as the other two; theres no sense of the intimacy (not necessarily friendly and certainly not sexual) that arises in any shared domestic situation. Cats hostility is always that of the outsider. We see Rachel and Ester having their first lesbian encounter, which moves from declaration to consummation with amazing speed. (But what would I know?)

I don't know how ironically Martyn meant her title, but I doubt that she intended us to see her sheroes as zeroes. But it's impossible to take much interest in them, because theyre dumb. Their reaction to the stash on their premises is to start snorting it. In itself this isnt implausible, but it makes not only the characters listless but the action; it's as hard to deal with dramatically as a stageful of boozers would be. At one point, somebody invokes Trainspotting, but that (I only know the movie, not the book or the play) had some narrative strength, deriving from the protagonist's attempt to stay clean.

Much of the acting is listless, too, though it tries to boost excitement by shrill displays of forced rage. Cheri Maracle as Rachel shines briefly when she talks about her ambition to transform the study of math by teaching it with passion. Ester, played by the author, never seems either clever enough to have devised her welfare- fraud scheme or stupid enough to have put it into practice. Keira Loughran as Cat is not much more resourceful than the others at close verbal combat, but she has more opportunities to strike out on her own, and she plays them with a hard-as-nails relish thats the only really gripping thing in the evening.

The play proceeds to a half-hearted climax. Theres a blackout, and on the night I attended, as the lights came up and the actresses moved forward for their calls, I heard, from two seats away, the most damning question that can be asked at the finale of any show: "Is that all, then?"

Black & White Photo: David Kinsman, Theatre Passe Muraille / Get the point? Cheri Maracle as Rachel and Sarah Martyn, the play's writer, as Ester. ;

WRINKLES

Winter Garden Theatre, Toronto

TORONTO - Breezing, not to say wheezing, into town with the least attractive title and logo in recent memory, Wrinkles turns out to be surprisingly not bad. Bits of it are even good.

The show (which I saw at a preview) is a revue, on the old-fashioned model: a collection of songs and sketches from a variety of pens, delivered by an interweaving ensemble of half-a-dozen hard-working performers.

Unlike many revues of the past, it has a unifying theme. Or, to put it another way, all the jokes are on the same subject. The theme, of course, is age and ageing -- though how old you have to be to qualify for the show's attention is left uncertain.

The evening begins with the redoubtable Douglas Chamberlain welcoming us, in what turns out to be the first of a series of recurring monologues, to "seniors boot camp." From now on, he tells us, we are geezers, and our role in life is to be annoying. (Later on, he will issue specific instructions on how best to carry this out, whether in the car or at the supermarket checkout.)

The message seems clear: This is a show about being 65 or over. But then the entire cast come on to do a bouncy musical number, and though some of them are initially supported by canes or walkers, they quickly toss them away. The songs title, probably grimmer than intended, is We're Still Alive, but its most insistently repeated phrase is "nobody on this stage is under 50," which lowers the bar considerably.

Basically, then, this is another entertainment for and about Baby Boomers -- who, somebody has realized, maybe from reading it in the papers, are no longer babies. These are people greatly exercised by the realization that, to quote the title of one of the show's better sketches, Paul McCartneys Fifty-Eight. (Serves him right, I say.)

If the Baby Boomers have discovered getting old, then getting old must really exist. Myself, Im just a little too old to be a Boomer, though I'm not quite as old as Paul McCartney, and our generation -- mine and Paul's -- doesnt have a name, which I find a relief. It means I can be exempt from all this ageist angst, and in fact I came out of Wrinkles feeling younger than I have in years. (If they want to quote me on that, I cant stop them, but it's not the intention.)

In practice, of course, the show finds its material where it can. The actors are mature but in excellent shape, and the people they play go up and down the scale. When the characters hit 70, the performers put on special voices. Anything to do with fading memory, fading strength or -- a great favourite -- fading libido that turns out not to have faded at all, is regarded as fair game.

This leads, as I may have mentioned before, to a certain amount of repetition. One sketch about Viagra may be OK; one sketch, with song attached, about a man's loss of erection may be OK; but having both seems excessively deflating. One writer, Frank Peppiatt, supplies a routine about a middle-aged woman disturbed by her elders continuing sex lives. He follows it with a routine whose punchline depicts a middle-aged woman being shocked by her elders continuing sex lives.

Some of the spoken humour is wretched, but the music comes to the rescue. There's something odd about it, though, a kind of temporal disjunction.

When the characters reminisce about the music of their youth, they are likely to mention Joni Mitchell, Eric Clapton or Blood Sweat and Tears. Boomer stuff, in fact. But the songs they actually sing are in an earlier style: mainstream American theatre music that suggests, at the very latest, the early 1960s.

At one point they go even further and beseech us to Bring Back Swing, apparently oblivious to the fact that somebody already has. (One of these performers actually appeared in Swingstep, for God's sake.) Swing, of course, is now just instant shorthand for nostalgia, but if these characters are meant to be remembering the real 30s and 40s thing, then they're a lot older than anyone else in the show. Most of the time, though, it's very pleasant to hear musicianly tunes that support lyrics you can actually follow and the actors can actually work with. One or two of them are rather solemn (I never knew playwright David French wrote lyrics) but many are funny. Especially well crafted are a clutch of numbers by Stan Daniels, who once wrote a cult Broadway flop called So Long, 174th Street. Two songs by other hands tell the old story of the man who trades in his wife for a younger model and gets taken. Both are good. The first is the more elaborate, the second (by Nancy White), the more effective -- or would be if its predecessor hadnt spiked its guns.

Its noticeably well delivered by Judy Marshak, the coolest person on stage. Her female colleagues are Denise Fergusson, whose persona is that of a maiden aunt who's been at the martinis, and Corrine Conley, whose hoity-toity demeanour wafts us back to the long-lost world of Elizabeth Arden. Two of the men specialize in suavity going to seed: Gary Krawford has the more genially harried manner, Brian McKay the more sonorous voice.

Heinar Pillar, who conceived the show (with Joyce Gordon) also directs it, smoothly enough, against a functional background of flats and obelisks.

2000-10-26-how-things-are-tragically-the:
Tanatalus plays in Denver until Nov. 30 it tours the United Kingdom from Januar

The tale of the Trojan war is the best tale ever told. It's being told again in Tantalus, a nine-play theatrical project that had its premiere last Saturday in Denver, Colorado, as a single 12-hour performance. Less than a great production, it is still a great and necessary event; and not just because of its length. Greek myth and Greek drama capture, as nothing else ever has, the ineluctable tendency of things to go wrong; nowhere else are the cruelty, the glory and the sheer capriciousness of human existence so starkly and vividly presented.

Tantalus is about war, and about human efforts, generally unsuccessful, to avert or contain both public and private violence. It is also about story-telling, and about acting, and it keeps reaching back into the pre-history of the events it depicts. In similar vein, one might outline the pre-history of this production. Forty years ago in England, director Peter Hall founded the Royal Shakespeare Company; he called on his friend John Barton, a Cambridge academic, to help him run it. Twenty years later Barton, still at the RSC, directed The Greeks, which told the Trojan story - - the war, its beginnings, and its murderous aftermath -- through abridged and altered versions of various Greek tragedies. About the same time Hall, now at the National Theatre, mounted a far more respectful production of The Oresteia by Aeschylus, one of the plays on which Barton had drawn for his opus. Barton spent much of the next 20 years writing Tantalus, covering the same ground he had traversed in The Greeks, but this time in his own words. Hall undertook to direct it (in collaboration with his son Edward) and the RSC to produce it, but they couldn't raise the finances. At which point Donald Seawell, founder of the Denver Theater Center and an old RSC patron, stepped in, to ask Hall how much he needed. Six million dollars? Seven? "Eight," said Hall, "to be on the safe side." So the money was provided; and the show became a co- production of Denver and the RSC, with actors from both countries. It has been in rehearsal for six months.

During this time the old colleagues' relationship itself went tragically Greek. Barton's original text (now published) ran to 12 plays, and he wasn't happy with Hall's demands for cuts. He walked off the show halfway through rehearsals and will be seeing it for the first time this weekend. This is doubly ironic, because Barton himself has been in the past a ferocious cutter-and-paster of other people's work; and because the show on the Denver stage has far more in common with his own previous work than with Hall's -- it is playful and trans-historical like Barton's The Greeks, rather than austere and ceremonial like Hall's The Oresteia. Hall has retained his attachment to masks, but this time they are not formal tragic masks but light coverings moulded to the actors' faces.

Tantalus himself -- whom the gods famously chained up with food and drink just out of his reach -- does not appear, though he is the ancestor of many who do. His story is told to us in fragments that are appropriately tantalizing, This is typical of the plays' strategy. The best-known Trojan-war texts are Homer's Iliad (which covers less than one-tenth of the 10-year siege) and his Odyssey; the action of the former is covered here in four lines and the latter in one. After them would come The Oresteia, whose events are likewise left offstage, and casually summarised at odd moments. Barton fills the space instead with less familiar narrative, drawn from the obscurer plays of Euripides and from cycles of epic poetry that survive only in fragments. A narrator-figure calls the result the "Saga of the Lost Bits." And if the bits sometimes contradict each other, that only reflects human inconsistency, especially with the unpredictable Greek gods in control. (They, unlike the Judeo- Christian God, signify how things are, rather than how we would like them to be.) Helen, we learn, may not even have gone to Troy; an insubstantial lookalike may have taken her place while she herself was spirited away to Egypt for the duration. The Greek general Agamemnon becomes an agonized liberal, trying to do the right and merciful thing and regularly failing. The pragmatic, unprincipled Odysseus probably does less harm; he is decent when he can afford to be, which isn't often. The great Achilles is an irredeemable boyish thug, his son a possibly redeemable one. The women, regularly raped, sold either into marriage or into slavery, survive as best they can, and get quite good at it.

The play begins, as did The Greeks, with the words "Who is to blame?" Each character might answer, "everyone else." The play itself perceives a deep, ineradicable flaw in human nature which means, paradoxically, that they may all be innocent.

Barton writes in short verse lines which are usually pungent, sometimes beautiful, and always compelling; they have the priceless ring of inevitability. His script is something between a tour-de- force and a masterpiece. Its weakness is that it often resolves into mere debate (not the same thing as the Greek convention of leaving violence offstage). The most powerful of the nine segments is one that cleaves closely to Euripides' great refugee drama, The Trojan Women. Some of Hall's cuts leave loose ends, but he was right to doubt the viability of Barton's prologue and epilogue; he has improved on the former, which now presents a group of modern girls (cultural tourists) being drawn into the action by a huckster- storyteller and becoming its chorus.

The production's greatest weakness is its lack of visual style. There are fine elements in the design (by a Greek, Dionysis Fotopoulos): watery entrances for the sea-nymph Thetis, flames that leap from the ground, the Trojan Horse represented by giant trundling wheels. But the costumes mix ancient and modern without much wit, and there are some devices that are momentarily effective but make no overall sense. Why do Agamemnon and Cassandra remove their masks for a love scene? Why is the Trojan king Priam on stilts? Greg Hicks, an English actor I have admired in the past, weakens both his Agamemnon and his Priam by adopting a monotonous singsong, but he has veteran compatriots who do very well: David Ryall playing an assortment of buffoonish kings (one of them making an intrepid final exit underwater), Alan Dobie as a chillingly blunt Odysseus, Ann Mitchell a doggedly crazed Hecuba. But the best are the American women: Annalee Jeffries as Clytemnestra and Andromache, Alyssa Bresnahan as Cassandra and Thetis, And we feel, in our minds if not in our eyes, the force of the play's central image: a rock that hovers over Tanatalus and may crush all humanity if it gets above itself, or maybe if it sinks below itself. It's no wonder dramatists and directors keep going back to the Greeks. They saw, and foresaw, everything.

YOURE A GOOD MAN, CHARLIE BROWN

New Yorker Theatre, Toronto

You're a good show, Charlie Brown, and I'd forgotten how good you are. Perhaps its because youre so well-meaning and mild-mannered and unassuming that you get overlooked.

I must stop this. There's no reason to feel sorry for You're a Good Man, Charlie Brown, which can never have been out of production since its premiere in 1967 (My press kit included a Peanuts chronology that omits that original staging, while listing the 1999 Broadway revival from which this new Toronto production derives. But thats producers for you: No sense of history.)

You might want to shed a few tears for the shows author, Clark Gesner, who is now dead, and even while alive never had another success, though he certainly did well enough out of this one. The U.S. critic Martin Gottfried once claimed there was a jinx on triple- threat writers -- those who do book, music and lyrics, as Gesner did -- since none of them ever had more than a single hit, and he may well be right. You might conceivably say the same of Charles M. Schulz, creator of the original Peanuts comic strip. He is also dead, and Peanuts was the only thing he ever did. But then, he was able to do it for 50 years, without ever growing stale, spinning out new variations on the same group of characters and the same idea.

Schulz's inspiration, very nicely captured in the musical, was to foist grown-up neuroses and a grown-up vocabulary on small children who in all other respects seem to be leading a conventional five- year-old existence: one that captures the 1950s and makes it seem a pattern for eternity. They go to school, fly kites, do homework (a book report on Peter Rabbit ...), play baseball, and have pets. (Or one of them does; others have fetishes.) When they suffer, as they often do, they do so very articulately. It's cute when you think of them as kids, and rather painful when you realize that you, the adult, are caught in exactly the same binds. The comic strip, every day another anecdote, gave Schulz the perfect controlled environment in which to carry out this unceasing experiment.

And the musical wisely makes no attempt to impose a plot. Its book is a series of sketches -- most of them probably transcribed directly from the cartoon -- and, like its source, it generally eschews punchlines, since its true to life, and life rarely provides a payoff. It just goes on, in a repetitive and compulsive kind of way thats both its comfort and its torment. Charlie Brown, nice though he is, will never win at baseball, kite-flying or romance, and will always have the feeling it's his fault; Lucy will always be unstoppably bossy; Sally will always be insistently self- justifying; Linus will always be super-bright but blanket- dependent; Schroeder will always occupy the musician's impenetrable space (him and his Beethoven); Snoopy will always lead a dogs life, secure, except at mealtimes, in his superiority to the humans among whom fate and the pet shop have unaccountably thrown him.

Especially telling is the contrast between Charlie Brown and Lucy -- the one more intelligent than he knows but fatally lacking in self-confidence and easily -- indeed, permanently -- punctured; the other dumb and loud and undeflatable. Watching her in her psychiatrists booth, charging Charlie Brown five cents for the privilege of learning that nobody loves him, including Snoopy, you wonder if she will really grow up to be a therapist or if (as seems more likely), she will compromise and become a CEO.

Charlotte Moore, who plays Lucy here, is conceivably the most accomplished performer on the New Yorker stage, but she is too knowingly brassy for the show: The style depends on keeping a delicate balance between innocence and experience, and she is weighted too far toward the latter. But Steven Gallagher is a perfectly articulated Charlie Brown and there is sweet-sour support from Daniel Murphy (Linus), Gab Desmond (Schroeder) and Cara Leslie (Sally), whose indignant and multi-faceted repudiation of the C grade she has received for her coat-hanger sculpture is the highlight of the show. (As she very pertinently says, if lack of talent is the issue, why should she be penalized for something that isn't her fault? Not to mention that her family's dry cleaning comes back on inferior coat hangers.) Brian Sills Snoopy is an engaging fantasist, finally taking off in a rendition of Suppertime ("bring on the hambone, bring on the bun/mamas little puppy loves every one") that's almost too insistently razzmatazzy for its context. The direction by Kevin Bowers (after New York's Michael Mayer) is as unobtrusive as direction in a musical can efficiently get.

The function of the songs is to drag into the light the thoughts and feelings that lie just below the characters surfaces, to make long musical lines out of captions. Sometimes what Gesner brings up is mush, as in the closing number, Happiness which exposes the sentimental cheeriness Schulz generally kept hidden. (Im actually a sucker for this, but it's a guilty pleasure.) Sometimes, as in Lucy's hectoring Little Known Facts or the title song or the glorious Book Report ("I work best under pressure/And therell be lots of pressure/If I wait till tomorrow" -- is Charlie Brown really a journalist?) its ace.

Gesner's original score has been supplemented by two new songs from Andrew Lippa. One, Beethoven Day, tries too hard; the other, My New Philosophy, gives a well-taken musical opportunity to the otherwise underserved Sally. Both numbers are anachronistically rocky for the company they're required to keep or the deceptively gentle world theyre meant to illuminate. Theres a second Peanuts musical, Snoopy, that has a better score and probably a sharper sensibility, but it doesn't have the charm of this one.

THE HOBBIT

Young People's Theatre, Toronto

TORONTO - Hobbits seem to have changed their habits. They have become far less bourgeois in their pleasures. That, anyway, is the impression given by the dramatization of The Hobbit at Young People's Theatre. It's hard to imagine Herbie Barnes' Bilbo Baggins, the only hobbit we meet, smoking a pipe or quaffing beer, which seem to be the main recreations envisaged for them by their creator, the late (and culturally belated) J. R. R. Tolkien. This is a health- conscious, socially and environmentally responsible, YPT-stamped Hobbit.

None of this is meant as a criticism of Barnes' splendid performance, or of the equally fine production of which it is the centre. Kim Selody's adaptation originated at the Manitoba Theatre for Young People with the same leading actor.

It is directed now by Jim Warren on what struck me, perhaps through association of ideas, as a rabbit-warren of a set. Designed by Glenn Davidson, it's many-creviced and multi-levelled, fitting both the hobbit's underground home and the inhospitable mountains through which he and his dwarf companions travel in quest of the dragon's treasure. Its central feature is a cave-like opening that can expand and contract, and that gives on to a sky-cloth (superbly lit by Bonnie Beecher) that can also function as a screen.

Here, a giant spider's web takes shape to entrap the travellers, with menacing arachnid legs at the corner of the picture. Here, parts of the story that cannot be done live -- the deliverance of hobbit and dwarves by a troop of eagles, their further escape concealed in a long line of bobbing wine casks -- are depicted in shadow-play; and so smooth are the transitions that we relish rather than resent the break in convention.

The dragon is projected across the whole stage; what looks like the whorl of a tree-trunk turns out to be his eye. Sound-wise, Cathy Nosaty's Celtic-flavoured tunes do Tolkien's clumsy attempts at verse a considerable favour.

I'm not sure what I think about Tolkien. I distrust the cosy Englishness of his vision, in which an idealized village pub becomes the centre of the universe. I resent the ease with which his creations -- admittedly against his will -- were adopted by the soppy hippie ethos of the '60s. I find his excursions into lower- class dialect painfully patronizing, and his humour, at best, awkwardly jolly. (When a character is meant to be plebeian and funny and evil, then it's a groaning matter.) I dislike the implicit glorification of feudalism.

But there is something admirably ambitious in his conversion of linguistic study into a hugely detailed personal mythology (hobbits were his hobby), and while his black-and-white morality can be irritating, it can also be bracing. You know which side you want to win and this, coupled with his storytelling gifts, which withstand any number of digressions, makes him a compulsive read. I read The Lord of the Rings trilogy at a comparatively advanced age and while confined to a hospital bed (making me an easy mark) and I found its scope irresistible, but The Hobbit makes an attractive, and certainly less pretentious, prologue.

The story, and an engaging delight in theatrical inventiveness, are what carry things at YPT. Inevitably, it's episodic -- the book is small-scale picaresque to begin with -- and things, as tends to happen in dramatizations of novels, get very bunched-up toward the end.

But most of the episodes work, and Bilbo -- adopting a mantra of "eggs, bacon, toast" to remind himself of more comfortable days -- gives the show a sufficient through-line as he battles his way through from timidity to heroism through a resourcefulness he never knew he had. Though both the actor and the character are grown-up, his quality is boyish; he's the Jim Hawkins of Middle Earth.

The scene that strikes strongest -- the most famous in the book and the one to which the production sensibly devotes most time -- is his encounter with Gollum, the omnivorous amphibian creature from whom he steals the magic ring that grants invisibility; Greg Kramer communicates a fine relish in the character's warped mind and evil syntax. ("What has it got in its pocketses, preciousss?") He also doubles impressively as the voice of the dragon, whose intentions seem basically similar. Indeed every creature the companions meet -- goblin, troll, dragon, spider -- seems intent on eating them; this is an orally-fixated universe.

Alon Nashman, bearded like a choral figure from the famous Tyrone Guthrie production of Oedipus, is impressive as Thorin Oakenshield, whose calamitous surrender to greed is the aspect of the story that suffers most from compression. Talking of compression, five actors between them play his dozen attendant dwarves; and the manner in which they each rush behind the scenes to emerge immediately and be greeted by a different name is brazenly enjoyable.

Lorne Cardinal's sonorous Gandalf is a less wizened wizard than I had expected, and less schoolmasterly. He ends the play by observing, in a significant-sounding voice, that there is more than Bilbo's magic ring than has yet been revealed, so maybe the YPT is contemplating (as Tolkien himself must already have been) a triple- decker sequel. I wouldn't mind; this show is their best in years.

I was privileged to obtain an audience with Dame Edna Everage on the day of her memorable meeting with the Toronto media at the Royal York Hotel. After the press conference, she received me in the hotel's Royal Suite; our meeting was suitably blessed by the presence of Dame Edna's good friend Queen Elizabeth II, in the form of a large framed photograph, obviously taken some years ago.

Dame Edna answered my questions with the frank fearlessness and the superb linguistic aplomb for which she is famous. Our in-person colloquium was supplemented a few days later by a telephone interview "to fill in the lacunae," as she put it. At this point Dame Edna was in Minneapolis, Minnesota, where she had gone to fine- tune the show -- Dame Edna, the Royal Tour -- which she brings to the Pantages Theatre this Tuesday. It was mid-morning and she was (she said) still clad in her peignoir. What follows is an edited transcript of our two conversations.

How does it feel to be returning to the colonies?

Well, I happen to be in many ways very innovative, very radical and in other ways very conservative, and I loved the old Commonwealth. When we were at school in faraway Mooney Ponds, Melbourne, we learned about Canada. I could actually draw the lakes. Like a little bunch of oak-leaves they were, sprouting. I've had a lot of invitations to come to Canada, and I've won an award in Banff -- lovely name, isn't it, Banff? Sounds like a brand of exclusive toilet paper -- and when I was young, my favourite show that I was taken to see was Rose Marie, and of course there were Mounties in that and I always had a picture of Canada infested with Mounties.

Did you feel that you were destined to be a performer?

Well, I did. In school I was the cynosure of all eyes. And of course my autograph book was full of things like "You Have That Spark, Magnetic Mark."

They called you "Mark?"

No they didn't. It was a figure of speech, Mr. Cushman. But people are drawn to me. You must admit, hardened old journo that you are, that was a good turnout this morning, and they listened, and they were, generally speaking, not impertinent. To return -- after a very long parenthetical route -- to your question, I didn't set out to be an actress. I never ever dreamt that one day I'd become a friend of Ingmar Bergman who is at this moment planning a film comeback -- Edna Gabler is the name of this picture -- and I think as Scandinavian shows go it will certainly have the edge on Mamma Mia.

Would it be fair to say you had a suburban upbringing?

My father sold vacuum cleaners from door to door, and he spent long periods in the country. It's not easy selling vacuum cleaners to people who don't have carpets. He'd save up and occasionally he'd get my mother a new attachment, a new optional extra. I'll never forget when he came home one night with his very first crevice nozzle. And my mother cherished that crevice nozzle.

I do feel that the moral values of Melbourne suburban life are very good guide-lines for the world. I think the next stage for me is to simplify, to go down, to say "I'm casting aside all of this and becoming an ordinary person again." I'm thinking of renouncing my damehood and just being Mrs. Everage. I rather miss that status. It would be courageous of me, in fact, to give all my lovely dresses to charity and wear just the ordinary, rather dreary clothes that you can see in Toronto any day of the week.

But obviously you didn't always feel this?

No, I didn't. I was very flattered when the Queen bestowed my damehood upon me for my services to culture. A lot of people, as you know -- well, you probably don't -- but the fact is that when you're in a position like mine there are a lot of envious people, and a lot of people say it's a spurious title. They claim I've bestowed it upon myself. I stay at Buckingham Palace when I'm in London. I have my own key. And I even have my own shelf in the refrigerator.

And of course the Queen and I meet. Now, it would be to betray a confidence if I told you what we discussed, but she's always sought my advice and then ignored it. So I take no responsibility for what that woman wears. Though I've helped certain American women. I persuaded Hillary to stop wearing those rather horrible little Alice bands. I nipped that in the bud. Tipper is a bit of a different story. She's really rather willful and femininity is not her specialty, I'm afraid.

How did the Queen convey the news of your damehood to you?

Well, she didn't say "I hereby confirm that you have a royal title." She just accepted it; she's a little bit in awe of me, frankly. I'm not in awe of anybody. I used to be a big fan of little Margaret Trudeau when she was quite an independent kind of a woman - - do you remember those days? And of course there's Margaret Atwood, whose books I adore. Danielle Steel and Margaret Atwood are my favourite writers. I don't think they've been together in the same sentence for a very long time, if ever.

I know how people receive a knighthood but what is the equivalent ceremony for a dame?

This is a little bit of an obsession of yours, isn't it, Mr. Cushman? There's an unpleasant probing tone in your voice. Well, you go along to Government House in Australia and they give you some little dry sandwiches and a little drink, the Governor shakes you by the hand and presents you with a velvet box and in there is a lovely ribbon with something you can hang round your neck. But if I returned my own damehood I'd do it very tastefully and it wouldn't spoil my friendship with royalty at all, I don't think. Because I think, between you and me, the Queen would like to be Mrs. Windsor. She'd give anything for anonymity. I haven't positively decided to return my damehood . But it's part of my becoming more accessible, becoming more ordinary. I've enjoyed my fame but now I think obscurity is beckoning me.

You could become famous for obscurity.

I could. I could be the most highly profiled obscure person you know.

There must be other dames, though, of whom you approve?

Well, little Dame Kiri Te Kanawa is a friend of mine. She's a little New Zealand singer. And Dame Judi Dench is a friend but I never thought her damehood suited her. She's very fond of hopping into royal garments, and she played Queen Elizabeth in that thing about the Globe, but she didn't convince me, and many people, including the critics, said I should have had that part.

Do you feel you have been typecast?

I'm myself in the theatre and I will be in Toronto, but I want people to know that I'm an actress. I'd love to join the company in Stratford, Ontario. I wouldn't mind playing small leads; but walk- ons, no, not at my time of life.

You got a Tony on Broadway?

A special Tony. There was no category I could fit into; I am uncategorizable. And I got the Drama Desk Award, the Outer Critics Award. I collected a shelf-full of hideous sculptures.

Do you feel prepared for the Canadian climate?

I've got sone humanely culled Australian animals who've donated their pelts to keep me warm.

Your manager, Barry Humphries, when you discovered him, he was just a struggling actor...

Struggling is the word. He was playing the part of a housewife -- he had to -- and I gave him some tips. And in the end the producer insisted I play the part. Well, can you imagine what a blow to his pride that was? It was a long time ago but the scars are still there.

How often do you go back to Australia?

Well, every year I revisit my roots. Fundamentally I'm Australian, but then I belong to the world.
