HONK IF YOU LOVE CHEESES

Tim Sims Playhouse, Toronto

TORONTO - The latest Second City revue has something in common with The Lion King: The best thing about it is its opening. And that opening is itself like that of The Lion King, and a very funny parody of it.

It appears to begin with a joke we've heard before, the one in which members of the cast sing settings of the regulations governing attendance at theatres. We are musically enjoined to turn off our cellphones, bleepers and digital watches, and forbidden to take pictures of anything.

This time, though, the subject matter expands, and we are told where we can buy our T-shirts and other memorabilia. Indeed some samples are brought on, and paraded around the stage, on the ends of sticks. It begins to seem like an amusing comment on commercial, or at least on commercialized, theatre. (The Second City, a very profitable franchise, is in no position to take the high ground here; but then, it isn't trying to.)

And we begin to notice that the sounds that are coming from the actors' mouths somewhat resemble African chants, and the aisles as well as the stage are filling up with performers -- which, with a cast of six, is quite a trick. A couple of guys in animal masks wander on -- an elephant and would that be a giraffe? -- and look somewhat surprised to be there. Anyway, they are gathering at the water-hole and there we are, in the dinner-theatre audience, taking the waters.

Also like The Lion King, Honk if You Love Cheeses (these titles get more and more mysterious) never returns to its initial level; and it doesn't have the same resources for taking up the slack.

It does make two departures from recent Second City tradition. One of these is an attempt at an overall shape; we are introduced early on to characters and situations that recur throughout the evening. This can be confusing, since the same actors appear in other and quite disconnected sketches, but there is something reassuring about it; it makes you more inclined to laugh at the material, which, considering some of the material, is just as well.

The second innovation is that this supposedly improvisatory troupe has gone, to some extent, back to improvisation: not just in the coda that they customarily tack on to the end of every show, but in the main body of the performance.

Twice they build numbers around suggestions from the house, and they are quite artful about the way they collect these building blocks. A couple in the audience are quizzed about where they first met. "At camp" said the respondents the night I attended, and two of the performers went into a long wailing love-duet with as many references to cabins, counsellors and enforced exercise as they could manage to cram in.

A later item began as a harangue about Hooters, delivered by a recruitment officer to a bunch of aspirant waitresses, they being us, or some of us. We were asked, among other things, to name rooms and pieces of furniture that might be found at our place of employment. The answers were solemnly chalked on a blackboard; and suddenly we were in the midst of an Agatha Christie spoof in which, as in some elaborate game of Clue, the words inscribed had to be worked into the solution of the crime.

It's probable that audience responses don't vary much from night to night, and that the cast have a firm structure that they can hold on to no matter what. But it's still pleasant. The Hooters sketch is good in itself (Sandy Jobin-Bevans, who seems rather tall to be a comedian, has exactly the right creased enthusiasm to put it over) and the Christie spoof is great fun, topping its resident sleuth with a visiting super-sleuth, who boldly tells us, "I know who did it and so do you", then backs off a bit and asks shyly, "So, what do you think?"

Making it up as they go along entails a strain of hesitant bravado that is rather appealing; unfortunately, the same quality distinguishes this company even in the bits that are supposed to be rehearsed, where it doesn't work nearly as well.

There is quite a good number about two women chatting endlessly in a mall to the despair of an accompanying child (Doug Morency performs prodigies of infant petulance in an attempt to capture their attention) and a very good, even imaginative, one about Blockbuster where, a once- idealistic employee despairingly notes, they now file Canadian movies under "foreign." That's all.

Especially surprising and, in the end, depressing, is the fact that spoofing The Lion King and The Mousetrap are the nearest the show gets to topical satire. There's no law; it's just that with an election brewing and health-care in crisis and the schools in disarray and newspapers shooting it out in the streets, they do seem to be passing up an awful lot of promising material. There is one number that looks like it's going to be about teachers having sex with students, but it stops short. (It does have a good punchline: a commodity in short supply elsewhere.)

There's even a sketch about cancer, which might count as being brave; it even has an idea -- that the medical profession, by definition, is in the business of profiting from human suffering -- that seems like it might be neat. But it would need more rigorous working-out than it gets here to escape seeming merely distasteful. But it does illustrate, on a large scale, a comic technique that's far too prevalent both in and out of this revue: take a dodgy notion and pummel it whimsically to death, hoping that if you go on long enough you'll hit something funny. Or at least that your audience will give in.

As for the show's recurring plotline: it concerns a couple of guys who go into partnership in what they call the human-fulfilment business, plus some of their clients and employees. The more vulnerable and exploitable of the partners is played by Lee Smart, a Second City veteran whose large frame and butterball countenance allow him to ring some fairly ingenious changes on the themes of gullibility and desperation, and who can sometimes get angry by way of contrast. (He has a freezingly genial smile.) Lisa Brooke is sharp, if too consistently abrasive.

I wasn't crazy about the two remaining cast members: Paul Bates being oily to the point of deliquescence; and Carolyn Taylor confusing comedy with exaggerated pouting and squealing. The director is Sandra Balcovske who, just to clinch the parallels with The Lion King, is a woman.

(From the National Post, Friday, November 10, 2000) I began my review in yesterday's Post of Dame Edna: The Royal Tour with the confession that I am constantly forgetting names. As my own byline had disappeared from the piece, I can only assume that the condition is catching. 

DAME EDNA - THE ROYAL TOUR

Pantages Theatre

As someone who is always forgetting names, I sit amazed at Dame Edna Everage's capacity for retaining them, especially when the names are those of people in her audience to whom she has only just been introduced.

I apologize for that use of the passive voice. It was wrong. There is nothing passive about the Australian diva and megastar -- megadiva, surely -- with her mauve bouffant, her jewelled spectacles that peer and intimidate like a twin-set of Regency monocles, and her endless wardrobe of shocking pink frocks, including one with zebra stripes that you could cross a street by. Above all, there is nothing passive about her relationship to us, her possums. She certainly isnt INTRODUCED to us; she doesnt even introduce herself; when she finds victims in the house she introduces THEM, to themselves, forcibly. First, she ascertains and vocally fondles their names; then she asks them questions, chiefly about their homes and what they -- the homes, I mean -- are like inside. (I thought beige was dead, but now I find it's alive and well and living in North York.") By the end of the 2 1/2-hour show, she has acquired some dozen of these dossiers, and what is prodigious is that she never lets any of them escape. She remembers which person goes with which history, and she manipulates them throughout the evening like a juggler playing with his balls. (Sorry.) Nothing is wasted; if she orders dinner for a hungry looking couple in Act One, then it arrives in Act Two, and they have to eat it. Onstage.

"I think real people are so much more interesting than celebrities, she coos, diabolically. If her act is anything it's an expose of the cult of celebrity: an exploitation of the twin ideas that fame in itself is a licence for unbridled egomania, and that people will do anything to be in its presence and have some of it rub off. When she interviews (i.e. patronizes, or matronizes) someone, shes like Joan Rivers, only more real.

On a literal level, of course, she isnt real at all; she's a fictitious character, invented, written and performed by the amazing Barry Humphries. This adds sting, but cancels offence; her victims aren't humiliated because they feel themselves to be part of the fiction, part of the show. On Tuesday night -- her Canadian stage debut -- she made instant if transient stars out of Carmen and Julie and Frank and Barbara and Ann and Steve and Nancy (whos tattooed) and Sandy and Sandys husband whose name, Sandy told us, is Harley. Like the motorcycle," Harley volunteered without being asked, for which impertinence he received a freezing rebuke from the Dame: "Do you often interrupt theatrical performances, Harley?

That sudden change of gear (an obvious metaphor in the circumstances) is Dame Edna at match-strength. So is the subsequent routine in which she gave Sandy a precious stone that she herself had received from an admirer in New York, described the murderous jealousies that this would inspire in Sandy's spouse and best friend, and ended up snatching the bauble back for Sandy's own good. And it must mark a new frontier in something-or-other when Edna learns from another couple the phone number of their mother, and calls the good lady up, right then and there; were used to seeing TV hosts do this sort of thing, but its somehow different when we're all in the same room. The recipient, by the way, took the call beautifully in her stride, almost as if she'd been expecting it, but of course being phoned by importunate strangers is now one of the recognized features of modern life.

Comedians before Dame Edna have drawn attention to the patrons up in the cheaper seats, but I dont know of any others who have cheerfully dubbed them paupers" and gone on dubbing them right through the show. She also takes it into her head that the punters in the side boxes may be deaf-mutes, and for their benefit she helpfully (and rapidly) repeats much of what she says in mime; though she does have to own up at one point to forgetting the sign language for arugula. Her head movements throughout are well worth studying, as are her facial expressions; welcoming those who have brought their spouses, "or significant others, or same-sex partners, she is overcome at the last item by a half-smirk, half- grimace that suggests she is shocked by her own tolerance.

Dame Edna, who was once an ordinary Melbourne housewife, has two grown-up children; and its notable that though she accepts her daughter's lesbianism (which doesn't mean that she accepts her daughter) she cannot bring herself to acknowledge that her son, Kenny, whom she adores, is gay. She gets the audience singing a song called any friend of Kennys is a friend of mine" and which at one point rhymes Kenneth with zenith.

She works into her patter, and even into her songs, knowledgeable references to such local landmarks as St. Lawrence Market and Church- and-Wellesley. "You cant say that Edna hasn't done her homework, she crows. I wish she hadn't said that; it seems anxious rather than outrageous, while the self-satisfied laugh that now punctuates her delivery sounds less like the Dame crowing over her own effrontery than like her creator exulting that the show is going well.

For the first time in my Everage experience -- which covers stage, TV and interviews -- I felt a gap opening up between the two of them; usually with Dame Edna its impossible to believe that such a person as Barry Humphries exists, which is the impregnable strength of the act. I laughed pretty much continuously; once I felt tears running down my cheeks; but I never felt transported as I have in the past. The fantastic spirals seemed less inspired, and the points less sharp, as if age were having a softening effect.

At one time, when she identified people in the audience, with exaggerated compassion, as senior citizens" and then kept coming back to them with a brisk cry of "senior! she seemed to be satirizing the whole idea that one could make old people feel better by calling them something else. If the act has one overriding target, its the cult of euphemism. She still calls people senior, but it now seems automatic. The end of the show, too, is a letdown, almost a cop-out, though it does belatedly explain the title. She tells us the Queen has asked her to take over the royal role in Canada, and though she at first protested that she had no infrastructure (thank God I remembered that meaningless word") but she was told she could create her own royal family. So she invites her chosen possums on to the stage and puts them into funny costumes. This I thought was unfair and, yes, embarrassing; she has the expertise in dressing up and they don't. And any comic could do it.

It remains to say that though Edna is not a first-rate song-and- dance person, Humphries is; and the difference is very cunningly split in the routines the Dame undertakes with her two Ednaettes, all the while sporting a winded, manic grin. The songs are in the old-fashioned English revue tradition, a tradition I happen to like: verbally loaded and with billowing piano accompaniment. This is provided by Wayne Barker, whom Dame Edna never once acknowledges and who is also repeatedly employed -- due presumably to some loophole in the musicians union regulations -- as a Polaroid photographer. Maybe Toronto has not inspired Dame Edna to her highest flights but that -- as she would be the first to agree -- is probably our fault rather than hers. What awaits you at the beautiful Pantages Theatre has its roots solidly in tradition, but the flowering is unique. And I suspect that it will bloom more outrageously as the weeks -- six of them -- pass.

I haven't mentioned the gladdies. Long may they wave.

JITTERS

Studio Theatre, Toronto Centre for the Performing Arts

David French's play Jitters was written in 1979, and it still stands up today. This is an achievement, especially in the current revival where it has a lot to stand up to.

It is a backstage piece, portraying the first preview, first night, and first morning-after travails of an imaginary play that appears to be of the family-fighting, hands-across-the-kitchen- table persuasion. Those who were around at the time have hinted that French based his own piece on real-life goings-on in the early days of Torontos Tarragon Theatre. There is a director -- of both the theatre and the play -- said to be based on the Tarragons founder (and French's own mentor), Bill Glassco; though here he more closely resembles a professor in one of our leading university drama departments.

French's method is to take a few strongly drawn types, throw them together in a situation of crisis, and let them slug it out.

There is the long-absent Canadian star who has had a couple of flops in New York and who is counting on this play to restore her credibility at home and also to carry her straight back to the Great White Way. There is the self-destructive hard-drinking Irish-born actor who ceaselessly rails at her for selling out, while secretly harbouring a great respect for her talent. There is the prim, mother- dominated actor, of Greek extraction, whose worst neurotic fears (hes a walking Greek tragedy) are confirmed when he learns the production doesnt have a prompter. There is the young actor fresh out of drama school. There is the director whose skills, at this stage of the proceedings, seem to be more diplomatic than creative. There is the promising playwright, whose second play this is. There is the stage manager, a hectoring martinet, obsessed with having the actors clock in. Somewhere offstage there is the Broadway producer they all hope will make their fortunes.

Jitters has a few resemblances to Michael Frayn's immortal Noises Off, which originated in London at about the same time. That, too, has a leading lady whose desire for a comeback makes her the power behind the production, and an actor whose colleagues have to keep confiscating his booze; and of course it has the same kind of ego battles driving it along.

Frayn's play, though, is a thoroughgoing farce while Frenchs only makes passing use of farcical devices; it turns out in fact to be an affectionate show-must-go-on kind of piece in which everybody ends up pulling together; in fact its sentimental, though not objectionably so. It also makes far less use than Frayn's of the play-within-the-play; we only see its opening five minutes, and they seem to be terrible: Canadian domestic drama at its turgid worst. Maybe, though, that's just the way this cast -- either by accident or design -- is playing it. Certainly the participants -- unlike those of Noises Off -- seem to believe they have a potentially good show on their hands; and if they dont, then theres not much reason for us to take an interest.

What happens is that final rehearsals before first preview get scuppered, largely through the feuding of the two leading players. Then there is mayhem just before curtain-rise when the male juvenile arrives very late and dead drunk, leaving the author -- paranoid at the best of times -- uncertain from moment to moment whether to don an unbecoming pair of pyjamas and go on in his own show. Anyway, it all works out -- how, we never quite discover -- and the last scene finds the company reacting to reviews in the local press that don't seem too bad, considering.

This, remember, is 1979, long before the existence of the National Post, for which they should probably thank their lucky stars, not to mention their lucky globes. Strangely though, the newspapers the characters flourish feature brightly coloured artwork, so either the production is trying to update the play or it's being careless.

Its certainly slapdash in other respects. The tone of the writing is primarily comic -- that much gets across -- but on the night I saw it the admittedly sparse audience failed to muster a single unanimous laugh. The only scenes that approach competence are the occasional conciliatory ones, which just about play themselves. I spent much of the evening replaying the dialogue in my own mind, and speculating on how amusing it might have been, given competent timing and intelligent inflection.

The best I can say for Eli Lukawitzs production is that nobody in it overacts. You feel that some of them couldn't even recognize a dramatic climax, let alone play one; it's all unbelievably listless.

The actor I liked best was Sarah Robinson, whose character -- some kind of wardrobe mistress -- barely appears. Samuel Owen, in black horn-rims and matching sweater, at least looks right as the dramatist; so does Allan Price as the drunken Celt, and he also seems to have the right temperament. But he never engages with Jane Moffat, who plays the homecoming queen as an amiable trouper without an ounce of glamour; their stormy relationship never actually happens, though its supposed to spark the play. Price plays the director as a middle-aged, ineffectual fusspot. (Mr Glassco, if its truly meant to be him, has ripened with the years into gentle sagehood, but at the time of the events presented here he was, by all accounts, a young pioneer.)

Other performances range from null to unspeakable. And who knows if the director could have done more with the cast, or they could have done more without him? One of the characters jovially remarks that "half of the audience come here expecting the set to fall down," which suggests the Tarragon has come a long way in the intervening 20 years, technically if not dramaturgically. But it must be possible to suggest poverty with more wit than is shown on this occasion. The physical design is not so much economical as grudging.

THE KABBALISTIC PSYCHOANALYSIS OF ADAM R. TZADDIK

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace

Adam R. Tzaddik would not call himself an observant Jew. But he is a studious one. For four years he has lived hermit-like in his apartment (what he has lived on is not revealed) immersed in the Zohar, an ancient Hebrew text that purports to explain that most insoluble of riddles, how God created himself.

However intellectually stimulating this may have been for Adam, he has not found it spiritually fulfilling. He claims, indeed, to feel deeply empty, if that isn't an oxymoron, or even if it is. So he signs up for therapy. In The Kabbalistic Psychoanalysis of Adam R. Tzaddik, the playwright Anton Piatigorsky presents us with 60 minutes worth of excerpts from Adams confrontations with his shrink.

Almost the first thing Adam says to his unnamed Doctor is that, since all psychiatrists are necessarily atheists, his must really despise him for his religious leanings. The Doctor doesn't exactly answer that (he doesn't exactly answer anything) but it does become clear that he sees Adams belief system as a challenge to his own.

In the plays most resonant moment, he proclaims works such as the Zohar to be what the world had to make do with before it discovered psychiatry: The author of the Zohar was actually analyzing himself, and Adam, in quoting the book, is effectively becoming its author. This equivalence is made easier by the fact that the author (I rely here wholly, of course, on what the dramatist tells me) is riddled with male-female, father-mother symbols. Pretty soon, this being a short play, Adam is dredging up his own most agonizing memories which have to do with incest, real or imagined.

The trouble with this kind of thing as drama is that, however painful the analytic routine may be for the doctor and the patient, it always looks easy for the playwright.

He is telling us things about his characters that he knew all along, so why not just tell us in the first place? Theoretically, the process of discovery has its own suspense, but in this foreshortened form it seldom works out that way. Reviewers here and abroad (the play has been done in New York and Montreal, as well as previously in Toronto) have compared this piece to Peter Shaffer's Equus but that play, with all its imperfections on its hoof, succeeded by putting the therapist at the centre of the play and letting us see what it meant to him. It was glib, but it was still affecting.

And it is also unfortunate for Piatigorsky's play that it arrives in the immediate wake of Terry Johnsons Hysteria, which makes far more moving and entertaining use of the psychiatric process. I couldnt care much about either Adam or the Doctor, and what we learn about them is much less interesting than what we always seem on the verge of learning about the Zohar; I put it that way because in performance the information flashes by too fast to be absorbed. And just in case we are about to follow it, the production drowns out the text at the end of scenes with appropriately anguished neo- Hebraic music, composed by John Zorn.

Chris Abraham's direction is accomplished, in a flashy high- style manner. The clinical relationship of desk and couch is liable to cause serious sight-line problems, so both characters here are in chairs. They do not however, face one another; the doctor sits behind Adam but at an angle to him, so they look like a detached pair of airline passengers. (Business-class; they have plenty of leg- room.) Each is bathed in a pool of light, a device of which Abraham - - as demonstrated at length in his Montreal production of The Possibilities -- is extremely fond. It's a striking effect, but the note it strikes is never varied. You long, however unreasonably, for someone to get up, and/or for the participants to look one another in the face.

The two sedentary performances are excellent, negotiating an extremely tricky script with great intelligence and unerring precision. Paul Fauteux, looking and sounding like a buttoned-up Albert Schultz, has all the scholarly shame, the defensive pride, of Adam. Terrence Bryant is a silkily impenetrable Doctor, professionally ruthless about winding up the session -- and indeed the play -- on time. He may, though, be more unfeeling than necessary, making a show of concern and implicitly acknowledging his own hangups, but still emerging as insufferably knowing.

That game-playing tone pervades the entire enterprise. Whatever the private feelings of those concerned, they come over all superior.

FIVE FINGERS

133 Bathurst Street, Toronto

The Five Fingers of Robin Fulford's play come together to deliver a blow. The title may also be open to symbolic interpretation, but I'm happier with the literal.

The blow is struck by a husband, Tuck, to his wife, Anna. The play takes us into their house, like investigators called to the scene of the crime. In the current performance, it takes us there with a bracing air of verismo. Theatres are traditionally described as houses, but this one actually is a house: at Bathurst and Adelaide, a couple of doors down from the Factory Theatre. There are practical reasons for this; the show is a workshop for which the author's own company, Platform 9, has been trying, unsuccessfully, to find a more orthodox home.

The play has existed in some form for the best part of a decade. As a one-act piece with the impenetrable title of Swahili Godot (whose significance may conceivably have been that the two characters are locked together but cannot communicate) it was performed in 1992 in Toronto and last year on the fringe of the Edinburgh Festival. While abroad, it began to develop a second act, which on Friday night -- at the start of a week's run -- received its first-ever performance.

It was also, apparently, receiving what amounted to its first real rehearsal; the director, Sarah Stanley (whose work here is by far the best I have seen from her), informed us beforehand that they had had no time to do more than talk the play's new second half at the table.

You wouldn't have known it from the performance; the two actors - - who carried scripts throughout -- flew. It seems that the only thing as effective as a thoroughly rehearsed cast is a thoroughly unrehearsed one. The first encounter of good actors with a fertile text usually sets off sparks; and for once an audience was there to fan them into a blaze.

About a dozen of us ("I like a full house," said the director appreciatively) were crammed just outside the living room, peering through an archway, for the first act, and into a studio room at the back for the second. The first part is largely alternating monologue. Tuck, a cleanliness freak whose distaste for the mess of married life has been aggravated by the arrival of a baby, variously fantasizes, storms and complains. Anna is drawn in less detail; her most notable characteristic is a wiry intensity that may derive more from the actress than from the writing.

It would be tactless to call her a human punching-bag, and systematic physical abuse is not the issue here, but her principal dramatic functions are to react and reminisce; she seems to have more memory than he of what drew them together in the first place. She recollects and re-creates their first meeting; they were in an elevator, and he wiped a smudge of toothpaste from her cheek. (This scene is evocatively staged underneath the arch, which provides a perfect confining frame.)

Now, in the disintegrating stage of their marriage, toothpaste has become something that he rages at her for forgetting to buy. Most men are likely to feel twinges of sympathy with Tuck's feelings of entrapment, but the author is merciless with him. He hasn't grown up; and when domesticity threatens to interfere with his work schedule -- or, worse, with his play schedule -- he explodes. Everything in that first half leads up to his hitting Anna; and everything in the second deals with the consequences of that irrevocable act. The effect, as we walk away at the end, is that of having witnessed the blow in slow motion.

Anna walks out, with the baby; Tuck begs her to come back; she refuses, though she does make a couple of brief business-like visits. There couldn't be much of a second act if she didn't. Dramatically, in fact, they have far more contact after they have broken up than before.

In the first half their scenes together are brief but compelling confrontations, the more riveting for being islands in a sea of lyrical soliloquy (though in Tuck's case the lyricism tends towards the jagged). We spend most of Act Two with Tuck, and here too he talks to himself a lot: necessarily, since there's nobody else around. But he is now far more concrete, far more focused on the present, and on what he wants but -- however pitifully he pleads -- is not going to get; his scenes with Anna (whose passport, in an incalculable mixture of pique and desperation, he hides) make that thoroughly clear.

I prefer the writing -- or at least the kind of writing -- in Act Two, though in both modes the author tends to repeat himself. What he is repeating, though, is worth saying, and even more worth showing; domestic dramas come and go, but this one is more painfully and individually honest than most.

It is also, of course, great fun to see it staged in this environment, and to see that environment so resourcefully employed. The living room action extends into the hall outside, and what must once have been the dining room; the scheme allows for some atmospheric lighting (by Rebecca Picherak), and when Anna looks at herself in a mirror, a stage manager holds it up for her: rather a Japanese touch. (Where did she glide in from?)

The move to the studio is an invigorating surprise in itself (we cluster in the kitchen while the equipment is being moved), and here, too, we get an extra dimension; some scenes are performed -- to great visual effect, and with perfect audibility as well -- in the backyard beyond; they seem appropriately chilly and groping. Inside, the central feature is a long table at which Tuck seems more isolated than ever, especially when on the phone to colleagues. (He seems be a loans officer in some financial institution. Need more be said?)

The actors, Ross Manson and Tamsin Kelsey, are presumably making up much of the choreography as they go along, just as they are exploring the text before our ears, and they hardly strike a false note; he exudes a boyishness that obviously thinks it's endearing, she manages to be firm and sensitive at once.

The idea is that each performance will build on the one before, and they are off to an excellent start. The play will probably resurface, sooner rather than later, in a more conventional setting, but I advise you to catch it where it is. Or maybe it will find another address (the owner apparently wants this one back) and become the first house-bound Toronto hit since the legendary Tamara. Which, by the way, was nothing like as serious or as affecting a play.

SLAVS!

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

Tony Kushner's much-feted double-decker Angels in America was a trenchant little piece about No. 1 ratfink Roy Cohn, adorned with some very good jokes and embedded in hours and hours of New Age whimsy that were tiresome at the start and unendurable by the close.

SLAVS!, his new play -- well, comparatively new, its been around in the U.S. since 1994 -- is, physically at least, a smaller-scale work; it plays for 90 intermissionless minutes rather than seven hours. It still manages to pack within those confines three acts and an epilogue, and its subject could hardly be larger. Its about Russia, during and after the last years of the Soviet Union. The mixture, though, is proportionately much the same, though this time the good parts, rather than being teasingly parcelled out through the entire work, come in a lump at the end.

Also at the very beginning: The show could hardly get off to a better start. Marked out on the stage floor, on John Jenkins' set, is a large white hammer and sickle. It turns out to be made of white confetti, and two substantial and impeccably Russian-looking women come on stage to sweep it off. While they work they debate the principles of dialectical materialism and their continued relevance or otherwise to the international working class.

The two babushkas (so identified in the program) are played by Maria Vacratsis and Randy Hughson, the latter of whom is a man. So this introductory scene is formally halfway toward the Monty Python sketch in which Eric Idle and Terry Jones (I think) appeared as two housewives with scarves on their heads who sat around in the laundromat, discussed existentialism, and finally put in a call to Jean-Paul Sartre.

The humour, though not up to the Python level, is still pretty funny, and it's abetted when more confetti falls from above to simulate snow. (Though when this effect is repeated later on, the law of diminishing returns kicks remorselessly in.)

The babushkas are chased offstage by a posse of apparatchiks who proceed to make speeches. These are the days of Gorbachev, and one speaker, seemingly one of natures filibusterers, makes a plea to stand fast against the tide of what calls itself reform. Another, by contrast, advocates that they should all leap vigorously into the future, and himself starts leaping all over the stage.

With only six actors in the cast, doubling and trebling come with the territory, and there is more cross-gender casting here. Brenda Robins and Maria Vacratsis deliver their tirades with much stomach- patting and squeaky baritoning, just in case were not sufficiently amused -- or sufficiently tipped off -- by the characters having names that sound like a bad translation of Gogol: names like Aleksii Antedilluvianovich Prelapsarianov. Both the orators fall dead -- one from too much talking, the other from too much jumping -- and that is Act One.

Act Two takes place in a room where the brains of old revolutionary heroes are kept, pickled. A party functionary (Ashley Wright) has wangled a post as guardian of these exhibits for a woman whom he would like to seduce. She, however, refuses his advances (though not the job) on the truthful grounds that she is having a lesbian affair with a doctor.

The doctor is a still-idealistic socialist; the sympathies of the guard (played with sardonic gusto by Kelli Fox) are, if anything, peasant and pre-Marxist. We take notice of this, and of the fact that love unites what ideology might put asunder, and of the surrounding visual symbolism.

It still seems very scrappy, and unfunnily cartoonish, and it doesn't account for a sequence, punctuated by blackouts, in which the two women get progressively (if those are your politics) drunker and more amorous.

By this point, I thought the play, considering the author's reputation and the amount of performing talent involved, to be a disgrace. Then the third act came along and knocked me over.

Its set in Siberia, under Yeltsin. The doctor from the previous episode, fervently played by Brenda Robins as a practical idealist whose disillusion has stopped miraculously short of cynicism, is ministering to the hopeless victims of radiation; we see one, a mute little girl.

In an earlier scene we have met a quietly smooth politician, given by Hughson the most restrained and effective performance of the evening thus far. He now reappears, and the childs mother, tremendously played by Maria Vacratsis, asks him what he -- not some abstract government, he -- is going to do about her situation.

It's a great wish-fulfilling moment: the kind of thing we have all, even in far less drastic circumstances, ached to ask of authority. The man, of course, has no answer -- except that he turns out to be a Russian ideologue of the newest and most frightening type, blaming everything on foreigners, financiers and Jews.

Kushner is a Jew and a leftist (he has said that coming out as a socialist is harder these days than coming out as gay) but to his credit, he doesn't have the woman reject fascist ideas in the name of proletarian principle; she merely says coldly that she is a Lithuanian, and that Russian nationalism is of no interest to her. Its left to the doctor to speak for the author: to say that socialism, whatever the crimes committed in its name (and she makes no bones about the impossibility of something like Chernobyl being permitted in the West), is still preferable to the alternative.

I hope shes right, but I'd feel happier about the play's position if it didnt (as the left, especially the theatrical left, still routinely does) sentimentally invoke Lenin, who may not have killed as many people as Stalin but was no teddy bear, either.

The epilogue reintroduces us to the two deceased politicos, who are in heaven and better company dead than alive; they are joined by the sick girl, now able to talk. She tells them, clearly, unemotionally and -- in Adanya Dunns performance -- with spell- binding fluency just how and why she died. Here the play finally achieves the tone of mordant, aching irony for which it has striven all evening.

It doesn't justify everything; the play's generalizations about the Slavic temperament -- all that vodka and desperation -- amount to no more than a series of literary gags. (A line about wanting to go to Moscow got the loudest laugh of the evening from the theatrically hip first-night audience, myself included.) But the good outweighs the bad, and Dennis Garnhum's production, uniting fidelity and flair, plays both to the hilt.

THE WEIR

Bluma Appel Theatre

Conor McPhersons The Weir, like many other Irish plays, takes place in a bar. In this case its a run-down pub -- a snuggery that looks more like somebody's dilapidated living room than a place of public entertainment -- in what we gather is an equally run-down village in the west of the country.

It is almost a private club, and the members get through a lot of beer -- bottled, to their disgust, since the tap is out of order.

But if the setting is conventional, the dramatic structure is not; at first, indeed, the play does not seem to have one. It unfolds principally as a sequence of stories told by the characters, and only later do we realize how craftily this succession has been graded.

There are five people onstage: the barman, a couple of regulars, an occasional and a newcomer. They tell these stories as monologues, as ways of showing off, getting comfortable, or just getting acquainted. The first tale we hear is a simple, and rather fragile, fairy tale, only mildly threatening, whose only immediate relevance is that it is set in the local community; it is in no way autobiographical.

The second is scarier, and though it doesn't relate directly to the speaker, it does concern people he and his friends know.

The third, which concerns a graveyard, comes straight out of the experience of the person who relates it and is disturbing; the only escape-clause is that the events apparently happened when the protagonist was running a high temperature, so he may have been hallucinating.

The men who spin these yarns are Jack, a garage-owning bachelor in his 50s; Jim, who works for Jack and gives him good racing tips, and who is somewhat younger and lives with his mother; and Finbar, who is married and prosperous and runs a hotel in the nearest town. He is making a rare visit, in the company of Valerie, a woman in her 30s recently arrived from Dublin, and the others suspect that he is making a play for her and that his intention is not so much to show her around as to show her off. They deprecate such behaviour, but that doesnt stop Jack, who has advance notice of Valeries arrival, from putting on a suit for maybe the first time in years.

Valerie, who seems shy but pleased by all this attention, also has a story to tell, and it's her own. It is about bereavement, and it is understated, riveting and deeply painful.

This is the second time The Weir has played in Toronto -- the original London production came to a WorldStage season -- and on neither occasion have I been able to look at the stage as Valerie's story reached its climax. There are elements of the paranormal here, too, but they are dwarfed by factual human tragedy. The mood in the pub naturally changes; whatever amorous designs the men may have entertained melt away, and their only concern is to make fumbling verbal gestures of comfort.

There is yet a fifth story, and Ill get to it. First, though, I must salute the cunning sympathy of the writing, the ease and economy with which life inside and outside the bar are brought before us; and the vitality of the language, which has the richness and muscle we expect of Irish drama but not the quaintness or the excess. The literate fluency is traditional, but the time is very much now.

The setting (by Francis OConnor) is from the bar at one side to the fireplace at the other, by way of the rain glimpsed through the dank window.

The acting, under Jackie Maxwell's direction, doesn't match the practised ensemble ease that we saw in the authentic Irish cast at Harbourfront, but it is still fine, warm, touching and funny. Barry MacGregor, an actor to whom bluffness comes natural, supplies a broad outline for Jack and then fills in the mans loneliness with a touchingly clumsy delicacy. Jim (generally referred to, even in his presence, as "the Jimmy fella") is Robert Persichini, who has a deliberate delivery, a slow-burn timing and a solid grace that are all his own.

John Jarviss Finbar, hands jangling in his pockets, shifting from one leg to the other as he wonders how and whether to play the seducer, is the picture of saloon-bar sophistication returned uneasily to its public-bar roots. Ann Baggley nicely sketches in Valerie's initial uncertainties, but gives a rather shallow account of her big speech, full of carefully planted pauses; it can hardly help being affecting, though.

Oliver Becker completes the quintet as Brendan the barman, quietly and humorously solicitous, still fairly young, and the only one who doesn't tell a story. Hes the audience; ultimately, it is for his benefit -- or so it increasingly seems to me -- that the stories are being told. He is the only one of the men with a chance of changing his life.

The last story is an encore for MacGregor as Jack, and it is soberly realistic. (The adverb is appropriate, despite the amount he and the others have put away.) He tells of his own foolish selfishness regarding his girlfriend of 30 years ago and how she slipped away from him when she moved to the city, of how he attended her wedding, of how he made a fool of himself at the service, of how he was touched by an act of kindness from a stranger, and how he still wakes every morning with, to put it less gracefully than he does, the memory of that girl in the room. The weir of the title is a local landmark, only once referred to, but it must be an image for the habits of a lifetime that can drown us all. Jacks story ends the progression by shaking off the supernatural. The moral seems to be that fairy tales are fine, but clap hands if you believe in people.

Apologies to Mairtin O'Carrigan, an authentic Irish actor whose performance in Jitters (as another authentic Irish actor) was misattributed in last week's review.

THUNDERSTRUCK

Factory Theatre, Toronto

The thunder in Thunderstruck is especially good, as is the lightning. Together they blow up a real McCoy of a storm, fearsomely created in lighting and sound. It's how the story starts. Lightning bolts invade the home of the Lasting clan, killing the father and mother of the house. This leaves their children -- three boys and a girl, all adopted -- to fend for one another, with the grudging consent of the local authorities. The three brothers are called, in chronological order, Rock, William and Fred-James. The sister, younger than any of them, is called Naomi, and she has a beautiful voice. When she is 20 she leaves home to tour as a country singer. A couple of years later she returns, brain-damaged. The brothers devote themselves to taking care of her, a situation that brings out both the best and the worst in them, laying bare all that divides them and, most essentially, all that unites them. The ending is drastic.

Thunderstruck is a play by Quebec writer Daniel Danis, premiered in Montreal nearly three years ago. It comes to us in an English translation by the ubiquitous Linda Gaboriau and in a production by the One Yellow Rabbit company of Calgary that has already triumphed at the Edinburgh Festival. (Much interesting Canadian work these days only reaches Toronto by way of Scotland.) So a play that must originally have been set in a rural area of Quebec now arrives carrying a strong whiff of the Prairies; theatrical Ontario is being set upon from both sides at once. The production taps into two deep- seated Toronto prejudices: a) that outside the metropolis, everything is wilderness; b) that theatre in other provinces is more audacious and imaginative than anything brewed here.

Thunderstruck is a remarkable example of text-based theatre, physically expressed. The four actors playing the siblings are the only ones who appear, and most of the time they stick to their own roles. But they are storytellers as well as impersonators, and sometimes they speak of themselves in the past tense and in the third person; they also, briefly, take on the voices of other characters. They begin the play as a chorus, recounting the history of the fatal storm, referring to their dead parents as "the father and mother, our own." As that suggests, they talk funny. "Unrile!" one of the brothers instructs another, this being apparently the family patois for "cool it." That probably sounds awful (and it does have its moments) but it works, with equal credit to the author, the translator, and the current interpreters who make it the material of a myth.

This is a folk tale but a modern one: The Lastings are devoted to their television and VCR, and deeply if skeptically concerned with the state of the health-care system. It's also a sort of psychological study, and the language has a function here, too. The last injunction given to the children by the parents, their own, was to "stay welded," and they do, chafing at the bonds but accepting them, often exulting in them. Like the children of multiple births - - who often communicate so well between themselves that they have less need than others to explain themselves to the outside world - Rock, William, Fred-James and Naomi were slow to learn speech. To encourage them their mother devised a contraption that she called "the Say-Sayer" (you put a new word in it and you get a reward) and this becomes the sacred symbol of their lives. In this production, designed by Terry Middleton, it's an intricate metal holder that exactly mirrors the structure of the house. It's false economy, though, to make it double as the family TV set.

That's my only cavil with the presentation. The production is directed by Blake Brooker and staged (which presumably means choreographed) by Denise Clarke; and the collaboration has produced strong, gentle work. Clarke also appears as Fred-James, the youngest and most delicate in feeling of the brothers, and she is especially fine. One of the play's most telling shifts of perspective is a quarrel between the older two that is relayed to us entirely throigh the voice of Fred-James, who speaks the words of both. Michael Green plays Rock, the oldest and most capable who cooks for the others and has the firmest connection to the outside world but is unthinkingly dictatorial in his own domain. Andy Curtis is William who has both admired and resented him for years ("when I was 10, I wrote on the red cardboard of the dictionary, 'my brother Rock is crazy'") and eventually takes a bloody revenge. There is a lovely moment when the trio stand side by side like Christmas figures, each of their faces illumined by a different-coloured lamp -- an effect that depends of course on both actors and technicians hitting their marks with absolute precision and thus typical of the show as a whole.

Elizabeth Stepkowksi as Naomi never gets to speak a coherent word, but sings hauntingly and has great physical presence. This she needs, since she spends much of the play in a harness, attached to a frame in the backyard, which is her brother's preferred site -- in warm weather, anyway -- for looking after her. (Who'd be an actor, I thought, as they winched her up.) The play may be saying something - - though nothing, I confess, very novel or profound -- about men's attitude to women. The brothers nagged and pampered her when she was small; adored her when she was well and could sing; treat her as a doll, though certainly a cherished one, when she isn't and can't. They still -- when they aren't prodding her, dosing her, dressing or making her up -- worship her. It seems that the lightning that killed their parents also entered her, leaving her with a tendency to toward phosphorescence; i.e. from time to time she lights up. For relief, once a month they go into town to party with select local girls and "untease that whoop-de-doo itch"; there were times when I was irreverently reminded of Seven Brides for Seven Brothers. They also live in a state of permanent mutual mistrust with what they call "the muncipalities" and it is the irruption of this outside world that precipitates the climax; a typical tale of a benevolent crowd of busy-bodies turning into a lynch mob. It's good to see a western again, even if it started out as an Eastern. This is my first encounter with the much-touted One Yellow Rabbit, and -- as an Anglocentric literary type -- I approached them, or it, all ready to be unimpressed. I was hooked.

GLENN

du Maurier Theatre Centre, Toronto

Near the beginning of Glenn, the young Glenn Gould calls to his mother that he has just worked out the structure of the Goldberg Variations. There must have been a parallel moment for the playwright, David Young, when he called to someone -- conceivably his director, Richard Rose -- that he had worked it out, too, and was going to build his play around it.

The resulting piece has become a Canadian perennial; first seen at the du Maurier in 1992, it was revived at last years Stratford Festival, and it returns to Harbourfront by way of the Centaur Theatre in Montreal. All these productions have been directed by Rose, and of the four actors in the current company, three have appeared in previous stagings of the play, though not always in the roles they play here.

The play does not precisely have four characters; rather, the one enigmatic figure of Gould himself is split four ways. There is the Prodigy, the precocious boy pianist; there is the Performer, who, still young, enjoys tremendous success, plus some severe criticism, on the concert platforms of the world, and eventually finds it all either too much or too little; there is the Perfectionist, retreating to the technological monasticism of the recording studio; and there is the Puritan, Gould at the end of his life, surveying his earlier selves with a sardonic though not embittered eye.

A partial hook is that Gould recorded the Goldbergs twice in his life, less floridly the second time than the first, and his life can be seen as a process of paring down. The play borrows something of the musics fugal form, alternating and intercutting the four Glenns (fair enough: Gould was fanatical about the possibilities of tape editing), letting them spy and comment on one another, and even indulge in the occasional four-way confrontation.

It sounds stimulating, and that's how it seemed when I saw it at Stratford, which was my first time with the play; it was dense, and sometimes confusing, but I assumed a second visit would clear some of that up. This time, however, I found myself tuning out more often than before, and not always feeling greatly rewarded by the parts that did hold me.

Sometimes the multiple focus twitches enjoyably. Gould did, undeniably, watch himself living his life, both at the time and afterward. So it's amusing when one Glenn watches another Glenn take a taxi, which turns out to be driven by yet a third Glenn (conceivably in psychological disguise) whose steering wheel is actually a red vinyl LP and who wants to discuss the maestros theories about music, to the maestros own embarrassed disgust. This is funny; I was reminded of Alan Bennett's evocation of Lawrence of Arabia, who "wanted his complete indifference to public notice to be universally recognised." Lawrence, Bennett said, used to don flowing Arab robes complete with scimitar and hoped, in this uniform, to pass unremarked in Oxford Street; Gould, a passionate hypochondriac, seems to have entertained similar expectations regarding his familiar uniform of cap, overcoat and muffler, but when he wore it in Manhattan in June, people talked.

The sight of the Gould quartet bound together in an entanglement of tape is an apt and witty visual image. There are even allusive sidelong references to Gould's questionable tastes in popular singers (Barbra Streisand and Petula Clark). But often the play seems the victim of its own mechanism, especially when all four constituent parts are involved. You grow to dread the shout of canon! invariably followed by the demand from one player that the others join him in some kind of word-association game.

There are two Goulds in public mythology: the musician and the eccentric. The musician, as Young himself is too smart not to know, is largely irretrievable in dramatic form, and giving the play itself some kind of musical shape doesnt solve the problem. Of course there can be occasional lines about technique and interpretation, but no sustained discussion and not much illustration. (We do, naturally, get to hear recorded snatches. Their main effect is to make us wish that the actors would shut up and let us listen to Gould playing Bach. Or to anyone playing Bach.)

The eccentric, of course, is far more theatrically accessible, and the play delivers him in bulk; we hear a great deal about Goulds reclusiveness and misanthropy and pill-popping. The most obvious thing about Gould is that he was a tease, and the script has enough of a sense of humour (I'm not so sure about the production) to deliver on this. Most of what we learn, though, could equally well be delivered to us biographically or anecdotally. That kind of conventional dramaturgy would probably come off very banal, so one can see why the author would go for something more ambitious. But it doesn't seem very much of a return for all that structure. And hints that Gould was some uniquely Canadian kind of genius merely prompt the question, "So what?"

If the play seems more distant than it did at Stratford, that may be because the audience in this space confronts it head-on rather then enveloping it. The staging looks very similar to before, the actors threading their way through a multiplicty of high-tech equipment.

The acting is down a notch in intensity, though Duncan Ollerenshaw (who has been with the play since its first workshop) repeats his appealing tremulous-sensitive performance as the Performer, who moves from loving to hating every moment of it. Brandon McGibbon's Prodigy is rather too much of an ordinary kid, but John Koensgen does a good, gnarled job as the Perfectionist. R.H. Thomson doesn't sound the depths of fright and pain that Richard McMillan (much missed since he disappeared into the jaws of The Lion King) brought to the Puritan, but he makes an excellent master of ceremonies, both crabbed and relaxed.

JACKIE MASON: MUCH ADO ABOUT EVERYTHING

Toronto Centre for the Arts

Jackie Mason has two phrases that he employs as props, to get him and us through two and a half hours of solo performance. They arent exactly catchphrases; a comic usually only repeats a particular catchphrase once in an evening, for recognition purposes. Mason uses his repeatedly. They are the nearest thing he has to breathing spaces. In other respects, he's unstoppable.

One phrase, applied whenever this most aggressively Jewish of mainstream comedians wishes to express disapproval of someone, is "Nazi bastard!" When I saw him on Broadway a few years ago he was applying it to any member of his audience who seemed reluctant to laugh; now, though, he seems to have mellowed and only uses it for people, or groups of people, who have aroused his displeasure in the outside world.

The other phrase is I don't want to pick on anyone (or, occasionally, "I dont mean to give offence"), invariably uttered immediately before he proceeds to do just that. One of the nicest things about Mason is that he isnt nice. Even at the end, just when he seems about to embarrass us by telling us what a lovely audience we've been and what a lovely city Toronto is, he salvages the moment by thanking us for catering to his egomania.

He does what he does extremely well. His delivery mixes English, Yiddish, and the spoken equivalent of scat-singing at machine-gun speed and with atomic intensity. It's just as well that hes sensitively miked. (On Broadway, the sound-mix was very harsh; every word came out as a bark, and I left at intermission. It wasnt that I didn't like him; it was just that I felt I'd had enough.)

His body is almost as ceaselessly active as his voice. he prowls the stage in a glossily tailored suit, with a stiff gait that proves surprisingly flexible, especially in the matter of -- literally -- bending over backwards.

He can sing and do impersonations; he offers a stunning Bing Crosby, especially on the low notes, and a rotten Frank Sinatra, for which he uses the same voice but different hand gestures. In speech, he expertly mimics Richard Nixon, Henry Kissinger, Jean Chretien (for local consumption) and Ted Kennedy, though he does them not with words but with assortments of guttural gibberish; Masons Kennedy converses in a rhythmic riff that seems to have been borrowed from Danny Kaye.

Most of the time, though, hes talking about social trends, especially those that come under the heading of style-snobbery. He lays into Starbucks and Evian and people who drive what they insist on calling sports-utility vehicles when it fact they're just trucks. (It looks like a truck, it drives like a truck -- I don't think he actually says it quacks like a truck.) Old people, he tells us, have a terrible time trying to climb into these vehicles, just as they have a terrible time trying to locate the cream and the cutlery in pretentious coffee-shops. Mason doesnt actually call them "old people"; he talks about elderly Jews.

His world is rigidly divided into Jews and Gentiles. They are good at different things. Gentiles like to stand in line; Jews push to the head of it, and sell refreshments to the schmucks standing behind them. Gentiles are good at basketball and coal mining; Jews arent. ("Can you imagine a yarmulke with a light on the front?") Jews are good accountants. (Even Gentiles don't want Gentile accountants.) Jews are good businessmen but also good consumers, especially when the desserts are free, at which point they magically forget that they're on diets.

And can you imagine such a thing as a Jewish farmer? (Actually I can, very easily, in Israel.) Mason never mentions the Middle East; when he discusses Jew-Gentile relations hes operating, for all his vaunted outspokenness, in a very safe and limited zone.

"They accuse me," he says, of dealing in stereotypes, but all Im saying is that people are different, right? What he's really saying is that large groups of people are different from other large groups, but that within those constituencies they behave with numbing consistency. What he's doing, of course, is taking anti- Semitic stereotypes, and, rather than denying them, glorying in them. ("Yes, we are smarter than you are. And were hypochondriacs.")

I doubt if this will lead to any increase in anti-Semitic feeling, except perhaps among Jews themselves, who may not like being lumped together like this, especially by an ex-rabbi. (Mason famously got out of the religion business when he found that all people liked about his sermons was the jokes. I think this was a little irresponsible of him. We could use some funny rabbis, God knows.)

This, of course, is the time to say that, of course, I have no time for political correctness. But then neither does anybody else I meet, so the battle against it hardly seems a medal-earning business. Were all so busy protesting our dislike of political correctness that there's nobody left over to be politically correct. (Yes. PC does exist, and it has its own spheres of influence, and it is a pain. But it doesn't present much of a threat to you or me or Jackie Mason.)

Masons role-reversal shtick is a bracing exercise for a time, but it does get to seem mechanical. So its a relief when, in the second act, he breaks away a little from his own well-cultivated patch, and talks about politics. He's funny when he turns to current events in Florida; presumably he's had his Bush-Gore routine all ready to go for some time now, but hes awe-inspiringly fluent in bringing it up to date.

He throws in some Canadian jokes, also presumably got up for the occasion. He does some great, though presumably not new, stuff on Bill Clinton and Monica Lewinsky, in which connection he plays the race card very well. (A Jewish girl is not interested in oral sex ... an oral surgeon, maybe.) I especially liked his ruminations on the presidential decision ("Its his field, he should know") that oral sex isn't sex. (All over the country, men were calling up hookers and asking for their money back.)

Mason's gibes at current pop-music sound merely, Im afraid, like standard Borscht-Belt disgruntlement (people have been making these jokes since Presley) but he seems genuinely appalled by Titanic: The Musical. Not the movie -- he loved the movie -- but the solemn-to-a- fault stage show, which he mysteriously characterizes as an empty- headed romp in which people did merry dances while the ship went down. (Apparently its all right to have the drownings serve as a backdrop to an invented romance between Kate Winslet and Leonardo DiCaprio.)

I bring this up because show business is one thing he seems really serious about: fittingly, because he is, at bottom, a traditional Catskills comic. Where he differs from the prototype is in not creating a biography for himself. Alan King, say, would spend his whole act telling us about his marriage, and whether or not he was telling the truth, he was establishing a character. Mason tells us almost nothing about himself.

It's also where he differs most from his current competition in town, Dame Edna Everage. Both pick on their audience, but Mason chooses just a couple of victims while Edna is more generous with her favours -- and more imaginative in the way she torments the recipients.

Most importantly, though, Edna is a character, and in the end, the one who's being most mercilessly satirized. Mason presents himself merely as a cranky but neutral commentator; he asks us to trust him.

What he does have in common with the Dame is the ability to fly. The best parts of his show come at the end of each half. He announces the intermission or the final curtain and then delays it, spinning out new ideas, and for the only time in the evening you dont want him to stop.

And the very end is charming. He tells us that we can leave but he doesnt see why he should. "So if you want to stick around and watch a little Jewish fellow doing nothing for a couple of hours ... " He does go, of course, and returns for the regulation bows, and gets the regulation ovation. The last thing Jackie Mason would ever be caught doing in front of an audience is nothing.

SMUDGE

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

There are certain plays you feel like a heel for disliking. Alex Bulmer's Smudge belongs in that category.

It is about a young woman who is diagnosed with retinitis pigmentosa, and goes gradually blind; and it is partially autobiographical. We are told that the character is not necessarily identical to that of the author, but that the experience is. We witness the protagonists anger, her rebellion, her humour -- which is very prominent -- and her, for want of a better word, acceptance.

The presentation in Alisa Palmers production is on a high level of professional skill, and the writing is at least adroit. It is also, though -- despite the personal commitment behind it -- generalized.

The author begins by plunging us, with admirable directness, right into the heart of the situation. Or so it seems: Sometimes says Freddie, our heroine and host, "I imagine myself a wild and famous silent screen star," one who has suddenly gone blind and who insists that nobody talk about it but that everything on the set be arranged to cater to her convenience.

And then you start wondering: Why a silent screen star? Why not a talking one? Or why not some other kind of prima donna altogether -- a queen, a politician or a rock star? Presumably the choice of image tells us something about the tastes and interests of Freddie herself; but it doesn't. Or the metaphor will be sustained throughout the play; but it isn't.

We move on to the scene in which Freddie receives the cruel diagnosis, and the even crueller prognosis. She ponders the vernacular habit of referring to a disease by its initials: RP, she says, like on baseball caps, or ski jackets. We cant be meant to believe that she actually said this, not at that moment and in the presence of authority, as represented by a doctor. Its the kind of bitter wisecrack that comes under the heading of "things-I-wish-I'd- thought-of-at-the-time."

The doctor then does what we all (in vain) long for doctors to do at such appalling moments; she displays some vulnerability of her own. She breaks down and sobs that she's in a terrible way herself, and that her husband or boyfriend has just left her. This is played with exaggerated sobs and strictly for laughs. After this double dose of the comedy of wish fulfillment, we are disinclined to believe anything.

Some things in what follows strike painfully home. Freddie talks about her diminishing vision, of how walking across the Second Cup to get some milk for her coffee becomes an agonizingly ludicrous experience. We watch strangers impatient when they dont realize her condition, and cringingly solicitous when they do. And we -- the sighted in the audience -- blush and laugh in recognition. We dont cringe ourselves, though, which is good; these scenes are tactfully short and sharp.

Slightly longer are scenes that show Freddie interacting with her therapist, or with her lesbian lover. Some of the tensions she has with the latter could arise in any relationship, and this, of course, is part of the point: Other emotions don't come to an end because of a physical disability. But we don't know enough about Freddie outside of (or indeed before) her blindness for these episodes to register much, and the play is awkwardly caught between being a case study and a full-length psychological profile.

Some of this may be due to Diane Flacks skilled but relentlessly life-of-the-party performance as Freddie. As a performer she is always on. This worked in Sibs, where she had good material and (in Richard Greenblatt) an equal partner; there she could be a counterpuncher. It lets her down badly in her TV series PR (she seems dogged by initials), where the material is atrocious and the focus, such as it is, is all on her and her energy.

That energy is a lot more controlled here. She is, after all, acting a real situation (by which I dont just mean biographically real) but it's one that's seen -- the word may be inapposite but I dont know a better one -- entirely from her perspective. She never steps back, never relaxes, and when she tries for vulnerability -- well, she can do it, but its like a stand-up comic saying, "but seriously, folks"; it comes too late.

Kate Lynch portrays a series of brisk but collapsible caregivers, personal and professional, without much variation. A third performer, Sherrylee Hunter, has little to do (little that's prominent, anyway) but does it well.

Carolyn M. Smith designed the sets and Andrea Lundy the lighting. The stage is divided by a translucent screen, behind which actions unfold in shadowy mime, obviously to give us a sense of Freddie's increasingly limited vision. (It may even relate to the initial silent-movie reference, though the visual styles are hardly similar.)

Its difficult to pay much attention, though, because theres always something going on in front. One moment, cuttingly written and played, shows Freddie, partially blind, shamed by an encounter with someone who is totally so. It jolts but, typically of the play, it goes nowhere. Maybe there's nowhere it could go.

Maybe this really is an unstageable -- or at least an undramatizeable -- subject.

THE DOLL HOUSE

Canadian Stage Theatre, Upstairs

The Henrik Ibsen play usually known in English as A Dolls House has become, at least in its title, more definite and less possessive: Pretty much the course of action that Ibsen recommends to his characters. The Doll House, in John Murrells sparky and speakable new translation, has been moved forward from 1879, when Ibsen wrote it, to 1912. So, at least, says the program, though I doubt if many would notice the difference.

Radical updating would anyway be pointless, robbing us of the thrill that always comes from discovering our own concerns anticipated in an old text. Ibsen's play, which climaxes in the most famous marital walk-out in world drama, gives the lie to the strange idea that feminism was some invention of the 1960s, though Ibsen himself professed to have no interest in what were known as women's rights. He was interested in human freedom, its uses and abuses; and he found marriage the ideal site on which to explore this. He wrote a great polemical play without being himself a polemicist, which is probably the way to do it.

The doll in Ibsens house is Nora Helmer; the householder is her husband Torvald, a banker on the brink of a major promotion. Torvalds favoured conjugal style might be called the Endearment Smothering; he obsessively calls his wife "songbird" and squirrel and professes to find her delightfully unworldly and impractical.

That is all he knows. Some years ago Nora saved him from a fatal breakdown by raising the money for a long holiday in Italy. Being short herself of ready kroner, she borrowed them from a shabby, disgraced lawyer named Krogstad and forged a signature to close the deal. Krogstad now threatens to tell the hitherto oblivious Torvald. Caught between her creditor's blackmail and her spouse's craven recriminations when he finds out, Nora grows up. She was already a clever manipulator; now she wants honesty and she wants knowledge, most of all about herself.

The last of the plays three acts contains two great duets. By way of prelude to the Helmers passionate break-up, we get a low- key union, clear-eyed to the point of cynicism, between Krogstad and Nora's equally needy friend Mrs Linde. It seems to be a kind of love; but then, as Nora says not long after, who knows what that word means?

This double climax remains thrillingly effective, but Vikki Anderson's production takes its sweet time getting there. I saw it a week into the run and I got the impression that whatever glue had held the performances together was starting to evaporate. Each actor seems to be operating separately. There is much forcing of conflicts; people get up and stride around on the least provocation, which is domestically unconvincing and also unsightly.

The setting, too, is unimaginatively shabby, although the director is a practised designer. I was reminded of Bernard Shaw offering assistance to the impoverished producers of another Ibsen play: "If I have a ten-pound note, they shall have it; if not, I can at least lend them a couple of decent chairs." In this context, the enlistment of James Kudelka to choreograph Noras tarantella (staged here for desperation rather than sexuality) looks like overkill.

Ben Carlson bestows on Helmer the same passion and personality he has brought to unpromising young men in Shaw Festival productions. Indeed, one began to fear for the plays finale; what would Nora have to complain about? But it works splendidly; we expect better from this Torvald, just as Nora does, and so we share in the bitterness of her disillusion. Carlson, as a good actor should, respects his character and fights his corner.

Fiona Byrne's Nora starts almost exaggeratedly giddy; you can see the exact moment of her transformation -- when she realizes, silently, that Krogstad will betray her -- and from that moment she never stops growing. The two actors meet, as Nora says their characters should, as equals; and though their last scene lacks its fullest measure of shattering suspense, it comes close.

Jordan Pettle's Krogstad is a fine study of shady self- justifying desperation, but its style and tempo -- very jerky and off-hand -- have nothing to do with those of the other actors. Melee Hutton's Mrs. Linde, meanwhile, is modest almost to vanishing point; in her scenes with Nora she is not so much confidante as stooge.

Raymond O'Neill has some poignancy as the stricken family friend, Dr. Rank, though the erotic potential of his scenes with Nora is severely diminished. (He came late into the production, having a couple of years ago replaced Peter Donat, who had given a memorable account of the same role at the Atlantic Theatre Festival; can you make a career of being second Rank?)

Ellen-Ray Hennessy brings unusual fullness to the tiny role of the Helmer family nanny. In this version she has only one child to chaperone -- half the number Ibsen specified. The reduction is damaging. It is important that when Nora slams the door at the end, she leaves behind it not one child but two; or, if you count her soon-to-be ex, not two but three.
