NEW FRANCE

Cameron House, Toronto

This is complicated, so pay attention.

TORONTO - In 1985, the theatre company called VideoCabaret began producing a 12-part sequence of what its writer and director, Michael Hollingsworth, describes as "comedies of manners," but which in fact amount to a comic-strip history of Canada. (The manners are very bad.) After adding new shows at a general rate of one a year, the project reached completion in 1999. Its overall title was The History of the Village of the Small Huts (a literal translation of the country's name) but the latest instalments, which bring the story up to the very recent past, have been labelled The Global Village; whether this is a whole new title or merely a sub-title is hard to ascertain.

Having in 15 years gone as far as it apparently intended to, Hollingsworth's troupe has launched a new five-year plan for doing the whole thing over again. They have kicked this off with a re- mounting of the show that began it all, an item called New France.

However, New France is itself sub-divided. It consists of four 55- minute plays; and you can tell they are separate plays, rather than just separate acts, because the cast takes a curtain-call at the end of each one. The four are being presented as two double-bills, in repertoire. The head spins. Just to make it rotate faster, you can take in New France in its four-hour entirety (plus generous intermissions) on certain days, matinee and evening. This is what I did, out of professional necessity, but I don't recommend it to the casual customer. I'm all for epics, but to keep you impressed over a whole theatrical day, a show needs to project a certain grandeur. VideoCabaret is into, at most, anti-grandeur.

I came in late on the original cycle -- three shows from the end, in fact -- but my enthusiasms and my reservations have remained fairly constant.

VideoCabaret's aim is to make their stage look as much like a television set as possible. They back this up with the usual specious rhetoric about appealing to "an audience raised on rock and TV" (so why not offer them something different?) but it has resulted in a distinctive visual style. Their stage is a small box, with low ceiling, raised floor and an unmediated black surround. Lighting pours down hard and bright, and the action does indeed look as if it's going on behind a screen. Each play is performed in a series of short scenes; five minutes, in this context, is regarded as a long time to go without a break. They haven't quite managed to achieve instant cutting from one episode to the next, but here the cabaret half of the equation takes over; at the end of each vignette, there is a black-out, then the lights go up to reveal -- with a speed that never ceases to amaze -- a whole new group of actors in place. It's especially impressive since there are only seven performers rushing in and out of costume, and one of them has the third play off.

All this quick change of course takes its toll, especially if you choose the one-day marathon option. It's the vehicle for an attitude toward characters and events that veers from off-hand to contemptuous.

New France covers the early period of French settlement in Canada, beginning in the 16th century and ending in the 18th. We see the French fighting and exploiting the natives, and both sides fighting among themselves, with the British joining in toward the end to take what they can from both.

The whites are consistently presented as cruel, scheming and corrupt, the Indians as just cruel and scheming. On a case-by-case basis, this could probably be justified, but over four hours it becomes achingly monotonous, if never actually boring. You begin to suspect the reason Hollingsworth keeps his scenes so brief is that if he went on any longer he might encounter somebody behaving decently, and he wouldn't know how to deal with it. In his chosen cartoon style he writes well, with a notable command of verbal rhythm, but it's notable that though his plays have the aura of comedy -- even torture scenes are played for giggles -- they are seldom actually funny. He and his actors are too busy sneering for the audience to feel much like laughing.

Each of New France's four constituent parts takes its title from a central character. The first, Donnacona & Cartier, shows the Iroquois chief of that name carried off by Jacques Cartier, pioneer French invader, to the court of Cartier's royal master, Francois I. Here he witnesses sexual and political intrigues that culminate in the incompetent aristocrat Roberval being put in charge of a new Canadian expedition, and being beaten soundly off by the Iroquois.

This is the best play of the four, largely because Donnacona himself is the only person in the show to be granted a modicum of dignity; he surveys the titled parasites around him with a sardonic bemusement that recalls the malcontent heroes of Jacobean tragi- comedies -- many of which were set, by their self-righteous English authors, in decadent French courts of precisely this era -- and he meets a grisly martyr's death. (So do many later characters, but their martyrdom is generally mocked.) Besides, the Parisian machinations, though only tangentially related to Canadian history, are compactly unfolded, and in retrospect one appreciates the change of scene.

The second play, Champlain, shows a new French adventurer establishing himself in Quebec, handing out land to his fellow colonists and allying himself with the susceptible Hurons against the intransigent Iroquois.

In Brebeuf, a fanatical and sexually suspect Jesuit who has loomed menacingly at the edges of the previous instalment dispatches members of the rival Franciscan order on doomed missions among the heathen, who finally catch up with him, too. In Frontenac, a foppish French governor presides over the annexation of the fur trade and also -- at wearying and complicated length -- over marital and extra- marital entanglements, precipitated by the arrival from the old country of fresh female stock. Unlike Donnacona, none of these three later titular characters really justifies his position; they are just three buffoons among many.

There are some unifying images: we begin with two Iroquois talking intently of beavers, and the subject recurs at least once per play. The author is also good at keeping seemingly irrelevant characters in motion, until their turn comes to join the parade. His actors have an absolute grip on the style, though their cod French accents gave me a headache, as if the Royal Canadian Air Farce were to set its sights on Quebec and keep them there for hours.

There is especially striking work by Billy Merasty as Donnacona; by Jonathan Fisher as the contrastingly sadistic Iroqouis chief Teganissorens, whose eye patch and gloating grin permeate three of the four sections; by Bruce Vavrina as Brebeuf, though he's more impressive on the sidelines than when he takes centre stage; and by Deborah Lambie, who executes a dashing gender switch as turncoat Etienne Brule, before she reverts to skirts as one of two calculating imported brides. The other, equally piquant, is Janet Burke, whose most notable previous role has been the puritanical Madame Champlain, a most unwilling immigrant and, on this show's showing, the first ever to ask if the winters are ALWAYS like this. Religion and its practitioners are presented with especially savage ridicule throughout, which is certainly the author's right, but he shows no inclination to explore why people might have believed, and the knee-jerk satire gets tedious.

Still, nobody could dispute the energy of the enterprise. The next batch is due in April; it's called The British, and I suspect that however appalling the French's behaviour may have been, we haven't seen anything yet.

THE VIC

Theatre Passe Muraille

This is a listless production, crammed with earnest but unfocused performances, of a first play that isn't ready. It neatly sums up a lot of what's wrong with the Toronto theatre. (The not-for-profit Toronto theatre, anyway; the commercial sector has other problems.)

The Vic, we are informed rather late, is TV cop-drama shorthand for victim; and Leanna Brodie's play is a study in victimhood, in how it gets invited and might be avoided. Set nominally in Winnipeg and scenically in limbo, it deploys its characters, all of whom are female, in four separate groups.

In one, a recent and severely damaged refugee from a cult is tended by her sister, an overseas aid worker currently in a state of burnout, and their well-meaning but baffled middle-class mother. In another, a PhD student, deeply depressed by the realization that her thesis is neither wonderful nor terrible but merely "adequate," enrages and is enraged by her girlfriend, an uneducated recovering alcoholic with a violent streak. In a third, a young, gifted and black filmmaker, who doesn't want to spend her career either trading on or apologizing for her race, signs on as assistant to an idolized and apparently world-famous director, and is sadly disillusioned. The fourth group consists of one person: an adolescent girl who keeps a diary on videotape.

There are vestigial links between some individual members of these set-ups, but essentially we are being told four separate stories in rotation, and sorting them out proves a hard task for everyone involved, not least the audience.

There is an intermittently recurrent framing device: Four of the characters are searching for a fifth, who is missing and feared dead. That the person they're looking for proves not to be the one you -- or at least I -- thought she was is either a cunningly devised red herring or just one more confusion: I'm afraid I vote for the latter. When we discover the truth of the situation, it's obviously meant to throw all we have previously learned about the characters into sharp and illuminating relief. But it doesn't, because in fact we haven't learned much about them; the author's chosen structure hasn't given her much time to tell us.

All of the characters are there to illustrate a theme: A couple of them are aggressors, most are at least potential victims, some are both. Some resist their fate, some collude in it, a few seem capable of escaping it altogether. But this is just theory. In practice, they are simply rushed onstage and told to confront one another. There is little feeling for any of the niceties, the half- tones, the hesitations that actually make up human behaviour. At one point a mother, who is anything but callous and who knows her daughter is in a fragile state, walks on and tells her one of her former associates has been found murdered, as unceremoniously as if she were reading the ten o'clock news. The actors are virtually compelled to go for the jugular, but with no solid ground from which to launch their attacks. So they come off awkward.

Waneta Storms, a gifted actress who has been turning up this year in consistently rocky circumstances, is the only one here to occupy her space onstage with any sense of either strength or repose; though, as the cultist living largely in a world of her own, she may have an advantage over the others. (She has a solo scene that seems to have come from some other play, but it is still the highlight of the evening.) Marjorie Chan as the solitary diarist is given the tenderest writing, and Moynan King as the reformed drunk the fiercest; and they both have their moments. Ann Holloway's turn as the swaggering sacred monster of the movies is embarrassingly overdone. But then she is isn't given any context.

That is partly the fault of the writing, but some blame must go to David Oiye, whose direction is atrocious. Steve Lucas has designed an all-purpose steps-and-ramp setting, with a withered tree- branch overhanging, that seems to have been left over from a run- down production of a Shakespearean history. Meant to accommodate everything, it suits nothing. Trying to treat the various levels as if they were hotel beds or domestic furnishings or even part of a credible outdoors, the actors get nowhere; and neither the lighting nor the staging contributes any atmosphere.

It's no accident that this year's best new plays -- Hysteria, The Weir, Elizabeth Rex -- have all been written in sustained scenes; I can't be the only person to be sick of watching plays with episodic television construction limping across inhospitable stages. (People sometimes claim the Elizabethans wrote this way. They didn't. And neither did Brecht, whatever else may be held against him.) But if a play is going to use this method, then a director has to find some kind of rhythm, and some way of capping the scenes. It isn't enough to dim the lights on one part of the stage, bring them up on another, and leave the performers to find their own way home in the gaps. (Are they meant to be in or out of character at these points? They look sheepishly undecided.) It may also make them bashful about starting again; the lack of flow and definition within the scenes reflects what goes on between them.

Anyone can make a mistake, but this play, according to the program, has been in preparation for three years and in workshop for nearly two. Surely, during that time, somebody might have noticed that its method was unworkable. Or has the workshopping of a play become an end in itself? On a related note: Could we put an end to the sickly, patronizing and increasingly common practice of letting the actors applaud the audience at the curtain. It usually looks desperate; and it's always presumptuous.

Clapping is our job. If we feel like it.

SCIENCE FICTION

Factory Studio Theatre, Toronto

There is the one about the two sinister strangers who snatch a mangy, destitute man from his mangy, destitute refuge at the behest of some mysterious outside authority; an example is Harold Pinter's The Birthday Party. There is also the one about alien forces who, confusing fact and fiction, seek the aid of some earthly practitioners of interplanetary fantasy; an example is Galaxy Quest. David Widdicombe's play Science Fiction borrows both these familiar motifs but still ends up as its own animal. Its origins may be mongrel, but, in this gloriously acted production, it plays like a thoroughbred.

The abducted professional fantasist is Spider, a once-successful sci-fi novelist who has fallen on evil times. He is crouching unshaven and otherwise dishevelled in a fetid hotel room, contemplating a refrigerator stocked only with dog food. (The dog is dead.) There's nothing very novel about Spider's plight -- if I had a dollar for every drunken novelist I've seen reduced to eating dog food, I could buy the next one a drink -- but both he and we are rescued from it, and in short order.

A young woman named Jill arrives. She is an omnivorous fan of Spider's work who has hitchhiked across the country to pay tribute and who encounters him being, as he frequently is, sick in a diner. Almost automatically, she starts looking after him, and even offers - - at no great risk, considering his condition -- to share his bed. They have a certain amount of inter-generational conflict; discovering in his room a cherished volume of Jules Verne, the patron saint of Spider's trade, she exclaims, "I never read anything old," as if afraid she might catch something. Jill's limitations, though, go with her strengths; shy but sure, she will be Spider's salvation.

Mostly she has to save him from Quint and Teddy, the two guys who come to take him away. Quint, the elder, is a former mercenary who, after being invalided out of service, was taken in by Teddy's family; Teddy, now orphaned, is his more-or-less faithful henchman, and very useful. Though physically small, he is able to hoist the sleeping, blanketed Spider over his shoulder, though he demurs at actually carrying him out of the room. Quint eventually lets on that his benevolent employers are aliens who want Spider to save the world; they recruit someone to carry out this amiable chore once every few thousand years. If Spider will co-operate, fine; if not, Quint -- also a devotee of his fiction but appalled by the state he has let himself get into -- will be more than happy to kill him, and perhaps take on the saving job himself, though he does seem to have it confused with world dictatorship. (He is one of Nature's fascists; cruel and servile at once.)

Killing is what Quint is good at, what he was trained if not born for, and the play takes shape as a duel between two rival ways of looking at the world. Spider's novels, we gather, were always fundamentally benevolent; the good guys were able to save the Earth or the galaxy or whatever, and it was worth saving. Quint wants to destroy, or at the very least to intimidate, and though statistically outnumbered (most people would rather be nice, and even Teddy proves a wavering ally), he is fearsomely powerful. He can get off on aiming guns at people, or by denying them their breakfast. The resemblance to Pinter's Goldberg goes quite deep. Quint too has come through a breakdown to find power in wielding power, and like Goldberg he threatens to run off with a play of which he is not technically the protagonist.

David Fox plays him magnificently, with remorseless weight and dazzling style. Quite the best-dressed person in the play (he has, admittedly, absolutely no competition), he wears his tie as tellingly as he wields his weapons; and he speaks with chilling casualness of the numbers he has killed. This is the most entertaining new play since The Drawer Boy, and Fox's appearance in both must have something to do with that.

As Spider, Hardee T. Lineham, who engagingly resembles Kelsey Grammer with a three-day growth, seems initially to be trying too hard; he delivers an initial soliloquy (not the author's best writing) in a resonant mumble that suggests he has something, possibly a microphone, stuck in his throat. He perks up as soon as he has people to act with, giving us someone to root for but not to gush over.

Kristina Nicoll as Jill is at once dowdily eccentric and magnetically attractive, and Dylan Roberts' Teddy is everybody's perfect foil. Ted Dykstra, who as director has done a masterly job of verbal and visual orchestration, speaks in the program of "this dream cast"; this is the kind of thing people say in their bios, when they're through thanking God or their mothers or whoever gave them the job, but this time it seems justified. This kind of acting and inter-acting provides real sensuous pleasure.

Steve Lucas, whose designs for The Vic I slammed yesterday, supplies four faultlessly evocative sets in a tiny space. There are times when the playwright's storytelling threatens to go off the rails, but like the heroes its hero writes about, it always finds a way out. Its long last scene keeps twisting beyond our expectations, and our central question -- do those space entities really exist? -- is played with brilliantly right up to the end.

SO MANY WORDS

Theatre Passe Muraille's Backspace

In So Many Words, a young woman pursues a celebrated writer to his hotel and -- after a great many well-chosen words -- goes to bed with him. That makes the second consecutive night on which I have seen this situation played out. The set-up in this play -- in which the man, the woman and the hotel are all up-scale and the two parties met that day on a plane -- is more plausible than the fantastic premise on offer just round the corner in the aptly named Science Fiction; but it isn't as dramatically real.

That doesn't matter too much since, unlike Science Fiction, Roger Rueff's piece isn't about story; it's about dialogue and ideas. It takes in place in Washington where the male protagonist -- a novelist whose works are better known for their intellectual than their emotional qualities -- has arrived to collect yet another award. His agent is waiting to greet him and in the first scene we watch her trying, unsuccessfully, to get rid of the preternaturally cool and determined young lady who has come straight from the airport to claim her own prize. In the second, this visitor finds herself up against a more formidable opponent, the novelist's wife. She discovers, at least to her own satisfaction, that the marriage is dead; the wife discovers that the intruder, who talks like a philosophy student, is an actress and lingerie model.

Next, our hero having finally checked in, comes the seduction. His admirer, after much probing, gets him to confess that he doesn't love his wife. She also reveals how much else she knows about him, including the well-guarded fact that he has a second career as a writer of high-class porn. (We have to take her word for it that it is high-class.) She offers -- and this time it is in so many words - - to make his fictional dreams come true. Either he confesses or his wife finds out, because the next sound we hear is that of her demanding a divorce.

Some uncomfortable truths come out about their relationship, with especial reference to his coldness both as a man and a writer. A coda brings back the agent who may love him in her way, and has the percentage to prove it.

The opening and closing scenes present us with brittle badinage on a high level: words used as weapons, offensive or defensive. The seduction is fun to watch, but seems to be acting out its own, rather common, fantasy: the one that says a rumpled middle-aged author will be an irresistible magnet to an amorous woman 20 years his junior. The marital battle cuts painfully deep, as does the expose of the author's psychological ruthlessness. It turns out that he has hugged to himself a hideous secret that gives him the energy to write.

I think the playwright overreaches in his choice of secret, and I don't believe he has properly calibrated the effect on the wife when it is revealed. (It would destroy her.). I'm willing to believe almost anything of writers, especially novelists, but not quite this.

To revert to my initial comparison: the characters here are more immediately recognizable than those in Science Fiction but they don't have the same theatrical blood in their veins; nor can they beguile us with long juicy speeches. The demands on the actors are severe; they have to maintain their poise and their pose to articulate the text and mine the subtext.

The staging is by the Actors Repertory Company, whose one previous show, Strindberg's Creditors, was another triangle piece conducted in duologues. What the script describes as "a well- appointed room" has been economically realized by the designer James Cameron, and the production, directed by Paul Lampert, is reasonably enjoyable; but the performances don't really cut it.

Both Brenda Bazinet as the wife and Jennifer Wigmore as the self- propelled sex object keep letting down their guard; Bazinet sometimes neglects even to raise hers, while Wigmore doesn't always sound as if she knows what she's talking about. Robin Ward, playing the most passive of the trio, has more legitimate cause to relax occasionally, and is, given the built-in implausibilties of his role, believable. Tedde Moore has the agent, a creature of lunches and reassurances, down 100%; 100% if you figure in her commission.

SALMON MIRANDA

Artword Theatre, Toronto

I have to break the news that Salmon Miranda is about a pair of young lovers called Sam and Miranda. It seems to me that if the girl were named Patty, we might have had a title that made more gastronomic sense, and I don't think the author was wise to bring the title that she does have explicitly, and whimsically, into the dialogue. Still, the play, especially in its earlier stages, is tasty.

Salmon Miranda has been announced, with an understandable blend of defensiveness and bravado, as a romantic comedy. Miranda, a non- graduating university student who works in a bookstore, spends the night with Sam, a waiter and -- at least by his own account -- actor, whom she met that evening in a bar. This is most unusual behaviour for her, but apparently standard for him.

We start the play in Miranda's apartment the morning after; the author, Leah Davidson, and the director, Sarah Armstrong, evoke a wonderfully fluid and convincing sense of post-coital confusion. Davidson herself, playing Miranda, is extraordinarily natural as she veers between nervous self-consciousness, stern efforts at practicality, and renewed surrender. By the end of the scene, the couple have agreed to extend the one-night stand into a relationship.

There could hardly be a play if they didn't, but there seem to be other good reasons. They are temperamental opposites who seem guaranteed to stimulate and enrage one another just about equally. Sam is the dynamic one. In the course of their first week together, he treats Miranda to karaoke, bowling and a much-increased alcohol consumption; she only demurs when he suggests they spend the weekend scuba diving. His restlessness has begun to get to her; and also, I may say, to me. At least I wished that Christopher Morris, who plays Sam, could find some way of letting up a bit -- in volume if not actually in energy -- since, even for an actor playing an actor -- indeed even for an actor who may be fantasizing about being an actor -- he seems excessively actorish.

Also, while Miranda just talks, Sam makes speeches; he seems to be a manic depressive, though we only get to see the manic side. He tells a long story about an exciting childhood experience riding the roller coaster at Canada's Wonderland. Miranda isn't too keen on roller coasters; she says she prefers merry-go-rounds. This, apparently, is the index of their differing temperaments, and the two of them then proceed to bat these handy metaphors all around the dialogue well into the second act. In a play whose best feature has been its overheard conversational quality, all this self- consciousness becomes a pain.

Act One ends with Miranda throwing Sam out; and that was all there was to the play when it was seen on the Fringe last year. In its new second act it gets more solemn, though it doesn't necessarily go deeper.

A year has passed; Sam comes back, of course, and they debate whether to start again. This time it's Miranda who wants to; Sam who has doubts. Miranda admits to having told lies of her own; Sam is revealed as a full-blown mental case. This is too much freight for the play to carry. Comedy as courtship-ritual is a necessary part of theatre, much neglected recently, but if it's going to work we have to like the characters concerned and believe they would be good for one another. I liked Miranda, but I decided that she would be better off without Sam. The play works hard toward the end to persuade us otherwise, and sending us out of the theatre to the strains of Ella Fitzgerald singing Let's Fall in Love was a great help.

All told, the play itself is likeable, and much preferable to the glum pretentiousness generally available elsewhere. These are real people, not -- at least not most of the time -- ciphers pressed into service to make a point. Morris is a proven good actor, even if I couldn't warm to him here.

My only doubts about Davidson as an actress are those that always occur when you see someone apparently perfectly matched to her role: Can she do anything else? (She did occasionally seem to be living beyond her technical means.) Anyway, both as actor and writer. she's warm, funny and a find.

THE VAGINA MONOLOGUES

The Music Hall, Toronto

The production known as The Vagina Monologues started as a solo performance, given off-Broadway by Eve Ensler, an actress and playwright. To put it mildly, it caught on. The cast was expanded from one to three; the show became a metropolitan phenomenon and an international franchise. It now tours the world.

It is a highly entertaining show, enlivening and even enlightening. In format, it could hardly be simpler (except, presumably, in its one-person incarnation). The three performers sit on stools, at microphones, and read. I still think they should at least memorize their opening remarks, when they're welcoming us in their own persons. There is, though, a good excuse, at least for one of them. The team consists of two American full-timers and a local guest; the latter position is rotated weekly, and its incumbent would hardly have time to learn the lines.

The guest star this week is Gloria Reuben, TV star, actress and singer, and she is tremendous, superbly limber and relaxed, both vocally and physically. She has the most spectacular routine of the evening, in which she plays a lesbian dominatrix who has become a connoisseur, not only of other women's vaginas, but of other women's huge variety of pleasurable moans. She demonstrates several, getting especial mileage from the WASP moan, daintily surprised, and the triple-orgasm moan, for which she draws spectacularly on her professional vocal prowess. (If you attend a later performance you may find Shirley Douglas or Sonja Smits in the home-girl role; I wonder how they'll get on.)

The Yanks on Reuben's flanks are Starla Benford, a wry comedian with a crackling forte that she knows how to hold, and Sherri Parker Lee, who looks and sounds as Southern as her name and does world- weary extremely well.

Reading or even reciting material is not the easiest task for an actor; the usual tendency is to overstress but under-characterize. Here, though, all three consistently, and exhilaratingly, hit the right note. The words they deliver derive from interviews conducted by the author with hundreds of women. The subjects were asked what they thought their vaginas might like to wear (the replies seem to have been wearyingly arch) and what they might like to say (the replies are instructively hilarious, with "slow down" the most popular choice). Some of the responses were turned into longer speeches -- one wonders with how much editorial intervention.

Some of the stories are sad: One 70-year-old woman tells of coming in her first boyfriend's car and never wanting to have sex again. Some are terrible: A Bosnian woman gives a grim, detailed account of multiple rape. (This is somewhat sweetened -- unwisely, I think -- by some flowery poetic commentary, but the horror comes through, and it's a tribute to the show that it can co-exist with the surrounding humour without either element feeling forced or devalued.) Some are stoically amusing, even while professing anger, like a description of visits to the gynecologist.

And most are celebratory. A young girl, who'd been abused by a male family friend, tells of a subsequent more pleasurable initiation by a sophisticated older woman. One woman is even allowed to tell, a little shamefacedly, of being awakened by a man who loved vaginas, especially looking at them. Apparently he wasn't too prepossessing in other respects, but it's reassuring to hear him given that much credit.

I found myself wondering defensively if there might not even, somewhere, be some lesbians who were lousy lovers. The show does, magically, include a celebration of the clitoris, the only human organ, we are reminded, that functions solely as a source of pleasure. The puritanical downside of this, we are duly reminded, is genital mutilation.

The show take its title rather freely. Sometimes the vagina is treated strictly anatomically. Sometimes it becomes a metaphor. It is certainly an opportunist show. But among its qualities is that of being the most vivid dramatization of The Joy of Sex, in several varieties, that we are ever likely to encounter.

THE VAGINA MONOLOGUES

The Music Hall, Toronto

The production known as The Vagina Monologues has come a long way, baby, since it was first unveiled in New York. It started -- in a modest way, so to speak -- as a solo performance, given off- Broadway by Eve Ensler, an actress and playwright. To put it mildly, it caught on. The cast was expanded from one to three; the show became a metropolitan phenomenon and an international franchise. It now tours the world dispensing wit, wisdom and T-shirts.

The T-shirts, by the way, reproduce the show's logo, in which the word "monologues" appears in rather small type. The resultant emphasis is all very wild and wonderful or, looked at from another perspective, rather coy and commercial.

The show more or less begins with the three actresses listing an enormous number of synonyms for "vagina" (most of them, I confess, new to me) and the cuteness of many of the words, at least as they deliver them, gets the audience thoroughly onside. Toward the end of the evening, one of the players delivers a more aggressive variant of the same routine; she goes into an extended rhapsody on one synonym we haven't yet heard, the commonest four-letter one. The vaunted intention -- of which I throughly approve -- is to reclaim the word as a source of celebration rather than insult, and though it's somewhat strenuous, it succeeds. The first-night audience roared its approval.

So the question arises: If they feel that strongly about it, and if we agree with them, why didn't they put that in the title? Well, there probably wouldn't have been as many radio spots. (I'm not sure about the T-shirts.)

I must stop pussyfooting around, if that's the phrase I want, and report that The Vagina Monologues is a highly entertaining show, enlivening and even enlightening. In format, it could hardly be simpler (except, presumably, in its one-person incarnation). The three performers sit on stools, at microphones, and read.

It's a little dashing, at first, to realize that this is all they're going to do, and I still think that they should at least memorize their opening remarks, when they're welcoming us in their own persons. There is, though, a good excuse, at least for one of them. The team consists of two American full-timers and a local guest; the latter position is rotated weekly, and its incumbent would hardly have time to learn the lines.

The guest-star this week is Gloria Reuben, TV star, actress and singer, and she is tremendous, superbly limber and relaxed, both vocally and physically. She has, in fact, the most spectacular routine of the evening, in which she plays a lesbian dominatrix who has become a connoisseur, not only of other women's vaginas but of other women's huge variety of pleasurable moans. She demonstrates several, getting especial mileage from the WASP moan, daintily surprised, and the triple-orgasm moan, for which she draws spectacularly on her professional vocal prowess.

All sexes in the audience seemed to enjoy this (probably for different reasons), and Reuben's colleagues were visibly impressed, though they prolonged their congratulations to the point of unprofessionalism. After all, we're the ones who paid for tickets. (Well, I didn't, but you will. If you attend a later performance, you may find Shirley Douglas or Sonja Smits in the home-girl role; I wonder how they'll get on.)

The Yanks on Reuben's flanks are Starla Benford, a wry comedian in the Whoopi Goldberg mould with a crackling forte that she knows how to hold, and Sherri Parker Lee, who looks and sounds as Southern as her name and does world-weary extremely well.

Reading or even reciting material is not the easiest task for an actor; the usual tendency is to overstress but under-characterize. Here, though, all three consistently, and exhilaratingly, hit the right note.

The words they deliver derive from interviews conducted by the author with hundreds of women. The subjects were asked what they thought their vaginas might like to wear (the replies seem to have been wearyingly arch) and what they might like to say (the replies are instructively hilarious, with "slow down" the most popular choice). Some of the responses were turned into longer speeches -- one wonders with how much editorial intervention. Obviously Ensler, like all investigators, found what she was listening for: Open at any page of The Hite Report and you find far more clinical answers to what must have been similar questions.

Some of the stories are sad: One 70-year-old woman tells of coming in her first boyfriend's car and never wanting to have sex again. Some are terrible: A Bosnian woman gives a grim, detailed account of multiple rape. (This is somewhat sweetened -- unwisely, I think -- by some flowery poetic commentary, but the horror comes through, and it's a tribute to the show that it can co-exist with the surrounding humour without either element feeling forced or devalued.) Some are stoically amusing, even while professing anger, like a description of visits to the gynecologist.

And most are celebratory. A young girl, who'd been abused by a male family friend, tells of a subsequent more pleasurable initiation by a sophisticated older woman. ("I thought -- when I grow up, I want to be a secretary too.") One woman is even allowed to tell, a little shamefacedly, of being awakened by a man who loved vaginas, especially looking at them. Apparently he wasn't too prepossessing in other respects, but it's reassuring to hear him given that much credit. Though I note that even the dominatrix aroused the displeasure of her neighbours because the volume of her own erotic moans, with boyfriends, was disturbing the building, so somebody must have been doing soemthing right.

The phrase "the myth of the vaginal orgasm" is never actually spoken, but it does sort of hover. I found myself wondering defensively if there might not even, somewhere, be some lesbians who were lousy lovers. The show does, magically, include a celebration of the clitoris, the only human organ, we are reminded, that functions solely as a source of pleasure. The puritanical downside of this, we are duly reminded, is genital mutilation.

The show, in fact, take its title rather freely. Sometimes the vagina is treated strictly anatomically. Sometimes it becomes a metaphor, and not always an exact one, for female oppression or for female sexuality. It is, in fact, a slippery subject, and the show is certainly opportunist. But among its qualities is that of being the most vivid dramatization of The Joy of Sex, in several varieties, that we are ever likely to encounter.

PETER PAN

Elgin Theatre

This year's Christmas extravaganza at the Elgin is a strange mixture of play, musical and traditional English pantomime. Ross Petty's previous efforts in this line -- Robin Hood, Cinderella and the others -- have been pantos through and through, loose-jointed entertainments based on stories that rank as folk-myths, without readily identifiable literary sources. Peter Pan, though, exists as a play: Well-known, revivable, less than a century old, certainly a classic, probably a masterpiece. Even the much-loved musical-comedy version of the 1950s simply stuck songs into the existing text: Something that shouldn't have worked but did, delightfully.

J. M. Barrie went public domain some years ago, so legally you can do what you like to his creations. The trouble is that, with Peter Pan, nobody in their right minds would want to do much. This is a first-rate adventure story that fills an evening, and needs no padding. (Most panto sources beg for it.) There are all those characters: Peter himself, the boy who wouldn't grow up; his Lost Boys and his fairy sidekick, Tinker Bell; the precociously motherly Wendy and her two Darling brothers; the spectacularly paranoid Captain Hook and his comparatively scurvy crew; mermaids, Red Indians, and the crocodile who swallowed an alarm clock.

The current version keeps them all, except that the Lost Boys have been joined by a few Lost Girls ("political correctness," muttered my own daughter, disapprovingly) and the Indians have gone, for equally obvious reasons. Petty and his team can't really cut loose -- they are stuck with Barrie's story -- but are they wedded to Barrie's words? No, bicarbonate of soda, no! And their own, though serviceable, aren't as good. They have also lost, or given away, Barrie's dark attitude.

The show's greatest asset is the boss himself. Four years ago, reviewing Robin Hood for Another Newspaper, I suggested Peter Pan (the real one) as an ideal future vehicle for Petty and his wife, Karen Kain, whom I have every reason to believe can fly.

I've got half my wishes: Petty is, as expected, a baroque, farouche, peruked and swishing Hook, equally adept at threatening, singing, bantering with the audience and collapsing in a heap. He also, according to tradition, doubles as Mr. Darling, here transformed from a would-be tyrannical paterfamilias to a cheerful Edwardian alcoholic. (The play has gained a London street-scene that seems to derive equally from Oliver!, Mary Poppins and music-hall, and features a cockney policeman who not only drops his H's but picks up them up in the wrong places.)

Sheila McCarthy has less fortune. She makes a proper airborne entrance, arms and legs akimbo, but all the complexities of the developmentally challenged character are gone and she is left playing cheerful straight-boy, not only to Hook but to Sharmaine Ryan's insistently flesh-and-blood Tinkerbell.

Jayne Lewis sings sweetly as Mrs. Darling and with engaging shamelessness as a vampy mermaid -- Esther Williams gone Mae West. The pirates are pretty funny, and the lost kids lively. Glen Kotyk's production also incorporates some lively fights and dances, and (courtesy Judy and David Gershson) terrible would-be contemporary songs.

There is also, in panto tradition, as much audience participation as the unusually heavy traffic will bear. We lose, though, the most celebrated example of spectator-involvement in world drama: Peter's plea that we save the poisoned Tink by clapping our hands. Presumably the idea of a threatened fairy was thought too alarming. Also gone are Mr. Darling's masochistic self-confinement to the doghouse, Wendy's fears for her bereaved parents, the pirates' real bloodthirstiness, and Peter's haunting loneliness: Everything, in fact, that makes the play creepily interesting.

We gain Ernie Coombs, aka Mr. Dressup, padding amiably around the plot on a rather loose lead. He presides over the final singalong. Traditionally, this is a panto's penultimate item, just before everybody troops down the palace staircase, married. Here, though, there can be no palace; and all the characters are already married, or too young, or incurably celibate. It makes for a really damping anti-climax; and it suggests that a Peter Pantomime really is a contradiction in terms.

To Jan. 6. (416) 872-5555

MURDER ON THE AIR

Limelight Dinner Theatre, Toronto

I see that last time I visited the Limelight, I complained about the food. However, sometimes standards in the arts can rise, and on this occasion I had no problems with the establishment's roast beef, which was very tender and juicy. My two companions tell me they were happy with their chicken, and we all liked the green salad. Likewise, the house red.

If the dinner at this dinner theatre has improved, the theatre has made no progress whatever. Only some names have been changed, presumably to protect the takings. Last year, the title was Murder on the Limelight Express. This year, it's Murder on the Air. The format, the atmosphere, even the storyline and the assembled character types, remain essentially the same. It was fun then, and it is fun now.

Jean Daigle -- star, director and co-writer for the company that calls itself Mysteriously Yours --was last seen, by me anyway, as Hercule Poirot. Now he's a tough American-style private eye, somewhere between Philip Marlowe and Mike Hammer. More of a Hammer, I think. He wouldn't have the patience to negotiate Chandler's tortured thoughts and tortured prose: He has a tendency to shout at people and he is rather stout -- something like Tony Soprano gone over to the other side.

Once again, he has a murder to solve, and once again he does it by interrogating the broadly drawn genre figures who make up the rest of the cast.

He also picks on members of the audience to assist him in his investigations, strolling round the room to find appropriate victims. Far more of this show happens between the tables than happens on the stage.

The story is set in and around a radio studio. Time and place are left vague but we seem, spiritually at least, to be in the 1940s, the Age of Welles. The station's presiding genius is called Orson Kane; its leading actress is named Rose Bud; and the joint is owned by a plutocrat, one (how could there be more than one?) William Randolph Wurst, who starts the action by turning up in his office, dead.

The Wurst, in fact, is over. Everything else, of course, has only just begun.

Everybody who knew William Randolph had, naturally, a motive for bumping him off -- and also had, inevitably, the opportunity to do so.

The late unlamented was about to sell the station out from under them, thus infuriating the entire artistic staff (one director, two actors) plus his own daughter, who hoped to inherit the operation, and the much-put-upon 40-year-old pageboy who wanted to marry her and had been told he could do so only over her father's dead body. (If I, too, may be allowed to do some recycling, of a sentence from my review of this show's predecessor: discarded mistresses, disgruntled employees, disninherited offspring: the dead man has been dissing everybody.)

So our detective subjects each of them to merciless verbal probing, interspersed with wisecracks, and we in the audience try to keep up with the clues.

At the end, we are asked to say, via ballot papers, who we think has done it. I, as usual, had no idea (I knew who I wanted it to be, but I was wrong, again) and naturally I cannot reveal the truth -- though I may hint that the guilty figure in this piece turns out to be not dissimilar to the guilty figure in the previous one. The intervals required for us first to ponder and then to vote seemed rather drawn out, but maybe I should have ordered more wine.

Daigle seems, if anything, better suited to his gumshoe role than to the Belgian sausage he played last time round. He seems completely unfazeable, even when audience members devise snappier comebacks than the ones he had planned for them.

The rest of the company are equally adroit. Not since Moliere, or maybe Gilbert and Sullivan, has a theatrical troupe reacted with such apparent enthusiasm to the task of playing the same stereotypes in the same cartooned storyline, every time.

They get their best chances, though -- and we get our best entertainment -- in a scene-setting prologue when everybody, at least as far as we know, is still alive. We watch them putting on their radio show, and it is very enjoyably spoofed.

Patrons are drafted to read small roles and supply the sound effects, and since they have never done these things before, the players have plenty of opportunity to ad-lib to their mistakes. ("I hear him coming up the stairs" -- pause as the new technician fumbles with her maraccas -- "drunkenly.")

I'm a sucker for this kind of thing and, judging from the reactions around me, I'm not the only one. In fact, this show, by giving its actors a chance to satirize themselves as well as the people they're playing, may have an edge on its locomotive predecessor.

Pondering the inevitable sequels, I look forward more keenly to Murder in Hollywood than to Murder on the High Seas. Though how about Murder in the Newsroom, with one of the suspects a gibbering, neurotic critic? That should please everybody.

Irving Berlin's White Christmas really is a great song, as fine an example as could be found of Berlins genius for matching his words to his music. It isnt a generalized greeting card; it's a first-person-singular song about someone who is missing out on everything except memories.

It only shifts into the second person in its last two lines, May your days be merry and bright/And may all your Christmases be white." Note how that coda, with superbly satisfying artfulness, reverses the title. Note, too, that the lines I've quoted are themselves in quotes; they arent a pat on the head for the audience, theyre what the singer is inscribing in all those Christmas cards he's writing. In fact, they're part of the story.

I confess I never got that last subtlety -- nor did I fully appreciate the quiet ingenuity of Berlins rhyme scheme -- until I read the lyric in Reading Lyrics, a generous and indispensable anthology just published by Random House ($61) and edited by Robert Gottlieb and Robert Kimball.

Gottlieb was, for too brief a time, editor of The New Yorker; he was also a publisher whose services to humanity include the midwifing of Joseph Hellers Catch-22. Kimball is a musical-theatre scholar who has edited sumptuous variorum editions of the lyrics of Cole Porter, Lorenz Hart and Ira Gershwin.

Reading Lyrics gathers the texts of more than a thousand songs from the American golden age, here defined as stretching from 1900 to 1975. It gets us, chronologically and temperamentally, from the supremely extroverted writer-performer George M. Cohan (flourished around 1905) to the supremely introverted writer-performer Dave Frishberg (flourishes around now.)

It is, among other things, the long-needed complement to Alec Wilder's pioneering American Popular Song, which as it happens was published just about the time Gottlieb and Kimball have chosen for their cut-off date. (Wilder, himself a composer-lyricist, is represented in this collection.)

Wilder's was a capacious critical study, devoted to composers; others have since tried to give lyricists the same consideration, but they have lacked the breadth and the sensibility -- sometimes, it seemed, even the knowledge -- to pull it off. Maybe its best, rather than giving us words about words, to give us the words themselves, and let the selection carry its own value-judgments.

The structure of the two books, though, is remarkably similar. Each deals with the major writers, here represented by a minimum of three lyrics and a maximum of 39 (thats Berlin's figure, earned both by quality and longevity). The others in the 30-plus category are Hart, Porter, Gershwin, Oscar Hammerstein and Johnny Mercer. Then, in both books, comes a coda or final chapter, mopping up important songs, one apiece, by writers who in the editors' judgment (some may disagree) dont make the full honour roll.

The two books also share an agenda, declared in Wilders work and implicit in this one. Though much of the material they deal with necessarily comes from shows and movies, they are concerned with the songs as individual entities that can be taken out of context. This probably explains why, while the authors are presented in order of birth, their songs are arranged alphabetically; we are asked to read the lyrics for themselves, rather than as parts of a score.

I don't think there's a song in this book that couldnt be done by one singer, or sometimes two, in a cabaret or on a CD. This doesnt matter too much with the earlier writers, in whose day theatre songs were pop songs, and who wrote in full awareness of that fact. It skews the record when we get to the 1960s -- the Stephen Sondheim generation -- and find ourselves rather arbitrarily confined to a menu of supper-club classics. So the choice from Sondheim's score for Follies includes two rather similar ballads, but not the magnificently evocative Waiting for the Girls Upstairs (an octet) or the venomously vengeful Could I Leave You (too scary, or too tied to its character, or both).

Even with the older songs, there can be problems. The received texts often depart from the originally performed ones, and the editors here seem to have relied -- except with the major writers whom Kimball has already edited -- on the published sheet-music, which often sanitized the songs or just shortened them. So we get a sinless, ginless reduction of Paul Francis Webster's I Got It Bad and That Aint Good, and a Thanks for the Memory in which Leo Robins wonderfully colloquial catalogue of bitter-sweet divorced reminiscence is only half the length it could be. (This song is the classiest of tearjerkers: I wouldn't trust anyone who wasn't reduced to a puddle by it, just as the technicians on the movie-set are said to have been when Bob Hope and Shirley Ross first recorded it.)

There are also some horrendous typos and mislineations, some probably carried over from the sources. Gentlemen, look what youve done to the last lines of Mercers Satin Doll and Jack Yellen's Hard Hearted Hannah. And Jerry Herman may have his limitations, but he would not (in I Won't Send Roses) have rhymed "find things with kind of things."

My first reaction to this anthology was that celebrated by so many of the songs: I fell in love. (How can you not, with a book that even recognizes the existence of forgotten men like Eddie DeLange and Ralph Freed?) Then, as in so many love affairs, I began to notice what was missing. The one really unforgivable omission is They Didnt Believe Me. Remarkable for its music but also for its uniquely-angled lyric (by one Herbert Reynolds, a.k.a. M. E. Rourke - - definitely a one-shot writer), its the first great and still- singable American theatre ballad, on a par historically with Alexander's Ragtime Band and St. Louis Blues, both of which do make the cut.

It's only slightly less startling to come to the end of the Noel Coward section and realize it hasnt included If Love Were All (Cowards "talent to amuse song), or to see that the game loser's By Myself isn't ranked among Howard Dietzs finest hours, or to find the beautiful, contemplative Too Late Now absent from the Alan Jay Lerner portfolio; Id trade it for On the Street Where You Live any night.

Most important totally-excluded lyricist: Oscar Brown Jr., jazz singer-songwriter of the '60s. Runners-up: Jon Hendricks, master of vocalese (and his colleague Annie Ross, for her virtuoso lyric to Twisted); Tom Jones, of The Fantasticks; the Marxist Marc Blitzstein; and Ann Ronell, who went from Willow Weep for Me to Who's Afraid of the Big Bad Wolf -- actually the Disney songs are an important sub-section the book neglects completely.

Its because the book gives you so much that you cant help wanting more. We discover that the American song was laughing at itself almost from birth: The flag-waving Cohan writes a sentimental song (Down by the Erie Canal) that he demolishes in an introductory verse:

The orchestras murder it near and far

It's usually sung by the female star,

The publisher gives her a motor car

And the chorus goes something like this.

(Frishberg, 55 years on, was up to the same thing in Another Song About Paris.)

P. G. Wodehouse, an Englishman on Broadway and as enchantingly deft in song as in prose, is as off-hand as Cohan but far more madcap, as in his song about Napoleon. (He was five feet high/But one tough guy/And I take after Nap.")

Then with Berlin, the immigrant alive to new American sounds, the Jew who wrote White Christmas, lyrics began to swing, and the best of them never stopped. This really is the secret; good popular songs have always been conversational, but the 20th-century American song, whether low-down or highfalutin', has been as alive to musical rhythms as to verbal. In fact, its made the two one. A showpiece example is Larry Harts Thou Swell: formal, slangy, jazzy, funny and tender all at once.

It all came together in the 1930s, when the Fred Astaire-Ginger Rogers movies, in a conscious response to the Depression, reached a zenith of fairy-tale sophistication, and inspired the best songwriters to some of their best work. This was echoed, at ground- level, by less-inspired glamour songs like Sam Coslow's Cocktails for Two ("in some secluded rendezvous ...), and balanced by more realistic New York subway-riding material from the remarkable Harold Rome (Life is a bitter cup of tea/Now I'm just salesgirl seventy- three/I used to be on the daisy-chain/Now Im a chain-store daisy.")

The editors do excellently by Porter and Berlin, juggling comic with romantic, familiar with obscure, and pretty well by Hart, though they largely stick to his most famous songs, with just a couple of classy rarities thrown in. The same treatment is given to Mercer, but he slips through their fingers; verbally resourceful and musically sensitive to an amazing degree, his tone of voice is yet extraordinarily hard to pin down (I know of no recorded collection that has managed it), perhaps because he had little to say, even about romantic love, though he said it angelically.

Some of the lesser names are revelations. Roy Turk, known for Ill Get By, made me chuckle with his Ain't That the Way It Goes, a song for two voices. ("I suppose you dance your best with Mary?/I always step on Rosie's toes/And yet Rosie says you dance divinely/ Aint that the way it goes?)

The team of Livingston and Evans, notorious for Mona Lisa, made me laugh out loud with a lubriciously detailed item called Femininity. Both these songs belong to the 10% in the book that Ive never actually heard, and under those conditions comic lyrics are easier to appreciate.

Love songs are much harder to judge. On the page they can look oddly shaped or obviously phrased; until you hear them with the music, you can't tell whether they're graceful or awkward.

There are one or two songs here that I suspect the editors dont much like themselves. They drily remark of Websters grandiose Love Is a Many-Spendored Thing that it can stand for an entire genre of overblown film anthems." (It comes here with a verse about meeting an oracular little girl in Hong Kong -- a sort of nature girl -- that was new to me and that makes it even worse.)

How do you read Reading Lyrics? Most of the time, if you're lucky, you sing along; the book is an implicit celebration of composers as well as lyricists, and of their Falstaffian partnership above all (not only witty in themselves but the cause of wit in one another). When you get to Martin and Blane's Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas you will, if youre like me, substitute the bittersweet movie lyric for the saccharine commercial one (where "until then well have to muddle through somehow becomes hang a shining star upon the highest bough").

And did you know that Haven Gillespie's Santa Claus Is Comin' to Town is "perhaps the most recorded song in American music history" (I didnt, but it figures) and it has a verse (ditto) and a second chorus in which Santa arrives bearing little tin horns and little toy drums, rooty-toot-toots and rummy-tum-tums (I did, and Im glad)?

And, maybe it's much too early in the game -- ah, but I thought I'd ask you just the same: What Are You Doing New Years Eve? Actually, that one of Frank Loessers isn't in there, but some of his funniest are. And so is that incredible patter number Ya Got Trouble by his (older) disciple Meredith Willson, four whole columns of it, and for that I'd forgive almost anything.

One of his most famous numbers, especially at this time of year, continues to be White Christmas. ; Black & White Photo: BING CROSBY IN WHITE CHRISTMAS: Giving voice to lyricists' dreams. ;

THE MERRY WIDOW

Jane Mallett Theatre

Franz Lehar, the composer of The Merry Widow was Hungarian, and the show itself was first produced in Vienna. Most of its characters, meanwhile, are citizens of some mythical principality in the very mittel of Mitteleuropa, but all of them are spending their time in Paris, for reasons either of business or pleasure. Pleasure predominates, since this is an operetta and in operetta life, given half a chance, is naturlich and naturellement just one mad whirl. Act one is a party at an embassy, act two a party at a private mansion and act three a party at, where else, Maxim's.

The gentlemen go through the entire entertainment in evening dress; the ladies in gowns of matching elegance except for interludes in which they either bustle around as roguishly upscale Parisian call girls or don milmiad frocks and pigtailed tresses to perform the peasant dances of their native land, looking inevitably like Valkyries working up to horned helmets.

So it all looks defiantly timeless: decoratively unrealistic in 1905, the year of its birth, and decoratively unrealistic now. Unrealistic, however, does not mean unreal; nor is it a licence to commit mayhem upon an unsuspecting script.

According to this new production, the librettists of The Merry Widow worked out topical references to Jurassic Park, the American election and even Mel Lastman (Toronto's profile must be rising if Central European diplomats are going around making jokes about our politicians). That's just in the first act; there are similar gags in the remainder, but I was too disheartened to note them. Now these interpolations may not contradict the show's costume scheme, but they certainly violate its spirit. They reduce a classic comic opera to the level of a Ross Petty Christmas pantomime, with the crucial difference that Mr. Petty knows what he's doing. Guillermo Siva- Marin, who directed this production and also takes credit for additional dialogue and -- God forgive him, for I never shall -- lyrics, clearly doesn't; at least I don't imagine that he actually set out to insult the intelligence of his actors, who delivered this stuff with the kind of desperate bravado that denotes deep embarrassment, or of his audience, who confirmed the performers' worst suspicions by stubbornly refusing to laugh.

It's possible that the Toronto Operetta Theatre caught this long- incubating disease from the Stratford Festival, who used to subject Gilbert and Sullivan to just this kind of stupidity; at least TOT has the excuse of being a small-scale outfit mounting its shows on a shoestring and for limited runs.

The piece itself the director seems to regard, equally patronizingly, as a silly charade interrupted by some pretty tunes. Lehar's tunes are of course more than pretty: They comprise a cavalcade of all that's best -- certainly all that's most familiar - - in European operetta, peaking in the untouchable Vilja. There is also the famous waltz, which in this uncredited translation is called Love Unspoken, and that rousing march of mystified misogynists whose refrain is "Girls, Girls, Girls" but whose printed title is Oh the Women, and which comes across as a sort of male can- can, or perhaps a can't-can't.

Lovely though they are, the melodies can sound stodgy or skittish if they're sung and played with flair, and especially if they're not not firmly anchored to the surrounding dialogue, of which there is a great deal.

The Merry Widow is based on the generally infallible Benedick- and-Beatrice or Fred-and-Ginger conceit of the couple who despise one another so much and so noisily that they have to be in love. She, Anna Glawari, is the free-spirited woman, left rich and happy by the timely death of her husband; he, Count Danilo, is the accredited rake who crossed her path once before. Both hail from somewhere very small and very broke called Pontevedro, and their union is earnestly desired by Baron Zeta, their country's ambassador to France; the widow is the only Pontevedrian with any money, and the baron doesn't want to see her throwing it away on some smooth- tongued foreigner. But he has other problems: He suspects, correctly, that his wife is deceiving him and he very nearly blunders into having his suspicions confirmed. These twin actions are laboriously set up but neatly resolved, the principal couple acting as good angels in the affairs of the secondary menage a trois.

So we need to believe in Anna and Danilo as strong personalities, and we need to sense electricity -- both positive and negative -- flowing between them. Fred Love as Danilo sings strongly and has the right air of decent worldliness in his acting, but his relationship to Barbara Hannigan's Anna is almost non-existent; she has no especial radiance about her -- she seems in fact rather prim, and it's very hard to tell what, at any given moment, she is either speaking or singing about; she trills, remorselessly.

As the straying baroness, Elizabeth Beeler is somewhat more credible, though Craig Ashton as her lover makes a wildly unlikely Parisian rake. Ian Simpson has an efficiently light touch as the Baron's all-purpose factotum, and Gregory Cross puts in some conscientious clowning as his employer, though he never once suggests a man whose world -- personal and professional -- is about to cave in on him. But then I don't suppose his director wants him to.

The story ends with an energetic double flourish of the double standard: The men in the cast upbraid the women for their indiscretions; the women, disguised in masks and decolletage, catch the men in the act, or as close to it as they're likely to get; and we end in the assurance that both sexes are frail, but women are smarter. (This counts as traditional comic wisdom, as preached by Europeans.) Something of this comes over, but never at an adult level.

The costumes are smart, and the sets look at first quite happy in their cut-rate state. Gradually, though, they develop their own kind of desperation. The luckless singers of one ardent duet are thoroughly upstaged by shadowy but very visible supers who take their places behind hitherto isolated bits of greenery and start moving them about. It looks in the half-light as if the scenery is trying to sneak away from the show without telling anybody; on top of this, the transformation, once accomplished, turns out to have been totally unnecessary.

The whole production, obviously intended to be elegantly naughty, is stalled at pretty and giggly. It does, though, make you want to see a rigorously opulent staging of the work directed by, say, Robin Phillips at, say, Stratford (on the assumption that the Festival has outgrown the urge to deface light opera): a production that might take the piece by the scruff of its merry widow and shake it out for real sex, real wit, real pain, and real romance. They're all there, waiting.

2000-12-27-it-s-not-easy-being-mean-thea:
The weeks leading up to Christmas were a terrible time for people in my racket, both practising and dormant. That at least is what I gather from reading them. Martin Knelman, an experienced critic of theatre and other things currently writing an entertainment column in The Toronto Star, used his space to examine an issue often pondered by people in the reviewing dodge, though probably not by many others: the use in ads of extracts from our immortal prose to make it appear that we endorsed the product more enthusiastically than was actually the case. He's against it.

Although Martin was complaining he seemed to find the whole matter fairly amusing, which I think is the right attitude. (I call him Martin because he's a friend of mine; also because this is John Frasers space and Im keeping it warm for him. John's a friend, too.) We critics spend a lot of our time misrepresenting the -- shall we call them works of art? -- that are placed before us, so we should not complain when we too get misrepresented. If we really feel passionately about it, then we should watch our language, so as to make life as hard for the advertising people as possible. This can be difficult. In a former existence I wrote that a disastrous play at London's famous Royal Court Theatre contained one very funny line. The play was then described in the listings as Very funny -- Robert Cushman, Observer". The PR told me that this expressed the managements genial contempt for critics. I couldnt help feeling that this contempt would have been more effectively expressed if they'd refrained from quoting us altogether. I also suspected that if they'd received any genuinely enthusiastic reviews, they would have used them. But the Royal Court was and is a very high-minded organization, and Im probably just being cynical.

Being misquoted is one thing. Being prevented from furnishing the quotes in the fist place is another. That, though, is what happened to Kate Taylor, my opposite number at The Globe and Mail, when she attempted to review New France, the two-part show currently being presented by the VideoCabaret company as the first instalment of their revived comic-strip history of Canada. She had to pay for her own tickets for the first part and was refused admission altogether to the second. These essential facts are not in dispute, though some of the details seem to be. Kate claims to have been intimidated by an anonymous bouncer; VideoCabaret say that, actually, they didnt buy in any heavies for the occasion and the guy in question was their own thoroughly unthreatening director, Michael Hollingsworth. Presumably there wasn't time for formal introductions.

The grounds for VideoCab's displeasure were that six years ago, Kate, seeing their work for the first time, had based an unflattering review partly on what her predecessors had written about previous shows, and that nothing she had come up with since had atoned for this. This surprises me a bit, since her review of the parts of the current show she did see seemed to contain about the same proportions of praise and blame that my own did; and theyve always been very nice to me. Kates subsequent complaints about this infringement on the freedom of the press were subsequently seconded by a Globe columnist, Russell Smith; and more surprisingly questioned by another Globe columnist, Rick Salutin.

Salutin -- we aren't really friends, though I admire his writing very much and agree with him 90% of the time -- has complained before about critics, not because of the harm they do to practitioners (a word I prefer to artists) but because of the harm they do to themselves: sitting in judgment all the time, we imperil our souls, or at least our senses of humour. I think there's something in this, though I guess Ill live with it. In the present instance he queried the custom of having a regular reviewer for each branch of the arts. Why not spread the load around a bit, allow for alternative voices? After all, even right-wing papers allow the occasional left-wing voice on their op-ed pages. (He should know.)

Well, for a start, arts writers dont divide quite as rigidly and predictably as political ones. Kate Taylor, and the Star's Richard Ouzounian, and I are very different people, of different ages and backgrounds, but our opinions diverge and overlap in ways that I certainly can't predict. (Well, sometimes.) Obviously I have a turf and a job to defend here, but I dont see how parcelling out reviews would work -- not at least unless we are talking about having two or more reviews per paper of each show, and I dont see any editor springing for that. If reviews were assigned on an ad hoc basis, then the situation would be even more arbitrary than it is at present. If it's a matter of fitting individual reviewers to individual plays, well, do either reviewers or practitioners want to be pre-judged on past records, which would be the only way of doing it? Isn't that, in fact, what VideoCabaret was complaining about?

I think they were within their rights to deny a reviewer free tickets. I doubt that they had the right to deny her entrance altogether. (Would they discriminate against non-publishing spectators in the same way?) I am sure that they were wrong to ask the Globe to send another critic; if they were going to take a stand they should have done it properly and gone voluntarily Globeless.

Obviously they werent about to do this because -- this is hardly a secret, nor is it shameful -- they wanted the free publicity that reviews bring. They dont give us free tickets because they love us. They have in fact, like all theatres at all levels of both economy and pretension, made a Faustian deal. (So have we; somehow the road to hell manages to be a two-way street.) And it's ratified every time they quote us, even when they do it accurately. Practitioners complain about the power of the critics, but it's largely they who have given it to us. People would forget what wed said if the ads didnt keep reminding them.

These days there's a new wrinkle in that situation because papers, with the blessed exception of this one, now accord plays star ratings, and the theatres seem much to prefer quoting them; they take up less space. They also look more judicial, but that's the harm of them. (They are also much less amenable to misappropriation -- unless, of course, you hire a press agent who can't count.)

They are cloaking a purely personal opinion in the dignity of statistics and perpetuating it, week after week.
2000-12-30-factory-unveiled-two-great-wo:
Near the beginning of the year, Factory Theatre introduced us to Florence Gibson and her play Belle, a richly written and richly imagined piece about black-white relationships in the industrial North, in the immediate wake of the American Civil War. It painted a broad but detailed canvas, was determinedly un-parochial, and used language more creatively and dramatically than any new Canadian play in ages.

Near the end of the year the same theatre presented David Widdicombe's Science Fiction, a hugely enjoyable take on the paranormal, the paramilitary, and the just plain paranoid. (It was also an auspicious directorial debut for Ted Dykstra.)

The Factory, like its blood brothers, the Tarragon and Passe Muraille, offered plenty of the regulation terrible stuff in between, and its actual production standards are very hit-and miss, but it deserves credit for giving us the year's two best new plays. It also brought us One Yellow Rabbit's Thunderstruck, which was elemental, and revived Michael Mackenzie's Geometry in Venice, which was a good idea.

Two achieved home-grown plays in a year may not seem much, but history (not to mention those revivals) suggests that you would have to be an incurable sap to expect more. The runners-up were at Tarragon: The delightfully funny Sibs, from Richard Greenblatt and Diane Flacks, may have been more of a revue than a play, but so much the worse for plays; Judith Thomson's Perfect Pie (with Nancy Palk at her best) was a solid slice of the rural.

The remaining members of Ontario's approved holy trinity of playwrights turned up in care of the Canadian Stage Company: George F. Walker's Heaven played like self-parody; Jason Sherman's Patience went on, and on, and on. It was technically a revival and, like a similar re-staging of David Young's Glenn, a disillusioning one.

Canadian Stage, as in previous years, took up some of the slack by not worrying too much about being Canadian. They did give us Brad Fraser's Outrageous, the year's best musical and, under its author's direction, the best performed. They also brought in The Overcoat, a magical spectacle from Vancouver, and enterprisingly followed that up by turning its director (Morris Panych) and designer (Ken MacDonald) loose on the fine British play Hysteria.

It wasn't a perfect match, and the actors, with the notable exception of Kristen Thomson, tended to get lost; but it struck any number of sparks. Soon after this came The Weir which was very moving, as productions of this uncanny Irish conversation-piece tend to be. Another worthwhile import (at Tarragon) was the American Tony Kushner's Slavs!, an ambitious survey of Russia post-perestroika, which started terrible and ended superb. It was acted by some of Ontario's best, though only Randy Hughson and Maria Vacratsis were actually at their best.

Nationalists take heart: In a crowded World Stage season -- which included Peter Brook, the Russian Gaudeamus, and the British National Theatre's intermittently magnificent Oresteia, we did as well as anyone, what with John Neville excelling himself in Krapp's Last Tape, and Robert Lepage, in The Far Side of the Moon, at his most beguiling, not least as a performer. He's underrated as an actor, perhaps because he makes it look easy. And, technical wonders apart, his stuff can be genuinely funny.

The Mirvishes locked up the commercial scene with The Lion King, Mamma Mia! (probably a very nice musical if you can stand the songs), and Dame Edna Everage.

They also brought Donald Sutherland impressively home in Enigma Variations; but they have yet to originate anything substantial.

Others' attempts at turning a profit were, as usual, woeful, based on un-bright ideas (a revue about ageing, a new musical of The Taming of the Shrew): apart, of course, from The Vagina Monologues, which happens to be an extremely well performed show.

There remains a yawning gap between the coterie and the marketplace, one that can only be filled by the classics. In 1999 it was triumphantly filled by Soulpepper, who perhaps aroused unfair expectations. Some of their work this year was very fine: a searching School for Wives and a re-mount of their heart-lifting Platonov (both directed by the invaluable Laszlo Marton) and a good account of Harold Pinter's Betrayal. But The Mill on the Floss wasn't worth their time (it didn't even feel like a Soulpepper production) and their first attempts at Shakespeare misfired: One production was cancelled, dampening the whole season, and the other, Twelfth Night, was only as good as its most experienced actors (very, in the case of Steven Sutcliffe's Sir Andrew) and rather self- consciously directed.

So Stratford retained its Shakespearean hegemony, expressed in three perfectly decent productions: a record that should be better but could easily be worse. Nearly everything else there was splendid. The house playwright appeared as a character, and a fascinating reticent one, in Timothy Findley's Elizabeth Rex which, as directed by Martha Henry, was a great experience but not necessarily a great play. The program told us it was about gender roles; I'm not sure we'd have known otherwise.

Even better was Euripides' Medea with Seana McKenna (this was a great year for the Greeks); and we also got Uta Hagen, another who makes it look easy, in Collected Stories, Brian Bedford, ditto, in Tartuffe, the best kind of romp in The Three Musketeers, and a musical Fiddler on the Roof that actually justified its place in the bill. The Shaw Festival had, for once, a lower profile; but The Doctor's Dilemma, Six Characters in Search of an Author and A Room of One's Own (with the Australian actress Pamela Rabe) were all first-rate, and She Loves Me a perfect delight.

A final word for three of our very best actors who this year scaled personal peaks: Diego Matamoros, poisonously bantering in Betrayal; David Fox, immaculately terrifying in Science Fiction; and Brent Carver, who was perfect in Elizabeth Rex and who proved in Fiddler that, given the material and the talent, there is no such thing as miscasting.

Black & White Photo: Peter Redman, National Post / Florence Gibson (left) with the cast of Belle, a play that brought imagination and rich language to the Toronto stage ;
