Until Feb. 4. Box office: (416) 504-9971.

ZADIES SHOES

Factory Theatre, Toronto

The new theatrical year gets off to a fine start with Zadies Shoes, a first full-length play by the 27-year-old Adam Pettle. It begins in cracking form, everybody racing ahead but under firm control, there is some bunching together at the rails somewhere around the middle, but the author streaks ahead at the end.

From which you may gather that this is a play concerned with horse racing. More precisely it's concerned with gambling, to which its hero, a young Jewish man named Benjamin, is addicted. When he first meet him he is watching a televised football game, on which he's had a minor and, as it turns out, unsuccessful flutter.

Its the track, though, thats his main preoccupation; betting big Gs on the gee-gees is both his downfall and, or so he devoutly hopes, his salvation. To fund his habit he has taken money from his Gentile girlfriend Ruth, a cancer patient who has despaired of conventional treatment and needs the cash to fly to Mexico for alternative therapy.

By this point Benjamin, too, is willing to try anything. He even, for the first time since his bar mitzvah, wanders into a synagogue where, meeting with an old religious man, he receives a hot tip plus some good moral advice. He neglects the advice but takes the tip. It's a longshot, but if it pays off, his financial problems, and conceivably his personal ones too, will be solved. Intermission hits with the ponies under starters' orders, making for the best cliff- hanging curtain in recent memory.

Its more than a matter of momentary suspense. Were involved with Benjamin, both for his failings and his good intentions, and also of course with Ruth. Both of them are in a position where the best that they can do is pray, as a musical-comedy hero in a somewhat similar situation once pointed out when asking luck to be his lady.

They share this condition with several of the other characters: with Ruth's elder sister, a curling champion wholly wrapped up in the outcome of her next and vital game, and with her younger sister, an eclectic cultist newly pregnant and equally wrapped up in that.

If that sounds schematic, it is -- and it's where the play is weakest. A disastrous meeting between the three girls goes the way the dramatist needs it to, rather than any way it plausibly would; nor are the two ugly sisters any more convincing when they change from monsters of self-absorption to angels of mercy. In these roles Torri Higginson and Juno Mills-Cockell hardly muster an ounce of conviction between them, and though Jackie Maxwells direction accurately shows off whats best in the play, it can find no mitigating nuance in what isn't.

This extends to some of the scenes involving Benjamin, whose gambling is apparently a family curse. The play's title refers to his granddad who came barefoot to Canada, having lost his shoes in a poker game. Benjys father, a successful doctor, is unable to bale his son out because of being similarly hooked; occasional flashbacks to their early relationship are painfully awkward, and also doggedly unrevealing.

Its more important, though, that Benjamin lives so vividly in the present; Jordan Pettle (the author's brother -- the evening is a riot of sibling revelry) makes his compulsive wrigglings between addiction and affection both painful and sympathetic -- painful because sympathetic -- and uncomfortably believable. (Could a nice guy be so selfish? Yes.) Kelli Fox as Ruth is chunkily enduring and good-humoured until she cracks, at which point her anger scalds. One character calls her "a rock," and it suits.

I fear that I haven't conveyed how funny the play is. The synagogue scenes have the weight of ages behind them, irresistible when both the timing and the anecdotes are as rich as those deployed by Paul Soles as a rabbinical horse-player, a combination of wise man and wise guy.

But, as the Levys rye posters used to concede, you dont have to be Jewish. Even richer, and certainly less predictable, comedy comes from Benjamin's racetrack friend and confidant, known as Bear, a recuperating gambler and junkie and alcoholic, and pretty together, considering. Randy Hughson's rollickingly sodden performance arouses a couple of seconds of misgivings (as in, hasnt he done this before?) followed by minutes on end of total bliss, culminating in as richly disorienting a final exit as I can remember. He has the script totally in his corner: A scene in which he desperately waits for a telephone not to ring is what should be known as a tour-de- farce, the fruit of scrupulously clever preparation, and all the more hilarious for having deadly serious underpinnings.

The character also functions as a moral force, an unexpected task that Hughson performs superbly, and is further folded into the plot by being Ruths sister's baby's father. (We also meet the curling sister's boyfriend, though symmetry seems the only reason for this.)

The set, designed by Sue LePage, is centrally composed of racetrack-stands. The thematic relevance is obvious but it means the indoor scenes, which is most of them, inevitably get shoved to the side. They survive, though, and the play, though composed of episodes, is not episodic. It wins by far more than a nose.

LARRY'S PARTY

Bluma Appel Theatre

---

Carol Shields' novel Larry's Party is a cool, inward account of the first 50 years in the life of a man. Larry Weller, born and raised in Winnipeg, accumulates two marriages, two divorces, one son and two careers.

Having taken a course in floral design, he rises to become manager of a flower-store. But on his first honeymoon he visits the Hampton Court maze in England, and there, "getting lost and then found," he stumbles into his vocation. He builds a labyrinth in his own backyard, exasperating his wife and precipitating their breakup.

He becomes a professional, and very successful, maze-maker; he moves to Chicago and meets his second wife, an academic in women's studies who specializes in the lives of female saints. When this union, too, exhausts itself, he sets up home and shop in Toronto. Finding his two exes in town simultaneously, he hosts a party for them, his current girlfriend and a small assortment of relatives and clients. And here his life, which seemed to have bottomed out, takes another turn.

Crisply and enchantingly written, the book is a minefield for dramatic adaptation. It has a story but no plot. It has a hero who, though no pushover, is essentially someone to whom things happen; even his floral education is the result of accident and maternal intervention.

The book, narrated in the third person, tells us much about his thoughts and feelings, but always in a guarded way, as if there were some final court of appeal yet to be heard from. It has little dialogue, except towards the end, and what it has reads more like a precis of conversation than like the thing itself; this is allowable in a novel but not in the theatre, where language has to stand up and be counted.

So if you are going to stage Larry's Party, then a musical seems a reasonable way to go, if only because of music's ability to speed things up. Here, though, it does not work.

The party that ends the novel is now used, not too surprisingly, as a framing device. Apart from that, everything is very literal. Richard Ouzounian, who wrote the musical's book and lyrics, simply squeezes in as much of the story as he can, in chronological order, where the original keeps pausing and recapping.

The novel, in fact, is something of a labyrinth, and that's rather satisfying. It also, I suppose, tells us that life is a maze; the novel dispenses this hardly revelatory information with a certain teasing grace, but the musical seems deadly serious about it.

Larry himself is somebody who wants to learn -- who does learn, about himself and about the limits and the potential of his own mind and body. What songs can do is make us free of his thoughts and feelings; and that's what these songs attempt, engagingly at first.

But the further inside Larry's head we go, the more we find it stuffed with the remnants of other musicals. Marek Norman's music is a continuous high-pitched drone (the orchestrations seem to consist entirely of plucked strings and plunked keyboards), and the lyrics buckle under pressure. Larry sings generic arias about being in love and being confused; the women in his life fare even worse. His first wife has a self-realization number that is one cliche after another; his Toronto lady follows it with something similar about being lonely yet defiant.

When Larry goes into a three-week coma, his son hastens to his bedside to unleash another power ballad; in the book he simply reads The Toronto Star (obituaries excepted) out loud, because he can't think of anything to say, and that might have made a more affecting number. All the strains and ambiguities in their relationship have been edited out in favour of bland affirmation; indeed, much of the material's quirkiness, starting with its very first episode, has been toned down. And when we get to the ending (not too satisfactory in the novel) we simply feel that, of three possible women, Larry has wound up with the most boring.

There are some brighter things in the score: a jolly song about botulism, for example, occasioned by the story of Larry's mother having once unintentionally poisoned her own mother-in-law, though staging the number in the presence of the guilt-stricken woman makes everybody seem remarkably tactless.

One of Larry's rich clients is a country and western singer, which occasions not the expected musical parody but a love song that gets touchingly reprised later on. Wit, though, is generally lacking, both in the writing and in Robin Phillips' direction and design. This is about the most lugubrious-looking musical I have ever seen. Black space surrounds a tall, transparent revolving structure whose maze-like qualities are rather quickly exhausted; a gift of a scenic metaphor seems to have gone begging. The arms of Larry's party guests stretch out from within it, and that is striking; things are less happy when the effect is reversed and the ensemble stands outside the action, doing aerobics while the principals emote. They also lie down, holding shrubs, to signify Larry's first, home-grown, maze.

No actor could do more for Larry than Brent Carver. He isn't obvious casting for Everyman -- he is too extraordinary an actor to seem an ordinary man -- but he contributes an undimmed spiritual generosity, a sense of easy tolerance, and of course a ringing voice. His face seems somehow rounder than usual, and his shoulders subtly and progressively hunch as he gets older. (The production is not otherwise much concerned with denoting changes in period or locale.)

Michelle Fisk adds some welcome astringency as his sister; Julain Molnar (academic wife) and Barbara Barsky (last chance) are also helpful. So, as Larry's father, is Gary Krawford, whom I coincidentally first saw, many years ago in New York, playing the lead in Stephen Sondheim's Company, a show to which this one bears some structural and spiritual similarities. If ever an actor could bring that musical's recalcitrant hero to life, it would be Brent Carver. Do it, someone.

Black & White Photo: Michael Cooper / Brent Carver as Larry, with Michelle Fisk as Midge: An extraordinary actor playing an ordinary man. ;
2001-01-15-my-name-is-jeff-man-behind-th:
His name is Jeff, and hes Canadian, and I bet you never want to read another opening sentence like that as long as you live.

Jeff probably doesn't either, though his feelings on the matter can hardly help being mixed. Jeff is Jeff Douglas, a 29-year-old actor based in Toronto, who has now been famous twice: a remarkable achievement considering that very few people actually know his name.

For them, Jeff is Joe, the guy who gave the patriotic speech in praise of Molson's beer in last years most celebrated TV commercial. It caught on; people would watch it again and again, for the pleasure -- especially when Joes voice hit screaming-pitch on the line about the beaver being a proud and noble animal -- of wondering, is this for real?"

Politicians, whose senses of humour tend not to be of the sharpest, decided that it was and, for them at least, Joe became an icon, giving Jeff his proverbially guaranteed 15 minutes of celebrity.

And the iconic status seems to have taken, because the news that Douglas was leaving Canada for Los Angeles has led to anguished questions about our national identity. We let a man star in a widely- applauded beer commercial with patriotic implications, and we still can't keep him? Let's sell the country now.

Carrie Fallis, Douglass Toronto agent, is bemused. "Jeff, she told me on Friday, is an actor; hes doing what actors do. Heading for Hollywood in the pilot season. What's the big deal? Still, any publicity is good publicity."

Douglas himself evinced the same mixture of gratitude and surprise when he spoke to me on Saturday from L.A. (Yes, he's there already, he just couldnt wait, get over it ... and anyway, my prestige has shot up in my neighbourhood since my kids friends learned that Joe called the house, though they had to be persuaded of it because who the hell is Jeff Douglas?)

"Movie and TV work, he told me, is slow in Canada in January and February. In L.A. it's the hottest time." Well, it would have to be hotter than Canada, but I appreciate that he wasn't referring to the climate. Actors are nomadic workers, and the way Douglas tells it, TV projects with an eye on the coming season, and even feature films, are falling off the trees this time of the year. They dont, of course, drop on everybody, but it makes sense for an actor with any kind of visibility to place himself in their path.

Douglas has that visibility, and it isnt all a matter of beer and beavers. He spent three years appearing for Disney in The Famous Jett Jackson (shown here on the Family Channel). No call seems to have gone out in Hollywood for ambulant Canadian icons, and Douglas has not been summoned south, like Paul Gross's Mountie, to demonstrate Canadian grit or even to provide a focus for Canadian jokes, though with the number of sitcoms that use the word "Canada as a knee-jerk cue for laughter, it can only be a matter of time before one of our own becomes the permanent fall guy in his own series.

When Douglas sits across the desk from a potential Californian employer the conversation will apparently go something like this:

So, your manager tells me you did some commercial. Who was it for?"

"Molson.

What's that?"

"Its a beer.

Oh."

No resonance, it seems. On the other hand, "its received with less prejudice down here. Nobody pigeon-holes me through it.

Actually, the commercial did lead to him being interviewed on American TV, and he thinks the mere fact that executives were seeing him and not knowing who he was or what he was talking about may have worked in his favour. They felt they ought to know, that something was happening that they didn't understand, and that they'd better grab a piece of it.

Douglas has a recall tomorrow for an independent feature called The Good Girl, movies being what he wants to do. Traditionally youre supposed to avoid the small screen if you want to work on the big screen -- why should people pay for you when they can get you at home for free? -- but that seems to be changing. TV shows are aimed a lot at people in their teens and early twenties, and thats the movie audience too. And I could end up doing a couple of pilots before I come back to Canada in March."

Well, that's news. We'd all thought hed left for good. Whats even more interesting is what he's coming back to do, what it is in his diary that Hollywood will have to arrange its schedules around. He's going to Edmonton to play Romeo in a new production at the Citadel Theatre. ("My name is Ro, and Im from Verona. I believe in peacekeeping, not swordfights. I want to marry my worst enemys daughter. Hey, I'm in love.)

It will be his second Shakespeare; he practised last year as Macduff, in a shoestring self-started actors' collective production of Macbeth, in an obscure theatre at Parliament and Yonge in Toronto. We got terrible reviews" he says cheerfully. "It was like they were trying to humiliate us. I got blamed for doing exactly what I was going for. But I was happy with it. The story got told.

So it turns out that Joe Canadian is really a theatre guy. (That should stand him in good stead in L.A., by the way; theres a lot of good theatre there. Well, think of the pool of unemployed actors they have to draw on.) And its obvious, even within the strict confines of a TV commercial, that Douglas is a good stage actor. Think of the way he modulates, before that screaming crowd, from shyness to hysteria.

Did he think it was funny? Yeah, I thought so. The tone is humorous. I'm not sure I have a clear understanding of the term 'irony" (would that everyone were so honest) "but I tried to make it funny. That doesnt mean I think everything he said is a joke. I believe in peacekeeping. I believe in diversity.

Another question I had to ask: We all know the cultural impression the ad made, but how much beer did it sell?

I read that Molson gained two market points as a result of the ad. I think that translates into between 20 and 40 million bucks." A financially savvy pause, because these days every actor has to be his own packager. "I wish I'd gone for a percentage."

STONES IN HIS POCKETS

Winter Garden Theatre, Toronto

---

TORONTO - Hard on the heels of David Mamet's film State and Main comes, from Belfast via London, a play rooted in a very similar situation. A Hollywood crew descends on a small community and, to put the matter as neutrally as possible, uses it. Mamet's film is set in New England, Marie Jones' play in old Ireland. More importantly, Mamet tells his story from the point of the invaders, Jones tells hers from that of the residents.

The result is that, appallingly though Mamet's characters may behave, we want their picture to get made. With Jones, we don't much care whether it is or not; we don't bear the movie people any particular ill-will, but it's the locals who count; whatever they want is fine with us.

Jones, on the evidence of her bio an extraordinarily prolific playwright and actress, has furnished a lively script, but there is no doubt that the immense appeal of the play lies in its format and its performance. There are many characters but only two actors: Stevie Ray Dallimore, who is gaunt and fairly tall, and Declan Mooney, who is shorter and rounder -- a classic duo.

Most of the time they play, respectively, Jake and Charlie, two youngish inhabitants of County Kerry who, along with 338 of their neighbours, are working as extras on what seems to be a period- piece manor-house romance with occasional gestures toward social conscience. The extras play "the dispossessed," which is something they seem to know about.

Both Jake and Charlie have a great fund of wit, as well as dead- end prospects. Jake has been to America and returned empty-handed; Charlie, former owner of a failed video store, has written a movie script that he hopes somebody on the set may look at. Both are angry and frustrated, though Jake's anger is much closer to the surface.

At any moment, though, either of them may change into somebody else. Mooney may start swanning around (he really does swan) as Caroline Giovanni, the fey and velvet-voiced American star of the picture, anxious to perfect her Irish accent by close (if brief) contact with some man who has one, and probably as well-intentioned as a person so cocooned in privilege can be. Or he may become Victor, the assistant director in charge of crowd control, who is Irish himself but tries to disguise it. Or Lewis, the terminally relaxed (or maybe just languidly exhausted) real director, who is English and who only manifests himself to the extras on very special occasions, and on whom, we realize, Victor is modelling himself. Or, with a terrifying rolling gait, one of the unit's security heavies.

Dallimore gets his chance across the gender-gap as Ashley, the continuity-person, gangling, vague and, in voice at least, fashionably London. He also plays Mickey, a stooped and cunning senior, revered as "one of the few remaining extras of The Quiet Man."

Mooney seems to be slightly the more virtuosic of the two, but in Ian McElhinney's production all the transformations are effected with dazzling grace, completeness and economy. There is pleasure in wondering who will morph next, and when, and into whom, and even in the bare-faced excuses a character will offer so that he may leave the stage and return immediately as somebody else. Sometimes he doesn't even bother to leave -- an actor may simply turn on his heel and transform himself in turning. Don't leave before the curtain- call, in which everybody we have met gets to take a bow in his or her own style.

Another character is Sean, a local boy who can't even get a job as an extra, though he's been obsessed by movies, or their glamour, since childhood. He's turned to drugs and, one night, having been thrown out of his own town's pub on to his own town's street for daring to approach the leading lady, he puts stones in his pockets and drowns himself.

Jake claims this as an extreme case of exploitation: the uncaring world of media and capital exploiting the rural Irish, materially and psychologically. (If there has been an Irish economic miracle, it doesn't seem to have reached this community.) When the film company, intent on wrapping up on schedule, seem about to refuse the extras time off to attend the funeral, battle is almost joined. Things are patched up and most faces saved, but scars have been exposed and will continue to fester.

Dramatically, this focus on the dead Sean is not too satisfying, because we have hardly met him. (I can only remember that Dallimore plays him because I recall him having a scene with Caroline, who's definitely played by Mooney.) So there has to be a lot of posthumous filling-in to make us care, and even that doesn't really work.

Indeed, despite some sublime comic moments, parts of the show are surprisingly heavy going; the actors, especially early on, have to do some of their pirouetting in a vacuum. There are certainly real issues here, the same ones touched on more subtly in such other recent Irish plays as The Weir and The Beauty Queen of Leenane: a rage to get out coupled with an even deeper rage that this should be necessary. Where the play really bogs down is in Jake's and Charlie's climactic decision to transcend their situation by "making their own movie." It's not so much wishful thinking as wishful writing -- the characters trapped in the playwright's metaphor.

What we will remember is the antics Jake and Charlie are forced into when the cameras are rolling, when they have to render homage to the heroine ("we have to look at her looking at us looking dispossessed") or witness an eviction without uttering a peep of protest, and we watch their heads bobbing from side to side, reacting to two principals who are still in their trailers.

Later, in a glorious set-piece, we watch the two of them going gamely and agonizingly through their own portions of a massed country-dance with, of course, largely invisible partners. (It isn't clear just when, or indeed if, this is supposed to have been rehearsed; maybe the producers just believe the Irish naturally got rhythm.)

At the end they corral Lewis, the director, and outline to him their ideas for a film about the deceased Sean. It seems surprisingly easy, considering the difficulties Charlie has earlier had unloading his script. Lewis listens politely and even makes a few suggestions. He finds the story too downbeat, and he thinks that Stones in His Pockets, which is what they want to call it, will be a real turn-off of a title.

Judging from the international success of the play, the laugh is on Lewis, but in fairness to him it should be pointed out that the dramatist, though keeping both the title and the suicide, has arranged things so that we go away cheerful, and that the actors have kept us happy almost throughout.

First seen nine years ago in Theatre Passe Muraille's backspace, Jump returns on the main stage: a stage that now looks more main than it used to and has been fitted out with -- of all dear old- fashioned heartwarming things -- a proscenium arch. The medium suits the message, since Jump is a 60-minute lampoon of the conventional marriage ceremony, which has been around for some time and which the show presents as something endearingly antiquated. Well, as something antiquated. For a one-joke affair, Jump is fairly ingenious.

It was written by Daniel MacIvor, though not much putting down of words on paper can have been involved; there is no dialogue. MacIvor devised a scenario, which the current director, Mark Lonergan, has reactivated; having missed the original, I can't say what changes he may have made.

Anyway, the conceit of the present show (though I probably couldn't have worked it out if I hadn't read the publicity) is that some bureaucratically minded government has redefined and codified the wedding ceremony, and renamed it a Jump. The traditional elements of signatures, vows, and gift-giving are streamlined, and all lead up to the Jump itself: The bride and groom are each required to climb a ladder (impressively revealed at the back of the stage and stretching out of sight) and demonstrate their commitment by leaping from it into one another's arms. Or not. So a regime intent on stemming the tide of unlicensed co-habitation by reasserting the sanctity of marriage has tried to make the ceremony more attractive by turning it into a combination of circus and Kafka. It doesn't make sense.

Of course there are those who would claim that marriage already IS a combination of circus and Kafka, and the show could perfectly well be a satiric cartoon based on that premise, using a theatrical vocabulary that has been common ever since the 1920s, or when experimental theatre started to call itself experimental.

The high-water mark of this kind of thing was the Absurdist movement of the 1950s, and this show often seems like Ionesco without words. The character billed as Man in Grey Suit (Clinton Walker, looking and leering like Eric Idle at his most jovial- sinister) might be a figure of Orwellian prophecy; he might equally well be a caricature of any present-day master of ceremonies. The bride, a.k.a. Woman in White (Severn Thompson), looks tearful, and the groom, or Man in Red Jacket (the very agile Scott McCord), looks out of it: No surprises there. The groom does take us somewhat beyond the norm; he finishes -- not to give too much away -- in a heap. It's a fitting conclusion to the day he's had.

For example: Inveigled into a dance with two kilted lasses who I suppose are bridesmaids (Girls with Dark Hair in Plaid Skirt 1 and 2: Aviva Chernick and Sarah McDonald), he ends up doing the splits, and is stuck like that for the longest time. The remaining characters are Woman with Purse (Anne Anglin), who is the bride's conventionally formidable mother and who gets to snuggle with the emcee, and Man in Overalls (Brendan Wall), a handyman who presumably comes with the hall.

A high point is the presentation of the presents. Everyone, it seems, has given a toaster; I don't know whether this is a rule under the new dispensation or whether it merely denotes a lack of imagination, or at least of co-ordination, among the happy couple's friends and relations. Either way, it's a tired joke in itself. But it's brought to life here by the sight of the bride trying to balance four toasters in a pile on her lap, while a cart laden with other toasters stands by her side. All then adjourn to watch a video of a toaster. The picture remains totally stationary, but they sit there gazing at it anyway. Finally, their attention turns to other matters, and so does ours, and just when we're least expecting it, the onscreen toaster pops. It's a neat moment.

Overall, though, the show falls into a species of comedy I find unendearing; treat your characters like automata and then mock them for following prescribed patterns. Marriage may well be a strange ritual inaugurating an even stranger relationship: All the more reason to explore why people sign up for it. (Or, if you want to extend the argument to gay couples, why they should WANT to sign up for it.) The ceremony is only as interesting as the people undergoing it; and each pair have their own history and their own motivation. If we don't know that, the spectacle becomes boring. Not to mention that it's a mime. (The presenters claim that it's something else, but nobody is going to believe them.)

DISCO GOALIE

Artword Theatre, Toronto

Jane Millers solo show Disco Goalie begins in darkness, pierced by loud thumping sounds that might be inspired by either half of the title. As the lights go up, we glimpse what looks initially like a huge spiderweb but turns out to be a hockey net. Before it stands our writer and performer, decked out in gloves, pads, helmet -- all the gear. The costume turns out to be a great sounding board; as well as talking to us, she sings a cappella, using her body as a source of percussive accompaniment, in the style of Bobby McFerrin. This is musically as well as technically impressive; the tunes, or fragments of tunes, that she sings may have originated as disco but - - initially at least -- she gives them some of the power and dignity of blues.

Which is all very fine, but does not in itself make a play. (Sporting pun not intended but gratefully received.) We need substance to get us through the evening, and Millers autobiographical monologue -- she uses her own name and has hinted in interviews that she is to some extent telling her own story -- wears increasingly thin. It starts promisingly; she tells, graphically and movingly but without self-pity, of being bullied at school, and of her parents' reactions when she told them about it. Her mother, very proper and straitlaced, instructed her not to cry because you're giving them a part of yourself when you do that"; her father ("my first feminist) advised her to hit back. She finds release in joining a hockey team and speedily discovers her niche as a goalie -- an aggressively defensive position of which her mother, who organizes the league, should thoroughly approve. Hockey becomes almost the most important thing in her life.

It improves her confidence, and hence her social life. But here a dichotomy opens up: On the ice, its her responsibility to keep the puck out; in her dealings with boys, and later with men, she lets as many in as possible. (The metaphor is her own, and endlessly reiterated.) Dancing, especially slow dancing, is the Dionysiac agent here. So the title supposedly sums up the conflict within her, or the two sides of her nature, or whatever; but really it doesnt, not in any dramatic or revealing way. There is just this girl who plays hockey and is sexually active -- and so what? Her description of her first boyfriend is wittily precise -- he was on the fringe of the popular group -- he wore glasses so he was attainable") but the account of her exploits progresses from mildly titillating to plain dull. She herself seems to come to this conclusion when, in her mid-thirties, she decides to give up on promiscuity and try for love. Her mother figures throughout in the story as a convenient, and endlessly shockable, opposing force, but she remains a very shadowy figure. Nobody else exists at all.

Even the music becomes an irritant. It gets to the point where every spoken line is interrupted by a few bars of some disco anthem. Lacking the usual instrumental trappings, we are thrown back, despite Miller's skill at body percussion, on the words, rapturously intoned as if they were gospel. (This time the pun is intended.) They don't stand up to it; and the effect would be monotonous even if we were dealing with a less constricted musical form. Miller is an attractive, energetic (God knows she's energetic) and technically versatile performer; and she may well have it in her to write speakable dialogue. What her range might truly be as either actor or writer is impossible to guess. The stage confessional may be cheap to produce, and it may be both great exercise and great therapy for the performer, but it's an achingly constricting form.

VINCENT

Theatre Passe Muraille, Backspace

The Vincent in Vincent is Van Gogh, as usual. Like the sugary Don McLean song of the same title, the piece soothes us with the implicit assurance that we, a safe century later, would never be such heartless philistines as to call a great painter a madman and even lock him up for it.

Essentially a lecture, very thinly disguised as a one-man play, it was written by Leonard Nimoy -- Mr. Spock of Star Trek -- presumably as a vehicle for himself. (At least, I assume the author is that Leonard Nimoy, and that is why he wrote it; the program is silent on both matters.)

A short time after Vincent's death, Theo, his art-dealing brother, takes his stand behind a lectern to tell the truth about the deceased. Behind him stands a wall full of Vincent's paintings, some of which he will eventually bring downstage -- half boastfully, half accusingly -- as the climax of both his speech and the play. He illustrates his story with extracts from Vincent's letters; whenever he gets to them the lighting changes and the actor leaves his post to assume the role of the dead man, speaking to us from beyond the grave. So the actor gets to play two contrasting characters; the play might have been called Vincent and Theo if Robert Altman's movie hadn't got there first.

Unfortunately, the play, unlike the movie, tells us almost nothing about the two men's relationship; and what it does tell, it states rather than dramatizes. Given the format, this is almost inevitable; the play takes the familiar scissors-and-paste approach of selecting a few documents and setting them up. Theo does, of course, have the inside track on some things. As a brother, he knows all about the grief Vincent caused his family when he set up house with a prostitute who was pregnant with somebody else's child. As a dealer, he is only too aware of Vincent's refusal to allow any of his work to be sold. He tells us, plausibly enough, that Vincent had impossibly high expectations of himself in every department -- art, religion, love -- and in effect set himself up to fail. None of this, though, seems to have eaten away at Theo himself; he reacts, at most, with mild exasperation. He seems to have no unresolved issues about his brother. Most of the time, it could be any narrator up there.

I don't know what Mr. Spock may have made of this double role; on the face of it, he would have been better suited to sensible bourgeois Theo than to reckless saint-and-sinner Vincent, but maybe he took on the challenge precisely to demonstrate that there was more to him than cold rationality and pointy ears. (The matter of Van Gogh's own famous ear is here approached by Theo with an appropriate air of pained self-consciousness: Yes, here it comes, the organ you've been waiting for.)

Gabe Bettio, who appears in this production (originally staged in Fort Erie), is certainly happier playing Theo; he projects a dry indignation both with the straight world that rejected his brother and the Bohemian world that led him to further excesses he certainly wasn't equipped to withstand. Theo's anger at the more robust Gauguin, whom Vincent hero-worshipped, comes over especially strongly. But when it comes to projecting Vincent himself, the actor is way out of his depth; he turns up speed and volume, by way of suggesting abandon, and he fails in the crucial task of making written material sound like spontaneous utterance: this in a man for whom, we are asked to believe, spontaneity was the breath of life.

The show's view of Van Gogh as persecuted (and self-persecuted) genius is perfectly conventional, perfectly predictable and, in all probability, perfectly accurate. The story and the work are compelling enough for the evening to maintain a low-burning level of interest, but it remains doggedly unexciting: a star-vehicle without a star.

Black & White Photo: Glenn Lowson, National Post / Gabe Bettio is happier playing Van Gogh's brother, Theo, than the great painter himself. ;
2001-01-20-on-stage-together-finally-oli:
They look as if theyre about to do a number, though it would be difficult to guess what it might be: three jaunty old gentlemen gazing determinedly into the future. Knowing, because of the instructions attached to the photographing, that only the future would see them. Together they represent a generation of great British acting: ended now and -- but we knew that a long time in advance -- irreplaceable. And such good taste in hats. (But where's Sir John Gielgud?)

Sir Ralph looks a trifle grim, and he could be so at times: not so much forbidding as unknowable. His off-stage life was the stuff of legend: he rode a motorbike around London (it could be seen parked around the National Theatre), had a fearsome capacity for alcohol, never bothered with an unlisted phone number. This dovetailed with his stage personality, which was a potent mixture of innocence and strength, with a speech-rhythm that was all his own: deliberate but fanciful. His voice and manner were so individual that it became possible to apply them in one's mind to roles that he had never actually played -- King Lear, for example -- and be moved by the result. Few actors have been so loved; watching him you often wanted to hug him, but knew that he would never let you close enough to try.

Lord Olivier, in the middle, is stoically smiling, and its possible that he was in pain; he often was in the last 20 years of his life, and the others may well be supporting him. The most active actor of his group -- a physical and mental swashbuckler -- he was eventually betrayed by his body, though never by his voice; and its possible that he gained a vulnerability that made him moving in a way he'd never been before. He, more than any of the others, is history; there will always be great eccentrics like Richardson and great chameleons like Guinness, but the conditions are no longer there to nourish heroes like Olivier: a man who honed his ringing, outsize skills in the theatre, successfully exploited them in the movies and emerged as the undoubted leader of a profession that now has no use for figureheads. Asked about his qualifications to be first director of Britain's National Theatre, he said in effect that there was no-one else; and he was right. He was not able to lead his company into its permanent home on Londons South Bank, but at least they named one of its three stages after him. (Its rumoured he hated it.)

Sir Alec looks the spryest: the least assuming, the most dapper. (He was also considerably the youngest: an up-and-comer when the others were already stars.) His prime qualities were spirituality and mischief; adjusting the balance between the two he was able to encompass everything from Hamlet to Star Wars; and, despite that latter brush with the supernatural, he always seemed more of the world, more of our world -- than his peers.

You felt that you might discuss politics with him, or the weather. All three prodigies won their spurs in the same theatre and decade, the Old Vic of the 1930s; in 1946 they were even members of the same company. But they never appeared together, all three of them, on the same stage or screen; so this image may be unique.

BURYING MICHAEL

Buddies in Bad Times

---

Michael was dead, to begin with. He died in Winnipeg, of AIDS. But he had expressed a wish to be buried in New Mexico; so Max, his lover, puts the body in the back of his car and sets off on the road with it, without telling anyone.

Max's earlier partner, a drag-queen named Albert, guesses what has happened and sets off in pursuit. Max is helped across the U.S. border by Frank, a young truck-stop attendant who deals with any kind of trouble by orally servicing the bearer. The car Max and Frank are driving is hijacked by Billy, a gunman who turns out to be harmless. The trio pick up Albert, who by now has been reduced to hitch-hiking; and they all live happily ever after.

Max, who has always led a pretty inhibited life in Canada, decides that this new mobile existence is what he really needs. He comes to realize that it is also what Michael wanted for him, and is probably why he made his deathbed request in the first place. My paraphrasing of the first line of A Christmas Carol was just a flippant way of getting this review started, but it now occurs to me that Ken Brand, the playwright, may indeed be offering a new post- seasonal version of the tale, with Max as a nicer Scrooge and the three other major characters serving, through their blithe disregard of approved social rules and roles, as the alternative-lifestyle equivalents of Dickens' cautionary ghosts.

Anyway, it is something to think about while you're watching the play. There isn't much else to occupy your mind.

About the most attractive features of the evening are the two road maps that hang throughout on the back wall of the set: one centering on Winnipeg, the other on Albuquerque and Santa Fe. A lot of us have fantasies of driving across America, and New Mexico seems as good a destination as any, even if we might not want to start from Manitoba.

Movies, though, are better placed than plays to bring the dream to life. The show feels amateurish, dependent on arbitrary bursts of energy from the actors. Terrence Bryant gives a credible performance as Max, casual and unforced but still focused; and he has been given some wryly contemplative speeches about his probable future in Winnipeg as "an AIDS widow." He does seem to carry a life with him.

Jason Jazrawy as Frank is a stagier figure but has plenty of bounce. The two are onstage together a lot, but though acting well individually, they never cohere; here and elsewhere, David Oiye's production flows about as well as a river of glue.

David Macniven makes awkward cameo appearances as some variously venal law-enforcement officers, before settling more happily into the role of Billy, the hold-up artist. Brian Sexsmith as Albert bears the bulk of the play's humour, and it seems a heavy burden. There is some momentary suspense in trying to work out whether he is giving an unconvincing performance of a woman or an unconvincing performance of a man dressed as a woman, but that of course is soon cleared up; he goes on to display all the warmth and humanity of Dame Edna Everage and none of the dexterity. He, too, improves as the play goes on; and he has the one moment that, catching me off- guard, made me laugh.

The main problem, though, is not these on-stage characters but the off-stage one. We are told nothing about the late Michael, except that Max loved him, and yet his name keeps coming up as if it were some kind of talisman.

Do I have to say this again? In the real world, a death from AIDS is horrible, though there are other equally horrific ways of dying. In the theatre it is, to put it brutally, only as good as the person who's dying it. It does not automatically bestow moral authority.

Since Michael doesn't exist dramatically, his plans for Max's future welfare are of minimal interest. And Max's own spiritual journey, which is what the play is meant to be about, is a subject raised and dropped as and when the author pleases.

If the other characters are meant to learn from him as he from them, that's even less substantial. As the story of a perilous journey, the play is flimsy, because there's no threat: little in the writing, less in the production. I suppose it preaches all- round tolerance; that isn't much to get for your time, but sure: God bless them. Every one.

2001-01-22-if-only-they-had-done-it-in-e:
TORONTO - Ferdinand Bruckner, German playwright of the 1920s, was a card. Under the name, his real one, of Theodor Tagger, he was also a Berlin theatre manager; and this double identity afforded him the rare pleasure of turning down his own first play. (He thought it was too sexy.) This is the one that has been translated as Pains of Youth.

It received its world premiere in Hamburg in 1926, caused a stir, and launched a lengthy and productive career. Neither the play nor its author have ever been well known outside Germany and Austria. They have attracted occasional attention in the outside world at times when youthful pain has been news: in the 1950s -- when the play's tortured, cynical and hyper-articulate characters were compared to those of John Osborne's Look Back in Anger -- and now. This production, by the enterprising Theatre Voce company, is the North American premiere. It's a trial, since the actors aren't up to the job, but it's an interesting one.

Ed Roy's production comes in an Expressionist wrapping, which initially seems reasonable in a piece born in the Berlin of Grosz and Kokoschka. As a prologue we are given two musicians, traversing the stage while playing piercing Teutonic jazz on bass and sax. We then get a look at the set: a striking design (by David Wootton) depicting a bedroom in which the walls don't meet, the furnishings are composed of huge piled-up books, and everything is tilted and angular; through a screen we glimpse the adjoining room, in which sizeable parts of the action will later be played in silhouette. A character spends a long time scrubbing the floor, in silence. Then someone comes on and speaks; and from that moment style disappears. The actors, as always happens in productions that don't quite know what they're doing, automatically lunge as close to realism as they can get. The set remains, of course, and it still looks good; but it's also unhelpful. I suspect that a design for this play should be either naturalistically detailed or absolutely stark. Truthfully, I don't know what the right style for the piece would be, but I'm sure this production hasn't found it.

The characters are mostly medical students or actual doctors: the women supposedly in their late teens, the men in their twenties. Most of them -- it's never quite clear how many-- seem to live in the same boarding house; the script is very sparse on background detail. (The stage directions say that it's set in Vienna, like Shakespeare's Measure for Measure, which notoriously mentions the place only once. Bruckner's dialogue goes the Bard one better and never mentions it at all.)

Marie, whose room we are in, is a recent and ferociously hard- working graduate. Her neighbour, Desiree, is a dilettante of titled family, infuriatingly capable of sailing through her exams on a minimum of preparation. In the course of the play, the two become lovers, each having tired of a previous male partner. The man who got into Desiree's life was a career nihilist named Freder, whom we see seducing the maid of the house, apparently for the sheer pleasure of turning her into a prostitute. Freder's union with Desiree must have been a battle of control freaks, with the man the predestined winner; Desiree has lots of bravado but no conviction and the imbalance, assisted by drugs, leads her to despair.

Marie has lost her boyfriend Petrell, a would-be poet, to a fellow student called Irene whom she despises and whom, in a fairly spectacular scene, she ties to a hat stand, by her hair. She calls it scalping her. (Coupled with a later suicide, this scene suggests Hedda Gabler with the gloves off.) I should add that Marie is, if not the heroine of the play, then certainly its emotional centre.

All the characters are young in years, but self-consciously old in disillusion. They are the children of the generation that lost the First World War, and -- psychologically at least -- they are living in the ruins; why study or practise medicine, one of them asks, in a world best left to die? They are quick to describe and analyze themselves, and even quicker to describe and analyze one another; the author seems to think that this constitutes characterization, and even action, but the result is that we find the characters at one another's throats before we've even been introduced. That might be exciting, except that most of the actors here are both physically too old for their roles and temperamentally too young; they can manage neither the willed sophistication of these chic dead-end kids, nor their underlying terror. What with everybody wandering into the room as if they lived there, through a confusingly non-existent door in this case, it comes off like a rogue episode of Friends.

Every relationship in this play is a matter of sex and power, with the two amounting to much the same thing, and cruelty can be surprisingly hard to act. The best performance, by miles, comes from the maid; Erin MacKinnon is tremblingly real as Freder's victim. She is noticeably less good, not bad, just ordinary, when she decides she likes her new life, and meets the others on equal terms. Like them, she has to work at it.

Fiona Highet, sashaying around as Desiree, works the hardest and the least effectively; Anne Page manages a certain balance as the pivotal Marie; Christopher Morris as Freder stops just short of twirling a melodramatic moustache.

Linda Prystawska is plaintive but otherwise vacant as the scalped Irene, and I forgot Joel Hechter's performance of her literary lover even while I was watching it. David Jansen rounds out the cast as a doctor who has done time for mercy-killing: a fortuitously topical touch that, like much in the play, twitches at the nerves.

The cast is much hobbled by Daphne Moore's translation (first staged in London) which isn't in English: not with lines like "even in science it's nearly always the charlatan and not the worker who finally attains the laurels," which would leave any actor gasping for breath.

The equivalent lines in German may well sound very hip and hard- edged; here they kill style and belief at once.

But something remains: the anxiety seems genuine, and compassionately meant. I don't know what Bruckner's subsequent plays were like; he may well have gotten slicker but I wouldn't be surprised if this were his best, the one he really meant.

MIDNIGHT SUN

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

Maja Ardal's play Midnight Sun is about hot music in a cold climate. In more scholarly terms, its about the impact of American big-band swing on the population of wartime Iceland. This is not a subject that gets explored very often in the theatre, or anywhere else; and in order to reduce its ramifications to manageable proportions, the author has zeroed in on an age-old romantic dilemma: Theres this cool chick, and she has to choose between a hepcat and a square. All three are native Icelanders, so the cool is literal as well, but the United States Army is also around, anxious to establish friendly relations with the locals, especially on the dance floor. Heard that before? There is perhaps more intellectual ambition here and less technical proficiency than in your average 1940s Hollywood soap opera with built-in cues for song, but the result is much the same.

Our heroine is Prila, who is going with an amiable young scientist named Petur. The two are just about to come to a life- long agreement, and it looks like we're all going to get home early, when, most frustratingly, a piece of Prila's past appears, an old flame whom everyone calls Kari Jazzplayer and who ran off to Denmark to play piano, though while there he switched to trumpet, which is certainly a lot more portable if youre going to keep hopping countries while theres a war on. He's also a piece of Petur's past - - his brother, in fact, and not at all pleased to find himself supplanted. So we settle in for an evening of Prila shuttling between two stupefyingly uninteresting young men.

Prila lives with her younger sister, Sissa, and their widowed mother, who seems to have a grudge against just about everything. Bodefully, she refuses to allow Sissa a party to celebrate her confirmation; the girl confides her frustrations to a race of little people beneath the floorboards, who apparently derive from Icelandic folklore but may also remind some spectators of the English childrens classic The Borrowers.

Caught between two stages of adolescence, Sissa is also caught between two cultures; Prila got a touch of the American pop bug when singing with Karis jazz group, but Sissa has been thorougly infected by it, by movies especially. When the Yanks arrive, she has what may or may not be fantasy encounters (it's very confusing) with GIs whom she addresses as Clark Gable and Jimmy Stewart, and who do indeed look like them. When she's with Jimmy, she quotes from The Philadelphia Story and she strongly resembles the interfering kid sister of that movie. That child, however, was a supporting character kept in her place; Sissa starts this play as if it were going to be about her, and though it turns out that it isnt, the damage has been done. In fact, it keeps being reinforced; the plays various plot lines, obviously meant to complement one another, instead get in one another's way.

Possible dream sequences apart, there is only one American in the play, a sergeant who is the base's radio announcer and disc jockey and also plays drums. He organizes a hop (a Big Band Bash or, as the locals have it, "Big Band Bass") to which only the Icelandic women are invited. Since this tactlessly clashes with the annual Midsummer Ball, the men have a double reason to be angry, and Petur orchestrates their resentment to get back at his jazz-obsessed brother and at the suspiciously swinging Prila. (This may not seem calculated to get her back, but Petur has obviously lost it.) When the Icelandic characters meet the sergeant and speak English to him, they do so in credibly Nordic accents, and this is effective; there is a feeling of two worlds coming into uneasy contact. Left to themselves, the natives speak just like you and me, and just about as entertainingly; the dialogue is flat, and there is no sense of anything going on below the surface. Not that the author is above inventing a few depths when it suits her; late on, the mother tells us all kinds of things we never wanted to know. (That is the curse of late-breaking exposition: Its always answering questions nobody asked.) Ardal, Icelandic herself, does make a point about the countrys women being more independent than either their own or the American men find comfortable; but in order to fully dramatize the culture clash she apparently has in mind, she would need to introduce us to more people. Just hearing about them, with no details supplied, doesn't cut it.

The production, by Andy McKim and Patricia Vanstone, does little for the play's credibility, especially on the domestic front. The set, by Vikki Anderson, is a multi-levelled affair and it doesnt look as if anybody lived there. (I have very few conversations on the stairs of my own house -- Alec Guinness on "one-foot-up, one- foot-down" acting.) Nor is it strong on visceral excitement; the staging of the first-act climax is extraordinarily half-hearted.

It does, though, boast a ruggedly charming performance, strong and deceptively still, by Kari Matchett as Prila; she sings well, too, in a casual tone thats a pleasing reminder of the many fine Swedish and Norwegian jazz singers who have arisen in the last half- century. (I've never heard any Icelandic ones.)

Matthew Edison is suitably stiff and uptight as Petur, and Jeff Madden, who smiles a lot, suitably devilish as Kari. Holly Lewis is defeated by the precocious outpourings of sister Sissa. While Nicky Guadagni has an even tougher time dealing with mom. She has to keep marching on, just when we've forgotten about her, and play stressful scenes with folded arms and eyes directed at the heavens; and having done that she is left standing around all high and dry at the end of them. Paul Braunstein copes cheerily, if none too subtly, with the burden of representing the entire American military presence; and all the actors, when required, play their own instruments, which is always impressive.

There is an additional performer, Greg Earle, who exists only to play the bass, which seems like cheating. Maybe they should have gone whole hog and made the show a full-scale musical; it does at least have more substance than either of the big swing shows that blighted the Toronto landscape the year before last. One of the better scenes here has a puzzled Prila coping with the lyrics of Chattanooga Choo-Choo ("What is this woo-woo?") and then sailing right through it without once looking at the paper. She and the combo also manage to leave out the entire middle of the song without consultation and without train wrecks, which just goes to show that jazz people can communicate at osmotic levels.

But why, when the American mentions Kansas, is he immediately asked if he knows Hoagy Carmichael, as Carmichael was an Indiana boy who at the plays's historical moment would have been in Hollywood? Anyway, Hoagy is constantly invoked, and the play ends with Prila singing his haunting Skylark. This presumably accounted for the cheers and stamps at the curtain -- either that or the world's gone mad. The Tarragon, which in the past has demonstrated a weakness for a dully pretentious new play, seems now to have opted for equally featureless banality.

MAKING PORN

Bathurst Street Theatre, Toronto

Pirandello's ghost needn't bother to get up, but Making Porn certainly exemplifies the interaction of life and art. It's about exactly what its title says it's about -- the production of pornographic videos, gay male division -- and two of its actors are actual porn stars, in San Francisco, which is where the play is set. So, at least, say the publicity, the program, and even one of the other actors in a speech at the curtain call. He also lays great stress on his two colleagues being lovers in real life, but here art and life part company; in the play they barely (oh dear, it's starting) have a scene together.

Making porn and Making Porn have something else in common: They both have to face the problem of what to put into the script between the sex scenes. Ronnie Larsen, who wrote the play, seems to have taken the challenge to heart, and has evolved a complex structure that boasts three separate but interconnected plot-lines.

There are the efforts of Arthur -- writer, producer, director and all-round sleazebag -- to produce his movie, i.e. to recruit a cast and pay them as little as possible; his biggest current expense is hiring a highly rated performer named Ray to play a lead in his new epic Cops. (Cops is all about policemen. And a plumber. I forget which Ray is playing. He doesn't spend much time in uniform anyway.)

There is the romance that blossoms between Jamie, Arthur's much- exploited assistant and live-in partner, and Ricky, a young law student fulfilling his life-long ambition of appearing in a porno flick; he dreams of being a star, but for the moment he comes cheap.

Finally, there is Jack, an aspiring but monotonously unsuccessful actor, whom we see auditioning for Shakespeare and for musicals, very badly. (I assume the effect is intentional.) He is straight but can only find work from the likes of Arthur: a fact that he tries, unsuccessfully, to keep from his wife, a legal secretary named Linda.

Getting all this together, and keeping it together up to the actual onstage shooting of the movie, makes for a long first act. Much too long, in fact, but there are some surprisingly good elements: surprising to me, anyway, since I confidently expected the show to be terrible. The demi-monde the play depicts -- a mirror of the wider movie world with its elastic critical and commercial standards and its self-intoxicated award ceremonies -- seems to be etched from experience; and Arthur, who sees himself as the Orson Welles of skin flicks, is a very convincing figure. As played by Butch Cordora (the characters' names seem drably prosaic compared to those of the actors), he is mean, hard-headed in some ways and myopically obtuse in others, and touchingly intent on getting the actors to respect his script --and not to say "dude" when he has written "guy."

The preparation of the more action-oriented sections of the movie is played for laughs, which seems a practical decision, given the nature of the theatre: a medium, by the way, for which Arthur expresses thoroughgoing contempt. (He'd probably approve, though, of the present management's policy of charging five bucks extra for a seat in one of the front three rows. What the big spenders get for their money is another question.)

Arthur's deteriorating union with Jamie (Adam Beckworth) is quite trenchantly outlined, and Jamie's compensating affair with the debutant Ricky (John Hensley) is convincingly tender. Jack's marital life with Linda isn't, but then I don't suppose any of those responsible for the play claim to be experts on heterosexual relationships. What happens is that Linda is shocked when she Finds Out, and insists on accompanying Jack to the set. The resulting scene requires all the actors to look incredulous, though not nearly as incredulous as the audience is feeling. Linda stops being shocked and gets thrilled by the commercial potential she sees in her husband's new career. (Not that he had an old one.) None of this is impossible, but it's written by numbers, and Kym Kristalie can hardly be blamed for playing it the same way.

Now, about those two authentic porn luminaries. Apparently they weren't in the show when it first opened (five years ago in Chicago) but their presence now is an example of standard road-company procedure: Cast a Name, from wherever, and however specialized. One of them, Jason Branch, is cast, presumably to type, as Ray; he seems a moody performer whose line-readings sound as if they're being phoned in on a very faint connection. The other, Blake Harper, goes the opposite route and plays Jack, which means that we have a gay actor acting straight in the role of a straight actor acting gay. It all comes out in the wash.

Act Two is much shorter, and much worse, and is dominated by the onset of AIDS. (At this point we look at the program and notice for the first time that the play is set in the early 1980s.)

One of the characters dies, though he does stick around, benevolently materializing at the top of a ladder, all decorated with Christmas lights. Ray refuses to work without condoms though Arthur declares Death Sooner: not his own, of course. He is, however, talked round by Linda, with whom he has virtually gone into partnership and who has suddenly taken to wearing mini-skirts. She seems to have given up on Jack, who is last glimpsed playing a messenger in what you can bet is a non-Equity production of Macbeth.

So it seems all but the two least sympathetic characters have got out of the porn business. It makes for a surprisingly traditional moralistic ending. This may not have been quite the author's intention, but by this point it has become unavoidably clear that his method in writing this play was to throw in anything -- farce or sentiment or social consciousness -- as long as it filled the space and bore some relation to the title.

Making Porn is, of course, junk; but so is everything in the current Toronto theatre apart from Zadie's Shoes and Stones in His Pockets, and this play is by no means the worst. The set is dominated by a free-standing door that at one amusing moment on Wednesday night refused to open, but otherwise Caryn Horwitz's production manages the transitions between scenes and episodes a lot more smoothly than has recently been the case in some higher-toned establishments. I note that she is now engaged in making a film of Making Porn, and that really should have Pirandello rattling his chains.

GIRLWRECKED

The Dovercourt, Toronto

Rana, a second-generation Canadian immigrant, remembers a relationship from her girlhood and its traumatic resolution. She was 11 when she arrived in London, Ont., having spent six years in her parents' home country of Mauritius. Initially assigned to Grade 6, she is abruptly promoted to 8 when the authorities discover that she can read Shakespeare, aloud and clear. Here she meets Roz, a red- headed girl, "skinny and scraggly," by whom she initially half- expects to be bullied. In the event, the two develop a friendship, and the beginnings of a lesbian romance. Both are distrusted by their peers: Rana for being foreign, Roz for just about everything - - the way she dresses, the way she smells. It all comes to a head with an especially vicious attack on Roz during which Rana behaves, in her own estimation, disgracefully. The memory stays with her forever, or at least up to the time that she tells us the story.

Storytelling is what this piece is -- a solo narrative written and performed by Soraya Peerbaye, who shares her protagonists ethnic background. Its a slight story but a compelling one, and might serve for a more elaborate play than we have actually been offered. We want to know more about Roz than Rana is able to tell us in this format. Even more importantly, we want to know more about Rana, knowing not being the same thing as being told. We can see that she wears a hijab, but though it's an important prop for the actress, we don't know to what extent it either intrigues or enrages her classmates. Rana is enraged and humiliated to find the word Paki traced on snow on her front lawn -- it seems her tormentors cant even get their racism right -- but the anger suggests complications in her, a hierarchy of prejudice, which is also unexplored, as are the lines of force that draw the two isolated girls together.

The framework for the play involves Rana reading, with caustically mocking restraint, a litany of how-to-hold-your-man principles from a teen magazine. This is intriguing, as is a later hint that Ranas and Roz's sexualities have diverged, but nothing much is made of either possibility.

It's not that one wants everything to be spelled out; rather, that a broader canvas might give the same subtleties more room to manoeuvre and more depth in which to resonate. And when it comes to violent action, or indeed to comic action, audiences have an unregenerate desire to see rather than hear about it. Even Greek tragic messengers delivered their casualty reports to someone; there was drama in the way their bulletins were received. The climax of the story is not that easy to take in as Rana tells it, so what might be called the post-climax -- when Rana tells us what really happened, as opposed to what she wants people to believe happened -- is in fact an anti-climax.

GirlWrecked is unsatisfying, but it is definitely talented. Peerbayes previous career has been principally in movement-based theatre; she and her director, Karin Randoja, have devised a choreographic staging built around the visual outline of a schoolroom. The outline presupposes a greater sense of academic place than the script actually supplies, but it enables Peerbaye, who seems to be making her professional acting debut, to move between, over and around two parallel rows of chairs with delightful, skipping grace. Her vocal authority is not as secure; words get lost, and the space, an echoing church basement at the Great Hall on Queen Street West, is not kind.

This apart, her delivery is delicate and acute, as is her writing. The main thrust of the show is verbal -- surprisingly so; and the words are precise, evocative and sometimes witty. When youre best friends, the early-teenaged Rana decides, "there can be no one else -- otherwise, it's polygamy." The later-teenaged Rana, a wallflower at a dance, refers to herself and her companions in rejection parading from the floor "like we're genuinely interested in examining the wall." Theres a vein of self-mockery here, gentle but merciless, that is very attractive. But it also seems too easy, and in the end too thin. As in nearly all one-person plays, however hard the narrator is prepared to be on herself, its still her story that we're stuck with.

CINDERELLA

Pantages Theatre, Toronto

Fairy tales are natural sources for musicals. Your characters can burst unselfconsciously into song without offending anybody's sense of realism, and you can even have a happy ending. Its a wonder it isnt done more often.

Richard Rodgers and Oscar Hammerstein II did it very well in their television version of Cinderella, which was first seen in a fabled live production in 1957, and has had two further small- screen outings since. It has also, inevitably and often, been reworked for the stage, for which it is in many ways a natural. Its main drawback is simply that it's too short; we get to the ball in double-quick time, certainly by theatrical standards, and of course once we're there, the story has no choice but to roll rapidly to its close.

Still, better too fast than too slow, and the touring production that has reached Toronto this week is a brisk piece of storytelling, light on the magic but ready with it when needed. It is, frankly, a much better show than I had expected.

Two pop stars, of widely spaced vintages, get major billing, so maybe they should be dealt with first. Deborah Gibson makes a spunky, practical Cinderella (never referred to as Cinders) except for her singing, which unfortunately sounds as if she has a hole in her teeth. She has to do a lot of vocalizing; Eartha Kitt, playing Fairy Godmother, has to do very little, and what she does comes out the same way it has for decades: as a mocking, sensuous purr.

This may not be quite what you would expect of her character, but then, this is no ordinary conception of the role. This is a therapeutically minded spirit whose main trick is not to turn mice into footmen and a pumpkin into a coach (though she does both to the usual throat-lumping effect) but to turn her ward into the mistress of her own destiny. She is a Do-It-Yourself Kitt.

The lady could, in fact, be more effectively imperious than she is. She can still turn a witty line, but her chief function here is to stand around looking extremely well preserved. She is indeed best when stillest, especially when making an unheralded, admonitory appearance at the ball. There is a strong hint in this adaptation that Cinderellas fairy godmother is actually her dead mortal mother returned, you might say, to Eartha.

Once upon a time, in a kingdom far away -- it was called England - - somebody waved a wand and turned the R&H Cinderella from a musical into a pantomime. This version, however, has little truck with that. Nobody plays to the audience, nobody steps out of character. The one apparent panto touch is the casting of a man, Everett Quinton, as the Stepmother, but his performance turns out to be the most serious and uncompromising of the evening. (The few bits of obvious clowning seem added-on and unwanted.)

This Stepmother is constantly on the verge of becoming a really interesting character: She is believably and chillingly cruel, worried about her own future as well as that of her offspring, obviously consumed with jealousy of her late husbands first wife, and taking it out on their daughter. This is the first time I have ever had any sense of what life in that household might have been like; and one's sympathy for the heroine, who apparently constitutes the entire domestic staff, increases tenfold.

NaTasha Yvette Williams and Alexandra Kolb are less successful at humanizing The Ugly Sisters (who aren't called that, but nobodys fooled). The writing of their roles has been coarsened down the years, to judge from what Ive read of the original production.

I have to rely on my reading, because that first TV version pre- dated the arrival of videotape. The current program credits Hammerstein with book and lyrics, but also lists Tom Briggs as having adapted the show for the stage "from the teleplay by Robert L. Freedman," presumably the one for the 1997 version starring Brandy and Whitney Houston. The Briggs text is a considerable improvement on that atrocity, but it probably falls short of the Hammerstein standard of urbanity.

Prince Christopher (not Charming, though Paolo Montalban seems pleasant enough) is shown fending off the matchmaking plans of his grumbling mom (Leslie Becker) and bumbling dad (Ken Prymus). These royal encounters are mildly entertaining, but they must once have been wittier than they are here.

The Sweetest Sounds, a later Rodgers song with his own lyric, has been imported to suggest the unacknowledged mutual yearnings of hero and heroine; sung before we have heard a note of the original score, it doesn't wreck anything, but it does spoil it, especially as it's staged in the most standardized of village squares, full of the most standardized village dancers. Here we really do seem to be in for a panto.

Gabriel Barres direction, James Youmans designs, and Ken Roberson's choreography all improve markedly later on, especially at the ball where the dancing -- until Cinderella arrives to wake the party up -- goes, literally and wittily, like clockwork.

There is, though, one excrescence in the staging: a strange double dose of Disney. As in the old cartoon, Cinderella at home is surrounded by friendly livestock, in this case one cat, one bird and four bewhiskered rodents, all co-existing in idyllic harmony. They are represented by puppets, worked Japanese style by visible actors. This is abruptly introduced and quite out of style with the rest of the production; it looks like The Mouse King.

What truly carries the show is what carried it first: the songs. The score is the best of Rodgers' late (i.e., anything after The King and I) period. Cinderellas In My Own Little Corner is the perfect set-up number, wistful but strong. (So who needs The Sweetest Sounds?) The Prince Is Giving a Ball, with its endless lists of improbable royal names, is very funny, or would be if the ensemble here seemed in on the joke.

The grand waltz Ten Minutes Ago is not one of Rodgers subtlest explorations of three-quarter time, but its sweep is exactly what is needed, not merely to accompany the ball but to carry us to the romantic heart of it. From there, duly enchanted, we move with perfect ease to the quieter consummation of the show's one authentic ballad, Do I Love You Because You're Beautiful. And there is more; not enough to make a great theatre score, but that was never the original intention. What we have is a makeshift, but of the nicest kind.

2001-02-03-play-portrays-killers-but-doe:
The miniature international festival known as Six Stages starts superlatively with a new work from DNA Theatre, headed by the much- feted but long-absent author and director, Hillar Littoja.

Paula and Karl is a home-grown piece on a home-grown subject: Remove the final vowel from one name and add it to the other, and you will recognize the source.

Putting Paul Bernardo and Karla Homolka on stage is not something I would have thought either possible or desirable. I would have been wrong. Frivolous though it may sound, the change of names adds the right amount of distance, gives the piece its own identity and helps remove any hint of exploitation. Mr. Littoja takes us inside his characters' heads. More crucially and completely, he takes us inside their world.

I mean that literally. The production revives an old form of environmental theatre that has fallen into disuse and that I never much liked in the first place. Here, though, it justifies itself.

The play is staged in a private house. We are greeted brusquely at the door, told to line up against the wall and escorted downstairs. What awaits us is a spacious basement living room with a kitchen in the corner. We are told we may stand, sit or wander as we like, even look into the adjoining rooms, but must get out of the way if the actors require it.

As one of the last to arrive, I found it difficult to decide which of those already present were actors; some I recognized as colleagues but others seemed remarkably relaxed and at home.

A video was playing, The Cider House Rules; I got quite caught up in it, since for a long time nothing else happened. Gradually it became clear the young blond woman slumped on the couch half- watching the movie, half-reading a book, and awesomely reposed was the only actor present; presumably she was Paula. Eventually a man joined her: her husband, Karl, home from work or somewhere.

As they greet one another, we in the audience switch automatically into a different mode; we start to judge the performances. At first they seem like what might pass in a normal theatre for good naturalistic acting; at these close quarters they appear artificial, the voices preternaturally clear, the sentences too precisely formed.

But as they go on talking, as Paula prepares Karl a sandwich and he eats it, as he proudly produces a large newly bought dildo and they play with it, as they begin casually alluding to somebody female kept bound and gagged in another room; as all this happens, the style begins imposing itself and the relationship becomes real, complete and frighteningly easy.

Veronika Hurnik's Paula, in particular, is more than just believable. It is the most completely, impregnably lived and inhabited performance I have ever seen; as closely detailed as the best screen acting but happening right there in front of us, unshielded and unedited.

During the action two detectives arrive, question the pair and ask Karl to show them around the house. We could have gone with them but it seemed more rewarding to sit and watch Paula as expressions of terror chased one another over her face.

Her role is perhaps the more rewarding, because it is the more varied of the two. Karl is pure unreachable bully: obviously capable of anything, though perhaps the most terrifying thing he does on stage is to crank up the volume of his CD player when Paula tries arguing with him.

James Thomson, having found the right implacable register for him, has to stay with it, but Ms. Hurnik is able to play both victim and manipulator, and to do strange things to our sympathies. When the police leave, having found nothing, she still knows the game is up and pleads with Karl to end it now; we know her motives have nothing to do with compassion and everything to do with self- preservation, but we want to believe differently and to side with her. One reason for respecting the play is that, at its close, it finds the right way of stopping us.

James O'Reilly and Randall Lanthier as the investigators are on a different level, giving good, even humorous, cop-show performances.

The play has been tightly and superbly edited; some loose ends simply add to the conviction. The real victim, of course, we never see, hear or even learn much about; the play would be intolerable, in every sense, if we did.

Despite its initial, and probably excessive, intimidation tactics, the production avoids the kind of superior stance that has traditionally accompanied this kind of presentation; it doesn't punish the audience for being there. It does what the theatre is supposed to do: show us humanity, which must include its phases of inhumanity.
