THE COMPLETE WORKS OF WILLIAM SHAKESPEARE (ABRIDGED)

Young Peoples Theatre, Toronto

Presented as a lunchtime production, or in some alternative theatre's studio space, The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (Abridged) would be just another stupidly unfunny revue. Presented, as it is now, by the most prominent and highly subsidized youth theatre we have, its a scandal. Not because its a bad show: That could happen to anybody. But because its premise, never mind its execution, strikes at the root of what the YPT is supposed to be about.

Basically the show's creators -- three writers, three actors, one director -- say Shakespeare is boring. They say this tongue-in- cheek, on the apparent assumption that if you say it often enough, you will somehow prove the reverse.

It doesn't work like that, though. Individually, they may all love Shakespeare but their collective creation -- or 95% of it anyway -- says, or shrieks, otherwise. Nobody of course is under any obligation to love Shakespeare, and there are plenty of reasons for finding the plays difficult. (All those funny words. And, according to this show, all those funny wigs.) If you as a practitioner find that the difficulties add up to tedium, then probably the best course is to give up and produce something else; theres plenty to choose from. If, on the other hand, you want to help your audience overcome their fears and enjoy the plays, you might do better by putting on a lucid and lively production of one of them than by indulging in two hours of nervous giggle. Which is what we have here: no comic focus, just a sequence of lurching from one weak idea to another.

The title actually suggests a folly of rather more grandeur than what is on offer. I expected to see the stage equivalent of a full- length cartoon that would somehow race through the basic plot-lines of all 37 plays in the canon, perhaps finding ingenious verbal links to take us from one text to another, perhaps even playing some of them simultaneously. It might not have meant much to anybody who didnt know all the plays already, but that was obviously going to be a built-in hazard anyway. (As it still is.)

It turns out, though, that the show proceeds on the assumption that a title mentioned means a play accounted for. The histories -- all of them -- are taken care of in a frenzied football commentary in which the brutal players are all kings: a full complement including Lear (whose play isn't a history) and Henry IV (Parts One and Two). But it would make just as much or as little sense with any other names.

The comedies, introduced to us as plagiarized works with identical plots, are similarly reduced to an all-purpose multiple scenario. Now, if they'd managed to act this out, rather than to deliver it as a gabbled synopsis that were supposed to applaud for its sheer speed, it might have been clever; but that would require a gift for creative pastiche that none of these authors seems to possess. To be fair, few people ever have; after 400 years, youd think that the anthologies would be crammed with successful Shakespearean parodies; in fact, there are hardly any. The style seems to be too protean for anyone to get a bead on. This show's approach -- alternating thou and "wouldst" and prithee with breezy references to hiding the salami -- does not cut it.

Sometimes the proceedings get quite academic; this is, after all, the Young Peoples Theatre, complete with study guide. The actors mention a 38th play, The Two Noble Kinsmen (one of them refers to it as "Chernobyl Kinsmen Shakespeare's contribution to geopolitics"); they say, correctly, that it is generally regarded as part of the Shakespeare Apocrypha; they then define that category for us as plays that are crap, basically and give Troilus and Cressida as an example of an apocryphal play that is actually quite good. Well, I dont know exactly how lofty an educational standard the YPT should be setting itself, but Im fairly sure that it shouldn't be in the business of spreading misinformation, especially misinformation about plays.

The Shakespeare Apocrypha is a technical, not a critical, term referring to plays of doubtful authorship. Kinsmen has long been considered one of them, though its status seems to be changing; Troilus never has. They then start telling us about Troilus, and are getting along all right until one of them mentions "Agamemnon, the Greek general, laying siege to Troy" and is greeted by cries of boring. It's not quite clear whats so frightening here -- Agamemnons long name or Troy's short one -- but whatever it is, it stops the show in its tracks and starts it apologizing.

I'm all in favour of teachers, in class or onstage, explaining things; I dont think they should be prostrating themselves before their audiences ignorance. I don't think the audience are much impressed by it, either. They know when they're being patronized.

If, for example, theyve seen Baz Luhrmanns film of Romeo and Juliet, which is a genuine example of making Shakespeare accessible, they may find this show's nudge-wink reduction of the play rather puzzling, since it parodies a performance style that only exists in other parodies. (As for the plot, Shakespeare himself satirized it much better in A Midsummer Night's Dream.)

The same goes for Glenn Davidsons quite ingenious scenic approximation of an Elizabethan stage, and for Sue Le Pages purposefully tacky Elizabethan costumes; they don't relate to how Shakespeare is done today, but only to how lazy comedians would like to think he's done.

Other plays that get comparatively full treatment are Othello, done as rap because of its black hero (I rather enjoyed this), and Macbeth, presented with startling satiric originality in Scots accents (this is where they really should have cried "boring"). And there is Titus Andronicus, whose hero appears in a TV chefs uniform to give us his patented recipe for cannibal pie; the joke, such as it is, must be lost on most of the audience since Titus is not, or ever likely to be, a set text.

And then there is Hamlet, which takes up the entire second half, as it would. Its given a skeletal run-through; mercifully, apart from the apparently obligatory audience-participation sequence in which some poor lady is hauled up to play Ophelia, it uses only lines from the actual text. This is an old idea -- schools do it -- but it gives the actors well-taken opportunities to display their nimbleness, especially when they have to do it again, faster, and then yet again, backwards. (They are Kirk Dunn, Joel Harris and Stephen Guy-McGrath and, insofar as I could distinguish them from what they were required to do, I thought they were all right.)

In the middle of this is the delivery by one of them -- not the one playing Hamlet -- of the "what a piece of work is a man" speech, all of it, spoken sensitively and unfussily. It stilled the house, and even got a round of applause. This, I'm sure, was the intended effect: an assurance that they do believe in the plays after all. But it does not, whatever they may think, atone for the rest of the show. It merely makes it look even sicker.

The program (like too many, and not just at the YPT) tells us less about the authors than it does about the lighting designer, but it lets on that they're called Adam Long, Daniel Singer and Jess Winfield; while the study guide, which seems to have exalted ideas about the shows educational potential, tells us it originated in the U.K. and has been kicking around for years. That is perhaps the most dispiriting thing about the whole enterprise: that the YPT brought this rubbish in, having presumably seen it in advance. (The director, Joel Greenberg, staged it in Toronto two years ago.) It will, I think, leave kids appreciation of Shakespeare exactly where it found it.

That is, it won't do any harm. But it's taking up space that might have been used to do good. Not sociological good, though that's what the YPT still seems to think its job is, but theatrical good, which is the only reason it has for existing.

2001-02-07-history-begins-and-ends-with-:
KEN CAMPBELLS HISTORY OF COMEDY (PART ONE: VENTRILOQUISM)

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, Toronto

Ken Campbell has been functioning in and around the British theatre for several decades now as an actor, playwright and director, though none of those classifications quite suits him. To the observer of his work they seem confining -- and they seem to seem like that to him, too. He still works with other people, but he may well have found himself as a solo performer, a raconteur who tells tales of the occult and bizarre with a gleeful gurgle in his voice and an air of casual conviction that is modestly spellbinding. The self-styled History of Comedy (Part One: Ventriloquism) that he brought to the Toronto Six Stages Festival shows him at his peak. Be advised, though, that it is not so much a history of comedy as a history of Campbell.

For as long as I can remember (which, where Campbell is concerned, is 30 years) he has been balding; he now has preternaturally bushy eyebrows to match the grey thatch. He walks briskly but unhurriedly onstage, giving the (grammatical erroneous) impression of being already in mid-sentence.

He starts talking about a Festival of Radical Ventriloquists that he attended in Kentucky, and he does so in the hypnotic tones that the late Peter Cook used in his immortal Beyond the Fringe monologue about working down the mines and not having the Latin to be a judge. The difference is that Cook was distancing himself from his character, obviously putting on a voice and somewhat sinister, while Campbell is affably himself.

He comes from a long tradition of British comedy. His roots are in the more eccentric aspects of the music hall, and I find it hard to describe him without invoking comedians who are not very well known in Canada. So indulge me. Like the melancholy-mad Max Wall, Campbell beckons us into a world of his own, though the welcome he extends is cheery rather than doleful. His voice can rise to pitches of outraged incredulity, expressed in the southeast London vowels, and the southeast London flamboyance, of the supreme British stand- up artist Frankie Howard. And he seizes on unlikely pieces of information and holds them up to the light with a schoolboyish enthusiasm that reminds me of my good friend Rob Buckman before he gave up comedy and moved to Toronto.

His act is in fact a collection of objets trouves, physical and intellectual. Behind him are two tables piled high with stuff: ventriloquists dummies (obviously -- and he tells us that in professional circles the word dummy" is frowned upon, the favoured term being "knee pal), pictures from his past, books including one virtuosically free of all words including the letter e." He tells us about his own life, concentrating on school days just after the Second World War when he and his contemporaries wrote away for teach- yourself-ventriloquism books and used the techniques they had learned to invent a universal non-verbal language with which to baffle the crazed war veterans who taught them and incidentally to bring about the destruction of the universe. He acknowledges that in the latter aim they were unsuccessful.

He also tells us about friends of his, the Plashwit brothers, who were nursed by dogs, and of the intense canine attachment developed by their kid sister, Nina (apparently the love of his life), and by how unshocked his own mother was when he told her. ("Remember Tim, she said mysteriously.) He tells us many details about these friends' father, who was probably an octuple agent," and about a 19th-century U.S. attorney who won hundreds of 19th-century dollars in damages for a dog-deprived client by delivering a passionate speech so moving that the recorder had to stop recording it. What the recorder did get down became the basis of the young Campbell's first professional ventriloquial act, a funeral oration that unfortunately drove the son of the deceased absolutely mad. He did, however, recover, and Campbell was eventually to re-encounter him, and the long-lost Nina, at the very same Kentucky festival that he began by telling us about.

You see how it goes. Campbell goes off at enormously lengthy detailed tangents (his act alludes, historically and geographically, to much of the known world and even more of the unknown) but he always comes back to where he left off, and then comes back to where he had left off before that. Its one thing inside another, like taking a Russian doll out of a Chinese box. Its amazingly fluent -- a great feat of memory, construction and conceivably spontaneous invention. I don't know if he makes any of it up as he goes along (he went on at my visit for 2 3/4 hours, which is excessive, though it was rarely boring), but he is never at a loss for well-chosen words. For an apostle of the non-verbal, he is a wiz with language.

Of course, we don't believe much of what he tells us. But then again, all the things he says that I can check up on are actually true. He did the eastern hinterlands of London -- what they used to call the Essex marshes -- and has the accent to prove it. He did, in the early 70s, found a troupe called the Ken Campbell Road Show -- I saw them. (Bob Hoskins was in it). He did write, direct and appear in epic day-or-week-long shows for a company he called the Science Fiction Theatre of Liverpool -- The Warp, which I didnt like but is being revived, and Illuminatus!, based on a cult book, which was amazing. So why shouldn't the rest be real? He seems to believe them.

He is fascinated by things -- the more arcane the better -- and the fascination is infectious. He talks of the psychic experience of "going through the wall on the other side of which everything seems funny; and I seem to remember reading that in real life he had to give up acting in plays because he found himself too amused by his colleagues' performances to concentrate on his own. He also tells us, with reference to performance conditions in primitive cultures, that you might say plush seats were the last nail in the coffin of real comedy." Well, that wasn't a problem in the back room at Passe Muraille. Believe me. Despite his logical mind, Campbell is not averse to the odd long-sequitur, so I doubt that his History of Comedy will have a Part Two, but if it does I hope we get to see it. If it doesn't, we could take this one again.

2001-02-10-a-small-scale-nuclear-play:
Mordechai Vanunu is the Israeli nuclear technician who gave photographs of his country's secret nuclear weapons program to The Sunday Times. The Israeli government kidnapped him, tried him for treason and sentenced him to 18 years behind bars. He is now in his 13th year of solitary confinement.

I Am Your Spy, a one-man play about Vanunu, is a joint production of two Vancouver companies, Rumble Productions and NeWorld Theatre, brought to Toronto as part of the Six Stages festival.

It is billed as a mixed-media production, a term that always seems to make those who use it feel very important and cutting- edge.

Here it simply means the show incorporates two working video screens, which today hardly seems a big deal. The smaller of the two screens shows us clips of talking heads, filling in some of the political and historical background of Vanunu's actions. The larger is used to present a blown-up image of the man himself, in his cell, as he would appear through prison surveillance-cameras.

Between the pictures is Vanunu himself, played by Camyar Chai, who also wrote the play (with Mara Coward), pacing a narrow stage- space which, according to the program, is exactly the same size as Vanunu's actual cell. We watch him trying to stay sane.

The effect is modestly hypnotic. Vanunu's first concern, chronologically speaking, is that his meal has not been served to him on time, depriving him of one of the psychological props that he needs in order to keep a grip on his day.

His next concern is whether or not he will receive a promised visit from his brother, his principal link with the outside world. We are left in no doubt that he is being held in conditions that are inhumane, if not actually inhuman. The same would of course be true of any prisoner in these circumstances, whatever his offence; but the play would not exist if Vanunu were any prisoner. All the same, it is only toward the end of the 65-minute piece that Vanunu starts talking about what he did and why he did it.

It amounts to a tiny treatment of a huge theme. The ethics of betrayal, and of the crazy-house world of nuclear armament, are more complex than the play ever comes close to acknowledging. The televised pundits make the most dramatic contributions of the evening; they reveal among other things that Daniel Ellsberg, author of The Pentagon Papers, learned via President Kennedy that if the U.S. were to bomb all the targets theoretically available to them, they would kill 600-million people.

This, it is pointed out, would make the Holocaust look like a minor conflagration; it would also, as another speaker says, destroy not just the present but the future.

The tone, though certainly more measured, is like that of Bertrand Russell's notorious denunciation of Kennedy and Macmillan as "more wicked than Hitler." Few would deny the Pentagon is a paranoid and self-righteous organization, but there really is a moral difference -- not to mention a practical one -- between a murderous scenario and a murderous reality. Hitler crunched more than numbers.

There is, after all, a case to be made for nuclear preparedness but nobody on that screen is ever allowed to make it. More crucially, the play has no mechanism for questioning Vanunu himself. He is alone on the stage, and the best the play can do by way of supplying a conflict is to have him put imaginary arguments into the mouth of his father, who has disowned him, and then answer them.

The only suggestion that there may have been some personal mixture in his motives is the acknowledgement that, as a Moroccan Jew, he felt in Israel like a second-class citizen. Probably the sharpest comment he makes is also the most flippant: If the purpose of the Israeli nuclear arsenal was to frighten the enemy, then wasn't he doing the government a favour by blowing the whistle and giving the enemy something to be frightened of?

The script, which combines extracts from Vanunu's own letters with the author's imaginings, is pedestrian; and though Chai's performance is perfectly competent, it is generalized: another nerve- wracked man in another prison drama.

I left the theatre perfectly prepared to sign a petition for Vanunu's release but far from sure he was right. (I actually felt more sympathy for him -- intellectually as well as emotionally -- at the time of his arrest and trial than I did watching the play.)

The production's tone is uncomfortably reflected in a jargon- ridden "writer's disclaimer" in the program: "Fiction is a double- edged sword. On the one hand, it allows the usurpers of the world to imprison history. Yet fiction also permits the artist to break free from the constraints of propaganda." In other words: It's all right if we do it. The Pentagon, from its own standpoint, might say exactly the same thing. Talk about double standards.

2001-02-10-the-play-s-the-thing-catching:
Robert Cushman is the National Post's theatre critic. See related letter " Shakespeare's politics: once more unto the breach" by Jeffrey MacIntosh, Toronto and Jens Andersen, Edmonton, on Page B12.

Adam Kirsch hits a whole row of nails on the head (The King's Playwright, Feb. 3). He is right, for example, about the mixture of brilliance, arrogance and perversity in Harold Bloom's Shakespeare: The Invention of the Human; the brilliance predominates but I too ploughed through Bloom's rhapsodies on Falstaff -- his favourite character -- wondering when he was going to stop telling us how wonderful the old fat man is and get down to explaining why. (He never does.)

Kirsch is right, too, about the politicized critics whom Bloom amusingly dubbed the School of Resentment: The ones who regard literature as a vast conspiracy against which somebody -- it's never quite clear who -- needs to be protected. They are not, perhaps, quite as monolithic a brigade as either Bloom or Kirsch might suggest. There are those who would damn Shakespeare for the sin of not being a 20th-century radical; those who praise him for having been one without telling anybody, writing his plays in a secret code that only they have been able to crack; and those -- a large group - - whose position is difficult to make out. This last bunch are so busy executing elaborate dances of disdain in the plays' general vicinity that it's hard to tell what they think; it's as if expressing an opinion about a work -- actually committing yourself to liking or disliking it -- would be unbearably square. Maybe what they truly resent is that Shakespeare can write and they can't.

And Kirsch is right in pointing out that Bloom and, say, the Marxist Terry Eagleton, actually agree with each other in detecting authoritarian sympathies in the plays, the only difference being that Eagleton condemns them while Bloom tries to explain them away, claiming that Shakespeare was really on the side of the rejected Falstaff rather than that of his former pal Henry V, "the mirror of all Christian kings."

What Kirsch doesn't say, though he goes on to demonstrate it, is that he sees these tendencies, too. He agrees with Eagleton, except that what Eagleton denounces Kirsch glorifies; at least, he wants gleefully to rub our noses in it which is, mutatis mutandis, a very Eagletonian position.

And I agree with all of them, but only up to a point. I think the matter is more complicated than any of them admit, though whether Shakespeare inserted the complications accidentally or on purpose I have no idea. Kirsch zeroes in on Henry V, but I think he underrates its complexity and overrates its importance among the complete works.

Henry V is explicitly a war-mongering, king-glorifying play. Shakespeare can often be opaque in his sympathies, but this time he leaves us in no doubt about what to think; in fact he brings on a narrator, the chorus, to tell us, half a dozen times. But this fact in itself should give us pause, because it's the only play in which Shakespeare does it. (Well, there's Pericles, but the chorus in that one is there only to guide us through a tangled picaresque tale.) It's as if he didn't trust himself to stay on the approved rails without subjecting himself to some kind of external restraint.

I have no doubt that Shakespeare, as a good Elizabethan citizen, believed in strong central government or that he got a kick from the idea of an outnumbered English army beating the hell out of the arrogant French; the play was written just 10 years after the defeat of the hulking Spanish Armada by a small, nimble English fleet, and the analogy must have been obvious.

But you can't make a whole play out of political correctness; it doesn't fill the space. I often think that Shakespeare was a more opportunist playwright than theme-hungry critics are inclined to admit; he writes each scene as intensely as possible, identifying with each character and each viewpoint as it comes up. So, as Kirsch says, Shakespeare is fully behind the Duke of Exeter as he threatens the French with extinction, managing to imply that it's their fault even though it's their country; and, no, he probably doesn't have much sympathy for the French when they bluster in reply.

But I think Shakespeare identifies with the French princess Katharine when she asks if it's possible that she should love the enemy of France, and with the Duke of Burgundy when he laments the devastation that has overtaken the land. That doesn't negate the patriotism. It's really the same divided message we're accustomed to in war movies: War is terrible but we want our side to win.

And there's more. Shakespeare famously kept Falstaff, with all his anti-heroic values, out of this episode of the history-cycle, though he had promised at the end of Henry IV Part Two to include him. (The entire Henry sequence is being presented at Stratford this year.) In this play, Falstaff's function is to die off-stage and be mourned in the most moving passage in the play. We know, and Shakespeare must have known, we have lost something. Falstaff's surviving friends tell us, uncontradicted, that "the king hath killed his heart" and they add, in what may be the best summary the play has ever had, that "the king is a good king, but." They then proceed to France, not exactly to subvert the glory, but to remind us that even a military band of brothers has its underside.

The king is a good king, the best in Shakespeare. (Well, look at the competition.) You can make a plausible case for the play as unadulterated hero-worship: Even Henry's toughest decisions redound to his credit and he ends up winning the war and getting the girl. But, seen from that angle, the play keeps including things it doesn't need. It's a big play (too big for its boots, perhaps) but I think it's fair to say that it doesn't show Shakespeare's imagination working at its whitest heat.

He was only half-way through his career when he wrote it. In the plays that follow -- the great tragedies -- the job of successful soldier-politicians like Henry is principally to tidy up the bodies. When generals take centre-stage, it's to disintegrate like Macbeth or be destroyed like Othello or die uncomprehending like Antony or Coriolanus. Lear, the only legitimate king among them, is brought to a ruined realization of the things he has neglected, among them the plight of the homeless. (The play uses that word.)

The heart of these plays is with the losers. And that's about as far from royalist triumphalism as you can get.

2001-02-13-one-man-five-mouthpieces:
VOICES

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, Toronto

Jeroen Willems is an amazing actor. He is Dutch, and he came to Toronto last week as the closing entry in the Six Stages festival in a solo performance.

With the exception of Paula and Karl, everything in this international mini-fest has been a one-person show and the standard has mostly been high. Also, blessedly, everything has been in English.

Willems has five voices in Voices -- five mouthpieces of international capitalism, gathered around a heavily laden dinner table in what seem to be the dying hours -- the liqueur, cigar and desultory dessert-eating hours --of a very fancy gathering.

Willems, who is both feline and forceful, passes from one chair to another, assuming a different voice and gait at each station. His physical grace in assuming and then maintaining each of these transformations is consummate. The vocal identities he bestows on each character are exact, his timing perfect, his inflections a joy, malicious and delicious. And he isn't even doing it in his native language.

Its possible his vocal virtuosity sometimes obscures the actual words he is saying, but I wouldnt lose sleep over it. The text, or most of it, is by Pier Paolo Pasolini, the late Italian film director, whose movies many of us for a few painful moments of the 1970s tried hard to persuade ourselves we liked.

It seems unlikely he meant the first four of this show's five monologues to function as parts of a play: They are separate character sketches, brought together here to illustrate the physical and intellectual structures that support multi-nationals.

There is a philosopher of sorts, distinguishing between those ordinary people who know they believe in nothing, and those equally ordinary people who believe in nothing without knowing it; there is a scientist; there is a manager. The attitude of each to the others is contempt, rising in intensity as we move around the board, though this is illustrated more in the staging than in the writing. At one climactic point, Willems gets to throw a drink in his own face, if you follow me; at another he gets to pinch his previous incarnation's helping of syllabub. (From where I was sitting, it looked like syllabub.)

What these characters say is often hard to follow intellectually; and even when it makes anecdotal sense, its hard to relate to anything else.

Pasolini, I suppose, is trying to condemn them out of their own mouths. But if mystification is what youre trying to attack, it hardly makes sense to add to it yourself, and it certainly isn't much fun to listen to. Also -- in a style I associate equally with 1960s Italian movies and 1970s English plays -- the piece seems to be presenting class warfare at the least interesting level. It's as if were being incited to revolution simply because the bosses eat richer food and have kinkier sex than the rest of us, but dont enjoy it very much. We're being asked to revolt against the privileged boredom of a mandarin elite, and it hardly seems worth the effort.

The last speech isn't by Pasolini at all, but by Cor Herkstroter, who gets program credit as "the chairman of the board of Shell International" and also -- in a fine display of barbed conscientiousness -- as co-author. (But is he getting royalties?)

So, for his last turn, Willems is impersonating Herkstroter, holding court among his sycophants and defending himself, and them, against the bad rap hung on them by the privileged mutterers of the West -- whose indignation at oil companies activities in the Third World has not, he notes, stopped them from driving their cars. He, too, of course, is meant to be condemning himself out of his own mouth. And if I read his speech in print, or heard him deliver it himself, I might well feel that he was.

But it doesnt work like that in the theatre. Herkstroter's ironies may be facile, but they are at least comprehensible, which gives them a distinct edge on Pasolini's. He transcends his intended role of devils advocate. And even if hes the real devil, he's preferable to the minor fiends around him.

The fact that his speech impales comfortable liberals (i.e. the audience) seems to have much impressed critics in Europe, comfortable liberals themselves, who seem to have found the show's format very novel and its viewpoint positively scathing. Essentially, though, its the same old, same old.

Except, of course, for Willemss performance, or rather performances. Starting out as the company's tame intellectual -- a daintily flapping logic chopper -- he moves through various degrees of camouflaged coarseness to arrive at Mr. Shell himself, whom he presents as unassuming but immovable, urgently courteous, suaver than suave. He strikingly resembles the smooth and fast gentleman salesman in the TV commercials for ING Direct.

His real set-piece, though, comes when he takes on the role of a lady diner, who conducts an intimate relationship with a pair of pantyhose and a high-heeled shoe that just happen to have been left lying about on the table among the brandy bottles. (It seems to have been quite a party.)

Willems gives a teasing performance of a tease, spinning out a detailed if obscure parable that does indeed concern diabolic temptation while the character's mind and body play out a separate drama of their own.

For a brief period, making louche use of a wig and a wine bottle, he is a man impersonating a woman impersonating a man: all the sexual levels you could want, with the added bonus of an assumed political significance ticking somewhere in the background.

The direction, by Johan Simons for Theatergroep Hollandia, matches the acting in world-class shimmer.

Black & White Photo: Ben Van Dunn, Six Stages Festival / JEREON WILLEMS IN VOICES: Feline and forceful characterizations. ;
2001-02-15-the-sheer-talent-here-is-deaf:
Until March 18. Box office: (416) 531-1827.

EARSHOT

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

There's an old critical theory, best expounded in Edmund Wilsons essay The Wound and the Bow, that holds that art is basically a hard- luck story. The creator has some kind of sickness, mental or physical, and exploits it. Its a romantic idea (or, more strictly, a Romantic idea), and these days we shy away from it. But it's a notion both exemplified and brilliantly vindicated in Earshot, a one- character play written and directed by Morris Panych. Randy Hughson performs the play, Ken MacDonald has designed it, and both their contributions are beyond praise, but everything stems from the author: The piece is a superbly mounted Panych attack.

Panych has apparently suffered all his life from over-acute hearing, an affliction he has bequeathed -- in, so to speak, amplified form -- to his protagonist, whose name is Doyle. (So says the program; I don't recall it being actually spoken.) A pain to Panych, the condition is a torment to Doyle. He lives in a spectacularly squalid one-room apartment, agonizingly aware of every audible detail in his neighbours lives -- and it seems that most details are audible if you concentrate. His complaint, he explains to some imaginary interlocutor, isnt deafness -- it's DEAFENING. The play's metaphor is similarly deafening in its obviousness, and quite magnificent in its effectiveness.

We like to think that the psychological barriers that separate each of us from everybody else are a curse; Doyle shows us that they are a blessing. He is forced to be super-sensitive to those around him and, even though he loathes most of them, he gets caught up in their lives to the extent that he hardly has one of his own. He rarely goes out. He was always, one suspects, a prey to inertia and he is now in its grip almost completely. He has no job, no friends, no prospects and only one ambition: to shoot himself. The plays title is double-edged, or rather double-barrelled.

Suicide is what he does, or wants to do, for love. Above him lives a paraplegic writer. Doyle recognizes the resentful rotation of the wheelchair and rejoices in the constant crinkle of rejection slips. Below lives a laid-off worker, whom Doyle judges, from the amount of time he spent on strike, to have been a longshoreman, and whose razor could dearly use a new blade. Offstage left is a senile woman calling for her dead husband and incessantly playing a 78 of, wouldnt you know it, Whispering. He hates the sound of all of them. But, offstage right lives Valerie, who works at a cosmetics counter and has a various but unfortunate love life and with whom Doyle is thoroughly and graphically obsessed. Tenderly, too: He rhapsodizes that there is nothing between them "except this wall" and that her skin is too delicate to be touched even by a sponge -- only the word sponge, the thing would not be soft enough.

She doesn't know he exists, so he is writing -- and mailing -- a suicide note to inform her. (He will, of course, be able to hear when she receives it.) We find him, at the start, composing this letter and excising the words "paradigm shift" with a shudder; shift reminds him of the only job he ever had (it lasted two nights) while "paradigm" sounds like 20 cents.

He is, in fact, quite a wit, and a cultured one -- incongruously so, in these surroundings. The wit falters somewhat in the middle sections of the play, but everything comes triumphantly together at the end, which presents a wonderful series of tragi-farcical reversals, culminating in Doyle's grudging performance of maybe the first charitable act of his life.

His living quarters are rendered by MacDonald (Panychs regular collaborator) in stunningly exaggerated perspective: life-size at the front of the stage and a virtual dolls house at the back. The furnishings are few and archaic; the phone is rotary, the portable record player might have adorned a teenage party of the 1950s. The bed -- wedged against the wall on the Valerie side of the room -- reveals naked mattresses whose foam seems about to break through some decidedly makeshift bonds; since the play has something of a Samuel Beckett form and flavour, it's tempting to christen these fragile fastenings Krapp's Last Duct Tape.

Doyle also has an endearing habit of fishing his used tea bags from the mug and throwing them at the shaving mirror, to which they stick; by the end there is quite an accumulation of them.

Unlike Beckett, Panych plays directly for our sympathy, but I find that honest. Certainly Hughson, a specialist in resilient derelicts, makes Doyle likeable, even in his eclectically crabby politics. ("I dont support welfare. I just collect it.") A giant on that foreshortened set, he plays the physical comedy to the limit (it seems possible that he may have to go through the whole play in his underpants, but propriety prevails) while vocally exploring the full range of the characters bemusement, anger and pain -- and his enjoyment of all of them. There is not a moment of dead air in his performance, and he has remarkable transformative powers; his face, pink and pouchy, sheds years when he harks back to his childhood and the memory of an operation that cured him of tinnitus and left him with something worse.

It's only February, and this, after Zadie's Shoes, is already Hughsons second virtuoso performance of the year; add in Slavs from last fall, and its his third of the season. At this rate, we won't need any other actors.

Panych's visual and verbal choreography of his own text is masterly. The visual, after The Overcoat and Hysteria, I would have expected; the verbal is an exhilarating surprise. The sound was designed by Derek Bruce, and it speaks, at appropriate volume, for itself.

A MIDSUMMER NIGHTS DREAM

Equity Showcase Theatre, Toronto

Good morrow, friends, says Duke Theseus in A Midsummer Nights Dream, when he comes upon the quartet of lovers sleeping in the wood near Athens: "Saint Valentine's is past." This line, surprisingly, failed to get a laugh on Wednesday night; maybe we were all too preoccupied with the filthy weather conditions through which we had struggled to get to Dufferin and Dundas to remember that it was still Feb. 14. We were also close enough to the end of the play to have begun worrying about the journey back. It seemed a dank, cheerless night on which to be seeing this of all plays.

It may, though, have been appropriate. According to Titania, the fairy queen, the weather in the Dream is awful, the seasons totally jumbled up, although she puts this down not to global warming but to the repercussions of her own domestic quarrel with her Oberon.

Certainly Chris Earle's production, this years joint venture by the professionals of Equity Showcase and the students of George Brown Theatre School, offers nothing green for our comfort. It is set on a flat disc of varnished wood, linked to the auditorium by wide steps of the same material. At either side of the stage is a stepladder; at the back of it is a murky grey curtain that turns out, when lit, to conceal Titanias bower.

Presumably, the hope is that this neutral setting will provide a launching pad from which the play can soar, fuelled by its own verbal and imaginative energy. That is to place rather too much trust in the powers of a mostly inexperienced cast, who can make the verse comprehensible but not transporting. But if the staging doesn't help them much, it doesn't hinder either, and the show is for the most part lively and intelligent. The Pyramus and Thisbe interlude is expectedly funny; so, less expectedly, is the long lovers quarrel. And at the close, when the fairies return by torchlight to bless Theseus house and its newly married inhabitants, there are some moments of authentic magic.

As usual, the production's most obtrusively original idea is its worst. Puck in the play's text goes also by the name of Robin Goodfellow, and maybe its this dual ID that has inspired the director to divide the role between two actors (actresses in this case) who are first seen kneeling and staring fixedly into one anothers eyes, and then proceed to split the character's lines between them. That those who talk to them still seem to think that they're addressing a single gentleman is only a minor irritant; its more damaging that we have lost one character without gaining two, since each partner now seems perversely to be acting less than half a role. It doesnt even help, as you might expect, in the scenes where Puck assumes multiple identities to mislead the mortals. And instead of talking to us, as Puck is required to do, they talk to one another, which is rude.

Of this right couple of Pucks, one (Melody A. Johnson) is a professional, and the other (Julie Tepperman) is a student. The licensed actors have in general been shrewdly distributed to bolster the learners. The most prominent card holder is Victor Ertmannis, who executes the now customary double of Oberon and Theseus. On this occasion, however, their respective spouses are played by separate actresses, so the merging of the two male rulers is as obscure in its purpose as the bisecting of Puck.

The professional Titania, Caroline Gillis, is very forthright and assured; the student Hippolyta, Janet Green, has few lines but demonstrates a talent for standing around looking thoughtfully beautiful, which is not a talent I would undervalue. Ertmannis himself plays a genially philistine Theseus, whose observations on the kindred qualities of the lunatic, the lover and the poet are as lucidly dismissive as Shakespeare must have meant them to be. His Oberon is much the same, but a touch more sinister. This actor seems unable to modify his native vocal quality, which is a ringing sneer; he even manages to make all things shall be peace sound like a threat.

The pro among the lovers is Graeme Somerville, who makes the amorphous Demetrius not only a person in his own right -- a rather prim, self-satisfied one who awakens to some kind of maturity -- but the anchor of his scenes: a double first, I should think. This has an excellent effect on his companions: Lysander (Brett Christopher) is less defined, but pleasant; Helena (Amber Lewis) blossoms delightfully when she has two men at her feet and a defeated rival at her elbow; and the thwarted Hermia (Jennifer Firestone) is a very effective spitfire.

Egeus, Hermia's heavy father, is played by Oliver Dennis, who almost makes the character interesting: not a first, but a rarity. His main employment, though, is to play Peter Quince, presiding over the Athenian Workers' Dramatic Society with charming concern and a script always at the ready. He commands a very youthful troupe. Even Bottom, the Dreams star role, is played by a student, Aaron Willis, who captures the serene assurance that is the heart of the character but doesnt have the resources to explore it fully. He too, though, makes a fine job of his awakening from enchantment (that is, he enchants us) and the Pyramus and Thisbe nuptial cabaret is, as aforesaid, a scream.

Every production seems to yield some treasurable new gag; my favourite this time was Starveling's silent challenge to Lysander (or was it Demetrius?) to put up his dukes when the courtier's heckling became intolerable.

As far as overall interpretation goes: Like every production of the Dream, this one has discovered sex. Whether Bottom actually has it off with Titania is left, as the play leaves it, undetermined. The scenes in which the lost lovers in the wood earnestly discuss who shall sleep with whom and at what distance are delightfully done. Theseus and Hippolyta begin the play with some heavy double- entendring about "the night of our solemnities" and Theseus' impatience for it; while the end rounds things off by having him, and others, knowingly underline every occurrence of the word "bed," which suggests somebody needs to grow up.

That, though, is not the play's last word: The immortals take over. And, what do you know, we emerged outside to find the skies clear and the road easy. Somehow, somewhere, a fairy couple must have shaken wings and made up.

WIT

Bluma Appel Theatre

Margaret Edson's play Wit arrives from the United States brandishing rave reviews and wearing every conceivable garland, including the Pulitzer Prize.

These facts, especially the last, are not automatically encouraging. The Pulitzer judges have a history of rewarding whatever ennobling drama is fashionable in a given year; and Wit, which is about a woman dying of cancer, seems all too obvious a candidate. Some years ago, they gave the prize to a piece of calculated uplift called The Shadow Box, which managed to be both cute and sentimental on the subject of cancer but could not bring itself to utter the word.

Wit, to its credit, has no difficulty saying it; and it is not, except towards the end and thus forgivably, sentimental. It is, however, cute; it begins with the central character appearing before us in a blue hospital gown and red baseball cap and asking briskly, How are you feeling today?"

This, she explains to us, is the standard hospital greeting, directed at a patient even when she is in the act of throwing up. She uses it to usher us into her own drama, of which she serves as both protagonist and mistress of ceremonies; and the convention involves repeated jokey intimacies that the audience laps up.

The heroine, Vivian Bearing, is a professor of English diagnosed at 50 with inoperable ovarian cancer and consigned to eight months of agonizing chemotherapy, at the end of which she dies. The play is performed on a generic hospital set and much of it charts Vivian's clinical progress, or lack of it.

It is, of course, moving, and the construction, which involves flashbacks to the patients past life, is remarkably deft and economic.

Indeed, for a first (and, by the authors avowal, only) play, Wit is extraordinarily accomplished; I'm tempted to use the word "slick. It doesn't have a single boring moment, and its Toronto presentation is ideal. I cannot imagine a tighter production than Glynis Leyshons or a more complete and affecting central performance than Seana McKennas.

All the same, I didn't much like it; and many of my doubts centre around the title. Much of the dialogue, and especially of Vivian's commentary, is witty in the conventional sense; the resident who has clinical charge of her turns out to be an ex-student of hers to whom she gave an A-minus; I wish," she murmurs ruefully, "Id given him an A, and the remark legitimately brings down the house.

But wit" here has a more specialized meaning, too: its the complex but light-hearted juxtaposition of words and ideas, set in dramatic conflict with one another, that distinguishes English metaphysical poetry, especially that of John Donne, whose Holy Sonnets are Vivian's academic specialty.

Everybody in the play goes on about these poems as if they were the hardest things in the language (actually, compared with, say, Emily Dickinson's, they are a breeze), and everyone, including Vivian herself, makes comparisons between Donnes unflagging intellectual rigour, the uncompromising demands Vivian made on her students and herself and the attitude of her doctors, who see her less as a person than as a research opportunity.

The case is rigged. Donne wrote erotic poems as well as religious ones, and the two categories overlap. Vivian can hardly have taught him without having come up against this, but we are meant to believe that her choice of subject reflects her own coldly ascetic nature; she has no friends, no lovers, no spouses -- no visitors. And though the fact is acknowledged it is never explored.

She also, it seems, has no interest in religion, though you can hardly approach Donne in purely secular terms. The poem "death be not proud is given a lot of attention, but even its peroration death thou shalt die" is not that baffling a paradox if you accept that its author, a clergyman, believed passionately in Christian resurrection.

One of the flashbacks shows us Vivians own university teacher returning an essay and telling her not to be sloppy, "This isn't Shakespeare. When Vivian is nearing death this teacher reappears (in what I devoutly hope is a dream sequence) to see her off with a line, not from Donne, but from Hamlet: Flights of angels sing thee to thy rest." There is subtlety in this progression, but the feelgood factor outweighs it.

Nor could I quite believe in a doctor (excellently played by Jim Mezon) who enters a room and briskly announces, "You have cancer, or in a nurse, the play's emblem of non-intellectual compassion, who doesn't know what soporific" means. In short, I don't think the play, clever though it is, justifies its own, to use the appropriate metaphysical term, conceit.

Alex Poch-Goldin, Joy Coghill and Kirsten Williamson give good acting support, and Ms. McKenna achieves a triumphant blend of technique and understanding. The role is written on one-and-a-half notes, which she never tries to soften or expand; she concentrates and distills, and the effect is spellbinding.

THE BEWITCHING OF MAX GUNTER

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, Toronto

Sky Gilbert is such an endearingly tireless self-publicist that it seems fair to review his new play with as much reference to what he has written about it as to what he has written in it. The Bewitching of Max Gunter has a subtitle tied to its tail: this AIDS play explodes ... Everybody duck.

"Everyone," says Gilbert in his press release, knows the typical AIDS play, and he goes on to list its constituent parts: the HIV- positive man awaiting death in his hospital bed, surrounded by relatives and friends. But, he asks, "what if HIV wasn't the cause of AIDS? ... What if men with AIDS werent guilty of anything? What if they werent victims? What if they were survivors & thrivers who got up from their hospital beds -- happy, promiscuous, & free of disease?" The answer, it seems to me, is that that would be very nice, even nicer than the moon being made of green cheese; and that the protagonist of such a drama, having arisen, would maybe do a little dance and then go home, as would the audience. It really wouldn't make much of a play. Oddly enough Gilbert seems to agree, because he hasn't written it.

In the first half he does seem to be sticking to his contract. We get Max, the bed-ridden hero, and his promised companions. Their encounters dont much resemble those in any AIDS play I remember seeing, but they do correspond to what might be called the platonic idea of an AIDS play -- an idea that most of us will gloomily recognize and that Gilbert has much fun lampooning. He isnt averse to a bit of gay stereotyping when it can help the show along, and his characters tend to be amusingly world-weary; Mark Christmann, playing Max, does this especially well.

Then there are the perfectly named Liz (Tracy Wright), Max's loyal woman friend, and a black hospital volunteer (Ryan Hinds) who puts his head cheerily round the door to ask how everybody is doing, and there are two other figures who require more detailed explanation. I'm not sure I can give it, but Ill try; the author- directors own published comments may help.

In the typical AIDS play, says Gilbert, there may or may not be a lover figure, the dreaded person who gave the homosexual AIDS. If such a character appears, the dying homosexual usually accuses his lover of killing him. That's news to me, but maybe I've been seeing the wrong plays. Anyway, Maxs lover, Thomas, does appear and is welcomed and doesnt get blamed for anything.

He does offer to perform oral sex on Max beneath the covers (Max declines) and then launches into a long speech about how Max should be out of bed eating plenty of vegetables and AIDS is just something invented by doctors and Max isn't sick at all. (In which case, we may wonder, why did he go to the doctors in the first place?)

Up till now, the actors have been reading from scripts, to demonstrate that this is just a play, for which the alleged dramatist takes no intellectual responsibility. When Thomas goes into his big number, however, he puts his book down, to show that he is speaking for his author. So it's unfortunate that Thomas, at least in Gil Garratts bright and shiny performance, seems more of a caricature than any of the supposed stick figures around him.

With one exception: Maxs monster-mother. To quote for the last time from Gilbert's typical-AIDS scenario: "[The patient's] parents come to visit, and though they are good-hearted people, they have prejudices, and find it hard to understand their sons disease"; he then adds, rather inconsistently, we know ... his parents are going to curse him. No we dont -- certainly not if they're the good- hearted people Gilbert has just claimed they are. Mother Gunter, however, (dad is dead) is not good-hearted and apparently never has been. She is selfish. and self-pitying. and does she ever have prejudices, and yes indeed she curses -- not so much her son as everyone else, especially everyone who isn't white. Her racism appears more rampant than her homophobia, though theyre clearly cut from the same cloth; in fact, her diatribes cause the black actor to leave the stage in protest. (Just what convention were meant to be in at this point is anybody's guess.)

Liz, trying to placate her, says, "Please calm down, Mrs. Gunter," or words to that effect, at which the old lady screams, Call me Goody Gunter! and the lights change and so does the parodic style (this must be the promised explosion), and suddenly we are watching a pastiche of The Crucible. Goody Gunter rolls around on what was once the hospital bed kicking her legs in the air and accusing people called Elizabeth and Mary and Tituba and Hecuba of having sent the Devil into her, and all we can tell for certain is that Ann Holloway, who plays her, seems to be having a good if exhausting time. (For some reason she never manages the Irish accent that her son says she has, and that he puts on when he's mimicking her.)

But it is possible to deduce that Mrs. Gunter is demonizing those she says have demonized her and that 17th-century persecutors of witches are being equated with modern haters of gays, not only in their intensity but in their effect. Homophobes have invented a disease and persuaded homosexuals to die of it.

As conspiracy theories go, it's remarkably simple and remarkably unpersuasive; it has too many deaths to account for. In a bizarre new twist on the old "my mother made me a homosexual" joke, we have "my mother made me a homosexual victim." Whether the theory extends to other AIDS fatalities -- to drug addicts or the children of drug addicts or to heterosexual victims, especially in Africa -- Gilbert doesn't say, inside the play or out.

Which is a shame, because though on this occasion he can neither think nor construct (his Ayn Rand play of last year, The Emotionalists, was far better) he still has a good ear; he writes very speakable dialogue, far better than that of some other, more highly rated playwrights. All he gives us here, though, are a few good jokes, a prolonged self-righteous scream and the opportunity to be out of the theatre within an hour, all posing as something daring and revolutionary. Sky, as they say, is the limit.

A FLEA IN HER EAR

Elgin Theatre, Toronto

I know what's expected of me, says the practised roue in A Flea in Her Ear, preparing to entertain yet another married woman in yet another hotel room, "but I dont know how to make it new." His plight is that of all the erotically propelled respectable citizens who inhabit classic farce, and part of the genius of Georges Feydeau, the Parisian master of the genre, is that at moments only the characters get to look into the abyss. Underneath the fin-de- siecle frocks and the ormolu gilt, its a bleak, mechanistic world.

It's also the plight of the director since, though the plays may have dark implications, those are not what make them work, and not why we keep going to them. Laszlo Marton, in charge of the Soulpepper revival of A Flea in Her Ear, is too intelligent a director not to know that what's expected of him is to make it funny; and he must know, too, that the best way to make it at least seem new is to make it socially and psychologically real. Unfortunately the methods he chooses contradict one another. The evening is an intermittently entertaining debacle.

People who try to summarize Feydeaus plots run the risk of ending, like the author, in a mental asylum, but here are the basics: Raymonde, the wife of insurance executive Victor Emmanuel Chandebise, finds her husbands marital performance flagging and suspects that he is squandering his resources elsewhere. So she has a friend write him a letter that will lure him to the notorious Hotel Coq d'Or (which she says in John Mortimer's probably free but indisputably excellent translation is not the Christian Science Reading Room) in hopes of an assignation. She will then burst in and surprise him. Unfortunately, everybody else she knows or is related to has a reason for arriving at the same hotel at the same time; unfortunately, too, the hotel porter is a dead ringer for her husband. Everyone collides; everything, with awe-inspiring infallibility, goes wrong.

Marton begins by parading the characters before us. All well and good: We are being shown a tight society inhabited by recognizable, not especially glamorous people who will be driven by lust, jealousy and the fear of discovery to behave like demented automata. A piano accompanies their promenade, and the pianist remains to underline, silent-movie fashion, every turn in the action -- every suspicion, every discovery, every flight and pursuit. While he plays, the actors freeze or move in rhythm. The plays central act, in the hotel, is essentially one long chase, which is here played out in an endless series of short, cute, stylized bursts.

Presumably the idea is that these moments will set off, or crystallize, the surrounding realism -- and it does not work. It destroys rhythm, it destroys narrative and it comes close to destroying the performances. The actors are troupers, and the script is a masterpiece, but there are only so many times that they can pick themselves up and carry on. There used to be signs hung in saloons that read: "Dont shoot the pianist, he's doing his best." I'm sure this one is, but hes killing the play stone-dead.

His accomplices, who made me feel equally murderous, are Andrew Massingham, who designed the movement, and William Schmuck, who designed the sets. The Hotel Schmuck is mainly composed of stairs, with the crucial bedroom shunted off to one side. The actors spend a lot of time executing debilitating steps on debilitating steps.

The social angle resides meanwhile in Diego Matamoross Victor Emmanuel, an uncompromising portrayal of a timid, prosperous Parisian bourgeois -- man as calculating machine. It is, at least to begin with, a fascinating, desiccated performance, but it lacks charm. This actor's dazzling series of performances over the last couple of years have all been as essentially cold characters. But to laugh at Chandebise -- or at any farcical hero -- we need to suffer with him, and Matamoros shuts us out.

And even if this might work for the insurance man, it doesn't for his double: Poche the porter, alcoholic and happily put-upon, should have an innocence about him that seems within the actors comprehension but beyond his scope. There is no joy in the quick changes of his double role -- a joy that was certainly there a few years ago when Bill Carr played the part at the Wolfville Theatre Festival in a production that had Soulpeppers licked at practically every point. (I have other memories, but to compare either show to the British National Theatre production of the '60s, which established the play in the English repertoire, would be unfair; it was maybe the funniest evening I've ever spent in the theatre.)

If the husband is disappointing, the wife is an outright disaster. Madame Chandebise should drive the play -- the jealous flea is in her ear -- and Liisa Repo-Martell has neither the right comic energy nor the right comic precision for the job. Nor, most crucially, does she have the air of outraged propriety that should make the character's prurience hilarious.

Cruelly enough, Colombe Demers as her confidante possesses all these qualities -- qualities that enable her to transform a theoretically dull role into the flashing centre of the production. She is matched only by Tony Nardi, who plays her Spanish spouse, a homicide named Homenides -- an unquenchable conflagration of jealous pride who takes his own obsession with sublime seriousness and thus makes it funny.

There are other good performances: from Tom McCamus as a Narcissus of the boudoir, from Ric Reid as the family doctor (another rescue job on a functional part) and from Stephen Ouimette in the poetically conceived role of a young man rendered incomprehensible by a cleft palate, though the actor could afford to be braver than he is, less afraid that we as well as the other characters will fail to understand him.

The middle reaches of the cast consist largely of actors of proven talent being strangely ineffective, but the lower orders include a delectable couple of maids (the kind everybody should have) from Melissa Moore and Patricia Fagan, and some dedicated acrobatics from Cliff Saunders as a perpetually priapic Prussian. These get applause, as does some virtuoso swinging from a chandelier, but such isolated moments are no substitute for a steady flow of laughter derived from character and situation; rather, they draw attention to its absence.

The production, amazingly from this director and this company, doesn't seem to trust the play. Its miscalculations, and their persistence through rehearsal, do however reinforce the Feydeau world view, which holds that human beings, having once launched themselves upon a collision course, will allow nothing to deflect them.

CLOUT

Factory Theatre

---

One of the two principal characters of David Young's new play is called Lionel K. Biggar. He is a press baron, and a vociferous apostle of material success who practices what he preaches; you might call him an apologist for the rich except that he never apologizes. The role is played, with great wit and presence, by R. H. Thomson, who starts the evening off by addressing his shareholders while looking like Lord Nelson. His enemies, he explains, have denounced him as a relic of the 18th century so he is humouring them and amusing himself by dressing up as one.

This opening routine is written, as well as played, with mischievous panache. It happens that the publisher of this newspaper, on whom L.K. Biggar seems to be closely modelled, has never appeared in naval uniform, past or present, at any office party that I've been invited to; but I was prepared to overlook this inconvenient fact and go with the flow.

Unfortunately, the author turns out to have his own misgivings; he reveals that Biggar's masquerade and vainglorious oration are things in somebody's dream: not his own dream, but that of one of Biggar's life-long opponents -- Trent, a left-wing journalist once fired by Biggar.

Trent, who comes before us bald and wearing the tattiest of hospital gowns, is dying of cancer, and the play is his fevered vision of Biggar behaving as he would like Biggar to behave -- except of course you can't control the way people and things turn out, not even, or perhaps least of all, in your dreams. But even with this mitigating subtlety, from the moment Trent declares himself, Clout loses its clout.

"Show me a good loser," says Biggar to the throng, "and I'll show you a loser." The play unhappily bears him out; it is the victim of its own chivalry. Politically it is on Trent's side; dramatically it is concerned not merely with giving the devil his due, which would be admirable, but also with stripping the wings off the angels, and it does this so remorselessly that it ends up as reverse agitprop, as devoid of real conflict as the conventional variety.

The two men find themselves chained together in a cellar, with diapers added to their former get-ups. Left and right, it is borne upon us as the characters thrash inseparably around the floor they need one another; it's an image, all right, but where do you go with it?

Plainly they have been kidnapped by some breed of terrorist; Biggar thinks it's an unscheduled installment of an ongoing toughening program that he has been inflicting on himself. Eventually their real captor appears: an implacable young female ecologist who loathes Biggar and despises Trent for having provided him with such feeble opposition.

After treating them both to some playful electric shocks, she gives Trent an assignment: torture the tycoon into seeing your point of view. We see Biggar pinioned to a slab of wall that has risen obligingly to the vertical for the purpose (what excitement there is in Richard Rose's production comes from the movement of the scenery) while Trent whips him.

But Biggar is contemptuous of Trent's ideas of cruelty, and certainly Trent's heart isn't in it; beating Biggar is his way of beating up on himself. The play, too, seems to be self- flagellating, desperately searching for some way of illustrating the personal inside the political. It comes up with the tiredest of devices. The two men, when young, loved the same girl. We flash back to the 1960s; Trent, a radical student editor, sends his girlfriend to discover the secrets of Biggar, the campus plutocrat. His scheme predictably misfires, and he becomes predictably jealous, while she becomes predictably pregnant. Trent behaves like a cad and Biggar, to Trent's great discomfort, like a gentleman. He can afford it, but still ...

So Biggar is better. That is what the script seems consistently, if surprisingly, to be saying; and the acting reinforces it. The writing does not permit Thomson to go on being funny but it does give him a shot at vulnerability, and he takes it very well, as he does the scorn and bluster that go with the territory.

Eric Peterson's performance of Trent, done on a single shrill and hectic note, makes a tiresome character even more so. Waneta Storms plays all the women, either because they're all faces of the eternal feminine (and the playwright does have the nerve to call one of them Eve) or because it's cheaper; she is woefully unconvincing as the tough terrorist, but very fine as the disputed decoy. There is one sequence in which she has to keep hurtling from one section of the past to another, and she keeps them beautifully distinct; she even blinks in character.

Trent gets the last speech, and it's an impressive one: tired, purged, presumably at the point of death, he speaks of opening up to some new truth "just beyond the scope of my thinking." Peterson kicks his tics and delivers it finely, as a serious balance to Biggar's comic overture. It might almost be the start of a play.

(From the National Post, Friday, March 9, 2001) A photo accompanying a theatre review of Gumboots in yesterday's paper was not, in fact, from the show. The review also carried an incorrect phone number for ordering tickets. The correct number is (416) 870-8000. The National Post regrets the error. 

GUMBOOTS

Pantages Theatre, Toronto

From the townships of South Africa comes the latest musical entertainment to wear its heart, and its title, on its feet. Gumboots are what were worn by black gold miners under apartheid to keep the water out. It came cheaper to the bosses than draining the mines. Since the workers were not allowed to speak to one another, they conversed by stomping their feet. And this, we learn largely from the program, was the origin of a dance style -- a physical equivalent of the blues, and equally adaptable. A group called the Rishile Gumboot Dancers of Soweto have refined, expanded and showbizified it, and their work is the foundation of this production.

Gumboots, then, is a celebratory show with elements of remembered protest -- you hardly get to be an international non-verbal hit any other way. (There is singing, plenty of it, but very little of it is in English.) It begins with half a dozen overalled and, of course, gumbooted men swarming on to the stage; four others will join them at various times during the evening, but this sextet remains at the centre of things. They begin the proceedings with an echoing hymn to Nelson Mandela; then they get down to business. The set is a scaffold resembling a mine-shaft; they take their places within it to mime the journey down. After rather lightly sketching in an essentially horrific existence, they break for an extended party sequence. Then they go back to work, more grimly this time. And they end, of course, with affirmation.

The physical vocabulary is initially compelling, but its the grammar that keeps us interested. The basic repertoire of foot stomping and leg slapping is extremely limited, but the rhythms that combine them are varied and sometimes exhilarating. (The director, Zenzi Mbuli, is both a choreographer and, though not in this show, a drummer.) The high-point, both visually and musically, is a train sequence whose prolonged percussive energy drives the audience happily crazy and sets them up for the restrained lamentation of the final section. This locomotive number is nearly as exciting as the best parts of Bring In Da Noise, Bring In Da Funk -- not quite, because the performers dont make the same individual connection with the audience.

Gumboots doesn't have the narrative and historical pretensions of Noise/Funk. It does, though, have a vein of self-patronizing cuteness the other show avoided. This is especially true, as you might expect, in the party scene. At one point, whether of its own volition or through commercial pressures, the show even flirts with the dread spectre of audience participation. Nobody actually gets dragged on stage, but a lady in the house gets congratulated on the whiteness of her teeth, as introduction to a song about it. (We also get asked to join in some singing, but it's not as if they lower a song sheet or get the sections of the house competing with one another. Besides, it doesn't happen till the curtain call, at which point anything rightfully goes.)

A guy sings a presumably self-mocking song called I'm Too Sexy, which seems to have put the camp into mining camp. Two more, imitating women, sashay and hip swing across the stage to the accompaniment of whistles (of the wolf variety), but are then wittily upstaged by another who simply walks. This celebratory sequence seems to make two points. One is human -- that people, even living in the direst circumstances, will still find means of having fun. The other is aesthetic -- a language born in sorrow will grow to encompass joy. Both are valid. But they are made at excessive length, to justify some rather commonplace fun and games.

The last sequence, though, is a real grabber, embracing a requiem for miners killed on the job and an ambiguous celebration that is also part lament, when the mine is finally closed. I like songs, and songs that join together to tell recognizable stories, so I am suspicious of dance revues passing themselves off as musicals. They seem to me part of the same homogenization of theatre that plunks popular musical movies on a stage and calls them shows; you appease the locals by giving them something they know and the tourists by dispensing with words. The SFX season at the Pantages is loaded with both; and Gumboots, already a hit in Edinburgh and London, has at the least been co-opted into the process. But its roots seem genuine, and the performing spirit is infectious.

Robert Cushman is the theatre critic for the National Post.

LILLIAN GISH: HER LEGEND, HER LIFE

By Charles Affron Scribner,

445 pp., $53.50

---

In 1944, Lillian Gish got fourth billing in an unmemorable movie called Miss Susie Slagle's. It was 20 years after her greatest triumphs and 40 before her death, but her name, says Charles Affron, "still meant something to moviegoers. Even if many of them would have been hard-pressed to say precisely why." His book, though it never manages to bring the actress to life as a woman, does explain why.

Just in chronological terms, her career was extraordinary. It began in 1902 when she was eight, with an appearance in Detroit as a threatened child in a touring melodrama that had begun its life in Toronto as The Little Red Schoolhouse but had been fitted out for the more raucous United States with the bodefully alluring title, In Convict's Stripes. She made her last appearance in 1987 in the film The Whales of August, co-starring with Bette Davis, who was younger but in far worse shape, and supported by Vincent Price and Mary Steenburgen. There could hardly be a more comprehensive rebuke to the accepted belief that child performers burn out early.

It is true, however, that she reached her peak young and her subsequent career was partly a refinement, partly an exploitation of what she had achieved then. She was the star and muse of Biograph Pictures, D. W. Griffith's silent movie repertory company: the eternal threatened maiden of the flickers raised to a higher power. Her acting life began when her alcoholic father walked out on her, her mother and her younger sister Dorothy. All three turned to the stage, and Lillian and Dorothy did well at it. They progressed from touring to New York, and from the stage to movies, which at that time were still based in the east; the exodus to Hollywood was only just beginning. They made their joint film debut in 1912, in An Unseen Enemy, and by the end of that year, Lillian had appeared in 13 pictures, of which Griffith had directed all but two.

She was the valiant child of a drunken daddy, so she took easily to melodrama, first on stage, then on film. She could identify with the stories and she internalized their firm, simple moral values. So did Griffith, and he added a messianic belief in the power of film that rubbed off on her -- to the point that, when talkies came along, she disparaged them as an adulteration of the pure art of the movies and especially of the pure art of acting. She may even have been right; certainly most of her contemporaries agreed with her.

Gish appeared in Griffith's most brilliant and most troubling movies. In the 1915 film The Birth of a Nation, with its stupefying glorification of the Ku Klux Klan, she was the flower of Southern womanhood, rescued from rape by a mulatto. In the epic Intolerance (1916), she is the spirit of time, eternally rocking a cradle: She is scarcely seen, but she is still the actress Griffith chose to hold the film's four plot-lines together. In Broken Blossoms (1919), she is allowed to die, whipped to death by a drunken father infuriated at his daughter for having taken refuge with a Chinese shopkeeper (billed as "the Yellow Man.") Dragged back, she hides in a closet, a terrified child, while her prizefighter parent batters on the door. Affron makes a persuasive case for this scene as one of the peaks of silent acting and an ironclad one for the picture itself as "the perfect introduction to the art of Lillian Gish."

The Sisters Gish were more of a double-act in life than on film: Dorothy, the sprightly disordered one, Lillian, the loving guardian, the self-conscious embodiment of American principle. Griffith seems to have driven her out of his company for her own good; he knew she had to be a star, but he had no place for any beside himself. She was never as big a name or as big an earner as Mary Pickford or Greta Garbo but she certainly stood for something. A lifelong Republican, she became a vocal supporter of the pre-Second World War America First Committee, taking stances ranging from the naive to the regrettable. But at least her isolationism was based on a genuine hatred of what she had seen in the previous war.

After the silents, she was, as Affron admits, famous for being famous. That's not to say her talking career was negligible. Returning to the stage, she triumphed in the very tricky passive- enchantress role of Yelena in the first major American premiere of Chekhov's Uncle Vanya. This book reminds us just how fecund and vital Broadway was in the '20s, '30s and '40s, and Gish was an important part of it. She still got roles in films too, including one near-masterpiece: Charles Laughton's terrifying The Night of the Hunter (1955), another film about hunted children -- a Griffith movie with its eyes open -- though by now Gish has graduated from victim to protectress.

She had always been adored by intellectuals who generally despised the movies; one of them, the vitriolic (and often insufferable) theatre critic George Jean Nathan, probably became her lover. One has to say "probably" because there seems no evidence that Gish, who never married, ever had a physical relationship with anyone. Nathan, though given a considerable build-up, fades out of the book, as he did from Gish's life; Affron never even tells us when he died.

Griffith, who does get an obituary notice, had also long been out of her life, though never, it seems, out of her thoughts. She never ceased to pay tribute to him as the greatest of all filmmakers, but on her reactions to his painful decline, (and on the details of that decline) the book is reticent.

Nor does it fulfill its announced aim of depicting an entire epoch in American culture. We register that Gish worked with many interesting people and had many famous friends; the names pile up, but few of them to much effect. The book is better on the legend than on the life, and best of all on the iconic early movies. Gish's own autobiography was subtitled The Movies, Mr. Griffith and Me, and though Affron manages to make us rethink the order of the billing, his own mixture remains essentially the same.
