2001-03-14-theatre-for-two-generations-t:
Undiscovered Country and After the Dance play in repertory at the Leonor & Alvin Segal Theatre (Saidye Bronfman Centre for the Arts) until March 25. Box office: (514) 739-7944

The Montreal Young Company, composed mainly of actors in their twenties, began operating last year with productions of Measure for Measure, Shakespeare's old parable play, and The Possibilities, Howard Barkers new one. These are plays in which raw actors can play ripe roles without the spectators minding too much; Shakespeare is protected by verbal style and chronological remoteness, and Barker never writes real people anyway. But the closer a play comes to contemporary naturalism, the more exacting our standards of belief are likely to be. This year, the young Montrealers have given themselves a tougher break.

Their chosen plays -- both rare and rewarding -- are Arthur Schnitzlers Undiscovered Country, from the Austrian 1910s, and Terence Rattigans After the Dance, from the English 1930s. These are plays with recognizable, if sometimes exotic, domestic set-ups. Their characters have homes to go to, including some that we actually get to visit. Both works, too, present delicate generational problems of casting and interpretation; they each concern the conflict between genuine youth and early middle ageing. So the audience has to make adjustments and allowances. But they are worth making -- these are two very stimulating evenings.

Schnitzler is a superb playwright of whom we still know far too little (though Toronto, at least, is about to get a basinful of him with two separate adaptations of his once-notorious La Ronde). Writing appropriately from Vienna, the cradle of 20th-century angst, he chronicled the sexual and social caprices and self-delusions of a war-doomed epoch.

Undiscovered Country, adapted by Tom Stoppard, though not that you would notice (apart from the occasional line like one about a man who wouldn't be caught dead with a suicide note), concerns a prosperous light-bulb manufacturer and serial philanderer named Heinrich Hofreiter. After ploughing more or less contentedly through his friends wives, he comes up against a much younger woman who makes demands on him that he cannot meet, though part of him would like to, and that circumstances finally allow him to evade.

He has a similarly ambiguous attitude toward his own wife. He loves her, and would like her to be happy; and if that would mean her taking a lover, he would be easy. That, at least, is what he thinks. When it actually happens, he is outraged, not so much out of jealousy as resentment. The lover, too, is guilty of the unpardonable sin of being young, and Hofreiter has had quite enough of youth.

Herr Hofreiter is not perhaps an admirable man, but he has the virtue of being clear-sighted: He can see through everybody, including, uncomfortably, himself. In this he resembles Chekhovs Platonov, another helplessly rakish hero whom we have recently got to know and to recognize as still one of our own. Indeed it's something of a shock that Hofreiter, unlike Platonov, finishes his play alive. But then Schnitzler's play was written a few decades later and a few thousand miles west of Chekhovs, and is by so much the more cynical.

If there is meant to be something heroic in Hofreiter, Shawn Campbell, the actor here, has not found it; he is rather snaky and oily. From the moment he comes on, though, he strikes a note of commanding intelligence that sets him apart from those around him, and he maintains it, barring a few lapses, throughout the play. By the end, he has imposed himself on his own terms. Amy Price- Francis, too, grows steadily as his wife, gracious and troubled, especially when she comes to measure out, with perfect candour, the depths of her erotic surrender. Both rise finely to the last act, in which the play does reach Chekhovian heights.

Hofreiter, returning from a duel, encounters his dead opponents unknowing mother (Kate Hemblen, also admirable) in the presence of his own wife. Schnitzler is a master of irony, and this scene is the tragic-comic variety made flesh. Stoppard made a cunning choice of English title. The undiscovered country," according to the Montreal program, signifies human behaviour. But when Hamlet coined the phrase he was talking about death, and that is as much on these characters' minds as love is. In fact, they go together.

There is plenty of encircling social comedy as well, especially in the middle act, which finds most of the characters holidaying in the Alps. Here, Hofreiter meets a hotelier (Robin Wilcock, excellently iced) whose heartless skill in personal relations leaves our Heinrich looking and feeling like an amateur. Other attractions hereabouts include a frazzle-haired mother-ridden poet (Eric Davis) and an explosively indignant guest (Shawn Riedle) whose anti- establishment tirades when his laundry goes missing prophetically approach Hitlerian intensity. There are also other characters whom one simply gets mixed up. Here we really miss the weight and experience that can create an identity simply by coming onstage. Even those playing their own young age come short of the essential worldliness.

Abundant doubling, though unavoidable, compounds the problem; and Bill Glassco's shoestring production does not provide much atmospheric support. His spare approach worked better in last years Measure (also, oddly enough, a sex comedy set in Vienna) than it does here.

In this regard Chris Abrahams production of the Rattigan has a distinct advantage. For one thing, it only requires one set, a Mayfair flat, which the designer, Vincent Lefevre, has managed with what seems in this context like stunning opulence. One scene is given over to a party that Abraham, also known hitherto as a distinctly puritanical director, has staged with remarkable mordant verve; it's the kind of thing you expect to see at the Shaw Festival (which should be noting his name). Then too, though Rattigan can hardly match Schnitzler for satiric intensity or philosophic breadth, he does have the edge as a story-teller. His play proceeds in a straight line, while Schnitzler's keeps moving into eddies and piling up parallels. With Schnitzler you would quite like to know what happens next. With Rattigan you cant wait to find out.

After the Dance was Rattigans second produced play, and his first -- almost his only -- commercial flop. He virtually disowned it, and it has only recently been reinstated. In fact it might be billed as Rediscovered Country, and it pairs excellently with the Schnitzler.

Rattigan gives us a society on the brink of the next war: the left-over bright young things of the 1920s versus the tough new generation who can see what's coming to them. It's like the continuing war between the Baby Boomers still stuck in the 60s and their younger successors who cant see what all the fuss is about. The differences are that a) in this play it's the younger ones who are in the majority and b) Rattigan's nostalgists make no pretense of being idealists. What they preach, and continue to practise is hedonism. This is a play about people who, when they drank, drank.

Presiding lush is Peter Scott-Fowler, who is rich and a historian, as far as hes anything. Like Hofreiter, he is amiably unfaithful to a wife who minds a lot more than she lets on. Like Hofreiter, he encounters a young woman who wants to reform him; the difference is that this one looks like succeeding. She gets him on the wagon; she gets him divorcing his wife; she damn near gets him writing that book hes supposed to have in him. It is, needless to say, a strain, and we wait to see whether she will succeed, our suspense diversified by our never quite knowing whether or not we want her to.

This, apart from narrative flair, is the play's great strength: It divides its sympathies very fairly. The intrusive Helen is both a pain and a paragon, and Michelle Monteith (who in the other play is overstretched in a middle-aged role) does full justice to both her aspects. So, conversely, does Robin Wilcock, who last year made a fine job of Shakespeare's lapsed puritan Angelo; he does equally well as Rattigans lapsed hedonist, for whom he finds the right quizzical weight to compel both our amusement and our sympathy -- even our respect. Kate Hemblen plays his wife, who doesnt take the pledge; and though the Mayfair drawl doesn't seem to sit on her lips with absolute naturalness, she moves easily within it, from drunk and happy to drunk and desperate. If she sometimes seems to be trying too hard, then so, it turns out, is the character.

The inner circle is completed by Joe Cobden, a new actor of remarkable ease and insistent promise, who contributes a delightful boyish cameo to the Schnitzler and here ripens, beautifully and almost effortlessly, into a permanent, and permanently sozzled, house guest. He is the play's commentator, and his commentary is, as he admits, outrageously self-interested. It is also, most of the time, absolutely accurate.

The others fit in with varying degrees of accuracy, but the frame sustains them. The protagonist has a habit of siting down at the piano and playing Noel Cowards World Weary, thereby acknowledging both a mood and a generational allegiance; his contemporaries are Cowards little ladies still dancing, his poor little rich girls with all their stitches dropped but still locked into their mad jazz pattern. Rattigan disapproves but he does not condemn, and he proves them still worthy of attention. The play probes less deeply into human nature than its Viennese companion, and moralizes more, but it is both honest and attractive.

Matching new talents to old plays, the Montreal Young Company is in some ways a paradoxical enterprise but it delivers a lot of what it promises, and its importance to the Canadian theatre, in terms of both actors and repertoire, extends beyond its home city.

AN ACRE OF TIME

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

The best thing about An Acre of Time is its stage. The Tarragon mainspace has been re-ordered so that the audience sits on three sides of a long rectangular platform; in such a small theatre, the feeling of the spectators surrounding the action can be very powerful. There seem to be two reasons for the arrangement. One is that it makes a nice change. The other is that it can give us the sensation of peering down into the inner workings of a society, this being what Jason Sherman's play is meant to be about.

At least that is half of what it is about. The remaining half concerns one woman and her personal problems. And though the author keeps trying to persuade us that each is a reflection of the other, the attempt is not convincing. We have two plays tied together with a fraying piece of string -- and they keep tripping one another up.

An Acre of Time is "inspired by" Phil Jenkins' book, which I have not read but which I gather is an impressionistic survey of the history of LeBreton Flats, a dilapidated piece of land by the Ottawa River. It was inhabited by the First Nations, appropriated by the French and English, run down and finally abandoned by everyone. According to its admirers, Jenkins' book is written in "poetic prose," but even with that liability it seems possible that the material it presents might have been fashioned into a workable semi- documentary theatre piece. Similar things have happened.

Sherman's play introduces a fictitious central character -- Julia Wright, a surveyor sent out by the National Capital Commission to help assess the Flats' potential for redevelopment. She has a personal connection to the region: Her young daughter drowned in the Ottawa River while on a camping trip with her father. (The couple have now, inevitably, split up.) This being the case, it seems unlikely that Julia would have accepted the assignment, but she seems to want to exorcise -- or maybe just exercise -- her memories.

She turns in what her superiors feel to be an unsatisfactory report, and the play shows her justifying it in flashback to a review board made up of the other members of the cast. The actors, an alert-enough bunch in the other roles they play during the evening, seem uncomfortable with this device. And so, apparently, does the author, since he has dropped it by the end of the show. Since this is hardly fourth-wall realism, he surely could have had Julia just talk to us; it might conceivably have given her a firmer position at the play's centre.

Julia spends some of her time fending off the advances of her boss, who has suffered his own bereavement, and of a boorish city planner, while succumbing to those of a young native filmmaker. (Like her, he is scouting locations.) She also has visions -- visions of figures associated with the area's past. She meets Samuel de Champlain and an 18th-century German practitioner of her own trade, as well as the entrepreneurial LeBreton for whom the flats were named. The tone of these encounters grows increasingly farcical. LeBreton, genial and accident-prone, sounds Cockney, but his six "nieces" (there seems some doubt about their true status) are done in as many different varieties of the English middle class, which at least gives the actress playing them a chance to show off.

We then get a play-within-the-play-within-the play, as one niece leads Julia inside a theatre where revue-like vignettes from the region's history are presented. The style resembles that of VideoCabaret's comic-strip chronicles, only not as expert and not as instructive. The cross-talking Jewish traders swapping gags about pogroms are probably unfunny on purpose, but that isn't much consolation while you're watching them. Brian Quirt's production is physically well manoeuvred, but if there is a comic tone here, he hasn't found it.

The play also keeps re-enacting Julia's last fateful conversation with her husband and child, without ever telling us any more than it did the first time -- as if reiteration in itself would move us. She also begins marking out an acre of ground with an old native measuring pole, to the bemusement of her Indian lover, who expected something more high-tech. ("Cutbacks?" he inquires. There are some good lines, and most of them are his.)

What she is doing, it transpires, is marking out an area for her own memory. That is a really forced metaphor, and it leads to an equally forced confrontation. Julia turns on the planner, who apparently is contemptible by definition, and tells him that whatever monstrosities he erects, he should leave an acre free to honour the past. She seems to be equating her own past with that of the territory, maybe of the country, and the equation does not hold.

Nor indeed do either of its constituent parts. We have learned very little about LeBreton Flats (nothing at all about its ordinary inhabitants) and not much about Julia. She keeps talking about her loss, but that doesn't mean that it has been dramatized. It is perhaps unfortunate for An Acre of Time that it arrives in Toronto after we have seen two productions of The Weir, which narrated the death of a child to far more devastating effect and managed to depict a society as well.

Pierre Brault, Timothy Hill and Kristen van Ginhoven do best among the supports. As Julia, Susan Coyne goes through the play looking and sounding glum, only flaring into life when she gets her tirade at the end. Even this, though, has only a momentary impact. It's as if the playwright were flogging himself into making some kind of statement. The play seems the theatrical equivalent of CanLit: aggressively good for you and very dispiriting.

ONE NIGHT STAND

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

The words Canadian classic inspire more dread than any others in the murky world of theatrical hype. The history books tell us that in the 1970s there was a golden age -- not just a renaissance, but a whole new world -- of indigenous playwriting. It must have been great fun if you were there at the time. Now, however, as revival follows revival, it looks like a bad joke.

The latest evidence is a restaging of One Night Stand, a great success in 1977 for Carol Bolt, who, sadly, died last year. She had updated it somewhat but, sentiment apart, it now seems a senseless piece, one that in teasing out a single situation manages to make 90 minutes of playing time seem like eternity.

The situation itself is basic but promising. Daisy, who is fairly young, and Rafe, who is younger, go separately to a club and pick one another up. Who actually made the first move remains a matter of debate, which is lifelike enough, but anyway they end up going back to her place: a high-rise apartment at Yonge and Eglinton.

Daisy is in a reckless mood. It's her birthday, but her married boyfriend has excused himself from the celebration, as have her best girlfriend and her boyfriend. Rafe is a twinkling stud of indeterminate background; sometimes he seems to be Latin, sometimes not. He also carries a tape-recorder around with him, maybe because he is a musician, maybe not. He has any number of stories. If consummation is delayed its not because Daisy is coy but because Rafe is, or maybe just because he never stops talking. Daisys frustration begins to communicate itself to the audience.

"I hate surprises," says Daisy, who works in a bank. "That's your problem," says Rafe, and it's not just a snappy comeback; its a diagnosis. At this point we seem to be in familiar dramatic territory: Rafe is the free spirit come to liberate Daisy from her respectable rut. If this were the 1960s, the inhibited partner would be the man, and he would have his life changed by some male playwrights fantasy in the form of an adorable, kooky nymph. More recently, genders have been reversed, and counter-cultural Galahads have taken to rescuing damsels who claimed to be quite happy in their distress but were wrong.

Rafe's behaviour, however, goes beyond the limits of endearing non-conformity into actual craziness. These are some of the things he does: He grabs Daisy's phone and is rude to her friends. He climbs out over the balcony into the apartment next door and returns wearing a scary animal-mask; he does this twice, managing on the second occasion to frighten the life out of Daisy, who by now is feeling understandably vulnerable. He calls an airline and books a flight to Peru on her credit card. Like many crazy people, Rafe cannot be argued with; he always has another answer. So far, so clinically accurate. But its as wearing in the theatre as it would be in real life, and every bit as tedious.

Rafe also blithely mentions having done time in jail for killing a woman. At this point it becomes really incomprehensible that Daisy, who may be horny and discontented but is not suicidal, doesnt throw him out: if not for her own sake then for ours. Alternatively, she might call the cops. As a matter of fact she does and, after a surprisingly long delay, they come to the door. (They seem to be Toronto's slowest.) She, however, manages to have them sent away by getting on the blower and doing some fast-talking to police HQ, who are remarkably understanding about it. (They also seem to be Toronto's dumbest.) If you think that sounds implausible, you should see what happens later.

Here we enter the territory of that which should not be revealed; but I can disclose that the plays denouement depends on Daisy having spent an unconscionable time in the shower with the water at full pressure and plugs in her ears. That at least is the only way I can explain her ignorance of the crucial events going on outside her bathroom door, which must have taken some time and made a considerable noise. There is a grim surprise ending that seems intended to prove something or to be the logical result of something else.

The only apparent reason for reviving stuff like this, apart from title-recognition value, is that it provides showy roles for a couple of actors. Making the characters credible is a harder thing, and giving them enough variety to fill out an evening may be impossible. At all events, it doesnt happen here. Stephanie Jones at least makes Daisy believably ravenous; a tall lady who has gone to the ball in a boldly striped top, she has a strikingly zoological look about her. She's a giraffe in zebra's clothing. Jason Cadieux's unrelenting winsomeness as Rafe is probably built into the role.

In one respect, seeing the hits of 25 years ago is cheering. Things have improved, even if they're still terrible.

CLOSER

Berkeley Street Theatre

---

At the first night of Closer, Patrick Marber's hit play from London, I caught sight of my old friend, Phyllis Stein, whom I had last encountered a year ago at this very same theatre refusing to be shocked by George Walker's Heaven.

Closer offers the same kind of come-on: warnings in the lobby about sexual content and explicit language, with smoking and strobe- lights thrown in for good measure, so I couldn't resist phoning Phyllis the next morning and asking her how she had got on this time.

"Well," she said with the hint of a girlish giggle, rather charming from a woman in her forties, "I wasn't shocked this time either. I must be a hopeless case. I know people in London got up in the stalls and protested -- you see I do read your paper -- but I think it's really the language they objected to. They couldn't see past that."

"You objected yourself," I reminded her, "to every other word in Heaven being 'f---.'"

"Heaven," she said judicially, "wasn't basically about sex. Closer is. If you're shocked by that, you're shocked. But the language is appropriate. And it's very specific."

"You can say that again," I said, knowing she was far too sophisticated to waste my time by doing so. "It's like a modern British La Ronde, isn't it, though with only four characters. Instead of a daisy chain, it's an eternal quadrilateral. They keep pairing and re-pairing strictly heterosexually and there seems no good reason why they shouldn't go on forever.

"The only thing is," I admitted, "I can't quite remember now who did what with whom and in what order."

"Oh!" she exclaimed "Men! The morning after, they never know a thing. All right, pay attention. Alice, she's a stripper, of no fixed abode, who picks up Dan -- remember, he's the obituary writer who wants to be a novelist. And they move in together, and Dan gets his book written, and when he's getting his picture taken for the jacket he makes a pass at Anna, the photographer, who rejects him. Then Dan accidentally sets Anna up with Larry, a dermatologist, right? And Anna and Larry actually get married. But Anna leaves Larry for Dan, though she says she still loves Larry. And Larry, who is devastated, takes up with Alice, but eventually Dan goes back to Alice again, but his jealousy destroys them and ... well, I don't have to remind you how it ends, do I?"

"No," I said hurriedly "please don't. But you're good. That was quite a synopsis. You should do this for a living."

"Well," she replied with surprising frostiness. "I don't. You do. So, tell me: Is it a good play?"

The things people ask you. "Yes," I said, very slowly, "I think it is. But it's limited."

"Explain."

That was easier. "You only see the characters at their crisis points. And since they are never together long enough for passion to subside, those crises are explicitly sexual. There must be more to them, to the people and the relationships and indeed Marber, who's more of a softie than people believe. But he hasn't put it on stage. What there is, is compelling. It's a kind of beneath-the-surface brutality you don't often see exposed."

"I'll say. You talked about who did what with whom. It's more a matter of to whom. And the ones doing are mainly the men."

"Oh dear, I thought that too, and I was hoping it was just male guilt. Alice is a real victim, isn't she? She doesn't act or talk like one, but she's -- what's the jargon -- objectified. There's her job, and Dan writes about her, and Anna takes pictures of her. The girl who played her in London was a real waif-type. Angela Vint, who does her here, is chunkier and saltier, which is sort of interesting but makes her seem less central."

"I knew you'd start mentioning the London production."

"Well, I did see it. What I mostly remember is Sally Dexter as Anna. She was very contained and completely sexual without ever trying to be sexy. The Toronto Anna, Gina Wilkinson, is aggressively bright, even when she's in pain; it's like every line is supposed to be an epigram. One problem in Dennis Garnhum's production is that nearly everyone is acting the accent rather than the character. Blair Williams as the doctor is an exception, but even he misses some transitions that ought to be there. Shaun Smyth as Dan I just didn't believe. He's a nerd in his first scene and a sharpie thereafter. Shows what the love of a good woman and a publishing contract will do."

"Perhaps they should have done it without accents."

"I thought of that; there's nothing here that couldn't happen in Toronto. But it's written in these English rhythms, and they impose themselves. When they do a Canadian play in London, not that they often do, or an American one, you expect them to do the accents. What happens here is that a very common problem gets exaggerated. Neutral lines get artificially coloured, usually with anger or self- pity. I know people think I have other obsessions, but that's the one I find myself going on about. That kind of acting isn't truthful and it punches holes in the play.

"But I liked the physical production. The play is set in rooms from an emergency ward to a strip club, which are done in modules; and for the last scene, in a graveyard, the whole stage opens up, right to the theatre's own brick walls. Peter Hartwell is the designer; it's brilliant.

"And now Phyllis, you have to tell me, what did you think of the famous cybersex scene?"

"Two men sending one another erotic messages, one of them pretending to be a woman? I thought it was a turn-on, like the scene in the club. And I loved the flushed eagerness on Blair Williams' face, and the irritation when he got a call from a patient: very funny. And you?"

"I found those scenes intriguing, but not arousing. The computer is actually a breakthrough: innovative and dramatically telling. But the sexiest scene for me was the first, the pick-up. All right, it's a male fantasy. But the detail is real; it's the most relaxed writing in the play. And how about the scene where Anna tells Larry, in great anatomical detail, what she and Dan did in bed, or on the couch?"

Phyllis paused. "I'm on my second marriage. And the first one ended badly; my ex was very jealous. I think he wanted to ask me those things, and if he had, I would have told him. As explicitly as Anna does. In those words. And with that grief and that anger. The play is about sex used as power -- verbally, hence the computer- scene, and physically. There's nothing new about it; we just have additional technology. A scene like that lays bare what all plays involving love or sex, which is nearly all plays, are really about but never say.

"Yes, it is shocking, in a good way. More than any nude scene. There should probably be an additional warning: No Nudity in This Play."

I was impressed.

"I think," I said, "I shall use that."

HOSANNA

Tallulah's Cabaret, Buddies in Bad Times, Toronto

----

TORONTO - Hosanna, the ageing drag queen with a fixation on Elizabeth Taylor, and Cuirette, his leather-clad roommate and bedmate, have returned to the Toronto stage sporting very broad, or "verra braid," Scots accents. I was initially convinced the action of Michel Tremblay's 1973 Quebec play had moved with them, to Glasgow; and it was a surprise, when they started dropping place names, to realize the action is still supposed to be going on in Montreal.

In Scotland itself, which reasonably enough is where this translation by Martin Bowman and Bill Findlay was first presented, the convention would have been transparent; when everybody talks like that, the brogue can belong to any time and any place. The language does restore to the play some of the salt that it presumably has in the original French; for us, though, it also sets up some quite specific expectations, and I can't see that the play would be harmed in any way if those expectations were indulged.

The characters would make very believable Glaswegians. As things are, you find yourself wondering how these two guys, who the dialogue tells us went right through the Montreal school system, managed to retain unaltered the speech patterns of their parents, and by what fluky coincidence they have ended up together.

Tremblay's play, which stands up better than most of its period, shows each of the two reaching self-realization through self- humiliation. Hosanna finds himself the victim of a cruel joke when he goes to a ball dressed as Taylor's Cleopatra; as he tells us in a long monologue, "everybody was dressed like her -- only better." What was meant to be a personal peak turns into Armageddon.

Cuirette, meanwhile, who has been maintaining that he is not really gay and that he is in fact a great womanizer, is similarly jolted into giving up his fantasy. "You are a man," he tells Hosanna as the latter climbs into bed with him minus the Hollywood-Egyptian lingerie, also meaning, of course, "I love a man."

In a way it's a puritanical rebuke, ten years ahead of time, to La Cage aux Folles (musical version), where the transvestite's anthem, "I am what I am," really translated into, "I am what I'm not." Either way, this kind of affirmation always comes across as sentimental, though doing it without music certainly makes it more palatable, as well as more economic.

Tremblay, despite the play's tough veneer, is certainly not averse to the odd tear-jerking platitude. When Cuirette leaves the house after a quarrel (the two spend the entire first act metaphorically at one another's throats) he stops in the doorway to remark, "You want to know something really stupid ..." There is the predictable pregnant pause, and then the equally predictable punchline: "I love you." The audience could probably say it for him.

A two-person play that is half bitchy recrimination and half tearful confession needs virtuoso performance. What it gets here, from a company optimistically designated Shockalot Productions, is decent to disappointing; Both actors look right and sound variable.

Director Wendy Thatcher (who, as an actress, is a mainstay of the Shaw Festival) staged the play in London with an actual Scottish actor, Alistair Hudson, in the title role. He plays it for her again now, and is absolutely fine in the give-and-take of the first half; haughtily funny with poignancy peeping through. This does not ripen, however, into the magnetic desperation that would be needed to carry us through the long monologue. Here he is perfectly sensitive, perfectly intelligent, but no more.

Cuirette is played by a local actor, Tony Nappo, who manages the accent perfectly but doesn't seem to have enough energy left over for the rest of the role, so the concept begins to seem self- defeating. To put it another way, he's often inaudible, though to be fair, the acoustics of Buddies in Bad Times' cabaret space don't help any. (The sightlines are nothing to write home about, either.) David Wootton's set is a colourful assemblage of bric-a-brac.

Theatrical legend holds that Hosanna's divided identity in some way mirrors that of Quebec itself. This is to pile ludicrous weight on a small but effective domestic drama. It also suggests that 30 years ago, people were so hungry for political theatre that they would swallow almost anything in its name.

ANNIE

Pantages Theatre, Toronto

The Great Depression is at its grimmest, and you are a little girl immured in an orphanage of semi-Dickensian oppressiveness, and the wealthiest and most influential man in America announces that he wants to adopt you. You are a sensible child; you hang in there.

Annie, the musical, has been hanging in since its premiere in 1977; and of course the comic strip from which it derives has been doing it for decades longer. The show worked 24 years ago, and it works now, infallibly. The recipe is simple: barefaced sentimentality accentuated by rampant cuteness but disinfected by humour, and with the mildest dash of social comment. It knows exactly how to moisten our eyes while sparing our blushes.

The best-known song in the score, though not the best, is the heroines incurably optimistic anthem, Tomorrow. When she first sings it, an outcast on the streets, its just one of those damnably effective Broadway things. In the second act she reprises it, in the White House, at a meeting of the Roosevelt cabinet. FDR is inspired by it and insists his advisors stand up and join in, even takes a chorus himself. By the end of the scene he has invented the New Deal. Of course we're not really asked to believe that an indomitable 10-year-old redhead was responsible for the salvation of America. But then again, perhaps we are.

Thomas Meehan's book is something of a masterpiece in the genre of having it both ways. Daddy Warbucks, Little Orphan Annies imposingly hairless saviour (shiny pate to her carrot top), tells her that his riches havent brought him love or happiness, though he cannot forbear boasting that he was still young when he made his first billion and in those days that was a lot of money." His mansion, full of fanatically loyal retainers genuflecting in rhythm, is both parodied and celebrated. So, at the other end of the scale, is the orphanage from which Annie escapes, administered by a heavy- drinking man-chasing harridan who forces her charges to chant "we love you, Miss Hannigan, and who has the disposition of a full- blown tyrant but not the efficiency. The script is not long on plot, but it does manage to throw in a certain amount of suspense centring on a dastardly plot by Miss Hannigan's jailbird brother and his floozie to pose as Annie's parents and capture a promised reward. They are, needless to say, foiled by Mr. Warbucks; when you can call in the president and the FBI all things are possible.

The book is better than the music. Charles Strouse wrote some of the best scores of the 60s, but Annie isnt on their level. Perhaps the most striking thing is the way in which it gets consistently worse as it goes on. It starts with Maybe, Annie's beautifully wistful dream of her lost parents; then comes It's the Hard-Knock Life, a spirited complaint for the massed orphans, and then Tomorrow. Next is Wed Like to Thank You, a mildly vitriolic chorale aimed by the New York homeless at the departing back of ex- President Hoover.

After that its downhill all the way, the decline only interrupted by You're Never Fully Dressed Without a Smile, a pastiche cheer-up song introduced as part of a wonderfully syrupy radio show, involving a smiley host, a limp-harmony girl trio, a ventriloquist and radio's only masked announcer." There are two back-to-back songs, NYC and Easy Street, that try embarrassingly hard to be show-stoppers, rousing and comic respectively, and are somewhat helped by their staging, but only somewhat. The last section of the show dissolves into a set of indistinguishable celebratory numbers, including a title song that seems to be promoting Annie as a mini-Mame or maybe -- when she comes down the staircase in her trademark red dress -- a baby Dolly.

Martin Charnins lyrics follow the same downward trajectory except that they arent as good to begin with. However, on this show Charnin wears two, or maybe two-and-a-half, hats. His was the idea for the show and he was its original, and very smart, director. He has also staged this touring revival, which is reduced in scale (I certainly missed David Mitchell's original spacious sets) but still spiffy.

Peter Gennaro's choreography remains expert fun, especially in the orphanage. Annies left-behind friends seem remarkably good- natured, expressing no jealousy whatever at her good fortune; they are also troupers. They are a riot in themselves, and riotously deployed, especially one called Molly (Danielle Freid), who is about five inches tall.

"Your days are numbered, says Miss Hannigan when she comes upon this tot being particularly rambunctious. She also swoops in after a production number yelling Do I hear happiness in here?" and, in a rare moment of philosophical calm, mutters, "Why any kid would want to be an orphan, I dont know. These are all, I assure you, very funny lines, at least they were when Dorothy Loudon delivered them on Broadway. As spoken here by Victoria Oscar they might as well be inaudible; and her dumpy, frumpy characterization lacks the sharp, manic outline Loudon supplied (as did Carol Burnett in the movie) and that is essential to both the part and the show.

Indeed none of the grown-ups here have the comic flair of the kids. Both the radio and the White House scenes go for about a quarter of their proper value; and was FDR's speaking voice really this effete? David Reynolds is no good at all at the cartoon-tycoon side of Warbucks though he is affecting when he shows his soft side, which is probably more important and certainly takes up more of his time. Marie Barlow is fine as his adoring secretary, whose adoration now seems more upfront than I'd remembered it. It may be a mark of the production -- an earnest of its earnestness -- that the most effectively sustained acting comes from Edward C. Stallsworth and Heather B. Stuart as Annies fake parents.

The two crooks play their assumed destitution so intensely -- he especially -- that we quite forget their crookedness. Instead we start thinking about life must be like outside the Warbucks stockade. This may be good for our souls but its bad for the show, and it prompts a thought about the timing of this revival; at the dawn of a recession, if recessions have dawns, it may not prove the most comfortable choice.

There are, after all, reminders all around us of what happens to Annies when they defy the cartoon rules and grow up. The role's creator, Andrea McArdle, is about to reappear among us as the dissolute Sally Bowles of Cabaret; one of her successors was Sarah Jessica Parker, whose stomping ground in Sex and the City is the same NYC so innocently and strenuously hymned here. Not that the current incumbent need worry about that yet; she is (or was, on the first night) Addison Timlin, who is all of nine. A mere swing -- that's less than an official understudy -- she nevertheless carried all blithely and confidently before her, as Annies should and almost invariably do. The cartoon-strip prototype had a dog, Sandy, so the musical does, too; he barely makes it into the story but of course he wins what's left of our hearts. This show will stop at nothing. But somehow you don't resent it.

THE BLUE ROOM

Poor Alex Theatre

Arthur Schnitzlers La Ronde, on which The Blue Room is based, is one of the few plays ever to have been banned by its author. Schnitzler, a doctor as well as a novelist and playwright, wrote it as a study of erotic behaviour in his native Vienna before the First World War.

Since every scene involves an act of copulation, it quickly became famous for what Schnitzler, who died in 1931, decided were the wrong reasons. He forbade performances in his lifetime and beyond. The play only became available in the early 1970s when the copyright ran out. At which point, of course, everybody jumped on it.

Some time after the deluge comes this version (billed as a free adaptation") by the English playwright David Hare, which updates the action to the present and to what the program describes as "one of the great cities of the world. The flavour of the dialogue suggests London, but the accents in this Canadian premiere place it in New York or possibly Washington.

As is well known, the play consists of 10 duologues. Two characters have sex, then one of them proceeds to another partner who in turn goes onto another, and the last one to appear rounds things off by getting together with the first.

Schnitzler probably meant each to be played by a separate actor but in Mr. Hares version, as in some others, two performers take care of all the roles. The play did sellout business in London and New York, due to the fact half the cast consisted of Nicole Kidman; even, for a couple of moments, of Nicole Kidman undressed. She was apparently sensational.

The Toronto production does not, of course, boast that kind of star power or that kind of eroticism; its two actors have their merits but they cannot provide the irreplaceable allure of Famous People Doing It.

Mr. Hare is not my favourite playwright but he has done a smart job here, and a snappy one. Updating the play inevitably means, though, depriving it of much of its original force. Schnitzler wrote of a society in which promiscuity was tacitly accepted but officially disavowed; advance the action to the 21st century and it no longer seems a very big deal. The play shrinks from an expose to an exhibition: a jaded display for jaded palates.

One tension in particular has gone: In Schnitzler's world the men always believe the women, barring a few obvious hard cases like actresses and prostitutes, to be more innocent than they are. There is a particular Schnitzlerian-type known, according to which translation you consult, as the Sweet Girl or the Little Darling, a charmer whom each lover believes to be available only to him.

The equivalent character in The Blue Room is a coke-snorting model; and the locale in which she gets herself seduced by a married man -- referred to by Schnitzler simply as The Husband and by Hare as The Politician -- has been moved from the private chamber in a restaurant so beloved of Mittel European drama to the standard hotel room. There is no sense of conventions being breached; the elegant cruelty of the Viennese version has evaporated.

The most obviously brutal scene is the first: a streetwalker has a taxi driver (originally, and more effectively, a soldier) against a wall. Subsequent encounters are more refined but less honest. The early scenes in Anthony Leo's Toronto production are very rushed; it seems remarkably easy to get laid. There are blackouts for the act itself.

The Blue Room is really a bitterly tolerant comedy about the lies people tell, to their partners and themselves, before and after sex; the one married couple we meet are the biggest liars of all. Of the duo here, both young, David Cook actually does best in older roles: as the husband/politician, equally complacent in both his aspects, and as a playwright consumed with authorial vanity: a sporting bit of professional self-satire on the part of both dramatists. Vanessa Hunt, by contrast, is best as Maid and Model, effortful when required to put on weight as the Actress and as the politician's wife, who should probably be played younger anyway; her old man certainly treats her like a child.

There is some beautifully moody inter-scene jazz sung by Melissa Stylianou; if she has a CD, I want to hear it. Her songs match the bittersweet final scene, in which an ineffectual aristocrat (delicately rendered by Mr. Cook) wakes up with the hooker and tries to persuade himself he did no more than kiss her eyes. It is the play's one romantic thought; she, however, is able to set him right.

The expense of spirit in a waste of shame": if you can imagine that great Shakespearean sonnet delivered with a shrug, you have the essence of the Schnitzler and, fitfully, of the Hare.

GOODNIGHT DESDEMONA (GOOD MORNING JULIET)

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

Recently, while reviewing an abortion of a Shakespeare romp at the Young People's Theatre, I commented on how few writers have ever managed to produce a passable pastiche of Shakespearean dramatic style. All credit, then, to Ann-Marie MacDonald, who in Goodnight Desdemona (Good Morning Juliet) does it very well. Unfortunately, though, thats all she does.

The good news first: Most of the play is, as you would expect, a spoof of Romeo and Juliet and Othello, and when listening to it I could hardly believe my ears. Here were newly-invented iambic pentameters that actually possessed the correct number of syllables and in which all the stresses fell in the right conversational places. More than that, there is a genuine feeling for Shakespearean wordplay, which also extends to a few passages of comic prose; and though MacDonald doesnt go in much for rhyme, I am sure that if she did she would get that right as well. Best of all, the piece is of a piece; it figure-skates with elan between passages of the original texts and the author's own new inventions.

It's a great bag of tricks, but what can you do with it? Not, it turns out, much. The play has been around since 1988, a Canadian standby if not a Canadian classic, but this is its first outing on a main Toronto stage. Its heroine is Constance Ledbelly, an untenured assistant professor of English who ghost-writes essays and lectures for her adored male superior, and then has to watch while he swans off to Oxford, new girlfriend in tow, to assume a post that should have been hers.

All that keeps Constance going is her pet theory about those two Shakespearean tragedies. She thinks they should have been comedies. Whats more, she thinks they once were; she believes in early, lost versions that included a clown figure who tipped Othello off to Iagos duplicity and had Romeo confess to having married Juliet, thereby bringing the Montague-Capulet feud to an end halfway through Act Three Scene One.

What, Constance wonders, would Desdemona have been like if Othello had not been duped into smothering her, or Juliet if she had not stabbed herself on her husband's corpse? The real answer to that is that they wouldn't have been Juliet and Desdemona, because those characters only exist within the dramatic structures set down for them. (Yes, there are sources, but the only currency they have is due to the plays they inspired. And anyway, the heroines meet bad ends in the sources as well, so killing them off was not just some misogynistic whim of the playwright.)

Admittedly, Constance is not the first critic to notice that the first half of Romeo unfolds like a comedy, or to doubt that the lovers passion would have withstood the strains of marriage. It seems doubtful, though, that Romeo would have got very far telling Tybalt to put up his sword because late last night they had become cousins; being the type he was, Tybalt would have taken this as an additional affront to the family honour and run him through on the spot. Indeed, one of MacDonalds best lines, given to a ghost, is beware of Tybalt; he hath not a sense of humour. It's even less likely that Iago's anti-Othello campaign could have been derailed by a passing jester. After all, King Lear had a fool, a very vocal one, but that didnt stop him disinheriting Cordelia and unleashing a whole chain of disasters.

Anyway, Constance, dejected and frustrated, has a dream in which she is plunged successively into the action of the two plays. In her waking life, she has worn a red hat that looks like a fools cap, which, given her preoccupation with lost manuscripts, translates easily into "foolscap," a neat visual pun. Now she finds herself playing the fool's part.

It works, too. She saves Desdemona who, reprieved from her death sentence, turns out a tougher warrior than Othello. (Perhaps this is why in the current production she is black while he is white. Or maybe it's colour-blind casting for its own sake. One never knows.)

Constance then proceeds from Cyprus to Verona, where things are more complicated. Romeo shacks legally up with Juliet and is tired of her the morning after. He prefers Constance, whom he thinks is a boy. Juliet also prefers Constance, whom she thinks is a boy, but is quite prepared to settle when she discovers that shes a girl. Constance, protesting that shes from Academe and not from Lesbos, first demurs, then consents. So they all go chasing, quite vigorously, through the streets, the graveyards and the bedchambers, and it starts resembling another play Shakespeare wrote, though with the homosexuality under wraps, called Twelfth Night.

It's also highly unsatisfactory, like watching a couple of greatly extended revue sketches. I know that's what critics always say when satire goes wrong, but its usually true.

The tone is too jokey for what the author is apparently trying to do. It may seem at times that she is mocking the fashionable "what if" varieties of Shakespearean scholarship, those that concentrate on describing not the plays we have but the plays the critics would like us to have. It turns out, though, that she is endorsing them. Constance is empowered by her imaginary experiences, and presumably goes back to Academe sane as hell and not about to take it any more. This kind of fantasy may get by as a brief essay in a learned journal, but it does not stand up in the theatre, where words have to take on the weight of flesh. And no intelligent person has ever thought of Juliet or of Desdemona as passive victims anyway; Juliet, for Gods sake, kills herself.

It isn't helped by having its author in the leading role. I say this with surprise as well as regret, since I have previously found MacDonald a very appealing performer. Actually, I still do; she has an eager-to-please spirit and excellent timing. But a performer is not necessarily an actress, and her range, both vocal and emotional, turns out to be limited; everything comes out as an optimistic squeak.

Her two role models are wearying company as well: Alison Sealy- Smith's Desdemona relentlessly bossy, Cara Pifkos Juliet relentlessly pert. In fact the best work in a female role comes from Juan Chioran in a brief butch turn as Juliets nurse; elsewhere, he parodies his own Stratford past with a booming Othello and a hissing Tybalt.

Alisa Palmer's production, too, is at its best as enjoyably busy Stratford send-up, though it, too, satirizes a received idea of Shakespearean production rather than the thing itself. The opening here-and-now scenes are painfully thin in acting, writing and direction. There could be some mutual disservice going on here. On the one hand, the play is not worth Canadian Stage's time and resources; on the other, this high-profile airing may even harm its continued prospects on the fringe and college circuits.

TIME AFTER TIME

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

Subtitled The Chet Baker Project, Time after Time is a Citizen Kane that makes the bad mistake of assuming that the character in whom we are really interested is the reporter.

The play is less about Chet Baker, the late jazz trumpeter and crooner, than about What Chet Baker Means to James OReilly, author and principal performer. Strictly speaking, it's about what Baker means to an anonymous but loquacious narrator, but since O'Reilly plays this role himself its hard not to make the identification.

He begins by telling us how, 10 years ago in a restaurant, on a date with the woman he later married, he heard a Baker record for the first time. He was transfixed by the sound of this haunted, tender voice from the 1950s singing I Fall in Love Too Easily, an outstandingly tender tune in the first place. Another actor actually sits at the table and attempts to score with the young lady, but he is upstaged by OReilly, hovering and commenting and grabbing all the best lines.

The show's first 10 anecdotal minutes are self-centred stand-up comedy and a pointer to how the rest of it is going to go. O'Reilly sets out to discover the truth about Baker, mainly by talking to people who knew him, and turning the results into the play were watching. (Or is he writing a book, or making a movie? Its very amorphous.) Occasionally the character of Chet himself appears, singing, playing and even -- as dictated by the others' memories -- talking.

The narrator is fascinated by the apparent discrepancy between the man and the music. How, he asks, could someone who sings and plays with such apparent sensitivity have been so appalling in his private life, abusing and deserting a succession of wives, destroying himself and his talent through drugs, and finally falling to a farcically ignominious death from an Amsterdam hotel window? The answer, of course, is very easily. A more interesting question might be: What kind of idiot expects there to be a one-on-one correlation between a performer and his performance in the first place?

O'Reillys surrrogate asks how Baker, the beautiful boy of American music, only 23 and personally and professionally on top of his world, could have sung and played with such awareness of loss and loneliness. Well, 23 years are quite enough for most people to gather some first-hand information on those subjects; and even if you have avoided the feelings yourself, you will have read and heard enough about them -- from popular songs, mainly -- to know how they are supposed to feel. Your audience will know, too, and between your assumptions and theirs the trick will be done.

The material helps, of course. A singer is a kind of actor: He will, by and large, sound sad on sad songs and happy on happy ones. Baker, as it happens, sang very few happy songs; wistfully romantic was about as positive as he got. There is a sentimental confusion in many peoples minds between a performer's emotions, which can be faked (the word is not pejorative), and his personality, which does tend to be the same on and off stage. Nothing in Baker's musical personality suggests he was a nice guy. Charming, yes.

The first time I heard Chet Bakers singing, I couldnt take it seriously; the voice was pallid, and the lyrical interpretation almost non-existent. Later I found, like many others, that the blankness had its own appeal, especially in its similarity to the piercing withered-leaf simplicity of his trumpet playing.

Oddly enough, though the play makes a big deal about Baker's unknowability (so that philosophically it has to be about O'Reilly, for what can any of us know about anyone but ourselves, and all that jazz), it presents a rather comprehensible, unpuzzling picture of him: He had too much too soon and couldnt deal with it, so he destroyed himself, taking a few others down en route. It is not a unique story.

There are two scenes in which a man and a woman -- probably the narrators younger self and his lady friend, at any rate played by the same actors -- argue about Baker's recording of his signature tune, My Funny Valentine, each of them taking a diametrically different position on each occasion. They debate whether the rhetorical questions the song poses ("Is your figure less than Greek?/Is your mouth a little weak?") are tender things to say to a woman or just insulting.

We seem to be talking less about Baker's performance than about Lorenz Harts lyrics, so here are a few facts: The song was written for a show, to be sung by a woman about a character actually called Valentine. Its sung in his absence, and that is how most singers of any sense and of either gender continue to sing it -- as an affectionate mock ode. The beloved cannot be insulted, because he or she never hears it. It's possible that Hart, who felt unattractive, meant it as a love song to himself, and it's possible that Chet, who had a highly developed sense of self-pity, also felt it that way. Another of his key tunes was Everything Happens to Me. That might be interesting, but the play doesnt get into it. Its more ambitious, and I suppose more intelligent, than a big showbiz bio like Jolson or Buddy, but it is no more illuminating.

Director Jim Millan gives it a smoky, moody production, and Martin Julien deals efficiently with all the male characters who aren't Baker or O'Reilly. But there are really only three reasons for seeing the show. One is Danny DePoe, who reproduces Chets singing and playing, not to mention his movie-star looks, with uncanny accuracy (though his native trumpet style, as exhibited in the intermission, seems far more muscular). He isnt an actor, but he is a presence, and his affectless line readings are just right; he is the right kind of hole in the play.

A second is the music itself, as dispensed by DePoe and an onstage trio. The third, the clincher, is the white-heat work of Philippa Domville, who plays the fallen idol's female survivors, each more damaged and vitriolic than the last. The actress, after a string of ladylike roles at the Shaw Festival, here reinvents herself and keeps reinventing. It's in the narrator's encounter with this parade of exes -- one of whom is herself a pathetic performer - - that the echoes of Kane are most deafening. Rosebud here turns out to be a plangent chorus of Summertime. The song itself was accorded a jokey mention back in the first scene, so presumably some kind of wheel is coming some kind of circle.

FAME

Pantages Theatre, Toronto

Up until Tuesday night at the Pantages, Fame had passed me by, and I rather wish that it had continued to do so. Fame, we are often assured by those who have it, can be a terrible thing. Fame--The Musical certainly is.

Though I missed the movie, and never caught so much as a single episode of the TV series, some basic information about the franchise had got through to me. I knew it was about New York kids attending a high school for the performing arts. David De Silva, who originated the film that set the cycle in motion, earns our goodwill by writing in the program about the importance of the arts in education. A worthy and sympathetic notion, though, is not enough; and though the stage production keeps proclaiming its own idealism, the actual product is thoroughly debased, an imitation of an imitation.

I gather that the musical takes themes, characters and situations that featured in the earlier versions, stirs them around a bit and changes the names. It certainly seems to be adhering to a formula. Its score is mostly new but it retains the title song from the movie, probably for identification purposes. Certainly the number itself, as rendered here, is no great shakes. It's an unshaded hymn to showbiz ambition, notably only for the odd fact that the character who belts it out eventually comes to a bad end. This could be mordant irony, but it's likelier to mean whoever planned the show was thinking one moment at a time.

The story unfolds in the early 1980s, in a gaunt rambling building that is about to give way to swishier premises at Lincoln Center, all this information being more succinctly conveyed in the program than it is from the stage. We follow an assortment of students who are variously talented as actors, dancers and musicians, and who train in all those disciplines while also having to maintain good academic grades.

We focus on three pairs of kids, one from each stream. All three couples have a similar dynamic, each consisting of one conformist and one rebel. The son of a virtuoso violinist, so straight that he even wears a tie on his first day in school though not thereafter, falls for an overly ambitious singer who just cant wait. A precocious ballerina whose obsession with dancing has so far kept her from having a social life is initiated by a gifted but angry hip- hopper whose graduating chances are threatened by his being dyslexic. A boy whose acting ambitions go beyond his previous success in commercials (I want to be a real actor, have you ever read Stanislavsky?") maintains a strange on-off relationship with a girl who at one point suspects him of being gay, when apparently all he is is dedicated.

The show tries hard to be rousing, and occasionally has a stab at being tough. One character dies of a drug overdose, a gesture at tragedy the production has done nothing to earn.

Even in its earlier incarnations, Fame always sounded to me like son of A Chorus Line: a series of confessional vignettes of aspiring performers, caught this time at an earlier period of their aspirations. As a full-blown musical, its like Hello Twelve, Hello Thirteen, Hello Love -- the big puberty number from that show -- indefinitely extended. It has, of course, taken on other influences as well. Bits of it are like a low-rent Rent, while the heroine, or anyway the noisiest girl, makes a final triumphal appearance atop a car that seems to have been driven over from Grease.

The show's residual documentary aspect makes its first half tolerable; there are scenes in class that are simplistic but interesting. In the second, the relationships take over, and with them the songs. These (music by Steve Margoshes, lyrics by Jacques Levy) are a deadening procession that never heard of subtlety or dramatic progression; most of them tell us, loudly and at length, what we already know.

An early number called I Want to Make Magic gives fair warning, as Nick the actor tells us, recklessly mixing his dramaturgical standards, that "I want to do The Lion in Winter/Brecht and Harold Pinter." He goes on to cite acting role-models including Jason Robards, who's a tough one to rhyme; his girlfriend, though, compensates later with a song bearing the all-time catchy title Think of Meryl Streep. The English and dancing teachers come to melodramatic musical blows over a students future; this is embarrassing, not least because its a break in convention. The show has acclimatized us to think of singing as something that kids do, and it's much too late for the grown-ups to join in.

Other students supply comic relief. A horny Hispanic tells the acting class about his erections, in a song called I Can'T Keep It Down. A black girl does some soul shouting about her eating- disorder; she can keep it down, and is overweight in consequence. The fat lady has sung, but the show is far from over.

Hot on her heels comes a big number in which Tyrone, the street- dancing champ, lets out his frustrations; its meant to be his showcase but its climax is a series of somersaults executed by somebody else. (The choreography, by Lars Bethke, who also directs, is the worst: as shapeless and cliche-ridden as anything gets.)

The English teacher does some more emoting about regarding her pupils as her children, since she never had any of her own; the actress is black, and she seems to be destroying herself up there, so she gets the regulation cheers from the white audience that thinks its hearing gospel, but less of them than usual, maybe because this is the third time in the evening the show has tried it on.

Finally -- or anyway at the lowest point -- the fame-crazed young diva who unwisely escaped to California, returns for an anguished workout called In L.A. that keeps restarting when you think it's finished and most of which she sings bent over sideways at an angle of 45 degrees, as if she didn't have enough pain in her life already.

I have to praise something, so let me say that the set, by Norbert U. Kolb, is authentically barracky. The cast are all too old to be credible high-schoolers, but that is not their fault, and maybe not anybody else's either. None of them deserves an individual mention, for good or ill. They all work hard, and achieve little. That, in a show about youthful hopes, is realism more bitter than anybody needs.

Black & White Photo: Carol Rosegg / FAME: Son of A Chorus Line with a bit of low-rent Rent and Grease thrown in. ;

ICARIA

The Great Hall, Toronto

The title Icaria suggests a re-telling of the Greek myth about the boy who defied his more careful father by flying too close to the sun and plunging to his death -- and that in fact is what it is. That at least is part of what it is. The boy's fate is mixed into a whole stew of family conflicts that are presented to us in scrambled and foreshortened form, not always comprehensibly. Icaria is devised theatre with a vengeance: technically skilled, sometimes evocative, often impenetrable.

It is the work of Number Eleven Theatre, a new group that grew out of a long-standing Winnipeg experimental troupe called Primus Theatre. Number Eleven is based in Toronto, but this show was prepared in Nova Scotia -- in Halifax, where it premiered, and in the small town of Granville Ferry, which seems to have left its mark. It has a very Maritime or just very Celtic flavour. Its four characters -- father, mother, son and daughter -- will tell one another folk tales with the slightest provocation and sing folk songs with no provocation whatever.

The creation of the show is credited jointly to its director, Ker Wells, and its four actors. The program lists 13 separate literary sources, but since the play lasts only 65 minutes, they can only be present in very compressed form. Their coherence, and that of the play itself as one scene melts into the next, is difficult to make out. The trouble with a dream play is that when anything goes, nothing counts.

The action is presented to us through the memory of Daphne (Elizabeth Rucker), the daughter, and it culminates in the suicide of Thomas (Alex McLean), the son. No motive is given, but we are at least invited to trace it back to a fight that Thomas once had with Pat (Varrick Grimes), his fisherman father.

Thomas says he wants to fly, citing historical precedents of people who almost made it. His father, home from the sea and wanting his tea, is unsympathetic, pointing out that "humans dont have the same muscles as birds." (This line has stuck in my mind as the simplest and most persuasive declarative sentence uttered in the course of the play.) While conducting this argument, they are performing aggressive acrobatics -- dad is a whiz at the old forward roll -- and stalking one another round the stage as if in a duel, only brandishing chairs instead of swords.

The correspondence to the Icarus myth is not precise. Icarus father, Daedalus, didn't try to stop his son from flying; in fact, he taught him how. He merely wanted him to pursue a sensible flight path. Here, though, it seems to have been elevated into a generalized image of paternal repression -- a symptom of everything that's wrong between the generations.

Later on, Pat appears on stilts to chase his son around the stage. There was a similar image of towering paternal terror in Ronnie Burketts puppet play Street of Blood, but it was far more effective there, partly because it was more imaginatively and economically done and partly because we knew enough about the characters to care.

The women have their tensions, too. Mother (Jane Wells), the only character given a function but not a name, tells her daughter a baleful tale and then hands her an outsize pair of scissors. We assume she wants her hair cut, but it looks more as though Daphne will stick the instrument into the back of the maternal neck.

Furniture and props in fact are a constant source of friction in this household. The family dinner table is an especially ominous place, though it also yields one moment of authentic magic: The tablecloth is whirled in the air, then unfolded and set on the ground -- suddenly we are at a picnic. At one point, we flash back to the parents wedding: the happy couple on stilts while their unborn children sing folk songs. At another, the two ladies do the keening while the men fight. The singing is fine, but the scenes have "experimental theatre," of a rather traditional kind, written all over them.

I was irreverently reminded of Coming Soon, the hilarious British comedy series shown recently on the Women's Television Network. In it, an intense London theatre group, in thrall to various fashionable prophets including our own Robert Lepage, go off to Scotland to prepare a new piece so they can qualify for a Scottish grant. (They failed the test for a lesbian grant.) Once there, they have to come up with something Scottish. Industriously researching the available folklore, and not being inhibited by any desire to communicate with their audience, they come up with what seems to be a play about the wind.

Icaria is a lot better than that; the people involved in it are accomplished (though Grimes doesn't have the weight to be a frightening father, even in this shows abstract terms), their motives are surely above reproach, and they obviously want to communicate. They dont much, though -- at least not with me. I can see that they know and mean what they're doing, and I liked their occasional lyricism when I wasn't feeling ground down by their portentousness. But for all the industrious application of local colour, there seems no particular reason for it to be going on where it does except a vague belief that these characters, being close to the water, must also be close to the earth.

It's no news, even in the theatre, that suicides are ultimately inexplicable. Square old Arthur Miller taught us that years ago in Death of a Salesman, but he rooted his play firmly so that at least we wanted to know. Icaria bequeathes us no more than a vague feeling that terrible things happen even in the best-intentioned families, leaving the mourners to mourn. It isn't enough.

PILEDRIVER!

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - There is something very comforting about the sight of a stage laid out as a fight ring. It brings shape and focus and the promise of spectacle.

The last century is full of plays that use boxing or wrestling as a metaphor for the class struggle or gender wars or whatever. Piledriver!, more aggressively upfront, uses wrestling as a metaphor for wrestling. It does get in to related issues but the writing is too thin and the performance too raucous for them to matter much. What count here are the fights.

There are about a dozen of them, very well staged in Bradley Moss's production, and intrepidly performed by four actors, including one woman, out of a cast of five; the fifth is the referee.

Inevitably, unless youre enough of a fan to appreciate the niceties, all that locking of hands round necks and bashing of bodies against ropes and canvas becomes monotonous -- unpleasantly monotonous, at that -- but there is a dramatic arc.

The characters are a small-time troupe, working the circuit from Edmonton to Toronto with a brief detour into the northern United States, in the late 1970s which apparently was just before wrestling lost its soul. The fights of course are faked, performed according to carefully worked-out scenarios, up until the last one, when latent tensions between the performers come to the surface and they start hurting one another in earnest.

So the theatre audience, after an evening of watching simulated simulated violence, gets to watch simulated real violence. That, it seems, is what a gig in Toronto will do to you.

Here life seems to be imitating art, because Piledriver! itself originated in Edmonton. It's a joint presentation by two companies: Three Dead Trolls in a Baggie, which does comedy, and Guys in Disguise, which does drag. Wes Borg of the first group and Darrin Hagen of the second collaborated on the writing and both of them appear in it.

The play grew out of their discovery that much of professional wrestling is gay. As one of the characters says, what else would you expect in a sport that consists of sweaty leather-clad male bodies groping one another?

The authors were especially fascinated by the career of a Western wrestler called Harvey Jones, who fought under the name of Killer Karl Kramer. Characters bearing both these names appear in the play, but this seems to be strictly a homage rather than an attempt to present opposing sides of one personality; the play doesn't go that deep.

The plays Harvey and Karl are long-time lovers. Harvey is the promoter who dreams up the storylines and refs the matches. Karl drives the bus and, though quite the nicest guy around, he is also the designated heavy: the wrestler whom the crowds are primed to hate and who must therefore lose every bout. (Karl says Harvey proudly, "loses better than anyone else in wrestling.")

Karl functions in the act like a warm-up comic. The real stars are Randy Rage, a long-haired stud cast as barbarian hero, and Rock the Cock, who affects a punk Cockney accent and is presented as the chipper challenger to Randys crown.

Randy is newly married; his wife, Angie, travels with the gang and gradually becomes an integral part of the show. Rock, a single thrown into close proximity with a couple of couples, is promiscuously gay with a preference for straight men. He is also ambitious to undermine Randy and take his place in the real world as well as the fantasy one.

In an older play, he would have gone about this by hitting on Angie (who does seem interested). In this one, he does it by successfully coming on to Randy. If you think of Randy as Othello, then Rock is a Iago who seduces him physically rather than intellectually. Indeed, at different times he seems to be Iago and Cassio and Desdemona. Randy, personally as well as professionally macho, gets to feeling very disoriented, and chaos comes again.

The play gets the atmosphere of the tour bus and small-town bars convincingly enough, and the sexual moves (an especially appropriate term in this setting) are neatly laid out. We hear again about homophobia being a mask for insecurity, and we learn something about wrestling as show-business, the small-timers itching for the big- time -- which in this time-frame, with the World Wrestling Federation looming, seems bigger and itchier than ever.

The characters, though, are not only mean but petty, the writing neither passionate nor funny enough to stir more than surface interest; and the acting doesn't do much to lift things.

As usual, the best performance, out of the ring at least, is the quietest: Wes Borg, co-author, as Karl, an ex-cop and ex-straight whose sexual orientation changed when he met the flamboyant Rocky, to whom he has been faithful ever since. Hagen, the other author, plays Randy, and the two of them have written themselves the most thoughtful scene, one in which they compare notes on the feasibility of changing lives and leaving wives.

The rest of Hagen's performance doesn't go beyond troubled swagger, while Joe Bird as Rock sticks in a groove of untroubled swagger. April Babigan has mostly to stand around being either annoyed or concerned, and cannot find much nuance in either. Jeff Page plays Rocky as the standard fussy queen in theatrical management, who italicizes every fourth or fifth word. It's entertaining for the first five minutes.

Buddies in Bad Times has done worse shows than this, but the company still seems to be taking its name with depressing literalness. Producing a good play would not necessarily be a sell- out.
