I, CLAUDIA

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

Kristen Thomson is the real theatrical thing. Her solo show I, Claudia demonstrates that she is a magnetic and versatile actress, but after her performances in Oleanna, A Streetcar Named Desire and Hysteria, that is hardly news. It also shows her to be a terrific writer, and that is news since she hasn't done it before. Her script has its faults -- an overall structure that doesn't work as it's supposed to and a wide sentimental streak -- but in a debutante, such lapses are forgiveable. What counts is that she can rock her audience -- she certainly rocked me -- on a regular basis with lines and moments that are hilariously funny, totally unexpected and unimpeachably true.

The title character of I, Claudia (that arch title is, I guess, another flaw; it suggests that if the pun were not available, Thomson would have been just as happy to call her heroine Gertrude) is a 12 1/2-year-old schoolgirl suffering the triple assaults of puberty, unpopularity and her parents' divorce. The last affliction has developed its own painful sequel -- her father's re-marriage to a lady named Leslie, whom he has introduced to Claudia as "a special friend."

Claudia, whose accounts of her own thoughts and feelings happily occupy the bulk of the stage time, recalls this declaration with devastating adolescent scorn: "I hate to be precocious, but I know a euphemism when I see one." She is even more dismissive of Leslie's physical endowments ("two flying saucers landed from outer space") and just incredulous about Leslie's suggestion that they should be girlfriends: "I thought, 'Leslie, look at yourself." I quote from memory, but I'll vouch for the tone if not the actual words.

Thomson lets Leslie have her own say, which we hear while she is being fitted for her wedding dress -- stressed herself and the cause of stress in others. She also plays two male characters -- Claudia's paternal grandfather, as disapproving of his son's new match as she is, and Drachman, her school custodian, who once ran a theatre in some mythical European country and is now our master of ceremonies.

To effect these impersonations, the actress appears before us in a series of half-masks, the kind that cover everything except the mouth. (They are part of a classic set, devised for drama schools by the noted Anglo-Algerian stage designer Farrah.) As usual with masks, one initially finds them forbidding and uncalled for. Also as usual, they proceed to impose themselves and to seem not only acceptable but essential. And as always with a good masked performance, you could swear that the flat faces -- Claudia's own anyway -- are changing expression as you watch. Much as I usually enjoy looking at Thomson's own face, the sacrifice seems worthwhile; she is neither an old man nor a 12-year-old girl, and the masks enable her to distance herself from the characters' incidental qualities while immersing herself in their realities.

That at least is the idea. It doesn't altogether work out because the subsidiary characters still don't seem very real or indeed very necessary. They are there to provide alternative views of Claudia's situation and they do to the extent that they provide physical evidence that there are other people involved. But the men offer very little in the way of perspective or cross-lighting; it's their presence as excess baggage that causes me to accuse the play of sentimentality. Drachman's accent, coming on top of his mask, amounts to a fit of the mumbles, while his philosophical showman's presence seems like something Ronnie Burkett might have dreamed up on an off-day, though it does give director Chris Abraham a chance to apply some modest but useful theatrical colouring. (How much he contributed to the performance is impossible to assess, but I suspect it was substantial; the show is tight.)

The grown-up characters we really get to know are those we never meet -- Claudia's parents -- but only and subtly through what Claudia says and doesn't say about them. Leslie's vulnerable- aggressive presence is entertaining, but even she operates at a tangent to Claudia rather than in tension with her.

It is she, Claudia, who makes the play; and when she is on this is incomparably the best show in Toronto. (There's no competition, come to think of it, even when she's off.) She has subsidiary problems: Her science project for one, and, rather closely tied to it, the fate of two pet goldfish whom she has named Romeo and Juliet, the wrong way round as she later discovers.

She is also aggrieved by the efforts of her mother, whom she calls "over-protective," to restrict her movements around town. She is also capable, after spending most of the play talking about the father, whom she clearly adores, of describing her mother as the nicest person in the world and concealing a sad poem she has written because she knows it would worry her. This is a revelation that tears at our emotions without exploiting them, as does her description of finding inalienable evidence, through pillaging her father's apartment, that he was involved with his new lady long before the divorce. She puts another stolen token beneath her mother's pillow in the hopes that this will bring her parents together: "I learned it in voodoo class," she says, and we believe her.

Claudia is at what you might call an aggravated awkward stage. She is immersed in teenage culture, as only an imminent ex-pre-teen can be, and her verbal reaction to any situation that affronts her is the ubiquitous "duh!" There are two riotous sequences of her dancing with self-consciously furious abandon in front of a mirror, and her career ambition is to be a VJ, but she doesn't feel cool enough to admit it to anyone. She feels especially intimidated by two contemporaries named Tracey and Stacey, whom one imagines as later versions of the twins who periodically make life hell for Bart Simpson; she also knows herself to be brighter than them in many respects.

Claudia is genuinely bruised but not mortally injured; she herself, with colourful variations, employs the analogy of a cocooned butterfly. As a writer Thomson seems to have observed many Claudias, then created this unique one; as an actor she hurls herself at the role with hair-trigger accuracy and a joy that envelops the house. I laughed till I cried, though the chances are I would have cried anyway.

Black & White Photo: Guntar Kravis / Kristen Thomson as Claudia, trying to come to terms with her geekiness and her father's new girlfriend. ;

SO IT'S COME TO THIS

Tallulah's Cabaret, Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, Toronto

So what it's come to is an amiable evening of raconteuring that could only with the most elaborate courtesy be described as a play, or even -- so low-key is it -- as a show. Emmett Foster, who wrote and performed it, describes himself at one point as an old man, though in fact he looks youthful but creased. Let's settle for well preserved. He has a lot to have been preserved from, including a Mormon upbringing, a mother who married nine times, major addictions to alcohol and cocaine, a wild gay life in Manhattan, and 18 years as personal assistant to legendary New York impresario Joseph Papp.

Foster's major asset in telling us about all this is his absolute naturalness. He walks on stage in black pants and sweater, sits on a stool at a microphone, and just talks. His major liability is that he seems to assume everything he talks about is intrinsically interesting simply because it happened to him, and it isn't. A woman with nine husbands certainly ought to be fascinating, if only as a case study in optimism, but we need to know more about her as a person than Foster seems willing to vouchsafe until late in the proceedings. Then he does start filling us in on some of her eccentricities, and especially on her cantankerous impatience when interrogated by doctors, but at this point he is talking about something else and he only brings her in as a reference.

We do gather that Foster's multiplicity of stepfathers only left him looking for a real one. He seems to have found a temporary paternal figure in a rich Californian who, without making demands on his body, financed him through university where he found a vocation in theatre. But the major force in his life turned out to be Joe Papp, for whom he functioned as chauffeur and gofer, confidant, minder and -- in the painful months leading up to Papp's death from cancer -- unofficial nurse.

When Foster talks about his boss, the piece comes to life. We get a clear picture of Papp as a driven egocentric who used people ruthlessly but did not manipulate or exploit them, much. In some ways he seems to have been rather naive. (Maybe egomaniacs have to be; they certainly can't afford a sense of irony.) He honestly could not see why Foster should not be at his disposal 24 hours a day, and really he was right; Foster connived at it and thrived on it. As he says himself, it gave his life purpose. He loved Joe and Joe maybe loved him -- he certainly protected and respected him. (The relationship was non-sexual. Foster praises Papp as a straight man who, before it became fashionable, took a stand on gay rights.)

His most revealing anecdote tells how, in the course of an extensive trawl through the city's sleazier hot spots, he lost Papp's passport the night before an international trip. The next day he tried ineffectually to cover up but soon had to confess. Papp made a swift phone call for emergency documentation, reassured Foster that he did not feel lied to ("a lie is when you say something to hurt people") and advised his protege, for his own good, to cut back on the drugs and booze. Papp literally had no time for other people but when he did find some, he used it. A man like that inspires loyalty, especially in a boy like that. The two ended up making a suicide pact: If either became incapacitated through illness, the other would arrange for euthanasia. This was to cause problems later. Foster tells us enough about Papp for his own purposes, but maybe not enough for ours.

For years, after all, Papp was maybe the most powerful figure in New York theatre. He started free seasons in Central Park, and had them institutionalized as the New York Shakespeare Festival. He parlayed that into the powerhouse downtown multiplex known as the Public Theater. For a time, he ran the theatrical component of Lincoln Center. He produced Hair, one of the most successful American musicals, and A Chorus Line, the most successful of all. He had a missionary enthusiasm for bringing theatre to audiences and players who might otherwise be excluded from it, for reasons of cash or culture or both.

He maintained his passion for Shakespeare and had lucid, often unconventional opinions about him, especially when it came to Troilus and Cressida. (When I met him, I expected to find a hustler. Instead I found myself talking to a scholar. That's not to say he wasn't a hustler as well.) I went to Foster's show hoping to discover more about Papp's theatre from somebody who had been there; at the least, more backstage stories that actually had something to do with what went on backstage.

Foster only mentions one actor, Meryl Streep, and one show, A Chorus Line; he paints a vivid picture of the off-Broadway first night, and how the entire audience went crazy and stood and cheered when the key changed and the brass blared on the closing number. This figures, not just because it was a great show and Papp's biggest hit (for years it funded the rest of his operation), but because Foster himself is temperamentally a Broadway baby, in love with the glitziest musicals. One would like to know how this sat with Papp, who often expressed disdain for Broadway but was not above making common cause with it.

To hear some of this, I would be prepared to sacrifice Foster's own thoughts on life, though to be fair these do become more compelling when he moves into his post-Papp period; if that relationship made him a person, then the person he is automatically becomes more worth listening to.

He laughs at his own coke-induced paranoia that led him to fantasize about being stalked by the authorities because of his homosexuality. (The joke proves double-edged; his Toronto audience seemed inclined to take the conspiracy seriously.) He mentions his own incredulity at not contracting AIDS, not to mention that of his friends. He also tells us he has given up on all his addictions including sex, the latter on hold until he finds someone he can commit to, which, he implies, he is "too chicken" to contemplate. He can be ruefully amusing, though his background and demeanour (I don't mean the Mormons) lead us to anticipate a higher standard of one-liners than he actually delivers.

His message to us is that we should be honest with ourselves, which is not likely to start any fights. There are both worse and better ways of spending an evening.

MANGIACAKE!

Artword Theatre

- - -

Drama is a tough medium, though we seem to be losing sight of the fact. More and more we are asked not to experience a play but to empathize with some narrator as he turns the pages of a family snapshot album.

This week in Toronto, three solo performers on three consecutive nights have offered us their own or somebody elses memoirs in shows that have ranged, in strict order of appearance, from the sublime to the iniquitous.

On Tuesday, Kristen Thomson in I Claudia went to the trouble of creating four characters, none of them obviously herself, and one of them, the title figure, a possible classic. On Wednesday, in So Its Come to This, Emmett Walker told us more than we needed to know about how it felt to be Emmett Walker, but compensated by imparting some first-hand observations on the more interesting figure of Joseph Papp.

On Thursday in Mangiacake! (a term denoting assimilated Italian- Canadians who are popularly believed to eat cake rather than bread), Charly Chiarelli spent two-and-a-half hours filling us in on the great experience of growing up as Charly Chiarelli.

So why should anybody care?

All this frantic confessing or, in Mr. Chiarelli's case, frantic exulting may conceivably be traced to the old culture wars on the topic of Appropriation. We were told that for white writers to write about blacks or for men to write about women was to appropriate the other person's experience, and not to be endured.

If you took both the race and the gender warriors seriously (admittedly few people did, and they themselves never seemed to), then you had to go all the way and accept that only a black woman was entitled to depict the experiences of a black woman, and that she had better not include a black man or white woman, even as a walk-on. Nor, logically, should you stop there: since the identity of each one of us can be broken down into any number of criss- crossing subdivisions, obviously the only kind of a play anyone is entitled to write is an autobiographical monologue. And it had better be performed by the author, since bringing in an actor can only send the appropriation to radioactive levels because actors always have their own agenda and theyre such egotists.

This seems to be the position at which Messrs. Foster and Chiarelli have arrived. And maybe theyre right, but it does seem to deal a death-blow to the idea of theatre as we have traditionally known it.

Mr. Chiarelli grew up in Hamilton, the son of Sicilian parents. He begins by telling us of a trip he took to the old country as a young man in the company of his new Irish-Canadian wife. He then flashes back to his boyhood and doesn't return to Sicily until after the intermission. He is a cheery, emphatic performer with a stocky build, flashing white teeth and matching hair, and he does not underplay. Describing a sadistic schoolteacher as a mean, cruel bitch," he draws out the words and illustrates each with a separate grimace.

He intersperses his chat with songs, which he performs in a pleasantly modified Vegas croon while accompanying himself on blues harmonica. (It's like listening to Tony Bennett and Sonny Terry taking alternating phrases.) One of the songs, called Crazy in Love with Italy, is your standard Tin Pan Alley travelogue ("Florence is divine/Michelangelo and history), the kind traditionally turned out by writers who had never been to the places in question. It somehow doesnt help to know that Mr. Chiarelli actually has.

What really makes the evening unbearable is its unrelenting positivity. Mr. Chiarelli wins every round. True, he gets beaten up at school by kids who call him a wop; but he gets his own gang to inflict violent retribution on his tormentors and even ends up as president of his school council. (I confess his election-slogans -- Put a wop on top" and "If youre a Jew, Chiarelli's for you" -- made me laugh.)

The second act has a rollicking section concerning his adult bout with testicular cancer but this, too, he beats, enduring the side- effects of radiation by smoking marijuana: a happily topical touch in view of this week's news.

There is supposed to be an overriding theme: Mr. Chiarellis acceptance that he is, in his scripts terms, a mangiacake rather than a wop and that this goes double for his kids. But the play takes shape as a mere series of anecdotes. Those set in Italy only left me longing, even more urgently than usual, for the next episode of The Sopranos.

Dramatists naturally draw on their own experience but that experience has to be mediated: invent some characters, hire some actors, put yourself in a bad light, change the names. Before he earned the right to compose Long Day's Journey into Night, Eugene O'Neill had spent three decades being Eugene O'Neill, and I mean being the playwright, not the man.

Of course, for all I know Mr. Chiarelli may have invented the whole thing, but it felt like he was telling the truth, and I mean that as an insult. Am I being too harsh? Well, it has been a long, lonely week, and Mangiacake! was the longest as well as the worst thing in it.

THE DRAWER BOY

Winter Garden Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - In the two years since it made its bow at Theatre Passe Muraille, The Drawer Boy, Michael Healey's play about myth-making, has made its own myth. Indeed, it was well on its way even on that first night. The sureness and steadiness of its narrative, its fresh approach to a familiar setting, the perfect teamwork of its three actors, and our complete unreadiness for what we were about to see (what, for a start, could the title mean?) combined to create a legend. In this revival, with the set glossed up for a bigger space and a commercial production but with the same director and cast, the magic still works.

The play is set in the early 1970s, on an Ontario farm run by two middle-aged bachelors, Morgan and Angus. Its heart is the story that Morgan tells Angus, every night, and that we hear toward the end of the first act. There was the farmer boy, Morgan himself, and the drawer boy, Angus, an aspiring architect -- that's the kind of drawing he did -- who went off together to serve in the Second World War. While stationed in London they met two young women -- "the tall girl" and "the taller girl" -- and two cases of requited love broke out. Tragedy struck when Angus, during the blitz, was hit on the head by a flying door and lost most of his memory. Still the two couples went back to Canada, had a double wedding, and happily worked the farm, until both the girls were killed in a driving accident. That's Morgan's story and some of it is true.

How much is true, and why Morgan invented the rest of it, is revealed by the arrival of Miles, a young actor researching a documentary play about farming; the reference, plainly, is to an actual and famous 1970s production called The Farm Show. Miles finds Angus to be an amiable simpleton who can do complicated sums in his head but forgets the names of people and things as soon as he has heard them. Morgan puts Miles to work in return for his keep; he has a sardonic sense of humour and has the city boy rising at 3 a.m. -- "to rotate the crops" -- and mucking out the cowshed with a fork. (Even Angus thinks this is ridiculous. "I'll get you a spoon," he volunteers.) Angus obsessively prepares sandwiches, which Morgan, with corresponding regularity, eats.

When Miles asks how it feels to be continually growing things in order to kill them, Morgan gives him a reply for the ages: "Miles" he says, tongue unfathomnably in cheek, "it's an emotional roller coaster." Miles's attempts to act this out, or to portray a neurotic cow terrified of slaughter if she doesn't give enough milk, apparently meet with little favour back at collective HQ. But he strikes gold when he overhears Morgan telling Angus his nightly tale. Without informing them, he has it put in the play and invites them to a run-through. Morgan is furious. Angus begins to remember things.

What eventually comes out is the story of a friendship -- a marriage, really -- that has withstood large amounts of suffering, cruelty, resentment and deceit, and will now have to carry the added burden of the truth. We are left in little doubt that it will continue, and that this is a good thing. The realization is moving and -- certainly in this performance -- remarkably unsentimental.

There is an irony here that maybe even the playwright hasn't noticed. Apparently, there was nothing in the actual Farm Show that resembled the story of The Drawer Boy. Nor should there have been since, when you think about it, the effectiveness of Morgan's story depends little on the characters having been farmers; it would have been touching whomever it had happened to. The Drawer Boy does tell us some interesting things about life on the land, and they are more compelling for being filtered through the author's own comedic sensibility. But what holds us is the very particular situation that he, as far as I know, has invented himself, and that radiates fascinatingly outward.

In part, of course, it's a tribute to the theatre itself. I have my doubts as to whether the effect on Angus of seeing his story acted out could really be as thoroughgoingly therapeutic as the play suggests, but I'll go along with it as a metaphor. Anyway, Healey caps it very craftily when he has Miles tell Angus the story of Hamlet, a character whom he once played and who had his own radical notions of drama as therapy. (It's also very funny, since Miles tells it in the first person, and the audience thinks for a few moments that he's alluding to his own student career rather than the Danish prince's.) Here it's Morgan who, though hardly a villain and certainly not a smiling one, turns out to be the guilty creature sitting at a play. No wonder he's angry.

Actually, one can sympathize with him. Most arguments about cultural appropriation are ridiculous; nobody owns history. But the direct personal experience of a living person is another thing, especially if you're going to parade it on stage in front of his neighbours. Miles, you feel, might at least have asked.

If he had, though, there would have been no play, either for him or for us. And what he does works out well, if at a cost.

It's at preserving this balance that Miles Potter's production excels. (He was in the original Farm Show but his work 30 years on seems a lot more tactful than that of his onstage namesake.)

David Fox's Angus retains its extraordinary power and especially its swift, decisive timing; his mind seems to be moving, with absolute assurance, backward and forward over the same minute patch of ground. The malice in Jerry Franken's Morgan is more to the fore than I remember it, but the complementary sense of stern concern remains unaffected. Tom Barnett's cavortings as Miles sometimes approach self-indulgence but never actually get there; in his other persona as concerned observer he's fine. It's not his fault that the moment at which he tumbles to the truth is the only one in the play that rings false, a contrivance for the author to get more quickly to the end. John Ferguson's spruce new set, complete with sky cloth, is unsuitably pretty but does no serious damage.

There have been a handful of fine new plays in the last couple of years -- mostly, like The Drawer Boy, from beginning playwrights -- but this remains the best.

FAMILY CIRCUS MAXIMUS

The Second City, Toronto

Second City's 50th revue is, mercifully, its best in years. It makes some departures from recent tradition. There is more music in it than has been customary and a lot more physical comedy, or at least a lot better physical comedy. The show has been directed by noted clown Michael Kennard, who in another life is half of Mump and Smoot (I dont remember which half), and he has the cast tying themselves in some highly impressive knots.

The title, as usual, is arbitrary. Family Circus Maximus is not a circus, despite its gymnastics; it is not big, let alone maximal (the cast is the standard half-dozen); and it is not a family show, though I took my own with no ill-effects.

The shows overall satirical viewpoint is easily described: It doesn't have one. It does have a shape, sort of. It begins with a prologue, acrobatically mimed and economically spoken by a new and engaging performer named Aurora Browne in the persona of a swan. The entire cast then unite in a song -- a good old-fashioned here-we- all-are-and-we-promise-to-be-funny opening number -- and then comes the first sketch, proper. It involves God, here seen putting the fear of Himself into a belated penitent who hasn't set knee in church for ages. (Look what I did to Job. And I liked him.) He reappears in the shows concluding number, involving an altercation between nuns and property developers. He is on the side of the nuns, which in this day and age is reassuring, and this second manifestation is what I mean by shape; in the shows end is its beginning.

The Deity -- bearded and bare-chested in appearance, raucous in delivery and Old Testament in temper -- is played by Doug Morency, a Second City standby, who most of the time is fully clothed, tousled and smoothly self-deprecating. He reminds me of John Cusack.

Morency teams up with Paul Bates, the group's resident fair- haired boy, for the evening's funniest item, one in which they appear as the Williamson Playboys, a very old-folkie act who claim to have invented Cajun music and have the seniority to prove it, since one is a centenarian and the other is his father. ("Our music has gone public do-main and we aint even dead.")

They also seem to have invented the infallible delaying routine rendered by younger troubadours as I really mean it or "without your trousers," but by these rugged pioneers as I beg your pardon. That is: One will sing the last line of a song, the other will musically beg his pardon, and the first will repeat it, thus implanting the key phrase firmly in the public ear and boosting sales, whether of sheet music, records or T-shirts. Having told us of this device they go ahead and use it, this proving that confirming expectations can be even more devastating than confounding them. You dont believe me, you go along and hear.

Also in the ring are Carolyn Taylor, a strapping female, and Jennifer Goodhue, a diminutive one, who makes an especially effective entrance as a midget Mother Superior, apparently propelled by a sub-habitual go-cart (i.e., a go-cart concealed beneath her habit). She also sings, rousingly, and I recommend her interpretation to the Stratford Festival, currently preparing The Sound of Music, since I feel it might add a a valuable new dimension to Climb Ev'ry Mountain.

The large and small ladies combine, literally, to play a pair of Siamese twins trying out for a job (I repeat, a job) as a cheerleader, not unlike -- very much not unlike -- the old Peter Cook-Dudley Moore sketch about a one-legged man who turned up at an audition for the role of Tarzan of the Apes, and was politely discouraged. The aspirants here are also discouraged, though not politely. We have moved on, in the general direction of cruelty. It is suggested to the big sister that she might gain the prize by having her companion surgically removed. You expect me, she asks, to kill my sister in order to become a cheerleader? Well yes, shrugs the person in charge, actually we do. One sibling reacts with aggressive disbelief, the other with the stoical self-abnegation of a floppy doll anticipating consignment to the attic.

I also feel benevolent toward a number about a neurotic young man whose father is both his fixation and his analyst, not so much for the spoken material as for a sequence in which the two of them, recalling childhood seesaw moments, lock arms and legs and rock.

Sandy Jobin-Bevans is the remaining member of the cast and he's good, too, though I cant think of anything in particular to say about him; this probably means hes the straight man. For the first time in ages, I felt sufficiently amused and impressed by the rehearsed part of a Second City revue to stick around for the post- show improvs. Some of these felt like set routines, easily adapted to the audience's nightly suggestions (which probably don't vary much themselves) but they were fun anyway. You beg my pardon? Go on and beg.

CABARET

Pantages Theatre, Toronto

- - -

Alma Cuervo was the best thing in Cabaret when it played at the Princess of Wales a couple of years ago, and in the somewhat reduced circumstances of the musical's return engagement at the Pantages, she incomparably is. (The show is part of SFX's "Best of Broadway" season, and it still comes closer to justifying that label that anything else in the package.)

She appears as Fraulein Schneider, the middle-aged Berlin landlady who breaks off her engagement to a widowed Jewish fruiterer under the looming threat of Nazism. Cuervo, whose career has been in plays more than musicals, gives a fine, strong account of a shruggingly accepting survivor of a woman, sheltered but worldly, and delivers her two solo songs with devastating power, musical and dramatic.

In one, So What, she psychologically kicks up her heels and proclaims that "you learn how to settle for what you get," especially in the matter of rent. In the other, What Would You Do, she reverses the coin, showing how a decent but unheroic person can settle because she's terrified of what she'll get, and dares her auditors, onstage and off, to condemn her.

These songs, written with an awareness of Brecht and Weill but not in their shadow, show Fred Ebb, the lyricist, and John Kander, the composer, at their best, unhysterically grown-up. And if there were a taste of justice in the world, they would bring down the house more conclusively than any of the score's more famous and flashier numbers. It's difficult, though, to get an audience on its feet for a question mark.

Cuervo also has a couple of duets with her admirer Herr Schultz, admirably played this time round by Hal Robinson. In the first, he presents her with a pineapple from his store, and they go into a tango with Hawaiian overtones. The second, a waltz, comes after he has impulsively proposed, and it sweetly celebrates their future marriage. Both numbers are charming with a touch of the absurd, and the two players convey this beautifully, but to make sure that we don't miss the point, the master of ceremonies of the eponymous Berlin cabaret is onstage behind them, silently -- but not gently -- mocking their feelings.

What chance, we are implicitly asked, does a mature Jewish- Gentile romance have in Germany, c. 1939? The production's overriding nihilism, though, takes the point further, acting superior to the possibility of any tender feelings between any two people, anywhere, anytime. That may not be the intention. It is the flavour.

When Cabaret was first produced on Broadway in the '60's, the numbers in the Berlin nightclub -- the sequence that begins at the top of the show with the emcee singing Wilkommen and climaxes near the end with Sally Bowles doing the title song -- were a commentary on the historical action, rather than a metaphor for it. The same was true of the film version in the '70s. The cabaret was only half of Cabaret. It was the more eye-catching, enjoyable part, so it's understandable that this revival -- directed in New York by Sam Mendes and choreographer Rob Marshall after an initial London staging by Mendes alone -- should make it the whole show.

"Life" according to Sally, "is a cabaret, old chum," and this production takes her at her word. The stories of Sally and Cliff (the musical's stand-in for Christopher Isherwood, who wrote the original Berlin Stories) and Herr Schultz and Fraulein Schneider and all the others, not to mention the rise of German fascism, are an extended cabaret-number; though, since Sally herself works at the club, some of this presumed onstage activity is actually happening backstage. I may be literal-minded, but I find this confusing.

It's swings and roundabouts -- Cabaret, in either of its major stagings, is a brilliant but problematic musical -- but the Mendes- Marshall version is the one we have here, and its flaws are the ones we have to reckon with. One of them is that it turns a supporting character into the star role, and by doing that makes it less rewarding. I remarked before that the emcee here cannot steal the show, because he already owns it. He's always around, leering and preening, and I got tired of him.

I suspect that the production concept determines the performance, but Jon Peterson seems more slinkily androgynous than his predecessor and, however much he may bare his fangs, he does not use them to bite into his songs. He also indulges in some below-Everage banter to the audience that may be a road-show addition -- I don't remember it from before -- and that probably bears little relation to how they carried on in the hotspots of old Berlin.

The conceit seems to be that the emcee, cavorting with his girl- and-boy band and chorus line, makes reductively uncommitted fun of everything, including the Nazis, but doesn't know what he's getting into. Giggles won't cut it anymore; a last tableau -- unique to this production -- shows him in a concentration camp, doubly stigmatized as a homosexual and a Jew. (Echoing the play Bent, he impales himself on the electric wire.)

You have to work very hard to earn the right to use Holocaust imagery, and it's difficult to think of a musical that could qualify. It's nice to know that the creators of this show think Hitler was a bad thing; it's also hard to believe that anyone in the audience needs to be told. What actually comes across is that the production, having run out of ways to shock us, is going for the ultimate.

Meanwhile, much of what was shocking in the original production, which eased us seductively and economically into the horror, has lost its sting; the emcee's gorilla song, for example ("if you could see her through my eyes, she wouldn't look Jewish at all"), which here comes right on top of, and is cancelled out by, a dialogue scene in which a stone is hurled through Herr Schultz's shop window.

The scene is very well staged. The song isn't; Marshall's choreography doesn't have -- presumably doesn't want -- the insolent finesse of Ron Field's (for Hall Prince, in the original) or of Bob Fosse's (for himself, in the movies). In the film, the Mein Herr number involved a lot of girls bending over chairs; here there are no chairs and we just get protruding posteriors.

Still, scenes and songs flow into one another very smoothly. The production knows what it's doing, even if it's confused about what it's thinking, and the staging is very assured. Joe Masteroff, the original librettist, still gets book credit, and he or someone has threaded an astute path though the myriad texts that this material has accumulated.

There are good performances from Drew McVety as a Nazi and Lenora Nemetz as a prostitute, and Hank Stratton does a decent job as the decent Cliff. Sally is Andrea McArdle who, eons, ago, was Broadway's first Annie. I was musing just a few weeks ago on what happened to feisty little musical orphans when they grew up. On this showing, it's nothing good. McArdle makes an earnest stab at the character, and she gives a touchingly tremulous torch-song rendition of Maybe This Time. But the English accent defeats her -- she seems to be groping her way from phrase to phrase, usually landing on the wrong word -- and the amoral playfulness of songs like Perfectly Marvelous (in character) and Don't Tell Mama (ostensibly out of it, but in it really) escapes her utterly. I hadn't realized before how good Michael Gibson's orchestrations are: seedy and reduced but capturing all the essentials.

HOW IS IT THAT YOU WANT TO LIVE?

Canadia Dell'Arte Theatre

- - -

The question How Is it That You Want To Live? is posed by a blind architect to one of his lodgers. It is almost the only thing he says in the play, though he does also ask the same man how he would feel if he saw a hippo coming down the street. Most of the time, inscrutable behind his eye-shades, he sits immobile, surrounded by empty grandeur. That is, he doesn't seem to have much furniture besides his chair, but he does possess a Henry Moore, or anyway a sculpture with a hole in it.

He may remind the drama-Harries among us -- that's a phrase a friend of mine once coined for people like me who obsessively compare plays to other plays -- of Hamm, the sightless chairbound protagonist of Samuel Beckett's Endgame. Like Hamm, he has a male companion to -- for want of a better term -- interact with and two other dependents living in confined conditions.

Hamm kept his parents in dustbins. Balthazar, this play's master builder, is the unknowing host to a married couple who look to be in their thirties and have taken up residence in Balthazar's crawl- space, which surprisingly affords them room to cook, eat and sleep. This is Beckett with a socio-economic context; someone even mentions the possibility of getting a job at K-Mart, though without much enthusiasm.

The piece is written, directed, designed (quite strikingly) and one-quarter performed by Peter Reitzel, who heads the Canadia dell'Arte Theatre, a troupe who are certainly Canadian and definitely arty. They have their own space and, judging from my own three or four brushes with them, a very select audience. There were 10 people in the house on Thursday and, in my experience of the Canadia dell'Arte, ten's a crowd. They don't seem all that concerned about communicating, even with the audience they do have.

This is true on the most basic technical level; Dennis Frey as Balthazar puts little energy even into the few, presumably significant, lines he does have. The company describe their play as "not so much a comedy as it is a reality." They add, "it is a battle of the ego deciding whether to side with the superego or the id." This, though probably meant to be helpful, is alarming. All the same, they have something.

The stage is divided between Balthazar's room and the couple's, and what happens in the latter is interesting and, given the premise, believable. Mr. Reitzel plays Richard, who understandably doesn't like being called Rich and who at the beginning of the day has a job, which he speedily loses. His wife, Elizabeth, is played by Julie Reitzel, who I take is Peter's wife, and they convey a powerful sense of intimacy. She has literary pursuits -- at least she is constantly either reading or writing -- and the deal seems to be that he will support her and help her pay off her student loan.

Naturally, this proves progressively more difficult; Christmas Day finds them reduced to sharing a couple of pieces of bread. Affection and resentment chase one another 'round and 'round as he sinks into lassitude and she into bitterness; the slightest thing will set them off but nothing conclusively erupts. The two Reitzels manage the subdued tensions very well, though -- as seems to be the way of this company -- they crack whenever something more extroverted is required.

On the other side of the wall the legitimate tenant, Edward (Michael Chipman, whose performance is indeed chipper but never quite takes), tries to make some kind of contact with his landlord. He puts on a periwig and reads to him from what may be a Restoration comedy; the dressing-up aspect is wasted on Balthazar, of course, but Edward is probably doing it for his own benefit. He also has a long, and pretty good, speech about cocaine.

The upshot seems to be that society is a house built by a melancholy man who may have good intentions but cannot see what he is doing, and in which artists -- if that is what Richard and Elizabeth are -- can only hope to scratch out an existence in a corner, on sufferance and unobserved. If they can accept that, they may not do too badly; Elizabeth says she's happy.

Occasionally, the two worlds collide; the couple tiptoe past the unseeing Balthazar on their way in and out, and once Elizabeth pauses to bestow a kiss on him. There is a confrontation half-way through that I totally failed to understand; maybe it's a dream (the production boasts a phantasmagoric score).

The ending is quite remarkably abrupt: when we finally grasp that the proceedings are over, we drift out without being detained by anything as vulgar as a curtain-call. Like the company's 1999 production of Ibsen's Ghosts, this new home-grown piece veers between scrupulous naturalism and portentous vagueness. The former is much preferable, but I doubt if the company see it that way.

HEDWIG AND THE ANGRY INCH

Bathurst Street Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - A short distance into Hedwig and The Angry Inch, I was shocked. This was not for any of the reasons that you or the creators of the show might expect.

It was not because of Hedwig, who is a German-born American- based former rock star reduced to playing a seedy dive in Toronto (impersonated, very convincingly, by the Bathurst Street Theatre) while her former lover headlines at a huge downtown stadium that Hedwig refers to as the SkyLab; all this I could take or leave. It was not because of The Angry Inch who is/are Hedwig's band, named after a small fleshy protuberance of which Hedwig, who was once Helmut, found herself in unwilling possession after undergoing a slightly incomplete sex-change operation. I am notoriously squeamish, but this job has hardened me and I bore the anatomical details, as detailed in speech and song, without so much as an inward shudder. It wasn't even because a show that has aroused terrific enthusiasm in New York and elsewhere now looks and sounds terrible; these things happen, often. No, what got me in the marrow of my bones was Hedwig's repeated complaints about her agent, whose name, she had the gall to announce, was Phyllis Stein.

Do you remember Phyllis? She is a splendid Toronto lady, well- bred and broad-minded, whose opinion I have sometimes solicited regarding some of the loucher entertainments around town. I was consulting her only last month about Closer, after which I felt she deserved a rest. But, after hearing her name bandied about from a public stage, I had no choice but to put in another call.

This is how it went.

ME (tentatively): Hello, Phyllis. Is it ... true?

PHYLLIS (suspiciously cheery): Hello, darling. Is what true?

ME: Don't bother. You've answered my question. You never called me darling before, and certainly not in italics. Phyllis, I don't want to sound like someone in a rock musical but you've betrayed me. You've gone over to the other side. You're in the show business. And you never told me.

PHYLLIS (a light laugh): A girl has to live. And I've always fancied the glamour. I thought some of it might rub off on me. Though mind you, when I met Hedwig, I thought it might be better if some of mine rubbed off on her. But I like to do a good turn when I can. And Hedwig needed one.

ME: You can say that again. But let's get this, if you'll pardon the paradox, straight. The person we see on stage is not Hedwig. The person we see on stage is Ted Dykstra, noted Canadian actor. And in New York, I gather, it was someone else.

PHYLLIS (nodding -- or so I assume): John Cameron Mitchell. He wrote the script. And Stephen Trask -- he wrote the songs -- was in the band. Such talented boys. They asked if they could use my name, and how could I refuse? They said it was just right for an agent.

ME: That sounds like their sense of fun. Just remember I saw you first. In Toronto, anyway. So you liked the show in New York?

PHYLLIS: Darling, I loved it. Such flash. And did you see the quote from Rolling Stone: "The first rock musical that truly rocks!"

ME: Well, they should know. The trouble is that rocking is the only movement it has. When Ted Dykstra sings his songs -- and he sings all of them -- all he does is prowl from one side of the stage to the other and back again. Like an actor impersonating a rock singer. And flash? The only visual element apart from Hedwig's drag - - and to be fair he does look about 14 feet tall when he first comes on -- is a series of slides depicting childhood drawings that Hedwig did back when she was Helmut. He was not, it seems, a visually gifted child. And they persist long after he's grown up, changed gender, changed country. Look, you've quoted Rolling Stone at me. Can I quote Stephen Sondheim to you?

PHYLLIS: If you have to.

ME: "Rock music is fine for rock concerts. Whether they're rock concerts called rock concerts or rock concerts called Hair or Jesus Christ Superstar ..." This was some time ago, you understand, but nothing has changed. Hedwig is a rock concert with unusually long monologues between the songs and I suppose it deserves credit for not pretending to be anything else. Except it is in a theatre, which arouses expectations. Now we're always being told that rock concerts have all the visual and visceral excitement that the theatre has lost. If that's true, I can't see that the answer is for the theatre to imitate what another medium is already doing better. But anyway, nobody seems to have told Jim Millan, who directed this one; it's drab. And meanwhile, as always, the score destroys any chance of developing story or character. And have you noticed -- unless they're outright camp like The Rocky Horror Show -- all rock musicals, however flippantly they start out, invariably end up with the hero taking the sins of the world on his shoulders? Think of Tommy. It's no accident that the first rock opera was JC Superstar. To those of us who never thought of rock stars as messiahs in the first place, it's pretty ludicrous. Especially since the volume of the music is always far in excess of any conceivable level of emotion in the drama.

PHYLLIS: But you're missing the real pain here ... Hedwig's divided body and divided nature, symbolizing the schism in all of us. It's no accident that she comes from Berlin ...

ME: And compares herself to the Wall. I know. Childish and pretentious, as usual. And yes, to save you the trouble of saying so, it's not my kind of music. But that's not the point. And in fact I've heard the New York cast CD, and I liked some of it. It has variety, and an occasional country sound -- Hedwig goes through a period as trailer trash -- and country tends to work dramatically, however limited it may be musically. And you can hear the words, or at least read them. (Which is the big rock cop-out, but we won't go into that.) And Mitchell as a singer has lyricism. Dykstra just bashes through everything, helped or hindered by the sound system. He's better when he talks -- he's a good actor -- but he doesn't have the real drag-queen glitter that the script presumes. But then neither does the script. There's one funny line.

PHYLLIS: Which I suppose you're going to be shameless enough to quote?

ME: You bet. Hedwig comes on wearing a fur, and says that some woman had asked her, "What poor creature had to die for you to wear that?" and that she replied, "My aunt Trudi." By the way, isn't Hedwig a Scandinavian name rather than a German one?

PHYLLIS: Don't stick your neck out. It might get chopped off.

ME: Ouch. Hedwig mentions other people but of course they never appear, and her patter doesn't bring them to life. Not her -- er, his -- mother, nor the American who seduced him in New York and procured the operation so he could marry her, nor Tommy Gnosis, her protege and nemesis -- he's the one who's supposed to be appearing at SkyDome. You'd think it might be fun to let us hear one of his numbers, so we could compare, but not a chance. Which reminds me, Phyllis, I have to ask. Remember, I didn't see the New York production. Were you Hedwig's agent there, too, or were you just dropped in here as another dab of local colour?

PHYLLIS: Darling, my lips are sealed.

Black & White Photo: TED DYKSTRA AS HEDWIG: He prowls the stage -- just like an actor impersonating a rock star. ;

GHOST TRAIN

Young Peoples Theatre, Toronto

"Every picture tells a story, doesn't it?" says the narrator at the end of Ghost Train, taking the curse off an ancient platitude by turning it sweetly into a question. The answer in this case has to be a delighted yes. The pictures in this show are stunning; not only does each tell a tale of its own but together they make a saga.

They do this with no more than token support from the text. The ostensible subject matter of Ghost Train is serendipitously the same as that of the new opera Iron Road: the building of the British Columbia section of the Canadian Pacific Railway by immigrant workers from China.

Betty Quan's script, based on a book by Paul Yee, tells this story from the point of view of Choon-Yi, a one-armed Chinese girl with an artistic gift, whose father leaves their village for Canada, promising to send for his daughter at a later date. When Choon-Yi is 16, the money for her passage arrives and she embarks on a long and nightmarish ocean crossing, packed tightly with other passengers in the hold of a steamship. When she arrives in Salt Water City, otherwise known as Vancouver, her father is nowhere to be found.

The rest of the play details her quest for him, which reaches its conclusion when, after several abortive attempts, she manages to paint a satisfactory picture of the "first car" -- the train to which her father and his compatriots have dedicated their labour and their lives. The completed picture turns out to have magical properties, but the mysticism is scrappy and unsatisfying. It's preferable, though, to the recurrent vignettes of life back in the village, scenes whose gossipy humour is extremely forced and -- given that it's directed at children -- patronizing.

The play's main flaw, though, is its failure to tell us much about the building of the railroad. The underlying assumption is that the Chinese workers were shamefully exploited. I can well believe it, but it isn't dramatized. Certainly, working conditions are shown to be tough, but what else would you expect on a major construction project in the middle of the 19th century? No evidence is presented that the Chinese labourers were worked harder or paid worse than anyone else; it's just taken as read. (And a sloppy comparison is made in the accompanying study guide between desperate Third World immigrants now, and these railwaymen, who at least had a definite job to go to.)

When we do get to see Choon-Yi's father at work, he and his companions seem rather cheerful, despite the dangers, and they show no signs of resentment. This is meant to be a key scene, or at any rate it's given pride of place at the end of the first act: a mystifying decision, since it suggests that the play is really not about Choon-Yi but about her father, though nothing else in the play supports that. The focus is otherwise all on her, and Karen Ancheta comes through with a determined and (at least on Tuesday morning) winningly throaty performance.

She gets sympathetic, if sometimes smilingly bland, support from Laurence Tan as her dad, from Denis Akiyama as the narrator, and from Richard Lee as a young restaurateur who befriends and woos our heroine and who has a second career as a carnival clown.

The only occidental character, seen in silhouette, is a ticket collector who gives Choon-Yi a hard time when she tries, appropriately enough, to search for her father by train. It's possible to mount a pungent drama about racism without letting us meet any of the racists, but it presents problems and they have not been solved or even, apparently, recognized.

Pierre Tetrault, artistic director of Young Peoples Theatre, is credited on this play with direction and dramaturgy, and his achievement in the first capacity far exceeds that in the second.

Donald Quan has composed a haunting musical score, though some occasional songs seem a needless concession to accepted conventions of children's theatre. (They also, in the China scenes, sound disconcertingly Western, even Wild Western; at one point, I expected the Magnificent Seven to gallop over the soundtrack.)

Glen Charles Landry is the set designer, but an additional phalanx of names is credited with visual creations, visual creations and visual art. That may seem like overkill but the results are inspired. At first, it seems that the production will be backed by slides: handsome but predictable. Then we notice that even if the pictures aren't moving, the camera is, pulling in and out as in a TV documentary.

In fact, there is a film running behind the play, but without upstaging it; rather enriching it with superb vistas of authentic places and faces. Three panels divide much of the acting area, each able to bear another set of pictures that can be faded in and out in time with the actors' movements. Shadowy scenes unfold within these compartments, especially useful for staging close-packed journeys by sea or rail. At one point, the train appears to be moving, because the film projected above it is moving, but in the opposite direction.

This is superb staging. It's enough to give "mixed media," that ghastly phrase for a usually ghastly concept, a good name.

Black & White Photo: Thomas L. Sandler / Denis Akiyama (narrator) with Karen Ancheta (Choon-Yi): journey of realization. ;

MOO

Alumnae Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Sally Clark's play Moo won a Chalmers award in 1988, and though I refuse to believe that it was ever very good, I imagine that a skilled production would at least make it look slick. The Alumnae Theatre, which used to be a respected professional company, has given it an amateurish revival in which all the actors are over- stretched, but if you can decode it you may discern in the text a recognizable Canadian quality, one that I would define as cute heartlessness. It can get cloying, but experienced actors on Toronto's classier stages have frequently managed to shine it up and pass it off as wit.

And, undeniably, the play starts with a smart idea. Sometime in the 1920s, to judge from the background music, Harry has his wife, Moo, committed to a mental hospital, claiming that she is actually his sister and that her furious denials only prove her insanity. Strangely, it takes the authorities the longest time to check out Moo's story, and by the time they do Harry has skipped town and shacked up with somebody else.

We are not, though, watching a tract about a man persecuting a woman. As far as we can tell, Moo is crazy, the proof being her continuing obsession with Harry, who first won her affection by shooting a gun at her. "I have this compulsive need" she says, "to be screwed around by someone. Not just someone -- no ordinary Tom or Dick will do; it has to be Harry." Treasure that line. It's as good as the play gets.

The attraction is symbolic; Harry is obsessed with Moo, too. The action unfolds over a further 40 years, much of which he spends mailing her postcards from exotic and unaccessible locations. She sets off in pursuit, generally finding that by the time she gets there, he has moved on. Occasionally she does track him down, and one of these reunions produces a son. In the course of Act Two this boy, tired of being reviled by his mother as ugly and stupid, revolts and goes off to war.

We also see Moo interacting with her family, especially with two sisters who disapprove of the goings-on, and whom she of course regards as pitiable prisoners of convention. The longer the play goes on, the easier it becomes to sympathize with the sisters' point of view.

When her relatives give her a 60th birthday party, Moo turns up accompanied by an admirer who gropes her furiously under the table, and whom even she admits to finding disgusting. She ends the play institutionalized once more, senile, visited briefly by a still- infatuated Harry and at greater length by a niece who used to admire her but who now reviles her, accurately enough, as a selfish woman who has wasted her life on a futile, not to say degrading, passion.

The niece also proclaims that she has no intention of letting the same thing happen to her. This may be a moment of genuine hope for the future of women, or it may be crushing dramatic irony; we simply don't know enough about the young lady to tell.

The play does not exactly endorse Moo, but it does present her as a force of nature whom we will enjoy spending two hours with: an Auntie Mame with consequences. Women like her certainly exist, as do men as helplessly feckless as Harry. Compulsive behaviour, though, is not necessarily compelling behaviour, and the play is one of that common breed that state a situation and then just keep repeating it (cf., currently, Hedwig and the Angry Inch, which at least is shorter and has songs).

Kristen Schiener's production is unable to keep the play in the style to which it would like to become accustomed. It has trouble moving with any kind of fluency from one short scene to the next, its furnishings sometimes misbehave (when I saw it, Moo had to bestow a sharp kick on a recalcitrant retractable bed), and it's sloppy at staging crucial physical actions. At one point Harry, stationed far upstage in the hope that we won't notice, gives his second wife a vague shove. We learn later that what he was actually doing was pushing her downstairs; who would have known?

Even worse, the actors -- mostly non-Equity -- seem to lack any sense of verbal timing, and the scenes between Moo and Harry completely lack sexual tension, which undercuts the play's entire premise. Brandon Barre as Harry has more ease than anyone else on stage, but not too much else. As Moo, Risa Gittelman seems (probably unfairly, since presumably she didn't cast herself) to be at the centre of a vanity production; she doesn't have the range, the authority or the sparkle for a character who sees herself and is seen by the play as a virtuoso creation.

The others, though they appear terrible, may simply be too young for their roles; the two who actually get to play young -- Darren Stewart-Jones as the son, Stefanie Drummond as niece -- are noticeably better than the rest.

Black & White Photo: Michael Cooper, Alumnae Theatre / MADE FOR EACH OTHER: Brandon Barre and Risa Gittelman as Harry and Moo. ;
2001-05-01-on-golden-pond-sinks-under-te:
Toward the end of CBS's live-drama production on Sunday night, we were treated to a full-length shot of a cameraman, though it may possibly -- since naturally they didn't linger on it -- have been a floor manager. On Golden Pond is a house-and-garden play, and earlier, in the middle of one of the indoor scenes, the camera had panned deliriously along a row of greenery belonging to the exterior. A boom microphone occasionally strayed into the top of the picture, but this may have been done on purpose, as a sort of live- production log. The awkwardness of many of the compositions was presumably accidental, suggesting that television has a lot to learn, or re-learn, about the art of catching drama on the hoof. Perhaps in acknowledgement of the abiding staginess of Ernest Thompson's play, we were treated to arbitrary views of the full set. The crowning moment of gracelessness came, fittingly, at the end: Julie Andrews and Christopher Plummer, the two stars, made their final exit by disappearing down the bottom right-hand corner of the screen.

Technical gaffes aside, On Golden Pond seems an odd choice for live production since it is, and probably always has been, so thoroughly dead. First staged in 1978, it's one of those Broadway confections (The Gin Game is another) that pretend to be honest in demonstrating that old people are not plaster-saints but pull back from showing them as anything worse than cutely cranky; that they are invariably cast with much-loved stars is the tooth-rotting icing on the cake.

The darling duo here are Norman Thayer, a retired English professor, and his wife, Ethel, of whose career, if she ever had one, we are not informed. She is pushing 70, he is turning 80. They have spent every summer of their 50-year marriage "on golden pond" - - their lakeshore residence in Main -- and here they are for another one. Norman's faculties are beginning to fail, and at one point he tells of getting lost on a familiar walk to the woods; strings welled up behind this speech to ensure that we didn't miss any of the poignancy. (Count your blessings: If this had been a TV film, it would have been drenched in tear-jerker music.) The play has no shame; it teases us by taking Norman to the brink, felling him with what looks like a fatal heart attack and then passing it off as a false alarm. The scene gives Ethel just enough time to display an improbably stiff upper lip; she is anguished, but unshakably well- bred.

Norman and Ethel have an only child, a daughter called Chelsea, now a 40-year-old divorcee. Long absent in California, she reappears with her new boyfriend, a dentist, and his son, a 14-year-old terror who represents everything in modern life that Norman detests and much he has probably never heard of. While the middle-aged couple go off to Europe, the old ones take care of the boy; and -- to nobody's surprise except the characters, he and Norman bond. The professor learns some new idioms; the kid starts to fish and even to read. Before, he dismissed the presence of books in the house as evidence that "they don't have cable." This is one of several indications that the script has been updated since '78. The juvenile language is more colourful than would have been tolerated, on the screen anyway, 25 years ago. Norman's ivy-league diction is now cut with coy hints at obscenity.

The thing is put together with undeniable slickness, and there are some good grouchy lines for Norman. Plummer, in great impish form, seemed to relish them -- and the enjoyment was contagious. There was also at least a hint of wickedness in it. The script tells us that the man could be a bastard, especially to his daughter. We are never shown any evidence of this, but Plummer at least made it seem a distant possibility. His reaction to the news that she has impulsively remarried in Brussels -- "get out of town!" -- could have been worth the price of admission, had there been one.

I imagine that Henry Fond in the 1981 film (which I avoided) was far less fun, being really frail at the time and unshakably noble. Katharine Hepburn, though, must have been an asset as his opposite number; when she called Norman "you poop," she must have given the word a real Pennsylvania tang.

Coming from Julie Andrews, still English after all these years, it merely sounded odd; and her acting hardly went beyond sweet reasonableness.

Still, this late reunion of the Sound of Music principles made a certain sense: With allowances for changes of time, place and accent, one can well imagine the von Trapps living out their declining years like this, lake and all.

Glenne Headly, woefully ill-at-ease, played the daughter, Sam Robards the prospective son-in-law, and Brett Cullen was saddled with the role that takes the lay to its lowest depths, that of Charley, the slow-witted mailman, who for decades has nourished a hopeless passion for Chelsea. "I love your laugh," Ethel told him, while plying him with coffee and biscuits; this was kind of her, since it sounded like a cross between a rusty hinge and a death- rattle, and it never stopped.

At the end we were shown a montage of highlights, and we got to hear someone -- the director -- congratulating everyone on their great work. The implication seemed to be that they had all come through some kind of historic ordeal. This really was unconscionable. Last year's Fail Safe, which must have been a far more complicated production, had none of the same glitches; and there was a time when all TV drama was live and nobody felt obliged to treat each play as a special event. That was also of course the time of black-and-white TV, so the plays seemed grittier all round. It was an accidental aesthetic but a real one.

On Golden Pond is a sentimental play about well-heeled, well- educated people with minimal problems -- the kind that Broadway, echoed by Hollywood and network TV, likes to call "civilized." They might just as well have shot it on a stage. It could hardly have seemed phonier. It might even have lent some charm.

THE EPIC PERIOD

Factory Theatre, Toronto

A native lawyer, reflecting on the difference between his ancestors' times and our own, decides that "vegetarian was the Ojibwa word for bad hunter."

I wish all of The Epic Period were like that, or at least that more of it were. The title suggests we are in for something dizzyingly ambitious, though the fact that there are only three actors in the cast (doing, to be sure, a certain amount of furtive doubling) should warn us to moderate our expectations. In the event, Sean Dixons play turns out to be a contemporary comedy of relationships, with a bit of the historic past clinging to it, and a bit of myth clinging to that. A pervasive air of tongue-in-cheek is meant, I think, to allow the elements to combine weightlessly into a whole. Its actual effect is to prevent any of them from really engaging the audience.

The comedy works best, especially in its romantic aspect. The embroiled couple are the lawyer, who is called Joshua but who also answers to the name of Bundle, and a soon-to-be-ex-nun, who was prophetically christened Moody. Just before the play starts, Joshua has helped Moody break her vows in the most decisive way; the action proper begins the morning after, with her attempting to throw him out. So this, at its outset, is yet another post-pickup play.

It turns out that their meeting was no random chance; Moodys mother has just died, Joshua was present at the deathbed, and he has been entrusted with a mission to the daughter. Its upshot is to send the two of them on a quest to a spot called Christian Island, a burial place for Huron converts of many generations before. While digging for treasure, they also continue to dig one another. Moody's discoveries in both these areas enable her to reach out toward her moderately estranged and thoroughly puzzled father, of whom, as it happens, Joshua goes in mortal fear. Not only has he debauched the old man's daughter but the old man happens to be his boss and he does indeed set out in pursuit of them, in a canoe and with a rifle.

When the three of them finally collide, bandying firearms and recriminations, the play -- 60 minutes into its 90-minute length -- comes to belated but exuberant life. We can even cut it enough slack to be somewhat moved by a scene in which Moody remonstrates with her father for the lack of attention he showed her mother, to which he more or less replies that he did the best he could. A kind of therapy ensues, facilitated by techniques of "shape-shifting" (which here seems to be a fancy word for role-playing) inherited by Joshua, a.k.a. Bundle, from his Indian ancestors. In the end, though, we dont know or care enough about any of the characters for it to matter.

The past is continually with us. Moody, through her mother, has Huron blood and her excavations bring her a message from her family past. (It may also relate to her own religious conflicts, though the point is hardly made.) There are brief historical flashbacks: A 17th- century Jesuit is seen admonishing a female member of his Huron flock, presumably Moodys ancestress. These sequences could probably stand bolder treatment than they get; in Brian Quirt's production, they are shoved to the side of the stage and intoned by robed and hooded actors who seem to be satirizing their own pretensions before even advancing them. The jokes here, whether past or present, come off nervous rather than joyous; neither period seems sure enough of itself to illuminate the other.

There was a similar uncertainty of tone in the recent An Acre of Time from the same director: the same see-sawing between solemn and jokey, as if to say we have all this Canadian history at our disposal and it's bound to be enriching, but we dont want to get too heavy about it. There is a lot of this in the current theatre. You may call it postmodern but you can hardly call it satisfying.

The play is also, perhaps less momentously, the second in succession on the Factory stage in which two male actors flank Waneta Storms. The lady appears on our stages as often as her husband, Randy Hughson (though rarely with him), and like him is always a welcome sight; she seems, though, to be generally less fortunate in her vehicles than he is. This time she takes as long to get into her stride as the play does, but when she hits it she is enchanting.

Herbie Barnes, last seen in the title role of The Hobbit, makes a cute bundle of Bundle, endearing in his insecurities, though passing them on rather too freely to his audience in the shape of diction that is swallowed or gabbled or both. And call me sizeist, or at least heightist, but I dont think the effect of his being slightly shorter than the object of his affections has been sufficiently allowed for in the staging. David Gardner's dad starts out disconcertingly low key but eventually reveals this to be a style, an effective way of conveying wounded bemusement. Steve Lucas's sets and lighting tickle the eye without much assisting the mind.

Black & White Photo: Nir Bareket Photography / ENDEARING AND ENCHANTING: Waneta Storms as Moody and Herbie Barnes as Bundle. ;
