ANYTHING THAT MOVES

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

Any way you take it, Anything That Moves is a very neat show. When it had its tryout last year (some tryout -- it won a Dora), I pronounced it, somewhat guardedly, the best new Canadian musical I had seen. I can now drop the guard: It is the best.

The show's shape and premise remain the same, but Ann-Marie Macdonald's book and lyrics, Allen Cole's music, and Alisa Palmer's direction have all been extensively revised and almost uniformly improved. The six actors -- two returners, four newcomers -- are all exemplary. Tim Howar is charming and euphonious as Joel, a shy and impoverished young florist who meets and falls for Jinny, a research scientist with a romantic backlog of men who are drunk or married or both.

Glynis Ranney, who acts as well as she sings, is splendidly edgy and hurting in this role. She even manages to surmount the proverbial hurdle of sharing a stage with something furry and four- legged, in this case a laboratory rat named Pat (one of the author's simpler rhymes) to whom she sings her first number, which is naturally drowned out by enthusiastic gurgles from the audience.

Jinny first sees Joel in the company of Tyrone, his flamboyantly gay best friend, and jumps to the conclusion they are lovers. Tyrone has all the show's best lines, or at least Juan Chioran makes them sound that way. The apex of saturnine, as fastidious in some respects as he is promiscuous in others, he sports an outstandingly twirlable moustache that he never actually touches. Judy Marshak is Jinny's mother, Fleur, addicted to alcohol and men but celebrating 15 years of abstinence from the former. She stops the show in the second act with a song called Menopausal Mama, far better integrated this time around than it was before. She now sings it to the other characters rather than to us. (Both parties enthusiastically respond.)

If Jinny has issues with her mother, so does Joel with his father, a military historian in a kilt played with sympathetic uptightness by George Masswohl. Usually remote from his son, geographically as well as emotionally, he is in town to bury a dead comrade. The officiating funeral director is a high-energy black lesbian named Alberta, who starts out, in Sandra Caldwell's performance, as the most overpowering of undertakers, every line a production number. This grows on you, and she later quietens down effectively. She also happens to be Joel's best customer -- an example of what a Dickensian character, speaking of the dramatic Unities, called "a kind of universal dovetailedness."

There is a lot of this. Each of the six onstage characters is dogged (or, as at least one of them would say, bitched) by the memory of another person, living or dead, who has to be escaped or accommodated. The musical shows our chosen half-dozen regrouping and at least potentially pairing-off. There are more question marks hanging over their destinies this year than there were last, when an epilogue tied up everything too neatly. One central problem remains: Jinny's belief that Joel is gay seems contrived, his failure to enlighten her even more so. Plenty of reasons are given -- she likes him very much but for the moment she wants a soul mate rather than a lover -- but they all seem like protesting too much. The theme of mistaken (sexual) identity is now, though, more central than it was: The show becomes a comedy about lying, and so successful as such that in the second act, when everybody convenes at a dinner party to which some are invited and others not, it almost seems to forget it's a musical.

Usually, though, it remembers in time and with enjoyable results. The subject matter may suggest the Sondheim of Company, but the show doesn't hit that level of acerbity or indeed of passion. It's a nice piece about nice people who deserve nice relationships, in a tone and style that recall the smaller U.S. shows of the '60s.

This means that as a lyricist, MacDonald is placing herself in the lineage of Sheldon Harnick, if not quite of Cole Porter. So one holds her to high standards. She meets them , with bright observation, lilting conversational rhythms and rhymes that surprise, usually in the right way. There are lapses, marring a couple of otherwise irresistible songs: "Diva" is not a good fit with "Mona Lisa," nor does "sucky" chime as she would like it to. (I won't quote the actual rhyme for fear of asterisks.) Otherwise she writes wonderful patter: A breakneck duet for Joel and Tyrone is an especial treat.

The ballads are less adroit. Cole's tunes are pretty enough but they tell us things we already know so they stop the show in its tracks rather than just stopping it. And while it may be funny to have Jinny ask despairingly "why can't a straight man be more like a fag?" it's foolhardy to make this the basis for an entire My Fair Lady parody. Inconsistent, too, since there are no other specific spoofs in the show. (Both shows feature flower sellers: Maybe that's the connection.)

Astrid Janson has designed a simple, pleasing and useful set, and the staging has improved immeasurably, up to the standard of Palmer's knife-edge work on Sibs. The choreographer, Valerie Moore, has obviously been invaluable: There are no big dance numbers, but this time around, Anything That Moves really moves.

Black & White Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann, Tarragon and Nightwood Theatres / Juan Chiroan, left, Judy Marshak and George Masswohl: Menopausal Mama is a second-act show-stopper. ;
2001-05-05-the-island-stands-apart:
To June 16. (416) 872-1111

THE ISLAND

Bluma Appel Theatre

- - -

To begin with, some history: In 1973 in Cape Town, Athol Fugard, the white South African playwright and director, collaborated with two black actors, John Kani and Winston Ntshona, on a play they called Sizwe Bansi Is Dead. It dealt with one of the most oppressive aspects of apartheid, the pass laws, and was surprisingly a comedy: it showed a black man beating the system by the desperate means of assuming a dead mans identity.

That same year the production travelled to the Royal Court Theatre in London, where its humour, anger and extraordinary authenticity knocked everybody out. It quickly returned in harness with a second, grimmer piece, The Island, about two prisoners in the notorious high-security fortress of Robben Island. The two plays then went on to conquer New York and, in 1977, even received major public production in New York.

Now, with apartheid gone, it is The Island that is staking a claim to survival. It was revived with the original performers at Peter Brooks Bouffes-du-Nord theatre in Paris in 1999, went from there to the National Theatre in London, and has now arrived in triumph in Toronto.

Sizwe Bansi was a protest play; The Island is a history play. The terms overlap, of course, but the latter is the more durable. Bansi was about a specific issue; The Island takes on an institution, one that still stands and, even if it crumbled tomorrow, could stand in imaginatively for political prisons everywhere. Robben Island is where Nelson Mandela was incarcerated, but even without that (and the play never mentions him) it would have the force of a myth.

The Island places another myth within the myth. It shows us two prisoners rehearsing their own version of what might be called the original protest play, Sophocles' Antigone.

That idea, probably Mr. Fugard's, may seem high-flown but is based on fact; there was an actor imprisoned on the island who attempted just that. Messrs. Kani and Ntshona themselves did time under apartheid, though in less extreme circumstances, but its probable that any black South African would know in his bones what the experience would be like.

The two appear here as cell-mates actually called John and Winston. John is the prime mover, the ex-actor who wants to do the play at the prison concert; Winston is his wavering collaborator, grumbling but loyal. Cast as Antigone, he more or less says, like Flute in A Midsummer Nights Dream, let me not play a woman." People, he rightly says, surveying his false breasts and straw- coloured wig, will laugh. Yes, says John very wisely, they will, but they can't laugh forever and then they'll listen.

Its hard to be sure after nearly 30 years but my impression is John has put on weight in the interim and Winston has lost it. Their mind-and-body double act has the same dynamic but different physical expression. Their acting is, if anything, even richer; physically, vocally, facially, each is complete to the core, while their rapport, after all these years as colleagues, goes beyond teamwork; they seem to breathe in symphony.

They begin the play with a 15-minute mime (not fun to watch, but necessary) of hard labour on the island beach: a special detail, even worse than the customary work in the quarry, aimed as much at their minds as their bodies. Then we find them in their cell where they can talk, quarrel, be human. Perhaps the most terrifying thing about the play, though, is the immediacy with which, when a knock comes at the door and an unseen guard confronts them, they revert to their officially sanctioned role as terrified automata, cringing at the double; its an act but it's real.

They don't spend all their time arguing about Antigone. They have a nightly ritual by which each of them alternates in the task of entertaining the other. One night Winston will tell John the plot of a movie (suddenly were reminded of Kiss of the Spider Woman, another two-prisoner piece, presented by the same Canadian producer, Garth Drabinsky, on the same stage); on another, John will act out the fantasy of placing a phone call home, inquiring after friends and family. Here, in the plays subtlest and most wrenching moment, John passes from amusing Winston to desperately reassuring himself as he asks about the wife who has stopped writing to him.

John is called to the governor's office and told his 10-year sentence has been commuted to three; he'll be out in three months. Winston, in brilliantly acted silence, tries to conceal his jealousy; then, gradually, as he describes Johns homecoming in cold, blistering tones we havent heard from him before, he lets it slip.

I used to think this passage too literary; I no longer do, though I could do without Winston telling John that he has the stink of freedom -- we've got there before him. It's probably unfair that were not told how long Winston is in for, and its not made quite clear how arbitrary the regime was; that two people could be given drastically unequal sentences for the same supposed offence.

The two men rally and we see their performance, noting that when John introduces them he mentions, according to form, not only their cell number but the fact that they're on "Diet G." Their take on Antigone destroys the Sophoclean balance, making Creon the racist tyrant, Antigone the unequivocal freedom-fighter. It's inevitable and stirring (one wonders if it will cost John his freedom) and not, even for a cushioned audience like us, sentimental. The actors -- who risked a lot to create the show -- have earned it, even if we haven't.

Performed by other actors, The Island would not be a great play and, outside this and Sizwe Bansi Is Dead (which I would like to see them do again, just to be sure), these may not be great actors.

But the play and the actors together are great, doing honour to the theatre and to the world. It is everything we were promised.

THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

Artword Theatre, London

The set for the first-ever Canadian production of Marivaux's The Triumph of Love is like a do-it-yourself kit for modest productions of 18th-century French comedy.

At the back is a flight of white steps leading up to a narrow entrance through which we glimpse a small rectangle of sky. A versatile vista, this changes from blue to mauve to back again, and once takes a dashing turn at being green. There are tall screens at the sides of the stage, bearing patterns of branches -- this play, like many another artificial comedy, is set in a garden. A few spindly trees stand up on stage, and there are also -- this is a philosophers garden -- a couple of formal but comfortable chairs.

A mirror confronts us from high on the back wall, reflecting the action before and below. Im not sure why, except two images for the price of one always make a striking effect. The trees, as it happens, look more convincing in reflection than they do in reality: Maybe there's an intellectual point there. The various parts do not really cohere, and a brown false proscenium that must be meant to unify them is downright ugly, but the design serves.

John van Burek's direction of his own translation more than serves: It is a considerable achievement. Its great virtue is nobody in it seems to be treading water. Every actor seems to know at every moment just what he or she is talking about and how it relates to what everybody else is talking about. This may not seem much to ask, but it is a surprisingly rare occurrence, certainly in a play as remote from us in time, place and convention as this one. I wont pretend my concentration never slackened, but I dont think theirs ever did.

In France, Marivaux's airy, trenchant studies of amorous deception have been making a comeback. Elsewhere, they hardly arrived in the first place, and though we know more of them than we did (this production follows on the same company's Game of Love and Chance last year), we still need careful guidance.

This is the story: The Princess Leonide wishes to make amends to the young prince Agis, whose family was disinherited -- and, it seems, decimated -- by hers.

She also has every intention of marrying him. So she seeks him out in the country house of the philosopher Hermocrate, who has watched over him since his childhood.

Since she would hardly be welcome in her own shape, the princess disguises herself as, as if you hadnt guessed, a man. Calling herself Phocion, she professes to be a travelling student, a sort of guru-collector who wishes to stay with Hermocrate in order to soak up his wisdom. With her she brings her servant, similarly transgendered.

To the ironies that traditionally accrue in a situation like this, Marivaux adds one of his own: Half the people Leonide encounters see through her masquerade and half dont, so the levels of deceit and awareness vary dizzyingly throughout. Shakespeare never thought of that.

We, inevitably, do think of As You Like It, what with deposed princes living in woods and disguised princesses conducting tutorials in passion and misanthropic scholars who claim to be above all that. However, unlike Rosalind, Leonide-Phocion is a ruthless flirt. To get close to Agis, she has to charm and disarm both Hermocrate, who knows she is a woman, and Hermocrate's bluestocking sister, Leontine (Marivuax can be brutally confusing with names), who thinks she is a woman. Coolly and successfully, she sets about making them both fall in love with her: Imagine Rosalind making a play for Jaques rather than laughing at him, and encouraging Phebe instead of rebuffing her.

She also has to buy and keep the co-operation of two of Hermocrate's male servants. Her own female attendant helps out here. Biology and the rules of theatre have their predestined way, and the play ends happily for some, cruelly for others. That is what comedy means.

I can imagine a production that went deeper than this one both psychologically and scenically, one that pointed up the pain and the sexual ambiguities, that made more use of emotional and pictorial chiaroscuro (the lighting here is very flat) -- one, frankly, with more money to spend.

Van Burek goes instead for speed and lucidity and achieves both. His translation is crisp, though occasionally coming up with words such as "whippersnapper" and wiseacre and "shenanigans" that are meant to sound colloquial, but dont. (A test: Can you imagine anyone using them in a new English play? They dont sound 18th- century either.) On the other hand, an observation such as "it puts a sort of fungus on your manly lineage," addressed by a gardener to his employer, is in context priceless.

In the virtuoso role of the faux Phocion, Amy Price-Francis, who was promising earlier this year with the Montreal Young Company, is endlessly charming and endlessly intelligent. She is not endlessly resourceful: She has to spend most of her time seducing one person or another and she does run out of changes to ring. Her few moments of royal whip-cracking are effective, and she governs the play: Without her or somebody comparable, it would fall apart. It will be interesting to see which major company snaps her up first.

She gets witty support from Helen Taylor as her maid, a role that disappointingly fades out, and rather unformed romantic opposition from Allan Hawco's young prince, though he does redeem himself with a moment of plain-speaking exasperation near the end. Michael Spencer-Davis is a nicely gnarled and mercenary rustic and Paul Fauteux a merry Harlequin, though excessively given to twirling himself around tree trunks.

The production has its tricky moments and most of them are inflicted on or by him. But then what do you do with a character called Harlequin? Is he a convention? Is he real? This version tries for a little of both.

That leaves the two crucial roles of the scholarly siblings. Ross Manson agreeably sketches in the outlines of Hermocrate, but he is not the absurd and noble presence that seems called for. Philippa Domville, retreating from her superbly full-bodied work in Time after Time into her Shaw Festival genteel mode, makes a chill spinster of Leontine.

Less funny and less incipiently passionate than they might be, they are also less sad. They do, though, share a fine proto-Wildean duet when each declares the intention of marrying the same person and puts on a fancy hat for the occasion.

In summary, this Triumph of Love is not quite a triumph but it is to love.

MOTHER TONGUE

Factory Studio Theatre, Toronto

- - -

This time around, the Factory Studio has been turned into a traverse theatre. That means the audience sits on either side of a platform that snakes down the middle of the hall. Unusually, the platform leads up to a small, conventional picture-frame stage. The platform recalls the runways of the Oriental theatre, and its used here for myths, dreams and monologues. The end-stage reeks of what we used to call kitchen-sink drama, and is in fact used here for scenes set in a kitchen. East versus West, real life versus fancy: These are what Mother Tongue is about, and Jim Warren, the director, and Glenn Davidson, his designer, have found an appropriate method of illustrating the contrasts.

I wish I could say the contents matched up to the packaging, but Betty Quan's play comes over as an ordinary domestic drama with a few exotic trappings -- and the trappings are actually less interesting than the domesticity.

It is a play about communication or the lack of it, and the theme has been assiduously worked out. We are in Vancouver, in the home of a widowed Chinese immigrant, who speaks only Cantonese. (Clever title, by the way.) She has two teenage children, both of them born in Canada. Mimi, her daughter, has won a scholarship to study architecture in Ontario.

Mimi's younger brother, Steve, is 16, and has been deaf since suffering an accident at the age of 11. Mimi speaks and thinks in English, though she tells us she sometimes dreams in Chinese. Steve communicates through sign language. As Mimi says, in the most poignant and pungent line in the play, he doesnt like to speak, since, not being able to hear himself, he is afraid that he might sound stupid.

Mother can understand only a few of her daughters English words and none of her son's signs, so she is doubly isolated. At some level, though, she wants it that way. She resents her daughter's independence, and especially dreads her imminent departure. ("A woman should only leave home to get married" she says, grasping helplessly at ancestral straws.)

And Mimi, though she may rage at her mother's intransigence, also fears she may be missing out on something.

She thinks of her dead Chinese father, and connects him with legends about an emperor and his daughter.

The father materializes from time to time. He is sympathetically played by Paul Sun-Hyung Lee, the picture of a hard-working shirt- sleeved immigrant entrepreneur, but these sequences never take off. They are lumpy, and somewhat soporific. Better are moments in which the mother talks directly to us -- in English -- about her hopes and fears when she first came to Canada, especially her fears. Jane Luk is excellent in the role, the unforced immediacy of her recollections contrasting with the fearful mask she wears in company. Steve (Sean Baek) also has his soliloquies but these poetic releases from silence do not universalize his plight; they obscure it. Marjorie Chan as Mimi does the bulk of the talking, both to her family and to us, but she never gets beyond a one-dimensional portrait of chippy adolescence.

She does, though, share in the most effective scene in the play: the one in which she and her mother square off over what the former sees as liberation and the latter as desertion. We can probably all respond to that conflict on some level. The trouble is that while watching, we feel sorry for ourselves or for people we know, rather than for the characters.

Sure, drama is meant to reach the general through the particular, but if the particular doesn't first come to life in its own terms, then a vital stage has been skipped. The characters are, at best, blanks who have struck a nerve. The misty superstructure, the elaborate play with different forms of non-communication, seem like an elaborate way of playing the multicultural card and the disability card simultaneously.

The father-daughter dream encounters seem a recurring theme for this writer: They recall a similar motif in her YPT adaptation of Ghost Train. (Though Mother Tongue, I believe, was written earlier.)

Ghost Train deals with the building of the Canadian Pacific railroad, a subject also treated, of course, in the opera Iron Road, recently seen at the Elgin. I drag this in -- by the heels, I admit - - because this may be my only chance to pay tribute to that stirring, gripping and moving Tapestry production. I hope it comes back.

THIS HOTEL

Theatre Passe Muraille

- - -

The stage is initially hidden from us by one of those red billowy things that, according to legend, used to be found in theatres all the time; I think it's called a curtain. It's very provocative. When it rises, it reveals a living room with a sofa, just like in the old days.

A man and a woman are there, and the woman talks about having the sofa re-covered. There is sex in the air. The couple are not married, at least not to one another. This is revealed when a door opens -- one of several on the set -- and in walks the lady's husband, carrying flowers. He is played by Randy Hughson and he looks, in these discomfiting circumstances, as amiably woebegone as only Mr. Hughson can.

He does what husbands, faced with disintegrating marriages, traditionally do. He leaves the house and checks into a hotel. And in This Hotel -- as the play's author, Alex Poch-Goldin, calls it -- he meets his life, broken into taunting fragments and rotating around him.

Not to hold out on you, This Hotel is a brilliant evening: masterfully written, acted, directed and designed. One of its hallmarks is a vivacious versatility. Steve Lucas's set is composed of simple units that keep revolving, with unnerving ease, to take us from bedroom to bar to dining room and back again.

Of the actors, only Mr. Hughson as the wandering cuckold Lester is confined to a single role. Alon Nashman, indeed, is billed as only one character, called The Bellhop, but he turns out to constitute the entire male staff: receptionist ("We treat you", he says with alarming cordiality, "just as ourselves") porter, valet, waiter, barman, and -- as the hotel likes to cater for every taste - - rent-boy.

He is, as he would have to be, super-knowledgeable and super- efficient, although something about his service -- maybe it's his intermittent oily accent -- does not inspire total confidence; we seem to be in an Expressionist hotel of the damned, presided over by Manuel from Fawlty Towers.

Brenda Bazinet's cut-and-dried style finds admirable expression (and also some expansion) in the hero's wife, who cheats on him to maintain his flagging interest and finds herself aroused and frustrated simultaneously; she also plays a frigidly flirtatious Southern lady who seems to have wandered into the hotel under the impression that it was Blanche DuBois' Tarantula Arms. (The bellhop has a speech that seems to confirm this, likening the place to a spider's web, with Lester, of course, the fly.)

Veronika Hurnik is a psychologically and physically damaged guest who plays an elaborate attract-and-repulse game with Lester, and also a French chambermaid who seems to be bearing the secret of life.

Richard Zeppieri plays all the remaining men, ranging from the wife's temporary stud (a nice study in bewildered brutality) to a bisexual husband looking for rough trade and then retreating from it in respectable alarm. He and Lester share an admirable scene in the bar, each shunning his own image in the other; it's counterpointed with Lester's memories, full of touchingly clumsy lyricism, of his first meeting, also in a bar, with his wife Arlene, whose name inspires him to some unaccustomed flights.

The advance word on the play (from a previous outing in the Fringe Festival) was that all the characters are aspects of the protagonist. I don't buy this, even if the author does. I think they represent parallels and possibilities; and while Lester may be imagining his wife's encounters with her boyfriend, his imaginings - - like his recollections of the marriage itself -- are meant to be substantially correct.

It doesn't matter; what counts is that we have a gripping, funny phantasmagoria with a dramatic logic that leads Lester to a breaking point that Mr. Hughson makes very moving.

There are weaknesses. I don't see the point of the Southern belle (and it's difficult to satirize a Tennessee Williams heroine, given that Williams himself, in his lesser plays, did the job so unintentionally well).

The hotel image, not to mention the spider-fly stuff, is not new, but Mr. Poch-Goldin (in a great advance on his previous play, Jim and Shorty) makes it his own; the curtain, framing the conventions of a door-laden bedroom farce, is a helpfully ironic touch. It's probably just as well that the maid delivers her message of hope in French, since we might not stand for it in English. Its effect is to send Lester back to his wife. This is the right thing for him, but their last confrontation does not suggest untroubled seas ahead.

It's a stark, questioning image, held to perfection by the director, Kelly Thornton, whose work throughout has faultless precision and panache. Playwright and director are also husband and wife; that, at least, says something hopeful about marriage.

HISTORY PLAY

The Great Hall, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Last year, Jennifer Tarver handily staged an unstageable Gertrude Stein play and called it Not Faust. This year, with equal theatrical authority, she has devised and directed a dramatic collage, a collection of excerpts from pre-existing texts arranged around a central theme.

The theme is Time -- that philosophical hold-all that has exercised the human mind since ... I dont think I can finish that sentence without seeming to enter the debate. Since the beginning of time? For as long as anyone can remember?

Abstract thought can be difficult to follow in the theatre, or maybe its just me, but it does seem every time I have been asked to attend to a meditation on the nature of Time, the true subject has turned out to be the workings of memory. The argument always seems to go something like this: There are these literalist mugs who cling to the idea of time being a linear progression, but in fact it's nothing of the kind, as can be seen from the way in which our minds jump about between past, present and future.

To me, this appears to be a false antithesis, between two totally different spheres of experience. To shift the battlefield from time to space: I have never been to Moscow; that does not mean I don't believe Moscow exists.

Tarver mounts her symposium on a long, narrow platform that divides the hall. It is designed by Jan Komarek and inhabited by three actors, all of them in full and impressive command of what theyre saying. The principal spokesmen, to judge from the list of sources in the program, are Aristotle and the 20th-century theorist J. W. Dunne.

Aristotle, as delivered by Peter van Gestel, is young, confident, and enthusiastic. He can afford to be since, to be linear about it, he got on to the scene early. Dunne, embodied by David Jansen as a pleasantly skeptical campus sage of European origin, describes the process of free association: Our minds wander from one subject to another, and within half-a-dozen mental moves we find ourselves in a completely different area from the one at which we started.

This is a universal experience, but he gives it a name thatId certainly never heard before: the memory train." We go from one station to the next, he explains, and, if the trip is not too long, we can take the train back, again stop by stop. Above his head and ours, small objects whiz along a pair of parallel lines resembling those in old-fashioned drapery stores, and presumably illustrating Dunne's theory.

In the 1930s, Dunne influenced the "time plays of J. B. Priestley, including Time and the Conways, seen at last year's Shaw Festival. Priestley used them as a pretext for playing Act III before Act II, thus ensuring an unending supply of easy irony of the if only theyd known" variety. It also depended absolutely on the audience experiencing time in linear fashion, even if the characters didnt. We had to know more than they did.

Priestley's are absent from History Play's core curriculum, but several other playwrights are present. We hear Cassandra, from The Oresteia, prophesying upcoming murders. There are repeated scenes from Thornton Wilders Our Town and Edward Albees Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? (Both involve characters called George, but they're played by different actors and I think the correspondence is just a coincidence -- if there is such a thing.)

Albees historian spars with the young scientist who was Aristotle a moment earlier and whom he accuses of undermining him and the whole tradition of secular humanism. Later, Martha, the historians formidable wife, recalls a (literal) boxing match she once had with him -- a memory that seems to define their whole relationship.

In Our Town, we watch the drugstore betrothal of the play's young lovers, as heart-rending when detached from the play as it is within it. Wilder makes us aware of all the possibilities they are passing up in order to seize on this one, and of course once you start thinking about the passage of time, there is nothing more poignant than young love, especially perhaps if it leads to something.

To drive the point home, we have heard Wilder's professor situating Grovers Corners, N.H., not only in historical but in archeological time, which makes us feel very small indeed. (Harold Pinters plays also appear in the credits, as do T. S. Eliot's Four Quartets, and they would certainly have been relevant, but if they actually put in an appearance, then I missed them. Proust, I guess, would have been just too obvious.)

None of this, either in isolation or in juxtaposition, adds up to more than a restatement of the obvious, but it is certainly well done. Van Gestel, as Wilder's fresh-faced young hero courting his true love and disillusion simultaneously, is almost unbearably real (the scene, like the play, makes us nostalgic for a probably mythical American innocence). And Jansen, whose roles include those of Wilders avuncular stage manager, is both soothing and probing, like a reassuring dentist.

Brenda Robins is accomplished in her various roles, but harder to believe. Her archeology lecturer is a comic turn; her young Emily in Our Town has an unshakeable edge of maturity, reinforced with a Glenda Jackson rasp; and when she recounts the Old Ladys tale of disaster from Voltaire's Candide (this is the lassy who in the Leonard Bernstein musical was easily assimilated but missing half of her backside), she loses the tone of bland, accepting irony that makes the horrors truly horrific. Besides, what is the speech doing here? It's remembering something that happened in the past? By that test, half of literature would qualify.

Robins does, however, have a great dismissive moment as Albee's Martha, dispatching the opposition with superb whiplash timing. Somebody, probably the designing Komarek, has furnished a fine sound score: The memory train seems to be one hell of a locomotive.

And the dramatic collage, whatever my qualms on this occasion, is a genre worthy of further exploration. It could, for example, tell us a lot about a specific time -- as opposed to a generalized Time.

THE MILLIONAIRESS

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

The heroine, for want of a better word, of The Millionairess is named Epifania Fitzfassenden. That, at least, is her married name; her maiden name, by which she prefers to be known, is Italian and even longer. Epifania Ognisanti di Parerga. Her husband is called Alastair Fitzfassenden, her solicitor, Julius Sagamore and her platonic lover, Adrian Blenderbland. All this mirthless elephantiasis is an accurate index to the texture of the play itself, one of Bernard Shaws last. The wheels still turn, and they still give off sparks, but the machinery is getting sluggish and the glow is subdued and intermittent.

Written in 1934, the play reveals the extent to which the 80- year- old Shaw had lost touch with the nature of the world around him. No shame in that, perhaps; except that he still persisted in writing as if he not only understood the questions but had all the answers. Epifania is -- to quote her author's description of one of his earlier and more endearing heroines, Saint Joan -- "a born boss.

The 1930s were a time when born bosses such as Hitler and Mussolini were bossing whole nations. Epifania is, in her own small way, their comic surrogate: a figure through whom we are invited to consider the problem of dictators and what is to be done with them, or how their energies are to be harnessed.

That at least is what Shaw says in his preface. We may note, from the extracts printed in the Shaw Festival program, that he didn't know what he was talking about. He reduces Nazi anti-Semitism to the regrettable failure of one genius to show proper respect for another: Hitlers throwing Einstein to the anti-Semite wolves was an appalling breach of cultural faith." Einstein, of course, was exiled, not murdered; other Jews, less celebrated, were also less lucky -- and this long before the full-blown Holocaust. Shaw may be forgiven for not foreseeing what Hitlers racial policies were to lead to; he cannot be excused for not seeing what they already were, or for trying to transfer the blame to the leader's followers.

The actual play never mentions Hitler or the international situation; Epifania, living in London, operates on a strictly domestic and even romantic front. So it might seem unfair to drag in Shaw's commentary, except that this production does, not only in its program notes but in its use of lines from the preface, transformed into snappy song lyrics to be sung during the scene changes: snappier, actually, than most of the dialogue, and more directly critical of Epifania herself and the money-mad values she represents.

Otherwise, we might theoretically be content to see the play as another comedy about a strong-willed woman who eventually finds happiness with an equally strong-willed, or at least strong- natured, man. In terms of plot, that is what happens here, but there are two obstacles to our enjoying the play on that level. One is that the play is half over before the central relationship is even introduced. The other is Epifania herself.

She begins the play by marching into her lawyers office, demanding a divorce from her husband: a champion athlete, but not in other respects the man she took him for. Her late and revered father, himself the descendant of a long line of millionaires, laid a condition on her future suitors: Like a less idealistic version of Portias dad, he had demanded they transform (ps)150 into (ps)50,000 within six months. Flukily, the bone-headed Alastair pulled this off by going into theatrical production. (The details are complicated, but they sound like The Producers in reverse.)

But the disparity in their minds and manners has led to discord, and to his using his boxing prowess to counter her skills at judo. Most audience members, without endorsing wife-beating as a general practice, are likely to sympathize with Alastair.

He has also acquired a contrastingly mousy girlfriend who has the significantly plain name of Patricia Smith, but who gains honorary entrance to the play's club by being affectionately known as Polly Seedystockings. She has one of the play's better speeches, about the difference between the people anyone can live with, like herself, and the people no one can live with.

Eppy, of course, belongs to the latter group. This makes her feel sorry for herself, and she takes it out on her tame suitor, Blenderbland, beating him rather seriously up. (This sequence is done here to music, which is clever but tends to take the edge off.) A doctor is summoned, and proves to be an unworldly and serenely dedicated Egyptian. She falls instantly in love with him and agrees to a test imposed by his late mother; she will go out into the world, penniless, and survive. So she does, in the process taking over an East End sweatshop and transforming a rundown riverside pub into a tourist attraction hotel, all beam and gleam.

Though admitting some limitations (such as being a lousy scullery maid) Epifania is loathsomely competent and successful, and contemptuous of all who arent. Shaw is still playwright enough to make us see the human costs of her entrepreneurship, or at least to tell us about them second-hand, but basically he wants us not only to admire his protagonist but to like her.

Unfortunately, on her first entrance he has her admit that she has no sense of humour, which makes her an awkward heroine for a Shavian comedy.

Lacking good jokes, successful actresses in the role have relied on ferocious personal charm; this apparently is what Katharine Hepburn did, and its certainly what Sophia Loren, who of course was the right nationality, did in the watered-down film. It's something the usually excellent Sarah Orenstein apparently cannot do, and initially doesn't seem to be trying.

Uniting all the least lovable qualities of Margaret Thatcher and Ayn Rand, she is nothing but bossy, with spasms of self-pity. Wriggle though she may, she cannot later escape from the trap she has dug for herself. She does strike a couple of wittily absurd poses as a rich woman trying to act poor, and conscientiously phrases a long speech about the joys of marriage, which seems like a last-minute attempt to turn the play into something it has not hitherto been.

Allen MacInniss production keeps hinting at uncomfortable contemporary parallels and then shying away from them. It is strange in other respects, too, because though its look, its sense of ensemble and its overall timing are very good, much of its individual acting is pretty bad.

The minimum requirements for Shaw performance, certainly at his own festival, are strong personality and uncluttered, unapologetic vocal line; the heroines uncertainties in both these departments here are reflected and magnified by her colleagues.

Nigel Shawn Williams as the supposedly charismatic Doctor can hardly get a line out without stumbling over it. Peter Krantz, though he has the right beefy demeanour for Alastair, is painfully wooden in any speech containing more than two sentences; and David Schurmann extends the already overlong role of Blenderbland by an unconscionable amount of dithering. This performance is one he has given many times before, though often to better effect.

Peter Millard's sweetly reasonable Sagamore is also an old acquaintance, but in this case it fits perfectly; and Severn Thompson has no problem winning sympathy for the sensible Seedystockings.

William Vickers and Donna Belleville are a welcome breath of stale air as the sweat-shop proprietors; you don't go to Shaw for working-class realism, but their brief scene at least acknowledges and explores how people live and react.

William Schmuck's sets, each first glimpsed through a sort of expanding spy hole, are a treat. Overall, though, the production tries hard to save the play from itself and fails.

LAURA

Royal George Theatre,

Niagara-on-the-Lake

- - -

NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE - Laura, says the song, is the face in the misty light, footsteps you hear down the hall. She is also, you may remember, the voice that floats on the summer night that you can never quite recall.

That Johnny Mercer lyric, more evocative than any of the lines in the play Laura, was written to fit David Raksin's indelibly haunting theme-music -- some of us in Niagara were humming it as we walked into the theatre -- for the celebrated 1944 movie. It was never sung in the film, but if you listen hard you can hear Woody Hermans vocal version playing behind the curtain calls at the Shaw Festival.

You also, in this atmospheric production, get to hear the tune rendered instrumentally by Charlie Parker and to listen, over and over, to John Coltrane playing Duke Ellingtons infinitely seductive In a Sentimental Mood.

There is also some older jazz on hand. Laura, the beautiful young copywriter whose murder in her own Manhattan apartment we are assembled to investigate, was a fan of "hot music," Louis Armstrong and Jelly Roll Morton: a taste deplored by several of her acquaintances, ranging from her permanent-bachelor friend Waldo Lyndecker, writer and self-styled connoisseur, to her janitor's wife, who claims her teenage son was being corrupted by Laura and her record collection.

In all, Laura reminds me of Lee Wiley, a sultry Southern singer of great distinction who was doing some of her best work at just that historic moment; bop was coming in, swing remained, but her heart and her rhythm were in New Orleans. People fell, and still fall, in love with the teasing promise in Wiley's voice, just as Mark McPherson, this plays splendidly named detective, though no necrophiliac, falls in love with Lauras portrait hanging over the mantel.

Laura began life as an unproduced play by Vera Caspary, then became a novel, then another play (the present one, written in collaboration with George Sklar) and then of course that film.

So any stage production comes weighted down with legend, accruing not only to the property itself but to the period from which it derives: the haughty 1940s, which have displaced the '20s and '30s as prime sources of American myth.

Both play and production are stronger on mood and even on character than they are on suspense. There is one diabolical twist in the first act but its very audacity lets the air out of the situation; it is hard, thereafter, to care very much who committed the crime, though there is a reasonable choice of suspects: five people seem to have had a motive.

What counts is the revelation of the number of men attracted to Laura like -- Im sorry, theres no other image -- moths to a flame: her dumb Dixiecrat fiance (this is the second Shaw Festival play in two days about a strong woman betrothed to a man unworthy of her), Waldo, McPherson, the boy downstairs. That, and the image of Manhattan high life, all smart talk and hard liquor. Good eating, too: Laura's success in the advertising racket apparently enabled her to employ a full-time cook.

Neil Munro's production cunningly hints the whole thing may be the smitten detectives dream. It is sensuously lit by Ereca Hassell and finely designed by Yvonne Sauriol, whose sets and costumes set off each other beautifully. McPhersons Dick Tracy yellow works especially well with the prevailing shade of dull ochre.

Ben Carlson, in a first-rate performance, wears the coat and the character most sympathetically. Jane Perry, playing the mysterious woman at the play's centre, has the heavy task of activating a period icon and is not equipped for it; her style is laboured.

Waldo, too, needs the high-strung ministrations of film noir music and lighting to achieve his full measure of eunuchoid menace (it also helps if he's Clifton Webb), but Michael Ball gives him a useful mixture of delicacy and bulk, and its a pleasure to watch him pattering across the floor or sliding along the sofa. The character seems to have been based on the waspish critic Alexander Wollcott, who was also the inspiration for The Man Who Came to Dinner, a role Ball is to play later this season: such a double comes seldom.

Mary Haney is superb as the cook; this is luxury casting in a stock part, as -- even more spectacularly -- is the triumphant deployment of Al Kozlik in the one-word role of a second cop. Stephen McQuigge also does well as the janitors kid besotted with the glamorous older woman. She gave him his very first kiss. That was Laura. But she's only a dream.

THE MYSTERY OF EDWIN DROOD

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE, Ont. - One of the liveliest musical numbers in The Mystery of Edwin Drood comes about halfway into the second act and is called Don't Quit While Youre Ahead. Beginning as a solo, it is gradually taken up by the entire 18-strong company. Musically and choreographically, it builds and builds, its excitement greatly enhanced by the sudden appearance of a stage- wide flight of steps on which all the performers can strut their stuff in delirious unison.

Obeying the precept of the songs title, they give us an encore, which is suddenly interrupted by the deflating announcement that it was at this point that Mr. Charles Dickens, who wrote the novel on which the show is based, laid down his pen for ever. He quit, leaving the rest of us behind. Cruellest of the cruel, the novel was a murder story, and we will never know definitively who done it or even -- since Dickens had yet to arrive at the discovery of the body -- if it was actually done. The actors, needing to complete the show, are on their own. Except that they have us.

The Mystery of Edwin Drood, the first interactive musical, is a smart, rowdily enjoyable and deeply unsatisfying show. It always was all of those things (it was first produced in 1985 in Central Park and then on Broadway, where it won most of the available awards), and the Shaw Festival production accentuates both its good and bad points.

A proper synopsis would take up all my space: Dickens' story -- set in a somnolent English cathedral town and centring on the disappearance from it of the rich, young, arrogant but essentially blameless Edwin Drood -- is complicated enough, but Rupert Holmes, who wrote the book, music and lyrics, has erected his own elaborate structure on top of it. We are in a Victorian music hall whose troupe is presenting its own Drood drama. The man who calls himself Your Chairman, who on an ordinary bill would merely introduce the acts and orchestrate the singalongs, now functions as narrator, though he retains his traditional fruity demeanour -- very much so, in Neil Barclay's performance.

There are various tensions and temperaments and non-appearances through drunkenness floating around among these artistes, and though they are not explored in much depth, they add to the mixture. A few of this cast, notably Our Chairman, do the beery direct-address thing very well. Others are more shamefaced about it; they also seem to have the patronizing idea that music hall performers, required to act dramatic scenes, would act them very badly.

It seems charitable to assume that theyre doing this on purpose, but its still painful to see John Jasper, the jealous opium- smoking choirmaster, last of Dickens' great tormented villains, transformed (by Michael Querin) into a vacuous marionette; or the Reverend Mr. Crisparkle (Douglas E. Hughes) become a mildly posturing stick figure. Melodrama, no less than music hall, needs to be played for its own values; camping it up is an admission of failure.

The show draws on yet another Victorian genre, by presenting the vanishing Edwin as a pantomime principal boy, i.e. played by a girl; Blythe Wilson has the piping voice for this convention but not the thigh-slapping spirit.

We, the audience, come into it when the Dickensian original has reached the end of its rope. We are invited to cast our votes on the questions outstanding. The company will then act out, and sing out, the remainder of the story as we have determined it. This is for real, and they have prepared material to cover any combination of choices we might make. It must have added hours to the rehearsal schedule, and that's without counting the understudies

Problem One is the identity of a mysterious detective who turns up late in the original text and is plainly someone else in disguise. At Fridays premiere (and, Im sure, at most performances in most productions) the house settled unanimously on a minor functionary named Bazzard, who in the first act had endeared himself to us by his very insignificance. Or rather, we warmed to him because his insignificance had been made so very significant; the Victorian actor cast in his role had complained that he, too, was an overlooked supernumerary, desperate for the big break. He had even sung a song about it, something about the walk-on's dream of seizing the limelight on, as the lyric neatly has it, some starless night. Guy Bannerman, the Shaw Festival actor who plays HIM, fairly hurls himself into this, with all the pent-up gusto of a performer who, to be frank, has not had too many juicy roles at Niagara himself. Of course we wanted to hear him do another number, and by voting for him we got our wish.

Our second and more onerous task was that of selecting the murderer. We are presented with seven candidates who had motive and opportunity for doing Edwin in. Being a Dickens student, I voted for Jasper, who, apart from being sexually repressed and a dope fiend, was jealous of young Drood's engagement to the beauteous Rosa Bud.

I was jeered at for making such an obvious choice, though that of course is why I made it: Dickens wasnt Agatha Christie trying to be born. The anointed killer when I saw it was the opium-den proprietress known as Princess Puffer, and here too I think the house was influenced by its desire to hear the performer sing again.

Personally I never knew that Corinne Koslo could sing at all, let alone that she could sing so well, and she faces her audience head- on with terrific buxom verve. I might also have fancied seeing the fair Rosa convicted: I would like to hear the actress, Tracy Michailidis, sing her way out of that since she seemed to me rather wasted on just being good. I could also have lent an additional ear to Jenny L. Wright, who plays the Oriental lady Helena Landless with what she herself winningly describes as "a geographically inaccessible accent."

We also get to vote for a happy-ending romantic couple, and we take pleasure in choosing the least congruous pair. This is because, frankly, we dont care -- and that is the show's major problem. All this audience participation is good, but not great, fun; and it comes on top of a script and performance that have not allowed us to believe in a single character and have been very sketchy about the actual story.

Much of Rupert Holmes' score is too clever for its own good, which means not clever enough. Make no mistake: For a first (and so far, alas, only) musical, its a fine achievement. The music is not inexhaustibly melodic, but it ranges impressively from invigorating rampages -- though the first and best suffers here from being performed with the house-lights up -- to at least one sweet ballad, Perfect Strangers.

Dennis Garnhums production has inspiriting energy; and its looks -- with credit to Timothy French's choreography and Allan Stichbury's good sets and better lighting -- are great.

PICNIC

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

Back in the 1950s, Kenneth Tynan, in an essay on the Broadway theatre, told of attending the Boston tryout of a new play, and then repairing to the director's hotel suite for the first-night party. There he found a committee of impromptu play doctors, rewriting the piece and then rewriting the rewrites, according to which overnight review they had read last. These desperate surgeries apparently worked: The play, Tynan reported, was "a tremendous success." It was also, he said bluntly, "a bad play." Tactfully, he refrained from mentioning its title.

A few years ago, Tynan's diaries, or bits of them, were published, and all was revealed. The play proved to be William Inge's 1953 Pulitzer Prize-winning Picnic, and you could have knocked some of us down with a feather. This, after all, is a famous play, one that has endured despite taking some other hard critical knocks on the way. A Broadway production a few years ago showed it to be unembarrassingly revivable, and Jackie Maxwell's adroit staging at the Shaw Festival confirms that verdict.

Picnic has even been called the best American play of its decade, an estimate that may take your breath away in the other direction until you pause to consider the competition. (The Crucible? Cat on a Hot Tin Roof? They're the work of better playwrights but they're not better plays.) The '50s were a great period for American musicals but a dreary one for American plays -- not that subsequent decades have done any better.

Clearly Tynan's blanket dismissal of Picnic was wrong. Picnic is not a bad play; it is in fact the best example of its genre. He was right about the genre, though, and about its inherent limitations. It's what he called a "mood" piece, the mood being "a sort of steamy, twilit ambience of pubescent yearning."

It all takes place in a small town in Inge's native Kansas, on and around a porch; the script actually calls for two porches but the tiny Court House space means that the lady next door has to live offstage and constantly seems to be bustling in from nowhere in particular. (What Christina Poddubiuk's set does show us, it shows excellently.)

On the porch, and presumably, though less believably, in the house behind, live Flo Owens and her two teenage daughters, beautiful Madge and clever, artistic Millie, each jealous of what the other has and she hasn't. The family has a lodger, Rosemary, a self-described "spinster schoolteacher" who proclaims so emphatically that she doesn't need a man that, by all known dramatic rules, she has to be lying.

Into their lives on the day of the town picnic drifts Hal, a well- muscled young hobo whom the author craftily contrives to have play the entire first act stripped to the waist. ("Can't you put on a shirt?" somebody finally snaps, in what may be the best line of the play.) He turns out to be a former student -- his football got him into college, his academic dumbness pushed him out of it -- and a fraternity buddy of Alan, the respectful and respectable young man whom everyone expects Madge to marry.

Naturally, Hal lures Madge away from Alan. Naturally, Rosemary is attracted to him, too, but masks her jealousy by getting drunk (illegally, Kansas being in every sense a dry state) and spitting vitriol at young people in general.

Give Inge credit for some subtlety; he does not, as you might expect, allow the stud to seduce the teacher, or even vice versa. Rosemary's pent-up feelings instead throw her more decisively than ever before into the arms of Howard, a local tradesman and her long- time semi-reluctant suitor. The two couples -- Hal and Madge, Rosemary and Howard -- brush up against one another, pass one another, but never collide. And this is dramatized in a long, virtuoso sequence of impromptu dancing -- superbly sustained in this production, which features some great jitterbugging to very appopriate music.

Neither the audience nor the characters (who by now have better things to do with their time) ever get to go to the actual picnic; after this scene, we don't need to. All the same, wouldn't you love to see a play in which the nice guy didn't finish last, or in which the spinster lady refused to be toppled from her lonely perch?

Apart from the dance scene, a real challenge, the play is probably foolproof, not that I've ever seen fools put it to the test. You cast it well, you light it well, you step back and watch the ingredients interact. The play connects with everybody's feelings of regret, and somehow -- despite the fact that it is set when it was written -- it has the comforting air of nostalgia.

When Tynan took in that Boston party, he told the director that the play's third act seemed to have come from some other play. The director, the redoubtable Joshua Logan, said that was probably because he'd written it himself. Doubtless he exaggerated; the last act seems of a piece with the rest, though Inge later felt he had copped out by supplying the approximation of a happy ending.

But even if he had insisted on frustration rather than fulfilment, that would not have turned him into Chekhov. There isn't enough at stake. Chekhov's characters are quirky and they sometimes die, or at least lose their cherry orchards. This play is thoroughly and professionally unboring -- something to be grateful for, especially these days -- but it is pat.

Patness infects the acting, too. Goldie Semple cuts a striking figure as Rosemary (she looks as I imagine Rosalind Russell did in the film, especially when wearing a hat) but when she goes through her drunk and jealous routine, a routine is what it remains. Fiona Byrne as the struggling Madge is correct without being exciting, as is Wendy Thatcher as her mother, suffering tight-lipped at the prospect of her daughter repeating her own mistakes, something we only fully realize at the very last moment. There's well-made drama for you: revealing and frustrating at the same moment.

Mike Wasko is fully alive in Hal's bravado and in his shamefacedness, and Mike Shara barely falters as the hapless Alan (originally played by Paul Newman -- the last time he ever lost the girl).

Lisa Norton wins all hearts and tickles all funny bones as Millie, the kind of awkward-age prodigy who seems to collapse time; i.e., when she grows up she will probably write the play we have just been watching.

Two older players bring worlds on to the stage. Jim Mezon, though maybe too insistently uninsistent, is Howard, the small-town sensual man, to the white-suited brow-mopping life. Jennifer Phipps is the neighbour whose existence -- a one-day marriage and subsequent enslavement to a bedridden mother -- is a distorted mirror of the other women's experiences and who lives, vicariously and with deceptive cheerfulness, through them. Effortlessly she reveals depths when nearly everybody else seems to be speaking lines.

PETER PAN

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

Productions of J.M. Barrie's Peter Pan fall into categories: those traditional and still in the majority, in which a lady plays Peter, and those gaining ground in recent years, in which a young gentleman does. No production, to my knowledge, has gone the whole hog, or perhaps the whole piglet, and cast an actual boy in the role, but a young actor who can pass for a boy can still automatically place the play in a more disturbing light. The boy may still refuse to grow up, but his play no longer has that option.

Dylan Trowbridge, who plays Peter at Shaw in the best all-round production I have encountered, gives us both the look and the essence of boyhood: vigorous, clear, energetic and sublimely selfish. Peter is the boy who runs away from his mother but still clings to her: The boy was heartbroken when he found that his real mother had locked the nursery window against him, so now he makes equivalent demands on the surrogate Wendy.

In the play's last section, when all but Peter have abandoned Neverland but when Wendy has promised to make annual trips to do his spring cleaning, Peter can forget to come for her for years on end but he will always do so eventually; he's still tied. She, though theoretically remembering, has forgotten in essence and in perpetuity simply by becoming a woman and having a daughter of her own. That daughter, a temporary substitute, will forget in her turn, and so will all their female descendants, "so long," Barrie's narrator tells us, "as children are young and innocent and heartless."

The catch is that Barrie himself, at sea with grown-up relationships, preferred children that way while knowing, Lewis Carroll-like, that he was going to be hurt by it. He was himself the Peter who refused to grow up and the parent (in his case an adoptive one) who was wounded when his children passed beyond him. The repeated questions of Fiona Byrne, this production's Wendy, as to what she really means to Peter, carry more than usual weight. They are not arch; they are potentially passionate and increasingly frustrated.

You didn't use to get that from productions of Peter Pan when I was a boy, but they were carefree cut-price affairs that didn't include the play's epilogue, which tells us most of this. That, as Captain Hook would say, is where the canker gnaws. (He does not, in this production, pronounce the "g" in gnaws, and personally I missed it.)

Barrie seems never to have stopped revising Peter Pan, whether as story, play or novel, and Christopher Newton has assembled his own text from the available variants. As a director, he is in top form; nobody stages literate spectacle better. Sue LePage designed the sets, and Kevin Lamotte the lighting.Very little is stinted. The flying is unprecedentedly prolonged and acrobatic, and only at one moment can you see the wires.

The crocodile (the one who swallowed a clock: We know what makes him tick) is of prehistoric proportions -- a veritable Moby-Dick to Hook's Ahab. The pirate ship is everything it should be, and for their ventures on land the buccaneers have a motorized sledge that might have been designed by Heath Robinson. The mermaids dance to the sound of Fred Astaire at his absolute vocal best. I did wonder, though, why Peter, at the end of the lagoon scene, uttered his famous line about dying being an awfully big adventure only after he had secured his escape.

There is acting going on, too. The lost boys are a varied and meticulously orchestrated ensemble, their scenes governed and taken to a new dimension by the inspired casting of the plumply mature Neil Barclay as Slightly Soiled, whom he makes a wonderful prep- school know-it-all. The pirates are less rewarding -- possibly less well-served by their author -- but they too have a champion in Bernard Behrens' divine Smee, though his role has been cruelly truncated. (The scene in which he and his shipmate Starkey meet the crocodile with their captain inside him has gone. No great literary loss perhaps, but why does the narrator bother to tell us that two of the pirates survived their defeat if we are never to learn which two?)

Jim Mezon's Hook lingers in the memory, as this actor's performances usually do, but it is too mild for its material. Hook, the periwigged pirate, is a baroque creation, even if he has doubts about his own authenticity. If a man is going to say, "Back, you pewling spawn! I'll show you all the road to dusty death," I don't think he should swallow the words, even if he is on the verge of being swallowed himself. Somehow this climactic shipboard scene is only a shadow of what one feels it should be. To be fair, it usually is; it was probably more richly imagined than written.

The production very tactfully spares our blushes by skating gently over the "do you believe in fairies" episode, but I question the wisdom of having Tinker Bell appear from time to time in the, so to speak, flesh: I found myself wondering for the first time why, instead of drinking Peter's poisoned medicine, she didn't simply spill it on the ground.

Overall, though, this production considerably surpasses the celebrated Royal Shakespeare Company production that was the first "serious" Peter. That felt like an essay on the play, or a journey round it; this is a realization of it, and a trip to its centre. It is the first straight Peter Pan that didn't make me secretly wish I were watching the musical.

TWELFTH NIGHT

Festival Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

I loathe bouzouki music, and there is a great deal of it tinkling away in the new Stratford Twelfth Night. The rationale is that this is Illyria, lady, and that what was Illyria is now Yugoslavia. That is hardly an idyllic locale these days, but the trappings of this production are early-middle-20th century, when presumably things were nicer; the twins wear a dazzling match of cream suits. There is a lot of street life, far more than the play demands or needs, though I grudgingly admit that most of it is put to good dramatic use. You might call Antoni Cimolino's staging the Balkanization of Twelfth Night.

I wanted to get the demeaning trappings out of the way, because underneath them is the best all-round production of this wonderful but elusive play I have seen in decades. There is nothing revolutionary about it; its theme is the traditional one of the madness of love, a distemper successfully worked through by nearly everybody in the cast. The exceptions are Feste, who was not affected in the first place, and Malvolio, who as an incurable narcissist (sick of self-love, says Olivia) is doomed to end in an undiminished fury of self-righteousness, aggravated now by genuine psychological pain. When he storms out vowing revenge, he is, to quote Tom Stoppard on Hamlet, stark raving sane.

There are eight crucial characters in Twelfth Night, which is one reason its such a devil to get right, and they are all well played, some of them outstandingly.

Even better than their individual strengths are the way they relate and interlock. The confrontation of Malvolio and Sir Toby Belch is the explosion of an antagonism that has obviously been smouldering for years. The way in which Olivia chimes in on Festes jokes, knowing not only the lines but the timing, denotes a life- long rapport between jester and employer from which the puritan steward Malvolio, however invaluable and good at his job, is pointedly and forever excluded; he stands outside, simmering.

The connecting lines are even visible when one of the participants is offstage. When Sir Toby boozily proclaims his devotion to his niece, we can feel her version of the story hanging menacingly in the air. The Stratford platform, which has been known to tear a play into disconnected strips, can also be a potent crucible for the union of disparate elements. So it is here, on a set by Peter Hartwell that consists of the familiar structure plus some lattice work.

The dominating presence, as in Robin Phillips' production 20 years ago, is William Hutt's Feste, slightly frailer now (his songs are miked) but with the same enormous shrewdness, patience and dignity. There is also, I think, more cruelty in his baiting of Malvolio; their encounters bring two views of life into collision.

This Feste has either experienced everything or observed everything (we dont know which and he isnt telling) and he meets the other characters on ambiguous ground. He is their economic dependent and their spiritual superior, which makes them into patrons afraid to patronize; the exception is again Malvolio, who pays for it. He is also, as a jester, very professional; Feste's jokes ("Dost thou live by thy tabor?" No, sir, I live by the church) are commonly thought beyond saving, but Hutt with calm authority gets a laugh with every one of them. When that voice says something is funny, you believe it.

The voice begins the proceedings, in recorded form, with a snatch of the closing song about the wind and the rain. It heralds an actual storm, the one that shipwrecks Viola, but before that we see Sean Arbuckle's Duke Orsino, apparently ingesting the musical food of love while huddling under an umbrella down by the shore, and practising what looks like Zorbas dance to boot. When an attendant asks if hell go hunt, you're tempted to murmur, "What, in this weather?" It seems like strange behaviour but it makes increasing sense; this is a violently lovesick Orsino, whose insecurity causes him to shout as well as mope, and who is capable of the final threat to kill the thing he loves.

Equally startling and equally justifiable is Michelle Giroux's coltish Olivia, who, once lured out of mourning, never looks back, perhaps because she never loved her dead brother too much in the first place. Tara Roslings lucid, graceful Viola is the most enchantingly accomplished Stratford debut I remember. Her sisterly grief is real; its beautifully brought out by the gentle embarrassment of John Dolan's sea captain when he realizes that in gossiping about Olivia's loss he has stepped on Violas: an early sign that the production cares, and is on the right track. This Viola can snap out of grief and into love, and can relish chance and adventure, without ever losing track of her deepest feelings. She is also, a real test in this role, as comfortable in farce as in romance.

Of the licensed farceurs, James Blendicks familiar impersonation of a decayed English colonel comes in ideally for a Sir Toby with an infinite supply of hip flasks. Domini Blythe is a superb Maria, housekeeper rather than chambermaid, economically extrovert and in control of every scene she enters. Michael Therriault, who enters the scene in cap and goggles -- has he driven to Illyria or flown? - - is a Sir Andrew Aguecheek who swings metronomically between assertiveness and subservience; caught wearing yellow, Olivia's least favourite colour, he strips off the offending garments as if in some ceremony of self-flagellation and returns in sporty stripes, which do him no favours either. He can do nothing, though, about his hair, which remains obstinately flaxen.

Hair is an obsession of Peter Donaldson's Malvolio, who sports a rebellious toupee and -- we learn -- sticks curlers in it at night. This is the broadest performance of the evening, or at least the butt of the broadest direction. The tango into which he forces Olivia at the height of his delusion is indefensible, physically if not psychologically: Where is the music supposed to be coming from? But even when pushed to the brink, the actor never topples over. This is a bold, thoughtful account of a man who embraces humiliation but still keeps something unsullied; you believe he thinks nobly of the soul. You dont feel sorry for him, you may not even respect him, but you accept he has a place in the world and the right to fill it.

Its wrong for Sebastian to be seen apparently getting out of bed with Olivia, just after their first meeting and just before their marriage; she isn't that kind of girl and he, a truthful lad and Viola's true brother, says in the last scene he is still a virgin. It's even more wrong for the priest who unites them to raise his eyebrows and virtually wink at the audience. Much of the comic business -- the duel, for example -- is funny by any reckoning; some isn't, and striving to please the public, as Feste promises, should not mean pandering to it or to your own worst impulses. There is richness and subtlety here, and I hope they survive the season unscathed.

PRIVATE LIVES

Avon Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

There are few plays whose plots are as simple and symmetrical, or as satisfying, as that of Noel Coward's Private Lives.

Elyot and Amanda, a tempestuous English couple now five years divorced, meet up unexpectedly when each is on a second honeymoon. In fact, they have adjacent suites in the same French hotel, and their encounter takes place on the balcony while each waits for the new partner to dress and emerge for cocktails. (It's that kind of play.)

Of course Elyot and Amanda are still violently in love, and of course they run off together to Paris, where Amanda conveniently keeps a flat. (It's still that kind of play.) Here they decline rapidly from bliss to blows, as they always used to and as they knew full well they would again.

They are discovered, locked in combat, by their pursuant spouses, the stodgy Victor and the silly Sybil. These two, having been forced into one another's company, begin to enact what amounts to a parody version of the relationship that they were intending to disrupt; that is, they forgo the bliss, for which they have not the wit, and go straight to the blows. Elyot and Amanda creep off and leave them to it.

In Coward's other familiar plays -- Hay Fever, Blithe Spirit, Present Laughter -- we know how the characters are able to maintain their enviable lifestyles; they are successful actors or writers or both. Private Lives furnishes no clue as to how Elyot and Amanda can afford their drinks, their dinners, their hotels or the glamorous globe-trotting to which they are both addicted. Apparently, they were born to it and take it as their right. That gives the play a fascinating kind of purity, and it is fitting that, in the 1960s when Coward's critical stock was at its lowest, it should have been a modest London revival of it that sparked off the Coward comeback, or what he himself referred to as "Dad's renaissance."

To my surprise, I have not seen the play from that production to this, and I realize that most of my impressions of it have been derived from the celebrated recording that Coward and his 1930s co- star Gertrude Lawrence made of the balcony scene, all clipped badinage with passion quivering decorously beneath. Speech rhythms are, I guess, a matter of fashion, but I could never take this combination of stiff upper lips and flaring nostrils at all seriously, either as acting or writing. It's very brittle -- and I would like you to repeat those words, Coward-fashion, with the accent on the adjective.

Coward was an adjective man. Brian Bedford, in his immaculate Stratford direction and in his own magnificent performance as Elyot, goes for nouns and especially verbs, and the result is unstrained revelation. Moment to moment, the play is beliveable; cumulatively, it is truthful.

Elyot is described in the stage directions as "about 30, quite slim and pleasant looking." Bedford is very pleasant looking and sounding, but he has admitted in interviews to being more than about 30, however generously you interpret "about," nor is he any longer what I would describe as slim. This, however, helps. Physically and metaphorically he puts flesh, not fat, on the character's bones and on the play.

The first-act reunion, in which Elyot and Amanda listen to a distant band playing Someday I'll Find You and talk feverishly about the potency of cheap music and the flatness of Norfolk while drawing ever closer together, has become a canonical example of subtext; talking about one thing and thinking another. In fact, the hidden meaning is so obvious that the text can hardly be described as sub.

What's remarkable here about Bedford's acting are the tenderness and the energy he infuses into Elyot's explicit declarations of love; yes, they're there in the writing, but not in how we usually hear the writing. Just as fine is the passionate tact with which he advances Elyot's, and Coward's, creed of gaiety in the face of mortality. If it sounded forced it would be embarrassing.

Best of all is the unbroken line of thought that carries right through his performance. Even when he makes an automatic joke about his mother-in-law, it's not a detachable gag but an integral part of his evolving but abortive relationship with his new wife, and an implicit step toward the predestined reunion with his old one.

He gets, of course, every laugh there is in the script. His timing on the first night when he spoke of the Catholic Church's non- recognition of divorce ("it's nice to think they'd sort of back us up") may even, from the look of it, have surprised Seana McKenna, his Amanda.

The play's middle act finds them fully enmeshed in the quarrels they have sworn to avoid, and they chart the onset of each squall and the eruption of the final storm in cartographic detail. They play excellently together, she the edgier of the two, he oddly protective, even in violence.

She has not quite his ease or his experience, and she has a fortuitous technical problem; by the time she has forced herself into the upper register of her voice and adopted an English accent that I can best describe as bohemian-suburban, she ends up sounding remarkably, if inadvertently, like Maggie Smith. The personality she projects is also remarkably Smithian, combative intelligence barely concealing stark terror. It happens to be right for the role, but it cannot help awaking echoes even for those of us who never saw Smith's Amanda, with or without Bedford's Elyot.

Coward once confessed that as a playwright, constructing a vehicle for himself and friend, he had been monstrously unfair to the supporting couple. Here he was being half-hard on himself. The function of Victor and Sybil is to provide foils and props for Elyot and Amanda. It is credible that Amanda would have turned to Victor, as solidly played here by Wayne Best, for temporary support. It is far less believable that Elyot could have endured two hours with Sybil, let alone an entire courtship; Sarah Dodd plays her shrill and flighty, but it is difficult to see what other option she has.

The cast is completed, and the symmetry enjoyably broken, by a maid who speaks only French, and that with a heavy cold; Kim Horsman is a champion sneezer and wheezer. John Lee Beatty's two sets are the kind that both demand and deserve applause, and Jane Greenwood's costumes effortlessly dazzle.

The sum total is as near a masterpiece as makes no difference.
