In repertory till Nov. 4.

THE SOUND OF MUSIC

Festival Theatre, Stratford

- - -

There is no excuse for the Stratford production of The Sound of Music. There is nothing wrong with Stratford doing musicals; they used to have a troublesome air of being brought in, but in the last couple of years West Side Story and, especially, the epic Fiddler on the Roof have looked like integral parts of the festival, classics among other classics and held to the same acting and production standards.

But nobody can do much acting in The Sound of Music, and the show itself has been feeble since its premiere 40-odd years ago. That it should since have mutated from family treat to camp cult doesn't make it any better. (The whole phenomenon of the singalong Sound of Music chills my blood; the news that somebody is planning the same treatment for Fiddler, a good show, freezes it.)

Let's start, as the show advises us to do, at the very beginning. In a musical, that means the music. This was the last of the Richard Rodgers-Oscar Hammerstein scores, and the least. Rodgers could hardly write a tune that wasn't catchy but there are only two here of any distinction: Sixteen Going on Seventeen, with its tongue-in- cheek lilt and, despite its lyric, My Favourite Things; John Coltrane didn't adopt those chord changes for nothing.

Everything else is jingles and dirges. There are also, to be fair, a couple of cynical duets for the show's two heavies, the Anschluss trimmers who want our hero, Captain von Trapp, to give in to history and get on side with the Nazis. These are surprising, since they were cut from the film (from which everybody knows the show) and are mordant to a degree that cultural amnesiacs do not associate with R&H. At least they could be; Kelly Robinson's production seems determined to destroy them with whimsical choreography, as if the show needed to be made more anodyne than it already is.

C. David Johnson, the likeable actor who plays the captain, has a rough time throughout, what with not being very imposing and not being able to sing, but he is never worse treated than during these two numbers, for one of which he should not officially be on stage at all.

As a romantic musical, the show is a non-event; its relationships don't exist, musically or dramatically. The juvenile couple get one nice number -- pointlessly extended with a lot of jumping on and off benches, presumably to prove we're in a musical -- and are then virtually dropped; the show keeps promising to explore the uncomfortable fact that the boy is a fascist but never gets 'round to it. (The film, oddly enough, did.)

The captain's ill-advised entanglement with a fashion-plate lady plutocrat, given an atrociously patronizing performance by Mary Ann McDonald, is similarly taken for granted; she's there and then she isn't. Meanwhile, the supposed central relationship between the captain and Maria, the governess from the convent down the mountain, simply isn't there. One of the captain's seven children tips Maria off that papa is in love with her, and she could hardly be more surprised than we are since there has been absolutely no chemistry between them: compare that to the similar situation in The King and I.

All the same, the revelation sends Maria back to the nunnery from which, as all the world well knows, the mother abbess sends her right back again with the adjuration to climb every mountain: advice whose vagueness is only exceeded by its volume.

This, for some reason, is taken to constitute a first-act climax. At least that's when they raise the lights and start selling the ice- cream. Cynthia Dale sings sweetly as Maria (the Dales, as well as the hills, are alive with the sound of music) and gets some feeling into her religious perplexities; in her domestic situation, though, she can be no more than pert.

Of the junior von Trapps whom she turns into a folk-pop group I cannot bear to write, except to allow that it isn't their fault.

That goodnight song must surely be Rodgers and Hammerstein's nadir, Hammerstein's especially. This is the show with cute kids, cute nuns, even cute Nazis; the appearance of a gauleiter in lederhosen gets a big giggle. Why the captain so staunchly opposes them, and whether Maria goes along with him through love or conviction, are questions left untouched. Don't say "But it's only a musical"; the authors wouldn't have thanked you.

The Festival stage's corners have been rounded off and the balcony has been covered with a shroud to suggest an Alp. The abbey scenes have some atmosphere: not so, the captain's estate. Given that Stratford should not be doing the show at all, the fact it has been done on the whole poorly may be taken as a perverse sign of integrity. I wouldn't push the point, though.

WHO'S AFRAID OF VIRGINIA WOOLF?

Avon Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

STRATFORD, Ont. - Edward Albee's Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?, as you doubtless remember, is about a middle-aged couple who are trapped with one another, and who for the duration of one drink- sodden late night and early morning virtually compel a younger couple to climb into their hellhole with them. Why have George, minor professor of history at a New England college, and his wifem Martha, daughter of the university president, stayed together all these years? For reasons of economic and emotional interdependence, and because, in some of the more twisted of the myriad ways available, they love one another. They sure know how to laugh together, mainly at other people, and we're always told that that's important. Why do the younger pair, Nick and Honey, a biology professor and his wife, stay in their hosts' living room and watch them tearing one another apart, while absorbing a considerable amount of the fallout themselves? This is a question that commentators have more frequently asked, but the remarkably fine revival at Stratford supplies an answer: Apart from being too drunk to move, they are having too good a time to leave.

The dynamics of George and Martha (named after America's first First Couple, for reasons that have little to do with anything beyond the author's playfulness) are fascinating, and they vary from production to production. In the 1962 original, Uta Hagen gave an exhilarating powerhouse account of Martha; she was a destroyer, literally and nautically, and the rest of the play had to get out of her way. Martha Henry's Stratford performance is equally aggressive, but she doesn't carry the same guns, and we are less inclined to see the play through her eyes. Peter Donaldson's George, the very soul and image of a cankered academic and a performance of consummate technical authority, is initially the more sympathetic.

For a start, in a 3 1/2-hour play that holds us mostly with its humour, he has the most elegant tirades and the snappiest one- liners. To his guests, he is aggressively patronizing; to his wife he is defensively patronizing, and he does have a lot to put up with. She humiliates him verbally in company, taunting him with his professional failures. And having cuckolded him verbally, she proceeds to do so physically, at least to the extent of Nick's alcohol-diminished capacity. (Nick's wife is immobilized on the bathroom floor at the time). However, George does play along with all this, even orchestrates it; he degrades Martha by letting her degrade herself and then pretending not to care about it. He is the cleverer of the two, and by so much the crueller.

As it happens, Henry's Martha in her swaggering, sashaying mode is rather forced; alone in the cast, she doesn't seem to be acting in her own voice but in something put on for the occasion. She is at her best (as she was, rather differently, in Long Day's Journey into Night) when the character is furthest from conventional lucidity -- most memorable when she sits silent on the floor, her mouth working convulsively in the intervals when she doesn't have a glass at it.

Sean Arbuckle and Claire Jullien are perfect as Nick and Honey, she, with a wide-eyed Mia Farrow touch, sinking steadily into girlish denial as the horrors mount around her. It isn't that the younger couple see in the older a warning of what they might become; it's that they are confronted with a mocking mirror of what they already are, except that they aren't even in love. The four play together, under William Carden's direction, with awe-inspiring precision and flexibility. The play, as always happens in great ensemble performances, grows stronger by the moment.

Stronger but not necessarily better. The conscious stages into which George and Martha, especially George, divide their games -- "Get the Guest," "Hump the Hostess" -- always seem to me like devices for the playwright rather than credible crutches for the playwright. So, too, with the most notorious crutch of all: their shared pretence that they have a child, a grown son. (They have an imaginary kid; Honey supposedly has hysterical pregnancies, though the truth, revealed by the author with old-time melodramatic relish, turns out to be even more hysterical.)

In some productions the child has been presented as Martha's genuine fantasy, one that George has gone along with but that he finally punctures as a kind of desperate therapy. In this one it's an acknowledged ploy that they can both use as a weapon: telling people he's a bad father, she's a bad mother. Martha plays the game best, so George kills the kid, so to speak, as an act of revenge that doesn't preclude a note of shared pity at the end. (It's like the finale of Look Back in Anger, and as ambiguously sentimental.)

Either way, it feels too cut-and-dried, as if reality and illusion were separable compartments rather than shifting mental states. It also occasions lyrical arias that I confess I did not, that late in the evening, want to hear. The play's length is justifiable; it needs to be relentless. Oddly, what slows it down is a major change in tone.

The standard argument against such criticisms is that Albee was not writing a realistic play at all but an absurdist parable. But this won't wash. Whatever may be true of his other plays (most of which I find deadly dull) this one has real, rooted characters in a real room with real walls and a real time-scheme. It even has a traditional Ibsenite structure, in which some things are left obscure but most questions are answered, including some we never asked. It also, now, has nostalgic appeal: It pinpoints the liberal Kennedy moment -- before Oswald, before Watergate, and above all before campus unrest; these academics had to make their own entertainment.

On top of this it has such mild pretentions as George's liberal attacks on what he takes to be Nick's heartless new scientific order or the fact that he happens to be reading Spengler's Decline of the West. This is all too scrappy to constitute a satirical comment on the American dream (title of an earlier Albee play), though George's speeches work brilliantly as part of his ongoing stand-up act. He has to sound off about something, just to keep the party and his own adrenaline going. No audience is ever going to take the play as anything other than a high-powered naturalistic play with a few odd bits sticking out. That, apart from the jokes, is why it plays so well; that is how these actors triumphantly play it.

HENRY IV PART ONE

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

---

HENRY V

Avon Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

The general word on last year's Stratford Festival was that it did everything well except Shakespeare. This year, that not- inconsiderable breach has been filled up in terms of quantity -- we have had four Shakespeare productions already, with one to come later in the season -- and of quality. The Shakespeares have been as exciting as everything else in what has been, if you can pardon The Sound of Music, an extraordinary opening week.

As an acting instrument, the festival company has come together more strongly and consistently than ever I remember. Look at its geological strata. It has William Hutt and Douglas Campbell, veterans of Stratford's commencement in 1953, as authoritative as you would expect and still amazingly fresh. It has mature players -- Brian Bedford, Martha Henry, Peter Donaldson, Seana McKenna -- who have been in and out of the festival in the intervening years and seem to belong there. And it has, at last, a solid, lively brigade of younger actors, some of them products of the theatre's new classical conservatory, which, to judge from the standard of speech and understanding up there, is feeding them the right stuff. Go to Stratford this year and you may hold the whole of the festival's history in your hands.

Talking of history, at the end of last week, Stratford continued its progress through the English chronicle plays on what might be called the Doughnut Principle, i.e., munchy but with a hole in the middle. Henry IV Part Two has yet to arrive, but the two plays that flank it are richly in place, as is the continuity between them: an especially remarkable achievement given they have been mounted by different directors on different stages.

Scott Wentworth's production of Henry IV Part One begins with a silent young man, whom we rightly take to be Prince Hal, dressed in neutral, modern black leather. This is not the cheeriest of beginnings, and it becomes downright perplexing when his father the king appears red-coated to meet with his advisors in what seem to be the fashions of the First World War. The next scene, the first to which Hal textually belongs, finds him in the company of Sir John Falstaff, who seems to have stepped out of some older production, being dressed in the style usually known as Merrie England. And at this point, everything clicks. Hal, surveying the king's world and Falstaff's, is having, in effect, to choose between the values of two kinds of past: one near, chilly and politic, the other distant, warm and seductively disordered.

Orthodox criticism gives the prince a choice of fathers; in this production, the actor playing Falstaff is the actual father of the actor playing the king, so Hal has to choose between father and grandfather. Visually, too, the mixed costuming is a cunning method of providing the best of all worlds; often we get the different periods side by side (by side) and Patrick Clark's designs are stylish enough to give us contrast without head-aching glare.

I confess to feeling apprehensive of Douglas Campbell's Falstaff. I have not always found him the subtlest of actors, and he has played the fat knight so often that I was afraid of getting a routine stroll through the role. I have rarely felt so humbled. Campbell's performance certainly bears the marks of experience but his ease is invaluable, not only to the actor but to the character. Falstaff may be perpetually young in spirit but it is age and a continual sense of having been here before that give him authority; everyone else in the play is his junior.

Campbell knows his way around this text, knows in his bones how to phrase it;he never sentimentalizes and he is also -- a surprisingly rare quality in Falstaffs -- very funny. The great tavern scene lives up to its reputation, both in the uproar it creates and in the frost that dispels it. When Falstaff, asked to explain his flight from the disguised Hal at Gadshill, snaps back, "I knew ye as well as he that made ye," he brings down the house: for once, a Great Shakespearean Comic Moment that works. After that, I could have forgiven the performance and the production anything.

Not, as it turns out, that there is much to forgive. Benedict Campbell presents a masterful Henry with an unfailing knack for saying the wrong thing. Wanting desperately to get through to his son, he cannot stop lecturing him; though he succeeds in regaining Hal's loyalty he can never believe that he has won his love, and the play ends with the gap between them still wide open. One of the ironies is that the king preaches the virtues of dissimulation to a prince who already knows more about them than he ever will.

Graham Abbey, who has been making a heartening progression through the ranks (he was D'Artagnan in last year's Three Musketeers), is a very fine Hal, simultaneously open-faced and close- hearted. He approaches kingsghip as a job, and he is a superb professional; he fights and kills Hostpur because it's expected of him, and his respect and regret seem genuine. He takes to the Eastcheap pub scene almost to the manner born; his comic timing is as good as Falstaff's.

Jonathan Goad's Hotspur lacks the right headlong pace, the sense of being carried away by his own excitement, but he is spirited, and especially sympathetic in the scenes with his wife (Jane Spence), which play like a happy sequel to The Taming of the Shrew; Shakespeare even changed Lady Percy's historical name to Kate.

Richard McMillan makes a pouchy-eyed politician out of Worcester; while, back among the lowlifes, two minor roles are cast from unprecedented strength: Barry MacGregor a stolid batman of a Bardolph, and Diane D'Aquila, an unusually sensible (and personable) Hostess.

The production is good at overlapping the disparate scenes, bringing them all into the same world. A huge map, spread across the floor for the rebels to plan their carve-up of England, stays in place when the king laments the country's fate to his son. Cloaked attendants change identity instantly from one scene to the next, and furniture displays the same obliging versatility. Only a small chorus of nuns seems puzzling; maybe they've wandered in from the musical down the road.

Henry V, directed by Jeanette Lambermont, wears a similar set of chronological bifocals. In this war play, we again have 1914-18 uniforms co-existing with medieval surcoats; since both styles, in Dany Lyne's design, are basically black, they go together well. Only the French are allowed colour and look full-bloodedly medieval, as if they lost the Battle of Agincourt by being militarily behind the times (which is historically true); unfortunately the Gallic males, with the exception of Michael Therriault's superb herald, are uncertainly played, though I thought I'd figured out by the last scene what Donald Carrier's pretending-to-be-weak king was up to.

The set consists mainly of a ramp, similar to that in the same director's As You Like It but far more appropriate. Behind it, ceaselessly projected, is video footage: close-ups of the principals, newsreels of marching mud-soaked troops. This may sound intrusive but it works very well, keeping a double focus. This is a specific historical war; it is also every war. It also poses the old double question: Death or Glory?

The play, which like its hero is the most opaque in the canon, never gives a definitive answer and the production, despite its obvious pacifist sympathies, never forces one either. Seana McKenna, a close-cropped Chorus, starts by addressing us with grim over- emphasis, punching every other word to make her meaning clear. Then, when she gets to the line about letting our imaginary forces work, she relaxes, as if she has now decided to trust us. She stays in firm but gentle control, giving all the choral praise of Henry its due, never ironizing until the epilogue when the script permits her. Much of what we see onstage contradicts or at least qualifies her, but that's fair enough; if the chorus told us everything, we wouldn't need the play. A solo cellist, Jill Vitols, both supports and modifies her with music that is alternately requiem and celebration.

Graham Abbey's Henry is still a young man easing himself into a role, and doing it consummately but at a cost. The cheerful face sometimes looks haunted. His patriotic war-whoops aren't set pieces; they're morale-builders, delivered to specific hearers for a specific purpose. In the big speech on ceremony, he almost wriggles spiritually free, but the summons of the outside world drags him visibly and painfully back to reality. He still snatches at humour whenever he can, with his soldiers and most notably in his wooing of the French princess. Sara Topham, who was Lady Mortimer in the preceding play and speaks French as enchantingly as she spoke Welsh, gives him a harder time, takes longer to melt, than most Katharines, and Domini Blythe makes her a watchful worried duenna; there is a sense, even as they kiss, that this match and the peace it symbolizes, will not last.

Diane D'Aquila makes the account of Falstaff's death as moving, if not quite as endearingly absurd, as it should be; she and her hearers are sitting in a line at the edge of the stage, their feet dangling into space.

Barry MacGregor completes his Bardolph by being spectacularly hanged on stage; this is becoming a convention, but I wonder if the point could not be more economically made. Similarly, Paul Dunn's excellent Boy is presented to us as camcording the proceedings; this maintains the overall performance metaphor but it robs us of direct comic contact. Keith Dinicol's Pistol and Thom Marriott's hulking Nym are welcome newcomers, and Evan Buliung's grumbling Williams is first-rate.

So, in a different sphere, is Bernard Hopkins' Archishop of Canterbury, smooth but shifty: This notorious bore of a character avoids boring us. Indeed, the house seemed spellbound by the entire show; certainly I was. The history plays, so history shows, are the best possible material for forging a Shakespearean ensemble. They have come through for Stratford; and Stratford has come through for them.

Until July 15. Box office: (416) 872-1212. Robertcushman@lycos.com

THE FULL MONTY

Elgin Theatre, Toronto

- - -

I doubt if I am revealing anything when I say that The Full Monty ends with six guys up on stage revealing everything. As has been the way with musicals, all the way back to Hair, the show goes coy at the moment of disclosure, which is not so much capped by a blackout as synchronized with it. There are, however, much odder things about this musicals closing number than that.

The strippers, as everybody will remember who saw the English film on which this American show is based, are new at the game: five blue-collar workers and one white or, counting another way, five youngish white guys and one oldish black. They have all been thrown out of work by a factory closure in their impoverished home town of Buffalo or, as it was pronounced in the movie, "Sheffield."

To raise some cash and revive their morale, they get up this stripper act. Comes the big night, comes the big number, and they start it with a song. Now, we have spent most of the evening watching them rehearsing , or just getting up their nerve, and not only have we not heard them practise a note, the prospect of their singing has never even been mentioned.

And another thing: Toward the end of the number, a great light shines. It proves to be the shows title, spelled out in giant neon letters, one word to a line. It looks hideous. It also looks expensive. So what's it doing there? The whole point of the story is that these men are broke. They have just about scraped together the money to hire the hall -- how could they afford all that glitz?

Or is it just that this is a musical, so it doesn't have to make sense?

The Full Monty, as you may have guessed, is a crass and charmless reduction of a funny and touching original. One of the worst things about it is the standard of performance in that closing number. Its too good. These guys are meant to be amateurs. Thats why we should be rooting for them.

A Jerome Robbins or a Michael Bennett might conceivably have devised a routine that would work as part of a musical while still keeping faith with the situation, but Jerry Mitchell, the choreographer here, has simply gone for flash. It isn't all bad flash; there's an audition number in the first act called Big Black Man that legitimately tears the place up, and its capped by another in which the whole gang loosen up their moves, macho-style, by thinking of Michael Jordan. But even that latter one has the feel of something thrown in to get us to intermission. It doesnt go anywhere.

It's impossible, anyway, to enjoy the show as just a series of mindless diversions, because it's trying to tug your heartstrings at the same time. This, however, is where it really degrades its source.

Part of the trouble may be the change of locale. Its not, God knows, that depression, economic and psychological, cant also strike in the United States (though John Arnone's elaborately skeletal set looks little like Buffalo, or like anywhere else). It's that the underlying assumption that an American audience couldnt possibly understand or sympathize with people from Englands post- industrial North is insulting to both parties, and this patronizing attitude seeps through the entire show. It's the same mindset that turned Fawlty Towers into the aptly-named Royal Payne, insisting on the way that Basil and Sybil were really terribly fond of one another.

Here, straightening out the characters' kinks and quirks , ostensibly making them more sympathetic, actually means making them less interesting and far less emotionally involving. Watching the film, one cared about the relationship between the tearaway young leader of the troupe and the son of his broken marriage. Here the boy is just another cute theatrical kid. And it doesnt help when his dad (Rod Weber, too bland for the dramatic weight he has to carry) starts crooning a lullaby at him.

This is one of a clutch of sentimental numbers that back up, one after another, at the end of David Yazbeks score. Its earlier sections are livelier. The opening ensemble, Scrap, a hymn of unemployment, captures a strong, angry mood that never recurs, and there are sharp observations, neat rhymes, and even a couple of genuine laughs in what follows.

Yazbek's tunes are less striking than his lyrics, but they are inoffensive until the home stretch when, for example, a song called You Rule My World, previously sung by a fat man to his beer belly, is reprised as a turgidly conventional soft-rock ballad. The composer has complained in interviews about the prevalence of musical-theatre scores that beg for cheap applause; he's right, but if he and his colleagues think that they have risen above all that, they should get the neon beams out of their eyes.

This show goes for every obvious effect it can manage. Terrence McNallys book dogs the footsteps of the movie, dulling or coarsening its impact at every turn. A sad-funny scene about an ineffectual suicide becomes forced, unfunny farce. The scene in which furniture repossessors are routed by the boys twanging their G- strings is still there; so is the abrupt termination of a rehearsal by a police raid. But neither scene has any force, party because of Jack OBrien's ineffectual staging, partly because the characters concerned no longer mean anything.

As for the scene in which our heroes break uncontrollably into their dance steps while standing in the dole queue -- the one great sequence that everyone remembers, the one that would seem to have real musical potential -- it's been transferred to the presumably less depressing setting of a funeral, where it goes for almost nothing. This may be because the scene is attempting to kill three birds with one stone; it also functions as a gay romance, and as a requiem for a dear departed whom we met, a whole act earlier, for all of two minutes.

Larry Marshalls big black man is energizing, and Daniel Stewart Shermans fat man is an appealing stereotype. Steven Skybell flaps competently about as the ex-manager living in fear of the bailiffs, though his is the most diminished character of all -- a supposed graduate of Wharton, one of America's top two business schools, but one who, if my resident management consultant is to be trusted, is seriously confused about the distinction between niche marketing and competitive edge, applying the former term to the concept of going the full monty when he really means the latter.

(Isn't it strange how glibly that phrase full monty now slides off all our tongues? Before the film came along, none of us had ever heard it. Im not even sure on which side of the pond it originated.)

Gay-friendly and feminist (or at least male-objectifying) though the show professes to be, all its women, save one, are shrieking caricatures, and ineptly played at that. The exception, and this productions nearest thing to a saving grace, is the veteran singer- comedien Kaye Ballard, who plays an elderly piano-lady come out of retirement to accompany the boys in their hours of need and glory. She regards them with a permanent gleaming smile, suggesting both great kindness and utter bewilderment -- personal, that is; professionally, she's almost unfazeable, though sometimes her resource -- "I can't play any slower," she complains of one hesitant strutter -- seems about to give out.

As a link with actual American show business, the character may have been written in to give the musical a link with something it knows about. Anyway, the actress and the script serve one another perfectly; every line is funny. To be honest, she seems to be acting in a world of her own. But it's a better world.

LONELY NIGHTS AND OTHER STORIES

Factory Theatre

- - -

Theatre Columbus, who work up their shows in rehearsal through group improvisation, have a winner.

Lonely Nights and Other Stories is a kaleidoscopic entertainment that deals, as announced, with people who cannot get through to one another or, worse yet, cannot even find another to fail to get through to. Here are people who cannot get a date, or sit tongue- tied in the presence of those they do have. Here are parents in search of children and children of parents. Here are sad apartments and sadder hotels. Here are rabid environmentalists who cannot even get desk clerks to listen to them.

Here, though it may not seem too likely, is a great deal of fun and as much sweetness as sadness. All the lonely people: The important question, as the show realizes, is not where they all come from but where they all go to.

The play is set, apparently, in the near future, though there is little about it that could not be happening already. The main differences are that the squirrels seem to be taking over, appearing everywhere anyone looks, and that the corded telephone seems finally to have disappeared. Cell-phones rule, cutting themselves out and their users off, and occasioning a telling joke about the way people communicate in prisons.

The setting is a picturesquely grey townscape, of which half the architecture looks vaguely Shakespearean -- curtained entrances, like at the Globe -- and the other half Dickensian. At a high window on the Elizabethan side sits a 3 a.m. radio announcer, telling us more or less that there are a million stories in the lonely city. Apparently, it has been raining for weeks.

This is not too prepossessing, and an extended group section that follows, all fretful hustle and bustle and mostly in mime, would probably be more enjoyable if one were seeing it for the second time and could appreciate where it was leading.

There are five actors in the cast, and initially it is not too easy to tell when one of them is either assuming a new identity or playing a recurring character. The hopeful sign is that, as the characters establish themselves, we want them to recur. And they do, in shifting combinations; the show begins to weave a cat's cradle of fragmentary encounters, even of fragmentary relationships.

The turning point for me was the moment at which a gawky lady who had interrupted somebody elses drama by trying to sell her a vacuum cleaner (surely a dying breed) was glimpsed knocking on another door, about to take centre-stage in her own story. There is something here of the insouciant loopiness with which Monty Pythons Flying Circus used to link its separate sketches; the vacuum hawker could well have been on her way to or from the Ministry of Silly Walks.

The writing of the show is credited to the director, Leah Cherniak, and to the actors, who are all in varying degrees splendid. One, Maggie Huculak, is sublime. The tallest actress west of Vanessa Redgrave, she plays with extraordinary grace and economy: a few strokes, a few words, and a character is solidly there.

She is the gently flailing salesperson who, asked to describe rather than demonstrate her product, begins by saying that "nature abhors a vacuum," and she is a maiden schoolteacher, etched with a wonderful stern dignity, who is mortally ill and whose plight moved me more in two minutes than did the whole of Wit put together.

Oliver Dennis specializes in gentle grotesquerie; he is a sci-fi nut of a receptionist whose courtesy is so understated as to be spectral, and an enforced celibate who, when other men tell him of their troubles with women, snaps that they're lucky to have the women to be troubled by, and -- more crisply -- a small-time private detective, English apparently, necessarily specializing in lost causes. His timing is superb.

Ker Wells is both touchy and touching as an illiterate ex-con, believably out for good behaviour, and very funny as a self- obsessed actor who talks to his mother as though she were his agent.

Michael Simpson does gruff, eccentric and cheerily desperate, notably as a man phoning every long-ago acquaintance in his address book before giving in and settling for phone sex.

Martha Ross lacks the presence and precision of the others (her night owls' deejay is over-insistent) but is fine as a lonely-heart rabbit farmer and a mother trying to make contact with a daughter on the other side of the world

All these people deserve some happiness. What's more, they get it. Relationships get tentatively launched; vital messages, through tortuous chains of circumstances, get delivered. Even the rain stops. Everybody breaks into a celebratory little dance, awkward but a delight. The emotional resolution that The Full Monty busts several guts to bring off, this show actually achieves. It should stick around.

THE DROWSY CHAPERONE

Winter Garden Theatre, Toronto

Despite appearances, The Drowsy Chaperone is not a satire on 1920s and 1930s musicals. It's a satire on people who love 1920s and 1930s musicals, and who also love satires of them. Its principal character, identified in the program as Man in Chair, is a gentleman of indeterminate years with a large record collection and a mind stuffed with theatrical trivia. He puts on an original cast recording, apparently issued as a 78 rpm album, of an imaginary 1929 show called The Drowsy Chaperone; and, to his delight and quite often to ours, the show takes physical shape before our eyes.

I pause here to remark that, for 78s, these seem to be very long- playing records, and that I know of no show from that period that was ever recorded by its stage performers, in full, dialogue included.

Man in Chair is played by Bob Martin, with an exquisite sense of controlled whimsy: That is, the character's whimsicality is out of control but the actor's isn't. The same Bob Martin wrote the show's book, in collaboration with Don McKellar, with Matt Watts given the intriguing, and as far as I know totally unprecedented, credit of associate writer. The same Bob was also one-half of the show's original inspiration; it was created to celebrate his wedding to an actress, Janet Van de Graaff, and the show-within-the-show actually concerns the threatened nuptials of a couple named, wait for it, Robert Martin and Janet Van de Graaff.

The in-joke worked well enough to be shown to the public at the 1999 Toronto Fringe festival, and from there it moved in expanded form for a run at Theatre Passe Muraille. At this point (with Bob in his present narrator's role but Janet playing Janet) the jest seemed to have more than run its course; blowing it up to still larger proportions for a commercial production, as has now been done, seemed like arrant folly. That at least is what I thought, and it shows how wrong I can be. The present version is not without problems but it provides plenty to admire and much to enjoy. How can you resist a show that starts with an accurate summary of every theatregoer's prayer just before the lights go up? "Oh God, let it be short -- nobody should have to stand two intermissions -- if it has to be a new Canadian play, let it not be a new Canadian play."

Well, The Drowsy Chaperone is short, has no intermissions, and far from being set in Canada, its main action seems to be going on in fairyland, or at the very least on Long Island. Prohibition is on, the Depression is not yet. The characters are showfolks, crooks, servants and the very rich. Janet the bride is an actress; Robert the groom is a goof. Their marriage is delayed by their own amiable stupidity and by a few plot complications. George, Robert's bald- headed best man, tries to keep the proceedings on track despite other characters' machinations. Janet is her producer's meal ticket and he does not want her to retire into matrimony; he owes money to a couple of gangsters who more than share his concern.

The producer's girlfriend is a dumb chorine who wants to be the star. Janet's mother is a dragoness, somehow lured into marriage with her butler. A continental gigolo makes a play for Janet but is deflected into seducing her sharp-tongued if somnolent companion, who is the chaperone of the title but a minor character nonetheless; she is an ineffectual guardian for Janet, who is a headstrong product of her time and place. "Here a girl can map her own/Life without a chaperone": Lorenz Hart, 1926.

They're all minor characters, and that is one of the aforementioned problems. There is nobody and nothing in this apocryphal vintage show we can latch on to. The man in the chair would have us believe that this doesn't matter, and that the enchantment of these old musicals lies in their silliness, in their unabashed stereotyping, in their shameless bad jokes, in their songs. Up to a point he's right, but he leaves some important things out, though he does allude to them in passing.

The real shows of this kind, or the best of them, starred people like Fred and Adele Astaire, and had scores by people like George and Ira Gershwin. Regularly, our narrator freezes the action to tell us about the actors we are supposedly watching; his capsule summaries of doomed careers are witty (and delivered with an enchanting blend of awe and regret) but of course these actors weren't real, and are being played by other actors anyway. This is not star quality. As for the score, which has been 50% overhauled for this production: Greg Morrison's tunes are very apt pastiche, and Lisa Lambert's lyrics are superb, in tone and in technique: I especially liked a feckless tap duet called Cold Feets and a wonderfully ruthless list song about disasters.

There is also an irresistible interpolation from another imaginary musical altogether. But none of the songs touch the heart or lift the show into a new emotional dimension, as the Gershwins or Cole Porter could. Also, there is a limit to how much enjoyment one can get from listening to bad jokes, even when they're bad on purpose and performed with panache. I suspect that the gangsters' malapropisms are meant to be funny in their own right; they aren't, but they sure try hard. Nor does the farcical action ever take off in its own right. In short, we don't care. I realize we're not supposed to; but the feeling still nags. It nagged me, anyway.

The show has been newly and transformingly directed by Daniel Brooks, who has previously demonstrated a witty way with weightier works and who is here equally fly with fluff. Christopher Richards, who designed gorgeous costumes last time round, has been happily retained. Of the cast, also half new, Dan Chameroy, vacantly beaming on roller-skates, sends himself happily up as what I suppose we have to call the hero, and Karen Hines as his opposite number does likewise. Frank Moore as the producer is dynamite, Paul O'Sullivan's best man is the best, and I withdraw my previous allegation that Don McKellar as the Latin lover looks like Hitler. Mary Lou Fallis, prominent comic soprano, puts in an overhyped appearance as a dea ex machina, and the lyricist plays the chaperone, whose bored song about the wonders of the world would be even funnier if she sang rather than talked it. I want to know: After this show and Honest Ed -- The Bargain Musical, could she write a show that would, please God, be equally comic but not a spoof? We need it.

The Winter Garden, stacked on top of the Elgin, is the nearest thing we have to a rooftop theatre, and the show might function best as did the late-night rooftop shows of the '20s: as a theatrical dessert, to be taken in after consuming something more substantial elsewhere.

To be honest, I lied somewhat about this show's lack of content; it has some, in the character of Man in Chair. (He does get out of it, quite frequently.) Before, he was the compere who stole the show; now they've given in and handed it to him. He tells us more about himself and about his devotion -- not uncritical but quite abandoned -- to escapist musical theatre. Other things about him we can observe for ourselves, and quite a character emerges; when he gets caught up in a production number, even more when the curtain calls go to his head, he becomes the audience as protagonist, and we realize that this is what the show was driving at all along. He is the star. He may even -- considering his sedentary posture and his tutelary relation to us, the other audience -- be the real drowsy chaperone. I never said the show wasn't clever.

INES DE CASTRO

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

- - -

"You talk about people as if they were abstractions," says Ines de Castro, protesting an act of inhumanity aimed in her general direction, and sounding very much like an abstraction herself. She is the Spanish-born mistress of 14th-century Portuguese Prince Pedro whose father, King Alfonso, regards her with considerable suspicion, their two countries being at war at the time.

The king eventually permits his ministers to execute Ines and murder her two young children. He sends his son to the front, hoping he will relieve the general embarrassment by getting himself killed, but Pedro confounds expectation by returning victorious at the head of his Portuguese men of war.

The king drops obligingly dead, and Pedro, succeeding to the throne, takes a grisly revenge on his beloved's enemies. The chief of them is tortured to death at a banquet, while Ines's corpse is exhumed, enrobed and enthroned, so that the people may pay her that homage in death that she was never accorded while alive. Ines, who seems to be a decent sort, if overgiven to philosophical speculation, comments from beyond the grave that this is not what she would have wanted.

The story, which is historical and has attracted previous dramatists, has been turned by British playwright John Clifford into a perfectly dismal play that is now 11 years old. It consists of people talking, and the fact that they have been given literate- sounding dialogue to spout does not make it any better. They never enact their predicament; they talk around it.

It is born in on us that killing people is wrong, and that men (it always seems to be men) who commit atrocities can always excuse themselves by citing similar crimes committed by the other side. I trust you find this enlightening.

The actors playing the royal and noble principals also double as a chorus, one of whose functions is to rub our noses in contemporary parallels. So a Portuguese Jew, who has seen how his co- religionists are being treated in Spain, gives a long description whose details -- victims being forced to dig their own mass graves - - are drawn from the 20th-century Holocaust.

There is also a very familiar-sounding passage about domestic violence. And, of course, descriptions of raped women and slaughtered or traumatized children resonate easily. If you don't come out of this play about medieval Portugal thinking of modern Bosnia and Rwanda, it won't be the playwright's fault.

I suppose it's petty to ask a man whose gaze is fixed on the wider picture to avert it long enough to bring to life the characters he is ostensibly writing about, and flippant to remark that his generalizations tell us nothing that we don't already know and are, in fact, exploitative. Sometimes the chorus speaks, with embarrassing condescension, for the common people for whom life, as it usually does, goes on. A meat seller, who would get on well with Sweeney Todd's Mrs. Lovett, talks about the war's depressing effect on her business: "You wouldn't believe what they're putting into pies." A torturer lets us know that inflicting ingeniously agonizing deaths is a living like any other, and that he personally is a good family man. Maybe Brecht invented this kind of thing. It certainly seems to have been around a long time.

More immediately, Clifford recalls the elaborately facetious phantasmagorias of Peter Barnes, who wrote The Ruling Class and The Bewitched. I don't like his plays much, either, but at least he got there first.

Ines de Castro is presented by Whetstone Productions, who say that they are "dedicated to developing and producing provocative scripts through physical exploration of the text using rhythm, music and gesture, and to fostering creative talent within an ensemble setting." This is to distinguish them from all those other companies which deliberately go looking for unprovocative scripts, which are fiercely opposed to creative talent, and which wouldn't know an ensemble setting if it advanced on them brandishing switchblades and singing the Jet Song. Why do companies insist on making these claims? Why don't they just shut up and do the bloody plays?

I'm also not sure about the "physical exploration" bit. Diana Kolpak's production looked pretty static to me, though the emphasis on rhythm and music may explain why the play starts with a lot of wordless chanting, and why some later speeches are aurally supplemented in a rather literal manner: If somebody in a scene mentions moaning, those outside it will moan.

The text, meanwhile, might have more luck in making banalities sound like profundities if the actors could bring to it something more dynamic than earnest complaint (for the good), silky sarcasm (for the bad) and shoulder-shrugging jocularity (for the poor).

Elyssa Livergant plays Ines, Ron Kennell her prince, Cheryl McNamara his cast-off spouse, Robert Tsonos the evil counsellor whose end you don't want to hear about, and Patrick Conner the king, who looks and sounds slightly younger than his son. This may be generation-blind casting, and Heaven forbid that I should be so literal-minded as to condemn it, but there is a built-in balance to such dramatic relationships, and it might be better realized by casting actors who at least approximate to the correct weight.

Completing the cast, and possessed of more presence and variety than all the others put together, is Dinah Watts as Ines's nurse, a relationship that, what with Ines being a strong-minded princess in an unfriendly land with a weak lover and two vulnerable kids, seems to have stepped out of Euripides' Medea. She also appears as Death, who comes for Ines and, this being the kind of play it is, tells us all about it. She does this well, and if I couldn't help comparing her to John Cleese as the Grim Reaper, that was hardly her fault.

ANTIGONE

The Great Hall, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Time has played some interesting tricks on Jean Anouilh's Antigone, which is fair enough since the play itself plays tricks with the Sophoclean drama on which it is based. Anouilh wrote his version during the Nazi occupation of France, and it must have been plain that his Antigone, defying Theban martial law by burying the body of her brother Polyneices after he has been declared an enemy of the state, stood for all the desperate heroes of the French Resistance. It could not be made too plain, however; and Anouilh was careful to give Creon, king of Thebes and Antigones uncle, arguments as good as his nieces.

This makes, of course, for excellent drama; the play, certainly in this taut new production by the Red Red Rose company, exerts a superb, unbroken grip. However, one vital element has gone irretrievably missing. I said we find Creon's arguments as good as Antigone's; actually, most of us will find them better. We no longer see Creon as a smooth apologist for collaboration; we take him at his own valuation as a conscientious workman, trying to restore order after a vicious civil war. When Antigone, having been caught at her corpse-covering, is brought before him, Creon -- her putative father-in-law as well as her uncle -- tells her not to be so silly and to go to her room. When Antigone makes it clear she will immediately leave it to re-scatter the earth that Creons guards have removed, he tries another tack. Does she, he asks, really believe all that superstitious nonsense about a mans shade being doomed to wander to eternity if it is not interred to the accompaniment of some pious words hurriedly intoned by bored and boring priests? Antigone admits that she doesn't.

This is where Anouilh departs most significantly from his source. Sophocles' Antigone does believe. His Creon does, too; he knows he is elevating laws of man above laws of the gods and, later on, the gods themselves tell him so. Sophocles play has been celebrated for centuries as a model of faultlessly balanced dialectic, but it actually leaves no doubt that Creon is a tyrant.

Anouilh, writing in an irreligious age, is far more ambiguous. His Antigone survives Creons assault by asserting that, superstition notwithstanding, the right thing is the right thing. She even withstands his assertions that the brother she mourns was actually a selfish thug. She finally breaks down when he reveals that he doesn't know if the body is even Polyneices'; it is just as likely to be that of his equally worthless brother Eteocles, who died fighting him and has been proclaimed a hero by virtue of having been in the right place at the right time. Creon then unwisely presses his advantage by telling Antigone about the happiness in store for her as the wife of his son Haemon, who loves her and whom she loves. Sensing that such mediocre pleasures will merely dull her idealism, Antigone jumps right back and opts for death. This is even less persuasive than the similar moment in Shaws Saint Joan, when the maid, having given up on her voices, goes to the stake only because it seems preferable to being locked up.

In the days of the Resistance, most of whose acts were suicide missions, it would have struck a chord. To us, it seems what Creon calls it: self-indulgence. Antigone, choosing death as an awfully big adventure preferable to growing up, appears to be auditioning for the role of Peter Pans ideal girlfriend.

The idea for which Sarah Phillips' production seems most pleased with itself is also its most questionable. It consists of eliminating Anouilh's impersonal one-actor chorus, and giving the lines to Antigone herself. The chorus function, apart from filling in holes in the story, is to expound a theory of tragedy; tragedy, we are told, differs from drama (melodrama might be a better word) in being calm, unhysterical, a matter of playing out pre-determined roles. A person has ideals, acts on them, and the machine is in motion. Letting Antigone herself tell us this may save an extra salary but it invites us, and the actress, to take her rather too much at her own valuation; she talks quite enough as things are, and now she is permitted not just to behave like a tragic heroine but to present herself as one.

This is not to attack the way Christine Brubaker speaks the choral lines; she does them impeccably. She is a little less successful when it comes to putting theory into practice, as Antigone herself. The characters salient quality is the one with which most actors have the most trouble: implacability. The temptation is always to work your way round it. When this Antigone berates her sister Ismene, whom she wants for an accomplice, she seems to be trying to persuade her: But Antigone would never stoop to persuasion. (Ismene says she sort of sees what Uncle Creon means; Antigone replies that she doesn't want to "sort of see" anything, which gives you the girl in a nutshell.) But she is very fine, the picture of a blackmailing waif, when she confronts Creon, and finer still, confused on the edge of her grave, in the last scene, shared only with a guard (Michael Healey, pricelessly embarrassed) whose intentions are good but whose emotional and intellectual resources are rigorously limited.

Richard Greenblatt plays Creon with a wry, weary reasonableness that I found almost totally convincing as argument and entirely so as characterization; only at the end does he seem insufficiently weighty and worn down; this, after all, is his tragedy as well -- he, too, has taken on a role he has to play -- and he loses as much as Antigone, with the extra twist that he has to live with it.

Haemon is bland and Ismene weak, but Elizabeth Brown as the nurse is excellent. She is played French -- or, presumably, French- Canadian -- and is constantly sliding between the original text (I assume it's the original) and the directors own new translation; Antigone replies in kind, and it gives their scenes an extraordinary intimacy. Anouilh, as you would expect, is masterly at supplying the kind of domestic detail the Greek tragedians disdained. This doesnt make his characters more vivid than Sophocles'; it makes them vivid in a different way. Probably it's a lesser way, and some of it seems excessively knowing. But it gets at least within striking distance of the ideal of tragedy that it propounds; and this production, beautifully set by Camellia Koo with a stark assortment of chairs and lamps, does it proud.

FOSSE

Pantages Theatre, Toronto

There is a telltale moment in the first act of Fosse. The band strikes up the opening bars of Hooray for Hollywood, and the cast of dancers, doing their job, perform a few steps to it. There are only a few because this song is the only one in the evening that never featured in a Bob Fosse stage or screen musical. It has been inserted, rather desperately, as narrative glue. It precedes a number that Fosse choreographed during his own time in Hollywood (his very first, actually, from the film of Kiss Me Kate), which itself is followed by a routine he devised for his stage show Dancin' as a tribute to Fred Astaire, set to a song that Astaire performed in another film Fosse himself had nothing to do with.

So this sequence represents, very roughly, the subject's movie period. To appreciate this, however, you would have to be an expert on Fosse's career, or at least be able to read the program notes in the dark. It is the same later on with a number done to the old song Dancing in the Dark (the real one, not the Springsteen pretender), apparently based on routines Fosse used to perform on television, with and without his first wife. Again, who would know? One can understand the show's creators -- Chet Walker, Richard Maltby Jr., Ann Reinking, in that chronological order of involvement -- wanting to avoid explicit narration, which might smack of the schoolroom or at least the PBS documentary, but they haven't come up with a comprehensible alternative.

The biographical approach, such as it is, is only fitfully employed. The idea seems more to illustrate Fosse's showbiz philosophy, which might be summed up as the world is rotten so enjoy it. We start with a languorous world-weary rendition of Life Is Just a Bowl of Cherries, and we end with a reprise of it. That's about it for structure. A mournful crouching creature at the side of the stage during the opening is probably the same one who reappears near the end as the downcast hero of Mr. Bojangles, a broken-down hoofer who spends most of his time in jail and probably represents Fosse's worst nightmare of the dancer's life. But we have had no sense of him in the interim.

So what we have is a staged anthology of song-and-dance routines - - the emphasis far more on dance than song -- that were originally created, for a variety of projects, by a man who was one of the two or three greatest Broadway choreographers. He was certainly the most distinctive -- the only one whose work can be identified at sight as being his -- and he was also the only one to parlay his stage success into movies and television. Some of these are still exciting. Big Spender, the dance-hall hostesses' massed come-on from Sweet Charity, remains a masterpiece: a symphony of sleazy costume and garish makeup, mockingly brassy music and minimal crooked- finger movement. Rich Man's Frug, noses and cigarette holders thrust aloft in a massed snobbery contest, is a satirical delight; it is also the only number that works better in this touring version than in the original production that we saw at the Ford Centre (as it then was) in North York, before it went to Broadway. This, too, derives from Sweet Charity: the last fun Fosse show before he decided that he had tidings to give the world, as in Pippin, Chicago, the film of Cabaret, and other explorations of his love- hate relationship to The Old Razzle Dazzle.

We get the trademark bowler hats, splayed feet, dark sets (reduced by Santo Loquasto to one dark set, and a gloomy one) and threefold formations. Fosse, having discovered the erotic potentialities of the trio in Steam Heat, went on exploiting them. He did it to great effect in individual shows, but when the results are placed end-to-end, it becomes wearing, however much he shuffles up the sexes. Cool Hand Luke (two males, one female) does not look all that different from Me and My Shadows (one male, two females), which immediately follows it. (And why in the latter do the two chicks keep singing, in counterpoint to the main lyric, about somebody called Dancing Dan the Safe-Breaking Man? The guy doesn't look like particularly like a break-and-enterer. You'd need to have seen Big Deal, the flop show in which the number originated, to answer that question. Most of us, of course, haven't.) A voice in my head began muttering, in the disjointed accents of Gollum from Lord of the Rings, "threesomes are tiresomes."

Unless my memory is failing me, the Glory sequence from Pippin, in which Fosse solemnly lets us know he was against war, and the orgy number Take Off with Us have been radically trimmed for the tour; I never liked the second one much, and I always hated the first, but there now seems no point in having them there at all. I Wanna Be a Dancin' Man, the Astaire homage, remains a delightful union of two apparent incompatibles, Fosse's tension and Fred's cool; they meet in the tilt of a hat. How To Succeed in Business Without Really Trying and Little Me -- two of the funniest shows Fosse or anyone else ever worked on -- have always been excluded: a pity, since the show could use some extra joy, especially now.

Even the wonderful extended closer, a skin-tight choreographic realization of the Benny Goodman warhorse Sing Sing Sing, is a shadow of its North York self; when the massed dancers perform the ultimate Fosse move -- the one that consists of leaping in the air while throwing out both your arms and letting your head follow -- they lack the proper abandon. Most of the dances here come off tight- limbed and heavy-footed.

Reva Rice, who does much of the singing and sounds a bit like Nancy Wilson, is a definite improvement on her predecessor; the other vocals, individual or group, manage to sound simultaneously loud and muffled. The orchestrations, even in their current tinny reproduction, are terrific; they are the work of Douglas Besterman, who recently won a Tony for his work on The Producers (as who didn't?) and, predominantly, of the great Ralph Burns, whom I would be inclined to nominate the hero of the evening. Livent, which originated the show, is nowhere mentioned in the program, and I suppose one would have to be naive to expect otherwise.

MILLERS COURT

Nightwood Theatre, Toronto

For the second time this year, the audience approaches a play by way of a meat elevator, this one taking us to the fifth floor of a building on St. Nicholas Street, at Yonge and Wellesley. Maybe the elevators in both cases were just plain old elevators, but while riding inside them I certainly felt like a piece of meat. The similarity goes further. The first play was about Paul Bernardo; the new one is about Jack the Ripper. The first play, I liked far more than did most of my colleagues; the new one I would challenge them, or anyone else, to like less. I suspect, though, that we will all agree: The amount of ineptitude on view here is awe-inspiring.

The piece centres on Mary Jane Kelly, the last of the Ripper's prostitute victims, who apparently met her end at the slum address in Victorian London from which the play takes its name. The show is the joint venture of two groups calling themselves Red Letter Theatre and Schmigeggy Productions. It was worked up in rehearsal by its five actors, one of whose number, Roxanne Deans, arranged their improvisations into a script; the results were directed by Adam Lazarus. They probably researched the historical record extensively, but the staged result suggests that they spent even more time poring over dusty manuals of what used to pass as experimental theatre. They proceed, earnestly, to throw their findings at us.

First, they give us painstaking naturalism. Mary Jane gets out of bed, while her landlord knocks at the door, demanding rent. Mary Jane performs her ablutions, which largely consist of taking swigs from a jug that we are meant to assume contains beer or maybe (and historically more likely) gin, but that she never persuades us contains anything stronger than mineral water.

Then it's off to the streets, which turn out to be full of expressionism; Mary Jane and two of her friends drape themselves round a handy post in grotesque attitudes likelier to frighten potential punters than attract them. This is presumably meant to illustrate their contempt for their clientele, but since they keep saying how much they need the money, it doesn't seem practical. We learn, in the course of the scene, that Mary Jane is pregnant.

The stage is then invaded by masks: The full company, in remarkably ugly visors, acting out some kind of street drama about the uncatchable, unidentifiable Ripper whom they seem to regard as a folk hero. Since they all speak in pinched accents suggestive of the English upper class, or caricatures thereof, I thought for awhile that they were slumming Victorian gentlefolk having a laugh at the expense of the working poor, but it turned out that they were meant to be actual 19th-century mummers impersonating Victorian gentlefolk doing the above. Either way, the performances they give with their masks on could hardly be more grotesque than the ones they have already given with them off, so the point, whatever it may be, is blunted.

Mary Jane's puritanical former boyfriend comes to call on her; they have a row, and she tells him to get out, which he does, without a murmur, in one of the least persuasive pieces of writing and staging I can remember seeing. She has a scene with a lady of charitable but patronizing intent, out to save her soul and body, whom she dismisses; and another with a working wife even poorer than herself, on whom she takes pity.

She drinks a lot and has a dialogue with a barman, who like her is Irish. The audience is beseeched in a program note to shout "To Ireland!" whenever these two give them the cue; soliciting audience participation in writing, in advance, may constitute some kind of record in naffness.

The motivation and identity of the Ripper are left in darkness, but a later choral scene (posh voices again) hints that it may all be the fault of society. There are two prominent male characters, each of whom we are led to believe may be Jack in disguise so the show may be credited with creating some suspense.

Mary Jane closes the proceedings with a detailed, posthumous account of her own disembowelling. Or maybe she's dreaming it in anticipation. We are left with the impression that, consciously or not, she was asking for it. That is probably a crudely reductive account of the complex web of destiny and victimization that the participants dreamed of creating, but I'm afraid it's the best I can do.

Jennifer Gillespie's performance of Mary Jane is slightly less awkward than what surrounds her, and that's the second-best I can do. Even the curtain call manages to be pretentious. The limpness of everybody's acting may be traceable to the lameness of everybody's dialogue, but, given that they all worked it out together, apportioning guilt is a frustratingly circular process. It seems safer and fairer to blame everyone.

2001-06-26-i-claudia-takes-doras-for-bes:
In New York, they have Mel Brooks; in Toronto, we have Kristen Thomson, and it is hard not to feel that we have the nicer deal.

Ms. Thomson, the author and sole performer of the play I, Claudia, won a Dora Mavor Moore award in both capacities, and while this may not be board-sweeping on the scale accomplished by Mr. Brooks's The Producers at the Tonys, it was still a heartwarming success.

She faced stiff competition in both categories (Seana McKenna in Wit would have been a shoo-in most years, and Zadie's Shoes was a fizzing new play), but the sheer attractiveness of both her and her performance -- not to mention the astounding fact of this being her first play -- had everybody rooting for her.

This has also been the year when a couple of operas divided most of the spoils for best musical, and justifiably.

The Canadian Opera Company's Billy Budd won for production, direction, lighting, lead male performance and -- inevitably -- set design. I must be the only person in Toronto who did not actually like Brian Thomson's hydraulic ship, but oddly, I still feel the award was justified, and it is hugely gratifying that Richard Bradshaw, the COC's dedicated chief, should have been rewarded for his inspired baton-waving.

Billy Budd, being old and British, could hardly win as a new Canadian musical. That prize went to the stirring Iron Road. I would have been happy for that show's very moving heroine, Zhenga Zeng, to have been acclaimed best musical actress, but Louise Pitre, in Mamma Mia!, was a reasonable choice.

The Irish actor Conleth Hill, superb in Stones in His Pockets, won over all the Canadian talent in Toronto, which must have been a nice consolation for losing out to Canadian Richard Easton in New York. Most gratifying-but-perplexing awards were given to Soulpepper's Platonov (supporting actor Diego Matamoros, and production). This being the very same wonderful show that won for best director for Laszlo Marton last year. The same director's brilliant School for Wives was not even nominated.

Other mysteries: Why did a play as poorly written as Ghost Train (a kids' show) get nominated for best play, when a play as brilliantly written and directed as Morris Panych's Earshot was shut out? In the independent (ie. small theatre) and young people's categories, the nomination of shows as weak as The Hats of Mr. Zenobe and as downright awful as The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (Abridged) suggest the Doras are still riddled with cronyism and/or sheer bad judgment.

The winning independent new play, rightly, was Chris Earle's Radio: 30. In all other independent categories -- acting, direction, design -- opposition was mowed down by a revival of Ibsen's The Doll House; it probably did not deserve quite as much as it got (though maybe it did when you look at the competition), but Shaw Festival actors Ben Carlson and Fiona Byrne were fittingly welcomed for venturing into Toronto.

The awards show itself, presided over and gently sent up by singer-comedienne Mary Lou Fallis and The Lion King's Jonathan Wilson, may have been the slickest ever.

TEMPEST-TOST

Third Stage, Stratford

Since the action of Tempest-Tost centres around the rehearsals for a production of The Tempest, it might conceivably have made sense for Stratford to program it alongside the Shakespeare play itself. But the similarity in titles might have confused the public, with people turning up for the wrong play on the wrong night, causing discord and confusion.

In the event, Tempest-Tost ends up in harmony and reconciliation, with some unresolved chords still thumping away underneath, which is a very Shakespearean effect. Richard Rose, who also directs, has adapted it, very closely and ingeniously, from Robertson Davies' first novel. This, published in 1951, concerns the amateur players of the Salterton Little Theatre (Salterton is an Ontario town not unlike Kingston), who are presenting both their first Shakespeare and their first-ever performance in the open air; their moving spirit, a Mrs. Forrester, insists on calling it "a pastoral." This in turn enables the Stratford designer, Graeme S. Thomson, to cover his roofed-in stage with greensward, which has the soothing and suggestive effect happily characteristic of pastorals.

There is a generosity of texture in Rose's play, a sense of life going on beyond what the stage has time to show us, that can only derive from its being based on a novel. However, unlike many dramatizations, it is not a bloodless canter through a series of predetermined events; leaving a lot of the book out, it allows us to savour what has been left in. It doesn't play like an adaptation, which is the highest possible compliment. This is despite the fact that most of its dialogue has been taken directly from the page, and that even some of the author's commentary has been cleverly incorporated into the spoken text. This actually improves on the original, since it neutralizes some of the more cloying notes in Davies' narrative voice: those in which the author seems to know everything and tells us what to think of it.

That said, a novel and a play are two different things, and Rose's production cannot always keep them in perfect balance. This is especially the case with the vital character of Hector Mackilwraith, the buttoned-up math teacher who gets himself cast as the virtuous Gonzalo and who, in virginal middle age, falls heavily for Griselda, who is 18 and beautiful. Griselda's rich family have lent their garden for the performance, and she, partly in acknowledgement of this favour, has been given the role of Ariel. Hector's passion drives him, touchingly and comically, to desperation. As a character in the modestly panoramic novel, he is first among equals. So he is in the play, at least in theory, but both the dramatic form and his own trajectory force him into the position of protagonist, without giving him the single-minded attention that would justify it.

Richard McMillan in the role offers not so much a superb performance as a series of superb performances. At first he is a fine Presbyterian cartoon: horn-rimmed, shiny-suited, oily-haired, moving in a stiff, jerky walk, head thrust forward and stomach pulled in. There is then a long middle section in which he seems to be treading water, gamely offering what amounts to a third-person report on his evolving state of mind. This is relieved somewhat in a scene -- one of the finest of the evening -- in which he listens aghast to two much younger men squabbling over Griselda's favours and is driven into an awkward defence of her honour. Even this, though, is not enough to prepare us for the tragi-farcical climax; the narrator in the novel can tell us things about Hector that the character in the play cannot enact. His final scene, however -- when the character has weathered both Shakespeare's tempest and his own - - McMillan plays with a chastened grace that is beyond praise.

Davies originally intended to build his story not around The Tempest but Twelfth Night, and in many ways that play -- which is in the current Stratford bill -- provides a better parallel. Hector, with his built-in rigidity and his painful endeavours to lighten up for love, is Malvolio to the unheeding Griselda's Olivia; and both ladies, as it happens, are being played this season by the same actress, Michelle Giroux. She has some difficulty locating the heart of Griselda (a problem shared by her authors), but she rises most sympathetically to her last scene with Hector, in which both have learned something and tacitly acknowledge it.

Around them swirl any number of subordinate conflicts. There is that, gradually simmering, between Mrs. Forrester, little-theatre politician and aspiring social butterfly, and the old friend, now a successful actress, on whom she has prevailed to direct the play. Lucy Peacock plays this visiting professional with great charm in her earlier sequences as silent, amused observer, and in her later as merciful goddess, but she can be unduly pushy in between; the text doesn't need as much help as she seems intent on giving it, and neither does the character, who is supposed to get her way through tactful forbearance. It doesn't help that her reason for being in town -- to dispose of her dead father's effects -- is the one important element that has been short-changed in the adaptation. Kate Trotter alternately flutters and bashes as Mrs. Forrester without ever getting her into focus. (Though the two women are contemporaries, Mrs F. is meant to appear older; in this production, partly through costuming, they come off as twins.)

Most of the actors, in fact, try too hard at the start; the production gets notably more relaxed, more humane and funnier as the evening progresses. Brian Tree exactly captures the pedantic pomposity of the professor playing Prospero; he ends praying for the advent of a university drama department staffed by people like himself, a prospect that Davies -- a former actor -- seems to regard with strictly muted enthusiasm.

Tara Rosling is almost uninterruptedly wonderful -- perhaps, indeed, the truest person on stage -- as the professor's shy daughter, cast in The Tempest as his shy daughter. Jonathan Goad is persuasively brash as the army officer cast as her Ferdinand and with eyes for every girl in the cast except her. And Michael Schultz promising, and sometimes much more, as his opposite number, a clever but unformed young man, recalled from university in England to minister to a sick offstage mother and to fall serially and helplessly in love.

Benedict Campbell is the music director whose sensual philosophisings we are not, I trust, meant to take as the last word in worldly wisdom. Two more authentic minor deities impose themselves toward the end: Les Carlson as the gardener whose concern for his lawn finally reaches real pride and passion, and Araby Lockhart as an elderly makeup artist, not much good at the work, but attaining fierce dignity as a defender of the emotionally downtrodden. There is something queasy about watching professional actors impersonating amateurs, unless the play is A Midsummer Night's Dream, but the sight of this troupe sitting in a long line on a bench, awaiting their first-night appointment with destiny, is enough to still any qualms. It becomes a rich, delightful evening.
