FALSTAFF

The Third Stage, Stratford, Ont.

The play the Stratford Festival is calling Falstaff begins with a prologue spoken by the symbolic character of Rumour. Since the play is really Henry IV Part Two, his main purpose is to bring us up to speed on what happened in Part One, and especially to remind us of the result of the Battle of Shrewsbury: King won, Rebels lost. By emphasizing the misleading reports that follow such an event (smooth comforts false, worse than true wrongs), he ushers us into this new plays sliding, rotten-ripe world. In this Stratford production, Rumours address is given an ideal delivery by Keith Dinicol, daintily sarcastic.

As good as the prologue is the epilogue, a speech so rarely done I had forgotten it existed. It is spoken here by Douglas Campbell, whom we have just seen as Falstaff, receiving his catastrophic comeuppance from his beloved Prince Hal, newly crowned as Henry V. Stepping nimbly away from his humiliation, he promises us a sequel to a sequel. His two identities blur; he is Falstaff, rejecting his own rejection, and he is the rubicund and orotund actor, part of the festival furniture, who has been playing comic leads here since the first season, 49 years ago. Either way, we are pleased to listen to him.

The space between these two elegant bookends is uneven: sometimes superb, sometimes rather dull. Scott Wentworth's mixed-period direction, as in Part One, is more notable for intelligence and lucidity than for imagination, which means it depends heavily on the skills and personalities of its actors. If the retitling has been done for commercial reasons (audiences don't want to feel theyve wandered into the middle of something, especially if they have), it also has a certain artistic logic; this, even more than Part One, is Falstaffs play.

Probably the crucial difference between the two productions is though Campbell has played the Part One Falstaff countless times before, this is his first attempt at Part Two. In Part One, he could greet the lines as old friends and concentrate on phrasing them, which he did with results that were often hilarious, sometimes surprising and never sentimental. In Part Two, he is far less secure. For an octogenarian actor to be essaying so lengthy a role for the first time is remarkable in itself, even if he does have a characterization all ready to fit it; and in fact much of what he does is excellent.

Dressed this time as a 19th-century country squire, he gives the role a firm outline, from his cynical beginning as a war profiteer, trading on a spurious reputation and some genuine diseases, through to the news of Hal's accession, at which his face lights radiantly up (I suspect the stage lights light up as well), and then down again to his final discomfiture, which is complete but economical.

There is nothing very probing, varied or original about any of this, but it is accurate and, when the vocal assurance is in place, very enjoyable. He can still build and relish the soliloquies; he can still toss off a perfect sardonic aside. The latter, in fact, is what he does best, but he can only do it when the words come out clean; and on the first night, though he didn't forget, he did fumble.

There is another problem. The most compelling aspect of Part One was Falstaffs relationship with Graham Abbeys prince, but in this play, with Hal increasingly alienated from his old life, the two hardly meet. When they do collide, on Hal's last trip to the Eastcheap tavern, a great scene comes to barbed if belated life.

Elsewhere, Abbey stints a bit on his character's world- weariness, and his delivery of the regulation speech about royal insomnia (it runs in the family) is very much by the book, but most of the time he is riveting. Even when king, he stays in his old black leather until the coronation. He gets more tension and control than I would have thought possible into the scene where he first threatens, then reassures, his brothers and the Lord Chief Justice.

Equally fine is his last-breath reconciliation with his father. Benedict Campbell (Mr. Campbell the Younger they would have billed him in the old days) plays the dying usurper as a man compulsively revisiting the past, both seeking and refusing vindication. He carries this habit, thrillingly, toward his deathbed, flinging open the chamber door to call rhetorically on other nations, putting a pillow on his head in mockery of the crown his son has prematurely taken from him, and incidentally recalling Falstaffs royal masquerade in the previous instalment.

The baronial scenes in this play are always hard to activate. This production gets them off to a compelling start with the conflicting accounts of Hotspurs death; his ghost wanders through the scene at one moment, and Jane Spence caps this with a powerful appearance as his widow. But the impetus is not maintained; the minor rebels are grey and there is a strange symbolic pseudo-battle in the middle of the peace conference. Bernard Hopkins' Archbishop has some good visionary moments, but I don't see why his every speech has to be a sermon.

Stratford this season has talent to burn, but it is surely a gratuitous conflagration that confines the great Richard McMillan to the role of the extremely functional Earl of Warwick, even if his revelation that Henrys death chamber is prophetically called Jerusalem gets probably its most quietly effective delivery in theatrical history.

Back in the part of the play with Sir John in it, Barry MacGregor completes his reliable Bardolph, equipped with a nose to challenge Cyranos but sadly deprived of his best scene. Diane D'Aquila's force and intelligence as the Hostess are as striking as they are unusual, but they dont seem to have much relation to the characters grasshopper mind. Kate Trotter's Doll Tearsheet is all right when she stops shouting, but the tavern is neither as funny nor as mellow as it should be, and not a patch on the equivalent scene in Part One.

The miraculous Gloucestershire episodes, which testify in loving detail to the persistence of rural and domestic life while princes and politicians kill and betray one another, are enlivened by a vivid bunch of recruits and by William Needles' aged Justice Silence, inexorably reminding his cousin that in his youth he was called "lusty Shallow" and not, as he now insists, "mad Shallow." Lewis Gordon plays the mad or lusty one, and though hardly one of the great or deep Shallows (like the Hostess, he isnt silly or voluble enough), he has a fine head-shaking moment at the end when he prophesies Falstaffs doom.

The confluence of so many Stratford veterans, besides being pleasant in itself, fits with the play itself, which is about age and change and the end of illusion. But, though the production has some neat overlaps and juxtapositions, the various parts never really come together and none of it matters as much as it should.

PRESENT LAUGHTER

Premiere Dance Theatre

- - -

With Stratford, Niagara, Soulpepper and the entire Follows family currently presenting his plays, Noel Coward now unquestionably ranks as Canada's national playwright. It is a puzzling situation, since his best work is so firmly rooted in the milieu of theatrical London between the world wars, but maybe imperial nostalgia has something to do with it. That, and an appreciation, also nostalgic, for well- crafted comedies, shrewdly based on the twin actorish preoccupations of sex and self-absorption.

Perhaps taking a hint from the title, Soulpepper's production of Present Laughter - Coward's last major comedy, written in 1939 - makes an ambiguous attempt to drag the play out of its own time and into ours. The play is set in the house of Garry Essendine, matinee idol and partial Coward self-portrait, which here could pass either as a genuine glamorous home of the period or as some contemporary rich person's handsome recreation of it.

Garry's manservant has a spiky punk hairdo, his manager sports a ponytail. Costumes, to begin with, could pass muster as from either era, but gradually they cut loose and so, very much, do the props; in the second act laptop computers and Starbucks coffee mugs are flourished with a sort of casual bravado. It all seems, as Coward himself might say, very silly, and - as he probably wouldn't, but I would - giggly.

It is also, obviously, deliberate; and deliberation is very much a feature of Joseph Ziegler's production. "She is crying," says Garry's Swedish housekeeper of his latest conquest, who has been ordered to get dressed and leave, "which makes her slow." (My favourite line in the play; it's the Scandinavian accent that makes it hilarious.) I don't know if the Soulpepper actors have been shedding tears, but something -- maybe a desire to escape from the famous clipped Coward style, maybe a determination to give the characters and situations their serious due, maybe nerves -- has made their pacing glacial. They don't actually take all the fizz out of the play, but they certainly flatten it.

The production is not so much bad as wrong, and this is especially true of Juan Chioran's central performance. Garry is a light-comedy actor whose success has enabled him to build a personal theatrical empire, surround himself with a devoted circle of admiring colleagues and charm the pants off everybody.

Now, the modern trappings make most of this ridiculous; Garry's kind of theatre does not exist any more, in London or anywhere else, and his kind of actor would be in Hollywood making millions in sitcoms, or jetting off to movie locations. He would not be about to set off (by boat, yet) for a six-week tour of Africa.

More important than any of this: Garry is sunny. That's what draws people to him. He reveals a dark side under pressure; that's what's funny. Chioran is dour and devilish from the start; you may believe that every woman he meets will fall for him (there's no accounting for tastes) but not that all his friends would confide in him; and when the play shifts gears into farce, with him as its victim, we don't feel for him. Technically, he is fine -- he gets all his laughs -- but temperamentally he strikes at his character's roots.

Individually, most of the performances are good; though Brenda Robins' metallic vamp exhausts her charms -- which are initially very striking -- within a couple of minutes, and Martha Burns as Garry's ex-wife exudes a dispirited air of wishing she were in some other play altogether.

Nancy Palk, however, keeps things efficiently moving as the omnicompetent secretary, and Patricia Fagan gets the show off to an excellent start, lying on her back in borrowed silk pyjamas and phoning to boast discreetly about her night of passion with the great man.

I must admit, too, that in a few cases the modern dress helps; it enables Michael Hanraham and Neil Foster to make something more definite of Garry's producer and director than the usual stick- figures. I developed a soft spot, too, for Rick Miller's angry young playwright who comes to mock and stays to worship. Best by far, though, is Joyce Campion, in a league and a world of her own as the housekeeper who dabbles in spiritualism and so may be said to be outside time in the first place.

All the same, this will not do. It is the second consecutive occasion (A Flea in Her Ear was the first) on which Soulpepper has spoiled a perfect comic mechanism by disregarding its ground-rules.

Some playwrights -- I name no names -- are big enough, free enough, poetic enough and frankly old enough to exist in several styles or time-frames simultaneously. Feydeau and Coward are not among them.

DREAM A LITTLE DREAM

Isabel Bader Theatre, Toronto

Apart from the Lovin' Spoonful, whose vocal sound was less accomplished but whose songs were better, the Mamas and the Papas were the best musical excuse for the 1960s. They offered warm and propulsive melodies, delightful harmonies and sweet, clever lyrics. I have never understood why, with all this craft and talent on your own doorstep, you North Americans got so excited about the Beatles.

Dream a Little Dream is the story of the Californian quartet, none of whom were actually Californian, narrated by the surviving Papa, Denny Doherty, who is now living back where he started, in Halifax. He does all the talking, with vocal and instrumental support from a six-person outfit calling themselves the Dream Band.

The press night started half an hour late: The musicians guitars had been stolen, and the producer had to send out for new ones. (Guitars, not musicians.) But even without this delay the evening would have seemed long: The songs remain lovely; what happens between them feels endless.

The choice of title is strange. Dream a Little Dream of Me is not a Mamas and Papas song. They didnt write it; it's an enchantingly relaxed tune from the 1930s, with lyrics by the fine and prolific Gus Kahn and music credited to a mysterious couple of surnames, Schwandt and Andree, that seem never to have appeared on anything else. Nor did the Mamas and the Papas sing it; Cass Elliot, the best- known and best-loved of the group and apparently something of a song sleuth, revived it as her first solo record and had a hit with it. It's performed here to warm us up for an account of her early death from a heart attack. After which, astonishingly, the show is over, without a word about the much later death of John Phillips, the groups mastermind and chief composer, or of the subsequent careers of his wife Michelle or of Doherty himself. We thought we were getting the story of the Mamas and the Papas, but it turns out we were only getting the story of Mama Cass.

Using her death as the climax provides an opportunity for cheap sentiment. That may sound cruel, but its what comes across. There is Doherty on stage. He has told us how he and Cass had been friends in New York in the early '60s, long before the group was formed, and that he had always loved her, though they had never been lovers. She had even asked him to marry her, but, he says, she was 300 pounds, and I wasn't man enough to deal with that." Thats a noble admission that loses some of its nobility when you think of it as being made every night to a paying audience. By the same token, his grief, though presumably genuine, registers as maudlin. Doherty, acclaimed in the publicity as a born raconteur, sounds here like a man who has told the same stories too often.

The script he and his director-collaborator, Paul Ledoux, have provided is not exactly a marvel of dramatic coherence. Misgivings set in early, as when Doherty recounts the familiar Grace Slick line about people who can remember the 60s never having been there as if we had never heard it before. There is a horribly overworked central image about his life being like crossing a stream, hopping from one stone to another, some flat and secure, some slippery and treacherous. At each turn of the story he gives a little leap, then tells us which kind of rock he has landed on. The slippery ones predominate, but that's life or, as some people call it, show business. Especially, of course, rock 'n roll show business. Theres another running gag in which Doherty tries to say the word "lawyers, finds it coming out as liars," and settles for "attorneys."

He goes on at length about his affair with Michelle -- which eventually broke up both their marriages and the group -- and about their improvidence and self-indulgence. If you like the music, you will have a fan's interest in the people behind it, but it is likely to be exhausted long before the show is.

There is some visual appeal: The band plays behind a scrim on to which are projected photographs (Michelle looks incredibly beautiful) and album covers and the like, and the juxtaposition is often effective.

Doherty still sings well, and he gets excellent musical help; Doris Mason, who does Cass, sounds at least as good as she did. If Phillips was one of the master songwriters of the era, second only to John Sebastian of the Spoonful, then Doherty was obviously a worthy collaborator, and we hear a couple of his later solo efforts that have some of the same toughness and invention; they are self- revealing without being weepily confessional.

The hits go by -- Monday Monday and Dedicated to the One I Love - - plus a few that turn out, in narrative context, to be uncomfortably apposite. They exist, though, as songs should, independent of any bleeding-heart relevance.

Anyway, for musical autobiography nothing beats that cheerful masterpiece Creeque Alley, which depicts the members of the group and their peers, scrabbling in and around Greenwich Village, just before they -- in various combinations -- made it. Maybe the show should have been built around it. It's sung here slower than on the record so, for the first time, you understand all the references. It's difficult to think of a pop songwriter since who has come up with rhymes and alliterations that are so great and sit so well on the music.

We probably have Cass to thank for the appearance of Rodgers and Hart songs on the group's albums, but it fits. Whether or not they knew it, Phillips and Sebastian, like Leiber and Stoller before them and Randy Newman coming up on their tail, were in the tradition.

FANNY'S FIRST PLAY

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

- - -

NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE - So commercial success is not everything. Fanny's First Play, originally produced in 1911, earned Bernard Shaw his longest West End run. It is now one of his least-performed works and is, in fact, one of his lesser pieces, a light reprise of themes -- among them the compromises of marriage, the iniquities of imprisonment, and the uncomprehending gulf between parents and children -- to which he gave fuller expression elsewhere. But it is deftly done, though the current lamentable production seems to be doing its best to disguise the fact.

It is a play-within-a-play. The outer shell introduces us to Count ODowda, whose distaste for modern life has induced him to withdraw from Britain to Venice, where he can dress in Mozartian regalia and, as he says, "shut out out the nineteenth century.

You mean," somebody objects, "the twentieth century.

To me," the count grandly replies, "the century I shut out will always be the nineteenth century.

Even in the twenty-first, that is still a good joke, and I reproduce it here to compensate for the Shaw Festival having cut it.

The count has sent his daughter Fanny to Cambridge, and as a graduation present he gives her a performance of an anonymous new play of her own choice, to be presented by professional actors and judged by professional critics (who, as the theatrical manager sagely remarks, come cheap").

In fact Fanny herself has written the play, and she has done it, as any forward-thinking young lady might, to shock her father.

The play itself is about children shocking their parents. Margaret Knox and Bobby Gilbey, whose fathers are business partners, have been unofficially engaged since childhood, though neither likes the situation much. In the real world, suffragettes are being sent down and locked up, and on one mad night the same fate independently befalls both Margaret and Bobby, though not for political reasons; each, in an excess of holiday spirits, has assaulted a policeman. As if this were not enough to bring their families to shame, each has made an undesirable acquaintance: Bobby has taken up with what an omniscient footman calls "a daughter of joy" and Margaret with a Frenchman.

We are told that rehearsals of Fannys play went badly to begin with because the director hadn't read it. Todd Hammond's Niagara production suggests not so much that he hasnt read it as that he hasnt listened to it. What Shaw said of Shakespeare is also true of his own work: The ear is the key to him. Both wrote in a heightened style that we have to accept as normal communication.

Shaw was often a verbal cartoonist, but the essence of a good cartoon is economy of line. What we get here, especially from the older characters, is gross and graceless caricature; if this is meant to be the fault of the fictitious actors then the joke wears very thin very fast.

The senior Gilbeys, in particular, seem to have stepped from some especially snobbish British B-movie of the fifties about people in trade. Peter Millard orates on a carpet, frothing and writhing; Nora McLlellan, with her trademark elongation of final consonants, seems unwilling to deliver a single line as if it might conceivably be addressed to some other sentient being.

Roger Rowland's Mr Knox, perhaps in compensation, is a mumbling nonentity. There is far more humanity, even some quiet passion, in Donna Belleville's account of his pious wife (Shaw always took religion seriously) but integrating this approach with the performances of her peers is, understandably, beyond her. The super- flunky is a role in which only perfection will do, and though Peter Krantz has the right impassive countenance he falls far short in vocal poise. He also muffs the plays best comic climax.

Severn Thompson, who plays Fanny herself, doubles as her heroine Margaret, though strangely, neither Fannys father nor the assembled critics seem to notice this. She plays both parts with the excessive flashing of eyes and teeth that are supposed to denote charm, but she does have some of the real stuff as well, and she comes noticeably to life in her scenes with Matthew Edison's Bobby, the neatest and best performance of the evening.

Simon Bradbury is fun as Margaret's champion Lieutenant Duvallet, especially in his long speech at the end, exalting the freedom of English family life over the constrictions of French. Its a surprisingly fluent oration, considering the characters earlier difficulties with the language, but after all, this is Fanny's first play.

Margaret declines to become the French lieutenant's woman, but Bobby does end up with his darling Dora, the Cockney lily, whom Caroline Cave plays her with more enthusiasm than accuracy.

In the play-without-the-play David Schurmann, who exudes weary urbanity, is disastrously miscast as the unworldly Count. William Vickers pipes and flutes absurdly as the senior critic, but the others are still very recognizable, especially the eternal brash young populist incarnated by Todd Witham. The way in which the whole tribe fall on the refreshments when their host's back is turned is definitely drawn from life. That, though, is a minor compensation. In a year when the standards of Shakespeare at Stratford have rocketed, it seems a shame that Shaw at Shaw should have plummeted.

THE MAN WHO CAME TO DINNER

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

- - -

NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE - There is a scene in The Man Who Came to Dinner that involves penguins. They arrive in a crate, onstage, and then, offstage, they escape and start waddling about. Everybody loves penguins, and audiences throughout this play's 60-year stage history have felt frustrated at having to hear about them rather than see them. There are, though, worse things than frustration, as is being demonstrated at the Shaw Festival, where the new production does let us see the penguins. They are not, of course and alas, real penguins. They are children dressed up as penguins, and they are not convincing.

They aren't funny, either, in part because they aren't convincing. However, the production, which is extravagantly misguided throughout, stakes a huge amount on the belief that they are. Our first glimpse of one of them, through a glass more or less darkly, is actually rather charming, but then they start appearing in full view, dogging the entrance of nearly every character in an extremely busy play. The theory seems to be that a failed joke becomes a successful joke if it is repeated 87 times. I can't recall the last occasion on which I saw a single gag hammered quite so remorselessly into the ground.

The play's protagonist is Sheridan Whiteside, an American literary and broadcasting personality of the 1930s, whom the authors, Moss Hart and George S. Kaufman, modelled extremely closely on their friend Alexander Woollcott, a critic and pundit who built a national reputation on a disgustingly ornate prose style and a huge capacity for being rude to people.

In the play he is entertainingly rude to almost everybody, but his principal targets are a middle-class family in the fictitious town of Mesalia, Ohio, to whose house he is confined one Christmas after breaking his hip on a patch of ice on their doorstep. He takes over the premises, exchanging cables and international phone calls with the rich and famous, receiving tribute from them (the penguins are a gift from Admiral Byrd), and occasionally welcoming them in person. He insults them, too, but in a fawning, friendly fashion.

The main action concerns Whiteside's unscrupulous attempts to thwart a romance between his secretary, whom he cannot afford to lose, and a local journalist. Later -- much later -- he repents, but this is only a necessity of plot; his championing of the artistic and romantic ambitions of his hosts' son and daughter similarly registers as one more method of spiting their parents.

For practical purposes, Whiteside is a horror, and it's a great indictment of all our moral characters that we enjoy him so thoroughly. At least, it should be. Michael Ball, who plays him here, has an incurably cuddly persona, and when he says that he is a cheery and gracious person by nature, it seems all too believable. He hardly has a bark, let alone a bite, so the play lacks a dynamic.

Still, he is an intelligent and accomplished actor, and it is a pleasure to watch him slump deep into his wheelchair, weighed down by misanthropy and smoking jackets. His shortcomings are, on the whole, the least of this show's problems.

Neil Munro, who directs, was responsible a couple of seasons ago for an enchanting production of the same authors' You Can't Take It with You, a whimsical comedy about a houseful of lovable eccentrics, Conceivably, he is trying to treat this very different play the same way. The Man Who Came to Dinner is a hard-as-nails extravaganza whose obsessively topical humour should have faded but hasn't; its sacred monsters are drawn, with libellous exactness, from life, and their professional craziness needs a realistic background to set it off.

Whiteside's unwilling host is not, as he is played here, a high- pitched maniac; he is an ordinary businessman, driven apoplectic. He has a sister who is a maniac, but her appearances do not need to be accompanied by spooky music; the actress, Mary Haney, can certainly do without it.

Noel Coward turns up, bearing the nom d'etage of Beverly Carlton, and singing his latest composition, a barbed pastiche actually composed by Cole Porter. Patrick R. Brown does a conscientious Coward impression, but conscience, as I have a horrible feeling I've said before, cannot make Cowards of us all, and he doesn't have the necessary heedless audacity. Anyway, his scene is ruined -- actually the whole play is -- by a sudden excursion into fantasy; he leaves the piano, which nevertheless goes on playing, and launches into a full-scale song-and-dance routine. Moments like this, and there are many of them even before we get to the penguins, suggest a director with no sense of humour desperately trying to prove the opposite.

Banjo, a.k.a. Harpo Marx, is more spiritedly done by Simon Bradbury (he's the only actor I've seen who doesn't try to squeeze in bits of Groucho on the side) but he goes on doing his shtick long after it's ceased to be necessary; we know who he's meant to be, and he should be speeding the action up, not slowing it down. (Did I mention the play runs three hours?)

Jane Perry is self-defeatingly effortful as a bitch movie star, but Laurie Paton is excellent as the secretary and Kevin Bundy surprisingly lively as her beau. Nora McLellan atones for her mother in Fanny's First Play with a more composed portrait of a matron not dissimilarly situated, and there are good lightning sketches from Richard Farrell as a doctor, Robert Benson as a radio producer, George Dawson as an entomologist, Al Kozlik as a manservant, and Jillian Cook as a cook.

Black & White Photo: David Cooper, Shaw Festival / A SLIP, A BROKEN HIP, AND IT COMES TO THIS: Jane Perry as Lorraine Sheldon and Michael Ball as Sheridan Whiteside. ;

SHADOW PLAY

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

- - -

NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE - Since Noel Coward was both a notable dramatist and a notable songwriter, there is a general assumption that he combined his talents in a body of first-rate musicals. It isn't true. His most substantial work in the genre, Bitter Sweet, is now sadly faded, and his subsequent operettas and musical comedies were not successful even when new. Many of his best songs were written for revues.

That leaves us with the sequence of one-act plays he wrote as vehicles for himself and Gertrude Lawrence, which were first produced in 1936 under the umbrella title of Tonight at 8:30. These nine playlets contain some of his best writing, and three of them are mini-musicals: Family Album, which is Coward in his lace- valentine mood; Red Peppers, a sketch about embittered music-hall performers whose effectiveness depends on whoever happens to be playing it; and Shadow Play,which is being revived as a lunchtime show at the Shaw Festival, and which is in part a musical about musicals.

Simon and Victoria, well-off and apparently brittle, have been married for five years; the gilt is rubbing off and the guilt is setting in. Each has another admirer waiting in the wings; Victorias is a harmless young man called Michael, and Simons is a more predatory young woman whose name (shades of Private Lives) is Sibyl.

Victoria has become dangerously addicted to sleeping pills, and on the night we meet her she is feeling especially low or, to put it another way, excessively high. She and Simon, with an older couple, have been to the theatre, and Victoria finds herself bitterly resenting the ease with which the people onstage could deal with their crises; when the pressure mounts, they could simply sing a song or go into a dance. Under the influence of the drugs, she starts re-imagining her own life as if it were a musical, sorting through her memories in an effort to discover what went wrong.

What she actually comes up with is a rerun of what went right: memories of her first meeting with Simon, their courtship, their honeymoon. There are no clues here to later disasters, other than our built-in awareness that young people grow older. We end up pretty much where we started, and the play does not dig as deep as it pretends.

Its surface, though, is very intriguing: sharp and economical in its depiction of the characters' over-privileged and over- stimulated milieu; highly suggestive in the way it intercuts past and present, dream and consciousness, speech and music.

Three of Coward's best songs weave through the action, whole or in fragments: Play, Orchestra, Play, which is in his finger-wagging Dance Little Lady-Poor Little Rich Girl vein of frenetic gaiety, and which later served as the signature to his cabaret act; You Were There, one of his most sinuous and insinuating ballads; and Then, a lesser-known number in which you can almost hear the masters voice, high-strung, keyed-up and reminiscent.

David Savoys production admirably captures the mood, with William Orlowski's choreography and Judith Bowden's designs making amusing, economical use of simple elements. Four couples -- the principals, the dalliances, the confidants, and a pair of domestics - - switch from characters to ensemble and back again.

Patrick R. Brown's performance of the Coward hero suffers from the same tentativeness that afflicts his impersonation of Coward himself in The Man Who Came to Dinner, but Patty Jamieson's Victoria is excellent. Jillian Cook and Guy Bannerman are the solid, sympathetic older couple who unnervingly advise their juniors to grab their happiness while they still can, and Karen Wood makes a notably pert maid.

HAY FEVER

Gravenhurst Opera House

Think of this summer's three full-length Noel Coward revivals as a pyramid. At its apex sits Stratford's Private Lives -- absolutely secure in its understanding of the play and of the techniques needed to get it across. At its base, balancing one another, are Soulpepper's Present Laughter and the production of Hay Fever at the Opera House in Gravenhurst. The former is thoroughly wrong-headed in its design choices, in its central characterization and in its rhythm; but at least it has a rhythm, and cleaves to it with considerable skill. The latter commits no egregious gaffes of interpretation, and it certainly doesn't try the fatal course of updating the play, but it proceeds, under Ted Follows' inert and muddled direction, in a series of badly timed fits and starts.

The director also appears as David Bliss, an apparently successful author of 1920s schlock novels married to a temporarily retired star actress, Judith Bliss, who grievously misses her public and compensates by putting on a non-stop performance for everybody else. This role is played by the director's own former wife, Dawn Greenhalgh; their offspring, and the companions of their offspring, account for the two junior Blisses, son and daughter, and for the quartet of outsiders, each one of them invited by a different family member to spend the same weekend at the family's riverside retreat (which they have somehow resisted calling "the Bower of Bliss) just outside London.

Whether the hosts have serious sexual designs on their guests is never too clear; somehow it's difficult to conceive of any member of the household concentrating long enough actually to get into bed with anyone. Besides, they don't seem to have any bodies. But they are all accomplished flirts, and by the end of the first evening they have contrived, almost without noticing, to change partners; each is necking with somebody else's former prey.

The visitors are greatly unnerved by this, especially as their morale has already been shattered by their having been forced to participate in a series of highly theatrical party games for which none of them possesses any aptitude. (Would you like to play the adverb game, in which you have to perform a designated action "in the manner of the word," up against a real-life West End star and her cubs? I thought not.) So, the very next morning, they all creep away together leaving their hosts, who have otherwise forgotten their existence, musing at the extraordinary way in which some people behave.

Coward himself once remarked that the play has long been a favourite with amateurs; it has a small cast and only one set "which must lead them, poor dears, to imagine that it is easy to act." He then added that he, as a humble professional, thought it one of the hardest he, or anybody else, had ever written.

He is of course right; the play demands huge technical accomplishment because it offers nothing to hang on to. It has no plot, no characters of any substance and no real subject; it says far less about sex than does Private Lives and far less about theatricality, on and off stage, than does Present Laughter. It consists entirely of behaviour, which can be delicious but has to be both precisely defined and seamlessly orchestrated.

The extended Follows clan behave their socks off, some of them more effectively than others, but each of them exists in his or her own cocoon; being related in real life doesn't seem to help them relate on stage. Getting them all on the same stage at the same time is obviously an administrative coup, but it is not the automatic artistic triumph that everybody concerned seems to think it is.

There is a certain kick in seeing the former Mr. and Mrs. Follows hurl marital insults at one another (Judith and David are probably going to stay together but they enjoy fighting), but that's as far as the chemistry goes. Dawn Greenhalgh's Judith has a brisk presence, but she is very bunched-up, a suburban leading lady rather than a metropolitan one.

Judith lives her life as if it were one of the rosy vehicles on which she rode to fame, plays with titles like Love's Whirlwind ("Is this a game? Yes, and a game that must be played to the finish.") Greenhalgh never suggests the abandon of a woman who can slip in and out of melodrama without even noticing. Nor does she have much truck with subtlety: "Men don't grow old like women -- as you'll discover to your cost, Myra, in a year or two" is a line that loses its effectiveness if it's hissed directly into the victim's face.

Ted Follows' portrayal of David as a bumbling fossil makes a change from the more usual crisp and suave interpretation, but it doesn't seem to suit the play as well. Samantha Follows' daughter is spirited but not much else; Laurence Follows' interpretation of son Simon as a languorous aesthete is a reasonable idea taken way over the top.

Among the guests, Edwina Follows barely registers as a terrorized flapper. Judith's sporty admirer has been turned into an American for the benefit of Sean O'Bryan (Samantha Follows' husband) and the transformation wears well; his is the only performance that comfortably inhabits the skin of its character. Stuart Hughes (Megan Follows' partner) offers an elaborate cameo of a stodgy diplomat -- all guffaws and unbendings -- but one that makes no connection to the rest of the play.

Worst of all -- certainly most disappointing, considering her track record -- is Megan Follows' account of that Myra Arundel who, according to Judith, "goes around using sex as a sort of shrimping net," She draws a cartoon of a drawling '20s vamp and goes through the play without modifying it by an inch. Just what possessed her to play the morning-after scene as if she were immune to the psychological hangover that afflicts all her companions? Smiling through it all, she leaves herself with nothing to act.

There is also a housekeeper, cast from outside the tribe. She was Judith's dresser, which Myra says is the only excuse for her. There can be little excuse, though, for Robin Craig's ostentatiously rude performance, and none whatever for her interpolated full-throttle rendition of Tea for Two in the last act -- the kind of nonsensical turn that begs for applause and gets it while sensitive souls shrink in their seats.

Applause for Dennis Horn's beaming set, though, is permissible; and the costumes, "co-ordinated" by Hilary Corbett, are bang-on.

Black & White Photo: Most disappointing is Megan Follows' (right) portrayal of Myra Arundel, who "goes around using sex as a sort of shrimping net." ;

TEMPEST

The Dream in High Park, Toronto

For some unfathomable reason, CanStage, mounting its annual open- air Shakespeare, has deprived The Tempest of its definite article. In the text itself it has made hardly any cuts, but the play -- Shakespeare's shortest apart from The Comedy of Errors -- still clocks in at just under two hours, sans intermission. There has been a fair amount of anxious modernizing of individual words, some of it reasonable, some of it downright neurotic.

The tinkering with the title may suggest that the director, Michael Shamata, intends to offer us a confessed adaptation of the play rather than the thing itself. In fact, he has provided a solid, conventional production that refuses to take off and that finds parts of the play absolutely intractable.

His Prospero is John Jarvis, with whom he worked happily the previous two summers in the equivalent pastoral set-up in Oakville. Jarvis is an excellent and lucid speaker of verse, and that is about the extent of what he gives us here. That is not in itself to be sneezed at; it gets him comprehensibly through the monstrous expository scene in which Prospero first tells his daughter Miranda all the things she doesnt know, then reminds Ariel of all the things they both know, and finally goads Caliban into recounting all the things that everybody currently on stage knows.

Anger and resentment, long pent-up, at the men who banished him and are now in his power, are the keynotes here, and they spill over. When he accuses Miranda of not listening, he seems to be taking out on her his feelings about his treacherous brother Antonio. That is fine as far as it goes, but this Prospero doesnt seem capable of anything else, and certainly not of being pleased or amused.

The performance becomes monochrome, and so in consequence does much of the play. Nor does it really pay off in its own terms; when Prospero renounces his revenge, the moment -- generally reckoned to be the climax of the play -- hardly registers. (What, I have sometimes wondered, did Prospero intend to do with his foes anyway? He never speaks of killing them. Did he intend to keep them wandering around his island in dazed perpetuity? And how would that square with his plans to marry his daughter to their leader's son?) And as for the great aria in which he surrenders his magic powers -- well, maybe William Hutt has spoiled us for hearing it from anybody else.

But then, this production has trouble with magic throughout. It greets the script's demands for spectacular effects grudgingly, as if it cant afford them and wishes they would go away. This especially applies to the set-pieces of the wedding masque and the phantom banquet, which here are meaningless.

One can sympathize with the desire to avoid any attempt at an ethereal Ariel; the part has been given to a tall actress, Tanja Jacobs, painted green like an alien in a science-fiction movie. She plays it neutrally, with no particular relationship to Prospero, loving or resentful or both, and with no especial yearning for freedom.

Also, it seems, she cannot sing, so her songs (mainly set as percussive madrigals) are relayed to us by a dubbed and presumably supernatural chorus. They seem to be done because theyre in the text and nobody quite liked to cut them.

There are four other sprites who trip around in white robes, topped by protective headgear that makes them look like bee- keepers. Their choreography (Mark Christmann is credited as movement coach) is uniformly unfortunate: a series of jerky shuffles. At the ding dong bell refrain that concludes the "full fathom five" number, they sway rigidly from side to side, perhaps in an effort to suggest pendulums.

The clown scenes, though, are well thought out, with Brandon McGibbon's Caliban a sympathetic butt for Oliver Dennis' very funny and nasty Stephano and Patrick Galligans fairly funny and timorous Trinculo. There is intelligence, too, in the handling of the courtiers who troop about the isle in modern formal dress, as if they had all been dining at the captains table when the storm struck. (Presumably they were too much the gentlemen to put on life jackets.)

There are a few vivid pangs of conscience in Michael Spencer- Davis' Alonso, though I despair of ever seeing this role accorded its full traumatic force, and some pleasant puttering from Keith Knight as Gonzalo. The young attendant lord Adrian (Ross Ward), generally a nonentity, is given some freshness by being played as a precocious juvenile, on the lines of Moth in Love's Labours Lost.

Alex Poch-Goldins silkily villainous Antonio works very well on David Jansen's pliant Sebastian. In the last scene, where these two have very few lines, the differences between them are sharply drawn. Antonio remains pointedly outside the circle of reconciliation, even turns his back on it; Sebastian is initially drawn into it, but eventually relapses into the orbit of his evil genius.

These monents are isolated, though, and easy to miss. It would take a far more tightly focused production, maybe in a studio setting, to relate them to the whole. The lovers -- Manon St-Jules as Miranda, Todd Hofley as Ferdinand -- are agreeable, she especially.

JEAN AND DINAH WHO HAVE BEEN LOCKED AWAY IN A WORLD FAMOUS CALYPSO SINCE 1956 SPEAK THEIR MINDS PUBLICLY

Artword Theatre, Toronto

The calypso referred to in the full title of what I had better just call Jean and Dinah may not be as world-famous as all that. At least I don't remember hearing it. But its certainly good and pungent. A big hit in the 1950s for the calypsonian Mighty Sparrow, it is sung from the point of view of Trinidadian men contemplating the departure of the Yankees from the island who have been monopolizing their women. It especially celebrates the fact that the formerly high-priced prostitutes -- girls called Jean and Dinah and Rosita and Clementina -- will now be available to them, cheap.

Tony Halls play -- a great success in Trinidad, Jamaica and the United States, brought to Toronto to coincide with Caribana -- looks at this situation from the viewpoint of Jean and Dinah themselves, some 40 years on. Jean has come by Dinah's place to persuade her to come out, as the two of them have done every year, for carnival. Dinah, the older of the two and half-blind, is reluctant to go. Besides, the two of them, as you would expect after all this time, have issues.

The patois, the accents and the thick local and historical allusions made a fair amount of the play incomprehensible to me. Around me, though, everybody was exploding with laughter and, making a few allowances for hospitable first-night enthusiasm, I think it's safe to assume they were right. Certainly the two actresses are magnificent, and you can feel the dialogue giving off sparks as Jean and Dinah survey their pasts, the men they have let themselves get involved with, the children who have been fathered on them (Dinah is at pains to point out she was a married woman and a nightclub hostess, not just a whore like Jean) and the vagaries of politics: "I never liked those Peoples National peoples," says Dinah of the nationalist government that came to power about the time the Americans left.

For all that, their conversation, which extends over the whole first act, does seem to go on a very long time. In Act Two, the convention changes, and we find ourselves actually at the carnival; not a specific carnival, past or present, but a distillation of all of them. Jean and Dinah play out a series of sketches in traditional masquerade roles. As a pair of sailors, mocking the shore-leave behaviour of the U.S. fleet, they seize the opportunity to hit on the men as they themselves have been hit on. (There is a certain amount of audience particpation here.) Dinah assumes the character of the Midnight Robber, an outsize gangster. Most pointedly, Jean plays Baby Doll, a role that allows her to accost any passing man and identify him as the father of her child. This is a role that strikes uncomfortably home, for both parties, and it melts into a painful scene about Jeans own son, ironically heralded by Dinahs crooning of another famous calypso, Brown Skin Gal, Stay Home and Mind Baby. (I do remember that one.)

Finally, we return to the present and the two women as they are now. By this point, however, the narrative thread has frayed, and a central question -- was Jean in any way responsible for the accident that robbed Dinah of her sight? -- seems especially inadequate to the weight it is meant to carry. Sentimentality, which has threatened all evening, finally senses a vacuum and moves in.

For most of the time, though, the saltiness of the language, and especially of the performances, keeps it at bay. Penelope and Rhona Spencer (cousins in real life, and too young for their present-day roles, but who cares?) are spectacular, intimately intense, audaciously exuberant. Penelope, who seems to have the more varied talent of the two, plays Jean with a wonderful squirrelling attack; Rhona, playing much of the piece from her bed and behind dark glasses, has sassy, somnolent authority as Dinah. Both chain-smoke throughout, but it doesn't seem to hurt their energy level. They share the stage with, and sometimes infectiously groove with, a percussionist, Richard "Popcorn" Cumberbatch, who is billled as Rhythm Man.

Overall rhythm, as opposed to individual performing rhythms, which are abundant, may be what this show, directed by its author, lacks. Even apart from that, it could use more music. But it is unquestionably joyful.

PERICLES

Coronation Park, Oakville

- - -

OAKVILLE - Only half of Pericles, Prince of Tyre is generally thought to be by Shakespeare. The first two of the play's five acts are usually palmed off on an unsavoury hack called George Wilkins, and they contain rhyming couplets of a lameness that one wouldn't wish even on him. Oddly enough, these are far less worrisome when heard than when read. Pericles, more than any other Shakespeare play, is a story -- a picaresque fairy tale, in fact -- and you take it as it comes; given a suitably magical staging, everything in it evens out. John Wood's production is lovely, taking full advantage of Oakville's peerless lakeside setting and is very neat and sensitive on its own account.

It begins with young prince Pericles discovering the powerful monarch Antiochus is living in sin with his own daughter. In a barbed line that suggests Shakespeare had at least some input into the play's opening, Pericles thanks the king for teaching "my frail mortality to know itself"; and that -- the vulnerability of the human animal to fate and fortune -- is perhaps the nearest the play has to an overriding theme.

Our hero spends the next dozen scenes on the run from the vengeful Antiochus and in the process endures more than his statistical share of shipwrecks and storms at sea. He woos and wins the beautiful Thaisa (a princess, of course), who apparently dies in childbirth during one of those tempests.

Her body is thrown overboard to appease the sailors, and Pericles' newborn daughter, Marina, is brought up by untrustworthy allies. When she is 16, her beauty and accomplishments provide unfair competition to their own child.

Rescued by pirates (in the nick of time, also of course), she is sold into a brothel, where she remains obstinately untouched. Finally, by beautiful coincidence, she is reunited with her father, whose grief has turned him silent and misanthropic. This father- daughter reunion -- by accident or design, this first of Shakespeare's last plays is much concerned with fathers and daughters -- hardly carries the emotional freight of the one in King Lear but it casts a comparable spell. Certainly it does here, staged and played with great delicacy and great economy.

Wood's production, in casual modern dress, is throughout both playful and trusting, with evocative traces of set (Michael Gianfrancesco) and beautiful lighting (Michael Kruse). A sail makes a ship, while for the last scene, in the Temple of Diana, a graceful set of columns appear, apparently from nowhere, as do a row of white lamps.

The immensely long entrances possible in this space are as beguiling as ever. There has also been some nifty textual editing. The acting is less authoritative than we are used to here (and also less audible, especially with the lake providing independent storm effects) but this play can take it. Its characters are not subtle and as a person its hero hardly exists; he is merely somebody to whom things happen.

Jonathan Eliot plays Pericles with a generalized down-home nice- guyness (a Prince of Canadian Tyre, perhaps) but manages to rise above it in the reconciliation, which gives him his one chance to act. Patrick Garrow is earnestly easy-going as the narrator Gower. Krista Sutton makes an unexpectedly mischievous Thaisa and John Fitzgerald Jay is smooth as her kingly father, a genial despot in naval togs.

Deborah Hay is not, to be unchivalrous, the radiant nonpareil the text suggests for Marina (and for just about every other Shakespearean heroine) but she plays her with a schoolgirlish determination that is refreshing in itself and also makes her survival in the whorehouse seem remarkably plausible.

Michael McLachlan does a similarly believable job on the town governor, who arrives as a customer and leaves a devoted (and, of course, successful) wooer. Melee Hutton makes a flinty impression as a sort of wicked-stepmother-by-default, and the brothel scenes ("Shakespeare at his most characteristic," somebody once said) are brought to life in most businesslike fashion by Michael Krek as an oily pander, by Chick Reid as a blowsy bawd and above all by Blaine Bray as their grumbling underling.

The three drive onstage in a red truck with matching caravan, from whence their professional operations are conducted. A similarly delightful touch is a silent vignette of Marina and her guardians' daughter sewing together; the outclassed companion drops too many stitches and leaves in tears. This is typical of the production in being funny and inventive, and in not being overdone. Productions of Pericles are still rare, and this is an ideal one see.

LA RONDE

Premiere Dance Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - The Soulpepper company return brilliantly to form with La Ronde, that century-old exploration of the sexual daisy-chain, recast in the form of a circle. It is remarkable in having a rigorous, even rigid, directorial concept that yet allows for great individual creativity from the actors. That is a rare combination.

It is not flawless. There is a kind of chocolate called a Viennese whirl and that is pretty much what Arthur Schnitzler, Austrian playwright and physician, gives us here; it is episodic by definition, and a synopsis challenges the resources of the English language in coming up with uncensorable synonyms for intercourse. In Jason Shermans new, Canadianized adaptation, a Hooker services an Athlete who screws a Maid who is laid by a Student who has an affair with a Wife who has sex with her Husband who debauches a Girl who is picked up by a Writer who fornicates with an Actress who seduces a Politician who finds himself in bed with the Hooker. Everybody, literally and figuratively, fucks everybody else.

Sherman has updated the action as well as transplanting it; his Politician -- actually a Senator -- was a Count when Schnitzler last set eyes on him; and there seems no particular reason for making an Athlete (a notably un-conscientious one -- he smokes all the time, despite yapping about his trainer and being back in time for curfew) out of the original's Soldier.

Sherman, whether on his own initiative or obeying orders, has repeated the gaffe made by David Hare in the more radical reworking that he called The Blue Room. We are not dealing here with timeless Shakespearean myth. Schnitzler was a great social, as well as sexual, chronicler, and when his play is cut loose from its historical moorings, some important things cease to make sense. The Student (Schnitzler called him a Young Gentleman) comes from a middle-class family that apparently can afford a full-time Maid and cook. He has a very Teutonic relationship with his tutor, and it cannot be naturalized merely by having them agree to meet at a pub rather than a cafe.

The Husband is patronizingly confident of the innocence of his Wife (a mature woman in this production); sexism and the double standard may not have gone away in the last century but they have changed their spots. Of course, much of human behaviour remains unchanged, but that would strike us more forcibly if we saw it revealed in an alien setting. It is, when you think about it, very silly to imagine that you can make a play "relevant" simply by changing its clothes.

Enough of that. In its own terms, Sherman's text is racy and occasionally witty. Herbert Olschok, a German director, builds a world around it. Astrid Jansons set is a forbidding and appropriately circular wall that revolves to uncover each new rendezvous. The actors trundle it around, each joining the scene- shifting parade after having played his or her first scene. Some of these sequences function as extensions of their relationships; some as commentary.

At the end, nine players are standing in line to present the prostitute who functions as both an emblem and a victim for all of them; she is the plays action reduced to its essence. Holly Lewis, playing this role, conjures us into the play from her first soliciting line -- half plaintive, half steely.

Something of the same note is struck by the other two young women in the cast: Stephanie Baptist as the Maid, who transmits innumerable shades of detail with a superbly light touch, and Patricia Fagan, who finds a native equivalent for the Schnitzlerian concept of the available Sweet Girl. They are all three cynical victims.

The production is, among other things, the best advertisement yet for the Soulpepper Young Company: Both Lewis and Fagan are members of it, as are Kyle Hawton, who plays the Athlete, and Allan Hawco, who was good as the punk valet in Present Laughter and is especially fine here as the Student, alternately callow and callous.

We see all the characters before, during and after sex, though the production somehow manages to avoid nudity. The avoidance is more intriguing than the reality would be. The early couplings are brutal and suggest that intimacy in this society always occurs standing up; later encounters are more urbanely comic. (They are also cumulatively less effective, but that has always been true of this play.)

They occur to wailing saxophone accompaniment -- Colleen Allen is the onstage wandering minstrel -- and have been brilliantly choreographed; Mark Christmann is credited as movement coach, as he was on the High Park Tempest, and the improvement in his work is sensational.

The first older character to appear is the Wife, who arrives for her assignation with the Student nervously disguised in layers of furs and scarves; you would know her for an adulterous woman a mile off. Her unnervingly flat delivery takes some of the juice out of the scene, but she develops a teasing Cheshire-cat quality in the scene with the Husband, played with delightful neurotic pomposity by Tony Nardi. He compulsively dusts off his pattering feet each time he hops into bed; indeed, their scene is a symphony of feet, their love making distinguished by the patterns their toes make. This is the most deeply ironic of all the scenes: The lawful couple have the most to conceal.

Oliver Becker is magnetically narcissistic as the Writer. Some things don't change, and his professional vanity, governing his sexuality and everything else, rings very familiar. Nancy Palk, though a little heavy on the prima donna and light on the vulnerable, partners him effectively as the Actress. At one point, straddling epochs and cultures, the two arouse one another by singing the Tango Ballad from The Threepenny Opera, the duet of a whore and her pimp. Dean Gilmour's Politician, excessively fussy in his first scene, finds the bittersweetness, clinging at romantic illusion and robbed of it, in his second, which is also his last.

It is not that these people are passionless but that their passions are brief and have the rest of their natures, plus the whole world, to contend with. This is the play's great insight, and it abides. Olschok's production may have inflated and solemnized the original but it has not, I think, distorted it. It runs three hours, but there is hardly a moment I would sacrifice. There is no flab on the performances. The lines of force between each pair of characters are drawn tight, and they can afford to take their time.

AN EVENING WITH HERSHEY FELDER

George Weston Recital Hall, Toronto

A most peculiar night at the lovely George Weston. Even its title was indeterminate. The program called it An Evening with Hershey Felder, but Felder didn't arrive until halfway through the proceedings. The marquee insisted the name of the attraction was Noahs Ark, but the musicians didnt even come in two by two.

Noah's Ark was in fact the centrepiece of the evening. It is a very earnest-sounding musical on which Felder and his partner, Kim Campbell, who has had some high-profile day jobs, have been at work since 1997. They presented us with some excerpts from it, he conducting and she narrating. It is a retelling of the Old Testament story that seems to lay heavy stress on the fate of the overwhelming percentage of the world's population that was left behind to drown, and on the general unfairness of it all. Noah also has cause to meditate on the unworthiness of his son Ham, who always seems to be the villain in any telling of this tale and who is here caught trying to seduce his brother Shems wife; he gets on board, just by having the right family connections.

The animals also seem perturbed by the fact that most members of their various species are about to be wiped out; they sang two songs but, survivors or victims, they were all drowned, by the orchestra. Felder wrote some advanced nursery-rhyme music for them, which sounded effective. His songs for the humans were less happy; James Barbour as Noah bellowed undramatically for ages in the very accents of Andrew Lloyd Webber: the anguished Webber, unfortunately, of the Phantom of the Opera rather than the sprightly one of Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat, which remains the No. 1 Genesis musical. Christianne Tisdale, as the beleaguered Mrs. Shem, was handed an especially insipid song lamenting the fate of her neighbours: "As I shall live and they shall die/I have no words to say goodbye."

The best thing to be said of Campbells rhymes is that they do truly rhyme, but they do so very predictably. There are one or two powerful images of catastrophe, but this whole skeptical approach to the biblical story is not as new as the authors seem to think. I don't know how the show might stage; its characters seem to do an awful lot of standing around emoting, but there would obviously be opportunities for spectacle. It could be more titanic than Titanic.

Felder, a dark-haired, compact and unforgivably youthful multi- talent, also gave us extracts from his recent Broadway show (he acts, too), George Gershwin Alone. I had not much warmed to what I had read of this, but now I would like to see it. It appears to be a biography of Gershwin fleshed out not only with his music, but with his own, or presumably his own, spoken and written words. Felder gave an excited commentary on Bess You Is My Woman Now, proudly describing how the music supports the text, while the song itself was patiently performed by Barbour and Tisdale. (Is this how it was done on Broadway? I thought it was a one-man show.) Felder had the very feel of Gershwin, innocently egocentric, both in his speech and his show-off playing of Rhapsody in Blue. He also led us in a singalong.

Before this, the same two singers demonstrated some of the pitfalls of performing Broadway songs out of context in a concert hall. Nobody ever knows how, or how much, to act them. While listening to his partner sing her half of I Loved You, from Carousel, Barbour stood with his hands in his pockets, to illustrate Billy Bigelow's feigned indifference; he has played the part onstage and I suspect the stance was carried over. In the theatre, though, he would have the chance to move around a bit. But in the wake of the National Theatre production of Carousel, this whole stolid approach to Rodgers and Hammerstein seems very outdated. Barbour's performance of Make Believe, from Show Boat, was extremely strange; some of his vowel sounds were grotesque, and at times he seemed to have only a glancing acquaintance with the melody. Tisdale sang sweetly in both selections.

The first half of the evening (without Hershey Felder) was devoted to Leonard Bernstein. The National Academy Orchestra, dynamically conducted by Boris Brott, played the most succulent of musical comedy lollipops, the overture to Candide, and really extended themselves in a suite of dances from West Side Story, which includes nearly all the best tunes. They even got the finger clicks and the shouts of "Mambo!" right, and I think I enjoyed the music more than I ever have in the theatre. Between these orchestral encounters, Glenn White, a superb young lyric baritone, sang Maria, a song I don't even like very much, and made some of the most beautiful sounds I have ever heard.

UNCLE VANYA

DuMaurier Theatre Centre, Toronto

When Soulpepper do Chekhov, with Laszlo Marton directing, they are the best. This years Uncle Vanya may be even better than last year's Platonov, even if it lacks the buccaneering appeal that comes from harnessing an unfamiliar monster of a play with sprawling action and a sprawling cast. Vanya is a far tighter work. It is also, obviously, a greater one -- one of the most searching, least sentimental analyses of human failure ever written and also one of the most compassionate accounts of the things that, struggling, we do to ourselves and one another. Its emotional impact here is tremendous.

Its physical impact is remarkable, too. One image after another clings to the mind, beginning with the sight of rain streaming down an almost-transparent curtain before the action begins -- a forecast of the storm that breaks out a whole act later and that here seems second only among dramatic tempests to the one in King Lear.

Once that curtain has risen, on a magnificently cluttered room on the Voynitsky family estate, miles from anywhere, people proceed to do amazing things. Sonya, the plain and devoted young woman who virtually runs the place, reaches out in friendship to Elena, her -- by local standards -- glamorous young stepmother. Elena flinches and takes a nervous swig from a wine bottle -- friend not being a word that has figured much in her vocabulary. Uncle Vanya, more agonizingly conscious with every moment of how he has wasted his life and hopelessly in love with Elena, imagines himself comforting her during the storm, picks up a chair, soothes and caresses it. Astrov, the local doctor, the most eligible man in the district, a prey to vodka and self-disgust but an ecological visionary, stands on furniture and makes speeches, at once passionate and absurd, about the need for forest preservation.

The professor -- Sonya's father and Elenas husband -- who selfishly and self-pityingly controls their lives, unveils his plan for selling the estate, to the fury of Vanya, who seizes the great mans papers and hurls them into the air. They lie scattered all over the stage, and Vanya's aged mother, who worships the professor, goes down on her knees and laboriously starts picking them up. When the professor finally departs, everyone -- the whole cast -- sits in silence for what seems like a minute waiting for him to make some great farewell pronouncement. It never comes. But we have had a hilarious moment of stillness to balance all the frenetic activity.

This kind of physicality is not what we expect in Chekhov, thought it is a direct descendant of what Marton, a Hungarian, gave us in Platonov. I described that play as "sprawling" and my abiding memory of it is of people spreading themselves out on sofas and on floors. They do the same here -- Vanya recklessly, Elena with a kind of provocative decorum, everybody else in between -- and though it seems extravagant, it never seems excessive or untruthful. It also appears very convincingly Slavic. (Maybe that isn't true. Maybe its a stereotype. But it is certainly wonderfully theatrical.) These people, or most of them, live on the land and through their bodies, even though we meet them in a confined space. Michael Levines set, without walls but compressing all the material of several lifetimes, is brilliant.

Four dazzling performances, intricately roped together, command the stage. Albert Schultz does perhaps his finest work as Astrov, whose mind and heart have nowhere to go and who is drinking and talking his way into oblivion. He is momentarily stirred by a love for Elena that she somewhat returns and whose discovery drives Vanya further into distraction. Schultz's Astrov has an open face (what we can see of it -- no actor looks better in a Russian beard) and the remnants of a generous disposition that can close down with a slap you almost hear. All Chekhov's doctors drink, but Astrov seems to be the best at his job in the circumstances and a likely surrogate for his author.

Liisa Repo-Martell, always good at waifs, seemed almost too obvious casting for Sonya, but she transcends type to create an emotional orphan, heartbreakingly businesslike, as sharp-tongued as anyone else on stage when her principles are challenged, but still the one who never lectures everyone else on how awful they and the rest of Russia are. Her speech at the end of hope deferred -- always deferred -- is as moving as we knew it would be. It is not helped by the intrusion of a Gregorian chant -- the productions one mistake - - but it is counterpointed as it should be by the unheeding ant- like activity of the rest of the household.

One of the many moments that is brought up shining new is the juxtaposition of Sonyas resigned lament for her own plainness with the immediate entry of Elena, looking beautiful. In Kristen Thomson's performance, Elena's is a restrained prettiness that is afraid of itself; she hints, more meaningfully than any other I have heard, at damaging affairs in the past. (This may be the point at which to compliment John Murrells muscular translation, which is a gift both to its speakers and its hearers.) She seems to have married the professor not just for security but to get away from sex. She can be stirred into a semblance of love and certainly into charity, but she retreats in horror when the going gets rough. She also drinks, more daintily than the men but just as compulsively. This is the subtlest of the performances.

Diego Matamoros Vanya is perhaps the most debatable, gone inordinately to seed, vociferously glorying in his own disintegration. All this is true, but there is little sign that Vanya could ever have amounted to anything at all; that, if not the Schopenhauer or Dostoevsky of his more fevered imaginings, he was at least a good farmer. Vanya is always catching himself out in his own pretensions, which is why he always goes to our hearts. When Michael Redgrave played the part, he literally made you laugh and cry at the same time. Matamoros has you doing both, but singly. His tirades are superb, and his final, crumpled demeanour -- hugging the threat of suicide like a fretful child -- irresistible. It's Astrov's task at the end to pull him out of it, wearily, since he shares some of the same condition. The duet between the two men in the last act and the electrifying rapprochement between the two women in the second are high-water marks of Canadian acting.

Robert Haley makers rather a pallid professor, very soft-spoken; its a decently accurate performance but hardly arrogant enough to push Vanya persuasively over the edge. Michael Simpsons Waffles, the ineffectual red-faced neighbour, is a touch cartooned but original in his vindictive pleasure at the fate of his long- absconded wife. Joyce Campion is a fine and unusually sharp-tongued nurse, and Charmion King something of a revelation in the tiny role of Vanya's mother; when she enters with her spectacles, her cigarette and her stock of pamphlets, she momentarily becomes the centre of the action. William Webster, bent double, makes an amazing impact in the still smaller role of the family servant and night watchman, consistently crossing the stage like a piece of mobile scenery. (But when is this actor going to get a good part?)

I mentioned, as I always do given half a chance, Redgrave's Vanya, the finest performance -- of anything -- I have ever seen and part of the finest production -- of anything -- I have ever seen (Oliviers, at Chichester and the National Theatre). So if I call Soulpeppers production the second-best Uncle Vanya of my experience, I trust it's clear that we are flying very high. At the end the rain-soaked scrim descends again, and we are left -- as I imagine they are behind it -- gasping and proud.

Black & White Photo: Uncle Vanya is a far tighter work than last year's Platonov -- and obviously a greater one. ;

The picture of Leanna Brodie as Isabella was taken by Michael Proudfoot. The National Post regrets the error. 

MEASURE FOR MEASURE

Withrow Park

- - -

Shakespeare in the Rough can get very rough. This Measure for Measure is a fresh and intelligent show, subject to spasms of embarrassing foolishness.

Having gone through the play's opening scene, the actors suddenly break into the prologue from Henry V, exhorting us to "eke out their imperfections and to think when they talk of horses that we see them" (not that anybody in Measure ever does talk of horses) and then proceed to read us our rights in the matter of not taking photographs and there being an intermission and so on.

It's weird; they are all too young to have seen the 1950s revue At the Drop of a Hat but both these little wheezes were tried out, to rather funnier effect, in that show.

When the intermission actually rolls around, things get even grimmer. The actors interrupt one of the play's key speeches, an odd one in rhyming couplets, to announce that it doesn't scan (it does) and that Shakespeare probably didn't write it (who says?) and that we may now all go and relieve ourselves. By now they have got a decent production going but they seem terrified that if they don't send themselves up they will be thought stuffy or, horror of horrors, classical. This kind of self-consciousness is not good for them or for us.

Sue Miner's production is especially distinguished by the quality of its exits and entrances, which is a higher compliment than it may sound. The action unfolds on a carpet surrounded by parkland; you can see the actors coming and going from a long way off, and the director uses the perspective to fill out the story and create something of a world.

This is a play in which different social classes come together under the impact of the, mostly arbitrary, law. Two consecutive scenes show us a remarkably muddled police-court case, about disorderly conduct in a brothel, and the religious novice Isabella pleading for the life of her brother, condemned for impregnating his girlfriend. We see the parties in both causes all together at the back of the stage, waiting for their hearings, and the effect is very telling.

It seems a shame, though, that, having included in this lineup the usually unseen character of one Mistress Elbow, the director has not found anything for her to do. She works her nine-strong company very hard, having them cover not only the scripted roles but a generous supply of supers as well. A whole posse of nuns patrols the environment, symbolizing the convent-life to which the heroine may or may not return. You half expect them to break into a chorus of "How do you solve a problem like Isabella?" but they are very effective.

The production is stronger on atmosphere than interpretation. The meaning of this notoriously ambiguous play hinges on our response to the character of the Duke of Vienna (Adrian Griffin), who abandons his realm in the first scene, leaving it in the care of the Puritan deputy Angelo, and then hangs around disguised as a Friar desperately trying to correct the excesses of both old and new regimes.

He could be an all-wise saviour, an unscrupulous manipulator or (most likely) something well intentioned but fallible in-between. He starts this production returning from what seems a rather mild night on the town and plays the opening scene with a hang-over; perhaps this is why he seems to have difficulty remembering, or even understanding, what he's saying.

In disguise, he is anonymous; in his own person, he wears shabby leather gear that makes everyone's acceptance of his authority hard to credit. Hints of his being a hypocritical playboy are never followed through; and it's impossible to care whether his final marriage to Isabella counts as coercion or as a happy ending.

Angelo (Michael Proudfoot) silently conveys embarrassment when he's offered the job and smugness when he gets it, but nothing when he actually talks.

Leanna Brodie's Isabella is much the most accomplished of the leading trio; she cannot bring off everything she tries for but she gives the character an unexpected capacity for humour, bred not of perception but of inexperience. When Angelo tries to blackmail and seduce her, she laughs; she simply can't believe it. When she tries to persuade her brother to accept death as the price of her chastity, she jollies him into it. She simply can't conceive of his saying no. It makes sense.

The most authoritative performance comes from Richard Alan Campbell as the cynic Lucio. Notable among the supports are Jane Moffat as the sensible justice Escalus, here transformed into a woman (who ends a day in court by going home with her assistant for a lesbian afternoon), and Anthony Malarky, a conscientious Provost in a security jacket.

Black & White Photo: David Leyes / LEANNA BRODIE AS ISABELLA: The play uses its surroundings well but gets silly at times. ;
