MACHOMER

Premiere Dance Theatre, Toronto

If the Simpsons were to take it into their heads to do a Macbeth spoof, they would probably make it one segment in a Halloween special and dispatch it in 10 minutes. They would almost certainly do it with great wit, and they might even manage to tell us something subversively instructive about the play itself.

Now consider Rick Miller's one-man show MacHomer, an international fringe hit for the last half-dozen years, now brought back to Toronto under the auspices of Soulpepper. (On the strength of his performance in Present Laughter, Miller now counts as a Soulpepper actor, and a good one.) It is all on its own and lasts an hour. It has only one idea in its head: to do a cut-down but largely authentic version of the original play in which all the roles are supposedly played by characters from The Simpsons.

If youre going to do a funny-voiced Shakespeare parody, you might at least have the grace to invent your own voices; all Miller is doing here is stealing somebody elses jokes. It's like the worst of old radio variety, or a desperate night at a comedy club. Macbeth and The Simpsons are both great texts but Miller has not made them illuminate one another, comically or otherwise. The limit of his verbal invention is to have his Homeric Macbeth wonder if that is a pizza he sees before him. Compare that to what the Simpsons themselves did with A Streetcar Named Desire or The Crucible or even, momentarily, the Witches scene from Macbeth. ("If it were left to you, there'd be nothing in the cauldron but newt-eye.")

Even on a voice-impersonation level the show doesnt work very well. Miller does an excellent Mr. Burns and Smithers (cast as Duncan and Malcolm) and a good Barney (an unlikely Macduff) but some of the others are very approximate. He seems unduly smitten with his impression of the tedious Captain McCallister, of whom we hear a great deal and who, since he plays First Witch, starts the proceedings off. Nor can Miller get very close to the real Homer. (He may be in good company; if you watch early Simpsons episodes, you notice that it took Dan Castellaneta a good two seasons to get the voice and character absolutely right. Since then, of course, nothing has been able to stop him: not even the frequently rotten scripts of the last few seasons.)

Homer plays Macbeth, for no better reason than that each is the protagonist of his own drama. So Marge, of course, plays Lady Macbeth, and here the show really runs into trouble because the two marriages have nothing in common. Can you imagine Marge urging her husband to murder? If you want to imagine it, youll have to riff far more creatively on the original script than Miller has even attempted.

The Macbeths famously have no children, which means Bart and Lisa are here confined to playing Banquo's son Fleance and Lady Mac's waiting gentlewoman. In the latter role, Lisa enters expressing her disdain for the crass commercialization of the whole enterprise. Yes, that is what Lisa would say. That is exactly what Lisa would say. But this show cant find any fresh way of having her say it. It throws in all the familiar characters simply so fans can cross them off their lists. I mean, our lists. But I can hear these voices, practically 24 hours a day and far better done, without leaving home. Whats the point?

The show's last Toronto outing was at Second City's Tim Sims Playhouse, virtually a cabaret space, and the move up in the world has not helped. It merely creates unreasonable expectations. There is now classier video footage behind the actor and a smoking cauldron thing for him to declaim from. There also seem to have been some changes in the script, which neither help nor hinder; I cant swear to it, but I dont remember encountering Sideshow Bob before, or the director character Jon Lovitz voiced in the immortal Oh Streetcar episode.

(Have you noticed, by the way, how Springfield keeps expanding and contracting? One week it seems to be a small town in which everyone attends the same church and sends their children to the same school. The next it's a metropolis with its own Lower East Side. If you deduce from this digression that I would rather be writing about The Simpsons than about MacHomer, you are right.)

In losing intimacy, the performance has lost some redeeming charm. Miller's speed and energy in keeping it going remain undeniable. But it is a stupid show, and Soulpepper has no business producing it.

THE SEAGULL

Avon Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

There are more ways than one to stuff a bird, especially when its The Seagull.

Soulpepper's current full-blooded Uncle Vanya, superb though it is, is not the only valid way of doing Chekhov. There is room for a cool diagrammatic laying-out of the characters and their relationships, or even for a nostalgic trip back to the mournful genteel tradition of which we have all heard but few of us have ever seen.

Certainly, after her fine and unsparing Cherry Orchard of a few seasons ago, one hoped for something definite from Diana Leblanc. But her Stratford production of The Seagull is frustratingly hit- and-miss, unrooted not only in any recognizable style but also in any recognizable time or place.

The set, to begin with, is a definite downer. For the first two scenes, which happen outdoors, Astrid Janson has supplied broad green strips of what looks like canvas, stretched out, one above another.

They are shifted around a bit when we move inside, and room is even made for a couple of doors. These supply a welcome touch of solidity, and may have something to do with the production's second half being a marked improvement on its first. Actors and audience get something to hold on to. We lose, somewhat, the sense that everything is happening in a void -- but only somewhat.

It doesnt even seem to be a purposeful void. The actors are in modern costume, and yet again I find myself fretfully observing that in a still-modern play, realistic as these things go, this is worse than confusing.

The characters keep dropping references we understand but that have nothing to do with the people we are looking at. They retain their Russian names, but who -- in Russia now or at any time in the last 70 years -- would be comparing a current star actress to Eleanora Duse?

Where now, in fact, is this plays whole world of resting or aspiring performers, driven or frustrated writers glumly measuring their achievement against that of Turgenev, of country estates whose visiting owners are at the mercy of their live-in managers who delight in denying them horses for a drive into town?

The structures have gone. The people remain, or their equivalents do, but we really could be trusted to notice that for ourselves. I know the effect is meant to be timelessly suggestive, but all it actually suggests is that the real costumes got lost in transit and that the performers are gallantly making do.

To be fair, a few of those in the smaller roles seem to benefit. Aaron Franks, in spectacles and leather jacket, makes far more than is usual of the financially challenged schoolmaster Medvedenko, who moves in the course of the action from suitless suitor to henpecked husband.

It is he who has the play's famous opening line, Why do you always wear black?, addressed to the contemptuous Masha, whom he loves and has the bad luck to win. Her even more celebrated reply -- "I'm in mourning for my life. Im unhappy" -- is delivered here by Sarah Dodd with fascinating snappishness, as if to say surely any fool could see that.

Thus begins an uncompromising performance, sad and funny, of a woman consumed by her own unrequited love for the young author Konstantin, and drinking to make sure the pain stays in place. (She has a secret passion and doesnt care who knows it.)

Lally Cadeau, too, makes much of Masha's mother, Polina, with her less demonstrative yearnings: She is married to the bullying bailiff but carries a permanent torch for the philandering doctor Dorn.

The richest of all these performances, though, is Brian Bedford's as the rapidly ageing Sorin, the one character in the play who has never been in love, though he has always wanted to be.

Indeed, as he tells us, he has never achieved anything he set his sights on, and he is now dying of it. (This is often held to be true of all Chekhovs characters, but it fits only a couple of them here.)

Bedford, mustering perfect technique in the service of perfect truth, presents an amiable joviality that gets eroded. In the course of two years, he goes from a dapper spectator to the prisoner of a wheelchair. He is also ineffectually, but not unperceptively, kind.

The only actor in the cast to make every line of Tom Stoppards jaunty translation tell, Bedford makes us hang not only on what he himself says, but on what everybody else says about him. We notice, for example, that his relationship with his nephew Konstantin is the only fulfilling one in the play, the only one in which the balance of affection is just about equal.

The play is full of allusions to, and quotations from, Hamlet (though I don't think these are as revelatory as the production, or at least the program note, would like us to believe) and Stoppard, who knows this territory, has added a few more.

He has not included the line about the pangs of despised love, though it's in depicting those pangs that Leblancs production is at its best.

There are numberless moments here of quiet heartbreak as the characters watch the passions of those they adore whirl inexorably away from them. Its when those passions come to the boil that the orchestration falters.

Martha Henry's crop-haired Arkadina seems uncertain just how actressy -- in the derogatory sense of being hollow and effusive -- this successful actress really is. We can see she enjoys playing lady of the manor, especially when she is just about to leave it. Dispensing a solitary rouble to be shared among the servants, she is in her element. (And they, silent roles all, are excellently played.)

We can guess what Konstantin means when he says his mother is good with the sick -- and when she tries to tend to his head wound while unable to stop her resentment of him showing through, at least some of the ambiguities get explored.

But when she abases herself in front of her wayward lover, Trigorin -- a fiendishly layered scene in which she is consciously acting what she genuinely and desperately feels -- she goes either too far or not far enough.

Peter Donaldson's Trigorin, a shambling predator disguised as an easy prey, has a similar problem in a different context.

He conscientiously avoids making an aria out of Trigorins great speech on the frustrations of second-rate authorship, but he loses some of its pain in doing so. He is fine, though, in his moment of sensual surrender to the adoring young Nina.

Konstantin and Nina may be the two hardest juvenile roles ever written, if only because the tragic ending is split between them. One gets the madness, the other the suicide. It would be so much easier to combine the two.

Michelle Giroux pins her Nina firmly on the girls hero-worship of Trigorin, with increasingly disdainful side-glances at a Konstantin whose existence she barely registered in the first place. ("A symbol if ever I saw one" she says --or Stoppard says -- when he presents her with the dead bird.)

This carries her logically through the first three-quarters of the play, but for the last quarter, something more than logic is required. And perhaps greater toughness: We don't quite believe this Nina will survive, and we should. She, unlike Konstantin, is a professional.

Michael Therriault cannot breathe life into the boy's literary theories -- love, on the whole, fares better than art in this production -- but his emotional, if not his creative, vulnerability is believable. Why does he kill himself? Perhaps to stop himself from turning into his uncle.

To round things off: Brian Trees insensitive drama-fancying bailiff is remarkably similar to his insensitive drama-fancying professor in Tempest-Tost. This actor never does anything false, so you cant call him mannered, but I wish he could find a different rhythm.

Rod Beattie as Dorn, the least self-lacerating of Chekhov's doctors, cuts a surprisingly slight and seedy figure. His good opinion of Konstantin's writing ought to count for more than it does here.

And so, unless I'm being impossibly sentimental, should his invocation of what other translators have called the "magic lake." This production could use some magic. It could even use a visible lake.

INHERIT THE WIND

Festival Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

I have never previously seen or read Inherit the Wind, but you develop a feel for these things. I arrived at Stratford expecting something gripping but hollow, and that is what I got.

The play is a 50-year-old dramatization, by one of those anonymous teams of Broadway writers, of a crucial trial in the American South of the 1920s -- one that pitted the advocates of Darwinian evolution against the defenders of Biblical creationism. A teacher, accused of contravening state law by mentioning Darwin in the classroom, found himself in court with his pious fellow citizens baying for his blood, or at least for a good stiff jail sentence. The teacher's name was John Scopes, and his case became famous as "the Tennessee (or the Scopes) monkey trial."

Prosecuting him, to the applause of the town, was William Jennings Bryan, three-time presidential candidate (unsuccessful) and a passionate fundamentalist. Ranged against him was the legendary Clarence Darrow, champion of unpopular causes, fresh from defending the accused in the sensational Leopold-Loeb murder case. The fate of the accused became overshadowed by the courtroom duel between these two men.

Some of the dialogue of Inherit the Wind is drawn directly from the court-record but the names - of the characters and even of the town itself - have been changed. That is the measure of how compromised and superficial the play is. It wants the privileges of fiction and the benefits of documentary without committing itself to either.

Darrow is renamed Henry Drummond, Bryan becomes William Harrison Brady. By any names, they are a couple of extremely juicy roles, and the performances here, by William Hutt and James Blendick, are super. Hutt gives Drummond an infallible dry wit, with an angry moral passion crackling beneath it. Its a relief to see the Darrow figure played thin and stylish, which he historically was, rather than with the sweaty bulk of an Orson Welles or a Spencer Tracy.

Its Brady, the feted local hero with a heart condition, who is the bulky, brow-mopping one, and Blendick's deep sonic boom suits him to perfection. He gives the man decency and simplicity as well as complacency, and makes a pretty distinction between self- righteousness, which Brady has, and self-satisfaction, which he hasn't: His past failures are visibly gnawing away at him. Because of the heat, those in court are permitted to remove their jackets, so we are treated to the rare spectacle of a couple of titans squaring off in their suspenders.

Their battle reaches its height when Drummond, denied the right to call expert witnesses in favour of Darwinism (since that doctrine is illegal, it cannot be heard in court), puts Bryan himself on the stand and cross-examines him about possible absurdities in his own beliefs. He brings up the usual problems. How come that the world didnt descend into chaos when Joshua stopped the sun coming up over Jericho? Where did Cains wife spring from? (As a Jew, I can't help resenting that when people go hunting for scriptural impalusibilities, they always turn to the Old Testament rather than the New.) But he only really gets Bryan on the ropes when he forces him to admit that the first day of creation might not, since it pre- dated the invention of light, have lasted the standard 24 hours. Maybe, suggests Drummond, it lasted millions of years.

Not for the first time when listening to a debate -- live, staged or televised -- you want to jump in and point out that the opponents have more in common than they might think. If they could both just agree that the Bible story is a metaphor, honour would be satisfied on both sides and civilization could move on. But of course life isn't like that, and drama cant afford to be.

Darrow-Drummonds role-reversing tactics must have been very dramatic then and remain highly theatrical now. But when the authors, Jerome Lawrence and Robert E. Lee, get away from the facts of the case and fall back on their own devices, those devices turn out to be very tired indeed.

Very much downplayed is the fact that the accused, here called Bertram Cates, actually sought prosecution. His was a test case, specifically engineered by the American Civil Liberties Union to expose the absurdities of creationism and the menaces of censorship. Cates here is a bewildered innocent, surprised to find everybody hates him and half-inclined to give up. He also has a romantic interest, a fellow-teacher who is also -- get this -- the daughter of the town preacher, a man whose virulent bigotry gives even Bryan pause.

Tim MacDonald and Claire Jullien, who play these two young puppets, understandably fail to bring their early encounters to anything like life. Only when she is forced to testify for the prosecution, and when he awaits the court verdict, do they seem like people.

Much else is left cloudy. The jury, traditionalists to a man, convict Cates (they have to -- he broke the law) but impose a minimal fine. What changed their minds? If it was the judge's unheard summing-up (C. David Johnson plays this part with dignity, which is all he's allowed), then what changed his mind, since he seemed as dead set against the prisoner as they were? Bryan is no Neanderthal. How does he reconcile his stance here with his earlier fight for womens suffrage?

There is a cynical journalist, modelled on H. L. Mencken, who goes around making free-thinking wisecracks that are initially very funny (Peter Hutt, who plays him with sour excellence, has the Hutt family timing), but get gradually less sympathetic. When he turns on Bryan in his hour of defeat, the chivalrous Drummond turns on him and calls him a vicious smart-alec attacking a noble man. As if we werent capable of noticing these things for ourselves.

When the schoolteacher prepares to skip town with her beloved, she says she has now read Darwin, and though she doesn't like what she's read she will defend -- well, you get the picture. Drummond nods his wise old head and gives her an atheists blessing. We know these issues are still alive, and we may amuse ourselves with fantasies of what Drummond might do to Stockwell Day if he got him up there, but really there is nothing in this play to disturb any audience liberal enough to go to a theatre and see it -- now, or any time in the last half-century.

Richard Monette has given it a full-bodied staging (i.e. a lot of actors well manoeuvred), on a set cunningly designed by Peter Hartwell to combine the spiritual with the topographic. Through stained glass, we glimpse townscape and landscape. In the early scenes, the townsfolk tend to stand around in a semi-circle, like the chorus in a musical. They seem to be waiting for Robert Preston to arrive and tell them they got trouble. When Bryan arrives instead, they do break into song: Hymns, of course, which they sing even on their way to prayer meetings. The point -- that this is a God-fearin community -- is made rather quickly, but they go on doing it, and a male trio singing an especially accusing spiritual at the start of Act II is very powerful. The population includes a Bible salesman, who is very ragged, and no wonder: There can't be anybody in town who doesn't already have what he's selling.

I have always been curious to see Inherit the Wind, so I can hardly knock Stratford for giving me the opportunity. They have the talent and resources to do it justice, and they have done so. But nobody had better take it for serious drama.

Black & White Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann, Stratford Festival / WILLIAM HUTT AS HENRY DRUMMOND: An infallible dry wit, with an angry moral passion crackling beneath it. ;

LOVE FROM A STRANGER

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE, Ont. - A character who proclaims in the first scene of an Agatha Christie play that "I want to live before I'm old and grey and dead" has almost a moral duty not to survive into the second. It's called irony. There may, though, be a greater irony to be mined in defying our reasonable expectations of the thriller genre by letting her stay alive awhile, and this is the path taken in Love from a Stranger.

It is not, strictly speaking, a Christie play; it is a 1936 adaptation, by actor and author Frank Vosper, of a Christie story that had been published a couple of years earlier. This may account for the dialogue, and even a couple of the characters, having more weight and flavour than those of your average Agatha.

The girl who tempts fate at the beginning of the action is named Cecily Harrington. After years of scrimping in a London office, she and her roommate, Mavis, have won a large cash prize in a sweepstakes. Mavis intends to use her share to travel. Cecily was all set to wed a stodgy fiance just returned home from two years in Sudan, but now she is having second thoughts. These are reinforced when a flaxen-haired young man calling himself Bruce Lovell appears from nowhere, ostensibly to rent her apartment, and sweeps her off her feet -- or at least off to lunch. (At the Savoy Grill, he remarks with impressive casualness.)

By the end of the first scene, and on 10 minutes' acquaintance, they seem mutually smitten. By the end of the first act they are engaged. At the beginning of the second act, they are married and happily ensconced in a very remote house in the country.

Here Bruce begins behaving very suspiciously. He commandeers the basement as a dark-room for his photographic habit and will let nobody else enter it. He claims that his own money is tied up and he must borrow Cecily's in order to buy the house. He gets her to sign documents that she does not appear to have read; there also seems to be a discrepancy between what he says the house cost and what it actually cost. He buries bottles of peroxide in the garden, leading us to speculate as to whether his hair colouring is truly God's work. He suffers unexplained dizzy spells and refuses to see a doctor about them. He removes from sight newspaper clippings, with pictures, concerning the recent trial in America of a serial wife- killer who got off by having a clever lawyer.

In fact, he acts so like a man with something serious to hide that we have a hard time believing him innocent, though by all the accepted rules of the game we know he must be. The truth of the matter I will not of course reveal. I will only say that the play takes shape less as a whodunnit than as a willhedoit (andifsohow). And that an early reference to Scheherazade and the Arabian Nights turns out to be thematically and materially crucial.

It takes its time, but the suspense steadily builds, and the last section, a masterful series of reversals, plays brilliantly with and against our expectations. Micheline Chevrier's production, barring a couple of weak performances, is well up to the standards of tautness and impeccability established by the Shaw Festival in these matters, and Brian Perchaluk's rural-fastness setting is as cozy a site for possible murder as could be imagined.

Lisa Norton and Mike Shara, as Cecily and Bruce, have some problems keeping their characters plausible in the early stages, but they squeeze every drop of narrative tension from their climactic duet.

Psychological tension, too: The criss-crosses here of attraction and repulsion may not quite be worthy of Strindberg, but they at least compete with the best of American film noir.

The supporting roles are no more than functional, but Laurie Paton's Mavis is an efficiently solicitous best friend, and there is more broadly entertaining work from Richard Farrell as the village gardener, who says things like "my rheumatics have been that bad," and from Helen Taylor as his buxom niece, who gets taken on as a raw but willing servant girl (and is roundly patronized for her pains).

Jennifer Phipps, as Cecily's busybody Auntie Loo-Loo, offers a model display of what might be called constructive scene stealing. As a genteel lady in reduced but not quite straitened circumstances, she is by turns protective, practical, overbearing and -- when the right expensive brand names are mentioned in her presence -- snobbishly coy.

Her instant changes of direction are very funny; she summons a world bounded at one end by tea at Harrod's (a reward earned by having registered her niece's apartment with the store's real- estate office) and at the other by cheap day-excursion tickets to the country, in the days when trains were trains and a coach with a corridor was a luxury. She is, as ever, real to her fingertips.

I was hoping that at the end she might ride to the rescue at the head of the U.S. Cavalry, or at least the local constabulary. But, as I said, this is a play that defies expectation.

THE RETURN OF THE PRODIGAL

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

This years Shaw Festival has been a downbeat affair, with the best productions -- Picnic, Laura, Love from a Stranger -- lavished on decidedly minor plays. The last production of the season, though, redeems nearly everything: The aptly named Return of the Prodigal introduces us to a brilliant and almost-forgotten playwright in a performance that shimmers, provokes and finally hits greatness.

St. John Hankin, the author, was a contemporary and colleague of Shaw and Granville Barker, and this play, an icily powerful social comedy, was performed alongside theirs in the advanced London theatre of 1905.

Set in the English county of Gloucestershire, a pleasant sort of buffer state between the West country and the Midlands, it concerns the Jacksons, a nouveau-riche family whose head is a self-made mill owner about to make still more of himself by standing for Parliament in the Conservative interest. His elder son, Henry, is also his business partner. Mrs. Jackson and daughter Violet sit and sew and receive company and generally acquiesce. The visitors are mostly drawn from the local gentry, who despise the Jacksons for being in trade but are prepared to overlook it for the sake of their money. Lady Faringford, the neighbourhood she-dragon, hopes to marry her daughter to Henry and is impatient with the girl's slowness at getting a proposal out of him.

The Jacksons have another son, Eustace, a ne'er-do-well who, after failing in an impressive variety of careers at home, was packed off in time-honoured fashion to Australia, with (ps)1,000 on which to make something of himself. He failed there, too: As he points out -- he can certainly talk with engaging fluency if he can do nothing else -- failure or success in one place will usually be duplicated in another.

He comes home and carefully collapses on the family threshold, feigning illness and exhaustion. Once the first flush of concern has passed, his father and brother start wondering what to do with him. He has an answer: They can support him, in return for his continued absence, since his continued presence would embarrass them and ruin their political prospects.

They do not, of course, take kindly to this blackmail; though perhaps even more disturbing to them is the philosophy with which Eustace backs it up. It is not, he points out, his fault that he was born without energy or willpower; given the choice, he would far rather be rich than poor. And even leaving the money out of it, success feels a lot nicer than failure. By what right do the successful punish the unsuccessful for the crime of getting less out of life than they do? Radical stuff then, this may hit even harder now. It strikes at the root of just about everything. It is the more powerful for being couched in a tone of insouciant irony -- the real thing, not our sickly modern counterfeit -- that never once raises its voice or lowers its guard. The play does at one point raise the spectre of a love interest, but Eustace and his author proceed to trample it blithely underfoot.

The values that Eustace observes under his parents roof are rampant, too, of course, in the world outside. Lady Faringford begins the play by envying Mrs. Jackson her new electric light because "lamps are so troublesome -- the servants are always setting themselves on fire with them -- and she maintains that same compassionate social tone throughout. She tells of a tenant who died of pneumonia through living in a damp cottage (so ridiculous ... as if all cottages were not damp") and of his widow who was promptly evicted for non-payment of rent, both events arousing the unaccountable indignation of Mr. Jacksons electoral opponent.

Eustace grasps the dilemma immediately and can see its consequences for those unfortunates who don't even have his advantages of a quick tongue and a rich father: "The strong must have the good cottages in order that they may grow stronger. And the weak must have the bad cottages in order that they may die off. Survival of the fittest, you know. Sounds quite topical, doesn't it?

The characters divide then, into the Jacksons and the rest, and the rest are the harder to bring off. So at least it seems in Christopher Newtons production, in which the minor nobility and their hangers-on are played as caricatures -- an effect that is especially disorienting in the early scenes, when we are still trying to sort out who everybody is.

Lady Faringford, as you may have observed, bears in her merciless snobbishness a marked resemblance to Oscar Wildes Lady Bracknell. The difference is that this lady's epigrams have perceptible consequences in the real world -- and that people occasionally answer her back. If Lady Bracknell were to say, I don't like this pernicious modern jargon about shopkeepers and gentlefolk being much the same -- theres far too much truth in it to be agreeable," the action would simply roll on to the next joke. When Lady Faringford says it, her daughter (prettily played by Susie Burnett) takes her up on it, and her mama has candidly to explain that social distinctions have to be ruthlessly maintained because without them people like themselves -- they have, after all, no real money -- would starve. Lady B knows these things but blots them out; Lady F admits them but carries on regardless. This makes her a fascinating study in selfish single-mindedness, but it imposes considerable strain on the actress, and Brigitte Robinson bends beneath it. Lacking both social and intellectual style, she seems to be dissociating herself from the character, as if fearful that she might be suspected of holding such horrible views herself.

Still, it is the family who are the heart of the play and certainly of this production. All five of them act superbly -- and interact even better. Ben Carlsons Eustace, stretched out in a hammock, with a straw boater perched rakishly on his outstretched foot, is a joy, perfect in both his impudence and his self-hatred. Patricia Hamilton, once she has disentangled herself from her guests, brings Mrs. Jackson to full life as a kind, unheeding woman, tirelessly capable of believing the best. Kelli Fox, having sat meekly on the sidelines for three acts, takes searing advantage of the fourth, in which she tells how much more hopeless, even than Eustace's, her prospects are.

The action finally resolves into a triangular contest between father and sons; their final scene, a battle in which ideas and emotions run on parallel lines, sends one of those new-fangled electric currents coursing through the theatre. Bernard Behrens is Jackson pere, trying to stand on his dignity but uncertain where it lies, his peppery temper compromised by the knowledge that he ought to feel affection for his black-sheep son even if he doesn't.

And nothing is finer than the relationship between Carlsons Eustace and Blair Williams smug, clever Henry; they don't like one another, they don't trust one another, but at some deep fraternal level they understand one another, and the knowledge brings them into occasional surprised alliance.

The Jackson house, as economically designed by William Schmuck, is creamily elegant, with beautifully etched rolling-hill vistas in the background.

Politically and psychologically, Hankins play seems to cut deeper than most of Shaws, though maybe its unfamiliarity has something to do with that. It unfolds with an undeviating logic, but spares us the accustomed Shavian sensation that the author knows all the answers and that all we have to do to be saved is listen. Hankin just keeps asking the questions; that's a cliche of a critic's compliment, I know, but this time it's true.

He himself had only one answer: There is much talk of suicide in the play, with drowning invariably the chosen method, and that is how Hankin, at the age of 39, ended his own life, a major loss to English drama. (He is the second drowned dramatist -- Frank Vosper, of Love from a Stranger, was the first -- to be premiered at Niagara in two days. If this is policy, I don't think it has a future.)

Hankin wrote at least two other plays -- The Cassilis Engagement and The Charity That Began at Home -- that are worth reviving, and one hopes that the Shaw may be embarking on a Hankin cycle to match its tour through the works of Granville Barker. If that leads to Christopher Newton returning as a guest director after he vacates the festival hot seat next year, then so much the happier.

WINGFIELD ON ICE

Avon Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

At the emotional climax of Wingfield on Ice, Walt Wingfield, a farmer with a past career in stockbroking, tells of cradling his just-delivered baby daughter. Newborn babies supposedly cannot see, but this one seemed to be greeting him with what he rather wonderfully describes as "such a look of skeptical appraisal as I've never received in all my life."

I felt like a skeptical appraiser myself as I approached this show. It is the fifth in a hugely successful series of one-man Wingfield shows, all of them written by Dan Needles, all performed by Rod Beattie, all previously seen at Stratford, and all unseen by me.

As a late arrival at the party, I feared I might be in for an evening of impenetrable coziness. My fears were unfounded. True, this is not the most jaggedly satirical evening you are ever going to encounter, but it has an agreeable tartness, is presented with unfailing skill (which I did expect) and is often very funny.

And, of course, there were things that surprised me, even if they were welcomed as old friends by everybody else.

For example, I have been assuming all year that the philosophically bemused, crusty looking old party in brown corduroy jacket, white-rimmed glasses and green eyeshades depicted on the posters (and now on the program cover) was Walt himself. Not a bit of it: He turns out to be Ed, old-fashioned editor of an old- fashioned local newspaper, who acts as a framing device. So, the play and Beattie's performance exist on three levels. Ed introduces Walt (Beattie slips off the jacket, and underneath are overalls), who introduces everybody else. Walt tells his stories and theirs in a series of letters to the cheekily named Ed that the latter must have been delighted to publish.

It is worth noting just how gracefully Beattie gives Walt's discursive prose the illusion of conversational ease without once resorting to forced hesitations or other rhythmic breakages. Delightfully impressive are the dozen different inflections he can bestow on the words "Yours sincerely, Walt," precisely matching each one to the tone of what has gone before.

Lost in the mists of time, or conceivably in the earlier scripts, is any sense of how Walt's citified past affects his position in the tiny township of Persephone, Ont., that he currently inhabits. He now seems as integral a part of the community as everybody else. He does sometimes affect an air of quizzical bemusement, but then, as a comic narrator, he'd have to. He can also, by the same token, be the fall guy; his wife Maggie's pregnancy occasions a hilarious sequence of verbal confusion around the phrase "the waters are breaking." He's talking agriculture, his friends and neighbours think he's talking gynecology, and his apparent callousness gets them very worried.

The first half of the show deals in similar, apparently disconnected, anecdotes. The farmer opposite, now retired, grumbles about his long-estranged brother who married a Catholic girl (this is traditional Orange territory) and has led a financially charmed life: "Lucky? He was carrying a tuba the day it rained gold." (This must be the Protestant obverse of "God help the Irish -- if it was raining soup, they'd be out in the street with forks" attributed to Dominic Behan, Brendan's brother.)

Walt's chum Freddy, who writes terrible impromptu poetry, tries to smuggle a dead goat into town and is stopped by a policeman who doesn't believe he's taking it to the vet and all but says, "this is an ex-goat." This particular escapade is stopped in its tracks by the onset of really terrible weather. A three-day ice storm descends, sealing off the township, making paths impossible and roads impassable, and suddenly justifying the play's title, which up to then we'd taken for a lark.

In the second act, the characters, co-existing in a state of siege, set differences aside and pull together. (Maggie gives birth.) All this is predictable and underlined in the commentary, but believable. Even the tale of the two brothers begins to veer toward reconciliation, though with a dark twist that lies somewhere between Chekhov and O. Henry. Beattie, in the course of the action, wears several hats, all of them Walt's. To summon the other characters, he relies on stance and delivery, all of it cleverly done, though when impersonating the women (Maggie especially) he tends to fall back on a generalized softness of voice. Sometimes the pressure slackens, taking my attention with it, but there is always something worth coming back for: not just good jokes but a humane spirit, a capacity for being surprised by things and sharing the wonder without going pop-eyed over it. The apogee of that, of course, is the line about the baby.

Douglas Beattie directed, and John Thompson, to quote the official credits, adapted the original set. (This is one of Stratford's more economical productions.) I can now join those who look forward to Episode Six, which will conceivably be called Wingfield and Chips. As in: off the old block.

GOOD MOTHER

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

Damien Atkins' new play begins with a quietly terrifying scene in which a woman in a kitchen clutches her head, lets slip the phone on which she was presumably dialling 911, and falls unconscious to the ground. The lights go down, to come up again on a hospital where the woman's husband waits for news of his wife's condition, desperately trying to control his anxiety so as not to alarm the young son who waits with him and whose own worry is able to co-exist with his craving for potato chips.

The balance of tension here is accurately observed and economically conveyed. A young doctor passes through, though only a junior member of the team, and a researcher rather than a physician, he reluctantly lets himself be drawn into providing some information.

The patient has had a stroke and is in a coma; she will not be the same woman when she comes out of it, not ever. Much of the scene's focus, though, is on the doctor's embarrassment, which is played -- by the author, as it happens -- for gentle but obvious laughs. He seems, as both player and playwright, to be offering comic relief that hasn't yet been called for. And since we are never to see this character again, we don't need to get that engaged with him; there is such a thing as too much human interest.

That is how it goes with Good Mother: scenes of genuinely piercing emotion alternating with others that are forced if not actually false. The spine of the play is the clinical development of the stricken Anne Driver, who up to now has lived up to her married name and been the driving force of her family. They have sometimes resented this but they have basically depended on it. Her husband, son and 18-year-old daughter now have to live without the sexy, intelligent woman they knew but with a helpless and initially incoherent person who disturbingly resembles her.

Anne, in fact, makes remarkable progress in the course of the play, but this only underscores the gulf between her and the woman she used to be. There are a couple of flashbacks to reinforce this point, but they aren't really needed. (The second, which comes in the form of a dream, is especially superfluous.) More helpful, really, is the casting of Seana McKenna, who usually plays strong, vibrant women and cannot help bringing those associations with her. She is the contrast, right there, and it is heartbreaking; that she is a fine and fiercely controlled actress in her own right doesn't hurt either, or at least it hurts in the right way. One may have wondered why she wanted to take on this part so soon after playing the cancer victim in Wit, but in fact the two roles turn out to be polar opposites. The pain of Wit lay in the protagonist being in full command of her faculties, almost until the end; that of Good Mother lies in her having lost them from the beginning.

It's moving almost beyond the call of drama, by which I mean it would take a lout of a playwright not to squeeze some legitimate pathos from the situation. There are, of course, plenty of louts out there, and I don't want to undervalue the skill, tact and promise Atkins demonstrates. But he is stuck with the familiar problem that attends plays about illness. There is only so far you can go in writing about the patient. Most of the emphasis has to fall on the actions and reactions of those around her, who in this case are very much around. The danger, of course, is that you end up writing an ordinary family-crisis play with a secret weapon up its sleeve, and that is often the case here.

Not always: The scenes involving the boy (Andrew Dodd) go on as truthfully, in writing and performance, as they began. Those with the father, played with affecting twitchy authenticity by Wayne Best, are fine, too, though underdeveloped. He becomes increasingly drawn to his wife's younger sister, a divorcee who is constantly around, ever-helpful and adoring (of both Drivers); this relationship naturally arouses the resentment of the two children. Most of what we learn about the sister she has to tell us herself; Jane Spidell copes very well in the role, considering. (She seems condemned this season to underwritten characters; in The Trials of Ezra Pound, she fared even worse.)

You would expect the husband-wife relationship, with its ramifications, to be the centre of the play, but it gets increasingly elbowed out by the problems of their daughter. Unfortunately, neither the writing nor the performance (by Michele Graff) of this role can raise it above the stock figure of the sullen teenager. Sure, she is at an age when daughters resent and fight with their mothers. Yes, she is now in a situation of uncommon stress, aggravated by the loss of her boyfriend (Shawn Mathieson), a relationship to which the play devotes a lot of time without ever bringing it truly alive. But wouldn't she, in the circumstances, make some effort? Would she blame everyone for everything all the time? The play eventually zeroes in on the relationship, cruelly misshapen but still oddly unaltered, between mother and daughter; but though it avoids sentimentality when dealing with Anne herself, it embraces it when presenting the two together.

There are two other characters. One is Anne's bouncy and largely unqualified nurse (Lisa Horner). Well-intentioned and full of earthly wisdom, she is a type but an enjoyable one; she too tells us more about herself than, dramatically, we need to know. The same goes, more damagingly, for a clinical psychiatrist (Kim Horsman) mainly distinguished by her briskness and lack of empathy; qualities that can certainly exist in doctors but here have no effect on the rest of the play and are therefore not worth the time they take to delineate. It's meaningless character writing, television-style.

We could, in the meantime, do with more information about the people who do matter. What business, for example, is Anne's husband supposed to be in? Miles Potter's direction is lucid scene by scene, but cannot prevent the play as a whole from straggling.

This, the last production of the Stratford season, is the only one of the four new plays on the bill that is truly, wholly new. The others have been an adaptation of a novel (Tempest-Tost), a semi- documentary (Ezra Pound), and the latest sliver of a continuing soap (Wingfield on Ice). It is also the most conventional: the one that could most easily have turned up somewhere else. This, surprisingly, is a hopeful sign: If Stratford is going to plunge seriously into producing new plays, as portended by the opening of the Studio next year, then it cannot wait around for special events, worthy to share a stage with Shakespeare and Chekhov. It has to be more eclectic than that, perhaps more modest, and it has to keep them coming. Good Mother may point the way to some good rowdy children.

PUPPETRY OF THE PENIS

New Yorker Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Nearly everything you have heard about Puppetry of the Penis is true. It does indeed consist of two men up on stage twisting their genitals into weird and, I guess, wonderful shapes for our delectation. It's also true that this is entertainment from down under, by which of I course mean the performing pair hail from Australia.

What has been falsely reported is that they perform in a state of full frontal nudity. True, they come on stage wearing classical cloaks that they duly and speedily cast aside, and they have no other garments beneath. But they do, throughout the proceedings, keep their shoes and socks on, as in some revue sketch about Englishmen making love. And one of them wears a funny hat; I think it's a pith helmet.

The two guys are named Simon Morley and David Friend. The former refers to the latter as Friendy. Friendy is the one in the helmet; he also wears a goofy grin and, by my unscientific calculation, demonstrates more than half of the couple's inventions or, as they call them, installations. For his facial wear, Morley favours the dry smile, and he also does most of the talking; in traditional comedy-duo terms, he is the straight man. As comics, they are very ingratiating. They swap roles a bit. But the rule is that one talks while the other does. Be assured that the evening contains no organ duets.

Their show's title, as they are keen to point out, undersells them. They don't just play with their penises; they throw in, liberally, their testicles and scrota. There will probably be sequels, with similarly alliterative titles. Stop trying to invent them and pay attention. The scrotum stretching, in particular, is taken to spectacular lengths. If the show on the first night seemed to be more -- or at least more vocally -- appreciated by the ladies in the audience, that may be because the gentlemen could never quite bring themselves to believe the actors' assurances that it didn't hurt. We felt their pain, even if they didn't.

Probably the most ingenious impersonation comes early in the act, when Friendy makes all his bits disappear from view and hops around the stage like one of his compatriot kangaroos. He calls this impersonation the Woman. Trailing this item closely in cleverness, and surpassing it in outrageousness, is the Hamburger, which I shall not attempt to describe, except to say that it involves a lot of folding and wrapping. They also do animals.

The performers have an assistant, who actually precedes them on stage, and announces himself as Priapus, ancient god of the phallus. He then retreats into the auditorium and films the show as it happens. (He seems to be better with a camera than he is at speaking lines.) The film appears on a large screen behind the actors so that we may get a good view of details we might otherwise miss. It's like watching a game at SkyDome. You don't know where to look.

Now, what has this production to tell us about sexual liberation? That is a complex question, with a simple answer: It tells us absolutely nothing about sexual liberation or sexual anything. (Except, of course, that there has to be a permissive climate for the show to get on in the first place.) The show is advertised as un- sexual; I would be inclined to call it pre-sexual. That puts it at the opposite extreme from the previous attraction at this theatre, the very verbal Vagina Monologues -- or, as I have come to think of it, Bridge of Thighs -- which might be called post-sexual. One show doesn't talk about it, the other only talks about it. On a strictly anatomical level, the difference between them is the difference between show and tell. Both productions, a little unfairly, seem to be aimed principally at women.

Both the differences and the similarities are reinforced by the presence in the current show of a warm-up act from the female comedy circuit: a British lady, now living here, called Wendy Vousden, who - - not unnaturally in the circumstances -- told jokes about the male body. Very blunt and aggressive she was, though maybe she needed somebody to warm her up, since her turn was nearly over before she said anything imaginative enough to be funny.

Having her there makes sense, though, because a) the audience, however broad-minded, is likely to arrive feeling queasy and is grateful for an icebreaker; and b) Morley and Friend, though sweet, have a limited repertoire and wisely ration their stage time to less than an hour. Even at that, they can get monotonous. At their best, though, they are hilarious. There is also audience participation; a lady is induced to go up on stage and help out. Friday's volunteer said it was her birthday and seemed to enjoy her surprise present.

I am uneasily aware that some readers may have tuned in hoping for a column of suggestive wordplay, and that I have short-changed them. It's late, but there is a line in Macbeth that goes "by the pricking of my thumbs." Perhaps we could try turning that around. I would just like to add that the two penis puppeteers struck me as being very -- um -- Australian. I don't think the show would work in any other accent.

SATURDAY NIGHT FEVER

Canon Theatre, Toronto

The Canon is the name that has been slapped on what was once the Pantages, the beauifully restored theatre at Yonge and Dundas where The Phantom of the Opera hung out for years.

It owes its new label to the involvement of Canon Canada Inc. and, according to the program, "exemplifies [the company's] commitment to the performing arts in Canada." Apparently, this commitment does not extend to preserving the name of a historic theatre chain, but there you increasingly go.

Whats happening on stage is a comparable act of cultural appropriation: a pitiful attempt to turn Saturday Night Fever into a musical. The 1977 movie, of course, was no such thing. It was a narrative picture that happened to involve a lot of dancing.

Its hero, Tony Manero, growing up poor in Brooklyn, lived for his nights at the disco and the picture let us get caught up in his excitement. But the dances were not the point of the thing, and they werent really presented as set numbers or as pieces of entertainment in their own right. Here, of course, they have to be: The stage production is desperate to give us something to applaud.

The stage show hews pretty closely to the narrative line of the film. Tony still lives at home, works in a paint store and fights with his unemployed father and devout Catholic mother. He still hangs out with a quartet of buddies and gets into fights. He is still the pride of the disco floor, and he still abandons one girl as a dancing and possible sexual partner and pursues another: a local young lady who works over in Manhattan and fancies herself as a social climber.

The implications of all this are bleak, but the show does its best to soft-pedal them. The film's dialogue remains (and sounds as flat as screen language usually does when spoken on stage), but it has been largely purged of profanity. The producers make no secret of this. In fact, their publicity employs the phrase "political correctness" not only without irony but with positive pride.

However, the efforts to turn Saturday Night Fever into family entertainment are constantly embarrassed by the elements of plot that keep turning up. This is now a show that presents a suicide and a gang-rape without providing any emotional context for them, and then hurries on as if they had never existed.

There is also a bewilderingly inconclusive and unnecessary sub- plot about Tony's brother, a self-defrocked priest, and a street fight that seems blissfully unaware of the prior existence of West Side Story.

When you talk about emotional context in a musical, of course, you are largely talking about the songs and how they fit in with the book.

Now, I always had a fondness, or thought I had, for the songs of the Bee Gees, if only because of the way in which they were anathematised by the strident prophets of rock. The two big tunes from the movie -- Staying Alive and How Deep is Your Love -- remain excellent pop songs. They bookend this show, the first coming right at the beginning, where it means nothing, and the other right at the end, where it is asked to mean far too much.

There really is a difference between songs intoned by disembodied voices on a soundtrack and songs sung by supposedly real characters in a show, and How Deep is Your Love sounds plain ridiculous when rendered as a fervent duet by two people who have just declared their intention of being only friends.

The other songs, whether new or carried over, divide into two categories. There are the dance- hall numbers, which are indistinguishable. (More Than a Woman is probably the best.) There are the dramatic numbers, which are equally generic but in a far worse genre. They may be sung by anybody who finds him- or herself in a situation of stress, details immaterial.

It really is very rude to start bellowing a ballad at an audience to whom you havent been introduced, and in this show nobody gets introduced. Tonys past and future girlfriends get to emote in this way, as does one of his friends. He himself holds out against it for most of the show, thereby greatly increasing his credibility as hero, but near the end he succumbs. Nan Knighton takes principal credit for the book, and in terms of character delineation and the careful integration of script and score, her work makes Mamma Mia look like Gypsy.

Arlene Phillips' choreography mainly calls for its dancers to be energetic, which they are. But it is very monotonous, number to number, and each individual routine seems to consist of a single step, endlessly repeated. We are expected to be impressed by the sight of a line of performers all raising their left arms, one after the other, in a partial salute to the show's (and the movies) logo. Its like demanding applause for a slow kick line. But then disco dancing, however gussied up, was never meant to be looked at for an evening, any more than disco music was meant to be sat down and listened to.

Nor are things much improved by the occasional lowering of a tilted mirror, in which we can study the tops of the dancers' heads. The routines look just as dull from above as from below. The mirror actually recalls the one the same distinguished designer, Robin Wagner, employed aeons ago in his sets for A Chorus Line, to rather better effect. His work here is unlikely to occupy a proud place in his portfolio (it's surely about time the display on a black backcloth of street signs, store names and even theatre marquees was laid to rest), and anyway seems in this touring production to be in an acute stage of disrepair. At one memorable moment on the press night, it started coming visibly apart.

There is, though, a rather sweet evocation of the Brooklyn Bridge with miniature cars crawling across it. (Which reminds me: the pieces whole premise -- for frustrated or self-deluded Brooklyn youth, the bridge as the pathway to an urban wonderland -- was anticipated in an earlier, similarly titled musical by Stephen Sondheim. Saturday Night, sans fever, was slated for production in 1954, but never actually got on till 50 years later, when it was resurrected in London and New York. It has a charming score, and deserves a small-scale production in Canada. Shaw Festival, Im talking to you. It's set in the 1920s, so it fits your mandate.)

Richard H. Blake does a good dancing-singing-acting job on Tony. Jeanine Myers looks properly cool as his lady, and if she seems to have trouble believing in the words she has to say, it's hard to blame her. Aileen Quinn, who had the title role in the film of Annie, has now grown into a good girl trying to go bad, which is food for thought. Rich Hebert and Suzanne Costallos as Tonys parents exemplify the professions wonderful propensity for acting its damndest, whatever the circumstances. (Just what are they supposed to be doing in the opening number, boogie-ing with all the kids?)

Not all the others are as conscientious, but they probably aren't being paid for their skills at characterization. By the same token, the choreographer is also the director, but she probably wasn't hired for being good with acting.

The show comes to us from a successful run in London, and also brandishing rave reviews from two separate papers in Chicago. London is no surprise -- its nostalgic embrace of anything that might be described as a rock musical has long been a joke -- but who knew Chicago was so easy to fool? Meanwhile, the professional theatre in general, and the musical theatre in particular, takes another merry step toward the grave.

2001-09-07-the-critic-who-spoke-to-me:
Robert Cushman is the National Post's theatre critic. His review of Saturday Night Fever appears on page B14. Obituary of Pauline Kael.

Pauline Kael was the first film critic I ever read -- and almost the last -- who seemed to be speaking to me.

By that, I dont just mean she had a button-holing colloquial style, though she obviously did. Most writers on film seemed to be operating from a realm of theory, to which I had no access. Some were purists who apparently admired only silent pictures; others revered European directors -- this was the heyday of Resnais and Antonioni -- whose films about the boredom of existence bored me as, I discovered to my delight, they did her.

None of them seemed to have anything to do with the experience, or at least with my experience, of enjoying a movie. None, for a start, seemed to have any interest in performance. They might occasionally analyze actors as icons, but they would never describe or evaluate what they actually did.

What immediately made me her fan for life was her demolition job on the film of West Side Story and her comparison of it to good musicals -- Singin in the Rain or anything with Fred Astaire.

Along with this went an exaltation of the best American "trash" (His Girl Friday, Duck Soup, Citizen Kane) over contemporary art films, along with an enthusiasm for the good new things that were managing to come out of Hollywood -- The Manchurian Candidate, Lolita, Ustinov's Billy Budd, eventually Bonnie and Clyde. Which didn't stop her slaughtering most other Hollywood movies, especially the piously well-intentioned ones, or liking Truffaut.

All this was before her tenure at The New Yorker, where she spawned a school of imitators who, she said, copied her style but not her opinions.

She was wrong there. They parroted her opinions as long as they knew what they were. When she wasn't around, you could see them hilariously hopping about, trying to second-guess what Pauline would have thought. You could never quite be sure because she was a merciless empiricist, too intellectual for show-business and too showbiz for the intellectuals: a very healthy if perilous position, and one shared by my other favourite critics, Kenneth Tynan and Walter Kerr.

She was always ready to lambast either the boobs or the snobs, and she could jump either way. Despite her breezy style, she was seldom funny. She is the only reviewer who has kept me reading compulsively without making me laugh. But you sensed that, beneath the unrelenting burrowing intelligence, there was an exasperated good humour. As in fact there was.

THE BALD SOPRANO THE LESSON

DuMaurier Theatre Centre

- - -

The plays of Eugene Ionesco -- Romanian by birth, French by adoption, stateless by temperament -- came violently into fashion in the 1950s and passed violently out again in the '60s. In the last few years they have been making a sly return.

Soulpepper's welcome double-billing of two Ionesco early one-act farces makes a fair case for the author's rehabilitation in its first half and an overwhelming one in its second.

The tag "Theatre of the Absurd" has done a lot more harm than good, but it applies to Ionesco if it applies to anyone. The Bald Soprano is a good entry point into his work; it was his first play (written in 1948) and derived, by his own account, from his experience of trying to learn English.

Amused and appalled by the stock phrases he found in his textbooks, he set about writing a play composed of just that kind of dialogue. Here are Mr. and Mrs. Smith in their living room complacently telling one another about the meal they have just shared, about their children and about their friends, the Bobby Watsons. (A large family, and every single one of them, male or female, is called Bobby Watson.)

Their friends the Martins pay a call and discover, in the course of an impeccably polite conversation, that they are married to one another. Ionesco may not have set out to satirize the expository techniques of the well-made play but he managed it anyway.

He also had a larger point to make about society. These people speak in dead sentences, therefore they are dead themselves. This is a rigged case; and even if we admit its partial truth (or regard it as a pleasant way of looking down on our neighbours), its point is rather quickly made.

Our continued interest is largely determined by how funny the author can make it, and his achievement here is uneven. At its best it is hilarious, especially in a fanatically logical sequence about a series of unattributable knocks at the front door.

Ionesco doesn't deal in non sequiturs; rather, he piles up the sequiturs until they cancel one another out. They need to be acted with a sort of deadpan panache, and of Soulpepper's central quartet, only Brenda Robins consistently has the hang of it, though Michael Hanrahan has a few red-faced moments.

Things perk up when a fire chief arrives (William Webster, looking alternately aglow and aghast) to tell anecdotes of virtuoso pointlessness, explain exactly whose fires he is and is not allowed to extinguish and generally supply a shoulder to be cried on. "A fireman," he explains, "is a confessor."

The play ends with language finally cracking apart, the cast screaming fractured platitudes at one another while -- a gratuitously frenetic touch in Jim Warren's production -- the stage revolves.

The show otherwise looks good, with its geometric moves on Glenn Davidson's sternly cosy set, though I wondered why, in a play that depends so much on references to a guidebook England that Ionesco at the time had never visited, nobody bothered with an accent.

The play leaves you thinking Ionesco had a great technique; but what could he do with it? Well, he learned, and fast, as is shown, appropriately enough, in The Lesson, written three years later.

This play, astutely directed by Chris Abraham, is a brilliant dramatization of the teacher-student relationship, written in terms of insouciant comedy and carried to the direst possible extremes.

A pupil comes to her professor's study for tuition towards her doctorate: a goal only modestly compromised by the fact that, though she can add one and one with perfect accuracy, subtraction utterly defeats her. Never mind: the professor will move on from arithmetic to philology. Gradually but also speedily (I'm sorry, the idiom is catching), the professor moves from patronizing pedagogy to bullying and from there to outright assault: anybody wanting a textbook study in schoolroom harassment need only see this play.

The professor's doubletalk is strongly reminiscent of Groucho Marx holding forth on the party of the second part, and there is more than a touch of Groucho about Tony Nardi's performance, forward stoop included; the part could probably be played with more demonic variety but what he does he does extremely well.

Meanwhile Liisa Repo-Martell, at her very best, takes the revolutionary step of playing the pupil as a real person with, at no cost to the humour, an unbroken and increasingly terrified emotional line.

The first play is a trifle, the second a masterpiece. Both offer the added attraction of Kristen Thomson playing a maid: In the first she's a pertly confident young thing who says her name is Sherlock Holmes, and in the second the professor's grumbling, motherly accomplice warning him that philology always leads to trouble. She is about 40 years too young for the latter role but she doesn't let it bother her and neither should you.

WOZZECK/WOYZECK

Bathurst Street Theatre, Toronto

So what fresh hells are these?

Georg Buchner's play Woyzeck, written in the 1830s, was the basis of Alban Berg's opera Wozzeck, first staged in 1925. Wozzeck/ Woyzeck, presented by the new and grandiosely named Theatre of Ideas, is a collage of the two works.

The disparity in the names of the two originals is due to a scribal error in reproducing one of Buchner's manuscripts, a mistake inherited by Berg. This production splits the difference by calling the principal character Woyzeck, while giving Wozzeck top billing in the title.

Buchner's play, discovered just in the early 20th century, was the last of its extraordinary author's four extant works. The others include Danton's Death, the greatest of all modern history plays, an especially impressive achievement when you consider that, at his death, Buchner was 23.

In his brief lifetime, he had passed at lightning speed from revolutionary enthusiasm to revolutionary disillusion. (A strictly radical progression, by the way. Nothing in his work suggests he would have become a conservative.)

The darkest of all his works is Woyzeck, whose protagonist is a tormented and, by all previous dramatic standards, inarticulate German soldier, at the mercy of his superiors.

The play's nightmarish quality is partly responsible for its magnetic appeal to modern directors, especially those of the Gothic twilight persuasion.

Even more attractive is the fact that it exists in four separate drafts, all of them different and none of them complete. We don't even know how the play was meant to end. For directors with delusions of grandeur, this degree of carte blanche has proved irresistible.

Berg's opera necessarily imposes a shape on the piece, though it comes at a price. Wozzeck/Woyzeck pursues an insight expressed 40 years ago by George Steiner in The Death of Tragedy. Steiner wrote that, though Berg's opera was superb as both music and drama, it distorted the play's central device by giving the hero an eloquent singing voice.

In the play, he just blushes and stammers, the impoverished victim of three cruelly fluent tormentors who between them drive him mad.

These are the Captain, to whom Woyzeck is batman and barber and who, at his most genial, addresses him as if he were an animal; the Doctor, who uses him as a guinea pig for bizarre dietary experiments; and the Drum-Major, who destroys the one meaningful corner of Woyzeck's life by seducing the mother of his child.

In this production, we get something that plays as a cut-down version of the opera -- the music rarely stops -- but in which some of the text is sung in German, some in English, and some, including all of the title role, is spoken.

In theory, it should give us the best of both worlds. In practice, it doesn't.

The show's director and originator is Misha Aster, a Canadian with extensive theatrical and operatic credits in the United States and Europe, and himself a figure of Buchnerian precocity. (He, too, is 23. We must wish him good health.)

This production is mounted with the co-operation of the Austrian Embassy, and its 21-piece orchestra is more or less evenly composed of Austrians and Canadians. Its five-person cast is similarly international.

This is a big deal. But the director's skills seem to lag some distance behind his aspirations. The production is staged on a large tilted disc with a hole in the middle that turns out to represent a pool. The design (uncredited, so presumably the director's) would probably remind me of Bayreuth, if I had been to Bayreuth.

So much empty space needs to be brought carefully and rigorously to life, and most of the staging here is ungainly and lethargic. Indeed, about the only scene with any physical energy is an elaborate beating-up episode. This is a giveaway in itself, especially when you consider that its violence is far in advance of anything specified in either play or opera.

Experienced actors would have their work cut out in these circumstances, but most of these players, naturally enough, are singers, with no particular physical presence. As Marie, Woyzeck's beloved whom he eventually murders, Renee Salewski sings beautifully and expressively, but she droops in speech and wilts in silence.

Nor does it help that, whether for reasons of economy or interpretation, the list of characters has been drastically reduced. Two of Woyzeck's oppressors, the Doctor and the Captain, have been combined into one, though Doug MacNaughton sings the lines written for the first in German (so he sounds more than ever like a proto- Nazi) and those for the second in English.

The Captain's is the first voice we hear, and the fact that I could actually understand him gave me high hopes for the whole enterprise. Later, I decided what I really wanted was to hear the whole opera sung in English, in a production as good as that mounted a few years ago by the Canadian Opera Company.

Anyway, though the bilingualism certainly has an effect, compressing these two characters into one reduces Woyzeck's predicament.

So, far more damagingly, does the merging of his friend, Andres, with the lecherous Drum-Major, who wins Marie principally through his confidence in the power of his uniform. (He wants to beget on her "a whole regiment of drum-majors.") Here, he is a stocky, ordinary young man in spectacles, a short beard, and a checked shirt. We exchange the tragedy of a baffled man -- alternately starved, bullied and cuckolded by those placed above him -- for the melodrama of the guy whose best buddy done him wrong. A lot of the piece ceases to make even dreamlike sense.

Jonno Roberts, the New Zealand actor who plays Woyzeck, looks authentically haggard, but the confused circumstances give him little chance to affect us. Paul Andres Mahr conducts John Rea's "chamber orchestration" of Berg's score. To me, it sounded scrawny rather than rich or stabbing -- but then the Bathurst Street Theatre is hardly Toronto's longed-for opera house.

Theatre Review

HABITAT

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Judith Thompson's confused new play seems obsessed at its heart with mothers and children, especially daughters. We begin with a girl called Raine, unleashing an aria of selfish teenage resentment at the bedside of her mother, who happens to be dying of cancer. The lights change, the soundtrack crashes, mother sits up in bed, and we get to hear the story of how Raine as a baby nearly choked to death in her mother's arms.

Her mother dead, Raine takes herself off to a group home that has just opened up on Mapleview Lanes, a leafy street in Etobicoke. The local residents, despite nice liberal principles, are not pleased by the advent of a dozen or so deprived, unruly youngsters, and they launch a protest. Spearheading it are another mother and daughter, Margaret and Janet, who don't get along; Margaret is a widow who has sunk into careless inertia since her husband's death, and Janet is a lawyer who confesses in a monologue that she doesn't like her own children much either.

Lewis Chance, the ambiguous figure who runs the home, has an intense telephonic relationship with his own mother in New Brunswick and tells a story that parallels Raine's, concerning the death of his baby brother. The remaining character is Sparkle, another inmate, a housebreaker and congenital fantasist who at one point claims to have killed his parents; a fey, out-of-the-closet Peter Pan who nurses an erotic obsession with Lewis that may or may not be reciprocated.

Thompson might conceivably have written a decent play about any one of these people, but spreading the load as she has, she is compelled to keep stopping and starting with all of them, often picking them up at an inexplicable psychological distance from where she dropped them. They do not, whatever unifying themes they may theoretically embody, make much of a mosaic. The worst of all is that these fragmented characters have been dumped into a sociological problem drama that demands conventional linear treatment if it is to work at all. Current theatrical economics may be the culprit, but it is hugely damaging that we never meet most of the kids the neighbours are complaining about; we simply don't believe the home exists. There is probably meant to be a connecting metaphor (these are all our children, society is a neglectful parent) but as it plays, Habitat is a mess, subject and method hopelessly at odds.

There are a couple of good speeches: Raine's first one, and Lewis' insistently jovial address to the community he has invaded. There are also some deep purple ones, and they are not excused by having Lewis, a prime offender, turn around and dismiss them as sob stories for suckers; Thompson still goes on writing them. (To wrongfoot the audience? That's a frivolous intellectual game.)

Margaret and Janet pay a call on Lewis, and he comprehensively insults them, though it would be in his interest to conciliate them. Maybe he's self-destructive, but that needs exploring. Maybe the author couldn't resist a flashy scene. She seems to be making it up as she goes along. Margaret has a series of encounters with Raine, whom she likes, and this quasi-maternal relationship is probably the play's best shot at reconciling its public and private themes. But the scenes are fragmentary, and it is never clear whether Margaret's abrupt reversion to the role of spruce homebody is triggered by Raine or by the conflicting excitement of defending her property values against the chancy Mr. Chance.

Katherine Kaszas' production is geographically awkward and emotionally stiff. Shawn Kerwin's set has furniture but no walls; this is a play about houses, but we never feel them. (Nice trees, though.) Near the end the furniture has to be moved, ludicrously. For the forty millionth time: Theatre is not television. Use short scenes at your peril. If you use them, find a style.

The sound effects are loudly clashing symbols. The actors go defensively for realism. Their success rate varies. Stephen Ouimette as Lewis is more charismatic than convincing. Holly Lewis as Raine starts strong but is defeated by her character's bewildering changes in attitude and even in intelligence. Corinne Conley's Margaret is trapped within a stereotype, and Kristina Nicoll's Janet is a blank. Luke Kirby's posturing Sparkle is the most irritating performance I have seen all year, but he is probably keeping faith with the text.

Apparently, CanStage were so pleased to have snagged a famous playwright that they went into production with a piece that, in its present state, should not have been done. The play inaugurates a co- commissioning program with the Royal Exchange in Manchester, which suggests two important theatres asleep at the controls.
