YOU ARE HERE

Theatre Passe Muraille

About halfway through You Are Here, Randy Hughson comes on stage and the audience wakes up. Partly this is the pleasure of recognition -- I haven't seen a play with Hughson in it for at least three weeks -- and partly it is because he radiates a contained energy unapproached by anybody else on this stage. It is a treat just to watch him rock backwards and forwards on his heels as he considers another characters dubious proposition.

He plays Thomas, a successful film director, and for an actor who rarely gets cast as a successful anything he is mightily convincing. He is far from being the central character. That position belongs to Alison, who makes most of her living as a celebrity journalist, and when Thomas first appears she is interviewing him.

Later she persuades him, not too plausibly, to direct a script that her psychologist-husband has written, and his initial reaction to it is worth recording: It is, he says, "very North American."

Asked to expand on that, he says that it goes on and on about its characters emotional states as if they were automatically of compelling interest.

Here Daniel MacIvor, the author and director, seems to be slyly mocking himself, or maybe trying to disarm criticism in advance. (Judith Thompson uses a similar tactic in Habitat, which opened the same night.) Because his play is an example of what Thomas is describing; it is all about Alison.

The first half of the play is her monologue, with illustrations. She sits on a chair in what looks, through an ingenious use of lighting, like a foreshortened black box. This has the effect of making Caroline Gillis, who plays the role and whose performance is technically unfaultable, look like a very big girl indeed, rather like Alice after drinking the potion.

Also like Alice, she recalls people from her past life, mainly her college days, and they pop up when she mentions them. They say something characteristic of themselves, she gives them a name-check (Richard! "Jerry!") and they go right on talking. It's like a sepulchral edition of This Is Your Life.

One of the visitants (played with some charm by Jim Allodi) is Alison's old roommate, who is defined, repeatedly, by his unwillingness to wear a watch since he wants his arms -- and, by extension, his life -- free. Another is the man she eventually marries.

There is also a female student whom she hates, all her life, for her apparent happiness and conventionality. We barely see this woman, learn nothing about her, but the author throws in an equally unrevealing final encounter as some kind of attempt at a climax. The point, probably a valid one, may be that we can all waste a lot of ourselves storing grudges against people who are really of no importance to us. But it isnt interesting, because Alison, however lyrically she soliloquizes, isnt interesting.

She is also steadily less credible, though her initial situation seems reasonable; she drifts into journalism, against her finer instincts, because she has to do something. Later, as the play begins to open out to include ensemble scenes, she becomes a film producer, and this is not believable, not of the woman we see.

Her experiences on set do permit the play to broaden into some mild satire on self-indulgent actors and manipulative directors: nothing very new, but at least there are some jokes.

Rather sharper is Alison's interview with the actress who eventually appears in her movie, and who adjusts her image, on a moment-by-moment basis, between brazenly commercial starlet and frustrated artist. Fiona Highet hits this off well.

All the characters become embroiled in a spiral of adultery, miscarriages, divorce, drink, drugs, the destruction of lives and the bitter evaporation of youthful ideals, displayed with civilized restraint across a restaurant table. It is, in fact, like a hundred other plays, but with an extra layer of self-consciousness.

Toward the end of each act, a character turns out front to reassure us that either the intermission or the final curtain will soon be upon us. These moments, presumably, are what MacIvor's program notes have in mind when they go on about honesty and breaking down the fourth wall and frankly admitting were in a theatre. Its kicking at an open door; Dr. Johnson pointed out, nearly 300 years ago, that no audience ever forgets it's in a theatre. Playfully underlining this can be fun; solemnly underlining it is a pain, though it seems to make those involved feel very cutting-edge. I think I might like some plays more if they didn't come wrapped up with sycophantic publicity and narcissistic manifestoes.

- Until Oct. 7. Box office (416) 504-7529.

SKYLIGHT

Tarragon Theatre

- - -

David Hare's plays are routinely praised for seamlessly blending the personal with the political. It would be nice if that were true. What actually happens is that he tears the two spheres into alternating strips, which then get pasted on to his characters.

In Skylight, which is certainly one of his best plays, there are only three characters, and two of them -- ex-lovers and political opposites -- get most of the stage-time. They are Tom, a restaurant mogul, and Kyra, 20 years his junior, who was once his employee and a virtual member of his family, and had a six-year affair with him. It ended when Tom's wife found out, at which point Kyra disappeared from his life. She now lives in a bleak North London flat and teaches at a bleak East London school, with a long, bleak daily commute between.

Both characters -- the powerful, perversely attractive man and the idealistic woman -- have their prototypes in earlier Hare plays; she, in particular, has been a recurrent figure. (Canadian content note: She used to be known in London as the Kate Nelligan role.)

Kyra is a more engaging figure than some of her predecessors, partly because it is only in the second half of the play that she starts haranguing anyone. We meet her on a snowy evening on which she receives two visitors from her past. The first is Tom's son, Edward, in his "gap year" between school and university, who tells Kyra how badly his father is handling his grief over his wife's death from cancer. The second is Tom himself, who, of course, wants Kyra back and is baffled by her current choices.

In the play's first, and better, half, Hare handles with remarkable skill the job of filling us in on the characters' past lives (it seldom sounds as if they are telling one another things for our benefit) while moving the new dramatic situation forward. We want to know what happened then and we want to know what will happen now.

It is all done on the arc of one continuous conversation, itself integrated with the ongoing domestic detail of Kyra's life. She is trying to cook dinner, and in Dennis Garnhum's fine Tarragon production, this is done with superlative realism. Food proves important in this play, and when Kyra eventually sets two places at table, it is a major climax.

One of the wonderfully fortifying things about Yanna McIntosh's performance of Kyra is the businesslike concentration she brings to all this; it makes you believe in her. Another is the quiet, sad, amused demeanour with which she watches Tom striding (physically and verbally) around her terrain, and the wry, laconic, perfectly calibrated way in which she replies to him; she never puts a foot or a word wrong.

Tom, whatever emotional wounds he may be bearing, has the implacable confidence of the self-made rich. Hare is a clever writer rather than a funny one, but he makes you smile at Tom's attack on that sloppy word "spiritual" and laugh hard at his declaration that a personal driver, whatever Kyra's conscientious qualms on the subject, is paid (and well paid) not to drive but to wait.

Thus far the personal and political -- which is mainly implicit - - run pretty much in tandem. And, by the way, the attraction between these two people is not only possible but extremely likely.

In Act Two, things come apart. Kyra delivers -- though McIntosh doesn't just deliver them, they flow out of her -- passionate defences of her work and blistering attacks on "the self-pitying rich" who mock her for doing it. (This play's six-year delay in reaching Toronto hasn't hurt it any.)

Like Shaw's Major Barbara, who worked in the identical part of London, she challenges Tom to come and see her at it. But by now the play has slipped its emotional moorings. It's as if the relationship were invented just to set up the speechifying. We find we have little idea of who she used to be and how it relates to who she is now. We may believe in the possibility of the six-year menage a trois in Tom's house, but we have no emotional purchase on it. We don't believe in the wife, from whose last days the play derives its title-image.

And we don't believe that Tom bleeds. Joseph Ziegler, stalking the stage with head and body cocked (and bearing a spooky resemblance to the author), has a sardonic edge but not an emotional one. There is no sense of his being a wounded bull who has fought his way up; Ziegler's is a second-generation swagger. The play is partly an exercise in class-reversal but it's equally hard to believe in McIntosh as the daughter of an ultra-conservative country solicitor. And yes, her being black has something to do with that.

The play is insistent that Tom and Kyra are in love but I couldn't care by the end whether or not this couple got together again, or why. I believed, though, in Tom's offstage relationship with his son; Brandon McGibbon's awkward Edward is immensely appealing and potentially infuriating. John Thompson's set looks too Canadian-comfortable, but the atmospherics (the occasional brush of snow on the window) are perfect. All faults allowed, this is still the best dramatic writing currently in Toronto, and McIntosh's is incomparably the finest performance.

Black & White Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / Robert Cushman says the performance of Yanna McIntosh (right, with Joseph Ziegler) is the best in town. ;

OTA

Artword Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - When it played at Harbourfront a few years ago, Robert Lepages The Seven Streams of the River Ota lasted about as many hours as there were streams, and at that it was still a work in progress. The show called Ota, presented by a group of recent graduates from the York University theatre program, plays for all of 90 minutes, and has the number of dramatic streams down to two, of which one now seems an insignificant tributary. It was given a long preview period at the Artword, followed by a tantalizingly brief official run. It must be brought back; it works extraordinarily well.

This is not a matter of cutting off surplus fat. Nobody who saw the original is likely to have wished it shorter; its length was not only part of its power but part of its charm. Like all Lepage's best work, it combined grandeur of theme and physical presentation with an engaging casualness in writing and performance. A delightful Feydeau-esque sequence about adultery is one of the things that has now gone missing. Like everything else it led, lightly but inexorably, to Hiroshima, from whose river the play takes its title.

Stephanie Saunders' adaptation makes no attempt to compare with the full version in richness, but it competes very well in imagination, intensity, wit and humanity. It takes one vital narrative thread and presents it in two segments.

In the first, set just after the war, an American military photographer, instructed to document the carnage, visits the stricken city, and falls in love with one of the living victims. Off to the side -- both of the stage and the story --sits a Czech- Jewish artist turned Buddhist monk discoursing on the peace to be found after surviving two holocausts. The role is played with sly strength by Rae Ellen Bodie, and survival is the plays theme, but it fits awkwardly in the new slim structure.

The love story, however, is beautifully done, told with very few words and staged with a deliberation that is measured but not portentous. Here, as elsewhere in Saunders production, the actors play with the kind of wise, shared rhythm that a director can inspire but not impose. Sherri McFarlane (who has her back to us throughout) and Adam Kelly make their union seem not only possible but inevitable.

If this sequence is the aftermath of the bomb, the remainder, set 20 years later, is the aftermath of the aftermath. Two young men named Jeffrey -- one American and tending a father sick with leukemia, the other American-Japanese -- encounter one another while lodging in the same funky (i.e., cheap) New York boarding house. Names apart, they seem to have little in common; they are, in fact, suspicious of one another. They turn out to have everything in common, and the revelation, which crowns a growing sense of shared kindliness plus an inspired recap of Abbott and Costello's "Who's on first?" routine, is very moving. Now, of course, more than ever.

The two Jeffreys are excellently played by Conor Green and Mike Realba. The latter -- the Japanese one -- has a delicate comic sense, especially marked in his scenes with a loud beat poet whose percussive hymn to the Hudson both intrigues him and keeps him awake. Could he not, this Jeffrey politely inquires, confine himself at night to working on the lyrics? This bard does his practising in the shared bathroom, and the very same bath also serves to develop photographs, which returns us to where we started.

Drew Nelsons set, which features sliding screens and slats that fall to the floor and start the play with a resounding crash, serves evocatively for the first sequence and cleverly for the second. A few performances are amateurish -- meaning they punch hard, but cant follow through -- but none are actually harmful.

What this short work and its long progenitor have that so many lack is mystery, which is not the same thing as obscurity. They make sense, but they also make more than sense. Anyone who still remembers alternately wincing and yawning through the pretentions of Hiroshima Mon Amour should find this show an antidote. More immediately, its advent -- and, if there is justice, its impending resurrection -- means that I have to withdraw my last week's assertion that Skylight offers the best dramatic writing in Toronto.

THE WALLS OF AFRICA

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace

Not surprisingly, many shows written and planned long before Sept. 11 have had extra resonances thrust upon them in the weeks since. Some of these are quirky: I wonder, for example, how Soulpepper's William Webster coped with his role in The Bald Soprano as the fire chief who tells householders that a fireman is much like a confessor. Some are fundamental: The meditations on Hiroshima in Ota turned on their axis from anguish recollected in tranquillity to tranquillity invoked in anguish. And some now seem amazingly daring, like the opening sequence in The Walls of Africa.

This play starts with an apparently Muslim woman, swathed in black from head to toe, regarded by a seated man. For a long time he just sits and she just stands. Then she starts to move, to undulate and, with artful thoroughness, to strip. Just what are we in for?

Nothing, as it turns out, especially religious or even explicitly political. The stripper is merely one of several erotic visions encountered or invoked in the course of the play by Mr. Pym, a middle-aged professorial gentleman living in what we assume is London in the 1950s. (The play mentions neither the city nor the decade explicitly but it reeks of both, though the characters are universal.)

Every evening, Mr. Pym comes home and goes straight up to his room, there to read or study or let his thoughts wander. Meanwhile, his landlady, a widow called Mrs. Fields, stretches out on her sofa, ever more languorously, with a glass of sherry, and tries unavailingly to attract his attention.

That a shy man, set in his lonely ways, may be so wrapped up in his own sexual fantasies that he cannot respond to the real, available thing even when it's spread before him is no great revelation, and one starts to wonder if the author, Hrant Alianak, will have anything else to tell us.

He hasn't, but he extends his theme artfully and compels our attention. He is his own director and he has scored and conducted the piece meticulously. The early scenes are wordless, and the principals' first extended conversation is almost drowned out by music. Mr. Pym is a great concert-goer (at the Albert Hall, I fancy) and he seems to bring the repertoire home in his head. Terry Crack is credited with this production's sound design, which makes especially intense use of some searing passages for strings.

When we do get to hear the characters talking, they turn out to be pleasantly and poignantly amusing. They find they have things in common, in addition to their complementary solitudes. Both have fond memories of visits to Africa before the war. Both are interested in Tolstoy, though her acquaintance is primarily biographical while his is philosophical. He is reading A Confession (surely a shorter book than the tome he is lugging about, which looks like half of War and Peace) and speaks with apparent approval of its author's late-life devotion to celibacy. She finds this perplexing, especially when considered from the point of view of Countess Tolstoy.

There is a delectable sense of constraint about these episodes, since even when Mr. Pym is persuaded to join Mrs. Fields on the sofa, he sits there with his hands locked to his sides and his hat in his lap. There is, of course, no tension like erotic tension, and these scenes are loaded with it.

Even after the walls of Africa have, figuratively, come tumbling down, all is not solved. He can hardly bring himself to call her by her first name of Elizabeth, while she seems all too eager to address him by his, which is Timothy. (This, by my computation, makes him Tim Pym.) She feels rebuffed, he feels hemmed in, and both, in different ways, feel guilty. And the play gets yet funnier and yet more painful.

It is superbly played. Layne Coleman, currently best known as director both of plays and of this theatre, returns to acting with a beautifully subdued, bound-up Mr. Pym, happy in his inhibitions or at least afraid of being without them -- gifted, probably for the first time in his life, with emotional power over someone.

Tedde Moore performs an emotional striptease at least as revealing as the literal one with which the play begins. She shows us a gracious, contained woman who spends the first half of the play releasing the temptress within herself and the second balancing her need and her dignity -- a matter now, not of preserving a social facade, but of salvaging her self-respect as a woman.

There is a striking contrast in visual and aural rhythms between these two -- he staccato, she flowing -- and also of dynamics: he necessarily on a single level, she modulating between a whisper and a mild conversational volume that, in this context, has the impact of a shout.

We should see more of Moore, who has been absent from our stages for a long time. We see, obviously, a great deal of Nicola Pantin, who plays the various mental pin-ups; she is impeccably alluring as all of them. Steve Lucas' twin-levelled set is, on this agonizingly cramped stage, a virtuoso deal.

THE SECRET GARDEN

Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - The Lorraine Kimsa Theatre, a name I rather doubt will catch on, is what used to be known as the Toronto Young Peoples Theatre. It commences its first re-christened season with one of the most dramatized of Victorian children's classics, Frances Hodgson Burnett's The Secret Garden.

This is the one about Mary Lennox, a spoiled but unhappy child of the British Raj, whose parents have died in a cholera epidemic and who at the age of 10 is sent back to England to live in her uncle's house on the Yorkshire moors. Here, she learns about love and nature and growing things. The rambling manor and its all-important gardens dominate this production, directed by the aptly named Jim Warren: aptly named since Glenn Davidson's elaborate revolving set is very warren-like. We are spun from rooms to passages, from indoors to out. Sometimes we can follow the progress of characters from one area to another; at others, actors, abandoned at the end of the scene, are left conscientiously miming in character as they are whisked away from us. They do their best to look happy about it.

Even when the scenery is standing still, its constant motion seems to have infected the production, which is chronically disinclined to linger over anything. As a result, crucial moments go for nothing. When Mary first meets her new guardian, the humpbacked and reclusive Mr. Craven, it is an occasion not of shock but of mild embarrassment, as if somebody had jumped a cue and turned up on the wrong bit of set. The redemptive ending, rather movingly set up, is rushed abruptly and gracelessly through, as though everybody on stage had a train to catch.

Still, some of the performances are strong, and the story is infallible. In India, Mary had servants to jump to her every command, and she has become a little horror in consequence. In Yorkshire, she is bucked out of that by Martha, the maid, who cheerfully refuses to dress her every morning. Bidden to play in the grounds, she makes friends with a robin (here a cheerful red- breasted puppet) and then with a crusty but good-hearted gardener. She discovers a deserted garden, whose door has been locked ever since Mr. Craven's much-loved and green-fingered wife fell from a tree to her death there. With the help of Martha's brother Dickon, who has a way with both animals and vegetables, Mary restores the place to its former glory. (The progressive greening is very well staged.) They used to call her Mary, Mary, quite contrary; now just see how her garden grows.

She next turns her attention to the stunted life indoors. Right from her arrival, she has heard strange cries, which Mrs. Medlock, the disagreeable housekeeper, dismisses as the sound of the wind "wuthering." (Both house and fable seem to have been designed by the Brontes, working in committee.) Eventually, she finds that these are cries of pain, coming from Mr. Craven's young son Colin, who never leaves his room and whom everybody, including himself, believes to be mortally sick. He is fretful and petulant, but Mary, who has first-hand knowledge of such things, bullies and cajoles him into life. Soon, she and the ever-obliging Dickon have him out in his mother's garden; and when his father, who has been hiding out in Italy, comes home it is to find the place simply bursting with symbols of regeneration. He allows his son back into his previously fenced-off heart and all ends happily. It could be unbearably mawkish, were the children not so unsentimentally believable.

Paul Ledoux's adaptation, which YPT first staged in 1991, is much better than the dark and confusing musical version that played on Broadway a decade ago, but it has, unavoidably, had to leave some things out. These include a melodramatic but helpful subplot concerning the family physician, Mr. Craven's cousin, who has his own financial reasons for wishing Colin's death; here he just seems to be an unaccountably bad doctor. (It doesn't help that both the Craven gentlemen are played, presumably through financial necessity, by the same actor. It cramps both their styles.)

The children are played by young adults, and played well, with a helpful leavening of humour. Ramona Gilmour-Darling makes no bones about Mary's initial awfulness -- in fact, she revels in it -- and shows too how it connects with her later role as a ministering angel. She always wants her own way, but her way becomes a better one. Derek Aasland is sure-footed as Colin, incorrigibly the young master, and Richard Harte makes Dickon likeable, which, given his alarming reserves of natural wisdom and practical charity, is an accomplishment. Kate Hemblen is a direct and charming Martha, though both her role and the story's social structure have been impoverished by the cuts. The grown-ups playing grown-ups are generally less impressive, with Tamsin Kelsey uncertain from one moment to the next whether Mrs. Medlock is an inhuman monster or just a human one; faced with the rejoicing at the end, she gamely changes character and smiles anyway.

ELISA'S SKIN

Tarragon Theatre Extra Space, Toronto

Carole Frechette wrote Elisa's Skin as the product of an exchange scheme between writers from Montreal and Brussels; the condition was that each author from one city write something inspired by the other. Inspiration comes in unpredictable ways, but for an outsider it is difficult to discern anything in Frechette's play that needs to have sprouted in Brussels, apart from a profusion of references to local landmarks. There is nothing in it that could not happen equally well if not anywhere in Canada, then certainly in Quebec. It does imply a European-style cafe culture.

Not that much in the play does anything so vulgar as happen. It is largely a monologue for Elisa herself, who sits nursing a drink at a patio table and talks about her love affairs. Two discernibly different men figure in her reminiscences, and while we are still trying to work out whether these relationships would have been sequential or juggled and whether they might still be going on, the author hits us with something else. Elisa starts talking as if she were the male half of a similarly remembered romance, although her voice and attitude remain the same. It is all very mysterious and the mystery, at least for me, diverts attention from what she is actually saying.

All is revealed when Elisa, speaking -- we may be tolerably sure - - in her own person, tells of a purely social encounter with a Young Man, who promptly manifests himself onstage. It is he, it turns out, who has put her up to this: to sitting around in public places and pouring out her emotional history. When she protests that she has only a limited amount of history to pour, he tells her to adopt other people's; it will be a kindness to them and therapeutic for her. So this is what she does: becomes a conduit for the extraordinary memories of ordinary people. Once we know this, her speeches become a lot less puzzling and rather more gripping.

The reason Elisa needs therapy is that she has skin problems. She constantly invites us to inspect her knees, her neck, her elbows, and see for ourselves whether there is just not too much skin there, falling in folds. (There isn't, by the way.) The cause, she learns, is that there are all these stories inside her, pushing to get out. This, plainly, is not a medical drama about middle-aged sag. It's a metaphor for something. I think it's about the writer -- I mean the writer in general, not just the author of this play -- about the need, the obligation, to give inarticulate people a voice; if you have the talent, don't use it -- you will explode. Taken literally, it just seems sentimental. Either way, the conceit tells us little about Elisa herself, and hers is the presence we are stuck with.

The writing of the play seems to be excellent; certainly John Murrell's translation is a string of pearls. There is a feeling here for the erotica of the everyday, coupled with a sensible regret that it doesn't actually happen every day. The incidents are believable, and so are the feelings that go before and after them. But it is still only one idea, repeated. The emotions Elisa reports are essentially disembodied, however physical the details; and Elisa, endlessly parading an unspecified sensibility, comes to seem like a Marguerite Duras heroine, only with laughs. Not enough of them, though: Like most solo plays that aren't very funny, this one, scarcely more than an hour long, becomes first monotonous and then boring.

This is not, as far as I can tell, the fault of Jackie Maxwell's production, which seizes on every piece of wit that comes its way. It has a prettily exaggerated little-town-square design by Ken Garnhum and mockingly moody lighting by Andrea Lundy. Tanja Jacobs matches them in style with a bold performance of a shy person. In a red dress with short, bunned hair and emphatic earrings, she seems constantly amazed and accepting.

She admits to being wide-hipped; she is also wide-mouthed and wide-eyed, and the eyes have a habit of migrating to the corners of their sockets and staying there, peering out in expectant disbelief. This happens especially when Patrick Galligan appears, as Elisa's occasional interlocutor; he shares with her a talent for pouncing, on both words and pauses, and though he obviously has far less opportunity of displaying it than she does, they are equally effective with it. Their few moments of duet and interaction are blessed ones.

TILLSONBURG

Berkeley Street Theatre

- - -

One of the attractive things about the new crop of Irish plays is that things happen in them: violent, exciting things. Sometimes, as in The Beauty Queen of Leenane, these incidents link up, pass through the characters and become a story; and the result is enthralling.

In Tillsonburg, a first play by Malachy McKenna, the events are scattered, rather than organic; there is liveliness but no real life. And it doesn't tell a story. It has three story-lines (not exactly the same thing) that have no reason other than geographical proximity to be occupying the same stage. Like a good sitcom, it is never quite boring, but never quite interesting either.

It has turned up in Toronto ahead of other highly-touted Irish (or English, or American) work for reasons of local pride; it is probably the first Irish play to be set in Canada. The author spent several summers as a tobacco-harvester in Southern Ontario, and those back-breaking, but companionable seasons on the farm were the inspiration for this play: that and a song called Tillsonburg by Stompin Tom Connors, which gives the author both a theme-tune and a theme.

McKenna seems to have split himself between two young Irishmen: Mac, who is a student, and Digger, who isnt. These two, pals since boyhood, come to work for Jon, who is in both personal and economic straits. Their only co-picker is Billy, who smokes a lot of stuff that isn't tobacco and is going crazy with it.

Mac and Digger get the lions' share of the stage-time. Both drink a lot, talk about girls a lot, phone their mothers and tell excellent jokes. They behave, in fact, like engaging young Irish buckos are expected to behave, at least on stage. (What with the rural setting and the ethnic humour, it occurred to me that the play might have been called The Paddy Fields.) They are also differentiated, to the extent that Mac is chunky and shy, while Digger is lanky and gregarious, though the physical differences may just be a matter of casting, and the pyschological ones have to be taken largely on trust.

In Act One we are told that this is their second joint visit to North America, the first having been a messy trip to New York. In Act Two we learn, far too late, about the traumatic events that befell them there; once again an author tries to give his characters a present by delving into their past. If he hasnt brought them alive first, this is self-defeating. The relationship is resolved in a burst of Boys Own Paper heroics.

Paul Essiembre gives a sturdy performance as Mac, and the author himself plays Digger; he has dealt himself some good lines and he deals them out again with full appreciation. There is, though, a disconcerting remoteness about his performance; he seems to go dead behind the eyes when he isn't talking.

Their employer is a man gamely defeated, and excellently played as such by David Ferry. (He says "eh?" with an authority that brings the Oldest Canadian Joke quivering back into life.) He has the beginning and the end of the play to himself, which suggests that it is all meant to be about him, but nothing that comes between really justifies it.

Jon is taking a battering from the weather, from the economy, and from his wife; she doesn't appear, having left him for a menacing figure known as Pete the Indian, whom we do meet and who seems to have stepped out of the pages of Mark Twain. Lawrence Bayne as Pete is called on to do little more than loom, which he does, effectively.

Pete also has a hold on Billy, whom he supplies with drugs and who fears and admires him in about equal proportions. Paul Fauteux is excellent value as Billy, whom he plays as a tousled, strung-out innocent, saying the first thing that comes into his head and wandering naked over to his co-workers bunks to discourse on the difference between the alluring graphics on a package of frozen burgers and the nasty grey stuff inside, and on the value of this as a metaphor for life.

That is about as deep as the play gets, though it does seem to have a submerged theme about fear of homosexuality, and a spasmodic one about territorial appropriation. Pete the Indian gets downright murderous about this, though it seems strange that he should choose a couple of Irish transients as his targets. But then there is nobody else available at the time. There is an attempt to tie all the narrative-threads together with melodrama, which is atavistically appealing; there may be only one Indian onstage, but the whites still get their wagons in a circle. At the end, there are the usual semi-regretful farewells.

The material is good enough for us to enjoy watching the actors acting, and Miles Potters production gives both text and performance plenty of rope. It also includes a terrific storm. Citizens of the real Tillsonburg are coming in to see the play on a gala weekend and this seems appropriate as well as admirable; the play gives the impression that the author selected a setting and then set about collecting incidents to fill it.

2001-10-20-pinter-commands-the-spoken-wo:
For 45 years, give or take, Harold Pinter has written the most commanding language in the English-speaking theatre. This is true whether or not you understand his plays, or even whether or not you like them.

There is no dialogue that matches his for snap, rhythm or resonance. He acts, too; and in recent years his acting has displayed the same ironclad wit and authority as his writing. Both talents were on display, full blast, on Wednesday at the Liberty Grand, where Pinter was the night's feted subject in Harbourfronts World Leaders series.

He read his most recent play, Celebration, which was staged last year in London. It is one of his lighter works, and conceivably his funniest. Two groups of people are celebrating at separate tables in a swish restaurant. Seated at one are an aggressively self-made businessman, his brother, and their wives, who are sisters. At the other is a smoother top dog and his wife. Between them flit the owner, his wife and a waiter.

I wouldnt claim that Pinter, flying solo, managed to keep all these nine characters absolutely distinct all the time, but the moments of doubt were remarkably few. Certainly he knew what he was doing, and his own enjoyment of it fairly bounced off his lectern.

Pinter was an actor before he was a playwright, and it would be interesting to know what his young performances were like. I suspect that success as a writer is what released his power and relaxation as an actor, and in recent years, with his dramatic output having slackened, a lot of the energy seems to have been re-channelled into performing.

In earlier years, he appeared occasionally in productions of his early plays, usually playing the aggressive wide-boy characters: Mick in The Caretaker, Lenny in The Homecoming. It would be great now to see him play Max, the overpowering father in the latter play. The vein of casual brutality that everybody has noticed in his plays is something that he brings out with relish in his acting; a few years ago, in a revival of his early play The Hothouse, he played the corrupt and hard-drinking director of a mental-hospital, and his barrel-housing power was, appropriately, intoxicating. Nothing, by the way, could have had less to do with the traditional, attenuated Pinter style."

But there is delicacy there. Both aspects were on show in his film performance in Mansfield Park, and both were rivetingly there in Celebration. The supposed top dogs here, as in other Pinter plays, spend a lot of time verbally humiliating their women, who respond in kind, but more subtly and hence more effectively. Pinter managed the coarse male aggression smashingly, but he was equally successful, roguishly feline, with the women, especially the one who taunts her partner with the exploits of her secretarial youth. ("I've been behind a few filing cabinets in my time.) Equally fine were his discreet, solicitous restaurateur, and a waiter liable to interrupt any conversation (May I interject?") with a jaw-dropping account of the famous people supposedly intimate with his grandfather: a roster that takes in most of the great literary names of the early 20th century, peaking with perfect comic pitch at "Thomas Hardy -- in his dotage."

Pinter's plays have always been about power (its one of the reasons actors like them so much) and most of his recent works have concentrated this theme into brief, naked parables of state oppression. There are political undercurrents in Celebration, but the focus is back on the sex-war. (The Caretaker, perhaps his gentlest play and still possibly his best, is one in which women are unseen and barely mentioned.) The new play revisits old Pinter territory with new joviality and expansiveness; and to watch the authors fabled reticence give way to the actor's needled flamboyance was an electric experience.

It eclipsed the tribute part of the evening: a staged dinner- party conversation about the Pinter oeuvre written by David Macfarlane and performed by some top Toronto actors. It had its clevernesses in its allusions to Celebration itself and to the dinner which most of the audience had just eaten as part of the deal, and it featured a delightful irruption-from-the-audience by Pinter's old actor friend Henry Woolf, now a theatre professor in Saskatoon. (At the risk of sounding Toronto-centric, couldn't anybody invite him to do a play here?). Mainly, though, it seemed forced.

FULLY COMMITTED

Winter Garden Theatre

I recently declared a bias against solo shows that are not funny. Fully Committed helps stoke my prejudice in the nicest way. It is a one-man play, it is very funny, and -- after a few doubtful moments - - it is totally beguiling.

The doubts come while the premise is being set up. Mark McKinney, ex-Kids in the Hall, comes on stage and the first thing he does is answer the phone. Having done so in his own voice, he shifts accent and position and starts playing the part of the caller, too. It seems impossibly arch, and you just wait for it to be over. Then there is another call, and he puts on another voice, and you realize that the whole play is going to be like that, and it becomes a convention rather than a gag, and not arch at all. You still wonder whether the author and the script can keep it up, but it soon becomes obvious that they can, and you go with it. In fact, you don't want them to stop.

McKinney plays Sam, a restaurant switchboard operator; he never says a word throughout the play that is not spoken on some phone line or other, external or internal. The text is very pure that way. It was written by Becky Mode, a New Yorker who has apparently logged time in the cafe trade, and it rings true. (That seems the appropriate phrase.)

Sam, to nobody's surprise, is an actor by vocation, and at least he isn't surviving between engagements by working among the waiters; though whether he ranks above or below them in the pecking order is an open question. He sits in a basement office, takes or refuses reservations and generally fends off the outside world.

He has a co-worker who today has failed to show up, so Sam has to take every call himself. Since this is a very fashionable, popular and expensive restaurant, he is generally juggling three or four calls at once; some callers are philosophical about being put on hold and others are not. Interestingly, the patient ones, as rendered here, are every bit as entertaining as the impatient.

Besides these, Sam has to deal with his employer, a sadistic prima donna of a chef who, also interestingly, seems to spend more time in his office or jetting off to celebrity junkets than he does in the kitchen; and with a temperamental Gallic maitre d'; and with various other more or less unhelpful colleagues.

In the few intervals he is allowed, Sam talks to his agent, or at least to his agent's secretary, about a part he may be up for; and to his widowed father in Indiana about the slim chances of the restaurant letting him come home for Christmas; and to a supercilious actor friend about the friend's success, which Sam clearly finds disgusting. Up above it is lunchtime; Sam, a virtual prisoner, gets very hungry -- a starving man amidst plenty.

The play has a classical sort of structure. Everything goes wrong for Sam initially; halfway through he descends into the mire (literally); and after that ritual cleansing, things start to look up. There is a hint that Sam has learned to play the world's game, but it looks more as if the world, through no intention of its own, has begun to play his.

I suppose there is some cheating here. We learn very little about Sam's personal qualities but we are on his side because he is the only person we see. The rest of the world consists of hostile voices trying to make his life miserable, which is how most of us see the rest of the world. And on this occasion we not only see it through his eyes, we hear it through his lips. No wonder we identify and take his small triumphs for our own. He even gets to tell the chef what he really thinks of his orange roughy. Stuff your Greek tragedies -- this is catharsis.

McKinney can make Sam little more than nice and, when occasion finally offers, quick-witted. That doesn't matter. We like him most because we admire his technical skill: the multiplicity of tones and shadings he comes up with and the precision with which he juggles them. They arrive, after all, in haphazard order, with no logical connections to smooth the transitions. (The first question actors always get asked is how they remember their lines. This time, even a spectator as jaded as I would like to know.)

McKinney is less adept at distinguishing the boys from the girls than Harold Pinter was last week when he read us his restaurant piece, Celebration. But maybe that's intentional; maybe that's New York. I'm still uncertain of the gender of Bryce, Naomi Campbell's assistant, who calls periodically to bark instructions about a table for 15 with a vegan menu and halogen lamps, while a gently complaining female senior citizen sounds like Alan Bennett. Never mind -- I enjoyed them both. Stephanie, the establishment's frazzled receptionist, does sound a very convincing transplanted English rose, with that London weariness that has taken over the whole culture, and I loved Mrs. Sebag, who is driven to hysteria by the news that her reservation has gone missing and has to stop yelling at the maid in order to scream upstairs to her husband for succour.

"Fully committed" is apparently upscale bistrospeak for "all booked up" -- which is what happened to the play when it was first done off-Broadway. After a long diet of worthy plays in small rooms and soulless shows in big ones, it is a treat to encounter a commercial success that actually deserves to be one.

Black & White Photo: Chris Bolin, National Post / Mark McKinney juggles a multiplicity of tones and shadings as he plays both ends of countless telephone conversations. ;

PICASSO AT THE LAPIN AGILE

Bluma Appel Theatre

- - -

Steve Martin's first, and to date only, play is one of those that brings together famous historical figures who never met, but should have. It ushers in Pablo Picasso and Albert Einstein, both of whom were in Paris in 1905 and who are here corralled in a cafe that the painter is known to have frequented. The physicist just happens to drop by.

What they have in common, of course, is that they are revolutionaries just about to happen, in a new century poised to do likewise. They are also great womanizers: something we have always known about Pablo and are just beginning to assimilate about Albert. So they discuss art, science, sex and genius, with additional contributions from the bar staff and clientele. Along the way they make a lot of jokes, or at least their author does. The result is less than a great play but, as presented by CanStage, is certainly a great evening.

The classic of this genre is Tom Stoppard's Travesties, which capitalized on the simultaneous presence in First World War Switzerland (or in Switzerland when everywhere else was having the First World War) of James Joyce, Tristan Tzara and Lenin. The difference is that Stoppard let the celebrities determine the shape and texture of his play, while Martin merely exhibits them. Martin sticks at simple addition, while Stoppard went in for dizzying multiplication. Also, Stoppard's jokes are strategic parts of the argument, while Martin's are there to make the party go.

Some of them, as you would expect from this author, are very funny. Almost at the top we get Einstein furiously ruffling his hair in order to look more like himself. (This is the professor's second appearance in a free-wheeling take-your-partners drama. Terry Johnson, in his play Insignificance, teamed him up with Marilyn Monroe.)

Later the Lapin proprietress -- who has had a fling with Picasso, like most of female Paris, apparently -- rounds on both men to tell them they only adopted their respective vocations in order to pick up girls. Einstein, who is just a year away from publishing on relativity and has no social life to speak of, calls this absurd, but it has a deeper truth. They both crave recognition, and the carnal kind is the best.The play is very good on sexual relationships, both in discussing them and -- with a swift, cartoon- like touch --displaying them.

When it comes to comparing their respective achievements, actual and potential, the two begin by scoffing at one another and end in deep mutual respect. Each is deeply moved by the other's visionary sense of design. This is very nice as far as it goes, but it leaves you wondering how the piece can possibly develop.

And then Martin surprises us, twice; his play really does get better as it goes on. Our heroes wonder who can possibly complete the new century's transforming trinity. Enter a giggling inventor, in a yellow checked suit, claiming to be the boy. Plainly he is a fraud (though he will probably do well). Then, thunder and lightning, and in blows a visitor from the future. The program just calls him Visitor, and I wouldn't dream of blowing his cover, but I will just hint that he is a pompadoured pop singer from Memphis (Tennessee, not Egypt).

I am not sure he really rates in this company (I mean, he's not Louis Armstrong), but compared to some of the other architects of the 20th century, he is a benign choice. The three of them look at the stars and see their names up in lights, the newcomer's much the biggest of the three. That, as he more or less says, is show business. And then a kitschy picture on the cafe wall disappears, to be replaced by Picasso's Demoiselles d'Avignon, striking awe into everyone. It's a deeply stirring moment. The play's tribute to genius comes alive, and feels felt.

The play looks good throughout: not just good but satisfying. It is directed by Randall Arney, who was responsible for its major American productions, on a gorgeously mellow, subtly raked set (designed by Scott Bradley, sublimely lit by Kevin Lamotte) that provides a superb cast with both a frame and a resting place.

The choreography, physical and verbal, is perfect. Jordan Pettle's Picasso falls a little short -- he is any fiery, attractive young man rather than this particular one -- but he rises to the play's climactic moments. Alon Nashman is a brilliant Einstein, impish and deep; and the supporting cast can hardly be faulted. Eric Peterson, speaking for the ageing and weak-bladdered ordinary man, pungently parades between barroom and bathroom; Geoffrey Bowes is sharp and solid as the patron of the Agile Rabbit (a Symbolist); William Webster is smart and stylish as a buyer and seller of masterpieces; and the two Great Pretenders are Ron Kennell, hysterically hysterical, and Blaine Bray, an unchallengeably authentic Elvis. (Sorry, it slipped out).

But the best are the two women: Cara Pifko, wounded but proud as one of art's recent conquests, and Michelle Fisk as the patroness, a Post-Romantic with all the sad, assured sensual wisdom that that implies. The play is a sketch, but it's a sketch with wings.

DIANA KRALL

Hummingbird Centre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Diana Kralls first two numbers on Friday night were a summary of her career to date. She began with a breakneck novelty, accompanied by her own prickly piano plus guitar, bass and drums. Then the 40 musicians seated behind her picked up their fiddles and horns and escorted her through a lush, slow ballad that she voiced in something between a murmur and a moan. So far has Canadas local girl come: from the West Coast pianist-turned-singer plying her solitary trade in, presumably, Nanaimo bars, to the high-priced siren whose promoters will spring for a symphony orchestra in every town.

Along the way she has evolved, or someone has created for her, an Attitude. She now comes on like the Gap-ad idea of a jazz singer: long black dress sliding off the shoulder, pouty lips, open-toed shoes with precipitous stiletto heels that made her initial traverse of the huge Hummingbird stage, from wings to piano, look decidedly perilous. Her image, however carefully fostered, doesn't sit quite comfortably on her, which is rather endearing. When she talks between numbers, which she does sparingly, it is usually to tell us on whose album she first heard the song she has just sung. Dispensing this information, she hovers between aloof and confiding. One half of her says, I'm just a beginner, learning from the greats"; the other half says, "Im a star.

Obviously what we are seeing and hearing is the result of a huge, and hugely successful, commercial operation. Critics are supposed to deplore this kind of thing, but actually the makeover has worked to Kralls advantage, and I don't just mean financially. True, she plays less interesting piano than she used to -- or maybe just less piano since her big new arrangements require her just to noodle against the strings. But it has given more character to her singing. I always used to find her a generalized vocalist; all the songs came out alike. Her up-tempo interludes with her trio still don't have much character; she had nothing new to say about I Love Being Here with You (the opener) or the now hopelessly shopworn Fly Me to the Moon.

The fans yelled for her to sing Peel Me a Grape, Dave Frishbergs cartoon of a femme fatale, with which she once had something of a hit. She refused, which was tasteful of her because her version of that song is horrific. She hasnt the humour for it; there is a difference between mock-deadpan and dead-deadpan. She did sing the more straightforwardly sexy Do It Again, but by eradicating any trace of demureness from the song and rendering it as a straight come-on, she lost all its tension.

That was among the stringy ones, and the orchestra helped kill it. But when they accompanied her on ballads, either lost or yearning, then something did emerge. It first peeped through on Maybe You'll Be There, which is not on the Sinatra album to which she assigned it but is a rare enough song to catch the ear.

It came more clearly into focus on Cry Me a River, the old Julie London anthem. It's a vengeful song and it suits Kralls sullen- goddess persona very well. She takes it harder and faster than London did and actually makes it more powerful and persuasive. There is also something dreamlike about her performance -- as if she were indulging a fantasy of retribution -- and this tranced quality turned out to work for happier songs as well -- sometimes in quite unlikely circumstances, as in her bossa nova treatment of the Gershwins 'S Wonderful, in which she seemed to be testing out the adjectives, or in I've Got You Under My Skin, which, after all, is about a kind of possession. She claims to have learned this one, too, from Sinatra, though her version has nothing to do with his; it might have come from an album called Songs for Swinging Catatonics.

Most of the arrangements are by Claus Ogerman, and heard in bulk, as on her new CD, The Look of Love (Verve), they are soporific. In smaller doses, with the singer actually there, they are quite compelling. Her vocal timbre is still off-putting; she either has or uses very little breath, so the words come out in short groups whose duration bears very little relation to their meaning and helps reduce the lyrics to mush -- a state to which they have already been brought by her apparent aversion to consonants.

Occasionally she does bite into a word -- as on Im not alone in the night" in Love Letters -- and the effect is contrastingly arresting. (It also helps that she does this song complete with verse.) Her showpiece encore of Joni Mitchells lugubrious A Case of You was almost completely unintelligible; all that came through was the title line, admittedly the best in the song.

The best -- or at least the best-showcased -- of her sidemen was the intent guitarist Dan Faehnle. Alan Broadbent, a superb pianist in his own right, conducted the band, whose physical presence, unlike Krall's, seemed oddly superfluous. The charts they were playing were the ghostly kind that seem to have been written to be piped in.

2001-11-03-a-dream-worth-remembering:
Until Nov. 18. (416) 504-PLAY

A MIDSUMMER NIGHT'S DREAM

Theatre Passe Muraille

- - -

The new all-female production of A Midsummer Night's Dream begins appallingly. A canoe appears at the back of the stage and the seven ladies of the cast disembark, looking like Indians from a touring company of Peter Pan who have been spending far too much time with the Lost Boys. They perform war whoops and tribal dances of rather less than high-school accomplishment; the fact that two or three of Toronto's proven best actresses are up there cavorting makes it all the more embarrassing.

It seems they are meant to be Amazons, back from a raiding party; they even get to playing football with a few, presumably male, severed heads. Tiring of this, they decide to put on a play: the one that we have come to see. And from the moment they utter its first words, everything changes and the evening becomes a treat.

The spine of Shakespeare's Dream is the marriage, announced in the first scene and celebrated in the last, of Theseus, Duke of Athens, and the captured Amazonian queen Hippolyta. Many productions try to ginger this up by making Hippolyta very dubious about this arrangement, and it usually looks like uphill work, unsupported by the text. Here, however, we have in a built-in subtext: the play presented from the Amazons' point of view. Whenever Theseus' name is mentioned, all the actors spit; in the world outside the play, he is their enemy. Waneta Storms as Hippolyta stands silent upon a rock, emanating stoic disapproval, while Diane Flacks as Theseus blusters around below. Their relationship retains its wit and edge right up to the close; and nothing seems to have been imposed.

Indeed, the wonder is just how smoothly the script accommodates an Amazonian (rather than feminist) interpretation. It is summed up in a tableau from the first scene: Kristen Thomson as the disputed Hermia stands, agitated, outside a knot of four men -- duke, father and two rival lovers -- who are presuming to decide her future. The general pattern is that men behave appallingly -- note the sadistic relish of Ruth Madoc-Jones' Egeus consigning his daughter to death or a convent, and the overweaning swagger of Karen Robinson's Demetrius -- while women who permit themselves to love them are very silly. Behold the relationship of Hermia and Helena (Catherine Fitch), rapt in reminiscence of their schoolgirl friendship before reverting to a competition in coyness, no holds barred and all claws bared.

Thomson's Hermia is the dominating performance from the moment she first flounces on, pouting and very much aware of her potential as a tragic heroine. She doubles as Bottom the weaver, in which she sometimes sounds like the two heroines of Absolutely Fabulous rolled into one. She seizes on the great amateur actor's ability to make every moment a performance, whether Bottom is improvising an apologia for the presence of a lion in Pyramus and Thisbe or bossing around his newly acquired retinue of fairies. Her handling of his awakening (one of the supreme moments in Shakespeare) suggests that, on their forays into the outside world, the Amazons acquired some crucial insights into the human condition.

In both her roles, Thomson overdoes some things, and she has a worrying tendency to repeat her effects: she is 10% infuriating and 90% irresistible. This has been, unquestionably, her year: by my reckoning she has played nine roles in four shows, one of which (I, Claudia) she wrote herself.

Kate Lynch's production is not only consistently funny, it is also consistently beautiful -- visually (Steve Lucas has designed a heavenly blue-drenched set, which he has lit magnificently) and verbally, a matter not so much of golden voices as of rigorously applied intelligence. Lynch must direct more Shakespeare; I found myself listening more intently than I have done at this play in decades, certainly more than at any Dream I have encountered at Stratford or in High Park. Storms and Flacks reverse their earthly royal genders to play Oberon and Titania; Storms' fairy king is wheedling, petulant but capable of grandeur, Flacks' Titania libidinous, capricious, but also tenderly protective. And when they confront the elements, they are majestic.

A few questions nagged at me toward the end. How would they manage all the instant doubling required of them in the final scene? They do it very smoothly and effectively. Whose is the offstage voice that keeps correcting the pronunciation of "Ninny's tomb"? (It sounds male. Maybe it's Shakespeare.) How would the Amazons deal with the insuperable fact that the play is a celebration of heterosexual marriage? The answer is that, despite a few continued naggings from Madoc-Jones' over-insistent Puck, they accept it, joyously. It seems that you can have your wedding cake and eat it, too.

That, of course, is inside the play. Outside it, they still have somehow to return to, and make sense of, their initial framework. They do it amazingly, though it would be unfair to reveal how. Let us just say that life holds out the unsettling possibility of imitating art. It crowns a superb production.

MR. RAISIN HEAD AND KID

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, Toronto

According to her biography, "Erika Batdorf has created, performed, directed and choreographed original movement theatre since 1983." I am not sure what movement theatre is, but on the strength of this double bill (which I saw at a preview), I can at least offer the reassuring news that it isn't mime.

It starts out as if it might be. The first play, Mr. Raisin Head, finds our creator-performer (she has a consultant director, Paul Lampert) in male attire, preening in front of a mirror while flicking her tongue contemplatively between her lips, suggesting the character she portrays is simultaneously vain and insecure. All this is tidily done, and it soon turns out that Batdorf talks as well. In fact, once she starts, she hardly stops.

And, in the course of delivering her script -- in two voices -- she unquestionably moves around, and in a disciplined way, but no more than you would expect of most actors in most plays.

The two voices belong to the guy at the mirror and the upscale lady he eventually marries. He sounds like he comes from the Bronx; she sounds strangulated-English. He has been trying to attract the attention of various people he calls Virtues (Truth, Purity and others), but they just look right through him, as if he were Mr. Cellophane in Chicago.

Feeling his inferiority and trying to better himself, he goes searching for culture, and at a museum he meets his future bride, who seems to regard him with amused contempt. During one of his sessions at the mirror, he decides he resembles a raisin and christens himself Mr. Raisin Head. Clinging unshakably to his metaphor (verbal wit is not the authors strong point), he decides his fiancee is a Grape, and of a superior vintage at that.

Still, they get together. The fact she insists on referring to art exhibits as "installations" only seems to make her more attractive in his eyes, and she presumably likes having someone she can impress.

Batdorf tells us in the program that I dislike numbness -- it is a mould I have to continually fight. Whether she is fighting it in herself or in others, she doesnt make clear. (She's being hearteningly modest if it's the first; presumptuous if its the second.) The piece has been promoted as "a monologue about self- worth," but its difficult for an audience to value a play's characters if the play itself hasn't done so first. The Grape lady in particular is a patronizing figure, patronized.

The second play, Kid, is much better -- more piercingly performed, more compassionately written and telling a more compelling story. Batdorf comes before us this time in what looks at first blush like a straitjacket with the ties undone. She announces herself as one of a pair of sisters, about to tell us a story about one of another pair of sisters. The latter couple are called Pinky and Stinky, and she is Stinky; Pinky never arrives.

Stinky is four and she lives in a garden under the dominion of a Mr. Mean Man, who persecutes her and her three friends: a Mr. Frog Man, a Mr. Mole Man and a Bird Lady. What we seem to have here is a tale of sexual abuse recounted -- to make the trauma bearable -- at two removes. It works as a fairy tale, with the horrors as relentless and as saddening as only a childrens narrative can be, and it reverberates as the author wishes.

When one of Stinkys companions looks at her and declares that she is "a grown-up person," something clicks; this is an adult who has been dragging around a child's memories, and a child's humiliation, all her life. (The absent non-smelly sister is presumably her everyday grown-up self.)

Batdorf has this time to animate five characters -- verbally, visually or both, plus drawing some of them on a blackboard -- and she does it admirably. Sometimes she seems to surrender too enthusiastically to the whimsy of her chosen medium, but that may be necessary for the sake of stylistic consistency, and anyway she always extricates herself.

2001-11-12-i-am-not-canadian-but-i-won-t:
Apparently I am part of a conspiracy. In his column in Wednesdays Globe and Mail, John McLachlan Gray accused me, along with Christie Blatchford and an anonymous front-page headline writer, of being suborned by the National Post to take part in what he termed a Tokyo Rose attack on all things Canadian. My own contribution to this remarkably offensive offensive was that I had written a less-than-enthusiastic review of Diana Krall's recent concert at the Hummingbird Centre in Toronto.

Let me get the ugliest part of this out of the way first. I have worked as a critic for the Post for three years, and during that time no editor, publisher or proprietor has told me either what to say or how to say it. I don't imagine that things are any different at the Globe, and I wonder why Mr. Gray finds it so hard to credit that writers on other papers might enjoy the same independence he does.

Now, it is true that early in my review I described Krall as "Canadas local girl"; in a Canadian paper, it seemed reasonable to acknowledge her Canadianness. It is rather a jump, though, to assume from that that any criticisms I made of her are caused by her being Canadian. Or rather -- this seems to be Mr. Grays main point -- that they are the result of her being Canadian and successful.

We've heard this tune before. We are always being told that Canadians have a national inferiority complex that makes them resent any of their compatriots who get ahead of the pack. (We hear it, amusingly enough, from both the left and the right, though usually in different contexts.) I don't see it. It seems to me that when a Canadian team wins an international game, or when a Canadian performer makes it in Hollywood, the enthusiasm across the country is deafening. It is true that success can inspire a backlash; but that has to do with imperfect human nature. There is nothing specifically Canadian about it. It has been known to happen in America. It certainly happens in Britain, which (I confess) is where Im from. Its weird, but the only evidence that Canadians have such a complex is their apparent compulsion to believe that they do.

This myth can obviously be very comforting to Canadians who are criticized; they can blame bad reviews on their compatriots' mean- spirited masochism. For my own part, I can see no way of dispelling it other than by subscribing to a sort of critical George Bush doctrine -- if I'm not with them, Im against them -- and giving all Canadian artists good reviews all the time. Perhaps this is what Mr. Gray wants; though I find it strange that, in his capacity as a playwright, he would rather be praised for his nationality than for his talent.

Actually, I find it hard to see what he wants through the contortions to which he subjects my review. A neutral reference to the orchestras fiddles and horns is construed as a sneer. I am told that I would have preferred synthesizers to a live band (I wouldn't, and never said so) and that I "saved [my] most withering contempt for Krall's fans," whom I never actually mentioned but whom I plainly felt to be dupes of a "commercial machine," a phrase he puts in quotes, although I never used it.

Here he seems to be joining hands with Kralls managers, one of whom disinterestedly wrote to the Post pointing out that his client had received standing ovations. Well, he has a job to do, but Mr. Gray must surely know -- as another correspondent has pointed out -- that standing ovations in big halls have long ceased to be a reliable index of quality either way. If an event is perceived to be large enough, audiences will practically enter applauding. This doesnt make them fools; it doesn't make them infallible, either.

I liked some things Krall did and didn't like others; and I dont think it takes a genius to note that, unlike Keith Jarretts, Krall's appearance is part of her package. But I don't think Mr. Gray was looking for nuance.

If I have any agenda regarding her, its this: Every so often a performer comes along and is hailed for rediscovering the classic American popular song. Those of us who love this music know that in fact it never went away and that dozens of singers, old and young, have been out there performing and preserving it for years, some of them extraordinarily well. Occasionally one of them catches the lightning, and it seems arbitrary which one. (It isnt just looks; you should see some of the sexy covers on the obscurer CDs in my collection.)

Before Krall there was Harry Connick Jr., and since her there has been Jane Monheit -- both American and, to my ears, her inferiors. One singer whom I prefer to any of them is Jeri Brown, who is Canadian. I did make a disparaging reference to a Joni Mitchell song in Krall's repertoire, but I try to spread my xenophobia around: The Krall arrangements that I described as soporific, at least when heard in bulk, are by Claus Ogerman, who is German; and her conductor, whom in other contexts I greatly admire, is Alan Broadbent, a New Zealander. Mr. Gray does give himself an out clause by suggesting it's not so much Kralls Canadianness as her not being from Toronto that I object to, but that doesnt wash: I like Robert Lepage.

He concludes his column by asking what Christie Blatchford and I would find to write about if we couldn't be anti-Canadian. I can't answer for Christie (except to say that I find it difficult to imagine her running out of subject matter), but I have been writing for this paper about theatre, mainly in and around Toronto, for the last three years and -- obviously -- 90% of the authors, actors and directors I have reviewed have been Canadian. I have subjected them to raves, pans and lots of things in between. And as long as I keep on doing the job, that is how I expect it to remain.

FIGHTING WORDS

Factory Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - The first image we see is a photograph: a gloved young man with fists raised and cauliflower ears. The first live person we see is a young woman, skipping rope. For a moment she could be any girl playing. Then we realize through the intensity of her exercise that she is an aspiring boxer, maybe fixated on the boy in the picture. A snatch of dialogue with another woman, slightly older and carrying a laundry basket, confirms this is indeed the case. It's a neat opening.

We are in Wales. In 1980, Johnny Owen, a bantamweight from Merthyr Tydfil, challenged a Mexican, Lupe Pintor, for the world championship. They fought in Los Angeles; Owen was knocked out, went into a coma and died a few days later.

Sunil Kuruvilla, a Canadian playwright whose plays up to now have only been seen in the United States, has taken this event, kept its factual antagonists offstage and told us the story through the eyes of three fictitious characters. Kuruvilla has had to invent people whose significance lies in their relation to somebody else real and unseen and make them live as more than representative figures. This cannot be easy, but he has managed it impressively well. We know these women didn't exist, but we believe they could have. Keeping them in action for the duration of a play is another matter, and here there are problems.

All the men in Merthyr have flown off to L.A. to attend on their hero and witness the fight. The women they have left behind are all as fixated on him as they are; the whole village seems to centre on boxing in general and Johnny in particular.

We meet Peg, obviously in love with Johnny, who used to let her box with him; her married sister Nia, more cerebrally attached to Johnny and with ambitions of becoming a BBC announcer; and Mrs. Davies, with whom the sisters apparently live.

Nia calls her husband George; Mrs. Davies, from an older generation, calls hers Mr. Davies. There are, we gather, problems with both marriages; and as nerves become frayed, the two wives begin dragging them to the surface. This, though, is an inconclusive sideshow from the main event: the struggle between the sisters over Johnny and the different things they each see in him.

The play is performed on a square platform, surrounded by hanging laundry. The laundry lines also get to double as the ropes of a boxing ring, the domestic turning into the epic; we are watching a metaphorical prizefight between Peg and Nia. That at least seems to be the idea, but the dramatic structure never really supports it; we are stuck at the level of two women naturalistically quarrelling, and the words don't fight fiercely enough.

Rosemary Dunsmore's production is sensitive, if sometimes slow, but it lacks emotional size. This becomes especially troublesome after the intermission. (A surprise -- I thought I had this pegged as a no-intermission play.) At the end of Act One, Peg breaks away and catches a plane to L.A. to see the real fight for herself. In Act Two she returns and tells what she has seen. It's a graphic speech. It's also a formal piece of classic storytelling, and it leaves her two hearers stranded between styles.

They are also somewhat marooned by their accents. The Welsh lilt, on the lips of non-natives, is apt to come out sing-song; and Linda Goranson as Mrs. Davies seems in particular to be operating within a limited expressive range.

Irene Poole is beguilingly gentle, but almost too consistently so, as Nia; a quirk of the play is that we are more concerned to learn the result of her radio audition than we are to learn the result of the fight. Jody Stevens is engagingly tough on the outside, fragile within, as Peg, but can neither maintain nor quite suspend her characterization during her long narration.

Both sisters turn out to be surprisingly good mimics; they can each put on the voice of Johnny's Mexican nemesis and communicate the hunger for success that he obviously possesses and that Johnny as obviously - and fatally - lacks. Indeed, we learn more about Lupe Pintor in those few moments than we learn about Johnny Owen in the entire play.

We also get a sharper sense of what Johnny meant to his community at large than we do of what he meant to the women we actually see, however much they talk about him.

With its fate-battered women and offstage violence, the play could be a distant descendant of Greek tragedy. What it doesn't have -- except conceivably for dedicated boxing fans who enter the theatre knowing all about the Owen-Pintor contest -- is an audience who carry the myth in their bones and can invest the proceedings with an overarching sense of doom.

CIAO, BABY

Berkeley Street Theatre Upstairs

- - -

Some notions, however attractive, may be too thin to make a play. Ciao, Baby is based on three volumes of verse by Gianna Patriarca, who came to Canada from Italy at a very young age.

They have now been worked into a four-person show whose subject, as you might guess, is growing up female and Italian-Canadian.

Toni Ellwand, one of the actresses in the current cast, has been trying for a few years to get this material onto the stage. Recently she called in the assistance of Paula Wing, an actress and playwright who also appears in the show and has arranged Patriarca's poems to tell a story.

At the beginning, a young girl arrives in Toronto with her mother and sister to rejoin the father of the family who has moved from the old country ahead of them. We watch this girl grow up on and around College Street, see her swap longings and experiences with two of her contemporaries, until we find the three of them grown up with daughters of their own, giving them the same headaches they once inflicted on their own mothers. Along the way the three of them also play other ladies of the community, sometimes to confusing effect.

The mood is generally cheerful and Patriarca, we are assured, avoids the confessional bleeding-heart mode in her writings. That, obviously, is all to the good. But it turns out here to have its downside. The emotions seem generalized, all the more so when a passage is split between three speakers. When we hear a monologue, we are presumably getting the poet's voice straight. When solos give way to trios the feeling is diluted and the verse, if it still exists, must be very free indeed.

The heroine's friends occasionally tease her about her habit of dropping out of social situations in order to sit down and knock out an ode, but her characterization doesn't go much beyond that. There is no real narrative, only chronicle, and the things that are recorded are commonplace.

There are problems at school, trouble with poppa for staying out late, worries about religion and dancing and sex and men: the stuff of any woman's life but of only passing interest unless you know her as an individual. Here the individual merges into the crowd, even at the moment of asserting herself. There is no binding motif: An early sequence about making wishes while watching trains pass is repeated at the end but cannot justify the prominence it is given.

Sue Miner's direction keeps it moving and alert, and the three actresses -- Ellwand, Wing and Lucy Filippone -- convey a pleasing air of quick-witted, sensual solidarity.

The token male is Charly Chiarelli, throatier than I remember him from his one-man show, Mangiacake, earlier this year (perhaps he has a cold), variously appearing as father, teacher, brother, husband -- all of them figures of mild oppression: Patriarca on the patriarchy. (The pun is hardly my own; the producers identify themselves as Matriarca Productions.)

There is mandolin and accordion music and at the end the women take a trip back to their roots. I love Italy but I still felt distant. This seems to be an entertainment for insiders.

2001-12-01-a-critical-response:
Simon Heath (letters -- Nov. 28), responding to Kate Taylors article on theatre critics, brings up again the old chestnut about the critics' (or reviewers') conflicting responsibilities to their readership and to the art form. We are always being asked about this, and I have never understood where the conflict is supposed to come in. If critics describe and explain their responses to the shows they see as lucidly and entertainingly as possible, they are doing the best they can by both parties.

People sometimes talk as if we were torn between the demands of the artists, who want us to say nice things about them, and of editors, who want us to pan everything because it makes good copy. This is a myth. For critics always to write raves might be good for individual artists, or at least for their egos, but it would not be good for the art form, and intelligent artists know that. Nor is it true that negative reviews are more fun to read, or even to write, than positive ones; in fact, the reverse is often true.

Michael Noon (letter -- Nov. 29) asks, although I cannot believe he means it seriously, why critics dont review a productions closing night and thus spare themselves and their victims the risk of "significantly reduc[ing] the revenues of many well-intended productions." (Aren't all productions well-intended?) There's a fairly obvious answer: If we like a show, and say so early in the run, we stand a chance of increasing the box-office takings.

My impression is that most theatres would rather take the risk and have us there. They do not give us free tickets because they love us personally or even because they revere our opinions. Reviews are a form of publicity; at the very least, they let readers know that a show exists.

Everything Ms. Taylor said in her article seemed to me 100-per-cent accurate. And it is not that common for the two of us to agree -- as I'm sure she would agree.

theatre critic, the National Post,
