REAL LIVE GIRL

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, Toronto

One for the record books: Real Live Girl is a musical whose title song is never sung. At least, I assume the show is named after the hit number from the 1960s musical Little Me: "Pardon me, miss, but I've never done this with a real live girl." It was written, obviously, to be sung by a man. Damien Atkins, author and performer of the current entertainment, is a man but he specializes here in songs written for women. He uses them to punctuate a first-person narrative about his struggle to express and acknowledge what he calls his inner girl.

Atkins, whose play Good Mother was produced at Stratford this year, is a clever writer and a more than clever actor-singer, but his new show suffers from an acute case of double focus.

The spoken and sung parts lead separate lives, though both have their attractions. Damien -- he uses his own name -- talks about the problems of growing up not only gay but as a girlie-boy. He offers a very funny montage of interviews with a succession of guidance counsellors ranging from smotheringly sympathetic to murderously hostile. (The latter counsellor, imported from England and hating it, tells him, somewhere around Grade Seven, "You've got to be prepared for the life of abject misery that lies ahead of you.") He tells us that at the age of 13 he could do a great Ethel Merman impersonation, but he doesn't let us hear it. In his later teens he preferred to hang out with girls, and he offers lightning vocal sketches of a few, though it's never clear whether he is presenting actual girls or just the ones in his head.

Quite early on he sings, with defiant petulance, I'm Gonna Wash That Man Right Out of My Hair. The show's publicity says he sings it as a reaction to a schoolyard bully (or at least as the reaction he wishes he'd had) but without that advance information I doubt I would have made the connection. The lyrics do not really fit the situation, and as the song progresses -- at some length, and incorporating sections that never made it into the South Pacific movie -- it pulls right away from its supposed context.

Another Rodgers and Hammerstein number, I Enjoy Being a Girl, has a kind of generic appropriateness. It has become, according to current political canons, a song that only men can sing, though, of course, they usually do it in drag. Atkins does not do the song in drag; he identifies with how women think and feel rather than with how they dress, and he stays in his own clothes throughout. At one point he goes into a kind of vocal drag, offering a series of quick- fire movie-star impressions, but he generally avoids the often cruel mockery that usually underlies the genre. He does not imitate specific performers, choosing instead to sing the songs for their own values. I would still rather hear them sung by real live girls but he does them very well.

Most of the selections are lesser-known show tunes. They include Craig Carnelia's moving Just a Housewife (from Working) and his more calculated but still effective Home Coming Queen (from Is There Life After High School); Just One Step, an overlong but interesting piece of vengeful desperation, from Jason Robert Brown's Songs for a New World; and I Had Myself a True Love, a superb Harold Arlen-Johnny Mercer number from St. Louis Woman. This last, a blues-opera lament, really needs more burnished tones Atkins' gently-pointed tenor allows, but he performs it skilfully, as he does everything he sings, his body language economically in sync with his voice.

But the songs, however much he protests to the contrary, tell us nothing about him except he has generally good taste. Each is a mask pulled tight over whatever may be the central Damien. (All right; they do tell us he's an actor.) I don't object to this, as I think there is far too much self-indulgent soul baring going on in the theatre; I merely point it out. And of course we cannot know if Atkins is really speaking for himself or if he has just invented a persona and given it his own name. When he talks about his macho father or when he speaks as his mother or his sister, we wonder if he is offering an accurate picture of his family, and what they think about it if he is.

David Oiye directed; John Hughes is the pianist. The show fits agreeably, if a little oddly, into its own self-created niche between drama and cabaret.

2001-12-11-mr-martin-is-a-tough-act-does:
Robert Cushman is a theatre critic for the National Post

THE PAUL MARTIN BUDGET SHOW

As a performer, Paul Martin is a critic's nightmare, because he doesn't have any mannerisms. He has no facial tics, he doesn't wave his arms in public, and though, in the course of his 65-minute budget speech he took the occasional sip of water, he never once mopped his brow. He also reads a script lucidly; unlike, say, the average radio newsreader in this illiterate age, he never emphasizes the wrong word in a sentence. He did read very fast -- too fast and too unemotionally for his words ever to pass as normal conversation - - but then he had a lot to cram in.

Confidence is obviously one of the things they teach you in politicians' school, but it must take colossal nerve to get up as Finance Minister in what everybody knows is a recession, and still act as if the good times are here. Well, maybe there were a few problems but nothing that Canadians couldn't lick. On and on the promises and predictions rolled, with never a hint that some of them might just fail to come true.

Now, considered simply as entertainment, budget speeches are boring. But history this year gave Mr. Martin something to talk about besides money. The first half of his speech was devoted to the "human tragedy" and its aftermath. I'm not sure that there's such a thing as an inhuman tragedy and the briskness of Martin's delivery told against him anyway. It was just another phrase, and not a very inspired one.

Anyway, tragedy as a concept is not a vote-catcher, so Mr. Martin presented recent events not as a disaster but as an opportunity.

It was an opportunity to feel good about our boys fighting on distant shores. It was an opportunity to strengthen our bonds with the United States -- and here. Canada's economy was inherently strong, and $23-billion were going into health care, there were going to be more tax cuts and no deficit. All of which was very good news, and you could hardly blame the minister's supporters for shouting "bravo" when they heard it. I, however, being professionally cursed with the tragic sense, felt the opposition parties were falling down on the job. Obviously they didn't want to spoil Mr Martin's big day but were there no skeptics, left or right, who felt moved to shout out "how?" This show lacked conflict.

In fact I heard no angry murmurs from the floor until Mr. Martin announced his plan for a $12 security charge to be added to every airfare; that really got them going. It came at the end of what may have been the emotional centre of the whole speech: the strategy for airplane security. Here I felt Mr Martin blew his top too early; the wildest cheers from his own side came on his first proposal, the one about having armed undercover cops on Canadian aircraft. If this was his strongest point, he should surely have saved it for the big finish. But big finishes are not perhaps his strong suit. He ended a paragraph on terrorists by saying, with machine-gun insistence, that we had to find out "who-they-are-and-what-they-plan-to-do." It sounded obvious.

Still, you can never be sure what will get the crowd going. A rallying cry about "education and innovation" (it even rhymes) woke only tepid applause. On the other hand, the phrase "facilitate cross- border trade in all parts of the country", brought the house down. As the act moved into its second half -- becoming a laundry-list like ordinary Budget speeches -- the mechanics of applause became more evident.

Then, when the clapping became frenzied, he got louder and more emphatic, and that excited them and they clapped even harder. At the end he even permitted himself the occasional gesture: the raising of a hand, the merest hint of an outstretched arm.

But he never followed through. As befitted a finance minister, restraint ruled.

SNOW WHITE AND THE MAGNIFICENT SEVEN

Elgin Theatre, Toronto

In Robert Altman's film California Split, which took overlapping dialogue to new heights of incomprehensibility, there was a just- audible recurring sequence in which George Segal and Elliott Gould challenged one another to name the seven dwarfs. Somehow, neither of them could ever manage to recall all seven at one time, and it was plain, from the frustrated murmurs all around the movie theatre, that nobody else could, either.

A few years later, there was a newspaper competition to name an eighth dwarf. My own nomination (un-entered) for a fitting companion for Sleepy and Dopey and Grumpy and, um, the others, was Filthy.

None of which is very relevant to Snow White and the Magnificent Seven, but relevance never seems to be of crucial importance to Ross Petty when he assembles his annual holiday entertainments. And besides, re-labelling the small septet, individually and collectively, has obviously been a major concern for him. Since the old title is politically beyond the pale, he has named them, as a group, after a movie of which you may well have fond memories. (Your juniors have probably never heard of it. Mine hadn't.)

Mindful of who holds the imaginative copyright on these characters, he has cloned the Disney figures as Pops and Duddy and Snoozy and Wheezy and Jolly and Blusher and Fingers (a startling departure, but he plays the balalaika) and has given them a theme song just far enough removed from Heigh-Ho, Heigh-Ho to discourage litigation. Actually, they seem to get rather tired of this number, and of whistling while they work, and they declare they would rather sing show tunes.

So, I'm sure, would Petty. His shows, built on the anything-goes model of English pantomime, keep making disconcerting lurches into sophistication. He himself adds to his gallery of villains by playing Snow White's wicked stepmother. It isn't a drag performance, exactly; he merely puts on a frock and does his usual dastardly stuff from inside it. He calls himself Queen Lola, just so he can vamp the hero while singing Whatever Lola Wants.

Snow White, played with unusual brightness and vivacity by Melissa Thomson, gets brighter and more vivacious than ever when she sings I Can Cook Too, from On the Town. She sings it to convince the seven of her housekeeping qualifications, so the song's double entendres go begging (even this new-millennium Snow White isn't that kind of damsel) but it livens the show up, no question.

Prince Charming and Muddles (both refugees from other fairy tales; you won't have heard of Muddles but I'll explain later) keep treating us to choruses of Brush Up Your Shakespeare. This is both a running gag and an in-joke. The Prince, in accordance with the Petty tradition of ritually sacrificing one classical actor every winter, is played by Graham Abbey, the last Stratford Festival's Henry V and the next one's Romeo.

He takes the song's advice to heart (though Snow White loves him anyway) and keeps favouring us with bits of Bard, from "my kingdom for a horse" to "soft, what light through yonder window breaks." (As they say in the trade: He isn't really going to do it like that, is he?) He does the good sport thing very well. He, like Snow White, is encouraged to be a lot funnier than panto juveniles ever were in my day, and he sings (a lot) and dances (a bit) with justified abandon. I think he should get together with the Shaw Festival's Ben Carlson and work up a club act.

Snow White is not one of the basic pantomime titles, and is in fact rather a thin story to take up an evening. Once you've done the mirror and the apple and the cottage, you're through. The Petty script, uncredited as usual, leaves out some of what tradition does supply. (No coffin, no nuffin'.) To make up the time, the show borrows from other pantomimes, mostly Cinderella. Muddles, sweet on the heroine but knowing better than to compete with the hero, is Buttons by another name; Eddie Glen plays him, well.

Other padding includes a mystifyingly irrelevant and extremely long scene in a gypsy encampment. Other characters include a moderately unscrupulous cat (Peter Deiwick) whose position is obscure but who seems to belong to Fred Penner.

Penner plays someone with a French accent called Oscar the Obvious and is also the compere. Thanks to him, the customary village green opening is withheld for about 15 minutes, and you may hope that you have escaped it entirely, but it finally clocks in, the boys still holding out their hands hopefully to the girls and the girls still tripping in dainty circles, before giving in and sitting on the boys' knees. I wonder if new choreography would be unconstitutional.

The magnificent ones hardly live up to their adjective; their timing is slack. Petty's own timing remains a pleasure, though it demands major co-operation from his audience. He was in luck on Saturday night when a disparaging reference on his part to Harry Potter produced ringing cries of "stupid" that had him digging deep into his fabled store of withering ad libs. This is not his best show (that would still be Robin Hood) but it's an improvement on the last few.

A CHRISTMAS CAROL

Premiere Dance Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Practice, in Michael Shamata's production of A Christmas Carol, seems to have made perfect. He has directed his own adaptation of the Dickens story three times before -- twice at Theatre New Brunswick, one at the Grand in London -- and it arrives in Toronto, care of Soulpepper, as calm, inventive, funny and moving.

John Ferguson's set takes the eye from the first moment: a handsome but neutral yard enclosed by three elegant walls, each incorporating three double doors. The resulting space can be inside or out, Scrooge's office or his house or street that takes him from one to the other. It can also be any or all of the locations to which the Ghosts of Christmas Past, Present and Future transport him in his providential dream. Here the production, much assisted by Graeme Thomson's lighting, becomes very fast and very fluid.

More exactly, it is fluid in executing transitions -- the doors closing on one scene as they open on another -- but very solid once the changes have been accomplished. Each episode flashes up and makes an impact. The picture of Scrooge as a boy at Christmas abandoned in a schoolroom is indelibly presented, the child alone in a pool of light.

Each of the various Christmas parties has its own separately joyous identity, even though each is attended by the same group of hard-working actors, playing an average of four roles apiece.

The sequence in which the dream turns to nightmare is a stark montage, as Scrooge sees visions of his own death and of the reactions -- flippant indifference at best, relieved loathing at worst -- that it inspires in the survivors.

A Christmas Carol usually takes well to the stage; it has an instantly appealing flavour and is short enough not to need hacking to pieces. But few versions have been both as faithful and as lively as this one.

Joseph Ziegler's Scrooge is perhaps too soft a touch, seemingly well on his way to joining the human race from the moment Marley's ghost gives him his wake-up call. But he is very affecting as he sees his past mistakes unveiled before him, and quietly harrowing when he pleads with them to stop happening.

After his awakening he is a delight, bubbling with relief and with the happy sense of his own absurdity. He doesn't reach the giddy heights scaled in the movie version (I mean the movie version) by Alastair Sim, who made you want to hug not only him but everyone within a radius of 50 miles; with Ziegler you would settle for 25. But he does execute cheerful contortions -- cartwheels, almost -- that the late Mr. Sim might well have had in his soul but could never have realized with his body.

John Jarvis plays all four ghostly visitants (Marley included) in a vivid assortment of fantastic get-ups. He is best as the silent, menacing Christmas Yet to Come; his Christmas Present, though authoritative, is a bit of a bully, bellowing admonitions that might be more powerful if they were understated. (They are certainly topical, especially the vision of the two children, Ignorance and Want.)

Tanja Jacobs is vigorously, toughly Dickensian as Scrooge's housekeeper, who ends up robbing his corpse. Oliver Dennis is a briskly sympathetic Bob Cratchit, and Susan Coyne, sharp and tender, authentically Dickensian in another mode, as his wife.

Note how sensitive the production is in the matter of Tiny Tim: It solicits our tears, not by parading a cute crippled child in front of us but by letting us see the effect on his parents.

There are four children in the cast, of whom Ross Ward is especially good; he plays the boy outside Scrooge's window on Christmas morning. He delivers his part in this dialogue from offstage, another tactful touch; the production then rewards us for our patience by letting him appear in Scrooge's room, staggering under the weight of the bird he has been instructed to buy. It isn't quite as big as he is, as he described it, but it will do.

George Orwell described Dickens as a man "generously angry," and though it's the generosity that registers most strongly here, the anger can be felt, too. Contributions to the Daily Bread Food Bank are collected on the way out, so we have a chance to put the moral glow that this story inevitably induces to some practical use.

I could have done without the Harlequin masks on the scene- shifters, and the scene of young Ebenezer's abandonment by his fiancee falls flat, though Ziegler's reaction to it doesn't. Otherwise all is splendid.

This Christmas Carol is accompanied by a generous selection of Christmas carols, including one that's better known as Greensleeves. The late Michael Flanders had a theory about the ubiquity of this tune in productions of period plays: He claimed it was composed by Henry VIII, and that every time it was used as incidental music, the royalties went to Royalty.

2001-12-22-a-level-of-intensity-randy-hu:
The Toronto acting world is a small one, a fact that can be both frustrating and comforting. Actors get used to working together, in constantly shifting combinations, and audiences enjoy matching them up. I have a porous memory for press releases, and these days I try not to look too closely at the program before the play starts. I like to be taken by surprise.

So this fall I found myself at Theatre Passe Muraille watching a play called You Are Here, by which I was less enraptured than some, when on to the stage, quite late in the first act and to my great pleasure and surprise, walked Randy Hughson.

The pleasure derived from the transforming energy and precision of his performance. The surprise derived partly from the fact that Hughson was playing a sophisticated and successful film director, though he is best known as an actor of colourful derelicts; he had started the year with a show-stealing performance of one of them in Zadie's Shoes and had gone on to another in Earshot, a show at the Tarragon that he had no occasion to steal since he was the only actor in it. (A set with a spectacular false perspective did give him some serious competition.)

Shortly after that it was back to Passe Muraille to play a bewildered husband in a phantasmagoric piece called This Hotel. Which is another reason that his being there in You Are Here was so unexpected. It was clear by now that Hughson was in demand, but surely, along about now, he was due for a rest.

Since then there has been Soldier's Heart, which has just closed at the Tarragon, and he is now in rehearsal for The Lonesome West, which opens at Canadian Stage in January. After that he does the commercial re-mount of Zadies Shoes.

I met him for lunch this week and asked him just how long this has been going on. He traces it back to the opening of Slavs!, at the Tarragon in the fall of 2000; since then he has done seven plays, plus the occasional TV and independent film, and has never had a day out of work.

I asked him what he thought was the quality that got him hired.

"I have, he said, a level of intensity. Its not difficult for me to access deeper souls. Also, I come from a working-class family and background and I use that part of myself. I have an Everyman quality. I'm very much in touch with my blue-collar roots."

He offered this self-analysis with the gentle assurance of a cherub. And, in fact, his performances are as notable not only for their sense of banked-up violence but for their remarkable sweetness, largely conveyed by offbeat but infallible comic timing.

The Lonesome West is one of the new wave of Irish plays -- written by Martin McDonough, author of the transfixing Beauty Queen of Leenane -- and is set in the same remote, poverty-stricken village. Hughson plays a 40-year-old man (his own age, exactly) whom he describes as "an adult male with a child's sense of justice and play and anger.

He is also one of two brothers, and opening rehearsals have been largely devoted to fights and accents. Hughson actually sounded Irish while we were talking; he admitted he was under orders to use it as much as possible. He also worried there might be an overlay from the Newfoundland voice he had just finished using in Soldiers Heart, then brightened up and said that he spoke with a Kingston brogue anyway.

Kingston is where he grew up. He studied English for a year at Queens University and then took the theatre course at Ryerson, from which he graduated in 1984. He spent six or seven years" acting in Saskatchewan and Alberta and came back to Toronto to find himself "not part of the stream of working actors; I definitely felt I was an outcast.

His turning point came in 1990 when Urjo Kareda, director of the Tarragon, cast him in a production of Judith Thompson's The Crackwalker.

Urjo," he says, "really stood behind me, then and afterwards. Gradually I started getting offers instead of having to audition. (He now generally knows what he will be doing a year in advance.)

I can make a living right now," he says, touching wood with a double layer of self-mockery.)

Another early triumph came in Whale Riding Weather, in which he struck me as the first stage performer I had ever seen who seemed to be acting with the whites of his eyes. In this he played another "very sinister fragile man-child fighting a sexual battle -- half- homo, half-hetero -- that I hadn't had to explore before."

It hasnt all been like that. "When I was younger, I was doing marginalized bad-assed emotionally disturbed young people. Ive got more comedic roles as I've got older.

Unusual among prominent Toronto-based actors, he has never played at either Stratford or Shaw, though not for want of being asked. I didn't feel the need to get settled there for a year."

He had played plenty of classics earlier, including Benvolio in Robert Lepages bilingual Romeo and Juliet, and he was Sir Toby Belch in Soulpeppers Twelfth Night. He also took on, and surmounted, the biggest classical challenge any Toronto actor has taken on in recent years, that of playing the title role in Daniel Brooks' extraordinary production of Goethe's Faust (Part One only, though hes still trying to talk Brooks into adding Part Two sometime).

"Thats the most work I've ever done in my life: full of hour- long philosophical monologues. He made them grippingly comprehensible, and his sympathetic quality can never have been more useful.

He performed a similar feat as the misanthropic recluse, tormented by over-sensitive hearing, in Morris Panych's Earshot. It was like memorizing a novel. I wrote lines all over the set; the audience never knew -- the set was so dark. Morris said he wrote it for me. He said it was me."

And was it? "Well, I dont suffer from advanced hearing. And that desperation isnt part of me. But certain aspects I could relate to. His loneliness, his isolation, his sense of removal from the rest of the planet. I reacted to the man's pettiness. And to his sense of humour about himself."

The last is plainly true. Quite apart from his talent, it's obvious why Hughson gets so much work. He must be a first-rate person to have in a company.

Obituary of Urjo Kareda.

Urjo Kareda went through three outstanding careers in and around the Toronto theatre.

First he was theatre critic of The Toronto Star, possibly the best Canadian critic there has ever been on a daily paper.

Next he was literary manager at the Stratford Festival, working closely with Robin Phillips, the artistic director, through one of the most fertile and energetic periods in that theatre's history.

Finally, he was an artistic director himself, in charge of the Tarragon Theatre from 1982 until his death early on Boxing Day.

The death was shockingly sudden, even though everybody in the professional worlds he had moved in -- worlds that are close but distinct -- had known of the drastic worsening of his health.

For the last few weeks Urjo's condition (friends, foes and neutrals always referred to him by his first name) had been the principal topic, spoken or unspoken, of every theatrical conversation in Toronto.

Apart from the threatened personal and artistic loss, there was the horrible irony of a man whose mind was his salient quality succumbing to cancer of the brain.

His career as a theatre critic was a classic case of seizing the moment. The years between 1971 and 1975 -- his time of office at the Star -- saw an upsurge in new playwrighting; really the birth of a new Toronto theatre. Kareda was its chronicler and its champion; he was searching, vivacious and enthusiastic and the impact of his reviews helped new plays and new audiences to find one another.

He became identified with the new movement but he ranged far beyond it.

He was an incisive, sometimes savage, analyst of the Jean Gascon regime at the Stratford Festival.

And he was versatile. Passing through Toronto on two occasions in 1974, long before I came to live here, I encountered his reviews of two major American musicals at the Royal Alexandra: A Little Night Music and Gypsy.

The music and lyrics of Stephen Sondheim, the acting and singing of Angela Lansbury, were anatomized with the same seriousness and described with the same excitement that he would have brought to either a new play or, another area of expertise, an old opera. His reviews had rhythm -- a great and rare quality.

His central passion, though, was for words. His move to Stratford -- Canada's theatrical establishment -- was seen by some in Toronto as a desertion but in fact it was logical: he liked working with texts and he got to edit the old as well as commission and encourage the new.

Much of a dramaturge's work is inscrutable from the outside but Phillips testified that, next to himself and the actors, Urjo had the greatest influence on what appeared on the festival's three stages. More new plays were presented than under any previous Stratford regime; none of them have turned out to be classics (for that matter, few of the new plays he acclaimed as a critic have stood up well to revival) but that was to be expected: masterpieces are rare. He did however commission new Canadian translations -- notably John Murrell's translations of Chekhov -- that are still in use today.

In his 20 years at the Tarragon (the roundness of that number is another ironic shock) he brought on such playwrights as Judith Thompson and Jason Sherman, and also gave a Toronto showing to American writers like Wallace Shawn and Tony Kushner.

In my own three-year term of office as a Toronto critic I have detected a weakness at the Tarragon for frail, earnest, over- literary scripts but I have also found that at least one of the most exciting shows of a given year would invariably emanate from one of the theatre's two stages: Sherman's It's All True, in Richard Rose's production; Daniel Brooks' amazing five-actor staging of Goethe's Faust; the very funny two-hander Sibs; Yanna McIntosh's coruscating performance in Skylight.

Innumerable playwrights have paid tribute to the nurturing that they and their scripts received from Kareda.

Less publicized has been the care he took with actors.

Randy Hughson got his first Toronto break in Urjo's production of Thompson's The Crackwalker and received constant encouragement from Kareda thereafter, culminating in the brilliant performance Hughson gave this year in Morris Panych's Earshot -- a show that was itself an all-round Tarragon Theatre triumph.

Kareda maintained a strong presence as a journalist, writing an arts column in Toronto Life and especially fine opera reviews in The Globe and Mail. He was also a valuable broadcaster, especially about music.

Two of the last things he wrote were a celebration of Toronto's actors and an everything-nailed-down rave review of Robert Lepage's Bartok-Schoenberg double bill at Canadian Opera.

Combined with the imminent return to Tarragon of Kristen Thomson's enchanting I Claudia -- a double Dora-winner and one of the theatre's great successes -- they make a fine memorial.

Black & White Photo: Chris Bolin, National Post / Urjo Kareda served as the artistic director of the Tarragon Theatre from 1982 until his death yesterday. ;
2001-12-29-an-earthy-star-kristen-thomso:
Profile of Kristen Thomson.

Kristen Thomson talked her way into her first role on the Toronto stage in 1994, and she has been a welcome presence there ever since.

The play was David Mamet's Oleanna, about the conflict between a young female student with failing grades and the male university professor whom she accuses of sexual harassment. In legal terms she wins the contest but many people have thought that the play was slanted against her. Thomson was one of them, and she went to the audition thinking, "this play bugs me so much I don't want to see anybody do it who isn't as irritated by it as I am."

She reflects now that "there are certain plays where it helps to be mouthy about them." Anyway, she got the job, played the part beautifully, held her own against the far more experienced and unrelated R. H. Thomson, and definitely arrived.

Now 36, she "didn't start acting until I was 22." She grew up in London, in "a very athletic family." Not being an athlete herself, she was quite withdrawn and, though she enrolled in a few acting classes in high school, she didn't much like them.

She went on to the University of Toronto, where she had friends who encouraged her to join them in the acting program at University College.

"That was very good for me. It's not a hobby course; it has to be a major. There's a strong academic component. You don't need it to be an actor, but it gives you a useful perspective."

(Two of her classmates were Waneta Storms and Ruth Madoc-Jones; she was reunited with both of them this year in the all-female production of A Midsummer Night's Dream at Theatre Passe Muraille.)

The course must have taken. Thomson went on to the National Theatre School and got her first job straight out of there when Miles Potter, now best known as director of The Drawer Boy, cast her in Dancing at Lughnasa in Winnipeg and Ottawa. She went on "getting decent work out of town," which led to Bob Baker, then director of Canadian Stage, asking her to audition for Oleanna.

That was the beginning of her breakthrough; it was consolidated by her appearances in two of George Walker's Suburban Motel plays, with the author himself directing: a decidedly un-academic experience for an actress of her background. "It was like being on a holy mission for everyone involved. George really pushes you to go out on a limb. He takes your mind out of the driver's seat."

It's one thing to make desperation compelling. It may be a rarer achievement to make the same impact as a character of rock-like sanity. She brought this off as Stella, the contented sister of the manic Blanche DuBois, in the Soulpepper revival of A Streetcar Named Desire. Diana Leblanc, who had earlier directed her in Skylight at Manitoba Theatre Centre, "wanted someone earthy for Stella" and was rewarded by a perfect performance, sensible and sensual.

It began a continuing association with Soulpepper which has since taken in a comic servant in The School for Wives, a contrasting pair of maids in an Ionesco double bill, and -- most arrestingly -- Yelena, the flame to the various male moths in Uncle Vanya.

When Laszlo Marton, Soulpepper's Hungarian Chekhov specialist, cast her in this she was taken aback. "Yelena is supposed to be beautiful. I'm not a dog, but I'm not beautiful." Not to be ungallant about it, the men in the play have little to compare her with, and Thomson brilliantly presented a woman not above trading on her looks, but frightened of the response to them; her response to a declaration was to reach desperately for a drink.

She is, as it happens, one of the most attractive performers on the Toronto stage, in terms of both looks and warmth; and the goodwill she has earned could be felt flooding across the Tarragon Theatre's studio auditorium at the beginning of this year, even though she was appearing there behind a set of masks.

The play -- undoubtedly Toronto's hit of the year -- was I Claudia, a series of monologues she had written; there are four characters, the principal one a pre-teenager recoiling from her parents' divorce. A child of divorce herself, she "wanted to write about that emotional territory." She did it, however, without wallowing.

The masks helped (she discovered them on a return visit to her old theatre school), provoking a wonderfully heightened blend of plaintiveness and farce. She won twin Dora awards as actress and playwright, though she has doubts about the latter category.

"Fundamentally, I don't believe that just because I wrote something, I'm a writer," she said.

I Claudia was largely improvised and then set down, and Thomson still can't see herself sitting at a computer and hacking out a script. The work on I Claudia goes on; it comes back to the Tarragon in January, slightly revised, and then moves on to the Belfry Theatre in Victoria. Nobody expects it to end there.

I calculated that in 2001, Thomson played nine different roles spread over four separate productions. Two of them were in the Dream (her Shakespearean debut): Bottom the weaver, with whom she had some problems that she traces to the character's multiple identities; and Hermia, whom she played as "a bit of a princess" delightfully and very boisterously.

"I tend," she says, "to have an abundance of energy that can get overpowering. But I've got not bad at accepting myself. I haven't come out limping or wincing from anything I've done."

Black & White Photo: Chris Bolin, National Post / Kristen Thomson didn't get into acting until she was in university at age 22. Her breakthrough came when she got the part in Oleanna. ;
2002-01-02-a-well-deserved-ovation-for-0:
robertcushman@lycos.com

(From the National Post, Friday, January 4, 2002) In Robert Cushman's roundup of the best theatre of 2001, the production of Zadie's Shoes was miscredited. Factory Theatre produced of Adam Pettle's "invigorating" play. 

The most gratifying Canadian theatre event of the year occurred in England, where Robert Lepage won the Best Play Award for his solo piece The Far Side of the Moon. It was gratifying because when this delightful work -- a triumph for Lepage as writer, director and performer -- was seen the previous year in Toronto, it was denounced by every critic, except this one, which is why I bring it up. Even in Toronto, most real people had loved it.

Also in London, The Royal Family, a revival of a whiskery American comedy about the Barrymores, sold out almost before it opened because it starred Judi Dench. She has been Britain's favourite actress virtually since her debut in 1957 (as Ophelia to John Neville's Hamlet) but it took movies and Oscars to make her this bankable. It couldn't have happened to a greater Dame.

In New York, a similar thing happened on a much larger scale when The Producers became the biggest show -- in terms of box-office takings, awards and impossibility to get into -- in the history of the world. This doesn't mean it has more to offer its audience than any previous blockbuster, though obviously its provision of laughs and showbiz and laughing at showbiz hit a nerve. It means the machine gets ever more efficient at exploiting the kind of success that nothing succeeds like. It also helped that it was a pre-sold title, though to nothing like the same extent as the Disney monsters that were ruling Broadway before it came along.

In Toronto, Adam Pettle and Kristen Thomson made auspicious playwrighting debuts. The year began invigoratingly at Passe Muraille, with Pettle's gambling comedy, Zadie's Shoes, followed in quick succession by a couple of mesmerizing monologues, Thomson's I Claudia and Morris Panych's Earshot (the latter a visual feast as well). Both were at Tarragon and both exhilaratingly performed, by Thomson herself and Randy Hughson, both of them blessedly ubiquitous during the remainder of the year.

After these three, though, things declined precipitously (apart from This Hotel, an intriguing play in a wonderful production), with established writers contributing some stinkers. Two welcome if belated imports: Skylight, with a superb performance by Yanna McIntosh; and Steve Martin's Picasso at the Lapin Agile, a treat as staged by American Randall Arney with a fine local cast.

Soulpepper, still Toronto's best hope, tripped over Feydeau and Coward, pulled themselves together with Schnitzler, Chekhov (especially), Ionesco and Dickens. Outside their loop, there was one brilliant revival, Kate Lynch's Amazonian Midsummer Night's Dream.

Stratford had its strongest season in years, gratifyingly rich in Shakespeare, and the Shaw Festival its weakest, redeemed at the end by The Return of the Prodigal. Two formerly promising Canadian musicals -- Anything that Moves and The Drowsy Chaperone -- kept their promises.

Big musicals, usually in tacky touring versions, were deadly, though The Full Monty at least gave us a chance to see Kaye Ballard. The generally moribund commercial theatre did, however, do well with plays. There were two dazzling imported two-handers, Stones in His Pockets and The Island.

There was Fully Committed, a hilarious solo stand by the voice of them all, Mark McKinney. I have often railed against one-person shows, but I confess this has been a great year for them. Add to the list the little-seen but compelling The Vindication of Senyora Clito Mestres, a Catalan performed here in English by an outstanding Yugoslav actress, Dragana Varagic.

This was also the year in which, at the behest of financial benefactors, new names were slapped onto two Toronto theatres: the Pantages became the Canon, and the plain old Young Peoples' Theatre became the jaw-breaking Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People. The generous donors might have shown even more generosity if they had allowed the previous titles -- one historic, the other usefully descriptive -- to remain. They would certainly have shown more class.

To end where I begun: The Canadian Opera Company's revival of the Lepage-directed double bill Bluebeard's Castle and Erwartung was the most majestic piece of theatre seen on a Toronto stage all year.

2002-01-10-two-sexy-solitudes:
PLAN B

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

Not to worry, but the separatists have finally got the referendum result they wanted, and Quebec is about to take its leave of Canada. Talks are underway. That is the situation depicted in Michael Healey's new play. In a hotel ballroom in Hull, Que., four politicians meet to discuss terms, just for the look of the thing; they all know and admit that the real decisions are being made elsewhere.

Representing Canada-as-we-know-it are Michael, the finance minister, who seems endlessly conciliatory, and Colin, a Saskatchewan senator, who seems rudely confrontational. Across the table are Mathieu, the Quebec premier, and Lise, who is minster for inter-governmental affairs, and has one with Michael. (I should admit that the play is ahead of me in making that joke, though the character who cracks it regrets it as soon as its out.)

Plan B is, among other things, the best political play Toronto, or maybe Canada, has seen in years. However, it is among other things. In interviews, Healey has said he is using political relationships as a metaphor for personal ones. Usually its done the other way round, and audiences will probably assume it to be the case here as well. Practically it makes little difference; the two levels get equal time and are mutually supportive. By the end, they are as one; some virtuoso passages of dialogue could refer equally well to the state of play in bedroom or ballroom.

The ambiguity is an integral part of the program; the play is shimmeringly accomplished but tantalizingly cool, even though it involves some high emotions. The first line, explosively lobbied across the table by Colin, is an obscenity that then appears, in deadpan French translation, as a surtitle at the top of the set. This, it turns out, is not a one-off jest; it's a thoroughgoing convention. Every speech in the play, English or French, is reproduced aloft in the alternative tongue. This can be very educational, especially when swearing is concerned. (Michael complains bitterly about the French language's inadequacy in this respect.) It also clues us in, wittily and unsettlingly, to the provisional nature of everything; and, of course, in a play set at a bilingual conference, it functions handily as something between a fact and a metaphor.

The centre is Michael, described in a line that seems destined to pass into legend as a man of successive sincerities. He is sincere when he talks on the phone to his family; he is also sincere when he tries to get Lise into bed and when he professes his love to her. In the other part of the forest, he is passionately sincere when he pleads with the Quebeckers to remain a part of Canada.

He can also turn, as they say, on a dime and become the ruthless politician, next in line for prime minister; and here, too, he obviously believes what he says, or believes that he does. Peter Donaldson plays him brilliantly as a sleek self-deprecator, alternating between an unassuming amble and a decisive pounce. Fine though he is, the voice I hear when I look at the published text is that of his author, an ingratiating but somewhat unsettling comic in his own right. And he has given the character his own name.

The only other figure of comparable complexity is Colin, whose belligerence, in Peter MacNeills performance, is twinned with humane guilt, ferociously denied. It all boils over in a francophobe diatribe he delivers in an empty room he knows to be bugged -- in French, so he will be understood by his enemies, and so they will know how well he knows them. John Dolan as Mathieu is mostly required to be interestingly suave, and Marie-Helene Fontaine as Lise to be interestingly alluring, in a mature, French kind of way (i.e. very); these assignments they carry off triumphantly. Pitch and timing in Richard Greenblatts production are just about perfect; while the set, by Glen Charles Landry, is geometrical in its elegance, protean in its efficiency and drop-dead in its handsomeness.

I found it hard to believe that an illicit liaison would be so freely discussed at the diplomatic table; and there are some melodramatic developments in the political action. But the play's two floors line up as neatly as the author hoped they would, especially when they each slope toward betrayal.

Along with this goes some verbal play that occasionally -- in a pregnant confusion over the word "trust," for example -- approaches Stoppardian resonance, though the general tone is closer to that of another serious British farceur, Michael Frayn.

This is Healey's first play since The Drawer Boy, and it lacks the narrative compulsion and the immediately engaging characters of its predecessor. But it is a broader achievement, taking its author into new areas of conflict: inter-sexual and -- at least in theory - - international, and making theatrical sense of both. We can stop crossing our fingers for him.

SLIP KNOT

Factory Theatre

- - -

In 1995 Vancouver, there live two old Germans, Second World War vintage, one of whom has lost his accent.

Fritz, the still-guttural one, is poor and part-Jewish and apparently had to do dreadful things in the death camps to maintain his cover. William, who is rich and successful, did far more dreadful things -- in both quality and quantity -- without the same excuse.

In the first scene of Ken Gass's Slip Knot, Fritz, who is mortally ill, pays a call on William and announces that he is about to go public with their past records. William kills him.

Judith, Fritz's daughter, knows about the murder, and at her father's funeral she makes eyes at William's son, Jonathan, who asks her back to the house. There is much saucy dialogue about the aphrodisiac effects of bereavement, and a fair amount of saucy action as well. Judith keeps referring to her Old Testament namesake, who gained access to the tent and bed of the tyrant Holofernes and killed him at the moment of climax.

This should count as fair warning, but Jonathan, lost to lust like a typical man, ends up sated and dead like Holofernes. (He, by the way, is pronounced throughout with the accent on the second syllable. I, having always heard it on the third, found this very grating but I acknowledge that there are two schools of speech.) So ends Act One.

Act Two brings together William and Judith, the surviving half of the cast, for a more elaborate cat-and-mouse, or sex-and-death, game. The play is billed as a thriller and it has a couple of twists that are genuinely surprising, as well as a couple that aren't. Much of the time, though, it seems to be nervously reveling in its own implausibility.

It also pauses from time to time to reflect on the Holocaust, and these moments, pinned as they are on to pasteboard characters in gimcrack situations, are intolerable. Together with the sexy overlay, they turn the play into concentration-camp chic.

In which connection: George Steiner once remarked on how sinister it was that "camp" should have become a vogue word for a flippant semi-style. I thought at the time that he was being over-ingenious, but a succession of plays and movies has changed my mind. This play may well have serious intentions as a sardonic fable of guilt and responsibility, but it could only realize them if it were written and performed with the icy high-comic authority of a parable by Friedrich Durrenmatt. Sarah Stanley's production is giggly and -- except in its enthusiastic sound and lighting effects -- insecure.

William, the eternal and invincibly amoral Nazi and a medical experimenter at Auschwitz and Dachau, is played by John Gilbert, who hovers, physically and vocally, between smooth and crinkly in the English manner, neither of them quite adequate either to the character's monstrosity or to his occasional qualms. On the first night he seemed unsure of his words, or at least of his phrasing.

Philippa Domville, by contrast, throws herself at the role of Judith with reckless abandon; a perplexingly uneven actress (wonderful in The Chet Baker Project, far from it in everything else), she tries to unite her two roles of temptress and avenger by adopting the winsome lisp of a Marilyn Monroe impersonator. She plays, somewhat too literally, the blonde bombshell.

Dmitri Chepotevsky starts well as Jonathan, who is both callow and callous, but his confidence eventually turns into coarseness. Les Carlson comes off best as Fritz, very trembly and ashen.

Not much is made of the play's being set in Canada. Nothing is said about this country's tolerance, or otherwise, of possible mass murderers, and one wonders if the characters' journeys were really necessary. Ex-Nazis have been known to thrive without ever leaving home.

THE DRAGONFLY OF CHICOUTIMI

Factory Studio Theatre, Toronto

- - -

THE DANCE OF THE DEAD

Berkeley Street Theatre Upstairs, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Dennis O'Connor gives an extraordinary solo performance in The Dragonfly of Chicoutimi as a man caught between trance and consciousness, between childhood and maturity, and -- most bizarrely -- between English and French.

He plays Gaston Talbot, a middle-aged Quebecois. As an adolescent Gaston witnessed -- may even have caused -- the drowning of an Anglophone playmate. The shock sent him into 40 years of silence. Now, finally, he talks, but in English -- a tongue he never spoke before. At least the words are English; the syntax remains French. The author, Larry Tremblay, is himself a French-Canadian who has never before written in English. (The play was staged in Montreal in 1995.) Playwright and actor together create an effect of tortured simplicity that is troublingly effective.

O'Connor is a round-faced, scant-haired man who looks somewhat Falstaffian; indeed, he played a good Falstaff in Toronto a few years ago, and he seems initially to be beaming benevolence. It turns out, however, that his Gaston has access to deep reserves, not only of confusion, but of hostility. A mask of hatred comes over the actor's face, and waves of it contort both his voice and his body. The speed of his transformations, and their whole-heartedness, are remarkable. He is, he says, "a child in an adult's body." Sometimes it seems to be the other way round.

Delving back into his memories, he recalls himself as a virtuoso artist of the Popsicle stick -- "the Picasso of Chicoutimi." He also remembers, and impersonates, his mother, whom he recalls, terrifyingly, as an implacable guilt-assigning monster. Finally, after much twisting and turning, he arrives at the event that traumatised him.

Kevin Orr directs with admirable tact. This, following Michael Healey's Plan B, is the second play in a week to use the linguistic divide as an image for the riven state of Quebec, though -- at least in this Toronto production -- Tremblay's piece works more potently in personal terms than in political. I wish it a longer life.

You can probably, if you try hard enough, find links between any plays. Gaston is perhaps possessed by the spirit of his dead friend Pierre. The Dance of the Dead, a cheerily named new musical that has also taken seven years to reach a Toronto theatre, gives us a whole stageful of unquiet ghosts, looking for a mortal body in whom to take up residence. It's set in a cemetery, to which a young man has come to commit suicide. However, he has chosen the one night of the year on which those who died with unfinished business (and who doesn't?) reassemble hoping for another chance. There are 20 of them, of various vintages; but once they have done their opening number, all but four take refuge in the auditorium and join us in watching the show. I hope they enjoyed it more than I did.

There are a few nice things going on here. One is a song called Double Your Trouble, supposedly written by a self-described blues singer (actually she seems to have been more of a torch singer) who passed away c. 1930 and who seems, on the evidence presented here, to have been some 10 years ahead of her time. The song itself is all right, but what I liked most is that she doesn't get up, come centre stage, and try to kill us with it. She sits on a bench at the side and sings it to the more recent revenante, whose favourite number it was during life and whose listening is as important as her companion's vocal. In fact, the two of them interacted.

Not much of that goes on, perhaps because most of these living dead are also walking cliches. The chanteuse died of a drug overdose, having previously discovered that the men in her life "didn't want me; they wanted the lady on the stage." Sandra Caldwell, who plays her, wastes little time on subtlety; hers is a relentlessly hands-on-hips performance, even when her arms are hanging down by her sides. Elizabeth Beeler gets somewhat more reality into her latter-day fan, a compulsive gambler who lost at Russian roulette. A third is a repressed homosexual. A fourth is a killer. Each of them pleads to be Edward's beneficiary. He chooses a recipient, but isn't happy with the results. So he changes the rules.

I was never quite clear what the rules were anyway. How come that Edward, now dead, was apparently able to stick around a whole year and monitor the fate of his soul in his successor's body? Why, if it comes to that, are these corpses still so concerned with the world of the living? I can hardly speak for the dead (though in this job ...) but the uncaring graveyard bunch of Thornton Wilder's Our Town seem to me a lot more convincing -- certainly a lot more compelling.

Scott White wrote both the book (which carries what drama there is) and the score, and he uses the characters' various ages as the pegs for an eclectic collection of songs. (To put it another way, he has tried to please everybody.) There are a couple of interesting tunes, but the lyrics -- aside from being carelessly rhymed -- are too clotted and contorted to carry the amount of exposition that has been wished upon them.

This is especially notable in Move On, a would-be gospel showstopper in which Edward, who has been doing some research (how?) tells his flock that all is now well with their survivors and that they themselves can now rest in peace. It must be the only revivalist number whose message is "stay dead." His contempo-pop ballads are as sententious and sentimental as everyone else's; and the whole thing is suffused in do-goodery. Though there is nothing explicitly religious about it, it has the flavour of Christian rock, that forlorn attempt to take back the Devil's music. It talks bold, about suicide and gambling and homosexuality, but it remains ineffably ingenuous.

Vinetta Strombergs' choreography is basic, involving lots of hand- waving, but she seems to have a cast of singers rather than dancers. Having them sit among us, though, is self-defeating as well as disconcerting; it throws the balance. Instead of getting the full effect of a vocal ensemble, you hear a single line being bellowed into your ear. And the words are frankly not the kind to which you want to get that close.

WALKING TO RUSSIA

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - As I was saying a couple of days ago, plays connect, or at least they cluster. Here, cold on the heels of The Dragonfly of Chicoutimi and The Dance of the Dead, is the third show in a week about deceased people walking. Coming up next: a piece called Mortality.

The young lady who goes Walking to Russia is doing it, or trying to do it, in a kind of hallucination. At least she did once; now she is dead and haunts the dreams of her parents. In fact, they are possessed by her; the family is Jewish, and she seems to be a new form of the traditional demon known as a dybbuk.

The characters live in Winnipeg, but both mother and father originally came from Russia. Father is a scientist and a Marxist, the kind of cranky, obstinate Jewish atheist who looks paradoxically good in a prayer shawl. He is obsessed with global warming, a natural preoccupation perhaps in a man who has moved from one cold climate to another.

One thing he has brought with him from the old country is a family recipe for an especially potent condiment, hot enough to revive a frozen child. The play is directed by Jennifer H. Capraru, who a few years ago -- for the same company, Theatre Asylum -- staged the admirable My Mother's Courage. This new one might be called My Mother's Mustard.

It is the first play of a new writer, Jonathan Garfinkel, and it does not hang together well. The daughter left home because of her vocational clashes with her father: He wanted her to become a scientist like himself, and she chose to be an artist -- worse yet, a religious artist. Her fatal, fevered walk was a metaphorical attempt to get back to her roots, spiritual as well as ethnic. The play is sprinkled with her lyrical monologues, but they make no connection with the rest of the drama; the actress, Ruth Madoc-Jones, goes devotedly through them but really she could be talking about anything.

The more mundane parts of the play are better value. Papa, on the verge of retirement, receives a visit from a former pupil, who offers him a job researching his favourite topic. It sounds like a great deal: a new lease on life, loads of intellectual stimulation, a shot at saving the world and the firm promise of a Nobel Prize. (It seems remarkably firm; I had no idea these things were rigged.)

The catch is that the work has to be done in Churchill, in northern Manitoba, a place even colder than Winnipeg, while our professor's wife has her heart set on moving to California. For years she has slaved as his unpaid secretary, sacrificing her own talents and her own ambitions; she also carries scars from his treatment of their daughter.

He rides roughshod over her -- as, obviously, he always has -- but gets his comeuppance in the course of a CBC interview. He is humiliated before the whole country, or at least that part of it that tunes in to Peter Gzowski. (or that used to; the play is set in 1999.)

The evening comes to life when Aron Tager, as the old man, receives the offer he cannot refuse; he plays with enjoyably grumpy feistiness throughout. Ann Tager-Page, his wife in real life, seems inhibited about recreating the relationship on stage; supposed to stand up to him, she is remarkably limp and toneless. Tenderness seems to become her better; she is far more at ease when the play flashes to show her relationship with her daughter, to whom she has passed on her own suppressed yearnings.

Jim Jones is fine as the former student. He also plays the iconic Gzowski, whose appearance is tactfully staged so that we see him only from behind. He looks, from this vantage point, amusingly convincing -- but his voice is way off.

MORTALITY

The Theatre Centre

- - -

I am beginning to wonder whether death is such a great dramatic subject after all: death in the abstract, I mean.

Hamlet, as eloquent on the subject as any character is ever likely to be, ended up talking only about the fear of death, confessing that the thing itself is something that nobody ever comes back to talk about. He manages to say this despite having spent time with a loquacious ghost bursting with news of the afterlife; somehow the prince's skepticism rings truer than all his deceased father's certainties.

So you can write about the fear of death, about the approach of death, even about watching the experience of dying, but never about the experience itself.

This may account for some of the odder aspects of Mortality, a new production from Ross Manson's company Volcano, which had great success a couple of years ago with Building Jerusalem. That, however unconventionally structured, was a play; Mortality is a revue with a cast of two actors, male, and two dancers, female. Manson has commissioned prose vignettes on the subject of death from three prominent Canadian writers and has contributed linking material of his own.

He starts with one of the actors, Martin Julien, coming on stage and trying bumptiously to make himself the centre of attention. (This is not a personal slur. He is merely performing as instructed. At least I hope he is.) He is then followed on and edged off by one of the dancers, who complains about having to work with such uncongenial colleagues.

It is unclear what these displays of professional jealousy have to do with the topic at hand (survival tactics, perhaps) but they seem like nervous ingratiation.

So does a later sequence in which Prospero's "our revels now are ended" speech from The Tempest is windily burlesqued, or maybe just delivered very badly. It comes to us in a film-clip, and the program contains a credit -- "screenplay: W. Shakespeare" -- whose defensive flippancy is all too revealing. The mini-movie seems to be a spoof of an old Hollywood newsreel. Almost insultingly scrappy, it is not a good advertisement for the concept of mixed media.

Back on stage, the performers, when they get down to it, don't seem to rub along too badly. The actors also dance, the dancers also act: all very respectably. Kate Alton is a helpful and adaptable choreographer, and in general it is the non-verbal sections that come off best. Julia Aplin, goggly-eyed, delivers a piece by Paul Quarrington about a child's falling off a jungle gym and sensing her own mortality for the first time. Her performance is intelligent, characterized by a kind of hyper-active primness, but the material seems heavily cute.

"You're saying, 'Get to the point,'" she keeps telling us; and yes, we are. The style is jokey without actually having any jokes. It is a relief when she stops talking and gives herself over, gracefully, to dance.

George Leach, mellifluous if monotonal, utters a monologue by Tomson Highway inspired, we are told, by the death of the writer's brother from AIDS. Gripping as long as it remains specific, or clinical, it proceeds to float away into impersonal lyricism. It only regains its force when the actor moves into wordless chanting.

A text by Carol Shields is spoken by Peggy Baker with, uniquely, some interaction from the other players. The dramatization is only partial, and only partially successful, but it includes some resonant observations that suggest both the attraction of the theme and its impossibility: "The moment of death occurs while we're still alive," and "Life marches up to the wall of that final darkness." It's when you get to the wall that the subject becomes intractable.

The most poetic thing in the evening is the sound of an old record -- Louis Armstrong playing and singing La vie en rose -- played on a wind-up gramophone that winds down. There is also very accomplished live music -- characterized by a saxophone as piercing as a flute -- written by John Gzowski and played by a trio with the composer at its head.

Martin Julien finally redeems himself with his rendition of a pungent poem by Stephen Dobyns, about Death going on strike and so rendering life meaningless, at least according to the rich and powerful who need it to grease their wheels.

The political angle seems somewhat parochial; Swift, in Gulliver's Travels, presented the prospect of eternal life far more persuasively as a curse for anyone. Death, as this show finally acknowledges, is something we can't live with or without. But for it to hold our attention in the theatre, we need to know something about the person dying.

Black & White Photo: Volcano Theatre / PEGGY BAKER AND MARTIN JULIEN IN A SCENE FROM MORTALITY: A mix of dance and theatre, it never gives us a reason to care about the dying. ;

THE LONESOME WEST

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - How are things in Connemara?

Martin McDonagh, living in London but of Irish name and descent, is the most naturally gifted playwright to have surfaced in the British Isles since Harold Pinter. He excels at all the basic things -- narrative, dialogue, character -- that a previous generation, in Britain as here, couldn't manage and pretended didnt matter. The result was 30 years of desiccated drama. Once again, the Irish have had to ride to the rescue.

McDonaghs The Lonesome West returns us to the remote Irish village that furnished both a setting and a title for his superb The Beauty Queen of Leenane. For sure the ol' place hasn't changed much. Like its predecessor, this play concerns people who basically live in a kitchen. Once again the burning of a characters hand on the all-important stove (stage right this time, rather than stage left) is a climactic event. Once again the reading aloud of a letter by the person who has just written it provides a showpiece scene and also has a crucial influence on the succeeding action. And once again that action concerns two family members living together in physical and emotional deadlock. It is conceivable that at some level they love one another, but what actually keeps them going is conflict.

Coleman and Valene, the two brothers of The Lonesome West, get rather more fun out of life than the mother and daughter of The Beauty Queen. They go out more, and their antagonism is slightly less deadly. Admittedly most of their excursions seem to be to funerals, and when we meet them they are just back from burying their father, whose head Coleman had playfully shot off in retaliation for a criticism of his personal appearance.

Valene agreed to pass this off as an accident (not that anybody in Leenane is fooled) on condition that Coleman sign over his half of their inheritance. So now Coleman, the wilder of the two, lives on the indulgence of his primmer brother. Meanwhile, Valene spends money on a brand new stove (in bright red, with the letter V imprinted on the front) and on an extensive collection of religious figurines -- acquisitions that Coleman regards with rancour.

But then these two men, now in their forties, have spent their lives destroying one anothers toys; and they are frozen in childhood rivalry, never happier than when rolling around in combat on the floor. Like the two women in The Beauty Queen, they delight in taunting one another with their sexual inexperience; their favourite insult is virgin feckin' gayboy.

The last scene finds them under orders to be nicer to one another -- if possible, to go over all their past grievances and apologize for their misconduct. So they try, but, as surely as happened to Elyot and Amanda in Private Lives, their attempted concord only leads to more, and more violent, discord. Some of the old cruelties they dig up really hurt. Besides, this is how they enjoy themselves.

This scene, like much of the rest of the play in Jackie Maxwell's CanStage production, is both uproariously funny and deeply painful. Colemans idea of home comfort is to pull his shirt out over his pants, revealing a momentary expanse of pot-belly; Randy Hughson takes full advantage of the rolling, childlike brutality, and of the sly, lacerating wit. Valene, less cunning than he wants to believe, is a mixture of violence and gentility. Benedict Campbell, beautifully pitched, gives him a prim walk that accelerates into a waddle.

As in The Beauty Queen, the central couple is supported by two other characters. One, played with poignant vivacity by Tara Rosling, is Girleen, a 17-year-old distributor of her fathers illicit whiskey. She nurses an unrequitable, almost Chekhovian, passion for the local priest, Father Welsh (or would that be Walsh? - - nobody seems quite sure, and neither, by the end of the play, do we), who suffers from what seem, in this region, to be fairly standard vocational agonies.

As Coleman kindly tells him, "You're a bit too weedy and you're a terror for the drink and you have doubts about Catholicism." (Hughson rolls off this reassuring catalogue with superbly off-hand assurance.) If he has lost his faith, the priest still has his conscience, and it racks him; David Storch, with a grey quiff incongruously crowning an otherwise sleek head of hair, makes him both tragic and absurd. He also talks as colourfully as anyone else in Leenane: "You didnt even cry when Holland knocked us out of the fecking World Cup" is his apocalyptic judgment on what he ironically takes to be Girleens heartlessness.

In The Beauty Queen the subordinate pair, though interesting, were kept subordinate. Here they are not quite secondary, not quite equal, and the play suffers from the split focus.

Nor, despite painting an apparently broader canvas, does it say as much about this desperate reach of Ireland as its predecessor managed subtly to suggest.

But if its overall structure is defective, what might be called its local craft -- its subtle banking of narrative detail to be explosively cashed in at a later date -- is often superb.

There is a third Leenane play, The Skull of Connemara, that we are still waiting to see and that may bring the whole trilogy into focus. (Don't hold your breath: The Lonesome West has taken five years to reach us.) McDonagh, riffing on earlier presentations of an idyllic rural Ireland, has created his own counter-world. It may be extreme, but you believe every word of it. The action may be dark but, because its inhabitants are so richly and idiosyncratically alive, the experience is exhilarating.

PSYCHEDELICATESSEN

The Second City

- - -

Second City titles never mean much. Psychedelicatessen is as arbitrary a name as any other, and more cumbersome than most. Do not let it discourage you -- the troupe's 51st show is its best in years, and by miles.

The early buzz has centred on the teams obligation to measure up satirically to the aftermath of Sept. 11. That may have something to do with it, but probably more important is the engagement as director of Chris Earle, a very pointed actor and playwright who is here the cause of pointedness in others. His half-dozen writer- performers are all in top gear; remarkably, there is not a dud sketch in the evening.

A few of the numbers relate directly to current events. Canadian troops arrive in Afghanistan and receive operational instructions from their American allies (Mind our stuff). A bevy of concerned Torontonians, or Torontonians who feel they should be concerned but arent sure how to go about it, gather on the terrace outside a party to puff smoke and pay homage to international crises ("Terror - - that's the topic, isn't it?").

Other moments evince a concern with air travel and especially with immigration. A malignant extraterrestrial applies for entry (occupation -- overlord) and damned if he doesnt get in.

A recurring character played by Paul Bates, who looks reassuringly bland and sounds tooth-baringly alarming, the alien turns like so many new arrivals to cab-driving, reverting to venomous type when a fortunately uncomprehending fare asks to be taken somewhere on College Street. ("You will pay for this!" I expected to.)

He is also on hand for the shows conclusion. I wouldn't want to give too much away so I will merely say that this finale also re- introduces us to other former acquaintances with accents, and that, whatever your previous feelings about Adrienne Clarkson, they will change.

Revue in recent years has become an end in itself, the comedy taking place in a whimsical never-never land inhabited only by standup comics. This one returns us to a recognizable Toronto, a recognizable Canada, a recognizable world. Even the obligatory embarrassment-in-a-restaurant sketch takes on a new dimension as a satire on the conventions of improvised revue itself, with Jennifer Goodhue, a pocket-sized fury, as a performer's nightmare of an audience participant. (It does go on a bit, though).

"Music With Borders," a salute to the Canadian troubadour market, has Paul Constable and Nathan David Shore, the groups two sardonic male heavies, providing nostalgically lachrymose impersonations of Gordon Lightfoot and Leonard Cohen, while Carolyn Taylor offers a Jann Arden in state of permanent vocal hiccup, and Aurora Browne a politely purring Diana Krall (Sony took the part/That once was my heart/America, you own all of me. Hang on, though; doesnt she record for Universal?)

Scenes of domestic discord, another Second City staple, seem this time to be about real people. Two Hispanic ladies passionately discuss the rival merits of baby formula and mother's milk; the breast advocate is rewarded by a strikingly healthy son able to sweep his provider up in a tango while taking nourishment.

As well as being highly inventive, these items occasionally cut surprisingly deep. An Italian-Canadian husband grudgingly agrees to turn down the sound on the TV when his wife requests some quality time. Another couple tries to rekindle the passion that had once briefly flared when the man returned unscathed from a subway accident.

My favourite sketch -- I think -- has the unquenchable Goodhue as a small child poured into a snow suit so that her estranged father may take her to see the Lord of the Rings.

Everything here rings true: the father's car horn honking outside; the child flailing, stifled, while her mother takes a long call from a sympathetic girlfriend; the mothers response when asked for a ring like the one that made Frodo invisible. ("Your father gave me a ring and he became invisible.")

I cant recall how it ends, and I have to admit that nearly every scene has trouble in finding a punchline. But then, who doesn't?

Black & White Photo: Rob Waymen / CAROLYN TAYLOR AND NATHAN DAVID SHORE IN PSYCHEDELICATESSEN: The revue exists in the context of Sept. 11, and it measures up to the challenge. ;

DREAMS OF BLONDE AND BLUE

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - For 15 encouraging minutes at the start, M.J. Kang's Dreams of Blonde and Blue seems to be off and more or less running. A young Asian woman appears before the curtain in the guise of a stereotypical Oriental sex kitten, all self-abasement and pidgin English. This, in a forward-looking Toronto theatre at the start of the 21st century, is somewhat startling; but there is a neat reversal. We discover that the young woman is an actress, auditioning in New York for yet another role as a prostitute and all too aware of what is expected of her.

Her name is Julia, and we follow her as she pays a rare call on her parents, who are immigrants from Korea. Father runs an unsuccessful restaurant, and when he talks to his daughter he speaks rather like the character for whom she was trying out: "You look like bimbo," he tells her. In his dreams -- which are staged for us - - definite articles are no problem. He imagines himself returning to Korea, running for prime minister, and getting in, on what seems to be a strident Americanization ticket, with Arnold Schwarzenegger brought along as celebrity guest.

In real life Father (that's how he's billed) has violently conflicted feelings about his adopted country. He has good reason to hate Americans, but he also wants to be one of them. He keeps having cosmetic operations, and he himself performs one on his restaurant. He switches from ethnic to indigenous cuisine and calls the new place Uncle Sam's Hamburger, a name that one feels would play better in any country of the world than the one he's actually living in. But then Father is a transparently terrible businessman.

His prime ministerial ambitions are never, after the initial fantasy sequence, mentioned again. This is a shame, since they are the most engaging part of the play, however unlikely. (Of course, the point of pipe dreams is that they are improbable. What strains belief is that Father should confide his to his wife and daughter.) After this, we are stuck with the story of Father's decline and fall, which is believable but dreary, not because he is a failure but because, dreams apart, he is a barely individualized failure. And at that, he's the liveliest character on the stage.

Everything is neatly symmetrical. Julia, who has betrayed another parental dream by dropping out of school, finds her personal life all too closely reflecting her professional one, especially in her relationship with a sadistic American boyfriend. Mother, a scientist by training, now focuses her energies on clothes, and especially on shoplifting.

Flashbacks to the old country introduce us to Father's own father and to his sister, even more spectral figures for whom we are nonetheless expected to feel. (The technical term for this is sentimentality.) A final retrospective shows us the childhood trauma, dating back to the Korean War, that shaped Father's attitude toward the two countries. It is, in fact, that trusty commercial- theatre device, the late revelation that explains everything.

One thing it explains is why the play is set in New York at all (as opposed to, say, Toronto). It certainly has very little New York electricity, even given that it takes place in Queens rather than in Manhattan. Steve Lucas, usually an excellent designer, this time contributes a dispiritingly anonymous set. And the director, Guillermo Verdecchia, is unable to extract much pace or excitement from either the text or the actors.

Most of the performances are glumly inadequate. Julia, played by the author herself, is drably overemphatic, and Mommy (Brenda Kamino) even more drably under. Paul Braunstein, playing various roles, is at least efficient; and Denis Akiyama as Father is considerably more desperately bright and incorrigibly sad. He, alone in the cast, has rhythm: that of a man hurtling optimistically toward disaster as -- to adapt Stephen Sondheim -- he careers from Korea to career. I'd vote for him.
