Until Feb. 17. Tickets: 416-872-1212.

THE GRADUATE

Canon Theatre, Toronto

The ways of titillation are strange. I considered crossing the ocean to see Kathleen Turner's momentarily nude appearance as Mrs. Robinson in the stage version of The Graduate, but I would not have crossed the street to see Jerry Hall, who succeeded her in the role in London. The presumed difference in their acting skills may have had something to do with this, but only in an indirect way; Hall, an ex-model, may have a better body than Turner, but the attraction lay in seeing a woman who wasn't best known for showing it off.

I never made the transAtlantic trip, but Turner and The Graduate have now obligingly saved me the trouble, touching down in Toronto en route for New York. I'm glad I saved my money. Turner, as rumoured, makes a brief and discreetly-lit appearance without any clothes on, and at other times looks very fetching in a slip. But her actual acting is on one note. It is quite an attractive note, with a foghorn quality good for getting off the occasional wry one- liner, but it never seems to belong to a real person.

Nevertheless, one misses her when she isn't there. She may not be giving much of a performance, but The Graduate isn't much of a play. Terry Johnson, one of Britain's best comic playwrights (Dead Funny, Hysteria), has adapted it from the Charles Webb novel and the 1968 Mike Nichols film, and he is also the director. I have never read the book, and largely forgotten the movie, but my impression is that Johnson has done a decent job of assembling the narrative into a series of short and reasonably shapely scenes. But he cannot, under either of his hats, prevent the story from running out of steam, both sexual and dramatic.

The closing sections of the first half are an especial drag, the audience applauding hopefully at the end of each episode only to discover that there is still another to sit through before they, like Mrs Robinson, can find relief in a drink.

The piece, with its West Coast setting just anticipating flower power, remains a prime example of that 1960s specialty, generational pandering. Now, however, it has two generations (maybe more) to play to: the Baby Boomers nostalgic for their own tame gestures of rebellion, and their successors who can convert the message of young- folks-good old-folks-bad to their own purposes.

Mrs. Robinson, not only alcoholic but unforgivably rich and middle-aged, seduces the virginal Benjamin Braddock, 22 years old and just out of college with all sorts of honours; and they both seem to be having a good time. Who could object? If there is any guilt, then presumably they share it. Well, Benjamin's parents are upset by his behaviour; and Mr. Robinson, understandably vexed, calls him a degenerate. But nobody expects us to take their opinions seriously; they're old. (And a clumsy farcical scene in which the three Braddocks visit some kind of guru-shrink makes damned sure we don't).

Benjamin gets off. But Mrs. R turns into a vengeful harpy, an evil force from whom the hero has to escape. She is shunted off to the sidelines, while Benjamin sets about wooing her virtuous daughter, Elaine, with whom he has fallen inexplicably -- or at least unexplainedly -- in love.

All three central characters, even though played by more-or-less movie stars, are wafer-thin, so one hardly cares what happens to any of them, except to wish they would hurry up about it. Jason Biggs doesn't have the chunky oddity Dustin Hoffman brought to Benjamin -- he is more of the conventional dreamer type, a latter-day Holden Caulfield signalling sensitivity -- but he does very well with the character's early awkwardness, which does suggest a kind of integrity, and with his later oddball determination. Alicia Silverstone squeaks and squawks with great conviction as Elaine, though I doubt if she does anything that fifty less celebrated young actresses could not have managed.

The two end up sharing breakfast cereal in bed, as some kind of ceremony of purity. This is in contrast to the behaviour of Elaine's mother, who devoted her energies to getting Benjamin into the sack and to stopping his mind from wandering when he was there. The latter activity provides the best scene in the play, as it did in the movie, though the preceding embarrassment in the hotel lobby is funny as well.

The play has, by current standards, an unusually large cast, and everyone else in it falls smartly into line, especially Victor Slezak's indignant husband and father, goaded into wielding an axe. Rob Howell's set, mainly composed of louvred doors, is witty and versatile, though somewhat chilly; it often leaves Turner, in particular, looking stiff and marooned.

Music of the period links the scenes, the selection going beyond the irritatingly wholesome Simon and Garfunkel tunes that adorned the film. Maybe the property would have worked better on stage if they had turned it into a full-scale musical. We could have had a real celebratory bash to start with ("We're throwing a party for our graduate/With Californian food that you'll be glad you ate") instead of remaining confined in Benjamin's bedroom while he avoids the revels.

I was about Benjamin's age when the film came out, and I remember my contemporaries thinking it a fine satirical thrust when a well- wisher sidled up to the hero and said "plastics." Here this famously economical career advice is delivered, more plainly and tamely, by Mr. Robinson; but I think now, as I did then, that it's the authors who come off smug and heavy-handed. We are meant to take the ironic point that the whole adult world and the people in it are plastic. But they could hardly be more plastic than the play.

SYNCOPATION

Winter Garden Theatre, Toronto

DESDEMONA: A PLAY ABOUT A HANDKERCHIEF

Artword Alternative Theatre, Toronto

I ought to like Syncopation. It is, in its way, a pioneering work: an example of a genre that has never existed before but that I have always thought should have.

Always is maybe pitching it a bit high; let's just say since 1978. That was the year in which Michael Bennett, the creator of A Chorus Line, mounted his follow-up production, a musical called Ballroom, whose main fault was that it was a musical. That is to say it employed the three elements of dialogue, song and dance to tell a story for which only two of them were necessary.

It was about unglamorous people finding a new vitality on the dance floor, and when they danced the show itself came gloriously to life. Unfortunately, they also sang, and not only were their songs lacklustre (though a couple of them have mysteriously survived), they were also unnecessary. Ballroom should have been something new: a play with dances.

Syncopation, by American playwright Allan Knee, is that something, and I wish I could be more excited about it. First performed in New Haven, Conn., in 1999, it is a two-hander, set on the Lower East Side of New York before the First World War.

Henry Ribolow, a 34-year-old meat packer and part-time dish- washer, has placed a newspaper ad for a dancing partner, someone with whom he might conquer the world. Anna Bianchi, who sews beads on dresses for a living, presents herself at Henrys studio, a bleak rented room in a tenement.

Change is in the air -- social, political and musical. The undulating sounds of ragtime emerge from Henrys portable Victrola, inspiring a whole menagerie (think foxtrot, think grizzly bear) of new steps. Oddly enough, the word "ragtime" is never mentioned in Syncopation, but then neither is the word syncopation.

Great subtlety perhaps, but what is in the play is thin and predictable. From the moment Anna, timidly and with misgivings, crosses Henry's threshold, you know the two of them will get together. Of course there are obstacles -- Anna is engaged to another man, Henry still lives with his mother -- but really the only suspense lies in wondering what mood the author will settle for at the end of the play. Will he soothe us with a happy ending or tease us with a bittersweet one? My lips, of course, are sealed; though I cannot forbear remarking that this, following The Graduate, is the second Mirvish presentation in quick succession whose denouement involves a fractured wedding.

The play's angle is that Henry, who believes dance will set you free and who dabbles in radical politics on the side, is actually more inhibited than Anna, so their relationship is syncopated, too.

Anna may be awfully concerned for her reputation; she is bashful when Henry asks her to take his arm, and when he suggests she raise her skirt a fraction to facilitate movement her shocked reply is, "Ive had enough freedom."

But it turns out she knows more about freedom than he does. She is fascinated, and eventually influenced, by a group of advanced women who congregate at a railroad station and are called the odd ladies; she is even more enthralled by an associated odd gentleman.

This, as the author rightly judges, was an explosive time in an exploding place, but very little of that ferment seeps into his play. We get a mild narrative (both characters are diarists, which helps with the exposition) but no sparks, either around or between them, not even when they dance.

Both actors, Cynthia Dale and Geordie Johnson, in fact dance very well. But dancing is not, after all, what they do, and they are unable to sweep one another off their feet or us off ours. Yet the play seems implicitly to demand that they should, and, of course -- audiences being programmed for romance -- we want them to. Maybe this play, unlike Ballroom, should have been a musical; it needs an extra lift.

Dales performance seems to want it to be; she delivers her emotions in tidy little packages, dispatching them swiftly, as if they were preludes to unwritten numbers. She seems constantly about to break into something, if not out in something. Johnson makes heavy weather of his Jewish-American accent and hence of his role.

Both performances, under Kelly Robinson's direction, are well- oiled but glib, signalling what the end of an episode will be before it has arrived. Of course, sizeable elements of this story have already been a musical. They called it Ragtime.

Comparisons of Paula Vogel's Desdemona: A Play About a Handkerchief (also American, vintage 1993) to Tom Stoppards Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead seem to me inept. Stoppard played absolutely fair with his Shakespearean source, figure- skating with the plot and characters of Hamlet while keeping them scrupulously intact; Vogel takes the three female characters of Othello and changes everything except their names and elements of their dramatic situation.

Before somebody points out that Shakespeare was just as high- handed with his own sources: His plays stand up in their own right, while Vogels absolutely depends on our knowledge of the original.

The result is tawdry and rather confusing. It also, by leaving all the men offstage, never engages with its real conflict.

The big joke is that this Desdemona seems to have slept with every man in Venice and Cyprus except Cassio. She also stands in, or lies down, for the prostitute Bianca on busy nights. Does this mean, the play indignantly asks -- or the publicity tells us that it asks - - that she therefore deserved to be murdered? (No, it doesn't. Next question.) Meanwhile, Emilia has been downgraded from Desdemona's trusty servant to her exploited laundress.

The play does make the occasional neat point about class, if not about sex, and Sue Miners production is as good as may be, given the painful inadequacy of two-thirds of the cast. Sarah Nevilles cockney Bianca, whose dialogue seems to traverse the erotic slang of three centuries, is marginally less excruciating than Anita La Selva's odious English deb of a Desdemona. (The author calls for the accents, but one hopes she didn't want them done this crudely.)

Brooke Johnson plays Emilia Irish and is far better at it -- and at everything else. But then Emilia always was the best role. Shakespeare's Desdemona, though, was a far more independent character than the one we get here, and her willow scene makes a far stronger feminist -- or just human -- statement than anything this play can come up with.

Still, Vogel went on to write the far superior How I Learned to Drive, so there can be such a thing as progress.

Until March 3. (416) 504-9971

CHEKHOV LONGS ... IN THE RAVINE

Factory Theatre Studio

- - -

The troupe known as Theatre Smith-Gilmour follow up its successful Chekhovs Shorts with Chekhov Longs. Note the subtle change in punctuation. The new show is uneven, but with searing moments of greatness.

The earlier program framed and adapted a bunch of the Russian master's short stories; it was omnibus theatre. The new piece concentrates on a single tale: the In the Ravine that gives the production its subtitle.

This staged novella, unlike the familiar Chekhov plays, concerns the peasants, not the gentry. We are introduced to the family of the Tsybukins, villagers who in the Russia of 1900 have done pretty well for themselves. They owe their prosperity to old man Tsybukin's talent for swindling his neighbours by selling them off-colour goods.

An ironic sign of this merchants success is that one of his sons, Anisim, has become a policeman. The other son, Stepan, is a simpleton but at least he makes an advantageous marriage. Father himself is encouraged to remarry. Anisim, who must have inherited some of the paternal talents, returns home in murky circumstances and there seems nothing for it but to marry him off as well. From here on, a cheerful narrative turns irreducibly, if still sardonically, tragic.

Theatre S-G is named for, and run by, Dean Gilmour and Michele Smith, who are this productions directors and, with the Company," its adaptors. They first hooked up 24 years ago while studying in Paris with the celebrated Jacques Lecoq, whose name is practically synonymous with modern mime. Their skills in physical performance are formidable and have been passed on to their fellow actors. All present are adept at sketching the physical outline of one person (or, on occasion, an animal) and then doing it just as adeptly for another. A wedding feast provides a showpiece opportunity; the cast switch roles and personalities at the drop -- or, more often, at the wearing -- of a hat.

They are less good -- at least Smith and Gilmour are less good -- at delivering text; and this play, which, despite the aesthetic trimmings, is a pretty straightforward rendering of its source, has a lot of text. Smith has a distractingly heavy French accent, though she still provides an amusing cartoon of the feckless Anisim.

Gilmour -- the only male on hand -- is more of a problem. He plays the central role of Tsybukin pere; he is also our host, establishing the village setting at the start with the aid of a couple of bricks. (The image is apt; brickmaking is the basis of the local economy, and a cruelly hard trade.) But his performance in both guises lacks weight and colour; also, though he has a reputation as a clown and favours us with a variety of conspiratorial smiles, he is not very funny. He is silently impressive at the end, when Tsybukin is a broken man, but he has not had much to fall from.

Three actresses complete the cast. Anne-Marie Kerr is properly agreeable as the new, and kindly, stepmother. The real excitement, though, comes from her daughters-in-law. Aksinya, the clever wife of stupid Stepan, is very reminiscent of another Chekhov character, the arriviste cuckoo Natasha, who fouls the nest of those politely helpless Three Sisters. Like Natasha, Aksinya enters into a family and, in the name of sound business and moral principles, devastates it. Colombe Demers makes her bloodcurdlingly implacable, though the fireworks they provide seem the province of the actress rather than the character. They are not quite rooted.

As a take-over artist, Aksinya gets her golden opportunity when the ex-cop Anisim gets arrested, leaving a bewildered bride, Lipa, who can now be described (and humiliated) as "the convict's wife."

In this role, Liisa Repo-Martell is astonishing. She enters, for inspection by her new family, with a shy smile that is more than an adornment; it seems to be her bodily essence. A person has come upon the stage, fully imagined and fully fleshed, and she remains there.

It is instructive to watch a scene in which she and her father- in-law converse while crossing the fields. The movement has to be stylized, and also true. Gilmour walks like an accomplished mime; Repo-Martell walks like Lipa, earnest, well-meaning, and striving to keep up. Her lamentation at her direst moment -- a sustained off- stage cry, unearthly but all too human -- is as harrowing a sound as I have heard in a theatre. It is like the stories one hears of Laurence Olivier's Oedipus: extremity made manifest.

Repo-Martell can also, as required of all the actors here, break off to assume other roles; and she does it, I think, more fully than any of them. (Her wedding guest, silently gossipy, is a hoot.)

In the three crowded years since she burst upon us, seemingly out of nowhere, in Soulpepper's Platonov, this is the finest work she has done.

To return to the show's punning title: the length can be excessive, the longings are superb.

The Adventures of a Black Girl in Search of God runs until Feb. 23. Box office: 416-973-4000. The Lost Boys runs until March 9. Box office: 416-368-3110.

THE ADVENTURES OF A BLACK GIRL IN SEARCH OF GOD

Du Maurier Theatre, Toronto

- - -

THE LOST BOYS

Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Djanet Sears uses space superbly. The Adventures of a Black Girl in Search of God, of which she is both author and director, unfolds on a deep, bare stage covered in what looks like, but probably isn't, baked sandstone. This design, by Astrid Janson, is wonderfully useful and suggestive, with Paul Mathiesen's lighting magnificently varying the contours. Scene changes, of which there are many, are immaculately handled, as are the movements of a cast of 21, including a singing-dancing chorus. Everyone and everything is in the right place at the right time. The show marks the debut of Obsidian Theatre, a bold new black company; and the overall sense of disciplined, but still spontaneous, conviction is very satisfying.

The play itself, which takes its name but nothing else from Bernard Shaw, is less impressive than the production, though it certainly aims high and wide. Its title character is Rainey, whose only child died at the age of eight and who is, understandably, still reeling. Once a religious seminarian, she turned to a career in obstetrics, then lost that vocation, too. She is divorcing her husband, a minister, though it is obvious they still love one another. She also has to cope with her father, a former judge; he is mortally ill but feisty, and now heads a squad of elderly urban guerrillas whose mission is to snatch demeaning black figurines ("lawn jockeys") from white property and repatriate them.

Down at the front of the stage is a trench, into which the cast periodically and joyously descends. It functions as a mass baptismal font and also stands in for Negro Creek, the Ontario area in which the play is set and whose black population -- recently, historically and successfully -- lobbied against a proposed change of name. The judge sees his own campaign as a continuation of that struggle. He also wishes not only to die at home but to have his funeral there -- an ambition with which Rainey, who is in denial where death is concerned, has considerable trouble.

There is, in fact, a lot going on here, some of it seriously serious. Rainey asks the age-old question about how, if God exists, He can permit evil and suffering. She is no more successful than anyone before her at getting an answer.

Exactly halfway through the play, she tells us the problem is not that she doesn't believe in God, but that she does -- a resonant line, but there is no dramatic progression either toward or away from it. Her husband, on the other hand, does not believe, but he continues in his job as a way of fighting for his community. This irony, once stated, remains unexplored; as does an additional late- blooming plot line concerning racist slogans daubed on his church, not to mention the revelation of an unspoken romance between the judge and one of his team.

Nor do we ever really discover how Rainey finally feels about her father's mannequin-rescue project. She starts by thinking it silly, but finds herself helping out with their most audacious project, a raid on the local museum. This occasions a rather delightful set- piece scene, but it exists purely as family comedy; it doesn't actually get us anywhere. Indeed, all the scenes involving the judge's gang are played for cuteness; they strongly resemble the old British film comedies in which senior citizens conduct lovable heists on fur dealers and jewellery stores.

The only hope of focusing all this is through Rainey's consciousness, but the writing doesn't do that; and neither does Alison Sealy-Smith's businesslike but opaque performance. Both author and actress fail to find a convincing mode for the character's frequent soliloquies. (Is she talking to us? Are we overhearing her? Or what?) All we are left with is a warm, fuzzy feeling when she (I think) finds God by accepting the people around her, including the fact that they die.

Walter Borden and David Collins are excellent as father and husband respectively, and Jackie Richardson makes a boisterous lady activist while also lending her gorgeous voice to musical interludes that range from gospel to scat.

The chorus (directed by Alejandra Nunez, choreographed by Vivine Scarlett) are similarly stirring, though their contributions seem increasingly a diversion from the drama rather than an illumination of it. Sears resembles Peter Shaffer, of all playwrights, in that she imagines scenes better than she writes them. She goes Shaffer several better, though, in staging them herself; and in that respect she realizes her vision to perfection.

There is another downstage trench in The Lost Boys, also designed by Astrid Janson; this one signifies the dugouts of the First World War. Four of R.H. Thomson's great-uncles perished in that fighting - - a fifth survived -- and in this one-man play Thomson tells us their stories, largely through reading their letters home.

There are some obvious objections here: We can hardly be expected to be as interested in his relatives as he is, and 2 1/2 hours (The Lost Boys clocks in slightly shorter than Black Girl) is a long time in which to listen to a single actor. But, for about four-fifths of the time, he surmounts them.

He doesn't help himself by dragging in obscure parallels with relativity theory or with his search for the death site of his own father, killed in a car crash. But he gets considerable assistance from the elaborate symphony of sound, film and lighting effects that has been orchestrated by his director, Jonas Jurasas; only toward the end does this become excessive.

What really counts, though, is Thomson's endless charm and resource in creating his characters, keeping them distinct and establishing his own commenting voice without overimposing it. As an actor with other actors, Thomson can sometimes seem guarded and academic; here he never strikes a false or unfinished note.

Black & White Photo: Glenn Lowson, National Post / Playwright Djanet Sears' The Adventures of a Black Girl in Search of God asks the age- old question: If God exists, how can He permit evil and suffering? ;
2002-02-16-only-one-road-worth-taking:
Road plays till Feb. 24. (416) 533-9231 Hollywood Bound closes tonight.

ROAD

Equity Showcase Theatre

- - -

HOLLYWOOD BOUND

Bathurst Street Theatre

- - -

Road is a fairly good night out about a truly terrible night out. It's set in England during the Thatcher years in a North country town that was once industrial but now, thanks to unemployment, is nothing. A narrator, a tramp called Scullery, invites us to walk with him down the main drag and to peer inside the houses: to look and listen as parents nag at children, husbands yell at wives, and all give back as bad as they get. Most of their energies are targeted at the approaching evening at the disco in the local pub. Already the threat of aimless violence hangs over the street, as does the promise of aimless sex; the local tarts are out in force, and it is hard to tell the amateurs from the professionals.

When I say that we are invited to take a walk, I mean it literally. This is a promenade production, in which the action unfolds in a series of scenes all over the theatre floor and the audience has its attention artfully directed to the next location or merely follows the actors around.

It's a form of staging that serves very well for plays about communities, as opposed to old-fashioned community theatre; we are voyeurs, not participants. It was popularized at the British National Theatre during the 1970s in revivals of medieval mystery plays and adaptations of Victorian novels about small rural towns. These were nostalgic shows; Road, which was produced at the Royal Court in 1986, was the first major attempt to use the technique in a contemporary setting. It was the debut piece of its author, Jim Cartwright (whose later plays include The Rise and Fall of Little Voice) and an instant success.

This Equity Showcase production mixes professional actors with graduating students of the George Brown Theatre School, and here, too, it can be hard to tell the amateurs from the pros. Everybody is very committed and adept. Everybody also sounds amazingly authentic: congratulations to Debora Joy, the dialogue coach, but the conviction here goes beyond vowel sounds. In Mark Wilson's production, the men tread barroom sawdust, the women flash suspenders, to the manner born.

All the same, the play, despite the premium it places on immediacy, seems remote, and I don't mean historically or geographically; we can understand these people, and we do not imagine things have changed much for them in the last 15 years. We start, sharply enough, with a young woman ironing her dress for the night while her mother shouts abuse and demands her money.

That sets the tone; the play's humour, which is real, is all rooted in insult or humiliation. When the author wants to prove that he has a heart, he writes lyrical speeches that certainly don't work as realism and aren't credible as a heightened expression of what the people might actually be feeling. "Joey's story" announces our host with an air of importance, and we are ushered into the bedroom of a young unemployed man who sees no reason to get up, ever, and of his wife who wonders where their lives have gone. You feel for their situation but not really for them.

The show's second half, when the joyless partying is over, contains a record dramatic amount of throwing up. A more or less catatonic soldier has been taken home by an overweight woman and just sits there while she tries to arouse him. There is obviously supposed to be a balance here of grotesquerie and pathos; what we actually get is a sustained leer followed by a brief bout of sentimentality.

The last big scene corrals two young men and two young women. The boys try routine seduction, the girls decide they want something more. So the boys give it to them: they pour gallons of wine and put on Otis Redding singing Try a Little Tenderness. This double stimulus induces a state of heightened awareness, prompting a series of truth-telling soliloquies. As an idea this is reasonable, but the actual words -- culminating in a group cry of "somehow I might escape" -- sound like things the author would like his people to say, rather than things they actually would.

The joylessness is laid on artificially thick, though some of this may have to do with Christopher Morris's performance as Scullery. He is a young actor worth watching but his performance here is a walking gloat with a scowl attached. His best moment comes outside the play proper; during the intermission we move to another room, representing the pub. Here Scullery is inveigled into singing Over the Rainbow. He does it beautifully (and, what's more, a cappella), conjuring up all the innocence that the song and, presumably the play, ache for.

The same anthem crops up in Hollywood Bound, a peculiarly aimless tale that originated at The Georgian Theatre Festival, where it was apparently known as The Company Cabaret: Meaford Goes to the Movies - - a more tactfully modest title in the circumstances. The new name looks especially rash when we see it emblazoned on the suitcases that the company of eight all insist on carrying early in the show. Their opening number, as you might have guessed, is Hooray for Hollywood, and you never saw so much choreographed hand-waving and knee-trembling in your life.

A through-line seems threatened but it rapidly disappears, as does any idea we might be paying tribute to the golden age of Hollywood musicals. Most of the stuff sung here is from films of the last 30 years: a period in which movie songs have, almost without exception, been dreck. Sometimes the show seems aware of this. A performance of the song from Titanic skewers not only the awful number and its awful singer but the conceit of the whole damn movie.

Krista Sutton, whose performance here is the bright spot of the show's first half, returns to even better effect in the second, when she tells Doris Day exactly what she can do with Que Sera Sera. That's just about it for wit, though Sandy Winsby, who seems to be the most experienced player around, manages to sing the song from Love Story with dignity. (No, I wouldn't have believed it either.)

The other performances come in various shades of gauche; sometimes this seems intentional, as when plump young Ken McClure sings the bashful Suddenly Seymour (from Little Shop of Horrors). He's also the one who does Over the Rainbow, in which he gives an accurate impersonation of Mandy Patinkin, whose overwrought interpretation seems to be supplanting Judy Garland's in the popular imagination, which is not a good omen. Nor is this show's benighted belief that it can take You Are Woman, I Am Man -- a funny song from Funny Girl -- and make it work by playing jokes other than the ones the authors had in mind.

Two even weirder examples of slapdashery: 1) Kevin P. Patterson, the show's writer (of what, exactly?) and director, wanders on at arbitrary moments during the first half to make announcements but is never seen in the second; 2) one of the songs is The Best of Times Is Here, which was never a movie song no how. It does, though, herald the intermission, so it might be accused of having relevance.

THE PIPER

Factory Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Colleen Murphy's new play takes up the old and frightening story of the Pied Piper, who lured a townful of rats into a mass watery grave and a townful of children into the intestines of a mountain. The Necessary Angel company and the Factory Theatre have pooled resources to employ 20 actors -- all of them good, and some of them among the best in town. Richard Rose has turned in a smartly drilled production, and Teresa Przybylski has designed mordantly mischievous sets and costumes. Don Horsburgh has composed a good if abbreviated musical score. So much talent can seldom have been so profligately abused.

To blame the author is also to sympathize with her, since she is one of her own principal victims. She has had a piercing insight into the original legend and what it might mean to us now, and has gone and buried it under a load of words -- long, elephantine words that seem intended to serve as social satire. (Some of the heavy- handedness may be the directors fault. Either he lacks a sense of humour or I do. Id say that on the first night the audience was on my side; there was little laughter, and what there was sounded scattered and self-conscious.) At the play's centre, panting for life, is a fable of institutionalized child abuse: A pampered society professes to love its children but actually neglects them and deserves to lose them.

It begins well, with an encounter between representatives of the play's two principal classes of victim. Tod, young son of the Deputy Mayor of Hamelin, meets Kingsley, described in the program (which tends, in pantomime style, to be more amusing than the play) as an Introspective King Rat." Kingsley, who sounds as if he once nested in the London School of Economics, knows intellectually about the depravity of the world but can never quite believe it when it happens, especially when it happens to him. When he quotes Nietzsche (which he does, repeatedly) you believe not only that he has read him but that he could, in a pinch, spell him; which is more than you could say for anyone else on stage, with or without a tail.

This is painfully demonstrated by the subsequent arrival of the Town Councillors, a round dozen of them. Their first appearance, rising from the ground to peer en masse over the edges of their conference table, is something of a coup, but everything else about them is agonizingly predictable, and they sink the play.

They are all corrupt, incompetent and competitively ambitious; and they equate polysyllables with wit. We know within five minutes that their author loathes them, but she has to keep them around in order to tell her story. So there they are, striking the same attitudes over and over: a cross between Friedrich Durrenmatt and Toytown.

The Mayor, humorously christened Pops Poppenheimer, is plainly meant to make us think of Mel with a dash of Mike; he presides over an administration that has sold off all the towns essential services, making itself vulnerable to rats and pipers alike.

To show the plays open-handedness there are a couple of hard- line feminists, belonging to a group calling itself Mothers Against Fathers, and an equally hidebound Russian lady who goes weak-kneed and dewy-eyed at the mention of Stalin. There must be more timely ways of satirizing the Left.

In the Robert Browning poem, from which most of us know the story, the Mayor and Corporation are the Pied Piper's undifferentiated antagonists. Corporation of course means something different to us than it did to the Victorians, and there is a clumsy song here to push the point.

In this version the corporate in-fighting takes up so much time that the evening is half over before the traditional action has started. The rats here are not an unwanted plague; they are an exploited underclass who come in useful as workers and, sometimes, as scapegoats. So when young Tod disappears, his father and mother - - who have been too busy with their own affairs, private and public, to take any notice of him -- find it convenient to blame the rats. They rise in revolt, and extermination is decreed. There is a horrible clashing of gears here, as between the old and new stories - - a conflict exemplified by the play's indecision as to whether its rats are people or rodents; it wants them both ways.

Anyway, this zany-looking young guy has wandered on stage, as unobtrusively as may be considering he wears a funny suit and plays a funny flute. (He also has a thing about insects.) Pink, the Mayors understandably bratty daughter, falls for him. Pops is furious but allows the match when the Piper, shyly and under duress, offers the traditional rat-disposal deal. He delivers, the furry guys drown, the town welshes, the piper takes the kids. And here, finally, the play begins to make emotional and intellectual sense.

When you read the poem, the disappearance of a townful of children registers as a pleasantly chilling cautionary tale. It is quite another thing when you have met a few of them and can imagine them vanishing just off stage; when you wonder whether Pink, the only one youve got to know, will escape being her own lover's victim; when you can actually see and hear the bereaved parents, however nasty they may be as individuals.

We remember that, in the council meetings, their main preoccupation was finding baby-sitters; they never wanted to spend the time themselves. They deserve what they get. And it shouldn't happen to anyone. This is provocative; and a second encounter between Tod and Kingsley, both of whom have endured a lot, rounds it symmetrically off. But you have to wade through a lot of facetious rubbish en route.

As for the actors, they are in there, wading with you. Julian Richings dominates as Kingsley, tirelessly reasonable even in the direst of extremities. This rat seems to have nearly as many lives as a cat, and needs them. Mostly we are glad to see him, though there are limits; at about the fourth resurrection I thought I detected a groan, suppressed but unanimous, all around the auditorium.

Melody Johnson is toughly interesting as Pink, Adam Kelly pleasantly spineless as the Piper (a Wandering Minstrel he, according to the program), and Rick Roberts and Maggie Huculak fight very fiercely as the selfish parents, who sometimes seem to have stepped out of another play.

Victor Ertmanis is better than I have ever seen him as the Mayor, a sadistic bumbler but with a few more qualms than his colleagues about the exercise of arbitrary power. The funniest of the town- hall bunch, with an unsteady walk and a crazy gleam in his eye, is Ross Manson as a sozzled preacher firing off tirades against the media.

Maria Vacratsis is criminally misused as the Stalinist, Richard McMillan scarcely less so as a nondescript functionary who always wanted children and finally gets to adopt a dozen of them; but his gently agonized expression as they, too, dance into oblivion finally justifies his presence.

The play is also a sort of musical, and Horsburghs music is stronger than Murphys words. The rats get a marching song that is dead-on Brecht-Weill. There is a love song for Pink that is icily melodic; and the Piper's tune turns out to be genuinely haunting.

CHRISTMAS AT THE IVANOVS

Poor Alex Theatre

- - -

Dancing into town, hot on the heels of The Piper, comes Cats, again. The Piper is largely about rats; Cats is entirely about cats - - which is its problem. (If there are any other fur-and-whiskery musicals, hovering and ready to pounce, could somebody please lock them up?)

Criticizing Cats at this stage is obviously like shooting kittens in a barrel. Here, however, goes.

Nobody will believe this, but when Cats opened in London -- way, way back in 1981 -- I enjoyed it. I even thought it was a good show. This had little to do with its position in the canon of Andrew Lloyd Webber, who had written better theatre music before (Evita) and would do so again (The Phantom of the Opera). It had a lot to do with Trevor Nunn, whose first commercial production this was.

Nunn was moonlighting from his job as director of the Royal Shakespeare Company for whom he had staged a sequence of wonderfully funny and/or moving productions, culminating in the epochal Nicholas Nickleby. There was a distinctive warmth about all of these shows (even Macbeth); they exuded a delighted trust in the resources of actors, audiences and the theatre itself.

Cats, an ensemble musical full of ragamuffin cheerfulness, was an extension of that tradition; unlike the later Les Miserables, which was a travesty of it.

Nunn plainly had a lot to do with that spirit. Though, since the show is not only through-sung but through-danced, much of the actual staging must have been the work of the choreographer, Gillian Lynne. But that was all right, too; in 1981, we were thrilled to see a British musical that could dance.

Cats, despite its cost and its spectacle, was originally an unpretentious show. When it opened in New York, it acquired a new layer of glitz, and lost some personality. (Also, some native colour. Cats is hardly community theatre but still, when a show's lyrics refer to Pall Mall and the Russell Hotel, it helps to have a cast with some idea of what and where they might be.)

Now, in the umpteenth touring version, restaged by Richard Stafford, we have tired glitz: a lethal combination. The current cast leap around a lot and seem very conscientious about it, but what they display is not so much energy as -- to borrow a distinction from Hal Prince, and one I cherish -- energeticness.

The dancing looks far less impressive than it once did. In fact, it looks startlingly ordinary: sub-Fosse routines only distinguished by the funny clothes the dancers are wearing and the length of time they keep going. (At the London premiere, the big Jellicle Ball number was greeted by wild applause and a piercing voice shouting Rubbish! Twenty years on, I have to acknowledge that the solitary heckler was right.)

One vital element that has gone missing is the original semi- environmental staging. John Napiers junkyard set and David Herseys lighting remain and are the most distinguished features of the show, but Napier's work is diminished by being stuck behind a proscenium. It's still a charming moment when a giant human boot descends from the flies to establish the physical scale of the proceedings; its even more delightful to notice that a discarded car licence plate bears the first three letters of the designers name; and the opening lightshow of cats' eyes gleaming in the dark to eerie electronic chords remains enticing. That, though, is before a single performer actually appears on the stage.

I said that the problem with Cats is that it actually is about cats. Well, all right, you and I, we should have such record- breakingly remunerative problems. But look here, the verses in Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats, the T. S. Eliot jeu desprit that supplied the shows inspiration and furnished its lyrics, are not about cats. They're about people, English types whimsically dressed up as cats, and it's their humanity that is the point. (Such as it is. The Eliot verses arent actually very good. They certainly arent very funny.)

In the show, all the effort goes into turning the humans back into cats. Satire has been sacrificed to cuteness. This has paid off commercially, to put it mildly. It's probably the ultimate tourist show. But it's hugely redundant.

People say that the trouble with Cats is it hasnt got a plot. Actually, the trouble is that it does have one. It isnt content to be a series of feline revue spots. It tries to link them together. So Macavity the Mystery Cat ("the Napoleon of crime") kidnaps Old Deuteronomy, who has to be miraculously brought back by the Magical Mr. Mistoffeles. The interim sequence in which the company moons about the stage, intoning we have to find Old Deuteronomy (a non- Eliot line) to an especially drab musical setting, has to be one of the most woeful moments in the history of the musical theatre. (It reminds you of the days when "English" meant amateur.)

More ambitiously, we have the reincarnation motif. One cat will ascend to kitty heaven on an outsized tire and come back after the show as somebody else. The choice falls on Grizabella, the scarcely seen Glamour Cat, who exists only to sing Memory and who we assume has had too many encounters with the wrong kind of Tom. (I don't, of course, mean Mr. Eliot). I would like to think that she is chosen so that she may return as somebody who won't keep singing that infernal song.

Its the scores low point, though Webber seems hamstrung throughout. He once declared that the poems' insistent rhythms practically dictated the tunes. He apparently thought this was a good thing; it isn't. This score should finally have silenced those who use "hummable" and memorable as terms of musical praise. I cant get the pounding melody of Mr. Mistoffeles out of my head. That doesnt mean I wouldn't like to.

- - -

Talk Is Free Theatre is a welcome new group, mainly composed of recent graduates from George Brown. Christmas at the Ivanovs, their initial production, is a Russian play from the late 1920s, banned at the rise of Stalin. It makes savage fun of the festive season, depicting a family (who are not called the Ivanovs) of the late Czarist era who go on being seasonably festive, even as each of them in succession drops dead.

Why attacks on Christmas under the old regime should have disturbed Stalin I don't know; I guess he was just a sentimental slob. But he certainly didnt like anarchy, and this play is determinedly anarchic, if that isnt a contradiction in terms (Even if it is, that never seems to have bothered the experimental theatre.)

The play also satirizes the police, the judiciary and the practice of locking accused people up in madhouses. The play was written by Alexander Vedensky. Additional material is credited by Daniil Kharms.

The Serbian-born director, Aleksandar Lukac, also adapted and, on top of all this, some of the actors are plainly making it up as they go along. In these circumstances it is difficult to assign praise and blame. Blame is due because the show's tendency to wander off into byways, and then into byways off those byways, can become more irritating than amusing. I don't want to upset anyone, but the characters have a related habit of disappearing up one anothers intestines, literally.

On the other hand, some bits, notably in the performances of Michelle Polak and Michaela Hayek, are genuinely chilling. Others are hilarious: There is one actor who looks, from certain fortunate angles, like Eric Idle, and -- with my mind thus set on Pythons -- I would not have been at all surprised to hear somebody say "hes not the Czar-king, he's just a very naughty boy." (Somebody very nearly does.)

Above all there is Kurt Smeaton, a young actor of stern authority and magisterial comic timing, who plays the Narrator. He gets to realize the dreams of actors and audiences everywhere by deconstructing the play and the other performances, while they are going on. He made me laugh uncontrollably. There ain't much fun to be had in Toronto at the moment, and this is worth your attention.

Black & White Photo: Nigel Teare, The Associated Press / A CAST OF CATS: Twenty years later, the flaws in a show that was never that good are really showing. ;

THE EDIBLE WOMAN

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - The protagonist of Margaret Atwood's 1969 novel The Edible Woman spends much of the book engaged to be married. There is a mid-story chapter that begins, "Marian was walking slowly down the aisle, keeping pace with the gentle music." We think for a moment that we have been fast-forwarded to Marian's wedding. It turns out we are accompanying her on a visit to the supermarket. Try bringing that effect off in the theatre. Or even in a movie.

Dave Carley's dramatization, which has arrived in Toronto from the Vancouver Playhouse, doesn't try. This is probably wise, but such wisdom multiplied comes out as folly. Like many such adaptations, this one keeps the narrative, most of the characters and even the dialogue, but loses the overall tone. In other words, it sacrifices what made the original worth reading in the first place -- in this case its wit -- and has nothing of its own to offer in exchange.

Marian, in her twenties, works for a consumer-research company; it's taken for granted she will have to leave when she marries. Her fiance, Peter, is a sleek young lawyer with the marks of success already upon him. On one of her questionnairing quests Marian meets Duncan, a preternaturally self-absorbed graduate student; he becomes Peter's rival, more in her head than in her bed.

Meanwhile, her roommate, Ainsley, has decided she wants a baby but not a husband and sets about seducing Marian's old college friend Len into performing the necessary biological operation; he, when he finds out what he has got into, is horrified. (He took Ainsley for a virgin -- a tribute to her acting skills. He prefers virgins. He shudders at the whole messy idea of birth.)

Under all these professional and emotional pressures Marian comes, horrified, to see herself as something to be consumed. She begins to identify herself with her food and -- in sympathy, as it were -- virtually stops eating.

The novel is in three parts. The first is narrated by Marian herself; the second is still seen entirely from her point of view, but told in the third person, as if she were now conducting a survey on herself; at the end, some resolution achieved, she's back on first. It's a puzzling device while you're reading, but it finally falls into place.

The play tries to reproduce it: Marian still narrates, and, in theory, the switch in pronouns should have a powerfully estranging theatrical effect. (Shall we forget the word "alienation"? Oh, I'm sorry, you already have.) In practice, it just glides by. This may have something to do with the central performance.

Marian is repeatedly said to be capable and intelligent, and the story loses all interest if she's played as some kind of idiot ingenue. Jillian Fargey goes through the first half of the evening on a simper; by the time she suggests some strength and intelligence, it's too late. Marian recalls that in her student days she scuppered an incipient relationship by making an ironic remark. The woman we see hardly seems capable of an ironic thought.

Some of the book's other characters have been conflated -- more, I imagine, in the cause of financial than of artistic economy. Ainsley now not only lives with Marian but works with her. Her other colleagues, the three "office virgins," are reduced to one who also doubles, improbably, as her supervisor. Duncan's two male room- mates, whom he humorously describes as his parents, are now also one.

If Duncan is half-orphaned, then so is the play; it feels drastically under-populated. This goes especially for a party scene in which everybody is meant to collide and pair off; designed as farce with underpinnings, it now just seems arbitrary. The introduction of a line of cardboard cut-outs to represent the actual guests is a real act of desperation.

There is a lot that seems desperate in Timothy Bond's production; it doesn't so much plan its effects as settle for them. We start with a tableau: Peter in the bath, fully clothed and humping (there really is no other word) an absent Marian. She's absent because she's at the side of the stage, telling us about it. But we don't concentrate on her commentary or on her detachment from her own body. We only register how crass Peter looks; and maybe we laugh and maybe we don't. It sets a tone all right, but it's the wrong one; it's the show that seems crass. (The incident is taken from the book, but it appears there at a later point and to more elegantly glancing effect.)

Later we get elaborate, and totally unnecessary, commuter scenes, to frame -- and obscure -- purely functional exchanges of information. They do nothing to create a sense of place or of time. The use of '60s songs (Atwood's text seems totally impervious to pop culture) does nothing to help us adjust to a world at once so like our own and so different from it, and Charlotte Dean's minimalist sets are garishly unhelpful.

The props, in a similar vein, are all mimed -- with one important, and obviously purposeful, exception. At the end Marian, in a gesture of self-exorcism, bakes a cake in the shape of a woman, and this we are allowed to see, though not very well. It is, after all, hardly a stage-size image. Even on the page it seems effortful, but there it doesn't matter as much. Drama may not be a higher form than the novel, but it is certainly a harder one; to use the appropriate imagery, one swallows a novelist's suggestions but one's stomach rebels when they take physical form on a stage. There, you have to believe.

Belief in this case is not much assisted by the acting, which is seriously substandard, certainly for this address. Tara Samuel is just about all right as Ainsley, and Daren Keay rather good as Duncan, though he is more your standard bohemian youth than the seriously creepy figure the author seems to have envisaged.

Alec McClure is compelled to play Len with a caricature of an English accent on the flimsy grounds that he has recently returned from working in the UK; given this, it would surely make sense for him to lose it when he, so to speak, loses it -- i.e. when the contemplation of Ainsley's fecundity reduces him to hysteria.

Lynne Cormack is doubly atrocious as the vestigial virgin (grimly cartooned) and as the heroines' censorious landlady. The latter character has been stripped of her original, more flavourful appellation of "the lady down below," which would counterpoint her with Marian's unseen bosses, "the men upstairs." This is hardly the most damaging decision of the evening, but it is one of the less accountable.

THE PIRATE WIDOW CHENG

Tarragon Extra Space

- - -

The magnificent Ronnie Burkett has raised the bar dauntingly high for practitioners of puppet plays. That's puppet plays as opposed to puppet shows. Burkett's achievements as a maker and manipulator of dolls are breathtaking, but they are not what you think about when you watch him at it. You concentrate on his accomplishments as actor and playwright.

In The Pirate Widow Cheng, the brother-and-sister team of Ann and David Powell enter these challenging lists and are defeated. Their previous productions have been for children, but they are attempting here to tell a grownup story with historical roots. Their technical skills are undeniable, though what they do here comes over as expert rather than exciting. Besides, it isn't the focus of attention. In this show the puppeteers are as much in view as the puppets, and -- as immediately becomes clear -- their talents do not extend to acting.

Nor, apparently, to writing. The script they have provided is sketchy in outline, cliched in detail. But we can't just ignore it and concentrate on the visuals. There is the outline of a story here, and -- like any audience given a sniff of a narrative -- we want to follow it and would love to be interested in it.

It certainly looks good on paper. The future Widow Cheng was a 19th-century Chinese entrepreneur who was sold into prostitution as a child but whose lot in life dramatically improved when she married a pirate. (Or, more accurately perhaps, when he married her.) He was good at his job but she proved better. Mr. Cheng's pirate fleet seems already to have ruled the waves, even in the face of the Imperial Navy itself. Mrs. Cheng turned it into big business, an armed extortion racket that earned the tacit co-operation of the Chinese government and may well have been less corrupt. Like a model capitalist, the widow retired while still at the top of her game and devoted herself to good works.

The most interesting thing about the Powells' presentation is their use of space. They occupy the whole stage floor. Black-clad, they move between an array of tables on which their wooden company - - who run into dozens -- are displayed. Two of these tables are later pushed together to create a ship: sort of like the forming of the barricade in Les Miserables, but with less fanfare.

Like Japanese Bunraku masters, the Powells let us see them manipulating their characters, but they are not purists. They employ a variety of techniques: at one point a whole sea battle is fought in shadow-play. Naturally this is impressive; or at least you feel it ought to be. But then it's over and you're stuck again listening to the presenters' voices.

Obviously, you don't go to a puppet show in order to listen. Except that, even at the humblest level, you do. Anyone who has been to a Punch and Judy show ("that's the way to do it") can vouch for that. And the Powells have a lot to say.

There is a framework in which, with miniature full-length suits hung from their necks like vests, they impersonate two published experts: Jorge Luis Borges, who turned the widow's tale into a short story and is played earnestly effete, and a Professor Dian H. Murray, who put him right on his departures from historical fact and is played anemically stern. (I don't know about Professor Murray but Borges certainly deserves better.)

They have no more authority when they turn to impersonating the pirates; the Powells, who apparently are British, play them in a kind of denatured Cockney accent. There are rude words aplenty, but the rhythm and spirit of slang are missing.

The same goes for the displays of violence (Mr. Punch still rules) and the cheerful acknowledgement, and occasional demonstration, of homosexuality below decks: The creators seem to be enjoying their sabbatical from playing for kids, but they still seem like pedagogues. It's very BBC.

So the characters never come to life. The principal puppets are striking enough at first glance -- both Orientally and marionettishly inscrutable -- but they don't grow in our imaginations; they never achieve the state of grace in which puppets seem to change expression. The performers exude a sense of unearned cheeriness; a story that might be worth hearing remains, for practical purposes, untold.

THE GOOD LIFE

Tarragon Theatre

- - -

Daniel Brooks's play The Good Life contains an amusing scene in which an actor gives an interview about a show he is currently rehearsing. This actor is also a playwright, though he hasnt written the play that hes puffing. This makes him the opposite number to Brooks himself, who has also been known to act but here functions only as author and director. (Directing is what he is best known for.) To add to the fun, the fictitious actor/playwright is called Dan.

Dan makes some pertinent remarks about the directions in which an audience's mind might wander while they're watching him on-stage. They might, for example, start thinking about the theatres splendid new washrooms: a line that went down especially well with the knowing first-night audience at the Tarragon, a theatre that has itself recently undergone just such a facelift.

You will have realized by now that The Good Life is a self- conscious play. Dan even tells his interviewer that nothing he says should be taken too seriously since he is just playing an acknowledged game, undertaken for publicity purposes only. Its decent of Brooks to put it that way, since he himself has been very articulate in interviews (and, to a lesser extent, in the program) about his intentions in this play. It's nice to know we don't have to take his pronouncements seriously.

Its always tempting to review plays in terms of their advance buildup, and I really should stop doing it, but some shows seem to ask for it. The Good Life is a play about love, or at least a play in which the characters make a lot of speeches about love. This is not a subject on which definite conclusions are to be expected -- though some distinction between "love" and being in love might be appreciated -- and Brooks has described his play as unfinished: structurally and intellectually a work-in-progress. This, he is honest enough to admit, is true of most plays; all artistic practitioners (this even includes reviewers) are likely to have further thoughts and to go on having them. Its the way things are.

That being the case, what's the big deal about this particular play, and why should an audience care? Audiences, skeptical but incorrigible, will have noticed by now that most plays have loose ends and frustrating final curtains; the most they expect is something that will be lively and engaging enough to keep their minds off those new washrooms. The audience, always and inevitably, is part of the theatrical transaction, but they aren't the ones who are there to do the work, and demands that they should pull their socks up and participate more always strike me as pretty dumb. The moment an audience tries to like or understand something, you have lost it.

The Good Life is part entertaining, part boring; the entertainment (there are good jokes) counts for a lot while youre watching, but the boredom is what you resentfully remember when its over. That passion fades, or that spouses stray, is not a revelation; we need to know about the people.

Dan is married to Gina, herself an actress. They sometimes seem about to take centre stage in an interesting play, one that is regularly derailed by the need to counterpoint their relationship with that of their also-married friends, Chris and Mary. One of these marriages looks happy, the other keeps erupting into fights, often in public; and, wouldn't you know, it's the miserable pair who stay together and the contented pair who split. There are also two younger characters; each arrives to chat up Dan for media purposes, and each serves as an erotic catalyst.

Dan is an articulate charmer in whom romantic love serves as a camouflage for selfishness. (I would like to add "or vice versa" but there is little evidence for it.) He even gets the play started -- very well -- with an acknowledgment, disarming in context though not thereafter, of the controlling role of his own ego. He is played by Guillermo Verdecchia; this makes a vital contribution to the general hall-of-mirrors effect, since Verdecchia was Brookss writing and performing partner for The Noam Chomsky Lectures, and other things.

He is beguiling at the outset, quietly insolent and self- possessed, and increasingly irritating later on when hes still quietly insolent and self-possessed. This may be because Dan emerges not just as a bastard but as a shallow bastard; he says things like our children don't belong to us, they belong to Disney, which sounds smart but isn't. (How many kids do you know who are truly owned -- not influenced, owned -- by pop culture?)

It may also be because Verdecchias range is limited; he can talk, he can even get angry, but he cant suffer, and the play does seem to want us to feel for him. Maybe he's a performer, not an actor.

The same may well be true of Bob Martin (the lanky comedian who plays Chris and whom I remember as the narrator in The Drowsy Chaperone), but for him it works. In the first place, his timing gleams; and in the second the man he plays is as wrapped up in his own ideas as was the Chaperone chap in his records of old musicals. The two performances are remarkably similar but both are truthful. Martin, in good, wry, stand up fashion, even rises to the challenge of a final oration in which he details the stages by which a physical love may be transformed into the love of an ideal: something of which he approves. His wife furiously dismisses this as plagiarized Plato, which seems about right.

Actually the whole play, according to its author, is modelled on a Platonic dialogue. (Not "platonic" in the vulgar sense, except that if you're talking about sex you probably arent doing it, at least not at that moment.) He also acknowledges many other sources, from Jane Austen to Ingmar Bergman. One he doesnt list is Tom Stoppard, whose The Real Thing much resembles The Good Life in its musings on love both licensed and adulterous, in its juxtaposition of two marriages, and in its autobiographical allusions; it also plays, though more whole-heartedly, with the relationship between life and theatre.

I am not accusing Brooks of pillaging Stoppard, merely pointing out that Stoppard had already covered much of the same territory, while managing to tell a story (The Good Life has just enough of one to be frustrating) and to depict characters who are more than mouthpieces. I should add, in fairness to Brooks's advocacy of ongoing creation, that I disliked The Real Thing when it first appeared and only appreciated it the second time around, though I would attribute this to a superior production; I don't think the text changed.

Brookss own production here is both nifty and stately, with scenes suggestively superimposed on other scenes and a satisfying use of microphones for the big speeches, one by each major character. Tamsin Kelsey (Gina) and Tracy Wright (Mary) as the wives have more physical presence than their partners but are starved for material, Wright especially. She is allowed to shout but Kelsey gets to smoulder and be decisive. Waneta Storms has little substantial to do as the lady interviewer, whose role in the action is ambiguous going on confusing; as her male counterpart, Luke Kirby has even less.

He does, however, get to deliver the evenings best line, one in which he takes aim at Dan's own writing and -- by an implication that the audience laps up -- at the play in which he figures. (That Daniel Brooks: He covers every base.) I also liked Dan's observation that it isn't subtext most plays lack, it's supertext. Too right.

BUNCHA' YOUNG ARTISTS FESTIVAL

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, Toronto

How do you dramatize an actual, recent and bloody event and explore rather than exploit it? Adam Pettle, who made an auspicious debut last year as the author of Zadie's Shoes, tackles that question in his new short play, Misha. Until about halfway through I doubted he'd cracked it. Then he does -- and rides triumphantly home.

Misha must have been at least inspired, if that's the word, by the Toronto murder of 15-year-old Matti Baranovsky, swarmed and killed when he refused to surrender a packet of cigarettes. It's presented as part of the Buncha' Young Artists Festival, a season of one-act plays presented by Theatre Direct, which specializes in plays by youthful writers aimed at yet more youthful audiences and which alternates between taking plays into schools and having the schools come to them. Not enough people get to see their shows. Their best work is excellent by any standard (I have to declare an interest: My wife is president of the board), and this play belongs with their best.

The author seizes on the fact that Matti, his assailants and the friends who were with him and were scared away were all Jewish. Misha is now the victim's name. This is a three-character play, with friends and killers reduced to one each.

Max, the friend, is also the narrator, plagued by nightmares ever since the event. Max recalls how Misha, a Russian immigrant, kept silent for his first three years in Canadian school, how he learned English from videos of Hollywood musicals, how he loved to play Shostakovich on the piano, how he was nervously preparing for a belated bar mitzvah (the earliest his parents could afford) and how he enthusiastically looked forward to losing his virginity on the weekend that proved to be his last.

How much of this is rooted in fact I don't know, but much of it seemed forced. We know, as we watch him in flashback, that he is going to die; and in the face of that brute certainty, psychology and human interest feel irrelevant, just as Max's traumas seem initially beside the point, the kind of thing you invent to fill out a play. We take Max's word that Misha was a nice, funny, intelligent boy, but would it have been any less horrific had he been none of these things?

The temperature changes when a Hebrew prayer is spoken and all three characters chime in on the "Amen." There is a chilling bond here. Its other face is Jewish anti-Semitism, expressed humorously by Max and Misha -- like many Jewish kids, they're embarrassed by their relatives -- and murderously by Aaron, the killer. He has fought in the Israeli army, (as did one of the youths in the Baranovsky case) and Misha attracts his animosity by seeming to personify Jewish submissiveness. In fact, he stands his ground; he has done enough running. It's Max, the streetwise Max, who runs and suffers for it ever after. (It's never explained why, having escaped, he didn't call 911.)

Max reflects that there is just one thing about Aaron he can respect: He didn't go on television and seek absolution through repentance. Neither did Max himself; but apparently everybody else in the school who had so much as clapped eyes on the deceased lined up to regale the chat shows with their memories. ("Misha once held open the cafeteria door for me." Cool.)

Pettle has a brilliant handle on grief culture, and the more the play opens up to wider issues, the more incisively the personal details strike home. Misha is not the central character -- Max is -- but he earns his titular position by being the figure in relation to whom all the other characters, seen and unseen, define themselves. The play takes on an independent life that is more than topical, more than anecdotal.

Zadie's Shoes showed Pettle's mastery of Jewish humour; the jokes here jar to begin with, but they get truly funnier as the play gets darker. (The bar mitzvah stories are a riot.) The closing sections of the play fall like hammer-blows, Max replaying the fatal encounter in his mind, over and over, trying to make it come out differently and always being brought up against the brick-wall truth.

Richard Greenblatt's production matches the tautness of the play, and the performances of Miklos Perlus (Max) and Daniel Stemer (Misha) grow with the writing. Aaron is hulkingly, loomingly embodied by Jacob Barker, who makes his first entrance swinging on a crossbar, commando-style. The play accords him a certain pity and a certain respect, and in so doing says something about the nature of terrorism and of counterterrorism; it may be timelier now than when it was first conceived. It does not dignify history -- what, in this case, could? -- but it does not degrade it either.

I saw one other Buncha' play last week: Martian Summer, by a Quebec writer, Nathalie Boisvert, translated (though it never sounds like a translation) by Bobby Theodore. This is another play about two kids growing up in shared solitude and another play that crucially involves smoking, though not of tobacco.

Peanut, a loner because she wears bifocals, and Kiko, an outcast because of a home life that is desperate to non-existent, are initially drawn together by a common hatred of dodgeball. Peanut is scared of the world, Kiko is mad at it; their friendship develops around a tabloid story they have read about an imminent landing by aliens.

They determine to meet the ship, reasoning that life in a distant galaxy has got to be better than here; in the linear, literal way in which they regard their fantasies, they might be an updated, transgendered Tom and Huck.

Peanut has a severely handicapped sister -- "a vegetable" -- and the two girls drag her with them to the meeting place, with predictably dire results.

This play, too, grows as it goes. It starts as just another rite- of-passage piece -- we are inured to plays about disadvantaged youngsters pooling their physical and psychological resources, and there is generally something voyeuristic about them -- but it becomes altogether richer and stranger. You get caught up in it. The wilder and faster the action becomes, the more believable it seems, both in writing and performance.

Soraya Peerbaye, gentle as Peanut, and Michelle Polak, driven as Kiko, complement one another admirably.

Jennifer Tarver's production handles some sizeable logistic challenges with impressive ease. The ending is beautifully, rackingly ambiguous.

MOJO

Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

Returning from holiday I find myself catching up with a seven- year-old British play that still provides a good, dark and dirty time. Also, for me at least, a nostalgic one. I never thought I'd see a Teddy boy upon the stage again: those teenage British toughs, or would-be toughs, of the 1950s.

Mojo is a first play by Jez Butterworth, who was born 10 years after the 50s ended. The play re-kindled a vogue for edgy, funny and nihilistic plays about small-time urban hoods. It offers the continuous possibility of violence, than which nothing is more dramatic. Butterworths handling of this constant threat and its occasional manifestation is brilliant. (That's a word his characters use a lot; it sounded anachronistic to me, though I guess he's done his homework. But I query his inclusion of laid-back. Very 60s.)

The scene is Soho, among the seedy clubs that battened on the rise of rock n' roll with its quickly manufactured local idols. The rising talent here is Silver Johnny, named for his suit, who up to now has been controlled by Ezra, a small-time mobster. Ezra never appears, for good and gruesome reasons. Somebody bigger, also unseen, has been bidding for Johnny's contract. We do meet Mickey, Ezras second-in-command and the oldest person on stage; and Ezras son, known as Baby, who seems to have been alternately abused and indulged and whose behaviour is consequently unpredictable; and a trio of minor menaces called Sweets, Potts and Skinny. Nearly everyone is on pills, and the second half shows them all under siege, little fish awaiting killer sharks.

If menace is the characters' style, it's also the authors; Butterworth is a beneficiary of Harold Pinters discovery that the cross-talk dynamics of Samuel Beckett could be mated to, and enriched by, the rhythms of cockney slang. Mojo begins with a long dialogue between Sweets and Potts, who understand little of what is happening around them, but sense that it's important. We sense the same, though we understand even less. But we're held, and we laugh. Butterworth is good at building up tensions and creating an atmosphere in which anyone will betray anyone else at any time, or would like to. This is not in itself, though, as rich or thick an effect as the author might think; like much thats aggressively hip, Mojo seems to have a few illusions of its own.

The first half is set in a small room, for which the designer, Lorenzo Savoini, supplies an exaggeratedly steep perspective that is more striking than helpful. The second half, in a bigger room, looks like standard realism, though there is no detectable change in the writing. When a full complement of interacting actors is on stage, Daryl Clorans production is excellent; when only two or three are gathered, it tends to the self-indulgent.

Dylan Trowbridge and Christopher Morris play the underlings' opening duologue for speed rather than sense, adding more mystification. Trowbridge at least looks good as the sickly Sweets, with a marionette walk and the face of an especially melancholy poodle. Morris develops considerable authority as the more confident Potts, half jocular, half jugular. But their Rosencrantz and Guildenstern act never quite pans out; if we are meant to see the action through their eyes, then the production is at fault, but I suspect it's the play. It wants to give equal (though no greater) time to Hamlet and Claudius -- Baby and Mick -- who are actually more interesting, but are cramped.

Blair Williams' Mickey anchors the play, as he is meant to, leaning hungrily forward. Mickey is a middleman trying for king, or at least kingmaker, though some of his actions remain baffling even after his motives are clear. Nor is it plausible that he should end up shedding tears over a relationship to Skinny -- a foul-breathed simpleton, much victimized by Baby and twitteringly well played by Damien Atkins -- that has never been established. The really sensational performance is given by Mike Shara as Baby, more childishly, insolently dangerous by the moment: dead in style, dead in period, and dead real.

Silver Johnny is played by Michel Protti, who also produces the play for Theatrefront. This company's self-proclaimed mandate is to push its members to "new emotional and physical limits." Protti certainly qualifies on the second count, since for much of his own appearance he is hanging upside down; it is good to meet a producer who is prepared to lead from the front and at such an angle. A refreshingly un-boring evening, worth hurrying to.
