GYNTY

Factory Theatre Studio

- - -

The heroine of Educating Rita, asked how she would solve the problems of staging Ibsen's Peer Gynt, cracked back with improbable smartness, "Do it on the radio."

The Theatre Columbus company have refined on this idea. They do it on the stage, and pretend they're doing it on the radio.

Five actors play between them the 50 characters of Ibsen's mammoth essay in the satirical-metaphysical-picaresque. They come before us in a detailed mockup of a broadcasting studio, standing at microphones, reading from scripts, and obeying the instructions of an unseen producer.

The director, Leah Cherniak, quotes as her inspiration the famous 1930s radio productions of Orson Welles. (Does she think that radio drama died out after that? Only in America.) A better reference- point might be Welles' stage version of Moby Dick, in which he sidestepped any realistic depiction of a whale or an ocean by presenting the whole thing as a rehearsal.

There is some ingenuity in Cherniak's plan, and some fascination in the way she works it out, but it destroys the play. And since the play is a great one -- the greatest after Shakespeare, I think -- that we hardly ever see, that is serious.

Peer Gynt is the archetypal fantasist; he fancies himself the hero of the folk tales told to him in his 19th-century Norwegian childhood -- he also just fancies himself -- and sometimes, thanks to his looks and charm, he gets away with it. He is also the uncommitted centre of his own universe.

In his middle years, he prospers as a slave-trader, and then goes adventuring in Africa and Egypt, but loses nearly everything. In his old age he comes home and faces death. He discovers that he, the great exponent of selfishness, the great wriggler-out of things, never had a real identity to lose; that he has proved unworthy of Heaven or Hell; and that he will be melted down -- by God's emissary, the Button-Moulder -- in a casting ladle. All that saves him -- provisionally -- is his continued love for the virtuous Solveig, who has waited for him for decades. This is a comedy: Peer ends up getting the girl, albeit in peculiar circumstances.

The original is in rhymed verse, and I suspect that it will never really work in English until some poet-translator does for it what Richard Wilbur has so wittily done for Moliere. The present version, unrhymed but with verse-sounding rhythms, is by the Irish dramatist Frank McGuinness: hence the new title Gynty, which seems rather silly here since the production drops the Irish accents half-way through.

Ibsen originally intended Peer Gynt to be read rather than acted; but it's in dialogue, and it has characters, and he was a playwright, and it's a play. Certainly it has to be one when it's on a stage. The relationships need to be realized, spatially and emotionally. It's hard to do this when the actors are bunched together, reciting. The convention eventually loosens up -- there must be a crucial moment when they drop their scripts, though I confess I failed to register it -- but not before it has done irreparable damage. And the disappearance of most of the studio trappings -- the mikes remain -- is confusing.

Worst of all, three separate actors share the role of Peer. This has been done before, on the insufficient grounds that performers of different ages are needed to represent his different stages. On radio, of course, this wouldn't apply; so the production is even false to its own concept.

Marcel Jeannin plays the young Peer on a pleasant but unvaried note of twinkling roguishness. David Jansen does the middle age, holding himself so far distant from the role that it virtually disappears. (This is especially true of his scenes as the would-be roue, abasing himself before the desert pin-up Anitra, she of the dance.) Oliver Dennis is the old man and much the best of the trio; his bleak refusal to let others have a happy family homecoming when none awaits him is the only moment of sustained feeling in the show.

Peer -- a character who combines the attractions of Hamlet, Falstaff and Lear -- is the greatest star role ever written, and should be played and received as such. (Step forward, Albert Schultz. Or Randy Hughson. Or one of the young lions of Shaw or Stratford.) Also, an audience needs a recognizable voice and body to unite a sprawling play that is always in danger of escaping beyond our grasp. Anyone who didn't know the piece would probably be lost here for much of the time. Peer may be Everyman, but even Everyman should have a face.

I know the trendy reasoning: that since Peer has no sustained identity, it makes sense to split him up. But that isn't what Ibsen was on about. Peer, despite his agonizings, does have a self, and a consistent one. But it's a limited self, a selfish self. He lives by the code of the trolls -- "be yourself and yourself alone " -- or, in the more helpful words of the translation I grew up on, " troll, to thyself be -- enough." Add to this the fatal advice of the Great Boyg to "go roundabout". It takes Solveig to break the deadlock, and it takes her forever.

All three Peers, when off-duty, do good work in minor roles: mostly male, though there is some gender crossing. Of the official women, Emma Campbell is a wondrously good and unforced Solveig, and makes instant and enjoyable switches into the various temptresses. (Her troll princess thpeakth with a lithp.) Martha Ross, though, is too trim and too bland for Peer's loving, scolding peasant mother; the richest mother-son relationship in world drama goes for practically nothing.

Indeed, too much is glided over, or simply cut, including some vital echoes and repetitions. This may sound masochistic but at three hours the play is too short. I admit to enjoying, shamelessly, the moments in which the actors stepped out of character and played actors.

For all I have said, the show is no disgrace. It is, obviously, a brave enterprise. But it is very frustrating.

ZADIE'S SHOES

Winter Garden Theatre, Toronto

BELLE

Factory Theatre, Toronto

The Factory, which in the last few years has had the best record for new plays of any theatre in Toronto, has two of its greatest hits on view again.

Florence Gibson's Belle is back at the home base, while Adam Pettle's Zadie's Shoes is being given a commercial run by the Mirvishes.

Both these authors were virtually unknown when their plays were first produced and the flaws in the two works stand out more sharply the second time around. But Belle remains the biggest play born in this city in years and Zadie's Shoes one of the most thoughtfully funny.

Zadie's Shoes stems, as its author has testified in interviews, from two traumas in his own young life: a diagnosis of cancer and an addiction to gambling. Both, we gather, are now in remission.

In the play, these two conditions are divided between two characters. Benjamin, an aspiring writer and practicing waiter, is an apparently nice Jewish boy and a devotee of the track as were his father and grandfather (or "zadie") before him. The cancer-victim is his girlfriend Ruth, who, having exhausted -- and been exhausted by - - the resources of conventional medicine, is about to fly off to Mexico on a more radical gamble: her life on an alternative cure.

Benjamin snaffles the money she was saving for their tickets and blows it on a bet, an act that is, to quote Ruth in a different but related context, "beyond selfish." He spends the balance of the play trying both to reverse his luck and win back her respect. One task proves easier than the other.

His road leads him, for the first time in years, into synagogue, where he meets an old man who doubles as tipster and confessor, a role in which Paul Soles delivers a lovely shrug of a performance.

He has, as you would expect, the lion's share of the play's jokes. Some of these are glib ("Jesus Christ!" exclaims Benjamin; "Wrong prophet," snaps back his new friend) but the best are splendid.

Equally funny, in a wilder and shaggier manner, is Randy Hughson as a recovering gambler-junkie-alcoholic, pressed reluctantly into service as Benjamin's partner in crime. Nobody is better at the comedy of bedraggled exasperation and he is, as he was before, especially fine when the character emerges unexpectedly as a moral force.

Benjamin himself is a problem. He talks a lot and -- as played by Jordan Pettle, the author's brother -- the character tends to disappear behind the words. He is uncomfortably real when he tries, like any guilty man, to charm himself back into his love's good graces. He plays with a kind of feverish casualness that stops short of a genuine addict's drive, and the feeling remains that, for all their good intentions, author and actor are letting Benjamin off the hook too easily. (Words run away with them as well as with him.)

Kelli Fox is admirable as Ruth, a believably good woman willing herself into desperate cheerfulness and genuinely moving when forced into anger.

The weakest elements of the play were always Ruth's two sisters and so, despite some re-casting, they remain. Deborah Drakeford is wooden as Beth, a curling champion preparing for her most challenging day on the ice. Tara Rosling tries far too hard as Lily, the kind of feckless spiritual eclectic we would once have called a hippie, now about to exchange generalized Earth-motherhood for a more specific maternity.

They are both formula characters with, especially in Beth's case, formula conflicts. Lily fits neatly into the play's plot, and Beth - - enslaved, like Benjamin, to the superstitions of good fortune -- into its theme.

Adam Pettle has an impressive sense of structure; but it is one thing to devise a pattern and another to bring all its elements to life. His vision, too, may be darker than his skills. Jackie Maxwell's production, with its bleachers setting, has been blown up without damage.

The major achievements of Belle remain remarkable.

Florence Gibson has dramatized and made comprehensible, without any hint of the schoolroom, a juicy chunk of American history: the reconstruction period that followed the end of the Civil War and of slavery.

She has told it through four representative characters who move from the South to the North -- two men, two women; two black, two white -- without ever appearing schematic. We follow the parallel, and sometimes conflicting, agitation for black rights and women's rights, and watch people with individual passions aligning and betraying.

She has fashioned a rich lyrical style, by spirituals out of Tennessee Williams, that usually avoids self-indulgence. The characters don't usually relax on it; mostly they hurl it at one another. The exchanges, in Ken Gass's production, are very well orchestrated.

Belle and her husband Bowlyn come from Georgia to New York after eight years' rock-hard saving, he to drive a cab, she to scrub floors. He loses his horse and she his job, both losses unintentionally caused by Nance, who is another kind of southern belle, the bleached kind, reborn as a suffragette.

She enlists them in her cause and for a time they are united, till sundered by sex and politics. Nobody gets what he or she wants - - not even Lackey, small-time exploiter turned small-time functionary -- but all survive for future conflicts.

Yanna McIntosh's Belle remains a shining success, not least because she humanizes an ideal: a character who stands, by right of race and gender, at the epicentre of discrimination and whom everybody admires.

I see that I originally described the play as "devastatingly funny"; I don't quite see where I got that from, but Soo Garay's Nance is still a marvellously witty creation, as well as a sad one, what with her brave but tattered rhetoric and her casual reference to Bowlyn's future fleet of taxis as "your vehicular conveniences."

Nigel Shawn Williams as Bowlyn lacks their precision, but does all right. Alex Poch-Goldin's shifty Lackey (or, as he wincingly insists "LackLEY") attracts the sympathy that invariably accrues to someone whom everyone else on stage considers despicable.

There is a fifth character. As in Zadie's Shoes, the heroine's sister proves the weakest link. (No fault, I think, of the actress, Janice Robinson, who is new and an improvement.) She stays down in Georgia, where she can usually be reached by flashback. The play seems to regard her as a prophetess, but Bowlyn calls her "your crazy sister" and he has my sympathy.

It's in her that the imagery and its delivery are the thickest -- she sounds like she's singing even when she's talking -- and most of the time I failed to understand her.

She takes over the last section of the play, leaving me wondering whether the other characters' return home was metaphor or reality for life or a visit, victory or defeat.

A small point: when Lackey alludes to the Ku Klux Klan, is he just acknowledging their existence or planning to join them? Probably it's the latter; he's a born loser. But why is he planning to go fishing? Of course, it's a nice thing to do in the South.

Note that Belle is a double act of cultural appropriation -- a white author writing about partly black history, a Canadian writing about wholly American history -- and that is a doubly good thing.

Black & White Photo: Heather Morton / Randy Hughson and Jordan Pettle in Zadie's Shoes, one of Toronto's most thoughtfully funny plays. ;

THE SHAPE OF A GIRL

Tarragon Extra Space

- - -

Joan Macleod's absorbing new play is about schoolgirl bullying. It's a monologue whose speaker, a mid-teen called Braidie, is neither full-fledged bully nor predestined victim; she inclines towards the first and plainly fears the possibility of becoming the second. Toward the close she looks at her best friend, Adrienne, who has been the prime mover in the near-fatal tormenting of their classmate Sofie. She sees, alternately, "a girl in the shape of a monster ... a monster in the shape of a girl."

This double image has appeared earlier, at intervals through the play, as Braidie absorbs the news reports of what is clearly the murder of Reena Virk. It is the realization that all Reena's schoolmates, not just those directly responsible, participated in the conspiracy of silence surrounding her death that pushes Braidie off the fence. The Shape of a Girl is a production of the Green Thumb young people's company in Vancouver, and a play about bullying from British Columbia -- site of the Virk killing and of the suicide of Dawn-Marie Wesley -- could hardly be more painfully topical. But this play would awaken fears and echoes at any time and in any place.

Macleod apparently began writing it before the Virk case, though it's hard to guess what the play could have been like before it found that focus. It might have been just another somewhat lyrical monologue about growing up female and misunderstood; Braidie, a Victoria girl, has literary inclinations and addresses her reminiscences to her absent brother Trevor. (Is she speaking aloud to an imaginary hearer? Is she writing letters? Or a journal? The riddling curse of the solo play reasserts itself. The more we hear about Trevor, the less substantial he seems.)

Braidie also has a fractious relationship with her mother, whom she refers to as "the voice of mom" and whose sole aim, as seen by her daughter, is to frustrate her every wish and generally ruin her life. This is darkly hilarious and rendered with ventriloquial accuracy. (Braidie speaks of her mother's "famous whisper-shriek" and describes life with her as "a crash-course in indignity.") But it still feels like padding. It has only a tenuous relationship with what really grabs us.

It's possible to wish that Macleod had not tied her play so closely to an actual event; that she had found another way of letting Braidie work out her salvation. But given the path that she has chosen (and maybe it was inevitable -- maybe we would have made the connection anyway and it's best to acknowledge it), she has followed it superbly. She traces the development of discrimination, beginning with Adrienne's invention, in Grade 4, of a game called Penalty Day, in which one girl is scapegoat for the duration.

As school progresses Sofie -- referred to as "It" -- is cast in this role full-time, to the point where, as Braidie observes with a mixture of wonder and shock, "even Sofie hates Sofie." When adolescence hits, Adrienne begins to take her boyfriend problems out on Sofie. This much perhaps is elementary. Subtler and more powerful is the observation of how -- on the rare occasions on which Sofie defends herself or when fate intervenes -- Adrienne herself acts the screeching victim, as if it were intolerable that she should be thwarted or that people should slip out of the roles that she had assigned them.

When Braidie finally finds it in herself to acknowledge and condemn the persecution -- including her own part in it -- the adjective she finds for it, after an enormous hesitation, is "despicable." Both the word and the pause that precedes it feel absolutely right: perfect as description, true to the speaker. Macleod's feeling for teenage girlspeak -- the rhythm, the vocabulary and the outraged conviction -- seems perfect; when she uses a term like "rancid" you feel that, if that isn't a current vogue-word, then it should be.

It is hard, though, to disentangle the writer's achievement from that of 22-year-old Jenny Young, whose performance, oval-headed and button-eyed, is a consummate wedding of mature technique to fresh impersonation. It is also, under Patrick McDonald's direction, superbly shaped; at its crucial point we feel that we are meeting Braidie in her prime.

The play's note of hope is perhaps not much justified by recent events, or by recent revelations about past events. But it has an emotional truth; the play earns it and so, I think, do we -- as audience if not as citizens. It feels right.

IN ON IT

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, Toronto

Daniel MacIvors In On It is another play about the impossibility of writing plays. This is the strategy. You write some crummy naturalistic scenes about the fallout from a disintegrating marriage, then acknowledge their crumminess in the hope this will prove disarming. You surround them with marginally less crummy scenes about the interaction of the two people who are presenting the first lot, then trust they will look good by comparison.

In On It is less arid, or at any rate less long, than such previous MacIvor works as The Soldier Dreams and You Are Here; and it does have its pleasures. One of them is a brief moment of mistaken identity that catches up actors and audience together in a blissful mental double take. Another is an opening speech, delivered by the author himself, tracing the external steps that can lead ineluctably to a fatal car accident.

MacIvor, who is also the director, is half the cast; he plays This One, the author of the play-within-the-play. Sharing the stage with him is That One, played by Darren ODonnell, another actor- playwright-director who here sticks to acting. The onstage relationship therefore mirrors the offstage one.

This One and That One are also lovers, though their relationship seems at the point of dissolution. They alternate roles in This One's play, about a man getting a fatal diagnosis and being left by his wife on the same day. That One objects that all This One's female characters seem to be drunks. Thats the least of the problems.

The stricken hero is given scenes with his grown-up son, who doesnt want to hear about his father's illness, and with his father, who is senile and doesn't recognize him. Later he meets the former partner of his wifes new lover and her young son. Its funny when the protagonist turns on his doctor, saying the resentful things we would all like to but never do. Other sections are less amusingly implausible. People can certainly be selfish and they can be shallow, but the behaviour here is shallowly shallow. I have been in some of the extreme situations presented here and I recognized no truth in the depiction of any of them. Perhaps the writing is meant to be bad, but that is no consolation when you're listening to it.

It's not as if all the soap-opera episodes illuminate, or are illuminated by, the predicament of the two presenters, unless you believe that one troubled menage is the same as any other. We learn how the guys met, and thats faintly amusing. This One has a thing about opera, which That One dismisses as cultural hypocrisy. Thats all. Otherwise, all we get are winks at the audience, as when the twosome hold up the poster of the show we are watching and start critiquing it. Or when we are told how people love a full-circle ending, and are duly given one.

Why bother? We all know theatre isn't real. We all know it can only tell a partial truth, so MacIvor is puncturing illusions that nobody holds anyway. Art about art doubtless has its place, but it's a small one. If plays cant be about anything else, then we may as well stop writing plays. The only immediate implication to be gleaned from this one -- or from This One -- is that homosexual authors have no business writing about heterosexual characters. I dont believe in this kind of ghetto aesthetics, and I doubt MacIvor does either. Certainly history is against it.

MacIvor's direction is fine, on a wide, bare, flat stage that concentrates the mind as wonderfully as, and more cheerfully than, the proverbial death-sentence. His acting, except when he is soliloquizing, is self-effacing to a fault, but O'Donnell, a fine figure of an actor, compensates in the focus and energy departments. The two do a delightfully daffy dance to the Lesley Gore record of Sunshine, Lollipops and Rainbows that recalls the sign-off of a Wayne and Shuster special.

I'm all in favour of plays that send you out humming. On the other hand, the same song was used to greater comic effect in the Thelma-and-Louise episode of The Simpsons. It makes you wonder why professedly experimental theatre should automatically get more respect than commercial cartoon television. But maybe it's unfair to invoke genius.
2002-04-06-minimalism-taken-to-the-max:
Closes tonight. (416) 937-4000

NIGHTSONGS FACE TO THE WALL

DuMaurier Theatre Centre

- - -

World Stage Preview is a short international season designed as a taster for the full-blown festival planned for next year. It has kicked off, imposingly, with a double bill from the Royal Court Theatre in London, both its components directed by Katie Mitchell, who was responsible for the memorable production of The Oresteia that came here two years ago.

Mitchell has always been known as a stylistic puritan, and with this program she has professedly gone into understater's overdrive. She has turned her back on such decadent frivolities as designed scenery and computerized lighting and sound effects. Her stage is furnished only by found objects. Question: Were they brought over from Britain or did the rules dictate that they be found anew in Canada?

Nightsongs, the first of the evenings plays and much the longest (90 minutes to its companions 18), takes place in a flat occupied by a young couple and their baby: The production scavengers have furnished it with a sofa and a pram, but not much else.

An interview inserted in the program associates all this economy with recent developments in the Danish cinema and the English novel. (On the first of these, I pass. On the second, all I can say is that my own impression of the current English novel, formed by such exuberantly panoramic writers as Jonathan Coe and Zadie Smith, is obviously out-of-date, but I like it that way.) In fact, the production style looks to me like Royal Court minimalism of a kind that has been in place for at least three decades. On its home ground, I used to regard it with grudging respect. Meeting it here I find the grudge lifting and the respect increased.

Nightsongs is by an apparently highly regarded Norwegian playwright, Jon Fosse. This may seem to reinforce the Scandinavian connection, but in the text as we hear it, nothing, nowhere and nobody seems specifically Norwegian; it sounds, in Gregory Motton's spare and demotic translation, as if it's going on in London.

It depicts a relationship that is miserable. The man hasnt left the house in ages. He spends his time lying on the sofa reading; he also writes manuscripts that are invariably rejected. His parents pay an embarrassed visit; the first, apparently, since the baby was born. The woman, craving release, goes out for the evening -- with a girlfriend, she says, though her partner seems disinclined to believe her. She does, indeed, eventually reappear with another man, named Mike (hes the only character who has a name, at least one that we ever learn). She is moving out to live with him.

Not all of the production's scenic elements are as ruthlessly realistic as the propaganda would have us believe. A rope-ladder contraption suggests, but does not resemble, a window. There are clock faces built into either side of the stage, and a large wristwatch hovering in space over the middle of it, like an unsmiling Cheshire Cat. These timepieces are reinforced by the recurring sound of a speaking clock, as heard on the British telephone system. All this is to emphasize that the scenes we witness, though not the intervals between them, are being played out in real time.

The principal duo nag, complain, feel sorry for themselves but never actually quarrel, largely because the man refuses to put up a fight. It's maddening, but it is not boring. The relationship is very real, especially in the way it sags without breaking. The mans reiterated assertion, whined rather than stated, that he thought the two of them were good together, has its own truth; certainly one can see how it would be true, and necessary, for him.

Maybe it is this fated interdependence that has caused Fosse to be described, or so we are told, as a 21st-century Beckett. I can see no other resemblance, though the actors accents occasionally make him sound like Pinter, while the grandparents' desultory attempts at polite conversation seem initially like early Ionesco: incongruous attempts to ridicule the banality of everyday speech. It turns out, though, there's a perfectly sober reason for them to talk as they do, and that its connected to the withdrawn behaviour of their son.

Not that his mate proves a paragon of decisiveness either. When it comes time to make a choice, she is racked by doubts. "I dont want things to happen" she says, and it seems to be a comment on the play.

Then we find out that things do happen, shockingly. A play about stasis turns out to be a declaration of its opposite; and very dramatic, considering. Paul Higgins as the man makes a surprising positive out of a collection of negatives; Sophie Okonedo is trenchant in a low-key way, maybe too low-key, even for a small space.

The afterpiece, Face to the Wall, is by Martin Crimp, who is prominent among younger English playwrights (and also among younger English translators). Here he employs a device that I suppose is daring but, in fact, turns out to be theatrically suicidal. A middle- aged man, fleshy and florid, appears to be pitching a movie to a couple of young Americans: a story about a killer mowing down four children. In full, eager spate he suddenly stops and asks for a prompt; this is supplied, he goes vigorously on, and then dries again, and again. We, of course, are uncertain whether the actor is really forgetting his lines, or whether this is a device. The longer it goes on, the likelier it seems to be the latter, especially since Peter Wight's performance is, between pauses, strikingly forceful and assured.

But it's never quite certain, and anyway the damage has been done; were too horrified by the spectacle (chronic actors amnesia has the fascination of a car-wreck) to have any shock left over for what he's saying. He starts to verbally brutalize the prompter, and I suppose this is meant to key in to the brutality he's narrating and, apparently, enjoying. He then sings a blues song about a murderous postman.

Real-life child massacres haunt us, and are obviously meant to; but in that context the tricksy little play seems a) tasteless and b) pointless: not a satire on media exploitation but the thing itself. In this instance, Katie Mitchell's direction seems minimal rather than minimalist -- less an artistic choice than a helpless bow to the inevitable.

2002-04-09-stoppard-gem-translates-so-we:
Until April 27. Box office: 416-368-3110.

INDIAN INK

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

My favourite Tom Stoppard story concerns a screenwriting offer he turned down because of a prior commitment to the BBC. You mean, said Hollywood, aghast, "you'd pass up a movie for a TV play?" Actually, said Stoppard (bashfully, one presumes) "its for a radio play."

Thats loyalty. Stoppard started in radio and went on to conquer theatre, television and film -- in that order and with an almost infallible sense of what belongs to each. Most of his successes, in fact, would be untransferrable from one medium to another. The exception is Indian Ink, a 1995 stage play that began life four years earlier as a radio piece called In the Native State. It works both ways. At CanStage, in a shimmering production, it brings the Toronto season to a sorely needed new high.

The play revolves around Flora Crewe, a fictitious English poet of questing intelligence and great personal attractiveness, who visits India in 1930, a year that ironically -- since she is supposed to be travelling for her health -- proves to be her last.

In the native state of Jummapur she encounters, and enchants, the Rajah who ostensibly governs the place, a young representative of the British government that supposedly controls the Rajah and -- most importantly -- an artist named Nirad Das, who offers to paint her portrait. While sitting, she composes poems -- poems that will eventually be published (posthumously, of course) under the title Indian Ink and will indeed prove to be, in a modest way, indelible. (The play's stage title makes a more reverberant pun than its radio equivalent.)

Crewe sends letters about her experiences to her younger sister Eleanor, back in London. Fifty years later, this correspondence becomes an important part of The Collected Letters of Flora Crewe, time and feminism having turned the once-neglected lady poet into a cult figure.

It makes me so cross, says her now-elderly sister, "that she missed it all ... Nobody gave tuppence about her while she was alive except to get her knickers off."

Eleanor now finds herself besieged by archeologists of Flora's past. These include the American academic who edited (i.e., heavily footnoted) the letters and is now surreptitiously researching a biography, and Anish Das, son of Nirad and also a painter.

The action criss-crosses between India and England, the 30s and the 80s. Partly it's about heredity and influence, and the unexpected ways in which these can work themselves out. With Indian independence a clear inevitability, Das the elder is a political nationalist and a cultural Anglophile, passionately devoted to Shakespeare, Dickens and -- above all -- Agatha Christie. (Civilizations, the play suggests, flatten at a distance; we are all cultural tourists, whether we stay home or visit.)

He never gets to the London he adores, but his son -- far more radical, artistically and politically -- ends up living there while deploring the continued British influence on his homeland.

Eleanor went out to India to visit her sister's grave, met another young English official and married him. Formerly a Communist, she became a sardonically observant lady of the Raj. Politics tend, in a Stoppard play, to be a function of whom you sleep with. Now Eleanor serves tea and homemade cake to visitors -- and laments that the tea, at least, never tastes as good as it did in India.

Stoppard is the best practising playwright in the English language, but his plays have always invited two kinds of suspicion: The simple, noticing that they contain ideas, assume they must be cold and difficult; and the solemn, noticing they contain jokes, assume they must be superficial. (One faction thinks them pretentious, the other not pretentious enough.)

Actually, the plays dont just contain jokes, they are made of them, in structure as well as dialogue -- serious jokes that blend and dovetail perfectly, and wrap up both the meaning and the actions. The only fault to be found with them is that the fizzy allusiveness sometimes leads to important plot points being sketched in rather than blocked out.

As for coldness: Stoppard must be the only dramatist who now writes intelligently about love, and the fact he does it with wit only makes his characters more endearing and -- often at unexpected moments -- more moving.

The heart of this play is in the encounters between Flora and Nirad Das, the Englishwoman and the Indian, trying to break through their ingrained notions not only of one another but of themselves. They proceed on at least three levels of contact and conflict -- sexual, political, artistic -- which of course overlap; when Das throws stones at the official English Daimler, whos to say whether it's an act of protest or of jealousy at a possible rival?

In Richard Cottrell's production these scenes come over even better than they did in the original London staging.

Fiona Reids Flora is, I think, unimprovable: perfect in sense of time and place, unimprovable in its style, pace and vulnerability. The wit is both verbal (You never mentioned Virginia Woolf, she is told after giving a literary talk. "I seldom do," she replies sweetly) and physical; Flora says she likes to wriggle her toes when shes working, and Reid shows her thoughts working excitedly through her feet. What she conveys most intensely is a proud, amused respect for her own integrity and everyone else's.

Sanjay Talwar as Das matches Reid in his sensitive alternation of eagerness and reserve. Their scenes include, by the way, the best- written nude scene ever -- a fortunate legacy of the play's radio origins. Das ends up painting Flora twice -- once with clothes, once without -- and the difference in the two pictures crystallizes all the plays themes.

All the minor Indian characters are excellently played. The Westerners, apart from Hazel Desbarats Eleanor -- and even she could vary her indomitability more than she does -- are less satisfactory. The footnoting U.S. scholar is clumsily done (his role is much enlarged from the radio version, and it seems a questionable decision) and Flora's pukka sahib admirer is dull, though the scene in which he takes her riding is pretty irresistible, staged as it is on a pair of pommel horses.

The staging throughout is lucid and graceful, and Susan Benson's designs, in which a translucent screen beautifully backs the whole width of the Bluma Appel stage, are the most exquisite the town has seen in an age.

Black & White Photo: Michael Mitchell / FIONA REID AS FLORA CREWE AND SANJAY TALWAR AS NIRAD DAS: the best-written nude scene ever. ;
2002-04-13-a-really-nasty-woman:
Medea closes tonight. (416) 973-4000. Inertia [Phase Two] closes tomorrow. (416) 538-9401.

MEDEA

Premier Dance Theatre

- - -

INERTIA [PHASE TWO]

Theatre Centre

- - -

The myth of Medea will never make a good feminist tract, unless you take a grimly apocalyptic view of feminism.

Medea, you will remember, was the sorceress who helped Jason, one of the more dubious Greek heroes, find and steal the Golden Fleece, cheerfully sacrificing members of her own family in the process. Euripides's tragedy finds the enterprising couple arrived in Crete, whose king's daughter Jason proposes to marry. Medea, not one to take rejection lightly, presents the bride with a poisoned robe, in whose embrace she dies an agonizing death. Her father, touching her body, shares her fate; this wasn't in the game plan but Medea gladly accepts it as a bonus. Then, so as to make Jason feel really bad, she kills the three children they have had together.

After that, in Euripides, she escapes in a magic chariot, presumably to live happily ever after, pausing only to cast a few well-chosen taunts in her faithless lover's direction.

Liz Lochhead's version, brought to World Stage by Scotland's Theatre Babel, changes this last development; Lochhead leaves the couple on Earth together, exchanging insults and recriminations.

Lochhead's text is described not as a translation from the Greek but as a new play "after Euripides." It includes a new scene between Medea and Jason's fiancee; Euripides left the latter young lady off- stage, but the encounter comes off as something he might well have written. It's like one of the catfights in The Trojan Women: The princess tells her rival, with patronizing sweetness, that Jason needs someone younger and that Medea should give in gracefully; Medea snarls back that older women know a lot more, which in her case is undoubtedly true.

All the Greek characters here speak in broad, and very salty, Scottish accents. This has an especially invigorating effect on the lower orders: on Medea's nurse (Carol Ann Crawford), loyal despite everything, and on the tutor (Lewis Howden), shiftier and more easily shocked, rising to a magnificent delivery of the play's lacerating messenger speech. Medea herself, the sinuous alien, has a European sound and stance that sometimes suggests Marlene Dietrich, seeing what the boys in the back room will have and serving it up with arsenic.

The chorus are also foreigners, but from closer to home. They are slave women, captured from neighbouring countries, and so speak with English, mainly Cockney, accents. They start by sympathizing with Medea, accommodating her views on Jason to their own on men in general; they are neutral, but intrigued, when she turns homicidal; and finally withdraw sympathy when the children are -- to use their mother's view of the situation -- sacrificed.

This is pretty much the trajectory they follow in the original, but it is far more immediate here than usual. The chorus, often an embarrassment, are among the triumphs of the script and of Graham McLaren's production. There are half-a-dozen of them, and they come alive not as a group of individuals but -- far more difficult -- as a group that is itself an individual.

Maureen Beattie's Medea is sulphurously, relentlessly uncompromising; a performance that proudly (and prudently) refrains from extorting pity, even her own. Jason, in Duncan Duff's performance, is not just a creep -- which seems inevitable -- but a wheedling chancer, going on about what a great sex-life he and Medea can continue to have when no one's looking. There is little here of the humanity that Seana McKenna and Scott Wentworth brought to the roles at Stratford two years ago. McLaren's direction is bleak, powerful, and brilliantly concentrated, with never a false or inflated moment.

- - -

The first line of Inertia [Phase Two] is, "Well, let's get on with it," which happens to be the last line of Jean-Paul Sartre's Huis Clos: the play (variously known in English as Vicious Circle, In Camera and No Exit) that corralled three sinners in a plush hotel room for an eternity of one another's company, and which itself ends with the famous discovery that "Hell is other people." (The play, whose celebrity is only equalled by its rarity, was scheduled but then cancelled for this year's inaugural season at the Stratford Studio. It would be good to see if there's more to it than its finale.) I thought I recognized one other Sartrean line --something about the lights never being turned off -- but otherwise this collage piece's main source is Chekov's Three Sisters, whose disconsolate heroines are here transformed into three nursing sisters who hate their work. The delightfully named OOmph! Group are the presenters, under the direction of Chad Dembski.

There is some fascination -- and even a few laughs -- in hearing the familiar lines juggled to fit a new environment, and there is some ingenuity in the way it has been done. But it becomes progressively clear that the Chekhov text is providing the show with its only interest and its only authority (the Sartre quotes only add a gloss of facile pessimism), and that the production is taking a free ride on a classic, illuminating neither its source nor anything else (as opposed to the Lochhead Medea, which is a genuine piece of work that does credit to Euripides, as well as sharing it with him).

Billed as "a multimedia collision," Inertia also features video screens and segments from the soap opera General Hospital, but these are just confusing. They also convey the feeling that the theatrical use of technology is a virtue in itself.

It does at least give us a nostalgic glimpse of the days when nurses, by virtue of wearing uniforms, were identifiably nurses. Sean MacMahon plays their one all-purpose patient who eventually and understandably discharges himself. The angels of mercy are Natasha Priest, the presently ubiquitous Michelle Polak, and Erika Hennebury, who rouses the house with a mockingly vamped rendition of a splendidly tacky pop song. Welcome to show business.

2002-04-17-for-this-he-hired-a-goyish-wr:
Adam Baum and the Jew Movie runs until May 4. Box office: 416-368- 3110.

ADAM BAUM AND THE JEW MOVIE

Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

NOVECENTO

Du Maurier Theatre Centre, Toronto

The 1947 film Gentleman's Agreement was courageous by Hollywood standards and craven by all others. It was the first big-studio treatment of anti-Semitism; Gregory Peck played a journalist who posed as a Jew in order to experience discrimination at first hand.

Darryl F. Zanuck, the mogul who made the movie happen -- and who was, almost uniquely among the studio bosses, a gentile -- asked one of the technicians what he had learned from working on it. "Well, sir" was the reply, "I've learned never to be nasty to a Jew, because he could be a Christian in disguise."

Around the same time, Samuel Goldwyn, a movie mogul who was emphatically not a gentile, apparently met with the WASP leftist screenwriter Ring Lardner Jr. (later of the Hollywood Ten and much later of MASH). Their encounter has inspired Adam Baum and the Jew Movie, a newish -- as in "funny, it doesn't look newish" -- play by Daniel Goldfarb, a young Canadian writer who lives in New York. It is intelligent, and it throws up some painfully amusing paradoxes, but it doesn't dramatize them.

The problems begin with Goldfarb's Goldwyn, who is here called Samuel Baum; the disguise is even thinner than Gregory Peck's but the dramatist won't own up to it. He sprinkles the dialogue with familiar Goldwynisms like "include me out" (as well as others like "leave messages to Western Union" that have been attributed to just about everybody). Better he should have called the guy Goldwyn straight out, or have invented his own manner of speaking.

Anyway, this Sam has been planning his own picture about anti- Semitism, and is both alarmed and incensed to discover that Zanuck is about to beat him to the punch. There is room in this town, he says, for just one Jew movie a year. (That is actually, by the standards of the time, a generous estimate.)

He has commissioned a script from a Nordic Oscar-winner called Garfield Hampson Jr., and Gar, after years of writing fluff, is delighted at the opportunity to exercise his social conscience. He favours the title Soil of Utopia; Sam doesn't, and who can blame him? Gar has done loads of research, and has tried to come up with a realistic account of American Jewry; unprejudiced, unglamorized. This, apparently, is not what Sam envisaged. For this he hired a goyish writer?

It is unclear just what kind of Jews Sam wants to put on his screen -- unclear to Gar, unclear to us, unclear perhaps to Sam himself. Anyway, he invites Gar to attend his son Adam's bar mitzvah party, there to see some real Jews.

Gar is appalled by the vulgar ostentation he beholds. Sam, definitively turning the tables, asks what right Garfield, the child of old money, has to criticize the ways in which first-generation immigrant paupers may choose to flaunt their hard-won wealth.

Sam, it transpires, would really like to make a movie as much like Zanuck's as possible. Hampson Jr.'s opinion of Gentleman's Agreement is similar to Sam Goldwyn's of a verbal agreement: that it isn't worth the paper it's written on. Baum Sr. thinks the movie -- scripted, incidentally, by the Jewish Moss Hart -- is the only kind of Jew movie an American audience will sit still for.

It's a good point, one of a few, but the play never amounts to more than a debating-piece. This works all right in the first half, which is a duologue in Sam's office; the characterization may be thin but the issues are strong, and we are further held by Sam's constant impish wrong-footing of his idealistic opponent.

But when we move to the Baum house, things get sticky, structurally and emotionally. We meet Adam, and observe -- indeed, have it thrust in our face -- his father's love for him. The time, remember, is immediately after the Holocaust, and a Jewish parent is going to be even more protective than usual.

It is also just after Hiroshima, and the fact that "Adam Baum" sounds like "atom bomb" is obviously not accidental. What good it's supposed to be is another matter. Is Adam Baum one portent of the future, and the Jew movie another?

Sam, we realize, knows in his bones what anti-Semitism is and what it can do, and he is entitled to fight it on his own terms. Well, all right, but the play ends with young Adam and his very secular father antiphonally reciting the boy's scripture portion -- a shameless (and, to this hard case, bootless) assault on the heartstrings. Enough already.

The sentimentality is enhanced by the performance of Richard Greenblatt, who is too young, too trim and too nice to play Sam. Goldwyn, by recent biographical accounts, was a monster, and he must certainly have been ruthlessly tough. How else could he have clawed his way up from direst poverty, and how can we be moved by his soft centre if we haven't first had to penetrate his his hard shell?

Garfield also seems amazingly innocent for a man with four Tracy- Hepburn pictures under his belt, but Rick Roberts plays him excellently as he steps blithely into all the traps his author has laid for him.

Alisa Palmer's direction speeds the first half along, and runs thoroughly aground on the second. Dylan Rosenthal's Adam is not so much written or directed as sacrificed; he looks right but is saddled, among other things, with one unbelievably crass joke.

The play also goes in for melodramatic padding. Sam gets alarming phone calls. By the time we find out what they're about (it's not what we thought) it's too late to tie the information to the theme. And talking of red herrings (which might be a good alternative title, Gar being the red and Sam the herring), Gentleman's Agreement has its uses as a stalking-horse but it finally gets in the way. We keep being diverted from Sam's feelings about his Jewishness to his feelings about the competition.

- - -

Alessandro Baricco, the Italian author of the monologue Novecento, seems to have been unsure what he had when he had it. Was it a short story or a play?

I think it's the former, but Tom McCamus' performance of it (brought to WorldStage by the Theatre de Quat'Sous of Montreal) makes that seem like quibbling. He is hypnotic. He plays Tim Tooney, a jazz trumpeter who worked a Trans- Atlantic liner between the word wars, and there met and befriended a miraculous pianist named Novecento who literally never left the ship; he was born there, abandoned there, adopted there, and you can probably guess the end.

The philosophic import of this is unclear, though the writer clearly thinks it has one; and there are some groaningly whimsical attempts at musical poetry (ragtime is described as "the music that God dances to when nobody's looking"). But as anecdote -- or a series of anecdotes, including a cutting-contest with Jelly-Roll Morton -- it is riveting.

McCamus, alternately awed and impatient, delivers it with hunched, sandy-voiced perfection. He works in chiaroscuro, as does Francois Girard's production, on a set (by Francois Seguin) that gradually reveals itself as a giant engine room.

Nancy Tobin, the sound designer, mixes the sounds of sea, ship and piano, cunningly and hauntingly. The show was here for three performances. It must return.

Black & White Photo: David Hawe, Canadian Stage / From left, Richard Greenblatt as Sam Baum and Rick Roberts as Garfield Hampson Jr. ;
2002-04-20-putting-the-ham-in-hamlet:
I, Claudia closes tomorrow. (416) 973-4000

HAMLET

Premiere Dance Theatre

I, CLAUDIA

du Maurier Theatre

- - -

The First Gravedigger in Hamlet, asked why the troublesome Danish prince has been sent off to England, replies that his eccentricities won't be noticed there, because "there the men are as mad as he." It's one of the few infallible laugh-lines in Shakespeare. Or it is when both the actors and the audience speak English.

In Lithuania they cut it. At least they do if the Meno Fortas company's production at Toronto's World Stage is anything to go by. Fair enough: It isn't a gag that travels. (Other cultures might agree with it, but they wouldn't find it funny.) And in Eimuntas Nekrosius' production it would backfire. This Hamlet doesn't have to set foot outside his own castle to meet men (though not women) who are at least as mad as he or, in several cases, madder.

The Production -- it seems to demand the capital letter -- has already moved on, but is worth considering as a phenomenon. It is sometimes interesting, sometimes exasperating, and often boring, though some of the tedium can be blamed on our not understanding what the actors are saying; the original text is projected on three separate screens, but they can hardly alert you to any subtleties of intonation.

The show also lasts four hours, despite substantial cuts; Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are dead, or at least missing, though nobody seems to have informed the surtitles, which still have Hamlet referring to his "two schoolfellows." Some of his exchanges with them have been transferred to other contexts, and there is much textual shuffling all 'round; scenes you think you have escaped are liable to ambush you later on.

The weather in Elsinore appears to be terrible, and the castle roof leaky; water drops on to the stage almost throughout, and several scenes are played around puddles. The stage is littered with impenetrably symbolic props, whose deployment accounts for much of the running time.

If the play is meant to take us on Hamlet's spiritual journey, then it fails. The hero drops in from time to time and broods, but is otherwise anonymous. The actor, Andrius Mamontovas, is a major rock star at home, but if his presence has a built-in significance - - voice of youth, and so on -- it stops at the national border. Claudius (Vytautas Rumsas) is easier to decode: a bull-necked boozer who shouts at everyone. He even bellows his way through his prayer scene, as if trying to bully himself into repentance. He is far from the conscience-haunted diplomat-king we usually meet, but he makes a lot of sense. And he does prove capable of playing the politician, when he persuades Laertes to murder Hamlet.

As it happens, Laertes (Kestutis Jakstas) is just the kind of young man to be duped, somewhat honest, but headstrong and smug, especially when lecturing his sister on the preservation of her virginity while standing, apparently, on top of his own cabin- trunk, all packed up for a good dirty time in France.

Daddy Polonius (Povilas Budrys) makes little impression, apart from being subjected to an interestingly grisly death from asphyxiation while holed up within, I believe, the very same trunk, and from being the youngest-looking old man ever while alive. He is forbiddingly bald and acts as an usher around the court -- two attributes he shares with Horatio (Ramunas Rudokas), who is accorded the most unusual interpretation of the evening.

The prince's chum, prized by him as the embodiment of stoical endurance, here becomes a burly, giggling neurotic, forever imitating the cock-crow that in the play's first scene sent the Ghost scuttling back to Purgatory. So eccentric is his behaviour that Hamlet lectures him on it, using the advice against overacting that, in a more conventional production, he would be addressing to the Players.

These professionals, by the way, have a hard job competing with the amateur histrionics going on around them, but they do their best, delivering most of their lines rolling around on rollers. They turn up later as the Gravediggers (three instead of the usual two), whom they play, uncompromisingly, as Clowns: i.e. determinedly stylized and grimly unfunny.

All this shouting, screaming and sawing of the air with hands leaves you wondering what the director can have left in reserve for the play's one episode of genuine insanity: Ophelia's mad scene. The answer, simply, is simplicity; the actress (Viktorija Kuodyte) comes on stage, says and does her stuff with great calm and stillness, and is both very effective and a great relief. By a similar paradox, the most consistently human person on stage is the Ghost, whose presence (he seems to have been preserved as a waxwork) haunts Claudius as well as Hamlet, and who here ends the play, bending over his son's corpse and sorrowfully beating a drum, as if bemoaning all the trouble he has caused.

This kind of Central or Eastern European production -- heavily- staged and ritually oppressive -- used to denote the director's dislike of the play, on grounds ideological or aesthetic or both. I don't think that's the case here. (Just as well; if you are bored by a play, your audience will be too, though not necessarily for the reasons you intend.)

I wondered if audiences in Lithuania are as familiar with Hamlet as audiences here; presumably they are, since this show -- which comments on the story instead of telling it -- would be incomprehensible to them otherwise. Nekrosius seems to be a clever but over-ingenious director, and Mamontovas a virtual non-actor; between them they scupper the play's emotional reality, the one element without which drama cannot sustain itself. To return to Hamlet's advice to the Players, he especially condemns "inexplicable dumb-shows and noise." This production is loaded with both.

To judge from that speech, with its references to "the modesty of nature," what Hamlet -- and presumably Shakespeare -- really wanted was, of all permanently unfashionable things, naturalism. Of course, that sounds crazy, since Shakespeare wrote in a profoundly unnatural medium; nobody really talks in verse, rhymed or blank.

But he and his contemporaries made it sound natural, and they obviously expected their actors to do the same. That is the genius of theatre; it starts with artifice and acts like it's real. For a wonderful proof, consider Toronto's own World Stage contribution, Kristen Thomson's I, Claudia. Thomson, performing her own script, wears a series of masks to play four separate characters. Masks are the convention of conventions but, having donned them, she makes no other stylistic concessions; she simply acts. (And you do feel you're getting a four-character play, not a one-woman show.)

The stubby, beseeching face of Claudia herself, the pre-teen struggling for a life in face of her parents' divorce and her father's remarriage, is already one of the great icons of the Canadian theatre. When the actress tilts her head, the mask can seem to change expression, from defiant to desolate.

We all know that the children of divorce blame themselves; Thomson's Claudia makes this sociological commonplace a stabbingly moving fact. When this show was first staged at Tarragon, I paused in my ecstasy to accuse it, glancingly, of sentimentality; I now withdraw the charge. I still think the play's two male characters are its least successful, because with them Thomson largely abandons wit and warmth for whimsy. But when she plays Lesley, Claudia's soon- to-be stepmother, the stage glows, and when she returns to Claudia herself, it positively explodes.

Watching these scenes, you cherish their creator; you also -- for reasons that transcend her representing us at our home-grown international festival -- feel proud.

THUNDERSTICK

Theatre Passe Muraille

- - -

I was fairly thunderstruck by Thunderstick. All its constituent parts work together: The writing rambles, the acting totally lacks conviction, and the direction is limp. For those who prize consistency in a work of art, it's something of a jackpot.

The title is apparently old Hollywoods idea of the American Indian name for a rifle. I owe this information to the author, Ken Williams, who mentions it in his program note but not, I think, in his play. (Its possible he did and I missed it. The proceedings were numb and left me number.)

Anyway, he gives us two contemporary Native Canadians whose weapons are the pen, or whatever you write with these days, and the camera. In other words they are journalists, working out of Ottawa, and they have been assigned by their masters to cover some complicated political shenanigans. They are also cousins who have not set eyes on one another for some time and are not too crazy about the prospect now.

The reporter is called Jacob, and the photographer, returned to Canada from an extended tour of the world's worst places, is called Isaac. We begin in Jacob's bathroom, watching him in the toils of a major hangover. (I cant help feeling that this reinforces, rather than mocks, a stereotype.) Eventually he throws up.

There is a toilet bowl on stage throughout the first act; sometimes it has a visible cistern, which means were at Jacob's place, and sometimes it doesn't, which means were in jail. Jacob and Isaac have been sent there after Jacob vomited again, this time over the Prime Ministers shoes. (The PM was giving a press conference at the time.)

Eventually they are turned loose, and set off in pursuit of their story. So, helplessly, do we.

Unfortunately, though the characters seem to have some idea what they're looking for, we don't. I said the intrigues were complicated; actually, theyre impenetrable. Theres something about a murder, and something else about a missing lesbian minister, and terrorists come into it, and so -- near the end, in time-honoured fashion -- do the Mounties.

It's possible the author doesn't care very much whether we understand or not, but I think this is rash of him. One of the theatres few natural laws is that an audience, given the merest whiff of a narrative, will do their level best to follow it; when they are unable to, they get frustrated and start to howl like beasts in the wilderness.

The second act is, in fact, set in the wilderness, or at least in Muskoka. The stage is now bare of sanitation, but it does have our two heroes car, which has broken down. This forces them to talk to one another -- about their childhoods and about their respective marital pasts, Jacob's being checkered and Isaac's tragic.

Jacob momentarily wonders how his ancestors would feel if they could see him now, lost in the open and scared of wolves -- a wry line that unexpectedly made me laugh. (It was the high point of the evening.) For a moment, there is the suggestion of a mood, but the actors prove unable to sustain it.

Here begins the tricky business of apportioning guilt. Of course, one can never really know; the author always gets the lions share of the blame, and its true that the storytelling here is confused, the comedy clumsy, the characterization less than rudimentary, and the theme indecipherable.

But though the actors may have been demoralized by the material, they seem, in turn, to have dragged it lower than it needs to go; these things tend to spiral. Ian Ferguson sometimes manages a coarse, blubbery energy as Jacob; Tim Hill as Isaac is simply lame.

The production looks as if the director, Paul Thompson, threw his hands amiably in the air and left text and performers to their own devices. The action happens on a pair of adjacent platforms, divided by a wriggly fault line. Sometimes the staging exploits this gap; sometimes it doesn't.

At the height of the drama, the players mimic a flight through the woods by running around the stage in a series of zig-zags; it looks like panic-by-numbers, and is unrelated to anything else in the show.

Somehow they get their scoop, whatever it is, and are rewarded. Jacob is given a job at the National Post (assistant features editor, in fact); Isaac turns one down. I'm not sure which of these is meant to constitute a happy ending.

THE HAPPY PRINCE

Nathan Cohen Studio, Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People, Toronto

- - -

Leslie Arden is the best hope among Canadian writers of musicals. In addition to her large-scale shows (best-known: The House of Martin Guerre), she has a portfolio of miniature musicals for children. The Happy Prince, now playing at the former Young People's Theatre, is one of them and it is a delight. Intended for six-and- uppers, it also offers more to adults than most of this theatre's teenage shows offer to anyone.

Arden's piece is a dramatization, both faithful and imaginative, of the Oscar Wilde story about the pangs and glories of the compassionate heart. For those whose memories of the original have, like mine, grown somewhat vague: A golden statue stands surveying a town, the one its subject ruled over when alive. Much admired locally for his splendour and his uncomplainingness (so they call him "happy"), the Prince is actually in anguish over the poverty and misery that were screened from him in life.

So he sends a swallow, which for personal reasons has delayed its migration, to relieve individual cases with the ruby from his sword and the sapphires that were his eyes. Finally, he has the swallow strip him of his gold leaf and distribute it at large. The swallow, refusing to desert the Prince, dies of the cold.

The statue, now blind and shabby, is pulled down by the town council (close relatives, apparently, of those who governed Hamelin when the Pied Piper passed through) and burned -- all but its leaden heart, which broke when the swallow died but, like Joan of Arc's, resists incineration. Prince and bird are taken up to Heaven.

I have undoubtedly made that sound mawkish, but Wilde didn't, and neither does Arden. The story is one of the best things its author wrote, and the musical is as witty and moving as its source.

The Children's Trio, a troupe founded by Arden, has originated five of these adaptations since 1982. Each has a cast of three, including the author-composer-pianist, who is also the very smart director. Her two colleagues here are Sherry Garner, who does most of the narrating, and Cathy Elliott, also responsible for the set and costume designs, which are done on the most stylish shoestring imaginable.

There is pleasure just in the perfectly balanced colours of the three players' cravats, or in the sight of them in the top townspeople's top hats. (Arden wears hers with particular flair.) The Prince himself is represented by a pair of golden feet; the swallow is an intricate hand puppet, manipulated by Elliott. She also supplies its voice and is equally eloquent speaking the lines or flapping the wings.

The swallow's initial delay in leaving town is caused by its having taken a fancy to a graciously waving reed in the river, much to the disgust of its friends. "This," they sing, "is a really dumb affair/She is certainly not in his class/There are plenty of swallows everywhere/Yet he's fallen in love with grass!" -- the abrupt descent to basics signalling one of Arden's most pointed meetings of words and music.

Humour and yearning alternate in her songs here -- and sometimes fuse. One of the Prince's initial beneficiaries is a young playwright, hungry and creatively blocked, struggling to complete a commission and remembering all the good advice he was ever given: "Somebody told you it's yours for the asking/If you haven't got it then you haven't tried/Somebody said you'd get out what you put into it/Somebody lied." ( Arden studied with Stephen Sondheim, and it shows.)

Following Wilde's text and expanding on it, she works in patter choruses and a sea shanty. Her outright ballads suffer from the soft- rock underpinnings that make nearly every theatre song written since 1975 sound the same, but only one number is a sore thumb.

It is, significantly, the only one not licensed by the original. Wilde wrote in a little matchgirl; he did not, however, give her dreams of running away and joining the gypsies. Arden does. At first we think she may just be teasing us with flamenco strummings and heel clicks, but they grow, inexorably, into a full number -- one that leaves us, at its end, exactly where it found us. Everything takes us further into the story, and it's an accomplished and beguiling journey. Children should take their parents.

THE MACKENZIE/ PAPINEAU REBELLION

Cameron House

- - -

From 1985 to 1999, the company called VideoCabaret occupied itself telling the nation its own story in a 12-play comic epic entitled The History of the Village of the Small Huts. They are now telling us again, reviving the original cycle, with a few amendments born of hindsight.

Part Three, first seen in 1987, has returned; and though I missed it the first time around I judge, from its resemblance to other segments, that its vision is unaltered and its style undimmed. As usual, every character who sets foot on the tiny, black-swathed cartoon stage is either a fool or a scoundrel, except for some who are both.

As a philosophy of history (and not just Canadian history), this is extremely plausible. As drama, especially given the short-scene format that comes with the VidCab territory, it has its limitations; as one disgraceful episode succeeds another, the revelations of corruption and incompetence become not just predictable but interchangeable. However, The Mackenzie/Papineau Rebellion is more tightly focused than other bits of the cycle, and therefore less monotonous. It has a strong story -- two in fact, told in alternating vignettes -- and though it may not dramatize the participants' complexities, it does at least suggest that they may, somewhere off-stage, exist. As well, the dark elan of the presentation remains seductive.

Michael Hollingsworth, author and director of the project, has perfectly defined its virtues and limitations in the clinching sentence of his auteur's manifesto: "The only thing one knows for sure is that the new boss will be the same as the old boss." So we get a style that seems to advocate revolt and ends up mocking it.

We have William Lyon Mackenzie, firebrand journalist and first mayor of Toronto, leading his insurrection against the oligarchic Family Compact, while, at the same 1837 moment, Louis Joseph Papineau makes his bid to replace the rich English rulers of Quebec with some rich French ones.

As ever, I find myself naively astonished at the sheer efficiency of the presentation: at the unerring speed with which seven actors, sharing 34 roles, switch between voices, wigs and boldly complicated costumes; at the accuracy with which they hit their marks in the blackouts on a stage scaled to look as much like a TV screen as possible (an inch out of place and they'd ruin the lighting on which the show largely depends); at the confidence with which they embody the chosen style. There is not a moment of uncertainty in the show.

Hollingsworth's script shows the way here; it has a remarkably confident tone. It uses anachronism without being silly or smug; it sounds, in fact, timeless.

Eddie Glen plays Mackenzie as a one-man ginger group; his face, broad in its own right, is protectively encircled by a halo of bristling ginger hair, and his voice bristles, too; he measures out his rhetoric like a pharmacist dispensing brimstone, so that a comparatively mild denunciation like "primeval" emerges as a fundamentalist "prime evil." Especially taking is his march downtown at the head of his pitchforkwielding troops; starting tremulously at Yonge and Eglinton ("thank God it's downhill"), he gains in missionary zeal as he passes the fleshpots of Summerhill and Rosedale, only to meet a rude military awakening somewhere south of College.

A fine orator but a lousy general (and not above exploiting his solitary tongue-lolling apprentice), his disillusion, when both his hopes and his troops lie in ruins, is still treated with something suspiciously resembling sympathy.

No such charity, and considerably less time, is accorded to Ostap Soroka's popinjay Papineau, excoriated by just about everybody including his own massacred supporters, each identified simply as "Patriote," just as every one of Mackenzie's men is billed as "Rebel." (The best way of attracting sympathy in a Hollingsworth production is not to have a name.)

The ruling English and French get it, naturally, in their stiff, preening necks. The twin commanders of Upper and Lower Canada compete in their lip-curling contempt for "the mob"; while the British governor, Sir Francis Bondhead (a name that, if it hadn't existed, would have to have been invented, probably by Dickens or Ben Jonson) comes off like a declining Roman emperor: murderously weak and nourishing a suspicious, though apparently unrequited, affection for a tough tycoon called McNab. Janet Burke as Bondhead gives the showpiece performance of the evening; she also plays three other roles, all of them male. (The few women in the cast, most of them Mackenzie's or Papineau's mothers, are played by men.)

Greg Campbell plays an escalating assortment of oppressors, at their summit Bishop Strachan, an ambulant snarl whose face clenches and whose teeth contort at the scent of anything or anyone to the left of Genghis Khan; one thinks of such contemporary holy rollers as Pat Robertson or Ian Paisley.

Some intermediate henchmen and turncoats come and go with confusing frequency, so that the show becomes rather muddy as a history lesson, but there is generally some sharply etched new arrival to pick up the slack: Bruce Vavrina as an anglophile veteran of 1812, expressing his contempt of all trimmers and moderates with a ferocious grin; or Patrick Conner as Lord Durham, the Governor General, who arrives like a courtly deus ex machina to do, as my children's Civics textbook describes it, the right things for the wrong reasons. The upshot, as always in VideoCabaret's chronicles, is a mixture of scorn and sadness; scorn wins out, but this time sadness gives it an unusually close run.

BREATH[E]

The Theatre Centre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Steve Lucas, one of the best and most ubiquitous stage designers in Toronto, has now turned to direction. He has declared himself to be uncomfortable directing actors -- a trait he shares with some other designers-turned-directors, and also with some directors who have never been designers at all. Unlike them, he has followed through on the logic of his convictions and has come up with a piece employing no visible human bodies at all. It offers us 30 largely hypnotic minutes composed entirely of sound and light.

This makes Lucas even more radical than Edward Gordon Craig, the harmless but extremely influential English eccentric who, in the early years of the 20th century, was proclaiming the supremacy of the director and the liberating importance of electric light. He thought actors would get in the way of his vision and proposed replacing them with life-sized puppets -- what he called ubermarionettes. (It never happened.) So at least he wanted simulated people -- characters of a kind.

Lucas's soundtrack (designed by Steve Gordon Marsh) comprises the insistent sound of a human heartbeat, much amplified and presumably multi-tracked, and the more subtly modulated sound of human breath. (The credit for the latter reads, "Breathing -- Jane Miller." Miller is an actress, so Lucas has had to compromise to that extent. But of course she isn't there; her contribution, too, is on tape.)

What we see on stage is a cloudscape, or maybe a fogscape; anyway, it's composed of drifting smoke, variously lit. It's contained within a receding series of proscenium arches, though we don't see them at first. When they are revealed, the sharply enhanced sense of a third dimension is a real coup. The audience sit in rows, in a kind of enlarged jury box; it only holds 27 of us, but then the show is given four times nightly.

It takes its shape -- I merely repeat what I'm told -- from Tantric philosophy; the program accordingly lists seven states of the mind and body, known as chakras. As a synopsis I found this less than helpful, but I acknowledge that the piece has a structure; I could feel it, even if I couldn't explain it.

Lucas knows what he's doing, imaginatively as well as technically, and his sights and sounds give considerable pleasure. I'm not sure he succeeds in his professed intention of putting the audience in a trance -- I'm not even sure that would be desirable -- but I did find my mind pleasantly drifting, sometimes concentrating on what was unfolding before me, sometimes thinking about other things entirely. This, admittedly, is what happens to me at many more conventional plays, but it's nice to know that on this occasion, the author has budgeted for it.

I see that I have tripped into defining Breath[e], at least implicitly, as a play. Let's see: Nearly 50 years ago, Kenneth Tynan, in one of my favourite pieces of theatre criticism, assessed the groundbreaking credentials of a new and plotless play called Waiting for Godot. He said Samuel Beckett was proposing a criterion for drama more fundamental "than any in the books: A play ... is a means of spending two hours in the dark without being bored."

He didn't say it was the only way, though of course not all the others would involve being, or even having, an audience. And, even if you're just thinking of time spent in theatres, you have to concede that the Greeks and Elizabethans, who did most of the formative work here, watched their plays in daylight.

Still, it's an appealing definition, though in one crucial way Beckett himself backtracked from it almost immediately. His subsequent plays all lasted less than two hours -- substantially less in many cases, to the point that when Tynan asked him to contribute to the erotic revue Oh Calcutta!, Beckett responded with a 30-second sketch in which an unseen person was heard to breathe, first in, then out.

He called this little joke Breath, and it seems to have been the partial inspiration for Lucas's more serious piece. It's more serious because he has actually put it on and it works.

It works well enough to wreak severe damage on another definition, one that I read in a British theatre magazine and have lived by for decades. It said that almost everything in the theatre could be dispensed with -- "even the play, if necessary" -- except for actors. Now Lucas has done without them as well -- and still produced a dramatic spectacle that involves the audience. (We wanted to applaud at the end, but weren't sure how, or whom.)

He has done it, wisely, in miniature; and he may not need to do it again. For most practical purposes, the old battered definitions will serve; a battery of plays without actors would prove very boring very fast. This one has the feel of a demonstration, an exercise, but a beautiful one. It is subtitled, in bashfully small print, "a sensual experience." I would substitute "sensuous" for "sensual" and recommend it highly.
