WELL,

Tarragon Theatre

- - -

Jonathan Wilson delivers in his new play Well, (the comma is part of the title) on the promise displayed in his previous piece, Kilt. You will note that, when it comes to finding names for plays, Wilson is the merry master of the monosyllabic moniker.

He certainly gets mileage out of this one, exploiting the various meanings of the word "well" almost to the limits of the dictionary. There is the kind of well you draw water from, or alternatively fall down, which is what Willie, the central character of this play, did when he was three.

There is the kind of well that you either do or don't feel; after being dramatically rescued, and becoming a local celebrity on the strength of that, the traumatized Willie was packed off to a mental hospital from which, 20 years on, he has now unofficially discharged himself. (He says he feels well, but he obviously has his doubts; others, including the authorities, share them.)

And there is the kind of hedging, qualifying "well" that people use in conversation, generally to play for time, and that denotes uncertainty. Carol, a television news reporter, is especially prone to this. As a child she fed on the story of Wee Willie in the Well, and she has recently done a "where is he now?" piece to commemorate the anniversary. Willie, on the run, catches the item on a motel TV. So he seeks her out, to answer her question, and to ask for her assistance in locating the scene of his former fame.

Willie, like many mental patients, is unnervingly straightforward; he has no defences. Carol seems to have nothing but defences, and they often rear up and hit her. (When we first meet her she is doing multiple retakes, caused by the word "deficit" always coming out of her mouth as "decifit." She never does get it right.) The play lines the two of them up in parallel, to show each eventually providing some of what the other needs.

They are both extremely well played. Aaron Willis is guilelessly and insistently watchable as Willie, and Melody A. Johnson, whose specialty is being vulnerably abrasive, is a sharp fountain of nervous energy as Carol.

Carol has been having occasional sex with her cameraman Quentin (played on an endearing note of rough-house bewilderment by Paul Braunstein), who would like it to be less occasional and maybe even official. When Willie falls -- inevitably and unthreateningly -- in love with Carol, Quentin's reaction is first violent, then understanding.

This three-cornered relationship is quirkily but solidly developed, helped by Wilson's flair for comic surprise, in individual lines and in whole scenes; Willie's opening speech to an unseen medical panel is a tour de force, as is Carol's first venture into Quentin's living quarters, a level of commitment from which she draws back appalled.

When it sticks to the present tense, the play does fine. When it reaches back into the past it runs, like so many other plays, into trouble. Willie's head is filled by the voice of a girl, whom we see and whom we take to be dead, and who is in fact inclined to goad and prompt him as if she were the ghost of Hamlet's father. Holly Lewis plays her, conscientiously though to little effect.

We also meet Willie's rural uncle, who is considerably more corporeal. Disillusioned by just about everything, he is now in the curio dealing business, and delivers rich, curmudgeonly tirades with which Richard McMillan is obviously having a lot of fun. (Too much perhaps, but as I also had fun listening to him, it would be hypocritical of me to complain.)

Eventually there are revelations about what really happened; and though they are not incredible, they are not burningly credible either ("Ding dong bell, Willie's in the well. Who pushed him in? That's where the doubts begin. Who got him out? That's what it's about"). Really, the author can tell us anything he chooses, and we don't have the evidence to call him out.

Whimsy creeps in, though not to the point of sentimentality. (Tears don't well up.) The last scene gets the play back on its feet, amounting to as much of a happy ending as we deserve.

Chris Abraham directs to the play's strengths, which are those of wit and unillusioned good nature. The evening confirms Wilson's place -- alongside Michael Healey, Adam Pettle, Florence Gibson, Kristen Thomson and the revered Morris Panych -- in the ranks of playwrights worth paying attention to. He has a voice and he uses it, well, well.

Black & White Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann, Tarragon Theatre / VOICE FROM THE PAST: From left, Holly Lewis, Aaron Willis and Melody A. Johnson in Well, Jonathan Wilson's new play. ;

THE BATTLE OF STALINGRAD: A REQUIEM

Du Maurier Theatre Centre

- - -

Georgia, Georgia, no peace I find. Rezo Gabriadze, a Georgian puppet-master and stage designer seeking a metaphor for the war that wracked his homeland in the 1990s, alighted on the devastating siege and defence of Stalingrad in the Second World War. The resulting piece, involving half a dozen puppeteers and a long list of recorded voices, has come to Toronto as the last offering in this year's World Stage Preview series.

Officially described as less a history than a lament, the show takes to extremes an honourable tradition of presenting cataclysmic events as glimpsed in flashes from the sidelines. Stendhals account of the Battle of Waterloo, in The Charterhouse of Parma, belongs in this line; and so does practically all of War and Peace. There was a celebrated dramatization of the Tolstoy novel that anticipated Gabriadze to some extent by using toy soldiers to demonstrate the Battle of Borodino.

In The Battle of Stalingrad, the events are twice distanced (thrice, perhaps, if you count the surtitles); not only are they acted out by marionettes but by marionettes who, for much of the time, represent farm animals. The inspiration here is apparently a war report about the landscape of Stalingrad having been covered with dead horses. The implications of that are very poignant, though not perhaps as poignant as the prologue of this production, which shows us a human body: a tiny, naked puppet, appallingly frail and vulnerable.

There is a matching epilogue, not quite as resonant, in which an ant mourns the number of his progeny stamped out in the campaign. We are meant, I think, to accept him as truly ant-like, rather than anthropomorphic, though obviously his plight has resonances for the fate of humans trapped in the same way.

Other times, though, the animal characters seem to be directly standing in for humans. So Alyosha, "a stage worker and transport specialist" and the nearest thing we have to a hero, is played by a horse, overloading a metaphor and diluting tragedy with whimsy. To put this in perspective: I am not a fan, either, of that American cartoon strip which presents the Holocaust in terms of mice. I love Animal Farm, but that has a consistent satirical tone; you know which are the animals and which are the humans, and why.

This show, too, uses both; you are expected to laugh indignantly at the humans and be sorry for the animals; which means taking a sentimental perspective and imposing it on the audience. Its one thing to concentrate on the marginalized characters who don't make it into the history books, but they need to live as characters.

I found the show visually beautiful, sometimes moving, but also confusing. It seems to be trying to be an epic and a collection of fragments, both at once, wavering between the sardonically mournful and the traditionally patriotic. Alyosha's relationship with Natasha, an actress, is hard to take hold of or to care about. I couldnt tell why the action shifts to Berlin before the war for a satirical look at intellectual cafe life. (I presume its satirical, since among the artists supposedly present are Bertolt Brecht and Franz Werfel, both of them well out of Germany by 1937, which is when this is said to be happening.)

The view of Stalin himself, and of the Russian brass in general, is very ambiguous. We feel the devastation, in a generalized way, and we also applaud the ingenious presentation of a train journey. We also note the presence of a Jewish wedding, complete with canopy, signifying, apart from its place in the plot, that life has a habit of going on. We assent to the proposition that war, any war, is hell, and that the helpless always suffer.

So Gabriadze has his metaphor. But it would have to exist more fully in its own right for us to take it to heart. It isn't just the use of puppets that makes it all seem small.

THERAC 25

Factory Theatre Studio

Adam Pettle, the rising young playwright of Zadie's Shoes and Misha, originally intended to be an actor. That career was derailed when he was struck by cancer; he survived, but the treatment left him with a depleted vocal cord, making full-time acting impractical. He has returned to the boards, though, in his own Therac 25, an early (1995) play, based on his own experiences in the cancer ward. His character, Alan, has suffered similar side-effects: "Hence, he says, the Tom Waits impersonation."

As a description this seems approximate -- Pettle's voice is at least an octave higher than the Waits growl -- but one sees what he means. Vocal range apart, there is a perceptible lack of professional finish in his performance; but -- given the subject matter and his own involvement -- this may be a positive gain.

The only other character, a fellow patient named Moira, is played by Patricia Fagan, a young actress who has given a string of notable supporting performances for Soulpepper over the last few years, and who here comes superbly into her own.

Moira, unlike Alan, is undergoing chemotherapy, and she has a far lower chance of survival. She has a set of caustic defence- mechanisms; among other things she puts an unconditional ban on the question "how are you feeling?" (Alans unthinking contravention of this rule, in a telephone conversation after their first meeting in the waiting room of the Princess Margaret Hospital, occasions one of the plays best sequences.)

Fagan, a fighting-spirit in a head scarf, is in unwavering control of her role; she times her author's zippy comebacks more smartly than he does himself. And this, perverse as may seem, is a problem.

Pettle, as his subsequent plays have confirmed, is a master of the wisecrack; his jokes vary in quality but the best are very good. They are, though, a double-edged weapon. They can speed a play appealingly along; they can also make it seem glib. Pettle's own character here is an aspiring writer, and the one-liners fall more naturally from his lips, rendered more credible, if anything, by his own somewhat unpolished delivery of them.

Fagan plays an aspiring social worker, and there seems no reason for her to be speaking the same language he does, and to be speaking it more adeptly. (Not to mention that he is Jewish and she isnt.)

The play is, of course, a love story, and it sometimes seems to be taking the Hollywood convention of meeting cute to grotesque extremes. Its as if Neil Simon had decided to write a cancer play: A Simon born a couple of generations later, into a climate that was by that time much more outspoken, but still cloaking his characters in a laughter that belongs to him rather than to them.

These considerations hobble the play in its early scenes but fall away as it progresses. (This is a short play and it rides to its climax in double-quick time.) It is an unconsummated, indeed almost undeclared, love story; and this fact, apparent from the outset, gives it more than pathos. The fact the characters are out-patients rules out the sentimentality endemic to hospital romances. We get to see the characters in the outside world: In their respective apartments (they never meet there but they talk on the phone), on a park-bench, in a church, where Moira throws up into a bowl of holy water.

The fact the play is born of grim personal experience predisposes you to respect the author's authority (and makes me feel slightly shamefaced about my own doubts). You also come to respect his skill, the way in which he plays off one kind of defensiveness against another. Moira's thin skin is matched by Alan's resistance to being physically touched; neither can get through to the other as they would wish. The tension builds to a stark, unsentimentalized ending; and one mourns the loss of a relationship; which -- in the theatre - - is maybe the most moving kind of loss there is.

The play is directed by Jordan Pettle, the author's brother, who is a successful actor, making the role-reversal satisfyingly complete.

COUNTERFEIT SECRETS

Artword Theatre, Toronto

It has taken the better part of 300 years but the plays of Pierre Carlet de Marivaux seem finally to be happening in English. We know this because one of them, The Triumph of Love, has become a film, playing in Toronto even as I type.

Some of us were able to steal a march on the movies last year, when the same play was staged here by John Van Bureks Pleiades Theatre company. That production was the central panel of a triptych. It had been preceded the year before by the same author's The Game of Love and Chance, and Van Burek's troupe has now completed the trinity with Counterfeit Secrets, which is his translation of Les Fausses Confidences. The play may well be the best of the three, but the production -- though intelligent and well worth seeing -- is the least successful.

The play is a knife-edged courtship comedy in which -- as suggested by the title -- just about every character is being doubly duplicitous. Some of them are never less to be trusted than when they are telling the truth.

Dorante, the son of a lawyer, infiltrates himself into the household of Araminte, a wealthy young widow with whom he has fallen in love. His agent in this scheme is Dubois, once his valet and now in the service of Araminte herself. He lets her know of his former masters passion (pretending hes doing so without Dorante's knowledge), embroiders matters by saying he's gone crazy with it, and waits for the tender-hearted Araminte to fall in return. Which she does, almost immediately; but there are, of course, complications.

Dorante, at the urging of a managing uncle, pretends love to Marton, Aramintes female companion; and she, too, is only too happy to reciprocate. Araminte is engaged in a lawsuit with a neighbouring count, and the prevailing wisdom is that this could best be settled if the two of them got married.

As Aramintes steward and legal advisor, Dorante is in an excellent position to frustrate this -- another test of his already compromised integrity. Araminte herself is highly uncertain about whether to follow her heart, and begins developing her own schemes and keeping her own secrets. There is a trap door beneath nearly everything anybody says.

Van Burek has given it a fittingly geometric staging, on a set (by Andjelija Djuric) that looks like an unused clinical ward into which somebody has mysteriously introduced an elegantly old- fashioned desk and chair. It's ages before anybody gets to sit down on the chair, comfortable though it looks; for the most part they have to deposit themselves on cruel high-backed contraptions that are moved and removed as needed. The walls are mobile, too; the actors push them around, often while talking.

Much of this struck me as wasted labour; the stage seldom looks much different when they've finished, and there are no crucial changes of locale in the play anyway. The main point seems to be to allow an occasional central position to a door with a small square window in it, through which the plays scheming servants can favour us with smug or menacing glances. These are effective, and they pay off especially well at the end, but Im not sure they're worth the effort.

The director has a firm grasp on the play, and his steel-and- gossamer translation is excellent.

Where he falls down is in his casting, or at least in one central piece of it. Arsinee Khanjian plays Araminte -- and seems piteously out of her depth. This is a play where language is a weapon -- one that needs to be wielded with absolute precision. Khanjian can muster neither the concentration nor the attack; losing the will to listen to her, we start missing out on bits of the plot.

Though the characters have secrets from one another, they don't have them from us; but its often hard to tell what Araminte is after. Her accent doesnt help, but it's probably sheer theatrical inexperience that is the main culprit. She looks as unhappy as she sounds -- frumpy, really, though neither she nor the other actresses are well-served by their costumes. (Julie LeGal, a Marton of more enthusiasm than finesse, looks half-dressed.) Araminte ends up as a puddle of hard-used innocence, which is surely sentimental; the lady may tell fewer fibs than anyone else on stage, but she has her own agenda and pursues it.

The best performance comes from William Webster as the uncle, who can turn on a dime from geniality to venom and who alone plays with the unfaltering pace and precision the text demands. Dawn Greenhalgh is amusing as Araminte's social-climbing mother, aghast that anyone should stand in the way of her becoming a counts mother-in-law.

Andrew Pifko is pleasant as Dorante, though without fully exploring the characters various levels of sincerity and deceit. Xuan Fraser is smoothly sinister as his servant, manager and -- the production strongly suggests -- lover. (The idea behind this particular beaux' stratagem seems to be that the two boys will live happily together off the widow's money. I doubt that even Marivaux meant to be that cynical.)

The modernish dress again leaves the traditional role of Harlequin (Thomas Hauff) out on a limb; with no spangled costume to hide inside, the actor is enforced to turn a clever idiot into a realistic character, and that is an impossibly tall order. He should exist on a different level from everyone else on stage; here, he's a schemer like the rest, and that is one more than the play needs.

SPEED-THE-PLOW

Jane Mallett Theatre

- - -

David Mamet's Speed-the-Plow is another of his plays about resentful male aggression. Abandoning the Chicago small-timers of American Buffalo and Glengarry Glen Ross, he now takes us to Hollywood, his second home, to meet men who have hit the big time, but are still small-timers at heart.

The play takes his familiar dialogue gambits and tragi-comic themes, but reworks them as satirical comedy. This may be inevitable. It seems impossible to write a Hollywood play that doesn't come out satirical.

The players here are Bobby Gould, who has been appointed head of production after years in the studio trenches, and his old buddy Charlie, whose career has always trailed at least a step behind and who is still toiling.

Now, with the walls of Bobby's office not even decorated yet, Charlie comes to him with a property: a prison movie with a major star. Charlie has only 24 hours in which to exercise his option.

Bobby, whose contract gives him the power to green-light one cheap (i.e. under $10-million) movie a year, is thrilled; he will take the story to the head of the studio, whose consent will surely be a mere formality. The project reeks of money, and Bobby and Charlie, prospective co-producers, are already counting it. (Bobby must, by most people's criteria, be rich already, but of course his standards are more exalted than ours.)

Trouble comes in the shape -- that seems the right term -- of Karen, the temp in Bobby's outer office whom he, in high-flying mood, has bet Charlie he can seduce. So he hands her a book -- a no- hope book that he has been entrusted with to give "a courtesy read" - - and asks her to come to his house that night and tell him what she thinks of it.

It's a novel about hope, despair, radiation and the end of the world; Karen finds it inspiring. She tells Bobby that this must be his movie, and he wins his bet. But he also lets himself be convinced, by her appeal to his nobler nature and to the motion- picture industry's power for doing good.

Next morning, as they are about to go into the crucial meeting and make their pitch, Bobby tells Charlie that he has changed his mind. Charlie is very upset.

This is a small, tight, witty play: The dialogue between the two men is prime Mamet (though it never rises to the comic poetry of his very best work) and the observation genially remorseless. But Hollywood is, after all, an obvious target, which makes it all the more important that it be hit sharply. It cannot afford to lose focus.

In this production by Jeff Seymour, an American actor-director who also plays Bobby, it sprawls. It literally sprawls. One side of the unwieldy Jane Mallett stage is taken up by Bobby's office; the other by his living room. Both are in view throughout. It seems a reasonably elegant solution (no designer is named) but the play is written in conventional long scenes, so at any given point half the acting-area is going to waste. Nothing is centred.

Seymour's own performance is competent enough. He seems to be aiming at giving Bobby a boyish vulnerability, or maybe that's his quality anyway, but he never confronts the question of how genuine - - or at least temporarily heartfelt -- Bobby's new-found idealism might be.

Bill Elliot's Charlie is stronger and meaner, and the resentment that seethes beneath his fulsome protestation of friendship makes itself felt. But the interplay between them is a shadow of what it might be, and when it erupts into violence -- as, in a Mamet play, it always does -- it merely seems surprising. It ought to seem surprising and inevitable.

Nor does it help that the production, well, pulls it punches; most of the incident occurs out of sight, behind a sofa. It has to be real, and seen to be real, to be funny; and it is funny, or supposed to be. The humour is that neither of the participants seems to regard it, really, as anything exceptional.

The part of Karen was originally played on Broadway by Madonna: a performance that I saw, but cannot remember a thing about. (It wasn't even memorably bad.) Here, maybe in a case of casting by association, the role goes to an actress best known for being the daughter of a pop singer: Joely Collins, daughter of Phil. But she turns out to be very good, with a warmth that I've certainly never seen brought to the role before. She cannot persuade us that the book she champions might be good (the passages Mamet lets us hear put paid to that) but there does seem a chance that she might genuinely believe in it without being an idiot.

She also rises, though not strongly enough, to the ambiguities that rise to the surface in the last scene, when the fight becomes a three-cornered one. Nobody here is pure, and the trap is laid, the point made, with a chess master's economy and finesse.

Seeing the play for the third time, I still wonder why Bobby doesn't solve his problem by pitching both pictures: one for the studio, one for himself. Given, though, that the choice has to be made, one ends up rooting for the corrupted Charlie rather than for the lady idealist; his need is more naked, and if a bad film has to be made, better it be one that some audience might actually enjoy.

This is a transitional work between the Chicago masterpieces where the guys tear one another apart without outside assistance, and Oleanna, the gender-war play in which the woman wins when the man self-destructs. Here everybody loses; some more remuneratively than others. This production draws most of the play's sting, but a little lingers.

THE TWO SIDES OF KURT WEILL

Gravenhurst Opera House and Arts Centre

FRIENDS, LOVERS, HUSBANDS

Berkeley Street Theatre Upstairs, Toronto

- - -

Kurt Weills well-documented pilgrimage from the theatres of 1920s Berlin to those of 1940s Broadway has made him one of the most contested composers of the 20th century. Fifty-two years after his death, the skirmishing continues. Here are a few of the principal positions:

1. Weill was an artistic renegade who showed real genius when writing dissonant, pugnacious scores for satirical operas with texts by Bertolt Brecht, and then diluted his talent by writing polite scores for polite American musicals;

2. Weill was a born melodist and popular theatre composer who was bushwhacked by Brecht but really found himself, and did his best work, when writing with the likes of Ogden Nash and Ira Gershwin;

3. When Weill went to Broadway he beat the Americans at their own game and, by virtue of his classical training and avant-garde roots, wrote more distinguished theatre music than did any of his adoptive compatriots;

4. Weill's European reputation has led to his American works being accorded a pre-eminence they don't actually deserve; i.e., his Broadway songs are taken seriously by music snobs who wouldnt give Richard Rodgers house-room;

5. Weill remained essentially the same composer throughout his career, and had a perfect right to write with whom he wanted, about what he wanted.

The last is the one I would now subscribe to, though at various times in the past I have flirted with all of them except number 3. (I like to think I invented 4.) Anyway, the thesis that Weill was, in all senses, a singular composer underlay the concert presented at Gravenhurst on Saturday, in the last of the seasons Pamela Wallin Cultural Weekends at Muskoka Sands.

Two singers, Catherine Malfitano and Joan Morris, performed, individually and in tandem, songs from both ends of Weill, with Morris's husband, composer William Bolcom, acting as accompanist and affable host. Early on, Malfitano sang Denn wie, am sich bettet ("as you make your bed, you must lie there") from Mahagonny; much later she performed One Life to Live from Lady in the Dark; and one sensed a direct line between the two of them that was due to more than the coincidence in lyric.

They're both fatalistic songs -- one grim, one cheerful -- though, oddly enough, the darker one is the one with more joy in it. There are good dramatic reasons for this -- the German lady believes in what shes singing about, the American is trying to convince herself -- but there is more to it than that. Heres my own modest contribution to Weill scholarship: Weill's Berlin songs have more rhythmic drive than his Broadway ones. They are, in fact, jazzier.

I put the word in quotes because the so-called "jazz" that Weill wrote with Brecht was actually an academic, mythologized approximation of American music. And yet these apparently ersatz up- tempo tunes are closer to the real American thing than the ones Weill wrote when he got geographically closer to the source. The Weill songs that swing, or at least can be made to swing, are Mack the Knife, Alabama Song, Song of the Tough Nut. One Life to Live and its equivalents are forced by comparison.

Where the American Weill excelled was in his ballads: Speak Low, My Ship, September Song, It Never Was You, the almost unknown If Love Remains. Alan Jay Lerner, who wrote a show with Weill, once told me he had to keep begging him to keep two thousand years of Jewish misery out of his tunes, but in fact connecting with the Broadway tradition of Hebraic melancholia (not misery) brought out much of the best in him; he was allowed to be emotional without putting his feelings between inverted commas.

Some of Malfitano's performances were marred by an aggressive (and, in a small house, excessive) determination to demonstrate that opera singers can be actresses, too. But she did give a properly scarifying Pirate Jenny, and a very fine rendition of the great bitter torch-song Surabaya Johnny, in which the resigned, anguished set of her head was as expressive as her voice.

Morris was another thing. In a Sunday morning discussion at the Muskoka Sands hotel, Bolcom described Weill -- with some reluctance, I think -- as the original crossover composer. Morris might, by the same token, be described as the paragon of crossover singers, a classically trained mezzo who has devoted most of her career to singing American popular songs. (She crossed over and stayed.)

So she and Weill, though new to one another, make a good match, and her radiantly sensible personality -- and voice -- make a welcome change from the line of doomy diseuses. She paid her respects to the German canon with a wittily vulnerable Barbara Song, and then moved on to the Broadway songs, making the yearning of My Ship and the resigned tenderness of September Song fresh and touching all over again.

Weills total output remains hard to judge. He was primarily a theatre composer, but though we often see his German shows (The Threepenny Opera is on at Stratford this season) we never see the American ones. In the meantime, I think of Weill as the great added extra in the Broadway pantheon: there were Gershwin, Rodgers, Porter, the whole amazing list, and then to make the mixture even richer we get him, too -- not quite of the tradition, but wonderful to have on its edges.

- - -

And what have we now? Well, in Toronto there is Friends, Lovers, Husbands, an unbearable new musical billed in the program as "a most civilized comedy!" Civilized, according to the lyricist and librettist, Nancy Phillips, means its not rock 'n' roll. Well, thats certainly a step in the right direction, but you dont arrive at civilization simply by going back to the cabaret/off-Broadway tradition of the early 1960s. It was limited even then.

The songs here are perfectly craftsmanlike. The rhymes rhyme, and a couple of Bob Ashley's tunes have original twists. (He also plays very good cocktail piano.) But they are smug, assuming the airs of sophistication and worldly wisdom, without ever earning them.

Blame, mainly, the -- for want of a better phrase -- dramatic situation. There is a sixtyish woman, a poet apparently, wondering whether to re-marry the louse she divorced 40 years ago. There is her younger self, who hovers outside the window and then comes in and makes herself at home. Home is rather crowded, owing to the presence of a large fairground horse, apparently there so that we can have one of those songs about life being like a carousel. Anyway, the two of them proceed to spend the whole evening discussing their life, and especially the men in it.

Their primary ex materializes. Not only is he outnumbered two to one but he has to spread himself even thinner by impersonating the male sex generally. We learn nothing solid about any of these people, and so can take no interest in any of the random reminiscences they insist on subjecting us to. All there is to ponder is why sexually explicit lyrics, when set to blue-rinsed show tunes, invariably sound so excruciatingly self-conscious.

Mary McCandless is Older Woman and Lisa Horner is Younger Woman. Cliff LeJeune plays Man -- valiantly, I thought, in a pixieish sort of way -- and I was touched that a man with so little hair on top should be depicted as still irresistible to women. Touched, but not convinced.

Black & White Photo: John Swannell / Catherine Malfitano gave a properly scarifying Pirate Jenny. ; Black & White Photo: The Associated Press / (KURT) WEILL: The great added extra in the Broadway pantheon. ;

Honour a theatre that stands by its writers. A couple of years ago Factory Theatre, in its studio space, took a chance on Beaver, a new play by a new playwright, Claudia Dey. It was savaged by the Toronto critics, including this one. Undeterred, Factory has now given us a new Dey, this time on its main stage. In the meantime, Beaver has been staged off-Broadway, where it has had a much warmer reception.

Beaver struck me as the work of a talented writer whose gift for language far outran her instinct for construction. It sprawled unbearably, though the New York staging may conceivably have made it tighter.

Dey's new piece, The Gwendolyn Poems, is even better written and rambles less, though it still lacks focus. It does, though, have the built-in discipline of biography, being the latest play about the poet Gwendolyn MacEwen. (They seem to come round once every two years.)

The play gives us MacEwen's deathbed reminiscences, or hallucinations; she died in her forties of complications from alcoholism. The framework, once established, is easy to forget, and most of the time we could just be watching a series of random flashbacks, featuring the more damaging people in Gwendolyns life. These include her photographer father, loving in a distant kind of way but separated from her, first by the disciplines of the darkroom and then by those of divorce; her mother, crazily embittered; and her first husband, Milton Acorn, fellow poet and about 20 years her senior.

His star wanes as hers waxes, and you half expect him to walk sacrificially into the ocean, or at least into Lake Ontario, like Norman Maine in A Star is Born. Getting wet, though, isnt his style; he has serious bathing issues.

The first half of the play shows us Gwendolyn facing these demons with considerable resource. The second half shows her falling apart, unhappy when drunk and worse when sober and a prey to DTs. In theory, one can understand how the later woman would develop from the earlier; in practise, we just don't see it happen. We gather that Gwendolyn is/was essentially life-affirming. Well, she would be, wouldn't she, being a poet and a woman and all.

There seems no pressing reason for most of the scenes to happen in the order they do, but individually many of them are a pleasure to listen to. Deys dialogue has real stage presence: heightened and electrically charged without ever seeming false. This is not, blessedly, an and then I wrote" evening; when poetry is called for, Dey writes her own rather than quoting her subjects (or so I am told; I am hardly a MacEwen expert). It works very well.

Words and feelings are brought superbly to life by Brooke Johnson, a hugely expressive actress who can change age and temperament in the flicker of an eyelash, and sometimes less. She has a comic-heroic presence that breathes sanity, making it all the more moving when she loses it. Barbara Gordon is brilliantly infuriating as the mother, forgetting and remembering things as it suits her.

I'm beginning to wonder if theatres that hire David Fox and Jerry Franken (together again after their joint appearances in The Drawer Boy and Stratford's Trials of Ezra Pound) get a rate. I am usually delighted to see them, either individually or as a team, but they got on my nerves here. Foxs Milton Acorn is a caricature of the eccentric artist, Quasimodo in a fright wig and a red-check shirt, and largely incomprehensible. Franken is surprisingly grey and mumbly as dad, though he compensates with an excellent performance as a prosaically kindly doctor who wants to save Gwendy (her mothers name for her, which tells you a lot about her mother) but is dubious about his chances.

Not all the best scenes are due to MacEwen's nearest and dearest being monsters; indeed, some of the best scenes are with her best friend, a sensible poet, played with refreshing solidity by Tamsin Kelsey.

Tony Nappo completes the cast as Gwendolyn's second spouse, an amiable Greek (his home country impresses his wife as being far superior to the Danforth) and also as Lawrence of Arabia, a life- long obsession of MacEwens who makes a sheik-like personal appearance just prior to the final curtain. This doesnt work, but then neither do any of the periodic references to him earlier on; this does seem to be a case of the author getting hung up on what she's read in the books.

The sky-cloth turns a welcome shade of deep blue for this last encounter; up till then, everything in Eda Holmes' production has looked dingy. This makes factual sense, Gwendolyn having lived for the most part in underlit basements, but it doesn't help concentration.

Black & White Photo: Nir Bareket / BROOKE JOHNSON AND DAVID FOX AS WIFE AND HUSBAND IN THE GWENDOLYN POEMS: The play's excellent dialogue is heightened and charged without ever seeming false. ;

In repertory until Oct. 27. Box office: 1-800-511-SHAW.

CAESAR AND CLEOPATRA

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

Your contemporary actress can look fetching, all done up in traditional temptress garb as Cleopatra, but your contemporary actor tends to look hopeless strutting around in a tunic. Though less frivolous reasons are put forward in the program, this must surely be one of the considerations that has prompted Christopher Newton, opening his last season as director of the Shaw Festival, to set his production of Caesar and Cleopatra not in its historical period but at the time in which Shaw wrote it.

That would be the late 1890s, and for a time it looks as if it's going to work. The curtain rises on a silent stageful of actors in khaki, playing cards, giving and receiving orders. They, we eventually deduce, are the Roman army of occupation in Egypt. While they putter about in their puttees, the voice of Newton himself fills us in on the historical background, in lines taken from one of the play's alternate prologues, supposedly spoken by the Egyptian god Ra.

The soldiers look as if they might be about to go into the other prologue, which is a group scene, but they never do. (I suspect a last-minute cut, since some of the characters turn up in the play's last scene without having been introduced. Anyway, it's a loss.)

William Schmuck has designed a multi-stepped and many-levelled set, which takes us from the Sphinx in the desert to an Alexandrian lighthouse to the roof of the queen's palace with beguiling ease, and even seems (through trompe l'oeil rather than hydraulics.) to go up and down. Newton deploys his large cast around and across it with his customary skill, and is particularly adept at positioning Caesar and Cleopatra themselves according to the shifting tides of their relationship. In Shaw's determinedly (and unhistorically) asexual reading, this is largely a matter of master and pupil.

Caesar is the closest Shaw came to depicting his ideal man: a political and military genius who also happens to be a convinced pacifist and humanitarian; since nobody else shares his principles, he has to fight everyone anyway. Basically, he is Shaw singing If I Ruled the World.

Cleopatra is the scared, superstitious schoolgirl whom Caesar teaches to be a queen but whom he cannot stop from developing into a tyrant; she is the everyday world at its sexiest. She cannot tempt him; he cannot convert her. When he sails back to Rome the political implications are cataclysmic but the personal cost amounts, for both of them, to no more than rueful regret. This is not tragedy, or even erotic comedy, but then Shaw thought both those genres frivolous.

Of course, both leads -- Caesar especially -- think and behave like Edwardians from the zenith of the British Empire, with historical names and in fancy dress. So do the other characters, colonized and colonizers alike. It seems to make sense to costume them accordingly, or so Newton and his literary advisor Ronald Bryden argue in their program notes. But the play is already full of jokey anachronisms, most notoriously in the figure of Britannus, Caesar's secretary from the land of the Druids, who behaves like the most censoriously correct of English civil servants. Putting him into a starched blue suit merely kills the joke by underlining it.

Nor does the modern dress do much for the more fustian passages, except bland them out. When people in this play are not exchanging Shavian witticisms they are saying things like "what ho" and "what say you to Mithridates of Pergamos?" You may want to believe that is Shaw making fun of the pompous chronicle plays of his contemporaries, but the truth is that it's a pseudo-Shakespearean style into which he fell quite naturally when confronted by history. (He did the same thing in Saint Joan).

Bryden may be right in claiming that previous productions of this play have drowned the text in spectacle, but this one is just as grandiose, only with different clothes on. It is juiceless; there are surprisingly few laughs. Maybe the play needed to be done, irrespective of period, on one of the Shaw's smaller stages. Then the characters could get at one another, and the ideas could get at us.

The program claims that this, Shaw's eighth full-length play, was his best to date. It was his most ambitious, certainly, possibly his most pretentious, but I doubt it could ever make as satisfying an evening in the theatre as Arms and the Man or You Never Can Tell, both of which preceded it. Still, it could be engaging and, in its own odd way, moving. As it is, when Caesar sails away and Cleopatra equivocally weeps (rather too sentimentally here), we don't know why it's meant to matter.

The lighting (by Kevin Lamotte) gives us a terrific blood-red sky for Cleopatra's disposal of her political adversary Pothinus, but is otherwise murky rather than moody. The low key that it sets for the first meeting of Caesar and Cleopatra at the Sphinx ("a dear little baby sphinx," she insists, not the great one) seems to infect Jim Mezon's whole performance. He is quiet -- very quiet -- and gentle and believably visionary, especially when he stares sad-eyed at somebody who has failed to meet his standards, but he lacks crispness and iron and the sense of boyish adventure, which is actually what keeps this conqueror going. He should be, in his own high-minded way, the most ruthless person on stage.

The more-than-promising Caroline Cave is splendidly in the moment for each stage of Cleopatra's progress, but sometimes seems to be getting them in the wrong order.

The rest are competent but unexciting. Apollodorus (Patrick R. Brown), the chivalrous carpet-fancier, works rather well as a Noel Coward aesthete either hugely or slightly ahead of his time, depending on which calendar you're using. (The wind-up gramophone that plays Jealousy is the nicest update in the show). Rufio (Guy Bannerman), Caesar's aide, is a kilted Caledonian, affecting in his last scene but underpowered earlier on. Britannus (Norman Browning) is as effective as circumstances permit; likewise Pothinus (Neil Barclay), less vulpine in a fez than he might be without. Ftatateeta (Sarah Orenstein), Cleo's murderously possessive nurse, seems to be trying excessively hard, in a thick, unplaceable accent shared by nobody else on stage.

THE OLD LADIES

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

- - -

NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE - The double author credits on The Old Ladies show us the whirligig of time still doing its status-reversing stuff.

The play, first staged in London in 1935, is a dramatization by Rodney Ackland of a 1924 novel by Hugh Walpole. Walpole, one of the most successful writers of his day, is now virtually forgotten, though its hard not to feel that an author disdained by fastidious litterateurs from Virginia Woolf to F. R. Leavis must have had something going for him. Ackland, never much more than a cult figure in his lifetime, has enjoyed a considerable posthumous revival, at Britains National Theatre and elsewhere. Some of his rediscovered plays -- Absolute Hell or The Dark River -- look like prime candidates for the attention of the Shaw Festival. Meantime, we have The Old Ladies.

It's a refined thriller, set in Polchester, a cathedral town that Walpole dreamt up and used in several books. Here, in separate but contiguous rooms in a thin-walled boarding house, live three women, each aged around 70; they are the only people we meet. The rest of the world communicates only by letter, and rarely at that.

There is May Beringer, the newest arrival, timorous and birdlike, with only enough money to keep her going for six months, clinging to the memory of her dead dog and -- more literally -- to a piece of ornamental amber, a present from a long-ago partner in what we take to have been an unfulfilled lesbian relationship.

There is Lucy Amorest, who seems, by comparison with her two companions, to be solid as a rock: a widow, anxiously awaiting news of the ne'er-do-well son from whom she has not heard for a year, and wondering whether a deceased male cousin has left her any money.

And there is Agatha Payne, who tells fortunes with playing cards and is apparently of gypsy origin, bodeful and resentful and -- at least to Miss Beringer -- deeply frightening. She loves bright things; she is deeply fascinated by Lucys possible inheritance and will, it seems, stop at nothing to get her hands on the newest lodgers flashing amber.

The action, on David Boechler's dollhouse set, moves between their respective quarters and also strays on to the staircase and landing. Lucy lives on the ground floor, while the other two share the upstairs; it's probably nobodys fault but this leads to scenes in their rooms seeming very cramped and -- even in the small Royal George Theatre -- remote.

The screws turn slowly but by the end -- with one woman a terrorized victim on the verge of a heart attack, another a prowling harpy, and the third a willing protectress with chinks in her armour -- they get, excitingly, to the wrenching point. And there are some satisfying twists to prolong the agony. The house takes on a double identity: prison and haven. Half of you wants the characters to get away, the other half is rooting for them to stay where they are since the outside world, from all we hear of it, has very little to recommend it.

James MacDonalds production does not quite trust the play; at least I imagine that that's why he has stuffed it with screeching music, film-noir style. (Some of it is actually drawn from the work of Bernard Herrmann, Hollywood's master nerve-scraper.) The two media, though, have different rules. In movies, its accepted that the music will do most of the acting. In a play -- certainly in a naturalistic play, which this is -- it seems silly.

Ackland knew about this; he was, apart from anything else, a master of atmospherics, with a crafty ear for domestic detail. In his last play, A Dead Secret, which I heartily recommend to the Festival as a most superior thriller set in Shaws lifetime but written after it (it's loosely based on the famous Seddon poisoning case), the dynamics of an overstretched, overcrowded household in suburban London are brought to shuddering life, partly through the use of music in real time: kids play singing games, a neighbour practises Just as Song at Twilight, of all piercingly annoying things, on the cornet. In the play and production at hand, you merely wonder where all that funny noise is supposed to be coming from.

MacDonald may be compensating for the crippling fact that his actresses are all too young for their roles. In accordance with Shaw Festival tradition, an erudite program note makes claims for the play that seem far in excess of anything that actually happens on stage. This time it has to do with the plight of elderly women, genteel and poverty-stricken, who have outlived the values they were brought up on and whom a new world is heartlessly abandoning. They are, in addition, deeply suspicious of the encroaching other, represented by the gypsy Agatha.

As sociology it's all true, and you can extrapolate it from the play when you think about it afterwards, but it has more to do with a synopsis of the action than with the action as it unfolds. Only in the third and last act is Agatha given some speeches about how she and her contemporaries would be better off dead. If we are to read these implications in for ourselves, then we need actresses who actually look and sound as if theyre 70. Otherwise the characters and the play are insufficiently pitiable, insufficiently cruel, insufficiently real.

Two of them here do make it, eventually. (I withdraw that "crippling and substitute damaging".) Wendy Thatchers Miss Beringer -- she never does get on first-name terms with the others - - finally has us sharing her fears, and Donna Belleville's Lucy is not only strong but subtle; a look at her is sufficient to tell whether she has just received good or bad news. But Maria Vacratsis's Agatha remains thoroughly external, exuding the idea of menace rather than its reality. She sounds, throatily, like a man and -- especially at her first appearance -- looks like one too; in a thick wig and a red wrap she resembles a Restoration fop or perhaps a modern judge, probably of the hanging variety. A good actress, she plainly knows what is required, but cannot find the desperation in herself; and the production has not centred her. It's a pretty good play, but it takes unduly long to declare itself.

DETECTIVE STORY

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE, Ont. - This is the Shaw Festival at its very best: the stylish reclamation of an imperfect but exciting play by a stageful of actors with skill and humanity pouring out of their ears. Sidney Kingsley's Detective Story, premiered in New York in 1949, is one of the last of the American verismo dramas that peaked in the '20s with The Front Page, and only died out when large-cast plays on Broadway became commercially impossible. Plays like these need to be crammed to bursting point with people; they depict buzzing workplaces that were thought to be seedily glamorous even in their own time, and now have period flavour going for them as well. This is the energy of life one step removed from the streets, transmuted into the energy of the theatre.

Detective Story depicts four hours (theatrically telescoped into three) in a Manhattan police station. Cops, suspects and witnesses come and go in profusion, but basically four cases are unfolding, ranging from a petty shoplifting to a death on an abortionist's table.

At the centre of the web sits Jim McLeod, a proudly incorruptible detective whose virtue is in danger of becoming its own disease. He has seen those he considers guilty go free, too many times, and is at least theoretically capable of taking the law into his own hands. One of his cases is a young man, a war hero for whatever that's worth four years on, who has stolen from his boss's till so as to impress his girl; he is transparently unlikely to reoffend, and even his wronged employer seems willing to drop the charge, but McLeod refuses to co-operate. The abortion case enrages him even more, and when the fake doctor seems about to cheat justice, McLeod beats him up. It then transpires that McLeod's loved wife -- the only softening influence in his life -- once had dealings with the man, and the revelation sends Jim, who is as Pentecostal about sex as about everything else, even further over the edge. Just about everyone in the cast -- his partner, the lieutenant who dislikes him but values his integrity, a cop-worshipping reporter who confesses that he'd be hanging around the station even if he didn't have the job, a velvet-tongued and possibly venal attorney -- lectures him on the dangers of his intransigence; and still he goes on.

They're right, of course; a cop who holds himself above the law is the devil, and nothing that McLeod says about the holes in the system is likely to make us feel any different. To that extent, the play is as unbalanced as its protagonist, if in the opposite direction. Nor, despite its air of outspokenness (and for a Broadway play of its time, it does talk very freely about abortion and, briefly, homosexuality), does it grapple seriously with the issues it raises. It never, for example, suggests that one answer to the scandal of illegal abortions might be to change the law. Kingsley's characters talk tough (another of his plays, Dead End, improbably provided a launching pad, via its movie version, to those B-feature comic favourites, the Bowery Boys) but his fictitious 21st Precinct seems remarkably clean; not one of its policemen is shown to be on the take. McLeod, you feel, has no kick coming about the company he keeps.

He isn't big enough to make a tragic hero; the reasons we're given for his behaviour -- chiefly, his revulsion at his father's abuse of his mother -- are Broadway-glib. In fact, his scenes may be the weakest in the play; as often in this kind of genre piece -- even The Front Page, which draws on farce and melodrama to create something that transcends both -- the milieu is more compelling than the story. The ingredients have changed -- there isn't much farce now, just the occasional hard-bitten laugh. There is still melodrama, and it's expertly thrilling -- but what continues to hold us is the sight of men at work, under a pressure that's second nature to them, and the vast spectacle of human behaviour. It's at least the illusion of realism; and apparently the original production was praised for its authenticity, by critics who had mostly been crime reporters themselves. (These days, we don't get the training.)

And here, Neil Munro's production displays a cunning that amounts to brilliance. It places action and performance of absolute precision within a ghostly surround. The furnishings on Cameron Porteous's set are of weather-beaten solidity but the walls are outline sketches; you'd call them blueprints except that they're in black and white. There are mouth-watering snatches of orchestral jazz -- Ellington or Miles Davis -- to introduce each act, but very sparing use of music thereafter.

The atmospherics (like those in Munro's superb production of The Petrified Forest a few seasons ago) are their own reward; they also promote style and discipline in the acting. Everybody's performance here is full to the brim, but nobody over-emotes; which is remarkable. McLeod's scenes, in particular, could lend themselves to Oscar-baiting emoting (there was a movie, and they probably did); Peter Krantz's performance is a triumph of buttoned-down restraint, a tour de force in reverse, and it's matched by Jane Perry's in the even more perilous role of the wife. Jeff Meadows as the embarrassed embezzler and Fiona Byrne as his hometown sweetheart play an equally perilous duet with comparable tact, though with a few more false notes.

There is a magical moment, halfway through the play, when William Vickers as the reporter, momentarily forgotten at the side of the stage, bursts back into our consciousness like a one-man Greek chorus, adjuring McLeod to "humble yourself, sweetheart, humble yourself." Presumably Jewish (McLeod calls him "Yossel," he calls McLeod "Seamus," which could be racial or professional or both), he moves through the play with sad, chirpy dignity, looking, with a piece of paper stuck in his hatband, like the Mad Hatter.

I'm tempted to call this the best of the supporting performances, but I could equally well say it of Neil Barclay's lawyer, as orotund as rotund, and developing a surprising moral weight to match his physical; or of Jim Mezon, grey and authoritative as the lieutenant. Really, the only way to do justice to this superbly orchestrated production is to put the whole cast in the lineup: Sarah Orenstein's shoplifter-for-a-day, who says "emotions are bad for me" and who rolls her eyes in shock when the personable young cop she has ruled out for being married is heard flirting with a client less particular; Robert Benson's paternal detective and Norman Browning's impassive one; Lorne Kennedy's silky abortionist; George Dawson's especially slimy crook; Simon Bradbury's visiting gangster from Sopranos territory; Al Kozlik's dubious philanthropist; Goldie Semple's fur-laden false witness; Jennifer Phipps, whose deranged complainant, reporting the atom bombs being manufactured in the next apartment, sets the tone for a day in the life; right down to Richard Farrell and Jillian Cook as a prosperous pair of robbery victims, barely visible but still -- like everyone else on stage -- alive and fully breathing.

MERRILY WE ROLL ALONG

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

THE RETURN OF THE PRODIGAL

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

- - -

The received wisdom on Merrily We Roll Along is that it has terrific music and lyrics, sabotaged by a story that insists, suicidally, on telling itself to us backwards.

The first part of the assessment stands without question. Stephen Sondheim's score includes a sweeping, propulsive title tune; two marvellous ballads, the wistful Good Thing Going and the searing Not a Day Goes By (the latter surely the most moving love song he has written); the electric Franklin Shepard Inc., a nervous breakdown in song; the propulsively engaging Old Friends, nervous and confident at once; and much else.

George Furth wrote the show's book, which is a radical adaptation -- and updating -- of a 1930s play by those Shaw Festival favourites Kaufman and Hart. The old friends arrayed for our instruction are Frank Shepard, composer; Charley Kringas, lyricist; and Mary Flynn, novelist and, later, critic. The three first meet on a New York rooftop in 1957, year of Sputnik. That's the last time we see them. The first time we see them -- two of them, anyway -- is in 1976 in Hollywood where Frank is now some kind of big shot. To adapt the words of the absent and embittered Charley, we "really don't know what he does," but he is visibly on the verge of his second divorce and is presumed to have sold out. The rest of the show looks at how, and why.

Furth's dialogue is smart and sometimes telling; line by line I prefer this script to the one he wrote for the far more successful Sondheim show, Company. The problems are in the narrative and the characterization. Merrily may basically be about three people, but it throws in lots of others as well, and they pull the focus. Dramatizing a three-way friendship makes severe demands on a show's time and energy; whether backwards, forwards or sideways, the participants have to be established both as individuals and as a group.

An abiding frustration of Merrily, through all the many revisions it has undergone since its premiere, is its failure to provide its principals with songs that really expose them; which is ordinarily what Sondheim does best. Charley has one cracker of a number (Franklin Shepard Inc.) but it comes early in the show, and nothing else in his role measures up. Mary is permanently and unrequitedly in love with Frank; people mention this from time to time, but little is actually done with it. Frank, when seen in Hollywood, looks less creepy than ineffectual. His major mistake seems to be his actress-wife Gussie who appears snobbish, selfish and a bitch- on-wheels. Nothing we see of her later (and we see a lot) either deepens or complicates that impression.

People who claim the show would work fine if it just pulled itself together and moved in a straightforward fashion are, I think, crazy. Ending the evening with Frank in his misery would just be depressing. Taking him and his pals back to their youth allows for some easy irony of the "little do they know" variety but it also supplies a more authentic poignance. Memories of the future do begin to affect our view of the past, and there are moments that radiate in all directions; when Frank and Charley audition Good Things Going, which becomes their first hit and whose first line is "it started out like a song" it's not just a love song but an image of their collaboration and of its eventual fate ("a good thing going, going, gone.")

And, just on its own terms, the picture of young people trying to make it in New York in the 1950s is joyously effective, with a pile- up of lovely numbers. Bobby and Jackie and Jack (about the Kennedys) is a dead-on pastiche of the kind of nightclub revue number Sondheim himself never got to write at the time; the extended tour-de-force, Opening Doors, is a whirlwind of wit and promise. The concluding rooftop trio, Our Time, lifts the heart and tears at it, simultaneously; it's as stirring and moving a closing anthem as any musical has ever had. I don't know whether it was the authors' idea or this production's to bring the whole company on at the end to reinforce the threesome, but it's a bad one. It reduces what should be their moment to just another finale in a musical.

Jackie Maxwell's production is generally better in small scenes than big ones. The three chums are fine: Tyley Ross a Frank who survives by never growing up, Jay Turvey a clowning Charley who's at once boyish and avuncular, and Jenny L. Wright an alcoholically acerbic Mary. (How nice of the show to make its integrity-figure a critic.) In the second line, Charlotte Moore hardly manages to soften the fearful Gussie -- what we see of her Broadway-Vegas rendition of Good Thing Going suggests the boys had sold out long before Hollywood beckoned -- but Glynis Ranney is very appealing as her marital predecessor, except when she elects to slay the audience, rather than the other characters, with Not a Day Goes By. Gary Krawford is excellent as Joe, the producer Frank cuckolds, and who may be the best-developed character in the piece; connect his dots and you get a person.

The show's perennial casting-problem (how old?) has been met here by using mainly young or youngish actors; two Shaw veterans, Nora McLellan and Peter Millard, are fine in their featured roles as Frank's in-laws but look rather incongruous in the group scenes. These are not happily written anyway; we are given two separate sets of hangers-on who exist only to be shot down. Valerie Moore's choreography is largely limited to basic stepping, except when it takes off into an ill-advised imitation of Bob Fosse's Rich Man's Frug. Judith Bowden's sets have an oddly anachronistic Art Deco flavour.

The show maintains its reputation; it doesn't, as they say, "work," but is more rewarding than most that do. And you will not be able to get those songs out of your head.

- - -

Saturday night at the Shaw saw the return of The Return of the Prodigal, last season's revelation in better shape than ever, even after an electrical storm that caused its last quarter to be played in a half-light. St. John Hankin's acrid Edwardian comedy about the survival of the unfittest goes into areas few plays of its period, or any other, ever reach. Christopher Newton's production is among other things one of the richest portraits of a family, in all its chaos and contradictions, that I have ever seen on a stage; Bernard Behrens, Ben Carlson, Kelli Fox, Patricia Hamilton and Blair Williams are a perfectly interlocking clan, though Carlson has spoiled with some lily-gilding what was once a moment of perfect comic insouciance. Brigitte Robinson is now in steely command as the local dragon, and Roger Rowland is a delightfully useless physician, making spirited conversation with the birds when nobody else will talk to him.

ALL'S WELL THAT ENDS WELL

Festival Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

The comedy about the physician's daughter who cures the sick King of France and asks as reward the hand of a deeply unwilling young nobleman is part of Stratford history. It was one of the two plays presented at the first festival in 1953 and has been revived every time Stratford has hit a major anniversary. It is now the opening show of the 50th season.

That original Tyrone Guthrie staging -- a modern-dress fantasia - - put what was then a neglected play on the map -- not just for Stratford but for the world. Richard Monette's new production isn't up to that legendary standard, but it's the best account of the play that Stratford has seen since. In part it's a love letter to the Festival stage itself, here seen in its pristine state, steps and balcony intact and unadorned, and bathed at the outset in the familiar but still magical dappled light.

This sets the tone for what unfolds as a sober fairy tale.(The play's first line is about death.) The costumes, designed by Ann Curtis, are beautifully cut strict Jacobean; set decoration hardly goes beyond pennants at the French court and a few plants at the country seat of the Countess of Rossillion. Everything is concentrated on the actors and the text, who come together in some surprising ways.

The key scene here is the one in which Helena, our heroine, persuades the King, worn out by previous doctors, to give her medicine a try. It's written in rhyming couplets, which look on the page like pantomime jingle. Lucy Peacock and William Hutt (who have played these roles before, though in separate productions) find depth and human contact in their exchanges, and also an unforced sense of ritual. Music sounds, softly, as Helena, who seems to be a holistic practitioner, charms the King, hitherto resolutely chairbound, into getting up and walking to his cure.

Hutt plays the pre-miracle King in a piping, querulous murmur that occasions the odd worrying moment: Is it characterization or has the octogenarian actor's vocal range finally shrunk? He settles the matter when up and ruling; rebuking the ungracious Bertram, who can think of Helena only as the poor relation in his mother's house, this king sounds positively like Lear working up to the disinheriting of Cordelia. (Previously he may have reminded you of one of Hutt's other great roles, Moliere's Imaginary Invalid.) He husbands his passions -- Hutt has always been good at keeping his powder dry -- but he nonchalantly asserts his authority in the last scene by delivering several speeches with his back to us.

Peacock, who excels at playing the heroine-as-governess or vice versa, commands the play as this one. Helena is the rare female lead in a Shakespeare comedy who does not cloak her determination in humour; she is frequently on the verge of despair but always pulls herself out. Her marriage to Bertram comes half-way through the play. He immediately ducks off to the Italian wars; she pursues him and takes the place in bed of a Florentine girl he is trying to seduce. This traditional comic device may be hard to take, but the psychology behind it -- about the power of sexual fantasy -- is disturbingly acute. Helena herself has a few graphic lines about it. She is, you might say, old beyond her years -- a good thing to be in a play where the old people are, by and large, the good ones.

Bertram's mother, the Countess, who cherishes her daughter-in- law and despises her son, is finely played by Domini Blythe, especially beautiful when she's angry. Bernard Hopkins is a jovial master-of-ceremonies as the lord Lafew, and Benedict Campbell a gnarled presence as the Countess's family fool.

Bertram's cubbishness, which matures into caddishness, is unsparingly portrayed by David Snelgrove. Bertram is a perplexing character because he seems to have so much right on his side; why should he be married off as payment for the royal doctor's bill? Yet nearly everyone in the play condemns him, and by the end of the play -- after his behaviour in Italy, and his worse behaviour in France, where he tries to lie his way out of trouble -- we agree with them. (Sara Topham, as his Florentine prey, has an especially neat speech, dissecting him and men in general.)

We also have to believe that he is better off with Helena and (more of a stretch, but after all it's what she wants) she with him. The truth -- a harsh one, as comic truths tend to be -- is that she knows what's best for them both, and that all her tricks are justified. This physician gives tough medicine.

It could all be funnier. Bertram's immaturity and his twists and turns and wriggles under pressure have their farcical side; so his dependence on his braggart sidekick, Parolles, and his near- neurotic disgust when this self-proclaimed hero is revealed as a fraud.

Tim MacDonald's Parolles is initially tame, his swagger outshone by his multi-coloured shirt, which could be the original technicolour dreamcoat. He only comes into his own when exposed and reduced to zero. From here he rebuilds himself: "Simply the thing I shall make me live" is his new credo, and what he is is a beggar happy with a steady supply of crusts, glad of his rags.

We need more of this unapologetic humanity in the last scene, which here becomes a tidy disposition of loose ends rather than a balanced exhibition of human strength and folly. "All yet seems well," says the King, summing up, and some actors have emphasized that seems as if to cast serious doubts on the marital happiness of Helena and Bertram.

Realistically, those doubts are obviously justified, but this may not be the moment for realism. Hutt slides over the line; we are allowed a happy ending -- rightly, I think -- but it could come at more of a cost.

Still, the title tells us what really counts: After his moralizing wrap-up, the King has an epilogue on the standard pattern, politely requesting our applause. Hutt has always been good at epilogues, and this year, on this stage, it's wonderful that he should have the last word.

MY FAIR LADY

Festival Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

To quote, unfairly, from the current musical at the other festival, the one at Niagara-on-the-Lake: "I saw My Fair Lady/I kind of enjoyed it." Actually, I thoroughly enjoyed it. I always do, once I'm there. I can never, though, get excited in advance about seeing it, and its accepted status as the Great American Musical makes me uneasy.

It isn't the greatness I question, it's the American-ness. Alan Jay Lerner and Frederick Loewe who wrote it were so un-American in style and subject matter (their other big titles were Brigadoon, Camelot and Gigi) they were lucky not to have been investigated by a committee. That is not a criticism of them; they were entitled to write how, and of what, they liked; and God knows they did it well. But it did cut them off from the vernacular energy, the slang and the jazz, that made many of us fall in love with the American musical in the first place; especially, perhaps, if we're not Americans ourselves.

My Fair Lady is based on a great English comedy, Shaw's Pygmalion, that is not just steeped in the class system (like most English comedies) but is explicitly about it. Its original Broadway production starred four English actors. You could make a case for it being the Great British Musical, transplanted at birth by some mischievous fairy.

Except, of course, that no Britons could have written or produced it, then or later. It may not have the American accent, but it does have the American know-how, the confidence of craftsmen at the height of their powers working in a form that was similarly situated. What it does is brilliantly brazen. You are supposed, if you want to turn a play into a musical, to reinvent it wholly; otherwise, why bother? My Fair Lady, however, retains extensive quantities of Shaw's dialogue, and sticks songs into it. This ought to be redundant: certainly irritating, probably boring. In fact, it's perfect. Lerner edited Shaw's text superbly, and seemed to know instinctively how and when to interrupt it. To early audiences, it must have been astonishing; to us, it just seems inevitable.

The show has a secret weapon. It's the best romantic musical ever written, but its romance is against the grain. Shaw himself denied that the tale of the professor of phonetics and the flower girl whom he teaches to speak like a lady was really a love story; but no audience has ever believed him. My Fair Lady finds its own place in the world by making real everybody's secret suspicions about Pygmalion. (One side effect of this is that the two pieces have been able to co-exist. Most musicals that attain this degree of success wipe out their source material.) Lerner makes stringent, and beneficent, cuts in Shaw's last two acts, and of course brings Higgins and Eliza together at the end. But his show has asserted its identity before that: in the scene where the transformed Eliza wanders disconsolate through Covent Garden while her former friends, not recognizing her, hum a reprise of Wouldn't It Be Loverly, which was once her song. It has no equivalent in the play, and it feels absolutely right.

In a program note, Richard Monette, director of the Stratford production, writes that "the musical ending is often seen as ambiguous." I don't think it is (why would Eliza come back to Higgins if she doesn't intend to stay? To have another go at him with the slippers?) and he hasn't staged it that way, but it might have been interesting if he had; it's about the only chance a director has to put an individual stamp on this show. Short of sheer ineptitude, all productions of it seem to come out the same. That's its glory and its frustration; both the humour and the elegance are immovably nailed down.

Monette's production gives full measure of both, especially the elegance, and makes one of the definitive proscenium shows look perfectly at home on the platform stage. Debra Hanson's costumes are glorious; they're most dazzling, of course, in the Ascot scene, where black-and-white gowns are set off against a black-and-white floor, but they're spiffy throughout, from Higgins' green suit for social occasions to the multi-coloured gear that enhances the costermongers' choreography.

On which subject: This show has done much to propagate some American myths about Britain with which I do not hold. One is that a mere academic would live in a mansion, attended by a full-time staff of nine capable of appearing impeccably uniformed even when roused from their beds at three in the morning. Another is that all cockneys are lovable wastrels who clutter up the streets with their knees bent and their thumbs tucked into their waistbands. Given this convention, the choreographer, Donna Feore, makes inventive and exuberant use of it, and is very well served by her dancers. She builds Get Me to the Church on Time, Doolittle senior's song before marriage, into a tour (probably inspired by the film) of the city's watering holes. It's jolly, but it goes on a very long time, and it refuses to wind down at the end when Doolittle allows himself to be taken off to execution, which is rather missing the point.

Colm Feore gives Higgins a touch of whimsy that suggests he knows how outrageous he's being; this softens him unnecessarily, but he gets the pedant's fervour, and he handles his songs brilliantly. Unlike previous Higginses, he insists on actually singing them; notes appear in A Hymn to Him and I've Grown Accustomed to Her Face that one never knew existed. Cynthia Dale's Eliza comes and goes: a well-timed line here, especially in the Ascot scene, a bright top note there, but overall cute rather than conquering. (It's a fearsome role, musically and dramatically, especially if you're not born to at least one of the accents.) The spark between the two of them is fitful, though her reaction when he first touches her during The Rain in Spain lights a torch. That number retains its effect as one of the great climactic moments in musical comedy. It's all in the placing, since the song itself isn't all that good; it has nowhere to go once it's started. James Blendick is amusing in Doolittle's dialogue, but has to coast through the songs, which is a downer. Barry MacGregor is splendid as Colonel Pickering: a better role in the show, where he's allowed to be a gentleman buffoon, than in the play, where he's the straightest of straight men. Otherwise, it's My Fair Lady: same as ever was.
