THE THREEPENNY OPERA

Avon Theatre, Stratford

- - -

STRATFORD - After My Fair Lady, The Threepenny Opera; after the most popular American musical set in London, the most popular German musical set in London -- the latter, admittedly, not a category for which there is huge competition.

If you think that Lerner and Loewe's view of the British metropolis was more mythic than real, you should consider the one that Bertolt Brecht and Kurt Weill dreamed up in 1928. Ostensibly set at the coronation of the young Queen Victoria in 1837, it presents a social, moral and legal structure that seems equally indebted to the authors' own Weimar Berlin and to a rather hurried reading of the novels of Charles Dickens.

It also gives off a pungent 18th-century odour -- naturally, since it is based, quite closely, on John Gays thieves kitchen classic, The Beggar's Opera -- while bits of it sound like the Germanic idea of 1920s America; Kurt Weill's music has the ferocious twang that at the time was thought of as jazz.

All these elements do come together to create their own world, but its very hard to recreate it, now, on stage. Stephen Ouimette, who directs at Stratford, is a fine actor who has hardly ever directed before. Considered in the abstract, as a debut production on a premier stage, his work is impressive. As a specific evening in the theatre, it is deeply unsatisfying.

There are two main problems with Brechts text. (There really aren't any with Weill's music.) One is its narrative incoherence, a fault it admittedly shares with its source, which, however, is more engagingly insouciant about it. Ouimette, I think, deals with this as well as anyone could.

The other is that it wants very much to shock, but 70 years of progress have made this goal increasingly hard to attain. This production starts with what has become one of the tiredest aggression gambits in the book: An apparently drunk, and certainly disorderly, actor pushes his way down the aisle, scattering restraining ushers in his wake. This one climbs up on stage, as they always do, and proceeds to sing the world-famous opening number, Mack the Knife.

However, what with his lurching gait and diction and the efforts of the other performers to stop him, the song gets drowned out. This is a pity, since Marc Blitzsteins translation (first heard in the shows legendary off-Broadway production in 1956 and the standard text ever since) turns out to contain rude bits that never made it on to the original cast recording, never mind the pop versions by Louis Armstrong, and Bobby Darin, and such.

I guess that hearing a hit song in a comfortable theatre (the Avon has been gleamingly refurbished) might count as bourgeois gratification, and the production is virtuously determined to deny it to us. Anyway, the device is never followed up; as the evening proceeds, the actors push about the various elements of Peter Hartwell's set, but that kind of thing happens in a lot of shows.

The story is the familiar one of Macheath, a.k.a. Mackie -- a criminal of impressive versatility, cold-bloodedness and sexual appetite -- who marries (or that's what he calls it) the daughter of the more respectably crooked Soho mastermind J.J. Peachum. Peachum, with the help of his wife and a bundle of whores, gets Mackie arrested and sent to the gallows. Thats all, except that it happens twice. The ending is a reprieve for the hero, the unlikeliness of which is paraded in all its ironic glory. (As it is in Gay; Brecht never claimed to have invented the alienation effect.)

Along the way, the actors pause to draw attention to how appallingly their characters are behaving and to how, society being what it is, they have no other choice. There are a lot of songs that say this, and even Weill cant altogether escape from the resultant grinding quality. All we can do is reflect on how deliciously shocking it must have sounded in 1928 and how often we have heard things like it since. It's not so much that it isn't true (though its not as unvaryingly true as the show would like us to believe it believes) as that its generalized. Only one line strikes freshly home, as spoken by Peachum, whose profession is the provision of rags and deformities to aspiring beggars. He says that the ruling classes are quite happy to force people on to their knees but can't stand looking at the results.

Brecht claims to be indignant at human depravity but, plainly, he digs it. This being the case, the best way to play both text and songs is lightly, so that we can share in the cynicism and, maybe, occasionally be caught off guard and bruised by it. This production, hoping to up the original ante, tries instead to rub our noses in it.

It doesn't help that though some of the cast can act and some can sing, very few can do both. George Masswhohl as Tiger Brown, the sentimental police chief, may be the closest to an exception; his line readings are a bit stiff, but this rather suits the character. He sings his portion of the Army Song duet with superb attack. (Credit too, and again, to Donna Feore, who has provided this number with discreet but brilliant choreography, mainly for rhythmically hunched shoulders.)

His duet partner is Tom McCamus as Macheath himself, and his far lighter but incisive voice makes a good match. But other parts of the score tax him cruelly, and the strain takes the bite off his delivery; even in speech, he gabbles. This shark has pretty teeth, dear, and a wicked smile and elegantly steely demeanour, but it isnt enough. (I break the rule of a lifetime by mentioning it but, for musical and other reasons, I would love to see him swap roles with Colm Feore in My Fair Lady.) Peter Donaldson as Peachum, too, lacks energy in his song; and here again it takes a toll on his talking, while Sheila McCarthy as his lady seems uncomfortable in both her aspects, pushing for a malevolence that isnt her.

There is some fine choral singing, though too little opportunity for it, and the younger women all have great voices. Blythe Wilson's Lucy, a jailer's daughter with riding crop, brings the house down with her Barbara Song; Diana Coatsworth as Polly sings a good, stark Pirate Jenny (admirably lit, by the way, by John Munro); and Susan Gilmour, as the non-piratical Jenny, makes the Solomon Song the most together sequence of the evening. But none of them makes much impact as a character; and Gilmour and her fellow sluts are disappointingly genteel.

The show pays off in its last act. Peachum squaring off with Tiger Brown threatening to flood the streets with beggars and ruin both the Coronation and the policeman's career is a sequence with real tension and authority. (Donaldson hits his stride here.) McCamus desperate in his cell while friends, enemies and cast-off loves line up on the other side of the bars is a memorable picture. The queen's mounted messenger, rising up from the orchestra pit, makes a delightful impression. After all that hard work, some authentically chilly winds do finally get to blow.

THE SCARLET PIMPERNEL

Avon Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

STRATFORD, Ont. - Well, let no one say that the play choices at this year's Stratford Festival lack thematic continuity. The Threepenny Opera, which opened on Wednesday, ends with a foiled execution. The Scarlet Pimpernel, which followed on Thursday, begins with several spiritedly unfoiled executions. Welcome to the French Revolution, which as we all know consisted solely of the serial guillotining of inoffensive aristocrats (no middle-class counter- revolutionaries need apply) for the entertainment of howling, cackling and mainly female mobs. But fear not: the Scarlet Pimpernel, flower of the British upper class, is coming to the rescue, in an assortment of funny get-ups, and fewer heads will roll.

Those that do, roll most persuasively; that first scene is, in its comic-opera fashion, not bad. What follows is an atrocity, with only three mitigating features. One of these is the overall slickness of Dennis Garnhums direction, especially in the matter of scene changes. Another is the sets themselves, designed by Cameron Porteous, which not only cross the Channel but bob about on it en route; the guillotine frame, minus its blade, remains a unifying feature, and should be put into storage awaiting the production of a real play about the Terror: Dantons Death, perhaps, or -- to show there can be such a thing as intelligent melodrama -- an adaptation of A Tale of Two Cities. Finally, there is Peter Hutt, whose performance as Chauvelin, the perpetually thwarted French agent, is smoulderingly hissable. That, however, admirably though he carries it off, is the key to what is wrong.

The sound of modern theatregoers self-consciously booing the bad guy is on the same level of loathsomeness as The Sing-a-long Sound of Music; they both denote an audience that feels smugly superior to the entertainment on offer and a production that wants them to. They can patronize this presentation of Chauvelin not because he is nasty but because, as a villain, he is farcically inept. Even when he's theoretically winning he carries on like a loser, boastful and accident-prone. He never presents anything resembling a threat. And this is supposed to be an adventure story.

I like swashbuckling romance. I loved the Stratford production of The Three Musketeers. That had its tongue from time to time in its cheek, but never so far in that it lost the audience's respect for the story it was telling. It enthusiastically piled on the narrative, and it never stood still. It helped, of course, that it was based on a masterpiece; nobody would apply that description to Baroness Orczys sturdy old potboiler. But she did give us in Sir Percy Blakeney, the fop as superman, a hero whos become an archetype, or at least a franchise, and this first story about his exploits ought to work dramatically. Indeed, it often has; the Baroness herself turned it into a play before it ever got published, and I'll wager that her version was superior to this one, which is by the late English playwright Beverley Cross. He takes a simple tale --one with surprisingly few surprises -- and tells it haltingly, abetted by a production that is far more interested in masked balls than in people.

The main people here are Sir Percy himself and his wife, Marguerite, a French ex-actress of former Republican sympathies. At least they seem to be former; that part of the tale is left muddy as is the question of how the Blakeneys, who fear they have fallen out of love, ever fell in it. One thing that has always puzzled me about the Pimpernel: He seems to have adopted the pose of a terminally languid dandy as a cloak for his daredevilling. In which case, what was he like before the Revolution made this cover necessary, and why has nobody noticed the difference? And what stage was he at when he met Lady Blakeney? Still, the important considerations theatrically are that his affectations should seem to be second nature and that both he and we should enjoy them; and the casting of the unalterably rugged Peter Donaldson in the role makes all this difficult. A heavyweight fop is conceivable (witness Donald Sinden, who played the Cross version in London), but not a morose one. Donaldson's Percy lacks innocence and a dancing wit, though admittedly the latter quality must be hard to convey when your best line, addressed to a hunchback, is "rung any good bells lately?" (A professor of English quotes this in the program as the sparklng summit of the plays humour, and who am I to disagree?) His more transitory disguises, once he crosses to France and gets down to the business of being damned elusive, struck me as remarkably transparent; but, of course, the officers of the Revolution wouldnt have seen Donaldson on stage as often as I have.

It might have been different. Obviously you don't go to The Scarlet Pimpernel for political complexity, but one passage in the novel that has stayed with me down the years and is not in the play is an exasperated remark of the hero's to the effect that a couple of the French toffs he had rescued positively deserved the guillotine for their ridiculous prejudices. Donaldson might have made something of that. As it is, its only in a couple of tender lines at the end that he reveals anything of his real quality.

Sheila McCarthy, his real-life wife playing his on-stage wife for the second consecutive night, seems to have lost any period style she may have possessed; her Marguerite is vocally and emotionally choppy. A couple of dunderheaded assistant pimpernels are given performances to match, and are unlucky enough to be involved in a fight scene, choreographed to music for the maximum of giggles and the minimum of excitement. I dont know, or wish to know, what Ian Deakin is up to as the Prince Regent, but I liked Brian Tree's huffy little turn as Lord Grenville.

ROMEO AND JULIET

Festival Theatre, Stratford

It's always a good sign when an audience at Romeo and Juliet laughs with, as opposed to at, the balcony scene. The lovers, despite some recurring premonitions, don't know at this early point that theyre in a tragedy; theyre giddy with the excitement of finding one another. They also get one another's words wrong; "what satisfaction canst thou have tonight? asks Juliet, when all he wants is an exchange of promises. Graham Abbey and Claire Jullien, in the new production at the Stratford Festival, sweep us up in their happiness, and the underlying precariousness of it seems all the more wrenching.

Miles Potter's production uses Elizabethan costumes, and even has the nerve to begin with the strumming of a lute. (Not only that, but at the death of Juliet, the lute plays something that sounds much like that all-purpose standby for period plays, Greensleeves.) It starts, or nearly, by filling the stage with the familiar crowd of serving wenches, carrying their familiar fruit baskets. It is, in short, extraordinarily traditional. It is also extraordinarily lively, giving the impression that although director and cast never went self-consciously looking for novelty, they often found it. Those wenches, for example, are not just decorative; they have a reactive part to play in the opening, and sexist, dialogue between two Capulet servants that sparks off the plays first brawl.

That and subsequent fights (arranged by John Stead) are exciting, varied and character-driven. Wayne Bests Mercutio is an accomplished and compulsive show-off; he has already provided a rivetingly sardonic account of the Queen Mab that still manages -- partly because of the way the other actors set it up -- to be magic.

No, in the middle of his duel with Nicholas Van Burek's Tybalt (more snake than cat), he feigns a death wound most persuasively. He's crying wolf; when he receives the real fatal hit, nobody believes him and he has, angrily, to joke them into paying attention. The complicity of Romeo, the would-be peacemaker, is starkly brought out, and so is the newborn fury that turns him too into a killer.

Some of this has been done before. But I have never previously seen the friar (David Kirby) who fails to deliver the fatal letter to Romeo played as a cheerful gossip, totally unaware of what he has unleashed. It makes perfect sense, and adds a brilliant new colour to the plays last movement. Nor have I ever known a production to be so bold with the irruption of the musicians into the scene of mourning over the drugged Juliet. This too makes sense, atmospheric sense, since looked at coldly this scene is farce; the Capulets are making a huge tearful fuss over somebody who isnt actually dead. (This scene, like some others, also brings forward a promising new clown in Courtenay J. Stevens.)

Abbey's Romeo, too, can laugh and be laughed at. His languishing over Rosaline, with whom he fancies himself in love before he meets Juliet, becomes a way of distinguishing himself with the boys: platonic locker-room talk. His despair after banishment is done, literally, flat-out. Art thou a man?" asks Friar Laurence, confronted by this self-indulgence, and the truth is that, no, he's still a boy. He doesnt really grow up until he hears the news of Juliets death and defies the stars, and then he does it, superbly, in an instant. (Though Romeo is never, ever, as inwardly mature as Juliet.) Abbey has the gift of authority even when quiet, rare on this stage.

Jullien's Juliet lacks his facility, but she is very appealing as she negotiates the shifting limits of the girl's obedience and independence. She too grows up in an instant: the moment at which Juliets parents -- with especial bitterness in this production -- desert her. The play is exuberant, early Shakespeare; with the built- in disadvantage that the lovers verbalize too much; they talk at times when the normal stricken person would only sob. Juliet, the more intelligent, suffers the most from this. Jullien at least makes us feel that the character is discovering her emotions in finding the words for them.

The production postpones tragedy until the last moment: in fact, until after the principals deaths. What is most deeply moving here is the reaction of those left behind; as, at a funeral, you feel sorrier for the survivors than for the deceased. The two bereaved fathers are strongly played, and their reconciliation accordingly momentous. John Dolan's Montague is thoughtful and dignified; Scott Wentworth's superb Capulet heads a riven household. He loves his daughter, but has no idea how to deal with her; he is deeply at odds with his young wife, especially when she starts mourning extravagantly over the dead Tybalt. I have seen Lady Capulets before who were in love with Tybalt, but never a Lord Capulet who seemed to notice. The man becomes a tyrant, which makes his final melting all the more affecting.

Some concluding words for Keith Dinicols Friar, best when tetchiest; for Lally Cadeau, who cannot make the Nurses endless reminiscences funny but is very good and watchful when she gets down to business in her mistress' service; and for Aaron Franks' bodeful Apothecary, impressively framed in his shop-front. A warm welcome to a production that touches heart and mind at once.

Fifty Seasons at Stratford is published by McClelland & Stewart at $60. Robert Cushman reviews Stratford's Henry VI: Revenge in France in the Post tomorrow.

At the risk of giving away the ending: the last line of my book Fifty Seasons at Stratford is "For what it has achieved, for what it has engendered, and for what it has provoked, the Stratford Festival is the best thing ever to have happened to the Canadian theatre."

That does not mean its productions have always been the best to be seen in Canada, though they often have been: equal to the best at any rate. It does mean that when Stratford commenced operations in 1953, there was very little English-speaking professional theatre in Canada, and that once Stratford had started, theatre started blooming all over the country. Maybe it would have happened anyway, but it happened this way. As it became an institution it attracted hostility, but even companies, classical or modern, that defined themselves in opposition to Stratford needed, for that very reason, to have it around.

As a classical and more especially a Shakespearean theatre, Stratford has access to the greatest source of energy available on any stage. Tapping it is always a challenge, but at least Stratford has the ideal platform -- literally -- from which to do it. That stage is one of the things that has made it, from the outset, the leading classical theatre in North America. The other is the enthusiasm and commitment of its actors and audiences, both remarkable for their long-term fidelity.

I knew some of these things before I started writing, but I became overwhelmingly convinced of them as I ploughed through 49 years' worth of reviews and articles made available to me by the staff and volunteers of the festival's extraordinary archive. (Was this a hard book to research? No. But it sure was time-consuming. And I can say, objectively and gratefully, that it is one of the most beautifully produced books I have ever held in my hands.)

My own interest in the festival arose, while I was growing up in England, from my enthusiasm for the work of its first director, Tyrone Guthrie, whose last great productions in London I was old and lucky enough to see. I wanted to celebrate Stratford but also put it in a critical perspective and, as far as I could, in an international context. It tickles me that, though Stratford is so very Canadian, it was an Irishman, grounded in the English theatre, who kicked it off, and that it owes its signature stage to the lucky coincidence of his convictions about producing Shakespeare.

What follows, taken from the book's first chapter, is about Guthrie and that extraordinary first season -- mounted under canvas, because nobody knew if the venture would survive. And about two plays that are in the season again this 50th year, as are two of those original actors.

On July 13, 1953, the curtain rose on Richard III, the first production of the first Stratford Festival. Only it didn't. There was no curtain, and that is perhaps the single most important fact about the festival. From that, sometimes in reaction to that, everything else has followed.

Today it's the rule rather than the exception for an audience to enter a theatre -- certainly a theatre with any artistic pretensions -- to find the set for the play all ready and staring at them. It happens even in proscenium theatres, which do have curtains to raise. A thrust or platform stage of course cannot have one, and it was a thrust or platform stage that was built for the Shakespeare festival at Stratford, Ont. This was revolutionary. The idea had long been talked about, dreamed about, but never before put so publicly and aggressively into practice.

Of the theatres erected in the English-speaking world since 1953 only a few have been designed in direct imitation of the Stratford Festival, but all -- certainly if they were intended to house a classical repertoire -- have had to take notice of its existence. It would be foolish to claim that the Shakespeare productions mounted on the Festival stage have been consistently more authentic or exciting than those staged anywhere else, but something about the place always suggests the possibility. And when it becomes a reality, a bond is created between the actors and audience, a bond that has kept the festival alive and loved for 50 years.

It might not have happened. It is doubtful that Tom Patterson, the trade-magazine journalist whose brainchild the festival was, had any idea of revolutionizing the staging of Shakespeare. Indeed, it's doubtful he had much interest in Shakespeare at all. Stratford was his hometown, and his main concern was to put it more firmly on the social and economic map. Like some other pioneers -- Lilian Baylis, for example, the Edwardian philanthropist who founded the Old Vic -- he fell in love with theatre only after he had started one of his own. But the man to whom he turned to realize his dream was a confirmed open-stager who had been yearning for the chance to create just such a theatre. He was also attracted to the idea of helping shape Canada's still-unformed cultural identity.

The man was Tyrone Guthrie, at that time probably the foremost director of Shakespeare in the world. He had been artistic director (though the term itself was not yet in use) of the Old Vic for most of the 1930s and the Second World War years, returning often thereafter; he had also directed at the English Stratford. All the theatrical knights and dames who dominated the English theatre of the mid-20th century had worked with him; Guthrie's actors, it was said, inevitably felt they were making history.

The critics did not always agree: Some of them found him lacking in high seriousness. Guthrie was constitutionally mischievous and irreverent, and he could never resist a joke. (Maybe it was the Irish in him.) He was also reputed to shy away from scenes of intimate emotion. (This was probably not the Irish in him.) The two essential qualities of a great director are intelligence and showmanship. Guthrie was a virtuoso of stagecraft, especially when great massed scenes were involved, and he had a knife-edged mind. Physically, as well as imaginatively and intellectually, he was eternally restless. Since the end of the war he had been a theatrical nomad: He lived in Ireland but rarely worked there. For three years, Stratford would provide him with something like a home.

Playing in tandem with the established stage favourite Richard III was the far chancier All's Well that Ends Well. Both, in their different ways, proved to be classic Guthrie productions.

Richard III thrust Stratford -- thrust Canada -- directly into the mainstream of 1950s Shakespearean staging. Herbert Whittaker of The Globe and Mail, the leading Canadian critic, said that it was such a production as nobody in Canada had ever seen before. It showed the director alternately -- sometimes simultaneously -- in his swirling and sardonic modes. He was equally adept at creating grandeur and at deflating it. This being a chronicle play, featuring a coronation and a battle, Guthrie and Tanya Moiseiwitsch (and Douglas Campbell, as arranger of the fights) filled the stage with bodies, richly costumed and intricately manoeuvred. The production was in a processional style to which the stage seemed ideally suited; it was the first of many great evenings for the flourishing of banners.

Richard III is also a study of a mass murderer, and Guthrie happily exposed its cruelty. Three of Richard's victims, condemned to execution on trumped-up charges, were dragged on stage having clearly been tortured, and then dropped to their fate through trapdoors. When the ghosts of those Richard had murdered appeared to him before the Battle of Bosworth, the last of them -- the decapitated Duke of Buckingham -- was holding on his own severed head. Alec Guinness as Richard presided gleefully over the bloodshed, literally over it: He delivered the opening soliloquy sitting cheerfully astride the balcony, thus allowing the architecture of the Festival stage to declare its crucial importance from the very first moment of the very first show.

Many found Guinness's performance brilliant but lightweight. Olivier's film performance, which was to fix the popular image of the role for the rest of the century and beyond, was still two years in the future, and though more majestically satanic than Guinness's imp-with-a-limp, it was to prove equally comedic. Most later productions have veered even more emphatically toward dark laughter, though few have had Guthrie's and Guinness's genuine sense of humour: They were almost certainly ahead of their time.

The Canadian response was bemused -- but ecstatic. A first-night standing ovation (not the automatic event it is now) lasted five minutes: an eternity in theatre time. Everybody knew that history had been made.

The second production proved equally important, but in a wider context. In a sense it may be the most important production Stratford has ever done, since it rediscovered -- no, discovered -- a Shakespeare play. All's Well that Ends Well was at that time rarely produced and even more rarely liked. It was one of the few remaining plays that literary critics felt safe in dismissing, while theatre critics seldom had a chance to say anything about it at all: Even The Two Gentlemen of Verona has a more illustrious stage history.

A poor French doctor's daughter wins the hand of a disdainful young nobleman by performing a miracle cure on the sick king, then has to follow her reluctant prize to the Italian wars and win him, through love and trickery, all over again; Guthrie put this Renaissance story into modern dress and made it both hilarious and enchanting. There was plenty of broad clowning in his treatment of the play's subplot, but the predominant mood was bittersweet, a delicate side of Guthrie's talent (and of Moiseiwitsch's) that critics often overlooked. The play emerged not as a dark comedy -- its traditional classification -- but as an honest, unillusioned one. The term "magic realism" had not then been coined, and when it was it signified something else, but it would have fitted the production perfectly.

In 1959 Guthrie was to recreate it at the British Stratford, and though he himself dismissed this revival as "cold pudding hotted up," he was in a minority: The critics mostly raved, and both actors and audience loved the show. A string of other notable productions of All's Well that Ends Well followed, and by the century's end the play was firmly established in the repertoire, a favourite of scholars and a magnet to directors; it had even played on Broadway. But Guthrie's 1953 Stratford production began it all, and has probably never been surpassed.

From the festival's more immediate point of view, it was the perfect complement to Richard III, an ensemble piece to balance that essentially one-man play. Helena, the heroine, certainly dominates, and she was dazzlingly played by Irene Worth (on alternating nights, she was the harridan Queen Margaret of the history play), but there are half a dozen other key roles.

Guinness played the ailing French king and Michael Bates was Lafew, the sharp-tongued lord. Douglas Campbell inaugurated a long string of comic successes at Stratford as the braggart Parolles. They were the visitors, and expected to be good, but at least two of the Canadians were equally impressive: the veteran Eleanor Stuart as the Countess and the young Donald Harron as her son Bertram, the play's cub of a hero. It looked as if the festival company might actually be a company.

The names from that 1953 program that now resonate most sonorously are those of three younger players who half a century later are essentially still there. Two of them, William Hutt and William Needles, are still on the Stratford bill in 2002; the third, Douglas Rain, is not, but he has returned often in the intervening years.

Hutt and Rain in particular were to become known as the Stratford actors par excellence, and Hutt is the company's undisputed leader. All three had significant small roles in Richard III as pawns of the hero-villain: Hutt was Brakenbury, the conscience-troubled Lieutenant of the Tower; Needles played the businesslike First Murderer; and Rain appeared as Tyrrel. These are roles that can go for nothing but that can also make their presence felt; the same goes for the Steward in All's Well, played by Needles. (In this production Hutt and Rain were walk-ons.)

All three actors were singled out in reviews: a cheering and accurate forecast for their subsequent careers and the identity of the company as a whole. Guthrie had predicted that it would grow its own lead actors, and it did so even more quickly than he might have envisaged.

People tended to patronize Guthrie after his death: Peter Hall in his published Diaries called him "that sad, mad Don Quixote of the theatre." But then people had patronized him in his lifetime as well, and many simply never knew what to make of him.

"I am an unashamed advocate," he once wrote, "of what dry-as- dust pedagogues call 'the play way' "; and in fact, no modern director has had a firmer grasp, theoretical and practical, of what the theatre is about. He may have been both too late and too early for the National Theatre of Great Britain, but he was absolutely on time for the national theatre of Canada. They may have named a theatre after him in Minnesota (they never did in Britain), but the Stratford Festival -- not just the stage, not just the theatre, but the whole buzzing organization -- is his real monument.

HENRY VI: REVENGE IN FRANCE, HENRY VI: REVOLT IN ENGLAND

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

The three parts of Henry VI were rediscovered by the English theatre exactly 50 years ago, and since then -- intact or compressed, on stage or television -- they have consistently occasioned some of the most exciting Shakespeare Britain has had to offer. Until now our own Stratford has never really faced up to them. There was a production in 1966 that stalled halfway through the cycle, and another in 1980 that crammed all three parts into one play. Leon Rubin has now come up, as adaptor and director, with a lucid and crafty version in two instalments, and a production that is a sustained adventure, thrilling for actors and audience alike.

Revenge in France takes us right through the French wars that are the subject of Shakespeare's Henry VI Part One. The revenge is that of the French themselves, casting off the yoke that was imposed on them by the late Henry V. The avenger-in-chief is Joan la Pucelle, who represents the Elizabethans vigorously unsympathetic idea of Joan of Arc, and whose task is made easier by the state of things in England; with the victorious Henrys son still a child, the realm is in the hands of a set of jealous, squabbling aristocrats, most of them somebody's uncle.

Their intrigues take centre stage in Shakespeare's Part Two, whose first half makes up the balance of Revenge. Henry VI is now grown and -- in the immortal words of 1066 and All That -- "such a Good Man that he was regarded as a saint, or alternatively -- especially by the barons -- an imbecile." He also marries an aggressive French princess, Margaret of Anjou, who can match any of the English lords for courage and ferocity, and is resented for it.

The Wars of the Roses are approaching, and they break out in Revolt in England, which accounts for the rest of Shakespeares Part Two and the whole of his Part Three. Here the House of Lancaster, Henry its titular head, loses the throne to the House of York, led by the Duke of that name and, after his (naturally) violent death, by his sons.

There are plenty of reverses, and -- what with the French wars at the beginning and the English at the end -- a good half of the action is devoted to battles. These have been staged (by the invaluable John Stead) with superb resourcefulness. They progress from cheerful hand-to-hand realism to a bitter, weary stylization, naturalism and symbolism triumphantly blend at the last when snow falls (as it historically did at the Battle of Barnet) while a giant figure of Death stands astride John Pennoyers set. This -- a metal bridge surmounted by a catwalk and bathed alternately in gold or silver-grey light -- proves to be both flexible and resilient, and comes with a great built-in archway.

If these were really Shakespeare's first plays (a vexed question) they were an extraordinarily ambitious way to begin. Part One, which takes some creative liberties with history, suffers from an excess of literal-minded rhetoric, as if not only the playwright but his theatre were still growing up, and stretches of Part Three are numbly written, suggesting that blood will have bloodlessness. It has three or four great scenes, though, while Part Two is wholly magnificent, with the knives temporarily sheathed it offers as vivid a picture of the shifts of power as you can find on a stage.

Its greatest role is Margaret, first seen on the end of a rope as prisoner of the Earl of Suffolk, who takes her home for his king and becomes her lover. Seana McKenna, defensive and flirtatious, plays this scene with wonderful wit; already she is on a journey and thereafter she hardly stops. Still demure when she reaches England, expecting a very different kind of spouse, she grows from kitten to tigress, both dismissive and defensive of her husband and agonizingly possessive of her young son.

Michael Therriault as Henry is delightfully guileless at his first appearance but hardly develops thereafter. This is a waste; Henry may not become powerful but he does become wise, and the scene at the Battle of Towton, where he observes the son who has killed his father and the father who has killed his son, should be the heart of the event. Here it isn't boldly enough staged, and Therriault fails to take, as Henry should, the whole agony of England into himself.

But there is plenty of compensation. Thom Marriotts hulking York grows a psychic inch at each appearance: First he is a cautious young law student; then -- newly ennobled -- an apprentice troublemaker, gaining in confidence; then a proud and full-grown rebel; finally, in a scene as cruelly staged as written, a bereaved father facing his own death. This is civil war, with victims and aggressors interchangeable, all capable of demanding our sympathy for atrocities identical to those they themselves have committed -- and, whats more, of getting it. Marriott has already been at Stratford for three seasons, during which I confess I barely noticed him. He must, like York, have been biding his time.

Jonathan Goad has been insistently promising for as long a time, but as Suffolk, noted for his insolence, he bursts through into the front line of ease and accomplishment. Dispatched at the end of one play, he returns at the top of the next as Jack Cade, the rebel as stand-up comic -- an unrecognizable transformation, though I wonder why a Canadian actor should be playing a Kentish character with a cockney accent.

Donald Carrier lacks the weight I would expect of Warwick the Kingmaker, but compensates with courtliness. The older nobility are solidly represented by Brad Rudy's Talbot, bluff soldier and francophobe; David Francis's Gloucester, doomed for his honesty; and Lewis Gordons Cardinal Beaufort, damned for his lack of it.

The best of the junior Yorks is Robert Hamiltons wavering Clarence, surprisingly since it's the least colourful role. Of his siblings, Rami Posner's Edward is too much the weakling, and Haysam Kadris Richard Crookback too foursquare to play the devil, though I could forgive him much for the insinuating way in which he croons, Clarence, beware.

Rubin has had the happy idea of translating some of the French characters lines into French; when La Pucelle, at lightning speed, turns around the renegade Duke of Burgundy, it helps that they speak the same language. Michelle Giroux's Joan is not allowed, as in the original, to go to the stake pregnant and unable to name the father. She does burn, however, ingeniously and in full view.

I cannot resist quoting once more from 1066 and All That, which says that one of the rules of the Wars of the Roses was that nobody was ever really king but that Edmund Mortimer ought to be. Mortimer's one prophetic scene is played by William Needles, a Stratford founder for whom veteran is too juvenile a word, and who can still show his juniors something about delivering a line with maximum economy and to maximum effect. Here, as in Romeo, too many players try to invigorate these early iambics by italicizing three words in a phrase or pausing three times, and the results are messy; even the sainted McKenna sometimes fails to hit her climaxes cleanly.

I have a few other questions and quibbles. If Cades mob deem literacy a capital offence, why do they hand out leaflets -- some of them, I regret to say, to the audience? The Cardinals death scene deserves to be acted rather than reported. Some plot lines and prophecies are left hanging, the Mayor of London looks about 17, and half the cast can't pronounce Westmoreland.

Otherwise, there are no complaints, and having written elsewhere that "for building a company, nothing beats the histories," I am delighted that both Shakespeare and I have been so vigorously vindicated.

2002-06-08-the-failings-of-bertolt-brech:
robertcushman@lycos.com

A mixed first week at the Stratford Festival threw up at least one extraordinary contrast in productions. The Avon Theatre, Stratford's proscenium house, offered The Scarlet Pimpernel, which is escapism run rampant, and The Threepenny Opera, which tries very hard to be anything but.

The Threepenny Opera is early Bertolt Brecht, written before he had become a full-blown Marxist, and before he had developed aesthetic theories to match his politics. It's tempting, though, to read the theories back into the piece; and indeed Brecht himself did so, on a lavish scale.

The word "Brecht" immediately summons, as in a verbal- association test, the word "alienation," though a better translation from the German is probably "estrangement" -- making the familiar strange. Spectators are encouraged to consider the broader social implications of the funny or tearful things that are happening in front of them; actors and directors are instructed to make it happen. This does not, as I understand it, mean that audiences are not supposed to feel, only think; it means that they should feel, and then think about their feelings.

Shakespeare may have invented alienation. Look at how subversively he calls attention to style and convention in, of all harmless things, As You Like It:

ORLANDO: Good day and happiness, dear Rosalind.

JAQUES: Nay then, God be wi' you, an you talk in blank verse.

Musicals are pure alienation. What could be less real, more disorienting, than the transition from speech to song? In theory.

In practice, audiences -- whether at an Elizabethan pastoral, or My Fair Lady -- have an incorrigible habit of picking themselves up and just going on believing. They'll swallow anything.

It's tempting to say The Scarlet Pimpernel, a dedicatedly tongue- in-cheek entertainment that doesn't even take its own melodrama seriously, is as estranging as you can get; camp, after all, is one of the basic alienation effects. But even my perversity has its limits; I am not going to claim that this show will jolt anybody into a more searchingly objective view of the French Revolution. The Stratford Threepenny Opera, though, takes itself very seriously.

A supposedly drunken actor wrecks Mack the Knife, the show's celebrated opening number, making it impossible for us to enjoy the tune or to follow the words. We are not here, the message plainly goes, to be charmed by Kurt Weill's greatest hit.

At later moments, Brecht's anti-capitalist, anti-Vice Squad lyrics -- "when we've had lunch, your preaching can begin" -- are belted out by the entire company, all lined up with their committed faces on. (Brecht's irony tended to stop short at his own pronouncements; he didn't want them undercut.)

The word is that Stephen Ouimette, who directed, and Tom McCamus, who plays Macheath, originally wanted to do the show in small- scale, rough-theatre style, maybe in a garage somewhere; and that their fierce intentions were defused when it turned into a big- budget Avon production. I wonder.

I've seen three previous productions of The Threepenny Opera, which is an appallingly difficult piece. The worst of them, thin- blooded and badly sung, was by Brecht's own Berliner Ensemble (though staged many years after his death). The best was a few years ago at the Donmar Warehouse, a small, though plush, theatre in London. Its Macheath was Tom Hollander, a truculent actor about five feet tall; as far as possible from a standard leading man, but charismatic as all-get-out.

This version updated the action, which Brecht set at the coronation of Queen Victoria, to an actual current Royal celebration; making it a lot more relevant, if that's your thing, than the original could ever have been to the author's 1928 Berlin. It, too, played -- and more creatively -- with the audience's expectations of Mack the Knife by withholding the song until halfway through the evening. It had style. It had coherence (most unusual for this piece). It had impact.

But it was a strictly theatrical impact. (The director, by the way, was Phyllida Lloyd, whose next musical was that great revolutionary statement, Mamma Mia!) It didn't change anybody's view of the world, though it may have reinforced it.

I doubt things would have been any different for the Canadian team if they had put the show on in a meaner space. They would have attracted the same liberal-bourgeois audience that comes to such a play at the Avon, though presumably fewer of them. It might conceivably have made them feel uncomfortable from time to time; but feelings, as Brecht taught us, are not thoughts, and neither necessarily leads to action.

Even at the Avon, Mr. Peachum's beggars can remind us of our own homeless. But it's only titillation.

It's hard to shock a contemporary audience. It can happen (when it does, it usually seems to happen in London) but I'm not sure how useful it is. It's impossible, now, to shock them with Brecht, however heavy the obligation to do so may seem. I also feel -- and, having examined my feelings, think -- that it serves Brecht right.

Black & White Photo: Courtesy Stratford Festival / Stratford's Scarlet Pimpernel is not a play that takes itself seriously, unlike The Threepenny Opera. ;
2002-06-11-four-musical-numbers-in-searc:
Until June 23. Box office: 416-504-9971.

SNAPPY TALES

Factory Theatre Studio, Toronto

In Snappy Tales four actor-singers rush around like mad things, performing in four miniature musicals, one of them so miniature it only lasts four minutes. The magic number further re-asserts itself in the matter of composers, a different one for each piece. There is, however, only one author, one lyricist and one director, and they are all the same man. He is Vincent de Tourdonnet, and he is a self-proclaimed satirist. He has taken four existing texts -- two literary, two dramatic -- musicalized and, in three out of the four cases, updated them. The results are interesting but, as you would guess, uneven.

We start with the ultra-brief one: The Doll's House, based on a story by Katherine Mansfield. (Id say the story if Id read it.) Two little girls of early 20th-century appearance peer over and into the lives of their dolls, imagine the mistress giving hell to the maid and reveal that they cannot wait to grow up and behave like that in real life. It's a satisfyingly mordant fragment, given music, by Stephen Eddins, to match.

Then comes The Good Person, based on (the program says "inspired by") Bertolt Brecht's play The Good Person of Szechuan. Brecht wrote a fable, set in a personalized China thats ancient and modern at once, in which three gods come down to Earth to give financial aid to someone deserving and discover -- not unexpectedly -- that the only worthy recipient of their alms is a prostitute. She tries to use the money they give her for charitable purposes and finds herself cheated and exploited left and right (i.e., screwed by clients and landlords alike). So she invents and impersonates a tough male cousin and, in his guise, finds herself acting as ruthlessly as everybody else.

De Tourdonnet pulls this story into present-day Toronto (the Good, he carefully reminds us), thereby giving it more teeth. The heroine uses her gods-given wealth to open a shelter for the homeless but soon, to her horror, finds herself operating a form of workfare. Some of Brechts pyramiding paradoxes have had to go, but the underlying point is not exactly hard to grasp, and it's a relief to be spared the original's Oriental whimsy; de Tourdonnets heroine is a more convincing hooker than Brechts ever was.

Before accepting her hospitality the gods are turned away from a restaurant; one hopes, for the sake of allusiveness, that the cuisine is Szechuan. The divinities themselves are an ecumenical, world-spanning trio: one token Confucius, one Santa Claus and one pre-Raphaelite fairy queen. Polemically this is the most powerful movement of the quartet and dramaturgically the neatest, but it's let down by J. Douglas Dodd's music, which has little character beyond cuteness.

The same goes for the score composed by Jim Kass for The Barnhouse Effect, which derives from a 1950 short story by Kurt Vonnegut. A scientist finds himself with the power to destroy any object -- any -- simply by looking at it and concentrating. This no- cost destructive capacity greatly endears him to the higher reaches of the U.S. military, though they are less charmed by his desire to use it to destroy destroyers, theirs included. The point has sharpened if anything in the intervening half-century, but it remains a single point. The story is awkwardly told here and is largely populated with caricatures left over from Dr. Strangelove.

These three pieces make up the first half of the evening. The second is occupied by Strange Medicine, which the program coyly describes as "based on an idea by Jules Romains." It is in fact a musicalization of Romains once-famous and now-forgotten comedy Dr. Knock. That play, subtitled The Triumph of Medicine, showed a GP descending on a new practice and revolutionizing it by persuading the local population that their bodies were merely an assortment of diseases waiting to happen and that they should dose themselves accordingly. The doctor gets rich, and so does the local pharmacist. The doctor is not a quack and he is not even primarily a profiteer; he is a fanatic.

Again, bringing this story into our own time sharpens its fangs, though its a weakness that we never really know what kind of medical system the protagonist is operating under, or just where in North America it's now meant to be happening. Besides this the musical, like the play it's based on, keeps cracking the same joke. Its a good and grim and pertinent joke but it does get monotonous. This habit of making one point over and over afflicts all the pieces on the bill -- all except the first, which only has the time to make one point, period.

Allen Coles music for Strange Medicine is by far the best in the show and maybe the best this prolific composer has composed for anything. An opening number in which the new physician is driven through the countryside by his predecessor and the predecessor's wife while they point out the beauties of the region is a particular delight, though a little long for its importance to the plot; it sways, as -- in the best staging of the evening -- do the three passengers, negotiating what seem to be hairpin bends on mountain passes. Grant Wenaus, the musical director, has designed some lovely vocal harmonies and also plays spiky, barbed piano throughout; the evening's overture, as he plays it, seems to promise better tunes than actually occur.

Barbara Barsky and Tracy Michailidis deal most efficiently with the various female roles; the men are Eddie Glen, a cheery, chubby fellow with a marked physical resemblance to the late Mel Torme, and Paul McQuillan, who at times seems far too nice a fellow to be credible as the passionate dispenser of Strange Medicine and at others seems just right. De Tourdonnet's staging manages for the first half to make a virtue of strict economic necessity, but the more ambitious last piece just looks starved.

This is an unromantic evening; the closest any of the components comes to a love song is a satiric tango and a besotted female patient who wants to be his very own hypochondriac. De Tourdonnet's lyrics, though, are not always tight or disciplined enough to fulfill his fierce intentions; these snappy tales snap less fiercely than seems to have been intended.

Black & White Photo: John Scully / Barbara Barsky, Paul McQuillan, Tracy Michailidis and Eddie Glen. ;
2002-06-15-the-doras-and-who-should-get-:
This year's Dora Mavor Moore Awards show appears to be the splashiest ever. The prizes are being dished out at the Princess of Wales Theatre on Monday -- The Lion Kings night off. The proceedings commence with a cocktail reception and end in Metro Square with something billed as Party with the Stars -- at least it does for us freeloaders and for those members of the public willing to shell out $150 for a VIP ticket.

With the Doras plainly shooting to be up there with the Tonys or even the Oscars, I feel like emulating my colleagues on the movie pages and offering my thoughts on who will win and who really deserves to.

Let it be said that these matters are less clear-cut in Toronto than on Broadway or in Hollywood. We dont breed blockbuster hits (though we import them), and we don't have enormous advertising budgets for kneecapping the opposition. We are a community, and it's a sure bet that at least half-a-dozen speechmakers will say so on Monday.

Still, the prizegivings have certain things in common. All are presented as races between the various suits (or, in our neck of the woods, the sweaters and jeans) who put the shows on; press releases and reports count the nominations garnered by each studio or theatre organization. I dont know why they think we care. Do most moviegoers even know which conglomerate financed their favourite flick?

In Toronto theatre, a company like Soulpepper may have a recognizable identity, since it presents classics and does so with a recognizable core of actors. But when a notable Canadian play comes along, I doubt that anyone by seasons end remembers whether they saw it at Tarragon, Factory, Passe Muraille or Canadian Stage.

Anyway ...

Best Play There are five contestants. There is no winner here as obvious as, say, Michael Healey's The Drawer Boy a couple of years ago. Healey's new and more complex Plan B deserves to win, but it had a mixed reception and besides, he won every conceivable prize for The Drawer Boy. I was glad to see that Alex Poch-Goldins witty and imaginative This Hotel got a nod, but I dont think it stands a chance. Nothing else was as entertaining as these two, but earnestness counts for a lot in Toronto, so I expect to see Daniel MacIvor's You Are There, Carole Frechette's Elisas Skin or Djanet Searss Adventures of a Black Girl in Search of God walk off with the trophy, in that order of likelihood.

Best Production of a Play I don't know what this means: presumably something to do with getting all the elements together and packaging them nicely. It's separate from best play or best direction, but in practice the best-produced show is going to look like the best-directed, and you wouldnt know the difference unless you were at rehearsals. In fact, the best-assembled shows were both at CanStage -- Indian Ink (the best play, as opposed to best Canadian play, of the season) and Picasso at the Lapin Agile -- but since these had the bad taste to be British and American plays with British and American directors, neither was nominated. Those that were: In On It, Skylight, Black Girl (my bet, though not my preference), The Island, and This Hotel (for which, lets hear it.).

Best Direction of a Play Laszlo Marton, when available, usually wins this, and should again for Uncle Vanya. My own runnerup: Kelly Thornton for This Hotel. Most vexing omissions: Kate Lynch's Midsummer Night's Dream and Herbert Olschoks La Ronde.

Best Actor in a Play Should be Alon Nashman (Picasso at the Lapin Agile). Diego Matamoros in Uncle Vanya was wonderful, but there were so many terrific performances in that show that it seems wrong to single him out, except perhaps symbolically. (Why not Charmion King as Best Supporting Actress? Too small a role to be noticed, I suppose.) John Kanis performance in The Island has been a legend for 30 years (as has that of his overlooked colleague, Winston Ntshona) so somehow doesn't count -- though we'd certainly all cheer for him. Peter Donaldson (Plan B) and Tony Nardi (The Lesson) are fine actors but theyve done better work elsewhere.

Best Actress in a Play This is the toughest: eight nominations. I can see nothing to choose between Yanna McIntosh (Skylight) and Fiona Reid (Indian Ink), but McIntosh had a potentially deadly role to enliven so Id go with her. So will the judges, since she's the newer girl and has two nominations. Though, as the other is for Belle, a repeat from last year, I can't see how its eligible. Tanja Jacobs is in with a chance as the performer of a highly regarded monologue (Elissas Skin), though in that area I preferred Jenny Young (The Shape of a Girl); I thought she was amazing.

The Musicals This is a farce. With the Mirvishes inactive, and Tarragon's Anything That Moves a revival, there were no new musicals. In the "best category, they've been reduced to nominating Damien Atkinss Real Live Girl, a standup act. I didnt much like The Piper but that surely deserved consideration at least as much. Why not simply suspend the category for a year?

In the production and direction areas, they've been further reduced to considering a Ross Petty pantomime and a thoroughly undramatic show about the Mamas and the Papas. I see no reason why Anything That Moves shouldn't clean up in every category allowed: direction (Alisa Palmer), actress (Glynis Ranney), actor (Tim Howar, though Damien Atkins is competition here) and -- probably -- choreography (Valerie Moore, though plays are also eligible here and there were nifty moves in a couple of them).

Real desperation: the appalling Saturday Night Fever is down for best touring production" though the Scots Medea (at World Stage) will obviously wipe it off the map.

Supporting Actor This can be male or female, play or musical. It has to be David Storch (The Lonesome West).

Design The years loveliest scenic design (Susan Bensons for Indian Ink) isn't nominated, though at least her costumes are. Also ignored: Scott Bradley's great set for Picasso .... Cheers, then, for Michael Levine (Uncle Vanya) closely followed by Steve Lucas (This Hotel).

All the above are in the "General Theatre, or big boys, division. In the smaller, or independent" (of what?) section, there is more of a tendency for two or three shows to sweep the board, like -- to name the most incongruous exemplars I can think of -- Titanic or The Producers. This year, the front-runners are Chekhovs Longs ... In the Ravine and -- my own preference -- The Walls of Africa. Though if Dennis OConnor doesn't win the best actor prize for his performance in The Dragonfly of Chicoutimi, I may very well get violent.

Until June 29. Box office: 416-531-1827. robertcushman@lycos.com

THE TURN OF THE SCREW

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

Henry James, that most resistible of great novelists (O the thinness of blood! O the long parenthesis-jammed sentences! O look who's talking!), had a relationship with the theatre that was loving but strained. He was a fan and he wrote plays of his own, all flops. But there have been many successful dramatizations of his novels and stories by other hands. The shorter ones, naturally, have been the more amenable, and The Turn of the Screw, that ineffably chilling haunted-house novella, has inspired several plays, at least one first-rate film and a Benjamin Britten opera.

A sheltered young governess, toward the end of the 19th century, is dispatched by a suave swell to his house outside London in order to take charge of his young niece and nephew. One of the terms of employment is that she shall take all responsibility for them, and never trouble him in any way.

The children turn out to be beautiful and charming. The only worrying factor is that the older of the two, Miles, has just been expelled from school for reasons that even his headmasters letter leaves uncomfortably obscure. The girl, Flora, is too young to have been sent away, and besides, in those days, girls werent.

The governess, whose name we never learn, sees two sinister figures around the place, appearing and disappearing, and she learns from the housekeeper, Mrs. Grose, that these must be her predecessor, Miss Jessel, and the master's former valet, Peter Quint, who had been lovers and who had apparently exercised an unhealthy influence on the children. To make things worse, both Quint and Miss Jessel are dead. The governess is convinced they have returned from beyond the grave to complete their corruption of Miles and Flora. All ends horrifically.

It is possible to read the book on two consecutive occasions and come to two diametrically opposed conclusions. The first is that the governess, who is also the narrator, really sees what she says she sees and is correct in her interpretation of it. The other is that she is a hysteric, besotted with the handsome employer, whom she only met twice, and determined to bring herself to his attention. She imagines the spirits (or, as she comes to think of them, demons) and misinterprets everything the children say and do, overrating their innocence and inventing their fall. Horrified by any manifestation of sexuality, she calls Quint a hound (not to mention a "base menial") and Miss Jessel a fiend, without actually knowing the first thing about either of them. The housekeeper who seems to be corroborating her suspicions, and whom she patronizes as an ignorant but honest soul, is actually just humouring her.

Keeping this uncertainty going throughout is a high achievement on James's part. I find his achingly fastidious style, which never makes a statement without qualifying it seven ways, a form of elegant hell, but I have to admit that he does actually achieve the subtleties he aims for. When a climax comes he is able to present it with comparative simplicity and to shattering effect. Reproducing this theatrically is, of course, a severe challenge.

Jeffrey Hatchers version, bought to Toronto by Theatre Kingston, has been praised (by its director) for preserving the ambiguities that previous versions have sacrificed. You could have fooled me. The governesss interview here ends with the employer silkily enquiring, "Have I seduced you?" This is an elaboration and a coarsening of a word used glancingly in the novel, and the motif recurs throughout the script. The governess's neurosis is stripped pretty bare in the play, and she is far more explicit about what the ghosts actually want of the children than her fictional inspiration ever was.

Meanwhile, Hatcher has jettisoned James's dialogue almost completely. His own substitute chat includes a long series of riddle games, not as tantalizing as they are obviously meant to be. He varies the story and even adds a coda, telling us -- as James never did -- what happened to the characters afterwards. (It isnt good news.)

It is probably impossible to put this material on a stage without coarsening it, and Hatcher has done a reasonable job, but where James created suspense, he creates impatience. We dont revel in the build-up; we just want to cut to the chase.

There is one central device that bestows a kind of claustrophobic sheen. The cast is confined to two actors. Michelle Mallen plays the governess, and gives a conscientious performance that sometimes buckles; at moments of severest crisis her passion descends into generalized urgency, as if she were defending herself against charges that nobody has actually made. Craig Walker, who is also the director, plays all the other roles: man, woman or child.

Actually he does one of each, with no change of costume; voice and stance are all. First he is the employer. Then he is the housekeeper, whom he plays as an old Scots biddy out of some old BBC television series, a choice that adds a note of feyness to the character who least needs it. From this he leaps back and forth into the character of young Miles, whom he plays uncannily well.

Little Flora we never see -- she is an invisible presence whom we imagine trailing along holding one of her elders' hands -- and we never hear her either; she is said to have been struck dumb by the traumatic events that preceded the play. This is not in the book. It's presumably been done in the interests of theatrical economy, and in the hope that it may provide some additional spookiness on the side.

But it's a mistake. We need to believe in the house and the children as real and normal if we are to be appalled by their supernatural takeover. A book can more easily get the best of both worlds, this and the next; a play really has to work at it.

TORONTO THE GOOD

Artword Theatre, Toronto

Something has gone calamitously wrong with Toronto the Good. (I'm speaking theatrically, not historically). The idea is intriguing enough: A scrapbook of life in the city in the 1890s, drawing on songs, pamphlets and journalism of the time. The songs seemed especially promising. The topical tunes of this period were often musically tame, but their lyrics, even when not very funny, teem with sociological interest. What appears on the stage, though, is almost totally inert.

There are some excuses. There are only five in the cast: Two men, three women, all of them constantly on the go. One of the quintet had to be replaced a week before opening; her substitute was unready to face an audience, and her uncertainty seems to have infected her colleagues. I have never known so many lines to be fluffed or mistimed in a single show, or heard so many songs so haltingly and illogically phrased. I have rarely beheld a cast so palpably uneasy about what they were doing. Two of the performers (Ann Bisch and Michelle Piller) display occasional verve. It would be cruel even to mention the names of the others. In the circumstances, it was irresponsible as well as foolhardy not to postpone the premiere.

I doubt, though, that all of the problems can be attributed to last-minute panic. The show, assembled and directed by Ronald Weihs, lacks focus. It sets up a contrast between a puritanically reforming Mayor of Toronto, William P. Howland, and the human impulses that go on cheerfully defying him: A bit like Measure for Measure, really.

But this conflict never takes off; after his initial proclamation, Mayor Howland -- here implausibly young and weightless -- disappears both from the stage and from our consciousness.

On the other side, there is the inescapable fact that few of the new freedoms -- of women to ride bicycles, for example, or to go out in boats with young men -- strike us now as remotely shocking. We need to be taken far deeper into the contemporary mindset if we are ever to understand why they should have been.

When it comes to depicting more radical vice -- the flourishing turn-of-the-century brothel-trade, for example -- the show becomes unhelpfully dainty. A police-court scene, in which a beaten wife pleads for her husband's acquittal because without him her children will starve, does strike an uncomfortable -- and uncomfortably modern -- note. But though the show gives a lot of time to the burgeoning of feminism, the whole issue seems cut adrift from the vice-virtue contest that is supposed to be governing the show. As sung here, some supposedly stirring hymns to emancipation are notable only for their feebleness. Nothing in this production ever seems to lead smoothly or pointedly to anything else.

Obviously it is meant to, or at least it was once. We of the press were handed a synopsis that reads like the fossil of some abandoned concept. It speaks of a pungent contemporary chronicler named C.S. Clark, and hints that he will be our narrator and tour guide. Well, one actor does do the bulk of the scene-setting, but he is never identified as C.S. Clark or anyone else, and he never gives the show any kind of tone: Certainly not a satirical one.

The first half is interminable. The second begins more promisingly, in a music hall. A comedian does an all-purpose introductory act that is devilishly hard to bring to life but does at least suggest, in its stream-of-consciousness versatility, a performing line that was to stretch in the next century at least as far as Jimmy Durante and Danny Kaye. Subsequent items, though, turn out as formless and arbitrary as the rest of the show, right down to a closer about coming to the end of the day -- a day that we never knew had started.

There is some amusement, as there generally is, in the recital of patent-medicine ads, many of which seem to have originated in the United States. And that's another thing: Most of the trends depicted in the show, and most of the music, could equally well be American or British. (One song, in and about a streetcar, strikingly anticipates the Trolley Song from Meet Me in St. Louis, though it's nothing like as good.)

There is little here that is specifically Canadian, let alone Torontonian. That could have been a point -- maybe Mayor Howland should really have been fighting for cultural protectionism -- but nothing is made of it. Indeed the only local interest -- sometimes the only interest of any kind -- lies in hearing the names of Toronto streets, trying to picture how they must have looked then, and comparing that with how they look now. I suppose it was a slip of the tongue that led somebody to give the address of one house of ill-fame as Sheppard and Adelaide; it must have been a hell of a place to get to, even then.
2002-06-21-everyone-s-a-winner-at-this-y:
Robertcushman@lycos.com

Michael Healey, stepping up to receive the Dora award for outstanding new play (general division), tugged at his hair and said, I don't believe this ... Robert Cushman seemed so sure I wouldn't win." Were I not even shyer than he is, I would have risen from my seat and shouted, "I wanted you to win.

I wrote last Saturday that Healey deserved the award for his play Plan B, but probably wouldnt get it since hed already won so big for The Drawer Boy, and the critical reception for Plan B had been mixed (i.e., none of the others seemed to like it as much as I did). But what do critics know? I've never been happier to be proved wrong.

The 23rd Annual Dora Mavor Moore Awards, as presented on Monday at the Princess of Wales Theatre, were among the slicker prize days in recent memory, though someone really must persuade the organizers that backcloths with stars on them do not represent the ne plus ultra in glamorous sophistication. Maybe they weren't meant to. One of the endearing things about the annual Dora show is that it seems intended as a parody of the Oscar and Tony shindigs.

Its also more egalitarian: People other than actors are allowed to make speeches and hand out awards; directors, producers, administrators, all sorts, though thus far theyve drawn the line at critics. As for hosting the evening, if the Tonys this year had Gregory Hines and Bernadette Peters trying to pass themselves off as a comedy duo despite looking as if they'd never met before, then the Doras had Diane Flacks and Richard Greenblatt, who are a comedy duo, or were a couple of years ago in their show Sibs. Needless to say, they wrote themselves better material than the Broadway scribes gave to Hines and Peters, and they delivered it better, though there is a limit to the number of jokes that can be squeezed out of Flacks's pregnancy, and they exceeded it.

Also, a certain self-consciousness clung to them; its hard for this kind of banter to sound spontaneous, and it didnt. They seemed to want to be a parody and the real thing simultaneously, especially when they went off into a musical number, celebrating the event's long list of sponsors to the tune (it eventually emerged) of Mack the Knife. This was the only warbling of the evening; music was otherwise confined to John Roby, pianist, saluting each of the winners by tinkling whichever show tune took his fancy at the moment. Next year, I'd like to see Healey host the event, either in his own droll solo person or in cahoots with his partner, Kate Lynch.

The show was also notable for a record number of ties in the voting (the award was split in four categories) and for the unpreparedness of the guest prize-givers in dealing with them. The award for male principal in a musical was presented to Damien Atkins in Real Live Girl, who reduced several participants, including himself, to tears by thanking his mother. (Yes, all award winners thank their mothers, but he really thanked her.)

Five minutes later it was announced he should have shared the title with Graham Abbey, usually of Stratford, for his work in Snow White and the Magnificent Seven. Abbey appeared and gave a good- sport performance to equal the one he offered last Christmas in green tights, tap-dancing with seven dwarves" (his description).

Later, a division of the spoils for outstanding touring production between Medea and Hamlet seemed to leave the representative of Harbourfront, which brought us both, uncertain of which tragedy she was accepting for.

The evening also featured no less than four acceptance speeches by Dean Gilmour -- a lot for a performer whose main talent is for mime. His (and his wife Michele Smiths) company, Theatre Smith- Gilmour, collected that number of prizes for their show Chekhov Longs -- In the Ravine. Three of them -- best play, production, and direction -- were plausible; that for the performance of Gilmour himself, who gave himself far more lines than he could interestingly handle, surely wasnt, especially since he was up against Layne Coleman (The Walls of Africa) and the magnificent Dennis O'Connor (The Butterfly of Chicoutimi). It was strange, too, given all the confetti aimed in its direction, that the really outstanding performance in Chekhov Longs -- Liisa Repo-Martell's -- wasnt nominated at all.

Among the musicals, as expected, Anything That Moves took everything that wasnt nailed down. Christopher Newton, presenting one of its prizes, referred to the show as Anything Goes, which the director, Alisa Palmer, seemed to take as a compliment, as well she might.

Glynis Ranney, outstanding actress in same, quipped how relieved she was that musicals were no longer lumped with opera. The rest of us were relieved, too, since it was a lunatic arrangement. The two operatic categories mainly consisted of the COC running against itself. The winners -- Ewa Podles, for her performance in Julius Caesar; and the Robert Lepage double-bill of Bluebeard's Castle and Erwartung for best production -- were predictable, pretty much in the best way. A prophecy: In the peripatetic world of opera, the winners are never going to be around to pick up their trophies.

Steve Lucas won the design award (independent) for Breath[e], which seemed inevitable as that show is nothing but design; it then transpired that he was meant to share it with the three gentlemen who designed The Girl With No Door on Her Mouth, a piece I regret having missed but will undoubtedly have a chance to see, since it also won for lighting (the same three guys), and two awards are more than enough to guarantee a revival.

Chekhov Longs shared its outstanding production citation with Hrant Alianak's The Walls of Africa, which also carried it off for sound design and best actress. The latter was Tedde Moore; and her prize -- the first of the evening -- was triply gratifying: a) she deserved it, though Dragana Varagic in The Vindication of Senyora Clito Mestres was stiff competition; b) its a comeback for her after years of virtual absence from the theatre; and c) shes the granddaughter of the actual Dora and it's nice that these things should occasionally be kept in the family.

Back in the general division, Garth Drabinsky also made a comeback when The Island, which he brought to Toronto, won for outstanding production of a play. I expressed my bemusement about this category last week, but if it has to exist it makes more sense to give the palm to a visiting show than to some arbitrarily chosen resident package. What, for example, makes Tarragon's Skylight, which was nominated, a more outstanding production than Soulpeppers Uncle Vanya, which wasnt? We all know awards are silly, but at least in the other slots there can be some attempt at objective judgment.

Uncle Vanya didn't win a thing, while Soulpepper's Ionesco double- bill, which I thought good but not on the same level, cleaned up: Tony Nardi, who made an especially generous acceptance speech, got best actor for his Professor in The Lesson; Jim Warren was feted for his direction of The Bald Soprano, and Victoria Wallace was dittoed for her costumes. David Storch in The Lonesome West won the award for best featured (i.e. supporting) performance, to my relief, and Yanna McIntosh in Skylight won for best female performance, to everybodys audible joy.

The Adventures of a Black Girl in Search of God, though not a musical, got best choreography (Vivine Scarlett), which is the award it deserved, and This Hotel got best sound design (Richard Feren, Torontos omnipresence of audio), which is something. Astrid Janson, winning set designer for La Ronde, paid tribute to the actors who had to trundle her creation around. It was a striking set rather than a beautiful one; where beauty is concerned, I still root for Susan Benson's translucent design for Indian Ink. And the Silver Ticket (or career achievement) award went to Bill Glassco, for many things but chiefly for founding the Tarragon.

Some obvious anomalies about the Doras scream to be corrected. It's proper that the authors of plays and musicals should only be eligible for awards at their works first appearance; its absurd that the performers and directors of the same shows can be nominated every time their show gets revived. (At this rate, the COC will be able to get prizes for that Bartok/ Schoenberg double-bill into infinity.) I have some sympathy with a colleague who inquires why The Island wasn't in the touring category (in which it would probably have won), considering it has been on tour for 30 years. And my own score as a prophet works out around 66.66%, especially if I'm allowed to count Michael Healey.
