2002-06-22-theatre-formed-a-strong-conne:
Robert Cushman is theatre critic of the National Post and the author of Fifty Seasons at Stratford.

Timothy Findley's Elizabeth Rex, staged at the Tom Patterson Theatre in the summer of 2001, was probably the most electric opening of a new Canadian play in the Stratford Festivals half- century of existence.

It generated its own sense of occasion: Here was a modern Shakespearean company performing a play about their equivalents on the other side of the world, 400 years ago. The play shows Shakespeares own troupe summoned to entertain Elizabeth I and finding themselves locked in mortal debate with her on questions of vital interest to both parties: love, gender, politics -- all kinds of role-playing.

Offstage, the Earl of Essex, the players' patron and the Queen's lover, awaited the executioners block; onstage, both parties tried to make sense of their lives

Set in a barn and staged in a converted sports club down by the Avon, play and production had tremendous atmosphere. This was a play that actors could latch on to and that exerted a corresponding grip on the audience.

But what really made it exhilarating was its architecture. It was written in two unbroken, richly peopled acts, each a great soaring arc of dialogue and action. Most current plays dont flow, they twitch; composed in short disjointed scenes, they behave like television scripts and often seem to wish they were. This one was bred of the theatre and belonged there.

Of course, Mr. Findley himself had been an actor. He claimed the experience had helped him as a novelist to tell stories and explore characters. And though his novels are what made him famous, his career both began and ended in the theatre.

Especially, it began and ended in Stratford. He was in the first company there in 1953. Alec Guinness, to whose Richard III he had played Catesby, thought well enough of him to take him back to London and pay for his further training. He worked there for a few years. He played Osric to Paul Scofield's prince in the first Hamlet I ever saw. And I wish, since I may be the only person now in Canada who saw the performance, I could remember more about it. As it is, I can only record the opinion of the theatre critic Kenneth Tynan, who thought it fell flat, but blamed this on the director (Peter Brook) not having a sense of humour.

In some respects, Mr. Findley's career parallels that of the English novelist Margaret Drabble. She, too, began as an actor -- at the English Stratford, indeed -- and she has continued to draw on the experience in her novels.

Unlike Mr. Findley, though, she has shown no serious signs of becoming a playwright. He, however, came full circle: In the last seven years, he was close to being Stratford's resident playwright. He lived there and was very much part of the life of the town.

By sad coincidence, his reminiscent foreword to my own book on the Festival was the last piece of his writing to be published in his lifetime.

There is more to come, of course. By the end of this 50th Stratford season, four new Findley plays -- more than by any other contemporary playwright -- will have been presented there in seven years. Apart from Elizabeth Rex, there have been The Stillborn Lover (1995), about a gay diplomat, and The Trials of Ezra Pound (2001), a semi-documentary, both of them exploring his favourite themes of personal and political loyalty.

This year, as part of the inaugural season in the new Studio (which I would not be surprised to find renamed the Timothy Findley Studio some fine morning), there will be Shadows, a one-act-play in which seven people confront their pasts at a spookily interrupted dinner party -- a situation that sounds quintessentially Findleyan.

Because both his energy and his reputation were so bound up in his novels, he seldom makes the lists of prominent Canadian playwrights and indeed the patrician tone of his plays sets them apart from those of his contemporaries and successors.

As a man, he remained very much part of the theatre. I have the impression -- I never met him -- he was someone whose taste and opinion counted. He was, almost independently of his plays, a theatrical icon as well as a literary one and is likely to remain so.

Elizabeth Rex towers over the others of his plays that we have seen so far (including adaptations of his novels, such as Not Wanted on the Voyage) and it is both satisfying and frustrating that it came so late. It was a wonderful way to end, but it might also have marked a new beginning.

THE SLEUTH-A-LONG SOUND OF MYSTERY

Mysteriously Yours Mystery Dinner Theatre, Toronto

I should know better by now, but always it takes me by surprise. Mysteriously Yours is a phenomenon among dinner theatres since it invariably provides both good dinner and good theatre.

The former may be the rarer half of the equation; I come from London (England) where people have been known to roll around on the floor after partaking of pub-theatre food, and not because the play was agonizingly hilarious. Even in Toronto the only real competition is the Second City set-up where you can wolf down huge quantities of good pasta before the show. Even there, however, you have to move to another room in order to be entertained. Here everything comes to you at the table, food and drama alike, and it's sometimes hard to tell exactly which commodity the waiters think they're serving up. My companion, as we gourmet critics like to say, expressed great satisfaction with the stuffed chicken. I can thoroughly recommend the roast beef and the sachertorte.

The gastronomic range is narrow but satisfying, and the same may be said of the plays. Each is a broad parody of a familiar story or film. The first time I went, the inspiration was Murder on the Orient Express, complete of course with Belgian detective.

This summer The Sleuth-a-Long Sound of Mystery offers us an Alpine music contest presided over by a Herr Straussberg, along with the Von Mousetrapp Twins, Hans and Ruppert, who have been winning the competition for 26 years straight, and a paranoid diva who not unnaturally resents this and who is called Julie Andrews-Lloyd- Webber.

The twins are accompanied by their remarkably faithful nanny Maria. Early on, a twin is shot and the distinguished detective Hercule Perrier, who just happens to be in attendance, involves all in solving the crime. Needless to say, everyone present has a motive, including several members of the paying public.

Here I must pay tribute to the company's capacity for painlessly eliciting audience participation. As the eating part of the evening draws to its conclusion, they move among the tables, issuing selected victims with lines of dialogue to be delivered at an appropriate moment. Somehow they manage to make spectators speak, sing and even yodel without embarrassing anyone. Jean Daigle, who always plays the presiding sleuth and is also both director and co- author, is the prime mover here. He moves things along in crackling fashion and has a particularly effective line in jovial bullying.

I wouldn't say that this or any other of the company's scripts is subtle as cultural satire. But the proceedings are always cheerful, often funny, and occasionally even witty.

The performers all seem to be resilient improvisers, as there is especially charming work from Laurence Prince as the twins, in whose mouths even rum-butter wouldn't melt, and from Brian Smith as the hard-pressed impresario (well, how would you like it if you had to give money back to 5,000 unseen but audibly rumbling Austrians?) who looks somewhat like John Fraser and not just because he wears a bow tie.

And the mystery does work in its own right, with the clues as conscientiously distributed as in a real thriller, which means, as far as I'm concerned, that they're totally baffling. I've never yet spotted the killer. No, I tell a lie.This time I did identify the correct suspect early on but then discarded my theory because it seemed too unlikely or, to put it another way, too obvious. I can't win.

The promised next show is Murder in Casablanca, and I imagine the management is already rounding up the usual suspects.

THE PLAY GOES ON by Neil Simon

Touchstone/Simon & Schuster $21.50

- - -

One of my favourite moments in a Neil Simon play comes in The Gingerbread Lady, when someone asks the protagonist, "Can I say something? and she snaps back, Only if it makes me laugh." This heroine, a compulsive wisecracker herself, seems to have released something in Simon. He seems to feel here the same carnival freedom he does when he writes books for musicals. "Yes says the hero of They're Playing Our Song, one such work, as he reports the breakdown of his car to the American Automobile Association, I'm a member; I even go to the meetings."

Much of the time, though, Simons jokes are fettered by the demands of psychological realism and the well-made play, often dealing with ostensibly painful subjects. This means the plays are frequently not as funny as one feels they might be -- the one- liners, though they usually make you laugh at the time, are oddly unquotable -- and also not as serious as they might be. This is not to accuse Simon of pandering. Like any decent writer, he writes up to his own limits. It has been his fortune -- in all senses -- that his limits have generally coincided with those of his audience.

Like the plays, this volume of memoirs, Simons second, goes down easily -- remarkably easily, given that it begins with the death of his beloved first wife and takes in two subsequent marriages that ended in divorce. There are plenty of good times recorded as well. At the point at which the book begins, Simon -- with Barefoot in the Park, The Odd Couple and Plaza Suite under his belt -- was already the most prosperous and popular playwright in the history of Broadway. This book chronicles the writing of more hit plays, and such lines-round-the-block movies as The Goodbye Girl. It also sees this quintessential New Yorker move, somewhat reluctantly, to California, and find that -- some of the time, at least -- he likes it. His relationships begin well -- the lovers' meeting is cute -- almost as if they were in a play or a movie, and naturally one cheers them on. There are also endearing moments of contact with children, step-children and grandchildren. All the same, it's largely a chronicle of loss and loneliness. Its told with an admirable lack of self-pity, but it speaks freely of pain, though it hardly ever makes us feel it.

Simon writes consummately for a live audience; he knows instinctively and precisely how to play with its reactions. (Many of his films, lacking that vital current between stage and auditorium, are dead by comparison.) His dialogue needs actors to bring it alive. The dialogue in this book, of course, does not have that advantage; and besides, the presence of dialogue is, in itself, questionable. It immediately -- unless you grant the writer the gift of total recall -- turns memoir into fiction. Which, of course, it may well be, but Simon does not seem to have any such deconstructive method in mind. He is merely trying to liven up his story the best way he knows how. You end up accepting the convention, but at a cost.

In part, the book is the autobiography of an autobiographer. Simon, in the period it covers, had increasingly taken to basing his plays on his own earlier life. "Writing, he says, is not always an act of creation. Sometimes ... its like a poison that inhabits your being, and the only way to get rid of it is to have the pen press deeply and quickly on the empty pages.... Those writers who go to the deepest and darkest of agonies are the ones who have lived there as well.... I wish I could go deeper, further, but then again I think as I do. I do make the effort if not the entire journey." That remarkably echoes the way many of us respond to Simon's plays: We think they're good and wish they were better.

The play he is introducing at this point is Chapter Two, about a novelist whose second marriage is threatened by his inability to forget his first. It contains a long speech in which the woman tells the man exactly what she thinks about the way in which he is underrating her and taking her for granted. It is, we are told, based very closely on a diatribe directed at Simon in similar circumstances by his own second wife, the actress Marsha Mason. In life, apparently, he thought it magnificent. In the play, I find it, Im afraid, stagy. But there you go. It helped the Simon-Mason marriage, but did not, in the end, save it. (Though Mason did play her own role, so to speak, in the movie version.) Their fictional equivalents -- in classic storm-weathering Broadway fashion -- do stay together; at least the audience is given no reason to believe they wont. The book tries to go more deeply into the failure of that marriage, and of Simon's subsequent one to a magazine writer, Diane Landers, but in neither case do we really find out why things fell apart.

Chapter Two was not, at the time, widely publicized as being autobiographical. Several of Simon's later plays were. There was the Depression idyll Brighton Beach Memoirs (maybe his best play, a seamless fantasia), drawn from his own adolescence, and its two sequels -- Biloxi Blues, derived fom his military service, and Broadway Bound, whose title suggests that its about the beginning of his writing career, but which is really about his mother, a martyr to housework and to life generally, sustained by the memory of the one night in her youth when she danced with George Raft. In real life, it had been George Burns, but Simon thought a Latin lover would sound more romantic than a Jewish comic. The story as told in the book has a charming coda, when the octogenarian Burns, appearing for Simon in the film version of The Sunshine Boys, is introduced to Mrs. Simon and recognizes her instantly.)

Simon is very interesting on how the plays depart from their historical moorings and why. This is especially helpful when he gets to Lost in Yonkers, which seems to be about the same characters as the trilogy but cannot be factually reconciled with it, almost as if it were going on in a parallel universe. He also, in confessedly self-indulgent style, uses the plays as pretexts to examine parts of his life that, incidentally, long predate the period the book is supposed to be dealing with. (So Biloxi Blues occasions reminiscences about his enforced stint as editor, and sole writer, of the official Army Air Force newspaper: "I was a tough editor .... I wanted to fire me but that didnt seem practical.")

The best bits, though, are the backstage stories about the triumphs and traumas of getting plays on. Simon says, more or less, that it's only when he's writing that he really knows who he is, and I suspect he knows it best when he's writing his plays, turning fact artfully into fiction rather than trying laboriously to turn fiction back into fact, as he is doing here. Which is as it should be: What interests us about a playwright is his plays.

robertcushman@lycos.com Obituary of Rosemary Clooney.

The first time I spoke to Rosemary Clooney I started by telling her, truthfully, that she was my favourite singer. It seemed the best way of starting, and apparently she thought so too since she laughed in a gratified (and, to me, gratifying) "I-think-I-might- enjoy-this-interview" kind of way. She laughed a lot.

This was in October, 2000, and she was on the phone from her house in California, about to leave for a tour that included a night at Roy Thomson Hall: her last ever gig in Toronto, as it turned out. We talked for an hour. Two things stay with me apart from the laughter. One was when I mentioned The Way You Look Tonight, a favourite song of mine that she had never recorded and that I thought she should; she immediately started singing it for me, as the most natural way of carrying on the conversation. (Breaking into song in the middle of speech was apparently something she did often.) She also interrupted me when I began likening her singing to Frank Sinatra's. "I'm not as good," she said firmly.

Maybe not, but I can't think of anyone in the pop-jazz-cabaret- standards spectrum who comes closer: Nobody else who so personalized her material while still respecting its native contours, nobody so adept at using rhythm to illuminate the meaning of a lyric, nobody with a voice so beguilingly layered.

It would have been interesting, if intimidating, to meet Sinatra, but it was never a consuming ambition of mine. (Just as well, since it never happened.) I really wanted to meet Clooney. Reading the tributes that have appeared in print and on the Internet since her death last Saturday at the age of 73, I have discovered that many others felt just as I did. Her audiences thought of her as a friend.

Applied to most pop singers, that would be cloyingly sentimental, but in this case it isn't. Clooney, more than any other performer, brought out, exemplified, the humanity in that most human of artistic monuments, the Great American Songbook. I did get to meet her in person, after her Toronto performance. She had a lot of physical problems even before the lung cancer that took her life, and her weight didn't help, and one wished that during her performance (which had mostly been superb) she had sat down more; the audience certainly wouldn't have minded, any more than we minded her sensible habit of wearing her glasses on stage. She was sitting, and obviously weary, in her dressing-room, but still she was a delight. "Miss Clooney --", one of her fans began. "Please," she said. "Rosemary." And so, for the rest of this story, it shall be.

As a performer, Rosemary dispensed a unique blend of joy and intelligence, wit and warmth: nice, but no pushover. Her humour, comfortably self-deprecating, bubbled over between numbers, playfully alluding to her million-selling career in the '50s without ever turning into a nostalgia act. ("I'm going to sing Hey There so you'll remember which one I was"; "Come On-a My House was based on an Armenian folk-song and sung by an Irish-American, so naturally we did it in an Italian accent"; "Don't try watching White Christmas if it isn't Christmas.")

She also talked a lot about her five children, her grandchildren on whose unruliness she was hilarious ("The kid's outta the will!") and, latterly, about her famous nephew, George.

There were other things in her past that she didn't allude to on stage: the strains of juggling the children, the career and a marriage (two, actually) to the philandering Jose Ferrer; the affair with Nelson Riddle, who orchestrated two of her best early albums; the breakdown that sent her, after witnessing the murder of her friend Robert Kennedy, into a mental hospital.

Most of her audience, though, was probably aware of them (there have been a couple of unsparing, though also unwallowing, autobiographies) and appreciated, even shared, the way she had turned herself around, into a new person and a new musician, with a happy new relationship, eventually a marriage, that was a large part of her salvation.

For the last 20 years she recorded for Concord Jazz, turning out an album a year, nearly all of them excellent, and constituting a legacy unapproached by any recent singer in the idiom. Working for a jazz label, and with small, stellar groups of musicians, liberated her; she may not have improvised but she swung, and her beat was unforced and irresistible. It enabled her to combine what had previously been disparate aspects of her musical personality. Before, there had been the infectious singer of up-tempo jollities and a sedate, mournful dispenser of ballads, plangent but lacking an edge. She needed to grow into her voice, or it needed to deepen to catch up with her. Even the best of her earlier albums (Blue Rose, with Duke Ellington; Love, with Riddle) pale in comparison to the Concords. Now, even her torch songs had a pulse and a tang; her version, for example, of One for My Baby, the ultimate saloon song, is the only one to compare with Sinatra's. Meanwhile, her comedic numbers were wryly incomparable. She made I Wish I Were in Love Again, the great anti-love song, sound swift and unanswerable, ending it with a laconic, spoken "Damn," the aural equivalent of a shrug of the shoulders. She sang Dave Frishberg's I Want to Be a Sideman with a delicious sense of the lyric's incongruity when coming from a woman and a matching embrace of its truth to the life of any working musician.

Her final album, Sentimental Journey, released last year, kicks off with the best version I've ever heard of That Old Black Magic, the only one that's neither tossed-off nor self-consciously torrid, and the only one in which the images -- the icy fingers and the elevators -- take on a solid existence. It also includes an awkward new song about Sinatra that's immediately redeemed by a real tribute: a performance of They Can't Take That Away from Me, whose first line is "The way you wear your hat"; for the nonce Rosemary changes "the way you sing off-key" to a decisive "on key." (Compare the way she just perceptibly isolates "the song that Crosby sings" in These Foolish Things, as a tribute to another colleague and mentor.) Yes, the breath grew short (to paraphrase September Song, another of her great ones) but she worked around it. Maturity -- a kind of sensual grandmotherliness -- became her; it seemed like wisdom. Late in her career, she was able to sing James Taylor's The Secret of Life, and sound as if she might actually have found it.

I envy those who really knew her. No singer can have been more loved.

THE HOUSE OF BERNARDA ALBA

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE, Ont. - The Shaw Festival production of The House of Bernarda Alba has "brave try" written all over it.

Federico Garcia Lorca's last play is one of the great unseen modern classics. The year of its creation, 1936, was also that of its author's death. A Spanish Republican, he became a Fascist victim during the early days of the Civil War.(The play remained unproduced in Spain for another 30 years.) Its subject is repression, and it has become a critical commonplace to regard the shuttered all- female household it depicts as a metaphor for the country itself, buttoned-down and beleaguered. I doubt, though, that it really strikes anyone that way when watching it now, especially in translation. It stands in its own right as a tight, inexorable march toward disaster -- an authentic tragedy.

Bernarda Alba, one of the more prosperous women in her Andalusian village, has five grown, unmarried daughters and has buried two husbands -- the second of them immediately before the start of the play. She now, with grim relish, declares an eight-year period of mourning. No men are allowed to cross the threshold, though prospective suitors are permitted, in accordance with tradition, to speak with their intended at her window.

A certain Pepe el Romano pays court in just this manner to Angustias, the eldest and (by virtue of her father's or stepfather's will) richest of the quintet, but it seems he has been conducting a more active dalliance with Adela, the youngest and most rebellious. Pepe is also desired by an intermediate daughter, Martirio, who is crippled and -- even more than her sisters -- embittered. All this we are told; Pepe himself never appears, nor does any other man.

The conflicting passions, and conflicting spites, of these three drive the play. (The remaining two daughters function mainly as chorus. They are Magdalena, dubbed "the hyena," though apparently just for the sake of the rhyme, and Amelia, whose only distinguishing feature -- at least in this production -- is that she has red hair.) They take up more stage time than their mother. Nevertheless, it is her play as well as her house. She controls the narrative. She, of her own choice, is doom.

Tadeusz Bradecki's production looks good, on a rich white courtyard set designed by Teresa Przybylski, and it clearly marks out the initial scenes of sibling rivalry. These get, intermittently, quite exciting, and the last act, which takes place in the early hours of morning and in which Fate gets seriously down to its appointed business of closing in, exerts a real ominous grip, much enhanced by Kevin Lamotte's lighting as it charts the pitiless onset of dawn. But, whatever the spatial limitations of the Court House stage, Bradecki was surely wrong to make such copious use of entrances from the auditorium. The daughters, when summoned by their mother, have to waste precious time climbing the steps from the lobby, when they should be gathering instantly like so many crows. An explicitly claustrophobic drama becomes diffuse.

Mainland European artists are commonly supposed to have access to depths of emotion unplumbable by the uptight British, a category that includes the Anglo-Canadians who dominate the Shaw (and most other Canadian theatres). This is probably a myth; and it is difficult to see any logical reason why a Polish director such as Bradecki should be more at home than a Canadian with a hot-climate play like this one. Certainly, some heat is missing here.

One might want to blame that on Richard Sanger's translation, but in fact it sounds direct and speakable, and if it lacks lyricism then so, by its author's own proud testimony, does the original. Lorca, a poet as well as a playwright, was insistent that in this play he had abandoned poetry for realism. Unlike such florid, and often static, Lorca plays as Blood Wedding, this one moves, purposefully and economically. There is poetry but it is the stripped-down poetry of action.

Though her daughters are the ones who scream or moan about their frustrated sexuality, the play's real passion resides in Bernarda herself. It is a passion, though, for the denying of passion, her own or anyone else's; and that makes her an almighty acting problem.

Glenda Jackson gave an atrociously externalized account of the role in London a few years ago, as a sort of walking ramrod. Nora McLellan at Niagara (in a performance nobly shorn of mannerisms) attempts something subtler and initially more sympathetic: a woman who is a victim of her own upbringing, a tyrannical tradition and a couple of no-good men. She does, in short, what has been done to her. But the play still demands that she do it with conviction; and the director hardly helps her by sending her on anguished walking tours of the stage, undermining her authority when she should be standing firm.

At the end, when the character turns into a mixture of avenging angel and hanging judge, the actress has to fall back on stonewalling; she simply cannot summon the grandeur.

She shares many of her scenes with an old servant on whom she leans for advice and who both fears and despises her. Not being one of the family, this woman serves a link with the outside world, bringing word for example of a girl who has been caught having non- marital sex and is about to be lynched for it -- the best news that Bernarda, whose own household may be running out of chastity belts, gets to hear from one end of the play to the other. Patricia Hamilton delivers these bulletins with some power, but there isn't a character there. Her relationship with her employer is seriously skewed; a confidante is not an equal, but this one is played almost as a superior. In caste-ridden pre-war Spain this is not credible. (It might be interesting to see a modern adaptation of this play, set, say, in Nigeria or Pakistan.)

Lynne Cormack's angular Angustias stands out among the daughters, as also does Susie Burnett's Martirio, a skilled tormentor of herself and others. Fiona Byrne's Adela, the only character in the play possessed of erotic pride, is unfortunately to the English Channel than to the Mediterranean. The Casa Bernarda also boasts a crazed grandmother who periodically emerges from her room cradling a lamb, as if in mockery of her enforcedly barren descendants; Jillian Cook plays her with most delicate dementia, but she suffers more than any of the others from huddled exits and entrances, as if the production were as concerned as her family to keep her out of sight. It is good, however, to see generally underused actresses such as Cormack and Cook given substantial roles. For all the inadequacies, there is the feel of a great play here.

Black & White Photo: Michael Cooper / Nora McLellan plays the matriarch of Casa Bernarda, a woman who is the victim of her own upbringing, a tyrannical tradition and two no-good men. ;

CANDIDA

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE, Ont. - The Rev. James Mavor Morell, Christian socialist, takes his duty to his North London flock very seriously, though he seems to regard them less as his parishioners than as his constituents. Morell is a tireless worker and an even more tireless orator; Blair Williams, who plays him at the Shaw Festival, wins our sympathy within seconds. Talking to his adoring secretary about all men being brothers -- everybody says it, nobody believes it -- he sounds witty and he sounds sincere. Then his curate arrives, and Morell changes the subject of his ongoing sermon; he is now preaching about the virtues of marriage in general, and about those of his own wife, Candida, in particular. Suddenly, he seems less attractive. He is still likeable but he sounds tactlessly, even tastelessly, boastful, and dangerously complacent. Our feelings about him remain in flux for the rest of the evening.

Jackie Maxwell's is the smoothest and most absorbing production of Candida I have seen, and the fluidity of Williams performance gives it much of its charge. Morell, who has taken his wife and her devotion for granted, is challenged for her love by Eugene Marchbanks, a hopelessly unworldly teenage poet. (The unworldliness is due less to his poetry than to his privileged position as the son of an Earl. He is an outcast from his family, but still.)

From the moment Eugene makes his move -- and its the husband he tells first, not the wife -- Morell is on quicksand: Not only does he have a rival but his own belief in himself, as his wife's protector and as a social activist, is called into question. Williams is younger than most of the actors who get to play this role, less sententious and more vulnerable, and he shows us a naturally resilient soul being harrowed. The close of the play finds him crouching, penitent and scared, on a touchingly low chair, like an overgrown schoolboy, which, of course, is what he essentially is.

Mike Shara's Marchbanks is a lanky faun, rolling on floors or hurling himself over sofas in ecstasies of adoration or self- abasement. This is absurd, but it is neither embarrassing nor unbelievable; it is done in precise rhythm with the characters emotions. Shaw had a peculiar idea of both poets and poetry, and much of what Marchbanks says is atrocious, whether hes inventing idylls of escape for himself and his beloved, or expressing horror (what Candida's father, with alcohol on his mind and breath, calls "the poetic 'orrors") at the thought of her having to chop onions. Morell points out that Eugene has no objection to menial tasks being performed by women with whom he doesnt happen to be in love; and here, as at many points of the evening, he is intellectually in the right. But of course, in Shaw, people in the right are always likely to get in wrong, and his greatest clowns are liable to be those with whom he is theoretically in agreement. It keeps the sparks flying.

What sets them alight is the fact that both Morell and Marchbanks are aspects of the author himself: Shaw the unstoppable talking and writing machine, and Shaw the platonic idolater of unattainable women. The problem with Candida is Candida herself, who is given little opportunity to justify the passions she inspires. She isnt even onstage very much. ("So I'm to be put up for auction," she says at the end, and it could be a resonant feminist line. But, to justify such pretentions, the play should have kept her around more. As it is, most of the energy goes into the two men squabbling over her in her absence.)

You can see why Morell clings to her; she runs his life. Marchbanks' infatuation is plausible on the assumption that shes the first woman who ever took an interest in him. But, theatrically, one wants more. In his extra-curricular pronouncements, Shaw was known to denounce Candida as an immoral woman who played with emotions she had no intention of gratifying. But that isnt really what he's written. He's given us an underequipped enchantress, almost begging an actress to fill in the gaps by coming onstage and radiating. Radiance is not really in Kelli Foxs armoury but she has charm and practicality, plus bags of intelligence, and they carry her the distance.

Candida, whatever its trimmings, is a conventional triangle comedy, confined to a single room within a single day. Those of us who enjoy Shaw for his craziness are apt to find its neatness tame. But Maxwells production reminds us that the well-made play has its own pleasures; there is a satisfaction in seeing characters arrive onstage at precisely the right well-motivated moment.

The set, designed by Sue LePage, is a very good space to be at home in, cosy and rambling at once. Bernard Behrens is slyly funny as Candida's ill-bred and impenitent dad, an entrepreneur who can always find the best excuses for underpaying his workers and with an eye continually open for a good deal; his daughter takes after him. He is the most Shavian character in the play, not so much because of his comedy but because he shows us, in the lightest way, what in the real world Morell is up against.

Laurie Paton is admirably sour and put-upon as the overworked typist (who decides, when finally given the chance to find out, that she has taken the pledge for beer but not for champagne), and Todd Witham is pleasingly ineffectual as the curate.

HIS MAJESTY

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

Drama is an obdurate medium, maybe a reactionary one. It likes kings, and has rarely succeeded in making heroes of republicans. It has, to its credit, no time for dictators or demagogues. Also, with rare exceptions like Henry V, it prefers its royals to be unlucky; in the interests of tension or pathos they have to be predestined losers (Richard II or Oedipus) or successful villains who finally get theirs (Richard III or Macbeth).

As monarchs themselves get thinner on the ground, so do non- escapist plays about them. Maybe the last to be written by an Englishman was Harley Granville Barkers His Majesty. It was also Barkers own last play (composed between 1923 and 1928) and, unless they decide to give stage-room to a couple of leftover oddments, the concluding item in the complete cycle of his work that the Shaw Festival embarked on in 1988, and that is one of their finest achievements.

Barker is never likely to knock his old mate Shaw off the perch of his own festival since he was neither as funny nor as prolific, but he may well have been more sensitively intelligent, and he certainly comes off as less complacent. His Majesty makes a great capstone. Never staged in its author's lifetime, and only once between then and now, it tumbles off the shelf far more approachably than did its predecessor The Secret Life. In fact, it's as fine and dense a political play as the 20th century has to offer.

It may also be the only good play ever written about an imaginary king, though its protagonist does have historical models. His Majesty, whose given name is Henry, is the deposed monarch of Carpathia, a country whose name sounds rather too cosily Ruritanian, but which seems to be standing in for Austria-Hungary. Kicked out after the First World War, he now resides in Zurich, raising chickens and keeping a gloomy eye on events at home.

The government there is presided over by a pedant-bureaucrat called Madrassy, who survived any number of upheavals by running the Ministry of Education for a succession of regimes that hardly knew they had one. Now it seems his luck may have run out; he faces challenges both from more radical elements within his own party and from a royalist insurrection without.

The king agrees to be flown into Carpathia (by a freelance English pilot), accompanied only by his wife and an unobtrusively invaluable aide. Henrys self-imposed mission is to prevent as much bloodshed as possible. He says he will stay if hes wanted, leave if he isn't. What's more, he means it; he truly believes in the dignity of constitutional monarchy. His queen, more of a traditionalist, wants him to stay, whatever, and she intrigues behind his back to bring this about. There is a dizzying series of alliances and counter-alliances, and people do get killed.

In Neil Munros production the first act, set in a Swiss hotel, is fidgety, marred by some nagging, weightless performances. Things pick up, and the play itself seems happier, when we move to Carpathia: first to a devastated chateau, home of a countess who is both the queens oldest friend and the mother of the rebel leader, then to a becalmed railway carriage which serves both as the king's headquarters and as his prison. It is also the site of a conference involving all interested parties.

This begins the play's second half, and from the moment the lights rise on half a dozen men around the table -- some of the more mysterious and significant with their backs to us -- we are away, in a massively textured world of realpolitik, slippery as ice, thick as mud. And we learn all over again why kings are so theatrically useful. The pressures of a nation are easier to summon when they bear down on one man who may relish the responsibility or loathe it but who is -- in every sense -- constitutionally unable to deny it. Even to abdicate is to make a royal gesture.

Barkers king is a mixture of urbanity and heroics. David Schurmann, who plays him here, is perfectly at home with the first quality and rises firmly and unfussedly to the second. His performance is, in its own terms, faultless, but the terms are familiar. This, for the Shaw Festival, is easy casting, but the play might benefit from an actor who could make the characters choices seem harder, and who could take us beyond regret and into agony.

A couple of years ago Schurmann played the equivalent role in Shaw's The Apple Cart, a play confessedly indebted to this one, but with the crucial difference that Shaw's king is not just intelligent and humane, like Barkers, but politically clever; he is a winner, which makes his play much slighter. (Theres far less at stake in it anyway.) The two performances, though, are identical.

Similarly, Michael Ball, who was a mixture of ally and antagonist in The Apple Cart, is in a similar position here as Madrassy. He too does all right by his own lights, and by his own sounds, which are those of vocal cords encased in whiskers, but one longs for an interpretation with less of the bumbler and more of the knife-edged pedant.

There is plenty of dead-on work at various levels: from Ben Carlson, who puts a rocket under the play as a right-wing Che Guevara; from Lorne Kennedy's unobtrusively resourceful Colonel; from Richard Farrell as another colonel, now demoted to caretaker and an expert at chess and munitions; from Dylan Trowbridge as a delightfully faceless (and virtually silent) officer; and from Roger Rowland as a farmer who, one scholar has observed, bursts on near the end like the asp-bearing clown in Antony and Cleopatra, both heralding and delaying tragedy.

There is also George Dawson, as a fascist-in-waiting who has been compared to Hitler but here comes on more like Goebbels, invincibly slimy. It is more than unfortunate that Munro has cut an exchange in which he recalls a former life blacking the boots of the king and his friends and reveals that he had been sent to prison for "optimism ... belief in the brotherhood of man, adding, I'm quite cured." Little time has been saved, and a whole dimension of the play -- perhaps its most chilling -- has been lost

The finest performances come from the women. Mary Haney as the queen schemes, bullies and -- in memorable silent agony at the end - - suffers with equal conviction. Sharry Flett is better than I have ever seen her, as the countess who goes in the play from one loss to another, and communicates grace through all of them. Their first scene together -- re-establishing an old relationship in drastically new conditions -- goes very deep. Also leave us not forget Severn Thompson as the countess daughter, an incipient partisan who already has the beret.

Most rewardingly, the play gets us into a world in which we can be moved by the feelings of respect or horror inspired by a monarchs fallen sword, even if the monarch has had to borrow the sword for the occasion. We can also see its absurdity. This is not one of the Shaw's perfect productions, like The Return of the Prodigal or Detective Story or Candida, but it winds up being as exciting.

Black & White Photo: Andree Lanthier, Shaw Festival / David Schurmann as the titular Henry in what may be the only good play written about an imaginary king. ;

A MIDSUMMER NIGHTS DREAM

High Park, Toronto

In theory A Midsummer Nights Dream is my favourite play. My affection is obviously shared by a great many other people, since I have yet to get through a year in this job without being required to attend a new production. If it isn't a Stratford spectacular, it's a bare-bones Equity showcase; if it isnt Kate Lynch trying out an all- female cast at Theatre Passe Muraille, its the Dream in High Park celebrating its 20th anniversary by bringing back the play that gave it both birth and a name. And if it gets increasingly difficult for me to see the play fresh and whole, it seems equally hard for directors and actors to convince me that they have. We're all haunted by the ghosts of past productions.

The ghosts can be laid; the Lynch ladies last year had me listening intently and delightedly to every line. The new Dream is conventionally shred-and-patchy, despite its publicized attractions of being both gender-bent and colour-blind. The first category of liberation consists solely of the casting of Alison Sealy-Smith as Pita (formerly Peter) Quince. Spelling apart, there's nothing about her performance, or even her costume, to suggest that she isnt sportingly playing the man as a man. (But do the clown scenes work as well with an actress in this role as they might with an actor? They dont. The dynamic between the characters is spoiled. Men behave differently when a woman is around, even when they outnumber her five to one.)

Racially mixed the show certainly is, though in a play whose characters are ethnically neutral to begin with (they're either fairies or Elizabethans with ancient Greek names stuck on) this hardly impinges. When it does -- when the actors translate occasional lines into what one assumes are their native dialects -- the device falls on its face. (It isn't like the French characters in Stratfords Henry VI periodically going into French, that makes a dramatic point.)

Musically, the show features a lot of homemade percussion, and this works better. When Bottom calls for the tongs and the bones, he gets the pots and the pans. Scenically, it affects a simplicity that turns out to be rather cumbersome. The multi-tiered permanent set looks like a Jungle Gym, and its very handy when the lovers start chasing one another. Things that look like hollow tree trunks are lowered from aloft, to provide hiding places for whatever immortal schemer happens to be standing underneath. Characters are painstakingly strapped into flying harnesses. It all seems to be a revolt against a realistic tradition of staging the Dream that hasn't existed in decades. Tricks are tricks, even if the audience can see how they're played, and these just slow up the action. Besides, we are watching this pastoral play in a park, surrounded by genuine trees. You can hardly get more naturalistic than that.

Richard Greenblatts production is full of ideas, but few of them go anywhere. We start with intimations of a police state. Theseus and Hippolyta make their opening nuptial speeches from an upper level and over a P.A. system, as if their wedding were a political charade. Threatening guards hold back the populace who are down on the ground floor as befits the lower classes. But they show no signs of being oppressed when we actually meet them, while the happy couple exhibit no signs of incompatibility whatsoever. Thats in performance; who knows what tension there may have been at rehearsal when the groom discovered that his bride was going to appropriate many of his lines, chiefly (do I hear a feminist axe grinding?) the more benevolent ones. This robs Theseus (Sanjay Talwar), never a complex figure at the best of times, of his one chance of development, from impassive figurehead to merciful prince. It does, though, rescue Hippolyta from her usual fate of standing around looking either adoring or resentful, so there may be a cosmic fairness about it.

Actually these two characters get their best breaks in a scene from which they are usually absent. It generally escapes notice that, in their initial slanging match, Oberon and Titania each accuse the other of having it off with their mortal opposites. In this production we see Theseus and Hippolyta, both presumably having had a last pre-marital night in the woods, drugged -- or maybe just exhausted -- in the trains of their fairy lovers. It makes an impression; and it pays off in the benediction sequence at the end of the play, when Oberon and Titania single out their old flames for special blessing.

That first fairy quarrel is the best scene of the evening, Oberon perched at the back of the auditorium in gold mask and cloak, looking and sounding like Darth Vader with a makeover. Walter Borden goes on to play the rest of the role in the same vein. Wake when some vile thing is near, hissed amiably into Titania's ear, is about as friendly as he gets, and it's a wonder that so malevolent a figure should take such a kindly interest in the fates of the lovers. He does show momentary signs of lightening up when he gets to the lyrical passage that begins "we are spirits of another sort" but then pulls back as if saying this isnt me. The production obliges him by cutting the rest of the speech. Maggie Huculaks Titania, initially promising, fades rather literally into the background, only recovering to register both shock and inhuman amusement at the thought of her dalliance with a mortal.

A boy, Adrian Morningstar, is a lively if unmodulated Puck. The mechanicals are very unfunny; one of them has a stutter, which I think tells all. Robert Perschini, with his buttery solemnity, should have been an excellent Bottom, and he has been given a fine ass's head (with tail extra). It deserves to make its first entrance from the centre rather than being hustled on from the side. He only comes to life when he acts Pyramus at the end, doing it with deadly and rather touching seriousness; as, even more effectively, does Matt Bois as his tragical Thisbe.

There are some nice touches in the lovers' scenes, especially the arrival in the forest of the lost Lysander and Hermia, scanning a map and wearing Mountain Co-Op knapsacks. Michelle Polaks Hermia is a very determined girl who at bedtime banishes her lover firmly to the far extremity of a very wide stage, and who is also good at karate. You never saw a maiden in less need of protection in the woods. Helenas startlingly modern line "she was a vixen when she went to school" rings very true. The fourfold brawl, as usual, goes on for too long with too much slapstick. But there's a treat at the end of it once the onset of darkness coincides exactly the fall of night in the real world. The Shakespearean foresight is staggering.

THE WINTER'S TALE

Premiere Dance Theatre

- - -

This has been an extreme week of Shakespeare. From A Midsummer Night's Dream to The Winter's Tale, from actors in High Park bellowing against the breeze to actors snugly indoors at Harbourfront, gently taking us and one another into their confidence.

Joseph Ziegler's Soulpepper production of The Winter's Tale is beautiful, but uneven. In style it probably owes something to the conversational chamber productions that Robin Phillips directed in the '80s for Stratford's Young Company (from which, eventually, sprang Soulpepper). It shows us characters exploring their emotions rather than flaunting them. This has its pitfalls.

From time to time, Tony Nardi, as the jealous Leontes, shouts. It's thrilling, and I'm unregenerate enough to wish he would do it more often. Leontes, the Sicilian king whose sudden jealousy of Hermione, his queen, and Polixenes, his best friend, comes near to wrecking everybody's lives, has some of the most complex, twisted verse in Shakespeare. Nardi, an actor who apparently has done very little Shakespeare, can shape it but -- except when he's at the top of his lungs -- he cannot colour it. So the poison that infects Leontes's mind becomes something we observe rather than something we feel; and his equally sudden acceptance of the truth and of his own guilt -- admittedly one of the hardest moments to bring off in the whole of drama -- lacks size and impact. Nor does Nardi seem all that interested in the penitent Leontes we meet toward the end of the play: a section in which the whole production goes slack before picking itself up for the closing epiphany.

That's the prosecution. The defence is that Nardi's performance is psychologically very acute. He even looks Sicilian (not that Shakespeare's comic locations count for very much) and from the start nurses an inferiority complex conceivably caused by his being shorter than everyone around him. He is a disaster waiting to happen; the wonder here is not that his jealousy breaks forth but that it has taken so long to do so. Once it has, it develops its own infernal logic. The more it's argued with, the stronger it gets; and Ziegler has been careful to devise groupings for its subjects that are innocent in themselves but inflammatory to one already enflamed. This Leontes is more psychological case than tragic-comic hero, but he's a very plausible case.

Soulpepper's two presiding actresses are at their best. I've never seen Susan Coyne do anything as fine as Hermione's trial scene; she too is quiet (except for her sudden cry "the Emperor of Russia was my father" which is proud and anguished at once) but with great variety and lucidity, and a radiant dignity.

Nancy Palk rattles the ears and heart as Hermione's champion, Paulina; confronting the king with his newborn child she virtually throws it at him, daring him to drop it -- a wonderful moment.

There is also work at court, of various degrees of sturdiness, from Oliver Dennis, C. David Johnson, Robert Haley and (strong casting in small roles) Jim Warren and Marek Norman.

Guido Tondino's sets are uneven. Sicilia is pictured with torchlit, if oddly Scandinavian, elegance, but taste abruptly departs when we reach Bohemia, where the sheep-shearing festivities take place in front of something resembling a large sheet of multi- coloured tinfoil.

The Winter's Tale is an audaciously bisected play that skips 16 years and changes countries halfway through its action. The greatest challenge for any director is to make the two parts seem like one, and Ziegler can't really make us remember in Bohemia what we've been through in Sicilia.

Our new acquaintances, though, are great company.. David Storch's Autolycus is the freshest, funniest and most inventive I have seen; the play acquires a new dimension when this quicksilver con-artist enters it, and Storch, perching on the edge of the stage to accompany his songs on country guitar, draws us right into it.

He has a fine lunk of a foil in Paul Thomas Manz's Clown, who in turn is set off by William Webster's shrewd and tender Old Shepherd. The pastoral love-duets, with Christopher Morris an unfortunately hangdog Florizel, go for almost nothing, but when she detaches herself to debate the rival merits of art and nature, Patricia Fagan's Perdita shows considerable spirit.

When Hermione, revealed by Paulina as a statue, comes back to life at the end of the play, her union with Perdita, her long-lost daughter, strikes deeper in this production than her reunion with her husband. At least, it does at first.

Through the evening, Ziegler has brought off a succession of visual coups, but strangely, the descent of Hermione from her pediment is not one of them; it makes less effect here than it has been known to do in far weaker productions, even though it has been handsomely set up and Coyne herself could hardly look more statuesque. Then, at the close, the characters are sent off in a chain, hand-in-hand. It looks weak until you realize that the order exactly mirrors their relationships. In the final moment Leontes and Hermione, believably middle-aged, are permitted an embrace; and this becomes a play about a marriage.

A CHORUS OF DISAPPROVAL

Premiere Dance Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - For sheer volume of output, Alan Ayckbourn long ago outran comparison with any other contemporary playwright. Unfairly, he is as talented as he is prolific. To find a match for him you would probably have to go back to the 19th-century novel, and especially to Balzac. Ayckbourn, too, though without himself slapping that label on it, has been assembling an ongoing Human Comedy, an amused, appalled depiction of a venal society at odds with itself: in his case, England from the late 1960s until now. With the exception of Bedroom Farce (a minor classic), the roster contains no outright masterpieces, but the canvas entire is an extraordinary achievement; once you've seen one or two sections of it, you want to collect them all.

Several of them are set in Pendon, an imaginary town whose location has never been disclosed but which it is tempting to identify with Scarborough, the North Eastern spa that has been Ayckbourn's base for years and where he runs a theatre-in-the-round where his own and many other plays get tried out. (Quite apart from his career as a dramatist, his record as a director, facilitator and encourager of other people's talents has been exemplary.) A Chorus of Disapproval introduces us to the Pendon Amateur Operatic Society (PAOS), who are engaged in putting on The Beggar's Opera. That link to a more canonical classic may well have been the cue for this new production by Soulpepper (they themselves are giving concert performances of The Beggar's Opera this summer), and the fact that the play was produced in London by the British National Theatre probably didn't hurt its chances either. Anyway, it occasions one of Soulpepper's best productions to date.

Ayckbourn likes playing games with time, and this show starts with a curtain call. PAOS are at the end of their first night, and the director steps forward to thank everybody, with especial reference to Guy, who stepped in at the last moment to play the leading role of Captain Macheath. Everybody applauds, then the curtain falls and Guy, turning to his fellow actors, finds himself the object of dirty looks all round. The rest of the play shows how he got there.

A Chorus of Disapproval isn't really a backstage play. It's less about a dramatic society than about a real society whose members -- some complacent, some insecure, and many mysteriously both -- are jockeying for position in rehearsal, just as they do in their everyday lives. The success or failure is not -- for us or for most of them -- a consuming issue. Backstage plays tend to be about professionals; I'm probably forgetting something, but I think this may be the first major play about amateur actors since A Midsummer Night's Dream.

The London production was nearly 20 years ago, and my memories of it are hazy, but Albert Schultz's production seems to have pushed the play more in the direction of a theatrical in-joke than did Ayckbourn's own. As before, songs from The Beggar's Opera itself are used to comment on the characters in the main story. A ballad about greedy lawyers reflects on the director, who in private life is a hopeless rather than actively crooked solicitor. The familiar "how happy could I be with either" follows -- though, in typical Ayckbourn fashion, it doesn't directly follow -- a scene showing Guy being fought over by two female admirers.

Soulpepper, though, go further and offer us whole routines. I confess to a slight queasiness at seeing skilled professional actors making fun of amateurs (as opposed to making fun of less skilled professionals, as in Noises Off) but the burlesques are so hilarious that I gave up worrying. There is also, reflecting Soulpepper's own status as established town favourites, a certain amount of self- satire. Nancy Palk wafts weightily about as a heavily pearled senior member, vocally insecure but financially impregnable, who -- in contrast to some of this actress' previous great ladies -- wants everything of Guy except his body. A speech recalling PAOS' disastrous production of The Sound of Music is all the funnier for being delivered by C. David Johnson, last year's Captain von Trapp at Stratford.

Schultz's production is a bravura success on every level. Cunningly and imaginatively staged, it also keeps the tricky balance between characters. This is a play with two male leads. There is Guy, who indeed is just a guy: a blank page on whom his new acquaintances can write whatever pleases them. Two married women -- one of whom has been having a lot of indiscriminate sex and the other very little sex of any kind -- throw themselves at him. He has a low-level job with a big company, and this leads three men (and their wives) to seek his help in a spot of insider trading. He makes no promises to anyone, but everyone assumes he has; meanwhile, he progresses from one role in The Beggar's Opera to another, ending up with the lead. David Storch makes him gently unassuming, and -- to his frustration as well as everyone else's -- as unknowable at the end as at the start. Or probably more.

This clears the space for Dafydd, the director, whom Ted Dykstra plays, entrancingly, as a Celtic mole with an enquiring stoop. He approaches the show with a professional commitment that he realizes to be somewhat ludicrous, given that his real job -- and his marriage -- are in tatters. A virtuoso scene shows him directing a lighting rehearsal while his wife and Guy, trying for a tryst, move in and out of the pools of illumination he insists on creating. As his spouse, Susan Coyne trumps her fine Hermione in The Winter's Tale -- a woman suspected by her husband and championed by everyone else -- with a beautifully detailed portrait of her exact opposite. Sharpness is her note: She is sharply frustrated, sharply angry and sharply in love.

Among the supports, Oliver Dennis gives great joy as an especially incompetent player, tiptoeing through his own zone of terror, with Denise Fergusson as the wife who protects him as well as she dares. I feel, as I always have, that the swinging couple (C. David Johnson and Nicole Underhay) are done with excessively broad strokes, and that the rich bore (Jim Warren) who decides that Guy is Scots and will not be told otherwise, can begin to bore us. But there is not a performance that is less than true or less than funny.

When he first emerged, Ayckbourn was routinely compared to Neil Simon -- on the grounds that they were both comic and both successful -- but the comparison has long ceased to make sense. Simon writes wisecracks, often very good ones; Ayckbourn comes up with a quotable joke. The funniest in this play is entirely a matter of situation, and it involves the person who hears it in depths of humiliation that Simon, as far as I know, has never plumbed; Ayckbourn being Ayckbourn, they are not prolonged.

Simon gives his characters little social or political context, and is therefore compelled, when he drops the clown's mask, to get mushy. Ayckbourn, the writer, hasn't a sentimental bone in his corpus. He can show suffering (and also embarrassment, a milder form of pain that is sometimes indistinguishable from it) and he never begs our pity for it. He can, sometimes though not in this play, be moving, but generally he is as unknowable as Guy himself, which can be frustrating. After all these years, he still confounds everybody's chief preconception about a commercial playwright: He tells no lies.

THE TWO NOBLE KINSMEN

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

- - -

STRATFORD - Theseus and Hippolyta are getting married, again, and, just as in A Midsummer Night's Dream, their progress to the altar is interrupted by a bunch of people asking favours. This time the suppliants are a trio of widowed queens whose husbands fell in the war of the Seven Against Thebes (read your Sophocles) and whose corpses, by decree of the victorious Theban tyrant Creon, lie still unburied. (Cf. Sophocles again.) The queens urge Theseus not to get married until he has put this right. His bride and her sister Emilia, who as Amazons know something about codes of honour, back the ladies up.

That's the first scene of The Two Noble Kinsmen. The second takes us to Thebes, where the title characters, Palamon and Arcite, both immaculate heroes, lament the state of their city but prepare to do their patriotic duty nonetheless. Battle is joined, Theseus wins, the kinsmen are captured and imprisoned, the bodies buried and the queens appeased. And at this point the action starts. What we have seen up to now has been mere prelude, a peculiarly luxuriant shaggy- dog story.

The Two Noble Kinsmen was published in 1613 as the joint work of John Fletcher and William Shakespeare, an attribution that most scholars have supported. It was left out of the First Folio, and only in the last 30 years have complete editions of Shakespeare begun routinely to include it.

Shakespeare wrote the first and last acts and one scene in the middle. It was his last writing for the theatre, and he seems to have been experimenting even beyond the corkscrewing verse monologues of Cymbeline and The Winter's Tale. The poetry this time is still more complex, but it's formal and outwardly directed, since the characters have no souls to search; they are figures in a chivalric story derived from Chaucer (who gets an unusually generous credit in the prologue). It's magnificent, but it is very hard to absorb in the theatre, and listening to those introductory scenes, in particular, is like groping your way through swathes of heavy silk.

It's a positive relief when Fletcher takes over. Palamon and Arcite, through their cell window, catch sight of Emilia and fall instantly, irrevocably, and almost simultaneously (not quite -- "I saw her first!" protests Palamon) in love. Immediately they are mortal enemies, trading insults in the same vein of high courtesy in which they once exchanged compliments.

Fletcher seems to have enjoyed taking them down several pegs, or maybe he couldn't help himself. He is -- at least in his comic mode - - a much underrated author, and still highly playable, sexually aware in a way that the Victorians thought decadent but now seems rather cool and funny. Sympathetic, too: There is a sub-plot concerning a Jailer's Daughter who falls for Palamon and sets him free (thereby anticipating the behaviour of future Jailers' Daughters from The Beggar's Opera to The Wind in the Willows), then, realizing she cannot have him, runs mad.

A program note suggests that the original audience would have found this a hoot. I doubt it. Did they laugh at Ophelia? (The echoes of Hamlet's girlfriend in these scenes, and of the Dream in some episodes involving a troupe of Athenian morris-dancers, are the clearest evidence that Shakespeare didn't write them; they're the work of an admiring but ambitious disciple.) The mad speeches contain some coded erotic truths. The Jacobeans would have laughed with the girl, not at her, and so do we.

We also like her a lot. She is saved when her doctor, a progressive mixture of psychologist and sex therapist, suggests to her workaday lover that he pretend to be Palamon. They live happily ever after, though under what identities remains unclear.

Obviously this is a play that Stratford should do, and Stratford, having waited for 50 years, has done it well: better than the Royal Shakespeare Company, which inaugurated its Swan Theatre with it, and which gave it a thoroughgoing Japanese appearance that merely made the play's own arcane conventions that much harder to get at.

There are samurai traces in the martial scenes here, but they are laid on lightly; the overriding style of David Gaucher's designs might be described as mixed heraldic. A sculptured horse's head protrudes provocatively from a pool, like the top half of a knight in some submarine game of chess. The set consists mainly of a forest of upturned spears, very suggestive when the scene is a forest, or indeed a prison, but distracting when the actors have to shoulder their way through it on other occasions.

The director is David Latham, principal of Stratford's five-year- old conservatory, and the cast is composed entirely of its graduates. They are a credit to the school, maintaining a high standard of liveliness and lucidity.

That is not to say they are all ideal. This is one of those plays with a built-in casting problem: Actors capable of meeting its technical demands are unlikely to be tempted by roles so thin. One would like to see Martha Henry, Seana McKenna and Domini Blythe parachuted in to lend proper weight to the bodeful queens. Colm Feore might make a superb Theseus, a role in which Jonathan Goad makes the common mistake of confusing authority with bad temper.

The verbal intricacies of Palamon and Arcite themselves might be unravelled by Graham Abbey and I'm not at all sure who else. The present duo, Rami Posner and Brendan Murray, seem to know what they're talking about in their first scene but can't communicate it. They improve immeasurably when they're given something immediate to act, alternating handily between the heroic and the absurd. (At least Murray does; Posner comes off rather sulky.)

The best in the main plot is Michelle Giroux's Emilia, whose voice drips with honeyed concern but whose demeanour is that of a Sphinx, as befits a heroine whose two suitors never think to ask her which of them she might prefer, and who doesn't seem to mind.

Deborah Hay, as expected, romps off with the play as the Jailer's Daughter, comic, pathetic, vulnerable and determined. She has great support from Michael Schultz as her shy Wooer; from Michael Therriault who does a whimsical double of doctor and schoolmaster, and who also delivers the prologue and epilogue with enormous charm; and from Thom Marriott as her father, a man-mountain with a lisp, at first sight a tyrannical clown but later a huge vat of concern, and not just for his daughter. Indeed, in there is a feeling of involvement from everybody in these scenes, both as actors and characters, and it's most welcome.

Fletcher's humanity softens us up for the return of Shakespeare, who proves as imposingly chilly as before, though more comprehensible. Palamon and Arcite fight a tournament for Emilia's love, the loser to forfeit not only his own life but those of his friends.

I don't know why Latham describes the sub-plot as "a dark strand." The darkness is all in this main action, with its kings and queens, knights and ladies, who talk of love but think only of death. A couplet that might serve as the play's leitmotif must haunt everybody who has read or heard it:

The world's a city full of straying streets,

And death's the marketplace where each one meets.

This is the last play of a supreme writer who was about to give it all up despite having three more years to live. There is no parallel renunciation in world literature.

HIGH GRAVEL BLIND / ETERNAL HYDRA

Studio Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

STRATFORD, Ont. - Stratford has its new Studio space, backing on to the proscenium Avon Theatre. Its stage is a full-size replica of the Festival Theatre platform -- steps, balcony and all -- but its black-box auditorium is much smaller, seating only 250. The theatre is intended for the unveiling of new plays and the investigation of unfamiliar old ones. This opening season is devoted entirely to new work, mainly short pieces presented in a series of three double bills .The first of these opened on Saturday.

"It is a wise father that knows his own child": that, reversing the usual proverb, was the conclusion of Launcelot Gobbo, the clown of The Merchant of Venice, after comically announcing his own death to the father who, "being more than sand-blind, high-gravel blind," had failed to recognize him. Paul Dunn, who was last season's Launcelot at Stratford, has written his own ingenious variation on this unlovable jest and called it High Gravel Blind.

His Launcelot, commonly known as Lance, is a Montreal ex- squeegee kid currently sharing an apartment, though not a bed, with Jessica, who makes something of a living as an artist -- more of one, anyway, than Lance, who is flunking bartender's school. Determined to better himself, Lance, to Jessica's unreconstructed Bohemian horror, puts on a three-piece suit and goes out in search of work. Or he would, if he didn't suddenly have visitors. At the door are Gord, the father who abandoned him as a child and has now come from Calgary to seek him out, and Margery, a born-again Christian and Gord's new wife.

Gord is the only character not to be named after a Shakespearean counterpart, probably because Shakespeare never told us Old Gobbo's first name. Jessica was of course the daughter of Launcelot Gobbo's employer Shylock, and Margery was the name of Old Gobbo's offstage wife. To complete the symmetry, Richard Monette, who directed Dunn in The Merchant, directs his play here, and does an excellent job. The play, though, is no pastiche. It goes off on its own track.

Chances are that Gord wouldn't recognize Lance even if he were in his usual gear, but the sober-suited young man he beholds is so unlike the pathetic figure he expected that he is completely thrown. Lance, having gone to unprecedented sartorial lengths to begin a new life, is less inclined than ever to confront his old one. He says that Lance is dead, and that he himself is another roommate called Rob. So the four characters sit down to discuss the departed.

The scenes that introduce the two couples are commonplace, but when the four get together the play combusts, an especially cheering progression for a young author whose previous play (for Theatre Direct) was a monologue. The situation is that of Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? -- its last act, anyway -- turned inside out; instead of an imaginary child being treated as real, we have a real, visible one debated as if he no longer existed. In many ways this is a more interesting situation, and certainly a more poignant one.

Booze flows less freely than in Virginia Woolf, since Gord is a recovering alcoholic who has reached the apologizing stage. He has a lot to apologize for, and Stephen Ouimette's tight-reined performance turns out to be the play's motor. Cunning games are played with our sympathies. We are inclined to be on Gord's side since he is on alien and bewildering turf, and a cruel trick is being played on him. But we come to see that Lance may have reasons other than fear and selfishness not to acknowledge this particular parent, who explodes internally at the realization, never quite articulated, that his son is/was homosexual. Nor can we ever be quite sure how close Gord may be to proving the wise father and knowing his own child and how much he too may be playing a self- protective game. (There is a running metaphor about clothes making the man; Lance is the creature of his own new suit, and Jessica, professionally, makes masks.)

Part of us wants to see a reunion between father and son; another part dreads a resolution so potentially sentimental. How it actually turns out I must not say, but I can promise that the ending is honest. Most of the play's comedy resides in Chick Reid's bustling Marg; Lance and Jess are well handled by Damien Atkins and Kimwun Perehinec.

The second play, Anton Piatigorsky's Eternal Hydra, is theoretically more adventurous and practically a lot less effective. It deals with the death -- in fiction, anyway -- of the fixed, solid character and the reliable authorial voice, ideas that seem a lot more provocative in the program notes contributed by the author and his director, Andrey Tarasiuk, than they appear on the stage.

Gordias Carbunkle, whose surname may signify eiher a jewel or a boil, was, we are told, a high-modernist author of the school and the stature of James Joyce. He left behind an unpublished masterpiece, long thought lost, which has resurfaced in the custody of Vivien Ezra, a scholarly custodian of Carbunkle's work and reputation who, as scholarly custodians will, has become fixated on her own idea of her subject, and even holds imginary conversations with him.

She takes the book to Randall Wellington, son and heir of Carbunkle's old New York publisher, who is less enthusiastic than she expected but offers to peg publication to the issue of a new novel, by a rising black female author, that just happens to have Carbunkle as one of its characters. Of course, her Gordias is not Vivien's Gordias, and Vivien demurs, while the-Carbunkle-in-her- mind stands at the side of the stage, begging her not to blow his last posthumous chance. It's a protracted, stationary scene, and all we really learn from it is that publishing, especially of old and difficult books that have not had the chance to age into classics, is not the gentlemanly business it once was, which most of us already knew.

The play's second, better half transports us to 1920s Paris (this, like High Gravel Blind, is a tale of two cities) to meet the real live Carbunkle, exploiting everyone with whom he comes into contact, especially if they're women. We meet two of these, who bear strong resemblances to the two we've already met, and the pattern is completed by the appearance of the senior publishing Wellington. We learn, again, that a talented man can also be a bastard, and that he can know it. This last factor makes him fairly compelling.

Ouimette, moving from Gord to Gordias, seems none too happy hanging around in the first scene as a thing in his archivist's dream, but he perks up considerably now, standing before a full- lenth mirror and inspecting himself with corrosive contempt. And so we see that Vivien's idealized view of Gordias is far from being the only one.

I seriously wonder if it took the advent of modernism, or the complications of post-modernism, to persaude people that human beings act and are seen differently in different companies. I even more seriously wonder, readers being adaptable creatures, whether the unreliability of the authorial voice is a matter of consuming interest to anyone except other authors. But then I'm a philistine; I once took part in a radio discussion of The French Lieutenant's Woman, in which the authorial voice was the only thing anyone else would discuss, while all I wanted to talk about was what a page- turner it was.

Meanwhile, back in the theatre: The solid, three-dimensional character may be a thing of the past, but the flash of personality remains the thing that keeps an audience awake, and this play flashes only intermittently. The supporting roles, all doubles, are played by Karen Robinson, Chick Reid and Paul Soles, in that order of effectiveness. None of them really pulls the words off the page, but then they are actors, not weight-lifters. Still, nobody expects seasons of new plays to be uninterupted triumphs, and if this is as bad as it gets, we'll be doing all right.
