RICHARD III: REIGN OF TERROR

Avon Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

STRATFORD, Ont. - Tom McCamus as Richard III seems, mockingly and insinuatingly, to be delivering the opening speech about the winter of everybody's discontent from the wings of the blacked-out stage. Gradually, lighting appears, and we realize that though his voice was indeed miked, he himself had been present all the time, curled up in one of the recesses of a steely and very built-up set, all stairs and alcoves.

Richard, we know, enjoyed sending his enemies to the scaffold. This Richard likes nothing better than to hang around on scaffolding. He also likes to curl up in trees, and there are several provided, all bent and weathered, not to say withered, rather like Richard himself.

The cluttered design (by Allan Wilbee) has its uses, especially for the leading actor -- the bottled spider of mad Margaret's curses has been given his web -- but it forces his colleagues into a series of deferential semi-circular groupings. This gives Martha Henrys production an old-fashioned air that its general intelligence and inventiveness hardly deserve. Its a relief all round when most of the architecture disappears, as it does for the last section depicting the protagonist's downfall. The trees remain, and they look increasingly like gallows.

The note of mischievous malevolence struck by McCamus (as indeed by Shakespeare) at the beginning of the play is maintained and expanded. This Richard is graphically and painfully deformed, and though he has learned to cope with his disabilities they are always liable quite literally to trip him up. He falls from his perch during the opening speech, and it is not a happy landing. Much later, at his coronation -- the moment of triumph he has shed so much blood to achieve -- he stumbles and falls. Many in the audience laughed, so I suppose that statistically the moment may be said to misfire, but I found it chilling; the actor has by now established the character as a man for whom humiliation is only a spur to more revenge.

He is not an especially charming Richard, but charm in this role may be an overrated quality. Those who are duped by him want to be duped, and there is a sizeable contingent, led by his own mother, that mistrusts him from one end of the play to the other.

Some waver. One of the play's subtler achievements is its observation of the way in which court alliances form and dissolve, according to the dictates of the moment. Magnetism -- a teeth- baring insistence that fluctuates between grin and grimace -- he has buckets of. He also has a Mick Jagger swagger. He can play the indulgent uncle at generous length, taking the future Princes in the Tower for extended piggy-back rides on his hump at dangerous speeds. One of the boys even gets to play, prophetically, with a dagger that Uncle Dick keeps hidden in his shoe, for emergencies. Its existence seems to be common knowledge, since in the last battle Richmond pulls it out and kills him with it.

McCamus is good at depicting Richards growing hysteria as his enemies close in on him, his mind audibly accelerating out of control. What he misses out on is stature, and I dont mean the physical kind. Laurence Olivier once said that at some point Shakespeare tells the actors of even his most wayward kings, "drop that -- you have to be St. George." He had the cornered Richard II especially in mind, and it never occurred me that the St. George rule would also apply to Richard III, who is all dragon.

But it does. At the close he is required to act like a king, first a guilty king, then a defiant one. McCamus' Richard doesn't have this in him (though McCamus himself probably does), and the last speeches, admittedly pretty stiff as written, go for nothing. They have, in fact, been heavily cut, and some of the plays power leaks away with them.

As it happens, Henrys editing of this long text is unconventional throughout. The execution at Pomfret of Rivers, Vaughan and Grey never seems to happen, though their ghosts turn up at the end, presented effectively as holograms (as are all the other ghosts). On the other hand, we do get to see scenes of backstairs intrigue and backstreet discontent that are generally excised and here prove worth the beholding.

The production moves fast but it never obliterates the actors. It's still fashionable -- probably it always will be -- to deride the general acting level at Stratford, but really we don't know what we have. This is a crack company, and everyones a person.

Scott Wentworth dies two fine deaths in two successive scenes: First as a superbly spoken Clarence, then as a fulsome voiced Edward IV, whom the news of his brothers murder dispatches at a stroke. (He seems, as far as I could tell, to have a stroke.) Peter Hutt is a bluff, rather disreputable Buckingham who makes the fatal mistake of thinking he can match his master, sick joke for sick joke; Wayne Best gives an interestingly equivocal Hastings, loyal to his late king to the extent of inheriting his mistress; and John Dolan makes more than most of the time-serving Stanley, though less than is there for the making.

The weeping queens, with Lally Cadeau's Duchess as their Mother Superior, are first-rate. Diane D'Aquilas Margaret is less a character than an ambulant voice of doom, but shes a powerful and economical voice. It might have been helpful to have Seana McKenna, who plays Margaret in this season's Henry VI plays, bring that biography with her into this one. (The "Reign of Terror" subtitle is designed to bring Richard III into line with the Henries, which have been given similar handles, but with the lack of continuity in other respects, I doubt that anyone will notice.)

Still, if McKenna had played Margaret, we would have been deprived of her striking Elizabeth, who begins as a self-pitying tippler, wallowing in incipient widowhood and then, when she has lost everything, grows up. The scene in which Richard, desperate, begs for her daughter's hand in marriage and in which she fools him into thinking hes succeeded, is the high point of the play, as these days it often is. Thats ironic, since it used to be denigrated, or even cut, as a mere reprise of Richard's celebrated coffin-side seduction of the Lady Anne (a scene that here lacks steam). In fact, it's far subtler and more satisfying, a duel instead of a walkover. Its the beginning of Richards end.

The end of that end is here very graphic, and it rhymes with the opening of the play. Richard is hanging head-down from a tree, only this time he's the naked and the dead. This is not far from the way in which the historical Richard's body was treated after the Battle of Bosworth. Its triumphal from one point of view, disgusting from another.

Graham Abbeys Richmond has been a stocky and mercifully unstuffy saviour; most unhistorical, since the real Henry VII was an extremely devious piece of work, but it's what the play the needs: a St. George who doesn't insist on his status. He's likeable, Richard is fascinating. You take your choice.

Until Aug. 4. 416-872-1111

FRANK -- A LIFE IN SONG

Bluma Appel Theatre

- - -

I have never seen the point of having a performer devote a whole evening to imitating another performer, especially when the one imitated is a singer whose authentic work is still easily available. Tom Burlinson's Frank -- A Life in Song does nothing to shake my skepticism.

Burlinson is an Australian (though born in Canada) who dubbed the singing voice of the younger Frank Sinatra in the biographical TV series that aired in 1991. Burlinson's voice was certainly a very close fit.

He has now expanded this impersonation into a full-length stage show in which he sings cornerstones of the Sinatra repertoire, from All or Nothing at All to New York, New York, and makes with the gestures as well. He captures the elusive Sinatra timbre unusually well, and he carefully copies as much as he can of the phrasing; his mimicry is at its most confident at the beginning of a song; but he tends to lose both tone and conviction at the end of a phrase: a problem that the original never had.

At best, though, it's a party-trick, good for perhaps two or three songs. The show is presumably aimed at Sinatra fans (who else would care?) but this fan, at least, wants none of it.

There are three levels to the Sinatra repertoire. First, and most importantly, there are the masterpieces of American popular song, songs that would have been classics even if Sinatra had never touched them, but are unquestionably the better for his attention. Burlinson gives us several of them. But these numbers -- I've Got the World on a String, I've Got You Under My Skin, Night and Day and (to a lesser extent) You Make Me Feel So Young -- offer infinite possibilities for interpretation; why would a singer want to limit himself by reproducing what another singer, however gifted, has already done with them?

Then there are the songs -- mostly written for Sinatra by his on- call team of Sammy Cahn and Jimmy Van Heusen -- that are good but only survive by virtue of his association with them: The Tender Trap, Come Fly with Me, All the Way. These, by and large, are the ones Burlinson does best, maybe because they will always sound like an imitation Sinatra, whoever does them.

Finally, there are the songs that nobody, including Sinatra, should ever have sung in the first place. My evening was shadowed from the start by the certain knowledge that, at some point in it, Burlinson was going to sing My Way. In fact, he saves it till last: a valedictory position in which it sounds even phonier than usual. Burlinson has not been doing it his way, he has made a point of doing it someone else's way. But he cannot claim to be doing the song in character either. This show is being mounted in a theatre, but it is almost totally lacking in dramatic content.

When Burlinson talks to us between songs, he does it solely in his own person. He seems an agreeable enough young man (or youngish - - he's 45) but the script he has given himself is atrocious. Purporting to be a casual barebones biography of Sinatra (whom he insists, gratingly, on referring to as Frank), it sounds like a bad magazine digest with no relation to normal human speech.

It is also stuffed with familiar anecdotes that the knowledgeable will be able to see coming a long way off. (Fair's fair; he does come up with a charming Sinatra quote about Johnny Mercer that I'd never heard before.) There are only two sequences of relief. One is a quick enumeration of Sinatra's good and bad personal qualities; the other, very near the end, comes when Burlinson talks, unpretentiously and with a modicum of wit, about Burlinson, or rather about his own fascination with his subject. In both of these there is some personality and the evening begins, belatedly, to make some sense.

His choice of songs is depressingly obvious. Sinatra's greatest achievement was his exploration and elevation, through album after album, of the American songbook, a legacy that extended far beyond what are accepted as his signature songs.

Burlinson, oddly, steers away from the few Sinatra recordings that might be considered directly autobiographical (Nancy, I'm a Fool to Want You, the entire September of My Years collection) but he sings only one song that would not immediately be tagged as "a Sinatra song"; it's Nevertheless, quite effectively linked to the breakup with Ava Gardner, and sung winsomely and well.

Indeed, Burlinson seems at his best on ballads; the contemplative tempo forces the performer to think through the lyrics, even if the thoughts he comes up with are another man's. One for My Baby remains moving, even at second hand.

In the up numbers, though, he is going, rather too enthusiastically, through somebody else's motions, physical and vocal, and so comes off like any other Vegas clone. When the supreme style and confidence of the master are lacking, the swingin' style becomes rather repellent.

Burlinson has good assistance from a pair of dancers, Aaron Cash and (especially) Mandy Carnie; their jitterbug routine is a treat. Even more of one is the sound of the original Sinatra arrangements (sans strings) played by an onstage big band.

Indeed, the evening becomes less a tribute to Sinatra than to Billy May, Quincy Jones and, above all, Nelson Riddle; their work, after all, was meant to be relayed to us by other people. Sinatra once said that he wished somebody else could learn to do what he did, so that his art didn't die with him. I doubt that he meant he wanted others to copy him; rather that he wanted them to sing popular songs as inquiringly as he did but on their own, equally independent, terms. In this context imitation, like other forms of flattery, is a betrayal.

Until Aug. 3. Box office: (905)-815-2021 robertcushman@lycos.com

MACBETH

Coronation Park, Oakville, Ont.

OAKVILLE, Ont. - The theatre by the lake, about whose natural charms I rhapsodize every summer, is mounting its first tragedy. The fall of night in an open-air theatre can always be counted on to supply second-act magic: a huge bonus when the play is a comedy. In Macbeth, of course the magic is required to be black, and nightfall proves up to the job. The background plashing of Lake Ontario, generally soothing, now sounds disturbing: the elements going unshakably about their business while humanity implodes. Meanwhile, the productions own thunder effects come on very strong.

Nature doesn't help the play much in other respects. Michael Shamata has more experience of this space than any other director, but he hasn't found much use for it this time. The green expanses between water and stage remain untravelled. Hopes that the invading English army might arrive by boat and then march down through the trees, merging with them to suggest that Birnam Wood could indeed be coming to Dunsinane, are not realized. Even the one tree at the centre of the acting area finds only a couple of roles for itself. Banquos murderers lurk round it. Lady Macbeth poses against it while beseeching the spirits, with a graphic gesture, to unsex her here and fill her up with cruelty. The spirits, incidentally, fall down on the unsexing part. Colombe Demers, both in her own right and in her relation to David Jansens Macbeth, is one of the most sensuously compelling Lady M's I have seen.

The central couple, at least as seen here, are death ships that pass in the night. He starts as a professional soldier, never more at ease that when caked in blood but with certain scruples about shedding it off-duty. When kingship is the prize, she is the practical agent who shows him the way to get it and makes sure he comes through. She would like, once the family firm has achieved its objective, to get out of the killing business; and she is mystified, even horrified, by his persistence in it. He is now the slave, not just of his own bloodlust, but of his own imagination, which keeps summoning new threats and new victims. (So she, when guilt takes hold, walks in her sleep and talks prose. He stays awake, and is a poet.)

The scene after Duncan's murder is the productions first turning point. He is appalled by his deed, but has already surrendered to it: high on blood. She, as she admits, has to get drunk to get through it; her reserves of determination are already beginning to be depleted. What keeps her going is her habit (marriage-long, presumably) of standing by her man. When he goes beyond her -- when he ostentatiously plans the death of Banquo without involving her -- she is devastated. With this groundwork laid, her remaining scenes of banquet and breakdown practically play themselves.

I wouldnt call Demers the most underrated actress in this part of Canada -- she gets good reviews and even award nominations --but she may, in proportion to her talent and versatility, be the most underused. Her high-comic work in A Flea in Her Ear and The Game of Love and Chance was exceptional, and here -- with a sulphurous voice, and wearing a stunning succession of gowns, formal and otherwise (she goes from beige to red to black to white -- far more variety of apparel than anyone else is permitted) she has every moment of her character's progress nailed down.

Jansen, in a far more alarming role, is less consistent. His baby- faced tyrant is best at suggesting a spiritual solitude. Remote at the start, even when receiving congratulations from his fellow- thanes, he is untouchable at the end, in a different world from everyone around him. He is less good at communicating what he sees there. He is at excellent at briefing Banquo's murderers, from whom he keeps a controlling distance; he is not the man to convince us that he actually sees Banquos ghost -- whom the production, prosaically and unwisely, refuses to produce.

This Macbeth ends up as a study in the banality of evil, ordering the slaughter of Macduffs family without a flicker of emotion; I suspect Shakespeare had something more excitingly demonic in mind. (He isn't helped by the fact that the real demon seems to be his servant Seyton, who doubles, among other things, as the Third Murderer who lets Banquo's son get away. You begin to wonder if hes doing this on purpose, playing a double game with the future royal family. Macbeth already gets double-crossed by the witches; he really doesnt need further competition in evil from his own entourage.)

The cauldron scene is effectively smoky, with one of the Three Weirds acting as medium for the prophetic apparitions; she is also apparently pregnant, the devil knows with what. (It is the character, not the actress, who subsequently appears as Lady Macbeth's gentlewoman, devoid of bulge.)

There is a good drunken Porter (Paul Fauteux) who briefly steals the show without stopping it, as is proper. Glyn Thomas does well by Banquo's lurking suspicions, as does Allan Hawco by Macduffs reeling bereavement. Malcolm (Philip Riccio) suggests a promising actor in need of basic Shakespearean training. He is involved, though, in the productions most rewardingly original moment: Duncan (Peter Elliott, who returns after death to do all the other old men) names Malcolm as his heir and teases out the announcement, just long enough to keep Macbeth in suspense and then tip him further over the regicidal edge.

The male characters wear shirtsleeves and leather jackets. This gives an unassuming air of modern-dress-by-default that is perfectly acceptable until you notice that the soldiers among them have guns in their holsters. This hardly fits the play's imagery, so famously preoccupied with daggers, and it makes the battle scenes look very odd. You feel that these guys would shoot first and ask rhetorical questions afterwards.

UNCLE VANYA

Du Maurier Theatre Centre

- - -

To caricature, but not by much: Most productions of Chekhovs Uncle Vanya concern a group of perfectly sweet, civilized people whose lives are wrecked by a selfish and pompous loudmouth, generally referred to as the Professor, who just happens to hold their fates in his hands. In Laszlo Marton's triumphant Soulpepper production (revived from last season), both sides have been reappraised. Robert Haley's Professor, a much improved performance, never obviously bullies anyone, never even shouts; he may indeed be the quietest person onstage.

Chekhov doesnt let us get a good look at this character until the second of his plays four scenes. He is briefly glimpsed in the first, but our knowledge of him is largely dependent on the testimony of others, and especially that of Uncle Vanya himself. Vanya, who has devoted most of his life to managing the Professor's estates, resents him for many reasons: his first marriage to Vanya's beloved sister and his second to a beautiful younger woman desired by Vanya himself; his literary reputation; his overall personal and professional success, as painfully compared to Vanyas own personal and professional lack of it.

Thats how Vanya sees it. When we get to spend some time with the Professor himself, we find he's a fretful hypochondriac, and as prone to self-pity as anyone else in the household. Certainly, he's selfish, and probably his books and articles (on "realism and naturalism and all that nonsense") are as useless and derivative as Vanya, once his blinkered fan, now declares them to be; but at least hes written them. For the first time in my experience, the Professors plan for selling off the estate, thereby giving everybody some money and a rest, sounds rather sensible. This doesn't let him off the hook. It's still clear by the end of the play that he is the only character incapable of feeling other peoples pain as well as his own. But at least hes allowed to have a case.

It isn't all gain. Some humour goes, and so does a sense of controlling malevolence: His refusal, issued from off stage, to let his daughter Sonya and her stepmother, Elena, celebrate their new- found friendship with some late-night piano-pounding does not come, as it has in other productions, like a blow in the face. But it does allow the other characters, all given flamboyantly full-blooded performances, the dignity of responsibility for their own suffering: a suffering that, most cruelly, refuses to kill them.

The play's last act finds Diego Matamoros Vanya, having failed - - twice -- to shoot the Professor, curled up, fetus-like, refusing to surrender the morphine he has stolen from Albert Schultzs Dr. Astrov: the man he suspects, groundlessly, of supplanting him in Elena's affections. (In fact, Astrov has merely got a little closer than his rival to first base.) The developing dialogue between these two actors has been one of the great achievements of Soulpepper's five year-history, and this current duet is a summit.

Astrov and Vanya confront one another now, brothers in futility, but dealing with it in different ways. Astrov, partly by virtue of his job and his passion for forest preservation, is the more active of the two, and the angrier. Schultz, in what seems to me more than ever to be his best performance, has ratcheted up the rage and bitterness since last year, even letting it inform the brisk environmentalist lecture he gives to Elena; he anticipates her boredom before she even declares it.

Matamoros, heartbroken and heartbreaking, sinks into his sulks. He has already lost most of his dignity in attempting to assert it. (Its telling that the Professor runs from him, not like a man in fear for his life, but like a man hiding from the club bore.) Now he has to surrender the final remnant along with the morphine. It liberates him in a sense; he goes back to his old hard-working life. But that in itself is a sentence.

The awareness of failure is Chekhovs constant subject, and he was to give it more complex symphonic treatment in The Three Sisters and The Cherry Orchard, but in Uncle Vanya, where the pain is distributed among a smaller domestic group, it hits harder. This is a play in which two adult characters, in rapid succession, appeal to a parent for understanding, and are ignored. It seems here like the most moving -- as opposed to depressing -- play ever written.

Kristen Thomson deepens and widens her study of Elena as a woman who for every tentative step forward takes several terrified steps back. Liisa Repo-Martell completes the central quartet as a notably unsaintly Sonya; all the characters in this play judge and blame one another and Sonya, for all her charity, can be as sharp-tongued as any. She may overdo the dowdiness; Sonya is in love with Astrov and, as American critic Eric Bentley once pointed out, we should feel that in turning her down he is, in very Chekhovian fashion, missing something. But she contributes greatly to the production's sense of place. This, in Michael Levine's superbly cluttered setting (which features a floor strewn with books, and a naked light bulb on a string), is a remote mud-caked Russia, in which people get desperately and uproariously drunk.

Marton, a Hungarian, gets us away from the genteel English- speaking Chekhovian tradition -- and also, to be fair, from the genteel Russian-speaking Chekhovian tradition; the Moscow Arts Theatre, at least after the revolution, was a privileged museum of bourgeois pleasures. The physicality of this production may or may not be especially Slavic but it is certainly exhilarating. Think of Matamoros love affair with furniture; he hides in it, and virtually makes love to a chair, caressing it as he fantasises about comforting Elena during a storm. Or think of Thomson, at her last moment, leaping into Schultzs arms, and him lifting her off the ground, when it's too late to do either of them good or harm. The supporting cast remains good, with Carolyn Hetherington, the only newcomer, an astringently understanding nurse.

MY FAIR LADY

Festival Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

The Stratford Festival's continuing cycle of American musicals effectively began in 1986, with a production of The Boys from Syracuse, Rodgers and Harts vaudevillean adaptation of The Comedy of Errors. The leading roles of the twin Antipholi were entrusted to two actors who might have been cast in the same parts had Stratford elected to do the original Shakespeare play: the companys two reigning juveniles of the day, Colm Feore and Geraint Wyn-Davies. Neither was known as a singer, but this score gave them testing romantic ballads to get through. The critics at the time expressed pleased surprise at how well Feore sang and sympathetic disappointment at how well Wyn-Davies, despite the triple Welshness of his name, didn't.

Sixteen years on, the two actors, both now valued commodities in the world outside and hence largely unavailable to Stratford, have returned to the Festival and to musicals. This season's production of My Fair Lady (also with classic lineage and a show that, unlike Syracuse, treats its source as an object to be venerated rather than gleefully plundered) opened with Feore playing Professor Henry Higgins. Wyn-Davies has now succeeded him in the role, and in the vocal department things seem much as they were. Feore may have been the most full-throatedly musical enry iggins in 'istory.

Wyn-Davies returns to the tradition, inaugurated by Rex Harrison and honoured by nearly every actor since, of pattering his way through the numbers. He is also less impish and acerbic than Feore, and far less impulsively energetic, but he brings far more lyrical fervour to the phoneticist's passion for the English language. Cuddly in his cardigan, where Feore was angular, he is surprisingly reminiscent of Kelsey Grammer in Frasier. Now, there would be a Higgins, pride just galloping for a fall; and he can sing. So, too, I believe, can his Daphne, Jane Leeves, who of course is English, and working-class English at that. (Northern, not Cockney, but I assume she could do both.) Of course shes too old for Eliza, but so is nearly everybody whos ever played her, with music or without, all the way back to Mrs. Patrick Campbell in the first Pygmalion.

Stratford's Eliza, Cynthia Dale, is of course not English, and certainly not Cockney. You feel the professor should be objecting, not to the ugliness of her vowels, but to their strenuous inaccuracy.

Admirably unfazed by the change in leading men, she has sharpened up Eliza's assertive and rebellious side to great comic and dramatic effect, in speech and especially in indignant mime, but she cant translate it into the more formal medium of song: Just You Wait, her impotent dream of revenge, is near to excruciating. (Not entirely her fault; the middle section of this song has some of the awkwardest lyrics the gifted but uneven Alan Jay Lerner ever penned.) In the gentler fantasy of Wouldnt It Be Loverly, though, where accent is a lot less important than mood, she is enchanting, as is the whole show, with special credit to Donna Feore's wistful choreography. At this point, Richard Monette's suave and captivating production lets us know exactly why we are watching the musical rather than the play.

Barry MacGregors Colonel Pickering remains a robust and amusing tower of strength. As Mrs Higgins, the musicals other guardian of decency, Joyce Campion deposits each of her pearls of wit and wisdom daintily and infallibly in the audience's laps.

Until August 11. Box office: 416-978-8668

ASSEMBLYWOMEN!

Hart House Theatre, Toronto

Greg Robic is a Canadian playwright, scholar and lyricist who a few years ago had a substantial and well-deserved hit with an oddball satirical musical based on Aristophanes' The Clouds, staying faithful to the originals structure but replacing its comic choruses with puposefully anachronistic lyrics fitted to familiar (i.e. out-of-copyright) opera and operetta tunes. He followed it up with a similar show derived from the same old masters Lysistrata. Now the two of them are back with their third collaboration which Robic has called Assemblywomen! Aristophanes called it Ekklesiazusai, and though I have even smaller Latin and less Greek that Shakespeare was once credited with, I believe that Robic's title is a fair translation. The play usually turns up in English, on the rare occasions it turns up at all, as something like Women in Parliament. This was a pretty revolutionary notion in ancient Greece, and it might even have rattled a few ears in 1918 Canada, which is where this production, for reasons that remain mysterious, purports to be set.

This time around, Robic has felt confident enough to propose himself a vote of thanks. A first-act song, listing the requirements for success in civil society, admonishes us "make sure you can quote all the plays of Greg Rouc." All? There have only been three. This kind of supposedly charming self-aggrandizement (there's a lighting- change to underline the daring deliciousness of it all) is premature; and though many in the first-night audience obediently fell about, I didnt. Aristophanes himself may have gone in for this kind of thing, but he had a corpus; even his surviving plays get him into double figures, and there must have been many more that are lost. Besides, he invented comedy. More importantly: even at this early stage -- especially at this early stage -- it was obvious that unlike Clouds (I cant speak for Lysistrata) Assemblywomen! wasn't going to work.

In looking for someone to blame, we should first go back to the source. As Robic himself has pointed out, the kind of comedy Aristophanes invented isn't our kind; it wasnt even the kind practised by the next generation in Greece. Down through the millennia stage comedy, whether satirical or romantic, has been about logical plot-lines and boy getting girl. The older kind lives on in revue, cabaret and early Marx Brothers; Duck Soup may be a greater Aristophanic masterpiece than anything by Aristophanes. Its an honourable tradition, but hard to revitalize over a whole evening in the theatre. Aristophanes started with an idea, and then spun out variations on it. It could be a great and subversive idea: most obviously so in Lysisatra where the women go on sex-strike until their husbands give up war. But even that one isn't developed; it's just repeated or -- when the author gets tired of it -- forgotten.

The original Assemblywomen (sans exclamation-point) must have struck even the Athenians a as a tamer re-run of Lysistrata. Here, the notion is that the women, led by Praxagora, tired of the self- glorifying and self-enriching antics of the all-male legislature, steal their clothes and, thus disguised, induce the assembly to dissolve itself and vote in a female government instead. Its typical of the author that the men, supposedly hobbled by having only their wives dresses to wear, still make it to the assembly first; the cross-dressing tactic, elaborately set up, is then dropped and only resurrected for a single self-contained scene. By most standards this is slapdash dramaturgy, but of course Aristophanes wasn't operating by most standards. The trouble is that the satirical points he makes, here at any rate, aren't sharp or novel enough to make us see things his way. We merely discover that the conventional wisdom that politicians are corrupt buffoons was equally conventional (and equally wise) 2,500 years ago. It is not a surprise. And the 1918 seating is, literally, neither her nor there. All you can say for it is that it does show us the women wearing the trousers.

Even Aristophanes felt something was lacking, because in this -- his last extant play but one -- he goes soft on us, as if nervous about attracting a young audience. In his second half he offers something approaching a love-plot. Praxagoras reforms include the abolition of money, free food for all and -- the one idea thats developed -- complete sexual liberty except that the young and beautiful have first to satisfy the old and ugly. (This may be the earliest, and potentially most far-reaching, instance of positive discrimination on record.) Praxagora's husband, Blepyros, formerly the loudest mouth on the Acropolis, is now plotting against her regime. They meet, both in disguise (they have their reasons; they also have masks), and most heavily fall for one another. However, both of them are firmly in the Attractive camp, and I'm sure you can work out the complications for yourselves. The situation certainly has some piquancy but it is quite remorselessly spun out.

At this point Robic and his director Marc Richard have to shoulder the guilt, or, more appropriately perhaps, face the music. My happiest memory of Clouds is of a wonderfully irrelevant number lampooning megamusicals and somewhat reminiscent (to put it tactfully) of Ya Got Trouble from The Music Man. Apart from its comic and lyrical merits, it came as a great relief in its American breeziness from the sedate European airs that made up the rest of the score. There is no equivalent number here. (The revelation that Bring Him Home, from Les Miserables, is lifted from Puccini, is no compensation. We still have to sit there and listen to the bloody thing.) The music here is taken from Donizetti, Sullivan and such, and it is very well sung by all concerned. But the numbers take a long time to sing, they repeat themselves, and there is a laborious archness about them that infects the whole evening: writing, performance and staging. Robic has a great fondness for polysyllabic humour. It works well when set to music, or at least to this kind of music. Between songs it just sounds pedantic.

Elizabeth Beeler acts fairly wittily, and sings spectacularly. Leo Wigglesworth, mobile in face, voice and body, is the obstreperous Blepyros. Lawrence Cotton is agreeably grumpy, leading the chorus in the first act and subsiding into it in the second. There are a couple of very good laughs. But the whole evening seems to be spoofing itself without having a self to spoof.

VAREKAI

Ontario Place, Toronto

People are saying that Cirque du Soleil's new show is uneven. They're right. Varekai, the Cirque's 14th spectacle, fluctuates between the merely amazing, the frankly unbelievable and the outright sublime.

Sublimity arrives early, in the production's take on the myth of Icarus (Anton Chelnokov), who here falls to Earth in the middle of a forest inhabited by a motley medley of beaked, winged and hooded creatures. What better protagonist for the Circus of the Sun than Icarus, who flew too high and had his wings fatally singed? This one, luckier than his classical prototype, survives, but is captured and trussed up. He is then hoisted aloft, and performs a breathtaking acrobatic dance, winding himself in and out of the net that constrains him. The moment at which he first seems to be throwing it from himself is ravishing. As visual poetry it beats anything in The Lion King.

It is matched, much later on, in a number billed as Aerial Straps. A black-clad figure, hanging on wires from his wrists, breaks to one side and is revealed to be two; he has a double, poised exactly behind him. The image of a person multiplying before our eyes is extraordinary. Hardly less remarkable are the synchronized pyrotechnics that the pair, all leathers and feathers, proceed to execute. (They are from England, of all places, and bear the impeccably public-school names of Andrew and Kevin Atherton.)

The Flight of Icarus is lyrical, Aerial Straps sensuous; the closing routine, Russian Swings, is a rumbustious fireworks display. A whole troupe of Russians (plus one Ukrainian and a Moldavian) perform on a matching pair of swings, one at each side of the stage. So far, so unsurprising, until the ever-widening arcs described by these liberated Slavs begin to reach 180 degrees. They then start to use the swings as trampolines, bouncing from one to another or landing in the folds of the huge circus tent. Again, you would expect nothing less from such accomplished swingers, but the heights to which they jump, and the complexity of the manoeuvres they execute while airborne (I still don't believe the scissor-kicks) and the sheer numbers involved become intoxicating. Don't try this in the playground.

When Cirque du Soleil, as one of the foundations of its identity, forswore animal-acts, it made an aesthetic gesture as well as a humanitarian one. Plenty of daredevilry remains, but watching the Cirque's routines you find yourself thinking not, as at any other circus, how dangerous they are but how beautiful. Some other items are almost on a par with those already described, notably a Georgian dance that shows what traditional Cossack steps would be like if executed by a small group of whirling dervishes. Even the more mundane acts are prodigiously charming, the trio of rope-twirling Chinese children billed as "Water Meteors" being charming prodigies as well. A juggler (the Mexican Octavio Alegria) does wonderful tricks with hats and sprays billiard-balls out of his mouth.

There are also clowns: a necessary evil in most circuses but a bonus here, a necessary change of pace and texture. A buxom libidinous soubrette (Mooky Cornish) makes audience participation a pleasure. Her male counterpart (Claudio Carneiro) is both her tormentor and her victim; he reaches his particular hell in an attempt to sing Ne Me Quitte Pas while chasing a spotlight that insists on doing just that. This too is an old gag, but it's made funny by having the torture carried to relentless lengths: at last, the Samuel Beckett musical, a man reduced to a robot. This couple also figure as a Papageno-Papagena Magic Flute subplot, against the more heroic love-interest of the principal figures.

I suppose I should have mentioned this earlier, but the show itself is late in getting round to it. Icarus encounters a woman (Olga Pikhienko) who does a graceful contortionist act on canes. He rescues her and they get married. It's hard to take much personal interest in them -- after all, we hardly know them -- and the two governing figures of the forest who seem to control their fate are similarly cryptic.

Also somewhat Mozartean, they are, according to the program, the Guide (Rodrigue Preteau) and the Skywalker (John Gilbey), benevolent and malevolent respectively; the latter, despite his title, wears a miner's helmet and resembles an outsized glow-worm.

The show may not add up as narrative, but nobody will be going to it for the story anyway. It is astoundingly colourful, thanks largely to the costume designs of Eiko Ishioka, and wonderfully lit by Nol van Genuchten. The set, designed by Stephane Roy, features a steep and perilous staircase that threatens to ascend into infinity but in fact culminates in an especially daunting catwalk; surprisingly little is done with it but along with a wilderness of poles, it makes an imposing background for an expanse of beautiful space. The score, a world music stew concocted by Violaine Conradi, pounds not only excitingly but helpfully.

Varekai, we are told, is the gypsy word for "wherever," and the impenetrable tongue into which the performers occasionally break may conceivably be Romany as well; I prefer to think of it as Cirquish. Only two of the cast of 50 -- the Guide and the lady-clown -- are Canadian, but the show is still recognizably ours in spirit, or at least recognizably Quebec's; directed by Dominic Champgane, from Montreal, it belongs to the same luxuriant streetwise culture as Robert Lepage. Cirque du Soleil is now one of Canada's greatest exports (there are currently eight different shows running across the world), and in its welding of international talent into a unified whole, it represents us at our best. Traditional circuses are multi-ethnic too, but in them the various acts go their individual ways; here there is unity, if not altogether of theme, then of energy and goodwill. At the end the entire company join in the swing celebrations, and joy, like the hero and heroine, is unconfined. Anyone who does not break at least a dozen times into spontaneous applause while watching this show, and who fails to stand and cheer at the end, is not to be trusted.

THE LUNATIC, THE LOVER AND THE POET

Tom Patterson Theatre

When Brian Bedford was a drama student in London in the 1950s, his classmates included Peter O'Toole, Albert Finney and Alan Bates. They were regarded as a golden generation almost before they were out of school. It says something about the British, and also the Canadian, theatre that of them all Bedford is the only one to have realized his potential as a classical actor, and that he had to come here -- or at any rate chose to come here -- to do it.

He is one of the world's three most accomplished Shakespearean actors, along with William Hutt and Ian McKellen. We really should boast about this more.

Bedford's one-man show, The Lunatic, the Lover, and the Poet is a distillation, and occasional expansion, of the Shakespearean work he has done since coming to Stratford in 1975.

He gives us extracts from many of the roles he has played there, and a few he hasn't. The scenes and speeches are arranged roughly in their presumed order of composition, and are linked by terse biographical narrative. (Bedford never speaks in the first person, either as Shakespeare or as himself.) The idea is that the writings reflect their author.

Sometimes, the connections seem simplistic, and Bedford probably leans too heavily and literally on the Sonnets as a key not only to the playwright but to the plays. The trajectory -- youthful exuberance, tragic disillusion, mature recuperation -- is one that the Victorians would have recognized, with their maps of the Shakespearean journey from "the Heights" to "the Depths" and back again.

That doesn't make it wrong. The stress on personality is academically unfashionable, and has been for decades, but everyone knows it's the right approach; not even academics actually believe that an author's identity is irrelevant, shameful or (the latest wrinkle) non-existent. And there is a frame here; the evening is never "and then he wrote."

Bedford's Shakespeare is fashioned to his own shining strengths as an actor: intelligence, wit and unsurpassed lucidity. He can get his mind and his tongue around anything. His Shakespeare - in this respect very unVictorian -- is a metaphysical poet, a theatrical John Donne, for whom ideas, compulsively explored and fastidiously juggled, are a conduit for emotion.

He starts, unexpectedly, with the sober Prologue to Henry VIII: unexpectedly, since the play may be Shakespeare's last and is certainly one of his least-known. It's revealing that Bedford should have chosen this, rather than the more flamboyant and open address to the audience that kicks off Henry V.

The Henry VIII speech doesn't appeal to our imaginary forces; it asks us to shut up and listen. It soberly ticks off what we can expect and what we cannot, and tells us to pay attention "for goodness sake." That's the emphasis that Bedford gives it, and the precision is absolutely typical; it banishes the phrase's colloquial familiarity, and restores its moral edge. He gives us the speech as a series of polished rounded sentences. After promising us tragedy (which he later delivers), he concludes "if you can be merry then, I'll say/A man may weep upon his wedding day," a jab that he infuses with a wonderfully mellifluous disdain.

He is at this moment the dapperest of lounge-suited actors, though by half-time the jacket and tie will have come off. He now starts talking about Shakespeare's early years, and makes the reasonable inference that the players who passed through the English Stratford were the inspiration for the barnstorming amateurs of A Midsummer Night's Dream: cue for his generously self-absorbed Nick Bottom, whose Yorkshire accent is a tribute to Bedford's own youth.

He gives us the saintly Henry VI, helplessly envying the life of a shepherd; "how many years a mortal man may live" jumps out at us with a desperate shudder. More provocative is his suggestion that Shakespeare's shotgun marriage to Anne Hathaway was the bitter source, years later, of Prospero's obsessive concern for his daughter's pre-nuptial virginity. It makes sense.

There are obvious gaps in the account of Shakespeare's progress: no mention of how political changes and literary fashions may have affected his work, and no Falstaff. There are also gaps in the subliminal account of Bedford's progress. Some of his most notable Stratford roles -- Richard III, Shylock, Benedick, Timon -- are missing, and I wish he had given us his Angelo from Measure for Measure rather than his Duke.

But we do re-encounter his Richard II, more sacramental and less of a tease than I remember, and his Malvolio; and see him sliding into beauty as Oberon, a role he has never played and still could. He also gives us Romeo's "soft what light through yonder window breaks" and reminds us that it is a speech made up of wordplay. The words come out as being about Romeo himself rather than about Juliet, which suggests that Bedford, a self-torturing rather than a natural romantic, would not have been good casting even when the right age. It is nevertheless fascinating to hear him scrupulously hunting down the images and securing every one of them.

His Hamlet, which he played in Liverpool at 21, must have been very exciting; he now has the nerve to offer us the most hackneyed soliloquy of all, "to be or not to be," to think it freshly through and to make us do the same. There is similar chutzpah in his reinvention (a different voice for each of the seven ages) of Jaques' "all the world's a stage."

As our predominant actor of Shakespeare's intellectuals, he must play Ulysses in Troilus and Cressida. And of course Lear, in whom the mind turns against itself; he here offers a note-perfect account of the great world-levelling scene at Dover cliff, an inviting sketch that one would love to see fitted into a full portrait. He passes from this directly into Macbeth's ashen "tomorrow and tomorrow and tomorrow" which he accurately interprets as the lowest of the depths. That brings us up to Prospero, another role that's waiting for him. "Our revels now are ended," loosed from its apocalyptic moorings in The Tempest, becomes a lyrical set-piece, but the great renunciation makes amends.

Finally, brilliantly balancing his admonitory prologue, he does Prospero's reclusive epilogue. In this he is at once the character acknowledging his dramatic situation, the author acknowledging the limits of his art, and the actor asking for applause. Without either tipping or overplaying his hand, he triumphs as all three.

2002-08-10-tale-of-two-theatres:
Robert Cushman is the National Post's theatre critic and the author of Fifty Seasons at Stratford (McClelland and Stewart)

For a Toronto-based theatre critic, summer used to be time off. Not any more. There is the Fringe and then, treading uncomfortably close on its heels its junior cousin Summerworks: each so stuffed with short-run events that some of us retire in confusion, not knowing where to begin, we never begin at all. There are open-air Shakespeares, more of them than ever, in parks in and around. There is Soulpepper, which has transformed the summer landscape.

Thats just in town. But for decades now the twin theatrical hubs of Southern Ontario have been the classical festivals, Stratford and Shaw, one named after a place, the other after a playwright. We take that for granted now but its rather odd. Of course, if the Shaw billed itself as the Niagara Festival, people might get confused. Would that be Niagara-on-the-Lake (as it is) or Niagara Falls? They're both tourist towns anyway, even without the theatre. If you tell somebody that you're taking a trip to Stratford, they will generally assume that youre going to see a play. With Niagara, theres always the possibility that you're going for the surrounding wineries or for the golf. Then again the name Stratford, worldwide, implies Shakespeare; and even though the festival dispensed long ago with the Bardic monopoly, you will nearly always find more Shakespeare at Stratford than you will find Shaw at Shaw.

This is a historic year for both festivals; that is a factual statement, devoid of value judgments. Stratford's season is its 50th. The Shaws marks the retirement of Christopher Newton, after an unprecedentedly long and successful reign as artistic director. Newtons achievement has been to establish a strong but flexible artistic identity in a town that often looks and feels as if it were built out of fudge. (People do live in Niagara-on-the-Lake, but it's always a puzzle, when one walks down the main street, to imagine where they can shop.)

As is well known, the Shaw Festival's policy -- not a mandate, since a mandate by definition is something youre handed by somebody else, and the Shaws choice was all its own -- has been to present plays written by Shaw himself or by other playwrights during Shaw's lifetime; as he lived for nearly a century, this is a fertile, and still accessible, field. A couple of years ago, this was amended to include plays set during that period but written after it. This year sees the first notable beneficiary of the extension: Chaplin, a play about the comedian written and performed by a long-standing member of the company, Simon Bradbury.

In fact, the Shaw has always been fairly liberal with its chronology. A case in point is its production this year of the Stephen Sondheim musical Merrily We Roll Along. This was written in 1981, and its action covers the period from the '50s to the 70s. (Or rather from the 70s to the '50s; it is, notoriously, told backwards.) So, even under the new rules, it doesn't qualify. But its based on a 1930s play by the classic Broadway team of George Kaufman and Moss Hart, so it squeezes in under the wire. The same is true of the Shaws previous two musicals: The Mystery of Edwin Drood and She Loves Me: By their sources shall ye admit them.

The Shaw Festival has a unity that does seem to radiate out from its titular figure. It explores a defined area of the repertoire, from the popular to the obscure, though avoiding the extremes of both. The masterpieces and the pot-boilers are given equal consideration -- they seem to be cut from the same cloth -- and there is an overall quality of inquiring urbanity that seems to derive from Newton himself. Three of this season's productions are his. Noel Coward' s Hay Fever, Newtons valedictory show, brings back Fiona Reid, an accomplished Coward comedian and a long- standing festival favourite. St. John Hankins The Return of the Prodigal, a deserved hold-over from last year, shows Newton and his team at their best. It's an Edwardian social drama with a satiric edge, and the practiced Shaw ensemble has all the skills it takes to play it; Ben Carlson and Blair Williams, two of the finest of the festival's younger actors, dig especially deep into the fractious but curiously understanding relationship between black-and-white- sheep brothers. The Shaw has just completed a largely triumphant cycle of the plays of Harley Granville Barker, culminating this year with the taxing but rewarding His Majesty. It is possible Newton will return as a guest to direct a similar series of Hankin. Heres hoping.

Newtons last production of Shaw at the Shaw is Caesar and Cleopatra, given a modern-dress treatment that somehow seems more persuasive in the program notes than it does on the stage. Otherwise, the patron-saint is represented by Candida, a play as compact as Caesar is sprawling. The production -- by Jackie Maxwell, Newton's designated successor -- is a good augury, since it makes an absorbing job of a play that can often be dull. It ranks at the top of this year's Niagara openings, along with the Prodigal and two productions by the long-serving Neil Munro: His Majesty and Detective Story, the latter an American genre piece that looks and sounds, like much of this directors best work, like film noir made flesh. Its also crammed to overflowing with vivid performances; sometimes one takes the excellence of the Shaw's regular players for granted, but this production is a reminder of what a priceless collection they are.

The Shaw, at least under Newton, has accumulated actors incrementally and held on to them greedily. It is rare there (except sometimes in the musicals, which make special demands) for a player to come in from outside to assume a leading role. It's likelier to happen at Stratford, where the continuity is real but more diffuse. This 50th year, in particular, is an occasion for continuity, retrospect and innovation.

One of the seasons two hottest tickets is King Lear, which brings Christopher Plummer, the Festivals first home-grown leading man, back to Stratford Shakespeare after an absence of 25 years, in a Canadian production by that most affable of British cultural legends, Jonathan Miller. The other is My Fair Lady, with Cynthia Dale as Eliza, and Professor Higgins played in succession by three more old Stratford heroes; Colm Feore played it at the beginning of the season, Geraint Wyn-Davies is currently in possession; he, in turn, will be succeeded by Richard Monette, director of the festival and of this very handsome production. Monette's acting appearances are even rarer than those of his Niagara opposite number Chris Newton (the two were Stratford juveniles together, decades ago) and this one is awaited with especial eagerness.

Monette is also responsible for an uncharacteristically austere staging of All's Well that Ends Well, with William Hutt, Stratfords undisputed doyen, as the King of France and Lucy Peacock as the medically gifted heroine Helena. Alls Well was one of the two plays presented at the first Stratford Festival; the other, Richard III, also gets a commemorative revival this year, directed by Martha Henry and with a chillingly funny lead performance by Tom McCamus. Those who wish to brush up on this history play's pre-history (always a problem in a piece where people keep referring to previously slaughtered princes, every last one of them called Edward) should brush up on the three Henry VI plays, which this year have been re-divided into two, subtitled Revenge in France and Revolt in England. In fact, they should be seen anyway since they offer a chance to see rare and exciting plays, vigorously and imaginatively done. An even rarer Shakespearean opportunity is The Two Noble Kinsmen, long regarded as apocryphal and delightfully done by young graduates of the festival's conservatory program. Contrastingly un-rare, but straightforwardly exciting, is this years Romeo and Juliet, directed by Miles Potter and with Graham Abbey and Claire Jullien as the lovers; Abbey, a past Henry V and presumed future Hamlet, does an especially winning job in a traditionally treacherous role.

Shakespeare dominates Stratford -- this year especially -- but does not set the tone in the way that Shaw does at the other place. Stratford can theoretically do anything, though it doesnt have the resources of a year-round national theatre that could systematically explore the world repertoire. (The best national theatres are, in practice, international theatres.) The line-up this year is more eclectic than ever before with the addition, to Stratford's established three theatres (Festival, Avon and Tom Patterson) of a new Studio space, long wished for and now opened -- to everybody's amazed delight -- exactly on schedule. Its stage exactly mirrors the Festival Theatres wonderful platform, but its auditorium seats only 250. It was planned as a showcase for new plays and rare classics. Retrenchment in the wake of Sept. 11 has removed the second plank of that program from this years bill, but the new plays are there in force: seven of them, of which six -- including a piece by the late Timothy Findley -- are presented two at a time. As I write, only one of these double-bills has opened; and its first half, High-Gravel Blind, an inventive riff by actor-playwright Paul Dunn on themes noticed when he was acting in The Merchant of Venice, is an auspicious start.

Stratford looks a more liveable place than Niagara. It is also a more edible place, the site of Ontario's greatest culinary explosion. The pioneering Church Restaurant, which transformed a previously dismal gastronomic landscape in the 1970s, how has an array of competition: the beloved Old Prune, the world-class Rundles, Pazzo, which offers excellent pizzas in the basement and haute cuisine appropriately above, and -- hidden coyly away in a shoppingstrip -- the sparky new Bijou. Elevated food is less easy to come by in Niagara (though elevated prices aren't) but either town, judiciously sampled, offers all the elements of a good time.

HAY FEVER

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

- - -

NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE - The Shaw Festival production of Noel Coward's Hay Fever has, most unusually for this play, a sombre beginning. Be reassured that it has a screamingly funny middle and end, but that opening is dark: literally.

Young Simon Bliss, son of the bohemian household in which the play unfolds, has drawn the blinds in order to contemplate a drawing of Lawrence of Arabia he has just completed. Sorel, his sister, reads a poem that Simon, justifiably, pronounces morbid. Actors playing this scene usually offer their lines half to the audience and half to the ghost of Coward, whom they are trying to appease by appearing as brittle and disembodied as possible. This couple, by contrast, are discontented young people having a conversation. They are setting up the rest of the play, to its great benefit, rather than filling in time before the arrival of the leading lady.

That lady, leading in all senses, is their mother Judith, the 1920s West End actress of sentimental melodramas (specimen title: Love's Whirlwind) gone into premature retirement and trying, with more enthusiasm than conviction, to conquer the role of country- house chatelaine.

Her husband, David, writes best-selling romantic novels of less than dubious quality (specimen title: The Sinful Woman). Judith never left the theatre in spirit and may soon return to it in reality: Meanwhile, the world is her stage, or at least the Thames Valley is. And it's catching. Sorel, the family member with the nearest approximation to a conscience, notes that "one always plays up to mother in this house; it's an unwritten law."

In Christopher Newton's production (his valedictory offering as the Shaw's artistic director) the differing degrees to which the clan members obey this law are very carefully marked out. The comedy's famous hook is that each individual Bliss has, without telling the others, invited a guest of the opposite sex down for the weekend. Partner-swapping ensues, wholesale but chaste, and worked out by the author with mathematical precision: The guests depart early, having been variously bruised, abused and -- most humiliating of all -- ignored. David is unselfconsciously, and Simon very self- consciously, exploitative. Sorel fights to be nice, or at least to be what the world calls normal, but she too gets sucked into the narcissistic whirlpool.

As Judith, Fiona Reid, like Seana McKenna in last year's Stratford production of Private Lives, displays the endemic tendency of Canadian Coward actresses to end up sounding exactly like Maggie Smith. Or rather, McKenna ended up that way, while with Reid it's an inescapable starting-point. This is initially disconcerting, but she goes on to carve out her own territory.

Smith's specialty is the comedy of alarm: Reid can do that, but what she gives us here is the comedy of wilful self-confidence; a woman whose dramas are her own invention, to be acted out strictly under her own direction. She enters from the garden wearing the kind of hat that might have provoked the French Revolution. Once launched into action she turns, repeatedly, on a dime. Having inveigled a helpless diplomat into kissing her, she cries out without missing a beat that "David must be told," and really does seem to believe that she is behaving, as she herself prescribes, with "absolute honesty."

She has at least three other moments for the anthologies. Speaking of a woman who "goes around using sex like a sort of shrimping-net" she irradiates what I have always thought a pretty vapid attempt at a comic line by topping it off with a brief illustrative mime. Remarking that "David's been a good husband to me, but he's wearing a bit thin now," she in effect ignores the comma, taking the line on one breath, treating the second half as a climax rather than an afterthought, and bringing down the house. Later, she discovers that same husband in the arms of another woman. According to Coward's stage-direction she observes them from the top of a staircase (a commanding staircase is de rigeur in a Coward play, and William Schmuck, the Niagara designer, duly provides one) and then comes down. Reid does nothing so commonplace. She is halfway down, by the normal method, when she sees them and executes the rest of the trip by coming down the banister in a sliding slump.

Michael Ball, in his best performance for several seasons, is sleekly self-absorbed as David, a mixture of lounge lizard and hermit crab. Mike Shara, who is cornering the Niagara market in willowy dilettantes, adds Simon to his collection, and Severn Thompson is Sorel, her fastidious intentions curdling into the most aggressive rudeness. (The director sees her development as the backbone of the play. It's apparent on the stage as well as in his program note, though maybe not to the decisive extent that seems to have been intended.) As in The Return of the Prodigal, one of the joys of Newton's production is the believability of this collection of monsters as a family. They belong together.

Hay Fever, famously, has no real plot, but it sure as hell has construction. For a play that its author claimed virtually to have improvised, it interlocks superbly. One thing leads, imperturbably but explosively, to another or, even more devastatingly, fails to. (The Blisses are better at furnishing cause than at recognizing effect: They seem to have invented collective amnesia.) A scene is provided for each possible male-female couple. Note the word "possible"; after the necessary expository scene at the top, no two Blisses are ever allowed to be alone together, because they would have nothing to say.

Among the victimized visitors here, Laurie Paton is sharp as the vampish Myra, the worm who comes closest to turning, and Kevin Bundy engagingly clueless as the sporty Sandy. He spectacularly initiates a running gag in which each of the guests in turn gets scorched by a breakfast hot-plate. This, breaking the oldest rule of comedy, is funny four times over: five, if you count the practised ease with which the Blisses themselves, hands wreathed in napkins, handle the situation.

This production defuses the complaint, once voiced by an English critic, that "the bores are more entertaining than the Blisses." This has its drawbacks; David Schurmann's diplomat and Lisa Norton's flapper make amazingly little of their embarrassed non-conversation on whether bullfights are crueller to horses or to bulls. Both warm up later. Note to old Shaw hands: In this production Michael Ball plays what would normally be the David Schurmann role and vice versa. Everyone is the better for it. The one extra character -- Clara, the theatrical dresser turned all-purpose domestic -- is played, to grim-faced perfection, by Mary Haney.

THE OLD LADY SHOWS HER MEDALS

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

Even now, nearly a century after the event, we are soaked in the front line imagery of the First World War: the mud, the blood, the trenches. We hear less of what life was like for those waiting at home. Certainly there are few plays about it.

Its a strange omission, since this was the great recruiting poster war, the one that mustered men by threatening them with the contempt of their womenfolk if they failed to join up. So one would like to know how those women felt while they kept the home fires burning, especially when the casualty figures started mounting up.

J. M. Barries The Old Lady Shows Her Medals, this year's lunchtime show at the Shaw Festival, does something to tell us. It's a one-act piece that was first staged in London in 1916, dead- centre of the conflict. It is a play of acceptance, not of protest, though there is nothing to stop us projecting onto it our own feelings about the needlessness of that war and the reckless incompetence with which it was pursued. Soldiers die and their mothers grieve and are proud. That remains true, whatever side youre on.

Barrie, the author of Peter Pan, has become a byword for sentimentality. But the definition of sentimentality is emotion in excess of the object, and its hard to see how that could be the case here. (If you want a sentimental play on this theme, try Bertolt Brecht's The Mother.) Typically, though, Barrie has given his situation a sweet-and-sour twist.

His heroine is Mrs. Dowey, a Scotswoman working as a charlady in London. Her friends and co-workers all have sons at the front, and boast about them ceaselessly. They trace the progress of the troops by moving condiments about on the kitchen table, and try to trump one another with the proper pronunciation of the various battlefields. Mrs. Dowey has no son -- she isn't even really a Mrs. - - so she pretends. She sends letters and packages to a Private Dowey (of the Black Watch) whose name she once saw in the papers, and produces replies that she mailed herself and that are actually composed of blank paper.

The inevitable happens: Pte. Dowey, home on leave, arrives to call her bluff. He is angry. He is also, it turns out, as lonely beneath his swagger as she is: no family, no girl. So the fabricated mother-son relationship becomes real, until the soldiers time is up.

Todd Hammonds production is uneven. He uses the theatrical equivalent of jump-cutting to speed up the story toward the end, and that is nifty. He is less successful in trying to turn Mrs. Dowey's trio of friends into a silent chorus, who apparently have the run of her basement apartment at the unlikeliest of hours. The three actresses concerned -- Maria Vacratsis, Wendy Thatcher, Donna Belleville -- are, amusingly enough, the same who make up the cast of the similarly titled The Old Ladies in the Royal George's evening bill. They are fine -- Vacratsis especially -- in the later and more sympathetic of their scripted interventions, but are oddly muffled at the start.

I acknowledge that Canadian actors have more important things to worry about than getting their British accents right, but the general floundering here is most unusual at the Shaw. When Pete Treadwell's Pte. Dowey (a performance more stolid and unyielding than the script requires) claims that a Scots soldier can do anything, one mentally adds "except get the voice right." He could also make more of the character's sudden burst of song, later taken up by Mrs. Dowey. It should be a Moment. (It would go to the tune of Yankee Doodle.)

Even Jennifer Phipps, who is English, tends to begin her sentences Cockney, though she has always arrived properly north of the border by the end of each one. There, though, criticism stops. I know of no actor who inhabits every role, to the smallest detail, more completely and less fussily than Phipps does, and here she is magnificent.

Her character is shy but decisive.When her friends gather and bicker, she stands quietly at the side, nervously aware of the falseness of her position, but she has plenty of spirit and, when roused, can discuss the disciplines of war more authoritatively than any of them. The look of horror that suffuses her face at the suggestion that she might be a pacifist -- part defensiveness, part genuine moral shock -- is tremendous. She has been living her fantasy to the full, and her scenes with her surrogate son are suffused with the sense of a dream finally realized. (The production, probably wisely, skirts the more troubling sexual undertones of this relationship. All the same, there are moments when she addresses him like a belated Wendy faced with a collective Lost Boy.) She also exudes a very Scots sense of pent-up mischief.

Her last scene is completely silent, and an honest heartbreaker. The emotion here is all about the character; our joy at seeing this actress in a commanding role again has to wait for its expression till the curtain call, which at the performance I attended gained a standing ovation. Both ladies -- the performer and the performed -- have earned their medals.

CHAPLIN

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

Mixed media is a fancy phrase that usually means getting the worst of several worlds, but Simon Bradbury, as author and performer of Chaplin, does the mixing as well as, if not better than, anyone I have seen.

Onstage, he is Charlie Chaplin, alone in his office-cum- screening-room, keeping colleagues and intruders at bay while running the rushes of The Great Dictator. Onscreen he is Chaplin again, trying to get his lines and business right, and spending a great deal of time, energy and exasperation saying "cut". When the canned Charlie and the live Charlie begin to interact, the one practically stepping off the screen to shake hands with the other, Bradbury's timing, in Neil Munro's production, is brilliant.

What, however, is it all for? The play is subtitled, mock- portentously (at least I hope it's mock), The Trial of Charles Spencer Chaplin, Esq. It presents its subject at a moment of crisis. It is 1940 and Chaplin, having held out against spoken dialogue for more than a decade, is making his first full talkie. He has always been his own director, producer, writer and composer; now even his acting involves him in a dual role.

The Great Dictator is of course the movie in which Chaplin exploited his own phenomenal resemblance to Hitler, or rather -- since the clown was famous first -- Hitler's phenomenal resemblance to him. Chaplin plays the dictator Hinkel, while doubling as his own familiar Tramp. In the latter role he gets to end the picture with an impassioned six-minute speech. It seems many of the people around Chaplin doubted the wisdom of this; and in Bradbury's scheme Chaplin himself comes to share their doubts.

Some of the points raised are commercial or political: Chaplin risks alienating the American public by making an anti-fascist, and hence pro-interventionist, picture, especially if he tops it up with a sermon. Others are personal or artistic: Chaplin's beloved little man has no place in so heavy a project, and Charlie risks killing off his own greatest creation. (This in fact happened; after this film, the Tramp never twirled his cane again.)

Bradbury's Chaplin brushes off most of these objections, but they lead him to confront a deeper problem. Alarmingly, Hinkel -- Chaplin's own invention played by himself -- starts haranguing him from the screen. How dare he presume to criticize dictators? Isn't he a dictator himself? And hasn't he built his whole career on the destruction of another human being? Chaplin got his start as a five- year-old in England, singing a comic song in the family music-hall act when his unstable mother went down with stage-fright. She never recovered, and ended her life in a mental hospital. Incidentally, the song he sang was about one Jack Jones, a snob who cut all his friends and relations when he came into money. "Being on your Jack Jones" is Cockney slang for going it alone. Chaplin has been, selfishly, on his Jack Jones ever since.

That's a neat verbal ribbon in which to tie up a theme: Bradbury is a writer. But the overall structure is strained. Chaplin surely had his guilts and insecurities but it is hard to believe that he would have embodied them in the figure of Hitler. (We can surely, without weaving elaborate psychological fantasies, give Chaplin credit for being ahead of his time and recognizing monstrosity when he saw it, even when it came wearing his own moustache.)

The Hitler-Hinkel whom Bradbury conjures up has to be, for the sake of providing an articulate opposition, improbably suave and coherent. Martin Amis, in his excellent and underrated new book Koba's Dread, remarks that it's possible to laugh at the big moustache, Stalin, but not at the little one, Hitler. He's right, now. But in 1940, when people knew less about Hitler, even his enemies could find him funny. Chaplin, who knew more than many, certainly could: He could hardly have taken the dictator as a subject on any other terms. And to be a worthy antagonist to his double, Hitler-Hinkel needs to be comic; a strutting, screaming buffoon. A short sequence in which Bradbury, live, gets to play him that way is the highlight of the evening.

Themes apart, the play staggers under the built-in curse of biographical drama, especially when it has a satirical or deflationary bent. The author has to keep pumping information as fast as he undercuts it. And even then a lot of interest is taken for granted: Bradbury has probably over-estimated the amount that most of us know, or care, about Chaplin. (I found myself leaning rather heavily on my memories of the Robert Downey Jr. film).

Add to this the similar curse on one-person plays, to which the technological trappings here add a special intensity. To keep faith with its own convention the play has to keep all other characters off stage. But it's one thing when the actor is cleverly conversing with his own image on a screen, and quite another when he's exchanging dialogue with the recorded voices of other actors playing the people Chaplin is trying to keep out of his room and his life. Some of these one-on-one dialogues go on a long time, and the effect is not only deadening but arbitrary: There seems no reason for the production not to cut its losses and get the interlopers off the phone and onto the set.

All these unseen folks, upbraiding Chaplin while feeding us the facts, make the play seem like a rogue edition of This Is Your Life, devoted to bringing its subject down instead of puffing him up. The method only works when Chaplin is persuaded to give an interview to a trio of journalists. We don't see them either, but at least the three voices can act among themselves. It's good radio. One of them asks Chaplin whether his anti-Nazism means that he's Jewish. (He wasn't.) The question goes unanswered, and the fact that it does is a tribute to Bradbury's dramatic tact.

You like Bradbury himself throughout. He is a champion actor of scrawny underdogs who here resists all temptation to play for sympathy but gets it anyway. He comes off, in fact, nicer than Chaplin is ever likely to have been. His technique is as winning as his personality; and when, on the first night, technology betrayed him -- a voice-tape kept repeating itself and he had to step out of character and call a halt -- we warmed to him all the more. On one level it was poetic justice; on another a heartening example of man asserting himself over the machine. (I suppose they can't keep it in.) The play is the first visible fruit of the Shaw Festival's augmented dramaturgical policy: adding plays set in Shaw's lifetime but written since. When this was first announced, some of us thought it would mean an instant diet of Tom Stoppard. We did not expect plays to emerge from within the company, or at least not this quickly. It's a hopeful start: The last production of the current regime pointing directly to the next.
