robertcushman@lycos.com

Five pairs of young actors are going in turn through the same scene. A married woman, planning to elope with the equally married hero, calls on him to discover why he failed to turn up for their assignation, and finds him still asleep. Have you ever, she demands, been on time for any of our meetings? His reply is "Rarely. But she perseveres, and by the end of the scene she at least has him out of bed. Sometimes -- the actors' interpretations vary -- she even gets him more or less dressed.

Laszlo Marton, the Hungarian director who has become the Soulpepper Theatre Companys annual visiting guru, is teaching a master class on Platonov. This is the massive apprentice Chekhov play he directed in Soulpeppers second and third seasons (1999 and 2000) and that in some ways has been its defining success.

The students are mainly young actors, recent graduates of George Brown College and the University of Toronto. They spent three weeks studying the play and preparing scenes from it, guided and goaded by Marton, culminating in an informal presentation earlier this month.

Some elements in the scene between Platonov and the impatient Sophie remained constant in all five versions. All Platonovs slept in their underpants. All got doused with water by their respective Sophies, two from the same massive basin. Each Platonov ended up running his hand up Sophie's leg and was -- somewhat unwillingly -- rebuffed, in a goodbye line that invariably combined rebuke and invitation. One Platonov ended up with a rackful of ties draped around his neck. Some Sophies were angrier than others, and some more importunate, and some Platonovs more emphatically hung over. Some Sophies banged louder on the door before entering, or even delivered the first part of the scene from outside it. Nor was it always the same door.

The students -- there were eight groups, of whom three chose to present other scenes from the play -- had the run of the rambling George Brown theatre building on King Street East and could perform in whichever room they chose, ranging from a comparatively formal meeting space on the ground floor to a garret-like studio upstairs. The action and the characters seemed to expand or contract obligingly.

It's wonderful" said Marton at the start of the presentation "to have such an old broken-down building. It has a life, it has a heart. He also quoted the great Italian director, Giorgio Strehler: our work is about the memories of our desires, disappointments and defeats."

On the second day of the class, he had reminded the students that Chekhov had accounted himself a failure -- this despite his achievements as dramatist, fiction writer, doctor, womanizer and philanthropist that he packed into a fairly brief life. So, not even the greatest are immune.

The student actors also had to draw on their experiences and bring those memories into the characters. This is standard acting theory as expounded by Stanislavsky and adopted (and adapted) by the New York Actors Studio, but Marton brings to it his own warmth, his own charm and his own passion for physical detail.

Theres a party scene in Platonov and two of the groups elected to present it. (An actress in one of them surprised everybody by making her first entrance from a fridge.) "Acting this scene, said Marton, is not about being old and Russian; it's about how you are at a party. You could be as knowledgeable about Russian literature as the British Museum itself; it still wouldn't help. Your body rhythm is very different, depending on what time of day it is, how long youre going to stay there, how many drinks youve had. It's difficult to have a conversation about your life at 8 or 9 in the evening; you need the magic of the night. A 1 a.m. line is not the same as an 8 o'clock line."

This sodden late-night feeling has come brilliantly to life in Martons Chekhov productions for Soulpepper. Everybody who has seen Diego Matamoros in the current Uncle Vanya virtually make love to a chair while lamenting the life he never lived and the woman he never had must have wondered where the idea came from. Matamoros says it originated with him ("I thought I need to hold something) and was edited and encouraged by Marton, but it must have needed the climate of the production, and of a whole way of working, to bring it about.

Matamoros, one of the 12 founding members of Soulpepper, is an associate director of the company with responsibility for training programs; he is probably the Canadian actor to whom Marton is closest, personally and philosophically. (Diego," says Marton, "is like my son.) Matamoros on that chair scene could be Marton on acting in general: It increases the variety of the moments you can have with an audience. If you dont have an object, you can't do it."

It's also a method that communicates itself to young people as the master-class scenes showed. The insistent physicality may even, given what Matamoros describes as "the fearlessness of youth, be easier for them.

You have" Marton told them "to make your own choices; thats how your work is going to be detailed and confessive. Matamoros echoes this: You must make decisions, you cant be a director's pawn." Marton advises and reacts, but he doesn't dictate, and yet its certain that the students were guided by what they had gleaned of his philosophy and his preferences. In other words, they wanted to please him.

The result was that each scene was recognisably a scene from a Chekhov play as it might be directed by Marton for Soulpepper, but all were different. Some moments were startlingly bold. I remember, from one of the party scenes, a shy young girl, first insulted and then kissed by Platonov, going into a state of visible meltdown. From an improvization near the beginning of the class I recall with delight the hunted hero burying himself under his mattress to escape the importunities of his mistress -- a picture that did not, alas, survive into the presentation. Criticism here is not the point, but my overall impression was that the women, given the more active roles, found it easier to connect with the play than did the men.

Marton has always claimed that he chose this play for Soulpepper, and subsequently for these students, because its about what happens to young idealists. But, really to grapple with the terminal lassitude that afflicts Platonov and his companions, you need to be an older kind of young.

This is Soulpepper's fifth year. It is also the fifth year of its association with Marton, and its fifth year of running master classes. One of the most impressive things about the company is that it proclaimed an initial commitment to training and has stuck to it.

Robin Phillips, in addition to directing the two productions of the company's first year, somehow found time and energy to teach as well. Matamoros and Albert Schultz, Soulpeppers artistic director, have given "Shakespeare intensives, and Marton has taken young actors through Ibsen and Turgenev as well as Chekhov.

Nor have all the people who signed up been theatrical beginners: Alon Nashman, one of the most highly regarded young actors in Toronto, was one of last years students and the experience, in Matamoros' estimate, led to his breakthrough performance in Picasso at the Lapin Agile.

An academy -- a postgraduate acting scheme for a dozen students a year -- is a vital part of the company's plans for a permanent home.

In reverse, seasoned Soulpepper actors such as Bill Webster and Martha Burns have been reborn" by the experience of teaching in the companys Youth Outreach program, which gives "the experience of theatre to teenagers who will not necessarily go into it professionally; Matamoros notes that the kid he is mentoring is going into commerce, but its a wonderful experience whatever you do." In effect, this scheme works in parallel with the acting classes, to teach audiences.

Soulpepper's academy scheme has some similarities to the four- year-old Conservatory at Stratford, whose graduates are already doing impressive things on the festival's main stages. It feels like a good time to be watching or working in classical theatre in Ontario. Marton certainly thinks so.

From October to June he runs his own theatre in Budapest, directing one production in a season of 12, and constantly teaching in the same academy in which he himself trained. In the summer he comes to his second home in Toronto.

"Its exciting for me, coming from a very small country, to think that this is really Canadian. These actors feel the work belongs to them -- theyre not imitators of another culture.

He'd already worked with many of the Soulpepper actors on a famous production of Three Sisters -- for a group called Masterclass Theatre -- seen at Banff and in Toronto in 1991. So when those actors reunited, I felt responsible for them." And what they've forged together -- Canadian Chekhov, paprika-flavoured -- is unique.

And, it seems, teachable.

(From the National Post, Tuesday, August 27, 2002) Jonathan Miller is the director of the production of King Lear playing at the Stratford Festival of Canada, starring Christopher Plummer. An incomplete name appeared in yesterday's National Post, due to an editing error. The Post regrets the error. 

KING LEAR

Festival Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

STRATFORD, Ont. - Christopher Plummers first entrance as King Lear is preceded by the sound of offstage cackling. The king then strolls on, arm-in-arm with his Fool, with whom he has apparently been sharing a joke, and pretty much ignoring the rest of the court assembled to hear his pleasure. His last entrance, with the dead Cordelia, is preceded by the sound of offstage crying, a transfixing feral moan that gradually resolves into the four most devastating monosyllables in Shakespeare. Between these two inarticulate extremes -- between heh, heh, heh, heh and "howl, howl, howl, howl" -- lies a magnificent performance.

It resonates with the quality of authority that the Earl of Kent famously salutes in his royal master, and that here translates as "bluff off-handedness." Plummers is a humorous, weather-beaten Lear who brooks no nonsense but whose idea of nonsense is anything he doesn't want to hear. Lear is the only one of Shakespeare's tragic heroes who speaks not a line of soliloquy. He sees no need to search his own soul and, since he has had years of absolute power, he feels there is nothing he cannot say in public. This feeling survives his abdication. He goes on expressing his feelings, whatever the cost, and eventually the expression takes the form of what the world calls madness.

Plummer can still the theatre, either with quietness or with rage. He treats the loyalty oaths of the opening scene as a pre- arranged routine, barely looking at Goneril and Regan as they pour out their rote protestations but keeping his head buried in the map of his kingdom. So when he explodes at Cordelia (better thou hadst not been born is memorably ironclad) and at Kent, the effect is titanic. Similarly, he plays the first quarrel with Goneril as a domestic row, outsize but prosaic, until he gets to the curse of sterility ("Hear, Nature, hear"), which comes terrifyingly out of nowhere.

Miller does the play few favours by pausing just before the storm scene. Actors and audience have to start the ascent all over again, and Plummer seems initially to be going through the motions. But maybe there is a point to it; this Lear seems to be enjoying the elements. What pushes him over the brink is the arrival of Poor Tom, unaccommodated man. This scene is a revelation, to Lear and to us. Usually its apocalyptic rhetoric, but Plummer takes it as a logical, irrefutable demonstration. Edward Bond called Lear "the greatest of all social critics," and that has never seemed nearer the truth. The apocalyptic is a mode that Plummer, maybe at the bidding of his director, shuns throughout, even in the great misogynist speeches at Dover.

The staging is consistently understated, sometimes to great effect. Gloucesters blinding, for example, is presented with the victim's back to us, leaving us to imagine the worst. At other times, it seems perverse. Lear's entry fantastically decked with flowers is made from one of the downstage gangways, allowing nobody a clear picture. He makes his last entrance not carrying Cordelias body, but dragging it behind him.

This doesnt stop Lear's own death from being moving, but it is less so than it could be, and less so than Plummer -- who is here at his uncanny, conversational best -- is clearly capable of making it. To be honest, Cordelia (Sarah McVie), earnest but unyielding, is not much more help to him in life than in death. The reconciliation is a one-sided affair, so the final terrible parting doesn't hit nearly as hard as it should.

Plummers return to Stratford Shakespeare, after an absence of 35 years, was bound to be a great event. Ones fear was it would be no more than that, that we would only see a star going through his paces. We don't. What we get is, in the best sense, a modest performance. You feel that the actor has parked his ego at the stage- door, so that we respond not to Plummer but to Lear. (At least until the curtain call, by which point he has earned his ovation.)

And the Lear we respond to, though not realizing every possibility in the role -- which would be impossible -- is very complete in himself, a vain, deluded but fundamentally honest man, bewildered into new experience and running with it.

The Festival stage is as naked and unaccommodated as Poor Tom himself. A table and chair are initially permitted; later on, we are denied even the joint-stool the text prescribes for the mock trial in the hovel. (This is a loss; the scene, sometimes the heart of the play, is unduly hurried and huddled.) The program doesn't even list a set-designer, though Clare Mitchell is credited with the costumes, which are sober, early 17th-century -- the plays own period -- and very helpful.

Indeed, the greatest strength of Millers direction, other than its line-by-line intelligence, is the sense of time, place and society that these clothes impart. We are in a theoretically ordered world in which great houses are surrounded by wasteland ("for many worlds around there's scarce a bush"), a world in which there are pieties to be transgressed and in which Bedlam beggars are the merest documentary realism, in which Kent's jovial reference to Lipsbury pinfold signifies an actual place.

Domini Blythes Goneril and Lucy Peacocks Regan, both imposingly wigged, are especially fascinating in this context, socially and emotionally. Tradition (which I am just old enough to remember) played these two as outright transparent monsters. A later mode, inaugurated by Peter Brook's famous production, presented them as reasonable women, sensibly averse to having their households disrupted. Blythe and Peacock take a middle way: They are born schemers, putting plausible grievances to malevolent use.

There is good work from Benedict Campbell as Kent, especially fine and firm at his king's death, and from James Blendick as Gloucester, another whose clothes help fix his courtliness. Maurice Godins Edmund is a cynical charmer, ironically poured into a Puritan suit, and Evan Builung a persuasive Edgar, in and out of disguise.

Stephen Russells Cornwall is a sadistic snake rather than the "hot duke" described in the script, but Ian Deakin makes a fine Albany, whose pedantic decency flares into outraged moral indignation, a development fatally underestimated by his wife.

Barry MacGregor's superannuated cockney Fool is excellent in its own right, but seems somewhat got at by his get-up, especially the floppy hat. He is also asked to bear more weight than the play affords him. Bringing him on in the first scene merely dissipates the effect of his first scripted appearance later on, and I remain sceptical of Miller's conviction -- reiterated now through at least four productions -- that the Fool should be as old as his master. (He is also, in this production, notably less funny than his master.)

Brian Tree is a superbly supercilious Oswald, a spaniel to his marrow, and collectors of tiny Shakespearean re-creations should note the brittle edge that Gary Folka brings to the virtually invisible role of Curan.

WALK RIGHT UP; SHADOWS

Studio Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

The double bills of new plays that have opened Stratford's new Studio Theatre have all fallen into the same pattern. Before the intermission we have had a more-or-less naturalistic, usually domestic issue-drama of the type of which we all profess to be thoroughly tired. It has invariably been followed by a free- wheeling experimental piece, the kind of boundary-bursting piece we all theoretically crave. And the tame old-fashioned offering has come out ahead every time.

That is certainly the case with the third and last of the season's two-headers. It starts with Walk Right Up, which is by a new playwright, Celia McBride, and which would be easy to dismiss as yet another illness play with a pat ending. It concerns Millar, who has had two strokes and is confined to a wheelchair, and his wife, Lily, an overpoweringly affectionate -- hence, controlling -- woman, who is now in the initial stages of Alzheimer's. These two have sinned against nature (certainly against credibility) by naming their son Brilliant and one of their daughters Poet. This must have been Lily's idea; she was once a writer, and one hopes that her books were less flowery than she is.

Poet has not become a poet. In fact, she is an actress, and has put her career on hold to look after her parents. She seems to have been something of a martyr about it, which may be why they have renamed her Pill. Anyway, she now has a movie job, and has handed over her caregiving role to her sister, who doesn't want it. The sister, whose name is Ella (the font of inspiration seems to have dried up when she was christened), in turn calls in Brilliant, a feckless pothead who initially evinces great enthusiasm for the task but who quits the house the moment somebody upsets him. Brilliant was once an actor but has long since given up the struggle, along with all other struggles. Ella -- we learn from a single line -- has a design business to run.

As you'd expect, much of the play is given over to recrimination. But it's barbed, focused recrimination, and McBride is very adroit at showing the sins of the parents reproducing themselves in the children, especially in a set-piece scene at the dinner table. The daughters are as aggressively protective as the mother, though Ella tries hard not to be -- self-consciously hard, in fact. As for the men, Brilliant's irresponsibility is itself a form of control. Millar, immobile and often silent, is the strongest person in the play, but his condition means this fact keeps taking us by surprise. His family treats him with well-meaning condescension and so do we; implicating us in this way is the author's smartest and most resonant device.

In Michael Shamata's production, Paul Soles admirably delivers the father's slurred speech and unimpaired feelings. Elizabeth Shepherd does finely by the intimations of his wife's crack-up, but lays on the smothering aspect too heavily. Kimwun Perehinec's Poet- turned-Pill lives rather too drably up to her second label, but Brenda Robins, with her quality of smiling edge, takes excellent care of Ella, and Damien Atkins (the author of Good Mother, last season's parental stroke play) gives his most incisive performance yet as Brilliant. Like Bereav'd of Light in the previous studio double bill, this play lets itself down with a platitude. At the end, Lily says, unarguably but unnecessarily, that "we all need help." It doesn't exactly match up to "reason not the need."

All the same, it was probably no accident Stratford opened this play on the same day as King Lear. It also has links to its companion piece, Shadows, which again shows us a group of artists, actual or potential, at the table, this time in the final stages of a dinner party. The host is Ben, a successful playwright, and the others seem to be his colleagues and acolytes. The play -- as its author, the late Timothy Findley, must have known -- is the acme of self- indulgence; unfortunately, it doesn't have the requisite audacity. It stops short at cheek.

Ben, a viperish piece of work, springs a party game; somebody has to reveal a dark secret that may or may not be true. Up to this point, not one of the characters has said or done a believable thing, and the game is incredible, too. But the author has a let- out; they're all playing another game. In fact, they're all would- be playwrights trying out ideas. This is offered as a surprise, and it is, but I'm not spoiling anything by revealing it. (Knowing it may even make the early stages seem better.) The winner will have his or her play performed on the main Festival stage; this is not, to be fair, the biggest laugh in the play but it is the most rueful. (Only one new play has ever been seen on that stage, and that was in 1961.)

Ben then proceeds to involve the audience. He orders the lights raised and asks a spectator to sip from one of the dinner glasses to see whether it contains real wine. On the first night, the chosen victim -- a fellow critic -- refused it as if it were a poisoned chalice, which in a way it was. His neighbour -- another fellow critic -- had fewer qualms and tossed off an unexpected response, with which Brent Carver, playing Ben, coped, I must say, admirably.

Anyway, it doesn't really prove anything. An author can play as many tricks as he chooses, and this play goes on playing them. It, too, ends with a cliche, though one spun out to greater length: a speech about how drama is composed of lies but that those lies may sometimes hit a nerve of truth. Undoubtedly: but this one never does, on any of the levels it keeps insisting on revealing. After so much smugness, this humility comes too late. And -- to reiterate a point made already this season -- it overrates the audience's fascination with the author's problems. The fact that all the characters are theatricals only makes it seem that much more incestuous.

The only convincing line anyone utters in this play is to the effect that Ben is a bastard, and since we have long lost track of who the speaker is or is pretending to be, or indeed of who Ben is or is pretending to be, it doesn't count for much. At different times, the characters invoke, by name, Noel Coward's The Vortex and David Mamet's Oleanna. Audiences are as likely to think first of Albee's Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf and later of Pirandello's -- well, anything really. They are not likely to think anything new has been added.

Dennis Garnhum probably does as well by the play as any director could, and Carver sports a new high-pitched voice with which he hits an appropriate note of sour mischief. He heads the bluest of blue- chip casts, including Robins (not as good as in the preceding play), Perehinec (much better than in the preceding play), Chick Reid, Karen Robinson, Gordon Rand and Stephen Ouimette, who is spectacularly wasted.

HAIRSPRAY

Neil Simon Theater, New York

OKLAHOMA!

Gershwin Theater, New York

- - -

I loved the first half-hour of Hairspray, and I quite liked the rest of it. Its a new Broadway musical, definitely a hit, based on the cult 1988 film. (My definition of a cult movie is a picture I heard a lot about but never got round to seeing.) It opened, improbably and unprecedentedly, in the middle of August -- between seasons, really -- and if nothing else comes along it will clean up at next year's Tonys.

As everybody but me already knew, it's the story of a well- rounded girl who makes good. Here is teenage Tracy Turnblad, in Baltimore in 1962, seen right at the top of the show, greeting the day from inside a bed thats been hydraulically raised to the vertical. (Prologue: Good Morning, Baltimore.) Tracy has a dream, about which she enthusiastically sings; its to dance on her local white-bread TV pop show, of which we immediately get a generous glimpse. (Ensemble number: The Nicest Kids in Town.)

Tracy confides her ambitions to her mother, a laundry worker. If Tracy is chubby, Mom is awesomely ample. (Character song: Mama, I'm a Big Girl Now.)

So far, so wonderful: a Bye Bye Birdie book married to a Little Shop of Horrors score. This pre-Beatles era was the last time pop music was of any use to the theatre, the last in which the music had narrative drive and the lyrics could be comfortably understood and might even conceivably be funny. This show's music (by Marc Shaiman) and lyrics (by Scott Wittman and the composer) are an amiable pastiche that propel the show along and raise a few laughs. The direction (Jack OBrien), choreography (Jerry Mitchell), sets (David Rockwell) and costumes (William Ivey Long) are rousing essays in the colourful-grotesque, and they never stop moving. Thomas Meehan, who, after Annie and The Producers, is Broadways man of choice for writing a cartoon, collaborated on the book.

The show hits its first roadblock about the same time Tracy herself does. Her dreams are blighted by the TV producer, who has her own hidebound ideas about what pass for good looks in Middle America, and by her daughter, who exemplifies them. They are a shrill duo -- the Wicked Witch of the West and child -- and they keep striking the same attitudes. (They have to, for the sake of conflict, but that doesn't help.) Mother has a number about her glamorous youth (When I Was Miss Baltimore Crabs) that takes us to the depths of dismal; it may be impossible in a musical to laugh at someone you loathe. Also, they seem more like an irritant than a threat. Even their star and host, Corny Collins (Baltimore's local answer, presumably, to Dick Clark), doesnt like them much, and he must have more clout than they do.

Worse still is when the show gets token-serious. It isnt just stereotypically unglamorous white people whom the villains are determined to keep off the air; once a month, their show has something called Negro Day, but the rest of the time, Baltimore's black population is unrepresented and unimpressed. (As one of them says, "every day is Negro Day at our house.") Tracy meets the black kids at her own school, mainly in detention class, and they teach her to really dance. She joins her cause to theirs, and -- along with a high proportion of the rest of the cast -- goes mock- heroically to jail for it. (The on-the-spot shuffle-and-tap routine in the women's prison -- The Big Dollhouse -- is a definite highlight, mainly for its tongue-in-cheekiness.)

Now, this particular battle for integration was a real one, but it was won a long time ago and Hairspray has no call to act so self- congratulatory about it now. As a friend remarked, it rings especially hollow when you look round the auditorium and notice a marked absence of black people. (There are plenty of fat people, though.) We take for granted, now, that any musical that can manage it will squeeze in an inspirational gospel number, and that the white audience will greet it with hysterical applause. Patronizing, I call it, and the anthem here (I Know Where Ive Been) is indistinguishable from all the others of its kind.

Its the only point at which the show gives up even the pretense of comedy, and it jars. Otherwise, energy and goodwill carry the day, especially when they cohabit in the person of Edna, Tracy's mother. On screen, she was played by Divine, the drag queen. The stage version honours this tradition, while modifying it in the direction of user-friendliness, by giving the role to Harvey Fierstein. (Whether they'll be able to keep the transvestite convention going when the show becomes a franchise is something we wait agog to discover.)

Now, you might argue that a show which goes on at such length about the acceptance-rights of big women is guilty of serious cop- out when it casts the biggest of them as a man. You might also note that Ednas first line in the show is to the effect that people like her and her family dont belong on television, and that she spends the rest of the evening fighting that assumption, and that nobody remarks on the inconsistency. It is also true that her role in the show really amounts to a series of detachable routines, and that what should be their highlight falls rather flat; this is an old- time vaudeville duet with her twinkling shrimp of a husband (the very admirable Dick Latessa) in which the writing runs out of wit when it is most needed. It doesn't matter; every word Fierstein's Edna says, or sings, or (this covers both the preceding) growls is funny: endearing, too. I wonder which Tony category this performance will be eligible for. As Tracy, Marissa Jaret Winokur has plenty of punch but not much variety, so her performance wears rather, how you say, thin.

In its essence, Hairspray is an old-fashioned 1950s comedy musical: songs and sketches marshalled into a mildly satirical plot line. But, coming in the wake of The Producers and Urinetown, it confirms a return on Broadway to American musical comedies that are recognizably American and recognizably comic. (Youve spotted the missing ingredient: Still, two out of three aint bad.) Such shows are still a (highly profitable) minority. The EuroDisney behemoths - - some are Euro, some are Walt -- continue to clutter the place up immovably: Beauty and the Beast, Les Miserables, Mamma Mia!, The Phantom of the Opera, Aida -- I am condemning the latter without seeing it and feel no guilt whatever. There is also 42nd Street, the revival of a revival, and Thoroughly Modern Millie, which is an imitation 42nd Street.

The best musical evening to be had on Broadway is the more honest, and certainly more thoughtful, revival of Oklahoma!, directed by Trevor Nunn. This started at the National Theatre in London and, by many accounts, was better there. But it's plenty good enough here, panoramically scenic (if the corn isn't as high an elephants eye, it would take an elephant to disprove it) and with Susan Stromans best choreography to date. Her dream ballet may not be as balletically impressive as the Agnes de Mille original, but it is more dramatically immediate, largely due to having the heroine, Laurey, dance it herself, rather than relying on a silent substitute.

Josefina Gabrielle's Laurey has been much criticized but I found her charming, and very detailed in the approach-avoidance games she plays with Patrick Wilson's Curly. Shuler Hensley is a wonderfully sung and acted Jud Fry, a gigglingly neurotic villain so understandable as to be downright troubling. Listening to the Rodgers-Hammerstein score, you don't just nod at a procession of famous songs (as you often do at classic musicals -- Kiss Me Kate, for example), you have a theatrical experience. After 60 years, these songs work.

MISS JULIE

Premiere Dance Theatre, Toronto

Man, according to August Strindberg, is the lord of creation, the creator of culture, while woman is "this stunted form of human being." He offers these cheerful definitions in the preface to his Miss Julie, probably the most famous of all one-act plays; and the most remarkable thing about them, apart from the casual assurance with which he tosses them off before proceeding to more important matters, is their lack of connection to the drama they are supposed to introduce. Strindberg wrote his share of misogynist plays. Miss Julie, whatever his intentions, isn't one of them.

Miss Julie, the daughter of an unseen and impoverished Swedish count, has the dignity that drama always bestows on the death- marked. Jean, the valet with whom she copulates in the course of a single midsummer night (it would be impossible to say who seduces whom) is a cold-blooded opportunist with ambitions, that will probably be fulfilled, in the hotel trade. Neither is a sympathetic character, though both are drawn from within, but theres no doubt which of them commands the greater respect. Its social rather than sexual equality that takes a beating in this play.

The play was written in 1888. Strindberg anticipated -- and with hugely superior economy -- the achievement for which John Osborne's Look Back in Anger was to be acclaimed 70 years later: that of putting the sex war and the class war on the same stage. He also managed to throw in religion. Miss Julie is oppressed by the Biblical injunction that "the last shall be first," which suggests that she, as an aristocrat, can never achieve salvation. Jean points out that, having submitted to him, she is now herself the last. Maybe Strindberg agreed. But in letting her accept her fate, he puts her right back at the head of the line.

To say Miss Julie is a power struggle is merely to say it's a good play; but it gives us that dynamic in a purer form than most. Its also one of the first avowedly naturalistic plays. Strindberg devotes much of his preface to saying so, and to proposing theatrical reforms that are now every theatres stock-in-trade. So, to restore the original impact, it's tempting to ignore the author's instructions and turn the play into a ritual.

This seems to be the intention of Herbert Olschoks new production for Soulpepper. Its extraordinarily uneven, swinging back-and-forth between brilliant and hopeless. It begins with Jean and his fiancee, the cook Christine, moving around the stage to music, like figures on a clock. It transpires that this is more than just a jazzy way of getting the show on the road; when the Count's bell rings from off stage, the two servants -- Jean, especially, with all his professions of independence -- start behaving like obedient automata. But it takes the whole length of the play for this to click into place. Last year, Olschok directed Soulpepper's La Ronde, with its 10 serial couplings, and at times he seems to be offering Miss Julie as an 11th. As in the previous show, a sax signifies sex; when Julie and Jean are off together, a lady saxophonist crosses the stage, soulfully blowing. Meanwhile, cupboard doors fly open and crockery tumbles from the shelves, to symbolize just how furiously theyre going at it. (The play takes place in a kitchen, though Peter Hartwells set, in greens and browns, looks more like a schoolroom. Maybe that's Scandinavia for you.)

When the characters are on stage there is plenty of pawing, with hands moving enthusiastically up and down legs. This is becoming a Soulpepper trademark, familiar from their productions of Chekhov. It's exactly what you expect in Strindberg: Desire is a given, and to keep illustrating it is underlining the obvious. In La Ronde the stylized techniques set off detailed realistic acting, with the heat coming from inside as well as out. In Miss Julie, with two of the same actors, this doesnt happen, or only sporadically.

Patricia Fagan and Tony Nardi are maybe the two outstanding actors of Soulpeppers second wave. (It's a tribute to the company that, at only five years old, it already has a second wave). In outline they have the characters of Julie and Jean down pat, but they have problems filling them in. Nardi conveys all of Jean's resentfulness, resolution and sullen magnetism, but his vocal limitations are nearly as troublesome here as they were in The Winters Tale. When he has a long speech -- like his reminiscence of spying on the young lady of the house when they were both children - - I found myself tuning out. Fagan -- tall, slim, wire-drawn intense and looking great in jodhpurs -- has the opposite problem; her arias, especially the self-hating ones at the end are riveting, but in dialogue she often falls back on all-purpose emoting. (The play feels under-rehearsed; some of it like a late run-through, with the actors still testing the weight of their lines.) She could become the best Canadian actress of her generation, but though shes the right chronological age for Julie, who's supposed to be 25, she doesn't yet carry the technical weight for the role.

Jane Spidell, who is certainly a comely Christine, gives the play an anchor in acquiescent normality, even when required to fall asleep, not slumped over the table as youd expect, but bolt upright in her chair. She only falters when she passes from piously lecturing her fallen mistress to angrily screeching at her, as if shed caught some kind of theatrical bug. And the three of them make the last scene, in which Jean, with Christine's silent approval hypnotizes Miss Julie to her doom, more persuasive than I have ever known it. Usually, I have lost patience with the characters by this point and would like to meet somebody else. At the end the production finds its rhythm, and comes through.

THE MAIDS

du Maurier Theatre Centre, Toronto

I can never consider the dramatic work of Jean Genet without remembering Kenneth Tynan's description of his play The Blacks as belonging to "that large category of avant-garde plays that sound more like masterpieces in description than in performance." The category, as far as I am concerned, is large enough to accommodate all of Genet's plays, including The Maids, which has been newly presented by Soulpepper.

The Maids is more bearable than The Blacks -- not least because it's much shorter -- but it has only one idea, which it keeps reiterating. This is that servants resent their employers while secretly identifying with them. Strindberg said the same thing in Miss Julie, Soulpepper's other recent opening, but he managed to say other things as well, and in about the same length of time.

Like Miss Julie, The Maids, first produced in Paris in 1947, has three characters. There are Solange and Claire, young-middle-aged domestics who are also sisters, and there is their mistress, known only as Madame. In the first section of the play, the cat is away and the mice are behaving accordingly. Claire dresses up as Madame and torments and patronizes Solange, whom she addresses as Claire. This is partly the girls' satiric comment on the fact that Madame always gets their names mixed up, but it's also a device for further titillating the audience. Who knows what incestuous lesbian identity swapping may be simmering beneath the surface? There is also some plot going on; by means of forged letters, the maids have framed Madame's lover on a charge of theft, and he apparently stands a chance of being sent to Devil's Island.

Genet's admirers tend to chatter enthusiastically about "ceremonial" and to claim that his plays bypass all the tiresome clutter of bourgeois drama and take us down to the roots of theatre, back to the Greeks and even beyond. That sounds all right until you encounter the plays themselves and discover that they're all talk. (The best Genet production I've ever seen was an English staging of his quasi-political play The Balcony that treated it frankly as dialectic, like Shaw without the jokes.) The dialogue may succeed in being perfumed and poisonous -- the fans tend to invoke the magic phrase "black mass" -- but that doesn't make it any less static. Some productions of The Maids up the ante by employing an all-male cast; Genet himself would apparently have approved, even though (or conceivably because) it adds another level of useless artifice.

Diana Leblanc's production, with real women, is the best I have seen; and though that isn't actually saying much, the back- handedness of the compliment is a reflection on the other versions, not on this one. Indeed, for the first third of the evening, I really thought they were going to get away with it. Nancy Palk as Solange and Martha Burns as Claire act out their initial masquerade with great emotional bravura and inventively stylish staging from behind a gauze. Or rather from between two gauzes, since the audience is seated on both sides of the stage. When the outside world is about to intrude, the curtains are whisked away and half the house finds itself confronting the other half. This is a striking moment , but it doesn't lead anywhere. For a moment, the audience may feel implicated in the charade, but the feeling wears off.

A phone rings, and we learn that Monsieur has got bail. Madame arrives and, having received the good news, sails off again, though not before the maids have tried to poison her. They prove, though, even more ineffectual at executing this scheme than they were at their previous one. The narrative tension, anyway, is not exactly overpowering; storytelling was far from being Genet's strongest suit, and he's at his worst when he stops playing games. In a sense, of course, he never stops playing them. The play's picture of domestic service has less to do with conditions in France in the 1940s, or at any other time, than with the author's fantasies. The Maids was inspired by, if not based on, an actual murder case, and awareness of this fact makes the play seem chilly in the wrong way: frivolous without being funny.

The exigencies of the plot sometimes force the actresses to behave as if they were in a detective story: They try for some realistic tension, though "the lamp will betray everything" is not a credible line, even in a melodrama. (Martin Crimp's translation is nevertheless a great improvement on the previous official version. This gives the production an advantage over Miss Julie, which is hobbled by a stilted text to which nobody in the program owns up.) Palk and Burns are a well-contrasted pair, the former towering over the latter but emotionally subservient to her. Burns makes especially bold choices, sometimes achieving an intensity that's not only white-faced but white-voiced. She seems, unfortunately, to have only one rhythm and one register, but the monotony is less damaging here than it would be in a more colloquial piece. Palk plays a worm that turns, or perhaps a jelly that sets; she has some memorable moments of stupefied helplessness, and she launches full-sail into a final vengeful tirade, though she cannot raise it from melodrama to the perverse tragedy its author seems to have intended. Both actresses go to heroic lengths, but they too seem in the end to be playing games. Maybe they're too nice.

Genet specified that the maids be between 30 and 35, and that's more or less credible here. He also said Madame was 25; no production that I have seen has taken him remotely at his word, though the sisters' jealousy might have a lot more edge if their tormentor were played as a patronizing youngster. This production goes to the opposite extreme by casting veteran Charmion King; she gives a flossily efficient performance but one that proceeds inexorably on its own tram lines, which only periodically intersect with those of the play. The production seems to be getting back on its own track when Claire, like one rising from the grave, dons Madame's dress -- or slips into her slip -- one last time; but this scene too peters out in verbal gestures.

The pundits used to label Genet as a theatrical absurdist, along with Beckett and Ionesco; this just shows how lazy pundits can be, since he had neither the starkness of the one nor the craziness of the other. He was rather the heir to the rhetorical tradition of the French classics, long after it died of inertia. As a homosexual who went repeatedly to jail (as a thief, like Monsieur, except he was guilty) he has enjoyed a sort of outsider's cachet; the Parisian intellectuals, led by Jean-Paul Sartre, adopted him as if he were a species of literary rough trade. English playwright Joe Orton -- also gay and with a record -- was to get the same kind of attention in the '60s, but his plays, riotously entertaining and far more seriously subversive, knock Genet's out of the ballpark.

FRANKIE AND JOHNNY IN THE CLAIR DE LUNE

Belasco Theatre, New York

For a discerning minority, Edie Falco is the hottest actress in America, currently enjoying simultaneous triumphs in three media. It seems safe to assume that she is as good in the imminent fourth series of The Sopranos as she has been in its predecessors. She gives the best of the many excellent performances in the John Sayles movie Sunshine State. And she is now appearing on Broadway in a revival of the Terrence McNally play Frankie and Johnny in the Clair de Lune.

These are three disparate characters, united -- at least as she plays them -- by a common quality: a crinkle-eyed world-weary toughness, especially when dealing with the opposite sex. (In the play, that's all she's dealing with. It is, and I trust you not to misunderstand the expression, a post-coital two-hander.)

All three are poised between hope and battered resignation. Carmela Soprano, being rich and married, is in a different situation from Marly in the movie and Frankie in the play, who are emphatically neither; but -- living on the edge of the law, and with a multiply unfaithful husband -- she has her own insecurities and her own strategies for coping. Dealing with Tony, she has consistently fought, winning battles if losing the war. When faced with the occasional tentative admirers the scripts have thrown in her path, she has let her face relax into a broad, wide smile, as she sends another illusion speeding on its way. The mixture of grit and grace is extremely attractive.

Carmela has an expensive wardrobe. As the reluctant motel manager of Sunshine State, a rumpled Falco goes through the whole film looking great in a tank top. She has inner style, born of wit and self-awareness. She doesn't expect much; her summing-up moment comes when she surveys herself in the mirror after what will likely be a one-night stand and lightly chides herself for her foolishness. And that note, which comes toward the end of the picture, is pretty much the starting point for her performance as Frankie in the Clair de Lune.

Frankie, too, is in the hospitality business -- she's a New York waitress. (The two characters share faded showbiz ambitions: Frankie wanted to be an actress, Marly's happiest days were spent as a kind of professional mermaid in an aquashow.) Frankie's Johnny -- Stanley Tucci, another Italianate actor with gangster connections; he is Capone's front man in Road to Perdition -- works in the same joint as a cook. They have been eyeing one another for some time, have finally gone out together, and have ended up at her apartment and in her bed. The play begins in darkness, to the accompaniment of noises that sound so exactly like two people having sex that one expects it to turn out to be something else. But no, it wasn't a joke, and the lights go up on the sight of two reassuringly middle-aged people, naked. Frankie, soon but not immediately, puts on a robe. Johnny is eventually persuaded to don his underpants, and struts around in them for most of the rest of the play.

The thing is, he is convinced this may be love, and possibly the last chance either of them may have at it, and he is reluctant to jeopardize it by vacating the premises. This is despite the fact that she, with no malice intended, would like him to go, or says she would, repeatedly. Now, where I live, if someone asks you to leave their home, you leave. If you don't, your behaviour is regarded as boorish rather than (as Johnny and his author would have us believe) charming. It's their first date, and already he's talking about marrying and having children. When Frankie says she is unable to have them, Johnny has an instant comeback: They'll adopt. Boy, he's cute.

The play (first seen in 1987) is the kind of purposefully bitter- sweet confection that is as close to serious as today's Broadway is prepared to get. Neil Simon writes the same kind of thing. So does Wendy Wasserstein. They never aspire to full-throated laughter or to deeply felt pain, and you know in advance that the ending will be neither happy nor the reverse. Indeed, suspense largely consists in wondering what compromise the author will manage to work out.

We all identify with broken dreams, and with the hopes of mending them, and McNally's play duly reels us in. It has also been cunningly scored for atmospherics. Frankie has left her radio tuned to the classical station (she doesn't seem the type, but apparently it was an accident) and Johnny calls the DJ and asks him to play the most beautiful music he knows. He obliges with the Debussy piece mentioned in the title, though he never names it; the characters reach the end of the play knowing less than we do. In a similar vein of cultural flattery, Johnny repeatedly quotes from Shakespeare, whom he finds difficult but rewarding, but he could as easily have been reading a Dictionary of Quotations as the Complete Works, since the lines he comes up with are invariably the most famous ones.

McNally indulges his characters but he does respect them, certainly enough to give the actors legs. If Tucci's Johnny becomes irritating in his unstoppableness, that is probably inherent in the role; and Falco, a woman coaxed out of a shell of exasperation and always liable to retreat back in again, crackles with life, wit and vulnerability. Her casual nude scene is incomparably more erotic than Kathleen Turner's celebrated turn in The Graduate, simply because you believe there's a real woman up there. If one thing unites Falco's three current performances -- disparate as they are in background, social status and even accent -- it's the sense they all convey of resilient women with reserves of intelligence that even they haven't fully tapped yet. You want to know what each of them is going to do next.

ABSOLUTELY CHEKHOV

du Maurier Theatre Centre

- - -

We take our pleasures where we find them. Soulpepper's Absolutely Chekhov is a program of five short plays, either by or about the Russian master. Two of them work well. The best moments of the evening, though, come between plays, when the actors double as scene- shifters. One of them is Oliver Dennis, whose unassuming demeanour conceals enchanting skills as acrobat and clown. While two burlier companions heartlessly grab all the lighter work, he is left to grapple all alone with the frame of a bed. He falls underneath it. He is almost crushed between its two ends. Finally, having apparently triumphed over the monster, he takes an unwary step back, and exits by somersault through an open window.

The plays themselves, made over by a bevy of current Canadian playwrights, are what Chekhov called his vaudevilles: the sketches with which he practised up for his major dramas.Theyre mostly farcical; an exception, placed at the end of the bill, is the one called Swan Song. It begins with the Falstaffian sound of an old actor snoring behind a curtain. He awakens to find himself in a deserted theatre, alone except for a sympathetic prompter (who apparently lives on the premises; at least, he seems to be pattering around them in a nightgown). The actor, once a star tragedian and now in the twilight of his career, relives and regrets old triumphs and current defeats.

William Webster, raging against the dying of the light, deals richly with the remembered glories and furiously with the present self-disgust. David Frenchs text allows him to close appropriately with Macbeth's out, out, brief candle -- the "poor player" speech - - after giving us tastes of Lear, Othello and even Hamlet. This -- the role furthest from Webster's own age and range -- is the best of all, with the prompter (Oliver Dennis, at rest) weighing in sympathetically with the prompt lines. The same device was used, at length, in the recent Christopher Plummer vehicle Barrymore. It is, of course, sentimental; and the director, Joseph Ziegler, could probably take it leaner and faster than he does, but it is very affecting.

Ziegler as actor commands the evenings other peak, The Dangers of Tobacco. This monologue finds him, in high Dickensian form, as an oppressed husband dragooned into delivering an anti-smoking lecture. The direction, by Albert Schultz, is very cunning. The stage is in the same sandwich formation -- spectators flanking the performers -- as for the concurrent production of The Maids. This is, on the face of it, the worst set-up for a play that consists of a man standing at a lectern. The production, though, turns this to comic effect; and Michael Healey, the adaptor, throws in a lot of good jokes. The speaker never says a word on his ostensible subject, except to remark that he himself rather likes a good puff now and then. What he does talk about, the words spilling aimlessly but compulsively out of him, is his miserable domestic situation, his monstrous wife, his six or seven -- he seems unsure -- unmarried daughters. (He practically invites his auditors to come and get them.) This is early stream-of-consciousness comedy, and very influential -- or at least prophetic. A friend of mine once characterized Alan Ayckbourns plays -- one of which Schultz directed with great success this season -- as speeded-up Chekhov; it's an accurate description but in fact Chekhov himself, in these apprentice pieces, was writing speeded-up Chekhov.

That doesn't mean you want a whole night of them. Previous Soulpepper productions have rewardingly brought out the farce in the full-length Chekhovs, but you cant expect too many brownie points for bringing out the farce in farce. Back in the days when audiences wanted more bang for their ruble, or just had longer attention spans, these playlets were much in demand as curtain raisers for plays too short to fill an evening. (Soulpeppers Miss Julie or The Maids would have been prime candidates for partnership.) Grouped together, they cancel one another out. It makes little sense to play The Dangers of Tobacco back-to-back with The Tragic Role, another piece (previously unknown to me) about a henpecked husband, though one apparently higher up the financial scale. It's set in cottage country, which I guess gives it Canadian flavour. Diego Matamoros, as a man lumbered with errands and parcels, calls for sympathy on his contrastingly unencumbered brother, who is Ziegler in role- reversal mode. The closing twist is visible someways off; it's comforting to discover that Chekhov had the same trouble with punchlines as everybody else. Adam Pettle is the adaptor; Daniel Brooks directs, modestly confining himself to a single corner of the stage.

The Bear, probably the best-known of the bunch, is a variation on the centuries-old Widow of Ephesus theme: a woman vowed to mourning is lured rapidly out of it by the advent of an unlikely suitor. In this case, hes come to collect a debt incurred by the late lamented. The production, again by Schultz, begins promisingly with Martha Burns, in mob cap and voluminous black, the very picture of determined Victorian bereavement. Thereafter, it loses all finesse. Jason Shermans script tips its hand by having a long-suffering domestic (Webster, otherwise lovely and moving jerkily from the hip as if stiffened by servitude) step out of context to exclaim "what I'd give for a hammer and sickle." All together now: Farce depends for its effectiveness on the performers' integrity and the audiences belief; it has less tolerance than any other form for cheap laughs. It also helps, in a whirlwind courtship farce, for us to want the characters to come together. They shouldnt beg for sympathy but their energies have to be focused.

Sherman is also the co-author, with Susan Coyne, of the new play The Old Business. This is harmless but pointless. It shows us Chekhov, reeling in retreat from the first-night failure of The Seagull, and having also to defend himself against those theoretically closest to him. Both his publisher- producer (Victor Ertmanis, shouting much as he did as Orson Welles a few seasons ago) and his ex-mistress (Nicole Underhay) accuse him of appropriating their stories for his play. The man's objections come oddly late -- he was around for the whole process, after all. Those of the woman, who sees herself as the model for his Nina, seem more substantial. His defence -- that Nina "endures" -- is suggestive, but would also apply to any other Chekhov character; they all endure, perforce, except the ones who get shot. Moments in this sliver of Chekhov's life echo or prefigure moments in his plays, both the long and the short ones, but the bits are arbitrarily assembled; we already know that imaginative writers hurt their friends and act wounded when told about it.

Fans of Matamoros and of Chekhov will be pleased to see how persuasively the one impersonates the other; he too endures (and he has a lot to put up with). Leah Cherniak directs the play, which it seems was originally intended to close the proceedings but now opens them, wisely leaving Swan Song to be the swan song. Or almost: There is a very taking curtain call, which brings the actors on singly, in the order of their first appearance. The accumulation is oddly touching: another of those unexpected fleeting pleasures.

ARTURO BRACHETTI

Canon Theatre, Toronto

Arturo Brachetti's one-man show calls to mind a mildly salacious joke that was going around when I was an undergraduate:

First Guy: "Doesnt Sally dress well?"

Second Guy: Yes, and so quickly, too.

Brachetti dresses very well and very fast. He is a virtuoso quick- change artist, a magician who does it with himself instead of with rabbits. He starts off with a bit of symbolism. He takes a white mask off his face; beneath it is another white mask, and then another. One has lost count long before he discards the last. In its own small way, this looks impossible: How can there have been room for so many layers? And this is a pointer to what he does for the rest of the evening. He will go offstage in one complicated costume, and return -- apparently instantaneously -- in another. However many dressers he has in the wings (the program only lists two), this is impressive. And it goes on impressing. For the whole two-hour show, our breath stays taken. That, however, is all there is to the evening. And it is not enough.

Brachetti, who began his career at home in Italy, nevertheless made his major breakthrough here in Canada -- in Montreal, at the Just for Laughs festival. This, on his current shows evidence, is surprising, because he doesn't seem to be much of a comedian: not a verbal comic, at least not in English, and not a great physical clown, either.

His director, Serge Denoncourt, and his designer, Guillaume Lord (both French-Canadian) have staged his act imposingly; it all takes place within and around a kind of revolving house.

The big set piece, cued by Brachetti's informing us that, like all Italian children, he grew up on American movies, is a long Hollywood montage in which he appears as one familiar icon after another. Its the ultimate drag-queen extravaganza, though more innocent than some. I dont mean it lacks sexual innuendo, merely that Brachetti shows no inclination to sneer at his subjects. This is refreshing but limited, since he neither characterizes nor impersonates; he simply shows up, suitably attired, and assumes an appropriate position.

The same goes for an earlier routine in which he acts out a western, switching between five archetypal characters. There is wit in the costumes (for which he himself is presumably responsible, since no one else is credited) and in the transitions between them, but little in what he does while wearing them.

He has the frantic eagerness-to-please of his compatriot Roberto Benigni, but he does not have much personality. Nor does it help that in his chats to the audience he draws attention to this shortcoming -- and even gets metaphysical about it. In the show's first half, he tells us about his childhood; he shows us supposed film footage of his family (and, of course, steps off the screen dressed as each one) and tells us about the local priest whose hobby was stage magic and who got him started.

In the second, he talks about a last conversation with his mother, who told him how proud she was of his success as the man of a thousand faces, and then added, (a little too conveniently for comfort) "But, Arturino, who are you really?" It sounds like one of those questions best not asked, or at least best not repeated in front of an audience.

Anyway, it gets dodged. Apparently, the television was on during their conversation, and they were interrupted -- oh coincidence! -- by the news of the lifetime-achievement Oscar being given to Federico Fellini. This prompts another ingenious, and technically impeccable, movieland tribute that culminates in Brachetti crying out, Thank you, Federico!

One would like to echo this with "Thank you, Arturo," but we are as far away from discovering the real Brachetti as ever we were. Which might not matter if he hadn't raised the subject in the first place.

He also includes some more mundane interludes, which, lacking a transforming spark, remain mundane. One of them involves a three- cornered hat, squashable into various shapes, whose versatility the maestro nonetheless overrates. (I wasn't surprised that a child in the audience failed to identify one of its wearers as Captain Hook. Who, trying to identify Hook, would look at his head?) Another is some shadow hand puppetry, which is clever but still the stuff of a hundred variety shows.

GODZILLA

Factory Theatre Studio, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - The new Toronto theatre season gets off to an appalling start with the English-language premiere of Godzilla. This play, like the movie franchise that begot it, comes from Japan, where it has achieved what can only be described as a monster success. Even the most popular Japanese plays usually run, we are told, for a mere two or three weeks, but this one has kept coming back on an annual basis -- like Anne of Green Gables over here, only not quite as sophisticated.

The play concerns a love affair between the celebrated 50-metre- long, 100-ton fire breather and earth leveller and an idealistic maiden of conventional human proportions whose name is Yayoi. That is the whole story. It is also the whole joke, and you could write most of it yourself. You know that Yayoi's family are going to object to their putative son-in-law, and so they do, at what feels like enormous length. (The play is actually quite short, but it seems interminable.) The author, Yashuiko Ohashi, does, to be fair to him, add a little twist: He proceeds to show us Godzilla's relatives voicing their own reservations. Theirs, though, are more easily and generously overcome; I guess they can afford to be big about these things.

Godzilla himself, whatever misdemeanours may be strewn across his past, is presented to us here as a gauche, well-meaning creature who tries very hard to watch where he puts his feet. A parable about tolerance and prejudice comes with the territory. It's so obviously built-in, in fact, that the author has no need to spell it out -- not that that stops him.

Here I have to confess my ignorance. Before seeing this play, I knew little of Godzilla beyond the name; in fact, I really could not have told him and King Kong apart. I had no idea that Godzilla was conceived by a Japanese film-maker in the 1950s as a sort of psychic compensation for what his country had endured at the end of the Second World War. I never knew either that Hollywood had added to America's imperialist record by appropriating the character but deleting the social comment. I learned this not from the play, which depends on but never mentions it, but from the press package; these days, though, I try never to read the package until after I've seen the play. (And of course the non-professional audience never gets to read it at all.) So, for example, I had no idea that Ultraman, the name bestowed on the heroine's vengeful former suitor, was himself a sci-fi icon from Japanese television. This, obviously, makes me a less than ideal audience for the play: a frustrated non-cultist at a cult entertainment. Still, my indifference to the genre never stopped me enjoying Little Shop of Horrors or The Rocky Horror Show, so I refuse to shoulder all the blame.

Godzilla is directed by Jim Millan for his very own Crow's Theatre company. I used to have a lot of respect for this director and his troupe, since my first encounter with their work was Brad Fraser's Unidentified Human Remains and the True Nature of Love, a sparky play excellently performed. Since then, though, my admiration has cooled, in the face of a line of indifferent scripts, messily produced. Last year's Hedwig and the Angry Inch was a nadir, but Godzilla lowers the ante still further, with a static production full of squawking actors, and with an ending as feebly staged as any I remember. It comes with the usual junk manifesto about plays that "question authority, social norms and accepted truths about history and our times." Accepted by whom? Most of Crow's self-selecting audiences are going to agree with the shows before they even start. This isn't a terrible thing in itself -- there are only so many opinions in the world, after all -- but it hardly seems like something to brag about. (It does seem to work, though. Reputations in Toronto not-for-profit theatre, once gained, are very hard to lose. And one way to gain them is by telling everyone, very loud, how revolutionary you are.)

Anyway, it hardly seems to apply to Godzilla, a thin slice of camp whose only gesture toward social comment is the suggestion that Japanese families have become very like American ones, or at least like American ones as depicted on TV. In other words, Japan, like the rest of the world, has watched too many sitcoms and has internalized its values. This joke, though, is short-circuited by the casting; all but two of the actors are Western, and there is no particular kick in seeing North Americans acting like North Americans. In other words, what we have is colour-blind (or at least ethnically blind) casting, working in the reverse of its usual direction but just as unpersuasively. Not that the two Japanese actors add very much; Jean Yoon's performance as the heroine's grandmother who once had a thing for a tadpole is as baffling as her character, and of course their presence means that the Westernization doesn't even amount to a consistent style.

The only tolerable performances come from those few actors who are allowed, now and then, to cool it. Melinda Deines' Yayoi is indeed more than tolerable; she's consistently delicate and sensible, and her opening speech (the play's best), describing the necessarily platonic nature of her love, promises better, wittier things than actually arrive.

Godzilla himself is played with pleasant aw-shucksiness by John O'Callaghan; he is portrayed as of human size, on the sensible grounds that attempts at spectacle would be self-defeating. (They would also be harder, but nobody mentions that.) He shares an agreeable guys-together pre-nup scene with his future father-in- law, played by Keith Knight. I took a special dislike to our Cinderella's jealous younger sisters, but it's probably not their fault.

On a more cheerful note: Daryl Cloran, one of our most promising young directors, has completed a year's internship at Soulpepper, with a workshop production of Edward Albee's The Play about the Baby. No more likeable than its author's other plays, it is still one of his wittiest and most riveting; and this production -- impeccably acted by Juan Chioran, Kate Lynch, Christopher Morris and Sarah Wilson -- was exemplary in its attention to pace and rhythm. It was given two matinee performances last Friday and Saturday. Soulpepper, or somebody, should bring it back.

WIT'S END II

Winter Garden Theatre, Toronto

Sandra Shamas is back, with another very funny update on her life and I-don't-think-they're-so-hard times. Wit's End, her previous show, had her in the wake of a divorce, ensconced in a farmhouse deep in the wilderness, or at least some miles away from the nearest town. Wit's End II finds her in possession. She even gets to pay off the mortgage.

Some of her material harkens back to her pre-rural days which, as an urban animal, I find a relief. Shamas has never reduced me to helpless laughter (unlike, say, the English comedienne Victoria Wood) but she does induce helpful laughter, which is not so much the opposite as the next best thing. She can take a cliche and twist it into a wisecrack, as when she tells us that she was mad at her body for so long that she'd forgotten what they were arguing about. Then she twists it still further, into something personal and imaginative, musing that she didn't have really have any reasonable quarrel with her body; it was holding up her head just fine.

On the subject of body image, she tells us of how she decided to celebrate winning an arts awards that entailed selecting a protege and commissioning a new work from her. She decided to go for a nude painting of herself by an artist who works from photographs. The photo shoot was an exposing experience that left her wondering "will she call me tomorrow?" When the painting was completed, she liked it, until it dawned on her (in a beautifully-rendered moment of mental double-take) that it was going to go on public exhibition right in downtown Toronto. Shamas is also very amusing on the differing reactions that the picture, now hanging on her wall, produces from her male and female visitors.

She talks about ageing (she's 45) and how she's read that among the first things to go are your nouns. This, apparently, has proved true for her, but the condition seems to be treatable; she could hardly tell us about nouns if it wasn't. Male-female relationships continue to take up much of her time on stage, but they are not explicitly sexual ones. If you live on a farm without being a farmer, then you need to import one; and apparently the thing to do in such a circumstance is drive to the nearest store and ask them if they have one in stock, or at least if they can have one delivered.

Later on, she finds a man to help her with the chainsawing. She enters into states of deep if taciturn communication with these men, and I think she goes on about them at rather too great a length. I don't know if what she's giving us is straight autobiography but, if it is, then maybe it could stand to be gingered up with a few falsehoods.

Her life takes another strange turn when she cancels her mortgage. To begin with, the finance company seems none too keen to let her out of its clutches. But once they've given in and the deed is done, or torn up (this isn't something that most of us know about), she feels at a loss.

Logic, even her own brand of it, seems to fly out the window. Owning her own home, she no longer needs to work. So she must give up being a performer. But she likes being a performer. What can she do to fill the void? She must get a job. We seem to have come round in a circle without our navigator having quite realized it. Or, to put it another way, the lady has left her non sequiturs dangling all over the property, and sooner or later -- maybe in Wit's End III -- she is going to trip over them.

Nor am I quite sure why her new landed state makes her decide that she must be a lesbian, or why she regards lesbian life as one long pajama party. A couple of real lesbians put her right on these points ("you're not a lesbian; you're just screwed up") and everyone heaves a sigh of relief. I don't want to reveal the sentiment with which Shamas leaves us -- it's a throwaway rather than a punchline and apart from it being unfair it wouldn't mean much in print -- but in its place it works just fine.

She fluctuates, like most people, between questioning and acceptance, and her lithe body language reflects this; she looks, sideways on, like a question-mark continually in the process of straightening out into a statement. A shrewd and likeable performer, she is clearly far from being at her wit's end. Still, I hope she will, at some point, return to the city.

GIRL IN THE GOLDFISH BOWL

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

Iris, the Girl in the Goldfish Bowl of Morris Panych's new play, lives in that bowl, figuratively at least, because its former inhabitant no longer does. He died, as goldfish will, and was flushed down the toilet by Iris' mother who has her own problems, as does everybody else in the household.

We are in a small Western Canadian town, one with a beach and a canning factory. It is 1962 and the Cuban Missile Crisis is happening offstage, though we do not feel it impinging on the characters to the extent that the author probably intends. Iris mentions it most, but then she is our narrator so she has the scope.

She is 11 and, at least by her parents' lights, irritatingly bright. Her father, an unemployed war vet who has a passion for geometry and spends most of his time standing at a draftsman's table, asks her: "Isn't it time you ran away from home?" (I should point out that he does love her, but he is having a bad day. He has a bad day every day.)

Iris is also told that she shouldn't use words that have more letters than she has years, a rule that she happily transgresses in nearly every sentence she utters. One of the forbidden words, this year at least, is "reincarnation." Iris is convinced that the body of Mr. Lawrence, her family's new and mysterious lodger, houses the returned spirit of her late pet, whom she called Amahl because he was bought in a mall. One reason for her theory is that when Mr Lawrence first arrives he is wet, or at least his clothes are.

Other people believe other things about him. Iris' mother sees him as a possible love object. Iris' godmother, a lodger of much longer standing who goes by the name of Miss Rose, sees him as a possible sex object. (According to the other females on the premises, this is how she sees every man.) Iris' father sees him first as a threat and then, in desperation, as an ally, a means of staving off the worst thing he can imagine, which is that his wife will leave him. Mr Lawrence himself seems bewildered by everything that is expected of him, and gives virtually nothing away about his identity; indeed the other characters all seem to know, or guess, more about him than he does. He is at various times suspected of being a spy, an escaped criminal, and a mental patient; and he does at one point express terror at the idea of undergoing a lobotomy.

There are shades of Harold Pinter's The Caretaker in the play, while at other points, with its earnest fish-conscious young heroine and its cramped dysfunctional family evokes comparisons as varied as Kristen Thomson's I Claudia and Neil Simon's Brighton Beach Memoirs.

It remains its own animal. Panych writes, here as elsewhere, with an uncommon, quirky blend of humour and compassion. ("I used to read," says the mother, being very precise about her vagueness, "but you know what words are like.") The author skirts whimsy without quite giving in to it, and is capable, as at the end of this play, of a sudden surprising harshness that is never gratuitous. He is not so great on narrative drive; you may be eager to hear what his people are going to say next, but you are seldom greatly concerned about what they are going to do. They also seem to have been somewhat arbitrarily assembled; there seems no reason for the presence of Miss Rose except to provide comic relief for a play that is comic already. Iris' vociferous disgust for the nuns who run her school is funny too (and presumably inspired by Panych's loudly- proclaimed rejection of his own Catholic upbringing) but it hardly connects with the rest of the play. Nor does the play get to grips with the relation, or lack of it, between Iris and her mother. What works surpassingly well, grounding the action with increasing firmness as it proceeds, is the parents' relationship. The woman who took a husband she didn't love, and found that time was unable to work the miracle; the man who hangs around hoping for affection, and dreams of finding it by transporting his wife to Paris where she will be seduced by the mathematical beauty with which the streets intersect and the Boulevards run into the Places.

Panych himself directs the play, splendidly. For design he has his regular collaborator Ken McDonald whose set here is unusually restrained and realistic. Much of the space is devoted to a staircase that boasts some spectacularly untrustworthy banisters; the family is on its uppers, unable to afford a television but with a very evocative collection of LPs.

Above all, though, this is a feast of acting. All five performers excel themselves. It is one of the play's oddities that Iris, the play's central figure, is far from being its most interesting and the repeated theme, that we are witnessing the end of childhood (like Eartha Kitt's on the day that the circus left town), is stated too insistently to be honestly felt. Panych obviously had fun finding her voice and writing her monologues, and we have fun listening, but there is self-indulgence on both sides. There is none though that I could detect in Kristina Nicoll's performance, with its hope and disillusion and querulous indignation. A couple of flash forwards to her adult self do little to enrich the play's texture but are marvellous, shocking contrasts in themselves. John Jarvis, whom I have usually seen being lucid and urbane, makes an extraordinary transition to the dishevelled and woebegone dad, constantly in his pajamas and gaining dignity in the act of sacrificing it. His brief moments of joy are delightful at the time and heartbreaking in retrospect.

It might be interesting to see his discontented spouse played by an actress less brisk than Brenda Robins (or one, as her husband might express it, with fewer sharp angles) but she does finely, and can create a great effect by very nearly smiling.

Tanja Jacobs' talents find outsize release as the louche Miss Rose, moving like run-down clockwork from her job at the factory to a social life as dissolute as she can manage; that is, she's canning by day and canned at night. At home, she seems always to be dragging herself momentously upstairs, in search of bed or bath; she looks like Luba Goy, one size larger.

Finally, Richard Zeppieri as Mr. Lawrence succeeds brilliantly in the daunting task of being simultaneously bewildering and bewildered. There are, one is convinced, scary things going on inside him. Or, more or less in the words of the 1940s song, which we get to hear perfectly updated to the swinging '60s by Frank Sinatra, I think he'd rather be a fish.
