THE SHAPE OF THINGS

Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Neil LaBute's The Shape of Things is a genuinely shocking play: maybe the only one Ive ever seen.

The shock is sprung by the plays narrative, and it is concentrated in one late revelation that feels like a blow in the face from an icy fist. It also feels thoroughly logical. It has roots; it's about people going to extremes, and the fact that you believe in them makes the shock last. I would hate anyone who had spoiled it for me in advance, so I will try to tread carefully.

The play's four characters are graduate students (median age, 22) at a liberal arts college in the American Midwest. We are principally concerned with Evelyn, majoring in fine arts, and Adam, majoring in English. Adam has a part-time job as a guard at the campus museum, and this is where he first encounters Evelyn, who is standing in front of a sculpture, a fig-leaved male nude whose prudishness she is all set to rectify. She has, literally, crossed the line that is supposed to separate the art object from the spectator. Later, she proves herself willing to cross that line metaphorically as well, which is far more alarming.

Adam will certainly be alarmed, though for the moment he is just inhibited and intrigued: intrigued enough to ask Evelyn for a date. Before you know it, they are lovers and Evelyn is making him over. Under her guidance Adam loses weight, dresses smarter, swaps his spectacles for contacts and has a nose job. He is also, we gather, having the best time of his life in bed. The transformation is duly noted by his friends: not, as Evelyn points out, that he has many. But we do meet Phil, Adams robustly philistine former roommate, and Phils fiancee, Jenny. In Adam's shy days, Jenny, fairly retiring herself, sat next to him in class but could never get him to take an interest. Now, however, he does, proving that the great thing about sexual confidence is that it does wonders for your sexual confidence. How far their dalliance goes is unclear, but it goes somewhere.

At this point, the play looks like it might be the American clone of Patrick Marber's English play Closer. We seem to be in for an evening of serious partner-swapping; what else would four characters get up to in a sexually charged setting? It doesnt happen, though; LaBute (best known for such movies as In the Company of Men) has more on his mind. He also writes more believable dialogue than Marber, or than most other current playwrights. His language is nervous, humorous and real; he uses the hesitancies and repetitions of youthspeak without ever becoming, like, you know, tongue-tied himself.

The play has also been widely compared to that most celebrated of all extended transformation scenes, Shaws Pygmalion: not, I think, very helpfully. In the first place, Eliza comes to Higgins asking to be changed, and in the second and more important, there is no explicit sex in their relationship. In Shaw, no one really gets hurt. Adam and Evelyn are wandering through a far thornier garden.

Evelyn repeats some advice given by her supervisor: Strive to make art but change the world. In the old committed days, that meant change society, on a broad political level. Evelyn, though, belongs to a generation that has largely given up on explicit politics (I don't actually believe this, but I'll go along with it), so she takes it to be the prerogative of the artist to use people, on an individual basis. Maybe without knowing it, she has taken the "but" out of that slogan and substituted an and. She wants art to affect people, on a visceral level --as the play itself does. Adam, for many reasons, is dubious about this. He keeps coming out with literary references that Evelyn fails to recognize. He belongs, in fact, to an older culture. He believes in boundaries -- as the play also does.

Its emotional sympathies are with the man (or perhaps I think so because mine are) but its strength is with the woman. Adams sins struck me as venial; Evelyn is not only breathtakingly manipulative but self-righteous, as only proselytizing artists can be. Notice, though, how the very names trip you up. The battle is unwinnable by either side. The plays penultimate scene all but screams "follow that." Its last scene takes up the challenge, successfully. Jim Guedo's CanStage production does superbly by it.

Amy Redford has been imported to play Evelyn; the Sundance Kid's kid seems to have trouble with theatre-sized projection but otherwise offers an accurately ruthless, driven performance; the character never apologizes for her actions, and the actress never apologizes for the character. Allan Hawco is a magic trick in himself; as the swathed nerd of the first scene, he looks and behaves practically middle-aged, and then grows gradually younger, outside and in. The other two are there to register, like the audience, varying degrees of shock. Jacob Barker shows, gradually, that a jock can have feelings. Amy Price-Francis (Stephen Sondheim once wrote a song called Multitudes of Amys; this productions casting seems designed to realize his vision) is very adept at showing a kind but baffled mind running for shelter.

One scene places most of the characters among the audience, to brilliantly unembarrassing effect. The plays London production, directed by the author, apparently used a deafening soundtrack by the Smashing Pumpkins that reportedly drove Harold Pinter and Lady Antonia Fraser out of the audience. I suspect my sympathies would have been with Harold and Antonia, and I applaud the decision to substitute a subtler, more varied score, culminating in Elvis Costello singing My Funny Valentine, with its own comments ("Your looks are laughable, Unphotographable") on life and art. The play doesn't need to deafen us, even if its author thinks it does. It also, despite the sex scenes, gets by without nudity. We are all long inured to the worst that playwrights can try to do us, but this one gets through our defences, as Strindberg presumably did when he was new. It's the best American play since David Mamet's Oleanna, and maybe better. Recommended, without reservation.

FILLER UP!

Artword Theatre, Toronto

The season that began so alarmingly with Godzilla has hit a further low with Filler Up!, a one-woman show so embarrassing that for long sections of it I could hardly bear to look at the stage.

My reluctance had nothing to do with the physical appearance of Deb Filler, the writer-performer: this despite the fact that her lifelong weight problem is the most prominently featured of the three things she is here to tell us about. (The others are her lesbianism and her Jewishness.)

Actually, Filler's shape is best described as comfortable, and she proves it, at the end of the show, by pulling on a pair of leather pants that, from all she tells us, would previously have been too small for her. This is one of the evenings two climaxes.

The other is her refusal to take more than a single bite of a freshly baked loaf of challah bread. Freshly baked, I should add, by her. We have watched her assemble and blend the ingredients with her own hands during the first half of the show, and during the second it has browned merrily in an onstage convector oven. It is, I suppose, a metaphor of sorts. But who kneads it?

Unmediated autobiography is the most perilous of all theatrical forms. If you dont warm immediately to the person doing it, it's all up. Nothing else is going to come along to tweak your interest; it's just you and her and her self-absorption. My own failure to invest in Filler has to do with the fact that, though she presents herself as a comedienne, and does funny voices to prove it, she seems to have no idea of how to weight a joke.

There are certain clowns (the late George Burns was one) who attain a state of comic grace in which literally everything sounds hilarious. Filler seems to have reached the opposite state. Trying to be ingratiating, she just sounds bossy; instead of throwing lines away, she belabours them. She didnt exactly win me over by breezily demanding a bigger welcoming hand than she actually received before doing anything to justify it.

She then started in on the jovial Jewish allusions that seemed, coming out of nowhere, like a calculated pitch to the hall. (Some of which, to be fair, responded. At the end -- critics are always being told they should mention these things -- there was even a standing ovation. As if you were surprised.) Im a Jew myself, and I still felt outnumbered.

I also felt shame: Shame at having hinted earlier this week that Sandra Shamas, who really knows how to do these things, might be less than a transcendent genius. Listening to Shamas' first-person narratives, you sometimes wonder how much of what she is saying is true. With Filler, you never doubt that all of it is, because you cannot imagine that anybody would have taken the trouble to make it up.

Anyway, the story she tells us begins in New Zealand, where she grew up as the daughter of two refugees from Nazi Europe. Both parents, mother especially, encouraged her to eat, and then worried when she got fat. So they sent her off to visit an aunt in the United States, who, by prior arrangement, deposited her in fat camp. She escaped from this after a day and ran back to auntie, a raucously vivacious soul who continued the family tradition by filling 'er up. Deb seems to have spent the intervening years shuttling between home, where she discovered her destiny as a performer, and New York, which is where she has pursued it.

A sub-plot concerns the present, pressing question of whether her now-widowed mother should come to live with her, a proposition on which both, courtesy of the intercontinental phone lines, blow ceaselessly hot and cold.

She tells us her mother has continued to call her even on the opening night of her Toronto run. Presumably, she will continue to do so on all the other nights. In other words, what was set up as a free-wheeling monologue turns into a play.

This is a miscalculation of unimaginable ghastliness. The shows only saving grace has been our shared pretence that she was talking directly to us, making it up as she went along. Now it thinks its a DRAMA. It's a mess: Neither fish, fowl nor good Yiddishe herring. (I didn't tell you that her mother was in the audience, in person, at the premiere. I didnt want to confuse you.)

Now, what can I salvage? Fillers recreation of her professional debut, singing an appalling homemade song to her boyfriend -- she had one then and he was a mistake -- is nice in its remembered awfulness. (Her other musical interludes are also awful but less intentionally so, despite the fact that she can actually sing. She picks up a guitar and does snatches of famous tunes with parody lyrics that are both heavy-handed and, well, half-baked.)

She does an amusing impersonation of her first lesbian partner, who accepted her tentative drug-propelled advances with a couple of off-hand monosyllables. She entertainingly recalls the name of her first movie role (Pudgy Earthquake Victim). She does a real routine about a hefty Hebrew maiden called Zaftige who personally parted the Red Sea, though Moses "accepted the award on her behalf and with it the perks. This should have been the end of the first half but, like the Red Sea post-miracle, it rolled relentlessly on.

Later on there is dignity in her telling of her father, a concentration-camp survivor, who persuaded the Russian liberators to let him enlist the help of the imprisoned German guards in baking bread. It's meant to offset the frantic jesting about diets and support groups but it merely overpowers them.

The recipe seems to have been exhaustively pre-tested. It boasts a co-writer (Lowery Marshall), a director-dramaturge (Molly Thom) and three other workshop dramaturges." It is produced by Filler herself and John Karastamatis, Toronto's smartest theatrical press agent, who must have taken leave of his usually impressive senses.

TO THE WALL

Theatre Passe Muraille

Andy Jones, the cordial comic from Codco, has a plumply unassuming air but grandiose ambitions. To the Wall, his new one- man show, is about the ultimate problems of good and evil, especially evil.

He tells us of a psychological condition that afflicts him, a sort of future-conditional deja vu; if someone is late for an appointment, Jones will immediately begin to worry about all the terrible things that might have caused this. He calls this sensation futur possible, peut-etre horrible. Many of us will recognize it.

For Jones, it's emblematic of the state of the world, and he calls God to account for it. In fact, he invites God to attend a public meeting (a first, as he points out) timed to coincide with the closing moments of this show. It will surprise nobody that this situation comes with a built-in anti-climax.

It shouldnt surprise Jones himself, since hes an atheist. However, he grew up in an extreme Catholic community in St. John's, Nfld. ("we were Hassidic Catholics") and the old habits of feeling die hard, especially in times of crisis. His own theory, rather a persuasive one, is that God felt lonely, and threw all the elements of existence at random into a series of parallel universes from one of which humanity emerged.

Bound by that initial commitment to chance and non-intervention, God then had to stand by when evil emerged. In other words Jones posits a creator but not a merciful one, or at least not one prepared to act on merciful impulses.

So what does humanity do in the meantime? Samuel Beckett (another lapsed Papist) asked this question, and Jones conducts himself pretty much like Beckett's tramps -- though since theres only one of him he has to be more lucid.

He spends his time pondering metaphysical problems and bringing them down to his own level. He considers the peculiar sex appeal of the stage performer: Here he is, a tubby badly dressed fella without very much hair who can imitate other peoples voices and make us laugh, and what he is really doing with these talents is sending out messages to the ladies in the audience saying "mate with me." He recalls the hellfire preachers of his youth, less interested in praising God than in damning Protestants, and invites us to identify the precise moment at which they start going mad. On the evidence he provides, I don't see how you could tell.

Jones also talks about stories so sad they would make bunny- rabbits weep; about the number of buckets of sand you would have to empty on the ground before they formed a perfect map of Newfoundland (and Labrador), and how you could not hope to do it without virtually unlimited time and the services of three young and attractive assistants.

He talks also about the exploits of his Aunt Mary, a small-town switchboard operator who eloped with a diplomat (she had to elope; he was a Protestant) and who acquired a perfect upper-class English accent that so intimidated Hitler, when her husband was posted to pre-war Berlin, that the memory of it stopped him from invading England. This means, I think, that even the good stuff happens for terrifyingly arbitrary reasons.

He keeps all these elements running in parallel, and promises us they will all come together at the end. They do, too, sort of; though, for reasons already hinted at, the show does dribble away at its close. Up till then, though, it's fine, and Jones himself is worriedly lovable. Pushed to the wall, I would say I liked it.

Until Oct. 27. Box office: 416-872-1212 robertcushman@lycos.com

THE LEAGUE AGAINST TEDIUM

Bathurst Street Theatre, Toronto

Simon Munnery is a famous unknown television comedian from Britain. The League Against Tedium, despite the plural implications of its title, is his one-man show. (Is there any other kind of show? This is the fourth solo bit to hit town this season, and the season is less than three weeks old. I begin to understand the concept of The Lonely Crowd.)

Munnerys League is successful in his, its, their declared intent; tedium is kept at bay. Tedium has, though, a less toxic but still dangerous brother called Monotony, and he proves harder to defeat.

Munnery seems to have done some conscientious research before coming to Toronto, and he throws in a decent smattering of local jokes. In essence, though, his is probably offering much the same show to us as he would to the folks at home. He specializes in dyspeptic one-liners, minimally connected, and liberally laced with sour whimsy.

We get a taste of his quality even before the start of the entertainment proper, as a series of texts unfold on a screen. Most of these are effortfully silly ("This show includes epileptics. No strobing, please) but a few are rather elegant (If you leave before the end of the show, you should be ashamed of yourself. If you stay to the end, you will be"). Perusing them, you wonder if the whole evening is going to be like that. It is, but the odds improve. It remains a collection of gags, but there are quite a few good ones.

Its only stand-up comedy, though, the stuff of a club. As a theatrical event, it's somewhere between ramshackle and non- existent. And it's best when it does least. Munnerys idea of spectacle is to come before us with a bucket on his head and to describe the reactions this get-up elicits from people on the street. He does this twice, once before the intermission and once after it. He makes some use of a video screen, on which appear images not only of himself but of his audience. It also reveals a series of famous visitors, from Socrates to Richard Wagner via the Ocean (I mean the Ocean is one of the visitors -- Munnery does seem to have thing about the sea), who make equally famous pronouncements so that Munnery can contradict them, which he does baldly and without argument. "Thus, he says, I win." No, he doesnt.

And, to be fair, I think he knows this. His is the comedy of a vanquished soul. His very title, when you think about it, breathes defeat. Having accepted this, we are free to applaud his gestures of defiance. Against cliches, for example, as when he questions the old saw that money doesn't grow on trees. ("Yes, it does. It's paper.) He asks why bees are attracted to honey, considering that they make the stuff (it must be vanity"). I was also very attracted to the peremptory instruction that I think sums up his philosophy: "Dont punish yourself. You deprive the world of its purpose.

Occasionally he does impressions. His Bob Dylan parody has the dubious distinction of being just as boring (i.e., obscure and inaudible) as the real thing. His Michael Caine act is far happier, and is carried on far longer. He says himself (and he may well be right) that the voice is addictive. Its also not too far removed from his own, which is New Cockney, a bilious sound that suggests the southeastern extremities of London encroaching on the centre and poised to take over. His black-rimmed glasses -- also the mark of Caine, of course -- go with the voice, even seem to be part of it. It's a barbed and jaundiced instrument, and it implies a view of the world.

On the totem pole of soliloquizing comics currently on view in Toronto, I'd place Munnery third; on top of Deb Filler but squashed underneath Sandra Shamas and Andy Jones. He shares some concerns with Jones -- they both go on about God -- but unlike Jones, he is not endearing. He is too cold to be cool, too noncommittal to be truly eccentric, a carper rather than a satirist.

But there is one thing he does better than Shamas. He deals with hecklers. He doesn't deal with them very subtly or inventively, but he does try. Shamas seems to regard voices from the floor as lese- majeste, and she gangs up on them. (Can one woman be a gang? Yes, if the rest of the audience is cheering her on.)

Aimless and fidgety as his performance often seems, he does end on a high. He recalls the true story of a BBC TV newsreader (he forgets which one, and so do I) who suffered a personal assault and remarked, when interviewed, that she had never known such terrible things could happen. But, says Munnery, pouncing on media narcissism, for years she had been reading the news. What did she think it was? A poem?" Well and clinchingly said. I had spent the most part of the evening teetering on the brink of liking him; now, at the very last, I fell.

2002-10-05-fish-friends-heavy-handed-sat:
Tarragon Theatre until Oct. 20. Box office 416-531-1827.

You want trends? I'll give you trends. The Tarragon Theatre seems bent on reinventing itself as an aquarium. Its main stage is currently occupied by Girl in a Goldfish Bowl, about a girl who fancies that the familys lodger is the reincarnation of her late wet pet. Now in the smaller room we have Fish/Wife, about a woman who is preparing a dish of sashimi for her guests and starts identifying with the raw material.

Rick Roberts, a good actor, here directs his own first play, a heavy-handed satirical fantasy with the occasional bright spot. Gwen is in her kitchen, with her thoughts divided between the menu and metaphysical speculation, when the dish shakes and water sprays up. Further experience reveals that the fish is alive, and that it reacts in this violent way whenever mention is made in its presence of death or dying or some cognate concept. Assisting Gwen in these discoveries is her lifelong friend Joanne.

Joanne has children; Gwen is married but childless. Her husband Rob is off in the next room, partying; Gwen has reason to believe that he is partying most enthusiastically with another old acquaintance named Sarah, whom she and Joanne have always resented. It is plain that they also, despite protestations of mutual devotion, resent one another. They also resent themselves, or the lives they are leading. I found the feeling contagious.

The two actresses come before us as clowns, in fright wigs and rouged cheeks. The play and production, in fact, signal their contempt for the characters from the first moment, leaving us wondering why we should be spending so much time in their company. (The play lasts only 50 minutes, but its more than enough.)

The raw fish dish is the only one that Gwen can cook, though her husband has uttered unkind thoughts as to whether it counts as cooking. Joanne is a strict vegetarian, and there are some fairly amusing exchanges on whether less strict vegetarians are transgressing their principles by eating fish. In their best moments, the two women recall the enjoyable bitching of Absolutely Fabulous, and Marjorie Campbell's performance as Joanne has indeed strong squawking echoes of the wondrous Joanna Lumley; bestowing gaseous condescension from a great height she commands attention to begin with but is exhausting by the end.

Lindsay Collins, as Gwen, is allowed to pace herself more, and so stays the course better.

She is helped by being the one to whom the really traumatic things happen; by the end of the play she is developing secondary fishy characteristics on her own account. But both performances nag.

There is some skill in the way that Roberts keeps us apprised of what's going on in Gwens marriage, and even what may have led her to this pass. But these suburban, or maybe just middle-class, tensions, have been explored a hundred times before. That doesnt make them irredeemable; Alan Ayckbourn regularly conjures high, sad comedy out of them, but then he bothers to understand his characters.

Roberts reaches back to the long-dead tradition of the Theatre of the Absurd, in which conventional people and conventional speech patterns are arraigned and invariably found wanting; he does with fish what Eugene Ionesco did with rhinos. We have seen over the last couple of years that some of Ionesco's plays still stand up (I doubt if all of them would) but there is a sense of wonder, even of poetry, in the way he approaches his subjects. He could also be very funny.

Roberts has some good lines, but the best of them -- something about recognizing the sound of mirthless laughter" -- rebounds all too easily on the play itself. It's fundamentally patronizing: an attack on undefended targets. (Or, of course, like shooting fish in a barrel.) And if the moral is that those who serve fish shall perish by fish -- or perish as fish -- then I don't think it's worth the trouble. There are some good macabre touches in the production, the best of them held in reserve until the very last second.

PROOF

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - David Auburn's Proof is an OK example of the kind of play that succeeds on Broadway, usually after a tactful tryout somewhere else, and goes on to win a Pulitzer prize. It is amusing and well put together; it is civilized, meaning that its characters are comfortably removed from the poverty line and have intellectual pursuits; it recognizes the existence of pain, but manages somehow to finagle a happy ending; and it takes place on a porch.

The porch and the house attached to it are in Chicago. Their current inhabitant is Catherine, who is 25 except in flashbacks, and is the daughter of Robert, who is now dead except in flashbacks and dream sequences. Robert was a genius mathematician who, like most in his field, did his best work early. His last years were pitted with mental illness, or as he himself more forcefully put it, he "went bughouse." It seems possible that Catherine, who dropped out of college to look after him, may have inherited both the genius and the disease. Those about her are more inclined to credit the second possibility.

Like The Shape of Things, CanStage's other current show, Proof has a powerful moment of surprise lurking in its armoury. A major difference is that in The Shape of Things (which is the kind of American play that doesn't win a Pulitzer) the revelation is integral both to the play's theme and to its plot. It simply couldn't be made any earlier than it is and, once made, it allows the action to proceed with no interruption and with accelerated force. In Proof, it's a neat way of bringing down the first-act curtain.

Catherine's main antagonist in the play is her elder sister, Claire, who has inherited the family skill with numbers to the extent of having a successful career in some kind of finance management. She now lives in New York and is about to marry her long- time boyfriend, unseen, who has lots of unspecified "connections." Having come home for the funeral, she takes charge of everything and, over Catherine's objections, arranges to sell the house. She also tries to take her sister off to New York for, as she tries to disguise but as Catherine quickly guesses, treatment.

Completing the cast is Hal, a former PhD student of Robert's, and now a junior academic in his own right. He plays drums in an all- mathematician rock band (the play has a lot of fun with the wild things that science geeks get up to in their spare time) and a long- time inarticulate admirer of Catherine. They come together in a scene of approach-avoidance-acceptance that struck me, romantic sucker that I am, as the best sequence in the play: best written, best acted, best directed. Boy then loses girl, in traumatic circumstances.

If the play stands or falls by Catherine, then in Martha Henry's production it does a bit of both. The role is played by Jennifer Paterson, a young Vancouver actress making her Toronto debut. (She gets an "and introducing" credit in the program, something I've certainly never encountered in the theatre before.) She is short and schlumpy and technically unprepared for the load of transitions her author throws at her. The latter liability means that, in a pinch, she falls back on unmodulated rage: a tendency that makes many of her scenes heavy going. Yet, despite her limitations, indeed partly because of them, she gets to the core of the character and is moving. Catherine has led a sheltered life. Her mind has had far more chance to develop than have her emotions, so she can be verbally sharp, even cruel, and she can be excruciatingly hurt. Paterson, who has a perfect heartbreak look, conveys all of this; her Catherine really could be an idiot savant. (I am not saying she is.)

In New York and London, the role has been played by a succession of stars, up to and including Gwyneth Paltrow. Maybe I'd feel differently if I'd seen one of them at it; not having done so, I have to say that I find such casting incredible. As far as the crucial relationship with the father is concerned, I suspect they would have presented loyal, glowing daughters (the standard Broadway model) rather than loyal resentful ones. This is not a part for glamour, least of all for glamour pretending to be something else, and anyway they must all have been too old. Paterson seems, if anything, too young.

However, her vulnerability risks making her sister seem stunningly unsympathetic, in every sense, and Henry's production does nothing to redress the balance. Tamara Bernier's Claire is pure polished brass, varied only in the wake of her dad's wake by an exaggerated hangover scene that has her wearing her hair Gorgon- style while moaning about "those physicists." She also torpedoes belief, not to mention subtlety, by singing an entire chorus of New York State of Mind as she waits to go home. A few hummed bars might be credible, but anything more seems like a sop to Bernier's own track record as a musical-comedy performer. And if it's meant to be a convention, couldn't the other characters, hometown loyalists all, be allowed to sing in reply that their kind of town, Chicago is?

Matthew Edison is excellent as the fresh-faced Hal, who squirms hard to be decent and in the second half of the play gets more accusations thrown at him than his behaviour seems to warrant. Hardee T. Lineham as Robert suffers from being strictly a creature of the past, meaning that his appearances keep halting the play just when we are keenest to learn what happens next. He has a long speech about the winter beauties of Chicago, which he delivers straight to the audience. But this may be what it's for; I can't think of any other function it serves, apart from giving the proceedings a spurious aura of poetry.

In the end, I don't know what the play's about. It certainly doesn't say anything of note about New York versus Chicago. As a study of fathers and daughters, it offers nothing new. More importantly, it can't revitalize the already familiar. In its treatment of varying attitudes toward possible genius, it plays out well as melodrama, but is maddeningly unspecific. As the author himself has admitted, there is no real need for the characters to be math whizzes rather than any other kind of clever. Compare, inevitably, Tom Stoppard's Arcadia, which also offers a female mathematical prodigy, whose preoccupations are integral to the themes of the play and whose theories we very nearly get to understand. Proof is a fair evening's entertainment, but it deepens my decades-long suspicion of what mainstream America takes for serious theatre.

EL PASO

Factory Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Michael Miller, the author of El Paso, writes excellent dialogue, and he comes out stinging. His opening scene shows Vivian, a black woman with terminal cancer, locked in bitter verbal combat with Junior, her neglectful and chronically unfaithful husband of 30 years. Junior once had a successful military career and may even have had a shot at becoming a general, but he is now in insurance.They live in Washington, D.C., but Vivian's hometown is El Paso, Tex., and she longs to go back there. In the next scene we take the trip for her, and almost immediately the play starts to unravel.

We are transported not only in time but in space. The date now seems to be shortly after Vivians marriage. Papa Spiller, her grandfather, already fears for her safety and tells his daughter Ida Lee, Vivians mother, to take his shotgun and go straighten Junior out. Ida Lee, however, has other concerns, mostly the succession of men in her life. She is a schoolteacher and both resentful and neglectful of her two daughters; the other, known as Tiny, works as a janitor in her mother's classroom, a fact her mother never lets her forget. To make things even more complicated, Papa Spiller, at some questionable point in the time scheme, gets ghostly visitations from a boy called Marcus, the child of Vivian and Junior (and therefore Papa Spiller's great-grandson), killed in an accident when his father should have been looking out for him. Vivian and Junior also have a daughter, Juanita, who, in what you might call the plays present-tense action, is struggling to get some belated professional qualifications; her relationship with her mother is edgy. (For her father she has, like nearly everyone else in the play, nothing but contempt.) It takes the audience the better part of the evening to get all this straight, and Philip Akins direction does nothing to lift the confusion. Nor does it help that several members of the cast are prone to fits of the mumbles.

This is a shame, because there are some powerful themes at work here. Papa Spiller's own parents were slaves; nevertheless, he has risen to be the owner of the biggest house in El Paso. But he and his family discover that there is more than one kind of enchainment, and that they are perfectly capable of manufacturing their own. ("Your house," Vivian yells at Junior, "was the hell of slavery, in blackface.") The middle generation grows up through the era of Martin Luther King and has to balance violence against forgiveness. There is also intermittent but inconclusive stress on disputed property, from houses to chinaware. I guess if the play's about anything, its about the tyranny of history and about the futility of blaming what you have become on what has been done to you. We get to hear a lot of recrimination; most of the characters are virtuosi of it. The effect is sometimes bracing, but cumulatively wearying. Its not enough that characters in the present should be dredging up the past; when we travel into the past, we find that they're still at it.

It also lacks focus. Miller has not written a Chekhovian ensemble piece in which all the characters contribute equally to a fluid pattern. He's writing more like Ibsen, telling a traumatic story backwards. But Ibsen had the sense to tell only one such story at a time, and -- since his generation had mercifully never heard of flashbacks -- he had to work hard at his exposition.

Watching El Paso, you keep wondering who the central character is meant to be. On the face of, its Vivian; we begin with her, shes in the direst straits, and the characters cluster around her sickbed. But it's Ida Lee, her monstrously selfish mother, who dominates the climactic scene with a violent transformation that is neither properly prepared nor credibly written. The protagonist might even be Tiny, the warmest and most tolerant figure in the piece (though certainly no pushover) and the one who, both figuratively and literally, travels easiest between El Paso and Washington, then and now.

When he writes a group scene, Miller seems to have problems keeping all his characters in play; the people in the middle are lively, but the others are reduced to implausibly mute spectatorhood. The production, which leaves them sitting around gaping, makes it worse. The contrast is a metaphor for the performances at large; most of them have their moments, but nobody is able to carry a character all the way through.

Kim Roberts, sharp-tongued and warm-natured, comes closest as the ironically named Tiny (I assume it's ironic, as the actress is anything but). Jeff Jones Papa is a fine figure of a sad, angry patriarch and he has a nice line in sarcasm, but psychologically he remains in his own corner, intoning. Satori Shakoor manages Vivians anger effectively, but can do little with her more passive moments. David Collins as Junior is hardly allowed to be more than a one- dimensional villain; every so often, the script tosses him a bone, in the shape of one or two grievances of his own, but it never develops them, though you can sense the actor straining at the chance. (It's not that Junior's cruelty isn't credible -- sadly, it is -- but that it has nowhere to go.)

Vivian spends much of the play locked in her bedroom; she and Junior berate one another through an invisible wall, like Pyramus and Thisbe having a succession of bad days. This is a cute enough idea, but it leaves the actors delivering tirades in no specific direction -- and, I would guess, with no specific direction, either.

Lili Francks has some rather shallow fun with the flirty side of Ida Lee. She cannot cope with the bitter old woman she turns into, but then she seems, like most of the play, to be written moment to moment, with no connecting line. Rothaford Gray is sweet as a suitor who marries her (or rather, whom she marries) and who swiftly repents.

The company in general has more energy than finesse, and the production lets them squander it; script and performance expend so much emotion on the small moments that they have none left for the big. I imagine that several strands of inexperience have become tangled here. The play may be about mothers and daughters, men and women, past and present, North and South, reality and dream. It cannot in reason be about them all.

Black & White Photo: Nir Bareket Photography / David Collins as Junior and Satori Shakoor as Vivian hash it out: excellent lines delivered in no specific direction. ;

A few weeks ago, Lynn Slotkin, who reviews theatre for CBC Radio, noticed that she had received no invitation to the premiere performances of The Shape of Things and Proof, the two opening productions of the new season at Canadian Stage.

Surprised by this, she e-mailed CanStage's press office to ask if there had been any mistake. She was informed, also by e-mail, the neglect was intentional: "We have removed you from the complimentary list at CanStage." She was of course at liberty to buy her own tickets and broadcast whatever opinions she pleased.

Producers have been known to fume at critics who have given them bad reviews, but they seldom take this kind of action. Indeed, Slotkin hadnt thought her reviews of CanStage productions had been especially hostile. She believed they had, like those of most critics covering the work of a company with so large an output, been mixed.

Martin Bragg, who holds the top CanStage post of artistic producer, denies anyway that its a matter of good or bad reviews. Like most people who have worked in the theatre for any length of time, he's used to both and inured to both. For him, it seems to be Slotkin's tone rather than her opinions that grate. He said, when I spoke to him over the weekend, this is about an individual -- Im not going to call her a critic -- who has been extremely destructive, personal and vindictive.

Grant Ramsay, CanStages director of public relations and promotions, takes a similar line. Slotkin's reviews, he says, have been "consistently mean-spirited, negative and personal."

I don't get it. I dont usually manage to hear Slotkin live on air, but I have been listening to tapes of four of her CanStage reviews from last season. All were of plays for which her enthusiasm was, at best, muted, which seemed a fair test. (Despite their protestations, I doubt CanStage objected greatly to the tone of the rave reviews -- three, by Slotkins own account -- she had given them over the same period.)

As a broadcaster, Slotkin can come on a bit strong for my taste - - like an overbearing mother handing down reviews rather than recipes -- but I could detect nothing in what she said that was malicious, and I always found her well informed and able to argue her case.

In at least one instance, the Judith Thomson play Habitat, her review was kinder than most -- certainly kinder than mine. Conversely, she liked Steve Martin's Picasso at the Lapin Agile, and especially its production, a lot less than I did; but there were others who disliked it more. Among the shows she liked are two -- Wit and The Lonesome West -- for which I shared her enthusiasm, and a third -- Goodnight Desdemona, Good Morning Juliet -- for which I find it inexplicable. Others would agree or disagree, in varying proportions.

There, in other words, you go: Diversity rules, and is surely to be welcomed. Bragg, Ramsay and their colleagues are as entitled to their opinion of Slotkin's reviews as she is to her opinions of their productions. Their course of action is another matter.

Before reviewing for CBC, Slotkin, a compulsive theatregoer in London and New York as well as Toronto, posted her opinions in her own on-line publication, The Slotkin Newsletter, which she still maintains. In this capacity, she never received or requested media tickets. And she says that even now, when she writes in the newsletter about a show she has already reviewed on CBC, she goes to see it again and pays for her seat. She had no quarrel with Ramsays claim that a theatre can hardly be expected to hand out precious free tickets to anybody with access to a Web site.

It sounds reasonable, too, for Bragg to say free tickets are given as a courtesy, and he, like any host, has a right to choose his own guests. But in fact its disingenuous. We are not dealing here with a straight hospitality situation: Your typical dinner invitation doesn't include the right to insult the cooking, at least not in public.

This is a business transaction. Theatres don't let the critics in free because they love us; they do it because they want good reviews, and in order to get them are willing to take the risk of receiving bad ones. Good reviews may send readers or listeners to the box office; they can also be torn into strips and used in ads. Indeed, press quotes have become the predominant mode of advertising plays. Critics, it occurs to me, must be the worst-paid copywriters in the world.

Its a Faustian bargain, with the difference that both sides can get burned. It would be morally healthier, both for the media and for the theatre, if we -- or, let us pray, our employers -- paid for our seats, and if producers refrained from using our reviews as fodder for commercials. (Producers complain, accurately, that a review is just one persons opinion; they then proceed to give that opinion the status of holy writ by exhibiting it on their own marquees.)

But the system isn't going to change: It works too well, not least logistically. It makes life easier for critics to be told where we have to be and when, and it's helpful for the theatres to know when were going to be around and to be able to give us seats from which we can at least see the stage.

We, too, should accept being quoted or even, if were unwary enough to give the opportunity, misquoted. Few things strike me as more absurdly pompous than the shrieks of reviewers claiming their deathless phrases have been taken out of context. We spend our lives misrepresenting plays and the people who create them. Who are we to complain when they misrepresent us?

I don't think this state of affairs is actually corrupt. Reviewers may be subject to all kinds of subtle pressures (most of them generated from within our own heads), but the lure of the complimentary ticket is not one of them. A freebie does not guarantee a rave, as any producer will ruefully testify. And shows survive both raves and pans, which are seldom unanimous anyway.

But if the system is going to work, then it has to operate on an equal-opportunity basis. If we're gong to be given privileges, we all have to be given the same ones. For CanStage, a publicly funded organization, to claim Slotkin can continue to review their shows if she pays her own way is, again, disingenuous. It places her in a false position in relation to the rest of us critics, and I dont blame her for refusing to accede to it. It also intimidates the other critics, who dont know if they will be next. (It won't, in practice, have this effect, but we're concerned with principles here.)

Robert Crew, who alternates with Slotkin as CBCs reviewer, has refused to cover CanStage shows until the ban is lifted, and he is doing the right thing. I would feel happier if CBC itself had taken a more explicit stand as well. The sanest arrangement is for theatres to send media tickets to the organization concerned, and for the organization to decide which reviewer to give them to. It should not be the producers prerogative to choose their own judges.

Bragg admits that in this instance CanStage may be shooting itself in the foot, since its constituency, certainly for its Bluma Appel main stage, largely overlaps with that of CBC radio: It's not serving us from a business point of view; we'll deprive ourselves of a prime marketing tool if we were to get a good review.

All the same, when I put it to him that a sort of unofficial pecking order applies here and that he would be unlikely to deny tickets to the Globe, the Star or the Post, he didnt deny it. Nor did he claim Slotkin had singled out CanStage for special abuse: "I think its just her style for everybody."

Probably there is a point at which a critic's continued rudeness or obtuseness justifies a theatre in taking preventive or retributive action. I don't think Slotkin has crossed that line, or even approached it; but I do believe critics should be held accountable. There is no point in calling them on matters of opinion, since these cant be proved, but they can and should be challenged if they make obvious factual errors, or if they seem insensitive to the ways in which shows actually get on to a stage. (This is a trickier area but -- in a collaborative form such as the theatre, where praise and blame have to be apportioned -- a crucial one.) But the best way to do it is to write a letter, or to demand time on the air. This means citing specifics. Barring a critic, or making him or her feel unwelcome, is a blunt instrument by comparison.

Its been tried before. In London, in the 1960s, Hilary Spurling, an especially bright critic who wrote for the Spectator, was removed from the free list at the Royal Court for saying, repeatedly, that that theatre's famous tradition of social realism was actually rather old-fashioned. The Court's directors, a famously sensitive bunch, were livid. Why, they knew they were revolutionary. People had been telling them so for years. Eventually, the Arts Council of Great Britain stepped in and Spurling was reinstated. The Royal Courtiers were left looking petulant. I would hate CanStage, a generally sane organization with a decent track-record, to go the same way.

Until October 20. Box office: (416)-975-8555 robertcushman@lycos.com

HOMAGE

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre

Is everybody these days writing the same play? I have now seen three in a row that feature family conflicts both within and across generations, cross-cutting between past and present, and a house that's about to be sold from right underneath its occupant. There was Proof, there was El Paso and now there is James Harkness's Homage.

I confess: The three plays don't have much else in common, and El Paso, which is extremely busy, stands at the furthest possible remove from Homage, which is distinguished by its reverential stillness. There are scenes when almost everybody in it seems to be asleep. We start with a woman puttering around in a kitchen. In a living room, a step down on a gently split-levelled set, two men sit in the half-light; one appears to be snoozing, the other to be reading. The two groups are under the same roof, but at different times.

The house, we learn, is a Southern Ontario farmhouse; and the woman, we see, is baking a pie. We watch her preparing it and putting it in the oven, with the kind of tranced respect we have been trained to accord to actors carrying out domestic tasks in realistic detail.

She is of course the farmer's wife, and her name is Anne. The farmer, Wilfred, whom we meet a little later, suffers from a cough whose seriousness he refuses to acknowledge. It seems likely it was caused by nearby industrial pollution, but the victim will have nothing to do with this idea or with the protest that some of his neighbours are organizing. His spouse, meanwhile, writes letters to her son Jim, who split for the city when he was still in his teens and has not been home since.

He's back now, though, now being a little bit later than then. He is the slumped young man and, following the death of both his parents, he has taken possesion of the farm. Both he and it are in dire financial straits. Nick, the man doing the reading, is actually an accountant, and is going through the books. Having done so, he pronounces that Jim has no choice but to sell up. But it's difficult to get Jim, who drinks a lot, to take this or anything else seriously.

The title may conceivably be a triple pun: home, homage, homosexual. Jim is gay, and mordantly flippant. He fled home because he felt stifled by farm and family, and craved creativity. Nick, his boyhood friend, stayed behind, despite having a cosmpolitan background (well, his parents were Italian) that Jim had always envied. This being Buddies in Bad Times, one assumes Jim and Nick had once had a sexual relationship, but it's never explicitly stated. Anyway, Nick now has a wife and kids, a circumstance Jim seems to regard with mild derision.

He also, after Jim's departure, did his best to look after Anne and Wilfred. That cough killed Wilfred, and Anne had gone rapidly downhill after his death. Jim, though, has found Anne's journal, and is marvelling at how well it was written. He realizes that the artistic expressiveness he left home to find was there on the farm all along. And I didn't realize until I started this sentence how very Wizard of Oz that sounds.

David Oiye's direction goes for a style best described as narcoleptic lyricism. This has its effective moments; the scenic overlapping means Jim and Nick can exchange memories and recriminations while Anne and Wilfred slumber on the sofa right alongside them. But for much of the time, it is just somnolent. Anne Anglim as Anne bestirs herself in her less trance-like moments, but there are too few of them. Bob Nasmith is excessively hoarse and subdued, even for someone in Wilfred's condition.

Andy Velasquez captures Nick's amiable stolidity but hardly varies it. Tom Barnett finds the appropriate quivers of self-hatred and self-pity for Jim, but doesn't seem quite to the manner, or mannerisms, born. (Barnett was also, more convincingly, the artsy intruder in another rural drama, The Drawer Boy. To adapt the old song: How Ya Gonna Keep Him Down on the Farm, After He's Seen the Farm? Twice.)

In theory, Harkness's decision to keep issues (big business, pollution, etc.) in the background and concentrate on the people is to be applauded. In practice, the politics sound like they might be more absorbing than the family dramas, which are thin.

The play does connect with the guilt many people feel over their parents, the regret for what has been missed, and this can be poignant. The play is well crafted, too, in terms of information revealed or withheld. But much of the time, the characters are going over old ground, slowly. David Fraser's set is of an unusual solidity for this address, and works very well.

Black & White Photo: Guntar Kravis, Buddies in Bad Times Theatre / Anne Anglim as Anne, Bob Naismith as Wilfred in Homage: Going over old ground, slowly. ;

In repertory until Nov. 2. Box office: 1-800-567-1600

THE SWANNE: GEORGE III -- THE DEATH OF CUPID

Studio Theatre, Stratford

- - -

STRATFORD - The Swanne: George III -- The Death of Cupid, written by Peter Hinton, might be described, inadequately, as a biographical- historical-fantastical piece about the young Victoria, pre-Queen.

The play is huge: It has a cast of 21, lasts for 3 1/2 hours and at that is only the first part of a trilogy. Stratford may or may not need this play; by the end, I was persuaded that it does, though I certainly had my doubts on the way through.The play, though, with its cast playing multiple Shakespearean roles, certainly needs Stratford.

Victoria's older self narrates the play, or at least appears from time to time sounding oracular. We actually begin before her birth, at the deathbed of her grandfather, the supposedly mad George III, surrounded by squabbling relatives. It seems to be modelled on a similar scene near the beginning of Richard III; and the play turns out to be riddled with Shakespearean echoes. Some of these are obvious to the point of being crass: "To flee or not to flee, that is the question," says a princess about to leave the country. Some are outright arcane; a nobleman's doxy called Jaquenetta gives birth in the streets. Jaquenetta is the name of the wench left pregnant at the end of Love's Labour's Lost.

What's more, most of the play is written in verse. Maybe all of it is. Some passages sound iambic; a few indubitably rhyme. I suspect that Hinton is not the author destined to rescue English verse drama from the irrelevance in which it has languished, almost without interruption, for some 350 years, but he can certainly muster the odd vivid image. A boy in an orphanage, where sodomy and flagellation are prevailing practices, bares his bum to show what he calls "welts as high as hot-cakes."

Much of the time, though, the style is estrangingly archaic. I'm sure Hinton doesn't need me to tell him that phrases like "fie, fie" or "hie thee to somewhere-or-other" or even "I know not how to turn" were hardly colloquial speech circa 1820; he is obviously trying for Elizabethan sonority. It's the opposite of Elizabethan, though; those playwrights' genius was to make an artificial form sound like natural speech, which is why their plays have survived. Hinton's dense, artificial style is quite hard to follow, and his storytelling doesn't help. There is a lengthy section in the middle of the first act that, while you're watching it, is virtually incomprehensible; it's a flashback that incorporates its own flash- forward. In the second act its relevance to the rest of the action is, piece by piece, revealed; and there's a definite feeling of release. Whether the later satisfaction outweighs the earlier frustration must be a matter of personal taste, but my advice to audiences is, hang in there.

I had better try to explain the title, as far as I can. Young Victoria, a snippy and studious teenager oppressed by mother and governess, says she will call the play (and she may mean this play, or a play within it, or both) The Swanne, because that's what ugly ducklings grow into. She may be referring to herself; she may not.

But the play is full of swans. The unfortunate Jaquenetta is described in the cast list as "a Swanne-marked woman"; and the toff who marked her is billed as "Minister of the Royal Order of the Swanne." A dish of roast swan is produced at one point, and a poor woman refuses to eat it. This seems to be an ultimate faux pas ("You mean to say you don't like swan?") but considering what the gentry get up to, she's probably justified.

As for The Death of Cupid; the young god of love appears to Victoria at one point, but it's one of the play's obscurer interludes. The general message, though, appears to be that pre- Victorian society is in the business of destroying love, and that only a few people, mostly in the lower orders, are interested in preserving it. It's the rich what gets the pleasure, it's the poor what gets the blame. You must have heard that before; it's the same the whole world over.

So: An extravagantly jerry-built piece in a largely sterile style, set nearly 200 years ago in a faraway country of which we know little. Why should we care? Well, an audience cares about a play if the author does, or at least if he cares enough. Hinton obviously cares inordinately; the sheer scale of his enterprise is proof of that, besides being an attraction in itself.

He has obviously fallen in love with the period,or with his own free interpretation of it. He often forgets that we know less about it than he does (casual references to the Peterloo Massacre and the Cato Street Conspiracy will leave most Canadian spectators forgivably baffled) and he has given his fictitious characters mirthless quasi-Dickensian names like Bobber Squich (oppressed) and St. John Voranguish (oppressor). In the end, though, you happily join him in the labyrinth.

The cast, several of whom either extend or excel themselves, are there before you. The author is also the director; his staging is excellent and he seems to have put the actors, with one lamentable exception, at perfect ease with the text.

The most memorable character, logically in so consciously theatrical a piece, is an actress: an old, blind, bald tragedy- queen, known as The Scarecrow, who arrives late and then virtually takes the show over; Diane D'Aquila, having already played a commanding hairless monarch in Elizabeth Rex, is even better here for being allowed absurdity as well as authority.

The next-best scene is a dagger-sharp confrontation between a sedan-bound King George and his eternal Prince Regent son; Prinny is Bernard Hopkins, who has rarely been better, and his old man is Ian White, who has never been better. Lucy Peacock transforms herself unrecognizably as the cockney wet-nurse who is the play's moral touchstone; Domini Blythe's quizzical blend of economy and integrity shines through three separate roles and three separate accents.

The young Victoria is Sarah McVie, who is sedately inquisitive; the older one is Lally Cadeau, whom I hope will let up on the booming in future episodes.

Margot Dionne, a returned Stratford luminary, also pushes mannerism -- in her case, a twittering primness -- to excess in her major role, but contributes a hauntingly still cameo as Mrs. Fitzherbert, the most noted royal ex-floozie since Nell Gwyn.

There are others, too, whom we will doubtless get to know some of better later on; the story will probably continue to double back on itself. I look forward to tuning in next season.

Black & White Photo: Courtesy Stratford Festival / Diane D'Aquila (left), as the Scarecrow, and Seun Olagunj as William. ;

RICHARDTHESECOND

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, Toronto

Matthew MacFadzean is an electric young actor, best known for playing toughs. He is very sharp and fluent, capable of infusing his lines with maximum colour and lucidity while operating at maximum speed. This quality comes in very useful in richardthesecond, a monologue that he has written himself and that often operates at the abstract level of music.

At least it does for me, because for much of the time I had very little idea what MacFadzean was talking about. His play comes out of a pop high-tech world from which I am at least a generation removed. His style and assurance as an actor, though, seem to carry over into his writing, so I feel inclined to cut him a lot of slack. He plays Richard the Excellent, a media-soaked raver (I guess that's tautological) whose preoccupations are reflected in Rebecca Brown's production by the presence of a couple of hyperactive video screens. MacFadzean has the stage to himself, but the screens allow some other actors to phone in performances. One of them gives a funny performance as a television news reporter putting stupid questions to young Richard and getting wiseass answers. I could be wrong, but I think this is one of Richard's fantasies.

Another is to identify himself with Shakespeare's Richard II; the show's opening and closing image is of our hero, seated, with a mirror ball and a Star Wars blade in place of the monarch's orb and sceptre. MacFadzean's thesis, lucidly stated in a program note, is that both Richards gain in awareness as their worldly fortunes sink. There is quite a difference, though, in what the two figures have to give up. Shakespeare's Richard forfeits real temporal power; MacFadzean's loses only popularity, and most of that he seemed to be imagining. In other words, MacFadzean's Richard is a much lower case, which probably explains why he is spelled in lower case.

He meets up -- on video -- with a spooky scientist; Gene is his name and genes are his game. He looks -- on video -- remarkably like John Lithgow. (I spent some time wondering whether the actor playing him actually was John Lithgow. I then noticed him sitting, in person, at the end of the row in front of me, and decided that -- since nobody was swarming him for autographs -- he probably wasn't. For the record, his name is David Francis.) Richard volunteers for an experiment of Gene's in, I think, cloning. Cloning is certainly mentioned; Richard even fantasizes, very amusingly, about what it might be like to have sex with his own clone. (At last, a partner who will know what he wants.) But all ends badly, or at least disillusioningly, leaving Richard carrying on not unlike the lobotomized hero of A Clockwork Orange. The story also recalls the futile rock-star-as-messiah fables that used to be so fashionable (Stardust, Performance, Tommy, and something with Paul Jones), though it's sharper than any of them.

Some easy targets like advertising and consumerism are amusingly assaulted, and MacFadzean has the admirable gift of satirizing a culture from a position deep within it. He also, all-importantly, has rhythm. In fact he has two rhythms, since at the end -- going further to meet me than I could go to meet him -- he goes into Richard II's despairing speech of self-realization in Pomfret prison, and does it admirably, continually coming up with new readings that make perfect sense. Stratford should snap him up: always assuming, of course, that he -- like his richard -- wants to be snapped.

Black & White Photo: Buddies in Bad Times Theatre / Unlike the Shakespearian Richard II, Matthew MacFadzean plays a raver and uses a mirror ball in place of the monarch's orb. ;
2002-10-19-hello-muddah-hello-fadduh-hel:
rcushman@nationalpost.com

The songs of Allan Sherman have come to town in a show called Hello Muddah, Hello Fadduh, and the title at least must be familiar. It's been in the North American bloodstream since 1963, when a comedy record of that name made No. 2 in the U.S. charts.

The song was the plaintive letter home of a boy whose parents had abandoned him to the mercies of summer camp. Since it was set to a very familiar tune -- Ponchielli's Dance of the Hours -- it was thought of as a parody-lyric, though it would be hard to say exactly what it was a parody of. The original, after all, has no words.

Lyric and music, seemingly incongruous, were a perfect match, rising and falling together: a deadpan list of complaints taking up the main melodic strain, then turning to an anguished plea ("take me home") that subsided into anguished blubbering ("please don't make me stay/I've been here one whole day.") Child or parent, everybody could relate.

The record's appeal crossed the Atlantic. I was commencing as an English undergraduate at exactly this time, and my contemporaries used to adapt the words to our own situation; we parodied the parody. (You're lucky; I can't remember any of our lyrics.)

The composer-performer was Allan Sherman. This was a name unknown to us, though as an inveterate haunter of record stores I soon became more familiar with it. He seemed to have three LPs to his name: all of them, I assumed, spin-offs from that initial hit. Apparently, though, I had this backwards. Hello Mudduh was a track from his third album, My Son the Nut.

Sherman had had a productive but checkered career as a deviser and producer of TV game and talk shows, but the early '60s found him out of work. He had been breaking his friends up with new words to popular songs, but when a record company finally took him up on the idea, it decided that life would be a lot cheaper if he were to attach himself to melodies that were in the public domain. So his first album was called My Son the Folk Singer. In between, a little prematurely, there had been My Son the Celebrity.

Investigation of the Sherman albums revealed further riches. Some of the songs I preferred to Hello Mudduh, partly because the executives occasionally relented and let him use better tunes. (Dance of the Hours really is an atrociously glutinous piece of classical lollipoppery.) I was especially fond of Sherman's adaptation of You Came a Long Way from St. Louis, which he turned into a primer on the French Revolution titled You Went the Wrong Way, Old King Louis. Actually this one has two great tunes, because its introductory verse appropriates the Marseillaise. Try singing along with this:

Louis the 16th was the King of France

In 1789.

He was worse than Louis the 15th.

He was worse than Louis the 14th.

He was worse than Louis the 13th.

He was the worst

Since Louis the First.

It may not be quite historically accurate (the assessment, I mean; the chronology is impeccable) but it's certainly funny. And notice how the rhyme snaps shut on the last line.

That song isn't in the show, but another of my exotic favourites is: a joyously literal interpretation of the Mexican Hat Dance ("but the Mexicans dance on your hat"), which manages to specify a different type of headgear in each stanza: like Irving Berlin, in You Can't Get a Man with a Gun, ticking off every known variety of firearm.

For the most part though, the show Hello Muddah, concentrates on domestic situations like the one depicted in its title song: "the kind of important moments in people's lives," according to Douglas Bernstein "that everybody can identify with."

Bernstein, who talked to me this week from his home in New York, is one of the two creators of the musical; the other is Rob Krausz, who also directs. It was done off-Broadway in 1992, and revived there last year. Krausz rediscovered the Sherman albums when his mother told him he had to clean out his old bedroom (a very Shermanesque situation) and shared his enthusiasm with Bernstein, whom he'd known since high school. The question then became: Did they try and find someone to impersonate Sherman. Or, in Bernstein's words, "do we have a big man with a crew cut and dark glasses, and fat, sitting in the middle of the stage, or do we tell a story?"

They went with the story: The saga of Barry Bockman and Sarah Jackman (whom Sherman once serenaded to the tune of Frere Jacques) who progress from birth through courtship, marriage, parenthood -- not all the way to death, but at least as far as Florida.

It's a classic Jewish-American trajectory, and certainly when Sherman first made his mark he was seen as an ethnic comedian: Alan King set to music. The titles of those albums, with their implicit obeisance to the classic Jewish mother, are evidence of that. They weren't being marketed to just a Jewish audience, though. This, as Bernstein says, was a time "when being Jewish was cool": when the hip comics were Mort Sahl and Lenny Bruce and (much the closest to Sherman, and not only for reasons of euphony) Shelley Berman.

Of course, Jews had always constituted a huge proportion of American comedians but until now those who became nationally famous had kept quiet about it.

The situation now is different again: Jerry Seinfeld's Jewishness is unmistakable -- far more than that of, say, Danny Kaye's -- but he has never, as far as I know, made any explicit comic use of it.

Sherman was, in his way, a pioneer: even a comer-out. He was one of those who found that Jewish suburban comedy could retain its local colouring, even emphasize it in a modest way, and still be understood. The family situations, after all, are universal. Before making its New York debut, Hello Muddah tried out in Phoenix and Kansas City, towns where, as Bernstein, notes, "there is not a large Jewish population." There were no problems.

Sherman's own moment was rather brief. He died in 1973, of problems connected with being overweight; he had also divorced, and his last years had apparently not been happy. Fashion has passed him by; his parodies assumed a situation in which Broadway and Tin Pan Alley were the musical lingua franca; and his whole gentle sensibility was pre-rock.

But if he himself was forgotten, Hello Muddah, the song, stayed around. Like all Sherman's best songs, it's a work of craftsmanship. Like some other comedy writers (Stan Freberg, Mel Brooks) he turned out to be a natural-born lyricist. Most musical parodies repeat a single joke; Sherman's tell stories.

Until Jan. 5. Box office: 416-872-1111. robertcushman@lycos.com

HELLO MUDDAH, HELLO FADDUH!

New Yorker Theatre, Toronto

Years ago in New York, I sat in on some auditions for what turned out to be a legendary flop musical, an item called Dance a Little Closer: lyrics by Alan Jay Lerner, who was absent that day, and music by Charles Strouse (Bye Bye Birdie, Annie), who was present. One applicant impressed everyone with an unknown song titled Juggling that lived up to its title in the dexterity with which it sustained its metaphor for the plight of a philandering husband. It turned out to be a cut song from an un-legendary flop musical called The Fig Leaves Are Falling, whose lyrics were by Allan Sherman. Upon hearing this information, Strouse slapped his thigh and said, Every lyric by Allan that Ive ever heard has been brilliant.

Sherman is better known, of course, as the author of comedy lyrics set to pre-existing tunes, the most famous being Hello Muddah, Hello Fadduh, which lends its name to the anthology of his songs that has now arrived in Toronto after two separate runs in New York. Juggling, alas, is not included in this show, but three other songs from Fig Leaves are thrown in toward the end, notably one of those what-has-it-all-been-for ballads, Did I Ever Really Live? It has an admirably terse lyric that steers clear of melodrama, and it might well be powerful in the right context.

It isn't in the right context here. Hello Muddah has been equipped with a story -- a man's life from cradle to within sight of the grave -- but that life seems to be so extraordinarily free of major trauma that the song seems pointless. Did he he ever really live? Not dramatically he didnt.

The show was put together by Rob Krausz, who also directs, and Douglas Bernstein, a skilled lyricist in his own right. If youre talking about parody lyrics, Bernstein once co-wrote a spoof of one of the songs from A Chorus Line that is funnier than all the editions of Forbidden Broadway put together. The script they have provided here is admittedly and intentionally the slightest, a succession of gag-filled pretexts for moving us from song to song.

But it's still a book musical, and that genre comes with its own built-in rules. Even if the book is just there to provide a framework for the songs, it should provide one that allows them to make sense. Alarmingly, Hello Muddah fails to do this even for the familiar numbers that are its reason for being.

Our hero's name is Barry Bockman, and he delivers his first song from his high chair. Its addressed to the little girl he will eventually marry; both she and the song are called Sarah Jackman, the tune being that of Frere Jacques. The song sends deadpan greetings to all the members of Sarahs very extended Jewish family. It may sound cute coming out of the mouths of babes, but it doesn't sound right.

Then there's the title number, that deathless musicalization of a boys desperate letter home from summer camp. Thats destroyed, too. "I've been here one whole day" wails the lyric, but here it's preceded (and interrupted) by dialogue suggesting that not only is it not young Barrys first day at the dreaded Camp Granada, it isnt even his first year. Some of the original's best lines have been cut, and the punchline -- a perfectly poised ending to a perfectly constructed lyric -- has been defused.

One thing that's unavoidably missing is the authors own voice. The song became a hit, 40 years ago, in Shermans own recording. He conveyed the boy's sensibility perfectly but made no attempt actually to impersonate him. Obviously, this option is not available to an actor, but without this kind of distancing effect the songs, which are slight, tend to wither.

It's even worse with numbers that were written to reflect no sensibility other than their authors; the spirit, that is, of an observant Borscht Belt comic, happily immersed in both domesticity and show business but wryly aware of their follies. These are smart songs, and they cannot convincingly be sung by dumb people. Shermans setting of the Mexican Hat Dance, tongue-twisting and devilishly rhymed, is here murderously entrusted to the hero's monstrous shopping fiend of a mother-in-law, on the pretext that she has just returned from a holiday south of the border. (A built-in hazard of this kind of show, for those who know the catalogue that's being plundered, is that you can see the songs coming from some way off. Sometimes you see them coming but they fail to arrive, leaving you to feel haunted by the ghosts of numbers that perished on the road.) This show came before Mamma Mia!, which uses the same cut- and-paste technique, but it hurts more here because Shermans songs, unlike Abbas, aren't junk.

There are a few occasions on which the numbers and the narrative actually match, and they feel like blessings. Grow, Mrs. Goldfarb (think glow, little glow-worm) was written in character as a husband's admiring commentary on the eating habits of his spectacularly overweight wife, and thats how its done here, with gentle precision, in contrast to the many numbers in which the staging, the acting and the sound system appear to be in a conspiracy to upstage the material. Also good is Crazy Downtown, in which a mature Barry and Sarah lie awake in the suburbs waiting for their teenage daughter to get home. The Ballad of Harry Lewis (who was "tramping through the warehouse where the drapes of Roth were stored") is a rousing closer, if you can accept a finale tribute to a character we haven't met before.

But other songs die on the vine. When Sherman rewrote Shine On, Harvest Moon as Shine On, Harvey Bloom, an ode to an astronaut, all the fun was in the pun. He might just as well have stopped after the first couple of lines (as he memorably did in such squibs as hello, young lovers, you're under arrest). Turning Mr. Bloom senior into Barrys employer, just so he can be dragged on stage to sing the whole song to nobody in particular, is an act of desperation.

It isnt the only one. The tone of the script is set early on when Barry and Sarah go to school. Their teacher refers to that great book The Canterbury Tales "by Cantor Barry." Apart from being a lousy philistine joke, this plunges us into a world of, to be polite, fantasy that has nothing to do with Sherman, who got his laughs from exaggerating reality. It also suggests that, contrary to all those rye bread ads, you do have to be Jewish.

Actually, I have nothing against ethnically stereotyped humour, as long as it's funny. The authors do come up with a few neat lines, but much of the show is stifling, especially a grossly protracted wedding scene. (The first-night audience lapped it up, but I don't think that does them any credit.) If this is meant to be the story of Barrys life then surely, somewhere in the course of it, he must have met at least one Gentile. Ghetto comedy loses its edge when the characters are no longer living in a ghetto.

Barry himself is given a charmingly tousled performance by Darren Baker, and Sandy Winsby offers an object lesson in the virtues of dry understatement. (He plays an accountant, and looks like one.) Everybody else tries far too hard; Jimmy Spadola, playing a relative whom even his relatives find irritating, almost makes a virtue out of shamelessness, but not quite.

Probably the best part of the show is a curtain-call medley, in which the performers step out of character and simply sock the numbers across. This is invigorating, and allows you to appreciate the songwriters gusto and craftsmanship, as well as his flair for attaching himself to catchy tunes. Charles Strouse was right: Sherman was a first-rate lyricist, born to write musicals, and it was Broadway's loss as well as his own that, after the fig leaves had fallen, he never got another chance.
