THE MIRACLE WORKER

Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People, Toronto

There are certain plays I would rather see at a young peoples theatre than anywhere else, even though they may originally have been written for grown-ups. The Diary of Anne Frank, which was given an excellent production at Torontos YPT a few years ago, is one of them; William Gibson's The Miracle Worker, the current attraction, is another.

Both belong in the category of humanitarian warhorses, well- crafted but simplistic. The Anne Frank play has to strain a bit to extract a hopeful message from the Holocaust but manages, at least in its original Broadway version, to send the audience home with the heroine's belief in the essential goodness of the human race ringing in their hearts. The Miracle Worker has an easier task, coming as it does with a historically certified upbeat ending.

As everybody knows, its the story of how the child Helen Keller, stricken by an illness that left her both deaf and blind, was rescued from darkness and silence by an indomitable 22-year-old teacher named Annie Sullivan. Annie had once been blind herself and had been raised in an orphanage. She could not teach Helen to see but she could teach her to speak and to love -- or at least to express the love that presumably had boiled within her during all the years in which she had lived like an animal, both the pet and the terror of her helplessly indulgent family.

The plays climax comes when Annie, after a long series of mental and physical battles, succeeds, almost beyond her dreams, in getting Helen to pronounce the word "water" -- the very same word that, as a brightly precocious infant, she had learned to speak before tragedy struck. Now she not only utters the word, she connects it to its meaning. This breakthrough comes, in the play, at the end of an unusually crowded day in which Annie has had to battle not only with Helen but with Helen's relatives. The Kellers, an old Virginia family still mentally re-fighting the Civil War, are divided against one another, and within themselves as well. Annie snatches victory from defeat with astonishing dramatic neatness. Her victory is, always and undeniably, moving. It is also, as the author arranges it, glib.

Annie is determined at all costs to spare Helen the institutional hell in which she herself grew up; the point is made through a series of aural flashbacks involving a brother who died there and whose voice, accusing her of desertion, continues to haunt her dreams. Meanwhile the Kellers try to deal with the monster in their midst: not the silent, violent child but the self-opinionated Irish Yankee they have hired to take care of her. Captain Keller (Confederate Army, retired; now in business) is on his second marriage, and he seems in danger of losing and misunderstanding both his children. His son by his first wife is a sarcastic cub who, of course, really craves his father's love. Critics have, in general, written these domestic scenes off as a total loss, and they certainly seemed like hopeless padding in the one previous production (in London, about 10 years ago) that I have witnessed.

Leah Cherniaks production, though, does surprisingly well by them. Greg Ellwand is credibly gruff as the Captain who never knows whether his dignity lies in supporting Annie or firing her. Stephanie Belding beams appropriately as the angel in his house, weak when hes strong and vice versa; and Paul Braunstein is excellent as the redeemable rat of a son who wanders through the play like a subplot waiting to happen.

In other respects the performance is less happy. Cherniak's YPT production of Anne Frank was grippingly claustrophobic (which admittedly comes with the territory); this time, though, her staging rambles. The first half seems to go forever, maybe because it combines the first two acts of what was planned as a three-act play, with cliff-hanging curtains carefully provided. Charlotte Dean's set -- a little house on the prairie masquerading as a modestly fine Southern mansion -- looks pretty enough, but its crannies and levels fillet the action into inaccessible little bits. What may be the crucial scene of the play -- Annies fight to get Helen to fold her dinner napkin -- is confined to a corner of the stage; the centre is occupied by the rest of the cast, standing in the half-light, looking uncertain how or whether to react.

Thus confined, the central conflict lacks its full blood- curdling effect; and the production seems anyway to be pulling its punches. As Helen, Mary Krohnert does efficiently all that is required of her, but there is not much individuality in her tantrums, and correspondingly little joy in her release from them. As Annie, Carmen Grant is tart, bold and occasionally witty, but there is little glow in her determination. She is more forceful when laying down the law to Helens household than in confronting the child herself. There is little chemistry between these two, and the impact is a fraction of what it might be.

Or maybe this is a play that only works the first time you see it. There are certainly no subtleties to be revealed at further viewings. (I sympathize with my colleagues who apparently have had to sit through it dozens of times.) That's what makes it ideal for a young audience, or rather what makes a young audience ideal for it. It is also informative without being patronizing, and this production enhances our education by projecting photographs of Helen's later triumphant progress. It shows us little, though, of what happened to Annie. And thereby hangs an oddity. The name of Helen Keller is rightly talismanic. The name of Annie Sullivan -- despite the enduring and worldwide success of this play celebrating her and named in her honour -- is still, to most people, unknown.

SWOLLEN TONGUES

Factory Studio, Toronto

In days when rhyming couplets were the rage,

They weren't much used upon the comic stage.

John Dryden and his Restoration friends

Found couplets ideal for satiric ends,

In lampoons written for a readers gaze;

And when the call went out for tragic plays,

Heroick Couplets were the style they cherished

For showing warriors who loved, then perished.

But as for comedies, when penning those,

Dryden and Co. did their best stuff in prose.

So Kathleen Oliver, poet, of Vancouver

Executes an unparalleled manoeuvre

When, in a play called Swollen Tongues -- her first --

She gives us comedy thats rhyming-versed.

(Translations from the French, however free,

Don't count; and nor, if you are asking me,

Does Caryl Churchill's tone-deaf Serious Money;

While Steven Berkoffs plays -- no, its not funny.)

I have one disappointment, I confess:

I'd hoped for comedy in modern dress

To match the modern words the author uses,

Some cutting comment on our time's abuses.

But were in period-comedy penitentiary

With costumes bought in from the 17th century.

Or maybe from the 18th. But, whatever,

The settings somewhere between now and never.

The themes that power Oliver's two hours' traffic

Are language, lust and love: some straight, some Sapphic.

Catherine wants Sonja, and woos her with verse;

Thomas the same, but Thomas verse is worse.

Thomas is Catherines brother; they've a tutor,

A Doctor Wise, who's Catherines secret suitor --

Though this last twist is wheeled into position

A bare two minutes before intermission.

A twist and a half, to no ones great surprise

The Doc's a woman, in a man's disguise.

(Were glad she sheds it; frankly she looked weird

In gown, specs, moustache and the briefest beard.)

One thinks of Candide, though more apropos

Would be the artifice of Marivaux.

(His gender-bending, though, is somewhat tearful.

While Oliver scorns bitter-sweet; shes cheerful.)

The English Restoration's undertext

Is here explored: Its sex farce is bisexed.

Shakespeare, as usual, also haunts our minds:

The Bacchae, too, because young Thomas finds

A new dimension in himself when set up

(You have to be there) in an Amazon's get-up.

In fact, all dramas here, as in a mirror. No,

I havent finished; did I mention Cyrano?

Lovers face off in poetry-contest fashion,

As if facility were a gauge of passion.

I find this dubious; but the mood's ironic,

And overall the author's tones a tonic.

Some flaws: Rhymes that are best described as "nearly,

Sentence inversion where the author clearly

Around the words has turned to meet the rhyme,

And padding -- Lord, she does this all the time.

Well, some of it: Her first line ends in work,"

And on its tail, gratuitously, comes "shirk.

What recommends her most to our attention

Is: She gets laughs -- usually by declension.

That is, shell step from staid and pedagogical

Down to the slangy or the scatological.

It's a tough life; and if she isn't Pope

Shes still a cardinal talent, a white hope.

The production is by Necessary Angel:

A venerated troupe on whom a changell

Quickly be visited, since Richard Rose,

Their founder and director, shortly goes

To the equivalent post at Tarragon.

In fact, he's there already. (He's a paragon.)

But in this period of overlap

Hes staged the present play, with all the snap

It merits. David Boechlers set's effective,

Especially in matters of perspective.

Among the cast, Ben Carlson's very fine,

Hitting the mark with Thomas every line.

He comes across as delicate, yet blubbery,

Even in hulking drag, out in the shrubbery.

None of the others is a perfect fit,

Though far more often than they miss, they hit.

Melody Johnsons cool can be sublime,

But she might vary it from time to time.

She's Sonja, self-proclaimed a happy slut.

Catherine's Karen Hines, bubbling but

A little over-eager. Nancy Palk,

As hinted earlier, talks much happier talk

And smiles more winning smiles, when Dr W.

Says, in effect, Let it no longer trouble you:

Im female." The play gains a firmer touch;

That choice of ambiguities was too much.

They end by welcoming us to "Lesbania;

I cant see why they don't say Lesbiania."

It would scan better and make better sense.

And, at the risk of sitting on the fence,

I liked the language, relished the best rhymes

(And eat your hearts out, Buddies in Bad Times)

And yet I left, aware of something lacking:

The play is weightless, less a feast than snacking

But it's a rich snack: rollicking and chic,

And -- at this point in history -- unique.

TWO WORDS

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

Two Words tells two stories. Both touch contemporary nerves while having the aroma, if not the actual credentials, of folklore. Originally set down by Chilean writer Isabel Allende, they have been combined into a play by Denise Blinn and Gabrielle Kemeny and staged by the multicultural Cahoots company. Blinn is also the director.

The Colonel, a successful though illiterate politician, is discovered in bed with his mistress, on whom he is dependent for the telling of stories. He craves one, it seems, every night. His lover used to sell her words in the marketplace, and she sold the Colonel two (unheard, of course, by us) that enabled him to win the election.

The story she tells now -- the tale within the tale -- concerns a judge, upright but implacable, who tries to entrap Nicholas Vidal, a famous local bandit, by locking his mother, a former prostitute, in a cage and leaving her there, in the heat of the town square, without food or water. Nicholas, the judge's mirror image, declines to ride to her rescue. The two are playing a game somewhere between poker and Russian roulette, and they are perfectly matched opponents. The mother commits suicide. The judge, who has refused appeals for mercy from the entire town, is forced to flee with his family. Nicholas intercepts them. Their survival depends on the bandit being seduced by the judges wife, previously an icicle.

The Colonel, hearing the story, identifies with the judge. Both fables, too, depict authoritarian men who find themselves in the power of women. But the parallels are not very close, and when the two plots finally converge, the effect is more confusing than enlightening. In terms, though, of making us want to know what happens next and of administering intermittent shocks, the adaptation is efficient. The dialogue (the playwrights own invention; there is none in the Allende originals) is appropriately spare and doom-riddled.

The production, however, seems constantly to be promising a richness of imagination it never delivers. It begins splendidly with the actors in the inner story creeping out, hands first, from under the narrator's bed. But nothing that follows matches up, except perhaps for the sight of the woman in the cage, which is a given anyway. There is, too, a preponderance of blank performances. Exceptions are the adaptor Kemeny herself, fittingly cast as South America's tantalizing answer to Scheherezade; Michelle Polak, first sullen, then searing, as the martyred mother; Xuan Fraser, insolently self-possessed as her brigand son; and Simon Casanova, whose fanatic judge might have stepped out of a newsreel.

There are now two plays in Toronto in which utterances crucial to the characters are withheld from the audience. In The Shape of Things, I desperately wanted to know what it was the lovers whispered to one another. But as for the two magic words with which Allende's storyteller empowers the Colonel, I really could not have cared less what they were. Obviously, this is testimony to my greater involvement in one play than in the other. But it also suggests that magic is magic and realism realism, however the two may have been combined in a fashionable formula, and that they have different codes. I resented the silence of Neil LaBute, even while grudgingly admitting he had the right, maybe even the necessity, to keep it. The silence of Two Words, though, is the kind that cannot be broken.

Black & White Photo: Michelle Polak, as a woman locked up to entrap her son, is first sullen, then searing, in this adaptation of two stories by Isabel Allende. ;

BULLY

Theatre Centre, Toronto

This seems to be the theatrical season of Stephen Hawking, the year in which the chairbound genius not only haunts the dreams of playwrights and their characters but bursts right out of them onto the stage. In Andy Jones' recent one-man show about good, evil and Newfoundlanders, an imaginary Hawking is featured, via video screen and sound system, as an occasional disembodied antagonist, his voice, or his voice box, piped in to pull the hero down from his more winsome flights. His role in Bully is more central, and he even appears in the flesh. Even here, though, he is a thing in the protagonist's dream.

Bully is the work of two young playwrights, Stephen Guy-McGrath and Steven Mayoff. As well as being half of the authorship, Guy- McGrath is half of the cast. He plays Eugene Michael Carter 2nd, a 10-year-old boy whose monogram spells out the most celebrated equation in modern science. This must have been a very thoughtful decision on his parents' part, though they haven't done too considerately by him otherwise. His father has left home; his mother spends most of her time bemoaning the fact.

Things are equally bad at school; Eugene is being persecuted by a 12-year-old who used to be his friend, and he ends up being seriously injured. He is a scientifically gifted boy (or, as his ex- mate would say, a geek), and he turns for consolation to imaginary conversations with the author of A Brief History of Time. In the light, if that's the word, of black holes, quantum mechanics and chaos theory he tries to make sense of his own predicament, and to imagine a way out of it. Alex Poch-Goldin plays all the other roles: Eugene's mother, his tormentor, the priestly and (it goes without saying) repressive teacher at his Catholic school, and Hawking.

This is a lively and ingenious piece that never makes full delivery on its promises. Eugene spends much of the play strapped into a harness, poised for flight. We acknowledge the boldness of the image and the intrepidity of the actor, but then we start to wonder what it's there for. We can see that Eugene has a lot to escape from; thoughts of the myth of Icarus invade our minds, and you might argue that Icarus, too, was let down by his dad (though, in all conscience, the old man did his best).

Ted Dykstra, the director, argues forcefully in the program that the play is really about the plight of a boy abandoned by his parents: physically by his father, emotionally by his mother, who thinks she's loving him when what she's actually doing is using him as the sounding board for her own grievances. But this doesn't really come across as central, not with Mr. Carter absent by definition and with the cross-gender casting giving us a Mrs. Carter who is stylized to the point of caricature. And though we can see why Eugene, himself a wheelchair case (we're never sure how seriously), should have adopted Hawking as a fantasy father, our understanding of their relationship is blurred by the fact that most of the time we don't know what they're talking about.

Or maybe I should speak for myself, as somebody who never even tried to read A Brief History of Time, much as I enjoy the title. Early on in this play the authors made me feel as if I really understood the Big Bang theory (though didn't I read somewhere that grave doubts have now been cast on it?), but the euphoria didn't last. I floundered, and so, as far as I was concerned, did the play.

At least, though, theory and dramatic practice unite in the central scenes, the ones showing Eugene's encounters with his playground nemesis, Harry Glassco. Maybe they aren't meant to be as central as all that. The play's title might well serve for any number of well-intentioned docudramas of the kind that get toured to schools. Probably the authors intended it to have a more complex resonance; it's possible to see that, in some sense, Eugene is being bullied by everyone else in both his physical and mental life, and that he is also capable of playing the bully himself. (The ending of the play, if I read it right, is scarifying.)

But in the end it's Harry's behaviour -- what you might call the classic bullying -- that carries the charge. It comes, though, doubly twisted. One variable is the suggestion that the two-year difference in the boys' ages, which once meant nothing, now means everything; if Time is the play's theme, then this is maybe the most striking observation on the subject that it offers. The other is that Eugene, testing out theories of infinite possibility, keeps re- playing the scene in his mind, testing out the different strategies he might have used. Whatever he says or does, the end result is always and ominously the same. What this is meant to prove scientifically I'm not sure, but theatrically it is very economical and very potent.

Guy-McGrath plays a very persuasive and engaging Eugene, victimized but not a victim, and Poch-Goldin complements him as a Harry with a similarly ambiguous glint, vicious but himself unmistakably boxed in. He also does sharp work as Hawking, though he has made some strange vocal choices; as a dream figure this Hawking is allowed both to walk and non-mechanically talk, but the accent he comes out with here is Central European. Did the actor actually want us to think of Dr. Strangelove? Or is this how Eugene, whose actual experience of genius scientists must be fairly limited, would think of him?

Anyway, this is not a squawking Hawking. And it seems to me that to make him a comic figure, as two shows have now done, is the highest and most merited of compliments. It's to acknowledge that his achievements have been so great, and his triumph over his afflictions so complete, that no amount of laughter can detract from them -- to treat him, in fact, like anybody else.

Some terminal thoughts, conceivably scientific: This play has a running time of 60 minutes. That may make it sound modest; nevertheless, it has been in the works since 1999, and has had three workshop productions. For what is presumably its prime outing, it has been staged way out west on Queen in a small basement theatre that, when I saw it on a Saturday night, was less than half full.

Now consider the production's credentials. Dykstra, its director, is one of Toronto's most talented and versatile theatre people: actor, director, composer. Poch-Goldin is one of our most highly rated young actors, and a promising playwright on his own account. They and the authors must wonder at times what it's all for.

That is the occasion as seen through a glass, a half-empty one, darkly. Lighten up. Treat the glass as half-full and it's admirable that they should all be so fully involved, and that a show worth catching should be there to be caught. Guy-McGrath and Mayehoff are clearly writers (and Guy-McGrath an actor) to watch. Bully for all of them.

Black & White Photo: Dean Baldwin, Theatre Centre / Stephen Guy- McGrath is Eugene, and Alex Poch-Goldin is everyone else, in this story of a scientifically gifted boy who finds solace in physics. ;

WOMEN WHO TALK TOO MUCH AND THE MICROPHONES THAT LOVE THEM

Poor Alex Theatre, Toronto

In this racket, you try to keep an open mind. Still, the very title of Micki Moore's one-woman show places a severe strain on anyone's reserves of faith, hope and charity. The first line of her actual performance wipes them out. She comes on stage, purporting to be a faded film star desperate for a comeback, and moans, in an intercontinental sort of voice, "I no longer vant to be alone."

That's about as witty as the evening gets. Moore's Garbo impersonation (why, at this late date in the history of civilization, would anybody want to do such a thing?) reaches its climax when she reveals that her career foundered, as recently as 1939, when she lost out to Vivien Leigh, whom she accurately describes as "wasp-waisted," for the role of Scarlett in Gone with the Wind. Well, that's news for cineastes. As a kicker she offers her own Central European take on one of Scarlett's most celebrated lines: "As God is my witness, I'll never go through Hungary again."

Moore not only performs this stuff, she wrote it.

Her subsequent vignettes are a little more up-to-date but are no more enlivening. She portrays a series of women who make public speeches with lamentable results. A tipsy mother at her son's bar mitzvah reveals her true feelings about her husband. (First the wedding scene in Hello Muddah, Hello Fadduh, now this. We've suffered enough. Or, as Mort Sahl is said to have said when the movie Exodus wound into its third hour, "Let my people go.") A lady convict sings the blues, but I've blotted most of this one out. A Presbyterian fundraiser reveals an innocent addiction to pornography and tries to get her congregation to invest in same; she also carries on a peculiarly unhilarious telephone conversation with her broker. An English aristocrat talks about celibacy and how often she's taken it up. (She is announced as Lady Penelope the Third. Call me an Anglocentric snob, but I have to point out that members of the English nobility -- unlike reigning monarchs and certain American millionaires -- do not have numbers after their names.) What all these women have in common is a propensity for dropping supposedly titillating hints about their sex lives, physical or mental. This may be a theme, but it seems more like a tic.

After each monologue, captions inscribed on a screen tell us on just which terrible TV shows the various ladies continued to make their confessions. Lest we miss anything, this information is also read aloud by a deep male voice -- very slowly.

For her last turn Moore portrays a Southern belle who married well, came to Canada and changed her originally Jewish name to Micki Moore. So it's autobiographical, though not, I would guess, very closely. Moore's own career has mainly been as a journalist and broadcaster; she conducts seminars on How to Be a Television Talk- Show Host. (Hey, that might make a show.) Her theatrical experience seems to have been limited, so for her to undertake a solo stage performance might be considered brave. Taking as her subject matter a parade of female narcissists strikes me as foolhardy. Vanity, vanity: All is vanity.

Black & White Photo: Before writing and staging her one-woman show, Micki Moore's career had mainly been as a journalist and broadcaster -- and it shows. ;
2002-11-08-the-return-of-the-king-actor-:
robertcushman@lycos.com Profile of Christopher Plummer.

For nearly 50 years now Christopher Plummer has been the right man in Canadian theatre at the right time. I am thinking particularly of his association with the Stratford Festival, and of his return there this year, in the festival's own 50th season, to play King Lear. He was last there in 1996, in Barrymore, but somehow that doesnt quite count. It was virtually a one-man play (the one other actor delivered his entire performance from offstage) and it was a semi-commercial production that had no organic relationship to the rest of the season. Also, it was done at the Avon, and Plummer had always been identified with the Festival Theatre platform stage - - which, in his glory days at the festival, was the only Stratford stage there was.

Plummers last appearance on that stage -- his last until now in Stratford Shakespeare -- was as Antony in Antony and Cleopatra, back in 1967. That's quite a gap, but somehow Plummer has remained a presence at Stratford and a presence in Canada. (He is in Toronto to receive an honorary doctorate from Ryerson University and to address the graduating class this afternoon at 2:30 in the Ryerson Theatre.) That is partly because he's on the Stratford board of governors and has been a faithful member of the audience. It also has to do with his unique position in the festivals history. He first appeared there in 1956, Stratfords fourth season and its last in the tent that preceded the building of a permanent theatre. He had actually auditioned for the first season in 1953, but Tyrone Guthrie, the director, had turned him down. Not, apparently, for any perceived lack of talent; it was more a matter of temperament. About the time he was doing Barrymore in New York, Plummer told me that Guthrie had thought me a bit of a playboy." He added: "He was absolutely right.

It was Guthrie's successor, Michael Langham, who invited Plummer to Stratford. He was already somewhat established outside Canada; indeed, he was on Broadway, acting with Julie Harris in Jean Anouilh's Joan of Arc play The Lark. The part that brought him to Stratford was the title role in Henry V. This made him, in his own words, the first Canuck to lead the company." (It had previously been headed by visiting luminaries such as Alec Guinness and James Mason.) It was Langhams first production as director of the festival, the start of what is to date its longest and probably most distinguished regime, and the Stratford careers of Langham and Plummer were to reman intertwined, right down to the 1967 Antony, which ended an era for both of them.

The Henry V was a historic production in several ways. With Quebecois actors playing the French roles, it seemed -- as the two warring countries made peace in the last scene -- to symbolize Canadas own hopes for national unity (1956, remember). And there at the centre of it was a 26-year-old actor with a clear shot at international stardom and with, as Langham described it, "the chemistry of a romantic classical actor -- a lot of sex, great charm, a natural comedic gift. In Plummer's own words, the Henry V zapped my career. From that time on, my name was above the title."

That cannot literally have been the case at Stratford, which has generally been very alphabetic and democratic about these things. But over the next 10 years he was undoubtedly the festival's star -- Stratfords, and therefore North Americas, top classical actor. He was Stratford's first Hamlet and Macbeth; he took in supporting character roles such as Sir Andrew Aguecheek (Twelfth Night) and Bardolph (Henry IV); and he especially shone -- in fact, glistened - - in the great swashbuckling roles: Mercutio, the Bastard in King John, Benedick in Much Ado About Nothing, and -- at the apex of panache -- Edmond Rostand's Cyrano de Bergerac. He may have been the last actor to play these characters without seeming implicitly to apologize for them.

Perhaps they connected to his offstage image. Plummer was born in 1929 in Toronto, where, he has said, "the remnants of Prohibition were in the air. I sniffed it at once, at the age of one, and said, This city is not for me. Safely removed to the more congenially cosmopolitan atmosphere of Montreal, he discovered ("when I was 15 and could safely run away from home") the delights of nightclub life, and he credits the great cabaret performers he saw there -- Piaf, Chevalier, Garland, Sinatra -- with awakening his interest in acting. (I couldnt believe all these wonderful people could hold an audience of drunks.)

Once a star he got caught up in the group he has called "the good two-fisted drinkers of our time": an international list that includes Richard Burton, Peter OToole, Albert Finney, Jason Robards Jr. and -- a recent casualty -- Richard Harris. Of them all Plummer, certainly when judged by his work in the classics, has been the great survivor. (He claims that one thing that preserved him is his love of food; he got too hungry to be a really dedicated drinker.)

So we had an actor who put in several rigorous seasons as leading man at Canada's premier theatre, became a movie star and was recognized as such, both on and off screen. (The Sound of Music -- still and perhaps ironically his most famous film -- came out in 1967, the same year as that Stratford Antony. One chapter began as another ended.) He was the local boy made good on a prodigious scale, at home and abroad. The fact that he and Stratford got started about the same time, and that Stratford then practically was Canadian theatre, had something to do with it. Nobody else has had quite the same impact, though Colm Feore and others have come close; William Hutt, the festival's undisputed doyen, is a different kind of actor.

And this year he has been back. Richard Monette, Stratfords director, who as a young actor played Eros to his Antony (we all wanted to become him ... I was in awe of him ... terrified ... little did I know that years later Id be offering him a job), collared him a couple of years ago across a restaurant table in London and told him he should really come back to play Lear or Prospero. He, then, marvelling at his own temerity, ("I wasn't even drunk") asked him if he was perhaps afraid of playing Lear. The answer came back like a flash: No, he wasn't.

Nor does he seem to be. The performance he gave on the August first night was superbly authoritative; it did not come across as the performance of a visiting star. It was obviously a homecoming, and the audience rose to it as such: the work of an actor at home in Shakespeare -- his vocal colour and control were exceptional -- and at home on that stage. (This, in Jonathan Millers production, had its famous facade naked and unadorned. No set designer was named, but in fact it was designed by Tanya Moiseiwitsch -- 50 years ago.)

He was believably this old man, this old king -- subdued for long periods, as if trying to get along with his daughters, then erupting volcanically. And since then, apparently, the performance has only ripened; Monette says that on the last night, on Wednesday, Plummer gave a truly great performance, much larger than it had been at the opening.

Also, it seems, more vulnerable. Domini Blythe, who as Goneril is on the receiving end of this Lears most devastating outburst, had not only never worked with Plummer before, she had never even seen him on stage. She approached the experience with the expected mixture of excitement and trepidation: I had heard that he was extremely temperamental. I'd also heard, though, that he loved women, and would only be difficult with men. In fact, he turned out to be wonderful to everybody -- very kind and non-judgmental.

She thinks his Lear took three or four weeks of performance to solidify. And then "three weeks or so ago, he just flew. It was all highly refined, and he achieved such freedom. At times when I'm on stage with him, he becomes so old and fragile. His eyes look like the eyes -- glazed and dull -- of people Ive seen in residences. Ive been watching him build it. It's not technical, it's organic."

Blythe has an anecdote that may or may not be significant: Chris likes to chat to people backstage at 6:30 or so, for about 10 minutes. And one evening I happened to mention that my dad, whos 80 and adores the play, was over from England and would be in tonight. I also said that Dad had been in Donald Wolfits Lear [Wolfit was the English actor-manager whose Lear was considered by many people to be the best they'd ever seen] in the 1940s, and Christopher's face just changed. He said, That was the first Lear I ever saw. I was 16 and they brought it to His Majestys Theatre in Montreal.' And he asked me where was my father sitting. The next morning, my father told me that Christopher's Lear was the greatest hed seen since Wolfits. And that was the night that he took off, for me.

It may just have been coincidence, of course. But it's good to think that an actor who incarnates a theatrical tradition in Canada should be so in touch with tradition himself. Monette says that "the world may remember him for The Sound of Music, but the theatrical profession will remember him for his classical work." Blythe says "he's one of the few actors who came out of this country who became well-known internationally but still kept the status of a great stage actor." He may even be the only one.

CONTACT

Canon Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - A lot of discontent was stirred up when Contact won the 2000 Tony Award for best Broadway musical. A musical is traditionally made of three things -- speech, song and dance, all delivered live -- and Contact is a show that has little of the first element and nothing at all of the second. It has music, of course, some of it even vocal, but none of it was written specifically for this show, and all of it comes canned, in pre-existing performances.

I think the fuss was unwarranted. Personally, I prefer shows that combine the three ingredients, but those that dont shouldn't be outlawed. For years, after all, Broadway, with a fixed and sickly smile on its face, handed out prizes to imported pop operas with no dialogue and virtually no dancing. Before that time -- 25 years ago - - the late Michael Bennett staged Ballroom, a story musical that was carried along by sensational dances and might well have done without songs. (It could certainly have done without the songs it actually had.) The form devised by Susan Stroman for Contact -- she calls it "a play with dancing" -- is perfectly valid, and was obviously waiting to happen.

How well it has happened is another matter. Contact is a thin mix. It's supposed to be about human contact, or the lack of it; but then, what play or musical isnt? Its actually three playlets with dancing, all of them concerned to some extent with erotic fantasy, though the first two are makeweights.

We begin with Swinging, in which a Fragonard painting comes to life. A high-born young 18th-century lady is decorously disporting herself on a swing, in the company of a complacent and equally well- bred gentleman who might conceivably be her husband. He alights and leaves the stage, to be replaced by a servant who had previously just been hanging around in the chiaroscuro. He takes our heroine higher and faster than she has been before, at least to judge from the delighted little yelps she emits. This morsel of choreographic double entendre is all the piece has to offer, apart from its music. The whole episode is played out to a single tune, Rodgers and Hart's My Heart Stood Still (a nod, perhaps, to traditional Broadway) as sparklingly fiddled by Stephane Grappelli.

Some spirited objections have been registered, not all of them by the Musicians' Union, to this shows borrowing its music from the record library. In theory I too would rather have my theatre music played by musicians who are actually there at the time; in practice, I concede that all the selections in Contact are meant to function as objets trouves, and no pit band would be likely to equal the performances we get here. Besides, I imagine that, at least under New York union rules, the local musicians were handsomely compensated for the rigours of not playing. (And indeed, getting ahead of myself a bit, I was seriously disappointed when the record of Beyond the Sea that gets spun in Contacts third segment turned out not to be Bobby Darin's.)

No words are spoken in Swinging, but there are some in the next item, called Did You Move? They are mainly expletives, delivered by a squat and menacing man who might conceivably be a gangster and who is visiting an Italian restaurant in Queens in 1954. (The program is more specific about this than the show is.) His bile is directed at the staff, for neglecting to bring him rolls, and at his meek and obviously long-suffering wife, for everything. He keeps wandering offstage in search of more nourishment -- this must be a buffet restaurant -- while barking at her not to move. She sits still as a mouse till he disappears, then starts indulging in increasingly vigorous danced flirtations with the waiters, to the sound of romantic music, from Grieg to Bizet. Always the music and the movement stop just in time, until the one time that they don't. This is ingenious and quite suspenseful, especially given Adam Dannheissers brutal performance as the husband. Stromans choreography is inventive, too, though its actual performance never catches fire, Meg Howrey as the wife being a lot better at being demure than at being aflame.

We don't hear any swing music in this piece, though it's conceivable that at that time and place it would still have been played. Its absence deprives the three parts of the evening of a second unifying pun, since the last and most substantial section -- which has the same title as the show -- is built on swing. It presents us with Michael Wiley, a 40-year-old New York ad-man who when he first meet him is receiving his umpteenth industry award but who nevertheless, or therefore, hates his life. He hates it so much that when he gets home he tries to hang himself. He fails; and is transported to a club of which he has previously heard. Its in the downtown meat-packing district, and its habitues pool-shoot by day and swing-dance by night.

The piece resembles the big-ballet numbers that used to wind up 50s movie musicals. The ones in which Fred Astaire or Gene Kelly would wander into some smoky dive and be captivated by some lanky seductress who was invariably unattainable and was usually Cyd Charisse. Michael's nemesis is a girl in a yellow dress who seems to him the incarnation of all he has been missing.

John Weidman's script makes no pretensions to depth, but it scores some fairly sharp points off award ceremonies and Manhattan celebrity and all that they entail. (In Michaels case this includes a barrage of phone calls from his deeply-concerned shrink.) As for the music and dancing: At first the club routines are executed a bit incongruously, to contemporary pop songs; finally, and presumably to demonstrate Michaels surrender to the swing culture, we get to hear Benny Goodman's Sing, Sing, Sing, the one tune without which any swing-related musical would apparently be incomplete. This exposes Stroman's choreography to damaging comparisons with Bob Fosses treatment of the same number; it isnt quite fair -- Stroman is trying to tell a story, while Fosse was having an exuberant abstract ball -- but it still leaves the routine here looking routine. Maybe it had more fizz on Broadway, and maybe the girl in the original yellow dress had more allure than her road-company successor (Colleen Dunn) can muster. As it is, it's difficult to see what Michael, played by Daniel McDonald with the right degree of awkward desperation, is getting so excited about.

Dannheisser reappears as an oracular bartender who bears a disconcerting, though probably intentional resemblance, to Michael Richards in Seinfeld. Thomas Lynch's sets are cavernously effective, both for the club itself which incorporates a louring Hopperish mural presumably held over from an earlier existence, and for the street outside, dominated by a gigantic Dont Walk sign that Michael, naturally, shows no inclination to obey. William Ivey Longs costumes are, as usual, excellent, glorying in cut and colour. The story exerts a modest romantic pull, and swing remains fun. Nevertheless the best part of the entertainment, as often these days, comes at the curtain-call which is a divertissement unto itself; the characters from all three instalments break loose from their moorings and cavort to the reconciling strains of Van Morrison's Moondance -- a newish tune that's good enough to be old.

ALPHONSE

duMaurier Theatre Centre, Toronto

If by some impossible twist of fate, a man crossed paths with the child he used to be, and they both recognized each other, they would both crumple to the ground, the man in despair, the child in terror.

That infinitely suggestive sentence occurs at the outset of Alphonse, a one-actor piece by Montreal writer Wajdi Mouawad. It has been brought to Toronto by the resolutely unpatronizing young people's company Theatre Direct, making a bold and rare incursion into a public theatre.

The earth-shaking confrontation it suggests never actually happens. What the play does is chip away at the idea, producing some fragments that are merely whimsical, others that are haunting. Alphonse is a schoolboy who one day fails to come home. His family - - father, mother, brother and sister -- seem more resigned than worried, but they do notify the police. The inspector is a humane but world-weary fellow who regards the assignment as a welcome change from the sordid criminal cases that usually come his way. He goes to Alphonse's school, interviews his contemporaries. Some of them are indifferent to the missing boy, regard him as a dreamer with no particular aptitude for work or games (other than marbles), but he seems to have had no real enemies and at least one close friend. Or at least a former friend. It appears that, of late, Alphonse has been keeping his distance.

Instead, he has developed a relationship with an imaginary friend, a boy called Pierre-Paul Rene, whom he dreamed one troubled night and who now fills his waking thoughts as well. And what Alphonse is doing, while his parents and siblings sit home for a week implausibly refraining from tearing out either their own hair or one another's, is walking down a country road inventing adventures for Pierre-Paul Rene. His friend can handle adventures, since he is described as "a gentle boy with a one-note voice who is never surprised by anything."

Alphonse himself, about to enter adolescence, is at the stage of being surprised by everything, not always agreeably. Even his first possible girlfriend scares him as much as she fascinates him, or at least his feeling for her does. Alphonse would gladly trade places with Pierre-Paul Rene, and in his mind this is what he does.

He sends Pierre-Paul Rene off on a mission. He is to journey to Pastryburg and confront the evil Flupan, who has stolen all the recipes for cake and turned the cooks into popcorn. The mythology here seems second-hand; besides, it's difficult not to think of Pierre-Paul Rene as a male Dorothy, from The Wizard of Oz, being sent on a mission by Peter Pan, or perhaps, given the schoolroom scenes, by Peter Pan crossed with Adrian Mole. Along the way he meets an old man who asks him the kind of questions ("Why does a tree grow tall? Why does a man grow old? Why does a river run into the sea? Why does the Earth keep turning?") that used to be asked in preachy pop songs and probably still are.

That's the worst of the play, but there is also a best. It comes out in a dark, troubling remark remembered by Alphonse's school friend: "A last dream, in Alphonse's opinion, is a beautiful story to tell." It sets the inspector's mind whirling, and ours, too. There is a magical rhythm in the writing that comes through admirably in Shelley Tepperman's translation, and it is set off well by the incursions of the adult world.

This is the strength, too, of the production. The direction, by Lynda Hill and Alon Nashman, is somewhat prosaic, save for the descent of a magical shower of popcorn, but Nashman's performance, narrating and playing all the characters, is ideal. There is a buoyant, bright-eyed quality about him that summons up both Alphonse and his alter ego. There are also a grace, speed and facility that enable him to change gears without crashing, and a toughness (not hardness) that serves beautifully for the grown-ups, who come over not only as believable people but as believable francophone people. Much of the heart of the play is in them: in the inspector who longs to keep the found Alphonse in the police station for an extra hour, just so the boy will look at him, and in the taxi driver who takes him home and worries about his health.

If the efforts of the adults to enter the mind of a child are more persuasively rendered than the thoughts of the children themselves -- well, the author is an adult, and maybe he is proving his own point. There is an anguish that comes over most of us when we recall pieces of our childhood, or at moments when we look at our own children. The play doesn't quite capture it, but it drops hints.

IN THE WINGS

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

Moment to moment, In the Wings can be very enjoyable, especially in its first and lighter half. It is a play about the theatre, that is largely set in a theatre. In fact, as far as one can tell, it's set in the very same theatre at which its currently playing. The actors seem to be having a good time spoofing themselves and their colleagues, and the first-night audience was more than happy to respond. As somebody once said about that ultimate brother-and- sister play, Tis Pity She's a Whore, the incest was sustained throughout.

It goes deeper, though, than mere in-jokery. In the Wings is based on a novel of the same name by the late Carole Corbeil, and it seems to have been at least partially inspired by a production of Hamlet that happened at Passe Muraille in the brave young days of 1983. The prince was played by Layne Coleman, who is now the director of Passe Muraille and of this production; he was also married to Corbeil. Nicky Guadagni, an actress and a close friend of Corbeil's, has adapted the book for the stage. In the Wings revolves around a projected production of Hamlet, and several of its characters, like Hamlet himself, are carrying the baggage of past relationships.

Most Hamlet-like of all, appropriately, is Allan, the intense and self-conscious young actor who gets cast in the lead. A serious manic-depressive, he is haunted by the memory of his father, up to whom he finds it extremely difficult to live. His Gertrude is Alice, who is trying to come to terms with the recent death of her mother. Old enough to play, if not actually to be, Allans mother, she is now having an affair with him. Jimmy, the director, has cast his own girlfriend as Ophelia. Then there is Robert, who is not part of the production. He is, in fact, a critic whose wife has recently left him and gone off with their son to Vancouver. Robert, rather ineffectually, is chasing an actress-singer called Louise, who happens to be an old flame of Allans, one whom he intermittently re- stokes.

I keep hearing that in the book (which I haven't read) Robert is an evil creature, corrupted by the power he wields. This is a view of critics with which I would not presume to argue (and besides, Corbeil herself was a reviewer before turning to fiction, though I never heard she was a cruel one), but it certainly isn't what appears on the stage. The casting, if nothing else, puts paid to it. If you want malevolence, you dont engage Michael Healey, a performer with an outsize but unemphatic presence who could not be unendearing if he tried. The man he plays has an unfortunate habit of offering personal compliments as if they were good reviews; he is also the only guy in sight who isnt getting laid. And he has trouble at the office. All this is to sympathize with rather than to hate. He is said (again I'm only repeating what I've heard) to earn redemption at the end, and we do see him, a lapsed Catholic, returning to confession and coming clean about his marriage. But since weve never met his wife, the scene, charmingly as Healey plays it, fails to carry much weight. In fact, good though it always is to see him, it is not at all clear what the character is doing in the play.

This of course is symptomatic of a fault that commonly bedevils adaptations of novels. There isnt enough time; there isn't enough space. Guadagni has fashioned some individually effective scenes, but characters are constantly presuming on information that we don't have, and then trying to slip it to us undigested. This is an especial problem with Allan, who has to keep repairing to his rich, cold stepmothers so we can hurriedly be filled in on his relationship to his father. (There are flashbacks. They dont help either.) Alice's love and resentment of her mother are handed to us with more ease, but they remain things we hear about rather than things we experience.

Still, for a play that comes to pieces as you watch, this has a lot to offer. It incorporates some wicked satire of the theatre, and believable portraits of actors as people; and it is, for the most part, very well acted.

Jonathan Watton, whom I remember being very promising in the first season of the Atlantic Theatre festival, fulfills that promise as Allan. He is febrile and magnetic, with an unstable conscience -- someone who attracts trust rather than love. He is at his best when scouring his stepmom's medicine cabinet, intertwining his own racing thoughts with the words of Hamlets "rogue and peasant slave" soliloquy. The intended parallels with the Shakespeare play work more strongly here than at any other point, and the words sound fresher than they often do in their official context.

Brooke Johnson stonewalls her way through Alices wounded- daughter moments, but as mother-lover she is very fine: strong and needy at once. She and Allan first meet when filming a sex scene for a TV play. It's directed by numbers and makes an amusing commentary on the erotic encounters that we witness, quite frequently, in the play itself.

David Fox enjoys himself, and pleases us, in a variety of roles, most notably the senior actor who is Claudius to Alice's Gertrude. (Fox actually was the Claudius in the real Passe Muraille Hamlet; he is Johnsons real-life husband. Go figure, but try not to hurt yourself.) John Jarvis, on a roll this year, is very funny as an alarmingly pretentious director, who seems to think hes staging the Marat/Sade. At any rate, his final tableau shows the drowned Ophelia protruding from a bath. Deborah Hay, though burdened with a couple of inexplicable songs, presents Louise as the kind of tough waif who flowers eternally on the theatrical fringe.

Steve Lucas' unit set is confusing when the action strays outside the theatre, but perfect when it stays home, as of course it would be. Coleman's production makes spare but pleasant use of the auditorium as well as the stage, and the sight of Healey arriving in the first row on the first night, and self-consciously waving to acquaintances (do we really do that?) is wondrous.

SIDE MAN

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

There is one scene in Side Man, Warren Leight's play about a lost generation of American jazzmen, that works better now in Toronto than it did four years ago in New York -- only one, but it happens to be the most important in the play.

It's the '60s. Three middle-aged horn men, hanging on to what's left of their careers after the onslaught of rock, hear for the first time a bootleg tape of the last tune played by the young trumpet prodigy Clifford Brown, just before a car crash took him in 1956. They are, of course, blown away. On Broadway the actors signalled their rapture by starting to finger imaginary instruments, in effect joining in -- an outrageously cute bit of business. The Toronto cast are far truer to the way in which actual musicians would behave and, incidentally, to the author's stage directions. They are very still. One of them occasionally slaps his fingers; another nods his head. The third, the play's title character, simply sits there, rapt. We can see right into him. We can hear what he lives for.

The scene comes halfway through the second act and it lifts the whole play. This is just as well, since for much of the time this production falls lamentably short of the mark. Its entire first act reminded me of miserable evenings spent in London watching English actors stumble through American plays -- a sensation I've never experienced in Canada before.

Side Man is one of those memory plays. It's narrated by Clifford, a jazz musician's son (as is the author). His parents had planned to name him Francis Albert, but something in the Sinatra connection went sour, so they named him after Clifford Brown, who died the year our Clifford was born. Gene, Clifford's father and the sideman of the title, met Terry, Clifford's mother, in the early '50s (though it feels more like the late '40s). She was studying classical flute; he was playing in clubs in New York and with big bands on the road, and it seemed as if the work would never dry up. Besides, he was good, and -- like many a fan -- she fell for him, his sound and his aura simultaneously. After Clifford's birth, the marriage goes violently sour. Gene is hopelessly unrealistic, believing there will always be gigs, that radio and TV will always need live musicians with jazz chops and that no reasonable soul would dream of leaving New York for, say, Las Vegas. Terry, the former ingenue, reacts by getting drunk -- angrily and bitterly and, on some occasions, almost fatally.

Gene hangs out with three fellow sidemen from the Claude Thornhill Band, a fine progressive outfit that Clifford oddly describes as "legendary" and "completely forgotten." (It can hardly be both.) It may seem strange that the four guys should find themselves working together on all their subsequent engagements, but have you never heard of dramatic licence? We meet Ziggy, who lisps, and Al and Jonesy, who ends up doing serious time for heroin and is therefore not on hand to hear the Brown tape. There is also Patsy, a waitress, who seems to go with every trumpet man in town, consecutively. (She marries several of them.) Between them these characters provide us with a capsule history of the bebop era and its aftermath; essential facts are fed to us with unobtrusive brilliance, and we get to feel what the life was like, why it ended and how its survivors are faring among the ruins. Or how they fared: "The present" in this play is 1977.

The domestic scenes take us nowhere we haven't been before, but they are tense and believable. If nothing in Terry's early behaviour foreshadows her later descent, then nothing forbids it, either. Anyway, the actors seem to find this aspect of the play much the easier to negotiate. Brandon McGibbon's Clifford is very plausible when interacting with his parents, usually with one of them at a time. He is thoroughly at sea in his role as storyteller, constantly sticking his hands into his waistband, in an apparent effort to look casual, and talking about jazz and the jazz life with a hushed reverence that suggests a square radio host trying to sound hip. Clifford isn't a musician -- he's a commercial artist -- but he grew up with the music and he would not be approaching it on tiptoe.

That's the trouble with Andy McKim's production as a whole. It looks all right; designer Sue Le Page has placed high grey windows in a brick wall that carries right on from the architecture of the theatre itself. But it lacks tone, it lacks rhythm, and much of the time the characters sound as if they don't know what they're talking about. Musicians wouldn't speak to one another in awed tones about Miles and Gil; they would all know who Miles Davis and Gil Evans were and would feel no need to put them in italics. Small things -- but they add up, destructively. Tony Nappo, Jim Jones and especially Oliver Dennis (the lisper) make a decent ensemble, but they are "characters" -- from any play -- rather than denizens of a unique world. Laura de Carteret as Patsy just overdoes things.

So, moving to the leads, does Jane Spidell in Terry's early scenes; she lays on the naivete with a trowel. She serves the later Terry, hardbitten and vociferously wounded, far better (though physically she hardly seems to age a day).

I have to say I missed Edie Falco, whom I saw play the role in New York and who is currently my favourite American actress. Actually, I missed her in two senses, since if I hadn't been at Side Man Tuesday night I would have been home watching The Sopranos. And it occurred to me that Falco's role as Terry was not unlike her later role as Carmela. Financial levels apart, both women's marriages follow the same, not uncommon trajectory: They fell for a maverick and ended with a brick wall -- though Gene makes Tony Soprano seem like the model of a solicitous spouse.

Gene doesn't get it; that is the gist of Oliver Becker's performance, which, though not immune to flaws of the production in general, is very subtle and complete. Compared to his buddies, Gene seems very sober and solid, a plausible husband and father. But that makes him even further removed from what the rest of the world calls normality; he doesn't need eccentricities to sustain him, he only needs the music. He really is a sideman; he's on the edge of life. Becker is a subtle and versatile actor who recently went grossly over the top in The Bear (in Absolutely Chekhov) but is here thankfully back on form. You believe that this unassuming, not to say empty, man can play like an angel. As indeed he does: I don't know whose records are subbing for him offstage, but they are gorgeous. The music, though heard only in snatches, is a huge emotional part of the play; like the Hamlet speeches in In the Wings (or come to that in Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead), these songs sound even more resonant in an unfamiliar context. For a last number, Clifford requests Why Was I Born, which, tellingly, is his mother's favourite. But what Gene plays, no less tellingly, is It Never Entered My Mind.

Black & White Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / Oliver Dennis, Tony Nappo and Oliver Becker play jazzmen trying to figure it all out in the age of rock. ;

INSANITY FAIR

Second City

- - -

The new Second City revue may be the leanest show the company has ever done. There is a fortuitous reason for this; one of the intended cast of six quit late in rehearsal, and some material went with him. With no disrespect to the missing person, what we are left with is very satisfactory. Ninety minutes including intermission may seem like minimal playing-time, but at least nobody gets bored. And a cast of five somehow seems more manageable, and friendlier.

This is the most political Second City show I remember, and also the most musical, though they seem not quite to trust themselves in either mode. Pat Kelly, a fresh-faced newcomer who can suddenly go sinister, kicks off as a short-trousered troubadour whose earnest serenade to the beauty of nature abruptly changes into an environmental diatribe arraigning, from the sound of it, everybody in the world over the age of 10.

Later he plays a Mephistophelean waiter at the top of the CN Tower, attending on two couples, both of whose conversations hover tantalizingly on the brink of full-scale explosion. "Revolve!" he commands periodically, and so -- lacking the resources of a fully- mechanized stage -- they do. They pick up their chairs and walk. Finally, they break into song. I would have liked both sketch and song to go on longer.

Paul Constable, whose hair is a forest, supplies some kind of connecting thread as a vice-principal dealing, over the course of three scenes with a somewhat specialized case of bullying. (The victim is singing Silent Night with the school glee club and finds, when she gets to the words "round yon virgin," that all the other voices have dropped out.) This brings back Kelly, who is nothing if not versatile, as the bully's father, the vice-president of a corporation, who informs the cowering pedagogue that he is a disgrace to the concept of vice. (Or something along those lines.)

Among the three ladies Jennifer Goodhue stands, or crouches, out as a high-velocity scuttler. She covers a wide age range, but is at her best as a senior who is both tyrannical and tyrannized, and who careens across the acting-area in and out of a mechanized wheelchair. She also careens behind the acting area, but in full view, since the production (by Michael Kennard of Mump and Smoot) makes excellent use of a scrim.

Carolyn Taylor and Aurora Browne share a surprisingly savage sketch -- by recent Second City standards, anyway -- in which they try to sell private health care using the techniques of the most blatant TV interview shows: The kind in which host converses with guest by asking rhetorical questions that seem to emerge from her mouth in large capital letters. My favourite bit, though, is a TV newscast, crammed with disasters, and with a heart-broken head- bashing puppet providing assistance "for the emotionally impaired."

They haven't come out with any good jokes about terrorism but are aware of it, and of the nervous, apocalyptic mood it induces. It's even there in a throwaway line in the opening scene. Good punchlines seem hard to come by, but the ancients probably had the same problem. Which reminds me: The Second Citizens aren't the first to notice the similarities between the names of Greek gods and those of sexually-transmitted diseases, so they should not act as if they are. That, though, is about the only item that outstays its welcome. This is a sprightly show.

1002 NIGHTS

Video Cabaret Cameron House, Toronto

In 1002 Nights, the delectable Tara Rosling plays a stripper. Take note: She appears before us in a dazzling set of golden undies, but that's as far as she goes. Such restraint may seem odd in todays theatrical climate, with actors shedding their clothes while playing people in all manner of professions, but there is a logic to it. For a stripper to strip would be theatrically redundant.

Anyway, Stella, the character Rosling plays in this one-woman piece, is more intent on baring her soul than her body. She is going through a personal crisis whose precise nature, in Simon Heaths script, remains somewhat muddy. She wants a change of career: She would like to give up lap-dancing for belly-dancing, a far more refined and subtle form of erotic art. Quite possibly, though, that's just a metaphor (though it's one that Rosling acts out very well). Stellas monologue has a number of different threads, which it alternates but never knits together.

First there is the theme of Scheherezade, who kept her head through a thousand and one nights in the royal Arabian bed, by telling the Caliph stories so beguiling as to leave him with no option but to tune in tomorrow. (Stella, who used some of her earnings to put herself through college, has read every one of them, which, as she correctly assumes, puts her ahead of most of us.) She never quite spells out the relevance of Scheherezades situation to her own, but you could say that they have both learned to survive by keeping men coming back for more: Stella, if we are to take her title literally, for one night longer than her predecessor.

Her other favourite literary reference is A Streetcar Named Desire, a play she says could only have been written by someone whose parents had named him Tennessee. (Actually, Mr. and Mrs. Williams named their child Tom.) She identifies with Blanche DuBois, striving to preserve some beauty in a fallen world: This despite the fact that her own parents has named after her Blanche's more practical sister. Her mother chose the name because she thought that hearing Brando howl Stella was just the most romantic thing, something indeed that she would wish for her own daughter; and she made the family watch the movie every holiday.

That must have been some mother. Still, it would have made a change from Miracle on 34th Street.

Moving from art to life, we have our Stella's experiences with an abusive boyfriend whom she met at the club: Stanley to her Blanche, perhaps, though she was smart enough to get away. And, Blanche-like again, we have her falling in love with a gay young man whom she also met at the club. This, unfortunately, is wrapped up in a coy, recurring fable in which he figures as a prince and she has dreams of flying. Indeed, we are never definitively told that this story is her own, though there seems little point in having it there if it isnt.

In short the piece, though never quite boring, is rambling and second-hand, though Ill admit that for a man to have written it at all is some kind of achievement; it doesn't sound ventriloquized. It is subtitled "A Search for Truth and Beauty," which is enough to put anybody off, but in Rosling's performance it finds what its looking for. She incarnates beauty, and eventually she embodies truth.

The latter part takes a bit of time. There is a vein of truculence in the script that she mines with excessive enthusiasm. You know how in life and in drama and on TV talk shows, which fall somewhere in between, women (somehow its always women, usually young ones) are always saying well excuse me! and "Hello?!" and "duh!" to denote sarcastic amazement. It's a tic that has long outlived its usefulness -- in fact it makes me wince. The tone, if not always the actual words, invades Rosling's performance when shes pouring scorn on the men behind the Arabian nights or the other men who have misinterpreted them ever since. (This includes the guys at Disney: tough really, considering the lengths they went to make Aladdin look feminist, but probably fair.) She blunts her points by underlining them. But she settles down, and eventually takes full bodily possession of her role; you cant see where the character ends and the actress begins. Her face is wonderfully mobile; it can warm you with a smile or it can seem to hold the grief of ages. Best of all, though, is her dancing. Shimmying, and shimmering, round the strip-club pole, she is entrancing. At the end of the play she goes into a celebratory step -- a sort of tap-and- grind -- that seems to be all Stella's own, nobody else's. Garnet Jones, her costume designer, and Claudia Moore, her choreographer, have done splendidly by her. Tanja Jacobs is the director who put it all together.

THE PLAY WHAT I WROTE

Wyndham's Theatre, London

DAMSELS IN DISTRESS

Duchess Theatre, London

- - -

I have seen Harry Potter live. At least I have seen Daniel Radcliffe, who plays him in the movies. Last Saturday night he was the guest star of a London stage production called The Play What I Wrote. He was very good.

You deserve an explanation. The Play What I Wrote features, and was written by, a pair of young British comedians named Sean Foley and Hamish McColl, known collectively as the Right Size. The show what they do is their tribute to an earlier, and frankly superior, English comic duo: Eric Morecambe and Ernie Wise.

To say that Morecambe and Wise were better than Foley and McColl is hardly an insult to the younger team. Morecambe and Wise were better than any double act since Laurel and Hardy. Their nearest Canadian equivalents would be Wayne and Shuster; both teams were national favourites whose TV shows made them national institutions. Both specialized in sketches that took off from familiar literary sources. In this line, W&S's "Wipe the Blood off My Toga" was a far more sustained and sophisticated effort than anything M&W ever attempted, but the British pair -- both, like so many great clowns, from the north of England -- had by far the more original and distinctive personalities. They were funny, so to speak, outside their material.

This was especially true of Eric Morecambe, a tall and well- padded man in shiny horn-rims, who was something of a genius. Ernie Wise, smaller and fairer and the straight man of the outfit, existed like all stooges to be tormented; in Ernie's case this meant being affectionately mocked by Eric for his "short, fat, hairy legs" and his literary ambitions. Every week Ernie, the most prolific of authors, would arrive bearing what he announced as "the play what I wrote." Every week, despite his partner's earnest attempts to stop it happening, Ernie's play would be put on. And Eric, generally cast as some variety of historical menial, would sabotage it.

Each play would contain a role for a visiting thespian -- Glenda Jackson, say, or Diana Rigg -- to whom Ernie would pay sycophantic court. Eric, appalled by this display, would stand on one side and exclaim, "You crawler" -- as subversive a comment on the celebrity culture as has ever been heard on network television. He would also disrupt the proceedings by sticking his head round the curtain and beaming. He might also, when subtler methods failed, slap his partner's face -- a ritualistic gesture that was surreal rather than violent -- or take the guest star by the throat. He once did this to Andre Previn. (When Andre questioned Eric's piano-playing abilities, Eric replied, in a sentence that passed into folklore: "I'm playing the right notes, sunshine, just not necessarily in the right order.") They were totally unsentimental, and totally unmalicious.

Morecambe died in 1984, Wise in 1999. In their heyday, the 1970s, more than half the population of the UK watched their BBC Christmas specials. Two generations of subsequent comedians have grown up in their shadow, among them Foley and McColl.

Apparently, when it was suggested to these two that they impersonate their great predecessors, they said the sensible thing - - i.e., no. It was then suggested that they do a show about two comics who were asked to play Morecambe and Wise and refused, and this they accepted. So their own theatrical entertainment mimics the shape of the classic TV shows.

Hamish is the Ernie figure -- an earnest amateur Shakespeare. Sean, the Eric equivalent, is bribed by a producer to pretend that Hamish is going to get his play on so that it can be turned at the last moment into the desired homage. A further twist is that the producer himself is a fake who is only looking for a chance to play his harmonica. When the show is at its height, there are three levels of ambition and dissimulation operating simultaneously. Or rather there are four, since Hamish, like Ernie, enlists a guest star to help out with his masterwork -- a different one at each performance.

The stage production trumps the original TV shows by keeping the guest's identity a secret until the moment of appearance. An actor who has filled this spot described it to me as "the biggest ego trip available"; the occupants have included such heavyweights as Ralph Fiennes and Simon Callow. (A running gag is that the man they're really after is Ian McKellen.)

This is the place that Master Radcliffe occupied on the night I went, and a smart, self-possessed kid is indeed just right for the job. The star's role is to take sides alternately with the stooge and the buffoon: to help humiliate one and be humiliated by the other.

The show -- directed somewhat unexpectedly by Kenneth Branagh, who must himself be on the guest-star short list -- has been a huge success; it is now on its second London run, and next year it will brave Broadway, though one can't help wondering how it will go down with an audience that doesn't get the references.

I myself spent the first, expository half wondering what all the fuss had been about, since the Right Size seemed to be the wrong fit. Morecambe and Wise were supernaturally natural performers, grand masters of the off-centre colloquial. (Eric, in particular, may have had the soul and grin of a zany, but he had the frame of a solid citizen. Both men were known for their sharply tailored suits.) McColl and Foley seemed, by contrast, cramped and monochromatic, though the third man, Toby Jones, was brilliant.

In the second act, though, they start to perform actual M&W material; within five minutes I was weeping with laughter and I hardly stopped until the final curtain. The superb original scriptwriter, Eddie Braben, has dusted off and augmented one of his superb original scripts, a French Revolution epic entitled "The Scarlet Pimple." Variety material -- stand-up, crosstalk, sketch and the occasional sitcom -- accounts for some of the best comic writing of the past century; work that, like all classic texts, stands up to new interpretation. McColl and Foley offer a loving comment on the prototypes, one that increasingly partakes of their glory and eventually becomes one with it.

The last scene shows Sean and Hamish lying blamelessly in bed together, as Eric and Ernie were wont to do onscreen. (Their TV shows depicted them as inhabiting a Platonic -- in all senses -- bachelor menage; in some ways Eric and Ernie anticipated Bert and Ernie.) A police car, siren blaring, tears by outside their window, and the two intone, in unison, one of the immortal duo's most famous lines: "He won't sell much ice cream going at that speed." They then turn toward one another and say, still in unison, "God, they were funny."

It's a perfect moment. Tears of laughter turn into tears of joy. And then the band strikes up, and the joy reaches sublimity level, as the boys go into their heroes' regular soft-shoe sign-off, a ditty called Give Me Sunshine. They recreate it perfectly -- a considerable achievement considering that Morecambe and Wise, who mastered all the skills of the halls before transcending them, were ace song-and-dance men.

There is more comic genius on show in London in Damsels in Distress, a sequence of three plays by Alan Ayckbourn, all set in riverside apartments in the city's newly fashionable Docklands. There are no continuing characters, but all the plays are performed by the same seven actors, who, for the first time in the author- director's long career, have been imported in bulk from his home base theatre in Scarborough, Yorkshire.

He has run this with imposing dedication for more than 30 years, while turning out double that number of plays -- an output as remarkable for its quality as its quantity.

The cast make a delightful ensemble, and though much of the fun of the project must lie in seeing each of them take on three widely varied roles, I found that the one piece I saw, Role Play, stood very well on its own. In fact, it ranks with Ayckbourn's best. What is most impressive about both play and performance is their ability to take characters over the edge of caricature and then somehow bring them back alive.

An engaged couple, believable and obviously at risk, are surrounded by grotesques (his drunken mother, her smugly philistine parents) and outsiders (the lap dancer from upstairs and her punch- drunk minder). The action is farce, with a couple of unfortunate gaps in credibility, but the people have real problems, and by the end even the most outrageous of them have been restored some measure of dignity.

Trilogies are in the London air this year, with Ayckbourn's trio matched by Tom Stoppard's epic political cartoon The Coast of Utopia. More on that to follow.
