JUST BETWEEN FRIENDS

Winter Garden Theatre, Toronto

ELAINE STRITCH AT LIBERTY

Old Vic Theatre, London

- - -

Bea Arthur and Elaine Stritch have a lot in common. Both are American actresses in their seventies with distinguished careers and distinctive voices, the word "distinctive" meaning, of course, that the noises they make, especially in song, are arresting rather than conventionally pretty. Both apprenticed at the same off-Broadway workshop, though apparently at different times. (At any rate, neither in her reminiscences mentions the other.) Both were offered leading roles in Golden Girls, a TV series that in celebrating longevity also managed to achieve it; Stritch turned the offer down, Arthur, as you may have heard, didn't. Both have stories to tell, and are telling them on stage in one-woman shows -- Arthur accompanied by a lone pianist, Stritch by a bouncing band.

Arthur got great notices when she tried her show out last year in the American hinterlands, but far cooler ones when she took it into New York. Her thunder had been stolen by Stritch who -- first off- Broadway and then on it -- scored the greatest personal triumph the city has seen in years. Having just seen them both -- Arthur in Toronto, Stritch last week in London -- I can see why.

Arthurs handicap in presenting a musical retrospective is that she hasnt actually done very many musicals. Those she has been in have mostly been high-profile, but in the most famous of them all -- Fiddler on the Roof, she played the matchmaker -- she barely sang. She was Lucy in the legendary off-Broadway production of The Threepenny Opera, and she gives us a song from the score, but not one she sang at the time. In fact, the only numbers that turn up from her performing past (since she sadly declines to sing a 1950s revue torcher called Garbage) are two from Mame, in which she played second banana to Angela Lansbury. One of these, Bosom Buddies, was originally a duet, so I guess it's logical that she only does half of it.

For the rest, it's all very arbitrary: songs from shows she wishes shed done or songs she presumably just likes. The latter category includes standards (Who Cares, Lets Face the Music and Dance, and a special favourite of mine, Fun to Be Fooled) that she dispatches very pleasantly and unfussily. Her voice is a flexible foghorn, and she seldom forces it beyond what it can achieve; also, and more importantly, she is a whale on colouring, but rarely over- colouring, a lyric.

Sometimes this isn't enough. She sings Some People, from Gypsy, and tells us how much she'd always wanted to play Mama Rose, though on this evidence she would have been very miscast; she doesnt carry the guns, and her Rose sounds more of a nag than a force of nature.

On the other hand, from Ballroom, a show composed by her accompanist, Billy Goldenberg, she takes Fifty Per Cent, a song usually guaranteed to bring out the screaming over-actress in any woman who sings it, despite the fact its supposed to be about settling for half. She banks it down, revealing it to be more specific and more affecting than I'd ever imagined.

She is very good at bitter. Pirate Jenny, the vengeful Threepenny Opera number that she offers in homage to Lotte Lenya, is hair- raising. It comes, though, with melodramatic lighting that is completely out of place in the casual impromptu entertainment she is pretending to offer us -- one that comes with the nudgingly ingratiating title of Just Between Friends.

Its conceit is that we are more or less in her living room and that she is talking directly to us, right off the cuff. For a time this works; she catches us off-guard by starting her performance with a string of recipes for roast lamb, and a couple of the defiantly off-colour jokes she tells are very funny. But her interplay with Goldenberg (an appealingly droopy and wizened figure, crouched at the ivories) looks and sounds appallingly unspontaneous; and her late avowal that she stepped on stage scared of being herself but that we had absolved her of her terrors is ludicrous. It's far too late for her to carry on as if this were her first night; we know shes being doing it for months.

And its not as if she reveals anything much about herself anyway. Most of her anecdotes are about other people, and she never casts herself in anything resembling a bad light. At times she can be unlovably self-approving: Musing on her TV triumphs, Maude and Golden Girls, she says, We picked a few bubbles, we broke a few taboos -- the kind of remark that might just be tolerable if offered to an interviewer on late-night TV, but not when planted right in the laps of a paying audience. If I were feeling cruel, I might describe her as a musical star who never was, revealing a self that never is. I'll settle instead for saying that her best numbers are worth experiencing, but that you have to shut out much of what lies between.

Elaine Stritch at Liberty is twice as long and very different. For a start, it's difficult to resist a 76-year-old woman who comes on stage in flapping white shirt and black tights, never puts on another thing, and gets away with it. Arthur fixes us with a patrician glare; Stritch shows us a tough mask that cracks, and she is tireless to the point of defiance about admitting her insecurities and indiscretions. She tells us about her long- preserved virginity and about her bad luck with men from Marlon Brando to Rock Hudson. She rhapsodizes (one of her few concessions to outright sentimentality) about her marriage, cut short by his early death, to English actor John Bay. She goes in moderately harrowing detail, laced with a little black humour, into her long history of alcoholism.

Confessional theatre is not my favourite thing -- I cling to the belief that actors are meant to refract their emotions through those of other characters, not to offer them to us neat -- but if its going to be done, it had better be done thoroughly and honestly. Despite all the name-dropping, Stritch skimps on her love-life -- we want her to tell us either more or less -- but her drink habit is as compelling to us as it was compulsive for her. Her script ("constructed by John Lahr, deconstructed by Elaine Stritch") is no masterpiece, but at least it exists. Its a serviceable frame, and it has something definite to surround.

To put it another way, Stritch has a musical history to go with the personal. Many of the London critics commented that her voice is not what it was; in fact it's almost exactly what it was: a rasp that sways. It's an attractive version of the Broadway belt -- soft- grained and hard-edged. By pausing, pouncing and driving a point home, she can squeeze the juice from a lyric and even from a melody; certainly from a rhythm. Her Broadway portfolio is not much more capacious than Arthurs, but at least it contains songs that are identifiably hers, and she sings them, if anything, better now than she did then.

From the 40s revue Angel in the Wings, her debut, she sings the tongue-twisting Civilisation (a.k.a. Bingo Bango Bango, I Don't Want to Leave the Congo) with unblushing insouciance; here, as in Broadway Baby (from Follies), her face looks blinkingly young. Clever lighting (originally by the great Jules Fisher) helps, of course, but in a show that never pretends to be anything but theatrical, that's acceptable. She does Zip, the mock-strip from Rodgers and Harts Pal Joey, and teases it out (that seems the right phrase) by telling the story of how she shuttled between theatres, and even between cities, when combining this one-song role with the job of understudying Ethel Merman in Call Me Madam; theres rather too much reconstruction-of-imaginary-conversations going on here, but it's fun.

There is nothing, alas, from Goldilocks, a flop show with some great songs, two of which -- Who's Been Sleeping in My Bed and I Never Know When to Say When -- would, by title alone, fit perfectly. But when she gets to Sail Away, written for her by Noel Coward, she makes more of Why Do the Wrong People Travel than anyone, including her, ever has before. And eventually theres Stephen Sondheims Company, with The Ladies Who Lunch and, even better, The Little Things You Do Together. Everything she sings has style, and intelligence, and authority; she even knows when to understate.

She does oversell Sondheim's I'm Still Here, a song that means something different, and something less, when removed from its context in Follies; it ceases to be a characterized chronicle and becomes a mere troupers anthem. Arthur, to her credit, explictly declines to sing it, though her pianist plays it as she takes her bows. In general, Stritch fares less well with unanchored songs that are supposed to serve as commentary, though theres one, the Gershwins' But Not for Me, on which she hits a splendidly appropriate note of vinegary regret. It's meant as commentary on her own situation; what sits in my memory, though, is not how the song illuminates her but how she illuminates the song.

THE BEARD OF AVON

Bluma Appel Theatre

- - -

Amy Freed, an American playwright, offers a fantasia on that reddest of herrings: the Shakespeare authorship controversy. The theory -- the plays could only have been written by a university graduate, preferably aristocratic -- is, of course, snobbish rubbish. I'd like to say Don't Get Me Started, but since I obviously have started, here are my own, mostly unoriginal, thoughts:

1. It's true the plays could not have been written by an "illiterate bumpkin" but there's no evidence that that's what Shakespeare was. He had a good grammar-school education whose curriculum has been painstakingly documented by modern scholars. Ben Jonson's famous comment about "small Latin and less Greek" merely means that Will was less good at these subjects than Ben himself was; it also carries the clear message that these were deficiencies Shakespeare easily overcame.

2. The supposedly arcane information contained in the plays was easily available in their printed sources, most of which we know.

3 Theatre people were in constant contact with courtiers and politicians; companies were obliged by law to have noble patrons. If there was anything Shakespeare couldn't work out for himself about top people's behaviour, all he had to do was ask.

4. Shakespeare's contemporaries all tackled the same kind of historical and political subjects that he did, and most of them give the impression that they know what they're talking about. Were all their plays ghosted by earls?

5. Shakespeare's immediate predecessors were known collectively as the University Wits. Their plays, for the most part, have not worn well. In other words, the graduate class had its chance and failed.

6. Some of the most erudite playwrights since, from Jonson to Stoppard, have lacked a college education.

7. One thing we do know about Shakespeare is that he was an actor. This seems a better preparation for writing effective plays than any amount of Privy Councilling and trolling around Italy.

8. If you're looking for first-hand experience in the plays, try the scenes set in fields, villages or taverns. You may wonder at a Warwickshire tradesman's son having created Hamlet; you should wonder more at the idea of the Earl of Oxford, currently most favoured of the pretenders, having dreamed up Bottom the weaver.

Or any of the other immortal low lifes. The Beard of Avon, in fact, has Oxford, on his deathbed, admitting to Shakespeare "I could never have come up with Falstaff."

Freed's comedy presents the lord and the player as collaborators, and her piece is actually a lot less subversive than she would like it to look. What she provides is a new riff on the theme of Shakespeare as inspired plagiarist, as the man who, according to Shaw, could tell a story so long as somebody else told it to him first, or who, in the words of Walter Kerr, was not only the playwright's playwright but the kleptomaniac's kleptomaniac.

Only here, instead of getting his plots from Plutarch, Holinshed or assorted Italian romancers, he gets them from Oxford. Or from Francis Bacon, or Lady Lettice Knollys or from Elizabeth I herself. Freed has had the bright idea of assembling all the authorial candidates who have ever been proposed, and making them bid for Shakespeare's services. Bacon, apparently, is the most hopeless hack of the bunch. The Queen, weary of ruling, fantasizes about being ruled, and comes up with the first draft of The Taming of the Shrew. We see it rehearsed, and Kate's submission speech has never sounded less embarrassing. Shakespeare improves the piece, of course, just as he does Lady Lettice's attempt at King Lear. (As she wrote it, it's all about the reading of a will.) As far as I could tell, the only play in the canon for which Freed denies Shakespeare any credit at all is Titus Andronicus. Hers is really a very orthodox argument.

Oxford remains the prime mover: a brilliantly gifted piece of sleaze who never saw a neighbour's wife he didn't covet, at least on his heterosexual days. He has a mind and a wit but he lacks concentration and the common touch. Both of these are supplied by Shakespeare, an untutored rustic who has a mild turn for rhyme but who, when we first meet him down on the farm, is unable to say anything about the rain except that it raineth, which he repeats three times. He escapes from Stratford and from his wife, joins the players and is taken on by Oxford as a literary front man. Before long he is supplying all the best bits in the plays. The two men are also, uneasily, friends. Their scenes together, as they both begin to realize which of them has the talent, are freshly conceived and excellently executed.

They take a long time to set up, though; and the play's first half is mostly awful. There is much cod-Elizabethan dialogue; we all know that our ancestors were readier with words than we are, but I doubt if their facility extended to speaking extempore in blank verse or rhyming couplets. (And, of course, pretending that they did makes impossible any serious examination of the link between how these people talked and how they wrote. So there goes the authorship question.)

We get ghastly parodies of early Renaissance drama, which Freed seems to think was composed of phallic gags and very little else; some terrible pre-Shakespearean plays have indeed come down to us, but none as ghastly as these.

David Storch's production is as uneven as the play: shameful in the bad parts, truthful in the good. The scenes at court are as clumsy as those in the barn, with Brenda Robins' Elizabeth a mere echo of all the player-queens who have preceded her (though, oddly, she sounds less than usual like Glenda Jackson). Stephen Ouimette's Oxford is uneasy at first but develops a fine wit-flicking style with a dark undercoating of self-hatred. Michael Spencer-Davis' Shakespeare is a complete success, buffeted but resilient. As an actor this Will seems ahead of his time; he asks about motivation, and complains "call you this direction?" when he doesn't get it.

There is a virtual sub-plot concerning Shakespeare's marriage. Anne Hathaway follows her husband to London, disguises herself as a whore and -- like one of Will's own comic heroines -- gains entrance to his bed without him recognizing her. This is a nice in-joke in a play that's full of them, but it barely connects with the rest of the action.

It does, though, enable Gina Wilkinson to display an equal talent for self-transformation; her Anne, a coarse harridan at home, becomes very warm and crushable when on the loose. Peter C. Wylde presents John Heminge, Shakespeare's colleague and eventual editor, as North Country actor-manager of what must already have been the old school; a weathered senior when he subjects Will to his first audition, he must have been a centenarian by the time he brought out the First Folio. Peter Hartwell contributes a burnished set that's a dead witty ringer for the platform stage at the Stratford Festival.

THE COAST OF UTOPIA

Olivier Theatre, London

About halfway along The Coast of Utopia, which is Tom Stoppard's umbrella title for a trilogy of plays about the Russian revolutionaries of the 19th century, somebody tells Alexander Herzen, you could be Minister of Paradox, with special responsibility for Irony. Its a position Stoppard himself could easily fill. If there were an election for it, he would win by a landslide.

Each of the three plays lasts some three hours. The total has been greeted by many British critics as a fascinating failure, though I would call it a flawed success. The plays opened in London last May, on the largest stage of the National Theatre in London and in a spectacular production by that theatres outgoing director, Trevor Nunn. The prudent and/or intrepid could see them all on one day, as I did just over a week ago. (It was the penultimate performance.)

It's a panoramic piece, but Herzen is the nearest thing it has to a hero. He's a crucial but somewhat forgotten figure: excoriated by Marx, favourably mentioned by Lenin (probably for the wrong reasons), more recently celebrated by Isaiah Berlin (Stoppards principal source) and, in the current issue of Atlantic Monthly, Christopher Hitchens. In the cast list to Stoppards part one, Voyage, he is described as "a would-be revolutionary." In part two, Shipwreck, he is a radical writer. In part three, Salvage, he's "a Russian exile." That neatly summarizes not only his trajectory, but those of the plays themselves.

Chronologically, they stretch from 1833 to 1865. So the halfway point, roughly, is Europe's year of revolutions, 1848. And the plays also stretch across the continent, moving westward. Part One is set entirely in Russia, where a generation of idealists is stirring, challenging czarist authority. Part Two shows them in flux, mostly banished from their own country, but deeply involved in revolts from Paris to Poland. In Part Three, most of them have fetched up in London, centre of one of the most reactionary governments but allowing refugees to live, plot and dream in peace. "Do poverty and liberty go together," asks one of them, or is it just the English sense of humour?

Stoppard is an emigre himself (from Czechoslovakia via India), and in part the play is the most elaborate, and the most ambiguous, tribute he has ever paid to his adopted country -- or, more accurately, to the country that adopted him. England is described, with a mixture of enthusiasm and exasperation, as "the rock against which revolution breaks." It tolerates you to death. There are worse ways to die.

Herzen certainly thinks so. We are told that in 1825, at the age of 17, he and a lifelong friend, Nicholas Ogarev, vowed, in memory of the failed December plot against the Czar, to devote their lives to perpetuating the struggle. The Herzen we meet is a socialist, but one increasingly distrustful of dogma, and especially of any doctrine that calls on its adherents to sacrifice their own or other peoples lives for the possible good of future generations: If we cant arrange our own happiness, it's a conceit beyond vulgarity to arrange the happiness of those who come after us.

I find that statement extremely sympathetic, not only in its own right but because it coincides with my own long-held opinion about Stoppard's moral qualities as a writer. We all know hes superbly witty. His jokes, and the texture they give his plays, are in themselves an affirmation that life might be worth living. Most political playwrights, certainly those of Stoppards own British generation, seem to want you to join them in their misery.

Herzen's mature position might be summed up as "free the serfs -- then we'll see," and its hard to quarrel with that. Hard for the audience, anyway; many of the other characters have no trouble doing it. His unfailing decency (the Paris barricades cured him of any taste for bloodshed) carries an inevitable theatrical penalty. Its probably no accident that the first play, in which he plays only a minor role, is by general consent the most enjoyable.

Its dominating figure is Michael Bakunin, who will end his days as an anarchist but who is essentially a serial enthusiast, embracing one fashionable philosophy after another. When we first meet him he's a military cadet, deeply into German idealism. Resigning his commission (study is difficult in the Artillery, owing to the loud explosions which are a regular feature of Artillery life), he then decides that physical reality has its points after all, and devotes himself to increasingly radical politics. Eventually, he gets himself sent to Siberia, but escapes. In the meantime, he deeply irritates his rich land-and-serf-owning father, sponges off his friends ("is there nobody who sees that the future of philosophy in Russia hangs on lending me a few miserable roubles?"), and exploits his four adoring sisters, who want to go to Moscow. Unlike their Chekhovian equivalents (and the resemblance is of course intentional to the point of pastiche), they actually make it there, quite often.

In fact, the play is bisected. Its first act takes place on the Bakunin family estate, and its second goes over the same period of time in Moscow, with several characters shuttling between. This yields a few nice ironies (and paradoxes), but it's needlessly confusing. When it comes to these kinds of structural games, Stoppard is no Ayckbourn, and there is more than enough to take in as things chronologically are. But the intellectual ferment of the time is wonderfully evoked, its passion and absurdity (literature is taken so seriously that the censor can close a paper over a hostile theatre review) exhilaratingly fused.

The second play is the most diffuse, though held together by the impact on the Russian emigres of the Europe whose libertarian ideals they, or most of them, had worshipped from afar. Karl Marx makes a brief appearance (hearing that Bakunin has been spending time with the working class, he asks what are they like?) and many critics seem to have found this disrespectful. They miss the point. Marx is the one character most of us already know something about, and besides, he wasnt Russian.

The last instalment is the soberest. Its history's fault rather than the author's than many of the liveliest characters have by now died off, but the play seems to share its exiled characters own sense that the real action is going on elsewhere. They would like to be back in Russia and so would we. (In another sense, they are perfectly at home. Like every character Stoppard has ever created, they all sound English.)

The earlier Stoppard play this one most resembles is Travesties, which showed us writers and revolutionaries becalmed in neutral Zurich during the First World War. But all those characters, including Lenin, were treated as historys clowns, and the narrating figure was the greatest clown of all. By contrast, Herzen, at the centre of this one, spends much of the last part making the same humane response to a series of off-stage cataclysms. Stephen Dillane, who plays him at the National, is intelligent but excessively dour: surprising, after his sparkling performance in Stoppard's The Real Thing, in a production that transformed my view of the play.

There is no lack of wit in the play. Sometimes it strikes very deep. A serf-owners' human holdings used to be described as so many hundreds (or thousands) of souls, and Stoppard can do a lot with that. But the humour proves hard to harness in performance. The main difficulty in Stoppards plays -- increasingly as time has gone on - - is their allusiveness. Almost every line is simultaneously a joke, a stage in an argument, and a chunk of exposition, and each needs to work on all three levels.

Nunns production is superbly organized, and visually stunning, with William Dudley's sets relying mainly on computerized projections on an Imax-sized screen; the camerawork scoops you into the action. It's thrilling, and a wonderful way of taming the vast Olivier stage, but it isnt what youd call intimate or laughter- friendly. The ideal Stoppard performers would perhaps be stand-up comics with university degrees, and not all this cast have the necessary skills. The best is Will Keen as Belinsky, the penurious and tubercular scribe whose road to revolution is literary criticism; he describes wonderfully funny and wonderfully touching verbal and physical parabolas.

Douglas Henshall is engagingly impossible as Bakunin, whom Herzen disowns but can never dislike. Guy Henry is imposingly languid as Turgenev, the greatest writer on display, who has Herzen's humanity without his idealism (he laments inter alia that "the word 'liberal has now entered the scatalogical vocabulary, like halfwit' or 'hypocrite ") and who, in one of the best late scenes, is brought up against a nihilist far more sinister and unyielding than Bakunin. His response is to put him into his magnum opus, Fathers and Sons. Earlier, life has imitated art imitating life by giving us an opening scene straight out of his A Month in the Country.

The much-praised actress Eve Best -- cast as Herzens wife, a Bakunin sister, and a Teutonic Mary Poppins -- was off at my visit, so a large hole in the plays' scheme gaped even wider. The characters' romantic and marital entanglements are obviously meant to parallel their intellectual commitments. Initially, this is fun. Young ladies fall for unresponsive idealists and wail I cant understand why they call it romanticism. Later, things get darker. Utopian sex proves as elusive as Utopian politics. A comrade seduces Mrs. Herzen; he in turn unites with the spouse of his oldest friend, Ogarev. But all this seems more a diversion from the main theme rather than an enrichment of it. Except, that is, for the scenes involving Herzens deaf son Kolya, whose death by drowning prompts one of the author's finest speeches: "Because children grow up, we think a child's purpose is to grow up. But a child's purpose is to be a child." Nobody (compare the TV play Professional Foul) writes more movingly and more acutely about children than Stoppard.

The response at the end was, by the standards of these marathons, muted. I can understand why. All the same, I want to see the plays again. There are rumours of this show visiting New York, and I can also imagine it being done at least as well by Canadian actors, though I doubt if we could muster such a physical production. I think, by the way, that the plays are too short.

THE DANISH PLAY

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

I was away when The Danish Play opened -- to laudatory reviews. I caught up with it a week into its run, and it seems to me extraordinarily overrated. God knows, its intentions are honourable. It's common knowledge that during the Second World War Denmark had the finest record of any occupied country in standing up to the Holocaust. A remarkable rescue operation that seems, morally at least, to have involved most of the population resulted in the ferrying to safety of nearly all the country's Jews. Beyond that, most of us know little of the Danish Resistance; Sonja Mills' play is in part an attempt to fill us in.

It's also the author's tribute to a member of her own family. Mills, who came to Canada from Denmark as a child, discovered that her great-aunt, a poet named Agnete Ottosen, had worked in the resistance. She was captured while on a courier mission, remained steadfast under severe torture and was sent to Ravensbruck -- which she survived, despite being subjected to Nazi gynecological "experiments." She even managed, after the war, to bear a son, though she ran afoul of her own country's bureaucracy by refusing to reveal the name of the father. Her behaviour became increasingly erratic, and she lost custody of the child, who grew up for the most part in an institution. In the end she succumbed to the tragedy she had managed, against all odds, to escape during the war.

There are two plays going on here, one on each side of the intermission. Both involve Agnete and four of her wartime comrades and post-war friends: Mads, a lawyer and part-time publisher; Michael, a gay playwright; Helga, Michael's sister, who runs a bakery; and Bente, who starts off as Helga's assistant. Their presence, though, is not enough to unify the evening; Michael, in particular, gets an excessively generous amount of attention. Presumably, both he and Agnete represent two kinds of marginalized figure, but this is never explored.

Individually, both sections are well-constructed -- the author is adept at dropping hints and springing surprises -- but the actual writing is undistinguished, chatty with some hopeful stabs at starkness. I except the interrogation and concentration-camp scenes, which are stark -- economically so -- among the best of their kind I have seen. The rest of the resistance story can hardly help being compelling, but the framing device of the survivors' annual reunion smells of soap opera.

The second act, less suspenseful but more interesting, is nonetheless waylaid by the fact we never know what proportion of Agnete's subsequent troubles can be blamed on her time in the camp. On the face of it, this would be enough to scar anybody, but the author seems to go out of her way to blunt this point with the character of Bente, who goes through many of the same experiences, including the medical ones, but who survives and is even happy. All right, they're very different women; we know Agnete is a difficult customer from the moment we see her applying to Mads for both a job in his office and a place in his underground organization. She might even be courting martyrdom, but again this isn't followed through. And it seems facile to treat Agnete's struggles with Danish red tape as on a par with her suffering under the Nazis, which is what she herself seems inclined to do, with only token contradiction from the script: A woman's right to choose single motherhood is not as momentous as the same woman's courage in defying the Gestapo.

One wonders, for example, if the Danish doctor who examined Agnete after her liberation was really as hidebound and unfeeling as the play makes her seem; while some of the objections to Agnete's parenting skills that are later raised by judges and social workers seem very reasonable. It sounds unfeeling, but I suspect the main reason Agnete is being treated as a tragic heroine rather than a sadly interesting case study is that the author is related to her.

The final catastrophe takes place offstage, depriving both us and the central character of the chance to add things up. Like the hero of an earlier Danish play (she even goes to see a production of Hamlet at Elsinore), Agnete comes to feel that "Denmark's a prison." Her friends, too, are given some desultory chat about the country's identity, including its posy-Viking colonial record. But if the author's aim is to question the idea of the nation-state (I got that from the publicity material, not the play), then she's telling the wrong story; Denmark's wartime history is glorious precisely because the Danes behaved differently from the citizens of other countries.

Kelly Thornton's production has one brilliant device: Agnete's interrogation and imprisonment are played out in the sharpest relief , on a small square of stage behind a scrim. The effect is both tactful and harrowing. (It's rather less tactful to use the same space for Agnete's later tussles with domestic officialdom, though it's certainly an efficient use of space.)

The rest of the direction is below the standard one would expect from the director of the superb This Hotel, as is much of the acting; the more workaday scenes are sodden, with nobody able to deliver as much as a believable conversational remark.

Christine Brubaker as Bente is a glowing exception; a scene in which she is confronted by a German soldier on the very eve of the Jewish evacuation is the tensest, fullest moment of the evening. Eric Goulem and Erika Hennebury also do well in a variety of purposely anonymous roles.

As Agnete, Kate Hennig is as split down the middle as the play itself. As the clear-eyed fighter of the play's first part, she is stridently wooden; as the character gets more impossible (or, if you prefer, more implacable), so the actress gets more plausible. Once pregnant, she's impregnable. The performance, of a woman locked up in her own logic, becomes very strong, even when revealing weakness; it has, in fact, a touch of the uncanny.

I AM YOURS

Equity Showcase Theatre

- - -

Judith Thompson's I Am Yours, first staged in 1987, is concerned with emotional need and emotional greed. They could well be the same thing. It's set in a bleak urban landscape that's willed rather than observed or created.

There is Toilane, a young man working as superintendent in an apartment block, who conceives an instant passion for one of the residents, an artist and teacher named Deirdre: Dee for short. He's especially crazy about her feet.

Dee, as far as we can tell, lets Toilane into her bed, or on to her floor, once and once only, and then tells him to get out and stay out. Well, almost. What she actually says is, "I know you're the super, but other than those kinds of things I never want to see you again." This might be described as not burning your bridges before you come to them.

Dee does, however, get pregnant. She has recently split with her husband, Mack, a bookseller, but she now lets him back into her life rather than acknowledge Toilane as the father. (The time-frame here seems somewhat murky.) Dee draws back at the last minute from having an abortion, decides to have the child and then immediately gives it up for adoption. She also enlists the help of her sister, Mercy, who has gone through life acutely conscious of being the less pretty of the two; it doesn't help when Dee tells her that she's better off that way. Mercy has been married herself, but the great love of her life, constantly remembered, is an older man who drove her to school when she was a girl and touched her in the car.

Completing the cast is Toilane's mother, Pegs; she's a single parent, he's an only child. Pegs has cleaned floors for a living, and she talks eloquently about the hatred she feels for her employers, and about the ingratitude of children once they get past the stage when, as she says, "they think you're Christmas." That line has stayed with me over the 15 years since the first production; in fact, it wasn't until I heard those words in the Equity Showcase revival that I realized that I had seen the play before. Everything else -- characters, action -- had escaped from me. There is a sort of justice in this. What Thompson's people say is more touching and believable, in this play at least, than what they do.

This is accentuated in the current production. Christopher Morris, a smouldering young actor, here establishes himself as a sensitive young director. (It's his first time out.) He may even be too sensitive for the play, since its earlier, more intimate scenes work better here than the full-scale battles that break out later.

The audience sits above and around a cockpit stage; for solos and duets the performers hug the sides of the acting area, very effectively. In ensemble scenes, though, they seem oddly reluctant, both physically and psychologically, to take over the arena.

The play talks a lot about love, but what it actually feeds on is anger. Dee, presumably, has scars, but we're not told much about them. What we actually see is a spoiled and breathtakingly manipulative woman who also happens to be an expert in blackmail, of both the actual and emotional varieties. She battens on her sister's insecurities; she threatens Toilane with a rape charge; she throws her husband out, begs him back, then banishes him again, all within the space of three minutes.

I thought for a moment that we were watching a cunningly collapsed version of the events of several months; but no, it's meant to be happening in real time.

Toilane falls for Dee at the same feverish speed, and the production is too gentle to get us into this emotional climate. Probably no actress could make Dee sympathetic; she emerges as someone who deserves what she gets, and also deserves to lose what she loses. But if we can't like her, we might at least be scared of her, or of what she describes as her "inner animal." Tracey Ferencz (who came late into the show) is altogether too careful and thoughtful for the role; she may be aiming for torment but she ends up playing spite.

The balance is further upset by the characterization of Toilane. In theory, his neediness is as sinister as hers. He is obsessively territorial; he has been a gay-basher; he has also done time. But when the story gets going we forget all of this; we merely see a not very bright young man being taken advantage of; especially since Benjamin Clost's performance is alive and sympathetic, down to his fingertips. Diane Hollingsworth lacks the panache for his mom, either in her semi-comic tirades or in her metamorphosis into the role of full-throated avenger. This is the play's set-piece scene, and it requires her almost to hypnotize her antagonists into surrender. But here, as earlier with Dee, it's difficult to see why they should sit quietly and listen to her. There's an element of personal feud here, plus a touch of class war, but nothing that's developed.

The remaining performances are fine. Adrian Churchill's Mack, very solid, takes full advantage of two of the play' s best speeches: one about a plague of bees behind his mother's pantry wall, and another recalling the humiliation of high-school dances.

Caroline Gillis as Mercy captures the still-lost girl within the grown woman; she's the one character who not only looks for love in all the wrong places but also, surprisingly, finds it. (One wouldn't put bets on it lasting.)

William Webster, the one survivor from the cast of '87, brings great tact and presence to three characters, plus the voice and silhouette of a fourth: the sisters' late father, who apparently is German.

That, at any rate, is the language in which, from off-stage, and from the depths of memory, he intones the phrase that gives the play its title. Its relevance remains mysterious.

"I am yours" is doubtless the kind of ecstatically surrendering avowal that most of the characters yearn to make; some of them even do, generally with dire results. Dee, the woman at the centre, never does and probably never could. Maybe that's the point.

ROBIN HOOD

Elgin Theatre, Toronto

They all come round again. Robin Hood was the first, and remains the best, of Ross Petty's attempts to kidnap the English pantomime, disguise it as a family musical, and demand ransom from a Canadian audience. (It robbed the comparatively poor to blackmail the relatively rich.) It first came among us six years ago, and I reviewed it then for some other newspaper, one that employs a star- rating system for plays. As I recall, I gave it 500 (out of four). Thats how good I and my own family felt.

Euphoria is wonderful but it does wear off, and though my kids have continued to escort me to the later Petty pantos, I have noticed their demeanour on these occasions becoming increasingly surly. This year they flatly refused to accompany me. I blame the schools. Their desertion has thrown me back on my own memories, which are unreliable. My impression is, though, that the musical component of the show is stronger than it was six years ago, but the comedy -- with one notable exception -- has gone off.

First, some basics. One reason Robin Hood makes a better Petty protagonist than, say, Cinderella or Peter Pan, is he doesnt come with a story, or at least not with one that has to be adhered to. He is a creature of folklore, commemorated in various tales and ballads, and really any one of them will do. At the Elgin we get the barest essentials. There is Robin the chivalrous outlaw, camping out in the greenwood with Little John and the guys. There is Robin's beloved Maid Marian: rich and beautiful and an orphan. There is the villainous Sheriff of Nottingham, who in this version cuts a few legendary corners by abducting the Maid and scheming, in the most dastardly fashion, to marry her for her money. (There should be a song about Carryin' Marian Home, but there isnt). There is England, depicted as one big village green, waiting for King Richard the Lionheart to hurry back from his crusade and liberate everyone. There is Marians chaperone Nurse Tickle, and the Sheriff's henchman Pinch. You will not find these last two in any of the books, but they are among the immovable pillars of the pantomime tradition: She's the Dame, hes -- Im not sure how to finish this sentence. He's the low-comic, indeed the lowest of the low, but in panto these usually come in pairs. In Cinderella, for example, they're the Brokers Men, though in my long experience of the genre I cant remember ever meeting the Broker. This time perhaps we do. The Sheriff could be the broker, since he's called upon to supply the other half of the act while simultaneously functioning as its outraged employer. "You're next door to an idiot," the Sheriff snarls at Pinch, and Pinch immediately moves a couple of steps away. I love that joke, always have, but I remember it working much better last time than it does now.

Im not sure why. It may be that Petty himself, playing the Sheriff, is resting too comfortably on whatever villains wear in place of laurels. He comes on stage and demands to be hissed, before hes done so much as evict a widow. Simon Bradbury, as Pinch, is a natural for this kind of downtrodden knockabout, but he seems out of sorts -- he's certainly starved for good material. So is Nora McLellan, whose Nurse Tickle is excessively broad even for a pantomime dame. In the old country these roles are always played by men. I don't know on what altar of political correctness this custom has been been sacrificed, but a man-hungry harridan is not funny when played by a woman. McLellan only comes into her own when theres music. Handed by a comic song that sounds like it dropped out of an especially uninspired ancient British musical, she takes it by the scruff of its neck and makes it work. She also presides, with genuine generosity of spirit, over the inevitable song-sheet sequence.

Both Bradbury and McLellan are veterans of the Shaw Festival. Bradbury is even required to revert on occasion to his posh voice, and I suspect this double-duty has put a crimp in his style. The sight of classical performers making exhibitions of themselves has almost been one of the prime attractions of these shows. It was inaugurated in the finest style by Pettys wife, Karen Kain, who, unless I have my memories crossed, was a delicious Good Fairy in Robin Hood Mark One. The series has never quite recovered from her retirement, but this year the management has mustered her opposite number from the National Ballet, Rex Harrington, to play what would have been her opposite number in the show, a black-clad Wizard of the Wood. Speaking, or at least pouting, for the first time on any stage, he proves less adept than Kain at delivering a comic line, but he does sing, which is more than she ever did. He also, of course, glides on and off and around the trees in the most gracefully sinister manner imaginable. His antagonist -- who functions surprisingly often as his partner -- is Sara Topham, Stratford Festival ingenue and a pert pirouettist on her own account. Both suffer, though, from the fact the story has no need of them; they can hover over the narrative, but they can take very little part in it. Pantomime characters, of course, thrive on irrelevance; but they need some function to be irrelevant to.

Stratford, past and present, also contributes Thom Marriott who, hulking and sulking, looks the very image of Little John. Steve Ross who, not being rotund, is by no means the image of Friar Tuck, but who has a snappy way with a one-liner suggests he's on the way to being hilarious, given the chance; and -- most blessedly -- Graham Abbey in the title role. Abbey cut his teeth in this environment last year as Snow White's Prince, in effect burlesquing his own Romeo before hed even played it. As Robin he makes similar hay of his recent Henry V, or -- going further back -- of his DArtagnan in The Three Musketeers, which admittedly was something of a spoof to begin with. He has now got past the good-sport stage, and functions as a comic presence in his own right.

Romantic leads in pantomime were born to suffer, to be endured by the audience and mercilessly mocked by the full-time clowns. Abbey does it to himself before anyone else can do it to him, and is the funniest person in the show. He can also recover himself and act the heroics for all they're worth, or almost: We were told that on the first night he had to go easy on the Fairbanks stuff because of a leg injury.

And he sings, well enough to hold his own against the more practised warbling of his Marian, Amy Walsh. The musical choices this year are more eclectic than ever, though the score evinces a special fondness for the lyrics of the late Alan Jay Lerner. Three of his songs turn up, two with Loewe and one without: Robin sings I Talk to the Trees, which makes a lot of sense for man in his position (even the line about how he met the King of France seems to fit); the citizenry perform an unblushing makeover on Brigadoon's Down on MacConnachy Square, which here becomes Down in Nottingham Square without another word being changed; and hero and heroine carry on a long-distance duet of Come Back to Me, though with her being held in durance vile it seems an unreasonable request.

The opening number is rather less sophisticated in tone; it is in fact the title-song from the old Robin Hood TV series starring Richard Greene. (Now, there was a good show.) It needs, obviously, no lyric-laundering, but the merry men have to sing it three times while waiting for their leader, whose unpunctuality was apparently notorious, to make his expected tree-swinging entrance. The delay goads them on to increasingly desperate choreography; by the third chorus, they are executing dainty twirls with their quarterstaffs. It all sets an agreeably jokey tone which, whatever my carpings, is never subsequently imperilled. Some first-night mishaps prompted prime ad-libbing from Robin and the Sheriff; I think we can assume there will be similarly fruitful disasters for the remainder of the run. As always, the program coyly refuses to name an author but it does for once list a director other than Petty himself: Indeed rather a distinguished one, Jim Warren. He may have made a difference, but I can't say I noticed.

THE CONJUROR

Isabel Bader Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - I never yet saw a stage magician whose tricks I could begin to decode. To me theyre all wonder workers, and probably in league with the Devil. Still, even by my credulous standards, David Ben ranks very high among the elect or, alternatively, very low among the damned. Some of his feats unfold within the space of his own hand; others need the width of a whole stage. He is juggler, illusionist, apparent mind reader, and occasional escapologist. He is also a historian of his own craft. What he isnt is much of an actor.

This deficiency matters since in The Conjuror (which he co-wrote with Patrick Watson, who also directs) Ben appears before us, in sober black though with a lock of hair hanging flirtatiously down over one eye, as an Edwardian globetrotter, bearing news of all that's best in the world of magic circa 1909. This quasi-historical framework has earned the show a past gig at the Shaw Festival, but it hangs heavy on the evening as entertainment.

The visual fustiness, which extends to the use as an assistant of a pigtailed junior mandarin, is obviously intentional. Less so, perhaps, is the irritating coyness of the Conjuror's patter, full of references to obscure young pioneers he has met on his travels: a promising doctor called Sigmund Freud, a certain T.E. Lawrence (who will become famous, or so it is predicted, as Lawrence of Egypt") and "a young painter named Pablo. It seems the Conjuror was able to give Pablo and his pal Braque invaluable help with a new style they were some way to stumbling upon and to suggest they call it Cubism."

Ben does not have the panache that might turn this laborious stuff into humour; he just sloughs it off, leaving it stranded somewhere between old-fashioned formality and contemporary casualness. Understatement is only a virtue when it is cunning and confident enough to count as statement. Anyway, the veracity of the act is shattered whenever Ben, like any other trickster, invites members of the audience up on stage as helpers or victims. They of course couldn't look less Edwardian, not even the one who turns out to be a plant.

All magicians need patter -- partly to distract our attention and partly to hold it. Nothing could be more monotonous than simply being dazzled for an evening. (This show lasts a full two hours, with intermission, which is pushing it for a magic act.) Most of what Ben does could function just as well within a simpler, speedier and -- it is to be hoped -- funnier framework. He starts by producing an endless succession of oranges from about his person and tossing them to the audience, which is ingratiating as well as dazzling.

He makes a spectator levitate, and later coaxes even more fearsome physical contortions from his own son. He saws a man, rather than the traditional woman, in half -- and does it with unrepentant relish. Most charmingly, he endows a handkerchief not only with the ability to dance but with a shy personality of its own; when he is brusque with it, you may want to use your own eyes to wipe the hankie. Half the show is, in the strict sense of the word, marvellous; the other half is dull. Choose.

2002-12-20-casablanca-with-an-order-of-c:
Indefinite run. Box office: 416-486-7469.

MURDER IN CASABLANCA

Mysteriously Yours Mystery Dinner Theatre Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Nostalgiacs, rejoice: Rick's Cafe in Casablanca is still open for business. This is thanks to the people at Mysteriously Yours, whose Murder in Casablanca is their best show to date. One of the characteristics that is most Mysteriously Theirs is that, in all the 60 years since the release of the totemic movie, neither the Cafe nor Rick himself appears to have aged a day.

Some things of course have changed. Back in the Second World War Casablanca, ruled by Vichy France, was a jumping-off post for anti- Nazis desperate to escape to neutral Lisbon. These days its a haven for environmentalists, all of whom naturally crave entry to Canada. But terror still stalks the streets of Morocco, and human life is cheap: Cheaper if anything, since even the Chief of Police, whom one would formerly have tagged as a consummate survivor, is no longer immune. At an early stage of the proceedings the body of this Captain Renault, still in his old job and still the suavest of the suave (The plane to Newfoundland, Rick. Youd like to be on it?) is discovered lifeless in the alley, obviously offed. The rest of the cast must decide who was in the offing. As is standard procedure at Mysteriously Yours, they enlist -- or maybe that should be extort -- the assistance of the audience in finding out.

First we eat, rather well; and from a menu appropriate to the locale. (I mean it includes couscous.) Next, actors move among us, sitting down at our tables and confiding personal information, such as why their characters hate all the other characters. This is good strategy: Motive before mayhem. Then the entertainment proper begins, and Jean Daigle -- director, co-author (with Brian Caws) and star -- takes command.

Usually Daigle appears in these shows as a guttural detective calling himself Hercule Parrot. This time, though, he appears as Rick, himself. The show is the better for the change. The Agatha Christie interrogation set-up still remains, in cockeyed counterpoint to a story from another tradition altogether. Meanwhile the movie Casablanca's mythological status makes it an especially fertile source for slapstick pastiche, and it's good to see the maestro moving right in there and getting his hands dirty.

Now Daigle is not exactly the reincarnation of Humphrey Bogart. This Rick may not, as I said, have grown a day older but he has unquestionably become shorter and fatter. Vocally, too, he is more aggressively hard-boiled than the elegantly laconic Bogie ever was. The character he really suggests is Tony Soprano, or at least Tony as he might have sounded had James Gandolfini been passed over in favour of Bob Hoskins. (The Sopranos, incidentally, must be high on the list of future targets for Mysteriously Yours -- it would certainly present a stimulating challenge to both cast and kitchen.) With a murder, and the love of his life, dropped on his doorstep simultaneously, Daigle shows us perplexity about to explode. He has to take it out on someone, so he takes it out on us. The audience at these plays always gets balloted on the killers identity; a permanent attraction is the scorn that Daigle invariably pours on those of us who guessed wrong.

The other actors conspire to take the action and characters of Casablanca to a new level. They draw out tendencies that the original authors may never have known they had. Along with a cop called Renault, the screenplay has made the show a present of a gangster named Ferrari. They take this coincidence (if thats what it is) and run, or rather drive, with it. We meet the incorruptible conservationist Victor Volvo (a performance by Brian Smith of virtuoso upstandingness), and his wife (Birgitte Solem, white- sheathed and demurely provocative), known to film-buffs as Ilsa Lund but here logically if somewhat laboriously revealed as Ilsa Lund- Rover. She of course is Rick's old Scandinavian flame, with whom he once shared an unforgettable time in the most romantic of cities. ("Whatever happens, we will always have Nantucket.")

Rick also has a newer, jealous flame, a role much expanded from the movie. There, she was the one who hooked up with a German, provoking from Renault the comment In her own way, she may constitute an entire second front. She was called Yvonne then. Now, of course, she is called Mercedes. Rick is tiring of her, maybe because she calls him Wick. (She does this because she has a lisp.) Mercedes is a singer, and she, or someone, knows the score. You expect to hear the inevitable As Time Goes By, but not perhaps the less-remembered Knock on Wood, delivered by Mercedes with all- purpose chic and some surprising new lyrics. ("Who's got cellulite? Weve got cellulite.") She doesnt do requests, or I might have been tempted to ask for The Lady is a Twamp, or better still Widin' Awound in the Wain. She is played by Barb Scheffler, incomparably.

Blaine Parker weighs in, at several stone, as Ferrari who smokes a villainous cigar (down these green streets a man must go). Gregg Taylor plays Renault and also, so he won't just lie around all evening, a cringing spy named Bugatti, in which role he manages a truly electrifying Peter Lorre impersonation: much the evening's best feat of mimicry. Spectators fulfill their assigned roles with gallantry and, in a few cases, cheek. At my visit three young people, seated not far from me, were pressed into service to play a camel and I thought they were excellent. I greatly admired the snap of the dialogue, and the unfazed alacrity of the ad-libs; I wonder if dinner-theatres are eligible for Doras. I came to Casablanca for the laughs and the eats. I was well-informed.
