2002-12-21-scrooge-tiny-tim-et-al-are-a-:
Until Dec. 29. Box office: 416-973-4000.; rcushman@nationalpost.com

A CHRISTMAS CAROL

Premier Dance Theatre

- - -

Soulpepper's A Christmas Carol, back for a second run, is as joyous, touching and resourceful as it was last year: theatrical magic directed to a moral end, and therefore doubly satisfying.

As a family experience, its credentials now extend from the auditorium to the stage itself. Joseph Ziegler repeats his fine performance of Scrooge; his wife, Nancy Palk, has taken over as Mrs. Cratchit (she's the one newcomer) and their son, Henry Ziegler, remains a creditably unmawkish Tiny Tim. Tim is of course the youngest Cratchit, and when we learn at the end that the reformed Scrooge became a second father to the boy, the justice of it seems even more poetic than usual.

Scrooge, as we all know, is a creature of extremes. The senior Ziegler is devilishly effective at the beginning of his journey, and angelically so at the end. Much less desiccated than most stage or screen Scrooges, he presents a still-vigorous man of business whose misanthropy is as much a matter of position as of disposition: not merely uncharitable but anti-charitable.

This robs some of his flights -- like the one about Christmas well-wishers being brained with their own pudding and buried with sprigs of holly through their hearts -- of their baroque hilarity, but it does suggest the coherent philosophy of a man whose head is as hard as his heart.

Surprisingly, he has a vulnerable imagination: a mordant sense of humour that starts to betray him immediately the ghosts come knocking. It softens, and takes him over, as he revisits his own past Decembers: observing himself as a boy, reclaimed from a miserable boarding school by a repentant father (it was clever of Dickens to suggest that sudden changes of heart run in the family) and then as a shy young man at his employer's party, dancing with his sweetheart.

Ziegler, in a charming moment of impatient nostalgia, demonstrates the steps. He dances, too, through his redemption: kicking off his shoes in an ecstasy of impromptu choreography. He gets full measure from the dialogue with the boy who reassures him that it is indeed Christmas Day and whom he dispatches to buy a turkey as big as himself: one of the great self-hugging moments in literature.

I have never understood, by the way, why Scrooge, in his last dream, is so slow to realize that the man in the grave is himself; he has been given enough clues, and the one thing he is not -- as Ziegler consistently and brilliantly demonstrates -- is stupid.

Michael Shamata's production of his own adaptation is both snug and spacious. It is suggestively set, by John Ferguson, in a box with many doors. At first glance it looks like a grim Victorian hallway; it can, we discover, equally well be an unexpectedly bustling Victorian street. (A small cast doubles, trebles and quadruples; this may not be meant to heighten the dream-effect, but it does.) Or the doors simply mark the boundaries and passageways between the past and the present, the actual and the possible. There are some lightning bravura effects, like the sudden appearance of Ali Baba from the recesses of the Scrooge-child's imagination, and the stage is smoothly parcelled out among episodes. If a scene is cramped, it's for a reason.

Thus, the poverty of the Cratchits' Christmas is stressed by confining it to one tiny, crowded table. (And the festive goose is pitiful enough to be a gosling.) I missed the sharp Dickensian outline of Susan Coyne's Clara last year, but Palk gives a warmly harried account of the role, and the increasingly excellent Oliver Dennis is a practically perfect Bob. He also plays countless other roles, in at least one of which, a receiver of stolen goods, he is unrecognizable: Good to know that he can play nasty as well as nice.

Patrick Galligan also brings grace to virtue as Scrooge's nephew, who exemplifies a more elegant level of hospitable poverty; his guests include Palk who -- in one of the evening's swifter transformations -- is languidly witty, and Tanja Jacobs who, in this and other roles, is enjoyably outrageous.

Some of the young adults are weak, but John Jarvis does a magisterial job as an unassuming narrator whose real business is to play all four ghosts. (Imaginative costuming by Ferguson.) As Marley in chains, he clanks and yanks enthusiastically; he goes on to make a bonhomous Ghost of Christmas Past, a silently menacing Future and a Present who splits the difference by alternating twinkle with glower. In the latter aspect, he can be almost too thunderous; the story and its images are making their own point with little need of underlining.

As usual Dickens stirs our consciences; and Soulpepper (and sponsor, Clarica) do us a favour by letting us contribute to the Daily Bread Food Bank on our way out.

George Orwell famously wrote that Dickens was an author whom both Left and Right tried vainly to kidnap. A Christmas Carol, being a straight-out parable, demonstrates even more plainly than his other works that he would not have cared whether philanthropy was public or private as long as it got the job done.

Black & White Photo: Cylla Von Teidemann / Soulpepper's A Christmas Carol, directed and adapted by Michael Shamata, runs until Dec. 29.
2002-12-30-the-road-to-chicago:
The film version of the 1975 Broadway musical Chicago works because we are fascinated by the intersection of celebrity and evil. Thats why it worked in 1975. And 1942. And 1927

Here is a bit of musical comedy lyric that Im fond of, a delectable slice of heartless insouciance. It's sung by a pair of theatrical agents to a nubile young woman who has recently been the death of her male protector. The chorus begins:

So here's a good tiding:

If men you are killing,

A talent youre hiding

To be a performer.

So be a performer

And soon youll be riding

(If God should be willing)

The crest of your life.

And it ends:

Unless you, God forbid,

Get hung for what you did --

Oho, you naughty kid.

Just fulfil this small request of your life.

You'll be happy all the rest of your

Long and healthy

(Knock wood)

Life!

That does not come from Chicago, show or movie, though it well might. The situation depicted and the philosophy advanced would fit right in there. It's from a stage musical called Little Me. The late, great and underrated Carolyn Leigh wrote the words, to music by the still-flourishing Cy Coleman. Little Me was staged on Broadway in 1962. The first Broadway production of Chicago was in 1975.

Im not accusing anyone of stealing (though I do remember being struck, when I saw that 75 production in previews, by the similarity of its first cynical spoken line to that of another, earlier show set in a criminal milieu, Irma la Douce). I'm merely suggesting that, in equating criminal and showbiz celebrity, Chicago was not as ferociously ahead of its time as it has become fashionable to believe.

Little Me's Belle Poitrine puts on a good show in court, is acquitted of murder, and becomes a star. She and the show then go on to other things. Chicago shows a jailful of jazz-age murderesses, chief among them the aspiring performer Roxie Hart and the experienced trouper Velma Kelly, who owe their eventual freedom, and stardom, to the grandstanding tactics of the razzle-dazzle lawyer Billy Flynn. It tickles me to note that it takes Chicago more than two hours to deliver the same message that Be a Performer socks over in less than four minutes, and that Be a Performer is funnier.

Chicagos prescient amorality -- or its prescience about amorality -- is generally held to account for its initial failure. A major flaw in this theory is the fact that the first production of Chicago was a success; it received generally admiring reviews and ran for more than 900 performances. It didnt take home many awards, but that was because it opened in the same season as A Chorus Line.

Revisionist history holds that A Chorus Line was a feelgood show that the sentimental audiences of the time lapped up in preference to the tough medicine offered by Chicago. Actually, A Chorus Line won because it was the better show (though Chicago has the better score). It also faces unpleasant truths just as squarely and -- since its characters are people rather than cartoons -- to more disturbing emotional effect.

Today, of course, a musical season that could boast both A Chorus Line and Chicago seems to belong to some unimaginable golden age. In fact, its riches extended even further than that. This was also the season of Pacific Overtures, the Stephen Sondheim/John Weidman musical about America's opening-up of 19th-century Japan to Western markets, layered and mournfully ironic. If you were looking for intelligence and adventurousness in musicals, that was the place to turn, but few people did, then or since. Some 15 years later, the same team came up with Assassins, a far more searching examination than Chicago of the links between violence, celebrity-worship and the cult of entitlement. I don't see Hollywood taking up either of these musicals in the near future.

Spectators at Chicago, in 1975 as in 2002, were having a good sophisticated giggle at the idea of universal corruption. This is the reaction the material has always provoked. It must have done so in 1927 when it first surfaced as a play based on an actual case, and it certainly did so in 1942 when the film Roxie Hart (starring Ginger Rogers but not a musical) took its place in the great tradition of hardboiled screen comedy.

Meanwhile, Broadway had given the world Anything Goes, Cole Porters 1934 ocean liner musical, in which a chorus of first-class passengers are tickled pink to find themselves on board with Public Enemy Number One, and sing a hymn in his honour; and Rodgers and Harts 1940 Pal Joey, an unwaveringly dark musical that happens to be set in a decadent Chicago clubland. That's another show always quoted as having been ahead of its time, but which was in fact a solid success the first time around.

Audiences are versatile animals; they can enjoy heart on one night and heartlessness on another, with no reference to what is supposed to be the Zeitgeist. Beware of pundits who tell you what you, as a product of your times, ought to respond to; they are, without exception, idiots.

The 1975 production of Chicago was brilliant. Even people who hated it could tell that. I know, because I was one of them. As a tourist, I appreciated the opportunity to collect three certified Broadway legends -- Gwen Verdon, Chita Rivera, Jerry Orbach -- in one evening and to see all of them operating at top form.

My problem was with the show's director, choreographer and presiding genius Bob Fosse. He had done a magisterially inventive and imaginative job, but I thought he was being self-indulgent. Not theatrically -- nothing could have been more disciplined -- but personally. When Orbachs lawyer went through his Razzle Dazzle number, he seemed to be standing in for Fosse, excoriating his own genius for playing theatrical tricks while continuing to play them, offering us delight while despising us for accepting it. (Rivera welcomed us back after intermission with a cheery, "Hello, suckers.")

If that was how Fosse felt, shouldnt he just put up or shut up? And what were those lines in Fred Ebb's lyric: Long as you keep 'em way off balance/How can they spot you got no talents? Did Ebb really want us to believe that he, or his composing collaborator John Kander, or the performers, or Fosse himself, were untalented? He knew they werent; we knew they werent. Wasn't all this mock self-flagellation rather sickly? And didn't it make the storys simple satirical point unnecessarily pretentious?

Fosse had been playing this love-hate game with his own abilities ever since directing the film of Cabaret. The original show (which he had nothing to do with) had handed him a metaphor, and he had run with it, all the way to his autobiographical movie All That Jazz. It made me angry, the more so because I admired almost everything else he did.

I no longer feel so strongly about it. Fosse and his few peers (Jerome Robbins, Gower Champion, Michael Bennett) have died, leaving no successors. They are, to put it mildly, missed. Chicago returned to Broadway in 1996, in a blown-up concert staging, and is still there. So the revival has run much longer than the original, and has generated the usual international spin-offs.

The word is that audiences have now caught up with the shows savage indictment of society, and have only to turn on the news to find contemporary parallels. The O.J. Simpson trial is frequently cited, though I can't imagine why. Simpson was a superstar before being indicted; Roxie and Velma are eternal wannabes.

But the real reason the show now slips down more easily is that, with Fosse no longer in control, it has shed its weight of personal obsession. It is a smaller show, but a more enjoyable one; an uncomplicated fable, rousingly performed. I had a great time at it. I caught the revival's first Velma, Bebe Neuwirth, who turned in the sleekest, most dynamic song-and-dance act I have seen in years. Watching her go through I Cant Do It Alone (she could), I found myself hoping that Ann Reinking, who both directed and played Roxie, was a lady with no malice in her heart; for she had to sit at the side of the stage during that number and watch Neuwirth steal the show from under her nose, eight times a week.

And now there is the movie, inheriting the old problems and adding new ones. People are still saying how topical it all is and how rotten we all are (or at least how rotten everybody else is), but not as loudly. A more pressing question seems to have taken over: How can you con a modern movie audience into sitting through a musical?

All the reviews I have read have said two things: a) this is the best film of a stage musical since Cabaret, and b) thats not saying much, considering the competition. I would not contest either point. But I am bothered by another repeated assertion: that Chicago's presentation of all its musical numbers as fantasies is proof positive that no other way is possible. We are told that audiences presented with characters gliding from speech into song as part of a story would hoot with derision, and probably tear up the seats.

This seems to me completely unproven, another example of theorists telling audiences how to behave. My, they're hip. Its certainly true that the numbers in Chicago wouldnt work as quasi- realistic character songs, but that's because that's not how they were written in the first place. Theyre the authors and director's commentaries on the action, and to perform them the actors assume the position of jazz, burlesque or vaudeville icons, fitted out with parodies of 1920s songs. (The parodies are exact: one-on-one, in some cases.) Both stage productions have been done on abstract sets, complex in the Fosse original, bare in the revival. In both we were, all the time and unmistakably, in the theatre.

This isn't really an option for a movie, and Rob Marshall, the director-choreographer, puts us where the story says we are: an apartment, a courthouse or (most of the time) the Cook County jail. The sets are stylized but theyre still places. The numbers can no longer be Fosses dreams, so they have to be the stagestruck Roxie's.

Most of the time, the writing and direction make this work. The one number in the original that is conventional conversational -- a funny female duet, very Kander-and-Ebb, called Class -- has been deleted. Dialogue that seems to be leading up to it is still there, so the cut must have been a last-minute decision. Presumably they realized there was no way of making it fit.

But something is still wrong. The picture looks like a musical -- the screen is full of flailing limbs and tapping feet -- but it doesn't feel like one. For all his Broadway experience (perhaps even because of it), Marshall seems as afraid of the genre as everybody else is supposed to be.

A review in Torontos Eye Weekly magazine has congratulated him on continually switching from the numbers to the plot "because theres nothing more tedious on film than four straight minutes of singing and dancing." Well, it's an opinion. I doubt if it would be shared by many people who've seen Astaire and Rogers, or Gene Kelly and Donald OConnor (separately or together) or, come to that, Joel Grey and Liza Minnelli in Cabaret, and it seems a strange position from which to judge musicals.

Its also a strange position from which to direct musicals, but it seems to have been Marshall's. He cuts so relentlessly and frenetically that we never actually get to see the performers perform. That negates the best reason for going to see musicals; it certainly negates what this show, in either of its incarnations, was about in the theatre.

Or maybe it's his stars whom Marshall distrusts. A couple of supporting players (Queen Latifah, John C. Reilly) get a chance to stretch out, and take it. But Catherine Zeta-Jones Velma is a blank with a slinky body attached; lacking the magnetic desperation with which both Rivera and Neuwirth flooded the role, she just seems unlikeable.

She has, admittedly, lost two of her best songs. Renee Zellweger has more to work with, and she makes a fine, fluffy Roxie, whose schemes seem to pop out of her head like speech balloons. Shes at her best in the trial which, significantly, is where the movie most departs from and expands on the show, and in which all she has to do is act.

Marshall has abandoned Fosse's louche choreographic trademarks (there are, as one reviewer has pointed out, no derbies) in favour of a more generic licentiousness, but in some ways he comes closer to the stage original than the revival does. The old relentlessness is back. This, as I may have hinted, is not necessarily a good thing. It draws attention to the show's main flaw: It keeps saying the same thing, over and over, in song after song.

So we're all either corrupt or gullible, except for those of us who are both, and every one of us harbours the jealous ambition to Be a Performer. Guilty. And what else is new?

Black & White Photo: Renee Zellweger in the new film adaptation of Chicago, which looks like a musical without feeling like one. Some of Zellweger's best moments are where all she has to do is act.
2002-12-31-the-shape-of-the-2002-theatre:
robertcushman@lycos.com

Old plays came to Toronto, new ones debuted, and faces new and old took to the stage

The more it changes. I've been glancing at my summary of Toronto theatre in 2001, and my first thought is that I could almost reprint it, changing only the names, and by no means all of them. At least I think my headings and links can stay the same. Lets see if it works.

AS FOR NEW TORONTO PLAYS ... THE YEAR BEGAN INVIGORATINGLY ... THINGS DECLINED PRECIPITOUSLY ...

Right. 2002s best new play was its first. Michael Healey's Plan B took the author of The Drawer Boy from the meta-theatrical to the sexually political. It unrolled less smoothly than its predecessor but ranged more widely and more deeply, and it spoke, sharply but humanely, in our theatre's most identifiable comic voice. I mean that almost literally, since my memory keeps insisting that Healey himself played the leading role, even though he didnt. (Peter Donaldson did, very well.) This may be due to Healeys having been so enjoyably in evidence later on, in the role of the craven critic in Carole Corbeil's In the Wings. He also wrote, or adapted, the most memorable segment of Soulpepper's Absolutely Chekhov. Both as writer and performer (I think of him as a performer rather than an actor) he is a master of verbal slapstick, a deceptive bumbler whose peregrinations always wind up on target.

After that, though, there was nothing. Well, almost nothing; Morris Panychs Girl in a Goldfish Bowl, the years second-best Canadian play, was likeable -- Panych writes very well for actors, and is also a superb director -- but unco-ordinated, a letdown after his previous triumphs with The Overcoat and Earplay.

In the Wings was a moderately endearing mess. Otherwise, on the Tarragon-Factory-Passe Muraille axis and beyond, the year yielded a handful of smartly staged mediocrities, a couple of ambitious disasters, and several numbing atrocities. Somewhat off the main drag there were three first-rate youth-oriented pieces: Adam Pettle's probing Misha, presented as part of Theatre Direct's Buncha festival; Leslie Ardens enchanting The Happy Prince, brought into what we used to call (some of us still do) the Young People's Theatre; and Joan MacLeod's The Shape of a Girl, from Vancouver to the Tarragon Backspace.

WELCOME IF BELATED IMPORTS ...

The Canadian Stage Company, despite its name, has a terrible record with Canadian plays but an excellent one with plays from abroad. Tom Stoppards Indian Ink was, strictly speaking, the best new play of the year. New to Toronto, that is: On British stage and radio it goes back about 10 years. It was given a superb wide-angle production by Richard Cottrell, dazzlingly designed by Susan Benson. Visually, this production bore the same relation to everything else seen on our stages as did Julie Taymors Frida to everything else seen on our movie screens.

As for American plays, these admittedly not so belated. Proof, which arrived all Tonied and Pulitzered, turned out to be nothing special (no more did the comparably garlanded and slightly superior Side Man at the Tarragon). Neil LaBute's The Shape of Things was electric; for thrills and surprises that were more than tricks, it was the most exciting evening of the year.

SOULPEPPER, STILL TORONTO'S BEST HOPE ...

I dont know how critics in Toronto stayed sane before this company came along. (Maybe they didnt.) Soulpepper's fifth year was an especially good one for its director, Albert Schultz. As Astrov in Uncle Vanya he gave probably the best performance of his career, while his production of Alan Ayckbourn's A Chorus of Disapproval was simply the finest thing seen on a Toronto stage all year. (Another contender for best new play, though this one, apart from being English, was 20 years old.)

Apparently it got into the season through a lucky accident. Soulpepper needed a companion to its concert revival of The Beggars Opera, and Stratford had snagged the rights to the more obvious Threepenny bit. The Beggars Opera, incidentally (I didn't review it at the time), turned out to be too insistently, or at least too fussily, musical. The few songs that worked were the simplest ones. But it did suggest that Patricia O'Callaghan, a magnetic Polly previously known only as a singer, might become a musical-theatre star.

In truth, all of Soulpeppers shows, apart from Chorus and the revived Vanya and Christmas Carol, have to rank as near misses, The Winters Tale being the nearest. But the sense remained of zest and commitment and of windows being opened onto territories we hardly ever see.

STRATFORD HAD ITS STRONGEST SEASON IN YEARS, GRATIFYINGLY RICH IN SHAKESPEARE ...

Yes and no. Stratford's 50th season suffered somewhat in comparison with its 49th, but the Shakespearean standard held. Christopher Plummer's King Lear surpassed expectation, which was running high. It had all the anticipated grandeur, more than the anticipated pathos, and a knack -- unleashed at stimulatingly irregular intervals -- for applying electric shocks to the text. Jonathan Millers production had a helpfully specific sense of time and place, but its supporting players seemed to be operating on a sink-or-swim basis. Like most critics I was rough on the young actress playing Cordelia; it occurred to me later that she might have stood more of a chance if her director, apparently distrustful of the plays redemptive element, had cut less of her role.

There was more detailed textual exploration, and richer company acting, in some less heralded productions: in Miles Potter's Romeo and Juliet, which found craggy contours in the Capulet household while playing bravely but fairly with a tragedy that for most of the time behaves like a comedy; in Leon Rubin's invigorating two-part Henry VI; in Martha Henrys Richard III, which was almost done in by a smothering set but which had a host of interesting people nestling in its crannies; and, on the edge of the canon, in David Lathams account of The Two Noble Kinsmen, a rewarding showcase for graduates of the Stratford conservatory.

Apart from Richard Monette's handsome staging of My Fair Lady, non-Shakespearean work in the main theatres was below par. The compensation was the opening of the Stratford studio with a season of seven new plays. Most of these would have looked standard on the Toronto circuit but there were a couple of exceptions: Paul Dunn's compact High-Gravel Blind and, at the opposite extreme, Peter Hintons sprawling The Swanne, first instalment of a promised trilogy. This is still impossible to judge. It seems foolhardy to build an elaborate critique of Victorian society on an incident that not even the author believes actually happened, but the size and energy made you want to come back for more. And it made a great workout for the company.

THE SHAW FESTIVAL HAD ITS WEAKEST ...

Not this year, though it was uneven. Christopher Newtons farewell season was distinguished by his superlative Return of the Prodigal (itself a return from the previous season) and by his moderately dark and very funny Hay Fever. (An insight into how Coward can be immoderately dark and sublimely funny was provided by the recent London production of Private Lives, starring an immaculate Alan Rickman and a wounded, shimmering Lindsay Duncan, which I caught at the end of its season in New York.)

Newton's successor, Jackie Maxwell, directed the only enjoyable Candida I have ever seen. Neil Munro's production of Detective Story was one of the best of his large-scale American genre pieces, and Munro also rounded off his Granville-Barker cycle with His Majesty, which demanded patience but amply rewarded it.

BIG MUSICALS, USUALLY IN TACKY TOURING VERSIONS, WERE DEADLY ...

As before, except Contact couldnt reasonably be accused of being tacky.

THE GENERALLY MORIBUND COMMERCIAL THEATRE DID WELL WITH PLAYS ...

Make that singular; the Mirvishes gave a wider showing to Zadies Shoes. Otherwise, the producers are waiting for The Producers. So are we all.

THIS HAS BEEN A GREAT YEAR FOR ONE-PERSON SHOWS ...

There were at least two this year, both female, that I can hardly bear to think about.

I now depart from last year's template with a few observations peculiar to this one.

UNDERRATED PERFORMANCES ...

Amy Redford in The Shape of Things; she attracted inexplicable animosity for being American and a film star's daughter, but in fact conveyed the character perfectly. Jennifer Paterson in Proof; similar, she was unquestionably immature technically, but that actually helped. And -- amazingly -- Ted Dykstra in A Chorus of Disapproval; nobody denied he was good, but nobody said that he gave the best performance of the year, which he did.

OVERRATED PERFORMANCE ...

Kate Hennig in The Danish Play, itself a strong, though certainly not unrivalled, candidate for Most Overrated Play. Actually, she wasnt half bad. But she wasnt half good, either, and I find the idea that the bad parts were a bold stylistic choice hard to swallow.

BEST PERFORMANCES OTHER THAN THOSE ALREADY MENTIONED ...

CHRONIC

Factory Theatre

- - -

Petra, the protagonist of Linda Griffiths' new play, suffers from what is probably Chronic Fatigue Syndrome, a condition that is difficult to treat and whose causes are unknown. The play takes the view that its viral, and even brings the virus onstage as a character. Virus is, of course, a word thats rife in our society - - virulently so, indeed -- and the author has no trouble spreading it around. The mysteriousness of the disease gives Chronic some of its initial interest. Its handiness as a metaphor, applicable to just about any situation, proves its undoing.

Petra works, necessarily part-time, in a small, ambitious software firm. Unless I was missing something -- and the dialogue gets pretty dense around these techies -- the phrase "computer virus" is never used in the sense with which most of us are familiar; rather, we are invited to believe that the information economy itself is working like a virus in our society; this company, at any rate, seems a lot more informative than economic.

Petra's co-workers are also her friends; one of them, Chris, is her boyfriend. When we first meet them, they have been together for six months, something of a record, it seems, for both of them. At some point in the second act, it transpires that they've lasted five years, though there is very little sense of time having passed.

Petras condition seems to be part of her attraction for Chris, who is very involved with her treatment and finds it a challenge. So, after an initial period of nervousness, does her younger colleague, Amber. A lesbian relationship seems about to blossom, in a scene where Amber sponges Petra down, though its diverted when Amber learns their boss Oscar, also young and geekishly driven, has fancied her for ages.

It's Petra who passes on this information, which dramatically comes right out of the blue. Nothing we have learned about either participant makes it sound either plausible or the reverse.

Meanwhile, Chris has an affair with Diane, Petra's doctor, a try- anything practitioner operating on the borderline between orthodox and alternative medicine; her specialty is hypnosis and she has a perpetually worried look. The person shes really attracted to is, of course, Petra. Chris, on first meeting Diane, contributes to the universal-virus theory of society by belligerently asserting that the Pentagon deliberately manufactured AIDS. This could, though, be meant as comic relief.

The play, in its earlier stages, is not as bad as all that makes it sound. It somewhat resembles Impromptu on Nuns Island, the new play from Michel Tremblay, in that its a debate with a storyline tagged on. Tremblay's story is the easier to follow, but at least with Griffiths you're spared the feeling that the author came to the party with all her ideas worked out years in advance. She does seem to be exploring, and theres a texture to her depiction of her heroine thats worthy of respect.

But the development is stagnant; at times Petra seems better, at times she seems worse, but the impenetrability of her condition makes it hard to know how or why to care. She conducts recurrent debates, which seem longer than they probably are, with the embodied Virus. He, like most of the cast, wants to possess her and obviously has a better chance than any of them; his invasion and her resistance are persistently restated, though admittedly it's hard to imagine what else they could have to say with one another.

The Virus is a peculiarly unhappy invention (dramatically, I mean, rather than medically, though that, of course, as well) who keeps coming on like Mephistopheles but going out like a pantomime Demon King without the charm. Eric Peterson, who has appeared these last few seasons in a succession of unusually irritating roles, cavorts mercilessly in this one, mincing any meaning that his lines might have.

Otherwise, Simon Heath directs a pleasantly cool production to which Caroline Gillis as Petra supplies a firm, unsentimental centre. I'm not sure what qualifications the character has to be considered a moral touchstone but the play implicitly treats her as one (even while denying that illness in itself makes anybody special) and the actress has the gravitas for it. Her authority may seem the greater because none of the other characters comes to life; though the actors seem to be doing their best, and the lines of communication between them are admirably unfussed.

The plays sense of humour is less than intermittent, but J. D. Nicholsen displays the occasional sharp glint of it as Chris; Graeme Somerville and Holly Lewis, as senior and junior nerd, are decent, if amorphous. As doctor Diane, Brooke Johnson doesnt get much beyond wearing a white coat and projecting shame-faced concern.

Andrea Lundy's lighting rings ingenious colour-changes on David Boechler's set, which is a vast quilted bed. All the world, it seems, is a sickroom, and that is the dispiritingly familiar conclusion to which the play conveys us. It's like having the sanity- is-madness rhetoric of R. D. Laing redirected from the mind to the body.

Petra, who has spent the play as a patient, now ministers to all the others, who have found blissed-out release from a stressed-out world. Some of them are even mimicking the most striking symptoms -- one that she herself describes as a kind of oral dyslexia, and which in her case takes the form of an inability to pronounce the word "home." Maybe she gets there in the end; I couldn't tell.

The play, though it fights against its fate, ends up as a rarefied disaster-of-the-week piece. Any deeper meaning dissolves on the tongue.

Black & White Photo: Nir Bareket / Eric Peterson, as the Virus, cavorts mercilessly, while Caroline Gillis, as Petra, supplies a firm, unsentimental centre.

SUNDAY FATHER

Berkeley Street Theatre

- - -

Just a week ago, in my summary of last year's theatre, I castigated CanStage for its terrible record with new Canadian plays. 2003 has barely dawned, and already the company makes a monkey out of me. From our first sight of the stage, which has been divided into three glistening compartments, Sunday Father, the new unburnt offering from Adam Pettle, is irresistible.

The tripartite set accommodates an action that moves swiftly through a variety of rooms. It also happens to match the plays cast list.There are three onstage characters: brothers Jed and Alan and Amy, Jeds wife. Others of course are mentioned without being seen: The most important of these are Jed and Amy's young son Daniel, and the brothers' father, a very successful lawyer.

Jed and Alan are the children of divorce. They spent weekends with their dad, and rounded off each visit by recording a tape, riffing on the activities of the day. These spoof radio-shows, brimming with hardly suppressed sibling rivalry, are recreated for us by the two grown-up actors as counterpoint to, and commentary on, the present-day action. Their catch-phrase introduction is "Hello, ladies and Gentiles."

The North American Jewishness that was spray-painted over Pettles earlier play, Zadies Shoes, is here applied with more surgical precision. Jed and Alan are, of course, Jewish. Amy isn't, a circumstance that breeds some tension between her and Jed, mostly expressed through uneasy jokes. It is not, though, the immediate cause of their break-up. Break up they do, and Jed finds himself on track for his father's fate of becoming a Sunday father. It probably suited his father. He doesnt believe it will suit him.

Jed and Alan have maintained a bantering relationship, centred on drinks and sports. Alan, unmarried and with a penchant for younger women, is a perpetual jock. So its ironic it should be Jed who's made a career in sports, at least to the extent of writing about them.

Alan, with apparent incongruity, has followed his father into the law; indeed he's followed his father into his fathers office. This was a painful course, because his father has always liked to make him squirm. Jed was the favourite; Alan resented it then and he resents it now, probably even more. His preferred Biblical excerpt is Cain and Abel.

At one point Alan tells this story, uncle-fashion, to an unseen Daniel, recasting it, to bitterly hilarious effect, in terms of contemporary Forest Hill.

At another, Jed, who is as much into Greek mythology as Hebrew, tells him in similar vein about the birth of Pallas Athene. This is also entertaining though not bitter. At a third, Amy does the bedtime routine with the legend of Pandoras box; one doesn't want to sound racist or sexist -- and the play is neither of those things -- but her goyish update sounds pretty pallid compared to the free- wheeling deconstructions offered by the two guys.

Not that that makes her a bad mother: But it's undeniable that Amy -- a psychiatrist with the physicians proverbial inability to cure herself -- gets less of a crack dramatically than the boys do. Even so, the play deals alarmingly well with the bitterness of divorce between two loving but incompatible people.

Especially cunning is a scene in which Jed and Amy recall their first meeting, so smoothly affectingly as to make the audience, sentimental slobs that we are, sniff a reconciliation; the possibility is then withdrawn and we -- acknowledging the truth -- take it without resentment.

A more serious glitch is one common to plays in which a major participant is glimpsed only through other peoples perceptions and other people's memories. The play, or its title, may link Jed to dad, but we never get a clear sense of what the old man is like. Clearly, he's overpowering -- he even dies in a lively way -- but that isnt enough. His invisibility may connect to Alans identification of him with God -- Abel's God -- but the fact remains that they can say anything, and we just have to sit there and take it. Why is he so terrible to Alan? Yes, parents have been known to play favourites, but this one's partiality strikes from beyond the grave. I dont want to give anything away, and its not an exact analogy, but I was reminded of one of my favorite Jewish jokes, concerning the Reading of the Rich Man's Will. "And to my no-good brother-in-law Louis, who said I'd never mention him in my will: Hello, Louis".

A last weakness is that the stage-right portion of the set goes unused until late in the evening. Otherwise the design (by Britta Gerecke, new to me and to Toronto) focuses attention admirably, apart from being smart and striking itself. Ive heard complaints that its too clinical and that it inhibits the actors; since the play has feeling to spare, and since the performers had no trouble making me laugh and -- towards the end -- cry, I'd be inclined to discount them.

David Storch's direction, especially of the actors, looked flawless to me. There are very few forced notes.

The plays themes interlock, but if you break then down you can say that it deals -- in ascending order of effectiveness -- with relationships parental, marital, and fraternal. The dialogue in Pettles previous plays has always flowed easily but has sometimes sounded glib; this time, given the characters and their circumstances, all doubts are squashed.

The brotherly scenes are duets as supple and uproarious as any I remember in a Canadian play. Ari Cohen's Alan is a wonderful sweaty- nerved lunk, a breathing compound of resentment, obnoxiousness, vulnerability and generosity.

Jed is Jordan Pettle, the author's own brother, who was also in Zadie's Shoes. His role there, an irresponsible charmer, was theoretically more complex than his role here, which is that of an emotional lightweight who is nonetheless honest and doing his best; the acting Pettle, more focused and economical than before, keeps him likeable without ever usurping the moral high ground.

Liisa Repo-Martell, whose previous appearances have nearly all been as physical or emotional orphans, seizes gratefully and rewardingly on her first chance to appear before a paying public in a well-tailored suit; she has a firm new vocal register to go with it and is, in the best sense, unrecognizable.

For once actors in a new play get to relish their roles rather than rescue them.

TWO WORDS FOR SNOW

Artword Theatre, Toronto

Commander Robert Peary, the celebrated Arctic explorer, and his assistant Matthew Henson have turned up on our stages these past few years with surprising frequency. They were minor characters in Ragtime; Father, that musical's self-proclaimed "forward thinker" went off with them to discover the North Pole, and was mightily surprised to find that Henson, holding the exalted position of first mate, was black.

Having done their bit to expose the token liberals inbuilt racism, Peary and Henson sailed right out of the show. (There is, of course, more about them in the novel.) But they have a whole play to themselves in Richard Sangers Two Words for Snow, which explores the ice trek's racial implications in more detail, and which premiered at the 1999 PlayRites festival in Calgary. It has now been remounted in revised form.

Sanger is a poet, and when I saw his play in Alberta, I described it as a work that was planned as a fantasia but emerged as more of a meditation. The meditative element is even more pronounced in this new version. In paring down his material, the author has refined it almost out of existence. We seem to be watching the preparations for, and the aftermath of, a drama that never actually happens.

As before, we shuttle between two parts of the past. We are in New York, in the Eskimo Room of the American Museum of Natural History. An aged Henson, almost an exhibit himself, receives a visit from Peary's son, anxious to preserve his fathers place in the history books. It seems the Commanders claim to have been the first man at the Pole is being disputed by Henson, in his own favour. Back we flash, principally to the Arctic-moored ship from which Peary and company plan their polar conquest.

The part of Henson is played, as it was four years ago, by Nigel Shawn Williams, who is most impressive in his older, more tired incarnation, looking weary and bleary at the younger Peary. As the fresher, idealistic Matt he is little more than nice. This is despite the fact that, even at this point, the character has a lot to be angry about. Not only is Peary denying him his place in history, conceivably even usurping it, he is also robbing him of the Inuit woman whom he possibly loves and certainly fancies. I recall this relationship carrying considerable emotional weight in the earlier production -- here it goes for very little. It seems to have been much abbreviated in the writing; and the actress, Lucie Idlout, looks sweet but is otherwise inexpressive.

This typifies the show as a whole. The Calgary staging was uninspired but lucid, with the occasional line that jumped out at you. Ross Manson's production, for his Volcano company, is arty and opaque, with a lot of moaning acting. Teresa Przybylski's set is bright enough to make you snow-blind, but the human confrontations are muted. The crucial showdown between the mate and the commander is staged apologetically and off to one side.

Some of the overall muffled quality can be traced to David Foxs playing of Peary. This actor can hardly set foot on a stage without dominating it, and his best performances are transfixing. Vocally, hes always ready to rumble. He invariably sounds as if he's acting through his whiskers, whether or not he's wearing any. Here he gives us sounds rather than words, attitudes instead of thoughts.

He is accompanied by Jerry Franken and Tom Barnett, the same two actors who supported his massive performance in The Drawer Boy. (The three of them were also together at Stratford in The Trials of Ezra Pound. I occasionally wonder if they have the same agent, and if he or she has negotiated some kind of package deal.) Barnett, the youngest member of the team, always seems to spend most of his time listening to the effusions of his elders. He certainly does so here, in the thanklessly functional role of Peary junior. Franken, the most versatile, appears in the more modern scenes as Dr. Boas, an ethnologist. His role, too, comes over as thankless going on pointless; and again, if memory serves, truncated.

This is odd, because Boas scientific work is theoretically central to the plays concerns. On which his own position, as a Jewish refugee from Nazi Germany where eugenics are about to take their most sinister turn ever, should cast an especially ironic light. The play erects a totem pole of racial oppression, carried out by comparatively civilized people. The whites -- to put it gently -- patronize the blacks, and they both exploit the Inuit.

It's revealed that Peary had brought back half a dozen Arctic natives from one of his earlier expeditions and put them on show. They had all died in New York -- of the cold. When I saw the play in Calgary, during a remarkably clement February, that revelation froze us, too. In Toronto -- where most of us are currently able to think of several words for snow, few of them printable -- it passes by with hardly a shiver.

Black & White Photo: John Launer / Lucie Idlout and Nigel Shawn Williams star in Two Words for Snow, which explores Commander Robert Peary's expedition to the North Pole.

FIVE FINGERS

Theatre Passe Muraille, Backspace, Toronto

The Five Fingers of Robin Fulford's play belong on the hand that delivered a slap to the face of a woman who lived with the man who struck the blow that ended the marriage that once filled the house that somebody-or-other must have built, sometime. It's an inexorable progression, and in its inexorability resides the greatest power of the play. Also its greatest limitation.

Two years ago, Five Fingers was actually performed in a house, at Bathurst and Adelaide. We followed the characters and the story around from one room to another. Fulford now believes that the audience on that occasion got caught up as much in the manner of presentation as in what was being presented, and he is probably right. But that doesn't mean they didn't respond at all to the subject, and in fact the story was more engrossing for being presented in a super-realistic context. It got, as I remember, very scary and very involving. It retains those qualities in this new production, but to a lesser degree. Directed by Wendy White on a stylized set of her own design, principally composed of three hanging drapes, it seems short, both literally and figuratively, of places to go.

There are Tuck and Anna, who were dating until she got pregnant, at which point they got married. Now that they're alone with their baby son, Tuck feels trapped and Anna feels exploited. One morning, finding no toothpaste in the bathroom, Tuck hits Anna. He immediately regrets it, or says he does. She leaves, and refuses to return. And that is all.

The show is produced by Fulford's own company, Platform 9, whose "mandate is to do original, issue-oriented plays." Those are the author's own words, and they raise a couple of questions. One: Who gave the company this mandate? If, as is probable, nobody did and it's their own idea, then it isn't a mandate, it's a policy. Two: Who, apart from a few benighted schoolteachers, wants "issue- oriented plays," anyway? A play may be inspired by an issue, it may engage with it, but that cannot be the sole point of its existence. Why do talented writers persist in talking like social workers? If Fulford as playwright came up with a play that could not be labelled and captioned as if it were an op-ed piece, would Fulford as producer feel obliged to reject it?

On this particular issue, most of us have our minds made up before we enter the theatre. We are not in favour of men hitting women or, come to that, of women hitting men. A play is hardly likely to contest that point. All it can do is take us inside the minds of the people involved, help us understand, maybe unsettle us a bit. This play, in its current form, does that admirably with the character of Tuck, and hardly at all with that of Anna. In sociological terms, she declines to get mired in the victim role. In dramatic terms, she's stuck with it. We get very little sense of what she may have contributed to this marriage, good or bad. She has very little to say for herself, or even against herself, and Suzanne Hersh, playing her, spends much of the play in recitation mode. She is too monotonously resentful, even granted that she has a lot to resent.

Tuck is more fully explored. (Well, the author is a man.) He is a boy-man who resents the erosion of his bachelor freedoms and tries to hang on to as many of them as possible. He also has a fierce distaste for bodily functions, at least other than sexual.

The two motifs come together at the moment of violence. He wants to get out of the house but cannot bear to do so without cleaning his teeth. Mark Cassidy, who has been given some excellent speeches, gets the character's rage across from the start, and does reasonably well by what passes for his remorse. I'd say that the play is emotionally on his side and intellectually on his partner's, but this seems to denote not so much complexity as incompleteness. It does, though, cast an interesting pall of guilt over the evening.

Fulford's original title for the play was Swahili Beckett, and in its present stripped staging it has a sense of unlocalized enclosure that fits into the Beckett tradition. It's impressive as well as oppressive, but it seems to deny its characters options. As an abstract issue, spousal abuse is simple -- it's the specific cases that get complicated. This play implicitly acknowledges that, but denies itself the tools for exploration.

Maybe, if I may contradict myself, it needs to be more of an issue play, to situate itself more fully in the wider everyday world. It's offered to us here as an elemental inferno, school of Strindberg, and in those terms it can only go half the distance. What it does, it does with style, constantly reworking its central image. We hear, for example, of fingers thrust into a vagina in the dark, and of the different meanings this has for both participants. Fulford is a writer, and it shows.

Black & White Photo: David Kinsman / Tuck (Mark Cassidy) feels trapped and Anna (Suzanne Hersh) feels exploited in Robin Fulford's Five Fingers.

WILLIAM AND JAMES

Theatre Passe Muraille

- - -

One historic function of the stage, much neglected in these penny- pinching times, is to provide spectators with an image of the kind of luxury in which they would all like to be living.

Theatre Passe Muraille, which can't be exactly flush with cash, has nevertheless put out nobly with its set for William and James. We gaze at the Victorian bedroom of an English country gentleman, done out in gilt, plush and crushed red velvet, plus a really hot- looking fireplace, tantalizing with the promise of even richer apartments, just out of sight.

David Wootton is the designer, and his work here is sumptuous, soothing and decadent, the latter in the same sense as a dozen boxes of President's Choice cookies placed end to end. Still, we cannot live just by gawping, and the sweetmeats here are less fun than the wrapping.

James is the master of this house, and William the young man he has picked up at a London party and brought home with him. James is married, but his wife lives conveniently far away, in one of two other establishments that he has dotted about the land. (One hopes, for the sake of James's credibility as a gentleman, that they are equally grand.) William, who looks pretty and sounds smooth, is carving out a career as rough trade and one night stand. He refuses in advance to stay longer than a night, to the dismay of James, who has decided, even before they go to bed together, that he wants love.

The morning after, James makes a proposal. William will stay in his house -- as friend, companion and sexual partner -- for a period of two years, at the end of which James proposes to die (of what cause remains unclear), leaving William an inheritance. William, hardly surprisingly, accepts. There are ups and downs in the relationship; at the end of the two years William, revealed as a far needier person than he would earlier have admitted, is also predictably in love.

I don't imagine that Robert Tsonos, the author, is telling us this story for its own sweet sake. But it's no great news that Victorian sexuality, homo or hetero, was a lot more complicated than its novelists and other official chroniclers were ever at liberty to disclose. Or that sexual relationships are power relationships, with money one of the greatest power sources available. That was true 150 years ago, and it is true now; but the choice of setting illuminates neither period.

It connects, perhaps, in a small way, when we learn that James, upholding the best of his society's values, likes to give to the poor, and that William, anticipating the worst of our society's values, says that it will simply spoil them. He adds that William only does it to make himself feel good. Unfortunately the obvious answer, which is "so what?" never gets made.

Otherwise, the play is escapist without being entertaining. Along with the stage-pictures we get the assurance of a well-staffed household (like My Fair Lady but with the chorus offstage) and the promise of elegant chat. Here Tsonos falls down; he does hit a consistent and acceptable tone, weighty without being antique, but it has no depths and the attempts at epigram are self-conscious.

To make a comparison the play itself seems to invite: Oscar Wilde's wisecracks, at their best, tell us something about the assumptions of the people making them, Tsonos' seem to be there because it's expected of them. A recurring debate about the meaning of a painting that the master has hanging on the wall of his room is especially dull; it's obviously meant to reflect on the characters themselves, but they're too flat to reflect anything.

Worst of all, perhaps, is the drawing out of the narrative. As a vignette, the piece might pass. Protracted over two years (real time) or 75 minutes (stage time), it really drags.

Mark Caven has a fine fit of anger when James pulls rank and declines to be a pushover; this comes late though, and one wishes that he had more backbone earlier. It's not so much that the character needs it as that the play does.

Michael Schultz, as William, preens as requested, both physically and vocally, but has exhausted his resources before his time is up. The director is George Pothitos.

Black & White Photo: David Kinsman / Mark Caven as James and Michael Schultz as William.

Peggy Lee

The Singles Collection (4 CDs)

EMI

Peggy Lee spent most of her best years recording for Capitol, and since EMI owns that catalogue, it's the products of that association that fill most of this box. There are also some token cuts from her fruitful intermediate period with Decca, and a couple from her apprenticeship as band-vocalist with Benny Goodman; the opening track, Lets Do It, reveals a Lee far more forthrightly and conventionally sexy than the veiled seductress were used to. Subtlety sets in on, of all things, The Atchison, Topeka and the Santa Fe, with Bob Crosby, and once she starts recording under her own name, the familiar Peggy with the subtle beat and the eggshell- finish voice -- at once soft, warm and unattainable -- arrives pretty much full-blown. But though she's consistent -- colonizing everything from pseudo-Latin novelties to '70s soft rock on her own unshakeable terms -- shes never monotonous; she thinks every song. For the first 10 years of her career, all her records were singles, so this can hardly be a complete accounting, but its an intelligent selection. The obvious things are here (Why Don't You Do Right, Manana, Fever, Is That All There Is) but so are some bewitching rarities: Alec Wilder's wistful Goodbye John and A Shade on the Blue Side, an otherwise unknown Hoagy Carmichael tune that allows her to be rapt and rhythmic at the same time. She gets inside her songs while standing outside her own image as a singer. Sinatra (of whom she's the nearest female equivalent) went for the dead-centre of the standard repertoire, but she weaves supply around its edges. The voice is misty, but the sensibility is made of steel.

MAMBO ITALIANO

Elgin Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - One of the moments I liked in Mambo Italiano -- one of the two, if we're going to be exact -- has a young Montreal woman of Italian parentage reflecting on what she found most frightening when she first ventured into the world beyond her own family. She discovered that out there, when people shout at you, its because they dont like you: They're really shouting at you. In Italian households shouting is the normal method of communication, and may even signify deep affection.

I can believe it, just as I can of Jewish households (personal experience) and Greek ones (a reliable informant). But put this behaviour on a stage, try and make a whole play out of it, and the results are coarse as well as deafening. In the case of Mambo Italiano they are even worse, since this one tries, not only to bludgeon us into laughter but also, mamma mia, to touch our hearts and even our minds. Since it doesn't have a thought in its own head, this last presumption is the crowning insult.

Steve Galluccio wrote the play, which has been a huge hit in Montreal in French and English. He gives us a wife, a husband, and their two grown-up children. The loudest of the tribe, is of course the matriarch who, almost equally of course, is called Maria. She bellows practically non-stop. Her husband, Gino, who is very rotund, can put up a token roar himself, but he mostly relies on self-pity and self-deprecation. Their daughter Anna, who is in her thirties, still lives at home, and is a mean screamer herself. Their son Angelo is a mute by comparison, but then hes artistic; like his author, he has a tidy career writing television sitcoms, though his success doesnt prevent his parents from telling him he should get a real job. He is also gay.

Egged on by his sister, who wants him to do her rebelling for her, Angelo comes out to his family. They are of course appalled. (I'm sorry to keep saying "of course" but it's that kind of play.)

Nino, Angelos boyfriend, is also upset, since he was very happy in the closet; the two of them used to enjoy themselves looking down from their window and making fun of Gay Pride parades. Nino meets Pina who, with no supporting evidence that I could see, regards herself as terminally unattractive but is desperate to get a man -- and she throws herself at him. (Pina may be the most demeaning, and least credible, piece of characterization in the play.) Before you know it Nino and Pina are engaged, to the relieved delight of Ninos mother, Lina. (I don't know why so many of the play's characters have rhyming names; maybe its practising to be a musical.) Since Pina, of course, is fiercely competitive with Angelos parents, they have to pretend to be actively proud of their son's sexuality. This is probably preferable to the cliched development we were all dreading, which would have involved them clutching Angelo and his lover to their bosoms, but the scene of competitive parental boasting has to be seen to be disbelieved. Anyway, it heralds an all- round family reconciliation. This occurs in adjacent confessional booths, for maximum cuteness.

The gay plot line concludes with one former partner further out than ever and marching in the parade (mercifully without his parents joining in) and the other going straight and getting married: Something, in other words, for everyone. To be fair, Nino's future heterosexuality is left in doubt; the suggestion, since its silent and economical, is the other moment in the play that I liked.

Did I say the play? There are three of them, going on by turns: The ear-splitting family cartoon, the sensitive homosexual piece and, raising its head at odd moments, the valentine to Montreal itself. They are not compatible. Nobody really objects to stereotypes; they are, after all, only watered-down archetypes, and archetypes always have a respectful press. There is nothing wrong with caricature -- it can, in the theatre as in the visual arts, be a very good thing. But it has to know what its good for, and that does not include tugging at our heartstrings. Mambo Italiano is that most moronic of dramatic oxymorons: A sentimental farce. You may be able to get away with this combination for 30 minutes on TV, but not for two and half hours on a stage. (I'm being unfair to sitcoms, the best of which keep sentimentality at arm's length. Seinfeld always avoided it, and then -- in its much-maligned final episode -- executed a mocking dance on its grave.) Like a sitcom, the play wants us to feel warm toward the four characters around the family dinner table, and cool toward all the others; and, as in a sitcom, this division of sympathies is purely arbitrary, unjustified by anything we are shown.

The nadir here is a prolonged bit of mystification about a dead aunt who may or may not have committed suicide. You might call it a mystery except nobody in the audience is interested in learning the solution. It seems Aunt Yolanda was a baffled life-force who wanted to teach her relatives to dance the mambo. You cant help feeling that her main motive for this was to provide her author with a catchy if barely relevant title.

But then Mambo Italiano takes a baffling approach to both history and language. Its older characters talk like Chico Marx. The play is set, according to the program, in the present. However, when Angelo, by way of providing a first-act climax, arraigns his elders for their petty-mindedness, he says they came to Canada from Italy "because of the war." His parents, though, look to be in their sixties at most. Maybe it was their parents who emigrated. But if so, why havent Gino and Maria learned to speak proper English? And, that being the case, why when they're alone together, are they speaking in broken English rather than in Italian? And how did this conceit work out in the French version? The answer to all these questions, except perhaps the last, seems to be: For the sake of cheap laughs. The cheapness might not matter if the laughs happened. But the humour is woefully predictable. When Poppa mentions the existence of a "homosexuale [NB that is not a typo] village," it's a foregone conclusion Mamma will ask how he comes to know so much about it.

The actors throw themselves into the style with what looks suspiciously like enthusiasm. I suppose Mary Long (Maria) deserves to be congratulated on the strength of her lungs, though shes overdoing things even by prevailing standards, and that Michel Perron (Gino) also warrants commendation for the expressive variety of his shrugs. There is matchingly shameless work from Ellen David as Anna, who compensates for nagging others by beating up on herself; from Penny Mancuso as Ninos beanpole ma, who mysteriously envies the slimness of a woman with far more meat on her bones than she has herself; and from Suzanne Le Nir as the predatory Pina, a pitiful victim of dramaturgical machismo: Her author exploits her for his own purposes, then heartlessly casts her aside.

As Angelo and Nino, Andreas Apergis and Joseph Gallaccio prove that quieter acting need not necessarily mean less simplified acting. The director is Gordon McCall, of Montreal's not-for-profit Centaur Theatre, where the show originated. The production's unsubtlety may be the result of a conscious decision to sell out to the forces of commercialism, but I suspect it happened naturally.

VINCI

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

Maureen Hunter's Vinci is an old-fashioned biographical- historical play, whose twist is that its central character never actually appears.

The Vinci in question is, of course, Leonardo, of that name and of that small Italian village. We know he was the illegitimate son of a lawyer and a servant, and that he seems to have been brought up by the people who more or less owned his hometown and who gave their name to it. On these foundations Hunter has erected the imagined story of young Pietro da Vinci who seduces Caterina, the family maid, despite being requested by his friend Bartolomeo, a novice of the priesthood, to leave her alone. Caterina becomes pregnant, and - - against all precedent for 15th-century Italian girls in her situation -- refuses to give the child, a boy, up for adoption. Instead, she goes into far less glamorous service with the chandler at the top of a nearby hill, and brings up her son, whose identity you can probably guess. He is, as you would also expect, a bright and precocious child and we hear her shouting encouragement to him as he plays, just off stage, with his pre-prototype flying machines. Hes always making things she tells a visitor proudly.

Meanwhile, Pietro, his oats mostly sown, makes an advantageous match with the richly dowered Albiera, who proves unable to bear him a child and is made to feel very guilty about it. Faced with the prospect of the da Vinci line dying out, Antonio, Pietros father, begins to think longingly of his grandson up the mountain, and puts all kinds of pressure on Caterina to surrender him. She resists, encouraged by Bartolomeo, who after a tour of duty in other parishes has returned to look after the souls in his native patch.

He is our guide to the action, and he provides a prologue and epilogue that show him, many years later, standing proudly in front of Leonardo's famous painting of the Last Supper. He has obviously kept in touch. Strangely enough, there is no mention in the body of the play of the young Leonardo evincing any kind of pictorial talent. The emphasis is all on his flair for making model planes. The painting is thrown in as cultural ballast. You might also call it cultural blackmail since, if we weren't aware of what the boy was later to achieve, we would not find the story of his first five years on Earth very interesting.

From what we are actually shown, the play might well be named for the place rather than the person: an everyday story of Renaissance countryfolk. Much of the drama centres on Caterinas proud fight to be a single mother. She seems, like her son, to be ahead of her time, but the characterization her author has devised for her is the combined product of sentimentality and wishful thinking. You dont have to subscribe to the philistine bromides of cultural materialism (which holds that all people and all art are products of the social forces acting at the time, that the idea of an unchanging "human nature" is a myth, and that no era has a chance of empathizing with any other) to suspect that people 550 years ago may have taken certain things for granted that we don't. The play is written in the kind of levelling schoolteacherly style that regards our ancestors as being just like us but in funny clothes.

Nursing sore memories of The Beard of Avon (the previous play at this address -- CanStage seems to making a policy out of trivializing genius), I can confidently assert that nobody wants an evening of mock-Elizabethan, which anyway would be anachronistic on its own account, quite apart from being in the wrong language. The trouble is not that the dialogue has no period flavour, but that it has no flavour at all other than that of cliche. At best, it suggests that the characters have been reading the wrong books. They can't make a plain statement without attaching a stale image to it. She hung suspended between life and death somebody informs us. "My sins, like pigeons, have come home to roost," laments somebody else - - we would get the point without the pigeons. You may notice, though, that both those quoted lines scan. One common characteristic of mediocre period plays is their tendency to fall unconsciously into blank verse.

Hunter can tell a story. Her play holds the attention more easily than do many that are, theoretically, better written. But she sets all manner of traps for her actors. Patricia Fagan keeps fastidiously clear of most of them. She manages to endow Caterina with a bit of passion and a great deal of dignity, though she cannot make us believe a final act of self-sacrifice that runs counter to everything for which she has hitherto been standing. Fiona Byrne is touching as the kindly, barren Albiera, thrown awkwardly into a tragic situation she did nothing to deserve. The two women share the best scene in the play, each of them bringing out unsuspected layers of feeling in the other. They are joined at its end by Craig Ericksons Pietro, who makes a believable playboy with an intermittently active conscience. Dylan Trowbridge is pleasing, though little more, as his younger brother, a character of little visible use.

As Antonio, a reluctantly heavy father who would rather cultivate his garden (literally), Robert Benson unwisely endorses every platitude his author foists on him. Gordon Rand worries amiably away at the role of Bartolomeo, without much success. Its never clear how central his character is meant to be. Are his struggles to realize his own vocation the point of the play, or are they merely a titillating side show? (I know Catholicism is a very theatrical religion, but aren't our playwrights succumbing too easily to the lure of the confessional? This play is the third in two months to make use of that all-too-convenient device.)

If the piece is about the priest's relationship to the artist, who presumably had his own vocational issues, then it's unfortunate most of it takes place in the years that have been left undramatized. The director is Dennis Garnhum, who seems recently to have been specializing in less-than-perfect plays. He generally puts a gloss on them without actually managing to elevate them. John Jenkins' set is a revolving contraption (also standard for history plays) that endeavours to suggest a da Vincian invention. And The Last Supper looks stunning under the lights.

LITTLE MERCYS FIRST MURDER

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

Melody Johnson is the actress of hard-boiled nerve endings. Her words fall out of the corner of her mouth in a belligerent squawk, shes full of sharp angles, and she has the air of an aggressive waif, hoping for the best but expecting the worst; her ideals have been trampled on, but they are always apt to reassert themselves.

In plays she always gives much the same performance (she showed greater versatility in a revue at Second City), but it's a performance I like, and she makes it seem right for every character she plays. For the central role in Little Mercy's First Murder its ideal.

This show is billed as a new musical, though its more a play with music; the songs punctuate rather than define the action. The book and lyrics are by rising playwright Morwyn Brebner. It has been very smartly directed by Eda Holmes. I enjoyed some of it, was impressed by more, yet found the whole thing crumbling in my mind before I had crossed the street from the theatre to the car park.

It's set in the well-known mythical city of New York, at an equally mythical date. The program swears it's 1942, but it seemed to me to bear a greater resemblance to the depressed 1930s. (There are references to the war, but I took them to refer to the coming conflict rather than the current one.)

Little Mercy is a young lady whose large mother has just expired with a knife stuck into her. So: Was it a Mercy-killing? (The script never actually makes that crack, but its implicit.) The cop on the spot thinks so, and he looks forward to seeing Little Mercy fry.

He nonetheless permits Mercy to visit the washroom down the hall, un-handcuffed and escorted only by a press photographer (this is not a realistic drama), and spends the rest of the show giving chase with Javert-like intensity. It takes him all night to catch up.

Mercy, meanwhile, has been on a tour of the citys infernal regions in the company of the cameraman, whose name is Weegee. He is apparently based on an actual person. I didn't know that, and presumably his voyeurism would have had more substance for those who did.

Anyway, he is professionally and personally attracted to disasters, and he never quite befriends Mercy, though he keeps looking as if he might. He also never buys her dinner, though he promised. Together they witness a fire, and see the rich people tramping into the opera. Mercy, who used to work in a library, comments sardonically on how the city houses its books far more handsomely than it does its people. Nevertheless, she was a great reader (the only one on the staff who was), and remarks on life's failure to measure up to the great novels.

She and Weegee wind up at a bar that boasts a variegated line-up of freaky performers. One of them, the headliner, we actually meet: Norma, a drag queen so smoothly convincing as to have the heterosexual barman completely in thrall. Mercy rebukes Weegee and the barman after theyve sung a misogynistic song (from the French). After that, its pretty much over bar the denouement.

It's a world-weary vision of a world worth wearying of, and some of it is delivered with style, a sort of downbeat swagger. But it ends up seeming pointless, and second-hand even beyond the dictates of pastiche, as if the author were trying to drape her own despondency in someone else's feathers. There isnt much story or much conflict, and the spoken lines have more the presumption of wit than its substance.

The music, by Jay Turvey and Paul Sportelli, helps a lot. It makes cunning use of Johnsons limited vocal range, cruelly pushing her highs and lows to make her seem more exposed than ever. The '30s -- or if you insist '40s -- come with built-in musical mordancy if you know where to look. This score takes in Broadway, Montmartre, Rio and Weimar (not much swing), with especial echoes of Marc Blitzsteins labour opera The Cradle Will Rock; the two pieces have a similar stations-of-the-cross structure, and there are at least two numbers that suggest either direct influence or a serious case of osmosis. One is a society ladys self-damning self-justification of her own patronizing attitude to the penniless, and the other is an ominous all-purpose protest song, improbably passed off as a radio hit of a time.

This latter contains Brebner's best efforts as a lyricist. Elsewhere she offers vague, sloppily rhymed words that don't match the music -- which, true to its imagined period, is the kind of music that absolutely demands precision. Theyre the kind of lyrics that sound impressive until you actually listen to them.

Maybe the most effective number is the first. The cast of six gaze cheekily out at us, singing no more words than la la la, as if to say, with more insolence than ingratiation: This is a musical, take it or leave it.

There has to be something to a script that can inspire its interpreters with this kind of confidence, and it persists throughout. Holmes staging, in sets by John Thompson, restores one's battered faith in what can be done in the smallest spaces. Even the projections behind a couple of scenes in a car are effective.

Peter Millard as Weegee fits comfortably into the shagged-out fedora and loosely-knotted tie that always signify either a hack or a private eye. Jeff Lillico is an unimpeachable Norma, bringing the house down with, or as, a little rumba numba. Tony Nappo, as her enslaved admirer, has everything it takes to make a musical comedy except a voice. Neil Barclay is a barrel-bellied cop, who has the best speech in the show, one in which he compares his own policeman's lot to that of his idyllic rural counterpart (probably as seen in the movies) and tells us, "my job is to protect people like you from people like you." Jane Johanson fills in neatly as everyone else. She and the director are also the co-choreographers, and they've done fine.
