CRIMES

Berkeley Street Theatre, Upstairs

The Crimes with which Adam Nashmans play are principally concerned are those committed in 1915, on a genocidal scale, by the Turks against the Christian Armenians. It also considers comparable atrocities, most crucially the Nazi slaughter of Europes Jews, and manages to glance en route at the current situation in the Middle East. All this, along with a slice of early-20th-century Canadian history, is piled on top of an approximation of a spy story. That's a lot, especially considering the play only lasts 90 minutes. In fact it's too much, while the play itself is much, much too little. Its scrappily written and staged, and its bad performances outnumber its good. All the same, it raises, and even answers, some interesting questions about the equivalence of evil.

Its long been an article of faith to many people, including myself, that nothing compares to the Holocaust: Not even Stalin's massacres, which were just as brutal and claimed millions more victims. But even such a dedicated anti-Stalinist as Robert Conquest has been quoted -- by Martin Amis, in Koba the Dread -- as saying he found the Holocaust worse than the Gulag, even though when pressed for a reason, he could only answer, I feel so." Amis himself suggests "the distinction may be that Nazi terror strove for precision, while Stalinist terror was deliberately random. The corollary of that may be that a potential victim had a better chance of being spared in Russia, where the terror was aimed at classes, than in Germany, where it was aimed at races.

As an English playwright once put it, perhaps a trifle optimistically, you could stop being a middle peasant; you couldn't stop being a Jew." There is, after all, no word equivalent to "genocide denoting the elimination of political opponents. Even the fact that the Russian midnight lasted so much longer than the German seems to make it less horrific. A terror that prolonged seems more porous -- its certainly less easy to pin down. And of course we know, thanks to the outcome of the Second World War, what the Nazi death-machine looked like. We found the evidence, and weve been looking at it ever since.

But the Armenians. Hitler famously invoked their fate as a kind of insurance cover for his own racial program: Who," he asked "remembers the Armenians? He had a point, although it didn't have the effect he would have wanted. The world has forgotten the Armenians, in a way that it hasn't forgotten the Jews. Holocaust denial is, in a sense, its own admission of failure. Nobody bothers to deny something that isnt still on everybodys mind.

The most effective scene in Crimes is a confrontation between our hero Tir, a Canadian of Armenian descent, and a sophisticated modern Turk who seems genuinely grieved to find his antagonist -- an anthropologist by trade -- digging up all that old stuff. One by one the Turk produces the same arguments (it was a long time ago, it was wartime, there were faults on both sides, anyway it's all a myth) that one can imagine being trotted out by an articulate neo-Nazi. The difference is that if such a man were a German it would be -- not an impossibility, certainly, but an anomaly. Germany has acknowledged its past in a way that Turkey hasn't.

To that extent, Nashmans proposed equation doesnt quite fit. But it has an emotional resonance, and there is an earlier scene in which the match is frighteningly precise. The play is full of flashbacks, and in one of them we see an Armenian woman killed during a death march that looks identical to those that followed the closing of the concentration camps. The Turks didn't have the technology for gas chambers -- no more than the more recent genocidal killers in Rwanda (an analogy Nashman doesn't get round to making, though surely an obvious one). There is a cold-bloodedness, an impersonality, to the Nazi assembly line that sets it apart. But not, I am forced to admit, as far apart as all that. Intellectually, Nashman (who is Jewish himself) has made his case.

Dramatically, though, he hardly begins. The play manages to be both thin and chaotic. Tir is part Jewish -- his father married a German-Jewish refugee whom he met on wartime service in London. (He had joined up to show solidarity with another persecuted race. It would be nice to believe that soldiers volunteered for the Allied forces in order to help the Jews, but I have my doubts.) Now, a mining conglomerate employs Tir to go to Turkey and verify the authenticity of a relic that hangs in a church whose land the company owns. This exhibit is a spear, supposedly plunged into the body of Christ on the cross. Tir ends up brandishing it against his Turkish opponent. (Is this meant to be a reversion to Christian warfare against Islam? Any deeper significance escaped me.) Before this happens, Tir -- whos shaping up to be anthropologys answer to Indiana Jones -- has been directed, by a series of mildly sinister strangers, from Amsterdam to Istanbul to Jerusalem, the last of which he wisely suspects of being a perilous place to visit. He has also taken a lot of drugs, mostly on the house, and has had erotic encounters that may or may not be hallucinations. It's certain that at least one of his trips has induced visions of his murdered Armenian ancestors.

Other glimpses into history are more prosaically presented. We keep zig-zagging between the present and various bits of the past, between one country and another, with captions unsteadily projected to tell us where and when we are. We see: Tir's grandfather as a child escaping from the death-march; the same boy taken into an Ontario refugee home specially established for Armenian orphans (an implicit rebuke to the later policy of none is too many," but dramatically a mere pious gesture to Canadian content); the boy as a man, running a fruit-store and squabbling with his two sons, who later squabble with one another. We also, as previously mentioned, see Tirs father in the army, and follow him to Berlin where he captures a German soldier who taunts him for being a Jew (which, if you can keep up with me, he isnt, though he feels a spiritual kinship). Dad gets violent, and we can't help mentally cheering him on, just as, later, we can't help cheering his son when, goaded, he turns on the Turk. Nashman probably wants us to feel this, and then feel ashamed of it; and he drives home the message that all this hatred must stop by bringing Tir to Israel. Which is morally admirable, but has no real impact because the action and the characters are so skeletal.

The dramaturgy is primitive, even leaving aside the chronological leap-frog. Most of the dialogue is naked exposition. Hrant Alianaks production -- designed, amazingly, by the usually excellent Steve Lucas -- is shabby. The supposedly atmospheric music, which often drowns out the actors, is especially painful. It seems to think the play is a movie -- probably of the made-for-TV variety -- and only draws attention to how much slicker it would be if it were.

Alon Nashman (no relation to the author, though theyve worked together before) plays both Tir and his father. Neither role has much use for his characteristic sense of mischief, but he works devoutly, and is charming when he rocks on his feet, simultaneously jet-lagged and stoned. Oliver Becker is powerfully smooth as the Turk, who trades in opium, and Michael Waller twitchily so as a German, who deals in diamonds, but isn't above handing out coke to total strangers in airport washrooms. He also plays the other German, the one who's anti-Semitic to the bitterest end. The other performances, other than that of the boy Garo Britsian, are miserable. Is it my imagination, or has the overall standard of acting in Toronto taken, this cold new year, a sharp and dispiriting turn for the worse?

DREAM MACHINE

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

The long-standing, or long-jumping, Calgary troupe that calls itself One Yellow Rabbit has arrived at the Six Stages festival with a largely hypnotic and wholly inventive tribute to the Beatnik prophets of the '50s. Dream Machine takes its name from a device invented by Brion Gysin, one of the lesser-known Beats, by which I mean that I'd never heard of him before. The show itself focuses on Allen Ginsberg and William Burroughs, of whom I had heard. No mention of Kerouac, but he's already had a show in Toronto, though it was nothing like as good as this one.

Gysin's dream machine, which if this production is to be believed looked like a silver decanter with holes in its side, was intended, says the program, "to transport the user into a waking dream state" and to produce "a drugless high." That could have saved a lot of people of lot of money, not to mention a sizeable amount of jail time. Its inventors hoped -- rather touchingly, I think -- that it would become "a common household appliance" but apparently "it never caught on." Anyway, the show aims to present a theatrical equivalent of that high, and -- though the spell wears off toward the end -- it succeeds.

It doesn't dramatize the lives of the Beats and, most of the time, it doesn't quote them. It starts, though, with one of Ginsberg's own poems: America, a magnetic compound of wit and paranoia delivered, with hair-trigger precision and four-wheel drive, by Michael Green.

Having made this initial splash, this actor takes a back seat to the other four in the cast, leading me to suspect that he is the only one among them who is not a singer. For the rest of the show is a musical, and virtually through-sung. In another part of the program Blake Brooker, writer and director, asks -- a bit rhetorically, at this stage in the game -- "could we create a musical without characters or plot?" Well, he has, or they have, and not all that surprisingly, since it's been done before, often. It used to be called revue, and it's a form with a respectable non- commercial history, as well as a lucrative commercial one. I'll bet there were Beat revues in the '50s, as there were certainly surrealist revues in the '20s and '30s.

Brooker's lyrics are a fine modern gloss on the Beats' own attitudes, very angular and stylish, and illuminating that broad strip of human life bounded by imperfect orgies and writer's block. "We are the Beats, clever and effete" chant the five performers in unison, bursting with their own dignity and alive to their own absurdity. There is, after all, a limit to how far you can go in passing self-gratification off as a form of benevolence, and the Beats do seem to have been intermittently aware of this. (The show stops singing for an exchange of letters in which Burroughs says that heterosexual intercourse is all very well but it's still like eating tortillas when you'd prefer steak, and Ginsberg replies that, actually, he's become a vegetarian. I hope that's authentic but if it isn't, my compliments to the author.)

Some of the self-mockery may be put down to this production's hindsight, but I don't think it all can. The music, mainly by David Rhymer, is very good: pungent and jazzy, as befits the time, and surprisingly melodic as well.

It's especially well sung by a rangy (both physically and vocally) and seductively confident enchantress named Onalea Gilbertson. Andy Curtis has the fair disdain of the Bohemian poet, of any ear, down pat. Brad Payne does some surprising backflips, while the remaining performer, Denise Clarke, is also the choreographer. Her inventions -- some languorous, some positively militaristic -- are very commanding, and faultlessly executed by all.

There are three musicians, half out of sight: Peter Moller, whose drums give the show a lot of its pulse, also doubles on percussive typewriter, and trebles on unearthly yells. The visuals (set by Chris Cran, lights by Cimmeron Meyer, costumes uncredited) are superb. I thought Little Mercy's First Murder was a stylishly mounted show (and not dissimilar in adopting an earlier decade's louche rebellion for its own purposes) but this one has it, well, beat.

It goes limp in its last stages, partly because its heroes come to seem seedier than the show itself has bargained for, partly because the writing becomes flaccid: The mystical self-pity outweighs the wit. Some of the later tunes sound like Kurt Weill, always a danger sign since he's so easily pastichable. Others are what you might call contemporary or what I might call bad. Most of the time, though, the show is superbly accomplished. And it makes you feel good, like a dream machine should.

Black & White Photo: Sean Denni / Brad Payne (left) and Michael Green help create a theatrical high.

PINOCCHIO

Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - The Theatre for Young People has put the boat out for its new version of Pinocchio. We don't see the boat, the one on which the woodcarver Geppetto goes in search of his lost puppet boy, until near the end, but it's worth the wait. It undulates enchantingly on top of an ocean made out of blue cloth. The joy of David S. Craig's production is that it faces every narrative challenge issued by a fantastical story, and solves each one in terms of simple theatrical magic.

Sometimes it's the magic of homemade scenic devices (Glenn Davidson is the designer), sometimes of acting, and often of both together. The climax comes when Pinocchio and Geppetto, having been swallowed by a shark of leviathan proportions, escape from its belly by making it sneeze and getting themselves blown out on the explosion. The effect -- as lights flash, sound rumbles, and the performers hurtle toward us -- is worthy of a 3-D movie.

It's a very long time since I read the Carlo Collodi book -- or, to give you an impression of just how long, since it was read to me - - but Eleanor Albanese's script gives a strong impression of fidelity. There are a few oddities and a few glitches. Pinocchio's famous retractable nose is impressively managed, but it's only allowed to do its lie-detector stuff in one scene. For the rest of the play, the hero's constant struggle between the demands of truth and the attractions of falsehood is barely felt at all. Indeed, apart from the recurring temptation of truancy, his moral dilemmas are skated over. When he makes his crucial choice in favour of unselfishness, he doesn't seem to have much to overcome.

There is -- despite a promise in the press release -- no Cricket to counsel the hero, or even to urge him to give a little whistle. Either there's been a hefty last-minute cut, or the whole business was a Disney invention. (I never saw the movie, but it's in my conscience -- I mean my consciousness -- just as it's in everybody else's.) This Pinocchio does have a self-appointed guardian angel, the Blue Faerie, but she's a simpering ballerina, wafting unaccountably in and out of the action. The horror of the island on which delinquent boys are transformed into donkeys -- Victorian child-correction at its literary extreme -- is underplayed.

There's an engaging cheeriness to the adaptation, though, that feeds on the story's theatricality and also on its Italian origins. The latter is a joke that sometimes wears thin (how many times do you want to hear the entire company sing Santa Lucia?) but it occasions some ripe performances: from Tony De Santis as an endearing Geppetto, and from Robin Craig as a Puppet Master, alternately flamboyant and cringing, with a fixed loathing for his major competition, the Opera.

There is also rich work from Andrew Moodie and Christine Brubaker as the Dickensian con artists Fox and Cat, here claiming to be of English origin, and who knows if it's they or the actors who are lying? These, and many other transformations, are much assisted by Teresa Przybylski's costumes, and by the masks of Trish Leeper, who is also responsible for the design of the puppets.

This brings us to the presentation of Pinocchio himself, which is the most obviously stylized aspect of the show and also, given the circumstances, the most literal. He's a puppet, so he's played by a puppet: not one of your Italian marionettes (we get to meet a couple of those and they comment on the difference) but a stringless figure of the Japanese Bunraku type, complete with on-stage manipulator (Ingrid Rae Doucet) to move his limbs and speak his lines. This is ingenious and arresting, but it does detract from Pinocchio's solitude. There are always two of him, which makes him seem less vulnerable. It does allow, however, for a last heartening coup de theatre when the puppet becomes a real boy -- though, oddly enough, this wished-for transformation is not something on which the script has previously laid much stress. But overall this is a delightful show, the best at this address in a long time. Make haste to Front Street. And always let your conscience be your guide.

The new director of Britain's National Theatre brings down the curtain

Nicholas Hytner, who is about to take over as director of Britain's National Theatre, has announced in advance that under his regime the National will no longer be producing musicals. They don't really belong there, he says, and anyway the company has already done all the good ones.

This seems, at first blush, somewhat dog-in-the-mangerish of him. As a guest director, he was responsible a few years ago for a production of Carousel that ranks as one of the National's most successful and enlightening musical revivals. It's as if, having had his fun, he's all set to stop other directors -- not to mention other audiences -- having theirs.

He has a point or two, though. If you wanted to be mean, you might say that, in this department, the National Theatre started at the top when it put on Guys and Dolls in 1982 and has been going downhill ever since. It's not just that that show, as written, is the best of all Broadway musicals; it's also that it offers uniquely rich opportunities to a company of actors rather than an ad hoc collection of song-and-dance specialists.

Since that date the National's own company strength has fragmented, and its productions -- of plays as well as musicals -- have increasingly become one-off affairs. When a musical appears in the repertoire -- as has happened with increasing frequency -- it has no longer been as a jeu d'esprit but as a building block, taking up a lot of time and space and holding out at least the possibility of transferring and making money.

Hytner's own opening lineup includes Jerry Springer -- The Opera, so we can take it that when he says he'll be abandoning musicals, he actually means mainstream Broadway musicals. (The English National Theatre has never revived an English musical, unless you count The Beggar's Opera.) For the most part, the National up until now has staged the brand-name shows everybody knows, a policy similar to that of the Stratford Festival, whose move into musicals was partly inspired by the National's example.

This has certainly been the case under the regime of the departing director, Trevor Nunn, who came to the National with a double reputation: as Britain's best interpreter of classic drama, Shakespeare especially, and as the director of Cats and Les Miserables. His National Theatre shows have included My Fair Lady, which has transferred to the West End, and Oklahoma!, a brilliant staging which followed Hytner's even more revelatory Carousel by conquering New York itself. (A confession: Years ago, the National commissioned me to write a report on the possible musical repertoire. In the course of it I asserted that there would be no point in the National Theatre doing Rodgers and Hammerstein. I hang my head.)

Nunn's valedictory musical is itself a departure, not one of the post-war behemoths but Anything Goes, Cole Porter's chef-d'oeuvre of 1934, set on that quintessential musical comedy location, a luxury liner. It has been rapturously received. I found it high on extravagance and short on personality -- which is exactly the reverse of how the show must originally have been conceived. Anything Goes enshrines the spirit of the '30s musical -- one of defiant, sardonic gaiety -- more completely than any other show, but while it trumps its genre, it does not transcend it. With their great songs and farcical scripts, these are wonderfully unimportant shows that originally tumbled onto the stage at the rate of a dozen a season. As far as I can tell, dancing was a lot less important to them than clowning.

Now, however, a revival of a '30s show is governed less by the nature of the piece itself than by generalized expectations about "the musical" as a machine for killing the audience with kindness. The pattern may well have been set by the overweening stage version of 42nd Street, which sacrificed all the grit of the movie in favour of an endless series of roof-raising production numbers. We are assaulted by the idea of entertainment, as if you could somehow manufacture innocence.

The highlight of this Anything Goes is the title number which, after its introductory vocal, builds into a full-stage, full- company tap number (Stephen Mears is the choreographer) that goes on and on and on through any number of styles and any number of combinations. It's irresistible, not least when Susan Tracy, a distinguished actress previously untaxed by the role of a battleaxe mother, stands in front of the line and shakes a leg that's as mean as her disposition. It provides, in its unexpectedness, a perfect illustration of what the song is about. It tumultuously closes the first act. But it's devalued when, 10 minutes into the second, a very similar treatment is given to the mock-revival meeting number, Blow Gabriel Blow, this time with minimal reference to the subject of the lyric.

Some of the smaller numbers, too, are fussily staged. To take a minute but significant example: In You're the Top, the line "you're Napoleon brandy" is here cued by the singer's catching sight of a glass of the stuff on a nearby table. Nobody delivering this paragon of list-songs should have to pause, for inspiration or anything else.

A major problem in reviving these shows: They were written, very specifically, as star vehicles, and we don't have the stars. Reno Sweeney, the nightclub evangelist, was the role that first defined Ethel Merman; here it's done by Sally Anne Triplett, who dances well but is so lacking in individuality that, whenever she came on in a change of costume, I failed to recognize her. Her leading man (John Barrowman), who should be cutely hard-boiled, has an unfortunate tendency to simper.

Simon Day, though, is first-rate as a titled buffoon of P. G. Wodehouse provenance (Wodehouse was one of the show's original writers), and Martin Marquez is fairly funny as the obligatory gangster, though he doesn't have the crumpled innocence the role calls for; when he disguises himself as a clergyman, he should look the part. As originally written, this hood was a superstitious soul, worried by his position as Public Enemy Number 13 and determined to rub out another mobster in order to promote himself.

That joke, alas, is no longer with us. The current, heavily adapted script was first staged at Lincoln Center in 1987, and I recall it being much more amusing there, partly because of more adept performers (Howard McGillin was a perfect cad of a hero, and Patti LuPone had charisma, even if she unforgivably swallowed Porter's consonants) and partly because the surrounding production, though grand, was not grandiose. The huge Olivier stage is no place to be intimate, and I suppose Nunn has given it and his audience what they both demand. But I wish he had approached the show as he might a minor Restoration comedy; gone back to the original, kept its structure if not all of its dialogue, and refrained from augmenting what was already a classic score. That would be a task for a National Theatre, and even Hytner might agree. The Shaw Festival used to do something of the kind with vintage musicals, though going to the opposite extreme of enforced economy.

Nunn's production of My Fair Lady (transferred to Drury Lane, where the Lerner-Loewe musical made its first London bow in 1958) is far more assured and has of course much more solid material to build on; not better, necessarily, but firmer. He does fall again into the British director's habit of treating the American musical as a giant box of candies of which not one can be left unsampled. Thus we get two extended Cockney knees-ups, where tradition and common sense call for only one. Higgins (Alex Jennings, wonderfully boyish in face and mind) looks set to deliver I've Grown Accustomed to Her Face all alone in the middle of a huge empty stage, and it promises to be tremendous, but then the director gets him travelling through London, haunted by the sight and sound of other flower girls. When it comes to Alfred Doolittle, the production seems to be mining a dark subtext that doesn't actually exist, either in the musical or in Shaw's play; the actor (Dennis Waterman) is plain surly.

But there are some inspired ideas, of which the best is perhaps the simplest. The interval has been moved forward so that the first- act curtain descends on a radiant but petrified Eliza departing for the ball -- a cliff-hanger, in fact. The Ascot scene has been revitalized by locating the action at a time of royal mourning; a scene we're used to seeing in white is now all in black.

Joanna Riding, a plucky Eliza, does especially well in that scene, showing off her new accent and her old ideas, but it's worth getting hold of the cast CD to hear her predecessor in the role, Martine McCutcheon. McCutcheon, a star of East Enders, brought a modern Cockney sound to the early unregenerate Eliza that made her songs and her whole character live as never before (though for the later, posher Miss Doolittle you're still best off with Julie Andrews).

Early on, a lyrical staging of Wouldn't It Be Loverly, full of character detail that's relevant rather than redundant, perfectly stakes the piece's claim to be a musical. Up to then, it's been Pygmalion with a patter-number stuck in; now, suddenly, it's a romance.

The end is as I've never seen it. Eliza stands impassive at Higgins' new demand for his slippers; she raises her hand, as if to throw them again; he raises his; they stand, locked; then they both burst out laughing. Maybe this will be a partnership of equals. It's about text and acting, two large parts of what a National Theatre is for.

Nunn's final farewell production is to be Love's Labour's Lost, deploying his Anything Goes cast. Shakespearean romance and Broadway romance have much in common -- both are composed of youth and cleverness -- and I hope the equation works.

THE PIANO LESSON

Du Maurier Theatre Centre, Toronto

Obsidian, Toronto's new black theatre company, bowed in last year with The Adventures of a Black Girl in Search of God, a show in which the performance outshone the text. In this, their follow-up production, the situation is reversed.

The Piano Lesson is one of a sequence of plays in which August Wilson has sought to dramatize the African-American experience of the 20th century, decade by decade. Wilson is a major American playwright whose plays are hardly ever seen in Toronto -- a shameful omission that it should not have taken the formation of Obsidian to repair. It would surely not have been beyond the capacity of CanStage or Tarragon -- two managements that pride themselves on showing us notable U.S. plays -- to assemble a group of actors to perform them.

Wilson's plays drive very hard. The Piano Lesson is his 1930s play, set in Pittsburgh in the home of an elderly man named Doaker, who shares the house with his niece Berniece and her young daughter, Maretha. Up from the South come Berniece's brother, known as Boy Willie, and his friend Lymon, with a truck full of watermelons. They plan to unload these and to return with the old family piano, of which Berniece and Boy Willie are theoretically equal owners; Boy Willie wants to sell it and use the proceeds to buy a piece of land, back where his grandparents were slaves. One other family member drops in from time to time: Wining Boy, a cheerful drunk who speaks of himself as a record star, and did in fact cut a couple of sides many years ago. And there is Avery, a preacher who is Berniece's suitor, and who finds himself pressed into service as an exorcist.

What the family has to exorcise is its past, represented by the ghost of a white oppressor who years before fell down a well in mysterious circumstances. He only manifests himself upstairs, out of our sight, but Berniece and others encounter him, and we hear their reactions. Much of the family's bitter history is enshrined in a set of carvings on the piano, with which Berniece is fiercely unwilling to part; you might say she treasures it for unsentimental reasons. So the action resolves into a duel between her and her brother.

Structurally, this is a solidly traditional, indeed old- fashioned play, on the Ibsen model -- the kind that confines itself to a single room full of people telling us and one another about their pasts. However, it keeps bursting those bounds, as indeed Ibsen himself did; it takes his title of Ghosts only a mite more literally than he did, and it shares his taste for conjuring symbolism from a nominally realistic setting.

Wilson's range of styles, though, is bolder. He is apt to forsake dialogue -- which in his hands can be rich, snappy or occasionally tender -- for monologues; and these range from lyrical reminiscence (Doaker recalling the sheer reliability of a career on the Yellow Dog railroad) to vaudeville schtick (Wining Boy on just about anything) to white-heat obsession (Boy Willie at the end of his tether).

And on top of all this there is, of course, music, which divides and defines the characters. Wining Boy still sings rural blues, the ambitiously contemporary Boy Willie shows Maretha how to play boogie- woogie, and Berniece, reaching far into the past, reveals an unsuspected affinity for religious chants that go back beyond gospel.

There's a thick texture here; when the characters talk about their family experience, it effortlessly takes on the density of American history. When Boy Willie talks about wanting land, the words are simple but the passion is palpable.

That, at least, is how good I think the writing is; I can't be sure, because in this production only snatches of it come through clearly. An acoustically unfriendly space is made even more hostile by a yawning, topless set, shabbily under-painted and grudgingly furnished. The play may transcend naturalism, but it needs to be natural before it can be transcendent.

Alison Sealy-Smith's production is awkwardly moved and sloppily spoken; in a play that depends on storytelling of one kind or another, the story is often very hard to follow. And the all- important music is ragged, and not in any Scott Joplin sense.

There is one shining light among the actors, and another that's modestly glowing. The shiner, giving a performance that rings clear of the surrounding mush, is Yanna McIntosh: Maybe too fresh and insufficiently careworn to be an ideal Berniece, but still wedding economy of means to accuracy of intent. The glow comes from D. Garnet Harding as Lymon, gauchely intent on finding himself a big- city woman. These two, blessedly, have a scene together -- one that shyly brushes against the edges of affection -- and it's much the best part of the evening. Suddenly there's rhythm, tone and contact.

Admittedly, the last exorcism in the play, involving Boy Willie, seems to be a case of a playwright gnashing his teeth and hoping for the best, and I doubt that any production could bring it off; this one, in which even McIntosh runs out of resources, hardly begins.

GEORGE EVANS

Top of the Senator, Toronto

George Evans, Toronto jazz singer, is dapper, wears glasses, has a hint of a beard, and moves around a lot. He has altogether the air of a white Sammy Davis Jr., and especially of the early '60s Sammy who was much influenced by Mel Torme and sang his way convincingly through intricately cool arrangements of some very good tunes.

Evans, who takes the stand in a bright red jacket such as I have never before seen on a singer of his persuasion, exudes the same kind of hip flamboyance as Davis; he even cocks his head and closes his eyes in the same manner to denote deep emotion. His voice, which is very agile, also summons other black singers with more traditionally respectable credentials; his low notes sometimes recall the echoing, roomy sound of Billy Eckstine, and when he gets impish he can go strangely cockney in the manner of Al Hibbler, who used to fill the role of clown-prince in the Duke Ellington band.

Unlike those true or false balladeers, though, he hardly ever sings slow. Whatever the explicit message of a lyric, Evans, at least in this engagement, which includes inter alia all 12 songs from his latest CD, always swings it.

This does have its pleasures, but the differences between songs get flattened out. I Only Have Eyes for You, a rapturous song, and Darn That Dream, a rueful song, exist here side by side in a kind of shoulder-shrugging no mans land.

To judge from his first two CDs, which came out some half-dozen years ago, Evans used to be a different kind of singer, less confident but more confiding, and more attentive to the contours of a lyric. But as his technique has grown (on Wednesday night he claimed to have launched a couple of songs in the wrong key, but it was hardly noticeable) so, apparently, has his sense of what is proper to a jazz singer. It seems to entail a lot of vocal shakes, applied just for the fun of it, some melismatic slurs, and some odd verbal stresses; a luxury-lounge account of The Very Thought of You included the line, "Im living in a kind of daydream," as if the key word were the conjunction. Frank Sinatra would not have approved.

One hazard of this quasi-instrumental approach, for all but the most inventive singers, is that the actual instrumentalists surrounding him are likely to do it better than he does. Evans is performing with an excellent and sympathetic quartet -- pianist Mark Eisenman, saxophonist Kelly Jefferson, the monarch of Toronto drummers Archie Alleyne, and (especially good) bassist Keiran Overs - - and there was a great and humorous rapport between the five of them. But in some of their solos the musicians seemed to be playing not only the music but the words, rather more expressively than the singer was singing them.

But there are no rules. I'm a Fool to Want You, which Sinatra (its co-author) used to sing virtually out of tempo, came up refreshed with a beat, and also with its melodrama somewhat defused, which was helpful. Where Have You Been is a lesser-known Cole Porter tune that its composer seems to have thought of as stately and sweeping. Its lyric, though, like most of Porter's songs, and has a subversive jauntiness that starts with a slangy title. Evans unceremonious approach matched it very nicely; two different brands of insouciance met and agreed.

The second set, which started with a straightforwardly propulsive This Cant Be Love was, as often happens, better than the first. It's not so much that Evans grew more assured as that we did; we started hearing the material through his ears.

Some of the lesser songs came out best. Make Me Rainbows and I'm Gonna Live Till I Die are rather generic numbers (that, in the case of the latter, is being kind) and Evans unstressed approach made them work as abstract essays in cheerfulness. And if you want to hear Alfie (personally I dont, but the club's lovely manageress had requested it), then Evans sings it as well as anybody is likely to. He makes it, in its own preposterously solemn words, something even non-believers can believe in.

THIS COULD BE LOVE

Poor Alex Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - There are a fair number of reasons why This Could Be Love could be terrible, which makes the fact that it's good all the more remarkable. Its a two-character musical, which is not a sub- genre with a very inspiring history, and the couple in question are identified to us only as He and She, which seems like economy gone insane. When we meet them they are at adjacent tables in some kind of bar (the sets are economical, too), each in the same position, seated but stood up.

Now, its probable that in real life both would feel too depressed and humiliated by their non-appearing dates to start making conversation, which is what these two do. If we grant that they might, though, it's quite possible they would, in a mood of defiant desperation, go off on an impromptu date themselves and that the night would find them in bed together, which sequence of events is what happens here.

What really challenges belief is that they should immediately decide to get married, even driving a considerable distance the very next morning to find a Cree chief empowered to officiate at weddings. (You never know when arcane bits of Canadiana may come in handy.)

The reasons they give for this behaviour may be even harder to get your head around. He and She, having both been burned by the traditional courtship rituals, jointly resolve to bypass all that. Theirs is a whirlwind anti-romance. They draw up agreements as to the conduct and goals of their relationship which He, the more anal- retentive of the two, insists on having written down in list form. (His hobby, the key to his character, is memorizing the names of capital cities that he has no intention of visiting.)

Of course they -- or should I say They? -- really are in love, and We -- I mean we -- settle in for an evening of waiting for them to acknowledge it, while they go through all the regulation hoops that tradition decrees for the occupants of two-handed plays about relationships, with or without music. I don't think Im giving away much by revealing that jealousies are caused by one partners previous experiences and the other's lack of them. Nor should it come as a great surprise that the pair split up in the course of the action and reunite at its end. We'd feel cheated if they didnt.

So we have a predictable story trying to pass itself off as unconventional; a double recipe for disaster. And yet the writing and performance make it work.

The author -- of book, music and lyrics -- is Brock Simpson, a charter member of the amoebic group of musical-comedy practitioners responsible, in various combinations, for two of the most delightful shows in recent memory: Honest Ed -- The Bargain Musical and The Drowsy Chaperone. This bunch have now formed their own company, Harry Gadsby Theatricals Inc. There is no such person as Harry Gadsby, and This Could Be Love is his first production.

The first thing you notice about Simpsons lyrics is that he knows what a rhyme is. This is quite rare. Russell Smith, a generally smart writer, had a recent column in The Globe and Mail lamenting such current deformations of the English language as the apparently incurable confusion between its and it's, and spoiled it by saying at one point that canine rhymed with mainline. It doesn't. Train-line rhymes with mainline, and if you cant hear the difference, theres nothing I can do for you. Pairing canine with mainline is not an indictable offence, but it could never give the same aural satisfaction as Lorenz Hart's mating of Yonkers with conquers.

This Could Be Love's first number, a mutual-attraction song thats invigoratingly breezy in words and music, is pure Rodgers and Hart (and the shows title may well be a homage to R&H's This Can't Be Love). Its second-act opener is a traditional softshoe duet of the kind Broadway audiences are currently lapping up as the eleven oclock number in Hairspray, though Simpsons is better written. You do wonder, though, what place this kind of pastiche has in a supposedly contemporary show, or whether a man who comes up with a couplet in which love is compared to a prick from an amorous hatpin, following it with "and this could be that pin," could ever sound at home in the 21st century.

The rest of the score proves that he can; that he can fit his old- fangled verbal dexterity into a varied succession of modern rhythms. This is something that neither of the previous Gadsby-group shows has tried. The heroine has a number called I Want (I think -- there are sadly no song-titles in the program) that sounds free-form but is in fact very tightly controlled, and it legitimately brings down the house. It's cleverness turned into joy.

Beside his songwriting talents, Simpson writes nippy dialogue and has a lively, if uncomplicated, sense of character. He has also given his characters interesting jobs. She is a department store's house detective, with the difference that her brief is to spy not on the customers but on her fellow employees; this breeds self-hatred, that the show explores, somewhat, but somehow cannot link to the main action. He has a career that is far more musically amenable; he writes advertising jingles, and we actually see him at it and believe what we see.

(Compare Theyre Playing Our Song, another two-character musical that was ostensibly about a couple of songwriters, but that could actually have been about anyone. This one is far more specific, and therefore far superior. Also, it doesnt have lyrics by Carole Bayer Sager, who, as somebody once said, probably thought that her names rhymed.)

It is predictable, but not stultifyingly so, that He, faced with writer's block, will make professional use of a tune that was supposed to be the couple's own private theme, thereby causing serious grief to She. (I curse Simpson for forcing me into these grammatical contortions. Why couldnt he give them names? What does he think he has here? Archetypes?) It looks like The End, but of course it isnt. The end, which is also a beginning, occurs in Helsinki (capital of Finland), where He finds personal and musical liberation -- "there under an alias/I'll be humming Sibelius" -- and where He and She solemnly commit themselves to not being committed, in a song that sounds like Sondheim's Being Alive turned inside out.

John Mitchells production is brisk, though spartan to the point of grubbiness. I imagine he would like to be able to afford more furniture, just as Simpson would probably appreciate more spacious musical arrangements than his own piano accompaniment can accommodate; his tunes deserve them.

Most of the costume budget seems to have gone on Krista Sutton (She), who is allowed an early release from the fluffy pink number that she wears to be stood up in. Jonathan Wilson (He) goes through nearly the whole evening in the same yellow bow tie with polka dots - - other things, too, of course, but thats what you notice -- and when he sheds it, it's a life-altering decision.

Both players seem to have been hired for their comedic rather than musical talents; both have a tendency to sing flat, and Wilson in particular seems fazed by harmonies. (I sympathize, but he's the one whos up there.) Both, however, compensate with energy, likeability and acting skills. Wilsons rabbitty enthusiasm, as a man who has survived a hundred put-downs, is very appealing, and Sutton is a fair stormer. Neither of them yields an inch to sentimentality.

The show seems aware of its own limitations in style and scale, and capitalizes on them. It satirizes itself, without ever cancelling itself out, which is quite a trick.

THE SEA

George Ignatieff Theatre

- - -

To see The Sea is to be reminded of what an extraordinarily good writer Edward Bond can be. Or at least how good he could be. The Sea is a 30-year-old play, written when Bond and the professional theatre still had some use for each other.

That relationship continued for about another decade, after which Bond seems to have decided that the theatre was just another irredeemable part of the capitalist world. He now writes only for uncorrupted amateurs, and young ones at that. I haven't seen any of his recent plays, but I do recall that earlier on, even when he seemed to be writing didactic parables, complexity, if not cheerfulness, had an incorrigible way of breaking in.

The Sea, from his earlier phase, is complex to the point of waywardness. Set just before the First World War, it's a comedy, and a truly witty one. Most of the wit is centred in the figure of Mrs. Rafi, a well-to-do widow who is the governing presence of the small coastal town in which she lives. (That town, as Bond wrote it, is in the south of England. In the current production, it has been moved to Newfoundland, with no especially ill effects. Indeed, in that setting, the sight of a Union Jack flying at a funeral carries an especially ironic charge.)

Mrs. Rafi has a natural authority, mainly expressed through bullying. Her most immediate victims are the more timid ladies of the town, most especially a Mrs. Tilehouse, who is her companion and who fears, respects and resents her in about equal measure. Mrs. Rafi is also an enthusiastic purveyor of amateur dramatics (though not of the kind that Bond would later favour) and one of the play's more hilarious scenes shows her rehearsing her colleagues in her own treatment of Orpheus in the Underworld, and putting them, appropriately enough, through hell. Some of her put-downs ("Jessica, do stop trying to look as if you had an interesting past") are inspired. It's difficult to resist a character who talks like that, even if her author would like us to see her as a symbol of everything that's evil in society.

He complicates the picture in other ways, too, because Mrs. Rafi is self-aware. She knows what she does to people, and claims, quite convincingly, that most of them enjoy it. She also prophesies that, when she is an old lady in a wheelchair, they will have their revenge. She has a long speech on that subject, and it's superb: concrete, funny and -- to invent a phrase -- self-pitiless. (Bond was to be less kind to the establishment monsters of his later plays, but they, too, tend to assert themselves in the teeth of his intentions.)

The best of Bond's dialogue has a stage presence equalled among living English playwrights only by Harold Pinter; his lines spring from and illuminate their dramatic situations, but also sound as if they might survive on their own resources.

Hazel Desbarats, playing Mrs. Rafi for the Actor's Repertory Company (a low-key Soulpepper), cannot muster the character's full force or energy, but she is very intelligent and very incisive. She rules the play as she does the village.

One of her less willing subjects is Mr. Hatch, the local draper. "Shopping," proclaims Mrs. Rafi, "is a lost art," and her efforts to revive it are principally at Hatch's expense; she keeps ordering stuff and then sending it back, getting him into deep trouble with his suppliers. She now cancels the biggest order of all -- for a set of blue velvet curtains -- and drives him mad. I still have a vivid memory of Ian Holm, in the play's original production, cutting up the fabric regardless into the required lengths, and then going at his customers with the shears; that intensity of manic obsequiousness is hard to bring off, and Alan Jordan, the current Hatch, manages the resentment but not the fury.

Mr. Hatch is somewhat crazy already: A man obviously ahead of his time, he believes that the Earth, and especially his town, is being invaded by aliens, and he has made some converts among the local male working class. It is this belief that brings him into Mrs. Rafi's irrevocable disfavour.

The play starts with a storm; Hatch is on coastguard duty; he angrily repels a foundered boat, whose two inhabitants he takes to be space invaders; one of them drowns.

The dead man happened to be the fiance of Mrs. Rafi's niece, on his way to claim her; so the chatelaine's wrath is understandable.

This is, indeed, no way for a coast guard to behave, and no amount of special pleading, his own about being too imaginative a man for his station in life, or his author's about the appalling way he's treated by the gentry, can put us on his side. (His later dementia includes an attempt to murder a corpse -- a very Bondian thing to do.)

Hatch, in isolation, is almost as vivid a creation as Mrs. Rafi, and we're meant, I think, to see them both as people too big for their environment, and either crushed or corrupted by it. But the relation between them is never driven through; one wouldn't expect it to be resolved, but here it disappears.

Instead, speechifying takes over. An old recluse (well played by Sam Malkin), who lives in a cave by the sea, delivers apocalyptic rhetoric about the end of a death-worshipping world that could fit a dozen other plays as easily as it does this one. The bereaved niece and her fiance's surviving ship mate fall in love, and they prepare to leave town -- thereby following Mrs. Rafi's advice but not, as is tartly observed, her example.

Both lovers are very high-minded, and there is a suggestion that the girl, who was Eurydice in her aunt's pageant, is likewise ascending from the inferno. But that's the kind of thing that sounds better in exegesis than in performance.

Brenda Bazinet's production is serviceable. It probably goes over the top in the funeral scene but is forgivably funny while doing it.

The opening storm is impressive, and so is the constant punctuation of military guns, practicing up for the coming carnage.

Brett Christopher and Janet Bourgeois bring unexpected life to the lovers, and Angela Fusco's Mrs. Tilehouse has amusing moments, principally musical. Robin Ward, too, is nicely befuddled as the local vicar, recruited first to play Pluto and then to eulogize a man he barely knew. He's quite a sympathetic character until the author remembers that he's an ideological enemy.

The play, like all Bond's best. creates a world and tells a story, albeit in fits and starts. He was a master craftsman, and it is the theatre's ill-fortune that he has, for what most of us would call practical purposes, abandoned the craft.

BOY GETS GIRL

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

Rebecca Gilman, author of Boy Gets Girl, has been hailed as the best new American playwright since David Mamet. This is unwarranted. She is a clever and intelligent writer (the two words are not synonymous) who dramatizes interesting subjects, and she may be developing a distinctive viewpoint. She has not matched it, however, with a distinctive voice.

Her expository dialogue is indistinguishable from anybody else's, and when she goes in for humour, the audience can usually guess her comebacks before the actors can utter them. So much for style. As for substance: as she says herself, her most successful plays have been about issues. Spinning Into Butter, the play that established her in New York, is her racism-on-campus play. Boy Gets Girl, which followed and is now receiving its Canadian premiere, is her stalking play. Its the more absorbing of the two, partly because of its novelty value. There havent been many stalking plays, though there have of course been several stalking movies.

Gilman has staked out an interesting area for herself -- her protagonists are capable women with moderately successful careers, pushed to their limits. She takes the workplace as her central setting. Theresa, in Boy Gets Girl, is a magazine writer, lately unattached. A friend fixes her up on a blind date with Tony, a computer engineer, slightly younger than herself, apparently charming, and very attentive: Disconcertingly so, in fact. When she declines to pursue the relationship, he refuses to take no for an answer. Theresa finds herself deluged by phone calls and flowers. It's embarrassing for her, and also for the audience -- emotional ineptitude is always painful to watch on stage, perhaps because it's so easy to identify with. We grow to dread the voice on the phone as much as Theresa does, which is a compliment to the play, even if a back-handed one.

What follows escalates, speedily, way beyond embarrassment. The calls become obscene, to be followed by threatening letters and worse. A restraining order is placed on Tony, but when he violates it, the police are unable to enforce it. Theresa is advised to leave town, get a new job, change her name: to sacrifice her identity, in fact. She is faultless, except perhaps in having discouraged Tony with insufficient firmness to begin with, and she is trapped. In Miles Potters production, the play makes us share her terror. This is a play with many scene changes, and after each revolution of Peter Hartwells smart, suggestive set we expect to find Theresa's nemesis lurking somewhere in the newly-revealed location. The denouement is as frightening as we have expected, though not in the way we have expected.

Seasna McKenna, perfectly cast, conveys all of Theresa's intelligence (which includes some wit), all her integrity, all her professional assurance and all her private panic. The last element she injects with great economy; it courses underneath, mounting in intensity but still kept down with just one devastating, hysterical moment.

Note this is not really a play about stalking; it is a play about being stalked. Kevin Bundy is a Tony suitably unsettling in his very blandness, but the mechanics of the piece mean he has to spend a lot of time offstage. The play isnt very interested in what might make him tick, settling for a few generalizations from a cop whos never met him. So there's a lot of stage time still to fill, and it's devoted to broadening the theme, contextualizing it, examining other ways in which men may objectify women.

Theresa has two very supportive male colleagues: Her editor, who offers her a refuge, and another journalist, who is the first to call the law. They could hardly be more loyal, but each -- at least according to the other -- has some kind of emotional design on her. Her fellow scribe is even insensitive enough to suggest writing a story on stalking, using Theresas ordeal as the hook. This makes her furious beyond words: literally, she refuses to discuss it. One sympathizes, but it means that nobody ever gets to ask the obvious question. Suppose she had never been involved, and he had brought a similar idea to her. He could hardly have written it without going into actual cases. Would she have minded then about whose privacy was being breached, whose trauma was being probed? And doesnt this go beyond male-female relationships? Don't we all project on to other people the things we want from them?

The two guys here do much of the play's legwork, functioning as they do as buddies, protectors, sleuths and sounding boards. They hardly have time to be people in their own right, and the actors have their work cut out to humanize them. Peter MacNeill slouches in comfortably pudgy mode through the role of the editor; John Jarvis has the edgier character, and sometimes pushes him too hard.

There remain three lively episodes in which Theresa, for interview purposes, visits an ageing film director famous for his obsession, offscreen and on, with womens breasts. Here, if you like, is the arch-objectifier, and Theresa gets very cross with him. She ends up quite liking him though, partly because he is engagingly shameless, and partly because he is both personally and professionally desperate. The role is played by Eric Peterson, who gives his best performance in ages. In recent roles he has been all over the place but here he is obliged to play all his scenes confined either to a desk or to a hospital bed. Thus restrained, he focuses his extravagance, channels it through the character, and not only relishes his generous percentage of the plays best lines but allows us to enjoy them too. I'm not sure what this character adds to the argument, beyond giving another twist to the kaleidoscope, but he's certainly good for the plays flavour, and for letting us see another aspect of the heroine. Its only with him that she's allowed to be both affectionate and in command.

This is, I suppose, a more prosaic play than the Bluma Appel's other recent Broadwayish imports, Wit and Proof. To put it another way: It has fewer pretensions, spiritual or intellectual, and is better off without them.

Black & White Photo: Lucas Oleniuk, Canstage / HE SEEMED SO NICE AT FIRST: Seasna McKenna plays Theresa Bedell and Kevin Bundy is her stalker boyfriend Tony in Boy Gets Girl.

FINDING REGINA

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

There are Josh, Rae and Annabel, and they all grew up together in Regina. Josh still lives there; the two women have moved away, Rae to Vancouver and Annabel to Toronto. They're now in their thirties, and we meet them in a Regina hospital, where they have assembled in the waiting area outside intensive care. Beyond the door lies a friend and contemporary, who has tried to kill himself. The last time our trio were together was at a funeral. In fact, these days they only meet when one of their group has either attempted or committed suicide, but apparently this happens often enough to keep them in touch.

Finding Regina is a first play by Shoshana Sperling, much of whose previous experience has been in stand-up comedy. She is from Regina herself, and the most successful portions of this piece come when she marries her personal and professional experience: that is, when she manages to be funny about her hometown. Outside the hospital it's minus 78 -- that's with the wind chill, though there's heated debate, if that's the right phrase, as to whether the wind chill actually counts. Anyway, the characters seem to take it in their stride, even the two of them who have bunked it to more temperate climes. (Who says theatre can't be a moral force? It probably does the Toronto audience a lot of good for us to have our own winter put into perspective. I didn't know whether to laugh in guilt or shiver in sympathy.) They don't complain much, or slap themselves, or blow on their hands, and they don't seem that bundled up under their parkas. When the action shifts temporarily to the cab of Josh's truck, two of them even attempt to have sex in it.

Behaviour like this seems to have characterized their teenage days, and it's left its mark. They have made typical choices, typical anyway of people in plays. Josh is still leading what he claims to be the same carefree existence, indulging in sports, dope and everything female that's available. Rae made a smart marriage, whose smartness is coming into question. Annabel is doing a PhD in women's studies, and the author, who plays the role herself, has fun with the way in which she wrinkles her nose every time one of the others says something politically questionable; she combines the moral certitude of Lisa Simpson with the belligerence of Miss Piggy. The set (by Tamara Marie Kucheran) takes clinical sterility to new levels of barrenness. There are also slides (sharply done by Graham Powell) that make Regina look like everywhere else, only more so. They suggest this would indeed have been a rigorous place in which to spend one's adolescence. But then, what place wouldn't?

Regina, from what we see and hear, is as companionable, or as claustrophobic, as any small town. Annabel tells us that, on alighting at the airport, she got a full update on the suicide's condition from the baggage handlers. Josh claims to know everything that's happened to everybody he was in school with, and a sequence in which he asks the women to test him on this knowledge is very enjoyable -- remarkably so, considering we don't, of course, know any of the people he's talking about. The interest seems to transcend both geography and generation. Even those of us who've never been to Saskatchewan, or who could not care less about the relative coolness of Bowie and Pink Floyd, may find ourselves drawn in. But when the play tries to work on a level deeper than that of a game show, it comes undone.

This is yet another retrospective play. The characters' present existences are pencil-thin, but keep feeding us bits of their pasts, so they can have something to react to. But it's all very arbitrary. Their author can make them say whatever it takes to keep the party going. That's all right when the only object is humour, but not when we're expected to have some kind of emotional response. What we learn is commonplace. Rae, the pretty girl in school, could have boyfriends without putting out, while Annabel's position was the opposite; jealousy results. Josh was a mindless stud, whose prodigious memory doesn't extend to recalling the identities of all the women he slept with; resentment results. Josh may also be insecure about his sexual orientation; denial results. Many of their reminiscences converge on their comatose friend next door, but naturally where he is concerned, we have even less of a reality check.

The actors in Kelly Thornton's production do all right when required to be funny, and flounder when obliged to be emotional. Jeremy Harris comes off best since Josh, Regina unregenerate, is spared most of the soul-searching; at least it's directed at him rather than from him. The other two have set speeches. Rae's, as delivered by Teresa Pavlinek, are shrill, and Annabel's, as unrolled at length by Sperling herself, are strident. They demand our sympathy, but never give us grounds for it. Numbness sets in, and so, only a little later, does boredom.

This is a common occurrence in the theatre so, to cheer myself up, I have compiled a list of the plays that have opened in Toronto this year that, whatever else, have not been boring. It's longer than I thought it would be: Wingfield on Ice, Sunday Father, Little Mercy's First Murder, Dream Machine, Pinocchio, This Could Be Love, The Laramie Project, The Sea, Boy Gets Girl and -- to prove that not being boring is not necessarily the same as being good -- Vinci.

STORMY WEATHER: THE MUSIC OF HAROLD ARLEN

Opening Night, CBC-TV

Harold Arlen, one of the giants of 20th-century American music and possibly the most gifted popular composer of them all, spent the last 15 years of his life in a state of deep depression, rarely venturing outside his own apartment. That is the premise of Stormy Weather: The Music of Harold Arlen, a celebration of his work that airs tonight in CBC's Opening Night slot -- though "celebration" may not, in these circumstances, be quite the right word.

Arlen's late-life reclusiveness (he died in 1986) is a historical fact. It may have had something to do with the fall from supremacy of his kind of song, but its immediate cause was the death of his wife, Anya, following a long period of mental illness.

Stormy Weather has Arlen (played by Paul Soles, who looks and sounds exactly right) wandering around his apartment (which also looks exactly right, at least to begin with). He's attended by a nurse, who wants him to watch a TV special about his work (presumably a repeat, since he's in it himself, and it's in black and white; we see bits of it, and they look mighty interesting).

Most of his attention, though, is devoted to the composition of a letter to the dead Anya: part reminiscence, part contrition. Affected by this double dose of nostalgia, he starts wandering around, opening doors. Gazing at the pills in his bathroom cabinet, he mutters, "they're turning me into a drug addict," and suddenly there materializes one of the opium-themed numbers he wrote for the Cotton Club in the '30s, Kickin' the Gong Around, done in a very decent approximation of its original Cab Calloway style.

After that, the visions get wilder. Every time Arlen enters a room, one of his hits gets up and hits him back. I've Got the World on a String becomes a number about puppets. It's the singer (Hawksley Workman) who's strung up, which seems to indicate a rather careless attitude to the syntax of the lyric. It's Only a Paper Moon becomes tuneless, toneless and generally repulsive. And those are just the happy songs.

Now, it's quite conceivable that Arlen, in his devastated condition, would have looked back at his early successes and found their light-hearted sentiments bitterly ironic. But it's unlikely that that's all he would have felt, and anyway, it hardly does justice to the songs themselves.

Arlen -- the composer of Stormy Weather, Blues in the Night and I Gotta Right to Sing the Blues -- fought all his productive life against being labelled a blues composer. His tunes were a unique combination of earthy and elegant. He wrote ballads as beautiful as Rodgers', rhythm numbers as effervescent as Gershwin's, and exhibited a sense of form that was probably the most adventurous of any.

Some of his songs' distinction came of course from his lyricists. He wrote with the best: Johnny Mercer, E. Y. Harburg, Ira Gershwin, even Truman Capote. Their contribution, though, goes unmentioned in this program, perhaps because it would complicate the sentimental view of Arlen's songs as the mirror of his soul. The omission probably explains the belief of one of The Globe and Mail's TV writers that after Anya's death, Arlen "never wrote another word." The truth is, he had written very few while she was alive.

It's curious, too, that Arlen, in a show presumably set in the 1970s, should keep imagining his songs being performed in the styles and accents of 2003. No wonder he was depressed.

At one point he wanders into a barroom and has to endure Rufus Wainwright, earlier the assassin of Paper Moon, wreaking even worse havoc on the more delicate I Wonder What Became of Me. And if you really want irony, the show has something worthy of Ken Russell: Anya's incarceration in a mental hospital inspires staff and patients to a ghoulish rendition of Ac-Cent-Tchu-Ate the Postive. At moments like these, you wonder if the performers and producers genuinely despise the material or if, even more alarmingly, they think they're doing it a favour.

A few of the pop people do have some idea. Debbie Harry looks as if she might carry off Stormy Weather itself, if she wasn't done in by the dissonant orchestration. Sandra Bernhard delivers a Come Rain or Come Shine that makes up in power what it lacks in pitch.

And there even are a couple of people who have spent their lives singing this stuff. Ranee Lee, apart from bustling about as the nurse, gets to sing The Man That Got Away. A much older jazz singer, Little Jimmy Scott, does Over the Rainbow, on which, to be honest, he inflicts melodic distortions that are every bit as extreme as those perpetrated by the younger folks. The difference is that his have some musical logic to them, and that his bizarre, haunted sensibility bears some relation to the song's.

It's clever, too, to have this, of all legend-encrusted numbers, sung by a man; doubly so when the man is one who sounds like a woman. Scott also sings, poignantly, I Had a Love Once, probably Arlen's last song, and one for which he did write the words. Best of all, Soles lip-synchs to Arlen's own recording (he was a fine singer) of his own favourite among his songs, Last Night When We Were Young.

It's always a sign of desperation when a show resorts to Busby Berkeley aerial shots of girls in geometric patterns in order to suggest Hollywood in the '30s, and the example here is no exception. In general, though, the production is technically fine. It blends its disparate elements very smoothly. But you keep wishing Arlen would heed medical advice and just settle down and watch that primitive TV tribute, so that that we could watch it with him, uninterrupted. It may have airbrushed his biography, but you can bet it had a more authoritative handle on his work than the show surrounding it does.

As background to the closing credits, the producers treat us to the old Jack Teagarden record of I Gotta Right to Sing the Blues, and it comes as something between a joke and a blessing. It's late but here, finally, is what it's about.

KINGFISHER DAYS

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

In Kingfisher Days, Susan Coyne plays Susan Coyne so confidently you'd swear shed been doing it all her life. She also wrote the script, which must obviously help. The play is, of course, based on her childhood memoir, which everyone except me has read. The dramatization brings her on in two guises: as an adult, doing the narration, and as a five-year-old child, doing the play.

My experience of watching grown-up actresses play little girls of five is rather limited, but I cannot imagine that many have done it more acutely or more completely than Coyne does here. Eyes shining and nose tip-tilted, she has the perfect attitude toward the grown- ups in her life: entreaty laced with blackmail. She is clear about everything, even the things shes puzzled by.

The story concerns one of several summers that she, a Toronto child, spent by the lake in Kenora with her family: a scholarly and abstracted father, a mother loaded with practical proverbs, and an assortment of siblings and half-siblings, right down to baby Andrew Coyne, here tagged, ornithology-fashion, as red-cheeks, tufted crest. Mother and father are the only family members who are portrayed on stage, but we get slides.

Susan has an additional father figure in the next cottage: a retired schoolteacher named Mr. Moir. Mr. Moir introduces her to literature -- to Lewis Carroll (Susan, like many well-brought-up and inquisitive girls, has a decided affinity with Alice) and, by subtle manoeuvre, to Shakespeare.

It goes like this: In a ruined fireplace, sole remnant of a cottage that once stood between the other two, Susan finds letters bearing the signature Nootsie-Tah. Nootsie-Tah is a fairy princess, banished for a time from her home in Peru and spending the interim (a thousand years) as lady-in-waiting to Queen Mab. Susan sends replies, of gradually increasing confidence and length. Nootsie-Tah is proudly illiterate but dictates her letters to a scribe, who of course is Mr. Moir. Susan dictates hers to her mother.

It could be cloying, and there are in fact a few letters too many; the situation is not in itself dynamic. But it holds us by working on two levels. We come to believe in Nootsie-Tah, her travels and travails, and we also enjoy keeping track for ourselves of the effect that composing her correspondence has on Mr. Moir. He's still a teacher, and a creative one with a flair for improvisation; he seizes, gently, the opportunity of opening a young mind and a young imagination.

He's given a jewel of a performance by Joseph Ziegler, very easy and crinkled but full of bottled-up gentlemans relish and meshing perfectly with Coynes implacable eagerness. We see two kinds of wonder feeding off one another, though I wish the play had found more room for the implicit running comparison, which occasionally breaks surface, to Alice and her creator or to Alice and her White Knight. Ziegler's Mr. Moir suggests what his Scrooge would have turned into, once the transformation had wholly set: a lovely creation alternated, rather than doubled, with the actor's drier account of Coyne senior, affable but aloof, and devoted to crosswords.

Martha Burns similarly combines the roles of mother (whose best scene, a cautious dip in the lake, is shown in silhouette) and of Nootsie-Tah, as whom she resembles a cross between Peter Pan and Tiger Lily, with a fair dose of the snootiness of Tinker Bell. Its a dashing performance, enlivened by entrances from and exits to all manner of unexpected places.

There is another theme running through the play, and no bones are made about it. Its Time, a subject that Coyne broaches in her own present-day person, right at the start of her introductory monologue. Most obviously it's the time that for a child, especially in summer, seems to stretch out for ever and for a parent rushes heartbreakingly fast. Hence, a call she receives on her cell-phone from her own daughter, in which the concerns of two generations crash together. Hence also the fact that she begins with a couple of false entrances, nervously wondering whether she's late, and appealing to the stage manager as the ultimate arbiter of all theatrical time.

Hence, yet again, her reference to the pleasure we must take in learning from the program that this play has no intermission, and will therefore be short enough for us to make it home in time to see the news. Here, I think, she confuses audiences with critics. Critics like plays to be short; watching them is our job, and the sooner we can clock off the better. Audiences like to get quantity for their money, though they will, all things being equal, settle for quality. As here.

By the end, Coyne has also mentioned geological time, the life expectancy of cloud forests and the accelerated chronology of adolescence. Nothing of this is any kind of revelation, but time, as experienced in regard to childhood, is an infallibly touching subject if linked to a believable situation, and so it is here.

Some of the script, especially the chat to the audience, is self- conscious. Correction: All of it is self-conscious. But thats rather the point, and Coyne makes most of it sound spontaneous and much of it funny. Ive only become conscious of her skill as a comedienne in the last year or so, and I'm charmed by it. I liked her reminiscence of her teenage shyness, and of how it defeated her mother's best advice ("Attack!") and eventually turned her into an actress. I even indulged the more blatant in-jokes, like her hesitation over the name of her director, Albert Schultz, who only happens to be her husband.

His production is sensitive and inventive, with a charming set by Ken Ganhum and magical lighting by Louise Guinand. And we learn -- or I did -- the true meaning of the phrase "halcyon days," for which you may look in the title.
