JOB: THE HIP-HOP MUSICAL

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - It gets harder and harder for a conscientious critic to find shows to which he can take his teenage children; the theatre may not be changing but they are. But Job, surnamed The Hip-Hop Musical, seemed a likely bet. I was told in advance that it contained no sex and no bad language, but I took them anyway.

They liked it. So did I. But I have to record that on the way out they remarked to me that, after an hour of listening to rap, they wanted desperately to hear some other kind of music -- any other kind of music. This, considering the sounds that pound through our house for much of the day and night, came as a surprise. (Driving home, I took them at their word, and subjected them to a standard- issue 1950s musical of no special distinction called By the Beautiful Sea. That, I thought, would learn 'em.)

As well as being an all-but-all-rap musical -- the first ever to cross my sheltered path -- Job, based on the Book of the same name, is a two-actor musical, the second to hit this town in as many weeks. The first was the comparatively conventional This Could Be Love, with two actors playing a character apiece in somebody else's script. In this case, the performers, Jerome Saibil and Eli Batalion, are also, as they would probably have to be, the authors; they wrote the lyrics and collaborated with Paul Bercovitch on the, well, music. Between them they play a multiplicity of roles, several of which they share. On at least one occasion a character passes from the care of one to that of the other, right in the middle of a scene.

All of which is very high-energy, high-pace and high-definition. Saibil and Batalion are not, at least according to the stereotypes that dwell in my head, your everyday rappers. They are white Jewish boys (they're both 22) from Montreal, and former scriptural and philosophy students to boot. Their lyrics throw in insouciant references to Hegel's Phenomenology and Immanuel Kant; and their subject matter, as already stated, comes from the Old Testament. In this very contemporary version, the prosperous and then inordinately long-suffering patriarch becomes Job Low, a rising record-company executive who abruptly stops rising. Jehovah is his boss, J. Hoover, of Hoover Records. Satan, a.k.a. Lucifer, is Lou Safire, VP in charge of finance, who snakily persuades the old man to test Job's company loyalty by stripping him of perks, shares, dental plan and most of his salary: everything in fact that makes the corporate life worth living.

This Job's tormentors stop short of giving him boils, though chances are they would if they could. But their incapacity in this regard does suggest a slight disconnect between the old story and the new setting. Nobody, whatever their opinion of the corporate culture and our dependence on it, thinks that it's in the business of dispensing divine justice. We may naively expect our employers to treat us fairly, but that's as far as it goes. It isn't even mildly surprising to find a music-business czar acting like a capricious, conceited and sadistic monster.

There are some who would say that the exceptionally mysterious ways pursued by the God of the Book of Job could well expose him to the same charges. But it's also true that most people find that idea worrying, and try to find some explanation for it. If you believe in God, you would like to think that the universe makes some kind of sense. Belief in music moguls who have turned their entire catalogue over to hip hop has no such corollary.

Batalion and Saibil seem somewhat aware of this, and even play with it a bit. Their primary personae in the show are a couple of squabbling narrators, known as MC Cain and MC Abel. The end of the show finds them arguing intensely (and just out of sight, which for some reason makes it funnier) about the moral, if any, of the story they have just told. Finally, they give up and revert to fratricidal type. This conclusion, which seems irritatingly abrupt at the time, makes more sense the more you think about it.

As it happens, Saibil and Batalion, or Cain and Abel, are often at their most endearing when they step out of their neo-Biblical roles and simply bitch at one another. Each is especially critical of the quality of the other's rhymes. What, one of them wants to know are "knishes" doing in there? (I think they go with "wishes" -- it's hard to keep track -- but I agree, it's far-fetched.) I suspect, though, that they and I would have our differences over what constitutes a good rhyme. To crib from the lyrical extracts from their score that were helpfully reproduced in last Tuesday's National Post: "Orwellian Twist" and "Machiavellian Twist" make an excellent rhyme; "launch" and "hunch" make a terrible rhyme. You can hardly deny the guys' zest and ingenuity in keeping the jingles coming, or at the musical sampling (Beatles to Beethoven) with which they vary them, but even at its best, the style gets oppressive.

The rhymes, the puns, the omnipresent short lines leave very little air, which is what my kids were complaining about. By the time the show got round to Job's comforters -- three sycophantic execs -- it had lost us, or at least me, though an earlier, and even oilier, board-meeting scene works very well. Characterization varies. The show can hardly to be said to make the best of a good Job; in fact, you never feel an atom of sympathy for him. But his wife -- a headscarved Hamptonian whose rise to academic tenure counterpoints his fall -- is a creation, and so is Hoover, who as befits his name is a vacuum, and goes around like an ambulant Tower of Pisa. Both these characters are alive, whichever of the dynamic duo is playing them.

The piece, charmingly unpretentious as it is, may turn out to be the high-water mark of the rap musical, just as that less intellectual Biblical treat Joseph and the Amazing Technicolour Dreamcoat was of the rock musical. (Joseph made fun of other pop- music forms. Job makes fun of its own. This may be preferable. It certainly seems more honest.) Saibil and Batalion are already at work on Job II, though they seem to have exhausted the original story. Maybe the theatre is changing.

THE LEAGUE OF NATHANS

Factory Theatre, Toronto

Whatever its other flaws, Jason Sherman's play The League of Nathans, 11 years old and now revived under its author's direction, hasn't dated. Its characters are Canadian Jews, and the focus of its attention is the Middle East. It deals, that is, with feelings and situations that have worsened, grown harder and more acute, but have not essentially changed.

There are three men who were boys together in Toronto in the 1970s: Nathan Isaacs, known as Izzy; Nathan Glass, known as Glass; and Nathan Abramowitz, known -- uniquely -- as Nathan. Conceivably Izzy gets nickname-status because he's a joker and something of a joke, Glass gets surname recognition because he's sombre and tough, and Nathan stays Nathan because he's too vaguely characterized for people to have any other kind of handle on him. Their friendship is sealed in a field; the three of them gather there one night in 1973 to pledge reciprocal allegiance in the kind of parody religious ceremony only possible to those who, at some level, believe. At their ages, 13 and each on the verge of bar mitzvah, well-brought- up Jewish boys really don't have any other option, however much they may resent it.

They talk, with teenaged flippancy and teenaged pugnacity, about Israel, or at least about the things they've heard from parents and teachers; about how Jews and Arabs treat, or might treat, one another, and about who has the right. Attitudes are beginning to take shape. Glass floats militant Zionism as the only safeguard against another Holocaust; Abramowitz says those who have been persecuted should be the last to persecute. This seminal scene is fluently written and staged, the boys' minds, bodies and personalities bouncing off one another, and merging closely enough to create a group identity. Most of the play's first half is lively; it switches constantly between past and present (which for these purposes is 1993) in a counterpoint that's usually bracing and never confusing.

The league of Nathans splinters, as far as we can tell, when Glass visits Israel and falls apart when he gets back. He is involved in a deadly attack on an Arab attendant at a Canadian gas station. He was, or so he tells Abramowitz before escaping back to Israel, a witness but not a participant. Now, 17 years later, all three Nathans find themselves summoned, from east and west, to a reunion to be held at a disused synagogue, of medieval origin, in Toledo, Spain.

The play then goes the way of the friendship, right off the rails. It seems unlikely that all three men would agree to keep this date; and belief is strained even further when we learn, as a surprise, who set the whole thing up. All this matters less, though, than the falsity of the supposed moral showdown between Abramowitz and Glass. When Nathan G. told Nathan A. about the gas station killing, he had made out that he was inside the car, watching two buddies actually commit the murder and scared to intervene; almost his first words were "it wasn't my fault, Nathan, I didn't do it." Now, hardened by years on the West Bank, he glories in the deed, claiming that it had rid the world of another potential Jew-killer. Such a transition is certainly not impossible, even if you reject the implicit assertion that all Israeli settlers subscribe to the ethical standards of Rabbi Meir Kahane. The problem is that neither of the Nathans seems to recognize there has been a transition. Nor, we must assume, does the author, unless he was hoping nobody would notice.

Glass never actually goes back on his story; what he does, in alternating blasts, is a) blame Abramowitz for not having offered him moral support at the time, though from the scene as we saw it, Glass was in too much of a hurry to have had time to accept any; and b) taunt him for not having lived up to his humanist principles by turning Glass in. (Why should he, if he believed Glass' protestations of innocence? He isn't a cop.) After pausing to sneer at his friend's "goyische wife"(ex-friend probably, ex-wife certainly) Glass asks him what, with all his high morality, he has achieved in his life. Nathan-who-is-called-Nathan collapses in a corner, whimpering in agony "I haven't done anything."

Michael Schultz, playing the beleaguered one, makes this moment very effective, though as his tormentor Rami Posner, required to be constantly on the attack, has been getting increasingly hoarse and forced. But the effectiveness is just that: an effect, and isolated. We certainly haven't seen Nathan the Good do anything, but who knows what he might have been up to between the short, sharp scenes? It's hard to make inaction register as a dramatic fact. The play leaves gaps in its development, and then blames the characters for them.

Abramowitz does do one thing: he writes, re-workings of Biblical stories. He inherited this habit, along with his sense of Jewish moral obligation, from his grandfather who used to tuck him up with mildly humorous elaborations of tales from the Old Testament. These tended to be supposedly redemptive fables with a destructive edge: Lot in Sodom, Noah's Ark. Nathan, progressing, has been trying his hand at a narrative of pure reconciliation: Joseph and his brothers. The end of the play comes when he finds an end to the story, thus occasioning the kind of hopeful finale with which outwardly cynical playwrights like to show that they really have hearts. (David Hare, in England, pulls this trick all the time.) The play's final statement seems to be: Reaching out to people is better than killing them. Few are going to quarrel with that, but I these characters don't fill it out much.

But there is, of course, a third Nathan, and he's the best thing in the play, Izzy is. Certainly, he seems so as played here by Ben Carlson, for several years the best youngish actor at the Shaw Festival and now -- after Swollen Tongues and this -- possibly the best in the entire Toronto catchment-area. Carlson is both solid and mercurial, an invaluable combination; he establishes his characters so firmly and so economically they can fly off in any direction and take you with them. Izzy is the conventional member of the league. He got married, went to run his father-in-law's factory in Winnipeg because it was the easy and expected thing to do, became a pillar of his community and bought bonds for Israel for much the same reason. If there's a Yiddish equivalent for homme moyen sensuel, he's it. He's shallow but he's also sincere, what he feels he really feels, if only for a moment. He can be equally moved by the picture of a maimed Palestinian girl and by the glimpse of a concentration-camp tattoo on the wrist of a man in the Spanish synagogue; the latter sight prompts an access of religious feeling that sends him, in the play's most resonant moment, searching for skullcaps for his and his friends' previously uncovered heads.

It's hard to believe Glass -- who refers to him bitingly as "that very funny man, Mr. Isaacs" -- can ever have had much time for him, but you can understand Izzy would have clung to both the other guys. Of all the characters in the half-dozen Sherman plays I've seen, Isaacs comes closest to be being a flesh-and-blood person. No, that's mean; he doesn't come close, he is.

A fourth actor, Ken James, doubles, rather too effortfully, as the grandfather and as another older Jewish man whom the Nathans encounter both on the plane to Spain and in the shul when they get there. He interrogates them about their places in the world and seems, like the similarly Strange Passenger of Ibsen's Peer Gynt, to function as a free-floating conscience.

The play may not have been overtaken by events, but it has been overshadowed by more recent plays, all of them written by Adam Pettle: Zadie's Shoes presents a fuller portrait of the wandering Jew as comic sage; Misha offers a more chilling picture of a violent Israeli vet; and Sunday Father has more amusing Biblical paraphrases that also form a more revealing dramatic arc (though, to be fair, you get a more detailed discussion in Job, the Hip-Hop Musical.)

Most of those plays are also funnier. Sherman's has the veneer of humour, but only two good jokes, one of which the script chivalrously attributes to Jackie Mason. (The other one is about the flight into Egypt, and it's really good.) Astrid Janson's set of textured walls stands around for the first act looking gaunt and imposing, and really comes into its own as the abandoned synagogue of the second.

LAST ROMANTICS

Berkeley Street Theatre

- - -

Charles Ricketts had a great success in 1924 with his designs for the first London production of Bernard Shaw's Saint Joan. Before seeing Last Romantics, of which he is one of the two central characters, I knew little else about him. Of his fellow-artist and life-long companion, Charles Shannon, I knew absolutely nothing. Michael Lewis MacLennan's play has dispelled some of my ignorance, but not enough.

One thing I learned was that Ricketts only turned to stage design late in life as part of an increasingly frantic effort to keep his and his partner's bodies and souls together. The Saint Joan connection isn't specifically mentioned, and there's no pressing reason why it should be, but you can tell that Ricketts must have been the ideal man for the job.

Shaw's play is about the end of the Middle Ages, or at least it keeps saying so, and Ricketts's own artistic sympathies seem to have stopped short not much later. A collector and museum consultant as well as a practitioner, he loathed the Impressionists and shuddered at the mere mention of Van Gogh. He became very unfashionable and all-but-unemployable. He was not very nice about it.

Ricketts and Shannon met as students. Shannon had seen himself becoming a commercial artist, but Ricketts saw higher things in him, thought him, in fact, a new Michelangelo.

Shannon seems to have had doubts about this, and the play shows him going so far as to consider settling down with a lady model. Ricketts is incensed, but all bets, amatory or artistic, are off when Shannon falls off a ladder, hits his head and loses, at the very least, his memory. Ricketts devotes the rest of his life, and of his monetary and psychological resources, to caring for his friend.

So it's a love story, but of necessity a one-sided one. Shannon narrates it, presumably from some mental plane of his own, but he's a blank even before his mind gives way. Oliver Dennis wins our sympathy in the role but not really our interest.

Ricketts, by contrast, is full of qualities, few of them likable. He professes to despise worldly success but is viciously jealous of those who achieve it; his possessiveness is, if anything, intensified by Shannon's accident; his tastes are obscurantist. We can hardly afford to mock him for that last quality -- time makes philistines of most of us -- but it adds to the dossier, and he is peculiarly arrogant about it, as about much else.

The actor, Julian Richings, sniffs out the character's meannesses with ferret-like determination and displays them with a thoroughness that may be forensically admirable but is theatrically monotonous. The man is meant to be the centre of an informal salon, but you can't see why he would attract visitors; he doesn't have the glamour.

What Ricketts does have going for him is his devotion, both to his friend and to the art he does like. Retained as an adviser by the National Art Gallery in Ottawa (the play breaks out in a sudden, though historically legitimate, rash of Canadian content), he hatches a complicated scheme for buying an Italian painting before which he and Shannon had once stood in youthful awe.

He is convinced that, if en route the picture can be hung on their own wall, the sight of it will shock Shannon back to his senses. "We're on the cusp," he cries, at every scent of an upturn in their fortunes, medical or financial. Richings does find a piercing truth in moments like these, and then the play comes temporarily into focus.

Most of the time, though, it sprawls, especially in its first half, which takes us back to the Gay '90s -- at undue and ultimately irrelevant length since the play is not, in any historical or polemical way, about homosexuality. Oscar Wilde is on trial, again, and everybody is talking about him, mostly disapproving of his lack of discretion. I doubt that we need another play that invokes Wilde as a dominating, though largely unseen, presence -- or at least it can wait until after someone has brought us Stoppard's The Invention of Love -- though when Oscar does appear, in Reading Gaol, he gets one of the strongest scenes in the play -- one absolutely devoid of both mannerism and aphorism, and played with sad strength by Michael Hanrahan. (It's the centrepiece of a triptych of celebrity; the same actor also plays MacKenzie King and the French painter Puvis de Chavannes.)

In the light of Hanrahan's forthright performance, it's ironic that many of the other characters seem to have stepped out of an especially campy production of one of Wilde's lesser plays. Ricketts illustrated all of Wilde's books except one, the fateful exception being Salome, whose pictures made Aubrey Beardsley famous.

He is played by Steven McCarthy who looks appropriately exquisite but seems to have taken a celebrated declaration of Beardsley's -- "of course I'm affected; even my lungs are affected" -- and extended it to the vocal chords; I could hardly understand a word he said.

I was equally foxed by Jonathan Crombie as a Canadian cultural flunky (strangely enough, he was far more at ease as an Englishman).

More comprehensible but equally mannered are Barbara Gordon and Kate Hennig as a team of aunt-and-niece lesbians who write novels under the collective pseudonym of Michael Field. They seem to be doing Bloomsbury with a vengeance and strictly from the outside in. Interestingly, when given the chance later on to drop the nonsense and express genuine anger or genuine concern, they both take it.

Vickie Papavs goes in and out of credibility as the model but is certainly luscious.

The acting, in fact, is a confusion of styles; Richard Rose has directed the scenery more sensitively than he has the performers. Charlotte Dean, the designer, has provided a set of mobile walls between which the characters gracefully glide. They are covered with empty frames, within which we are to imagine the Ricketts-Shannon collection of old masters, lovingly assembled and painfully disposed of.

MacLennan wrote the admirable play Grace, seen in Toronto a few years ago, and there are hints of another fascinating piece buried somewhere here. But it hasn't got out.

Amidst franchised mega-musicals, a selection of oft-overlooked plays by the Bards contemporaries gleams

LONDON - The Royal Shakespeare Company, rival of the British National Theatre since the two were created in the 1960s, has fallen on hard times. That at least has been the word these last few years; I have rarely been able to check it out for myself since the RSCs recent programming, in Stratford-on-Avon and especially in London, seems almost to have been designed to confuse. One never knows where they are, who they are, or what they're doing.

Adrian Noble, the artistic head and a fine director of plays if not of companies, has largely abandoned the RSC's London base at the Barbican (a space everybody hates, but they have to be somewhere), proposed tearing down the old "jam-factory" theatre on the banks of the Avon, and seems to have abandoned any idea of maintaining a permanent acting team.

Like the National, the RSC is about to change directors. Michael Boyd, youngish and still fairly unknown, is taking over, and he inherits at least one hopeful sign. Last year, in tandem with the regulation Shakespeares in the big house, the RSC mounted a season at the smaller, newer Swan Theatre of five lesser-known pieces by its patrons contemporaries, performed by a self-contained group of 28 actors. The whole season has now transferred to the Gielgud Theatre on Shaftesbury Avenue.

Its amazing. In the heart of the West End -- a theme park crammed with internationally franchised musicals and pop-song collections masquerading as theatre -- stand five plays, in rotating repertory, from the period academics insist on calling early modern.

The plays stand up, no question. All the same, I found myself at the Gielgud wishing I were seeing them at the Swan, which, of all the platform-stage houses built in the last half-century, is the only one to match the Canadian Stratford for impact and intimacy. It also became clear that, for all its enthusiasm and dedication, this was not a strong company. There was a lack, as in so much English theatre now, of actors who were a) experienced and b) good.

At the highest level, there was only one. Antony Sher is a star who, almost uniquely in his generation, has dedicated himself to the theatre -- and to the classical theatre (and this company) at that - - and the two plays in which he appeared were much the best. Sher is a gleeful and consummate technician for whom display has sometimes seemed an end in itself, but here he had roles that could soak up all the energy he threw at them.

In The Roman Actor by Philip Massinger, Sher played a mad emperor (if that isn't tautological), a sadistic tyrant with two fatally soft spots: for his empress (filched from another man who is executed for the impertinence of having been there first), and for the theatre. Naturally, his favourite woman cuckolds him with his favourite player.

Sher gave a silky, mesmerizing account of a man nine-tenths convinced of his own divinity, and if the barefaced audacity with which he switched between manhood and godhead seemed to belong to the actor rather than the character, the process was too enjoyable to occasion much complaint.

Massinger has fallen out of scholarly favour. The Victorians liked him because they thought he was moral; their successors have disdained him, probably for the same reason. (The Revels Plays, the premier publishing series in the field, has yet to issue any of his plays.) He thought this play to be his best, and the production (by Sean Holmes) suggests he was right. It has a good, clear political story, told by the company with great commitment, and its use of three plays-within-the-play, all impacting on those who act and those who watch them, is metatheatre as teasing and effective as anything before Pirandello.

The critical stock of John Marston, who flourished on the cusp between Elizabeth and James, fell in the last century as surely as Massinger's rose. Marston could never have been described as wholesome; his plays present a corrupt court world with lickerous relish, though he always pays lip service to some kind of moral order.

The Malcontent, his masterpiece, allows him the best of both worlds, being about a deposed and (by his own account) virtuous duke who returns disguised as a scrofulous and highly articulate cynic, a Prospero with a three-day stubble and a vocabulary virtuosic in its offensiveness. Sher seized on the part and gave it the soul of a mole, burrowing into human nature and finding it, to his delight, even worse than hed suspected. He looked mole-like as well, though straightening up, literally and impressively, for the happy ending. (This is a play in which murders are plotted, copiously, but never performed.) The production, by Dominic Cooke, moved the action to a Latin American dictatorship, which was not greatly illuminating, but at least bestowed an identity and some nice visuals.

Shers principal antagonist in both these plays was Joe Dixon, a strapping young actor not yet fully formed; he delivers strong outlines but sometimes seems to have boxed himself inside them. In The Roman Actor he had the title role, the unwordly star at the imperial court, entrusted with a speech in defence of his craft that became an anthology-piece. Dixon delivered it well but as a performance. It would surely be a richer irony if it seemed to come from his heart.

In The Malcontent, he was a ruthless but incompetent usurper, and gave us rather too much of the incompetence and too little of the ruthlessness; he was no threat. But he smoked a cigar with style.

Gregory Doran, the cheerful and formidably knowledgable young director who devised and ran the season, also directed The Island Princess by John Fletcher, the most obscure play in the quintet. (At least, it was the only one I'd never seen before.) It was also the trickiest, for Fletcher, the hit commercial playwright of the post- Shakespeare generation, is a very slippery writer. Facile is perhaps the word; he wrote easy, conversational verse that sits especially well on the lips of caddish young men, a type he seems to have drawn from life and that remains permanently modern.

The Island Princess is an adventure story set in what we now recognize as Indonesia. The Christians (Portuguese, but we're meant to identify) square off against the heathen (everybody else). The original audience would certainly have recognized and relished passing parallels to English colonial adventures, but to us its tempting to read the whole play as a progressive-minded satire, and a priest -- dressed up here like Osama bin Laden -- does have a bitter speech about Western exploiters. Hes also the villain in disguise, pushing his own agenda, but that irony, or whatever it is, went for very little since neither his villainy nor his rhetoric came compellingly across.

When the cultures square off at the end of the play, it's made clear that the Christians are always right. The titular heroine, formerly a fanatic, ends up embracing both the faith and the body of the handsomest invader.

The play, in fact, keeps falling in and out of seriousness. It's sophisticated by default, and though Dorans production, with a gamelan band, had fun and drive, the actors couldnt keep up with the currents. Maybe they lacked practice, both in their careers and in the preparation of this play. In Doran's scheme, all the plays were given short rehearsal periods, partly for economy and partly to recreate Elizabethan spontaneity. But the words can hardly come as speedily to us as they did to our ancestors. (There are those who claim the Elizabethans never rehearsed, but it seems unlikely. When Shakespeare wrote a burlesque rehearsal in A Midsummer Night's Dream, was he satirizing something that didnt exist?)

In Edward III, its the English who are always right, even -- or especially -- when they're laying waste to France, at an early stage of the Hundred Years' War. This chronicle, the earliest play in the bunch, has been attributed to Shakespeare, and has now been officially accepted into the canon. (Im not sure who makes these decisions.) But it seems unlikely. He would already have written the Henry VI plays, which are far more accomplished, and he is unlikely, at any date, to have come up with a phrase like "dusty heaps of brittle sand." (Come on now, which is it? Dust or sand?) The only passages that might sound Shakespearean concern King Edwards attempted seduction of the (married) Countess of Salisbury, and they are like the early word-drunk comedies like Love's Labours Lost.

Later on, the king goes to war, and faces other moral tests, but ends up always taking advice and doing the decent thing. There is a pattern here and it came through, but not very grippingly. It's like Henry V without the introspection, and David Rintoul, in the title role, gave it little more than a round voice.

There was one fine performance, from Michael Thomas as the vanquished French king, who passed effortlessly from a real man to the emblem of a ruined land -- the kind of double focus all these plays require. The same actor made an admirably despicable spy in The Roman Actor.

Weakest of the shows was the one outright comedy, Eastward Ho! which, as written, is a seamless collaboration between George Chapman, Ben Jonson and Marston. I had heard mixed reports of this show, and feared it might come out as a cheap romp. Watching it, I rather wished it had. This is one of the city comedies that were among the periods best inventions, partly a celebration of the thrift and honesty of London tradesmen, and partly -- perhaps mainly -- a satire on it.

Here it was hard to tell what it was, and the production was so slow that it was even harder to care. Much of the plays delight lies in its evocation of the town itself, complete with place- names; here, surely, was a case for projecting a map onto the back wall, rather than making us blink at a dark surround all night. The pivotal character, a scamp of an apprentice named Quicksilver, could hardly have been less like his name, but his goldsmith employer (Geoffrey Freshwater, an old RSC hand) at least spoke like a human being and, while on stage with him, other actors tended to do the same.

There were other good performances in all the shows, but not enough. (The women were uniformly weak.) And there are rewards in all the plays, enough to make the season seem more than the sum of the parts. I hope Doran does it again (he says he will) and I'd like to see our theatres -- Stratford most of all -- try some of the same. I can't imagine seeing any of these plays as often as Im required to see Shakespeare, without going mad, but there could be no richer or more helpful context for any Shakespearean theatre. In no other period do you get such a sense of drama inventing itself.

And we might even do them better. We dont necessarily have better actors, but our classical companies -- Stratford, Shaw, Soulpepper -- are better at keeping them together and letting them ripen -- better in fact at texture.

Coincidentally, the National Theatre has just opened a main- stage production of one of the best-known Jacobean plays, John Webster's The Duchess of Malfi. This is a more elaborate show than any at the Gielgud, and some of its ideas work well, especially the translation of the madmen, sent to torment the Duchess, into a sadistic video. This, you will have gathered, is a modern-dress production, directed by Phyllida Lloyd (Mamma Mia!), and the set seems to represent a football terrace.

Whenever somebody dies (which is often -- this is the classic tragedy) he or she gets up, walks to the stands and surveys the rest of the action. So the Duchess, killed off four-fifths of the way through, is kept in our minds, a neat solution to an old problem. Before retiring, each victim delivers a final speech to us -- an inspired notion, since these last words are proverbial meditations (Webster called them sentences), not natural speech.

Unfortunately there is little of this verbal sensitivity elsewhere, and the overall acting is poor. Janet McTeer's Duchess is diminished by whats going on around her and, as her brother, Will Keen, who knocked me out with his hysterical intensity in The Coast of Utopia, gives the same performance over again, augmented by a lot of crotch-grabbing. He leaves no doubt of his characters incestuous motivations but tells us nothing about them. He also sounds a lot less patrician than the jumped-up steward whose marriage to his sister he resents. Maybe the production is telling us that, in a pop- star age, all social roles are reversed, but it isn't carried through.

This, of course, is one advantage Canadian actors have. They are spared the crisis so neatly summed up by Alan Jay Lerner: "An Englishman's way of speaking absolutely classifies him/The moment he speaks he makes some other Englishman despise him." We are luckier, and should make the most of it.

Black & White Photo: Jonathan Dockar-Drysdale, Royal Shakespeare Company / Claire Benedict and Antony Sher in The Malcontent. Sher stands out among RSC performers as a star of the highest level.

TIME AFTER TIME: THE CHET BAKER PROJECT

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, Toronto

The good things in Time After Time: The Chet Baker Project remain as they were: the music, the moody and smoky staging and the playing of the female roles, all of them by the same actress.

The major change since the show's Toronto debut two years ago at Theatre Passe Muraille is in the casting of the central character. That character is not Chet Baker himself; he is still played by the trumpeter Danny DePoe, who continues to offer superb simulacra of Baker's piping, pleading way with a musical phrase and of his affectingly affectless singing. He also has the sulky looks for Baker the babe magnet, and is reasonably convincing when speaking the tactfully few lines he has been allotted. If he seems out of it dramatically, that's hardly inappropriate for Chet, who lived much of his surprisingly long life strung out on heroin and who drifted through marriages and other relationships without, apparently, giving a damn -- indeed, without giving anything.

Chet was a star -- a pop star, even, which is rare for a jazz man -- but he isn't the lead here. That distinction goes to Ted, his would-be biographer, a role previously played by the play's author, James O'Reilly, but now entrusted to a real actor, Randy Hughson. The change is of less benefit than I had hoped; Hughson's anxious, amiable presence -- part bear, part cherub -- is welcome on any stage, but the pleasures of having him around are diluted by the fact that it is not until the show's end that this fine actor is given a chance to act. At that point he is allowed to contemplate, through pained and narrowing eyes, the approaching shipwreck of his character's marriage. Up until then he has functioned as a link man and raconteur. It isn't enough.

One assumed when O'Reilly himself played Ted the role was at least partly autobiographical. Even now one needs to believe it for the piece to have any dramatic interest at all. We first meet Ted looking back to his first date with his future wife 10 years earlier; they hear the Baker recording of I Fall in Love Too Easily. The couple are smitten with Chet and with one another. It doesn't occur to them to give any credit to Jule Styne who composed it, though it's possibly his second-best tune, the best being the same Time After Time that gives the play its title and which we also get to hear.

Ted embarks on a quest to find the man behind the sound and soon enough, like many before him, finds himself asking how such a creep could have given voice to such beauty: or, more specifically, "where did the sadness in those songs come from?" It's an outstandingly dumb question that presumes a one-on-one correspondence between artists and their art; and a long, long line of creative bastards has given it the finger. As it happens the only clues that can be found in Baker's work are morally discouraging; its beauty, though real, is almost entirely narcissistic.

Not for nothing was Chet's theme tune My Funny Valentine.

Ted's own drama, contemplating the fascinating question of whether he's fallen in love too easily, is relayed to us in fractured form; Hughson stands and watches while another actor plays his only-ten-years-younger self. The narrator may be the protagonist, but heaven forbid that we should get too close to him. You can call this hall-of-mirrors stuff post-modern if it makes you feel better, but it's dramatically useless; Ted isn't nearly as interesting as Chet, but it's Ted who hogs the stage. We end up with a pretentious frame surrounding a scissors-and-paste bio-drama: the kind of thing in which Benito Mussolini's musician son has to be given a scene, just to give Chet an excuse to let off his most famous stoned one-liner. ("Yeah, man, it was a drag about your dad.") Figures more central to Baker's life make more reasonable appearances, but the men at least are seldom convincing; Russ Freeman, pianist and arranger on the crucial sessions of the 1950s, is given lines that sound as if they came from a magazine interview. That isn't how people actually talk, and Shaun Smyth, who plays all the supporting male roles, cannot convince us otherwise.

The women are another matter; they seem to have been more imaginatively written, and Philippa Domville plays them in dazzling succession. They range from a buxom groupie at an early recording session to a line of justifiably aggrieved ex-wives, culminating in Ruth, an aspiring singer and fully-achieved lush who is the most hard-bitten (by Chet, principally) and hard-biting of them all.

One thing you could say for Baker; he had excellent taste in tunes. They are terrifically played here by DePoe and a backing trio, in a style that some might call retro or neo-classic but that many of us think of as just the natural way to play this music. It may not be better than what you might hear in a club most nights of the week, but there's a special thrill in hearing it in a theatre: just as a song, in any play that isn't actually a musical, always comes as a treat; it's like playing hooky. Jim Millan's production is highly atmospheric; and though Steve Lucas' set doesn't help much, dominated as it is by a bed slung awkwardly and precipitously in space, his lighting certainly does.

HEART OF A DOG

Artword Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - A dogs life is much like a mans -- nasty, brutish and short -- only more so. That is as much of a message as I can glean from Heart of a Dog, a show in which presentational flair considerably outdistances clarity of intent.

The piece has a complicated history, and comes at us from a number of cultural and linguistic removes. It started out in 1925 as a novel by Mikhail Bulgakov, the Russian writer whose affection for the old order (see his play The White Guard) and skepticism toward the new made him a special pet of that tolerant old sentimentalist Joseph Stalin. Bulgakov's work got banned, this story included, but he himself was protected; he was even given a theatre to run, to keep him out of trouble.

Anne Nenarokoff, a Canadian writer, turned the Russian book into a French play, which was presented last month by Theatre francais de Toronto. This, in turn, has been translated into English by Nenarokoff and her husband, John Van Burek, and the production has been remounted by the same director with most of the same cast.

We are presented with Professor Philip Philipovitch, a doctor practising in Russia in the early post-revolutionary period, whose specialty is rejuvenation by transplant and whose waiting room is regularly crowded with those who can afford his fees. Expanding his patient base, he inserts the sexual organs and pituitary gland of a dead young man into a living dog. It works.

The dog gets up on its hind legs, puts on a suit of clothes and talks, though less decorously than the doctor, his assistant and his nurse would wish. (What we hear of his conversation sounds innocuous enough, but things have moved on since the '20s.) His bathroom habits are distressing, and he takes to sneaking into the nurses quarters. And he gets into bad company, chiefly that of a housing apparatchik intent on expelling the doctor from an apartment suite of counter-revolutionary spaciousness. But then he was an ill-bred dog in the first place.

My opening citation of Thomas Hobbes was glib, like everybody elses, and requires some modification. The celebrated Hobbesian estimation of human life referred to man's fate and behaviour if not put on a leash by authority. Sharik, the former canine, is plenty leashed; he has, indeed, two kinds of authority to contend with: that of the medics who made him and that of the state.

The two are not working in concert. The bureaucrat's suspicions are fully justified; the professor may claim that he was trying, under laboratory conditions, to create "a good Socialist citizen, but his truer feelings seem reflected in his reference to this farce that calls itself a revolution."

He thinks that he, like his author, has friends in high places, but he is brutally disabused by the end. (His nurse, scenting danger, has already attempted a getaway.) So the overreaching scientist comes off almost as a freedom fighter. This may be intended as complexity, but it registers as confusion; we are never sure what is being satirized.

Sharik, meanwhile, takes his place, alongside the heroes of such more-or-less contemporary Russian plays as Mayakovskys The Bed Bug and Erdmans The Suicide, in a gallery of unregenerates making their scruffy individual protests against the brave new world.

He differs from them, though, in apparently wanting to join it; his protest lies not in what he does but in what he incorrigibly is. On two legs or four, he's a walking objection to the idea of human perfectibility, but the play doesn't seem to like him any more than it likes anybody else.

This may not be the case in the novel, which I havent read but which I gather begins with a monologue for the mutt. This might be enough to put us in his corner, or his kennel, but the stage version isnt having any. It keeps everybody at paw's length.

Satires on Practically Everything sound fine in theory, but they get very wearing in practice. As narrative, the play unrolls slowly and, despite its clinical setting and even more clinical air, muddily.

Jean-Stephane Roy is obviously a director to watch, and what he does here is very watchable. It is easier, though, to admire than to enjoy. It is impressively balletic in its deployment both of the performers and of Rudy Braun's sets. The doors are especially graceful.

The actors sometimes wear masks and sometimes exaggerated makeup (though in todays theatre, any makeup looks exaggerated). This gives a distancing effect, presumably intended and conceivably enhanced by the fact that some of the performers are playing in their second language. The effects of this probably arent intentional, but I certainly found the thought processes of Patricia Marceau's nurse hard to follow.

There are vigorous commedia turns by Eric Goulem as the junior medic, and by Martin Albert as the housing man, though breathing new life into this familiar caricature of a slimy functionary is pretty much impossible.

As the dog, Rafal Sokolowski gives, perhaps logically, about the most human performance of the evening. He never sentimentalizes and always seems, at least metaphorically, to be sniffing at his acquaintances' trousers.

He is rivalled for fullness of effect only by William Webster's chief organ grinder, whose eyes have a demonic glitter especially impressive for having to transmit itself from beneath a pair of ferociously bushy eyebrows. At a moment of especial stress he declares that his hair is standing on end -- and so it does, great grey tufts of it. He is, though, rather likeable, as vainglorious scientists go; having the secret police on your tail tends to rank you among the good guys, even if you are in the Frankenstein business.

Besides, there's a cultural thing going on here; Philip Philipovitch would like everybody else to be addressed by name and patronymic like himself, and has a hard time calling anyone Comrade. What audience that has been warmed by Chekhov and chilled by Orwell could fail to sympathize?

AWAKE AND SING

Equity Showcase Theatre, Toronto

Clifford Odets' Awake and Sing is a landmark play that still lands. It was written in 1935 and was the defining production of that fabled New York troupe the Group Theater. The Group transformed American drama and later infiltrated American film by combining the political with the aesthetic. There had been other champions of ensemble performance and of socially conscious plays, but the two concerns had never come together in this fashion. This being the Depression, there was a lot to be socially conscious about. There were also whole areas of American society that had hardly been put on stage before, except for laughs. Odets, an actor, a socialist and Jewish, just pushing 30 when he wrote the play, was, quite literally, the playwright the Group, and the times, had been looking for.

Awake and Sing is set in the apartment of the Berger family in the Bronx. Nominal head of the house is Myron, who once went to law school but has made nothing of it. Effective head is his wife Bessie, and she is very effective. She is especially keen on controlling the lives of her children. When daughter Hennie gets pregnant by a man who promptly disappears, Bessie makes sure that she marries a helpless admirer whom Hennie doesn't love and for whom she makes very few allowances. Son Ralph meanwhile has fallen in love with a girl whom we never meet, largely because Bessie has forbidden her from the house. The family has one comparatively prosperous member, the small-time capitalist Uncle Morty.

The political content, though, is more in the air than on the stage; we can link the oppression of the junior Bergers to what's going on in the world outside but only one character makes explicit connections, and much of his fire has gone out. This is Jacob, Bessie's father, an Eastern European of the old radical school, who still rails against the bosses and the politicians, but whose ideals are regarded by most of the others as a joke; he divides his time between grumbling, bestowing sad admonitions on his grandchildren, and retiring to his room to play Caruso records. The cast is completed by wiseguy Moe, a wooden-legged casualty of the First World War and now a bootlegger; we gather that he once pressed his attentions on Hennie, with some success, and that he would like to press them again.

You want the good news? The play fulfils its own Biblical injunction; it is awake and, nearly 60 years on, it still sings. There are is some melodramatic twists, which we happily swallow, and there are some lyrical flights, which we don't Odets has some very strange ideas, that may be ideologically mandated, about what constitutes a happy ending, and he overwrites like mad as if to convince himself that he believes in what he's saying.

Most of the time, though, he operates through humour used as a weapon. His Jewish-American dialogue was recognized at the time to be the best that Broadway had heard, and it has hardly been bettered since. It isn't Neil Simon (too serious) and it isn't Arthur Miller (too funny) but it probably made both of them possible. Only David Mamet, with his deadly crazy flights of fancy, has gone beyond it.

You want the bad news? One wants to scream the title at the current, horribly inadequate Toronto revival. It's mounted by an almost new organization calling themselves the Co., one of whose two moving spirits is Dean Gabourie, a young director with a respectable track record. For the first few minutes, which find most of the Bergers simmering at the kitchen table, it looks as if he will know how to orchestrate the play, and in particular how to adjust its volume controls. The promise is not fulfilled. This is a tin-eared production, with one unfortunate distinction; it gives us a Jewish family that apparently has never learned to shout.

It does operate under a number of handicaps. One is the theatre; the upstairs auditorium at Equity Showcase is an echoing church- hall. (There's a basement, which most other shows use; it's no treat to sit in, but it does allow for concentration.) The acoustical problems are compounded here by a topless setting of bits and pieces. The production seems very keen on re-creating the world just outside the action; we get a soundtrack of period news and period music, and lines of washing hang from the ceiling above us; for some reason the auditorium is drenched in gloom, even when the play is not in progress. We get to see grandpa Jacob poking about his room in silhouette. None of this extraneous stuff compensates for the lack of life at the centre.

Hardly any of the actors are up to their roles. Their indvidual inadequacies rebound on one another, so that the show always looks as well as sounds wrong; people are always hanging around the stage in awkward positions, or hugging the walls, or facing off as if they know they are supposed to be angry with one another but have no idea why. Hennie and Moe play their altercations as a series of unmodulated snarls; it's impossible to believe that there could ever have been any attraction between them.

Poor downtrodden Myron spends one whole scene with his head to one side and cupped in his hand, as if he had a toothache; this might work in a boldly stylized production (though I doubt that's what the play needs) but here it just looks strange.

A few performances have their fits and starts, but the only one to come consistently to life is the rebellious Ralphie of Aaron Willis. Conceivably he's helped by playing close to his own age, but there is a current running through him. It's easy to sympathize with his sufferings at the hands of his mother; here, indeed. it's all too easy. Bessie Berger, as written, is one of the great Jewish matriarchs; a monster, perhaps, but a force of nature. She's gone through a lot to keep this family together. Danielle Bourgon plays her, irritatingly and often inaudibly, as a mere whiner. She, or her director, or both, seem deaf to irony, deaf to anger, deaf to rhythm; when Bessie rounds on her son, reminding him of their poverty, and says "I bought a new dress every week? A lover I kept?" you would swear the actress believes that the woman really did these things. The question marks she couldn't hear? There have, I think, been cuts; I have seen one other production of this play and my principal memory of it is hearing Bessie mow down all dissenting voices with the repeated scornful phrase "another county heard from!" In this performance I heard that just once and even then I barely caught it. If we cannot both respect Bessie and resent her, the play crumbles. The best that can be said for this show is that makes you want to see someone else (Soulpepper possibly, the Shaw Festival definitely) tackle the play.

Black & White Photo: Clifford Odets' Awake and Sing was the defining production of New York's Group Theater.

THE DOMINO HEART

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

Suspense in the theatre comes in many forms. A rarefied example can be found in the first scene of The Domino Heart. This new play by Matthew Edison, previously known and valued as an actor, has a cast of three, of whom two are dimly visible at the start of proceedings. The third is fully lit, and she begins talking to us, or to herself with us as a surrogate. Half an hour later she is still at it, and we, remarkably, are still paying attention. We do wonder, though, whether she will at some point get round to interacting with her companions or whether we are in for a whole evening of monologues.

As it turns out, we get the latter, with trace elements of the former. This is a play that follows its heart: metaphorically, of course, but also literally since it chronicles the transplanting of an organ from a dead body to a live one, which rejects it, with great regret, and thence to another, which accepts it, thank you very much. Structurally, the piece is a cardiovascular La Ronde, right down to a last sequence which brings us back to the character with whom we started.

It isn't her heart of course, at least not technically. It's her husband's. The lady, beautifully played by Rosemary Dunsmore, is Cara, an academic, and she was married to Peter, a writer. For a short time she betrayed him with one of her students. She confessed it and was forgiven. So at least it seemed; Peter made no secret of how much he had hurt her, and he detailed, graphically, how she had wounded his heart. (A metaphor here, of course, but only barely.) Then he died in a car crash, leaving her with guilt, despair and a young daughter.

Also with her husband's organ donor card. The designated host body belongs to Mortimer, a clergyman, elderly but -- since the part is played by David Fox -- vigorous. We meet him on the night before his operation. He is partly engaged in composing a sermon, out of a mixture of habit and enjoyment. As it happens, he has lost his faith, but he still has considerable hope and abundant charity. He too, though, has the abuse of love on his conscience; a lifelong bachelor, he once rejected a female admirer who subsequently killed herself.

We learn, having taken our leave of Mortimer, that there were surgical complications and that he died on the table. The domino heart -- is this really an exact metaphor? -- ends up inside Leo, an advertising high-flyer and part-time insider trader. He is, scarily, only 33 when he receives it. Even more alarmingly, his connections have enabled him to jump the waiting list.

Leo, of course, has been abusing his body for years, in the guise of not denying it anything. When we first see him he is, as near simultaneously as possible, sipping a cognac and smoking a cigar. An early highpoint of Raoul Bhaneja's performance, which is flashy in the best sense, comes when he changes, with visible smugness, from one silk shirt into another.

Leo has also been abusing everybody else. He admits, with what comes over as cheerless bravado, that his profession exists to cheat the public and that he is exceptionally good at it. His cynicism is spiced with self-hatred, a corrosive mixture that burns especially fiercely when he considers his relationship with his mother, a penniless immigrant who was raped at 17 (Leo was the result). In our last sight of him, he seems to be raising a gun to his mouth. It turns out to be a cigarette lighter -- a slower way to go.

So we have one character who may have caused a suicide, another who is quietly committing it, and a third who, as we finally discover, has actually made the attempt. Add them up another way: We have one person who had love but abused it, one who wanted it but refused it when offered, and one who has spent his life denying its existence. The parts don't quite interlock; even in narrative terms, Cara's life is finally affected by Mortimer but not by Leo (though, in fairness, she would like it to be). The asymmetry is frustrating, though admittedly if everything did add up neatly, we would probably be complaining of glibness.

I have a built-in resistance to plays composed of sequential soliloquies, unless they are delivered by Kristen Thomson in masks, or are as potently intercut as in Kennedy's Children years ago. But even setting my prejudices aside, the form lets the subject off the hook. In drama, as in life, love is easier said than done. Edison writes about it eloquently, sometimes movingly, but I still wanted to see his characters slugging it out, one with another, rather than telling us all about it afterward.

On the strength of these monologues, he could probably write excellent dialogue. This is his first play to be produced, and it's a hopeful debut. Nothing sounds forced, and the writing has set off some superb performances.

Dunsmore, whose demeanour suggests the control she's lost, projects a racking bitterness, which breaks down into innumerable fine gradations, and which she finally and inspiringly transcends. Fox's beaming gentleness, which usually serves to mask mountainous reserves of rage, here reveals only more gentleness, which is a treat. Bhaneja has more limited opportunities (it may be a tribute to the author's own moral fibre that this dubious character is the only one who seems to be drawn from the outside) but he takes them with great bite and crackle.

There are no blank spots in any of the performances, a tribute, at the very least, to Michael Kessler's casting, and a strong indication that his direction, though properly invisible, has been both responsive and responsible.

SWEENEY TODD

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

"Mrs Lovett," sings George Masswohl's Sweeney Todd, escaped convict and ascetic avenger, to Fiona Reid's cheerfully practical purveyor of meat pies, "how I've lived without you all these years I'll never know!" Sweeney the barber has slit the throat of a man who threatened to reveal his secret and deliver him to the law; she, desperately short of raw materials, has pointed out what a sin it would be to let a juicy, newly dead body go to waste.

Sweeney has just been balked of killing the man he was really after, the judge who once had him transported on a trumped-up charge so as to have easier access to the beauteous and virtuous Mrs. Todd, and the disappointment has sent him over the edge, into universal and murderous misanthropy. In Mrs. Lovett, who fancies him, he has found the ideal partner. The deranged visionary meets the businesslike amoral functionary. It's the combination that makes atrocities possible. In bringing them together, and showing just how and why each needs the other, Stephen Sondheim's musical touches greatness.

Sweeney Todd derives from a play by English dramatist Christopher Bond, who took the archetypal melodramatic figures of the demon barber and his culinary partner and supplied them with a back- story. It was Bond, taking a hint from The Count of Monte Cristo, who made Sweeney the victim of a judicial frame-up that he learns, on his return, to have had consequences that outrun his most feverish nightmares: The judge raped Todd's wife, who went mad and took poison. Joanna, the couple's daughter is now the judge's pent- up ward whom he, pushing his passions forward a generation, now plans to marry.

Bond's play, closely followed in Hugh Wheeler's spare musical book, springs at least one superb narrative surprise; Sondheim's music, which is virtually continuous, carries, colours and deepens the story, driving through it like the "perfect machine" to which the chorus compares the hero's compulsively turning mind.

Sweeney's obsession is of tragic proportions (there are very few musical protagonists of whom that could be said) and his murderous fury spends itself as relentlessly and as self-destructively as Macbeth's.

Morris Panych's CanStage production is imperfect but the size, emotional rather than physical, is there. Visually it lacks some of the expected Panych panache, and Ken MacDonald's set is a disappointingly conventional collection of scaffolding, steps and catwalks. Sweeney's tonsorial parlour, where much of the most crucial (and bloodiest) action takes place, is remote from us; it can, as it turns out, be trundled closer to us but the effect, when it comes, is laborious and belated.

Panych staged the wonderful mime drama The Overcoat (which is returning to Toronto as part of this year's WorldStage season prior to opening in London) and he is his own choreographer here. He keeps the commenting crowd in ceaseless motion, sometimes fussily and occasionally to the point of coyness.

Some scenes, though, he stages brilliantly. The second-act opening, in which the citizens of London, unknowing cannibals, thump their tables and demand "more hot pies," is more uproarious and more chilling than I have ever known it before. (The song is called God, That's Good.) The madhouse outbreak, which empties a covey of lunatics into a town already sufficiently crazed, is superbly done. The "city's on fire" song that accompanies it inaugurates an almost unbroken and superbly resourceful musical sequence that carries the show right through to its final scene. Here Sondheim fully justifies his own claims about music as an ideal engine of suspense. I was on the edge of my seat throughout.

Musically, the performance is very strong. Bruce Kellett's musicians play what I assume are cut-down versions of Jonathan Tunick's original orchestrations, with the vital parts intact. The opening Ballad of Sweeney Todd, with its seductive rhythm and its eerie chords that seem to have risen from the murkiest depths of the Thames, is as potent as ever, more interesting and more haunting than Mack the Knife, to which it bears a scene-setting resemblance. It recurs as narrative punctuation, and you listen avidly every time. (And as for lyrics, when you hear the early expository couplet "And what if none of their souls were saved / They went to their Maker impeccably shaved," you know you're safe with the show.)

The company does full justice to the choral writing, which is the finest in any musical in decades. Among the solos and duets, Pretty Women is as yearning a ballad as Sondheim has written, perversely lovelier for being sung in duet by the bereaved Sweeney and the arch- enemy he is about to dispatch. The crashing, discordant Epiphany carries Sweeney persuasively over the brink of madness before the famous duet A Little Priest in which he and Mrs. Lovett celebrate their new mass-catering system and spell out the ingredients. I seem to be the only person who doesn't find this one of Sondheim's best lyrics, but the rollicking waltz tune carries it, making it the outrageously effective first-act finale it is designed to be.

For all the heartless jollity, this is a moral show. It is a dark show (as opposed to a merely cynical one like Chicago, whose movie audience is swallowing it quite happily as escapist entertainment) but though it sympathizes with Sweeney, and gives him energy, it isn't on his side. The verdict on him is pronounced very simply and effectively by the simple-witted apprentice Tobias: "You shouldn't hurt people, Mr. Todd."

It's capped by another violent narrative twist (which some strange cuts make less powerful than it should be), but it isn't contradicted. The hero's passion, in approved tragic form, spends itself, leaving the title song to make a sombre summing-up -- not, as it's sometimes misinterpreted, "we are all guilty," but "psychopaths are more common than you think." Panych's production, which mercifully refrains from poking its fingers at the audience, makes the point very well.

The two lead performances are admirably balanced. Masswohl, principally a singer, keeps a brooding grip on the role, occasionally and effectively breaking into a kind of speaking-on- pitch. His face is a bland mask that only cracks at the last, posthumous moment, but this is surprisingly effective; the man is essentially unknowable. Fiona Reid makes Mrs. Lovett's spoken lines as flavourful, and funnier, than I have ever known them, radiating a merry, conscienceless practicality; she anybody's cockney mum. In what is effectively her musical debut, she does astonishingly well in some very tricky songs, rarely faltering in pitch and never in rhythm, and never missing a lyrical point. The only number that defeats her is By the Sea, Mrs. Lovett's dream of a coastal retirement, perhaps because it's the only song in the score that is a number, to be performed rather than acted. (A campy staging doesn't help her, though it's presumably meant to. )

There are especially good supporting performances from Shaun Amyot as Toby and Mary Ann McDonald as a mysterious, premonitory Beggar Woman. Damien Atkins, bent double and speaking in a kind of piping sneer, is too grotesque for the beadle but sings his parlour ballads very amusingly. Regan Thiel chirrups sweetly enough as Johanna who, after spending two acts playing the simpleton, turns out to be a determined chip off her dad's block, and Tyley Ross is very pleasant as her sailor lover. This is a self-described "musical thriller" that fills both halves of that prescription to the limit and beyond.

2003-04-01-showing-up-the-americans:
The Royal Shakespeare Companys performances in Ann Arbor, Mich., and Harlem have given our festival something to compete with

In the first two weeks of March the Royal Shakespeare Company brought three productions from England to the University of Michigan, in Ann Arbor. For two of them, Coriolanus and The Merry Wives of Windsor, this college date was originally meant to be the end of the road. However, after being enthusiastically greeted on both sides of the Atlantic, they will now be playing at the Old Vic, the historic London theatre that used to be run by Ed Mirvish and will soon be run by Kevin Spacey. The third RSC show, an adaptation of Salman Rushdies Midnight's Children, has already moved to an equally historic theatre, the Apollo in Harlem. It closed there this weekend.

When Midnight's Children opened in London in February, British critics rated it as a brave try at the impossible, and this has been the general American reaction as well. Rushdies novel, which rhymes the post-war history of India with the personal history of a child born on the precise dot of independence, is a long and crowded work that tries hard to be a masterpiece and has the impertinence to succeed. The theatrical version apparently derives from an aborted TV serial, and in that form it might have stood a chance. But when reduced to 3 1/2 hours of stage time, epic novels invariably come out scrambled -- both too long and too short.

Midnights Chldren plays New York under the auspices of Columbia University, which had also been co-sponsors of the run at Ann Arbor. The two Shakespeares were solely the responsibility of the University of Michigan itself, and in particular of its Music Society, which every two years hosts a campus residency by the RSC, discussions, tutorials, and lectures as well as performances. Ann Arbor is one of the American towns closest to Canada, and not just geographically. Very much dominated by its university, it feels like a lived-in place, rather than a collection of strip malls. It is also practically a dormitory town for our own Stratford Festival.

One wishes that there were a Canadian university as enterprising, as well-equipped (Ann Arbor's Power Center for the Performing Arts, where the shows were housed, is of amphitheatre proportions) and -- most of all -- as richly endowed. Failing that, it would have been nice if one of our other theatre organizations could have picked up on the RSC's presence in the neighbourhood and whisked them over the border. In fact, Don Shipley, the artistic director of Torontos WorldStage, which starts its 2003 season next week, had entertained hopes of doing just that. But the dates didnt match, and as Shipley himself says, discussion for future seasons is -- in the non- university sense -- academic; with du Maurier's name-sponsorship forcibly withdrawn, it seems certain this year's WorldStage will be the last.

Friends of mine at Ann Arbor, enthusing over Coriolanus and The Merry Wives, and especially over the claritry and vitality whith which the actors delivered the texts, said, but of course, you take that for granted. I think they were being kind: not in regard to these two shows but to the RSCs work in general. There was a time in the 1960s, and another time in the 70s, when the RSC set the standard for Shakesperean production around the world. The record since has been erratic. One can't get over-confident on the strength of a couple of shows, but these two were very encouraging -- much superior, in terms of acting consistency and overall liveliness, to the company's London season of rare Renaissance plays, which was certainly adventurous but in which the enterprise outstripped the execution.

It may be wrong to speak of the RSC as a company; at any given moment it is likely to be several companies, and even in Ann Arbor there were two entirely separate groups of actors -- one for Shakespeare and one for Rushdie. This diversity, as Ive complained before, can breed confusion, both artistic and logistic; but it also gives the chance for a particular team to strike out excitingly on its own. There are times when it can be a positive advantage for the left hand not to know what the right hand is doing.

The two Shakespeares,like the Jacobean quintet, had started their lives at the intimate Swan Theatre in Stratford-on-Avon, but they were far more successfully blown up for a larger space. This was especially true of Coriolanus, a magnificent play set early in the history of Republican Rome, which here looked panoramic. The play depicts an aristocratic caste bred in a cult of war, of which the central character, trained by a bellicose mother, is the most enthusiastic adherent. Searching for a recognizable equivalent, David Farr, the director, came up with Japanese samurai. I dont know that it helps either the audience or the play to subsitute one remote culture for another; one female character tip-toed daintily about like a minor figure from The Mikado, and even in the battle scenes -- the most detailed and elaborate in Shakespeare -- the stylization got in the way; it was hard to follow what was going on. Much of the time, though, the trappings could be tuned out. My own hunch is that Shakespeare and company, taking the verse form for granted, thought that they were writing realistically. Certainly this is true of Coriolanus, in which the language is extraordinarily supple and forceful; colloquial humanity asserts itself through an apparently formal, structured medium, and the thrill lies in the tension between the two. The central scenes, in which a newly emergent populace asserts its will against the hero, and succeeds in getting him banished, convey a sense of a society on the move, history in motion, that's almost unmatched in drama. It's hard to realize that potential on stage (if only because, in these straitened times, there never seem to be enough bodies available) but this production, after some faltering, brought it off.

Greg Hicks, who plays the title role, is pretty much unknown outside the English theatre, but is a star within it. He has been with the RSC, on and off, since the 1970s and apparently was greatly surprised to be asked, at his time of life, to play a hero whose arch-enemy describes him as a "boy of tears." Hicks, though, is one of those ageless actors, graceful and with a steel-tipped, light- baritone voice in superb control of the plays tirades. When Coriolanus, whose shyness matches his arrogance, is obliged to put on the robe of humility and beg the peoples votes for the consulship, he finds the process impossible to take seriously; but he cannot laugh it off, and Hicks shows us exactly how his incredulity hardens into rage, and why that should lead him to march on Rome at the head of an alien army. He has a core almost of steel; not quite though and, when his mother, wife and son come to plead with him to spare the city, he is unable to refuse them.

This is the only production I have seen in which his boy (who has only three grudging lines in which to show himself a chip off the old block) makes the first visible dent in his father's armour. It is left to the matriarch Volumnia to drive the blade home, and drive it she does. Alison Fiske, who makes her a wonderfully unyielding Tory matron, is an actress I have admired since the '60s, when I saw her at the Open Air Theatre, Regents Park, playing Jessica in The Merchant of Venice with a burnished warmth that practically jerked me out of my deck chair. Fiske is one performer here who, at the very end, benefits from the kabuki treatment. She returns to Rome, knowing that in saving her city she has sacrificed her son. She has no lines, but the production permits her a tremendous silent scream.

The Merry Wives of Windsor, at the other end of Shakespeares range and his only play set firmly in his own time, is also transplanted: to the late 1940s, with small-town post-war England beginning tentatively to feel its oats. This very relaxed production, directed by Rachel Kavanaugh, is not the most hilarious Merry Wives I have seen, but its laughs are warm and honest, and leave you feeling good. The end-of-play reconciliation is a small epiphany. Ford (Tom Mannion), the cuckold in his own imagination, misses out on the virtuoso displays of farcial self-torment with which most actors of the role bring down the house; but I did believe, more firmly than I usually do, that he was jealous and that it hurt.

There is a genial, gentlemanly Falstaff by Richard Cordery, who had shone in Coriolanus as a dangerously suave Menenius, the glad- handing patrician posing as the people's friend; as Sir John his enforced indignities are accentuated by his being as tall by nature as he is round by padding. His followers, too, usually nonentities, become recognisable saloon-bar types -- "spivs," people have called them in those dear old black-market days -- and the lovesick Master Slender comes similarly to life as a tongue-tied county booby. The wives themselves (Lucy Tregear and Claire Carrie) are very pleasant plotters, with enough contrast to keep us interested. Hicks turns up as a firebrand French spluttering with a bloodlustn (not all that unlike Coriolanus, really) and Fiske is his housekeeper -- or, in this dispensation, his charlady -- Mistress Quickly; this character's running joke is her unstoppable garrulity, and she finds a rhythm for it that seems absolutely right for both periods.

For the first time in years I felt, not that British Shakespeare productions had things to teach the Canadian models, but that they were giving us, as they should, something to compete with. Both these shows have young directors. One hopes that they will be an integral part of the RSCs new regime, and that a once-great company will be great again.
