THE BLUES

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

Hrant Alianak, the veteran dramatist and director, is currently bringing off a grand slam at Theatre Passe Muraille. Upstairs in the Backspace (confusing, I know, but that's how it is), there is a remount of The Walls of Africa, his excellent, and excellently acted, play from last season. On the main stage downstairs, we have The Blues.

The Blues is also a revival, though from a more remote time. It was first staged in 1976, and its reappearance now is very encouraging; it shows how much Alianak has improved as a playwright. It also holds out some hope the Canadian theatre may have grown up a bit; like most of the plays that have been resurrected from the supposed golden age, it suggests that in the '70s it was such an exciting novelty for Canadians to be writing plays and getting them on that each new arrival was greeted as an instant classic. Something of that attitude still persists, but not as strongly; and the plays, or some of them, have got better.

The Blues, set in a New York bar in the early '50s, is a nostalgia-trip even as written. For a brief time we can have fun just drinking it in; Steve Lucas has designed another impeccably evocative set, and there's a Billie Holiday record playing. In fact we get to hear a lot of Holiday; at least two more of her songs are piped in during the proceedings, and one of the play's four characters, a tart called Ripples who's been jilted by her abusive protector, identifies strongly. As Aldo the barman remarks, Ripples' conversation is peppered with titles from Billie's repertoire. (She's lost her old flame -- or he's changed -- so she's got a right to sing the blues, and now she covers the waterfront, with no detour ahead, at least until the real thing comes along.)

Not all the play's literary borrowings are as frankly acknowledged as its Holiday snaps. A Salvation Army lass, name of Virginia (yes, there are jokes) wanders into Aldo's bar and tries to convert him to temperance, and he seduces her after spiking her milk: a sequence of events unlikely, except by its sheer barefacedness, to surprise anyone who has ever seen Guys and Dolls. Having fallen heavily for Virginia, Aldo says that what he sees in other women drunk, he sees in her sober, and you wonder if he knows he is reproducing, verbatim, the opening of Kenneth Tynan's classic essay on Greta Garbo. The remaining character is Tyrone, who writes hardboiled fiction; the play itself, since we hear him doing the occasional narrative voice-over, may be one of his stories, but the Alice-in-Wonderland point is not pursued. Tyrone has the enviable ability to type out his stuff in the bar, very fast, and to read it aloud even as he does so.

One of the sentences he lays on us -- "this is a story about passion, bloodshed, desire and death: all the things in fact that make life worth living" -- shows him to be a plagiarist of prophetic gifts, since it's the opening statement of the musical Irma la Douce, whose English version didn't come along until 1958. Still, Tyrone is the best reason for seeing the play, or at least Eric Peterson's playing of him is. Peterson, nailing down his recent return to grace in Boy Gets Girl, starts his performance by tossing his fedora at the hat stand. it lands perfectly, to his amazement and -- to judge from the look that creeps into his eyes -- terror. Later on, he has two long, bravura speeches, magnificently delivered. The first is a catalogue of imagined carnal delights, towards the end of which the actor, still without pausing for breath, mounts the bar and struts along it, Cagney-fashion. The second, less well-written but just as irresistibly spoken, this time with punctuation, is about seeing Citizen Kane and not getting it the first time but having it haunt your memory and having to go back for a second and more rewarding look. I can't see what it's doing there except passing the time, but like its predecessor it brings down the house as if it were an especially spectacular musical number, which in a way it is.

All the characters get to do at least one aria, with the neat exception of David Bolt's stoical Aldo; he does at one point embark on his life-story, but the others shush him before he has completed a sentence. He's forgotten that the bartender's role is to listen to everyone else's troubles while keeping quiet about his own. The defrocked Virginia greets her fall by fantasizing, again with very few pauses, about a future career submitting to every sexual degradation she can conjure up at such short notice; Janet Burke, emphatically wide-eyed, gives the speech amusingly, though it's hard not to apply to it the best line in the play that Aldo, in a different context, delivers to Tyrone: "Tyrone, you're showing me a side of yourself that I don't particularly want to see." I have already mentioned Ripples' name-that-tune recollections: Linda Griffiths puts them over as a mixture of self-pity and bad temper, but that may well be how they're written.

None of these characters interact, or even come to life. It's as if pop-art archetypes were guaranteed to be touching or hilarious with no extra effort, and that all an author had to do was assemble the cliches. The spectators, meanwhile, can congratulate themselves on spotting the references; this, as you will have gathered, is something for which I'm a sucker , but I was bored nonetheless. It's amazing that a writer as demonstrably talented as Alianak should ever have come up with such a piece of aimless camp, and it passes belief that critics across the country should ever have acclaimed it. (It was praised for its satire. Of what?) Crazy I call them.

Black & White Photo: David Kinsman / David Bolt, left, and Eric Peterson in Hrank Alianak's campy barroom effort The Blues.

THE NOTEBOOK

duMaurier Theatre Centre, Toronto

Toronto's WorldStage, which without its duMaurier sponsorship is in imminent danger of being puffed out, seems at least to be going out in style. The fine opening production of its maybe-last season hails from Belgium, though of its four actors, one is Polish and another -- the only woman -- is of Scots parentage, and sounds it. It is based on a novel, also Polish, and is performed, at least for this gig, in English. The cast are responsible for the adaptation and they must also have directed themselves, since no one else is credited as having done it. The spare, stylish and disciplined show they have come up with suggests directors may be a dispensable species.

The story is set in an unnamed country during an unnamed war. It's clear, though, that the author, Agota Kristof, was writing about her own Poland and that the war is the Second World one. We have occupiers who are Germans, supposed liberators who are Russians (and whose first action after conquest is to hang up pictures of their leader and forbid all criticism) and a brutally abused minority who are all too clearly Jews. At the centre of the play are twin boys, whose mother is apparently off to do a spot of collaborating, and who wants to leave them in a border town in the care of her own mother, known locally as the Witch. The grandmother's response to her daughter's request is typically barbed ("For 10 years you didn't give me a thought. You never came, you never wrote") but she takes the boys in, threatening to "put them to work." What she actually does is neglect them, making them sleep on a bench in the kitchen, barely feeding or clothing them, and leaving them unwashed. They don't seem to mind.

In fact, they become chillingly self-reliant. They toughen themselves by exchanging blows and insults; this imperviousness to physical or mental pain comes in very useful later. They also become their own home-schoolers, with the help of a Bible and a dictionary. These endow them with a formality of diction (they scour the dictionary for "synonyms and antonyms") that the neighbouring adults find deeply disconcerting. They explore the forest. They become adepts of the black market, and supplement their income by performing conjuring tricks in cafes. They acquire a kind of sex education, supplied in various ways by the handicapped girl next door, by the housekeeper of the local priest and her soldier-lover, and by the occupying officer who's been billeted with their grandma. They observe the Jews being marched out of town to their deaths. They learn the techniques and the dangers of crossing the national frontier. They write down all their experiences and observations in a notebook, and their narrative gives the play its frame.

They are, to put it mildly, dispassionate. They do seem capable of what might be called kindness. For example, having discovered that the priest has been touching up their young neighbour, they ask him for money in order that they may pass it on to the girl and her ailing mother. ("Have you any idea what you're doing?" he asks. "Yes, sir," they reply. "We're blackmailing you.") They do not seem capable of love, hate and fear. They come to prefer the bracing indifference of their grandmother to the clinging affection of their mother. The extent of both their practicality and their amorality is revealed when they finally have dealings with their father, formerly a POW, now a refugee.

Presumably the twins are meant as studies in the distorting effects of war on childhood. There could hardly be a timelier subject, and it certainly resonates. We recognize the spectacle of children old before their time but immature forever. It's ambiguous, though. These are very special cases, or -- since they are psychologically if not physically identical -- one special case times two. Not every evacuee can have undergone experiences so consistently brutish, or have reacted by going to such extremes of self-regimentation. At times we seem to be witnessing the convergence of two recognizable Central European traditions. One is the fable of the wild child in a hostile landscape. The other is satire of a rigid educational system that's all facts and no feelings. It's a rich mix, but the more poetically compelling the piece becomes, the less you feel like generalizing from it.

By "poetically compelling" I don't just mean that it's written in verse, or at least in brief, unmodulated sentences that are laid out in a line apiece. This does give it a hard, blow-of-the-fist sort of quality, of the kind that's to be expected when inhuman events are relayed in the levellest of tones. But the impact resides more in the visual style, which is swift and almost totally unencumbered by furniture, and in the sense that the actors, having worked up the text and the staging themselves, are making you a present of the results.

As the brothers, Gunther Lesage and Robby Cleiren go through the entire play in shorts and singlets, and with visible bulges in their pants; they are implacable in their innocence. All the other roles are shared, with a fine disregard of gender, between Ryszard Turbiasz, whose thick voice, ranging between a roar and a whine, hits an especially happy medium as the wavering priest, and Carly Wijs, the Scots lady, who when playing the predatory maid adds a dash of sensuality, even of warmth, though the latter quality is turned abruptly off.

There is a fair amount of humour in the play, not quite all of it black. The Notebook, though more or less complete in itself, is only the first half of the story. The second is called The Proof and is being given at alternating performances. I look forward to catching up with it, since the present instalment has left me asking a bunch of questions, of which the simplest -- though by no means the least urgent -- is, what happened next?

Black & White Photo: Raymond Mallentjer / FROM LEFT: Performers Robby Cleiren, Carly Wijs, Gunther Lesage and Ryszard Turbiasz adapted this spare, stylish and disciplined show for the stage.

THE PROOF

duMaurier Theatre Centre

- - -

You've heard about the terrifying telegram: the one that read simply "ignore previous telegram" when there had been no previous telegram. The two linked productions, brought to World Stage by the Belgian company De Onderneming, are something like that, though from a critic's point of view maybe even scarier. In this case, there has been a previous telegram but, memory being what it is, it's impossible to ignore. You're confused already.

Let me try to explain. The Notebook, which I reviewed on Thursday, and its sequel The Proof, are based on a trilogy of novels by Agota Kristof, who is Hungarian and not, as I previously and carelessly assumed, Polish. The Notebook presents the experiences of twin boys scrambling for survival in an unnamed but guessable Central European country during the Second World War; it takes its title from a journal supposed to have been kept by the pair of them. At the end of the play, after the country has passed from Nazi occupation to Communist dictatorship, one of the brothers, now aged fifteen, escapes across the border. The Proof tells what happens to him afterwards. And almost the first thing we learn is that nearly everything that's in the notebook (and therefore in The Notebook) was a lie. For a start, the two brothers we thought we saw were only one, or at least one and a fantasy companion. These means that nearly everything I wrote in my review was a lie, too. I fell right in.

The Notebook was about not letting anything take you by surprise; it was linear and Brechtian, complete with captions. (Many of these on the first night failed to appear. I'm not sure whether this was an accident, or the production's own jokey little tip-off as to what was in store.) The Proof, by contrast, is dark-cornered and full of surprises; they are relentless, disorienting and finally very moving. It's impossible to discuss either play without giving stuff away, and if you plan to see them, which I strongly recommend, you might do better not to read this review until afterwards. Bravo, the Internet.

In The Notebook, none of the characters were named. In The Proof, nearly all of them are. We discover that the boy who crossed the border was called Lucas; the brother whom everybody tells him he imagined was named Claus. We start by getting a look at Lucas's life before he escaped; one seedier, though less primitive, then the story that was told before. He was more engaged with the community around him, but essentially even lonelier. (Before, he said that the woman under whose roof he lived, now dead, was his grandmother. She wasn't.)

Twenty-five years later, with international tensions reduced, Lucas returns to his homeland. He says he is looking for his brother Claus. What's more, though again nobody will believe it, he finds him. The two brothers had never shared an evacuee existence; Lucas had made that up to assuage an unbearable loneliness. They had been separated at four years old, when their parents' marriage broke bloodily up. (I doubt if papa and mama did their twin sons any favours by giving them anagrammatic names,either). Claus's life, though more comfortable than Lucas's, has been every bit as unhappy; maybe more so.

Reviewing The Notebook, I tried hard to see the twins' plight as emblematic of the fate of children in times of war. I was wasting my time. War obviously doesn't help, but it turns out to be only the backdrop to an agony that could happen anytime, anywhere. Nor do I take much stock in the idea that the boys are symbols of a divided Europe, even if it's what the author herself thinks. As surely as Oedipus, Claus and Lucas are pursued through their lives by childhood trauma, aggravated by adult cruelty and folly, their own included. (The young orphaned Lucas in an institution is a very nasty piece of work; Claus is a coward.) It may not quite be tragedy, but it's as close to it as our age is likely to get, and it's presented with unflinching, and ungloating, honesty. Claus believes Lucas's story, but he cannot bear to admit it, and the last part of the story shows us why.

In the end, despite the false trails and changes of front (gleefully aggravated here by having a company of four cover all the parts), it all adds up. Well, nearly all; there are still some puzzles and ambiguities, including the minor one of why we're constantly told that Lucas plays the harmonica, when we actually see him playing the accordion.But I don't believe that the play's ultimate goal is mystification, and I wouldn't have much time for it if it were. The story that emerges by the end is the one we're meant to believe. Anyway, I'm sticking to it.

Underrunning the narrative is the idea of storytelling itself, as a device for validating a life. As somebody says, rather extravagantly, "He who writes nothing is lost/He has merely passed through life without leaving a trace." And in Eastern Europe, whose soul so long resided in banned books, that may not be altogether a joke. Lucas writes his notebook, though he apparently pieced it together very quickly and long after the events it purports to depict. Claus puts his experiences into poems which are described, unsurprisingly, as "definitely not amusing" but powerful, and are published semi-anonymously. He writes them under the unsympathetic eye of his mother, who keeps comparing him unflatteringly to his long-lost brother. And this theme must account for an early, grimly funny digression about a would-be writer who falls apart when his loving but overpowering sister actually gives the opportunity to write . (He's also a smoker who would give it up except that, being an alcoholic, he doesn't have the will power.) There's a strong whiff of incest in all the story-lines, as indeed there was in The Notebook, though it seems less taken for granted in town than in the country

As in The Notebook, the actors have made their own adaptation, and perform, superbly, under their own joint direction. The mood though has changed. The Notebook was light, a perverse pastoral; The Proof is heavier, more detailed, more citified. The same actors play the brothers, Gunther Lesage as lanky Lucas and Robby Cleiren as chubby Claus, but where the previous style was about denying feeling, this is about showing it; even repression here is a kind of demonstration. Ryszard Turbiasz supplies a balancing slyness, and can be very funny. Carly Wijs exchanges the flirtatious Scots of her earlier roles for sardonic London. Your last chance of catching both plays is today, and you should take it. They're wonderful.

Black & White Photo: Courtesy De Onderneming / Robby Cleiren, left, and Gunther Lesage reprise their roles (sort of) from The Notebook in its sequel, The Proof.

GLENGARRY GLEN ROSS

Premiere Dance Theatre, Toronto

A WOMAN IN WAITING

York Quay Studio Theatre, Toronto

- - -

I doubt whether fewer cigarettes will be smoked in Toronto in future merely because the duMaurier name, and with it the duMaurier sponsorship, have been forcibly removed from the World Stage festival. I doubt if many duMaurier customers will even change their brand loyalty. Apparently the state may continue, without hypocrisy, to profit from the sale of tobacco, while forbidding valuable cultural institutions to do so. And one of the most valuable will probably cease to exist. Somebody somewhere must be feeling very virtuous.

Meanwhile, for this year at least, the World Stage show goes on. It even goes on when one of its principal actors has to bail out. Last Wednesday, the first night of David Mamet's Glengarry Glen Ross, from Chicago's Steppenwolf company, was cancelled when one of the cast -- the lead, in so far as this paragon of ensemble plays has one -- had to return home for family reasons. Another Steppenwolf actor, Rick Snyder, was brought in next day to replace him. Steeped in the style but not in the role, he had to carry a script. By Sunday afternoon, when I saw the show, he was in flawless command of the text -- the immaculate succession of starts, stops, hesitations, overlappings and aggressive-defensive obscenities that make Mamet at his best both the supreme stylist and the most cunning naturalist among living playwrights -- but was physically reined- in. It was like seeing what would obviously be a fine performance, with a week still to go before opening night.

Glengarry is the third great U.S. play about that fundamental national figure, the licensed huckster. It completes the trilogy that was begun by Eugene O'Neill's The Iceman Cometh and whose centrepiece, obviously, is Arthur Miller's Death of a Salesman. Indeed, Mamet's whole play might be considered as both an extension and a refinement of a crucial scene in Miller's: the one in which Willy Loman, down on his luck, asks his boss for a break and winds up fired. Mamet's piece gives us four front-line sellers whose business is persuading the unwary to buy what we may safely assume to be worthless properties in Florida. Shelley Levene (a.k.a. the Machine, the Snyder character) was once the champ of them all, and is now the most desperate. But all of them both despise and depend on their office manager (who in turn depends on the unseen bosses above him, as they do on the even more shadowy figure above them).

Like Willy Loman, they all --even the younger, slicked-down hot- shot whose figures should win him a Cadillac -- keep harking back to old heroic days, when men were men and went out and found their own suckers -- sorry, clients -- without needing some jumped-up office boy to point them in the right direction.

A surprising amount of commentary on the play seems prepared to take them at their own valuation: This despite Mamet's own warning that we should never trust the things that people say; that language invariably lies for its own advantage, and the speakers' real feelings can only be glimpsed when they shut up. (Some silent despair at the end of this play makes the point very graphically.) The old order may be giving way to the new, and the new may be more soulless, but there still seems little to choose between them. These guys are in the business of cheating the gullible, and they always were. And however they may talk about old-school loyalties, they will cheat on one another as readily as they will on anyone else. We know why they do it; we don't meet their families as we did the Lomans, but we hear just enough to appreciate the pressures. We can even feel sorry for them.

But the most sympathetic character in the play is, fittingly, the least voluble: A terrified buyer, torn between fear of his wife and a touching loyalty to the man who wants to fleece him. He is beautifully played here by Peter Burns.

Oddly enough, this quintessentially American play was first produced, in 1983, by the National Theatre of Great Britain, which had earned Mamet's trust with its production of his earlier American Buffalo. Steppenwolf, though, has the U.S. patent on the play; and Amy Burton's new production, both aurally and visually perfect, shows why.

It has two settings. One is a strip-mall Chinese restaurant, where you can just about taste the MSG from looking; this is where the characters gather in pairs to bitch, scheme and do business. The other is the office itself, the morning after a break-in; someone has stolen the all-important client list. Seeing the place spectacularly trashed, we also register how it must have looked before, and the combination is explosively funny.

The cast includes David Pasquesi as the star shark with a bewitchingly literate line of patter, Matt DeCaro, Tracy Letts and Alan Wider, and there is no fault in any of them. Each, by the way, is a completely different physical and emotional type to his counterpart in the equally fine and believable English production, which argues a great richness in the play. Everyone's timing is a delight. Words may be as untrustworthy as Mamet says they are, but they can still give great joy; in this play, and in this production, every one of them counts.

- - -

The festival's substantial South African component began with A Woman in Waiting, conceived and written by Yael Farber and Thembi Mtshali. It's an autobiographical one-woman show, a monologue with some music, for Mtshali, a commanding and attractive performer who is in her fifties and who was a lead player in Ipi Tombi, the black African musical that went round the world. She is also a national TV star. Once though, she was a Durban live-in domestic,with no apparent future.

The cruelties of apartheid predictably give the show its greatest impact, hitting harder for coming after a few years of happily sheltered childhood. Perhaps the most moving part tells of the bonds that she could not help forming with the white babies she looked after, while not seeing her own child for a week at a time. (She prayed that, at least, none of her charges would grow up to be a policeman, brutalizing blacks.) She got her break when the daughter of one of her employers heard her singing in the kitchen, and insisted she audition for a show. It's truer than usual to say that the rest is history, and a lot happier than history usually is. Critics in other countries have complained that she slides over some important matters and that she devotes too much time to celebrating her own success. I can agree with the first complaint but not with the second. It seems to me she's earned the right.

TAMARA

Graydon Hall Manor, Toronto

World Stage's Canadian content section kicks off with a revival of Tamara: officially a play by John Krizanc, but better known as the "legendary environmental theatre event" (the press release's precisely accurate description) that effectively launched Richard Rose's Necessary Angel company in 1981. Rose has now moved on to become director of the Tarragon, so this is his full-circle farewell.

As everyone knows, the show unfolds before a limited audience in a stately house: all over it, since the actors -- 10 of them -- keep splitting up, moving off into different rooms in different combinations, and we can decide which of them to follow. We become - - not our own dramatists, exactly, since the script has been written and we can't amend it -- but our own story editors. And of course, with the action multiplying amoebically, however we choose, we miss a lot. At the same time, we maintain the perverse belief that the bits we saw were the most important ones.

The effect, however close we may get to the actors, is not to make the event more real but to make it more artificial. For a start, the house is standing in for the Italian mansion of Gabriele d'Annunzio, poet and icon, in 1927. A possible but unpredictable Fascist, d'Annunzio is being wooed by Mussolini to give legitimacy to his regime. On this particular night, d'Annunzio awaits a visit from the Polish artist Tamara de Lempicka, who is going to paint him and whom he wants to seduce. (Given the slippery political climate, a possible theme, for her picture or for the play itself, might be D'Annunzio Denounced.) Others in residence are d'Annunzio's housekeeper, a pianist who is also his former mistress, an aspiring ballerina who wants his patronage, and an all-purpose male artist. There is also a brutally mannered policeman, keeping tabs for Il Duce. Below stairs, sometimes literally, are a valet, a chauffeur and a maid. Both echelons may contain spies, probably Communists. Two separate characters turn out to be Jewish ex-gondoliers.

It's a magnificent gimmick. It's impossible not to be awed by the production's logistics, by its sumptuous layout, and by its sheer synchronicity. It's impossible, too, not to be tantalized by the thought of what you might be missing (not to mention the screams, gunshots and door-slams that always seem to be going on somewhere else, and the vintage Rolls in waiting at the front door) and to at least consider coming again and making other choices.

It's seldom given to an audience to stand in a kitchen and watch, at close quarters, an actor preparing and then eating a frittata, as John Gilbert's d'Annunzio does here. After he'd performed this feat, I rather drifted away from the Commandante (as everybody calls him), so, come the end of the piece, I was unsure what the upshot of his story was, or why he was thought to be so important. I realized I had seen even less of the title figure; indeed, I wondered whether her status was some kind of joke on the theme of hope and meaning deferred. (Tamara and Tamara and Tamara.) But no, I'm sure she must have been existing like mad, even when out of my sight. On the other hand, I remember spending more time with them when, as a tourist, I saw the original production, and I didn't find them all that compelling even then. I do recall that the actor playing d'Annunzio was a lot closer to the dwarfish historical figure than is the bluff, upstanding Gilbert, but neither player was able to bring him to life

This time, while aiming to spread my favours as equally as possible, I ended up spending most time in the company of Victor Ertmannis' Fascist cop, and of Ellen Dubin as the kind of maid whom everybody ought to have and whom most, as far as I could tell, had. There was much plotting and counter-plotting going on here, and a lot of angry or ironic statements about the strange people whom politics can, figuratively or otherwise, put you in bed with. Yes, some surprising or just misguided people supported Fascism. But this isn't news, and the play doesn't make it new.

When the show was first done, Rose and Krizanc announced that they were commenting on Fascism by reducing the element of Fascism in the theatrical experience itself -- i.e., by giving the audience some choice. However, all of Rose's subsequent productions that I've seen have had a perfectly orthodox relationship between show and audience, so either he's dropped this dubious theory or he's surrendered to Fascism himself. Krizanc, since writing Tamara, has not had a very obtrusive theatrical career, but he has written for film and television, in both of which, of course, the choosing is done by the camera.

His writing here is melodramatic going on portentous. "I know the difference between an artist and a whore," says d'Annunzio. "A whore has better morals." The ballerina, who has exhibited racist tendencies, is told: "You will never be a modern dancer; you can move, but you're not free." The style, or lack of it, affects the acting. The performers, with a couple of exceptions, are very assured, but they're mostly engaged in striking attitudes. This kind of intimate exposure is supposed, theoretically, to lead to acting of rare truthfulness (it did a couple of years ago in Paula and Karl), but here it's up-close and impersonal.

Halfway through, and again at the end, the valet brings us all back together to inquire solicitously as to how we're getting on. At such moments, the show takes on a strong resemblance to Mysteriously Yours, the whodunit dinner theatre, which is every bit as interactive and usually better written. You get a full meal, too, though Tamara does offer wine, both preparatory and dessert, coffee and cake. I had fond memories of that cake from the '81 production; in fact, I thought it was the artistic highlight, not only of the production but of the entire one-time-only Toronto Theatre festival, of which it formed a part. In the intervening years, the standard of the patisserie has gone down but the performance level has gone up. That's true not only of Tamara but of the Canadian theatre in general. You have to hand it to Tamara -- it must be the most successful play nobody has ever seen.

RICE BOY

Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

Sunil Kuruvilla is a young Canadian writer of Indian descent. He studied at the Yale Drama School, and his plays have been done in the United States before being seen here -- circumstances that have made him a thing of wonder in Canadian theatrical circles. That may be unfair, not least to him. On the evidence of last season's Fighting Words and now of Rice Boy, he is one promising local playwright among several.

The strengths of Rice Boy are its tenderness and its occasional wit. Its weakness is its fragile, overloaded construction. It's about a boy in a tree. Tommy is a 12-year-old from Kitchener whose parents have periodically taken him on trips back to their relatives in India. On one of these, his mother drowned; his father has never recovered from the loss. That's in the play's past. Much of its present is devoted to a more recent visit. This throws Tommy into contact with his slightly older cousin Tina, who has crippled legs and is about to be given away in an arranged marriage. The marriage of Tina's own parents has been in a state of suspended animation ever since her father discovered his wife's infidelity with the local doctor. The household, whose women are considerably stronger than its men, is completed by a grandmother and a serving girl; the latter is the former wife of a fish-peddler who still comes to call, for professional and other reasons. This last thwarted relationship is probably one more than the play can take.

These Indian scenes are framed by, and interspersed with, scenes in Canada. In India, Tommy would climb to get a view of the neighbouring town, and would report on it to Tina, whose condition prevented her from leaving the house. Back home, Tommy still spends time aloft -- partly in memory of Tina, with whom he fell into a kind of love, and partly, it seems, scanning the horizon for some place in which he might belong. Both as a Canadian in India and as an Indian in Canada he feels displaced. (His father, a math professor in India and a pizza worker here, feels the same but articulates it less keenly.) Tommy goes so far, having read the description of a missing boy on a milk carton, to offer himself as a substitute to the bereaved father, a meter reader in St. Jacob's, Ont. It works for both of them, for about a day. It's a surprisingly touching scene, of a kind one has never seen before.

This is a play of hopes and regrets -- Tommy's hopes, most everyone else's regrets -- much of them over lost or inaccessible partners. Tina is caught in the middle, with a family able to build up her dreams and slap them down again within a single sentence. (Her mother, preparing her for marriage, says, "Eventually you will be unhappy but not in the beginning.")

The word "Chekhovian" comes to mind, and with it the reminder that the evanescent feelings in Chekhov's plays are encased in symphonic structures, interweaving themes and characters within solid, act-length scenes. Kuruvilla, like most current dramatists, writes in short breaths. His brief scenes do have a theatrical identity. They don't look, as so often happens, like displaced fragments from a film or TV script. But knitting them together is a challenge, especially with the double time-scheme added in, and Micheline Chevrier's production doesn't meet it. The overall pace is limp. One scene baldly stops, another as baldly starts, when one wants them to melt into one another.

Some end on a confrontational note that may be intended as defiance but comes over merely as petulance. This is especially the case with Tommy himself. In the hands of Zaib Shaikh, an actor too old in years and too young in technique, he remains a literary construct. So do most of the others: Granny, played by 90-year-old Zohra Segal, is more impressive as a presence than as a characterization. Sanjay Talwar as the cuckolded Uncle reiterates his mastery of the mild and the accident-prone. In one of the play's best scenes, he and his brother, Tommy's father, return drunk and gloomy from a meeting with Tina's future spouse and in-laws, trying intently to persuade themselves that all will be for the best: so intently that they fail to notice Tommy, following behind them, has fallen down a well. When they do discover it, they take it in their stride, even if he's failed to. For them, it seems to be an everyday occurrence.

The play abounds in telling patches of local colour, but they play as isolated effects. We learn, for example, that Indian television companies trawl the city streets and, having found the prettiest girl, make her newsreader for a day. Or, to be more exact, for a half-hour. It seems to be the summit of Tina's ambition. Imali Perera plays her attractively, capturing all the impatience, physical and emotional, of a girl apparently doomed to the opposite. She is the most compelling figure in the play, but she still gets lost in the shuffle. Her journey ends in a question mark, but the pressure is so low that it seems more like a comma.

Black & White Photo: Lucas Oleniuk / Imali Perera (left) as Tina and Zohra Segal as Granny in playwright Sunil Kuruvilla's tale of hopes and regrets.

YIIMIMANGALISO: THE MYSTERIES

Elgin Theatre, Toronto

- - -

OUTLYING ISLANDS

du Maurier Theatre Centre, Toronto

- - -

In the beginning is God, dressed in a sarong of many colours. He announces his identity, plus the creation of the world, in the short, clipped verse lines characteristic of the English medieval mystery plays, from one of which his lines are in fact taken. A chorus of angels hails him in liturgical Latin. Then the beat to which they're singing gets syncopated, and they break out into an explosion of song and dance as wild and joyous as you are likely to encounter on any stage. Within its opening five minutes, and in three separate modes, Yiimimangaliso: The Mysteries has declared itself, and the hand it shows is a dazzler.

The production is the brainchild of Mark Dornford-May and Charles Hazlewood, respectively the director and conductor of the Broomhill Opera, which operates out of Wilton's Music Hall in Londons East End. They were invited to stage an opera in Durban, South Africa, and, while there, conceived the idea of a show that would utilize the talents and traditions of the countrys township choirs. When they held auditions, they were overwhelmed with applicants eager not so much to get on to the stage as to get a job. They emerged with a show that has gone round the world.

It's a multiple, post-apartheid example of the story that was told to us earlier in this World Stage season by A Woman in Waiting, and was unforgettably exemplified, long before that, by the international progress of John Kani and Winston Ntshona in Athol Fugard's plays. South Africa may not send much theatre to the world, but when it does it catches fire.

This show is a superb matching of talent to material. There are four sets of mystery plays extant, including the Chester cycle, which this production has taken as its source. They were performed, and presumably written, by the tradesmens guilds of the time as a user-friendly method of retelling Bible stories. In other words, they are amateur shows. There have been some fine professional revivals of them, but all have suffered from some degree of self- consciousness. The performers here were technically amateurs when they started out, and they recast the plays according to their own talents, personalities and traditions, which is what the originals must have done. They also share their predecessors bent for creative anachronism. It's a safe bet that local stars were born on the city streets of the 14th and 15th centuries, and their performances might well have taken on the international circuit, had such a thing existed.

Only a minority of the lines come to us here in Middle English. The rest are in a variety of African tongues, including Zulu, Xhosa and Afrikaans; a line spoken in one language is quite likely to be answered in another, and all are regularly reinforced and transfigured by music. Actors double as musicians, playing mainly on a variety of pots and pans.

The story proceeds from the creation to the revolt of Lucifer and his supporters, who are cast into a pit surmounted by gleefully realistic flames. We go through Adam and Eve, Cain and Abel, and -- a favourite set piece in all the mystery cycles -- Noah's ark, which may be the first English sitcom: With no biblical warrant, all the versions capitalize on Mrs. Noahs respectable reluctance to set foot on board and leave the neighbourhood. Noah, as played here by Sibusiso Ziqubu, has the dimensions and demeanour of Porky Pig. His reception of his sailing orders is, fittingly, a high-water mark of the shows linguistic freedom; meaning is transmitted mainly by incredulous cries and obedient looks. (Noah also has some trouble getting the chickens on board.) The flood's end is greeted by a swelling, and moving, chorus of You Are My Sunshine. The sons and daughters-in-law, bid to go forth and multiply, make enthusiastic exits.

The Old Testament, as far as the mystery writers were concerned, ended with Abraham and Isaac. (In other words, they leave out everything that might count as Jewish history.) We fast-forward, come to the start of Act Two, to the Annunciation, and follow the Jesus story through to the Resurrection. The Nativity is heralded by the tossing on to the huge, bare stage of a bale of hay and the crisp announcement: "Bethlehem.

A similar shorthand is employed for most of the scenes. I was slightly taken aback by the ease with which I, a nice Jewish boy, picked up the references, but then I had a post-war English education, with religious (i.e., Christian) instruction still embedded in the curriculum. This may have messed with my mind, but it taught me something about the icons and sources of Western civilization. Politically and socially, I'm in favour of the secularization of education; culturally, its a problem. The abandonment of the King James Bible, even in churches, has already made it far harder to speak or understand Shakespeare, and some of todays kids might well be confused by parts of The Mysteries.

Vumile Nomanyama plays both God the Father and God the Son -- an obvious double that I've never seen executed before. An authoritative, sharp-tongued actor, he makes a peremptory deity, proud of what he's wrought and aggressively aggrieved when it lets him down. His transformation into Jesus is announced by having him join his mother in a dance. Off comes the sarong, and hes human and vulnerable in a pair of short pants. He, in turn, teaches his disciples to dance; I wouldnt swear that Judas (Steven Hicks) has two left feet, but you can see his persecution complex growing.

The company have a Beggar's Opera in their repertoire, in which Nomanyama plays Captain Macheath; that I'd like to see. In their production of Carmen (which they are alternating with The Mysteries) the title role is played by Pauline Malefane, a presumably versatile actress who in this show is a vibrant Virgin. Andries Mbali is a sly, red-suited Devil, tireless at his job and equipped with horns for his role in the New Testament, though not in the Old.

It isnt all fun. The Massacre of the Innocents is harrowingly done. The mothers are singing lullabies when their babies are torn from them. The soldiers are black-clad secret police, and their leader (Zorro Sidloyi, a striking bass) joins chillingly in the singing as he closes in for the kill. The elements of the show come as effectively together here as they do in the sequences of celebration, of which the last would have any audience on its feet.

- - -

From the Traverse Theatre, Edinburgh, comes a show far more subdued, and far more baffling, but also with its share of atavistic elements. Outlying Islands, a new play by David Greig, is set just before the Second World War. Two clean young Englishmen, just out of Cambridge, have been sent to one of the remotest of the isles that dot the Scottish coast to study the bird life. They take up residence in what was, as little as a hundred years earlier, a pagan chapel. The place is now uninhabited, though leased by an elderly sheep farmer, Kirk by name and also by puritanical nature, who is now their remarkably surly guide. His closely watched niece makes up the company.

It transpires that the ministry that financed the trip has interests beyond birdwatching. They actually want to use the isle and its non-human population to test the efficacy of -- hold your breath -- anthrax. This news provides an undeniable frisson for us and for the characters. The two boys are shocked to their ecological boots. Mr. Kirk has already delivered himself of some observations on the corruptions of modern life (Women are uncovering their heads! Cinemas have arisen!") that make him sound like one of the railing prophets who got left out of The Mysteries. He is more amenable, though, to some of the other ways of Mammon, and starts calculating what he stands to make from the government in the way of compensation. Battle is joined. And the old man, who shouldnt have been drinking, drops dead of a heart attack.

This leaves Ellen, the niece, free to come out of her shell. Both the young men lust after her -- though John, the virginal junior of the two, is ashamed of his feelings, and Robert, who got himself a sexual reputation at college, isn't. Ellen, who doesn't subscribe to her uncles view of the movies and who has a particular passion for Laurel and Hardy, describes her two potential suitors, not imperceptively, as "Laurel and Laurel." There is a charming sequence in which the three sing The Trail of the Lonesome Pine, a song that makes a memorable appearance in Stan and Ollies Way Out West. Ellen, who has seen the film 37 times, can sing all of it; Robert, who has seen it once, can sing some of it; and bashful James, who has never seen it, can just about join in on the title phrase the last time round.

All this love-interest part of the play is well developed, at least until it succumbs to the misty portentousness that envelops everything else. Themes -- war and peace, paganism and Christianity, freedom and inhibition, the birds and the bees -- are picked up and dropped again, and it's hard to see how they're all meant to cohere. Lyrical dissertations on the migratory and nesting habits of the petrel must be meant as metaphors of the human action, both on stage and off in the wings of history, but I couldnt make any specific connection.

Robert, whose mental and imaginative processes are especially obscure, is given a monotonously pushy performance by Laurence Mitchell. But Sam Heughan makes a nice, fresh John, and Lesley Hart an emergingly edible Ellen. Robert Carrs Kirk has a strange pinch- vowelled accent, but this is a Scots company, so I imagine it's authentic. Philip Howard directs, rather slackly, on a split-level set that might be more evocative if it were less dingily lit. Even a cave should have its moments of illumination.

THE MAGNETISM OF THE HEART

Premiere Dance Theatre, Toronto

- - -

GAGARIN WAY

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, Toronto

- - -

Deconstruction can be hard to appreciate when you don't know what the targeted work looked like when it was still constructed. The Magnetism of the Heart, brought to World Stage by the Polish company Teatr Rosmaitosci, is based on a 19th-century comedy called Maiden Vows by Aleksander Fredro. Fredro is apparently Poland's national comic playwright; on its home ground this production has been described as an assault on "the most holy of sacraments of the Polish stage," which could be either an accolade or a denunciation, depending on who's talking.

I had to make what acquaintance I could with the original, via Surtitles, while watching what had been done to it, and I couldn't see that anything very disrespectful was going on. The production certainly gets wild at times (though definitely not in the sense of being undisciplined) but it is also continuously wonderful. It struck me as an attempt to reclaim a play that must have suffered the fate of classic comedies around the world -- i.e., staged too often, with a kind of automatic, antiseptic jollity, and taken seriously, as a piece involving real people with real feelings. Laszlo Marton did the same thing, though far less elaborately, in his Soulpepper production of Moliere's School for Wives. Fredro is known indeed as the Polish Moliere, though on the evidence of this play, which is concerned with the duplicities and vulnerabilities of erotic love, he had more in common with Marivaux.

The show is directed by Grzegorz Jarzyna, an enfant terrible who stages each of his shows under a different name, presumably on the sound principle that it's harder to hit a moving target (for this play he's called himself, or herself, Sylwia Torsh). The main strategy here is to move the action steadily forward, from one era to another, as the evening progresses. Everything starts buttoned- up and fairly conventional. By the end, characters are chasing each other across the stage, shedding clothes as they run, then lying down and rutting vigorously to the accompanying strains of the Bee Gees' Stayin' Alive. Though since this 1970s music seems to be coming out of a 1930s radiogram, it does appear that the aural elements of the show have here streaked ahead of the visual.

The maiden vows of the play's original title are taken by a couple of sisters, Aniela and Klara. They make, as you might guess, a mutual promise to steer clear of men. Each, of course, has a suitor; Aniela is besieged by Gustaw, a cynically resourceful young rake, and Klara is being pursued by Albin, a dry-looking stick who is of indeterminate age but has apparently been hanging around for years (though probably not, as Gustaw disgustedly claims, for 50 of them.) Gustaw takes all their destinies in his hands and steers matters to the expected amatory conclusion. He does it by playing mind games, whose elegant cruelty is here played to the hilt. But so is the explosive joy that results. It's like Les Liaisons Dangereuses with a happy ending.

As the pace gets more hectic, the scenes get shorter. A few are limited to a single line. No 19th-century playwright is likely to have written this way, even in Poland, but then Jarzyna (or Torsh) is credited with adapting the text as well as directing it, and with the terms so plainly declared we can hardly complain of distortion. Anyway, it's not as if the director has indulged in the tedious contemporary sport of sneering at his author. The keynotes of the evening are lightness and grace, of a consistency and accomplishment whose likes we rarely get to see.

The sets, by Magdalena Maciejewska, are magic, and the music and soundscape (the latter incorporating a whole barnyard of country noises) inspired.

The performances are intensely, sometimes clownishly, physical, but never forced or grotesque, and the actors speak with similarly understated finesse; it's rare to find yourself laughing at the delivery of lines in a language you don't understand, but I did so here. Magdalena Cielecka (Klara), who is slimness itself, has an entrancing scene in which the fashion of the moment has her standing at a writing desk, her bustle undulating with indignant expectation. Maja Ostaszweska (Aniela) has the wittiest mouth movements I remember seeing, and is also very touching. Redbad Klynstra (Gustaw) makes a sublime Byronic entrance. And Cezary Kosinski (Albin) lopes magnificently. We last see him taking a shower, which, considering the enthusiasm with which the aroused Klara has just laid him, he probably needs.

The cast is completed by the girls' mother, Gustaw's uncle and a surly servant whose essential superiority to his arrogant employers reaches its conclusion when he takes centre position at the curtain call. I suppose this class consciousness might be considered revolutionary, but it's actually pretty standard in modern production of bourgeois comedy, and the text, as far as I could tell, gives plenty of pretext for it. The entire septet comes together, without benefit of words, for the most riotous breakfast scene since Hay Fever. Or, on the remote chance that it's the dramatist's inspiration rather than the director's, before Hay Fever.

Gagarin Way is a first play by a young Scottish dramatist, Gregory Burke, brought to World Stage by our very own Crow's Theatre. It premiered in Britain in August, 2001, just in time to avoid seeming terminally quaint. "We might," says one of the characters, "make political violence fashionable again." He now seems a little late, and the political violence that he actually pursues is almost endearingly old-fashioned. Still, not everybody can hijack a plane; you have to make the most of what you've got. The play centres around the kidnapping of a multinational upper manager by a pair of disaffected workers who propose to shoot him, as a gesture or an example. Or whatever: They aren't very clear themselves.

The play starts out very funny. It takes place in a computer factory in Dunfermline, Fife, and it kicks off with a discussion between Tom, a former student (politics and philosophy) working in security in the hope that something better will turn up, and Eddie, anarchist, autodidact, and -- we later learn -- psychotic. It's a laugh, though rather a snobbish one, to begin the play, bang, with Eddie the punk sounding off in the broadest and most profanely demotic Scots about Jean-Paul Sartre and someone else whose name sounds like "John Jenny" but actually turns out to be Jean Genet. It's even more of a gas because Eddie's contemptuous assessment of Genet's criminal chic and Sartre's glorification of it is right on the button. (He points out that Genet, celebrated for the time he spent in the clink, must therefore have been pretty ineffective at his chosen vocation of thief and concedes that Sartre certainly had a nose for a catchy title. Being and Nothingness: That's going to draw the crowds.)

We meet Gary, an old-style socialist whose grandfather fought in the Spanish Civil War. And with Gary comes, all trussed-up and temporarily unconscious, their chosen victim, Frank. When unwrapped and revived, Frank discomfits them by not being Japanese, and in fact being local, though since removed to the Home Counties. And hereabouts the play stops working properly.

It goes on being funny, if sometimes with excessive winsomeness: Eddie, berated for not bringing balaclavas to the party, protests, "You can only get woolly ones -- I'm allergic to woolly." There is also a fair amount of pungent political comment, though the most pungent comes from the captive Frank, who has been around and seen it all and is disgusted with capital and labour alike.

In fact, Frank -- at least as played, or spat out, by Hardee T. Lineham in an untraceable accent -- is the most menacing figure on stage, which may not have been the intention. Aidan Devine's Gary is like a cartoon shop steward, too sweet and worn down for his sanguinary intentions to be taken seriously.

Shawn Doyle's Eddie is more believably murderous. I called him an anarchist because it's a label that Gary pins on him and that he accepts, but politics don't really concern him except as farouche debating points; he's too anarchic to be an anarchist. Violence is what gives him the real buzz; he says so -- and rather too often, as if his author had run out of other things for him to say. I didn't lose belief in him, but I did lose interest.

Matthew MacFadzean, whose previous line of toughs might have made him obvious casting for Eddie, instead plays Tom, the fall guy, and does him very well.

All round, Jim Millan's production is better at getting laughs than at conjuring danger; it plays, in other words, to the script's strengths and fails to camouflage its weaknesses. When violence does come, it's surprisingly ineffective. Burke writes juicy dialogue, and is probably a coming man, though maybe not as preternatural in his accomplishments as his publicity might suggests. This play was produced in Britain at the National Theatre, and it's being claimed that Burke is the first playwright to have achieved this with a first play. Of course it was in 1967 -- pre-history -- but the National once gave a main-stage premiere to a play called Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead by an untried writer named Tom Stoppard. And there have been others since, such as Patrick Marber with Dealer's Choice.

In one way, though, Burke moves us on. Earlier left-wing British playwrights, like Edward Bond or Howard Brenton, anticipated this play's kidnap-the-capitalist or pinion-the-politician scenario, and though they usually gave the captive some decent arguments, if only to pass the time, they never left any doubt as to whose side they were on or who would ultimately win. In Burke's world such certainties, maybe even such hopes, are gone. Hence the mockery, hence the fury, hence the despair. The title derives, by the way, from a street name in an actual Scottish mining town. They wanted to name it after a Soviet hero, and the first astronaut (or, as Frank wearily corrects his captors, cosmonaut) was the most famous one to hand.

The Magnetism of the Heart, meanwhile, is the subtitle of the original Fredro play, and a very apposite one.

Black & White Photo: Peter J. Thompson, National Post / Gagarin Way is Gregory Burke's first play.

100

du Maurier Theatre Centre, Toronto

- - -

This year's World Stage season, now at its halfway mark, has brought us some stunning evenings of theatre: far better, I can tell you, than the World Theatre seasons that became legendary in London in the '60s and '70s, but were often simply boring.

Don Shipley, buyer-in-chief for Toronto's international bazaar, has stocked it with exceptional taste and skill, but he, like everyone, has his lapses. One of them is an apparent willingness to be impressed by any show that has won prizes or praise or both on the fringe of the Edinburgh Festival. The Edinburgh fringe is an overstuffed annual jamboree that distributes its favours with indiscriminate enthusiasm. The agreeable but hardly overpowering Gagarin Way got raves there, and not just because it was Scottish. Now we have 100, an English show which comes bearing a Fringe First (Edinburgh's equivalent of an Oscar, and about as trustworthy) and which plays like an unwitting parody of everything denoted by the dread phrase "experimental theatre."

All the elements are in place, all the signs that have denoted the avant garde for 70 years and counting. It is presented by a company that calls itself theimaginarybody. The eschewing of capital letters has long been taken to signify virtue (I've never understood why), and this lot climbs further up the sacred mount by abjuring spaces between words as well.

There are five actors, dressed in different varieties of white smock, and there are cubes for them to sit on. One of the actors carries a piece of fruit. The stage floor is shiny black, though it does assume other shades, including an interesting dappled one, when the lights change. And the action, as you might have guessed, is set in limbo.

It's set there literally, which I guess is a point in its favour. I mean, we're not just dealing in arty metaphor here. Of the five characters, four have just died. The fifth is an old lag, there to show them the ropes. He tells the newcomers that they must each select a memory from their lives, to stay with them always. And he means always. Everything else they will forget. If they either cannot or will not come up with such a key moment their fate, though unspecified, will be awful. One imagines they will join the truly lost souls, neither good nor bad, hot nor cold, milling hopelessly about in the ante-room to Dante's Inferno.

Three of the four deceased are from London; this seems a bit skewed any way you take it, but the idea was presumably that the company would draw on the world it knew and that the audience would respond accordingly. Two of the three knew each other in life; in fact they were lovers who died together in an accident. The third is an executive high-flyer whose career was cut short by a brain disease.

The lone foreigner has a French accent, but that's probably just the actor; he comes from an unspecified African village where he antagonized his fellows by telling them the world was round. It may be irreverent of me to be reminded of Michael Flanders' Reluctant Cannibal who got clobbered by his peers when he tried to persuade them that eating people was wrong -- it may even be racist -- but I can't help it.

All the candidates act out scenes from their pasts, with the other actors dropping their immediate identities to help out in supporting roles. These episodes can take place in offices or parks, or on underground trains, or at speed-bike races. Whatever the setting, it's summoned up with the aid of some bamboo sticks, which apparently are standard issue on the doorstep of eternity. These implements are unquestionably versatile -- it's even possible that in jungle scenes we are watching bamboo canes playing bamboo canes - - but that's because they're featureless, and I groaned every time the actors started twirling them. It's like watching a drama school exercise going on for 60 minutes.

Sometimes the proffered memories fail to pass muster with whoever the authorities may be, while a successful application is signalled by the shining, in the audience's eyes, of a battery of bright lights. It seems unlikely, though, that we're being offered a whole new mythology of the afterlife. Rather we're being told, none too subtly, to make the most of our earthly lives while we have them -- to Seize, in fact, the Moment.

A suffocating air of piety, earnest but not earned, afflicts the entire enterprise. People wrote plays with similar settings and themes in the 1930s; there's an especially ineffable English version called Outward Bound, in which death is an ocean liner. This new treatment, with several decades of the group-creation ethic at its back, is even sicklier.

The writing is credited to Neil Monaghan, with input from Christopher Heiman (director) and Diane Petterle (producer). Between them they have achieved a remarkable level of watery banality: not a character, not a situation, not a single line comes to life. One doesn't care how these people have spent or misspent their lives. One is only aware of the show's creators hovering over them, tut- tutting.

The show comes with one of the most touchingly overbearing press releases I have ever encountered. It's an orgy of name dropping. The production team invoke Chekhov (Michael, not Anton), Lecoq (there is some mime), Stanislavski (who would have taken to his bed had he seen the sloppy generalities that pass here for acting) and Gabriel Garcia Marquez. The director, in his program bio, carries this quest for glory by association to even more tenuous extremes, informing us that he studied acting at "Cygnet Training Theatre (Patron Peter Brook)." Gosh. The actors, we are told, have between them worked with Peter Hall, Trevor Nunn, Mike Alfreds and Katie Mitchell. So have many: What I want to know is, would any of these directors work with any of these actors again?

The current script, though, may not be a fair test. It offers its players nothing to bite into, especially given that the cast we see is not altogether the same as the one that first worked the show up. But what they come up with is very forced. It's possible, listening to their back-slapping line readings, to conclude that they must have been hired for their physical skills, but it's not as if any very extraordinary demands are being made on these. It's no big deal for actors to suggest a subway ride by swaying from side to side while hanging on imaginary straps; it's been done.

I spent a lot of time resenting Lawrence Werber, who plays the hellish host, for acting the nag when he should have been acting implacable. There turns out to be a reason for this (it's the show's one half-decent surprise) but I still think he could have used more variety. He, by the way, is saddled with the device that gives the play its title; his charges have to make their decisions before he can count up to the magic number. I can't explain why this seems to me to epitomize the evening's quality as nothing else could, but it does.

Black & White Photo: Neil Mountford, World Stage / Matthieu Leloup must choose a single memory he wants to keep.

Until May 11. 416-504-9971

HOME IS MY ROAD

Factory Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Florence Gibson's new play, Home Is My Road, has a couple of exceptionally powerful speeches lined up in its closing stretch. Both are delivered by the same performer, Brenda Robins, though as two different characters. In the earlier sections of the play the doubling is confusing since Robins' admirable qualities do not include a facility for vocal or physical disguise, but by the end we have our bearings where she is concerned. Unfortunately there are other confusions, in both script and production, that are not so easily sorted out.

Most of the play is set in Romania, 12 years ago, though both of the women Robins plays are Canadian. One is an adoptive mother and the other desperately wants to be. The latter, whose name is Grace, comes to Romania in the meltdown period after the dethroning of Ceausecu to buy a baby from an orphanage. Eventually she acquires one only to find herself up against its mother.

Meanwhile, back in Canada, a woman who went through a similar adoption process some 20 years before, is writing letters to her daughter: a daughter who has quarrelled with her, as daughters will, and has gone off to Europe to try to locate her birth mother. The speeches both women deliver are great self-lacerating odes to the power and the pain of motherhood. Yes, says one, I know it will make me an impossible person, possessive and unreasonable, but it's still what I want. Yes, says the other, before entrusting her sentiments to the mail, adopting a child has made a loving monster of me, but I still wouldn't change a thing.

I have made it sound as if Robins were the star of the show. She isn't, but -- with no disrespect to her colleagues -- the play might be better off if she were. She carries the theme. But it's only very late on that we realize that it is the theme; there have been many detours on the way. She's offstage for much of the play, and when she is on most of her scenes are played out behind a symbolic slatted rope curtain that runs the width of the stage; it doesn't make her invisible or inaudible but it does make her remote.

Gibson, as she showed in her previous play Belle, can write dramatic poetry unmatched by any other playwright in Canada. There are flashes of that quality in this play, but they are rare, maybe because the story doesn't spur the style. Belle, you may remember, dealt with the experiences of American blacks and whites, post- Civil War, post-reconstruction. Its five fictitious characters were living creations, but their actions and reactions reflected and were governed by the broad swathe of history that they inhabited. Times changed, and so did they. Home Is My Road also starts from a historical, post-cataclysmic situation, but doesn't advance from it. The characters are left to their author's devices, and these turn out to be scattered.

Much of the play is devoted to Esme, the girl in search of her mother. (She does once mention a father, but fathers in this play are marginal figures.) She falls in with a family of gypsies (or Roma), one of whom, a young man named Stefan, first tries to rob her and then becomes her lover. Esme becomes convinced she is of gypsy birth and at one angry moment goes so far as to tear up her Canadian passport to prove the point. Stefan thinks she's being self- indulgent, a conclusion the audience is likely to have reached before him. From an unsympathetic point of view, which is the obvious one to take, she's having an unusually elaborate teenage tantrum, rejecting the parent who loves her in favour of one she is highly unlikely to find. She is also making a shallow and romantic identification with a people she knows almost nothing about.

The gypsies she meets are more than usually displaced, constantly pushed from one side of the border to the other and at the mercy of an exploitative if not quite conscienceless local bureaucrat. The family also includes Stefan's sister, Trinquet, and their brother, Fedora. Trinquet's husband is an imprisoned activist; she also has a baby. Fedora is mentally handicapped. They are a play in themselves, a play on which Gibson has expended a lot of stage time and energy but that doesn't co-exist very well with the drama of motherhood and adoption that finally takes precedence. Plainly the author has chosen Romania as her flashpoint, since it offers a graphic example of Western women indulging their thwarted maternal urges at the expense of actual mothers too oppressed or impoverished to resist. (At least, that's one way of looking at it. It doesn't hold up when you consider the children in those fetid state orphanages who actually were orphans.) By that token, young Esme, the indulged child, is playing out the maternal drama in reverse. But making the exploited family gypsies only adds extra baggage. It's Trinquet's child that's in dispute at the end; Stefan's fecklessness and Fedora's slow-wittedness help bring this situation about. But it all seems a needlessly cumbersome way of setting up a fine final scene.

The characters all present hefty acting problems, and in Ken Gass's production each of the actors seems stuck in his or her own corner trying to work them out. Patricia Fagan's forthright Esme is the only one who ever seems to be making contact with anyone else, and even she becomes increasingly rigid as her behaviour becomes increasingly impossible. Arsinee Khanjian does her best stage work yet as Trinquet, but she is stuck with being a nobly suffering symbol for both her gender and her race. Belle, in Gibson's previous play, had to shoulder similar burdens but was given far feistier material to work with.

Even Gibson's ear deserts her when it comes to working out a dramatic language for the Roma characters, who are given a kind of pidgin English, denuded of articles and spiced, in Stefan's case, with the occasional saucy pun. The role reduces Brandon McGibbon to a state of permanent, and not always comprehensible, sing-song. Sean Dixon does a lot of enthusiastic grunting as Fedora. There is also a character billed as Dumptruck, played by Dragoslav Tanaskovic, the production's music and sound designer, who stands around playing authentic-sounding accordion music; it's never clear whether he's meant to be there or is just a piece of atmosphere made flesh.

Black & White Photo: Nir Bareket / Brenda Robins and Arsinee Khanjian in Home Is My Road.

RUSSELL HILL

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

- - -

Chris Earle's Russell Hill takes its title from a grassy spot by a Toronto ravine. Several subway passengers clambered to safety there after a crash in August, 1995, in which one train rammed into another at Dupont station. Three passengers were killed and many others injured. It was the worst accident in TTC history. I had completely forgotten about it.

The fact that I could may be part of the play's point, though both play" and "point are dubious words in this context. Earle, whose roots as both author and performer are in comedy and revue, has here written a collection of speeches and sketches. The presumption is that they have some connection, metaphorical rather than factual, to the disaster, and the basic set is a subway platform: An imposingly realistic design by John Thompson that also turns out to be remarkably versatile. It needs to be, since the scenes we witness happen all over town and beyond.

The best is a chance encounter between two former lovers who reminisce about their break-up. He, who initiated it, wants to be told that he didnt cause her any pain. She begins by saying sweetly that he didnt, and then goes on, at ruthlessly hilarious length, to prove to him that he did. This is a virtuoso speech, both in the writing and in Shari Hollett's performance, which is both unhurried and unstoppable. When it does stop, the stage, with appealing incongruity, is taken over by Frank Moore, playing a crooner who seems to have jetted in from Las Vegas, or at least motored down from Casino Rama. Tuxedoed and with a hand microphone, he unleashes the full lounge treatment on a honeyed anthem to Toronto, leaving us to ponder yet again why lyrics that would pass without question if they celebrated New York or Chicago should sound so absurd when aimed at home.

It's just as well this sequence exists because the rest of the show, despite being exceedingly well acted and directed, is dire. Its the second Tarragon play in succession to begin with the author chatting up the audience. Susan Coyne, in Kingfisher Days, got away with this by pretending, charmingly, to be embarrassed; Earle blows it by pretending, embarrassingly, to be charming. We know he can be charming in other contexts, but here his very skills betray him; hes too confident for words. Of the items that follow, one, a young woman's letter to a penpal, is dully written but redeemed by the intensity of Mary Francis Moore's delivery. Others dont seem to be redeemable at all. They include a commuters address to the lucky beggar" in whose basket he regularly drops a coin; a thwarted tryst between two women lingering in a pool at a Mexican resort; and a number in a massage parlour. This last item comes early enough for us still to expect some connection between what we see and what we've been told the evening is about. Our confusion at there being no such connection is exploited by having Earle himself say what we're thinking. This may be meant to be disarming. It isnt.

Theres a late scene in which a young film assistant comes to the door of a local householder, explaining that a picture about the accident is to be shot on his street: a movie-of-the-week, apparently, with oodles of suspense and a heroic young doctor in the starring role. One welcomes this segment for its humble relevance, and for its touch of satire, but it has other merits, too. An unspoken sense of loss makes itself felt behind the politeness of the resident (Frank Moore again), while Earle does his best acting work of the evening as the gofer, trying to be brash and polite at the same time.

But he also has a monologue, in what we take to be his own person. He tells about waiting for a streetcar at 1 a.m. and being shouted at by a gang of youths in an SUV to "get a f---ing car. After initial fury, he decides this admonition hides great wisdom, presumably about the impending death of public transport. Earle can't be blamed if his story reminded me of Alan Bennett's vicar in Beyond the Fringe, recalling the employee -- of, coincidentally, the London underground -- who stopped him when he was entering an area marked No Entry by saying hey, Jack, where do you think youre going?" and caused him to ponder on where, indeed, do any of us think were going.

Earle also treats us to some whimsical musings on the modern impossibility of separating tragedy from comedy, apparently under the impression that is some revelatory idea. He talks about the escaped passengers emerging at Russell Hill on a summer evening, and of the sense of relief, and even of well-being, they must have felt, and how illusory such a feeling must be, in the grand scheme of things. Because the thing about disasters is, you never know when they're going to happen. Tell me something I don't know.

And presumably the point of all the disconnected vignettes is they each carry the possibility of catastrophe. Only they dont: Unless you take the view that any human story, taken far enough, will explode, in which case any selection is arbitrary and, almost by definition, boring. Or maybe the whole fragmented structure of the show is meant in itself to be an example of dicing with disaster. Or, to switch cliches, of skating on thin ice. But it doesnt cut any.

The invented scenes are intercut with extracts from the train driver's testimony at the inquest. Earle plays the questioning lawyer, and the others take turns at playing the driver. Of them all Sam Earle, aged nine, is the simplest and most effective. Earle senior has decently forsworn any intention of dramatizing, or otherwise sensationalizing, the crash itself. But he's still invoking documented suffering, and in that light the games he plays are every bit as cheap. Chris Abrahams direction gets everything possible out of the text, and is very slick technically. The one cast-member I havent yet mentioned is Robert Smith; he's good too.

Black & White Photo: Michael Cooper, Tarragon Theatre / Mary Francis Moore, Frank Moore, Robert Smith, Shari Hollett and Chris Earle in Russell Hill, based on the 1995 subway crash in Toronto.
