Until Apr. 27. Box office: 416-973-4000.; robertcushman@lycos.com

THE SYRINGA TREE

du Maurier Theatre Centre, Toronto

Pamela Gien, author and performer of The Syringa Tree, is a South African living in America. So her one-woman play sails into World Stage under two flags. It's a quasi-autobiographical piece, entirely concerned with her youth in and around Johannesburg, but it was worked up in L.A. and premiered in Seattle. Its now in process of going round the world and being turned into a movie.

The festival has billed it as part of "Indaba -- celebration of South African culture" and it makes a neat pair with Thembi Mtshalis A Woman in Waiting, the solo piece that inaugurated the celebration three weeks ago. Each is a first-person account of growing up under apartheid by a woman who found adult success as an actress and writer.

There are, however, notable differences. Mtshali sticks, as far as we can tell, to the facts of her own life and uses her own name; Gien grafts her recollections onto an invented narrator whom she calls Lizzie. Mtshali's piece is a monologue done entirely in her own voice; Gien's is a play in which she plays all the characters, about 30. And Mtshali is black and Gien is white.

Its unusual in the theatre to hear the story of apartheid told through the experiences of a white liberal. We start in 1963, when Lizzie is six. Her father, a doctor, is a self-described Jewish atheist, her mother a lapsed Catholic. Lizzie, of course, is looked after by a black nanny, Salamina, who shortly after the play begins gives birth to a daughter of her own, named Moliseng. Lizzies father delivers her, but her existence has to be kept a secret; she has no papers. We follow the growing-up of both girls, their mutually devoted companionship and their inevitable enforced divergence.

Lizzie's parents are outstandingly decent people and, given the circumstances, model employers; they protect their servants, take risks for them, and say thank you when they knock off for the day. Compare this to Mtshali's memories of life as a domestic, and in particular to her story of the woman who, when she turned up late for work after being scooped from her home by a police raid, accused her of lolling in bed with her boyfriends. Mtshalis accounts of the white children she couldnt help loving are not that dissimilar to the relationship between Salamina and Lizzie, and if Salamina has the luckier deal, she doesn't have Mtshali's escape route into the theatre.

At first Lizzie is able to see the racist world beyond her home as a sad joke, personified by the Afrikaans pastor next door who has passed his bigotry on to his family. My father knows, says his daughter, Lizzies occasional playmate. "God tells him everything." Maybe somebody should write a play about them, the bad guys; it would probably be unsettling but it could be instructive.

Reality crashes in on Lizzie when Moliseng disappears from a township hospital and Lizzies mother, breaking unwritten rules and probably some written ones, drives there through the night in search of her. Lizzie, also disobeying orders, crouches in the back seat. A later, starker trauma comes when Lizzie's grandparents' house is invaded by "freedom fighters from Rhodesia" (the words are attributed to the South African police though its hard to believe theyd have chosen that term) and her grandfather is killed.

According to interviews, this murder and the birth of Moliseng are the only incidents in the play that Gien took directly from life. But they are enough to make the play feel autobiographical, and, as in every other example of the genre from Long Day's Journey into Night on down, this creates problems. You don't know what to believe, and you feel less credulous than you would toward a work of avowed fiction. After the killing, Moliseng leaves her employers house, apparently ashamed of her people. Is this an act of foolishness or nobility? It could be either, or both. But it is told, not dramatized. Its the author's creation, so she has a duty toward it. She can't just pass it off as a historical enigma.

Gien begins the play on a swing, beneath the tree of the title that symbolizes home. (The sense of place, despite a spare and evocative set and soundscape, by Kenneth Foy and Tony Suraci respectively, is willed rather than communicated.) She brings to her multiple roles a graceful, limber body that can contract and expand like Alice under the influence of cake, and an impressive armoury of voices: every role an individual, no duplicates. The piping tone she uses for young Lizzie -- the one we hear the most -- is ingenious but can be tiring; its a relief when she starts channelling the the grown-ups, especially when theyre Lizzie's parents, as humorous as thy are humane.

One begins to wish for our narrator to grow up, though when she does it's nearly the end of the play and all rather a scramble. We arrive at the Soweto riots, and a 14-year-old Moliseng becomes politicized. Lizzie emigrates, marries, has a child but refuses to take a trip home, even after the arrival of democracy and despite her continuing love for her old and still-exemplary dad, which I thought weird. Eventually she does return, under circumstances it would be unfair to reveal.

I can say theres a kind of reunion, and its moving. And I found myself slightly uncomfortable at being moved, because of something sentimental in the implied picture of blacks and whites. I was also uncomfortable at my own discomfort, because the situation is not one of which I have direct experience and I have no right to judge it -- not as theatre but as life.

That's the semi-autobiographical factor kicking in again. The Syringa Tree is on almost every level a more accomplished and sophisticated work than the more straightforward A Woman in Waiting, but though the black solo voice may not in itself be more trustworthy than the white multiple one, it is still, at this juncture and on this subject, easier to accommodate.

KAFKA IN LOVE

Hart House Swimming Pool, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - The last production of what may be the last World Stage Festival was mounted at the weekend for four performances only. Kafka in Love was a Canadian production from a group called Autumn Leaf Performance. Billed as a water-opera, it was a mixture of live aquashow, pre-recorded music and film. Presented in the uncommon theatrical surroundings of the university pool at Hart House, and an unlikely bet for touring, it may be remembered by those who saw it as a super- curiosity.

The premise is that we are in Berlin in 1936, year of the Olympics. A German aquastar, Gerti Wasner, has prepared a piece of performance art that's been banned by the Ministry of Propaganda, since it purports to describe her affair, 23 years earlier, with Franz Kafka, a writer of whom the Nazis would have been unlikely to approve even had he not been Jewish. (In one of the few spoken passages in the work, Kafka is officially described as a bug; presumably Goebbels had read Metamorphosis.) Gerti, played here by Kirsten Johnson, takes the plunge anyway, abetted by six chlorinated- water nymphs drawn from the ranks of the Toronto Synchronized Swimming Club.

Projected on a screen above the pool is a film about the Gerti- Franz romance, though its unclear whether this movie is meant to be understood as part of Gertis own project or of the Canadian director Thom Sokolowski's project about her project. The movie shows us a Kafka disillusioned with his fiancee back home, and ripe for a fling. Those are not terms one would usually apply to the tortured author of The Trial and The Castle, but this work suggests that, like some other writers who have presented themselves as sexual incompetents (Philip Larkin comes to mind), Kafka was holding out on us. He seems, apart from anything else, to have been quite the looker back in 1913; there's a nice moment early on when his screen-image is reflected in the waters beneath.

Of course the film could be romanticizing; its Kafka after all as an actor (Avi Phillips, playing opposite the young Gerti of Kelci Archibald). He recites pieces of anguished prose in voice-over, and he does a fair amount of walking down passages that are, well, Kafkaesque, and that look as if they were photographed in another part of Hart House. But really there is not much to distinguish him from any sensitive young man, and even though he and Gerti do some happy splashing of their own (they met at an Italian spa), the twin spectacles dont do much to illuminate one another.

The live one, though, is more fun to watch. Patricia Edwards is credited with swimsuit design, and she has come up with a dashing set of ensembles in primary colours. The matching cloaks that they discard before getting wet are especially elegant. The "synchronized choreography" that Debbie Sands has devised is not especially inventive; I guess options in these circumstances are fairly limited, but there must be ways of deploying the chorines besides gathering them into Busby Berkeley starfish formations, a trick the show falls back on twice.

Still, they do it very well. A couple of them turn up at one point wearing tall cylindrical hats decorated with wrap-around photos of Kafka himself: presumably to signify the depth, or height, of Gerti's infatuation.

Other, non-human things, float upon the waters -- cushions bearing relevant artifacts: a bowler hat, an open book, a pen and paper. And, when the two lovers succumb to passion on-screen, the pool is filled with lighted tapers, an effect that can be counted on to be magical, even on dry land. John Denniston's lighting is very moody around here, and the music, though I couldnt tell you what piece was playing at the time, is haunting. Here the piece does, appropriately, come together.

The score, opera or not, is about the last thing in the evening one notices. Its a tapestry of pre-existing compositions that blend into a continuous plangent blur suggestive of exposed nerve endings.

At the end of the show the present-tense Gerti, having executed her gesture of defiance, announces that she accepts the new order, and dives in one last time. Whether she really meant that from now on she would stop hugging her memories of decadent Czech writers, or whether she was executing a coded gesture of resistance, I couldn't say. The piece seems to be riding on its audience's built-in responses to a famous author and an infamous epoch; it has nothing decipherable to tell us about Kafka or love or Nazism or any combination of, or antagonism between these things. The idea of a play in a pool has real appeal, and so up to a point does the reality, but such pleasures as this one provides are abstract, which in this case is a polite word for kitsch.

One would have liked World Stage to end with a grand finale rather than a hollow bonbon. It would have been more in keeping with a festival that this year has been remarkably impressive.

There have been lapses of course. There was Horse Country, for example, an American two-hander that followed in Beckettian tradition by presenting a comic double act and hijacking it for higher purposes. It ended up making a valid enough point about the national tendency to interpret the pursuit of happiness as the right to be entertained. But this insight hardly justified the penitential unfunniness of the endlessly circling dialogue that preceded it. Its usually a bad sign when ones main response to the actors is admiration for their feat in remembering their lines.

Otherwise, the most disappointing shows were British (100, Outlying Islands), Canadian (Tamara) or a mixture of the two (Gagarin Way). I grieve for both my countries.

Canada's honour, though, was redeemed by The Overcoat -- at least, I imagine it was. I didn't see it this time round but, on the assumption that it was as good now as it was when it played at Canadian Stage three years ago, it brought the seasons score of masterpieces to five, the others being The Notebook/The Proof (Belgium), The Mysteries (South Africa), Glengarry Glen Ross (U.S.A.) and The Magnetism of the Heart (Poland). Thats a feast in just one month. We shall miss World Stage, though I hope against hope we shan't have to.

Black & White Photo: Autumn Leaf Performance / Production least likely to go on the road: Kafka in Love requires a swimming pool for full effect.

Until May 10. 416-870-8000.

1984

Studio Theatre, Toronto Centre for the Arts

The worst mistake made by Tribal Productions' stage version of 1984 may be its neglect of the novels roots in George Orwells England. Or it might be the decision to use Winston Smith's ordeal in the cellars of the Ministry of Love as the frame for his whole story, thereby letting us know his chief torturer's identity from the start rather than springing it as a cruel surprise. Or it could be the wholesale sentimentalization of the story and characters. Or mabe its some other misjudgment. There is no lack of gaffes from which to choose.

Fairs fair: Tribal is a shoestring operation and most of its actors are non-Equity. Toronto's more affluent theatres can come up with work just as naive and pretentious as this, but they usually lend it a gloss and authority that makes the evening easier to get through. Putting the most celebrated of dystopian novels on the stage is a challenge for any company, and Eli Lukawitz, director and principal adaptor, has managed to get quite a lot of the story up there. He has even had a couple of good ideas. Chief among them is the prominence he gives to the telescreen announcer who is the face of the Party in Oceania. Whether inciting its members to hysteria in the daily Hate sessions or feeding them the latest over-production figures, she is always the same woman; and, in Tara Beagan's performance, the most compelling figure on stage. Though, of course, she isnt on stage as the others are. That may help her, as may the fact that she doesnt have to pretend to be a character.

One difficulty in dramatizing the book now is that the calendar year 1984 has come and gone. Orwell was enormously prescient because he was enormously observant; to adapt one of the Party's own slogans, he sensed the future by knowing the present and the past. But his nightmare of universal terror did not come to pass exactly as and when he said it would. (Nor has it now, despite this production's earnest efforts to persuade us otherwise, with an opening montage of Bush, bombs, Osama and Saddam, the last admittedly looking very like Big Brother.)

Now this is no problem when reading the book. One simply adjusts to Orwells vision, which in many respects is a naturalistic one. On stage, a theatrical genius might be able to keep Orwells theme and narrative while abandoning the homely details of the vision and transmute the particular into the universal. Anybody less gifted would be well advised to follow the original, and let the audience do its own transmuting. This production is done on a grey abstract set of obelisks and cubes, and with its actors fitted out in futuristic one-pieces rather snazzier than the drab overalls specified by Orwell, so it's probably going for the universal. In the theatre the universal, though, has an unfortunate habit of turning into the anonymous, which is what happens here. I don't think I heard the word London spoken from one end of the play to the other. Maybe theyre trying to make it an allegory about Canada. Maybe they just cant do the accents.

Here's an example: Parsons, the eternal Boy Scout, the cheerfully sweaty and unflinchingly loyal workhorse on whom the Party depends, and who calls Winston and everyone else "old boy," is English-lower- middle-class English -- to the core: not so much in what he is as in what he says. Andrew Penner's performance is at least on the right lines but the juice has gone out of the role. Others fare far worse; indeed, the productions capacity for misreading the characters is almost inspired in its consistency. Mrs. Parsons, the harried mother who lives in terror that her indoctrinated kids might turn her in for thoughtcrime, is played as a metallic vessel of menace.

I mentioned sentimentality. In the book the imprisoned Winston meets a drunken woman, also called Smith who, after vomiting copiously in front of him, says why, I might be your mother. Thats all. Here he meets a younger, very sober woman who says she might be his sister, and the production seems to want us to believe her. It even tries to make a Moment out of it. Winston himself is played (by Samuel Owen, who also worked on the script with Lukawitz and Ben Bain) as a whining, downtrodden zombie. The idea seems to be that he is only awakened to rebellion by his affair with Julia. There are two objections to this: 1) Winston is already thinking heretical thoughts and doing heretical things -- like keeping a diary and talking to proles -- long before he meets Julia, and not even this adaptation can disguise the fact; 2) Winston, as acted here, shows no sign of awakening at any point whatever. Lauren Brotman's Julia is the nearest thing to a passable performance, but she too is sentimentalized, or perhaps idealized. When Winston tells her "you're only a rebel from the waist down," the sexy Julia of the book takes it as an excellent joke, not that this Winston seems capable of making one. Here, she stalks off the stage, miffed. If theyre trying to turn her into a feminist flagbearer, theyve got the wrong girl.

The third principal, Don Tripe's O'Brien, is a smiling cliche of a villain, unlikely to have taken anyone in. In fact, the flashbacks that break up his interrogation of Winston come as a relief, one doesnt want to hear a sustained debate between two characters who dont appear to have a brain between them. The production is noticeably short on sex and violence: a forbearance that might be virtuous in other contexts but is nonsensical in this one.

Lukawitz can be forgiven for failing to stage the Two Minutes Hate convincingly, and he may even be forgiven for messing up the ending. It takes place, after all, mainly in the protagonist's head. He cannot be forgiven for muffing the lovers' arrest, which only needs to be played as written. Plumbing the depths of the unpardonable is Winstons capitulation when hes faced with the horror of the rats and shouts out "do it to Julia." He isn't allowed here to do it of his own accord; O'Brien has to plant the idea in his mind. So he's spared the ultimate humiliation, and the audience is spared the point of the fable. The stupidity of this hardly bears contemplating. There's also a whispering chorus, letting us know from the outset that we are in for an abysmal evening.

CONFEDERATION

Cameron House

- - -

Here we go again. Confederation, which is about what its title says it's about, is the fourth installment of Video Cabaret's comic- strip history of Canada. This project has always been noted for the boldness of its staging, the reductiveness of its text and an acting- style that has partaken of both qualities. Nothing much has changed.

Except in one respect. The History of the Village of the Small Huts, which is the mischievous overall title of the project, is now on its second complete go-round; and Confederation is, fittingly enough, a reconstitution of elements from the first cycle.

As I understand it (I wasn't around for the previous try), five plays, of which Confederation is the first, have been distilled from what used to be two, dealing with the fortunes of Canada during the later 19th century -- what Michael Hollingsworth, the author and director, calls, with surprising anglocentricity, "the Victorian age."

Though material has apparently been added, simple arithmetic suggests that each of the five new plays will be briefer than each of the two old ones, and Confederation in fact clocks in at an unprecedented 75 minutes without interval. It feels too short but I didn't want it to be longer, if you follow me.

The stage is crammed with people itching to inscribe their names on their country's destiny, or at the very least on its future highways and hotels.

Here is John A. Macdonald, with a bibulous nose and before his knighthood (the latter being a difficult concept to accommodate), scheming to turn Canada into a Dominion, and then to have dominion over it.

In his Ontario corner is George Brown, scribbler, and in his coin- de-Quebec George-Etienne Cartier, distinguished by a castellated hairstyle, heaped-up in the middle and with a protruding wisp on either side, that's extraordinary even by this company's standards of baroque wiggery-pokery. After stringing them along and having his way with them, Macdonald hangs them both out to dry, leaving each to salve his wounds as best he may. Cartier resorts to guttural splutters, Brown starts The Globe.

Meanwhile in Montreal, Wilfrid Laurier, very insistent on the proper pronunciation of his Christian name, is preening in opposition. And under his influence comes the student Louis Riel, fresh out of the seminary, where he has soaked up the free-thinking texts of Voltaire while enduring the hell-fire denunciations of a thunderously bigoted Bishop Laurier.

The bishop stands out among the play's characters by virtue of being a full-fledged monster rather than just a fool or a knave. The clinching touch of grotesquerie is added by having the role played by a woman; Aviva Armour-Ostroff, in a performance as fearsome as her name, wields a very mean crozier. There is a similar cross- gendered enthusiasm in Elizabeth Brown's George Coles, "a portly man": his own complacent description and a riotous understatement, since his padding could fit out a Falstaff and still leave a bit over.

The two ladies also play ladies, though to less effect than is usual in this series; there is the regulaton amount of philandering but it has little effect on the body politic. It seems to have been included in the play out of habit. The men, as is customary, correspond to everybody's private opinion of politicians: They're venal and incompetent, even when these qualities would seem to cancel each other out.

Patrick Conner's Macdonald, who gets what he wants, is as much the clown as Brown and Cartier, who don't. (The show takes it for granted that what he wants is a bad thing, though the case is unproven, and anyway Video Cabaret thinks that about everybody.)

The cast acts with great forcefulness and enthusiasm; as Laurier, Bruce Vavrina, a veteran of the style, adds a touch of delicacy. Dylan Roberts' Riel is almost sympathetic but then his character is still a young thing, and very oppressed. At the end he takes himself back to Manitoba to foment resistance.

It's a "watch this space" kind of moment; obviously in the next play he will become important, thus giving the production licence to Get Riel.

I usually begin my Small Hut reviews by paying tribute to the precision and ingenuity of the black-box staging. I'm beginning to take it for granted, but it's as fine as ever, seven actors crammed into a tiny space, with a huge number of lighting areas, and always managing to hit the right spot. (And the right spot, conversely, always managing to find them.)

The speed of the transitions continues to take the breath, as does the speed and the complexity of the costume changes; Armour- Ostroff, at the operation's sharpest end, plays seven roles, most of them recurring. Astrid Janson and Julie Kenton designed the costumes, which are grotesquely splendid, and Brad Harley the props, which are splendidly grotesque.

The pace and the trappings give the proceedings an aura of wit that the script may not actually support. Full-throated laughs are few, though there's one terrific exchange about safeguarding the rights of minorities, especially those of that notorious minority, the rich. VideoCabaret gives very good cartoon. But it does get monotonous.

Black & White Photo: Michael Cooper / Patrick Conner as John A. and Aviva Armour-Ostroff as his wife.
2003-05-05-the-bard-s-unsinkable-play:
Not only is Love's Labour's Lost the first great romantic comedy in the English language, it is also the first great anti-romantic comedy. Four young men vow to dedicate themselves to three years of celibate study and, of course, are immediately derailed by the appearance of four young women. Then when, after the customary ration of advances and rebuffs, all seems set fair for a quadruple wedding, Death steps in and checkmates the revels.

At the height of the play's mirth, the Princess of France, who is on an embassy to the King of Navarre, receives news that her father has died. Courtship is put on hold. The Princess and her three ladies tell the King and his three lords that, if they wish, they may resume their suits in a year and a day, the interim to be spent on reflection and good works. It doesn't seem that long, but it is, as Berowne, the joker in the king's pack and the comedy's central character, pointedly remarks, "too long for a play." This, one of Shakespeare's earliest Elizabethan dramas, is only just beginning, and already it's deconstructing itself.

The end of this play is moving, in a unique fashion. Obviously we shed no personal tears for the late King of France; we have never met him, barely heard of him. What hits us so hard is the fact of mortality and, especially, its intrusion in a comic context. It casts doubt -- sober, uncynical doubt -- on all happy endings, including those in Shakespeare's other comedies. When the messenger arrives, Navarre's local inhabitants have been presenting a farcical pageant of the Nine Worthies. "Worthies, away," says Berowne, virtually cueing the lights, "the scene begins to cloud." It's magnificently self-conscious writing, absolutely sure of its effect.

Love's Labour's Lost is a pastoral, a form in which little happens but in which behaviour and language stand out in the sharpest relief in what the poet Marvell called "a green shade." The setting is soothing, the mood astringent. Much of the dialogue is wordplay: characters scoring off one another, misunderstanding one another. This poeticizing and logic-chopping are among the bad habits of which the women hope to cure the men by imposing their 12 months' penance. Shakespeare is satirizing his more self-indulgent contemporaries, but is also having a grand time beating them at their own game. In theory, the play is full of hopelessly obscure jokes; in practice, they are beautifully built up and always relate to the people making them. I don't think I have ever seen a bad production of Love's Labour's, and I don't remember hearing or reading of many. The play is magic.

Antoni Cimolino's Stratford production, if not among the greats, offers a good measure of delight. Santo Loquasto has set it (discreetly) and costumed it (richly) in the French modes of the late 18th century; the women's white dresses in the last scene knock your eyes out. Graham Abbey, perhaps influenced by the director's idea that the men lack "social graces," makes a surprisingly surly Berowne; his great speech of self- discovery ("and I, forsooth, in love") is played for anger, rather than for the overflowing joyousness of being carried away against one's will. It's a matter of opinion, but I know which interpretation I prefer. Still, he has no trouble controlling either the play or his fellow students, especially in the great scene in which each in turn is unveiled as an apostate. Shane Carty takes the now conventional gauche view of the King, and successfully runs, or shambles, with it. Dana Green's Princess forces her merriment but is charming when serious; Michelle Giroux is suitably metallic as Rosaline, Berowne's dark lady; and the minor lords (Stephen Gartner, Caleb Marshall) and ladies (Sarah McVie, Deborah Hay) get more definition than usual. There are useful contributions from James Blendick in the major role of the Princess's chamberlain and Les Carlson in the very minor one of her forester.

The courtiers' compulsive chattering is echoed in their rustic dependents. Brian Bedford gives a lovely account of Don Armado, lost in dusty dreams of grandeur, peering with mystified gentleness at everything that pertains to the real world and especially at the country wench, Jaquenetta, Dulcinea to his Quixote. His page Moth (Jacob James) is both too tall and too old for his role, but so quick and responsive that we can let it pass. This central comic trio is wonderfully completed by Jonathan Goad, an entrancingly light-handed and full-blooded Costard. The pedants (Brian Tree and Barry MacGregor) are adequate, which is another way of saying disappointing. “The Worthies show” falls flat, partly for this reason. It's character comedy, and it can't work unless all the characters have been established. It's played here for slapstick, as if it were “Pyramus and Thisbe”. These amateur actors trip themselves up; the production doesn't have to do it to them. This faltering in the comedy robs the last-minute tragedy of its full impact. But this is still my favourite play, and it's here in much of its glory.

AIDA

Canon Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - As Aida, the captive Nubian princess, and her Egyptian lover Radames, climb into the tomb in which they are to be buried alive, they sing the show's big ballad at one another. We know it's the big ballad because this is the second time they've done it; and they sing at, rather than to, one another because Aida is the kind of overblown and inhuman musical in which emotion is something you flaunt rather than something you feel. Still, you have to give the two characters credit. The song is about the need to simplify existence, which they are about to do in a big way; it's called Elaborate Lives, and it must take remarkable fortitude to come out with such philosophical gems when you and your sweetheart have just been condemned to elaborate deaths. If they weren't in the wrong civilization you'd call them Stoics.

Aida is of course the Disney musical of the Verdi opera. It junks the original score (perhaps mindful of an earlier Broadway musical called My Darlin' Aida, which didn't and flopped) but keeps close to the original narrative. Radames, Egypt's military wonder boy, is in line to marry Amneris, the Pharoah's daughter, and he makes her a present of Aida, of whose royal lineage he is unaware. Her identity is known, though, to her similarly enslaved compatriots for whom she becomes a rallying-point: a situation that escalates when her father, the king, joins them in jail. Meanwhile Radames' father plots to assassinate the Pharaoh, thus speeding his son's accession to the throne; Radames and Aida fall gradually and inexorably in love; and Amneris wrestles with conflicting impulses of jealousy and nobility. Also, in this version, she has a vein of pampered silliness, played for laughs, which the authors pick up and then discard with amazing arbitrariness. The show was in terrible trouble pre-Broadway and it suffers now from a frantic uncertainty of tone. I would guess when they were patching it up all concerned just kept grabbing for the nearest effect.

Apportioning responsibility for the musical's book may be a matter for archeologists rather than critics; it seems to have been assembled in layers. The program credits Linda Woolverton (who wrote the stage version of Disney's Beauty and the Beast), who gets a line all to herself; and then adds Robert Falls and David Henry Hwang, who are billed as a team; Falls is also the director. Their work here is, to put it as kindly as possible, utilitarian. I never thought I would mourn the demise of the through-sung pop-opera, but this is one show that might do better without dialogue. The gulf between text and songs is unbridgeable; they are different kinds of humdrum. The score is by Elton John, who writes music of no discernible merit, and Tim Rice, who is a slightly more interesting case. Rice was always a slapdash lyricist, but his work used to have sparks of humour and even of intelligence. (Compared to those here, his lyrics for Evita were works of slashing political insight.) Rice has written about Pharaohs and such before; a song here called Another Pyramid has a couple of lines that awaken faint echoes of his funny lyrics in Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat, but that's all. The show begins and ends with a solemnly intoned musical lecture called Every Story Is a Love Story. Actually, every story isn't and musicals might do us a favour if they acknowledged the fact, or at least stopped preaching about it. It's significant that pop music -- at least the kind of pop music that gets into theatres -- should have started to get heavy about love just when it lost the ability to imbue the subject with any tincture of romance, wit, sexuality or individual feeling. The bulk of this score is composed of power ballads as turgid as they are interchangeable. For a couple of numbers John and Rice go back to their presumed roots in rock 'n' roll; a strange decision since the songs in question are the only ones that seem meant to advance the plot, so the fact that you can't make out the words is exceptionally damaging. It's also odd that they are also the only numbers to involve an older character, in this case Radames' villainous dad, but maybe the authors are acknowledging that rock is now seniors' music. The actor concerned is Mickey Dolenz, on whose performance I would prefer, if only for sentimental reasons, to remain silent: not so much in deference to his past as one of the Monkees (I'm not a believer), but because he once directed a stage version of Bugsy Malone, a show even worse than this one but which he came very near to rescuing.

The only thing more heavy-handed than this Aida's attempts at drama are its attempts at comedy. Amneris is handed an old- fashioned dress-parade number -- by a pool, yet -- that demonstrates what an empty-headed clothes horse she is. (Do I dare tell you that it's called My Strongest Suit?) She later has a heavily innuendoed scene in which she tries to get Radames into bed. This is the same Amneris whom we are finally meant to accept as a figure of grace and mercy. Maybe this is the Disney tradition showing through; you could only get away with this kind of inconsistency in a cartoon. Aida is the first Disney stage show not to have started out as an animated feature, but old habits die hard, especially when they've proved lucrative. It's a tribute to Lisa Brescia that her Amneris ends up dignified and even moving. The story itself helps; its closing sections made me want to see the opera again.

Jeremy Kushnier is a Radames bland in bearing and strained in song. Paulette Ivory's Aida can be vocally overbearing, but that seems to go with this musical territory; everybody wants to be a soul sister, however slight the provocation. Her acting, though, is admirably feisty and direct; she earns her place as both national and romantic heroine.

Wayne Cilento contributes choreography whose only function seems to be to reassure the audience that they're watching a musical. It makes the men look especially absurd; a cohort of archers, bidden to make all speed to the docks, waste valuable time by pausing centre stage and posing with their bows and arrows. The evening's only trace of distinction comes from Bob Crowley's sets and Natasha Katz's lighting, superbly colourful co-conspirators. Much is the show is a symphony in red; one scene lines up Amneris in orange, Aida in pink, and Radames in basic tawny, all of them posed against a purple sky. There are also a couple of stunning trompes l'oeil. But even here there are lapses; young love is symbolized by a star- spangled firmament with a crescent moon slung so low that it might be awaiting the exertions of an especially unambitious cow. One of the few rules in movies, according to the late Pauline Kael, is that "all pictures set in ancient Egypt are ridiculous" and the show seems scared that the same rule might apply to the stage. The setting is chronologically and ethnically nondescript; it's an approach but it isn't a style. And Crowley's costumes, apart from Amneris' authentic royal gown, are less good than his sets. An occasional scenic resemblance to The Lion King only points out the poverty of what's going on in front: an attempt to please everyone while committing to nothing. I don't know if the audience for musicals is as stupid as the show would like it to be; people stood and applauded on the second night but maybe they were being polite.

Black & White Photo: Peter Redman, National Post / Jeremy Kushnier as Radames in the Toronto production of Aida.

HOTEL LOOPY

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

- - -

Here's a health to Rick Roberts, actor of this parish: recently returned to it, in fact, after a spell working in the United States, a fact that has earned him a surprising number of column inches in the local rags.

He justifies them all in Hotel Loopy, a show for which he is one of seven writer-performers and in which he has one solo scene that must be the funniest thing in town. It involves him speaking into a phone, a long red one to match the noses worn by everyone in the cast. (Hotel Loopy, it had better be confessed right now, is a clown show.) He tells his friend at the other end -- who is unheard, unseen, unidentified and, let us face it, non-existent -- that the audience isn't laughing.

This, of course, immediately starts the audience laughing, nervously at first and in isolated pockets. Roberts then describes the quality and quantity of this laughter, thereby provoking more of it. Certain words in his commentary are especially likely to set us off. He remarks on this fact, thereby ensuring they set us off all over again.

Interestingly, the laughter -- at least on the night I went -- never becomes full-throated or unanimous, but some individual peals are hysterical. This creates its own tension; every one of us feels alone in the actor's grip.

Audience reactions are, I suppose, fairly predictable, but Roberts must have to improvise his routine to some extent. Whatever the case, his control is cast-iron. Indeed, I was probably wrong in describing the scene as a solo; it's a duet played with the house, or perhaps a symphony in which he, with a maestro's affected negligence, conducts us. It's the most creative use of audience participation I have ever seen.

Hotel Loopy is indeed set in a hotel. It resembles Garbo's grand one in attracting famous guests who like to parade down the staircase, and John Cleese's Fawlty Towers in being in a state of dilapidated chaos. The latter resemblance extends to the sudden death of one of the guests and the staff's subsequent efforts to dispose of the body.

Roberts is the bellhop, with a Manuelian habit of dropping the guests' bags. His audience-involving habits declare themselves quite early in the show, when he crosses into our space, promising not to embarrass us by singling out individuals, and singling out individuals just to impress on them that he won't embarrass them. This, he reassures us, is not a kids' show. It has a fourth wall. He knows, because he's just cleaned it.

The show's strongest point is the deftness with which it demolishes its own pretensions; its weakest is the pretensions themselves. Theatre Columbus, the company responsible, is a long- established comedy-and-movement troupe with an uneven track record, and this is an uneven show.

Its credentials warm the heart. The cast includes some of Toronto's best-loved actors, and some of its most notable playwrights. (In a couple of instances, these are the same people.) All, as already noted, are in clown makeup and costumes. For those playing the hotel staff this involves striped pyjamas of a distinctly jailhouse cut.

The producers quote the mime artist's spiritual mentor Jacques LeCoq: "When the actor comes on stage, wearing a small red nose, [he is] entirely without defense ... The clown is the person who flops, who messes up his turn." These are resonant sentences, but the clown's vulnerability, his scapegoat quality, is much diminished when everybody is somebody's fool.

Michael Healey presides as the hotel manager, greeting every untoward thing that happens by looking, as is his wont, amazed but not surprised. Dropping and then hanging in at the hotel piano is Scott McCord as Louis the lounge act, hell's answer to Billy Joel, breathing lascivious-sounding greetings into his microphone and whispering his way, as imperturbably as incongruously, through what he claims is his trademark rendition of Rhinestone Cowboy.

Both of these actors are unforced fun. Less so is Marjorie Campbell as (I think) the proprietor's wife, interrupting illicit trysts with her frenetic cleaning, as if to prove that a vacuum abhors Nature.

Crossing over to the guest list: Marthas Ross also seems to be trying too hard, or her portion of the script does, as a self- proclaimed famous writer who claims to recall assignations with the manager on the beaches of their youth. Kristen Thomson, as a visitor very rich and very easily provoked, has surprisingly little to do except, at the end of the show, give birth. (She has looked convincingly pregnant earlier on.) She does get, all too briefly, to intone a blues to Louis' accompaniment, including a line that sounds like "I'm not Judi Dench." Maybe she isn't, but I can't think of a Canadian actress who comes closer.

The prize turn on this side of the register is Alon Nashman's; he plays Tom Cruise, or at least plays an actor playing Tom Cruise, who in turn does not wish to be recognized, despite having adopted the thinnest of disguises, or at least it would be thin if Nashman bore the slightest resemblance to Cruise in the first place.

You're lost, aren't you? So was I, and I'm not convinced that all this blurring of lines and confusion of roles (where's that fourth wall again?) is justified by the amount of laughter it raises. In his own right, though, Nashman is very appealing, whether descending the staircase, singing along with the Sammy Davis record of What Kind of Fool Am I without quite knowing the words or at least the phrasing, or grandly taking on Louis to play "the Soundtrack to My Life."

His antics lead to a kind of showdown but it doesn't count for much. Nor do Healey's head-scratching reflections (he always sounds like he's scratching his head, even when he physically isn't) on humanity being divided into those who find life too short and those who find it too long. Nor does the (possibly related) fact that the play ends with both a baby and a corpse in view. The show prides itself on being inconsequential, but even inconsequentiality has consequences, the chief one being that it's difficult to keep it funny over a space of nearly two hours. (An alternative might be to make it menacing, but Leah Cherniak's production hardly tries for that.)

There are longish periods when Hotel Loopy becomes, to clean up one of its own jokes, Hotel Droopy. When it is funny, though, it's sublime.

Black & White Photo: John Lauener, Tarragon Extra Space / Who are these clowns? They are, from left, Michael Healey, Kristen Thomson and Rick Roberts.

SALOME

Barrymore Theatre, New York

Al Pacino, Marisa Tomei, Dianne Wiest and David Strathairn headline, under the direction of Estelle Parsons, in what is billed as Oscar Wilde's Salome: The Reading. In other words, your money (were talking Broadway prices) buys you an impressive quantity of star power, even if the stars havent learned their lines. The bargain is a fair one, as the stars are blazing. Indeed, even the downside has an upside, since actors who appear with scripts are automatically excused from getting into period costume or strutting about in front of period sets. When, as in the case of Salome, the period in question is Biblical, this can save a lot of embarrassment.

Salome, the play, is a curiosity of curiosities. Wilde wrote it in 1893, in French; it was then translated into English by an unknown hand. (The translator credited in the published text is Lord Alfred Douglas, but authorities doubt the truth of this, and in fact Douglas denied it himself. He said if he had written the translation, it would have been much better. Maybe Bosie's indignation at being held responsible for what he considered inferior goods does something to explain his subsequent bad behaviour.)

Wilde's play inspired Richard Strauss opera, whose success, as is often the case with musicals, has eclipsed that of the original. The play is hardly ever revived, which is unfortunate because, though lush and eccentric, it is very good. It tells the familiar Biblical story: The prophet Jokanaan (John the Baptist) is imprisoned in a cistern in the palace courtyard for railing at Herod the Tetrarch of Judea, and especially at his marriage to his brothers widow, Herodias. Salome, Herodias' daughter and the object of her stepfather's unrequited lust, is fascinated by Jokanaan, who angrily declines to have any bodily contact with her. Herod begs Salome to dance for him, promising any reward she fancies, even to the half of my kingdom. She does her show-stopping number, the one with the veils, and asks for the prophets head on the famous silver charger. Herod reluctantly gives her what she wants; she bestows on the mouth of the dead Jokanaan the kisses that the live one had refused. Herod, in a presumed mixture of jealousy and disgust, orders her killed.

All this is economically dramatized in one continuous and concentrated scene that yet finds space for a telling accumulation of sidelights; as well as text, we get context. We hear the squabbling Jewish sects, forever arguing points of doctrine. We get some insight into the new Roman Empire, to which an admiring Herod owes his authority (hes very impressed that the current Caesar should have found time to write a satire attacking the Stoics). Above all, we are made aware, through the thundering admonitions of the Baptist, of the new cult that is advancing on Jerusalem from Galilee, and that represents a threat to just about everyone onstage. Jokanaan advises Salome to seek out Jesus (whose actual name is never mentioned -- he's simply the Man) and ask forgiveness for her sins. She shows no sign of having heard what he's saying. Herod, who takes a livelier interest in the world around him and is something of a humanitarian in his spare time, approves of some of the miracles whose report has reached him: "I hold it," he says, a good deed to heal a leper. But there are limits. He knows when his power is really being challenged. "I allow," he insists, no man to raise the dead.

Wilde seems to have been inspired by the swift barbarity of the story and by the contrasting luxuriance of the atmosphere in which it unfolds. His style massages the palate like a bunch of ripe grapes, slowly crushed and savoured one after another; it lingers on detail. Much of the text comes in list form. It begins with Herodias page describing the strange look of the moon ("she is like a woman rising from a tomb") while his friend the Young Syrian, who later kills himself rather than watch Salome throw herself at Jokanaan, rhapsodizes on the Princess extraordinary beauty. It's difficult to keep track of who is celebrating which. Salome professes her adoration, first of Jokanaan's body, then of his hair, before finally settling on his mouth -- she has an atlas worth of topographical similes to bestow on each feature. Herod, who seems to owe his literary colouring as much to the Arabian Nights as to the New Testament, has an astonishing list of consolation prizes -- peacocks, pearls, crystals and emeralds with miraculous properties - - to offer Salome in exchange for her requested delicacy of tete du Baptiste sur le plat.

The scripts calculated excess seems to call out for rich, ripe, oratorical acting -- the kind for which English actors, raised on Shakespeare, used to be recruited in order to bestow a semblance of class to the supporting roles in Hollywood epics. That, in the current production -- an Actors Studio project that has been percolating in private for years before braving the New York masses - - is just what it doesn't get. The actors go as far as is humanly possible for the demotic, the naturalistic and the conversational, in fact for the unabashedly American, and once we get over the initial shock to our expectations, it works. This is where Parsons' informal staging proves its cunning. The pretence of reading is by now just that (Pacino, in particular, negotiates great verbal parabolas without once glancing at the text), but it helps keep convention at bay. A large, and very uneven, supporting cast sits on nondescript benches and rostra, chiming in as required. Meanwhile, the four leads share, roughly speaking, a couple of styles between them.

The more solidly traditional work comes from Strathairn, who makes Jokanaans imprecations lucid and imposing without ever sliding into gratuitous rhetoric, and from Wiest, a splendidly forthright Herodias, whose disdain for symbols and omens (the moon is like the moon, that is all) stands in refreshing contrast to the mental habits of virtually everybody else onstage. These are timeless performances.

Tomeis Salome, by contrast, is violently, sulkily contemporary. If she's a princess, she's a Jewish-American one, and her dance is little more than a series of sulky gyrations. Herod, one feels, is rather easily aroused. But then Salome is the archetypal Hollywood brat, and Tomei unerringly conveys the headlong selfishness of a child trained to get everything she desires and to acknowledge no other horizon.

The driving force, though -- onstage and apparently behind it -- is Pacino, who has been experimenting with Herod for ages. My companion mused aloud on the reasons for the actors long fascination with the role. The best reason I can think of is that it allows him to show off.

But he shows off very creatively. The only other time Ive seen him live was in a production of American Buffalo in which he was like a parody of Method acting, all mumble and mannerism. Here, though, he really communicates, though certainly in an offbeat way. He proves at the end that he is fully capable of the grand manner; for the most part, though, he offers us insecurity enthroned.

His Herod is as egotistical as Salome, but brainier. He knows what he wants: He wants her, as once he wanted her mother. (That passion has long faded, as Wiest's Herodias, steeled in contempt, bitterly acknowledges -- not, one suspects, that she fancies him much either.) But he is restrained by fear of just about everything. He fears Caesar and he fears the supernatural, so he does his best to ingratiate himself with both. He speaks, repeatedly, of an enemy, the King of Cappadocia, on whom he tries, childlike, to unload all his fears. It is that king, not he, who tells lies, and who will be summoned to Rome and crucified, and who will be eaten of worms as the prophet has foretold. When he hears of the rumoured new Messiah, he reaches heights of sublime petulance. ("This Man must be found and told that I forbid Him to raise the dead.") The catalogue of luxury goods with which he tries to buy Salome off is hilarious and frightening.

His wheedling and whining becomes, undeniably, a little monotonous, but then so, I suspect, would any other treatment of the role. He has certainly found its heart. Reading the play after seeing Pacino perform it, I found myself unable to imagine it done in any other way.

Black & White Photo: Sara Krulwich, The New York Times / Al Pacino (here with Marisa Tomei as Salome), the driving force behind this production, has had a long fascination with his character, Herod.

MISALLIANCE

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

Nobody ever accused Bernard Shaw of being self-effacing. He liked to write himself into his own plays, not only through his ideas, which can be blessedly hard to pin down as both he and his characters keep contradicting themselves, but through his perceived public personality. The central character (i.e., principal chatterbox) of Misalliance is John Tarleton, Edwardian underwear millionaire, self-made and self-taught, with a literary reference to fit every occasion. "Read Darwin," he will say when the conversation takes an appropriate turn, or "Read Chesterton." When the topic that arises is the Superman, Tarleton's recommendation is "Read Whatsisname." And he doesn't mean Nietzsche.

A bust of Whatsisname, a.k.a. GBS, and another of Ibsen, Whatsisname's playwrighting idol, adorn the set for Neil Munro's production of Misalliance, which opens this year's Shaw Festival. (It's also the first production of the new Jackie Maxwell regime, though in style, quality and personnel it's indistinguishable from the old Christopher Newton one. I'm not complaining.)

There's a moment in Shaw's text at which an incensed young man lashes out and smashes the nearest available object. In this production, that object is the Shavian head. "I never liked it much," says the next arrival, surveying the debris.

The director makes the author's presence felt in other ways as well. He begins with a film clip of Shaw, delightedly presenting his right "profeel" (his pronunciation) to the camera, before turning round and, with equal satisfaction, showing off his left. The message seems to be that you never know where to have him but he's always in control.

The play itself, as already noted, is pretty self-referential to begin with, not only in its incidental little jokes but in the larger joke that constitutes its very nature. It's subtitled A Debate in One Sitting (though an intermission is permitted), and it's like a parody of the popular idea of Shavian drama: all talk, no action.

Actually, Misalliance has plenty of action, much of it bizarre. What it doesn't have is plot. As for the chat, Hypatia Tarleton, daughter of the underwear magnate, complains repeatedly that her family and friends do nothing, but of course in doing so she's merely adding to the volume. (Pun intended. To put it another way: She can talk. And does.)

The title seems to derive from Hypatia's insecure engagement to an overbred young runt named Bentley Summerhays, but the last thing anyone cares about, either on stage or in the auditorium, is whether this match will go through. Hypatia prays for adventure to fall from the skies, and so it does when a plane crash-lands onto her father's grounds, piloted by an old friend of her fiance, and with a Polish lady acrobat as passenger.

This leads to amorous complications, but you could hardly say the play is about them. Nor, despite the protestations of its preface, is it about the relationships of parents and children; that's merely a subject that gets vigorously discussed from time to time. In the end it seems to be about itself, about its cheekiness in bending our ears, and its success in not boring us while doing so.

And, yes, it's probably about a privileged section of English society that is neither as secure nor as virtuous as it would like to believe. In that respect, it's a light-hearted preview of Heartbreak House, a more sombre Shavian talkfest that ends with an impromptu air raid, a more sinister attack from the skies. Munro pushes the resemblance as far as it will go, and probably farther; he begins with the sound of an aerial takeoff and ends with the characters huddled together in anticipation of another descent.

It's a prickly, enjoyable production that falters only when the director lets his own sense of humour, which is heavy-handed, get in the way of his author's; and a uniformly expert team of actors ensures this doesn't happen very often. Only two performers cause misgivings, and they, I suspect, are obeying orders.

One of them is Pete Treadwell as the would-be assassin of Tarleton, who long ago done his mother wrong. This character, a downtrodden but volubly politicized cashier, emerges from a portable Turkish bath brandishing a revolver (which earns him the name Gunner) and proclaiming, "I am the son of Lucinda Titmus!" Later, confronted by evidence of immorality in the Sussex countryside, he utters the dumbfounding prophecy, "Rome fell! Babylon fell! Hindhead's turn will come!"

It must be very difficult not to make him funny, and no other actor I have seen has tried, but Treadwell, who plays him as a genuine skulking menace, brings it off. The idea presumably is to make his subsequent description of the wage slave's appalling lot hit home, and to make his bullying at the hands of his betters seem despicable. Both these things happen, but they could have happened anyway, and been even more effective for the change in tone.

The opposite fault -- pressing too hard for laughs -- afflicts Sharry Flett's Mrs. Tarleton in her exaggerated efforts to make the Polish lady, who speaks the language perfectly, understand English. Mrs. Tarleton is in some respects a blinkered woman, but she doesn't deserve to have this kind of stupidity attached to her; indeed, she emerges later on as the wisest and most charitable person in the play, and when Flett is allowed to take this opportunity she does, beautifully.

Nobody is right, nobody is wrong, everyone is fallible and therefore funny, everybody has a case. That's the key to Shaw, and this company knows exactly how to turn it. Lorne Kennedy is a bantamweight but thoroughly persuasive Tarleton, spryly phrased and with solid Northern roots, and Michael Ball gives the wittiest performances of the evening as Lord Summerhays, ex-colonial governor, sinking into old age with every ironic nerve twitching.

Of the youngers: Laurie Paton plays the acrobat with suitably perfect poise, finding juice in every syllable; Mike Shara, beefily cast against his usual type, wins an excellent hearing for the proudly philistine Tarleton junior who would have infuriated his author had anyone else created him; David Leyshon snivels gently as Bentley; Graeme Somerville makes an ambiguously clean young Englishman out of the aeronaut, who has a better build-up than he has a role; and Jane Perry's pivotal Hypatia deserves the last word.

That indeed is what the text gives her, but she doesn't get it here. The production substitutes a final clip of Shaw himself, smiling, with infuriating assurance, as if to say, "There! I knew best." He didn't always, but in this instance he did. It seems a shame to contradict him.

Black & White Photo: Michael Cooper, Shaw Festival / PLANE CRAZY: Jane Perry as Hypatia and Graeme Somerville as Joey Percival in Misalliance.

BLOOD RELATIONS

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

The classic theatrical treatment of the Lizzie Borden axe murders is now just half a century old. I refer of course to the finale number from the revue New Faces of 1952. ("Oh, you can't chop your momma up in Massachusetts / And then get dressed and go out for a walk. / No, you can't chop your momma up in Massachusetts; / Massachusetts is a far cry from New York!") But Sharon Pollock's play Blood Relations comes in a very honourable second. It was first staged in Edmonton in 1980, has been constantly revived ever since, and now gets a slap-up outing at the Shaw Festival, in the space where the cosy English thrillers used to be.

I would not dream of being frivolous, but I can't resist pointing out a bedrock similarity between the revue and the play. Both deal with their subject matter by putting it in an explicitly theatrical context. In the New Faces item, Miss Borden's trial and acquittal in her hometown of Fall River, Mass., are presented as part of the weekly hoedown, complete with square-dance calls. ("Cross your fingers, knock on wood / Local girl is making good.")

The Pollock piece gives us psychodrama. We meet Lizzie in 1902, 10 years after the bloody events, still living with her sister Emma in the house where their father and stepmother met their grisly ends. Lizzie is also conducting an affair with a Boston actress -- this is historically accurate -- who comes for tea every Sunday. On one of these occasions, The Actress -- that's how she's tagged throughout -- asks, presumably not for the first time, "Lizzie, did you do it?" and gets an evasive answer, also probably as usual. But this time Lizzie, playing to her lover's strengths, goes on to suggest a charade. The two of them will act out the events leading up to the killings. Lizzie will play Bridget, the maid, and The Actress will play Lizzie. And in this way perhaps the truth will come out.

There are serious problems with this framework, but what stands inside it is pitilessly gripping. Lizzie lost her mother when she was two. Her father, a rich skinflint, took another wife whom Lizzie detested. At 32, Lizzie is still unmarried, still at home, in defiance of all the rules laid down for her age, class and period. Her parents resent this, and she resents them right back. (Her sister, older and equally a spinster, doesn't seem to get the same flak. But then she doesn't give it either.)

Apart from striking Lizzie while trying to bully her into marrying a man she barely knows and doesn't like, her father is planning to sell the family farm right out from under her. To top it all off, he takes an axe to his daughter's pet pigeons, thereby giving her ideas. Strangely enough, she seems to blame her misfortunes more on her stepmother than on her father, whom she protests she still loves. But she takes a chopper to the both of them anyway; we see her raise the murder weapon on each occasion, before the merciful blackout.

That at least is the conclusion to which the experience of impersonating Lizzie drives The Actress, and it seems logical, indeed inexorable. The historical Lizzie got off, but her assumed guilt has passed into folklore. We hear a bit of her counsel's defence, and it's very unpersuasive. He says, basically, that no well-brought-up lady could possibly have done such things, which is the flip side of the stifling condescension that sent Lizzie bananas in the first place.

Eda Holmes' production reinforces, quietly and superbly, the enveloping sense of doom. Victims and killer alike go soberly about their business, wrapped in invisible shrouds.

Michael Ball and Nora McLellan, the latter's performance being the best I have ever seen her give, are gravely controlled as the parents, meaning well and acting mean. Laurie Paton plays The Actress, which effectively means she plays Lizzie, and she is sharp and solid as a rock. Jane Perry, who is so to speak the official Lizzie, suggests that the haunted woman finds considerable release in assuming the comparatively cheerful role of the maid. (Both ladies, in their different ways, grant Lizzie a corrosive sense of mischief.) Sharry Flett is mild and drawn as Emma, whose absence from home on the crucial day made, as they say at awards ceremonies, the whole thing possible.

Paton, Perry and Flett (they sound like a team of solicitors) are all performing striking doubles vis-a-vis their previous night's roles in Misalliance. They are also the only actors who appear in the play's outer action, Flett's Emma having graduated over the years to the role of nagging conscience, or perhaps just nagging voice of propriety.

Pollock was probably right to go for something more complicated than a bald murder story. But the hares she starts don't actually run. Why, for example, does Lizzie play Bridget rather than any other character? There's no indication that her performance as the maid influences the way in which The Actress interprets Lizzie. How do we account for the scenes in which neither of them appears?

The play ends with Lizzie denying she did it, then turning on The Actress and saying "you did." At least, that's what happens in this production; in the published script she turns on the audience. It makes no sense either way. We may empathize with Lizzie's plight, but that doesn't convict us of anything.

There's no suggestion that The Actress has twisted the facts, or come up with a new discovery. Everybody has always believed Lizzie was the killer, and it's not as if we have any way of checking out the play's veracity as we watch it; few of us have the facts of the Borden case at our fingertips.

Actually, Lizzie's guilt is what makes the story interesting. Certainly it's what makes it dramatically interesting. In recognizing this, The Actress at least shows that she knows her own business. And most of the time, when she's not splashing out of her depth, the playwright does too. Jump like a fish, jump like a porpoise; all join hands and habeas corpus.

Black & White Photo: Michael Cooper, Shaw Festival / CHOPPY PERFORMANCE: Jane Perry, left, as Miss Lizzie, and Laurie Paton as The Actress.

Robert Cushman is the author of Fifty Seasons at Stratford (Madison Press/McClelland & Stewart).; rcushman@nationalpost.com

Five Shakespeares, a Greek element and two musicals

You never know till you get there. But at least on paper, the line-up for this year's Stratford Festival is one of the most adventurous there has ever been. In fact, in terms of the plays selected and the stages they're being deposited on, it may be the most adventurous ever.

Start, as is proper, with the Shakespeares. The safest bet, though I'm probably jinxing it by saying so, looks to be The Taming of the Shrew, at the Festival Theatre, the opening show of opening week, and the only one of the canon's proved crowd-pleasers to occupy the flagship stage. It has other things going for it as well. It's directed by Miles Potter, whose Romeo and Juliet was last year's best all-round Shakespeare, crowning a steady Festival ascent that had previously taken in a fine grapple with Greek tragedy (Medea) and a decent new play (Good Mother). He'd already covered himself with glory by directing The Drawer Boy in Toronto, not to mention being the namesake of and inspiration for one of its characters. It would be tempting to say that no one is hotter than Potter; actually he's not that kind of fire-breathing director, but he's better than some that are.

His Kate, formerly his Medea and his Good Mother, is his good wife, Seana McKenna. McKenna was recently hailed in a Toronto Life profile as the first lady of Canadian theatre; I can think of a few contenders, but I don't think anyone could doubt her present pre- eminence among Stratford actresses.

An ungallant but unavoidable observation; McKenna is playing opposite a Petruchio (Graham Abbey, the Festival's current young lion) from the generation below her own; it will be interesting to see if the production wants to make anything of it. It's been done before (a 20ish Peter O'Toole once tamed a 50ish Peggy Ashcroft at the English Stratford) but then what hasn't?

There have also been productions, both in and out of Stratford, that have dressed the actors in cowboy hats and boots, which this production has been advertised as doing. It's one way of taking the well-known chauvinist curse off the play, though how far that curse actually exists where audiences are concerned is open to doubt. One has almost to apologize for pointing it out, but the Shrew has an unusually consistent history of being damnably entertaining.

The season's only other brand-name Shakespeare is Antony and Cleopatra, a play sublime but booby-trapped. It's at the intimate Tom Patterson, a move that may deflect some of the Burton-Taylorish assumptions that persist in clinging to it.

It's directed by Martha Henry, whose track-record in this space (Richard II, Elizabeth Rex) is outstanding but who is still, as a director, somewhat underrated. Her leads are Peter Donaldson and Diane D'Aquila, Stratford trusties branching out; I anticipate a grizzled, bitter-sweet approach, but it's only a guess.

Meanwhile, the other two main-stage Shakespeares are plays that people, including me, have been saying would never again be risked there. Antoni Cimolino directs Love's Labour's Lost, his first production since his admirable Twelfth Night two years ago. This, for all its apparent obscurity, is an enchanting play and one with an especially glorious Stratford record. (Some people still have dreams about Michael Langham's 1950s production.)

Pericles, seen here only twice before, is directed by Leon Rubin; he works a lot in the east, which sounds right for this magical mystery tour of a play, and was also in charge of last year's invigorating Henry VI plays in which Jonathan Goad, now cast as Pericles, gave a breakthrough performance.

This year's sheer volume of Shakespeare -- five plays -- is encouraging, given what the festival is supposed to be about. Some of it may be attributed to Richard Monette's declared determination to mount the complete works in the course of his regime, though now his contract's been extended he may relax the pace somewhat. (If he doesn't, Timon of Athens, Henry VIII and Cymbeline will all make their bows in 2004.)

Monette's own production of Troilus and Cressida -- one of the greatest plays but, again, seen at Stratford only twice before -- connects with what may prove to be this season's most memorable feature, and certainly looks like its bravest: its Greek component.

This, a long-gestated Monette project, looks remarkably wide- ranging. It's one thing to put on Greek tragedy; Stratford's record here, though not exactly abundant, goes back to Oedipus in the second season. Greek comedy, we hardly ever see; the cynic in me murmurs there may be a reason for this but I'm prepared to put him on hold while I await Aristophanes' The Birds, directed at the Patterson by an actual Greek with the almost too-perfect name of Nikos Dionysios.

Meanwhile, Stratford's new Studio theatre gives us an intriguing variation on Aeschylus' Oresteia trilogy: that is, it begins with Aeschylus' own first part, Agamemnon, and then proceeds to two 20th- century French plays that roughly parallel his second and third: Jean Giraudoux' Electra and Jean-Paul Sartre's The Flies.

It sounds stimulating and -- for the actors, who will have to play the same characters in very different plays -- a challenge. And to cap all that, we'll get a second dose of Sartre, a production (postponed from last year, when 9/11 prompted a wholesale drawing in of horns) of his elegant vision of hell, No Exit, a play far more often discussed than staged -- at least I've never seen it. All right then: Even I have never seen it. Nor have I seen The Birds or this particular Electra or The Flies, so I have much to look forward to; criticism has been described as conducting one's education in public, and mine has been much neglected.

There's more. Last year's studio season, the first, was wholly devoted to new Canadian plays. This year, there's only one: The Acts of Venus, being the second part of Peter Hinton's The Swanne: Princess Charlotte, another trilogy, whose first installment was delivered last year.

Those of us who were both bemused and fascinated by it back then will welcome another chance to figure out what it's supposed to be about. In the Tom Patterson there's a new-old Canadian play: Anne Chislett's Quiet in the Land, winner of the 1983 Governor General's Award and set, like so much else, in the First World War.

That's not mentioning the musicals. The King and I is the big one, the only non-Shakespeare on the Festival stage, with Victor Talmadge as the King and Lucy Peacock as I. (This will be nostalgic for me: I first saw Peacock as Eliza in My Fair Lady. I thought musicals were what she did.) At the Avon, there's Gigi, which was the first-ever stage version of a classic screen musical, and thus the first step on the road to the Disneyfication of Broadway; aren't you glad you're not young any more? This will be the third Lerner- and-Loewe show that Monette has directed. Can Brigadoon be far behind?

The Avon, which may fairly be described this year as Stratford's haven from experiment (well, it has a proscenium arch), is also home to "the family experience": a somewhat unfortunate label, I feel. This year it's The Hunchback of Notre Dame, which at least stands a fair chance of being better than last year's Scarlet Pimpernel. Chef d'oeuvre time: Brian Bedford directs and stars in Coward's Present Laughter, which sounds ideal.

Some of this has to work.

Black & White Photo: Michael Cooper / Seana McKenna as Katherina and Graham Abbey as Petruchio in a westernized version of The Taming of the Shrew opens Stratford next week.
