ON THE TWENTIETH CENTURY

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

I missed the train. I'm referring to the gleaming art deco monster that devoured the stage, dividing and combining and revolving and all but jumping in the air, when On the Twentieth Century was given its Broadway premiere in 1978. This is a musical about monsters, mainly of the sacred theatrical variety, and the train, the 20th Century Limited that chuffed its luxurious way between Chicago and New York in the Twenties and Thirties, is its emblem as well as its setting. Its a show whose keynote is extravagance: extravagance of decor, of expenditure, and of personal behaviour. Placing it on one of the Shaw Festivals smaller stages is, in some ways, to deny its nature. The production, by Valerie Moore and Patricia Hamilton, is mostly delightful, but you do sometimes feel the pinch.

The year is 1932. Oscar Jaffe, a habitually impoverished but unsinkably buoyant actor-producer-director, is fleeing from the collapse of his last show while already planning an even more spectacular next. He cannot afford to board what the title song calls the luxury liner between N.Y. and Chi at the station, but once it's moving he climbs in through a window and takes possession of the most desirable compartment.

Also in transit is Lily Garland, once Oscar's discovery, protege and mistress, now a movie star. Oscar schemes to pry her loose from Hollywood, from her current beefcake boyfriend, and from a rival manager, and re-sign her, personally and professionally. Ben Hecht and Charles MacArthur (the authors of the greatest American play, The Front Page) created Oscar and Lily in a play, Twentieth Century, that subsequently became a movie with John Barrymore and Carole Lombard playing roles that might have been written not so much for as about them.

The musical is the adaptation of one crack duo by another. The book and lyrics are the work of Betty Comden and Adolph Green, and theatrical monsters were their stock-in-trade. (One has, sadly, to speak of them in the past tense since their extraordinary 60-year- and-some collaboration ended when Green died last year. Its good that he should have this production as a memorial, though it obviously wasnt planned that way.)

As screenwriters they provided the fuel for Jack Buchanan's self- proclaimed genius director in The Band Wagon and for Jean Hagen's silent movie queen ("if we have brought a little joy into your humdrum lives, it makes us feel like it aint all been in vain for nothin ") in Singin' in the Rain. You can see traces of both these characters in Oscar and Lily. Comden and Green surveyed the world they grew up on, and later in, with affectionate irony, and they did a lot to keep it alive, at least in our thoughts. They were also high on professional eccentrics: as in this show Mrs. Letitia Primrose, a crazed moral reformer plastering the locomotive with stickers announcing the end of the world and warning sinners of the consequences. She has a song on this theme called Repent: Like you I once was wild./Men shouted 'oh, you kid!/A life of shame I led/ And dirty doings did. That last line is pure Comden and Green. They adored mock formality; they loved to take a cliche and twist its tail. Maybe the funniest lyric line in this show is "But, but, but, but, but, but, but ...", sung by several characters in succession when in receipt of unwelcome news. You might expect to find it in a very bad novel. Set to music in all its shamelessness, its artifice proudly exposed, it scintillates.

The music to which its set is Cy Coleman's. Coleman was a natural collaborator for Comden and Green. Like them he's urbane, a wit, and one of the last upholders of a great tradition. Hes the jazziest Broadway composer since Harold Arlen. In this show, however, he put the rhythm largely on hold. Lily, Oscar and their cohorts, who behave operatically, are given opera and operetta parodies to sing. Its a lovely notion, and sometimes it works: when the stars, temporarily reconciled, are cooing Our Private World at one another, or when Oscar stages a mock-death scene out of Puccini. The title number that sets the train in motion is marvellously elegant and propulsive, and occasionally the jazz breaks through, which is a relief. But rather too frequently the show comes over as the idea of a wittily over-the-top extravaganza, instead of the thing itself. Some of the score is inert, including a quarrel duet that notably fails to end the first act with a bang.

Inevitably, some of the weaknesses are accentuated in this production. Paul Sportelli's cut-down orchestrations are very neat, but one does crave a bigger sound. It's a pleasure, as always at the Shaw, to hear unamplified singing (and there always seems to be some actor in the cast whom you never suspected could sing, and can), but though most of the performers can project their voices or their personalities over the band, they cant always get both across at the same time. Which brings us to the matter of star power, in a show thats supposed to be about it. Every actor I have seen in the role of Oscar has had to struggle uphill, trying hard to be dynamic and debonair and not bringing it off, and Gary Krawford here is no exception. But then he doesn't have the material; though the script keeps insisting on the chemistry between the two leads, it never makes us feel it, and Oscar's solo songs always seem to be in a losing competition with Lilys.

One reason for this is that his are static proclamations, while hers tell stories. We first meet her in flashback, a catarrhal rehearsal pianist propelled into stardom by Svengali-Jaffe and let loose on a song called Veronique, about a French heroine who inspired a nation by refusing her favours to Bismarck. ("Veronique, she close her door/And start the Franco-Prussian War"; its like a parody of the Les Miserables view of history, avant la lettre.) Later she gives us Babette, in which she's a Somerset Maugham heroine: the only example I know of a song that successfully lampoons a whole style of spoken drama. Patty Jamieson is especially taking as the earlier, humbler Lily (real name Mildred Plotka) of whom of course we don't see much. There are some blanks and glitches in her prima donna stage, as if she were saving herself for her coloratura moment, which admittedly is stunning when it comes.

Brigitte Robinson cannot quite sustain Mrs. Primroses big number, but she has a manic determined twinkle thats thoroughly right. Patrick R. Brown, long and lugubrious, and William Vickers, rotund and desperate, do terrific work as Oscar's aides, for whom life is one long loyalty test; Brown looks rather like Adolph Green, which is not only appropriate but helpful. Evan Buliung is funny as Lily's narcissistic performer though he doesnt equal the ecstatic acrobatics that made a star of Kevin Kline when he created the role.

Valerie Moores choreography is excellent; the more people she has to move, the merrier. Especially nifty are the mass embarkation, and the whirlwind imbroglio She's a Nut, which sweeps up the cast, the storyline, and the audience. We even get -- something I'd hardly dared hoped for -- the prescribed glimpse of Mrs Primrose clinging indomitably to the front of the engine. Indeed, whatever qualms I may have about its scale, Yvonne Sauriol's locomotive design is a sleek treat in its own right, with the journey helped on its way by playful little devices like a toy train (used rather too often) and what seems to be a tunnel at the end of a light. Her costumes are superb. Unusually in a musical, the second act is better than the first. By the end joy is unconfined, even if the show isn't.

Black & White Photo: Andree Lanthier / Gary Krawford as actor- producer-director Oscar Jaffe and Patty Jamieson as his once protege and mistress Lily Garland.

WIDOWERS' HOUSES

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

I know people who can't stand Shaw, but who make an exception for Widowers' Houses. It was his first play, originally staged in 1892, and in some respects it's a crude one, but its crudity is bracing. It is free of the sound of the author congratulating himself on his own cleverness. Widowers' Houses is an "issue" play, but like all the best of its breed it transcends that label and becomes a moral play, though not -- to echo a distinction made by one of its own characters -- a moralizing play.

The issue here is slum landlordism. The deeper themes are poverty and responsibility. Harry Trench, a young London doctor on a holiday jaunt to Germany, falls in with Sartorius, a self-made gentleman of mature years and ample income, and his daughter Blanche. Harry and Blanche are mutually attracted, and he asks for her hand. Her father is glad to grant it, since Trench, though of modest personal means, is aristocratically connected.

Back home, Trench discovers that his future father-in-law's wealth derives from buying up decayed properties, letting them decay further, and squeezing rents out of impoverished families who have nowhere else to go. Trench, revolted, wants nothing to do with the business or its proceeds, until Sartorius points out to him that he is already profiting from it; he holds a mortgage on one of the properties. By now, however, Harry has alienated his fiancee by asking her to live on his salary. She, who has a temper to match her father's and is far less adept at controlling it, has him shown the door.

In the play's last act, the climate changes. Sartorius discovers there is more money to be made by improving his houses, thereby upping the compensation when railways and town planning call for their demolition. He is given this tip by Lickcheese, formerly his highly efficient rent collector but dismissed for authorizing some desperately needed repairs. Lickcheese has since become adept at insider trading, and is now a figure of oily prosperity himself. For the scheme to go through, Trench's consent as mortgagee is required, and he sullenly refuses to give it. But he is talked round, the lovers are reconciled, and the drama concludes with all proceeding in to what will undoubtedly be an excellent supper. There is a happy ending for all the characters except the unseen ones: Sartorius' tenants, who are still destitute and will shortly be homeless as well.

Many of Shaw's plays conclude in this way, with a festive finale beneath which the relevant social evils continue to fester. However, as the plays get progressively more talkative and diffuse (and also, to be fair, funnier and wider ranging), so the bonhomie tends to overwhelm the indignation. Here there's no mistaking it. The lines are drawn halfway through the evening, when Sartorius sets about demolishing Trench's illusions. Like all Shavian capitalists, he makes a very good case. People need somewhere to live; any improvements he put in would be stolen and burned for firewood; the situation is regrettable but it cannot be helped. Lickcheese, while railing at Sartorius' meanness, says much the same thing. Trench, convicted of fecklessness for never having examined the sources of his own income, can find no answer. He refuses to play the hypocrite by swallowing Sartorius' late conversion to the cause of slum clearance, but sex -- as powerful a lure as money -- destroys even these defences.

Joseph Ziegler, director of the Shaw Festival production, says in his program note that Shaw "offers us no hint of a solution." This isn't quite true. Before catechizing Trench, Sartorius says, "I assume that you are not a socialist, or anything of that sort."

"Certainly not," says Harry, indignantly. Shaw himself, of course, was a socialist, and he is here offering us the glimpse of a loophole, one that his characters immediately close. In other words, this is the best kind of propaganda play: the kind that keeps the propagandists offstage.

The roles have been cast largely against type, with varying results. Trench, an unthinking young hearty in Shaw's description, is played by Dylan Trowbridge as slight, intense and idealistic -- "boyish," as the stage directions prescribe, but in a more vulnerable way. It works, though, and Trowbridge's alternating bouts of passion, shame and confusion give the production much of its energy. There is a further injection from Peter Millard's Lickcheese, less cringingly Dickensian than his name and some of his lines might suggest, but solid and biting -- occasionally too much so, since he steps out of character to underline a few of his points. (Shaw isn't Brecht.) His insidious geniality in the last scene is very good.

Jim Mezon, with massively domed brow, curled grey moustache, trim beard, and walking stick rampant, brings his familiar quiet authority to Sartorius, and commands the stage as usual. I don't know why he goes sentimental instead of stern when reminding Blanche of his own mother's poverty, or why he relapses into Cockney while he's doing it. Or rather, I think I do know why, and I also think it's a mistake.

Blanche herself is a problem, partly because though she enriches the play, she also overflows it; everybody else is in a bitter parable while she's in Hedda Gabler. Her tantrums seem to have been inspired by one of Shaw's own lady friends. Her furious relations with her father and with her intended are more than the main action requires, but need more space if they are to register in their own right. (She also seems to be conducting a sado-masochistic relationship: a minute role, admirably filled out by Susie Burnett.) The production errs by bringing her final seduction of Harry down almost to the level of farce. Their last clinch needs to be passionately sustained if it's to bear the weight the author places on it. Lisa Norton has to strain hard, and mostly in vain, to reach the full dimensions of Blanche's passions, or indeed of her snobbery. If Sartorius has the vestige of a social conscience, she ("I hate the poor -- if they must be provided for, let somebody else look after them") has none, as he ruefully recognizes. It isn't her fault -- few things here are anyone's individual fault -- but she comes as close as anyone to being the play's villain.

Christina Poddubiuk has designed a versatile setting that blossoms especially in its third and last incarnation as a lamplit drawing room, a cosy bastion against the outer darkness.

Black & White Photo: Michael Cooper / Dylan Trowbridge as Harry Trench and Lisa Norton as Blanche in the best kind of propaganda play -- one that keeps the propagandists offstage.

THREE SISTERS

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

The fourth and last act of Chekhov's Three Sisters has been described as the high-water mark of modern drama. I find that accolade a little grudging; I think the summit is occupied by the third and fourth acts together. In Jackie Maxwell's production -- the last of the Shaw Festival's opening week and Maxwell's own first show as artistic director -- this sequence, comprising everything that happens after intermission, is a straight trip up Parnassus.

In the play's first act, we've watched the genteel Prozorov sisters try to maintain a civilized life for themselves in a country town a thousand miles from their longed-for Moscow. Civilization in this case means conducting cultured conversation with the artillery officers stationed nearby.

Act Two has shown the cultured dream thinning out; the women's adored brother, whom both they and he hoped would be a university professor, sinks into the life of a petty civil servant, drunk, henpecked and a cuckold. The third act takes place against the background of a town fire and, under pressure, nearly all the characters look at themselves and see themselves as failures. At its end, Masha, the middle, married sister and Irina, the youngest, each make a bid for a compromised kind of happiness. Masha confesses her love for the battery commander, also married, and Irina decides to accept the proposal of a kindly, homely ex-officer who adores her but whom she doesn't love. The whole long scene is an extraordinary crescendo of desperation.

The last act sees the soldiers ordered to leave town, Masha distraught, Irina's fiance killed in a duel and oldest sister Olga settled into the position of school headmistress, a job she swore she'd never take. It isn't quite tragedy. The cheerful sound of the departing military band spurs Olga to deliver the most measured of the play's many paeans to a happier and less constricting future, and Irina declares her intention to stop feeling sorry for herself and work. That's half the picture. The other half shows brother Andrei pushing a pram, containing a child that probably isn't his, as well as an old army doctor, far gone in vodka and nihilism, declaring everything meaningless.

This production keeps an exemplary balance, with Kelli Fox possibly the best and certainly the strongest Olga I have ever seen. She makes solid sense of every line she utters (a quality not universally shared by her colleagues) and her every reaction is a full one.

It's a truism that any good production of Chekhov makes certain lines strike you as if you'd never heard them before, though I sometimes wonder if this is as true for Russian audiences as for us foreigners, who are continually being exposed to new translations. Susan Coyne's version at Niagara strikes the occasional false note, but it is also full of perfectly chosen revelatory phrases, simple words in which the characters give themselves away for all time. Andrei (magnificently played by Ben Carlson) tries, in that incendiary third act, to tell his sisters what a wonderful woman his wife, Natasha, is. It's an uphill job, because he's lying, to them and to himself. Finally his shame overwhelms him -- "my dear sisters, my sweet sisters, don't believe me, don't" -- and he leaves the stage in something between tears and a cold sweat. Kulygin, the outclassed schoolmaster, says, "I love Masha, she's very special" -- nice greeting-card sentiments to be sure, but he's talking about his wife. And never before have I really appreciated Masha's refusal to enter the house that was her family's inheritance but that has now been colonized by her sister-in-law.

Olga begins the play with a calm celebration of Irina's birthday, and this too carries a lot of weight. The assured staging directs our eye to the happiness at the centre of the stage, and it takes a few moments to register the presence of Masha at the side, with discontent visibly gnawing. After this, the production takes something of a dive, with much of the acting becoming generalized, seemingly aimed more at creating a "Chekhovian" mood -- hesitant enthusiasm undercut by nostalgia -- than at transmitting specific meaning.

Chekhov's characters, especially his men, are notoriously prone to "philosophize" and to mock themselves for doing so, but maybe we should give them more credit for meaning what they say when they say it. Caroline Cave's Irina only achieves full definition when her world falls apart; her understated grief is very well handled. The attraction between Masha and Vershinin (Kevin Bundy) becomes an incoherent subplot; he barely emerges from the uniformed ranks around him.

Tara Rosling's performance of Masha is anchored by her delivery of a snatch of rhyme, idly repeated when first we meet her, desperately reprised at the close, and equally striking at both ends. The abandon of her parting with her lover is very fine, as is the devastation that follows it, and the deadly accuracy with which she lets a laugh break through her torpor when her husband (Douglas E. Hughes) tries to amuse her by putting on a false beard. What passes between these poles, though, is a blur.

The relationship of Andrei and Natasha (Fiona Byrne) comes over, by contrast, as sharp as a boxful of tacks. Cruelly, Chekhov shows us its best and worst moments in direct succession. At the end of Act One Andrei proposes, and at the start of Act Two they are parents, and Natasha is well down the road from shy to shrew.

What sets the production unshakably on its feet is the fight between Natasha and Olga -- insofar as Olga can fight -- over the fate of the superannuated nanny, Anfisa. It's a clash of two world views. Anfisa herself cowers between them, in yet another of Jennifer Phipps' uncannily complete embodiments of a tiny role.

Then comes the first of the parade of self-scourgings: the doctor's, delivered by David Schurmann. This actor's voice is ineradicably placid, more than one expects in this role, and you can feel him placing his words, but he is very powerful, and it's good to be reminded that the doctor was a gentleman before he was a bum. In the last act he gives some curt advice to Andrei, then, as always, gets distracted. You find yourself wishing, for both their sakes, that he could have said more.

Sue LePage's sets, filling the wide stage, make every moment look good. They also echo the play's increasing harshness. The last scene, the only exterior, makes us feel the town's isolation, and its imminent desertion, in our bones. It's only autumn, but there's a cold wind blowing through the farewells. The end, by drying its own tears, should bring on yours: not floods, perhaps, but well- tempered drops. This has been a very good first week.

Black & White Photo: Michael Cooper, Shaw Festival / From left, Kelli Fox as Olga makes solid sense of every line, while Tara Rosling's Masha and Caroline Cave's Irina round out the titular characters.

THE TAMING OF THE SHREW

Festival Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

The Stratford Festival's opening production of The Taming of the Shrew is set in the Wild West, or at least in its legendary movie equivalent. Two obvious questions: Is this illuminating? Is it fun? The answer is that it isnt always either, but that its enough of both to be worth anybody's while. Most importantly, Miles Potter's production sets off two lead performances that are in perfect command of the stage, the text and the audiences pleasure. Graham Abbeys Petruchio and Seana McKenna's Katharina exemplify what Stratford is, or should be, about.

Abbey's Petruchio is a Clint Eastwood hero, laconic and dangerous, with Morricone music heralding his entrance. (If youre going to turn a comedy set in Renaissance Italy into a western, theres obvious sense in making it a spaghetti western.) Presenting Petruchio as the strong, silent type sets up an interesting tension, since he's the most talkative character in the play. This is a Petruchio who can quell a frontier saloon with a glance, a gun and a twirling rope, plus a few card tricks and the odd reference to his deceased father. One of the production's nicer touches is the suggestion that the late Antonio was the terror of the county, and that Petruchio now has the use of his reputation. He also uses what you might call rhetoric, though even when hes at his most boastful, its on the level.

Level is the word for Abbey's delivery throughout. He rarely raises his voice, trusting to the fact that Shakespeare, presumably on purpose, has given him lines more colourful and sensible than are available to any other man in the cast. Abbey is adept at finding humour in his lines, rather than laying it on and gouging it out. He's nervous before meeting Kate (he checks his gun) and then, like most Petruchios, falls in love with her at first sight. But, having once paid his lyrical tribute to "the prettiest Kate in Christendom," he doesnt dwell on it. He is very businesslike, and the whole taming process is an uphill struggle, not a step to be taken for granted.

I wonder why no production I have seen has marked the turning point in Kates career: the moment at which, when Petruchio belabours a servant, she interposes with patience, I pray you, 'twas a fault unwilling. It must be the first time in her life that she has said a word on behalf of another person. Nothing else, though, is missed in McKenna's performance. She terrorizes would- be suitors with a rifle, and beats her younger sister Bianca up real hard. She is also age-conscious, and not just in respect to Bianca. She never gets over Petruchios reference to her as his elder, though I wouldnt say she makes a meal of it. Obviously she meets her match, in all senses, in Petruchio. Everyone else in town, male or female, is an idiot.

The conventional romantic interpretation of the play is at work here, but it's tested more rigorously than usual. This Kate never stops fighting. She isn't happily playing Petruchios game by the time they get to their sun-and-moon controversy. He has to work for her acquiescence, and he looks a bit silly when he gets it.

Her famous, or notorious, submission speech is delivered, with house-stilling virtuosity, to three separate recipients. Much of it is aimed, formidably, at the Widow, who turns up in the last scene as Hortensios bride -- a role I have never seen given such importance, or perhaps just never seen so well acted (by Lally Cadeau) as it is here. The gain to the play is enormous. Kate obviously loathes her on sight, as a complacent harridan. Some of the speech she directs at herself, as she tries to work out what her married role will be -- how much she owes and how much she is owed. The third audience is Petruchio, who is served gracious notice on what he can expect. She's on her knees at the end of the speech; when he demands a kiss, he has to join her there to get it. I wouldn't say this solves all the plays problems, but it gives them a healthy airing. When the couple go off to bed at the end, one is not only happy for them but relieved.

The badlands setting lends unusual plausibility to Katharinas words about husbands putting their lives on the line for their wives' protection, and it lends credibility to other bits as well -- to Lucentio's claim, for instance, that he killed a man the moment he hit town. But if you want to prove that Shakespeares text fits perfectly into this new landscape, you should play the game according to the rules. Theyre broken when you start mucking around with the place names, or for that matter changing "argosies" to shipments and "galliases" to goldmines. On a related point, we all agree that standards of Stratford verse-speaking have shot up, so couldn't they learn how to stress quite simple words like "satiety" and "choleric"?

The supporting actors seem to be on a loose rein, though probably no looser than in a conventional production. There's a lot of anxious subdivision of lines for laughs that dont come, especially in the courtship scenes with Bianca, plus the regulation number of phallic gags. (Save it for Aristophanes, later in the season. He holds the patent.) But most of them some of the time -- and some of them most of the time -- manage to zero in on their characters and their material.

Wayne Best successfully reinvents Grumio as a bowlegged cowpokes sidekick, as gabby as Hayes, and Donald Carrier as the amorphous Hortensio manages to impose himself in three separate identities: as earnest citizen, witless wooer and occasional moral compass. Jonathan Goad's Mexican Tranio is wildly excessive as a servant, but witty when impersonating his master. Paul Soles' Baptista looks and sounds exactly right as a white-coated senator in the making, and Kyle Blair gets some bashful humour out of Lucentio.

I liked Les Carlsons bemused Vincentio, who apparently came from England and kept his accent, and developed a soft spot for Barry MacGregors Pedant (now known as the Man from Mantua), who has two accents, one real and one fake, and gets confused between them. Deborah Hay's Bianca seems too dumb and mean to attract even this gang of admirers, but she makes some sense in the last scene, which she plays drunk. Indeed, everything comes satisfyingly together at the denoument, and when a production of a Shakespeare comedy has achieved that, it's achieved virtually everything.

Black & White Photo: Michael Cooper / PERFECT COMMAND OF THE STAGE: Seana McKenna as Katharina and Graham Abbey as Petruchio.

THE KING AND I

Festival Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

The Stratford Festival's opening week of politically incorrect theatre continues with The King and I, the fourth and last of the major Richard Rodgers-Oscar Hammerstein musicals. Rodgers' score is his last great one, and Hammerstein's book, which takes large historical and biographical liberties, is maybe his most ambitious feat of dramatic engineering. It's also an honest attempt, by a 1951 Broadway liberal, to present not so much a clash between two civilizations as a nervous encounter.

The King of Siam, in 1863, imports British governess Anna Leonowens, to help civilize (i.e. Westernize) his offspring and, eventually, his kingdom. This being a musical, the King and the teacher fall in love; this being an uncommon musical, their feelings remain not only unconsummated but undeclared. In the meantime, the show tells us, they learn from one another, and so perhaps, on a personal level, they do. Theoretically, their two cultures are meant to be mutually instructive as well. In practice, it's a one-way street. Everything the show and its audience would endorse -- free speech, the abolition of slavery, respect for authority rather than prostration before it, romantic love -- is here championed by the West and, at best, grudgingly accepted by the East.

The show's cuteness quotient is actually more troublesome now than its cultural complacency, though the two are likely to reinforce one another. I remembered the show's last scene as a deeply moving encounter between two people who never told their love and are about to be parted forever, without so much as a farewell duet to see them through. Very dignified, I'd always thought it. I must have blotted out the intrusive part played in it by the royal brood whose tears, on this occasion, pre-empted my own. I never got past the lump-in-the-throat stage, and I didn't even stay at that point very long.

Frankly, I have always found Getting to Know You, Anna's song- and-prance in the schoolroom, one of the more resistible items in the R&H canon; its jogtrot lilt and doggedly earnest lyric foreshadowing the later degradations of The Sound of Music. The other songs, though, are lovely: peaking musically in the sweeping serenity of Hello, Young Lovers and theatrically in the joyous, foreshortened Shall We Dance.

The show's artistic peak, though, is not a song: It's the ballet The Small House of Uncle Thomas, Tuptim's interpretation of Harriet Beecher Stowe. This sounds like a recipe for disaster -- two ethnic stereotypes for the price of one. But the masks, the sounds, the costumes, the Jerome Robbins choreography (with Eric S. Robertson executing fearsome acrobatic leaps as the wicked king) create a world and a style of their own. Tuptim's dramaturgy is as ruthlessly selective as Hammerstein's own, and her Uncle Tom is a minor figure, present only by right of title.

Debra Hanson's sets are imposingly palatial. The singing is mainly lightweight; the hallowed young lovers (Anne Marie Ramos and Charles Azulay) are pleasant, but their amplified top notes shriek. The two leads are not heavy vocal roles; the singing of Gertrude Lawrence, the original Anna, was erratic, and that of Yul Brynner, the once and forever King, bizarre.

It's the film, with its pitch-perfect dubbing, that has established false expectations, certainly in Anna's case. One does want the actors, though, to sing right up to their own limits, and neither Lucy Peacock nor Victor Talmadge does that. They tend to talk their songs, which makes them not more dramatic but less. Talmadge ruins his A Puzzlement song that way, not helped by fussy staging. Otherwise he makes an excellent king, fast and light without any loss of authority. Peacock, though, never goes out to meet him; she seems touched only at the start of Shall We Dance or when, with her back to us and her reddish-brown hair cascading down it, she listens to Helen Yu, as the King's number one wife, sing Something Wonderful. One wants Anna and the king to be funnier together. If they were, they might go on to break our hearts.

Black & White Photo: Michael Cooper / Lucy Peacock as Anna and Victor Talmadge as the King.

Antony and Cleopatra may be the first play ever written about stardom

ANTONY AND CLEOPATRA

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

- - -

STRATFORD - One of the problems with Antony and Cleopatra is that though a lot of things happen, very little changes. True, there is the little matter of an adjustment in the balance of the power over most of the known world, but even that is a foregone conclusion.

When the play starts, Mark Antony and Octavius Caesar are officially joint rulers of Rome and its dominions. But Antony, spending all his time playing around in Egypt, has already effectively abdicated. He rallies and struggles as the play proceeds, but his political position is at the mercy of his passion for Cleopatra, and that never alters. Neither, mercurial as she may be, does hers for him.

So the challenge is to keep us interested in the ebbs and flows. Martha Henry at Stratford gives us an intimate staging in one of the Festivals smaller spaces, though at times it seems to be aping the epic as far as is possible; soldiers, in the plays innumerable battle scenes, march up, down and around, much as they would probably do on the main stage.

There are some cliches and rough edges, and most of the supporting acting is inexplicably (and inexcusably) dull, but the gains outweigh the losses. We can concentrate on the people, and together or apart the two leading players stand, and eventually fall, in triumph.

Peter Donaldson's Antony is a man with a past, and knows it; he wants everyone else to know it too, and -- depending on the circumstances -- to adore him for it or to commiserate with him. Sartorially or cosmetically, he has few pretensions; he goes through the play in a brown jerkin, and when he speaks of "this grizzled head" (laying it, in a moment of operatic self-pity, on a block) he is being precisely accurate. But then this Antony doesn't need to dress up to convey authority; he really was what everyone says he was -- the great general, the charismatic politician -- and inside himself he still is. Only time and desire have changed the game and left him stranded.

This is a superbly clear performance. Donaldsons searching, decisive manner of speech is equally an asset to him as an actor, to us as an audience and to Antony as a character. Given a chance to command, he takes it, whether hoisting Cleo on his shoulder for a night on the town or sweet-talking Caesar or Pompey at a summit conference.

But his age betrays him twice over: in his refusal, born partly of fear, to take young Octavius seriously as a political rival, and in his knowledge that Cleopatra is his last great fling, causing him to cling to her desperately. He is shamefully convincing in his sadistic rage when she flirts with Caesars ambassador, and he hits the very nerve of Antony when he pours out his thanks to his servants -- partly because he really means it, and partly (as Enobarbus sardonically comments) because it's good for his image. The same double instinct is at work in his, initially botched, suicide.

The only thing the performance lacks is the capacity for excess; when Antony calls Cleopatra triple-turned whore or calls for "one more gaudy night," the words don't pull their weight. This keeps him from being a great, as opposed to a very fine, Antony. Theatrical history, though, suggests that there may never have been a great Antony, with the possible exception of Michael Redgrave; and even fine ones are rare enough to treasure.

Diane DAquilas Cleopatra is another very lucid performance, perhaps too much so: hers is a brilliant surface that never cracks. She shows us, skillfully, how her need for Antony parallels his for her; handsome and vocally sultry, she's younger than he but still aging, and she obviously feels vulnerable.

All the domestic details of their relationship -- the opening flirtation, the jealous banter, her fastening him into his armour -- are perfectly done. But this Cleopatra is too much the lady; she can't muster the fishwifes fury with which Cleopatra greets the news of Antonys marriage; the messenger should tremble for his life, and this one has no occasion to.

In the last act, where she assumes the mantle of Antony's Roman honour -- or where she helps herself to his image, he having no further use for it -- there is no transcendence; she simply glides through it.

Maybe this is right. Maybe Cleopatra should keep us guessing, a trickster to the end. She's a survivor; even her suicide is a survival tactic, and unlike Antonys, its beautiful. It's also her final joke.

One thing this production lacks, though, is humour, a deficiency that especially weakens Cleopatra's scenes with her maids, of whom one is inadequate and the other weird.

Nor, though its common practice, is there any reason to play the clown (Bernard Hopkins) of the last scene as a self-consciously winsome messenger of death. He doesnt have to be a barrel of laughs, but if he were innocently businesslike (You want asps? I got 'em) he would be more truly sinister.

Wayne Best as Enobarbus has his moments as a commentator, but he misses an astonishing amount of the role, including all of the wit and most of the soldiership. And when his anthology account of the queen in her barge had to be underlined with music to make its point, I felt like going home.

Antony calls Caesar boy, an insult I have never seen taken so literally as it is here with Caesar played by Paul Dunn, an actor barely out of teenage roles. It startles at first, but imposes itself as it goes along; prematurely silver-haired (a Caesarean family trait, perhaps), Dunn conveys Octavius's hero-worship of Antony, and his concomitant resentment, and the increasing confidence of a born diplomat reinforced by the callousness of inexperience. His closing speech, though, is excessively perfunctory: Caesar may be in genuine awe of his dead adversaries, or he may be furious at being cheated of Cleopatras presence at his triumph; either way he ought to feel something.

There are bits of business -- Pompey goes jogging, Cleopatra gets a massage, Enobarbus and Menas arm wrestle -- that seem merely fussy.

There is also a full contingent of messengers, running on and falling into exhausted heaps as if it were a rule of their (Eastern?) union.

The production is best when most direct. A set (by Allan Wilbee) that initially resembles a high-diving platform proves itself when it turns into Cleopatras monument. Its invasion by the Romans, lethally confusing in most productions, is superbly staged here.

I've used the word "image" a couple of times; and it may, in its modern sense, be the theme of the play. Antony, Pompey, Enobarbus all perish when what they think of themselves, and what they want the world to think, lose contact with what is practically possible. Caesar survives because his ambitions, his values and his achievements are in exact alignment; Cleopatra has it both ways, the only protagonist in Shakespeare to die in satisfaction rather than in agony.

It may be the first play ever written about stardom -- and its fate (which may be poetic justice) has been to fall victim to its own legend. More of it than usual comes to life here.

Black & White Photo: V. Tony Hauser, Stratford Festival / Peter Donaldson's Antony is a man with a past, and he knows it. Diane D'Aquila's Cleopatra is another lucid performance.

GIGI

Avon Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

STRATFORD, Ont. - There is a line in Gigi, both the movie and the stage show, that always sticks in my throat. "Paris," it says, "is a suburb of Maxim's." It's meant as a joke, of course, but to an uncomfortable degree it's where the show is coming from. Alan Jay Lerner, who wrote the script of both versions, had years before penned the screenplay of An American in Paris, and in its viewpoint Gigi is the ultimate American-in-Paris musical. It takes a populous and complicated city and reduces it to a set of wealthy, well- dressed people with nothing on their minds except their palates and - - overwhelmingly -- their own and other people's love affairs. All they have to worry about, apparently, are where their next truffles and Veuve Clicquot are coming from and where their last lovers are going.

The expounder of this vision, the musical's narrator and raisonneur, is Honore Lachaille, belle epoque boulevardier extraordinaire; or, to put it in the most convenient shorthand, the Maurice Chevalier role. Honore is the uncle of Gaston Lachaille, a playboy less comfortable with the routine, who finds solace in the humbler home of a lady known as Mamita, and her grand-daughter Gigi. Gigi's precise age is left coyly unspecified, but she's a schoolgirl. She's rapidly maturing, though; and Gaston, as all the world knows, comes to realize that she was trembling on the brink while he was out yonder somewhere blinking at a star. He falls in love.

The film, based on the novella by Colette, came out in 1958. It was Lerner's and Frederick Loewe's first work since their stage triumph with My Fair Lady, and it was another instant classic. It's like My Fair Lady without the Doolittles; it shuts out the workaday world. A stage version, with a few extensions to the script and score, reached Broadway in 1973, looking exactly like what it was -- an attempt to cash in on an already famous property. It was, as things have turned out, the first in a long and depressing line of such things, but people were choosier then and it flopped.

The show does try to distance itself from Honore's viewpoint more than the film did. Gigi's great-aunt, a hugely successful courtesan who elects to tutor the girl in such crucial matters as the distinctions between diamonds, is a dragon more monstrous here than she was in the movie; Honore himself admits, or complains, that his world is changing. But its existence in the first place is probably a figment of his author-lyricist's imagination. Lerner was married eight times (is this the definition of a romantic?) while Honore avoids wedlock like the plague. But the author admitted he identified with the old roue, or with roues in general, and that's where the show's heart is. Some of the suspense hinges on the question of whether Gigi will become Gaston's mistress or his wife. Audiences now might question whether the latter would be necessarily the happier fate.

You have, in short, to put some of your feelings on hold to enjoy Gigi. The film made it easy: It had sumptuous settings, an archetypal cast, a tight screenplay, one of the best scores ever written for a movie musical, and Paris itself. The show forfeits some of these advantages and dilutes others. The authors did not reinvent their original creation; they merely made it longer. Of the five new songs, only one (The Earth and Other Minor Things) is very interesting, and the additions to the book are padding. The second act seems to go on long after the story is essentially over.

Since the film itself has yet to disintegrate, Gigi is in the strictest sense a useless show. But comparisons seem to matter less the further away you get from the Main Stem. Broadway and Hollywood were in direct competition in a way Stratford and Hollywood are not, though to admit as much may be to relegate the festival to the level of superior summer stock.

Richard Monette's production is hardly at pains to disguise its origins -- it begins by projecting credits on to a pretty water- colour front cloth -- but it's livelier than either of the others I have seen (both British). Cameron Porteous' revolving sets make up an enjoyable pastiche of Parisian paintings, from Dufy to Lautrec, and the couture is the height of haute.

There is even a scene with real emotional resonance. Everyone's favourite number in the film is I Remember It Well, the duet of the two old lovers Honore and Mamita. So it is here; the temperature changes in the theatre from the moment they meet, and when the music starts you can feel the audience silently singing along. But we get more than a reprise. Domini Blythe has her own way with Mamita, not gently contradicting her amnesiac partner as Hermione Gingold did but complementing him, rapt in her own reminiscence. Hers is a lovely, delicate performance altogether, and her concern for her grand-daughter's fate is the most touching thing in the evening.

James Blendick's dapper Honore, by contrast, hews close to the Chevalier model, though in a voice more crusted with port than champagne. His singing sounds much stronger, full of new highs and lows, than it did last year in My Fair Lady. (It may help that Honore Lachaille's songs are more laid back than Alfred Doolitle's.) A minor puzzle in the production is why these two players and most of their colleagues sport French accents, while a couple do not. Patricia Collins' Aunt Alicia is imperiously English, assaulting all of her lines like some Lady Bracknell of the demi-monde, and reaping a reward on the few occasions when they're actually witty.

As Gaston, Dan Chameroy's point of origin is uncertain, and his performance also wavers. He deals resoundingly with the title number -- the one in which he admits, more or less, that he has grown accustomed to Gigi's face -- but he misses the sardonic snap of She Is Not Thinking of Me, a song I much prefer. Nor does he look quite right for the most eligible bachelor in Paris; there is a sulkiness to his lip and an aggressiveness to his chin that suggests the other, rather less sensitive Gaston whom he played in Beauty and the Beast. (Can an actor make a career out of playing characters with the same name in stage versions of movie musicals?)

As Gigi herself, Jennifer Gould acts and sings most refreshingly, but her final transformation works no magic; she is more attractive as a hoyden than as a heroine. Gaston's previous flame is played as such a screaming ninny as to cast serious doubts on our hero's taste, and there is too much anxious scampering about, with Donna Feore's choreography confining itself to regulation twirls and can- can lines. Nor is the production exactly chary of ethnic stereotypes, but then neither is the material; a guy can't even install a telephone without interpolating a "vive la France." "There must," proclaims Gigi, when failing to understand the lovestruck Parisians, "be more to life than this," but the show never even hints as to what that might be. Paris is Paris Again: a suburb fit for tourists.

One of the problems with Antony and Cleopatra is that though a lot of things happen, very little changes. True, there is the little matter of an adjustment in the balance of the power over most of the known world, but even that is a foregone conclusion.

When the play starts, Mark Antony and Octavius Caesar are officially joint rulers of Rome and its dominions. But Antony, spending all his time playing around in Egypt, has already effectively abdicated. He rallies and struggles as the play proceeds, but his political position is at the mercy of his passion for Cleopatra, and that never alters. Neither, mercurial as she may be, does hers for him.

So the challenge is to keep us interested in the ebbs and flows. Martha Henry at Stratford gives us an intimate staging in one of the Festival's smaller spaces, though at times it seems to be aping the epic as far as is possible; soldiers, in the play's innumerable battle scenes, march up, down and around, much as they would probably do on the main stage.

There are some cliches and rough edges, and most of the supporting acting is inexplicably (and inexcusably) dull, but the gains outweigh the losses. We can concentrate on the people, and together or apart the two leading players stand, and eventually fall, in triumph.

Peter Donaldson's Antony is a man with a past, and knows it. He wants everyone else to know it too, and -- depending on the circumstances -- to adore him for it or to commiserate with him. Sartorially or cosmetically, he has few pretensions; he goes through the play in a brown jerkin, and when he speaks of "this grizzled head" (laying it, in a moment of operatic self-pity, on a block) he is being precisely accurate. But then this Antony doesn't need to dress up to convey authority; he really was what everyone says he was -- the great general, the charismatic politician -- and inside himself he still is. Only time and desire have changed the game and left him stranded.

This is a superbly clear performance. Donaldson's searching, decisive manner of speech is equally an asset to him as an actor, to us as an audience and to Antony as a character. Given a chance to command, he takes it, whether hoisting Cleo on his shoulder for a night on the town or sweet-talking Caesar or Pompey at a summit conference.

But his age betrays him twice over: In his refusal, born partly of fear, to take young Octavius seriously as a political rival, and in his knowledge that Cleopatra is his last great fling, causing him to cling to her desperately. He is shamefully convincing in his sadistic rage when she flirts with Caesar's ambassador, and he hits the very nerve of Antony when he pours out his thanks to his servants -- partly because he really means it, and partly (as Enobarbus sardonically comments) because it's good for his image. The same double instinct is at work in his, initially botched, suicide.

The only thing the performance lacks is the capacity for excess; when Antony calls Cleopatra "triple-turned whore" or calls for "one more gaudy night," the words don't pull their weight. This keeps him from being a great, as opposed to a very fine, Antony. Theatrical history, though, suggests there may never have been a great Antony, with the possible exception of Michael Redgrave; and even fine ones are rare enough to treasure.

Diane D'Aquila's Cleopatra is another very lucid performance, perhaps too much so: Hers is a brilliant surface that never cracks. She shows us, skillfully, how her need for Antony parallels his for her; handsome and vocally sultry, she's younger than he but still aging, and she obviously feels vulnerable.

All the domestic details of their relationship -- the opening flirtation, the jealous banter, her fastening him into his armour -- are perfectly done. But this Cleopatra is too much the lady; she can't muster the fishwife's fury with which Cleopatra greets the news of Antony's marriage; the messenger should tremble for his life, and this one has no occasion to.

In the last act, where she assumes the mantle of Antony's Roman honour -- or where she helps herself to his image, he having no further use for it -- there is no transcendence; she simply glides through it.

Maybe this is right. Maybe Cleopatra should keep us guessing, a trickster to the end. She's a survivor; even her suicide is a survival tactic, and unlike Antony's, it's beautiful. It's also her final joke.

One thing this production lacks, though, is humour, a deficiency that especially weakens Cleopatra's scenes with her maids, of whom one is inadequate and the other weird.

Nor, though it's common practice, is there any reason to play the clown (Bernard Hopkins) of the last scene as a self-consciously winsome messenger of death. He doesn't have to be a barrel of laughs, but if he were innocently businesslike (You want asps? I got 'em) he would be more truly sinister.

Wayne Best as Enobarbus has his moments as a commentator, but he misses an astonishing amount of the role, including all of the wit and most of the soldiership. And when his anthology account of the queen in her barge had to be underlined with music to make its point, I felt like going home.

Antony calls Caesar "boy," an insult I have never seen taken so literally as it is here with Caesar played by Paul Dunn, an actor barely out of teenage roles. It startles at first, but imposes itself as it goes along; prematurely silver-haired (a Caesarean family trait, perhaps), Dunn conveys Octavius's hero-worship of Antony, and his concomitant resentment, and the increasing confidence of a born diplomat reinforced by the callousness of inexperience. His closing speech, though, is excessively perfunctory: Caesar may be in genuine awe of his dead adversaries, or he may be furious at being cheated of Cleopatra's presence at his triumph; either way he ought to feel something.

There are bits of business -- Pompey goes jogging, Cleopatra gets a massage, Enobarbus and Menas arm wrestle -- that seem merely fussy.

There is also a full contingent of messengers, running on and falling into exhausted heaps as if it were a rule of their (Eastern?) union.

The production is best when most direct. A set (by Allan Wilbee) that initially resembles a high-diving platform proves itself when it turns into Cleopatra's monument. Its invasion by the Romans, lethally confusing in most productions, is superbly staged here.

I've used the word "image" a couple of times; and it may, in its modern sense, be the theme of the play. Antony, Pompey, Enobarbus all perish when what they think of themselves, and what they want the world to think, lose contact with what is practically possible. Caesar survives because his ambitions, his values and his achievements are in exact alignment; Cleopatra has it both ways, the only protagonist in Shakespeare to die in satisfaction rather than in agony.

It may be the first play ever written about stardom -- and its fate (which may be poetic justice) has been to fall victim to its own legend. More of it than usual comes to life here.

THE HUNCHBACK OF NOTRE DAME

Avon Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

This adaptation of The Hunchback is a show in which things have gone so comprehensively wrong that it's difficult to know where to start laying blame. One might finger Victor Hugo himself for writing a novel so thickly-plotted nobody could hope to dramatize it in its entirety and still make sense. But he did not, after all, ask to be dramatized; though since his book has rarely been off the stage or screen since he wrote it, you might say he was offering an implicit invitation.

Those who have accepted it have usually taken liberties. In the words of the Stratford program, disassociating itself from such practices, previous versions have mucked around with "significant story points and even character destinies. I think the last phrase means that, in the past, happy endings have been imposed. There will, we are assured, be none of that kind of carrying-on here.

Jolly good. But unless you have eight hours of playing time at your disposal, such fidelity is likely to be self-defeating. Incident is not the same thing as action. In this show, plots, counterplots, playlets within the play, alchemical experiments, hysterical accusations of witchcraft, whippings at the pillory, stretchings on the rack, near-rapes, a hanging, and the occasional outbreak of true love succeed one another upon the stage at a pace I can best describe as a quick trundle. Along with them comes a motley horde (there really is no other phrase) ranging from Quasimodo, the deaf and deformed bell-ringer of the title, to that more elevated human gargoyle, Louis XI of France. And we are given no reason to care about anything that happens or anybody -- man, woman or beast - - that it happens to.

Rick Whelan has supplied a two-toned script, and neither tone is happy. Some of it is stiffly archaic and sounds like a bad old translation, the rest is gracelessly modern and sounds like a bad new translation. (I was worried sick" says a court lady to her returning swain.) The narrative method is equally inconsistent. We start with the actors telling us how the novel came to be written and filling us in on its earliest action: The depositing of the infant Quasimodo on the steps of Notre Dame and his adoption by the sinister archdeacon Dom Frollo; this prologue has some dignity and is, in retrospect, the highlight of the evening. The third-person voice is then dropped, only to return abruptly in the second half. One thing that plays and musicals have taught us about Paris is that its streets have always been crammed with picturesque, bloodthirsty rabble. So it is here, and a member of the crowd will sometimes step forward to fill us in on what the people are thinking. This habit grows until we reach the gypsies' assault upon the cathedral, and their repulse at the hands of Quasimodo. The cast, exhibiting no visible signs of shame, turns around and tells us about these exciting events; after all its put us through, the production throws its hands in the air and admits it doesnt know how to stage its own climax.

Dennis Garnhum, director and dramaturge (a double duty that may not have been a good idea) adds some incongruities of his own. The pet goat of the gypsy heroine Esmerelda is played by an actress, mounted on a trolley and holding up a pair of artificial forelegs: a piece of stylization that connects with nothing else in the production. Esmerelda herself has to be carried after being tortured, but a mere scene later she is running all over Notre Dame defending her virtue. Earlier she has enacted a marriage of convenience with the errant poet Pierre Gringoire, who according to the program notes loves first Esmerelda, then her goat, and finally and even more alarmingly the stones of Paris. Gringoire is played by Dan Chameroy in a vein of cringing comedy, with a voice that's a distant relative of Olivier's Richard III, suggesting were at a crookbacks convention. He does get a couple of intentional laughs, which puts him ahead of anyone else in the cast.

Nicholas Van Burek is affecting as Quasimodo, and probably benefits from the fact the hunchback's deafness makes him a man of few words. It is belatedly explained to us that he can lip-read; though this doesn't account for his apparent incomprehension when brought before a kangaroo-court earlier in the proceedings. Jennifer Gould is a spirited Esmerelda, though unable to convey the innocent strangeness that keeps her and society in a state of mutual incomprehension.

Stephen Russells Frollo has some initial presence, but is the victim of the most ineffectual series of exits and entrances ever visited upon a tormented villain. A couple of minor performances are irredeemably atrocious; the others are held hostage by a literally unspeakable text and a production that leaves them exposed and unsupported. Alexander Dodges sets, mainly in black-and-white photogravure, are reasonably atmospheric.

This production is the latest in a line of schoolroom classics marketed as "family entertainment." But it's far too dark and cruel for younger children, while those old enough for it would have a much better time at Pericles or The Taming of the Shrew. The show is the worst I have ever seen at Stratford, but something has to be and this will pass. What is more worrying, and should occasion some serious head-scratching at head office, is that it's a show aimed at no imaginable audience.

THE ADVENTURES OF PERICLES

Festival Theatre, Stratford

- - -

One of Shakespeare's last and most unruly plays, Pericles is also one of the few in the canon to employ a full-time narrator. He is John Gower, medieval poet, and he returns from the grave to tell the story. Or, as he puts it in the first of the endearingly clunky couplets that make up his role: "To sing a song that old was sung / From ashes ancient Gower is come."

Leon Rubins Stratford production takes this hint with bewitching literalness. At the beginning of the show the entire stage is swathed in white, billowing silk; it undulates like the ocean on which much of the action will take place. Up through a trap door shoots the figure of Gower himself, in his underpants, his head and body also painted completely white. A transfixing figure even before he opens his mouth, he turns out to be even more compelling when he does. Thom Marriott, who came to notice as a steely Warwick in Rubins Henry VI productions last year, here manages the surprising feat of tempering the steel with whimsy. His is a resourceful, playful and magisterially resonant performance, and it places him on the top shelf of Stratford actors.

The story into which he so seductively draws us is a picaresque, of a kind Jacobean audiences seem to have lapped up. Its hero begins as a self-cast Prince Charming, seeking the hand of the daughter of the King of Antioch. He recoils on discovering that she is committing incest with her father, who would kill him for the knowledge, and spends the next three acts as a royal refugee. En route he scoops up the more moral daughter of a more benevolent king but is shortly parted both from her and their daughter, the sea- birthed infant Marina. A 20-minute intermission allows the child to grow up 14 years and to face down threats to her own life and virtue. The key at the end is reunion.

At Stratford, once the silks have been dispersed, we find ourselves looking at the outlines of a ship. The masts and tackle frame the acting area, and the play's succession of far-flung locales takes shape within them. The action of Pericles has been described as a whistle-stop tour of the Near East; Rubin, who has worked extensively in Asia, and designer John Pennoyer push it farther and take us round the Middle and Far Easts instead. As far as I can tell, Arabs inhabit Antioch; Turks live in Tarsus, where Pericles relieves a famine and is scurvily treated for his pains; the Japanese rule Pentapolis, where he enters a martial-arts contest to win the hand of his bride, Thaisa (or should she be Thai?); and Indians appear to have colonized Ephesus, where the same lady undergoes a miracle cure at the hands of a boy swami on whom the play's great leap in time has no visible effect whatsoever. All this, abetted by Bruce Gastons music and Donna Feores choreography, is magic, taking up all the cues for showmanship that are built into the play.

The play's problem is its hero, who has no striking characteristics, apart perhaps from all-round decency; he is simply someone to whom things happen. Jonathan Goad does more than most to individualize him. He's an impetuous young man, running cheerfully into danger in the first scene, though with enough sense to get out of it quick; and he matures into an impetuous older one. It takes time; in the long scene in which he meets his daughter, he has to be drawn out of the catatonia to which he succumbed when he lost her. (He also stopped shaving.)

Once brought alive, though, he can hardly contain himself; even when her identity has been established, he cant stop himself demanding further proof, just for the joy of it. The humour here is probably the actors rather than the character's, but it makes the scene even more affecting than usual. Technically, Goad has still to discover legato; he bounces up and down on the lines, rather than letting them flow. But then, as Pericles is buffeted by fate, so any actor who plays him gets knocked about by the text, which is so corrupt that it never made it into the First Folio. It improves spectacularly as it goes along, but its first two acts, where the character has to be established, are in wretched shape. It must be hard for an actor to get an emotional purchase on it.

Lear and Cordelia, Pericles and Marina: Fathers and daughters provide the most moving moments in Shakespeare.

Nazneen Contractor does her part in the duet with a determination that would rouse any hypochondriac from his stupor. She lacks the unforced grace that should cling to these fairy princesses as of right, but she's a fighter -- a quality that has previously served her well in Mytilene, where Marina is sold into a brothel and talks her way out of it.

This, however, is the one part of the show where the exoticism gets out of hand -- though maybe Rubin is trying to show us the underside of The King and I. The brothel staff speak in prose, usually a sure sign that Shakespeare, whatever the plot says, was thinking of home. We should recognize these people, as he certainly did. The trappings come between the actors and their reality, and also between them and the jokes. Michael Therriault gets most of his prescribed laughs as Boult, the assistant pimp (the richest, if hardly the longest, part in the play), but its a strain. Sarah McVie, in a surprising role for last years Cordelia, makes an admirably businesslike Bawd.

A trio of fishermen put in a more respectable word for the working class, with Robert King especially good as the skipper. That's back in Pentapolis, where Karen Ancheta makes an unconventionally pert Thaisa. I could have done with more wryness and maturity than Charles Azulay brings to her father, a well- meaning monarch trying to give his blessing to two young people who are mad about one another anyway but are bent on playing Romeo and Juliet.

In all, the production is a delight; and, coming at the end of a most uneven opening week, it's a fair haven such as might have been welcomed by the storm-tossed Pericles himself.

Black & White Photo: Michael Cooper / Thom Marriott is transfixing as the medieval poet Gower, back from the dead to act as narrator in Shakespeare's Pericles.
