TOP GUN! THE MUSICAL

Factory Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - For a measure of how far civilization has declined, recall that 50 years ago Alan Jay Lerner and Frederick Loewe wrote My Fair Lady. They did not write Pygmalion -- The Musical. They had enough respect for their source material and for themselves to offer an interpretation rather than a rip-off. Since then, of course, the musical has dwindled from a genre to a suffix, to be tacked on to any property for which audiences might conceivably feel nostalgic. The creators of Top Gun! The Musical have noticed this phenomenon and are out to satirize it. Their source is the 1986 Tom Cruise film, but their show is not actually a musical of the movie. It's a musical about people who are attempting to put on a musical of the movie. So really it's Top Gun! The Musical! The Musical.

This may sound interestingly complex in theory, but it's rotten in practice. The production was a box-office smash at last year's Toronto Fringe Festival, proving yet again that in those hectic circumstances, audiences (not to mention critics) are liable to drop both their guard and their standards. Now that it's been remounted in its own right, its deficiencies gape.

They start with what the show apparently thinks is its smartest idea: the fact that Top Gun itself, being about aerial warfare, is the dumbest possible basis for a musical. Now, it's quite true that in the real world similarly hopeless projects are attempted all the time. I wonder if the authors realize that their title is only one syllable removed from something that actually happened, rather briefly, on Broadway in 1990 and that was called Shogun: The Musical. The question is: How much time do you want to spend making fun of this? We all treasure The Simpsons' immortal Oh, Streetcar, and some of us recall a movie called The Tall Guy, starring Jeff Goldblum and Rowan Atkinson, that involved a musical version of The Elephant Man. ("Somewhere up in heaven, there's an angel with big ears.") But the numbers in these cases never took up more than a few minutes of screen time, which is just the amount they needed in order to be funny. Beyond that a bad song is a bad song, whether it happens accidentally or on purpose.

Denis McGrath (book and lyrics) and Scott Wise (music) presumably realize this, which is why they've given their spoof a backstage frame. Unfortunately, the songs in the "real" story are no better than those in the fictitious one: worse, if anything, because they're sincerely turgid. Of course, it's possible that they're meant to be spoofs as well. There's one, a solo for a leading lady in need of a break, that is strongly reminiscent of the Music and the Mirror number in A Chorus Line, though it is not, as far as I can see, being played for laughs. In fact, I don't know how seriously the show's creators mean us to take their outer narrative; and, what's more, I don't believe they know either. I think they just drift from moment to moment, grabbing at whatever effect seems within reach. But you can hardly expect to keep an audience's attention for 90 minutes without offering them a foothold in something.

I admit my credentials for judging Top Gun! The Musical may be precisely the wrong way 'round -- that is, I have never seen Top Gun but I have seen a lot of musicals. The show may have been filled with satiric jabs at the movie that I totally failed to appreciate; though, in all honesty, the full Saturday-night house I saw it with didn't seem to be laughing all that much either. (They did clap at the end, though. I don't want to rig the case.)

I do know, because the publicity has told me, that the show wants to bring out the film's homo-erotic subtext, and there is one character, a gay actor, who's very insistent that Iceman, his role in the musical, is Maverick's real love interest. (I assume you know who these people are, even if I don't. Anyway you, unlike me, are under no professional obligation to confess your ignorance.) A once- male character, named Goose, has been recast as a woman. But the show-within-the-show is so obviously doomed, by incompetence as well as intractability, that we can't give a lick what they do to it.

Four weeks from opening, the creative team discover that they've been denied the rights to You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin', which they were planning to interpolate; "let's just say they're the Unrighteous Brothers," quips the director, in a fair example of the script's level of wit. It turns out not only do they not have the rights to that song, they don't have the rights to Top Gun. The producer who brings this news wants to push on anyway because it will be great propaganda for the war in Iraq; he's a fanatical U.S. vet, maybe still a practising General. Up until his arrival, I'd assumed the scene was Canada -- how else to explain the knowing references to David Mirvish and Garth Drabinsky, which, in substituting name-dropping for humour, had served early notice of the kiss of death?

The producer sings a song about putting asses in seats, but since the actor playing him has a trick of gabbling not only his dialogue but his lyrics, I couldn't tell whether he was hoping to achieve this end by filling his show with right-wing content or by eliminating all content whatsoever. Whichever it is, he manages to rile the director, who has ideals. This is surprising, because earlier on he has sung a very similar song called Forget the War. At politically charged moments like these, you wonder if the show wants to be Smoking Gun, The Musical.

The director is conflicted anyway because he's just come off Apocalypse Wow, which apparently lived up to the first word of its title but not the second. There is also a leading lady who arrives two hours late and puts the moves on the director, while demonstrating none of the charm or glamour necessary to get away with such behaviour. But why go on? Colin Viebrock's production, apart from being visually untidy, is extremely slow; every joke is given plenty of time to die. There is a cast of seven, of whom surprisingly few can sing. Dmitry Chepotevsky can (he plays Maverick) and he is also agreeably goofy. Alison Lawrence is more solidly appealing as the faithful stage manager who does most of the work (this is believable) but she is defeated when obliged to sing a generic blues that appears to think "biscotti" rhymes with "latte." One critic has compared this dreck to The Drowsy Chaperone, which, whatever its limitations, had excellent lyrics. When will they ever learn?

Lurking behind all this there may well be some talent and good intentions. Some of the tensions within the company are well observed. But consider: The cast sends us away with a reprise of Asses on Seats. Is this neo-Brechtian cynicism, or what? Everybody knows that, other things being equal, a show with songs is less boring than a show without songs, but it's time to stop trading on this circumstance and calling the results "a musical." It happens at every level, but at least the old mega-musicals (remember them?) had stories that they genuinely wanted to tell us. I never thought it possible, but Top Gun! The Musical made me nostalgic for the high professionalism of Aida (The Musical).

Black & White Photo: Top Gun! The Musical is a musical about people attempting to put on a musical of the movie. When will they ever learn?
2003-06-21-divining-dora-our-theatre-cri:
The four outstanding shows of the 2002-2003 theatre season in Toronto were A Chorus of Disapproval, The Shape of Things, Sunday Father and Sweeney Todd. Of these, all but the first were produced by the Canadian Stage Company: a surprising fact, perhaps -- given that CanStage also puts out a lot of middlebrow junk -- but a fact nevertheless. Despite this, CanStage don't get no respect. This places them at the opposite pole from the Tarragon Theatre, which gets oodles of it and whose productions have snagged a record number of nominations for this years Dora Awards. With these circumstances in mind, let us look at whos up for the Doras, which are being handed out on Monday night.

We had better start in the General (i.e. big, or at least bigger) division, with the contestants for Outstanding Production of a Play, which is not the same category as Outstanding Direction of a Play, a fact that must have many ordinary theatregoers confused. The best productions are the ones that at least look the best-directed, and if you weren't at rehearsals, how do you know otherwise? Maybe the Production trophy should be renamed Best Wrapped Package, or just Most Enjoyable Evening, though I admit that neither of these has as high-toned a ring. My own nominations would naturally be the first three shows listed in my opening sentence. (The fourth is a musical.) In fact, Neil LaBute's The Shape of Things has been shut out, not only from this category but from all the others, while Sunday Father has done hardly better. Being American, The Shape of Things was ineligible for Outstanding New Play; it was, though, incomparably the most exciting new-to-Toronto play of the season, and it was also well done, with fine performances by the indigenous Allan Hawco and -- though some people would say but -- the imported Amy Redford. So what gives? Xenophobia?

A Chorus of Disapproval has been nominated, and obviously it would be my choice: a funny and truthful play, in an English style thats not too easy to crack, brought off triumphantly by nearly every member of a large cast -- Soulpepper at its best. What probably will win (on the Oscar principle that its been nominated for nearly everything) is Tarragon's Girl in the Goldfish Bowl; this wouldn't be a disgrace, though the show was a classic case of the whole being less than the sum of its parts.

Soulpepper got a second nod for its Absolutely Chekhov compilation; surprisingly, since, as one would expect of a bill of five one-act plays, it was uneven.

One of the remaining nominees, Spark Productions Romeo/Juliet Remixed, was R&J in a disco, literally. Out of tenderness for my ears, I avoided it, but I gather it was an event. As for the others, Tarragons Russell Hill and Factory Theatre's revival of The League of Nathans, I don't know how they got in there. Russell Hill, to be fair, had everything going for it except a play. Is this what "production" means?

Outstanding Production of a Musical should, of course, be Sweeney Todd, and its in with a chance. It has a huge advantage in sheer quality of material. It will very likely lose, though, to Little Mercys First Murder (Tarragon), which seems to be another of those board-sweepers. Otherwise we have the barrel-scraping that's customary in this category: Brookstone's A Dixie Gospel (I didnt see it; it was probably wonderful); Theatre Non Nobiss Snappy Tales, which had its moments, but still; and, I give you my word, Ross Petty's Robin Hood.

Outstanding New Play was Adam Pettle's Sunday Father, no question. It hasnt been nominated. Just to rub it in, the same playwrights respectable but lesser Therac 25 has been. (Because it's autobiographical? Because it's about cancer? Because it has fewer jokes?) Anyway, that being the case, good luck to Morris Panych, author of Girl in the Goldfish Bowl; he may need it, as hes up against Sonja Millss The Danish Play (autobiographical at one family remove, and with very few jokes), which has been wildly overrated in every department. Also up are Chris Earle's Russell Hill, which proves that jokes aren't enough, and Matthew Edisons The Domino Heart; if there were a "most promising" award, the latter would win it in a domino heartbeat, but a play composed of sequential monologues leaves me, at least, unsatisfied. Oddly, Susan Coynes Kingfisher Days, Tarragon's second-best new play (after the Panych) has gone unnoticed in all particulars, though my impression at the time was that everybody loved it.

Outstanding New Musical: We're talking about the writing here, are we? The prize will undoubtedly go to Little Mercy, though Snappy Tales probably has as good a score, at least in the bits that were composed by Allen Cole. In both shows, the music far outclassed the words. Greg Robics Assemblywomen! was also nominated, presumably by people who didnt see it. (As Frank Sinatra once sang, they have to fill their quota.) The year's best musical, far and away, was This Could Be Love, which doesn't qualify here since it came from the Independent (i.e. small) theatre sector -- which, however, has no separate category for musicals. You lose some, you lose some.

Outstanding Direction of a Play: This ought to go to Albert Schultz for A Chorus of Disapproval. Hes really blossomed as a director; not only was this the seasons best-acted and funniest show, it was also its best-staged. That apart, I wouldn't begrudge it to Morris Panych, for his own work on his own play, and would feel surprisingly cheerful about it going to Chris Abraham, whose staging of Russell Hill is responsible for whatever credibility this piece has. Also up: Brian Quirt for Through the Eyes, a one-man show, so you really can't tell, and Leah Cherniak, whose nomination for The Miracle Worker (at YPT) must be a pious gesture. This was approved, when Jim Guedos The Shape of Things or Diana Leblancs bold stab at The Maids or (if you want a kids' show) David S. Craig's Pinocchio werent? Oy, in such a world we are living.

Outstanding Direction of a Musical: This has to be between Eda Holmess handling of Little Mercy's First Murder and Morris Panych's handling of Sweeney Todds multiple ones. My heart is with Panych (such flaws as I noted on my first visit had mostly vanished or turned into virtues by my second), but my money is on Holmes. And she made an extraordinarily good impression, recently reinforced by her production of Blood Relations at the Shaw. If by any chance Panych does win in all four (you heard me) of his nominated categories -- well, theres nobody who could make a better job of all those acceptance speeches.

Outstanding Performance by a Male in a Principal Role, Musical: Sweeney Todd is the most demanding role in the musical repertoire, and I don't see how you deny the palm to anyone -- in this case, George Masswohl -- who makes a go of it. So he wasn't ideal; who, since Len Cariou, has been? Peter Millard was nice in Little Mercy, but theres no comparison. Graham Abbey is up for his Robin Hood, but he won last year, and for essentially the same performance.

Outstanding Performance by a Female in a Principal Role, Musical: This will go to Fiona Reid for her Mrs. Lovett in Sweeney Todd. Or there will be riots.

Outstanding Performance by a Male in a Principal Role, Play: Ted Dykstra in A Chorus of Disapproval. No contest. But there could be, since his perfectly gorgeous, or gorgeously perfect, performance was a) nearly a year ago and b) in a comedy. Also, Richard McMillan is up for Through the Eyes, a taxing solo turn, though not his best work. John Jarvis (Goldfish Bowl) and Ari Cohen (Sunday Father, its only look-in) were both splendid, and Im glad they're there, but no. Stephen Ouimette, pulling up his socks, or his Elizabethan hose, halfway through The Beard of Avon? Gimme a break. Most overlooked actor: Ben Carlson, the best thing in both Swollen Tongues and The League of Nathans, and, superbly, unshowily versatile.

Outstanding Performance by a Female in a Principal Role, Play: This will be Kate Hennig for her uncompromising (i.e. unnatural) performance in The Danish Play. Though it could just be Rosemary Dunsmore in The Domino Heart; she was impeccable and she was monologizing. I'm happy Brooke Johnson got a nod for her handsome and heroic work in The Gwendolyn Poems, and surprised that Nancy Palk and Martha Burns were passed over for their similar qualities in The Maids. They were both, in the end, too nice for their roles, but I wouldnt hold that against them

Outstanding Performance in a Feature Role in a Play or Musical (and, I might add, by a male or female; we get real indiscriminate at this point): This is going to be either Eric Peterson for what amounted to a comeback performance in Boy Gets Girl, or Joe Ziegler for his hilariously downtrodden lecturer in Absolutely Chekhov. I liked them both, though I liked them even more in The Blues and Kingfisher Days respectively. And what, pray, happened to David Storchs Autolycus in The Winter's Tale? Actually, I shall root for Bruce Dow's tonsorial mountebank in Sweeney Todd, since I underrated him at first and would like to make amends.

Outstanding Design (of various kinds): John Thompson is in line twice over, for his sets for Little Mercys First Murder and Russell Hill (that subway), and could justifiably win for either. So, probably, could Andrea Lundy, who lit both of them. Jay Turvey and Paul Sportelli are up for Little Mercys sound design/composition, but it's a musical and they're its composers: ditto with the Snappy Tales guys. As far as Im concerned, theyve had their nominations. How do you tell the sound-score from the score?

Outstanding Choreographer: Suddenly we have our own breed of director-choreographers, since Morris Panych and Eda Holmes (with Jane Johanson) are nominated in both categories: This doesn't make them Robbins and Fosse, but the footwork in Sweeney Todd and Little Mercy was excellent. Also named is Tracy Flye for Robin Hood. This has to be a gag; no Petty panto is ever going to feature awardworthy choreography. It's not what those shows are about.

Outstanding Musical Direction: Bruce Kellett (Sweeney Todd) should be a shoo-in. Though so too, working in a more modest musical context, should Marek Norman (A Chorus of Disapproval).

So much for the Generals. On the proliferating Independents I have, for the most part, to pass; I didnt see enough. Id like to see Krista Sutton get Best Actress, for This Could Be Love, and don't see why she shouldn't; the show itself should be in the omnibus Best Play or Musical section, but, like I said, it couldnt get a break. Best Actor, from what I saw, was Alex Poch-Goldin in Bully, with honourable mention for Matthew MacFadzean, another soloist, in richardthesecond, a play that he wrote.

Which reminds me: This years Dora host is the incontestably adorable Kristen Thomson, who two years ago won both author and actor prizes for I, Claudia, and our hearts along with them. I have fond hopes that she will bring out the beloved Claudia mask, and that she will make fewer jokes about her pregnancy than did last year's emcee, Diane Flacks. Are they going to make fecundity an official qualification?

2003-06-23-the-best-part-shes-ever-had:
Elaine Stritch at Liberty opens tonight at the Elgin Theatre, Toronto, and runs till Saturday. At the box office, all Ticketmaster outlets, 416-872-5555 or ticketmaster.ca.; robertcushman@lycos.ca

After a lifetime on the stage, Elaine Stritch feels she is finally 'free up there' to do and say as she pleases - hence the title of her show

Elaine Stritch performs her autobiographical show, Elaine Stritch at Liberty, this week in Toronto, looking very liberated indeed in a man's shirt and black tights, the latter revealing a truly remarkable pair of legs. On more formal occasions she dresses up, casual but elegant. Her previous booking was in Chicago, and when I met her there last week, at the Ritz-Carlton Hotel, she was a symphony in beige. She wore taupe (her word) gaberdine slacks, a silk blouse, a Paul Davis knit tie, her favourite sweater -- given to her by her maid in New York ("her name is Nancy Torres and she knows how to pick 'em") -- and a lapel pin held over from her first- act costume in the Toronto and New York production of Show Boat, 10 years ago.

And does anyone still wear a hat? Stritch does. She's her own answer to the withering question that she asks in The Ladies Who Lunch, the Stephen Sondheim tour-de-force that she introduced in Company, in 1970, and that remains a cornerstone of her repertoire. It tops off the ensemble perfectly. It's also utilitarian ("I can put eight rollers in front of my hair, put a hat on, and I don't have to have my hair down when I'm not working."), and that combination is basic Stritch.

When she is working, she wears the tights-and-shirt outfit ("it's very comfortable"), causing John Lahr, theatre critic of The New Yorker and her writing collaborator on Elaine Stritch at Liberty, to look up at her during one of their sessions and dub her "an existential problem in tights" -- a remark that went right into the script and that she calls "a gorgeous line." Lahr also threw in references to "things like Samuel Beckett," and indeed Stritch, with the yearning cragginess in her voice, could be very good in Beckett.

Right now, though, and for the last two years, she has been offering what may be the most personal of one-woman shows: some of her signature songs from musicals, linked by the story of the consuming passions of her life -- for the theatre, for the men she has loved, and for the bottle. They are intertwined, though not, as it turns out, interdependent. She has been able to do without the last of them. The show is its own provisional happy ending; she has been able to score the biggest success of her career after staying on the wagon for 15 years.

She was talked into doing the show by her producer, John Schreiber. "He said school will start at 10. Somebody hits me with a schedule, I'm there. It's when I'm left to my own devices I am scr- r-ewed. Royally screwed."

When Sondheim came to see the show, and she told him how terrified she was, he said, "Elaine, terror becomes you."

I asked her if performing was where she went to get away from her insecurities, and she referred me to the name of the show. "One day John Lahr put a little note in his pad, At Liberty. He said, 'I've been kicking around some ideas about what this show means, and it means you're at liberty to say any damn thing you want.' I said, 'That's the title, John, that's the title.' But I don't actually mean that I'm free to say anything I want ... Because I'm on the high side of 70, and older people can say exactly what they want, but I don't feel that's what the show's about. I feel that I'm free at last by feeling secure, and I accept my life, and I'm not sore about anything, and I do feel free up there. I do not feel that liberty offstage. I hope I will someday. I'm working awfully hard on feeling secure after the curtain comes down. That is so difficult for me, because I'm leading a sober life in every way, so I'm fully aware of how tough it is to relax. It is tough for a dame like me to put her feet up and say, 'I'm gonna have a bran muffin and a cup of tea or look at the ocean or take a walk.' I can't get there."

She seems to have the tea part down all right. Our meeting at the Ritz took place over a civilized tray of Earl Grey (it followed a prolonged period tramping the hotel's capacious lobby and cafe area to find a table quiet and comfortable enough) and it all seemed rather English. This seems fitting, since Stritch lived in London -- at the Savoy -- during the '70s and '80s. A TV series, Two's Company, in which she played the rich and hyperactive employer of Donald Sinden's imperturbable butler, made her Britain's favourite American broad. Her only marriage was to English actor John Bay. His nephew, George Bay, joined us at the end of the interview; he lives in Chicago and produces English muffins -- a commodity, by the way, unknown in England.

The marriage, by Stritch's own account, was a great one. "And maybe it's like all things that were just great, it was brief." It was cut short by her husband's early death. "So I don't know about that love business. I know I had something very special with John. And there wasn't a lot of emphasis on the obvious -- I mean the sexual -- it was just wanting to be with somebody. I haven't had anything like, since John died, the feeling of calm I had when he was alive. I almost reverted right back to the nut that I was before I married him." Nowhere during our conversation did she sound more serious and, well, sober than when she said that.

Her feelings about the brevity of love are somewhat contradicted by her memories of her own parents, who were married, lovingly, for 74 years (she emphasizes the number, with what sounds like a mixture of pride and incredulity) and who died, at the ages of 95 and 96, "within 12 hours of each other."

It sounds like an ideal way to go, and Stritch's supportive Catholic upbringing should not, by all the rules, have sent her off the rails. But she was experimenting seriously with alcohol when in her teens, while nourishing "a basic desire to be just about anybody else. If I'd meet a nurse, I wanted to be a nurse. I don't mean act a nurse, I wanted to be the nurse. It's only very recently that I'm looking in the mirror and saying, 'You're OK.' I mean, I had to get to be 77 before I could say this, but I don't care how long it took. But, you know, where the hell have I gone? I haven't played my part, ever, until now."

Taking this last remark literally, I pointed out that not many actors get to play themselves the way she's doing now. She agreed. "And let me tell you something, it's the best part I ever had. Because an awful lot of rehearsal went into it (I'd wanted to say that, but she beat me to the punch).

"A guy said something to me at the opening-night party in New York. He just brushed by me and said, 'Elaine, you're the best thing in it.' Isn't that divine? I've been looking for him ever since because I would marry him, by mail, on account of that one line. But he hasn't got in touch, so I don't think he wants to spend the rest of his life with me."

As the show reveals, she has spent two-year portions of her life with Gig Young and with Ben Gazzara; and also, which the show doesn't reveal, with Joe Allen -- yes, there really is a Joe Allen - - "the restaurant guy. He was cut from my life, for time reasons, and he never came to see the show. (Which sounds like poetic justice. Gazzara did come, and said, "Elaine, I didn't know you were that talented.")

With all this high-powered competition, I wondered how John Bay, who wasn't that well-known, had plucked up the courage to propose. "He didn't. I did. I knew it was on his mind, so I just made it easier for him. He replied -- and I credit him in the show -- 'Well, why not?' " The way she tells it, he said it a lot like Jack Benny. He was a connoisseur of comedians and achieved his greatest success playing Groucho Marx in A Day in Hollywood -- A Night in the Ukraine. He was Groucho: "most extraordinary," as Stritch says, "because he looked like Jack Kennedy." He also did a one-man show as Groucho in which, with the author's "be my guest" consent, he sang Send in the Clowns with altered lyrics: "Isn't it rich/Isn't it queer/Finding the deeds to the ranch/In your brassiere?" Hearing that sung by Stritch imitating Bay imitating Groucho is an experience.

An admiring journalist in Chicago wrote of her, "She's straightforward, she's honest, she's upfront, she's foulmouthed," and Stritch relished all the adjectives except the last.

"I thought, God, if there's one thing -- and it hit me, it's an example of me being the strong woman that everybody thinks, and I cried when I read this. There's no word in the English language I hate more than foulmouthed, and to call a woman that ..." Aggrieved, she spelled out for me, but did not actually say, the four-letter words she has never used in her life. "Foulmouthed?" she concluded. "Jesus!"

The strong-woman image derives, of course, from the roles she's played in musicals -- take-charge dames in the Ethel Merman tradition garnished with her own flavour of acidulous: Joanne in Company, or the luxury-cruise hostess of Noel Coward's Sail Away. Her sound is an individual cross between musical comedy and drawing- room comedy. In fact she's only done seven musicals in the whole of her life, not all of them hits, but they've been enough to establish her as one of the queens of Broadway. "As a singer," she says correctly, "I'm a hell of an actress" -- and I'd add that, though she may not have the greatest range or the purest tones in the world, the notes she does hit are in tune.

She's actually done more plays than musicals, her favourite being Edward Albee's A Delicate Balance, which she played in a New York revival some half-dozen years back. Chicago's Steppenwolf company has asked her ("and it's funny they would") to do Sweet Bird of Youth. "And to do that, at my age, would be to fulfill Tennessee Williams' advice, because he told me before he died (here she adopts an accent best described as Southern-nasal), 'I don't care how old you get to be, Lainie, Sweet Bird of Youth -- it'll never be done till you do it.' Isn't that marvellous?"

It could be. Between such engagements she remains, like any actor, At Liberty but with a twist. She can go on doing this show for the rest of her life, energy and longevity feeding off one another in a woman who knows she's a legend but has figured out how to work around it.

In repertory until Aug. 29. Box office: 1-800-567-1600.; robertcushman@lycos.com

NO EXIT

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

Jean-Paul Sartre's Huis Clos has taken up permanent residence in the modern consciousness as a new vision of damnation, one in which the fires and tortures favoured in the Middle Ages are replaced by subtler and more economical methods. Three lost souls, each specially selected for the capacity to get on the nerves of the other two, are locked up for eternity in a Second Empire drawing- room. Ninety minutes of this is enough to bring them to the realization that "hell is other people."

The play, variously translated as No Exit (Stratford's choice), In Camera and Vicious Circle, is a college-course favourite and a staple of student theatre groups, but its professional productions, at least in English, are rare. On the evidence of this Stratford production, that strange combination of celebrity and obscurity is justified. The idea is indelible, the execution flat.

It may seem unreasonable to complain that the characters never come to life; they are, after all, dead. But you never believe that they could have lived. Besides, Sartre was an atheist, and his inferno is really a conceit, in which the things living people do to one another are carried to their ultimate conclusion. At least that's the idea. It isn't how the play works while you're actually watching it. To the extent that it works, it works as a vision of the afterlife.

There are two women and a man. The man, Cradeau, was shot as a deserter (the play was written at the end of the Second World War), and though he would like to claim status as a conscientious objector, his motives seem to have been a lot shadier. He was also, in the great tradition of French intellectuals, very mean to his wife. Interestingly, though he is quite willing to accept his status as one of the damned, he is very evasive when it comes to accepting detailed responsibility. He is the first onstage, and the play, not too surprisingly, is written largely from his point of view.

The women are denied even his limited measure of complexity. They're sketched in with almost contemptuous lightness. Estelle is vain and a man-chaser; she killed her baby because motherhood was too much trouble, and drove its father to suicide. Inez is a lesbian and a secretary, and those really are the only things we learn about her.

Sartre's eschatology is notably materialist. His characters have brought their bodies with them, and they are still wearing the clothes that they once stood up in (which are not, probably, the clothes they were buried in). Maybe the inmates are in for more physical torment than the authorities let on; the three unsupported circular pouffes that are the room's only furnishings are surely going to be hell on their backs.

We assume the characters do have physical frailties because they still have physical desires. Cradeau and Estelle would like to have sex together, but are frustrated by the jealous presence of Inez. The same would be true if lust were to strike in some other combination.

Over eternity, one could presumably get used to being watched; what these characters can't stand is being disapproved of. They are narcissists, who nevertheless depend on others for their validation. There are no mirrors in this room, so they can only find their reflections in one another's eyes. They can't escape those others, because the lights are never turned off and their eyelids appear to have been surgically removed. By an especially cruel twist, they are able to see the people who were once in their lives carrying on without them and saying unkind things into the bargain.

Put it like that, and it's no wonder Sartre's conclusion has passed into the language: Hell is other people, if you have to be locked up with them forever. It's so obviously true that it hardly matters who the other people are. Even one's nearest and dearest would probably pall. The play's choice of characters seems arbitrary; anyone would do. (Being confined with these three for a mere hour and a half is an infernal sort of experience for the audience, but I don't think that's meant to be the entire point.)

So the play seems frivolous, in a Gallically philosophic kind of way. I have a friend who thinks that what Sartre really meant was "Hell is other French people." He may have something there.

That said, there are probably subtler gradations of cruelty in the script than are realized here. Jim Warren's production is the staged equivalent of an intelligent reading. Everybody shouts when required, laughs when required (most noticeably when they realize the implications of the play's celebrated punchline), and nobody digs very deep. They seem, for hand-picked mutual torturers, to be letting each other off very lightly.

Claire Jullien as Estelle flounces about the stage, looking very blond and fetching in a blue dress but exhibiting the character's shallowness rather than exploring it. Chick Reid's Inez is flinty and hectoring, as if that were what defined a lesbian. Stephen Ouimette's Cradeau is somewhat subtler, imprinting himself on the mind as a man with a pervasive mental wince. His last illusions collapse when, doubled up in mirthless merriment, he announces, "I'm dead -- I've gone into public domain," one of the few memorable phrases in a disappointingly flavourless translation by U.S. poet Paul Bowles.

There is a fourth character, the bellboy who shows the principals to their room. As played by Andrew Massingham he is obseqious and opaque, which are the right qualities. I shall think of him as the spiritual (if that's the word) cousin of the minor devil who, in a recent New Yorker cartoon, inquired solicitously of a new arrival, "And now your choice for all eternity -- ranch, blue cheese or Italian?" Getting to choose: That could be a worse hell than Sartre's.

THE BIRDS

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

There's only one thing harder to revive in the modern theatre than ancient Athenian tragedy, and thats ancient Athenian comedy. The Stratford Festival this year is giving us both, and it has begun what I think of as Greek Week with a comedy, thereby going where very few major companies have gone before. Aristophanes The Birds is, like all his extant plays and presumably like all the vanished ones as well, an essay in the farcical-satirical-musical-lyrical. Its Stratford production honours this medley and comes up with its own -- a mixture of the beautiful and the boring.

Greek tragedy is comparatively accessible to us because it tells a story. Aristotle, a model critic who observed practices rather than making rules, declared that plot was the soul of tragedy. Greek comedy, by that criterion, is soulless; it has situations, usually one per play, but hardly builds a narrative out of them. It is also soulless as we might use the word, because it isn't interested in character, either. Its people are front men, for ideas or for routines.

Aristophanes wrote his plays during the war between Athens and Sparta that ended in the ruin of both. Typically, his plays show us beleagured Athenian citizens trying either to knock some sense into their society's head or, more often, to opt out altogether. The Birds gives us a couple of these voluntary refugees, Pisthetairos and Euelpides, who set out in search of Tereus, a mythological malefactor whom the gods turned into a bird, a hoopoe, and who they hope might point them in the direction of a superior city. Finding themselves surrounded by birds -- of radiant plumage, suspicious mind and hostile intent -- they have a brainwave: Why dont the birds found their own aerial city, independent of both men and gods? Their hosts welcome this idea with open wings, and elect, or at least accept, Pisthetairos as their ruler. They call their new realm Cloudcuckooland, a name that has rung in legend ever since.

Before becoming the birds masters, our two Athenians were in imminent danger of being their victims, trussed up to have their eyes pecked out. Dressed here in khaki, like desert explorers, they somewhat resemble Hope and Crosby in the old Road movies, awaiting immersion in the cannibal pot before, with one bound, they were free. And indeed, though theoretically social equals, they have the makings of a classic master-servant duo: Pisthetairos the pompous and Euelpides the put-upon. The latter, as usual, is the more grateful role, and Bernard Hopkins makes a lovely job of it, alternately downcast and joyful, and binding the modes together with a George Formby accent. He finally melts our hearts when, dispatched by his friend on yet another errand, he turns and says, with genuine tears, I wish to God you'd do some of the work. Then he goes off and, though the play is only half done, never comes back. Nor is he even mentioned. Aristophanes, you see, does not subscribe to our sentimental notions of human interest. For us, though, who are saddled with them, Euelpides' absence dampens the play almost beyond repair.

Anyway, after hes gone, Pisthetairos receives a series of visitors who represent the worst elements of his old home, and of course want a place in the new one. They include a priest, a poet, a quack scientist and, plague of plagues, a professional informer. Pisthetairos out-talks them all, and even fends off a challenge from the gods, largely by appealing to their greed. He has a barbecue going, and Herakles, one of the Olympian delegates, is super- heroically hungry.

Scholarly opinion has it that Pisthetairos is satirized as an exploiter figure, instituting a new tyranny as bad as the old. I dont get it. He comes across as the underdog enthroned, cheered on by his author. I see from the program that the great Bert Lahr played the role in an American production, and it needs a clown of that calibre (though I can't think of any equivalent in the Canadian theatre, except perhaps Heath Lamberts) to hold the show together. Keith Dinicol here is heavy-going, though I have to salute his handling of what is, after all, the play's central moment. "Why not be birds?" he asks rhetorically for himself and partner, and then -- as both the wonder and the practicality of it strike him -- he says it again, hushed: Why not be birds?

His ponderousness elsewhere infects, or at least is shared by, the rest of the cast. What read in Dudley Fitts translation like snappy cross-talk exchanges seem, in Nikos Dionysios production, to go on forever. There are some fine visuals, notably in the huge costume creations -- traditional masks, robes and platform soles -- that Teresa Przybylski has run up for the various divinities, but they, too, weigh the action down. I except the more delicate apparition of Iris, the messenger goddess, who appears hovering on wires and suspended from a crane, this time of the non-avian variety.

But then "Why not be birds?" The choruses -- sung, danced and spoken by the birds themselves -- make a very persuasive case for it. The radiance that classicists have always found in these passages comes through in Fitts' verse, whether delicate or ribald. Dionysios' choreography, not actually very Dionysian, isnt up to much except in its more menacing, foot-stomping or beak-crunching moments, but the singing is lovely, and though Michael Vieiras music is uneven, at its best it's ravishing. When these elements come together, they make you catch your breath; you feel in touch with something great.

Aristophanes' plays are like topical revues, and modern productions, when they happen at all, often fillet his texts and use them as pretexts, for their own agendas. There is little of that here, other than a studded rocker costume for a passing parricide and an interpolated reference to weapons of mass destruction. Part of me applauds this fidelity to the original, full of references to local celebrities who aren't even in the history books; another part suspects that we might better honour the spirit of Aristophanes by being less obedient to the letter. He was a free-wheeling writer and we should maybe free-wheel right over him, though some pretty horrible things have been known to happen when people try. Anyway here it is, The Birds, and well worth catching, as long as you go prepared.

PRESENT LAUGHTER

Avon Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

Stratford, Ont. - Garry Essendine, the protagonist of Noel Coward's Present Laughter, is not a playwright. That is one thing that differentiates him from his author. Another is that, though Coward himself tended to see the outside world in terms of the theatre, he did at least see it. Garry seems unaware that it exists at all. Otherwise, as has been recognized ever since the original 1942 production with Coward in the lead, the play is autobiographical, not as a literal record of events but as the distillation of a small but seductive world.

I doubt it has ever been recreated more completely or more scintillatingly than it is now at Stratford, where Brian Bedford gives it direction that is nearly impeccable and a central performance that is absolutely so. Garry is a London matinee idol, whose success has enabled him to build a personal and professional empire. Its wheels are turned by two men -- his manager and his producer, and two women -- his secretary and his not-quite-ex wife. They have to attend to his ego and, quite often, his love life as well as his career, and they frequently complain. However, as he never tires of reminding them, without his talent there would be no machine to maintain. Garry has achieved, purely as an actor (and probably, though we never really hear about it, as a director), the kind of eminence that it took his creator the exercise of half-a- dozen talents to attain.

His charm and his susceptibility to flattery expose him to the attentions of a succession of younger admirers (female, to protect the innocent). They arrive at night on his doorstep, claiming to have lost their latch keys, and emerge from the spare room the following morning, demanding breakfast from the resident domestics and collapsing into tears when their host and lover turns out to have only the haziest recollection of their existence. They can be dealt with.

A more serious threat emerges in the person of Joanna, who is the wife of one of Garry's male associates and the mistress of the other. (It's impossible to remember which relationship is which. The two men are indistinguishable, even when they're on stage together.) Joanna, as the Essendine entourage all agree, "is not one of us," but this is not a fate she seems at all willing to accept.

There's a relaxed quality about Present Laughter that makes it Coward's most attractive comedy. This is especially true of its first act, which sets up Garry and his lifestyle with no apparent signs of haste, even though a plot-line is already ticking meticulously away underneath. In its second act, with characters threatening to burst inopportunely out of rooms, the play becomes explicitly farcical, but it works throughout as a subtler kind of farce, one in which it's not the hero's reputation or physical well- being that is in jeopardy, but his place in his own mental world. Garry is about to embark on a taxing tour of Africa (nobody denies that he's a hard worker) and, as people never cease to remind him, he's getting older; the play's title comes from the Shakespeare song that tells us "youth's a stuff will not endure." He needs to be admired, needs to be in control, and though he may be the most intelligent person on stage, he is not necessarily the cleverest. He does, though, have untouchable style.

Bedford, from his first dressing-gowned entrance (descending the staircase that naturally dominates Michael Yeargan's beautifully lined Art Deco set), holds all the contradictions in balance. He is graciously tetchy, well-meaningly self-absorbed. As in Private Lives, he plays the Coward style without once aping the staccato Coward voice, thereby doing the play the greatest of services. Every line, whether a direct thrust or a glancing blow, is flawlessly timed, but the technique always illuminates the character.

He makes us love Garry (and like him, which is not the same thing) but he never sentimentalizes. The play is, in fact, a more unsparing self-portrait than can be found in Coward's diaries, autobiographies or other published pronouncements. People actually get to attack Garry for his self-centredness; he even gets rebuked for his "finger-wagging tirades," which sound very Cowardian. Which only reinforces the cardinal tenet of Coward's, and Garry's, own faith: that the theatre is all-important and therefore, of necessity, the place in which you tell the truth.

Seana McKenna is in dagger-sharp form as the perfect secretary, and Domini Blythe charming as the presumably perfect wife, though she is best when she too gets down to business. (I wish she didn't keep her hat on so much; it makes her look temporary.) The live-in staff are of golden quality, with Brian Tree imperturbably pertinacious as Garry's valet, and Patricia Collins something near sublime as his housekeeper who is a sloucher and a chain-smoker and a spiritualist and Scandinavian -- almost an embarrassment of riches for any actress.

There are a couple of flaws: Sara Botsford's Joanna is merely haughty, not much of a threat, and Michelle Giroux has an exaggerated initial idea of what a star-struck English deb might sound like, though she straightens out later on. Tim MacDonald is frighteningly accurate as her male counterpart, a solemn young playwright who comes to attack and stays to worship, and who has travelled all the way from Uckfield. (This is one feature of the play that defies export; to the English, English place names are hilarious. Just take it from me: Uckfield is a scream.) This character strikingly exemplifies the play's double nature. He allows Coward to let off steam, via Garry, with a cri de coeur about theatrical pretension, but is then slotted smartly into the structure, right up to the final curtain.

Which reminds me: All of Coward's major comedies -- this one, Hay Fever, Private Lives and Blithe Spirit -- end with a character or characters tip-toeing off the scene, leaving others to face some outstandingly cacophonous music. This is what a later dramatist, in a different connection, called "withdrawing with style from the chaos." In its way, it's a philosophy.

THE HOUSE OF ATREUS: AGAMEMNON, ELECTRA, THE FLIES

Studio Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

Over the last few decades, theatre companies have mounted mar- athon productions that stitched together some of the extant Greek tragedies to tell a continuous story (John Barton's The Greeks) or that re-crossed the same ancient territory in a giant succession of new scripts (John Barton's Tantalus). Stratford's The House of Atreus has elements of both these approaches, but is its own absorbing animal.

It starts with Aeschylus' Agamemnon, which is the first part of the only surviving Greek trilogy, The Oresteia. Agamemnon, King of Argos, son of Atreus, returns home from his 10-year generalship at the siege of Troy only to be murdered by his wife, Clytemnestra, and her lover Aegisthus. It's a revenge killing, with a multiplicity of motives: Clytemnestra hates her husband for having sacrificed their daughter Iphigenia so that the gods would send the Greek fleet a favouring wind for Troy; Aegisthus' family has been at war with Agamemnon's for two blood-soaked generations. The vendetta is pursued through Aeschylus' two subsequent instalments, in which Agamemnon's surviving children, Electra and Orestes, avenge their father and are pursued for their pains by the Furies, goddesses of the ancient unrelenting code for which our own civilization's metaphor is "an eye for an eye."

The Stratford venture, however, steps aside from Oresteia II and III, and instead offers us two dramatizations of the myth from 20th- century France: Jean Giraudoux's Electra and Jean-Paul Sartre's The Flies. The first was written under the approaching shadow of the Second World War, the second during the German Occupation. Each reflects the preoccupations of its time and, in these productions, is costumed accordingly. The Agamemnon designs, meanwhile, are as conventionally classical as you're going to get these days. Each of the plays has a different director, but the actors are the same. One of the enterprise's pleasures is to watch them going through stylistic hoops, not to mention ageing, while preserving their identities.

In Agamemnon, most of the cast are in the chorus, the most talkative in any surviving Greek play; it accounts for at least half the text. David Latham's production, which uses Ted Hughes' magnificent mailed-fist translation, accepts the chorus as the play's principal character, or in this case collection of characters; this is a resolutely un-stylized presentation, with no masks or massed speaking. It works most of the time. There is one moment when the chorus is explicitly, and rather comically, divided against itself, wondering what to do as the king is noisily dispatched off stage. Dividing up the speeches, for clarity and colour, is one thing; setting up artificial conflicts between the choristers is another, a drain on the actors' energy and the audience's concentration. It also highlights the uneven level of accomplishment within the ranks. The older ones do best; Walter Borden dominates, as a sedentary brooder perched on the edge of a two-stepped dais that's the central design feature of all three plays; but Maria Vacratsis and Ian White are strong too. Their juniors feature underdeveloped voices and a couple of speech impediments.

Part of the chorus' role is to fill us in on the backstory of the Trojan War, and to act as a sounding board for the principals, especially Clytemnestra, a monster with a lot of right on her side. Karen Robinson in the role is sharp and glittering as a newly honed dagger, but she seems to find the long speeches a trial. She dives into them with tremendous energy, but is then reduced to bobbing about. If the lady protests too much, it's true of the actress rather than the character.

Flaws acknowledged, this is still one of the best realizations of a Greek tragedy I have seen. Its strength is to present a single inevitable action while summoning the infinity of shadows that surround it. The Greek and Trojan armies, like this play's avengers, were caught up in an endless futile round of murderous self- justification. They knew it, but couldn't stop it. The play is amazingly timely, and has been for 2,500 years.

It seems more urgently topical than its two younger companions. These too draw on the audience's knowledge of the background, but they're hampered by telling stories they don't actually believe in. Giraudoux, in Electra, holds the problem pretty much at bay by sheer force of wit, and the great strength of Leon Rubin's production is its unwavering sense of serious playfulness.

The play has two commentator-figures, both deliciously played. Sean Arbuckle's beggar is a figure of barbed whimsy who asks the higher-ups all the impertinent questions that the deferential Greek chorus never got round to. The other is a gardener, to whom the troublesome Electra is about to be married off; Rami Posner spends the first half of the play standing expectantly on the edge of the action with a posy in his hand. Dismissed at the start of the second half, he delivers an anti-tragic manifesto on the virtues of cultivating one's garden rather than populating graveyards. Borden and Topham crop up again as his relatives. He, as a pompous judge, spoils his effects by swallowing his words, but she, nothing if not versatile, is a delight as his perpetually randy wife. Promising for the past two seasons, she has reached the arrival stage. The onlookers are completed by a trio of malignant schoolgirls (Julia Donovan, Julie Tepperman, Randi Helmers) who, we discover, are the Furies. They age before us in time with Electra's growing appetite for revenge.

She, played by Sarah Dodd with exemplary implacability, begins the play like Hamlet, unaware her father was murdered but knowing something is rotten in her mother's marriage. Mother and daughter share a mutual loathing; Robinson's Clytemnestra burns all the clearer for being relieved of her tragedy-queen responsibilities. Orestes, banished, returns, and the oft-dramatized reconciliation of brother and sister is played out again; they sleep together and she wakes up with knowledge and a motive, after which they're no stopping her. And then there is a twist. The usurper Aegisthus asks Electra to join him in saving the city.

Giraudoux was writing in the age of appeasement, and he ended up serving in the Vichy government. From this perspective his drift looks shabby. But the fit isn't precise; coming in the wake of Agamemnon, we still think of the story as Greek. Unfashionable for decades, the playwright's time may be coming again if he can be done with this degree of style.

Sartre's The Flies, by contrast, is stuck in its own time. Narrative continuity goes by the board, since the play re-enacts much of the action of Electra, but we still feel we're seeing another facet of the same prism. The flies are the latest incarnation of the Furies, welcomed by a guilty Aegsithus as a means of intimidating his subjects. In Peter Lichtenfels' production they're gas-masked figures whose fingers perform an unremitting hand- jive.

A graver problem is that Sartre's characters do little but talk, and not nearly as entertainingly as Giraudoux's. This time it's Orestes the avenger who gets away from Electra. Dodd's performance is a good as before, bar a few moments of sentimentality in which it's her turn to protest too much. Johnstone, a cipher in the preceding play, comes to life here as Orestes takes on the task of the "necessary murder": a killer, and unrepentantly so, let the Furies -- whose role at the end is ambiguous, if not downright confusing -- pursue him as they may. He is, in fact, the existentialist hero of the Resistance, and one might accept him more happily if Sartre didn't let him proclaim himself at such length. Aeschylus' Furies were eventually absorbed into a humane judicial system; Sartre's just go on buzzing. We've had a theatrical crash course in the descent of man.

I have left the dominant performance till last: Scott Wentworth's Aegisthus, who in each play presents a radically different aspect of the same unmistakable man. He gives the closing moments of Agamemnon an electric shock, when he appears out of nowhere, undressed to the nines as killer and gigolo. In Electra he's the consummate pinstriped politician, Claudius in the play's Hamlet pattern. In The Flies, he's a variant of the same, but with a death wish. Witty, poised, and effortlessly powerful, the actor is a national resource. He also, in the unity he finds in diversity, incarnates the achievement of these productions as a whole -- an audacious concept, excitingly fulfilled.

Summer is the season of Shakespeare in the park, wherein nature provides the scenery, the lighting and much of the atmosphere

They call it The Dream in High Park even when, as this year, the play happens to be Twelfth Night. For many people there is only one legitimate open-air Shakespeare, and all others are pretenders. An actor friend who in the 1960s played two seasons at the Regent's Park Open Air Theatre in London told me that patrons, usually American, would call up and ask if A Midsummer Night's Dream was playing that night. Told that it wasn't even playing that year, they remained undeterred; couldn't you, they would plead, do it tonight anyway?

Because it has fairies, and a team of accident-prone rustics putting on a play, A Midsummer Night's Dream has an undeserved reputation for innocuousness. It's the play of choice for introducing children to Shakespeare, and outdoor presentation -- a pretty setting for a pretty text -- seems to go along with that. Also, outdoor theatres tend to be cheaper to attend than indoor ones (The Dream in High Park is free, although there is a suggested $15 donation), so taking the family is an easier proposition.

Shakespeare's own theatre, the Globe, was, of course, an open- air theatre, though urban rather than vernal. The roofless Elizabethan playhouses were modelled on bustling inn-yards, not on quiet parklands. Ironically, A Midsummer Night's Dream may originally have been one of Shakespeare's few indoor plays. There's evidence it was written as a celebration for an aristocratic wedding, to be performed in the banquet hall after supper (just like the plays of the artisans Pyramus and Thisbe is, within the play itself). Doubtless it had an afterlife on the public stage, but neither venue would have allowed for real trees, which are the selling point for modern alfresco Dreams: "a wood near Athens," with real wood.

The other plays in the open-air Shakespeare canon are there for similarly literal reasons: Twelfth Night (the runner-up, set largely in a countess' garden), As You Like It (a forest) and The Tempest (a desert island). These are also, of course, well-known comedies with wholesome auras.

Then there is Love's Labour's Lost, which happens entirely in a royal park and is the premier pastoral play in the language, but it's regarded as obscure, and so counts as a risk. As also, in this context, do all other Shakespeare plays, and anything written at any time by any other playwright whatsoever. Canadian theatres, to their credit, often take such chances.

Actually, doing any play in the open air is risky, and what is at risk is, in all senses, concentration. I'm not referring to the trivial distractions, such as airplanes and mosquitoes. I mean that plays in parks are, of their nature, very difficult to focus.

I now propose to get autobiographical. In my youth, I was involved in two open-air Shakespeare shows. At 15, I played Fabian (encouragingly described in the text we used as "this unnecessary character") in a school production of Twelfth Night. It was done in a garden, but, most important, it was done in front of a house. Having that unifying facade to act in front of, and to walk in and out of, was a great help.

It was a golden English summer, and everybody, actors and audience, felt enchanted. Our Malvolio grew up to be a playwright, while at the other end of the cast, furniture was moved about by half-a-dozen 12-year-old pages, one of whom was called Alan Rickman. I would like to say that his talent was immediately recognized by his seniors in the cast, but it wasn't.

Some 20 years later, the three of us -- Malvolio, Rickman and I - - were fortuitously reunited at a theatre reception. I doubt if any other old school production, or indeed any other old school, was as well represented. Malvolio was married by now to an actress, a very good one, and he tried to explain to her what it had been like. "Well," he said, "there was Peter Brook's Dream, and there was Twelfth Night." He was probably right.

My other memory is less happy. Some half dozen years later, I directed a troupe of Cambridge undergraduates in a production of A Midsummer Night's Dream at, of all places, Stratford-on-Avon. (Talk about coals to Newcastle.) One of the local hotels had fostered a legend that the play had first been performed under a spreading oak tree on what were now the hotel grounds.

It seems doubtful to me that Stratford would ever have been a touring date for the Globe company. Will himself, who had left home in order to leave home, would not have been keen -- and, anyway, somebody pointed out that the strain of oak in question was introduced into England a century after Shakespeare's death. But the management kept their tradition going for a couple of years.

Oxford had brought a production the previous year. Now it was our turn. We didn't do a good job, or at least I didn't. The play, performed all over a sprawling greensward, had no particular identity. Also, this was one of England's less golden summers, and my memory is that it rained every night. The audience was under cover, but the actors weren't. One night, the downpour was so torrential that the performance was adjourned after half-an-hour to a rehearsal tent, the cast pretty much making up the moves as they went along. Also, they didn't have to shout, and the play suddenly acquired intimacy and a shape. I was converted on the spot to the idea of the Dream as nuptial cabaret.

Even out in the wilderness, I'd observed that the second half of the play, after darkness had fallen, was much better than the first. This led me, when reviewing some professional park show years later, to refer to "the blessing of night that falls upon the just and the unjust open-air production alike." It's impossible to resist. And, of course, when the natural lights go out, you bring on the artificial ones, and with them you can be selective. The play ceases to be flat and acquires contours.

What we call interpretation is largely a matter of lighting. Shakespeare's audience, who got the plays fresh, may not have needed it, but we, who often know them too well, need the help. Shakespeare himself, in his later years, must have discovered this when his company opened a candlelit indoor theatre, the Blackfriars, which took more money (partly because it charged more) than the Globe ever had. This, by the way, is the space for which that other supernatural favourite, The Tempest, was first designed.

Not that I don't have pleasant open-air memories as a spectator. I saw my very first Dream as a kid, in Regent's Park, and very delightful in a solidly old-fashioned way it was. The following year, I saw a comedy there called The Romanticks, by the author of Cyrano de Bergerac, about a pair of self-elected star-crossed lovers whose parents had to push them together rather than pull them apart. If the title and the theme sound familiar, that's because the play later became the source of the musical The Fantasticks, which was to run some 40 years off-Broadway. I must be one of the few people who has seen the play but not the show.

Regent's Park standards in those days were thought to be pretty tatty, but they were spruced up circa 1960, largely by a future director of Canada's Stratford, David William. Stratford's current director, Richard Monette, also has a Park past. I got my first glimpse of him when, a temporary expatriate, he played Lorenzo there in The Merchant of Venice. (His Jessica, coincidentally, was the future Mrs. Malvolio, referred to above.) Last time I went, Judi Dench was there, directing The Boys From Syracuse. Regent's Park, like other classical theatres, has succumbed to the lure of the musical.

It's also got far more architectural, and more fenced-off, since the days when God painted the scenery. High Park, too, goes in increasingly for built-up sets. But spaces with natural features beyond the regulation greenwood are at a huge advantage. I am regularly bewitched by the lakeside setting of Oakville's Coronation Park, which confers a benefit on any director who cares to use it, and where the sight of people on the distant horizon who may or may not prove to be part of the play is its own added attraction.

Far less decorative, but almost equally spacious, is Withrow Park, where Shakespeare in the Rough has evolved a style that has benefited such unlikely choices as Othello and Measure for Measure. They use the outlying space to fill in the characters' biographies between the written scenes. It's almost like getting two plays.

Maybe the ideal parkland theatre is Britain's Glyndebourne Opera House, where you experience the show indoors, with perfect acoustics, and then picnic between the acts. It's getting the best of both worlds. Pastoral -- what the poet Marvell wonderfully evoked as "a green thought in a green shade" -- is a marvellously seductive form, from the Renaissance to Into the Woods -- but it isn't a realistic one, and natural scenery may be contrary to its nature. Besides that, I'm pampered, and I doubt if the outdoor experience can ever be ideal for a play. But it can undoubtedly be fun.

THE CORONATION VOYAGE

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

A kind of history was made last Saturday. The Shaw Festival's main stage was given over, for the first time, to a play by a living playwright. Not only living but Canadian; and French-Canadian at that.

It wasn't, strictly speaking, a new play. Michel Marc Bouchard's The Coronation Voyage has been around since 1995, during which time it has been widely produced in both French and English. It sits well on the festival stage; it has the size and the assurance. It's a big play. It's even, some of the time, a very good play; but only some of the time.

It's set in 1953, on board a liner travelling from Montreal to Liverpool, with a complement of passengers bound for the crowning of Elizabeth II. We focus on two families. One consists of a Montreal mafioso known to us only as the Chief and his two sons, Etienne and Sandro, each born of a different mother. The Chief is escaping the country, with official connivance; and he and his boys will assume new identities when they get to the other side.

The second group contains Monsieur Gendron, a government minister, his wife, Alice, and their daughter Marguerite, all holding good seats for Westminster Abbey. There is a link between the two parties. Marguerite is a pianist, and will be playing Chopin at a gala concert in London. She has inherited this gig from Etienne, a musical prodigy whose career was ended when two men from a rival mob, by way of putting the frighteners on his old man, slammed the piano lid on the boy's fingers. The Chief now faces a threat to his other, younger, son; the equally unnamed Diplomat who holds the family's new passports, and hence their fates, in his hands -- or, more likely, in his stateroom safe -- refuses to surrender them until the Chief grants him a night in bed with Sandro, who is 13.

When I first saw the play, in Vancouver in 2000, the audience seemed to take this plot development in stride. In Niagara, it produced shock waves more palpable than any I have felt in a theatre since the night the world first heard about the blinding of the horses in Equus.

So what, theatrically speaking, are all these people doing in the same boat? Bouchard is obviously too serious to have thrown them together just for kicks, Grand Hotel style. There must be some symbolic intent in presenting us with a collection of Quebecers, en route to the ultimate Anglophile celebration. The ministerial party makes this stick. Gendron himself, in thrall to a government he more or less despises, is torn between loyalty (or, of course, careerism) and self-loathing. His wife has already made her choice; she lost three sons on the Dieppe beaches in 1942: All of them, she insists, sacrificed to the ambitions of the English. She has a lacerating speech in which she puts her view of the case while her husband, rather feebly, pushes the official line about standing by the allies.

Also travelling first class (this is not an economy play) are three over-the-moon young ladies on this trip of a lifetime after winning a competition for girls named Elizabeth. They and their attendant protocol officer (amusingly played by Glynis Ranney) provide comic relief that is genuinely funny, but they also have an obvious relevance to the play's treatment of what might be called patriotism-once-removed. The themes come together when the three tin Lizzies are taken painfully through the etiquette of the royal curtsey, with the minister's daughter standing in as queen.

Apart from being very entertaining in itself, this rehearsal proves a catalyst in the relationship of Marguerite's parents. It's a fine scene, finely acted. Donna Belleville is stylishly sozzled as the angry Alice; and though it seems odd to cast a so emphatically Anglo actor as David Schurmann in the role of the minister, he plays it very well; nobody, indeed, does world-weariness better.

But that leaves the other half of the play unaccounted for; and what the Chief and his sons have to do with the state of Quebec or of Canada, or anyway with their relation to the mother country, is beyond me. They do provide a link to another of the play's concerns, but it isn't a happy one. "Historians," intones the blackmailing Diplomat (who, as played by Peter Krantz, intones practically everything), "always disagree on one point: history." He's such a wit. We've seen a sort of illustration of his thesis in the discussion of the disaster at Dieppe, but it isn't really all that much of a disagreement. Nobody gives Alice an argument as to what actually happened; they merely differ over whether it can be justified.

All right; now get this. The Chief has brought along a tame Biographer to write his memoirs (i.e.: to tell his story to the world in the way he would like it to be believed). When the Chief finds himself entrapped by the Diplomat, the Biographer recites, in counterpoint, the ways in which the Chief might deal with the situation if he were still the Chief. The world probably divides between those who find this kind of thing profound, and those who just find it profoundly tiresome. It isn't an effective dramatization of two levels of reality, because only one of them gets dramatized. It's a single conventional action that keeps getting interrupted so that we may be told, over and over, that one of the characters would like things to be different.

It's probably not the actors' fault, but whenever I've seen this piece the Biographer has established himself, very quickly, as the character I would most like to see dropped overboard. Apart from being irritating in itself, his running commentary has the inevitable effect of knocking all the dramatic stuffing out of the Chief. I have a horrible feeling that this may be intentional, but I'd still rather watch The Sopranos. The Chief is a hollow man, striking attitudes. He still has to present an iron facade; and for that Jim Mezon, who plays him, is certainly your man. But he could do this role in his sleep.

Jackie Maxwell's production has an imposing air. Ken MacDonald has designed the kind of big-boat setting on which you keep expecting the characters to break into a number (and the way they're posed at the beginning, they look as though they very well might). The actors' delivery could have been stamped by the Department of Weights and Measures: It's very weighty and extremely measured. It's quite a surprise, on reading the published text, to discover that though Linda Gaboriau's translation may sometimes be stiff, it still bears a marked resemblance to normal conversation. There is a theoretical point in jacking up the style of the performance to match the heartlessness of the action, but it isn't sustained. The production, like Marti Maraden's three years ago, goes soft on us, mainly in the scenes between the embittered Etienne and the embarrassed Marguerite.

Dylan Trowbridge and Susie Burnett act as if they can't believe the awful things that are coming out of their mouths; instead of inhabiting their lines, they apologize for them. She is better in her scenes with her family, but he is equally strained when confronting his father, maybe because his antagonist is less a person than an idea.

Jeff Lillico's Sandro, however, is very good, and the more heartbreaking for being the one character who is permitted, from time to time, to be cheerful. And the play's ending is superb: a reverberating denouement with an innocently implacable smile on its lips. The sins of the fathers are visited upon the fathers, or at least on those who don't know how to atone. One in the play does, the other doesn't. It's a semi-fearful symmetry.

DIANA OF DOBSON'S

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

Cicely Hamilton was an English actress, writer and suffragette; and she has been a footnote, if that, in the theatre history books. Diana of Dobson's was her first major play, originally staged in 1908 and a success then and for decades afterwards. It then fell into disuse, but it has been rediscovered in the last dozen years.

Now, at the Shaw Festival, it is receiving its first ever Canadian production. It's a find.

It is part angry satire, part fairy tale -- which is not, come to think of it, an uncommon combination. Dobson's is a drapery store in South London and, as far as its employees are concerned, maybe half- a-grade above a sweatshop. Diana, surname Massingberd, is one of the female sales staff. She shares an on-site dormitory with half-a- dozen of her fellows, all of them liable to have their subsistence wages docked still further if they break any of the establishment's numerous petty regulations.

(The Edwardian drapery business, at once exploitative and paternalistic, seems to have been a world unto itself. Contemporary writers -- H. G. Wells in Kipps and Harley Granville Barker in The Madras House -- use it when they want to portray capitalism in its purest form.)

Diana, daughter of a doctor who died and left her penniless, is by virtue of her middle-class upbringing more bitter, more outspoken, and hence more often in trouble, than her workmates. Suddenly, she comes into money, (ps)300 of it. For comparison purposes: Her shopgirl's wage is five shillings a week, while a young ex-guardsman can live, though not as comfortably as he'd like, on (ps)600 a year.

Diana decides to blow her windfall on a month of luxury in the Swiss Alps, and the Parisian gowns to go with it. Thus attired, and posing as a widow, she attracts the attention of the guardsman's managing aunt, who thinks her nephew's only hope is to marry money, and even of the bashful fellow himself.

He proposes; she reveals her true financial status; he is shocked. Stung, she challenges him rhetorically to try earning his own living, as she has had to do. Surprisingly, he takes her up on this; unsurprisingly, he can't cut it. What happens after that, you will have to attend the play to discover.

It's an oddly constructed piece, with a profligate habit of picking up characters and putting them right down as soon as they have served their turn. That the denizens of Dobson's should be dropped in this way is fair enough: They exist to make points about wage slavery and -- in the person of one who's about to become a bride on the grounds that anything would be better than her current life -- about marriage. The two themes are closely entwined, and this first scene prepares the ground.

But one wants to see more of the tycoon whom Diana encounters in Switzerland and for whom, it turns out, she once worked. He is not a nice man -- as a self-made success who's made his way from errand- boy to entrepreneur, he believes the weak deserve to go to the wall - - but he is an unapologetically vital one, and he recognizes the same quality in Diana.

In fact, he falls for her, thus giving the cue for a scene the author unhappily failed to write. They argue the relation of boss and worker very energetically, but are not allowed to come to grips with the allied question of the relation of husband and wife. It's true this is raised elsewhere, but what might be the sparkiest part of the puzzle is missing.

In terms of character and language, the play lacks texture. It plays, compared to other Shaw Festival discoveries, like hand- me- down St. John Hankin or Granville Barker. It's also very free with its coincidences. But it lives, because the issues it raises are firmly embedded in its action and because the same battles, or their descendants, are still being fought.

Then, too, it comes from a time when even serious playwrights were expected to tell stories; and this one keeps you agog to know what will happen next. There isn't a boring moment in it.

The director, Alisa Palmer, keeps the narrative going, though in other respects her production is rather shallow. The Dobson girls are allowed a surface quality apiece -- one chirpy, one sour, one pert, one peevish -- but then fall into an undifferentiated litany of complaint.

This unfortunately includes Severn Thompson's Diana. There is no special edge to her rebellion, no difference in pressure as she engages with her various companions. She has enough force and charm to carry the play, but she filters them through a fixed smile that lifts only in the very last scene -- an unusual mixture of pain and whimsy, set among the down-and-outs on the Thames Embankment.

Goldie Semple plays the mercenary matchmaker of the mountains, so dazzled by Diana that she starts humming the Merry Widow waltz. Hers is an elegant, seemingly self-generated, performance that might look very well in an Oscar Wilde revival but comes off here as an isolated turn. That she gets laughs is a good sign; that she also gets exit applause is not. Patricia Hamilton is agreeably agreeable as her confidante, or acquiescent acquaintance.

But the best performances in this female-driven play come from the men. Peter Hutt is hard and intelligent, with the right perverse streak of sensitivity, as the rag-trade king who has parlayed the rags into riches for himself and more rags for everyone else.

Evan Buliung plays the cashiered hero with remarkable delicacy. Outwardly a slice of well-bred, dunderheaded brawn, he has more feelings than anyone would believe and, with very few words to help him, he shows them first struggling for existence and then breaking through. More of a buffoon than he would like to be, he is yet less of one than everybody thinks. "Everybody," in this case, includes Diana, and when he accuses her of not having noticed what was going on inside him, he is right. We noticed, though, and the credit is the actor's.

Black & White Photo: David Cooper, Shaw Festival / Diana Donnelly as Kitty Brant and Severn Thompson as Diana Massingberd in Diana of Dobson's -- part angry satire, party fairy tale.
