THE PLOUGH AND THE STARS

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

Sean OCaseys status as a world-class playwright rests on his first three full-length plays, an informal Dublin trilogy written in the early 1920s and providing a worm's-eye view of the birth of modern Ireland.

The Plough and the Stars was the last to be written, following on The Shadow of a Gunman and Juno and the Paycock, but the earliest in chronological setting. It unfolds around and against the Easter Rising of 1916, the event that sparked off those Irish troubles" that have yet to exhaust themselves. The play's skeptical view of what had become a cherished patriotic moment caused riots at its first production in 1926, and led to its author spending the rest of his life in England.

OCasey called the play a tragedy, as he did its two predecessors. Everybody else, though, thinks of them as tragi- comedies, and its their humour, and the way it leavens and thus highlights the pain, that has kept them alive.

Neil Munro's Shaw Festival production of The Plough has some powerful moments, especially towards the end; but it is penitentially slow and morose. This earnest approach may be due to an understandable horror of the comic stage Irishman, but however honourable its motives, it has caused much of the play's appeal to leak away. Several of the cast seem to have their mouths full of cotton-wool, and the small quadrilateral of an acting-area proves unkind to a play thats a kind of off-centre epic.

All three Dublin plays show history impinging on a group of tenement dwellers who have more than enough to cope with already. Those in The Plough fall into three inter-connected groups. There are Jack Clitheroe, a former officer in the Irish Citizen Army (precursor of the IRA) and his young wife, Nora, who is pregnant and lives in justified terror of Jacks returning to the colours. There are Nora's uncle, Peter Flynn, and her cousin, the Young Covey, and the carpenter Fluther Good. Their main occupations are arguing and drinking, though Fluther, when we first meet him, has been three painful days on the wagon.

Finally, there are the older, husbandless women: Mrs. Gogan, who has a consumptive daughter, and Bessie Burgess, the only resident whose sympathies, about which she is relentlessly outspoken, are with the British. The First World War is, of course, in progress and Irish boys, Bessie's son among them, are fighting abroad in the trenches as well as here on the streets. The others run what might be called an apolitical gamut: Most of them would be Fenians if push came to shove, but they would rather it didnt.

OCasey's own attitude to the warring factions is to call down a curse on all their houses and a blessing on those trying to survive inside them. He himself was a lifelong Socialist, who abandoned the nationalists when they turned out to have no interest in economics. But he still reserves his sharpest satire for the character whose views most closely reflect, or at least caricature, his own.

This is the Young Covey, who carries around "Jenersky's Thesis on the Origin, Development an Consolidation of the Evolutionary Idea of th Proletariat, a title he pushes on all he meets, including a prostitute who is consolidating her own proletarian role by trying to pick him up.

This encounter occurs in the second of the play's four acts, which is set in a pub. Outside, an orator is delivering an authentic, blood-curdling speech of the period: When war comes to Ireland, she must welcome it as she would welcome the Angel of God!" (Patrick Galligan, looking sinister, plays his onstage doppelganger.) Inside, the characters are fighting their own wars: mostly verbal, though the two widows come to actual blows.

It's a tame contest, though. Wendy Thatchers Bessie has a gaunt presence that comes in useful later, but neither she nor her antagonist (an excessively lugubrious Kelli Fox) raises much dust. Neil Barclays publican seems forever to be halting brawls that haven't actually started.

In the third act, the rising happens: Offstage, the rebels occupy the post office and the British shell them. Onstage, the tenement people gleefully seize the chance of a little looting -- though not, in this production, gleefully enough.

They aren't the soaks and pretenders of OCaseys earlier plays; they hold down jobs and they display a real, if erratic, solidarity that cuts across barriers. Nevertheless, O'Casey, the most unselfconsciously Shakespearean of modern playwrights (with the blessing that he didn't write in verse), wrote them as clowns, with identifying routines that need to be played to the hilt.

They arent. Uncle Peter, as played by an unsuitably healthy Simon Bradbury, sinks without a trace. Hes meant to be a wizened old man with an excitable streak: He imagines that everything said by the Covey is intended to annoy him, whereas in fact only half of it is. Ben Carlson fires off a few effective rounds as his tormentor, but their comic relationship never happens.

Benedict Campbell comes off better as Fluther, and his silent sinking under the influence is a miniature tour-de-force; or, considering his weakness, a tour-de-faiblesse. But there should still be more gusto, more verbal energy, in a character who can tell the Covey, "It would take something more than a thing like you to flutther a feather o' Fluther. And so it goes for all of them.

O'Casey, who could write comic poetry, fell flat when he tried for the romantic kind, but here -- in the garishly coloured scenes between Jack and his little red- lipped Nora," as they both insist on calling her -- the productions restraint is an asset. Mike Shara and Fiona Byrne act with tact and discover passion; she even brings off a descent into madness at the end.

The last scene, showing the risings aftermath with the army clamping down, is altogether the best; we finally get to feel the pressure of outside events. I don't know if the Cockney Tommy is aiming for impersonal menace, or if he's simply having trouble with the accent, but the Dubliners scurry and rally admirably; and Fluthers decision, when evacuated for the night, that there would be nothing "derogatory" in playing cards in a Catholic church, is a lovely grace-note. Then theres a shocking climax, and an equally shocking release of the tension.

It was O'Casey's own climax as well: None of his later plays is as good. So at least it seems when you read them -- they are hardly ever staged. It might be interesting to try.

Black & White Photo: Andree Lanthier, Shaw Festival / Mike Shara and Fiona Byrne as Jack and Nora Clitheroe: With tactful acting, they discover passion.

THE TEMPEST

Theatre at the Lake, Coronation Park, Oakville

- - -

TWELFTH NIGHT

The Dream in High Park

- - -

I wondered, while travelling to the Theatre at the Lake, if the shipwreck that begins The Tempest was going to be staged on the lake or even, when the passengers quit the vessel, in it. That really would be worth the drive to Oakville.

It doesn't happen. The scene is presented right down front in the main acting area, on a large wooden structure with deck-like qualities. As it's still daylight, with no chance of fancy effects, we get to see who the characters are and can make out what they're talking about. This lucidity turns out to be a constant feature of Miles Potter's production, and it's most welcome.

It comes, though, at a price. The set has to remain in place for the rest of the show, thereby blotting out most of the view. The stage's famous oak tree, which here seems to be growing through the middle of the ship, remains unused. The lake itself, this theatre's primary source of enchantment, is barely visible, and the attendant wide open spaces have to remain unused, though they would seem ideally suited to showing us the various groups of castaways groping their way around Prospero's island.

As Prospero himself, David Ferry seemed on the first night to be suffering recurrent crises of memory quite distinct from the character's. Telling Miranda about their expulsion from Milan, he informed her it was old Gonzalo who was "given this job," not a turn of phrase you'll find in the First Folio or any edition since. There were several of these impromptu substitutions; and they had an impressive habit, not only of making narrative sense, but of scanning as well.

Ferry is a very intelligent actor with an impressive technique. He can, for example, take a complicated subordinate clause and relate it back to the sentence he first thought of, all on a single breath. In a character as complexly articulate as Prospero, this is a great asset. He is firmly in control of the marathon expositions of his first scene, properly angry at "our revels now are ended," and stirring, in a subdued way, for the great renunciation. But he cannot fill the great gap in the play's structure -- the fact that though Prospero completely controls the play's front and back ends, he is largely absent from its middle, merely dropping in from time to time to see how his magic is going. In these incursions, Ferry suggests a friendly conjuror putting in appearances at a children's party, rather than a dedicated avenger calculating just how far he can go.

He is, on the whole, an amiable Prospero; and this creates problems. Prospero's obsession with his daughter's virginity may be warped prurience, or it may be passionate concern. But it really doesn't make sense as daddy's little joke. Caliban, meanwhile, is even more sympathetically played by Oliver Dennis, especially fine when getting helplessly drunk on the sailors' liquor and singing his doomed song of freedom. When we're told he tried to rape Miranda, we frankly don't believe it. Prospero keeps him in leg irons, which he can loose with a wave of his wand (an effect I've never seen before) whenever he needs his slave to do some log-hauling. The relationship could hardly be more graphically exploitative, so one expects something more explosive at its resolution than this Prospero's expression of mild regret. Nor does his relation with Ariel (played, in a mystic monotone, by Deborah Pollitt) really go anywhere, though it's nicely set up, with Prospero scrupulously adjusting the remaining length of service in the spirit's contract.

The clues here are in the text, and Potter's attention to its details is his defining mark as a director of Shakespeare. It isn't enough to carry him through the sweeping reunions of the last scene, which pretty much falls apart, but it illuminates many of the earlier ones. The courtly conspirators (Patrick Garrow and Patric Masurkevitch) are unusually compelling; in a Napoleonic costume scheme, these two wear tricorne hats as a badge of villainy. The clowns (Larry Yachimec and Andy Pogson) not only get their full complement of laughs but get them on the lines. Tova Smith very nearly balances the innocence and eagerness in Miranda, though her Ferdinand (Jonathan Geenen) plays ardour mainly in terms of a toothy grin. There are four attendant spirits who play the goddesses in the masque and -- in the production's most imaginative moment -- end up bearing away the relics of Prospero's art: his books and the pieces of his broken staff. Their greatest service, though, is to help out with the songs: "Come unto these yellow sands" is authentically enchanting.

- - -

There is nothing of this quality in High Park's Twelfth Night, but it's lively, the best thing here in several summers. Once again the stage is a built-up area: There's a triple-tiered set, whose upper levels are frustratingly under-used, all done up in various shades of blue. Olivia's taste in garden furniture is bizarre, but it has its uses: I've seen the plotters in the letter scene hide in many places in my time, but never behind turquoise obelisks.

The best feature of David Storch's production is its briskness. I've grown up on autumnal melancholy Twelfth Nights, and I like them, but my favourite character, Fabian, refers to the action as "matter for a May morning" (Twelfth Night itself, of course, is in January, but we won't get into that), and Harold Bloom has written that he's never seen a production that was mad enough. He might have liked this one.

One reason for its speed is the director has cut all the more obscure jokes. You would not believe what this does for the running time. He's also reversed the order of the first two scenes. This is now common practice, though why any director should want to begin with "What country, friends, is this?" rather than "If music be the food of love, play on," beats me. (First, the magic; then the exposition. Please.) Anyway, when we do get to David Collins's Orsino, making his musical requests, he turns out to be passionate, edgy and neurotically intense. ("Enough, no more" must make the minstrels quake behind their lutes.)

Genevieve Steele's Olivia is a bubbling flirt, who can't wait to get out of mourning. Zainab Musa is ill-prepared for Viola's lyrical flights, but, by accident or design, casts a refreshingly unsentimental light on her "patience on a monument" speeches. She and her twin, Sebastian, are both black. (They all look the same to Illyrians? Surely not.)

The multicultural casting even admits an American Sir Toby (Bruce Gooch), a vigorous country rake. Sanjay Talwar's lanky Sir Andrew is conventional but very appealing when he proudly acknowledges that many do call him fool. Chapelle Jaffe is a good, managing Maria, and Michael Spence a Feste with a rough sense of humour and a gimpy leg; I apologize in advance if it's the actor's own. But the most accomplished performance is Michael Spencer-Davis's Malvolio, whose mandarin repression is explosively released when he goes into yellow stockings and cross-garters, topped off on this occasion by a jockstrap. Definitely a creature of extremes, he still does not merit the shock ending his director has devised for him. I said this was a lively production. It's even, line-by-line, intelligent. But I wouldn't claim it was thoughtful.

Black & White Photo: Canstage / Sanjay Talwar as Sir Andrew Aguecheek locks swords with Zainab Musa as Viola in Twelfth Night in High Park.

NO MAN'S LAND

Premiere Dance Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - In future years people are going to tell their children how William Hutt, in Soulpepper's production of Harold Pinter's No Man's Land, trod daintily around a carpet, taking elaborate care never to actually touch it, in order to get at a glass of whisky. Hutt plays Spooner, an unsuccessful poet (or so he says), who finds himself in the house of Hirst, a successful poet (or so he says).

Hirst has apparently met Spooner in the literary reaches of North London ("do you often hang about Hampstead Heath?") and asked him back for a drink. Or for many drinks: There are few things in this play of which one can be sure, but if there is one near-certainty it is that Hirst is an alcoholic.

No Man's Land was first staged in 1975 by Britain's National Theatre, directed by Peter Hall and with performances by John Gielgud and Ralph Richardson that became legendary. I wouldn't claim that Albert Schultz's production, in which Hutt squares off against the Hirst of Peter Donat, improves on the original, but it's comparable, and in a couple of ways I prefer it. It makes less grandiose claims for itself; it has a homelier, more approachable setting (by John Thompson) and is played as the highest comedy. Pinter uses the English language better than any other living dramatist, and the wit of this production's first scene, both spoken and implied, has the audience purring with suppressed delight.

Hirst has success, or its trappings; Spooner, envious and possibly admiring, wants in. Spooner, whose speech sometimes suggests a pastiche of T.S. Eliot, has, we gather, sunk fairly low in the world, and earns a crust by clearing the tables in the pub where Hirst picked him up. Now he sits in the corner, stooped at attention, looking like an especially unkempt professor, in white crumpled hair and a brown corduroy suit. Anxious not to offend his host, or to seem to presume (hence his careful circumlocution of the carpet), he can still not resist tilting at him whenever possible, and Hutt's presentation of these discreet jabs is a miracle of sustained timing. He presents a civilized mind, angry at its own corruption; as with Gielgud, our awareness of the actor's own cultural status adds a teasing element to the effect, but does not create it.

As Hirst, Donat has to work harder at creating the massive cocooned eccentric than did Richardson, who could just be. Donat is a hawk-like figure with claws for hands; claws that twitch convulsively in expectation of the next drink, and a voice that's somewhere between a bark and a croak. He says comparatively little, but his impassivity in itself keeps Spooner on the hop. Barely moving from, or even in, his chair, he still commands the room until, after falling to the floor, he leaves it, slowly and on all fours. ("I have known this before" says Spooner; the first utterance, mournful and oracular, of what is to prove a recurring refrain.)

Suddenly, Spooner is surprised, by Foster and Briggs, two younger Londoners who seem to be Hirst's minders, and are not at all pleased to find their turf invaded and their authority potentially challenged. More vicious cat-and-mouse games ensue. The play declares itself an up-market reprise of Pinter's masterpiece, The Caretaker, presenting the same triangular power-struggle between the resident, the intruder, and the guardian -- or, in this case, guardians.

It takes a swerve when, next morning, Hirst reappears transformed, dapper in blazer and cravat. Pinter is a cricket fanatic, and Donat looks here as if he might be on his way to Lord's for a Test Match. For that matter, all four characters have the names of famous cricketers, and there is a sequence in which Hirst and Spooner debate, in cricketing terms, the talents of a former mutual lady friend; though the punchline -- "in other words, did she google?" -- has now, of course, taken on different connotations.

It may seem strange that the two men, apparently new acquaintances the previous night, should now be discussing in some detail a shared past. As a matter of fact, it is strange, and two rival explanations -- neither, of course, confirmed nor denied -- suggest themselves. One is that Hirst, on the previous night, was just too drunk to recognize Spooner, and that was Spooner was biding his time. The other -- which I think more likely, and certainly more interesting -- is that Hirst is fantasizing again (he addresses one of his servants by a different name) and that Spooner, with brilliant improvisational skills, is continuing to play up to him, working off a real resentment in an imaginary framework.

The reason I find it more interesting is that the gilded world the two of them now conjure up, of country houses and university and smart adultery and tea on the lawns -- is fine brittle satire, but is inescapably second-hand. It has nothing like the reality of the play's present, which reasserts itself in Spooner's last desperate speech, listing his qualifications for the role of Hirst's companion. Hirst might, Spooner suggests, address a literary society of which he is secretary and which meets upstairs at the pub, the room, the milieu, and their implications for both men leap before our eyes. This speech is one of the high-points of contemporary drama and, as spoken by Gielgud, it was a perfect fastidious marriage of text and performance. Hutt's delivery was, on the first night, a trifle ragged, but he superbly conveyed the need behind the cadences.

Schultz's direction orchestrates the battles with an acute sense of who sits where and who moves where. Especially sweet is the moment in which Foster and Briggs, sniffing defeat, make as one for the drinks table. The two wide boys are admirably played by Stuart Hughes, who has a daintiness of threat that suggests Mick Jagger, and Michael Hanrahan, though his accent sometimes prompted the suspicion that he would be happier if his character were Irish.

Each of them is granted a set-speech, one about Balinese girls who are thoroughly available at home but untouchable when they sign up at London language schools, and the other about the impossibility of ever finding your way out of a West End thoroughfare called Bolsover Street. Such is the power of Pinter that for years after the premiere, Londoners who had seen the play and who found themselves driving toward Bolsover Street, would freeze in terror.

I have never been happy with the ending, in which Hirst's announcement that he is changing the subject "for the last time" is taken to entail universal stasis. Even in so verbal a piece, this seems to place excessive weight on a mere turn of phrase. (A play on words in a play on words.) But it has a chilly effectiveness, especially here with Donat at once terrified and terrifying and the octogenarian Hutt, who has been using his quiet and silky side, suddenly sounding out like King Lear. He is a phenomenon. The new Toronto season starts here, at what may very well prove its highest point.

Black & White Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / William Hutt plays the unsuccessful poet Spooner in the Soulpepper production of No Man's Land.

HAPPY DAYS

Premiere Dance Theatre, Toronto

- - -

"That is what I find so wonderful," says Winnie, the heroine of Samuel Beckett's Happy Days, "a part remains of one's classics to help one through the day." I have that line handy because it is reproduced at the head of the press release for the new Soulpepper season, of which Happy Days is the second triumphant production. As a slogan for an ambitious theatre company, it strikes me as disingenuous. The classics, as experienced by Winnie, are a few literary fragments disconnected from their sources, part of the mental and physical detritus of her life. If they help her through the day, that isn't necessarily a compliment to them.

Or maybe it is. The distinction of Beckett's vision, certainly in this play, is that it's pitiless without being heartless. Winnie, a presumably middle-class woman of dainty tastes, sits buried in a mound of earth -- up to her waist in the first act and to her neck in the second. Plainly she is being encroached upon, by time and by the routines of her existence. A program note says this is "considered by many to be Beckett's most cheerful play," but if that's true it suggests that those "many" have a talent for optimism equal to Winnie's own. The play may well contain Beckett's most cheerful character, but that's not the same.

It's another presentation of the things that we do in order, as one of the tramps in Godot put it, "to give ourselves the impression we exist." The things in Winnie's life may be even more disturbing than those in the lives of Vladimir and Estragon, since her lifestyle is closer than theirs to what most of us are likely to experience as quotidian reality. Winnie's day starts with the ringing of an alarm clock -- at a volume that scares the living daylights out of the audience, but Winnie takes it in stride. (Or would, if she were in any position to have a stride.) Once awakened, her day revolves around a few simple props: a parasol, which at one exciting moment catches fire, a capacious handbag, a gun -- this last apparently confiscated from her husband.

The pleasures she takes in these possessions have, she realizes, to be carefully parcelled out; if she got through all of them too soon, who knows what emptiness would engulf her? The bag and its contents, in particular, are treats to be carefully rationed out. And she has to judge, very carefully, the time to sing her song. Apparently she knows only one, The Merry Widow Waltz; the second time it's appeared in a play in two weeks.

The play unfolds in two dimensions: the metaphysical one, presenting a cross-section of Winnie's existence, one day very like another; and the temporal one, tracing the progress of a relationship. I mentioned Winnie's husband. His name is Willie and he apparently lives behind the mound. We hear little from him and see less. But the back of his bald head occasionally pops up, while his wife admonishes him on how to protect himself from the sun and how best to re-enter his burrow. (Backwards, on all fours.) Occasionally he reads ads from the newspaper, chosen for their sardonic content ("smart boy wanted") or replies, even more sardonically, to Winnie's incessant questioning: Asked to define a hog he replies, with feeling, "castrated male swine."

The end of the play finds Willie putting in a more extended personal appearance, appearing in front of the mound in evening dress, then crawling up it, encouraged by an expectant if somewhat disparaging Winnie. ("Not quite the crawler you were, Willie. Not quite the crawler I gave my heart to.") Whether he is trying to get at her, as she excitedly anticipates, or at the gun, is a moot point. Whether, if the latter is the case, he intends to use it on himself or on her is even mooter.

Michael Simpson plays Willie perfectly, but the play of course belongs to its Winnie, Martha Burns. I approached her performance with some trepidation since, though I have always respected Burns' acting for its intelligence and imagination, I have often felt these qualities betrayed by a lack of vocal colour, a tendency to droop and hence to make every line come out the same. Unexpectedly, this matters far less in the context of what is virtually a monologue. Here, she can make her own rules and set her own rhythms. Her timing is consummate; she is the wittiest Winnie I have seen as well, incidentally, as the comeliest. She is also, behind her debonair smile, the most frightened, and therefore the bravest; the most conscious of the things she is fighting not to recognize. Her recurring mantra -- "This is going to be another happy day" -- is, like her whole performance, beautifully poised between delight and despair. And -- though the author must of course take ultimate credit for this -- the sight of her face sticking out of the earth as the lights go out on Act Two is irresistibly funny.

Some of the lightness of touch can presumably be attributed to Vikki Anderson, who is both the director and designer. The mound, as she has envisioned it, is an extension of Winnie herself; it spreads out around her like a hoop-skirt. There is also a false proscenium, which points up Winnie's own occasional awareness of being a character in what was once an avant-garde play. She talks about a couple who came to look at her and asked what she was supposed to mean, stuck there like that -- the kind of joke Beckett had already played in Endgame. Anderson may also have speeded up the play by cutting bits of it. The end comes very abruptly, and I missed the line in which Winnie exhorts the laboriously climbing Willie to "put a little jizz in it."

Some streamlining, though, is forgivable. Line by line the play, like just about all of Beckett, is perfectly judged, but it pushes its one image excessively hard. You forgive it, because the metaphor is so strong, but you get the point early and you don't have the (comparatively) huge casts of the earlier plays to compensate. Nor do you have the ferocious economy of the later playlets, to which this one looks forward. "What a curse, mobility," says Winnie, apparently speaking for her author, who was to supply his actors with progressively less room for manoeuvring.

To end where I begun, a Beckettian thing to do: The word "classic" is applicable here, not in the general sense of something rather old, but as denoting a particular style, the one that's the opposite of "romantic" and whose gift is to find joy in rigour. Soulpepper, with No Man's Land and Happy Days, has now richly delivered on that style twice in two weeks. Next, the sternest test, is Phedre, as classic as plays come.

PHEDRE

Du Maurier Theatre Centre, Toronto

- - -

Inexorable, says Theseus, king of Athens, in Ted Hughes translation of Racine's Phedre, "that is the word for the gods." It's also the word for the play in which he is -- I use the word advisedly --caught: the world of Racine is one of omnipresent trap. Its characters, drawn from Greek tragedy, sometimes see themselves as the pawns of destiny, but destiny only means forces within themselves. When they take action, whether its to escape these forces or to help them along, the results are invariably appalling. Just like life, really. When he makes his pronouncement, Theseus thinks things are as bad as they can possibly get. He is wrong.

Racine, writing in supposedly rational 17th-century France, never mocks his myths. Almost alone among the modern playwrights who have plundered the Greeks, he seems to believe passionately in the stories he is telling. He alters them, of course. Phedre, which depicts the consuming desire of Theseus wife for her husband's virginal stepson, is based on Euripides' Hippolytus, and the difference in titles tells us much about the plays. Euripides was more interested in the young man, and Racine, celebrated for writing "she-tragedies," in the woman. Then, Racines Hippolytus is not Euripides untouchable ascetic; he is in love, with the captive princess Aricia. This looks suspiciously as if Racine were throwing in the neo-classic equivalent of a Hollywood romantic interest, and this may indeed have been the case, but he turns it to characteristic account.

Phedre only learns of Hippolytus' love half-way through the play. Until now, passion and shame have been combusting inside her. Now jealousy is added to the mix, pushing her into the abyss on whose edge she has been trembling from her first appearance. She becomes, for the first time, consciously malevolent. And since she is a high- principled woman, with a strong sense of family honour (daddy is a god, with an important position in hell) the guilt helps destroy her.

Racine offers no naturalistic crutches to either his actors or his audience; his concentration makes Shakespeare look slap-happy. Soulpepper's Phedre is brave and ambitious. Im not sure how successful it is because, frankly, I dont know what I want from Racine, certainly not from Racine in English. Even in France, the play's exalted reputation weighs it down; outside it, we have to add to the legend of the stupendously moving Phedres of the past (all of them French) the general consensus that Racine's fanatically economical poetry is untranslatable. We approach the play asking for the moon, knowing we wont get it, and wondering how much to settle for instead.

There is something very lunar about Daniel Brooks production, which Dany Lyne has set in a wasted chamber backed by a series of sternly receding arches, each framing a door harder than its predecessor to squeeze through. Andrea Lundy's lighting punctuates the action with uncommon boldness, switching abruptly from one state to the next, and sometimes settling with cruel insistence on the face of a single actor. Phedre and Theseus, in particular, look under the white beams as if their souls have been stripped.

There is a matching soundscape (by Richard Feren), which hums behind much of the dialogue, quietly but distractingly; between scenes, and far more helpfully, it blows up a storm. This may be meant to suggest the approach of the sea-monster who plays a crucial role in the play's catastrophe; it also sounds like the roar of an express-train, hurtling toward disaster, which is by no means a bad metaphor for the action itself.

The staging pushes the play to a higher pitch than does Hughes translation, which is gratifyingly speakable but is not on the same level as his Agamemnon, currently at Stratford. His blood-red poetic talent may not have been in tune with Racines. Being English, he can't resist bringing the characters down to Earth; Tanja Jacobs as Phedre's meddlesome confidante (a role she may be too young for) is allowed more or less to tell her mistress that being unlucky in love runs in her family and that she really should pull herself together. Racine certainly wasnt humourless but his jokes, usually sadistic ones, are in his texture rather than his text. Hughes script is in verse, but it doesn't rhyme; the couplets, the strict form that strains the passions to breaking-point, are what make Racine terrible, just as they're what make Moliere funny.

The production seems split between Racines demands and Hughes concessions, and Brooks' grip on the acting is far less rigorous than it is on the effects. It's a famous moment in theatrical history when Phedre asks for a chair; it shows how far gone she is, since people in French tragedy seldom do anything so undignified as to sit down. Here they sit all the time, admittedly on very unwelcoming high-backed seats that seem to have come from the demanding workshop of Charles Rennie Mackintosh. (At a moment of high passion, one of the chairs gets knocked over, and its thrilling; then another one is, apparently for the sake of symmetry, and its an anti-climax.)

Once seated, the actors are tempted further into chattiness, with attendant gestures, and each gesticulation lowers the temperature; I wanted to tie their hands to their sides, especially in the opening expository scene where we're more aware of the characters trying to explain what they mean than of what it is they're explaining.

As Phedre, Nancy Palk makes a thrilling first entrance, swathed in veils, keeping her back to us and hugging the walls, the very picture of libido at the end of its tether. One wondered if she could keep it up; in fact she does, but with not enough variation. The power remains but its indiscriminately channeled, with crucial changes in the characters mental state going unregistered. She is the most sensual of Anglophone Phedres (of those I've seen, Diana Rigg was nun-like and Glenda Jackson downright spinsterish) and she has the technical and mental resources for the role; but not, perhaps, the temperament. She is a generous actress trying to feed an insatiably ravenous role; and though that may sound an ideal arrangement, it doesn't quite balance.

Phedre is not, despite the legend, a one-woman show; and one great virtue of this production is that it emerges as the tragedy of a whole family, and indeed of a kingdom. (Three people die; the rest are devastated.)

The play has been cast up to the hilt, with actresses of the standing of Kate Hennig and Patricia Fagan drafted to deliver brief bulletins of bad news, though their chief contribution is to stand around paying mutely eloquent tributes to doom. Jonathan Watton has the looks and the air -- not insensitive but callow -- for Hippolytus, though his verse-speaking is in urgent need of attention. Diego Matamoros, though not quite one's idea of a man with a thousand ravishments on his resume, is a fierce, uncompromising Theseus; uncompromising because I, at least, had never realized before just how mean and vindictive this character is. William Webster makes amends for his earlier fidgets with a finely focussed account of the great messenger speech, and Yanna McIntosh -- whom Soulpepper should start pelting with major roles -- is a vibrant Aricia; the most sensible character in the play but as incapable as the others of stopping tragedy in its tracks. To make us feel that may be achievement enough.

Black & White Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / A she-tragedy? Diego Matamoros as Theseus and Nancy Palk as the title character in Phedre.

PORTRAIT

Artword Alternative Space

- - -

A man in his 30s and a woman in her 20s stand side by side. He does most of the talking. He tells her, and us, that he is a success, a man of destiny, adding charmingly that I'm important. You arent. She, politely unimpressed, says that she, a rising young artist, can give him true immortality by painting his portrait.

This little scene, schematic but crisp, kicks off Portrait, a new play by Marisa Victor. What follows is that he (no names are given) accepts her invitation and visits her studio, a poverty-row garret with a rotary phone and a dysfunctional toilet. She professes to be a dedicated artist, emphatically uninterested in material rewards, and to have innovative techniques that will allow her to capture on canvas the man within. Skeptical but intrigued, he goes along. He, of course, fancies her (she seems ambivalent about him) and their involvement, whether or not its sexual, eventually harms his marriage. She meanwhile gets a taste -- a substantial taste -- of what it's like to be fashionable.

In some ways, the play resembles The Shape of Things. A woman professing to be an artist takes a man and, in making him the subject of his art, changes him. In this case, though, the subject knows from the outset that he is the subject, and he starts, unlike Neil LaBute's nerd, from a position of power. We get role reversal rather than violent humiliation.

The painter, meanwhile, most unlike LaButes scarily undeviating heroine, has her doubts. She doesnt know whether she's any good; she doesn't know whether she wants to paint portraits or devote herself solely to abstracts; she lives in constant fear of having sold out. Or she says she does; maybe shes just being manipulative. But even her manipulations point to actual insecurities. The audience, which starts out thinking its been summoned to watch a shiny idealist put a crass materialist in his place, gets its preconceptions knocked about. The woman also believes herself to be privileged, by virtue of her potential if not of her achievement. She's a believable study in arrogance.

So, also, is the man, but less interestingly. He goes through credible but predictable motions. It might help if we had a clearer idea of just what it is he does that's made him rich and famous at 37. (He seems to be some kind of captain of industry, but one cant be sure.)

Then again, the casting may be skewed. Stephen Near, though perfectly competent, seems young and light for his role, and sticking a scrub of beard on his chin does not bestow charisma. Grania Maguire, on the other hand, looks and sounds exactly right as the blond transformer, convincing enough to override some first- night insecurities. In fact, the whole production, under Lindy Zuckers direction, appeared unfinished, with the actors still too far from one another's throats.

The play is the second show from Allegoria Productions, whose "mandate," it says here, is to produce provocative and entertaining new and classic plays interpreted to focus on Canadian social, political and environmental issues (i.e., to do the same as everybody else). I don't know who told them to do it; if nobody did and its all their own idea, then it isnt a mandate. A mandate is, by definition, something you get handed. There's a comic comment on this kind of language in the play itself, when the heroine says, "I have a commission for a self-portrait." At least I hope it's comic. The authors ear is, in general, very good -- and talking of ears, the script contains a mini-lesson on the right way to pronounce Van Gogh.

Theres a very sharp first-act ending. It feels, indeed, so conclusive that it's disconcerting to find it followed by an intermission rather than a curtain call. To put it more brutally, the situation is slight and the development prolonged. The play holds the attention, even so.

SHE STOOPS TO CONQUER

duMaurier Theatre Centre, Toronto

- - -

A wise British director once said that there is nothing much you can do with Oliver Goldsmith's She Stoops to Conquer, a play so inherently sturdy, charming and amusing as to resist anything you might call interpretation. I am not sure whether Albert Schultz, who has directed it for Soulpepper, is of the same mind. My guess is that he is trying to do something with the play. My problem is that I can't make out what it is. And this may well be because he himself never quite decided.

She Stoops is mistaken-identity comedy raised to a higher power. The plot premise is that Young Marlow, a London gent, mistakes a private country house for an inn. The psychological premise is that this misunderstanding suits him just fine. Marlow is terrified of women of his own class but a wolf with females of the lower orders. He has been sent to woo an heiress but, taking her for a barmaid, sets about seducing her instead. She, knowing the truth and attracted by him anyway, takes respectable pleasure in leading him on and then confronting him. Goldsmith, a shy and dissolute young man, based Marlow on himself, and the character still rings true, 200-and-some years on.

Did I say "rings"? Obviously this play is full of people falling into error and then, abruptly, realizing the truth. In this production, every time either of these things happens -- indeed every time there's a twist of plot or a change of mood -- the moment is signalled by some kind of bell tone. (Actually it's the twanging of a harpsichord.) You would think, after the dire experience of A Flea in Her Ear a few years ago, that Soulpepper would have learned the folly of stopping plays in their tracks by underlining the comic points. But, no, here they go again.

To be fair, the effect this time is less destructive. The play does survive. But all this nudging is patronizing to the audience and no great compliment to the actors, who should be playing the transitions themselves, rather than standing around with invisible thought balloons coming out of their heads. The production has the odd effect of turning the play into the opposite of what its first audiences liked about it. In 1773 it was welcomed as an oasis of realism in a desert of sentimental artifice. Here it goes right back into artificiality.

Some of this seems to be intentional. Patricia Fagan plays Kate Hardcastle, the heroine, as a girl who likes striking and then mocking attitudes. When she's alone with her cousin Constance (Molly Atkinson), the two of them enjoy exchanging confidences as if they were the heroines of what another character calls "a whining modern novel." That's neat. But this Kate never lets up. Flitting between her indulgent father (pleasantly played by Oliver Dennis) and her bemused lover, she is less a sensible young lady who knows what she wants and how to get it than a dyed-in-the-wool designing minx. Some of what she does is clever, but the smiling arabesques that she describes all over the text are too much. This is an actress who should be relaxing into her own charm, not sqandering it. Marlow takes it for granted that every serving girl is a tart; Kate doesn't need to act the part quite so enthusiastically. Stuart Hughes' Marlow is an unexpectedly searching portrait of a gentleman-lout, but hard though the couple play together, there is little spark between them, and no particular delight in the happy ending.

Delight, in fact, is what the show lacks -- delight and warmth. Most of the jokes land, but they do so in isolation, without the joy that should make a pyramid of them, each level more welcome than the last. That takes personality, and the right blend of personality. Paul Manz makes the scapegrace Tony Lumpkin a persuasively dropsical figure, rather lightly touched in. I can't hold it against him that he isn't especially funny; funny Lumpkins are even rarer than funny Falstaffs.

As his doting mother Mrs. Hardcastle, Fiona Reid, not surprisingly, is funny. When she complains of her husband's "Gothic vivacity," she transports us into another world of wit, one in which an actress can suck all the juice from an adjective and then come back in triumph for the noun. She can also drop an aside in the audience's lap more purposefully than anyone else on stage. The problem isn't that she's acting in a different style from everybody else but that the production makes no allowances for the fact -- it just has her swoop on, do her stuff, and swoop off again. It also robs her of the one chance to make her character human when, lost in her own back garden, she fancies she's met a highwayman and offers her own life in exchange for her son's. The cute staging hereabouts - - actors waving fronds, pretending to be trees -- stops us caring about that or anything else.

There is, despite Astrid Janson's high and handsome set, little sense of domesticity, though I did enjoy the set-piece scene in which Mr. Hardcastle's lumbering servants (led by Michael Simpson's immovable Diggory) convulse at the memory of one of his ancient stories. Jordan Pettle gets an unusual amount out of the second- lover role of Hastings, whom he plays as a caustic commentator, full of sound judgment except when his own interests are at stake. He is not, admittedly, the smoothest dispenser of 18th-century prose. But this only points out a gap in Soulpepper's record as a classical company. Very few of their successes have been in plays written before, say, 1830. She Stoops, indeed, is one of the few dead- centre English classics they have even attempted, and maybe we were naive to expect that they would romp through it. The play's subtitle is The Mistakes of a Night; this production only makes one real mistake, but it's a big one, and the night is full of it.

Black & White Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / Molly Atkinson (left) and Patricia Fagan are cousins who enjoy exchanging confidences as if they were the heroines of what another character calls "a whining modern novel."

THE SWANNE: PRINCESS CHARLOTTE (THE ACTS OF VENUS)

Studio Theatre, Stratford

- - -

When the first instalment of Peter Hinton's trilogy The Swanne bowed in at Stratford last year, it proved to be an elaborate exercise in the what if or "just suppose" school of historical drama. We were told that Princess Charlotte, daughter of George IV of England (a.k.a. the Prince Regent, Beau Brummells fat friend, that one) had a liaison with her valet, who happened to be black, and that she gave birth to a son. Some complicated baby-switching ensued; and as the play enfolded, continually changing time-frames and social strata, we watched the boy hounded from pillar to post, finally landing in the dressing-room of an old, blind actress.

Theres no question of the boy, whose name is William, challenging the succession; his colour alone would declare him illegitimate. Nor do I believe that Hinton believes he actually existed. This is awkward; Shakespeare, for example, may have told all kinds of lies about Richard III, but he probably thought he was telling the truth, so his play carries weight as a view of history. Hinton's story is a fairy tale; so the picture of 19th-century England (and, by implication, of other times and places as well) that he attaches to it can never quite be taken seriously.

That's the downside. The good news is that for much of the time the sheer scale of Hintons ambition, which sometimes verges on the insane, generates its own energy, carrying cast and audience along with it. The newly-opened Part Two, subtitled Princess Charlotte (The Acts of Venus) strikes me as a great improvement on its predecessor, though that may partly be because it has that predecessor to build upon. The gain is in density of theme and atmosphere, rather than narrative. If your main pleasure in the theatre is the simple one of knowing what happens next, you will be frustrated. Hinton offers nothing as straightforward as a sequel. He goes back over the same ground, showing it off from different angles. We have, by the end, moved on a little chronologically, but not much.

As before, the play is presented to us as having been written by the future Queen Victoria, four years before her accession. It seems she has spent a lot of her girlhood (she must be 13) reading Elizabethan and Restoration plays. That at least would account for the strange, if colourful, lingo spouted by the staff and clientele of the brothel (largely, but not exclusively, homosexual) in which much of the play takes place. Victorias view of the state of England is far from what we think of as Victorian. (But then, who knows what goes on in the minds of impressionable young girls before they become virtuous wives and widows?) She also shows great disgust for the rich, especially her own relatives, and great sympathy for the poor; as well she might.

Her play has a chorus-figure, the goddess Venus, who comes to Earth in search of her son Cupid. In other words, she is Looking for Love in all the Wrong Places. (She's one of several mothers here in search of sons). What she finds among humankind is love destroyed and distorted, though it probably doesn't need her presence to point this out.

What else happens? The play keeps switching between periods. In 1817, Charlotte has her affair and her baby, while St. John Voranguish, the royal whoremaster, falls in love with a street girl named Jaquenetta, who also gives birth. She was formerly -- flashbacks within flashbacks -- the mistress of Fred Dobing, an actor in a touring company run by and starring a Mrs. Cox, who is devoted to the Greek classics and is in fact the younger self of the blind Scarecrow from Part One. Fred quits the stage in favour of political agitation; he gets mixed up in the Cato Street Conspiracy, a sort of pre-Victorian Gunpowder Plot, which here inspires some of the simplest and strongest writing and playing of the evening. Meanwhile -- so to speak -- in 1833, the now-adolescent William takes refuge in the brothel, and is pursued there by the authorities, who seize the excuse to tear the place apart. The scenes in the brothel and theatre go on a lot, maybe because Hinton enjoys writing them, but they do have relevance. "I do value words and what they mean" says Jaquenetta, in what I take to be the plays key line. Life would be better if we told the truth, respected style, loved honestly, paid decent wages, refrained from raiding gay bath houses, and maybe abolished the monarchy. I think thats the message.

There is little continuity between this year's casting and last year's; about the only survivors are Seun Olagunju as William, Julia Donovan who sports a royal lisp as Charlotte, and Diane DAquila who as the Scarecrow seems more than ever to be having both the role and the time of her life. Some of the actors seem to have trouble getting their tongues around the lines, which is surprising, since the author is also the director and, in terms of atmosphere and staging, an excellent one. The newcomers include Jane Sidell, superb as Jaquenetta; Scott Wentworth invaluable as Voranguish, in both tough and tender moods; John Dolan, very strong as Fred; and Sara Topham, hard-bitten as the only whore without a heart of gold. Ian White makes a quick, sharp impression as the conspirator Thistlewood, and Margot Dionnes oddly distanced style of acting suits Venus very nicely. As the bawd, Maria Vacratsis is uncharacteristically aloof.

There is surprisingly little humour, apart from the use of long words in sexual contexts, but the overall drive and colour compensate. Next year, presumably, we'll get Part Three. And at some point, surely, all three plays must be staged together, maybe in a single day. I think there's a very good chance that we would be blown away.

TROILUS AND CRESSIDA

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

Richard Monette's production of Troilus and Cressida has two shining virtues. One is the intelligence that informs the speaking and staging of each individual scene; whether wittily, passionately or despairingly, the characters relate. The other achievement is really the former writ large; all these episodes are forged into a pattern.

Like most directors, Monette places his intermission at the point where Troilus, the youngest prince of Troy, wins the love -- and the body -- of Cressida, whose father has defected to the Greeks and who is liable at any moment to be sent to be join him. As we watch these precarious sweethearts embrace, courtesy of Cressida's uncle Pandarus the super-bawd, two other couples are spotlit at opposite corners of the stage, reminding us what, in this play's society, love actually means. There are Paris and Helen, whose legendary passion caused the legendary war that is now in its seventh weary year. And, representing the Greek camp, there is the spoiled hero Achilles and Patroclus, his companion -- or, as he's described by the scabrous Thersites in the only explicit homosexual reference in any Shakespeare play (and I'm not forgetting Richard II), his "masculine whore."

There is a matching tableau at the end of the play when all pretenses of love and honour are in tatters: Troilus, Cressida, Pandarus, Thersites, each in desperate isolation. I am not suggesting these unifying devices are earth-shakingly original, or that this is the most imaginative production Monette or anyone else has ever directed at Stratford. It may, though, be one of the most lucid, and with Troilus that could be more important. A very great play, it can also seem a very diffuse one. Its themes are tightly knotted, and the Trojan War itself bestows some appearance of unity. But in fact Shakespeare drew on two sources and two groups of characters. Half of the play is taken, however sardonically, from Homer; the famous "anger of Achilles," the war-hero who refuses to quit his tent and fight the Trojans until Patroclus' death stirs him to fury, is reduced to a highly ambiguous fit of the sulks, and he kills Hector, his chivalrous Trojan opposite, not in single combat but in a vicious ambush. Troilus and Cressida, though, seem to have been inventions of the Middle Ages, and it can sometimes seem a mere coincidence they are occupying the same space. Even at the end, in the chaos of battle, the various actions do not so much unite as -- to use the kind of abrasive image the play itself delights in -- rub up against one another.

I had to miss this production's first night and, having heard some disparaging reports, I found myself wondering when the bad stuff was going to start. It never does. Even the notorious superimposition of Nine Inch Nails' Closer to God at the end of the play failed to bother me. I don't think it helps much, but it lasts for all of 30 seconds, and is pretty much inaudible anyway. It does, though, enable the management to post a sign in the lobby warning of "offensive language," which must be a first for Stratford Shakespeare. Actually, all of Shakespeare's plays, by censorship standards, contain offensive language, and none more than this one, but the general assumption is the pure of heart won't notice.

"Wars and lechery ... nothing else holds fashion" is Thersites' uncontroversial summary of the action. This production clearly enjoys getting its hands dirty in both areas. But it also bears down on the words and ideas that insistently cross the narrative lines: Value (who, or what, is worth fighting for?), Taste (sex is for epicures), Time (the great leveller, the great destroyer and -- mercifully -- the great anaesthetist). By the end, we have a clear notion of what the play is about. David Snelgrove is an excellent Troilus, at once sincere and self-indulgent. He has the guts, when convinced of the banished Cressida's infidelity, to play self-pity and hysteria for what they are; and he manages the transition to pitiless warrior admirably. Claire Jullien shows comparable nerve by taking Cressdia seriously; beset by insecurities, she still means her vows. She begins to crack when Troilus, at their parting, keeps harping on his constancy and her possible falsehood. She senses, suddenly, that it's all about him. Her reception at the Greek camp ("kissed in general") is played as a virtual gang-rape, leaving her no recourse but her own wits; her final yielding is given a graphically sexual staging that, for once, makes sense.

I can't say the same for the public rutting of those smoochers Paris and Helen, nor for Pandarus' feeling-up of a young male servant who ought to be running rings round him. Not that there isn't plenty of warrant elsewhere for Bernard Hopkins' playing Pandarus as a busy, voyeuristic old queen. He's putting Cressida in Troilus' bed as a substitute for being there himself. Note that when the lovers are parted all his sympathy, all his concern, are for the boy. There's kindness in his performance, too, and a progressively harrowing presentation, vocal and physical, of Pandarus' "diseases." He's as much emblem as character.

Stephen Ouimette's Thersites could probably be more emblematic; his individual scenes are salty enough but his presence doesn't infect the air. As Ulysses -- the self-appointed spokesman for order and logic in a world that rejects both -- Peter Donaldson is expectedly trenchant. He's the clever outsider, needed but disliked, and dispatched on the more distasteful errands. One of these is the confrontation of Jamie Robinson's sinister narcissist of an Achilles, a sun god on the skids, who keeps his Patroclus (David Shelley) in a subtly observed state of uncertainty, never knowing which way, sexually or otherwise, his hero is going to jump.

Also good are Jeffrey Renn's buffoonish Ajax and Ian Deakin's trim Nestor. Among the Trojans, Tim Campbell places the ageing golden boy who is Paris, and Geordie Johnson makes a splendid Hector, the nearest thing to a tragic figure. It's he who, having marshalled all the arguments against the war, abruptly changes face and gives it the green light -- for reasons of prestige. This inconsistency, which used to worry critics into convulsions, is the play's starkest image of the way the world actually goes, then and now. There are also some exceptionally sharp cameos: Paul Soles' Priam, Paul Dunn's priestly Helenus (a character in four lines and a gesture), and Joanna Schellenberg's Cassandra, a still and scary irruption in what is already an impressively balanced council scene. (This year at Stratford, Cassandras -- this one, and Sara Topham's more spectacular turn in Agammenon -- have been good news.)

Some excessively nervous cutting deprives us of some of Ulysses' best lines and of Ajax's gruff epitaph for Hector. But the play that remains makes sense.

Festival Theatre, Stratford

- - -

QUIET IN THE LAND

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

- - -

STRATFORD - Not only is Love's Labour's Lost the first great romantic comedy in the English language, it is also the first great anti-romantic comedy. Four young men vow to dedicate themselves to three years of celibate study and, of course, are immediately derailed by the appearance of four young women. Then when, after the customary ration of advances and rebuffs, all seems set fair for a quadruple wedding, Death steps in and checkmates the revels.

At the height of the play's mirth, the Princess of France, who is on an embassy to the King of Navarre, receives news that her father has died. Courtship is put on hold. The Princess and her three ladies tell the King and his three lords that, if they wish, they may resume their suits in a year and a day, the interim to be spent on reflection and good works. It doesn't seem that long, but it is, as Berowne, the joker in the king's pack and the comedy's central character, pointedly remarks, "too long for a play." This, one of Shakespeare's earliest Elizabethan dramas, is only just beginning, and already it's deconstructing itself.

The end of this play is moving, in a unique fashion. Obviously we shed no personal tears for the late King of France; we have never met him, barely heard of him. What hits us so hard is the fact of mortality and, especially, its intrusion in a comic context. It casts doubt -- sober, uncynical doubt -- on all happy endings, including those in Shakespeare's other comedies. When the messenger arrives, Navarre's local inhabitants have been presenting a farcical pageant of the Nine Worthies. "Worthies, away," says Berowne, virtually cueing the lights, "the scene begins to cloud." It's magnificently self-conscious writing, absolutely sure of its effect.

Love's Labour's Lost is a pastoral, a form in which little happens but in which behaviour and language stand out in the sharpest relief in what the poet Marvell called "a green shade." The setting is soothing, the mood astringent. Much of the dialogue is wordplay: characters scoring off one another, misunderstanding one another. This poeticizing and logic-chopping are among the bad habits of which the women hope to cure the men by imposing their 12 months' penance. Shakespeare is satirizing his more self-indulgent contemporaries, but is also having a grand time beating them at their own game. In theory, the play is full of hopelessly obscure jokes; in practice, they are beautifully built up and always relate to the people making them. I don't think I have ever seen a bad production of Love's Labour's, and I don't remember hearing or reading of many. The play is magic.

Antoni Cimolino's Stratford production, if not among the greats, offers a good measure of delight. Santo Loquasto has set it (discreetly) and costumed it (richly) in the French modes of the late 18th century; the women's white dresses in the last scene knock your eyes out. Graham Abbey, perhaps influenced by the director's idea that the men lack "social graces," makes a surprisingly surly Berowne; his great speech of self-discovery ("and I, forsooth, in love") is played for anger, rather than for the overflowing joyousness of being carried away against one's will. It's a matter of opinion, but I know which interpretation I prefer. Still, he has no trouble controlling either the play or his fellow students, especially in the great scene in which each in turn is unveiled as an apostate. Shane Carty takes the now conventional gauche view of the King, and successfully runs, or shambles, with it. Dana Green's Princess forces her merriment but is charming when serious; Michelle Giroux is suitably metallic as Rosaline, Berowne's dark lady; and the minor lords (Stephen Gartner, Caleb Marshall) and ladies (Sarah McVie, Deborah Hay) get more definition than usual. There are useful contributions from James Blendick in the major role of the Princess's chamberlain and Les Carlson in the very minor one of her forester.

The courtiers' compulsive chattering is echoed in their rustic dependents. Brian Bedford gives a lovely account of Don Armado, lost in dusty dreams of grandeur, peering with mystified gentleness at everything that pertains to the real world and especially at the country wench, Jaquenetta, Dulcinea to his Quixote. His page Moth (Jacob James) is both too tall and too old for his role, but so quick and responsive that we can let it pass. This central comic trio is wonderfully completed by Jonathan Goad, an entrancingly light-handed and full-blooded Costard. The pedants (Brian Tree and Barry MacGregor) are adequate, which is another way of saying disappointing. The Worthies show falls flat, partly for this reason. It's character comedy, and it can't work unless all the characters have been established. It's played here for slapstick, as if it were Pyramus and Thisbe. These amateur actors trip themselves up; the production doesn't have to do it to them. This faltering in the comedy robs the last-minute tragedy of its full impact. But this is still my favourite play, and it's here in much of its glory.

Anne Chislett's 20-year old Quiet in the Land is a historical piece, respectable but schoolteacherly, about Ontario's Amish population and their principled resistance to serving in the First World War. It has obvious local relevance for Stratford (the village it depicts is just down the road in the Waterloo direction), and it tells an interesting story. Christy Bauman, de facto head of the community, becomes its rigorously traditional bishop; if there is such a thing as a militant pacifist, he's it. His son Yock, a problem since childhood, does the unthinkable and joins up, eventually returning in a state of shocked disillusion. This seems too easy. What if it had been the Second World War? What if Yock had helped to liberate a death-camp? The language never ignites, and the characterization is pat and cozy. This is especially true of its more humorous scenes, which concern naughty housewives who regard the telephone as the work of the devil but can't resist sneaking a call when the neighbours give them the opportunity. I admit that there's a ready audience for this kind of writing; the matinee I saw played to a full house and a standing ovation. Shakespeare should be so lucky.

The play is also structurally skewed; the real threat to the Amish establishment turns out to come not from the heretical Yock but from a devout contemporary who burrows from within. But this theme is established weakly and belatedly, and we sit through it, waiting impatiently for the prodigal to return; the more so since Michael Therriault plays Yock with a force and economy that nobody else comes near to matching. Andrey Tarasiuk has staged the play with impressive expansiveness, spreading the township across the length of the platform stage, but he has not concealed the play's soft centre; at times, especially with the older women, he accentuates it. Stephen Russell has some fine fiery moments as Christy, but his workaday intransigence cannot help getting monotonous; Robert King weighs in agreeably as the voice of jolly moderation.

Black & White Photo: Michael Cooper / Dana Green ss the Princess of France and Shane Carty as the King of Navarre in Love's Labour's Lost.

THE PLAY'S THE THING

Premiere Dance Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Four years ago, on a momentous evening, Diego Matamoros' opening speeches as Sandor Turai in The Play's the Thing offered proof beyond doubt that Soulpepper meant business. This was the opening production of its second Harbourfront season, back in 1999. It had taken us by storm with its inaugural two plays the previous year, and had since mounted a good one-off production of Our Town at the Royal Alex, but these had the feeling of special events. This by contrast was the first exposure, Soulpepper's and ours, to what would have to be the company's normal buckle-down circumstances.

From the moment the lights went up, we knew that things were going to be all right. In fact, we knew it even before they went up, as we gazed at the preliminary sight of three cigars glowing in the dark. It was an invitingly cheeky moment, to be followed by more elaborate outrageousness as the three smokers took us through the opening of Ferenc Molnar's comedy. This deals with the problem of exposition by having the three men -- all, we gathered, theatre professionals -- discuss the problem of exposition. How easy it would be, muses one of them, if one of the characters could simply step forward and tell the audience who they are and why they're here. Which is just what he proceeds to do.

The director, Laszlo Marton, was later to be responsible for Soulpepper's memorable productions of Chekhov and Moliere; here, on his home ground -- both he and the play are Hungarian -- he took the pulse of that opening sequence, and of the entire play, perfectly. Matamoros, in the role of a highly successful boulevard playwright - - suavely impudent, tongue exactly poised in cheek, as deadly serious as only assured playfulness can be -- set the tone, a quiet one, bursting with suppressed comic energy, and the rest of the cast took their time from him. Nothing was forced. The Canadian theatre, or a piece of it, had discovered style. It had grown up.

Not to keep you in suspense, Matamoros' performance in the current revival is as good as ever it was. As before, he is delightfully reinforced by William Webster as Mansky, his authorial colleague, jovial or nervous depending on how the wind blows; Jim Warren as an impromptu prompter; and Michael Hanrahan as a butler so resourceful and punctilious that he might have been invented by P. G. Wodehouse. As indeed he partly was; Wodehouse adapted the Balkan original, and if he didn't interpolate jokes of his own (I bet he did) then he put the originals into spruce and sparkling English.

He was also responsible for changing the play's title. It was originally Play at the Castle, and it is to a castle (which seems to double as a hotel) that Turai, Mansky and their composing collaborator have come to meet the leading lady of their new comic opera, script and score in hand. Molnar's is a highly -- indeed exorbitantly -- theatrical piece, and there's a play within the play. But Wodehouse's Shakespearean handle is more specific than that. The play, it turns out, is the thing in which Turai catches the consciences of the diva Ilona, and more especially of Almady, the vain, older married actor who is laying siege to her.

Ilona, as it happens, is engaged to Albert the composer, who is young and romantic and behaves as if life were something for which he'd written the music. He and his two friends overhear Almady apparently making love to Ilona in the room next door (the castle walls, it's explained, are very thin) and she apparently not rebuffing him. Albert is ready to destroy himself and his career and -- this is what really rattles them -- his librettists' careers as well. So Turai devotes what remains of the night to writing a play ("one is either a playwright or one's not") that both incorporates and excuses the incriminating words that had wafted from Ilona's boudoir. He then blackmails the miscreants into learning his lines and performing them on the ensuing evening.

Having got this far, pretty much on wings, the play and the production sag a bit. It's a one-idea piece, after all, however glittering that idea may be. There's an inconclusive subplot concerning the best ways of ministering to Albert's state of mind, and Molnar should not have attempted, just before intermission, to reprise the comedy of self-consciousness with which he commenced operations. What was delicious the first time around is tiresome the second.

But everything rights itself in the last act, when Turai's new play is rehearsed. He's fashioned it, we discover, not only to repair young Albert's illusions but to teach the philandering Almady a lesson. C. David Johnson repeats, and may even improve upon, his masterly performance as the ageing matinee idol, ritually humiliated by every line he is enforced to utter. There are two new arrivals: Allegra Fulton, a vast improvement on her predecessor, gives Ilona a wit and also a sense of caring that enrich the play's texture immeasurably; Jonathan Watton's Albert gangles charmingly. Some shows have the quality of a smile, and this one is a veritable Cheshire Cat: teasing, immovably assured, and lingering long after you might think you've seen the last of it.

Black & White Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / Diego Matamoros (right) as Turai is as good in Soulpepper's current production of The Play's the Thing as he was in its original four years ago. He is delightfully reinforced by William Webster as Mansky.

When you pack this much theatre into one city, you're practically guaranteed some brilliant performances

LONDON - Theatre in London is split in two, like everywhere else only more so. One half is a game reserve for the ubiquitous mammoth musicals. Toronto has its long-running productions of The Lion King and Mamma Mia! London's West End has them both, along with others like The Phantom of the Opera and Les Miserables that have run their course with us, and still others (Chicago, Fame, Stomp, Grease) that keep coming back for short seasons here, but over there have settled in for solid runs.

This precise situation is never going to be duplicated in Toronto or any other North American city outside New York. We don't have the stages, the audience, the tradition or the tourists. (Though we will get The Producers before they do.) So I wouldn't say in looking at the West End at the end of this hot summer, I have seen Toronto's future. I would say I have seen its present -- everything the traffic will allow -- multiplied.

As in Toronto, these globally anonymous shows are balanced by others that have some connection to their audience. Again, there are more of them. But here the difference isn't simply one of numbers. London has something no North American city, including New York, has or is ever likely to have: a system of subsidized repertory theatres mounting plays on their own premises, and transferring some of them into commercial houses. This makes for a rich menu.

It's unusual these days for a West End management to originate a major production that isn't a musical. It can happen, though, and it has done so now with a piece by, of all forbidding foreigners, Pirandello. Absolutely ... Perhaps (known in English textbooks as Right You Are -- If You Think So) was a revelation; all the things one has been told about Pirandello and never believed -- that he was a great comic playwright, that his plays are seething with Sicilian passion -- turned out to be true.

It helped, obviously, to have an Italian director (and designer) in Franco Zeffirelli. The play, offering us factually incompatible but desperately held accounts of a single domestic situation, keeps pulling the ground from underneath us, and so does the production.

It isn't quite true to say this show exists independently of the subsidized sector. The repertory tradition has helped create the audience for it, and Zeffirelli himself directed regularly for the National Theatre in the glory days of its first director, Laurence Olivier. Some of his present cast worked with him there, notably Olivier's widow, Joan Plowright, now the star attraction in what is nonetheless an ensemble piece.

The National itself has just sworn in its fifth director, Nicholas Hytner, an intellectual and a showman. The showmanship has been evident in his opening season, notably in his modern-dress production of Henry V. This is superbly mounted on a wide open stage, with actors jumping in and out of Jeeps, and much commentative use of video -- the king's rallying speeches, after being delivered live, are promptly repackaged as unusually eloquent sound bites.

The best thing I saw at the National was a revival of David Mamet's Edmond, about a man's descent into the urban inferno: a contemporary Woyzeck except that Mamet's protagonist -- who walks out on his wife, goes pussy-shopping, gets a gun and ends as a convicted murderer at the sexual mercy of his cell partner -- is articulate. He talks, but he has no centre. Kenneth Branagh, sliding between reason and rage, plays him brilliantly.

The Royal Shakespeare Company, similarly, has done great West End business with Brand, Ibsen's gruelling verse-play, by casting film star Ralph Fiennes as the pastor who makes untenable demands on his family, his flock and himself. Artistically, the results are less successful; Fiennes, following the rule book for actors playing fanatics, acts on one note, in his case a nagging one devoid of the whirlwind intensity that might shift the character's weight. Still, mountain-peak Ibsen is always more bracing than horsehair-sofa Ibsen, and there is one very fine performance from Claire Price, radiant as the hero's long-suffering wife.

Shakespeare's Globe, combining the charms of novelty and antiquarianism, remains a prime tourist attraction, almost the symbol of London's renaissance. Its actual standards are very uneven. I saw a real rarity -- Dido, Queen of Carthage, Christopher Marlowe's first play -- crassly staged but redeemed by two leading actors who could not only speak the verse but act it.

A brand new house, the Hampstead Theatre (replacing a makeshift old one), introduced London to our own Adam Pettle with a production of his Sunday Father that seemed mysteriously unaware that the play is a comedy. On this evidence, we do their plays better than they do ours. But, of course, we've had more practice.

The vogue in new British plays is historical-biographical. Most complex, in the spider's web manner, is After Mrs. Rochester, which presents novelist Jean Rhys through her life, her work and her obsession -- indeed identification -- with the madwoman of Jane Eyre. It takes three actresses to play her, all of them good. Polly Teale adapts and directs for the Shared Experience company, known for accomplished, if sometimes precious, literary reworkings.

The National offered Nick Dear's Power, with the young Louis XIV taking his first steps toward absolute monarchy by playing one finance minister, the feckless Fouquet, off against another, the calculating Colbert. (In romance terms, this is Man in the Iron Mask territory.) Tolerably smart, this is distinguished by the Queen Mother of Barbara Jefford, a classical veteran who can dispose of an opponent by snapping "I want him dead" as if her tongue were the axe.

Terry Johnson's riveting Hitchcock Blonde (ex-Royal Court Theatre) is a tale of two exploitations. There is a movie academic's seduction of his research assistant while investigating a lost fragment of early Hitchcock, and the maestro's own clammier and more complex relationship with the girl who stood in for Janet Leigh in the Psycho shower scene. Much depends on Hitch himself, played here to lip-smacking, syllable-rolling perfection by William Hootkins (an American, surprisingly). More great use of video -- actually, the best ever -- in William Dudley's designs.

This play just carries off the palm from Nicholas Wright's Vincent in Brixton, which concerns the historically dubious love affair of the young van Gogh and his middle-aged, depressive London landlady. I saw it in a non-air-conditioned theatre on the night before the hottest day in the city's history, and since the play's attractions include the cooking of realistic meals in a fully functioning Victorian kitchen, it's a tribute to the writing, the acting and the audience that all of us survived. (For once it seemed right that they should applaud us.)

This is a quiet, beautiful play, lit up by the transcendent performance of Claire Higgins, one of England's finest unsung actresses. A whole life's progress -- defensiveness, awakening, heartbreak, rage and new resolution -- was mapped out in her face. English acting is not always what it's cracked up to be, but when it is, it can make your heart swell.

Black & White Photo: Adam Butler, The Canadian Press / At Shakespeare's Globe, Marlowe's first play was blessed by leads who could not only speak verse but act it.
