THIS IS OUR YOUTH

Berkeley Street Theatre Upstairs

According to rumour, This Is Our Youth, a physically exciting and verbally brilliant piece by the American Kenneth Lonergan, is autobiographical. That figures; it was his debut play, and first-time dramatists, like first-time novelists, are traditionally expected to write about themselves. It would also explain an otherwise puzzling circumstance: A fresh and urgent play, that opened in New York in 1996, is actually set in 1982. Lonergan, the playwright, was a late starter. This was his youth.

It still feels contemporary, even after the further gap of the seven years the play has taken to reach Toronto. In fact, when the characters start bitching about the President, it comes as a shock to realize that they are talking about Reagan rather than George W. Bush. The play concerns kids with rich Manhattan parents who are devoting most of their post-high-school days to doing and dealing drugs. There may be fewer of these around now than there were in the indulgent '80s but there are some. Even when the characters, in retro mode, put on a record of Little Richard singing Tutti Frutti and start jiving to it, you know, then as now, they owe what knowledge they have of the steps to multiple viewings of Grease. You may be struck, only when the play is over, by the poignant fact that you have witnessed the end of the LP era. Only when I thought about it later did it strike me that I had been watching a stage full of adolescents minus computers -- though I had registered the related fact that, even though they say "like" a lot, they are, for professed drop-outs, remarkably articulate.

We meet Dennis, whose father has got rid of him by buying him a split-level apartment (well, the sleeping area is two steps up from the living room); and Warren, Dennis's long-time friend and hanger-on, whose father has simply got rid of him. Thrown out, Warren has helped himself to $15,000 of his dad's money and now turns up at Dennis's place. Dennis starts to devise complicated, constantly changing schemes by which the two can have a good time and still make enough of a profit selling coke to return the loot before Warren's father gets mad. Dennis, who in other respects fancies himself like crazy, lives in mortal fear of Warren's father getting mad; he considers Warren's father a dangerous gangster, though Warren apparently doesn't. Warren, whose general attitude toward Dennis is one of giggly subservience, goes along; though he is also tempted to do some big spending on a date with Jessica. Jessica, according to Dennis at least, is the first good-looking girl to show any interest in Warren in years. She is the only other character.

Woody Harrelson's direction is, at the start, almost excessively manic. It finds itself rapidly, though; the energy level is exhilarating in itself, and he knows how to vary it. Fabrizio Filippo, who plays Dennis, suffered a foot injury during rehearsals, but the resultant limp actually helps. It makes Dennis, whose rhythm is determined by whatever he happens to be on, seem more driven than ever, all hopped-skipped-and-jumped-up. He's a self-appointed golden boy, proud of his prowess with women (he demonstrates this by screaming abuse on the phone at his semi-estranged girlfriend), with clients and at sports. Constantly in motion, he maintains a punching bag in his apartment -- two punching bags, if you count Warren. Late in the play, reality hits him and he crumples; but it's reality seen on his own self-dramatizing terms. Filippo simultaneously arouses our pity for the character, our amused contempt for what the character's saying and our admiration for his own skill at delivering what amounts to a massive prose aria.

Marya Delver cleverly plays Jessica as a girl caught between convention and rebellion, which of course is another convention. She has a knack for delivering cliches ("I don't take advantage of the city's facilities, and it seems like a total waste") as if they were earnest truths, then catching herself doing it.

Marcello Cadezas, who was the driving force in assembling this production, has ironically cast himself as Warren, who is neither driving nor a force. In fact, and it may be the most clever thing about the play, Warren is two people. With Dennis, he's the addled loser his companion needs him to be. With Jessica, and even on the phone with his father, he's still nervous (watch the way Cadezas scratches his leg in moments of stress) he's thoughtful and even, sometimes, lucid. His two scenes with Jessica are elaborate rituals of approach and avoidance, beautifully outlined in both writing and performance. Warren's two halves come together when, emboldened by all he's gone through, he attacks, very sensibly and moderately, a few of Dennis's grosser illusions.

The play's flaw is it has no definable centre. Warren, the only character onstage throughout, is the protagonist by default, but Dennis has the flash, the charisma and the breakdown. As a group portrait, though, it doesn't quite work, since Dennis and Jessica barely connect. We are left with a cross between a genre painting and a jigsaw puzzle. That, though, is unlikely to spoil anybody's fun. The play's title, which suggests something out of the beatnik era, verges on self-parody; is it a boast, a rebuke or a take-it-or-leave-it declaration? The play turns out to be all three, tempered by humour and the merest dash of nostalgia. It has the zing of a Look Back in Anger, which was the granddaddy of all This Is Our Youth plays, minus the self-righteousness and with a better narrative.

This, give or take, is still our youth. Just as it always was.

Black & White Photo: Warren (Marcello Cadezas) beats up on Dennis (Fabrizio Filippo) in a play directed by Woody Harrelson.

REMNANTS

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

- - -

The Old Testament tale of Joseph and his brothers has inspired modern authors from Thomas Mann to Tim Rice and Andrew Lloyd Webber. Now, in what is effectively the opening production of the new Tarragon regime, we have Jason Sherman's Remnants, an extremely clever and ultimately moving attempt to wed the old story to the Jewish experience in the first half of the 20th century.

The title is, at the least, double-edged. It recalls the old Jewish idea of the saving remnant; those few who survive the worst catastrophes, to bear witness and to carry on. More prosaically, it can mean the scraps in a tailors shop that may, perhaps, be stitched together to make a new garment. That is how this plays Joseph gets his multi-coloured coat. Jacob, his father, is a prosperous Jewish tailor in 1920s Poland. Ten of his sons help in the business; the other two, born to Jacob's second and better- loved wife, get more generous treatment. Young Benjamin, a mute, stays home as his father's pet; Joseph is a yeshiva student.

The older brothers traditional jealousy of the favourite son, with his pesky dreams, is cursorily treated. I never thought I would write such a thing, but I found myself missing Rices wit. What is interesting is more specific. The brothers are Communists, planning to unionize the store; they suspect Joseph of being their father's spy. (Their shifting political commitments are deftly handled throughout.) They plan to kill him, but, as in the original, Reuben the eldest stays their hands; he proposes packing Joseph on board a boat to New York. By some mischance it docks at Halifax instead, and Joseph, having got past the immigration authorities, begins a Canadian odyssey.

He works for four years in a Toronto sweatshop but is fired when the owner, a Mr. Pottinger, tries unsuccessfully to involve him in precisely the kind of union-busting activity of which his brothers had accused him back home. Pottinger, of course, is Potiphar, but he has no wife; he tries to seduce Joseph -- physically as well as politically -- on his own account. This may score high as dramatic economy, but considering everything else that's going on, its a bit much. After more adventures Joe finds himself, thanks to his prowess at interpreting dreams, in the service of Mackenzie King, currently (1932) between premierships; history may not be able to offer Sherman a Pharaoh, but it has done him the favour of dealing him a King. And in an even snugger fit, the dream of the fat and lean kine turns out to signify seven years of Depression followed by seven more of wartime resurgence.

Comes the war, and Joseph is appointed the PMs representative on immigration; which of course makes him complicit in Canada's infamous anti-Semitic quota system. As you'd expect, his brothers, desperate to escape from Poland, unknowingly become his clients, and he plays out with them the same cat-and-mice game that was adumbrated in the Bible, played for even higher stakes: agonizingly high, in fact.

Sometimes the play has to spend too much energy connecting the Biblical dots, getting from one incident to another. But even these scenes travel fast. The strength of the play, much the best of Shermans that I have seen, is that its built like a fable, almost like a cartoon, more concerned with story and its implications than with character. (Sherman's previous scriptural update, Patience, based on the less-tractable Book of Job, died on its feet, endlessly probing a protagonist who had never come to life in the first place.) In an ideal world one would like to know more about Joseph and especially about the corrosive effect on him of either concealing or denying his Jewishness, but one settles for him here as a providential enigma. Most of his brothers, probably for budgetary reasons, spend the evening in the wings; they are represented on stage by Reuben, kind but weak, and Judah, bullying but effective. As they move between those poles, and as history itself changes them from predators to victims, they take on not individual complexity but collective texture. This is more than enough; the long-delayed reunion and forgiveness ring true on all sides.

Line by line, the play is cleanly, piercingly written, with occasional funny lines that are more than funny. Told that his father must have been a nice man, Joseph says that he wasn't, except to him, which tells you something about Jacob and more about Joseph. "Dont you find that power corrupts?" Joseph is asked, and replies "absolutely"; which would be the glibbest of gags if he himself were not becoming, at the very least, compromised.

Richard Roses production, his first as Tarragon's boss, is also his best in ages: gaunt, speedy and very well acted. Graeme Thomson's designs, built of trunks and suitcases, rescue the oldest of refugee images; and his lighting is amazing, especially in its pinpoint use of a downstage scrim shaped like an outsize portrait frame. Dmitry Chepotevskys Joseph is best in his days of quietness and comparative innocence; called on for complexity, and especially for implacability, he stonewalls. Alex Poch-Goldin and Alon Nashman, though, are superb as the principal brothers, offering essences but not caricatures, and as many other characters as well; Poch-Goldin is especially delectable as an English butler, condemned and reprieved on strict Genesis principles. There is a great double by Victor Ertmannis as a sardonic King (rather a flattering portrait, I suspect) and a Polish peasant, first Jacobs employee and then his protector, and Jerry Franken does fine work as a variety of elders, from Jacob himself to the Canadian mandarin in charge of keeping Jews out. The play ends at Jacob's deathbed, the patriarch looking backward and forward -- to today's Middle East -- with equal bitterness. Then the brothers and the righteous Pole join hands in hope; the moment courts sentimentality but avoids it. The old story and the new make a handsome couple.

Color Photo: THE CAST OF REMNANTS, FROM LEFT: Jason Jazrawy, Dmitry Chepovetsky, Alon Nashman (background), and Alex Poch-Goldin.
2003-09-26-a-well-deserved-encore-gents:
2 PIANOS, 4 HANDS

Elgin Theatre, Toronto

- - -

The best scene in 2 Pianos, 4 Hands remains the one in which the teenage Ted Dykstra, played by the present-day middle-aged Ted Dykstra, is told by an angry conservatory examiner, played by Richard Greenblatt, that he will never make a concert pianist. He has the talent, but he has squandered it through lack of discipline. Dykstra crumples at the keyboard. The audience, even those members of it who never took piano lessons, goes rigid in sympathy. The effect, I think, goes deeper even than the near-universal experience of having an adolescent dream crushed. It's about having a door slammed in your face at any time of your life, and knowing that the slamming was justified.

It rather queers the pitch of the succeeding, balancing scene in which its Greenblatts turn to shed years and Dykstra's to play the dismissive tutor. It seems that Greenblatt, who has also been a classical student up to now, has decided to play jazz, and he embarrasses his tutor, his audience and us by trying to sound hip, on and off the piano. He too gets his comeuppance, a funnier one than his partner's but less touching.

Returning to Toronto after having gone round the world for seven years, both with and without its performer-creators, 2 Pianos, 4 Hands remains a unique show. Comedy at the keyboard is a fairly common commodity, but its usually a solo proposition, and I certainly can't think of any other piece that welds a series of musical jokes and domestic sketches into a dual autobiography that resonates. Nor can I think of another that utilizes the same combination of talents. Versatility is not uncommon in Canadian theatre (it's almost a necessity for survival), but the accomplishments of Dykstra and Greenblatt -- each a respected actor- musician-writer-director -- are ridiculous. Here they get to show off all of it. (Andy McKim is listed as consultant director, which I assume means the other two prepared the production and he looked it over.)

They take us through encounters with intimidating or inspiring teachers, dead composers who make terrifying technical demands ("thanks a lot, Mr. Bach!") and parents who attack them for not practising enough when theyre young and for getting the whole thing out of proportion and practising too much when theyre older. The show, incidentally, is rather educational, especially about the naming of chords.

Much of the detail is plainly fanciful. I stand to be corrected, but I don't believe Dykstra and Greenblatt, a.k.a. Teddy and Richie, actually grew up together in Montreal and played together in duet competitions, at one of which Dykstra got humiliatingly lost in the Hall of the Mountain King. I wonder, too, whether their ambitions were as consumingly, exclusively musical as they would have us believe. Was theatre something that both of them just fell into later, as a last resort? (They've done very well if it was.) But the essence is believable.

The short, shock-headed Dykstra is the more resourceful and malleable clown of the two, especially adept at childish terrors and tantrums and at protruding from the piano stool at impossible, anguished angles. Greenblatt, taller and thinner, is a strict straight man with a touch of the Borscht Belt, a kind of thinking man's Bud Abbott. They are, as some of the world now knows, a great team. They end, after a couple of sharp scenes depicting the scuffles of the young almost-musicians, as middle-aged men reflecting on what might have been. They then play -- ostensibly for one another, really of course for us -- seriously and without interruption. Here, and especially in an encore rendition of Sheep May Safely Graze (thanks indeed, Mr. Bach) they convince us that they are indeed, as they claim, "two of the best players in the neighbourhood" and that it's a good neighbourhood.

Black & White Photo: Peter J. Thompson, National Post / Ted Dykstra, left, and Richard Greenblatt started their hit show about aspiring pianists seven years ago.
2003-09-29-from-the-school-of-mamet:
Until Nov. 1. 416-368-3110.

BLUE/ORANGE

Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Joe Penhall's Blue/Orange was first staged in 2000 by the National Theatre in London, where it won every available award. On the evidence of the new Toronto production, it deserved them. As usual, its CanStage that has brought us the play; as usual, we wonder why it had to take so long.

Playing at the downstairs stage at Berkeley Street, Blue/Orange starts in remarkably similar fashion to This Is Our Youth one flight up. Two young men are squaring up to one another loudly, and one of them, ceaselessly on the move, is demanding coke. Only he means Coca- Cola -- not that he doesnt have a taste for some harder stuff as well -- and his antagonist is warning him off it, along with all other sources of caffeine. The hyperactive one is Christopher, of African parentage and now living in Shepherd's Bush, West London.

He's just completed 28 days in a mental ward and is entitled to go home. He wants to, or at least he thinks he does, or at least he thinks he does most of the time. Bruce, the junior psychiatrist in charge of his case, wants to keep him; he thinks Christopher could still be a danger to himself and others. He has Chris tagged as a case of Borderline Personality Disorder.

Enter Dr. Robert Smith, Bruces superior and supervisor, who points out that this is a very vague diagnosis: Borderline of what? Robert wants to send Chris home for a variety of reasons, of which the least controversial is that the hospital is short of beds. Obviously, though, he has his own agenda, as (less obviously) does Bruce; and the play develops into a power-struggle.

Chris has real problems. When he cuts open an orange -- any orange -- he pronounces its inside to be blue. He also claims to be the illegitimate son of Idi Amin; Robert seems inclined to take this possibility seriously, though Bruce cant, and neither, I imagine, can most members of any conceivable audience. The play does not go very deeply into questions of race, though all three characters play the race card when it suits them. Chris, whose feelings of persecution may or may not amount to clinical paranoia, is likely to describe all who cross him as fascists -- including his neighbours who, Bruce points out, are blank. Robert advises Chris to go home and listen to some reggae; Chris, of course, is not Caribbean, and the remark would be patronizing even if he were.

Penhall, like other young British playwrights, is an avowed fan of David Mamet. In the program for the National production of Mamet's Edmond, he describes the play as a response to all those worthy drones bemoaning the end of socialism. It was the end of worthiness. He and his peers have apparently turned their backs on the sermonizing of the David Hare-Howard Barker generation, just as that lot rejected the soft-centred nostalgia of John Osborne and Arnold Wesker, who also thought they were rebels. Each generation thinks it's the toughest until a new lot comes along, at which point the incumbents turn all sensitive and rebuke the intruders for their lack of finer feelings. Its pathetic, really.

For the moment, though, Penhall and company are writing political drama that isnt doctrinaire; please note that failing to make the expected liberal noises is not the same thing as being right wing. For what they're doing, Mamet, with his electric sense of personal confrontation on society's margins, is the best reference. Theres a brief bit in Blue/Orange, celebrating an offstage characters cooking skills, that recalls one in Glengarry Glen Ross; maybe it's an homage.

Structurally, the play shapes up like a three-sided role- shifting Oleanna, with a similar final movement. A character -- Bruce, in this case -- finds that what he thought were casual remarks have been taken out of context and used as evidence against him.

It's a continuously exciting play, building conflicts that never let up in dialogue, that is both stinging and believable. This too is our youth, not just in London; and numerically more representative of it than is the play upstairs. Its also skewed. Most of it is a struggle between the two physicians, and the audience is inevitably going to take the side of the younger; hes up against authority, therefore vulnerable, and he also seems to be talking sense. At least he isn't talking nonsense on the scale of Robert, who is still quoting R. D. Laing on madness being the real sanity and who also seems grammatically impaired. (He recites a line by Allen Ginsberg: "Human is not a noun, he is a verb.") I have no desire to knock Chris Abraham's production, which is very tense and, within its limits, visually striking; note the use of the sets single doorway, especially in relation to the perpetually hovering senior shrink. But it does accentuate the imbalance. In the first scene R. H. Thomsons Robert is a psychiatrist as one of the Monty Python team (probably the late Graham Chapman) might have presented; his beard, cords and sports jacket are impeccably realistic, but he seems to be on speed: tic-ridden, manipulative, and a bully. He's the paranoid, obsessively defensive about his own position and his own research. Is the play really telling us that the lunatics have taken over the asylum? It seems, at this date, a bit simplistic (though it might ironically confirm some of Robert's own wilder theories.) In itself its a riveting display, and Thomson does quieten down considerably in the later scenes, but the damage has been done; we simply dont credit a thing he says. Except one thing: He speaks of the damage Christopher will suffer simply by being locked up with older and undoubted psychotics. And after the play is over, a few more of his arguments feel more convincing than they did at the time. It's to the play's credit that it nags at you like this, but we could, I think, have had more of that at the time.

Kevin Hanchards Chris is as real as acting gets. His accent, for starters, is dead to rights (credit to Ned Vukovic, the dialect coach, for the sound of all three performances) and he manages a role that is one outburst after another without ever losing his own control. He is febrile, obviously, and tortured, and surprisingly funny; apparent innocence is mixed in him with a residue of slyness, and however much he contradicts himself he always seems, at that moment, to be telling the truth. Darren Keay as Bruce has the unenviable task of playing straight guy to a couple of crazies (Im speaking theatrically, not clinically) but he does it with increasing confidence and also with increasing ambiguity; he suggests, by the end, that he can, when cornered, be as petty as anyone else. This isn't a perfect show, but it's alive.

Black & White Photo: John Hryniuk, Canstage / R.H. Thomson, left, as Robert, Darren Keay, standing, as Bruce and Kevin Hanchard as Christopher.

Happy End is in repertory until Oct. 31; The Royal Family until Nov.23. Box office: 1-800-611-SHAW.

HAPPY END

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the Lake

- - -

THE ROYAL FAMILY

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the Lake

- - -

AFTERPLAY

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the Lake

- - -

Kurt Weill and Bertolt Brecht crammed half-a-dozen of their best songs into the score for Happy End, which is a gangster musical set in a weird European idea of 1920s Chicago. There are the sinuous cautionary tales known as The Sailors' Tango; Dont Be Afraid; the Song of the Big Shot, which has also been translated as the Song of the Tough Nut; and the defiant Ballad of the Lily of Hell. There are also two nostalgic odes to improbably exotic hangouts, whose names, if nothing else, reflect Brechts deviationist affection for Rudyard Kipling: the Bilbao Song, about a rundown bar, and the Mandalay Song, about a short- order knocking-shop. Above all there is Surabaya Johnny, the most haunting of all torch songs, in part because it tells a story.

Despite these riches, the show -- planned as a follow-up to the runaway triumph of The Threepenny Opera -- was a resounding flop at its Berlin premiere in 1929. The songs, though, and the burgeoning Brecht-Weill mythology, have guaranteed it an afterlife; and it's now reached the Shaw Festival, as the second and presumably more serious musical of the season.

Nobody knows who wrote the book of Happy End. Brecht himself only took credit for the lyrics, and the script is ascribed to a mythical "Dorothy Lane." It seems it was mostly the work of Brecht's amanuensis Elisabeth Hauptmann. Brecht had a habit of screwing his female collaborators (in every sense) but this time even Hauptmann was reluctant to take responsibility. Thats understandable. Its a laboriously drawn-out piece in which long sections about a gang of bank robbers headed by a feared female mastermind called The Fly are alternated with shorter ones about the travails of a Salvation Army lieutenant popularly known as Hallelujah Lil. While on a safari for souls, Lil meets and falls for Bill Cracker, the toughest guy in the gang. The romance of Bill and Lil is bedevilled by the usual on-off misunderstandings, presented with a careless contempt that falls someway short of being satire. Guys and Dolls has nothing to fear from this one.

Michael Feingold's confessedly free adaptation seems very pleased with itself; it obviously knows more about North American pop culture than Brecht and company ever did, but in exhibiting this knowledge it pads the show out to even greater lengths. The characters include a Charlie Chan knock-off who is a pain from beginning to end, and the gang are given the impossible task of seeming dangerous and incompetent at the same time.

The Niagara staging also begins on an odious note of self- satisfaction. Happy End at the Shaw Festival? say the cast, as if congratulating themselves, "Impossible!" However, once this obstacle has passed, and after we've got through an interminable mock interrogation scene that leads precisely nowhere, Tadeusz Bradeckis production, much abetted by Jane Johansons choreography, takes on a hard-edged identity that is very satisfying. The handling of the big mission scene, revolving around an anthem called The Liquor Dealer's Dream, is a model of pace, tension and surprise.

I wish I could say as much for Blythe Wilson's performance as Lil; her acting is stilted but worse -- she doesnt seem to know how to build her songs. She unleashes all the anguish and bitterness of Surabaya Johnny in the first chorus, leaving herself with no further options, and the song, for once in its life, fails to be moving.

Benedict Campbell presents Bill as the kind of middle-aged businessman-crook that Brecht always said he wanted Mack the Knife to be. Its a stylish performance, with plenty of relaxed presence, but it too has nowhere to go. Guy Bannerman and Neil Barclay are good among the crooks, and Jeff Lillico, as an apprentice punk called Baby Face, even better. His amusing counterpart on the side of light is Mike Nadajewski as a Salvationist who faints a lot. As The Fly, Glynis Ranney reasserts her supremacy among Ontario's singing actresses, though she cannot explain the character's ascendancy over the gang; nobody could.

Theres a political message at the end, though Id call it hasty rather than happy. The main attraction remains the music, very well served up by its director Paul Sportelli, though the virtuous lack of amplification prevents all of the syllable-clotted lyrics from coming through. But the names of Brecht and Weill do not in themselves make a good musical; On the Twentieth Century, the season's other musical, though more of a strain on the festival's human and technical resources, is a far better show

- - -

I dont know if it influenced the programming but The Royal Family, the last opening on the Festivals main stage, has something in common with Twentieth Century. The leading male character in both is a thinly disguised portrait of John Barrymore. In The Royal Family, he's played by Peter Hutt, who is raffish, roguish and right. It isn't just, or even principally, his play; we get the whole Barrymore clan, their surname changed to Cavendish. First staged in 1927, its one of the bustling Broadway comedies, traditionally lucky for the Shaw, that were churned out over the decades by George S. Kaufman and Another. In this case, though, the other is not Moss Hart, who brought inspired craziness to the collaboration, but Edna Ferber, who brought mainly sentiment; she wrote Show Boat, and theatrical dynasties seem to have been her obsession. In Martha Henrys production, we do grow to love this one, though we might love it more if Patricia Hamilton had brought more wit, and certainly more savour, to the Cavendish matriarch, determined to live and die in harness. Goldie Semple, though, is in terrific form, in fact the best I've ever seen her, as the star of the next generation, the Ethel Barrymore figure. She gives brilliant expression, physical and vocal, to the character's -- and the plays -- main joke, which is that the more she professes indifference to the theatre, the more theatrical she gets.

Norman Browning offers a bluff variation on this theme, as an ageing in-law in desperate pursuit of a vehicle, and Caroline Cave in the ingenue role is all the authors could have hoped and more than they deserved. Jillian Cook has a high old time as the maid, whom she plays Irish but whom you can bet your life was written black.

- - -

Afterplay, the seasons lunchtime show, has closed but deserves a memorial. It's actually after two plays, and if that too sounds Irish -- well, so is the author, Brian Friel. He brings together Andrey from Chekhov's Three Sisters, and Sonya from his Uncle Vanya, some 20 years after the end of their respective plays; they meet in a shabby cafe in Moscow. So Andrey got to Moscow, even if his sisters didnt, and they even further down on their luck than when we last saw them. Friels speculations logically have no more value than anyone else's, but we accept his version because we are seeing it on a stage. Ah, we say, that's what happened to them; thank you, Id always wondered. Friel isnt Chekhov; his characters, after some delay, make explicit confessions of their shameful secrets, rather than letting them seep out between the lines. But his idea tickles us, and is plausibly carried out.

Simon Bradbury and Helen Taylor had some trouble locating the right register, but were admirable once they'd found it; Daryl Cloran directed.

Black & White Photo: The Shaw Festival / Simon Bradbury as Andrey Prozorov in Afterplay.; Black & White Photo: The Shaw Festival / Nora McLellan as Kitty LeMoyne Dean in The Royal Family.: (Photo ran in all editions except Toronto.)
2003-10-03-characters-would-like-to-have:
Until Oct. 12. 416-975-8555.; robertcushman@lycos.com

PLAY MURDER

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, Toronto

- - -

In four years on this beat, I don't recall seeing a good new play at Buddies in Bad Times. Standards of performance, too, have been, to put it gently, variable. Still, the company is now entering its 25th season, so maybe I've just struck a bad patch. Buddies itself seems to be getting nostalgic for past glories; it is celebrating its anniversary with a revival of a 10-year-old play by Sky Gilbert, founder and former artistic director. This too is bad, but it's bad in a confident way.

Bits of it are even good. Gilbert is a talented nuts-and-bolts playwright, with a first-rate ear; he can set his characters at one another's throats with a few well-chosen lines, and can even show them being convincingly and touchingly affectionate. After every such scene, though, his play dissolves in giggles; maybe he feels he owes it to his image.

Play Murder keeps jumping styles and time-frames, and generally sending itself up. It's about Libby Holman, a real-life torch singer of the 1920s and '30s who was also a minor Broadway star. In the latter capacity she introduced at least two standards, Moanin' Low and Something to Remember You By. In 1931, she married Zachary Smith Reynolds, heir to a Deep South tobacco fortune. The following year, aged 20, Smith, as everybody calls him in the play, was found dead, shot. Libby was widely suspected of his murder, but a grand jury investigation (unmentioned in the play) found insufficient evidence to try her. The official verdict was suicide. Libby went back to performing, but her future career was, understandably, jinxed.

This may not have been solely the result of her tragic past. Her records suggest she was a terrible singer, uncertain of pitch and doomy of manner. (That is not a prerequisite in a torch singer; Helen Morgan was dainty in her suffering.) In her later years, Holman grew pretensions as a folk and blues singer, and took herself very seriously indeed. She seems to have been totally lacking in humour, which in a popular singer is a pretty crippling limitation.

It's also one that Ellen-Ray Hennessy, who plays her here, is blessedly unequipped to present. She is all wit and a lot of sexiness, the latter a quality she can laugh at without losing. (The real Libby certainly looks sultry in photographs, and may well have been more fun off stage than on, but I still can't imagine her laughing at herself.)

Hennessy also has the ability to change mood on a dime, to be savage one moment and pitiable the next. Her Libby is an elongated jazz baby, running on nicotine and alcohol, frustrated by her husband's Southern home, by his disapproval of her career and, it seems, by his impotence. She delivers the play's excellent last speech, in which she sums up her life mordantly but without self- pity, with absolute command.

Libby is in a lesbian relationship that survives, though possibly only as a friendship, into her marriage, something that particularly riles Smith. The play, though, never holds course as an examination of Southern homophobia, or of its racism, a subject even more briefly broached. Somebody suggests that Libby's problem is that she expects life to be like the movies, though there's been no previous mention of this expectation, or indeed of the movies.

As for the lady and her music, Hennessy, who's meant to be drunk at the time, slurs her way incomprehensibly through one of Holman's trademark songs. Before the acts, we hear Bessie Smith, who was pre- Libby, and during the action itself we get bits of songs that are mostly of Holman's period, and one of which, What Is This Thing Called Love, she actually recorded. But it isn't her version we hear. The recordings are unmistakably of the 1950s; Sarah, Blossom, Chet and Mel are among the voices that float by. (So do those of Jane Russell and Marilyn Monroe.)

My first suspicion, which I discarded, was that the author- director couldn't tell the difference and thought, like many, that old songs were just old songs. My second was that he shared my opinion of Libby's singing, and much preferred these later models. My third, desperate but probably accurate, is that the anachronism was intentional and meant to be "commentative." It goes with having the actors step constantly out of character to comment unfavourably on the dialogue they've been given or the dance number they are suddenly required to perform.

Jason Cadieux, who as Smith shares the acting honours with Hennessy, gets a speech -- quite magnanimous, considering -- in which he first laments his position as a straight man surrounded by homosexuals, and then switches to complaining about being a straight actor in a gay play. Gilbert seems to think tricks like this are what make a gay play.

Occasionally -- when Libby steps out of time to remember later conversations with Tennessee Williams or Tallulah Bankhead -- the playfulness justifies itself, but for the most part Gilbert is so busy satirizing his story he never gets around to telling it. To put it another way: There's no point in deconstructing something that was never constructed in the first place.

Much of Act Two is taken up by a jokey reconstruction of the fatal events, volubly resented by the characters as characters and by the actors as actors. The audience, though, is in no position to join in the fun; it's not as if most people will enter the theatre as experts on the case.

I found myself thinking of Blood Relations, the Lizzie Borden psychodrama revived at this year's Shaw Festival, which also takes too much knowledge for granted. For all I know, Gilbert was consciously spoofing Sharon Pollock's play when he wrote this one. But the final impression is that he's sneering -- at his characters, his actors and his audience -- which is unfortunate, because he isn't a sneery writer.

Steve Lucas has designed a multi-chambered set, the grandest I've ever seen on this stage, though sadly underused for most of the evening. Ann Holloway plays Libby's drama coach, a would-be grande dame who recalls being booed when she appeared in The Wild Duck as a senile grandmother (this is not surprising as there is no such character in The Wild Duck). She is atrocious, but she may conceivably be doing it on purpose. Jane Johanson, having been instructed by the text to do terrible choreography, has gone right ahead and done it. She also plays Libby's love interest.

I read recently that even Daniel MacIvor has grown tired of writing plays about plays; it's the best theatrical news I've heard in ages.

Black & White Photo: David Hawe, Buddies in Bad Times / Ellen-Ray Hennessy as Libby with, from left, Jason Cadieux as Smith, Jane Johanson as Louisa, Marc Gushuliak as Ab, Ann Holloway as Blanche.
2003-10-06-comedic-revelation:
Indefinite run. Box office: 416-343-0011.

ARMAGET-IT-ON!

The Second City, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - The response of the late James Durante to warnings of Armageddon was "Armageddon outta here." Jimmy could make anything sound funny, but I think we might agree that the line in itself has an elegance missing from the title of the new show at Second City. As a pun, Armaget-it-on! is even more forced than such previous entries as When Bush Comes to Shove, What Fresh Mel Is This and -- leaving personalities out of it -- Psychodelicatessen.

Here, though, carping stops. Those previous titles merely grabbed at names in the news and left it at that; the shows themselves had nothing to say about Toronto's mayor or America's president. The last one, The Bush League of Justice, had nothing to say about anything. This new show does have a running concern with the idea of apocalypse, and from time to time with the more joyous idea of getting it on. It even seems to be advocating one as an antidote to the other, or at least as a way of taking your mind off it. It gets it on itself by being one of the funniest of recent Second City revues, and much the most thoughtful.

Don't be alarmed; I mean only that the premises for many of the sketches are more original and ingenious than usual. The faces and bodies on the stage are mostly familiar, and so are the satirical targets, but the approaches are fresh.

An early number takes on the Canadian melting pot and the Middle East at the same time, and even involves its performers in a bit of acting, building a relationship as well as firing off gags. Sandy Jobin-Bevans, the company's laid-back straight-arrow guy, has taken advantage of a cheapo TV offer and bought his Jewish roommate, the tousled and insistent Matt Baram, a ticket to Israel: one-way. He thought, or so he says, that his friend would welcome the chance to get back to his roots. "Dude," says Baram, patiently indignant -- he can also be frisky, though not here -- "I'm from Edmonton."

Another double header: The diminutive Jennifer Goodhue, who by length of service and force of personality is now the company's star, plays a motivational speaker exhorting her audience to stop doing the two things that impede success (thinking and feeling), and meeting her own ultimate challenge when asked to find work for a suicide bomber who is not good at his job; i.e., he's still alive.

Naturally, the show eventually arrives at Osama bin Laden himself, shooting a new video under the frustrated eye of an American director who uses Method methods; he gets the old anger going by rekindling his client's early-morning rage at finding there was no milk for his Cheerios. This, I suppose, is an obvious idea -- the video, not the breakfast cereal -- but it's executed with a lot of brio.

The best-sustained item presents Canadian soldiers in the Second World War wondering when, if ever, the Yanks are going to get onside, while expressing their own dark suspicions about root causes. ("I hear we're only here for the wheat.")

Coming up to date, we are reminded of the never-to-be-forgotten trauma of the blackout: 4/11. (The lights, they claim, went out at 11 minutes past 4 p.m., and that does sound about right.) People playing solitaire on their computers lost their games and will never get them back. Others were sent home because their jobs were deemed inessential. Imagine how that made them feel.

With ultimate logic, the show also takes on the Second Coming. Jesus Christ returns, courtesy of MTV or similar, to answer questions and perform a few miracles, which do not include the Blue Jays winning the World Series. "Look", says the host, "she's Jesus, not God." (I should have mentioned that the Gospels got the gender wrong. Also that Jesus, in the person of the feisty and imposing newcomer, Jamillah Ross, is black.) This number gets in good lines at the expense of all the Toronto newspapers including, I confess, this one.

Consumerism in general and The Gap in particular are done over twice. These of course are more conventional targets, but both blows land and both are freshly twisted. Especially piquant is the one about the lady who is persuaded by the store to buy a young Mexican girl, whom she can wear as a stole. Goodhue plays her purchase; she has the right dimensions and the right agility, and seems delighted to be of use. The show even gets away with a sketch about neighbouring couples playing Truth or Dare and discovering predictably unpredictable things about themselves.

Then there are the songs, few but fine. One is a madrigal about a maiden on the local club scene who finds herself the victim of a one- stand knight. That's her line. Mine -- which I wish I'd invented but have actually plagiarized from another song -- would be that her mother never told her there'd be knights like this. Actually the real delight here is the sight of Goodhue, who sings the ditty, lolloping round the stage between verses, deciding that she likes it, and then lolloping again.

Goodhue later gets to play Simon to Baram's Garfunkel, and they both look very well cast. They are planning a Broadway musical that will do for them what Mamma Mia! did for ABBA; i.e., recycle all their hits in the least congruous contexts possible. Baram also has a solo, with the most stinging lyric of the night, in which he apologizes to the U.S. for the ways in which we're better than they are.

Paul Constable, an alarmingly self-assured fella next door, and Naomi Snieckus complete the cast, who as always write their own material. So we can't attribute the rise in quality to the intervention of some outside author, though it's quite possible that Steven Morel, the first-time-out director, was more rigorous in his editing than some of his predecessors have been. The only serious complaint can be that the show bears further witness to the death of the punchline. Nobody can find a neat way of ending anything, and, as always, I sympathize.

HEAD TO HARBOURFRONT

A reviewer on Amazon.com described Janette Turner Hospital's latest book as "dressed-up pulp fiction." 2003-10-14-the-howls-of-wolfgang-amadeus:
Until Nov. 1. at the Bluma Appel Theatre. Box office: 416-368-3110.

Some years ago I met an academic, high up in a U.S. theatre department, who was trying to show what a fearless rebel he was. "I think Peter Shaffer is a big load of nothing," he proclaimed heroically. It struck me that, in the circles in which he moved, he would be likelier to be torn to pieces for praising Shaffer, but to my shame I didn't mention it.

Part of the reason for my silence may have been that, though my own opinion of Shaffer's plays was higher than his, it wasn't that much higher. Amadeus (not his best play, incidentally) was still new at the time, and I thought it a plodding chronicle with a couple of incandescent moments. Despite all the tireless rewriting Shaffer has undertaken since the play's London premiere in 1979, that is still what I think.

But I also believe some of the attacks on the play to be misguided and in a peculiar way self-serving. Most of them, of course, hinge on Shaffer's portrayal of Mozart, the play's title character (Amadeus, "beloved of God," being the composer's significant middle name) but not its star role. That distinction goes to Antonio Salieri, Mozart's older contemporary, a minor talent tortured by the appearance on the scene -- his scene, since he's official composer at the court of the Emperor Joseph II -- of a major one. Mozart is presented as a childish, foul-mouthed buffoon, and no conceivable kind of artistic genius.

There are several answers to this. One is that some people seem to have naive and starry-eyed ideas about the personal behaviour of artists. Another is that Salieri is the play's narrator as well as its protagonist, so the Mozart we are offered is quite explicitly Salieri's Mozart; and Salieri, to put it mildly, has baggage. A third is that even this Mozart is no fool; on the admittedly rare occasions that he talks about music -- the only thing he really cares about -- he does so with sense, humour and point. I am no student of Mozartian biography, but I see nothing impossible in the idea of the man on that stage having written that music.

Salieri finds it all too possible; he also finds it unbearably unfair. Mozart's genius makes him, in his own estimation, a mediocrity, and he asks for the sympathy of us, his fellow mediocrities, in the audience. In his own way, Salieri is Mozart's greatest fan; and the play's best writing comes when he describes the effects on him of Mozart's successive compositions. This led John Simon, the critic of New York magazine, to pronounce the play (on its first Broadway production) absurd on the grounds that mediocrity, by definition, can never appreciate genius. The subtext here is, of course, "I, John Simon, appreciate Mozart; therefore I am no mediocrity."

But I'm afraid that if we accept Salieri's drastic either/or definitions, then Simon, since he is plainly not a genius, is a mediocrity, like most of us. If genius can be appreciated only by other geniuses, then genius is going to be playing to empty houses. Actually, the play shows, in its portrayal of a bitchy and improvident Mozart, it's perfectly possible to be a genius in one area of your life and mediocre or worse in all the others. Conversely, Salieri is an initially decent man who quite consciously turns himself into a villain. The play's real, burning subject is jealousy.

This comes to a head in a searing speech at the end of the first act, in which Salieri acknowledges his feelings, renounces his previous ascetic life and dedicates himself to the destruction of his rival -- which, in the second act, he accomplishes. But, tremendous as it is, this speech is a dead end; because it isn't just about jealousy, it's about God. Salieri, a religious man in a religious age (well, more religious than ours), has offered his musicianship to God, only to find God choosing to speak through Mozart, instead. Now, if this were merely a metaphor for any kind of artistic inspiration, it might wash; but Shaffer (and here, I think, it is Shaffer, not Salieri) seems to be taking it literally. He's making claims for Mozart he wouldn't make even for Bach or Shakespeare or Rembrandt. But if God speaks through any artist, he must be speaking through them all, including, come to think of it, the bad ones.

Anyway, it throws the play off track. "My quarrel is with God, not with Mozart," Salieri says, thereby entering the realms of the undramatizable. God isn't onstage, Mozart is; and we get a school- drama rendition of the rest of the composer's brief, unlucky life, with Salieri pushing the buttons. Much of this amounts to a tour of Mozart's greatest hits, each opera mined for possible biographical relevance. Sometimes this is effective, as when The Magic Flute leads to Mozart's rejection by the Freemasons, previously his only benefactors. Sometimes it's Hollywood kitsch, as when the ghostly Commander in Don Giovanni is identified with the composer's own father, of whom we have till now scarcely heard. Along with that you can take the earlier episode in which Mozart sits down at the harpsichord and transforms a humdrum march of Salieri's into what became the first-act finale of Figaro: the composer at work, just like in the movies.

Morris Panych's CanStage production is visually stunning; inventive up to the very last moment and a great improvement on the stodgy original. Ken MacDonald has set it in a bare, off-cream room into which are lowered a succession of flats, some ugly but all striking. Salieri, like the psychiatrist in Shaffer's Equus, is a role that any actor can play. I don't really mean that; it has to be an actor of great technical resource and personal command. But the personality has to be the actor's own, because the writing is faceless. David Storch, after an uncomfortably doddery beginning, eases into a performance of great economy, intelligence and, when called for, wit; though he doesn't have the transformative power for that first-act climax. Matthew Edison's Mozart starts excessively slapdash, but he, too, collects himself later. The two share a fine late scene -- a new addition, I think -- that does bring their relationship poignantly into focus.

Salieri has a couple of stooges whom he calls the Venticelli, professional gossips and a shameless narrative device. They make Salerio and Solanio of The Merchant of Venice look like live wires. Indeed, all the supporting characters in Amadeus must count as cruelty to actors, apart from Mozart's long-suffering wife, given an unfortunately lumpen performance by Shauna Black, and the Emperor Joseph, whom Robert Persichini makes vaguely benevolent and offhandedly funny.

The play's close finds Salieri claiming to have killed Mozart and nobody believing him; he's denied even that shot at immortality. The irony is compounded, of course, by the play itself having rehabilitated a previously forgotten composer, to the point where Cecilia Bartoli's record company can let her make an album of Salieri's Greatest Hits. They don't sound bad; if that's mediocrity, we should all be so lucky. The same, I think, is true of the play; and you are unlikely to see a better staging than this one.

Black & White Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann, CanStage / Matthew Edison as Mozart is excessively slapdash in the beginning but manages to collect himself.
2003-10-17-so-much-to-gain-from-a-minor-:
Until Nov. 16. Box office: 416-536-5018.; robertcushman@lycos.com

HELEN'S NECKLACE

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

- - -

Helen is a Canadian woman, at large in an unnamed Middle Eastern city, and she has lost her necklace. "Lighter than air" is her description of it. Its pearls are plastic, and it has little monetary value, but it means a lot to her, and she is understandably upset at its disappearance. So she goes all over town looking for it.

En route, she meets a number of locals of both sexes, some of them more fluent in her language than others, all of them with problems of their own. A mother, in denial over the death of her young son, finally admits that the corpse that possesses her mind is that of her own child, not that of a neighbour's. Helen, abashed, recognizes that, compared to such a loss, that of a mere necklace matters little. But she still wants hers back, and her quest next takes her to a building site. Here a man lectures her on the state of the city and on what it's like to live in what is in effect -- maybe in reality -- a bombed-out refugee camp. His cry, and that of his people, is "We cannot go on living like this." He advises Helen to adopt it as her own, and she does.

I can't see that she has earned the right. The play is by Carole Frechette, the Montreal dramatist whose Elisa's Skin was seen in this space two years ago. She writes with a certain grace; or so at least I judge from John Murrell's translations. And she has won the Siminovitch Prize, which in Canadian theatre is the most prestigious award going, or at least the most lucrative. So I am probably in a minority in finding this piece tenuous, pseudo-lyrical, and -- in its arbitrary linking of large and small sorrows -- meretricious.

It's slightly more fun to watch than its predecessor, which was sternly anchored to a cafe table; this one's heroine gets to move about, mostly in a mimed taxi with an amusingly cavalier attitude to other traffic. But after the encounter with the bereaved mother, everything is anti-climax. Helen may come to accept the unimportance of her necklace in the scheme of things, but the play doesn't. It continues to treat the necklace as a potent symbol of something, and so, more alarmingly, does Helen herself. It stands, I would guess, for all the meaning that has leaked from her life.

But if I am seriously to believe that Helen cannot go on living like this, and to be affected by it, then I want to know how she is in fact living and how she has been living in the past.

We gather that she was part of a legation and that she stayed behind when her compatriots went home; the play also treats itself to a brief flashback about a break-up. It isn't enough. The indigenous characters are in specific predicaments. Helen seems to be suffering from a generalized Western malaise, calculated to appeal -- lazily -- to the audience's feelings of privileged guilt. We end on the customary note of modified hope, the two sides -- epresented by Helen and her driver, who has been patiently dropping her off and picking her up all day -- giving to, and learning from, one another.

Susan Coyne is Helen, insecure but determined; she has a shy smile that speaks volumes. I cannot fault her performance, but I have to confess that after her funny and passionate work of the last couple of years (at Soulpepper and elsewhere), I find its built-in literary droop is something of a letdown -- not in skill but in what's demanded of it. It has a sober charm to it.

As does Sanjay Talwar's assumption of all the other roles, though he seems so determined not to overact that they tend to blur, not at their edges -- you always know which is which -- but at the approach to their insides. Why his overtaxed taxi driver speaks much better English at the close of the play than he does at its beginning I cannot begin to explain.

Eda Holmes' direction is sensitive. The event as a whole is mildly interesting, mildly boring, and very Tarragon.

robertcushman@lycos.com; Until Nov. 9. Box office: 416-504-9971.

TIGER OF MALAYA

Factory Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - A good story goes a long way, and Hiro Kanagawa, an experienced actor but a new playwright, has one in Tiger of Malaya. It's drawn from recent and still resonant history, and that helps keep it interesting.

At the end of the Second World War, the Japanese General Yamashita, who had earned the tigerish soubriquet by his skill at taking Singapore from the British, was put on trial for the atrocities committed in the Philippines by troops under his command. The play is concerned less with the actual trial than with its preparation and its aftermath. It centres on Yamashita himself and on the two American officers assigned, with less than his full co- operation, to defend him.

There is no question here of the accused pleading that he was merely obeying orders. He was the one giving the orders, and the question is of whether he gave the right ones, and whether his men would have taken any notice if he had. Yamashita, who regards the proceedings as victors justice, has already given himself up for lost. His main concern is whether he will be honourably shot or dishonourably hanged. However, when roused to defend himself, he claims that the situation in the last year of the war was so chaotic he had no hope of controlling it.

His American counsel believe him. They also discover that he had been a moderate, opposed to the war, tolerated by the Japanese high command only because they couldnt do without him. They think he is being railroaded by a vengeful General MacArthur (who never appears, though his recorded voice is heard), and they could well be right. However, though Yamashita may not be guilty as charged, he may still have things on his conscience that escaped the official indictment. He is a haunted man from the beginning of the play. Toward the end, he tells his lawyers -- by now his friends -- the terrible truth. One of them is disgusted, the other reacts with a kind of barbed tolerance.

There is a lot going on here, and though it mostly works as narrative, its theme hangs in tatters. If Kanagawa is attacking the integrity of war-crimes trials in general, at least when carried out by the winners, he hasn't made his case. Nuremberg (to which the play makes occasional sidelong allusions) may have been imperfect but it was also indispensable, and the play simply isn't big enough to cast any light on the worlds abundant supply of later hideousness; the most it can offer is a few automatic twinges.

Structurally, too, it is split. Yamashita, as played by Denis Akiyama, is a compelling character, quiet and grey and charming and powerful. Continually moving toward and then away from us, he is consistent even in his inconsistency. His defenders, who have as much stage time as he does, also have issues, both regarding him and between themselves, and their roles are less successful.

They seem to have derived, by osmosis rather than direct imitation, from other characters in similar circumstances. Captain Lederman, the conscientious young Jewish intellectual, might have stepped out of The Caine Mutiny. His superior, Colonel Hilroy, is a kissing cousin of Rod Steigers redneck sheriff in In the Heat of the Night. He's a salty Southern bigot whose sympathies turn out to be surprisingly wide -- he has, in fact, a history as a civil rights champion. The American colonel and the Japanese general have something in common -- neither of them is what the world would take them to be. But the point is only made at the end, and faintly at that. Before that, the play seems to be tugging in different directions.

Neither the writing nor the acting is well served by Ken Gass' direction, which is forceful but flat; it forges ahead, disdainful of nuance and heedless of pitfalls. Each performer is left to find his own rhythm, and they rarely cohere. As Lederman, Jordan Pettle, though likeable as always, is tentative, often reduced to smiling through. Ken James has a whale of a time as Hilroy, who is indeed a whale of a role, though perhaps a beached one. His elegant bluster, when he takes his clients case to a higher court, is the evenings high point, at least as entertainment. It is, of course, a solo turn.

Two women complete the cast, and neither has a happy time. Ginger Ruriko Busch plays Daisy, a Californian of Japanese parentage who is interpreter for the defence. Her mixed race seems to be her qualification, not only for her place on the legal team but for her place in the play. It produces additional tensions, mostly described rather than presented, that the play doesn't need, or at any rate can't use. Both the character and the performance are ineffectual.

And then theres Rosario (Aura Carcueva), a figure whose taunts and entreaties fill the generals nightmares. Dramatically she is irritating, as phantoms often are. She gets in the way of what is, after all, an exciting tale, the more so because it's only late in the second act that we have any idea what she's talking about. She turns out to be the inhabitant of a village where the general discovered the worst in himself. He doesnt actually say, "The horror! The horror!" but he seems to be thinking it.

But presenting this information in a kind of stationary flashback, split between narrative and re-enactment, deadens its impact; even Akiyamas performance becomes incoherent. (The war criminal traumatized into facing his responsibility is another familiar trope, from The Andersonville Trial to Judgement at Nuremberg.) And the production makes no allowance for Rosario's existing on a different plane from the other characters. She simply happens, like everybody else. Her image, which begins and ends the play, is presumably meant to haunt us as it did the general, but nobody seems to have told the lighting designer.

Still, despite everything, this is a play with a subject and with a certain amount of weight. It's both an impressive debut and the best new play at Factory in some time, probably the best since Belle. (It's a co-production with the National Arts Centre, and the show goes to Ottawa after its run in Toronto.) And, in a world in which something like Miss Saigon not only makes millions but is taken seriously as a compassionate look at East-West relations and the aftermath of war, it's a humane corrective.

Until Dec. 7. Box office: (416) 314-2901.

SCARAMOUCHE JONES

Winter Garden Theatre, Toronto

All the world, or so Cole Porter once said, loves a clown, a proposition thats put to a hefty test in Scaramouche Jones.

This is a one-man play performed by Pete Postlethwaite, the British actor whom Steven Spielberg is said to have described as the best in the world. Postlethwaite has greeted this accolade with amused self-deprecation; and I suspect that Spielberg, if he said anything, was inadvertently paying tribute to a breed of actors who dont exist in the United States, and who may be an endangered species even in the United Kingdom. They cut their teeth in regional repertory (Postlethwaite is recognizably a northerner), progressed into the national classical companies and became character actors in film and on television. A few (Bob Hoskins, Patrick Stewart, Alan Rickman, Brenda Blethyn) hit the right role and became stars; Postlethwaite's break was In the Name of the Father.

Since the early 1970s, which is when he came to London and when I first began watching him, he has never to my knowledge given a bad performance. He is a remarkable blend of tough and sensitive, capable of putting his vulnerability on hold when he plays a sneak or a villain. This particular abnegation is not required of him in Scaramouche Jones, in which he is all gentleness, reacting with resilient amazement to a brutal world. His Scaramouche is a circus funnyman on the tip of his 100th birthday, though looking wonderful for his age. Postlethwaite, phenomenally unpushy for a solo performer, is soft-edged without ever being soft-centred.

The play he's in, written by Justin Butcher, is another thing: little more than a contrivance. We meet Scaramouche in the last hour or so of 1999. When the millennium expires, he expects and intends to die with it. This will be satisfyingly symmetrical since he was born on the stroke of midnight, as 1899 yielded to 1900. He was the son of a gypsy prostitute in Trinidad; his fathers name, as he repeatedly informs us, was Legion (for we are many") but his mother told him that daddy was an Englishman and he hugs this information to himself with pride. He will in fact end up in England, but he doesnt get there until both he and the century are half done.

Before that he was orphaned, kidnapped and sold into slavery; his master is a North African snake charmer with whom he is reasonably happy, and from whom he learns many things, including classical Latin. In his thirties, moving eastward across Europe, he connects with his gypsy roots, an experience that gains him a brace of cruel beatings, both from his own folk and from the authorities plus a mockery of a marriage.

The Second World War finds him in Italy; he is sent to a concentration camp at Split in Croatia, where he is put to work as a gravedigger. Here he discovers his talent for comedy; he makes funny faces to amuse the children who are about to be machine-gunned and tossed into the pit.

His path here recalls, but varies from, that pursued by Roberto Benigni in Life Is Beautiful; the latter's clown character came into a camp and put his known comic talent to use, whereas Scaramouche only finds his vocation in extremis. Postlethwaite, mercifully, is less benign than Benigni; he doesn't ask to be loved, and the show, by virtue of that, stops short of being offensive. But it is very suspect.

The idea seems to be to give us a clowns eye view of the last century; Scaramouche, though he has plenty of troubles of his own, is initially shielded by geography from the worst public events -- he occasionally refers to them as distant rumours -- but is then brought right up against the periods defining atrocity. But we all know that the 20th century was a chamber of horrors, and a dramatist who wants to exploit them has to earn the privilege. Butcher's account of the camp at Spalato (a.k.a. Split) seems to be a Holocaust compendium; it has gas chambers and execution pits. In reality, the one, at Auschwitz and Treblinka, replaced the other, which had flourished, if that's the word, on the Russian front. Maybe Ive been misinformed, but its news to me that there were gas chambers in the Western camps; they were confined to the extermination centres of Poland. In the West there were prisons and transit camps; they weren't pleasant, but neither were they slaughterhouses. The designated victims were moved on. The play seems to be taking a free ride on history, and on our pre- conditioned reactions to it.

After the war, Scaramouche moves on to England, having acquired a surname, courtesy of a friendly Welsh customs officer who -- rather surprisingly -- recommends Jones as a good old English name, rather than fiercely reserving it for the Welsh. Maybe he's being ironic. Here our hero becomes a clown, apparently a very successful one. We arent told the details. The second 50 years are skated over; what we thought would be the intermission turns out to be the final curtain. We do see Scaramouche, before embarking on his autobiography, shaking his head over the news from East Timor, in implicit recognition that humanity hasnt improved much. What is ducked completely is the really interesting question: How could a man with his experiences embark on a career as a children's entertainer? How did he use his memories? How, in fact, did it all work? There is a running image of Scaramouche, as one trauma succeeds another in his life, acquiring layers of white faces, till he finally graduates to the professional white of clownage. I didn't find it very illuminating. What is more subtle and less pretentious than the rest, is the theme of the colonial child hanging on to his Englishness, as England itself shrinks and the Empire disappears.

Otherwise the script is journeyman work; it tells its story, isnt boring and includes a couple of good jokes. And it provides a vehicle for a masterful actor, one who neither misses nor belabours a beat and whose body is as controlled and expansive as his mind and voice. In Canadian terms,Id say he combines the earthiness of Randy Hughson with the fastidiousness of Diego Matamoros. (He has also become the movies' best imitation Canadian, courtesy of performances in The Shipping News and Between Strangers.) It's great to have him among us. I wish he were here in a play.

Black & White Photo: Peter Redman, National Post / Postlethwaite plays a 100-year-old clown in Scaramouche Jones.

BHOPAL

The Theatre Centre, Toronto

- - -

The story and subject matter of Bhopal are historical, and calculated to make an audience feel angry. The calculation succeeds. The writing and presentation, by contrast, make the audience feel irritated, and that cannot have been the intention.

Rahul Varma's play concerns an industrial and environmental catastrophe that came to a head 20 years ago. The firm of Union Carbide was manufacturing pesticide at a factory in Bhopal, India, using a gas with highly toxic properties. In the surrounding areas, babies and animals were dying. In 1984 there was a gas leak, and an explosion. The resulting death toll is reckoned at 20,000 and rising. Union Carbide's American bosses shut the plant down and offered compensation on a scale that the Indian government, at least initially, thought derisory.

Varma's original intention was to write a documentary play about all this, but over the years of working on it, he gave his imagination freer rein, especially in the matter of inventing characters. So at least I gather from interviews included in the press kit that the management, like most managements, helpfully hands out to the critics. (Please don't stop; we'd be lost without it.) Mere audience members are denied this information, though it would not only be in their interests but in those of the play to have at least some of it included in the program. The spectators certainly deserve to be told that of the seven characters onstage, only one bears the name of an actual person. This is Anderson, CEO of Carbide International, and it can be no coincidence that he, despite being given a performance in which effortful brashness seems to be standing in for brutal confidence, is the most compelling, three-dimensional figure around.

It's to the playwright's credit that he allows even this man, whom he plainly despises, a case. He tries to do the same for the characters he has made up, but paradoxically they seem far more like stick figures, all on hand to represent something, with bits of human interest pasted on.

At least Anderson is history's pawn rather than his author's. The others display all the drawbacks of fact-based drama and none of the advantages. They include a lady doctor (Canadian, presumably for the sake of audience identification) who is on to what is happening and whom the local authorities are trying to silence -- at least until the factory blows up, at which point they decide they need her help. There is a Canadian diplomat, sent to extricate her, and weaseling around between the various factions. The doctor has little use for his services, and the play doesn't seem to need them much either.

The Indians include a senior economics minister whose political tune changes abruptly but inconclusively in the course of the play, and the factory manager, who was educated in the United States and who says that by taking the job, he's helping his people and his country. He probably means it, but once installed, he cuts corners and tries to cover up the results. He's also having an affair with his assistant, whom he gets pregnant.

This woman, named Madiha, emerges -- also abruptly -- as a key figure in the play. She is in violent denial over the prospect of her baby, like those of the slum women around her, being born with appalling defects. She is set against Izzat, who is just such a woman and just such a mother. The doctor wants to send Izzat and her child to the U.S. -- for treatment and as live propaganda. Izzat plays her and the company off against each other, getting what she can from each, though the play's structure is so confusing, jumping around in time and space, that it's hard to keep up with what she wants or at what stage she wants it.

The play eventually zeroes in on these two women, affording the actresses more extended opportunities than are available to anyone else in the cast. But what it offers with one hand, it takes away with another. As Izzat, Yashoda Ranganathan is saddled, among other things, with the convention that obliges any play set anywhere in Asia to begin and end with a woman reciting an inexplicable fable. Imali Perera's Madiha never recovers from the bald, bad writing through which she is required to convey her love for her boss and her hostility toward everybody else. There might be a play in her relationship with her opportunistic lover, but it cannot co-exist with everything else that's trying to go on. Her final gesture is merely that.

A charitable assumption would be that the play doesn't have time to treat all its elements in depth, and so has to resort to shorthand. Anyway, what happens is that the fiction keeps crowding out the facts, though the facts are far more compelling.

I am feeling friendlier than I used to toward "issue" plays. The issues usually have a built-in fascination -- this one certainly does -- and they generally come attached to interesting stories; that's how they got to be issues in the first place. Bhopal never actually forfeits our attention, and it has no trouble making our blood boil over corporate greed and managerial negligence. That, though, is the easy part. It fritters away our goodwill by devising stock confrontations for stick figures, going off at soap-opera tangents and leaving its political points hanging. The current Tiger of Malaya (another issue play with an Asian setting) suffers from some of the same diffuseness, but survives by being the story of a particular man and pushing that story through to its conclusion.

Most of the acting ranges from the overheated to the half-baked, and though Guillermo Verdecchia's production manages a few neat instant transitions in the earlier scenes, it does little to clarify what's going on. On the first night, some of the lighting cues were crazily out of sync; either that or the director has an exaggerated belief in the powers of darkness.
