Instead of comedies, John Neville's acting company starts with Ibsen's masterpieces

The three last plays of Henrik Ibsen are among the mountain- peaks of European drama: bleak, bracing, glistening and inaccessible. More prosaically, all of them -- Little Eyolf, John Gabriel Borkman, When We Dead Awaken -- are set within easy walking distance of the nearest icy heights, and all have protagonists who dream of scaling them. The hero of the last -- Ibsen's "dramatic epilogue" -- even looks as if he might make it.

The plays are rarely produced; but last weekend, all three were given rehearsed readings at Hart House under the aegis of the veteran (for once, the word seems justified) actor and director, John Neville.

The event was partly a fundraiser for the threatened Hart House Theatre itself, and partly a shop window and possible launching pad for Neville's own dream of a new acting company in Toronto, one he has roguishly christened the Classical Theatre Conspiracy. It's unclear whom its members would be conspiring against, but the CTC's stated aim of bringing the city famous old plays it would never otherwise see has an obvious similarity to that of a company that started operations here six years ago.

In an interview with this paper, Neville hinted he is less than impressed with Soulpepper (for whom he has acted and who gave his memorable performance in Krapp's Last Tape an extended life after its initial showing at World Stage.) If Neville's Conspiracy does get off the ground, it will be inevitably perceived to bear the same adversarial relation to Soulpepper that Soulpepper, despite vehement denials from both sides, is thought to hold with the Stratford Festival.

And Neville does seem, in this impromptu trial run, to have exposed a chink in his rival's armour. With a few notable exceptions, like Don Carlos and Phedre, Soulpepper's choice of repertoire has tended to the lightweight, or the comparatively recent, or both. This of course is a characteristic it shares with Stratford (when it isn't doing Shakespeare, and sometimes when it is); with the Shaw Festival, and with practically every other classically-based company in the English-speaking world. They all spend most of their time doing comedies. There are sound reasons for this, both commercial (people like to laugh), and artistic (most of the world's best plays are comedies); but it can lead to some of the sterner masterpieces -- those late Ibsens for example -- being, to use an appropriate phrase, frozen out.

My hopes for the weekend were not high; the plays are difficult, the company (though not its individual members) was untried, and readings seemed a half-hearted substitute for actual productions. I could not have been more wrong. The plays were fascinating, and one of the evenings -- the middle one, not to keep you in suspense -- was transcendent.

There were, it turned out, several ways of doing rehearsed readings. Little Eyolf, directed by Neville himself, gave us the most conventional; actors moved around, just as they might in a proper staging except they happened to be holding books in their hands. It was also the weakest; since there had been no time to make he movement meaningful.

More than almost any other Ibsen, this play risks turning into self-parody, a problem that begins, at least to unsympathetic Anglophone ears, with the title. Eyolf is a 10-year-old who fell off a table while his parents were off making love, and was crippled. By the end of the first act he is dead, drowned, leaving his parents with a burden of guilt even heavier than the one they started out with.

All these plays are about the mortal conflict between love and vocation. All have a hero surveying his past achievements and wondering if they are worth the suffering caused to the women in his life. The women, angrily and volubly, wonder the same thing. In Eyolf, the hero is a would-be writer, repulsed by his wife's sexuality; anyway, he has neglected her, first to pursue a dubious muse, and more recently to go on mountain hikes with his son. With the boy gone, he clings with suspicious closeness to his half sister, whom he calls his "big Eyolf."

The play ends on a note of acrid ambiguity, with the central couple promising to devote their lives to the children of the neighbouring poor. The actors, led by Robin Ward and Brenda Bazinet, tried fatally to downplay and naturalize everything. Only Eyolf himself (Andrew Chalmers), too young to be self-conscious, seemed to be acting his lines rather than apologizing for them. It was clear the play, if done well, could be shattering, but doing it well is hideously hard. The frankness of its sexual content is amazing; the imagery in which it's couched risks seeming coy and evasive.

John Gabriel Borkman, a magnificent play and the best-known of the three, was more formally staged, with the actors at lecterns. There were always, however, more lecterns than speakers; a character could move from one to another with terrific effect. The allowances one had instinctively made for Little Eyolf turned out to have been misguided; this was the way to do it. Graham Cozzubbo, clearly a director to note, gave a production that, however economical, was a production, with superb lighting and sound.

Superb acting too. Borkman is a financier whose dreams of glory (power for himself, betterment for all mankind) were ended when he was caught with his hand in the till: a scenario with plenty of parallels then and since.

Released from prison, he has prowled in an upstairs room for eight years, while his embittered wife waits below, trusting in their son to clear the family name. The family have all been supported for years by the wife's twin sister, whose love Borkman sacrificed in order to placate an influential rival. Elizabeth Shepherd's splendidly uncompromising Mrs. Borkman might have allowed herself a touch more light, and Dixie Seatle, her pliant but equally determined sibling, a touch more shade, but their duelling duet was spellbinding.

Gary Reineke, erect and high-domed like the legendary Broadway showman George Abbott, found in the title role an unexpected note of sardonic whimsy, and fell short only in the final scene when Borkman, a miner's son, ventures out into the upper air and is killed by it. Borkman is a tragic figure, in a foreshortened way; he is also a monster of egotism, as are the two women. The comic aspects of this are underlined by Borkman's faithful clerk (a lovely performance by Keith Dinicol) who cheerfully points out that the function of friends is to minister to each other's illusions. Indeed we had been laughing already, at the characters' sheer brazenness, but there was nothing defensive about the laughter; it never undercut the play. This production deserves an extended life. It could even have one as a reading; Al Pacino ran Salome that way on Broadway.

When We Dead Awaken, which Cozzubbo and Neville co-directed, offered a third, intermediate way of staging; the actors sat round a long table, slanting away from us. This worked both formally and realistically; the play is mostly talk. This is the "last play" to end all last plays -- its authors' obsessions, whittled down to their purest form. Most of his plays proceed by recapitulation, but they generally progress forward at the same time; this one has little action, and that little is frail; the mountain air still stimulates but it has grown very thin. This time the guilty hero is a sculptor of, for once, genuine accomplishment; the wronged woman is his former muse and model, whom he used for his masterpiece, and then abandoned. (What really seems to bug her -- shades of the marriage in Little Eyolf -- is that when she posed nude, he never made a move. I don't think I'm vulgarizing.)

Meeting again, they lure one another up into the snow, and die happily ever after. The roles call for actors of transfiguring power: David Gardner's old artist was crinkly and sensible but hardly charismatic, better at disillusion than at dreaming. Dixie Seatle, the only performer to appear in more than one play, fixed here on a single effective note of mordant seductiveness, effective but limited. All the same, the power and intelligence of this actress, who is well-known but seldom seen, were a revelation. I hope that her reinstatement on the Toronto stage is one of the things for which the Conspiracy is conspiring.

GOODBYE, TIM HARDIN

The Poor Alex Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Right at the beginning of his first hit song, If I Were a Carpenter, Tim Hardin rhymed "lady" with baby. Four hundred years earlier, Shakespeare, through the mouth of Benedick in Much Ado About Nothing, had expressed withering opinions about people who do that, and they are still valid. To be fair, the meandering folksy quality of Hardin's tune -- and indeed of his lyric -- is not of the kind that leads you to expect great rhyming precision, and the song does have its own plaintive appeal.

He was to improve on it, though, with the tender, bemused Misty Roses, a song of adoration shot through with previsions of loss; and with Reason to Believe, an honest look at a lovers infinite capacity for self-delusion. In Goodbye, Tim Hardin, a play in which he is the only speaking character, Hardin includes these two songs on the very short list of his own favourites. He has good taste.

But then we dont know if it's really his taste, or that of Bill Ballantyne, who plays him here and who is also the author. The two men apparently met once, in the 1970s when Hardin was playing a gig in Toronto. He suggested tea at the King Edward Hotel (Ballantyne got stiffed with the bill), and it may be that confidences exchanged over the sandiwches and pastries found their way into the present script. Otherwise we don't know what the sources are. Since the play is subtitled An Imaginary Life we can assume a fair amount has been made up.

Hardin was a junkie who acquired his habit in the army, before his musical career even started. The havoc wrought by his heroin habit on his life and his talent is, if youll pardon the expression, the substance of the play. His greatest successes were in the mid-1960s. We meet him in 1980, in a rundown apartment in Los Angeles, on his last night before dying of an overdose. He was 39. If Pete Postlethwaite in Scaramouche Jones is the spryest centenarian imaginable, then Ballantyne here is about the most grizzled guy never to have made it to 40. Hes in danger of having his poetic licence endorsed.

It's a two-man show. In one half of the stage, Ballantyne plays Hardin; in the other, David Matheson plays -- and sings -- Hardin's songs. At the outset, Ballantyne seems a delightful performer, telling his story in tones of gentle amazement, as if he didnt quite believe his own life; his voice and eyebrows arch in unison. It gradually dawns on us, though, that this is all he can do -- or at least all that his own text will allow him to do.

His Hardin is fun when reminiscing about his poverty days, hanging out in Greenwich Village with his fellow folkies Fred Neil and Phil Ochs; the three of them would eat substantial meals at upscale places like the Algonquin and the Russian Tea Room, before making their escape through the mens room window. (It's left unclear whether they were ever able to pull this stunt more than once at any one restaurant, but in retrospect Hardin seems to have been practising up for tea at the King Eddie.)

They would also spend time in clubs, listening to Thelonious Monk and Miles Davis. Again, there's a suspicion that Ballantyne, a jazz fan (and a pianist in another life) is projecting his own tastes onto his subject, but its true that Hardins own songs are more musically interesting than those of most of his contemporaries, which is probably why they attracted good people like Bobby Darin. Ballantyne has Hardin talking lovingly about harmonies, as well as quoting with relish, if no particular relevance, from Shakespeare and Yeats. We can also cheer him on when he mocks the fresh- scrubbed protest-folk that immediately preceded him, and especially when, contemplating a later generation, he excoriates "that idiot Scotsman with no sense of rhythm" -- this turns out to be Rod Stewart, who was to have a hit with Reason to Believe, a song that deserved a better fate.

Ballantyne-Hardin is out of line, though, when he implicitly tars Darin with the same brush; you have only to listen to their respective albums of standards to hear the difference -- Darin was all rhythm. And without Darin's hit recording of Carpenter and his subsequent versions of other songs, Hardin would hardly have had a career.

It would be good to hear from the play something about how Darin came across these songs, and about how these and other covers affected Hardin's immediate prospects. The whole period of his success is skated over; he goes from hopeful to has-been without a beat. Ballantyne blames everything on the drugs, but one would like a few more specifics.

A lot of time is given to Hardins marriage to an actress, Susan, who we are told was perfect. (She inspired The Lady Came from Baltimore, a song Matheson doesnt sing.) Their relationship started out idyllic and ended wretched; after trying her best on many occasions, Susan left him. Again, it was the drugs' fault. It may well be true, but the only insight the play has to give us, delivered as solemnly as though it were a revelation, is the familiar one that heroin destroys trust. The same kind of hollow generalization is applied to the subject of crooked managers: "They don't just want your money, they want your soul." No, they dont; they just want your money.

Royalties alone should have kept Hardin in reasonable comfort, even if he could no longer write or perform, but he died bankrupt. Again, one wants less verbiage and more facts. Meanwhile, Matheson sings 10 Hardin songs, and the wistful innocence of his performances, set against the regret of Ballantynes monologues, establishes the counterpoint that was obviously intended. It exists but doesn't develop. I should add that Ballantyne's own command of the stage stays firm until the end, and that on the occasions when he goes for laughs, he gets them.

GODFATHER KNOWS BEST

Mysteriously Yours, Toronto

- - -

In the course of enthusing over Mysteriously Yours' previous production, Murder in Casablanca, I speculated that a logical source for the troupes next spoof might be The Sopranos. Thats the last time I try to influence the course of modern drama. The producers have taken me up on the idea, or maybe they had already had it, and I must confess that it doesn't work.

Godfather Knows Best is based on an earlier Mafia epic, but the principle is the same. As in all shows at this dinner-theatre enterprise, actors move among us somewhere around the dessert stage and fill us in on the details of their pasts. Those of us who have been here know that very shortly someone will get whacked, and we will spend the rest of the evening guessing the identity of the killer. We also know that everyone will have had an opportunity and an abundance of motive.

And so it proves here. Don Provolone is about to relinquish the savoury cares of office and has summoned to his farewell party representatives of the other major families: the Asiagos, the Mozzarellas, the Parmesans, the Romanos and the odoriferous Blue Cheeses. (All these subsidiary characters are played by us. Most of them are undemanding, requiring us only to eat, drink, and pay attention.) Soon enough, one of the Don's sons bites the dust. A detective, played as always by the redoubtable Jean Daigle, conducts the investigation.

Now you dont usually find cops playing prominent roles in gangster family sagas, so in order to recruit one, this show has gone outside its core material to a totally unconnected TV show. Daigle appears before us as Inspector Columbo. But this mixing of myths is a weakness; it suggests the basic source isnt rich enough. At first blush, this seems absurd; The Godfather films are full of memorable characters. But when you think about it, none of them, apart from Brando's Don, have become mythic (i.e. they are not conducive to impersonations). Compare Casablanca, in which not only Bogart and Bergman, but Howard, Rains, Greenstreet, and Lorre, have taken on existences in our shared imagination. I still think The Sopranos would have yielded more opportunities; but I suspect the whole Mafia world, at least as depicted in our favourite fictions, is so inbred that when you bring an outsider in to open it up it simply shrivels.

Anyway, it doesn't throw up many good jokes, which are what Mysteriously Yours relies on to keep the engine running. The plot turns on a conspiracy to involve the Provolones in the processed- cheese business, a business that true sons of the old country hold to be degenerate. The authors should be congratulated on their heroic restraint in never once referring to Don Provolone as the Big Cheese; and they have managed to work in a nice line about the kind of cheese you would expect to find in Muskoka. But there is not much to take your mind off the mystery; whose thinness may be attested by the fact that, for the first time, I was able to guess correctly who did it. There is still some fun. The action is whipped along by Daigle, who does his usual inquisitorial act -- bullying with a touch of bemusement. Of the rest, Brian Smith stands out as consigliere, Tom Dugan, "an Italian stuck in an Irishmans body," whom he plays with a richness of accent and cringe that we never got from Robert Duvall. Other characters include the Dons banished son, Michael, and his peculiar son, Frodo (a slave to slices); their very blowsy sister Connie; and the importunate Kay; they are all recognizable, but though the actors work hard, neither they nor the writers are able to strike many sparks. As always, though, the cast show extraordinary skill in remembering the names of those spectators whom they have dragooned into the action. The food, this time with an Italian flavour, remains above dinner-theatre standard; and the service is better than you'll find almost anywhere.

THE ADVENTURES OF A BLACK GIRL IN SEARCH OF GOD

Harbourfront Centre Theatre

- - -

The commercial restaging, for an extended run, of last year's inaugural production of the Obsidian Theatre Company is a breakthrough for black theatre in Toronto. The first-night reception was understandably tumultuous. It hurts, in the circumstances, to say that the play isnt very good.

The production is. Djanet Sears, who wrote The Adventures of a Black Girl in Search of God, also directs it, and (with Alejandra Nunez), composed it. The latter is very important. The show employs a vibrant singing-dancing chorus who are said to represent the heroines ancestors, though I can't see how this could be clear to anybody who hadn't read the program. When I reviewed the shows first production, I wrote the chorus seemed "increasingly a diversion from the drama rather than an illumination of it." This is still true; what seems additionally evident at a second viewing is that the chorus seems designed to give an air of size and unity to what is actually a play of bits and pieces.

The most interesting piece, and potentially the largest, is a matter of old and new history, but this too is something on which the program is rather more informative than the play. The action unfolds around Negro Creek, a corner of Southern Ontario named for the black soldiers who were settled there after the War of 1812. In 1995, a white council, presumably for reasons of misplaced political correctness, decided to rename it but were opposed by members of the black community, furious at the denial of their history. This protest is the ground bass of the play, (and its success is theoretically the dramatic climax) but its so submerged as to be almost out of sight. This is partly because the actor charged with relaying it to us has, despite many admirable qualities, a tendency to gabble; but it's never really dramatized anyway.

It's rather loosely tied to the guerrilla campaign of some Negro Creek seniors to repossess certain black historical artifacts -- some demeaning, some not -- from white properties. Their culminating raid, presented with a wealth of comic detail, is conducted on a museum and involves the participants posing as cleaners. It proves too much for the health of the ringleader, a retired judge who has been living on borrowed time. This is a fact with which his daughter, a former obstetrician, has enormous difficulty in coming to terms. Her own child died at the age of eight, and the mother has since veered between blaming herself and blaming God; she is the black girl of the title, which has been creatively pinched from Bernard Shaw. She asks the eternal question of how a divine authority can permit so much suffering; its a rhetorical question (and the rhetoric is powerful), and she gets as little answer as she expects.

She has a surrogate on hand to pose it to; her husband -- estranged, though they still love one another -- is a minister, though his vocation seems to be social rather than spiritual. Challenged to justify the ways of God to man, or to woman, he replies: "Im in sales, not marketing." It's the best line in a play not short of good lines.

The play also has a generous spirit. What it lacks is coherence. It strays off into whimsical sidebars, and the heroine, whose quest should unify the play, is frequently displaced. Karen Robinson, the revival's principal newcomer, gives her more passion and presence than she had before, but she cannot help ceding pride of place to her activist dad, who has the action, the glamour and the jokes. Walter Borden plays him, as before, with crafty wit, while David Collins, also as before, plays Gods sales rep with fire and a twinkle.

Also held over and still looking good are the sets (Astrid Janson), the lighting (Paul Mathiesen), and the choreography (Vivine Scarlett). The last, along with the singing, retains its power but arouses doubts. Its rooted in black church music, which is as stirring here as it usually is; but it seems unambiguously celebratory for a play whose final gesture seems almost secular. There is space for argument here, and a Greek tragic chorus, to which this play's ensemble has been compared, might have paused to provide one; so, indeed, might a Greek comic chorus. But that doesn't happen here. The music seems to exist for its own sweet sake (and for some uncommonly nifty scene shifting).

None of which is to deny that the production's rebirth, with Mirvish Productions acting as midwife and upping the size of the cast from 21 to a phenomenal 23, is an event, and it deserves to be seen.

HOCKEY MOM, HOCKEY DAD

Factory Theatre Studio, TORONTO

- - -

TORONTO - A lonely man and a lonely woman, each of them separated from a former partner, find themselves occupying the same space for one morning every week. So what do you think is going to develop between them? Well, in real life, probably nothing: People are notorious for their skill at missing boats. But this is a play, and it isn't by Chekhov, so something has to happen.

The options are of course limited. We know there will be some kind of romantic involvement. It will end happily, or unhappily, or with a question mark; everything has been done before. But there are good reasons why it has; given charm, humour and performing skill, we can hardly help being interested, even involved.

Michael Melski's Hockey Mom, Hockey Dad has these qualities, plus a setting that's commonplace in the outside world but unusual to the point of being exotic in the theatre -- a double recommendation. As you will undoubtedly have guessed, our two characters, Teddy and Donna, encounter one another at ungodly hours on Saturday mornings while escorting their respective sons to hockey practice. The boys are already on the ice by the time each scene has begun; we never see them but we hear a lot about them. We watch their parents shivering in the bleachers, and making whatever supportive noises come naturally to them. Teddy bellows encouragement; Donna lets hers out in a deliciously self-conscious monotone.

They live in a small town in Cape Breton. Teddy is a school janitor and Donna a supply teacher. Teddy is rough, in a cuddly sort of way, and very ready. Donna is quiet and withdrawn. So it's Teddy who has to make the running, while Donna, who carries more emotional baggage than he does and certainly hugs it closer, begins to thaw -- as she must if there is to be any action at all.

The author is adept at filling in details of the characters' off- stage lives, Donna's especially; when she hints what a struggle it has been to find the money for her son's equipment but how she had to do it anyway, we very much get the picture, economically and emotionally.

Whether we are intended to see the whole Teddy-Donna relationship as a kind of hockey game, I cannot say. It seems to me the play toys with the idea whenever it wants a handy metaphor, but drops it very quickly. It's much better at showing how the practicalities of the game -- from carpooling to violence -- affect the lives of all four characters: the two on stage and the two just off it.

David Ferry's Teddy looks his name: chubby, weathered and enduring. A specialist in the comedy of desperation, he feels disappointment keenly, and has obviously known a lot of it, but he tries breezily to rise above it. (As cheerleader for a team that loses every game, he needs to.) Ferry's ebullience rarely lets up, and his energy never, but there are nuances within the bluster.

Nothing in Irene Poole's performance of Donna can top, or even equal, her first fish-out-of-water moment: one that leaves it ambiguous whether she is doing her earnest best to play the approved version or is simply making mock of the whole concept. But her subsequent delicate wariness, hardening under pressure, is both accurate and effective. Her character is given more of a chance to develop; she may seem the more passive, but in fact it's she who acts and Teddy who reacts.

It was probably a mistake to give the slender play an intermission -- then again, it may go with the subject matter -- but the first, funnier half, since we are forced to consider them that way, is his and the second hers. It's in this half that the play comes nearest to making the game itself resonate. We learn things about Donna that seem predictable in retrospect (a tricky concept, I know) but strike home at the time. Violence is the issue; she hates it and blames Teddy for exposing her son to it; he argues that it's a good toughening process. Both have a case, and as they talk passionately past one another you want them, more than at any other point of the evening, to be together.

Rosemary Dunsmore's direction wastes not a single moment, either during the scenes or between them; and Glenn Davidson's set is good enough to freeze your toes off. The play has already had an extensive life out East, and looks a very commercial proposition. I mean that in the nicest way.

HELLO ... HELLO

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

This unbearable musical is set in the future, and the future is in polka dots. They are sprinkled remorselessly across the back of John Thompson's set, which is otherwise shiny and silvery, like a nightclub trying desperately to happen. It could give you a headache, but then so could the show. The design never tells us where, in what the script calls "a megalopolis," we are supposed to be but, in terms of glitz and emptiness, the material and its staging make a perfect match.

Hello ... Hello seems, rather confusingly, to have been conceived as a satire on glitz and emptiness, maybe even as a lament. Its moving spirit -- as author, lyricist, performer and (for want of a better term) assistant composer -- is Karen Hines, who may be best known for a series of solo clown shows, about a young woman called Pochsy; the latest, Citizen Pochsy, has yet to reach Toronto. Pochsy's specialty is the bland acceptance of the intolerable; she dispenses coyness laced with doom. Hines' persona here is very similar, and it proves unexpectedly more monotonous when she's teamed with other players than when she's at it on her own.

She plays Cassandra, who works in a boutique called the Abyss. (After the Gap, there was nowhere to go but down.) Visiting a graveyard to mourn her late husband, she meets Ben, who is paying similar devotion to his deceased girl-friend. With all this in common, plus a shared tendency to sing flatly, they fall in lust, and even in love. In the second act they have a child. Cassandra learns of her impending motherhood through some kind of pregnancy- test involving a dead rabbit. I couldn't follow the details, which are buried somewhere in the most protracted musical number of what comes to seem like an endless series. I can testify, though, that in this song the author attempts to rhyme "suspects her" with "trimester." We have all been so beaten down by lyrical incompetence that these days we hardly bother to wince when mere monosyllables are mis- mated. But failed attempts at trick-rhymes are intolerable.

Ben is very high up in a company that manufactures expensive baubles for the delectation of people who have been persuaded they need them, and it's just as well he has the money and position he does. In this society, medical care is only available to people who are very rich or who appear on television. It is also a society that has abandoned all the things that are pleasant without being profitable. Their absence is marked in a recurring litany -- "I remember deer," "I remember bananas," "I remember artists" -- spoken by characters who may indeed remember but can only go through the motions of regret without the comprehension. We are being presented, in fact, with Our Own World If We Don't Watch Out. Unfortunately the satire is more joyless and sterile than anything, now or to come, that it could conceivably be satirizing.

Cassandra, whose ex was an artist and who may have shared his fatal sensitivity, withers away in this climate, but has nothing to wither away from; she mopes, in a high-pitched monotone, from first to last. Her moments of joy are especially alarming, flashing artificial brightness like the teeth in a dentifrice ad. (This may well be intentional; that doesn't make it good.)

Ben, played by Peter Oldring with a rampant quiff and a modicum of boyish charm, apparently survives better because he feels less.

All other roles are played by Aurora Browne and Steven Morel, the latter a veteran, in one capacity or another, of most of the better small musicals of the last few years. In fact, though, there aren't many other roles; these two actors mainly function as a chorus, filling in every inch of the narrative before, or sometimes even while, it happens. Alienation was surely meant for bigger things than this. They also deliver a lengthy prose-poesy prologue, so ornate as to be impenetrable. I could hardly wait for it to stop, and the first song to begin. Then the first song began, and hope died.

The melodies, composed by Greg Morrison ("with Karen Hines" says the program), fall like water on the brain, though the synthesized harmonies -- Morrison plays the entire score solo on an electric keyboard -- supply some astringency that helps a bit. Chris Earle's production hits, I imagine, precisely the note of glossy self- satisfaction for which he and his collaborators were aiming.

COOKIN AT THE COOKERY

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Alberta Hunter was 82 when she first appeared at the Cookery in Greenwich Village. She was resuming a career as a jazz, blues and cabaret performer, after a 20-year hiatus spent working as a nurse. At the time of her comeback, she was a wiry, bun-haired woman, wizened and wise-looking, who did not so much sing her songs as deliver them in a commanding rhythmic rasp.

In Cookin at the Cookery, subtitled The Music and Times of Alberta Hunter, the great survivor is portrayed by Jackie Richardson, who has a very powerful voice, is a considerable way short of 80, and could not reasonably be described as wiry; "ample" would be more like it. She is a warm, overflowing performer, while Hunter in her Cookery days, though certainly not ungenerous in her approach, was economical and kept her own counsel. Richardson might be a persuasive Bessie Smith or Pearl Bailey, maybe a Dinah Washington. But what she really does best, and does here, is Jackie Richardson.

Does this matter? I think it does, because Hunter is serious history. We think of Bessie Smith, the archetypal singer of classic blues, as a figure from some heroic age before the flood, but Alberta takes seniority even to her; she actually wrote Downhearted Blues, the song with which Bessie had her first hit record in 1923. In the '20s, Hunter was a part of the Chicago jazz scene, then of the wider New York entertainment scene; and she topped the decade off by going to Europe, playing opposite Paul Robeson in the first London production of Show Boat. She continued through the Second World War, and of course when she returned to singing in the 1970s, her age was a great part of her attraction.

All of these facts, except perhaps the last, are mentioned in Marion J. Caffey's script. (It would be straining courtesy to call it a play.) Caffey himself has successfully staged it around the United States, and he directs it here as well. Like most shows of its kind, it is jerry-built, awkwardly written and haphazardly researched. Most of it seems meant to represent Hunters opening night at the Cookery which, we are given to understand, she took as the cue for a full-scale bout of autobiography. Richardsons lack of resemblance to the aged Alberta is something of an issue, as is the failure of Dale F. Jordan's shiny split-level set to look anything like the actual Cookery, which was a cosy check-tablecloth sort of cafe. These objections would be pedantic if the script and production achieved firm compensating identities of their own, but they don't so they arent.

We flash back, a lot, to Albertas childhood in Memphis, where she was raised by a single mother whom Richardson -- somewhat confusingly -- plays herself. The young Alberta is done by Montego Glover, an American actress who is billed simply as Narrator but in fact is much more. We are told the two women remained close but the mother never once saw the daughter perform. Years later, during the Korean War while her daughter is off entertaining the troops, Mrs. Hunter dies. This sends Alberta into a breast-beating rendition of I've Got a Mind to Ramble, punctuated by cries of "these are really the blues." But this is cheating, since, for all the time mother and daughter have spent on stage together, we never get any real sense of their relationship. It's as if the song couldnt be trusted to make an impact on its own, but has to be artificially pumped up.

Albertas sexual abuse at the hands of a school friend's father occasions a melodramatic tete-a-tete but is then forgotten; her lesbianism is brought centre stage for two minutes and never referred to again. If these things aren't important to the drama, why bring them up in the first place? It feels like filler.

Much worse is the shows apparent ignorance of the music its supposed to be celebrating. When Alberta first arrives in Chicago (in 1917!) she lets off a couple of choruses of Swing Brother Swing, a number that dates, as its name suggests, from the 1930s; Billie Holiday sang it with Count Basie, who is even mentioned in the lyrics. Alberta then tells of singing a ballad, Two Cigarettes in the Dark, and getting booed by a jazz-hungry audience. Really they should have fallen down and worshiped her for her prophetic powers, for this song too dates from the '30s and sounds it. Hunter recorded it, at that much later period, in London. The show grabs at random items from her discography. But if the most impressive things about her were her longevity and versatility, then it's short-changing her by not keeping the times and genres distinct.

Hunter worked in Chicago with Louis Armstrong. That much is true. The show has the two of them performing the duet routine on When the Saints Go Marching In that Satch did with Danny Kaye in The Five Pennies, c. 1960. This has nothing to do with Alberta Hunter; its just generic showbiz, like most of the piece.

Here, though, critical schizophrenia sets in because, to tell the truth, the number is a riot. Glovers Louis is perfection -- the singing, the mugging, the spirit, everything -- and though she doesn't actually play the trumpet, we don't for a moment doubt that she could. With just a stoop and a cackle, she also becomes the living image of Barney Josephson, the venerable entrepreneur who brought Hunter back, and whose worshipful introductions of her and the other idols whom he booked into the Cookery often lasted nearly as long as the acts themselves. (In his younger days Josephson did more for racial integration than any other manager in the history of nightclubs. The show neglects to mention this, and it also -- more surprisingly --makes no reference to the film Remember My Name, to which Hunter contributed as both singer and composer and which did as much as the Cookery gig to re-establish her.) Glover doesnt have the strongest singing voice, but considering all her other talents it would be churlish to hold this against her. In the first half of the evening, she comes close to stealing the show.

The second half, however, finds Richardson taking such firm possession of St. Louis Blues that it hardly matters whom shes meant to be impersonating. Hunter at the Cookery was a suggestive imp; Richardson is a salacious steamroller. Nor can I imagine the real Alberta indulging her audience by having them clap along to Sweet Georgia Brown, though the theatre audience obviously enjoyed it.

Richardson is forced, by her own persona and the script's deficiencies, to play your stereotypical red hot mama, which Hunter wasn't. Indeed, for a production that makes a great show of decrying stereotypes, this one seems remarkably dependent on them. I wonder, for example, where it's documented that the supervisor who dismissed Hunter from her nursing job was both white and monstrously patronizing.

You get some of the authentic Alberta, more vinegar than syrup, in her appeal to her club audiences to remember to call their mothers. In general, though, I suspect that the less you know about the subject, the more you will like the show.

TEQUILA VAMPIRE MATINEE

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - There are a lot of elements jostling rudely for attention in the title Tequila Vampire Matinee, and so there are -- too many, in fact -- in the work itself, which I need hardly say is a musical. It also stands heavily indebted to some more celebrated tuners: Some of the debts are built into the structure and explicitly acknowledged (I Pagliacci) and others are not (The Rocky Horror Show). Confused and derivative though it is, it still manages to have its own flavour. It is an original, and to be welcomed.

Its written -- book, music, lyrics, kit and caboodle -- by Kevin Quain, who is also in it. Quain is best known (though frankly not by me) as a kind of underground troubadour, operating mainly out of the Cameron House on Queen Street. This is his theatrical debut piece, and I think he means it as a myth.

At any rate, its impossible to work out when the story is meant to be happening. Most of it unfolds in a saloon, in a Western town that everybody calls San Something-or-other, and is probably somewhere near the Mexican border. (That's where the Tequila comes in.) The setting has all the trappings of a dime novel from the 19th century. But most of the characters belong to a vagabond theatrical troupe, one of whom has her starry eyes set on the bright lights of Las Vegas, which didn't have any lights until the 1950s.

Go figure; the show leaves you plenty of time. It starts with a puppet prologue, performed by Punch and Judy. I dont know if these figures, originally Italian, have ever been as popular in Canada as they were on the English beaches of my childhood, but they must have some currency, or Quain wouldnt have used them. So you'll probably remember that Punch has a big nose and a bigger stick, the latter of which he uses to belabour Judy, who loves him, until she's senseless. Lest you should think Punch a mere misogynist, I must point out that he administers the same treatment to everyone else, chortling, in the authorized version, thats the way to do it" as he does it. Here, though, we only get Punch and wife. The excuse for their presence is that the chief of the itinerant actors, known as Big Daddy, is a puppeteer, among other things, and that Punch is his favourite glove (though he actually has all the debonair charm of Ed the Sock). In fact, Big Daddy identifies.

And the reason for this is that he is in love with, or at least very possessive of, Sugar Plum, the blond ingenue who dreams of Vegas. He is tormented by the thought that she might leave him. All this is revealed in a roadside episode that takes place before a front cloth, and very long and very cramped the scene is. But then the cloth disappears, the bar is revealed, and with a full stage at its disposal the show begins to go, if not with a swing, then with an attractively crooked lope.

The saloon is owned and run by a square-jawed young man called Ramon, and both he and it are on their uppers. Ramon sings, very well, about leading a dogs life, and anyone old and lucky enough to remember a hit song -- or monologue to music -- called Life Gits Tee'jus, Don' It? will recognize the mood, and the idiom, immediately. Big Daddy and company descend on the place (I mean that pretty much literally), and Big Daddy, who seems to have gone to the same theatrical school as the King and the Duke who caused such problems to Huck Finn, sweet-and-fast-talks Ramon into letting him and his strollers use the place as their theatre.

Also in the company are Lulu, who is a lesbian, and Twitch, who is a pyromaniac, though neither of these attributes play as significant a part in the action as we are led to believe they will. Its more important that Ramon falls for Sugar Plum, leading her to realize that there may be more to life than getting beaten up by her old man. Big Daddy, getting wind of this, suffers all the tortures of jealousy. After singing a lament of his own, to a tune strongly resembling Help Me Make It Through the Night, he puts on a wind-up record of Veste la giubba to emphasize the point.

Unfortunately, Big Daddy has been presented as such a louse that there is no future, on even the most farcical level, in having us root for him as a broken-hearted clown. Its no use trying to persuade us that Mr. Punch has feelings. This reduces the impact of the set-piece scene.

The show goes on (that's where the Matinee comes in) and it proves not to be the expected burlesque bill but a rather expert pastiche of classic bedroom farce, part Moliere, part commedia dell'arte. It also parallels the real-life situations of the characters performing it. Its rich and its clever, though not as rich or clever as it would obviously like, and indeed needs, to be.

It is something, though, and it's funny, as the show frequently is, often at the times you least expect it, which of course are the best times. Quain has written a kind of Brechtian country score, down-home music that suggests home is about to be repossessed by the bank. And if his lyrics have no special distinction, plus the usual quotient of bum rhymes, at least they don't sound as if theyre trying to be clever.

Ted Dykstras direction is lethargic, but that, once we're past the preparatory stuff, doesn't matter, and could even be intentional. A laid-back musical may sound like an oxymoron, but this could be one of a kind. The choreographer, Dawn Naser, hasnt come up with any notable steps but shes arranged some entertaining groupings.

The cast are excellent. J.D. Nicholsen's Big Daddy is powerful if, as already indicated, irremediably unsympathetic. Amy Rutherford's Sugar Plum is a delight, popping her eyes and fluttering her lashes like one of Fiona Reids demurer heroines stripped of her sophistication. Brendan Walls Ramon has looks, humour and a voice. As Lulu, Shelley Simester reveals herself a mistress of the lost art of deafening an audience in song without artificial aids, and as Twitch, a shaven-headed buffoon accurately described as "the reason children are afraid of clowns, Stephen Sparks is sensationally deft, bodily, facially and vocally. That's the way to do it.

Quain himself appears as Maestro, a pianist, and Dragoslav Tanaskovic is Vladimir, a bass player. Both have vestigial parts in the action, which they discharge with the inimitably out- of-it quality peculiar to acting musicians. Otherwise, they're the band. As to where the Vampires come in; they don't, hardly, and when they do it's ridiculous. But not to worry: As Big Daddy and Co. would doubtless say to an unruly audience: What do you want? Blood?"

CABARET

The New Yorker Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - According to the program, this production of Cabaret was "inspired by" the one directed by Sam Mendes in 1998 in New York. To be honest, there isn't much inspiration on offer at the New Yorker but the lineage is certainly recognizable. Cabaret has been on a downward slope ever since Hal Prince's brilliant original staging in 1966. Prince's production was about the rise of Nazism in 1930 Berlin; Mendes' was about how deliciously naughty we are; Jordan Allison's is about how deliciously naughty we would like to be and how heavy-handedly we go about it.

Allison is a 20-year-old who has raised nearly half-a-million dollars to get this show on and to direct it himself. Hats are off to him for his enterprise, but maybe even that much money isn't enough to get this show looking right in even a small commercial house. The costumes are schlumpy beyond the call of the Depression (just what is that dress Fraulein Schneider wears to her engagement party?) and the conceptual conceit that the whole show is taking place within the confines of the Kit Kat Klub -- that every character is a cabaret-turn and every scene a number -- never stands a chance, for the stage is just a neutral space. Merely putting the musicians on stage doesn't cut it; lots of musicals do that. So the scenes in Fraulein Schneider's boarding-house, which we have no alternative but to take literally, are more than usually confusing. You never know whether you're in a room or a passage.

Nor has the budget been stretched to employ actors who can do it. People have always complained about this show that the performers cast for Sally Bowles and the Master of Ceremonies -- even those who are actors rather than musical-theatre people -- have far too much star-quality to have ever been working at a dive like the Kit Kat. Well, not this time. Neither here has a spark of wit, and both galumph through their roles. Barbara-Lynn Redpath's characterization stops short at a horsey English accent. A smudged carbon of innumerable previous Sallies, she does just one thing that's original -- she sings the title-song tremulous and choked-up rather than defiant, as if really torn at the prospect of parting from Clifford. It doesn't work, but it was worth a try. Stephen Sheffer also shines in one song, his soft, defeated crooning of I Don't Care Much. Otherwise, his emcee is epicene by numbers.

Brian Wigg's Cliff is intelligent if colourless; though he would be wise to talk his way through his four lines of song. (They are all that remain to him in this latest re-ordering of the John Kander- Fred Ebb score. Credit Allison at least with cutting Mein Herr and Maybe This Time, two songs from the movie that have been creeping into theatre editions and have no business there.) Allan Price, though his accent is more French than German, has a decent go at Herr Schultz, but Julia DeSotto is a bossy Fraulein Schneider, devoid of soft spots. The more she bellows about her vulnerability, the less we believe her. None of the principals has much of a voice; more importantly, none is very adept at putting over a number.

I don't know why the production has given star-billing to two unknowns (Sheffer and Redpath) in a cast of other unknowns. This is supposed to be an ensemble piece. It was a bad day for Cabaret when the emcee became the star role. If the show is about any individual characters, it's about Sally and Cliff. The emcee isn't a character at all; he's the compere who steals the show but -- as I pointed out last time this musical hit town -- you can't steal a show that's already been handed to you.

Dancing in the club numbers consists of simulating sexual intercourse in various positions: A narrowing-down of options that must, so to speak, have taken a lot of heat off the choreographer, Monica Morrow. She does vary the pattern at the beginning of the second act by having the chorus adopt a swastika formation, like Springtime for Hitler without the laughs. (Well, unfortunately, not without the laughs.) The staging of the famous, or perhaps notorious, Gorilla song -- "if you could see her through my eyes/ She wouldn't look Jewish at all" -- is crass. It's done as a fast tap number. The lulling seductiveness of evil -- which is what the song is about, what the show is about -- flies out the window.

Which raises the question: What is all the giggling and squealing for?As Prince staged it, the cabaret was meant to be a lure, a symbol of the forgetfulness that made fascism possible. The idea was moralistic, in the American way, but it had its own logic and followed it through. Since then, what the movie famously called "divine decadence" has become an end in itself; something with which to titillate, and then to shock. Recent productions come close to blaming Weimar nightlife for the Nazis, which is absurd. The flamboyantly gay emcee is identified with the forces that, as he must have known, would destroy him. As they do: In a closing image that was invented by Mendes and looks like it's becoming standard, our host comes before us as a concentration-camp victim. In that earlier, slicker production, this seemed like a desperate attempt to top all the evening's previous shock-effects. In this more cloddish version it seems, oddly, more honest.

And the production has developed some power in its second half; the single stone through the window of Herr Schultz, the Jewish greengrocer, remains more frightening than any of the painted menaces in the club routines. (At this moment, it's possibly more frightening than it's ever been.) It's a tribute to Kander and Ebb and to their librettist, Joe Masteroff, that their material, even in these reduced circumstances, still seems immensely strong. And there, since I can feel my own candour ebbing and since most of those concerned are very young, I shall stop.

Until Dec. 7. Box office: 416-504-9971.

(nod)

Factory Theatre, Toronto

- - -

(parenthetically, there is always something pretentious about putting a play's entire title either in lower case or in brackets. this one does both. what's it supposed to prove? and how are you meant to pronounce it?)

(nod) is about a family. There are a mother, two sons and a daughter. There was also, once, a father, but one day he got up, left the house, climbed into his boat, sailed it across the local lake and drowned. Mother, too, has just met a watery end -- in the bathtub -- as the play starts, but that doesn't stop her from playing an active and voluble part in the succeeding action. Her children, all now adults, strive to come to terms with their parents' legacy, which was pretty damaging. The house is in a rotting state of disrepair, and so are the children's psyches. They were all disappointments to their mother, and she was a nagging burden to them. They remember mama, and she comes back to haunt them.

Father is not afforded the same corporeal presence, probably because of mysterious, unknowable circumstances in both his life and his death. He is merely a shadow, intermittently projected on to a video screen. It must also be in his honour that the cast, at regular intervals, sway and hurtle around the stage as if they were in the opening scene of The Tempest. They also have a habit of humming What Shall We Do with the Drunken Sailor, which they do with the air of people who are furnishing us with a vital clue to something.

The show is produced by Theatre Gargantua, a troupe with a commitment to mime, music, mixed media and such. But however much of a collaborative effort the production might have been, its text is the work of a single author, the actor and playwright Rick Roberts. Roberts gave a terrific performance in last season's Hotel Loopy, in which he delivered a monologue that was a marvel of gratification perpetually delayed. He never, when writing for other actors, gives them comparable opportunities to delight. His previous play, Fish/ Wife, was trim but desiccated, its two characters patronized abstractions. This new one is less shapely, and outstays its welcome even at 80 minutes, but it strikes more chords on the way.

None of the family members is favoured with a name; they are identified as Mother, Sister, Brother, Young Brother and Tenant -- the last a young girl who has taken up residence in the basement, and whom even the other characters treat as some kind of symbol. All this stylization affords some very effective shortcuts; the family pressures are served up neat, often as sour jokes. Brother (Michael Spence), who can hardly get out of bed, pursues a fitful career as a janitor, this being the nearest he can come to realizing the maternal ambition for him to become a famous scientist. Younger Brother (Aaron Willis) was in the womb when his father departed, and emerged with a hunched back or, as his mother prefers to put it, with very bad posture. Both of these performances have an individual wit, as well as the required ensemble enthusiasm when it comes to reeling, writhing and fainting in coils.

The women are less fortunate. Erica Buss (also the production's sound designer and not, I suspect, a performer much at home with words) finds little in Sister beyond aggressive self-pity. This is a quality she seems to have inherited from Marjorie Campbell's Mother, who dispenses it with a relish that grates on the audience as much as it does on her relatives. (It certainly explains why Father left home, though the place's crumbling state is apparently his fault.) The Tenant (Lori Nancy Kalamanski) makes little impact and has little chance.

The play is billed as "for anyone who has ever had a family." That takes in most of us, and most of us will find something to respond to. Not enough, though. I've managed, so far in my critical life, to resist quoting Tolstoy's celebrated observation about every unhappy family being unhappy in its own way, but the time has come to throw in the towel. This unhappy family has certainly found its own way, but the show's insistence on mystification and -- if there is such a word or even if there isn't -- mythification means that the specifics are barely established and never explored. I appreciate that the play doesn't want to be a soap opera but all the jumping around in time and space or between present and past, fantasy and actuality, can not make it into anything else. And those trappings aren't necessarily as thrilling as they're often assumed to be. Jacquie P.A. Thomas' direction is well-drilled but not especially imaginative.

(As for the title. It's more than possible that the whole play is a dream. And Sister, who's narcoleptic, is the likeliest person to be dreaming it.)

Black & White Photo: Michael Cooper / Erica Buss as Sister, Lori Nancy Kalamanski as Tenant (in the background), Marjorie Campbell as Mother, Michael Spence as Brother and Aaron Willis as Younger Brother in the Theatre Gargantua production of (nod).

MOSLEY AND ME

Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

- - -

When I first heard that Adam Pettle's new play was to be called Mosley and Me, I fancied that it might concern somebodys encounter with the old leader of the British Union of Fascists. That would be a good challenging subject for a nice Jewish boy playwright, especially one whose plays are now being done over there. It turns out, though, that on this occasion Pettle is not broadening his horizons but narrowing them. The play, set in a bagel shop in Montreal, is the latest to have reached the boards with his name attached -- and, though it has its occasional charms, much the least interesting.

The plays first-person character -- he doesn't actually narrate it, but he does top-and-tail it -- is Nathan Mintz, whose family has been making and selling bagels for generations. He is an unwilling inheritor; he studied creative writing at university because, he says, "that's where the big money is," (hollow laughter from a substantial part of the house), and he still dreams of a career in screenwriting.

Johnny Mosley is his new assistant -- for baking, not writing, though he has an influence on the latter as well; he has, after all, inspired Nathans narrative. Johnny is an ex-con and a Gentile. (Though, as Nathan explains, bagels arent really Jewish in origin; they're Austrian, like Hitler. They're certainly stateless now.) The two men have one thing in common. They are both crazy for poker. Nathan has a regular game going in the back of the shop, at which Johnny soon becomes a valued player.

Nathan can be a something of a schlemiel. He thinks, for example, that Guys and Dolls is the greatest movie musical ever made. (The show, yes; but the movie?) But hes still, to make a connection that we can hardly help humming along with, good old reliable Nathan, though subject to fits of insecurity and temper. Johnny, it turns out, will go recklessly and maybe ruinously for any kind of gambling. Initially, he has a beneficent effect on the bagel business -- which has been, figuratively speaking, in the hole -- and he helps restore Nathans morale about his writing. But the differences between the two assert themselves, and there is a scam.

Johnny (Mosley) and Nathan (Me) are all of the shop and all of the play. The other poker players are described and spoken of, never seen; ergo, we never see a game (though play and production do add a chapter, or at least a footnote, to the history of theatrical realism by showing us Nathan and Johnny actually making bagels). I confess that I usually fall asleep when forced to watch a card game, either in real life or on stage or screen. The British play Dealer's Choice was an invigorating exception, but that put a whole complex dynamic before our eyes, the kind of thing that Mosley and Me only attempts at second hand. Just hearing a game described, either before or after it happens and even when there is cheating involved, turns out to be even more enervating than witnessing one.

The friendship the play describes is sketchily portrayed, so its threatened dissolution seems like no particular threat. It jerks the play partially to life but not completely.

Vikki Anderson's production (for her own company, DVxT) may be too grandiose for the small story within it. I know people said the same thing about Pettles last play, Sunday Father, but that play was big enough to look after itself, and it dealt far more wittily and suggestively with the Jew-Gentile contrast, which here is surprisingly lacking in flavour. The director is also the designer; a couple of dirty beige slabs summon the basic setting well enough, but when, quite late in the game, they move around, they seem to be echoing the plays own sudden rush into action without much helping it. The relevance of the huge 17th-century painting that hangs, half- obscured, behind one of the flats is something I am still trying to figure out.

The casting, though, could hardly be bettered. Mosley is one of Randy Hughson's less blustery performances, combining a hulking strangeness -- it isn't exactly menace -- with what seems to be an innocently inquiring warmth. When the screws are turned on him, or at least when he talks about it, his body and his personality seem to tighten, so that what previously seemed genial expansiveness gathers into a single forceful stream of desperation.

Alex Poch-Goldin, who gets better at each appearance, is his opposite: a man who tries to be guarded and defensive, but is actually wide open. The Montreal neighbourhood, unknown to me, in which the bakery is situated, is called Mile End. This is also one of the East End neighbourhoods that would have been one of the late Sir Oswald Mosleys stomping grounds in the 1930s (a London equivalent of Torontos Christie Pits), so maybe there's a connection after all.

SUR

Artword Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - There is a musical sequence in Sur that sums up the enterprise as well as anything could. It comes a short way into the second half. There is no listing in the program, but the song seems to be called Six Little Sparrows and it's an elimination number, on the order of Ten Green Bottles, in which each verse announces the disappearance of another character. It's performed here by half-a- dozen South American ladies of the early 20th century, who are on their way to discover the South Pole. (I'll get back to that.) Accompanied by music with a vaguely Latin pulse, they all skip to the centre of the stage, converge, clap hands and skip back again. They repeat this routine six times, without variation, and at the end of it every one of them is still standing. There is a complete disjunction between the words and the staging. And so it goes, throughout.

There is also no connection between the genteel perkiness of the song and the toughness demanded of these women to get where they're going; and this too is a constant. Sur (Spanish for south) is adapted and directed by Ronald Weihs, from a short story by the veteran American fabulist Ursula K. Le Guin. It's set in 1909-10, after Captain Scott's first failed expedition to the Antarctic but before his legendarily disastrous second. "If Captain Scott can do it," says one of our heroines, in what the playwright declares to be his favourite line, "then why can't we?" (She chivalrously refrains from mentioning that Scott couldn't do it.) The idea, having once taken root in her mind, spreads from country to country across the South American continent as if by bush telegraph, in a sequence that stands out from the rest of the evening in possessing a certain amount of dramatic reality and even a little wit. Having pried themselves free from protective or disinterested menfolk, our six recruits take ship with a kindly if patronizing captain, who deposits them on the outer shores of Antarctica, trusting they will have a nice holiday and get down to some serious knitting. The sea - voyage through decreasing degrees of latitude is charted in a song, one with the temper of a nursery rhyme and the tempo of a dirge, whose refrain, endlessly repeated, is "there's land to the South, so I've been told." One reason for welcoming this show's intermission is the hope that the performers might use their time out to learn another tune.

Despite the songs, Sur is not a musical; it seems to be using music because, in group theatrical creations drawn from either literary or documentary sources, that is one of the things one does. The show has been in preparation for half a year, and has gone through two stages of workshops: a fact that suggests -- not for the first time -- that good intentions and long rehearsals are no guarantors of authenticity. One thing that "workshopping" (a word we could probably do without) is supposed to achieve is a high standard of physical reality. To put it at its most basic: In this show about polar exploration, you would expect the participants to look, sound or act cold -- even to the extent that we feel it ourselves. The way this lot behave, and the way they're kitted out, evoke nothing more extreme than a brisk day in Southern Ontario.

When two of them actually reach the Pole (the others having stayed at base camp) they do try to summon the appalling climactic conditions, but by then it's too late. They also refuse to leave any markers to show subsequent explorers that they made it. The story's sly conceit is that while it can't be proved that a couple of women succeeded where Scott and Shackleton failed and where Amundsen had yet to venture, it can't be disproved either. This tale and its characters are avowedly fictitious, but who's to say that something like it couldn't have happened?

No one, that's who. But the what-if style of narrative is far easier to sustain on the page, where the author is in full command of the tone, than on the stage, where everything -- certainly on this occasion -- shrieks out that the whole thing is impossible. However much the text may go on about women's endurance and adaptability and about their superior knowledge and skill in matters of diet and housekeeping, nothing persuades us that it could have been done --not by these women with their finishing-school manners, aptly reflected in a school-play standard of acting.

Actually, that's unfair. I have recently seen two high-school shows that, for inventiveness and sophistication, left this one choking in the dust -- or, as I suppose I'm obliged to put it, gasping on the ice.

2003-12-08-and-the-allusions-just-keep-o:
The finale of Slings and Arrows airs tonight on The Movie Network at 10. It repeats beginning Dec. 19. See www.themovienetwork.ca for details.; robertcushman@lycos.com

A couple of weeks ago Bravo! aired a TV profile of Richard Monette, the artistic director of the Stratford Festival. Despite its lurid title, The Madness of King Richard, it was remarkably tame. It started well, with its subjects revelations about an unhappy childhood that caused him to seek an escape route onto the stage, but these hints of a divided nature were never followed up. Amazingly, there was no reference to, let alone exploration of, what Monette has elsewhere identified as the great crisis of his professional life: the onset of the paralyzing stage fright that ended his successful career as an actor and caused him to take up directing instead. There were tantalizing glimpses of his breakthrough performance as the drag queen in Michel Tremblays Hosanna, but those of us who know his acting mainly by report would like to have seen more.

One thing the show demonstrated is that there are a lot of people who can do impersonations of Richard Monette. It ended with a whole montage of them, the best one coming from actor Dan Chameroy. All the same, the most devastating Monette impression is probably done by Monette himself, who can take a sly delight in playing up to his own perceived role of the outsize actor-manager, rolling out the syllables and savouring the vowels. He is, paradoxically, an actor- manager who these days hardly ever acts, but who remains very much an actor's director.

Meanwhile, in the miniseries Slings and Arrows, Stephen Ouimette is playing Oliver Welles, artistic director of the New Burbage Theatre Festival. New Burbage is a big-time small-town operation that bears a strong resemblance to Stratford. It specializes in Shakespeare, swans swan about in its neighbouring river, and its flagship stage, from what we can see of it, is similar to the Stratford platform, though its lobby, with its huge sweeping staircase, is that of the Canon Theatre in Toronto. (And it's impossible to believe that the one could lead to the other.)

Ouimette is also giving his Monette. Its a wicked assumption, especially when hes handing out first-night benedictions in the dressing rooms, but presumably an affectionate one; Ouimette is a pillar of the Stratford company and will be both acting and directing there in the coming season.

The play that's about to go into rehearsal as the story begins is Hamlet, and the new text runs in parallel with the old one. Oliver gets killed off (by a truck labelled "ham") at the end of the first instalment. He hangs around in subsequent weeks as a ghost, and this, plus the appearance in one episode of a pair of argumentative undertakers, is certainly meant to remind us of Hamlet -- though, as this is television it's likelier to make us think of Six Feet Under. Also, Oliver dead and devoid of Monette mannerisms is a lot less entertaining than Oliver alive and loaded with them.

This is partly because Olivers spectral function is to illuminate things that happened years ago, and that we dont care about. He was in a three-cornered relationship with Ellen Fanshaw, the festival's past and present leading lady (she's aged from Ophelia into Gertrude), and Geoffrey Tennant, a former enfant terrible of an actor who went mental in the middle of playing the Prince, walked off, and was never seen again, at least not on that stage. Now hes Olivers successor, trying to breathe life into what he has accused of being a moribund, commercialized organization. However, where The Madness of King Richard could have used more facts about the past and less gush about the present, Slings and Arrows lives only in the present. It's six hours of onstage drama and backstage gossip.

On that basis, I've been enjoying it a lot, though Im not sure how much of my pleasure derives from knowing the territory. The cast is crammed with Toronto theatre favourites doing cameos. Julian Richings and Robert Persichini, for examples, are delightfully Dickensian as the modern gravediggers. The script is the work of three actor-writers -- comedians Mark McKinney and Bob Martin and the very legit Susan Coyne -- all of whom are, admirably, in it; Coynes nervous, harried secretary is an especial treat. They have wound the allusions very tight. Geoffrey has taken over not only Oliver's theatre but his new production of Hamlet, and the more the series zeroes in on the play, the more absorbing, entertaining, and even moving it becomes: The closer the focus, the bigger the picture.

Geoffrey and Ellen, past lovers, are played by Paul Gross and Martha Burns, real life husband and wife, and they make -- I'm talking about their acting -- a terrific team. But the reverberations go deeper; the Hamlet Geoffrey has to direct is a movie hunk (Luke Kirby) whom nobody thinks can do it. Gross himself, fresh from his TV success in Due South, played Hamlet at Stratford four years ago and, though he wasnt treated with that degree of contempt, he got some patronizing notices, my own probably among them. But as Geoffrey, he has all the glamour, the wit, the intelligence and the bravura of a heroic actor, a breed that can take on comedy as well as tragedy. The festival -- the real one -- should re-engage him.

At times he seems to be playing Albert Schultz (who, just to confuse us some more, makes a fleeting appearance at Olivers funeral, playing heaven-knows whom). But at a deeper level, Gross too is playing Monette -- not the personality but the history. His Geoffrey is an actor who has grappled with personal and professional trauma by redirecting his energies. The authors, intentionally or not, have taken the two public sides of Stratford's director -- the populist and the idealist -- and divided them between their two male principals.

The result doesn't offer much ammunition either to those who believe that Stratford has sold its soul or to those, like me, who think its doing all right but sometimes sails a lot too close to the wind. In fact the show ducks the question by making its villain an outsider: an American sponsor -- a sort of Wicked Witch of the South -- who wants to give the main stage over entirely to musicals, throwing on some Shakespeare in the two smaller houses for those who like that sort of thing while plastering the Bards face all over town, just like it's done in the English Stratford. (I once swore a mighty oath that I would never use the phrase "the Bard" but in this context it seems appropriate.) Her cat's-paw in all this is New Burbages nervously ambitious general manager (the McKinney role), but he is saved by actually witnessing a performance of Hamlet: Rather like the Puritan in Shakespeare in Love whos swept protesting into Romeo and Juliet and stays to cheer with everybody else. Well, it was his first time; and the manager, too, acts like it's the first Shakespeare he's ever seen. How long has he been in the job?

Theres also an oleaginous critic called Basil (Sean Cullen) whose role is less important than the advance publicity led some of us to believe. Are they trying to tell us something? Now, Basil cant be me; I'm thin. All the same, the only paper anyone is seen reading the morning after the Hamlet premiere is the National Post. What did I think?

Probably not the same as the New Burbage people themselves; our perspectives would be irreparably different. Still, Geoffrey, when things look desperate, reassures his cast that they have one thing working for them -- the greatest play written in 400 years. I prefer Lear, but I see his point; there's no play as malleable, as pregnant with associations, as Hamlet.

Slings and Arrows, a confessedly incestuous exercise, a mixture of in-joke and love letter, is at its best when feasting off the allusions, and they keep coming. Some people believe that bits of Hamlet, served up in other contexts, are more stimulating now than the play itself can ever hope to be. It's a heresy I would like to reject but suspect may well be true. The irony, a cheering one, is that the snippets of Hamlet always make you want to see the play again, hoping that the next time will be the one. That does unite us.

Black & White Photo: Stephen Ouimette (left) and Paul Gross star in Slings and Arrows.
