CINDERELLA

Elgin Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Certain marks on the body of Cinderella at the Elgin lead me to believe that dramaturgy has been committed. For a start, the program, for the first time in my experience of Ross Petty's annual holiday extravaganzas, lists an author. In fact it lists a dozen; Malcolm Heenman gets the principal credit for "script adaptation" (adaptation from what remains a murky question) but he seems to have had the assistance of the director, Jim Warren, and about half the cast. No doubt about it: This pantomime has been in a workshop, and I don't mean Santa's.

This, by the standards usually prevailing in these parts, is a very thoughtful show. We all know that Cinderella went to the ball in a coach magically made from a pumpkin. This version seizes on that fact, and works back from it. Cinderella's family, the village they live in, and -- as far as I could make out -- the kingdom that surrounds it, are all economically dependent on the pumpkin crop. But there seems to have been either a devastating blight or a profligate Halloween; and in order to send Cinders off to meet her Prince, her Fairy Godmother has to commandeer the only remaining pumpkin in the neighbourhood. It's supply-side economics: Subsidize the upper classes and their posh parties, and the benefits will filter down to the community, or at least to the pretty and deserving. For once it seems to work.

Not only is there thematic unity; there is also motivation. It's traditional for Cinderella to make a cheerful, sparkling entrance among the merry villagers in the opening scene -- which, considering the way she's being treated at home, makes no psychological sense. In this version however, Cinderella has no initial reason, apart from the threat of universal starvation, to feel unhappy about anything. Her father, Baron Hardup (his traditional name in English panto), has gone off to repair the family fortunes. No sooner has the first number been cavorted through than he returns, accompanied by a newly acquired wife, whom he must think is rich because she's immensely tall and dresses flashy, and her two dowdy and ungainly daughters. The new arrivals take one look at their beautiful new step-relative and decide they don't like the competition. So the heroine's persecution at their hands is not a given; we actually see it evolving. And if you want to know why her loving dad doesn't intervene -- well, it's partly because his every word is a malapropism so nobody would understand his protestations if he made them. But it's mainly because he spends most of the action in a debtors' prison, for non-payment of pumpkin tax. And if you want to know why his daughter allows herself to be domestically exploited, it's because she's being blackmailed; her stepmom won't allow her to pay prison visits unless she toes the line.

Jennifer Gould's Cinderella needs all this rationalization, because she's an unusually spunky and sensible heroine who backs down for no one. She hasn't even been nourishing any particular ambition to go to the ball, though when somebody mentions the idea she thinks it quite a good one. (She'll be able to ask the king to pardon her father; the show is not just conscientious about narrative continuity, it's obsessive.) About all she has in common with the regulation pantomime ingenue are good looks and a radiant singing voice. Her romantic interest is similarly non-traditional. In the old days across the sea, he would have been played by a strapping female with handsome legs and powerful lungs, and would have been known generically as the Principal Boy. That variety of pantomimic cross-dressing tradition having lapsed, the role has to be differently conceived, and the new Petty convention, increasingly evident over the last few years, is to make him funny. Thus, Adam Brazier's Prince Jack (they tell him to act charming but it doesn't take) is a moon-faced conservationist with a good heart but no social graces.

Turning the romantics into comics undoubtedly makes their scenes more interesting, but it does make life tough for those other performers who would seem to have being funny as part of their job description, and to whom the script and direction are a lot less helpful.

In most Cinderellas, the star role is Buttons, the page-boy clown who adores the leading lady, helps her with the chores, and wins all hearts when royalty steps in and makes off with his happiness. Cliff Saunders, possibly the first balding Buttons in theatrical history, is given coarse mechanical routines, and if his heart is breaking he keeps it to himself. He's quite easily bought off by being made Mayor, an occasion for topical jokes that the show, most uncharacteristically, denies itself. Meanwhile, Dandini (Jonathan Wilson), Buttons' opposite number in the Prince's suite, has been given more opportunity than usual, and slightly better material, and is a definite threat.

One regular attraction of the Petty pantos is the spectacle of some Stratford or Shaw Festival luminary, letting his hair down. This time it's Don Harron, a leading Stratord juvenile as recently as 1955, who plays the tongue-twisted Baron and is expectedly endearing. The Fairy Godmother is played by Erin Davis, famous radio and TV host. She gives, I suspect, much the same performance live as she does canned; that is, she's very assured, very enthusiastic, and speaks to the other actors and to the audience as if she were conducting a phone-in.

The producer himself plays the evil stepmother, thus combining his usual function of hissable villain with the less accustomed one of pantomime dame. The two don't go well together. You see, children, the Dame -- the more durable aspect of the transvestite tradition -- is meant to be a sympathetic figure; when the show is Aladdin or Dick Whittington, he/she is the hero's feckless but loving mother, man-hungry but harmless. She's also supposed to be dowdy. Danny LaRue, Britain's premiere drag queen, once played the Dame and it didn't work at all; he looked too good in the frocks. Petty has the same problem; svelte and sneering, he crowds the pitch for his ugly offspring (Mary-Ellen Mahoney and Karen Skidmore) who fight back gamely but with diminishing returns.

This production has more comic talent than it knows what to do with, and that is not a compliment. When mama leads her brood in a morale-boosting rendition of Everything's Coming Up Roses, we have no idea how to take it. Is it a character number? Is it a spoof? Are they hoping for a show-stopper? Or are they just hoping?

It also stands out uncomfortably by virtue of being a good song. The other music is bullying shlock, of the Lloyd Webber persuasion or worse. Pantomime (the show bills itself as a musical, but it's kidding) has always interpolated the popular songs of its time, but this of course means that its numbers just get worse. I suspect that Petty knows this, and that it's the Roses song that actually reflects his own taste, which is why he makes such a big deal of it.

As for production values, there are real ponies in the transformation scene (a first here, I think); and, as far as I could tell the dancers from the dance, the corps, especially its male members, seem capable of more than is asked of them. This isn't the best of the series that I've seen -- that would be the last Robin Hood -- but it's better than the last few.

Black & White Photo: Jim Allen / Adam Brazier as the socially ungraceful Prince and Jennifer Gould as the sensible heroine Cinderella.

THE UNDERPANTS

Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

- - -

YOUNG WIFE: Where have you been?

WIFE'S FRIEND: I've been to the theatre. A new comedy. Sternheim.

WIFE: Should I see it?

FRIEND: Wait for the adaptation.

I quote -- well, paraphrase -- from memory, but I think I have the gist of the exchange, and especially of the punchline. It's Steve Martin being self-referential, and it appears in The Underpants, his adaptation of a German comedy, pre-First World War, by that very same Carl Sternheim, that the Shaw Festival once presented under the title The Unmentionables and that has been billed in England as The Knickers. (Truly, as an earlier and more faithful translator than Martin once noted, an inexhaustible subject.) My memories of the Shaw production, which was excellent, suggest that we didn't actually have to wait for the Martin version, but now that we have it we might as well enjoy it.

The underpants, or whatever they are, belong to Louise Maske, the stay-at-home wife of Theo, a junior civil servant with rigorous ideas about practically everything. She is out in the street one day, watching a royal parade, and the sight of the king so excites her that her undergarment falls to the ground. She rapidly picks it up, but not before the sight has excited at least two men, both of whom make their way to her husband's house and ask to rent a room. He, scenting profit, divides the available living space between them; they, scenting Louisa, agree to the arrangement; and Louisa's friend and neighbour, scenting vicarious fulfillment, eggs her on to accept the advances of at least one of them.

Exhibitionism, fetishism, voyeur-ism and, in Theo's case, avarice and possessiveness, which could just be two names for the same condition. Sternheim was writing a satiric account of a society of uptight obsessives, what the 17th century would have called a comedy of humours, something that resembles farce but is more concerned with depicting a society than with pursuing individual manias. (Has anyone ever seen a real German farce? Does one exist? The idea chills the blood.)

Martin makes it a farce, pushing the characters over the line that separates mere obsessives from demented automata. Certainly that's how it appears in Daryl Cloran's extremely fast, furious and meticulously timed production. Sternheim depicts civilians who are fanatically nationalistic and have a military sense of order and obedience; it's easy for a modern audience to see them as fascists in embryo and to congratulate the author on his foresight and themselves on recognizing it. This version, however, forecloses on any sense of prophetic subtlety; as the actors career around the stage, their arms begin forming Nazi salutes and their legs start executing goose-steps.

It's quite funny the first time. Martin, whose ambition seems to be to cross Tom Stoppard with Woody Allen, also crams his text with double entendres (in the original, the situations are sexual but the dialogue is decorous, which has its own humour) and he also works in some genuine verbal wit. "You're here under false pretences," says one suitor, to which the other replies, "What other kind are there?" I'd never thought of that.

This, unusually, is a one-door farce; no entrance is laggard, every one of them is a surprise, and the crucial aperture takes pride of place on Lorenzo Savoini's cunning set, which is a few skewed notches away from being realistic. Dana Osborne has designed clever costumes, the prize exhibit being the candy-pink number worn by Holly Lewis' Louisa. It not only decorates her, it deliciously defines her, as she pouts and minces about the stage, weighing up the pluses and minuses of erotic surrender and never really surprised by anything. In herself, she makes the show worth seeing.

Her spouse, though, almost makes it worth missing; Brian Marler plays Theo as a roaring, stomping bully, and has to work uncomfortably hard at it. It seems wrong for him, and it's wrong for the character; Theo, even in this coarsened version, is a complacent tyrant who takes his own authority for granted. He's the linchpin in what Sternheim planned as the first instalment of a comic epic about the German bourgeoisie, and the end of the play finds him comfortable enough to contemplate (and he's very contemplative, in a smug way) starting a family. I don't want to give anything away, but the sequel shows Theo's and Louisa's son, Christian, as an ace social climber, watched from the sidelines by his doting parents. That play is called The Snob.

Louisa finds herself the victor of her wooers' hang-ups. One, a self-styled poet, would rather write odes about his passion than consummate it; Evan Buliung makes him a farouche artist in narcissism, in what amounts to an amusing reprise of his performance of On the Twentieth Century. By contrast, Dylan Trowbridge, also on leave from the Shaw, breaks new ground as his rival, a timorous barber (Jewish, which allows the adaptation further leeway in the matter of mordant comic prophecy), so jealous of the poet that any passion for the lady melts into second place.

The actor shows an unsuspected talent for physical comedy and gives a splendidly uninhibited account of a deeply inhibited man; he's always been good at internalized neuroses, but now he shows he can externalize them as well. Kate Lynch gives an aptly gloating account of the confidante, and William Webster makes a welcome if belated appearance as Theo's ideal lodger, a puritanical monarchist. There is also a kind of deus ex machina (by definition, an ever tardier arrival), an invention of the adapter's, and one that shows him striving his hardest to be funny. The role is played by yet another good actor, Christopher Morris, who seems singularly ill- suited to it.

Cloran, one of our best young directors, apparently chose the piece to test himself in farce. He passes -- after the sloppiness of just about everything else we've seen recently, the discipline of this show comes as a tonic. All the same, just to clinch the case, I'd like to see him attempt a whole-hearted example of the genre -- a Feydeau or a Ben Travers or something American -- rather than this hybrid. By all means see this adaptation, unless you're a real purist, either about farce or (somebody must be) about Sternheim, in which case -- wait for the real thing.

Black & White Photo: Daryl Cloran, Berkeley Street Theatre / "I just made you say underwear!" From left, Evan Buliung, Holly Lewis and Dylan Trowbridge in The Underpants.

THE PRODUCERS

Canon Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - The film The Producers was a satire; the stage show is a celebration. Partly it celebrates the movie, and the myth that it has turned into in the 35 years since its creation. But most of all it celebrates the great gleaming entertainment machine that used to be the American musical, and in so doing gets it up and running and funny again. That makes it something for us, the public, to celebrate as well. Also something for us, the local public, to be proud of, as the performance by this Canadian cast is top-notch. They may not want our help in rebuilding Iraq, but theyd be dumb not to let us help them rebuild Broadway.

Let me, as if we were two characters in an exposition, inform you of what you undoubtedly know: Mel Brooks conceived and wrote The Producers, and it concerns two impresarios -- the veteran Max Bialystock and the neophyte Leo Bloom -- who raise millions more than necessary to produce a musical called Springtime for Hitler in the expectation that it will close on opening night and they can disappear with the balance. (The show wont run; they will.)

Sean Cullen plays the overbearing Max ("the man who invented Theatre in the Square -- nobody had a good seat"), a role for which neither his voice nor his personality are large enough. He rolls his eyes very expressively, though, and a spot of ad-libbing late in the evening gave hope that he will loosen up as the run proceeds. Michael Therriault is magical as Leo, the inhibited accountant who first attracts Max's attention by spotting a lacuna of $2,000 in a Broadway show capitalized at $100,000. (Oh yes, the time is 1959.) Therriault has done musicals at Stratford, but we know him best as a classical actor. He establishes the character immediately, as an adorable tussle-headed bundle of neuroses. But it's in song and dance that this Leo blooms -- first venting his fantasies, with soft shoe and ringing tenor, in I Wanna Be a Producer, just one guy and a chorus line; then succumbing to the attentions of a pneumatic, Amazonian Swedish showgirl in a number euphemistically titled That Face, which involves a lot of bobbing up and down behind sofas. This is a twist the movie never gave us: Leopold Bloom Gets Laid.

Apart from taking to the medium like one born to it, Therriault appears to be creating his own character while his colleagues look as if theyre faithfully following tracks that were laid down three years ago in New York. Many of them, though, do it with a skill and panache that might just as well be original: Paul OSullivan as Franz Leibkind, chicken-raising Nazi author of the worst play ever written; Juan Chioran imperiously swish as director Roger De Bris, also the certified worst, whose personal and professional credo is Keep It Gay; Sarah Cornell, six foot four of Scandinavian delight (That Face, That Body, That Accent); and the burly Steve Ross, who appears every five minutes in a different costume. And the ensemble singing and dancing are marvellous.

Susan Stroman directed and choreographed the show; Robin Wagner designed the sets, and William Ivey Long the costumes. They are Broadway's current A-team, the people who get called for everything. Stroman's direction (her first) keeps the show moving and also knows when, briefly, to let it breathe. She also delivers her best comic choreography, whose wonderful mad touches include a chorus of chickens shaking a wing to the music or, in one extreme case, extending it into a Nazi salute. She gets nuns dancing the hora, which must be a first, and repeats her trademark device of bringing on the girls from unlikely places -- in Crazy for You they poured out of a car; here they emerge from a row of filing cabinets. She even finds an equivalent for the climactic overhead shot in the movie that showed us the Springtime for Hitler chorus line in swastika formation; I wont give away details except to say that it involves Wagner (the designer, not the composer) paying homage to his own famous tilted-mirror set for an earlier Chorus Line.

Brooks book, in collaboration with Thomas Meehan, follows his screenplay very closely (all the funniest jokes derive verbatim from the film), except in the closing sections, which are the weakest. He also wrote the score, which of course incorporates the two songs that were in the picture. Springtime for Hitler itself remains the best; apart from the insouciant outrageousness of the words (winter for Poland and France) the tune has an insane Hollywood-Viennese lilt that's absolutely right. Brooks is not an outstandingly original composer (Prisoners of Love, the other movie holdover, slithers into Bill Bailey Won't You Please Come Home within seconds, and I would like to set a tune detective on most of the newer numbers), but there is an unassumingness about his pastiches that gets them by; this score, unlike most that try to recreate the Golden Age, is not soulless. It benefits greatly from Doug Bestermans orchestrations, which sound as if he had a ball. And the 1940s vocal harmonies in Springtime are killers. My favourite new song, partly because of OSullivan's dynamite performance, is Fritz's Haben Sie Gehort Das Deutsche Band?, which is in a mode that might be called Swingkraut and sounds like something a very young George and Ira Gershwin might have knocked off while no one was listening. Brooks music is, surprisingly, more interesting than his lyrics, which race along all right but are good-humoured rather than actually funny. In a song like Where Did We Go Right? (the producers are ruined because Springtimes a hit) the punchline is given away in the title, though there is one couplet folded in there that made me laugh: "Oh, we knew we couldn't lose/Half the audience were Jews."

The show The Producers is far gentler than the film. This is partly because the movie Max was Zero Mostel, who could be threatening even when benevolent -- especially when benevolent. It's partly because the show is a full-blown musical; Max and Leo have numbers and are thus endearing. But mainly it's because the movie itself exhausted all the shock value there was in the material. The show is nostalgia for the film. Camp is a loaded word in connection with Nazis, but having had its harmless fun with Hitler, the show is permitted to divide women into young nymphomaniacs and old nymphomaniacs, and -- while being itself the most heterosexual of musicals -- to bring the rest of the genre out of the closet in Keep It Gay. (This, by the way, was once the presumably innocent title of a song by Rodgers and Hammerstein.) None of this is especially incendiary, but if there had been no movie and The Producers had appeared in 2001 as a totally new show, I doubt that they would have been allowed to get away with it. But they have, as Max and Leo did, and we can feel happy for it. "If you've got it," sings Ulla the sexpot Swede, "flaunt it." They have, and they do, and we love it.

Black & White Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / Sean Cullen and Michael Therriault play more endearing versions of Max Bialystock and Leo Bloom in the stage version of The Producers than their counterparts did in the film.

This has been a miserable year in the Toronto theatre. In terms of new Canadian work from established writers, it was frightening. We had Adam Pettles Mosley and Me, unambitious and mildly disappointing; Florence Gibson's Home Is My Road, ambitious and seriously disappointing, and Jason Sherman's Remnants was panoramic and the only play of the year to be both funny and moving on any kind of scale. It gives me no pleasure to say any of the above, but the truth is the truth.

Otherwise there wasnt much. Susan Coyne, who has been coming into her prime as a character actress, has also been making stealthy advances on the profession of playwright, progressing from translator to collaborator to TV scriptwriter to adapter of her own childhood memoir Kingfisher Days. This was charming, as was her own narrating performance in it; next step awaited with interest. Another actor, Matthew Edison, made a promising writing debut with The Domino Heart, a series of linked monologues: a reasonable way to start though not, one hopes, the way that hell go on. Yet a third actor-playwright (we grow them here), Chris Earle, gave us Russell Hill, a portentous revue with a stunningly persuasive, not to say versatile, subway-platform set. From Montreal, Carole Frechette's Helen's Necklace was one of those ultra-sensitive pieces that make me wish I were home with a book.

Most of these plays were stuck in their own past or present back yards. So it was a relief when, at the end of the year, two plays turned up with, by our standards, exotic settings and resonating themes. Tiger of Malaya, about Japanese war crimes trials, was no masterpiece, and Bhopal, about murderous multinational malfeasance in India, was weak and muddled in both writing and production, but their stories at least set the adrenalin running.

Im not claiming things are much better elsewhere, though the ever-accumulating backlog of foreign plays makes it hard to be sure. (When are we going to catch up with the Tom Stoppards and Terry Johnsons?) The American This Is Our Youth (Kenneth Lonergan) and the English Blue/Orange (Joe Penhall), both given good Canadian productions this year, were lively evenings but in familiar moulds: the nihilistic teenage play, the mental-hospital power-play. (The latter is actually an ingenious melding of social and generational conflicts, doctor-patient crossed with doctor-doctor.) One sat through both crossing off their good points but without surrendering. And they were the best. We saw nothing else from the U.S. except the documentary Laramie Project, in which content again trumped form. The British import (or touring stopover) Scaramouche Jones offered a fine, gentle solo performance from Pete Postlethwaite but little else; it was an essay in the sentimentalization of once-disturbing themes; no wonder it was a hit. Peter Shaffers Amadeus, an earlier example of the same kind, was revived by Canadian Stage, and so imaginatively, under Morris Panych's production, that one almost forgot to question it's being done at all. Maybe it was to keep us up to date with Shaffers revisions; he is a tireless rewriter, and most of his changes here were for the better.

Panych at CanStage also directed the musical highlight of the year: A revival of Stephen Sondheims Sweeney Todd with a worthy performance by George Masswohl and a wonderful one by Fiona Reid. For size and power, this was the highlight of the Toronto year. (It even compared favourably with the COC production of the Peter Grimes that may partially have inspired it.) This year's Dora Awards reached a new plateau of irrelevance by denying prizes to Sweeney while heaping them on a smaller homicidal musical Little Mercy's First Murder, which was passingly stylish but cumulatively monotonous. It derived prestige of course from being done at Tarragon, which gets automatic respect, rather than at CanStage, which never gets any. Next years jury, obeying this rule, may even give musical prizes to Karen Hines Hello...Hello.

Actually, the best new small Canadian musical of 2003 was the hole-and-corner This Must Be Love, traditional in wit and style but innovative in thought, with honourable mention for the determinedly oddball Tequila Vampire Matinee which blew up quite a storm once it got started. Though here's a rule for aspiring musical makers: don't make fun of the form -- certainly not in your preliminary pronouncements -- until youve mastered it.

For sustained fun we had to wait, as usual, for the summer, when the classical companies get going. Soulpeppers revival of Harold Pinter's No Man's Land was the show of the year, something to make you purr with delight. The coup of getting William Hutt back on the Toronto stage was matched by the sublime wit and craft of his performance, which in turn was complemented by Peter Donats self- transformation and his antagonist, and by the sheen of Albert Schultzs production. Beckett's Happy Days, with Martha Burns, was nearly as good. The other new shows weren't. Phedre, staged by Daniel Brooks, was an imaginative raid on the near-impossible, but Nancy Palks performance looked increasingly like a fine actress beating up on herself. Schultzs She Stoops to Conquer tried much too hard to be funny. A word for John Neville's emrbyonic Classical Conspiracy, whose Ibsen readings pointed out peaks still to be scaled; Soulpepper's choices are getting dangerously cosy.

The Shaw Festival, under its new director, Jackie Maxwell, had an up-and-down year. I liked Maxwells own production of Three Sisters, with its use of a wide stage to emphasize loneliness, and applaud her courage in mounting a newish Canadian play, Michel-Marc Bouchards uneven The Coronation Voyage, though I can't really blame the tourists who stayed away: What's in it for them? These were the departures; other shows fell into the established categories. Shaw himself was decently served by Joseph Zieglers production of Widowers Houses, though I found it less revelatory than most, and by Misalliance, which sometimes seemed to succeed in the teeth of its director, Neil Munro. Blood Relations was a good home-bred alternative to the traditional English thriller (production better than play) and the two musicals could hardly have been more contrasted or, in their own ways, more ambitious: On the Twentieth Century, a dauntingly coherent comic opera, and Happy End, which survives on its Brecht-Weill songs and nothing else. I also had one of the best hours of my life at a reading, directed by Christopher Newton, of Cole Porter's blessed musical, Jubilee.

Stratford came in for some belabouring: I'm not sure why. They gave us Sartre and Aristophanes, even if they didnt seem to know what to do with them, and Aeschylus and Giraudoux, whom they got very right. The home-grown House of Atreus -- one story from three authorial points of view -- was a triumph. There were first-rate productions of Troilus and Cressida and Pericles, and good ones of The Taming of the Shrew, Antony and Cleopatra and Loves Labour's Lost. The Swanne trilogy continued on its infuriating and fascinating way. Only the musicals were confounding; I doubt that Stratford needed either The King and I or Gigi, except financially, and I'm certain it didnt need them both in one season. For boulevard theatre at its best, though, you could hardly beat Brian Bedford in Present Laughter. Stratford still offers our best display of actors: Peter Donaldson, Seana McKenna, Graham Abbey, Scott Wentworth, Diane DAquila, Jonathan Goad, Thom Marriott -- and Michael Therriault who limbered up at the festival for his Toronto appearance in The Producers, a show that, what do you know, damn near lived up to its hype.

robertcushman@lycos.com

Where The Producers is concerned, I may be part of the backlash against the backlash. I got caught up, just from reading about it, in all the excitement surrounding the show's smash opening in New York in 2001, and yearned to see it there immediately. When it became clear this wasn't going to happen, I began to develop a skepticism bordering on hostility, a feeling much enhanced by the production's clean sweep of the Tony Awards. The number that was performed at the Tonys didn't look too hot on the small screen, and anyway there had to be something wrong with a show that won all those prizes.

Besides, Mel Brooks wasn't a real composer and this had to be an ersatz score. I lost interest in catching up with the show once its original cast had departed. I knew it would be done in Toronto sooner or later, and if I was going to see replacements, I decided I would wait for them to come to me. (I think, as things have turned out, I was right about this.) I also virtuously refrained from listening to the CD, in the belief that when you do hear a score in the theatre for the first time, you ought to hear it fresh. (I was right about that, too.) Anyway, it took the better part of three years for The Producers to get here, and that made it seem like the day before yesterday's news. I didn't expect it to be bad, exactly, but I didn't expect it to be wonderful either.

In the theatre as elsewhere, low expectations frequently turn out to be justified, but there are times. ...

I was delighted, by the sheer fun and confidence of the thing, from the moment the curtain went up; actually, from before the curtain went up, since this show has an energizing overture. When did you last hear an overture at a musical? When, come to that, did you last see a curtain? By mid-point of the second act, I had surrendered. (Just as well, since it's at this point that the show, its plot line diverging from that of the original movie, takes something of a dive.)

Brooks' music may not be on the highest level, even as pastiche, but it has sparkle and versatility. It sounds right in every style it attempts, and at each point of the story that it serves. Maybe at this point it takes an inspired amateur to write a traditional showbiz score and do it with love; the professionals, hacks and geniuses alike, have moved on to other things. The score and the show have got under my skin. The thought of them, the sound of them (I have now played the CD) make me smile. I went back last week for a second look and, away from first-night pressures, enjoyed it even more. In the leading role of Max Bialystock, the understudy was on. I can't claim it was a star-is-born occasion: Steve Ross, who normally -- and excellently -- plays half-a-dozen minor roles, sings better than Sean Cullen, for whom he stood in, but is no great comedian. Actually, there are running gags in the script that neither he nor Cullen has brought off. But this is obviously one of those shows that work whoever's in them.

Not that I would want to be deprived of Michael Therriault -- his frame, as in a Hirschfeld drawing, seemingly reduced to arms, legs and top hat -- going through his I Wanna Be a Producer number, accompanied by a bevy of chorus girls, every one of whom, including the Bette Midler look-alike on the end, is taller than he is. The actor's joy in executing Susan Stroman's choreography fuses with the character's at bursting out of his shell. So contagious is the expression of this Leo Bloom's desire to be a producer "with a hit show on Broadway" that one loses sight momentarily of the fact that what he and his partner Max are actually shooting for is the mother of all Broadway flops.

Which brings me to a flaw in The Producers -- a tiny flaw, perhaps, and insignificant in the great scheme of things, but someone has to point it out. The story, in its stage version, doesn't make sense.

It did in the film, sort of. It all boils down to what they do to Springtime for Hitler, the title song of the certified worst play in the world. Now it's unclear, in both versions, whether Franz Liebkind, the play's pigeon-raising Nazi author, actually planned his masterpiece as a musical or whether that's just something that is done to it by the terminally camp director Roger de Bris. We never learn either what was in the piece apart from its famous title number, or just where in the evening that number was supposed to occur. In the movie it seems to be the first-half closer; in the show it's apparently both the finale and the first appearance of the leading character, which suggests Liebkind was indeed quite the master of dramatic construction.

Anyway: In the movie, the theatre audience sits through the number in exactly the kind of frozen horror on which Max and Leo are banking. Then on comes LSD, the actor cast as Adolf, who, stoned, departs from the text and calls everyone "baby." This incenses Franz ("the fuhrer never said baby!"), and disarms both the audience and the critics, who decide the whole thing is a delightful spoof. You may think them rather easily amused, but at least the film is trying for some kind of cause and effect.

There is no LSD in the show. Franz himself is cast as Hitler, having won the role with his knockout rendition of what remains my favourite number, Haben Sie Gehort Das Deutsche Band. Franz apparently is Herr Broadway; he must have spent his refugee time in New York sneaking into the balcony of every musical in town. "That's our Hitler," shouts Max, understandably on one level, perplexingly on another; didn't he want someone bad? We'll never know, since Fritz has a mishap on the first night, and is replaced by Roger the director, who stops the show. This time, a star is born. (Boy, in Juan Chioran's performance, is he ever.) But Roger's performance is absolutely of a piece with Roger's production, and we can only assume the audience loves both. So Max and Leo are defeated, not by fate, but by their own incompetence at assembling even the elements of a flop. Which, after all the buildup, is less interesting.

Maybe the show is making a savage comment on the tastes of Broadway audiences; though in fact circa 1959, which is when it's set, hit musicals tended to be good. (Some of them were even funny, in a way that The Producers itself is the first show in years to revive.) More likely, Brooks and his colleagues are trying to have their kuchen and eat it. The rest of the show bears this out. Max, Leo and Franz go to jail, and put on a show there, Prisoners of Love. In the movie this was just another scam. On stage, it's the prelude to another Broadway hit, starring, and presumably directed by, the same Roger de Bris. Logically it would be just as bad as Springtime for Hitler (which presumably is still running, though with God-knows-who in the lead) and it would bomb; that kind of freak lightning doesn't strike twice. But at this point all the show cares about is sending us away happy.

And it does. There are a few gestures toward post-Chicago cynicism ("It ain't no myst'ry,/If it's politics or hist'ry./The thing you gotta know is,/Ev'rything is show biz.") but the stage Producers, unlike its cinematic forebear, is a feel-good entertainment. Whatever shock value there was in the idea of singing and dancing Nazis has long since departed. And maybe there's a kind of justice in that. There's a famous line attributed over the years to a variety of Broadway savants who were going through tryout hell: "If Hitler's alive, I hope he's out of town with a musical." Now here he is, in town in a musical -- a figure of fun in an especially Jewish example of a form that was virtually invented by Jews. It can hardly be a complete revenge, but it's a sweet one.

Kristen Thomson, already in line for being Toronto's favourite actress, clinched the title in March, 2001, when she appeared at the Tarragon Extra Space in the solo piece I Claudia. In this she gave three fine performances and one enchanting one, the last being as the title character, a lonely and indignant schoolgirl. She also -- who knew? -- wrote the piece herself, subsequently carrying off Dora Awards in both her capacities.

The first night was the most joyous I remember attending in Toronto, local girl making better than we could possibly have imagined; since then she has performed the show in Victoria, in Hungary and at World Stage, and she is now back with it again at the Extra Space (Dec. 30 to Feb. 8). We'd like of course to see her do something else, and even write something else. (She's also taken time off to have a baby. How selfish can a lady get?) Meanwhile, I Claudia remains a treat that everyone should enjoy. It lifts the heart just to see Thomson put on Claudia's mask: an icon already.

She is just one of the heavier hitters descending on Toronto theatres after the holiday lull. Talk about versatility: Ronnie Burkett -- actor, dramatist, director, singer and, oh yes, master puppeteer -- brings his latest piece, Provenance, to CanStage's Berkeley Street Theatre (opens Jan. 9). Burkett has just won the annual Herbert Whittaker/Drama Bench Award; this is administered by the Canadian Theatre Critics Association, and we done right. He is also, after Robert Lepage and the Cirque du Soleil, the Canadian theatre artist whose name means most abroad.

In the Tarragon main space, Judith Thompson directs her own new play, Capture Me (Jan. 6). The cast includes Soulpepper's Nancy Palk and the husband-and-wife team of Tom McCamus and Chick Reid. At the Passe Muraille Backspace, the admirable Randy Hughson and Jane Spidell make up the company of Tom Walmsley's Blood (Jan. 22), in which they play a brother and sister who are, apparently, more than usually tight-knit. Kate Lynch directs.

Martha Henry, first lady of Stratford and maybe of Canada, makes a rare Toronto appearance in Michael Frayn's Copenhagen at the Winter Garden (Jan. 7, at last.) Her colleagues in this multiple- award-winning English piece about war, nuclear physics and moral responsibility, are two Shaw Festival luminaries, Michael Ball and Jim Mezon, and Diana Leblanc directs. This show is a co-production from Ottawa's National Arts Centre and Halifax's Neptune Theatre, and won high praise in both places.

In Ottawa itself the NAC, under director Marti Maraden, stages Hamlet (Jan. 8). Tom Rooney, one of the young actors most esteemed by his peers, plays the prince, while a strong supporting cast includes Fiona Reid and Ben Carlson, two actors who to date have played criminally little Shakespeare, and -- with enough experience in that vein for seven -- Stratford's veteran of veterans, Douglas Campbell.

Campbell started his career long ago in Britain. This month brings to Toronto three great Britons (an appearance by any one of whom would be an event) in a single show: Vanessa Redgrave, Ian Richardson and Donald Sinden. Their vehicle is The Hollow Crown (Princess of Wales Theatre, Jan. 27); the anthology-chronicle of jovial skeletons in royal closets that has been a Royal Shakespeare Company standby since -- are you ready for this? -- 1961. (Which reminds me, the Toronto production of The Mousetrap closes this month.)

Restrospecting for a moment: I apologize for omitting Adam Pettle's Sunday Father from my survey of 2003, the more so since it was one of the best plays of the year. I should also have shed an angry tear over the enforced demise of duMaurier World Stage. This festival's last lineup included some work that was inept and some that was agonizingly boring, but it also brought us masterpiece productions from Poland, Belgium, South Africa (The Mysteries) and the United States (Glengarry Glen Ross).

And I have to pay a tribute to the late Alan Bates who, apart from his fine film career, was one of the best of the post-war generation of English stage actors. (He managed, in a peculiarly British fashion, to steer an even course between movie star and jobbing thesp.) Canada didn't see him at his best; he was miscast in a dull production of The Master Builder that came to the Royal Alex a few years ago, and -- at Stratford in 1967 -- seems to have been a low-key Richard III and (in The Merry Wives of Windsor) a forced Ford.

He was a great ironic actor -- savage or tender, depending -- rather than a heroic one, and also a man with great historical timing -- he was in the original productions of no less than three epoch-defining British plays. In John Osborne's Look Back in Anger he was Cliff, the stoical best friend; in Harold Pinter's The Caretaker he was Mick, the flash, menacing brother; in Simon Gray's Butley he was, finally, the protagonist, the seedy academic falling apart. He was even better as the shiny-smooth protagonist of Gray's subsequent play Otherwise Engaged. Like Albert Finney, his classmate (the word "class" applies here in both its senses) and contemporary, he kept getting better as he got older. He won a Tony for his last stage appearance, in Fortune's Fool, after Turgenev. I wish we could have seen it.

2004-01-05-the-performances-critics-tend:
robertcushman@lycos.com

The theatre can do without theatres; actors, in the last resort, can act in open spaces. It can also do without playwrights; actors, if forced, can make up their own lines, sometimes as they go along. And God knows, directors are expendable.

Actors, though, cannot be got rid of. Plays that do without them have occasionally been written. Two examples that come to mind, oddly enough with almost identical titles, are Breath by Samuel Beckett (running time: approximately one minute) and Breath[e] by our own Steve Lucas. But the idea is unlikely to catch on. In the end, a theatrical event depends on just two sets of participants: a group of people doing it and another group of people catching them at it.

For all that, actors are neglected. True, they get applause, adulation, sometimes even money, but they also get taken for granted. The Siminovitch Prize, the most lucrative theatrical award in Canada, has now been given in successive years to a director, a playwright and a designer. This year the same cycle starts all over again, with no hint of recognition for the people who have to get up there and make the shows happen.

Harley Granville-Barker -- who was, successively and successfully, actor, director, dramatist and scholar -- declared in the last of those incarnations that "the art of theatre is the art of acting, first, last, and all the time." Critics, even if they pay lip service to this fact, tend to give precedence to playwrights and directors, whose work is easier to intellectualize and, very often, easier to describe.

Here, anyway, is my own attempt to make some amends: a list, more or less chronological, of the performances -- and, sometimes, groups of performances -- that most thrilled and delighted me, in and around Toronto, in 2003. It omits some that were highly praised in other quarters, but it is, all the same, substantial. We are living in a climate of good acting.

- Most blazing supporting performances: Yanna McIntosh in Phedre; Sara Topham in Agamemnon

- Blazing (and witty) supporting performance: Montego Glover in Cookin' at the Cookery. Honourable mention: Juan Chioran and Paul O'Sullivan in The Producers

- Welcome visitor: Elaine Stritch (at Liberty)

- Most pleasant surprise: Nora McLellan in Blood Relations

- Most scandalously underused performer: Jennifer Phipps, the best actress in Canada (seriously), and a long-serving member of the Shaw Festival company, but whose only role last year was the minor one of Anfisa, the nurse, in Three Sisters. As always, she brought a world -- the world of the play -- on stage with her, unforcedly filling out every moment of her character's progress and connecting all the dots. Do you remember the moment in Shakespeare in Love when the hulking Jim Carter, as the actor playing the nurse in Romeo and Juliet, was asked what the play was about and replied "well, it's about this nurse"? When Phipps was on, Three Sisters was a play about this nurse.

Until Feb. 8. Box office: 416-531-1827.

CAPTURE ME

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

The title of Judith Thompson's new play is mysterious, as is a fair amount else. At a guess, Capture Me is an unspoken invitation issued by Jerry Joy, the play's heroine and a junior kindergarten teacher, to Dodge, the older man to whom she was married for seven abuse-riddled years and who now seems set on reclaiming her. He has come back into her life with the threat, largely unspoken but understood by both of them, that he will at some point kill her.

Jerry is making other, and perhaps more conscious, claims on the possessive instincts of at least two more people. One is Aziz, an Arab refugee whose unseen daughter is one of her pupils. Dodge is not the kind of man who needs a pretext for jealousy, but if he were, the evolving relationship between Jerry and Aziz might provide one, though it remains platonic. Aziz, who is much shocked by Western manners and morals, would countenance nothing else. Jerry, adopted at birth, has also just discovered the identity of her biological mother, a doctor named Delphine, and has been making silent phone calls to her, leaving Delphine to fear that she too is being stalked. When Jerry finally finds the courage to declare herself, Delphine declares herself touched and pleased but unwilling to meet. She is in fact dying of cancer.

The remaining member of the play's group is Minkle (Thompson's characters have the most picturesque names), Jerry's friend and colleague, as outspoken, especially about sex, as Jerry is reserved, and the one person whose help and advice never has to be solicited. She is an unusually cheerful character for a Thompson play, though she has her own lurking demons. The others are fully paid up denizens of an inferno that seems made up, in equal measure, of Toronto now and the good old human condition.

Some of the writing has the power one expects from this writer, and some has a charm one doesn't, notably a scene in which Jerry instructs Aziz on the proper etiquette at a Canadian child's birthday party. About a third of the way through, the parts seem to be shaking into a coherent, and potentially fascinating, pattern. Jerry and Aziz seem to represent the innocence and fragility of human happiness, and Dodge, who explicitly compares himself to Iago, is everything that threatens it. But the moment passes, or rather it's prolonged without effective action to sustain it.

As Delphine, Nancy Palk has a fine first-act speech, brilliantly delivered, exploring her own conflicted reactions after hearing from her daughter. She's a soul in fear, hiding within an eroded shell of professional capability. But the second half finds her telling a story of childbirth and comparing it, at great length, to an exploding volcano. Note, she doesn't say it is a volcano; she says it's like a volcano. It was said long ago that metaphors are dramatic, similes aren't; and this one, a self-conscious slab of Fine Writing, just about eats the play.

The biggest flaw, though, is the failure to develop the relationship between Jerry and Dodge; it just keeps being restated. We do get to see how it started. Dodge was Jerry's professor, and she appears in flashback in his office, protesting that his teaching has offended her religious susceptibilities. Talk of the devil. She does, and it arouses him, which in turn fascinates her. Randi Helmers, all blond Nordic idealism, is even better at playing the young Jerry than she is at playing the sadder-but-wiser figure of the main action. Tom McCamus does glamorously Satanic very well but his role really consists of just two scenes, endlessly repeated. He is the sexy psychopath, repeatedly cropping up to terrorize Jerry, and he is the acknowledged sinner, lecturing a class of delinquents on the crimes for which they have been condemned and of which he knows himself to be guilty. These tracks run endlessly in parallel; they never converge.

Michael Dean Wint gives a sweet account of Aziz, though the character is irritatingly idealized, and even more irritatingly vague. We're never even told which country he comes from. Jerry isn't told either; indeed she says she never even asked. This is plain unbelievable. (Some of the romantic interludes between the teacher and the immigrant had me yearning irreverently for the comic treatment Zadie Smith gave to the equivalent relationship in White Teeth.) Aziz only develops complexities after he's left the scene, promising "to do what must be done." The more cynical characters suggest he's gone home to wreak vengeance on the men who killed his family. So maybe Jerry has fallen for two violent men in succession. Or maybe she hasn't; maybe they're opposites. There's a tableau in which Dodge and Aziz both appear silent at the back of the stage that could mean anything.

As Minkle, a Thelma in search of a Louise, Chick Reid grabs every opportunity she's given. But, good though the actors are, they all hit false notes on occasion, as when they break up their overwrought lines with the kind of melodramatic pauses that have nothing to do with real-life patterns of speech and little, I fancy, with real- life patterns of thought. What they do have to do with are memories of other actors' acting. A less indulgent director might have ironed this out, but here the author is the director. She also, in her twin capacities, presents at least three scenes that may or may not be dreams. This may be a teasing ambiguity; it may, as I think, be simply confusing.

The idea, perhaps, is to show that Jerry, in ironic contradiction of the title, has at least the potential to be mistress of her own fate. So probably she has, but in the play she remains a victim, not of other characters but of her author. There seems no reason other than dramatic convenience for the authorities to be unable to protect her, especially as she shows no inclination either to return to Dodge or to apologize for him. There seems no reason for her mother to be dying, or indeed to be making long speeches about volcanoes, except that both circumstances fill out what comes to seem like a willed vision of darkness. The play can sometimes evoke terror; it doesn't explore it.

COPENHAGEN

Winter Garden Theatre, Toronto

- - -

TORONTO - Few theatregoers, I imagine, actually thrill in advance to the idea of a dramatized debate on nuclear physics, especially one in which two of the three participants are genius scientists who left to themselves would probably be conversing in equations. But in Copenhagen, which reaches us six years after its London premiere, Michael Frayn brings it off, using the technicalities as both the springboard and the metaphorical armoury for an examination of motive and morality.

In 1941 Werner Heisenberg, probably the most brilliant German physicist of his time, visited his old friend and teacher Niels Bohr, Danish, half-Jewish, and living -- so far more or less unmolested -- in his occupied country's capital. Nobody knows what they said to one another, and their own subsequent testimonies are contradictory and inconclusive. It is, however, a safe bet that they talked about atomic weapons and about the prospects of either Germany or the Allies developing them. Heisenberg, who after all initiated the meeting, may have been asking Bohr for information, either political or theoretical, or he may have been trying to issue a warning, or he may have been requesting a kind of absolution from a man his fellow scientists called "the Pope": an implicit instruction not to help Hitler build a bomb. This last is the interpretation the play seems to find most interesting and, in the end, most persuasive.

It is also the most controversial. Heisenberg may not have been a card-carrying Nazi, but he remained in Germany and worked for the government. It is easy to think the worst of him. Frayn is unusual among playwrights in that he likes to believe the best of people, but he is also a comic writer, sometimes a satirist, and no pushover. Here, working like a scientist himself, he tests and retests the meeting, playing it out three times with different results. He also harks back and forth to Heisenberg's other visits to Copenhagen: in 1924, as Bohr's eager student and -- very quickly - - his favourite, and in 1947, when the two men met again, irreconcilable in post-war bitterness.

In a way, the play takes place in the present. The three characters -- Bohr, Heisenberg and Bohr's wife, Margrethe -- are all dead, and they review their lives, and especially this one incident, from some kind of limbo. This means they can be quite shameless about reminding one another, for our benefit, of what they already know. But then, how else are you going to spend eternity? Together or apart, the trio trade memories, excuses, recriminations and mathematical formulae as if there were no tomorrow, as for them of course there isn't. And as, Margrethe grimly suggests, there may be for none of us, thanks to "this wonderful machine" her husband, a thoroughly nice man, made possible with his inspired discoveries in the 1920s.

Heisenberg says there are two things for which he is remembered: his visit to Bohr and -- his own great discovery -- the uncertainty principle. This concerns the movement of particles, but the play uses it as a bridge -- a facile but effective one -- to get at the uncertainty of human motive. Not only can we never be sure what other people think or want, neither can they. Heisenberg unquestionably impeded, probably prevented, the development of the German bomb by leading his superiors to believe it couldn't be done. He may have misled them, for reasons of conscience, or he may have been telling what he thought to be the truth because, as the Bohrs point out -- he gently, she caustically -- he hadn't done the sums. (Of course it didn't help that all the people who might have put him right were Jewish.)

Anyway, he spent the rest of the war working on uranium 235 in a cave (literally) with no hope of applying it practically -- i.e., destructively -- and in imminent danger of blowing himself up: pure research, pure happiness. Meanwhile Bohr, that nice man, having shared in the great evacuation of the Danish Jews to Sweden, proceeded to the United States and worked, in a small but supportive way, on the device that devastated Hiroshima.

Frayn was a journalist and then a novelist before turning to the theatre, and he continues to keep all three options open. He is not, I think, a natural playwright but he has turned out better than many who are. He sets himself huge technical problems -- reinventing full- scale farce in Noises Off, full-scale debate in Copenhagen -- and solves them. The range seems effortless; a whole act of Noises Off is virtually silent while this play is nothing but talk. The chat is sometimes overwhelming, the characters dispensing information, technological or historical, faster than we can keep up with it. But most of the time Frayn's skill at weaving his tapestry is remarkable. Apart from the crucial meeting, the recurring threads, each reinforcing the others, include the memory of Bohr's son, drowned in a boating accident with his father helpless to save him; Heisenberg seeing his country brought to ruin by war, twice; his internment in England, where his kindly hosts bugged him as ruthlessly as the Gestapo might have done; the irony of good, or indeed bad, intentions. And time has been kind to the play if cruel to everything else. Anything that touches on lethal weapons and who might have the right to use them, or on the politics of occupation, strikes deeper now than it did in 1998.

Diana Leblanc's production, played with minimal furniture against a set of translucent screens, imposes some needless visual and musical flourishes. The lighting, though, is superb and both the placing and the orchestration of the actors first-rate. The performances themselves are even better than those in the admirable British original. As Margrethe, the judge and observer, Martha Henry is as watchable as she is watchful. As Bohr, Michael Ball finds a new use for his familiar bumbling-academic persona; Ball always seems to be padding inquisitively through his lines and the historical Bohr, endlessly modifying his utterances, must have done much the same thing. Bohr's strongest term of disapprobation is "interesting," and Ball wields the word like a self-sharpening knife.

Ultimately, though, the play is about Heisenberg, and it's Jim Mezon's performance that dominates, even when he sits with his back toward us, so that we focus on his bald head and protruding ears, a big man who might be asking for forgiveness or demanding justification; probably he thinks they're the same thing. Vocally he may hit the note of anguished perplexity too hard and too often, but he communicates an enormous amount through it. He is a man, or at least a consciousness, never at rest. Even though the play may settle for a sympathetic view of him, you sense that he himself could never settle -- in life or after it.

PHAE

Factory Theatre Studio

One of the less easily pronounceable titles of recent years, Phae turns out to be short for Phaedra. She was the mythical princess, wife of Theseus, who destroyed herself and others with her passion for her virginal stepson Hippolytus. The story was most famously dramatized by Euripides, who named his play after the boy, and by Racine, whose Phaedre is firmly centred on the woman. Now here comes a young Canadian actor and playwright, Julian Doucet, keeping the Racinian focus and the Euripidean scorn of romantic sub-plots; and setting the whole thing down in a contemporary Deep South trailer park. It works remarkably well.

Doucet plays Hippolytus, though his best acting moments come before the main action, as he talks about the Greek legends he has learned about in school. He gets to wondering what all them old gods might be doin' right now, on account of all the spare time they must have on account of not havin to listen to folks' prayers, what with nobody now believin' in them an all. The schoolteacher who set our heros mind working in this way is Miss Minerva, and Doucet is pretty smart all around with his classical references. Before marriage, his Phae was a Miss Judge; the original Phaedra was the daughter of Minos, who presided over the sentencing of the dead in the underworld.

The American South is a mythology in itself, and Doucet's cunning is that his white-trash characters are aware of this and of their own place in it. They read the tabloids; they watch daytime TV. And though having the hots for your stepson may rank fairly low on the Jerry Springer scale, it's enough to bother Phae. She may not be burdened by a queens responsibility toward her subjects, but she does care what the neighbours think. She seems noticeably less eaten up by guilt than her dramatic predecessors -- her fatal compulsion seems more like simple selfishness -- but her lust, fear and anger are real enough. The fear is both of her own passions, and of her husband, Big Daddy, king of the trailer park or at the very least of his own particular trailer.

The anger, as well as the lust, is directed at the unresponsive Hippolytus who gets on better with animals than with people and who likes to hang out in the woods dressed only in shorts. (He is one character who gets to keep his Greek name, though it turns out this is only because his late mother couldnt pronounce hippopotamus, which would have been her preferred pet name for him.) These people have size, even if the play looks at them cockeyed.

At the moment of unavoidable truth, Leanna Brodie's Phae lets out a feral cry worthy of her Racinian prototype. It's an inspired touch to have her afflicted by a (phantom) lump in her breast, which weighs her down as surely Racines Phaedre was crushed by her consciousness of tragic guilt. Instead of the nurse, Oenone Phae has for confidante and go-between, Una, proprietress of the local beauty salon. Caroline Azar in this role, like Brodie in hers, gets the best of both worlds; both of them are credible inhabitants both of their immediate society and of the long tradition that they have lately joined.

None of their colleagues brings this off, and the dreaded question "what for?" begins to haunt the evening. The play wants to have fun with the myth and the milieu, while simultaneously evoking the old tragic thrill; the subtitle "a trailer park trashedy," with its air of amused condescension, gives it away.

Daryl Clorans production is sure-footed with the drama and the blacker comedy, club-footed with the overt light relief. Doucet's young Tarzan is not very interesting in either the writing or the acting, and the chorus (Kimwun Perehinec and Tova Smith as a couple of gossips under the hair dryers) are downright tiresome. Nor does anybody, including Oliver Becker who plays him, seem sure just how fierce and fearsome Big Daddy is meant to be.

At only 90 minutes, the play in its later sequences begins to seem long. But the language is rich and the promise great; and both the concept of Phae and Brodie's execution of it a treat.

Them gods aint just stayin home bein' lazy; they's a usin all that free time to wreak havoc with human lives, just the same as they always did. And you know sumpn? With no more of them divine responsibilities to worry about, they's a-probably enjoyin' it more'n they ever did.

Black & White Photo: Factory Theatre / LEFT TO RIGHT: Caroline Azar, Leanna Brodie and Oliver Becker in the Factory Theatre production of Phae.

PROVENANCE

Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

Ronnie Burkett has a bad habit of making the rest of theatre look unnecessary. Not only is he a virtuoso puppeteer, he is also a playwright, actor and director able to stand comparison with any in the country. All these talents are on abundant display in his new piece, Provenance, which is uneven but unmissable.

Burkett continues to do wonderful things in the string-pulling line; he can make his marionettes waltz, skate (ice or rollers) or - - it sometimes seems -- blush. There is a bewitching delicacy about these puppets, even in repose; they have been carved for character. He gets some of his best and tenderest effects, though, when he abandons the strings and simply cradles his creations in his hands. There is a third convention, one in which he assumes a character by wearing him, her or it as a headband, but this is too remote, physically and emotionally, to be effective. There is an overall sense that, as far as simple puppetry is concerned, Burkett has been everywhere, done all of that and is now after other things. Or maybe it is we who, taking his mastery for granted, are looking for the other things. Either way, Provenance challenges both creator and audience simply as drama.

It even attempts poetic drama. He begins by setting three of his characters on little chairs and having them deliver intercut monologues in verse. This is asking more of us than is reasonable. It's the start of the show, we haven't yet adjusted to the physical scale, and its hard to focus on the words when you arent sure of the bodies from which they are supposedly issuing. Only one member of the trio grabs us from the outset, though all three prove crucial to the subsequent action. At least I think they do; the reappearance of one of them is so long delayed that I could only identify him through a process of retrospective elimination. I had almost no memory of what he had said.

The figure who springs to life proves, fortunately, to be the heroine. She is Miss Pity Beane, raised in a small Canadian town by her gay father and his companion. The latter, whom she calls Uncle Boyfriend, seems to have been her formative influence. Pity is a creation to rank with Mrs. Edna Rural, the sheltered housewife of Burkett's Street of Blood. Both of them are superficially inhibited ladies who keep surprising us and themselves with their reserves of strength and daring. Pity has grown up self-consciously plain and worshipping beauty, which she identifies with a painting that she found reproduced in a school library book. It's in pre-Raphaelite mode, and depicts a young man (androgynous in aura, like many of Burketts inventions, but technically male), bound to a tree in a glade like Saint Sebastian awaiting the onset of the arrows.

Pitys fixation on this picture leads her to art-history college, where she gives a presentation on it, fiercely defending her ideal of beauty, and indeed the whole unfashionable notion of beauty itself, against the scorn of the academy. This speech (in prose) is as good and funny as theatre writing gets, an overflowing torrent of intellectual passion mixed in with a kind of desperately innocent scurrility. "I'm not, she screams at her professor, even interesting enough for you to dismiss as beautiful"; think of all the warring ideas that line gathers up. (The unseen professor's name, by the way, is Turcott, which I take to be a mischievous homage to Iris Turcott, dramaturge both for Burketts Theatre of Marionettes and for CanStage, which is presenting the show.)

Pity, aided by a travel grant from the late Uncle Boyfriend, sets out to track down the original painting and determine its provenance: its physical and intellectual history. She locates it in a brothel in Vienna, whose proprietress is a glamorous aged lady named Leda. Leda is another of the soliloquizers we met when we came in, a woman whose sexual experience is as vast as Pitys is limited. She is even more loquacious than Pity and a lot less entertaining, affecting a style of Euro-worldliness Burkett embraces with excessive enthusiasm and at excessive length.

The provenance of Provenance seems to be an examination of the whole mystique of bodily beauty. Pity's virginity qualifies her for a single night as a sex worker (one client, specialized tastes) from which she emerges physically unchanged but emotionally enriched. Encouraged by Leda and others, she learns that ordinary can also be beautiful, which is just as well since it's what most of us have to get by on. Its a cheering conclusion, and -- as Pity more or less said to the professor -- I couldnt care less if it's sentimental. But I don't quite follow the steps by which we have arrived at it, and I dont understand, except in the vaguest way, what Leda herself has to do with it.

So Professor Turcott, or his literary-dramatic equivalents, would probably judge the play a failure. And so might I, if it werent for all the great stuff that crops up on the way. There are engaging subordinate characters, like Leda's tolerant husband (I was less keen on the philosophical monkey to whom he seems closely related), and an old American customer at the whorehouse, enamoured for decades of a black lady who looks like a Josephine Baker figurine and has the jazz-dancing chops to justify it. Pity has another tremendous speech that begins as an uproarious demolition of pretentious high-school dramatics and modulates into a searing account of pain and humiliation. I know that people have accused Burkett of wallowing in or exploiting violence, but they're wrong. He is, of course, by the very terms of his trade, a manipulator, but he is not manipulative. Compare Provenance to the recent Scaramouche Jones; that dealt in second-hand atrocity, this gives the real, newly imagined thing. Pitys pitiful story is matched by a long speech for a terrified young soldier in the First World War. This returns us to verse, a pounding verse, doggerel in metre but not in content, and delivered by Burkett with relentless power, horrified and horrifying.

He is of course onstage throughout, and his energy and concentration are amazing, keeping the show going even as he lovingly deposits its dramatis personae in spacious closets at the side of the stage; puppets, you feel, never had it so good. Burkett also sings, though I feel that the showbizziness of the numbers he did in Street of Blood suit his voice better than the dour morsels of Continental cabaret he has dreamed up here. (You probably have to dress up to sing songs like these; probably in what I cant stop myself from calling liederhosen.) Since there is no separate design credit, he must also have painted the painting and created the dollhouse-against-a-landscape that constitutes the set.

I would guess that Burkett attracts more passionate enthusiasm than any other theatrical figure in English-speaking Canada. I would also guess that it's justified.

RESTITUTION: AN IRISH-CANADIAN RHAPSODY

Factory Theatre, Toronto

A series of misadventures kept me from the opening of Restitution, but I could hardly avoid noticing a marked chilliness in the reactions of those colleagues who were present. Having caught up, I have to say I found the play less of a trial than did the other reviewers, and less long as well. They were complaining that the show had robbed them of three hours of their lives; on the night of my visit, it clocked in at a mere two hours twenty.

It remains a rum piece, and by its close a vexatious one. I also have no idea what kind of play it is trying to be. Consider this: The date is 1882, the place the Ottawa valley. There are two brothers, Stephen and Seamus, whom their late father brought to Canada from Ireland when they were both small boys. Now grown up (physically anyway) and with kids of their own, they enjoy a fraternal relationship which would be like that of Cain and Abel, except that both of them are Cain. Seamus begins the proceedings by dealing a fatal knock on the head to Stephens son James for the crime of touching Seamuss favourite horse.

James is an accomplished harpist who was all set to go to Toronto to study at the Academy of Music. When Stephen's wife hears of her loss she says what any Irish mother would say if her musically gifted boy had been snatched up to heaven: He's forgot his harp. I suppose thats a funny line, though I cannot imagine what the right tone would be for delivering it; in this production it comes out of nowhere.

I dont think it's appropriate to compare Michael O'Briens play to those of Martin McDonagh. Its true that O'Brien's characters tend, like McDonaghs, to be violent, vindictive and Irish, and that they say "feck" a lot, though not as often as McDonaghs do. But McDonagh's plays (pre-eminently The Beauty Queen of Leenane) are tightly plotted and well motivated. O'Brien merely tells a tale, which is his right, but doesnt it ramble.

I confess to bearing him a grudge for a politically correct version of Oliver Twist that he committed for the Young Peoples Theatre a few years back, but I also confess that he can write. His lines and speeches have rhythm. But his scenes don't, either in themselves or when placed against one another, and so neither does his play.

Stephen's wife commits suicide, obliging him, once the priest gets to hear about it, to dig her body up and remove it from consecrated ground. Seamus, though he does feel bad about some of this, seems to think he can pass it all off with a few apologies, though he later throws in some cash as well.

This turns out to be mistaken generosity; Stephen promptly hires three local nondescripts to hunt Seamus down and crucify him. He spends the rest of the money on moving to Toronto, in order to pursue a career as an author, which seems a bit arbitrary.

Eight years pass, and we find ourselves in the big city, still never encountering a soul who isnt from the ould counthry. This second act, as cheerfully bloody as its predecessor, might be Torontos answer to Gangs of New York, though, alas, without the spectacle.

Stephen writes and even sells idyllic stories about his beloved brother's untimely death, though the bottom falls out of this market when Seamus reappears. (Crucifixion is obviously not what it once was: I mean, we're not talking resurrection here.)

The feud is on again, despite the best efforts of Seamuss daughter, who was always a reconciler, and has now got her to a nunnery. This gives OBrien, at his lowest ebb, the cue for a few jokes about the habits that nuns get into under their habits.

Meanwhile, in the opposite corner, there is the ghost of Stephen's father (Seamus's too, of course, but he only appears to Stephen), a mountainous apparition who carries a chain. I initially took this, since the action takes place around Christmas, to be a jovial reference on the spirits part to Jacob Marley, but he turns out to have more personal reasons.

He was a mean old man, to put it mildly, who now claims credit for having, among other things, caused the great Irish famine, and he has terrorized his sons into being terrors themselves. All ends comparatively happily, for those still alive. One of them, probably speaking for the author, blames all the suffering on religion, or maybe its just Catholicism.

And sometimes the characters feel their pain like pain, and sometimes they don't; it seems to depend on whether the playwright, at any given moment, is after a laugh or a shudder. I can best describe the style as brutal whimsy. It's seldom actually dull, but if theres a way of making it theatrically coherent, Sarah Stanleys production hasn't found it.

The Factory here adds to its record of mounting the unsightliest shows in Toronto. Most of Carolyn M. Smith's set consists of a raised tilted disc; it might be an impressive ground for action, except that the cast are seldom allowed to act on it. Most of the time, they are huddled in corners at the sides. This is all right for the more soothing scenes, of which there are a couple, but most of the play is confrontation, and the actors have no room in which to square off. They look and sound unruddered. According to the program, the director is currently teaching at the National Theatre School -- not, I hope, on the uses of theatrical space.

Richard McMillan is an actor fully capable of either full- blooded melodrama or comically understated angst. As Stephen he seems to be switching at random between the two. As Seamus, John Dolan varies between a grizzled cackle and a grizzled moan.

Kelli Fox, in a variety of roles, comes off best, except when, for economy's sake, she dons a moustache and flat cap and tries to pass as a male desperado. Lisa Norton has only one role, but her character is so inconsistent that she too seems to be playing several. She does each of them well but cannot connect them.

As the dead da, Jefferson Mappin gets the play off to a tremendous start with a fine anecdote (misleadingly fine, as it turns out) about a bear. His barnstorming later gets monotonous, but he may not have any choice. The company is completed by Alon Nashman, a fine actor whom God probably never intended to play an Irishman, and certainly not, as here, half a dozen of them.

Black & White Photo: David Hawe, Factory Theatre / A RARE MOMENT OF SQUARING OFF: from left, John Dolan, Alon Nashman and Richard McMillan in Restitution: An Irish-Canadian Rhapsody.
