RAY JESSEL

Top of the Senator, Toronto

Ray Jessel -- he was Raymond Jessel then -- was the last man to write words to Richard Rodgers's music. He was brought in as a replacement lyricist on Rodgerss final show, I Remember Mama, in 1979. Before that he had collaborated with a Canadian composer, Marian Grudeff, on a Broadway musical about Sherlock Holmes. Before that, he and Grudeff were in Toronto, writing numbers for the well- remembered Spring Thaw revues. And before that -- well before that - - Jessel was growing up in Cardiff, Wales. He is, as he tells us in his cabaret show at the Senator, a Welsh Jew -- a rare ethnic species; unless we mate, were gonna die out.

Jessel, who is 73, took to performing at the piano a couple of years ago, doing his own material of course. These days he writes both words and music, usually with his wife, Cynthia Thompson, as co- lyricist. He has a thoroughly charming presence and, like most songwriters, very little voice, not that that matters; he knows perfectly how to pace and point a lyric.

He is a short, endearing man with wispy grey hair tied with a bow at the back that he musses when he wants to look like Albert Einstein. He does this in a number called I'm a Genius, whose rhymes are indeed ingenious, but which is not actually very funny, maybe because the premise on which it's based (Einstein as egomaniac) is not very persuasive.

Its almost the first thing he does, and I found myself with the same tepid response to its immediate successors: a spoof on songs about towns entitled Oxnard, a place he introduces as being two hours drive from Los Angeles (where he lives) or three if you're lucky; I'm All Right Now, a "serious" song which turned out to be yet another essay in the laughing-to-keep-from-crying genre whose classic is I Get Along Without You Very Well; and a Noel Coward parody, which gets the musical tone dead to rights but is way off on the lyrics. (They sound more like Paddy Roberts, a classically unfunny English songwriter of the 50s and 60s.)

All the same, Jessel is building huge likeability through these numbers, so when the good songs do start coming, they sound wonderful. One is That Old Kurt Weill Song, which gets Weill's Bilbao Song in a presumably affectionate hammerlock hold and pins it to the floor while also taking a savage detour in the direction of Surabaya Johnny (I'd like to cut your throat, Johnny/Cause you only sing one note, Johnny.) He can do French as well, as in Mon Amour, for which he dons a beret (which both suits and transforms him) and unwinds a magically disconnected succession of Gallic names and phrases. And then theres The Shakespearean Tragedy Rag (didn't T.S. Eliot once make mention of one of those?), which is not only hilarious but very sound on Shakespeare; and Life Goes On, a serious song that works and puts a fresh spin on the inconvenient human capacity for surviving heartbreak.

Mostly, though, Jessel's ballads are his weakest work, written in a torch-jazz style that seems to have been preserved in aspic from the 50s. Those songs, to put it bluntly, have all been written. Jessel, as he tells us in numbers like Whatever Happened to Melody, is a hopeless nostalgic or maybe, on the strength of I Want to Sing a Show Tune, a hopeful nostalgic. But I think hes got it wrong. The acknowledged fact that they're not writing them like that any more means that it's no longer possible to write them. This doesnt mean that writers who treasure the Broadway and Tin Pan Alley traditions have to surrender to rock or rap. It means they have to take the tradition and expand on it, as has been done by Stephen Sondheim and Cy Coleman and David Shire and the great Dave Frishberg (of whom Jessel sometimes reminds me) and as may be done, though its too soon to tell, by the latest generation of New York show-writers.

Jessel offers a couple of songs from a work -in -progress, a musical version of Moll Flanders entitled, as you might well guess, Moll; there's a pub rouser that might have come from Lionel Bart and a love song that might have come from anywhere -- Defoe's cynical matter-of-factness is not, I suspect, on this shows agenda. Jessel is joined on these and other numbers by our own Theresa Tova, a contrastingly overpowering (and much taller) performer: so powerful in fact that its sometimes hard to tell whether she's spoofing her songs or selling them straight.

I've left out a few treats: a song that knocks Cabarets Two Ladies into a cocked hat, and a satire of all songwriter retrospectives called And Then I Wrote, whose punchline is "and then I wrote And Then I Wrote: which is this song." Fairer than that he could not say. I may have qualms about some of Jessels material, but there's much I like; and the man himself is a modest marvel of showmanship.

WRITTEN ON WATER

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

Somebody in Written on Water, groping for the right expression with which to describe a piece of writing, says "it's so ... precious." The same word had been on my mind all evening, and not in any complimentary sense. Michel Marc Bouchards play takes us back to dramatic territory that we havent visited in decades, and that very few of us have missed.

It takes place in a long, high-ceilinged room in what may once have been an impressive house but is now a ruin. The windows have been blown in. Outside, a young man wanders, wearing what looks like a pair of angel wings. Inside, a bevy of much older people discuss life, love and the pains of senior citizenship.

The room, it transpires, is called the writing room. We are in a small town, recently devastated by a flood, whose elderly inhabitants used to gather together to share the literary records of their existence. These have now been washed away, and need to be reconstructed from memory. So, at least, thinks Samuel, who presides over the writing and reading circle. Some of the others understandably feel they may have better things to do with what remains of their time.

The mid-20th century was full of plays set in elegant and/or dilapidated residences in which cultivated people, in the shadow of cataclysm, convened to exchange attitudes and aphorisms. Jean Giraudoux and Jean Anouilh wrote them in France, and their disciples, Christopher Fry and John Whiting, in England. The fashion never really spread to North America, though. If any part of this continent were to be hospitable to it, that part would, for obvious reasons, be Quebec.

But things have changed. The tradition of wit, which is what kept those older plays more or less afloat, seems to have died out. Maybe it survives in Bouchard's original French, but there's little sign of it in translation. If people on stage are going to talk at, rather than to, one another for a couple of hours, the least they can do is be funny. The audience at the Bluma Appel was obviously waiting, in some desperation, for them to start.

The town, we learn, was in a bad way even before the waters broke. All the young people had left for more populous parts, with the exception of Danny, the one lurking outside with the appendages. (I still dont understand those.) He spends the first part of the play longing to be let into the writing room, and the second actually inside it and happy to be there. I think he didnt know when he was well off.

He seems to want life to be even more literary than Samuel would like to make it. "If only," he enthuses, we could actually become metaphors. It sounds like a terrible idea to me, but in a way Danny has got his wish. He and the other characters seem more like figures of speech than figures of flesh and blood. It's as if the incredibly annoying Biographer of Bouchard's The Coronation Voyage had taken over the whole play. Theres a whole thread of narrative about a missing cat. It seems to exist solely so that the old phrase about letting the cat out of the bag can, for a second, threaten to turn into a physical reality. Its the liveliest moment of the evening.

I'm far from sure that Bouchard endorses Samuel's preference for words over deeds. Some incidents suggest he doesnt. Two women in the group start a long-delayed relationship. A man and his wife insist on facing up to the facts of old age. Young Danny gets to make love for the first time -- or so he, at some length, tells us. There is a fairly bracing attack on the euphemisms that, in todays world, obscure actual experience. But the play settles into a recurring rhythm: People make gestures of independence; the patriarchal Samuel calls them to heel.

I can see that some interesting questions are floating around here. Can things be said to exist if they aren't written down? Does the composition automatically distort the event? Does plain writing beat fancy? Can literature survive?

There may even be some kind of allegory of Canada or Quebec, though the state-of-the-nation defence seems to me increasingly the resort of desperate dramatists and even more desperate critics; it can be applied to virtually any play.

I cannot speak for Bouchard's earlier plays but, of the recent ones, The Coronation Voyage was overblown, but told a substantial story. It even had suspense. Down Dangerous Passes Road was an anecdote gasping for significance. It went on about its characters pasts without ever giving them a dramatic present.

Written on Water has the same fault but worse. We are told, for example, that Samuel treated his late wife badly but are given no reason to care. The play is lifeless, punishingly so, and Micheline Chevriers production, though it has no technical faults that I could discern, fails to animate it.

As Samuel, David Fox is, as usual, massively, dangerously genial - - a quality that can be electrifying in a supportive context but seems arbitrary outside it. The others -- Jerry Franken, Barbara Gordon, Carolyn Hetherington, Doris Chillcott and, as Danny-come-to- judgement, Jordan Pettle -- are visibly doing their best but seem, as a group, to be fussing rather than feeling.

Franken, acting crotchety, probably comes off best, though he and Fox (how often have they acted together?) strike surprisingly few sparks off one another.

Bouchard at least makes stimulating demands on his designers. Judith Bowden responds with an appropriately lofty acting-chamber, dominated by a long and draughty wall that makes its impressive way to an upstage point, where it meets a shorter one. The room's third wall is as invisible as its proverbial fourth. So a presumably oblong space becomes, from the audience's point of view, a triangular one; its an old device but it usually works, and it does here. In all other respects, I think youd be better off at Restitution.

Theatre Passe Muraille Mainspace

BLOOD

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace

- - -

After a short break for renovations (new looks for lobby, box office and bar) Theatre Passe Muraille reopens its doors, both sets of them, with re-stagings of plays that have already been seen elsewhere in Toronto. Both are two-handers, depicting domestic partnerships in extremis.

Sean Reycraft's One Good Marriage was first seen at the Summerworks Festival. As often, a one-act play that must have knocked em dead in those crowded, uneven circumstances looks somewhat orphaned when asked to take up a whole evening on a main stage. Critics may not mind (we prefer short plays, especially in winter) but paying audiences may crave more quantity if not, on this occasion, quality.

That, though, is their affair. One Good Marriage is a well executed work. Its title is only partly sardonic. Stewart and Steph, its two characters, seem to be surviving, even though their wedding was the cue for a large-scale disaster. The exact nature of this catastrophe is not revealed until the end of the play, so I obviously have to shut up about it as well.

The two of them tell their story as if in front of some informal tribunal. They are colleagues as well as partners. Shes a teacher; he's the school librarian, though he has no taste for -- or presumably in -- books. ("It's not" he says of his job a book thing.) Grimly amused, they recall the washroom graffiti that were the kids acknowledgement of their relationship prior to tying the knot. They also tell about their honeymoon, a bad job (due to faulty booking arrangements) that they made the best of. Or, as they put it with bland expressions that come out barbed, "we got to know each other."

This talent seems to have stood them in good stead during their subsequent joint career as the innocent harbingers of apocalypse. Tragedy can kill a relationship, but it can also cement it. There are hints, in the ways Stew and Steph delicately but continually put one another down, that in other circumstances theirs could have been One Bad Marriage, maybe One Rapidly Failed Marriage. Now they seem to be in for the long haul, like those happily married couples in Strindberg or Albee.

Some of the writing is glib, as when a neighbour is described as kind of scary, in an anorexic-with-a-Honda kind of way. What kind of way would that be, exactly?

More damagingly, here is a built-in structural flaw. The plays vested interest in springing its final surprise keeps it at arm's length from the characters' interaction. We cant quite evaluate their reactions because we dont know what they're reacting to. The play's qualities as a thriller are at war with its qualities as psycholgical exploration, though both are real.

Both are excellently presented in Shari Holletts production, with fine performances by Jeff Miller (who looks like Kevin Spacey) and Mary Francis Moore; he is merry on the outisde and mean underneath, shes the reverse. Steve Lucas's set, one of those open- to-the-back-wall jobs they specialize in at Passe Muraille, isn't boring.

Ive been thinking about boredom, as people in my line of work naturally tend to. It may have got a worse rap than it deserves. It comes, after all, in varying intensities. There is the insupportable boredom that emanates from a really stupid, talentless play or musical, but we havent had one of those since ... well, for a few weeks. (There's no need to be gratuitously cruel.) There's the boredom tempered by grudging respect, as in Written on Water; something seems to be going on, even if its impossible to discern what. There is the boredom that may not actually exist but that we as an audience plead in self-defence, when a play thats deficient in all other respects stubbornly insists on holding our attention; think Restitution.

On the highest level, there's the boredom that periodically surfaces in a top-quality work like Ronnie Burkett's Provenance. This has passages that, by general agreement, dont work, but even those that do can exhaust our attention. Theres a long speech in Provenance that's moving, harrowing and superbly written and performed. Nevertheless, about two-thirds of the way through, my mind -- after duly acknowledging that it had been moved and harrowed -- switched off until the next thing came along. The scene went on being superb; it just did so without me.

And then there's the boredom of Blood. This seems to be due to a discrepancy between the intensity that the play itself keeps taking for granted, and the conviction of what actually happens on stage, not to mention the inherent limitations of the two-character play. Tom Walmsleys couple are brother and sister and -- as someone once said of the Jacobean sibling-drama Tis Pity She's a Whore -- the incest is sustained throughout.

Noelle, recently released after doing time for drugs, has an opportunity to make $500 if she can put up with an extra male for a threesome. The only partner she can come up with is her brother Chris, who has also been an addict but hasn't been in jail. He is, rather ostentatiously, trying to reform. (Once he wanted to go into the church.) Chris and Noelle have never had sex together, but it seems they both wanted to. The opportunities for dramatizing guilt, rage and tenderness are considerable, and are duly utilized.

This is one of those plays that will make most who see it feel they have led sheltered lives. There is therefore a considerable fallout of midddle-class guilt, which translates into a willingness to believe what were told. And yet, despite some high intensity in the writing, we dont.

Some of this may be due to the play's habit, endemic to duologues, of dropping the names of people we never meet. In One Good Marriage this doesn't matter; its a demonstration piece and we can be be given what information we need as we go along. Blood is naturalistic -- in structure, anyway -- and has to rely on hints.

The name that comes up most often is Martin, an evil genius (and former lover) in both characters lives. He's meant to inspire terror but, because we never get a chance to check him out, he doesn't. He doesnt work as an offstage Pinteresque menace either; were told too much about him, even if we're not told enough.

The play, which premiered 10 years ago at Factory, has a golden reputation, so it could be that Kate Lynch's production doesnt drive hard enough. Jane Spidell as Noelle starts it off with a terrific low-key monologue, but seems thereafter to be trying to be tough. When she answers the phone, she doesnt say "hello," she says "go." Spidell makes that sound terrifying, but she can't bring the same urgency to more extended passages; some recurrent technical flaws the night I saw her suggested she may not have made peace with the person she's playing.

Randy Hughson may be too easygoing and endearing for the circumstances. When he does occasionally snap into gear, he can be powerful. John Thompson's set -- high, deep and bare -- reminds again of the wonders that can be wrought in what seems, at first sight, one of Toronto's most limiting spaces.

I grew up with the Royal Shakespeare Company. I was in the English equivalent of Grade 9 when Peter Hall founded it in 1960, and my undergraduate years, 1963-66, coincided with the company's first glory period. So the RSC has been part of my life, and so have the four actors, all among its early pillars, who are now in Toronto performing The Hollow Crown -- a show that is itself an RSC institution, one that dates back to the company's very first year.

It may be eliding the truth to say that Peter Hall founded the RSC. What he did was take over the artistic direction of the Shakespeare Memorial Theatre at Stratford-upon-Avon, and radically expand it. He opened a London base at the Aldwych Theatre; he admitted non-Shakespearean plays, including new ones, to the repertoire; he tried to create at least an approximation of a permanent company. The Royal" tag was bestowed in 1961, thus creating a brand name that, in the words of another director, Bill Gaskill, had "everything going for it except God.

One of Halls appointees was a Cambridge don, John Barton, who had firm and fruitful ideas about the speaking of dramatic verse. Barton was to develop into one of the finest of all Shakespearean directors, but his initial encounters with professional actors were bruising. As a salve, in that first 1960 season, he devised and directed an evening of readings by and about the Kings and Queens of England": The Hollow Crown. Its first private showing was successful enough for it to be given a Sunday-night showing at the Aldwych the following year. The critics came, and raved. The show went into the main bill and has remained a standby ever since, suitable equally for school tours and the West End: cheap to mount, requiring no learning of lines and providing a showcase for company stars, actual or potential. The list includes the four who are doing it here, in what amounts to an RSC franchise rather than an official production; none of them has worked in a full RSC production for at least 20 years. The three men are still listed in programs as RSC Associate Artists, but this seems to be shorthand for "actors who are working somewhere else.

To take them in order of their first RSC appearance: Ian Richardson was in the original 1960 company, arriving in the middle ranks (billing was hierarchical in those days) after playing Hamlet at a major rep. Today this would be unthinkable: A young actor with that kind of credit would insist on playing star parts straight off or would go into TV, which is one reason why standards have declined. Richardson made an immediate mark playing fops and minor villains. From 1962 he was getting leads on the order of Oberon, Cassius and Coriolanus. One of the keystones of the Hall-Barton approach was an emphasis on the metaphysical wit of the language, and Richardson played this with exemplary relish and lucidity; he could also, when he turned on his high trumpet tones, be terrifying. It was an influential voice; you could hear RSC juniors doing unconscious imitations of it. Length of service had something to do with this; he is the only member of the current quartet who has acted before with all of his colleagues. He stayed, almost nonstop, until 1975, by which time his mastery of his means was exhilarating to watch. Since then, he has done little theatre, though his cold- blooded Prime Minister in House of Cards is about as classic as TV acting gets: a modern Richard III.

Vanessa Redgraves stature as a film and stage actress hardly needs comment. You might claim, though, that the RSC made her. In 1961 a West End appearance in Ibsen's The Lady from the Sea had established her as one of Britain's best young actresses, rather than just the daughter of the great Michael Redgrave. The same year Hall, always a greedy snapper-up of talent, needed a Rosalind (in As You Like It) at short notice. Redgrave -- apart from her unquestionably being, as the text prescribes, more than common tall" -- delivered a melting, magical performance, in a perfect production by the late and very fine Michael Elliott; for audiences of the right generation she will always be the Rosalind, just as her father will always be the Uncle Vanya. She stayed for another year, to do The Taming of the Shrew and Cymbeline, then left to conquer the world . Shes never been back, but the mark she left was indelible.

Donald Sinden arrived in 1963 as an actor dedicated to the theatre (hed started out at Stratford in 1945 and '46) but best- known as a light comedian in British films. He was eased in with a couple of supporting roles, then took the major one of the Duke of York in the great history cycle The Wars of the Roses, a performance in which you could feel the enthusiasm of an actor claiming his birthright. (The RSC discovered actors; it also rediscovered them.) He left but kept coming back: staking an undisputed claim as a grand master of Restoration comedy in The Relapse, playing a superbly funny -- and disturbing -- Malvolio in a Barton Twelfth Night that remains definitive to everyone who saw it; finally surprising everyone as one of the most powerful and moving King Lears of our time. Sinden has a sonorous instrument and formidable timing, tunable to both comedy and tragedy. He may also know more about theatrical lore and tradition than any other actor alive.

Alan Howard arrived last of the four in 1966 -- as a young actor known but not well-known -- and lit a fire almost immediately, playing a degenerate Renaissance princeling in The Revenger's Tragedy: for a new director, Trevor Nunn, and opposite Richardson, whose decisive break it also was. He was also the last to leave, staying until the early 80s. He, too, had a trumpet voice (lower register) and a great command of rhetoric; he was the broadsword to Richardsons rapier. He was an unmatched actor of heroes, Henry V and Coriolanus, who explored their insecurities without mocking their strengths. He also showed, in Wild Oats and The Forest, both plays about players, a delightful talent for self-satire.

All four of these actors, in different ways and at different times, helped define the RSC and its style; a style whose influence has now gone round the world. And all, incidentally, say they would like nothing better than to go back. And from what I've seen recently I think it needs them.

THE HOLLOW CROWN

Princess of Wales Theatre

This Royal Shakespeare Company standby contains only one piece of writing by Shakespeare. You might call it the title number or, since we hear it at the beginning of the evening, the overture. It's the famous speech in which Richard II invites his supporters to sit on the ground and tell sad stories of the death of kings, death being the ultimate mockery lurking inside "the hollow crown that rounds the mortal temples of privileged folk like himself. Ian Richardson, in the current version, delivers it like a virtuoso, packing enormous variety into a dozen lines. A light laugh accompanies the phrase all murdered." A mordant, threatening grandeur surrounds "the hollow crown itself.

It turns out to be a misleading introduction, since little else in The Hollow Crown -- a collection, assembled 40 years ago by John Barton, of prose and song by and about the Kings and Queens of England" -- carries comparable weight or even pursues comparable themes. For a start, Richardson and his distinguished compeers -- Vanessa Redgrave, Donald Sinden, Alan Howard -- never at any point sit upon the ground; they take their ease in handsome straight- backed chairs or, when the moment demands it, march downstage and address us standing up.

Then again, few of the stories they tell are especially sad, and not many have to do with the death of kings. The monarchs they chronicle, all the way from William the Conqueror to Victoria, did die of course, and sometimes the fact is mentioned, but a vital part of the Shakespearean equation is missing. The dramatic point is not just the contrast between celebrity and mortality; it's that these people had power, and with that power went responsibility, and that they were always agonizingly aware of it. Its what makes them dramatically interesting. Otherwise theyre just a collection of ordinary ladies and gents who led privileged lives and wore heavy head furniture, and the show is just gossip.

It does regain its dignity at the close, when it dips beneath the horizon of history and gives us the departure of King Arthur, as narrated by Thomas Malory. This has nothing to do with political reality, but it's potent myth about kingship -- and it's stirring. There are a few comparable moments on the way through. We get Redgrave as Mary Tudor, the "Bloody Mary who went on to burn all those Protestants, drawing a shawl awkwardly around her as if to give herself courage when outfacing a rebellion. (There is, I think, an implicit contrast with the celebrated and far more assured speech -- which we dont hear -- given by her sister Elizabeth, when mustering her troops at Tilbury: I know I have the body of a weak and feeble woman" and all that stuff.) She is equally moving as the condemned Anne Boleyn, protesting her innocence while the juggernaut of the Tudor succession rolls over her. There is Richardson as the absolutist Charles I, on trial for his life and confronting a judge (Sinden) who might as well be speaking a different language; a clash not just of character but of fundamental principle. The change to a constitutional monarchy may have been a giant step for mankind but it was a death blow to a certain kind of English drama. There has barely been a good play written about a British monarch since.

Most of The Hollow Crown is a grab bag, but even on those terms the best bits are generally the sad ones. The death of George IIs wife, as recounted by her physician, might equally well be the death of any woman, but Sinden delivers it with a gruff tact, edged by wit, that makes it very affecting. Most of the show, though, falls over itself to be entertaining, as if it were afraid of losing our attention.

Back in 1961, when it first appeared, it was a novelty, the first staged anthology; it may also have owed some of its success to the presence in its original cast of Max Adrian, a great actor who was also a great camp comedian. He could make anything funny. He may, though, have blazed a dangerous path for his successors. It can be oddly reassuring to see that luminaries of the classical stage can behave as desperately as lesser mortals in the quest to get laughs; all the same, the spectacle of Sinden and Howard verbally wrong- footing one another through selections from The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (a history, not a newspaper) is not an edifying one. The musical support, too (by a singer-guitarist, Stephen Gray) is predominantly smirky.

Redgrave, who cannot only create a mood but cast a spell at a moment's notice, does the best sustained comic turn as a 15-year- old Jane Austen, at work on what she cheerfully admits to be a thoroughly biased History of England (Mary Queen of Scots good; Elizabeth I bad, very bad). She manages, pretty much, to get us laughing both with the material and at it. Even she, though, has run out of steam by the time she gets to Victoria's description of her own coronation.

Sindens fine-brandy comic technique remains 100% proof, but he too ends up repeating his effects. Richardson does a jolly Charles II announcing his marriage, but is heavily dependent on a self- deprecating guffaw. Howard is the most starved for good, or at least suitable, material; he is best reciting a poem by the saintly, tortured Henry VI -- a role of whose Shakespearean equivalent he gave a memorable account in the 80s.

And there's part of the rub. We have here three actors whose combined resumes would include a pair apiece of Lears, Hamlets, Benedicks, Coriolani and Richards of both denominations; plus an actress who has played a definitive Rosalind and five separate Cleopatras. I was looking forward as much as anyone to seeing all this talent and experience on a single stage. What I had forgotten is how little opportunity this show (it isn't a play -- doesnt pretend to be -- and I wish people would stop calling it one) gives its actors to interact. All they can do most of the time is smile, appreciatively and looking as if they mean it, at one anothers performances.

I found myself compiling mental lists of four-handers (Shaw's Don Juan in Hell? Claudel's Partage de Midi? Becketts Endgame? -- well, perhaps not that one) that might allow them to strike some sparks off one another. I suspect, too, that The Hollow Crown works better as a divertissement within a regular repertoire than when carted off around the world as a four-star entertainment in its own right. The four stars are here, and I wouldnt advise you to miss them, but don't expect to see them stretched to anything like their full capacity.

THE WELL BEING

HAMLET

National Arts Centre, Ottawa

- - -

A last-minute gap in the studio program at the National Arts Centre has been providentially filled by the arrival of mouthpeace, a South African troupe specializing in narrative and instant physical inventiveness. Their show The Well Being (already seen in Edmonton and Winnipeg) is an essay in the allegorical-ecological. Some of its text is simplistic, some is a little bemusing, but the performance itself is enchanting.

The piece is the joint creation of two actors, Andrew Buckland and Lionel Newton, and a director-designer, Lara Foot-Newton (who is Lionel Newton's wife). They differ from most South African companies that visit us, especially the improvisational ones, in being white. All the characters -- and between them Buckland and Newton play multitudes -- have pungent Afrikaans accents. This even includes a couple of frogs who act as chorus and who have a vested interest in the fables subject matter, which is water.

A prosperous community, identified as The Valley (a neat fit for Ottawa), endures its first flood, which makes them sulky; and then drought, which drives them crazy. The catalyst for these catastrophes is the rape of a village girl called Flo. Her assailant is the minister, a Reverend Caketon. After a certain amount of tut- tutting, his parishioners close ranks and drive Flo out. She takes refuge on top of a hill and begins digging a very deep hole. When the floods cause a mass exodus of BMWs, Flo is left alone, visited only by an amorous porpoise, with whom she has a child. When the valley-dwellers return and find themselves faced with thirst, they become convinced that Flo, by now a universal scapegoat, is secreting water at the bottom of her hole. (Dont bother; the play has already made that joke.) They call her a witch and a "wild woman," and march on her hill with murderous intent.

We automatically assume that any South African play, even now, will have something to say about apartheid; and it may be that Flo - - whom we never hear speak -- is meant to be black, as her persecutors are undoubtedly and uniformly white. But it seems likelier that Flo is meant to be a force of nature; her second name, as if her first were not symbol enough, is Deluge. The director writes in a program note of her country being violated, and though she also mentions rape statistics in times of war and congratulates her male colleagues on their unique empathy with women's feelings (I didn't get this but Im obviously not the best judge), its devastation of the environment that the show has most on its mind.

This must be the purpose of the porpoise: He shows the natural world fighting back. But what counts most is the joyousness with which the production presents his courtship of Flo, the two of them romping together in an ocean of paper strips. I should explain that the play begins with a roll of paper unfurled across the floor. As the play progresses, the actors, for their own various purposes, tear it up; by the end of it the stage is awash in paper and watermelon seeds. Flo's child is represented by a watermelon; in a subsequent scene the frogs do outrageous things with it. (It calls to mind the famous exchange from The Producers: "Actors are people." Have you ever eaten with one?)

The citizenry, who include a couple of sodden British ex-pats plus indigenous gossips of all sexes, are caricatured. But they are certainly funny, and after all the story is being told in shorthand.

Some of the fun comes from the speed with which Buckland and Newton, a double-act in black singlets, somersault (sometimes literally) from one role to another. They both get to play Flo, probably to keep her mysterious. It may by now be no novelty for the theatre to chill us with the evocation of a lynch mob, but the scene is still a powerful one. And if our amphibian hosts hover on the edge of cuteness, their earthiness keeps them from falling in. They end up, though, taking delightful headers, dutifully followed by swarms of invisible tadpoles, into the well that gives the play its title. God bless them and all who sail, swim, float or wallow with them.

- - -

My trip to Ottawa allowed me to catch the penultimate performance of the NAC's mainstage Hamlet. I had heard good things of Marti Maradens Shakespeare productions (she is the director of the NACs English Theatre as well as of this play) and this one justified them. It was a conventional staging, clear and lively, on a very Stratfordian set: all stairs, rostra, and ladders.

The least successful thing about it was its one innovation: An apparent attempt to suggest the whole play was being presented by the company of Players who turn up in it as characters. What this amounted to in practise was a series of mute, surprised encounters between, say, the Player Queen and the real Queen, as if the former were holding a mirror up to nature and the latter just didn't know where to look. These interludes were confusing while they happened, and completely forgotten once they were over. The concept may also be held responsible for the weirdest intermission-placement (halfway through the play scene) of any Hamlet I have seen, but it allowed the piece to be done in, of all avant-garde things, Elizabethan costume. We even got a traditional Ghost, in a silvery-grey cloak and a thorny crown. It may even have inspired a piece of luxury casting: Douglas Campbell, doubling a First Player proud of his craft with a First Gravedigger corpulently confident in his. If William Hutt is the elder statesman of Canadian acting, then Campbell is the roving patriarch.

It was altogether a strong company. Fiona Reid gave Gertrude credit for more intelligence than do most actresses, and was notably more attached to her son than to either of her husbands.

Ben Carlson was a Horatio with almost too much personality to stay in his place as onlooker. People are always asking why Hamlet didn't just kill the King and get it over with; you wondered why this Horatio, so kind and capable, didnt do it for him. He also seemed, in the mad scenes, to be in love with Ophelia on his own account.

Victor Ertmanniss Claudius, pure villain, and David Schurmann's Polonius, mild dodderer, were limited conceptions, competently executed. Michelle Monteith, like many Ophelias, was nothing in particular while sane but admirable when demented. Her whispered delivery of the line about rue -- "we may call it herb of grace on Sundays" -- was new and imaginative, the sound of a convent-girl gone horribly wrong.

Which leaves us with Tom Rooney (currently of TV's This Is Wonderland), the productions raison detre, and the first Hamlet in ages to hold me as a whole person in a story rather than an actor in an anthology of diploma pieces. Hamlet, according to the Gravedigger, is 30, which usually comes as a surprise. Rooney, pushing 40, made no special attempt to shed years, but then he has a spectral face and precise voice that make him seem ageless -- own brother to Yorick, and bearing the same twin marks of the jester and the corpse. With the hyper-ironic Ian Richardson in Toronto with The Hollow Crown, I found myself wondering whether Richardson's youthful Hamlet may not have been much like Rooney's: a joker who is not a dyed-in-the-wool cynic; a man who genuinely wanted to think the best of humanity and whose will has been shattered along with his ideals; a prematurely old mind yoked to a still-young soul. He has counted Claudius out from the start, and hardly bothers to disguise his contempt. He treats his mother with a mixture of respect and bitter disillusion. His solid flesh soliloquy is quiet and helpless: uncomprehending despair in a fallen world. He works the miracle of bringing "to be or not to be" alive; he unpicks it as though it were a metaphysical poem, a series of conondrums to which he would genuinely like an answer. Some scenes -- the hysterical triumph after the play, the quiet acceptance before the duel -- are as good as I have ever seen them. He is technically impeccable. He is also, without sentimentalizing, very likeable. If he can play the part again, and play it soon, he could be the Hamlet we have all been waiting for. Stratford and Soulpepper should be knifing one another for his services.

NEW CANADIAN KID

Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People, Toronto

The title of "gibberish coach" is a novelty among Toronto theatre credits, though we can probably all think of past productions that sounded as if they might have employed one. The job is serious business, though, in Dennis Foon's 20-year-old play, New Canadian Kid, now available in a sparkling new production at Torontos young peoples theatre.

Gibberish, in this play, is what comes out of the mouths of people whose actual language is English. English, meanwhile, issues from people who, in reality, can't speak a word of it. It's an aural equivalent of the reverse games that Peter Shaffer, in his Black Comedy, played with darkness and light. That play was a farce, and much of Foons piece is funny as well. But it has, this being the YPT (all right, the LKTYP), an instructive purpose. We are taken inside the heads of a boy named Nick and his mother, new immigrants to Canada from a place called Homeland. In particular, we follow Nicks progress in school.

Every child's first day at school is mystifying. Nick's is mystifying multiplied. Two classmates, a boy and a girl, seem well- disposed enough toward him and are certainly curious. They are revolted (read, surprised) by the aroma that comes from his lunchbox; he seems to be bumping up against a meaningless wall of sounds and symbols. Foon is considerate enough to throw us some entertaining clues as to what their words mean. Hockey, for example, is called, as far as I could catch it, schlamstick while "mapleleafo" seems a slamdunko for the Canadian flag. Nick, in one of the shows less convincing moments, seems uncertain whether to stand or sit while O Canada is being played, though surely after the first couple of seconds he would just imitate the other kids. He begins very soon to make connections; not unexpectedly he makes them far quicker than his mother. At first it was she who had to quiet his fears when he longed to go back home. Pretty soon the roles are reversed. There is also a father who never appears, since hes too busy making a living, though not, as we are carefully informed, in his old job as a teacher -- an example of theatrical economy overlapping with real-life economy.

Of Nick's two peers, the girl is called Mench while the boy is called Mug. What is it with those names? Anyway, they both live up to them. Mench acts like a mensch, as they used to say in my family, and becomes Nick's staunch friend, while Mug turns out to be a bully. He ends up scrawling the word sgak on Nicks wall. This may be a generalized insult or it may be an epithet reserved for Homelanders. The latter seems the likelier but the point, though danced around at length, is never very firmly made. Sean Baek, who plays Mug, is of visibly Asian descent, leaving you wondering whether he was cast simply because he was the best for the role (hes certainly good, sliding very believably from neutrality to aggression) or whether the production intends some comment on the attitudes of older immigrants toward newer ones. There is much to be said for what is usually called "colour-blind casting" but the phrase itself is ridiculous. It suggests that an audience can wilfully edit the visual information with which it is presented; and it can't.

Richard Harte, clad in various shades of green, makes a charming Nick, feeling his way through a minefield with great humour and delicacy. Claire Calnan as Mench has the same qualities in even greater abundance, and her role may be trickier because her character has more choices. She is especially touching, and especially sure-footed, when Nick brings her home to meet his increasingly isolationist mother, setting off what threatens to become an incipient culture clash.

Laurel Paetz's Mother is less convincing than her juniors, maybe because the play has been written from their point of view rather than hers. There is something dutiful about the writing of her role - - she remains the outsider in ways the author may not have intended - - and hence something forced about her playing. "Chillex," as they say in gibberish when they want someone to back off.

Leah Cherniak, in a theatre notorious for good intentions muddily transmitted, delivers a production that impresses immediately with its clean-edged elegance and subsequently with its wit and resource. Its mounted on a new thrust-stage formation that encourages economy and rewards concentration. Victoria Wallaces design, incorporating a revolve on the platform and a giant blackboard behind it, is neat, and Todd Charlton's sound score is terrific.

At a 60-minute running time, the play's conceit never becomes coy or its message strident. It ends on an honest note of qualified hope. The audience, mostly nearer eight than 108 (those are the stated parameters), were gratifyingly quiet while the show was on and gratifyingly noisy when it was over. The gibberish coach is Michael Kennard, of Mump and Smoot, thanks to whom this new profession begins its life at the top.

Verve's diva series covers Ella, Billie, Blossom and more

Divas are the opposite of singers. Let me try to put that in a more conciliatory way. People who enthuse about "divas seem to adore them for qualities that have only a tangential connection with music; for the amount of noise they make, or the degree of hysterical intensity they can inject into a song, irrespective of its text. The cult originated among the soprano-fanciers of opera, and found a natural home in the more melodramatic areas of pop, starting in Motown. It's dispiriting, though, to find that even in the saner world of jazz, everybody is trying to get into the act.

But thats how it goes at Verve, which calls the latest recycling of its catalogue of female singers the diva series." Recent convulsions in the record business have made that catalogue even more impressive than it used to be. The Universal Music Group has swallowed up not only Verve but Decca and Mercury, who, from the 30s to the '60s, recorded between them hordes of jazz or jazz-pop singers. The resultant riches are almost too embarrassing to contemplate.

For an extreme example take the figurehead of the series, and maybe of jazz singing in general, Ella Fitzgerald. She spent 20 years at Decca and another 10 -- her greatest -- at Verve. George Evans, the Toronto vocalist who compiled her volume and most of the others, can hardly have known where to start. In fact, he starts with some of her early, inescapable tracks (A-Tisket, A-Tasket, Mr. Paganini and what is probably her most beloved scat extravaganza, Oh Lady Be Good) and ends with two even more familiar warhorses from her famous Berlin concert, Mack the Knife (the one where she forgets the words) and How High the Moon. In between comes what inevitably seems a random sampling from her Songbook years; those in which, under the tutelage of Verve's founder, Norman Granz, she worked her way through the best songs of the best American composers, creating not so much definitive performances as definitive collections.

These tracks are as soothing or as invigorating as ever, but they dont mean as much cut loose from their original moorings. The standard complaint against Ella in this context has always been that she neglects a songs lyrics. She does not, perhaps, dig very deeply into them, but she doesn't obstruct them either. The sheer loveliness of her voice, and the unpretentious joy that she takes in the music, keep you listening and let you construct your own interpretations.

Also, there's a wry humour in her voice thats often overlooked and that works beautifully as long as she or her producers trust it. It comes out very clearly in the latest track on this disc, a song called I Said No, which has a typically witty Frank Loesser lyric that she sings perfectly, first time around; she then does a second chorus that she seems to have written herself and that leaves you wondering whether she understood what she was singing about in the first place.

The disc will certainly get a lot of play in coffeehouses, but so much of this material has been repackaged before that it seems anodyne. If you want to give Fitzgerald a serious listen, youd do better to pick up one of her Verve albums (they're nearly all on CD) in its entirety.

Sarah Vaughan's voice matched Ellas for range, precision and flexibility, though Ive never warmed to it as much. Its beauty is grandiose rather than approachable, and if Ella's approach to lyrics might be described as neutral, Sarah's sometimes seems positively destructive.

Along with the grandeur goes a disconcerting coyness of tone; when, in Misty, she compares herself to "a kitten up a tree, it sounds all too apposite. It can even grate when she isnt singing words: Ellas scatting on How High the Moon is exhilarating however often you hear it; Sarah's sounds sterile. We know she can do it; there's no sense of surprise.

Shes at her best singing with small groups, but Mercury (for whom she recorded) more often backed her with big orchestras, and this selection reflects that. Theres nothing wrong with that format, but the combination of big band and big voice is overpowering. There are Vaughan performances (Embraceable You, for example) that take my breath away, but none of them are here.

Carmen McRae, now: an unfailingly intelligent musician, she was capable of both sabre-toothed precision and amazing warmth, sometimes within the same song. You can hear her move from one to the other and back again on her disc's first track, Falling in Love with Love. Then comes a melting I Only Have Eyes for You, followed by a Speak Low that cuts right into the song's curt, ominous rhymes (our moment is swift / like ships adrift"), which in turn gives way to a hovering Midnight Sun that is, in the songs own words, "icy- white and crystalline," with a zany Comes Love waiting further down the block.

These early Decca sides of McRaes (she was in her thirties) are her best work; she was given great repertoire and inventive arrangements, and the tight format of what were meant to be commercial albums kept her from self-indulgence. Also, her voice was pleasanter then; later, she sounded jagged for jaggedness' sake. This is the best volume in the series.

Billie Holiday's entry draws on her careers middle period, self- aware while avoiding the masochistic depths (at least as relished by her more ghoulish fans) of her final husk-voiced recordings. Some of her best work is here, the serene Easy Living and its bitter counterpart Dont Explain, along with Good Morning Heartache, a Speak Low even better than McRae's, I Wished on the Moon, and the inevitable-but-welcome God Bless the Child. (Though the final track, Lady Sings the Blues, is an odd choice unless it's trying for some kind of name recognition.)

The anthology treatment has never hurt Holiday -- indeed she sounds better in the context of other singers. So many of her instinctive innovations have become common coin that you need to hear her successors to realize how good she was.

Anita ODay, Fitzgeralds main rival at the real Verve, sang a similar standard repertoire, usually in looser settings and with wilder results. She's undervalued as a lyric interpreter (like McRae she can be acerbic or even disconcertingly tender) but you really listen to her for high-velocity madness; there can't be many singers who are at their best in Tea for Two.

This is a good collection, though the inclusion of Peel Me a Grape is a reminder that nobody should be allowed to sing this song except Blossom Dearie. Its mysteriously missing from Blossoms own bouquet, though we do get her original unrivalled performance of Dave Frishberg's other early masterpiece I'm Hip. Dearie, at once wide-eyed and pungent, sings (and plays piano) with understated wit, as in They Say Its Spring, an obscure song that once heard refuses to leave your head. She can also, out of nowhere, touch you deeply with Someone to Watch Over Me, a song I had thought I wanted never to hear again.

Dearie whispers; Astrud Gilberto murmurs. With her the moment is more important than the music, so she of all of them may have the best claim to be a diva. True, divadom is supposed to be about attitude, and Gilberto sounds too modest to have one, but that can be an attitude in itself. Anyway, she remains identified with the Brazilian music that did us all a favour in the 60s, and since it still sounds enchanting, so does she. On some of her later tracks (I Haven't Got Anything Better to Do) she sounds good in her own right.

At the opposite extreme of force and guts, Dinah Washington's disc is a joy, as she bends a wide variety of songs to her own will and leaves both them and us the better for it. Nina Simone is more problematic but she, like most of her peers, is heard here at her most disciplined and rewarding. The lineup includes her classic, naked reading of Porgy, the self-descriptive I Put a Spell on You and Wild Is the Wind, a movie tune that she makes sound like the folk song it's trying to be.

There's an extra album, The Ultimate Diva Collection, which samples all the above singers (in, wastefully, some of the above songs) alongside others, like Peggy Lee and Shirley Horn, who deserve representation in any future batch, as indeed do several men -- Mel Torme, Bing Crosby and Fred Astaire are all in the inventory - - if there should ever be such a thing as a Divo Collection. There are brief, hurried-seeming liner notes by the ubiquitous, in these latitudes, Will Friedwald, and the artwork is uniformly hideous. Maybe such exaggerated portraiture goes with the title.

CHINA DOLL

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

Nora Helmers, the heroine of Ibsen's A Doll's House, slammed the door on her husband, her family and her whole past life in 1879. That of course was in Norway, but the sound reverberated around the world. By 1920 it was making a major contribution to the emerging feminist movement in China. The prostitutes in the teahouses of Shanghai took a particular shine to it, and were even referred to as "Noras." This is the kind of long-range, far-reaching effect that theatre buffs dream of. It makes us feel we may not be wasting our lives.

It sounds, in fact, too good to be true. But the facts are there, set out in the program for Marjorie Chan's new play China Doll, and justifying what might otherwise seem an intolerably cute title. Su- Ling, Chan's heroine, grows up during the last years of Imperial China and the first years of the republic, and her life is changed when a local draper with an activist past hands her a samizdat copy of the Ibsen play.

Su-Ling is not a prostitute, though she might as well be; she is a poor girl -- of, as they say, good family -- who is about to be purchased as the second wife (i.e., first concubine) of a local rich man. She has been brought up, very strictly, by her embittered grandmother, who is a servant in the house of the designated husband. The play charts the awakening of Su-Ling; everything in it is a flashback from her first line, which is "I am walking towards the future."

Those words have a particular resonance because Su-Ling has spent her life, since the age of five, with her feet bound. This traditional method of making a woman attractive to men was on its last legs, so to speak, at this time, but the news hasn't reached Su- Ling's community, where the custom is rigorously enforced.

It seems to work, too, at least in the sense of having turned Chinese men into a race of foot fetishists. Merchant Li, Su-Ling's benefactor and the only male we actually set eyes on, has an orgasm when measuring her for her tiny shoes -- and he's one of the enlightened. It was he who, long before making a Nora of her, taught her to read -- to the fury of her grandmother, who believes, with reason, that literacy lowers a girl's market value. The only other character is a servant girl with whom Su-Ling is forbidden to play when they are both children, and whom the grandmother bullies unmercifully when she turns up later as Su-Ling's bridal attendant.

Chan does a good job of suggesting the progress of history through the interaction of only four people, as does Kelly Thornton's clear and deliberate production. There is, however, a downside. The pattern can hardly help becoming schematic, and though the play is never boring, the slow pace gets oppressive. This is partly because the outcome is so predictable. We know, even without the opening line, that the show will end with the heroine having her own Nora moment, and we want her, for her sake and our own, to get it done and get it over.

We can't get too excited over the obstacles she faces, because they're mainly external. There is little complexity in Su-Ling or in anybody else, just the occasional faltering when the play feels the need of it. Ibsen always denied having any interest in women's rights, but that's his problem; the play speaks louder than its author. All the same, the best productions of A Doll's House are those that suggest the husband might also have a case, and -- most importantly -- that Nora has been partly complicit in her own oppression. There's nothing like that here.

We do encounter, though, at least one other literary analogue. At one point we hear a Chinese version of the Cinderella story, with special emphasis on the slipper. The foot motif actually looms larger than the doll theme, and is more deserving of a place in the title, but it isn't very satisfactorily worked out. The climax is Su- Ling's tearing the wrappings off for herself , and here the production, previously cool and open, goes melodramatic on us. Red lights flash and music jangles while the protagonist, behind her semi-transparent bed-curtains, is obviously up to something. What it is, we can't quite make out, and though we find out soon enough, the moment has passed. It's cheating.

Meanwhile, much has been made of the "Lotus slippers" -- ceremonial shoes, intricately designed -- that the bride herself must prepare and embroider, first for her betrothal and then her wedding. It turns out that Su-Ling is no good at embroidery and has to get the besotted Merchant Li to do it for her. She has, in other words, no stake -- not even an aesthetic one -- in the system she's abandoning.

We see nothing of her allotted husband, who wants to have a China doll that he can call his own, and that he is apparently prepared to break -- literally -- if she doesn't give satisfaction. We see far too much of the grandmother, whose function is to be either a bully or a nag, sometimes both at once, and who is very poorly played. Nothing is more theatrically lethal than an unsympathetic role, ineptly acted; it drains the stage. The actress, who seems too young for her role, is allowed a couple of vulnerable moments, and is tolerable when tearful. Chan herself plays Su-Ling, and her acting, whether downcast or perky, faithfully reflects both the charm and the limitations of her writing. John Ng's Merchant Li is likeable, but fuzzy at the edges.

As the servant, outspoken but chained to her social role, Keira Loughran brightens the scene every time she appears, and irradiates it whenever she opens her mouth. None of her colleagues has anything like her discipline or her attack. Maybe the contrast is intentional, meant to denote a difference in class, but it ends up seeming more like a difference in culture; she sounds, in her immediacy, far more North American than they do.

Loughran also makes a few ghostly appearances, most delicately executed, as Su-Ling's mother, who vanished into the work of the teahouses. This is another thread, the rebellion of the sexually exploited, that the play sets in motion but fails to pursue; its themes and characters go on and off like Christmas tree lights, rather than having the steady glow of Chinese lanterns. That, though, is a lot to ask. This is a first play, and an ambitious one, and it's worth attending. You learn something from it, and that's always a pleasure.

THE ADVENTURES OF ALI & ALI AND THE AXES OF EVIL

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

There are Ali Hakim, named after the peddler in Oklahoma!, and Ali Ababwa, named after the genie in Aladdin. They come from the unmapped country of Agraba, and right now they are in Canada, hell- bent to entertain us. They are also out to earn a buck by any other means possible, including hawking anything that isn't nailed down, and to get asylum.

That is the premise behind The Adventures of Ali & Ali and the Axes of Evil, a funny, scattershot show that has come to us from Vancouver, having existed before that as a radio comedy item. The Axes of Evil is a terrorist group from whom the two Alis are pledged to protect us. We in the theatre are particularly at risk because, we are told, terrorists are likeliest to strike at groups of people enfeebled by boredom.

Camyar Chai (Ali Hakim) and Marcus Youssef (Ali Ababwa) are respectively of Iranian and Egyptian extraction, though their characters seem to stand for the entire Middle East. (Well, almost. They dont stand for Israel. Not in any sense.) Their humour, though, is double-edged. They are likely to strike at the whole multiculturalism industry or at least at what it has actually become. Broadly but gleefully, they present mini-dramas in which immigrant sons who wish to assimilate clash with immigrant fathers who dont. One of the unregenerate dads is a butcher, who seems to be engaged in chopping up beavers; I'm not sure whether this would make him an exceptionally bad Canadian or an exceptionally good one. To be honest, I'm not even sure if Ive seen any plays that resemble the ones theyre skewering, but I'm sure I would hate them if I did. Anyway, I get the idea.

Ali and Ali also tell us about Agraba's native religious cultists, the Sammites, who worship Sammy Davis Jr. It seems that moderate Sammites, who might settle for a chick and a martini, have been overcome by frenzied hard-liners who insist on singing themselves hoarse and tap dancing until their feet are worn into stumps. I was hoping this notion would turn into a running gag -- maybe they could impersonate themselves into an identity crisis -- but in fact it makes just the one appearance. (Possibly just as well. The show isnt always that prudent.)

The Alis are more imaginative in their self-satire than when they are taking on the opposition. Their George Bush jokes are weak, and their Tony Blairs are worse. On the other hand, it would be hard to resist the earnest anti-terrorism operative (Pakistani, with a maple leaf) who turns up in a series of nifty video bits to lecture us on the degree of danger we are in. The bottom rungs of this very Canadian ladder are Decaf (which I think means "you can go out and play") and Double Double (which might mean go out and play but wrap up warm.) Near the top, and frightening, is Boot Cut, a level of terrorism alert brought to you by the Gap.

This Dr. Mohanides Panir (his name as it appears on the screen is much longer, but I can only pass on the edited version that theyve squeezed into the program) appears three times and may, like this sentence, outstay his welcome. There is, to be sure, a classic law of comedy known as the Rule of Three, but nobody said it was immutable. In a similar way, though I enjoyed the way the twosome kept buttering up Ian Hanomansing ("celebrated handsome brown fellow"), they exhausted my patience when they made him the supposed hero of some future movie epic about the Iraq War, one that might be entitled Saving Private Ryan's Football Jersey. There's an idea here, but it goes on forever and is carried entirely by narration. Here we could really use some film clips.

There is a third member of the cast, a white actor named Tom Butler. He plays two roles. One is the Alis long-suffering stooge (they dress him up like some houri out of Kismet and address him, in full knowledge, as Tim) who gets to reflect bitterly on the fine career he had in movies before coming to this pass; the other is a kilted theatre manager who marches periodically on whenever the act threatens to overstep some kind of mark. This last extra layer strikes me as a rather craven safety net ("You dont believe these guys are outrageous; well he does"), but the character sort of justifies himself when he delves into his own historic past to recount the last battle of William Wallace. He moves between the chilling and the absurd, from the grisly details of Wallace's execution by the English to the claim that his severed head was placed upon a pole -- and then they killed him. This shows that even Dead White European Males have their historic grievances, and that they can be just as sincere and just as self-indulgent about them as anybody else.

And so it is with the Alis. One of them has lost his fiancee; the other wants to send money home to his imprisoned wife. It's laid on thick but it isnt dismissible. The pair, like most double acts since 1955, have a whiff of Waiting for Godot about them, and their battered-but-hopeful act allows them to get away with an ending that is probably soppy and definitely touching. Chai and Youssef are wily, charming performers who know how to work an audience and one another. I was in their pockets from the moment one of them told a rude story about a leprechaun (great accent, by the way) and I remained there, despite some restive moments, until the end, which features a surprise appearance by their sponsor Osama bin Laden, who isnt really much into the arts but figures he might as well give it a try. (They suggest that he improve his outfit's image by re- branding it al-Qaeda 2.0.)

Guillermo Verdecchia collaborated with the two stars on the script and he is also the director. His production is not what you would call polished, but chances are the show wouldn't work if it were.

THE SYRINGA TREE

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

I have now sat through The Syringa Tree three times in six months, and the fact that I have been able to do so without going mad argues a solid strength in both the play and its subject. The piece, a quasi-autobiographical monologue about growing up white in apartheid South Africa, was brought to last year's World Stage by its author, Pamela Gien, who gave it a fine, physically liquid performance marred by an oppressive winsomeness.

The protagonist-storyteller is, at the start of the action she recounts, six years old, and the actress-author, though she had no trouble impersonating some 30 other characters en route, kept her in a state of pucker-voiced innocence practically through adolescence.

Now at CanStage the role is being alternated by two Canadian actresses, Yanna McIntosh and Caroline Cave, between whose performances I find it almost impossible to choose. One at a time or in conjunction, they blow their authors performance out of the water while lifting her text up to the sky.

What neither of them can do is disguise the plays lack of focus. It's never too clear whose story it's meant to be. The narrator is Elizabeth Grace, whose father, a doctor, is a self-described "Jewish atheist" and whose mother is a cheerfully lapsed Catholic. The couple are exemplary white liberals, doing their very best for the surrounding community and especially for their own black servants. Chief among these is the Xhosa nanny, Salumina, who dotes on her Miss Lizzie and is doted on in return. The first significant thing that happens is Saluminas giving birth to a "pickaninnie" (thats the word they all use) of her own, a girl named Moliseng. Lizzie bonds with her as well; probably her first real inkling of the system she lives under comes when she instructed that the presence in the house of Moliseng, who lacks the proper papers, has to be kept secret. Her first real fright comes when the child is seen by their neighbour, an Afrikaans minister.

Two traumatic sequences of events mark Lizzie's growing-up. One is the temporary loss of Moliseng in the chaotic local hospital system; the story of Mrs Grace driving to the rescue, car windows tightly closed, is the tensest sequence of the evening. The other is a bloody attack on the farm of Lizzie's grandparents, carried out by insurgents from Rhodesia whom a white policeman describes, with improbable restraint, as freedom fighters; this, you may feel, would hardly have been the time or the place for political correctness, but it is a forcible reminder that the play comes to us from the United States, where the author now lives and where theatrical punches are still habitually pulled.

Showing us apartheid through the dawning awareness of a well- disposed child is a cunning way of mediating its cruelty; its also, presumably, true to Giens own experience. But its usefulness diminishes as the child grows older, which may explain why the later scenes seem rushed. We flash forward to Elizabeth at university; it's the time of the Soweto riots and Moliseng is in the thick of them. The upshot sickens Elizabeth and she, like her author, leaves the country -- a development that was foreseen by her father who loves his country but had warned her "don't ever make this place your home."

She doesnt come back for years; and I wonder now, as I did last year, what took her so long. Not even the collapse of the hated regime can sway her, let alone any desire to see the man she still affectionately refers to as my old dad. (The play teases us, too calculatingly, with the possibility that her mother may be dead. I was reminded of the episode of The Simpsons, set in the future, in which Lisa phones home to announce her engagement, to be greeted by a delighted Marge saying "I wish your father could be here to hear the news" and then adding but he isnt back from work yet.) What draws Elizabeth back is news of Salumina and Moliseng; and it makes both her and the play look self-indulgent.

Moliseng's name is literally the play's last word, which by both actresses is first affectingly crooned and then stirringly proclaimed. But for this to be any more than sentimental, Moliseng would have to be the central figure (as opposed to figurehead, which she briefly is). And for this to happen, Elizabeth would have had to hog less of the limelight than she does. Even the story of her stricken grandparents is interrupted by her memory of an earlier, happier trip that netted her a nice new pair of pickaninnie pants. This is downright confusing, and anyway, weve had quite enough cuteness already. The play is also pretty cavalier with its symbolism. The tree of the title is Lizzies special childhood refuge: a place to swing from, a place to hide. But then it sort of spreads. Moliseng in Soweto is rhetorically exhorted to "hide ... climb the tree." Any tree, apparently, will do.

The play is another of the off-Broadway semi-serious type -- heartfelt, moderately funny, and safe -- that CanStage brings us every season. I'm not knocking this; somebody has to do it, and they do it well. On this occasion, under the play's original director, Larry Moss, theyve done it superbly, and twice over. Of the two performances, Caves is perhaps the more surprising. One expects McIntosh to be magnificent (she has a track record of it) and a standing ovation is guaranteed here from the moment she opens her mouth; it takes five minutes to realize that Cave, a Shaw Festival ingenue whose acting muscles are rippling with unsuspected strength, is headed in the same deserved direction. Both of them use the little-girl voice, but discreetly. McIntosh simply states it as a fact; Cave plays with it more. Both can be hilarious. McIntosh is black and Cave white; this doesn't matter -- both are required to play characters of both races, and anyway one-person plays make their own rules -- but it does make a difference, to both their perception and ours: Which is why I don't find "colour-blind casting" a useful term. Cave brings more harried, humorous detail to the Grace parents who, as characters, are the play's richest creations, or recreations; McIntosh is a more rooted Salumina, and a more mischievous Moliseng, roles that she inhabits but that Cave has more visibly to impersonate. As the older Moliseng at Soweto, McIntosh is thrillingly defiant, Cave movingly tremulous. McIntosh has richer fun with the young Lizzie, Cave is the more lucid as the narrating Elizabeth. But frankly, from the first moment, which finds Lizzie hanging upside down from her swing (superbly lit, like the whole play, by Louise Guinand) you know that you're safe with either actress and blessed with both. To indulge in one final quibble: McIntosh, on this stage, is born incandescent, Cave achieves incandescence, and the play, through their ministrations, has incandescence thrust upon it.

RUNE ARLIDGE

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

As a comparatively new Canadian, and one wholly indifferent to sports, I had no idea until this week who Roone Arledge might have been. Thanks to kind friends and helpful press packages, I have now learned of his fame as a sportscaster and TV executive, and I could even understand the single sidelong reference to him in Michael Healey's Rune Arlidge, whose title character, a woman, was named after Mr. A. by a father who was a fan. What I don't understand is why Ms. A. is the title character, because she never properly takes her place at the centre of the play. Neither, unfortunately, does anything or anybody else.

This is a three-act play, a long-neglected form well worth resurrecting. The action begins in 1994, and ends 15 years in the future, a time about which the play, mercifully, bears no apocalyptic tidings. It seems that life then will be much the same as it is now; even print journalism still hangs on. The people the play depicts have gone even further downhill than they had when we first met them, but that was to be expected.

The scene throughout is a dilapidated Ontario cottage on what one suspects to be a fairly stagnant bit of lake. Here, when we start, lives Mrs. Frances Arlidge, whose husband left her, and who is taking this and other things out on the world and especially on her two early-twentyish daughters, Michelle and Rune.

The three of them have an abrasive relationship. Frances usually communicates with the girls by swearing and moaning at them, and they give at least as good as they get, at least in the profanity department. Frances is also given to delivering long retrospective monologues about, for example, how she and her ex came to buy the cottage and what a terrible idea it turned out to be. These narratives are often funny and always fluent: "How do you speak in paragraphs?" Rune asks her, and even while enjoying them its possible to share her incredulity.

According to Frances, a lack of empathy is what causes relationships to fail; she should know (and, to be fair to her and her author, she knows she should know). Also according to Frances, Michelle is tough and takes after her, while Rune is sensitive and vulnerable and needs protecting. Frances may be right, but the difference doesnt register dramatically. In the first act, we perceive the sisters just as a double-act up against their mother, and the play, lacking a foundation, never recovers.

Things do happen: Michelle, doped-up and promiscuous, is revealed to be pregnant, while Rune, currently a student, is visited by her boyfriend and receives a surprise proposal, which does not work out. Act Two, which takes place now, is almost wholly uneventful. A series of strokes has robbed the once-vocal Frances of speech; she can only grunt. She gets very little sympathy. Michelle has a 10- year-old daughter with whom she is already replicating the relationship she had with her own mother. Rune has a new, and startlingly boorish, fiance. The ways of the heart are strange, especially when fuelled by desperation, but it's impossible to believe these two could ever have got together: Not that the guy isn't well-meaning -- he may, come to think of it, be the best- intentioned person on stage -- but still.

Act Three shows us Michelle more like her mother than ever, while finally bringing Rune herself into something like focus. Re- encountering her oldest flame, who is still burning, she delivers some wise words about how knowing the kind of person you are, and why, is no help at all in changing it. There is a Chekhovian sense of boats having been burned, mainly while nobody was looking.

Its Chekhov perhaps mediated through the homelier tragicomedy of, say, Alan Ayckbourn. (I once quoted a friends description of Ayckbourn as speeded-up Chekhov; Healey, in this play, is slowed- down Ayckbourn.) There are recurring images to bind the piece together -- leeches, canoes and toast are prominently featured -- and the self-perpetuating mother-daughter dynamic is wincingly recognizable whenever it appears. It's what we grab on to. But it's also a bit obvious, and since Rune herself is supposed to stand somewhat outside it, it pulls the plays focus.

Leah Cherniaks production is strong on mood (thanks are due to Charlotte Dean's set and Kirk Elliott's sound design) but less so on pace and coherence. Good actors abound. Fiona Reids phrasing of Frances fretful arias is expectedly expert, but more impressive is her silent pain later, her face and hands expressing her longing to have another vengeful go. One still never knows who this woman is, especially socially.

One does know what Rune does; she's a newspaper columnist, but there's no particular dramatic reason for her to be so. Jane Spidell is excellent in the role, and at moments extraordinary, the moments being the gentle ones in which she exposes a capacity for love combined with an incapacity for letting it happen. Julie Stewart is probably louder, not just in decibels, than Michelle needs to be, but I wouldnt fault her too heavily for it.

Severn Thompson is a believable terror at 10 years old, and a sultry, incisive one at 25. (Her role includes a near brush with incest, horrific because casual.) Rick Roberts is charming as Runes loser of a suitor, and Ari Cohen works very hard as his loudmouth successor who has to carry far too much of the middle movement. The same act concludes, however, with a lovely speech, a stumbling evocation of the might-have-been, beautifully delivered by John Dolan. It suggests that the play's real subject might be time. But then, of what long play could that not be said? Healey's previous plays have marked him as our most humanely intelligent playwright; nothing here makes you doubt his talent, but structure and content are way out of whack.
