THE TRIALS OF JOHN DEMJANJUK: A HOLOCAUST CABARET

Harbourfront Studio Theatre

The musical Cabaret, in its most recent incarnation, ended with a flash-forward to the death camps. The nightclub master of ceremonies, who had guided us through the rise to power of the Nazis in Berlin, was suddenly transformed into a pyjama-clad victim of the Holocaust. Many people seemed to think this terribly brave, but it struck me as an awful, and awfully cheap, idea: The musical genre straying into territory to which it had neither the vocabulary nor, in this case, the time to do justice. Now along comes The Trials of John Demjanjuk, subtitled A Holocaust Cabaret, which takes up, almost literally, where Broadway's Cabaret left off and which might be described as an atrocity about atrocities.

John Demjanjuk is the Ukrainian-born Cleveland auto worker who was put on trial in Israel in the 1980s, accused of having been the man known as Ivan the Terrible, a sadist remarkable even among the guards of Treblinka. He was convicted, but was acquitted on appeal. He returned to the United States, where, two years ago, his citizenship was revoked; he now awaits further judgment.

The show tells his story, or at least dances around it, in what we all fondly imagine to have been Weimar nightclub style. A wailing- voiced announcer, who might be Cabarets emcee reincarnate and who expounds the same mordantly escapist philosophy, teams up with a rouged, red-wigged chanteuse who doubles on accordion and suggests Sally Bowles run hopelessly to seed. It made sense for Cabaret to use cabaret, since it was a style that flourished in Germany in the early 30s, which is when and where the show is set. It had been stamped out by the time of the Second World War, which is when this play's events begin. In adopting it, the show is trying to cash in on the legend of the style's eternal hard-hitting relevance (Brecht and Weill and all that) and also, of course, to shock us. Its saying: You never thought such material could be handled in so flippant a manner -- guess again.

Behind this lies the assumption that we have never considered the issues for ourselves and need to be jolted into doing so; its undoubtedly sincere -- solemn theatre people have an unlimited belief in their own commitment and everybody else's apathy -- but it's mistaken. And besides, it isnt enough to be politically incorrect; you also have to be good at it.

The author, Jonathan Garfinkel, originally wrote the piece as a poem, though one hopes his poetry isnt fairly represented by the song-words he's served up here. He doesn't seem to know what a rhyme is. I know poetry doesnt have to rhyme, but if its going to try, then it had better do better than "Porsche" and of course. The "of course," by the way, signifies shameless padding, of which there is plenty; Garfinkel is also a great one for inverting the natural order of words so as to push the one he needs to the end of the line. If we are to consider these as lyrics, then they are the worst I have ever heard -- and I've heard some doozies.

The nadir comes in the material for the prosecution and defence lawyers in the Jerusalem trial, each concerned with his own glory and his own agenda, each treating the courtroom as his stage. (Defence counsel is the one who drives the Porsche, of course.) This conceit -- the law as showbiz, the lawyers as prima donnas -- is not as outrageously novel as the production seems to think it is. It was given a thorough workout in Chicago, another Broadway musical and from the same composers as Cabaret. There is no reason why the poor theatre shouldn't borrow from the rich; the latter has a lot to teach. But I wish the experimentalists wouldnt give themselves such airs while doing it.

When the real-life Demjanjuk trial began, I rejoiced that the real Ivan had been found and looked forward to his conviction. I then began, grudgingly, to admit that there seemed to be serious doubts about his identity. I imagine many people felt the same. Its to Israel's credit that his appeal could be both made and upheld, though the show doesn't seem inclined to get into that. It does, though, maintain a scrupulous ambiguity about the man accused. He might be a decent family man, helplessly railroaded (vignettes of his life in Cleveland are among the shows better moments), or he might be the Devil incarnate. He is given a haunting, mocking double (psychic, not physical) who might be the Ivan inside him or might be the real Ivan, somebody else altogether who really did those things. Thats in theory; in dramatic practice, he's your standard sinister Nazi, a sneering psychopath strongly resembling Ralph Fiennes' performance in Schindlers List. There are also scenes of Demjanjuks service in the Russian army, from which he was captured and appropriated by the SS. He is seen with a fellow conscript, who is a Jew, and the two of them are played as a bad cross-talk act. It's an intentionally bad cross-talk act, but that doesn't help. The bold questions the play claims to be asking -- chiefly, would we behave any better under comparable pressures? -- have been asked a hundred times before and a lot more clearly, and the answer must always be the same: No, very likely we wouldnt. Now tell me something about this man.

Frank Moore as Demjanjuk does seem to be trying and, as far as possible, succeeding. He is, by turns, dignified, sinister and frightening. He also, it turns out late in the proceedings, can sing, while most of his colleagues seem to have been selected for their inability to carry a tune. Their acting varies: At the low end are Dmitry Chepotevskys inner Ivan and the duelling lawyers of Dov Mickelson and Michael Rubenfeld, each of them a platitude on legs; at the high is Clinton Walker as a Treblinka survivor, recounting unspeakable memories that chill the soul, just as the show's creators knew they would. Whether they have earned the right to use them is another matter; on the evidence of the rest of the evening, I would say not. Christine Brubaker, whom I have greatly admired in other circumstances, is here pointlessly abrasive as both performer and composer. Jennifer Capraru's portentous production includes such high-school drama cliches as a whispering chorus echoing significant words from the main dialogue.

We may no longer be able to regard the Holocaust as something uniquely horrific -- not after Cambodia, Rwanda and what we know of the Gulag. None of them should be treated as pretexts for showing how clever and daring you are. Its immoral; its also self- defeating, since nothing can be more shocking than the facts. Treat them soberly, or don't treat them at all. Where mass human suffering is concerned, there are worse sins than being boring.

DR. CHEKHOV: WARD 6

Factory Theatre, Toronto

After their successes with Chekhov's Shorts and Chekhov Longs, the troupe known as Theatre Smith-Gilmour has come up with a third instalment they have heroically refrained from calling Chekhov Medium. Dr. Chekhov: Ward 6 derives the first part of its title from the Russian writer's parallel career in medicine. Ward 6 is a novella he based on his experiences of visiting and working at a remote hospital in Siberia, and this show is a dramatization of it.

In a life of less than 50 years Chekhov achieved greatness as a writer of both drama and prose fiction (a very rare double), while also working full-time as a courageous and conscientious physician. Indeed, his conscientiousness, as exemplified in that trip to Siberia, helped kill him. And he was a great success with women. Yet he died convinced he was a failure.

To the rest of us, this must seem extraordinary, as well as oddly reassuring. One thing that must strike us now, though, is the continuity between the different areas of his life. It isn't just that there are doctors in his plays and medical themes in his stories; it's that the qualities of shrewdness, kindness and total lack of sentimentality that seem to have characterized him as a doctor all carry over into his writing.

Ward 6 is one of his bleakest tales, though the telling is, as always, cheerfully practical. It's set mainly in a hut, the most decaying part of a decaying hospital, "a hundred and fifty miles from the nearest railway station." This hut is the mental ward, inhabited by five patients and a brutal porter/ attendant. We meet one of the inmates, Ivan Dimitrich, a poverty-stricken gentleman who could never hold down a job, could never form a relationship and became convinced that everyone was out to get him: which, in time, they did, condemning him to his present incarceration with no hope of reprieve.

The doctor in charge of the hospital, Andrey Yefimitch, arrived in town full of benevolent intentions. But he got ground down, became hopeless and listless and has not now set foot in Ward 6 for years. But one day he wanders in and starts a conversation with Ivan. These two defeated men, one of them deranged, have probably the best minds in the neighbourhood (a familiar Chekhovian pattern - - think of Dr. Astrov and Uncle Vanya) and they engage together. Ivan rages, Andrey counsels resignation, basing his stoicism in the fact that we're all going to die anyway. (His own life, though as lonely as Ivan's, is of course comparatively comfortable -- as Ivan doesn't hesitate to point out.)

The story, having hooked our interest with the patient, turns out to be about the doctor. An ambitious assistant overhears him in friendly conversation with a madman. The local authorities urge him to take what turns out to be a disastrous vacation. When he returns, he has no job, no money, and pretty soon nothing at all. He too is consigned to Ward 6.

This is Chekhov anticipating Kafka, and it's better than Kafka, because it is rooted in observed reality rather than the author's neuroses. Ivan Dimitrich, like Josef K, feels he must have committed some unidentifiable crime and that he will be punished for it, but we understand what has brought him to this state and why other people perceive him as they do. We also understand, all too well, the bureaucratic politics that destroy Andrey, and his own hopeless vulnerability to them.

Michele Smith and Dean Gilmour, founders and guiding spirits of the company that bears their names, stay faithful to the story's form while altering its flavour. They are expert mimes who bring the tradition of commedia to everything they do.

Their staging here is, as always, swift, graceful and imaginative. They can, with the minimum number of beds and bodies, create the close-pressed, hopeless hut at a moment's notice. These, in the atmosphere they create of a world with its vital passages blocked up, be the best-staged asylum scenes since Peter Brook's Marat-Sade.

But the production can also be distressingly cute. It's pleasing, when we are told that Ivan Dmitrich was a great reader, and hands unknown fling a book at him, which he insouciantly catches; it's excessive when more volumes are immediately flung at him from all sides, however nimbly he fields them. And it gives a misleadingly playful impression of what his life was actually like.

At the heart of the story is a series of debates. It takes great verbal authority to get these discussions from page to stage, and this is just what Theatre S-G, as a showcase for Smith and Gilmour themselves, is least able to provide. Gilmour gets things off to a fine and steely start as narrator -- it's a shock to realize he is also to play Ivan, a role whose anger he transmutes into something beamishly Dickensian, but swathed in a nightgown, he does give the character a gaunt, compelling physical presence.

Smith as Andrey has the perpetual sad smile of Pierrot; her holy- fool innocence does something to suggest the doctor's plight, but doesn't begin to do justice to a character who is as much his own victim as anyone else's. (Chekhov would never have countenanced it; he was always especially hard on his own trade.) Far more damaging is Smith's heavy French accent, which obscures the sense of the text while dulling the senses of the audience. Even Andrey's most startling insight -- "So long as prisons and madhouses exist someone must be shut up in them" -- goes for virtually nothing.

In Chekhov's Shorts and Longs, some of the dramatic slack was taken up by actors of the calibre of Colombe Demers and Liisa Repo- Martell, but there is no supporting work of that quality here. As the Postmaster, the doctor's nearest approach to a friend, Paul Fauteux works hard, and somewhat successfully, to supply the sense of coarse quotidian reality the show otherwise lacks, and Ann-Marie Kerr, who plays a number of roles, is most prominent as Andrey's housekeeper, forever poking her head around the corner of the proscenium like a cuckoo popping out of its clock. It's nice, but it has nothing to do with the real world.

I should end, though, with a concession, maybe a confession. Among major writers -- certainly major modern writers -- Chekhov is a figure almost uniquely sane and likeable. Therefore, we all want to kidnap him -- that is, to remake him in what we take to be our own image. That is what Theatre Smith-Gilmour have done with him, both before and now. They have as much right to do so as anyone else. And at least they have an image.

Black & White Photo: David Leyes / Ann-Marie Kerr and Dean Gilmour in Dr. Chekhov: Ward 6, the last instalment of Theatre Smith- Gilmour's Chekhov trilogy.

TAPE

Gladstone Hotel, Toronto

There is always an attraction in seeing a play outside the confines of an orthodox theatre, though the refreshment comes from the change itself, rather than from any specific virtue in the new locale. This is the case even when a play is produced in its "real" setting, since what is now known as site-specific theatre is no more real than any other form. To a purist, it may even be less so. A play set in a hotel room, and actually performed in one, undoubtedly offers a jolt, but how do we account for the presence, amid all this authenticity, of ourselves, the spectators, each of us keenly conscious of the others' presence, and all of us more clearly visible than we would be in any old conventional space? The further you go toward realism in the theatre, the more artificial you become. The paradoxes of theatrical representation are, as always, enough to make your head spin.

Tape is a one-act play set in a seedy hotel room in Lansing, Mich. It receives its Canadian premiere in a seedy hotel room in Toronto -- or, in charity to the managements feelings, in one of the few rooms at the now-trendy Gladstone on Queen West that the renovators have not yet reached. Eighteen of us voyeurs are squeezed in two packed rows along one wall, otherwise everything is as time and nature left it, though some fortuitous new holes in the peeling wallpaper make the atmosphere even more atmospheric. The show is the inaugural venture of Crate Productions, whose stated aim is "to engage non-traditional audiences in alternative venues." Im not sure of the definition of a non-traditional audience, but I'm fairly sure I don't; all the same, I was glad to be there.

The play, first seen in New York in 1999, is the work of a rising dramatist, Stephen Belber, who has a new play due on Broadway this season. His past credits include being one of the team responsible for The Laramie Project, which means that, going strictly by the numbers, he is currently the most-produced playwright in Toronto.

In conventional surroundings Tape would probably seem decent but ordinary. Here, the veracity of the setting and the closeness of the quarters give it more tension and impact than it might otherwise have. It starts with one of those one-upping contests between old buddies that I suspect of being more common in American drama than they are in American life. Jon and Vince were friends in high school. Jon is now an aspiring filmmaker on the edge of achievement; his first picture is about to be shown at the Lansing festival. Vince has come from California -- where he works as a firefighter and, more steadily, as a drug dealer -- to cheer his old pal on. That at least is how it seems at first.

We are in Vinces room. (Jon, we assume, has a much smarter one somewhere else.) It turns out that the two of them have issues, long- simmering ones, over a girl named Amy whom they both dated and on whom Jon may or may not have forced his attentions. The title refers to a piece of recorded evidence, and also, I fancy, to the sticky bonds that still envelop the three characters. For Amy, conveniently, is also in Lansing. She works there, in fact, as a lawyer and, from the look and sound of her, a high-flying one. She has her own story, and it trumps the egos of both the guys. This is a Rashomon in which we are fairly sure whom to believe.

There are no great shafts of wit or insight in Belbers individual lines, but he builds up a powerful cumulative picture of male insecurity. As Vince and Jon shift positions we come to understand -- sometimes immediately, sometimes in retrospect -- why each needs to believe the worst of the other. More subtly, we also understand why each needs to believe the worst of himself.

The play offers an ironic take on the old saw about nice guys finishing last, the teaser being the difficulty of working out which of these guys might, at least in comparative terms, be the nice one. The verdict, such as it is, is a surprise. For the actors, required to be aggressive in a confined space, the main problem seems to be finding the right level: not just of intensity but of volume. The urge to underplay leads John Gordon (Vince) and Chris Reynolds (Jon) into a pair of performances too restrained to be credible. It's only when Vince lights up a joint, and Jon partakes, that their mellowness begins to make sense -- becomes, in fact, a style. (Vince has come well supplied with dope, and also with drink. When the play starts, the floor is already littered with stove-in cans.)

Once properly poised, they stay satisfactorily on target; Gordon taking Vince's angry pain and hanging it out to dry, Reynolds Jon contriving to seem smug and open-faced at the same time. Kate Meehans Amy comes on like an ice goddess out on a date, as if the heroine of Neil LaBute's The Shape of Things had wandered into a David Mamet play and proceeded to show the boys what tough really was. Here too the play twists an old maxim: It may be that hell hath no fury like a woman scorned but here the fury is caused not, as the men would like to believe, by what they did in the past but by what they're doing now.

Chad Dembskis production might make more inventive use of the space (which is, after all, the selling point) but its intelligent about character. And the room gives an ineradicable performance of its own, one that's enhanced every time someone opens the bathroom door or lifts the window to give us a peek at Queen Street. Every overheard sound contributes, and every surly bulb of neon. Come to Toronto if you want to shoot a film about Lansing. You could show it at both festivals.

BETHANY'S GATE

Theatre Centre, Toronto

The most influential theatrical practitioners in Toronto may be the clowning duo known as Mump and Smoot. Their own appearances may be infrequent, but they are always turning up, as directors or coaches, in the credits for other peoples productions. Or their names may just be listed among the acknowledgments in the program, as is the case with Bethanys Gate, a show with unmistakable symptoms of Mumps and Smootiness.

Bethany's Gate is a short, rather sweet lampoon of classical ballet. All the performers wear shiny red noses, an unusual occurrence in ballet but very much in accordance with the technique of Pochinko clowning, which is the brand espoused and disseminated by M&S. The noses carry with them a couple of built-in advantages, both fully exploited here: They make the performers look slightly funny, no matter what they're doing; and they function as a uniform without destroying anybodys individuality. If anything, they accentuate it.

The story concerns a princess who is the victim of a magic spell, a swain who hopelessly falls for her, and a corps of animals. The ending is happy, if you discount the fact that the principal characters are dead. It is, in fact, what philistines, myself included, will recognize as basic ballet. Whetstone Productions, the group presenting the show, seems to be composed of performers who are not primarily dancers, at least not in this idiom, so the piece has an unfortunate tendency to look less like a parody than like the real thing done badly. This is not, however, catastrophic.

Bethanys Gate has been advertised as "a ballet within a play." I don't think the thing the ballet is within can truthfully be described as a play, but it does involve a lot of talk, much of which is amusing. The eight actors, or whatever they are, purport to be members-in-exile of the National Ballet of Gorgontrevich. We are never told precisely where Gorgontrevich is, but one would guess it to be somewhere in the East End of Central Europe. I deduce this from its former inhabitants' accents, which are ripely generic, and from the slide show of their homeland with which they favour us early on. This suggests that Gorgontrevich is one of those picturesque states whose main industry had better be tourism. Otherwise, its in trouble. Not that it isnt anyway, what with the revolution that has driven out the dancers (monarchists to a person) and with the terrible memory of what its citizens tremblingly refer to as the Great Schism.

Most of this valuable knowledge is relayed to us by the troupe's artistic director, one Nicholas Denouement, who also dances the role of the hero, for which he seems frankly a little long in the tooth. He begins the evening in fairly standard fashion by forbidding us to use cameras (unless, he notes while adopting a becoming pose, we use them to take pictures of him) and goes on to tell us the history of Bethany's Gate, the Gorgontrevich National Ballets national ballet. It seems the original choreography (1793) was lost for a couple of centuries and has only recently been rediscovered, though what we see might easily have been assembled from guesswork by any reasonably competent dance teacher at an elementary school.

Nicholas is played, in a wittily captured vein of pained egomania, by David Tomlinson, though you have to dig deep in the program to disinter this information. Meagan OShea appears as Madame Zola, who in turn appears as the bewitched and bewitching Bethany. The madame seems -- one feels free to mention this now that the girth of opera singers has become a matter of open debate -- somewhat plumper than one expects of a prima ballerina. Indeed, the relationship of Nicholas and Zola -- he evasive, she adoring -- is strongly reminiscent of that of Kermit the Frog and Miss Piggy.

This brings us to the dance itself, in which the creatures surrounding the unfortunate Bethany (and her gate) are all, of course, offering red noses to a blue lady. This raises a question: Do the appendages belong to the characters in the ballet or to the dancers portraying them or to the actors portraying them? And then again: Are the lumpen movements of the chorus actually a choreographic comment on the assembled beasts of field and forest (indistinguishable on stage, if not in the cast list) or are they just bad luck?

Not that there aren't some pleasing performances going on here. I liked the coyly flirtatious Mina (Diana Kolpak) and the shy but intense Patina (Kathleen LeRoux), and was greatly struck by Eeejit (Hadrian Abbot) who is both surly and burly and looks like Rick Salutin in tights. But, frankly, if Whetstone Productions really expect us to see any interaction between the characters in the ballet and those of the Gorgonetrevichers themselves (or do we, with special reference to the name Zola, call them Gorgons for short?) then Whetstone Productions is fooling itself. Both levels are far too sketchy to permit that kind of carry-on.

There is some musical pleasure. The original Gorgontrevich score must have gone the way of the original Gorgontrevich steps, but we are treated instead to Bernstein and Borodin -- the overture to Candide and dance music from Prince Igor. The former is always a delight to hear, and those in the know can sing along to it, as its principal melody is that of the song Oh Happy We. You can also, if you had the same kind of warped musical upbringing I did, annoy your neighbours by singing the Borodin, as it's the tune that turned up in Kismet as Not Since Nineveh.

Though the show lasts only an hour, it does have an intermission. For this, however, we stay in the auditorium -- which, considering the available lobby space at Theatre Centre, is a good idea.

As our hosts put it, we bring intermission to you. They also bring trays of doughnuts and bottled water that we are allowed, indeed encouraged, to buy. The doughnuts are a dollar apiece; "dollars to doughnuts" used to signify long odds but the economy has changed.

More intrepid patrons can buy kisses from Mina or have their faces sculpted in cheese (a traditional Gorgon art form) by Patina. We have here an exemplary combination of hospitality with entrepreneurship, one that our more established theatres might well emulate. I look forward to being served by company members at CanStage (wine and cheese) or the Shaw Festival (tea and crumpets).

Bethanys Gate is directed by Kolpak and Tomlinson, and written by them "with the company." Original music is by James Fisher, who has CDs for sale though not during the intermission, and choreography by OShea. Lighting is credited on one slip of paper to Sharon DiGenova and on another, far more plausibly, to Oskar Gongonzovich.

Black & White Photo: Diana Kolpak / David Tomlinson as Durwin (he also co-wrote the work) and choreographer Meagan O'Shea as Bethany.

THE RIDE DOWN MT. MORGAN

Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

The climax of Arthur Miller's Death of a Salesman comes when the protagonist, Willy Loman, commits suicide by crashing his car. The same author's The Ride Down Mt. Morgan, premiered a full 42 years later in 1991, begins where the older play stopped, sort of. Its hero, Lyman Felt, is revealed to us in a hospital bed, his presence there being the result of his having driven full-tilt down the icy hill referred to in the title. Its at least possible he was trying to kill himself.

From Loman to Lyman is a long haul, and not just chronologically. Suicide was the only thing at which Willy L. ever succeeded. It seems to be the only thing at which Mr L. Felt has ever failed. In his youth he was a promising poet, published in The New Yorker, and a friend of James Baldwin; he then switched to selling insurance, a field in which he is now a mogul. (The world may be full of poets- turned-insurance-men, but there can be few who were that good at both.) Willy had an extramarital affair on the road, but it wasnt really crucial to his downfall. Lyman may owe his present prone position to the fact that he has had two wives, simultaneously.

"That's bigamy! said a shocked Margaret Dumont to some leering proposition of Groucho Marx, to which Groucho replied well, its big o' me, too. Lets be big for a change." Lyman thinks, at least some of the time; he sees himself, in his less guilt-wracked moments, as an explorer, an adventurer and a man who really loves women. And though the play has some moral and intellectual quarrels with this position, emotionally its on his side. It can hardly help this, because it's written from his point of view.

Miller's original title for Salesman was The Inside of His Head, and he might well have resurrected it as at least a subtitle for this play. Receiving the news that both his wives have been called to his bedside, Lyman gloomily imagines the course of their inevitable meeting. We see his imaginings played out, and they seem to be 100% accurate.

From their home in New York -- probably an East Side townhouse -- comes Lymans legal partner, Theo, svelte and businesslike and attended by divorced daughter Bessie, who takes the situation even worse than her mother does. Bessie rages; Theo just faints, though she has some bitter things to say when she comes to. From the immediate neighbourhood comes Leah, also prominent in the insurance business but with a very different style. Theo puts her down as a kind of leftover hippie, the kind, in Theos estimation, who never bothers to wash her underwear. She's earth-motherly, and a literal mother as well, having born Lyman a young son whom we never see.

Subsequent encounters between the parties seem to be in real time; Lyman, however, reserves the right to disappear through a hole in the bed when the discussions get too heated, then to reappear at the side of the stage and lose himself in reminiscence. In other words, there are flashbacks. Technically there is nothing very challenging about this, but the mood and style are very difficult to hit off. The present production is both the play's Canadian premiere and the first offering of a new company called Birdland Theatre; it has had a nightmarish preparatory period -- the word "jinxed" hardly seems adequate -- that has included the deaths of two of the principal people involved, one of them the director, Cameron Wright. Ones heart goes out to all involved, and it seems cruel, however necessary, to point out that the element most missing from the show is playfulness.

Part of this is the plays fault. Its structure is comic -- the first scene between the wives borders on farce, and is framed as such -- and its texture tries to be, but it lacks both the verbal and the narrative inventiveness to keep its ideas afloat. Lyman declares that, after a lifetime of subterfuge, he wants to tell the truth, and the truths he tells are comic ones, of the painful variety; of how he has been bored in both his marriages, and used each to alleviate the other, to the benefit of all concerned. (There is one brief, funny scene that shows this system in action. It seems to work, at least in the short term.) He talks a lot, but -- intentionally or not -- his words form a smokescreen; we never get a real sense of what either union was actually like.

You start to wonder, impertinently and perhaps irrelevantly, what it all means to Miller himself, thrice-married though only sequentially. There is little of the social resonance you get in his earlier plays (from All My Sons, via Salesman and The Crucible, to A View from the Bridge). Like Harold Pinter, whom he otherwise little resembles, Miller has tended to write about rich people since becoming one himself, and the air in his later work seems less nourishing. I know there have been suggestions that Lyman's behaviour is a comment on the ethos of the 1980s, but I've never believed that selfishness, greed or hedonism were inventions of that decade. Besides, those qualities in Lyman are the most attractive ones in the play. He has a lively mind, which is just as well considering the amount of the play that takes place there.

The role calls for the wit, the style, and the passion, both intellectual and sexual, of a Christopher Plummer; indeed its difficult to think of another Canadian with the weight and range to play it. Ron White manages the elegant ironies very well as long as hes sitting up in bed, but when he starts getting up and burrowing into his past, he cannot find a full man there.

The production has apparently been staged by the actors themselves, in accordance with their director's presumed intentions, but the results are ragged. Pace slackens; exits and entrances seem drained of energy or purpose; the set takes economy to the point of drabness; crystals hanging from the ceiling cast flickering, distracting reflections throughout. Kate Trotter as Theo has some memorably angry moments, and a provocative semi-mad scene near the end, but Zorana Kydd does little to suggest what Lyman's second wife may have had that his first didnt.

There is good, impeccably dressed support from Peter Van Wart as Lymans lawyer, the voice of conventional decency (i.e., he wonders why his client didn't just have an affair the second time around) and really excellent support from Marium Carvell as a nurse who, if she were free, might well elicit Lyman's third proposal. Melissa Kramer plays the thoroughly ungrateful role of the thoroughly ungrateful daughter, who admittedly has much to be ungrateful about.

No Miller play is dismissable, and this one has more substance buried in it than anything by Edward Albee, on whose territory it seems sometimes to be trespassing, but it needs more, from everybody.

Color Photo: Guntar Kravis / Melissa Kramer, Ron White and Kate Trotter.

AFTER THE FALL

Equity Showcase Theatre

For anyone in Toronto with an obsessive interest in the life and loves of Arthur Miller, now is the time. At Berkeley Street, we have the Canadian premiere of The Ride Down Mt. Morgan (1991), which takes us inside the mind of a high-flying bigamist. Miller himself has been married three times, most famously to Marilyn Monroe, and its all been perfectly legal, but still one senses a resonance.

That play has now been joined by Equity Showcase's revival of After the Fall (1964), which is far more blatantly, not to say notoriously, autobiographical. Or perhaps the word is self- referential; or even self-indulgent. Actually there's no even about it. After the Fall may well be the most self-indulgent play ever staged.

It lasts three hours, and it contains some stunning scenes, all of them about marriage. You have to wait for them, though, and you spend most of the wait listening to the protagonist talking. Sometimes he talks to other characters, but for much of the play he harangues an unseen auditor who may, according to his authors preface, be either God or his shrink. (The heros shrink, not the playwright's or the deity's.)

My own impression was that he was addressing a meeting of Angst Anonymous. To the portmanteau words invoked above, I would add "self- flagellating" and, especially, self-justifying. I would stop short, though, of "self-serving." Millers unremitting uprightness may get on your nerves -- it does on mine -- but this is a work of agonizingly honest intent. You respect it, even while glancing furtively at your watch.

Distancing himself, Miller has made his surrogate a lawyer, name of Quentin. He too is thrice-spliced. His first wife is, well, his first wife -- acquired, one imagines, before he got successful. His second is Maggie, the Marilyn figure, here transformed from an actress to a singer, though working as a switchboard operator when first he encounters her. His third, who hovers on the plays margins radiating wisdom and understanding, presumably parallels Inge Morath, the Swedish photographer who became Miller's last, and lasting, spouse. Here she is named Holga and is German. When Quentin meets her she is a tour guide at a concentration camp. He was too callow for his first marriage, and unable to cope with his second (who could?); now he hopes to prove worthy of his third.

My people died in this place, says Quentin at the camp. "They also built it." He is referring, one imagines, not to the Jewish race but to the human one. Miller's gloss on his title is that the expulsion from Eden endowed humanity with the power of moral choice, and that humanity has been trying to wriggle out of the responsibility ever since. Cains first instinct when charged by God was to deny responsibility. Miller quotes that primal evasion in the introduction to this play, and goes back to it in the actual text of The Ride Down Mt. Morgan.

Quentin feels guilty about everything, including his attempts not to feel guilty. His conscience casts a frustratingly wide net. His father went bust in the 1929 crash; his mother blamed his father at the time and has gone on doing so ever since. Some of this has rubbed off on Quentin himself, but its hard to see exactly what.

He also seems to feel bad about his brother, though this relationship is very sketchily drawn. (Perhaps Miller trusted us to take it for granted. His plays are full of fraternal tensions. No wonder he keeps harking back to Cain and Abel.)

Later, Quentin, like Miller, goes through McCarthyism. His old professor, summoned before the committee, commits suicide. Quentin has stood by him, personally and professionally, but still feels inexplicably responsible. Another friend is subpoenaed, and opts to be a friendly witness. (The original production of After the Fall was directed by that most celebrated of name-namers, Elia Kazan. Those rehearsals must have been fun.)

It's practically impossible to write boringly about the blacklist, and these scenes are duly gripping. But the fog that surrounds them, in the shape of Quentin's musings after and even during the event, is almost impenetrable. I have seen two productions of After the Fall, and at each of them my main response to the actor playing the lead was one of amazement that he could have remembered all those lines, followed by admiration that he should have made sense of them.

In this production, Joseph Gallaccios memory is impeccable and his phrasing mostly lucid, though he sometimes confuses natural with casual. As for characterization, there is none, nor is any possible.

Anyway, were waiting for Marilyn, or Maggie. There's an earlier character, who in this production looks more Monroevian than Maggie herself does, and may be said to function, both psychologically and dramaturgically, as a pneumatic tease.

But when the real Maggie finally appears, near the end of the first act, she gives the play an electric shock. When Quentin first meets her, she's just a girl on a park bench, nervous and eager, arousing his protectiveness ahead of his libido. (This is a far cry from Millers first encounter with Monroe, which occurred when she was an official Hollywood sex goddess.)

In London a few years ago, Maggie was played by a mercurial black actress, suggesting that we were watching a play about what might have happened if Arthur Miller had married Billie Holiday. In this production shes a stocky gamine, so it's more as if Miller had hooked up with Judy Garland; Lesley Faulkner, a find, is erotic vulnerability personified, a dream when she's nobody in particular, and a nightmare when she supposedly has the whole world at her feet.

Like Marilyn -- or Billie or Judy -- Maggie is drug-dependent and impossibly demanding and impossibly needy. Her scenes with Quentin are riveting, the circumstances are extravagant, but the dynamic, the ebb and flow, seem to be those of any couple, magnified. Even Quentins habit of lecturing her, as he does everybody else, rather than talking to her is believable; he would, and its his only line of defence.

The play has been accused of exploiting Monroe, but I don't agree; I think it makes her live. The mastery of domestic tension stretches back into Quentin's first marriage, especially when his first wife gets jealous and begins bristling at every ring of the phone. Mind you, however heavy the authors guilt trip, its still hard not to hear him crowing, somewhere behind it all, "I've been to bed with Marilyn Monroe."

Rod Ceballos' staging is excellent, especially in a final sequence in which Quentin silently confronts everybody from his past, present and future. The production is especially commendable, considering the special circumstances of Equity Showcase. Many of the large cast are inexperienced, some dont have union cards, and there are several performances by actors who are either too young for their roles or just not good enough.

But it doesnt matter. One adjusts. One adjusts better, in fact, than at The Ride Down Mt. Morgan, which has a cast of seasoned but largely miscast professionals, a kind of soft-centredness to which actor-driven companies like the new Birdland Theatre are especially prone. (One of Soulpepper's great achievements is that, whatever traps they may have fallen into, they've avoided that one. They've never seemed outclassed by their plays.) In other respects, After the Fall made me feel better about Mt. Morgan, just as the author himself seems to have done. In the later play, he leaves off blaming himself and lets cheerfulness break in. It's a great relief all around.

Black & White Photo: David Sweeney / Joseph Gallaccio as Quentin and Lesley Faulkner as Wife No. 2, also known as Maggie.

ROGUES OF URFA

Artword Theatre, Toronto

Araxi Arslanian's grandfather survived the Turkish massacre of the Armenians during the First World War. She herself has survived Arterio-Venous Malformation, a brain disorder that kills most of the people it afflicts. Her play Rogues of Urfa, which she performs herself, is a solo piece that tells these two stories in alternating slabs, narrated by protagonists whose kinship is revealed only at the end.

One doesnt want to make light of so much real suffering, but the mixture doesnt take. The monologue form is always perilous, and here it has the effect of reducing an individual medical case- history and the virtual elimination of an entire people to the level of a couple of hard-luck stories. Plays about illness are always a tough proposition because the pain, in most cases, is nobody's fault; ergo, there is no conflict. If such a subject is to have any dramatic life, it has to be approached from other points of view besides that of the sufferer; otherwise, the play becomes a mere complaint.

The Armenian holocaust obviously presents different opportunities and different problems. The event may be said to have set the tone for the 20th century; Hitler famously said the world's amnesia about the Armenians made him feel safe about eliminating the Jews. The details are horribly familiar: the families burned alive in their own homes, the mass graves dug by the victims, the death marches, the war obscuring the whole operation. (At that, there seems to have been more international protest over this genocide than over the later one -- not that it did any good.) Only the gas chambers are missing, but doubtless the Turks would have got around to those if theyd had the technology and if theyd had numbers as great to dispose of. It's a story that still needs telling, and it provides some duly harrowing moments here. But it is diminished -- not only in scale but in emotional impact -- in being presented so much as the story of one man. Arslanian's forbearer comes from the town of Urfa, identified as the birthplace of Abraham (and so presumably identical with the Bibles Ur of the Chaldees).

I am a young man of the city, he says, "its secret prince." Many times he repeats this rubric, whose first part may be unexceptionable, but whose second is never supported: His story supplants that of his granddaughter every time. It functions, in fact, as a form of aural ID -- one that starts out mildly irritating and ends up screamingly intolerable by the end. He and two friends escape from one of the forced marches and take refuge with the French army; returning home after the war they find prejudice as rampant as before -- another example of history, so to speak, anticipating itself. The trio are presumably the titles rogues of Urfa but there is nothing very colourful about them to justify the appellation -- and it also seems to devalue the intercut story of Arslanian herself, which is surely meant to be equally important.

That it is literally her story is only made explicit at the very end, when her father addresses her by the author's own first name; but it has been plain enough all the way through. She begins by telling us how, as a schoolgirl in Canada, she tried to present a puppet play on the Armenian experience, and how her classmates laughed at her; initially one assumes that this was racial prejudice, but it turns out that she was exhibiting the first symptoms of AVM. Admitted, full of hope, to the National Theatre School, she is forced to leave -- by what seems, from her account, to have been a monstrously unsympathetic administration -- when she started having seizures. Then came a spell at university and an eventual breakthrough into the professional theatre, where she went through hell at the hands of colleagues who referred to her as "Seizure Sally." This seems to refer to her appearance in a Toronto production of Our Country's Good for which, nonetheless, she won a Dora -- an event she has recalled in interviews with, it must be admitted, justifiable satisfaction.

One sympathizes, sometimes painfully, with her constant feelings of being excluded, but still feels that one is only hearing half the story; however appallingly people may have behaved to her, the laws of the theatre dictate that they should be condemned out of their own mouths rather than hers. George Orwell said that an autobiography should only be believed when it shows its subject in a bad light, and the same applies even more to a play-length soliloquy. Everything Arslanian tells us may be factually true, but it doesnt make good drama.

In pursuing her drive toward self-vindication (or, if jargons your dish, self-empowerment) Arslanian may actually be short- changing herself, since she seems competent as a writer and skilled as a performer. A big lady, she throws herself enthusiastically into the angular bits of mime-to-music that her director, Rebecca Brown, has either devised or permitted to mark the transitions between her two principal personae. None of her characters is much characterized, but she shifts very confidently between voices.

The conclusion, that survival runs in the family, comes across both hurried and sentimental; one can feel happy at the escapes of both generations without regarding them as more than a fortunate coincidence. Recurring references to sand and "white light" are not enough to unify the play's two halves. As a person Arslanian is fully entitled to her convictions on this score -- she has probably more than earned them -- but as a dramatist she needs to persuade rather than affirm.

The Artword Theatre hosts this production, but did not originate it; all the same, despite the horrors that it relates, it's very much in the house's familiar folksy feel-good mould.

Black & White Photo: Randy Brown / Araxi Arslanian won a Dora for her work in Our Country's Good.
2004-03-29-the-musical-brat-pack:
robertcushman@lycos.com

The Top o' the Senator, Thursday night, was as packed as I have ever known the place. The occasion, a cross between musical set and media junket, was the Canadian debut of young British singer- pianist Jamie Cullum. Cameramen hunkered down at the front of the room obliterated the lower half of the stage, enabling the star to make a highly effective surprise entrance. There he suddenly was, standing atop the piano and giving out, unaccompanied (well, obviously), with the verse to Cole Porters I Get a Kick out of You.

Cullum is one of the current crop of musical juveniles singing standard songs (sometimes) in jazz settings (also sometimes); they might be described as a musical Brat Pack, especially considering that that phrase, in its original movie context, was a pun on the name of Frank Sinatras bunch. Other members are American Peter Cincotti and Canadian Michael Buble; their godfather, who trod the same path a decade ago and has recently shown signs of returning to it, is Harry Connick Jr. Of them all, Cullum seems to me the best -- though I'd add the rider that he's the only one of the newcomers Ive seen live and that hes a more exciting act in person than he is on disc.

One thing I chauvinistically like about him is his un- Americanness. British singers attempting this repertoire often end up sounding mid-Atlantic -- which means from nowhere -- but there's a vestigial rasp and snarl in Cullum's vocals, a sound that would once have been called Cockney but is now just classless-ubiquitous, and that lends humour and an edge.

It isnt hostile; Cullum himself comes across as a nice young man, fresh out of college. Its both self-aware and self- deprecating, and it comes in especially useful in the chat between songs, a part of the business in which very few American singers have managed to avoid sounding pompous. Cullum's laid-back introductions are a point of rest to set against his manic physical activity. When he gets around to actually playing the piano, he's liable to stand up and attack it, Jerry Lee Lewis fashion, or reach inside it to take prolonged solos on its strings. Physically slight, temperamentally impish, aggressively mobile, he suggests Mick Jagger cast as a supper-club Frodo.

When he gets into the chorus of I Get a Kick, hes a born-again post-rocker, pounding out a rhythm that could be called enraged swing, but sensitive to lyrics, especially the ones about cocaine; as he shruggingly says afterwards, the song might have been written yesterday. Later he does I Could Have Danced All Night, very convincingly, as the hangover from a rave. He includes the verse to this one, too, which is most unusual for someone who isnt Julie Andrews.

He also does more recent stuff, including Jimi Hendrix' The Wind Cries Mary and Jeff Buckley's Baby, You Shouldve Come Over, making a better musical case for the former than for the latter; he didnt do much for the lyrics of either. (He was much clearer on the standards, or maybe it's just that I know those words backwards anyway.)

But a lot of his show just merged, enjoyably. At one point he wandered away from the piano for an engaging saunter through Singin' in the Rain. It seemed to follow on logically from what went before, but Ive still no idea how, musically, he got there.

His sidemen, Geoff Gascoyne (bass) and Sebastian DeKrom (drums), played superbly and were loyal foils.

The CD Twentysomething (Verve, to be released here May 11) unhelpfully adds a band, which sounds like an afterthought and, along with the lack of an audience, accentuates the cracks in the singers voice; rough would be better. And most of those welcome verses are missing. There are several of Cullum's original compositions, which tend to start better than they finish; the title number has a terrific premise (what do you do with an arts degree?) but degenerates into an aimless list. The best is a song called It's About Time.

Like all his contemporaries, he has been hailed as being, and damned for not being, the new Sinatra. Its a pointless comparison, if only because the Sinatra whos being invoked never existed at any given time; he's an essence of the singer, distilled from a career of 50 years. None of the newcomers has the sweet sound of Sinatra in his band-singing twenties; they've gone straight for the burned- out, world-weary voice without having gone through the years it took its owner to earn it. To put it another way, they sound like Bobby Darin, first and best of the post-Sinatras, but without the vocal energy. Cullum, despite reproducing a Sinatra interpolation on Kick, sounds the least like an imitator, which means he may have the best chance of emulating the original and making the songs his own.

Of the others, Cincotti is the one being marketed most simply as a jazzman; his self-titled CD (Concord), recorded last year when he was 19, features just bass, drums, sax and his own piano, on which he is strikingly clever and assured. (His Erroll Garner impression on Spinning Wheel is a warm musical joke.) His singing is boyish going on brash, best of all on Miss Brown to You.

Michael Buble, who also has a self-titled CD (Warner/Reprise), has the richest voice of the bunch -- certainly the smoothest -- but is really being sandbagged with Sinatra. Not only does he sing the songs (a Summer Wind thats here more of a feckless breeze), he even sings the arrangements; Billy Mays familiar chart on Come Fly with Me is reproduced, so we can sing along with Buble singing along with Sinatra, a sort of double karaoke. It's fun to play in the car. Buble could probably deliver better; on his quiet concluding track (That's All), he does. Maybe hell turn into Vic Damone. One song, the Latin perennial Sway, turns up on both discs. Bubles is the Arthur Murray version; Cincotti actually sounds like a kid longing shyly for a dance, which is unusual on this kind of song, and makes sense.

Connick, now the senior of the juniors, has a new CD, Only You (Sony), composed of songs from the '50s and '60s, a period less musically rich than he seems to believe, or maybe it's just that his choices are odd. (Who wants to hear more of More?) His singing is sleepier than ever -- Dean Martin on the wagon, perhaps -- but it yields some unexpected rewards, notably on a doggedly pleading Save the Last Dance for Me. His arranging -- his greatest talent, I think -- is excellent. For Once in My Life sounds fresh (for once in its life) with what appears to be the relentless plucking of whole banks of strings.

THE TERRIBLE FALSE DECEPTION, SMOKE

Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

Rafe Macpherson describes The Terrible False Deception, of which he is the author, as "a four act play in 40 minutes, or 42 with laughs." He also tells us that there is no intermission between the acts, which might be surprising in other circumstances but is only to be expected in these. He must know, because he obviously planned it that way, that his play has a title tautological enough to worry Al Franken. This befits the piece, a merry exercise in which the same four actors repeat the same actions four times over, while speaking completely different lines each time around.

They also appear throughout in the same costumes and on the same set; the designs suggest they are appearing in some elegant period comedy, perhaps something by Marivaux. (He wrote Les Fausses Confidences, which there is nothing to stop somebody translating as The Terrible False Deceptive Confidences.) At the beginning of Act One, a middle-aged woman, perhaps a servant or a confidante, enters, takes a letter from a desk, and places it in her bosom; and if that's not shorthand for comedy of intrigue, I should like to know what is. A young man in a uniform, a hussar or dragoon, follows her on, and is followed in his turn by a youngish lady, posing and flirtatious in a white dress; these two must be the romantic interest, married or otherwise. Last on is an older man; he is clearly the older man.

These actors are not, though, speaking period dialogue, or indeed any kind of dialogue having anything to do with plot. Instead they are telling us what, as actors, they are thinking. They are thinking dissatisfied thoughts about the script, the production, and the talents of their fellow performers i.e. of one another. In Act Two they go through the same motions, but this time speaking the lines that were set down for them. Apparently the play they're in isn't French at all, it's Russian. It can't be Chekhov; rather it suggests those formidable Russian names one encounters in textbooks on the history of drama, names like Ostrovsky and Griboyedov. These masters have seldom been well served by their translators, and the quality of what we hear on this occasion richly confirms what we already know to be the opinion of the actors. They are forced to say things like "I cannot drink, and I trust never will I."

I'm a sucker for this kind of in-jokery, and I loved it when in Act One, Angela Fusco, as the actress playing the housekeeper, or whatever she is, picked up a hat and remarked that there was no earthly reason for her to do such a thing, but that she had been given absolutely NO direction. I liked it even more when Patricia Yeatman, as the actress playing the countess, or whatever she is, outlined the way in which she would deliver a big speech, starting quietly and ending very loud and throwing in arbitrary pauses of the kind guaranteed to impress audiences -- all it of course preparing for the Act Two pay-off in which, at the identical moment, she delivers just such a speech in just such a fashion. Macpherson (who has a day job as a dresser at Mamma Mia!) has provided only basic satire of the conventions of classic comedy, but he's stiletto-mean when dealing with conventions of actors.

Act One is billed as Theatre of the Self-Aware and Act Two as Theatre of the Unaware. Act Three is Theatre of the Underwear, which may make you think that at this point the author began to get a bit desperate. This time the actors are talking about their sexual fantasies; in this act they probably aren't actors at all but real people at a costume party. Act Four (Untitled) gives us another twist, the performers lamenting just how foolish they were to get involved in such a pretentious pseudo-experimental piece as the play we've been watching, and indeed are still watching. It's no wonder that one of them starts speculating on the possibility that they are all dead and in hell. Also, there's been hanky-panky over their contracts. But a play can't escape the charge of being too clever by half just by owning up to it -- and thereby augmenting the offence. "Too clever by half" is indeed a mathematically accurate estimate; the play stops being entertaining smack dab in its middle, or when it aims to be something more ambitious than a poor man's Noises Off. However, the laughs accumulated before then do allow the play to chalk up 41-and-a-half of the 42 minutes it's aiming for. It's well performed, with Kyle McDonald (who seems excessively callow) and Wally Michaels playing the men, though it might work better as an excuse for more established classical actors to send themselves up rotten.

Vinetta Stromberg directs the play, which she first mounted at the Toronto Fringe in 2002. The afterpiece, Smoke by Michael Maclean, was done by the same director at the Fringe of 1997. It's a morose monologue about a man with a craving for SOMETHING, whether it's tobacco or something more spiritually nourishing. The titular metaphor also curls around the character's description of his father's death and funeral, which seem to be the central disorienting events in his own life. It renewed my suspicion of all one-person plays that don't involve laughs, songs or Kristen Thomson. Otherwise, you might just as well read them as see them. Actually, it's the kind of piece that people always say, wrongly, would work better on radio. In fact radio drama depends even more than the theatre on action and on the contrast of personalities; the stage, when deprived of these things, still can't help giving you something to look at. Here it's Hume Baugh, with a face and voice that are open but ravaged. He does a good job, but not good enough to hold my attention, which had wandered within five minutes of the start.

THE RED PRIEST

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

Antonio Vivaldi became accustomed to going to parties, some of them given by nobles or even by kings, at which the house band would play The Four Seasons. This was before the days of royalties, even from royalty, but he knew it was doing him good in the world, and it was flattering besides. All the same, he began to wish people would realize that he had written other things as well, and he found himself listening to his greatest hit with gritted teeth. So much I have learned from Mieko Ouchis The Red Priest, in which Vivaldi is one of the two characters. Once a feted and fashionable composer, he is slipping from favour and is, as he prophetically tells us, only a short time away from a paupers grave. If you adopt the Peter Shaffer view of musical history, he is Mozart and Salieri combined, the doomed genius and the jealous cynic in one.

This might also be called the play in which Amadeus meets Arcadia. The other character, known only as the Woman, is the wife of a French aristocrat. She feels imprisoned in her marriage, which to her is symbolized by her husband's precise patterned gardens. Vivaldi is hired to teach her the violin; a wager has been made that, in a mere six weeks she will perform before the current king, who only happens to be Louis XIV. She professes little interest in learning -- and less aptitude. Vivaldi is a practised instructor; he spent years teaching convent girls, back home in Italy, and is theoretically in orders himself -- hence the play's title.

There is much initial mistrust between the two, even stretching to mutual contempt. They are both unhappily trapped in their social roles and take their feelings out on one another, with the difference that she can vent some of her feelings out loud while he is constrained to keep his under wraps. But the ice melts, and music brings them together; they even fall, chastely, in love. I wouldnt say this was predictable -- I didnt feel involved enough to wonder what would happen next -- but it's no great surprise, either. Much of the text is made up of the two characters' embittered soliloquies; some of these are interesting, especially those that feed us information about the composers past life, but they stand still, luxuriating in their own images instead of surging forward.

The duologues are as carefully laid out as the grounds of Monsieurs chateau, but they are hardly more exciting. We understand that The Woman's marital predicament is humiliating and may well be about to become even more so, but we never feel it. Conceivably she would be more interesting if she had a name, but I can appreciate the tact of not giving her one. Vivaldi is a historical personage, she is an imaginary one; so making her his equal by calling her Madame Something would ring subtly false. But then, why has a real composer been dragged in in the first place? It helps atmospherically, of course, to be able to have his music playing in the background, more or less continuously, but it feels like cultural ballast.

The play, especially in its earlier scenes, reads better than it acts, or at least better than it's acted here -- this despite the fact that the same cast and director have already done it in Calgary and Edmonton and that the playwright is also one of the performers. The worldwide commercial success of Two Pianos, Four Hands is said to have been limited by the difficulty of finding actors who can play the piano. It must be even harder to find an actress who can play the violin.

Ouchi fulfills this part of her own assignment admirably; she succeeds especially well in the presumably daunting task of charting the pupils progress from unbearable to really rather good. (Its hard to play bad on purpose.) Her non-instrumental playing, though, is pinched and suburban; lines that were presumably meant by their author to glitter -- and that look, on paper, as if they had a chance of doing so -- are delivered, also by their author, so that they droop. The Woman may be miserable in her position, but she should look and sound capable of filling it. Ouchi can be poignant when crushed, but in her haughtier moments, which are most of them, she presents no challenge.

Ashley Wright's Vivaldi is more fleshed-out, with a good line in acid self-torment, but no sparks fly between the two of them.

Ron Jenkins' production looks elegant enough on David Boechlers formal landscape of a set, but its pulse is slow, as if presuming on a dynamic that hasnt actually happened.

The play has a subtitle, Eight Ways to Say Goodbye. This derives from a game the Woman plays with herself, reeling off the different excuses she might give for leaving her husband. When she plays it for the last time, at the very end of the play, there's a twist. Vivaldi, shortly before this, gives his own version of the same routine, prophesying the steps by which he will approach his own demise. Terse and pungent, it's the best speech in the play, maybe because it summarizes actual events rather than filling out an author's frail fancy. He then adds a ninth step: Be forgotten for 200 years." So he was, and the words reverberate.

But the reverberations have nothing to do with what has gone before, where Vivaldi, apart from the tunes and the odd biographical snippet, could be anybody. Amadeus, for all its faults, had some ideas about what Mozart and his music may have meant to his contemporaries. It also had a vulgar energy of which no one could accuse The Red Priest.

2004-04-05-when-ustinov-was-king-peter-u:
From Fifty Seasons at Stratford by Robert Cushman (McClelland & Stewart). Peter Ustinov died on March 28 at the age of 82.; Obituary of Peter Ustinov.

As artistic director of the Stratford Festival from 1975 to 1980, Robin Phillips most successful tragedy, beyond a doubt, was King Lear, mounted in 1979 and 80 as a vehicle -- there really is no other word -- for Peter Ustinov. From one point of view this was a throwback to the days of Frederick Valk as Shylock: a star journeying to Stratford to play a single role. From another, it could not have been more different. Valk was a titanic actor recreating a role that he had already made his own. Ustinov was a charmingly informal performer essaying not only Lear but Shakespeare for the very first time.

His classical credentials, in fact, were slightly more impressive than that might suggest. In the 1950s he had played a memorable Peer Gynt -- live, uncut, spread over two evenings and in a rhyming translation -- for BBC Television, and Peer in his old age contains strong intimations of Lear. (In his youth he recalls Hamlet and in his middle years Falstaff. It must be the best part ever written.) One of Ustinov's own early plays, The Moment of Truth, was about a senile military head of state modelled about equally on Marshal Petain and Shakespeare's king, and Ustinovs original title for it had been King Lears Photographer. He had been obsessed with Lear for years.

Ustinov believed the play to be about senility. This was the cause of Lear's capricious behaviour toward his daughters in the first scene; this was the real diagnosis of his madness in the central scenes. When he claimed he would do such things, what they were yet he knew not, but they would be the terrors of the Earth, the reason he didn't know was that hed forgotten.

Vocally, of course, the terrors of the Earth were beyond Ustinovs range. Some critics complained of his failure to release the full power of the verse, as if this were some kind of wilful omission on his part, but the obvious truth is that he didn't because he couldn't. He made no attempt to outroar the storm or to create it with his voice. "Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks," he modestly suggested, and left the winds to get on with it.

He made no bones about Lears impossible behaviour, but he was funny (as Lear certainly should be) and charming and pitiable: too easily pitiable, perhaps, to be truly moving. There seemed, really, to be nothing for Cordelia to forgive. It was understandable that Kent and the others should want to look after him, less so that they should revere him. Could he, for example, ever have been a great warrior? Then again, we were dealing here with a man, not a monolith.

In 1959 Charles Laughton, once Ustinovs colleague in corpulence in Spartacus, played King Lear at Stratford-upon-Avon and, despite some sublimely moving moments, failed. One reason was that he offered a small-scale performance in a traditionally scaled production: the kind that Phillips, preparing his own staging, referred to as a "Stonehenge" version.

Stonehenge can work -- it worked for Olivier's television performance -- but it would not have worked for Ustinov. Phillips cushioned him with a detailed realistic production set in his favoured 19th century. This was not an unprecedented idea: Trevor Nunn, three years earlier, had used the same period for a Lear starring Donald Sinden, another actor whom many people thought of primarily as a light comedian.

Phillips' production was more crammed than Nunns with realistic and domestic detail: This was an epauletted, cigar-smoking Lear, addressing family and friends from his favourite armchair. It helped that these pictures were framed within the Avon proscenium: It is difficult to imagine Ustinovs Lear commanding the Festival stage.

He had sympathetic support from Douglas Rain's Gloucester and Jim McQueen's Kent, and steely opposition from Richard Monettes Edmund and (in the second season) the Goneril and Regan of Martha Henry and Patricia Connolly. Above all he had William Hutt, pausing halfway through his own parade of Lears to offer a Fool whose stinging jokes were tempered by the sense that he knew -- in this case from experience -- exactly what the old boy was going through. Those who never saw Ustinovs Lear cannot quite believe that he brought it off. But plainly he did.

Black & White Photo: One of Ustinov's own early plays, The Moment of Truth, was originally titled King Lear's Photographer.

NUMBER ONE AND JAMIE

Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People

Alone among Toronto theatres, the former YPT seems to be on a roll. Where the other houses are, at best, treading water, this one is actually improving.

It even seems to be developing a style, one characterized by narrative drive and geometric neatness. These qualities, which were evident in this season's revival of New Canadian Kid, are even more forcefully present in the new and more ambitious, Number One and Jamie. It is, in fact, over-ambitious but thats a good fault, certainly at this address.

Usually, when a childrens theatre mounts a two-act two-hour production, it's of something borrowed from the adult repertoire. Paula Wing's play, by contrast, is custom-made. Jamie is a 10-year old whose problem, like most peoples, is fear.

His parents, currently together, have repeatedly split up in the past, which is enough in itself to make him insecure. His mother doesnt help by constantly worrying about him, though not about the things he worries about. (We don't meet his father; he works long hours and probably wouldn't have the time to put in a personal appearance.) Predictably but still amusingly, Jamie is embarrassed rather than reassured when his mother insists on collecting him from school.

Besides the terrors that really haunt him reside at home; he has a paper route in his own apartment building; fearful of what may lie in wait behind doors or around corners, he counts every one of his early-morning steps.

He lives in special fear of the unseen woman in Apartment One, whom he calls the Gorgon. When he does meet her, she turns out to be the wheelchair-bound landlady. She doesnt mind being called a cripple; "There are," she says, "worse things than insensitivity." Its a refrain with her that there are always worse things; a woman with a sharp and salty tongue, she listens in on her tenants' conversations, both live and telephonic, and is convinced that people are out to get her. She is, in fact, as scared as Jamie, though more entertainingly aggressive about it. She is especially afraid of a blue car parked outside, and part cajoles, part threatens, Jamie into trailing it. Spy and spymistress communicate first by walkie-talkie, later -- at Jamie's insistence and to Number Ones disgust -- by cellphone.

The chase is complicated by Jamies encounters with another lodger, an elderly Hungarian who qualifies, by current theatrical usage, as a second-generation refugee; he escaped, that is, not from the Nazis but from the Communists.

The riddles are only partly solved by the end; frustrating at one level, this is reasonable at another and a considerable compliment to young audiences. What Jamie has wandered in to is the world of adult sorrows, a world in which terrors persist and admit no easy solutions.

A less fruitful complication is Jamie's relationship with his friend of his own age, a boy whom he calls Risky Phil, because he's so risk-averse. Phil is as nervous as Jamie, but his response is to retreat into elaborate technological fantasies. The author is getting at something here but its not clear what it is.

Micheline Chevriers production unfolds in pools and strips of light, admirably designed by Christopher Dennis. Around the twilit edges of Deeter Schurig's ghostly set there lurk and skulk menacing anonymous figures in trench coats and fedoras. It isn't clear why the nightmares of a 21st-century child should be haunted by figures from 1940s film noir (maybe Jamie has been allowed to stay up too late watching television), but they are effective, if ultimately overused. We get into Jamies mind; we understand why, when his flat is burgled, he -- for complicated but childishly logical reasons -- should feel guilty about it.

The relationship between the plays two titular figures is not as central as the author presumably wants it to be; too many other elements jostle for our attention.

Still both Number One and Jamie are admirably played. Robin Craig makes a splendidly witty and fretful spider at the centre of the web; Keir Gilchrist copes very engagingly with what may be the longest role ever written for a pre-teen. (He is the play's narrator as well as its protagonist.)

As his contemporary, Demetrios Matthews has more trouble projecting, and their scenes together are murky. Deborah Drakeford is frazzled and funny as Jamie's mom, Harve Sokoloff capable but predictable in a role that may not permit of anything more.

It remains one of the best plays seen in Toronto this season; more compelling than most of the supposedly grown-up plays we have recently been offered and at least as intelligent.

Color Photo: Daniel Alexander / Demetrios Matthews plays Risky Phil and Keir Gilchrist the titular character in Number One and Jamie.
