PELAGIE

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

Many, perhaps most, musicals are based on something else. This rule seems to hold good everywhere except in Canada, where the best shows, with the odd happy exception like Leslie Arden's Happy Prince, are originals. Adaptations here tend to fall into the category immortally labelled by Mary Rodgers as "why musicals," which means, according to her friend Stephen Sondheim, why bother?

It seems a harsh question to put to Pelagie, a show with epic ambitions over which many people have bothered hard for a period of seven years. Still, it has to be asked. I havent read Pelagie-la- Charrette, the novel by Antonine Maillet that serves as source; but on the evidence presented at CanStage I would guess that its undramatizable, musically or otherwise.

The main action covers a five-year period, from 1773 to 1777. The characters are Acadians, survivors of the Great Expulsion; 20 years before, they were violently uprooted from their homes in New Brunswick by the British and shipped to the coast of Georgia. Now, with their oppressors up to their eyes in the U.S. War of Independence, it seems possible for them to make the trip home, overland, by wagon. The moving spirit in this daunting endeavour is Pelagie herself, widowed mother of three, a tireless taskmistress and cheerleader, pulling her cart or having her family pull it like an idealistic Mother Courage. As they travel through Louisiana, Massachusetts and points progressively north, they lose some members of their party and acquire others.

So this is the story of a journey, and as such a theatrical minefield. The obvious technical problems are the least of it; in Michael Shamata's staging they are neatly, and at times impressively, solved. The real handicap is that the structure is, by definition, picaresque, meaning it's just one damn thing after another. There is very little room for cause or effect, and no overriding idea that might compensate for the lack. The characters - - partly through the nature of the narrative, partly through deficiencies in script and score -- are all cardboard cut-outs; their only function is to strive, and -- this being a post-pop- opera musical -- they have the anthems to prove it.

As Pelagie, Susan Gilmour sings powerfully, sometimes beautifully, but the woman never comes to life. She is least believable when in love, a condition that seems to have been wished on her for no other reason than its part of her job description as a musical heroine. Her sweetheart, sung with matching robustness by Rejean J. Cournoyer, is a dashing skipper of a privateer. Theirs is an on-and-off kind of courtship, because hes constantly away performing daredevil feats other people tell us about afterward. He does get to perform the onstage feat of saving Pelagie's cart from falling off a bridge (which, periodically descending from the flies, is the chief architectural feature of John Ferguson's set). I tried to believe this was a thrilling dramatic climax, rather than a transplanted circus act, but I couldnt. Despite conscientious efforts to maintain Pelagies status as a Strong Woman, the romantic relationship is a throwback to the maiden-in-peril and hero-to-the- rescue days of Rose Marie and The Desert Song, though without the melodic sweep that made the old operettas, in their own terms, credible.

Even more damaging than the show's failure to create compelling individuals is its failure to create a compelling community, since the latter is what it keeps telling us it's about. "I will bring back / Many people / To Acadia / THIS MUCH I VOW" sings Pelagie, which tells us nothing except that the shows creators have an all- too-conventional idea of how to bring down a first-act curtain. Again, the problem seems inherent in the material.

No one (including the authors in interviews) can help comparing this musical to Fiddler on the Roof; it even has a capering violinist. The older show, however, doesnt begin with an expulsion; it ends with one, and we have had time to feel for ourselves what its people were being expelled from. We've also had the chance to get to know them as individuals in a particular place, rather than as a crowd on the road. Both pieces have a wedding scene early in the second act. The one in Fiddler is moving because we know the bride and groom, and what they and their parents have been through. (That's why Sunrise Sunset has become the ultimate Jewish wedding song; it expresses universal feelings through individualized mouths.) Pelagie unites two young people who have hitherto expressed barely a flicker of interest in one another. The ceremony is followed by a song for the heroine, expressing her conflicted feelings as mother and woman; it sounds both generalized and arbitrary.

The evening is mostly score; the characters never meet a crisis they dont want to sing about, sometimes, as in the above example, they seem to have invented the crisis for the sake of singing the song. They always sing exactly what they mean; you sit there all evening hoping someone will discover subtext. There are no unforced emotional peaks, though there are a couple of comic Cliffs; Cliff Saunders and Cliff Le Jeune seize avariciously on every scarp of light relief thats thrown to them. Mostly, though, the performers, able and vigorous though they all are, have nothing to act.

Allen Cole's music avoids the Les Miserables level of turgidity, but even at its best it offers stray haunting phrases rather than whole rounded tunes. Vincent de Tourdonnet's lyrics merely plod, somewhat erratically. When he ends a line with a reference to the brine you wonder what could be wrong with the simple word "sea." (It turns out that it wouldnt rhyme with time; but then, of course, neither does "brine.") The stand-out number, suggesting the show might have found a style of its own, is one of the folkier items -- a very old mans song about "the wagon of death." This sounds like a leitmotif in preparation, and it's no surprise when the wagon itself appears. It is a shock to find it driven by a red- dressed woman whom I took at first to be a camp-follower but who turns out to be Death herself.

The show's central conflict is revealed, very belatedly, to be between her and Pelagie; or, if you like, a race between their two wagons. I wont reveal the outcome except to say the story seems to end merely because the show has been running rather a long time. The productions last-ditch attempt to prove this really has been a show about Acadia is, almost literally, to run up a flag and wait for us to salute it.

My own throat remained unlumped, still longing for some sign of irony, of genuine romance, of unpumped passion, above all of wit. I wonder if there's any chance of Nellie McKay writing a musical.

Black & White Photo: Lucas Oleniuk, CanStage / A MAIDEN-IN-PERIL AND HER HERO-TO-THE-RESCUE: Susan Gilmour as Pelagie and Rejean J. Cournoyer as Beausoleil in Pelagie.
2004-04-15-a-grand-couple-of-grannies:
BEAUX GESTES & BEAUTIFUL DEEDS

Artword Theatre, Toronto

- - -

This will probably come out ruder than I would like, but the most dispiriting thing about Marie-Lynn Hammond's Beaux Gestes & Beautiful Deeds, other than its title, is the authors appearance in it. The show is a barely dramatized memoir, and it reawakens my prejudices, which have been known to extend all the way up to Long Days Journey into Night, against plays in which the characters' main claim on our attention is that they are related to the author. Having the author there in her own person compounds the offence.

Hammond, a Montrealer of mixed Anglo-French descent, stands centre-stage flanked by two actresses playing her grandmothers, one from each half of her inheritance. On her right is Elsie, a society lady with a lively past, two dead husbands, and a drinking problem. On her left is Corinne, also twice widowed, poor all her life, and the mother of 10 children. During the Second World War, Elsie's son met one of Corinnes daughters; they fell in love and married, the result, obviously, being Marie-Lynn herself. When they meet, very near the end of the play, Elsie and Corinne prove to have just one thing in common: They both disapprove of the match, Corinne, with her Catholic convictions, on religious grounds and Elsie, with her social insecurities, on snobbish ones.

Their encounter hardly qualifies as a revelatory confrontation. All the same, it raises the pressure of a play that has hitherto consisted of two parallel monologues, intercut with songs. These are delivered by the narrating author; one of her early offerings I at first took, unfairly, to be her own special lyric to My Favourite Things. (The melody did turn out to be slightly different.) I confess I didnt know until afterward that Hammond is a prominent Canadian singer-songwriter, and that she fronted a successful folk group called the Stringband.

The songs she offers here, the English ones anyway, have nondescript lyrics and whiny tunes; the French ones have a bit more muscle. They are all commentative numbers, designed to tell us about her grandmothers with an especial emphasis on what she herself thought of them: "Elsie" we are informed, more than once, was a wild one who, in the First World War, "slept with young men home on leave." The effect is of musical finger wagging. One of Elsie's flames was a daredevil pilot, who subsequently became both her second life partner and her flying instructor. Elsie's ambitions as an aviatrix, certainly bold for the time, are celebrated in the productions logo, somewhat misleadingly since it isnt that important in the play's scheme of things, nor, given that she's supposed to be sharing the limelight equally with Corinne, should it be.

There are hints that Marie-Lynn herself has inherited Elsies wildness, but not much can be made of it. The characters exist in different time frames and different conventions and they can never interact. Hammonds presence, in fact, does no favours to anybody, including herself. She seems intrusive, because the play's focus is really on the two grannies. Their theatrical dignity is undercut by the implication that their real importance lies in her being their descendant. The non-appearance of the generation in between doesn't help much either.

It wouldnt be quite fair to dismiss the play as a piece of nothing. The old ladies are excellently played, to a degree that would hardly be possible if the actresses werent able to draw at least the outlines of their existence from the text. Maria Ricossa's Elsie, the lacquered neurotic shell of a good-time girl, is somewhat by the book (or at least by a David Lean movie) but is still meticulously done. As the bedraggled Corinne, Deborah Lalonde- Grover gets a weary witty shrug into her voice as well as her shoulders; she's a woman whom life has beaten down but who isnt beaten. The performance has a lovely unsentimental spirit. It completely inhabits the womans skin, and also her soul.

The play, a great success 20 years ago, has been restaged by its original director, John Van Burek. His Pleiades Theatre has previously mounted a string of Marivaux productions that have been the best things seen at the Artword, and I rather wish he were continuing to make his way through the old master's complete works. They are far more pertinent than this much newer piece. It may once have been thought a piercing study of opposing cultures, but all it really does is sketch a couple of positions. It seems parochial, and there's too much of that going around as it is.

robertcushman@lycos.com

Andy Bey's recording career took a while to get going. But his new CD proves it has been worth the wait

In the Fifties and early Sixties, there was a fine sibling vocal group in the United States known as Andy and the Bey Sisters. One of the sisters, Salome, subsequently moved to Canada, to become a bright light on the Toronto musical and theatre scene. Andy Bey, the brother and the main musical mind behind the group, embarked on what has proved to be a distinguished but troubled existence as a singer- pianist.

Some of the troubles were matters of temperament; he seems to have had little taste or talent for the politics of the music business. Some were to do with health; he was diagnosed HIV- positive, though he has not developed full-blown AIDS. His recording career hardly got going until the 1990s, by which time he was in his sixties. But it has been worth the wait. His new release, American Song (Savoy Jazz), strikes me as the best ballad album by a male singer since Frank Sinatra's late masterpiece She Shot Me Down.

The first Andy Bey solo CD I heard, a live set recorded in Zagreb and released on a Polish label, was called As Time Goes By (Jazzette; good luck in finding it) and one thing it revealed was that, for Bey, time went by very slowly. I would continually come to the end of a six-minute cut and realize that, not only had he spent all that time singing just one song but he had sung only one chorus of it. I also realized that, despite this, I had not been bored. He has a hypnotic voice and delivery.

The delivery is, nearly always, quiet and exploratory. The voice itself, though, suggests other possibilities, being a capacious bass- baritone in the tradition of earlier black crooners such as Billy Eckstine and Johnny Hartman. Bey has something of Hartmans uncanny smoothness, though where Hartmans reflected the suavity of a drawing room, Bey's suggests the contemplative ambience of a half- empty bar. It is, now at any rate, a somewhat ravaged voice. There are shards of gravel in the vibrato that add texture without hurting the tone. But he can also move, without apparent strain, into an unblemished falsetto that presumably owes something to early singing in church. The contrasting heights and depths suggest the flexibility of Sarah Vaughan but applied with the stillness and economy of Shirley Horn.

His American revival (few people can have heard the Polish disc, though in some ways it's my favourite) began in 1996 with Ballads, Blues & Bey (Evidence), his haggard voice, weathered but forceful, matched to his musing piano. It includes a desolate Willow, Weep for Me, in which the falsetto becomes truly eerie and which is marred only by one of those interpolated codas that singers seem compelled to throw in to convince us that theyre singing jazz. (The obediently tearful willow is exhorted "better do it while you can as if there were some danger it might stop.) Theres an amazing Embraceable You in which the words come to papa, come to papa, do" - - more or less spoken -- just about jump off the disc; on the repeat chorus, he sort of growls them.

His superb assurance does have its downside. When he goes off on a wrong tack there's no way of stopping him, and on the two faster tracks here -- You'd Be So Nice to Come Home To and Yesterdays -- he seems to be confining his accompaniment to the same bass riff played over and over. In the liner notes he professes himself extremely proud of this device, but it gets very monotonous. What the disc most splendidly reveals is his affinity with the music of Duke Ellington and especially of Ellingtons collaborator Billy Strayhorn. In a Sentimental Mood is perfect for him; he revivifies Im Just a Lucky So and So, on which most singers knock themselves out to be cheerful, by sounding perilously surprised, as if he can't believe the luck; and his Day Dream -- credited to both composers but sounding, in its pent-up yearning, overwhelmingly like Strayhorn -- is probably definitive.

For his next outing, Shades of Bey (1998), Evidence gave him a band. The opening track is Like a Lover, a Brazilian tune fitted out with a roseate English text; it's in the category that I think of as nature-ramble lyrics. He manages to make it sound sensible, with an economical, matter-of-fact delivery. He even, with a new rumble in his voice on the low notes and remarkable purity in the high ones, gives it gravitas. Going outside the usual parameters of the Great American Songbook, he discovers, among other things, Nick Drakes River Man, which fits the canon very nicely; it sounds like Nature Boy, only intelligent. Thelonious Monks Straight No Chaser (songified as Get It Straight) doesn't suit him; it's far too quick and abrupt. But there are two lovely Ducal things. Pretty Girl (originally Star-Crossed Lovers, from the Shakespearean suite Such Sweet Thunder) is calmly beseeching; Blood Count, Strayhorns last tune, written while he was dying of cancer, is very moving. Retitled The Last Light of Evening, its been fitted out (by another singer, Dominique Eade) with a lyric that cunningly keeps its options open; it might, just, be a love song but it keeps faith with the composition's identity as a premonitory requiem.

Bey did record at least one album in the Seventies and Koch Jazz has reissued it. It's called Experience and Judgment, and it shows more of the former than of the latter. The cover photo shows the singers head encircled by what appears to be one of the rings of Saturn; and the music, shapeless period funk, is appropriately spaced-out. The songs are agonizingly inspirational, and even more agonizingly inept. Bey wrote several of them himself, and the opening of his Celestial Blues should give you an idea: "We must get closer to the essence of life/ But be aware that it takes courage and strife. The advice is topped off by a resonant howl. Beys voice, naturally, was springier then that it is now and one would like to know how it sounded on real songs.

The new CD, though, is loaded with them. The voice is more haunted than ever but also warmer. (The mix seems to favour it more than usual.) There are a couple of voice-and-piano tracks; the others feature a small group, with probing arrangements by fine pianist Geri Allen, who also plays on two of the best cuts. The opener is Never Let Me Go, a remarkable song full of short naked lines, that gets to the core of Bey's talent; he is dignified and vulnerable, simultaneously.

He sings Angel Eyes complete with verse, which freshens the song considerably; moves wonderingly through the unearthly superlatives of Midnight Sun while still keeping some hold on reality; and even brings out a hard-bitten quality in It's Only a Paper Moon that is certainly there (its a Barnum-and-Bailey world/ just as phony as it could be") but that escapes most singers. A Latinate Speak Low is only half successful -- it gets melodramatic -- and the Ellington numbers this time are uneven. He pays more attention than is wise to the hack words of Caravan (its possible he thinks they're spiritual; God figures heavily in his liner-note acknowledgements), and though he approaches the decidedly worldly heroine of Satin Doll with appropriate wariness, Johnny Mercer's gloriously hip-and-flip lyrics are really beyond him.

He remains best when slowest. Ellingtons Prelude to a Kiss comes over beautifully contemplative, with a Frank Wess tenor solo maintaining the questing mood. Lush Life, Strayhorns upmarket barroom soliloquy, might have been written for him, and his performance challenges Hartman's great version with John Coltrane -- an end-of-tether narration that moves from defeat to despair. It develops at the end into an extraordinary series of wordless monosyllables ("heh heh" is prominent) that isn't quite scat singing, though it keeps the beat going superbly, more like scat acting. It takes over where the rather gauche lyric, very much a young man's work, leaves off; this is experience and judgment.

Late comebacks are fairly common in jazz, especially perhaps in jazz singing. This is a late arrival, and every bit as welcome.

Black & White Photo: Steve Berman, The New York Times / Andy Bey's new CD, American Song, reveals a voice that is more haunted than ever but also warmer.

COOKIN AT THE COOKERY

New Yorker Theatre, Toronto

- - -

Theyre still Cookin' at the Cookery, and I am still the spectre at the feast. I wouldn't want to rattle my chains too indignantly; the performances in this purported biography of the jazz, blues and cabaret singer Alberta Hunter make this an enjoyable evening. Jackie Richardson, though totally unlike the wiry and vinegary octogenarian who held court in the 1970s at the Greenwich Village boite that gives the show its name, is an experience in her own right. All the same the show, now transferred from the Bluma Appel for a commercial run, retains its original stunning indifference both to the facts of its subjects life and to the intelligence of its audience.

Maybe its ignorance rather than indifference. The song list in the program gives a small but significant clue. It includes a song titled My Handy Man Ain't Handy No More. There certainly is such a song -- a complaint about a partner's flagging virility so blatant it hardly qualifies as double entendre -- and the real Alberta very likely sang it. But Richardson, impersonating her, doesnt sing it here. She sings an earlier song -- a prequel, if you like -- that was certainly in Hunters repertoire, titled simply My Handy Man. Since this number, as you might guess, has precisely the opposite message, you would think someone -- writer-director Marion J. Caffey, perhaps? -- might have noticed the difference. This is in a show in which we are adjured, not once but twice, "to tell it like it was, if you're gonna tell it all."

It gets worse. Hunter was born in Memphis around 1895 (that's what she told The New Yorker), to a mother who apparently never saw her daughter perform, so distrustful was she of all music that wasnt church music. But this same mother is shown quizzing her daughter on who wrote the St. Louis Blues. Alberta answers, correctly, that it was W. C. Handy; she even throws in a reference to Handys Memphis Blues, thus getting extra credits for both musical knowledge and civic pride. Alberta seems to be about 10 at the time. Handy published St. Louis Blues in 1914.

The show isn't big on musical chronology; either that or, as I noted before, it's trying to credit its heroine with prophetic gifts. She starts her career, in the Chicago clubland of the teens and twenties, by treating the patrons to songs from the Thirties. (One of them is Swing, Brother, Swing, which belongs to Billie Holiday and no one else. It has little to do with Hunter stylistically, and nothing historically.) She teams up with Louis Armstrong to sing When the Saints Go Marching In, in a barefaced pilfering of a routine that Armstrong performed with Danny Kaye in a 60s movie.

The guiding principle seems to be that any old song will do, the operative word being "old." Hunter enjoyed a phenomenally long career, which naturally encompassed many different styles. Thats one reason why she's interesting. For this show, however, as for so many others, all pre-rock music is the same, and it makes precious little difference whether you're using it for purposes of derision (the old fashion) or nostalgia (the new one).

The non-musical scenes are crummy. Extended conversations between Alberta and her mother never get beyond platitudes. It then tries to use the relationship as a tear-jerker. Mama died while her daughter was off entertaining the troops in the Korean War. Obviously, Hunter would have felt terrible about this, but it wasnt her fault, and the show hasnt earned the right to lay a guilt trip on either her or us. The message seems to be that this is what taught her how really to sing the blues. It cheapens both the woman and the music.

The show makes a brief and justified fuss about the indignities to which black performers were subjected in the clubs and on the vaudeville circuit. It doesn't see fit to tell us anything relevant about Barney Josephson, the club owner responsible for Hunter's comeback. When Josephson, who was white, was in school, he got beaten up for befriending a black classmate. In the 40s he ran Cafe Society, the first truly integrated nightclub in New York (any patron making a racist remark was ejected), and took a lot of heat for it.

Barneys brother Leon, who had been involved in a plot against Hitler in 1934, was one of the first victims of the Un-American Activities Committee. The Hearst press went after him, one columnist implying that he was a junkie and concluding, with no supporting details, "and there is much to be said about his brother Barney."

Not in this show there isn't. He's presented just as an ancient Jewish gentleman, endearingly doddery if tight-fisted. I somehow feel that he and Alberta would have had things to talk about.

If the writing insults the career its meant to celebrate, the performances more or less make amends. Richardson, who acts as commandingly as she sings, is motherly in a way the childless Hunter never was; the real Alberta seems to have gone direct from daughter to universal aunt.

Richardson, whose voice is richer and rounder than even the young Hunters, does not, probably cannot and maybe need not affect the leathery parlando that was the hallmark of her subject's late period, which is the period that really matters; without it, it is doubtful anybody now would know or care about her. She also goes in for the kind of audience participation antics to which the real Alberta would never have stooped but that producers of these kinds of shows seem to think are mandatory. (I trust CanStage isn't planning to insert them in next seasons production of Aint Misbehavin'.)

She does, though, put a rich, authoritative stamp on everything she sings, and especially to those Hunter wrote herself, from My Castle's Rockin, sheer joy, to Ive Got a Mind to Ramble, sheer devastation. (There's also The Love I Have for You, which, I'm afraid, is sheer schmaltz, at least as presented here.)

Strictly speaking, Richardson and her co-star Montego Glover share the central role; Richardson plays the older Alberta and mother, Glover plays the younger Alberta and everyone else, to which latter assignment she brings a caricaturists edge. As lithe and winning as ever, she is less of a threat this time around. Its definitely Richardson's night.

A lot of performing also gets done by the folks out front who, on both occasions that I have seen the show, have been warmly demonstrative. It's amazing how enthusiastic a theatre audience will be, one that would never go to a jazz club, if you can persuade it that what it is hearing is jazz.

Black & White Photo: Bruce Singer, Canstage / Jackie Richardson is unlike the wiry, vinegary Alberta Hunter she plays, but puts a rich, authoritative stamp on everything she sings.

THE LAST 5 YEARS

Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

- - -

I sat through the first night of The Last 5 Years, a two-handed musical that is almost through-sung, wearing a smile that must sometimes have broadened into a grin. Some of the laugh lines in my face could be attributed to the laugh lines in the songs; there are some very funny lyrics here. But more of them derived from sheer pleasure in the craftsmanship of what I was watching and, especially, hearing. I also felt a tightening in my throat, because the story the show tells is both painful and believable, and in my fists, because I desperately wanted to know what both the author and the characters were going to come up with next.

This last matter, as it happens, is a little more complicated than is usual in a musical. Jason Robert Brown -- the 33-year-old New Yorker who wrote the music, the lyrics and what little there is in the way of dialogue -- tells the story of Jamie and Cathy, who in their mid-twenties meet, fall in love, and get married. Jamie is Jewish and Cathy Gentile. Jamie is a precociously successful novelist, Cathy an enduringly unsuccessful actress. Jamie has bags of self-confidence, Cathy has very little. Temperamental and professional differences drive them apart. The show tells the story from both their points of view, alternately. Only Jamie's journey is shown to us chronologically, from first date to breakup, and Cathys in reverse. They meet only at the midpoint, when Jamie proposes, occasioning the one real duet in the show. The concept can be hard to keep straight in your head, but its a piercingly original image for the relationship of two people who are -- to resort to a rather less original image -- like two ships passing in a five-year night.

Apart from neatly combining the suspense of forward motion with the built-in pathos of flashback, the device keeps us guessing about where to bestow our sympathies. We start with Cathy, just after Jamie has walked out; she's the victim and we're on her side. Then we switch to Jamie, who has just seen Cathy for the first time, hugging himself over having finally found a Shiksa Goddess (thats the songs title) after years of intra-ethnic dating: "I've had Shabbas dinners/on Friday nights/With ev'ry Shapiro/ in Washington Heights." I already liked the show, but those lines in that song crashed all my defences.

Exhilarating as the number is, it doesnt actually make you like Jamie; hes too bumptious, too full of himself. And -- though generations of nice Jewish boys will know the feeling -- isn't it just a bit shallow to fall in love with a girl mainly because she isn't Jewish? Its a possible criticism of the show that it doesnt develop this theme, although there is a later tour-de-force song: a homemade Talmudic fable delivered as a prelude to handing Cathy a Christmas present. But mainly the show pursues other things.

We follow Cathy's self-consciousness about a second-rate tour she's in (I think youre really gonna like this show/Im pretty sure it doesn't suck) and her anger when her frail hopes collapse ("You can't spend a single day/Thats not about/You"). We see Jamie exultantly taking calls from his agent, and Cathy barely able to place a call to hers. We see Cathy, whom the shape of the show has hitherto landed with all the down numbers, finally get an exultant work-out with the scores nearest approach to a traditional show tune, a sardonically joyous routine set in her dressing-room in Ohio. We laugh and suffer with her through a humiliating sequence of auditions. We watch Jamie move up and move on, and we're inclined to resent it as she does, but we also come to realize that he has a point, and to acknowledge the truth in his line -- one of the bleakest ever sung in a musical -- I will not lose because you can't win.

Eventually we give up judging. We recognize that these are two people who love one another and that, however much we want it for them, that just isnt enough. The show is apparently autobiographical, based on the authors first marriage, but it plays as an independent creation and, by the end, a very moving one.

The show is, obviously, post-Stephen Sondheim. Brown's lyrics don't have the undeviating tautness of Sondheims but they are usually on target, sometimes brilliantly so. Musically, Brown adopts Sondheims technique of using high discordant notes to convey anger or anguish or both. The central duet, too, begins by recalling Sunday in the Park with George, and has later phrases that fleetingly recall the early, tender So Many People. (And I assume that recurring lyrical references to "rolling along," apart from revealing a taste for internal irony, are a homage to Sondheim's own time-reversal musical.)

But, as a composer, Brown also goes a very individual and encouraging way. He wrote Songs for a New World and the score for Parade, but this is a huge advance. For one thing, it's the first theatrical song cycle to tell a coherent story. Andrew Lloyd Webbers Tell Me on a Sunday hardly counts, and anyway it was a staged concert piece. For another: Forget about Rent, tear out your Hair, cast a pitying look back at Theyre Playing Our Song, which had a faintly similar theme -- this is the first time that a contemporary pop sound has been made to work dramatically.

The score is eclectic but unified. Some of the songs rock, a couple are countrified, and there is an overall obeisance to the ethic of the singer-songwriter, but Brown never once resorts to the spineless generalities that the pop world takes for profundity. Everything, musically as well as verbally, is specific to these people and this narrative. He has also written his own orchestrations, in which a cello sound takes unwonted and haunting precedence.

They are superbly played here, by a chamber group under the direction of Marek Norman. Daryl Cloran's staging could be more helpful in providing a context for each number, but he seems to have led his actors straight to the heart of the material. Blythe Wilson starts out angry, just as she did when singing Surabaya Johnny in last year's Happy End. That was a mistake; it left her nowhere to go. Here her fury is a devastated, and devastating, beginning from which she rebuilds herself: fiercely, charmingly, humorously, and -- at the end, as a hopeful Juliet in braids -- heartbreakingly. Her performance, if I can trust my CD speakers, has more edge than her predecessors in New York; Tyley Ross, on the same evidence, has less. He is a capering kid, not too believable as an intellectual, and his diction can be distressingly muddy, but he has his own way of getting at the character. He presents a naturally selfish guy, who still has a searing capacity to care. And he too can be funny. Sets (Kelly Wolf) and lighting (Kevin Lamotte) are neutral but undistracting.

The show repeats itself a little, and it leaves out things we would like to know. But it offers 80 minutes of undiluted pleasure. This is the best evening in the Toronto theatre since No Man's Land. It is the best evening in the Toronto musical theatre since ... I honestly don't know how to finish that sentence but whatever landmark I am searching for dates back way beyond the last five years.

Black & White Photo: Lucas Oleniuk / Blythe Wilson and Tyley Ross are superb in Jason Robert Brown's musical, the best evening in Toronto theatre since No Man's Land.

SIMPL

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

- - -

Katl Valentin, whose name is just about familiar from social histories and theatre textbooks, was a German comedian who flourished before, during and after the First World War but more or less sat out the Second. He wasn't Jewish and he wasn't political. Peter Froehlichs play Simpl, in which he himself plays the leading role, is an attempt to bring the man to life, to recreate his routines and to investigate why he either chose or was forced into silence.

It makes for an interesting evening, sometimes an entertaining one, but it doesnt have much urgency. Froehlich is an authoritative performer with an impressive number of verbal, physical and musical skills, but he is not a great clown. Valentin apparently was; at least, the whole show rests on that assumption. He has been described as the German Chaplin, though from what we see here the two had little in common, even leaving Charlie's politics out of it. Valentin -- at least Froehlich's Valentin -- was not ethereal or balletic, and he was not primarily a mime. He did songs, monologues and sketches, and he also played the tuba, always a laugh-getter of an instrument. His hometown, which he seldom left, was Munich. He worked in that citys cabarets, from one of which, the Cafe Simpl, the show derives its vaguely punning name. An alternative title, on similar lines, might have been My Funny Valentin.

Karls chief comic persona, as presented here, is that of belligerent innocent, a bull with the world his china shop; a vocal Harpo Marx with a healthy infusion of Groucho, though with the physical solidity of a Sid Caesar (who comes especially to mind because he did very good Teuton). The prize number here shows Karl wreaking methodical havoc in a radio studio, careful always to enter through the effects door (and to close it behind him) and refusing to leave until he gets exactly what he wants. It's funny, but it's something short of uproarious.

The same goes for most of the material. The songs give off a pleasing air of craziness without being especially amusing, though its possible of course that they have lost something in translation. Valentins career is apparently well documented on records and in film shorts, and Froehlich put the show together from these sources, along with memories of his own father, who was a fan.

Piety, though, may have misled him. This doesn't seem to be the kind of rich comic text that another actor can walk into and make his own. Valentin's public, which included many famous intellectuals, seems to have thought he was a genius. This makes life difficult for anybody attempting to walk two and a half hours in his shoes.

It isnt a one-man show. Valentin had a female partner, Liesl Karlstadt, who, in accordance with a long tradition, discovered a gift for comedy while trying with all her might to be serious. Actually, its Karl who discovers it, and she becomes his off-stage counsellor and on-stage punching bag: If he's Caesar, she's Imogene Coca.

Nicola Lipman plays her efficiently and sympathetically. Liesl, we gather, is in love with Karl. He, as it happens, is married, a fact thats mentioned precisely twice, though you would think it would have had some bearing on his conduct in such turbulent times Liesls predicament is treated in hardly more detail; Karl's indifference leads her to attempted suicide and a mental hospital, but the build-up to this is perfunctory. She merely, as in some old biopic, asks plaintively why Karl can't see her as a woman.

There is a third member of the team, Karls accompanist, Gerhard Krachmann. He is played by Peter Tiefenbach, who supplements his reliable musical talents by acting as a solid straight man in the sketches. His dramatic gifts are somewhat overtaxed, though, when he has to a) fill us in on the march of history by treating his colleagues to tidbits from the newspapers and b) represent the rise of Nazism in his own person. He takes to strumming the piano in a brown shirt. He goes from doing this within the act to doing it in real life -- there is no clear demarcation, and the elision, though doubtless meant to be suggestive, is merely confusing.

So is much of the historical background. Karl doubtless lived to some extent in a world of his own, but it still strains belief to hear him wondering, in the late 1930s, where his old friend and admirer Bertolt Brecht could have got to. (Brecht, a wily bird, skipped the country in 1933, within 24 hours of the Reichstag fire.) Like Brechts Galileo, Valentin kept his options open; invited to tea with Hitler, he talked non-stop so that the Fuhrer wouldn't have the chance to ask him any embarrassing questions. But the rising pressure of terror, the possible cost to Valentin if he had got out of line, is bewilderingly underplayed.

He kept out of trouble but he got up the Nazis' noses anyway. In his comedy he presented anti-social behaviour without condeming it - - a tactic guaranteed to enrage totalitarians, or perhaps politicians of any stamp. Froehlich gives Valentin, or has found somewhere, a penetrating comparison between the audience response to political humour ("they laugh because they want to punish someone) and to his own (they laugh because they cant help themselves"). That sounds right to me, and I have no doubt that the second is preferable. It might not excuse Valentin if he had been an active collaborator, but apparently he wasnt; he never joined the Party.

The question of whether he stopped performing out of disgust or because he had no choice sounds as if it should be compelling but it never is. Nor is the question of what he should have done. Valentin's choices never concern us -- perhaps because the show has not decided how much of a biography, as opposed to a celebration, it wants to be.

We do see Karl and Liesl making a brief post-war comeback. They play red-nosed refugees, bombed out of their home, attempting to load their belongings on to a cart that keeps tipping. It's far from a barrel of laughs but it makes you understand why Samuel Beckett was another Valentin fan. The couple can't go on; they must go on. Richard Rose's production seems to be trying for a mixture of dourness and drollery, though the balance tips decisively toward the former.

Color Photo: Jean Levac, Tarragon Theatre / Peter Tiefenbach, left, plays a solid straight man, while playwright Peter Froehlich takes the role of Katl Valentin in Simpl.

UNITY (1918)

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

- - -

I wondered, while watching Unity (1918), whether all Canadian drama used to be like this. Rumour suggests that it did; that once upon a time, not so long ago, everybody was writing and producing wordy and worthy historical dramas with multiple plotlines and irritating poetic streaks, plays that implicitly ordered their audiences to pay attention because a) these things really happened and b) they happened here. How did people stand it?

The thing that happened in this case was an epidemic of influenza that took millions of lives just as the First World War was ending, and that had an especially devastating effect on Canada. Plays in this genre tend not to be set in big cities (though they're often performed there; this one started out in Vancouver) and Kevin Kerrs piece takes place in Unity, Sask., a real place with a symbolically useful name.

The characters, though, are fictitious. They include a trio of teenage girls -- one shy, one saucy, one sensitive. The sensitive one keeps a diary, which I think is fair warning. The saucy one is enthusiastically convinced that the world is about to end, and would like to get some fun in before it does, preferably with a nondescript young man popularly referred to as the Preacher. Most of his contemporaries are of course at the front, and the girls, especially the shy one who has a special attachment, are eagerly awaiting their return. When they do come back, those we meet tend to be sick or blind or married.

We are probably the better for being reminded that 1918 saw a forgotten apocalpyse on the heels of the well-remembered one. We dont get much else out of it, though. The play is two years old, so it cannot be accused of cashing in on SARS; now, of course, the sight of a whole population going about its business in surgical masks does offer a familiar jolt, but there's no particular merit in that. Nor is the mere fact of loss going to affect us much, unless we have some insight into the people who suffer it. Here they are so many marionettes, all awaiting their turn to die or be mourned.

There is one sweetly personal moment when the diarist gets to meet the local hero for whom she has been darning and mailing socks. There's also the piercing image of one plague victim, condemned by the laws of quarantine to shuttle back and forth by train without ever being allowed to get off. I dont know whether or not this is drawn from life, but I did get the feeling that a documentary approach to what actually happened would be more compelling than the evening of free association were offered here. It's an unfocused fantasia on the subjects of sex (frustrated) and death (achieved), in which the flu is only intermittently present.

Some variations on the theme are, so to speak, left over from the war. Others find expression through the character of a young Icelandic woman who has inherited the family gravedigging business (there must be limericks about this) and is generally resented. (She's played black. Colour-blind casting is all very well, but I dont see why it should preclude some attempt at an appropriate accent.) Like nearly everybody else, she makes flowery speeches. The showpiece one is given to the blind soldier. It turns out that he lost his sight not, as we first thought, in a gas attack but by gazing between the thighs of a prostitute the night before. His former story makes a lot more sense, on every level.

Chris Abrahams production frames the play handsomely without doing much for its insides; it may even have obstructed them. Actors are sculpturally disposed across a wide, wide-open set, designed by John Thompson and dominated by what I took at first to be a couple of tall crosses (emblems of mortality) but which are, more prosaically, telegraph poles. A slatted road runs across the front of the stage and then proceeds to climb up what would otherwise be the proscenium; a few intrepid actors attempt to climb after it, or on it, but not very often. There are not, after all, many situations that cry out to be played at an angle of 45 degrees.

It is all superbly lit by Andrea Lundy, whose dawn comes up, twice, like visual thunder. The director has not, however, managed to infuse much energy into the performances; the holes at the top seem to have let the air out, and the actors -- some of whom have good track records -- are indistinct and anonymous. A couple of biddies who serve as the town's communication system are especially badly served, stuck in a trench at the back of the stage and having to compete with the sound of their own machinery.

At the end the cast join in a hymn to Canada. They sing it well - - it's not the national anthem -- but it's as if the play had suddenly remembered its own title. And a dull season gets, at its last gasp, even duller.

UNIDENTIFIED HUMAN REMAINS AND THE TRUE NATURE OF LOVE

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, Toronto

- - -

I have found that in the minds of British critics who have some acquaintance with Canadian drama, Brad Frasers name leads all the rest. Its a little hard for us to think of him as our breakout playwright, simply because in the last 15 years he hasn't written many plays. But this new production of the piece that made his name explains why he has gone down so well all over the world, while also serving as a bracing reminder of how welcome his voice was here back in 1990. Theatrical writing with this much wit and presence is still uncommon. At Buddies in Bad Times, where this revival has landed, it's practically unheard of.

There are long titles and there are cryptic titles: Unidentified Human Remains and the True Nature of Love manages the unusual feat of being both, though the play itself is not especially either. The remains are those of the female victims of a serial killer at large in Edmonton. (The location may well have significance for those who have lived there, but for the rest of us it could be any city.) Love is sought, in some form, by each of the plays seven characters, most of them sexually active though not as much as theyd like to be, all of them in a mess.

In terms of plot, the multiple-murder story has not worn well, least of all in the gloating narrative vignettes of death and dismemberment that set the tone for it and for which the cast turn into a chorus. The play has few pretensions as a whodunit, and though it's being billed as a thriller, it only comes to life in that vein toward the end when one of the characters, confronted by some clues best described as bloody obvious, is abruptly transformed into both a detective and a one-person vigilante squad. (The implicit comment on the efficiency of the Edmonton police force is not flattering.)

In terms of theme, however, the two halves of the play go very well together. The image of sexually motivated murder looms over the everyday action, an extreme instance of the potential for cruelty latent in any relationship. Most of the characters come to recognize this in themselves; some confront it.

To get down to cases: We meet David and Candy, who once experimented as lovers but are now better cast as roommates. (Their apartment is a point of relative stability on Philip Beesley's urban jungle of a set, whose other components change identity by the minute.) David, who greets his co-habitant with "honey, Im homo," is described as a professional faggot, which means he gets all the best lines.

He is also a professional waiter, though he once had passing success as an actor; his new career derives from what I remember a film character in a similar situation describing as "a wild, untamable desire to keep from starving to death." Besides, hes good at it. He's sought out by his busboy Kane, who plainly adores him but is scared of doing anything physical about it. Part flattered, part annoyed, David reaches his lowest point by starting to humiliate Kane and maybe his highest by stopping.

Meanwhile, Candy oscillates between Jerri, a lesbian admirer whose attentions are as persistent as Kane's and who gets treated with equal capriciousness, and Robert, an intermittently abusive bartender. Candy also has a career: Shes a book critic, though very little is made of the fact; she isnt, for example, branded as a metaphorical serial killer on her own account. (This is an admirable gesture of self-restraint from Fraser, who has posted his own frank opinion of critics on his Web site.) And in yet another meanwhile, there is Bernie, who can't do without women but who also seems to hate them and who desperately craves his friend David's reassurance.

The foibles, dates and destinies of these people are interwoven in quick-changing scenes, as if the concept of Friends or of Sex and the City were being stripped of glamour and played for real. The play also makes the most resourceful use yet of phone messages recorded and overheard. The comic pressure, partly because of the seriousness of the stakes, is raised very high, and in one sustained sequence erupts into farce. Both of Candys current attachments visit her at the same time. David, who was all primed to go out for the evening, changes his mind. Miss all this? he says. "You must be crazy." He could be speaking for us all.

Crows Theatre, which first produced the play in Toronto and has yet to do anything else as good, remounts it now under the same director, Jim Millan. I remember his original production, with Brent Carver as David, as being sleeker and more precise than this one; here, cast and audience alike seem to be clinging to the comedy because they are unsure of everything else, with the inevitable result that it's less funny. (And time, probably, has nibbled at the play's edges.)

The performances are mostly fine, but they all have moments of flabbiness -- times when theyre mouthing lines with no clear sense of who theyre talking to or why. Damien Atkins, barring the odd lapse into sentimentality, is impressively and enjoyably in command of David; likewise Mary Krohnert as Candy, continually getting knocked off her perch and climbing back up again, and Jenny Young as Jerri, unrecognizable from her last Toronto appearance, in The Shape of a Girl. As Kane, Philip Riccio grows steadily in definition as the character grows up. Tony Nappo is blusteringly, and blisteringly, believable as Robert, whom the play, if not Candy, drops with excessive abruptness. Michelle Latimer copes gamely with a psychic hooker who beats the brunt of the more portentous writing. Only Brendan Wall falls short; a good actor, he cannot muster either the weight or the torment that the play seems to demand of Bernie -- without, admittedly, giving him much to go on.

Some things that once played inevitably now seem arbitrary. Most of the play's muscles, though, still flex. The appetite is whetted for Fraser's new one, which has the enticing title of Cold Meat Party and is due next season at Factory Theatre. Already, we hear, it has been a wow in Manchester.

HAIRSPRAY

Princess of Wales Theatre, Toronto

- - -

If you were to judge Hairspray by the coherence of its plot, which is not an exercise I recommend, you would not be impressed.

In Baltimore, a teenage girl, overweight by conventional beauty standards, conquers all rebuffs to get into the dancing chorus of her favourite TV pop show, and eventually gets crowned Miss Teenage Hairspray 1962. In beating down doors for herself she also manages to open a few for her black friends, who are being marginalized by the local network. Thats all. If the show weren't so energetic and entertaining, it would be unbearable.

It gets you on its side from the first moment, which shows you our heroine, chubby Tracy Turnblad, on her back -- in bed, which has been propped up vertically, and singing about getting up in the morning, which she proceeds to do. She shing-a-lings her way through Good Morning, Baltimore, a song whose lyrics pretty much set the tone for the evening in their lovably cheesy optimism ("every day is an open door") and in their opportunism (there's the flasher who lives next door, which is sort of funny in its casualness while letting us know that this show is to be squeaky clean with the just the occasional dab of sleaze to maintain its self-respect.) The music sets a tone, too; you cant, looking back, tell one tune from another but each one, or nearly each one, is infectious when it happens.

The hidden master of the current Broadway musical -- and indeed of the current Toronto musical -- may well be Thomas Meehan, who collaborated on the books of both this show and The Producers; and who long ago wrote the script for Annie; he knows, in other words, how to make musicals work as cartoons. (And probably Hairspray, like The Producers, tames the film that it adapts.) Cartoon is an apt mode for Hairsprays slice of pop history; the show takes us back to that peculiar rock 'n' roll interregnum between the reign of Elvis and the ascension of the Beatles -- a bubblegum time still sufficiently in sync with older modes for to use square old words like "square." One number is called Welcome to the 60s, and it sounds ironic; this is really the pre-60s, with Motown just beginning to break and Connie Francis still a force in the land. It's an era memorialized in its own time by Bye Bye Birdie; but for Hairspray, Marc Shaiman (music and lyrics) and Scott Wittman (just lyrics) have written almost an entire score in a style that Birdie used only for occasional spoofs. In this show, it's the odd traditional Broadway number that comes across as pastiche.

The TV show that Tracy so desperately wants to be part of seems to be an extension of her high school; indeed most of its performers are her fellow students, including Link Larkin, resident-heartthrob and aspirant Elvis. We have spent several scenes thinking that Tracy is worshipping Link from afar, before the show thinks to slip us the information that hes really been quite near all the time. (The fact that in this production he looks a good 10 years older than she does abets the confusion.)

The principal threat to Tracys ambition is the show's producer, Velma Von Tussle, who hates her for her unglamorousness, epitomized by her weight and her big bouffant hairstyle. Velma's ideal of beauty is her daughter Amber -- svelte, blond, untalented, and another of Tracys unexpected schoolmates. Velma and Amber are of course the shows villainesses; and though villains are supposed to be fun to watch and to act, these two just get in the way. They aren't people you love to hate; they're simply irritating. Velma herself is an ex-beauty queen, the former Miss Baltimore Crabs. That is not a funny enough idea to sustain a whole song, but she sings one anyway.

Apart from being a second-grade schemer who never looks like winning, Velma is a racist; she denies it (I love Sammy Davis Jr, and hes Negro and a Jew), but shes aghast at having black people or black music on her show, even though everybody else, including her star DJ, seems to think it a great idea. Tracy certainly does; she spends a lot of time in detention (her hair has obstructed her classmates' view of the blackboard) and the black kids she meets there help make her a dancing star.

Tracy's mother Edna, initially shocked by her daughters ambitions, soon changes tack and gets right behind her. If Tracy is plump, Edna is mountainous, and the show is about empowering her as well. At least, thats supposed to be the idea; though, as I noted when I saw the show in New York, your credibility in proclaiming that Big is Beautiful is somewhat compromised when you cast the biggest woman of all as a man. It's best, though, not to tell this show to get serious. On Broadway Edna was played by the gravel- voiced Harvey Fierstein, as endearing as hilarious. Jay Brazeau, who plays it in Toronto, goes through the same motions, voice included, but the life and the warmth and the outrageousness aren't really in him. Nor is Vanessa Olivarezs Tracy up to the standard of her predecessor; when she dances, which is what shes meant to be about, it isn't an event. But she sings well and acts appealingly, and it's neat to have a veteran of American Idol in a show about its innocent TV predecessor.

Susan Henley is bland as Velma, and Charlotte Moore, cast as a trio of dominatrices (if thats the plural), plays each with the same half-hearted Satanic grin. Fran Jaye has some vocal swagger as Motormouth Maybelle, a matriarchal black DJ who talks mainly in rhyme, and who also sings the inevitable "believe-in-yourself" number; these songs in musicals are all indistinguishable, and theyre all guaranteed to floor a white audience that thinks it's getting soul as surely as the folks at Cookin' at the Cookery think theyre getting jazz. Anyone who objects to the stereotypes in The Producers should really be shocked by Hairspray; at least The Producers has the wit to play them all for laughs. Hairspray stops being fun when it stops being fun. In this version, it has two performances that show absolutely the right way to go, sharp outlines delightfully filled out. One is Jennifer Stewarts as Tracy's tearful and eventually triumphant best friend; the other is Tom Rooney's as Turnblad Senior who runs a joke shop (the Har Har Hut) and dresses the part. He describes himself as "a crazy loon," so Rooneys three-month passage from Hamlet to Hairspray may not be as much of a stretch as it looks. But he gets maximum underplayed impact from every spoken line, and he is obviously having a whale of a time in song and dance. His affectionate duet with Edna -- a sort of loud soft-shoe -- is the number most improved from New York.

The most deteriorated is a womans prison routine that now looks and sounds like a blurred copy of the Cell Block Tango from Chicago. Some knowing echoes from earlier musicals (Edna keeps quoting from Gypsy) are clearly designed to keep the buffs happy: but I have no idea whether a scene on a compartmentalized beehive set that resembles The Telephone Hour in Birdie, is meant as an homage or merely indicates the director, Jack O'Brien, and the designer, David Rockwell, are running short on ideas. This isn't something they do very often; OBriens production has great pace and involvement, and Rockwell's scintillating backdrop is, by Kenneth Posner, even more scintillatingly lit.The costumes by William Ivey Long, usually a wizard, are disappointing, even the outsize fashions for Edna, though she's great in her working garb as a laundress. Jerry Mitchells choreography may not be strikingly imaginative, but it sizzles, as do the corps that performs it. The closing number is called You Cant Stop the Beat; and even if you could, you wouldn't want to.

- Indefinite run

PYGMALION

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

THE IMPORTANCE OF BEING EARNEST

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

The opening production of this year's Shaw Festival is a treat. One of the more delicious things about it is its unfamiliarity -- a surprise, perhaps, considering that Shaw's Pygmalion is generally reckoned one of his most popular plays and is probably still the one likeliest to crop up in schools. But I have only seen one previous professional production of it, though I must have seen half a dozen of My Fair Lady.

That, of course, is the reason; the musical has preempted the play. It has not, however, killed it off, which is what was done to the plays (name them if you can) that gave birth to Oklahoma!, Carousel and Cabaret. In this instance, there is room for both versions, and one wouldn't want to be without either.

Inevitably, the original now seems to be full of cues for song that nobody picks up. It's quite a jolt to hear Eliza Doolittle say, rather than sing, that she can do without Henry Higgins, and it's an electric shock to find him telling her in speech, rather than us in song, that he's grown accustomed to her face. Note, though, that the songs of which those lines remind us -- even the latter, a love song that never mentions love -- are among the tougher numbers in the My Fair Lady score; and that the play provides few pointers to the gentler ones. Nowhere in Pygmalion does Eliza fantasize about life being loverly -- certainly not with somebody's head resting on her knee -- and nowhere does her dustman father profess his faith in a little bit of luck or make a song and dance, even a purely verbal one, about getting to the church on time. My Fair Lady is a soft- edged romance; Pygmalion is a hard-edged one.

It is a romance in the sense of being a love story, despite Shaw's own protestations to the contrary. This famous play's actual title is now one of those meaningless, taken-for-granted labels (like Hay Fever); but it refers back to the Greek legend of Pygmalion, the artist who sculpted a woman, Galatea, so beautiful that the gods allowed her to come to life and marry him. Shaw's 1913 equivalent (not a very close one, come to think of it, but he's the one making the comparison) is the professor of phonetics who teaches a Cockney flower girl to speak like, and thus to pass for, a duchess. "Galatea never does quite like Pygmalion," said Shaw, flying in the face of myth. He said it, not in the play itself but in a narrative sequel affixed to the published text and explicitly designed to disillusion its readers. It tells how Eliza married, not Higgins, but the helplessly adoring Freddy Eynsford Hill. Nobody has ever wanted to believe this. I don't believe Shaw himself believed it. It's true that , in real life Eliza probably would have married Freddy. But she wouldn't have done it in the comedy Shaw actually wrote; as you can tell from comparing the play, which is effortlessly witty, with the epilogue, which is effortfully smirky.

Jackie Maxwell, responsible for the Niagara production, quotes the epilogue in her program note as one of her guiding lights. Frankly, I wouldn't have known if she hadn't told me, certainly not from the fine show she's actually put on the stage. It's a panoramic presentation, splendiferously designed by Sue LePage, and with lighting and sound, by Kevin Lamotte and Marc Desormeaux respectively, that make the opening in the Covent Garden rainstorm thunderously effective. The text incorporates some scenes that Shaw wrote for the 1938 movie; these afford us glimpses of two vintage taxis and of Eliza, in silhouette, forced into taking her very first bath by the professor's ruthlessly motherly housekeeper.

These extra episodes come in the printed version with an authorial running commentary, some of which the production retains and puts into the mouths of small-part players, representing the London poor who also seem to be moonlighting as scene shifters. They also speak some, though by no means all, of the original play's stage directions, in accordance with a strange convention that declares it late, departs early and seems arbitrary throughout. The director appears here to be operating on what Shaw himself might have identified as the Todgers principle: Reviewing one of Henry Irving's heavily cut Shakespeare productions, he likened Irving's treatment of the text to the culinary habits of the Dickensian Mrs. Todgers, "a-dodgin' around among the tasty bits with a fork and a- eatin' of 'em."

The tasty bits that Maxwell has picked out are socially conscious bits; they supply details of what it's really like to be poor. But they aren't necessary; the play itself -- through Eliza's mouth, and her father's, and even Higgins' -- tells us all we need to know of the constriction and deprivation from which the heroine's fairy- tale transformation allows her to escape. It's what was left out of the musical, and it's the real difference between the two. Poverty here isn't a jolly knees-up about the joys of beating the system; it's Doolittle senior, spokesman of the undeserving poor, accepting an unwelcome legacy because it's all that stands between him and the workhouse. That's a fairy-tale too, of course, and a hilarious one, but its implications are anything but.

Doolittle's prose arias are here superbly delivered by Simon Bradbury, with cock-sparrow gusto and a rare -- very rare -- instinct for the construction of lines, speeches and entire scenes. Rhythm: It's why Eliza's celebrated lapse into the vernacular is still bloody hilarious in the play, but why they could never get it to work on Broadway when they wedged it between choruses of the Ascot Gavotte.

Lorne Kennedy makes a dapper Colonel Pickering, and the genteel- poor family of the Eynsford Hills are nicely differentiated and also nicely connected, Jillian Cook's Mama having apparently bequeathed her mild snobbery to Catherine McGregor's unsteady Clara (in whom it ceases to be mild) and her gallantry to Adam Brazier's wistful Freddy. Nora McLellan's Mrs. Pearce is a fine figure of a domestic, and Patricia Hamilton's Mrs. Higgins is, in her grace and authority, the mother Shaw probably wished he'd had.

Jim Mezon endows her undentable son -- the male chauvinist who puts the pig in Pygmalion -- with the glee of a schoolboy, the passion of a pedant and the empathy of an elephant, which is just the right combination. Tara Rosling's Eliza resorts too easily, even after her elevation, to what Higgins earlier describes as "detestable boo-hooing" but is in all other respects enchanting, especially when, in standing up to her hooray Henry, she starts to penetrate his defences. The two of them chart a clear and exhilarating line through the long and potentially repetitive duet that constitutes most of the play's second half. And by the last line, which states precisely the opposite, you know by the end that Eliza will marry Higgins and not Freddy, as surely as if they were characters in a musical.

The festival's production of The Importance of Being Earnest is by contrast, or even without the contrast, appalling. As the work of Christopher Newton -- whose eye, ear, and taste are usually as fine as any director's in Canada -- it is almost incredible. What, given that Wilde's text depends even more than Shaw's upon absolute rhythmic certainty, are we to make of a production that allows Jack Worthing to interject a "yes, quite" into his first scene, and Lady Bracknell an even more unbelievable "uh-huh" into her last? Why, in a play whose characters live by a social code that permits them to do or say anything so long as it doesn't involve an obvious breach of decorum, does Algernon not merely grab Jack's plate of muffins but stomp on his foot and leave him unfunnily hopping? Why does Miss Prism keep pawing Canon Chasuble? Is she afraid that otherwise we wouldn't realize she fancied him?

In fairness to the director, he may have resorted to slapstick to compensate for his younger actors' inability to get their laughs on the lines. And in fairness to them, very few young actors can cut it. With tradition dead (though it should surely be alive at Niagara if it's alive anywhere) you have to work hard to acquire the technique; and of course by the time you've acquired it, you may no longer be young. Of the insecure quartet here, Evan Buliung's Jack comes off best; he can afford a certain heavy-handedness, since he is both the oldest and something of an outsider, his upbringing having been, so to speak, handbagged. He makes a fine thing of his surprise appearance in mock mourning -- or would if the staging allowed him to take full advantage of it.

David Leyshon's Algy is woeful, a supposed wit unable to feel his way to the end of an epigram. As Gwendolen, Fiona Byrne comprehensively violates the character's own dictum that in matters of grave importance style, not sincerity, is the vital thing; in place of self-absorbed hauteur, she offers aggrieved pettishness. Diana Donnelly's Cecily is a fine red-headed figure of a gal but too beefy in shape and manner for anyone to compare her to a pink rose. The tea-table scene, a usually infallible piece of situation comedy, falls flat because both young ladies are far too blatant in their rudeness. Certainly they should have their claws out, but the claws should be sheathed in the silkiest of gloves.

So should be those of nearly everyone in the play, though in the case of Lady Bracknell the gloves need to be lined with lead. Goldie Semple, like many recent Bracknells, is a looker, an idea with which there is nothing wrong. Not looking like a gorgon does not, however, absolve her of the responsibility of behaving like one; Semple's phrasing of one particularly famous line (it would be unfair to say which) is inspired, but she undermines herself by being both physically restless and vocally fussy.

Indeed, if the younger performers haven't yet learned how to do it, the older ones seem to have forgotten. Bernard Behrens' Chasuble has some nice scattered moments of scandalized propriety; Brigitte Robinson's Prism is not only cheap but forced. The best performance is given by Robert Benson as the manservant Lane; in the few moments he's on stage he creates both a credible past and an interesting present. In the even smaller role of the butler, Guy Bannerman melts charmingly into tears at the happy ending, and there are some excellent groupings as that ending is approached. But that is about all.

Wilde's masterwork is a farce of manners, which makes it a one- of-a-kind achievement. It's constructed of jokes, and even if you know them by heart, there can still be joy in hearing them perfectly told. To muff them is to destroy not only the author's aesthetic but his meaning. In Pygmalion, Higgins complains of high society that "the silly people don't know their own silly business." In The Importance, written 20 years earlier, they know it all too well, and if the actors cannot convince us that they know it, too, the play is pointless.
