2004-05-11-bet-on-this-classic-american-:
Three Men on a Horse

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

- - -

Meek and mild Erwin Trowbridge of Ozone Heights, N.J., makes a living writing verses for greeting cards -- a living that's as modest as he is himself. He also has a talent, an uncanny and infallible one, for doping the horse races. He never bets -- he would never take such a risk -- but on one rare, rebellious day he wanders into a New York bar where he encounters three professional gamblers, who naturally regard him as a gold mine. These guys give Three Men on a Horse its title, though there is never any doubt that the protagonist is Erwin.

He is currently being given a sweet, lanky and altogether captivating performance by Kevin Bundy, and if everything else in this Shaw Festival production matched his charm and restraint, there could be unbounded joy in Lakeville. Before getting into why it doesnt and there isnt, I should supply a few details about the play itself.

It was staged on Broadway in 1935, very successfully, and is the joint work of John Cecil Holm, who first had the idea and wrote it down, and George Abbott, the master showman who knocked it into performable shape. Abbott's record at picking winners wasn't quite as infallible as Erwins, but it was impressive and phenomenally durable, and this comedy found him at his peak, an eminence that he occupied for at least four decades.

It isnt the wittiest comedy ever written or the most inventive; it spins out its one idea to dangerous lengths. But that idea is a solid one, and it connects to something beyond itself. Erwin, both as versifier and as tipster, is a creature of inspiration. He is in fact an artist (it doesn't matter whether or not he's a good one) and, like most artists, he combines total confidence in his gift with a terrifying awareness that it may disappear at any moment. Did I say he was modest? I really meant that he was humble -- a much finer thing.

The play fits into the favourite Niagara category of "classic American comedy" (a cupboard that must by now be dangerously close to bare), which has occasioned some of the best evenings on the Festival stage and some of the worst. The bad ones are those that blow the plays up to suit the supposed demands of the space and of its audience -- an audience that the management sometimes seems to consider remarkably undemanding. The nadir, a few seasons ago, was a production of The Man Who Came to Dinner that looked as if it had set out to undermine the play.

The current show, directed by Jim Mezon, isnt in that miserable league, but it exhibits some of its fondness for making jokes at the expense of the material. It features a running gag about the failure of the stage machinery to function properly. Thus, when the curtain first rises, it doesnt; it gets stuck halfway up. Even if you find this kind of gag amusing the first time, your later laughter is likely to be inhibited by the suspicion that some of the mistakes might really be mistakes.

I don't know how Abbott himself directed the play, but from all I've read about him -- and especially from the insistence of his star pupil, Hal Prince, that the famous Abbott touch was not about pace but about logic -- I am sure he would have hated the shenanigans here. They send out the most damaging signal possible for a comedy: the message that those concerned think that what they have isnt actually very funny.

The fault goes deeper than mere trappings. As an actor, Mezon never overacts -- the reverse, if anything -- but as a director he seems to be encouraging his colleagues to make up for his own lost time.

Some of the performances are embarrassingly exaggerated. Not all: Bundy, as previously noted, is a tower of strength, and not just metaphorically. Erwin does some spectacular worm-turning at the end, but even before that, he knows his own mind and shows it. This Erwin is no patsy. And neither is Patsy, that being the name of the principal horse-player. Simon Bradbury, pulling off a grand slam after his performance in Pygmalion, has a touch of Paulie Walnuts about him; generally genial, he turns speedily and frighteningly businesslike when he gets nasty. (These guys are not, as far as we can tell, mobsters, but they obviously have connections.) Peter Hutt, hulking, and Jeff Lillico, fresh-faced, complete an excellently contrasted trio.

As an observing barman, Peter Millard is almost too restrained (that sounds perverse, I know, but its true). As Erwin's bullying brother-in-law, Douglas E. Hughes keeps just about on the right side of caricature. The exit applause gained by Anthony Bekenn's tyrannical tycoon reawakened my suspicion, which I thought Id laid to rest, that the Shaw audience appreciates nothing so much as really bad acting.

The women, apart from Jillian Cooks cameo as a hard-boiled reporter, are horrific, though there are tantalizing signs that they don't have to be. Catherine McGregor, as Erwin's nagging but loving wife, is quite pleasing when she stops behaving like some kind of vibrating toy. As Patsys moll, a former showgirl, Glynis Ranney speaks in a voice that sounds like the product of a cheap tour through the continent of Europe but is probably meant to suggest a Jewish upbringing in one of the outer boroughs of New York City. Or maybe its a homage to Lotte Lenya. Anyway, it's an accent standing in for a characterization. Ranney, who has spent most of her career in musicals, seems to be working excessively hard to prove herself legit, and I suspect she could do far better with far less effort.

Erwin's specialty, at least as shown here, is writing Mothers Day cards, so Saturdays premiere had great, if necessarily fleeting, topicality. The appeal of Cameron Porteous' sets and costumes will probably prove more durable; they are solidly rooted in the Depression without being in any way depressing.

Erwin can only perform as a race-track prophet when riding the bus home; he tries to recreate the experience in the mugs' hotel room, but he cant, not even when one of them pipes up with an encouraging "fares, please." This is in the script, and its funny; I don't think it's enhanced by having the entire gang doing an elaborate mime. On the other hand, theres an addition to the texts last moments that's a definite improvement.

As in The Man Who Came to Dinner, a character written as black -- an elevator operator, in this case -- is played white, presumably so that nobody need feel demeaned. On the other hand, no black actors have been engaged to play parts that were written white but could plausibly be either. I would call this getting the worst of both worlds.

- In repertoire until Oct. 29. Box office: 1-800-511-SHAW.

Color Photo: David Cooper, Shaw Festival / From left, Jeff Lillico as Frankie, Glynis Ranney as Mable, Peter Hutt as Charlie, Simon Bradbury as Patsy and Kevin Bundy as Erwin.
2004-05-13-the-old-men-by-the-tree:
robertcushman@lycos.com

KITE

Tarragon Theatre Backspace

- - -

If Winnie, the heroine of Samuel Beckett's Happy Days, were to get up out of her mound of earth and encounter another person equally intent on making purblind proclaimations about the joyous rightness of things, the result might not be unlike the scenario depicted in Kite. And if the meeting turned into a squabble, as it almost certainly would, and if it took place beneath a tree, then we would certainly be reminded of Waiting for Godot. As we are here.

Rick Roberts, the author and director of Kite, is far too smart not to know he had that comparison coming; it is in fact built into his play. He offers variations on Beckettian themes, variations that are in some respects more naturalistic than anything you would find in the works of the master, and that in others are more fantastic.

The antagonists are Man One and Man Two, both very old and living in what, from the sound of them, are real-world high-rise apartment buildings. They meet on top of a hill overlooking what, from the sound of them, are real-world urban noise and chaos. Each claims to be having a "wonderful day" and disputes the right of the other to say the same. Man One is flying a kite, which naturally gets stuck in the branches of a tree. His objective, as an acting teacher would say, is to recover it. Man Two has an assignation with a much younger and apparently very beautiful woman whose name, he says (when he can remember it), is Sheila. He is wearing a nice Italian suit for the occasion. His objective is to persuade Man One to leave and stop cluttering up the scenery.

Man One is falling apart, literally. Quite soon after we meet him, he loses a tooth; and thats just a start. He is, though, in full possession of his marbles. He talks volubly and logically. Man Two is in better shape physically, but is mentally much likelier to drop off. In the wit combats with which they, like Vladimir and Estragon, pass the time, Man One invariably has the better arguments; but he cannot make then stick because Man Two refuses to acknowledge them.

The play is about the indignities of old age, as manifested in physical and, to some extent, mental decay. Thats all it's about, but the subject is big enough in all conscience: universal, indeed. It's taken here to extremes, at some sacrifice to even metaphorical credibility. The kite flyer and the datemaker are not merely old; theyre centenarians. (Incidentally, have you had enough of kites as images of aspiration? Me too.) I know hope springs eternal, and we all make fools of ourselves, but honestly.

All the same, the humiliations visited upon the couple do ring painfully true. Man Ones disintegration prompts some trompe l'oeil effects of the kind that Roberts as director is, as he showed in his earlier play fish/wife, a master. (I don't want to spoil it, but Man One turns into a headcase.) Man Twos intended does actually come within binocular length but to what end? (I dont want to spoil that either, but the young can be very cruel. And they can really rub your nose in it.)

I haven't been much of a fan of Roberts' previous plays. This one had me divided. Its initial stretches, especially some non-verbal ones, I found tedious. Then the play began to interest me, though without ever making me feel that it had carved out an identity independent of its spiritual source. Later still, it produced some passages of real resonance, and my engagement with it deepened. But as it worked itself out, it lost me again; all its points made, it still kept making them. Overall, though, I would call it Roberts best work to date.

It is superbly served by half its cast. Oliver Dennis, who has given an inordinate number of fine performances these last few years, here gives the finest yet. His Man One is a figure in whom dignity and grievance fuse to create real anger. His predicament makes him ridiculous, but he never plays ridiculous; the writing takes care of that. He is not, however, permitted a worthy match. Man Two is played by a woman, which immediately gives the proceedings an unwanted touch of the cutes, and also takes away much of the sting, seeing as this character is the one whose predicament is sexual. There are actresses who, even en travestie, could match Dennis for power, but Marjorie Campbell is not one of them. Piping and preening, she cannot help playing the thing as a joke -- with intelligence but without weight, physical or spiritual. Talking of spiritual weight: Dennis, I realize, must now be playing this piece at night while rehearsing Lucky, in Soulpeppers forthcoming Godot, by night. Could an actor's existence get more existential?

- Until May 23. For ticket information call 416-531-1827.

Black & White Photo: News Service / Oliver Dennis, left, and Marjorie Campbell play bickering centenarians in Rick Roberts' play Kite.
2004-05-14-eight-unanswered-questions:
robertcushman@lycos.com

CONSECRATED GROUND

Factory Theatre

- - -

Halfway through its action, Consecrated Ground reveals the reason for its title. George Boyds play is set in 1965 in Africville, a shantytown in Nova Scotia, maintained by the Halifax city authorities as a black ghetto. The houses have been left to rot, a garbage dump and an abattoir have been installed virtually on the premises, and the place is infested with rats. They attack a baby boy, whose mother is busy raising some of the evenings few laughs by taking a broom to other, presumably mechanical, rats who are scuttling over the floor of the next room. The child dies (if you detect a slight uncertainty of tone in this juxtaposition, you will not be mistaken). The mother, Clarice, whose family has lived in Africville for generations, demands that her son be buried, not in the nearby cemetery, as seems customary, but on the "consecrated ground" of the village itself.

First Question: Where have Clarice's ancestors, of whom she often speaks, been buried? She gives no indication that they are not in the cemetery along with everyone else. She has suffered a terrible tragedy, but does that give her the right to change the local burial regulations?

Second Question: Since Clarice was not alone when the rats appeared in her kitchen, why didn't she dispatch the friend who was with her to look after the baby? And why does she feel no apparent guilt about not having done so? Most mothers would be prostrated by the death of a child, however it happened. Clarice shows no emotion but anger, some of it directed at the white folks (who certainly bear a heavy load of responsibility for having let Africville degenerate into a slum) and some at her husband, Willum. Willum, who unlike his wife has no sentimental ties to the place, wants to accept a government offer to move into the city where, he points out, he can have a real job and they can have a real home. The author presumably wants us to feel that both sides have a case, but he tilts the play heavily in favour of Clarice, who is accorded all of the dramatic privileges of a tragic matriarch and none of the responsibilities. This may be self-defeating. I found myself inclined to favour Willum, since he at least listens to his wifes arguments while she shows not a shred of respect for his. (Hes also far better acted, but we'll get to that later.)

Neither of the above questions is posed in the play, let alone confronted. It might be a richer, more textured piece if they were. The play was first staged, fittingly, in Halifax in 1999 and was nominated for a Governor-General's Award the following year. Unity (1918) has actually won this award; like the Pulitzer down south, it seems to have more to do with Worthiness of Subject than with anything else. The buy-out/expropriation/ethnic cleansing of Africville actually happened, and the facts, and the authors indignation over them, do set off some sparks, especially when the process actually gets underway. But the action halts and hops from one scene to another, with issues picked up and quickly dropped.

The production, by Obsidian Theatre, does the play no favours. Obsidian made a bright beginning with Adventures of a Black Girl in Search of God, hardly a great text but a lively one (and with some resemblances to the current piece, the defence of Negro Creek being a later, lighter equivalent of the defence of Africville) and vibrantly staged and performed. They have been floundering since. David R. Collins direction here is limp, hardly able to build a scene, let alone a play. No lines of communication open up between actors; people barely look at those to whom they are supposed to be talking, and few lines are uttered as if the speaker actually expected a reply.

Kevin Hanchard as Willum is the only actor to play with consistent force and fluency; his performance here is not up to his brilliant work in Blue/Orange, but then neither are the circumstances. He shares the best sustained scene in the play with Tom Clancy (Norman C. Owen), the junior bureaucrat sent to enforce the city's will and not much liking it; like all well-meaning men in impossible situations (see the conscientious clergyman in The Crucible) this token white man emerges as protagonist by default; he's the only character permitted complexity. As the minister and de facto community leader, Nigel Shawn Williams comes through in fits and starts; he certainly has authority but, like anyone, he could use some help. Far more in need of it are the women in the cast: Shakura SAida as Clarice, Lili Francks as an elderly all-purpose babysitter, Abena Malika as the local tramp, named Groovey. None of them is bad exactly but they are all amateurish, indistinct and unable to hold or vary a feeling.

Third Question: Is the government guy Groovey is said to be involved with the same Tom Clancy who spends so much of the play bustling around the place? If he is, its odd they don't have any scenes together. If he isn't, its even odder that the matter is mentioned at all.

Fourth Question: How is it that Groovey has time to move to Montreal and then come back again, while the infant body still lies unburied?

Fifth Question: Whats Groovey's purpose in the play anyway?

The remaining male character is Doublespeak (Troy Adams), who accepts the government's offer and later regrets it: a good scene that should have been followed up. His family is moved out in a garbage truck. Clarice and others claim this is part of a systematic process of humiliation. Clancy says it was a one-off mistake.

Sixth Question: Which of these is true? Were never told, and it matters. Doublespeak justifies his name by talking with a stammer.

Seventh Question: Just what is this supposed to add? The play ends with a funeral. I suppose it would be naive to make my Eighth Question a simple Why? So I will ask instead: Shouldnt the staging make it clear that this is the end, rather than leaving a painful moment of uncertainty between the last notes of the burial hymn and the first claps of the curtain call?

- Until May 30.

Color Photo: Obsidian Theatre / Shakura S'Aida plays Clarice, a mother who demands that her baby son be buried in the Nova Scotian village of Africville.

2004-05-15-the-producers-if-you-ve-got-i: Mel Brooks's film was a satire. His stage show is a celebration of the great gleaming entertainment machine that used to be the American musical. Susan Stromans direction keeps the show moving and breathing, and her comic choreography is her best. Brookss pastiche music is unassumingly accurate -- better, surprisingly, than his lyrics. The Canadian cast is top-notch. "If you've got it, flaunt it." They have, and they do, and we love it. (Canon Theatre, 244 Victoria St., 416-872-1212. Open run.)
2004-05-17-a-relative-bargain:
City for Sale runs to May 30. Box office, 416-703-1725. Invasion Free Since 1812 runs indefinitely. Box office, 416-343-0011.

CITY FOR SALE

Cameron House, Toronto

- - -

INVASION FREE SINCE 1812

Tim Sims Playhouse, Toronto

- - -

Two ventures in topical satire, one of them disappointing and the other downright dismal.

VideoCabaret have paused in their cartoon-epic re-enactment of Canadian history to zero in on a slice of life both more recent and more geographically confined. City for Sale, written and directed by Deanne Taylor, is set, say the handouts, "in a lakeside metropolis whose leading citizens have sold out the public trust and public assets." Much of the action is concerned with said citizens' attempts to dispose of a couple of bits of town that have escaped their favourite developers: a patch of waterfront and an island. A bridge and airport are mentioned.

There are, as they say, no prizes. However, one thing that differentiates this show from the Village of the Small Huts history cycle is that those plays name names, real ones. City for Sale is comparatively coy with characters who are, theoretically, imaginary. They include Oscar Price, a media mogul who has the whole town in his hands; Nick Wolfe, a skilled and lascivious lobbyist who has done a lot to put it there; and a Mayor Hamwell, formerly in retail, and bringing to high office a chronic condition of foot-in-mouth and truly horrendous hair.

The VideoCabaret style remains the same as ever: innumerable short scenes, played on a small square box of a stage; harsh, fierce lighting; eight actors making dazzling quick changes between equally dazzling costumes and wigs. (Lights by Andy Moro; togs by Shadowland.) But the structure, and the roguish pretence of fiction do not go well together. Taking at least some responsibility for her characters, Taylor has supplied them with elaborate plots and counterplots; in fact, she has written a play rather than the usual VideoCab revue. A lot of it concerns Nick Wolfes love life, if love is the word; he has three influential or ambitious women on a string, which customarily contributes to his success, and eventually proves his downfall. It only takes one worm to turn.

I dont know how much of this is true but, though I'm always willing to believe the worst of people much richer than I am, the sex here gets in the way of the politics, and indeed of the satire. I wouldn't say that VideoCabaret have gone soft and opted for, horror of horrors, human interest, but they are asking us to take a certain interest in their characters feelings while denying us any sustained acquaintance with them. Of course they try to be as heartless as possible, but the cuteness of the concept has dulled their edge.

Theres something else that undoes them. This story has a happy ending. The good guys win. It isn't in VideoCabaret's nature to admit that there are good guys, and they go through some of the motions of defaming their own side: the chorus of islanders (John Alcorn has written them a couple of neat songs) who stand up against the forces of Price Media and its cynically branded Greenworld project are a bunch of floppy idealists, and probably vegans; Mac Mackenzie, the left-wing councillor who wins as mayor when scandal catches up with his opponents, has to get into bed -- metaphorically, you understand -- with some dubious fellows. But it looks like window dressing. Rather more effectively, the forces of greed are allowed to assert, calmly, that though theyve lost the battle, they hasnt lost the war; all politicians may not be the same but all politics are. The play has one deathless plutocratic line: I like to do business with governments; they own all the best stuff.

Seven members of the hard-working, hoop-jumping cast are absolutely fine: Janet Burke, Patrick Conner, Beverley Cooper, Greg Campbell, Shari Hollett, Ruth Madoc-Jones and Stephen Sparks. The eighth, Anand Rajaram, verges at times on the sublime; it would be tempting to say that as Mayor Hamwell he hams well, but in fact he is gentle and lost, and both speaks and looks the very poetry of haplessness.

Second City is never likely to betray its heritage and go in for storytelling. Invasion Free Since 1812, the troupe's "55th Sketch Comedy Revue," has at any rate the series' best title in recent memory. It suggests that the show will be more sardonically political than usual, and the director, Bob Martin, says himself that the show will be a little louder and a little angrier than its predecessors. Alas, the best title hides the worst show.

Being Canadian here means, as it usually does, having an attitude about Americans. You wouldnt think that playing that for comedy, now, would be all that hard. The shows polemical set piece gives us a couple of rabble-rousing young Republicans (and they do look very good in their bow ties and red suspenders) blaming every one of the world's evils, and every one of their government's policies, on Osama bin Laden. The trouble is, this isnt just their punchline, its the show's; the writers' thinking is every bit as lazy as that of the people theyre lampooning. (And like them, theyre relying on their audience agreeing with them before they've started.) The number touches, heavily, of course on Iraq; but there is only one line about Abu Ghraib, the scandal that, whatever your thinking, has changed the whole profile of the war. These are supposed to be improv comedians, able to adapt to breaking news rather than go with what they had in rehearsal.

The show also digs into more distant U.S. history for a poison- quill exchange between Thomas Jefferson and Benjamin Franklin that may mark a new low in pointlessness. It says nothing about them or us. (You want to lock the performers in a room with the CD of Stan Freberg's History of America, so they may learn how these things should be done.) Its matched by the very next number, the free- association ramblings of an old woman in church. I have sometimes lamented Second Citys inability to think up punchlines, but here, where what has gone before is so feeble, you hardly notice.

There is some better material, though the bad stuff tends to crowd it out. There is an endearing running gag about Paul Martin opening up the first marijuana counter at Shoppers (an experience that takes him, in succeeding scenes, back to the '60s), and a sharp one involving Paul Constable as a radio DJ whose station format keeps changing while his patter remains the same. There are some sketches about marriage that may make you wince as well as laugh -- in fact, wince rather than laugh. There's one about a gay man applying for maternity leave, from a boss who has a virtuoso line in office psychobabble-with-gestures; Naomi Snieckus hand-jives (and word-jives) her way through this splendidly. A tribute to Rochester ("the Winnipeg of America," and did I also hear it referred to as the "home of Jack Benny"?) makes a delightful closer. The performers -- the others are Sandy Jobin-Beavans, Jamillah Ross and Matt Baram (a cross between Woody Allen and Harpo Marx) -- are fine. They are also the writers, however, so one's congratulations have to be muted.

Black & White Photo: Michael Cooper Photography / VideoCabaret presents City for Sale, set in an unnamed lakeside metropolis, a bridge and airport are mentioned.
2004-05-20-all-the-king-s-horses:
robertcushman@lycos.com

DEATH AND THE KING'S HORSEMAN

Artword Theatre, Toronto

- - -

The Nigerian laureate Wole Soyinka wrote Death and the Kings Horseman in 1976, and it became an instant classic. A Toronto production was planned, and then cancelled, in 1987. It has finally reached us in a joint production by AfriCan Theatre Ensemble and the Artword Theatre that might, it if it had more distinction, be called a disaster. As it is, its simply a disgrace.

The play is set in a Nigerian town in 1945. The king of a Yoruba tribe has died and custom decrees that his Horseman, one of his highest officers, follow him in an act of ritual suicide.

The play has a five-act structure, on the Greek model, and Act I shows the Horseman, egged on by his Praise-Singer, announcing his intentions to the women of the market, who form the singing-dancing- drumming chorus of a play that's both tragedy and comedy.

Act II takes us to the British Residency, where the plans of the District Officer to attend a party at the European Club (its first in ages, apparently) are disrupted by the sounds of uproar in the town. These two acts are written, obviously, in disparate styles -- the first florid and ceremonial, the second prosaic and clipped.

The two modes begin to impinge on one another in Act III, in which a black police sergeant, under white orders, makes a comically ineffectual attempt to stop the immolation. They collide in Act IV, which sees the return of the Horseman's son, back from studying medicine in London and finding himself caught, angrily, between two worlds.

Act V is full verbal confrontation between two modes of life, not to mention two views of death. There is a final twist that is not in the least surprising -- and was probably never meant to be.

The performing challenges it presents are obviously enormous. They are faced here by a catastrophically unpractised cast who seem to have been given no help whatsoever. The director, Ronald Weihs, is probably right in claiming the play has no subtext and that the actors should simply "let the words do the work.

This, though, as many Shakespeare productions have all-too- grimly revealed, can be perilous advice. However rich or vigorous the language (and lack of subtext is not always a virtue unalloyed), it still has to be pitched, directed, shaped. At the very least, it has to be spoken clearly. This production gets off to a typically thoughtful start by playing a vital expository duologue on the steps of the auditorium, behind the backs of most of the audience. Baffled at the outset, it takes us ages to catch up.

I cant believe it was Soyinkas intention to shut out a non- African audience (he writes in English, after all), but we do need help. Not that the script always gives it: When the exasperated District Officer asks the Horseman, Must you people always speak in riddles?" all but the most committed multiculturalists are likely to sympathize.

I confess I found the strictly English scenes easier to understand. I did not, though, find them any easier to enjoy. They are just as feebly acted, and if anything -- since they don't have the crutch of ritual to help them along -- even worse staged. The Officer's wife is condemned by the vagaries of the set to play an extended scene half-hidden behind a downstage grille.

I remarked last week, when reviewing Consecrated Ground, that some of its performers were amateurish without being bad. Those here are amateurish and bad, at least at delivering lines. Some of them do have other talents. The singing is all right, the dancing lively without being especially inventive and Donald Carr, playing the Horseman, gives a remarkable physical account of the long self- hypnotized approach to sacrificial death.

"Your eyes are glazed like those of a courtesan says one of the spectators, but its true not just of his eyes but of his whole gleaming, twisting body. That, though, is just one side of the character. The other is the sensual man who has relished his life (the juiciest fruit on every tree was mine") and who still clings to it, especially when it takes the form of a new young wife. I said the play was both tragic and comic: The Horseman is a man whom Fate has cast in a tragedy who often seems to feel that he would be more at home in the other genre. Like his son, though in very different ways, hes conflicted, and the results are agonizing. At least, that's what I suspect was going on. But I can only guess.

I have always thought it more of an insult than a compliment to call a performance "sincere." But, when skill is lacking, sincerity can be something useful to fall back on. And there are moments late in the evening when both Carr and Ian Morfitt (as the District Officer) communicate an awareness of what their characters are going through and of what they stand for. They can't project it, but we know they care. At such moments, the cultural clashes that are at the plays heart (and which could hardly be more topical) make themselves felt. The plays bold classic outline, and the way the action is disposed within it, are convincing proof that this is an author who aims high and has the right to do it.

I am not convinced this is a great play, as opposed to a play with greatness in it. To believe that, I would have to see a production that turned all the fine words into weapons. In the current circumstances, even accepting that they're fine is an act of faith.

- Until May 30. Box office: 416-366 7723 ext. 290.

2004-05-22-city-for-sale-coyly-discloses: The familiar VideoCabaret Canadian-history style (short scenes, fierce lighting, dazzling quick changes by the actors) remains the same in Deanne Taylor's play about the attempted selling-out of "a lakeside metropolis," but the material is coy, declining to name real names. 2004-05-25-a-musical-renaissance-this-se:
robertcushman@lycos.com

This theatre season in Toronto has not been notable for very much. But it has managed to do one unexpected thing. It has born witness to a renaissance of the musical, a form that, for as long as any of us can remember, has had a glorious past but has only intermittently had much of a present. It has a present at present; signs are that it may even have a future.

By "the musical" I mean the American musical, whose fortunes may not, strictly speaking, be Canada's problem. But they send us the shows anyway so it's in our interest that they be good. The season has brought four new, or newish, American shows, and between them they cover the waterfront of available styles. They also connect with some of the best of the older shows, which, as it happens, are on abundant display at this years classic festivals. This week sees the opening of Urinetown, which, if reports are to believed, revives the tradition of the satiric or microcosmic musical in which a town, usually rotten, stands in for a whole country, or maybe for Western civilization in its entirety. As John Kander, composer of Chicago, has delightedly observed, "corruption never goes out of fashion."

Neither does simple gaiety; or even when its unfashionable, it's popular. The Producers puts us back in touch with the tradition of burlesque, using that term in both its senses: of broad lampoon and of even broader sex-farce. It's what Cole Porters musicals were like, in between the sophisticated songs (and sometimes even during them; Porter, outside the ballads that made it on to the Ella Fitzgerald songbooks, had an unbridled taste for double-entendre). Its a gals-and-gags show, spiced up by the act that some of the gags happen to be about Nazis. It's also a reminder, such as we haven't had in years, of the power of positive choreography.

So, in its way, is Hairspray, which is the first decent contribution in years (actually the first ever, apart from Little Shop of Horrors) to the rock n roll movie-exploitation genre. That may not seem like much of an achievement until you consider the cut- price road-company horrors that have been loosed upon the world in recent years: Saturday Night Fever, Footloose, even Grease, which was a decent stage musical before being revived as a cheapo copy of its own film version (i.e. an adaptation of an adaptation). Instead of their imitation high spirits, Hairspray offers the real thing: real humour, real professionalism, real energy. It nearly has a real story.

The Producers and Hairspray are Broadway products to the bone. Their size is part of their appeal. Urinetown, though rapidly transplanted, started off-Broadway, which is probably its spiritual home) and it's playing here at the Bluma Appel, rather than the Royal Alex or the Princess of Wales.

The Last 5 Years, which completes this season's quartet, will always be a small-house show, and not just because it only has two characters. Unlike its companions, it is not overtly nostalgic, but it too is part of a tradition, that of the intimate psychologically- driven musical. Even in its use of contemporary rhythms, it is doing for its own time what Gershwin and Sondheim, among many others, did for theirs. The same claim has of course been made for a long line of would-be theatrical rockers, but they didnt have theatrical flair or theatrical training. Jason Robert Brown has both.

Brown wrote other shows before The Last 5 Years, but he certainly counts as new and, at 32, as young. That is one of the cheering things about this batch of shows; theyre all the work of new writers, new at least to the musical theatre. All right, nobody expects Mel Brooks to follow The Producers with a whole stream of new musicals (age apart, how many scores can you write as pastiche?) but the others look good for shows to come. Brown, in particular, is routinely grouped with Adam Guettel, Michael John LaChiusa, Andrew Lippa and others, as adventurous composers whose new musicals are getting on. They are not, for the most part, getting on Broadway (and when they have, they haven't lasted) but that worries me less than it probably worries them and their agents. The American musical, for reasons of finance and demographics, can never again be simply the Broadway musical.

What counts is that it should maintain the best of Broadway craftsmanship. This -- after all the years of Anglo musicals, Anglo- French musicals, Anglo-Scandinavian musicals (Mamma Mia!), even American musicals trying to be Anglo musicals (Jekyll and Hyde) -- seemed to be falling into disrepair. You notice it in the music; you notice it even more in the words. (A couple of seasons ago, in a real gesture of despair, the Tony went to Contact, a ballet posing as a musical.) Certainly the old hands noticed. The above quote from John Kander is taken from Colored Lights (Faber & Faber, $34.50), an instructive and entertaining book of conversations between Kander, his inseparable lyricist-collaborator Fred Ebb, and an interviewer, Greg Lawrence.

Ebb: "I don't think many people writing today even know hasically what constitutes a rhyme."

Kander: Many contemporary lyrics dont rhyme not because they are intentionally not rhyming but because the people writing the lyrics dont know the difference.

This isn't just pedantry. A sharp rhyme makes a sharp point, and helps to create sharp stories about sharply-observed people. Dull rhymes mean dullness of effect, besides being a form of aural torture. Crystallizing meaning is something that songs, and hence musicals, are uniquely equipped to do. And it seems -- miraculously - - that knowledge lives on. It may have skipped a generation, but it's back. The lyrics in Hairspray may be fallible in this regard but frankly, if Hairspray were as bad as things got, wed be living in a golden age.

After seeing Hairspray Ebb, less charitably, "wanted to write and tell [its authors] to listen to Frank Loesser, which would be good advice for anybody." It would, though my own guess is that Marc Shaiman and Scott Wittman, the writers in question, have already taken it. We all have the chance to take it, as spring gives way to summer and the Stratford Festival revives Guys and Dolls, the greatest of Loessers five Broadway musicals. Of all the old masters he may have the most to say to us now, because he came to the theatre by a roundabout route. Before and during the Second World War he wrote lyrics -- and later, music -- for musical movies. He brought a blue-collar sensibility into popular song. In every respect -- except wit, accomplishment and the fact they were both composer lyricists, he was the opposite of Cole Porter, whose Anything Goes is also on the Stratford bill this year. The Complete Lyrics of Frank Loesser (Knopf, $75.00) -- the latest in a handsome and invaluable series that has previously covered Porter, Lorenz Hart, Ira Gershwin and Irving Berlin -- allows an overview of his career. It's no news that in Adelaide's Lament, the confessions of a love-lorn, bronchially challenged showgirl, Guys and Dolls contains the greatest of comedy lyrics:

You can spray her wherever you figure the streptococci lurk

You can giver her a shot for whatever shes got but it just wont work

[Kander and Ebb rightly point out that, for whatever reason, streptococci is funny in a way that "streptococcus" could never be]

And again:

You can feed her all day with the vitamin A

And the Bromo Fizz

But the medicine never gets anywhere near

Where the trouble is

If she's getting a kind of a name for herself

And the name ain't his,

A person can develop a cold.

Has there ever been a better build?

But this is only the culmination of a long line of Loessers working-girl songs, most of them written for Betty Hutton in the movies. For a turn-of-the-century New York seamstress:

Oh, the sewing machine, the sewing machine,

My pride and joy

If I didnt have my sewing machine

I'd marry James McCoy.

But I bobbin the bobbin, and pedal the pedal,

And that's the end of Jim,

Cause by night I get so weary

I dont even look good to him.

Or, on the oddities of a jive-talking boyfriend (this was 1942):

He says, Hep, hep, with helium,

Now, babe, we're cookin'!"

And other expressions, to wit:

He says, "Were in the groove

And the groove is good-lookin.

He sounds like his uppers don't fit.

Loesser would protest I'm in the romance business," but even when writing a love song he could hardly help writing funny: From Love Me As I Am:

And dont try to make any changes;

It wouldnt be worth your tears.

Don't try to make any changes -

My mother's been trying for years!

In an age suspicious of romantic ballads (rightly, considering the overheated specimens that have plagued the theatre in recent years) Loessers demotic off-handedness sounds mighty congenial.

Richard Rodgers and Lorenz Harts Pal Joey (1940) comes, chronologically, between Anything Goes (1934) and Guys and Dolls (1950), and its composer and lyricist also fit temperamentally between the urbane Porter and the street-wise Loesser. Pal Joey, opening this week at the Shaw festival, is famous as the first of the hard-boiled musicals: a distant ancestor of Kander and Ebb's Chicago, and set in the same city. It shares the musical bill at the Shaw with Adam Guettel's Floyd Collins, one of the most adventurous of the new wave. Guettel also happens to be Rodgers' grandson. In more ways than one, the line carries on.

URINETOWN

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

- - -

I wouldn't want to give away the beginning. Still, I have to say, even before the overture is played, Urinetown is hysterically funny. The overture itself is hilarious; its a parody, with every taut dissonance in place, of the opening music from The Threepenny Opera. Then comes the first song; and thats great, too. In fact, for its first 10 minutes, Urinetown is musical-comedy heaven.

That first number is delivered by a loquacious cop named Lockstock. (It later transpires he has a comparatively silent partner called Barrel.) Lockstock is here to tell us about "Urinetown the musical. Not the place." We won't see the place, he informs us, until Act Two, though he does warn us: It's filled with symbolism and things like that.

Lockstock is assisted in his narrative duties by Little Sally, a presumably orphaned waif who feeds him questions like "Is this where you tell the audience about the water shortage?" Lockstock shushes her: Youre too young to understand it now, but nothing can kill a show like too much exposition. The title of the number is Too Much Exposition.

Urinetown is a satire on matters political and environmental. It is also a satire on the idea of doing a musical satire in the first place. This higher or self-referential level provides most of the jokes. Or rather, most of the joke, because the show keeps making the same one in different words. I laughed heartily to begin with, but less heartily as the idea -- "the central conceit," to quote Lockstock slightly out of context -- kept coming back for more. But I have to confess that when it comes around the last time it does so with a twist that justifies most of what has gone before. Urinetown (The Musical) plainly thinks its very clever and very funny. It overrates itself on the second count but is absolutely accurate on the first.

At the risk of burdening this review with too much exposition: The water shortage became a drought, and this gave the government the excuse to hand over all toilet facilities to a private corporation, the Urine Good Company, which runs them on a fee-for- use basis at a handsome profit. Any citizen found hoarding (though that may not be the right expression) is consigned to the dreaded Urinetown, the musical theatre's answer to Room 101.

The corporation is run by the ruthless Caldwell B. Cladwell, who has a corrupt senator in his pay. (Senators in musicals are always corrupt. This is an inviolable tradition that may have originated in Ancient Rome.) He also has a daughter, whom he was unwise enough to christen Hope. Hope is a college graduate and an idealist. She believes in love. She takes an upstanding but confused young man named Bobby Strong, and, by having him listen closely to her beating heart, turns him into a hero. He leads a rebellion. This being a musical, it succeeds. This being, as it is at pains to assure us, an unconventional musical, the revolution has consequences undreamed of in most shows, even the ones that keep singing at us that dreaming is all-important.

According to Little Sally (and if you haven't heard it from her, youll have heard it from Urinetowns abundant pre-publicity) another item that could kill a show is a bad title. She's obviously right. Look at Les Miserables. This show has Les Mis in its sights from the get-go, though it only closes with it toward the end. In Urinetown, as not in Les Mis, we are actually told why the people are revolting.

It cannot, however, avoid taking on board some of its target's deficiencies. The actual narrative, as heroes and villains and attendant rabble are manoeuvred into position, tends to trundle. The fact that its being played for laughs rather than sentiment makes less difference than you might think.

Greg Kotis had the idea, which is inspired, and wrote the book, which sometimes isnt. (Give it credit: It is, in the circumstances, remarkably un-scatological. That's a relief.) He also, with composer Mark Hollmann, wrote the lyrics. These have both point and point of view, and they are, when not cramming in too many syllables to be comprehensible, decent. But there is no special joy in them; even I, who love to quote lyrics, feel no urge to quote any of these. Cladwell's big cynical number, Dont Be the Bunny, might be better for an occasional change of animal.

The show does have three great and glittering weapons: the music, the staging and the performance. Hollmanns score is super- pastiche; it takes in the styles of just about every musical in circulation while maintaining its own delighted voice. The opening Threepenny Opera strains are its Ground Zero, though its greater debt is to the next Brecht-Weill piece, that classic among dystopian musicals, Mahagonny. (Actually, Urinetown is better satire than Mahagonny. For one thing, it makes sense.) The music also draws on sunnier sources like Bye Bye Birdie and The Music Man; at least I can't think of any better analogue for the rapped-out Cop Song than the latter show's Ya Got Trouble, Urinetown (The Place) being River City with the river dried up. One song, Run Freedom Run, sort of mutates, starting out by mocking Broadways idea of country and finishing by crucifying its notion of gospel. The audience claps along as if it were the real thing, leaving you wondering on whom is the joke. A late anthem, Tell Her I Love Her, impales French musical epics in all their pomposity, while the finale, I See a River, is a wonderfully vacuous piece of sturdy uplift.

John Randos direction and John Caraffa's choreography, both imported from the 2001 New York production, supply a great, zany commentary. It's a delight to see a staircase wheeled into position so that Hope and Bobby may serenade one another, Tony-and-Maria- style. Indeed, one of the great joys of the show comes in seeing the insufferably virtuous romantic leads taken down a lot of pegs. Bobby meets just the fate you would want for him. As for Hope, whose divided loyalties make her both heroine and hostage: It was presumably the scripts idea to have her spend most of Act Two gagged and bound to a chair, but I imagine it was the productions to have her contributing enthusiastically to one of the numbers from that position.

There is much fun, too, in the staging of the insurrection, when the mob have Cladwell on the run and Lockstock over a Barrel. Suddenly everyone starts walking in slow motion. It's about this time, too, that Little Sally makes an unexplained and unexpected appearance on roller skates. And just as the show begins before its beginning, so too it continues after its close with the company twirling around in a celebratory dance that looks like something left over from Fiddler on the Roof. Come to think of it, Cladwell has earlier executed some melismatic cadenzas that outdo If I Were a Rich Man. Which is fair, because he really is.

The actors maintain the high standards we are coming to expect from homegrown casts in American musicals. David Keeley as Lockstock is butter-smooth, as genial as he is sinister; as Miss Pennywise, the unappetizing proprietress of the even less appetizing Public Amenity No. 9, Mary Ann McDonald reveals a gratifying talent for tuneful overacting; Stephen Patterson and Cara Leslie are straight- faced star-crossed carollers; Frank Moore is an efficient Mr. Big; and Jennifer Walser's Sally is everything you would imagine an omniscient moppet to be. As for the downtrodden poor, they are deeply unsavoury and spend most of their time in a sewer. What else would you expect?

robertcushman@lycos.com

AH, WILDERNESS!

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

- - -

According to a theory expounded by an American critic in the 1930s and much quoted ever since, the plays of Eugene O'Neill move us not because of their writing but because of the emotional cost to the author in setting them down. Ive never really bought this idea, or at least Ive never seen why it should apply to O'Neill more than to any other dramatist. But it does seem to work, in a kind of reverse gear, with Ah, Wilderness!

The first thing everybody notices about this play is that it is, unique in the O'Neill canon, a comedy, and a gentle one at that. Its a nostalgic piece, recalling comfortable family life in what the stage directions call "a large small-town, in 1904 Connecticut. Its a play many other American playwrights might have written, and several have. All such plays have a strong element of wish fulfillment, but O'Neill was unusually upfront about that element in his. The Miller household of Ah, Wilderness! represents, he said, the way I would have liked my boyhood to have been."

Even without that admission we would probably guess that Richard, the 16-year-old son of the house, with his moods and his shyness and his fondness for what his elders regard as subversive literature, was a stand-in for the author. We can also compare him to O'Neills later self-portrait as the tubercular Edmund Tyrone of Long Days Journey Into Night, with his tyrannical father, morphine-addicted mother and drunken older brother. You don't have to consult the biographies to know the grimmer version is much closer to the facts (even though it piles on the darkness with as much calculation as Ah, Wilderness! ladles out the light) Richard and Edmund have certain things in common, notably a fondness for reciting poetry; Swinburne is a favourite of both. And we follow each of them through a single rite-of-passage day; in Richard's case it happens to be the Fourth of July. Edmund and the Tyrones make us appreciate why ONeill had to will himself into a holiday mood and create Richard and the Millers. Its the implicit contrast that makes the comedy poignant as well as charming and funny.

It is both of those pleasant things in surprising measure. O'Neill turns out to be remarkably adept at writing big, festive dinner-table scenes, at mining the humour in family relationships and especially at turning people around to show off their lovable weaknesses. He could be a Gentile Neil Simon, though without the extractable wisecracks; the laugh-lines here (and there are many of them) come out of the situations. Joseph Ziegler's production is something of a twin to his lovely Soulpepper staging of Our Town, and it contains especially fine work from Norman Browning as Richards father, a newspaper editor torn between the firmness he thinks he owes his boy and the indulgence he is naturally disposed to grant him. The latter, of course, always wins out, but the actor makes every twist convincing. Even the familiar facts-of-life episode, in which father dutifully tries to instruct his son before realizing to his relief he doesnt have to, comes up fresh.

It isn't all idyllic. Nat's brother-in-law Sid is a dubiously reformed alcoholic whose weakness has torpedoed his long courtship of Nats sister. (One of the old songs that the play deploys to rich atmospheric effect is Waiting at the Church. It doesnt go down well.) Sid is a joker, but a sad one; William Vickers cleverly balances the jovial with the shame-faced. He must represent the O'Neill family drinking problem, slightly displaced. He is thus well placed to commiserate with his nephew on his first hangover. Richard has spurned the day's patriotic celebrations, as befits one who dreams of seeing Pierpont Morgan driven in a tumbril, and he feels, temporarily, spurned by the nice girl to whom he has given both his heart and his warmest selection of verses. So he seeks consolation in one of the towns most disreputable taverns (sternly realized in Christina Poddubiuks set design), where he considers the attractions of the juice and the flesh, before deciding against both. This is most unlike the real O'Neill, who was well acquainted with sex and booze at an even younger age; but that's the point. Jared Brown, good in the role throughout, is especially persuasive in his tentative foray into the lower depths, particularly when he tries to defend the virtue of a lady who doesnt want it defended.

The Miller women are slower to come into focus, but Wendy Thatcher steadily establishes herself as Richards mother, sharp- voiced and soft-centred, and Mary Haney proves a subtle presence as his valiant, disappointed aunt. Some supporting performances are coarse-grained (Lisa Norton makes far too hardened a trollop), but there is a forceful cameo from George Dawson as the town bigot, Richard's putative father-in-law, and a delicate one from Graeme Somerville as a barman.

Watching Ah, Wilderness! with its author's biography in mind is a little like seeing the young Judy Garland in the similarly nostalgic setting of Meet Me in St. Louis while knowing what was to become of her. Indeed, the wartime success of that movie set off a cycle that included a musical version of ONeills play, a cult classic called Summer Holiday. O'Neill's dream, set near the beginning of the Depression, had by the decades end become Americas. It's an impossibly rosy picture; it ends, almost as a premature inversion of Long Day's Journey, with Mr. and Mrs. Miller pledging mature love and expressing confidence in their sons future. Its so sweet it hurts. But it feels earned, or at least entitled. It isn't the cost that's paid that moves us; its the cost thats avoided.

- In repertory until Oct. 8. Box office: 1-800-511-SHAW.

PAL JOEY

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

- - -

Richard Rodgers, composer, and Lorenz Hart, lyricist, were the greatest songwriting partnership of the 20th century. Pal Joey is probably the most revivable of their musicals and certainly the most revived. A moderate success in its first Broadway outing in 1940, it came back in triumph in 1952, causing many people to claim that it had been ahead of its time. It has, from the outset, had the reputation of being pioneer work, and that reputation is deserved. But pioneer is not necessarily synonymous with good, and the show, in my experience, never works as well as one wants it to. The new Shaw Festival production, though it certainly has its merits, is another in the line of disappointments.

Pal Joey was the first realistic musical comedy. (There had been realistic operettas, notably Show Boat.) Realistic is a relative term in musical theatre, since real people don't sing, but what it means here is that script and score combine to tell a coherent story about believable characters. To adapt a Kenneth Tynan definition of serious drama that I have always liked, they present a view of life from which the pain is not left out. Musical comedies of the 30s, notably those written by Rodgers and Hart themselves, had left the pain almost entirely out; when it crept in, in the superbly despondent lyrics Hart wrote for the teams best ballads, it never had much to do with the rest of the show. And now here, suddenly, was, of all unprecedented things, a musical about a failure.

Pal Joey is based on a series of vignettes by John O'Hara, about a small-time singer and nightclub emcee. They are presented, in arresting syntax and even more arresting spelling, as letters written by "yr old pal Joey to a bandleader-friend, or former friend, whose star is rising as inexorably as Joey's is standing still. Bitterness and jealousy, submerged at the outset, take increasing command of the correspondence.

The musical supplies a plot. Joey, whose looks and charm are both his blessing and his curse, can never keep his hands off an available broad (in his vernacular, mouse"); he is also a compulsive fantasist, whose pick-up line consists of spinning yarns about an imaginary country-club childhood. Newly arrived in Chicago, he meets Vera Simpson, a rich married woman who doesnt believe a word he says but likes everything he does.

She stakes him to his own club, but ends the affair when the going gets risky. Its a serviceable story, though not enough happens in the first act and too much in the second, which involves a confusing set of blackmailing schemes -- a structural imbalance, by the way, that's the precise opposite of the one you find in most musicals.

The strength of the show's book is its consistency of tone, rooted in the seedy clubland it depicts. Every character in it is unashamedly venal, apart from one innocent. ("And she, Rodgers liked to point out, was stupid." I dont want to impugn the shows integrity, but actually she emerges as rather smart.) It must have had quite an impact in 1940; musical audiences were used to dirt, but not to dirt with a purpose.

In one vital respect, though, the musical's script betrays the spirit of O'Hara -- even though OHara himself wrote it. (Or co- wrote it. Much of the work seems to have been done, uncredited, by the original director, George Abbott. That gives Abbott, also the co- author of Three Men on a Horse, two shows in this years Festival. I'm surprised more fuss hasn't been made of this.) We lose Joeys narrating voice. Maybe Broadway wasnt ready for a first-person musical, but without that unifying consciousness Pal Joey becomes just another show, scene into song into scene.

Which brings us to the great uncomfortable secret. Because Pal Joey is Rodgers and Hart's most adventurous work, it has generally been rated as their best. But it is, by their standards, a second- rate score. Yes, it has Bewitched, whose velvety candour ("Vexed again, perplexed again/Thank God I can be over-sexed again) always sounds bracing, especially if you grew up with the bowdlerized pop version. It also has I Could Write a Book, but I suspect this song's popularity derives from being the nearest thing in the show to a conventional love song. Its really rather ordinary. It also has nothing to do with the people who are supposed to be singing it, being the same kind of precocious boy-girl duet the pair had been turning out since Manhattan, 15 years earlier.

None of the songs fit very well with the dialogue (and the transitions are usually awkward); OHara's characters speak with their own voices; Hart's sing with Harts. In his earlier shows this was a joy; here its a liability. He knew what was needed, and he tried, but he tried, as in the self-consciously frank" numbers like What Is a Man and Den of Iniquity, too obviously hard. That leaves the nightclub numbers, brassy parodies that Rodgers, in particular, seems to have enjoyed writing. They sound, in retrospect, like his farewell to jazz; three years later he would, professionally speaking, have divorced Hart, married Oscar Hammerstein, given birth to Oklahoma! and embarked on a career of respectability.

The best of all the spoofs, an arch horticultural parade called Flower Garden of My Heart, is ruined here by having its performers portrayed as tuneless incompetents; it's only funny if it's done solemnly. Most of the time, though, Alisa Palmers production is solid and Amy Walshs choreography lively. William Schmuck has designed some economically stylish sets, one of which seems to be paying tribute to the original, or at least to a widely reproduced photograph of it.

There are good performances, with Adam Brazier -- who acts, sings and dances extremely well -- playing Joey as his own worst enemy, loud of mouth but essentially innocent, "fresh" in a double sense. This is original and plausible, at least until Vera throws him out, when the script gives him the cue to turn venomous, and he passes it up. As his mistress, Laurie Paton looks stunning, speaks her lines with unfailing wit and joins the swelling ranks of fine actors you never imagined could sing so well. Her acting and singing, though, haven't fused; and her rendition of Bewitched is undercut by restless staging. Vera is supposed to be a woman of complete social and sexual assurance; she shouldn't be breaking up her reverie by wandering aimlessly around the room

Lorne Kennedy is too effortful a tough guy as Mike, the club owner; Neil Barclay, by contrast, is effortlessly in style, more so, indeed, than anyone in the show, as the gangster Ludlow Lowell. With Jenny L. Wright as his moll, he does right by both his scenes and his songs. Whether this character should have songs is another matter. The fact that he has shows how much this musical is stuck in an older tradition in which anyone could sing anything. Most revivals have assigned his numbers to somebody else.

They would actually sit rather well on Joey himself: not as a performer but as a character. One of the more tantalizing things about Pal Joey is that so many of the numbers almost work as commentary, as if the show were a concept musical waiting to happen. Joey's brash audition song You Mustn't Kick It Around happens to be my favourite thing in the score, but I still found myself wishing someone would ignore his advice and kick it in precisely that direction, even at the cost of wholesale rewriting. As it is, when Joey does the boastful Happy Hunting Horn, a long number that could be commentary, as if it were part of the plot, I get nervous. I remember that Mrs. Simpson is expecting him to join her in the car outside; and I am sure she is one dame who just hates to be kept waiting: a real Uptown Mouse.

A MIDSUMMER NIGHT'S DREAM

Festival Theatre, Stratford

- - -

Shakespeare set A Midsummer Night's Dream in a wood near Athens. Leon Rubin, director of this year's opening show at Stratford, sets it in what the program assures us is an Amazonian rain forest, full of trailing tendrils and inhabited by fiends bearing fronds. There is no reason why these two visions should conflict.

Shakespeare was no literalist, certainly not in this play, and calling the characters Athenians obliges nobody to dress them up in tunics. Rubin, though, seems to think there's a problem. He tries to solve it by cutting all specific mentions of the place out of the play. This is a mistake on several levels, and it comes near to sinking an otherwise buoyant occasion.

For one thing, he has to keep coming up with verbal substitutions, and keeping track of these becomes a distracting kind of game. In the text, when Oberon, king of the fairies, instructs his servant Puck to throw love-juice in a young mortal's eyes, he tells him to identify the man "by the Athenian garments he hath on." Here his clothes become "civilian garments," leaving you to wonder just who, in Oberon's mind, might qualify as a civilian. (Somebody urban? Not a soldier? Not a fairy?) Athens itself becomes simply "the city" which sounds unhappily generic. The specific is always better than the general, and the name "Athens" comes with legendary associations that are important to the play. Much is lost by the changes and nothing gained; and that's not even counting the occasions on which they muck up the verse. In this play, even more than in its author's others, metre matters.

And another thing: Bottom the weaver is no longer a weaver. Nor do any of his fellow performers in the artisans' interlude of Pyramus and Thisbe retain their trades. Doubtless Shakespeare chose these somewhat arbitrarily (bellows-mending must have been a specialized trade, even in Elizabethan England) but they help give the characters an identity, both as individuals and as parts of a society. Here they could be anyone. Indeed, their first entrance suggests they might even be professional thesps, down on their luck and glad of a gig. By the last scene, that's cleared up; they are, indeed, "hard-handed men who work in -- um, the city --here." All the more reason, then, for us to know what they work at.

All of which is a shame, because there's some beautiful stuff going on here. There are trapezes for the fairies to swing from, though these are not used -- as they were in the famous Peter Brook production a generation ago -- as metaphors for the characters' magical powers. The acrobatics here are far more intrepid, using the whole vertiginous height of the Festival stage, but they aren't organic; they function as discrete production numbers.

Down among the mortals, there is plenty of nimble character- development. Theseus and Hippolyta start the play with a formal tango, which suggests passion held severely in check -- on her part, anyway. The relationship is sustained, though it doesn't hold when, as is customary, the duellists morph into being Oberon and Titania. The actors simply have to start over. (This, admittedly, has been the case in every production I've seen that has tried it.) For all that, Jonathan Goad's performance of the twin monarchs is a notable achievement, in deft control of every mood and every nuance. His lady, Dana Green, doesn't have the same degree of authority or finesse, but she does pretty well.

The young lovers held my jaded attention from first to last, which is a feat. Shepherded by heavy- father Egeus (Brad Rudy, humorously illuminating a really rotten role) they immediately show welcome signs of diversity. Suck-up Demetrius (Jeffrey Wetsch) has put on a jacket for the occasion; heart-throb Lysander (Haysam Kadri) ostentatiously hasn't. They tend to merge as the evening goes on, but that's unavoidable. Helena (Michelle Giroux) is, delightfully, a besotted teenager, trying out faithful-dog poses, and also a uniformed and prissily conscientious student. "She was a vixen when she went to school" says this Helena in a revelatory new reading, intimating that her rival Hermia is a drop-out and probably a slut.

This indeed is how Nazneen Contractor, in her first scene, seems to be playing her, which makes her later emphatic protection of her virginity hard to credit. We all know the play's about sex, and any production that finds it necessary to break up a single line with four separate spasms of heavy breathing is surely working too hard at underlining the obvious. Still, the quartet's awakening, having learned their respective erotic lessons, is done with rare conviction and is the most moving sequence in the play.

Bottom's awakening is very fine, too, and Thom Marriott's whole performance a treat. He makes little of his transformation scenes, possibly inhibited by a skeletal ass-head that obscures him without actually disguising him. But as the obsessed amateur actor -- big, fresh-faced and not a man to mess with -- he is superb. He is perfectly good natured; he merely knows, deep in his being, that what's best for Bottom is best for the play; and he could well be right. The actual Pyramus-and-Thisbe show is among the funniest I have seen, irradiated by this Pyramus' total belief in himself and his part: He really is a good actor, whatever his audience may think. Among his fellows, Donald Carrier makes a studious Peter Quince, younger than most and seduced, to his own annoyance, into mispronouncing "Ninny's tomb" just like everybody else; and I really loved Snout (Anthony Malarky), formerly the tinker, and the only one I have seen to be overcome with bashful pleasure when addressed as "sweet and lovely Wall."

Nicholas Van Burek supplies a stolidly mischievous Puck, rather lacking in charm. This makes the play's ending cooler than I suspect was intended. It's hard, in fact, to detect any overall vision behind the production; it goes in for quick-fix solutions, and its pleasures have to be taken as they come. This may be the price of severing the play from its roots.

Shakespeare wrote two Athenian plays, and both of them are in Stratford's opening bill. I hereby serve notice that if, at the appointed time, I find myself confronted by something called Timon of the City, I shall require some very serious explanation.

- In repertory until Oct. 31. Box office: 1-800-567-1600.

THE COUNT OF MONTE CRISTO

Avon Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

There are certain novels that defy dramatization by virtue of their thematic range and psychological complexity. Alexandre Dumas' The Count of Monte Cristo is not one of them. It is a complicated story with a very simple thrust. Those complications, however, fill many hundreds of pages, which constitute another kind of headache for an adaptor, especially one shooting for a playing time of two and a half hours.

An even bigger problem is that the complications are a large part of the point. The implications of this may not have been taken sufficiently on board by the new version at Stratford, which is a resourceful staging of a dog of a script.

The Count of Monte Cristo, as is well known, is the ultimate revenge fantasy. Edmond Dantes, a young Marseilles seaman, is thrown into prison on a trumped-up charge of plotting for the restoration of the Emperor Napoleon. He has been framed by three men, of whom two are motivated by jealousy, sexual or professional, while the third, a local magistrate, acts from mixed motives of ambition and self-protection.

During his 20-year incarceration in the dungeons of the Chateau dIf, Dantes meets a fellow prisoner, the Abbe Faria, who tells him of a fabulous treasure buried on the isle of Monte Cristo. Dantes escapes, digs it up and becomes unimaginably rich. He takes the title of Count of Monte Cristo, and sets about rewarding his friends and, more importantly, punishing his enemies. His plans take him years to mature and months of intricate plotting to execute. He virtually plays God and finds, eventually and inevitably, that he has overreached himself.

Marshall Bordens adaptation remains fairly faithful to the first half of the narrative (the imprisonment part, which, mathematically speaking, is more like the first 10th) and takes wild liberties with the rest. A couple of his inventions are ingenious, but they all have the effect of diminishing the story, and not just in terms of bulk.

His Monte Cristo (the man, not the island) has no stature, no grandeur, and -- most crucially -- nothing to repent. In the novel, Dantes drives one of his foes to suicide and another to madness; the third, who happens to be the slimiest, he deprives of some millions of francs but eventually lets off. In this play, sword in hand, he takes each of them on in single combat, which is very decent of him, not to say heroic.

It's true that the man who wrote Monte Cristo also wrote The Three Musketeers (in fact, he wrote them simultaneously, a believe- it-or-not achievement in itself) but they're very different works. Dantes is no DArtagnan, and neither he nor his novel is a swashbuckler. When the action moves to the money-mad salons of Second Empire Paris, it comes close to being social satire on the scale of Balzac.

At the centre of it -- by sheer force of will, personality and bankbook -- sits Monte Cristo, spinning his spiders web schemes, and in their intricacy lies much of the book's appeal. There is probably no way of realizing them on stage other than by dividing the play over two long evenings. (I think that would be worth trying; Dumas, I learn from the Stratford program, tried it himself with his playwright's hat on.)

But back in the real world: Those who havent read the novel may feel differently, but Borden seems to me to have reduced it to a tale not worth telling. Some of his choices, even given his built- in time limit, are thoughtlessly destructive. He gives Dantes an ally and protector, thereby robbing him of his monomaniac solitude. He throws in a sentimental illegitimate-son motif, and supplies an unqualified happy ending in place of the ambiguous one in the original. He goes in for lines like "Fernand de Morcerf, I hold all your tomorrows in my hands." In fact he scoops up every cliche, verbal or theatrical, that offers itself to him.

A program note tells us that, in Dumas, "the good guys are good; the bad guys are monstrous." This isnt true; even when he wrote melodrama, he peopled it with characters of some vigour and even subtlety. In this version, though, the least suggestion of a mixed motive is ruthlessly ironed out, notably those belonging to the magistrate Villefort and the drunken innkeeper Caderousse, the latter of whom seems here to have stepped, along with his wife, straight out of Les Miserables, and I don't mean the novel.

The protagonist himself is done in by having his role divided between a young and an older actor -- inexplicably, since his contemporaries in the story are allowed to do their own ageing. This is probably the single most damaging decision of the evening: It reduces the performers, David Snelgrove and Brad Rudy, to sounding a single note apiece (ingenuous and implacable, respectively); it robs the audience of any handle on the central character; and it drives a final, decisive nail into the coffin of the hero's singularity. It also stifles the one potentially touching moment in the piece, when the Count re-encounters his long-lost fiancee and she instinctively but silently recognizes him.

Andrey Tarasiuks production has its own share of received ideas; you couldnt, apparently, set foot in a tavern in Marseilles in 1815 without finding the customers whooping it up in a production number.

Dana Green as Dantes' intended and Thom Marriott as his benevolent employer suggest at least the outlines of characters; other performances are simplistic, but the director has not allowed his actors to make fools of themselves as they did in last year's Hunchback of Notre Dame. And what might be called the hydraulic aspects of the staging are impressive. Guido Tondinos set starts as the deck of a ship; floors, walls and sails then rise, fall and slide to create all the other locations. Its ingenious and graceful.

The designer's idea of making the ocean a unifying image falls down, though, in the second, land-locked, act; the Comte de Morcerf's receiving room is done up in a shade of aqua-marine that could give the hardiest guest the collywobbles.

Black & White Photo: David Hou, Stratford Festival / Count 'em: Andy Velasquez, Andrew Massingham and Jeffrey Renn.
