GUYS AND DOLLS

Festival Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

The name of the classic American musical comedy Guys and Dolls arouses very joyful feelings in the hearts of members of the audience, and even of dramatic critics, whenever it is displayed upon a playbill. This is a show that dates back to 1950, and ever since that year it is well known for providing members of the audience, and even dramatic critics, with evenings of great merriment, and also of tunefulness. And I have to say, right off the bat, that this Stratford Festival production is definitely one of those evenings, and that there is a smile on the lips of everyone who leaves it, and probably a song in most of their hearts as well.

But in the breasts of dramatic critics, though probably not of members of the audience, the prospect of witnessing a new production of Guys and Dolls is apt to provoke trepidation. For when reviewing such a production, it is a point of honour among certain of these critics to pay tribute to the style and spirit of the late Damon Runyon, on whose short stories of the gamblers and showgirls and other characters who congregate around the Times Square district of Manhattan this musical is based; and this tribute is not too easily paid, for Runyon is an author with many distinctive qualities, one of which is that he is such a writer as hates and despises the use of the past tense. He is also such a writer as has no objection whatsoever to the deployment of long sentences, and indeed takes a positive pleasure in deploying them.

Another very clever scribe who is now deceased and who is named Abe Burrows writes what is called the book, or script, of Guys and Dolls, after many other scribes try and fail. And an even cleverer guy named Frank Loesser, also deceased, is given first shot at writing the music and lyrics, and no other shot is ever necessary because when it comes to fitting words to music and music to words, this Loesser is maybe the smartest guy to operate on Broadway in the 20th century or maybe on any street at any time.

One of the original producers is Cy Feuer, and he is still with us though naturally a most senior citizen, and in fact he recently writes a book titled I Got the Show Right Here, which is a title he borrows from the opening line of Guys and Dolls: Namely and to wit, "I got the horse right here, from a song called Fugue for Tinhorns, which is a trio with overlapping words and notes and a very classy way indeed of commencing a musical comedy. On the matter of Guys and Dolls, Feuer says the secret of Loesser's and Burrows' success is that, not being dramatic critics, they are faithful to the spirit of Runyon but not to the style because they know that when spoken, either on stage or screen, said style is likely to fall flatter than any pancake. So the big love duet of the show is called Ive Never Been in Love Before, whereas in strict Runyonese it would of course be called I Am Never in Love Before, which is by no means as mellifluous or as romantic.

The parties who sing this duet are Sky Masterson, the highest roller among all the hotshots in New York, and Sergeant Sarah Brown of the Save-a-Soul Mission, whom he inveigles into travelling with him to Havana but whom he brings home safe and sound. This ill- assorted couple make up what is called the serious love interest. There is also a comic love interest, which is furnished by Nathan Detroit, sole proprietor of New Yorks most respected floating crap game, and Miss Adelaide, who sings and dances at the Hot Box nightclub and is Nathan's fiancee of 14 years standing, though whether standing is her customary position during this relationship is a question I am too much of a gentleman to pursue.

These two affairs of the heart are most cunningly intertwined in the plot, though according to Feuer's volume, one or the other of them will always dominate depending on where the show is being played. For example, in Philadelphia, where the show first tries out and which is a very respectable town, it is a show about Sky and Sarah. In New York, which is by no means as respectable, it becomes a show about Nathan and Adelaide.

I have to say that Stratford must be a very respectable town indeed because here Sky and Sarah walk off with the show. Indeed, Scott Wentworth is indubitably the best Sky Masterson I ever see. He plays the part at Stratford before, 14 years ago, and it may well be that he is 14 years too old for it now, and indeed his voice frays a little and he is not helped by his costume, which is surprisingly drab. But his command of the stage and of the idiom are absolute, and he delivers his lines with such wit and economy that they sound like the funniest remarks in the show, which is not a possibility I ever contemplate before now.

Cynthia Dale plays Sergeant Sarah, and I have to say that I never enjoy her singing as much before as I do here, especially when she sings Ill Know and If I Were a Bell. Geordie Johnson plays Nathan Detroit and is both amusing and endearing, though more than somewhat hyperactive, even for Nathan, who is a great worrier.

Sheila McCarthy as Miss Adelaide is likewise very funny in spots, though the Brooklyn honk she adopts is by no means original for this kind of role. The plush delivery case from which she emerges to sing Take Back Your Mink looks like a very Hot Box indeed, though the overt eroticism of routine itself is surely misplaced. Likewise, the fast tempo at which this Adelaide is forced to deliver her Lament is most unfair to her, depriving her of laughs even on such a line as if shes getting a kind of a name for herself, and the name ain't his," which is only the single funniest line ever written in a musical. The proof of this comes in the second act, where she gets to sing what is known as a reprise at a much more reasonable pace and slays the audience three times in the space of a single chorus.

Kelly Robinson's production is generally cold to begin with, perhaps overawed by the size of the stage and by the triptych of unwelcoming arches that dominate Debra Hansons set and that pay inadvertent tribute to the Festival Theatre itself by looking 1950s Shakespearean. But it warms up when we get to Havana, as is appropriate; while in both the crap game ballet and the Save-a-Soul revivalist meeting, Michael Lichtefels, the choreographer, and his jumping jack-knifing performers come up aces.

The songs Luck Be a Lady and Sit Down Youre Rockin' the Boat have me walking on air while glued to my seat. The latter number is led by Bruce Dow as Nicely-Nicely Johnson, whose girth is commodious and whose voice is practically a counter-tenor. His pal Benny Southstreet (Shawn Wright) is also somewhat refined, and even shy. For real roughneck flavour, such as distinguishes the original production, which is cast practically from off the streets, we must rely here on Harry the Horse (Nigel Hamer), who is truly threatening. His friend Big Jule (Grant Linneberg) looks and sounds solid enough, though personally I think that bringing him on in a Cadillac with two beautifuls in attendance is a ploy that is somewhat desperate.

The forces of good, however, need no artificial support, being impeccably represented by Patricia Collins as General Matilda B. Cartwright and by Douglas Chamberlain as Brother Arvide Abernathy, who here sounds Scottish rather than, as is customary, Irish.

By the end, cast and audience come to an understanding common at performances of this piece, which is that none of us can believe our good fortune at being involve. If you ask me who, apart from Wentworth, is the star of the show, I can only say that the show itself is the star. With every production it looks more like Broadway's masterpiece, though of course to some of us it always is.

MACBETH

Festival Theatre, Stratford

- - -

The notorious jinx on productions of Macbeth has often seemed to be working overtime at the Stratford Festival, whose main stage has groaned over the years under the weight of half-a-dozen versions, none of them successful. Last Friday night, the curse was lifted: not completely or definitively, but with strength, imagination, and a couple of star performances of which one is praiseworthy and the other superb.

John Wood's production is notable among other things for its defiance of current wisdom. Most people believe (I do myself) that these days the play stands its best chance when mounted in a small space, acted by a small cast, and set in some kind of timeless limbo. Wood, with no apparent qualms, manoeuvres a full company over the full festival platform, and even has the gall to state in the program that the play is set in Shakespeares 11th century." Obviously this is not quite the 11th century that you find in the history books, but it does oblige the actors to wear pre-medieval helmets in which they could easily look ridiculous but somehow dont. Scotland stands pretty much where it did, with bagpipes and even the occasional bold stab at an accent; but the play does not degenerate, as it often has at Stratford, into a procession of anonymous warriors clad in plaid. The production likes spectacle; it is the first in my memory in which Birnam Wood looks for a brief moment as if it might really be coming to Dunsinane. It also creates a social world. Servants and other dependents bustle through its stately homes; witches and other outcasts, forming an alternative order, huddle around braziers on its blasted heaths.

Tricks are played with the order of scenes, but they justify themselves. At other times the text is treated with jaw-dropping, and possibly misguided, reverence. Shakespearean collectors are afforded a rare opportunity of seeing the Hecate scenes, which few scholars think are by Shakespeare and nearly all productions automatically cut. Mythologically, Hecate is the goddess of night, in charge of evil spirits. If she has a function in the play it may be to create a hierarchy of bad. If you want to know which witch is which, then she's the witches' witch; even the Weird Sisters are afraid of her. As played here though (by Joyce Campion) shes an ineffectual old biddy of whom the junior crones -- a businesslike corpse-robbing bunch, led by Rita Howell -- can hardly wait to see the back of. I dont see the point, unless it's to underline what a fool Macbeth was to listen to any of them. The traditional view is that the scenes were written in by Shakespeare's contemporary Thomas Middleton in an effort to turn a hit play into a musical, and thats probably right.

Wood throws in a couple of puzzling musical interludes of his own. He ends the tragedy with a dirge for the Macduff clan, as if the play had really been about them -- a belated suggestion, not to say an untruthful one. At the front end of the evening, Lady Macbeth has starred in a hootenanny cabaret, for the benefit of visiting King Duncan. (It isnt enough that she's going to have him murdered? He has to suffer this as well?) It seems an over-elaborate way of demonstrating how two-faced she is.

But all such lapses can be forgiven just for the staging of the murder-scene itself, with the Macbeths hovering in darkness at opposite sides of the main acting-area, which is bathed in an inverted pyramid of white light. (Gil Wechsler, the veteran lighting designer, has done inspired work throughout, but this is his masterpiece.) They have shut themselves out of the daylight world; they have also erected an impassable barrier within their marriage.

Lady Macbeth, practical and unimaginative, thinks that one killing will do the trick, and after that they can reign happily ever after. Macbeth knows or suspects better, but he allows himself to be drawn along; the first murder snaps his conscience, and he becomes a full-time monster, leaving his wife far behind and on her own. That is the orthodox reading, and this production sensibly follows it. When Graham Abbey as Macbeth returns from killing Duncan, saying simply "I have done the deed, he says it in the voice of an incredulous zombie. And from there he fatally rebuilds himself. Abbey shows us the process in meticulous detail; he takes us, as any successful performance must, inside Macbeth's mind. What he finds there, though, has more sinew than colour. The very qualities that I have always admired in this actor -- lucidity, intelligence, a complete absence of mannerism -- may betray him here. Macbeth is the trickiest of the tragic heroes because -- unlike Lear, Hamlet and Othello, whom he meet in something approaching normal circumstances -- he has no ground zero. He only speaks a single line before the witches are at him. The actor has to tell us who he is by injecting some personality, maybe even some eccentricity of his own, and this Abbey either neglects or fails to do. Technically, this is a fine performance that meets every challenge. As a stage in the evolution of Graham Abbey, its interesting and encouraging. As a portrait of Macbeth, it is wanting.

Lucy Peacocks Lady Macbeth is common-sense operating, at least in her early scenes, on the level of neurosis. Her invocation to unsex me here" is matched by the contemptuous cradling gesture with which she dismisses her own experience of motherhood; the spirits have answered her, sooner than she knows. I have never seen an actress fail with the sleep-walking, but hers is one of the best. It, too, is staged in startling, brilliant illumination, but this time with the actress in the centre of it, roaming and crawling over a giant white sheet: She is in bed but her eyes never close. The audacity of the conception is matched by the performance, which plumbs depths of despair I never imagined were in this actress. This must be the performance of her life. The director again does too much in bringing her on, unscripted, to find her suicide-weapon but you can see why he wanted to give us a final look at her.

The concentration that marks both these performances, especially in their scenes together, extends through the cast. The various thanes and princelings may lack presence (Michael McLachlan, though probably promising, is not only too young for Macduff but, even more damagingly, too short as well) but you always know what their scenes are about. A couple of minor roles are exceptionally well played. William Needles, with half-a-century of Stratford work behind him, makes the Old Man both a believable part of the fabric and a moral force. Robert Persichini freshens the Porter's speech by making it both the original "knock knock" routine (which it is -- read the text) and the credible utterance of a tired man on a cold night. He then sticks around as a useful member of the Macbeth household before being led off -- not, one hopes, to execution -- by the invading English. He seems to have been promoted to butler for the banquet scene; this has been staged with very few guests, so everyone of their appalled reactions counts. Even Banquo's ghost is a no-show, which in a production otherwise very hip to the supernatural, seems inconsistent; and -- in a full-stage, as opposed to a studio, version -- is surely a mistake.

TERRACOTTA WARRIORS

Elgin Theatre, Toronto

- - -

The principal character of Terracotta Warriors is Qin, First Emperor of China, a position he attained in 221 BC by the time- honoured method of doing in his nearest rival, who would undoubtedly, had things turned out differently, have done likewise to him.

Qin begins this "action-musical" in fairly spectacular fashion, by defeating his enemy in battle. It may be the nicest thing he does all evening. Once he has been coronated (I quote the word employed in the program synopsis, which I take to mean the same thing as being crowned, though possibly, given the mores of the time, more painful) he settles down to the usual imperial pursuits.

He ruins his mother's love life by having her lover torn apart by five strategically placed horses. He roots out conspirators, actual or imagined. He collects concubines, whose ultimate fate is to be buried alive when he himself has snuffed it; during his lifetime, he has inflicted the same penalty on the authors of displeasing books. The forbidden texts themselves he has cast into the flames, in what the program calls "the world's first cultural revolution"; it might also have credited him with the world's first, and possibly most effective, gun-control registry, since he has similarly incinerated a pile of equally forbidden weapons.

Among Qin's more positive achievements was the building of China's Great Wall, though it's a safe bet the labour practices on this project weren't what we would call enlightened either. All told, the First Emperor, to give him his contractual billing, is not the most endearing choice imaginable as hero of a musical.

This, though, may be to apply alien criteria to a form that advertises itself as "an entirely new genre and a new brand." (The italics are mine, and they denote dread.) Dennis K. Law, MD -- writer, producer, director and originator of the action-musical -- has now created two of these shows. The first, Of Heaven & Earth, played only in Vancouver, which is also where Terracotta Warriors originated. Law, abruptly dropping the mission statements about introducing traditional Chinese performing arts to a wide Western audience, says that his invention "was inspired by the need for something new on the Broadway scene." It seems a little premature to make that claim for a form that has yet to travel south of Toronto. It is also suicidally irrelevant, since the best chance of doing something new "on the Broadway scene" has always been to forget about Broadway. Do what you want to do, for the audience you have, and if it's alluring enough the big boys will come begging. Law's notes must, I feel, have strayed into the program by mistake; they read more like a pitch for investors than an aid for audiences.

When it stays close to its proclaimed roots -- as a display of Chinese music, dancing, acrobatics and martial arts, strung on a narrative thread -- Terracotta Warriors is quite impressive. Its costumes are gorgeous. Its performers, of whom there are going on 100, have energy, discipline and skill, though they never make you feel, as Chinese opera performers have been known to do, that what you are watching is not physically possible. The curtain call is the most enjoyable part of the show, but there are occasional moments en route that strike home dramatically. The sight of the doomed authors, trying pathetically to pull their writings out of the fire, is affecting, and a scene of self-immolation by hanging manages to be delicate and brutal at once. Mostly, though, this is a series of set pieces, and therefore specially subject to the law of diminishing returns. It's possible, if you keep one eye rigorously trained on the synopsis, to see how the scenes fit into the story. It is not too easy to care.

Now it's true that action-musicals are being puffed as "more amazing than heart-warming, more visual than emotionally appealing." That may be. There are a couple of gymnastic Asian dancers in this year's musicals at Stratford, and what they do is far more exhilarating than anything that happens here, partly because there's less of it. It's still possible for audiences familiar with even the less sophisticated Western entertainments -- cheerleading, perhaps, or Radio City Music Hall -- to feel that they've seen some of this stuff before: A waving banner is a waving banner, whatever angle it's being held at. And even old Broadway may have got ahead of this show; there are American musicals that have used Oriental theatre techniques far more imaginatively than anything that's on offer here, musicals from Pacific Overtures all the way back to The King and I. The latter show, in fact, has bequeathed a romantic subplot to Terracotta Warriors. Here, too, the monarch's favourite girl enters on a doomed romance in defiance of her lord and master; here, too, the young lovers kiss in a shadow and meet sticky ends.

Indeed, despite its avowed indifference to "comedic dialogue, tuneful songs and light-hearted romance" (all those things we're all so bored with), the show seems as bound to Broadway aesthetically as it would like to be commercially. Though it has live traditional instrumentalists, it also uses a pre-recorded score that suggests, at its most adventurous, Leonard Bernstein ready to rumble. Its stage-stealing role is that of the Emperor's chief eunuch, who starts as his pander and confidant but ends up despising him. Purse- lipped and in a permanent hunch, he's like a cross between Rigoletto and the emcee in Cabaret. His thoughts are relayed to us from the side boxes by a soprano who does the only singing -- indeed has the only words -- in the show. She performs half-a-dozen songs, two of which sound like the theme from Love Story. It's obviously not the show's fault that I don't understand the language, but surely a translation would have been in order, or at least surtitles. It might have been our one chance of learning something not only about the eunuch but about the Emperor himself, of whose thoughts and feelings we know as little when we go out as when we came in. A tyrant as protagonist is problematical enough; a tyrant who's also a cipher is impossible. It's Springtime for Hitler without the laughs.

There is a basic throne-room set, in heavy red with fat encrypted pillars, that can hardly help looking like one of the more grandiose restaurants at Queen and Spadina. It's interspersed with some etched backdrops that are far more pleasing. One of them depicts the afterlife, in which the ghostly warriors of the title are present en masse. "After death all men are equal and the Emperor is mocked and the lovers triumph in a ghostly celebration." So concludes the synopsis, or almost. "What an incredible journey of the mind!" it adds, prudently furnishing its own rave review. Under the circumstances, I need hardly apologize for quoting so liberally from the program. If it's going to encroach on my territory, the best I can do is encroach back. Besides, there are times when the publicity for a show can be more entertaining than the show. It can certainly be more revealing.

Black & White Photo: Flip Publicity / When it stays close to its proclaimed roots -- as a display of Chinese music, dancing, acrobatics and martial arts, strung on a narrative thread -- the action-musical Terracotta Warriors is quite impressive.

TIMON OF ATHENS

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

Would you prefer a timely Timon or a timeless Timon? Both are on offer in the new production at Stratford, one on each side of the intermission, and both are riveting, the first perhaps more than the second. The disjunction is not the fault of the production; it's built into the play, one of Shakespeare's least seen, possibly written in collaboration and almost certainly unfinished.

Timon of Athens starts as a satire, one that can tilt either toward comedy or tragedy. Timon is a rich man and a compulsive giver. All Athens flocks to his house, to flatter him and suck him dry. He ends up ruined, and finds not only that his former friends refuse to help him out but that, somehow, he owes them money and they are dunning him for it.

As another poet was to put it, nobody knows you when you're down and out. Timon, having discovered the truth of this, proceeds to live it. He betakes to the woods and becomes a hermit, living on roots and spewing vitriol at all who visit him -- a company that, for one reason or another, includes nearly everybody who was a part of his former life. His bitterness is unrelenting; the only thing that cheers him up is the prospect of his hometown being destroyed by the army of Alcibiades, a military hero who also feels ill- treated by the powers that were.

The play's first half is all bustle and chatter, its second all stasis and diatribe. Its hero stands an equal chance of being cut in two, but the great triumph of the Stratford production is that Peter Donaldson's Timon is believably the same man throughout. He is a rugged actor, hardly one of nature's golden boys, which makes the glass-smooth composure of his prosperous days seem all the more impressive. There is a force to this Timon's benevolence, a sternness, a point-blank refusal to believe that life could ever be anything other than what he wants it to be. You feel that none of his beneficiaries would dare refuse his bounty, even if they wanted to.

When bankruptcy threatens, he positively exults in the thought of how happy they will be to show their gratitude. Flying so high, and with so much power in reserve, he can only be in for the most tremendous crash. Usually it's an instant reversal, but Donaldson cunningly contrives a transition. Stumbling out of Athens, he turns to curse the place, and can hardly believe what he's saying. He has to fight, not to find the words, but to force them through his lips. Later, of course, the dam having burst, they will flow unstoppably.

Stephen Ouimette, the director, much aided by his designer, Lorenzo Savoini, sets the play now and, very possibly, here. For the first half, which looks white and luxurious, it works brilliantly. The senators of Athens, who seem also to function as its bankers, are for the most part a collection of bloodless veterans, but their leader (Robert Hamilton) is young, a Bay Street high flyer in request at all the best parties. Those bashes are especially well staged. Ouimette, who made his directorial debut a couple of years ago with a Threepenny Opera that was terrible but talented, here makes good on that scattered promise.

There is wit in the way Timon's friends lap up his feasts, greedily appraising the cuisine, and even in the way his servants stand behind the guests' chairs. The various lords, sketchy in the text, are thoroughly and consistently individualized, never more so than in their responses, clumsy or lascivious or both, to the dancing hookers (a masque of Amazons in the original) sent to lure them onto the floor. Their apogee comes when they severally weasel out of their obligations to their benefactor. Each scene gets special treatment. Lucullus (Ron Kennell) is ferrety and implacable, sipping wine as he holds forth on the ways of the world. Lucius (Robert Persichini) is smooth, blubbery and evasive. We catch him at the beauticians', removing the cucumbers from his eyelids to stare incredulously at the messenger come to inform him that Timon is broke. Finer still is the scene in which the flatterers convene at Timon's last banquet, convinced he has been having them on, and wondering what delicacies he has in store for them this time. They are wonderfully shameless.

These scenes could have been written yesterday. The later ones could have been written at any time; they seem to have been sculpted out of rock. Here the modern dress begins to outwear its usefulness - - a wilderness, after all, is a wilderness, whatever the period. This section is hobbled also by the consistency of Timon's invective, which is magnificent but monotonous. He takes on all comers but gives each much the same treatment. Even his faithful steward (a heartfelt performance by Bernard Hopkins, though more commentator than character) is excused from the general curse on the strict condition that he prove the only honest man.

The character who survives best is Apemantus (Tom McCamus), the cynic/philosopher, who haunts Timon's prosperity with unheeded good advice, ostentatiously swigging Evian while everybody else knocks back the Chardonnay. In this 21st-century world, he looks like a remnant of the 1950s, with specs and cap and a satchelful of Sartre. Visiting Timon in his cave, he arrives by bike (sans crossbar) to mock him for playing the amateur misanthrope while he himself is the professional. Timon feels much the same about him, and they have an enjoyable if excessively long slanging match, one that the production cleverly varies by giving Apemantus an early false exit, apparently in fear of his life.

Making Alcibiades (Sean Arbuckle) a contemporary guerrilla seems very forced, and putting his two mistresses into fatigues even worse. Timon genially urges them to spread disease in Athens, and if they don't look like whores his advice rather loses its point. The production seems to want to make a statement about war, while the play uses it only as a means to a rather hurried end. Alcibiades' dilemma as to whether or not to spare his homeland has always seemed perfunctory, and never more so than here. Nobody knows the chronology, but it seems a reasonable bet that Shakespeare abandoned Timon first for King Lear, a far more nuanced study of madness and ingratitude, and then for Coriolanus.

If the last scenes remind us of anything contemporary it's Beckett. Donaldson's Timon is allowed the comfort of an umbrella straight out of Happy Days, and he brandishes his despair like an ambulant version of the despotic Hamm in Endgame. "I am Misanthropos and hate mankind," he proclaims, standing waist-deep in a pit holding a spade above his head. It's ridiculous and it's undismissable. If Timon never lets up, then neither does the actor. Donaldson may not have the gale-force power one dreams of for Timon's tirades, but he has unfaltering lucidity and a superb vein of gnarled humour; the play acts a lot funnier than it reads. It's unforgiving laughter, culminating in Timon's bequest to his countrymen of a tree from which to hang themselves. This, impeccably drawn-out and timed, is the climax of a major performance, and the climax too of the play. The hero then simply disappears. This is nobody's idea of well-made drama, and Timon of Athens may well be, by academic standards, a bad play. But it's a great bad play.

ANYTHING GOES

Avon Theatre, Stratford

- - -

I don't approve of the Stratford Festival's presenting two big musicals in one season. However, if theyre going to do it, they could hardly have chosen two better shows. I expected Anything Goes, the second, to be a letdown after Guys and Dolls. I was wrong.

The two make an instructive couple, being similarly flavoured products of different theatrical eras. If Guys and Dolls (1950) is the musical-comedy masterpiece, it got that way partly by paying attention to the Rodgers and Hammerstein revolution of the 1940s, with its emphasis on story and character. However, for the kind of world it represents, it bypassed the backwoods primness favoured by R&H and went back to the unreformed metropolitan musicals of the previous two decades, a raffish breed of which Anything Goes (1934), with music and lyrics by Cole Porter, may be the prime example. The gangsters and showgirls and even the missionaries who populate Frank Loessers musical are the staple figures of Porter's. Indeed, the earlier show directly anticipates the later in making one of its central figures a female evangelist. It's typical, though, of Porter that his lady does her soul-saving as part of a cabaret act.

Like Guys and Dolls, Anything Goes is a New York show. Its setting is a luxury liner chugging its way across the Atlantic, but thats a technicality; the passengers and even the crew bring Manhattan with them. Its there in every word they speak, and especially in every note they sing.

It's true those notes don't have the cumulative theatrical effectiveness of the ones in Guys and Dolls. Porter was probably a better composer than Loesser (lyrically, Id say they come out even) but each of his songs has to stand alone; they are prime numbers all right, but they dont add up. You're the Top is exhilaratingly clever but it could be sung by anyone. Adelaide's Lament is laugh- out-loud funny because it could only be sung by Adelaide. Porters Blow, Gabriel, Blow may be a more rousing gospel spoof than Loessers Sit Down, You're Rockin' the Boat but its never going to bring down the house in the same way, however hard the performers work at it; we dont have the same attachment either to the people singing it or to the situation they sing it in.

That's not to say that Anything Goes has a bad book. It has a good one, though it's hard to know whom to credit. Even in 1934, the first script, by P.G. Wodehouse and Guy Bolton, had to be revised, by Howard Lindsay and Russel Crouse. The current text, by Timothy Crouse (son of Russel) and John Weidman, is a further adaptation, prepared for a Lincoln Centre revival in 1987 and since accepted as standard.

The antiquarian in me would like to see the original given a try, but the realist -- who once tried to read it and gave up -- admits we are better off without; its fault is not that its frivolous but that it works its jokes to death. The new version whistles along, winking at the spirit of screwball and, remarkably often, recapturing it.

The basic plot remains the same. Billy Crocker, millionaires runner and bon vivant, has stowed away to woo Hope Harcourt, heiress, who is engaged to Lord Evelyn Oakleigh, Englishman. Billy has two allies: Reno Sweeney, old flame and nightclub evangelist aforesaid; and Moonface Martin, criminal. Moonface, who spends much of the show disguised as a minister, is surprisingly harmless considering that he ranks as Public Enemy No. 13. (In the original he was superstitious and desperate to improve his rating, a gag they should have kept.)

That's all you need to know, except that at one point Billy is mistaken for Public Enemy No. 1, and feted by all the celebrity snobs on board. So you might say the show, unlike Guys and Dolls, has a satiric point to make as well as being a celebration of the permissive society that was trying to surmount or ignore the Depression. The title song is about both these things.

The sound of that tune in the overture, closely followed by a briskly syncopated You're the Top, is enough to raise the spirits, and they stay raised throughout. The original score, which contains five standards, has been augmented by other Porter songs, though I cant help noting that the only one that really works (Easy to Love) was written for the show in the first place and then cut. Porters songs aren't quite as interchangeable as he (or his estate) might like to think. Even if they can't be said to advance the action, they do rise from it with surprising ease -- far more naturally than those in Pal Joey.

Anne Allans staging and Patrick Clarks set are both, in different ways, built of steps, and they show one another off to great effect. The title number, somewhat cramped for space, never reaches the delirious heights of the one in the current, highly praised London version, but in other respects I prefer the Stratford production. It's lighter and wittier, it carries the story better and it is, by and large, better acted.

The major flaw is the casting of the incurably ladylike Cynthia Dale in the powerhouse role of Reno, whose first line, which is also her first joke, depends on her not being a lady and whose subsequent material, both spoken and sung, is fashioned accordingly -- for Ethel Merman, which is probably the best indication of how wrong Dale is. The best of her here, though it still isn't right, is her rangy red-haired visual line. (She looks strikingly like the late and stylish jazz singer Marian Montgomery, who also played this role once upon a time, even less happily.)

Michael Gruber is a smooth if somewhat squat leading man. Understudy Dayna Tekatch was, at the performance I saw, a delightful Hope, if strained by one of her songs. And Jimmy Spadola is about as ebulliently lunar as a Moonface could be. (Well, he might grin a little less.) As Moons moll, Sheila McCarthy sports another terrific profile -- she seems to be chewing gum with every inch of her body -- and is on top of every opportunity shes given; a shame there aren't more.

Douglas Chamberlain earns his passage with the way he says, "Crocker, I didn't know you were Chinese" (its a long story), and as a duo whom we always knew were Chinese, the brothers Jason and Julius Sermonia not only dance like devils -- as do a large percentage of the cast -- but act like them as well.

I doubt the ships captain and purser should look so much as if they've been promoted from the chorus. It should be more of a surprise when they join in the fun. And though it may well be necessary to turn every number into a showstopper (what other identity do they have?), it makes the last couple of songs feel exhausting.

One isn't sorry to see the show end, unlike Guys and Dolls, where one resents the last scene simply for being the last scene. But while it lasts, it's joyful, and that joy is in itself a statement.

WAITING FOR GODOT

Premiere Dance Theatre, Toronto

- - -

The Soulpepper production of Waiting for Godot, with William Hutt as Vladimir and directed by Albert Schultz, is good but not great. This is a slight disappointment after the same partnership's work on No Mans Land, which was great. But let us count our blessings.

Chief among them is Hutts performance as the senior of Samuel Beckett's two tramps, spending their days by a barren roadside awaiting, more or less patiently, the non-arrival of their presumed patron Mr. Godot. Hutt putters around the stage with his usual superb physical grace and also with his usual superb physical wit. As Spooner, the minor poet in No Man's Land he used these attributes to create a man in a social relationship, a man at once cunning and obsequious. Here, where the characters have no biographies and few visible means of support, he puts the same methods to different ends. An actor in Beckett can hardly create a character from the outside; he has to fill out the role with his own personality, his own experience, and his own technique; and the richer these are, the richer his performance is likely to be. Hutts are of course exceptionally rich; his being 84 has something to do with that, but not everything. This Vladimir moves daintily, partly because he is feeling his way with an old mans caution, but also because he is putting tentative toes into a metaphysical void. He has been burned, or maybe frozen, before.

As far as attitude goes, he is an instinctive but timorous humanitarian. He is genuinely outraged by the brute Pozzo's treatment of his tethered slave Lucky, but he can be intimidated into dropping the subject. Besides, he has ignoble instincts of his own; he, too, likes to have someone to despise. Just about every character in Beckett loves to subvert his own or the world's pretensions, and Hutt, as you would expect, flicks off these deflationary remarks with superb finesse. Vocally and emotionally, though, his finest moment -- the productions one real revelation -- comes when he faces the Boy who, for the second time, brings Mr. Godots excuses for his non-appearance. Desperately, angrily, though knowing the answer in advance, he begs the messenger to acknowledge that they have played this scene before; that, if this is a nightmare, it is at least a real one. He wants that much validation, that much dignity. Of course he doesn't get it.

This is the darkest patch in what is otherwise a fairly light- textured production. Eric Bentley once wrote that if you enter a theatre where Godot is playing you can feel the author's despondency cutting through you like an icy wind. I can see how that could be true, but I confess that I have yet to see a performance at which it seemed to be happening. Maybe, 50 years after the plays premiere, we are just too accustomed to Becketts inferno; we know about it even if we haven't seen the play. We know that Vladimir and his partner Estragon are filling in time and calling it living, and that that's what we all do, but -- just to prove the authors point for him -- we can live with that. We are inclined less to deplore the futility of their cross-talk than to enjoy its bravura; they are after all, among the theatres great clowns.

Schultz's production is lucid and almost continuously entertaining; and it pushes neither a tragic nor a comic interpretation; it seems to take the play pretty much as it comes. It lacks an overriding identity; its first image, which is deceptively witty, has little to do with its last, which is disconcertingly cute. The latter description would also do for Andrea Lundy's lighting, which allows the sun to set and the moon to rise with amusing abruptness, and for John Thompsons set which is conventional to the point of being reppy. All this has perhaps to do with an insistence on the plays overt theatricality; the funniest bit may be when Jordan Pettle's Estragon, desperate for an escape route, nonetheless recoils from the direction of the audience, and Hutt, casting his own glance out front, mutters, more or less, I don't blame you. Theres a moment like it in every Beckett play. Theyre all in part about actors taking their time on stage.

The relation between Hutt and the much younger Pettle is less rich than one had hoped; it seemed like inspired casting, considering the telepathic closeness with which they once played Lear and his Fool, and the age-difference should have added a whole new contour to the play. There is a fresh, tender dimension when this Vladimir comforts his companion, who has fewer intellectual resources and very sore feet, but it's intermittent. Pettle has less flavour and definition than his partner; as in other of his recent performances, he short-changes his own considerable charm with an excessively casual delivery. It isn't until the second act that they begin truly to complement one another, in their mournful duet on the subject of "the leaves." Then, when Hutt makes Vladimirs last stand -- we have kept our appointment, how many can say as much? -- Pettle cuts him wonderfully down to size with his simple "millions." (You can do few crueller things to a person than to answer his rhetorical question.) Then, too, its Vladimir who encourages Estragon's more vicious impulses, but it's Estragon who has them. For all the difference in their ages I did begin to consider them as two halves of one person, not an interpretation with I usually have any truck: soul and body, air and Earth, Don Quixote and Sancho Panza.

As of course, in a bitter variation, are Pozzo and Lucky. Oliver Dennis tortured servant, wispy-haired and wispy-bodied, is movingly mimed and, in his one long speech, superbly spoken. The scrambled message of doom is taken more deliberately than usual and is, by being almost comprehensible, so much the more disturbing. Joseph Zieglers Pozzo is superb at his first appearance, as much dandy as bully, taking a real if patronizing interest in the tramps' predicament, and desperately eager for their good opinion. My apologies to the director: This is another revelation, that the play is not just about two pairs of mutual dependents, but that the lines cross. But when this Pozzo returns, blind, the performance dwindles, handicapped by surprisingly clumsy staging that places his collapsed body far upstage and half out of sight. This obscures the tramps' vital, shifting reaction to his helplessness, while his famous epiphany about Time -- they give birth astride of a grave -- emerges devoid of sting and devoid of agony. This in turn lessens the impact of Vladimir's even more celebrated reprise ("astride of a grave and a difficult birth"), which should in turn lead up to his encounter with the Boy. But then Hutt, as noted, does that magnificently anyway. If this production has not been born great it stands a good chance, as the run progresses, of achieving greatness.

2004-06-22-family-warfare-never-looked-s:
RUTHERFORD AND SON

Court House Theatre,

Niagara-on-the-Lake

- - -

The title Rutherford and Son suggests one of those early 20th- century dramas about power struggles in some family business in the North of England. The suggestion turns out to be accurate. The play is set in a big house on the Yorkshire moors in 1912, though its not as you might expect about trouble at t'mill, or even about trouble in t'insurance company. Rutherford and Son run a glassworks. And despite the patriarchal title, which accurately reflects the principles on which the firm has been run, the strongest and cleverest characters in the play turn out to be women.

As was the author. Githa Sowerbys play, a success in its own time, fell into neglect until 1991, when it was reprinted in the same anthology of New Woman Plays as last years Shaw Festival choice, Diana of Dobson's. That turned out to be an attractive but unsatisfactory piece. Rutherford is grittier and more compelling.

It starts deceptively. John Rutherford, the self-made master of the glasshouse, runs his home as dictatorially as he does his factory. He storms, for example, if he is kept waiting for his dinner, though he thinks nothing of keeping everybody else waiting until he is ready. So the play's first movement shows us the rest of the family hungrily anticipating his arrival. There his Ann, his spinster sister, stiff and resigned. There is John junior, who was being groomed as heir to the business (it would presumably save re- painting the signs) but showed no taste or aptitude for it and fled to London; he has now returned accompanied by his wife, a former office worker, and their infant son. There is Richard, Johns younger brother, who like the proverbial fool of the family, has gone into the church; and who has been cowed by his fathers bullying into acting more foolish than he really is. And there is Janet, their sister, unmarried like her aunt and, from the initial look and sound of her, as rigorous and puritanical as her father. They all have grievances and frustrations; and, as they gloomily unload them upon one another, it's hard not to be reminded of the old Monty Python sketch in which two flat-capped Northerners competed furiously over which of them had less to eat as a child and which had to dig more coal before breakfast.

When Rutherford senior arrives and calls the clan to order, the play and the characters break their bounds. He is in a professional and emotional bind; the business is in financial trouble, and though he claims, apparently sincerely, to have built it up for the sake of his children, he actually despises every one of them. Son John claims to have invented a new manufacturing process, one that might save the firm from ruin. He wants to sell it to the highest bidder; his father is determined to get it for free. Meanwhile, daughter Janet turns out to be a lot less repressed than everybody took her to be. There are awkward joins in the construction -- the author seems at her wits' end to find a place in the plot for Richard -- but the action rolls over them. You are agog, as in all the solid plays of this time, to know what happens next.

There are two major outsiders. One is Martin, the Rutherford foreman who becomes, by a powerful irony, the emotional trustee of three conflicting family members, and who buckles under the strain. The other is Mary, Johns wife, to whom old Rutherford has hardly deigned to speak since her arrival. By the end of the play, he has to. It might have been better had the author refrained from bringing this fact explicitly to our attention -- wed noticed it for ourselves -- but it's a superb device anyway, signalling a radical shift in the balance of power, and expertly prepared.

Jackie Maxwell's production makes a strong case for the play, with a couple of large lapses. Early on, an expository duet between John and Mary has been played on an exaggeratedly high pitch, as if both participants knew they were supposed to be upset, but had no idea why or how much. Even in the play at large, neither of these performances is quite right. John is a difficult role, a weakling with genuine abilities, self-absorbed and also self-destructive; the elements are all there in Dylan Trowbridges performance, but uncertainly dispensed, so one isnt always sure if it's the actor or the character who's vacillating.

As Janet, Kelli Fox is stunning, in two successive modes. As the black-clad housekeeper of the opening, she is a one-woman Wuthering Heights, barbed and boding. Then the mask comes off: She has to face her father, with both the accumulated bitterness of decades as an unpaid servant and the reality, already compromised, of her one chance at happiness. The griefs and the accusations come pouring out, white-hot; and the actress never indulges, never lets up, never hits a false note. And thats without reckoning the complexities of her last appearance which is composed about equally of erotic devotion and stony devastation, and which finally resolves into a silent declaration of independence. In The Return of the Prodigal a few seasons ago, Fox finely played a woman who was in a similar position but resigned to it. Here she gets to fight the battles and, from the audiences point of view, to win even those she loses.

Peter Krantz makes an arresting figure of Martin, torn between loyalties, though it's hard to believe in the feudal strength of the bonds to which he finally surrenders; you keep wanting him to stop being Frankenstein's monster and turn into D. H. Lawrence. Mike Shara adds a leaven of hapless humour as the reverend Richard.

Rutherford himself is Michael Ball, an actor who has been regularly cast as tyrannical capitalists and has often, as in Hobsons Choice and The Matchmaker, endowed them with unsuitably soft centres. Those plays, though, were comedies, so they may have seemed to be asking for it. This one gives no scope for lovability; and Ball, though he can never quite seem as if he were made of granite, rises finely to the occasion. Rutherford is not all monster; there is shrewdness, even occasional tolerance, in the way he deals with people to whom he is not related; his passion for the family firm is real, however destructive of his actual family. It ends up being both his downfall and, in a woundingly ironic reversal, his salvation. You can see it coming; which makes it all the more satisfying.

- In repertory until Oct. 9. Box office: 1-800-511-SHAW.

His accent wanders between north and south, which is conceivably intended to make a subtle geographical point but is in practice confusing.

HITCHES

There is a scene in which an aggrieved village-woman invades the Rutheford home and takes improbable possession of the living-room; she is played (by Donna Belleville) as if she were, accent part, an avenging banshee from an Irish play of the same period.

(This kind of confrontation, in which both parties aim at passion and only achieve petulance, seems to be a recurring weakness in Maxwells work; there was a scene just like it, and involving one of the same actors, in last year's Coronation Voyage.)

Nicole Underhay as his bride has even more trouble with the idiom, so much so that she often sounds simply inadequate; but the shape and meaning of the character are working away inside her, and they are in large part the shape and meaning of the play.

It may not have been the author's intention that this turn into a play about Janet, but she certainly provided the ammunition.

2004-06-23-women-on-the-edge-of-a-war:
WAITING FOR THE PARADE

Royal George Theatre,

Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

This seems to be Kelli Fox's week for being incandescent. The night after opening in Rutherford and Son, she appeared, peroxided almost out of recognition, in Waiting for the Parade, giving an equally striking performance in a totally dissimilar role.

She is one of a quintet of wives, mothers and daughters doing their bit on the Calgary home front in the Second World War. Fox's character has a husband serving abroad and reported missing. She takes up with another man, to the strong disapproval of some of her friends and the envious tolerance of others. Conflicted and fuelled by alcohol and music (she likes Elmer's Tune, though it's a controversial choice), she takes off into a great tirade in which affirmation dukes it out with despair.

Throughout the play, she is a vibrant, practical voice to whom the audience instinctively warms. Once again one admires this actress's energy. I don't mean that she shouts or runs around a lot, but that she zeroes in on her character's emotions and projects them with maximum intensity and minimum fuss. She is, as far as I can tell, absolutely in period. And it's refreshing to see an actress who has specialized in being solitary or rejected getting her man: two of them, in fact.

Those men, like all of their gender, remain offstage. The five women have the play to themselves. Just about every notable Canadian actress seems, at some time or another, to have appeared in John Murrell's play, which was first staged in 1977 and has been constantly revived ever since. It belongs to the snapshot school of Canadian drama; a historical situation is researched, representative characters are devised and given group scenes and solo scenes that it is hoped will accumulate into some kind of meaningful mosaic. The technique now seems old-fashioned, though it is still in frequent use (vide, most recently, Unity 1918) and is seldom as well-handled as here.

Murrell's greatest assets are his sympathetic ear and his resourcefulness at mixing and matching. Four of his characters work, in uneasy alliance, at a voluntary organization whose name and precise purpose are unspecified but which seems devoted to entertaining the troops, chastely, and bolstering the morale of any passing civilians. (Qualifications seem to include the ability to sing harmony.)

The fifth woman is a ringer, a German immigrant, non-Jewish, whose father has been interned. She is an object of suspicion to most of her neighbours, and the play's means of demonstrating this are initially glib; when she's heard singing Lilli Marlene, the Canadians, who apparently were unaware of the song's origins, immediately remove it from their playlist. Complexity dawns, however, when some of the other women begin to welcome her as a friend, with losses that parallel their own. Others don't, or they vacillate. Battle lines aren't drawn, exactly, but there are stimulating skirmishes.

If the play is meant to make a larger statement about women and war, as the author's program note suggests, then Linda Moore's prosaic production hasn't brought it out. The interest remains anecdotal. But they are involving anecdotes, and the performers are afforded at least the opportunity to dig beneath familiar surfaces. (How many male playwrights have written five good parts for women in one play?)

Laurie Paton matches Fox's performance with her quiet, dark and witty work as the German. Donna Belleville gives a brooding, peremptory account of an older woman who loses one son to war and another, a conscientious objector, to peace. Jenny L. Wright plays a young wife tethered to an ageing slob of a husband, and is lively if somewhat cartooned; hers is the one off-stage relationship that never comes clear in our minds, but then this character, with her reiterated worship of Leslie Howard and her uncritical trust in Mackenzie King, is something of a caricature.

The women's institute, or Calgary canteen, or whatever it is, is run by a bossy, self-important and self-consciously elegant person who is patronizingly beastly to the German, and raises her colleagues' hackles as well. "I don't like that woman," says one of them, repeatedly, apparently voicing the general opinion.

Unfortunately, it seems to be shared by Helen Taylor, who plays the hate object and delivers a flat performance that never suggests she might have a valid point of view, or even feelings of her own. It's true that the dramatist has left the character out in the cold, but it's the actress's and director's job to bring her in again.

- In repertory until Oct. 9. Box office: 1-800-511-SHAW.

Black & White Photo: David Cooper, Shaw Festival / From left, Helen Taylor, Jenny L. Wright, Donna Belleville and Kelli Fox keep the home fires burning in Waiting for the Parade.
2004-06-24-clever-stuff:
robertcushman@lycos.com

NATHAN THE WISE

Harbourfront Centre Theatre

- - -

There is a character in Nathan the Wise known as the Great Patriarch. He seems to be the head of the Orthodox Church in 12th- century Jerusalem. He is very keen on burning Jews at the stake. He is also not above instructing a Christian knight to carry out a murderous ambush on Saladin, the famous Arab sultan to whom the knight just happens to owe his life. The Patrriarch stands out among the people in this play for his malevolence. The others are about as nice a bunch as you could hope to encounter in a serious drama, especially one set in the middle of the Second Crusade with the three relevant religions poised at one another's throats.

Strangely, all this benevolence does not add up to blandness. Nathan the Wise presents a conflict of good intentions. It's a comedy since the conflicts are, with conscious artificiality, resolved, but it could just as easily turn tragic.

It was the last work of Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, major 18th- century German novelist, philosopher, playwright and -- I am pleased to note -- critic. Lessing was the son of a pastor and an object of scandal in his time for his inquisitive tolerance of other faiths; one thinks of him as a born-again humanist. The title character of his play, who shares much of his own benevolent skepticism, is a rich and universally respected Jewish merchant, a sort of Shylock in reverse, complete with a much-loved only daughter. He comes home from a trip to find that she has been rescued from burning -- not at the stake -- by a passing Knight Templar, the very same ex-captive whose life was spared by Saladin.

Knight and maiden are naturally primed to fall in love, which, after some hesitation on the young man's part ("A Christian love a Jew? Well, why not, this is the Promised Land") they duly do, with Nathan's ecumenical blessing.

Nathan, meanwhile, has been summoned to the court of the Sultan who, as he well knows, wants to extort gold from him. Saladin is, however, an exceptionally civilized potentate. He puts a question to the Jew: Which religion -- Jewish, Christian or Muslim -- is the true one?

Nathan is far too canny and skeptical to give a direct answer. Besides, he doesn't have one. Instead he offers a parable, designed to show that though there may be a truth, it is unknowable. Saladin is enchanted, and proclaims Nathan his friend for life. Good old reliable Nathan, not called the Wise for nothing, offers him the money anyway.

Saladin, to get back to the other part of the plot, released the Templar because the young man reminded him of his own deceased brother. There are all sorts of fairy-tale tangles going on here, and they are resolved in a series of revelations and reunions that might have raised the eyebrows of Shakespeare or Moliere, not least because the ending they inspire, though happy, is far from conventional.

Lessing, in fact, turns romance against itself -- the point presumably being that though it would be lovely if everybody were as tolerant as his characters learn to be, it isn't likely. It certainly wouldn't have been so in Jerusalem then, and it seems achingly unreachable now, hence the impulse for this revival. Nathan, so kind and clever and urbane, is a historically improbable figure, a backward projection of Lessing's own Enlightenment hopes, and Saladin, glamorous figure though he was, can hardly have been that noble. The play's considerable achievement is to make us believe in them dramatically, using wit as a fence against sentimentality.

Tim Albery's Soulpepper production is good on argument but short on atmosphere. The clarity of the former is underlined by Sharin DiGenova's lighting, while the vagueness of the latter is reflected in Dany Lyne's set, which is overall sandy. This looks impressive at first, but once we have paid our respects to the fact that the Holy Land is basically desert, we remember that Jerusalem itself must, even then, have been a built-up area. There is little sense of a city's life being led, and a log across the middle of the stage, conceivably symbolizing a barrier between the races, serves mainly as an impediment to traffic.

Costumes are mixed, Nathan approximately modern, everyone else approximately medieval. But if the Jew doesn't inhabit the same period as everybody else, we lose the sense of how perilous his position is. (The play itself is hardly so familiar that we need to be jolted out of any pre-conceived notions about it.) Yes, he's an anachronism, but the point doesn't need underlining. What the production chiefly lacks is danger.

In which connection, the only flaw I could detect in William Webster's Nathan is an excess of affability. Nathan has been through things, and though Webster is very moving in the moments at which these memories explicitly surface, they should surely be a part of him throughout, sewn into his coat. In all other respects, he is very fine. He embodies Nathan's moral qualities in a way I suspect few other actors could, he radiates humour and, yes, wisdom, and he is in total command of a complex text. (Edward Kemp's translation is in colloquial, barely identifiable verse.) His telling of the long religious fable is superb, and it calls out an answering quality in Andrew Moodie's suave Saladin, who can turn on terror in an instant, but knows to use it sparingly.

The play's Achilles heel may be its attempt to make a protagonist of an ethically perfect figure, while the character who goes through the most twists and travails, and so should technically be the hero, is the Templar. It's a tricky role and Dusan Dukic, though occasionally caught a step behind his own dramatic progress, does well by it.

The daughter is a surprisingly insubstantial presence, to whom Cara Pifko brings little besides an innate perkiness. Karen Robinson is jarringly bourgeoise as the Sultan's scheming sister. (She sounds, if you'll pardon the stereotype, more Jewish than anyone else in the play.) Among the Christians, there are good neutral performances by Barbara Gordon as the daughter's duenna and by Derek Boyes as a conscience-torn friar, but the most striking is David Calderisi's Patriarch, political to his fingernails.

There is yet a fourth culture represented, in the person of a temporarily non-whirling Dervish, charmingly played by Vik Sahay, who crosses all lines; he partners Nathan at chess and works as the Sultan's treasurer, a post for which he has neither the heart nor the qualifications. He quits, disgusted, and sets off for India, telling Nathan, who hesitates to join him, "if you can't live your life in the instant, you'll always be the slave of others."

It may be the most resonant moment in the play, though it doesn't seem to lead anywhere, but maybe it's balanced by the last image, which is one of acceptance, and is very well staged. The show doesn't yield the same tingle of discovery as such earlier Soulpepper rarities as Don Carlos and Platonov, but it's a fascinating evening and a heartening one.

- In repertory until July 31. Box office: 416-973-4000.

Black & White Photo: Guntar Kravis, Soulpepper Theatre / Cara Pifko as Rachel and William Webster as Nathan.
2004-06-26-anything-goes-worth-flying-ov: The Cole Porter songs in Anything Goes are prime numbers, but they don't add up to make a story. All the same, this is a joyous example of the old, raffish metropolitan musical, with a good, screwball book, light and witty staging, and good performances (though Cynthia Dale is no Ethel Merman).Every number's a showstopper, which is joyful if exhausting. (Avon Theatre, Stratford, Ontario. Runs to Oct. 31. 1-800-567-1600. www.stratfordfestival.com).
2004-06-26-hutt-putters-around-and-steal: As Vladimir, Samuel Beckett's senior tramp, William Hutt putters around the stage with his usual superb physical grace and physical wit. He moves daintly, partly because hes feeling his way with an old mans caution, partly because he's putting tentative toes into a metaphysical void. Albert Schultz's Soulpepper production is good but not great, though it stands a chance, as the run progresses, of achieving greatness. (Premiere Dance Theatre, Harbourfront. Runs to July 1, Aug. 20-Sept. 24. 416-973-4000).
2004-06-26-jonathan-goad-is-in-deft-cont: Leon Rubin's production, set in a rainforest with trailing tendrils (not to mention vertiginous trapezes), has no detectable overall vision: Its considerable pleasures have to be taken as they come. Among them are young lovers who hold attention from first to last; an Oberon (Jonathan Goad) in deft control of every mood and nuance; and a superb Bottom (Thom Marriott). But cutting references to Athens and the tradesmen severs the play from its roots. (Festival Theatre, Stratford. 1-800-567-1600. www.stratfordfestival.ca.)
2004-06-26-rutherford-and-son-s-stronges: In this play from 1912, there's trouble at a Yorkshire glass- making firm run on patriarchal principles -- though the strongest and cleverest characters are, like the author, Githa Sowerby, women. It's a gritty and compelling piece, with a strong narrative that ends with a woundingly ironic reversal. Michael Ball rises finely to the role of the tyrannical Rutherford; as his daughter, whose griefs and accusations come pouring out white-hot, Kelli Fox is stunning. (Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake. Runs to Oct. 9. 1-800- 511-7429. www.shawfest.com.)
2004-06-26-the-doras-and-the-winner-is-o:
Picking winners for this year's Dora Awards is a more than usually frustrating occupation, because the nominations in most categories are more than usually grotesque. True, the 2003-2004 theatre season in Toronto was not a bright one, but it wasn't quite as gloomy as the Dora voters, by both their inclusions and omissions, have managed to suggest. Something is wrong with the electoral process -- maybe it's log-rolling, maybe it's the theatrical equivalent of tactical voting, but it should be looked into.

We start with the General Theatre division. "General" here means larger, a capacious domain that can accommodate anything from the Princess of Wales to Theatre Passe Muraille, but that does include most of the venues most people, including this critic, are likeliest to have visited.

Outstanding New Play: This, as is perhaps appropriate, is the most vexatious category of all. I thought the best new work of the season was Jason Sherman's Remnants, followed by Ronnie Burkett's Provenance, which was one-half disappointing but the other half superb. Neither play was nominated. The omnitalented Burkett, who might have qualified in three other categories, has this year been shut out of all of them. Could this be backlash after all his previous acclaim?

Of those that are up there, my money would be on Trey Anthony's da kink in my hair, even though I didn't see it. Or maybe, given the competition, because I didn't see it. The most respectable of the rest is Marjorie Chan's China Doll, though I doubt it made anybody's heart sing.

Confederation's claim to newness rests on a technicality, as it's a reworking of an earlier play in Michael Hollingsworth's ongoing cartoon history of Canada. The whole cycle probably deserves a special prize, but singling out this installment looks like an act of desperation.

The two remaining contestants are unbelievable. Peter Froehlich's Simpl, a tribute to an old German comedian, was a decent evening's entertainment but only marginally a play. Michael O'Brien's Restitution - An Irish-Canadian Rhapsody was generally regarded as appalling; I actually liked it more than most, but not to the point of calling it good. The most surprising omission is Carole Frechette's Helen's Necklace, which everybody else seemed to think was wonderful; I suppose I should feel vindicated but I actually feel vaguely indignant.

Outstanding New Musical: This always occasions a certain amount of barrel-scraping, sometimes reaching as far down as Ross Petty Christmas pantomimes. Not this year, though Petty's Cinderella (one of his better shows) was as deserving of a nod as the nominated Pelagie, which was deadeningly worthy, or Hello ... Hello and Top Gun! The Musical, which were deadeningly worthless.

That leaves Tequila Vampire Matinee, which was original and fun. Betcha Top Gun gets it, though (its camp apparently struck a chord), unless there's an Acadian sympathy vote for Pelagie.

Outstanding Production of a Play: This, if it means anything, means Best All-Round Show (Without Songs).

This, by any sane measure, was Soulpepper's No Man's Land. It wasn't nominated. It's tempting to accuse the Doras of an anti- Soulpepper bias (the company, along with CanStage, is regarded as Establishment and therefore suspect), but I'd say that in most respects Albert Schultz's bunch have had fair treatment this year.

This oversight, though, is a huge one; and paranoia has a right to be rampant. And then again, just look at the competition. For thoughts on China Doll, Confederation and Simpl, see under Outstanding New Play above.

Remnants (Tarragon) deserves to win for its combination of writing, acting and direction. The Syringa Tree (CanStage, so I contradict myself) probably will win. You alternate two admired actresses in a solo turn that goes straight to our liberal hearts and what else do you expect?

Outstanding Production of a Musical (or Best All-Round Show With Songs): How exactly do you compare The Producers, brought in on a big scale, with the home-brewed product? Well, if you have to, The Producers clearly wins (and at this point it could probably use the comfort). I certainly wouldn't repine if the glory went to The Last Five Years (American piece but new Canadian production), but there's a better chance that it will go to Cookin' at the Cookery, though it's nothing like as good a show, and -- lest we forget -- is also brought in. I see Tequila Vampire Matinee is in there too, so maybe it has a better shot at New Musical than I'd thought.

Outstanding Performance by a Male in a Principal Role -- Play: The standard here is very high. Jim Mezon (Copenhagen) was very fine, and I am happy for David Ferry (Hockey Mom, Hockey Dad), Rick Roberts (hilarious in Hotel Loopy) and, even though I didn't see him, Dennis O'Connor (Le Visiteur). And I lament the exclusion of Kevin Hanchard (Blue/Orange). All the same, if it doesn't go to William Hutt (No Man's Land) we have forgotten what both words and acting mean.

Outstanding Performance by a Female in a Principal Role -- Play: This must be a headache. Yanna McIntosh and Caroline Cave are both up for The Syringa Tree, and the canniest thing would have been to finesse some kind of joint nomination. Forced to choose, I imagine the jury will vote for McIntosh, though if it were me I'd be inclined to avoid the issue and plump for Martha Burns (Happy Days), who was just as good. (And dare I say that I was more impressed by McIntosh's unlisted number in Phedre?) Nicola Lipman (Simpl) was good, but doesn't stand a chance; likewise Jane Spidell, nominated for Blood, but deserving it more for Rune Arlidge. Department of Seriously Uncanny Coincidence: The author of Rune Arlidge this year won our awed admiration by donating part of his liver to the author of Blood. That certainly puts awards in perspective.

Outstanding Performance by a Male in a Principal Role -- Musical: Michael Therriault in The Producers, and I don't want to hear any arguments. (Therriault's co-star, Sean Cullen, is also nominated and will be hosting the ceremonies. Hello, Sean.)

Outstanding Performance by a Female in a Principal Role -- Musical: Jackie Richardson (Cookin' at the Cookery) will get this in a cakewalk, though it's a shame that it's at the expense of her co- performer, Montego Glover. Why wasn't she entered under Supporting? Or, as they call it here, Feature? The rest are filler, though can anyone explain to me why Susan Gilmour, Amy Rutherford and Sarah Cornell (the wondrous sex-object of The Producers) were nominated, while Blythe Wilson (The Last Five Years) wasn't?

Outstanding Performance in a Supporting -- sorry, Feature -- Role in a Play or Musical: Another bulging category, the more so as it contains the entire cast of Confederation, billed as Ensemble. So joint nominations are allowed. Assuming they don't win by weight of numbers: C. David Johnson (The Play's the Thing) was a repeat performance and Brandon McGibbon (The Producers) honestly wasn't that good. It's down to William Webster (Phedre) and Juan Chioran (The Producers). Chioran's was the flashier role, if that means anything. Actually, it was the flashiest role of the year, and he did it better than the guy on the Broadway-cast CD.

Outstanding Direction of a Play: Albert Schultz (No Man's Land) isn't there. Richard Rose is, twice: deservedly, for Remnants, and undeservedly, for Simpl. Sarah Stanley (Restitution) boggles the mind. Larry Moss (The Syringa Tree) -- well, he didn't do anything wrong that I could see. What about Morris Panych (Amadeus)?

Outstanding Direction of a Musical: Again, two different worlds. Susan Stroman (The Producers) beggars, in every sense, the local product. If the home team gets it, then Daryl Cloran (The Last Five Years) deserves to win; Marion Caffey (Cookin' at the Cookery) doesn't, but very likely will. While we're at it:

Outstanding Choreography: I don't see how this could not be Stroman.

Outstanding Musical Direction: I want it to be Marek Norman (The Last Five Years).

When we get to the various design awards, we're even further into the comparison of incomparables. Let me say merely that Robin Wagner's sets and William Ivey Long's costumes for The Producers were all they should have been; and the costumes, by Astrid Janson and Julie Renton, for Restitution were well up to VideoCabaret's fantastical standards. Andrea Lundy picked up three of the six lighting nominations; I'm rooting for her work on Phedre.

In the Independent (or Very Small) Theatre division, I didn't see enough to have many opinions. I was no fan of Dear Boss (up for New Play) or of (nod), another Production nominee).

I did like Rebecca Northan (Female Performance) in Dear Boss, though she faces stiff competition from Kate Meehan (Tape). Eli Batalion has a deserved Male Performance nomination for Job: The Hip- Hop Saga, though his partner in this two-man show mysteriously doesn't. Clinton Walker has one for The Trials of John Demjanjuk; Frank Moore hasn't, but should have.

The various nominations for Theatre for Young Audiences managed to ignore both New Canadian Kid and Number One and Jamie at the resurgent YPT (now renamed the Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People). Opera is none of my business, but I would choose the Canadian Opera Company's Die Walkure for Production, and, beyond a doubt, Laura Claycomb's heavenly Gilda in Rigoletto for Performance.

2004-06-26-the-first-10-minutes-of-urine: All toilet facilities have been handed over to a private corporation that runs them on a fee-for-use basis. A musical satire on matters political and environmental that's also a satire on the idea of doing a musical satire in the first place: It's not always as funny as it thinks it is but certainly as clever. The score is super-pastiche that retains its own delighted voice; the staging adds its own zany commentary; and the first 10 minutes are musical- comedy heaven. (Bluma Appel Theatre, 27 Front St. E., 416-368-3110. Until Labour Day weekend.)
2004-06-26-waiting-for-the-parade-gives-: This is Kelli Fox's season for being incandescent. Here, she is vibrant, with maximum intensity and minimum fuss, as a Second World War wife whose husband is missing in action and who takes up with another man, to mixed reactions from her friends. She and Laurie Paton join the long line of Canadian actresses who have given outstanding performances in John Murrell's 1977 play about five Calgary women doing their bit on the home front.
