ROMEO AND JULIET

Home Depot Theatre

ShakespeareWorks is an organization, involving some of our best actors, that for the last half-dozen years has been taking Shakespeare workshops into schools. It is not the only group to have done this but it is has, by all accounts, done it very well. It has now moved on to, literally, another stage, and a purpose-built one at that. A platformed playhouse has been erected in Ashbridges Bay Park at the eastern end of the Beaches -- a theatre paid for, built by and named after the Home Depot company. It is, as befits such patronage, an impressive testimonial to the things that can be done with wood.

It has a thrust stage, not unlike the one at Stratford, though where that one bristles with sharp points, this one is rounded off. Behind it is an array of steps and balconies that pays notional tribute to the Elizabethan theatre but also strongly resembles a grand old-fashioned movie house. In place of the screen is a large hole affording a view of Lake Ontario and the cycle path in front of it. I have heard people speak philosophically of open-ended theatre, but this is the first time I have ever sat in one.

In theory, we are getting the best of both worlds -- the shelter of walls and a roof with the grandeur of a natural setting. In practice, I fear we are getting the worst; the structure may well keep out the rain (this couldn't be tested on Friday night) but it doesnt keep out the cold, while our view of the outside world is severely circumscribed. The passing traffic, mechanized or human, doesnt get absorbed into the picture, as it does at the arboreal theatre in Coronation Park; it just distracts.

The stage itself is fine, though this inaugural Romeo and Juliet doesn't do much for or with it. The rearguard action that ShakespeareWorks has been fighting against the erosion of literature in our schools is vital, and the more there is of it the better. But we aren't starved in Toronto for summer productions of Shakespeare alfresco, and though the casting for this show looked, on paper, as if it might outclass the opposition, it hasnt worked out that way.

Anyone coming fresh to the play (which should surely mean much of the target audience) would, I think, be baffled by the first quarter- hour. The prologue has been cut, though "two households both alike in dignity" is an idea that would surely have appealed to the sponsors. The course of the opening brawl is disguised by percussive accompaniment, aimless rampaging, odd little sub-fights and sheer bad speaking.

Later, R.H. Thomsons production does have some good ideas. I liked the rejigging of the text that enables Tybalt to punctuate the ball scene with explosions of wrath rather than spending himself in a single outburst. This mixed-up Capulet kid is portrayed (by Michael Rubenfeld) as a spluttering sociopath who prowls the streets of Verona cracking a bullwhip, and who meets his end when Romeo, in a clear case of poetic justice, garrottes him with it. In the graveyard finale -- the best scene in the show -- the peripheral characters hovering outside the tomb speak in apprehensive whispers, which is both sensible and atmospheric.

But the effective moments remain isolated. They have no afterlife and fit into no coherent rhythm. This is particularly sad as the director seems to be trying to make the separate scenes illuminate one another, sometimes by overlapping them. That's good in theory; in practice it means having Juliet's gallop apace, you fiery- footed steeds obscured by the dead bodies being carried off from the previous scene. And when scenes arent being thus rushed, they are often -- especially in the Capulet household -- agonizingly drawn out.

Proven actors come off mediocre or worse. Sarah Orenstein, after all her fine work at the Shaw Festival, plays a Lady Capulet who initially hints at having been soured by early motherhood but whose later emotions seem to have got snarled up in her veiled headdress, which resembles an ornate hairnet. (The costumes are generally unhappy. When Paris, who is most drably got-up, asks Capulet "what say you to my suit?" you fear the old man will actually tell him.)

John Dolans elderly competence as Friar Lawrence is welcome under the circumstances, but he does nothing truly interesting until the last scene, when he approaches the drugged Juliet in an obvious state of mortal terror. Lynne Griffin's Nurse is all right, once she gets past an atrociously fussy first scene, though her "marry with the County" speeches are grimly misdirected.

The only truly successful performance, the only one with both fire and logic, is Blair Williams' Mercutio, who infuses good old traditional swagger with a sense of inner anger, lashing himself into a frenzy in his Queen Mab cadenza as if fearful that he might at any moment run out of metaphor.

The title roles have been given to two young performers who have done well in modern plays but are ill-equipped for this one. They are done in at their first encounter by staging that banishes them to the side of the stage while what seem like acres of space remain unoccupied in the centre. They rally for the balcony scene, which is done with a nice blend of playfulness and apprehension, but fall apart thereafter, both individually and as a team.

Allan Hawcos Romeo is the better, though happier fooling around with the boys than with the love stuff. Mary Krohnerts most notable previous role was Helen Keller in The Miracle Worker, which may not be the best preparation for long passages of Shakespearean verse. It may even be counterproductive; the pre-miracle Helen threw herself about in frustration at not being able to express herself in words, and Juliet seems to be behaving much the same, waving her arms when language refuses to work for her. She is about the brattiest, worst- tempered Juliet I remember seeing; I suspect there is an intelligent performance going on underneath but it doesn't stand a chance of emerging. She isn't helped by having her potion-speech interrupted by the ghost of Tybalt, an appearance as uncalled-for as any he can have made during his lifetime.

The other juveniles include two pleasant studies in gaucherie: a Peter (Richard Harte) who comes on like Steve Buscemi, and a Benvolio (Ryan Field) who likes to hang backwards down flights of steps, like some kind of urban sloth, a habit that later spreads to all the other junior Montagues.

Audiences are handed a Shakespearean Insult Kit, which may be left over from ShakespeareWorks educational program. Choice epithets are arranged in two columns of adjectives and one of nouns; we can mix and match as we please. So if I wanted to describe anyone connected with the show as a mammering, clay-brained canker-blossom (Im not saying I do and I'm not saying I don't), the company would have only itself to blame.

MAN AND SUPERMAN

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

- - -

"I wish says Enry Straker, Cockney chauffeur from the days when automobiles were automobiles and only the select and wealthy few could afford to own them, that I had a car that would go as fast as you can talk, Mr. Tanner." On Saturday at the Shaw Festival, every reviewer in the house must have rushed to copy that line down, while the response from the audience was uproarious. Enry had expressed perfectly what we had all been thinking. Ben Carlson plays Jack Tanner, self-described Member of the Idle Rich Class and author of The Revolutionists Handbook, and the exhilarating velocity of his delivery is only matched by its clarity, intelligence, charm, passion, self-mockery and wit. This is a wonderful performance, an individual creation that is a walking textbook on how to act Shaw.

Its the driving force of a tremendous production, one that was greeted at its premiere with an ovation of a fervour I have never encountered before at this festival and rarely anywhere else. (For an audience to stand up and cheer is standard politeness these days, but it's still unusual for it to refuse to shut up and leave when the lights are raised so that the actors have to take their calls all over again.) The volume of the applause was commensurate with the volume, in another sense, of the performance. This production is a six-hour affair, including a generous interval for lunch. It includes not only the basic comedy of courtship that constitutes the standard acting edition but the long tangent, in the form of a dream, that Shaw stuck in halfway through and that is generally known as Don Juan in Hell. In this, John Tanner takes on the identity of his namesake and supposed ancestor, Juan Tenorio, the lecher of Seville. Remembering that The Importance of Being Earnest is also in this year's repertoire, you might say he is Jack in this world and Juan in the next. This infernal interlude is crammed with orations that are among the longest, and mercifully among the best- turned, that GBS ever dreamed up.

Though the production is running through the season, the complete version can only be viewed this month. My best advice is to beat the doors down now, perhaps shaming the management into bringing the whole thing back next year. The shorter version will no doubt continue to be excellently performed, but it is unlikely to have the same impact.

It may also look rather odd. The director, Neil Munro, and his designer, Peter Hartwell, seem to have planned their staging on the sensible principle that a play which has to incorporate a scene in Hell can hardly afford to look realistic. So, though the costumes reflect the plays Edwardian origins, the settings could be anywhere. The first act, in particular, looks as if its going on in a rehearsal room; it's lined with benches and filled with chairs and tables that can be arranged to give the actors all the support they absolutely need and not a sofa or bookshelf. At the back is a screen on which the characters, who are, after all, myths-in-waiting, can cast their shadows before making their entrances. Tanner's motorcar gets similar skeletal treatment, and delighted applause, in the next scene. Shaw being notorious for his love of paradox, it seems appropriate that this season there should be a realistic car onstage in Pygmalion, which doesnt demand one, but not in this play, which does; and that both should work perfectly.

Munro and Hartwell delight in playing games with our expectations. When we get to Hell, we find four bare chairs side by side and dread that we are in for a static four-sided debate; in fact the chairs are only once occupied, and then as a joke. Most of the scene finds the actors roaming around a plush red operatic Hades, complete with yawning smoky grilles, but roaming always with purpose. Each of them seems ideally placed at every moment; the visual orchestration matches the verbal, and helps make it possible. And so it is, too, in the more conventional scenes. The play is a duel between Tanner, the self-proclaimed rebel against convention, and his ward, Ann Whitefield, who is set on marrying him. In each act they have a duet; each time they start on opposite sides of the wide stage and come gradually together, grudgingly or, at the last, passionately. Ann is that recurring Shavian figure, the respectable woman whose virtue allows her to be both shameless flirt and ruthless predator, but whom we cheer on because we know shes made the right choice, and that he will be the better for it. Fiona Byrne plays her very prettily and guilefully, if without the magnetic power that Shaw envisaged for this vessel of what he was pleased to call the Life Force.

And what has all this love play to do with Don Juan in Hell? Not much, actually; or, at least, the connection hangs by a thread. For centuries, poets and dramatists have been re-casting the legendary womanizer as a philosopher; Shaw, being Shaw, makes him a Puritan as well. The Devil (Benedict Campbell, courteous and implacable) is a sentimental hedonist, whom we have glimpsed on Earth as a Spanish brigand; backed up by the Statue who was Juan's earthly nemesis (David Schurmann, courteous and very placable, known in the waking world as Roebuck Ramsden, pillar of moderately enlightened society) he makes horribly irrefutable speeches about mankind's essentially destructive nature. Juan nevertheless refutes them, claiming, whatever its lapses, humanity strives for perfection; evolution continues to evolve. Ann, present as Dona Ana, grasps from this that her purpose is to help the process by finding the best father for her child. In other words, the whole gigantic digression provides the unconscious motivation for her behaviour in the main action. But, basically, what we have here are two plays for the price of one, and I personally am not complaining, especially given how well they are both being done.

I admit that the barebones production tends to maroon the older female characters, who need a society to belong to: Sharry Flett, good actress though she is, is in no way credible as Anns browbeaten mother. (If its any consolation to her, she looks far too young.) But there is a phalanx of good men. Evan Buliung may be too modern, too aware of his own absurdity, as Ann's hopeless poet- suitor, but his is still a delightful performance, and the herald of a future star. Straker is a gift of a role, but one that a surprising number of actors fumble; Patrick Galligan nails every thought and every syllable. There is solid work from Graeme Somerville and Guy Bannerman as a pair of Irish-Americans who serve to people a sub-plot, along with Lisa Norton who plays Ann's opposite number with unflinching unpleasantness.

We also get a glimpse in Hell of Jennifer Phipps, who plays Ann as an older woman and finds as much wit in five minutes as her colleagues do in five hours. The production knows what it's doing at every moment, down to when it starts lowering the curtain, with one vital speech still to go. Carlson, with whom this review must end as it began, unabashedly detaches himself and delivers it down front, marvellously. Earlier he has won applause in the middle of a scene with his magnificent delivery of a speech composed entirely of antitheses. I have never, in the non-musical theatre, felt an audience to be so completely with an actor; and never can the solidarity have been more deserved.

- Man and Superman in repertory until Oct. 9; Don Juan in Hell until July 25. Call 1-800-511-SHAW.

robertcushman@lycos.com

THE TINKER'S WEDDING

Court House Theatre,

Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

John Millington Synge wrote one famous full-length play, The Playboy of the Western World, and several that are lesser-known and shorter. The Tinker's Wedding is one of these, and is being given a lunchtime production at the Shaw Festival.

Like most of Synge's plays, this one is set among the peasantry of backroads Ireland, who are depicted as a voluble set of cunning loons. Young Sarah Casey has taken it into her head to marry her companion, tinker Michael Byrne. The priest in the County Wicklow village where they abide agrees to perform the rites, on payment of 10 shillings and a freshly made tin can. Michael's mother, Mary, who dearly loves her pint, sells the can to buy booze, and some hell breaks loose. The priest washes his hands of all three vagrants, and they assault him. He begins formally to anathematize them, and they run away in terror.

Synge was one of the founding writers of the Irish dramatic renaissance of the 1900s, and Dublin's notoriously shockable press and public were regularly scandalized by him. The Playboy caused riots, just apparently by using the word "shift." The Tinker went unstaged in its author's short lifetime, but it was published and, as expected, vilified. This time, though, it wasn't sex the critics were on about but religion.

They seem to have been unperturbed both by the probability that Sarah was already living with her intended, and by the gynecological implications of her marital yearnings coming upon her, as her man puts it, "since the moon did change." They ignored what they elsewhere denounced as Synge's slurs on Irish womanhood; what infuriated them was his view of the Irish priesthood. The parson here is venal and stupid, though no more so than the tinkers.

The common view is that the play is on the side of the latter, as being in tune with the natural world, and it's true they seem to have more notion than the priest of how to have a good time -- at least, old Mary does. But really each side is as bad as the other, and the play makes no bones about it. The great strength of Synge's plays is their total lack of sentimentality.

Their greatest weakness, though to be sure it's often reckoned a strength, is the elaboration of their style. He writes fine and flavourful, when he confines himself to simple sentences, as when the priest tells his tormentors, "Let you leave the road, and not be plaguing me any more."

But it's seldom he does so confine himself. "Is it raving mad you're going, Sarah Casey," asks her putative mother-in-law, "and you the pride of women to destroy the world?" The second phrase, pungent as it is, blunts the direct impact of the first. Words in plays are weapons, and should be, and these are too frequently muffled.

So the first duty of a production is to rescue the conflict, and to turn the lines of text into lines of force running between the characters. This is something that Micheline Chevrier and her cast only occasionally accomplish. Most of the time we are conscious of a decorative noise going on, without much specific meaning. The delivery is in a style that it's impossible to resist describing as Synge-song. (And it isn't a matter of accent, it's a matter of phrasing.)

Nora McLellan comes off the strongest as old Mary, with her face, as the playwright himself might put it, as black as a chimney- sweep's that's just after comin' down half-a-dozen flues one after the other, the way she'd be rollickin' about the stage with her arms flailing, and the smell of the drink upon her voice as clear as it might be upon her breath, and she a good 20 years too young for the part, with the vigour of 10 women inside her.

Trish Lindstrom as Sarah is fierce but undecipherable, and the way the two women are going on at one another, you know one is hammer and the other is tongs, but you couldn't say which is which and what they might have on their minds. David Leyshon is refreshingly laconic as the tinker, and he a mere pawn in the game, despite having his name emblazoned in the title in full view of the whole Niagara region and the blessed tourists besides.

The priest is described, just before his entrance, as "a big boast of a man with a long step on him and a trumpeting voice." So it's a grand surprise when he turns out to be none other than little William Vickers, and he less a boast than a modest understatement with a prim, pettish sort of walk and a voice to match. And though it's long we've known him to be a fine, funny actor, he carries no overtones here of the princes of the church, the way he'd rather be handing out condolences than maledictions, and any angry woman might snap her fingers at him and devil the consequences. He puts up, in short, not much of a fight.

The play is a tricky one, and some of the tricks are its own fault, but there's more to it than gets a proper airing here.

- In repertory until Sept. 5. Box office: 1-800-511-SHAW.

Color Photo: David Cooper, The Shaw Festival / Trish Lindstrom as Sarah Casey and David Leyshon as Michael Byrne.

2004-07-16-a-double-bill-with-the-requis:
THE DUMB WAITER / THE ZOO STORY

Harbourfront Studio Theatre

- - -

I will, any day, take minor Harold Pinter, which The Dumb Waiter is, over major Edward Albee, which The Zoo Story is. Soulpepper's new double bill gives us the opportunity to take them together. Both go down smoothly, and both go down very well, especially the Pinter, which is practically impeccable.

There are two of them in every Pinter play, or at least in many, especially the early ones: Two wide boys, two wise guys, engaged in nefarious and often mysterious pursuits, threatening others while feeling threatened themselves. They are the Irishman and the Jew who abduct the unfortunate hero of The Birthday Party, the two servants who stand guard over the alcoholic novelist in No Man's Land. They are, in an especially subtle variation, the two brothers in The Caretaker, who are barely on stage together but palpably bonded nonetheless. In their purest form they are Ben and Gus, who have The Dumb Waiter to themselves.

Ben and Gus, as we not too gradually learn, are gunmen, employed on a regular basis by an unspecified organization; it might be criminal or it might, to judge from the resources it apparently has at its disposal, be quasi-governmental. They are clearly Londoners, though when we meet them they are in Birmingham, in the basement of a big house awaiting the arrival of their latest victim. It's the usual arrangement, though Gus, who seems unhealthily given to questioning and complaining, thinks the sleeping and catering arrangements represent a decline from what they're used to. Both men are nervous. Ben, the senior partner, tries to relieve his feelings by reading and re-reading the newspaper; Gus would like to make some tea, but is frustrated by the facilities.

Around 1960, when this play was first produced (it seems to have been written in 1958, maybe as a trial run for the far more complex Birthday Party) Pinter acknowledged three influences on his work: Beckett, Kafka, and American gangster films. All are in evidence here, but he seems to have left another off the list: The BBC Light Entertainment Department. He is writing in the style of such radio and TV classics as The Goon Show, Hancock's Half Hour and Steptoe and Son; barbed cross-talk routines in which Cockney-influenced banter climbs into absurdity before boiling over into exasperation. Or maybe it isn't an influence; maybe it's a bred-in-the-bone affinity. Ben and Gus squabble over the problems that surround common phrases concerning the boiling of kettles (or, to be as precise as they might like to be, the boiling of water in kettles). Their patience is further tested by the activity of the dumb waiter itself, a miniature elevator device used in big old houses to transmit orders to kitchens below. This one starts making demands on them ("Scampi!") that they are very ill-equipped to meet. Someone, it seems, is playing games with them, and cruel ones.

Ben and Gus are played, respectively, by Michael Hanrahan and Stuart Hughes, the same actors who played the equivalent roles in Soulpepper's No Man's Land. Part of the point of this production is to let us see what was then a subsidiary couple, operating in its own right. The compliment, and the promotion, are justified. They have a few problems with the accents but none with the rhythms, which are far more important. We begin with Hughes doing some modest calisthenics, mainly involving the putting-on of shoes; Hanrahan, lying on his bed, watches with disgust. There are shades of Laurel and Hardy, especially on Hughes' side of the equation. Already we have two modes of humour, two modes of tension; and Ted Dykstra's production subsequently plays both to the hilt. The two men sitting back to back, in complementary perplexity, are a rich sight. Steve Lucas' set exudes genteel damp, and John Lott's soundscape is first- rate, from the off-stage roar of traffic kicking itself and the play into gear to the minatory creaking of the dumb-waiter itself. The only possible quarrel with Dykstra's direction might be that the characters' interaction is so detailed, the surprise ending is not much of a surprise -- but that seems a small price to pay.

The same two actors supply the other half of the evening's raison d'etre by appearing in The Zoo Story, another duologue and one that starts with bird-song instead of with motorbikes. If The Dumb Waiter was among Pinter's first plays, The Zoo Story was Albee's very first or at least the first to be admitted into his canon. It's a more ambitious piece. The Dumb Waiter is pretty much a self-defining mechanism (and so more enjoyable to us than to its original audiences, who wondered what it meant); The Zoo Story undeniably opens on to wider vistas, and not just because it takes place in the open air. Jerry, the urban outcast who keeps the respectable publisher Peter glued to his Central Park bench with stories of his lonely childhood and lonelier adulthood and of the landlady whom he hates and of her dog who hates him, has a statement to make about love. His question as to why, if his feelings have no value, the word "love" was invented in the first place, is a resonant one, and it crowns a brilliantly-witty monologue. It does not, for me, erase sickly sentimentality that suffuses this as it does so many plays by Albee (and that you never, repeat never, get in Pinter), or the air of warmed-over Kerouac that Jerry brings with him. It's a play very much of its period, and Albee was unwise to update it, as he recently has. Peter might just have sat still on his bench in innocent old 1959 but at any later date he would have turned and ran in two minutes. And the religious undertones in the characters' names (Jerry for Jesus) and in the climactic action are very suspect.

What is exciting, as often in Albee, is the play's aggressive humour, along with -- very well staged in Diana Leblanc's production -- the battle for the bench. We're always being told that Pinter's plays are about territorial battles; this one of Albee's really is. Hanrahan, with his pained and bashful smile, gives a beautifully complete account of Peter; Albee has now written a prequel dealing with Peter's marriage, but in light of what Hanrahan implies here, with his smile and the nervous crossing of his legs, it hardly seems necessary. Hughes takes longer to get inside Jerry's skin; he seems at first to be paying unconscious though certainly timely tribute to the young Marlon Brando. But he has found his voice by the big speech, and it's a hypnotic one.

CYMBELINE

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

As many people must have noticed, the Shakespeare plays that most move an audience are not the great tragic ones that are officially supposed to. I don't think I have ever cried a drop at Hamlet or Macbeth, and though I have shed tears at King Lear they have not been at the tragic finale but at the reconciliation of Lear and Cordelia that comes a whole act earlier and constitutes a kind of false happy ending.

It's the epiphanies, genuine or bogus, that get you every time, which means the plays that most reliably tickle the tear ducts are the comedies, and it sometime seems that the more improbable or convoluted their resolutions are, the more power they have. The most bizarre of all is Cymbeline, a fairy tale trying to pass itself off as a history. Its new Stratford production, only the third in the theatre's history, certainly choked me up, and I mean that in a very good way.

There is more sheer story in Cymbeline than in any other Shakespeare play, including a sizeable amount of stuff that has happened before the curtain goes up. Imogen, daughter of Cymbeline, a vestigially historical king of ancient Britain, has married a poor but valiant gentleman named Posthumus whom her furious father has now banished. Cloten, the king's loutish stepson, has been paying court to Imogen, egged on by the Queen, his transparently evil mother. Meanwhile, or rather a long time ago, Imogen's own two brothers have vanished, stolen in infancy.

All of this is explained in the first scene by a First Gentleman, who like all first gentlemen knows everything, to a Second Gentleman, whose ignorance is, even by second gentleman standards, phenomenal. David Latham's production gets rid of him, and turns the entire exposition into a monologue, delivered by a young actor, Kyle Blair, who subsequently appears as a soothsayer, a singer (for the heavenly aubade "hark, hark, the lark") and Jupiter, who makes a late visionary appearance, supposedly perched on an eagle. He is, in short, the play's hotline to the supernatural, a function he discharges with charm, even though I suspect someone older and more waggish might have better filled the bill.

I rather wish Latham had not backed off from the gentlemen's scene as written, if only because its bald-faced outrageousness sets the tone for much of the play. One of its author's last works, it's full of shameless theatrical devices, many of which echo characters and situations in the earlier ones. Harold Bloom, writing with his customary blend of brilliance and pig-headedness, has convinced himself that the play is a sustained essay in self-parody. I don't see how any production could hope to get this across, and I suspect Shakespeare was merely enjoying himself working the conventions, laughing with but not at them. He comes across as a mellow master who is mostly holding his material at arm's length but who can sometimes find himself overwhelmingly involved with it.

He certainly piles on the styles. The action stretches to include an invasion of Britain by the forces of Rome, whose general bears the twice-Latin appellation of Caius Lucius but whose staff officers seem to be a far later breed of Italian, with names ending in a vowel. One of them, Iachimo, is a major-league Jacobean villain, who makes a wager with the exiled Posthumus on his wife's chastity and goes to great duplicitous lengths to make it appear that he's won. There are also scenes in the Welsh mountains, where the king's lost sons have been brought up as extraordinarily noble savages, and where, inter alia, they deliver the most exquisite dirge in the English language over a character who happens not to be dead.

In narrative terms the bits all fit together with fiendish, seemingly casual ingenuity. Making them belong to the same dramatic world is another matter, and productions tend either to place the whole thing within some kind of unifying scenic frame or to play each component for its own value as vividly as possible. Latham takes the latter course, and generally succeeds; visually, the production is no particular shakes (though it offers an unusually intelligble staging of the oddest battle scene in Shakespeare), but it confirms its director's talent for dealing lucidly with wildly difficult texts.

To play the Wicked Stepmother he has Martha Henry, at her silkiest; she wears a fur collar and carries a pet ferret, making it hard to tell where one ends and the other begins. Nobody would be taken in by her for a moment, but then hardly anybody in the play is. She is able, through sheer mastery of words and the spaces between them, to build solid relationships with other characters, most notably her unsavoury son, in which role Ron Kennell gives the tastiest performance of the evening.

This Cloten is the ultimate spoiled child, very funny as a vain fool, he is also dangerous, not least to himself. Imogen tells him that her husband's "meanest garment" means more to her than Cloten's whole person, and he obsesses on the phrase, theerby activating not just a fetish but a whole extra plotline. I have never seen this played half as entertainingly or half as convincingly.

Claire Jullien doesn't dominate the play as Imogen is traditionally supposed to; but she acts with delicacy and strength and a surprising humour: "I see a man's life is a tedious one" she remarks in her male disguise ( I must have mentioned the male disguise), and delights the house. She also masters the more testing tragi-comedy of waking up beside what she takes to be her husband's headless corpse; this is Shakespeare milking a situation to its absurd limits, as was the fashion among his younger contemporaries, and then transcending it.

Her two major male foils fall short, though in opposite ways. Dion Johnstone shows promise as Iachimo, but mere promise in so juicy a role hardly cuts it; he looks more smooth-tongued than he sounds. If Iachimo is a gift of a part, the jealous Posthumus is a pill, a character who pushes to the limit the convention that, however foully a hero may behave, he's still a hero.

Dan Chameroy rages energetically but looks disconcertingly sulky. He seems in fact like more of a Cloten; since the two men are said to take the same size in clothes and are never on stage together, maybe they should be doubled. (Makes at least as much sense as doubling Theseus and Oberon.)

Of the other young actors, Gordon S. Miller likewise shows promise as the younger lost boy, and Stephen Gartner definite achievement as the elder. As their guardian, Stephen Russell sports a beard and manner apparently left over from his Mennonite performance in last year's Quiet in the Land; as the faithful servant Pisanio, Bernard Hopkins is a ministering angel who gets progressively stronger as he flutters progressively less. Old reliables on the margins are Brian Tree and, as an enchantingly urbane family doctor, Ian Deakin.

Which leaves Cymbeline himself, a title character who has far more title than character. James Blendick plays him with booming stolidity, which turns out to be an advantage. The king spends the last scene hearing the plot unravelled and having his family restored to him. He has a lot to respond to and, rather than trying to make each reaction top its predecessor Blendick greets each with level delight, rather as we do. It's the family reunions that make these comic denouements so deeply effective; boy getting girl is nothing, but wife restored to husband (Imogen is the only heroine to go married through an entire play), brothers to sister and, above all in Shakespeare, daughter to father -- these have the power of myth.

We believe because, against all the odds, we want to believe; there is no way for the multiple revelations of Cymbeline not to be funny, but that only adds to their joy. Anyway, that's how it works here: Mine eyes, as someone says in the similarly impossible All's Well That Ends Well, smell onions.

Theatre Review

TRANSLATIONS

Premiere Dance Theatre, Toronto

- - -

With a few exceptions such as Uncle Vanya and the current Dumb Waiter, Soulpepper shows have not been noted for distinguished design. However, Francis O'Connor's set for the new production of Brian Friels Translations raises standards not just for Soulpepper but for Toronto theatre in general. The play takes place in Ireland in the early 19th century, in a cottage that doubles as a hedge- school supplying a liberal and largely classical education to the surrounding peasantry. Here, executed in some holy mixture of stone and Styrofoam, its an edifice that exploits stage dimensions of height and depth one hardly knew existed. Imposing though it is, it's neither overpowering nor unbelievable. Its textured walls and floor frame, cradle and very likely inspire the actor; a big rickety staircase calls cruel attention to the fact that one of the inhabitants is lame and another habitually tipsy; wide doors at the back swing open to reveal glimpses of the country with whose fate the play is centrally concerned and to give periodic entrance to the English army that controls that fate. Whenever redcoats appear upon the stage (O'Connor -- who despite his name is English, not Irish -- also designed the costumes) the dramatic temperature changes. The play is also wondrously lit, by Kevin Lamotte; his opening burst of morning sunshine is fair dazzling and his evening shadows are burnished.

Friels play, now just over 20 years old and incomparably his best, is about the political power of language, not just in making the rules but in defining the territory. The hedge-scholars (all of them adult) speak only Gaelic and, in an impressive number of cases, Latin or even Greek. The dominie and his son alone speak English, and that mainly for interpretative purposes. Into the district comes the army, conducting an ordnance survey, which means they are rationalizing the local place-names, which in turn means they are, most of the time, Anglicizing them. The soldiers of course speak only English, so they have brought their own interpreter, who happens to be the schoolmasters other son, a character whose loyalties are ambiguous. Though the details are only hinted at, the situation is explosive; a major Irish rebellion lies in the recent past and the spectre of the Great Famine hovers, with grim irony, over the future.

Whether the characters are supposedly speaking English or Gaelic, we always hear it as English, and Friel's achievement in establishing and maintaining this convention is remarkable. There is never any confusion, at least for us; the characters' confusion is richly exploited -- first for comedy, then for polemically charged drama in a debate between an Anglophile Irishman and a Hibernophile Englishman, finally and most unforgettably in a love scene poignantly conducted across the linguistic divide.

The setting, and the authors use of it, are marvellously original and suggestive; its tempting to describe this as the kind of history play that Chekhov might have written had he ever delved into his country's past. One hopes, though, that he might have been tidier about developing his narrative. The political action is largely in the hands of two off-stage characters called the Donnelly twins; as a friend of mine once put it, speaking with the double authority of critic and teacher, they never made it to class, so the bloodier part of the action never comes into focus. Neither, and more crucially, does the possible part in it of the schoolmaster's two sons; and the faintness of the action infects the characters. It ends very finely, with a scene that begins by echoing the finale of an earlier Irish classic, Juno and the Paycock (two sozzled old men intruding unawares on a scene of tragedy) and then expands and explodes in unexpected directions. It includes a great speech by the teacher, Hugh, who seems, liquored or not, to be the authors mouthpiece; he reveres the past, lives in it in fact, but he also knows both the inevitability of change and the probable cost of it.

Hugh is played by Diego Matamoros at his best, meaning that he has the authority to take over the stage from the moment he sets foot on it, and the intelligence and technique to keep it in his grip. His performance is a monumental study in wryness. Indeed, in this production by Ben Barnes (artistic director of Dublins Abbey Theatre) all the Irish characters are well played, both as individuals and as a group; the sight of this motley group lining up defensively against the wall when the soldiers come is a memorable one.

David Storch, who has one virtuoso tirade, makes an urbane, troubled figure of the brother who got away, and Gordon Rand a complex one -- hopeful, bitter, crushed -- of the one who stayed. The play is in part a love story; Patricia Fagan, after an initial bout of arms akimbo acting, blossoms romantically before settling on a note of tough heartbreak, superbly sustained. Michael Simpson gives a pleasantly fey account of an old man whose classical studies have led him to serious contemplation of marriage with the goddess Athene (living in the past can be carried to extremes); and Liisa Repo-Martell is expectedly piercing in the emblematic role of a village girl traumatized into silence.

The English, as so often in Ireland, are a problem. Oliver Dennis offers a gentle cartoon of the commanding officer; pleasing enough at the start, but underpowered for his later roll call of the new English place names, which should fall like a series of hammer blows. This is the climactic scene of the play, its image of colonialism in action. Its rendition here is one of the few points at which this production falls short of the London premiere two decades back.

Another, more lengthily damaging, is the performance of the junior officer who falls in love with Ireland, with its topography and with at least one menber of its population. He's meant to be a naive young man; as Philip Riccio plays him he's merely silly, unbearably so in the first act, compensating somewhat but not enough in the second. The performance admittedly spares us the burden of worrying too much about the character's ultimate fate, one of the things that Friel, undoubtedly by intention, leaves vague and open- ended. The technique is effective up to a point but frustrating beyond it. It makes the play, to my mind, less than the masterpiece it was proclaimed at birth, but still undoubtedly a marvel.

The Royal Shakespeare Company's director, John Barton, stopped by Stratford recently to share a few tips

John Barton is the eminence grise of the Royal Shakespeare Company, a semi-official position he has held now for nearly half a century. Formerly a Cambridge don, he joined the RSC at its inception in 1960, as assistant to the artistic director. Bartons own first ventures as an RSC director were unfortunate; he had not crossed the gulf between working with undergraduate actors and working with professionals. But he persevered, creating the anthology show The Hollow Crown (which, in its umpteenth incarnation, came this year to the Princess of Wales Theatre in Toronto) and working with Hall, as editor and co-director, on The Wars of the Roses, a sequence of Shakespeare history plays that proved to be in itself historic. By the end of the 60s he was back in the saddle as a director in his own right, with a particular talent for the comedies; his Twelfth Night, All's Well That Ends Well, Love's Labours Lost and Much Ado About Nothing were tart, beautiful productions that I never expect to see bettered. Actors seem to have regarded him, affectionately, as the ultimate absent- minded professor -- bearded, cardiganned, and given, according to legend, to chewing on razor blades. You wouldnt have thought it possible to be both tense and teddy-bearish, but Barton seems to have managed it.

He himself talks of his "phony academic reputation; I got a fellowship at Cambridge that I wasn't expecting, and I wanted to stay a student so that I could act and direct." At Cambridge there was plenty of opportunity for both. All this activity, though, was strictly extra-curricular; neither Oxford nor Cambridge has ever had a theatre faculty, a situation of which Barton, who expresses great distrust of university drama departments, thoroughly approves: I learned more by falling on my feet and doing things.

His university background clung to him, at least as far as the critics were concerned. He was constantly described as the RSC's most scholarly director though in fact, he was liable to take more liberties, especially textual ones, than any of his colleagues. Ian McKellen, who worked with Barton as an undergraduate and was in his RSC productions of King John and Marlowes Doctor Faustus, both of them ruthlessly edited, has this to say about about him: "I wish people would stop calling him academic; hes actually a great vulgar showman."

For years, says Barton of his early time at the RSC, "I did all the fights, then I got very interested in language, words, etymology." He built himself a reputation as the world's foremost practical expert on the speaking of Shakespearean verse. There have been books, TV shows, videos and workshops that he has conducted all over the world. He has just been in our Stratford, working with a cross-section of festival actors, ranging from the comparative veteran Seana McKenna (this year's Queen Katharine in Henry VIII) to the comparative neophyte Haysam Kadri (this years Demetrius in A Midsummer Nights Dream).

Barton's way in these workshops is to concentrate not on Shakespeare's plays but on his sonnets; things turn up there he says "that always turn up in the plays," and they are of course both more independent and more concentrated than speeches out of context would be. Each participant gets to do a sonnet from a shoret-list of 15 to 20, and is given three days to prepare it: I get them to do it in their own way, then we find out the important things.

McKennas assigned sonnet was "When my love swears that she is made of truth." (Second line: I do believe her, though I know she lies.) First, she delivered it once through, out loud. Then, as she tells it, Barton said "there, youve got it, now follow the argument more." Another actor, Shawn Wright, less experienced in Shakespeare (he's part of this season's musicals company), tackled the same sonnet, and elicited the opposite response: Youve got the argument, its clear; now you could loosen it up.

McKenna describes Barton as "a wonderful diagnostician -- he knew where to start with this particular author." And also, obviously, with these particular actors: With you, he would say, "we have to look at this first"; and this, McKenna explains, could be the motion of the whole speech or a particular poetic detail.

Actors at sea, according to Barton, play a speech as a series of questions, instead of as a continuous statement. Anyone who has experienced the nagging style of performance that disfigures modern plays as often as classic ones will know what he means. "Actors," he also says, tend to generalize without thinking; and his primary weapon in fighting this tendency is to tell them to look for the antitheses. The sonnets are loaded with elegant oppositions, and making them clear and sharp is the best way of making sense of these packed poems, for both speaker and listener.

Moving on to the plays, Barton points out that "to be or not to be" is both a good antithesis and a good question. It also turns out that this most familiar of all soliloquies is the best one to encourage clarity of thought in a workshop since it is (and in all my years of Shakespeare-watching, I'd never noticed this) the only one that doesn't have an I in it.

Kadri had as his sonnet "Who will believe my verse in time to come/if it were filled with your most high deserts?" which he chose because it was lyrical -- not as knotted as some. It contains a line about the author's lines being yellowed with their age, and this was one of the phrases -- and one of the facts about the words themselves -- that Barton ("use the words") employed as a guide- line. (He also advised, sit in a tub, read a sonnet.)

"At first I was really nervous -- not too positive with the piece. Now I'm more comfortable, its less daunting of a task," Kadri said. Hed been pausing too much: I took out a couple of caesuras that were breaking, I'm not afraid to cold-read Shakespeare now. You know it's all there for you, waiting in the text.

I had hoped that Barton would offer drastic comparisons between the British and Canadian ways of approaching Shakespeare, but he wasnt making any.

"The same questions come up wherever you are: You cant take skills for granted. Actors now come to the RSC from TV, not from rep" where, in the old days, they would have done a lot of Shakespeare. Drama schools don't necessarily teach it; they're preparing people for films and TV. But people pick it up quickly. In principle, actors want to belong to a permanent company, but films distract them. That, though, may be less of a problem in Canada, where the distractions are fewer. The Canadian Stratford does have a high degree of continuity, and it shows.

Kadri, who trained at the University of Alberta, is also a graduate of what is now Stratfords Birmingham Conservatory, and he found Bartons approach "not radically different." He's still learning, but so is everybody.

McKenna, who has been at it for upwards of 20 years, says it took me a good decade to feel I could juggle with it a bit. Part of it's confidence, being able to speak as quickly as you think.

She notes that Barton was directing as well as instructing, asking the actors questions, and telling them to ask the literal questions that they found in the text. "Hed say even ask a rhetorical question as if you don't know the answer.' "

How much full-scale Shakespeare directing Barton will do in the future, though, is dubious. "Technically Im an advisory director at the RSC. Im working with Michael Boyd, the new artistic director, on his new production of Hamlet. This will be the seventh time I've worked on Hamlet, though I've only directed it myself once. Ive come to feel that Ive done every Shakespeare play I want to do. Perhaps now I'm more useful as a contributor."

Matt Dusk and David Mahogany cast themselves in the moulds of legends

Bono and The Edge, of U2, wrote a song called Two Shots of Happy, One Shot of Sad that they intended for Frank Sinatra. He died without recording it, which, from the point of view of his legacy may be just as well. Not that he didn't, from time to time, record far worse things, but this one is so obsequiously tailored to his perceived image that any performance of it he might have given would have sounded like self-parody. And though that is not a trap he always avoided, he usually did.

The song has now fallen into the hands of the 25-year-old Canadian singer Matt Dusk, the latest performer to cast himself in the Sinatra mould and one whose tone and angle-of-attack do, at moments, sound surprisingly like the original.

It's the virtual title track of his first CD Two Shots (Decca, a sign of the copycat times that a newbie would-be crooner should get a major-label contract first time out) and the singer does indeed get two shots at it, one at each end of the record; though, as usual in these circumstances, the vocal is identical on both mixes. The singer's backing groups include the Toronto Symphony and the Royal Philharmonic; and he claims, at a frighteningly young age, to have found his spiritual home in Las Vegas.

The title song's title idea isn't bad, but it isn't sustained. The lyric, grabbing at one pre-packaged image after another, comes to sound like a Frank Sinatra free-association test: "I'm just a singer, some say a sinner/ Rolling the dice, not always a winner"; "We were walking together down a dead-end street/Mixing the bitter with the sweet." The worst of it is that the authors obviously thought they were being sophisticated. Most of the new songs on the disc (from a number of different teams, though the name Robin Smith crops up on many of them) are the same, only worse. None of them have any inner logic. Something called Cold as Ice, aimed at some presumably faithless lady, is a catalogue of random reproaches. Lonely Road, whose title alone sounds warning-bells, is foolhardy enough to end with a moaning coda about "the long, long road." Other songs tell us that "when love is young, the air is sweet/forbidden fruit is all we eat" and that "life goes on like a carousel."

Some of Dusk's phrasing on Miracle, one of the more rhythmic items, would certainly have raised his idol's eyebrows: "Remember the bolt that came out of -- breath -- the blue." Nobody is going to die of suspense waiting for the end of that thought. He sings it twice, with no variation. For somebody who is being touted as a jazz singer -- or indeed any kind of singer -- he doesn't seem very inventive.

He does have a voice, and some technique; and if you want imitation-Sinatra, you do get someone who seems to have gone to the source, rather than to Jack Jones or Bobby Darin. It seems, understandably, to be the insouciant Sinatra of the '50s and early '60s who has captured his imagination, but the material on which he tries to recapture this approach is more like the turgid stuff to which the master surrendered in the '70s and '80s. The great lyricists took their inspiration from their own sensibilities and the common speech around them; these take it from other songs.

The sad fact is that love songs in the classic American tradition can no longer be written. The older writers still trying it end up sounding like hacks and the younger ones like hicks. This doesn't mean that the existing repertoire has to be retired, though of course anyone singing it faces daunting comparisons. Dusk does two songs that might be called standards: Fly Me to the Moon, hardly the cream of the Sinatra crop and sounding here like the Basie version with its teeth drawn, still appears a masterpiece of coherence in this company; the Beatles' Please Please Me (with "girl" changed to "love," I assume for political correctness) is sung and arranged with ludicrous solemnity, and slowed down to what must be meant as a sensual pace, though in fact it sounds nothing like as sexy as the cheerfully lustful original.

Dusk himself is part-author of two of the songs. One, The Theme from Loaded Gun, is the worst thing on the disc, a James Bond knock- off ("he plays the game, like a moth that finds love in a flame") that hasn't the wit to be a spoof. The other, a song called Five, is the best, an original idea that is followed through and isn't chained to an antiquated structure.

If Dusk sounds at times like a boy sent to do a man's job (though less so than his peers, Peter Cincotti and Michael Buble) the American Kevin Mahogany sounds man enough to overpower any song or setting you could throw at him. A string of excellent albums on big labels had led me to believe he was a singer who could sing anything. So indeed he is; but there are some things that are more suited to him than others. When he appeared last month at Top of the Senator he offered a tribute to the late Johnny Hartman, the gentlest of all accredited jazz singers -- almost a crooner -- but one authoritative enough to be John Coltrane's performer of choice on one of the best vocal albums ever made. Clint Eastwood used his recordings on the soundtrack of The Bridges of Madison County, which brought him a posthumous fame greater than any he had known in his life, and made rather odd Mahogany's introductory claim that he was now "in some ways ignored."

Stranger still, certainly in live performance, was the sight of him singing Hartman's songs -- nearly all ballads -- in, for the most part, Hartman's manner. He is a mountain of a man, with a barrel chest from which issues a magnificently rich, resonant and flexible voice. He is in perfect control of it and had no trouble scaling it down. But he looked like a man who should be singing the blues, urban style (well, he is from Kansas City) and it was both a thrill and a relief when he actually did.

The Hartman program is preserved, recorded live, on To: Johnny Hartman, the first release on his own label, Mahogany Music. He does Fools Rush In, Body and Soul, In the Wee Small Hours of the Morning, and does them well, reproducing Hartman's delicate, purposeful placement of words and his way of electrifying an unexpected word; his air of being polite but no sucker. But while Hartman made you feel that this was the way to sing these songs, with Mahogany it only seems like a way. Cutting back on the dynamics robs his voice of its identity. You are spared the visual incongruity of the live experience, but the disc becomes monotonous. The faster numbers are all bunched at the end: a Nature Boy in which subtle rhythmic phrasing helps, blessedly, to take your mind off the words; a fun Kiss and Run; and two Ellington-Strayhorn songs that suit Mahogany far better than they did his model, Satin Doll and an exciting scat- filled Take the A Train.

A companion disc, Big Band, finds the singer in far more congenial surroundings even though the Frank Mantooth Jazz Orchestra -- the big band principally in evidence -- sounds, like so many now, more like a sleek screaming machine than a living organism. One song, Moonlight in Vermont, turns up on both albums; though it is, on the face of it, better suited to the quiet ruminative approach, the extrovert version, though it robs us of Mahogany's evocative emphasis on "Icy finger-waves," is far more invigorating.

Other songs Mahogany refurbishes are One for My Baby, the one with which Matt Dusk's Lonely Road rashly courts comparison, and that he makes not just haunting but ghostly, and the melodramatic I'll Never Stop Loving You, on which he's disarmingly smoky. Two roller-coasting blues, Centrepiece and In the Evening, confirm him as Joe Williams' natural heir. He doesn't have Joe's majestic smoothness, but maybe that will only come with Joe's silver hairs. Both those tunes, incidentally, were even more exciting when he did them at the Senator with just a trio; a big band helps set a context, but he doesn't need it to swing.

As if to prove it, the last and best cut on the Big Band disc, a light-footed Don't Get Around Much Any More, is done with just piano. Compared with his previous discs, these two are curtly- produced reach-me-down affairs, but I know of no better male singer working this territory.

THE COMEDY OF ERRORS

Coronation Park, Oakville

The Gardiner Expressway was further than usual from living up to its name on Tuesday evening, and I arrived in Oakville to find Antipholus of Ephesus in full protest against being shut out of his own house. For those who don't know, the reason for his exclusion is that his wife, unaware of the difference, is entertaining his identical twin brother, Antipholus of Syracuse. The boys were separated at birth, and the Syracusan one has been roaming the world, in search of his long-lost sibling. He has come finally come to the right place; but for some reason that Shakespeare never got around to explaining, it never once occurs to him that this might be the reason that people he has never met keep behaving as if they have known him for years. He puts it down to black magic, and cannot wait to get away.

The Antipholi have twin servants, both named Dromio and similarly split. Masters and men are no better at telling one another apart than anyone else in town, and for an Antipholus to send a Dromio on an errand is a recipe for disaster; the messenger will invariably end up reporting back to the wrong headquarters. Though the text never explicitly mentions it, the farcical action depends on both sets of twins not only looking but dressing alike, something else for which the author never bothered to account. These conventions accepted, the piece runs like clockwork.

In view of my late arrival, I have to describe my reaction to Miles Potter's production as tentatively positive. I can confidently assert that it demonstrates its director's customary and praiseworthy determination to make every line work. This includes the punning comedy routines that make up most of the Dromios' roles; the actors, Cliff Saunders and Murray Furrow, cannot make all the jokes funny, but -- like Big Jule in Guys and Dolls, rolling his blank dice and trusting to his memory of where the spots formerly was -- they provide a very clear indication of where the laughs ought to come, and why. This, since they are both efficient and endearing performers, is remarkably satisfying.

They both wear funny fezzes, this being a modern dress production set in Turkey, in homage to where the city of Ephesus formerly was. Their bosses, meanwhile, wear matching white suits. Matt MacFadzean is equable and agreeable as the visiting Antipholus and Patrick Garrow fiercely voluble as the resident one; if the former, suspecting witchcraft, goes through the play being very, very afraid, then the latter, who gnaws through his bonds after being imprisoned on a double charge of debt and insanity, goes through it being very, very angry.

Mary Ellen Mahoney gives a commanding performance as the Ephesian brother's jealous wife, who is one of the things he's angriest about, and Severn Thompson a sweet one, sometimes too liltingly lyrical, as her more malleable sister. The boys' long-lost parents are touchingly played by Thomas Hauff and Terry Tweed.

"Touching" is not the first quality normally attributed to The Comedy of Errors but it in this production it's a salient one. Potter apparently aims to do as right by the themes of loss and reconciliation as he, and most other directors, do by the slapstick. Neither quality is played here to the utmost. The comings and goings at the barricaded house are nicely handled, and there is some entertaining business with rope, but I have certainly seen productions that were more hilariously inventive. And I have heard of -- though not actually seen -- productions that were more moving and mysterious.

The climactic moment at which all four brothers set foot on stage together could raise both more laughs and more tears than it does. But there are nice subtleties as the show winds down. The Antipholus pair seem somewhat guarded about their own reunion, as if still perturbed by the likelihood that one has lain with the other's wife, though presumably pleased to have found their mum and dad.

As for the Dromios -- well, they're only servants, so nobody cares who their parents are. But they're left alone on stage to get acquainted and, after a few moments of shy caution, they arrive at the joyous conclusion that, having entered the world together, they will "go hand in hand."

Shakespeare himself was the father of twins, one of whom died young, which may explain why this play has more resonance than you might expect. In any event, in addition to its qualities as farce, it stands as the first of those comedies of reconciliation which, as I argued recently in reviewing Cymbeline, are powerful precisely because of their improbability.

The production, like the last few in Coronation Park, obscures the enchanting lakeside setting with its own built-up one. I appreciate that the play needs the suggestion of a house -- certainly for the scene where I came in -- but I want both.

robertcushman@lycos.com

This year, I paid my first visit to the Resurgence Theatre Company in Newmarket, and was enchanted. This summer Shakespeare troupe operates in a vernal setting whose charms are enough to shake my previous allegiance to the Festival of Classics' lakeside auditorium in Oakville.

The shows are staged in a tent, pitched right at the edge of Fairy Lake, a stretch of which is visible behind the stage Its a smaller patch of water than you get to see while watching a play in Oakvilles Coronation Park, but having it framed by the theatre itself makes it seem even more magical; it's a part of the show, even if it isn't being explicitly used. Its the kind of best-of- both-worlds effect -- natural and sheltered -- that ShakespeareWorks must have been aiming for with their Home Depot Theatre in Toronto, but Resurgence has been cannier in its structure and luckier in its view.

It helps, of course, if the stage setting harmonizes with the natural one; Resurgences Much Ado About Nothing (which closed on Saturday) was greatly enhanced by a simple, elegant design from Glenn Davidson, a compact interior that gave naturally on to the vistas beyond. You don't get this any more in Oakville, where built- up sets have recently been obscuring the landscape, or at the Dream in High Park, which admittedly has no lake to call its own but where even the surrounding trees tend to be obscured by elaborate facades. I have some quarrels with David Ferry's production of Much Ado but, taken all around, it was the second most enjoyable Shakespeare so far this year, bettered only by Stratfords Timon of Athens.

My reservations have to do with the question of how many liberties its permissible to take with Shakespeare. Actually, permissible" is the wrong word, because nobody is in a position to issue the permits; "sensible would do better. The great French director Louis Jouvet is said to have replied to a correspondent who had accused him of betraying Moliere's intentions, Tu lui as telephone?" In the words of an English critic, to whom I owe that anecdote, Shakespeare's number doesnt answer either, and I am constantly surprised at the confidence of reviewers who write as if they had some personal hotline to him.

I have, for example, seen a notable Edmund in a Stratford King Lear accused of not seeming villainous enough (he should have worn a hump?) though, since Edmund scores with two out of the three women in the play, which is no bad average, it seems reasonable enough to me to play him with a certain charm. This year, some of my colleagues have arraigned Ron Kennell, a brilliant Cloten in Cymbeline, for being "grotesquely comic. From my reading of the text, I would say that was precisely what he was intended to be.

And there I go, talking about intentions; Im not immune. Let me put it this way: An author, especially a dead one, may not have provable intentions, but a text does have an identity, which can be tested in performance. If what an actor says or does is in plain contradiction of what the story is telling us, and especially if he seems visibly embarrassed about it, then we can be fairly sure that something has gone wrong.

I find that I can take almost any amount of re-locating Shakespeare, in time or space; the plays themselves are full of anachronisms (the classic example is the clocks in Julius Caesar) and the original actors probably wore Elizabethan gear, with a few trimmings. That doesn't mean our players should go into doublet-and- hose, since what was a neutral convention to Shakespeare's audience would have specific (and possibly unhelpful) connotations to us.

I do rebel, though, when a director persuades himself that changing the scene necessitates changing the words. This isnt because re-writing Shakespeare is morally wrong; its because the results always sound silly. One of the minor villains in Ferry's Much Ado announced that he would have his lady love call me her sexy Borachio as she is wont." Both halves of that line are newly made up, but the first does not belong to the same world as the second. As a rule of tongue: If you're going to put new words into the characters mouths, keep to words that would have been current when the originals were written.

Ferrys chosen time frame was the tail end of the Spanish Civil War. His Arragonian soldiers came not to Italy but to the Basque region of France. They were all Republicans -- an International Brigade, in fact -- which made it a bit ticklish that their leader, Don Pedro, is a prince and is constantly addressed as such. In this production they called him either "major or commondante," and there was no way it ever sounded natural. (Cf. the lengths to which people go in Stratford's Midsummer Night's Dream to avoid mentioning Athens, or a recent Macbeth in which they got very coy over the word "Scotland.)

Other characters became monsieur" or "citizen or comrade." The plays other minor villain was called Comrade Conrade, which was funny, but not funny enough to justify the concept. Don Pedros bastard brother, the malcontent Don John, turned into his sister Dona Juanita, motivated by unrequited love for Claudio, the juvenile lead.

It's seldom wise to pronounce a Shakespearean performance definitive; a better one is always liable to charge around the corner and flatten you. But I feel fairly safe in asserting that Irene Poole was the best (because the only) Dona Juanita I shall ever see. (She was very striking to begin with, especially in her brooding silences, but vocally she ran out of steam. Don John is a one-note role; Dona Juanita turned out to be a two-note one.)

She returned at the end to throw a damper on the play's merry- making. This balanced the opening, which changed the announcement that Don Pedros men had suffered few casualties to the news that they had suffered a whole heap of them. So all the fun and games were overshadowed by the reality of war. This is in flat contradiction of the text, which disposes of the war in the first half-dozen lines and never mentions it again. Its a post-war play. It doesn't seem credible that people with a bloody conflict still on their hands would devote themselves so whole-heartedly to amorous intrigue.

(Another rule: If you're going to update the plays, dont fix on a specific historical event. The parts wont match up. And if you get in an argument with Shakespeare, you are not going to be fighting from strength. He got there first.)

A frame, however, is less important than what you put inside it. The individual scenes and relationships in Ferry's staging were lively, detailed, intelligent and inventive. I liked the ongoing sense of a household, and I especially liked the head of it, Don Allison's subtly comic Leonato.

Only the constabulary scenes misfired, with gendarme Dogberry (Stephen Guy-McGrath) underlining his malapropisms as if he were aware of them, and Verges (Brendan Gall) played, for laughs, as a half-wit. This, apart from being in terrible taste, misses the point, which is that Dogberry patronizes the colleague who is marginally more capable than he is.

Paul Eves Benedick, once he had shaved off his Hitler moustache and combed back his Hitler forelock (strange adornments for a man of his politics) emerged as a crisp and worthy Benedick, though Camilla Scott played his Beatrice not just as possessed of a fury but as unable to exorcize it. She sang beautifully, though "sigh no more, ladies, passed in various moods around the cast, became the plays theme song.

For once, the witty lovers yielded in interest to the sober ones. Christopher Morris, immeasurably improved since his Florizel in Soulpepper's Winter's Tale, played Claudio, with great resource, as a passionate cad, a heartfelt opportunist. Carly Street turned Hero from an ingenue to a buxom defender of her own rights and other people's, wounded and forgiving. This Hero was the heroine, with a new closing speech to clinch the point, and though this may have been a distortion of the original, it was also -- consistency be damned -- an improvement.

Black & White Photo: Richard Bain, Stratford Festival / Ron Kennell, left, as Cloten in Cymbeline. Some critics found his portrayal too grotesquely comic," but that seems to have been the intention.

GOODBYE, PICCADILLY

Red Barn Theatre,

Jacksons Point

- - -

The Red Barn Theatre, north of Toronto on the shores of Lake Simcoe, has been operating since 1949, which makes it Canadas longest-running professional house. It has atmosphere as well as history. It's a link to the largely vanished days of summer stock, though these days it casts its shows individually, rather than maintaining a company for a season. In recent years it has neither received nor invited much critical attention. Its current artistic director, Jordan Merkur, seems to want to change this; and he has lured us in with a fairly new play (meaning a play not yet seen in Toronto) by an experienced television writer, Douglas Bowie.

Goodbye, Piccadilly is an entertaining and touching domestic drama with a misleading title. Half of its characters are Canadian and half British, and those from over there are paying an extended visit over here, but though the play is indeed about a culture clash, it isn't one thats primarily expressed in national terms. There is -- or, until just before the action starts, there was -- Brick, a long-serving mayor and general public benefactor, who has just been awarded the Order of Canada. He has a wife, Bess, and a daughter, Bobbie, who is 47, thrice-married and childless. Bess is on the phone, filling in her friends and the audience on her current circumstances, when she gets another call, informing her that her husband has died of a heart attack, in London. This is doubly shocking to her since she thought he was still in Canada, on a week- long canoe trip; hes been taking one at this time every year.

More surprises are in store. There appear from England Kitty, who claims she had an affair with Brick when he was serving there during the war, and Cecil, their son, a forever-young middle-aged man. A video, recorded by Brick himself, confirms their story. He has of course been seeing his English family once a year, for a week at a time. (It's amazing that he got away with it, but then most of it happened in the days before cellphones.)

Bess, an unyielding woman of the old stock, still refuses to believe that the pair are anything other than gold diggers. And -- though she's the only one who wants to fight it -- battle is joined.

Brick and Bess run a country inn, and Brick has bequeathed his English family a half-interest in it. Collaboration being impossible, the place is split in two very separate halves; the Bess- Bobbie sector continues to offer plain fare and hearty outdoor activities, while Kitty and especially Cecil go in for duck stew and evenings with Oscar Wilde. As the inn turns out to be such a focal point, its a serious weakness in the play that its existence hardly registers during the entire first act. It makes much of the second half look arbitrary. The counterpointed vignettes of rival hotel management are funny to begin with but they quickly become tiresome. Cecils Wilde routine is barely believable, and Bobbie's attempt both to puncture and to rescue it with a Fawlty Towers imitation is flat-out incredible.

But there are other things the play does very well. If I was gobsmacked by the baldness of the exposition, I have to admit it gets the job done, and very efficiently. The growing rapprochement between Bobbie and Cecil -- the aging younger generation -- is cunningly charted, and the second act brings further revelations from Cecil and his mother that are movingly written and delivered, and that deepen the issues with which the play is concerned. It's pushed too hard in the closing scenes, whose arteries get clogged with sugar and reconciliation, but the point is made that though blood may well be thicker than water, there are other human bonds more potent than either.

The play is that recurring phenomenon in the Canadian theatre, a good commercial piece with no commercial theatre to go to. The leading non-commercials in Toronto, with the likely exception of CanStage, would think it beneath them, though it might just -- by virtue of a Second World War flashback at its start -- scrape under the wire at the Shaw Festival.

Merkurs production features a unit set that cannot accommodate all the demands made upon it. Some exterior scenes involving rock climbing are especially awkward (and not especially necessary). The acting is uneven, though the springing of the plays main surprise - - the high point of the evening -- is beautifully handled by all concerned.

Brick, though dead, appears on stage, both in his testamentary video and as a commentator and observer. Reg Dreger's performance, however, falls short of the stature that all his survivors keep claiming for him. (Imagine this role played by someone like David Fox. It could transform the play. It could also, of course, capsize it.) Diane Hollingsworth's Kitty keeps being shunted to the side of the action and she looks excessively dowdy, especially considering Bess dismissive description of her as "a showgirl. (She did, we are told, have a brief shot at singing for the troops). But she sounds absolutely right, very caring and considerate, modestly dignified, generous in anger, worn out but not worn down.

Cecil initially seems to be composed of gay cliches; apart from the Wilde and the cooking, hes a devotee of musicals, though he draws the line at what he calls the dreaded Andrew Lloyd." As that phrase shows, Bowie has a very good ear, verbal and musical, though he seems to me inconsistent in making Cecil a fan of Les Mis. Anyway, partly by working through the stereotypes and partly by working around them, he brings the character -- faultlessly embodied by the actor, Stuart Dowling -- to quirky, solid life.

We get a far stronger sense of what life was like for Kitty and Cecil, during their one week a year with Brick and their 51 weeks without him, than of what it was like for Bess and Bobbie with the proportions reversed. It seems to me, too, that the effect could have been much the same had Brick found his secret life in Toronto or Montreal. Bess would have had just as much to be hurt by and to condescend to.

The balance, as I may have hinted, is tilted against her. We can tell, if we think about it, that she has been seriously hurt, but what we actually see and hear is a snobbish, unyielding woman behaving foully to some perfectly nice people. Brick, you come to feel, must really have been a brick to have stuck with her. Nonnie Griffin's performance, though perfectly competent, does little to modify the impression. Arlene Mazerolle looks far too young for Bobbie, whose chances of future childbearing are said to be remote, though I gather that in fact she is exactly the same age. This may mean that we should reconsider our preconceptions about the relationship of age to appearance, but I doubt if this particular play is the one in which to try out such radical notions.
