THE LAST EMPRESS

Hummingbird Centre

- - -

Warm on the heels of the Chinese musical Terracotta Warriors, which was about the first Emperor of China, comes the Korean musical The Last Empress, whose title saves me the trouble of balancing this sentence.

Terracotta Warriors originated a long way away from the country it depicted -- in Vancouver, to be precise -- and it aimed, fruitlessly, at cracking Broadway. The Last Empress, by contrast, is a native Korean project -- it started in Seoul -- and has already been to Broadway, via London. It is performed here, as it was not in New York, in the original Korean, with English surtitles.

Language apart, though, it is as Westernized an enterprise as the other. In some respects it seems rather more so. I am no expert on Asian choreography, but if the routines we see here represent authentic Korean dance, then Korean dance and the routines at Radio City Music Hall must have sprung from a common source.

The Last Empress is inoffensive but -- despite all the arm- waving and leaping about -- inert. It is, though, very instructive about a slice of modern history of which most of us will know nothing; and there are worse things to do with your time in the theatre than spend it learning something.

The show certainly beats Terracotta Warriors in the matter of its title figure, on whom it keeps its eye firmly fixed throughout and who appears to have been more interesting in the first place. She is Ja-Young Min, who in 1864 was recruited from common stock to marry the boy king of Korea, a country then known as Chosun.

As the two of them grew up, they found themselves facing the defining dilemma of traditional cultures in the 19th century (and indeed since): whether to stick with the old ways and isolate themselves or embrace modernity, meaning in practice doing business with the strongest foreign power around. The king being one of those good weak monarchs of whom Shakespeare's (and historys) Henry VI is the paradigm, the decisions were taken by his far more powerful wife. She favoured progress, with caution, and encouraged a deal with Japan. When the Japanese proved too overbearing partners, she switched allegiances to China. This eventually resulted in her murder at the hands of a band of samurai commandos. The killers were afterward put on perfunctory trial in Hiroshima and, naturally, acquitted.

The trial serves as the shows prologue and epilogue, and is itself preceded by footage of the atom bomb falling, 50 years later, on Hiroshima itself. The association seems, to put it mildly, meretricious, but it's an accurate forecast of the show itself; like the Occidental pop operas that have obviously inspired it, it will grab at anything.

International realpolitik makes itself felt half-way through the first act when naval envoys from Germany, France and the United States arrive and, perched in crow's nests, demand trading rights:

We dont foresee that you will be the least bit argumentative

So please ignore the man owar that acts as a preventative.

Those lines aren't from The Last Empress; they're from the Please Hello number in Stephen Sondheims Pacific Overtures, which shows the Western powers, earlier in the century, exerting similar pressures on Japan. I cant be sure, of course, but I doubt if the Korean lyrics include anything so elegantly cutting; the surtitles certainly don't. The show does function, though, as an unwitting sequel to Pacific Overtures. It shows the Japanese doing unto others what had previously been done to them. The Europeans aren't exactly squeezed out. They return in Act Two, in a number that looks more than ever like a reprise of Please Hello, mounted on stilts and with national emblems adorning their tall hats. But its the Asian nations themselves who have to fight it out.

They do it, though, to Euro-American music. Its ironic that Pacific Overtures, a Broadway show about cultural infiltration, should have embodied its theme with music that got purposefully less Eastern as it went along, while this one -- an indigenous Asian musical on Asian themes -- should sell out to the foreign devils from the moment it gets started.

I mustn't be hypocritical about this; if the show had used authentic music throughout, it would probably have bored me. But it is dispiriting that Hui Gap Kim's score should sound at its best like second-drawer Rodgers and Hammerstein (or, more specifically and predictably, like outtakes from The King and I) and at its worst like the filler between the big numbers in the flossier Andrew Lloyd Webber shows. (The kings father, a semi-villain, is pursued by chords that seem to be urging him toward the title song from The Phantom of the Opera.)

None of it is terrible, but -- as in all the Europop shows -- there is an air of painting-by-musical-numbers about the way the show is laid out. The queens difficulties in conceiving serve as the cue for a sorcerer's fertility dance. A faithful solider-lover, straight out of old operetta, appears at intervals just long enough to have enabled us to forget his existence. There is, of course, an anthem of hope at the end of the evening.

There is also some humour; at least, I think that is the purpose of the sequences in which counsellors in squabbling squadrons bend their knees and jump backwards while arguing over the future of their country. They seem, if the translation is to be trusted, to be singing lyrics made up of stirring abstractions in polysyllables. Maybe In Ja Yang's original lyrics are more truly lyrical but, from my experience of the equivalent Anglophone shows, I wouldnt bet on it.

The show, under Ho Jin Yuns direction, looks impressive. The designer, Dong Woo Park, keeps his stage high, deep and sparsely decorated. The backdrops and icons with which he does adorn it make a corrspondingly greater impression, and are mostly in sombre reds and glittering golds.

The only performer to make much of an impression across the language barrier is Tae Won Yi in the title role. She sings powerfully, especially as death approaches, though I have to say that is a long time in coming.

Her acting is hampered by the fact that the character is granted little complexity. People who agree with her politics love her, and those who don't hate her, but that gets us nowhere. The important contradictions should be within her, and they don't exist.

Evita, with which this show has been freely compared and which probably did much to inspire it, is by comparison a masterpiece of psychological insight and political acuteness. The Last Empress, though, tells a better story.

THE TWO GENTLEMEN OF VERONA

Shakespeare in the Rough,

Withrow Park, Toronto

- - -

Shakespeare in the Rough is, as its name proclaims, the poor relation among the summer classic festivals. I'm not referring to its standards, which can be high, but to

its setting. Its in the middle of the city, just off the Danforth, without a scenic waterway in sight. The setting has no natural line of demarcation; it simply stretches away in all directions. These spaces can provide extra-long exits and entrances, and sometimes they can even be used to fill in an entire back story to the main action; Measure for Measure a few years ago did this very strikingly.

This years production of The Two Gentlemen of Verona, a play not too rich in subtext or plot complications, confines its extra-mural activities to having a few characters trot off to catch the boat from Verona to Milan, while a steam whistle sounds offstage. Mostly they go to the port on foot though one, who's always late, uses a bike. As it happens, both Verona and Milan are land-locked cities, but The Two Gentlemen isn't very strong on geographical substance, either.

Its one of Shakespeares earliest comedies, mostly notable for the way in which it forecasts the mature ones. Here, in sketchy form, we find fickle, featherbrained young men wooing witty, steadfast young women whom they don't deserve but whom they nonetheless get. The text is a riot of puns and of images pursued more for their own lyrical sake than for anything they might tell us about the characters.

Dean Gabourie has given it a pleasing, light-hearted production in costumes whose main reference point seems to be the 1930s, and with music to match. At one point, a scratchy vocal performance of Who Is Silvia?, surely the best-known passage in the play, is brushed aside in favour of a far jauntier rendition of It's Only a Paper Moon, to ukulele accompaniment. This jovial piece of sacrilege is the only outright violence done to the text in the entire evening, unless you account the moments of torture, swift but recurrent, occasioned by the refusal of all concerned to pronounce Milan with the accent on the first syllable. It may not be modern but its metrical.

There are a few other additions. Shakespeare in the Rough prides itself on making the plays accessible, and it likes to ease its audiences into them. This means putting off for as long as possible the dread moment at which a line of actual script has to be uttered. This time a vaudeville stage has been erected, on which appears a performer announced as Sir John Eglamour to declaim a soliloquy composed of fragments from King Lear, Much Ado About Nothing, Romeo and Juliet and As You Like It. Hes the kind of 19th-century barnstormer whom Mark Twain immortalized in the characters of the King and the Duke in Huckleberry Finn, and the idea here seems to be to have us laugh at his hamming so that we will better appreciate the more informal style that lies in wait for us. It's an unworthy tactic, mocking the old to make the young look good.

Later on, members of the company burst into more or less appropriate snatches of Cole Porter (Brush Up Your Shakespeare) and Noel Coward (Why Must the Show Go On?) accompanied by other members of the company on accordion, trombone, drum and washboard. The effectiveness of these depends on who happens to be doing them. Some of the actors can sing, some can't; just as some of them are good at cross-talk routines and some arent.

Its brave and sporting of the production, though, to keep so many of the jokes in, however hopeless, and most of the actors play up gamely. Sanjay Talwar, an actor not previously at his best in Shakespeare, presents Valentine, the more ostensibly heroic of the two gents, as a floppy poseur, unable to resist striking attitudes whether mocking at love or falling headlong into it. Proteus (Adrian Griffin), his opposite number, is less amusing, but then his is an ungrateful role, a cad (especially in this production's choice of fashions) who never achieves the dignity and glamour of outright villainy. The two heroines have far better chances and they are far better taken: Pip Dwyer languishes loyally, with some nice fits of anger, as Julia, and Gina Clayton plays a clever Silvia, alternately swooning over her swain and running exasperated rings around him.

The blazer-and-boater style could as easily come from the late- Victorian period as from the decade between the wars. It suggests Jerome K. Jerome's humorous classic Three Men in a Boat (To Say Nothing of the Dog), especially as this play does have the best role ever written for a dog, that of Crab, the obdurate cur owned by the servant Launce, whose devotion to him may be the sincerest emotion in the play.

Crab is here played by a rotating team of canines, perhaps as a safeguard against the dreadful things that befell their species in this park last year. The one I saw (and presumably the others as well) wore a little white ruff, which could be either the productions sole jokey gesture to Elizabethan costume, or a homage to that most literate of television hounds, Wishbone, the thinking dogs Snoopy.

With all their advantages, though, none of these pets are likely to steal any scenes from Jameson Kraemer's Launce, a solid clown (doubling on trombone) who gets all of his laughs without ever pushing for them; he does have the best material. His rival comic, Speed (Jane Miller, playing as a man, or perhaps a boy), has to work harder for fewer results. Since he/she is the company biker, you might say that the role -- all wordplay, no character -- is tough peddling.

The supporting cast includes a Hispanic Thurio (Carlos Diaz), who contemptuously addresses his rival as "Sir Walentine"; a Duke who looks like John Gielgud but does not, unfortunately, sound like him; and two outlaws, one of whom seems to have stepped out of Robin Hood while the other might be a deserter from The Pirates of Penzance.

- - -

A few departing thoughts on this year's offerings at Summerworks. Almost sure to make a reappearance is The Arabian Night, by Roland Schimmelpfennig, a name that sounds a lot too good to be true, but apparently denotes Germanys most fashionable young playwright. Five people wander, haunted, up and down the stairs and elevators of an apartment block thats been visited by mysterious failures of power and water, and meet extraordinary fates. A woman wakens from a tranced sleep to remember nightmare experiences in a harem; another woman goes looking, more prosaically but implacably, for jealous revenge; a man meets a bewildering number of willing temptresses; another ends up, Alice-in-Wonderland style, in a bottle; the caretaker, self-conscious about his overalls, tries to cope.

The story is told to us through their alternating monologues. This isn't as new an idea as some seem to think, and I doubt that the play means much, but it's very well written and it grips. Ross Manson directed it beautifully, with live exotic musical effects, and there were fine performances from Philippa Domville (always better at being vulnerable than in the hard and glossy roles she usually gets), David Jansen, Zaib Shaikh and -- a born monologist, in addition to his other talents -- Michael Healey.

Healey wasnt the only prominent playwright to remind us of his acting roots. Adam Pettle, whose performing career virtually ended when his voice was shredded by throat cancer, proved he still has expert shy timing in Fish Shack, in which he played a cop in a jumpsuit. Bonnie Greens play started with a very funny pause, but had little else to recommend it; it played like a spoof of some non- existent genre with a lame excuse for a storyline and an equally lame performance from a character who, unhappily, hardly stopped talking.

Robert Fothergill's Borderline was an attempt to confront the Rwandan massacres, and when it got to grips with them -- with the horrific details and with the question of responsibility -- it was very powerful. It short-changed itself, though, by coming wrapped in a love story between a Canadian aid worker and a possible Hutu killer. To be sure, this particular catastrophe has built-in Canadian content, but the approach trivialized the drama, and forced the production into a style of half-baked naturalism. Documentary may not be the only way to go with a subject of this magnitude, but it surely needs the kind of austerity one would expect a documentary to provide.

Theatre Review

AS YOU LIKE IT

Theatre by the Bay, Barrie, Ont.

- - -

The last, positively the last, of the Shakespeare summer wine, Toronto region, is also the headiest.

Barrie's Theatre by the Bay lives up to its name in the most literal sense; it's housed in a square tent that does indeed stand on the edge of a bay. However, since the tent is fully closed-in, the water's proximity has to be taken on trust while you are actually watching the play. What you lose in atmosphere, you gain in concentration. Daryl Cloran's production of As You Like It, with the audience on four sides of the stage as if it were a boxing ring, is seriously funny and also seriously serious. It brings out complexities the current, perfectly pleasing production in High Park hardly seems to have noticed.

The period is announced in the publicity, as "the Ragtime era," though I would guess the director was influenced less by history than by the novel and maybe the musical, since he singles out two of their real-life characters, Harry Houdini and Henry Ford. (I should note that, though there are magic tricks in the production itself, there aren't any motorcars.) There's ragtime piano playing as we enter; Marek Norman, who also composed the music for the High Park version, has come up with a wholly different but equally delightful score here, including a closing theme that had me humming down the highway. Initially the music seems to be issuing from an on-stage Victrola that Orlando, the dispossessed hero, smashes to the ground the moment he enters to complain about his wrongs. We aren't used to this kind of violence in As You Like It, and it makes a bracing beginning to the play; it carries over into Orlando's desperate scrap with his tyrannical brother Oliver and, of course, into the wrestling match at court, which is one of the most exciting I have seen.

The verbal conflicts are as tightly wound here as the physical. Lorenzo Savoini's set is composed of three overlapping rostra; in the court scenes they're covered with tarpaulins, which are removed when we get to the Forest of Arden to reveal a surface cracked and mottled. The various levels come in handy for sight gags; "trip, Audrey," says Touchstone, and she does. More importantly they are used very fluently and intelligently to underline who, in any given dialogue, has the upper hand. What ultimately makes Cloran's production so rewarding is that he doesn't, barring a few forgivable gaffes, try to pump energy into the text; he draws energy out.

He does this despite having in Jacklyn Francis a Rosalind who, while not actually bad (the play could not survive a bad Rosalind), is disappointingly bland. Rosalind is the play's thermostat, and a very active one. Half romantic abandon, half devastating common sense, she keeps plunging the characters, including herself, from a hot tub into a cold shower and back again, like a one-woman sauna regime. Francis's performance hardly keeps up. She has some nice abashed moments early on, but abashment is not most of the time what Rosalind is about. Her two principal foils, in fact, come close to outshining her. Tova Smith makes a witty Celia, at her sharpest when, mouth agape, she falls instantly in love. Brett Christopher gives Orlando, normally a very cardboard lover, anger and ardour and an unusual sense of the ridiculous. In fact, he conveys the outrageousness of Rosalind's masquerade, as a woman pretending to be a man pretending to be herself, more acutely than she does.

Benjamin Clost's Touchstone does conjuring routines, mainly involving his walking stick. He looks like a Samuel Beckett clown revived by a spell at a spa, and, sprawling with the suitcases of the entire refugee party, he looks to have stepped right out of Waiting for Godot, a Lucky who gets lucky. With both vocal and physical bravura, he revivifies the entire role, including his opening gags about pancakes and mustard that Shaw once claimed would have any self-respecting audience yelling for its money back. Brian Marler's Jaques, a pocket nihilist with a Byronic streak, works similar wonders with his casual, sardonic treatment of the Seven Ages of Man. He nods appreciatively at the foresters' downbeat, bitter songs ("most friendship is feigning, most loving mere folly") but is still mensch enough to proffer a drink to an exhausted old man.

Jane Spence's Phebe, strapping and blazing-eyed, gives the play an electric shock when, at the halfway mark, it most needs it. Her instant passion at the sight of Rosalind, staring at her and oblivious to everyone else, is very funny. It also -- a recurring strength of this production -- makes a strong dramatic fact of an element that too often gets taken for granted. Other examples are the friendship of Rosalind and Celia and the bloody napkin that scares Rosalind into a swoon. Another is the sadistic insecurity of Duke Frederick that permeates his entire palace. Brian Paul, genial until crossed, plays this to the hilt before switching, as is now customary, to the other Duke who is genial throughout. There is another excellent and less-expected double from Christopher Kelk as the play's two old men: Adam in town, Corin in the country, and rock solid as both. Matthew Deslippe's Oliver, strong and devious when he's a brute in a suit, seems at a loss when he goes native and reforms, but Alastair Forbes' lanky Silvius is very sweet, and even the minor servant Dennis, as inconspicuous a character as you could find in the Folio, takes on in Alex Dault's performance a brief, obsequious personality of his own.

In addition to Touchstone, the production sports another, more prestigious prestidigitator: Hymen, god of marriage, who puts in a personal, scripted appearance to preside over the quadruple marriage at the close, and an unscripted one, in tall hat and opera cloak, at the very beginning when, unfortunately, none of us has the faintest idea who he is. Even at the end, the casualness of his demeanour works against the effect the production wants him to make. The slack is picked up, though, by the song "wedding is great Juno's crown," which somehow works better as a company sing-along than it would as a solemn hymn. This in turn is undercut by Jaques' misanthropic departure, deplorable but oddly sympathetic. Balance is then restored by Rosalind's epilogue, which Francis does charmingly, winding up with a little magic trick of her own. The final effect is of illusion gently punctured but not destroyed, the final flavour of joy tempered by tartness. Where As You Like It is concerned, this is neither a revolution nor a revelation. But it is a pleasure.

Black & White Photo: Mandy Ridgers / Taylor Trowbridge, left, as Audrey and Ben Clost as Touchstone in Daryl Cloran's production of As You Like It.

THE SWANNE: QUEEN VICTORIA (THE SEDUCTION OF NEMESIS)

Studio Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

I am happy to report that, with its concluding instalment finally in place, The Swanne floats. It also rocks.

Peter Hinton's trilogy, unrolled over three consecutive Statford seasons, is as formally ambitious a work as the Canadian theatre can ever have created. Most of it purports to be a play written by the 18-year-old Queen Victoria immediately before her accession to the British throne: an allegory of the state of England with special emphasis on its underside. But as well as this play-within-the- play, we have the outer spectacle of Victoria -- "Drina," from her first name, Alexandrina, until her accession requires something more triumphal -- actually composing it. Here in Part Three, we have more of Drina herself than ever before. Her relatives get wind of the play and naturally they hate it, especially her mother, the Duchess of Kent. They tell her to destroy it. The question is how much of the world she has imagined, will the young monarch take into her future life.

Karl Marx said he wasn't a Marxist, and it's very possible that Victoria herself was no Victorian. All the same, this is the queen who refused to sign a law against lesbians, not out of tolerance but because she refused to believe that such women existed. Hinton's Drina, if we are to take his fantasia literally, must have gone into extensive denial in order to turn into history's Victoria; which may very well be the point. Drina's play deals, sympathetically and enthusiastically, with most varieties of sex, but the relationships it favours are the homosexual ones, male or female. Part Two ended, more or less, with a raid on a gay brothel. Part Three begins, more or less, with the public hanging of four of its clients, who make gallant ends. Meanwhile, the brothel-madam sits in the stocks, pelted with everything a generous law allows.

In an adjoining part of the action, two orphan youths, once lovers, roam London in search of one another and also of the truths about their respective parents. One of them, William, is black, the illegitimate son of Drina's late aunt Charlotte, his existence concealed by a vast conspiracy. This is known as confusing the royal issue; and it's the main reason Drina has written her play. Her mother's lover is pretty scathing about it:

The flaw in the premise is obvious.

An illegitimate child, no matter what colour, cannot become monarch of England.

Therefore, all the scandal Drina portrays is completely unconvincing.

Some of us raised that objection when we saw Part One; and in acknowledging it now, Hinton both confronts and disarms us. As he does again, a bit later:

Criticks are cruel and take revenge on the art

they wish they had the courage to create. But whatever nonsense people write about you,

there is a truth in it somewhere.

I call that decent. Those lines are spoken by the Scarecrow, a tragic (sorry, tragick) actress now old, bald, blind and committed to Bedlam who has functioned throughout the trilogy as the spokesperson for what Drina plainly sees as the subversive power of the imagination. Her play also finds plenty of room for more explicit protest, whether open and bloodily dispersed (the Peterloo massacre) or covert and betrayed (the Cato Street conspiracy). Victoria was a closet radical. Who knew?

If you don't know your early 19th-century English history, you may find these events confusing. I learned mine in school and I found them confusing, what with the allusiveness of the writing and the scrambling of the chronology. The published text, just out, puts dates on the scenes; the staged version can't be that helpful. The situation is worsened, of course, by the gap between productions; we're asked to remember characters whom we haven't seen for a year and who, in many cases, are now played by different actors. (They are also, in many cases, less well played, but we'll get to that.) We are also expected, unavailingly, to remember what the swan symbol itself is all about -- I never really grasped it in the first place - - while the subtitle The Seduction of Nemesis is plain confusing. Is Nemesis, fate, the seducer or the seduced, and either way what does it mean? On a smaller matter, what does the Duchess mean by saying that Drina's "notions of love are picaresque?"

Is that really the word she's after?

But the course, as we have now learned three times over, is supremely worth staying. The narrative pieces interlock and so, though more here has to be taken on trust, do the themes. Publication confirms what was suspected two years ago -- that the play is in verse. It's informal verse, hence the uncertainty, but it's tight enough to keep the dialogue, written as it is in an exuberant mixture of new formality and old slang, from spilling right off the edge of the stage. It's also muscular and very often witty. Two years ago I accused Hinton of indulging in quaintness for its own sake; I withdraw the charge. And as before, one revels in the energy with which he has filled the stage, both as writer and director.

Some of it goes into the names he has invented, which are Dickensian and then some -- fearsome names like Dud Grudge, for an exploiter of orphans. Sometimes, admittedly, we get more name than character. The program listings for the crowd scenes have rather more flavour than do the scenes themselves. For the most part, though, the staging is masterful.

Diane D'Aquila, whose scarefying Scarecrow has been the cycle's figurehead through all three plays, reaches greatness. Poignant, dignified and unerringly funny, she hits the mark with every line she utters. This accuracy, which goes hand in hand with economy, shows up the majority of her colleagues who handle the language with what, considering that the author is also the director, must be remarkable sloppiness. Nearly everyone acts in italics, and on the wrong words at that. There are exceptions: Margot Dionne is delightfully dotty as one of William's possible mothers (he has several), Michelle Giroux is in fine fastidious form as a repentant whore, and I enjoyed Michelle Fisk's broad turn as an unrepentant one, though I didn't believe in her for a moment.

Tanja Jacobs brings off a brilliant double as a bawd in the inner play, and in the outer one as Victoria's mama who seems aware of the coupling and resents it, though with so much multiple casting going on I don't see how the audience is supposed to notice. I approved of Thom Marriott's vigour and Donald Carrier's ambiguous gentleness. Brad Rudy lacks the definition that his predecessors brought to the tormented-villain role of St. John Voranguish, "a whoremaster"; Lara Jean Chorostecki moves in and out of correct focus as Drina/ Victoria; and as her hero William, Seun Olagunju is likeable but rushed. Though I was happy to see him finally reunited with his Jeremy, I was as glad the author keeps their rejoicings brief.

Their meeting occurs in the middle of a major outbreak of Canadian content, with all the more sympathetic characters in Drina's drama taking ship to found a New London. One of them has been over here before in less propitious circumstances ("no man's been ta 'ell and live to tell of it ... unless ya been to 'Alifax") but now their hopes are higher. They join in song; there may be irony here, what with their creator about to forsake them and embrace her royal destiny, but one's instinct is to share the joy, not so much for the characters or their situation as for the scale and achievement of The Swanne itself.

We are told that it took Victoria three years to write her play; it has taken Hinton 11. He has been a director for years, but The Swanne is his first play I've heard of making up for lost time, but this is amazing.;

Black & White Photo: Richard Bain, Stratford Festival / Lara Jean Chorostecki as Drina in Stratford's The Swanne: Queen Victoria (The Seduction of Nemesis).

KING JOHN

Tom Patterson Theatre

Stratford, Ont.

- - -

In the days, which must be at least 50 years ago, when King John was a popular play, its most celebrated scene was usually referred to as "Hubert-spare-mine-eyes.

This is the episode in which Hubert, the nasty king's imperturbable confidant, undertakes to put out the eyes of the captive child Arthur (who has an embarrassingly strong claim to the English throne) but is overcome by the boys pleas for mercy and ends up his devoted protector. Its one of several scenes that are excellently done in the new Stratford production, with Aidan Shipley as a trusting Arthur who would melt any heart, and Tom McCamus a Hubert, walleyed on his own account, who undergoes a wrenching transformation whose results are with him for the rest of the play.

Antoni Cimolino's stern staging holds back on the obvious pathos and emphasizes the brutality, which, of course, makes it even more pathetic. This aborted blinding emerges as the second-most horrific scene in Shakespeare, and the production, consciously or not, echoes Peter Brook's famous staging of the one that surpasses it, the actual blinding of Gloucester in King Lear. Arthur is bound to a chair by two henchmen, and pushed onto his back, ready for his jailer to apply the hot irons.

There is an odd thing about this scene, though; its the only one in the play in which blinding is so much as mentioned. The kings instructions to Hubert were to kill the boy, and once the scene is over, everybody reverts to that assumption. The dislocation is typical of the play. It is full of powerful confrontations, but they don't cohere.

This could be because Shakespeare, like Hubert, had a fit of conscience. He was writing in a militant Protestant culture, in which the customary view of King John -- he who signed the Magna Carta and lost his washing in the Wash -- was that he was an admirable if sometimes misguided fellow who had the guts to defy the Pope. Shakespeare (who ignores the charter, though not the washing) portrays him, probably with greater accuracy, as a despicable fellow who had the guts to defy the Pope.

The speech in which he does so, though stirring enough in a xenophobic way, seems to have wandered in from another play. And if we take it in context, it sounds like the bluster of a weakling trying to impress himself and everybody else -- which is how Stephen Ouimette plays it.

John, as the production is at pains to point out, is a mama's boy. The show starts with a succession of spotlit tableaux: three male characters -- John, Arthur and the Bastard Faulconbridge -- each seen with his mother. This is fine as far as it goes, but it does not, chronologically, take us far enough, since none of the ladies survives into the plays second half. (One of them doesnt make it past the first scene.) I'd say it was an interesting sidelight, rather than a governing image.

That is no reflection on the maternal performances. Martha Henry makes, as you would expect, a formidable Eleanor, a dowager whose influence on her royal son can certainly be believed to stretch from beyond the grave. She is seen happily playing with the captive Arthur while John plots the boy's death, a touch sympathetic and macabre.

As Constance, who fights for Arthurs rights with a fervour that embarrasses him, Diane DAquila seems at first unsuitably subdued, but she rises superbly to her scene of crazed bereavement in which, like all the best players of madness, she is heartbreakingly logical. (Constance, in what must have been a far grander manner, was one of the great roles for the passionate likes of Sarah Siddons. It occurred to me that the actress whom D'Aquila plays in The Swanne would have had it in her repertoire.)

Lally Cadeau makes more than most actresses of Lady Faulconbridge, who has, not too blushingly, to tell her son how she was seduced by Richard the Lion-Heart. He approves, but then he would, wouldn't he? And, while were with the women, Keira Loughran makes a highly promising Shakespearean debut as Blanche, married off as a peace offering and torn in emotional halves when her English uncle and French husband resume hostilities.

The play keeps doing things like that. People continually break faith or change sides, and John himself is a virtuoso of deceit. The trouble, dramatically, is that he isnt very dynamic or whole- hearted about it, as if Shakespeare, writing a patriotic play (and John's enemies, unlike Richard III's, are foreigners) couldnt quite give up the idea that he might be reclaimed as a hero. I wonder if it might be more effective to cast a heavyweight actor in the role, one who would let the weakness peep through an initially confident facade. Ouimette, nervously pacing his palace, is a neurotic from the outset. His performance is perfectly accomplished and perfectly credible, but you do wonder what this man is doing at the centre of an action-packed play.

Shakespeare seems to have wondered, too, since he has him progressively abdicate control. This sounds as if it should be more interesting than it is; Shakespeare abdicates too, allowing the king a vivid but strangely foreshortened death.

The problem has always been there, and it explains the tradition whereby the usurping John has himself been usurped, theatrically, by the far more attractive Bastard, who is vigorous and funny and observant and, despite some of his own protestations, good-natured. Jonathan Goad, who gets better and better, gets off to a fine start by sitting cheekily on the throne when no one is looking, and proves especially good at easing his way through the sparkling soliloquies that were their authors breakthrough in colloquial characterization. (So at least says Harold Bloom, and it's one of his more insightful observations.) Equally fine is his handling of the concluding this England" speech, which he delivers not as a jingoistic proclamation, nor as a fashionable exercise in debunking, but quietly, alone on the stage, as if he hopes it might prove true but is by no means sure.

This fits right in with a intelligently ambiguous production, which is set in the late Victorian period (helpful for telling nationalities apart) and emphasizes carnage, perhaps unnecessarily since we know what war costs. More impressive are the scenes of diplomatic chicanery. The papal legate is as smoothly nasty as the most bigoted Elizabethan could have desired. Bernard Hopkins plays him on a silken note that can be monotonous, but is impressive when cajoling Dion Johnstone's ambitious young Dauphin, who proves a chillingly apt pupil and (an apt invention) treats his new wife appallingly. Peter Donaldson has more to offer as an actor than the presumably well-meaning French king can accommodate.

The principal feature of Santo Loquasto's design is a mobile platform, which is mostly useful and can sometimes surprise us. There are also striking sound and lighting effects, at their best and boldest for the death of Arthur.

THE HUMAN VOICE / THE ELEPHANT SONG

Studio Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

A character is on the phone, and we can hear her but not the person to whom she is talking. Drama offers a writer no challenge like this, or so experience suggests. In 99 plays out of 100, it's met with a monologue that sounds like:

"No, I don't love you any more ... Yes, I have burned all your letters ... Yes, I can tell that you're angry ... Oh, I see, you're coming straight here, by taxi, with the pearl-handled revolver that you keep in the top right-hand corner of your desk, underneath the box of typewriter ribbons that you never got round to throwing out after you bought the computer, and you're going to shoot me because you've decided that I'm a heartless bitch, and you should be here in half an hour, traffic permitting ... Yes, I'll put out the cat ..."

The blessed 100th play is Jean Cocteau's The Human Voice, which premiered in 1930 and is entirely made up of one of those one-sided phone chats. A woman is talking to her ex-lover, who has dumped her quite recently. One of the play's signal virtues is that the man never seems, on a technical level, to be putting words into her mouth.

Emotionally, he is; she is the one who is still in love, which means she is, to a great extent, at his mercy. So she tries to accommodate him. We can make a very good guess at what he is saying at the other end, but neither she nor the author stoops to quoting him directly. Character and dramatist retain their dignity. She is no puppet, and he no puppeteer.

There is no indication her current malleable state is her normal one, or that she might not snap out of it at some future time. We get vivid glimpses of a tougher woman in the peremptory way in which she addresses the other callers who intrude on her party line, and who sometimes cause her to lose her connection. (And we thought our phone system was a pain.) These interruptions are expertly used to vary the texture and even to inject a little humour.

From what she says, and from the look of her rumpled but elegant bedroom, not to mention her silk pajama suit, we judge her to be a sophisticated lady, probably with a career, who has put her glossier self on hold.

Her ex is apparently a lawyer. She is terribly understanding as she tries to keep him on the line while avoiding sounding jealous or dependent -- two incompatible objectives. We can work out not only what the man is saying, but also what he's probably thinking. One guesses that a part of him is concerned while a larger part wishes she would stop clinging, and we can sympathize, though more for her.

We get to see her clearly from inside and out. By the end of the conversation she has the telephone cord wound round her throat, which of course suggests suicide but also emotional envelopment. "I'm wearing you", she tells him, with emphatic playfulness. She's also wearing the play.

Lally Cadeau plays her as a woman whose flesh is ruling her head, and whose anxiety is trying desperately to pass itself off as cheerfulness. This is a seamless, generous performance that never hits a false note. It shows us both what the character is and what she was.

Jim Warren's direction and Sue LePage's design are perfectly key. The new English version is by John Murell, possibly our best playwright and certainly our best translator. I had thought of this play, on the rare occasions I thought of it at all, as a mere exercise for its author and actress. I was wrong.

Its companion piece, Nicolas Billon's The Elephant Song, does come across as an exercise, though a talented one. Its author is 25 and this, his first play, lacks a defined centre. It eventually emerges as a play about mother love, or the lack of it. A young man was denied affection by his mother, an opera singer more concerned with the affection of her public. She gave her son a stuffed elephant called Anthony, but that is no compensation. When we meet the boy he is in a mental hospital, still holding fast to Anthony.

The most powerful moment in the play -- though one that completely breaks with its otherwise naturalistic conventions -- comes when the mother (Barbara Dunn-Prosser) appears from out of nowhere, singing, beautifully and unaccompanied, a Puccini aria. But to get to this point we have to go through a prolonged cat-and- mouse game between the boy and the head of the mental hospital, who is not the psychiatrist who's actually been treating him. That doctor has disappeared, and the action begins as an investigation into his absence. In the course of this the patient -- who as he says himself is crazy but not stupid -- gets to tease and taunt the physician, even to twit him a bit on the state of his marriage.

We have met this kind of institutional duelling in plays before: in Equus, in Blue/Orange and even -- to stretch a few points -- in David Mamet's Oleanna, while the effects of living with a demanding diva were explored, recently and at some length, in Michel Tremblay's Impromptu on Nuns' Island.

I am not suggesting plagiarism or even influence, merely that the playwright is bound to have a tough job making this territory seem new. In this context, some of his accomplishments work against him. He seems too clever, too good at dialogue and building up tensions, to get by on youthful freshness. The protagonist's delight at setting false trails seems to have infected the author. By the time we get to what's really on their minds, it's too late for us to care.

The play has the same direction and design team as its predecessor, here doing more conventional work. Mac Fyfe as the troubled young troublemaker is an arresting addition to the theatrical gallery of the beautiful and the doomed. Stephen Ouimette, who plays pouch-eyed professionals as well as anybody, goes conscientiously through the required paces as the head head- shrinker but cannot bring him to independent life, perhaps because the character, for all the time he spends on stage and all the lines he gets to speak, has been endowed with very few qualities.

Maria Vacratsis seems uncomfortable with the remaining role, that of a nurse whom the patient mocks unmercifully -- though usually behind her back -- for being overweight, and who finally emerges as a substitute mother. Or maybe it would be more accurate to say that he emerges as a substitute son. Either way, it needs more investigation than it gets. Played as a surprise climax, it just seems glib.

The play inspires the mixture of future hope and present disappointment for which the standard word is "promising."

KING HENRY VIII (ALL IS TRUE)

Festival Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

The first play ever to be presented on the Stratford Festival stage was Richard III, and the platform has always seemed to be a natural for the histories. It offers scope and sweep for the massed scenes, and stark concentration for the contrasting moments of solo introspection. It's been years, though, since one of the chronicles was last mounted there. Lacking name recognition, they have been banished to Stratford's smaller spaces. Richard Monette's Henry VIII, his best Shakespeare production since The Tempest, is a tingling reminder of how much we have been missing.

Henry VIII is an atypical history. It contains no wars, nor even the threat of any. Its spectacular scenes depict not battles but processions. It seems only to have acquired its familiar title because the editors of the First Folio wanted it to fit in with the other histories. It previously bore the less regal name of All Is True, a name that some recent editors have restored as has (in square brackets) the current Stratford billing.

Such gossipy but non-committal titles seem to have been a defence mechanism for Elizabethan playwrights as they drew closer to the history of their own times. There's another play about Henry called When You See Me, You Know Me while one on Elizabeth herself is breezily labelled If You Know Not Me, You Know Nobody. Anyway the Folio editors did Shakespeare a posthumous favour; All Is True could be about anything but Henry VIII is one English monarch who, thanks to Hans Holbein, Charles Laughton, and those half-dozen wives, has marquee value.

The play only takes in the first one-and-a-half wives. It covers the divorce and death of Katharine of Aragon and the courtship and coronation of Anne Bullen, and culminates in the birth of Anne's daughter, the very same Elizabeth. It also presents the pomp and downfall of the all-but-all-powerful favourite, Cardinal Wolsey. Shakespeare's junior contemporary John Fletcher is reckoned to have been a major collaborator on this play, and, style apart, the play reflects his expertise at dramatizing contemporary court manners, especially the less savoury ones.

Ann Curtis's set gives us the Stratford stage at its most starkly elegant, while her rich Tudor costumes, also stark, make it swirl. The pattern, very clearly and skilfully realized in this production, is of ceaseless frolic and intrigue, punctuated by dark nights of the soul, spotlit when good fortune gives out. Big, lively, stage pictures regularly give way to big, lonely solo performances, each able to command the stage when his or her moment comes.

The character who bridges both these worlds, while never quite belonging to either of them, is the king himself. Like his current Stratford stablemate King John, Henry is a Protestant hero -- he founded the Church of England, after all -- caught in an ambiguous light. Once again Shakespeare hedged his bets, but this time to far better effect. We never get the goods on Henry, and he never gives anything away: He has just a couple of asides and no soliloquies.

Graham Abbey plays him superbly as an isolated and detached young man rapidly reaching authority. Though he starts in the familiar hands-on-hips pose, he is no fat Holbein cut-out: He is a golden boy, and caparisoned as such. At first he seems passive, in willing thrall to Wolsey. A momentary imputation of tyranny arouses him to anger, and the scene shakes. As the cardinal seems about to thwart his divorce, so he becomes more his own man, and these eruptions, generally of a single syllable, become more frequent and more feared. But he remains ambiguous. Any number of motives are imputed to him, by himself or others -- guilt over marriage to his brother's widow, love or lust for Anne, desire for a male heir, anti-Papal sentiment -- and they all seem, in their moment, genuine. Obviously, he can compartmentalize.

He is terrified that Anne will die in childbirth, then, when he hears that she has born him a daughter, he is devastated. He pulls himself together, of course -- partly for the look of it, partly from genuine parental pride -- and when Cranmer prophesies the child's glorious future, he listens in wonder that's tainted with disbelief and even more with disappointment. He still wants a son. At the play's last moment, he spots a likely future mother, Jane Seymour (at least we can tell it's her if we look at the program), and we know that all is up with Anne. None of this is in the text, but it's better than what's in the text. I preferred this performance to Abbey's Macbeth, but I suspect that he had to play Macbeth first in order to give it.

Kicking off the line of royal victims is the Buckingham of Raymond O'Neill, an actor of great presence never previously tapped, making his farewell to the crowd, every inch the noble martyr. His successors are contrastingly unsentimental. Walter Borden, climbing a new rung as an actor, effortlessly projects Wolsey's insolence, deviousness and vindictiveness, plus his confidence in his own powers. He has a crooked smile. Nor is he magically transformed when misfortune strikes. "Farewell, a long farewell" is played not for pathos but for irony -- he's sure he'll be on top again. When he finds he won't, he doesn't crumble but he does repent, because there is, after all, nothing else for him to do. His new piety seems genuine; he remembers he's a priest. On one level, this is opportunistic writing, on another, it's perfectly believable.

The most sympathetic character in the play is Katharine. Knowing this, Seana McKenna declines to play for it. Defying Wolsey or pleading her own case in the divorce court, she is lucid and splendidly angry. Anger persists, laced with weariness, through her interview with the cardinals (a tricky scene she redeems) and even at her death, where she pursues her mental vendetta against Wolsey almost to the end. Finally, when she tells of her heavenly vision, and even more when she makes provision for her attendants, she is sublime.

Monette's production has its share of cliches. An unidentified prisoner stumbles across the stage in the middle of someone else's conversation, to remind us that Tudor England was a dangerous place, as if we didn't know. A pair of celebrity-spotting gentlemen turn up (twice in the text, three times in the production ) to rubberneck at the royal festivities. One of them is Scottish, the other's accent wavers but could be Irish, and they're both very full of themselves and very camp. This makes a kind of sense -- if you know not them, you know nobody - but it's overdone.

The plum role of the Old Lady goes for nothing because the actress (Chick Reid) is not in fact old, and by the same token I'm sure, though I can't prove, that Lord Sands (Steve Cumyn) should be a dirty old man rather than an exquisite young one. However, Sara Topham is a spirited Anne, most of all in the dumb-show of her coronation; Stephen Russell's Norfolk powerfully leads the jackals of the court, and Brian Tree and Steven Sutcliffe are fine as the persecuted Cranmer and the persecuting Gardiner, though I nourish a secret desire to see them switch roles. One of the best things about the show, though, is that their altercation, which comes after most of the stars have departed, is no kind of anti-climax. The play makes sense; and though this isn't the first modern production to bring that off, it's one of the few. This has been a good season for Stratford and a better one for Shakespeare, with the supposed lesser plays coming through like gangbusters.

It is said Cirque du Soleil has scouts at the Olympics, but one wonders if it should be the other way around

CIRQUE DU SOLEIL: ALEGRIA

Ontario Place, Toronto

- - -

Early on in this Cirque du Soleil extravaganza, a revival of one of their greatest hits, there is a trapeze act. It starts quite gently, making audience members feel that they too might have swung that high and that wide in their playground days, if only someone had had the stamina to push them. Even when the performers pass ever more wildly across one another's flight paths, while hanging in impossible positions, there is still something very soothing about the grace and confidence with which they do it. They tell me that the Cirque people have talent scouts at the Olympics. Personally, I think it should be the other way around.

Indeed its hard, while watching the assorted gymnasts of the Cirque, not to conclude that we sent the wrong people to Athens.

Reviewing a Cirque du Soleil show is a tough gig, because the best parts, which are most of them, put you into a state of trance, and their worst into a state of boredom; and neither state is conducive to acts of critical analysis. Alegria (a Spanish word meaning "joy") does give us a way in by pretending to have a structure, maybe even a story. It purports to present an equivalent of the medieval Feast of Fools, at which social ranks changed places, kings becoming clowns and vice versa. So it seems that all these magicians of the body -- whose tricks depend on skill, not legerdemain -- have invaded some kind of castle, at which they are understandably welcome guests. But I dont recommend that you worry about it.

Marvel instead. Marvel at the somersaulting contortionists, who don't seem to have anything as inflexible as a bone in their bodies. Then there are the men who hold the Russian bars, a receding set of flexible horizontal springboards from which another set of men take off on vertigo-defying leaps, only to find that the first set of men have, quite literally, raised the bar, so that they have to land on a higher plane and then take off from that, even more extravagantly.

But then raising the bar is what the Cirque du Soleil is about. They have a fire-eater whose fire-eating is actually the least of his accomplishments. Anyone, he seems to be suggesting, can put flaming brands in their mouth; what really separates the men from the boys is the ability to encircle your body with rings of the stuff and juggle them at lightning speed. There's the man who seems to be flying through the air supported only by two large red ribbons. And there are the daredevils, whom I assume to belong to the same family -- this is a circus, after all, and theirs is a very traditional circus act -- who spin around near the highest point of this biggest of big tops, before dropping down to trapeze-level where other relatives, swinging equally hard, will catch them by their legs. I dont think there are ever more than three people in one of these formations at any one time, but even family dependency has its limits.

There is also a strong man who looks like hes employed as a bouncer but, as it turns out, wouldn't hurt a fly. More to the point -- since there are, famously, no flies on the Cirque, nor any other form of non-human life -- he wouldn't hurt a person. I guess that he, and the shows friendly though not over-hilarious clowns, are part of the narrative of which, as I have said, I could make little. There is, though, a scene at the end of the first half that is probably a part of it and that is extensively enchanting. It involves the sprinkling from a sack, onto the stage-floor, of a myriad of little slats and widgets that form into a miniature circular railroad track. Behind this there is a big black slab with a hole in it, suggesting a wall designed under the influence of Henry Moore or Barbara Hepworth. There is a snow-storm; it huffs and it puffs and it blows the house down.

The onstage characters have, I think, scurried to safety; but, just to let us know how it feels, with a mighty wind and a massive blower, the snow, in the form of numberless grains of confetti, is propelled at the audience. We rouse ourselves for the intermission, happily covered in the stuff. I have seen this effect employed before, in an entertainment called Slavas Snowshow in which it was used more lyrically, but that doesn't make it any less effective here.

The worst feature of Alegria is its music, which consists mainly of a trite titlesong, endlessly reprised. The sets, costumes, lighting and choreography, however, make glowing amends. I doubt if even the Cirque has a performer able to hold his breath for two hours, and it certainly isn't possible for a mere spectator, but most of us will sit there imagining the feeling.

NOTHING SACRED

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

In the opening moments of George F. Walker's Nothing Sacred, a 19th-century Russian bailiff is enthusiastically beating a peasant. (The emancipation of the serfs is only a couple of years away, so the bailiff is enjoying his privileges while they last. He claims, sounding as though he believes it, that the peasant is enjoying them as well.) Onto the scene come two young men. One of them is Arkady Kirsanov, the kind-hearted son of the landowner on whose estate this is happening. The other is his pal Bazarov, self-described nihilist. Arkady asks Bazarov, whom he reveres, if he can't put a stop to this distressing scene. "Yes, I can," says Bazarov, in a cool tone that makes no promises as to whether or not he actually will.

As it turns out, and in the most immediate sense, he does. Bazarov is one tough customer, and pretty soon he is beating up the bailiff. But he probably means more than that. He means that he knows how to destroy the political system that allows such things to happen. The questions then become, whether he will get the chance to put his theories into practice, and how they will work out if he does. The play doesn't answer them and there's no reason why it should, but it puts them, trenchantly and suggestively, in motion.

Nothing Sacred, which was first staged in 1988 and is being given a brave and brilliant revival on the main stage of the Shaw Festival, is a reordering of the Ivan Turgenev novel generally known in English as Fathers and Sons. (On my bookshelf it's Fathers and Children, which the translator swears is more accurate, but it's a fact that the children whom the novel shows in relation to their fathers are uniformly male.)

It's a good play, maybe its author's best, and some of its merits derive from its source. The two writers have widely different sensibilities; to put it very crudely, Turgenev was a landscape painter while Walker is a cartoonist. Walker, as is his right, changes Turgenev a lot, but it can't be a coincidence that his characters here, however much he buffets them about, have stronger legs and generally warmer hearts, than those in his original, contemporary work. The play is also very funny; by quickening the pace and sharpening the angles, Walker brings out the element of farce that inhabits most of the great works of Russian realism.

There is, though, a price to be paid. If you take over another writer's characters and situations and then change some of his narrative but not all, there are liable to be inconsistencies. Where the Kirsanov household is concerned, the play stays close to the book. There is Arkady and there is his father, Nikolai, who runs the estate, conscientiously but reluctantly, since it's his inheritance from his own father, and who wants to be a nice man, and often succeeds. There is Nikolai's housekeeper, by whom he has a child -- another son. There is Nikolai's brother Pavel, who, like him, once professed liberal principles, but has now most emphatically abandoned them. He takes pride in adhering to the old values, though they aren't necessarily the old Russian values; his favourite society seems to be England where the rich know their place, its obligations as well as its privileges. He and Bazarov naturally get on one another, and take great pleasure in doing so. Eventually they fight a duel, as they do in the novel, though here it has a very different outcome.

Bazarov's story differs greatly; and so, as a result, does his character. His relationship with the beautiful chatelaine Anna Odintsov is different (and so is she). His relationship with his own skills as a gifted, and unsentimentally practical, medical student is different, or at least less thoroughly explored.

Most crucially, his relationship with his own parents (much humbler than the Kirsanovs) has disappeared, taking with it half of what, if his title is to be trusted, Turgenev meant his novel to be about. The Bazarov of the book ends up as a doctor in his father's village, where he has been able to put at least some ideals into practice. Walker's Bazarov finishes, still a cuckoo in his friend's family's nest, where he is a figure of acute tragi-comedy. The Niagara program note claims that Walker's Bazarov is "a good deal more likeable than Turgenev's."

This may be true at the beginning of their respective stories, where the stage nihilist, as fanatical as his literary counterpart, still has the emotional advantage of being, literally, a figure of flesh and blood, and also benefits from being given some of his author's best jokes. It isn't true at the end, when Turgenev's Bazarov has simply been through more than Walker's, and has grown up because of it, and is by so much the more sympathetic.

One of the great attractions of the play is the way it organizes its people and events into evolving groups, affected by distinctions of class and age but not governed by them. This geometric quality is beautifully reflected in Morris Panych's production, which is remarkable for its wit and clarity. (At least it would be remarkable from most directors; from this one it's par for the course.) Ken MacDonald's set, wide open at sides and top, is enhanced by sudden bursts of colour and dominated by shifting, projecting patterns of lines, circles and arrows.

This being nominally Russia, I thought of 1920s Constructivism, though the program, more sophisticated in such matters than I, cites the equally Russian, but exiled, Wassily Kandinsky. There are also, when the patterns start popping, reminiscences of Saul Bass, the great designer of Hollywood title sequences, so it's perfectly logical that the evening should start with a rolling of credits.

Beneath and in front of these scenic fireworks there are plenty of human ones. As Bazarov, Mike Shara seems to have taken his cue from an instruction that's issued, somewhat incongruously, to another character altogether, but that happens to suit him perfectly: "Your attitude should be one of muted insouciance." He is the revolutionary who knows all the answers, sees no need to shout them out, and is sourly amused by all who disagree with him. He doesn't hate, but then he doesn't love either; and he does visibly grow up -- not politically (the play doesn't give him time) but emotionally.

Arkady, the central consciousness of the book, is here stuck with being his friend's progressively puzzled shadow, but Jeff Meadows, with a round and open face, makes him credibly decent. As a third companion, an eager sycophant who apparently lives to be rebuffed, Dylan Trowbridge gives an exceedingly bold performance; bold because it takes the chance of being unsympathetically ridiculous and features a whinnying laugh that would be unbearable if it weren't so truthful.

Jim Mezon starts off his Kirsanov pere with a bluff authority that must be second nature to him, but deepens it with a loss and loneliness that seem wholly specific. I wished Benedict Campbell might take Pavel's self-willed (and self-wounding) foppery to more extravagant lengths, seeking out the dignity in absurdity, but on his own more compact terms he is excellent. The scene in which the two brothers exchange nocturnal confidences is the evening's finest.

It's a treat to see Tara Rosling, one of our premiere actresses of waifs and strays, getting as Anna the chance to play elegant; she makes an especially striking entrance in a blue dress that perfectly sets off the colouring of the surrounding chairs and tables: This is especially cunning as it isn't actually her house, but then the production makes no pretence to naturalism. She has trouble, though, filling in the role, which has been ruthlessly transformed into that of a bomb-throwing revolutionary, an invention abrupt in itself and having nothing no visible connection to the rest of her.

Finally there are the servants, all admirably acted. Trish Lindstrom, as her master's mistress, plays sola. Four male attendants are established separately, and then, in one of the play's most satisfying strokes, come together -- first in a search party, then at a deathbed -- as a selection of varied individuals with a common interest. They are the whip-wielding bailiff (Patrick Galligan); his victim (Andrew Bunker), subsequently transformed first to a robber, then to Bazarov's gauchest but most important disciple; a superstitious bodyguard (Micheal Querin); and the Kirsanov family's senior retainer (Richard Farrell).

The last, who has seen everything, is especially impressive; he is the one who is commanded to be mutedly insouciant, and the funny thing is that he already is. His insouciance is in fact so muted that his superiors never notice it, which is their loss. The joke is that the oldest character in the play is also, inside himself, the most radical, and though he himself may not do anything with it, somebody will, sometime.

HARLEQUINADE

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

- - -

Here's a poser. The Deep Blue Sea, Terence Rattigans best full- length play, was first staged in 1952, two years after the death of Bernard Shaw, so it would be ineligible for production at the Shaw Festival, whose original rules limit the repertoire to plays dating from the patron-saints own lifetime. It wouldn't even qualify under the new amended guidelines which permit plays that are set in that period but written later; The Deep Blue Sea, like most of Rattigan's work, is set in Time: The Present. If the festival people wanted to produce it (and they should) they would have to rationalize the situation somewhat like this: Plays arent written or produced overnight, so Rattigan must at least have been thinking of this one in 1950, which would have been time present when he started writing. Such logic is not unheard of

No such sleight-of-mind would be necessary to justify a production of The Browning Version (1948), Rattigans best one-act play and a minor masterpiece, but the festival hasn't programmed that either, though I'm sure it will one day. What it has offered us to be going on with is Harlequinade, which was originally devised as an afterpiece to The Browning Version, and is a very light satire on the theatre. This is its first professional Canadian production, and, more surprisingly, the first time that any play by Rattigan, once the monarch of the West End boulevards, has ever reached Niagara.

It presents Arthur and Edna Gosport, a long-serving and popular acting couple, who are on the road as Romeo and Juliet, long after it has ceased to be appropriate. Edna is closer to 40 than to 14, much closer, and as for Arthur, best not go there. But they soldier on, bickering and bantering but devoted, to their profession and to one another. We meet them dress-rehearsing, at their latest touring date. Another opening, another show: If Harlequinade reminds us of Kiss Me Kate (which came along a year later) its partly because the married stars in both the play and the musical are based on that most celebrated of acting couples, the Lunts, who at this time were not just a legend but a living one.

Its great fun, though it needs to be seen in relaxed circumstances, either paired as originally with something more substantial or done on its own, as here, as a lunchtime diversion. It went over especially well at last week's premiere with a largely pro audience who laughed as knowingly at the actors playing it as at the actors they were playing. Peter Hutt is especially delicious as Arthur, looking in his balcony-scene costume like a superannuated buccaneer, earnestly essaying a "little leap" that he has never tried before and that throws his partner into deep confusion and then sportingly giving it up, devil-may-care in what passes for his private life, and devoted to his craft even in the grimmest of circumstances. Goldie Semple as Edna lacks his lightness of touch, being more the battle-axe and less the butterfly than the role seems to warrant.

When Harlequinade first appeared, it was hailed as the best backstage farrago since Sheridan's The Critic two centuries earlier, a position it continued to maintain until being decisively displaced by Michael Frayns Noises Off. Like Noises Off it runs out of energy but it does so far sooner and with less discrimination. It stops making jokes about the theatre and throws in a more mundane farcical subplot. This concerns a previous professional engagement of Arthurs at this very same Midlands town, during which he absent- mindedly got married and unknowingly fathered a daughter. That child is now grown up and presents herself, with her own husband and her own baby. This blast from the past naturally throws Edna into even greater perturbation than did Arthur's little leap; it qualifies, when you think about it, as quite a big leap. Arthur himself isn't much perturbed; he is in fact imperturbable. (Twenty years before, hed managed not to notice the General Strike. This is taken as a great joke on the self-centredness of actors, though they are hardly the only people who live in worlds of their own and are oblivious to politics.) This insouciance is an admirable quality in its way, but it does rather disqualify him as the hero of a farce.

The subplot isnt that bad in itself; and it's firmly nailed down here by Diana Donnelly as the very voluble lost girl and Graeme Somerville as her very taciturn spouse. But Neil Munro's production is at fault in presenting the play as if it were about Arthur and Edna. It isnt. Its about their stage manager, Jack, who does all the play's work while they get its glory. (This is art imitating life.) It's Jack who has to cope with all the turmoil while fending off a crisis of his own, in the shape of his fiancee who wants him to get out of the theatre, like now. He also has many of the sharpest lines, some about how the audience loves the fact that Arthur and Edna are actually married, some about the role of arts subsidy -- a new-fangled thing at the time -- in taking plays to audiences who dont want to see them. These last have been cut in the current production, which is surely rather craven of the Shaw. I dont agree with the sentiments either, but they're funny in context.

Kevin Bundy's performances as Jack is no more than amiable; and consequently neither is the play. Jack is a soul in agony; the hero that every farce needs. (Noises Off is an exception; it presents a group in agony. But the lack of an identifiable protagonist may explain its obstinate refusal to come to a final boil.)

I should not, though, get too heavy about Harlequinade. A decorative style of Shakespearean acting and production, fashionable in the 1930s and already fading fast in the 40s, gets entertainingly lampooned; Judith Bowdens decor is a monument to the Higher Tat, all the way down to an etched backdrop that looks more like Venice than Verona. But doubtless the Gosports had a Merchant in their repertoire as well.

There is a delightful performance from Jennifer Phipps as Arthur's mother, a Dame, now playing the Nurse, who always has a bottle and some advice handy, and is thoroughly indomitable; and another from Bernard Behrens as a small-part actor who detests the business and is highly domitable. David Schurmann puts in a flavourful appearance as a morose manger, Peter Krantz drifts periodically and silently across the stage, looking even more menacing than usual; and Mark Adrians makes a definite shy mark as a super, entrusted at short notice with the single line "Faith, we may put up our pipes and be gone." Rattigan himself, as First Musician, spoke this line in an undergraduate production at Oxford; and he claimed that his delivery of it always brought a perceptible frown to the brow of Peggy Ashcroft, who had been imported from the professional stage to play Juliet, and was supposed to be acting dead at the time. He wrote The Deep Blue Sea for her, regardless.

FLOYD COLLINS

Courth House Theatre,

Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

Twice this season, the Shaw Festival's first-night audience has rightfully erupted. The first occasion was the full-length main- house production of Man and Superman, a triumph of expansion. The second is the production at the intimate Court House of the off- Broadway musical Floyd Collins, a triumph of compression.

Floyd Collins, with music and lyrics by Adam Guettel and book by Tina Landau, is a compressed epic to begin with. It's based on a historical event, and is set in 1925 in Kentucky, an area of the country that didn't have to wait for the Great Depression in order to be depressed. In Barren County (a name almost too good to be true) the 37-year-old Floyd goes exploring the neighbourhood network of subterranean caves, hoping to discover a new one that he can open up for pleasure and profit. He does find it, but a rock falls on his foot, trapping him. The rest of the show chronicles the attempts, increasingly elaborate and well-publicized, to rescue him.

It's literally true to say that a story unfolds on two levels. Down below there's Floyd in his loneliness and his desperation, neither of them as unvaried as you might expect. Up above, there is what the show's publicity claims to have been the first media circus. The first reporter on the scene is a rookie from Louisville, Ken., named Skeets Miller, who turns out to be the only man small enough to squeeze through the hole at the top of Floyd's cave and actually talk to him. Skeets' coverage eventually won him a Pulitzer -- that's outside the compass of the show, but we do learn that his initial story has been syndicated in thousands of papers. Floyd learns it too and is impressed, even though he doesn't know what "syndication" means. Skeets sums up in himself the divergent forces at work; he forms a genuine bond with Floyd but he also profits from his predicament. And like Floyd, he has unrealized dreams, he wanted to be an operatic baritone, a revelation at which Floyd heartily laughs.

Skeets' initial dispatch lures in a host of other reporters, print and film. A mining company arrives, offering to take over the entire rescue operation, at no charge. They're in it for the publicity, of course, and their boss is a bully. Nevertheless, he does sincerely want to help, or so it seems, and he persists after most others have given up. Floyd's own family is deeply riven. His fundamentalist father is tempted by all the money on offer; brother Homer, the proud owner of a new Model T, hops between agonizing over Floyd and posing for the newsreels; and sister Nellie, Floyd's favourite, is newly out of an institution and distrusted by everybody else. Add in the other locals and the vast assembly, mostly unseen but felt, of gawkers, sympathizers, refreshment concessionaires and hucksters. There's a brisk trade in souvenirs.

Guettel's score, his professional debut, is remarkable; far from conventional Broadway but very theatrical. He picks up the folk rhythms, reinforced by the Aaron Copland frontier sound, that his grandfather Richard Rodgers put to memorably jaunty use in Oklahoma!, and takes it much further and, as is appropriate, far deeper. (For that matter his mother, Mary Rodgers, wrote a score for Once Upon a Mattress that her dad found rather startling.) There is a long sustained solo for Floyd at the start, taking him from hope to disaster, that's a tour de force. It's an aria, really; and when late in the show we get to a threatening, doom-laden reprise of The Ballad of Floyd Collins (heard more innocently at the start), then we really do seem to have arrived at bluegrass opera of an intensity and sophistication to challenge Porgy and Bess or Sweeney Todd. It's this that seems to me the musical and dramatic climax, rather than - - as claimed by the show's expert musical director, Paul Sportelli - - the actual double finale, which is certainly moving but goes on, for my taste, a little long.

It isn't always the easiest show. A static musical is pretty much a contradiction in terms and Floyd, for obvious reasons, doesn't move about much. He is ingeniously released from his bondage for some yearning (and ultimately wrenching) fantasy sequences. Even while he's immured his author and composer give him interesting and even funny things to say. All the same one tends to feel relieved when the action shifts upstairs and the conflicts get more physical and more explicit.

Not everything is perfect here, either. The Collins family are late developers, theatrically speaking, and the character of Nellie, though beautifully sung by Glynis Ranney, is something of a cheat. The sympathy between her and Floyd is musicalized but it isn't dramatized. Still, overall this is a neat and gripping script, and sometimes a very funny one.

Talking of humour: When I heard the original cast CD and when I saw a London production (which didn't have the resources) of the number that I, in my unregenerate way, liked the best was Is That Remarkable. In it, a trio of reporters, overhearing things and invariably getting them wrong, send their scoops down the phone lines. It has a jazzy, urban bounce and it gives Guettel the chance to show that he can write snappy lyrics with the best of them. It is, in fact, the nearest thing in the score to a traditional show tune. Eda Holmes, who is both director and choreographer, has staged it very well with the three hacks, in a diagonal line, moving all over the stage in a series of predatory jumps and crouches -- I think it's a tribute to her production that it doesn't stand out. She and her team hold us just as firmly for the more demanding stuff. The staging, on a set by William Schmuck largely composed of mounds of newsprint, is beautifully fluid, moving us in and out and up and down with enchanting ease and unending ingenuity.

Best of all in Holmes' production are the performances she gets, from a cast who plainly know they are in on something special and are on fire to share it. Jay Turvey as Floyd, apart from singing like a lark, plays brilliant variations on the theme of a smile -- optimism got him where he is and it remains with him, even his bitterness has a tang of benevolence in it. Jeff Lillico's Skeets and Jeff Meadows' Homer are both excellent foils to him and pulsating characters in their own right. There is strong work, too, from Peter Millard, Kevin Dennis, Douglas E. Hughes and Ben Carlson. The unmiked singing is, as usual at Shaw, a rich treat; the offstage voices singing responses to Floyd's halloos, as he feels his way through the caverns, are more haunting than any electronic echoes could hope to be.

I was shocked when the reviews of Man and Superman failed to mention the overpowering audience response which, even if you didn't like the production, was an extraordinary happening in itself. (It wasn't the standard Pavlovian ovation, and you could tell the difference.) So, just in case there are any similar lapses this time: The audience at Floyd Collins, from at least halfway through the evening, was bursting with suppressed excitement, and when the time came to release it, they -- or rather we -- exploded. But then the whole show is an explosion. And, as Floyd himself has cause to confirm, an explosion in a confined space is really something.
