MIRANDOLINA

Harbourfront Theatre Centre,

Toronto

- - -

The Italian play we know in English as Mirandolina is actually called La Locandiera, which translates roughly as The Female Innkeeper. Mirandolina, the heroine of Carlo Goldoni's 1753 comedy, does indeed keep an inn, one in Florence inherited from her father, and keeps it very well. Her male guests adore her, or most of them do; the smitten ones we meet are a rich Count and a poor Marquis. The one holdout is a man referred to in Soulpepper's program as the Cavaliere and in the actual (uncredited) text as the Knight. It's nothing personal; he resists Mirandolina because he resists all women. So she sets out to humble him.

She'll make him fall in love like any other man and maybe then he'll know what kind of fool he am, er, is. And that's exactly how it works out. This task accomplished, Mirandolina turns her back on the encircling gentry and -- this is not a spoiler -- bestows it on Fabrizio, her only visible member of staff, to whom she had promised it all along, this arrangement being something else bequeathed to her by her departed dad.

Mirandolina is a play with a slender story, beautifully put together. Its story could well seem very conventional: Attractive working woman has fun with the nobs and snobs, puts them properly in their place, and ends up with her true love, who is of satisfyingly humble birth. That's one way of looking at it, and it may very well be the right way. But it isn't the only way, and Laszlo Marton's Soulpepper production tries for something more complicated.

As in many Shakespeare comedies, there are awkward bits left over at the end, and a production has the choice of sweeping them merrily under the carpet or leaving them exposed and throbbing. In Marton's version, there is pain on view. Mirandolina arouses in the Knight a passion that neither of them can control. He ends up wounded and she ends up scared and more than a little guilty; when she falls into her potboy's arms, it's not because he represents love, it's because he represents shelter. She's settling.

I quite enjoyed the show, but it frankly doesn't work. This is surprising, coming from the director who showed us all the dark comedy in Chekhov and Moliere, but this production is listless. The central fault is not in the interpretation but in the casting, or at least in one piece of it. Sweet or bitter, if the play is The Taming of the Misogynist, then that man's humour had better be there from the beginning, a fact in the play, upfront and kicking. Stuart Hughes was the best thing in last year's Soulpepper production of the faintly similar She Stoops to Conquer, but there he played a paralytically shy man rendered bold in the presence of a social inferior, preferably female. The Knight he plays here seems creditably devoid of class consciousness, and has no noticeable inhibitions whatever. He is presumably meant to be a hard-bitten soldier, but as Hughes presents him he is, at most, a cashiered cadet with a dissolute air. He does his best to play the roaring boy, and he has some good howling moments when his defences crumble, but it's hard to understand why his hostess should regard him as such a challenge.

This of course rebounds on her performance as well as on his. Mirandolina is supposed to be a woman everybody falls in love with, and there could hardly be better casting for that than Kristen Thomson, for looks, personality and a sense of all-round capability. It's the way she runs her house, as much as anything else that attracts the men. The production's best scene shows her seducing the Knight by cooking and serving him the perfect ragu: Ah, those Italians. Her smile and her decolletage don't hurt, either.

Marton's visual inventiveness (or the physical inventiveness he inspires in his actors) remains intact; the production's abiding image is of Thomson draping her shawl over her own head and the Knight's, then withdrawing, leaving him lost and floundering. It sums up their relationship. But things are seldom that precise. Thomson is firing on all cylinders, but indiscriminately, and it's hard to follow what's on the woman's mind or why. She's plainly meant to be more than a tease, but her actions are too cruel, too relished, for us to take her as a defender of sensible womanhood. She only gets it together at the play's epilogue, a routine farewell to the audience that she endows with half-a-dozen shades of meaning, flashed out in dazzling succession.

The whole cast goes off in all directions; not as unhappily as in Marton's production of A Flea in Her Ear, but with similarly jerky results. Diego Matamoros' Marquis is physically extreme but vocally subdued: an odd combination, and one that prevents the central joke of the impoverished aristocrat from coming through clearly enough to be funny. (There's one like him, boasting of his lineage and terminally cheap, in every Goldoni play; he may have disdained earlier stock figures, but he wasn't above inventing his own.)

Michael Simpson does better at the Count, especially when his pride flashes out and drives him to a duel. Richard Zeppieri makes a loutish, possessive Fabrizio, but I suspect that's director's interpretation rather than actor's choice, and there's nothing wrong with the way he does it; plus, as you might tell from his name, he's ethnically right. Also passing through the inn are a couple of penniless actresses, posing as noblewomen, and battening off each of the men in turn. One is played blowsily and well by Diana Leblanc, and the other sleekly and even better by Jennifer Gould. Paul Manz is charming as the Knight's man, who, in a delightful touch, is as gone on Mirandolina as everybody else.

The costumes are non-specifically modern, thereby compromising one of the play's principal attractions, the view it affords us of a distant society complete in itself. Astrid Janson's set, though, is timeless, a high chamber whose altitude accommodates a huge quantity of fully burdened laundry lines. A breeze blows enchantingly through the sheets as the play starts; a rainstorm, delightfully summoned through Andrea Lundy's lighting, is the cue for everything to be brought inside. This gives us a link to the play's most celebrated scene, in which Mirandolina does the ironing while fending off the Knight's advances. Which, he asks plaintively, means more to you, that linen or me; and Mirandolina, practical as ever, tells him.

THIS IS OUR YOUTH

Berkeley Street Theatre

- - -

So, it's welcome back again to This Is Our Youth. Or This Is Our Youth Again. Or Sex and the City Goes Legit. The American play, seen in Toronto a year ago, has returned with two of its three roles recast with names, or sort of, from movies and television. The occasion has increased my respect for Kenneth Lonergan's script. If it can survive this cast, it can survive anything.

To recap: The play concerns three New Yorkers, all in their twenties and all with prosperous parents. Dennis has his own apartment and deals drugs; he is more or less permanently wired. Warren lives with his father, whom he hates, and seems to spend most of his time both hanging out with Dennis and hanging on to him; he's a human punching bag, to whom Dennis turns his attention when he's done with the actual punching bag that adorns his room. Jessica crosses their path as a possible date for Warren. As Dennis puts with his customary charm, she's the only good-looking girl his friend has had a shot at in years.

Lonergan's play is avowedly autobiographical (This Was His Youth), which explains why it's set in the 1980s. But, barring the absence from the characters' lives of PCs and CDs and the presence of hostile references to President Reagan rather than President Bush, it could be happening now. (This Is Still Our Youth, or a fragrant sample of it.)

Juvenile speech patterns, we realize, have stayed, like, remarkably unaltered down the decades. The characters talk in a mode that might be described as self-stylized, and within that framework the author's turn of phrase is impeccable. "You're really harsh, man" says a petulant Warren after Dennis has dealt him an especially vicious put-down, and the choice of word is perfect. Equally impressive is his skill at building scenes.

The peak here is the first encounter between Warren, unpractised lust trying to look cool, and Jessica, mild disinterest that feels obliged to act polite. With the help of some smoking and some dancing (to Tutti Frutti on vinyl, nostalgia squared, as it were) they adjourn to the penthouse suite at the Plaza -- though even now Jessica appears willing rather than keen. En route we learn about the death of Warren's sister, a topic the playwright puts to explosive use in the second act, as a partial and very persuasive illustration of Warren's angry, wounded relationship with his father.

The physical bones of Woody Harrelson's former excellent production are still clearly visible but the flesh has decayed to the point of decomposition. The two newcomers are devoid of theatre experience and they have the lack of technique to prove it. They both gabble and mumble; one of them has little idea of projection and the other has none whatsoever.

The former is Katharine Isabelle; a scene that requires her to get angry is totally beyond her, but otherwise she makes a reasonable stab at Jessica's well-intentioned blankness, as she oscillates between a permissive lifestyle and the desire to be back at her mom's before curfew. She's amateurish, but on screen this might be a passable performance.

The one given by Jason Lewis (the Sex and the City dude) would be intolerable in any medium. He speaks in an unvaried subterranean drawl, but his inaudibility is only the half of it. It's clear from the lines you can hear that he has no idea how to phrase his author's language and no appreciation of either its shape or its wit. The great cadenza in which Dennis suddenly develops the ambition to be a film director might as well not be there. He does admittedly look at home on the stage, even if he doesn't sound it; he slouches and pounces and punches as if he were enjoying it. Even so, one looks achingly back on the dynamic things Fabrizio Filippo did with the role last year, and especially on how he managed to integrate an enforced last-minute limp into Dennis' general jumpiness. It might take a full set of crutches to galvanize Lewis.

I don't recall Marcello Cabezas, the original cast's sole survivor, being as exaggeratedly high-pitched and hysterical last time around as he is now, but maybe he feels obliged to make up for the languor of his colleagues. (He is the moving spirit behind the whole production.) Having nobody to bounce off, and no rhythm to fit into, he is bound to seem forced, but he still transmits Warren's puppy-dog self-abasement -- he always seems to be presenting his bum for Dennis to kick -- and his dignity when, with nothing left to lose, he asserts himself.

Last year, Warren, because he has more stage time than anyone else, seemed to be the central character by default. This time he's the central character as of right. Between them, the trio run a gamut of incomprehensibility; but Cabezas at least has energy and focus. His colleagues just made me angry, as did the people -- Cabezas, under his producer's hat, included -- who hired them. What are they doing here? There must be any number of good young actors, in and around Toronto, who could use the break; there must, come to that, be any number of American actors whom one would welcome to chance to see. Why bring in rubbish?

Black & White Photo: Dawn Alexander / Marcello Cabezas, left, and Jason Lewis in Kenneth Lonergan's play -- back for a second Toronto run, but with semi-famous actors.
2004-09-10-he-sang-what-he-wanted-duets-:
robertcushman@lycos.com

For iconic singers in their twilight years, recording an album of duets is beginning to seem like tempting fate. Frank Sinatra's two CDs worth turned out to be the last records he ever made, but at least he was still alive when they came out. Ray Charles' Genius Loves Company (Concord Jazz) has turned out to be a memorial tribute in a more literal sense than anyone can have wished.

It adheres to the Sinatra pattern in teaming its star with a dozen other name-singers from various musical backgrounds. (And some tracks are produced by Phil Ramone, who was responsible for the entire Sinatra project.) It differs from its predecessor in that the performers on each song don't owe their apparent proximity to the miracle of overdub; they were actually there in the studio together.

This, though, turns out to make less of a difference than you might expect. There is a sad lack of interplay on most of these performances. The most exciting -- really, the only one with excitement -- wasn't done in a studio at all; it's a live encounter with Van Morrison on Morrison's own song Crazy Love, for a TV awards show. You can feel the audience spurring them on; more importantly, you feel the two men (and Charles probably has more in common with Morrison than with any of his other partners here) spurring one another on. It's practically the only occasion on the entire disc on which Charles ventures a spoken ad lib.

It's the last cut on the album but it was recorded first, in June, 2003. The studio sessions began the next month and concluded nine months later, and they find Charles not only in progressively lower spirits but also, obviously, in progressively worse health. Charles actually fares worse here than did Sinatra, who was paired much of the time with singers who had no affinity with his very specialized kind of music and to whom, in many cases, he had never been (and indeed never was) introduced. His voice was ragged but, at least on a few songs, still powerful.

Charles gets a more imaginative selection of songs (Sinatra's were all his old warhorses) and a pretty good and varied bunch of people to do them with. And there is a logic, which there never was with Sinatra, in teaming him with singers from across the board because, as everybody has said, he himself was the great defier of genre.

At the same time he was never what you would call versatile; he may have embraced every kind of song but they had to submit on his terms. I don't mean that he desecrated or defiled them, but that extraordinary voice -- with its wails, moans, peals and chuckles and its unfailing sense of narrative logic -- was more individual than they could ever be.

I first encountered Charles in the early 1960s when he was going, though I didn't know it at the time, through his country-and- western phase. I Can't Stop Loving You was a big hit for him, and though I never found the song very interesting, I lived each time it was played for the moment at which he told the choir that was dogging his footsteps to "sing the song, children." A wonderful blend of serenity and chutzpah, a laying on of hands coupled with a wink at the congregation.

After that, a lesser hit but one I preferred, came You Don't Know Me, a sublimely self-pitying number that probably wasn't meant to appeal to my teenage angst but did anyway. Anyway, he gave it dignity and he gave it agony, apparently without trying. He didn't have to emote, his voice was emotion. And though these were both country songs, it never occurred to me for a moment to think of him as a country singer.

I didn't know, either, about Charles the jazz or blues or rhythm- and-blues singer, or Charles the singer of standards. I didn't even know he played the piano. (It wouldn't have made much of an impression through all those strings anyway). I found out a lot, in very short order, when I saw him on -- and I refuse to say "of all things" -- The Perry Como Show. Perry's choral director, of course, was also called Ray Charles (he took, in self-defence, to billing himself as The Other Ray Charles) and the two indulged in a little banter before the first Ray -- the black, blind one -- started singing Georgia on My Mind, which had the same electrifying effect on me that it has had on everybody else who's heard it.

It still does. And I still don't quite know why. Other good singers have sung it very well, before and since (the road, in this case, goes back to 1932) without making the same connection. Charles, meanwhile, doesn't really sing it any differently from the way in which he's sung countless other tunes, and yet something -- some yearning quality, I suppose, though that sounds inadequate -- fuses singer and song.

It's not even as if anyone really knows whether he's singing about a place or a girl; the authors (Hoagy Carmichael and the mysterious Stuart Gorrell) never came clean about it, and neither did Charles. (The state of Georgia had no such doubts and has adopted the song as its own.) All we can be sure of is that Ray longs passionately for something and wants, with every fibre of his voice, to tell us about it.

Something of the same thing happens when he sings the song Ruby (which is about a girl) and which jumps out from an album of songs with women's names in their titles, all of which he apparently treats in exactly the same way. He does tend to sound best when he's singing about the unattainable, and this perhaps has its counterpart in the tone of outraged bewilderment that characterises his best comedy numbers: Hit the Road, Jack or, my own favourite, Busted.

Of all these touchstone songs, the only one to turn up on Genius Loves Company is You Don't Know Me, on which Charles kindles at least the embers of the old anguish. His songmate is Diana Krall and she complements him nicely, being equable but not bland. (And after what the camera did to her in De-Lovely, one is rooting for her anyway.)

Better though is Norah Jones, who on the opening cut, Here We Go Again, sounds -- to my surprise -- like a veritable soul-daughter to The Man; it's a very quiet and easy duet, and Charles has a laugh in his voice of which one would like to hear more.

Natalie Cole, whose father was Charles' earliest influence and who has herself become a very reliable singer of all kinds of standards, joins him for Fever, which, from the opening bass vamp on, can't help sounding like an out of place tribute to Peggy Lee. It might have been better to have heard one of Charles' songs that Peggy featured, Hallelujah I Love Him So or, even better, Tell All the World About You; Brother Ray the considerable songwriter is not represented here. Charles can't sound feverish anymore, and Cole's attempts at backchat don't work.

The saddest pairings are with figures from comparatively contemporary pop. Elton John, bringing his own Sorry Seems to Be the Hardest Word (with melodramatic strings), sounds like the most self- important voice in popular music, at least until the ludicrously spectral Michael McDonald turns up to weigh down Goffin and King's Hey Girl, though Charles himself does manage to emit a few sensual gleams through the general listlessness. He sounds like a very old man when he joins James Taylor on Taylor's Sweet Potato Pie, but the track is pleasant easy listening, with a father-and-son air to it.

The country singers don't do too well. On Do I Ever Cross Your Mind, Charles actually sounds more country, or at least placid, than ever, but when Bonnie Raitt joins in, singing in exactly the same way, it's too relaxed to be interesting. Charles matched with Willie Nelson for It Was a Very Good Year sounds like a good idea, and Nelson's matter-of-factness is initially endearing; Charles, though, sounds genuinely toothless -- even his phrasing is suspect -- and it's distressing. Sinatra (to whose arrangement this one is heavily indebted) was only 50 when he recorded it. You don't want to hear two genuinely old men singing about when they were 35, though their last unison line is powerful.

Happier, bluesier things: B.B. King (Sinner's Prayer) still sounds gritty and powerful, and still plays ringing guitar; Charles' piano doesn't sound as good, but he gets down to business by the end. This is, as expected, the most sympathetic pairing. There's good rapport with Gladys Knight (Heaven Help Us All) as well; she sings good gospel, as of course does he, though the production is chintzy, especially the choir.

And then there's Over the Rainbow, with the melody coming up so overpoweringly in the intro, you expect to hear Charles duetting with the ghost of Judy Garland. What you actually get is Johnny Mathis. You also get Charles singing a song that's almost completely wrong for him. He once, in an interview with Whitney Balliett, spoke of songs he loved but couldn't sing. Stardust was one of them. The reason, I think, is that Stardust, like most of Over the Rainbow, is a contemplative, generalized kind of song. Charles had to sing in the first person; he wasn't a philosopher, he needed to want something, a woman or a state, it didn't matter.

Rainbow only gets that personal on its last line -- actually, its coda -- and then, and only then, Charles makes it really poignant. It's worth it, perhaps, to realize that about him. And there is something touching about this tribute from Charles' peers and disciples, about its spirit if not about its execution. Sing the songs, children.

2004-09-16-too-frank-also-too-johnny:
Until Sept. 26. Box office: 416-366-7723.

FRANKIE & JOHNNY IN THE CLAIR-DE-LUNE

Jane Mallet Theatre, Toronto

- - -

Frankie and Johnny are sweethearts. At least they are on the night we meet them in Terrence McNally's play. Previously they have been co-workers in a New York greasy spoon, she a waitress, he a short-order cook. At the end of their first date, they go back to Frankie's apartment and into her bed. And, oh lordy, how they can love.

I suppose it's to the play's credit that it's explicit about the physical nature of human relationships, especially the messier ones. Both Frankie and Johnny are in their 40s and neither of them is a conventionally glamorous figure; there is plenty of material here about sagging flesh and flagging energy. But if the laughter this arouses is to be sympathetic rather than queasy, we need both to believe in the characters and to feel for them. McNally, one of the most successful of American playwrights, writes realistically about their bodies, but when dealing with their minds he is apt to get mushy. It's a very Broadway thing -- the desire to write romantically without being sentimental -- and it's likely to trip up. Nobody holds it against McNally that he's slick -- it's quite an achievement to keep us interested in two characters and one situation for two whole acts -- but he can also be glib. And he's inadequately served by the newly fledged BirdLand Theatre, whose second flight this is. The production gets the rhythms only fitfully correct, and neither of its performances comes fully alive.

The dynamic is that Johnny wants to hold on to Frankie while Frankie has her doubts. Both of them have been bruised in the past, both by family and partners, and these are the differing ways in which they react; he's a battered optimist, she's a wry pessimist. Both, needless to say, have shattered dreams; she wanted to be an actress, he didn't want to be a cook. And then there is the coincidence of their names, which the play brazenly, and I suppose charmingly, exploits by having Johnny call in to a classical music DJ who flatly refuses to believe it, but who anyway plays for them what he announces simply as "the most beautiful music ever written." It's Debussy's Clair de Lune; we know it, they don't. It goes with the actual moonlight that's streaming full-glow outside; they tell us so, and we believe them.

There can be no quarrel with the play's atmospherics; we believe that this is New York, and we can smell the food in the cramped apartment. Not all the cultural references are musical. Some are literary, and they work less well. Johnny, an autodidact, has a Complete Shakespeare in his locker; he's working his way slowly through it, or so he tells us, and he keeps quoting from it. But the book might just as well be a Dictionary of Quotations, because somehow all the lines he comes up with are the famous ones. And it's at points like this that McNally's writing becomes dangerously coy.

The play was first staged in 1987, and it was revived on Broadway a few years ago with Edie Falco, alive in every nerve end, playing Frankie. Falco's resilient spirit and crinkled, world-weary smile are difficult images to erase from any role, and Zorana Kydd who plays it here (also BirdLand's Artistic Producer) is ill-equipped to compete. She gets the outline of the character well enough, especially in its resentful aspects, but she seems to have only two modes of performance; she's either exclamatory, which can be wearing, or passive, which can be dull. Peter Van Wart's Johnny is competent but raucous; his dreams of a perfectly imperfect love never achieve lift-off. Rod Ceballos' direction lacks any sense of thrust-and-parry, not only between the characters but between the play's various levels of wit; these, being stage New Yorkers, are always making jokes, and the production seems uncertain of when they mean it and when they don't. The play reaches its predestined, qualifiedly happy ending with nothing much seeming to have happened, inside the characters or out.

2004-09-20-remembering-glassco:
Obituary of Bill Glassco.

The reviews will be universally positive for founder of the Tarragon Theatre

Bill Glassco, who died last Monday of throat cancer at the age of 69, had one more year of life than he had expected. His doctors had predicted his death a year ago, but his illness went into remission, bestowing on him what he described to friends as a miraculous bonus. It was typical of him that he could sound genuinely joyful when saying that, with no hint of either sanctimony or martyrdom.

As has been said many times during the past week, Bill Glassco was one of the first gentlemen of the Canadian theatre. He was also truly a gentle man, and possibly never more so than during those last years. His place is secure in Canadian theatre history as one of the architects of the 1970s revolution, which combined the creation of our first school of indigenous playwrights with that of theatres and companies dedicated to their performance. In 1972, with his then-wife Jane Gordon, he founded the Tarragon Theatre, of which he remained artistic director for a decade, and which became Torontos flagship house for new plays.

Among the playwrights he championed were John Murrell, Judith Thompson, James Reaney and David French. He directed every one of French's plays, from the first, Leaving Home, which inaugurated both the Tarragon and its author's cycle of plays about the Mercer family and their emblematic progression from Newfoundland to Toronto, down to the most recent, Soldiers Heart, which brought both author and director back to the Tarragon after a long absence. The list also includes Jitters, the backstage comedy that was the Tarragons greatest financial success in Glassco's time, in which he himself is generally reckoned to be one of the characters. His reign at the Tarragon was before my time in Canada. When I came here he was helping to form what we now know as CanStage, a company formed by the merger of CentreStage (which he had also directed) and Toronto Free Theatre. It was not initially a very happy marriage, and both Glassco and Toronto Free's Guy Sprung had left before the new entity achieved its own identity. Anyway, I thought of Glassco principally as a nurturer of dramatists. He was certainly that, but what I have learned from talking to his colleagues -- and just about everybody in Ontario theatre was a colleague of Bills at some point, as were many beyond -- is that he was a nurturer of all theatrical talent.

On consecutive days following his death, I found myself talking about him to Andrey Tarasiuk, head of new play development at the Stratford Festival, and to actor and director David Ferry; casual conversations that turned into impromptu interviews. The stories they told me -- even the words they used -- were eerily similar. Both credited Glassco with starting their careers; both had been spotted by him when they were students at the National Theatre School in Montreal. Tarasiuk, who thought he wanted just to direct plays, was informed that he was going to run theatres -- as he has done, notably, before going to Stratford, the peripatetic young peoples group known as Theatre Direct. Glassco took him on at the Tarragon and, as he says, made him do everything: production, stage management, directing and associate producing.

One of Bill's great strengths said Tarasiuk, using an acting metaphor but not just talking about actors, "was to cast an individual and encourage him on a certain path. He also had the ability to work in a team with all his collaborators -- not just with the playwright and the actors, but also with the designer, the stage management ... he worked on a basis of friendship with all the production personnel. He believed that success depends equally on all the parts. It was an illustration in mentorship."

It obviously wasn't planned that way, but next year at Stratford, Tarasiuk will in effect be paying tribute to his mentor by directing James Reaneys Sticks and Stones, the first play in his Donnelly trilogy -- a bold project to which Glassco gave a home at the Tarragon 31 years ago, after seeing a workshop of it in Halifax. Among the actors involved in it, in both Halifax and Toronto, was one to whom Glassco had already given a break, Ferry.

It might be truer to say that Ferry spotted Glassco than that Glassco spotted him. In 1972, when the aspiring actor was in his third year at the NTS, the Tarragon production of Leaving Home came to Montreal. Ferry remembers being mesmerized ... by the recognition I felt. The young lead was Frank Moore (who, 32 years on, has just finished playing the big, bad businessman in Urinetown), and Ferry, a Newfie himself, found "his energy, presence and Canadian sound, electrifying. I wanted to be an actor like that right away. There was also an electric feel of commitment to the telling of Canadian stories that was reflected in the talk that Bill gave to the audience after."

A few weeks later Ferry was visiting friends in Toronto, and espied -- outside a butchers shop in Rosedale -- a Volkswagen with a bumper sticker: Have You Been To Tarragon Lately? "This long drink of water with a Buddha on a chain round his neck gets out, and I recognize him as Bill Glassco. Without even thinking, I went right up to him and gushed about the French play and told him that I thought it would be a good thing if I went to work for him at Tarragon. Of course, I was clueless as to the etiquette of the business, but he was generous enough a man to say he would consider it." The audition Ferry eventually got (for the title-role in David Freeman's You're Gonna Be Alright, Jamie Boy) was unconventional. Glassco took him and his girlfriend out for a drink: I remember going on passionately about her at one point while she was away from the table, and Bill asked me to immediately do my audition piece right there in the bar with the passion I was feeling about my girlfriend. The punchline? "He cast me right there."

Ferry confirms Tarasiuks description of the Tarragon atmosphere in those days: The thing that one felt working for Bill in those days, for better or worse, was that you became part of a family. It may seem simple now, but walking in the front door of Tarragon to be greeted by all those photos of Canadian playwrights on the walls was to give us a sense of being home. He adds that "the place was very late-60s in its ambience." Though I can't speak to that, I can testify that in his later years -- the sage, white-bearded years -- there was always a touch of the ex-hippie about Bill. He seems, indeed, to have been quite the sage even in his younger days.

It wasn't only anglophone dramatists whom he championed in the 70s; he also introduced the plays of Michel Tremblay to the world outside Quebec. He translated them, in collaboration with John Van Burek, and he staged them at the Tarragon. Strangely, though Bill himself was from Quebec, his command of French was not at this time especially good; before embarking on the translations, he had to take language lessons from his schoolteacher-cousin, Jane (the other Jane Glassco in his life, and someone to whom I owe much of my own friendship with him). Quebec, too, became his chosen home in his last years; it was there that he embarked on his last major enterprise. This was the Montreal Young Company, which he started in 1999, at the Saidye Bronfman Theatre, as an opportunity for emerging professional actors (especially anglophone Quebecers, who tended to get lost after emerging from the NTS) to play the classics. The company played two interesting seasons and then went into hiatus, a state from which it was set to return -- and still is -- next year. (Glassco was a genius at fundraising). His continuing commitment to young talent was additionally evident in his choice of the outstanding young director, Chris Abrahams, as his deputy. I remember his incredulous delight when he told me that Abrahams, who directed a stern version of Brechts Fears and Miseries of the Third Reich in the first Montreal season, had fallen in love with a neglected play by Terence Rattigan, of all old-fashioned dramatists, and was bent on staging it in the second; the play was After the Dance and it proved excellent.

It's an open secret that Bill himself was not an especially inspired director of plays (though I have good memories of his Montreal Measure for Measure) but it's more important that he was an inspired and inspiring director of theatres -- and a great and apparently selfless facilitator of talent. Ferry remarked to me that Bills uncle (or was it his great-uncle?) was a poet and added some of that poets heart was definitely deposited in Bill. Bill was also a musician. I used to run into him into CD and sheet-music stores in Toronto, and we had talked about doing a show together on Harold Arlen. He was an accomplished pianist, and in the last few years he recorded a couple of homemade CDs, to be distributed among friends. One of them -- with his daughter, the actress Briony Glassco, supplying some vocals -- was devoted to Gershwin. His funeral (at Hart House last Thursday) ended, unconventionally but surely very movingly, with everyone present singing They Can't Take That Away from Me. It's a great epitaph, but even better is the one with which his close friend Mary Kerr relayed the news in an e- mail: "Dear Bill G. died today. He is free and through and clear. I am very sad."

Black & White Photo: Dave Sidaway, CanWest News Service (The Gazette) / Bill Glassco, ex-hippie, talent nurturer, Canadian.

PRIVATE JOKES, PUBLIC PLACES

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

- - -

Oren Safdie, son of a famous architect, has written a play in which two other famous architects -- fictitious -- pass judgement on the final-year project of a young student and are very nasty, both to it and to her. The title is Private Jokes, Public Places. I have no idea whether the play itself is a private joke, but it sits very uneasily in the public place that is the Tarragon Theatre.

I lied when I said that the two judges are architects. One of them, a German, is; the other, who's English, is only a critic but he carries on as if he had the authority of a practitioner that should, I suppose, be a lesson to us all. Margaret, the student, is a Korean-American (the play takes place in a city that might well be New York, though theres nothing to stop it being Toronto) and her diploma piece is a design for a community swimming pool. The fourth and final person on stage is Margarets professor, who likes her.

There are other characters, but they're unseen; they are Margaret's classmates, and they are presumed to be sitting where we are. This is a public judging, before an audience. The author sets a trap for himself here, and Alisa Palmers production pushes him enthusiastically into it. The characters dont have to talk to one another, because they're too busy talking to us. They -- the two pundits, especially -- are showing off. This may well be because of the kind of people they are. In practice, though, it's difficult to distinguish between the characters showing off and the actors doing it.

Even as written, the play suffers from a damnable lack of conflict. (Its full of people shouting, but that isnt the same thing.) There is this idealistic but also practical young woman and there are these two well-fed establishment bullies picking, and occasionally hitting, on her. It's obvious whom we're going to side with. Margaret wants her building -- imaginary but on an actual site -- to serve the people who would use it, and is also averse to tearing up a tree that would stand by the side of the pool. What could be more admirable? Her opponents are enraged by her refusal to fit into any recognized movement; anything with "ism" on the end would do. At one point Margaret, who gets increasingly emboldened as the action progresses, says something tactless about the failure of Modernism. The critic immediately rears up: "The Modernists? You criticized the Modernists." Thats the level of caricature were dealing with. Margaret, meanwhile, turns into Joan of Arc.

Maybe Safdie intended a little more light and shade; maybe he intended there to be some right on both sides. It's hard to tell here, because the actors' scrambled delivery makes the arguments impossible to follow. (Think of the lucidity of Copenhagen, which showed, both in its writing and in this years Toronto staging, how ideas and the people holding them can be made dramatic. Or of the Shaw Festivals Man and Superman.) The production tips its hand from the beginning by having the men deliver their opening speeches from off-stage, making it impossible for us to apprehend either who they are or what they're talking about. M. J. Kang -- whose performance, since she's played the role in the plays three U.S. outings, cant be blamed on the current circumstances -- never gets beyond playing Margaret's nervousness. Victor Ertmannis as the Englishman does begin by acting like a human being, but has turned by the end into an angry buffoon. Dan Lett, by contrast, starts out unbelievably snide and snarky as the German, but develops some subtlety in the final stages. David Jansen come off best; his role as the mild- mannered teacher effectively prevents him from screaming at anyone. His mildness is probably meant to be suspect, but his interventions come off here as so may draughts from an oasis.

This is the third time in two weeks that an American play with credentials has fallen flat on a Toronto stage. This Is Our Youth is a commercial production and Frankie and Johnny in the Clair de Lune an independent one, but from an institutional theatre with the Tarragon's tradition, one expects more. Then again: Maybe I missed something but I failed to see on Tuesday night any sign of tribute to the theatre's late founder, Bill Glassco. Not a picture on the lobby wall; not so much as a slip in the program suggesting that the night's performance -- the start of a new season -- might be dedicated to the man who got the place started. I was shocked.
2004-09-24-catching-up-with-the-parade:
robertcushman@lycos.com

BROADWAY: THE GOLDEN AGE

- - -

There's a Rodgers and Hammerstein musical titled Me and Juliet that contains a song called Intermission Talk. It's sung by the ensemble, who are divided between cynics sneering that "the theatre is dying" and enthusiasts proclaiming that "the theatre is living." The latter, of course, get the last ringing word. This was 1953, part of the era in which R&H themselves were the kings of Broadway, though most of the shows they mention in the song are musicals, not plays. The period 1945-60 was a prosperous and creative time for musicals; it was also the era of Arthur Miller, Tennessee Williams and the late Eugene O'Neill.

This, roughly, is the period commemorated in Rick McKay's documentary Broadway: The Golden Age. It begins with a clip of Carol Channing, in her prime, singing Before the Parade Passes By from Hello Dolly, which is scary, though not as alarming as the sight and sound of Channing herself in interview, 40 years on. Her face is almost entirely masked by dark brown shades while her voice, which once ranged from squawk to croak, is now just croak. She's talking about what a unique experience the live theatre is, and she seems to imply -- or maybe it's the context that does it for her -- that Broadway and the theatre are the same thing.

Two things about the film are already clear: It's hung up on divas, and it takes a scattershot approach to its material. There are at least two movies here -- one about the shows themselves, and the other about the offstage lives of the people involved in them -- and they're recklessly intermingled.

McKay himself came to New York as a stage-struck youth from Beech Grove, Ind., and found -- like everybody before him, no matter when they arrived -- that it wasn't what it was, that the parade had in fact passed by. So he set out to talk to and record as many as he could find of the people he'd read about in newspapers, magazines and history books. He corralled an impressive number of celebrated interviewees, most of them heroically averse to fancy Hollywood notions such as facelifts. (They tend to be shot in unflattering and unvarying close-up.) He could not, understandably, bear to sacrifice a single one of them. They are of various vintages, so it never becomes clear just what the boundaries of Broadway's golden age might be.

Some speakers look back -- as spectators if not as participants - -as far as the 1930s, though it's a fact that even then Broadway types were fondly remembering the wildly productive days before the talkies and before the crash. Most would zero in on the '40s and '50s, though some would extend the glory days into the '60s. Why else begin with Hello Dolly? But then some might pinpoint that show as the start of the decadence. Stephen Sondheim analyzes the phenomenon of the Compulsory Standing Ovation (he's about the only one who analyzes anything) and it's arguable that Dolly was the show that began it.

Broadway still produces new musicals; it no longer produces new plays. There is at least as much here -- perhaps surprisingly, given the film's sensibility -- about drama as about musicals. Everybody, musical or legit, names as their favourite performer Laurette Taylor, who created the mother in The Glass Menagerie. She never made a talkie, but McKay has dug up a screen test that shows her to have been as breathtakingly natural as her admirers claim.

The same can't be said for those who are held up as her peers. Kim Stanley, caught in an onstage clip from Bus Stop, looks and sounds Hollywood sincere, while Marlon Brando, also described as a guy who might have wandered in off the street, has always seemed to me stylized as hell. But maybe I've seen too many Brando imitations.

As this suggests, much of the film's content has been determined by what film and TV clips are available to back up the interviews. There can be no other reason for devoting a whole segment to Robert Goulet and his insecurities about being in Camelot. Another self- contained section re-tells the familiar story of Shirley MacLaine's discovery as an understudy in The Pajama Game. This time, though, MacLaine gets to do much of the telling, and she's charming.

Carol Burnett tells about sharing an apartment -- and sharing a dress -- with four other aspirant actresses when she first came to New York. (That kind of struggle still goes on, of course, but it's only interesting when the people doing it have become famous.) Most contributors talk about how much more camaraderie there was then than there is now, and it's probably true; there were more shows, therefore there was more of a community. One gets a sense of everything being less desperate, less pretentious, largely because going to the shows was so affordable. We hear how people shuddered when top price rose to an unheard-of twenty dollars. No wonder Broadway was part of the culture then, while it's just a tourist attraction now.

Other reasons are offered for the decline. West Side Story is rightly singled out as a capstone of the period and given extensive coverage. On the other hand, its abolition of the distinction between singing and dancing ensembles is also cited as another nail in the coffin. The use of mics, which crept in in the '50s and is now universal, is unanimously denounced; I wouldn't argue, though I can't help suspecting that in Shakespeare's time, when roofed-in theatres first appeared, there were Elizabethan barnstormers who looked back to the good old days and swore that all this new- fangled candlelight was killing the drama.

McKay ends up acknowledging that today's young audiences and performers may in time look back upon this as a golden age. I don't think he really believes this, and neither frankly do I; but anything's possible. Perhaps, in 40 years' time, people will think back fondly to the great days of 2004 when Broadway had theatres.

Rating Three

2004-09-27-i-gave-it-a-chance:
pppeeeaaaccceee runs until Oct. 10. Box office: 416-504-7529.; robertcushman@lycos.com

PPPEEEAAACCCEEE

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

- - -

Darren O'Donnell, the talented creator of Boxhead and White Mice, wrote and directed pppeeeaaaccceee with Rebecca Picherak. The triple spelling is presumably connected to the fact that the show has three actors, playing three roles. It would be inaccurate, and maybe even insulting, to suggest that they are playing characters. Most of time they talk -- mainly among themselves, though sometimes they're looking at us -- about life Before, During and After the Revolution. We'll get back to that.

First though, they ask us to engage in "an imaginary group hug." They acknowledge that it may seem silly, but say that it's our last, best hope. An hour-and-a-quarter later it transpires that this ethereal love-in was meant to envelop the whole show. At the beginning they tell us to close our eyes. At the end they say we can open them again. Of course if we follow their instructions we won't see any of the show, so I doubt they mean us to take them literally. In any event, I strongly advise against it. The visual aspect of the production is much its strongest point.

Is there irony here? Maybe not, but there is whimsy, which amounts to a weaker version of the same thing. It permeates the evening. The precise nature of the Revolution is left undisclosed, but it seems mainly to have been one of consciousness. It probably involves the redistribution of wealth, but the trio seem more concerned with its effect on their egos, which it has diminished, and their love lives, which it has enhanced. The language in the early stages of the show is dialectical, or maybe metronomic. Before the Revolution there was X, after the Revolution there is Y, and Y is, always and axiomatically, superior.

Of course, it's possible they've been brainwashed. One thinks of the poor beasts in Animal Farm, willing to put up with anything rather than have Farmer Jones back. Orwellian satire, though, does not seem to be what the show has in mind.

From Vladimir Lenin to Mike Harris, the word "revolution" has acquired so much unsavoury baggage that you'd think people would be wary of using it, even in the theatre, without at least defining their terms. But here it is again, a mantra rather than a program. The most specific the show gets is when it starts taking about the theatre; it's very self-referential. Before the Revolution, the actors muse, there was Clapping and there were Bows. "What" asks one of them "was all that about?" They try going through the motions, to find out what it was like, and they can't continue; it's just too ridiculous.

Now this, apart from being thought-provoking in itself, creates suspense; it starts you wondering how, come the end of the evening, the actors will deal with their own curtain calls. Because they do take them, and the audience does applaud; at least, it did on the first night, and I think we can assume that it will be just as incorrigible throughout the run. The actors stuck to their guns; they didn't prostrate themselves in front of us. They resorted, instead, to one of the oldest cliches of new theatre; they started applauding us.

The first time I ever saw this done -- probably not the first time it ever was done -- was in Peter Brook's production of The Marat-Sade, that play about the lunatics literally taking over the asylum. It conveyed, very powerfully, the actors' contempt for the audience. Since then, of course, it has come to signify something milder: the actors' patronizing of the audience.

That isn't how it's intended, of course, but it's how it always works out, even in the hands (again, literally) of nice peaceful people like the ones doing pppeeeaaaccceee. Because consider this: The relationship between stage and auditorium is a power relationship. While the play lasts, they are in control. They are up there, in the light, doing their thing; we are in the dark, paying respectful attention, even when hardly understanding a thing that's going on -- as is very much the case with this show. (I'm generalizing, of course, from my own reaction, but the vibe I got was that most people were as baffled as I was.) Only at the end do we, the spectators, get to reverse the balance: to assert our authority as customers, sometimes even paying ones, by bestowing or withholding applause. When they start doing it, usurping our privilege, they aren't displaying sweet solidarity; they're trying to hang on to power. And, by the way, applause is not some toadying invention of bourgeois society; it's been going on for centuries.

Some lines in the piece (I am tempted to elongate the spelling, but self-control rules) are evocative, even scary: "The roots of my teeth have turned to liquid" is one that stays with me. The word rhythms are good.

The set (by O'Donnell and Naomi Campbell) is impressive, a huge billowing white drape that must mask a very solid stepped structure, since half-way through all three actors climb up the curtain and perch at its top, in a sort of crow's nest.

Intrepid though this is, it ushers in the most confusing part of the entertainment. The three are hiding from something, and they're still (they say) in a theatre. A caption informs us that is now "during the Revolution." The show, without sense and without warning, breaks its own time frame. Since its initial try-out last year (which I didn't see) the play has apparently made some concessions to conventional narrative, and this could be one of them. But it strikes me as ill-advised. The abstract portions at least have some charm. This bit, which hints that the revolution may not have been as bloodless as all that but which isn't letting on, manages to be both didactic and obscure, which is not an appealing combination.

The actors play together with dedication and what looks like confidence; among other things, they apply a fine sense of shape and variation to a long section in which they take turns proclaiming "I am an idiot," which may be an especially heartfelt form of Revolutionary Self-Criticism. Greg MacArthir is the most winsome of the three but not to excess, Maiko Bae Yamamoto is contemplative but worried, and Ngozi Paul is questioning but tough.

They are, respectively, caucasian, Asian and black, but there doesn't seem to be any special significance in that. The show distinguishes itself from the fiascoes that have so far littered the new season, in that the people on stage seem to have a very good idea of what they're about. What they don't do is communicate that idea to the audience.

Last Thursday I stated, wrongly, that there was no visible tribute to the late Bill Glassco in the lobby of the Tarragon Theatre. The theatre has, in fact, posted a blow-up display of its press release announcing his death. I apologize.

SNOWMAN

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, Toronto

- - -

Greg MacArthur is currently functioning in Toronto as both actor and playwright. He's one third of the cast of pppeeeaaaccceee, (a title I am getting quite tired of typing) but, though theres nothing wrong with that performance, he is shown off to better advantage as author of Snowman. Its an unsatisfying but resoundingly talented piece, the most interesting new play I remember seeing at Buddies in Bad Times, whose new season it opens.

It's set in the far and frozen north, in a small township whose inhabitants seem to be marked by their loneliness, their transience, or both. Here is a guy named Denver and his partner Marjorie; some years ago, after existing on the fringes of petty crime, they pointed their noses toward the north and followed them. This is where they ended up.

Denver survives by renting videos, stolen from his previous employers down south. (You'd think his stock and clientele would by now have have exhausted one another, but he does in fact talk about expanding.) Marjorie doesnt do much of anything; shes drugged-out and depleted.

Their closest friend in town is Jude, a soulfully beautiful young man (Denver reckons he'd be a sensation in town, though here he passes unnoticed) who woke up one morning to find that his parents had walked out on him. Jude first wandered into Denver's store asking to rent some gay porn, of which Denver has a good supply, all of it German. As Jude doesnt have a TV or VCR of his own, Denver lets him use his and Marjories living room. Jude is a good supplier of coke, which, Denver notes, is easier to obtain in these latitudes than feta cheese: much easier.

It's only Denver who really takes to Jude. Marjorie doesn't much like him or, as far as we can make out, anyone else. Jude in turn becomes fixated on Denver. Dialogue scenes between these people are brief and rudimentary; they tell us most of their stories in monologues, which are both the plays greatest strength and its greatest weakness.

Hovering on the edge of the action are a bunch of vaguely threatening Nintendo-hungry teenagers. Theyre vital to the atmosphere and, as it turns out, to the story, but we never actually see them.

There is a fourth player whom the author cunningly holds in reserve, sending her out on the ice comparatively late in the game. This is Kim, a government archeologist, who has arrived from the big city to investigate a discovery of Jude's. He has found a human body, male, perfectly preserved in ice for what may be centuries.

Denver gets really attached to this Snowman, who also seems to take on a symbolic significance for everyone else in the play; he represents something they want or lack or resent. Kim adds to the emotional mix by developing the hots for Denver; indeed, she fancied him, just from his name, even before she met him. She is a past- mistress, however, at keeping an emotional distance.

Monologue seems a fitting mode of expression for all these separated souls, and the ones MacArthur has written vividly evoke both the physical and psychological landscape. In their last-gasp lyricism, the speeches feel very Canadian (and not just because of the climate) but they have a distinctive voice, sawn-off and weather- beaten. Denver's tone is especially compelling; hes an urban animal who is yet quite at home in the tundra, a born exile.

The narrative technique helpfully absolves the director from the necessity of actually staging some very tricky episodes in which frozen human limbs get tossed about, to macabre or farcical effect. But of course this avoidance of whats generally identified as drama becomes a problem. The characters may not be able to connect but we would like to see them try, rather than just hearing about it. The piece comes off as a dramatized novella rather than a play; and, short though it is, it becomes tedious.

David Oiye's production is lucid and sympathetic. David Fraser has designed a glistening set as well as lighting that's both sensitive and sensible. The acting is excellent, with Eric Goulems glowering, stoical Denver keeping the centre firm, and Paul Dunn (another talented actor-playwright, though presently visible in only one of his guises) radiantly quivering as Jude. As Marjorie, drab and dangerous, Philippa Domville effects a pitch-perfect transformation from the brittle, upscale ladies she usually plays; Marjorie is an ice-maiden too, of course, but Domville has found a new battered voice to go with the curlers and the housecoat make a lot of difference. Kim is more recognizably icy. Veronika Hurnik gets both the metropolitan sheen (by local standards, anyway) and the inner chill.

All the characters, in the famous Thoreau phrase, live lives of quiet desperation, and the play shows that just getting out of the rat race is no solution; even just below the Arctic, both life and despair go on. The play extends hope to its characters and then withdraws it, while leaving us in no doubt that they will survive. It isnt the most enlivening conclusion, and the play sputters out. But I have great hopes for the playwright.

robertcushman@lycos.com

Lately," says George Evans, Toronto singer and record producer, the girls seem to have been having all the fun.

Hes introducing a CD compilation that's intended to restore the gender balance while also striking a blow for national pride. It's titled Here Come the Boys, and subtitled A Canadian Crooner Collection. Ambiguity beckons, because Evans liner note goes on to speak of "Canadian male jazz vocalists" -- a triply endangered species in the marketplace. Crooner never appears -- perhaps its assumed to be a synonym. I doubt, though, that's how most people hear it. A "crooner," to most of us, suggests something more sedate, more armchair-comfy and more adhesive to the melody, than a jazz singer, who is assumed to be aggressive and iconoclastic.

But then one remembers Bing Crosby, who would generally be considered a crooner par excellence, could also swing as hard as he wanted whenever he wanted, and probably do so more naturally than any other white man who ever lived.

Evans has collected male vocalists from across the country, singing either standards or new songs in the standard tradition, and if crooning and jazz are adjacent categories, then all these guys seem to be operating at the point where they brush edges, neither excessively stuffy nor excessively far-out. All but one have jazz musicians accompanying them, for the most part excellently, and they sound happy with the arrangement (and the arrangements).

This, as Evans remarks, is hardly the first period in which male singers have been outnumbered by female; he refers to a similar tidal wave of girl singers in "the heyday of the jazz/pop long- playing albums of the 1950s." He might have gone further than that since, at every period of pre-rock pop, the rank-and-file singers have mainly been women. But however good or popular the best ladies have been, the governing figures of each era have been male: Jolson, Crosby, Sinatra. (And it's certainly the case in rock.) Despite the immense success of Diana Krall and -- if she counts -- Norah Jones, and the lesser achievements of Jane Monheit and Stacey Kent, its still arguable its the men who make the running. It's Harry Connick and Michael Feinstein (and maybe now Jamie Cullum) who have exemplified the ways these songs are sung, and inspired imitative schools of singing them. Not that that's much consolation to their less-celebrated brethren.

Its even more discouraging if youre from here. I can think of no male Canadian singer who's made an international dent, no vocal equivalent of Oscar Peterson. To adapt an old line about Broadway: From what Evans tells us, most of the singers here are making a living, but they certainly aren't making a killing. Nor can I identify any Canadian style of jazz-pop; the singers on this disc might just as well be American.

All the tracks are from the vocalists previous solo albums. The oldest on hand, and he sounds suitably elder-statesmanlike, is also the best-known, though his fame doesnt rest on his singing. This is Gene Lees, who has a higher profile as a critic and lyricist, and who naturally sings one of his own songs here, Dreamer, set to one of Antonio Carlos Jobim's fragile, beautiful melodies. Lees writes earnest, pastoral lyrics that are not greatly to my taste -- I call them nature-ramble lyrics -- and I can't recall a single funny line in any of his songs. (His criticism can also be pretty humourless.) His singing, by contrast, is pleasantly conversational, and though he has long lived in California, he is surrounded here by Canadian musicians who confound geography by playing expert Brazilian.

Another of Lees lyrics turns up, presumably by design, as the next track. This is Waltz for Debby (to Evans music), an undeniably sentimental song about a little girl growing up that is guaranteed to melt the heart of any father. It really has to be sung by a man and is done here with quiet authority by Joe Coughlin (from Vancouver), another veteran and probably the most accomplished performer on the CD. He knows exactly how far he can push his voice and the song.

The subdued quality of these performances is typical of the album. Most of the singers are plaintive and nearly all sound polite. Maybe this is a Canadian style (though I've always had my doubts about our national stereotype) though I suspect it has more to do with the current boyish fashion in cabaret singing and even more with the still-potent memory of Chet Baker, who in the 1950s perfected the art of being uninflected. Nobody here takes passivity to the oddly charming lengths Baker did, but the majority transmit that sense of what it takes to be cool; they put a lot of effort into sounding effortless.

One of the best is Adam James (Montreal) who has more edge than most and offers an intelligent, brusque reading of Cole Porter's Get Out of Town, the only time when a familiar song is thoroughly freshened. Neither John Labelle (Montreal) with Ive Grown Accustomed to Her Face nor Pat Lacroix (Toronto) with Young and Foolish quite brings that off, though Lacroix -- who must, from his bio, be neither young nor foolish -- reveals unexpected power when he gets to the end, and Labelle, the most Bakerish of them all, does suggest what Chet might have been like had he ever been inclined to growl.

Tim Tamashiro (Calgary) rounds off the disc with a forthright account, more Nat Cole than Sinatra, of In the Wee Small Hours of the Morning, striking a presumed blow for gay pride by refusing to change any pronouns.

Denzal Sinclaire, one of the more high-profiled men on the roster, does a Lucky Day thats cheerful but no more; the song can hardly help being a throwaway and I suspect sounds better on its original CD, in the company of numbers more challenging to Sinclaire's well-travelled chops (the notes assign him to Toronto and Montreal and Vancouver).

Much the same goes for John Alcorn's (Toronto) Falling in Love with Love, taken from a disc entirely devoted to Rodgers and Hart. On its own it sounds like all-purpose hip lounge lizard, a treatment no better or worse suited to this than to any other song.

The most interesting tracks are those where the material is the least familiar. John Neudorf does Stevie Wonders Creepin, and is hauntin'. Vincent Wolfe applies the regulation soft-sensitive voice to an R&B tune, You Just Don't Know, with surprisingly satisfactory results; he proves one of the best lyric interpreters on hand, even though the lyrics are basic. Ted Hawkins (Toronto), who does have an R&B voice, tackles Who Will the Next Fool Be?, a Charlie Rich song, and turns it most rewardingly in an early-hours nightclub direction. John Gilbert (Montreal) offers You Bring Out the Beast in Me, a song written in the flippantly amorous 1950s style associated with Bobby Troup. It is, as you might guess, an animal-catalogue song. A couplet like youre a pterodactyl/with whom I could be tactile deserves more credit for enterprise than achievement since it doesnt rhyme. ("The urge to merge" does rhyme but is scarcely new.) The pleasantly cynical Meet Me at No Special Place ("and I'll be there at no particular time") could use a harsher delivery from Tory Cassis (Toronto) who, in a gentlemanly way, underplays its wit.

And then there's the highly experienced Kenny Colman, who sounds most like a traditional crooner; hes like Tony Bennett but with less gravel. He alone sings with a big band -- one of the biggest, the London Symphony Orchestra. Johnny Mandel conducts, and the tune is a good one of his own thatId never heard before: I Won't Believe My Eyes, with unexpectedly down-to-earth lyrics by Marilyn and Alan Bergman, who are usually among the archest nature- ramblers. The track comes late on the disc, so the strings are a surprise, and a pleasant one. Colman is impeccable, smooth but not smarmy. And finally (well, not really; it's Track 2) there is George Evans own contribution. This is Lullaby of the Leaves, technically a standard but one not often heard, and a very welcome choice. He has the craggiest voice on the disc (completely belying the roguish pose he strikes in his photo) but also one of the roundest. He makes inventive phrasing choices, and if he throws in some show-off high notes at the end, he has earned the right. Only some rather dated scatting betrays him. And hes done both his peers and his listeners a service by assembling the disc. It's a superior sampler, whose built-in contrasts make it especially good for the car.

robertcushman@lycos.com

All this week we're updating membership in the Academy of the Overrated, the pantheon introduced 25 years ago in Woody Allen's Manhattan.

- - -

Let us be clear. Overrated is not the same thing as Bad. Billie Holiday is overrated. That doesn't mean she wasn't a fine singer. It means that, for reasons that have more to do with politics and biography than with music, she has been accorded excessive reverence by people who would hardly acknowledge the existence of other singers -- Frank Sinatra, Peggy Lee, Rosemary Clooney -- who have sung the same repertoire to equal effect.

With the exception of Randy Newman, every pop and rock act since 1965 has been overrated. As Aaron Wherry pointed out here on Wednesday, there is no way, irrespective of their actual talent, that any of them could have lived up to their hype.

Laurence Olivier and Marlon Brando are overrated, since they were neither as moving nor as funny as some of their contemporaries. And to turn from interpreters to originators: Modern Drama is overrated. I don't mean mere "modern drama," the bread-and-butter new plays that our theatres turn over on a regular basis; that is routinely overrated, or the reverse, according the whims of journalism. We know that. I have in mind the founding fathers, the dramatists who flourished in the last quarter of the 19th century and the first half of the 20th, the ones who were canonized by American theatrical academic Robert Brustein in a 1960s book called The Theatre of Revolt.

Brustein's pantheon consists of Henrik Ibsen, Anton Chekhov, August Strindberg, Luigi Pirandello, Bernard Shaw, Eugene O'Neill, Bertolt Brecht and (a desperate choice, since here overrated does mean bad) Jean Genet. Samuel Beckett didn't make the cut, on the grounds that he just didn't write enough plays. For my purposes, this was just as well, as there is no way Beckett is overrated. You may not like what he did, but it was necessary and he did it perfectly.

Brustein's main criterion for selecting his writers was that they made audiences feel uncomfortable. Or most of them did. Here I want to drag in another American critic, John Simon, who once asked rhetorically "Do you think Ibsen was a nice man? Or Pirandello? Or Strindberg? Or Brecht?" with the clear and correct implication that they were not. He then pointed out that Chekhov, bucking the modernist rules, probably was a nice man. This is reflected in his attitude toward his characters (which is charitable, but not sentimental) and may explain why he is the only one on the list whose plays audiences consistently enjoy. He isn't overrated. Indeed, when you add on his short stories and his work as a doctor, you may conclude that we have yet to do him justice.

Shaw seems to have been a nice man, too. He only gets into Brustein's book on sufferance, treated with deep suspicion for having had the gall to write comedies, and optimistic ones at that. The others -- Strindberg, Pirandello, O'Neill, Brecht -- make excellent clubs for critics to beat their readers (and directors their audiences) over the head. I am not dismissing any of them -- though in Brecht's case it's tempting -- and I am not trying to discourage anyone from reviving their plays. Last year in London, I saw a Pirandello (not about the theatre) that justified the claims that are made for him; Stratford's Long Day's Journey Into Night is deservedly legendary. I would be happy to be further persuaded. But I do think that they, and the vision of theatre they have bequeathed to us, are limited.

Robert Fulford this week outlined a couple of the reasons why critics overrate particular artists. He left out the least flattering to our trade, which is identification. To promote a writer is, vicariously, to share in the glory, or to hope to. This can lead to resentment. John Osborne, it seems, never forgave Kenneth Tynan for the widespread belief that Tynan's review of Look Back in Anger had been crucial to the play's success and hence to Osborne's whole career.

Sometimes identification can go further. F.R. Leavis, a critic once hugely overrated and now the reverse, seems on some level to have believed he actually wrote the novels of his hero, D.H. Lawrence. Certainly, he used Lawrence as a stick with which to beat all novelists except the few whom he could accept into his Great Tradition. Unfortunately, he made these few seem like moralizing bores, which is what, among other things, they are.

The most insufferable of them, by far, was Henry James, parading his exquisite sensibility in never-ending, minutely qualified sentences. The only Great English Novelists who are not overrated are Jane Austen, whose sparkle not even Leavis's approval could quench, and Charles Dickens. Anthony Trollope isn't overrated, partly because he's still recovering from decades of being underrated. It goes without saying that all living novelists are overrated, with the exception of Zadie Smith. And maybe Philip Roth.

Anne Kingston, introducing this series, came up with the complementary category of the Untouchable, meaning unquestionably great. Proust plainly belongs there, even though I've yet to finish Remembrance of Things Past. I can tell from what I have read that it is not overrated. I'm surprised by the inclusion of Freud. It seems to me that people have been tearing him down for ages, to the point where he has become underrated.

That leaves Shakespeare. His reputation has been endangered by the critics whom Harold Bloom calls the School of Resentment, and even more by the unfocused rhapsodies of Bloom himself, which are enough to make anyone resentful. But he remains the greatest field of energy in the English language, maybe in any language. Theatre critics are able to put his reputation to the severest practical test; there are no other authors whose work we could watch so often without going mad. Despite all the praise that has been heaped upon him, he is not overrated. (I suspect he was a nice man, too.)

THE UNEXPECTED MAN

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

- - -

If what we're told about North American tastes is true, then Yasmina Rezas plays are, or ought to be, deeply unfashionable. Experience, though, proves they arent and oughtn't. This French lady writes the kind of plays that used to be described as "civilized": plays about economically comfortable Europeans with mainstream cultural concerns. Despite this handicap, her play Art has been a worldwide success. The Unexpected Man has done less well, which is understandable, but it has done all right, which is deserved.

It's a more challenging piece than Art. It has two characters instead of three, much less action and fewer jokes, though it may have more wit. Where Art was concerned wholly with the foibles of cultural consumers, this play has a creator as half its cast. Hes a novelist, and the plays title is also the name of his latest book. It's also a description of him, at least in his relation to the other character, who is a female admirer of his work and with whom he finds himself alone in a confined space. She knows who he is, but to him she could be anybody. As they wonder whether or how to make contact, we listen to their interior monologues, or -- since they are sharing a compartment on the express from Paris to Frankfurt -- their trains of thought.

He describes himself, right at the start, as an embittered man, ill at ease with the world of things; he makes a fetish of it, though one suspects he would like to be lured out of it. Meanwhile, he is having a good discontented time, complaining to himself about his sleep habits, about his bowels (whatever, he wonders rhetorically, happened to Ex-Lax?), about his daughter, who has committed the unforgivable sin of getting engaged to a man who's inaudible, and about his oldest friend, who has in effect deserted him by taking up with a comparatively young woman. (Youth, it is clear, is the enemy.)

His travelling companion, too, has lost a close male friend -- in her case, to death. He wonders why she, unlike any other woman on a train, isnt reading. She in fact has a copy of his latest in her bag, and is pondering whether she dare bring it out and, if so, when. In his head, hes defensive but curious; in hers, she's flirtatious but scared. In ours, we're fascinated but impatient, wondering whether either will make a move, whether the monologues will ever become dialogue. We may even, if weve travelled on English trains, remember that the alarm system there is called the communication cord. We make silent bets on whether they will, metaphorically, pull it.

Its a slender thread, but it neatly ties together the intellectual, the emotional and the mundane, and -- in Christopher Hampton's more than admirable translation -- it has just enough suspense to hold us. It's surprising, given the authors reputation, that the play hasnt been given a higher-profile Toronto staging. Physically, it demands little; spiritually, it could take more.

Chris Abraham's production, though perfectly intelligent, is economical to a fault. The performances, by a grumbling Les Carlson and a musing Deborah Kipp, are accurate but low key. It should be possible to probe further into these characters' interiors -- into her yearnings and his discontents -- and emerge with more colours.

In London these roles were played by Eileen Atkins and Michael Gambon, two of the best, and though it's considered bad critical form to suggest alternative casting for a given production, it's hard here not to start thinking of possible Canadian equivalents. (Eric Peterson and Seana McKenna were the two who tugged hardest at my imagination.) But this is still the most recommendable play in Toronto, and I recommend it.
