THE RAT PACK: LIVE FROM LAS VEGAS

Canon Theatre, Toronto

- - -

A New York taxi driver once told me of a trip to Las Vegas during which he had seen Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin and Sammy Davis Jr. doing their joint nightclub act. He had dropped a hundred bucks for the privilege, which -- this was 1967 -- was very serious money indeed. "But," he said, "for three celebrities like that, you don't mind paying it."

I probably wouldn't have minded myself, given the cash and the opportunity. All the same, I found my cabbie's choice of words perturbing even then, emphasizing as it did the fame of the performers rather than their talents. At least, though, the celebrities he was getting were the real things. The Rat Pack: Live from Las Vegas, which is the latest in the line of necrophiliac tribute shows, asks our indulgence for a trio of imitators. The actors make no attempt to reinterpret either the people or the material; they merely try, with varying degrees of success, to reproduce them. The show started its life a few years ago at an ungainly shopping-precinct theatre in the far western end -- as opposed to the central West End -- of London, and it is an appropriately suburban entertainment, karaoke done for money.

In theory, it should offer more dramatic interest than most of its kind. It has three subjects, so there is the possibility that we will see them interact. That, after all, was the attraction that drew Vegas patrons in the '60s. The premise is that we are watching one of those evening get-togethers at the Sands Hotel. But sitting sober in a theatre is not like sitting sauced in a club; watching an acted show that's been scripted and rehearsed is not like rubbernecking at an all-star party that traded on its freewheelingness and probably did contain a fair quantity of genuine ad libs.

There is also the question of whether the stars are being celebrated for the right reasons. We are being asked to admire all three of them here not for their vocal or comedic skills but for their status as rich, hard-drinking, skirt-chasers: swingers whose connection to musical swing is purely coincidental. Compared to what they actually had to offer, it's an image that's at best irrelevant and at worst rather repugnant.

This show's sense of period, as of everything else, is coarse- grained. The big-band orchestrations sound authentic and are great to hear, but the set is anachronistic, and so are many of the songs. In the interests of delivering as many greatest hits as possible, the evening is filled out with numbers that entered these guys' repertoires decades later: The Candy Man, Mr. Bojangles, New York, New York and Mack the Knife, on the last of which the singer, Stephen Triffitt, seems to have Sinatra's version confused with Bobby Darin's.

That, though, comes late. At first glance Triffitt, an English performer who has made a career out of Sinatra imitation, seems to have his man down cold. He has the insolently cool profile, the cock of the head, the subtly swaying arm, the hooded eyes that close to focus a note or a mood, the clinching rhythmic foot. He also, to a most unusual degree, has the metallic texture of the voice (though not its compensating warmth) and a good copyist's idea of the phrasing.

However, by the second line of the first song, the cracks show. Copying isn't enough; indeed it's antithetical to what the real Frank was about. He essays two Sinatra stereotypes: the imperious Lothario (Luck Be a Lady, The Lady Is a Tramp -- would FS ever have dealt two Ladies back to back?) and the saloon sufferer (Angel Eyes, One for My Baby), but nothing in between. Nor does he have much authority in comic banter -- though in this he may be uncomfortably close to the real thing. Sinatra could be a great emcee, but as an interacting comedian he was a bully.

Mark Adams, when singing, sounds exactly like Dean Martin. This may be no great trick; Dino's voice is one of those anyone can do, like Jolson's and Durante's. Nor do Adams' appearance and manner have much of Martin's endearing cragginess; his face indeed seems to be cut from the same unwrinkled cloth as his shiny serge suit. But he does capture excellently Martin's pivotal position as both the funniest and, in his way, the most courteous of the group; the booze jokes ("the difference between a drunk and an alcoholic is a drunk doesn't have to go to the meetings") still work.

Sammy Davis, master impressionist though he was, could never manage to sound like Sinatra. I offer this consideration as balm to Rashad Naylor, who can't sound like Davis, and is too tall to look like him, either. His singing starts out wrong, with That Old Black Magic done at about a third of the frantic Sammy tempo, and gets worse. His dancing is better, but he doesn't get to do much of it. The supposed dynamo of the act never sparks, and stops the show from working even on its own constricted terms. Three mature and beefy chorines, performing timelessly awful choreography, are another handicap.

Even less relevant is the finale. Triffitt sings My Way, which, apart from being another anachronism and the worst song ever written ("without exemption," says a lyricist friend of mine, without compunction), gives the lie to the rest of the evening. We thought it was about three men and now it turns out to be about only one. There follows what seems an endless series of encores. Well, it sounded like some of the audience wanted them. In London, the show has been running for two years in the real West End. That, whether you judge the event as music or as theatre, is a truly depressing thought.

MATT AND BEN

Poor Alex Theatre, Toronto

- - -

This is a sweet surprise. Matt and Ben is a one-act fantasia about how two struggling young actors surnamed Damon and Affleck might just possibly have come to write an Oscar-winning movie script called Good Will Hunting that also, by some strange coincidence, provided plum roles for them both.

The play is itself a funhouse reflection of the story it tells. It was created by two American actresses, Mindy Kaling and Brenda Withers, who played it themselves at the New York International Fringe Festival and then did it again, very successfully, off- Broadway. The New York director, David Warren, has now re-mounted it in Toronto for macIDeas, the indie-commercial concern that wisely brought us This Is Our Youth, then unwisely brought it back. Two local ladies, Hilary Doyle and Jane Spence, now play the two guys, and play them very well. In fact text, staging and performance reach a collective level of accomplishment and delight that leaves every one of the season's previous openings in the dust.

The way the play tells it, the script for their breakthrough film fell literally into its authors' laps. There they were in Ben's Boston apartment (which, in Michael Gianfrancesco's colourful cock- eyed design, bears a suspicious resemblance to a playroom), working away on a screenplay based on The Catcher in the Rye. Their working methods consist of Matt's reading the book's dialogue aloud and Ben's transcribing it word-for-word on his much-prized computer. Matt expresses some doubts about this, on the lines of "If this is so easy, why hasn't anyone done it before?" But Ben isn't having any.

Then suddenly, down from the sky by way of the ceiling, there appears a typescript bearing the title Good Will Hunting with their own two names attached as authors -- Matt the thoughtful achiever being billed, in defiance of the alphabet, above Ben the blowhard slacker. It seems too good to be true. It also seems as if the play is trying to deny the real-life Damon and Affleck any credit for the work that made them; but, by a twist that it would be unfair to reveal (and that you wouldn't believe if I did, but that makes perfect sense at the time), it manages to have things both ways. Kaling and Withers make fun of Matt and Ben, but they don't actually denigrate them.

You could hardly call the play a satire of the celebrity culture, if only because it's quite explicitly part of that culture itself; I mean, the authors wouldn't be wasting their time writing about a couple of losers, right? Nor is it fair, though it seems popular, to denigrate the piece as an extended Saturday Night Live piece, since it is a) coherent and b) funny. It's a riff based on the assumed resemblances between the two men and the roles they played in the movie, though the play dramatizes this without ever becoming as maudlin or repetitious as the film. Its Matt is no charismatic genius, but he is energetic and ambitious. Its Ben is a goof, but one who has his own agenda and is capable of being hurt.

The play, like every crosstalk comedy written after 1955, has echoes of Waiting for Godot, and there's at least an acknowledgment, in the suggestion that the characters first met when getting up Vladimir and Estragon as a high-school drama exercise. (Matt, typically earnest, asks Ben if he can do a French accent. Ben offers to learn one from his brother Casey, who took French for a year.) It's very acute, and very entertaining, about the jealousies and the frayed but enduring loyalties between two young men who bonded as kids and have come to take their relationship for granted. It's done as cartoon; one of the best sequences shows us the teenage Ben creatively disrupting his buddy's painfully serious rendition of Bridge over Troubled Water. But that doesn't make it any less truthful.

The crucial element in the style is, of course, having women play the roles. Doyle, whose background is in revue, and Spence, whose background is in Shakespeare, have mapped out a perfectly proportioned middle ground that accommodates the best of both. Indeed you might say they pass on into one another's territory. Doyle's fair-haired Matt is the more detailed and inward performance, Spence's bumptious brunette Ben the more extrovert, outsize in enthusiasm, outsize in hurt, though never ballooned out of proportion. (I have a sneaking and possibly unreasonable respect for Affleck as an actor, based on the fact that I first saw him in Shakespeare in Love, in which he sported not only an excellent English accent -- presumably not learned from Casey -- but a real sense of style.)

Each of the actresses gets to play one other famous figure, while her principal character is offstage somewhere, either on an errand of mercy or having a huff. Spence appears as Gwyneth Paltrow, urging Matt to follow her own example and go for it, whatever it is. The funny thing is, you don't at this point think of Spence as a woman playing a woman; you think of her as a woman playing a man playing a woman. But then the last thing I saw her in was As You Like It.

Doyle's apparition is a terminally crotchety JD Salinger, apprising Ben of the extreme improbability of he or anyone else getting the rights to Catcher or to anything else in its author's legendarily slender oeuvre. This, I suppose, is where Ben grows up. "No wonder no one's ever done it before," he muses, or words to that effect. I found myself thinking what a blessing it is that nobody has ever been allowed to turn the book into a musical (I bet they've asked), since it would undoubtedly come out as You're a Good Man, Holden Caulfield.

Whether they're playing male or female, singly or together, the performers' timing is of exemplary crispness, as is the production as a whole. Its ending is surprisingly touching, and it only takes 70 minutes to get there.

CUL-DE-SAC

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre

- - -

Daniel MacIvor is at the peak of his performing form in Cul-de- Sac. It's a solo show that he also wrote and which is directed, very well, by his old colleague Daniel Brooks. MacIvor, without ever leaving the stage or changing a costume, plays some half-dozen roles, but his pivotal role is that of Leonard, a gay man who lives at the end of a dead-end street. (That is a non-judgmental statement of fact. Leonard does at one point toy with the idea of it being a metaphor, but he wisely and rapidly discards it. Unkind critics may end up having similar thoughts about the title, but this one is inclined to stifle them. More or less.) Some of his neighbours would like to exchange the dead-end designation for the one in the play's title, which they think more seemly, but Leonard, who knows what the French actually means, has his doubts about that.

Leonard is a magnificent creation, a gushing fountain of witty self-deprecation, unable to get to the end of a sentence without restarting or qualifying it three times. He's a character built out of speech rhythms. (These, he points out, are not Australian, even if they sometimes sound it, thereby echoing in reverse a line of the late Peter Allen's: "For those of you who are wondering, is he or isn't he? Yes, I am Australian.") He also worries about whether his life would have been different in the unlikely event he got into hockey and about his inability to sing. Leonard's relationship recently ended, and his search for consolation proves fatal. He is, even when we meet him, dead, and the play tells us, among other things, how this happened.

It begins with a terrifying onslaught of sound and light that suggests the mother of all thunderstorms, but which signifies the approach of death. The sound makes its way right down the street and back up again. The technical effects in Brooks's production are stupendous; Richard Feren designed the sound and Kimberly Purtell the lighting, which includes an amazing red wash that encircles Leonard at crucial moments, lending an especially sinister shade to his fingernails.

With all this going on around him, I felt I could happily have listened to Leonard all night. Maybe this was an overenthusiastic response -- anyway there turned out to be no chance to put it to the test. Though Leonard keeps returning as our narrator and guide, the focus shifts to his neighbours, testifying (to the audience? the police? God?) as to how they felt about him in life, and how they feel about him now he's gone. They also air several of their own hang-ups. Unfortunately they have little interesting to say about the protagonist, and their author has little interesting to say about them. (Leonard's own remarks about them are almost unfailingly amusing, but that doesn't amount to dramatization.)

The performance level, too, slips from brilliant to merely clever. A married couple, needling one another about their sex life or the lack of it, inspire a back-and-forth routine of vocal quick- changes; it's like watching a Ronnie Burkett show without the puppets -- and also without the humanity.

Some of the other locals, thankfully, are not at home, but we do get to meet: a cranky veterinarian, forced by the pressures of retirement to get belligerent about his lawn; an opera queen whose enthusiasms run to nudism and Gilbert and Sullivan (The Pirates of Penzance is a leitmotif in the play, though I don't think the reasons go beyond playfulness); and, briefly, a lawyer.

There is also the lawyer's teenage daughter who set out to write a novel but, in every sense, lost it. She refers to stuffy and unsympathetic adults -- which in her experience seems to mean all adults except Leonard -- as "knobs." She is much the most engaging of the bunch; all the same , we've been spoiled in recent years for piquant studies of female adolescence, and this one comes in a distant third to I, Claudia and Girl in a Goldfish Bowl.

The group portrait amounts to no more than another chorus of "all the lonely people," and there's no particular irony or power when none of them realize the full horror of what happened to Leonard in the third hour of his last morning, that none of them, in fact, can put a name to the noise.

We discover it, and the realization entails a second astonishing performance from MacIvor, as physically tight as the first is endearingly floppy. The son et lumiere complement him by going into scary overdrive. But that's all. MacIvor is extravagantly talented, but all that talent is employed to such little effect. Correct that: His work is usually plenty effective, and never more than here. Say instead that it's effective to so little point. As the presentation of one man's fate, Cul-de-Sac is self-sufficiently powerful. What surrounds it is padding.

OMNIUM GATHERUM

Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

- - -

Dinner parties are among the few things in the world harder to arrange than plays, since for parties you don't usually get to rehearse. So hats should be off to the director and cast of Omnium Gatherum, who have had to cope with both challenges at once.

Here the party actually is the play; what's more, the normal hazards of serving and eating are accentuated by the fact that, for most of the performance, the dinner table is slowly revolving. There is an obvious technical reason for this; it means all seven actors (there is an eighth, but he's a late arrival) get equal time for acting with their backs to us. But we may also be reminded of the restaurants with spectacular views that you find near the tops of tall buildings: places like Windows on the World at the World Trade Center. Maybe I'm imagining the allusion but, since Omnium Gatherum is concerned with matters arising from Sept. 11, it seems apposite.

And there I just about run out of compliments. The play is a collaboration between two American writers, Theresa Rebeck and Alexandra Gersten-Vassilaros, who in the wake of the attacks found themselves incensed by the unmediated screaming of partisan opinions that passed for debate on TV and in print. Their reaction is understandable. Unfortunately, all they've done in their play is to reproduce the phenomenon they're deploring. Their characters are mouthpieces shouting past one another.

The party-thrower is Suzie, who runs a billion-dollar gracious- living business and is thus reminiscent of Martha Stewart, though much sillier. Her guests include an English intellectual journalist, neo-conservative but anti-Israeli and a very big drinker, who is bound to stir thoughts of Christopher Hitchens; a courtly Arab scholar who suggests a somewhat idealized Edward Said; and a bellicose novelist who everybody tells me is Tom Clancy.

There are others less easily tagged: a black woman who is apparently a minister, and a feminist whom the novelist thinks, wrongly, must be a lesbian. The gourmet meal, each of whose courses gets lovingly described, is wasted on her, since she's both a vegan and allergic to walnuts. They all, even Suzie, are writers of some kind; the only common ground they have is their hatred of the book reviews in The New York Times. Otherwise, they spend the night at one another's throats, disagreeing about literally everything. As the last topic clicks into place (the environment, I think), Suzie gives an approving gurgle. This is the kind of stimulating conversation she was hoping for.

I doubt that any sane hostess would knowingly assemble so rudely ill-assorted a bunch, and I also doubt that they would proceed in such an ordered fashion from one subject to the next. Real-life conversations go off at tangents. But then this, we learn, is no real-life party. We only learn it, though, very late in the show, and the revelation involves the authors in breaking what had seemed to be their own rules. David Storch's production has tried earlier to suggest that all is not what it seems, with flashing lights and loud noises and gusts of smoke, but it isn't enough to dispel the pervading air of ham-handed naturalism.

The seventh diner is at first conspicuously silent. He turns out to be a firefighter who was one of the rescuers at the twin towers. Suzie, roguishly donning a burqa, ushers in a surprise guest whom she announces as a real-live Arab terrorist and who plays that role to the hilt. Some physical violence gets mixed in with the verbal.

But if this is meant to be a party at the end of the world, or even if it isn't, then much of what we've heard is bewilderingly trivial. What is the point of the vegan lady's disquisition on her love life? Why does the black lady sing? Why does the Hitchens chap proclaim not just that humanity has been at war for all of its history (indisputable), but that peace is undesirable -- a position I cannot imagine even the contrarian Hitch espousing? These characters are made of straw. And is all the gourmandizing meant to make us feel guilty? The gap between rich and poor is a huge issue but, given that it exists, it's of very minor interest what specific luxuries the lucky ones choose to indulge in.

To be fair, the constant emphasis on food gives the play some metaphorical, if not intellectual, coherence. And to be even fairer, it is never actually boring; the state of the world takes care of that.

There are two admirable speeches for the Arabist. Both are finely delivered by Nigel Shawn Williams, an actor who is moving into maturity at full gallop. Fiona Reid, playing Suzie, never once slips outside her character; she turns crassness into poetry. It seems, all the same, a waste of her talents. Brenda Robins as the feminist acts well but with an unsuitable brittleness. Sam Kalilieh is vivid as the terrorist, Andrea Scott largely unnoticeable as the minister, and Ashley Wright powerfully quiet as the fireman -- though when he finally gets a big speech, one obviously intended to stop us in our tracks, it turns out to be a routine recap of familiar horrors. The crudest figures are the Englishman and the novelist; at least the performances (by James Macdonald and Hardee T. Lineham) make them seem. The tableware glistens becomingly.

Toward the end Suzie, proudly surveying her convocation, invokes the play's own awful title; but the irony, if that's what it is, rebounds on the authors. They have no apparent reason for bringing these people together other than as a means of paying lip service to a popular fallacy, i.e. that it is their bounden duty to write about their country's trauma. Unless they have something individual to say about it, it isn't. Their conclusion here, as unexceptionable as uncontroversial, is the one reached years ago, more wittily and succinctly, in the song of The Reluctant Cannibal: Eating people is wrong.

HAUNTED MASTERS

Spadina Museum,

Toronto

- - -

As a treat (I wouldn't call it a trick) for the Halloween season, a new company billed as The Troubled Souls Co-op has taken over the top floor of Spadina House, next door to Casa Loma, and mounted a quadruple bill of phantasmal playlets. The title Haunted Masters derives from the fact that each segment is based on a short story by a celebrated writer. This is a touring production, in the sense that the audience goes walkabout among different rooms, depending on which chamber is deemed most conducive to scaring the life out of us with the material at hand.

The plundered scribes are, in order of appearance, Henry James, D.H. Lawrence, Edith Wharton and Charles Dickens. Not having read any of the tales in question, I cannot judge how faithful the dramatist, Gene Franklin Smith, has been to his originals. From the fact that he has set the Dickens episode in 1952, some 80 years after its authors death, I deduce that he is not above taking certain liberties. At any rate, each of these pieces stands dramatically on its own feet. None of them plays like an adaptation. Each moves fluently from scene to scene within its confined space.

The James is the subtlest, and also the most fully realized. In its authors peculiarly uptight Anglophile New York, a man tactlessly asks his former betrothed to act as his go-between with another woman. Both incipient partners have a fascination with death, which the spurned one balefully exploits. Somehow, the intended couple never get to meet; every date is broken, and the relationship dies of attrition, as do both its constituent parts.

Lawrence's The Border Line is a more literal ghost story, at least as done here. A young man named Alan marches off to war (the First World one) and is killed. Katherine, his enthusiastically pawed beloved, takes up with Alan's old chum Philip, whom the late hero has always despised as being "on the wrong side of the border." Katherine is German, and after the war she drags him off to the fatherland where she, her sister and Alans ghost treat him with the charming contempt reserved in Lawrences fiction for men who don't measure up to their creator's exacting standards of ramrod virility.

Il Canile is a Wharton story, re-titled and also (Ive looked it up) re-located. It now takes place in a Renaissance Italian world in which noblemen entrap unfaithful wives and their suspected lovers and have them stabbed, garrotted or cast into dungeons. That seems to be the game of the husband in this play, but hes foiled by his wife and her dangerous pet dogs. Not that that lets her off any hooks; She finds herself on trial for witchcraft and murder, with the hounds cited as her familiars. The transposed setting has inspired some heavy-handed stylization, with everyone in masks except the heroine; even she spends much of the time heavily veiled.

The last play is the most cheerfully ghoulish. The Bride's Chamber (Dickens called it The Ghost Chamber) finds a young British couple with an exorcism to arrange spending a night in a room that 100 years earlier was the site of dreadful deeds. A Victorian miser who had arranged his wife's demise appears to plead for absolution. His auditors seem unwilling to indulge him. They presumably are Smiths invention, tossed together with a ghostly host (or ghostly guest -- Im not sure who has the property rights here) who is authentic Dickens.

Patrick Conner's direction is weak on period style but strong on murky atmospherics; the final piece is positively Grand Guignol. It suffers from having no role for Soo Garay, who is the most striking of the four performers, whether as Jamesian vampire or Lawrentian vamp; the Wharton, in which she has to appear faceless, bent and croaking as the entire Venetian judicial system rolled into one, defeats her.

Jaclyn Francis, pallid in the first exhibit and understandably oppressed in the third, is lively in the other two, especially when acting vindictive. Stephen Sparks, absent in Part One and neutral in Two and Three, gets an enjoyable outing as the guilty spectre in the last. Craig Stanghetta seems overtaxed by the demands made on him, and especially by the cockney accent that he seems to think is the voice of 20th-century England.

The author presides over the evening, ushering us upstairs into the performing space and jauntily informing us that the house itself is haunted. I saw no sign of it myself but I emerged from the evening pleasantly spooked.

VIGIL

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

- - -

You have been summoned from another town to the apartment of your aunt, who has sent you a letter informing you that she is mortally ill. She is your only living relative. You enter the room and, naturally, you ask the woman lying in bed in front of you the same question that would rise to the lips of anybody in your situation. You ask her when she is going to die. You expect her, obviously, to hurry up about it.

That is the first scene of Vigil, a startling two-character play by Morris Panych first staged in 1995 and now revived under its author's direction. The man is called Kemp and the woman Grace, though we owe this information to the program rather than to the dialogue, in which neither name is ever mentioned. There are good reasons for this: Kemp, who works in a bank, is a buttoned-tight middle-aged man, not the type to get on first-name terms with anyone; while Grace utters, in the course of the play, hardly any words at all.

That first line of Kemps, as hilarious as it is abrupt, is followed by a blackout. The play proceeds through a series of such scenes -- some of them very short, a couple silent -- during which, offstage, the seasons pass. Kemp, who had envisioned acting the angel of mercy for two days tops, finds himself stuck with the role for the best part, if thats the right phrase, of a year. He cooks Grace innumerable butterscotch puddings and takes her (unseen by us, but he mentions it) to the bathroom.

She, meanwhile, eats, knits (a lot) and looks surprised, as well she might. Kemp's remarks about the desirability of her early demise never let up; in fact, they become more insistent. He even goes to the lengths of rigging up a suicide machine for her, a Heath Robinson contraption that, depending on which string she pulls or button she pushes, can either electrocute her or knock her on the head. (It also incorporates a noose, though Kemp doesn't dignify this with an explanation.) Grace seems intrigued.

This is, of course, a one-joke situation. But there are several mitigating circumstances. One is that many (though not all) of the jokes restatements are very funny. Another is that this is one of those rare, liberating plays that actually breaks a taboo. Kemp gives voice to the silent thoughts that hover around many death- beds. And he has to do it more than once, or we wouldnt believe that he meant it.

In some respects, Panych lets us off easily. It isn't, after all, Kemp's mother lying there. And it isnt as if he was that close to his aunt. He saw her, we discover, just once during his extremely miserable childhood, and never forgave her for not coming back.

His parents, meanwhile, never forgave him for not being a girl. He claims, surprisingly, that they tried to turn him into a homosexual and, even more surprisingly, that they failed. Kemp is asexual and proud of it, though for somebody whos never experienced physical contact he pronounces on it with suspicious authority.

(Maybe he should have been a priest; at one point he says, "not being a Catholic, I didn't know how misery and self-loathing can be a religion." He sounds a bit jealous.)

He is also an arch-Scrooge, making bilious pronouncements on Halloween and Christmas as he peers out through one barely opened window. He resembles, in this position, Clov in Samuel Beckett's Endgame, reporting back to his blind and chairbound master on the desperate state of the outside world. And yes, this is, among other things, a Beckettian double act, as what double act is not? Kemp also looks forward, if thats the right phrase, to the protagonist of Panychs own Earshot, who tried to shut out the world with earplugs. Panych writes great misanthropes.

The one joke, to sum up, is on Kemp himself, and he knows it; he's the one in love with death. It's just that he wants Grace to be the one to propose. She, in her mind at least, is rather spry.

Then, in the second act, theres a revelation that explodes nearly everything. The ramifications even allow for something approaching a hopeful ending, one thats brought off without either sanctimony or sentimentality. The writing throughout is heady, made of crisp, weighted lines that float.

Panych's staging is matchingly confident, as is Ken MacDonald's crafty, crooked setting, which suggests a Canadian Chagall. The actors are two of the best, though they are not equally well cast.

Martha Henry, her mouth a perpetual O, is wondrous as Grace, contemplating the intruder as if he were an alien species, which in part he is. Her expressions, witty and wistful enough at the time, seem doubly so with benefit of hindsight.

Brent Carvers Kemp is technically impossible to fault (though on the third night, when I saw the show, he had some edgy patches) but also hard to believe. This is the first time I have seen Carver play a role that is other than life-affirming; even his Tartuffe relished life for himself, at whatever expense to others. Hes at his best here when Kemp, against all the odds, develops a twinkle, packing his suitcase and talking hopefully of travels with his aunt. This is his journey's end, and a touching one.

The earlier stages have twinkled as well, but less convincingly; Kemp's negativity can be funny, but it emerges here as whimsical rather than desperate. It's not that Carver avoids the darkness; he is obviously making a serious effort to explore it. We know from the past that he can be as fine in tragedy as in comedy, but black farce -- the grubby ground between the two -- seems at the moment to be foreign to him.

Color Photo: Lucas Oleniuk, CanStage / How long has this been going on? Martha Henry as Grace and Brent Carver as Kemp in Vigil.

robertcushman@lycos.com

The golden age of the American musical was the 1920s, when people had money to spend and no television or talking pictures or long- playing records to spend it on, when there were 50 shows running in New York at any given time, and when Florenz Ziegfeld, the master showman, was exciting the senses with his Follies and taking a flyer at narrative art with Show Boat.

The golden age of the American musical was the 1930s, when the Depression sent scores of the brightest talents out to Hollywood but also when those who remained, presumably feeling that they had nothing to lose, did some of their best work, and when the great songwriters -- Cole Porter, Rodgers and Hart, the Gershwins -- were at the height of their powers.

The golden age of the American musical was the 1940s and 1950s, when the era of great songs gave way to the era of great shows, with enough overlap to keep everybody happy; the time when Oklahoma! ushered in a long line of musicals with stories that made dramatic sense and numbers that were there to help tell them; the period that produced the dozen or so shows that constitute the Broadway musical repertoire.

Obviously, the above statements cancel one another out. Each, though, has something to be said for it, and last week they were all advanced with equal earnestness by Julie Andrews, in her capacity as narrator of the six-part series Broadway: The American Musical (PBS, and available on DVD).

Of course, the contradictions werent her fault; she was reading somebody elses script, instructing us in the basics of Broadway history as if she were running the little von Trapps through their scales. The cheerleading tone was preserved even into the series' last instalment, though if the Cameron Mackintosh/Andrew Lloyd Webber/Walt Disney musicals were presented to us as any kind of golden age, it was as a golden age of marketing.

The choice of Andrews as front woman for the American musical has been criticized on the grounds that she is and sounds anything but American. But the series offered us such a tourist's view of the musical that it seemed appropriate to have a brisk foreigner as guide. Or would you rather have had Carol Channing showing you around?

Nobody, given the amount of ground it had to cover and the amorphous audience it was addressing, can have expected this series to be anything but superficial. In the six hours, I counted just one provocative comment: Stephen Sondheims observation that West Side Story, despite its dead bodies, has a happy ending. But, accepting the limitations, they did a good job. They zeroed in on a selection of representative shows, and tried to relate each in its artistic and historical context. Newsreel and performance footage came movingly together in the treatment of On the Town, for example, a wartime show about sailors on leave grabbing 24 hours of happiness, watched by an audience for whom every goodbye might prove final.

Illustrative scenes came from all over, mostly from whatever might have strayed onto television. This often meant The Ed Sullivan Show (including, amusingly, the mild spoof on Sullivan himself in Bye Bye Birdie). A clip from the original Guys and Dolls revealed to me why Sam Levene is regarded by those who saw him as the irreplaceable Nathan Detroit. William Tabbert, standing at a piano singing Carefully Taught from South Pacific, flanked by Rodgers and Hammerstein themselves, showed how angry that song is. I realized for the first time how right Alfred Drake, with his Shakespearean sound, must have been for the cowboy hero of Oklahoma! (The 40s and '50s were the golden age; certainly the most confident one.)

When they showed movie clips they were refreshingly honest about it, and they generally stuck to films involving the stage performers, many of whom -- had anyone thought of recreating numbers in the TV studio? -- are now seriously unavailable.

That we never saw or heard a song complete was, given the program's documentary rhythm, forgivable. Numbers done full-length, with nobody but Sondheim or Hal Prince allowed to comment on them, would be another show, and one Id like to see; as I would a history of Broadway seen through the drawings of Al Hirschfeld, present here purely, and less interestingly, as Grand Old Man.

I would have liked more about performers generally; they started off beautifully with Bert Williams, Ziegfelds black star and plainly one of the great comic artists, and with Ethel Waters, but then lost interest. I would have liked more cross-referencing -- people talking about shows they weren't in. The series ran out of steam in the '80s, which -- considering most of the shows it was talking about -- was no coincidence.

THE ART OF ROMANCE

Tony Bennett (Columbia)

- - -

I didnt go to Tony Bennett's recent concert at Roy Thomson Hall because my previous visits had suggested that he wasn't varying his repertoire much, a feeling that reviews of his current tour had done nothing to dispel. On record, though, he continues to explore new songs -- new to him, anyway -- and even at 78, to refine his singing style. He is one singer whom age becomes; the husk in his voice is still some way short of becoming a croak and he sounds, at his best, generously thoughtful.

His new CD, The Art of Romance, plays to his strengths as a balladeer, with one excursion -- The Best Man, a Nat King Cole hit from the 40s -- into the ruefully comic. Bennett has probably explored the American songbook more thoroughly than any big-name vocalist short of Ella Fitzgerald, though unlike Ella he has mainly steered clear of composer collections. He hasnt yet reached the all- passion-spent philosopher stage, and chances are he never will; he still sounds emotionally in the thick of things.

Sometimes too much so; Harold Arlen's Don't Like Goodbyes, one of his more recondite selections, is a theatre song that exists in two variants, to be sung either by a mature character or a young one; Bennett opts for the young version, and confuses the matter still more with a reckless choice of pronouns. The best are two old warhorses that he refreshes simply by taking them gently and intently through their paces: I Remember You and the finest Gone with the Wind I have ever heard.

Over-dramatization remains his besetting sin; he kills the ambiguities of Stephen Sondheim's Being Alive by talking, sometimes shouting, its key lines. He also goes in far too often for self- deprecating chuckles. Johnny Mandel, last of the classic arrangers, supplies rich charts and is composer of three of the tunes: Little Did I Dream, which has a sub-par Dave Frishberg lyric; Where Do You Start, a short-winded song about divorce that Bennett almost transforms; and Close Enough for Love, which is quietly, perfectly done.

JULIET (AND ROMEO)

Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People

- - -

Gender reversal has been going on in Shakespearean stagings for a good long time -- about 400 years, in fact -- but title reversal is a new one on me. The avowed aim of Guillermo Verdecchia, director of Juliet (and Romeo), is to tell the old story from its heroine's point of view, or at least to put her at its centre. He succeeds, more or less, with the invaluable assistance of several people, including William Shakespeare.

It was Shakespeare, after all, who kept Romeo off-stage during the crucial fourth of Romeo and Juliet's five acts, leaving it to the leading actress to carry the most exciting part of the action while the leading actor sulks. Juliet defies her parents, drinks the potion and gets entombed alive while Romeo is cooling his heels in banishment. It's no wonder that, in most productions, she has been the star. One sometimes wonders how Romeo came to be such a romantic talisman outside the theatre, when inside it he is so often, though not quite always, the second banana. Third, if he's up against a good Mercutio.

Verdecchia's truncated eight-actor version does its best to de- emphasize the hero even further, for example, by transposing the text so that we get our first glimpse of her before encountering him. For the earlier parts of the play, Ieva Lucs' Juliet repays the compliment, falling spiritedly and touchingly in love. One of the show's best ideas is to have the couple speak much of their initial duet in unison, bonding before our eyes. The balcony scene is fun, too; the production is good at mapping out relationships, even if it's decreased their number. In the later, more testing sections, however, Lucs tends to summarize her emotions rather than act them. She arrives at the end of a process without taking us through the steps.

An actor playing Romeo has a tough enough time, even without having his name pushed into parentheses as if he were some kind of afterthought. Toby Malone is stocky and well-intentioned, and speaks with a broad Australian accent that seems designed to test the limits of multiculturalism. It serves him best in the scenes with his male friends, though the production, intent on letting us see him as something that happened to Juliet, has cut the best of these. Chances are it would cut his fight scenes, too, if they weren't so inconveniently vital to the plot.

In fact, the fights are here taken very seriously, as you may judge from the program, which lists a Fight Director, Simon Fon; then lists him again, as Designer and Builder of Weapons; and also throws in an Assistant Fight Director. The specially designed weapons are mainly knives, and the combats are tense and very nasty. Even with such limited manpower, the production manages to convey more of what is actually happening in the various brawls than do some that are filled with bodies. Everyone knows that in the opening scene the servants bite their thumbs at one another as a sign of contempt. This is the first time I have seen Tybalt repeat the gesture in order to goad Mercutio, and it makes a lucid prelude to their duel.

Mercutio is excellently played by Benjamin Clost, who jokes the Queen Mab speech without guying it; and his pal Benvolio is reasonably played by Karim Morgan as an earnest peacemaker who survives into the second half by appropriating lines that customarily belong to Romeo's servant.

A more noticeable casualty of the reduced casting is Juliet's mother. Peter Smith as Capulet has to speak for both mother and father. He handles his new single-parent duties most interestingly, presenting a man who loves his daughter and would like to understand her but who has no gift for it and so falls, through frustration and a short patriarchal fuse, into tyranny. When the Nurse tries to intercede for her charge, he strikes her. This should supply a straight line into the Nurse's own frightened betrayal, but Rae Ellen Bodie, having handled her moment of protest rather well, fails to make the connection.

Juliet's defiance of her dad seems to be, if not on the production's mind, then on the publicity's. It describes the play as "a cautionary tale" involving "disobedience of parental authority," thereby aligning itself with an old and, I thought, discredited critical tradition that condemned the lovers by referring back to Elizabethan handbooks on family values. If you can find me a Shakespearean heroine who disobeys her father and doesn't have the play on her side, I'll buy you a drink. The only obedient girl in the canon is Ophelia, and look what happened to her.

In this play, the young show up the old, and nothing in this young people's production contradicts that. Its sense of period is rather puzzling. It has an Italianate setting, complete with steep perspective and checkered floor, fit to induce nostalgic sighs in anyone who remembers 1950s picture-book Shakespeare; the costumes, similarly, are off-the-peg Renaissance. However, the torches Juliet teaches to burn bright are plainly electric, and so is most of the music. If the aim is universality, it doesn't work, but it doesn't destroy anything either. Of course Shakespeare's own last line foreshadows the new title, but then there aren't many rhymes for Juliet.

COUPLE OF BLAGUARDS

Winter Garden Theatre, Toronto

- - -

Once upon a time, Frank McCourt, who was later to write Angelas Ashes, and his brother Malachy, a sometime actor, pooled their talents to create an autobiographical entertainment. It dealt with their poverty-stricken childhood on the worst street in the Irish city of Limerick and with their subsequent emigration, not both at the same time, to New York where, on the show's evidence, they had a very good time. They performed the piece, often making it up as they went along, in the pubs and barrooms of their adopted city. Gradually it solidified into a play, and a successful one. Eventually the brothers tired of performing it and it passed into the hands of other, professional actors, two of whom have now brought it to Toronto.

I don't know what the McCourts are like as performers, but I suspect the show worked better when they were doing it themselves, primarily because the authors have supplied no characterizations for other actors to seize upon. There is nothing in the writing to distinguish Frank from Malachy or Malachy from Frank. The first act is entirely devoted to Franks boyhood -- grim at the time, fairly funny in the telling -- but what happens to him could equally well have happened to his brother, and there is nothing distinctive about the way he reacts. When Frank takes a ship across the Atlantic just before the intermission, there seems no particular reason for him rather than Malachy to be doing it. Indeed, when its revealed in the second act that Malachy went on the same journey just a little later, one feels distinctly had.

Worse than their anonymity as individuals is the lack of any dynamic between them. There is no reason beyond the accident of birth for them both to be in the same play. This matters less in the first act, where some unity is bestowed by the fact of their belonging to an identifiable community. They grew up in the poorest part of a depressed town. There was a lavatory outside their house: not theirs, the whole street's. "Worse than the ordinary miserable childhood, says Frank in Angela's Ashes, is the miserable Irish childhood, and worse yet is the miserable Irish Catholic childhood."

In the book, thats a source of both anger and laughter, with the anger predominating. In this earlier hack at the same material, everything is played for laughs. Its true that we hear of a drunken and often absentee father, and of the infant deaths of too many McCourt siblings; the loss of one young brother and the account of the father's taking him for burial provide the play with its only touching moments. But for the most part, we hear about bigoted priests instructing impressionable schoolboys on the Seven Deadly Sins, with special emphasis on the horrors of "the Lust. The implications of all this are horrific, as the McCourts themselves in other contexts have testified, but here it's presented, if not as endearing, then certainly as amusing. Which it is, though its effectiveness is lessened by the fact that weve heard it all before. Irish Catholicism at its most parochial is rather an easy comic target, certainly a much-battered one.

Frank is played -- man, boy and casual acquaintances -- by Jarlath Conroy, an actor in the sly-voiced, sharp-featured Irish mould that traditionally inspires adjectives like ferrety" and "weaselling; by way of variation, I would like to describe this latest exemplar as stoatlike." He is more competent than compelling. Howard Platt, an actor of greater bulk and greater resource who is also the director, plays all other roles, before settling down in the second act to being Malachy.

Here, with both brothers arrived in New York, the show splits its focus and becomes thoroughly arbitrary. We get alternating pages from their stateside careers, assembled with no shape and no logic. Frank gets a job looking after canaries, and glues them to their perches to conceal their deaths on his watch. On military service, he meets a girl who introduces him to the glories of his own countrys literature. Malachy, after reading a speech from The Playboy of the Western World, gets an acting job from a director who seems easily pleased. The father, a shadowy figure in the first act, turns up in the second to make emotional demands on the brothers and us; so, with even less preparation, does their mother, the Angela of the ashes. A third brother, never so much as mentioned before, also puts in an appearance, under the apparent impression that we've known him all along.

The show remains mildly entertaining, and seems to be making very few claims for itself -- which, considering its overall pointlessness, is a blessed mercy.

Black & White Photo: David Allen / Howard Platt, left, and Jarlath Conroy in Frank and Malachy McCourt's autobiographical tale.

NOT MY STORY

Artword Theatre, Toronto

- - -

The first lines of Silvija Jestrovic's Not My Story are actually from Chekhovs Three Sisters. It turns out that the woman delivering them is auditioning for the role of the middle sister, Masha. Her own name, also very Chekhovian, is Sonya. She comes from what was formerly known as the former Yugoslavia, and is now living in a city in Canada; we assume its Toronto. Her speech over, she laughs with her unseen judges about the obvious suitability of her Slavic accent for a play that is about Russians, even if it's going to be done in English. She laughs, but she probably isn't joking. More sort of desperate.

Flanking her are two other women, her expatriate compatriots. The three arent literally sisters, but if you go looking for resemblances to Chekhovs ladies, you can find them, in fractured form. In place of Olga, the reluctant headmistress, meet Lela, who announces herself as an art history teacher but has been forced into more exotic pursuits. For Irina, who planned a marriage of convenience with a man she didn't love, we offer you Nena, who actually ties the knot with a gay Canadian in order to get citizenship. He has his own agenda; she's a photographer, hes an aspiring model, though his real talent seems to be for mixing juices.

This is a play about people denied outlets for their talents and ambitions. The author comes from a background similar to those of her three heroines, and so do two of the actresses. The stage is repeatedly occupied by moments of anger, frustration and even fleeting happiness that feel authentic.

There is not much, though, to hold them together. Chekhovs characters, to pursue the analogy, existed within a society, and their drama is framed by the arrival and departure of a military battalion whose members crucially affect their lives. They also have a fire and a fatal duel to speed their lives along. These women are, by definition, on the fringes. They can't even yearn for Moscow because their Moscow is what they ran away from. Things indeed happen to them, but the events don't register, and so we get no sense of change or growth. It proceeds in brief, isolated scenes that frequently seem about to turn into something interesting but never quite make it; they end before they can take hold.

Dragana Varagic, who plays Sonya, is herself a formidable actress. Her own situation, as a performer whose ethnicity may be denying her some of the breaks she deserves, parallels that of the woman shes playing. Varagic fills her up with the bitterness of rejection and the wit of survival, and I would watch her play Masha or any other Chekhov heroine any time.

But Varagic is also the director, and thats a mistake. It looks as if her energies were divided, and the production exists in a permanent state of droop. This applies not just to the scenes but to the spaces between them, which are filled with really irritating piano music.

One of the play's misfortunes is that its central characters are all in essentially the same predicament; so Sonya's friends cant help but seem like paler echoes of herself. Given this, Cynthia Ashperger (Lela) and Rena Polley (Nena) play with constant determination and intermittent success. Ashperger comes on especially strong in a surprise-revelation scene that takes us down one of the plays more promising false trails; Polley is the only one of the trio not to sound authentically Central European, conceivably because she isn't. The production may be taking its cue from a theory Sonya advances at the start, about the irrelevance of accents to the higher scheme of things; she varies it later by saying what a gas it would be were she to perform pregnant.

Some plays -- Chekhov's, for example -- are big enough, and have become mythic enough, to stand up to that kind of thing. This one isnt exactly in that class. If it isnt specific, it's dead. It's about different cultures, for Gods sake.

The last words spoken in Not My Story are "lets begin." They're at the wrong end; we'd been waiting to begin all night.

Color Photo: Steven Miric, April Productions / Rena Polley and Jason Jazrawy in Not My Story, starring and directed by Dragana Varagic.

ON THE MOON

Peter Cincotti (Concord)

- - -

Peter Cincotti, singer-pianist, was 18 when he made his New York debut in 2002 (at the Algonquine, no less); 19 when he cut his first CD for Concord, sounding pleasant but slight. He repeated four of the same songs, a lot more forcefully, on the Montreux Festival set Voices of Concord Jazz, an apparent attempt by a nice-great label to get some of the way back to its roots.

Cincottis upward trend continues on his new one, On the Moon, which has some very encouraging stuff. Neither his voice nor his piano are startling in themselves, but he applies them intelligently, the voice in particular. He wrote or co-wrote four of the songs, which range from the dreadful (He's Watching, a trip back to the land of I Believe) to the interesting (I'd Rather Be with You). He takes on Raise the Roof, from one of the two recent musicals of The Wild Party, and tries far too hard to make it live up to its title; that kind of full-bloodedness comes naturally or not at all.

If he doesnt have Broadway savvy, he does have street smarts; he kicks off with a cheekily aggressive St. Louis Blues (though what does he mean by "she wants for powder"?). Two other songs about places are from the department of Songs Everybody Knows But Hardly Anyone Sings: Bali Hai, which, with harmonica and multi-tracked vocal, sounds very sinister, and I Love Paris, given a take-it-or- leave-treatment, suggesting that if we hated Paris, he wouldn't be much bothered.

It may be my nostalgia kicking in, but the two best tracks are revivals of old pop hits: the Drifters' Up on the Roof, which is a delight to hear as a solo, and Eddy Arnold's sublimely self-pitying You Don't Know Me, which here completes a progress from country via Ray Charles soul to stark cabaret jazz.

NO GREAT MISCHIEF

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

- - -

Alistair Macleod's No Great Mischief is a novel in the form of an imaginary memoir. This makes it one of the trickiest kinds of novel to adapt for the stage, since such attempts are liable to result in one character doing most of the talking. The problem is exacerbated when, as often happens, the narrator turns out not to be the crucial character -- when he is stuck telling what is essentially someone elses story. The Tarragons treatment of Macleod's book, crafted by David S. Young with the help of the cast, suffers severely from this displaced focus and pays heavily for it.

R.H. Thomson, who does the introspective monologist better than most, appears here as Alexander, fictitious present-day scion of the historical clan Macdonald who moved from Scotland to Cape Breton in the late-18th century. He's quizzical and observant, but that isnt enough to make a protagonist. As a child, Alexander lost both his parents to an accident on the ice; most of his family, including his elder brother Calum, last of a long line of Calum Macdonalds, went down the mines; but Alexander opted for dentistry and now lives and works in Windsor. Calum, who was told at 15 that he was now the man of the house and tried to be, lives in a doss-house in Toronto, the victim of an uncontrollable temper and a violent disposition. He is played by David Fox who, not for the first time, veers between being genuinely powerful and just overpowering. The framing action starts with Alexander paying him a regulation visit, and end with the two of them, at Calums instigation, taking a last fateful drive back to Nova Scotia. Calum is the dynamo of the action, but it's Alexander who gets the stage time. Even when Calum is present he's likely to be acting out what his brother says about him. This happens, most damagingly, at what proves to be the fateful moment in Calums career. In other words, the story is illustrated, but its not dramatized.

And then there's the Curse of Canadian Content, here present in a peculiarly virulent and self-defeating form. If the purpose of Canadian drama is, in the old phrase, to allow us to tell our stories to one another, then the trouble with this story is that it is told rather than shown. Sometimes there's both, but when there is, the telling outweighs the showing.

If one gets brownie points for setting a play in a region of Canada other than that in which its being performed, then its held to be especially virtuous if that region is Cape Breton, because of the musical opportunities. Every member of this cast can play some kind of instrument (Fox plays the spoons) and there is dancing even at the curtain-call, but the all the fiddling and capering do nothing to speed the play along.

Richard Rose's production adheres to the traditional rules for folksy ensemble theatre, with the actors loyally miming livestock and voicing sound-effects. Nancy Palk, the only woman present, has a sharp few moments near the beginning and a sustained vignette near the end, but is wasted in between. Geoffrey Pounsett is charming as somebody referred to, even more delightfully, as "serious grandfather;" and Jody Richardson shakes things up a bit as a shady American relative who makes a surprise appearance, which is good, and an abrupt disappearance which in a play, as opposed to a novel, is simply frustrating.

I started feeling unexpectedly tender toward A Couple of Blaguards, the strictly commercial Irish piece to which I was rude a couple of weeks ago, and which also assumes that we will be fascinated by a family whom it does nothing to bring to life. No Great Mischief may conceivably be more intelligent, and it is unquestionably more serious, but A Couple of Blaguards is, from time to time, funny. And it doesn't behave as if it thinks it's doing us good.

CANADA HOUSE

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, Toronto

- - -

When a play is titled Canada House and is largely set in a bar of that name, and when it also concerns the activities of a company called Dominion Inc. whose logo is boldly emblazoned on the back wall of the set, it's reasonable to assume that symbolism is being committed.

So, in intention at least, is prophecy. J. Karol Korczynski's play takes place far enough in the future for one of its few amusing lines to be a reference to the Stockwell Day Memorial Golf Tournament, which, to judge from the script's overall tone of voice, is not very far at all. Canada House is one of those allegories about what's in store for us if we don't watch out. Dominion Inc. -- a neatly sinister pun -- is the project of a bold young entrepreneur with aggressive ideas for the mixing and marketing of non-medicinal drugs.

For putting these schemes into practice, he expects and receives respect, in the shape of rewards and awards, from a think-tank known as the Social Market Foundation. He is also into grinding the faces of the poor, big time. For his next trick, he plans to introduce Social Robotics, by which he means reducing your employees to a state where they will do anything you tell them to, the more immoral the better.

I can believe this. What I can't credit is the story that goes with it, at least not as it's told here. Probably for economic reasons, we only meet three characters, slim pickings for a dystopia. There is ruthless Ray, the aspiring dope king, who lives his life as a revenge for the day strikers occupied his father's factory and whose one exploitable weakness is his dependence on kinky phone sex.

There is Sally, a gnarled and feisty ex-everything, who services him in this regard and thus has a hold on him, but who also, by extreme coincidence, becomes one of his wage slaves, except she doesn't get wages. Commuting between them, as an old associate of Sally's and a new employee of Ray's, is Louis, a walking shrugging cliche from Quebec. They all talk a lot, so much so that we are near the end of a long first act before anything remotely gripping happens. I know it's a highly unfair comparison, but I kept remembering the operatic version of The Handmaid's Tale, a not dissimilar cautionary tale that was no more subtle but at least looked good and moved fast.

Canada House itself is a last-chance saloon where the regulars express themselves through karaoke and the occasional comic monologue. Atmospherically, this is quite convincing. The author, according to his bio, has been there, so he can't be accused of vicarious slumming. Dramatically, though, he dawdles, wallowing in local colour while leaving big holes in both the narrative foreground and the political background. He manages, against all odds, to end on an optimistic note, but that too seems self- indulgent, the kind of rallying cry best left to the audience's own response. Throughout the play, speeches -- hopeful, caustic or despairing -- are delivered to extra unseen characters who remain, at least in this production, obstinately unbelievable. The case is not much better with the ones we do see.

The director is Graham Cozzubbo, whose work earlier this year on The Ibsen Project I greatly admired, but who cannot make this piece function. The stage at Passe Muraille Backspace always looks at first glance dauntingly cramped, but it has in the past proved surprisingly flexible. Cozzubbo and his designer, Lee Wildgen, have made one huge scenic miscalculation that starts by being irritating and ends by robbing the play's climactic scene of any effect it might have had.

The actors flounder, each in a different way. Wendy Thatcher, perhaps in reaction to the constrained gentlewoman roles that generally come her way at the Shaw Festival, plays Sally's outspokenness not as the woman's natural mode but as if she were trying to impress someone. As Ray, Brian Marler deals entertainingly with his and the play's best moment, a creepy parody of an Oscar acceptance speech; everything else he plays with an embarrassing lack of conviction. As Louis, Daniel Kash seems to be staking everything on his accent and losing. The sense of the role, and hence of much of the play, drowns in the sound. The Canada House Collective, presenting the show, has plans regarding political theatre that sound virtuous, if not especially original. One can only wish them, and us, better luck next time.

Color Photo: Wayne Sujo / Wendy Thatcher and Daniel Kash can't stop talking in J. Karol Korczynski's dystopian tale.

In this period of post-election recovery, we decided to forgo the angry ragings of Marilyn Manson (yesterday at Massey Hall), for the softer sounds of Sufjan Stevens. The quiet singer/songwriter has, perhaps hastily, been lumped in with a number of similar souls as leaders of a new folk. JAZZ

REMEMBERING MABEL

Mercer: Volume 2

Joyce Breach

(Audiophile)

- - -

SEPTEMBER SONGS

Wesla Whitfield

(High Note)

- - -

Much of the finest singing of classic American song is being done by those performers, cult rather than popular, who cluster somewhere around the cusp of jazz and cabaret. These CDs are by two of the best.

Joyce Breach, bred in Pittsburgh, based in New York, offers the second in a planned trilogy of albums drawn from the repertoire of the late Mabel Mercer. Mercer, the doyenne of Manhattan nightlife, was an unassuming woman whose fans perceived her as regal, but whose authority was leavened with a refreshing raucous wit.

Breach's persona is in a lower key. Her singing is soothing, sensible, and quietly confident, with a hint of remembered sadness in the voice. Looking in the other direction, this can become grave apprehension, as in Cole Porter's After You, an apparently happy song that is also a heartbreaker. She's a fine contemplative singer, notably in Love-Wise, which comes to the conclusion "you're perfect for me." Her understatement does wonders for This is All I Ask, a testament of a song that can be unbearably overbearing.

Sometimes her keel is too even. Two worldly Cy Coleman tunes, When in Rome and The Riviera, suffer from a lack of laughter in the voice. Keith Ingham, a fleet and sensitive pianist and arranger, leads a trio with support from bassoonist Laurie Goldstein. Especially pleasing is his mournful obbligato on Blame It on My Youth, one of the few famous songs here, and one that Breach does well -- title notwithstanding, it's a song that needs maturity to do it justice.

Breach's opening tune is While We're Young. It's the closer on Wesla Whitfield's September Song, whose opener is its title track. This gives the album a shape; it's bookended by songs about seizing the moment, at different times of life.

This disc focuses on three composers, and should perhaps have a big "W" logo: Wesla Whitfield warbles Wilder, Weill and Warren. There may just be too many elements to make a satisfying whole, but song by song, it's lovely.

Whitfield, from San Francisco, had classical training but not a classical career. She does evanescence exceptionally well. She can spin out flowing lines and then cut them off -- especially on September Song -- with what sounds like brusque regret.

Her backing groups include the Kronos Quartet, whose chamber sound in Weill's Speak Low sits intriguingly over a pulsating trio led by the singer's husband, Mike Greensill. These strings can swing too, as in Jeepers Creepers, which crops up with delightful abruptness halfway through a medley. Whitfield is at her best on I Had the Craziest Dream, a bittersweet song on which, uniquely, she emphasizes the bitterness, without letting it quite take over.

POND LIFE

Factory Studio Theatre

- - -

There are these two heterosexual couples, one married, one not, the former having invited the latter over for dinner. The married man is called Dick, and the living-together guy is called Richard. Dick's wife is named Sandy, short for Alexandra. Richards partner is named Daisy, which looks at first like a break in the pattern, but it turns out that she is thinking of adopting the stage name of Alexandra Rampage; she is, God help us, a singer-songwriter.

It seems at first that we are in for an absurdist satire about interchangeable suburbanites, on the order of Ionescos The Bald Soprano. However, the tone soon shifts to something more resembling Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf only nastier, if you can imagine, with the twist that here it's the hosts rather than the guests who are the aggressors. Their opting for full-length names rather than diminutives is the outward sign of that. Not that the modest hosts are any bargains either.

Pond Life takes its title from an inaugural discussion between Dick, whos a doctor, and Daisy on the mating habits of frogs. These, as the play progresses, begin to seem preferable to the habits of humans, mating or otherwise. Its an elegant piece, though a bit over-extended for what it is, written and directed by Gord Rand, an excellent actor most recently seen in Soulpepper's Translations.

Richard and Daisy are late, which enables Dick, once he's through with his biological lecture, to while away the time putting his hand up his wifes skirt. Just as shes beginning to warm up to the idea they hear noises and -- despite the fact that they're expecting visitors -- react as if they had burglars. With a skilful tackle, the normally meek Dick brings the rugged Richard to his knees. This is about the last aggressive thing Dick does in the play since, once the apologies have been made and food has been proffered and refused and drinks accepted, the black-clad Richard reveals himself, proudly, as a life-style bully. He's cool with it because its cool on him. He says so himself and, interestingly, nobody gives him any arguments.

The ostensible reason for the get-together is that the two women are friends at work. It turns out that the bonds between -- and across -- the couples are more complex than that. There have been amorous complications in the past, and they threaten to persist in the present. (Nobody here gives much thought to the future.) Also, Dick and Richard are business partners, nefariously trading in human embryos. Dicks job gives him the access. Toward the end the worm does turn, but that just makes him seem even wormier. Sandy's bubbling innocence begins to seem a lot too true to be good. Daisy is high on vanity and colonic irrigation.

My usual reaction to plays that inform us how rotten we all are (we in the audience being, by definition, as middle-class -- and therefore as guilty -- as the people we are gaping at) is to ask to be told something I don't know. There is nothing revelatory about arraigning our society as a collection of unhappy breeders, festering in slime. But it can be done well or badly, and Rand does it well. Its uncommon for a play to sustain an insouciantly bleak comic tone as persistently and successfully as this one does. It only falters, as plays so often do, when the characters start talking about other characters whom we havent met and in whom we don't believe. At these moments the script does raise its voice, break out in sobs, lose its own cool. But there aren't many of them.

Rands direction, on an economic and fastidiously virginal set designed by Chad McMillan, is even more aassured than his script. The actors, mostly non-Equity, are perfectly in style, with Ryan Blakelys nervous goodwill as Dick and Jeanie Calleja's nervous good humour as Sandy bending under pressure but, alarmingly, never breaking. Kerry McPherson's Daisy delivers her character intact, though she sometimes rushes out to grab her egotism rather than letting it come to her. As Richard, who uses boorishness as both an armour and a weapon, Ryan McVittie is insuperably insufferable. Which is, of course, a compliment. Note that in a mixed-doubles cast, both male actors are named Ryan. Is this a sign of the times? How long has it been going on? Was it confusing at rehearsals? Note too that it's a name that cannot easily be shortened. That, on the play's showing, is scary.

Color Photo: In Pond Life, living in the festering slime seems preferable to the everyday cruelties of the characters.

BIGGER THAN JESUS

Factory Theatre, Toronto

- - -

Rick Miller is best known as author and performer of MacHomer, in which he showed that he could recite the text of Macbeth in the voices, all the voices, of the characters from The Simpsons. This was clever, since he was doing, live and solo, what it takes more than half-a-dozen unseen actors to accomplish on TV. It was also pointless, partly because he was merely imitating the characterizations that others had created, and partly because his extended party-trick cast no light, satirical or otherwise, on either Springfield or Shakespeare.

Miller's new show, Bigger Than Jesus, is better than MacHomer, far better, and also much more ambitious. It's a seriously comic inquiry into Christianity, and especially into the reputation and historical effects of its founder. Parts of it are brilliant and other parts silly. Mathematically the silly parts predominate, but the brilliant parts are the ones you'll remember.

Miller appears before us as a black-clad young man whose self- effacing vocal manner co-exists with absolute physical and technical command. He is, he tells us, 33 and a lapsed Catholic, two highly significant circumstances. The second of them prompts him to structure his show in the form of a Mass, a unifying concept that, from this non-Catholic perspective, fails to unify. I just had to grab at the different sections as they passed.

One of the best of them comes at the beginning. Miller gives us a slick, fast, witty lecture on the Gospels as history. His conclusion is that, in that light, they don't amount to much, having been written down centuries after the events of which they profess to be eyewitness reports. He comments on the threat that dissenting Jewish sects posed to the Roman government of Judea. He explains, grimly and dispassionately, the physical details of crucifixion. He outlines the paradoxes of a revolutionary preacher having been adopted as a symbol of political and religious repression, of a charitable activist being used to promote intolerance, of a Jew becoming the arch-pretext for anti-Semitism. None of this, of course, is new, but Miller, stating rather than hammering, makes it urgent.

Much of what follows is, unhappily, not so much a development of the argument as a series of whimsical re-statements. There is a long sermonizing turn by a black-sounding preacher who has the fervour of a fundamentalist but the humour of a humanist; that may sound like a stimulating combination but it plays like self-indulgence, Miller back in funny-voice mode. There's a flight on something called Air Jesus. There are frequent returns to the MacHomer fallacy that pop- culture references are automatically hilarious: The four evangelists are compared to the Beatles (Mark is Ringo, Matthew is George, Luke is Paul, John is John) and, in a re-enactment of the Last Supper with toy-figures, H. Simpson himself reappears as Judas. In sequences like these, Bigger Than Jesus is smaller than Jesus Christ Superstar.

It always looks good; the show is presented by Necessary Angel, which seems appropriate, and is the company's first production by its new director, Daniel Brooks, who is also credited, with similarly solemn overtones, as co-creator. This, following Cul-de- Sac, is the second occasion this season on which, through timing and technology, Brooks has taken a one-man show to a higher plane. There is especially striking use of instant video, affording us overhead views of Miller in crucified pose, this nice inquiring young man turned into a bewildered martyr.

The show's second great sequence does indeed come when Miller himself turns into Jesus; or rather into a cross -- pun not intended but welcomed -- between Jesus and a baffled comedian facing a tough house. He delivers, very well, some of the most challenging sentences in the New Testament, ending with "love one another." He pauses. "Any questions?" he asks hopefully. He tries a few more quips. All of them die. He still goes on standing there. This says something, something both moving and disturbing, though I'd hesitate to say exactly what. The show also demonstrates, unexpectedly though not too surprisingly, that Miller can sing.
