SIDE BY SIDE BY SONDHEIM

Bluma Appel Theatre

- - -

I spent some of my time at Side by Side by Sondheim smiling and tapping my feet, but rather more of it groaning and grinding my teeth. At moments I even averted my eyes. This 1976 revue, designed to make audiences more aware of the music and lyrics of Stephen Sondheim, may have outlived its historical purpose. Its subject has become a cultural icon; people who don't like his funny, beautiful, probing and unnerving songs by now are never going to like them. And, as things have turned out, he's written nearly as many musicals since this retrospective as he had before it.

None of this, of course, need prevent Side by Side from furnishing a decent evening's entertainment. This CanStage revival, though, arrives loaded with handicaps. Some of them are inherent in the piece itself. One is the opening, a coy and genteel arrangement of Comedy Tonight. (The song is meant to be a celebration of low comedy, for Jupiter's sake.) Another is the closing, a medley of, basically, song titles that's equally cloying and even more insufferably knowing. The mandated two- piano accompaniment, though perfectly well executed, imposes a conservatory sound that knocks the guts out of the music

Then there's the matter of casting. The first London-New York production was built around and sparked by two first-rate singing comediennes, Millicent Martin and Julia McKenzie. None of the four Toronto performers is in that league; they obviously get the wit of the lyrics, but they are very self-conscious about putting it over. The original was held together by the dapper, deadpan narration of Ned Sherrin, who wrote and delivered disposable jokes that nobody else seems able to get away with.

Eda Holmes' production dispenses with a separate narrator, turning her cast into a quartet of singer-dancer-talkers. I confess that when I heard about this I thought it a good idea, a way of bestowing unity and fluidity on what could easily become a stop-and- go succession of disconnected songs. I had reckoned without the discomfort level of actors, as opposed to raconteurs or stand-up comics, asked to deposit uncharacterized material in the audience's laps. It's even worse when the banter is divided between them, and they have to pretend that it's spontaneous. And when new and supposedly topical lines are shoved in among the old, it becomes positively painful.

John Thompson has designed a Shakespearean history kind of set, full of steps and darkness and varied by some sharply etched projections. There are a few other visual effects; I liked the strip of blue that unfolded when the I Remember singer got to the word "sky" and folded up again at the song's regretful end, but I was totally baffled by the snowfall that accompanied Send in the Clowns.

The costumes are uniformly unbecoming. A few of the ensemble numbers give Holmes a chance to show her skill at directing actors and text; the magnificent Someone in a Tree, a combined history- philosophy lesson set to a steadily climbing beat, is done with an exemplary blend of delicacy and force. (But how one misses a full band at the finish.)

Most of the conversational bite of You Must Meet My Wife, a barbed duet from A Little Night Music, comes through. I wish they hadn't cut Barcelona, a post-coital number that's one of the rare theatre songs that does what we are always told they should do, i.e. the work of a one-act play. Sondheim in the '60s and '70s wrote many songs about discordant marriages, and this show makes a theme of them. Holmes ends several of them by bringing on a third, silent partner at the end. She must be trying for a through-line, but it comes off as just a mannerism.

I wonder, rather than employing a full-time choreographer, Jane Johanson, if Holmes might not have done better by devising her own, as she did this year for Floyd Collins. The result would probably have been homelier, but it might have been tighter, and this material, in this setting, doesn't really need the old razzle- dazzle, which in any case here seems like enthusiastic winsomeness.

There's a paradox about taking Sondheim's songs out of their original settings; they might seem less equipped for independent life than the self-sufficient tunes of, say, Cole Porter, but they can sometimes drag enough of their contexts with them to give the actors something to act. The corresponding danger, especially in the solo numbers, is that the performers will try too hard.

Here they all do. Dan Chameroy does it least and comes off best. His seasons at Stratford, mainly in plays, have sharpened his interpretive skills; he does a stabbing Could I Leave You, here transformed into a song about a literally gay divorce, a passionate Marry Me a Little and a yearning Anyone Can Whistle, topped by a pardonably flaunted falsetto.

Jay Turvey, so good in Floyd Collins, seems lost without a consistent role to play, but he does manage a lovely I Remember. The allocation of songs is hard on him, and harder still on Julain Molnar, who only comes into her own in The Boy From ..., a hilarious bossa nova spoof that she does toothy and bespectacled. Mary Ann McDonald is the most effortful, and sometimes her efforts pay off; she strains every nerve to make I'm Still Here the show-stopping climax of the evening, but the song only works if the singer is a star, or at least a former star.

An evening like this should leave you wanting more. There is, after all, far more good Sondheim available, even within this show's foreshortened time frame. But, in fact, you want less. It all feels long, and that's wrong. Very wrong.

Black & White Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / Dan Chameroy, left, Julain Molnar, Mary Ann McDonald and Jay Turvey in Side by Side by Sondheim.

BECKETT & BRECHT

Theatre Centre, Toronto

- - -

Newly decked out with a lobby that's almost welcoming and an auditorium that's almost comfortable, Theatre Centre at fashionable Queen and Dovercourt recommences operations with a double-bill that pays tribute to the two gods of 20th-century drama. In Beckett & Brecht, Beckett is represented by a selection of his own playlets, then Brecht by a newly-written piece in which he is the pivotal figure. For this and other reasons, the first part comes off the best.

Its contents are described in the program as Beckett Shorts, designed perhaps to be worn with Tom Stoppard's Jumpers. Beckett was notorious for insisting on absolute fidelity, not only to his dialogue but to his stage directions. He was also justified, at least for his later and briefer works. In these, the image defines the play; a production that tampered with it would have nothing left to work with. Jennifer Tarver, the director here, has her work cut out -- and does it very well -- constructing the pictures, pacing her three performers and engineering neat transitions from one piece to the next.

The first of the quintet, also the best-known, is Not I, in which a woman billed simply as Mouth, this being her only visible feature, pours out the contents of her memory, at fever pace, to a silent hooded Auditor, who looks like a human question mark. Every time the speaker slips into the first person, she corrects herself and reiterates that the experiences she's describing are actually somebody else's.

Scenically, Mouth's mouth is the merest pin point cut in a black drape. It's a striking effect, though the velocity of the words (flawlessly delivered here by Barbara Gordon, as defensive as she's desperate) and the eye-aching darkness make concentration difficult. In fact, one is quite often bored. But it's a creative kind of boredom, one that keeps jerking the mind back to attention. Guilt has its uses.

It doesn't work in That Time, the piece that lends its name to the collection and gives us a grizzled protagonist (David Jansen) sitting motionless while stereo speakers on either side of him offer two conflicting versions in two registers of his own voice, of a cherished and/or rejected incident from his past. Beckett keeps his images very specific and that, as always, is a blessing. He may set the interpreters endlessly arguing but, from moment to moment, he is the least cloudy of writers. All the same: I can't see that That Time adds anything to what he said earlier and better in Krapp's Last Tape. The knife is dulled, but he still persists in twisting it.

It's twisted further in the two mimed plays, Act Without Words I and II (done in reverse order). Here, of course, the stage directions are the plays. In one of them, a pair of adjacent sleepers are prodded awake in their sacks (this is emphatically not the Ritz) by a long pole that emerges from the wings like an old- style vaudeville hook, except it's to start the act rather than stop it. One man, very grumpy, stumbles resentfully into life, the other, far cheerier, begins his day with a brisk series of physical jerks. But ultimately it makes no difference. Each ends up precisely where both began. In the other, the torture is refined; a solitary figure (Paul Fauteux) is bullied by whistles and tantalized by an inaccessible bottle of Evian (the branding being, I assume, the production's tribute to the author's adopted homeland). Life is a series of Pavlovian reactions, culminating in the grave. Beckett has tapped in to the secret of farce -- human beings depicted as automata are funny.

The last bit of Beckett, Catastrophe, was new to me and a revelation. It has three characters, two of whom get to walk and talk. A male director and his assistant arrange a male model in a suitably humiliating pose. They might be arranging a gallery installation, but it turns out they're rehearsing in a theatre. This is not only -- who'd have thought it? -- Beckett going in for showbiz satire, it must also be his ironic apologia for the hoops through which he put his own actors or the holes and corners to which he confined them. It makes a superb first-act finale. Sam Beckett was a gentleman and a showman.

Bert Brecht was just a showman. And it's a bumpy decline here from SB to BEBE, which is about Brecht and his women, in relation to whom he was a bastard. We meet three mistresses and -- proudly announcing herself in the funniest line -- one wife: Helene Weigel, the original Mother Courage and co-founder of the Berliner Ensemble. Four actresses tell us how he exploited them domestically, sexually and professionally. The earliest, Elisabeth Hauptmann, claims to have done most of the work on The Threepenny Opera. How much and how vital remains unclear, but there was plainly no reason to deny her either credit or royalties, both of which Brecht did.

The show, a collective creation directed by Jennifer H. Capraru, retells some interesting history but is too fragmented and dispersed to work as drama. Stylistically it invokes the spectre of Berlin cabaret. Maybe it's time to acknowledge that this vein has been definitively mined. Of the new songs, only one (The Exile Song, lyric by Morwyn Brebner) gains from being heard rather than read. It's sung by Camille Stubel, whose angular Weigel is the most commanding performance. As Ruth Berlau, last and looniest of the partners, Ruth Madoc-Jones is undone by a patter-song that is too fast, too clotted or both.

Mention is made of Brecht's slippery testimony before the Un- American Activities Committee. Meanwhile, Beckett, who never struck political poses, was working heroically for the French Resistance. Brecht's best line is confined to the program: "A theatre which cannot be laughed in is a theatre to be laughed at." Right on, Bertolt. But Beckett's jokes are better.

robertcushman@lycos.com; The Winter's Tale runs until Dec. 23. Box office: 416-973-4000; Aladdin runs until Dec. 31. Box office: 416- 872-5555.

Shakespeare never wrote a Christmas play. Neither, as far as I can determine, did any of his contemporaries. Elizabethan England was an aggressively Christian society, to the extent of imposing fines and worse on any citizen who stayed home on a Sunday. But this didn't mean the popular theatre was expected to dramatize Biblical stories, or to deal explicitly with Christian themes; the whole idea smacked of blasphemy. There was even legislation forbidding the mention of God's name. Subject for Discussion: Religious censorship always undoes itself since it inevitably fosters secular-humanist entertainment.

That's not to say that Elizabethan and Jacobean playwrights, soaked as they were in Christian ideas, didn't automatically include them in their plays. Obvious examples are Shakespeare's last plays, which tell stories of resurrection and reconciliation. For Christmas associations, The Winter's Tale, at Harbourfront's Brigantine Room, recommends itself, if only by its title. As it turns out, though, it is only by its title. The semi-professional group Theatre Kingston has brought the play to Toronto as a seriously seasonal offering. The production is good, but it doesn't make its advertised case.

It starts with a string band playing carols, and ends with all the actors harmonizing on Once in Royal David's City, some of them in tune and others not. Both top and tail are, of course, pasted on. Within the actual play there are occasional iconic gestures. The costumes are Victorian, which gets us thinking Dickens. The court of Sicilia initially boasts a couple of Christmas decorations; when the action darkens, when the crazed king Leontes orders his wife, Hermione, dragged off to prison on suspicion of adultery, the holly wreaths get dragged too. When Hermione is displayed as a statue in the magical last scene, she's in a Madonna pose.

Then there is the young prince Mamillius, who says "a sad tale's best for winter" and who dies of a broken heart when his mother is put on trial. In this production, he hangs around posthumously, holding a teddy bear. He also gets to speak the mid-play chorus, which gives us crucial information, here drowned out by guitar accompaniment. He is around to cast a blessing on the finale and generally acts like a Christ-child.

This is Sunday-school sentimentality, and it contradicts the play. Leontes, after 16 years' penance, gets back a lot, including his wife and the baby daughter he left to die of exposure. But he doesn't get back his son. Some things can't be atoned for.

"Thou met'st with things dying," says the old shepherd at the play's turning point, "I with things new-born." If the text suggests any Christian festival, it's not Christmas but Easter, whatever the weather. But, as usual in Shakespeare, the myths are mixed. One character glancingly compares himself to Judas, but the play's official deity is pagan Apollo, and Leontes' crowning folly is to disobey the Delphic oracle.

The strengths of Craig Walker's production are intelligence, intensity and -- in a space not generally employed for anything larger than a poetry reading -- intimacy. Royal Sicilia is signified by a carpet; rustic Bohemia by a rug.

The play, contrary to critical tradition and the director's program note, emerges most compellingly as psychological realism. At least, it does in Matthew Gibson's performance of Leontes. This is a paradox; Leontes is a notoriously unrealistic character whose jealousy, as in a fairy-tale, flares up out of nowhere five minutes after his first entrance. Gibson does his best to pave the way by imbuing his initial speeches with a suspicious sneer; once inside his fantasy, he is riveting. Each self-torturing image comes drenched in sweet reasonableness, every outside attempt to argue with his obsession pushes him deeper into it. This is paranoia defined, a gnarled and treacherous script superbly navigated, keywords pounced on and illuminated without ever halting the flow. He's less successful with the repentant king, whom he plays on a single beatific note that's initially arresting but turns swiftly sanctimonious, and I don't know how he'd manage on a bigger stage; but in the first half his Leontes is almost -- not quite -- the best I have seen.

None of the other performances compare, including Gibson's own double as the young shepherd, a.k.a., Clown. In fact, the pastoral scenes flop. The Autolycus (Ivan Sherry) is in the audience's face without ever making contact, while the young lovers have little charm and no finesse. The last redemptive movement makes little sense because we don't believe in the redeemers, including, back at court, a Paulina who's less a moral fury than a nag. Hermione (Jennifer Roblin) plays her trial scene with quiet power, and the good Camillo (Peter Aston) is nicely professorial, fittingly so since by day the actor is a professor, of microbiology and immunology, which must be another source for good. That the play both preaches and exemplifies charity is undeniable, but the shiver it unfailingly provokes when the statue comes to life pre-dates Christianity. It's ancestral.

If you think a happy tale best for winter, then Aladdin, this year's Ross Petty pantomime, at the Elgin, is a good buy. This story, too, is multi-cultural. Originally part of the Arabian Nights Apocrypha, it was transported by English panto to a music-hall idea of Imperial China, complete with comic laundry. This version pulls it to back some kind of Middle East; at least it's ruled by a Sultan (Kyle Dadd), surnamed Redundo because he says everything twice -- a joke that bears repetition better than you might anticipate, or expect.

On the other hand, its music and dancing are funky, even hip- hoppity, and its broader comic accents Maritime. Ted Dykstra's direction is, by the standards of the genre in general and Petty in particular, ferociously disciplined -- even the song-sheet sequence is over double-quick -- and there is a writer (David Finley) who dares to sign his name and has no reason to be ashamed of doing so.

There is, hooray, no village-square scene: ergo, no merry villagers. Adam Brazier, in the title role, maintains the good new Elgin tradition of a plucky hero with classical-theatre chops who can laugh at himself. The star performance, though, is Jennifer Dale's as a librarian-narrator who gratifies her fantasies and ours by morphing into a svelte, limber Genie of the Ring. In her first guise she sings, charmingly, Pure Imagination, the best song ever written by Anthony Newley and Leslie Bricusse. In her second, she swivels, with as little cue-for-passion as Leontes, through Diamonds Are a Girl's Best Friend, in the course of which she, too, strikes a Madonna pose, i.e. she sticks in a few bars of Material Girl. (Moulin Rouge has much to answer for.)

She is also good at putting down her producer, whose villainous Abanazeer ("brassiere" for the grown-ups in the audience) is uncommonly, well, restrained; usually in Petty's panto performances, one senses a real farouche actor trying to get out, but this year he seems to be taking a nap. The special attraction is Bret "Hitman" Hart," whose Genie of the Lamp is an acting debut as impressive as any professional wrestler is ever likely to make.

2004-12-20-broadway-s-last-real-jazzman-:
robertcushman@lycos.com

This year the American musical lost two men from its last great generation of writers, the group that first made its mark in the late 1950s and early '60s. That doesn't mean that no talented lyricists and composers have emerged since; but Fred Ebb, who wrote words, and Cy Coleman, who wrote music, each managed the kind of consistent, productive career that has been denied to their successors. Both started when costs were still just about containable, and a writer was allowed a speedy second chance.

Ebb's first Broadway show was Flora the Red Menace (1965), which introduced Liza Minnelli; Coleman's was Wildcat (1960), Lucille Ball's first musical and also, to no one's surprise, her last. Both flopped, but each was followed within two years by what turned out to be its writers' masterpiece; Ebb, with his composer John Kander, wrote Cabaret; Coleman, with his lyricist Carolyn Leigh, Little Me.

Coleman and Ebb never collaborated, though it was talked of, and they might have made a good team; each was known for writing smart, hard and witty songs. Coleman, with whom I'm concerned here and who was my second-favourite contemporary composer, died a month ago of a heart attack, and that death, at the age of 75, was a shock. He fell sick, suddenly and dramatically, at a first-night party (though not for one of his own shows, that would have been too much). He had always seemed, in his life and his work, to be boyishly buoyant (he had one of the most distinctive, pealing laughs I have ever heard), and he had half-a-dozen projects on the boil. There had been a late- life marriage, a daughter and a rejuvenating return -- with a glossy New York club booking -- to his early career as a jazz-flavoured singer-pianist.

There was something very satisfying about that, because it was in the Manhattan cabaret scene of the '50s that Coleman had found himself as a composer. A concert prodigy (he played at Carnegie Hall when he was seven), he had switched to jazz, formed his own trio and started writing songs. These immediately became favourites with late- night singers, including the two cult monarchs, the matronly Mabel Mercer and the effervescing Bobby Short. To this day, in what remains of New York cabaret, Coleman's songs are probably sung more often than those of any other composer later than Cole Porter. Meanwhile, his tunes had been taken up by performers with a far wider constituency: Frank Sinatra, for whom he composed Witchcraft, and especially by Peggy Lee (who herself wrote some songs with him) and Tony Bennett, both of whom recorded an album's worth of Coleman material.

These songs included It Amazes Me, which is about sophistication caught off-guard; The Rules of the Road, which is about sophistication getting dumped and drowning its sorrows in a kind of stoical bravado; and The Best Is Yet to Come, which is about sophistication facing a glorious erotic future. The last, written in 1959, somewhat belied its title by turning out to be not only the best song of Coleman's career but the best non-theatre song to be written by anyone after the end of the Second World War. Introduced by Bennett, but recorded definitively by Sinatra with Count Basie, it makes stunningly resourceful use of one simple, muscular melodic idea and a rhythm that, through all its undulations, never lets up. It's a song that's supremely confident but never behaves like a bully. It also has a Carolyn Leigh lyric ("you think you've flown before but you ain't left the ground") as snappy and driving as the music. Leigh, whose qualities included an endless joy in and flair for rhyming, matched her collaborator not only in worldliness but in occasional unexpected vulnerability. In On Second Thought, about regrets and trying not to phone, she finds a sung equivalent for the spirit of Dorothy Parker -- something, incidentally, that Parker herself, in her few songwriting efforts, signally failed to do.

Leigh is usually considered Broadway's second-best female lyricist, first place going to Dorothy Fields, who belonged to the really great generation, the pre-war one. I think I prefer Leigh, certainly as a partner for Coleman. He split up with Leigh after their first two shows (because of her insecurities, or so it's usually claimed) and teamed up with Fields. Their first show, Sweet Charity (1966), is probably Coleman's best-known; it's scheduled for a revival next year. It's terrific entertainment, and its score is probably the last from a traditional Broadway musical to have entered the cultural bloodstream. But there is more energy than inventiveness; some of the wit has gone, from the music as well as the words.

Here's a paradox. The theatre was lucky to have Coleman; in his group of Broadway composers, he ranks second only to Stephen Sondheim. And yet it's not certain that the theatre is where he belonged. Little Me is his only great show, though it was never a great hit. A merciless spoof of show-business autobiographies, its durability seems threatened, not by the writing -- nearly everything in the score and in Neil Simon's book is hilarious -- but by the impossibility of finding a comedian capable of taking the right cartoon approach to the show's multiple leading roles. (They were written -- all seven of them -- for Sid Caesar.) Constructed of episodes, sketches really, it allowed Coleman and Leigh to write in their discrete pop/cabaret style, which was their best style. And indeed at least three of the songs have become extractable standards.

That's not to say that his later work is negligible. He wrote an intentionally overripe comic-opera score for the art-deco farce On the Twentieth Century; a jazz -- well, jazz-pop-Hollywood --score for City of Angels, a staged film noir with its own built-in commentary; a soul-sleaze-gospel score for The Life (1997), which is about Times Square prostitution and contains a song called The Oldest Profession that's about the only full-throated roof-raising diva number of the last three decades that doesn't insult its audience's intelligence. These are all substantial shows, even though none of them is quite satisfying. Coleman, as you'd expect from his background, was a stylistic jackdaw, but his essays in style went beyond pastiche; there was always something of himself in them. He used to have a trademark: the Coleman march-tune (Hey Look Me Over, Pass Me By, It's Not Where You Start) that sounded like a generic rouser but always turned out to have flair, spring, amusement. One show, the circus musical Barnum (1980), was largely made up of tunes like this but they all turned out to be worth paying attention to; indeed, they were the only things in the show that were.

There were also bolts of sheer melodic sweetness. Barnum has a song for Jenny Lind that you can imagine the legendary nightingale having actually sung. City of Angels boasts what may be the last great torch song. Coleman was the heir of George Gershwin, who made jazz work in the theatre, and Harold Arlen, who didn't quite but wrote magnificent songs anyway. That makes him unique among his peers, and with no apparent successors.

He was also, to the end, a matchless performer of his own songs, as demonstrated on a recent CD, It Started with a Dream, and on a 30- year-old LP that should be reissued. I once asked him about the apparent cult of self-laceration among cabaret performers. He didn't want any part of it. "No," he said, with that laugh, "I've done my suffering. I love what I do, and I'm lucky." And that, in everything he did, comes across.

2004-12-27-toronto-plays-were-foreign-to:
Next Monday: my customary list of the performances of 2004 that afforded me the most delight.; robertcushman@lycos.com

Imports got here late, but thank goodness they got here when they did

The best new play seen in Toronto this year was Michael Frayns Copenhagen, which is six years old and British. This has been quite a year for Frayn in Canada, what with Noises Off coming back in delight at Stratford. It has indeed been quite a year for Frayn in North America, with his Democracy triumphing on Broadway. This play about Willy Brandt will undoubtedly get to Canada -- even to this part of Canada, sooner or later, though on recent evidence it will probably be later. Meanwhile, we salivate.

The best Canadian play seen in Toronto was Morris Panych's Vigil, which is nine years old. None of the later competition could match it for wit, daring or oddball good-nature. This has also been quite a year for Panych, whose stereoscopic direction of George Walker's Nothing Sacred was one of the events of this years Shaw Festival.

The best other play seen in Toronto was the almost aggressively modest Matt and Ben, which was also -- under the baton of its original New York director, David Warren -- one of the sharpest productions, never missing a beat or a laugh.

I readily concede that there are more pressing subjects to be considered than the rise to Hollywood stardom of Damon & Affleck Ltd., and that they could well occasion finer, deeper, more searching plays. The trouble is we didnt see any of them. Very likely they weren't being written.

What we got instead was self-importance. The paradigm, if only for its title, may have been Omnium Gatherum, an exchange of pre- packaged positions on the state of the world after 9/11, in which most of the production's and the performers energies were taken up by the technical demands of a revolving dinner-party. That was American.

Our own brand-name playwrights went round in circles: Michael Healey with Rune Arlidge, never dull but never finding its focus; Brad Fraser with Cold Meat Party, intermittently funny and sometimes approaching Joe Orton territory, but not ice-hearted enough to be at home there; Judith Thompson with Capture Me; David S. Young with No Great Mischief (after Alistair Macleod); Deanne Taylor's VideoCabaret show City for Sale. These all had worthy aspirations, as of course do most plays. Nobody sets out to be bad, which makes you wonder why so may companies feel compelled to issue manifestoes proclaiming their good intentions; what do they think everybody else has?

I noticed over the year, as one home-grown would-be epic succeeded another, a family resemblance between the Tarragon, Toronto's most prestigious independent theatre, and the Artword, one of its least: two households both alike in Worthiness.

Worthy one-person plays were, as usual, much in evidence, some of them written by their actors. Two, though, stood above the pack: Daniel MacIvors Cul-de-sac (I cant share the general enthusiasm for his writing, but as a perfomer he's transfixing) more for its riveting performance than its writing, and Rick Miller's Bigger Than Jesus. These shared a director, Daniel Brooks, who is obviously good at this kind of thing. With them should be ranked Ronnie Burketts super-puppet-show Provenance, not his best and sometimes frankly boring, but at other times blindingly brilliant. There were promising writing debuts from two other actors; Marjorie Chan with China Doll and especially Gord Rand with Pond Life.

Worthiness afflicted the musicals, especially Pelagie at CanStage. It even afflicted the commercial musicals, with Terracotta Warriors and The Last Empress teaching us lessons in Asian history but doing very little else. The most sadly newsworthy event of the year was the failure of the blessedly frivolous Hairspray to sustain a commercial run, despite a terrific home-grown cast. Nor did the slightly edgier Urinetown take this town to the extent that was hoped. Cheeringly, though, the best musical did, on its own terms, the best business; the two-handed The Last 5 Years at CanStages second space.

Now to the companies: The most thrilling performance of the year was Ben Carlson's Jack Tanner, matching velocity to verbosity, in the Shaw Festival's Man and Superman. Listening to it was like watching a high-wire act. The show was also a triumph for Neil Munro, a wildly uneven director here in perfect control. The Shaws second most exciting night was another musical, Floyd Collins. Stratford came through with a batch of unfamiliar Shakespeares -- Timon of Athens, Henry VIII, King John, Cymbeline -- and scored with them all, in roughly that order of achievement. It also offered more outstanding female performances than seemed plausible. And, come to think of it, it offered, or completed, the biggest and best new Canadian play, Peter Hintons trilogy The Swanne, which cannot be compared to anything.

Soulpepper offered an unbroken run of good productions but no great ones, making it, according to your angle, either their best or worst season to date. Also, apart from ShakespareWorks, whose inititial production belied their name, it was an unusually good summer for alfresco Shakespeare, with David Ferry's Much Ado about Nothing (in Newmarket) and Daryl Cloran's As You Like It (in Barrie) good by any standards. A word, too, for Marek Norman, who composed totally different scores for both this and the High Park As You and was also the ace MD for The Last Five Years.

2005-01-03-toronto-stage-s-2004-bliss-li:
robertcushman@lycos.com

Here are the stage performances, in and around Toronto, that afforded me the most delight in 2004. It is not a categorical list of the best, which is impossible to quantify; it is an accounting, almost certainly incomplete, of the acting whose memory makes me smile or, in certain cases, tingle.

Martha Henry, Jim Mezon and Michael Ball in Copenhagen, as classy a start as a year could wish

Ronnie Burkett in Provenance, not just his puppeteering but his acting, especially his creation of Miss Pity Beane, spinster (and if his writing was uneven, there were still some virtuoso speeches).

Keira Loughran, lighting up China Doll (and when she moved to Stratford, she showed great promise in King John).

Jane Spidell, a moral centre, in Rune Arlidge.

Yanna McIntosh and Caroline Cave, taking solo turns in, or possibly under, The Syringa Tree.

Blythe Wilson, a musical treat, in The Last Five Years.

Oliver Dennis, at his increasingly-frequent best, in Kite. (Good in Godot, too, and cruelly miscast in Translations.)

Leslie Faulkner, best-actress-new-to-me, a magnetic Monroe surrogate in After the Fall.

And at the Shaw Festival:

Simon Bradbury, squeezing all the juice from the dustmans arias in Pygmalion.

Kevin Bundy, a serene nebbish in Three Men on a Horse (and surprise casting at that).

Kelli Fox, delivering a one-two punch in Rutherford and Son (in which she was excellently partnered by Michael Ball) and Waiting for the Parade (in which she was matched by Laurie Paton). In both, Fox delivered white-hot passion under finger-tip control. Lets admit, or proclaim, that she was the actress of the year. In Toronto, earlier, she'd even been good in the ramshackle Restitution.

Ben Carlson in Man and Superman; for virtuosity, stamina and the audience's sense of being present at a breakthrough, this was the acting event of the year.

Mike Shara in Nothing Sacred, Peter Hutt, star, and Jennifer Phipps, cameo, in Harlequinade; Jay Turvey, Jeff Madden and ensemble in Floyd Collins.

At Stratford, an extraordinary quartet of actresses in or hitting their prime: Lucy Peacock in Macbeth; Diane dAquila in The Swanne, and also in King John; Lally Cadeau in The Human Voice; Seana McKenna in Henry VIII, and also for one sublime double-take in Noises Off.

Not to mention: Peter Donaldson, magnificent in Timon of Athens (and the Shakespeare production of the year); Scott Wentworths gambler in Guys and Dolls and Sheila McCarthy's moll in Anything Goes; Sara Topham's young thing and Barry MacGregors old one in Noises Off; Ron Kennell, plus Martha Henry and ferret, in Cymbeline; Jonathan Goad in King John; Graham Abbey and Walter Borden in Henry VIII.

And at Soulpepper:

William Hutts Vladimir in Waiting for Godot, rackingly conveying the human need for contact and reassurance (and Joseph Ziegler's Pozzo doing the same, though, strangely, only in Act One); William Webster, Andrew Moodie and David Calderisi -- the good, the nice and the nasty -- in Nathan the Wise; Michael Hanrahan (especially fine) and Stuart Hughes in The Dumb Waiter and The Zoo Story; almost everyone in Translations, but especially Diego Matamoros (and did I mention the set?); Kristen Thomson, suddenly finding her best form in the last five minutes of Mirandolina.

Around the parks and elsewhere:

Jane Spence making Phebe, a mall role, the most dynamic character in As You Like It (Barrie), though Benjamin Clost's Touchstone was competition; Christopher Morris making Claudio, an impossible role, the most interesting character in Much Ado About Nothing (Newmarket); Tom Rooney, a boiling Hamlet (Ottawa) and Albert Schultz; a gentle one (Soulpepper).

And back in the metropolis:

In Hairspray -- Jay Brazeau, not quite Harvey Fierstein but few are; Michael Torontow, rescuing the juvenile lead; Jennifer Stewart, a bulls-eye cartoon.

In Urinetown -- David Keely, a cop made out of soap; Jennifer Walser, a witty, wistful waif; Stephen Patterson and Cara Leslie, crucifying the love interest; Spence, again, and Hilary Doyle in Matt and Ben.

Ross Manson in Cold Meat Party; also, Amy Price-Francis, whose British accent (flat Mancunian) was found wanting by many. But what would I know? I only grew up there.

Daniel MacIvor in Cul-de-Sac, and Rick Miller in Bigger than Jesus -- two impeccable solos.

Jordan Pettle, returning to form in Small Returns; Jennifer Dales Genie of the Library, and Adam Brazier's Aladdin, in Aladdin; Matthew Gibson, best-new-actor-to-me, negotiating the minefield of Leontes in The Winter's Tale. And in Vigil, Brent Carver, virtuosically loquacious, and Henry, mostly silent and wholly wonderful.

The most improved and consistent Toronto theatre was the Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People, whom I can now forgive for their cumbersome new name.

2005-01-10-one-fine-day-canadian-writer-:
Trout Stanley runs until Feb. 8 (416-504-9971), Little Dragon until Jan. 30 (416-504-7529) and Bea's Niece until Feb. 6 (416-531-1827).

I was gearing up, through most of a week loaded with unsatisfactory Toronto premieres, to denounce the whole idea of encouraging new Canadian plays as being cruel to audiences. Then at the last moment came Claudia Deys Trout Stanley at the Factory Theatre to blow my ill-humour to smithereens.

Dey, whose language has always been striking and whose dramaturgy has sharpened with every play shes written, here delivers a masterwork. It depicts an outlandish world and makes us believe in it. In remote B.C., somewhere between Grizzly Alley and Misery Junction (names that are apparently as authentic as they're evocative), live Grace and Sugar Ducharme, 30-year-old twin sisters whose parents, referred to as the holy mother and father, died 10 years ago, bequeathing them the town garbage dump.

Grace -- a glamorous figure in thigh-high boots, sky-high hair and provocatively zippered front -- now runs the business single- handed; Sugar has worn her mother's dirty-pink tracksuit every day since becoming orphaned and in all that time has never left the house. She manufactures what she calls "tragic figurines" for which, she says, there is quite a market. Factor in that the twins were meant to be triplets (they call their stillborn sister Duckling) and that the day on which we meet them is their birthday, on which terrible things usually happen.

Sugar is about to end her life of quiet desperation with a rope but is foiled by a male intruder who, despite appearances -- he wears a stolen cop suit -- is probably not the suspected killer of a local stripper-cum-Scrabble-champion. He, too, has lost his parents, but then they treated him appallingly. Among other things they named him Trout Stanley. (Asked about this, he says simply, its a fish name.) Having rescued Sugar, he woos her in one of the funniest and most ecstatic love scenes in recent, or any, memory.

Grace returns bearing a gun, and a three-way battle ensues, in the course of which it becomes clear that Grace, who may not be as liberated as she looks, has engineered Sugars reclusiveness from motives both selfish and concerned. The play turns out to be about love and release. The details may sound Gothic, but there is not a hint of camp. This is simply a play about people who live at extremes, of climate and feeling. The narrative gets a little muddy toward the end, but for the most part it unfolds logically, confidently and surprisingly.

It is also joyously written. Tense, witty verbal duels, in which repetition is a signpost to the characters' desperation and the author's control, erupt into soaring prose arias. The play pays homage to the fierceness that lies around us without ever becoming folksy. It even gets away with fiddle music.

Eda Holmess production is all but faultless, with a great ear for phrasing and eye for placing; Kelly Wolfs set and costumes are delightful and Andrea Lundy's northern-lights lighting is glorious. Melody A. Johnson sometimes has you hunting for her words, especially when they come at the ends of sentences, but she makes even this seem right for Sugar, who in her hands is a perfect compound of woe and wonder. It's hard, too, to imagine any improvement on Michelle Girouxs Grace, who sounds as good as she looks, or on Gord Rands Trout, a shy guy who has made himself bold.

One thing that bodes well for Trout's and Sugar's future together: They both dislike martial arts, finding them "too sudden." This would make them an unsympathetic audience for Keira Loughrans Little Dragon (Passe Muraille), whose Chinese-Canadian heroine, a first-year student at Queens, decides rather late in the play that she is the illegitimate daughter of Bruce Lee. Even before this, she has begun to find her identity through kung-fu and its analogues, all of which are helpfully differentiated.

In Marion de Vries' production, every scene is staged as a martial-arts contest; the fights are directed by Richard Lee, who might well pass for the son of Bruce and in fact gets to play him, or his apparition. The choreography ingeniously underlines the action -- we appreciate just who is kicking who's ass, psychologically speaking -- but over a whole evening it gets to feel mannered. Anyway, the plays first half is a lively though unfocused romp through campus life with race-and-gender undertones; when the main issue arrives, it seems contrived. Loughran is a promising writer and she remains an interesting actress. Strangely awkward at portraying her protagonists conversational life, she excels at bringing her thoughts to the surface. Michelle Polak gives fierce support as a jealous-Jewish-lesbian co-student.

At the Tarragon, third stop on our theatre's Axis of Good Intentions, an evening yet more diffuse: Bea's Niece whose title, apart from being a false rhyme and a false pun, is a false pointer to what David Gows play might be about. Anne (Maria Ricossa), a novelist on a psychiatric ward, does indeed have a wise and wacky Auntie Bea (Patricia Hamilton, minus the proper zaniness) prone to offering worldly advice, e.g., "Scotch, a gun and some opium are the three things you need most to be a lady." Or maybe other-worldly, since she may not really be there; she also doubles, or the actress does, as a female rabbi. But she doesnt seem any more central than does Anne's husband (John Bourgeois), who certainly is dead, or her harried, pregnant shrink (Fiona Highet, floundering), whose fractious relationship with her patient may really be the play's spine. But the characters and their concerns, plus references to the kabbalah, are just dotted about the dialogue as the equivalent literary and religious symbols are dotted about the stage. The play never gets a grip, and so neither does the audience.

Richard Roses production seems little concerned with orchestrating text or performances, but on April Viczkos essence- of-clinical set it does look good, with an especially dashing trompe l'oeil effect, which, coming right at the start, proves the best thing in the evening.

On the heels of Hotel Rwanda, Hollywood's take on Africa's troubles, comes a screening of a new documentary, Liberia: An Uncivil War, by Jonathan Stack and James Brabazon. Part of the ongoing Hot Docs series, Liberia looks at events in the summer of 2003, when rebels in the west African nation, already in control of 70% of the country, stormed Monrovia. Stack stayed in the capital while Brabazon travelled with the rebels, and what emerges is a balanced, terrifying and sad portrait of a once-proud nation in political tatters. Monrovia, settled by freed American slaves in the 1800s, has long considered itself the little brother of America, but since the end of the Cold War in 1989, relations cooled, and by 2003 little aid was forthcoming from the United States. Liberias president, Charles Taylor, promised to step down once peacekeepers arrived, but no one would send them before a ceasefire. The screening will be followed by a Q&A with Stack. A Whistle in the Dark plays until Feb. 5 (416-368-3110); The Bear until ; The Glass Menagerie until Feb. 26 (416-368-3110).; robertcushman@lycos.com

A new group calling itself The Company Theatre gets off to a magnificent start with a show that has everything. A Whistle in the Dark (Berkeley Street Upstairs) is a relentlessly compelling play, 44 years old but new to Canada, given a flawless ensemble production with a great performance at its centre.

Tom Murphy's play, written when he was 24 and at the start of a long career, shows us the Carneys, a patriarchal Irish family, most of whose members are living in England. Their code is one of violence, verbal and physical.

Michael, the eldest son, is trying, like his namesake in The Godfather, to turn his back on it. However, his Coventry home has been invaded by three of his brothers: the hulking Iggy (short for Ignatius), the taciturn Hubert and the flash sardonic Harry, who is borderline psychopathic and, unhappily, a natural leader. They are now joined by two visitors from the old country: the boys dad, an ex-cop who claims, probably rightly, to have made them what they are, and Des, the youngest brother, baby-faced and raring to prove himself.

Looming ahead is a battle with a rival clan of expatriates. Everyone looks forward to it except Michael and his wife Betty, reviled by her in-laws for the double crime of being a woman and English.

On my way out of the theatre, I heard three separate people joking that their own families were just like that. In fact, there are chords here that will resonate with almost anybody. Take away the fists, the knuckledusters and the broken bottles, and the tensions at work here -- the jibes, recriminations, occasional bursts of affection and the incessant jockeying for position -- are universal. There are strands that have to do with the condition of the working-class Irish male c. 1960, but the play goes beyond that. Michael is the emblematic figure of the man struggling to escape his heritage. Nothing that he tries, reasoned protest or accusing silence, seems to work; it merely exacerbates his siblings angry sense that he sets himself above them. As was famously noted by another Irish writer, each man ends up killing the thing he loves, and there are many ways of doing it.

The orchestration of all this, with the narrative excitement inexorably rising, is a prodigious achievement. The language, as one expects of an Irish play, is rich and witty; it is also, as one doesn't always expect, forceful and economic, looking forward to Martin McDonough, rather than back to O'Casey and Synge. (There is no profanity, but the dialogue hits just as hard for all that.) The characters may be mostly thugs, but they are inexhaustibly varied, and one of them is a major creation.

This is the boys DaDa, a timorous windbag posing as the hardest of the hard, and given by Joseph Ziegler what may well be the performance of his career. He is at once immense and delicate, courtly when he first pays his respects to the lady of the house," very funny when he deplores the unhealthy effects of trees ("all that carbon dioxide"), piteous when in his cups and revealing the depths of his own desperation, scarifying when he climbs on a chair to play the sentimental tyrant. Most terrible of all, and most brilliantly revealed by the actor, is his ability to shut out any fact or argument he doesnt want to hear, right down, in a moment of blackest comedy, to the play's climax.

The producers have imported an Irish director, Jason Byrne, whose work is a revelation. This is the tightest yet richest production imaginable, with not a move or word wasted, and every performance crammed to the limit. Michael is Jonathan Goad, who finds the right mind and stance for the role and has the perfect name. No character has ever been more pitilessly goaded, by himself and by others. Sarah Dodd plays his wife with a fine blend of pity and anger and a perfect sense of time and place. David Jansen is creepy and amusing as a Carney hanger-on, Oliver Becker brings weight and an occasional disconcerting gentleness to Iggy and Aaron Poole endows Hubert with a smile that's the visual equivalent of a snarl.

The remaining brothers are played by Company Theatres two artistic directors; Philip Riccio is the baby-faced Des and Allan Hawco the magnetically dangerous Harry, loaded with discontent. These are the two most unpredictable characters in the play, because one of them has the glimmerings of a conscience and the other hasnt. One doesn't know, either, what else this company has in store, but it has made the most stunning debut since Soulpepper's Don Carlos. It may even, judging by its aesthetic and by much of its casting, be Son of Soulpepper.

Also highly recommended: The Bear, Chekhovs one-act farce about the boorish landowner who comes to collect a debt from a widow and ends up collecting her instead. (Its an old story; the Romans had a word for it, if not the Greeks.) This is given in the Grange Room, a beautiful if defiantly un-Russian chamber at the AGO. Christopher Morris' production is boisterous, inventive and adventurous; Madame's first appearance is a scream. It is also surprisingly delicate; this is Chekhov, after all, and David Ferry is touching as well as hilarious when, against all his wishes and in defiance of his own best interests, he finds his misogyny melting. His lady (Nicole St. Martin) is less accomplished, but still tears some delicious strips off the memory of her late unlamented.

Coming down some steep steps: The Glass Menagerie (Berkeley Street Downstairs) has most of the musical and atmospheric trappings that Tennessee Williams specified, but in Chris Abrahams production they come off more doomy than delicate. There are also audibility problems, due to a yawning set and some exaggerated accents. Rosemary Dunsmores maternal belle is the hardest to hear and also the hardest to take, making the woman so terrible a nag that the collapse of her dreams has no emotional impact, which means that the play doesn't, either. As the withdrawn daughter Laura, Michelle Monteith similarly overdoes the wan and winsome, but she is touching in the scene with her Gentleman Caller, whom Seann Gallagher makes the most likeable character in the play. Williams may have intended us to deplore his breezy philistinism but, in this hot-house atmosphere, it comes as a relief. Ironically, too, this caller is a gentleman; he smashes fragile glass unicorns and more fragile feelings, but he's genuinely sorry about it.

2005-01-26-a-loving-labour-but-with-its-:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Love's Labour's Lost at the NAC until Jan. 29 (613-755-1111). 'da Kink In My Hair runs to Feb. 27 at the Princess of Wales Theatre (416-872-1212).

NAC production misses the details, while 'da Kink needs filling out

Marti Maraden, outgoing director of the National Arts Centre's English Theatre, has recruited an extraordinary number of our best actors, including at least four of my personal top 20, for her valedictory Shakespeare, Love's Labour's Lost. Unhappily, the whole doesn't amount to more than the sum of the parts, which means, by cruel theatrical arithmetic, that it adds up to less.

This early comedy, a word-drunk piece trying to get sober, is magical but tricky. As a pastoral it needs a sense of place, which isn't achieved here by a platform set built from anonymous timbers and a louring backcloth dotted with strange shapes, neither of which suggest parkland or much of anything else, except perhaps dead fish. John Pennoyer has also designed 18th-century costumes that are elaborate but, especially for the women, constricting.

The themes and relationships are accurately sketched in but not fleshed out for the most part. There is, tonally speaking, insufficient light and insufficient shade, and little of the speed with which one keeps giving place to the other. Juan Chioran comes off best as Don Armado, knight of the bedraggled countenance; the mournful Hispanic accent gives him, of course, no trouble, but it does sometimes seem to be taking over the characterization. Ben Carlson has all the pace, energy and intelligence for the jesting Berowne, and it's a pleasure to hear him phrase the big speeches; but he misses out on the sheer glee of self-mockery when he, too, falls in love.

There are also surprisingly few sparks between him and his dark lady Rosaline, played by Yanna McIntosh. Casting a black actress in this role sounds intriguing but works out awkwardly. When Berowne's friends cast aspersions on his lady's complexion, by which they textually mean just her hair and her eyes, they sound not merely rude but racist. It's especially perplexing since the arch-mocker (Nigel Shawn Williams as the King of Navarre) is himself black. Maybe some comment is being made on intra-racial prejudice, but I rather doubt it. Colour-blind casting and colour-specific casting seem here to have collided. Of course one wants to see McIntosh in Shakespeare, but I doubt if Rosaline, an underwritten joker, is her part, any more than Kelli Fox is a natural for the Princess of France, whom she plays with a charming but unvaried smile. I would like to see these two gifted actresses exchange roles.

The veteran David William makes a properly courtly, if excessively detached, Boyet; Peter Froehlich and David Schurmann make little of the pedants' cross-talk act but have nice moments, of confusion and rebuke respectively, in the concluding show of the Nine Worthies. The whole production, indeed, perks up in its last movement, which is the acme of bittersweet. The messenger of death makes his infallible effect, allowing Fox to play naked pain, which she does superbly, and McIntosh to administer an extra silent sting in the play's tail. And the song of the Owl and the Cuckoo has been beautifully set by Marc Desormeaux, with its verses cunningly distributed among the players. This, if nothing else, is a labour won.

The last show that Ed and David Mirvish presented at the Princess of Wales was Hairspray. They have now replaced it there with another hirsute extravaganza. This suggests a consistency of vision usually deemed rare among commercial managements, and we should acknowledge it.

By all accounts 'da Kink in My Hair was extravagant only in spirit when it made its bow two years ago on the Toronto fringe, and when it subsequently appeared at Theatre Passe Muraille. It was a homely, rambling comedy-drama about a Toronto hair salon with an exclusively black, and exclusively female, staff and clientele. Cheerful enough on the outside, it got its real grip by allowing the customers to deliver a series of monologues that celebrated the joys of life while detailing the stark odds against them, in the shape of prejudice and cruelty both without and within their own community.

The pattern is still there, but it has been complicated by the producers' turning the show into a musical. This in itself is a very good idea; and it has obviously been carried out with the enthusiastic co-operation of the author, Trey Anthony, and her director Weyni Mengesha, who has herself supplied music and lyrics. It has not, though, been carried far enough; the numbers are good, and excellently performed, but there are too few of them to create a style. Nor has much thought been given to the way they affect the rest of the show which goes on as if it hadn't been informed about the changes.

A musical can afford even less than a play to waste time, or to stop and take deep breaths. We now notice how thin the connecting scenes in the salon are. The author herself plays the proprietress, and is very warm and entertaining, though she seems happier talking to the audience than to the other characters. But then, apart from some funny business over botched take-out orders for lunch, she hasn't given herself much to do except to be welcoming. She's everybody's confidante, but she apparently isn't meant to hear the other characters' deepest revelations. So there's neither contact nor conflict; the women merely come and go.

The confessors, all well played, include an elderly woman joyfully re-discovering sex with a neighbour, a career-woman who, in order to prove herself, is running dangerously on empty, a movie- star returning to the old neighbourhood and letting us know about her lesbianism (this sequence is the most forced, as if the show had suddenly decided that it was being way too heterosexual and had better get more inclusive) and a church-sister who has lost her son to schoolyard violence. This last is the most painful, but not altogether for the right reasons. It's too raw a situation to be trotted out and then discarded. It feels formulaic.

That doesn't stop it feeling real, as do most of the stories. This is a rare example of our city's inhabitants getting to state their case on a big stage. More music, and better musical staging, might turn it from a series of fragments into the rich social tapestry it needs and deserves to be. More imaginative design might make the salon itself into a glistening image of community rather than the arbitrary setting it now seems. (Both the dialogue and the program notes affix symbolic value to hair, but you have to take their word for it.) At the moment, the alternation of songs and monologues makes for a half-baked Chorus Line without the overriding suspense.

One speech, and one performance, take the show to a different dimension. The last soliloquy comes from a Jamaican girl, recently arrived, whose openness first wins our heart ("why Canada so cold?" she asks with enchanting plaintiveness), then breaks it with a harrowing tale of family abuse, then warms it again with hope. The role is played by d'bi.young, who inhabits each of its moods so completely as to make you feel in the presence of a new major actress. Her speech melts into an ensemble number and, this time, that's the wrong decision. She deserves her own space and her own applause.

robertcushman@lycos.com; Take Me Out runs until Feb. 12 at the Bluma Appel Theatre, 27 Front St. E., 416-368-3110.

Clever baseball play's structure just seems out of whack

Never really hits it out of the parkYou would expect a play called Take Me Out to have something to do with baseball, and in the case of the new show at the Bluma Appel, your expectations would be correct. But there is, of course, more than one kind of outing, and the action here is set in motion when the star player of a U.S. team publicly declares himself to be gay.

Hold those thoughts and add another. To take somebody out can also mean to dispose of him, and this story does involve slaughter on the diamond. (And you thought hockey was a rough game.) That makes the title a triple pun. Im impressed.

Im also confused as to what the piece's real subject might be. Not that there's anything confusing about the narrative: Richard Greenbergs play, a Tony winner in 2003, has great drive, much humour and hardly a dull moment, and the CanStage production (which introduces Toronto to one of the most prolific and successful of current American dramatists) honours all those virtues.

It is also, like so many garlanded Broadway (and off-Broadway) plays, a bit glib and brittle, with characters who can be unnaturally articulate. Just to make things more complicated, it seems aware of these tendencies and concerned to avoid them. It raises some painful issues and it seems wary of making them pretexts for platitudes, but in doing this it ends up ignoring them. Pain -- as opposed to lyrical regret -- has no place in its last scene. The most obvious of its titles meanings turns out, if only by default, to be the important one. At its core, the play is a celebration of the game. Life's a mess; let's play ball.

Darren Lemming, the player who comes out and who, despite his surname, seems anything but self-destructive, is black as well as gay -- half-black, anyway. He is also supremely confident (people say he behaves as if he were God, and he doesnt contradict them), having gone through life hitherto without encountering any kind of discrimination; this, as his adoring financial advisor tells him, makes him an extraordinarily fortunate person, a statistical freak.

At first his luck seems likely to hold. His teammates take his declaration in stride, though their behaviour toward him in the showers begins subtly to alter. (The play is punctuated with shower scenes. I hope theres a warm-water clause, as well as a nudity clause, in the actors' contracts.)

The antagonism gets less subtle when a spectacular new pitcher arrives, an uncouth orphan named Shane Mungitt, from one of three redneck states -- he isn't sure which. He gives an interview to the press, full of abusive references to the kind of guy hes now expected to share a locker room with, and is suspended. After making a public apology, hes allowed back. But things only get worse.

It's a possible virtue in the play that Darren, far from being a noble martyr, is not very likeable. It's a definite flaw that he isnt very interesting, either, and that his crucial relationship with an old buddy, a player of equal talent who shines as a bigger star by virtue of playing on a lesser team, never comes to life.

This opacity is reflected in the performance of Thom Allison, whose surface assurance shows little sign that things might be churning underneath. Nothing much, in writing or acting, seems to be going on inside Darren; hes all smooth declaration.

Shane, by contrast, the racist homophobe (words much too big for him), is full of sullen life and loaded with motivation; he had a horrendous childhood, and baseball has been his lifeline. Mike Shara plays him with electrifying conviction as a mix of rugged resentment and blank incomprehension. Making us understand the bad guy is a laudable dramatic aim, but here the author's very success paints him into a corner. On the face of it, Darren and Shane are the prime antagonists, but the play more or less abandons any conflict between them. They have, after all, nothing to say to one another.

To be fair, this point is very well and wittily made in a late scene in which the two are brought together by a third player, name of Kippy, who talks as if he had wandered on to the field out of a library, which indeed proves to be the case. (He claims to have been a late developer, baseball-wise, and here he is playing on a major team. I've no idea how credible this really is, but I had trouble believing it.)

Kippy tries to build bridges; to make Shane, for instance, understand the subtle differences between calling someone a coloured person and "a person of colour." He doesnt get very far. Kippy is for much of the time the plays narrator, its puzzled mouthpiece, though he, too, fades before the end. While he's around he is, in Matthew Macfazdean's earnest and beaming performance, excellent value. Its significant, though, that a character so peripheral to the plot should loom so large in the play.

The same goes for Darrens money man, a repressed soul who is turned, by having a ballplayer as a client, into a rabid fan. David Storch is brilliant, twisting and turning through ecstasies of vocal and physical discovery. In discovering baseball he becomes part of America; and if the play is indeed a celebration of the game, then he, the outsider, is its prime celebrant. He has half of the final scene and all of its final moment. For practical purposes, his is the star performance. He does not, however, get a star curtain call, though two other actors do. I cite this as external evidence that the play's structure is out of whack.

As a further bonus we get Randy Hughson exercising his talent for rapid-fire good-humoured exasperation as the team manager. Morris Panych directs with what, borrowing from a song, I will fall back on calling his usual flair. And Ken MacDonald, placing the world within a locker room, designs with his.

The production is of comparable, though not identical, quality to that of A Whistle in the Dark; it falls short mainly because the play does. Where the Irish play is fierce and undeviating, the American is, at the crunch, wavering and sentimental. Both, though, are very funny. Among other things.

2005-02-05-making-sense-of-the-merchant-:
robertcushman@lycos.com

There are two Shakespeare plays that deal with race, and both of them are set, at least partly, in Venice. Othello begins there and then moves speedily to Cyprus; that island, though, was a Venetian colony and the city-state's politics are never left far behind. The Merchant of Venice switches throughout its length between Venice itself and a place, of uncertain geographical provenance, called Belmont

Belmont is a fairy-tale spot, and you might say the same for most of the settings of Shakespeares comedies, even the ones with recognizable names. Theyre nearly all in Italy, a place that for Elizabethan England combined the attractions of accessibility and exoticism. If you could afford it, you took a trip there. If you were among the majority who couldn't, you stayed home, read romances, watched plays or maybe wrote them. The towns Shakespeare fantasized about seem to have been interchangeable; he named them Padua, Verona, Milan or Messina, according to his whim or source material, but he hardly bothered to research their differences.

Venice was something else. (So was Rome, but the dramatists, beneficiaries of a firm classical education, reserved that location for tragedies.) Venice was a world power, political and economic, the first great mercantile state, maybe the first melting pot. If you wrote about it, and especially about its merchant class, you were dealing with contemporary reality. You were specific. You mentioned gondolas. You mentioned the Rialto, with some knowledge of both where and what it was. You showed awareness of the city's dependence on foreign trade and its consequent prickly relationship with its own resident aliens.

In his fine new film of The Merchant of Venice, Michael Radford has seized on this. He naturally shot his Venetian scenes in Venice, capitalizing on that places timeless capacity for looking like itself. (Anyone whos been there will know what I mean. It's like being on the stage of a play set in Venice.) And, approaching the play's most notorious problem head-on, he starts with captions filling us in on the position of the Jews in Venice in 1596, which is as good a date as any for the plays composition. He tells us about ghettoes and curfews and about the Jews being forced to make their living as usurers and to wear red hats as if they were, well, yellow stars.

Here he goes in some respects beyond Shakespeare, who mentions none of these things, though he may (unconsciously?) imply them. The play does, however, tell us just how good Christians were accustomed to behave toward Jews when they met them on the street (or on a bridge over a canal): They jeered and spat at them. Here we see Jeremy Irons's Antonio doing just that to Al Pacino's Shylock, which is slightly -- though only slightly -- more disturbing than hearing about it. A Shakespeare film, even more than a stage production, is necessarily a comment on the play. Radford makes his comment by providing a context, one in which people buy and sell and walk about and bring their lines to recognizable life. We see the characters anti-Semitism, and maybe the plays, as a moment in history. That doesn't let anyone off the hook, but it does lend a clearer view.

I'm a traditional humanist on this. I think the play makes perfect sense if Shylock is taken as pure villain, who deserves to be robbed of faith and daughter and ducats, but it isnt a sense I would want to sit through. Meanwhile, I cling to the idea that in drawing him (again unconsciously?) from the inside, Shakespeare made Shylock comprehensible and, to a degree, sympathetic. Shylocks villainy is, in any case, on a far smaller scale than that of Barabas in Christopher Marlowe's cartoon tragedy The Jew of Malta, but that only makes him more disturbing and, in the history of anti- Semitism, more dangerous. You don't believe in Barabas. You do believe in Shylock. I certainly agree with the Canadian Jewish Congress that The Merchant shouldnt be taught in schools until the students, too, are able to contextualize.

Pacinos Shylock, ethnically unassailable (The thing about Italian families, according to Kaye Ballard, who came from one, "is they're so Jewish"), is a masterly portrait of suffering and ancient grudge (a line the movie cuts) hardening into implacability. The most eloquent case this Shylock makes is not "hath not a Jew eyes?" but his speech at the trial, vitriolic and exquisitely reasoned, calling Venetian society on its ownership of slaves. This, too, is the kind of specific historical matter you don't find in the other comedies. (And Radford has a black halberdier standing by to underline the point.) In some ways, though, the most interesting performance is Ironss Antonio, whose melancholy is all down to his love for the lightweight Bassanio (Joseph Fiennes is very lightweight); borrowing from Shylock to finance his friends wooing of Portia, Irons seems almost to be courting martyrdom. There is nothing new in this interpretation, but I have never seen it given so much presence, maybe because I've never before seen Antonio played by a star.

Nor have I ever seen his incipient immolation so powerfully staged, the victim bound to a chair to surrender his pound of flesh. The tension of the trial is screwed to the uttermost. One is left with a feeling of unacknowledged kinship between Shylock and Antonio (either of whom might theoretically be the title character); both doomed outsiders, they are the biggest men in Venice. In a more rational world they might be friends.

The theme is pursued into the last scene at Belmont, which is not the anticlimax it has generally been reckoned. (Belmont is played by Luxembourg, which doesn't look like itself.)

The lovers have had their spat over the rings that were meant to be pledges of everlasting love. Lynn Collinss Portia, hitherto more powerful in Venice than at home, says she will give Bassanio a new ring, and asks Antonio to hand it to him, making him the agent of his own emotional undoing. She had always seemed a touch jealous of her husbands friend, even while saving his life; now she has both men where she wants them.

Most productions in my experience have ended with one character left alone on stage: either Antonio or Shylock's daughter, Jessica, now married and Christian. She, too, is fondling a ring, the very turquoise that Shylock's friend Tubal (the admirable Allan Cordunner) had said she exchanged for a monkey. Was he lying? Misinformed? One would like to know.

Either way, Jessica has been snubbed by the other Gentiles, even though she is now theoretically one of the goodies. Even Shylocks enforced baptism may well have been viewed by the Elizabethans as a happy ending for him, though the film certainly doesnt see it that way. I lied when I said The Merchant is about race: Its conflicts and prejudices are all religious. But of course one easily blurs into the other. The Nazis burned scrolls and synagogues; they burned converted Jews as well.

You don't need modern dress to make the point. Radford makes it, very powerfully, by going precisely in the opposite direction.

Color Photo: Sony Pictures Classics / The enforced baptism of Shylock, played by Al Pacino in Michael Radford's film, may have been viewed by Elizabethan audiences as a happy ending for the Jewish character, but the movie doesn't see it that way.

robertcushman@lycos.com

From its panting title on down, Poochwater (Theatre Passe Muraille) is a mangy dog of a piece. It was first seen at the Toronto Fringe Festival, and it returns to town bearing Dora awards and four-star reviews. This is the kind of funny thing that happens on the way from the Fringe, where plays with mild appeal stand out from others with no appeal whatever.

There are a couple of appealing ideas rattling around in Mike McPhaden's play, but they do no more than rattle. It starts with a man coming into a ratty apartment intent on returning a wallet he has discovered in a park and whose contents declare it to be the property of a Mr. Martin Poochwater. Mr P. is apparently out, so his benefactor, a meticulous and ingenuous type, prepares to leave him a long letter of explanation. When he comes, however, to sign it, he finds he cannot remember his own name. The apartments owner returns and, discovering a stranger on the premises, makes a belligerent citizens arrest, using a neighbouring old lady's cane as enforcement.

The locale is a U.S. city, soon after the end of the Second World War. At one point there is a power failure. The two men, cast into darkness, find that as ex-GIs they can converse in Morse code, and the realization causes them to drop their antagonism and become, cautiously, buddies. This is a sweet sequence, certainly the best in the play. Otherwise, the choice of time and place seems gratuitous. The publicity material makes claims about the play showing a turning point in the history of America, but to transfer this to the text itself is really to take the will for the deed. A few hints are dropped about Americans' consuming religiosity, but none of them is specific to the period.

The 1940s setting is also supposed to dictate a bold performing style, deriving from the films of the period. Im glad they told me that, because otherwise I might have maligned the performances by describing them as oversimplified. The author himself plays the intruder, whom he makes both google-eyed and google-mouthed, and Jeff Miller is his rough-and-ready-but-good-hearted assailant. They arent bad but they are certainly insistent, not to mention loud.

There is one narrative revelation, which can be seen coming a long way off. To be fair, I don't think it's meant as a surprise. The first intimation of memory loss is powerful. This man, who can remember most other things, has forfeited his identity. Its a universal nightmare, and our stomachs lurch in sympathy with his. But the feeling dissipates as the writing becomes irrepressibly cute.

Our hero likes to see his life as a series of equations, which he scrawls on the apartment door. His host storms at the vandalism, and we agree with him, though maybe not for the same reasons. The real objection is that, though the writing-on-the-wall gag is all right the first time, it goes on, and on, and on. The show, which apparently first clocked in at 40 minutes, now runs for 70. Thats another funny thing that happens to plays on their way from the Fringe.

- Poochwater runs until Feb. 27 at Theatre Passe Muraille, 16 Ryerson Ave., 416-504-7529.

- - -

Poochwater's choice of time frame at least allows for the introductory playing of some nostalgic period records -- from the war itself rather than its aftermath. But then, the two characters are themselves inclined to nostalgia.

This leads me to a more exotic fringe, the one inhabited by those popular singers who partake of both cabaret and jazz. The best of them specialize in the intelligent reshaping of familiar songs, thinking them through, without obvious fireworks, and emerging with something fresh and touching.

A recent recorded example is Eric Comstock's singing of Imagination, with its whimsically conversational Johnny Burke lyric (and matching Jimmy Van Heusen melody). This occurs on No One Knows (Harbinger), a remarkably refreshing album that announces something rare: the presence in the genre of a young male singer whos worth taking seriously.

Comstock is a New York singer-pianist with a talent for landing on the right unexpected word and making it sound logical. He seems to have shed what was previously a nondescript preppiness. His voice is still light but it has body and it takes him to most of the places he wants to go. He can swing, crisply and modestly (like the young Jack Jones of the 1960s, before his style got bloated). His rhythm lets him rescue a potentially maudlin song like To the Ends of the Earth.

His repertoire is very impressive; it streches beyond the standard suspects to Paul Simon and Oscar Brown, Jr. He has even, most rarely in these latitudes, found an interesting new song, Easy on the Heart, with music by Charlie Haden and coherent words by Arthur Hamilton, the man who wrote Cry Me a River and who knows how to explore a conceit rather than exhaust it.

Even better is Comstocks title track, a magical discovery of a song by Billy Strayhorn, Duke Ellington's cohort, that, indeed, No One Knew.

There are misses: Ellington's Dont Get Around Much Anymore, whatever its lyric seems to say, does not work as a slow ballad. Making a march of If I Had My Druthers, a song in praise of laziness, is a joke that just seems perverse. (And given the speed he goes at, Comstock might at least have included more of Johnny Mercers lyrics.) Mostly, though, either doing lost-love songs or lost-in-love songs, Comstock is excellent. Superb musicians (Wycliffe Gordon and Frank Wess) offer rich support.

Carol Sloane's Whisper Sweet (High Note) is also named after a rare song, by the great stride pianist James P. Johnson. It includes the wonderful injunction be persuasive," which is what Sloane does, though she doesn't so much whisper as murmur sweet. But its a full- blooded murmur, and may be the most beautiful vocal sound anyone is making in jazz at the moment.

She can navigate the testing vocal line of My One and Only Love unaccompanied and not sound as if shes showing off. Where or When conveys its message of deja vu with insinuating urgency and runs to a very creative second chorus whose melodic variations still tell a story. The wistful This Time the Dream's on Me is taken at an unusually brisk tempo, with the magisterial Norman Simmons playing super-saloon piano. Sloane's seamless phrasing makes the implicit pain sound casual and offhand but nonetheless real.

For so thoughtful a singer, she can be cavalier with lyrics: What promises to be a definitive reading of The Night We Called It a Day is maimed when she reverses the meaning of the songs entire middle section, and her inaccuracies on Heres That Rainy Day (Burke and Van Heusen again) are hair-raising or, to purists, hair-tearing. Otherwise, this is a perfect disc -- the reigning singer in the field at the height of her powers.
