2005-02-12-mamma-mia:
Royal Alexandra Theatre - 260 King St. W. - 416-872-1212

The score for Mamma Mia! is drawn from ABBA hits of the '70s, and in this production they are shoehorned into a story that in no way concerns them. Instead, the musical's script raises issues about marriage and parenthood, and ends in a lame reprise of most of ABBA's hits: a pop concert, in fact. But for nearly five years now, the audience has been greeting each song with a thunderous clap of recognition. Not only do they applaud; they laugh. Indefinite run.
2005-02-17-shaw-fest-takes-the-american-:
Even enthusiasts of American musicals can have their doubts about the extent to which they have taken over the classical theatres in Canada, just as they already had in the U.K. (Not, ironically, in the United States, which doesn't have a classical theatre.) So the appearance of a musical on the mainstage of the Shaw Festival (1- 800-511-7429) -- which has previously kept them pocket-sized -- may be regarded as a two-edged sword. Still, the show itself is one of the best: Gypsy, lyrics by Stephen Sondheim and book by Arthur Laurents. Nora McLellan, who has given good Ethel Merman in the past, takes on the Merm's greatest role, the archetypal battleaxe stage mother, in a production by Jackie Maxwell. There's a smaller show as well, the return, from two seasons ago, of the Bertolt Brecht-Kurt Weill Happy End, German of course but set in an imaginary U.S., with some of the duo's best songs, if hardly their best script. Stratford (1-800-567-1600), meanwhile, offers another Sondheim, the festival's first attempt at a show for which he wrote both music and lyrics, the late masterpiece Into the Woods. More populistically, if there is such a word, there's Hello Dolly, which Noel Coward memorably described as a show he didn't like but hugely enjoyed. It's a common reaction. Dolly herself is usually cast with a personality whose mere appearance at the top of that staircase gets the crowd cheering. But the show is based on a distinguished play (The Matchmaker), and Stratford has cast a real actress-who- can-sing, Lucy Peacock. This may be a first. It should certainly be an event.

Color Photo: Into the Woods.
2005-02-19-autobiographical-explosion-of:
Poor Alex Threatre, 296 Brunswick Ave., box office 905-881-6546. Until Feb. 26.

Tick, Tick ... Boom! driven by its songs rather than story

Certain theatres, even some that are strictly for rent, with no overall artistic direction, develop identities. They have good or bad karma. The Poor Alex, cramped and intimate, is one of those with good. I dont recall ever seeing a bad show there. Tick, Tick ... Boom! keeps up the standard.

The show is a fascinating fragment, the fascination deriving from its proximity to a much better-known work by the same writer. Jonathan Larson is the lyricist and composer who wrote Rent. He devised this piece, in 1990, while waiting for that break, or for any break. Its autobiographical, and it's all about his fear and frustration at the prospect of turning 30 without having got anywhere. As all the world knows, he died on the very day he seemed meant to get there, the day Rent was due to open. The rest is history that he never got to see. Watching Rent with that in mind is poignant enough. Seeing Larson's own story is doubly or triply so.

Tick, Tick ... Boom! (the title refers to the countdown to an explosion threatening within the protagonists head) is not what youd call a sturdy piece. Larson wrote it for himself to perform, just songs on a linking thread of monologue. After his death, David Auburn (the playwright of Proof) reshuffled the bits and turned the show into a three-hander. There is still the hero, Jon, trying to blend Broadway and rock in a new musical that would do justice to both; meanwhile, wouldn't you know, he waits tables. There is now Susan, his girlfriend, a dancer turned dance teacher, who wants to leave New York and take Jon with her. There is also Michael, Jon's boyhood friend and cold-water flatmate, who has given up an acting career for something in marketing. With a new apartment and a BMW, he seems well on the way to becoming one of the yuppie scum who are excoriated in Rent, though hes treated a lot more sympathetically. For one thing, hes gay, which in a Larson show is enough in itself to put you on the side of the angels (or at least of the Angels in America).

What happens between and around these three is thin and predictable, but there is an overall impetus deriving from the impending workshop of Jon's musical, Superbia (in fact, an unproduced Larson title). It happens, it's liked and it leaves its composer wondering what now, which is very much like life. (The show is pronounced too rocky for Broadway, too big for Off). But at least he has something to celebrate on his 30th birthday. In real life, Rent is still six years off.

What makes the show, though, is the songs. The tunes, with a couple of exceptions, are at least as driving, infectious and melodic as anything in Rent, and the lyrics are noticeably better. For one thing, they have humour, something lacking in Rent (except perhaps for Tango: Maureen). For another, there is no portentous recitative. The script may be slight, but it serves to keep the songs from falling over one another. There is a lovely, sexy thing titled Green Green Dress, and another titled Why that Jon sings about himself and Michael, which is poignant, witty and specific: "When I was sixteen/Michael and I/Got parts in West Side/At White Plains High./Three oclock, went to rehearse/In the gym./Mike played Doc -- who didnt sing --/Fine with him." Note how easily and pointedly the rhymes fall. There aren't many rock scores you can say that about.

The reference to West Side Story, lyrics by Stephen Sondheim, is no accident. Sondheim, Jon's idol and mentor as he was Larsons, is the shows fourth character, though he remains offstage. His voice, the genuine article, is heard on an answering machine toward the end, and it's touching. He's also all over the score, in the form of homage and plain, though maybe unconscious, borrowing. A song titled Sunday is a hilarious spoof of its namesake anthem in Sunday in the Park with George, though its not about Art but about Brunch. A ballad starts off like Send In the Clowns; a tongue-twisting argument number recalls the virtuoso Your Fault in Into the Woods, but then goes off at breakneck speed in its own direction, which happens to be Country.

And the whole birthday motif in the plot is reminiscent of Company.

That doesnt make Larson a copycat; he just knew to steal from the best. One dialogue scene finds Jon wandering among the alien corn (i.e. Les Mis posters) on Broadway, and lamenting that theatre music is still 60 years behind the times. This isn't true. For better or worse, there's no new music on Broadway now that could have been heard there, or anywhere, in 1930 or even in 1950. That very much includes Sondheim, however traditional his craftsmanship. That craft was his greatest gift to Larson, who never equalled it but might have done, and meantime had his own energy. He was especially good, as in the opening numbers of both his shows, at fury.

The Toronto production, by a new group called Getting Up, isnt great. Mario DAlmonte's direction is sluggish, and the design unimaginative. Dean Armstrong is initially too pixieish for Jon's desperation, but he grabs hold of it in the crucial workshop scene and never lets go. Daphne Moens is miscast, physically and vocally, but Michael Dufays has charm as Mike.

The songs still sound good, though they sound better on the New York cast CD. Larson at his death was one year younger than George Gershwin when he died. They both brought outside forms, rock and jazz, to Broadway, in bastardized form, of course, but the theatre is always a bastard. Im not about to compare them in terms of quality, but the quantity bears thinking about. Think of the dozens of shows Gershwin put out in his lifetime, and the one that was all Larson could manage. The system has broken down: Thats really what Tick, Tick ... Boom! is about. Anyway, to adapt John O'Hara, Jonathan Larson died on Jan. 25, 1996. I don't see any way of not believing it, but I still feel cheated.

Color Photo: Mark Uhre, Mitchell Marcus / Dean Armstrong takes time to warm up to the lead role but hits the right notes after the workshop scene.
2005-02-24-videocabaret-makes-riel-impac:
Video Cabaret shows usually feature around a half-a-dozen actors but look -- with their short scenes and quick-change black-box stagings -- as if they have casts of thousands. Of course, these days half a dozen might as well be a cast of thousands. The latest re-staged instalment in Michael Hollinsgworth's tragic-comic-strip History of Canada is The Red River Rebellion (Cameron House, to March 20) with Louis Riel, Wifred Laurier and John A. Macdonald among those caught in VidCab's invariably unflattering light. Other recent Toronto arrivals are small-scale and make no bones about it. Cast Iron (Tarragon Extra Space, to March 13), written by Lisa Codrington and performed by Alison Sealy--Smith, presents the memories of a woman from Barbados dying in a nursing-home in Winnipeg. It's a joint production by Nightwood (women's theatre) and Obsidian (black theatre). Question: does this make it twice as specialized, or only half? There are two speaking actors (and a third who's almost mute) in "Pinter & Pirandello" (Artword, to March 6), which is not an imaginary confrontation but a double-bill in which each half concerns love, jealousy and fantasy. Pinter's The Lover is the better-known piece, originally as a TV play (it still bears the traces); Pirandello's I'm Dreaming, But Am I? will be new to all but experts, though its title would, of course, fit nearly everything its author ever wrote.

2005-02-25-from-steam-to-shakespeare-tom:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Robert Cushman, theatre critic for the National Post, is the author of Fifty Seasons at Stratford.; Profile of Tom Patterson.

Tom Patterson jump-started the history of theatre in this country, even though he had no such thing in mind. It's tempting to say that this is a very Canadian state of affairs, but in fact its the way things seem to work all over.

In 1951, Patterson was a trade-magazine journalist who saw his hometown of Stratford, Ont., in economic decline. Its major industry -- steam train repair -- had closed down, a victim of technological progress. Patterson decided that one thing that might replace it was tourism, and that Stratfords greatest asset in this regard was its name. After all, the town wasn't just Stratford; it was Stratford on a River Avon, with swans. It cried out for a Shakespeare festival.

Patterson's initial idea was to present a single Shakespeare play, alfresco, in a bandshell down by the water. That it came to more than that was due to the coincidence of Pattersons dream with that of Tyrone Guthrie. Guthrie, the leading Shakespearean director of the mid-20th century, had long felt that the plays needed to break free form proscenium stages and onto platforms that had the freedom, though not necessarily the exact dimensions, of the Elizabethan theatre. He had been experimenting in Britain and elsewhere with makeshift open stages; now he made a purpose-built platform the condition of his coming to Canada as first director of the Stratford Festival. And so that it might be big enough to call itself a festival, he insisted on a program of two plays.

Patterson went to Guthrie because he couldnt get Laurence Olivier. He had sold some remarkably far-sighted city fathers on his idea, and they had funded a trip to New York where Olivier was then working. Patterson failed to meet him but he had proved, not least to himself, that he was prepared to go to the top.

He phoned Guthrie at his home in Ireland, and found himself talking to the one man both bold and humble enough to hop on a plane and check out the mad ambition of some amateur he had never met. By the end of his trip it was agreed between them that Stratford would have its festival with Guthrie directing. It opened in 1953. Two years from inception to completion is astonishingly quick progress.

Guthrie brought with him a designer, Tanya Moiseiwitsch, some technicians and four actors, including two stars, Alec Guinness and Irene Worth. Everyone else involved was Canadian. It was a big company and a good one; two of its members, William Hutt and William Needles, will be in this year's Stratford company. Most of them had been working mainly as amateurs or in radio. There was, at that point, hardly any English-speaking professional theatre in Canada.

Moiseiwitsch's new stage, surrounded by a circus tent for its first four years and by a concrete structure thereafter, was to influence theatre architecture all over the world. Meanwhile the company itself inspired the formation of other companies, other festivals, other regional centres, across Canada. It eventually led to the birth of new Canadian playwriting.

Of course, the influence wasnt always acknowledged. In many quarters it was actually resented. But even the opposition took shape within the theatrical world that Stratford built. And everyone present at that first night in 1953, knew they were in at the birth of something more than a single theatre.

One of those bitten was Patterson himself. For publicity purposes Guthrie fostered a myth that Patterson had been inspired by his visits to European classical theatres while on wartime military service. In fact he had barely visited a theatre and had never seen or read a Shakespeare play. It seems that like some other pioneers (Lilian Baylis, for example, the Edwardian philanthropist who created Londons Old Vic, and who was Guthrie's own mentor) he fell in love with the theatre only after starting one of his own.

At the end of the Festival's first season he was already planning a new touring venture, the Canadian Players, which he ran with one of the imported British actors, Douglas Campbell (who is still here). He went on to found or consult with other Canadian theatre projects, and he remained part of the Stratford organization itself until 1969. His initial position was general manager. He was popular with the company, though more seasoned administrators seem to have regarded him with a mixture of affection and exasperation.

Relations with the festival were sometimes strained after his departure, but all fences were mended in later years. He was a welcomed figure on both formal and informal Stratford occasions, and the festivals Third Stage was re-named after him. Stratfords debt to him is incalculable, but so are those of the Canadian theatre and of Canada itself.

Color Photo: Tom Patterson, left, in 2002 with Chris Yaneff, designer of the poster for Stratford's first season.
2005-02-26-miller-s-plays-resist-labels:
robertcushman@lycos.com

Some years ago I decided that, what the hell, I should spell out my standards as a critic. This is what I wrote then, and what I hold to now: I want the theatre to make me laugh, cry, tap my feet or hold my breath. I think that covers everything."

Arthur Miller, who at the moment of his death two weeks ago was the most honoured playwright in the world, never wrote anything that challenged admission in the foot-tapping category. He wasnt best known, either, for raising laughs, though in The Price he created one character, an old Jewish dealer, who convulsed the audience practically every time he opened his mouth.

Miller could certainly make us hold our breath, both for the scope and depth of what he attempted and the skill with which he brought it off. In The Crucible he brought a historical period to life, used it to illuminate another and -- a very rare feat in the modern theatre -- told a remorselessly gripping story. He showed the same narrative flair in All My Sons. In After the Fall he laid bare a marriage with an honesty that transcended autobiography (and incidentally redeemed an otherwise hideously long-winded play.) In the one-act A Memory of Two Mondays -- a play thats been forgotten since a short piece with a big cast has trouble finding a home -- he painted one of the great dramatic genre-pictures. The late plays (post-1970) are of interest only because they're by the man who wrote the earlier ones.

It all comes down, though, to Death of a Salesman, the play that makes everybody cry. Technically, it's an amazing achievement. I dont believe any play up to then had made such extensive use of flashbacks to denote overlapping states of memory and consciousness, and Im not sure any has done it as successfully since: all this while maintaining an inexorable forward momentum. It's also, and this is what really brings on the tears, the best modern play about the dynamics of being a family, about the way in which its members tear at one another, and try to reassure one another, and then tear again, because they just don't agree or they just dont understand.

Think of the choreography at the end of Act One. Willy Loman, the disintegrating salesman, and Biff, the son on whom hed pinned his hopes, are at their usual loggerheads. Happy, the other son, comes up with a business plan that sounds tempting. Biff is intrigued and Willy is over the moon. So is Linda, Willy's wife, but she expresses her enthusiasm a bit too forcefully for Willy, who feels crowded. So he yells at her, for agreeing with him. Biff, incensed for his mother, yells back. Willy, ashamed, backs off, and it all blows over. Till the next time.

As an undergraduate, I directed Salesman with a cast of other undergraduates. We were all young, all English, and yet we latched on instinctively to this American family of whom even the youngest was 10 years our senior. I was amazed by how little I needed to say about these scenes. They simply clicked into place, and they moved like express trains.

I was less enamoured of Miller's preface, with its insistence on the plays status as a tragedy. It seemed enough to me that it was a very good play, very moving (I used to sit in the audience and feel those sobs welling up around me) and obviously universal. Bringing in academic categories was, I felt, opening an unnecessary can of worms, and research revealed Miller had done just that.

Right from the start, there were those who couldnt forgive him for being a Broadway playwright with aspirations.

The suspicion persists, or so I judge from Barbara Kay's article on Miller in the National Post. She finds Salesman "more pathetic than tragic, largely because she thinks Miller blames Willy's fate on a capitalist society of which she herself approves. Well, it wouldnt bother me if Salesman were an anti-capitalist play, the salesman victimized by the hollowness of his own value system. But it isnt. Miller himself pointed out that the most decent character in it is Willy's neighbour Charley, a businessman whose values are not essentially different from Willy's. He just happens to be better and more cautious at putting them into practice.

Oddly enough, much the same criticism has been levelled at the play from the Left as from the Right. Kenneth Tynan, who revered the play, thought it couldnt be a tragedy because Willys fault lay not in his stars but in the fact his employers didn't have a proper pension plan. It was left to English playwright John Whiting to point out that Willy dies not because of the flaws or even the merits of the system he works under but because he is a weak and deluded mortal man. His job does indeed encourage his fatal belief that you can get by on a smile and a shoeshine. But if he were denied that, he would have found another way of screwing up his life and his family. He's like Chekhovs Uncle Vanya (in one of the few plays thats comparably affecting), who liked to believe that, dealt a better hand, he might have been a Schopenhauer or a Dostoevsky. The play knows better.

Chekhov can make me laugh and cry, sometimes simultaneously. His plays, not tragedies, are better than most tragedies. They're better than Miller's. But Salesman is a tragedy, even if it defies the so- called laws of tragedy," which in any case arent immutable. Theyre just theories, devised by humans to describe plays written by other humans. They don't even fit all the plays they're supposed to. Aristotle, from whose Poetics they all derive, confined himself to analyzing just one play, Sophocless Oedipus Rex, and even that defies the formula in a rather important respect: Its hero doesnt die. (Sophocles later killed him off in another play.)

Kay tells us that "in a Shakespearean tragedy, the protagonist, prompted by a 'tragic flaw,' offends against the moral order of things. That sounds all right, but what exactly is Hamlets tragic flaw"? That he fails to kill his uncle? He seems to be more the wrong man in the wrong place. (A victim, really. Like Willy Loman.) And if "suicide is cheating, dramatically speaking (take that, Willy, you wimp), then among the cheating plays are Othello, and Phedre, held to be the very model of a French classical tragedy, and Antony and Cleopatra, a double suicide. It really doesnt leave very much.

It does leave King Lear, and you can indeed trace a straight line from Lear's terrible mistakes in the first scene to his death in the last. But I doubt if anyone watches that ending thinking it was really all Lear's own fault and at least the moral orders now been restored. I dont want to be flippant, but I suspect the restoration of moral order" in Shakespeare is mainly about the necessity on an open stage of leaving someone in authority to order the removal of the bodies. Tragedies don't tell us that things are all right "as long as hierarchies are observed, though I can see why conservatives would take comfort in thinking so. They tell us that things go wrong. Always. That's why we need them.

I think now that Salesman, whose heros fate is shaped by his society but not determined by it, belongs among them. I certainly dont hold it against Miller that he failed to celebrate America's virtues and strengths." That wasn't his job. Its never been any dramatists.

Shakespeare, of course, covered himself by never writing about his own time and place, but reading between the lines of Lear or Troilus and Cressida, I don't sense a man in love with his own world. Euripides was run out of Athens, and Ibsen never stopped telling his fellow Norwegians how much he despised them. Even Chekhov said that the purpose of his plays was to make his fellow countrymen look at themselves and see how empty their lives were. Perhaps, as Kay says of Miller, in doing so "he weakened his claim to timelessness. It's really too early to tell. So far, though, they both seem to be doing pretty well. The academics say that comedies aren't just plays that make you laugh" and that tragedies aren't just "plays that make you cry." But nobody has come up with any better definitions.

Color Photo: Dennis Clark, Getty Images / Arthur Miller, seen at a staging of The Crucible in 2002, took his last bow on Feb. 10 at his home in Connecticut.

2005-03-05-unless-gets-lost-in-translati:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Unless runs through Feb. 23 at the Bluma Appel Theatre, 416-368-3110.; Bat Boy: The Musical runs through April 16 at the Bathurst Street Theatre, 416-872-1111.

Most of Unless gets in the way. I am referring to the new play at the Bluma Appel, not to the Carol Shields novel on which it is based and which I haven't read. In a novel, strands of story and groups of characters can be laid out in parallel, so to speak, and can make a satisfying pattern. In a play, you want to know what the main narrative is, and how everything else contributes to it. This applies even to Chekhov, whose symphonic structures are built around what are essentially thriller plots: Will they save the cherry orchard? How many excuses can they come up with for not going to Moscow? Whom will Uncle Vanya shoot and whom will he miss? When lesser dramatists try the same kind of juggling act, they are doomed. Most of what's on stage at the Bluma seems to be there purely because it was once on the page somewhere else.

The adaptation of Unless was begun by Shields herself, and completed after her death by her daughter Sara Cassidy. It is, fittingly enough, about a mother and daughter -- at least, that's the only part of the play that grabs you. There is Reta Winters, a fairly successful writer of what she calls "light fiction," who lives with her family about an hour outside Toronto. And there is Norah, the eldest of her three girls and a university student. Without warning, Norah drops out and joins the homeless. Reta, naturally, is devastated.

Reta, at her first appearance, speaks pregnantly of undergoing the "useful monotony" of happiness. This, it seems, is not enough for Norah, who takes up daily residence on a downtown street corner, wearing a sign inscribed with the single word "Goodness." It's an intriguing situation, with built-in emotional pull. We feel sorry for Reta and curious about Norah. But our questions remain unanswered; we learn virtually nothing about Norah, even in the rare scenes in which she actually appears.

Mostly we watch Reta accommodating other things and other people. The play may be telling us a harsh truth: that, even for a virtually bereaved parent, life goes on. But it feels more like padding. We witness Reta at work on her new book -- scenes and characters take shape before our eyes. We hear her accept compliments from her new agent (in New York, yet) and see her fend off his attempts to rewrite her. She deals, in turn, with an inept interviewer, a kaffeeklatsch of friends, her other children, who are given very little dramatic presence, and her doctor husband, who has almost none.

She also writes letters to editors, complaining about the persistent marginalization of women. And somewhere in all this we are presumably meant to piece together the sources of her daughter's desperation. The mother observes and expresses; the daughter internalizes and explodes.

But a character has to exist in her own right before she can illuminate something or somebody else, and Reta doesn't. Her scenes with other people are just sketches, overlong and under-amusing. Most of the time, though, she addresses us directly, which is even more enervating.

The title is a literary conceit about the significance of seemingly innocuous words, conjunctions and such. In a similar way, that old novelistic touchstone, the authorial consciousness, has been transported to the theatre unmediated, and has, as usual, wilted there. Nicola Cavendish, the actress charged with embodying it, is capable but no miracle worker.

Roy Surette's production itself enjoys switching between levels: upper and lower, darker and lighter, illusion and reality. The overall flavour, characteristic of new plays at this address, is of CanStage doing CanLit. (Such shows tend to come from somewhere else. This one is a co-production with the Arts Club company of Vancouver.)

It seems somehow typical that the most ambitious dialogue sequence is also the most frustrating. It involves Reta's mother-in- law, previously incapable of making conversation, suddenly finding her voice when left alone with the agent. The staging frantically signals that it's meant to be funny and touching, but one just wants it to stop, since, somewhere else, the story of Reta and Norah, which is all we're interested in, is finally showing signs of coming to a head. Celine Stubel brings some intensity to Norah. Phillip Clarkson's costumes are excellent; they have more colour than anything else in the show.

Norah's chosen piece of pavement is at Bloor and Bathurst, which places her kitty-corner from the Bathurst Street Theatre, the home of Bat Boy: The Musical, at which she might have a slightly better time, as did I. This off-Broadway import derives from stories published in the Weekly World News about a creature found in a cave in West Virginia who was indeed half bat and half boy. (I only know what I'm told.) If, as seems likely, the WWN is the campiest of tabloids, then it stands to what you might call reason that its creepiest scoop was just asking to be turned into a spoof musical. I'm not sure anyone else was asking. Just about every musical you see today is a spoof musical, and they aren't all The Producers or Urinetown, not by a long shot. Those shows have internal consistency: The Producers is about the theatre, and Urinetown is a sustained riff on a certain theatrical tradition. (It's a satire on satires, something that shouldn't work but does.)

Bat Boy, by contrast, just lurches. It starts with a chorale intoning "hold me, Bat Boy, touch me, Bat Boy," an amusing take on all the sickly Messianic musicals from Jesus Christ Superstar to -- the real prototype -- Tommy. By the end, when the Bat in Bat Boy has triumphed over the Boy and he's reverted to sucking blood, including his girlfriend's, in quite a big way, the ambience is more that of The Phantom of the Opera, with appropriate crashing chords in the score. Somewhere en route, Bat Boy has been taken in by a local family and taught to speak BBC English, with the help of BBC tapes.

This is so we can be reminded of My Fair Lady, though the relevant song seems to have strayed out of some other, and thoroughly undistinguished, musical altogether.

The low point, of the writing and particularly of the staging, comes when the lovers take to the woods and are surrounded by papier mache animals, as if that in itself constituted a parody of The Lion King, or indeed as if a parody of The Lion King were self-evidently a good thing.

For the most part, Laurence O'Keefe's music and (especially) his lyrics are neat, if inevitably cloying. He does seem to like the musical as a form. The book writers (Keythe Farley and Brian Flemming) give the impression that they despise it but would quite like to cash in on it. They are cynically irresponsible -- when all else fails, they hint that they're being serious about the way we treat outsiders. (An evening of parody is difficult to sustain, especially if you neither like nor understand your target.)

Bat Boy's adoptive family are turned into arbitrary monsters, especially dad, who is a veterinarian, and our second underwritten medical man this week. I wondered if he might be suffering from some kind of post-Vietnam, or maybe post-Gulf trauma. That could make him two kinds of vet. The surrounding gap-toothed gap-brained rustics don't pass muster even as caricature.

Michael McGinn's production is hearty (not to mention overmiked) rather than inventive. The cast all pitch enthusiastically in, with Jayne Lewis and Laura Caswell doing especially well as -- again -- mother and daughter. Jay T. 2005-03-12-half-life-celebrates-and-pond:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Half Life plays at the Tarragon Theatre, 30 Bridgman St., 416-531-1827, through April 3.; A Suicide-Site Guide to the City plays at Buddies in Bad Times, 12 Alexander St., 416- 975-8555, until March 20.

John Mightons Half Life, the dramatist-mathematicians first new play in eight years and a beauty in every department, runs at the Tarragon for 90 packed minutes. Packed but not rushed: The play, which is set in an old people's home, has an enchanting air of relaxation. If it is advising us to make the most of the moments we have, then it is practising what it preaches. Except that it doesn't preach; it celebrates, and mourns, and ponders.

Its opening scene is exemplary, setting up characters, action and themes. Two middle-aged people, Donald and Anna, he with a mother in the facility and she with a father, make conversation in the waiting room. In his first speech, Donald talks about a party trick hes developed -- he will start telling a story and when, as invariably happens, he is interrupted, he will check on whether his hearers remember what he was saying. Sixty per cent of the time, theyve forgotten. Later he and Anna get to talking about dogs. Donald, a neurologist, says reassuringly that they "don't have a very keen sense of time." Anna, a designer, muses that that must account for their capacity for devotion: Every moment is a new moment for them. Their hurts are forgotten.

Both Donald and Anna are currently single, and we are primed to expect something to develop between them. So are they. But their attraction turns out to be a stalking horse for the play's real romance, which is between their octogenarian parents. Annas father, Patrick, was a code-breaker during the war (this is important), and - - though a heavy smoker, drinker and grump -- he still has his faculties.

Donalds mother, Clara, is beginning, sweetly, to lose hers. ("Is your mother happy here?" Anna asks. My mother is always happy, Donald replies, "but she's not often here." He may not be quite right on the second point.) Clara becomes convinced that she and Patrick knew and loved one another 60 years ago. Patrick neither confirms nor denies it. It may be fantasy, but the more I think about the play the less inclined I am to think so. The play is about forgetting or remembering things, not about making them up. The point is made near the end when a scene that we might well have taken for a dream is shown, in the deftest manner imaginable, to have been real.

If Mighton's writing is both luminous and tactful, then so, too, are Daniel Brookss direction and all of the performances; the various excellences are inextricably knit. Carolyn Hetheringtons Clara, still deeply concerned for her son if vague about some of his details, has extraordinary grace, a sensible and sensitive woman with her edges blurred but her essence unimpaired. Eric Peterson has a mischievous gleam, and a lurking sense of hurt, as Patrick. Neither actor strains after senility (Peterson in fact seems younger than he does on Corner Gas) but both convey the sad, not bitter, comedy of a Romeo and Juliet in reverse -- they would like to marry, but their children disapprove.

We wouldn't survive, Donald says, "if we remembered everything." Even computers, he points out, have limited memories, and he seems to think it's a point in their favour. But he can still be saddened by his mothers lapses, and grieve in advance his own daughters forgetting of that intensity of happiness only available to 10-year-olds. The role, a flawed raisonneur, finds Diego Matamoros at his incomparable best. He plays a fine mind, a gentle soul, a wearied and maybe despairing man. His spiritual and intellectual opposite is the local clergyman, dismayed by Donald's tendency to prefer machines to people but otherwise finding good in everything. His beaming optimism can seem fatuous but, when you get beyond the veneer, a surprising amount of what he says makes sense. Randy Hughson's performance takes the Reverend repeatedly to the edge of farce then, just as regularly and in the nick of time, rears back.

I still havent done justice to the economy of the plays story- telling, or to its feeling for the quotidian reality of life within an institution and also beyond it. This is encapsulated in Maggie Huculak's nursing assistant, who cares about her charges, and may possibly be exploiting them, and who is loved by them and then, when a much-needed better job comes along, is gone from their lives. It is there, too, in Barbara Gordon's embittered resident who cries out, in the plays bleakest and funniest moment, I want to be treated like a senior citizen. (She is. Thats the trouble.) If Laura de Carteret's Anna has less definition than the others, that may be because she has been written mainly as a foil, the artist to Donald's scientist, and because she, unlike him, is denied scenes with her parent. There is also a last dying fall that, as staged here, registers more as an inconclusive thud. Otherwise, no complaints. Springing some great tricks but playing no games, this is on occasion both subtle and satisfying: a permanent play about evanescence.

- - -

Its rough luck on Darren ODonnell to have opened A Suicide- Site Guide to the City in the same week as Half Life. It sort of spikes his guns. A first-person stand-up act, O'Donnell's piece is offered, both implicitly and explicitly, as an antidote to conventional plays with plots and characters.

He has a point. When it doesnt work, all that dramatic machinery can get very oppressive. Suicide-Site, which is just him and us (and him a commanding actor, though not quite as good at this kind of thing as Daniel MacIvor), is a better night out than Unless or No Great Mischief or Poochwater or Bat Boy: The Musical or Omnium Gatherum or ODonnell's own last show, pppeeeaaaccceee, which he wrote but didn't act in. But it isnt as good as Half Life or A Whistle in the Dark or Trout Stanley, all of which opened this year. (And its only March. We grumble, but at this rate we'll be having a golden age.)

O'Donnell, who greets patrons in the lobby both before and after the show, claims to be playing himself, since hes tired of doing impersonations. Having met him (though not in the lobby), I would say hes doing a good job. But of course, this kind of acting is just as artificial as any other, and he isn't even making it up as he goes along. Indeed, he draws attention to this fact, telling us when he wrote the various parts of the script, and commenting on the differences between himself then and now, which don't seem that great. He also introduces us to his sound man, his lighting designer and an onion he uses to make himself cry. If hes telling us that all theatre is fake, his own included, then we know already. And nobody, apart from a few guilt-ridden professionals, cares. (To be fair, Daniel Brooks was sounding off just as self-indulgently a few years ago about how no show is ever ready, and nothing deserves good reviews. I hope hell forgive me my rave for Half Life.)

That leaves us with what O'Donnell actually says. Sometimes he's ruefully funny, especially when genially presuming on the entire audiences feelings of middle-class guilt. Other times, hes imaginatively chilling, as when he talks about his own suicidal impulses. (Though the tour promised in the title unhappily never materializes.) When he gets to the reasons for his angst, he's not so hot. He admits to not feeling as upset as he might over 9/11, on the grounds "the enemy of my enemy is my friend." He doesn't seem to realize that this cuts both ways. Osama bin Laden would be an implacable enemy of anyone and anything presented at Buddies in Bad Times, which would make ODonnell the buddy (in bad times) of George W. Bush. Do you ever get the feeling that political debate is polarized between the jerks and the knee-jerks?

He also riffs on Richard Floridas theory on the rise of the urban creative class (i.e. us and him) without really taking it anywhere. But he has fine timing, and he clearly wants to say something. Like I said, there are worse ways.

2005-03-19-writerly-muscle-in-my-mother-:
robertcushman@lycos.com; My Mother's Feet runs through April 2 at the Berkeley Upstairs, 26 Berkeley St., 416-368-3110.; Macbeth runs through March 27 at the Theatre Centre, 1087 Queen St. W., 416-504- 7529.

Our first sight at My Mothers Feet is the welcome one of Tom Rooney, talking and, from time to time, blinking at us. He does both with a shy charm whose potency is increased when he adds to the mix a conspiratorial, self-deprecating smile.

Rooney, who last year went triumphantly from Hamlet to Hairspray, is here playing a man named Dan. On the floor by his side stand, strangely, are a pair of prosthetic feet. They are intended, he tells us, for his mother, who has lost the feet she was born with. He proceeds to riff on this subject, firing off a series of apparently heartless puns concerning what Fats Waller would have called the old ladys "pedal extremities. It appears she was attached to them for more than the usual reasons, or at least Dan's imagination makes it seem so. She was a very active and controlling person, and as soon as he was old enough, he used his own feet to get as far away from her as possible. She is now, he says, de-feet- ed." The outrageousness of this culminating zinger induces mixed feelings -- I think I let out an admiring groan. Which is to say: The joke is terrible but it makes its point.

This opening sequence establishes what the rest of the play confirms: that Gina Wilkinson -- a first-time playwright already known as an actress and, to a lesser extent, as a director -- has a striking if erratic way with words, one that compels attention without always rewarding it. The play's ideas are thinly stretched over its action. For a start, there is the matter of the feet themselves, which hardly earn their place in the title. Not until the last scene do we learn how Dans mom came to be deprived of her original pair, and by that point weve forgotten about them. They have played no part in the intervening imagery or the intervening story.

That last phrase may be misleading. This isn't a sequential sort of play; there is no "now to it, except in Dan's narrating mind. What we see is what he chooses to tell us, and we follow him back and forth across the years. As a boy, indeed, well into adolescence, he was not so much mothered as smothered. He was encouraged to believe in his own superiority to those whom his mama calls peasants" or "hoi polloi, meaning, apparently, just about everybody else in the world, especially teachers. Even on the brink of manhood he is compelled, before going out on a date, to stand still, protesting, while she hems his trousers. (This is a very well- observed scene.) Just how intense the mother-son relationship becomes I should not reveal, but youll probably have guessed anyway.

Dan finds himself a bride, which is rather surprising, though we may be meant to feel that he has rushed into marriage -- or been rushed -- rather too precipitately, as if he has something to prove. The newlyweds move as far from Dans mother's home as they can manage without emigrating, and they have a son, whom Dan adores. When the marriage breaks up, the wife, for some unexplained but dramatically convenient reason, makes no attempt to gain custody. Jane Spidell, with no physical alteration, plays both mother and wife, and is admirably chilling as one and admirably warming as the other. I suppose the two are meant to be aspects of the same woman, but I can't see where, beyond the obvious, that gets us.

Completing the cast is that most unassumingly versatile of actors, Jerry Franken, doubling as Dans understandably ineffectual father and as a more assertive small-town cop who, we note, addresses him as son." Dan goes to him because he becomes convinced his mother has tracked him down and is stalking him (even, he says aggrievedly, at Dominion). He takes his son off on a rite-of- passage camping trip into some symbolic-sounding woods where they meet with a realistic-sounding bear. But then Dans wife's name is Ursula, meaning "female bear, a genus against which his mother, who thinks in unforgiving images, has prophetically warned him -- though we only hear the prophecy after we've seen the marriage.

Probably the whole play is more metaphorical than Ive made out, but then I have a literal mind. Its beautifully directed by Micheline Chevrier, who makes simplicity and concentration into a style. Deeter Schurig's suggestively vernal set helps. So, very much, does John Munro's lighting. What comes over, though, is an extended case study with no apparent reason for being except as a flexing of writers muscle. Wilkinson does have muscle to flex. She writes well about sex, which is rare in plays, and gives Ursula a wonderful speech on the subject. She can get into a mans voice, too, which is just as well, as Rooney's Dan does most of the talking. He does it magically, with great lucidity and lightness of touch, especially in the matter of whimsically distinguishing man from boy. He seems to be able to play any age, and he hereby joins my short list (available on request) of actors who should play Peer Gynt: In fact, he's at the top of it.

All the same, if the play is meant to be an exorcism for its central figure, it doesnt come off, in part because he is so central. Plays with narrator-figures outside their action can, sometimes, work: e.g. Henry V and Our Town. Plays in which the narrator is also part of the story are far dodgier, though they have proliferated ever since The Glass Menagerie and are now a positive plague. One character gets privileged over the others, and the evening becomes a series of shortcuts.

For a contrast, admittedly an exalted one, look at Macbeth. It leads us inside its protagonists head, but doesn't demand that we take up residence there. Peter Farbridge, playing the role for the Modern Times Theatre Company, makes a highly intelligent tour guide. However, he looks and sounds neither warlike nor haunted, and even in an avowedly non-realistic production, these are handicaps.

Farbridge, with his director, Soheil Parsa, is one of the founding members of Modern Times, a company that has been in existence for 15 years, and has been doing this play intermittently since 1995. Parsa's staging, with a cast of nine, is both imaginative and ingenious, and since its billed as an adaptation, one can hardly complain of the liberties it takes.

In fact, most of these are very effective -- the text is cut, but its also embellished, with silent actions depicting scenes that usually happen offstage.

Much of the show is about scarves, long ones. Sometimes they enfold the actors, enabling them to play the witches (known here as the wayward sisters"), who are elastic in number, sometimes stretching to include the entire company. Other times, the scarves are unfurled, so that the players can attach themselves by them to posts, or to other actors. It's also about robes. Duncan is completely enclosed, face and all, within a gold one, through which there issues, muffled but recognizable, the voice of Alon Nashman. Maybe this is to suggest the unreachability of kingship, maybe it's so that the same actor can more easily double as Macduff, a role he plays with contrasting immediacy. In this version, we actually see him discover the kings body -- which is, come to think of it, his own. Malcolm, as heir apparent, sports a matching golden cravat, but Macbeth himself stays strictly dun-coloured. He may have murdered his way to the throne, but he still isnt a king, not a real one. Well, I presume that's the idea.

The production does have a habit of undercutting some of its own best moments. There is, for example, a first-rate staging of what I would call the cauldron scene except that the cauldron has been eliminated, along with all the savoury ingredients that are customarily tossed into it. (Fillet of a fenny snake is off, dear.) It culminates in a brilliantly resourceful staging, much the best I've seen, of the show of Banquos royal descendants -- which also, incidentally, caps an unusual and very rewarding emphasis on the muted ambitions of Banquo himself (Brendan Murray). You can see why Macbeth is spooked by it. We dont need him to go into a manic war dance, as if to show what a very bad boy he is now becoming. Similarly, a spare suggestion of the massacre at Macduff's castle is only cheapened when the assassins go on another choreographed rampage.

This is a multicultural staging, aesthetically speaking, with a multi-ethnic cast, urbanly speaking.

Those of us who long to see the sexy Iranian lady from 24 play Lady Macbeth get a mini-preview from Stavroula Logothettis, who is Greek, though it's unfortunate she doesnt bring much to the role beyond the idea that the lady uses her sexuality to enmesh her man.

And you get that from every production. The director himself plays the Porter who has lost most of his jokes but gained a reeling encounter with the drug-addled grooms who get framed for Duncans murder, two gentlemen who in more conventional circumstances we seldom get to meet. It's a more than fair exchange. The production doesn't plot much of a course for its two leading characters, but it leads us excitingly into the world that surrounds them.

In the background is Jane Spidell as Tom's mother.; Colour Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / The avowedly non-realistic production of Macbeth makes extensive use of wardrobe props such as scarves.

Gypsy opens at the Shaw Festival on May 7; Into the Woods opens at the Stratford Festival on June 3.

Sondheim makes his characters sing as if they were talking

Stephen Sondheim, composer and lyricist, celebrated his 75th birthday on Tuesday, and much of theatrical New York, both practitioners and fans, celebrated it with him. There was a 12-hour marathon concert of his songs the previous Saturday, admission free, and a formal gala on Monday, proceeds to the encouragement of new playwrights. The honours and the affection are deserved. For 35 years now -- the breakthrough show in this regard was Company in 1970 -- Sondheim has been Americas pre-eminent musical dramatist. He may well be her best living dramatist of any kind.

In a book of interviews that appeared a couple of years ago (Sondheim on Music by Mark Eden Horowitz) he himself offers the clearest description I have encountered of what he does, and the best clue as to why it works so powerfully: "I've discovered over a period of years that essentially I'm a playwright who writes with song, and that playwrights are actors.... Ill go upstairs, and Ill get back into the character of Wilson Mizner [in the show that was then called Wise Guys but eventually reached the stage as Bounce], and I'll start singing to myself. It'll take me a while to make that transition, because its been a couple of days since Ive been Wilson, but I'll get upstairs, and I'll be Wilson."

I would add that he gets to be Wilson -- or Sweeney Todd or the Baker in Into the Woods or Desiree in A Little Night Music -- in a concentrated form. Songs, even the intricate musical scenes that Sondheim often writes, are comparatively brief things. They can crystallize speech patterns -- and, through them, thought patterns and feeling patterns -- in ways unavailable to most spoken drama, whose methods are longer and messier.

Richard Rodgers (with whom Sondheim collaborated, not too happily, on the 60s musical Do I Hear a Waltz?) got close to the heart of it when he said, Steve has a curious way of making people sing as if they were talking.

People in real life dont usually express themselves in rhyme, to musical accompaniment, but the unlikeliness of the feat -- making an outrageously artificial form sound colloquial -- is a large part of its attraction.

It also, when done well, gives a feeling of inevitability. The same is true, of course, of Shakespeare -- people don't talk in blank verse but he and his contemporaries persuade you that they do, and that the beat you hear is the pulse of common speech or, in soliloquy, of a mind inventing itself. In theory, musicals should do for us what verse drama did for the Elizabethans. It doesn't often work out that way in practice, but Sondheim has come closer, more often, to making it work than anyone else.

Colloquial lyrics were nothing new in American song when Sondheim began his Broadway career in the 1950s. They had been perfected in the 30s by Cole Porter and Lorenz Hart and Oscar Hammerstein and all the other writers of the songs we now call standards. Mostly, though, they had been stand-alone things, expressing nobodys sensibilities but their authors'. Hammerstein, who was Sondheim's mentor, lacked the verbal wit of some of the others but he went beyond them in putting song at the service of character and narrative; his people, for the most part, sing what they mean. Sondheim took the next step, and nobody has yet got beyond it. He restored the wit, and not just as decoration: He uses it to point up the gap between what people say and what actually drives them. Sometimes theyre conscious deceivers, more often theyre in the grey area between self-assertion and self-doubt, giving themselves away without knowing it. Wilson Mizner in Bounce (which has yet to reach New York but is full of good songs) is both -- he's a con-man from America's Gilded Age, but his greatest victim may be himself.

Sondheims own term for this, borrowed from Methodspeak, is "subtext," which hes defined as giving the actors something to act. There isn't much of it in his lyricist-only debut in West Side Story (some way to start a career) -- there's so much action in that show that there just isnt time. But its there in Gypsy, the next one, with its whirlwind theatrical mother blinded by her own ambition. It works wonderfully, of course, for comedy, including farce.

There's a recurring character in Sondheim's work, the complacent self-glorifying male, who gives himself away with every word he utters. He is given classic status (literally) in Miles Gloriosus, the braggart soldier of A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum, whose establishing number is an impatient command: Bring Me My Bride. He reappears as the peacock Count of A Little Night Music, pluming himself on the devotion of his wife and his mistress: The song is titled In Praise of Women. He splits amoebically into the two Princes of Into the Woods, commiserating on the agony of falling sequentially in love with every fairy-tale princess in the book. "Ah well," they conclude in unison, back to my wife.

They sing, most of these guys, rhapsodic tunes. Being his own composer has expanded Sondheims dramatic resources enormously. He writes beautiful music; his melodies are astringent, which may explain why theyre so often undervalued in a world that equates bloatedness with emotion, but they soar; he also writes ironic, searching music. Often the two modes co-exist: Sweeney Todd eulogizes Pretty Women, harmonizing with the Judge who raped his wife and whose throat he plans to cut; a discontented wife in Follies uses a suave and sweeping waltz to ask her rich husband Could I Leave You?, a question less rhetorical than it may seem, considering the offhand bitterness of the subsidiary questions that go with it. ("Not to fetch your pills again / Every day at five, / Not to give those dinners for ten / Elderly men / From the UN-- / How could I survive?")

Or in Company, a trio of husbands sing Sorry-Grateful, spelling out their conflicted feelings concerning the married state. They are upfront about their doubts, and about the impossibility of resolving them, and the tune, which is sweet and plangent, blesses and absolves them. But its unsettling harmonies suggest there may be doubts even about their doubts. Everybody identifies with this; it exemplifies Alexander Pope's description of poetry as what oft was thought but ne'er so well expressed.

Company, usually regarded as quintessential Sondheim, is in fact an anomaly. People (including me) have described him as the bard of modern Manhattan, but its his only show to be set entirely in the time and place at which it was written. Follies, Assassins, Bounce are all, in different ways, American panorama. Pacific Overtures, one of my two or three favourites, is a complex conceit, deeply funny and deeply sad, about the Western powers "opening up" of Japan during the 19th century. One number, Please Hello, a multiple pastiche for a succession of diplomat-admirals making blandly outrageous demands, is so faithful to the history that it's been adopted as a teaching aid in schools.

He hasn't often originated his own projects. Hes been drawn in by collaborators: by Hal Prince, who has produced and/or directed about half his shows; or by his librettists: Arthur Laurents, James Lapine or (specializing in the political shows) John Weidman. But he has immersed himself in each subject and emerged, I imagine, slightly different from when he went in. I suspect, if I can pursue this extravagant analogy a little further, that Shakespeare worked the same way: Burbage or someone said remember that old play about King Leir [yes, that was the spelling] and his daughters? and -- after protesting "oh not that old thing again" -- he threw himself into it. I imagine, too, that if youd had a drink with Shakespeare at the Mermaid Tavern, the conversation, though interesting, would not have been on the philosophical level of Hamlet's soliloquies or Lear on Dover cliff. Sondheim in conversation is unflaggingly humorous and penetrating. His eyes light up when he pounces -- the only word -- on a new idea.

But the wisdom -- again the only word -- that comes at the end of Into the Woods is something else. It's distilled from the characters experience, and presumably the authors, but it transcends both.

And then it's on to the next. Perhaps the best birthday tribute he can be paid is that everybody who cares wants to know what that will be.

Peter and Mary have been married for seven years, without an itch. They tell us so, in one of those expository conversations that is plainly being conducted for the audience's benefit rather than their own. Indeed, they are standing side by side and looking out front, so that there may be no doubt about the matter. They say theyre happy, so we know they arent.

We gather that they have a child, and are thinking of adopting another, from China, which apparently is the fashion these days. Not that they couldn't produce a second baby on their own, but Mary just doesn't have the time for all that pregnancy, not to mention its exhausting aftermath. In fact, we speedily learn that she is pregnant, but intends to have an abortion early next week, a course of action of which Peter thoroughly approves. He does worry a bit about her having to take the morning off work to have the procedure, but he reasons that her bosses will be delighted when they learn the reason. No more of that troublesome maternity leave.

The play Peter and Mary inhabit is called The Leisure Society, and they are fully paid-up members of it. We can tell as much by looking at their furniture, Marian Whaks set being so sleek that I thought for a moment I had wandered into the wrong theatre. (The Factory isnt known for visual elegance, or for plays about those who live in it.) They are also, as you may have gathered, rotten, and their author, Francois Archambault, spares no pains to tell us so.

For example, though they often mention their baby boy, and have a monitor in their living room so they can hear him if he cries, they never once mention him by name -- he is always just "the baby, an appurtenance. This is certainly repellent. It is also unbelievable. Here, as elsewhere in the evening, one hears the disagreeable sound of cards being stacked.

On the evening we meet them, Peter and Mary are having an old chum over, a recently divorced man named Mark, whom they feel they have, in some unspecified way, outgrown, and whom they have invited so that they may announce the end of the friendship.

This also strains belief; adult friendships often wither away but they aren't usually brought to such formal conclusions. Anyway, this purpose crosses tracks with another: Peter and Mary have promised one another a threesome, and it dawns on them -- or, to be more exact, it dawns on Mary -- that Mark would make the perfect third wheel. However, Mark, who is noisily enjoying his newly minted bachelorhood, has brought along his casual sex-partner (not his girlfriend), Paula, and Peter thinks for a time that he would like to have her along instead. (Peter, Paula and Mary; where have I almost heard that before? The answer, I guess, is blowing in the wind.) But the best-lay plans prove as fallible as the best-laid ones, and things work out differently.

It all seems fairly harmless, except perhaps for the one who gets left out, but the author seems convinced these shenanigans constitute a critique of our acquisitive civilization. His tone, which is icy, suggests it, and his program note, which is positively frozen, confirms it. It's the rich what gets the pleasure, yet again. The corollary must be that sexual experimentation is the privilege of the privileged, which sounds pretty snobbish to me.

It also sounds frivolous -- in a world full of war, starvation and oppression, an earnest playwright spends an evening tut-tutting about sex? This seems to be where the theatrical Left meets the Christian Right. There are offhand references to some of the characters less forgivable foibles -- hitting one anothers children, for example -- and these are credible, but they are mentioned only in passing.

That's not to say the play, first seen in Montreal, is a write- off. In its own hermetic way it works. It's economical, proceeding in a series of short, speedy, sawed-off scenes that are sometimes cruelly funny. It efficiently parades its characters heartlessness and exposes their loneliness. Bobby Theodores translation is so good that it doesn't sound like one. Ken Gass's direction is high- gloss, with especially searching performances from the two men: Geoffrey Pounsett is Mark, boyish and hollow, to the life; Richard Zeppieri does a masterly job on Peter, whose bravado is rather less than skin deep and who ends in an emotional pool filled about equally with sulks and shame. Carolyne Maraghis Paula is visually compelling, but aurally monotonous. The same goes, in more complex ways, for Irene Pooles Mary; she is sharp, throaty and intense, but she does not have the lightest of touches, and this weakens the impact, not just of her comic moments but of her sad and furious ones. Still, she leaves an impression, one -- and I mean this as a compliment -- of authentic misery.

I don't deny that the play gets down to being a persuasive anatomy of a particular marriage. What bugs me is the attempt to blow it up beyond that. That and the sense, implicit from the title onward, that the author is prejudiced against his characters from the start, which in turn prejudices me against him.

There could hardly be a greater contrast than Blackbird, both in ambience and in effect. Adam Rapp's play is the second offering from Crate Productions, who do site-specific shows, and who seem specifically specific about finding the grubbiest sites available and putting on newish, shortish American plays inside them. Their first one, Tape, took place in a room of the old Gladstone Hotel that the renovators hadnt yet got around to. Their new setting makes that one look palatial -- its a squatters' loft at Yonge and Gerrard, up several flights of alarmingly rickety stairs (though next door to a good Vietnamese restaurant). It stands in for a poverty-row room in New York, inhabited by two young people, a man and a woman whose bodies are prematurely decaying. It looks the part.

The couple are lovers, sort of. Baylis is incontinent, an affliction he owes not to his service in the Gulf War but to a civilian accident suffered when moving furniture into the home of people in Manhattan's own leisure society. Froggie is an ex- stripper (they met at her place of work) now largely confined to bed with hepatitis.

Shes a druggie, naturally; they both are, but shes more serious about it. One of her favourite phrases is get me some heroin": Baylis thinks she'd be better off with vitamin pills, and actually persuades her to take some. She has run away from a middle-class home, not, it transpires, without reason. His disability pay is hardly enough to cover their medical bills, let alone everything else. The floor, naturally, is littered with their detritus. Kimberly Purtell's production spares us little.

The story begins with the characters shouting abuse at one another, so that the play risks being another exercise in seeing how much squalor a well-brought-up audience will take. (Theres no limit.) It ends in a kind of tenderness, so it also risks sentimentality.

It comes closer to the latter, especially in its title, which refers to a presumably symbolic bird pecking away outside. Its also set on Christmas Eve, but it manages to keep that irony serviceable and, eventually, touching. The action largely hinges on Baylis's attempts, once he realizes the desperateness of Froggie's condition, to haul her out of it, and we find ourselves pulling for both of them. That is not, perhaps, the highest function of drama, but its a good one. It means we believe.

The performance is compelling without being ideal.

The two actors are also the producers, and both seem to be viewing the proceedings somewhat from the outside. There is very little variety in Chris Reynoldss Baylis; there is more in Kate Meehan's Froggie, but she's all shell -- her toughness, meant to be only flesh-deep, never cracks.

But they play well together, and it's a compelling evening, in this environment, a riveting one.

Site-specificity may be a gimmick, but here it's a necessary one: It makes you feel trapped.

THEATRE

AIN'T MISBEHAVIN

At a time when musicals arrive with threatening titles like Wicked and Les Miserables, one welcomes the promised gaiety of Aint Misbehavin', surely the cheekiest double negative in the annals of popular song. It was of course the title of one of Fats Waller's greatest hits as composer and performer (the other was Honeysuckle Rose) and it gives its name to one of the best-loved of all songwriter revues, not so much a biography as a celebration of his music and milieu. First staged in 1978, its very much an ensemble piece; however, its revival by CanStage is a frank vehicle for Jackie Richardson following her success last season in Cookin at the Cookery (and it has the same director, Marion J. Caffey). In Cookin', Richardson played Alberta Hunter; in Ain't Misbehavin' she plays Fats -- the whole cast does -- and it's a role to which, gender apart, she seems far better suited.
