2005-04-09-wicked-proves-its-not-easy-be:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Wicked runs through April 24 at the Canon Theatre, 244 Victoria St., 416-872-1212.; Fishwrap runs through May 1 at the Tarragon Extra Space, 30 Bridgman St., 416-531-1827.

The title Wicked is an understatement. This musical, a hit on Broadway last season, is diabolical. One thing that can be said for it, though, is that it has a nerve. That's what it takes to begin a show that's meant to be a sort of parallel text to The Wizard of Oz with a song proclaiming, just like the first big number in the classic movie, that "the wicked witch is dead."

Which old witch? Well, not the one you thought. The musical begins close to the end of the familiar story, with the death of the Wicked Witch of the West -- as opposed to her sister, the Wicked Witch of the East, whose flattening by a stray house from Kansas set the original revenge plot in motion. Through the magic of flashback, we now get to see that plot from a new angle. Glinda the Good Witch, who seems to make a career out of hanging around near the corpses of rival sorceresses, volunteers to tell us the truth about the newly deceased, whose name, this is news, was Elphaba. It seems Elphaba wasn't really old, nor -- more important -- was she really wicked. Those were just malicious rumours spread by the kind of people who write stories and believed by the kind of people who read them.

There is, of course, a fallacy here. There is no "truth" about fictitious characters, waiting to be uncovered. The only reality the Oz characters have is the one bestowed upon them by their original author, L. Frank Baum. There is nothing to stop subsequent scribes from using his fictions to create their own alternate universe. But there are certain rules that need to be followed if the exercise is to be any fun.

Wicked trades on our knowledge of the basic story, especially in its MGM incarnation. Its book (by Winnie Holtzman, from a novel by Gregory Maguire) gets a few chuckles from the sidelong glances it takes at the adventures of Dorothy (who never actually appears), the Wizard, the Tin Man et al., just as Tom Stoppard's Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead gets huge laughs from the exactness with which it dovetails with Hamlet. Wicked, however, after yapping at its source's heels for most of the evening, runs away from it when the going gets rough. Narrative consistency goes by the board. I defy anyone to make sense of what happens at the end of this show to the Witch and the Scarecrow.

Elphaba here isn't a villain; she's an abused minority of one, being the only person, even in Oz, with its Emerald City, who is green. She owes her complexion to a dalliance of her mother's with a mysterious stranger who passed through town bearing a talismanic bottle of something that looks like mouthwash.

It seems nobody in this society is born a witch; you have to learn it. Elphaba and her crippled sister, Nessarose, go off to the local equivalent of Hogwarts (someone must even now be at work on Harry Potter: The Musical, though maybe they're still trying to get the rights), where another student is the fair, spoiled and crushingly popular Glinda, who progresses from persecuting Elphaba to feeling sorry for her.

Elphaba, the spunky waif, comes over as the Liza Minnelli character (even, piquantly enough, the Judy Garland character), especially as performed here, very well, by Stephanie J. Block, fresh from playing Liza on Broadway in the unrelated Boy From Oz. Kendra Kassebaum, despite having the right spun-sugar voice and looks, gets less out of the co-starring role of Glinda, which is unfortunate, as Glinda has the more to offer. Her attitudes and actions oscillate, while Elphaba simply goes from being misunderstood to being even more misunderstood. Even when she accepts the supernatural identity everybody is trying to force on her (in a strenuously unmemorable Act One finale titled Defying Gravity), it doesn't lead to her doing anything even vaguely malevolent. Anyone looking for the moral complexity of Into the Woods ("witches can be right / giants can be good / you decide what's right / you decide what's good") is going to be disappointed.

It's not easy being green, but it has its compensations. Elphaba can make an environmental statement without even opening her mouth. She also stands up for the animals, who are being prevented from teaching in schools (Timothy Britten Parker is both charming and touching as a learned goat who becomes a learned scapegoat) and even from talking. Oz is turning into a police state, and Elphaba wants to stop it. The show makes a great parade of being against stereotypes, but it's sacrificed a lively original to a virtuous stereotype of its own. It may act brave, but it doesn't even have the guts to deliver the unhappy ending its own narrative logic clearly demands. Earnest and preachy, it's one of the new-style humourless musicals, only with a few jokes thrown in. The tone is pop-Oprah. Or is that a tautology?

This brings us to Stephen Schwartz's music and lyrics. Schwartz used to write tinkly pop scores (Godspell, Pippin) relieved by the occasional really nice tune. He has progressed to writing bombastic pop scores (Children of Eden, this one) also relieved by the occasional really nice tune. The prize here is I'm Not That Girl, a sweet addition to Broadway's treasury of plain-Jane laments, sung by Elphaba when she believes the cutest boy in school fancies Glinda rather than her. (She's wrong, of course.) The girls' closing duet, For Good, also has appeal. It's surprisingly quiet, for one thing, and its key line -- "who can say if I've been changed for the better -- I have been changed for good" -- if not the wittiest pun you've ever heard, is still neat and makes a point. But the other emotional numbers, especially Elphaba's various epiphanies, simply scream the place down (they also bring the house down, but, given today's debased tastes in musicals, they would), while most of the humorous ones are very self-conscious. A word about trick-rhymes: They work only if a) they're part of an overall playful style; b) they reinforce metre and sense; c) the author can keep them coming, unforced. Schwartz incorporates them as and when they occur to him, then stops. He and his librettist also go in, a lot, for words like "rejoicify" and "disgustified." I don't know what Yip Harburg, who wrote the lyrics for The Wizard of Oz and for whom the invention and up-ending of words were the brilliant expression of a puckish imagination, would have said about these. But I can imagine, and it wouldn't be pretty.

I doubt he would have approved of this show's take on the Cowardly Lion, a caged cub who seems a very poor exchange for Bert Lahr rhyming "dinosaurus" with "king of the faurus." Or of its Munchkins, who are remarkably large. Or indeed of the Wizard himself -- the show is at pains to prove he's a charlatan, but we knew that coming in. The actor, David Garrison, spends the evening frantically searching for something to play. Joe Mantello's production also looks terrible, with heavy costumes and an even heavier set. The renowned Eugene Lee has designed a set of doors that regularly slide apart to reveal what appear to be the interstices of a giant clock. It takes up a lot of space, that being the only excuse I can think of for Wayne Cilento's constricted choreography, which rivals his work on Aida for atrocity. The whole thing resembles a Ross Petty panto, with a slightly larger budget and considerably less wit. Come back, Bat Boy, all is forgiven.

David Macfarlane's Fishwrap takes us into the lair of a freelance journalist who seems, at first glance, to be living in Beckettian squalor, as if this one-man play were Krapp's Last Laptop. It turns out he has the renovators in. Also, he has lost his regular arts column and his bicycle. So far, so autobiographical; we have learned as much from interviews with the author in various papers, including, quixotically, the one that fired him. Vogel, his onstage alter ego, has also contracted a tropical disease and been deserted by his wife, and these things -- as revealed in those same interviews -- are fictitious. Much of the play is a duet for Vogel and his alter ego, an older, harder-bitten (though not, in his case, by African insects) journo called Teddy. So much I learned later from consulting the printed script. In the piece itself Teddy's name isn't mentioned, and in fact I never even guessed there were two of them. I merely thought that the actor, John Jarvis, was talking in funny voices.

The gripes about the newspaper business are the play's most amusing things, and not just, I fancy, to professionals. Too many of them have been given away in advance, but there are also lines about the habits of builders that had me laughing hard. I was moved, too, by the moment of realization concerning the absent Mrs. Vogel, and intrigued by Mr. Vogel's apparent inability to distinguish his feelings for her from his feelings for his bike.

In fact, the play and Jarvis's performance, as acrobatic physically as vocally, kept me happy until the last stretch when both turn mawkish. Vogel recalls, at lyrical length, his first job, a paper route that included, talk about wheels turning full circle, an old journalist. We are meant to be touched, and I wasn't.

Colour Photo: Joan Marcus / PUTTIN' ON THE WITCH: Kendra Kassebaum as Glinda and Stephanie J. Block as Elphaba in the touring production of Wicked.
2005-04-16-nightclub-acts-to-a-higher-po:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Ain't Misbehavin' runs through June 25 at the Bluma Appel, 27 Front St. E., 416-368-3110.

This week's column is about singer-pianists. One of the greatest of them all, from the mid-1920s to the early 1940s, was Thomas Fats Waller, whose songs and personality are celebrated in Ain't Misbehavin', a show that was a Tony-winning hit In New York in 1978 and has been a staple ever since. In its CanStage revival it remains what it always was, a nightclub entertainment, magnified to a higher power. It sags in a few places but it's a welcome chance to encounter real singing, real dancing and real music in a Toronto musical.

The show is not a biography of Waller, and nobody gets to play him. Or rather, everybody gets to play him. His repertoire is shared among the entire cast, split, in this instance, six ways. It was only five ways in the original production -- two male, three female - - and the addition of a fourth woman is unwarranted. There is simply not enough material to go around. This may be the first time ever that Fats has been stretched thin.

This is an ensemble show; even so, Jackie Richardson, following her success in Cookin' at the Cookery, has been given a star entrance and star position in the curtain call. Between times, though, she is a shining member of the group, her face, a perpetually smiling moon, lighting up the stage and her voice warming it. Her buoyant I've Got a Feeling I'm Falling far surpasses that of Broadway's Nell Carter, whose voice sounded as if it were being squeezed out of a tube of toothpaste.

Divine Brown is efficient and enticing (she sings Squeeze Me), Starr Domingue energetic but arch (she sings Yacht Club Swing, one of several period pieces that get mugged into incomprehensibility) and Kim Richardson game but extra (she doesn't get a solo). The men, on the other hand, are fully extended: literally so in the case of David Lopez, whose limbs are uncannily loose and whose persona is that of mocking Harlem devil. He makes 'T Ain't Nobody's Biz-ness If I Do a wonderfully joyous hedonistic hymn: more effective, in fact, than his more showily depraved Viper's Drag, an ode to the reefer that is, in every sense, long drawn out. His horizontal contortions here demand to be described as "slithy," the portmanteau word Lewis Carroll assembled from "lithe" and "slimy." Doug Eskew is the most physically Walleresque of the gang. He is indeed mountainous, being about as long as he is broad. His is that robust complaint (to himself or a friend? -- I'm never sure) Your Feet's Too Big. He also has a rich voice and a winning grin that is more optimist than cynic, more Satch than Fats.

That's something Ain't Misbehavin' has never got right. It knocks itself out transmitting its hero's ebullience, but that was something of a mask. Waller, a compulsive eater and drinker, was a troubled man. The show hardly lets us see his demons, and we seldom get to hear his one-eyebrow-raised one-liners. The nearest we get to Waller the satirist is Lounging at the Waldorf, a spiky instrumental to which Richard Maltby, Jr., the show's first director, has set some sardonic lyrics. As Fats himself famously remarked, though not in this show, "I wonder what the poor people are doing tonight."

The mask does drop for the climactic company number (What Did I Do To Be So) Black and Blue, chillingly and beautifully sung. A hit at its birth in 1929, the song was found embarrassing by later generations, but has lately been reclaimed as a song of both protest and pride. According to Bobby Short, of whom more in a moment, it is not about black and white at all, but about tensions within the black community between the light-skinned against the dark. However you hear it, certain lines ("I'm white inside / It don't help my case") always sound shocking. Here it's a stark statement, beyond anger.

Andy Razaf wrote the words for that, as he did for Honeysuckle Rose, the title song and several others. I tell you since the program doesn't. Waller composed much of the show's music, but by no means all, and he never wrote lyrics, though, as always with these anthologies, it's what the words say that guides the choice of songs.

I also think some people would be interested to know that the raucous and jivey That Ain't Right, one of the production's highlights, was the work, words and music of a young and decidedly unsmooth Nat King Cole.

The show seems to have acquired more spoken lines than I had remembered, most of them unfortunate. Otherwise Marion J. Caffey's direction and choreography are whirlwind. There is neat design by Phillip Silver, a generic cabaret across which balls of light chase one another like soap bubbles. The band, under William Foster McDaniel, is terrific. You will have a good time.

- - -

Bobby Short once said that he loved Waller's music but always felt inadequate performing it, perhaps because, though his own urbane cabaret style could encompass the blues, it stopped short at vocal barrelhouse. (Short's style depended on not worrying what the poor people were doing tonight.) Nor could he hope to emulate Waller's ferocious skills as a stride pianist. All the same, in later life he recorded an excellent album of Razaf lyrics, many of them to Waller's music.

Short, who died a couple of weeks ago at the age of 80, was the premier New York supper-club performer of his generation, really, of all generations. Indeed, I sometimes suspect he not only epitomized the style he perfected -- a mixture of cut-glass elegance and down- home energy -- he actually invented it. Born into a large, poor black family in Danville, Ill., he helped support his family as a child performer on the vaudeville circuit. Then he went back to school. He had found himself attracted to songs he was too young to sing, and he set out to learn about them and the life they represented. As a young man he established himself in the nightclubs of Hollywood, then of Paris, then of New York. When the thriving cabaret world of the '50s collapsed, under the double onslaught of TV and rock, he scuffled, but at the end of the '60s he secured a short gig at the Carlyle, a dowager among Manhattan hotels, an engagement that was extended and in fact ended only with his death. His status as a New York landmark was cemented by his appearance in Woody Allen's Hannah and Her Sisters. Woody takes his coke-snorting young girlfriend to see Short at the Carlyle and, when she proves unappreciative, tells her "you don't deserve Cole Porter."

Short's recording career, nearly all of it available on CD, falls into three periods. There are the youthful albums of the '50s on Atlantic (my favourites are Sing Me a Swing Song and The Mad Twenties), on which he explores the show-tune repertoire. Then, still for Atlantic, there are the sets he made near the beginning of his Carlyle comeback. These include a couple of legendary concerts with his friend and inspiration Mabel Mercer, which more or less set off the New York cabaret revival, and a series of double-length songbooks (he described them as "public services") exploring Coward, the Gershwins, Rodgers and Hart and -- definitively and self- definingly -- Porter. At their best they capture him at his best, as florid as before, both vocally and instrumentally, but with an increasing depth both of timbre and feeling. His vibrato-laden voice really did improve with age. Finally, for Telarc, there were a series of old-master albums that became increasingly jazz- flavoured. After the death of his long-time bassist, Beverly Peer, he abandoned the trio format and fronted a crisp small band. To hear how his style evolved, listen to his versions, successively less flippant but no less witty, of the Vernon Duke-Ira Gershwin number I Can't Get Started. He must have sung this a thousand times but, at every live performance I heard, he kept it fresh.

He started out, and I suppose remained, one of high society's pet exotics. His affectations must, at first hearing, have been as alarming to Sinatra buffs as to rock fans -- perhaps more to the former -- but once you listened beneath the mannerisms, you found an extraordinary attention to the twists and nuances of lyrics, an infallible nose for jokes and surprising tenderness. I would rank him among the half-dozen best male interpreters of classic popular song, beside Sinatra, Mel Torme, Fred Astaire, Johnny Mercer and a floating sixth who might be Dick Haymes.

He said last year that he was retiring from the Carlyle. Then he changed his mind. Then he died, of a leukemia diagnosed only a few days before. He was a courteous and, I think, a kind man. I thought he would go on forever. In an important way he probably will.

-

Robert Astle's self-performed monologue is so wispy it barely exists. A blind piano tuner fishes around in the interstices of his instrument, and finds objects that remind him of his unhappy past life. If this story -- a melodramatic one -- is worth dramatizing, then why not dramatize it, instead of just telling us about it? The acting is as tentative and unformed as the writing. Closes tomorrow.

2005-04-23-seven-days-of-quirky-despair-:
robertcushman@lycos.com; The Seven Days of Simon Labrosse runs through May 1 at Artword, 75 Portland St., 416-366-7723, ext. 290.

I have not been a great cheerleader for the plays of Carol Frechette, but The Seven Days of Simon Labrosse is her best that I have seen. It is more eventful than the others, and it's the first one to have made me laugh.

It's quirky, even if some of the quirks are excessively whimsical. Even its subtitle, A Darkling Comedy, is something of a deterrent that way; it isn't the darkness that scares, it's the cute diminutive.

Simon Labrosse is a young man who needs to get a life and, even more pressingly, a job. The landlord is pounding on the door of his one-room apartment, demanding weeks or months of back rent, while Simon's attempts to pretend he isn't home grow increasingly frantic. Otherwise, he spends his evenings recording taped messages to send to his girlfriend, Nathalie, who is in Africa "helping the helpless." His days he devotes to looking for work. He has a different scheme for each day. Sometimes he goes house to house; other times, he presses his services on strangers in the street.

On his first day he offers himself as "an emotional stuntman" -- someone who will feel your pain. Unfortunately, the customer whose door he darkens is an aggressively angry man who likes to feel his own pain, and reacts much as people in ancient times used to do to unwelcome vacuum-cleaner salesmen. On his second, a lady at a cafe is first intrigued but then appalled when he suggests she employ him as her imaginary movie director, going through the motions of filming her life as if she were a star and the world her audience. (Well, isn't this what everybody wants nowadays? Apparently not, when it comes down to it.) He approaches a couple and suggests himself as a finisher of their sentences, which are, like most people's, chronically incomplete. At first this seems like Simon's best idea yet -- it certainly makes for the play's best-sustained scene -- but all he achieves with it is to set his two prospective clients off in different, and antagonistic, directions. Simon has an infallible knack of exacerbating other people's insecurities, while doing nothing to alleviate his own.

His private life goes much the same. Nathalie doesn't reply to his tapes, and though he remains stubbornly optimistic, he does begin to wonder at her silence.

Now, when you consider the play's title, you may think Simon's apparent confidence in the speed and efficiency of Canada Post to be, shall we say, touchingly exaggerated. They are supposed to get a package all the way to Africa, and to bring another one back, in just a week? Especially as Simon seems unsure of just where on the continent Nathalie might be -- all he remembers is that the country is one of those that ends with an "a." As noted, the play's whimsy is sometimes close to unbearable.

It does, though, give us a window into desperation. We come to realize just how much Simon needs to hope, and how little hope he reasonably has. It is clear early on that his love is unrequited, and the girl of his dreams almost precisely that.

There is another layer. Simon's tale is presented to us as a play within a play. In an attempt to give himself an identity and his existence a meaning, he has hired two actors to play the supporting roles in the story of his recent life.

Unfortunately -- nothing in Simon's world ever happens fortunately -- the actors have issues of their own. One has apparently been engaged mainly because her name also is Nathalie. Given half a chance or less, she will prattle on about the state of everybody's internal organs, especially her own. She is studying this; it seems to bring her great joy. Leo, her opposite number, feels no joy at all. He suffers from a neurological disorder that makes him incapable of uttering a cheerful word. Whenever Simon's script presents him with one, he freezes, and the play with him.

This, too, seems at first insufferably arch, but as the play goes on it becomes funnier and, with that, sadder. Simon is incorrigibly nice, and it seems part of his reason for putting the play on is to raise money to get Leo cured. Fat, the world being what it is, chance.

The production at the Artword is presented by Pleiades Theatre, who up to now have specialized in producing classical French plays. Now they give us a modern one. (Frechette is French Canadian, but her sensibility, especially in this piece, is straight out of the Parisian drama of the 1930s: gentle satire with a punch.)

But it is also presented "in association with" the Montreal Young Company, whose founder, the late Bill Glassco, had intended to direct it, and to whom the show is a tribute. Michael Shamata is now the director, and an adroit one, the production simple and visually clean. Two of the three performers are Young Company alumni.

The exception is Mike Hughes, whose Simon, a battered but unquenchable innocent, has the air of a white-faced clown who's gone out without his makeup.

Manon St-Jules pitches the actress Nathalie a little hard, but gets the parts she plays -- a series of studies in withdrawal -- very well. The prize performance, though, is Paul Fauteux's as Leo, consumed with rage himself and spreading it over every role he plays.

In practical terms, this means he gets to deliver a series of furious arias, at least one of which -- as a courier who arrives with a much-awaited package and is not happy about it -- he executes with virtuoso panache. He can build to a climax, puncture it, then pick up the pieces and build again.

The translation is by John Murrell, the English master of the tirade, and it, too, is a virtuoso job, though it makes you wish yet again that he was spending his time on his own plays rather than other people's.

2005-04-30-worldstage-makes-virtue-of-ne:
robertcushman@lycos.com; World Stage ends tomorrow at Harbourfront Centre, 416-973-4000.; Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme closes tonight at Berkeley Street Upstairs, 416-534-6604.

The WorldStage festival, left for dead a couple of years ago, has recreated itself this year in minimalist form. Every show has been a solo performance of some kind. This can only have been a financial choice, even if dressed up as an artistic one. Still, there have been some interesting events.

The best I encountered was My Arm, written and performed by a shaven-headed Englishman named Tim Crouch. Some of its appeal lay in the games it played with the idea of confessional theatre. Crouch tells his story in urgent though unhurried tones that convince you that he is being autobiographical.

Gradually, you come to realize he can't be. He is in far too good physical shape. The man whose story he tells has done horrible, irreparable things to himself. He tells us he lost a finger. We count. Crouch has 10 of them. Also he talks about his hair, of which he has none.

The person he talks about seems, as a boy, to have been on the vulnerable end of an intense sibling rivalry. As the climax of an escalating series of attempts to gain attention, he raised his right arm in the air. He never lowered it again, leading in time to the breakdown of his whole body. But he did get the notoriety he craved, and more. When he moved to London he got taken up as an art object; a whole exhibit was devoted to him, under the title Man- I(n)festation. A cultural entrepreneur acts as his producer, and is said to be at the back of the theatre, checking up. It was, I think, this detail more than any other that persuaded me for the longest time that the guy was for real.

Crouch, an experienced actor, has created a character, even while making no attempt to imitate him. This aesthetic runs through the whole show. For props, he uses objects he borrows from the audience. But he casts them, so to speak, against type; any thing -- a credit card, say -- can stand in for any other thing, or for any person. He trains a camera on these objets donnes and they appear, enlarged, on a video screen, still stubbornly themselves but also convincing emotional correlatives for the ingredients of his story. The use of video is indeed extraordinary. The narrator mentions his mother's death; she did not, as far as we can gather, drown, but he shows a clip of a woman wading out to sea, and the sense of loss is overwhelming.

The show has its limitations. Its commentary on the art scene gets nowhere in particular. Crouch does, though, come up with a one- line mantra that works both as satire and as common-sense affirmation: "Art is anything you can get away with."

Laurie Anderson, in my heretical view, doesn't get away with it, at least not in The End of the Moon. This is the fruit of her unlikely tenure as artist-in-residence at NASA, and is a series of anecdotes and observations linked, as far as I could tell, by free association. Some of them are delivered from an armchair, others from the podium on which she plays her electric violin. The sound is pleasant, but it all fades into a single blur.

At one juncture she announces a 30-second pause, which duly happens. This is cute, though hardly provocative. And her use of video is not nearly in the same imaginative league as Crouch's. Where she falls shortest, though, is in her delivery, which is even in pitch and tempo (like Crouch's) but without an edge (unlike Crouch's).

It all comes at you through a mic, which depersonalizes it even further. The total effect is undeniably hypnotic, as presumably was the intention. But the trouble with hypnosis is that it puts you to sleep. I felt, especially when the ritual cheers rang out at the end, that I was watching an unclothed empress.

The other shows I saw lacked even Anderson's sense of occasion. Bombshells was a set of four monologues written by Joanna Murray- Smith and performed by Caroline O'Connor. The characters are girls or women in states of quiet or noisy desperation: a bride who marries "for the sake of the dress" (is this credible any more?) and goes on the day from exultation to despair; a "yuppie mum" overwhelmed by everything (this is credible, but it isn't fresh); a widow who experiences an unexpected awakening (the best of the bunch); a teenager in a talent contest (grim caricature masquerading as affection). Every one of them is a stock figure, and the writing is rarely funny or sympathetic enough to compensate. O'Connor, an actress-singer-dancer of Anglo-Australian-Irish extraction, gets to use all her skills and all her accents, and she is a trouper. Rosebud, another U.K. import, gave us Orson Welles waxing autobiographical, its structure apparently determined by the availability of recyclable anecdotes. A scissors-and-paste job, without the ghost of an original viewpoint, Mark Jenkins's script told us little about the work and nothing about the man. But what else would you expect of a piece that takes its title from the Citizen Kane conceit that Welles himself dismissed as "dollar-book Freud"? Christian McKay's Orson came to life just once -- when his voice broke in the middle of a list of abandoned projects.

- - -

There is some fine cosmpolitan theatre, from closer to home, in Moliere's Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme, as presented by Theatre Francais de Toronto. This is famous as the play whose parvenu protagonist learns from his newly engaged philosophy teacher that he has spent his entire life speaking in prose.

Guy Mignault, a radiant beanpole, makes the discovery a blessed event, and he is scarcely less engaging when receiving dubious instruction from his fiercely competitive tutors in fencing and dancing. Mignault's Monsieur Jourdain goes through the entire play being duped, and you feel happy for him. His folly, born of joy, is nobler than other people's wisdom.

As often in Moliere, the play's first half, where the hero's foibles are exhibited as in a revue, is more rewarding than the second, in which the plot grinds into gear. In Diana Leblanc's production, though, everything glides along wittily, smoothly and even subtly. There is good work from Marie-Helene Fontaine's Madame Jourdain, exasperatingly sensible, and from Paul Essiembre and Jessica Heafey as scheming or saucy servants. In Sarah Balleux's design, the actors are sartorial centaurs, 17th century below the waist and 21st above. It works, as does nearly everything else.

Quentin Tarantino has said the sign of a good film is that it makes you want to go home, eat some pie and talk about it. With that in mind, our Popcorn Panel features film buffs feuding in this space each week.

- - -

THIS WEEKS PANEL:

- Chris Knight, the National Posts chief film critic

- Tara Ariano, the editor of the Web sites Fametracker.com and TelevisionWithoutPity.com

- Robert Cushman, the Post's theatre critic

THIS WEEK'S PIE: Peach.

THIS WEEKS SUBJECT: The Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy

CHRIS: After more than 20 years of trying, The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy arrived in movie theatres last weekend. The radio series on which all other versions of the Guide (books, TV miniseries, computer game, etc.) are based first aired in 1978, about a year after the opening of Star Wars, a science-fiction property that is almost exactly unlike The Hitchhiker's Guide. I only mention it because it, too, is about to finally wrap.

While laity of the churches of Douglas Adams and George Lucas are no doubt thrilled by these developments (and as a pantheist, I claim membership in both groups), 20-odd years seems like a bit of a wait for the Sixth Coming. How can any mere movie be worth the wait when the wait is measured in decades -- and when we already have several exciting and popular versions of the story? Its one thing to know where your towel is, but I cant help wondering if there comes a time when you should throw it in.

TARA: I haven't been waiting; I've never read any of the books. I can report, however, that at the showing I attended -- opening night at the gigantic Paramount Theatre here in Toronto -- there were many nerds attending in full geek regalia. A couple of them, decked out in their robes with their towels around their necks, stomped out about halfway through, and a dork quorum a few aisles behind us spent several minutes through the closing credits loudly registering their complaints.

Coming in without any baggage, however, may be the exact reason I liked the movie as much as I did: It was silly and British, very well cast (particularly Sam Rockwells George W. Bush-channelling Zaphod Beeblebrox, at whose every line I couldnt help giggling), intermittently pretty to look at and peppered with random acts of violence and cruelty. I understand that it wasn't completely faithful to the source material, but to complain about that is, I think, to ignore the fact that books and movies are different media, and that sometimes there has to be a love interest. Even nerds need to let girls, with their icky love talk, into the clubhouse.

I guess this is all by way of saying that I hear there were supposed to be three-breasted aliens at some point, but I didn't miss them.

ROBERT: I know the Hitchhikers Guide, not through the books, which Ive only skimmed, but through the original radio series, of which I was a devoted fan whenever I remembered to tune in. And it does seem to me that the story's radio origins are the most important thing about it.

Once you add visuals, you slow down the flow of jokes, which is what happens in the middle of this movie. It's no accident that the best performances are the disembodied ones: Stephen Fry, whose inhuman geniality is perfect casting for the voice of the Guide itself; Alan Rickman, hilariously lugubrious as Marvin the Paranoid Android; and Helen Mirren as the supercomputer.

Of the ones who appeared, Im afraid I thought Rockwell a real pain, just flailing around; weve seen this brainless macho hero a hundred times before and funnier. I was glad when he lost one of his heads; at least we were free of that gag. But Martin Freeman is very nice as Arthur Dent (I'm English -- I know how to queue).

But it all gets bogged down in the action parts, which tend to look the same these days whether they're in Star Wars or Galaxy Quest. The picture gets a terrific boost though, when Bill Nighy appears toward the end. Its worth the price of admission just to hear him say, "I do not know this cheese of which you speak." And the closing sequence, when the Vogons attack Arthurs new house, is great on every level. As is the theme song for the dolphins.

CHRIS: It's true, the jokes originated and still work best in the ether, where one can imagine hyperintelligent supercomputers, Vogon constructor fleets, two-headed men or (if you like) three-breasted women without worrying about how to film them.

By its very nature, the Guide (and Adams's humour) is about superlatives -- the worst poetry, the ultimate answer, the infinite improbability drive, etc. Try filming someone imbibing the best drink in existence, said to have the effect of being hit with a slice of lemon wrapped round a large gold brick. Cant be done.

On the other hand, one could view the movie as an expensive trailer for the Guides other incarnations. I was surprised to see a lot of youngish folks at the screening I went to, and if even 1% of them track down the books -- well, they'll be even more surprised.

As for the towel toters at Tara's screening, theyre probably also writing angry letters to Peter Jackson for failing to include "the cleansing of the Shire" in his Lord of the Rings trilogy. Some folks will never be satisfied, and I reserve the right to be one of them.

TARA: Thats true of so many books -- that the images in the movie can't possibly live up to what we imagined, or that our very favourite lines had to be jettisoned for the sake of forward motion. Believe me, I had plenty of bitter criticism to heap on the film version of Mansfield Park a few years back, so I feel for you, Chris.

But then I suppose the counter-argument is that a story should be strong enough, in its most essential elements, to exist in two separate media, and to mean different things to those who consume them in each incarnation. The Hitchhiker's movie isnt going to be the same product to me, with absolutely no knowledge of the series beyond the number 42, as it is to you, evidently steeped in it. The challenge for the filmmakers is to please us both, even if they didnt film exactly what may have been in your mind. But if they can't please us both, they'd probably be glad enough to know that movie fans dug it -- it couldnt have been just the bathrobers that put it in the No. 1 slot in its opening weekend.

ROBERT: I went with an 18-year-old who has read the entire trilogy -- all five books of it. His comment, which struck me as very reasonable at the time, was that though the film was enjoyable, it was bound to frustrate those who knew the original and confuse those who didnt.

I'm relieved to hear from Tara that he was wrong on the second count. Having now read more myself, I'm torn. Im impressed with some of the restructuring and bothered by some of the additions and omissions. Zaphod didnt have to be as annoying as Rockwell makes him; he's like an inferior version of Kevin Kline in A Fish Called Wanda. Part of me enjoyed the love plot; another part wished they'd refrained from putting it in. It was like MGM softening up the Marx Brothers after their anarchic days at Paramount.

But the basic flavour comes through, and though thats not all you could wish, its probably all you could reasonably hope for. It starts good and finishes good. Thanks again for the fish.

2005-05-07-two-sides-of-alice-dont-quite:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Robert Cushman's reviews of the Shaw and Stratford festivals will be appearing during the week in Arts&Life.

Susan Coyne is emerging as a very funny writer even as she has, over the past few years, emerged as a very funny actress. Her new play, Alice's Affair, contains a line about an unfashionably conformist university that I can barely restrain myself from quoting. It contains several more that wouldnt make much sense if I did quote them, but that work splendidly in context. Coyne, in short, can write verbal comedy and she can write situation comedy.

Unfortunately, the play in which these qualities are being exhibited doesnt add up. Part of it is about a middle-aged woman trapped in what seems to be a constricting marriage; another part of it is about the various relations between literature and life; and one part seems to have been superimposed upon the other.

The eponymous Alice was once a creative-writing student with a demanding teacher regarded by many, notably himself, as charismatic. He is dismissive of Alice's writing, though he would probably claim that he was being cruel only to be kind. He also, we gather, toyed with her emotions, and maybe with her person as well. She certainly wouldn't have been the only student he had had this kind of relationship with.

Flash-forward to now, or thereabouts, and Gregory, the predatory professor, is being buried. His ex-students, who for our purposes are Alice and her friends and contemporaries, gather at the graveside to pay tribute. Afterward, they adjourn to Alices summer cottage and interact. There are Jane, a gold-plated confidante who cant understand why Alice is so shocked at her having a string of boyfriends; Cheryl, who has forsaken her earlier ambitions for lesbianism and good works; and Marie, Cheryl's partner and a psychic. And there is David, who was once Alice's lover and -- her husband being tied up in the city -- would like to be again. David is the only one of the group who has stuck to writing, quite successfully, though he is haunted by the likelihood that Gregory would not have approved.

The trouble with all this is that Alice, the linchpin, is not credible as a writer. I dont mean that she couldnt write; theoretically, anyone could. I mean that her author hasn't told us much about what kind of writer Alice ever wanted to be, and that she lets us forget about those ambitions for most of the play. The mature Alice could be any discontented woman tempted by any importunate men. The ones in question don't seem to be any bargains (both the late Gregory and the extant David come over as unstable egomaniacs) but that doesnt get us very far.

In its attempts to bridge the gap, the script plays some games. We start, entertainingly enough, with one of Gregorys lectures, a series of showy put-downs. Then, as a sort of student's revenge- fantasy, we get the first part of Alice's current biography, presented as a series of scenes in which Gregory is dragooned into playing supporting roles. (In one, hes a waitress.) Then, more or less straight, we get the old buddies reunion; this, giving a stageful of talented actors a chance to pull together, is the most fulfilling part of the play, and certainly of Eda Holmes's production. It culminates in a seance, which in turn leads into a dream sequence in which everyone concerned seems at their wits' end. Much earlier mention has been made of William James (author of The Varieties of Religious Experience) and of Harry Houdini, and both in some sense materialize, but not to any clarifying effect.

Martha Burnss Alice is self-effacing almost beyond the call of duty, at least until she takes a late opportunity to lose her temper. Daniel Kashs Gregory is enjoyably arrogant while alive but an uncalled-for irritant when dead; and neither Brenda Robins (Jane) nor David Jansen (David) bring anything fresh to their roles. Brooke Johnson, though, is amusing as Cheryl, a super-malaprop who mangles not just words but whole proverbial phrases; the joke becomes mechanical but I kept on laughing anyway. As Marie, a disconcertingly practical oddball, Nancy Palk is toweringly delightful. The proceedings are rarely dull, but they're rarely satisfying, either.

- - -

Trying, an autobiographical piece by Canadian-American Joanna McClelland Glass, is as smooth a ride as Alice's Affair is bumpy, but its less interesting and equally lacking in any visible point. Unless, that is, the author, who for dramatic purposes has renamed herself Sarah Schorr, is out to prove what an exemplary secretary she once was. She performed that office nearly 40 years ago for Francis Biddle, former attorney general for FDR and a judge at Nuremberg; and, apart from a tendency to repeatedly split her infinitives, she seems hardly to have done a thing wrong. (She does get pregnant, by a husband who apparently no longer loves her, but thats a matter for sympathy, not blame.) She reminds her employer, now 82 and appearing under his real name, of an illustrious liberal past that he seems irascibly in danger of forgetting, and teaches him to use a Dictaphone. This cross-generational two-hander is painless but bland, right down to the obligatory final scene in which Sarah, through a carefully phrased phone conversation, informs us of her patron's death. One problem is that the fragments we're vouchsafed of Biddles former life are more dramatic than anything we see or hear him do now. Another is that an octogenerian hero is apt to be a drain on a plays energy level. Paul Soles, though, without any obvious cheating, keeps this one burning fairly bright; he is crotchety without being obnoxiously endearing. An actress less pretty than Caroline Cave might provide a stronger counterweight. Also, in a play that's full of quotations (as the lady said of Hamlet and might also have said of Alice's Affair), shes prone to attacks of poetry-voice. The play probably invites them, but it might have been better to refuse the invitation. Otherwise, Marti Maradens production effectively dispenses light and shade, while Christina Poddubiuk's study-set, crammed but not cluttered, looks a beautiful place to live and think in.

- - -

Steve Lucas has designed an equally fine though contrastingly bare set for Sky Gilbert's Rope Enough, the kind of vast empty room in which anything can happen and almost anything, including Gilberts production, can look good. The title pays homage to the Hitchcock film Rope, and also (though nobodys acknowledged it) to the highly revivable Patrick Hamilton play on which the film is closely based; and they in turn derive from the 1920s Leopold-Loeb case in which a well-heeled male couple, disciples of Nietzsche, murdered apparently for kicks. In this updated version an equally swank duo, disciples of Derrida, murder or claim to have murdered, for a kaleidoscope of reasons. Maybe they want to subvert conventional ideas about gays; maybe they want to confirm them; maybe they just want to have fun. Their author-director, as capricious as they are, plays with all the possibilities, to surprisingly provocative effect. He muddies the waters, though, by throwing in a subplot about a self-proclaimed gay role-model who goes about having unprotected sex. Perhaps we're meant to think of him as the real killer; perhaps we're meant to think him a cool joke at the expense of the plays raconteuse, a friend who keeps insisting she isnt homophobic and may be standing in for the rest of us. The acting is uneven, meaning that by conventional standards it's often awful but that it gets its points across and can sometimes be very tense; Gavin Crawford as the more articulate accused exemplifies all these things.

- - -

Chekhov's Heartache is the fourth, no less, of Theatre Smith- Gilmours dramatizations of the masters short stories. They have drawn this time on two of the bleakest, Peasants and Peasant Women, which here appear even bleaker since the original's spare, swift narrative movement turns into a trudge when acted out; no matter how swiftly and adeptly the four actors switch character, their patented style (lots of mime and vocalized sound effects) transforms questioning tragedy into dogged gloom. The junior players, Clare Calnan and Monica Dottor, are fine, but the troupe's founders weigh the show down. Michele Smiths face can transform itself into a mask of pain but the sense and flavour of English speech continue to elude her. Dean Gilmour lacks both the range and the power for the acting problems, which here include an especially damnable blend of cruelty and hypocrisy, that he insists on setting himself.

- Alices Affair plays through May 29 at the Tarragon, 416-521- 1827. Trying plays through June 11 at the Berkeley Street Theatre, 416-368-3110. Rope Enough closes tomorrow at Buddies in Bad Times, 416-975-8555. Chekhov's Heartache plays through May 29 at the Factory Studio, 416-504-9971.

robertcushman@lycos.com

In 1999 William Hutt played Prospero in The Tempest at the Stratford Festival for the third, and what was widely assumed to be the last, time. The assumption was a natural one. Hutt was 79, and Prospero, the magician who at the end of the play breaks his staff and drowns his books, is generally recognized as the greatest of all valedictory rules, maybe signifying Shakespeare's own farewell to the stage. According to rumour, this was not only going to be Hutt's last Prospero. It was going to be his last performance on stage.

"I don't know whether I should apologize to everyone," said Hutt, between rehearsals for this year's festival, at which he is playing Prospero again. "I don't think so. I never said I was going to retire. I did say, very pointedly, that I was going to take a year off, which in fact I almost did. Except I did some directing that next year." (The play was Oscar Remembered, a piece about Lord Alfred Douglas, and featured Michael Therriault, who had been Hutt's Ariel in 1999.) "But because of my age and my saying I was taking a year off, the media made a retirement thing out of it. That's how I viewed it."

To be fair, the festival's publicists never said Hutt was retiring. But they never denied it either. They knew a good angle when they saw one.

This time, though, the retirement is official, right? "Absolutely" says Hutt. Then he elaborates.

"It's my farewell performance on stage. I'll do films and televison if they come along, of course. And if somebody actually thinks 'Oh, maybe he'd like to direct a play, that's perfectly acceptable. I can just sit there and tell everybody what to do. Or just sit there, and hope they'll do it."

There seems little doubt that they would. Hutt is by almost universal consent our greatest actor. Few actors would argue with a man who is the object of so much respect and affection. And it's not just longevity or that he is part of the fabric of our major theatre, having been at Stratford virtually continuously since the first season in 1953. It's the risks he took after he became a legend. Following his failure to retire, he did things that no actor in his eighties is supposed to do. He went on playing leads at Stratford. Some were parts he had played: the King of France in All's Well That Ends Well and Feste, a performance of legendary repose and command, in Twelfth Night. But in 2001 he also took on a massive oratorical role as Clarence Darrow, defending the evolutionary cause in the American courthouse drama Inherit the Wind. (He and his creationist opponent spend much of the play in shirtsleeves and braces, inspiring the National Post headline "The Suspenders of Disbelief.") He then took a remarkable left-hand turn, returning to the Toronto stage for the first time in decades, to appear in two modern classics with Soulpepper.

"I loved working with Soulpepper. Without them I'd never have got the chance to play either one of those roles." The roles were Spooner in Harold Pinter's No Man's Land, in which he was astonishing, and Vladimir in Waiting for Godot, in which he was scarcely less so, despite being slowed down by arthritis and some initial memory problems. "If I'm going to go out, at least I'm going to go with a little panache, not fade away."

And so it's back to Prospero. And talk about coming full circle, this -- as far back as 1962 -- was the first unequivocal lead role he ever played at Stratford. He doesn't remember much about that performance, except the "distinct pleasure" of playing scenes with his Miranda, a brand-new Stratford ingenue named Martha Henry, and the Ariel of the late Bruno Gerussi. He does recall, though, that Michael Langham, then director of the festival, though not of that production, must have been impressed: "He said, 'This should lead to Richard II very soon.' And it did."

Langham is one of the three Stratford chiefs whom Hutt (who has worked with all eight of them) regards as having had the greatest influence on his work. "I learned more about acting from Michael than anyone else. He's a brilliant choreographer; he made us understand clearly the picture he was making with our bodies. We weren't just standing here because he'd told us to."

Robin Phillips "taught me the importance of stillness and thought. He told me I could bounce along perfectly well as I'd done in the past, I'd make money, but that there were more levels to my career than I thought there were." One of those unexpected levels has in fact become something of a legend. "People would come up to me over the years and say 'The part you've played that meant the most to me was ...' and I'd think 'Please, please, let it be Lear or James Tyrone.' But what invariably comes out is Lady Bracknell."

That towering dowager (six-foot plus, with Hutt playing her) in The Importance of Being Earnest occasioned one of Phillips's most celebrated directorial notes, when he remarked: "Lady Bracknell can walk through a room without disturbing one speck of dust." That, Hutt found, was a message he could apply to every role: "It's not just about standing still, but if you're going to do something, do it that deftly, with that much concentration, so it means something."

Richard Monette, the current Stratford director, "has kept me alive. When he took over, 13 years ago, I was over 70. Most directors would have said, 'We'll find whatever we can for you, of course we will,' and proceed to find very little. But Richard has really made a place for me in this organization. I think he thinks I'm very valuable to it." (He does.)

Monette directed Hutt's previous Prospero, and he's also directing this one. Hutt is still re-thinking the role, especially the famous "Our revels now are ended" speech, which virtually prophesies the end of the world. "There's a temptation, because it's a famous aria, to soften it, but" -- and at this point in our conversation Hutt hammered out his words, savouring the meaning of each one -- "I think he's really angry, and sardonic and almost in despair. I hinted at it last time, but this time I said, 'I'm going to go for broke.' "

Then there is Prospero's renunciation speech, one that for the audience is likely to carry even greater emotional baggage this year than it did in 1999. For the actor it's a huge technical challenge, building up one detail after another. "You have to do it in such a way that it's not all one note. And what changes the music is a change in attitude. You start by admiring and invoking the spirits, then you say 'Let me tell you what I've done' -- and that includes the claim to have raised the dead, like Lazarus. He's snatching at equality with God, and he has to eventually forgive himself for that. The mood changes again. I wasn't able to do that in '62. My sense of music wasn't acute enough."

It certainly is now. "I was very fortunate. When my voice changed, it dropped in exactly the right place. Some people's drop in very odd places. Rod Stewart, God knows where his voice dropped to." It's a surprising comparison, but one knows what he means.

The Tempest turned out not to be Shakespeare's final play. And there are rumours Hutt might yet be seen again on a Stratford stage in something less demanding -- perhaps in a cameo role for Monette's own farewell season, two years down the road. ("If I'm still active - - and alive. Because I owe Richard a lot.") This season anyway we have that voice, and that stillness, and they are sovereign.

I've been catching up with some CDs of Broadway musicals, most of which we have yet to see in Canada.

The big exception is Gypsy, just revived at the Shaw Festival. The album of the 2003 Broadway revival, starring Bernadette Peters (Angel -- that's the label, not the lady), confirms my belief that those who have criticized Nora McLellan's Niagara Rose for being too soft, vocally or temperamentally, are off-track. There are many ways of playing Rose. And not even a managing mother has to yell all the time to get her way. It can be done with charm.

Peters in fact has less voice, or anyway less belt, than McLellan. And yes, a Rose whose most fully realized number is a buoyant Together Wherever We Go, closely followed by a flirtatious Small World, may be said to be missing something.

But Peters is a superb actress (though I don't know of her ever doing a non-musical play) who works through text as well as music. And one advantage of the CD over the LP format is that it has more space for linking dialogue -- even, occasionally, for whole scenes.

The climax of any performance must be Rose's Turn, in which her vicarious fantasy of burlesque stardom gives way to breast-beating recrimination and then to triumphant and/or grotesque affirmation.

That's already quite a palette. But the defining moment -- the one that nails the interpretation -- comes just afterward. Rose's daughter, now famous as Gypsy Rose Lee, has overheard her and says "you really could have been something, Mama"; to which mama replies "If I could have been, I would have been, and that's show business." I don't know how Ethel Merman delivered that line, but I imagine she sounded matter-of-fact and not too bothered. Angela Lansbury, my favourite Rose (one of the half-dozen best performances I've seen of anything), made it accepting and therefore healing. Tyne Daly infused it, memorably, with bitterness; she wasn't reconciled to anything.

Peters offers a synthesis; she knows she should give up but it still deeply hurts. This is one torn, neurotic lady. And the lead- ins to Everything's Coming Up Roses and to Rose's Turn itself can never have sounded more terrifyingly driven -- which, riding over the rough bits, is pretty much how she does the songs themselves. What you get is a thin-skinned woman willing herself to be thick- skinned -- trying, if you like, to be Ethel Merman. Merman's own recording (now on Sony, including some bonus tracks) remains the benchmark, as original-cast albums nearly always do, not just for her performance but for everybody else's, orchestra included. But this is a worthy supplement.

- - -

I wonder if The Frogs (PS Classics) would qualify for the Shaw Festival. GBS is a character in it, but it doesn't take place in his lifetime. (I'll get back to that.)

"The time," says Nathan Lane, sounding perplexed, "is the present. The place is ancient Greece." Lane is playing the god Dionysus, in an adaptation of the Aristophanes comedy by Stephen Sondheim and the late Burt Shevelove. (A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Parthenon?) In the original, Dionysus, whose job description includes responsibility for the theatre, journeys to the underworld to bring back Aeschylus and/or Euripides to revitalize the drama, and also public discourse.

Here the candidates are Shakespeare and Shaw, which may not seem like much of a contest, though Shaw himself is both the title and the subject of one of the best songs, joyously sung by Lane. ("The mind with such velocity--/All right, there's the pomposity./But that's just Shaw.") Shakespeare gets a beautiful setting of Fear no more the heat o' th' sun, which must be the most notable of Sondheim's rare collaborations with another lyricist. Then, as in the Greek, there is the Frogs' chorus, delivered as Dionysus crosses the Styx. The amphibians here ("not your hoity-toity intellectuals/ not your hippie-dippy homosexuals") represent the forces of solid conformity, or perhaps liquid complacency, i.e. they stick in the mud. The satire may be somewhat generalized, but this is still a wonderful piece of choral writing, witty and relentless. If the show seems to run out of steam in its second half, that may be Aristophanes's fault; he wasn't hot on plot. (I am not quoting.)

The musical started out in 1974 in the Yale Swimming Pool -- good for frogs, bad for acoustics. It reached Broadway 30 years later, "even more freely adapted" by Lane himself. He is becoming omnipresent in musicals, and especially on recordings of musicals, which is fair enough as he must be one of the most musical comedians ever. (His hysteria was wrong for his namesake in Guys and Dolls, but maybe he was frustrated by having so few songs.) He's very good in the title role of Sherry! (Angel), a surprising recorded resuscitation of a 1967 flop, based on The Man Who Came to Dinner.

The play, in a revival of which Lane appeared a few seasons back, didn't exactly cry out to be musicalized, then or now, but given that the thing was done, it doesn't sound bad.

James Lipton, better known now as the obsequious host of Inside the Actors' Studio, wrote the lyrics, which are quite adroit. To his clout in getting this project on a major label, add that of the cast, which also includes Peters (rather wasted), Carol Burnett (doing a luscious cartoon of a predatory star), Tommy Tune and, though he barely sings, Mike Myers. His character is based on Harpo Marx; who can say whether he got the voice right?

Sweet Smell of Success (Sony) should have been a Toronto musical; it was one of Livent's lost projects. It reached New York in 2002, and was generally attacked. The CD makes it hard to see why. This adaptation of the classic '50s movie about Broadway columnists, press agents and other underworld figures relies too much on a gossips' chorus, but is otherwise loaded with atmosphere. Also with melody: Marvin Hamlisch comes up with ballads (I Cannot Hear the City and Rita's Tune, though the latter seems to have suffered damage since the Toronto workshop) that I wouldn't have believed he had in him; the moody '50s sound seems to have liberated him. (Though I've always suspected that his strictly '70s score for A Chorus Line would have got more respect if somebody else's name had been on it.) Craig Carnelia is maybe too gentle a lyricist for this milieu, but his work is still good.

John Lithgow, as the Burt Lancaster-Walter Winchell figure, took most of the knocks; they said he couldn't sing. Well, he doesn't have the voice -- or, more important, the flair -- for his 11 o'clock number, a mocking song-and-dancer titled Don't Look Now. But he sounds superb, deadly accurate, as the merciless potentate with the steel-trap column and the steel-trap mind. Listen to him ticking the day's items on or off; he's a dictator in a double sense. Again, it's about the acting.

2005-05-21-walker-revival-full-of-surpri:
robertcushman@lycos.com

Adult Entertainment plunges mordantly into sex and violence

Revivals, revivals. A 35-year-old theatre and a 20-year-old company are each celebrating their anniversaries by bringing back one of their greatest hits.

In the case of Factory Theatre (b. 1970), that should perhaps be two of their greatest hits. Or, alternatively, one-third of one of their greatest hits. In 1997 and 1998, the Factory presented Suburban Motel, a cycle of six plays by George F. Walker, all of them set in the one room suggested by that title. They are now reviving two of them. First off, Adult Entertainment.

Walker's Suburban Motel is, to understate matters, a long way from Neil Simon's Plaza Suite, which had a similar linking idea. It could be on the edge of any Canadian city -- indeed, in the current instalment, only a single reference to "the Crown" clues us in that we are even in Canada. That would be the Crown in its legal aspect. Our four characters here are all legals or involved with legals. There are Max and Donny, who are cops; Pam, Donny's estranged wife; and Jayne, Max's girlfriend, who is here for a tryst. She is also a lawyer, and she has an angle. She has a client who is technically guilty but whom she would like to get off, by incriminating the client's notably vicious boyfriend. She asks Max to lean on him. Max agrees. And if you think this makes Max seem bent, you should meet Donny. He's way over the edge.

This, of course, is the world Walker subsequently explored, and is still exploring, in his TV series, This Is Wonderland. Or rather it's a complement to it. I don't remember seeing many cops in Wonderland, crooked or otherwise, and though the lawyers who are its stars have their quirks, they don't seem to have compromised themselves as Jayne has. On the other hand, the TV show lets us see the clients, the wrecked or endangered humanity that is only an off- stage presence in the play.

I have to confess that I prefer This Is Wonderland. I like its humour, which is often uproarious, its sense of the city, its variousness. It has texture. Its alternating storylines engage me more than does the concentrated portrait of four souls in purgatory that we get here. It feels like life, while Suburban Motel, or at least this part of it separated from its original siblings, feels like a very thin sliver of it.

I say this rather nervously because, as a piece of writing for the stage, I can think of absolutely nothing to say against Adult Entertainment. It's taut, it's funny, it's mordant, it's surprising, it's full of sex and violence. It manages the considerable feat of presenting a stageful of self-loathing characters without either patronizing or endorsing them. Its vision isn't theirs. The events are those of a nightmare (literally, in one scene) but the play itself stays sane. The language doesn't sing, but it snaps. And there is one recurring line for Jayne, one to which she clings for assurance when things begin to fall apart, that is every bit as good as it thinks it is.

I have similarly mixed feelings about Ken Gass's production, which is good but doesn't feel ideal. Its best sequence comes at the very beginning and is, strictly speaking, extraneous. Or so I judge from the printed text, whose first stage direction begins "Jayne Johnson and Max Malone are having sex." Then a phone rings and the play starts, and the abruptness of this sets the tone for what follows. Here, though, instead of the characters being discovered, we see them coming into the room, careering around it, pulling off clothes, arriving on the bed. It's well and wittily choreographed, and it puts the "adult" into adult entertainment; we become thinking voyeurs, noting that Jayne is in two minds, and Max very much in one. It's a flaw, though, in the production and maybe in the play, that this isn't followed through. We may be able to work out intellectually how much Max is driven by desire, and how Jayne is split between lust and calculation, but we seldom feel it.

The performers are fine, but they hold us as actors rather than as characters. Jane Spidell, playing her near-namesake, is flamingly talented, and she looks right, but she has to work at the hard- boiledness and also, more curiously, at the vulnerability. Ron White as Max is a solid centre to the action, but he sucks emotion in rather than letting it out; he may be meant to be strong and silent but there must be more going on inside him than the actor lets on. David Ferry as Donny, the former vice-squad man who has been warped by hanging out with hookers, is coiled and cute, in a nasty way, but not really dangerous, and maybe physically wrong; the script says he's large, and Ferry is medium. Linda Prystawska seems initially out of her depth as Pam, but she improves, and makes the most of the play's best line, in which diurnal life incongruously intrudes. She may be the vessel -- not the mouthpiece -- for the play's ultimate message, which is that, though you can't touch pitch without being defiled, pitch will touch you anyway, so deal with it. Next up, The End of Civilization, in which Max and Donny ride again.

The kind of play Adult Entertainment is has worn better than the kind of play The Anger in Ernest and Ernestine is. But genres aren't shows, and the latter piece, which the Theatre Columbus troupe have brought back for their 20th birthday, gave me a better time. What the suburban-motel piece is for its opening few minutes, this one is for its entire length: a danced duet of approach and avoidance, consummation and revulsion. The show was written in 1987 by Leah Cherniak, Robert Morgan and Martha Ross. Cherniak directed it, and does so again now, with Rick Roberts and Jenny Young replacing her co-authors as the actors.

Ernest and Ernestine are a shy pair, doomed to become one. He lives in an anal-retentive world of his own; she has what he calls "pizazz," though it seems more like she's sort of flaky. (She thinks it's smart to leave teabags in the pot, which I think would be grounds for divorce.) But they get married, as they would, and set up house in -- apparently -- a basement with a furnace in the living room. Their breakfasts show where they're headed. Ernest takes his time, counting every cornflake; Ernestine, rushing off to work, performs a ballet, more frantically scrambled at each successive rendition, of chewing, swallowing, dressing, cleaning and farewelling.

There are a good number of reasons for being prejudiced against this show, starting with the title. (Do Ernests marry Ernestines? If so, they deserve all they get.) There is the revelation in the program that Theatre Columbus's founding figures -- its Christopher and Christabel Columbuses -- studied in Paris at the fabled feet of Jacques LeCoq; we have suffered too much over the years in the names of mime and clowning for this to seem anything but a threat. There is a sequence in which the couple try to deal with their unruly furnace by strict adherence to the rulebook, which they read aloud; this seems like one of Eugene Ionesco's gratuitous illustrations of the absurdity of words, people and everything else. There is the fact that everything is predictable; it's a given that these lovebirds are going to end up hating one another. And so they do, without ever quite ceasing -- which is also predictable -- to love one another.

You don't have to have been in a committed relationship for all this to strike home; just having shared a space with someone will usually do the trick. But this piece makes it fresh and makes it clever. It also makes great technical demands on its performers, demands that Roberts and Young meet with almost insouciant assurance. She incorporates a heel-clicking Highland fling (or is it Latin?) and even a touch of ventriloquism without turning a hair; he shows how every man, when he thinks himself alone, can be his own Bruce Springsteen. One especially nice touch: Ernest and Ernestine are never more united than when they can join their anger and focus it outward, against all the forces that would punish them for having driven the wrong way up a one-way street. Maybe that's meant to be another metaphor for marriage.

- Adult Entertainment runs through June 12 at the Factory, 416- 504-9971. The Anger in Ernest and Ernestine runs through June 5 at Theatre Passe Muraille, 416-504-7529

2005-05-28-crazy-nights-at-the-walkerlan:
End of Civilization runs in repertory until June 12 at the Factory Theatre. 416-504-9971. Evita runs until June 5 at the Princess of Wales. 416-872-1212.

And more revivals. One of them is revelatory, or at least one scene in it is. Theres a duologue in George F. Walker's End of Civilization, one of the two plays from his Suburban Motel cycle that Factory Theatre is remounting, that's unlike anything in any other Walker piece I have encountered. The thing is, its normal. Or at least, its about people who have recently left a state of being that most audiences would accept as normality, and who are still reeling from the shock, unable to adjust. Most Walker characters are at the end of their tethers; and though this is routinely described as being "disturbing, it really isn't, because we can't imagine them ever being at the other end.

Here we meet Henry and his wife, Lily: Henry has lost his job, and has reached the desperation stage as regards finding a new one. So he has come to the same anonymous motel room we know from previous plays (excellently realized, in all its just-short-of- seediness, by Shawn Kerwins set design), so that he can use it as a base from which to present himself for even more interviews; and Lily has come along, to give him support. But of course, with their house on the line and their kids staying with relatives, all the strains of their marriage are coming to the surface. Lily resents Henrys assumption that, just because she's never had a job, she would be incapable of finding one now to help out. Henry is fearful of being mocked, by his wife or the world. Already dangerously angry, he has begun to take pills.

As well as being brilliantly written, this scene is cunningly placed so that it functions not as exposition but as exploration. The performances, by Dennis O'Connor and Brenda Bazinet, illuminate every beat of conversation, every flicker of tension; a partnership turns, before our eyes, into a pair of resentful solitudes.

OConnor, a weighty actor in every sense with a shock of white hair, comes on like a cross between Falstaff and Lear; his railings against the state of a greedy, heartless world take on a farcical kind of grandeur. It has to be farcical because this is a Walker play, after all, and one of the marks of a Walker character is an insouciant acceptance of the awful. (The characters revel in it; the author, somehow, doesnt.) As he sinks deeper into Walkerland, Henry comes under suspicion of mass murder -- not of the men denying him work, but of his fellow applicants, whom he despises as disgusting ass kissers... depressing."

Lily, however, doubts he did it: "I just can't see him killing people. Especially if they weren't management.

Investigating the case are Max and Donny, the same two world- weary cops whom we can meet alternate nights in the companion- piece, Adult Education.

Here they are onlookers rather than prime movers, and it suits them better. Ron Whites Max, not so much hard-boiled as over-easy, is especially good, now that hes allowed to stick strictly to business. Donny is more involved; it turns out he was at school with Lily, and he gets very upset when she discovers the easiest way for a woman alone in a suburban motel to make some money.

Not that Donny has anything against professionals (matter of fact, he's obsessed with them) but he has standards.

Donny is crazy" in Max's estimate, "sick in Lilys; and David Ferry is, as before, expert but perhaps too endearing. But then his place in the action is rather strange; he isnt at its centre, but he won't stay on the periphery either. Walker delights in messing with his audience's expectations, both of chronology (this play has an ultra-confusing time-scheme, of which I cannot even now make perfect sense) and of symmetry. Donny, by common consent of all who meet him, needs help. One thing he could maybe use is a play of his own.

The cast, in Ken Gass unimpeachable production, is completed by Jody Stevens, obvious but not objectionable as the hooker down the hall. End of Civilization is the best play now in Toronto, as bleak, funny and pertinent now as at its premiere seven years ago -- when, incidentally, it had a definite article to its name. More downsizing.

- - -

From further back in theatrical history, not to mention historical history, Evita returns to confirm its reputation as the best musical to come from the firm of Tim Rice and Andrew Lloyd Webber, whether working separately or together.

Rices more sardonic lyrics wear particularly well; the syllables tend to sit jerkily on the notes, but they have point and attitude, especially in the opening Oh What a Circus, the commentary of someone called Che (sort of Guevera, but only sort of) at the funeral of the temporary secular saint Eva Peron. Musically the number is a pre-echo (a preprise, perhaps) of the show's hit tune, Don't Cry for Me Argentina, and its good to hear it so comprehensively desecrated.

And when Che remarks of all the mourning that its good for the country. In a roundabout way" we are hearing political analysis with more edge and resonance than we usually get in musicals, especially in the 25 years since. Also it sounds unforced, not overly impressed by its own toughness. Rice was always a joker. These are his best, and most serious, jokes. They are the wittiest lyrics Webber has ever had to set. And yes, that does include Cats.

Rice is less impressive when he tries for Broadway wordplay of a more traditional kind. When Eva in her glory sings "The people adore me. So Christian Dior me, it's like bad imitation Dave Frishberg. (Frishberg wrote Peel Me a Grape: Best way to cheer me -- Cashmere me... New Thunderbird me -- you heard me." Hear the difference?) And when, in the Big Song, the lady proclaims herself "Dressed up to the nines. At sixes and sevens with you, it's pitiful. Its also a shock to realize that the tune itself consists just of its title phrase and some plodding padding. Webbers Latin pastiches, though, have energy, especially the tango and the brisk parade of Eva's discarded suitors as she sleeps her way to the top. Her rise from direst poverty is very well presented, evoking both sympathy and revulsion. Keeping these divided aims in balance proves much harder, though, once she's made it. There are gaping narrative holes -- the bane of the sung-through musicals, where everything has to be conveyed through lyrics which arent up to the job. Why did Eva throw herself at Juan Peron, rather than at any other of Argentinas ambitious soldier-politicians? What did she see in him? What did they promise, that made the people support them? What did they see in her -- or, as Che puts it, all too rhetorically who is this Santa Evita?" Just a Latin-American Princess Diana? The answers to these and other questions can be found in the program more easily than on the stage. Che's verdict -- "she did nothing for years -- seems all too accurate, dramatically if not politically. That does not make for a satisfactory heroine. Or even a satisfactory anti- heroine

And that's another, even more important, thing. The show has no characters. Peron himself is a cipher. The most emotional song goes to his discarded mistress, whom we have never met before and never meet again. (Im told that in the movie, they gave this number to Eva. Smart move; she could use it.) That leaves Che and Eva, a commentator and a symbol. They never meet, never make contact, not even when they sing a duet. It leaves an emptiness.

His is the better role, a brave cynic who keeps getting beaten up for being ironic. Bradley Dean sings in the choppy falsetto that now seems inseparable from the genre (it wasnt originally) but he has the right mocking posture.

Eva Peron was, obviously, a hard case; Kathy Voytko sounds as hard as the nails that proverbially get scratched on chalkboards. But of the charm that she must also have had -- what Rice's scansion forces her to describe as a little touch of star-qualitee' -- there is no trace. She can go dreamy when required, but her passion is petulance.

The shows strongest point was always its staging and that remains, with Larry Fuller, the original choreographer, "reproducing" the original direction of Harold Prince, who now has an "entire production supervised by" credit. The emblematic groupings are still striking, especially the nine naval officers who move in tight formation, three abreast, and signify Power. Theres also a recurring tableau vivant of Argentinian nobs, looking and sounding as if they had dropped in from the Ascot scene in My Fair Lady. It's a quarter century since the show's London premiere, but half the cast still sounds English. Evita is the best of all the pop operas, or rock song-cycles, or whatever you want to call them, but that doesnt constitute a claim on immortality. You let down your people, Evita. You were supposed to have been immortal. But in the end you could not deliver.
