2005-06-01-both-these-ends-justify-the-m:
Journey's End is in repertory at the Court House Theatre, Niagara- on-the-Lake, until October 8; Happy End at the Royal George Theatre until October 28. 1-800-511-SHAW

NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE - The Shaw Festival production of Journey's End is, to use the appropriate vernacular, a jolly good show. This famous play about the trenches of the First World War (written 10 years after the event) was the first English theatrical word on the subject, and -- at least until Oh What a Lovely War came along, to do for the enlisted men what Journey's End did for their superiors - - the last one.

R.C. Sherriff, whose first play it was, had an astonishing success with it that he never managed to duplicate. He went on writing into the 1960s, usually plays on ostensibly serious subjects that emerged as irredeemably cozy, with all problems easily solved. Journey's End is cozy too, in a way. It focuses almost exclusively on the officer class, all of them apparently dedicated to preserving the social and moral codes they learned at public school in new and appalling circumstances. But the play transcends its apparent limitations. Sherriff, writing from personal experience, shows how desperately these men, mostly very young but a couple in early middle age, need the memory of home comforts and home beliefs. Sometimes it seems that that's what they're fighting for.

We are in a dug-out in France in 1918, the British troops awaiting the last major German offensive. Captain Stanhope, the company commander, barely in his twenties, is a good and popular officer who can only keep himself and his men together by drinking. Osborne, his second-in-command and indispensable confidant, is a placid ex-schoolmaster who reads Alice in Wonderland. Their comrades include Trotter, jovial and unimaginative, who came up through the ranks; Hibbert, who has cracked and wants out by any means available; and Raleigh, the youngest and newest recruit, who knew Stanhope at school and hero-worships him. He also happens to be the brother of Stanhope's fiancee, and Stanhope, already prey to self- torment, lives in fear that the boy's letters home will expose him as the alcoholic wreck he feels he has become. War, from these men's perspective, lives up to its reputation of being 90% boredom and 10% terror. They live for the next revolting meal and the next essential cup of tea. What lies ahead is the near-certainty of injury and death, a prospect brought even closer when orders come for a reconnoitering party to get information by taking a prisoner. Osborne and Raleigh are chosen to lead it.

Christopher Newton's production, relaxed and amused in its first half, gets very tense in its second. It does take a few surprising short-cuts. The Colonel (Anthony Bekenn) is far too reminscent of Stephen Fry's C.O. in the War According to Blackadder, jovially unperturbed about sending his subordinates into harm's way. Evan Buliung's Stanhope carries the play, as he should, but he does so by hitting the same high-strung note with hardly any variation; still, when he brings out the good in the terrified Hibbert by appealing to him to do the decent thing and stay with the other chaps, he gets well away with the trickiest scene in the play. Conversely, Patrick Galligan's Osborne could afford to let up on the sweet reasonableness just occasionally, but his is still an affecting performance; when, left alone and sick with fear, he lets down his guard for a silent moment, and it's a very moving one. Jeff Meadows' Hibbert is good, William Vickers' Trotter even better and Jeff Lillico's Raleigh ideal, progressing from juvenile enthusiasm by way of a shocked forced maturity to a final uncomprehending agony. The trench cook, Private Mason, is a role that Simon Bradbury could probably play in his sleep, but he is as wide awake as the character himself. When he too goes up the steps to battle, a whole wider world of combatants comes into focus. We never do find out exactly which, if any, of the characters gets out alive. It's the most honest ending possible.

Tadeusz Bradecki's revived production of the Bertolt Brecht-Kurt Weill musical Happy End looks as good now as it did two years ago, given a stylish visual bite by its designer Peter Hartwell, and with every move precisely plotted. It's the piece itself that continues to disappoint; the songs are some of Weill's best, but though they help set the mood, they have almost nothing to do with the action. This, tossed off by Brecht and his collaborator Elisabeth Hauptmann and then ascribed to a mythical "Dorothy Lane," is slight to begin with: an encounter between some fairly inefficient gangsters and a deatchment of the Salvation Army in a mythical Chicago. The confessedly free adaptation by Michael Feingold makes it seem even more drawn-out, and is as laborious as the electronic contraption through which the gang's mastermind, The Fly, sends them their orders. Feingold's lyrics aren't that great either, though they're now the approved English version. The piece ends, in a thin echo of The Threepenny Opera, with the two sides uniting to battle the common enemy, Big Business. But the mob, even in the 1920s, was big business. (I'm not sure about the Salvation Army.) Brecht seems, by the way, not to have heard of Prohibition. His hoods are small-time shakedown artists.

Cast changes are up and down. Ben Carlson, standing in for Benedict Campbell until mid-June, hasn't the misanthropic weight for public enemy Bill Cracker. His singing voice, so pleasing in She Loves Me, here sounds hoarse, which might seem right but isn't. Something about his presence leads us to expect a serious love- plot, which doesn't materialize. This might be intentional alienation but I don't think so. Glynis Ranney, though, far supasses her predecessor in the role of army sweetheart Hallelujah Lil, especially in the way she builds the great torch song Surabaya Johnny from innocence to ashes. She's sweet voiced, but believably tough. It probably isn't Jay Turvey's fault that I couldn't wait to see his sinister Japanese mastermind get whacked and was severely disappointed when the whacking proved temporary. Among the other original-cast survivors, I especially liked Jeff Madden's Baby Face and Donna Belleville's Major Stone. She, incidentally, is the first of two Salvationists of her rank to appear at the Shaw this season; Major Barbara follows shortly. Times being tough all over, as both Brecht and Shaw keep reminding us, I wonder if the two shows can share the uniforms.

Colour Photo: David Cooper, Shaw Festival / Jeff Lillico as Raleigh, William Vickers as Trotter and Evan Buliung as Stanhope in Journey's End at the Shaw Festival: jolly good show.
2005-06-02-the-difficulties-of-playing-o:
robertcushman@lycos.com; In repertory at Stratford's Festival Theatre until Oct. 28.

THE TEMPEST

Festival Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

At the age of 85, and playing Prospero for the fourth time, William Hutt can still surprise us. In what he insists will be his last stage performance, Hutt takes the old magician of The Tempest to new extremes. We first see him with his hands shaking as he lifts his staff to start the storm that will shipwreck his enemies. Our next sight of him, and our first hearing, comes when his daughter Miranda pleads with him to break the spell. For a moment his anger, still on the boil and fused with pride in his own accomplishments, seems directed at her. Then it dissolves into gentleness, suddenly and completely.

These reversals, constantly repeated and immaculately executed, underpin Hutts whole account of a man who takes a plays length to determine whether the rarer action is in virtue or in vengeance. He's probing Prospero's emotions and the colours of his words at the same time. There are speeches in his long tale to Miranda of how they came to the island that struck me as though I had never heard them before. He relives the love he had felt for his usurping brother Antonio, as well as the pain of his betrayal.

He goes to the furthest edge with our revels now are ended, that prophecy of doom deceptively packaged as a nostalgic farewell. Its prompted by Prosperos remembrance of a second plot against his life, and by his possibly guilty rage at Caliban, the exploited "demi-devil" responsible for it. Hutt has spoken in interviews of his desire to take this speech to its nihilistic limits, and he does. I think he takes it too far (does Prospero really feel only contempt for "the cloud-capped towers" whose dissolution he predicts?) but that's a matter of interpretation, not execution. It's thrilling to hear him ride the wave of his passion and to see it crash clear into the next scene, to break only when Ariel, who isnt human, challenges him to remember that he himself is. The pause before he bows to the inevitable, which is mercy, is going to be legendary.

He is also from time to time very funny, especially when wryly surveying the instant love affair of Miranda and Ferdinand. The mood is catching; in Richard Monettes production the youthful absurdity of this pair is played up (by Adrienne Gould and Jean-Michel LeGal) far more than usual. They can be delightful, she especially, but they can hardly have Hutt's capacity to switch moods, to go the brink of farce and then step back from it. Once set on their course they stay there.

Most of the actors make strong initial impressions they fail to reinforce. The courtiers in the wreck are clearly distinguishable, which is uncommon, and when they come ashore it looks as if Monette will be able to make their plottings as compelling as he did in his production with Hutt six years ago. It's not to be; the scenes are still less boring than in most productions, but only Gonzalo (Bernard Hopkins) strikes any fresh sparks with his vision of an island Utopia. The toffs costumes may be authentically Jacobean, but they look constraining. And their varying degrees of guilt and repentance, which are crucial, are here routine.

Prosperos relations with his servants are also rudimentary. Ariel (equally well played and sung by Jacob James, with strange Struwwelpeter fingernails and stranger poses) is faithful with a touch of impatience, and that's that. Nor do you have to believe that the play is a commentary on colonialism to want there to be more going on between Prospero and Caliban; Stephen Ouimette is surprisingly subdued, though he grumbles and rhapsodizes as required. Brian Tree, a commanding and properly nasty Stephano, dominates the clown scenes. Steven Sutcliffe's Trinculo has one nice touch: a ventriloquist himself, he gets very spooked when Ariel ventriloquizes him.

The productions one lapse from basic coherence is the betrothal masque, with the text cut and the dancing prolonged, considering the choreography, beyond reason. The best that can be said is that it makes Prosperos loss of temper very understandable, though since it's staged for exit applause, that connection gets obscured. After that, though, it's plain sailing, with Hutt at his peak in the speech of renunciation -- which, incidentally, struck me as being far more about the character than about the actor. Maybe I used up my responses on the latter score in 1999, when we all thought he was retiring; which isnt to say I wont be crying buckets if they let me in to his farewell performance in October. Until then, concentrate on experiencing verse acting at what is currently its highest stage of development.

Colour Photo: David Hou / In his speeches to Miranda (Adrienne Gould), Hutt probes Prospero's emotions and the colours of his words at the same time.
2005-06-03-good-golly-he-likes-dolly:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Until Nov. 6. 1-800-567-1600

HELLO, DOLLY!

Festival Theatre, Stratford

- - -

Lucy Peacock doesn't find herself in Dolly Gallagher Levi, the matchmaking factotum of Hello, Dolly!, until she reaches her big number. I don't mean the title anthem in the restaurant; I mean the first-act closer, Before the Parade Passes By, in which Dolly -- one of the show's two potentially merry widows -- affirms her decision "to rejoin the human race."

You can feel Peacock seizing on the preliminary dialogue in which she asks her late husband's blessing on her new departure; at last the actress has something to act, and it carries her right through the song, for which she mysteriously finds more voice than she had for her any of her earlier excursions, when the orchestra regularly drowned her. (William Hutt in The Tempest also husbands his resources, but more excusably and more productively.)

She also excels, when she gets to the title routine, at showing the woman's delight in returning to her old haunts and being courted; but the truth she brings to it only exposes the falseness of the number itself. It isn't about the character who's supposed to be singing it, and it certainly isn't about acting; it's about star status, justified or otherwise, getting cheered for coming down a staircase.

It doesn't help that the staircase here is less impressive than the one the designer, Patrick Clark, has provided for the miserly Mr. Vandergelder's hay-and-feed store back in Yonkers. Peacock does fine when she gets to sit down and vamp Vandergelder in the restaurant, and she's the only Dolly I've seen to take genuine pleasure in the adventures of the young lovers in the other part of the plot -- one thing she has in common with Prospero, for those who crave thematic parallels.

But most of Dolly is shtick, for which she isn't equipped. To play Dolly you don't have to be able to sing, exactly, but you must move the Earth with your voice. Peacock doesn't come from that tradition or have those skills, whether for the outrageous camping of Motherhood or the ragtime raucousness of So Long, Dearie. (An 11 o'clock number if ever there was one; it comes from nothing and goes nowhere.) Even the earlier dialogue bits defeat her; she sounds foggy and choppy, with an accent, Gallagher rather than Levi, that comes and goes.

The best all-round performances come from Peter Donaldson, whose Vandergelder is a sustained display of wit, and from Christina Gordon in a minute but evocative turn as a street trader. There is some delight, too, from Dayna Tekatch and Kyle Blair as the snivelling Ernestine and her swain, dragooned into exhibition dancing. As Mrs. Molloy, the other widow, Robin Hutton sings sweetly but hardly acts at all. Laird Mackintosh has some spirit, plus prancing-pony legs, as Cornelius Hackl, and Lawrence Haegert and Amy Walsh fill in nicely enough as the fourth couple.

None of them, though, can really compete with the athletic dancers in the Waiters' Galop, especially the ones who wield spatulas as if they were Indian clubs. Michael Lichtenfels' choreography throughout is in a different world from his work on The Tempest, though the number that's simply called Dancing is less rapturous than it should be; when the late Gower Champion staged it, it just about defined the spirit of musicals, or at least of musical comedy.

Susan H. Schulman's direction is rather more prosaic than that, though it tells the story well and has a good sense of humour. It has plenty of colour, too, especially in the costumes.

I never understand why audiences infallibly applaud revolving stages for revolving, or dancers for high-kicking in unison; surely that's the least you'd expect in either case. But I confess to being a Pavlovian sucker for anything that appears on stage in the likeness of a train, and the one here is dandy. It's featured in Put On Your Sunday Clothes, a joyously expectant number that's one of my two favourites in Jerry Herman's score. (The other is Elegance, which isn't by Herman at all but by Bob Merrill; which may explain why it has a couple of rhymes that are spectacular. Or, as it has to be pronounced here, spectackular. Its spruce pleasures are, in this production, spoiled by over-elaboration.)

Which brings me, at last, to the show itself. Its source, Thornton Wilder's vintage farce The Matchmaker, provides wit and style and a modicum of wisdom; the adaptation, by Michael Stewart, adds a bit more wit and considerable slickness. The score, if not the most distinguished in Broadway history, is like the whole piece an honest and successful attempt to make an audience feel happy. The tradition it inagurated could easily turn stupid and mechanical, as was demonstrated in Herman's very next diva-showcase Mame. But Dolly, anchored to earth by its setting in turn-of-the-century melting-pot New York, has substance. It's taken me 40 years to admit it, but Hello, Dolly! is a great musical.

Black & White Photo: David Hou / Lucy Peacock excels at showing Dolly's delight in returning to her old haunts, but she isn't equipped with a voice that moves the Earth.

2005-06-04-playing-ibsen-forward-is-an-i:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Hedda Gabler runs through June 12 at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, 416-975-8555.

There seem to be two reasons why Hedda Gabler gets more productions than almost any other Ibsen play. First, it has only seven characters; and second, one of those seven, Hedda herself, is a role every leading actress feels she owes it to herself to play. God knows why.

For a woman who's been tagged as the female Hamlet, Hedda displays a remarkably narrow range of feelings, nearly all of them disagreeable. She's snobbish, she is -- to put it very mildly -- manipulative, she's frigidly flirtatious and she's cruel. That might seem to put her in good dramatic company: "Macbeth, after all, is a mass murderer, but he has a conscience about it, and his conscience, to a great extent, is the play. Hedda is determinedly self- righteous about her faults, though she does, at what is probably her most engaging moment, admit to being a coward, unable to break free from the conventions she professes to despise. Somehow, though, in the world outside the play, she has gained the reputation of actually being the rebel she would like to be. Either that, or it's all society's fault."

Somewhere in the reams of interviews that preceded the Volcano company's disastrous new production there is a reference to Hedda's being "ahead of her time." She isn't; she's behind it. Within the play itself we see her old schoolfriend Thea Elvsted earning Hedda's hatred by doing what she herself is scared of doing -- leaving her marriage to befriend the dissolute but presumably gifted writer Eilert Lovborg.

A full decade earlier, and even more decisively, Ibsen had shown us Nora slamming the door on her doll's house, in a play that used to be denigrated as an ephemeral pamphlet compared to Hedda Gabler but that now generates far more electricity.

There is another sense in which Hedda is old-fashioned, to the point of being an anachronism, and it's much more interesting. Like other Ibsen protagonists, Hedda, daughter of a general, dreams of being a tragic hero, and finds herself in a context that has no use for such a thing. In Ibsen's fallen, tragicomic world, vainglorious master builders lose their footing and tumble off towers, and disgraced industrialists, dreaming of a comeback, keel over and die in the snow.

Hedda, to avoid a scandal and the threat of sexual blackmail, makes a cleaner end by shooting herself -- offstage -- with her late father's pistols. Judge Brack, her would-be seducer, famously greets this event with the shocked observation that "people don't do such things," a remark whose irony is doubled by the fact that Hedda had used exactly those words to mock the behaviour of her husband's aunt in leaving her hat lying on the sofa. Suicide is reduced to the level of a social faux pas. You can see why Hedda would want out, even though she has been complicit in the system when it suited her.

That at least is what happens in the play Ibsen wrote. In Judith Thompson's adaptation, as directed by Ross Manson, Brack's last line has gone. In exchange we get a long, hallucinatory speech about horse-riding that Yanna McIntosh as Hedda is required to deliver between gunshots while dragging herself bleeding around the stage. The lady is thus deprived even of the final freezing dignity that her author granted her, though I have a suspicion that Manson and Thompson believe that in giving her a dying aria they are building her up rather than bringing her down. The speech itself connects with Hedda's earlier demand that her husband buy her the horse he promised and that he can no longer afford. That incident takes up one line of the original; in this version it seems to go on for petulant pages.

The play was written in 1890. Here its first half has been advanced to the beginning of the 20th century. After the intermission we find we have jumped still further forward; the time is The Present and the place (to judge from a single interpolated joke-line about Queen's University) is Here. The inspiration for the time shift seems to be the wonderful new book Lovborg has written about the future, a choice of subject audacious enough to put the fear of God into Hedda's placid husband, George, who is in competition with Eilert for a university post. That's the dramatic point, not whether Lovborg personally thinks the future will be good, bad or indifferent; he doesn't say, not in Ibsen. Thompson, though, has decided the matter for him: The future is going to be awful. Accordingly she takes us first to within hailing distance of the First World War, and then to the world as it is today, and we all know what to think about that.

The idea panders to our modern mania for making old authors agree with us, but it does nothing to illuminate Hedda herself. It also emasculates the play's shock-horror climax. Hedda's new living room affords no stove in which she can burn the manuscript she thinks of as Lovborg's and Thea's child; she has to mess around with a fire bucket instead.

Anyway, it's impossible to believe she is destroying the only copy: not in a world in which Kinko's stays open 24 hours in case, as stated by the late, great Mitch Hedberg, you should wake up in the middle of the night feeling you need two of something. The updating is distracting for the audience and, I would guess, a hindrance to the actors.

Manson and Thompson have of course a perfect right to use the basics of Ibsen's play as a jumping-off point for their own original creation. But that isn't what they've done. They've stuck close to their source, while pausing from time to time to pad it out with the occasional new line or even scene of their own. Some of these underline what's already there; others strike out from it, but without getting very far. It makes for a long evening.

Like everyone, I looked forward to seeing McIntosh as Hedda, and like everyone I seem to have been guilty of arbitrarily matching star actress to star role. McIntosh looks striking in her red dress, and Teresa Przybylski's deep white set allows her to take some commanding upstage poses. I admired, too, the convulsive movement of her hands when she begins to contemplate literary infanticide. But what McIntosh has always projected best is fearlessness and generosity, qualities that are pretty much the antithesis of Hedda. Nor does she do justice to the brittle comedy inherent in a woman who makes jokes at everybody else's expense while life plays its bitterest joke on her. She offers instead a kind of majestic resentment, monotonous and rather forced. Even more effortful is the boyish Brack of Nigel Shawn Williams, floundering in a vain attempt to do suave.

Ann Baggley's Thea is wooden in everything that pertains to Ibsen but a touch livelier in some added moments that allow her to get cross with the heroine. There is lovely work from Alon Nashman as a conciliatory George, a worrier wed to a wife who wanted a warrior, and a charismatic turn from Tom McCamus, whose Lovborg is a tousled charmer in the Dylan Thomas manner. He is acting in a different style from everybody else, more obtrusively modern (i.e. he gabbles), but that may be part of the concept; he is the Harbinger of the Future, after all.

Tanja Jacobs seizes every opportunity afforded by the role of Aunt Juliana and then a few over. George's auntie, fussy but kind, is the nicest of the nice people to whom Hedda considers herself superior. Another of her butts is the maid Berthe, played by Cynthia Ashperger, who in this adaptation gets to state at great length her objections to the new lady of the household. Come the new millennium she gets real bossy, and starts addressing her employer by his first name. So I told a lie; the play does have a new subplot -- the development of the servant class.

The fast-forwarding also permits far more detail than the original provided, not only about the contents of Lovborg's book but about what he and the other guys get up to when they're out on the town. I confess I always used to find Ibsen's 19th-century reticence on such matters rather trying. I see now that I didn't know when I was well off.

2005-06-07-of-cats-brothers-and-hot-rela:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Cat on a Hot Tin Roof is in repertory until Oct. 29; The Brothers Karamazov until Sep. 24. Box office: 1-800- 567-1600

CAT ON A HOT TIN ROOF

Avon Theatre, Stratford

THE BROTHERS KARAMAZOV

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

- - -

Tennessee Williams' Cat on a Hot Tin Roof, superbly revived at Stratford, is a three-act play unlike any other. Its action is continuous -- the first line of each new act is a repeat of its predecessors last -- and maybe some hardy director will one day pick up on that and play it straight through without intermissions. It might then shake down into a seamless whole, a single rushing stream on which the lights keep shifting. As it stands, and has often been pointed out, it keeps changing shape and focus while maintaining a ferocious hold on its story.

Act One is a duet between Brick, the crippled, alcoholic football- hero son of the Southern millionaire Big Daddy, and his wife Maggie, self-surnamed the Cat. Or rather its a solo for Maggie, who is desperate that she and Brick should have a child so that they can grab a major share of the family fortune, with sullen interjections from Brick, who wants as little as possible to do with Maggie, especially sexually, and is drinking to forget. Act Two brings Brick up against Big Daddy himself, whose birthday it is. This act is more truly a double, for though the father does most of the talking, he does goad his son out of his cage. Brick's shame is that a relationship with his best friend Skipper, that may or may not have been homosexual, led Skipper to kill himself. Big Daddy has terminal stomach cancer but thinks he's been reprieved; Bricks revenge is to tell him the truth -- an unaccustomed thing in these latitudes or indeed, as the play repeatedly tells us, anywhere. Act Three is an embattled ensemble for the whole family, including Bricks lawyer- brother Gooper and his wife Mae, who have five kids with a sixth on the way. If there's a central figure here it's Big Mama, who, having spent two acts in volubly happy denial, has to cope with the facts and, after taking time out to melt into a piteous puddle, does so.

What binds all this thrillingly together, in the writing and in Richard Monettes direction, is character-conflict and atmosphere. The scene throughout is Brick and Maggies bedroom, where they get no privacy. Lorenzo Savoini's set is a series of tall shuttered window frames, open to a darkling sky, with a balcony outside that, we assume, runs right around the house. Here Gooper and Mae's brood - - the no-neck monsters as their aunt Maggie unfondly calls them -- run wild; they also erupt into the room itself. Interruption at tense moments is a residential hazard in this house since Big Mama, whether from hospitality or paranoia, forbids locked doors. Its a brilliant theatrical device, which emerges here as a series of perfectly timed explosions. The culmination, one of the great grotesque scenes in modern drama, is the kids unctuous rendition of Happy Birthday, with the parents who coached them looking on: a real all-American moment.

Monette's estimate of Williams in general, and this play in particular, is higher than mine; I don't feel that were in the presence of Greek tragedy, modern style. Id call it high-grade melodrama -- a form I like -- with a human face. But the idea of playing the longer, lyrically-charged speeches downstage and out- front works very well; each major character gets to reflect or suffer in solitude before returning, newly enlivened to the fray. (Fray, in this play, is just another word for life.) Both Cynthia Dale as Maggie and David Snelgrove as Brick seem freed up by their Southern accents. Hers sometimes courts caricature, but she projects a very fetching mix of daintiness and sensuality, aiming her body like an arrow at her husband, and faltering only when she reaches the peak of rage that provokes him into throwing his crutch at her. He, alternately brooding and taunting, gives his best performance to date.

The gap in the electric fence is James Blendick's Big Daddy, a perfectly intelligent reading of the lines minus the crude elemental force for which they cry out. (Williams thought the character his best-written, and he was probably right.) Without that power, the old man's arraignments of "mendacity" -- the plays last best chance of establishing a universal theme -- seem like special pleading. Its not the actor's fault, though, that Williams' decision to bring him back in the last act seems more mistaken than ever; he would be more powerful, as first envisaged, as an off-stage howl of agony. Lally Cadeaus Big Mama, dolled-up and smothering, is perfect; you see just where she is coming from and just why her husband cant stand her. Brigit Wilson is a properly screeching Mae, and Thom Marriott a superbly deceptive Gooper; at first just a set of dentures in a suit, he comes into his professional kingdom at that infallible theatrical stand-by, the squabble over the will.

Fathers-and-Sons, the engine that drives the second and finest of Cat's acts, is the whole motor of The Brothers Karamazov, where at least three of the four title characters have some motive, personal or philosophical, for offing their dad. I have a hunch, unsupported by research, that Dostoevsky's novels rank second only to Dickens in frequency of dramatization, mainly because each of them is, among other things, a murder story. This is the aspect that Jason Sherman has seized upon in an ingenious adaptation that gradually reveals itself as a continuous trial-scene, with the evidence presented as a series of flashbacks and flashbacks-within-flashbacks. And even then there turns out to be a false bottom to the whole thing.

There is also a sporting, though probably foredoomed, attempt to do justice to the books ideas along with its story. Briefly: Dmitry, the prime suspect in the murder of Fyodor Karamazov, is trying to find his own tortured way between the belief-systems of his older and younger brothers. Dmitry is admirably played by Jonathan Goad, who gets a drunk scene that summons all the quicksilver self-hatred of the Dostoveyskyan hero. He is obviously the most dramatically viable character, unless you count the father himself, red-bloodedly rendered by Scott Wentworth as the Big Daddy of St. Petersburg, coarse but vital. Ivan the agonized atheist (Shane Carty) and Alyosha the monk-in-training (Peter van Gestel) are merely mouthpieces, though Ivan's famous fable of the Grand Inquisitor, his case against official Christianity, is at least given a chance, and a deftly-staged one. But you feel, as earlier with the stinking corpse of Father Zossima, that it's included because its too famous to leave out.

The fourth brother, the bastard Smerdyakov, is also the narrator; hes played by Ron Kennell, in sneering mode, and is maybe one device too many. The women, apart from a dependably fastidious and dependably mysterious Michelle Giroux, are woeful. It's a mystery how an actress as good as Dixie Seatle could end up so thoroughly patronizing the character she plays, while Dana Green's Grushenka, the whore desired by two generations of Karamazovs, seems inspired by the legend that this was a role once coveted by Marilyn Monroe.

These lapses apart, Richard Roses production is first-rate, an endlessly resourceful re-shuffling of chairs and tables to create instant new locales, peopled by an ensemble who start out resembling a church congregation, then morph into courtroom spectators and participants, and are always specific and always involved. Shermans ear is liable to go tin (somebody says "uber-bad"); still, this is probably as good a three-hour version as anyone could come up with. But it can't shake -- probably no version could -- the feeling of a book hanging in the wings and denying the play any chance of autonomous life.

INTO THE WOODS

Avon Theatre, Stratford

- - -

As usual with Into the Woods, I was in tears when the curtain came down. This composite fairy tale, with music and lyrics by Stephen Sondheim and book by James Lapine, has the most moving finale of any musical since Carousel. And in that respect it may well be better than Carousel: That shows Youll Never Walk Alone is an infallible throat-lumper, but it would probably work just as well at the end of any sad story with an uplifting finish. Children Will Listen, the choral number that concludes Into the Woods, makes a general statement about parents and how they habitually both love and fail their children. Its import is universal, but the impact stems from its direct connection to the action we have been watching. And it isn't heavy; it moves easily into a reprise of the title tune, which is a cheerful cautionary tale.

You could apply that description to the whole show, with the rider that the cheer has a darkness to it and that that combination, increasingly complex as the evening proceeds, here makes a masterpiece. It helps that the material is mythic to begin with, and so slides naturally into song. Here are the familiar stories of Cinderella, Jack and the Beanstalk and Little Red Ridinghood, told simultaneously with their destinies intertwined (a little later, Rapunzel gets added to the mix). Here, too, are the newly invented figures of a Baker and his Wife, a childless couple promised offspring -- by the Witch next door" -- if they can beg, borrow or steal a set of ingredients that happen to be the property of the other characters. Into the woods they all go, as in some new Midsummer Night's Dream, to find their fortunes and even their identities. Act One ends with all the nice peoples ambitions achieved, all the wishes granted; as the final song is to say, tying everything yet more firmly together, "wishes are children. The second act shows how those children grow up.

The giant whose partner was slain by Jack on his last trip up the beanstalk comes down to exact revenge. But if theres guilt, there are plenty of people whom Jack can share it with -- as is demonstrated in a breathless cat's cradle of a number called Your Fault, a sort of musical Gordian knot that gets savagely cut by the Witch, with a song of her own. The Witch, who in another part of the show is a helpless grieving mother, represents the way things are -- which doesn't mean that its how they should be, or that they cant be altered. The last part of the play finds the characters, or some of them, joining forces to destroy the Giant, knowing both that it's the only thing to do and that the Giant also has a case. Even the Wolf who (temporarily) devoured Red Ridinghood may not have deserved to die. As the Witch says, unanswerably, ask a wolf's mother." Such even-handedness as this is rare in the theatre. Its rarer still outside it.

The most immediate joy of the show, now as at its premiere 18 years ago, is the way in which it juggles and combines its sources. You never know who is round the next corner, or what the ramifications will be. The Bakers Wife, needing a slipper for the Witch's potion, finds it on the foot of Cinderella, in flight from the Prince's ball. She also reveals how dazzled she herself is by the Princes image ("they say that hes charming), an infatuation that will have an ironic sequel much later in the evening. The links are in the script, but also in the score. Sondheim has written shows that are richer in free-standing melody, but none in which the themes are so tightly and scintillatingly interwoven. The last batch of songs tear equally at the mind and the heart. If there is in any musical a more poignant line, set to more healing music, than sometimes people leave you/halfway through the wood," I haven't heard it.

At Stratford the show gets a production from Peter Hinton that's visually imaginative and textually lucid; it makes some connections, such as Prince Charmings farcical fear of blood, that Id never noticed before. I still prefer the pastoral setting of the first New York production; it seems to me that if you first charm an audience with traditional greenery, you can more effectively shock them when things start to go wrong. Dany Lyne's setting, in which the trees are spare and blood red, is as grim as ... well, as Grimm. (Most of us never learned as kids that Cinderella's sisters, who werent ugly, cut off bits of their feet in order to fit into the slipper. Its in the story and in the show.) Some things here, like the Giant's descent, are actually understaged. Others are extraordinary, notably Rapunzel's tower, which is co-terminous with her long, long dress, and the Wolfs last two-course meal.

Talking of swallowing, some of the costumes do just that to the actors. Susan Gilmours Witch is fatally lacking in wit, but she's hardly helped by being costumed first as some sort of green-swathed fertility symbol ("you should see my nectarines is not a funny line when she shakes her ass to show them growing on her) and later as a dominatrix. (She's supposed to be beautiful. Each to their taste, I suppose.) The Baker and his Wife are flour-faced Gothic figurines, but here the actors do break free; Mary Ellen Mahoney develops intelligence and humour, while Bruce Dow simply and breathtakingly develops. His is the character who learns and suffers most; the emotional core of this production is his last encounter with his father to whom Peter Donaldson, classical casting paying off in spades, brings unprecedented power.

Kyle Blair is a fine fresh-faced Jack, and his exultant singing of Giants in the Sky is the musical thrill of the evening. Then there are Jennifer Waisers bratty Little Red, Dayna Tekatchs Cinderella, and the princes, Thom Allison and Laird Mackintosh, whose Agony, a contest in romantic narcissism, is as always the comic peak. (I can't pause to explain why Mackintosh's theres a dwarf standing guard" is the shows most hilarious line, but trust me.) Allison also plays an excellent Wolf, producing a ringing voice from within a very literal-minded animal suit. As Cinders' late mama -- who is usually left unseen -- Barbara Dunn-Prosser stalks the stage majestically and sings to match. Bethold Carriere's musical direction is customarily impeccable, except that Your Fault isn't fast enough. Hello, Dolly!, Stratford's other musical, is a great show as musicals go; Into the Woods is a great show as anything goes.

Naughty wives and rural lives: Fallen Angels was deemed quite shocking in the 1920s.

FALLEN ANGELS

Avon Theatre, Stratford

WINGFIELD'S INFERNO

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

- - -

The Fallen Angels of Noel Coward's 1924 comedy are called Julia and Jane. Each of them lives in a frightfully, not to say frighteningly, expensive flat in Central London. At least, we can see for ourselves that Julia does, and we have no reason to believe that the circumstances of Jane, who resides on another floor of the same apartment building, are any less luxurious. Both women are married, and though we don't know what their respective husbands actually do that yields such riches, we assume that it's Something in the City. Off duty, they're solid tweedy chaps whose main preoccupation is golf.

Julia and Jane have more in common than a postal address and identically placid marriages. Each, long ago, had a premarital fling with the same fella, a debonair Frenchman (he must have been debonair) named Maurice, who whisked one of them off to Rome and the other to Pisa for romantic times they wish neither to forget nor to repeat. Or so they say.

Now, with their off-putting spouses off putting, the ladies learn that Maurice is about to arrive in London, news that leaves them all a-tremble. This is Act One and it's promising. They settle down to await his arrival, fortifying themselves with food, drink and memories; nostalgia turns inevitably to competitive recrimination, culminating in a spot of outright physical violence. This is Act Two and it's hilarious, certainly in Brian Bedford's Stratford production. It's also a tour de force, since it's kept going entirely by the two old campaigners, with a maid popping in occasionally to provide sustenance. The lover eventually turns up, and so, less eagerly anticipated, do the husbands. This is Act Three, and we won't go into it.

The play was deemed quite shocking in the 1920s, whether because it showed respectable married women with erotic pasts, or because they actually talked about those pasts, or because they got plastered while talking about them. There's still a kick to it, not in the sex but in the lovingly orchestrated rudeness. Seana McKenna plays Julia and Lucy Peacock Jane, and they are Absolutely Fabulous. (The resemblance is more than passing, especially in the falling- down-drunk bits.) Both ladies are wonderfully served by the designer, Susan Benson, especially when they put on their party frocks. They are not so much dressed as sheathed, and they do battle accordingly.

McKenna, a rapier in green, makes the initial running, scoring point after point with the nasal drawl, as of somebody who feels temporarily superior, that she perfected in Private Lives. The first act is hers, but then she is playing on home ground. Peacock, a blunderbuss in red, seems at an initial disadvantage; personally, I felt very relieved when she took off her formidable hat and began to make herself comfortable, and I wouldn't be surprised if she did too. She proceeds to go from strength to delirious weakness until, thoroughly sozzled, she becomes the helpless victim of inanimate objects that should by rights be on her side. The goings-on around this point are sublime; Bedford's direction combines the verbal precision of his previous Coward productions with the physical madness of last year's Noises Off.

The maid in this play was always a good role in a quiet long- suffering sort of way (they call her Saunders because her predecessor's name was Myfanwy, and who can blame them) but here she is something else. Someone, it seems, has got hold of a previously unknown text in which she is good, not only at her own job, but at everyone else's. She is musical, far more so than her employers, and she knows exactly which golf clubs you should take to the links at Chichester. Omnisicient and omnicompetent, she is a female Jeeves, the only one I have ever seen on a stage. (Male clones are quite common.) Joyce Campion, at once meek and imperturbable, steals the show, an especially neat trick considering that neither leading lady ever lets go of it. That's ensemble, I guess. The last act, by its author's admission, is weak; it depends heavily on the long-delayed arrival of Maurice, who here is not sensationally smooth; while the husbands seem to be duffers, whoever plays them. The play does show Coward practising up for Private Lives which has exactly the same shape, only better.

Wingfield's Inferno, the sixth of Dan Needles' plays-for-one- actor about the ex-stockbroker who turned to farming, takes its name most obviously from a fire that destroys the Orange Lodge at Persephone township, leaving our hero-narrator Walt Wingfield lumbered with the task of raising money for its reconstruction. There's a metaphorical meaning too, of course, drawn from The Divine Comedy; Walt seems uncommonly literate for both his spheres of action, which may partly explain why, though liked, he always feels something of an outsider.

I wouldn't say Walt goes through his own personal hell, but he does periodically invoke a particular circle of Dante's penitentiary where reside frauds, hucksters and, by logical inference, insurance companies. The last are a recurring theme in this show. It might have been called Wingfield's Insurance.

The theme, as is customary, is first broached by local newspaperman Ed before the baton passes to Walt himself via his Letters to the Editor. The structure remains the same as in previous Wingfield plays; a series of anecdotes, mostly farcical and each apparently self-contained, all find their resolution in the denouement, like a whole team of shaggy dogs kept on a single leash.

Once again Rod Beattie, under the direction of his brother Douglas Beattie, plays Walt and all who come in contact with him. Serene and quizzical wife Maggie, stuttering brother-in-law Freddy, an assortment of self-interested lodge members and over-ambitious horse trainers, a baby and a dog: All are brought to instant life with the crinkling of a brow, the twisting of a larynx or the popping of a pair of eyes, the last being the distinguishing feature of a glorious new addition to the cast, a glad-handing member of parliament with a porous memory and a capacious thirst

The previous episode, Wingfield on Ice, reached its epiphany with the birth of Walt's and Maggie's daughter Hope. This new one tries for something of the same effect with less success; it feels like repetition. But there is plenty of joy en route, in Walt's slapstick encounters with skunks, animal and human, and in the tale of a dead- cert winner of a racehorse, done in by a change in the weather. Through it all Rod Beattie, a one-man carnival of baffled humanity, is reliably amazing.

In Jonathan Coe's wonderful new novel, every major character takes a turn at being the narrative consciousness

THE CLOSED CIRCLE

By Jonathan Coe

Alfred A. Knopf

384 pp.,

$35

- - -

Jonathan Coe's new novel is wonderful: You can't wait to get to the next page and dread arriving at the last. It will, however, and despite the customary publishers' claims that it "stands on its own," make no sense to anybody who has not read its predecessor, The Rotters' Club. Which is no hardship whatsoever, as The Rotters' Club is also a terrific book. The Closed Circle, though, is better.

The Rotters' Club is about a group of bright, awkward teenagers growing up in the 1970s in Birmingham, then one of the dourest of British cities. It's also about their parents, and both books are, among other things, virtuoso exercises in the alternation of points of view. Every major character, with a few significantly opaque exceptions, gets his or her turn at being the narrative consciousness.

The spectacular finale of The Rotters' Club is a 30-page continuous sentence in which a painfully sensitive and socially hopeless boy named Benjamin Trotter expresses his joy and wonder at the world after his first sexual experience with the girl of his dreams. Many thought that the author went too far, but I disagree. It's a perfect expression of the character's state of breathless ecstasy, and it has one hell of an ending. Avert your eyes if you don't want to know this: The couple meet a man in a pub who prophesies that they will have a long and happy life together and that Mrs. Thatcher will never be Prime Minister.

Coe is very good at dropping these bombshells from the real world. He does it again, more literally and even more shatteringly, when Benjamin's older sister and her boyfriend, at the height of happiness, go out for a night at a Birmingham pub, which is then blown apart by an IRA bomb in the worst terrorist act yet to have happened on the British mainland. The sequel, set 30 years later -- today, in other words -- makes similar use of public events. The more domestic ones, such as the threatened closing of the city's BMW works, are splendidly used to bring the characters and the times into focus. The Iraq war, by contrast, simply (and not very satisfactorily) looms in the background. Tony Blair is almost a character in the book, often invoked but never actually present.

Remember Y2K? The Closed Circle begins with accountants and musicians -- Benjamin is both -- rushing to back up their files. Ben, whose contemporaries all expected him to turn out to be a literary-musical genius, has in fact produced nothing; he has also settled for a companionable, childless marriage. He has never forgotten his first love, and has made no effort to.

Of his male contemporaries, two are now journalists. One is a London high-flyer who married rich (he always wanted to, despite being the son of a shop steward) but whose ambitions are dashed when he's promoted to literary editor, not what he was hoping for. The other, still in Birmingham, wants to write an analysis of Britain's new Far Right, linking it to the advent of New Labour. But the pieces won't stay in place. Blairism, with its fondness for international capital, epitomizes much of what the neo-Nazis detest. Things are complicated. Everybody's instinct is to run for cover.

The latter scribe's ex-wife, still his and everybody else's friend, is haunted by the memory of her elder sister who disappeared in the earlier novel. She herself is currently on the rebound, at one point hooking up (incongruously, and she knows it) with a millionaire executive who has bankrupted one company after another, never failing to let a handsome compensation package hit him on the way out.

There is also Benjamin's younger brother, Paul, who used to lurk in his room reading Friedmanite economics and gloating over "the death of the socialist dream." Now he's a Labour MP. Privately, he disapproves of the war; publicly, he sits on the fence; eventually, he votes for it -- for strictly non-political reasons.

In the first book, he was seen only from the outside. In this one, we're allowed inside his head. Coe, being a humane and humorous writer, allows us to sympathize with him. That's not the same as approving of him. All the other characters despise him (even his girlfriend acknowledges that "his sense of humour was surgically removed at birth") and their author seems intellectually on their side. But even in The Rotters' Club, Paul performed the nearest thing to a heroic action: He saved someone from drowning. Here he proves as accident prone as his brother, falling recklessly, almost self-destructively, in love. Obviously, it can happen to anyone.

The Rotters' Club was at times confusing. It was hard to keep track of the characters, or at least of the links between the generations. In The Closed Circle, everything comes clear. The title refers in a minor jokey way to a right-wing think-tank (Paul's a founding member), and in a major serious way to the resolution of everything in the plot that had previously been left hanging: People and incidents we might have forgotten are brought cunningly back to mind and their significance revealed. This isn't coincidence, or not very often.

The new movie Crash deals in coincidence, and it's sometimes brilliantly effective. The Closed Circle trumps it by dealing in logical surprise. The crowning revelation is so masterfully sprung, so immaculately timed, that I laughed aloud in sheer joyous satisfaction.

Coe and his younger compatriot Zadie Smith have got me reading novels again. Both fuse sharp comedy (though hers is wilder) with formal ambition (his is more controlled) to create panoramic social satire with pain beneath. As a stylist, Coe hardly puts a word wrong.

Really, of course, The Rotters' Club and The Closed Circle are one big novel, with the second half making final sense even of what seemed the most strained device of the first -- the introduction as a framing device of a boy and girl from yet a third generation. They close the circle and then open it again: "the two of them," in a miraculous closing sentence that I think I can quote without spoiling anybody's fun, "wanting nothing more from life, at that moment, than the chance to repeat the mistakes their parents had made, in a world that was still trying to decide whether to allow them even that luxury."

HEDDA GABLER

Buddies in Bad Times

12 Alexander St. - 416-975-8555

In Judith Thompson's adaptation, directed by Ross Manson, Ibsen's 1890 play has its first half advanced to the beginning of the 20th century and its second to now. In the world of Kinko's, we are asked to believe that Hedda is destroying the only copy of Tesman's manuscript. The play's famous last line is cut in favour of a new dying aria for a bleeding heroine. Yanna McIntosh's Hedda (Dora- nominated) mainly projects a majestic resentment, monotonous and rather forced. Closes tomorrow.

JOURNEY'S END

Court House Theatre - Niagara-on-the-Lake - 1-800-511-7429

A jolly good show. R.C. Sherriff's classic play about the trenches of the First World War focuses almost entirely on the English officer class, but transcends those cozy limitations. It shows how desperately these men, mostly very young, need the memory of home comforts and home beliefs, when what lies ahead is the near- certainty of injury or death. Christopher Newton's production, relaxed and amused in its first half, gets very tense in its second. In repertory through Oct. 8.

HAPPY END

Royal George Theatre - Niagara-on-the-Lake - 1-800-511-7429

Tadeusz Bradecki's revived production of this Brecht-Weill musical, set in Brecht's favourite mythical Chicago, is given a stylish visual bite, with every move precisely plotted. The songs are some of Weill's best but the book, drawn-out and laborious, is almost contemptuously slight. Cast changes are up and down, with Glynis Ranney's Hallelujah Lil (she sings the great Surabaya Johnny) one of the ups. In repertory through Oct. 28.

THE TEMPEST

Festival Theatre - Stratford

1-800-567-1600

Verse acting at its highest stage of development. At 85, and playing Prospero for the fourth time, William Hutt can still surprise us. From anger to gentleness and back again, reversals -- constantly repeated and immaculately executed -- underpin Hutt's whole account of a man who takes a play's length to determine whether the rarer action is in virtue or in vengeance. The pause before he bows to the inevitable is going to be legendary. In repertory through Oct. 28.

HELLO, DOLLY!

Festival Theatre - Stratford

1-800-567-1600

Lucy Peacock doesn't find herself in Dolly until she reaches her big first-act closer, Before the Parade Passes By. At last the actress has something to act. Most of Dolly, though, is shtick, for which she isn't equipped. The show itself is an honest and successful attempt to make audiences feel happy; the production, though prosaic, has humour, colour and good dancing. Peter Donaldson's skinflint widower is the best and wittiest performance. In repertory through Nov. 6.

AS YOU LIKE IT

Festival Theatre, Stratford

- - -

And so, for the second time, we go into the woods. The Stratford Festival's opening week concludes with As You Like It, in a good conventional staging with a couple of publicity points. One of these concerns the sound of the show. The other concerns its look. They go together.

As You Like It has a lot of songs. Stratford has commissioned new settings of them from Steven Page of Barenaked Ladies, and the Ladies en masse have laid down instrumental tracks to which the resident actors can sing along. There's something quixotic about commissioning a group primarily celebrated for its lyrics to provide music to someone else's words, but as things have turned out Shakespeare and Page sound like they might be a team with a future. The songs are agreeable light rock; the more sombre ones are especially effective -- or maybe it's just that they crop up in the best parts of Antoni Cimolino's production. When it comes to a lighter entry like It Was a Lover and His Lass, the show starts acting as if it would like to be an old-fashioned rock musical. The tune itself is nice, as are they all. If having a Barenaked Ladies credit in the program drags in some additional spectators (I think it might) then so much the better. Though if it's part of a larger scheme to tap a huge new Stratford audience, it can only be described, with acknowledgements to Bob Geldof, as a Band Aid solution.

Second point: The score is nostalgic, a '90s group creating a '60s pastiche. That's the period in which the production is set. There's a sense in which nearly all contemporary productions of Shakespeare are set in the '60s, but this may be the first since the hangover days of the early '70s to get so aggressive about it. It summons "the summer of love," though the summoning has been done more emphatically in the advertising than on the stage. Now, if you want to take this seriously, it's wrong. As You Like It has nothing to do with any kind of summer. Listen to those songs. The early ones are all about rough weather and winter winds; a late one celebrates springtime, the only pretty ringtime. That means love, all right, but it also means rebirth; and it's not unusual for productions to illustrate the progression by giving the Forest of Arden bare- branched trees before the intermission and green, leafy ones after. That's not an option with Santo Loquasto's set, which matches Barenaked Ladies with bare-naked ladders. Five of the stepped variety represent the forest, and they are not equipped for foliage.

I like the set, but Loquasto really scores with his costumes, which are eclectically specific. Rosalind and Celia, virtual orphans at the usurper's court, are in school uniforms for their first scene, nightgowns for their second; they are, chillingly, dragged from their beds to be banished. Wicked uncle Frederick (Stephen Russell, very tight-lipped) is a military dictator of Latin American provenance, who interrogates suspects by ducking them in a pool, one that's also available for merrier purposes in the forest, where love, peace and headbands rule. As for '60s unisex: it should in theory be ideal for Rosalind's male disguise. In practice, it isn't; when girls could be boys anyway, the masquerade loses its point.

At one vital moment, the costuming mugs the script. "Alas the day," cries Shakespeare's Rosalind when she learns that her beloved Orlando is loose in the same wood, "what shall I do with my doublet and hose?" That's a line that soars and laughs. This Rosalind says "what shall I do with my clothes?" a line that stumbles and falls down. When a design concept clashes with the text, then obviously it's the concept that should go, not the line. In fact, both could stay. Audiences, especially audiences willing to take ladders for trees, aren't that literal-minded. The same mistake was made in last year's As You Like It in High Park, but we expect better of Stratford. Don't we?

A Hare Krishna wedding, topped off by a cheeky "just married" sign, doesn't quite measure up to the solemnities of the last scene. The fact is, the "summer of love" was dumb, a time of sappy sentiments and songs, and you're lucky to have missed it. The Beatles' All You Need Is Love was a joke, possibly an intentional one. This was a period that got high on the word "love" without ever wondering what it meant. As You Like It glorifies it too, but it asks questions. Rosalind, the cleverest woman in Shakespeare, falls headlong in love and then debunks every romantic illusion and emerges still a lover. She's completely vulnerable and completely witty, which is why audiences have always fallen in love with her.

Which brings me, reluctantly, to this production's greatest disappointment, which is Sara Topham's Rosalind. It's disappointing both in light of the actress' track record and of the initial impression she makes here, sitting at the tip of the stage and staring straight ahead, the picture of stark misery waiting to be aroused. But the awakening never comes. There is probably a vibrant performance of Rosalind going on inside her, and occasionally it breaks surface, but most of the time she simply fails to fill the space.

It's remarkable, with this central flaw, how much of the play still works, and works well. Ensemble scenes, in court or country, are intelligently directed and responsively played. Orlando's meeting with the banished Duke (Barry MacGregor, unabashedly decent) is beautifully layered, with Dan Chameroy leading the lords in the winter wind song, as cheerfully bitter as the weather it describes; William Needles, in lovely form as old Adam, reminding us that William Hutt isn't the only prized survivor of Stratford's first season; and, as a permanent outsider, Graham Abbey's eloquent Jaques, an embittered casualty of the sexual revolution. As Touchstone, Stephen Ouimette finds laughs in lines that most actors have left for dead, a feat that he manages by cleaving firmly to his role as a professional sophisticate desperate to maintain his superiority when cast among yokels. The more seriously this show takes itself, its text, and its actors, the better it is.

2005-06-18-therapy-s-the-thing-hard-ques:
Revolutions in Therapy closes tonight at the Artword Theatre, 416- 366-7723, ext. 290.; rcushman@lycos.com

There are exceptions, but new plays of the narrative kind are usually frustrating. Maybe its the hype that invariably precedes them, but they always seem to be holding out the promise of searing new insights into our lives and the society that shapes them. Not surprisingly, they fail to deliver. They also run out of steam as stories.

It isnt culturally respectable to say so, but you can generally get a better time at old plays. This doesn't have much to do with nostalgia, except of a purely esthetic kind; it can be pleasant to be taken back to times that were more confident about the theatre than ours is, and so produced more confidently entertaining plays. The reason is that we approach an old play, even when it's one that we havent seen before, without illusions. We have a good idea of what such a play has to offer. It comes from another time and the lives that it may have professed to change are long since over. We can enjoy watching these people swimming around in their natural habitat, and can learn something about what their world was like. And if they do turn out to have something to say to us directly, well, thats gravy.

A new play is unlikely to tell us anything about our own time that we don't already know. Except, that is, on a factual or anecdotal level, which explains why documentary drama, on stage or screen, is often more exciting than the made-up variety. There are stories around us more compelling than those any dramatist could invent. And maybe there is something self-defeating in the whole idea of narrative fiction. Look, as I devotedly have for four whole seasons and will again, at 24. It provides just enough character interest for us to keep watching without hating ourselves, but basically it's about generating suspense, an art that it may have refined to its purest condition yet. Every episode keeps us on the edge of our seats, and every episode is frustrating. The real-time component is part of this. We watch the minutes being counted off at the side of the screen, and at first we feel comforted; theres plenty of time before we have to return to the real world, and plenty of time for this weeks crisis to be defused. But even when it is, there has to be another one left unresolved, to keep us hungry for another week. This may be pleasurable, but the last instalment is always a letdown. This is partly because the climax of every series except the first has been weak in its own terms, but the chief reason is that, with no more cliffs to hang on to and nothing else from the experience worth preserving, we feel squeezed, empty.

Some of these thoughts went through my mind while watching Revolutions in Therapy, a new production from a three-person group who call themselves STO Union. This show (it is emphatically not a play, and the emphasis is theirs) is partly about finding alternative ways of describing and even alleviating personal angst, and partly about the relation between performers and audience. There's no automatic reason why these two things should be considered together, and by the end the proceedings have drifted off, but every so often one part brushes up against another with stimulating results.

Early in the proceedings one performer, Tracy Wright, asks another performer, Nadia Ross, about the pain she's suffering. Ross gives a fancy answer that Wright, rather refreshingly, says she doesnt understand. Ross starts telling a story instead about a man who underwent terrible bereavement. This hooks us, but she breaks off, and the show starts worrying aloud about the nature of narrative and in particular about the morality of suspense, about the fact that our desire to know what happens next makes us value a perpetually delayed future at the expense of the present moment, which, even when were not listening to stories, is no way to live our lives. She is in fact asking that most terrifying of all questions: Are we having fun yet?

STO Union is not offering documentary, and it certainly isn't in the classical revival business, but it is striving for something real." After Wright is through interrogating Ross, Ross interrogates Wright. (Both speak through microphones, which seem to give them protection by making them sound impersonal. When deprived of them, the performers act naked and scared.) It seems both have been through psychoanalysis, and are unimpressed. As a different form of therapy, and a different form of theatre, they offer "meditation, though, frankly, if they hadn't told me that thats what it was, I wouldnt have guessed.

However, they second-guess themselves. Just why," one of them says to another, "should they, meaning us, be interested in what you have to say?" I paraphrase, but not by much; anyway, it's a good question, and one that more companies should ask themselves. Later on they try to enlist us still further by walking among us, and trying to see things from our point of view. It's audience participation minus most of the embarrassment.

You want real? In her projection of pain and fear Ross, who is co- writer and co-director as well as performer, is as real as real can be; which means of course that she is acting, very well indeed. Jacob Wren, who is her co-co-writer/director and who makes a late appearance just as we are beginning to wonder if there was a mistake in the program, doesnt act at all and probably cant. But the fact that he seems to have no right to appear on a stage in front of a paying audience doesn't make him any more genuine. Wright, who occupies a less exalted position in the hierarchy (she's credited with "artistic collaboration") falls, in point of stage presence, somewhere between the other two. But the fact that one makes such comparisons proves that this is a show like any other. Acknowledging the existence of the audience makes no difference; neither does having one of the actors complain about the role shes been given.

Artifice doesnt cease to be artificial merely by drawing attention to itself. It might conceivably be different if they were making it up as they went along, but though the script grew out of improvisation in rehearsal, it is now just a script, as set in stone as any other. (Paradoxically, this method seems to work best when the aim is naturalism, as in the films and plays of Mike Leigh.) When Wren comes on, it's to take over Ross's role, she having apparently been overcome by the agony of it all. Thankfully, she reappears, but by now the metatheatrical stuff has killed off everything else.

Ross resumes her story but its no longer as compelling as it was before. Maybe thats the point. She still talks about pain, as do the others, but the urgency has gone out of it. Connections are made, or at least alluded to, between individual anguish and our condition as members of a capitalist society, and they sound convincing but not overwhelmingly so. Most of us, after all, know plenty of people who seem to be getting along all right and not having breakdowns. The particular condition the performers describe is not universal, and we don't really know if they have experienced it themselves or if they're just pretending. If its the former, then the assumption that they speak for all of us is presumptuous; if its the latter, then it's presumptuous and deceitful.

The production looks excellent, played out against a screen with an abstract design composed, as far as I could tell, of pieces of Kleenex. This periodically fades, to show video clips of the natural world, which are pretty, though their relevance is mysterious. What they mainly add is a layer of sentimentality. All right, the piece isn't a play, and in some ways thats a relief. But its still theatre, and therefore subject to the theatrical obligation to make interesting use of its audience's time. If we are to do without story, we need a good substitute. Revolutions in Therapy may have its subject confused with its method. Theatre often does function as therapy, both for its originators and for its recipients, but that isn't what it's for, and to claim otherwise is self-indulgence. This show, which is about to represent Canada at a festival in Stuttgart, asks some hard questions but it comes up with some mushy answers.

Colour Photo: Courtesy Artword Theatre / Tracy Wright and Nadia Ross hook us in at first, but then the show starts worrying about narrative and suspense.; Colour Photo: KIEFER SUTHERLAND IN 24: art determined to generate suspense.

BLUE MAN GROUP

Panasonic Theatre, Toronto

- - -

On my way Sunday to the Panasonic Theatre, formerly the New Yorker, and don't you hate these name changes, I encountered a nice lady who asked me if I was going to the boycott. This took me slightly aback, since a boycott, by definition, is not something you go to; its aim is to keep you away. But I knew what she was getting at. She meant was I going to the demo across the road from the theatre, organized by the local entertainment unions to discourage us from patronizing the Blue Man Group, who have opened operations in Toronto without benefit of union-approved contracts.

My sympathies here are all with organized labour, and I felt a twinge of guilt when I heard one of the speakers opposite asking us not only to refrain from seeing the show ourselves but to encourage other people not to see it. If anyone's in a position to do that, I am. Still, a job's a job, and I have to do mine by saying that if you're looking for highly skilled undemanding entertainment, the Blue Man Group will provide it. If, on the other hand, you are in search of a life-changing experience, you can pass this one up. The show is by turns charming, boring and annoying.

As everyone must know by now, the three original Blue Men (Matt Goldman, Phil Stanton, Chris Wink) started out in New York in the late 1980s as street performers, in the business of administering harmless surprises to equally harmless passersby. Since what they did qualified as performance art, they moved into the art scene (for which they claim they were too irreverent) and then out again, into an off-Broadway theatre. From there they expanded worldwide, becoming something between a conglomerate and a cloning device.

Three men -- it's impossible to tell which of the names in the program are actually theirs -- appear before us, as the show's creators used to do in the days when they had the time. They are wearing tight-fitting cobalt-coloured masks, which make them look as though they have painted themselves that way. They don't say a word. That's another prejudice they have to live down -- not only are they blue-faced black legs, they're mimes. Still, they don't put on insufferable airs about it. It's just the way they are.

Their main talents seem to be percussion-pounding and juggling. They pound vigorously and rhythmically on drums and other less conventional instruments --not, obviously, until they're blue in the face but until they have a right to look that way. (There are full- time musicians backing them up, very well.) At the same time, they toss marshmallows back and forth, catching them in their mouths. A lot of candy-munching gets done in this show, and the chomping too is rhythmic. Breakfast cereals are also consumed. Whatever Equity's qualms, none of these actors looks like going hungry. They also do a certain amount of regurgitating, but keep it surprisingly within the bounds of good taste. They have perfected a form involving gum balls that might be described as oral action-painting.

They project a certain amount of personality, really a remarkable amount considering what is plastered all over their faces. Their range of expression is narrow but sharply defined. Two of them can look aghast at the things the third has done, while the third can look innocent, or maybe just oblivious. (It's what's known in the trade as "who? me?" humour.) They can also be appealingly inhuman. When, as we knew they would, they lure a spectator onstage, they don't -- of course, they can't -- humiliate her verbally, as more conventional comics might do. Just sitting down with her at a table for what feels like minutes on end, they prove that silence can be far more intimidating -- and, yes, far funnier -- than any words. Eventually they relent and instruct her by example in the fine art of eating Twinkies in public.

It wouldn't be true to say that the show's humour is strictly non- verbal. Some of the best parts involve words; they just happen to be written rather than spoken. Even before the proceedings proceed, we are disarmed -- at any rate, I was -- by a stream of neon messages, making sly fun of our expectations as a group and of some of us as individuals. One audience member, who may or may not have existed, was advised on how to cure a headache by thinking of it as a cow. (I think, in retrospect, that this was the highlight of the evening. But my tastes may not be typical.) The show proper plays gentle mind games, concerning our inability to follow three sets of messages at the same time, and our determination to try regardless. There is also a short diagrammatic film, with recorded commentary, on the subject of modern plumbing (the one thing that binds our society together).

There is also, in this very high-tech show, a constant effort to debunk technology, or at least to remind us of its existence. You may remember an episode of The Simpsons in which Sideshow Bob went on television to denounce television, winding up by remarking that he was perfectly aware of the irony, and viewers needn't bother to write in and tell him. He was of course on a TV show within a TV show. The Blue Man Group never get as sophisticated as that (the closest they get to satire is a feeble routine about the dance movements of rock stars), but they seem to be saying much the same thing.

That must be what has got them the name of post-modernists. That and their disregard of narrative conventions. But in the latter respect, they're no more advanced than any old-fashioned revue or variety bill, while their penchant for blurring the line between stage and auditorium would hardly have surprised the Marx Brothers or even the more primitive anarchists of my London youth, the Crazy Gang. It was probably also anticipated by old shows that I've read about but have never seen, like Hellzapoppin' or the Parisian revues of Robert Dhery. The recent Toronto show Revolutions in Therapy was kicking at the same can, though more cerebrally. Wherever there's theatrical convention, or any kind of convention, there will be a corresponding urge to tear it down, and it can be fun. I bet it was great fun when the original Blue Men were mentally goosing people on the streets of downtown Manhattan. But when that's the only idea, and when the techniques employed keep repeating themselves, then a show, even if it only lasts 90 minutes as this one does, can get monotonous.

It can also get desperate, as in this production's occasional resort to video footage of things supposedly going on off-stage. Why does mixed media, which certainly sounds exciting, always end up seeming such a cheat? Anyway, the whole thing builds, for want of a better word, to a prolonged finale involving music that's relentless, strobe lights that are more so, and the swathing of the audience in endless lengths of tissue paper. Some people whose taste I respect, and whom indeed I live with, thought it the best time they'd had in ages. To me, it felt like forced celebration, which is why I left feeling angry. There were Blue Men waiting in the lobby, who when asked if they will pose for photos with audience members, reply very politely that they will. That's right; they talk. But maybe they aren't the True Blue Men.

Colour Photo: Tyler Anderson, National Post / Protest or not, the Blue Man Group are highly skilled and undemanding, but they won't exactly change anyone's life.; Colour Photo: Blue Man
