THE DONNELLYS: STICKS AND STONES

Studio Theatre, Stratford

- - -

Diane D'Aquila, leading actress in Stratford's Sticks and Stones, made a charming curtain speech on opening night. She recalled the 1970s, when Canadian drama was beginning to wake up and new plays were tumbling on to stages. Many of them, she disarmingly admitted, were not very good, but she was obviously making an exception for James Reaney, author of the trilogy The Donnellys, of which Sticks and Stones (premiered 1973) is the first instalment. Reaney, she said, had been one of those "leading the charge"; and he was present, now an octogenarian, to receive an obviously heartfelt tribute.

After which, it seems churlish to report that the play now looks like something that was probably very exciting if you were around at the time. It takes the familiar Canadian trope about telling ourselves our own stories to wild extremes; it's so concerned with modes of storytelling that the story itself never gets told. It takes place in the township of Biddulph, not that far from Stratford. Its climax and raison d'etre is the murder-by- incineration of James Donnelly, an Irish-born farmer, and four members of his family. This happened in 1880, but the play has a fluid time scheme that allows the event to be echoed, pre-echoed, forecast, remembered, described and even lampooned. The one thing it doesn't get is dramatized.

This is partly because the author still has two-thirds of his trilogy to go, and he's saving it up; but it's still frustrating. (And, given the free conventions he employs, there'd be nothing to stop him from staging it twice.) Frustrating, too, is the way in which the play piles on background material so that it obscures rather than illuminates. Back in Catholic Ireland, Donnelly had been a "whitefoot," meaning someone who refused to run with the right mob. This label followed him to Canada, and it may have been his murderers' principal motivation. But there are plenty of other conflicts to choose from. As well as Catholics against Catholics, we have Catholics against Protestants, Irish against English, rich against poor, white against black and, for a fleeting couple of sentences, Grits against Tories, Donnelly being a Liberal voter in a region ruled by Conservatives. Donnelly also arouses the jealousy of any number of land-grabbers, and is undeniably bloody-minded on his own account. He kills a man in a brawl, and spends seven years in jail -- one year, as it happens, for each of his children.

As well as being drunk on its own history, the play is drunk on its own style. Back in '73 a professor declared Reaney a better dramatic poet than Eliot or Yeats; that's doubtful, but the text, which is in prose, does contain some pungent sentences, along with chunks of exposition naive enough for a school play. It's folkweave drama in excelsis, with games, fights, dances and even a traditional theme tune, the powerful ballad of John Barleycorn, that has to be manhandled into relevance. Characters switch from playing scenes to delivering first- or third-person narration, and the company keeps forming itself into a chanting chorus. It's very uninvolving, and also very confusing; I kept longing for the actors to thin out a bit, so that those remaining might get a chance to interact, or at least to clue me in on who they were supposed to be. The Donnellys' enemies may have been varied and many, but here they seem interchangeable, like so many snarky shadows.

To succeed now, when we are no longer overawed by Canadian content for its own sake, the play would need ruthlessly lucid acting and direction. Andrey Tarasiuk's production gets lost in the thickets so liberally planted by the author; it looks and sounds as if getting the show onstage had left no time for getting it clear. People start shouting before we can tell what they're shouting about, and they hardly ever stop. Some of the younger actors are lamentable. Occasionally there's a good barbed scene; the best involves an itinerant priest from Kentucky (David Snelgrove, recycling his Cat on a Hot Tin Roof voice) refusing absolution to a suborner of killers (Andrew Massingham) who wants to confess without actually admitting any guilt. Reaney sees Donnelly himself as a figure of tragic intransigence; Robert King cannot make him anything more than a stocky malcontent.

The play's final flaw may be its most crucial: Reaney seems less interested in portraying the Donnellys than in vindicating them. He was apparently roused to write the play by reading a book that takes a far blacker view of his protagonists than he does (and is in fact called The Black Donnellys). He seems, from the noblest of motives, to be fighting a literary battle; he even puts his opponent into the play, in the guise of a travelling medicine showman who mounts a caricatured version of the Donnelly case while the real Mr. Donnelly looks on. This, if you don't know the background, is baffling. It's puzzling enough even if you do. We're offered a parody of something that we never got straight in the first place. There's also a scene involving the Governor-General and his wife that plays like Video Cabaret without the finesse. Actually I'd like to see the VideoCab gang get their hooks into this stretch of Canadiana. And, having a weakness for epics, I'd still be interested to see the remaining two- thirds of this one. As pages of theatrical as well as national history, they deserve respect. But I'm not convinced that they deserve reverence.
2005-06-25-the-inside-track-on-the-doras:
robertcushman@lycos.com; The Dora Awards are presented at the Winter Garden Theatre on Monday at 8 p.m.

Once again, in the brief interregnum between the announcement of the nominees for this year's Dora Awards and the prize-giving itself, we contemplate who deserves to win, who actually will win and who isn't even in the running but should be. As usual, the theatre awards are divided into two main sections, General and Independent. These correspond, more or less, to what used to be known as Mainstream and Alternative. Or perhaps -- since some of the theatres in the General section would still think of themselves as being Alternative, or at least as being alternative to other theatres in the same category -- we should simply call them Big and Small.

Big first then. There are five nominees for Outstanding New Play, and if critical response, general buzz and actual merit are any guides, John Mighton's Half Life should get it in a walk. The next- best contender, in my book, would be Claudia Dey's Trout Stanley, but if there is a threat it will be Rick Miller's Bigger than Jesus. At least, I think of it as being Miller's play (or his stand-up comedy routine), though it's in fact credited to him and his director, Daniel Brooks. I don't think it's a play, though I'm well aware the same has been said of many of the most notable events in theatrical history. The two remaining slots are filled by Keira Loughran's Little Dragon and David Young's No Great Mischief. I'd like to say that I can think of any number of overlooked candidates, but I can't. In fact, I can't think of one.

OUTSTANDING NEW MUSICAL This year the choice is down to two. (Remember, they have to be Canadian.) One is Aladdin, the Ross Petty pantomime, credited to David Finley. The other is Guy Mignault's Autour de Kurt Weill, which I didn't see but assume will win on cultural grounds.

OUTSTANDING PRODUCTION OF A PLAY Once again, the smart money is on Half Life, which was outstanding in text, performance, direction and design and has most (not quite all) of the nominations to prove it. And once again, Bigger than Jesus will be the competition. Take Me Out (a.k.a. "the baseball play") was a good production, let down by one major performance and the no-better-than-all-right quality of the text. Most puzzling nomination: The Leisure Society, on two counts -- it was a thoroughly overrated piece, but if people thought it was so good, why isn't it up there under New Play? And why did it get the nod in this category over two superior Factory Theatre all- rounders, Trout Stanley and the Suburban Motel double-header? The latter, one of the best-liked shows of the year (there were reservations in this column, but that's typical), hasn't been nominated for anything. Incredible.

OUTSTANDING PRODUCTION OF A MUSICAL Now we're talking. American musicals qualify for this one, so it's a straight fight between Hairspray and Urinetown, the latter having the edge, as it's the smaller, smarter and, all things considered, better show. Wicked hasn't been nominated at all, which is a pleasant surprise. The two Canadian shows mentioned above are in here as well, as is Ain't Misbehavin', but I can't believe any of them is a threat.

OUTSTANDING DIRECTION OF A PLAY Daniel Brooks is running against himself with Bigger than Jesus and Half Life. I hope he wins for the latter. Ken Gass is nominated for The Leisure Society, though I feel again that it should have been for End of Civilization, one of the Suburban Motel plays. I'm glad Joseph Ziegler got a nod for his Soulpepper Hamlet and sad that Ben Barnes didn't for his Soulpepper Translations. Also nominated are Eda Holmes for Trout Stanley and (yes, I do go to the odd French thing) Diana Leblanc for Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme.

OUTSTANDING PERFORMANCE BY A MALE IN A PRINCIPAL ROLE: PLAY This is the most perplexing category of all. Rick Miller is up there, of course, for Bigger than Jesus, as is Daniel MacIvor for his solo turn in Cul-de-Sac (which sounds like one of the trickier parts of a driving test). They were both excellent, but I think that Miller will probably win. However, I also think that one-person shows should be in a separate category, the requirements of acting on your own being so different from those of doing it with other people. Nominated in the latter, less flashy, section are Eric Peterson (my choice) in Half Life, Paul Soles in Trying and Stuart Hughes in Soulpepper's Pinter/Albee double-bill. All fine, but no more so than Dennis O'Connor in End of Civilization or than a whole bunch of Soulpepper actors: Michael Hanrahan, Hughes's opposite number, or William Hutt in Waiting for Godot, or Diego Matamoros, Gordon Rand and David Storch in Translations. Rand was also brilliant in Trout Stanley, but Matamoros beats him out as the year's most taken-for- granted talent since the plethora of nominations for Half Life includes none for his performance, which was, in its quiet way, almost the best male acting of the season.

OUTSTANDING PERFORMANCE BY A FEMALE IN A PRINCIPAL ROLE: PLAY "Male," "female" -- why so clinical? Whatever happened to those useful words "actor" and "actress"? Anyway, this one is clear-cut: Carolyn Hetherington must win, both for the sheer grace of her performance in Half Life, and for her status as a mature performer of whom few of us were properly aware. Also, there's not much competition, though Melody Johnson was pretty riveting in Trout Stanley. And what, pray, about the unlisted Martha Henry in Vigil?

OUTSTANDING PERFORMANCE BY A MALE IN A PRINCIPAL ROLE: MUSICAL This has to be a contest between Jay Brazeau, the mountainous mother in Hairspray, and David Keeley, the oleaginous cop in Urinetown. Brazeau's role does come with built-in natural advantages. I guess Tom Rooney's delightful performance as her hubby doesn't count as "principal." But who knew he could sing and dance?

OUTSTANDING PERFORMANCE BY A FEMALE IN A PRINCIPAL ROLE: MUSICAL Jennifer Waiser's Little Sally in Urinetown, no contest. The competition is thin: Divine Brown plucked from a cast of equals in Ain't Misbehavin', two by Mary Ann McDonald, and Vanessa Olivarez who, in the lead role of Hairspray, was close to being bad. Maybe they should have let Jay Brazeau qualify in this category.

OUTSTANDING PERFORMANCE IN A FEATURED ROLE Simple mathematics show this to be the most crowded pigeonhole of all. But they insist on lumping everybody together: male, female, play, musical. Of the half-dozen assembled I vote for Mike Shara in Take Me Out. I note that Fran Jaye got nominated for belting one of those indistinguishable supposed-to-be-soul numbers in Hairspray, while Jennifer Stewart, the life and real soul of that particular party, got nothing.

OUTSTANDING SET DESIGN Francis O'Connor for Translations. Some people claimed it overwhelmed the play; it didn't, and I'd be rooting for it even if it had. Costume Design Dunno. Maybe Sarah Balleux for her dual-focus duds (ancient below, modern above) in Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme. Lighting Design Kevin Lamotte's work on Translations glows in my memory. Sound Design Search me. I remember there being some terrifying noises in Cul-de-Sac, courtesy of Richard Feren.

MUSICAL DIRECTION Here, too, one takes excellence for granted, though Stephen Woodjetts (Urinetown) was noticeably good, perhaps because he appeared on stage. But I think I favour Marek Norman, who after his nominated work on the High Park As You Like It went on to compose a totally different score for the same play in Barrie, proving twice over that a Canadian can provide great Arden music without being Jann or even a Barenaked Lady. Choreography John Carrafa, Urinetown, exhilaratingly funny, just beats Jerry Mitchell, Hairspray, merely exhilarating.

I have to be less categorical about the Independent categories, because there was much I didn't see. Nonetheless, I shall be both shocked and furious if A Whistle in the Dark doesn't get Outstanding Production, as it was the best show of the season, period. Ditto for Joseph Ziegler as the play's patriarch, the performance of the year, any divison, any category. I am already incensed that there is no nomination for the director, Jason Byrne; do the judges think that those seven impeccable performances orchestrated themselves? This, considering the similar neglect of Ben Barnes, must be what is meant by the luck of the Irish.

Best actress in this division will, I hope, be Barbara Gordon in Beckett's Not I, with honourable mention for Jenny Young in The Anger of Ernest and Ernestine. Yanna McIntosh is also nominated for her Hedda Gabler, though it seems perverse to acclaim a fine actress for a performance so far below her best. Best new play in this sector: Gord Rand's Pond Life would be fine with me.

Awards are silly and unfair, and it's foolish for anyone, onlooker or participant, to get agitated about them. But the fact that we do is a sign that both we and the activity that's up for grabs are alive and somewhat kicking.

Colour Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / John Mighton's Half Life should be a lock in the Outstanding New Play category.; Colour Photo: Bigger than Jesus, with Rick Miller, is in the running in several categories.

2005-07-02-the-musical-s-decline-greatly:
robertcushman@lycos.com

Ethan Mordden is a New York author of both fact and fiction who, over the past eight years, has published a decade-by-decade history of what he terms "the Golden Age of the Broadway Musical, from 1920 to 1980. He has given us Make Believe (treating the musical in the '20s), Beautiful Mornin' (the 40s), Coming Up Roses (the 50s), Open a New Window (the '60s) and One More Kiss (the '70s). There has, obviously, been a decade missing, but he has now accounted for it with Sing for Your Supper: The Broadway Musical in the 1930s (Palgrave, $38.95). The completed six-volume chronicle, which mentions nearly every show and has something crisp and analytical to say about most of them, is a unique achievement. Mordden seems to have read every script (and every source of every script), studied every score and -- but of course -- listened to every album. He is also a very entertaining writer, and at times an infuriating one.

Right at the start of Sing for Your Supper -- up in the acknowledgements, in fact -- he describes himself as someone who believe[s] the art has been locked in a spiral of degradation ever since Babes in Toyland." Babes in Toyland, music by Victor Herbert, appeared in 1903, long before Morddens Golden Age even got started. So obviously hes joking. But there's maybe a part of him that wishes he wasn't, that would like to move the decline of the American musical as far back as possible and get it over with.

The other side of that coin is visible in yet another of Morddens books, one that appeared last year and, though not officially included in the Golden Age series, is written in the same style and format. Its called The Happiest Corpse I've Ever Seen: The Last 25 Years of the Broadway Musical (Palgrave, $38.95), and it announces itself as a jeremiad on the way things are now. You will note that though, like all the Golden Age books, it takes its title from a song lyric, this time the song in question does not belong to the period being discussed; the phrase comes, instead, from Cabaret (1966). It's as if Mordden couldnt bear to defile his title page with anything from a present he so thoroughly despises.

His introduction confirms the feeling: The musical has become the province of "inarticulate idiots specializing in worthless forms based on exhausted old song catalogues and the staging of movies. Present-day America has summoned up a new kind of musical, coarse and uneducated. Thus prepared, and feeling an instinctive sympathy with the proposition advanced, one settles down for an enjoyably destructive read.

It doesnt materialize. The generalized denunciations keep coming, it's true, and the book's last sentence expresses a repugnance that is itself repugnant. But when he comes to examine the shows, Mordden finds an amazing amount to like. The post-Golden Age musicals over which he rhapsodizes include La Cage aux Folles, The Rink, Rags, the superflop Carrie (unpredictable, and that is the best theatre possible"), Nine, My One and Only, Dreamgirls, Crazy for You, The Mystery of Edwin Drood, City of Angels, Aida (!), Urinetown, The Producers (so that doesnt count as a staged movie?), Grand Hotel, Titanic, Sweet Smell of Success, Kiss of the Spider Woman, Side Show, Ragtime (though he finds its politics too left wing), both versions of The Wild Party and the five most recent New York Sondheims. He lists some "absolutely humourless shows, which sounds both accurate and damning, but most of them turn out to be among his favourites. When he devotes a chapter to the European pop- operas," one sniffs blood, but -- though his tone is rather evasive - - he finds nice things to say about them, too. (Les Miserables, that compendium of cliches, is stupefyingly described as "the one with the best lyrics.) In fact, Mordden, after all his attacks on the dumb and the ignorant, here turns around and starts castigating the snobs" who pounce on isolated flaws in these works to denounce the whole genre. Not that that stops him from casting Tim Rice into outer darkness for one notorious non-rhyme in Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat.

So what, other than the obvious monstrosities from which no period is free, doesnt he like? He doesn't like Mamma Mia!, praise the Lord, and he calls Hairspray "stupid junk, though that term would be better applied to something like Side Show, a portentous show about Siamese twins, without the brains to match its ambitions. Mordden has always been soft on solemn musicals, though he's also capable of conducting a joyous examination of The Producers, which, as he points out, is the old baggy-pants comic show reinvented.

I agree with him about some shows, not about others. I share his pessimism, though not its violence. The reasons for the decline of the musical are clear enough: rising costs leading to rising ticket prices leading to fewer shows and no middle ground between massive hit and instant flop; a falling-off not so much of talent as of avenues for talent; most important, the gap, first apparent around 1960 and widening ever since, between music thats pop and music thats dramatic -- able, that is, to explore story and character. Once upon a time the best musicals -- a Guys and Dolls or a My Fair Lady -- were also the most popular. Now, that's the exception. Maybe the best new writers, the Adam Guettels and Michael John LaChiusas, should resign themselves to being minority entertainers, though that must be hard when you're working in a form that in the past has made so much money. Mordden says that the only people who really understand musicals are gay men and Frank Rich. Maybe thats the problem: too small a demographic.

He seems inclined to blame todays audience for not being as intelligent and literate as its ancestors, who got all the references in Cole Porter. Maybe, but a writer taking this attitude should not misspell Occam (of Occam's razor) on his own second page. Mordden's great virtue is that he knows a lot; his great vice is that he cant bear to appear ignorant about anything. He also hammers bad jokes into the ground. One actress, notorious for getting cast in flops, he chases down the decades, announcing that at her third-grade Easter pageant, some parents demanded their money back, though admission had been free." Hes a very witty writer, except when he's trying to be funny.

He finds the '20s a thrusting era in which an inconsequential form became consequential partly because people like Gershwin were writing the music, partly because of Show Boat, which revealed huge new possibilities of musical storytelling. These remained mostly dormant until the Rodgers and Hammerstein shows of the 40s, while in the 50s everybody joined in. Innovation became the norm. He thinks this persisted into the '60s, though I don't; I think thats when the form began to calcify. Witness Mame, one of his real faves, which tells us (in the song that gives his 60s volume its title) "the fellow you ought to be is unconventional while remaining unshakably conventional itself. And then the 1970s, which yielded the last major show, A Chorus Line, that was also a huge hit.

The '30s, oddly, were a period of stasis. At the outset of Sing for Your Supper, Mordden makes a couple of statements about the decade's shows that are both surprising and true. One is that they werent very adventurous. The other is that they werent very political. Brother, Can You Spare a Dime, the depression anthem, was a theatre song, but it was atypical. (Even its very politicized lyricist, E. Y. Harburg, never wrote anything else like it.) There was Porgy and Bess, but that was an opera; it didn't influence anything, though it's still ahead of everything. There were also Gershwins comic operas about presidents, which were smart but harmless, and Marc Blitzsteins labour opera The Cradle Will Rock. Mordden, whose conservatism has been growing increasingly peevish (perhaps because the musical is a traditionally liberal form), does manage here to be fair to Blitzstein, whom he described in another book as a braying stooge." Otherwise, it's an era of great songs, so many that when discussing Jerome Kern's Music in the Air, Mordden doesnt even mention that it contains The Song Is You, one of the most-performed standards of all. And its a time of stars. It saw the arrival, bang in 1930, of Ethel Merman, whose Cole Porter vehicle Anything Goes is quite rightly the decade's most-revived show. Sing for Your Supper is the name of a Rodgers and Hart song, and is less celebratory than most of Mordden's titles. Its about tuneful survival, and thats just about right for the '30s.

ORPHEUS DESCENDING, AND THE MEASURE OF LOVE/ RUTH DRAPER ON TOUR

Stratford Festival

- - -

In the Deepest South setting of Orpheus Descending, Seana McKenna stands out as the only person in town with an Italian accent. It makes her the least operatic individual on stage, something that could only happen in a Tennessee Williams play. Her character, known as Lady Torrance, is the daughter of, to quote the local gossips, "a wop from the old country" who made himself very popular by opening a wine garden back in the days of Prohibition, but then, quoting again, "made a bad mistake. He sold liquor to niggers." Some prankish citizens burned down his establishment, and him with it. What Lady doesn't know, though everyone else does, is that the ringleader was the local dry-goods merchant whom she subsequently married and who now, 20 years later, lies dying upstairs.

It has been a loveless, childless marriage anyway, and it has left Lady with her own inner conflagration, a dry and bitter fire that here lights up the stage. McKenna's performance, magnificent even by her own recent standards, is a compact of anger, need and a storekeeper's practicality; it denies self-pity and substitutes, to the play's great benefit, a whiplash wit. Most of her key scenes are with Val Xavier, a young itinerant musician who, by vague mythological association, gives the play its title. In Miles Potter's production these duets are superbly orchestrated, and just as superbly performed, with lines of force between the couple sometimes spanning the whole depth of Peter Hartwell's spare, evocative set.

Jonathan Goad gives a marvellously practical, unselfconscious account of Val, a tougher role than Lady since he exists less in anything he actually does than in what he says about himself and what other people, including his fevered author, see in him. His temperature is "always a couple of degrees above normal, same as a dog's." He is coming, at the age of 30, off a successful career as a stud; his prized possessions are his snakeskin jacket and his guitar, autographed by Leadbelly, Bessie Smith and others. (Goad can sing and play, which helps keep the character rooted.) Lady distrusts him, is drawn to him, and in her own way uses him; the town tramp (a smashing performance by Dana Green, low-down and lyrical) whose rich family pay her to do it somewhere else, sees in him a vulnerable fellow-spirit and wants to get him away; a painter (a too-young Sarah McVie) with failing eyesight and mystical leanings, associates him with a vision of the Risen Christ, and falls on her knees before him. (I should perhaps have mentioned that the play is set at Easter. An earlier version was filled-to- bursting with Christian imagery, which still seems more central to it than Orpheus-with-his-lute.) The artist-lady is also the sheriff's wife and the sheriff is not pleased.

His jealousy, though, is not what precipitates the play's catastrophe, which is plenty catastrophic, involving lynching and blowtorches and flesh-tearing dogs. The various strands of the action themselves resemble a pack of dogs, running wild in different directions. The play has a lot of story but not much plot. It is possibly the ultimate Williams work, sweaty and lyrical, shrewd and naive, wild-eyed and wide-eyed, sometimes hypnotic, sometimes ludicrous and quite often both at once. There are frequent lines, and occasional whole scenes, that cut like knives. There is also a lot of intentional humour in the portrayal of the way a small town wags. And the underlying horrors, as we have recently been reminded, are real.

The cast is stuffed to extravagance with Stratford stars. Thom Marriott's sheriff is worthy of one of the best brooding Westerns; an intruder lurking shamefacedly at the back takes off his hat and stands revealed as Scott Wentworth, playing a single vital scene; Michelle Giroux is a chillingly efficient nurse, held in reserve to the last act. Fiona Reid and Brigit Wilson make an enjoyable pair of scandal-mongers, though if there's a flaw in Potter's direction it's in his handling of their opening exposition, which is too busy to be clear. Besides, it's unfairly true that Southern speech, however authentic one knows it to be, always sounds exaggerated when coming out of non-American actors, and one needs time to adjust. The ending, too, is a bit forced (and in excess, for once, of what the author ordered). But between those poles the performance is awesome. It doesn't prove the play a masterpiece, but it makes it unmissable.

The Measure of Love, Nicholas Billon's new play, is a duologue for two old friends from convent-school. One, who was a free- spirited girl, became an actress; the other, who had once, in her innocence, thought herself the result of an immaculate conception, became a nun. Might it not have been more interesting if they had exchanged destinies? Anyway, here they are; the actress has written a play to apprise the nun of some things in their past that she should know about, and they proceed to act some scenes from it, the nun, who has had no prior warning, proving to be a remarkably talented sight reader.

Some of this involves hearkening back to a school production of Romeo and Juliet in which they were the lovers, except that the sister-in-charge didn't approve of that kind of love and altered the play accordingly. We hear some of her reformed text, and it doesn't make sense, even in its own terms. Just what were the doomed couple, rewritten as just friends and cousins, doomed for?

Billon's own play, like his previous Elephant Song, has more contrivance than substance. One of its ostensible themes is memory, but nothing is made of the announced fact that the actress may be losing hers. However, what is revealed about the nun is touching, and Fiona Reid's face registers the news and its consequences. There is also a nice contrast in the ways she and her colleague, Diana Leblanc, address the audience to express their solicitude for one another: Leblanc urgent and conspiratorial, Reid bemused and benevolent. Jean-Louis Roux directs.

The play forms a double-bill with Ruth Draper on Tour, devised and directed by Raymond O'Neill. Ruth Draper, who died in 1956, was a world-famous American writer and presenter of comic and dramatic monologues. This show presents Lally Cadeau in a selection of these pieces, linked by extracts from letters that Draper wrote to a friend while shuttling between capitals. Sometimes the monologues are set in the cities she's travelling to, sometimes they aren't. The letters make her sound very pleased with herself, and the impression carries over into the vignettes themselves, which are intermittently amusing but seem snobbish and sheltered when dealing with Draper's own upper-middle-class, and sentimental when dealing with anyone else.

All of which is rather unfair to Cadeau, and very unfair to Draper. There are two CDs of her work on sale in the lobby, and these reveal that what her contemporaries said about Draper was true: She was a genius. Her ear was fantastic. She found and maintained a different accent for everyone, and that without ever leaving the vocal confines of the United States. Cadeau never captures the vein of crazy comedy with which Draper can catch you deliriously off guard. Draper was always hard-edged, while Cadeau's edges are soft. Then again, Draper's monologues are never soliloquies; her characters are always talking to somebody. Her admirers always praised the way she seemed to fill the stage with her unseen interlocutors; Cadeau can't do that and neither, probably, could anybody else. Most importantly, Draper wrote these pieces for herself; she did them perfectly, and there is no point in varying a single pause or a single inflection. The script supplies no compensating context, so the actress' task is hopeless. Buy the discs.

2005-07-09-open-air-shakespeare-takes-on:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Much Ado About Nothing runs in High Park through Sept. 4, 416-367-1652. The Taming of the Shrew runs at the Home Depot Theatre, Ashbridge's Bay, through Aug. 7, 416-872-1111.

The first two plays in Toronto's annual parade of open-air Shakespeares are comedies, as these alfresco entertainments generally are. Both are set in Italy, as Shakespearean comedies tend to be. Both have been visually updated in their new productions to the early 20th century, which again is par for the course. Both are sex-war pieces, and that's no great surprise, either.

Much Ado About Nothing, which is early middle Shakespeare, might be described as a refinement of The Taming of the Shrew, which is just early. In Much Ado the central couple, Benedick and Beatrice, tame one another, with a little help from their friends. (It might be argued that that's also what the couple in the Shrew do, but more of that later.) The smoother play of the two, it also gets, from James Macdonald for the Dream in High Park, the suaver production. The time frame is the 1930s; the ambience involves straw hats and checkered tablecloths. A musician, Jonathan Monro, sits at the piano and plays ragtime tunes, which in the '30s must have counted as nostalgia, of his own composition. They are excellent, and his setting and performance of Sigh no more, ladies makes you wish that the play had more songs. He also acts, doubling as the minor villain Borachio and doing it rather well.

The production starts with a simulated battle, sounding a solemn note that never gets repeated. And no wonder; it's true that the play starts with soldiers returning from the wars, but that's a mere pretence for getting everybody in the same place. As the show proceeds, it goes in for a lot of all-purpose merriment, but it gets stronger and more specific as it goes on. It's kept on course by Juan Chioran's Benedick, which lacks somewhat in physical swagger (the actor, who is pencil-thin, seems more drawing room than barrack room) but nothing in wit or honesty. He keeps, when tricked into love, a delightful balance between Benedick's pride and his passion, and his reconciliation of the two -- "the world must be peopled" -- is a triumph, wisdom reduced to absurdity and all the wiser for it. He, too, can sing; Benedick as written probably can't, but nobody here is going to mind that he does.

Jacklyn Francis's Beatrice takes longer to assert herself, not rising above routine until the church scene, where she simultaneously declares love for Benedick and seeks revenge on Claudio, the man who has broken her cousin Hero's heart. After that, she never looks back. Historical note: A traditional test of Beatrices at the church is whether they can avoid raising a laugh with the peremptory demand to "Kill Claudio." Francis actually goes for the laugh and, getting it, persuades you that Shakespeare may have intended it all along.

The errant Claudio himself, a shallow fortune-hunter whose worst vice is his sincerity, is given a very fair hearing by Brett Christopher. Xuan Fraser as Don Pedro has a good lonely moment when he all but declares his own love for Beatrice, but fails to follow it up; it could, after all, be the reason that he conceives the plot to push her and Benedick into one another's arms. As his treacherous brother Don John, Anousha Alamian is melancholy in a beret. Jim Warren gets the outlines of Dogberry, the complacent copper, but can't make him funny, possibly through lack of supporting manpower. I have seen Dogberry effectively played as a Sicilian carabiniere, as an Indian policeman serving proudly under the British Raj (hence the malapropisms) and even -- if you can credit such outrageous avant-gardism -- as an Elizabethan country constable. But wherever you put him, he needs a context. In all, this is an enjoyable production, with one commanding performance; it's often superficial but it's never actually false.

Last year David Ferry directed a good Much Ado in Newmarket. He's now moved on, or back, to The Taming of the Shrew, for ShakespeareWorks' Home Depot Theatre (there's a real come-on of a name) in the Beaches. His production is rougher than the High Park show and, in its opening stretches, crasser, but it ends up more interesting.

This time the Italy on stage purports to be that of 1913, with Fascism beginning to raise its head. (Its dominance in the '30s is something the Dreamers in High Park don't seem to have noticed.) Most of the time, though, Italy serves as an exotic backdrop with some funny associations, which is probably much how it functioned for the Elizabethans. There is a town-square band for atmosphere, but characters heroically refrain from eating ice cream.

The first half here is full of one-off gags that don't work, making the stage look untidy. But there are some good comedians on board, and they gradually assert themselves. Christopher Morris's Tranio is a boon from the start, and he helps speed the subplot along. Dylan Roberts's Biondello is a plump little joker who looks and behaves like Lou Costello; by a rather different token, Don Allison's father, Baptista, is a dead ringer for The Sopranos' Paulie Walnuts. Paul Braunstein's Grumio has no antecedents that I can spot, but he makes an excellent complainer. Peter James Haworth's Hortensio has a stammer, which sounds desperate, and it comes and goes, which is confusing; he's also required to do Irish, which is a terrible idea, but he's a benign presence when given the chance. The widow who snaps him up in the last scene is allowed to prowl the stage unscripted earlier on, while another character is given a spurious wife who has to stand there saying nothing while all hell erupts around her. I can see that a director staging the Shrew may feel compelled to do his bit for gender equity, but this is ridiculous.

And for the last time -- though I know it won't be the last time - - if directors feel compelled to update Shakespeare verbally, could they at least ensure that their emendations fit the metre? Could they, for a start -- this goes, too, for the last Stratford Shrew -- learn how to pronounce "choleric"?

This brings us, sort of, to this production's two leads, neither of whom, up until the intermission, seem to have a clue about speaking -- and hence acting -- Shakespeare. Paulino Nunes's Petruchio has the look of an adventurer with a good heart, but he gabbles. Elizabeth Saunders's Katharina seems to be mumbling even when she shouts. There are some good ideas in their love-at-first- sight encounter, but hardly any nuance. We can see that this Kate is a misfit, abused by her family. As her goody-goody sister, Bianca, Marion Day is not only a tease, which is usual, but a bully in her own right, as long as nobody bigger is looking. Saunders comes suddenly into her own at Petruchio's house when she delivers -- as a soliloquy -- her speech about going hungry, and makes it both powerful and searching. Petruchio tames her, as the text indicates, by holding up a mirror of her own behaviour. Nunes, playing his last card, rolls on the floor and throws a tantrum; she laughs, at him and at herself. Game over.

The last scene is splendidly staged, with Saunders's reading of the so-called "submission" speech both lucid and moving, and Nunes capping it with the offer of his own hand, followed by a brisk triumphant goodnight. Ferry's choice of period at this point pays off. In a more liberal society the scene would be ridiculous; here it seems like the only way out for two people who are essentially outcasts, and who are still wearing the raggedy clothes that Petruchio prescribes (a point out of which most productions obliviously weasel).

I don't know quite what comes over this show at half-time, but I imagine nightfall has something to do with it. We can't actually see Lake Ontario, but we're aware of it. And the couple of trees that we can see, through the theatre's open back wall, look lovely.

MAJOR BARBARA, THE AUTUMN GARDEN

Shaw Festival

The last, and very memorable, image in the Shaw Festival's Major Barbara is of Ben Carlson as Adolphus Cusins, professor of Greek, gazing with mixed feelings at a pile of explosives. They are, thanks to an agreement he has just entered into, part of his inheritance. He is to be groomed for succession to the armaments firm of Undershaft and Lazarus. Current proprietor: Andrew Undershaft, millionaire. Its a double connection since Adolphus is about to marry Undershafts daughter Barbara, who, as an officer in the Salvation Army ministering to the poor of East London, gives the play its title. Cusins shares Barbara's charitable values but not her religious beliefs. He abhors Undershaft's beliefs, which boil down to selling guns to anyone who can pay for them, but develops a grudging respect for his values, of which the chief is that the most corrosive of all crimes is poverty. No wonder hes conflicted.

The play, first staged in 1905, still resonates, what with its discussion of where exactly charity begins and its prophetic view of the military-industrial complex. Undershaft tells his son Stephen, who wants to go into politics, that he will end up passing whatever laws best suit his fathers interests. The arguments are as brilliantly marshalled as in any Shaw play, though it remains true that once you've heard them, you've heard them. The paradoxes may dazzle the first time around, but on subsequent encounters you greet them as old friends -- congratulating yourself and the late author whenever they seem to strike particularly close to home. The characters are sharply etched, but they offer the actors little opportunity to take us by surprise. It can happen; it happens in that last moment of Carlsons, which occurs, significantly, after the last words have been spoken and the play is officially over. But mostly one judges the performances not on what hidden depths they may uncover, but on how well they phrase the lines.

The play is a three-sided contest, with a large corps of kibitzers. In Joseph Zieglers mostly admirable production, the major flaw is the major. Whatever disagreements they may have with her, Barbara's father, her fiance and practically everyone else find her inspirational. Diana Donnelly's Barbara, though, seems less a saint than a prig, lacking both in intellectual passion and in the confident wit with which she -- an earls granddaughter -- bosses the working classes into obedience. This spoils the plays second and most obviously actable act, set in the Army shelter. A series of ironic reversals, culminating in her colleagues' decision to accept tainted money in order to maintain operations, pulls Barbara's rug, or her prayer-mat, out from under her. She ends in (temporary) despair. Here it hardly registers.

That matters, though, less than it might, since Shaw -- whatever lip service he may pay to his heroine -- is actually more interested in the men in her life. After some preliminary bouts in the East End, they come to grips in Undershafts model factory -- a veritable garden city -- where the tycoon convinces the poet to work from the inside and "make war on war." (The play almost persuades you that its that simple.) This scene, which could be just endless talk, is here riveting. The iron fist of Benedict Campbell's Undershaft is so well concealed within his velvet glove that it sometimes threatens to disappear altogether, but his is a fine confident performance nonetheless. Carlson's Cusins is a model of mischievous lucidity, infused with racking doubt.

The supporting chorus is split between drawing-room and slum. Mary Haney as Undershafts estranged wife commands the former, with an entertaining portrayal of an imperious woman pretending to be meek. She is supported by Evan Buliung as an endearing chump with a talent for blurting out the emabarrassing platitudes in which everyone secretly believes, and by David Leyshon as the ineffable Stephen who, with his serene confidence about family values and the difference between right and wrong, seems destined for success, if not as a politician, then as a political columnist. The East Enders vary in quality, but Patrick Galligans Bill Walker is a first-rate bit of rough, Sharry Flett screeches and wheedles to great effect as Rummy Mitchens and Jenny L. Wright is unobtrusively accurate as a junior Salvationist. The library and the shelter are gifts to any designer with imagination and a budget, and Christina Poddubiuk accepts them gratefully; she surpasses herself though in the trickier last scene, an observation deck commanding vistas of vertiginous prosperity

The late Lillian Hellman is best known theatrically as an author of melodramas, good (The Children's Hour, Montserrat) or bad (The Little Foxes, Toys in the Attic). So The Autumn Garden, a mild success on Broadway in 1951, comes as a surprise, and a pleasant one. Crammed as it is with characters in potentially explosive relationships, it might be described as melodrama that fails to happen, and is all the more truthful for it. There are two marriages on stage, both unhappy but both destined to endure. There is a long- standing friendship that is never going to develop into anything else. There is an engagement and that isn't going to go anywhere either. A wise critic once said the tragedy in Ibsens plays is that things turn out not to be what they seem, while the tragedy in Chekhovs is that they turn out to be exactly what they seem. By that criterion, The Autumn Garden is Chekhovian.

It is so in more superficial ways as well, since it presents a stageful of characters interacting in an enclosed setting that, like them, has seen better days. We are in the living room of a house near New Orleans that survives by taking in summer guests, all by now old acquaintances. This could be the more decorous side of the Southern discomfort currently running riot in Stratford's Orpheus Descending. The widowed owner awaits the return from Europe of an old flame, a raffish painter whose own wife has grown accustomed to his seasonal infidelities. Another widow watches in distress the involvement, unacknowledgedly homosexual, of her son with a predatory (unseen) writer, and is watched in turn by her own martinet of a mother. The son, meanwhile, is affianced to the niece of the house, who has been charitably imported from France and would like nothing more than to go back there. A retired general announces his intention of divorcing his wife, who acts as if she hasn't heard. Few of these people are nice, none are happy and most are tormented by what might have been, but all are interesting, if only because of their waspish (or could that be Waspish?) tongues.

Martha Henrys direction errs, I think, in ignoring the plays original three-act structure, so that its most obviously dramatic scene doesn't so much land as thud. Otherwise she adroitly maps the play's shifting emphases and unexpected confrontations, and lets us relish the sharpness of its dialogue. She has an A1 cast. Only David Schurmann as the general seems miscast; he goes through the motions of agony but his civilized facade refuses to crack. Wendy Thatcher, though, does an unflinching job on his spouse, while Patricia Hamilton is a splendidly pointed matriarch. Sharry Flett, Goldie Semple and Laurie Paton offer a trio of touchingly fastidious studies in distressed gentlewomanliness; Flett plays the central role of the chatelaine, which, on the heels of her Cockney pauper in Major Barbara, qualifies her for this years Niagara medal for versatility.

Mike Shara is a blushing juvenile and Jim Mezon a wine-and- weather-beaten commentator, but the most spectacular performance comes from Peter Hutt as the returned prodigal, a wonderful study in self-hatred perpetually deferred. He knows hes no good, as husband, lover or artist (his pictures are perpetually unfinished, and God knows how he maintains his cosmopolitan life-style) and he compensates by jovially patronizing everyone he meets. He's also the drunkest person on stage, which is saying something. He finally intrudes on the sleeping-quarters of the emigre niece, thus precipitating the nearest thing to a show-down. The girl, whom everybody takes for stupid though she's probably the wisest person around, is played by a striking newcomer, Charlotte Gowdy; she's tall, less gauche and more beautiful than the author seems to have envisaged, but that does no harm at all.

robertcushman@nationalpost.com; A Midsummer Night's Dream runs through Aug. 6 at the Jelinek Cork Shakespeare Stage, Coronation Park, Oakville, 905-815-4049. The Dispute closes today, 4 p.m., at the Robert Gill Theatre, 214 College St., third floor, 416-966- 1062.

Journeys do not generally end in lovers meeting. Shakespeare may once have said they did, for the sake of a rhyme, but his own comedies, and classic comedy in general, give him the lie. From old Athens to old Hollywood, a comic journey begins with lovers meeting. It then throws obstacles in their paths until the final fade-out, at which point it brings them back together and leaves them there, for better or worse. Usually it's for better, though there's always a cynical temptation to think otherwise. And there are some plays in which the author genuinely seems to be on the side of the cynics.

This week has brought two excellent productions of contrasting comic masterpieces, one fair and familiar, the other black and rare. The famous one is A Midsummer Night's Dream, which Miles Potter has directed for the Festival of Classics in Oakville in a production that goes far beyond being "good for an open-air show"; it's simply one of the best Shakespeares to come along in years. It isn't too easy to say why; Potter's work isn't critic-friendly, in the sense of supplying easily visible concepts for reviewers to chew over. This production is in modern dress, but there doesn't seem to be any agenda to that, beyond simple accessibility. But the overall impression is that the director approached his text and his actors with an open, alert mind and tried to get the best out of both. It works. Dialogue and characters spring into life, and make one another funny, with layers. Even the story seems fresh.

It grips, in fact, right from the start. The Dream is an unusual case, in that its lovers have met, and are embroiled, before the play starts. Its fairy king and queen have been married for, presumably, eons; its mortal boys and girls are in an amorous tangle when we first meet them. The first scene is a quarrel, and it's especially well done here, as an escalating crash of juvenile egos, and one adult one; in the heavy-father role, Michael Spencer-Davis, a pillar of middle-class respectability relishing the prospect of his daughter's immolation should she defy his wishes, is the only Egeus of whom I have ever wished to see more. Shauna Black's Hermia must have been the prom queen at her Athenian high school; a virginal flirt, secure in her own prettiness, she brings her teddy bear along on her flight to the woods. Tova Smith's Helena, a bespectacled geek clutching an album of her adored Demetrius, painstakingly spells out every thought that occurs to her, and wallows unstoppably in every emotion. The young men, as usual, have less personality, but Darren Keay and Matthew MacFadzean make the most of what they are given; when, much later, they all awaken from their dream, MacFadzean's Demetrius gets the strangeness of the play better than almost anyone in the cast. The long four-sided quarrel in the forest is very carefully built, with the slapstick applied only at strategic moments. The progressive tearing and shedding of clothes is an especially riotous running gag and -- please don't misunderstand -- a revealing one.

The interplay within the Athenian amateur actors' group is equally rich, with Spencer-Davis doubling as a Peter Quince who comes to rehearsal equipped with a beret and a chair marked "director." He's plainly read all the books, and is very prompt with textual notes and vocal exercises. The latter are mainly aimed at Mark Lancaster's Flute, a bass who, cast as Thisbe, is very reluctant to force himself up into a soprano. He hates his role but, in one of the production's inspired touches, it takes possession of him; his dying speech is actually rather moving, capping a scene that up to then has been hilarious. Murray Furrow's Bottom takes direction less well, and stages at least one spectacular walkout. He is delightfully bumptious at his first appearance, disappointingly routine when hidden within his ass's head, but magical when he, too, has his awakening. The succeeding brief scene when he rejoins his friends is much the best, from all hands, that I have seen.

In a production notable for its humanity, the superhuman fare less well. J. D. Nicholsen, a Shakespearean debutant, makes a strong initial impression as Oberon but doesn't vary it much. He has the air and appearance of a laughing buccaneer, suggesting Captain Hook before his traumatic encounter with the crocodile. Indeed, there's a strong flavour of Peter Pan about this section of the play. Claire Jullien, a rather elocutionary Titania, arrives attended not just by a single changeling child but by a whole troop of Lost Boys and Girls, all apparently abducted from a fancy-dress party. They do not, as you might expect, turn up later as Peaseblossom, Cobweb & Co.; those roles are taken by the four largest of the mechanicals, which is a very neat effect. The prize of the fairy kingdom, though, is Deborah Hay's captivating Puck, a resentful show-off forever stealing up behind Oberon and failing to surprise him.

Whom does that leave? The court figures aren't too hot, with Jason Mitchell's Theseus played for one-note geniality and Jane Spence wasted as Hippolyta. There's an amusing transgendered treatment of major-domo Philostrate, who comes equipped with what can only be spelled as a Philophax. The ending is genuinely happy, for the audience as well as the cast. Nightfall does its accustomed work, but I think this show would be magical even at matinees.

- - -

A brand plucked from the annual bonfire of the Toronto Fringe: Kate Lynch, who herself directed a fine all-female Dream a few seasons ago, now stages an anti-Dream, in the shape of The Dispute, a once-neglected but recently reclaimed piece by the French 18th- century master Marivaux. It's also, and perhaps more significantly, an anti-Tempest.

Two young men and two young women, each one brought up in ignorance of anyone else's existence save that of a couple of guardians, are finally unleashed into the brave new world that has such people in it. Such people, that is, as one another and -- even more -- themselves; they have not, up till now, been allowed mirrors, either. The whole is a controlled experiment, conducted by a Prince and his mistress desirous to find out which sex is the more fickle. The result -- as A falls for B, who returns her ardour but is then attracted by C, who has had her own thing going with an equally susceptible D -- is pretty much a draw, though the ladies score higher on narcissism. This is brought out with especial deliciousness by Egle (Carly Street), patiently explaining her own beauty and her rival's ugliness to said rival, Adine (Robin Schisler), who feels the same in reverse. The two men (Geoffrey Pounsett and Brendan Murray) are at least prepared to be pals; or, as an uncredited but British-sounding translation has it, "mates." The four of them have childish emotions trapped in mature bodies, which is pretty much the predicament of Shakespeare's quartet, except that they grow out of it. Marivaux's point seems to be that we never do, though social conditioning may help us to disguise the fact. His geometric precision becomes, inevitably, predictable, but it's compelling anyway, because it's so witty and so persuasive.

Lynch's production has a light touch and a dark heart. The central foursome are admirably framed by Tim Campbell and Jayne Lewis as the courtly manipulators and by Camille James and Jeremiah Sparks as the keepers who, Egle charmingly says, don't count as attractive because they're so black. It all sounds good and looks terrific, with the amorous or jealous tussling delightfully choreographed. The group responsible, the Sweat Company, announce that their purpose is to match "powerful, challenging text" to "bold, expressive, physicality." I detest such manifestos but have to admit that, in this case, what is promised gets performed.

2005-07-21-you-get-what-you-need-from-cl:
Bus Stop is at the Royal George Theatre until Nov. 27; Belle Moral is at the Court House Theatre until Oct. 7. 1-800-511-SHAW.

BUS STOP

Royal George Theatre

BELLE MORAL

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

Everybody is nostalgic for roadside diners, and the one designed by Sue LePage for the Shaw Festival production of Bus Stop looks good enough to be franchised. The play itself, William Inge's Broadway hit of 1955, also calls up memories of a neater if not happier time, a period in which dramatic characters got together to interact in confined spaces for tightly limited periods -- and emerged the wiser for the experience. Truths are told, destinies are linked and even the remaining loose ends have a tidiness about them. Of its kind, Bus Stop is about as good as it gets.

It has the double advantage of seeming both fresh and familiar since, though famous as both a play and a film, it is not often seen, at least not in these parts. A blizzard brings a small busload of people -- a driver and four passengers -- to an overnight halt some 30 miles west of Kansas City, which, as the local sheriff has patiently to explain, isnt in Kansas even though they themselves now are.

First to disembark is young Cherie, a self-pronounced chantoose who claims that she is being abducted. Bo, an equally youthful cowboy from Montana who was in K.C. for the rodeo, caught her club act and was dazzled. She liked him, too; at any rate they went to bed together. (Everythings up to date in Kansas City. They've gone about as far as they can go.) He woke up convinced they were in love and engaged and wouldn't hear otherwise. So here they are, en route to Bos ranch, with his protective older buddy, Virgil, along for the ride. The remaining traveller is Dr. Lyman, an old soak of an ex- teacher, who quotes Shakespeare and comes on to young girls, in this instance to Elma, high-school student and part-time waitress. She too gets dazzled but only temporarily, thanks to the good advice of Grace, whose diner it is and who herself is taking advantage of the extra-long stopover to have a fling with the bus driver.

All in the course of the night discover something about love and tell us what it is. Grace learns to settle, Elma learns to wait, and the doctor learns to give up.

Bo and Cherie, the central couple, share a more complicated educational process. He, with some assistance from his friends wisdom and rather more from the sheriff's fists, discovers that you can't always have what you want, especially if what you want doesnt want you. She, finding that hes more vulnerable and less experienced than he let on, melts. Her decision is also influenced by her realization that neither her past nor her probable professional future bear much thinking about. (Her performance of That Old Black Magic as part of a wayfarers' cabaret halfway through the night doesn't suggest any kind of threat to Doris Day.) So the expected Broadway happy ending has its dark underside.

The buckaroo and the chantoosie-floozy are American legends, with Cherie carrying additional mythic baggage from being played on screen by Marilyn Monroe. Its a tribute to the two actors here that each of them can embody the archetype and still find the person within it.

Nicole Underhay, in a fluent and firmly centred performance, explores all Cheries permutations of hurt and pride; Martin Happer's Bo has a blithe swagger that's a very plausible anagram for innocence. Hes even, by the end, managed to make the characters boorishness likeable, which is quite a feat. (My hazy memory of the movie is that it finessed this matter by filling in all the back story, and showing it mostly from Bo's point of view.)

Jackie Maxwell's production gets the personal rhythms and the rhythms of the diner flowing smoothly into one another, with Grace and Elma brought firmly to life by Mary Haney, shaking her feathers like a satisfied mother hen, and Diana Donnelly, a perceptive listener and eager participant. Michael Ball is a fine drawling sheriff and Norman Browning a good self-hating lush. Peter Krantz supplies a melancholy ground-bass (actually, he plays guitar) as Virgil who, like Antonio in The Merchant of Venice, bows out of his young friends life when a lady bows in.

Virgil may supply a literary subtext as well as a homosexual one. He shares a name, after all, with the Roman poet who was resurrected to become Dantes guide, philosopher and friend through the first two-thirds of The Divine Comedy.

Or maybe my mind is running that way after seeing Ann-Marie MacDonald's Belle Moral, a new play that's loaded with literature. The title, puns apart, denotes a big old house not far from Edinburgh, and the time is the end of the 19th century. The references run from partially submerged prophetic gags about Kafka and Proust to more topical and explicit invocations of Wilde and Shaw, to outright quotation from times past; Shakespeare gets paraphrased, while the plays best speech is a poem by Robert Burns, the one about mice. Paul Sportellis score includes strains of Clair de Lune, which turn out to be a musical pun. And then there's Darwin.

Pearl MacIsaac, the de facto mistress of Belle Moral, is an amateur biologist concerned to push evolutionary theory further forward, or perhaps backward; her project emerges as the endeavour to find a genetic link between humans and dogs. Or, failing that, nicer ways for the one to treat the other. "We still organize our societies" she says, "as though we alone had been created in the image of a god in whom we profess no longer to believe." I wish the bulk of the play were as good as that line at taking ideas and rubbing them together.

Pearl's father recently died; her mother, who was thought to have carried a strain of insanity, committed suicide shortly after giving birth to Pearls brother, who has grown up wild and whimsical. But it never works up any steam, and when its resolved the surprise is less in the resolution itself than in the fact that it has one. The jokes are almost continuous but seldom funny, and they don't add up to a comic structure.

It reads better than it acts; better anyway than it acts here. The director, Alisa Palmer, has given a weightless play a heavy- handed production. Judith Bowden's pannelled mural of a set looks impressive at first glance, but it proves very impractical for the plays succession of short, shifting scenes; we spend ages watching furniture being trundled around in the half-light. The actors, too, are stuck in glue; the art of conversation sounds, most unexpectedly at the Shaw, in steep decline. The Scottish accents may be a hurdle even Fiona Byrne, whose overall lucidity as Pearl is a mercy, is sometimes strangled by hers. Jeff Meadows antic flourishes as the brother are exhausting. Peter Millard plays the family doctor with a rank lack of conviction. Brogues apart, he has a tough job functioning as the play's melodramatic villain and all-purpose reactionary. Donna Belleville does reasonably well by a barely characterized maiden aunt. The best writing goes to, and the best acting comes from, Bernard Behrens as a decrepit retainer amusingly addressed as Young Farleigh.

2005-07-23-the-singers-and-the-songs-juk:
robertcushman@lycos.com

About 40 years ago Billy Wilder made an especially cynical movie titled Kiss Me, Stupid that everybody loathed but that I rather liked.

Its about a couple of small-town amateur songwriters (one of them Ray Walston) trying to sell some material to a visiting singing star, an alcoholic womanizer (played by Dean Martin and named, lest there should be any misunderstanding, Dino). The price of success for the writers is to put Walston's wife in Martin's bed, though they finally jib at this and substitute the local good-time girl (Kim Novak). The film wasnt really a musical, but it had of necessity a few songs, and it counts as the last movie to have an original score by George and Ira Gershwin.

George had been dead for a quarter of a century, and Ira was in retirement, but every so often he would come out of it to fit new words to his brothers unused melodies. In this instance he faced the challenge of writing songs that would sound as if they might be the work of neophytes without actually letting down the Gershwin family name. I'm not sure that he found the right balance, and at one point he seems -- gracefully -- to have given up altogether. There's a sequence in which a conscience-stricken Walston, probably dubbed, sings a heartfelt ballad written for his wife, and its a beauty, certainly in that context. Its called All the Livelong Day - - Ira had wanted to add and the Lovelong Night" but his prudishness overcame him -- and I left the theatre longing to hear it again.

I never got the chance. Nobody, it seemed, recorded it, then or in all the years and all the Gershwin tribute albums since. In fact, Ella Fitzgerald had made a single of two songs from the film, but they were never reissued. They are, however, available now, on a two- disc anthology of her '50s and '60s singles, all re-released, titled Jukebox Ella (Verve).

All the Livelong Day is not, in truth, quite as lovely as my memories of it, and I think the tempo is too fast. But its still worth hearing, with an especially tender last section, and Ella, of course, sings it beautifully. Its one of her soothing numbers. The pairing, I'm a Poached Egg (Without Toast), is great fun. It's meant to be a parody of the kind of losers list-song that Ira perfected in I Cant Get Started, but it's jaunty enough to pass as the real thing. It could easily have turned up as one of the obscurer numbers on Ella's epic Gershwin songbook with Nelson Riddle; indeed, both arrangements, though uncredited, have Riddle all over them.

The rest of the package shows that Fitzgerald could be as infectious and inventive with ephemera as with classics. None of the songs became hits, though some of the 50s ones (Too Young for the Blues or The Silent Treatment) are quite good. There are also a couple of wonderful oddities: versions in German -- recorded, perplexingly, in Denmark -- of Youre Driving Me Crazy and Mr. Paganini, which swing more, if anything, than they do in English. (They also, when Ella abandons words, give the bizarre sensation of a singer scatting in a foreign language.) A 1962 recording of Desafinado reminds us that Ella was one of the first North American singers -- maybe the first -- to latch on to the bossa nova. There's also something she wrote herself, in '64, called Ringo Beat, whose message, more or less, is "we used to swoon over our idols; now let the kids have theirs." Coming from a more calculating singer it would sound, then or now, like unconscionable pandering (and why choose to celebrate that particular Beatle?); from her, obviously meaning it and having fun with it, its sweet.

At about the time Ella recorded that, Mark Murphy was beginning to break through as the jazz singer of his generation, with a beautifully controlled voice and an unfettered imagination. Hes gone on ever since, and has sometimes seemed to be progressively -- a double-edged word -- losing touch with his material. He has made some very forced and ugly sounds, no pleasanter for the fact that he was obviously making them on purpose. But his new one, Bop for Miles (HighNote), actually recorded in 1990, shows him near his best. It was made live in Vienna, and seems to be a seamless suite of songs associated with Miles Davis, though some clumsy edits suggest that originally there were pauses. It works best, though, when one song plays directly off another; when a fast, ruminant (as in both thoughtful and cud-chewing) All Blues goes into a wild Summertime that refers to the melody just often enough to keep itself grounded, and thence, by seasonal association, into a super-speedy Autumn Leaves, which has little to do with the mood of the song (these leaves aren't drifting, they're driven), but works anyway. Murphy blurs the line between words and sounds, and sometimes between song and speech, and on the later tracks this gets wearing. Squeezing the songs out in an alternating assortment of grunts and falsettos, he sounds as if he might be in physical pain. But he ends in fine form, with a barely lyricized version of Milestones, one of his warhorses from way back. He is backed by a small, fierce band that, strangely for a Davis tribute, has no trumpeter. But perhaps Murphy himself is the trumpet.

A far quieter, but in her way equally spiky, performer is Patti Wicks, who sings and plays (very good) piano. Love Locked Out (MaxJazz), her first album on a more or less prominent label, won me over immediately with its first and title track, a fairly rare Ray Noble song with an ultra-rare verse. The tone of this is admonitory, which seems to suit her well; hers is a stark, guarded kind of voice that sends the lyrics at you in short, clipped phrases. She sounds oddly like the 50s cabaret performer Frances Faye, who played mostly for laughs. Wicks deals mainly in ballads, so she needs the right ones, songs with an edge. Cole Porter suits her perfectly; she sings After You, one of his more romantic avowals, but still with a presentiment of doom behind it. She also does well by Rodgers and Harts great It Never Entered My Mind, Cy Coleman's self-mocking Would You Believe and the vengeful An Empty Glass. (She can't match Peggy Lees fast, clipped version of this, but I doubt anyone could.) On a more sentimental song like Blue Gardenia, you long for something more liquid. Wicks can also be heard, in more informal form and working with an Italian trio, on Basic Feeling (Jazzmates).

Wesla Whitfield is a singer who combines fine technical equipment with a probing and highly intelligent approach to lyrics. On her latest, In My Life (HighNote), she finds new, unforced ways to phrase songs ranging from I Have Dreamed, done rhythmically for once, to Wrap Your Troubles in Dreams, which here sounds like hard- won wisdom. Her accompanist, Mike Greensill, is one of the best there is.

Freddy Cole is his own accompanist. Hes spent most of his career trying both to escape and exploit the shadow of his brother Nat. He sounds far more gravelly than King Cole ever did (though who knows how his voice might have aged, had it been given the chance?) and now sounds pretty much his own man. His new one, This Love of Mine (HighNote), is mellow rather than memorable, but it's pleasant and has fine musicians and interesting songs. The latter range from the fairly new, such as Bob Dorough's Just for Now, to the long- neglected Out in the Cold Again, on which Cole sounds sad, certainly, but still warm.

2005-07-30-a-cruelly-effective-wild-duck:
robertcushman@lycos.com; The Wild Duck is in repertory through Sept. 3 at Harbourfront Centre Theatre. Olympia runs through Sept. 19 at the Premiere Dance Theatre. 416-973-4000.

Ibsen's The Wild Duck is usually described as a play about two kinds of lies -- the high-sounding ones known as ideals, imposed from without and generally fatal, and the more mundane falsehoods that people tell themselves, and hope others will believe, just so their lives will be bearable. "The truth will set you free" goes up against "humankind cannot bear very much reality," and loses. The description's accurate but it sounds, and is, schematic. Laszlo Marton is a director more interested in people than in abstractions, merciless in his eye for detail, charitable in his overall vision. In his production for Soulpepper, one of the finest things he or they have achieved, The Wild Duck is revealed as the most moving play ever to be written on a subject that's painfully specific: cruelty to children, across two generations.

Do what you want to the grown-ups, shouts the play's commentator, Dr. Relling, but leave the child alone. It's a thrilling moment, because Relling, who prefers to remain as drunk as possible for as long as possible, doesn't usually rouse himself to that degree of passion. It's also wrenching, because we have met and fully believe in the child he is trying to protect: Hedvig, the adoring daughter of the feckless photographer Hjalmar Ekdal and his protecting wife, Gina. And it's mordantly ironic, since the man he's cautioning is himself the victim of a kind of child abuse; this is Gregers Werle, who grew up hating his father, a businessman who once engineered the ruin and imprisonment of his partner, Hjalmar's father. Old Werle has, in fairness, supported the Ekdals ever since, but then he may have another motive; Gina once worked for him and he might be Hedvig's father. Certainly Gregers believes he is, and he, the play's idealist, makes it his mission to purify the Ekdal marriage by letting in the truth.

Up until Gregers moves in on them, the Ekdals are a reasonably happy family group, and certainly a tight-knit one; the staging makes that last metaphor tangible, showing the three clinging devotedly together at their first joint appearance and desperately, in a kind of fearful parody, at their last. The heart's blood of the production is Martha MacIsaac who, 20 herself, makes a tearingly convincing 14-year-old, radiating love and trust toward her undeserving dad, hurt but forgiving as children are when he forgets a promised present, devastating when she, afraid she's lost him, is herself devastated. There isn't a trace of winsomeness or false sentiment about this performance, and its closing stages, even if you don't know what's coming, are heartbreaking.

Chekhov may have been laughing at The Wild Duck when he wrote The Seagull, whose heroine, when an admirer gives her the eponymous bird, asks him, "Is this some kind of symbol?" (Well, words to that effect.) Ibsen's duck is several kinds of symbol, and the characters, Gregers especially, are all too aware of it, only their interpretations differ. It could be the truth that needs to be brought to the surface; it could be the lie that needs to be destroyed. Prosaically, it's Hedvig's wounded pet living, along with sundry other creatures, in a surprisingly capacious loft. In Csorsz Khell's set, sparse and starkly lit, this seems to be located beneath the family living quarters, which is even more surprising but allows for some thrilling descents.

There is a creepy bond between Hedvig and Gregers; they are, after all, half-siblings. Brent Carver's Gregers is a haunted fanatic with a residue of charm, a one-man cult who suffers, in Frank McGuinness's adaptation, from "the wrong of believing he's always right"; he can't understand why his nostrums aren't working as prescribed and goes on applying them regardless. The phrase "creeping Jesus" comes to mind, as he insinuates himself through doorways, rubbing his fingers like Uriah Heep. It takes a Hjalmar to see him as a saviour, just as it takes a Gregers to hero-worship Hjalmar. They could be a revisionist Othello and Iago, Gregers a destroyer who means well and Hjalmar an incorrigible self- dramatizer who turns on his daughter -- not his wife -- as savagely and as unbearably as Othello on Desdemona.

Diego Matamoros's hollow Hjalmar, another damaged son and an inventor who hasn't decided what to invent, is disarmingly as well as disturbingly funny at first. Indeed, part of the play's greatness is that he goes on being funny even when the tension is screwed tightest. But his callousness when playing the role of injured father is hard to watch, if only because it's so hard to disown. Matamoros's searching performance could represent any of us at our weakest.

The cast is all-round impregnable, starting with the flunkies (Derek Boyes and Philip Riccio), discoursing in gossipy whispers while preparing a bowl of punch, and moving up through Alon Nashman's deluded demoniac, making a person out of two lines and an alcoholic exit, up to David Hemblen as Werle senior, a tycoon in the quiet twilight of his powers, and Brenda Bazinet as his last mistress. William Webster is magnificent as Old Ekdal, a fantasy monarch in his own domain, a lost and humiliated beggar outside it. (The play may be said to take in elder abuse as well.) Maggie Huculak's Gina is less patient than most; when Hjalmar picks a melodramatic quarrel with his wife, she yells right back. I disagree with the conception but I can't fault the execution. Joseph Ziegler's Relling, angry rather than morose, is irresistible.

Olympia, by the Hungarian Ferenc Molnar, Soulpepper's other new show, starts with a sabre-toothed Brenda Robins and a doleful, pooch- faced Michael Healey (also the adapter) brazenly telling one another what they already know. We've had that joke, in the same author's The Play's the Thing, and here, since the characters aren't working theatricals, it's less thematically relevant.

What they are is Austrian aristocrats relaxing at a spa in the last glow of the Empire. The play was written in 1928 but seems to be set shortly before the First World War put an end to all that. Essential information is that Austrians despise Hungarians, though they sometimes find them useful, and should on no account fall in love with them. So of course Olympia, our heroine, does just that, with a humble cavalryman.

The play sets itself up as a trifle, then shows its teeth. Albert Schultz's production is elegant in looks and movement but the bite is intermittent. Kristin Booth is far more at ease with Olympia's heartache than with her cruelty. Stuart Hughes plays her unintended, who has tricks of his own, and does it well, especially in his earlier, shyer moments, but there needs to be more going on between these two people than is apparent here. Frank Moore appears as a deus ex machina, striking a single beaming note that is highly effective to begin with but whose returns steadily diminish.

There are, though, two riotous performances. One comes from Oliver Dennis, whose accident-prone intelligence officer is high farce. The other belongs to Nancy Palk, whose imperious, if not actually imperial, turn as Olympia's mama is high comedy, which means she puts a shiny gloss on some very base impulses. Apart from being continuously funny, she conveys what the show otherwise lacks: the sense that these people act as if they own the earth, and like it that way. When she utters the best line in the piece, something about the good old days when kings could eviscerate troublesome commoners, no questions asked, she makes Lady Bracknell seem like one of nature's democrats.
