2005-08-06-this-merchant-is-an-easy-sell:
The Merchant of Venice runs in Withrow Park through Sept. 5. 647- 438-6742.; robertcushman@lycos.com

As is well known, there were officially no Jews in England in Shakespeare's time; they had been expelled in the 14th century and were not readmitted until later in the 17th. It is therefore unlikely that Shylock in The Merchant of Venice could have been drawn from life, at least as far as his Jewishness is concerned. A new book, of which more later, argues that he is in fact based on a race of usurers closer to home, the Puritan moneylenders of Elizabethan London. Thats quite persuasive; Shakespeare, like anybody working in the theatre, would have had every reason to attack the Protestant extremists who wanted to close him down, and Shylocks rabid dislike of music (hardly a Jewish characteristic) certainly marks him down as one of the killjoys.

Whatever. The play still calls him a Jew, and that is something with which we are stuck. Even the new production by Shakespeare in the Rough doesn't try to change that, though it has given the role to an actor who is not only gentile -- Native Canadian, in fact -- but a woman. I'm not sure if this counts as gender-blind casting; I would expect that to mean giving a woman a crack at playing a man (or vice versa), but here Shylock is turned female.

Its hard to judge the validity of this idea because in this performance it hardly gets to first base. Jani Lauzon has little of the fire, the wit and the depth of both hatred and suffering that make the character interesting.

All the same, if this is gender-blind casting, then the concept seems necessarily to entail tone-deaf casting. Men and women talk and behave differently in one anothers company than they do when left to themselves, and Shakespeare was quite smart enough to know this and to write accordingly. If you're going to perform a sex change on a major character, then you also need to do something far more radical to the text than just altering the pronouns.

(There are a few more ambitious rewrites. I was wondering how they'd cope with "I had it of Leah when I was a bachelor." Its become I had it of Nathan when I was a young woman. Call me reactionary, but I think the old line is sharper.)

It is fun to see Shylock turned into a Jewish mother, but he has after all only one short scene with his daughter, though its elongated here by having them sing a duet. This comes just after the speech about hating music.

Otherwise, Sanjay Talwar's production is lively and intelligent, with some sharp editing and an excellent use of Withrow Park's deep perspective to remind us of characters who are theoretically offstage. This troupe still has the inside track on open-air Shakespeare within the city, even if, compared to luxurious High Park, its a dirt track. Michael Blake does an excellent double as the Prince of Morocco and Gratiano, though I still wonder why no actor ever plays up the latter characters melancholic streak. The shifting moods that Carly Street uncovers in Portia, especially in the casket scene, put her on a different plane from the rest of the show, and her disguise at the trial is amazing.

But that's another thing: This is a play in which the heroine has to dress up as a man in order to be taken seriously as a lawyer. It's a sexist society as well as a racist one (an eclectic design that takes in crinolines and cellphones does nothing to change that), so its impossible to believe that this Shylocks enemies, so free with the anti-Semitism, wouldn't take hostile note of her womanhood as well.

Now for that book. It's Shadowplay: The Hidden Beliefs and Coded Politics of William Shakespeare, by Clare Asquith (HarperCollins, $34.95), and my friend John Fraser has prophesied elsewhere that it will create a stir equal to that occasioned by Stephen Greenblatts justly acclaimed Will in the World. Personally, I doubt it. Asquith takes the now-accepted view that Shakespeares parents were Catholics, forced to hide their religion in a Protestant England that was virtually a police state, and that he inherited their beliefs. She goes beyond it in declaring that the plays' real purpose is to fortify the old believers and preach the cause of tolerance to Elizabeth and James I, all the while evading the censors.

This raises some questions. Did Shakespeare have only one theme over some 40 plays? How did he manage to be both plain enough and subtle enough to get away with it all those years? How, come to that, have audiences ignorant of their real meaning managed to enjoy the plays for four centuries? Asquith has an answer: Shakespeare disguised his real concerns beneath "great universal dramas" that he was apparently able to conjure up at will, even though his mind was really on something else. At one point, she concedes, someone must have objected and he was forced to abandon his main preoccupation while writing, among other things, the two parts of Henry IV, featuring Falstaff. This would mean that he was able to do some of his very best work, including the creation of his greatest comic character, with one hand tied behind him.

Asquith, a Catholic herself, is fighting her own corner. She comes remarkably close to implying that England's conquest by Philip of Spain would have been a good thing, though even Elizabethan Catholics, mindful of how the Spanish had treated the Dutch, might have had second thoughts about that one. She also, at the last minute, suggests that most of Shakespeares best fellow-playwrights were playing the same game. Years ago I reviewed a production of John Fords 'Tis Pity She's a Whore, a tragedy whose characters include a Friar (mostly good) and a Cardinal (definitely bad), and I remarked then that there was a book to be written about the shifting attitudes of Renaissance dramatists toward the Catholic Church "treated both as venal superstition and moral authority, sometimes within the same play." This is not the book I had in mind. England had been Catholic for centuries; the Reformation was recent. So of course there were mixed feelings.

Asquith does, as noted above, have some pertinent comments on individual plays. She persuades me, more or less, that Jaques in As You Like It is a portrait of Ben Jonson, though I was shaken by her failure to notice that a brief scene in the same play to which she attaches great weight is in fact one of those perennial Elizabethan jokes about cuckolds horns. Her literary scholarship is altogether pretty shaky. She confidently asserts that the apocryphal Edward III is the only play Shakespeare failed to revise for publication, though half the plays werent published at all till after his death. She gets characters' names in The Tempest wrong, and can't decide whether the king Macbeth murdered was Duncan or Donald. John Fletcher, one Jacobean playwright she doesnt like (he was a Protestant), is accorded sole authorship of Henry VIII and The Two Noble Kinsmen, two plays that she also doesnt like; everyone else thinks they're collaborations. The Shakespearean scenes in Kinsmen are so like him at his latest and knottiest that I can't imagine the facile Fletcher having written them. As for Henry VIII, Asquith describes its opening scenes as masterly pastiche ... exactly in Shakespeares style. Heads, you win. Her magnanimity in allowing that in this play "Wolsey, Norfolk and Buckingham are all given noble farewell speeches" is flawed by the fact that Norfolk doesnt have a farewell speech -- because he isn't going anywhere. Nor do I see why the very moving death scene given to the impeccably Catholic Catherine of Aragon somehow doesn't count.

The only honest response to Asquiths claims is a simple one: We dont know. She, however, keeps advancing her theories as though they were proven facts, so the book comes to read like a gushy historical novel: Shakespeare v. the bad guys.

The contrast with Greenblatt's speculative biography is extreme. He gives us a Shakespeare at war with himself, and his pages are studded with perhapses and supposings and let-us-imagines. He never tries to pass conjectures off as facts, which of course makes them more convincing. He, too, lays great stress on Shakespeare's Catholic heritage, but is convinced that he settled for scepticism instead; he wasnt anybodys martyr. Greenblatt is especially good on the possible story behind the sonnets and on the unprecedented depth of characterization that started with Hamlet. On The Merchant he remarks that though Shakespeare may not have known about Jews, he certainly knew about Judaism; he heard the Old Testament every week in church. Asquith writes as if the question of anti-Semitism had never been raised. Greenblatt, too, of course, is fighting his own corner (which, so you'll be warned, happens to be much the same as mine), but he does it with more grace. To echo the truly Shakespearean pun of his title, his is the best Will in the World.

2005-08-13-pitres-annie-goes-great-guns-:
robertcushman@lycos.com

Louise Pitre in Annie Get Your Gun is, to mangle a song title, as wonderful as falling in love. At least the experience hit me that way because, though I have admired Pitre on occasion, I have never before seen her in a show that I liked. As Irving Berlin's Annie Oakley, she sings as well as any leading lady I have seen in Toronto. In between her numbers, and during them as well, she acts, bringing out all the facets of the character she plays.

Make that both the facets. Annie is brash, and she's naive. Any complexities in her role result from the rubbing together of those two elements. Her first appearance, certainly in Pitre's performance, is a delight; she's in hot perplexed pursuit of a bird she's just shot off some lady's hat. She's a phenomenal backwoods sharpshooter who takes that ability enchantingly for granted but has no idea that it's something the outside world would call a talent and therefore marketable. But she learns, fast, through challenge contests and world tours with Buffalo Bill's Wild West Show and an instant requited passion for the show's own champion hotshot, Frank Butler. Both career and romance go wrong, but only for as long as it takes to give the musical a story.

Pitre plays both the joy and the heartache full out, but tactfully; this isn't a crying show. The defining moment of her performance is the rueful glance she bestows on her trusty rifle before launching into You Can't Get a Man with a Gun. The song itself is a tour de force that finds neat and funny rhymes for almost every known variety of firearm. She makes it even better by linking it fully to the personality and predicament of the woman who sings it.

She is equally persuasive in the gentler numbers, in the incredibly bewitching Moonshine Lullaby or in I Got Lost in His Arms, a song that musically and lyrically is an object lesson in the arts of tension and release. This show has a great set of songs; if they don't quite add up to a great score, that's because their placement is often arbitrary. I Got the Sun in the Morning is a joyous swinger, and I wouldn't be without it, but there's no dramatic reason for it to appear at one point in the show rather than another, or indeed in this show rather than any other.

But then the show itself is no great piece of architecture. The book (by Herbert and Dorothy Fields, revised on this occasion by Don Carrier) doesn't have a second act. After the intermission it simply stands around finding lame excuses for Annie and Frank, who have split arbitrarily up, not to get together again until the last possible moment.

The two leads sing, between them, all but one of the songs, so it's unfortunate that this production is virtually Frankless. Pitre has the warmth and colour to sing Annie without belting like Ethel Merman. (Actually, to judge from the cast album, Merman in this role didn't belt like Merman, at least not all the time.)

Frank has fewer specifics to fall back on; he's a Broadway baritone or nothing. Billy Ray Cyrus wears a cowboy hat to the manner born, and acts rather sweetly from underneath it, but his soft-grained country voice doesn't have the tone, range or rhythm for his songs. We know, as their big duet tells us, that anything he can do she can do better, but it shouldn't be quite such a foregone conclusion.

The production at Massey Hall is in semi-concert form. That is, the actors, while wearing their costumes and knowing their lines, have to thread their way around the orchestra, which takes up most of the stage and accounts for a good half of the vaunted "company of 50." Still, it's good to hear a big band playing a big-band score. And Donna Feore's direction is very resourceful, even working in some choreography, nearly all of it good.

The supporting cast has virtually nothing to play, a fact that Sandra Caldwell's vibrant presence in the especially thankless role of Dolly Tate makes particularly hard to bear. The others do their best, but Buffalo Bill remains an avuncular cipher and his manager, Charlie, a grinning stooge, while Chief Sitting Bull would surely be denounced as a comic travesty if only his jokes were funnier. The ways of political correctness are strange. This version retains the poisonous ending, in which Annie gets her man by letting him think he's the better shot, but deletes I'm an Indian Too, a harmless number whose absence saps some badly needed energy from the end of the first act. In its place we get the cast pacing hopefully around the stage in yet another encore of There's No Business Like Show Business. In its proper place that much-misunderstood song is splendidly done, with Pitre's Annie visibly seduced into embracing the travelling life. It isn't an explosion of theatrical pomp; it actually dwells on the seamier side. "The towel you've taken from the last hotel ... the roustabouts who move the show at dawn ... the closing when the customers won't come." Mind you, this Annie has already had her run extended, and justly; the sheriff won't be escorting her out of town just yet.

- - -

The roustabouts who move the Cirque du Soleil presumably work unionized hours, and don't have to do anything at dawn, or not very often. When the Cirque hits town, it settles here for a while. Corteo, its latest presentation, purports to have a theme, as most of them do. This time it's a requiem for a dying clown who looks back on past circus experiences (probably a metaphor for life, but don't think about it). However, unless I'm getting blase, this edition lacks something, both in beauty and in daring. The skills are awesome, of course, but life and limb go, for the most part, remarkably unimperilled. The distinguishing characteristic is the frequent appearance of what might be children but are probably very small adults. One gives the show its most delightful sequence as she floats out over the audience, attached by a harness to five balloons, while her daddy-clown asks for her to be given back. This time around, though, the Cirque, with its long intermission for selling the maximum amount of merchandise, seems more business than show.

- - -

At the smaller end of town this year's SummerWorks festival has come up with at least one real winner. This is Essay (Theatre Passe Muraille), by Hannah Moscovitch, in which a first-year history student provokes her teacher by handing in a paper about a woman he deems unsuitable. She isn't, though, making a feminist protest (as she memorably says, "It's only an elective"); in fact it's he, one short generation older, who berates her for being insufficiently feminist and gets in trouble for so doing. The twists are endless, and are both aggravated and manipulated by an apparently gleeful professor who has the two of them in his power. Or so it seems. The situation could never be resolved, but it could be further complicated, and I gather the author plans to extend it. In its present state it's tautly directed (by Michael Rubenfeld) and acted (by Jordan Pettle, Claire Jenkins and Richard Greenblatt). Chekhov said that if you bring a revolver onstage, you have sooner or later to use it. This production proves the same to be true of a box of Kleenex. It's quite a debut.

The File, by Greg Nelson (Factory Studio), is a timely piece about ethical principle and government surveillance and the proper or permissible limits of both. It holds as argument, but never transcends it. Two excellent actors (Michael Spencer-Davis and Sarah Dodd) play four characters, courtesy of instant flashback. They spell out the issues, whereas Essay lets us do our own spelling. Democrats Abroad (Passe Muraille Backspace) is a monologue by Chris Earle, a vision that I think and hope is exaggerated of a repressive U.S. flooding Canada with disillusioned soldiers and dissident celebrities ("every city got at least one Baldwin"). If the premise seems glib, Earle's writing can be amusing and heartening, and his performing is spot-on.

In Kathryn: Starring as Herself at Last (Factory), an octogenarian performer, Kathryn Albertson, proves that having appeared on Broadway and being a recovered alcoholic do not, in themselves, make you Elaine Stritch. I think she might be happier talking to us off-the-cuff than acting out a script that her life story fails to justify. Your Palace in the Sky (Palmerston Library) suffers from the delusion that some banal fictitious stories will take on significance if you paste them on to the 1985 Air-India crash. The result is inept and, considering the real suffering involved, insulting.

- Annie Get Your Gun runs through Sept. 3 at Massey Hall, 416- 872-4255. Corteo runs through Sept. 11 at Ontario Place, 1-800-450- 1480. SummerWorks closes tomorrow.

THE LARK

Festival Theatre, Stratford

- - -

The Stratford production of The Lark, Jean Anouilh's Joan of Arc play, is a fine one, with a consistent approach, rigorously maintained. It is more intense and less ebullient than most shows on the main Festival stage -- and its worth noting that the Stratford audience, belying the bad rap that it so often gets, was palpably hooked. So was I. But I doubt that either the style or the tone is right for this play.

The director, Michael Lindsay-Hogg, has updated the setting by 500 years, from the 1430s and the last stages of the Hundred Years War to the 1940s and the German occupation of France. Its true that Anouilh, writing the play soon after the Second World War, can hardly have helped drawing on the experience of occupation, collaboration and resistance for his dramatization of Joan, liberating her country from foreign invasion and getting burned alive for it. But that doesn't mean that he was assuming an exact correspondence between one well-defined historical period and another. Costume plays can be helpfully punched up by non-specific modern dress -- but here there are specifics, and they don't match. Charles the Dauphin, the snivelling symbol of French legitimacy, could hardly be less like Charles de Gaulle. Theres no modern European equivalent for the ecclesiastical court by which Joan was tried and condemned, and I doubt that Vichy collaborators, lay or clerical, would have been as scrupulous in their proceedings as Anouilhs priests appear to be. We also have to cope with an enemy commander whom both history and the play say is English -- the Earl of Warwick, in fact -- but whose bearing and insignia declare him every inch a Nazi.

The courtroom of Rouen, as directed by Lindsay-Hogg and designed by Eugene Lee, might be a Gestapo interrogation-centre. The lighting is cold and spare, and emotions are battened down. This hardly accords with Anouilh's playful, almost fairy-tale, view of history, in which Joan's career before her capture is brought to us through a series of flashbacks.

The play, done here in a Cold-War adaptation by Lillian Hellman that is a compact of Brodway efficiency and beleaguered Broadway liberalism, is an odd experience for audiences who grew up on Shaws Saint Joan. The two plays naturally cover the same historical ground and there are whole scenes in the French play that paraphrase, parody or parallel the English one. Then suddenly it strikes out on its own. Robert de Beaudricourt (Brian Tree), Joans first helper, is as puzzled and blustery as in Shaw, but he is given a butter- fingered sexual interest in the Maid that she, intriguingly, knows just how to parry; in Shaw, such thoughts would never have entered anyone's head. Anouilh's Dauphin starts out as an echo of Shaws, a grown-up child needing to be chivvied into manhood, then acquires an idenity of his own, less petulant, more selfish, more worldly. Steven Sutcliffe develops him brilliantly.

Anouilhs Warwick is a domesticated version of Shaw's ruthlessly polite politician, more genial and less cynical in his humour. That at least is what I get from the script, which I first encountered in a less businesslike translation by Christopher Fry. Graham Abbey's Warwick seems to me a virtuoso exercise in playing against the text; the character, who does indeed speak of the power of propaganda, becomes a club-footed Goebbels magnified to the scale of Richard III. Its a mordant, compelling piece of acting, consummately world- weary and therefore dangerous, but there isnt a laugh in it.

In this production the Inquisitor is a woman, a prospect that doesn't seem much likelier in the 20th century than in the 14th, but that does enable Martha Henry to draw all eyes while sitting motionless at the tip of the stage, dark-suited and completely silent, for the entire first act. Nobody can have expected this Spanish Inquisition, and when she does finally speak (she does the accent) her words burn. They do not, however, convince; their brand of misanthropy, much reiterated as the play proceeds, seems abstract, something made up out of the dramatist's own head.

The story of Joan of Arc, says the wise fool Dauphin in the plays last line, is a story that ends happily. At least thats what Anouilh wrote; Fry transferred the line to Cauchon, and Hellman cuts it entirely.

Anouilh, more sentimental, gives us one last flashback, to the Dauphin's coronation, supposedly Joan's finest hour, and leaves it at that. Its the kind of spectacle that would normally set the Stratford stage ablaze, but here its staged like a child's birthday party, as if downbeat were the point. This set the seal on my belief that the production was on the wrong track. But it's as fascinating as many right ones.

2005-08-20-follows-flowers-in-fool:
robertcushman@lycos.com; In repertory through Oct. 1 at the Harbourfront Theatre Centre, 416-973-4000.

The character of May in Sam Shepard's 1983 play, Fool for Love, is generally reckoned to be his first fully drawn female character. I'd go further than that. All the characters in this piece have more life in them than any in his previous works. It was the best play Shepard had written up to that time, and I have yet to see another of his to match it. Previously he had put down supposedly mythic American figures -- cowboys, gamblers, rock 'n' rollers -- and let them stew in their own jargon. The results were static, and very boring. In Fool for Love there is action and there are tightly coiled conflicts, and the language, because it carries that tension, sings.

Cowboys. For some reason, of which the likeliest is sheer coincidence, they are all over our stages, all of them figures who in some sense are working the rodeos, some in triumph, others in desperation. The leading man of Annie Get Your Gun peers amiably if nervously from beneath his ten-gallon hat and suggests that once upon a time you could, if you were the star of Buffalo Bill's Wild West Show, get a girl with a gun. The heroes of Bus Stop, at the Shaw Festival, and of Fool for Love, newly revived by Soulpepper, have a harder time of it, one that seems to get worse with the years. Bo, in Bus Stop, from the 1950s, has to be taught how to treat a lady, but at least his job still makes sense. He has a ranch and it pays. Eddie, in Fool for Love, is an anachronism and knows it. Like Bo, though in rather different circumstances, he feels himself predestined to a certain woman, and he has some kind of future to offer her. Bo's Cherie, being '50s Broadway, was just naturally bound to accept it. May, 1980s off-Broadway, may well feel the same, but her destiny remains open to question. As does Eddie's.

Really, he's in two kinds of myth. There's the obvious western one, and there's also one that seems to go back to the Greeks. Its nature is only revealed late in the play, and Fool for Love is not yet enough of a classic for a critic to feel happy about giving away the ending. Anyway, Eddie and May have a long-time on-and-off relationship that is clearly unbreakable and that both are trying to break, Eddie in the way he behaves, May in the way she reacts. Eddie has been away a long while and now he's come back to where he left her, which happens to be a motel room in the Mojave Desert. Steve Lucas's striking set reduces this to its bare essentials, which are very bare indeed. Ted Dykstra's exciting production has them bouncing literally and audibly off the walls. Every crash, every door slam reverberates, courtesy of John Gzowski's sound design, as if the characters were in an emotional squash court.

The game has a spectator. Quietly and rather contemptuously at the side of the stage sits an Old Man, who comes from a different dimension but is taken entirely for granted. He represents a heroic past that may not have existed but that still exhausts all Eddie's efforts to live up to it. He also knows crucial things, about both of them. Eddie and May, naturally, are jealous of one another. She suspects him of being with a presumably rich woman called the Countess, who has indeed followed him here, though the nearest she gets to putting in a personal appearance is when the headlights of her car are seen shining from outside, an effect that's both scary, especially for Eddie, and funny. May has a date with someone called Martin. He does appear, to Eddie's discomfiture; not that he proves to be any kind of threat -- he's endearingly mild-mannered, and Eddie gets rather protective toward him -- but the fact that he exists at all is an unwelcome surprise.

Stuart Hughes gives a delightful account of Eddie, who always seems to be entering with a new piece of professional gear, ostensibly for some practical purpose or just to keep in trim, but really to impress May and -- above all -- to reassure himself about his own identity. (At one point he sports two coils of rope and a revolver.) He has the physical image down perfectly, but Fate plays unkind tricks with it. Having ducked out of sight for fear of the Countess, he is forced to play a long sequence on the floor, propelling himself around with his hands in order to conduct a conversation.

Megan Follows's Meg has less room for physical manoeuvre but more for emotional, and she goes to superb extremes of rage and tenderness. She has a tougher mind than Eddie, though it does her little good. I remember seeing Follows giving a whole string of fine performances in the great early years of the Atlantic Theatre Festival, and it's a treat to see her picking up now where she left off then.

Shepard's character successes in this play aren't confined to the heroic, or even the mock-heroic. He shows that he can also create a playable stock figure in the shape of Martin, whom Kevin Bundy makes into a very appealing slice of milquetoast. It occurs to me that though the play's title most likely refers to May it could equally apply to any of the cast -- even to the Old Man, despite his claims to have got it all together in a past life. He is, though, the least successful part of the play, not because of his casual breaking of dramatic convention -- that in itself is a triumph -- but because the news he brings is less exciting, and far less amusing, than the things we see and hear unfolding in the present. Frank Moore, unrecognizable from his smooth roles in Urinetown and Olympia, commences this one with great grizzled authority but fails to vary it. The play itself is more successful when mining the recent past than when invoking the ancestral. In the end, its murkier revelations aren't necessary. May and Eddie stand plenty tall without them.

2005-08-23-when-stratford-does-marlowe-i:
robertcushman@lycos.com; In repertory until Sept. 24.

EDWARD II

Studio Theatre, Stratford

- - -

Christopher Marlowe's Edward II starts with an exultant soliloquy by Piers Gaveston, the new king's old favourite. "Old," that is, as in "well-established." This is unusual; generally, if there is any exulting to be done at the top of a Marlowe play, it will be done by the title character. Edward the Second, king of England, only appears on stage after Gaveston has graphically outlined the high times --make that gay times -- that they will be having, with a whole realm as their playground. Then Edward enters, bullied by his barons, who aren't having any of it.

That is the way the play goes. Edward is nearly always at the mercy either of his friends or of his enemies; he rarely gets a chance to act for himself, and when he does, the results are nearly always disastrous. It is, all the same, his play throughout; it begins with his accession and ends with his death, hideously murdered in the dungeons of Berkeley Castle.

In the new Stratford production -- the festival's first ever Marlowe and one of its shamefully few ventures into any of Shakespeare's contemporaries -- David Snelgrove plays Edward with a boyish doggedness that seems right at any given moment but doesn't vary much; it leaves unsounded the depths both of Edward's vulnerability and of his suffering, though it excels in showing off his vengeful streak. To be fair, Edward as written does not so much develop as endure. As often happens in Elizabethan plays, theatrical sleight-of-hand allows the years to slide into one another. One moment, Edward is the youthful king, the next he's the father of a 12-year old boy, and not too long after that he's "aged Edward," and it must be hard to know where to mark the transitions. Snelgrove's Edward looks and sounds no older at the end of the play than at the beginning, though he does look dirtier, as well he might given the appalling degradations of his imprisonment. His captors seem motivated partly by simple sadism, partly by the hope that he'll commit suicide and save them the bother of regicide. Here, they're out of luck; Edward hangs on, with a toughness that may, we are led to believe, be the last trapping of kingship. He harps pitiably on the contrast between his present state, but he displays no inner growth, which is why his role is less rewarding, both for actor and audiences, than the Shakespearean Richard II, which it so plainly influenced. Richard attains a sardonic awareness of his own responsibility and of the vulnerability of all mankind; Edward is left complaining that his only fault was to have loved too much -- which, in the world of this play, would certainly have marked him out for destruction.

Richard II is a play about a kingdom as well as a king. Edward II goes through the history-play motions -- the barons complain about the state of the realm and about the king's lamentable failure to make war on foreigners -- but you don't really feel that Marlowe was interested. He wrote plays about aspiring supermen, who may use their societies but aren't really involved with them. In Edward II, probably his last play, he focuses for once on powerlessness rather than power, but it's the same theme in reverse; we merely get to spend more time with those who suffer the pain than with those who inflict it.

The play is not quite as heartless as that makes it sound. When the barons, who don't mind Edward being homosexual but object to his lavishing high offices on a comparative commoner like Gaveston, ask the king, "Why should you love him whom the world hates so?" Edward replies, "Because he loves me more than all the world." It's a piercing moment, but it changes nobody's mind. Also, it probably isn't true; Gaveston has his own agenda, and we never know how much affection may be mixed in with his ambition. Jamie Robinson gives him an effectively insolent performance but without the weight either for his initial dreams of glory or for the sudden access of nobility that in an Elizabethan play invariably accompanies incipient execution. Edward's replacement favourites are nimbly done by Nicolas van Burek as Young Spencer and by Ron Kennell, who is absolutely right as the obsequious scholar Baldock (and extremely wrong as the Archbishop of Canterbury).

There are a few cliches in Richard Monette's production. The play's final scenes themselves can hardly help being harrowing, but the effect is lessened when Edward's jailers and murderers, who are supposed to be minor aristocrats on the make, are played with a coarseness that would seem excessive in an end-of-pier melodrama. It's their refinement that should really chill the blood. I also never want to see another slow-motion battle. Otherwise the play is given all the speed and clarity it needs, plus a brief orgy to show it's up to date. It's an emblematically-styled production in which you can tell that Gaveston is a spendthrift; he has an extra suit of clothes. Scott Wentworth as Young Mortimer goes from junior rebel to king in all but name, without changing out of his red tunic. He gives, as expected, a glittering demonstration of the ruthless ambition that marks him out as Marlowe's favourite; he falters only at his defiant end, which he shouts when he should be taking it coolly for granted. James Blendick and Walter Borden do some expert harrumphing as the king's rougher opponents. Michelle Giroux plays Edward's queen, whose masochistic devotion -- first to her husband, then to Mortimer -- she seems to find it hard to credit. This gifted actress' comic sense often seems to trip her up; there's a constant air of tongue-in-cheek about her. It does work here for the tremulous hypocrisy of her later scenes, wishing her husband dead "so it were not by our means."

Marlowe may not have been much interested in the sweep of politics, but he knew all about realpolitik. It's probably what killed him.

2005-08-26-defile-it-under-r-for-raunchy:
popcorn@nationalpost.com

Quentin Tarantino has said the sign of a good film is that it makes you want to go home, eat some pie and talk about it. With that in mind, our Popcorn Panel features film buffs feuding in this space each week.

THIS WEEK'S PANEL:

- Chris Knight, the Post's chief film critic

- Tara Ariano, the editor of the Web sites Fametracker.com and TelevisionWithoutPity.com

- Robert Cushman, the Post's theatre critic

THIS WEEK'S PIE: Cherry.

THIS WEEK'S SUBJECT: The 40 Year-Old Virgin

CHRIS Sitting atop the box office last weekend was the politically incorrect and oh-so-funny 40 Year-Old Virgin, which earned a respectable US$20-million and will surely almost double that this weekend as the love-in takes hold -- moviegoers and critics alike adore this film.

Down at No. 4 after six strong weeks, the politically incorrect and almost-as-funny Wedding Crashers, now having taken home (as Tara would say) 177.6 million tasty crab cakes.

These films are both R-rated and raunchy, and both star men- children (man-children? man-childs? whatever): Steve Carell as a hirsute but otherwise stunted-at-puberty type who collects comic books and action figures; Vince Vaughn and Owen Wilson as a pair of ladykillers who suddenly realize in the midst of their youthful shenanigans that "we're not that young."

So why the boffo box office? Are North Americans trying vicariously to recapture their own youth and (in Carell's case, anyway) innocence? Or could it be the simple fact that nothing else this summer has been so grownup and at the same time so damned funny?

TARA "Recapture," nothing -- the characters in both Crashers and Virgin are just about as mature as my friends and I are. (I can't recall how many times my sister and I have sat around playing videogames and trash-talking each other with such political incorrectness that if we spoke that way to strangers, we'd probably get arrested.)

How much Virgin and Crashers have in common beyond their ratings is debatable; however, there is something to be said for a comedy that goes all the way to the joke -- whether it involves a bad word or a boobie -- instead of pulling up short for the sake of the children. The scene in Virgin in which Paul Rudd commandeers a camcorder wouldn't have worked if the producers had been forbidden to show the Smart Tech TV screens broadcasting the image of his ass ... so thank God they weren't.

ROBERT Well, I haven't seen Wedding Crashers, but I'd guess that the success of The 40 Year Old Virgin is because it is funny. And charming. In a way it's trying to have it both ways. It's sex-farce mingled with romantic comedy, and it's the latter element that wins out. Catherine Keener is a wonderful sexy-sad older woman -- well, she may well not be older than Carell physically but she has to be emotionally -- so it's rather like seeing The Graduate with Anne Bancroft allowed to win out, which everybody always wanted anyway.

And it's well-constructed; the jokes build and pay off, right across the movie. I don't think it's all that wonderful, but I'm not sure it's better than the movies I avoid after seeing their trailers. A new Hollywood sex comedy for people who don't like new Hollywood sex comedies.

CHRIS I do like Hollywood sex-comedies, as long as they give me credit for intelligence. That seems to be where people are connecting with these films. And I don't even get all the jokes (are you really gay if you like Coldplay?), but I don't care -- I appreciate that the filmmakers trust me to figure out where to laugh rather than feed me lame cues like the word "man-whore." (Yeah, I'm talkin' to you, Bigalow.)

In fact, the films are weakest when they fall back on the tired tropes of the genre: Wedding Crashers' trash-talking grandma; 40 Year-Old's drunk date from hell. We've seen these characters in other movies, but there's a lot we haven't seen -- although we're sure to see some copycat comedies in a year or so. Sigh.

TARA Another reason that I think Virgin was maybe a tiny bit better than Crashers is that, its grabby premise aside, all of the events in it seemed like they could have actually happened. The reasons for Carell's Andy to have given up on women at some point in the past rang true. His co-workers' unidentifiable feeling that Andy was off somehow (virgin, serial killer -- what's the difference, really?) seemed believable. And the notion that someone as innocent as Andy could win over a woman as world-weary as Trish wasn't so outlandish when the film did such a great job showing his many layers of heartbreaking sweetness.

Maybe it's robbing the movie of its scandalous R-rated frisson to put it this way, but at the centre of all the raunch (which is always fun) was a very sweet, G-rated love story (which is hard to pull off without its seeming twee). Aw!

ROBERT I think it achieves that by glossing over the question of how Andy actually feels about his virginal status. The movie never makes up its mind whether he's happy with it or resents it. (His embarrassment at the poker game becomes embarrassing in itself, which is maybe a sign it's truthful.) And his buddies -- I suppose it's plausible that they'd be concerned to get him laid, but not that it would become an obsession, even if they are working out their own frustrations And you want to yell at them -- or I did -- when they actually try to stop him from getting together with the woman who's right for him, apparently just for the sake of prolonging the plot. I did think the mother-daughter shouting matches were very convincing; straight from the world of Judd Apatow's sadly bumped Freaks and Geeks -- which I think was a greater achievement than this picture.

NEXT WEEK'S PIE: Pumpkin.

NEXT WEEK'S SUBJECT: The Brothers Grimm

2005-08-27-fresh-prince-of-soulpepper-sc:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Hamlet is in repertory through Oct. 1 at the Premier Dance Theatre, 235 Queens Quay W., 416-973-4000. The Comedy of Errors runs through Sept. 3 at Heritage Park, Barrie, 1- 866-735-9243.

Albert Schultz is an outstandingly lucid Hamlet and an outstandingly likeable one. The two things go together. Schultz, it turns out, speaks Shakespearean verse with a clarity, discipline and colour that will stand comparison with any actor in Canada short of William Hutt. His soliloquies in particular are unclouded windows into a mind that will consider any question, see it from every angle, passionately pursue each argument and still end up dissatisfied.

To be or not to be -- a speech that comes, strictly speaking, out of no dramatic situation except the restlessness of Hamlets own thoughts -- leaves him bereft of any reason for not committing suicide but still with no intention of doing it; in fact, it's the prelude to some especially feverish activity. Or take the two matched speeches "O what a rogue and peasant slave am I" and How all occasions do inform against me, which sing the same tune in different keys. In both, Hamlet, with his revenge unachieved, adopts the comparative method of self-laceration, measuring his own inactivity first against the Player who's reduced himself to tears by reciting a tragic lament, and then against the Norwegian army marching to conquer a worthless patch of ground. Both actions are essentially ludicrous, and Hamlet knows it. But he ends both speeches by metaphorically slapping himself on the back and promising to emulate them; he will be a man of action, if it kills him. The irony is that the more measured of his two conclusions -- "my thoughts be bloody or be nothing worth" -- leads only to the deaths of Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, who arent worth it. He does kill Claudius, his real enemy, a whole act later, but thats a reflex decision when he finally finds himself hurled into the middle of the revenge tragedy that he has been circling around all evening.

The earlier, more melodramatic (and more celebrated) the play's the thing in which I'll catch the conscience of the king proves far more practical. He has laughed at himself for in effect playing the Player with his cry of "O vengeance," but in fact his command performance goes on as planned, Claudius unmasks himself on schedule and Hamlet feels at liberty to kill him. He then, of course, stabs the wrong man. Hamlet the play is like a giant staircase, rearing up in the darkness and with some vital rungs missing. The gaps make it only more satisfying. Its as illogical as life, and the character with the best mind in the whole of drama is at the heart of it, trying to make sense.

Schultzs Hamlet is a sensitive guy emotionally as well as intellectually. He is unusually well-disposed toward most of the people he meets, with the obvious exception of Claudius, and also of Polonius, whom he treats with a contempt untempered even by the grudging affection for the old man that most Hamlets manage to squeeze in somewhere between the lines. Welcoming the Players, he is courtesy itself, and when he rouses himself from his initial misery to greet Horatio (Oliver Dennis, anxiously supportive), his whole spirit seems to light up. This is one of many occasions on which the actor seizes the plainest implications of the text and makes them a dramatic fact. Both the gentleness and the bashful histrionics were features of Paul Gross's Stratford Hamlet -- for the same director, Joseph Ziegler -- but they make more organic sense this time around.

The reverse of his benevolence is a bitter disillusion when it's abused. Longing to believe the best of Ophelia, he turns on her, with brutal venom, when he suspects her of betraying him. When after her death he proclaims his love for her, you dont actually believe him, but you believe that he would like to believe himself. The chief outward forms of his "antic disposition" are a white flapping shirt and bare flapping feet that, given the actors broad face and frame, make him look endearingly untidy. Real madness occasionally threatens but never materializes, which is a reasonable choice. What Schultz doesn't crack is Hamlet's vein of mordant hysteria, the dark defence reaction after hes seen the Ghost or scared the king or killed Polonius. He is fine in the healing stoicism of the last scenes and in the fun of the duel before it turns mortal. This is a Hamlet with an open face and an open mind, open to everything. The strain kills him. He dies, you might say, of young age.

There is an extracurricular pleasure just in seeing Schultz on the stage again, for the first time since Uncle Vanya three years ago, and watching him, Soulpeppers artistic director, interacting with a stageful of company regulars. No one would accuse Soulpepper of failing to promote themselves, but the one achievement they have neglected to publicize is the one that has probably won them the greatest following: their creation of a flexible recognizable ensemble. It's much in evidence here. William Webster is a dazzling Polonius, flashing up wit from every line while combining the crafty politician with the self-satisfied buffoon. His family, in this production, convinces as a group. Patricia Fagan's Ophelia may be her best performance yet, not so much for the taunting sexuality of her madness (its very good but Ive rarely seen a mad Ophelia who wasn't) but in the far harder scenes of sanity where she presents a sheltered girl crucified by her own obedience. She listens lovingly to her brother Laertes (Seann Gallagher, technically ungainly but essentially accurate) but is terrified of her father, especially when he's being solicitous.

Oliver Becker, much improved from last year, is a shabby Claudius. This makes sense. The king envies his nephews popularity (which here is unusually plausible) and is no glamorous villain. He has committed one murder and would prefer to leave it at that; he would rather like to play the good uncle and would very much like to repent, though neither proves possible. So he reverts, with cold efficiency, to crime, at which he remains very good. His dependence on his wife remains, and is partly reciprocated. Nancy Palks Gertrude is a small but affecting study in hopelessly divided loyalties.

The director himself plays a good Ghost and a better Gravedigger, though Claudius's recoil from the latter as if he had seen the former is best described as a nice try; the production is too full of doubling for this example of it to have registered as anything special. Denmark's a prison but in Peter Hartwells economical set it seems to be made of Norwegian wood. Each scene is encircled by the actors who arent in it; this encourages concentration, theirs and ours, though the idea overreaches itself when characters already dead get up and start haunting the final massacre. If this is intended to suggest encroaching doom, it's too late; it hasn't been that kind of production. Zieglers great merits are the quality of his storytelling, the depth and texture of the relationships and the fact that the actors always know what theyre talking about -- even in the opening battlements scene, which is about the people in it and not, as often, about getting the show started. Later on, R and G (Sanjay Talwar and Derek Boyes) arrive with a full subtext, as if somebody had written a whole play about them and they had read it. Schultz's Hamlet may be the observed of all observers, but he is also the observer of everyone else. He has left his mark on the character; the character, I suspect, will have done the same to him.

A lighter Shakespeare: I hated the first scenes of Theatre by the Bay's Comedy of Errors, but by the show's end I admired it very much. I shall return to it next Saturday, but as that is its last day, I advise you to see it now.

2005-09-03-the-comedy-of-errors-at-theat:
In Richard Rose's production of The Comedy of Errors, the Shakespeare play with a double dose of twins, Ephesus is a town composed of transparent cages. In the first scene, the refugee merchant Aegeon is confined in one of them while he tells his long tale of woe. It seems more monotonously woeful here than is strictly necessary, while the Duke who judges him is a cardboard tyrant. The cages are rearranged to form adjacent chambers, from one of which the jealous wife, Adriana, harangues her patient sister, Luciana, who is doing aerobics in the other. For street scenes, the frames that define the cages are realigned into an urban maze through which the Ephesian natives obliviously rush, each one minding his own business at a furious rate.

It all seems very inhuman, as much in itself as in the society it depicts, and not much fun at all. But as the show progresses it develops personality, humour and even warmth. The frames are manipulated with an agility and inventiveness that matches the constant reshaping of the furnishings in Rose's production at Stratford of The Brothers Karamazov.

The identical Antipholus brothers -- one a resident, one a tourist -- suffer identical identity crises and carry identical briefcases, which they use as offensive weapons. Master-servant relationships are defined here by the varying ways in which beatings are given and received. The serving Dromios (Kyle Horton and, with a slight edge, Michael Rubenfeld) take their punishment with grimaces and jokes, each in an individual rhythm. The Antipholi (Brandon McGibbon and, with a definite edge, Brendan Murray) are respectively piqued and outraged. The highest-definition performance is Philippa Domville's pregnant Adriana, whom the pressures of farce bring ever closer to premature delivery; she gives a new meaning to the term "hysterical pregnancy."

The last scene is a joy, Victor Ertmannis's condemned Aegeon entering into the spirit of things by laying his own head upon the executioner's block, then wondering why nobody notices. There's a lovely surprise ending that, even with only one performance to go, I shouldn't give away. Let me just say that it's the perfect way to end a play about twins.
2005-09-03-a-matter-of-pride-writer-iden:
robertcushman@lycos.com

Eleanor of Aquitaine, wife of Henry II of England and mother of Richard the Lion-Heart and that unhappiest of royal villains, King John, had a busy life. She has also had, posthumously, a busy stage career. She has played juicy supporting roles in scripts by William Shakespeare, Jean Anouilh, Christopher Fry and even Alfred, Lord Tennyson. In the 1960s she attained to Broadway and subsequently Hollywood stardom, opposite her husband, in The Lion in Winter. (Henry, of course, was the lion.) She has now received the ultimate accolade: her own one-woman show.

Eleanor of Aquitaine: Mother of the Pride, written by Catherine Muschamp, gives us the lady on what we assume is her deathbed having what we assume is her last dream. She imagines herself defending her life and works before a tribunal composed of her deceased opponents, of whom there were many, Eleanor being a combative personality who lived into her 80s, by 12th-century standards an astonishingly ripe age. The charge on which she is arraigned is one of heresy. As far as I know, no ecclesiastical court of Eleanor's own time ever accused her of such a thing, but in this play the word has a meaning that's vaguer in one sense and more specific in another. Eleanor is on trial for being ahead of her time, for being a Strong Woman.

So she was, but she wasn't unique in that, even in her own time. Her mother-in-law, Matilda (familiar to readers of 1066 and All That as Matilda-or-Maud), was a great rattler of kingdoms. Eleanor, though, had a bigger kingdom to rattle than most. She was in fact married twice. Her first husband was Louis VII of France. They divorced after failing to produce an heir, something that was generally taken to be Louis's fault. (I have brushed up on the period in Simon Schama's marvellously racy History of Britain.) She then married Henry, an alliance that gave them dominion over much of France and most of Britain. Of the children she bore him, eight survived at least some way into adulthood, a phenomenal figure for the time. Eleanor was also responsible for introducing the French cult of courtly love into England, a bit like Jackie Kennedy bringing culture to Camelot. Henry and Eleanor were a great power couple, but they grew apart, politically and sexually, Eleanor spending many of the later years of Henry's reign locked up in a castle.

Here she gets to state her case, with no one to answer her. This is a miserable way of doing business dramatically, and it short- changes history as well. As often happens in this kind of piece, we feel not that a conflict of people and issues is being explored but that a writer is championing a character through a feeling that she - - it usually seems to be a she -- has been neglected by everyone else. Frankly, I don't believe that Eleanor was prophetically championing the cause of women; I think she was championing the cause of Eleanor. Good for her, and maybe good theatre, too, but not when her principal antagonist is presented only as a buffoon who used to be good in bed but has aged into a tyrant who takes mistresses, one of whom Eleanor arranged to have killed. (The Middle Ages may well have thought of this as murder. They wouldn't have called it heresy.)

Many of Eleanor's previous theatrical appearances have been on the fringes of plays about Henry II and Thomas Becket, and we get to hear something about their quarrels here, probably because they're too famous to leave out. We learn little of what part Eleanor may have played in them, and nothing about their importance to the separation of church and state. Nor would you guess that Henry virtually founded English common law, which has influenced the world. Harping on their domestic troubles, Eleanor comes off as a whiner.

She also seems to be a liar. She accuses Henry of murdering two of their sons, whom she had encouraged to rebel against him. (These were not nice people, despite the efforts of The Lion in Winter to pass them off as endearing squabblers in a medieval sitcom.) She says that one of them, Geoffrey, was killed by the forcible insertion of a poker "in his orifice."

This is the identical nasty end that awaited a later king, Edward II; for graphic details, see the current production of Marlowe's play at Stratford. But the historical Geoffrey died, without foul play, in a tournament. Why has Muschamp borrowed somebody else's horror show? Is she setting Eleanor up as an Unreliable Narrator? That would be a useless exercise, since the play gives us nothing against which to measure her. Or has the author decided that that is just the kind of thing Henry would have done, and consequently that he must have done it? Muschamp, a feisty octogenarian in her own right (raised in Canada, incidentally, though now living in France), seems to have identified with her heroine altogether too closely.

Eleanor has a heart, not to mention a poetic streak. She says that when a boy was flayed in her presence, her tears fell "like mineral water poised on stalactite." Here, as at many points in the show, I wondered whether the play was written in blank verse or whether, like much half-baked historical drama, it just fell into the rhythms. Visual interest in Jean LeClerc's production is confined to the red heraldic cloak from which Eleanor unwraps herself at the very beginning of the evening and in which she re- swathes herself at the end. The actress, Chapelle Jaffe, seems confident enough but delivers most of the text on one note, a peremptory staccato bark.

- - -

2005-09-10-recalling-redgrave-s-class-ac:
robertcushman@lycos.com

The greatest performance I have ever seen was given by Michael Redgrave in the title role of Chekhov's Uncle Vanya. I find it hard to put a date to it since I saw it, and the equally great production, directed by Laurence Olivier, of which it was a part, three times over a period of three years. In 1962, Vanya was one of the three plays in the opening season of the Chichester Festival Theatre in the south of England. It was revived there the following year, and was then taken to London as part of the inaugural season of the National Theatre, of which company, as of Chichester, Olivier was the first artistic director. I hitchhiked from London to see the two Chichester versions and then, having started university, hitchhiked to London for the National Theatre one.

So my memory of Redgrave's Vanya is a composite. I think the performance grew over time but obviously it was my first exposure to it that had the greatest impact. I discovered in later years that I hadn't been alone; that many people who had seen it at much the same impressionable age as me thought it not only a great performance (people of all ages were agreed on that) but a transforming experience. One contemporary whose choice of career it influenced was Alan Strachan, a British director and writer who was to work with Redgrave in his last years, and whose excellent biography of him, Secret Dreams, has just come out in paperback (Orion, $19.95).

The core of the character and of the play -- the greatest moment, I think, in all modern drama -- comes when Vanya, the frustrated and exploited estate manager, tries to shoot the Professor who has proposed selling the family home from under him, and misses. "It was heartbreakingly moving," Strachan writes, "but also side- splittingly funny." That's absolutely accurate, though I think I'd reverse the order; one laughed first, especially at Vanya's anguished cry of "missed again," and then registered the abyss of tragedy beneath the farce. But in fact the two reactions came so close together as to be virtually simultaneous. We talk fairly glibly of being made to laugh and cry at the same time, but this may be the only occasion on which I have known it to happen.

What we saw was a man wasted; even sadder and funnier than that, a man self-wasted. Redgrave, a tall and handsome man with a superb voice, heroic in other roles and potentially glamorous even in this one, laid the groundwork early. When he first comes on, Vanya describes the Professor as a buffoon who has spent his life regurgitating ideas about "realism" and "naturalism" -- "things that intelligent people have known all along and the stupid ones don't care about anyway." It's a great line, one of my all-time favourites, but it tumbled out of Redgrave's mouth just a little too fast, unstable, as if he were compensating for something. Vanya is in love with the Professor's beautiful young wife, Ilyena, curses himself for not telling her when there was time, fantasizes about what their life might have been like and then curses himself again for having such ridiculous thoughts. Redgrave's Vanya was continually catching himself out in his own folly. He brings Ilyena flowers, and finds her kissing his contemporary, the local doctor -- a prelude to the greater humiliation of the failed murder attempt. The last act finds him hugging his own failure, refusing to hand over the drugs with which the doctor, Astrov, fears he may kill himself.

The rest of the cast was all-round fantastic: Rosemary Harris, Joan Plowright and the legendary Sybil Thorndike were all in it, and all at their best. Harris and Plowright, playing a brief scene of happiness, cruelly dashed, seemed to be living rather than acting. You'll understand that when, a few seasons ago, I described Soulpepper's Uncle Vanya as the second-best I had seen, I was giving very high praise. I had always assumed that it was the product of a group of star actors who had arrived at ensemble by mutual consent; Strachan's book persuades me that I had greatly underrated the force of Olivier's direction, and he reminds me how superb was his staging of the shooting scene, all over the open stage.

Olivier himself played Astrov, and though he was seldom my favourite actor I vividly remember the weariness ("I shall have to perform your autopsy -- do you think I shall find that interesting?") with which he signalled that the two men were brothers under the skin, both worn out before their time. And overlaying that, of course, was the mutual respect of two great actors. Twenty-five years earlier, Redgrave had played Laertes to Olivier's Hamlet; Redgrave's eldest daughter, Vanessa, was born during the run, and Olivier famously announced the event at the curtain call with the words "A great actress has been born" -- speaking, Strachan notes, "with what then must have seemed emotional hyperbole but which now seems extraordinary prescience."

Olivier wasn't always that generous, and Redgrave's first and only season at the National was unhappy. His memory began to fail him, a painful circumstance that it took years to diagnose as the onset of Parkinson's disease, a condition that slowly but inexorably removed him from the stage and even from the screen. His Vanya turned out to be not only the summit of his career but its climax, and it's possible to see its overflowing nervous energy as both a herald of his illness and an index to his psychological condition. Strachan, whose book is exemplary in its linking of its subject's personal and professional life, identifies Redgrave's twin demons as drink and guilt over his bisexuality -- not the condition itself but the pain it must have caused his wife, the fine actress Rachel Kempson. They stayed married, though, and devotedly -- her late career blossomed as his faded -- and they did, after all, found an acting dynasty. It may, unfairly, be what Michael Redgrave is now best known for. When we think of "the Redgraves," we think of Michael's son, Corin, and his daughters Lynn and Vanessa and their offspring, though in fact both of Michael's parents were actors, and the family tradition stretches back even further.

Vanya, a frightening portrait of a failure, might be called the great anti-heroic role. But Redgrave also played all the heroic ones; and though I never saw his Lear, Hamlet or Antony, I think I may well have concurred with those who thought them the best of our time. He also, of course, had a major film career that stretched from The Lady Vanishes to The Go-Between by way of The Stars Look Down, Dead of Night and The Dam Busters. Strachan reminds me that in the '50s it was customary to speak of Redgrave, along with Olivier and John Gielgud, as one of Britain's three greatest actors. By the time of his death he had been supplanted in that pantheon by Ralph Richardson, though, actually, all four belonged there. Redgrave also seems to have suffered from being dubbed "an intellectual actor"; if that means "emotionally cold," then he wasn't -- he was the most moving of them all, far more so than Olivier. He was certainly an intellectual man: university-educated, a former schoolteacher, a great reader and a fine writer. He wrote probably the two best English books on the craft of acting (The Actor's Ways and Means and Mask or Face), a nightmarish novella on the same theme (The Mountebank's Tale), a couple of unmade screenplays, including an Antony and Cleopatra that sounds as though it would have been wonderful and a first-rate dramatization of Henry James's The Aspern Papers -- natural-born Shaw Festival material if ever I saw it. He must indeed be the best documented of all modern actors, both by himself and others. British critic Richard Findlater wrote an excellent study of him (Michael Redgrave, Actor) in the '50s. Redgrave himself, with Corin's assistance, wrote a rather disappointing autobiography (In My Mind's Eye), and now Strachan has both completed the story and enormously filled it out. The result is the best biography of an actor since Simon Callow's of the similarly conflicted Charles Laughton. And though Strachan is a less graceful writer than Callow -- or than Redgrave -- his intelligence, his sympathy and his wide-ranging sense of theatrical history could hardly be bettered.

He is the subject of a biography that has just been released in paperback.; Black & White Photo: (Book cover of Secret Dreams.)

MEASURE FOR MEASURE

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

- - -

This year's Stratford Festival is ending in an orgy of orgies. A brief gay group scene has been added to Marlowe's Edward II; it couldn't be called irrelevant but it does risk obscuring one of the play's main merits, which is that it takes homosexuality for granted, something that wasn't to happen again in English drama for close on 400 years. Meanwhile, a new production of Measure for Measure begins in a strip club, one that's obviously doubling as a brothel, all tastes obliged. The merrymaking here comes to an abrupt halt when the joint is raided, by troops under the command of Angelo, deputy to the Duke of Vienna.

This is strange, because it's only in the subsequent scene -- or, as Shakespeare would have it, the first one -- that Angelo is given the authority that would allow him to conduct such an operation. It's handed to him by the Duke, who announces that he's leaving town, trusting that the notoriously ascetic deputy will clean the place up in his absence. Even in pure showbiz terms, it might have been more effective to start with this sober exchange and then to bring on the debauchery -- which is what Shakespeare's text, in a slightly more restrained manner, actually does.

Once out of the gate, however, Leon Rubin's production, set by John Pennoyer in various shades of contemporary Gothic, offers an engrossing account of a perenially fascinating, if perenially frustrating, play. Measure, unlike Edward II, actually is a play about sex. Angelo's crack-down on vice involves the resurrection of a disused law forbidding non-marital sex, and the consequent condemnation to death of Claudio, who has got his fiancee pregnant. Isabella, Claudio's convent-bound sister, goes to plead for his life; and Angelo, as aroused by purity as only another puritan can be, offers a deal: Claudio's life in return for Isabella's virginity. She refuses, appalled. This being a comedy, there's a way out, but it requires a lot of manipulation.

Most of the intriguing is in the hands of the Duke, who has stayed around, disguised as a friar, ostensibly to see whether Angelo can live up to his own pretensions. In fact, hardly anybody in this play can. Angelo's fall is obvious. Isabella seems to care far more for chastity than charity; when the terrified Claudio suggests that she might take Angelo up on his offer, she verbally flays him alive. The Duke makes three. He, too, starts out denying the claims of the flesh; the end of the play finds him proposing to Isabella.

All three roles are strongly played at Stratford. Jonathan Goad's Angelo starts out a sincere, if bloodless, young idealist; he then falls almost visibly apart in his two long interviews with Isabella, which he rightly identifies as scenes of mutual temptation. He also, hardest thing of all, keeps us with him through the play's last judgment, by which time he is a tortured shell, riven with self- disgust, who welcomes his own unmasking.

There is less of a straight line through Dana Green's Isabella, but there is a succession of exciting moments. She is as much the legalist as Angelo himself, and you can feel her locking minds with him even as she shrinks from locking bodies. Thom Marriott's Duke is well-intentioned but congenitally manipulative; like his fellow principals he learns painful things about himself -- a process implicit in the play and that Marriott takes further than any actor I've seen, though not, to my taste, far enough.

Jeffrey Wetsch is a touching if sometimes incoherent Claudio, and Paul Hopkins makes, in both senses of the adjective, a sympathetic Provost. The low-lifers admirably capture the play's shifting view of vice, as a trade to be condemned, condoned and, finally, tolerated -- much where we are today. Andrew Massingham's Pompey is an inventive and ingratiating music-hall pimp, who gets fine comic support from Shane Carty, Brendan Averett and Stephen Gartner. Mistress Overdone is played with majestic lewdness by Diane D'Aquila, this season's Mistress Underused; she doubles as a very aged nun, and bends double to do it. It's made clear throughout that the religious life is terrible for the posture; the disguised Duke, who looks more padre than friar, has a permanent stoop, as of one bending over forwards to gain people's confidence.

The Duke's return is most cleverly staged. This final scene has to seem like a big public event; this small-cast production brings it off by involving the audience; the scripted spectators, waving flags or petitions, are placed among us; Don Carrier's Lucio, clown prince of the underworld and a whimsical blend of satirist and sycophant, is delightedly and delightfully in his element. The revelations and reversals are excitingly done, and Marriott's Duke dispenses justice and mercy with humour as well as humanity -- which is what the text suggests and most productions studiously ignore. Then comes the unscripted kicker. Isabella, given no lines, greets the Duke's closing proposal with silent dismay; another man is hitting on her. This isn't a new interpretation; in fact it's standard modern. But the production hasn't prepared the ground. This Isabella's spiritual vocation has never seemed more than an exaggerated passing phase; and there has been definite chemistry, and not of the father-daughter variety, between herself and the Duke. For once in a staging of this play, a happy ending looks justified, and denying it seems a gratuitous slap in the face. So I doubt this production's end as I doubted its beginning; I was also disturbed in the middle by frequent re-writes, not all of them of passages that are impenetrably archaic. This is becoming a most irreligious habit, and it can't be good for the souls of actors or audiences. Other than that, everything's very fine.

2005-09-17-when-in-rome-do-as-the-briton:
robertcushman@lycos.com

They still talk the same way in Capitol City, a.k.a. Forum Town, only more so. If the HBO series Rome is to be believed, every soldier and civilian in the time of Julius Caesar spoke with a British accent. The place used to be a bit more multicultural than that; indeed, in the 1950s, a peak period for movies set in the ancient world, Britons were rather a depressed species.

Jimmy Porter had something to say about that. He, you may remember, was the hero of John Osbornes Look Back in Anger, the breakthrough play for the new wave of English drama in 1956. Jimmy, like his author, won an undeserved reputation as a spokesman of political protest. In fact, his discontents were rather vague, and very self-centred, and it's a safe bet that he -- again like his author -- would have turned very reactionary in succeeding decades. Jimmy could, however, be an entertaining cultural critic, and the play's success was largely due to the appreciative laughter he drew from a like-minded audience who werent used to hearing their own feelings about, for instance, the stodginess of the posh Sunday papers given voice on the stage.

He struck a similar nerve when he turned his attention to the Hollywood epics whose lascivious ladies were invariably attended by husbands so weak and meek "theyd probably give some poor English actor the part. They were bound, Jimmy correctly theorized, to be cuckolded by the handsome gladiators, all of whom were American and most of whom were Victor Mature.

It was all a matter of class, in several senses of the word. Even in a progressive picture such as Stanley Kubrick's Spartacus, Kirk Douglas and Tony Curtis may have been the heroes but they were still slaves. For patrician villainy, Kubrick cast Laurence Olivier, for beauty Jean Simmons, and for weight, both physical and intellectual - - weight allied to wit -- Charles Laughton and Peter Ustinov. Ustinov actually played a slave dealer, probably not a profession for a gentleman but still many steps up the ladder from the slaves themselves.

Besides, he was a comic character, and in North America British actors have traditionally been reckoned good casting for clowns as well as kings. They are supposed to be good with words, funny words as well as noble ones. Indeed, in Canada the comic tradition, or its derivatives, may well have lasted longer. As far as I can determine, when Tyrone Guthrie started the Stratford Festival he insisted on his Canadian actors using their own accents, but there may have been some slippage over the years; at least, I suppose that the constant complaints about Stratford actors doing imitation English must have some basis in something. I can't say Ive ever heard it myself, or at least not until the current production of Edward II. In this the royals and barons are all impeccably, and very effectively, Canadian, but the jailers and murderers sound as if theyve come from the slums of London, and I don't mean London, Ontario. As it happens I think that making them lower class at all is a misreading of the text, but leaving that aside: What are 20th-century Cockney accents (they aren't 21st) doing in a play written 400 years ago and set 200 years before that?

In a show like Rome, of course, the problem shouldnt arise; the characters would have been speaking in Latin anyway, so any variety of English speech is an artifice, an American accent every bit as good as a British one. But this opinion does not seem to have been shared by the moguls in the United States, who used to star a Yank or two for box office and fill up with Brits for tone. The pattern persists, though nowadays your Gwyneth Paltrows and Matt Damons try their best to fit in vocally, and do so far more persuasively than Marlon Brando, say, peacocking his way through Mutiny on the Bounty.

When in Rome you do as the Britons do; and, just to be on the safe side, you had better be British. Perhaps this has to do with its being television; the mostly American directors have done time on Deadwood, The Sopranos, Six Feet Under and Sex and the City, and the general ambience seems like a stew of all of them, but the casting is strictly Masterpiece Theatre. Well, a bit of Shakespearean training never did any harm, especially when its allied to a talent for cheeky comedy, and most of the actors in the series are thoroughly qualified in both.

It's a shame that the writing doesn't give them more of a chance to show it. The scripts are trying desperately to be high-flown political drama and low-down steamy soap opera at the same time. The Romans, we are implicitly assured, may have had funny names and worn funny clothes (the assembled Senate looks, as ever, like the steering committee of a Turkish bath), but really they were just like us. We are briskly told that a wounded soldier is under the medics," but the medics themselves, mindful that this was all happening a long time ago, use words like "mayhap. Theres nothing wrong, of course, with mixing periods and styles; as with any other kind of writing, anachronism depends on having an ear. My memory tells me that I, Claudius, the progenitor of all these series, had it; I recall John Hurts Caligula bringing his horse into the Senate and murmuring his life has expanded so much since I made him a Consul." That's characterization, exposition and a good joke, all in one; that's wit.

Rome offers us only an invitation to "more lunch -- dormouse, perhaps? I suppose thats informative, but it does seem dragged in. Its not as if American TV writers can't be witty, even elegant, when dealing with their own time and place. Compare the unfailing mixture of brutality and formality in The Sopranos, or the new and highly promising Prison Break, in which one convict (the terrifying Peter Stormare) says to another, You're a mercurial man" -- now theres a good Latinate adjective -- and then, as if justifiably pleased with himself, repeats it.

The actors in Rome may have been cast for style, but they cant supply what's lacking in the script. Each is thrown back on what he or she knows best. The guys in the fictitious human-interest roles do all right, but really, who needs them? There are two stand-outs, however: Kenneth Cranham's Pompey, with a face as gnarled as a road map and a mind to match, is at the centre of the shows political scenes, which are its best. And the superb Lindsay Duncan, as an especially resilient matron, has just the mixture of fire and ice that the series seems to be aiming for, but has so far been given little opportunity to display it. She plays Attia, mother of the future Emperor Augustus and an all-round decadent; she has a high old time whipping slaves, bedding most available males and bullying her sullenly defiant daughter. She has to work terribly hard at it, as the population acknowledges; outside her villa, someone has scrawled "Attia fellat omnes. Its strange that the graffiti artists should be writing Latin while everyone else is talking in English, but maybe the producers felt they couldn't risk a translation. Mostly they reckon, correctly, that there's a special appeal to sex and violence when they come with cultural trappings. And I have heard stranger dialogue. I still treasure the memory of Robert Taylor in Quo Vadis who, while Nero fiddled and Rome burned, reassured a small boy, Don't worry, son, we'll get you out of this."

Rick Miller's Bigger Than Jesus is a seriously comic investigation of Christianity. Parts of it are brilliant and others silly, but though the latter predominate, it's the former you'll remember. Miller's self-effacing vocal manner co-exists with absolute physical and technical command. The best sections include a slick, fast, witty lecture on the Gospels as history and a sequence when Miller turns into a cross between Jesus and a baffled comedian facing a tough house. Through Oct. 15.
