Robert Cushman is the National Post's theatre critic.

THE PEOPLE'S ACT OF LOVE

By James Meek

Harper Collins

391 pp., $34.95

- - -

Most English readers confronted by Russian novels have a love- hate relationship with the characters' names, so evocative and so confusing. Them and their patronymics. James Meek's The People's Act of Love is an English novelist's brilliant reduction and provocative updating of the world of the Russian classics, and it begins with an implied joke on the subject. At the age of 12, Kyrill Ivanovich Samarin, a natural rebel, asks if he can take his uncle's name rather than his father's and become Kyrill Pavlovich instead. He's told this isn't allowed. So he asks to be called just Samarin, and so he is, right through the book.

The same first sentence, packed but not forced, also mentions dynamite. Flash forward nine years and the Russian Revolution has begun. We meet Samarin again, a fugitive in Siberia, claiming to have escaped from the White Garden, a Tsarist prison camp in the Arctic, along with a fearsome criminal known as the Mohican, who chose Samarin as a companion so that, when their food ran out, he would have someone to eat.

The publisher's blurb speaks of "a story of communism and cannibalism," and while the novel may not exactly equate the two, it does present them both as, shall we say, extreme tendencies. Not that they are the only ones on view. At the time of the action, the Red victory is assured but not yet secured. The Whites are still fighting and the town of Yazyk, where most of the story happens, is controlled, along with the neighbouring railroad, by a brigade of Czechs who came to fight alongside the Russians in the First World War and now cannot wait to get back to their own country, which has only just come into existence.

All that keeps them in Yazyk is their commander, Captain Matula, who is both crazy and malevolent, and who cannot bear to give up his dominion over men, territory and -- his special passion -- horses. "It's pleasant to be king of Siberia, sir," says his second-in- command, Lieutenant Mutz, "no-one's surprised you don't want to go back to being a sales representative for a light-bulb manufacturer in southern Bohemia." Some English reviewers have compared Matula to Kurtz in Heart of Darkness, but Matula is actually the more convincing creation. In his case we know what "the horror" is.

Yazyk is principally inhabited by a cult whose members have castrated themselves (or, in the case of the women, hacked off their breasts) to be closer to God, and who refer to themselves as "angels." They, like the Czech Legion, actually existed, and Meek brings them superbly to life in all their pettiness and all their fervour.

The saner people in town include the majority of the Czechs themselves, and Anna Petrovna, generally known as "the widow," a self-trained photographer with a son who has moved here for personal reasons and is, or has been, an object of desire for at least three of the surrounding men. "Anna Petrovna," muses Samarin on first hearing of her from the chief of the castrati, "that's the kind of name that allows you to imagine any kind of woman." In fact she's every Russian heroine, a warm-blooded Tolstoyan woman who has strayed into a nightmare Dostoevskian landscape. Humanly fallible, humanly angry, she is one of the book's two identifiable points of reference.

The other is Mutz, a dogged and conscientious secular Jew whose ambitions are to win Anna, to get rid of Matula and to lead his men safely home. He can't win 'em all, but he does a very respectable job against crazy odds. Not all this novel's antecedents are European: It has a definite whiff of Catch-22, and not just in the military scenes.

The cast is completed by the approaching Reds, already split between decency and the rulebook, and a shaman from the forest who dies of drink, maliciously supplied by someone unknown. The book is in part a murder mystery, and one whose neatness takes a second reading to appreciate fully; it's also full of surprises that actually surprise.

Meek, as well as being a novelist, is a prize-winning foreign correspondent for The Guardian, and he plays the reporter-as- historian with glittering precision. One section is a roll call of the Czechs who have gone missing, and it's done with gaunt unsparing wit. His prose reflects the harsh, dazzling white light of the tundra-and-taiga setting.

If much of the action is horrific, the tone is humane. "The people's act of love" is Samarin's phrase for revolution; the castrates of Yazyk might describe their own self-mutilation in the same terms. In the end, Samarin comes to them, begging them to take the knife to him, to destroy the human impulse that, twice in his life, betrays him. We judge these people by their failure to live up to their own terrifying ideals; even Matula has a grotesque moment of generosity.

For Samarin, who preaches what would later be called "perpetual revolution," the Reds are only temporary allies on the road to a gulag of which the Tsarist White Garden is a mere prophecy. And in fact his dream is shared by the last local remnant of the White regime: "It doesn't matter who rules, whether it's a prince of the blood or a Marxist, as long as they're Russian, and as long as the peasants fear them ... fear should shine on them like light."

The book is a grim study of fanaticism and an act of faith in its limits. It is also funny; the author's command of irony is pitch- perfect, but he can also be more tenderly amusing; the Czech legionaires, beneficiaries of both styles, are a gallery of deft sketches, and the last pages make you feel glad for the survivors among them, the humane pragmatists. A book whose author likes to play with names closes with the feeling that the Meek might inherit the Earth after all.

2005-09-24-soulpepper-s-cryptic-triptych:
robertcushman@lycos.com; The Long Valley is in repertoire at Harbourfront Theatre Centre until Sept. 29. 416-973-4000. The Affairs of Anatol runs at the Artword Theatre until Oct. 9. totix.ca

E.Y. Harburg, the lyricist of the Depression anthem Brother Can You Spare a Dime, used to say that until he wrote that song there was no Depression. John Steinbeck might have made the same claim for such emblematic novels as The Grapes of Wrath and Of Mice and Men, and also, it seems, for the short stories with which he began his career in the early 1930s.

I say "it seems, since I have never read them. However, I have now seen a dramatization of three of them, titled The Long Valley, presented by Soulpepper as the last production in its seven-year tenancy at Harbourfront, and the characters in all three seem very depressed, though not necessarily depressing.

They aren't on the poverty line; few of them are even near it. But the cold winds of a devastated society are blowing around them and have worked their way inside. These people have gone beyond loneliness and into isolation, a self-willed solitude rendered more intense by the fact that most of them have legal partners. The Long Valley, a locale as much psychological as geographical, takes us back to a time in which folks had, as the saying goes, to make their own entertainment, and the ways in which the women in particular choose to amuse themselves can be disconcerting.

In the first tale, a farmer's wife devotes herself to growing chrysanthemums and makes a present of some, in a nice pot, to a passing tinker; hes strangely reminiscent of the peddler from Oklahoma! (the musical, not the state) though the lady is no wanton Ado Annie. But this fleeting contact is enough to arouse a new feeling in her that her husband, driving her to an unaccustomed night on the town, can register but not explain.

The second shows us a woman getting her kicks by buying a snake from a biologist and watching it eat a rat.

The last concerns a well-to-do married lady who has turned her garden into a bird-sanctuary; her most loved pet is a white quail, and she orders her husband to kill a cat whom she thinks is threatening it.

This cryptic triptych is played by, respectively, Liisa Repo- Martell, Ann-Marie Kerr and Colombe Demers, who also make up a group calling itself This Is a Bird. Under this umbrella they have adapted and, it seems, staged the stories. (No director is listed, though Chris Abraham is named as dramaturg.) This collective credit has led to allegations that the show doesnt really count as a Soulpepper show; in other words, that This Is a Bird is a cuckoo in the nest. I can't see why, though I will admit that the play seems a strange choice as an end-of-chapter production, since it bears little resemblance to any previous Soulpepper production except The Mill on the Floss, which it's much better than.

Its a frail, uneven but haunting piece that faces two old- established problems at once: the challenge of literary adaptation and the curse of the multiple bill. The acting is naturalistic, at least at speech-level, but there is also much mime; the work bears some resemblance to that of Theatre Smith-Gilmour (with whom several of the cast have done time) and though it doesnt have that company's shaping visual imagination, or its editorial skill, it does have a more affecting emotional core. It has been well designed by Julie Fox, who places sheets of what look like corrugated iron at the back of the stage, and lays another on the floor to simulate -- very convincingly -- a creaky old jalopy on a bumpy rural road. It's also been well lit and even better sounded, if thats the word, by Jan Komarek.

The leading ladies vary. Kerrs orgasmic snake-fancier is acting by numbers. Demers has a commanding swagger as a Lady Macbeth of the aviary (playing opposite an actor, David Jansen, who was in fact her Scottish thane a few seasons ago) but this episode too remains book- bound, a possible black comedy in a state of suspended animation. It's the first one, the least obviously eventful, that works best.

Steinbeck's dialogue in Of Mice and Men always struck me as the most urgently speakable I had read in a novel, and the language here has something of the same charge. Youre nice," says Jordan Pettles farmer, trying to locate the change that has come over his wife, then "You're strong"; and the change in adjective is very revealing.

Repo-Martell is a quietly quirky actress, and Pettle a casually downbeat actor, so they don't exactly set off fireworks, but they do create a landscape, their own personal dustbowl. The men also fit into a pattern, one of destruction born of frustration: The tinker smashes the pot, the scientist throttles the snake, the husband shoots the quail. In the last story, two of the women act as ghostly doubles for the third, and the three wind up in an aggrieved enigmatic group. This works, perhaps better than it has a right to; what might have been an evening of fragments falls into a whole.

- - -

One of Soulpeppers more underrated productions was of Arthur Schnitzlers La Ronde, that celebrated daisy-chain from old Vienna. The same author also wrote Anatol, another sequence of heterosexual encounters but cut to a different pattern, depicting just one man and his apparently inexhaustible succession of women. It's less often done, at least in its original form, though in the early 1960s it inspired at least two musicals.

One, a Broadway confection with a gorgeous score and an unworkable book, was titled, with unfortunate lack of foresight, The Gay Life. The other, which I actually saw, was a very arch entertainment called Parasol, which should tell you something, done on British television but starring -- I'll give you 100 guesses -- Canadas own William Hutt.

Both those adaptations of course were more about setting than substance, more sachertorte than Sacher-Masoch. Schnitzlers play, though very witty, is as sobering as most studies of the Don Juan myth; eternal cynic or, as here, eternal romantic, Lothario leads a lonely life. This may or may not be true to life, but it's certainly very consoling.

It's a tribute to Schnitzler (and to his translator, the all- around theatrical genius Harley Granville Barker) that in its new production by a company called Glastonbury West, who have re-named it The Affairs of Anatol, the play still seems good. The odds against it are heavy. There are a few interesting things in Sue Miners production; the stage-floor (designer, Jackie Chau) looks as if Gustav Klimt had got constructively down on his hands and knees, and Anatols ladies are allowed to watch one another's scenes, as a mocking or pitying chorus; they, like their sisters in The Long Valley, end up in a mutually protective group, probably with more reason.

Individually, though, they range from the ineffectual to the actively embarrassing, with the notable exception of Kathryn Winslow, who is both subtle and supple as a respectable old flame wondering what life might be like on the other side of the tracks.

As Anatol himself, John O'Callaghan, gives a performance of simpering inadequacy; the guy may be a loser but he isnt supposed to be a stooge. It may partly be the contrast but as his pal Max -- who has a thinner address-book but probably a more fulfilling life - - James S. Murray seems to get more engaging by the moment. A young actor named Daniel Abrahamson makes his professional debut as a waiter and a valet; whether this is the start of a great career I couldnt say, but he is very good at looking professionally pained.

2005-10-03-billy-crystal-tightens-up-his:
Runs until October 9. (416)-872-1212; robertcushman@lycos.com

700 SUNDAYS

Canon Theatre

- - -

Billy Crystal's father died when Billy himself was 15; 700 Sundays is Crystal's calculation of the number of precious days father and son were able to spend together in and around the family house in Long Beach, N.Y. Crystal Senior loved his family and they loved him back, but he had to stint on quality time since he worked two jobs. One was as manager of the legendary Commodore Record Store in Manhattan, a pioneer in the marketing and even the production of jazz. The other, stemming from the first and a source of great pride and delight for his son, was as an emcee at a jazz club. What with one thing and the other, a lot of great musicians passed through the Crystal home. Crystal has a story about his grandmother solicitously asking Louis Armstrong -- at a Jewish Seder, no less -- why he didn't just cough it up. I hope it's true.

Embroidered or not, the mixture of jazz and Judaism obviously made for a rich childhood, and they make for a fine, fun show. An autobiographical monologue that's a cross between a play and an especially elaborate stand-up comedy act, 700 Sundays is performed with a winning mixture of shrewdness, charm and bounce. There's a set representing the outside of the house; Crystal strolls on, in front of it, and starts talking about his family, as it was in -- mainly -- the 1950s. He begins with the family car, accidentally totalled on its first day by the local Mafia boss, whose extravagant offers of reparation Mr. and Mrs. Crystal proudly refused. Then it's on to the grandparents, a ripe collection, at least as depicted here, who spoke Yiddish ("a mixture of German and phlegm").

We get to see these people in projected photos, with which Crystal rightly calculates we will identify. ("We all have the same five relatives; they just jump from album to album.") Some he acts out, in a series of percussive vocal cameos. At one point, he combines the two modes by impersonating a home movie of an aggressive uncle who fancied himself king of the barbecue; read his lips, if you dare. His most sustained impersonation is of his Aunt Sheila, "who always told the truth," and whom we see -- in a Great Chronological Leap Forward -- on the phone in Florida, ceaselessly mobile despite having a titanium hip, telling a friend about her daughter's lesbian wedding, while occasionally deigning to throw a remark at her husband ("Leonard, get the car!"). This sequence is the funniest thing I have seen on a stage in ages, and a bit touching as well.

In parallel with this, we have the black musicians, who called young Crystal "Face" and seem to have adopted him as a kind of mascot. His mother's brother, the founder of the Commodore firm, was Milt Gabler, who among other things wrote lyrics for Duke Ellington tunes and produced some of Billie Holiday's most notable records -- including Strange Fruit, on which her regular label wouldn't take a chance. Billie, we learn, took Billy to his first movie. Worlds combine when the family take their first and only holiday together, in the Catskills, and Billy falls in love with the borscht-belt comics. His future is decided -- by him anyway -- and he starts to amass a repertoire. Act One ends with him doing a terrific mime to Spike Jones' You Always Hurt the One You Love - a commentary on a parody.

Act Two goes more for the heartstrings than the funny-bone. Billy's father, already reduced by the demise of the store, dies of a heart attack: ironically, on the day on which his son, moping over a lost girlfriend, had shouted at him for the first and only time. (I trust that this also is true. It's not the kind of thing anybody should make up, and Crystal seems trustworthy). Billy's mother promises him that, broke though they are, he will go to college, like his two brothers before him, and she works heroically to make it happen. It's none of my business, I suppose, but I wondered why his Uncle Miltie, by now a big wheel in the music business, couldn't have helped out.

The story sags a bit as Billy stumbles into puberty, with his genitals developing not only a mind but, in his telling, a voice of their own. It's one joke, prolonged. There is also more than seems necessary about his career on the school basketball team. He speaks touchingly, but at too much length, about the void -- in his heart, in his mother's heart, in the house -- left by their bereavement. This can't be argued with, and of course we identify. But there remains a problem about getting up in front of an audience and telling them, without the mediation of a playwright or of other actors, about your own feelings, especially if the feelings are a credit to you. Elaine Stritch at Liberty, the other major Broadway confessional of recent years, got around this by concentrating on adulthood and dwelling on the dark side, while also throwing in more actual performance than Crystal does -- which, considering that we go to see these people because they're performers, was a good thing. Neil Simon, in Brighton Beach Memoirs, trod much the same social and psychological territory as Crystal. He made a full-scale play of it, which I think is more satisfying, if only because it puts paid to worries about the boundaries between fact and fiction.

Crystal also deals with his mother's (much later) death, which left him, as he says, "an orphan at 53." He is quick to acknowledge that this, or something like it, happens to everybody; but, charming though that is, it doesn't quite dispose of the matter. He is, after all, getting paid and applauded for telling us how much he loves his parents; and of course he wouldn't get to do that if he weren't already a star. Whether that disqualifies him from being a worthy audience surrogate, I'm honestly not sure. But he's appealing, and immensely talented, and projects decency without priggishness, which is an accomplishment. Des McAnuff's production, apart from the trifling matter of being 30 minutes too long -- Crystal does three hours, all on his own --puts him in a perfect light.

2005-10-04-french-revolution-for-dummies:
robertcushman@lycos.com

With the customary acknowledgements to Letterman: The Top Ten Reasons why Les Miserables is the worst musical ever written. Well, all right: the musical with the least forgivable ratio of commercial success to artistic bankruptcy.

1. I DREAMED A DREAM The name of the show's most prominent song is itself a case study in redundancy. What else would you do with a dream? Note that this show, which started life as a French song- cycle drawn from the Victor Hugo novel, was hammered on to the stage by the Royal Shakespeare Company, whom you would expect to have some sensitivity to the English language. They approved that lyric, the rest of which is as vapid and generalised as its title. They also approved the accompanying melody, which is reprised, with minute variations, whenever something emotional seems called for, and which must constitute about 50% of the score. Claude-Michel Schonberg, the composer, is no marvel of melodic fecundity.

2. MUSIC The tunes he does write are grindingly repetitive in themselves. They come in two flavours, moaning (the ballads) and bullying (the choruses). Neither is equipped to explore the characters or to forward the story; each song endlessly repeats things that we already know. This score, copyright 1985, sets musical dramaturgy back 40 years. This being a through-sung musical (meaning there's no release), the plot, of which there is much, has to be carried by those even whinier mini-melodies that think they're recitative. Any lyricist setting them is bound to end up writing doggerel.

3. LYRICS Not that that obstacle should let these writers off the hook. The English lyrics are by Herbert Kretzmer, a decent craftsman (as is just observable in Master of the House, the evening's one gesture towards wit), but one who seems to have no horizon beyond show business. A story that needs to be freshly imagined is told through stale images ("no song unsung/no wine untasted") that derive from memories of other shows. ("Additional material" is credited to James Fenton, a respected poet who was fired as original lyricist; apparently some of his work remains, but Fenton slumming is indistinguishable from Kretzmer soaring.)

4. CHARACTERS There aren't any. There's Jean Valjean, the stolidly saintly reformed convict who, in the immortal words of Forbidden Broadway, "significantly changes France by being an all- around nice guy." There's Javert, the policeman who hounds him through the decades (and eventually the drains) and whose implacability is matched only by his incompetence; the arm of coincidence being longer than that of the law, he keeps running into Valjean but never manages to nab him. Both men are monochrome. Youth is represented by an extraordinarily lifeless love-triangle.

5. ONE DAY MORE At the end of a very long first act, and in blatant imitation of the Tonight ensemble in West Side Story, all the cast sing about how they have things to do tomorrow. Don't we all?

6. REVOLUTION Much of Act Two is devoted to Parisians mounting the barricades; actually just one barricade, which seems unrealistic of them. This (Forbidden Broadway again) is "not the big, famous French Revolution but a little later, one you didn't think you knew anything about." Not, I suspect, that most of the audience does know, even when it's over. We are never told what the issues are; the only Establishment figure on view is Javert, so the people seem to be revolting against one malevolent cop. They might as well be the Parisian rabble of The Vagabond King, about to break into a rousing chorus of "to hell with Burgundy," except that this bunch wouldn't know any tunes that good. This is a show for people who like to drool over revolutions, especially doomed ones, without being bothered by anything as sordid as politics.

7. KIDS, ESPECIALLY THE ONE WHO'S THE LOGO That would be Cosette, the waif with the sunken eyes, who, as an orphan, sings a song that makes Oliver! seem like searing social realism. But then so does the whole show. Even more shamelessly, there is Gavroche, chirpy child who sings about little people and who waves a little banner while his elders wave a big one. Ain't that cute? His principal function is to wring our hearts by being slaughtered on the barricade. This isn't as stomach-turning as the use, in the same authors' Miss Saigon, of real footage of real orphans, but it's on the way.

8. STAGING This hurts. The show was directed -- 20 years ago but it's still their production -- by John Caird and Trevor Nunn, who were previously responsible for the RSC's Nicholas Nickleby, the peerless model of how to stage a novel while making a glowingly humane theatrical statement. Nunn, who has proved himself a great director a dozen times over, here gives us stereotyped groupings, a revolve that spins as if someone had lost control of the controls and no human content. The story is clearly told, but that's all.

9. Stars Somebody, for some reason, sings a song of that name, and the sky starts twinkling. This happens twice.

10. STUPIDITY See 1 to 9 above.

Notwithstanding clause: The touring version that's arrived in Toronto is in pretty good nick. Randal Keith is a ringing Valjean (his song Bring Him Home is, let's be fair, a cut above everything else in the score, both melodically and dramatically) and Norman Large is amusing as Thenardier the scoundrelly innkeeper, more Dickens than Hugo but that's a blessing. Most of the singing is excellent, though the composer's addiction to long, high endings does nasty things to the vowels. The sound-design (by Andrew Bruce) has always been first-class; you can hear every word, whether or not you want to.

2005-10-07-proof-s-critics-are-divided:
Quentin Tarantino has said the sign of a good film is that it makes you want to go home, eat some pie and talk about it. With that in mind, our Popcorn Panel features film buffs feuding in this space each week.

- - -

This week's panel:

- J. Kelly Nestruck, Arts & Life reporter

- Robert Cushman, the National Post's theatre critic

- Tara Ariano, the editor of the Web sites Fametracker.com and TelevisionWithoutPity.com

This week's pi: 3.1415 ...

This week's subject: Proof

- - -

Kelly: Proof, adapted from David Auburn's Pulitzer Prize-winning play of the same name, features Anthony Hopkins as a once-great mathematician gone mad and Gwyneth Paltrow as his daughter, who worries she may have inherited his neurological tendencies along with his numerical talent. Though well within the parameters of the crazy-genius genre, Proof moves to the head of that class for depicting mental illness as the enemy of creative thinking rather than its quirky ally.

And yet, while the film avoids some (psycho)tropes, other cliches -- like the yuppie sister with jojoba for brains -- abound. Is all that talk about imaginary numbers and Sophie Germain just a disguise for an inert drama about a quarter-life crisis? Does Proof follow old formulae or is it a unique prime of a film?

Robert: Well, the play's original author is on record as saying the play could just as well be about any kind of genius, so I guess the math is merely top-dressing. I wasn't crazy about the play -- it seemed the kind of safe, semi-serious thing that gets Pulitzers and these days represents Broadway's nearest concession to original drama. For a while, I thought I'd like the film more as a glossy TV movie-of-the-week, and with about as much visual oomph. But that wore off and irritation set in.

The thing is: The actress I saw play the lead in Toronto was believable, because she was young and unpolished. I thought Paltrow was very good, but she was wrong. She's a star, undisguisably; her face and her spirit catch the light. They can make her up and dress her down as much as they like -- she still looks more beautiful than her supposedly elegant sister, who wasn't just a nag but a frump. And of course they pared away what edges the play had. I came to the end thinking: What was that?

Tara: I think I must be getting old (or am past my quarter-life crisis, at least), because I rebelled against the film's manipulations and stood firm in my annoyance with Paltrow's Catherine, identifying instead with Hope Davis's level-headed Claire. I get that we're supposed to feel so sympathetic toward Catherine, the delicate genius-cum-self-sacrificing saint, but the truth is that it's extremely tiring to deal with a depressed person who won't or can't help herself. Reviews I've read have made Claire out to be this bourgeois nightmare, oppressing Catherine with her inadequate care and stupid suggestions, but to me she seemed, if insensitive, at least well-meaning.

Having experienced her father's spiral into mental illness (that drove away or killed the wife and mother no one mentions even once - - what did happen to her?), it's natural for Claire to try to "square away" Catherine however she can, and with the limited resources at her disposal. To say that depressed people are self- involved due to their illness gives us a reason for Catherine's resistance to her sister's ministrations, but it's a shoddy excuse for her acting like a sullen teenager. Since the movie starts a week after the death of Catherine's beloved father, that might be unfair - - but it's no less fair than the movie's treatment of its one functional, employed non-genius. I've got your back, Claire! And I also appreciate a nice conditioner!

Kelly: Well, Catherine was just treating others the way her parents taught her. And by parents, I mean screenwriters Auburn and Rebecca Miller (daughter of playwright Arthur, by the by). They treat Claire with disdain because she's not like them and pretend as though the mother never existed because she's inconvenient to the plot. They make math geek Jake Gyllenhaal run after -- and briefly overtake! -- a car so that they can pretend Proof is worthy of being filmed. And they make Catherine even more intransigent than she is in the play so that they can include a scene of her dashing through an airport.

While I don't think I can prove that Proof was a bad movie, I do think it is possible to show conclusively that it was not a very good one. QED, yo.

Robert: Well, they also threw in a party scene and a hitting-the- sack scene, both of which are only narrated in the play. But I can't say I felt a wiser person for having seen them, or for having met a peculiarly stiff representative of the math faculty. It's a desperate play-into-movie technique. Meanwhile, Claire's character and back story are pared down quite ruthlessly. I didn't share Tara's sympathy for her -- there just wasn't enough to her to arouse any feelings -- but maybe I should have because the cards are so stacked against her. I mean, how dare she be nasty to Paltrow?

Meanwhile, Gwyneth and her boyfriend get the few mildly funny lines, which will always predispose me in someone's favour. The flashbacks drove me wild --just as I'm getting vaguely interested in the story, I'm whisked back to Anthony Hopkins being Celtic and mystic (with a line written in, I noticed, to explain his origins). I can't see what was added to his first appearance by his second, third, fourth or whichever.

Tara: Yeah, the father character just goes back to my main point, which is how dicey a proposition it is to build a production of any kind around a character who's mentally ill: He couldn't add much to the proceedings because of all his crazy. Add him to Catherine and you end up with a film half-anchored by characters who've lost their moorings (I'll forgive your math puns if you'll forgive my boating metaphors), which, naturally doesn't work.

I never saw the play, so I can't compare it, but the film felt plenty stagey on its own -- the settings were claustrophobic, the dialogue was stilted and the staging was generally just static. The running and the party and the sex didn't make it feel any more as though we were in a three-dimensional universe. And the point of the enterprise was to remind us that it's important to believe the people you love, even if they don't shower regularly or probably know how to balance a chequebook? Talk about a story problem with extraneous information.

2005-10-08-staring-down-melodrama-three-:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Enoch Arden closes tomorrow at the Theatre Centre, 416-538-0988. The Monster Trilogy closes tomorrow at Buddies in Bad Times, 416-975-8555. Banana Boys runs through Oct. 16 at the Factory Studio, 416-504-9971.

Alfred, Lord Tennyson wrote a narrative poem titled Enoch Arden, about three inhabitants of an English seaside town. Enoch himself was a mariner, eventually a shipwrecked one; Philip was his friend since childhood and a miller; and Annie, loved by both of them, married Enoch but then, despairing of his long absence, gave herself to Philip. Needless to say, Enoch returned and underwent what I can best describe as a crisis of renunciation. The story shows all three of them behaving with exemplary nobility.

Richard Strauss set this poem to music, a combination of disciplines that is technically known as "melodrama." Now comes Judith Thompson, who has utilized the work of both men to create a two-character piece set in the present day and titled Enoch Arden by Alfred Lord Jabba and his Catatonic Songstress. Jabba is a mentally disturbed man, possibly schizophrenic, who lives (this is Judith Thompson, after all) in a halfway house in Parkdale. His catatonic songstress, and fellow-inmate, is named Ciel. Jabba undertakes to perform the poem, partly, we suspect, in order to show off, but also, by his own account, to jerk his companion out of her stupor and into the redeployment of her talents as a singer and pianist. These turn out to be considerable; the two moments in the play at which Kristin Mueller's Ciel bursts into song are electrifying.

The original narrative obviously runs the risk of seeming melodramatic in the more familiar, non-musical sense. Enoch could fairly indulge in enough self-pity to float a musical by Andrew Lloyd Webber or Claude-Michel Schonberg. But Tennyson kept such indulgence at bay, Strauss disdained it and Thompson looks it in the eye and stares it down. There's no denying that Jabba jabbers. He claims that the poem is really his story, and says that he once held an audience spellbound with a complete recitation of it. (He confesses that many left at the end of the first hour, but the survivors liked it.) He identifies, we note, with Enoch or Philip, depending on who is the loser at any given moment, and he takes off on virulent rants at the winner. We can place him; and, having done so, we can sympathize without having to swallow everything he says. His motives seem confused, not least to himself, but at least the friendship he proclaims is real.

The piece has its flaws. You'd have to be Jabba, or maybe Thompson, to believe that the past and present characters display an inevitable affinity, and anyway we don't have time to take the poem on board before grappling with how it's being used. (Read it first; it's shorter than Jabba would have you think.) Maria Lamont's direction could hardly be more sensitive, technically or textually; the show's atmosphere grabs you from the start. It takes time, though, to appreciate the accumulating skill and speed with which Thompson alternates levels and styles. The same versatility and virtuosity characterize John Fitzgerald Jay's Jabba, as assured in measured Victorian verse as he is in frantic hyperactive contemporary prose (in his mouth they sound equally natural, which in fact they are) and able to switch instantly from one to the other without dropping a stitch. This is an amazing performance; where has this actor been all our lives? The show closes tomorrow; I imagine it will reappear somewhere but it's worth catching now at the Theatre Centre, the ideal space in terms of its location (way out west on Queen) and, despite recent face-lifting, its general air of unsettlement.

- - -

Also worth hurrying for (to Buddies in Bad Times), and also concerned with weird, is The Monster Trilogy by RM Vaughan. This started life, per the title, as three separate monologues, but in the current production (by Moynan King) they have been intercut. The governing one is for, and about, Susan Smith, the spurned South Carolina woman who murdered her two children by strapping them into her car and driving into a river, and is here seen in prison at work on a series of videos that she intends to send to Oprah, Springer and Barbara Walters, so that they and the world will understand. She is juxtaposed with two fictitious (as far as I know) "monsters," also female. One, who talks to us direct, is a burly cop who expresses racist sentiments, has probably warped the life of her son and is not getting much satisfaction from either her job or her husband. The other is a minister, who seems to derive a suspicious amount of pleasure from officiating at the funerals of teenagers, and who does her justifying to an unseen Monsignor. (Wouldn't that make her Catholic? Did the Church start ordaining women when I wasn't looking?)

The writing is notable for its wit: not just in the sense of being funny (though it is, very, especially when the policewoman is talking) but in how it probes into peoples' minds through the texture of their speech. Vaughan presents a frighteningly persuasive picture of Smith, who goes, before our very ears, from speaking in terms of what she has done to what has been done to her. She claims to have killed her children to spare them the pain of living without her, and then of course outlived them, to embark -- on this showing - - on a career as a successfully self-justifying victim. Kirsten Johnson, whose video image appropriately takes up more space than she herself does, inhabits her completely.

But is the author presenting a moral equivalence between this woman and the other two, or is it just that the show's publicity suggests that he has? All three characters may be guilty of sins against the young, but to equate verbal racism or even perverse parenting with actual child murder seems to me political correctness gone mad. I think I'd feel that way even if Ann Holloway's cop, miles the best performance I have seen her give, were less endearingly uproarious than she is.

On the third part of the puzzle I have to suspend judgment, since Caroline Gillis's Reverend is so monotonously artificial that I lost the ability to follow what she was saying. But I couldn't detect any implication that she had personally disposed of the young people she was burying, so her sins, too, seem of a lesser order: thought crime, perhaps. If the point is "you think these people are monsters -- think again," well, two of them aren't, not by comparison with the one occupying the cell downstage left -- whom Vaughan does make us understand but not, I think, forgive. I don't understand, either, why St. Teresa of Avila descends at the end; nor would I have known it was her if the program hadn't told me. Still, this is the best new writing I have seen at Buddies since I started doing this job.

- - -

Banana Boys, by Leon Aureus from a novel by Terry Woo, is about five young Chinese men growing up in Canada: second-generation immigrants caricatured, so the title reminds us, as "yellow outside, white within." The scenes presenting them as a group are rambunctiously enjoyable, even when the mood is desperate; it's notable that when kidding around they show themselves as adept as any whites at imitating blacks. The rub is that the two who are meant to interest us the most -- one who burns out on dope and a fast-track business career, one who's pressured into becoming a doctor though he wants to be a writer -- are the closest to stereotype, not ethnic but dramatic. The bonds binding them to their friends are frayed, to be loosened or tightened as suits the script, so the action winds ineluctably down. Nina Lee Aquino directs a strong, flashy production, with a high-energy acting quintet: Richard Lee, Derek Kwan, In-Surp Choi, Dale Yim and David Yee, who is the most incisive, as the youth most alert to, and angry about, racial slurs. He's also the one who looks the least Asian, and I wondered -- this seems to be my week for racial insensitivity -- whether this should be put down to Occident or design.

Colour Photo: R. Kelly Clipperton / John Fitzgerald Jay inhabits the role of Jabba, while Kristin Mueller has stunning moments in the Theatre Centre's production of Enoch Arden.; Colour Photo: David Hawe / Ann Holloway does an uproarious turn as Constable Margaret Chance in The Monster Trilogy.
2005-10-15-tales-from-the-hood-powerful-:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Born Ready and Pusha Man are in repertory at Theatre Passe Muraille through Oct, 19; Better Parts is at Passe Muraille Backspace through Oct. 29, and Fish Eyes is on through Nov. 5. 416-504-7529.

Theatre Passe Muraille, in a vigorous protest against the Toronto stages customary fixed-run routine, is devoting its fall season to nine new plays, performed in repertory. The program is called Stage 3, on account of its triple-barrelled marketing slogan word.sound.power." You have to love those dots.

First off are two double bills, one on each of the theatres stages. Passe Muraille's co-producer is the Obsidian Theatre Company, the city's leading black group, but the overall program might be called ecumenically ethnic. The opening main-stage show, though, is very black; two plays by a new writer, Joseph Jomo Pierre, that sound to my sheltered ears like authentic ghetto- blasters. (Pardon my archaic expression.) That goes especially for the first one, Born Ready, in which a young man known as B-Side announces, "Im from the hood, and adds, You know what a hood is? A hood is something that you pull over your head to conceal yourself." If you want word power, there it is: language that travels, sardonic and anxious and menacing and defeated all at once.

Born Ready (whose original title was Born Ready To Die) is an extended flashback; it starts with a shooting, and then has killer, victim and witness telling us how they got there. The killing has less impact than the talking. The one woman of the three announces herself right off as "the official ride-or-die Bitch, the iconic Peggy Sue, subservient to the fullest. This may be meant to be ironic -- Cara Rickettss smouldering performance points it that way -- but dramatically she gets the subsidiary role, one that embraces some stark memories of childhood in an orphanage, but also contains the cloudiest lines in a script that's best when it's most specific.

B-Side (whose every line, as spoken by Mike G-yohannes, rings like a challenge) talks about the pecking order of poverty, and of how he rose right up it when he got himself a gun. And of how, as a gang leader, he felt both elated and uneasy. (You doing dirt with your fam.... You sipping that ghetto-fabulous juice. To 200 or so people you are actually the shit.... But that all changes.... And a nigga got to live up to the hype." I quote directly.) Blackman, a little shyer (at least thats how his author plays him), grew up even more deprived ("my aunt raised me ... if moms had hard times, my aunt had it worst), with a nervous, fascinated awareness of women. B-Side seems, by contrast, to have marched right into his sexuality, along with everything else.

There is a limit to how much you can do in a play with monologues, even when theyre as strong as these. Eventually Pierre brings his characters together, but he still has them talking past one another; the knot doesn't tie, and in that regard Philip Akin's production doesnt help any. Atmospherically, though, its fine, played on flights of fire-escape steps backed by Passe Muraille's resident catwalk. The inner city has seldom come this powerfully to a Toronto stage.

The companion piece, Pusha Man, is more of an ensemble number, though it, too, gives the impression that it would be happier as a set of solos. Ricketts and G-yohannes reappear, this time as a young couple -- well, two young people who've had sex -- named Sarah and Benjamin. It starts with Sarah all but giving birth in an alley and Benjamin nervously promising that help is on the way. It turns out that he doesnt mean the doctor. He means the local dope dealer, Pusha Man himself, a.k.a. Absolute. David Collins is monstrously cool in this role; he makes a singing entrance and seems like an updating of Porgy and Besss diabolic Sportin' Life. He turns out, though, to have less of the Devil about him than of God, and a disgruntled God at that. (Your poor asses dropping your last five dollars into a plate that I ain't never going to see, that aint funny. Goddammit, buy some food!") He does make Sarah feel better, though the womans role in this play surprisingly in the circumstances, is even more passive than in the other. Absolute's main concern is to make Benjamin, who wants to run away from fatherhood and just about everything else, face up to life. The script I read was short and rather snappy, especially in the Pusha Man's exasperation with his own lingo. ("No mellow, no yellow, no fellow, I dont even wanna hear nothing that sounds like it.) But it seems to have got elongated in rehearsal, with passages both mystical and mystifying; I can just about understand why Benjamin, in worm-turning mode, puts on Absolutes trousers, but it beats me why Absolute has Benjamin suck his breasts. I would guess that Pierre, having given us the facts in the first play, is aiming for myth in this one, though he's more poetic when he's being real. But man, he can write.

- - -

Both these plays, Born Ready especially, are aiming, as far as I can tell, for theatrical rap. Metaphorically, that is; the words arent in rhyme or even in verse, and any music is strictly incidental. But the worlds the same, as are the attitudes, though they're critiqued. Better Parts, first on at the Backspace, is theatrical rap; Nicole Stamp -- author, performer and director -- tells her own story, in couplets, to musical backing, though both her rhythms and those of her accompanist (Paul Clifford on bass) have a variety and sophistication way beyond hip hop.

This show is, in fact, a total joy. It's Stamps story of her walk home from a temping job, fantasizing about a life of comparatively rich and famous, being taken home to meet the families of exotic men from villages Ill never see/called Clinton, Ontario, or Sault Ste. Marie." Finally, in one of the few successful examples of meta-theatre I have ever encountered, she envisions herself performing this very show on perhaps this very stage, watched by "actors and actors' families/as Toronto audiences always seem to be, the acting contingent observing well, she's funny but she isnt any better than me." (Between Stamp and Pierre, I havent had so much fun quoting in weeks.) She is funny, enchantingly light and sure of touch. And, considering she's doing triple duty, remarkably the opposite of self-indulgent. Her show lasts less than half an hour.

It's also, of course, a hard act to follow: and Fish Eyes -- written and performed, but not directed, by Anita Majumdar -- is much, much, much too long. Not specifically autobiographical (or so Id guess), it tells of Meena, a Canadian teenager who is being groomed for a dancing contest in her familys native India, and would much rather not go. Meanwhile she's hopelessly infatuated with the most popular boy in school, who is, of course, thoroughly taken up with the most popular girl.

This is pretty tired territory, and the ethnic component doesn't make it any fresher. It might work better if it zipped along, but Majumdar and her director, Gregory Prest, insist on lingering over every step of the story. Counterpointed with our heroine is her fanatical dance instructor, known as Aunty, who is still locked in mental struggle with the British Raj, one member of which once broke her heart in what she insists are parallel circumstances. The tone is mostly humorous without actually being funny, though there is the occasional sharp joke, as when Meenas white-bread ideal is overheard referring to his equally pale girlfriend as "my bitch," thereby casting an interestingly envious light on the plays next door. Majumdars acting dexterity, as she slips in one role and out the other, can't be faulted; neither can her skill in the dance, which she manages to satirize and celebrate at the same time.

2005-10-22-nostalgic-farce-a-long-way-fr:
robertcushman@lycos.com

Harold Pinter's Nobel Prize for literature is only the third time in the past 40 years that the award has gone to a playwright. The Italian Dario Fo won in 1997, and then you have to go back to 1969, when the recipient was Pinters own hero, Samuel Beckett, who in any case is nearly as important for his novels. Its cheering, just as a matter of genre chauvinism, that drama has been invited back to the grown-ups' table. And it's justified because Pinter, like Beckett, occupies a theatrical space that is wholly his own. If ever the phrase "legend in his own lifetime" were justified, its here.

It happened, too, amazingly early in that lifetime. He was 28 when The Birthday Party was pretty much mocked off the stage, inspiring all the same a groundswell of support that ensured a responsive hearing for The Caretaker two years later. That play (which, most fortuitously, Soulpepper is reviving next year as part of its inaugural season in the Distillerys Young Centre) had a cultural impact still unmatched by any subsequent English play. Suddenly there was this thing called Pinter: tense, witty, enigmatic and amazingly confident in its placing of words and moods and actions and people. And so it has continued.

Scenically, his plays divide into the rough (everything up to The Homecoming in 1964) and the smooth (everything since). The former, infused with the idioms and the terrors of his London Jewish boyhood, are the more obviously resonant, but the latter find a comparable music, clipped rather than flowing, in the theoretically petrified rhythms of the English middle class. However cloaked the emotions, the language is pellucid and the jokes among the funniest in modern drama. And he has a gift denied to most of his contemporaries and successors; he creates great characters. A wise director once suggested that Davies, the tramp in The Caretaker, may be the last role created by a British playwright that future actors will yearn to play, though on the strength of William Hutt's Toronto performance, I'd be inclined to add Spooner, the poetaster of No Mans Land. Pinters plays keep passing the revival test; if they aren't classics, nobody's are.

- - -

One of Pinters more unfortunate, but short-lived, effects was the creation by other writers of mechanical "comedies of menace" written in imitation Cockney. Far more important has been the arrival in his wake of a whole generation of seriously comic playwrights, boulevardiers with muscle. One of the best of them is Alan Bennett, whose Habeas Corpus, a big success in London in 1973, has just received its Toronto premiere at CanStage. There are two mysteries about this. One is why its taken so long. The other is why it's happening now. It looks and sounds a long way from home.

Habeas Corpus is a comedy from the '70s thats set in the 60s, though from this distance of time and space the distinction may be difficult to discern. The scene is Hove, an especially respectable adjunct to the seaside resort of Brighton, which itself has always seemed respectable enough. Beneath the prim exteriors of course, lewd passions can rage, and they do here.

Our central character is Dr. Arthur Wicksteed, a physician with a consuming non-professional interest in women's bodies, notably excepting that of his wife, Muriel. She, long weary of being ignored, thinks longingly of a diminutive former admirer, now president of the British Medical Association and, naturally, in town for a meeting. The Wicksteeds have a spotty and miserable son whose name, Dennis, his father can never remember, this being one of the play's less happy running gags. There is also the doctors unfulfilled sister, Constance, who is persuaded that her problems would be solved if she had bigger breasts, and who sends away for a pair of false ones. These duly arrive, as shortly afterward does a man whose job it is to fit them. He encounters the wrong lady, and she, with pleasing symmetry, is run into by the wrong gentleman. This leads to double-entendres and the promise of worse.

Meanwhile -- there has to be a meanwhile -- the Wicksteeds, father and son, each have an assignation with the same visiting sex bomb; of the two she prefers Dennis, since she believes he is mortally ill and will therefore be the ideal official father for the baby she happens to be carrying. And further meanwhile there is the local vicar, a bucktoothed clown in whom lustful fantasies cohabit with a virtuous desire for Constance, who doesnt want to be virtuously desired, and there is the unmarried mother-to-be's own mother, a battleaxe recently returned from the colonies and shocked by everything she sees.

If all this sounds farcical, that's because it is. Bennett himself apparently calls it a farce without doors. But hes only the author; what would he know? The fact is that the entire first act depends on an assortment of characters all with nefarious and conflicting designs on the same small piece of living space, and this space had better be demarcated by something, even if it isnt doors. Otherwise the play isn't funny, and if it isn't that, it cant aspire to be anything else, such as deep. Morris Panychs production is unrelentingly open-plan, with no concessions to domestic or any other kind of realism. Ken MacDonald's set is a gleamingly clinical framework, forbiddingly adorned with X-rays, including one of a foot in a high-heeled shoe.

One gets the point. Humankind is a bag of bones, destined for the grave, and entitled to as much sensual gratification as possible before it arrives there. "This," say at least four people in the course of the evening, in varying shades of delight and dismay, "must be what they mean by the Permissive Society." There's a nostalgic phrase for you. The whole piece is nostalgic, in that it keeps echoing what other British playwrights of the time had already done better, notably the late Joe Orton, whose What the Butler Saw beats Bennett hollow in using brilliant farce to present a satiric indictment of British morality. Orton, however, had a throughgoing heartlessness that few could equal (though many have tried, including Pinter). Bennett is nicer and sadder, but though this play seems to celebrate and mourn in about equal measure, its final mood is one of oddly spinsterish distaste.

The actual dialogue jokes are less than Bennetts best, and anyway, good or indifferent, they involve references and idioms that current Canadian actors and audiences are likely to find foreign. Fiona Reid, who can time any line to its best advantage, is the most at home as Muriel; and Joseph Ziegler, playing his second cynical doctor in a row, is a bearded elf, caught between a twinkle and a leer. The most emphatic treat, though, is Melody A. Johnsons Constance, as demanding as she is dolorous until her moment of expansion. As her clerical admirer, David Storch is upstaged by his own set of falsies (the dental ones); he is funnier in his other, quieter role as an aspiring suicide whose efforts nobody notices. Cyrus Lane does all right as Dennis, and so does Tara Rosling as the vamp, though she has to work at it. The others are at sea; Astrid Van Wieren seems to be channelling a character, a premature Maggie Thatcher, whom she knows must exist but can't quite reach. Sheila McCarthy, as an omniscient choral housekeeper, has a more sophisticated version of the same problem -- she's constantly on the edge of the right style. But she's saddled with an annoying and unnecessary role: Why should we need someone to tell us this is a cartoon?

- Habeas Corpus runs through Nov. 5 at the Bluma Appel, 416-368- 3110.

CRITIC'S PICK

HELLO DOLLY, SO LONG STRATFORD

This weekend sees the closing of all but one of the Stratford Festival's main stage productions. Pride of place has to go to The Tempest in which, on Friday, the magnificent William Hutt as Prospero gives his farewell performance. Hutt has emphatically stated that this signals his departure from the stage, not necessarily from acting, and that he has no intention of shedding last-night tears. Saturday sees the closure of the much-underrated Cat on a Hot Tin Roof, The Lark and Fallen Angels. On Sunday it's curtains (or would be if they had them) for As You Like It and the great musical Into the Woods. Only Hello Dolly remains, for one more week.
2005-10-29-aunties-brew-up-bitter-tea-ha:
robertcushman@lycos.com

Anna Chatterton and Evalyn Parry, known collectively as the Independent Aunties, are two performers who appear, like so many others, to be better than their material. Sympathy is tempered by the fact that they write the material themselves.

They are appearing in the Stage 3 season at Theatre Passe Muraille, in a quintuple bill, in which four of the five plays occur after the intermission. The one that comes before, obviously the longest and theoretically the most substantial, is titled Frances, Mathilda and Tea. Frances, who is short and in black, and Mathilda, who is tall and in red, are genteel middle-aged ladies of the Victorian era, and tea is what they are taking: a birthday tea in honour of their mother, who is dead. It is somewhat surprising to find them as part of an avowedly experimental season on a contemporary Toronto stage, and dispiriting to find them living up so completely to received ideas about Victorian womanhood. If the tea table itself isn't enough of a tip-off, we find them to be repressed, spiteful and generally lacking the advantages of more enlightened generations. They spend this day, and presumably most others, playing mutually exploitative mind-games.

Mathilda likes to taunt Frances with allusions to her own happy and productive days as a memsahib in British India, though even if she's fantasizing, which seems likely, its strange that she should feel obliged to identify her late spouse as "my husband Charles" every single time she mentions him. Frances likes to trap Mathilda into playing physically humiliating party games. There is a revelation at the end but the characters have been so little explored, their milieu so much taken for granted, that it is difficult to care about what has been revealed. The best you can say is that both actresses, especially Parry as Mathilda, are good at the voices.

Their cartooning skills are further deployed in the succeeding playlets, collectively billed as The Mysterious Shorts. They arent all that mysterious, and they don't all seem short, but the first one qualifies on both counts. It gives us Gertrude Stein and Alice B. Toklas, conversing in brusque non sequiturs drawn from Stein's own writings. It goes on just long enough to establish the ladies identities and then abruptly stops, which is probably appropriate.

Next they play female reporters from a 30s or '40s newspaper movie, bereft of their scoop and also of any wit or point that might carry the sketch past the initial pleasure of recognition. Parry at least manages a super parody of Rosalind Russell (the program credits both His Girl Friday and The Women) at her toughest, with a touch of Katharine Hepburn thrown in, a matter not so much of vocal tones as of vocal angles. Then, even more protracted and less amusing, come the 1960s, which are really cartooned, giving us Chatterton as a frustrated housewife named Petronella and Parry as a dubious emissary of liberation known as SuperStacked.

The last segment, pegged to the 1980s and titled A Drop Dead Gorgeous, Tanned, Thin Sweet Valley Adventure, gives us, at last, a good joke: only one, and it's pretty much given away in the title, but weve learned to be grateful. A golden generation of complacent California girls (and a few boys), having gone to sleep one night truly content, wake to find that all their charms have been stolen. They have, in fact, Lost Their Adjectives.

The breathless tone of the eras teen fiction is, I am going to assume, accurately captured, though the story doesn't make sense. The thief turns out to be not some dumpy and dumped-on outsider but a girl whom our twin heroines (identical, we're told, but with nothing else in common -- all right, two good jokes) had always regarded as a serious threat; which she couldnt have been unless she had Adjectives of Her Own. Taken as a whole, the evening suggests that women were oppressed but inwardly rebellious in the 19th century; achieved style, if not actual independence, from the 20s to the '40s; and frivolously blew it in the '60s and after. It also indicates that white gentiles are as vulnerable as any other of the ethnic groups represented in Stage 3 to stereotype and to self- stereotype.

- - -

The Alchemy Theatre, a small-scale operation specializing in the classics (which seems, in practice, to mean just Shakespeare), offers a Julius Caesar that is most successful with the funeral scene in the Forum. This, considering the lack of resources, may appear surprising, but in fact the enforced economy here works better than many other productions half-hearted attempts at spectacle. Half a dozen actors, clustered in the auditorium wearing beaked masks, make an excellent symbolic crowd, and their few spoken lines function as they should: as brilliant shorthand for the shifting emotions of a crowd.

Brutus (Kyle McDonald) unpacks his oration with logic, and with a palpable self-satisfaction in that logic. Antony (Chris Cocoluzzi) then wipes him off the popular radar with a delivery of the friends, Romans, countrymen speeches that superbly blends genuine passion over Caesars death with a ruthless skill in manipulating his own and his hearers' emotions. I really didn't want him to stop. Alone in the cast, he has a real sense of pace. Even more important, the rhythms of his speech match those of the characters thoughts. He is less successful in his subsequent scenes, in which it seems the actor rather than the character is dangerously pleased with himself.

Brutus is played with intentional smugness, which is justifiable up to a point, but should not constitute the whole performance. Signs of humanity -- toward his wife or his page -- are ruthlessly obliterated, or maybe were not noticed in the first place. True, this is a political play from which nobody comes out well -- an honest political play, in other words -- but the characters are complex men, not bugs.

Simon Michellepiss nondescript production hardly lives up to his company's high-sounding slogan ("Classical Theatre for the Modern Mind"). It consists of lines spoken more or less intelligently but without much depth, and of bodies shunted rather awkwardly around a confined space.

The black drapes, off-the-peg togas and inexperienced cast are all economically understandable, but they take a toll. So does the textual editing that has the minor conspirators, an ignoble bunch, returning as Brutus's and Cassiuss staff officers, who are the opposite. (And, in one case, commit suicide to prove it.) The most ingenious rewriting is applied to Casca, the number-three conspirator and, textually, the number-one assassin. In this version he doesnt get to stab Caesar in the back or anywhere else, but he does change sides, ending up as one of those men whom nobody likes.

Still, that central scene is really exciting, far more so than it usually is. Or perhaps I should say than it used to be, because Julius Caesar, in theory one of the most popular plays and one of those we all studied in school, is these days hardly ever done. I don't know why it's slipped so far down the charts. Its certainly not for lack of relevance. I think its because of all the tragedies it offers the least scope for sex and violence. Or anyway for sex.

- - -

It's fitting that John Mighton should have won this year's Siminovitch Prize. His Half Life has created more ripples than any new Canadian play since The Drawer Boy. Equally gratifying is the plays current success (in its original production) in Glasgow. Its rare for a play to cross the ocean, in either direction, and to be applauded with the same seriousness on both shores.

- Francesca, Mathilda and Tea and The Mysterious Shorts run through Nov. 6 at Theatre Passe Muraille, 16 Ryerson Ave., 416-504- 8980. Julius Caesar closes tomorrow at the Alchemy Theatre, 133 Tecumseth St., 416-998-7503.

2005-11-05-dame-s-vengeance-not-so-sweet:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Dame Edna: Back with a Vengeance closes tomorrow at the Royal Alexandra, 250 King St. W., 416-872-1212. Second City: Reloaded runs indefinitely at 51 Mercer St., 416-343- 0011.

Dame Edna Everage is a star, and you are not. That is her message, now and forever. All the same, now that she's Back With a Vengeance, I fear she's slackened off. When I first saw the Dame, she was far from the megastar she has since become. I know people whose memories go back even further than that, to when she made her London debut as plain Mrs. Everage from Melbourne, determined to make it in show business and to be accepted as an idol among idols, and to do it by the simplest means of all: by standing on a stage and telling us all about herself. Hers were the dreams of an everyday housewife: pure stardom, celebrity in its most concentrated form. These days we take her surname for granted. We forget that there was once a time when, given the appropriate Australian twang, it actually meant something.

She had of course to make compromises on the way up. She had to sing and dance, like any run-of-the-mill trouper. She also had to tell jokes, but that can never have been a hardship, since her humour depends on her certain knowledge that we, her public, will be fascinated by whatever details of her life she deigns to share with us. She in turn has taken a kindly and increasingly persistent interest in the details of ours, especially of those of us who are married and female. She remains in essence a housewife talking solicitously to other housewives; it's probably the secret of her success.

Over the years, like any artist, she has kept refining her craft, but she may now have refined it too much. She has a new and cozy rapport with her pianist, but her musical routines are beyond perfunctory and beyond tacky. I realize that that is supposed to be the point, but they are also beyond functioning as parody. The spoken parts of the show consist almost entirely of Dame Edna interrogating selected members of her audience or, as she puts it, "empowering" them. Edna prophesied what Oprah wrought, and Edna can still out-wreak her.

Now, her victims have asked for it; at least they've purchased tickets near the front of the theatre, which is nearly, though not quite, as rash as arriving late for an Everage show, something that gives you a 100% chance of being singled out. (The first night's statutory latecomer claimed that he had come from the City Hall parking lot. The Dame pointed out that she'd come all the way from Australia, and she'd made it on time.) Most of them are happy to play along.

As ever, she retains total recall of those she has selected, of their names and what they have confessed. And she keeps returning to them throughout the evening, never letting go. This is impressive, but it was more dazzling in the days when she interwove these interjections with more elaborate dissertations on the follies and foibles of her near-peers among the world's famous (always so humble in asking for her advice) or indeed among her own family: "homeopathic" Kenny or prostate-stricken Norm or perpetual bridesmaid Madge. She more or less confesses that she has nothing left to say about this latter group, which is understandable, but she has nothing to take their place. Gone, too, are the rich ruminations with which she favoured us last time she was here, on modish words like "infrastructure" and "arugula." Her show, in fact, lacks texture. Even the ceremonial waving of the gladioli is an anti- climax. It doesn't have anything to top.

She can still be hilarious, in ways that are hers alone: a creation apparently independent of her creator. (It becomes increasingly hard, in reviewing Dame Edna, to mention the name "Barry Humphries" without feeling stupid.) She retains her magnificent improvisatory command of the English language: "Is your soap taupe?" she asked a lady who had admitted to having a bathroom decorated in that colour, which can't often happen. And, to the customary waves to the paupers in the balconies, she now adds a judicious comment on the few empty seats. They were purchased in advance by subscribers, who are now dead. What other explanation could there be?

Visiting Dame Edna and the new Second City show in the same week, I became aware of a new theatrical rule. When a married couple is inveigled onstage, as happened at both entertainments the nights I was present, the husband will always be called Michael. Also, audience participants have become increasingly talented. The Second City's Mike and his wife, roped into a scene about someone else's marriage, showed themselves to be expert mimes. A lady cast as Dame Edna's mother in her final skit burst into song, and tunefully, to the Dame's noticeable displeasure.

Second City: Reloaded is the troupe's first revue in their new and cozier space opposite the old one. It's also one of their best shows, with a manic quality I have never seen from them before. One number finds the cast running round the auditorium like slavering dogs. Anand Rajaram, who is especially good at it, returns at unexpected intervals to slaver some more. He also gets the show off to a terrific start as a Sikh taxi driver who discomfits his Toronto passenger by revealing a Scots accent, and helps with a terrific close-to-finish as an Arab pizza-maker suspected by his customer (Matt Baram, a walking nervous breakdown) of having mingled parts of the previous owner in with the pepperoni. This is the show's take on terrorism, fear of.

Another thing: Improv, previously confined to a separate slot at the end of the evening, now crops up within the show itself. Paul Bates pounds out heartfelt (by him and us) letters of protest to Telus Mobility and Rogers Cable, and then takes suggestions for further indignant missives; one to Highway 407 really inspired him.

There are flaws. If there are ways of being funny about either Karla Homolka or breast cancer, which I doubt, this show hasn't found them. Nor has Second City ever been much good at musical numbers. There are two here, placed back to back, as if to get them over with. Back on the credit side place a number where the cast go orgiastic and anti-environmental at the sight of a Hummer, and a bit set at an Argos game whose changes of mood require real acting, and get it.

2005-11-12-beyond-goodness-and-evil-gene:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Goodness runs through Nov. 27 at the Tarragon Extra Space, 30 Bridgman Ave., 416-531-1827.

High up among the Great Unanswerables, right next to "why do bad things happen to good people?" comes "why do good people do terrible things?" Why, in particular, do they turn on their neighbours and become participants in genocide? Goodness, Michael Redhill's new play, asks this question intelligently, absorbingly and -- as was almost inevitable -- frustratingly.

Part of the frustration is inherent in the method he uses, which is quasi-autobiographical. The story is told to us by a man, a writer, who says his name is Michael Redhill, though he is at pains to point out in his introduction that he is actually being played by an actor called Jordan Pettle. "You'll be in good hands with Jordan," says Redhill by way of Pettle, and so we are. This endearingly unassuming actor is here at his best, his habitual casualness, which can sometimes be excessively low-key, functioning to convey a quick mind, sensitive and inquisitive antennas and a capacity for feeling acutely embarrassed. His performance is in sharp and obviously intentional contrast to those of his colleagues, who -- as things in his dream or perhaps in his nightmare -- are acting in primary colours.

The character known as Redhill comes before us bearing two pieces of baggage: a failed marriage and a Jewish heritage, both of which, I believe, he shares with the real-life Redhill. The rest of his story is probably less factual. He tells of going to Poland after his divorce to find out about his many relatives who were killed in the Holocaust. The villagers he meets have little to tell him. They even wonder whether, amid the many holocausts of the 20th and 21st centuries, this one was really so special. Redhill starts wondering, too. Stopping off in London on his way back to Canada, he meets a mysterious man who refers him to a mysterious woman who tells him a mysterious story, which of course comes to life before our eyes.

It concerns Matthias Todd, an accused genocidaire put on trial by his victims' compatriots. Exactly which war, and which massacres are being referred to, we are not told; there are of course many candidates. The storyteller, whose name is Althea, had been Todd's jailer. The accused, when we flash back to his imprisonment, is an old man who may be unfit to plead. His prosecutor is ferociously convinced that this is a sham, and that Todd is in full command of both his mind and his memory. Todd's daughter, with equal passion, contends that he isn't.

Both sides are agreed that Todd's murderousness didn't spring from nowhere. His own family had been slaughtered by members of the ethnic group whom he himself went on to target, to whom he had already given both personal and ethnic offence. So we have a complex situation standing in for any number of other complex situations. To drive home the genericness of it all, the actors lace the action with singing, whose provenance varies from African to Eastern European and back again.

On top of all this, we have Redhill himself. The other characters suggest that his interest in them may have much to do with his own bitterness, not so much over his ancestry as over his ex-wife's infidelity with his best friend. He doesn't deny it. Philosophically, though, it seems irrelevant. Of course we all have agendas. Next question. Meanwhile, the story of Todd-in-prison takes on its own life but not its own meaning; his possible amnesia is another red herring. The tale's bloody end is revealed to us ahead of time, but this gesture toward Brechtian alienation, like most such gestures, does nothing to stop us getting involved. It doesn't even kill suspense. Effective though this is, the play ends up in a double bind. A situation cannot symbolize other situations unless it is first itself. But it can't become itself when it's continually nudging us about how representative it is. A play set in Iraq, say, might conceivably illuminate events in Rwanda, or vice versa. A play set everywhere is a play set nowhere. One ends up resenting the characters for being so voluble about their feelings and so secretive about the facts.

The Volcano company production, directed by Ross Manson and designed by Teresa Przybylski, brings Redhill's limbo to stern visual life. The Tarragon's Extra Space becomes a dungeon with one small door. Some of the cast seem to have been chosen for musical rather than dramatic credentials, and, as often happens with musical- theatre performers gone legit, their acting loses in subtlety what it gains in force. This is especially the case with Bernadeta Wrobel as the daughter, and it's also true of Lili Francks as the reminiscing Althea, who starts off in an immensely strong accusatory tone that she then hardly varies. Jack Nicholsen's prosecutor is contrastingly silky-smooth, but he, too, keeps hitting the same note. Tara Hughes as the younger Althea, exposed to an arch-enemy's possible humanity, has the chance to move between sympathy and implacability, and takes it. Ambiguity is built into Victor Ertmanis's role as Todd, and he's able to function both as contemptuous warlord (in Nazi terms, he's more Goering than Eichmann) and, more memorably, as bleary-brained survivor. He also has a set piece about a mass killing, designed both to shock and to make us, the good people in the audience, acknowledge our own capacity for evil. It succeeds on the first count, as well-written accounts of atrocities tend to do, much less in the second, which remains a debating point. A play that poses urgent questions never finds the right people to put them to. Maybe, as Redhill's Polish villagers told him, they don't exist. But it's strange that a piece that compels attention almost throughout leaves you with so little.
