Kevin Spacey, beginning his second year as artistic director of the Old Vic, is playing Richard II, and everybody is very relieved. Spacey offers something new in Richards; not the traditional mellifluous martyr, nor the more recent mordant ironist exploiting his own humiliation, but an arrogant playboy monarch who never dreamed that power could have limitations.

Spacey is one Hollywood star whose vanity projects justify themselves. It may seem a leap from playing Bobby Darin (in Beyond the Sea) to playing Richard but the two characters, as he presents them, share a lust for the limelight and a certain doomed cockiness. They also demand that the actor master new skills, and Spacey swings Shakespearean verse as confidently as he swung Mack the Knife.

He appears in a modern-dress production by Trevor Nunn, whose themes are surveillance and publicity. Everybody is on show, and most of the characters collaborate with the process. John of Gaunt delivers his famous lament for England -- "this royal throne of kings" -- directly to a news team. After his death, the footage is cut up and replayed, to the specifications of whoever wishes to profit from it. Gaunt's son, the usurper Bolingbroke (Ben Miles), inherits his father's skills and refines them; everything he says and does is calculated for public consumption.

Spacey's Richard also plays to the cameras. His problem is that he does it without calculation and enjoys it too much. He barely troubles to conceal his boredom with his squabbling barons. Only once they're banished is he able to stretch out at ease -- apparently in his favourite nightclub -- though even here he is as likely to snap at his cronies as to indulge them. He has authority; his decision to go in person to the Irish wars seems, for once, to be more than a mischievous whim. His return, to find himself virtually deposed by Bolingbroke, gives full vent to his talents for angry self-pity. I have never heard "what must the king do now?" delivered with such savagery. Richard never stops talking but it's not until his last scene in prison that he has a soliloquy, or -- in this production's terms -- that he has no camera to play to. The ex- king's driven self-discovery, however, is the one point at which Spacey's performance falls down. It's more a matter of equipment than of understanding; he just doesn't have the notes in his voice with which to move us. The episode, though, in which he's visited by his loyal groom is unusually touching.

It's the kind of human detail at which Nunn, the best Shakespearean director there is, habitually excels. He both burrows into the text and builds a world around it. Modern dress can sometimes be a too-easy option, but it can also help supply a rationale for every scene, and that's what happens here. The strange semi-farcical interlude of the York family conspiracy has never made as much political or psychological sense as it does in this production, though I thought the Duchess's arriving at Bolingbroke's court in a motorcycle helmet was a bit much -- surely she could have taken a taxi.

Visiting London's theatres from Toronto currently inspires a sense of deja vu. They have, of course, the same musical franchises ours do, plus a couple of incipient ones such as Mary Poppins and The Woman in White, while revivals of Journey's End and You Never Can Tell make the West End look like a mini Shaw Festival.

And then there's Schiller. Next Tuesday in Toronto the Goethe- Institut has a video presentation on "Rediscovering Friedrich Schiller as a political playwright." Schiller, once practically a synonym for Neglected European Dramatist, is now hot even among insular anglophones. Canada led the way, with Soulpepper's inaugural production of Don Carlos. The same play was a West End hit last season and it's now been succeeded by Mary Stuart, in a production by Phyllida Lloyd that was acclaimed at the intimate Donmar Warehouse but looks punishingly bleak at the full-sized Apollo Theatre. The translation is an awkward compromise between ancient and modern, and the costuming is similarly split. Or rather it's segregated, along gender lines; women in period frocks are oppressed by men in modern suits. The contrast helps us to tell the gents apart, but -- despite the efforts of two fine actresses, Harriet Walter and Janet McTeer -- it does little for the ladies.

Kristin Scott Thomas is magnificent in an even less familiar classic, Luigi Pirandello's As You Desire Me, as a sleazy-nightclub singer who may be somebody's long-lost wife. Or, this being Pirandello, may not. Bob Hoskins plays her brutish protector and seems uncertain why he's doing it. The supposedly unpredictable play is predictable. We know we're going to be told that identity is unstable and unknowable and we sit there waiting for the penny, or the lire, to drop.

And much the same is true of the season's new dramatic hit, Heroes. Written by a young French playwright, Gerald Sibleyras, it has been translated by Tom Stoppard, whose jokes are expectedly good in a, for him, unexpected mode, i.e. they aren't quotable out of context. A bewitchingly verdant set (by Robert Jones) frames three enchanting actors: Richard Griffiths, John Hurt and -- especially good -- Ken Stott. They play a trio of old soldiers plotting their escape from a First World War veterans' home. It's a given that they won't succeed, or even seriously try. We watch them squabbling and reconciling and generally acting bittersweet on their way to the play's inevitable dying fall. It's been packaged like that more interesting French three-hander, Art, and I expect it to arrive at the Royal Alex -- or, if a post-Broadway tour falls through, at CanStage -- around 2007.

TIDELINE

Factory Theatre

Long plays are back in fashion. Hot on the heels of The Trials of Judas Iscariot, a brilliant three-and-a-half hour show whose characters are in purgatory, comes Tideline, which goes on for three hours and forty minutes, is not brilliant and whose characters are also in a kind of purgatory. In this one, though, the audience joins them there.

Wajdi Mouawad, a French-Canadian playwright of Lebanese extraction, sets the last two-thirds of his piece in a recently war- torn land that he coyly refuses to name, but that is distinguished, at least in this staging, by the rockiness of its terrain and the readiness of its inhabitants to behave like symbols. Before we get there, however, we have an hour or so to kill. We start, promisingly enough, with a young man named Wilfred bounding onstage to tell an unseen judge about how he was having the best sex of his life when the phone rang to tell him that his father had just died. You may wonder what he said about this to the lady in his bed, or she to him, but such prosaic concerns are far beneath the play's notice.

We do learn that Wilfred's mother's family won't let his father be buried next to her because she died giving birth to Wilfred and they blame the father for it. This genuinely haunting situation, occasioning a couple of touching flashbacks, is set up at length over the play's first act and is then never alluded to again.

What happens instead is that Wilfred, with the court's permission, takes the body of his immigrant dad back to the old country for burial. He first meets a highly dispensable blind poet who recites the opening verses of the Iliad, though we don't appear to be in Greece. He then encounters a lady singer, and they gradually accumulate a whole retinue of the young dispossessed, who go tramping the land in search of a suitable gravesite so that Dorothy -- I mean Wilfred -- can fulfill his quest and go home. The corpse they carry is represented sometimes by a body bag and sometimes by a living, talking actor. Finally, after an especially interminable lyrical interlude, they commit the old man to the sea. Hence the title.

Wilfred's companions have all lost their own fathers, bloodily. So there's a bond. But there's no way that his condition matches or illuminates theirs. This attenuated fantasy could only be passed off as a universal fable by visionary direction and actors able to turn the lines, some of which have potential, into poetry. Bill Lane gives it a painstaking, plodding production, staffed by a cast who aren't up to it. Michael Rubenfeld does well as the Wilfred of the first act, blushing and gesticulating like Woody Allen thrust into Hamlet, but he merges into the crowd later on. His companions preach, mutter or -- in the case, after a couple of neat cameos, of Dylan Trowbridge -- shout; true, his character, a would-be terrorist, is supposed to yell, but it must be possible to do it with more nuance. Andrew Moodie has some fun as an imaginary film director who seems to represent Wilfred's narcissism, and no fun at all as an equally imaginary medieval knight who represents his childhood and whom he grows out of.

It's that kind of play, bypassing the specific to aim at the universal, and achieving only a kind of ponderous whimsy. It's intended as an act of remembrance. Mouawad, as stated, was born in Lebanon; you'd think there'd be a play there, one that might illuminate atrocity instead of just referencing it from time to time. If the besetting sin of Anglo-Canadian drama is to be parochial, then that of French-Canadian drama is to be cloudy and portentous. In this instance, I'll take le vice Anglais.

Colour Photo: Ed Gass-Donnelly / Michael Rubenfeld plays Wilfred like Woody Allen thrust into Hamlet in the first act of the three- hour, forty-minute play Tideline.

robertcushman@lycos.com; The Dishwashers runs through Dec. 18 at the Tarragon Theatre, 416-536-5018. Crowns runs through Dec. 10 at the Bluma Appel, 416-368-3110.

Morris Panych's The Dishwashers is the second play in succession (The Optimists was the first) to arrive on the Tarragon stage with an idea, a setting, a group of characters and no development.

Panych directs it himself, and it comes, like all his productions, with a startling set by Ken MacDonald. On this occasion the most startling thing about it is how uncharacteristically realistic it is. MacDonald takes us into the bowels of a vauntedly classy restaurant, down to the cheerless depths where the crockery is reunited with the cutlery and both get resparkled. It's tempting to describe the space as cluttered but in fact, close-packed though it is, its extremely ordered. And the detail is extraordinary, from the bits of tomato obstinately clinging to a plate to the steam that rises from the machine as yet another cleansing cycle nears completion.

Presiding over this process is Dressler, who alternates between a grinding cynicism about the way the world works and a touching faith in the higher culinary motives of his bosses upstairs. He takes enormous pride, for example, in being a part, however lowly, of a trade that could recognize an artichoke as a potential gourmet treat where others might have seen just a prickly green thing." Being a dishwasher seems here very much like working for a newspaper.

Labouring alongside him is Moss, an old and very sick man ("riddled with cancer, Dressler says briskly, and thats the best thing about him"), kept on apparently through charity, though whose charity is long left a mystery. Into this setup there is thrown, as there always seems to be in workplace plays, a young newcomer: not, for once, a student but a hotshot investor, name of Emmett, who had found he wasn't so hot.

The play is in part a tribute to Panych's father, who slaved for years in a comparable environment. Its problem is that environment is all, apart from a handful of really funny lines, that it has to offer. The space between the beginning of the play and its end is filled by having the characters revolve in their predetermined patterns. Dressler oscillates between obsequiousness and officiousness, without ever quite losing his humanity; hes an ex- con, and still has a few scams going. Emmett is sometimes resigned to dishwashing for life, and sometimes rebellious; his attempt, capitalist though he is or was, to form a union, is the nearest thing to a plotline, but it, too, seems like filler. His conflicted state is indicated by his inability to finish a sentence without contradicting himself; this trait is especially evident in a final scene thats genuinely surprising but that twists its screws a few times too many to be satisfying.

As director, Panych begins the first act by having the stage furniture play some poltergeist tricks of its own, and the second by having the three principals do a little dance. Both these devices are delightful, but they have nothing to do with the rest of the show. The second, though, lets the rubicund Randy Hughson, who plays Dressler, show how very light he is on his feet. This actor is a puzzle. Most of his recent performances have been the same, filled with desperate bluster, but each has seemed absolutely right for the character he is playing. His pace and comic timing are great helps, of course. Ditto Eric Peterson as the aged Moss, though he has in the circumstances to go for slowness rather than speed. Jonathan Crombie is good, though fuzzy in outline, as Emmett; and Daniel Karasik makes an excellent impression as a last-minute recruit.

Crowns is about hats. They line the side of the stage, and they also weigh down most of the text. Half a dozen black ladies, and one black gentleman, discourse in disconnected monologues on the importance of wearing gorgeous headgear to keep up morale and appearances in the segregated South. Regina Taylor's script -- there's no way its a play -- is adapted from a book by Michael Cunningham and Craig Marberry, and I can see that on the page, with photographs, the vignettes could have considerable anecdotal and historical appeal. Recited on a stage with no continuity, they are paralyzingly dull. There is a sliver of a through line, about a teenager from the North sent to live with her high-hatted relatives, but it doesnt amount to anything. She does a bit of rap; most of the show's music is gospel. The audience is dragooned into clapping along. This must be the most desperate of CanStage's annual attempts to build a show around Jackie Richardson. She is in great voice, as are all the cast, but theres no way this is a musical, either. The show is dire.

I could happily have devoted my entire column to The Last Days of Judas Iscariot, but it has already come and gone. The director, David Ferry, roped off a corner of the yawning Fermenting Cellar in the Distillery District to serve as a suburb of Purgatory, where a catatonic Judas comes to trial, and animated it amazingly. Dramatist Stephen Adly Guirgis is a lapsed Catholic, though he might equally well be a vexed secular Jew. With exhilarating wit he applies New York street talk, leavened with much learning, to the problem of Judas (ultimate villain or ultimate victim) and all the moral and political problems that radiate from it. He doesnt have any answers. An evening in which the surprises never stopped coming was peopled by, among many others, Irene Poole, racked and ringing as Judas's lawyer; Sanjay Talwar, her fawning opponent with a fez; Alon Nashman, Sigmund Freud as coke fiend and, as surprise-witness Satan, Diego Matamoros, immensely powerful, imperturbably cool. Pray that some at least of them will be back.

Colour Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / Jonathan Crombie, left, and Randy Hughson in a scene from The Dishwashers at the Tarragon Theatre.

robertcushman@lycos.com; The Goat or Who is Sylvia? runs through Dec. 10 at the Berkeley Street Theatre, 416-368-3110. The Amorous Servant runs through Dec. 11 at the Artword Theatre, 416-872-1212.

It is rare these days for a play to sport a double title, especially one whose second half asks a question that its first has already answered. Such is the case with The Goat or Who is Sylvia?, Edward Albee's latest. I give nothing away in revealing that Sylvia is a goat, indeed the goat, the new love object of a man who, up until shortly before the play begins, has been perfectly happy with his wife.

A more perplexing question is, why is Sylvia? Why, that is, did Americas senior practising playwright choose to build a play around this particular compulsion? He is clearly not concerned to examine bestiality for its own sake, an omission for which most people will be grateful. Maybe he was just challenging himself to write an entertaining play on an unlikely subject, in which case he passes his own test with flying colours -- this is possibly his wittiest play. Most likely he is pursuing his ongoing project of anatomizing the American marriage and how it copes with shock. Though if he wanted to shock us, hes too late. The audience with whom I saw the play seemed composed mostly of senior citizens, and they lapped it up, especially the ladies.

Martin, the goat-fancier, is 50 years old and an acclaimed architect. (If world drama has taught us anything, it is that successful master builders are peculiarly prone to bizarre infatuations and tragic falls.) He is devoted to his wife, Stevie, and she to him. But when Martin, on a trip to the country, comes face to face with Sylvia, he is smitten, and embarks on a full- blown affair. When Stevie finds out she is, of course, devastated.

Albee has long moved on from the clangorous marital warfare of Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? to something subtler. Here, as in his previous Play About the Baby, he gives us a textbook happy marriage, one moreover that prides itself on its tolerance. The couple's teenage son, Billy, is gay, and theyve coped with that all right. (Well, sort of.) Indeed Billy has been boasting to his friends about what an exceptional advertisement for wedlock his folks are. But apparently there are limits, and Martin crosses them. Billy thinks so, and so does Stevie, who coats her fury in a savage humour that takes us back to the earlier Albee. Martin, by contrast, is the kind of man who cant get angry. He can be aloof and ironic, especially when people misuse words in his presence, and he stews in his own compound of helpless guilt and injured innocence. When he is roused to defend himself, in the play's most reverberant sequence, it's on the universal subject of involuntary sexual arousal. He is not, at this point, talking about goats.

For a play that has been eagerly awaited since its New York premiere in 2002, The Goat has received a strangely muted Toronto staging. Micheline Chevriers production, at CanStages secondary address, has two things going for it. One is the set, designed by Judith Bowden. Its clean lines do the hero's profession proud. Its slatted walls have an appropriate air of barn door, and its imposing central arch might be the frame for a Greek tragedy, which is what, at its bloody finish, the play surprisingly but logically becomes. Not to give anything away, but tragedy may have had its origins in ritual sacrifice, and the word itself means "goat-song."

The other asset, a vital one considering he's on stage throughout, is R.H. Thomsons Martin, a delicate, worried portrayal of the cerebral brought up against the visceral. Its high time that Paul Dunn progressed from playing teenagers, but his Billy is accurately self-absorbed and accurately lost. John Jarvis, though, is lumpen as the family friend who lets the cat out of the bag, or the goat out of the pasture. And though Gina Wilkinson seems to have the right tragicomic idea about Stevie, she hammers that idea into the ground. Her touch is as heavy as Thomson's is light.

- - -

According to John Van Burek, Canada's champion of 18th-century comedy, the plays of Carlo Goldoni fall into three periods: Early, when Goldoni was in thrall to the commedia dellarte, its stock characters and plots; Late, when he had developed his own far more realistic approach; and Intermediate, which is a bit of both. The Amorous Servant, which Van Burek has translated, very well, and directed, less surely (and in which he also acts, quite creditably) is Intermediate, but I suspect it might be more profitably treated as if it were Late. It concerns Florindo, a young man thrown out of his fathers house through the wiles of his stepmother, and Corallina, a maidservant who looks after him, lives with him (platonically) and falls in love with him (probably). He certainly falls for her, at least for a time. She, though, tells him that he would be far better off with a girl of his own station, and fixes him up with one, while she stakes out a male coeval for herself. The scene in which Corellina and Florindo make their positions known represents an extraordinary clashing of gears, between one school of drama and another, one political era and another. Tradition, social and theatrical, wins out, but not without regrets, on stage and certainly in the auditorium.

This, the play's central scene, suffers from being staged somewhat off-centre, a miscalculation emphasized by the geometric precision of Michael Gianfrancesco's charming set. The productions first act is altogether stretched very thin, with too much strenuous clowning draining the blood from a story that, though not remarkably complicated, becomes hard to latch on to. The characters arent necessarily played to commedia type. Dov Mickelson's Arlecchino, for example, is his own kind of buffoon, a sweet amalgam of Chico and Harpo Marx. But he has some coarse colleagues, and the show doesn't take hold until after the intermission.

Its only at this point that the two best performers are allowed a scene together. They are Christine Brubaker, a heartwarmingly practical Corellina, and Jerry Franken, who clowns as much as anyone, but with authority and economy, as the hoodwinked dad whom she calls mi padrone. The translation retains many Italian phrases and they work beautifully, making the play seem just strange enough; some of the actors even do accents. This duet sets the plays denouement in motion. Goldoni, an unassuming master craftsman, gathers all his threads together, and the process is very satisfying. This is the play's English-language premiere; watch for other countries to follow.

Colour Photo: Lucas Oleniuk, Canstage / Stevie (Gina Wilkinson) is understandably devastated when she learns of her husband, Martin's (R.H. Thomson), affair with a goat, in Edward Albee's latest, The Goat or Who is Sylvia?

JIMMY

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre,

Toronto

- - -

Playwrights have been saying for centuries that life's a dream, but few have been as earnest about it as Marie Brassard, author, director and sole performer of Jimmy. Jimmy is a self-described "homosexual hairdresser" who came into being 50 years ago as a thing in someone's dream. The person who dreamed him was a U.S. army general who was due to ship out to Korea the next day but never made it on account of he woke up dead.

Jimmy, whose imaginary existence had been cut off at a moment of unconsummated passion, was forced to spend the next half-century in whatever limbo unemployed dream-figures inhabit, waiting to be dreamed up by somebody else. Eventually somebody obliged, that somebody being an actress.

I've heard this story before, or one very like it. I'm thinking of Pirandello's Six Characters in Search of an Author, in which figures from an abandoned play wander into a theatre and ask the director and his troupe to put them out of their agony by completing their drama.

The difference is that Pirandello's play really is about the theatre; it makes some true, if obvious, points about the ways in which life's raw material is inevitably distorted and simplified when it gets into the hands of a playwright (and let's not even talk about actors).

Brassard's is not really about dreams; it captures the textures and rhythms of dreaming, but its central device is not so much playful as whimsical. We may well invent people in our dreams, but those people don't then hang about and crop up, with full biographies attached, in the dreams of others we haven't even met.

It all seems to be a pretext for a play about love, one that's periodically poignant but overwhelmingly sentimental. In the general's dream Jimmy falls in reciprocated love with a young soldier -- chances are the general identified with the soldier and died of shame at the thought.

The actress wants to make Jimmy over as her lover, and he naturally recoils, quite graphically. Eventually, Jimmy is reunited with his G.I. courtesy, I guess, of the suddenly generous actress if she's still the one doing the dreaming. Moral: Happiness is only possible in sleep, and at that somebody else has to do it for you.

Remember that an actress is actually playing Jimmy. Here we move from text to performance, which is on a higher plane. Literally: The whole show unfolds on a ledge perched in the right-hand corner of the stage.

Our first sight is of Brassard, inscrutably androgynous, with her bare back toward us and a braid of thick black hair running down it. There's a mirror behind her and a screen beside her, both supplying reflections and refractions.

When she turns toward us she's Jimmy, in a bulging suit with a flapping shirt, a loose-hung tie and a smartly folded pocket handkerchief. Later Jimmy will use this napkin to wipe himself after masturbating, having been aroused at the thought of a fish. (He again had his back turned, but he will still apologize for having done such a thing in front of us. If the actress is still an actress, the audience is still an audience. Keep up.)

When Brassard speaks, it's with the voice of Jimmy, which comes to us, through a distorting mike, as a cracked baritone that bears little resemblance to the sound of a homosexual hairdresser or of any other human being, but is undeniably striking.

Later she adds the voice of the actress, then alternates between them; and so quick are the transitions that at moments you would swear that she is speaking with two tongues at once. It becomes apparent that Brassard is not only playing the actress, she is that actress; which may explain, if not legitimize, some bewilderingly irrelevant interludes about her relationship with her mother.

The identification is clinched when, suddenly, the technology fails and Brassard apologizes to us in her own unmediated voice. It's a startling moment, as such breaks in convention always are, and you even wonder whether it might not be genuine. In fact it's woven so closely into the text that it had to be planned. (Maybe that's why the audience was kept waiting for ages before being allowed into the theatre; we were being softened up for the idea of technical glitches.)

So this is really another play about the theatre and like most such, more notable for technique than for substance. In a funny way, though, it backfires: Jimmy emerges as an interesting and affecting character, Brassard doesn't. Whether that constitutes a victory or a defeat, I wouldn't presume to judge.

Black & White Photo: Simon Guibault / Marie Brassard plays the title, and only role, in Buddies in Bad Times' production of Jimmy.
2005-12-10-corpse-deserved-death-but-par:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Last Will and Videotape runs indefinitely at Mysteriously Yours, 416-468-7469; Movin' Out runs through Dec. 31 at the Canon Theatre, 416-872-1212.

The corpse that provides the pretext for the latest interactive mystery from Mysteriously Yours is that of a multimillionaire (nobody says he's multi, but anything less would cut very little ice these days) by the name of William Randolph. He seems, however, to have little in common, richness and deadness apart, with the late Mr. Hearst. Nor, more surprisingly perhaps, does he bear any notable resemblance to Hearst's most celebrated fictional equivalent. This show is not a spoof of Citizen Kane. It isn't really a spoof of anything, except perhaps itself.

That's a pity. Mysteriously Yours has always been far more concerned with being funny than with being thrilling, and it has thrived in the past on parodying such highly recognizable sources as Casablanca and The Godfather. (The two shows in question are each being given occasional performances during the holidays.) When left to its own devices, it's left with its own devices and nothing more. This dinner theatre still provides both dinner and theatre of a higher quality than that combination would generally suggest, but in the new show, Last Will and Videotape, it's coasting.

Anyway. The centenarian Randolph has left behind a baby-doll wife whose protuberances might themselves be murder weapons and who is greedy, a daughter who is grasping, her videographer boyfriend who is covetous, unctuous Uncle Shecky, who is after every nickel he can get, and the family lawyer. All expected handsome handouts in the will of the deceased, so all had a motive to decease him. There's also a pianist, though he's there to finger rather than be fingered. This is, I believe, the first Mysteriously Yours production to feature a musical number: a spirited company rendition of Well Did You Evah, with new lyrics that would probably not have amused Cole Porter.

And, most important, there is Jean Daigle, the troupe's protean resident sleuth, appearing this time as a Newfie cop. Daigle's zest and his quick-thinking authority never cease to impress me, and this time he gets to play another role as well; he appears, in screened flashback, as the murdered man, of whom one can only say that he had it coming, no matter whence it came. We see him about to make another will, which can only mean trouble. I wonder if some day some higher-minded theatre group might kidnap Daigle and force him, for more glory but probably lower wages, to play Moliere or Feydeau. They could give him back later, and everybody would win. I should add that his solving of the case seemed to me, on this occasion, exceptionally clear. I actually understood who had done it, and how, and why. I always guess wrong, but this time I felt like kicking myself.

I saw the alternate company for Movin' Out and they were as impressive as the A-team celebrated in the Post by my colleague Michael Crabb. I cannot in fact imagine any improvement on James Fox (no, not that one, though he is also English), who played piano and sang the Billy Joel songs. That includes Joel himself; Fox is grittier. The musical highlight of the evening was his rendition, in a screaming growl, of We Didn't Start the Fire, a ferocious catalogue of American icons from the end of the Second World War to the Kennedy assassination. ("JFK blown away, what else do I have to say?")

It wasn't, for me, the choreographic highlight. The evocation of the Vietnam War that Twyla Tharp had arranged on the main stage looked to me pretty generic, whether it was going for the pity or the terror. Movin' Out is by current standards an unusually good show, but I would question the general assumption that the music and the staging are always in perfect sync. Quite often one outpaces the other. Tharp, for example, gets a grave and lovely romantic duet out of the unpromising Just the Way You Are: "I don't want clever conversation" ... a sensible decision when you're about to rhyme "hard" with "are."

Or maybe that line's a sly prophetic comment on the show's lack of any kind of conversation. It isn't quite true that it has no spoken words, but for the most part song and dance have to carry not just one another but the characters and story. It reinforced my doubts about using pre-existing songs in a narrative musical (as opposed to a revue). The show never plumbs the stupid depths of Mamma Mia! and its songs are far better in the first place. They are used as commentary, and the show is strict enough about this concept to deny Fox, or whoever, to sing Joel's Piano Man -- because that would, inescapably, be a song about him. Tharp had great success with a ballet based on Frank Sinatra songs, but there was no story and they danced to records. This one, with the music present, is close enough in feeling to a conventional musical for it to become frustrating that the characters don't have a chance to sing their own songs.

It also hurts that the characters don't have much character, only names: Brenda and Eddie and Tony and James and Judy, all chosen because they crop up in Joel songs -- that arbitrary. The three boys go off to war, and one is killed. So that's why Vietnam was fought: for the sake of romantic symmetry. Back home in Long Island, the remaining quartet drift and decline, but love and redemption somehow prevail, and all ends sappy, I mean happy, with the dead one giving his ghostly blessing.

Joel's songs really are dramatic, in their lyrical detail and in their dramatic sweep, and I'd far rather hear an original musical from him than from Elton John. Tharp's choreography, thrillingly emphatic in its mix of flashing lights and flashing legs, similarly matches yearning and aggression. At its best, the show has the same kind of excitement as the great dance musicals West Side Story and A Chorus Line. But its form prevents it from taking that extra, how you say, step.

2005-12-13-jonathan-james-moore:
Jonathan James-Moore

In 1966 at Cambridge, as the May Week show for the university's Amateur Dramatic Club, I directed a Feydeau farce, Hotel Paradiso, writes Robert Cushman. In the supporting role of Monsieur Martin, a barrister of overflowing geniality somewhat impeded by a spectacular stammer, I cast, on impulse and without audition, an imposing red-haired first-year undergraduate who had begun to establish himself as a magisterial comic presence at the Footlights and whose name was Jonathan James-Moore [obituary by Alan Strachan, 24 November].

It turned out to be the smartest casting decision I ever made. In the short term, Jonathan gave a virtuoso performance that stopped the show every night of the run; in the long, our association began a friendship that, reversing the usual order of things, developed into the longest, happiest and most productive working relationship I have known - though this time he was the one doing the directing.

It was in the BBC Radio Light Entertainment Department, some 15 years after our first meeting, that I wandered into his office at one end of Light Ent's fabled corridor to say that I had an idea for a Radio 3 programme on musicals, and would he kindly produce it? We made a pilot, which led to a series - eventually to half a dozen of them - which at his suggestion we called Book, Music and Lyrics; and which in turn led, over the course of 20 years, to other shows, both series and one-offs, of which our joint favourite - not only because it involved a series of wonderful trips to New York - was Sweet and Low Down, an informal history of Manhattan cabaret. We proved, I think, that it was possible to treat popular music on radio and to be entertaining without compromising anyone's intelligence: our subjects', our listeners' or our own.

As a producer, Jonathan was simply the best: shrewd, encouraging and endless fun to work with. About halfway through our two decades, he became head of the department. Jonathan prided himself on his political skills, but he must have been the least bureaucratic of BBC chiefs, and certainly one of the best-loved.
2005-12-17-pop-goes-the-pantomime-singal:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Snow White and the Group of Seven runs through Jan. 8 at the Elgin Theatre, 416-872-5555.

They call it a family musical but its still a pantomime. Just four years ago Ross Petty's panto subject at the Elgin was Snow White and the Magnificent Seven. The seven were small and therefore sort of traditional, even if they did take their group description from Hollywood, with a distant nod to Japan. Now the same story has come round again, this time thumbing a couple of noses at tradition, with a double dose of Canadian content.

Snow White and the Group of Seven pays homage on its backcloths to the local painters on whom it puns, but the people who live in the cottage where the heroine finds refuge aren't artists, at least not in that sense. Theyre a pop group, and three of them (Ryan Malcolm, Gary Beals, Billy Klippert) are -- Ill fess up, I only know this from the publicity -- alumni of Canadian Idol. Six of the seven are brothers -- the characters, I mean, not the performers -- and the seventh is their dad. He's played by Alan Frew, who was a Canadian idol before there was Canadian Idol, and who presides over the pack with an air of exasperated authority and in an accent of ripest Caledonian.

Well, why not? The original story of Snow White is bare-bones simple: Mirror, Dwarfs (not Dwarves, cf. the pedantic Prince of Into the Woods), Apple, time to go home. Something has to fill out the evening, and pantomime has always been cheerfully eclectic in its choice of filling. Despite what you may have heard, there is nothing revolutionary about having the cast break into current pop songs rather than show tunes. In the UK, where the panto form originated, they've been doing it for years, grabbing at whats middle-of-the- road topical in music as much as in humour.

But, here the music becomes part of the plot. The Group have rented what used to be the Dwarfs cottage in order to re-hone their act. This could mean that they're woodshedding in an actual woodshed. When Snow White moves in she becomes their manager and sends them out on the road, this being the cue for a miniature pop concert in which the boys show off all the different styles they can imitate. Needless to say, it's while theyre away seeking their fortunes that Snow Whites evil stepmother comes to call, bearing the poisoned apple. Only this time it's an apple-flavoured cookie, and the queen is disguised as a Girl Guide. O Canada. By the way, Snow White's fondness for apples has been carefully set up earlier in the show. This is something new: a pantomime with exposition.

Even newer, its a pantomime with deconstruction. At the climax, through some postmodern jiggery-pokery that went right over my unsophisticated head, the traditional fairy-tale ending is declared inoperative, and the forces of good and evil do battle with contrasting rock songs as their weapons The jury that decides the victor is composed, of course, of young members of the audience, and they have far more to do than most children who get pressed into panto service. They have, for one thing, to be hectored by Sean Cullen, whose role in the story is unclear (he keeps emerging from behind the mirror) but who works around it as a narrator-and- commentator figure. By the way, the voting is rigged and all ends happily. I dont think that's a spoiler.

David Finley's script is more cheerful than funny, and it can also be rather cumbersome. It gives Snow White a group of animal buddies who are so attentive that her official septet of protectors seem superfluous: How many friends can a girl have and still claim to be persecuted? But the shows heart is in the right place, and the recruiting, for the second year running, of Ted Dykstra as director gives the proceedings a renewed shot of energy and purpose. Hes ruthless with the conventions. There is no initial gambolling on the village green; there's no village green. Instead there is, courtesy of Tracey Flyte, choreography worthy of the name. And the inevitable singalong is down to just one chorus, with no competing comics setting the house against itself. Make a quick exit and you can miss it altogether.

One of the production's reforms has long been a feature of Pettys pantos. It consists of making the romantic leads interesting. They, this year, are another pair of ex-Idols. Elena Juatcos Snow White is a capable, sensible heroine of the kind pioneered in Disney's Beauty and the Beast (the film, not the show). Jamie McKnight is endearingly helpless as Prince Willie Wanderoff, who keeps getting lost. He even looks lost, though his beloved doesn't, when the two of them break into a duet, but then he has some cause to be -- the words that come out are only loosely attached to the situation, even by pantomime standards.

Apart from doing good musical service, the group act, at least as well as is called for. (Of course, playing wannabe pop stars is something at which theyve had practice.) Eddie Glenn manages to be endearing as the Princes comic sidekick, despite being handed some ropy material. And then there's Petty. As ever, he plays the villain, who in this case has to be the wicked queen. But this is one place where tradition strikes back. The pantomime dame (middle- aged comedian in drag) has always been a sympathetic character, definitely on the side of the goodies, and combining the huggable with the hissable doesn't work. The updating, too, seems to have left Petty behind. Some of his humour is whiskery (do the kids really appreciate a reference to Seinfeld's Soup Nazi?), and though he throws himself into his glam-rock number with admirable ardour, I suspect that his heart, like mine, is still with the show tunes.

Colour Photo: Bruce Zinger / The Idols have musical talent and are convincing as wannabe pop stars.
2005-12-21-short-plays-bring-out-politic:
THE WRECKING BALL

Theatre Centre

- - -

The code of conduct at The Wrecking Ball is simple. Some half- dozen playwrights are commissioned to write, in the course of a week, plays based on events in the news. The resulting texts -- which tend, for obvious reasons, to be short -- are then given barely rehearsed readings for one night only by an intrepid group of actors. At last Sunday night's show, the third of the series, both writers and performers constituted a fair cross-section of Toronto's finest.

Ross Manson, speaking for those in charge, cheerfully announced in his opening address that one of the authors had broken the rules. This was Michael Healey, who under the title Generous offered a scene already written from a play already scheduled (at the Tarragon). A six-hander, it displayed more craft and polish in its writing, if not always in its performances, than anyone was likely to come up with when composing under the gun. Its topicality, though, could not be faulted, as it showed a minority trying to maintain itself in power through foul means (fair ones obviously not worth considering) and foul language. It was Healey back somewhere close to his Plan B turf but with more wicked humour; whether he can keep up this vein of cheerfully black comedy over a whole play -- or even whether he intends to -- we wait, eagerly, to discover.

Of those who played the game, the best was Claudia Dey. A brief like the Wrecking Ball's will bring out either the journalist in writers -- usually the cartoon journalist -- or, as in Dey's case, the poet. Oil shortages were her starting point; her Slick Says it was the Land of Plenty and the Plenty was Mine was a monologue, set in the foreseeable future, for a disempowered U.S. gas-pump attendant, lamenting a way of life that has gone from unsustainable to unsustained: "no more garage suicides," and people are actually walking. Dey might be the Randy Newman of Canadian playwrights, giving a voice to those whom progress, or at least progressive thought, has left behind. Gord Rand, who played the title role in Dey's Trout Stanley, gave the piece perfect voice.

Adam Pettle's The Bleachers was similarly oblique in structure if not in tone, drawing on the reappearance of an old news item. Two teenage girls, their speech rhythms perfectly captured by author and actresses (Patricia Fagan and Monica Dottor), complain and smoke and goof off from class, before going off to kill the mother of one of them. Slight, and apparently written in just one day, it still showed Pettle making a welcome break from his recent folksy domestic plays, in the general direction of his powerful Theatre Direct play, Misha.

In between playlets, Alon Nashman and Tanja Jacobs, both seen to advantage throughout the evening in more conventional roles, appeared as, respectively, Harold Pinter and Ann Coulter, reading from his Nobel acceptance speech and her book. They presented a powerful image of two people with no interest in listening to one another, ever. Pinter, naturally, was the more elegantly stylish, but Coulter, to my discomfiture, and probably against the organizers' intentions, got off the most effective line -- something about liberal discourse (liberal being her mysterious term for left- wing-of-all-persuasions) consisting of saying "Bush lied" to a college audience pre-programmed to cheer.

The two remaining Ball-Wreckers played with this temptation, if finally skirting it. Both took on Iraq. (So did Dey's play but more obliquely.) Alex Poch-Goldin's Doublespeak was a monologue for a Bush speechwriter, a Republican with doubts, in mental search of an America worth fighting for. That's interesting, but it never came to life; the too-easy satire of its opening hung over it throughout. Matthew Edison's Captive Audience tried to get everything in: Christian peacemakers, torture-planespotters, Islamist terrorism and CIA abduction, America blackmailing Canada (10% back on softwood lumber) and Canada playing, I do believe, hardball. The common thread seemed to be that everyone was in some sense a hostage or a hostage-taker. Edison may have the makings of an epic play here, but at the moment it's a mess, in shorthand.

So when Manson calls, as he did on Sunday, for more political plays on Toronto stages, my response is "yes, but." Not if they're diagrams or animated slogans; Political theatre can be as escapist as any other kind of theatre, but it depends what you want to escape from. Besides, everything is political; or so said singer- songwriter Claire Jenkins, halfway through a half-time set in which she also sparred in a kind of musical slapstick with her violinist partner, Tom Howlett. Jenkins' best number, The Band Played On, shares a title, obviously, with a famous song of the 1890s. It also, less obviously, has the identical subject and situation to She Didn't Say Yes, a Jerome Kern delight from 1929.

Black & White Photo: Though playwright Michael Healey did not play by The Wrecking Ball's rules his previously written scene was topical.
2005-12-24-a-year-of-great-ensembles-loo:
robertcushman@lycos.com

This has been the year of great ensemble productions in and around Toronto. The five most exciting events of the year were A Whistle in the Dark, Half-Life, The Wild Duck, Orpheus Descending and The Last Days of Judas Iscariot. Each of them offered the high theatrical pleasure of a sizeable group of fine actors, all interlocking in a flawlessly orchestrated account a major play. Though I doubt that any of the plays would qualify as tragedies in a classical sense, they all dispensed generous quantities of pity and terror, shot through with laughter.

A Whistle in the Dark was the Canadian premiere of an alarmingly powerful 40-year-old play by the Irish dramatist Thomas Murphy. It was the first offering (there has yet to be a second) of a group called Company Theatre, who imported another Irishman, Jason Byrne, to direct it. He orchestrated a terrifying study of family violence, fuelled by social, sexual and political grudge, building to the extraordinary image of an old man striving to deny the horror that he himself had unleashed.

John Mighton's Half-Life, the year's best new Canadian play -- indeed the only item on the list that wasn't a revival or an import - - was as seemingly gentle as Whistle was aggressive, a study of the middle-aged watching their elders slipping away or, even more disturbingly, refusing to. It was the best offering of the year at Tarragon, though it must strictly count as a visiting production, mounted by Necessary Angel under their new artistic director Daniel Brooks, whose record there, so far, is impeccable.

The Wild Duck showed Soulpepper at its finest. Laszlo Marton stripped all didacticism from Ibsen's play (possibly his masterpiece) to show it as a searching tragi-comic study of self- delusion, which we already knew, and psychological cruelty to children, which we didn't, at least not with this degree of intensity. Some scenes were almost unbearable to watch, and not for sensationalist reasons.

Orpheus Descending had Miles Potter directing an absurdly strong Stratford cast (in the small Tom Patterson space, which made it seem even richer) in a Tennessee Wiliams play whose excesses, initially enjoyable as Southern Gothic, went on to make transfixing sense. It shared with Whistle and The Wild Duck the ability to keep spectators on the edge of their seats, both dreading and willing an inexorable climax.

The Last Days of Judas Iscariot, directed by David Ferry, was a political, religious and anachronistic extravaganza by an off-beat American playwright, Stephen Addy Guirgis, working with a wit and audacity well beyond the refined canons of Broadway or, indeed, off- Broadway. Loose-jointed and confessedly imperfect, mounted in an improvised space in the Distillery for a few performances, it was probably the freest and most exhilarating show of the year for actors and audiences alike (and they were sometimes hard to tell apart).

Part of the fun in this town is in seeing a loose-knit group of exceptional actors forming and re-forming; even those identified with the major companies get to play outside from time to time. Of those five top shows, Diego Matamoros was in three, going from a quiet, alert scientist in Half Life to a glorious, dangerous fool in The Wild Duck to a flamboyant, angry Satan in Judas; no actor can switch more electrically from a purr to a shout. Joseph Ziegler, Alon Nashman and Jonathan Goad were each in two. Nashman in Judas brought off a delightful double of Sigmund Freud and Doubting Thomas; Goad's stud in Orpheus was one of three outstanding performances he gave at Stratford, along with his beleaguered son in Whistle; and Ziegler's paterfamilias in Whistle, a cowering blowhard, was the male performance of the year. The female performance of the year was Seana McKenna's Lady in Orpheus, a superb combination of the passionate and the sensible, the tormented and the outrageously funny.

Just outside the charmed circle was Trout Stanley, outside only because, with a cast of merely three, Eda Holmes's production had to offer a narrower range of kicks. They were superb: Melody Johnson, Michelle Giroux -- two highly distinctive actresses, perfectly cast - - and the protean Gord Rand. (I borrow that description, gratefully, from one of our best playwrights.) Claudia Dey's play was the second best of the year, another stage in the development of a writer who was always wonderful with words and is increasingly good with stories and characters. She confirmed this in miniature with a monologue in the one-night Wrecking Ball, the last show of the year as Trout Stanley was the first. Otherwise, the best new Canadian writing was in Essay, a short piece by a new writer, Hannah Moscovitch, seen at Summerworks and surely to be seen again. After that there's a gulf, which is not too alarming in retrospect (how many good plays do you expect to see in a year?), but can feel so at the time.

There were other golden moments, though. William Hutt, making a graceful, but unsentimental, farewell by finding new and fiercer things to do with Prospero in The Tempest; Albert Schultz, who is some decades off having the same aura, but who brought a comparable skill and freshness to Hamlet; John Fitzgerald Jay giving a stunning wild-eyed performance in Enoch Arden; Mike Shara and David Storch, doing scary and delightful things in Take Me Out, which was also the best of Morris Panych's abundance of productions this year. Factory Theatre had a good year, Buddies in Bad Times had maybe their best times ever; and Theatre Passe Muraille bestirred itself with its Stage 3 season, which brought forward promising voices in Joseph Jomo Pierre and in Nicole Stamp, who was irresistible.

The best visiting show was Billy Crystal's. It was a terrible year for musicals unless they were festival revivals (the Shaw's Gypsy with Nora McLellan coming into her own, Stratford's Into the Woods). But at the big spots in town, Evita was tired, Wicked wicked (and not in any new-fangled positive sense) and Les Miserables miserable. There was far more fun and melody in Jonathan Larson's TickTick Boom at the sadly departed Poor Alex. Actually, the best musical I saw, by far, was the televised version of Jerry Springer: The Opera, which is the boldest and most inventive departure in the genre in years. There seems little chance in the Toronto that rejected Hairspray, Urinetown and even The Producers while embracing Wicked, but can we see it on stage?

Colour Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / Carolyn Hetherington in John Mighton's Half-Life, the year's best new Canadian play -- a study of the middle-aged watching their elders slipping away or, even more disturbingly, refusing to.; Colour Photo: Perter Redman, National Post / William Webster, Brent Carver, Diego Matamoros and Martha MacIsaac in The Wild Duck, which showed Soulpepper at its finest.
2005-12-31-a-peek-at-the-year-ahead:
robertcushman@lycos.com

One thing can be safely prophesied about the Soulpepper company's opening season at its new home in the Distillery District. The Young Centre, which Soulpepper will inhabit on what its artistic director, Albert Schultz, describes as "a time-share basis" with the George Brown Theatre School, will have the most inviting lobby in Toronto. Open even now for unofficial peeking and official ticket-buying, it's a long, spacious-seeming room with a bookstall promised at one end (an outcrop of Leonard McHardy's beloved Theatrebooks) and -- it warms my heart just to type it -- a functioning fireplace already blazing at the other.

Those who can tear themselves away will find that beyond the lobby there are theatres: two main stages, of which the larger looks like a more flexible version of the Harbourfront Centre Theatre that has housed many of Soulpepper's best productions in the past, plus a black box and a cabaret. Nine plays have been announced for the two principal spaces, amounting to a year-long repertory that will give the company a continuous presence unprecedented in the annals of non- commercial theatre in Canada -- or even, with the single and more grandiose exception of the National Theatre in London, England, outside it. (Urban institutional houses usually take summer holidays, while festivals shut up shop in the winter, as Soulpepper itself has previously done.) I think that's exciting.

Exciting, too -- maybe satisfying is more the word -- is the lineup of actors, which includes nine of the 12 founding members, as well as a bunch of others who have become closely associated. If I single out the young Martha MacIsaac, it's because I should have done so last week when retrospecting about The Wild Duck, for whose emotional impact she was largely responsible. There are also -- borrowed or plundered or whatever from the Shaw and Stratford festivals -- Ben Carlson and Jonathan Goad, of whom young actors hardly come any better.

To clarify: I like it when companies stay together -- I think it's the best way for a theatre to establish an identity -- but I think, too, that its members benefit from getting out and about now and then. I also feel, perhaps contradictorily, that our best actors, of whom there are a remarkable number, constitute a floating super-ensemble anyway.

Soulpepper's other strength has always been its programming, of plays that you can't see anywhere else. As far as I can tell, of those they're doing next year, only one (The Importance of Being Earnest) has been given a major production by any other Toronto company within the last 20 years. And yes, that does include King Lear. This is par for their course; of those they have staged in their preceding eight years of existence, only one (Twelfth Night) has turned up anywhere else in the past two decades. And yes, that does include Hamlet. The cause is not exactly timidity in other theatres -- they have their own, more domestic, fish to fry -- and the picture is of course different if you bring in Stratford and Niagara, but Toronto is supposed to be a theatrical metropolis in its own right. Some of the plays Soulpepper has done (Our Town, The Bald Soprano, The Lesson, a couple of one-act Chekhovs) even I had never seen before, anywhere, ever. One (Olympia), I'd never even heard of. They got to some of the rarer European classics in their catalogue (Don Carlos, Platonov, Nathan the Wise) ahead of London, which is supposed to set the pace in these things.

The coming season plucks only one play (Gogol's The Government Inspector) from that old Continental shelf. It's contrastingly heavy on plays from the second half of the last century: Ionesco, Pinter, Stoppard, Mamet, all of whom have been at sometime tagged with the absurd "absurdist" label, and who do have family likenesses. Something's been left out, and consistently so. Of plays written in English before 1900, Soulpepper has done only a few Shakespeares and She Stoops to Conquer. I have a hunch that older English plays are harder than older foreign ones, which get done after all in modern translations, but there are some rich pickings out there, all unpicked.

I spent a few days in November at the pleasantest theatre I know, the Swan in Stratford-upon-Avon, watching the Royal Shakespeare Company's Gunpowder season (now transferred to London), consisting of Elizabethan and Jacobean plays that were considered, in their own time, censorably dangerous. They still seemed apposite now. There were two rapier-sharp studies of villainous realpolitik, both prudently set in and around ancient Rome: Ben Jonson's Sejanus, which I'd never thought would work but did, and Philip Massinger's Believe As You List (retitled, for good reason, Believe What You Will), which I'd always thought would work, and did. There was Thomas Middleton's The Old Law (retitled, for no good reason, A New Way to Please You), a riotous comedy about enforced euthanasia for octogenarians (already an endangered species in 17th-century England, one would have thought), leading to all kinds of heartless scheming by hopeful heirs. The only mild misfire was Sir Thomas More, which has one startling speech that's probably by Shakespeare but otherwise played like a lesser Man for All Seasons. And these, remember, aren't even the recognized classics of the period. We have a long way to go.

The Stratford Festival, at least, is making a start. It staged Marlowe's Edward II this past year, and is doing Webster's The Duchess of Malfi, directed by Peter Hinton, who seems ideal casting, next. It's throwing in a Moliere and a Corneille as well, but I don't know how much credit it will get. Stratford can program Aeschylus, Aristophanes, Giraudoux, a couple of Sartres and Peter Hinton, all in one year, and still be accused of playing safe. It can cram six of the riskiest Shakespeares into two seasons, and still be found wanting against the RSC, though the latter balanced its Gunpowder adventure with a Shakespeare lineup consisting of As You Like It, Twelfth Night, A Midsummer Night's Dream and -- as a mad experimental gesture -- The Comedy of Errors.

Endnote: Several members of the super-ensemble mentioned above are featured in the upcoming Lord of the Rings, of which you may have heard. One among them is Carly Street, a newcomer who's relevant here for a coruscating performance in a rare Marivaux (is there any other kind?), The Dispute, that was a jewel on the 2005 fringe. She went on to play a fine Portia in Shakespeare in the Rough's Merchant of Venice. Look out for her. I'm told she can sing, too.

2006-01-06-vanity-project-leaves-actor-a:
Until Jan. 15. (416)-504-7529.

HAMLET (SOLO)

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, Toronto

- - -

A few years ago Robert Lepage came to town with a one-man Hamlet that was very hi-tech and, if memory serves, made occasional surreptitious use of an extra actor. Raoul Bhaneja, offering his own solitary take on the play, has no truck with such extraneous aids. He comes before us, unsupported by tricky lighting or sound effects, a sensitive young man in a black sweater that takes us right back to the old existentialist days of Jean-Paul Sartre. To be, that is the question.

For setting, Bhaneja has a simple brick wall, against which, when one or another of the characters he plays feels specially intense, he bangs his head. In another sense, he's banging his head against a brick wall all night. The question arises, just as it did with Lepage: Whats the point? And the answer comes back the same now as it did then: There isnt one.

It's not as if Hamlet, the character, doesn't provide enough to keep any actor occupied. Even in a conventional production, we have to spend a lot of time in that actors company, and the experience can get very wearing if he doesnt click. Whether he does or he doesn't, one thing that usually makes the evening go faster is the presence of other actors in other roles, adding texture and promoting interplay.

In such circumstances, Bhaneja might make an interesting Hamlet; he is in command of the text, suggests an active mind and has a compelling line in instant hysteria. This surfaces to especial effect just after he's seen the Ghost, and later when he turns, with an unusual degree of spite, on his errant mother. He also offers the occasional new reading. The air bites shrewdly; it is very cold, uttered on the battlements as he awaits his ghostly father, becomes "is it very cold?" This Hamlet is apparently such a skeptic, he cant even trust his own senses. But its hard to see the character or to develop any feeling for him, because he has to keep stopping and turning into other people.

The best of his multiple performances is probably Claudius, who begins as a stereotypically jovial villain but then develops a tormenting conscience that he has to abandon when his talents for conspiracy, plus the need for self-preservation, prove too great to resist. But a man can only do so much, and Bhaneja begins to run out of voices. Some of those he rings in come from the British Isles, where he has in fact worked; his Polonius sounds Welsh while his Rosencrantz and Guildenstern -- Hamlet's fellow students, mark you - - are oafishly Cockney, like heavies from a Guy Ritchie movie. Horatio, by contrast, is so gentle he almost fades into the brickwork.

Visually, Bhaneja manages the instant changes very well. He and his director, Robert Ross Parker, have developed a graceful repertoire of movements and gesture that enables one character's action to merge into the next ones response. Especially striking is the sight and sound of Ophelia sobbing even, it seems, as Hamlet and company leave the stage. The aural hand-overs are trickier; theyre done at the same unnatural speed that a ventriloquist uses to switch voices with his dummy. The text has been keenly and ruthlessly cut (one whole soliloquy gone, and not a sign of Fortinbras) with an eye to comfort and clarity; I still wonder, though, if someone unfamiliar with the play would know what was going on. Probably the most commanding lines are interpolations: Bhaneja's brisk calls, in his own person, for lights, "intermission," and blackout The last carries an inescapable subtext of "There! I've done it." The production is a vanity project, but it differs from most in leaving the impression that the actor, as well as the audience, deserves better.

2006-01-07-the-songs-will-live-on-foreve:
robertcushman@lycos.com

You know it when you hear it, but it's hard to put a name to. Its an area of song bordered on four sides by Broadway, Hollywood, jazz and the pop marketplace sometimes known as Tin Pan Alley. It held sway in the United States, and also conquered most of the Western world, during the first half of the 20th century. It was celebrated and chronicled in 1972 by Alec Wilder in a book titled American Popular Song that was immediately hailed as definitive, and has remained so. Tony Bennett, when asked about it, said simply, "Its the Bible."

Wilder's title, however, prompts a few questions. The urban style he celebrates wasn't the only kind of music before 1950 to be both popular and American, even if it was arguably the best, and certainly got the most attention and the most airplay. More recently, admirers have been referring to the the Great American Songbook, but that carries the implication that the book is now closed. There is also Classic American Popular Song, which is the title adopted -- with some misgivings -- by two writers, David Jenness and Don Velsey, for a new book (Routledge) that is an avowed sequel, and a less avowed supplement, to Wilders.

This is a book that had to be written, though one hardly dared hope that it would have been written this well. Its lively, intelligent and awe-inspiringly thorough. So was Wilder's, but his tone and approach were different. He was both a distinguished composer and a distinguished curmudgeon, and his very personal book (published by Oxford, and still very much available) has an engaging air of being made up as it goes along. Though neither Jenness nor Velsey is a professional academic, theirs is a more obviously scholarly work -- which doesn't make it immune to the odd factual howler. Several of these concern Duke Ellington, whose highly collaborative ouevre slips through their fingers as it did through Wilders.

The new boys have different axes to grind. Wilder, who subtitled his book The Great Innovators, 1900-1950, believed the world came to an end, musically speaking, in, at the latest, 1965. Jenness and Velsey, whose subtitle is The Second Half-Century, 1950-2000, think it still goes on, if in commercially diminished terms, and they make a persuasive case.

There is an overlap. Wilder ignored his 1950 cut-off date to pursue the later careers of Irving Berlin, Richard Rodgers, Cole Porter, Harold Arlen and their lesser-known peers. (Jerome Kern and George Gershwin were already dead.) Jenness and Velsey retrace these steps and amplify them. They are dead right, I think, in their assessment of the splendours and miseries of Rodgers and Hammerstein v. the earlier Rodgers and Hart. And theyre wonderful on Arlen -- the very first song they treat is his snappy, unknown I Love a New Yorker, which put me on their side from the start. They are also able to do justice to Wilder's own songs, which he, of course, had to ignore.

Like Wilder, they insist they are concerned with theatre songs only to the extent that they can be sung and understood out of context. This was all right for Wilder, who wrote of an era when theatre songs were pop songs, and were more or less interchangeable between shows. Post-1940, musicals had greater dramatic identity, and songs are more firmly tied to sources. They cannot be ignored, though, because they're too good -- as good, our authors claim, as their predecessors, and they have the arguments and analyses to back this up.

So they tie themselves in a few knots, claiming, for example, that comedy songs are outside their purview. They turn out to be inconsistent about this, though not, to my taste, inconsistent enough. We get discussions of West Side Story minus Gee, Officer Krupke, and of Guys and Dolls (Frank Loesser is rightly one of their heroes) minus Adelaides Lament. They do, however, persuade me of the merits of Ive Never Been in Love Before, the one song in the latter score that I'd always dismissed.

Among later theatre composers, they pay rapturous attention to Cy Coleman, whose superb jazz-influenced songs may never have received serious treatment in print before. (I wish he could have lived to see it -- he died in 2004.) They are also properly admiring of Coleman's much undervalued lyricist Carolyn Leigh. They deal more systematically with lyrics than Wilder did, and a few word men, such as Johnny Mercer, get sections of their own.

Stephen Sondheim gets a chapter more or less to himself, pointing out (apparently it still needs to be said) that his work isnt cold and that his music is as good as his lyrics.

Its also noted that in his later scores he's often abandoned the old compressed song structures. This, plus his frequently unromantic subject matter, makes him a distinctively contemporary figure, even outside the theatre.

Unlike Wilder, Jenness and Velsey don't hate rock, but they dont think it has much relevance to the tradition theyre discussing. They do admit the influence of the singer-songwriters, from Dylan on. The irony (they're politer about this than I would be) is that these writers have been praised for doing what Sondheim and a few of his theatrical successors have done better: without formlessness and -- since they're dramatists -- without the self-pity that too often gets equated with honesty.

As exceptions, with which Id concur, the book names Joni Mitchell and especially Randy Newman, a dramatist manque with dynastic ties to old Hollywood.

In a book that gets in nearly everything (I count myself an aficionado but was amazed at the cabaret songs I didnt know), one notices the gaps. The most glaring omission is Oscar Brown, Jr., who shone in the '60s and unites any number of traditions -- he came from jazz, he was a singer-songwriter, he worked in the theatre, he wrote both love songs and protest songs, he had links to rock and even to rap. When it comes to technical analysis, the authors devote more space to harmony than did Wilder, who was a melody man.

This makes their book harder work for a layman, but you can usually see what they're getting at. It helps, of course, if you already know the songs, but everybody knows some of them, even now. That is the greatest hope for the Classic Song: Its attracting young singers, young writers, young listeners. It will never again be the popular form, but it will survive.

There is little analysis, musical or historical, in Ken Blooms coffee-table book The American Songbook: The Singers, The Songwriters and The Songs, but there is plenty of fact and anecdote, lavish illustration, and the occasional quite biting opinion. (Nat King Cole did all his good work in the '40s; Bobby Darin had "absolutely no depth." Ear of the beholder.)

The book is arranged in three biographical sections. First come the singers, a long but inevitably incomplete list: The fine Johnny Hartman makes it into the blurb but not into the book and there are no entries for figures as smooth as Vic Damone or as quirky as Shirley Horn. Then there are the bandleaders, but only a few: My favourite, Woody Herman, is missing.

Finally, the real meat of the book, there are the composers and lyricists. Bloom omits most of the post-1960 show-writers on the grounds -- a plain man's variant on Jenness and Velsey -- that they had no pop hits. Interestingly, though, when he does write about them, he does so in terms of scores rather than songs. (He is, I suspect, more a theatre than a pop or jazz animal; he has an equally handsome companion-book on Broadway.) Im puzzled by his references to the title song of Bye Bye Birdie -- I didnt think it had one. Most fascinating are the minor figures: I never expected to read a whole page on Sidney Mitchell and Lew Pollack (They wrote At the Codfish Ball for Shirley Temple.)

The sidebars include lavish song lists, happily not confined to the obvious hits, and my favourite story, about a songwriter with a stump instead of a hand, using it to pound a man's head against a saloon bar. That's Harry Woods, said a friend when the cops came. "He wrote Try a Little Tenderness."

Agins, The New York Times / The new book pays rapturous attention to superb songwriter Cy Coleman.

HUMBLE BOY

Tarragon Theatre

- - -

Bumble bee, Humble Boy. Charlotte Jones' clever and charming play, five-years old and English, begins with a snatch of Rimsky- Korsakov's flute specialty, and follows up with the entrance of Felix Humble, an overweight young man who makes straight for the large hive in the corner of his parents' garden. The bees, however, have flown, or been evicted.

Felix is a research physicist working on String Theory, which is apparently an attempt to explain everything. (It tries to reconcile relativity and quantum mechanics, two theories that are incompatible.) As a friend of his mother's says, "If you have to research anything, everything would be the thing to research."

By that exacting standard, Jones' play doesn't quite add up. It doesn't find a connection between all of its elements, which include not just the habits of bees but the flowering of roses, the nature of grief and of love, a touch of class conflict and the plot of Hamlet. Felix's father, a biology teacher and amateur entomologist with a consuming desire to find and name a new bee species, has died, and his mother is about to re-marry, with a man of whom Felix violently disapproves. The Claudius to her Gertrude is the retired owner of a fleet of buses; he's also something of a Polonius, being the father of Felix's cast-off girlfriend. This Ophelia, though, has gone anything but mad; though she did get a bit angry, she has pulled herself together, borne a daughter, and become a nurse. There is also a gardener who wanders on and off, telling Felix things about Nature; I thought he might equal the First Gravedigger, but I turned out to be very wrong.

In more recent British terms, Humble Boy may be said to explore Tom Stoppard themes in Alan Ayckbourn territory. The cosmic concerns, though, don't always mesh with the domestic. You may say that Felix is trying to make sense of his own life as well as of the universe, but that's terribly vague. It's a gap in the writing, and also possibly in Richard Rose's production, that it never establishes Felix at the centre of things. He is a Hamlet without soliloquies, hence an unprivileged Hamlet, just one point-of-view among several. Dean Paul Gibson plays him delightfully, a self- tormenting brain in a shell both physically and emotionally gauche, but if he undergoes any kind of spiritual journey (as other characters keep hinting he does) the steps are far from clear.

Humble's mom is granted a recognizable epiphany -- a reversal of her Shakespearean prototype -- and Fiona Reid carries off the transformation triumphantly. Transformation is the word, since in the earlier part of the play she's been depicted, with relish, as both shallow and selfish, qualities on which Reid deploys her high- comedy skills, starting with an entrance in which she radiates impatient disdain through dark glasses atop a black funeral dress. You wonder why Felix should want to redeem her, but you're pleased when he does.

It's a fine actors' evening all round, with every character given both a solid place in the ensemble and at least one triumphant solo. Nicola Lipman all but stops the show as an exploited dowdy who, asked to say grace, revolts by loading it with any number of qualifying clauses; it doesn't take up much space on the page, but while she says it, time is suspended. Michael Ball is enthusiastically boorish as the unsuitable suitor who is allowed a mind, heart and wracking memories of his own; he also has a Glenn Miller fetish he's carried into the digital age. Sarah Dodd plays some of her moments of wit and wisdom rather too obviously as moments, but she's still immensely captivating, making sense and practicality sexy. She has a love scene with Felix that dissolves into farce but leaves you feeling, even as it does so, prepared to kill the author if she doesn't allow the two of them to get back together. Ian D. Clark rounds out the company as the gentle horticulturalist. The women, by the way, are named Flora and Rosie. In this pastoral setting it seems appropriate that even the director should be called Rose.

It's a show to be relished for its constantly shifting surfaces rather than for its dubious depths. It has wit, both structural and verbal, and a mastery of tone. The flute comes back at the end but there is no sting in the tail. Felix's, and the play's, last words are the very same with which Hamlet surrendered himself to fate: "Let be." Or, as the original spelling might very well have had it, "Let bee".
