2006-01-14-too-many-stories-not-enough-d:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Homechild runs through Jan. 28 at the Bluma Appel, 416-368-3110. Bombay Black runs through Jan. 22 at Theatre Centre, 416-538-0988.

CanStage has a habit of mounting its bigger plays -- bigger, that is, in intellectual and emotional scope, such as The Goat or The Shape of Things -- in its smaller spaces and its smaller plays in its biggest. The latest example of this vice versatility is Joan Macleod's Homechild, a conventional domestic drama set in an Ontario farmhouse surrounded, on the wide stage of the Bluma Appel, by a lot of rocks.

Perched at the back on some of these as the play begins is a very young girl making a speech. What she is talking about is hard to distinguish since the actress (Lara Jean Chorostecki) is required both to shed years and to talk in a Scots accent while addressing the audience from what seems a very long way away, and the combination defeats her.

This gets the evening off to a confusing start from which neither the play nor Martha Henrys production ever really recovers. Its hard to concentrate on Scene Two when you're still trying to come to grips with Scene One, and so on down the line.

The overbearing ruggedness of Astrid Janson's set seems partly prompted by the plays depiction of an isolated way of life that is under present threat, but it may also owe something to a supposed larger, historical theme. I say supposed" because, as so often happens, that theme is more evident in the publicity and the program notes than on the stage. A hundred years ago, give or take, Canadas population was swollen by an influx of British children, dispatched by orphan charities, who were badly treated when they got here. The play is concerned to expose this ancient scandal, but it doesn't get around to it until the evening is almost over.

We're told, finally, about a brother and sister who came over from Scotland and were heartlessly separated. The brother, now 80, is Alistair, who owns the farm and who never talks about his sister but dreams of her constantly; hence, we eventually work out the mysterious prologue. Their story, though, doesnt seem all that terrible in proportion to the amount of time weve been kept waiting to hear about it. Indeed, and rather self-defeatingly, it pales in comparison with what we're told about their lives back home with their mother.

Alistair has a stroke, and his secret comes out, prompting his daughter, Lorna, who left for the city and feels self-conscious about it, to track her aunt down and effect a reunion, even though Alistair protests, bitterly, that it's the last thing he wants. The scenes involving father and daughter are the best, and the best acted, in the play. Eric Petersons Alistair starts out as merely another in his line of cranky old men (this is his third play in succession portraying some kind of invalid and the second in which hes been hooked up to a saline drip) but goes on to have a haunted, touching scene in which he gets to interact with his phantom sibling. He follows it up with a volatile mix of shame and anger that eventually and thrillingly explodes. Brenda Robins, always at her best when not required to play brittle, does an admirably straightforward, caring job on Lorna.

Barbara Gordon, a late arrival, is just as unsentimentally sympathetic, though it's hard to believe in the past she's said to bring with her. Others in a blue-chip cast -- Patricia Hamilton, Randy Hughson, Tom Rooney -- seem to be there merely to kill time as friends and family, though the capacity of Hughson and (especially) Rooney to make passably amusing lines sound like sparkling epigrams is much appreciated. Nor could I see what was added by Joyce Campions role as another old orphan girl, apart from the mystery of why she has kept her (London) accent while her Scots contemporaries have lost theirs. Anecdotally, there is too much going on. Dramatically, there isnt enough.

- - -

Much the same could be said of Anosh Irani's Bombay Black, though the anecdotage here is first-rate. The title refers to a cheap drug, "a mixture of hashish and boot-polish, available but not recommended at the dance parlour that's the plays setting. Its also a fair description of the desperate circumstances of the play's three characters. Apsara is an exotic dancer, Indian-style; that is, she really can dance, with her clothes on, and the customers can't touch. Padma is her mother and, for want of a better word, manager. (The mother-daughter relationship has all the coziness of a cross between Gypsy and The Beauty Queen of Leenane.)

Kamal is a bookseller who comes to see Apsara dance -- oddly, as hes blind. But it turns out the three have a shared village past -- one that explains Kamals blindness -- and the play unfolds partly as a love story, partly as a study in the oldest of all dramatic subjects, the ethics of revenge.

It isn't diffuse like Homechild but it does flag, partly because some scenes go on way too long (especially a couple of chaste erotic fantasies), partly because the script consists almost entirely of duologues.

On the rare occasions when the entire cast is allowed onstage, the author does nothing with them and can hardly wait to get them off again. Nightswimming, the group that developed the play, go on in their program note about having a bold visual style" well, Camellia Koo's set is striking with its carpet and swinging bed, and there is, obviously, dancing. Apsara is good at her job and looks especially terrific at the start, in silhouette. But basically the play is all talk.

It is, however, very good talk: pungent and lyrical and sometimes witty. Line by line, Irani never hits a false note. The actors, however, under Brian Quirts direction, hit several. They are liable to pump feelings into lines that dont need them, or to stonewall in the face of situations that do. Not that they don't have their moments. Anita Majumdar doesn't have the chops, or maybe just the experience, for the emotional assault-course that the play wishes on Apsara, but she can be touching and she can be tough. Sanjay Talwar (recently very funny in The Trials of Judas Iscariot) is sweet but doesnt have the variety to sustain Kamals essentially passive role. Deena Aziz's silky Padma is enliveningly cynical at the start, but when the play calls for passionate extremes, she settles for melodrama. Still, clap hands; there could be a dramatist here.

2006-01-18-how-julie-met-the-boy-friend-:
Julie Andrews asked me, on the phone from Los Angeles, if I remembered Educating Archie. As one whose childhood occurred in England in the 1950s, I certainly did. It was a BBC radio comedy show, very popular with the younger set since it revolved around a ventriloquist's dummy, a perpetual schoolboy named Archie Andrews. It ran for years, with many changes of cast, but the 15-year-old Julie was one of the originals.

Half a century on, she mused for a moment on the bizarre phenomenon of a sound-only ventriloquist act. Mind you, in those halcyon days, people even accepted radio conjours.

"You played Archie's girl-friend," I said.

She corrected me with the crisp friendliness that has defined her from those days to this. "Not exactly. I was the girl next door." That she was, a well-behaved young lady in contrast to the more mischievous young females with whom Archie spent most of the show getting into scrapes. Actually, young Julie's verbal exchanges with Archie were the merest prelude to the real reason for her presence on the show -- her weekly song.

She was already a stage and radio veteran, part of an act known as Ted and Barbara Andrews and Julie. Barbara was her mother, Ted her stepfather. They toured the country's music halls, and were also mainstays of an even more venerable radio variety series, a lunch- hour relic of the war called Workers' Playtime. Gradually, Julie became the mainstay and focus of the act.

"I had a genuinely freakish voice, with a huge range and an adult larynx. I could sing operatic arias." She made her West End solo debut, doing just that at the London Hippodrome. She was 12. She became a solo attraction.

Her subsequent Broadway and Hollywood career is fabled: My Fair Lady, Camelot, Mary Poppins (P. L. Travers, the fearsome author of the original stories told her "you're too pretty, but you've got the nose for it"), The Sound of Music, Victor/Victoria, plus non- singing roles in satirical comedy (The Americanization of Emily) and even a Hitchcock thriller (Torn Curtain). But it all started, theatrically, with The Boy Friend. That was the show that brought her to the United States in 1954, and it's now the show with which she has made her debut as a director. Her production, first seen at the Goodspeed musical-revivals house in Connecticut, has been touring the U.S. and it opens tonight at the Royal Alex in Toronto.

The Boy Friend was already a British phenomenon when first it played New York: A loving period re-creation of the tunefully absurd musicals of three decades earlier ("a new musical of the 1920s" said the posters) that set London long-run records. The London producers wouldn't release the West End cast, so an entirely new British team was recruited for Broadway. Julie was cast as the heroine.

The original U.S. opening of The Boy Friend is famous for having had trouble on the road. At least, that's what I'd thought; "We didn't go on the road," said Julie. "We had all our troubles in previews in New York." In full view, so to speak. "Cy Feuer [of the producing team, Feuer and Martin] thought the show needed to reach an extra level; that what had been a sweet piece of lace in London wasn't viable on Broadway, where the ante automatically goes up. There were ... disagreements." Sandy Wilson -- the show's author, lyricist and composer -- was barred from the theatre, as was the British director Vida Hope. Feuer himself took over and the show was a hit -- though less of one than in London.

So who was right? "They were probably both right -- and I don't say that just to be tactful. The producers were right in their own terms, though maybe they weren't wildly tactful about it at the time." (Wilson, to judge from his autobiography, certainly thought they weren't. He decided in the end to take the money and gracefully walk.)

Julie, during all these battles, was keeping her head down, a nervous 20-year-old new to Broadway, "learning on my feet, very fast. All I knew when I came to the States was how to belt out a song and," she says diplomatically, recalling those valuable early days on the halls, "how to deal with certain audiences. Thank God for variety."

There's always been steel behind that English propriety. One remembers Alan Jay Lerner, one of her idols and mentors, recalling her rock-like solidity in the even more fraught pre-opening circumstances of Camelot: "She makes you wonder how the British ever lost their Empire." And the current, very entertaining, British stage version of Mary Poppins, in which the title character becomes almost a supporting role, makes you reflect that being Julie Andrews can't be as easy as she makes it look.

Her own production of The Boy Friend falls, by her account, between the poles of the delicate London and brash New York originals. The show, she says, has a "sweet inanity -- it's endearing. You have to steer a course between being camp and arch, and 'aren't we being funny?' " The show is set in Wilson's idea of the '20s musical idea of the French Lido; the designer is Julie's first husband, Tony Walton. "Visually, we've borrowed from Raoul Dufy, who was painting the South of France at just that time; he has a radiance that transports us to that period. Of course, people now don't know what the musicals of the '20s were like, but we've tried to make it like bubbles in a glass of champagne." On previous legs of the tour the production has been greeted, she says, "either with condescension or outright delight. I hope that audiences will come out smiling and toe tapping." In her first venture as a director, Julie seems to have been having a feel-good time. "I'd love to do more directing. It's been nervous-making, but I'm fond of my company, I feel they're my family. And they tell me the Royal Alex is a beautiful little theatre, just right for the show." Well, up here we think it's quite big, but after the barns they've been playing in, we know what they mean.

THE BOY FRIEND

Royal Alexandra Theatre, Toronto

I can never think of The Boy Friend, Sandy Wilson's "new musical comedy of the 1950s", as a parody. I suppose it qualifies as pastiche, but even that word suggests a degree of aloof calculation that hardly fits. I've said in the past that Wilson, who knocked this show off as a very young man around 1953, used the '20s style quite naturally, as if he really thought that was the only way to write musicals. His subsequent shows give the lie to that, but though some of them are interesting, none have been anything like as successful. On this show, he landed on a peculiar kind of home base, and created a peculiar kind of masterpiece.

It's a crystallization. Wilson squeezes the '20s form to its essentials, which he sees as charm, innocence and verbal and musical ingenuity. Sometimes he improves on the originals. The carefree love duet, I Could Be Happy with You, which defines the show, is far more delicate and elastic than I Want to Be Happy, the Vincent Youmans tune that must have inspired it, while Wilson's Room in Bloomsbury is at least as desirable a residence as Noel Coward's Room in Bloomsbury. Each of the songs has a teasing modulating verse to set it up, while the multiple rhymes and the air of precocious wisdom that they generate are pure '20s if not purer: "He is simply a necessity/If you want to get on/And we may as well confess it, he/ Is our sine qua non." Only Stephen Sondheim in Follies was to catch the tone so exactly, but he used it to make extra-curricular points. Wilson revels in it for its own sake.

One thing he neglected, though, was narrative. A real '20s or '30s musical comedy -- No No Nanette or Anything Goes -- has a profusion of storylines that are positively Dickensian compared to The Boy Friend which gives us boy getting, losing, and re-getting girl with the absolute minimum of complication. Love at first sight is a lovely thing; it saves so much time. There are no comic sub- plots, principally because there are no comics. One thing The Boy Friend lacks that its models had is bad jokes. It doesn't have many good ones either, but there are a few. Anyway, Polly Browne, at finishing school in the south of France, falls in love with Tony. Each thinks the other is poor, which shows how nice they are, but they're both really rich, which shows how happy they'll be if the niceness ever runs out. At one point Polly thinks Tony's a thief, on remarkably flimsy evidence, but she realizes he isn't when he turns up at the Carnival Ball wearing a Pierrot costume. Or something. The show's last act has nothing to do but postpone this reunion with a series of divertissements, most of which in this production do divert.

The Boy Friend is a hard show to get right, partly because we are now further from the '50s than the '50s were from the '20s. It's all old now, and likely to be packaged as generalized nostalgia, which was certainly not Wilson's attention. It can easily be either too quaint or too raucous. Julie Andrews, who was Broadway's first Polly and directed this revival, gets the tone mostly right, though some of the details make the teeth clench. I accept that the ensemble of Polly's friends and fellow flappers have to squeal from time to time, but they shouldn't be doing it in quotation marks. Polly herself (Jessica Grove) has to try to be sweet, which is a self- defeating exercise. Her Tony (Sean Palmer) is good on demeanour but short on personality. Wilson's devout belief in what he was doing can make us believe, too, and even care, but it doesn't happen here.

The show looks, however, great, especially when there's dancing going on. I don't think I've ever seen a bad Charleston on stage; I guess you have to do it well to do it at all. But the two routines here -- the first a pas de deux, the second a pas d'everybody -- are exceptionally knock-out. John DeLuca is the choreographer; Andrea Chamberlain (Maisie) sets them alight as she does everything else she touches, even the dialogue. Rick Faugno, her vis-a-vis, is no great actor but his feet hardly touch the ground. The still-great Tony Walton has designed a second-act set that brings the Riviera to refulgent carnival life, and the still-great Richard Pilbrow has lit it superbly; he ends one night-time number with a positive sunburst, but nobody said musicals were realistic. Paul Carlin is charmingly embarrassed as a reluctant older swain; Nancy Hess as the head mistress (that's one of the jokes) who ensnares him is insufficiently formidable but can certainly sing. A great production of The Boy Friend (the best I've seen was a London revival directed by the author) can be both intoxicating and enchanting. In this one, you settle for intoxication.

Black & White Photo: Diane Sobolewski, Mirvish / Polly (Jessica Grove) falls in love with Tony (Sean Palmer), and then the trials of true love begin.
2006-01-21-attack-of-the-cloned-sons-a-n:
robertcushman@lycos.com; A Number plays through Feb. 11 at the Berkeley Upstairs, 416-872-1111; Return plays through Jan. 29 at the Tarragon Extra Space, 416-531-1827.

Caryl Churchill is doing A Number, and a very good one, on the subject of cloning. Churchill, an unflaggingly active British dramatist since the 1970s, has written plays that range from the brilliant (Top Girls) to the atrocious (Serious Money). But she has always been an original, nobody's clone.

A Number presents a father and his sons, three of them out of an unknowable quantity: "a number," as the play says in its very first line, a phrase that's arresting and has become downright chilling four lines later. Thirty-five years ago, the father, whose name is Salter, traded his anti-social four-year-old son in for a newer test- tube model. (The original boy's mother, unstable, according to Salter, was dead. "She was one of those people when they say there has been a person under a train and the trains are delayed, she was a person under a train.") The scientists executing the process took advantage of the opportunity to produce more than the one clone. One was sent home with his dad; the others were dispersed.

Now, in just under an hour's playing time, Salter is confronted by three of his sons in turn: the original called Bernard, the replacement also called Bernard and one of the random others, name of Michael. His issue have issues, or at least two of them do. Bernard 1 not unnaturally hates Bernard 2, for whom he was dispossessed. Both of them, also for understandable reasons, hate their father. One of them always has.

Arguments about nature and nurture have presumably been going on since Adam and Eve fell to wondering where they'd gone wrong with Cain and Abel (who, not to give too much away, are relevant). I don't think the play has as much to say on the matter as some critics have claimed. But it has a lot to say about the perils of fatherhood and the needs, fears and resentments of sons, and it says them in short, unpunctuated speeches that come so fast upon one another that they virtually overlap. In these duologues one character will complete or anticipate another's thoughts, sometimes accurately, sometimes not. Audience and actors are kept on their toes.

Salter, the father, is a study in overlapping all by himself. Repugnantly cold-blooded (see again his description of his wife's death), he still wants, like everyone, to think well of himself. He takes some responsibility for his failure with his first son, though he admits more than perhaps he knows. Nothing in the play is more chilling than his telling how he felt perfectly safe leaving the house because he knew that the boy would be too scared to get out of bed. In the same breath, though, he will boast of how hard he tried with his second. And perhaps, by his own lights, he did. He initially sees the cloning revelation as a chance to make money, and he never quite gives up on the idea. Thinking in the play's own terms, one wonders what Salter's own bringing-up was like: Is there any cause in nature, or nurture, that makes these hard hearts?

For the second time this CanStage season (The Goat was the first), a notable play has been given less than it deserves. David Storch has mounted it traverse-style, on a strip of stage with the audience on both sides. This sounds as if it should aid concentration, but in fact it hinders it. With just two actors squaring off at any given time, we spend the evening looking at their profiles and our fellow-spectators' faces. As Salter, Gary Reineke strikes a nice initial balance between the suave and the shifty, but never moves beyond it. The role was created in London by Michael Gambon ("the great Gambon," Ralph Richardson called him), who can switch in an instant from geniality to terrifying cruelty, and the play must have been a whole different experience.

The three sons are played of course by the same actor, and Shawn Doyle does a fine job of differentiating them. With no obvious physical effort, he conveys the in-grown hardness of the elder Bernard, the deepening disillusion of the younger and the cheerfulness of the human experiment Michael. That's the play's kicker; Michael, who presumably was fostered, is happy, and nothing Salter can say will make him declare otherwise. All it took, apparently, was not being raised by Salter, though without Salter, Michael, and the indefinite number of Richards, would not have been. As Michael himself says, as if knowing how out of place he must seem in a Significant Modern Play, "Sorry."

Traverse-staging works better for Return (The Sarajevo Project) which has a larger cast and more action. This show, to which we have been looking forward for about four years, is enjoyable and disappointing in about equal measure. The disappointment stems from it being a small domestic play, born of international co-operation and on a large international theme. Theatrefront, a Toronto troupe that includes some of the best younger practitioners, sent a deputation to Bosnia and worked with actors there on a story that would illuminate both sides. The cast of the resultant production comprises two of theirs and three of ours.

One casualty here is the Western superstition that theatre gets more exciting, and certainly more physical, the further you go East. The most adventurous staging here is also the lamest: a recurring flashback to the carnage of war that gets no more convincing, and no less confusing, however often it happens. The main part of the play concerns the return to Sarajevo of Tarik, a young man who escaped and who now brings with him his new, and pregnant, Canadian wife. He also brings papers that will enable his Serbian family to emigrate to Toronto. Only, they don't want to go.

A huge national tragedy is of course the sum of many small ones. But, even given that, this play (written by the company with a dramaturge, Sue Balint, and directed by Daryl Cloran) gets sidetracked. It can be very acute, and funny, when dealing with cultural differences; the most reverberant line is the one that Tarik's vegetarian bride (played delightfully and touchingly by Holly Lewis) utters when offered Turkish coffee: "Do you have decaf?" Much of the play, though, is taken up with deciding how much of a bastard Tarik is (Christopher Morris deals well with the ambiguities but he doesn't have much to go on) and on how he treated the girl he left behind him, who subsequently took up with his younger brother. It's a story of love and jealousy that could be happening anywhere, and though that may be the point, it isn't a very interesting one.

On these limited terms, the play and production more than hold attention. The visiting players are Alana Dzebo, radiantly angry as the ex-fiancee, and Tanja Smoje, gently luminous as Tarik's sister. Dylan Trowbridge splits that difference as the brother, who's both powerfully angry and enforcedly quiet; he lost his tongue in the war. The same actor doubles (they all do) as a Canadian peacekeeper, whose one scene opens windows through which the rest of the play gazes only fitfully.

Colour Photo: Chris Gallow / Alena Dzebo as Jasna and Dylan Trowbridge as Emir in Return (The Sarajevo Project), a small production resulting from international co-operation that is enjoyable and disappointing in equal measure.; Colour Photo: Lucas Oleniuk / Salter (Gary Reineke), right, traded in his antisocial four-year-old son 35 years ago for a test-tube model who was further cloned. Shawn Doyle plays three of the man's sons, who confront their father in A Number.
2006-01-28-biteless-delivery-makes-lyric:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Letters from Lehrer runs through Feb. 25 at the Berkeley Downstairs, 416-368-3110.

When Richard Greenblatt decided to do a one-man show about Tom Lehrer, he naturally wrote to his subject, full of hope and admiration, requesting the old musical satirist's permission and, if possible, his blessing. He got the first, grudgingly, but not the second. "If all this isnt enough to discourage you, Lehrer wrote, outlining his reservations, let me know, and maybe I can come up with some more."

This correspondence continued over about three years, with neither man changing his tone or his stance. Its incorporated in the finished show and is the most obvious reason for the show's title, Letters from Lehrer. There seems, however, to be a secondary cause. Greenblatt sees Lehrer's songs, including those written in the early 1950s around the time when he himself was busy being born, as a coded message directed at him personally. He doesnt believe this literally, of course, but he cant help thinking of them that way. He first heard them in the '60s when, as the child of a left- wing couple who had quit the Communist party in 1956, he was himself becoming politically aware. The songs spoke to him, and Greenblatt's show is about What Tom Lehrer Means to Him: a blend of recital, commentary and spiritual autobiography.

The mixture doesnt take. Its nice to hear the songs again, at least the bits that you can hear. It doesn't matter that Greenblatt doesn't have a voice. Neither did Lehrer, but he had killer diction and phrasing that nailed every joke. Greenblatt has an even, biteless delivery that makes mush of the lyrics (a muddy amplification system doesnt help) and he seems to be on vocally distant terms with the tunes. He plays better piano than Lehrer, but even that seems counter-productive; his performance of the songs is keyboard-directed rather than audience-directed.

Nor am I sure that the songs can bear the dramatic weight Greenblatt wants to place on them. Lehrer stopped writing and performing 40 years ago, leaving Greenblalt feeling, by his own account, personally abandoned. The songs we have are the products of two separate bursts of creativity: in the 50s, when Lehrer wrote and performed them as a sideline while pursuing a scholarly career in mathematics; and in the early '60s when he resurfaced as in- house minstrel on the TV satire show That Was the Week That Was.

I remember, if I, too, can get autobiographical, the first batch making a great impression at my school when they were new. They were, in those days, unbroadcastable, but we lapped them up via the records and the published songbooks. What attracted us about them was the bloodthirstiness, and the occasional sex. We thrilled to the comparatively mild Hunting Song (the protagonist bags "three game wardens, seven hunters and a cow) and to the more advanced cynicism of My Old Home Town, I Hold Your Hand in Mine, The Wienerschnitzel Waltz and The Old Dope Peddler (he gives the kids free samples/ because he knows full well/that today's young innocent faces/will be tomorrows clientele"), not to mention Lobachevsky, the ultimate paean to cheating on exams.

Greenblatt doesnt sing any of these, and I don't think their absence is solely due to the familiar limits of anthology shows. The songs don't fit his thesis. The ones that he sings from the 50s have a more obvious political edge: The Wild West is Where I Want to Be (about nuclear testing), I Wanna Go Back to Dixie ("I aint seen one good lynchin' in years) and We Will All Go Together When We Go, in which he's the apostle of apocalypse. These certainly place Lehrer at the sharp end of what Greenblatt calls the 50s liberal consensus" but its a stretch to call them protest songs.

Most of them are lethal parodies of various kinds of pop song, something Greenblatt's uninflected delivery tends to obscure. When, in the '60s, Lehrer took on The Folk Song Army, he was irked not just by the folkies self-importance ("it takes a certain amount of courage to get up in a coffeehouse or a college auditorium and come out in favour of the things that everybody else in the audience is against, like peace and justice and brotherhood") but by the fact they wrote terrible songs. Greenblatt does later on make a valid point about the morale-building virtues of preaching to the converted. He might have added that, anyway, the Right does it just as much as the Left.

It was Lehrers superb craftsmanship, rather than the uniqueness of anything he was saying, that set him apart in the '60s since, by this point, satire was not only hip but pop. Nor has the kind of thing he was doing ever gone away; Jon Stewart is doing it now, and to bigger audiences. This makes it difficult to accept Greenblatt's view of Lehrer as the light that failed. Its true for him, obviously, but thats not enough to hang a confessional show on.

The best part of the performance is not Greenblatt on Greenblatt or Greenblatt sings Lehrer but Greenblatt speaks Lehrer. Lehrer's style in prose was sabre-toothed self-deprecation. He used it in his liner notes, and he's evidently still using it in the occasional interview and in those letters. Whenever Greenblatt quotes him, the evening lights up. I especially approved Lehrers dictum that the only worthwhile response to a joke is laughter; applause means merely that the audience agrees with you. (There was a bit of that going on, the night I saw the show.) I must also say that theres one, entirely apolitical, number that Greenblatt puts over excellently, the breathless rattling-off of the periodic table as a Gilbert and Sullivan patter song; I'm in awe of any non-scientist who can even remember it.

Colour Photo: Lucas Oleniuk / Richard Greenblatt's one-man show received more applause than laughter.
2006-02-04-ring-finale-is-golden-gotterd:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Gotterdammerung runs through Feb. 12 at the Hummingbird Centre, 16-872-2262. John and Jen runs through Feb. 11 at the Walmer Centre Theatre, 416-927-7880.

I have no wish to poach on any music critics preserve, but I would like to state that, considered purely as theatre, the Canadian Opera Company's new production of Gotterdammerung is as stunning a feat of staging as I have seen in Toronto. One image alone is enough to make the history books: that of the scheming Hagen standing at the back of the stage, the outline of his bald-eagle head piercing the shadows, while Brunnhilde, alone downstage, unveils her plans for self-immolation. I don't know how one divides the credit for this between direction (Tim Albery), design (Michael Levine) and lighting (David Finn); the collaboration is seamless and inspired.

The production is especially rich in what must, I suppose, be one of the primary Wagnerian skills, that of holding a single picture for a very long time. The palace scenes in this production are set in a high-tech corporate office, around a boardroom table that gets larger, scene by scene, as the power games get nastier. There is a matching power in the way that characters sit impassive in their designer chairs, listening to their rivals emote. When Hagen dreams of his Nibelung father, the two communicate by computer, the screens glowing red in the greyness. A battery of lights burns with a matching red for any scenes involving fire. The horizon is crisscrossed by electronic cables, doubling as the threads of destiny spun by the Fates in the opening scene. Theres even some legitimate humour when the Rhinemaidens turn up as a coy trio of bathing belles.

Not everything works. A truly frightening chorus of men in suits (the Harry Rosen choir, my companion called them) lose some of their impact when they start pounding the table with spears. Staging, synopsis and surtitles taken all together cannot make clear what happens at the triple apocalypse -- one flood, two fires -- of the operas grand finale. But the whole cycle has been an international-sized triumph of which Richard Bradshaw, conducting as dynamically from his general director's office as from the pit, must feel immensely proud. I look forward to the apotheosis in the new opera house with Das Rheingold, the remaining instalment of what, thinking in megamusical terms, we might call The Ring of the Lords.

At the opposite physical extreme of musical theatre the Acting Up company, which made its debut last year with Tick, Tick ... Boom, takes firm steps forward with John and Jen, a sturdier piece in a much superior production. One of the attractions of this two-person American show is that it ought to be terrible but isn't. In the first half, set in the 60s, John and Jen are brother and sister; she, the older, goes off to study in New York and becomes a counterculture warrior, he goes off to fight in Vietnam and becomes dead.

In the second, set in the 80s, Jen and John are mother and son, she having named him after the sibling whose end has left her with a load of unrealized obligation; the permissive teen has become an over-protective adult and her boy, of course, resents it. They fight; in the end they reconcile.

It sounds schematic and it sounds sentimental. In the first act, it seems outrageously neat that one family should provide such an exact microcosm of the split within America. There's even a duet titled You Don't Understand that spells it all out. The catalyst, a vivid offstage presence, is a borderline abusive father against whom Jen revolts while Jon takes him as a model of manhood. (Theres also a mother, but we learn almost nothing about her.) In the second, the positive ending seems, in retrospect, inevitable. But it doesnt seem so at the time. There's a battle going on, a commonplace one certainly, but real, and moment to moment the show rings true. It can't avoid -- doesnt want to avoid -- the cuteness endemic to American musicals about families or the uplift endemic to American musicals about anything, but it sails through them. We dont, after all, see many musicals that focus closely on brothers and sisters or on mothers and sons, and this does both and does it honestly. The first relationship moves from bonding to conflict, the second the other way, and that grand scheme is very effective.

This is almost a through-composed musical, so at moments of high emotion, the characters stop singing and start talking, rather than the traditional other way around. Tom Greenwald's lyrics are unflashy but attentive, with the occasional spark of wry wit; the first Jon complains that though his sister advised him to metaphorically hit a home run, she was never there to see him literally do it. (Her never coming home throughout her years at college is about the hardest thing in the show to believe.) Andrew Lippa's music isnt as melodically rich as his later score for The Wild Party, where he has all the styles of the 1920s to play with, but its a cunning feat of tension and release

The performances, under Michael Jones's direction, are musically and dramatically first-rate. Stephanie Roth is both concerned and abrasive as a woman in whom the two qualities run together, the more so the older she gets. Kyle Blair, the superb jack of last year's Stratford Into the Woods, now plays boyhood again, twice, and he has great fun emphasizing the two Jons different varieties of disgruntlement. He also has a great capacity for playing anger, excitement and hurt; he can be soaring and searing at the same time.

Were often told that the problem with doing satire is that the status quo is a satire in itself. I think it's more that oppositional comedy is an industry, and we're running out of shock. Torontos Second City regularly pays tribute to topicality, generally about the United States, with some kind of punning title, and then proceeds to domestic business as usual. Things are the same back source. In Chicago, the first Second City recently unveiled its 92nd revue, Iraqtile Dysfunction, which has even more merits than the current Toronto show but has nothing to say about Iraq.

Well, almost nothing. I liked a number in which a janitor called Abdul is thoughtlessly branded a terrorist by everyone at his office, except for one kind lady who offers him Girl Scout cookies, and is gratefully told "I like you. Dont come to work on Tuesday." Next thing we know, he's being interrogated.

But that's another scene, largely inhabited by characters from still others. Everyones a running gag. One of them is an ex-CIA agent who subsequently shows up on a PTA committee, and finds that another mother has told her son the date of the Spring Fair, which was supposed to be a secret. (We have two choices. We could re- schedule, but that would be difficult. Well have to shoot him.) A candidate for the priesthood is subjected to a word-association test to see if he's gay. I think that's political; its certainly funny. The show is slick and inventive, with a blessed touch of madness. Even a routine about a married couple forced into conversation by the breakdown of their TV comes up fresh. ("Do you want a drink?" Im an alcoholic. "Is that a yes or a no?")

One performer, a dangerously cherubic naif named Brian Gallivan, is a likely candidate for star-alumnus status. His finest moment comes when, in a wheedling Hispanic accent, he goes through the bag of a member of the audience commenting incredulously on what he finds there. This was a genuine improvization. Believe me -- I stayed for the second show to check.

Black & White Photo: Michael Cooper / On the bed, Brunnhilde (Frances Ginzer) and Siegfried (Christian Franz), with Rhinemaidens (Allyson McHardy, Colleen Skull and Laura Whalen) in the Canadian Opera Company's production of Wagner's Gotterdammerung.; Colour Photo: Joanna McDermott / John (Kyle Blair) and Jen (Stephanie Roth) in Acting Up company's John and Jen, a two-person American show that ought to be terrible but isn't.
2006-02-07-no-wallowin-time-in-these-cor:
In repertory through March 25. 416-866-8666.; robertcushman@lycos.com

OUR TOWN

Marilyn and Charles Baillie Theatre, Young Centre for the Performing Arts

- - -

Good morning. Its a bright and early day in the city of Toronto in the province of Ontario. At least it is for those of you who live there and are eating your breakfast while you read this; and the rest who live some place else or just plumb got up late, well, youll have to use your imaginations. Which is what Mr. Thornton Wilder would have wanted you to do.

Wilder wrote this play, Our Town, back in 1938; it uses a bare stage to present three days, spread some years apart, in the life of a place called Grover's Corners, N.H., even further back in the 20th century. We're talking about horse-and-buggy days, moving on to early automobile days. Wilder wanted us to laugh and cry and wonder, and maybe hold our breaths our little, over people bein born and fallin in love and marryin' and dyin', sometimes ahead of their time. All the satisfaction of it and all the futility. And you know what? He brings it off, just about completely.

Of course, he doesnt do it all by himself. He has the best help. Some of us are still chokin up and feeling the glow from last week when that old Soulpepper company -- they're only eight, historically speaking, but they're already part of the landscape -- opened their new theatre with this very play. Its very warm and practical and inviting -- the theatre and the Young Centre complex its part of and the Distillery complex it's part of -- and it's in a nice situation. You can walk out the back door and see clear down to Lake Ontario; least you could if some public benefactor would take a stick of dynamite to that darn Gardiner Expressway.

Now this first night of Our Town ended with a standing ovation, which wasnt at all surprising. Thing is, it began with one as well, and you know that aint usual. Here's how it happened. The play is narrated by a Stage Manager who talks directly to the audience, very much like I'm talking to you now. Hes played by Albert Schultz, whos Soulpepper's artistic director and the man most responsible for getting them to where they are today. Literally. So we file into the theatre, and there's Albert, which is how everybody refers to him in these parts, alternately movin bits of furniture around and just standin and lookin' out at us. Then the lights go down, and our eyes meet his and everybody stands up and cheers. And it's not so much him saying "Welcome to my theatre, which you might expect, as us welcoming him.

As for the rest of the evening; well, you cant say fairer than it not only lived up to that beginning, it topped it. Same goes for Alberts own performance. Everybody says Our Town is sentimental. Well, it can be if you don't do it right; but, apart from having enough discreet charm to make the entire bourgeoisie turn green, he keeps steering so we don't get a chance to wallow. When hes asked whether people ever realize their lives while they live it," he says "the saints and poets, maybe." I always thought that was kind of a phony line, but here its all in the maybe. He does it as a sort of rigorous shrug.

Well, that's Joseph Ziegler's production all over, a real model of tact and control. He directed this play for Soulpepper at the start of their second season, and it was like a testimony that they were here to stay. Its even better now, thanks in large part to Martha MacIsaac, who tore all our hearts out last year in The Wild Duck and now lacerates them all over again. She plays scholarly young Emily who pairs up with George, the baseball champ next door. She and Jeff Lillico make the scene where they plight their troth over mimed sodas in a minimalist drugstore, sad and funny and touching like it always was. She makes the last act, where shes one of a bunch of dead people all sittin' on chairs to represent a graveyard, devastating like it never was but was always supposed to be. Young Miss MacIsaac gets very earnest about lovin' and bein loved, and her disillusion when she revisits her past and sees everybody taking everything for granted is terrible.

Sittin next to her in that cemetery is Miss Nancy Palk, who plays her mother-in-law and has never been better. We know from the start that she's going to die, and the knowledge makes her delicacy and her enthusiasm very moving. She has modest ambitions that won't be fulfilled; she makes us feel delight in small pleasures and grief that they cant be larger. Then theres Oliver Dennis as her doctor- husband, all upright and caring; while as the other parents there's John Jarvis, a newspaper editor who's a bit pompous and a lot shy, and Jane Spidell who struck me at first as over-brisk but who justifies it when she gets to that flashback in Act Three. And thats not the half of it because in the outfield --doin their bit in the bit parts, you might say -- are such folks as William Webster, with a bitterness carved out of granite, Charmion King shedding easy tears at a wedding and leaving the hard ones for us, and old Diego Matamoros readin' us a geology lesson, and some terrific kids and more.

It's the authors opinion that, not only are our lives the only ones weve got, they're the only ones the universe has got. He wrote this play just before a war, about a time just before another one. The crazier and more fragile the world gets, the more poignant the play seems: poignant and maybe terrifying. But not depressing; in fact, in this production, which is as good as this play is ever gonna get, it's positively uplifting. Some lady actor, posin as a member of the audience, asks whether our town has any culture or beauty in it. Well, our town does, and this is part of it. Seems like the city of Toronto and the province of Ontario ought to be tellin people about it. You have a good day.

Black & White Photo: Sandy Nicholson / Ah, young love! Martha MacIsaac and Jeff Lillico help to make Thorton Wilder's Our Town the best it's ever going to get.

THE GOVERNMENT INSPECTOR

Marilyn and Charles Baillie Theatre, Young Centre for the Performing Arts

- - -

Soulpepper have paired their production of Our Town, an ambiguous celebration of small-town life, with The Government Inspector, an unambiguous attack on it. If the first production is perfect, the second is hit-and-miss. The hits are ecstatic. The misses include some jokey references to the companion play and to the company's new theatre, which may be meant as self-mocking but come off as self- hugging. Soulpepper are neither young enough nor old enough to be begging us to love them.

The entire evening, though, is about self-conscious theatricality, and to determine why Morris Panych, directing his own new adaptation, should have taken this approach (other than that it comes naturally to him) we have to go to the end of the play and work back. Nikolai Gogols comedy, set in a particularly backward Russian backwater, is probably the most celebrated mistaken- identity joke in world drama. A washed-up young man from St. Petersburg is mistaken for an investigating official by the local authorities, who load him with bribes to conceal their misdeeds, which are legion. Its practically a modern myth. (Its descendants, as noted in the program, include a classic episode of Fawlty Towers.) As the play races towards its final curtain, it takes in two Textbook Great Moments; Panych has seized on these and built a whole style around them. In the first, the town's mayor, learning he has been tricked, goes ballistic and turns on the audience. "What are you laughing at?" he yells at them. You're laughing at yourselves. This really stopped them in their tracks in Russia in 1838. Whether it could have the same effect now I doubt, but Im certain that Panychs concept hasn't helped its chances. There is no shock in having a play suddenly go meta-theatrical on us, when it's been frantically meta all evening. A few minutes later the story concludes, with a reversal that turns the assembled councillors into a row of open-mouthed petrified dummies. This is a second celebrated moment that always has difficulty living up to its legend. To help it along, Panych has added a surprise coda. I cant, of course, reveal what it is, but I will say that in seeking to avoid an anti- climax he has come up with a bigger one.

The principal carrier of the shows theatrical virus is the impostor himself, Khlestakov, a penniless junior clerk with literary aspirations. At least that's how Gogol wrote him; in this version, he's a stranded out-of-work actor. I think that somebody who falls into playing a part, and comes half to believe in it, is funnier as an idea than someone who does it for a living. There are plays, including a famous Russian one called The Forest, in which actors are mistaken for the people they act, but The Government Inspector wasnt meant to be one of them. I cant push the point, though, because the role, concept and all, allows Diego Matamoros to emerge as the great farceur we always knew he could be. Some of the in- jokes actually help him; a riff on Panych's success with another Gogol adaptation, The Overcoat ("a play without words where everyone just ran around to music") certainly made me laugh. It's just a preliminary, though, to a scene that remains essentially as its author wrote it, in which the mountebank gets gloriously drunk on alcohol, flattery and his own unbuttoned fantasies -- a progress only impeded by the after-effects of the fish he was served at supper. Both vocally and physically, the performance becomes a series of triumphant swoops and shameful lurches, each shading delicately and with increasing velocity into the next. Earlier, broke at his inn, he has given us similarly sharp contrasts between misery and bravado; later, he greets supplicants while reclining on a divan, head resting on hands, like Groucho Marxs idea of sexy. Youre never sure whether Khlestakov is an innocent masquerading as a trickster or vice versa; and neither apparently is he. His manservant has been rewritten as his more level-headed fellow- actor; Oliver Dennis, the only quiet person on stage, is our old friend, the straight man who's funnier than most of the clowns.

Panych's adaptation falls between stools, at its best when it sticks closely to the original while sprucing up the chat a bit, at its worst when inventing unnecessary sub-plots. These include having the mayors dumpy daughter (Deborah Hay, delightfully twitching and squawking) dejectedly wooed by the local health officer (Ben Carlson, looking forlorn beyond the call of duty), and having the other functionaries, not so much bureaucrats as kleptocrats, appeal to the supposed inspectors generosity by making the town look even worse than it is. This goes nowhere, and anyway it obscures what the play is angriest about: Not that the characters try to paper over abuses but that the abuses exist in the first place. The purpose, of course, is to invite comparisons with recent Canadian scams, but rubbing the audience's noses in contemporary relevance is pointless; a play either resonates or it doesn't. Here the satire starts strong and then peters out, William Websters mayor whipping both town and play into shape with tremendous force in the first scene and then running on empty. Nancy Palk plays his wife as a towering lascivious virago; she does it well but I rather wish she wouldnt. The others merge into a group, apart from John Jarvis and Ted Dykstra who, as a matched set of capering gossips, are a two-man group of their own.

However, there seems never to have been a production of The Government Inspector, starting with the very first one, that wasn't criticized for farcical extravagance, so that element may, just possibly, be inherent in the play. Panych's actual staging is, on its own hectic terms, excellent. He arranges the characters, each of them costumed by Judith Bowden as a separate joke on Russian couture, into close-packed tableaux of greasy corruption; in between scenes he gets them dancing in the kind of frenzied gallop that usually serves to conceal a set-change but here distracts us from the fact that Ken MacDonald's design, a cartoon in steep perspective, is staying very much the same. I think audiences will enjoy the production very much; I'd like to think that, if some of the choices had been different, they would have enjoyed it even more.

2006-02-11-playing-a-so-so-hand-the-gamb:
The Gambler through until Feb. 19 at the Artword, 416-872-1212; The Real McCoy runs through Feb. 26 at the Factory, 416-504-9971.; robertcushman@lycos.com

Fyodor Dostoevskys short novel The Gambler is a highly dramatic work composed under highly dramatic circumstances. Dostoevesky was under the gun when he wrote it, committed to writing two books more or less simultaneously (the other was Crime and Punishment) with the knowledge that if this one was not delivered on time, he would forfeit to his publisher the rights to his complete works. Unable to write fast enough, he engaged a secretary, a young woman with an understanding nature and excellent shorthand skills. He dictated the story to her, and together they had it ready for delivery at the last moment of the 11th hour. Soon after this was accomplished, the young woman, Anna Grigoryevna, became Dostoevskys second wife.

Ronald Weihs's dramatization of The Gambler (the last production at the Artword, at least in its current location) splits the playing time and the stage space between the story itself and the manner of its composition. This is an interesting idea, or so it seems to begin with, and practical, too; it enables David Ferry, a good actor who is at least 20 years too old for the title role, to put quotation marks around the incongruity by jumping back and forth between playing the character and playing his creator.

The fictional protagonist is a 22-year-old tutor called Alexei, whom we meet dancing attendance on his employer, an impoverished Russian general, and all his family. The clan has fetched up at a German town unequivocally named Roulettenberg. They send Alexei to the casino to try and recoup their fortunes. He succeeds often enough for his employers to get dangerously hooked, and finally, he succumbs himself. Dostoevsky, a serious gambling addict, knew what he was writing about.

He also put into the story another real-life addiction -- his hopeless love for a woman named Polina, a name he here bestows on the General's stepdaughter, who has Alexei on a string and is pretty highly strung herself. Fyodor (thats the program billing for the author-as-character; the name Dostoevesky is sprung on us later, as if it were some kind of surprise) makes the connection himself, and we wait for the two Polinas to come together in a dazzling coup de theatre. If the outer and inner stories have so much in common, they ought to collide at some point. It never happens; Ferry merely keeps crossing from the side of the stage, where hes Fyodor, to the centre, where's he's Alexei, and back again.

Fyodors courtship of his adoring stenographer (Claire Jenkins, doing her best) is both prosaic and insipid. Theres no indication that his gambling continued to plague the earlier years of their marriage, though that's what happened and it would seem to be relevant. Instead we get some stuff about Fyodor gambling on getting his book finished, or maybe on proposing, and the gamble paying off. He proposes; she accepts; happy ever after.

The dramatized story itself is a little livelier. It's a doggedly literal adaptation, until it runs up against scenes it cant stage, at which point it throws its hands in the air and hopes for the best. Molly Thoms production suffers about equally from lack of imagination and lack of resources. In the book, the casino scenes are made feverishly thrilling by the presence of a mob of spectators, egging the principals on, giving them good and bad advice, sometimes making off with their winnings. Here all we get are generic recorded crowd noises plus a roulette wheel that doesn't spin. (Economy? Symbolism?) There goes the atmosphere, there goes the whole thrust and flavour of the story.

What actors there are suffer from double-trouble. Irene Poole plays the stepdaughter, icily and effectively, but has nothing left over for the very different role of the General's gold- digging mistress. Brett Christopher does well as a decent English gentleman, not so well as a dubious French one. The machinations of these people, murky enough in the book, become impenetrable in the play. Karl Pruner gets his one role of the General completely wrong, as a colourless martinet instead of the virtuoso of self-abasement that hes meant to be. Jennifer Phipps plays a grandmother who arrives to lose her fortune at the tables, when her family were counting on her to die quietly in Russia and leave it to them. She brightens things up, but shes an eccentric English lady rather than a possessed Russian one. Ferry and Poole do get some erotic tension out of their later scenes, but he's too leathery to encompass the tutor's frenzied vulnerability, either to desire or to the game. A line in both play and novel says that the Russians have never understood roulette. Maybe thats why they had to invent their own brand.

And talking of inventors: Andrew Moodies The Real McCoy is another case of writing-by-numbers, but one that doesn't even have Dostoevsky to fall back on. Its source, far less amenable, is Life. It's a biography of Elijah McCoy (1844-1929), born in Colchester, Ont.

That about exhausts the Canadian content, since McCoy was educated at Edinburgh University and spent his adult life in and around Detroit. Its an astonishing story; McCoy, the son of escaped slaves, had a remarkable career as an engineer and inventor, his signal achievement being the invention of a lubricating device for industrial machinery. Customers wary of being fobbed off with imitations would make a point of asking for "the real McCoy." So a man of whom few people have heard has nonetheless become a proverb. This is mentioned in the publicity but, strangely enough, not featured in the play.

As a black genius in a prejudiced society, McCoy faced huge pressures, and the play mentions them from time to time. But it doesnt find any consistent way of dramatizing them. In fact it lacks any central conflict, personal or political. Elijah is disowned by his fundamentalist father and, tragically and prematurely, loses two wives. But these things seem to happen just because they happened. They carry no weight, and the characters are either stereotypes or ciphers. McCoy's scientific career is more intrinsically interesting, and there's an amusing sequence in which - - apparently to stop his second wife from nagging him -- he creates an ironing board, a lawn sprinkler and a pair of waterproof boots, one after another, just like that. But the comedy of this has no connection to the rest of the play, which also moves fast but only because there is nothing it wants to linger on. And the play is full of loose ends: Elijahs parents cant afford to send him to college, but next thing we know he's there, and across the Atlantic at that; there's a line suggesting that one of his employers is going blind, but thats the first and last we hear of it.

Moodie is his own director, and may have set himself an impossible task. At any rate the production is scrappy and much of the acting feeble. A major exception is Maurice Dean Wint who endows the adult McCoy with a courteous nature that expresses itself chiefly by speaking (and writing) in fluent polysyllables. A minor one is Kevin Hanchard, who starts as the boy McCoy and then moves on to the heros best friend, who is unable to live up to Elijah's gospel of self-help and self-reliance: a noble and necessary doctrine in science but limiting in terms of personal relations. There's the glimmer of a theme there, but it never burns.
