robertcushman@lycos.com; Leo runs until March 19 at the Tarragon Extra Space theatre, 416-536-5018.

LEO

Tarragon Extra Space

- - -

There is a special joy in hearing and seeing a piece of theatre unfold at top speed with all its moments packed and none of them blurred. That's what happens in Leo, an unflaggingly accurate production of an outstanding new play.

The playwright, Rosa Laborde, is the Canadian child of a refugee Chilean family. Her play depicts three young people growing up in Chile before, during and just after the Allende years. There is Rodrigo, an idealistic political activist, and Isolda, a pragmatic political activist. Finally there is Leo, a poet, for which Rodrigo admires him, and apolitical, for which Isolda despairs of him. "Thank God," says Isolda to Leo, "there are the Rodrigos in the world. Imagine what would happen if there was just you and me." To which Leo quietly replies "I do."

That, in a deft and devastating way wholly typical of the play, shifts the ground, from the political to the personal. Rodrigo, Isolda and Leo are close friends; they are also interlocked lovers. In the course of the play each of them has sex with each of the other two. Isolda and Rodrigo are engaged -- since the age of 11, apparently -- but there are times when Rodrigo's benevolent fanaticism is too much for her and she turns to Leo instead. He reciprocates, but she is concerned when she hears him murmur Rodrigo's name in bed. Each member of the trio has a moment of jealousy, finding out about the other two. The tensions disturb them but do not destroy them. They have, after all, other, desperate things to worry about.

Leo may be a political skeptic but he has an interest in fashioning a rebellious ancestry for himself. He claims that his father fought alongside Che Guevara in Bolivia and vanished in the Bermuda Triangle. (The truth is considerably less romantic.) One way or another, he's an easy mark for Rodrigo's enthusiasm, and when the Pinochet coup comes, he finds himself following the love of his life (Isolda, after being captured, presumably tortured and released, has fled the country.) In this respect the play resembles Kiss of the Spider Woman; ideologically uncommitted men sacrificing themselves for their male lovers' principles seem to be a Latin American tradition. But this may be a coincidence. And if it is derivative, who cares? The play unfolds within the title character's memory; at any rate it begins and ends with Leo, tied to a chair and beaten by invisible hands, spitting out possibly meaningless words like "imperialism," "socialism" and 'totalitarianism" ... "words to live by ... words to kill for." Philosophically, I would guess that Laborde is closest to Isolda, the humane empiricist, but she has entered into each of her characters equally.

The play's emphasis on triangles -- Bermudan and eternal --has inspired Graeme S. Thomson to design a three-cornered set, with the audience on all sides, and Richard Rose to direct a similarly shapely and hard-edged production. Scene succeeds scene with an exhilarating combination of velocity and detail, grace and force. (The play is billed at 75 minutes and comes in shorter.) We are never allowed to forget that these doomed exploding characters are terribly, pitiably young.

Cara Pifko, very fresh and immediate, does her best stage work as Isolda; Sergio Di Zio captures both the strength and the naivete of Rodrigo (watch his shoulders shake as he gets stoned for the first time); and Salvatore Antonio, whose sharp nose and inquiring chin give him a bizarre resemblance to Rowan Atkinson, is a brilliantly mercurial Leo. Actually the three work so well together, both in the writing and the acting, that assigning them individual qualities feels arbitrary. Their chemistry is infused with what I take to be an authentically South American kind of wit. "The truth is," says Isolda to the boys, "that alone neither of you is all that much but if you were combined you would make the perfect man."

"I've had that same thought," says Rodrigo.

"It might not," says Leo dryly, "have been what she meant." Marcelo Puente's guitar music suits so well that I hardly registered it was there. It's embarrassing to admit but I can't think of a thing to say against any aspect of the show.

Black & White Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann, Tarragon Theatre / Cara Pifko and Salvatore Antonio make up two thirds of a cast so good together that 'assigning them individual qualities feels arbitrary.'
2006-02-16-to-be-frank:
To Be Frank

He made his first comeback in the 1950s - and then he kept coming back, again and again. Now Sinatra is singing from beyond the grave in a new West End show. Robert Cushman analyses why we still get such a kick out of Ol' Blue Eyes

Nostalgia and technology have brought Frank Sinatra back into fashion. Supremely great popular singer though he was, that may not be a good thing. All those Rat Pack retrospectives, whether theatrical recreations or repackaged CDs, play to an idea of early 1960s sophistication that was superficial at the time and is rather embarrassing now. They concentrate on the booze, the womanising or at least the talk of womanising, the Las Vegas high-rolling, and the stagy camaraderie, rather than on what was important: the Kennedy-era liberalism (apparently racist jokes by or about Sammy Davis Jnr were quite liberating in their day) and, most of all, the music.

When, in the middle of one of those Clan shindigs, Sinatra goes into a solo song, whether a curt, commanding "Luck Be a Lady" or a yearning soaring "I Have Dreamed", the mood changes; we are somewhere else, and so is he. It seems that he can't help himself; suddenly, he's concentrating. In between, though he may be the master of these revels, he seems out of place. Compared to Davis and Dean Martin, both natural clowns, he seems forced in his banter and somewhat surly; on screen he could be a compelling if stylised actor; but in what is supposed to be his natural habitat, carousing with his buddies, he is heavy-handed, something between a grouch and a bully. Maybe this is the real Sinatra, but it's a reality one would rather not know about.

In all probability, it's just one of many real Sinatras. I have my doubts about the super-hologram version of Sinatra that's about to open at the London Palladium, though they have less to do with my feelings about Sinatra than with my feelings about the theatre. But at least the director, David Leveaux, seems in interviews to have a genuine feeling for his subject; he has summed up Sinatra's artistry by saying that "his relationship with song was conversational yet deeply musical" and his fascination by saying that "it is impossible not to get personal with Sinatra because he is certainly going to get personal with you."

Personal and yet impersonal; or perhaps, super-personal. The great paradox of Sinatra is that he brings to his songs a unique inescapable personality and temperament - not to mention a tumultuous and controversial biography, of which his public is thoroughly aware - and yet puts all this at the service of his material. He disappears into the music, and then reappears in what I can only call purified form. He sheds, for the duration, everything that isn't pertinent to the song, or at least to his interpretation of the song. (His conception of "Let's Face the Music and Dance" is different from Fred Astaire's; come to that, his conception of "The Song Is You", in the 1980s is different from his idea of the same song in the 1940s.)

Part of this has to do with the fanatical precision of his diction. He sings consonants. He sings "Night and Day", where everyone else sings "Nightanday". It sounds like Sinatra, because nobody else does that, but at the same time it's copybook Cole Porter. This is what the man wrote; this is what you are going to hear. And there is, always, the implication that you have never really heard it before. The fusion of arrogance and humility is unique, and irresistible.

As a singer, Sinatra is a great actor. He expresses himself but at one remove, through a text. And just as great English actors define themselves through their performances of the greatest English plays, finding their own voices through the formal challenges of Shakespearean verse, so the great American singers are recognised by their treatment of the great American songs; they, too, have to make an artificial form sound natural, and more exhilaratingly natural precisely because of the artifice.

And Sinatra has an advantage over Gielgud and Olivier; he was there when the tradition was coming into being. He grew up with it; by the time he started seriously singing, in the 1940s, the repertoire - Gershwin and Porter and Arlen and Mercer and Rodgers and Hart - was already half-formed. He helped to codify it. It's an astonishing body of work that has gone in and out of style but has never gone away. It is in fashion now, and identified with Sinatra, even though many other fine singers have performed it. When a Rod Stewart or a Michael Bublé records an album of standards, it's hard to say whether they are doing it because they want to be Sinatra and therefore sing those songs, or because they want to sing the songs and so cannot help but ape Sinatra.

They, like Rat Pack imitators and enthusiasts, can only sound superficial because they have, as actors say, no centre. They either show off or are dull; either way, they think it's about them. Sinatra didn't sing about himself, he sang from himself, and it's a distinction I'd stand by, though I think some of his more bellicose fans might have trouble telling the difference.

There are of course songs in which Sinatra sounds directly autobiographical - charmingly in "Nancy", unbearably in "My Way" - but they're a minority. And even "Nancy" is as concerned as much with itemising his daughter's qualities as with expressing her father's feelings. For the most part Sinatra is singing about common experience, or occasionally about a very particular other experience; we assume that he is drawing on similar experiences of his own but we have no proof and we don't need it. It's showbiz lore that his bruising relationship with Ava Gardner in the 1950s informs In the Wee Small Hours, his first great ballad album, but you don't have to have heard that to be moved by the music. There's no self-pity in his singing of "Glad to Be Unhappy" or "Last Night when We Were Young", just wry, searching, majestically structured readings of magnificent songs. Read up on Sinatra's actual behaviour at the time, and it's a lot less ennobling, a lot more self-indulgent. But one is in the past, the other is for ever.

This insight, this dramatic quality, grew with time. Sinatra's career falls into four periods, in each of which he was affiliated with a different record company. As boy-singer for the Tommy Dorsey orchestra on RCA, he sounds appealing but callow, additionally constrained both by the big-band format and by most of the songs. His contemporaries were struck by his apparent belief in his material (we, who are used to hearing him sing as though he means it, tend to take it for granted), and by the sheer tender beauty of the voice. That we can still hear, as we also can, in his pop-idol years with Columbia. The warmth on these is overwhelming; so is the vulnerability that makes his performance of "Someone to Watch Over Me" something like definitive.

These were the years of the string-laden, swoon-inducing Sinatra. He wasn't yet a swinger, to listen to in the musical sense. To listen to his impeccably cheerful version of the light-hearted "Five Minutes More", one of the biggest hits he ever had, is to be surprised by the chances for rhythmic variation that he passes up, missed opportunities that he was to repair when he re-recorded the song in the 1950s for Capitol.

The Capitol years were, by common consent, his finest. They offer the best of both worlds, the charm and the vocal bloom of the preceding period offset by a new rhythmic variation and a fierce intelligence. His technical and interpretative mastery are in perfect sync. He seems to revel in taking the measure of classic song after classic song. This, not coincidentally, was the age of the LP; singers who were more than cabaret cultists had the chance to explore the catalogue and, on occasion, to add to it. These were the years of his unsurpassably melancholy "One for My Baby" and his unsurpassably happy "You Make Me Feel so Young". The last stage began in the 1960s when he started his own company, Reprise, which he quickly sold but for which he continued to record. There was no immediate break in style but the voice became grittier and, if anything, more interesting.

It was a long period, which went to schizophrenic extremes. At its crassest there was "My Way", ill-written and bombastic, which unhappily still counts for many people as his identity-song. It gets, anachronistically, into all the Rat Pack tributes; my opinion of the Palladium show will rocket up if they have the guts to leave it out. It's not just that it's a terrible song; it's that its blatancy is a direct contradiction of everything that the true, subtle Sinatra is about.

But there were compensations. He took the measure of genuinely dramatic pieces like "Ol' Man River" and the "Soliloquy" from Carousel, songs he had sung in the 1940s when he neither the depth of voice nor of sensibility to do them justice. "Ol' Man River" is a triumph of imaginative empathy; he isn't black, it's decades since he's been downtrodden, but he gets inside the song and its bleak message ("tired of livin' and feared of dyin'") of universal suffering. He had maybe his finest hour recording a bossa nova album - a style he'd never sung before - with Antonio Carlos Jobim. He takes it over; or let it takes him over. On one track, "Dindi", you can actually hear him being humbled, amazed by the mysterious beauty of the song. This is a pop singer? He sounds like the wisest, most compassionate man you ever met.

As a person Sinatra was at his most appealing when acknowledging contradictions and obligations. ("I've been over-rewarded in my life and that's the truth." "An over-privileged adult ought to do something to help under-privileged children". "Whatever else has been said about me is unimportant; when I sing, I believe I'm honest".) Most of us are capable of both good and bad behaviour, but his position gave him more scope in both directions; my own guess is that, even outside music, he did more good in the world than harm. But it's the music that counts; 60 years of self-expression that mostly transcended self and still have the power to touch.
2006-02-18-dont-believe-the-hype-award-w:
robertcushman@lycos.com; I Am My Own Wife runs through March 4 at the Bluma Appel Theatre, 416-368-3110.

An East German man named Lothar von Beerfelde spent much of his life, and certainly the most fulfilling parts of it, dressed as a woman and going under the name of Charlotte von Mahlsdorf. Lothar/ Charlotte, whose biography presents anyone writing it with a pretty problem in pronouns, spent his childhood under the Nazis and much of her adulthood under the Communists. Lothar's father was Nazi to the core, and showed it in the way he treated his family. Charlotte devoted her life to preserving parts of her country's nobler past, turning her Berlin home into a museum notable for its collection of furniture and -- her special passion -- old gramophone records. Being homosexual made her an easy target for official blackmail, and the Stasi pressured her into serving as an informer. But she survived the regime and ended up honoured for her cultural activities, if pilloried for her snitching.

It's an intriguing story, or sounds as if it should be. An American writer, Doug Wright, has turned it into a very dull play, which he has called I Am My Own Wife. Those words, or so the play assures us, were Lothar's own answer to the question, posed by his mother while she was hanging out the laundry, of when he was going to settle down and get married. It's a catchy label; also a catch- penny one, since Charlotte's sexuality is one of the many things about which the play has almost nothing to say. It comes to us from New York loaded with awards: a Tony, a Pulitzer, an Obie (since it cleaned up Off-Broadway before cleaning up On) and God knows what else. However bad things get for new Canadian plays -- and this season has been dire -- we can at least comfort ourselves that we don't dole out prizes with such reckless abandon as they do down south. Not, of course, that we have as many prizes to dole.

And not that they have many plays to choose from, or not many that make it to Times Square. Those that do make it seem, increasingly, to be live movies-of-the-week, dedicated to shining a sympathetic spotlight on someone who is ill, unbalanced or in a sexual or intellectual minority. Everybody gets to feel compassionate, and the plays invariably make their way to CanStage. (I'm not knocking the management for this. It's a public service, since we've heard these plays talked about and want to see them. But they don't add much lustre to the resume.) I Am My Own Wife has an added cachet: It's a one-man show (though it might be a test case for gender-blind casting) and almost bound to occasion a virtuoso performance.

Stephen Ouimette is the actor in the Toronto production and he delivers, outlining Charlotte with delicacy and dignity. His first appearance raises the highest hopes; she enters impressively through a pair of double doors in the centre of the back wall, defuses the moment by realizing she has forgotten something, exits apologetically and returns bearing an ancient horned phonograph of the kind that plays cylinders and hypnotizes dogs. (Charlotte is devoted to that old HMV or RCA logo -- depending on where you grew up -- and it could be the single most endearing thing about her.) She has, she tells us, "funfzehn thousand records." Unfortunately, though, Ouimette cannot devote all his energies to playing Charlotte. He has, without changing his dress, to play a load of other characters, including the author himself.

This is what really wrecks the evening. Wright is determined not just to tell us about Charlotte but to tell us about his fascination with her, rather than showing us by writing a real play about her. Nor do we even learn much about what that fascination might have been, beyond the fact that Wright is gay himself. It's somewhat reminiscent of Richard Greenblatt's recent show about Tom Lehrer, but Letters from Lehrer, whatever its flaws, was at least up-front about its real subject being Greenblatt himself, and it provided backup: Greenblatt told us in detail why Lehrer's songs were so important to him. (And of course the fact that he was performing the show himself made it more immediate.) Wright, who first heard about Charlotte from an American reporter-friend in Berlin, gets bogged down in the minutiae of his own trips to and from Germany. He seems to have had a lot more co-operation from Charlotte than Greenblatt did from Lehrer; he got interviews and had access to letters.

One that we hear is from a friend and colleague of Charlotte's, a gay antique dealer whom she shopped to the Stasi. He wrote from prison, with no recriminations. But for all the weight and time this episode is given, it remains an anecdote, diverting our attention to a subsidiary character who, since he never comes to life, either, isn't worth the trouble. Years before this, the young Lothar killed his father, to stop him from persecuting, and probably killing, the entire family. He went to prison for it. Charlotte tells us this, and we are given no reason not to believe it, but we are given no clues as to how these events actually affected her, and little sense of what it was like to grow up a non-Nazi in Nazi Germany. Stuff happens, that's all.

We're told toward the end that there is considerable doubt as to how effective an informer Charlotte actually was. We are also told that we will probably never know the truth. That indeed seems to be the point of the play and of the structure the author has chosen: that we can never know about Charlotte or Wright, himself or anyone. And I believe it; it's old news. I still think it would have been better if Wright had gone ahead and guessed, and come up with either a sustained monologue for Charlotte or -- probably less effective -- a conventional play with characters and a story.

The piece that we have is directed by Robin Phillips, of whom, especially now when we see so little of his work, it seems a waste. He gives it an elegant and, as far as I could tell, a sensitive production, with a few unnecessary touches. The sound system turns up the echo when Charlotte has something particularly poignant or harrowing to say; the play may need the help but the actor doesn't. Hirsham Ali's set is austerely handsome; museum clutter, or something resembling it, is occasionally visible behind the scrim but, once past the first sighting, it's more frustrating than evocative. Louise Guinand's lighting is alternately discreet and striking. Wright says that Charlotte is a transvestite without being a drag queen; she goes through the play, as she apparently did through life, in a plain black dress. Susan Benson is the impeccable designer, though, as she's another great neglected talent, it seems a waste of her, too. Still, Charlotte's status as the least spectacular cross-dresser in theatrical history points to something; she was, as the play tells us, a survivor. And popular culture has taught us that in Germany, the arch-survivors are women: Mother Courage, Fraulein Schneider, anyone played by Marlene Dietrich. In wanting to be one of them, Lothar was joining hands with history, and Charlotte was being practical.

Colour Photo: Shin Sugino / Stephen Ouimette plays Lothar/Charlotte von Mahlsdorf, a cross-dresser who spent his childhood under Nazis and adulthood under Communists.

2006-02-25-sex-violence-and-the-religiou:
robertcushman@lycos.com

Curtains are coming back. That doesn't mean theyre coming down, with a satisfying whoosh, like in the good old days. The drapes that have been hung downstage, first at the Young Centre, for Soulpeppers The Government Inspector, and now at the Passe Muraille Backspace, for Three Squares a Day, are frail, temporary things that have to move sideways to reveal or conceal the riches within. Still, they're a start. For decades now it's been taken for granted that audiences, when they arrive in a theatre, will be gratified to see the set there waiting for them. Its supposed to liberate them from bourgeois notions of concealment and titillation.

Ive never quite bought this. Seems to me that if a set isn't good, then you don't want to spend any more time looking at it than is absolutely necessary. And if it is good, then it will seem even better with the element of surprise.

Enough with the heavy irony. The curtains in the two new shows arent there just to be decorative or nostalgic. They are trying to tell us something. In the case of The Government Inspector its that the show we're going to watch is a consciously artificial celebration of the theatre itself. In the case of Three Squares a Day it's that the show were going to watch is a peep show. This latest offering from veteran playwright Tom Walmsley begins with Patricia Fagan, delectable in a flaming-red negligee, entering to push the curtains aside. What lies behind, designed by Kelly Wolf, is a life-size inhabited etching of a small-town Canadian kitchen. It oozes cartooned conventionality. The program, with an unusual degree of up-frontness, has already alerted us to what the style and the targets are to be. A play about the religious right, it promises. Sex. Violence.

So then. We are in the house of Morgan, who runs a security company that specializes in strike-breaking, and his wife, Candace. They are evangelical Christians, very much into God, breakfast cereals and excruciating snack foods. They read, often aloud, a newspaper that looked, from where I was sitting, exactly like the National Post but that sounds like a cross between a local gossip sheet and a supermarket tabloid. It features stories about how fast Hell is filling up.

Morgan gives a roof and a job to his older brother, Thomas James, who used to be a drug-taking, free-loving leftie but has taken a partial step toward his brothers good graces by converting -- like Walmsley himself -- to Catholicism. But he's one of your progressive social-justice Catholics. He translates right-wing economic theory as "the poor have too much money and the rich don't have enough, which he thinks is the opposite of Christian. By contrast, Morgans idea of a political position is to contemplate the terrorist armaments that may be aimed at the United States and to say, Its a disgrace those weapons aren't aimed at Canada."

Candace seems, on the surface, to be ready for debate. When Thomas James comes up with the de rigueur references to camels and needles, she goes so far as to tell him, with sweet pity in her voice, that he does not understand. This is as close to a meeting, or even a battle, of minds as the play gets. As dialectic, it's a frost.

A related but deeper flaw is that Morgan and Candace are hypocrites. Their favourite social activity is to attend "Arabian Nights, for couples only, involving wine, nudity and whatever else. (If it cant make me pregnant," Candace says, "it isnt sexual relations.) We also learn that Morgan has been getting it on with every available young woman in his catchment area. I know that fundamentalist ministers are continually getting caught out in real- life scandals, and last Sunday's New York Times said that the Bible Belt has the highest divorce rate in America. But a clash of values is more interesting dramatically if the values are sincerely held. And besides, the religious right is far more frightening if we assume it means what it says.

So we have to fall back on the sex and violence, which, fortunately, are good. One sibling beats the other up, and the scene is very well staged; tactfully, too. The comic mainspring is that Candace is hot for Thomas James and progressively less coy about it. Morgan, who is sterile, wants his brother to father Candace's child. What he has in mind is artificial insemination via a turkey baster. This, by Candaces definition quoted above, would of course count as sexual relations, maybe with a pun on relations," but anyway it isnt what she has in mind. TJ, despite some mental twistings-and- turnings, agrees with her. The play resolves into a neat satirical sex farce, lampooning the striving and decorous middle class. It's like the German classic The Underpants, seen recently in Toronto and at the Shaw Festival. Walmsley isn't as good as Carl Sternheim at keeping his eye on the object, but he does pretty well.

- - -

Kate Lynch has given the play a very witty production. Jordan Pettle, an actor who exudes amiable doubt, is an unlikely choice for the ironclad Morgan, but he makes his charm work for him, presenting a bully so sure of his own righteousness and so adept at double- think that he hardly has to work at it. He also looks, as the plot requires him to be, easy to deceive. David Jansen is a powerful, easy, ambiguous presence as TJ: ambiguous because the dramatic weight of his Catholicism remains a secret between the playwright and God. But the most perfect of the three squares is Fagans Candace; theres a new comic boldness in her playing, a perfect matching of means to ends. She gets both the shimmying temptress bit and the mental solipsism that makes it possible. Like Candace, she invents her own outrageous conventions and makes them work for her.

- - -

Kurt Weill's 1941 Broadway musical Lady in the Dark also made its own rules. Two years before Oklahoma! it proposed a new equality between book and score. Moss Hart's voluminous script is about the psychoanalysis of a fashionable magazine editor baffled by her life. Weills chameleonic, echoing score (the best-known song is My Ship; the best is This Is New) and Ira Gershwins tricky lyrics depict her dreams. The show's account of, and faith in, analysis is simplistic and its conclusions dubious (the heroine needs only to find the right man), but there is a haunting, ambitious quality to it. It has never had a major American revival, partly because the central role, created by Gertrude Lawrence, is a terror. Donna Murphy might have the best shot today at the necessary mixture of brittleness and warmth. Last weekend's production by the Toronto Operetta Theatre (at the Jane Mallett) was a non-starter in almost every respect.

Some of the performances, in Guillermo Silva-Marins production, were so inept one didnt know whether to be embarrassed by them or for them. Not only could most of the cast not speak or move, they couldn't sing, at least not in the sense of making themselves heard over the orchestra: that includes the leading lady, Elizabeth Beeler. The only bright spot was Thom Allison, the one recruit from the regular musical theatre, who got regulation camp laughs as an art editor and did coruscating song-dance-and-patter work in the musical bits, especially as a judge at a trial conceived, Chicago- style but years earlier, as a circus.

- Three Squares a Day runs through March 12 at Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, 416-504-7529.

robertcushman@lycos.com

Are musicals the last bastions of cultural nationalism? Even in this age of global co-production, each show zealously, or jealously, proclaims its point of origin. The pop operas of the last century often seemed as rootless in their stories as in their musical styles, but they were still identified, by their creators and everyone else, as the British (and occasionally French) invasion.

The imminent Lord of the Rings has its world premiere at a Toronto theatre, under Canadian management, and its cast boasts half a dozen members in good standing of Canada's roving super ensemble, but it still comes to us from another country, and I dont mean Middle-earth. Its origins, creative and entrepreneurial, are British, and it debuts here, as has been freely acknowledged, largely because there was no suitable theatre available in London. We know that if its a success, a theatre in London will magically open up, as of course will one in New York, still regarded as the ultimate test. If it can make it here, it still has to make it there.

As for the native Canadian musical, there hasn't been one that the outside world would recognize since Anne of Green Gables (and none before that). But that may be about to change. In May, The Drowsy Chaperone opens on Broadway. This is a show that has already progressed from the status of nice overstretched joke in its first Toronto outing to that of thorough delight in its second. We now wait to see whether its American production, which has already gone down very well in Los Angeles, can take it up a notch without losing the original's naive crafty charm.

Chaperone is in the category of affectionate spoof, a genre that in the past has produced hits of the magnitude of The Boy Friend (British) and Dames at Sea (American). One thing that argues for the integrity of the new production is the retention, among an otherwise all-American cast, of the original narrator, the very droll Bob Martin, who set the shows tone and without whom it is difficult to imagine. It may be an augury that Chaperone owes its New York booking (at the Marquis) to the early demise of Andrew Lloyd Webbers The Woman in White; we are coming to rely on parodies and revivals for injections of the traditional musical-comedy delight that has otherwise vanished in a sea of humourless self-importance.

Which reminds me: The show is directed by Casey Nicholaw, who already has a huge Broadway success with Spamalot, the musical of Monty Python and the Holy Grail. This is coming to the Canon Theatre in July and August as part of the Mirvish season. Wicked received the same kind of limited-run exposure here last year, and it obviously marks a retrenchment from the days when The Producers and Hairspray were set down for open-ended runs that unexpectedly closed.

I confess to some uncertainty over which country has bragging rights to Spamalot. The source material is obviously very British, and so, for all his current expatness, is Eric Idle, the musical's co-author and Python-in-residence. All the same, the power of the production (Mike Nichols being the man ultimately in charge) and its magnum-scale confidence are definitely American: one thing, at least, that Spamalot has in common with Camelot. The tone, though, to judge from the cast recording, is American with a difference, and that difference could only be English. Spamalot is a theatrical Tristram Shandy, a musical that is in part about doing a musical. So is The Producers. But The Producers is insiders' spoof (which is perhaps why it failed outside New York and as a movie); ultimately, it believes in the conventions, even takes them for granted. Spamalot is baffled by them; when, in a number titled The Song That Goes Like This, it lampoons the entire corpus of the Lloyd Webber ballad, it communicates -- very effectively -- a bafflement that such things should exist.

Meanwhile, we continue to get old musicals, mainly, though not entirely, American ones. The Stratford Festival, still working its way through the standard classics (My Fair Lady and Guys and Dolls have now come around twice each), this year reaches South Pacific, but twins it with the primal British show, Oliver!. The Shaw Festival, which last year joined the main-stage musical game with Gypsy, follows it with High Society. CanStage is about to give us Hair, and has already announced The Rocky Horror Picture Show for next season.

As for when and how the latest, surprisingly rich, Broadway crop will reach us (The Light in the Piazza, Dirty Rotten Scoundrels, The 25th Annual Putnam Spelling Bee), there is as yet no word. Meanwhile, we have some catching up to do. Recent Toronto productions of Jason Robert Browns The Last Five Years and Andrew Lippas John and Jen have reminded us how little we still know of the new wave of American composers, most of whose shows -- not all - - are too small for the commercial producers but don't fit the identity of most of our non-profits. Lippa's The Wild Party is worth investigating, and so is the exactly contemporaneous show with the same title and the same source by Michael John LaChiusa, both of them acrid explorations of the 1920s style and ethos. The LaChiusa show I most want to see, though, is Hello Again, his update of Schnitzlers La Ronde, which has some stunning musico-dramatic scenes.

Browns Parade, a grim show about a Southern lynching, has yet to be seen in Canada, even though it started as a Livent project. Anyone who saw Brent Carver as the victim, reprising his big number at the Tonys, must have been a) profoundly moved; and b) aghast when he lost the prize to Martin Short. (Also one of ours, but patriotism, as Edith Cavell said, is not enough.) And talking of Livent authors, Lynn Ahrens and Stephen Flaherty, who wrote Ragtime, have gone on doing fine work. Their A Man of No Importance, from a movie about a shy, gay Dublin bus conductor who lives for amateur theatre in general and Oscar Wilde in particular, is full of good things. So, even, is their ill-fated Seussical, though its delightful numbers never find a story to unite the songs and the Dr. Seuss characters and lingo.

2006-03-10-dickens-would-approve:
robertcushman@lycos.com

I am about to give away the opening line of the new season of The Sopranos. It's actually an old line, practically a proverbial one: "Nobody ever went broke underestimating the intelligence of the American public." I will refrain from telling you the context in which the line is spoken and the response that it gets.

Anyway, it has to be there as a cheeky acknowledgment by the show's creator, David Chase, of the extraordinary anomalous position his gangster-chronicle now holds on American television. The Sopranos, by making no compromises with its own intelligence, has rated that of its audience very high. It doesn't have the numbers of American Idol, but it hasn't gone broke; very far from it. And I'll bet that over the years its residuals will be higher.

To see and hear the familiar title-sequence again -- James Gandolfini's Tony Soprano driving home while Woke Up This Morning plays on the soundtrack with its pounding refrain about getting yourself a gun -- is to experience an extraordinary rush: to wonder, too, how we ever got by during the show's long hiatus. I think it's the best opening any TV show has ever had, clueing us in on the man and his world without speaking a word. That sequence apart, though, almost the most revolutionary thing about The Sopranos (ironically, given that title) is the way it does without music, or at least without music that would not realistically be playing in the course of a particular scene. (And even the opening song might conceivably be on Tony's car-radio.) The show never brings in extraneous scoring to tell us what we are supposed to be feeling. Other cable shows have followed its example, but on the networks, it wouldn't be allowed; it would be like doing a sitcom without a laugh-track. It must be one of the reasons Chase keeps giving thanks that the big boys turned him down.

That's not to say that The Sopranos isn't manipulative; all drama is. It has involved us from the start in one simple conflict; it has built a huge edifice on a single hinge. It's usual to say that the show is constructed on a kind of pun; it's about a man who supports, and is supported by, two separate families, the one under his roof and the Mafia.

That's true, but the main point is that within both these sets of relationships Tony is capable of behaving either well or badly. He is unfaithful to his wife, almost automatically, but he loves her and values their marriage; he is proud of, and worries about, his children. A representative middle-class man, really. He is in denial about the mother who wanted to have him killed (here we get less representative) and is recklessly, even dangerously, indulgent of the senile uncle who plotted it with her; indeed, one of Uncle Junior's dramatic functions is to make Tony look good.

Professionally, Tony can be more compassionate than one expects of a mob-boss or every bit as brutal. He can feel rage and pity at the murder of a teenage stripper in a way that mystifies his associates; he can also cold-bloodedly engineer what is, by general consent, the most shocking event in the story so far, the killing of his nephew's helpless stool-pigeon of a girlfriend. The writers even managed to up the ante on that the following week. "We haven't really talked about Adriana," said Tony to Christopher. We anticipated some serious soul-searching, but it turned out they only wanted to discuss how to make sure the feds didn't find out.

That's a wonderfully light-fingered example of the serious way in which the show plays with our feelings. It's a tantalizing process; we like Tony, and we cling to any signs that he may be redeeming himself, only to have them dashed the next moment. And still we keep coming back for more. It was all pre-figured in the very first episode, when Tony's wife Carmela said to him "the difference between us is that you're going to Hell and I'm not." That remark has echoed down the years (Carmela apologized for it a couple of seasons later) and it comes back, hauntingly, in the new season.

All of which suggests that Chase and his colleagues are working on a very large canvas indeed. Successful TV series can go on for a long time, but few of them do more than add one similar set of incidents to another. In fact, before The Sopranos, I don't know of any American show that did. I do know of some in Britain. Dennis Potter, Britain's premier television playwright, realized after turning out dozens of one-off dramas that he had a far more capacious vehicle to hand in the serial format previously reserved for literary adaptations. The results were Pennies from Heaven and The Singing Detective. Alan Bleasdale wrote the uproarious, unruly GBH, a comic epic about local politics that kept throwing off new characters and sub-plots lie a dog shakes off fleas. The fashion spread to more obviously popular forms; Between the Lines (shown over here as Inside the Line) was a series about police investigating other police, which managed to place individual stories within a developing narrative and was brilliant until it disappeared up its own plot-complications. It also anticipated The Sopranos in its ruthlessness about killing off sympathetic characters. The Sopranos, though, has gone it one better by being the first crime-series not to be told from the point of view of the cops.

Some British critics grumbled about "the death of the single play," but they should have been celebrating TV's discovery of its own greatest potential, the development of a narrative scale unavailable to theatre or movies.

It had, however, been grandly exploited in the past by another form combining the highest quality with the highest popularity: the 19th-century novel. This too usually came out in instalments, and made great use of cliff-hanger endings; Charles Dickens' motto was "make 'em laugh, make 'em cry, make 'em wait." It was also, like The Sopranos, obsessively concerned with sex and violence. (What else is there to write about?) And if the sex in those novels is discreet, sublimated even, the violence is up-front and ferocious. Dickens in England, like Dostoevsky in Russia, wrote murder-stories, frequently about people being battered to death.

One thing Dickens didn't go in for, which the TV practitioners do, was sequels. But other Victorians did. Anthony Trollope, underrated until recently, wrote giant sequences of novels, and if his bishops and politicians seem decorous on the outside, their in- fighting is as merciless as any criminals'. These writers used the long form to create fierce social panoramas, and their descendants do the same. The Sopranos, like the Godfather movies which dealt with a more grandiose criminal era, presents the business-ethic carried to its logical extreme. That isn't the most interesting thing about either work, but it helps.

Chase has said that he originally wanted each episode of The Sopranos to be complete unto itself. We must be grateful that he either decided or was forced to orchestrate a novel on video. He also says, somewhat contradictorily, that he has always had the total arc of the series in his head, though he famously refuses to tell anyone including the actors what it is. But while keeping us waiting for the pay-off, he has managed to create something extraordinarily complex. The characters, surely the best written and best-acted bunch in TV history, keep expanding, keep playing off one another. Some become icons that their actors can't shake off; Gandolfini in his movie roles always seems like Tony Soprano playing dress-up, while Edie Falco has been able on stage and screen to become someone else entirely, though she never sheds Carmela's crinkled grin. The point is not that one kind of acting is better than the other, but the show has been able to accommodate both (and I may have imagined it but I think there's a subtle, almost unearthly, shift in their styles to accommodate a new development in the upcoming series).

Themes echo, symphonically; Christopher, almost quitting the gang, plays out the one thing we want Tony to do and know he never will. Perhaps the best-loved episode of all and certainly the funniest -- Pine Barrens, in which Christopher and Paulie get lost in the woods -- can afford to keep Tony on the sidelines, though he's still the controlling presence; the series trusts its minor characters, even if their boss doesn't. And we're kept aware throughout that Tony's Jersey mob is only part of a wider criminal world. Everyone's expected to knuckle under to New York.

This awareness of a broader context is one thing that has made it more exciting than its most notable successor, Six Feet Under, which, for all its brave qualities, remained a brittle domestic soap. (And undertaking is a business more inherently limiting than racketeering, though I guess they have a symbiotic relationship.) The influence of The Sopranos has of course extended beyond cable; 24 wouldn't have been able to take the long-range risks it has without that example. It also has a conflicted hero, though Jack Bauer's personal issues, unlike Tony's, always seem to be more alluded to than dramatized.

The first two episodes of the new season are as accomplished and audacious as any that have gone before -- they certainly took me by surprise. They also demonstrate a learning-process; an ambitious idea that didn't quite work in the last batch has been refined and perfected. It's depressing that this, even though stretched out over two years, will be the last of The Sopranos but uplifting too. Long- form is a great thing; too long is deadly. Chase obviously knows when to stop; and I trust him when he says he knows how.

2006-03-10-the-beeb-does-the-bard-bbc-ca:
robertcushman@lycos.com

BBC Canada is doing unto Shakespeare what the Great Kleptomaniac so prolifically did to his own precursors. It is recycling him. The series Shakespeare Re-told, which reaches us after being shown last year in the U.K., presents newly scripted modern-dress adaptations of four of the most popular plays.

The problem here, of course, is that Shakespeare's own company at the Globe would never have dreamed of mounting seasons entitled, say, Holinshed Re-Chronicled or Plutarch Plagiarized. They weren't in the business of drawing attention to their sources. They wanted their audiences to enjoy new plays for their own sakes. Shakespeare Re-told wants its audiences to enjoy new plays for the sake of old ones. How they would strike people with no knowledge of the originals I can't say, but I doubt if, with that umbrella title, many of them will be watching anyway. The theoretical target may be viewers who have dim memories of the plays, from school or from the occasional past production, and want some painless clarification. But it doesn't work like that. The new scripts are knowing, sophisticated affairs that play games with the Shakespearean stories and joke with the Shakespearean texts. These aren't new creations exploiting Shakespearean ideas, like Edward Bond's Lear or Tom Stoppard's Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead. These are parasites, of varying degrees of entertainment-value.

Not surprisingly the one tragedy in the lineup, Macbeth (March 12; 9 p.m.) works the best, since here the comic touches freshen up the original story rather than going into competition with it. It even makes good fun of the play's own scary reputation. "It's bad luck to call him by name", says someone of the protagonist; "just call him the Scottish chef." The Scottish chef is Joe Macbeth, so named not only in homage to Shakespeare but also possibly to a 1950s gangster film that was an earlier exercise in the same updating genre. Joe presides over a swank restaurant kitchen in London; one night, putting out the leftovers, he meets a trio of orange-suited garbage-collectors who tell him "three Michelins coming your way. Joe." They're right, and thus emboldened Joe -- encouraged, of course, by his wife -- takes his carving knife to Duncan, Irish kingpin of the city's restaurant empire. It fits; gourmet ratings are their own battlefield while celebrity chefdom may be as near as our culture gets to hereditary kingship. (Malcolm, Duncan's official heir-apparent, has put himself out of the running by being an ex- vegetarian.) Peter Moffat's script has a mordant wit on its own account: "In another life," says Duncan, en route to slaughter, to Lady Mac, "I'd make a pass at you." "In another life" she replies "I'd let you." Moffat also clears up the vexed question of the Macbeths' missing child; they had one, which lived just long enough for his mother to give him the breast, once. The bell that calls Macbeth to murder emanates from his cellphone; "what, in our house?" becomes a smooth "murdered -- here?"; "beware Macduff" is "Look out for the big waiter"; and the banquet scene with Duncan's ghost is brilliantly re-imagined. James McAvoy (the faun from The Chronicles of Narnia) is a fine, bristly young protagonist; and the upshot, if not tragedy, is very high-grade melodrama.

The comedies, by contrast, suffer from a brittle brightness that owes something to Shakespeare but more to upper-class British sitcom. Sarah Wainwright's The Taming of the Shrew, which aired on March 5, is the only script in the group to depart significantly from its original's storyline, though not far enough to become its own thing.

The sex war is more spiffily fought in Much Ado About Nothing (March 19, 9 p.m.), a play with less to apologize for. Benedick and Beatrice (Damian Lewis and Sarah Parish) have become sparring newscasters on local TV. This seems a very good metier for them, and David Nicholl's script allows them to play the right kinds of wit: twittishly insistent in his case, sharply defensive in hers. All the storytelling is clever, though the framing for infidelity of the bride, Hero (who does the weather but has trouble with the word "meteorologist"), is even less plausible in a world of cameras and text messages than in one of eavesdropping and disguises. Dogberry the bumbling constable is here Mr. Berry (Anthony O'Donnell, himself a veteran Shakespearean clown), an officious but surprisingly competent security guard. Intertextuality is here confined to having Beatrice coach Benedick through one of the Sonnets ("let me not to the marriage of true minds...") and it works, elevating them. It's better than any of the verse in Much Ado itself, a play that depends for its zing on Shakespeare's comic prose and seems to lumber without it. Again, the elimination of familial bonds -- Beatrice is no longer Hero's cousin -- weakens the action. One post-feminist touch, however, is very telling; this Hero doesn't forgive her slanderous Claudio just because he's apologized.

No more does Helena in Peter Bowker's A Midsummer Night's Dream (March 26, 9 p.m.) settle for being some boy's lapdog. This play is probably the toughest assignment of the bunch: a symphonic structure that's light as a feather and tough as steel -- and one of the few Shakespeare plays that he seems to have made up. This version, set in a kind of honeymoon theme park, is a brave, sometimes charming but unsuccessful try. Oberon and Titania are still disrupting the climate with their marital squabbles ("Why do you think the weather's so weird nowadays? You think it's global warming? No chance.") though they're more equal than they were back in Athens, and he apologizes for playing practical jokes on her. The mortal marriage they're trying hardest to repair is that of Theseus and Hippolyta (a.k.a. Theo and Polly), the original play's authority figures, here doubling as Hermia's parents. It's labour lost since, even with actors as splendid as Bill Paterson and Imelda Staunton, those characters aren't very interesting. The final nuptial celebrations, somewhat altered, do cast an approximation of their customary spell, with the Rude Mechanicals providing the cabaret. They are the resort staff (security again) with Johnny Vega's Nick Bottom a stand-up comic who was once a professional. His encounter with the fairy queen is sweet. ("I'm Bottom, but you can call me Booty." "They call me Titania." "I'm not surprised."). Vega has the perfect blend of shyness and assurance, and you want to see him play Bottom for real. That's the feeling left by the series as a whole; it leaves you hungry for the genuine article. Which may even have been the intention. But it's a self-defeating one.

Black & White Photo: BBC Canada / In A Midsummer Night's Dream, Johnny Vega plays Nick Bottom, a stand-up comic who meets the fairy queen.
2006-03-11-past-perfect-far-from-it-but-:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Past Perfect runs through April 2 at the Tarragon, 416-531-1827; The Rochdale Project runs through March 19 at Theatre Passe Muraille, 416-504-7529); Kafka and Son runs through March 18 at the Al Green Theatre, 416-504-7529.

In Past Perfect, Michel Tremblay's most recent play, four people take turns telling Albertine, a young Montreal woman, how impossibly self-centred and self-dramatizing she is. She doesn't deny it. This simplicity, as of a Greek tragedy minus the earth-shattering themes, is characteristic of veteran playwrights who have already done narrative structure. And as the play proceeds, Tremblay's embracing of monotony does to some extent pay off. To put it another way, the later scenes are less boring than the earlier ones.

This, at the Tarragon, may have as much to do with performance as with script. The central character has figured in many previous Tremblay works, most elaborately in Albertine in Five Times, in which five different versions of her, aged from 30 to 70, held the stage simultaneously. Past Perfect rounds off those decades by going further back. The year is 1930, and the heroine is 20, working in a restaurant and in a deadly sulk about that and everything else, especially about having lost her boyfriend to her own sister. Her first conversation is with her mother, who does the janitor's work in their building. (The janitor whose work she does is her husband.) Albertine mocks her mama for wearing her good straw hat while working and mama chides Albertine for wearing her best Sunday dress on a Thursday. She then realizes that Albertine is actually wearing her sister's best Sunday dress and deduces correctly that this is all part of a hopeless scheme to win her beau back. As Nancy Beatty plays her, Albertine's mom is so subdued you expect her to sink through one of her own scrubbed floors.

She's dynamite, though, compared to sister Madeleine, who is portrayed by the hitherto-promising Claire Calnan as beyond dowdy. Not only has she been robbed of her one nice frock by the woman she's sharing the stage with, but she delivers her lines, many of which are perfectly sensible, in a mixture of shout and squawk.

She may have been forced into operatic mode by Leah Cherniak's staging, which has the two girls chasing and haranguing one another all around their living room. It isn't very effective and it isn't very believable. The most devastating conversations between two people usually occur when the participants are sitting down; if they are on their feet, it's for some practical reason, not because a director thinks it will look striking. There are some pretty stage- pictures here, composed from cigarette smoke and the changing positions of the furniture on Yannik Larivee's revolving set, but they're offset by obtrusively brutal lighting and constant back- projections of tearful early movie queens, from whom Albertine is said to have derived much of her world view. Having made its point in about two minutes, this footage keeps coming back, not just to haunt the leading lady, who is having a tough enough time as it is, but to upstage her.

As Albertine, Caroline Cave is required to act in a state of continual climax; she hits a few peaks cleanly and powerfully but in between she is simply strident. The Greek comparison may be apposite; she's Electra, right down to her adoration of her (absentee) father. More prosaically, she's a very recognizable type of neurotic narcissist, and the production does her and us no favours in taking her at her own inflated valuation. Something is wrong when a talented actress spends so much energy acting badly.

Admittedly there are things in the text, at least in this translation, that would defy any actor's attempts to act natural. The exposition is shamelessly naked, and period atmosphere consists of people saying repeatedly that they're "in the middle of a Depression." The play only perks up when we meet the two last arrivals, who have identifiable attitudes and the specific details to back them up.

One, the only family member with a sense of humour, is Albertine's fat, gay brother (Jeffrey R. Smith), who gets a frosty response when he asks her to forget her own problems for a moment and think about his. The other, delightfully played by Brendan Gall, is the sisters' Gentleman Caller, who, when Albertine protests her undying love for him, says in effect that if that is love he doesn't want it; it feels too much like being smothered. She, of course, declaims that she'll never get over him, though, on the evidence of the five later Albertines in the earlier play, she actually bounced right back.

- - -

The Rochdale Project is a collective enterprise memorializing another collective enterprise: the alternative college, squat and drug- exchange that is part of 1960s Toronto mythology. As a play, it's hopelessly split between story and scrapbook. There are six principal characters of whom five are hippie stereotypes; an amateur dealer, an airhead, an earth-mother, an autodidact and a designer of geodesic domes. The sixth (Melissa Good, whose performance lives up to her name) is an ex-Mennonite dragging around a personal secret which -- in a classic example of a dramatic no-win situation -- she refuses to divulge until long after we have guessed it. She is also the character who takes the firmest stand to keep Rochdale open, as it succumbs to debt and disorder, though it isn't clear why she bothers.

The cast, under Simon Heath's direction, performs cheerfully and efficiently. They seem to belong less to the age of Hair than to that of Rent, especially in the matter of non- payment. They even start the second act Rent-style, all lined up, though they don't sing at us.

- - -

Kafka and Son is a thrilling adaptation of an unmailed letter from the novelist to his overbearing father, whom he blames or credits for making him the incredibly influential wreck he was. "You're a true Kafka," he tells his dad, "in loudness and in presence of mind"; the term "Kafkaesque" obviously meant different things back then. Its more familiar connotations are brilliantly realized in Mark Cassidy's production, which situates young Franz, menacingly lit and mostly in a fetal position, in one makeshift cage after another, with a slanting overhead grille completing the effect. Alon Nashman's performance of both roles is flawless, vocally, physically and imaginatively: what, in light of Kafka Junior's tortured timidity, you might call a tour de faiblesse.

THE ARAB-ISRAELI COOKBOOK

Berkely Street Theatre Upstairs

- - -

Here is an uncontroversial compliment. The Arab-Israeli Cookbook is the most mouth-watering play in Toronto. It tantalizes the tastebuds more than any play since Saturday, Sunday, Monday, Eduardo de Filippo's celebration of the bedrock Neapolitan values of work, home and pasta.

Both plays devote a lot of stage time to food: cooking it, eating it, talking about it. The current one derives from a research trip to the Middle East, undertaken in 2003 by Robin Soans. Soans, an English actor with an uncanny vocal resemblance to the great Alec McCowen, interviewed scores of Israelis and Palestinians: Jewish, Muslim, Christian. He discovered that, whatever their differences, they had one thing in common: a consuming interest in consuming.

So not only are they like one another, with virtually interchangeable cuisines, they are like everybody else, in or out of war zones. We all cling to simple pleasures, in the face of all the pressures that assail us. That's a humane observation, but it isn't necessarily enough to make a play.

The script that Soans assembled from his interviews supposedly allows each person to speak in his or her unmediated voice. This suggests that all of his subjects spoke English. If a translator was involved, that immediately introduces another level; and there are some speeches, which, translated or not, are too neatly turned to pass as verbatim reproduction. One dish is described as having "a stiff whiff of antimacassars and mothballs." That sounds like a phrase that's been tidied up. In a conventional play, that might not matter, but it does in a piece such as this, which stakes everything on authenticity. The script is notably short on stops and starts. Everything sounds like a soundbite.

You notice this more because the play is, considering its setting, remarkably short on conflict. It is so intent on demonstrating its characters' common humanity it neglects the things that divide them. Jews and Arabs only appear together in one scene, set in a hummus store, where the sight of an unguarded bag sends everyone into terror. It's the most dramatic scene, though it violates the evening's premise. (Was Soans himself present at this incident? Did one of his subjects tell him about it? If so, who? And how can that person guarantee the accuracy of everyone else's dialogue?)

Most of the rest is monologue, a form that is even more limiting than usual here because for the most part the speakers talk only of their own communities. We hear that the two sides live in a state of mutual fear and resentment, but only in passing. We are mainly told how each group feels about its own friends and neighbours.

Surprisingly, given the alternative theatre's reputation for leftiness, we are made more aware of the Israelis' sufferings than of the Palestinians'. Maybe Jews talk more. More likely, it's a matter of suicide bombings lending themselves more easily to exciting set-piece narrative than harassment at checkpoints. Whatever you think of it politically, it's a weakness dramatically. The underlying grievances on both sides are barely mentioned, let alone discussed. The play does, though, perform a valuable service in giving a voice to the region's Christians, consigned to the sidelines on a good day, caught in the crossfire on a bad.

One of them comes closest to being the play's voice. She has a compassionate heart and an austere outlook, as well as being one of the best cooks, and she doubts any of the grassroots attempts at understanding -- inter-cultural sports, protesting mothers, etc. -- will bear fruit. She might be passing ironic judgment on the play.

She's played with dignity by Barbara Gordon, one of seven performers giving multiple accomplished performances. But that too is a problem. Sometimes when an actor you thought was still playing an Israeli is now an Arab, it makes a point; other times, it's confusing. Beyond that, the actors are in the same bind as the script; they try hard to be conversational and end up falling into familiar stage rhythms. Victor Ertmannis, whose roles include the hummus-maker and a bus driver on what's virtually a suicide route, is the most persuasive. The others are David Fox, whose familiar massive presence accommodates surprising versatility, Mark McGrinder, Jeff Miller, Kimwun Perehinec, and Maria Ricossa as a widow who could afford to live anywhere but stays in Israel because it's where she feels humanly connected. The play is directed, with great attention to culinary detail, by Joel Greenberg, who three years ago staged The Laramie Project, a venture in the same documentary style that concentrated, more successfully, on one sensational story in one town and let it ramnify. Here the ingredients remain obstinately scattered. They don't, in fact, cook.

Colour Photo: Barbara Gordon shows off her acting chops in multiple roles.
