THE INNOCENT EYE TEST

Royal Alexandra Theatre

Michael Healey's new comedy switches between being a sex-farce, a political homily, a meditation on art and a rogue episode of 24. None of these elements work, partly because they get in one anothers way, but somewhere in the plays confused heart are some thoughts on how Canada should be conducting itself in the world.

Set in a swish Tuscan hotel, the show has a multi-national cast of characters -- they seem indeed to come from practically everywhere except Italy -- but the protagonist is Canadian, and one of his fellow guests keeps calling him Canada. This happens so often that we too start to think of him as Canada, and by the end he finds himself taking what amounts to a national stand on international relations, especially regarding the United States. The upshot is that it's bad for us to sell the Americans plutonium, a stash of which is kicking around one of the plot lines, but good to sell them paintings. Good for our pockets and very good for their souls.

These are worthy thoughts but they arrive late and in a hurry. The part about the painting has to do with Samuel Kneck, the man who is Canada, being an art-dealer. He is in Tuscany at the bidding of Darryl Plate, a Las Vegas entertainment mogul who is opening a museum back home and wants to acquire a Mark Tansey painting whose title, The Innocent Eye Test, is also that of the play. The painting depicts a cow in an art gallery gazing enchanted at the picture of another cow. Darryl, who had bid for the painting sight unseen, is enchanted when he actually sees it. He, the plain man smitten, identifies with the cow. This is the best scene in the play. But it doesn't relate to anything else, and Darryl himself has nothing to do with the nuclear-enrichment thread thats going on elsewhere. Thats the trouble. The play may aspire to be an anti-farce, purposely running its jokes into the ground, but that's hard to bring off. We're left with the trappings of the form, without the unifying energy.

Also present are an Irish married couple who may or may not be terrorists (or Irish, or indeed married); a young woman who has psychic powers and for whom Samuel falls heavily; and a Ukrainian, carrying a briefcase identical to Sams. We expect the two bags will get confused, and when they dont we feel half cheated, half relieved. A cliche has been avoided. Then they do get confused, but only half-heartedly, and it feels like the worst of both worlds.

Up till now Healey's writing, like his acting, has always been funny whatever else; but here, where that gift is vital, it seems to have deserted him. There is some charm in the character of Daryl, who envisages an art gallery where a moving walkway whisks the spectators from picture to picture, finally depositing them in the gift shop. Sounds to me like the logical gallery experience; I can't see why Sam, with his pesky Canadian conscience, has anything against it. Tom McCamus, cast against type as Daryl, does a very good job of whisking on his own account; he, like his character, seems to be doing his damndest to get the show on the road. Gord Rand, a boundlessly surprising actor, as the man from Ukraine, lugubrious but hopeful, does a remarkable job of acting in his underpants; and C. David Johnson has himself a nice little comic cadenza in the second act. But nobody else is much good. Kevin Bundy, usually fine with lovable losers, is merely bland as Sam; Lisa Norton is a blank; and Tanja Jacobs seems to have given up, especially on sounding Irish.

Accents are a problem all around, especially as half the characters are pretending to be from somewhere theyre not. One of them is juggling three nationalities simultaneously. This creates a problem with audibility, exacerbated by the Royal Alex acoustics and the open spaces atop and around David Boechlers sets. The first act, by the hotel pool, looks hideous. The second, in Sam's suite, looks hideous and unbelievable. Its back wall is adorned by what appear to be the eyes of the Mona Lisa; it seems you don't have to go to Vegas to get your art dumbed down. The same uneasy compromise between God and Mammon characterizes the show as a whole. Mirvish Productions, doing their bit for Canadian drama and one of its best writers, get an inferior example of both, while author and interpreters seem to be aiming at some coarse idea of "commercialism" and missing. The designer and several of the actors are veterans of the Shaw Festival, and Christopher Newton, whose production has pace but not much else, is that theatre's distinguished former artistic director. The whole thing does resemble a bad night at Niagara-on-the-Lake, posh theatre letting its hair down when it had much better keep it in place.

Black & White Photo: Bruce Monk, Mirvish Productions / Samuel Kneck, right, represents our country amongst the multi-national characters in The Innocent Eye Test.
2006-03-18-summoning-darfur-s-frightenin:
robertcushman@lycos.com; The Monument runs through March 23 at the Berkeley Street Downstairs Theatre, 416-368-3110; Hanas Suitcase runs through April 23 at the Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People, 416-862-2222.

Colleen Wagner's The Monument begins with a long monologue, spoken by a teenage soldier named Stetko who awaits execution. He had been convicted of participation in multiple officially sanctioned rapes and murders, committed during a guerrilla war. He admits his crimes, looks back on them with shame mixed with a certain amount of pleasure, expresses some resentment at being the object of victors' justice, and claims, predictably, that he was mostly motivated by peer pressure and the need to prove himself sexually. He also talks about his girlfriend who should have visited him but hasnt.

The speech is somewhat generic but compelling; both the narrative and the emotions are believable. At the end of it, Stetko is approached by a woman named Mejra who will let him escape if he will then do whatever she wants. He agrees, and the rest of the play depicts their wanderings through a war-torn landscape. The transition takes the play to a different level, and a far less satisfying one.

Obsidian Theatre has revived the play, which was first seen here 10 years ago. The original production was set somewhere in Central Europe. Obsidian, restoring what were apparently the authors intentions, sets it somewhere in Africa. Either fits -- which indicates the play is lacking in specifics, the things that make drama happen.

Stetko's promised submission to Mejra involves walking around with his hands tied. Having him thus powerless, she starts hitting him, hard. At first this is rather satisfying; the man who committed unspeakable violence against women is getting a dose of his own medicine. But as it goes on, our sympathies shift. Whatever may have happened in the past, in the dramatic present, the victim is now Stetko or, as Mejra calls him, Stinko.

We learn, as Mejra herself does, that violence begets violence and that revenge turns hollow. But we already knew that, and the play keeps repeating it, with the minimum of human content that might make it seem fresh. The couple eventually arrive at the mass grave of Stetko's victims, one of them, unsurprisingly, Mejras only daughter, and they erect a grisly makeshift memorial, the one in the title. Symbolically presented, it makes for a powerful image, one on which the play should really end. But it doesnt.

Nigel Shawn Williams's production, designed with appropriate bleakness by Shawn Kerwin, is atmospherically strong if sometimes gratuitously underlit. If it gets monotonous, that's probably unavoidable. The same goes for the performances. Garnet Hardings sullen boyish bravado in his opening speech is exemplary; his subsequent oscillations between subservience and defiance give him little room to manoeuvre. Yanna McIntosh, avenging fury crossed with grieving survivor, has even less; her authority cannot be faulted, but the role has her punching far below her weight, even if the punches are literal.

- - -

For a contrasting lesson in how to bring atrocity home, see Hanas Suitcase. This production by the former Young People's Theatre is based on Karen Levine's book about two Tokyo schoolchildren who became fascinated by an exhibit in their citys Holocaust Education Centre -- the suitcase of Hana Brady, a young Czech girl sent to Auschwitz via Theresienstadt -- and, aided by a teacher, set out to learn more about her. As their investigations proceed, Hanas story takes shape in their minds and before our eyes.

Emil Sher's dramatization is remarkably successful, give or take some strenuously chatty exposition, and Allen MacInnis's direction is superb. On Teresa Przybylskis clever and elegant set, worlds collide. The screen doors of the Japanese house slide open to reveal silent grey figures trudging their way toward the camps. Thats all it takes: that and the brief use of a balcony level as the perch for an impassive SS guard.

The perkiness of Siu Ta and Richard Lee, grown-up actors playing the Japanese kids Maiko and Akira, can be hard to take, but it serves a purpose; they initially see the plight of the European Jews as a kind of video game. Only gradually do they come to recognize the horror and sheer helplessness of it. They and their teacher (admirably played by Jean Yoon) dominate the first half; Hana, her brother, George, and their parents are silent presences.

In the second act, they come to vocal life. Hana and George's incredulity at the remorseless restrictions as the Nazis crack down (the most frightening part of the story, because it's the easiest to identify with; the camps are beyond being moving) is echoed by Maiko and Akira, shocked for them and recoiling with them. Their words become interchangeable, and the ripples spread out among the Canadian children, watching from the auditorium. George, the only survivor, now lives in Toronto, and has attended a performance. The reverberations on that occasion -- he appears in the play as an adult as well as a child -- can only be imagined.

Jessica Greenberg plays Hana, Paul Dunn the young George, Eric Trask (who is especially fine) and Sarah Orenstein their parents and other adults. The re-enactment takes us all the way to Hanas consignment to the gas chambers. Its all handled with great tact, but no soft-pedalling.

There is another dimension to the story and to the production. Hana was one of a group of child artists who documented life in Theresienstadt, and some of their drawings, hidden and recovered, are projected. The show has undertaken its own project of research and reclamation. It confirms the rocketing of standards at this theatre under MacInnis's stewardship. It also, by concentrating on one reality, summons the corresponding reality of Darfur far more powerfully and movingly than The Monument, which is explicitly angled to do so. It also makes you wonder if, in Israel, schoolchildren are undertaking similar projects on Hiroshima.

Colour Photo: David Hou / Yanna McIntosh and Garnet Harding have little room to manoeuvre in their roles in The Monument.
2006-03-21-the-sopranos-returns-after-it:
I am about to give away the opening line of the new series of The Sopranos. It’s actually an old line, practically a proverbial one: “Nobody ever went broke underestimating the intelligence of the American public”. I will refrain from telling you the context in which the line is spoken and the response that it gets.

Anyway, it has to be there as a cheeky acknowledgment by the show’s creator, David Chase, of the extraordinary anomalous position his gangster-chronicle now holds on American television. The Sopranos, by making no compromises with its own intelligence, has rated that of its audience very high. It doesn’t have the numbers of American Idol, but it hasn’t gone broke; very far from it. And I’ll bet that over the years its residuals will be higher.

To see and hear the familiar title-sequence again – James Gandolfini’s Tony Soprano driving home while “Woke Up This Morning” plays on the soundtrack with its pounding refrain about getting yourself a gun – is to experience an extraordinary rush: to wonder, too, how we ever got by during the show’s long hiatus. I think it’s the best opening any TV show has ever had, clueing us in on the man and his world without speaking a word. That sequence apart, though, almost the most revolutionary thing about The Sopranos (ironically, given that title) is the way it does without music, or at least without music that would not realistically be playing in the course of a particular scene. (And even the opening song might conceivably be playing on Tony’s car-radio.) The show never brings in extraneous scoring to tell us what we are supposed to be feeling. Other cable shows have followed its example, but on the networks, it wouldn’t be allowed; it would be like doing a sitcom without a laugh-track. It must be one of the reasons Chase keeps giving thanks that the big boys turned him down.

That’s not to say that The Sopranos isn’t manipulative; all drama is. It has involved us from the start in one simple conflict; it has built a huge edifice on a single hinge. It’s usual to say that the show is constructed on a kind of pun; it’s about a man who supports, and is supported by, two separate families, the one under his roof and the Mafia. That’s true, but the main point is that within both these sets of relationships Tony is capable of behaving either well or badly. He is unfaithful to his wife, almost automatically, but he loves her and values their marriage; he is proud of, and worries about, his children. A representative middle-class man, really. He is in denial about the mother who wanted to have him killed (here we get less representative) and is recklessly, even dangerously, indulgent of the senile uncle who plotted it with her; indeed, one of Uncle Junior’s dramatic functions is to make Tony look good. Professionally, Tony can be more compassionate than one expects of a mob-boss or every bit as brutal. He can feel shock and pity at the murder of a teenage stripper in a way that mystifies his associates; he can also cold-bloodedly engineer what is, by general consent, the most shocking event in the story so far, the killing of his nephew’s helpless stool-pigeon of a girlfriend. The writers even managed to up the ante on that the following week. “We haven’t really talked about Adriana” said Tony to Christopher. We anticipated some serious soul-searching, but it turned out they only wanted to discuss how to minimize the possible fall-out.

That’s a wonderfully light-fingered example of the serious way in which the show plays with our feelings. It’s a tantalising process; we like Tony, and we cling to any signs that he may be redeeming himself, only to have them dashed the next moment. And still we keep coming back for more. It was all pre-figured in the very first episode, when Tony’s wife Carmela said to him “the difference between us is that you’re going to Hell and I’m not.” That remark has echoed down the years (Carmela apologised for it a couple of seasons later) and it comes back, hauntingly, in the new series.

All of which suggests that Chase and his colleagues are working on a very large canvas indeed. Successful TV series can go on for a long time, but few of them do more than add one similar set of incidents to another. In fact, before The Sopranos, I don’t know of any American show that did. I do know of some in Britain. Dennis Potter, Britain’s premier television playwright, realized after turning out dozens of one-off dramas, that he had a far more capacious vehicle to hand in the serial format, previously reserved for literary adaptations; the results were Pennies from Heaven and The Singing Detective. Alan Bleasdale wrote the uproarious, unruly GBH, a comic epic about local politics that kept throwing off new characters and sub-plots like a dog shakes off fleas. The fashion spread to more obviously popular forms; Between the Lines (shown over here as Inside the Line) was a series about police investigating other police, that managed to place individual stories within a developing narrative and was brilliant until it disappeared up its own plot-complexities. It also anticipated The Sopranos in its ruthlessness about killing off sympathetic characters. The Sopranos, though, has gone it one better by being the first crime-series not to be told from the point of view of the cops.

Some British critics grumbled about “the death of the single play” but they should have been celebrating TV’s discovery of its own greatest potential, the development of a narrative scale unavailable to theatre or movies. It had, however, been grandly exploited in the past by another form combining the highest quality with the highest popularity, the nineteenth-century novel. This too usually came out in instalments, and made great use of cliff-hanger endings; Charles Dickens’ motto was “make ‘em laugh, make ‘em cry, make ‘em wait.” It was also, like The Sopranos, obsessively concerned with sex and violence. (What else is there to write about?) And if the sex in those novels is discreet, sublimated even, the violence is up-front and ferocious. Dickens in England, Dostoevsky in Russia, wrote murder-stories, frequently about people being battered to death.

One thing Dickens didn’t go in for, that the TV practitioners do, was sequels. But other Victorians did. Anthony Trollope, underrated until recently, wrote giant sequences of novels, and if his bishops and politicians seem decorous on the outside, their in-fighting is as merciless as any criminals’. These writers used the long form to create fierce social panoramas, and their descendants do the same. The Sopranos, like the Godfather movies which dealt with a more grandiose criminal era, presents the business-ethic carried to its logical extreme. That isn’t the most interesting thing about either work, but it is important.

Chase has said that he originally wanted each episode of The Sopranos to be complete unto itself. We must be grateful that he either decided or was forced to orchestrate a novel on video. He also says, somewhat contradictorily, that he has always had the total arc of the series in his head, though he famously refuses to tell anyone including the actors what it is. But while keeping us waiting for the pay-off, he has managed to create something extraordinarily complex. The characters, surely the best written and best-acted bunch in TV history, keep expanding, keep playing off one another. Some become icons that their actors can’t shake off; Gandolfini in his movie roles always seems like Tony Soprano playing dress-up, while Edie Falco has been able on stage and screen, to become someone else entirely, though she never sheds Carmela’s crinkled grin. The point is not that one kind of acting is better than the other, but the show has been able to accommodate both (and I may have imagined it but I think there’s a subtle, almost unearthly, shift in their styles to accommodate a new development in the upcoming series). Themes echo, symphonically; Christopher, almost quitting the gang, plays out the one thing we want Tony to do and know he never will. Perhaps the best-loved episode of all and certainly the funniest – Pine Barrens, in which Christopher and Paulie get lost in the woods – can afford to keep Tony on the sidelines, though he’s still the controlling presence; the series trusts its minor characters, even if their boss doesn’t.. And we’re kept aware throughout that Tony’s Jersey mob is only part of a wider criminal world. Everyone’s expected to knuckle under to New York.

This awareness of a broader context is one thing that has made it more exciting than its most notable successor, Six Feet Under, which, for all its brave qualities, remained a brittle domestic soap. (And undertaking is a business more inherently limiting than racketeering, though one obviously feeds the other.) The influence of The Sopranos has of course extended beyond cable; 24 wouldn’t have been able to take the long-range risks it has without that example. It also has a conflicted hero though Jack Bauer’s personal issues, unlike Tony’s, always seem to be more alluded to than dramatized.

The first two episodes of the new season are as accomplished and audacious as any that have gone before; they certainly took me by surprise. They also demonstrate a learning-process; an ambitious idea that didn’t quite work in the last batch has been refined and perfected. It’s depressing that this, even though stretched out over two years, will be the last of The Sopranos but encouraging too. Long-form is a great thing; too long is deadly. Chase obviously knows when to stop; and I trust him when he says he knows how.

THE LORD OF THE RINGS

Princess of Wales Theatre, Toronto

At the curtain calls for The Lord of the Rings, the stage itself rises up and takes a bow. It deserves to. It has been giving a flawless performance all night, and a breathtakingly versatile one.

Not only does it revolve, which perhaps is no big deal, it also rises, falls, divides and subdivides, frequently doing all these things at the same time. The multiplicity of levels and compartments is great for battle scenes, of which there are many, and for overall speed; the various strands of a complicated story can overlap, which is exciting in itself.

The theatrical version of J.R.R. Tolkien's trilogy has its faults, most of them coming unshakably with the territory, but scenically, technically and imaginatively, its a marvel.

Under Matthew Warchus implacably disciplined direction, hardly any of the effects are gratuitous. The bad guys look really bad. The first Black Rider, suddenly unleashed from nowhere, is as majestically scary an apparition as I have seen in a theatre, a giant skeletal amalgam of horse and man. This, like the presentation of the man-eating spider Shelob with visible actors pulling her giant legs, may owe something to the animal acts in The Lion King, but it's creative imitation.

The virtuous people get their share of spectacle as well. When Aragorn, the returning king, finds himself short of living soldiers to fight the armies of the Dark Lord Sauron, he calls on the Warriors of the Dead who arise, shrouded in mist, from what looks like a huge vat of seaweed: a thrilling finale to the second of the show's three acts and a really smart recruiting idea. One can think of many places now where it might come in handy.

Rob Howells sets, a forest of invention with withered branches as the governing motif, pull not just the stage but the auditorium into Middle Earth, as does Paul Pyants lighting, which, in its beauty and variety, calls for the coining of new superlatives.

With three books to get through, the show can hardly afford to waste time so it starts before it starts with its real heroes, the hobbits of the Shire, already on stage, indulging in simple hobbit pleasures, such as trapping fireflies and releasing them again.

We have a solid base to start from and, some three and a half hours later, to come back to, since the show includes the culminating episode of the Scouring of the Shire, which is more than the movie-version did. It's a noble choice, but as a payoff it doesn't pay off. It feels rushed, not so much in tempo as in lack of weight. Thats something that keeps happening, and its the main flaw.

The adaptation, by Shaun McKenna and the director, is outstandingly intelligent. Resourcefully, it brings in shadow-play and a disembodied narrator to handle the exposition that's left over from the earlier book The Hobbit. It later proves neat at telescoping: cutting out swathes of narrative and binding the remaining bits together. It keeps its eye firmly on the essential object, the Ring of Power, the original weapon of mass destruction; on the quest of Frodo to destroy it; and on the torments, physical and mental, of Gollum, who's enslaved himself to it.

Tolkiens books, of which Im an admirer but not a devotee, have two big things going for them. One is our involvement in a reassuringly simple struggle of good against evil, the Dark Lord Sauron and his underlings vs. everybody else. The other, which helps guarantee the first, is the sheer scale of the story, which amounts to a ready-made mythology, something you can get lost in. It makes up for any amount of cardboard characterization and sheer bad writing.

It isn't for song and dance. Everybody has denied that Lord of the Rings can be turned into a musical, including those who've actually been doing it, and its true that the songs here are mainly used as dramatic lubricants -- glorified incidental music, really -- rather than as things in themselves.

Mainly, but not always. Early on theres a full-scale, stage- filling hobbit hootenanny. It's irresistible -- Peter Darling's choreography is top notch-- but it relates to nothing in the show. It looks and sounds, by the way, very Cape Breton. The score is the work of an Indian, A.R. Rahman, and a bunch of Finns, Varttina, with an Englishman, Christopher Nightingale, co-ordinating; but its clear that while here theyve all gone native.

There is one song that works dramatically, holding our attention, deepening the action, projecting the characters. Frodo and his friend and servant Sam cheer up their weary selves by hymning one another's heroic deeds, then Gollum reprises their tune, turning it into a lacerating investigation of his schizoid self. Michael Therriault, whose Gollum suggests Ariel re-inventing himself as Caliban, here sets the seal on a performance that has already slithered into theatrical glory.

Comparably fine is Evan Buliung's Aragorn, a piece of genuine heroic acting, supple and plangent.

Some of their peers among Canadas best-singing actors -- or best actors period -- are shown to less advantage. Brent Carvers Gandalf is too little the tetchy teacher, too much the saintly sage. Carver's great qualities are vulnerability and mischief, and Gandalf doesn't have much of either.

Richard McMillan as the turncoat wizard Saruman has little to do but stand around in whiskers; and Dion Johnstones Boromir is killed off before he can come to life. The show simply doesnt have time for him, or for most of the other Fellows of the Ring.

Gabriel Burrafoto (Legolas) and Ross Williams (Gimli, Welsh like in the movie) are just token dwarf and elf respectively; Owen Sharpe and Dylan Roberts as the junior hobbits are lively, but I couldn't tell them apart. Shawn Wright gets some of the show's few laughs as the spokesman of the Ents, who guard the trees and, with the aid of wires and stilts, look like them.

James Loye and Peter Howe, the two principal British imports, play Frodo and Sam; and are admirable, though the show skates over Frodos inner struggles on Mount Doom (which, given the books exclusively male worldview, might not be too far from Brokeback Mountain). I'm not sure that what happens at these climactic moments would be clear to anyone who didn't already know.

Some of this has to do with the absence of an important character, the title character in fact. The lord of the rings is Sauron, who forged them and whose power depends on them. He doesnt make any personal appearances in the book, either, but he lives there in what people say of him.

We are told he has shrunk his being to a single malignant all- seeing Eye. Thats quite an image, one you would think a production high on visual coups would want to capture. But it doesn't even try. It proceeds to miss out on the one really moving scene in the book, the one in which the new king and all his court kneel to the dazed heroic hobbits.

As an unsatisfactory substitute we get a wedding ceremony at which the guests, in one of the show's less happy design choices, look like a convocation of beekeepers. But this is to carp. At its worst, the show is far better than doubters ever thought it could be. At its best, its wonderful.

All politicians are egomaniacs, most are corrupt, many are idiots and more than a handful, regardless of party, are indictable crooks. Or would be if there were any justice. Which there isn't.

I have no trouble believing any of this. Even if I wanted to be skeptical, my ongoing exposure to VideoCabaret's comic-strip history of Canada would have worn down my resistance long ago. There are other side effects, though, of being told exactly the same thing about every participant in every chapter of our continental story. You may not lose belief but you do lose interest.

"The only thing one knows for sure is that the new boss will be the same as the old boss." That, taking the words out of my mouth, is Michael Hollingsworth, author and director of the cycle, in his program note. He adds: "What is going to happen has already happened." It happens all over again in Canadian Pacific Scandal, which is Part 6, coming around -- like the whole enterprise -- for the second time. The new bosses, alternating as the show proceeds, are John A. Macdonald, boondoggling over the contracts for the new Canadian Pacific Railway, and Alexander Mackenzie, whose thing is temperance. (It's the Caledonian Age of Canadian politics.) Forced to choose between the colourful carpetbagger and the prohibitionist prig, the voters naturally end up plumping for the latter. Others present include Wilfrid Laurier, who is pompous, and -- the closest thing to a sympathetic figure -- Louis Riel, who goes insane.

I speculated when reviewing an earlier instalment that one reason for VideoCab's habit of working in short, sharp scenes is that they dare not linger on any episode or character for fear of stumbling over something complex, someone who had done something admirable or at least defensible. No chance of that happening here. The problem is that as one surveys this troupe of venal marionettes, one rapidly -- by the end of the second scene, in my case -- ceases to care who is screwing whom. Somewhere off stage, of course, are the ordinary Canadians who are really being screwed, but the play is such a closed system that they barely register. The chief pleasure is the homely one of seeing famous figures from the history books getting their pants pulled down. It's a revenge on school.

The designs (from a team headed by Andy Moro, set and lighting, and Astrid Janson, costumes) are still dazzlingly brazen, the quickness of the changes nearly as unbelievable. As for the actors: The Campbells are coming, the two arch Scots being played by Richard Alan Campbell (MacK) and Greg Campbell (MacD), dour and braw respectively. Jim Jones is, in accordance with VidCab tradition, a truly terrifying bigoted bishop, and Kerry Ann Doherty stands out, in every sense, as a pudding-bellied Alexander Galt.

- - -

VideoCabaret have been at it since 1985. The state of highly skilled monotony that it has taken them 20 years to reach is attained by the two-girl team known as Independent Auntie in 50 minutes flat. Their show Clean Irene and Dirty Maxine, resurrected from the SummerWorks festival of three years ago, is billed as "A Deadly Comedy"; well, they said it. This show, too, harks back to schooldays. It's a rhymed cautionary alphabet. Anna Chatterton and Evalyn Parry, writers and performers, tell us about a gaggle of contemporary urban females, all of whom come to bad ends, from Arty Mary, felled by her own pretensions, to Yoga Lola, caught for keeps in a compromising position. (They do admit that there are certain letters they bypass.)

Sometimes, though not often, one thing leads to another. Arty Mary is confronted at her own exhibition by Busy Lizzie, a critic who -- braver than most in the trade -- tells her what she thinks to her face, before taking off on her own doomed trajectory, too driven to look where others are driving. Chatterton and Parry use their voices percussively and their bodies pneumatically. They're especially good at bending their bodies into complementary shapes. Their physical wit, however, is not matched by their verbal, which stops short at relentless brightness. Their point seems to be that to want anything, or to be anyone, is to invite disaster, but they don't prove it. Even my favourite of their creations, Quaker Fanny, meets an arbitrary end, unless you're prepared to take her soubriquet very literally. You've heard of an idea looking for a show. This is the reverse.

- - -

The bulk of plays from the past 300 years were written for curtained proscenium arch theatres. They can work on open or platform stages, but there's much to be said for seeing and performing them in their natural habitat, especially if you're a student trying to find out how their parts fit together. Most new theatres, especially academic ones, go for the platform look, but York University has just opened a new house, the Sandra Faire and Ivan Fecan Theatre, in traditional proscenium formation -- handsomely done up, what's more, in traditional plush red.

It's part of York's new Accolade Project, which officially opened last Monday. The project is an arts centre, spread over two buildings, that people have been hoping and planning for through most of the 30 years that York's fine-arts faculty has been in existence. It also contains performance, rehearsal and exhibition spaces for music, dance, film and visual arts.

Phillip Silver, York's dean of fine arts and a distinguished stage designer in his own right, has done much to bring the Accolade Project to fruition. For him, the single most important thing about it is that it will give students in all disciplines the opportunity to work in facilities of the highest professional standard so that they'll be prepared for similar environments in the real world. If they're lucky, that is.

ESCAPE FROM HAPPINESS

Factory Theatre

- - -

In 1992, when the Factory Theatre first staged it, George F. Walker's Escape from Happiness was in three acts and took three hours. It has now slimmed down to two of each. Not having seen the original production I cannot say if the compression is responsible for the plays disjointed feel, as if its constituent parts arent quite fitting together. It could be bred in the bone; this being Walker, it could even be intentional. Like most of his plays it is funny, a bit suspenseful, and generally more fun than many other people's. It also has two separate plots that don't cohere, even though most of the characters are involved in both of them.

There are 10 people in the cast, which was unusual 14 years ago and is phenomenal now. The gender-balance rivals Noahs Ark for strictness, and the women are without exception the stronger. Nora, in whose east-end Toronto house we are, is the eccentric mother of Elizabeth, who is a lawyer; Mary Ann, who is a flake; and Gail, who is married to Junior. Junior starts the play with a bang by being found lying on the floor with a chair rammed into his chest, having been rather severely beaten up. Gail wants to call the police, but Nora advises against it. She herself was married to a policeman whose name was Tom and who once burned down the family home. A man exactly resembling Tom now lives upstairs; Nora claims that he isnt her husband but nobody believes her and, no spoiling, we aren't expected to either. We also meet the two guys who did it to Junior and who it is assumed were involved with him in some kind of drug deal, and two cops who come to investigate. One of the latter is female with fancy college training, the other, old-school male, was once Tom's partner, though the play makes less of that than you might expect. Maybe their relationship was a casualty of cutting.

Theres the family story and theres the crime story, and they're united by emotional volatility if by nothing else. The question why do you say outrageous things? receives the answer "to bring the truth into focus, and to get things rolling." Which could be Walker copping, you should pardon the expression, to his own method. Nora is trying to hold her family together, though that's neither as clear nor as central as it might be. (It doesnt help that the other plot requires her to spend long periods off-stage. In custody, if you must know.) Shes sharp-tongued and somewhat saintly; non- family members cower when she talks to them, especially when she's doing it for their own good. She's played by Clare Coulter, whom I havent seen on a stage in years and who makes, apart from some vocal blurring, a triumphant return; Nora lives by her own logic, and Coulter never deviates from it for a moment.

None of the other ladies in the cast has quite the same degree of unforced confidence. As Gail, Rebecca Auerbach starts surly, and then has to spend the rest of the evening backtracking, which she does quite successfully. Mary Ann has left her husband, and puts implicit trust in a shrink who has told her to be authentic; she does this by telling her sister Elizabeth, so repeatedly that it becomes a running gag, not to be ashamed of being a lesbian. (Elizabeth isnt. Ashamed, I mean.) It must be difficult not to play Mary Ann as a comic turn and Catherine Fitch, though certainly spirited, doesn't bring it off. No offence, but I found myself fantasizing about having this role played by Mary Lynn Rajskub, the wonderfully tactless Chloe of 24.

And maybe Kiefer Sutherland could play Elizabeth who, if not quite in the Jack Bauer class, does have a habit of taking the law into her own hands --ironically, as she's on a personal crusade against police brutality. Shes also very tough on her own father. In both cases shes right but self-righteous. Cast, as frequently before, in a killer-dog role, Irene Poole again gives a tornado of a performance, the kind you root for even while feeling that at certain moments the lady's pushing it. If Poole prompts that response occasionally, Nola Augustson's college cop, over the top without a springboard, gets it all the time.

The gentlemen are notably quieter, though they all turn out to have interesting things to say for themselves. The two crooks, a father-and-son act, are far more eloquent threatened than threatening; Oliver Becker positively blossoms under duress, while Jamie Robinson goes electric in what looks like a nothing role and suddenly isnt. Junior is an underwritten role, but Brandon McGibbon gives him a personality, sort of rabbity. R. D. Reid makes, at the very last minute, a thought-provoking case for the policeman and his unhappy lot. Ken Gass, the Factorys artistic director, directs artistically (apart from one very forced grouping near the beginning); Layne Coleman, his opposite number at Theatre Passe Muraille, has nipped around the block to play Tom, with great shamefaced authority. He isn't exactly a moral centre, more of a litmus-test; his family have to figure out how to respond to him. Pending better times, which may come, this usually involves making him soup.

Tom and Junior have some kind of scam of their own going, which I couldn't follow. This is an example of an overall problem. There is plenty of life on stage, but its hard to believe in what happens off it, either now or in the past. The title refers to a theory that Nora and her family have spent their lives purposely making themselves miserable. Quite conceivably they have, but it just sounds like something people say. The play is supposed to be unified by the idea that its a rough world out there, and getting rougher, so the best thing to do is to be nice to our relatives. Walker's plays have a tough mouth and a soft heart, and the combination worked better across the sprawling canvas of This Is Wonderland, a series that might have gone on forever (though it sadly didn't) and therefore didnt need a shape. A play does; and I still think that Walkers best is his Turgenev adaptation, Nothing Sacred, which came with one built in.

robertcushman@lycos.com

I see that Time has described The Lord of the Rings as a definitive megamusical. I have some problems with that. Im not sure that it's grammatically possible to be A definitive anything (please be more definite with your articles, Time) and anyway, "megamusical" is an exceptionally ugly word of which I had hoped we'd seen the last. Ive just discovered that my spellcheck doesnt recognize it. Good ol' spellcheck. Its standards are so self- effacingly high, it doesn't recognize the word spellcheck, either.

Also, if we have to use it, the term megamusical has certain specific connotations that The Lord of the Rings, big and expensive and musical though it undoubtedly is, doesnt quite match. Megamusicals, also known as pop-operas, are a recent, though extinct, breed, in which meaning, story and character get drowned in non-stop helpings of vocal and instrumental soup. They dont have spoken dialogue to help them explore, expound or be funny. They are, almost by definition, dumb.

This doesn't stop them being, for those who like them, very effective. It may even help. Shows like Les Miserables or Miss Saigon seem to deliver emotionally in a way that The Lord of the Rings doesn't. So, for that matter, do dumb shows of a later, more modest stripe such as Wicked or Mamma Mia!. They scream their audiences into submission. The Lord of the Rings is blessed, or cursed, with intelligence.

Note that I said "intelligence," not intellect. Theres nothing deep or complex about the Tolkien trilogy on which the show is based. Its an invigorating adventure story, with good and evil clearly marked out, even when individual characters slide between them. The source's appeal, as I noted in my initial review, is closely bound up with how much there is of it; with the way it creates a world, using sheer narrative energy to build a new mythology, practically from scratch. I was one of those who doubted whether it could be effectively adapted for the stage. It had, after all, taxed the resources of three long films.

Well, there are things missing that are definitely missed, and some that are there but rushed. All the same, the adaptation is remarkably successful and clever. It respects its original's shape; like the books, it starts in the Shire and ends there. It craftily combines two of the originals battles, and deals in brilliant shorthand with the complicated sequence of Frodos betrayal by Gollum to the spider Shelob, his capture by the orcs and his rescue by Sam. I actually prefer the show to the movie. The latter lost me during its second instalment, when it turned into an endless series of fights, prolonged for their own sake. The show, for all its compression, gives more breathing space to the characters, and even as spectacle it's more exciting. Live theatre, when it works, always is, precisely because of the odds against it, especially now, when we know that a movie's vaunted "cast of thousands" has been computer- generated. The staged warfare isnt altogether free of self- indulgence. It occurred to me that one reason the orcs keep losing is that they spend too much time leaping up and down on their sprung snowshoes and not enough smiting the enemy. But the battles are thrillingly choreographed, in a style that draws both on Japanese martial arts and British productions of Shakespeares histories, and you can actually follow them. And just to see the stage bathed alternately in gold and blood-red is a stirring experience.

The show does have an identity problem. We were constantly assured before its opening that it wasn't going to be a musical, but it seems uncertain what kind of musical it doesn't want to be. I cant really judge the lyrics, which tend to be tongue-twisters, Elvish chants or otherwise indecipherable, though Im sure they're better than the jolly ditties with which Tolkien peppered his own text. Most of the songs are used as a kind of vocal underscoring, a new convention and an effective one, more notable for isolated haunting phrases than as whole melodies. There are times, though, when the score harks back to old ways.

One is the hoedown at the Prancing Pony inn, which could be the best ethnic dancing (if hobbits count as an ethnicity) in a musical since Fiddler on the Roof. There is a difference, though. When the Jews and Cossacks do their challenge-dance in Fiddler's inn, it tells us about their relationship, which is a large part of what the shows about. The face off between hobbits and men tells us nothing and goes nowhere. But its so much fun one would hesitate to cut it. The same cannot be said of the periodic retreats into pop-opera conventions that are the only boring things in the show: the love duets that fail, just like the film did, to persuade us that this story has any interest in women; and worse yet, the five minutes in which the elf-queen Galadriel sings at us that we're in Lothlorien and that it's a nice place to be, both of which we already knew. It also obscures what is important about the scene -- Galadriels temptation by the power of the ring, and her victory over it.

The temptation of power is the storys emotional core. It's there in the show, most centrally in James Loye's Frodo, but not yet as clearly or as strongly as it should be. At the moment the most conflicted character on stage, Brent Carvers Gandalf, is the one whose inner struggles are supposed to lie in the past. The production needs some rewriting and redirecting to clarify who some of the characters are, what they want and why they talk so funny. The four hobbits, though, are already funny in the right way -- as Tolkien clearly wanted them to be, but better than he managed, since his own sense of humour was heavy-handed; the word "donnish" might have been invented for his jokes. The master-servant relationship in his book is remarkably similar to the one in Pickwick Papers. I wonder if Tolkien would have acknowledged how much Sam Gamgee owes to Sam Weller. Probably not. He disapproved of all English literature later than Beowulf. He also denied that his ring had anything in common with Wagners; they're both round is as far as he'd go. Well, of course. Both convey unlimited powers, both corrupt their wearers and all who covet them, both cause brother to kill brother and both are discovered floating in a stream. Otherwise, nothing in common. Still, some of the staging in Lord of the Rings is Wagnerian in its grandeur, or what one imagines "Wagnerian" would have been like when Wagner himself still had a say in it. Its also, in its own way, as imaginative as the magnificent new-style Ring at the COC. To have combined this with the human element is an accomplishment.

- - -

Friday night is music night at a Toronto vegetarian restaurant, Le Commensal at Bay and Dundas, where I recently discovered a singer. (Doubly serendipitous; I wasnt looking and I'm not a vegetarian.) Her name is Beverly Taft; she was singing jazz-tinged standards and making them sound fresh without tricks. I especially liked her transformation of The Way You Look Tonight into waltz time, bring out all out of what Alan Jay Lerner, in another song, called its "tender fun." Even better was a relaxed and rapturous Blue Skies, lightly swinging, one of those occasions on which, as the song itself more or less says, everything suddenly goes right. She was singing with just piano. She has a CD with ensemble accompaniment and a broader repertoire, titled How Ya Gonna Keep 'Em Down on the Farm, so called because it was recorded near one. It doesnt, alas, include that song, which is surely ripe for rediscovery by a respectable singer, but it does have Im an Old Cowhand, complete with verse and wittily phrased. I recommend the lady and the venue; together when they coincide, separately when they don't. A subsequent trip to Le Commensal yielded pianist Norman Amadio, one of Toronto's most unassuming treasures.

2006-04-07-the-lord-of-the-rings:
The Lord of the Rings

Theatre

Princess of Wales, Toronto

The parade of images in Matthew Warchus's production of The Lord of the Rings is ceaseless and astonishing. The Black Riders are truly terrifying, especially the first one who appears out of nowhere as a spectral compound of man and horse. The senior Orcs travel on great curved snowshoes; other ranks push themselves into battle on sinister crutches. The Ents, on stilts and held up by wires, do a superb job of looking like trees. The stage itself is a spectacle, constantly moving up, down and around, splitting apart and coming together again. It even takes a bow at the end and nobody could begrudge it.

This show, reputedly the most expensive yet staged, has spent its millions wisely. Practically too, as devices work strictly to serve the story. Rob Howell's set, superlatively lit by Paul Pyant, is an arrangement of branches that makes an environmental statement as well as a narrative one; and unlike the film it includes the last episode, in which hobbits chase the polluters from the Shire.

The obvious problem remains: how, in one three-and-a-half-hour show, do you adapt a book that barely fitted into three long films? Warchus and his co-adaptor Shaun McKenna have done it cleverly, cutting out great patches of plot and sensitively binding the remains together. This show is intelligent, but it isn't satisfying. The sheer proliferating bulk of JRR Tolkien's trilogy is a major part of its attraction. Reduced, however cunningly, it loses weight and even urgency.

Most of the score, by AR Rahman and the Finnish group Varttina, is serviceable, underlining rather than advancing or creating the plot.

The British actors James Loye and Peter Howe play Frodo and Sam admirably. Most of the rest are Canadian. Gollum is superbly played by Michael Therriault, who a few years ago was a fine Ariel; now he's a Caliban, malevolent and tormented. Evan Buliung's Strider, glamorous even in tatters, is that rare commodity, a genuine hero. The others make less of a mark or have less of a chance.

In this show the human element fights hard and sometimes wins, but the mechanical element, which is after all a human invention, is wonderful. Robert Cushman
2006-04-08-american-buffalo-lacks-exuber:
robertcushman@lycos.com; American Buffalo runs through April 29 at the Young Centre, 416-866-8666.

When its animal, an American buffalo is a member of a threatened and depleted species. When it's mineral, it's a coin that has a similar rarity value, though the price it will fetch is largely determined by its physical condition; which, come to think of it, must be true of the bovine definition as well. David Mamets play American Buffalo embraces both meanings, the first as metaphor, the second as plot device, though theres a certain amount of crossover between the two.

Mamet's three characters see themselves as businessmen, robber barons, rugged individualists of the type that made America America. That was a long time ago. Now -- in 1977, to be exact -- it's tough to get a break, especially if youre trying to scrape a living on the back streets of Chicago, within earshot of the El. Donny, the most grounded of the three, runs a second-hand store. Bobby, a young addict, is Donnys gofer. (A junkie in a junk shop. Ha.) Teach, as Damon Runyon might have put it, does the best he can, a profession as overcrowded in Mamet's Chicago as it was on Runyon's Broadway. He is always angry. The first thing he says when he walks into the store is F---in Ruthie, which he repeats five, or it might be six, times. What this Ruthie may or may not have done to him is immaterial. The point is that, in Teachs mind, someone is always doing something.

As in Mamet's next play, Glengarry Glen Ross (which is both a refinement and an expansion of the same territory), the characters spend much of their time planning a break-in. Donny sold a buffalo nickel to a collector for what he now considers a ridiculously low price. So he wants to get it back and take the rest of the man's hoard while hes at it. He enlists Bobby to help him with the job, and Teach angles himself in, too. But none of the three wholly trusts the others, and things fall apart.

Mamets dialogue no longer has the thrill of novelty, but it still has both music and muscle. In this play, he depends less than usual on the fast overlap and more on the built-up aria. He famously makes poetry out of profanity; he also shows his characters, who have imaginative minds but limited horizons, striving toward a philosophy. Commonplace words become witty through artful repetition; concepts compress and crash together. Teach insists on packing a gun in case "God forbid, something inevitable happens."

Stuart Hughes's production for Soulpepper is lucid (something not to be taken for granted in handling Mamet) and reasonably entertaining but, by the standards of both play and company, disappointing. It lacks both terror and exuberance. Victoria Wallace's set, piled high with bric-a-brac and deep and wide as well, is breathtaking at first glance, but inappropriately charming as the action proceeds. (Her costumes, though, are excellent).

Ted Dykstras Teach plays things very close to the chest. Hes a hunched ball of resentment from his first appearance to his last, his accent sounds right and his obscenely slicked-down hair tells us exactly who he thinks he is. Dykstra gets to the soul of the character, but he misses the equally important outward flourishes. Teach's paranoia should be baroque in its excess; this is a man who can say of someone he has never met and of whom he has barely heard, "guys like that, I like to f--- their wives." And at the end, both performance and production literally pull their punches. Teach administers a savage beating, or so he has done in previous stagings; here it's down to a single blow. Its followed by a fit of destructive rage to which neither his heart nor his hands seem committed. If its any consolation, he's a lot better in the role than Al Pacino.

Jeff Lillico's Bobby is appealing but unsuitably healthy, even wholesome. Michael Hanrahan comes off best with an understated, compassionate performance as Donny. Donny is compassionate, up to a point. He looks out for Bobby, again up to a point, and dislikes violence. But it is he who sets the plot in motion, out of a mixture of greed and pique, planning a crime to avenge an imagined slight. A saint he aint, but Hanrahan shows us little of his underside. Think of Donny as Tony Soprano to Teachs Paulie, with Bobby as a cross between Christopher and Anthony Jr. I don't know if Mamet was a direct influence on The Sopranos, but he certainly helped make that show possible.

- - -

A higher-toned American classic from the previous decade, Edward Albee's Whos Afraid of Virginia Woolf? is a play that, like American Buffalo, retains its stylistic zing long after its shock effect has worn off. As ostentatiously long as Buffalo is disconcertingly short, it sets its sights not just on America, but on the whole civilization of which its a part. At least, it can't be for nothing that George, the history professor, brings down the second-act curtain with a reading from The Decline of the West. And of course he, an ageing history professor, spends some of the play sparring with Nick, a new appointment to his college's biology faculty.

Not that I think any of this means much; were all much more concerned with the bloody feuding between George and his wife, Martha, and with how they bait Nick and his wife, Honey, who step so unwarily into their marital lair. And with how much they all drink; thats something that had disappeared by Mamet's time. George and Martha, America's first first couple; the names must be significant, or maybe theyre just their authors little joke.

In other words, the play's intellectual superstructure is a pretentious irrelevance, but the wit-combats work like a charm. They were very well orchestrated in Ron Ulrich's just-closed production at the Neptune Theatre in Halifax, which was better than almost anything weve seen in Toronto this year. Nigel Bennetts dry, suffering George made the running in the first 1 1/2 acts, as Georges tend to. George, for whom defence is the best offence, has the choicest wisecracks.

Sad, flamboyant Martha, of course, has her share, and it was no surprise that a flaming-haired and flaming-mouthed Fiona Reid made the most of them. What was revelatory was the way she, with Bennett's collaboration, transformed the last act, practically drawing a map of the character's sickness and despair. It concerns, you may recall, the couples fantasy of having a son, and Georges methodical destruction of it. I have never believed either in the fantasy or in the self-aware cut-and-dried games the two of them play with it, but I believed this time in the results, watching Reid, as if on an operating table, unravelling and, just possibly, reravelling again.

Geoffrey Pounsett was a good, pugnacious Nick, and Mary Ashton a perfect mouse of a Honey. Both couples are childless; that must portend something, if portentousness is your thing. George and Martha, for better and worse, have stayed together; one doubts if their juniors will have the same luck, or lack of it. As in American Buffalo, the characters -- the two principals, anyway -- end by reclaiming something of their best selves. That looks more sentimental in Albee than it does in Mamet, but this production, by never letting go of the bleakness, made it touching.

10 DAYS ON EARTH

Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

Ronnie Burketts marionettes can move you in ways unavailable to actors of mere flesh and blood. In his new piece, 10 Days on Earth, he shows us a man named Darrell who has a chronological age of about 50 and a mental age of about 10. All his life he has lived with, and been cared for by, his single mother. One night she dies in her bed. Darrell simply thinks that, for whatever reason, she doesnt want to get up. So, for the 10 days denoted in the title, he goes about his business, making himself sandwiches, taking the bus to and from his job at a shoe-shine stand, talking to his few friends and preparing for Halloween.

Since Darrell behaves like a child we react to him as powerfully as if he actually were one. And because he's a puppet, we don't feel manipulated; he does that for us, so to speak, and its all in plain view with Burkett, the master of all puppet-masters, standing at the top of the stage, pulling all the characters strings. When Darrell, small, neat and dignified in his suit and bow-tie, returns home each evening and calls out to his non-appearing mom, the effect is heartbreaking and, because it's been pared down to essentials, not at all mawkish.

At least it works that way the first couple of times. After that, of course, the effect begins to wear off; I didn't actually resent the repetitions, as theyre so clearly part of the package, but I began to wish for something more. Burkett -- who is, as usual, his own writer, director, designer and supplier of all the voices, including some nifty singing -- is at pains to supply it, but he isnt always successful. He has spoken of the play as being a celebration of maternal love, a description calculated to elicit an incredulous blink, since Ivy, Darrell's mother, only appears briefly and in flashbacks. But at second blush, it's true. We feel the quality of her love through the effects of its forcible removal; and the more you think about it, the more overwhelming it seems. In the one extended encounter between mother and son, she catches him masturbating and counsels him to do it behind closed doors, like -- as she all but spells out -- she does. It sounds embarrassing, if not grotesque, but in fact it says something serious about the needs of both of them, and does so seriously and -- if its the word I want -- touchingly.

Theres also a powerfully suggestive scene in which Ivy, on her one night out a week, re-encounters Darrell's father (and namesake) who refuses to go home with her. But a prologue that sets up the whole situation is confusing, and some of the supplementary material feels like padding. One of Darrell's friends is a homeless man called Lloyd, this being a pun on Lord; he thinks hes God -- literally -- and he despises his creations, except for Darrell, who shares his lunch with him. Lloyd has two angry tirades; the first one makes a point, the second just repeats it.

Darrell also has a girlfriend named Patsy, with whom his scenes are shorter and more effective. But most of his feelings are directed towards a storybook character, a smart red-coated hound called Honeydog with whom he identifies and whose adventures are, at regular intervals, acted out. Its characters are on wires thicker and more visible than those of the humans in the main plot; we have, in fact, a puppet show within a puppet show, which may be a first. These inset scenes give us a taste of Burketts technical virtuosity, especially when a homing pigeon collapses inwards and turns into a multi-coloured balloon. These interludes may be visually striking but they're verbally dull; the introduction of a sheep called Blanche DuBaa comes off as a pale imitation of Sesame Street ("Meryl Sheep, a sheep's sheep" -- is she still around?). Whats worse, they have no discernible relevance to the main action. Honeydog and his protege-companion, a duck named Little Burp, may invert the mother-son relationship of Ivy and Darrell, but that doesnt get us far.

The play's final gesture is sad but hopeful; there are people who will look out for Darrell but they'll never replace what hes lost. Its nice but unsatisfying. Ever since the superb Street of Blood, Burkett seems to have been looking for a story spacious enough to match his talents; this isn't it, and his decision to stay aloft of his characters, rather than moving among them as in previous shows, seems to me regrettable. Left to operate on their own scale, his creations seem, paradoxically, not less like puppets but more. The show completes a season of CanStage productions that have, without exception, been disappointing or worse. It doesn't break the jinx, but it puts a dent in it.

robertcushman@lycos.com; Hair plays through June 17 at CanStage, 416- 368-3110.

The best scene in the CanStage production of Hair involves a character called Margaret Mead, who is played by an actor called Matthew Boden. (You get the drift.) Margaret is one half of a safari- suited couple who, on some cost-conscious combination of honeymoon and anthropological survey, wander into the precincts of The Tribe. The Tribe are the 1968 New York hippies who are the show's collective protagonist. Margaret is fascinated by them and asks them all sorts of questions about their beliefs, their style preferences (especially that all-important Hair) and their sex lives. She is, of course, especially intrigued by the last item. Margaret looks tousled and rangy, like Elaine Stritch, and she talks as Stritch might have done had she allowed her long residence in England to affect her accent. Some of that style and crackle carries through when she eventually breaks into song, making her, in this company, just about unique.

The trick casting means that Margaret ends up, like all the other outsiders in the show, as a joke. (The insiders are treated, as they treat themselves, with stultifying solemnity.) The strange thing is, though, that the show places its audience in exactly the same position as it places Margaret and her partner, Hubert. It even has them entering from the auditorium to prove the point. It addresses us as if we, too, were tourists. When the show was new, it paraded its characters as if they were on a reserve; now that its old, it exhibits them as if they were in a museum. Its nostalgic, all right. When did you last hear the word psychedelic"?

The numbers, which take up most of the show, tick off the prescribed attitudes as briskly and impersonally as if they were items in a catalogue. We get, in rapid succession, songs about astrology (Aquarius, obviously), drugs (Hashish), sexual variation (Sodomy), race (Colored Spade) and somewhat displaced Beatlemania (Manchester England). These are all reasonable subjects for songs (except perhaps the first, which isn't a reasonable subject, period), but they could be sung by anybody. Later on we get Flower Power Peace March, Hare Krishna and, by way of a love song, Claude Is My Acid.

Claude is the show's nearest approach to a hero. Hes just received his Vietnam draft card, and cant quite bring himself to burn it. That, God knows, was a real dilemma for a lot of people, but Claude isn't real. He's a cipher, torn -- or so the show would have us believe -- between the value systems of his friends and of his family. Since the former are an amorphous sentimentalized mass and the latter are revue-sketch caricatures, it isnt a very exciting contest. The show keeps forgetting about it, anyway, and then has the nerve to try and milk it for pathos. Its suggested a couple of times that Claude's best course would be to escape to Canada, and it's never made clear why he doesnt. Still, the idea does net the show some extra laughs since, as we all know, audiences who are Canadian always find it funny to hear their country mentioned by people who arent.

Robert A. Prior's production has come in for a hefty collection of brickbats, most of them deserved, but the real fault lies in the material. Even Galt MacDermot's music, much the best thing about it, is catchy but thin. James Rado, who collaborated with the late Gerome Ragni on the book and lyrics (the latter mostly clumsy, occasionally perceptive), has apparently reworked the script to make the narrative firmer. It is indeed clearer than it was in its original Broadway production, which I saw in its London incarnation and remember as being an energetic bore, but it isnt any stronger.

Apparently, it once was. William Goldman, in his invaluable study of late 60s Broadway, The Season, describes the contrast between the show's origins at New York's Public Theatre and the commercial transformation that made it a hit. When it started, Goldman says, its informality felt genuine and its anti-war message heartfelt. (Also imaginative; it involved toy tanks.) Uptown, it became a matter of making the right noises, as loudly as possible. And so it has remained. Act Two presents a kind of minstrel show involving the assassination of a black Abe Lincoln (you cant accuse the show of missing any bases) that somehow develops into a battlefield phantasmagoria. Were undoubtedly meant to open our eyes and think of Iraq, but the whole thing feels now, as it did then, like cashing in. It also invites mortifying comparisons with Twyla Tharp's Movin' Out.

Priors program note describes the show as celebrating the 60s attempt "to alter the course of human evolution. (Wow. And you thought mere political change was a challenge.) He then comes down to Earth and tells us how many thousands of times the songs got covered. He reinforces his own staging with a nonstop light show that's at its best when it's abstract and at its worst when its specific. If two guys are singing a song about The Flag, and actually holding on to one while they do it, showing us a projection of the thing as well seems kind of superfluous. Stephen Huess choreography can be pleasing; the highlight is Good Morning Starshine, which has The Tribe swaying in rhythm while sitting entwined on a giant bed. Their singing; though, is mostly screechy and often toneless. The black women are especially bad in this respect, which may be an attempt to defuse a stereotype, but I wouldn't want to bet on it.

The acting doesn't have much more character than the singing. Jamie McKnight as Claude seems like a nice young man. Craig Burtanowski as Berger, The Tribes head honcho and main mouthpiece, does have a personality, but it isnt an attractive one. And so ends a CanStage season that has sometimes offered interesting plays, and sometimes satisfying productions, but never both at the same time. I see that the management has abandoned Passion," its slogan for the last few years, in favour of "Humanity," which ought to cover everything. Though I also note that next season's opening title is Of Mice and Men, which, apart from its dismaying cautionary connotations, would seem to get us at best only halfway there.

robertcushman@lycos.com

Critics are always being asked about their responsibilities. Recently, we have been handed a new one. A few weeks ago, I was on a panel at which one of the speakers from the floor asked whether, in keeping with the new spirit of the age, we reviewers didnt feel a special obligation to be nice to shows that might bring tourists back to Toronto.

The show my questioner had in mind was, of course, The Lord of the Rings, a show that, as it happens, I liked. But I hadn't been prejudiced in its favour by the advance publicity: rather the reverse. That long buildup, you may recall, was all about the economic benefits that would accrue to Toronto from the presence of a big hit musical. We heard a lot about the unprecedented amount of money and technology involved, and about the show's being based on a hugely successful book that had already spawned three hugely successful films. It seemed to be trading heavily on name recognition; it was, in fact, a spinoff. Really, its a wonder it turned out as well as it did.

David Miller, the Mayor, approves of it. In an article in last Sundays Toronto Star, outlining a vision for the city's golden future, he looks to a time when Lord of the Rings is still playing." It's Exhibit A -- indeed its the only theatrical production mentioned by name -- in his eulogy of the citys arts- boosting program.

The Lord of the Rings may or may not be successful in attracting the foreign hordes, but I cannot believe that it forms part of any vaunted "Toronto cultural renaissance, if only because it has so little to do with Toronto, or indeed with Canada. Yes, it does include some of our best actors, a couple of whom are doing some of their best work. But the material, the production and the initial impulse and financing are all British. It's a close call, but I'd say that the big Livent musicals from a decade ago, Show Boat and Ragtime, were slightly more Canadian. They were American in their writing, their staging, their subject matter and most of their casting, but they were at least produced here. And they did attract American audiences, as did the same companys money-spinning import The Phantom of the Opera and the equivalent shows that have been brought in by the Mirvishes.

But none of this constitutes a culture, let alone a renaissance. Nor, despite all the fuss thats being made about it, does the concurrent opening of a batch of new performance and exhibition spaces: What somebody once called the edifice complex." Personally, after years of enduring the cramped seating and barnlike acoustics of the Hummingbird Centre, I'm delighted that the Canadian Opera Company is about to have a new home. But the exciting thing here is not that the COC will have "a world-class facility (whatever that means) but that it has a world-class production of the Ring cycle to put inside it. The only art form for which buildings, in themselves, are a major achievement is architecture, and in that respect Toronto has a long way to go before it becomes Chicago.

A culture is not something that a city creates for tourists. It's something that a city creates for, and with, its own inhabitants. If tourists want to join in the fun while theyre passing through, fine, but thats not what it's about. Toronto keeps talking about becoming a theatre centre to rival London or New York but it seems prepared to skip a few stages to get there. Both those cities had strong theatrical traditions long before the visitors arrived. Britain's National Theatre has been, by and large, a roaring success. But it had already been one for 10 years, in makeshift quarters at the Old Vic, before moving into its purpose-built complex on the South Bank. (And that Old Vic success grew from uncounted years of previous tradition.) Broadway has become something of a joke, and it certainly is marketed to tourists, but those tourists are only interested -- certainly I was when I first visited New York -- because the place has an aura, accumulated over decades during which it catered primarily to New Yorkers.

Tourists, anyway, are fickle. They are only around for part of the year. Managers in London know this, and in the off season they concentrate their marketing strategy on attracting the home audience, or a larger proportion of it than would be coming anyway. Tourists are limited, too, in what they want to see. They want to see musicals or, given the appropriate surroundings, classics. They dont want to see new plays unless theyre established commercial hits, which Toronto has never found a mechanism for creating. And, frankly, why should they? The plays are unlikely to speak to them. New plays don't have to be parochial, but they do imply a shared frame of reference, which a theatrical metropolis has the time, and the resident audience, to develop.

The Toronto success story of the past decade has been Soulpepper, which neither plays nor markets itself to tourists. So I was told a couple of years ago by Albert Schultz, the artistic director. I wondered whether the move to new premises in the Young Centre might have changed that, but when I spoke to him last week he assured me that it hadn't. He did say that subscription audiences -- local by definition -- had doubled, and that his focus was on attracting the four million people who live within 25 minutes of us." (He also said, and I heartily agree with him, that Toronto has spent far too much time feeling sorry for itself over the fallout from SARS and 9/ 11.) Soulpepper, by the way, shares the Young Centre with the George Brown Theatre School. One of the most exciting of all Torontos new spaces is the National Ballet School on Jarvis. These cant be tourist attractions. They're investments in the culture of the future.

Soulpepper doesn't do new plays, but it has built a new Canadian company. The best prospect for our citys theatre is the simultaneous flowering of Soulpeppers classical policy with the fostering of new plays at theatres like the Tarragon, Factory and Passe Muraille. This past season has been a terrible one in the latter department, though before rushing to judgment we should remember that a) always and everywhere, more people have been good at acting in plays than at writing them; b) history teaches that any theatre that devotes itself to new plays will spend 90% of its time producing junk. The best we can hope for is that some of it will be lively, temporarily engaging junk. And, to be fair, some recent seasons have come closer to meeting that quota. It's an unglamorous hope, but it's the best we have. And tourists wont help us achieve it.

Near Bay and Wellesley, theres a condo development where the new opera house was once intended to be. It's called Opera Place -- in other words, what we have in place of an opera. We can wave all the flags and chant all the slogans we want, but if we put all our faith in new buildings, imported musicals and an audience of transients, they will be what we have in place of a culture.
