2006-04-28-tearin-up-the-stage:
BOYGROOVE

Diesel Playhouse, Toronto

- - -

Everything new is old again. If I were looking for a historical precedent for this amused deconstruction of the boy-band phenomenon - - and I suppose I am -- I'd go back to a musical of which the creators of this show have probably never heard and which they are certainly too young to have seen. Not to mention that it happened on another continent. I'm referring to Expresso Bongo, a British musical from the 1950s about a young rock-and-roller whose agent finagled him into stardom and got ditched and kicked in the teeth for his pains. That's Boygroove's story as well, multiplied by four.

The endearing similarity between that show's Bongo Herbert and the four close-harmonizers of Boygroove, who are called Boygroove, is that nobody, including themselves, thinks they're any good. They are among those chapters in pop history that the official culture refuses to take seriously; the show proceeds on that assumption and does nothing to challenge it. You can't imagine anyone writing a show this disrespectful about the Beatles or any other group or performer with pretentions; even the Supremes, in the Broadway musical Dreamgirls, got respect. But satirizing the Backstreet Boys is kicking at an open door. Not that kicking at an open door can't be fun.

It certainly is here; and, rather unusually, it gets to be more fun as it goes along. One reason for the delayed impact is that it takes time for the group to register as a group. And one reason for that is the performers' own cleverness. The actors who play Boygroove also play all the other people in their lives. In practical terms, this means that at most given moments the quartet is actually a trio, while the fourth member moonlights as their agent or their choreographer and harangues them.

There aren't many new jokes to be made about agents or choreographers, but this show does a spirited job of recycling the old ones.

Some things have changed since the '50s: Back then, the manager would have been a lone shark (and quite possibly a loan-shark as well); now, he's one of a whole school. He doesn't have to peddle his proteges to the Corporation; he is the corporation, or one of its spokes. He still gets disposed of, quite early on. His shafting is the agenda for the boys' first real scene together. They have, of course, had group numbers, but one of the more surprising things about the show is that most of the songs are filler. Aaron Machri's music and lyrics exaggerate the real generic thing just enough to seem comic, as do the moves laid on by Kay Grigar, but no song really takes the stage until the boys make their last goodbye (with The Last Goodbye).

By then, we've come to know and even like them. There is Andrew (Andrew Bursey), listed as The Sensitive One, a pudgy creation whose conscience troubles him because making a lot of money and laying a lot of girls hasn't left him with much time to save the planet; he has his own pet cause -- "Stop Right There, Hunger!" -- and when he mentions it, he gives a deeply-felt salute. There is Jon (Jon Paterson), The Bad Boy, lean and mean but not so much that he doesn't have dreams of being the first rock-star in outer space, which I can't help thinking is not the best idea either he or the show has ever had. (Well, maybe it is the best he's had.) There is Lance (Scott Walters), The Gifted One, he who spurns the groupies and whose belated emergence from the closet is the immediate cause of the group's implosion. And there is Kevin (Matt Alden) who is billed as The Leader, but whose most positive quality seems to be not being any of the others. The actor compensates, though, with a brief sketch of George Michael, skimming discreetly from a busted tryst to a waiting helicopter.

Boygroove's almost-nemesis is a rapper called HypeTastic; he tells the rock press how much he hates and despises the wholesome foursome, and they tell the pop press how they wish he'd just be tolerant like they are. I told you there was nothing new under the lights. It's just like Cliff Richard refusing to take the Beatles' bait when they made fun of him. But though with Cliff one always felt that he never quite got the point, Boygroove in these disputes make a lot of sense. In all, they're pretty realistic about their place in the world. They know they're a perishable commodity; at the height of their fame they reckon that they have three albums left in them, at most, plus maybe three movies "if our bodies hold out." I think it's Kevin who says that he wants to make $24-million before it's all over and frets that so far he's only made one. But those are the early days; he retires with $30-million. Clearly he has his eye on the ball, and so (despite a few wastes of stage time, like Kevin's girlfriend and an interlude involving Mr. and Mrs. Tom Cruise) do Chris Craddock's script and Kenneth Brown's direction. Both are fast, astute, and friendly with attitude. And if you want to find the Diesel Playhouse, it's where Second City used to be before moving across the street; and the chairs, tables and drinks remain the same.

- Until June 4. 416-971-5656

2006-04-29-the-gulf-between-accuracy-and:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Care runs through May 28 at the Tarragon Theatre, 416- 531-1827. Sparta runs through May 8 at Theatre Passe Muraille, 416-504-7529.

Diane Flacks plays all the women and Richard Greenblatt all the men in Care, a play they have cooked up together after the fashion of their delightful Sibs a few seasons ago. The characters they create this time -- the principal ones, anyway -- are easy to identify with; to believe in, as Jon Stewart might put it, not so much.

Steve and Ellie are a married couple, young-middle-aged, who have had their first baby. They cope, or fail to, with disturbed and sleep- less nights, the unequal division of labour (pun not intended, but Ill go with it anyway), the precipitous decline of their sex life and the fact that Ellie's career is on hold while Steve's seems poised to take off, thus provoking further resentment. These may not quite be universal themes, but theyre common enough to keep most audiences interested. More specialized, but still eminently recognizable, are the cultural tensions. Both Steve and Ellie are Jewish, but they differ in how they want their son to be brought up, he opting for secular and she, rather to his surprise, for religious.

Both have outside interests. Steve may be having an affair with a colleague; its never quite clear how far they've gone, and we don't see much of the relationship anyway. We do, on the other hand, see a great deal of Ellies father, who is dying of cancer, tended to at home by a succession of cartoonish cameo caregivers, and who, in his pain and his grouchiness and his craving for a Montreal bagel with all the cholesterol, is the most compelling character in the piece. We also get to meet Steves personal trainer and Ellie's masseur; and we are vouchsafed a couple of visions of God, seen here as the greatest Cartoon Cameo Caregiver -- or Withholder -- of all.

There is a geometrical imbalance in the show, and in the strengths and weaknesses of both the material and the performers. The most important emotional lines converge on Ellie in her triple capacity as daughter, wife and mother. But Flacks is not a very resourceful emotional performer, and with her at its centre, the play is sketchy. More precisely, it's revue-sketchy. She is fine as the various agency crones hovering at the bedside (especially funny as the short-tempered one whom her patient calls a Polish Nazi), but as Ellie herself, shes stuck on a single resentful note of grievance that never rises to grief.

So Greenblatt becomes the fulcrum. He doesnt have the widest range of any actor in the world, but he has a laconic strength that encompasses wit and that serves him very well as the old man. As Steve, though, he's less a person than a predicament, which in fact is the play in a nutshell. The issues are real enough, but they're journalistically familiar and they havent been made fresh. Theyre a series of jokes, surprisingly few of which get laughs. Eda Holmes directs sharply and speedily, with the baby cleverly represented as something between a projection and a hologram, but the show is as clear an example as I can remember of the theatrical gulf between mere accuracy and truth.

Sparta, a new play by Sarah Martyn, is self-referential on a couple of levels. The author apparently grew up on a farm, not unlike the one that occupies the stage here, in a small Ontario town similar to the one that gives her play its name. What's more, one of her characters, a young woman who's returned to the farm and to her highly dysfunctional family to celebrate her 25th birthday, is an aspiring writer. She decides to write a story based on the life around her, and reads some of it to her parents. They are aghast, as was I, though for slightly different reasons. As far as I could tell, what she reads out is a direct transcript of a conversation that we heard a couple of scenes before. This suggests that Christina, which is the young ladys name, has either an impressive memory or impressive shorthand skills, coupled with a staggeringly literal approach to the concept of "writing about what you know."

Whatever it is, it gets totally and unexpectedly dropped in the second act, which is all melodrama. Its melodrama that's partly rooted in researched reality. The farm, like many small farms, is going under, and father Marvin's only way out is to sell it, which he refuses to do. (If nothing else, the play supplies a grim counter- narrative to our theatres most familiar depictions of Ontario farming, the Wingfield series, of which the latest, Wingfields Inferno, opened this week at the Royal Alex, after its success at Stratford last year.) Marvin's wife, Carol, is a schoolteacher, and there is little sympathy between them; she does suggest that, if he ever read King Lear, it would strike a chord, but he's obviously not a reading man. He certainly has little sympathy with Christinas literary ambitions, especially as shes eking out a living as a waitress in order to realize them. Carol gives her family advice, which they resent, even when it's good. Christina's siblings, much older than she, are Alden, who worked in a bank but has quit to offer what his father regards as dubious help on the farm, and Mary, who is a high-flying Toronto lawyer. There is a rule, which I cannot explain, that the ostentatiously smart member of any theatrical family will be called Mary.

Martyn writes well about family tensions in the abstract, so to speak, but she is less good at tying them to a specific story. The action founders on a couple of revelations, the first highly predictable, and the second a total and unbelievable surprise, though certainly not unprecedented either in literature or in life.

The actors are left clinging. Hilary Fennell makes an impressive professional debut as Christina, hugging her own misfortunes without wallowing in them, and Ryan Hollyman is agreeable as Alden, who doesnt say much and keeps physically in the background, for neither of which one can blame him. Laura Wilson is good, too, in a rather conventional hausfrau way, as Carol. But Bob Collins Marvin is a very low-key tyrant, and having him take a long tour around the stage taking his feelings out on the furniture does nothing to enhance his credibility. Aviva Chernick's Mary carries no conviction, even (I suspect) to herself. She, too, spends much time lurking in corners, but with far less motivation, unless you count a possible fear of the big scene that lies in wait for her near the close of the play.

As you may have gathered, Layne Coleman's direction does little to help the play or the actors; surprising since, as hes currently demonstrating in Escape from Happiness a few blocks away, hes an excellent actor himself. But he puts his current cast in impossible positions on Steve Lucas's equally unhelpful set. Meant to represent the farmhouse kitchen, it has lost most of its walls and narrows to a point at the front, like the prow of a ship. Characters stand there, with their backs to everyone else, and make speeches, leaving you wondering where in any conceivable room they could be. There is also the least convincing dinner-table scene I have ever witnessed. I did, though, believe in the coffee inside the mugs that the actors kept brandishing. I'm sure it was instant. I'd bet the farm on it.

Colour Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / Diane Flacks and Richard Greenblatt play all the roles in Care, a play they wrote for themselves.; Colour Photo: Aviva Armour-Ostroff / Hilary Fennell plays Christina and Bob Collins is her father, Marvin, in Sparta, a play about small-town Ontario farm life.
2006-05-05-he-said-she-bedded:
MATHILDE

Young Centre for the Performing Arts

- - -

A man and a woman face one another in bitter, bodeful silence. Then they start talking. It transpires that they are a married couple, middle-aged and well-off, and that she has just returned from serving a 15-month prison sentence. Her crime was corrupting a minor; she bedded a 15-year old boy. She is a writer, her husband is an oncologist. He seems to have spent the last few days gathering up the physical evidence of their former life, and neatly packing it. "I've become the box king," he says.

Critics have it easy. It was simple enough for me to do my own packaging job, to write "it transpires" and then lay out the relevant information. It must have been much harder for the author of Mathilde to dispense it in the form of a conversation between two people who know it all already but never once seem to be going over it again just for our benefit. My hat is off to the French playwright, Veronique Olmi, for writing an expository scene that flows naturally, easily and with suspense; she never appears to be willfully withholding her revelations but she times them all for maximum effect. And I'll keep the hat off in salutation to her Canadian translator, Morwyn Brebner, whose original plays have never satisfied me but whose actual writing skills have never been in doubt; she comes up here with dialogue that's charged with wit and freighted with both the affection and bitterness of shared experience. Mathilde, the wife, says how tired she became, in her pre-prison existence, of being "the perfect accessory for the well- to-do oncologist." The husband, Pierre, recalling how her literary friends passed the time that she was serving, recalls "the number of dinner parties your incarceration saved from tedium."

As exposition gives way to explanation, we discover that Pierre and Mathilde want one another back -- he's more explicit about it than she is -- but that they are both unwilling to let go of their respective grievances. Whether their reunion would be a good thing, or how long it might be expected to last, are questions the author necessarily leaves unanswered. (My own guess is that routine would conquer, with all the negative and positive fall-out that entails.) The tensions, apart from the extra fillip of the wife's criminal record, are familiar enough, and the characters are of the kind we often meet in upscale drama. But the author makes them fresh and presents them with a fierce concentration that seems, from this side of the Atlantic, peculiarly French.

They could indeed be archetypes, and Nightwood Theatre's very fine production (which gives the Young Centre's second space its professional baptism) presents them as such. Mathilde herself is like Jean Anouilh's idea of Antigone, a no-half-measures heroine whose revolt happens to be sexual rather than political. She says little about the actual affair (though Pierre throws in what he takes to be the telling detail -- that her teenage lover went along with the law and claimed he'd been exploited), but when she does talk about it she exults; she says that it was like discovering her body, maybe her sexuality, for the first time. And, as with Antigone, one is torn between admiring her and telling her to get a grip. Martha Burns lacks something in vocal steel, but the spirit is there; she strikes directly, sometimes frighteningly, at the spirit of non-compromise -- and at the desperation when it threatens to break down. And when she wears a white raincoat, she looks like Paris transplanted.

Tom McCamus' Pierre is her perfect rumpled complement, the pragmatist pointing out that she thinks she's got problems; he lives every day with the imminence of death, even if it's other peoples'. Affability may come easy to him, but it takes a battering. Each of them is an expert at searching out the other's tenderest points; and though the man is, on the face of it, the injured party, that only makes him better at it. Tenderness has a habit of flaring up as well; in fact, the depth and texture of a marriage are present here as they are in few other plays. (It's stretched a bit long, even at 80 minutes, but that's another thing, and in this case a minor one.) The play builds to a fitting near-climax, reflecting both their vocations. The novelist relates her feelings; the physician writes them down. The notes are read back; she doesn't believe them. Both performances occasionally fall into the forced aggression that is most actors' default mode; otherwise Kelly Thornton's direction, tightly focused on a stage sandwiched between two slices of audience, is flawless.

- Runs until May 27. 416-866-8666

2006-05-06-bad-acting-teachers-a-witty-d:
Play is a feat of comic writing and acting

Sky Gilbert's new play is called Bad Acting Teachers, a title thats less straightforward than it looks. It leaves you wondering at just whom Gilbert, who these days is a theatre professor himself, thinks he is taking aim. His targets could be bad teachers of acting, or people who teach bad acting on purpose (there could be quite a market for that) or teachers of acting who are also bad people. Gilbert, the most vociferous gay activist in our theatre, if not our culture, is also quite the moralist, and that last definition turns out to be the one he has in mind. This is a play about power trips.

It isnt an especially profound play about power trips, but it is an entertaining one, the best-sustained feat of comic writing, acting and direction to appear in Toronto in ages. The structure could hardly be simpler, which means that bringing it off is a tour de force. A young actor, seeking to improve on his already decent professional credentials, seeks help from three charlatans in succession. A silent opening sequence tips us off. It's a trailer, composed of significant moments from the encounters that make up the main play. The first teacher punches our hero in the chest, the second slaps his face and he flees the presence of the third, who is showing ominous signs of executing a panther-like spring.

Number One is Finn Gunn, a cowboy-booted veteran of the alternative theatre of the '70s, nostalgic for the days of people putting on plays in tiny spaces without any money (so whats changed?) and of "speaking to farmers about farmers." Or, in Hollingsworths case (that would be Michael Hollingsworth, now of VideoCabaret; Gilbert isn't afraid to name names, or at least to drop them), there was "good old-fashioned decadence, not like the fancy decadence you get nowadays."

Finn, put over by Jason Cadieux with hilarious faded swagger, seldom has a drink out of his hands. His notions about acting are difficult to make out through the resultant haze, but they seem to involve the student getting in touch with his inner man, plus a massive amount of wrong-footing, physical and psychological.

I can't work with you, he says, "if youre afraid of me," an ultimatum that on the intimidation scale must come out just ahead of act naturally. He then tops it by throwing what appears to be an epileptic fit. I have seen few funnier sights recently than that of Jefferson Guzman, as the Actor whose name we never learn, attempting to escape the room by creeping turtle-like across the floor, while his mentor lies writhing a few feet away from him. What he most wants to do is leave without paying, which really gets Finn where he lives.

Number Two is Ismene Popoff, who commiserates with the Actor over the violence hes suffered from Finn. If Finn, for macho reasons, preferred working with men, Ismene, rendered to life by Ann Holloway as a would-be Earth mother from an even earlier cultural era, likes to interact with women. She believes in "mortifying the flesh," which she finds easier with women because, if I'm deciphering my notes properly, they're vaginas.

Our boy, lacking that genetic predisposition, isnt too sure he wants his flesh mortified but, after a wittily played round of cat- and-mouse, he consents, on condition that it wont hurt too much. When it does, and he protests, she accuses him of wanting to rape her. He counters that this is unlikely, since he's gay, but this cuts no ice with her. (The hierarchies of victimhood can be damnably tricky to establish.) He makes his second precipitate exit of the evening, pursued by cries of "you rape me with your privilege." It's a little disappointing to see her turn into a stereotype of the resentful feminist, and more so that the characters never really engage, but were dealing with cartoons here, and this is a funny one.

Number Three is Reginald Architruc, who commiserates with the Actor over the violence hes suffered from Finn and Ismene. If Reginald has theories about acting, he keeps them to himself, along with his hands, at least to begin with. What Reginald has, or says he has, is contacts -- he seems to be as much agent as teacher -- and he uses them to get his young male clients into bed. He's a snake in snake's clothing, if snakes wear pink. He can even promise Hollywood if, amusingly enough, his prey will conceal being gay. He asks what man, with a couple of token British exceptions, has ever succeeded in being both out and a star, and the Actor is abashed to discover that he cant name one. So, probably, is the audience.

Gavin Crawfords Reginald sports an English accent himself -- whether it's meant to be natural or affected, I can't say -- and is altogether a fawning, preening, dangerous person. Finn, in the first scene, rails about Stratford; Reginald manages, in a single paragraph, to bitch about the festival and about Finn for being fired from it. (Poor Stratford; gets it coming and going.) Reginalds own name-dropping is of the sleekest brand. His prize anecdote concerns fellating Edward Albee. It seems to be his favourite seduction gambit. You neednt, he tells the Actor, think of me as a predatory teacher (I paraphrase slightly) because I'm so obviously behaving like a predatory teacher. So it doesn't count. As a comment on the debased postmodern idea of irony, that cuts pretty deep.

It spurs the Actor finally to assert himself, on behalf of all students, acting or otherwise, who have ever served as scapegoats for their instructors' hangups. It's probably too explicit a statement to be believable, but it is undeniably satisfying, not least because it holds true for many relationships besides pedagogic ones. Most of what goes before is undeniably slight and parochial, but enjoyably so. Gilbert writes great witty parabolas of wounded self-aggrandizement, impeccably delivered by three of his cast and sympathetically suffered by the fourth. Everything is phrased and timed well; placed well, too, on a wide set, helpfully stripped of all but essential furniture. Appearances can be deceptive, but on this evidence Gilbert himself is rather a good acting teacher.

- Bad Acting Teachers runs through May 7 at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, 416-975-8555.

robertcushman@lycos.com

2006-05-06-wingfield-s-inferno:
ROYAL ALEXANDRA

260 King St W. - 416-872-1212

The sixth instalment of the Walt Wingfield saga might also be called Wingfield's Insurance. The rural township's Orange Lodge burns down and stockbroker-turned-farmer Walt is put in charge of its reconstruction. Anecdotes, apparently self-contained and mostly farcical, come together at the end, like a team of shaggy-dog stories on a single leash. Rod Beattie, playing everybody, is reliably amazing. Through June 4.
2006-05-08-upped-in-charms:
This year's Shaw Festival begins with one of the old boy's most infallible creations. Not that he was so old at the time; Arms and the Man, written in 1894, was only Bernard Shaw's fourth play. He called it, with his tongue only partly in his cheek, "a romantic comedy." It's really an anti-romantic, anti-heroic and anti- idealistic comedy that finishes by setting up more palatable ideals of both heroism and romance. It borrows its title from the first line of The Aeneid, and brings the assumptions of that bellicose epic down to Earth. It takes for its setting a real and recent war in the Balkans. Later conflicts in that region have made this one look positively cozy, and Shaw himself, whimsical as ever, can't help making it mock-picturesque. It was the first of his plays to be turned into a musical -- a downright comic opera in fact, The Chocolate Soldier. This incensed Shaw, but in a way he was asking for it. The Shaw Festival team gives it to him all over again.

Jackie Maxwell's production is as cute as a whole row of buttons. The approach has its charms, but it ends up selling the play short. It starts very well; at least once we've got past a prelude treating us to a series of dollhouse views of the

upper-crust Bulgarian manse in which the action takes place. When the stage buckles down to its prescribed business representing the heroine's bedroom, we get a fine duet between Raina Petkoff, the daughter of the house, and Captain Bluntschli, the Swiss mercenary in flight with the defeated Serbs, who climbs into her chamber, begins by threatening her and ends by throwing himself on her mercy, which is freely granted. Raina, whose father is a senior officer and whose fiance, Sergius, is

a cavalry-charging hero, has a

starry-eyed view of war, which Bluntschli, the professional soldier who has just spent three days under fire, systematically deflates.

He makes her angry, but he also makes an impression. Raina is

Diana Donnelly, who has gained enormously in charm, humour and authority since playing Major

Barbara last season. Patrick Galligan, torn between politeness and fatigue, is enchantingly deft as Bluntschli, whose native genius for logic and logistics is enhanced by his being the son of a hotel tycoon and whose holster is stuffed not with ammunition but with far more useful chocolate creams.

The first scene, then, is beautifully written and beautifully played. After that, things slide. The production becomes soft- centred, even by chocolate-cream standards. The men come home, Sergius acting passionate and petulant by turns. He is an inveterate poseur, but that doesn't mean he has to strike literal poses every moment. Mike Shara can hardly utter a line without resting his fist on his brow, his elbow on his knee, or his leg on a convenient rock: sometimes all three at once. In between gestures he gives a good, if lightweight, performance, but all this pantomime subverts part of the truth about Sergius, which is that he partly sees through his own pretensions. As Raina partly sees through hers, when it gets to the point that they see through one another's, their relationship is -- quite cheerfully -- doomed.

In a program note Maxwell describes the characters as "wonderfully eccentric." But they aren't; they're conventional people, vigorously drawn, which is where the fun lies. Peter Hutt catches the tone perfectly as Major Petkoff, who only wants to settle into his comfortable old life and his comfortable old coat. Peter Millard gets close to it as the servant Nicola, though for some reason he plays his crucial line about having the soul of a servant as if it were an expression of anger rather than self- satisfaction. (Characters in Shaw rarely get angry; those who do almost invariably look ridiculous.) But the maid Louka (Catherine McGregor) is played as a fiery feminist, rather than a clever and sexy girl with an eye to the main chance, while Nora McLellan's Petkoff mama, having been very helpful to begin with, progressively loses touch with reality. It may be that the overpowering turban she wears in company leaves her with little option.

William Schmuck's costumes and Sue LePage's sets increasingly dominate the evening, driving out the real humour. The Petkoffs are awfully proud of their library, "the only one in Bulgaria." Shaw's stage directions make clear that it has very few books but is "a most comfortable sitting-room," not terribly grand. Here it's a yawningly wide chamber, furnished with intimidating elegance and with no books whatsoever; they must all be shelved on the fourth wall. It's the kind of design that gets audience applause, especially in Niagara, but does nothing for the play. Jokes pass unlaughed-at; the recouplings of Sergius and Louka, Bluntschli and Raina, have no tension. Galligan remains delightful, but he lacks force; the energy that should leave the other characters gasping at the close is a shadow of what it should be. ("What a man!" says Sergius, flattened by this whirlwind of an anti-hero, and then adds, "Is he a man?" The curtain falls on the question.) Donnelly forfeits her poise and, worse yet, her timing. Raina's final admission of love for her chocolate-cream soldier should be the play's romantic peak; its anti-romantic peak as well. It's hard to forgive a production that lets it pass as a non-event.

- In repertory until Oct. 29.

1-800-511-SHAW

2006-05-08-where-there-s-a-will-there-s-:
robertcushman@lycos.com

Tara Rosling gives an extraordinary performance as Catherine Sloper, the shy, plain heroine of The Heiress, betrayed by the two men who should love her the best. At least she sees herself as plain, and most of the other characters agree with her. The audience doesn't. The audience sees a woman of great physical and intellectual potential whose upbringing has deprived her of all confidence. At the end of the play she gains it, at the price of losing everything else.

The Heiress is an adaptation, by Ruth and Augustus Goetz, of the Henry James novel Washington Square. "Suggested by says the printed text; the Shaw Festival program denies James even that meagre credit, though it's full of other information about him. It reminds us of the often-noted fact that though the stage-struck novelist was never able to write a sucessful play of his own, his tales have consistently provided the basis for other peoples hits. Everybody gains, including those of us who find the books unreadably precious and who are grateful to the plays for providing us with easy access. The Heiress, first staged on Broadway in 1947 and a repertory staple ever since, may be the most successful of the lot. The Goetzes are presumably responsible for the narrative craft and James for the psychological complexity. In this production its gripping entertainment that never insults the intelligence.

Catherine is the only child of Dr. Austen Sloper, a prosperous New York physician of the mid-19th century whose wife died young. He has never stopped comparing Catherine to his wife and finding her wanting. His daughter's only talent seems to be embroidery and that's not enough. Help her to be clever," he asks his sister, sounding helpless; "I should so like her to be clever. He wants someone who will sparkle in his drawing-room.

Roslings Catherine might well be capable of cleverness, even of sparkle; she can say intelligent things and she can even laugh. But shes been told so often that she's dull that she's retreated into dowdiness. When she tries to break out, she tries too hard and gives up. At her first appearance she looks stunning, but self-conscious. And her voice, repressed and tremulous, is that of someone who has marshalled her thoughts and then lost all trust in them.

I wondered if this sound would be enough to see the actress through the play. It turns out that it is; the dynamics dont change much but the intensity does. Her voice carries her from repression to awakening to abandon to agony, and finally to a denial, like burning ice, of herself and everyone else. Catherine, for the first time in her life, is wooed, by a stylish but feckless young man named Morris Townsend. She falls headlong and unconditionally in love. The doctor has Morris pegged as a fortune-hunter, probably with good reason. Catherine survives the imputation that nobody could over her except for her money, though the scene is painful to watch; her world collapses when Morris seems to prove the doctor right.

Neither father nor lover earns a second chance. What keeps the play grown-up is that we are never sure that Catherine has made the right choice. Justice is on her side; the chance for happiness, however compromised, may not be. Accused of being cruel Catherine replies, in a line that sounds famous even if youve never heard it before, yes, I have been taught by masters!" A sense of tragic inevitablity haunts Rosling's performance here. Locking herself up in her father's Washington Square mansion, shes trapped in his estimation of her.

Mike Sharas Morris helps keep the options open; few actors can do sincerity as he can, and when he professes his love for Catherine there remains the tantalizing possibility that he isn't wholly faking it. There's little plumbing of ambiguous depths in Michael Balls doctor, but in its conventional way his unbending paterfamilias fills the space. As his widowed sister, and everybodys confidante and hanger-on, Donna Belleville grows steadily from dramatic convenience to person in her own right; she's also an audience surrogate, hoping against hope -- and against reason -- for a happy ending.

- In repertory until Oct. 7.

2006-05-09-i-m-going-for-broke-william-h:
In 1999 William Hutt played Prospero in The Tempest at the Stratford Festival for the third, and what was widely assumed to be the last, time. The assumption was a natural one. Hutt was 79, and Prospero, the magician who at the end of the play breaks his staff and drowns his books, is generally recognized as the greatest of all valedictory rules, maybe signifying Shakespeare's own farewell to the stage. According to rumour, this was not only going to be Hutt's last Prospero. It was going to be his last performance on stage.

"I don't know whether I should apologize to everyone," said Hutt, between rehearsals for this year's festival, at which he is playing Prospero again. "I don't think so. I never said I was going to retire. I did say, very pointedly, that I was going to take a year off, which in fact I almost did. Except I did some directing that next year." (The play was Oscar Remembered, a piece about Lord Alfred Douglas, and featured Michael Therriault, who had been Hutt's Ariel in 1999.) "But because of my age and my saying I was taking a year off, the media made a retirement thing out of it. That's how I viewed it."

To be fair, the festival's publicists never said Hutt was retiring. But they never denied it either. They knew a good angle when they saw one.

This time, though, the retirement is official, right? "Absolutely" says Hutt. Then he elaborates.

"It's my farewell performance on stage. I'll do films and televison if they come along, of course. And if somebody actually thinks 'Oh, maybe he'd like to direct a play, that's perfectly acceptable. I can just sit there and tell everybody what to do. Or just sit there, and hope they'll do it."

There seems little doubt that they would. Hutt is by almost universal consent our greatest actor. Few actors would argue with a man who is the object of so much respect and affection. And it's not just longevity or that he is part of the fabric of our major theatre, having been at Stratford virtually continuously since the first season in 1953. It's the risks he took after he became a legend. Following his failure to retire, he did things that no actor in his eighties is supposed to do. He went on playing leads at Stratford. Some were parts he had played: the King of France in All's Well That Ends Well and Feste, a performance of legendary repose and command, in Twelfth Night. But in 2001 he also took on a massive oratorical role as Clarence Darrow, defending the evolutionary cause in the American courthouse drama Inherit the Wind. (He and his creationist opponent spend much of the play in shirtsleeves and braces, inspiring the National Post headline "The Suspenders of Disbelief.") He then took a remarkable left-hand turn, returning to the Toronto stage for the first time in decades, to appear in two modern classics with Soulpepper.

"I loved working with Soulpepper. Without them I'd never have got the chance to play either one of those roles." The roles were Spooner in Harold Pinter's No Man's Land, in which he was astonishing, and Vladimir in Waiting for Godot, in which he was scarcely less so, despite being slowed down by arthritis and some initial memory problems. "If I'm going to go out, at least I'm going to go with a little panache, not fade away."

And so it's back to Prospero. And talk about coming full circle, this -- as far back as 1962 -- was the first unequivocal lead role he ever played at Stratford. He doesn't remember much about that performance, except the "distinct pleasure" of playing scenes with his Miranda, a brand-new Stratford ingenue named Martha Henry, and the Ariel of the late Bruno Gerussi. He does recall, though, that Michael Langham, then director of the festival, though not of that production, must have been impressed: "He said, 'This should lead to Richard II very soon.' And it did."

Langham is one of the three Stratford chiefs whom Hutt (who has worked with all eight of them) regards as having had the greatest influence on his work. "I learned more about acting from Michael than anyone else. He's a brilliant choreographer; he made us understand clearly the picture he was making with our bodies. We weren't just standing here because he'd told us to."

Robin Phillips "taught me the importance of stillness and thought. He told me I could bounce along perfectly well as I'd done in the past, I'd make money, but that there were more levels to my career than I thought there were." One of those unexpected levels has in fact become something of a legend. "People would come up to me over the years and say 'The part you've played that meant the most to me was ...' and I'd think 'Please, please, let it be Lear or James Tyrone.' But what invariably comes out is Lady Bracknell."

That towering dowager (six-foot plus, with Hutt playing her) in The Importance of Being Earnest occasioned one of Phillips's most celebrated directorial notes, when he remarked: "Lady Bracknell can walk through a room without disturbing one speck of dust." That, Hutt found, was a message he could apply to every role: "It's not just about standing still, but if you're going to do something, do it that deftly, with that much concentration, so it means something."

Richard Monette, the current Stratford director, "has kept me alive. When he took over, 13 years ago, I was over 70. Most directors would have said, 'We'll find whatever we can for you, of course we will,' and proceed to find very little. But Richard has really made a place for me in this organization. I think he thinks I'm very valuable to it." (He does.)

Monette directed Hutt's previous Prospero, and he's also directing this one. Hutt is still re-thinking the role, especially the famous "Our revels now are ended" speech, which virtually prophesies the end of the world. "There's a temptation, because it's a famous aria, to soften it, but" -- and at this point in our conversation Hutt hammered out his words, savouring the meaning of each one -- "I think he's really angry, and sardonic and almost in despair. I hinted at it last time, but this time I said, 'I'm going to go for broke.' "

Then there is Prospero's renunciation speech, one that for the audience is likely to carry even greater emotional baggage this year than it did in 1999. For the actor it's a huge technical challenge, building up one detail after another. "You have to do it in such a way that it's not all one note. And what changes the music is a change in attitude. You start by admiring and invoking the spirits, then you say 'Let me tell you what I've done' -- and that includes the claim to have raised the dead, like Lazarus. He's snatching at equality with God, and he has to eventually forgive himself for that. The mood changes again. I wasn't able to do that in '62. My sense of music wasn't acute enough."

It certainly is now. "I was very fortunate. When my voice changed, it dropped in exactly the right place. Some people's drop in very odd places. Rod Stewart, God knows where his voice dropped to." It's a surprising comparison, but one knows what he means.

The Tempest turned out not to be Shakespeare's final play. And there are rumours Hutt might yet be seen again on a Stratford stage in something less demanding -- perhaps in a cameo role for Monette's own farewell season, two years down the road. ("If I'm still active - - and alive. Because I owe Richard a lot.") This season anyway we have that voice, and that stillness, and they are sovereign.
2006-05-09-great-american-songbook-bad-a:
HIGH SOCIETY

Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

Already this new season the Shaw Festival has given us the good (The Heiress) and the indifferent (Arms and the Man). Here, in unwished-for symmetry, comes the bad.

There have been at least three attempts to make a stage musical out of High Society, and none of them have worked. There's no way they could. The given elements not only fail to jell; they cancel one another out. The immediate source is a 1956 movie, from the twilight years of the MGM musical. It has a pleasant but unremarkable score by Cole Porter, who was also in his twilight; it's significant that the best number, Well Did You Evah, is a recycling of a Porter song from 20 years earlier. It's also significant that the number is remembered not for its intrinsic qualities but for being a duet for Bing Crosby and Frank Sinatra, stepping outside the story and virtually playing themselves. This really is the decadence of the movie musical; it celebrates not the performers' skills but -- to coin a word we undoubtedly need -- their famousness. It is also, of course, a hard act for later performers to follow. (Louis Armstrong's in the picture, too, literally playing himself. That's an impossible act to follow, and none of the stage versions have tried.)

The movie is itself based on a famous play, Philip Barry's The Philadelphia Story (1939), which became a classic film in its own non-musical right. Cary Grant and Katharine Hepburn are in it; that means we have two generations of legend to contend with. The play, and all its derivatives, concern the melting of an ice-maiden; Tracy Lord, beautiful and self-righteous society heiress -- all this year's Shaw shows seem to be about heiresses -- is about to marry George Kittredge, "so humourless he's funny," who has worked his way up from the bottom (of a coal mine). No one approves, least of all Tracy's once and obviously future husband Dexter, who is -- well, he was -- Cary Grant and who lives conveniently next door.

Barry's play is not so much an American classic as an apology for one. It's neither as wise nor as witty as it thinks it is. But it's well-made, and doesn't take too kindly to having songs poked into it. The High Society movie gets around this, just about; there are Porter's songs, generic and few in number, and there is the story, and they go their separate ways. ("End of song" says Satchmo at the start of the picture; "beginning of story." And so it goes, throughout.) But you can't write a show that way, not these days, so adaptors, with the blessing of the permissive Porter estate, raid the catalogue for additional songs in the forlorn hope that they will fit the action. The inevitable dehydrating result is a score made up not of songs that people just have to sing in these circumstances, but of songs that it's not quite possible they might. The styles don't match, despite the authors' shared social context; Barry was genteel, Porter was rude. It's even worse when the song is a standard; the present version (which was done without much success on Broadway in 1998) throws in Just One of Those Things and It's All Right with Me, and it's as disorienting as hearing Macbeth's "Tomorrow and tomorrow and tomorrow" in the middle of Othello. The obscurer songs are more fun, though I'm Throwing a Ball Tonight and You've Got That Thing are so dragged in you can practically hear their screams Their titles get heavily dropped in advance, allowing buffs extra time to squirm.

Occasionally, gold is struck: I Worship You, a beautiful song well sung (by David Leyshon) works miraculously well as an expression of George's feelings about Tracy; I'm not sure where a self-made, self-proclaimed philistine gets off with his references to the goddesses Isis and Astarte, but the imagery is apt for the subject if not the singer. In fact, given the hopelessness of the enterprise, Arthur Kopit's script is a credible job; he has shuffled the movie songs into a new and sensible order, and he gives a sizeable portion of the second act a coherent identity as a post- midnight pastoral after the fashion of A Little Night Music, with couples rearranging their destinies in the stately home's stately grounds. If the show has an unsung heroine, it's Susan Birkenhead, whose "additional lyrics" to some of Porter's tunes actually match the originals for wit and far surpass them for dramatic relevance. She has turned what used to be the High Society Calypso into a running commentary by the Lord family's servants on the antics of their employers. It's a good unifying idea.

It's debased at Niagara by Kelly Robinson's busy, coarse production. So is much else. Who Wants to be a Millionaire, one song from the film that might stand a theatrical chance, is performed by the scenery rather than by the two important characters (Patty Jamieson, who is adequate, and Jay Turvey, who is reptilian) to whom it is supposed to introduce us. About the only things to praise are William Schmuck's sets, imposing indoors and magical out, and the Dexter of Dan Chameroy, whose acting flows nearly as effortlessly as his singing. But all depends on Tracy. Camilla Scott is a decent character actress and she can sing a ballad in an anonymous kind of way. But her fizz is forced; and she has the emotional vulnerability and comic finesse of a sledgehammer.

High Society is a famous title. That must be why it's there. But if the Shaw Festival is committed to doing mainstage musicals (which seems to me a dangerous gambit), it cannot let famousness govern its choices. There isn't enough to go round.

- In repertory until November 19.

2006-05-18-the-dummy-s-a-metaphor-dummy:
THE VENTRILOQUIST

Factory Studio Theatre

- - -

Larry Tremblay's The Ventriloquist is not about ventriloquism -- or not in any literal sense. True, it does begin with a man who has a doll on his knee, a doll played by a live actress. The doll represents a girl who has just celebrated her 16th birthday, her form of celebration being to cut off her blonde braids. For her present, she asked her mother for a Parker pen. What she actually received was a frustrating set of Chinese boxes. By the time she got to the last one, she needed a magnifying glass to view the contents, a glass she usually uses to view her stamp collection. The girl seems angry. The ventriloquist seems intimidated. So ventriloquism is a metaphor, and the play is really about adult control and childish resentment. Or vice versa.

No, it's really about literary ambition, especially among the young. The doll morphs into Gaby, a young woman writing in her room, behind a locked door. She now has her Parker pen and she uses it to write, effortlessly, the most beautiful stories and the most beautiful novel the world has ever seen. She wants to be better than Balzac, and she succeeds.

No, it's really about the power of fiction, and life's tendency to imitate art. The things, some of them atrocious, that Gaby writes about tend to come true.

No, it's really about psychiatry as abuse. Though apparently in her own room, Gaby is simultaneously in the consulting chamber of Dr. Limestone, a therapist with unorthodox methods and a controlling personality, who is identical to the ventriloquist, and who's treating her for writers' block. He has a prospectus, which apparently guarantees a cure if the patient obeys its demands. He gets Gaby to tell her story, and her stories, while stripped to her underwear. He has a compensating story of his own, about how his mother once stripped him to his underwear and forced him to eat onion soup. He hates onions. Gaby has already composed a story about a girl who fell in love with a beautiful young man who was actually an onion. Ah, the power of disguise.

No, it's really about sibling rivalry in its cruellest form. Gaby had an adored brother called Edgar, also a writer -- an acclaimed poet. He met a horrible end. Gaby wrote about it. But before this, or maybe in a parallel universe, Gaby took him her story; and he read it, admired it, made off with it and was furiously jealous of it.

No, it's really -- well, intermittently -- about the outside world trying to get inside the heads, and the rooms, of children. While Gaby sits creating fictions and/or interacting with Dr. Limestone, her door is knocked on by her father, her mother, who subsequently dies of shock at her son Edgar's fate, her sickeningly pious friend Lea whose birthday gift to Gaby was -- yes -- her prized stamp collection and who got called foul names for her pains, and a Dr. Mortimer who comes with parental recommendation but who sounds every bit as predatory as Dr. Limestone. She's also called on by Balzac, who isn't pleased to hear that Gaby has gone into competition with him and calls her the same names she called Lea. This seems to be Harold Bloom's theory of the anxiety of influence turned inside out; it's the older writer who's anxious, and how.

No, it's really about Africa, and the Europeans' fascination with it. Dr. Limestone takes over Gaby's story and makes it about Edgar, who takes the manuscript of the novel to an African village and reads it to a riveted audience. While he reads it, his skin turns black and heavily-tattooed, to the fascination of a woman called Flybelly, who seems to be Gaby's alter ego and who, towards the end of the reading, cuts off her braids. Edgar is played by the same actor as Dr. Limestone so what we took to be colour-blind casting isn't. In fact Edgar is Doctor Limestone and he and Gaby end by hurling insults at one another, sexual and literary.

No, it's really about ...well, get this. An epilogue finds Dr. Limestone back with his doll on his knee (it's now her 27th birthday), while his mother shouts at him through the door, telling him it isn't right to shut himself up like that and he should get a life. So the whole thing has been a man's projection of his own hang- ups onto an imaginary woman, which is maybe what art is, or maybe just what men are. And the play itself has been a set of Chinese boxes. And the ventriloquist's name is Parker.

It's clever, to the point where cleverness becomes silliness. Everything adds up, or at least everything in the play has an echo somewhere else, but everything cancels out. It has its compelling moments, and its witty ones, including Gaby's declaration that she doesn't "want to be like those stupid girls who think the world doesn't revolve around them." But Gaby and Dr. Limestone and their various appurtenances are never more than their author's own dummies. And the fact that this may be the point doesn't make it any less frustrating. Keith Turnbull's production of his own translation is kept afloat by Meg Roe, an actress new to Toronto, as the gabby Gaby. Nigel Shawn Williams is fine at the play's top and tail, which put him in shy mode, but he doesn't have the fluency or the authority for the shrink in the middle. French-Canadian drama seems to be going through an aridly self-conscious phase, at least judging from the examples that reach Toronto of which this is the latest

There is, as it happens, a corker of a play going around about the interaction of truth with storytelling, one that tells a really good story itself. It's The Pillowman, by Irish playwright Martin McDonagh, whose The Beauty Queen of Leenane knocked us out a few years ago, and whose The Lieutentant of Inishmore is a hit in New York. It's been done all over Canada, even by students, but the Toronto theatre has yet to stage it. This may not be Toronto's fault -- the rights to major plays are held up for years by the prospect of first-rate tours that never materialize -- but it's the Toronto audience's misfortune.

- Until May 21. 416-504-9971

2006-05-24-a-deadpan-evening-with-the-wi:
STEVEN WRIGHT

Elgin Theatre, Toronto

- - -

Somewhere in the course of his two-hour show at the Elgin last Thursday, Steven Wright admitted to being 50. This puts him closer to my age than to my children's. All the same, they were the ones who introduced him to me, mainly by playing me tapes in the car. This is their favourite method of broadening my horizons. It seems to work better with comedy than with music.

To Wright, though, I had some resistance. I had been far more susceptible to his more manic disciple, Mitch Hedberg, who died unexpectedly a couple of years ago. Hedberg is the guy you still see in trailers for stand-up shows on Comedy Central, easily identifiable because hes the only one who suggests that stand-up might actually be funny. Hes the one with the juiced-up weirdly italicized delivery who says "when I was a boy, I used to lie in my twin bed and wonder where my brother was." In some ways he recalls the incredulous observational style of Richard Pryor (when I first heard him I assumed he was black, which he wasn't) minus the political content. I surrendered the moment I heard him.

Like Hedberg, Wright dispenses one-liners and two-liners in oceanic quantities, in an order over which he presumably has some control -- he sounds too assured to be shuffling them on the spot -- but which seems quite arbitrary to the rest of us. He redefines deadpan, to the point of vocal somnambulism. The sentences emerge at a level pace from a throat lined equally with gravel and molasses. I found him, in sound only, rather pointless.

Still, I agreed to take my two sons to his appearance in Toronto, or to let them take me. (Apparently, he likes it here. We were his audience of choice for his DVD.) I promised the Post that I would file a piece on the unbridgeable generation gap.

Sorry. My boys fulfilled their part of the deal; they were gone from the moment Wright strolled on stage and unleashed his first joke. Trouble is, so was I. I don't see how Im expected to resist a man who says -- without preamble, as if we had just boarded his train of thought -- that he wished the first word he ever uttered had been quote so that, just before he died, he could round it off by saying "unquote."

Hes been known to say, quite audibly, that if we can't hear him, it's because hes in parentheses. Hes fascinated, first, by words, and, secondly, by behaviour as it's dictated by words. He's the Wittgenstein of stand-up comics, and he looks as the philosopher might if hed been dragooned into appearing in a production of Waiting for Godot. (Alternatively, he looks -- and sounds -- like an undertaker who lives, as opposed to loves, his work.) The visual element makes all the difference. He doesnt actually do much. He has three chairs on stage, and he divides his time between them with scrupulous fairness. Occasionally he picks up a guitar, and even plays it, while he sort of sings. That's all. But his presence, which is as powerful as downbeat gets, automatically gives his act a structure.

I used, he says, "to be a narrator for bad mimes," and though it takes a moment for the concept to sink in, it sounds reasonable. Like Lewis Carroll, he pays words the compliment of taking them literally, and then observes the chaos. You can't have everything. Where would you put it? He rubs concepts together. "I stayed up all night playing poker with tarot cards. I got a full house, and four people died."

Unlike most comics, he casts few aspersions on his own personal life. If hes been a failure with girls, he doesnt let on. Well, he does say on one of his tapes my girl has a queen-size bed and I have a court-jester size bed, but it isn't one of his best. Hedberg took the same idea to far wilder heights, when he fantasized about being visited by a king and saying "Hey, your majesty, we have a bed just your size", adding How come you kings are all the same size? and adding to that "We got one for your lady too." Hedberg, a comedian with exclamation-points, got excited by absurdity; Wright takes it as it comes. He doesn't do cadenzas that well. He had a surprisingly long and coherent routine last week about picking up a hitchhiker, but it never really got better than his chilling initial question to his passenger, How far do you think youre going?

Ask Wright a silly question ("did you sleep good?") and you get a disconcertingly sensible answer (no, I made a few mistakes). At the supermarket checkout he asks to buy the divider that separates his purchases from the next customers; asked why, he replies "you don't know the people I live with." I think this is the closest he comes to making a social statement. All the same, a view of human relations lurks darkly in everything he says.

I don't know why the kids have been keeping him from us; hes very grown-up. Maybe its just that the young have more time and energy to visit comedy clubs, so stand-up becomes part of their culture. (Of course, most children are comedians by nature. It's only when they start doing their routines for an audience beyond their own family that we should get nervous.) It's also true that most stand-up is awful; people spewing out fragments of supposed autobiography in no particular order. Wrights genius is to embrace the random as a principle while keeping his distance. He doesnt bore us with his personal problems or invent imaginary ones. Indeed, he doesn't seem to invent things at all; he just finds them. No wonder he's an idol.

robertcushman@lycos.com

2006-05-26-man-truly-lives-up-to-his-nam:
CRINGEWORTHY

Theatre Passe Muraille

- - -

Things certainly seem to be looking up at the end of the season. Cringeworthy apparently came into existence because Alex Poch- Goldin, playwright and actor, had thought up a wonderful name for a character and needed a play to go with it. This isn't the generally approved method of writing plays, but it's probably as good as any other. The result certainly justi-fies it. Cringeworthy is more than praiseworthy. It is very nearly raveworthy.

Mr. Cringeworthy lives, at least during his onstage hours, in a basement office in London in 1912. (An exceptionally cold winter, if the play's to be trusted.) He is a serious man of business, as is demonstrated by the presence, on Joanne Dente's evocative set, of two separate desks: A large flat one, to be worked at, and a roll- top, to make the back wall look good. He is in the moneylending dodge, with opium-trafficking and a little procuring on the side. He also subscribes to charities, and has testimonials on his walls to prove it. Scrooge might have been like this if he'd done some backsliding and discovered how to make his conversion pay.

Into Cringeworthy's web stumbles a hapless Italian named Luigi Tarantella. His brother in the old country has run up a debt he has no means or intention of repaying, offering Luigi as security. After offering a brisk run-down of all the nasty things that can happen to defaulting debtors, Mr. C. takes pity on Luigi, who is starving, and offers to ease his pain by bringing his wife, Angelina, over from Naples, all expenses paid.

We can guess that Cringeworthy intends to put Signora Tarantella on the game, and so he does. But he proceeds by easy stages, first sending her out to have innocent suppers with rich gentlemen, then employing her on drug drop-offs.

There are hints that Cringeworthy gets at least half his kicks from the power he wields over the couple, though personally I think he's mainly in it for the money. (He calculates interest by the quarter-hour, if not the minute.) But his crooked benevolence undoubtedly has an effect on their married life. Luigi claims to have found a job, though more likely he survives by stealing food. Angelina finds him out and comes to despise him and, very likely, hate herself.

Cringeworthy, meanwhile, has his own problems, chiefly venereal. He is writing an epic poem about his own disintegration, composed entirely in limerick form. It's very picturesque, though some of its rhymes are suspect. I'm prepared, though, to accept that as a reflection on the character rather than on his author's skills.

In fact, Poch-Goldin's ear, both as author and as actor of his own protagonist, is almost, though not quite, flawless. He relishes both the character and his background, and they take shape together. A mass of Victorian and Edwardian details, gleaned from other plays and other books, fuse into an individual creation. Literature becomes life, a shared fantasy relished on both sides of the house that first feels like history, and then like a premonitory mirror of our own time.

We believe in Cringeworthy's rise from pauperized slavery in a northern pencil factory, in his fanatically exact exactions, in his taste for sweet baked goods with his tea, in his ambiguous musings on a freer future, in his obsessive twitting of his victims' eating habits and their inability to indulge them (the word "linguini" really gets him off), and in the havoc he obsessively wreaks on their personalities and on his own.

The only flaw in the play, and in Chris Abraham's otherwise impeccable production, is that after a riveting half-hour they start to seem drawn out.

Short though the play is (85 minutes, going on 90), it begins to feel long. In its second half the scene keeps shifting from Cringeworthy's den to the Tarantellas' hotel room and back again, and a metronomic predictability sets in.

Both apartments, incidentally, are visible throughout, with no discernible gap; leaving me to imagine during the first part of the play that Cringeworthy was so conscientious, or just so cheap, that he slept in the shop.

Paul Fauteux and Tara Nicodemo are brilliant as the Tarantellas forced to dance to Cringeworthy's tune, he endearingly pitiable -- before selfishness and resentment set in and leave him merely pitiful -- and she increasing her stature as she loses her innocence.

They also, for extended periods, speak Italian like natives, which neither of them are.

This may be the best three-hander to hit one of our stages since The Drawer Boy; it's certainly (with the possible exception of Poch- Goldin's ear- lier This Hotel) the first time since then that this particular space has been so alive with the sounds of discovery and surprise.

- Until June 11. 416-504-7529

2006-05-28-taking-help-from-those-who-ne:
According to the Web site of the Ontario Coalition Against Poverty, which was scheduled to picket last night's gala opening of the Stratford Festival, the black-tie audience members climbing out of their limos "may not know much about Shakespeare but they are all experts at keeping us in poverty." This is because, "They are a Who's Who of the rich and vile (including members of the Ontario Government)." I don't know how much OCAP members know about Shakespeare but, by accident or design, they chose a remarkably pertinent play at which to stage their protest. The show kicking off this year's festival is Coriolanus, which actually begins with an anti-poverty riot. OCAP didn't let on whether they intended to demonstrate outside or disrupt the actual performance, but we were in for an evening of total theatre.

Coriolanus starts with starving citizens swarming the streets of ancient Rome. They're turned aside by a smooth-talking patrician, Menenius Agrippa, who persuades them that the senate has their best interests at heart. He may even believe it. There are many ways of interpreting the scene and the play: left, right and neutral. As usual, Shakespeare turns a merciless eye on all varieties of self- interest, while maintaining complete understanding of those who practise it. The citizens think their prime enemy is the warrior- hero Caius Martius, later glorified as Coriolanus: "Let us kill him and we'll have corn at our own price." They're wrong; Martius is a raging snob, but he's no politician, and certainly no economist. His fellow nobles pressure him into running for office, and have no hesitation in discarding him when he proves a liability. After he dies, a victim of just about everybody in the play including himself, political life goes on exactly as it did before.

At the risk of sounding like Menenius, I think OCAP's methods on this occasion were similarly confused. It isn't clear whom they were targeting. It could've been the MPPs in the audience, whom they hoped to embarrass into raising welfare rates by 40%. I hope they succeeded, but I doubt that they achieved much beyond making themselves feel better. It could have been the opening-night festivity, though this seems rather an inconspicuous symbol of conspicuous consumption. Or it might have been the Festival itself, which "speaks to a... tradition in which poor and homeless people are swept from sight to make way for an annual play pen for the rich."

I haven't myself noticed much poverty and homelessness on the streets of Stratford, Ont., but of course that could just be a tribute to the ruthlessness of the sweeping process. I did, though, telephone John Spencer, a retired Anglican pastor who has lived in Stratford and been involved with the festival for 20 years, and who corroborated my impression that Stratford is actually one of Ontario's more affluent communities. He also mentioned the theatre's record in helping members of the community who are in need; "The festival," he said to me, "is basically not just another Stratford factory." That's one of the ironies. OCAP are picketing an institution most of whose members, like most people working in the arts, would agree with them.

I sense a kind of reflexive philistinism here, a feeling that classical theatre is just a fancy way of grinding the faces of the poor. I haven't heard of any poverty protests at major hockey games, though seat-prices there are at least as prohibitive and the stars earn money beyond any theatre actor's dreams. It's true that the festival gets public money that might, in theory, go to poverty relief instead (hence, presumably, references to the festival's "Queen's Park sponsors"). But (a) that wouldn't happen even if all arts subsidies were removed tomorrow; and (b) the amounts involved are, certainly by European standards, pitifully small. Which helps explain why the prices are so high, and why the repertoire is so commercially weighted. But that's another story, and probably one that wouldn't interest OCAP very much.

What is at work, obviously, is a visceral anger that such inequalities should exist, that there should be poverty in a society that is demonstrably capable of producing great wealth. And they're right; it's wrong, indefensibly so. But that's a situation that indicts all of us above the poverty line, which would include some of the organizers of OCAP. After that, it's all finger-pointing, an arbitrary matter of where you draw the line: How much money is anyone allowed to have and how are they allowed to spend it? It's symbolism, and symbolism is important -- as Shakespeare knew and as everyone in Coriolanus knows, except the hero. But as a soldier, though not as a civilian, Coriolanus grasped one principle that OCAP on this occasion has forgotten: Choose your battlefield.
2006-05-30-addicted-to-suspense:
Last week saw the end of a months-old television tradition, by which Fox TV kept our nerves pleasurably jangled for two solid hours. At 8 p.m., they gave us the first season of Prison Break, the story of Michael Scofield, design genius from Chicago, who gets himself consigned to the citys Fox River penitentiary so that he can spring his brother, consigned to Death Row for a murder he didn't commit. Michael framed himself, so to speak; his brother Lincoln was framed by crooked politicians, a phrase that here, as in most dramatic latitudes, is a tautology.

This was followed at 9 p.m. by the longer-established 24, which has just completed its fifth season of the adventures of Jack Bauer, the wild-card super-agent of Los Angeles' Counter Terrorism Unit (CTU). The common device here is that the action of each series is supposed to unfold over a single day and in real time, one hour per episode. Over the years, Jack has saved the city and the country from bombs, viruses, nerve-gas, presidential assassinations and -- this last seasons ultimate weapon -- presidential treason. Both shows run on the same fuel: the plan that, once per episode, goes catastrophically wrong, only to be rescued and then threatened anew the following week. Both have wildly implausible storylines but extremely persuasive underlying assumptions. Both feature affectless superheroes with an occasional glint of fallible humanity.

It seems like a dream now, but the very first time we saw Jack Bauer he was peacefully teaching chess to his teenage daughter. It may be the last peaceful moment hes had, certainly the last involving any member of his family. Before that first hour, or episode, was out, his daughter was well on her way to being kidnapped by terrorists. A short time later, his wife was in the same predicament, and by the end of the day, or the season, Jack, a broken man, was cradling his wife's dead body in his arms, mumbling I'm sorry.

His anguish was understandable. So was his shock, though it was hardly greater than ours; were hardened now, but five years ago popular TV series didnt kill off sympathetic major characters. That he should feel guilty was also understandable, though it wasn't quite rational. It's true that his wife was killed by his traitorous ex-mistress but the treachery, though obviously not the lechery, was something he had no way of knowing about. (Neither did anybody else on the show, probably including those who write it.) Its also true that Jacks family had only been in jeopardy in the first place because his enemies wanted payback for his activities as a super- counter-terrorist; but he'd rescued them and placed them in what he had every reason to believe was a safe place.

The surprising thing is that Jack's authors, too, seem to hold his familys fate against him. Or at least they do occasionally, when it suits them. The producers have been quoted as saying that the final season of 24 will have to end with Jacks death "because he's a tragic hero."

John Doyle, The Globe and Mail's TV critic, has coupled Jack with Tony Soprano as men who are shown to be rotting within, even if some unthinking viewers are dazzled by their machismo. Hes right about The Sopranos, a morally aware show that never takes its eye off the object. But 24 doesnt have that kind of texture or that kind of seriousness; it's all about suspense, at which it's brilliant, perhaps unprecedentedly so. Tragedy needs a protagonist with some talent for introspection; serious drama needs writers with some capacity for analysis. Jack and his creators dont have time for either.

The moral crux is supposed to be Jacks readiness to inflict torture; we are seduced into applauding behaviour from him that we would condemn in the real world, and then we feel ashamed of ourselves and start asking questions. But in practice the show lets both us and its hero off the hook. Jack mistreats only people whom the viewers know in advance to be thoroughly bad guys with specific information about imminent outrages. This is in fact the ticking bomb scenario that U.S. authorities invoke whenever they want to justify torture (or whatever they, at that moment, feel like calling it) but of which they have yet to adduce a single concrete example. Life, it seems, is not as neat as 24.

Only once does Jack seem to have suffered pangs of conscience while on the job. It was in season three. On the orders of the president, who was himself yielding to the whim of some blackmailing fanatic, Jack put a bullet through the neck of CTU's then-current boss, murmuring "God forgive me" as he did so. It looked like a real character-crunching moment. It has not, however, been alluded to since.

One corollary of the real-time convention is that it doesn't permit flashbacks. It doesnt seem to allow for much in the way of mental retrospection either. Once youre dead on 24, you are, with rare exceptions, dead; and unmourned to boot. The amount of collateral damage Jack's exploits leave in their wake has almost become a running gag. There should be a permanent memo in all CTU agents' e-mail: "Never go on a mission with Jack Bauer. He will survive. You wont." Civilians, too, have bitten the dust only to be instantly forgotten, this season in record numbers.

The show derives much of its force from connecting with threats that are all too real, and it probably performs a therapeutic service by exhibiting and temporarily defusing them. It never mentions 9/11, but it obviously exists in its shadow; this season, it even risked what can best be described as a mock hijack. But Jack himself strides through it all, leading 95% of an unexamined life. Hes an action-hero, combining agility and cunning (no wonder he's good at chess) in a tradition that stretches all the way back to Gilgamesh via Odysseus. And like his predecessors, he has a weapon with quasi-magical powers that only he can wield. In his case, it's a cell-phone that can download or transmit anything with stupefying efficiency.

24 has obviously been a great influence on Prison Break, which went on hiatus with the escape effected but everything else still to play for. The next season should perhaps be re-titled Prison Broken, though that sounds like something you do to incarcerated pets. There was a new last-minute wrinkle; an old con revealed the whereabouts of a $5-million stash on the outside. Judging from the looks on the faces of the guys who overheard him, the next season could turn into Its a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World minus the slapstick. For its part, 24 looks like its turning into The Manchurian Candidate. Last we saw, Jack was on a slow boat to China, in the hands of sinister captors who have their own uses for him.

Im addicted to both shows, but I find that my withdrawal symptoms are worse if I miss an episode of 24. I'm desperate to know what happened but I know that if I catch up later, having already been given a summary of events, there will be very little there for me. The pretense that all these events are happening in one day is no longer believable; though it was in the first series, the only one in which you actually felt night giving way to day and day to night.

Prison Break isn't as viscerally exciting, but it has a richer spread of characters, what with Michael having involved half the prison population in his plans. And with character comes humour, which may actually be detrimental to suspense; it allows all concerned to relax.

Politically, both shows could be said to be ahead of their time. 24 has featured a black president, who was a saint, and Prison Break has had a female vice-president, who is anything but. For a time, 24 seemed to be grooming its own villainous Veep, and its perfectly possible that the writers, who notoriously make it up as they go along, abandoned this idea only when they realized that Prison Break had beaten them to it. So they broke another taboo, and put their own president Logan through a series of U-turns. First he was a weasel, then a villain, and finally -- with virtuoso efforts from authors and actor -- he was a just-about-credible villainous weasel, Nixon with a touch of Bush. Seeing which, the Prison Break team struck back and -- in a dazzling display of fancy narrative footwork -- had their own Commander-in-Chief assassinated (another network convention gone bust) and speeded his deputy into the Oval Office. Where she now sits, all ready to wreak havoc in Season Two, as corrupt and right-wing and vindictive as they come.

These are odd politics for conservative Fox, but then this is the network that brought us The Simpsons, which in its prime was the most subversive show on television. It knows the value of being in touch with the times. And both Prison Break and 24 are very much of their times in their preoccupation with corporate conspiracies.

President Logan was obsessed with oil, and his strings were being pulled by a still-unmasked bunch of smoothies who were probably rolling in it. Prison Breaks VP was originally in cahoots with something called The Company, which employed her to put paid to environmental bills. Obviously, energy conservation is not a priority for the evil masterminds of either show, but I think they might conserve some of their own by simply joining forces across the commercial break. Their aims and methods seem remarkably similar.

Actually, there's something at work here more fundamental than the zeitgeist. There's the nature of drama. It is, as all the textbooks say, about conflict; and theres no excitement, moral or physical, in being on the side of the overdog. Drama is, by definition, against authority, whether thats government or something beyond. So Prison Break takes its characters from the most marginalized section of society; while CTU, though an official organization, is a maverick one, in constant danger of being wiped out.

24's long-term prospects seem infinite; there's always another day. Prison Break is unlikely to achieve comparable longevity, due to its confining premise, not to mention its confined premises. Even if they contrive a means of throwing the whole cast back in the slammer, nobody is entitled to play more than one Get Out of Jail card. On a personal-relations level, I think Michael, who after all is not a career warrior, may have a faint shot at happiness, even though his lady of choice rounded out the season by taking a drug overdose that may or may not be fatal.

Jack and Audrey were granted so many tender reunions that one knew for certain their relationship was doomed. Jack, even if he has to spend the whole of next season in China, will just go on as one of the walking wounded. But he will walk tall, or as tall as Kiefer Sutherland can, and his wounds will only bleed on very special occasions.
