2006-05-30-taking-help-from-those-who-ne:
OCAP is protesting Stratford theatre, but it's reliant on aid

According to the Web site of the Ontario Coalition Against Poverty, which was scheduled to picket last night's gala opening of the Stratford Festival, the black-tie audience members climbing out of their limos "may not know much about Shakespeare but they are all experts at keeping us in poverty." This is because, "They are a Who's Who of the rich and vile (including members of the Ontario Government)." I don't know how much OCAP members know about Shakespeare but, by accident or design, they chose a remarkably pertinent play at which to stage their protest. The show kicking off this year's festival is Coriolanus, which actually begins with an anti-poverty riot. OCAP didn't let on whether they intended to demonstrate outside or disrupt the actual performance, but we were in for an evening of total theatre.

Coriolanus starts with starving citizens swarming the streets of ancient Rome. They're turned aside by a smooth-talking patrician, Menenius Agrippa, who persuades them that the senate has their best interests at heart. He may even believe it. There are many ways of interpreting the scene and the play: left, right and neutral. As usual, Shakespeare turns a merciless eye on all varieties of self- interest, while maintaining complete understanding of those who practise it. The citizens think their prime enemy is the warrior- hero Caius Martius, later glorified as Coriolanus: "Let us kill him and we'll have corn at our own price." They're wrong; Martius is a raging snob, but he's no politician, and certainly no economist. His fellownobles pressure him into running for office, and have no hesitation in discarding him when he proves a liability. After he dies, a victim of just about everybody in the play including himself, political life goes on exactly as it did before.

At the risk of sounding like Menenius, I think OCAP's methods on this occasion were similarly confused. It isn't clear whom they were targeting. It could've been the MPPs in the audience, whom they hoped to embarrass into raising welfare rates by 40%. I hope they succeeded, but I doubt that they achieved much beyond making themselves feel better. It could have been the opening-night festivity, though this seems rather an inconspicuous symbol of conspicuous consumption. Or it might have been the Festival itself, which "speaks to a ... tradition in which poor and homeless people are swept from sight to make way for an annual play pen for the rich."

I haven't myself noticed much poverty and homelessness on the streets of Stratford, Ont., but of course that could just be a tribute to the ruthlessness of the sweeping process. I did, though, telephone John Spencer, a retired Anglican pastor who has lived in Stratford and been involved with the festival for 20 years, and who corroborated my impression that Stratford is actually one of Ontario's more affluent communities. He also mentioned the theatre's record in helping members of the community who are in need; "The festival," he said to me, "is basically not just another Stratford factory." That's one of the ironies. OCAP are picketing an institution most of whose members, like most people working in the arts, would agree with them.

I sense a kind of reflexive philistinism here, a feeling that classical theatre is just a fancy way of grinding the faces of the poor. I haven't heard of any poverty protests at major hockey games, though seat-prices there are at least as prohibitive and the stars earn money beyond any theatre actor's dreams. It's true that the festival gets public money that might, in theory, go to poverty relief instead (hence, presumably, references to the festival's "Queen's Park sponsors"). But (a) that wouldn't happen even if all arts subsidies were removed tomorrow; and (b) the amounts involved are, certainly by European standards, pitifully small. Which helps explain why the prices are so high, and why the repertoire is so commercially weighted. But that's another story, and probably one that wouldn't interest OCAP very much.

What is at work, obviously, is a visceral anger that such inequalities should exist, that there should be poverty in a society that is demonstrably capable of producing great wealth. And they're right; it's wrong, indefensibly so. But that's a situation that indicts all of us above the poverty line, which would include some of the organizers of OCAP. After that, it's all

finger-pointing, an arbitrary matter of where you draw the line: How much money is anyone allowed to have and how are they allowed to spend it? It's symbolism, and symbolism is important -- as Shakespeare knew and as everyone in Coriolanus knows, except the hero. But as a soldier, though not as a civilian, Coriolanus grasped one principle that OCAP on this occasion has forgotten: Choose your battlefield.

2006-05-30-the-imperfect-crime:
TOO TRUE TO BE GOOD

Court House Theatre,

Niagara-on-the Lake

Shaw Festival

- - -

The last Bernard Shaw play to begin at Niagara with a parade of masked medics was, logically enough, The Doctor's Dilemma. The same device is now being used to launch the later and lesser-known play Too True to be Good, the pretext being that the action begins in a sickroom. Here lies a very rich, very spoiled and very protected young lady who is suffering from the measles. Suffering still more is the human-sized Microbe who -- big laugh -- has caught it from her. He keeps up an embittered running commentary on the first act, which in print at least, is very funny. It is destroyed here by a ghastly performance from William Vickers who shouts, moans, coughs - - does everything except simply and humorously talk. Shaw once told an actor that it was impossible to overact in his plays. He had a point. But there is a difference between purposeful extravagance (this play is sub-titled "a political extravaganza") and the underlining, and consequent undermining, of every joke.

A gaffe like this is likely to be the fault of the director rather than the actor. Which is strange because, in most other respects, Jim Mezon's production is exemplary: It's the Shaw Festival's best Shaw production in the last couple of years and a cast-iron example of what this institution is for. It has a terrific trio of central performances. Nicole Underhay is a ferocious ball of perfectly-targeted energy as the Patient rescued from hearth, home and hypochondria by a couple of neophyte crooks who steal her insanely valuable pearl necklace so that all three of them can live on the proceeds. Kelli Fox is a lot of fun as the Nurse, a cockney con-artist who cheekily passes herself off as an Italian countess. Blair Williams plays the brains of the operation, or the intellect minus practicality, though his true vocation has always been for preaching.

The burglary takes up the first act. At the end of it, the Microbe announces that "the play is now virtually over but the characters will discuss it at great length for two more acts." ("The exit doors" he adds, "are all in order.") This of course is Shaw poking characteristic fun at his own loquacious reputation. It also happens to be pretty much true. The three tricksters arrive in an unnamed "mountainous country" that could be in North Africa, the Middle East or the Caribbean. There is a British force here commanded by Col. Tallboys, an amiable blimp with ambitions for a knighthood. He is played by Benedict Campbell, who has never been better and who wields a teapot with true-blue English aplomb, at one point jabbing it an opponent's ribs. The actual work of the regiment is done by the omnicompetent Pte. Meek, based on Shaw's friend Lawrence of Arabia and played by Andrew Bunker with sublime self- effacement. This is a master-servant role-reversing relationship as old and infallible as the hills. It also contributes to the play's intended air of vertiginous dislocation. It's 1932 and a world still reeling from the last apocalypse is preparing, half-knowingly, for the next. The Burglar's speeches about having destroyed cities and civilians hit very hard. He also discourses on the higher centres (the mind) that govern him and the lower (sex) that preoccupy the Nurse, and the impossibility of satisfying either without the other.

The play itself must carry some of the blame. It was, in the '60s, the first of Shaw's late plays to be rehabilitated, the first to show that the farce of ideas, increasingly divorced from social reality, carried a greater kick than critical tradition had acknowledged. But the traditional objections remain; Shaw's characters can say anything at any time, and it's a challenge to keep them rooted and consistent. The paradoxes -- a microbe infected by a human, an atheist who casts out his believing son -- become mechanical. To counter this, a production has to fire on every cylinder of personality, not just -- like this one -- on most of them.

A lot depends on the final speech. The preacher, left alone, preaches, his situation being that he has to, despite not knowing what to say. Traditionally this has been taken as Shaw's own confession, the author once more tipping his hand, this time in despair. He always denied it, but we don't have to believe him. Certainly the speech works best with that tension behind it. Williams' skill remains; so, very much, does his likeability. But the passion, though it sometimes appears on the horizon, isn't there yet.

- In repertory until October 7. 1-800-511-SHAW

Colour Photo: Shaw Festival / In an irony true to the play's name, the young lady sick with the measles has infected the microbe with the same disease.
2006-05-31-seeing-through-it-all:
THE INVISIBLE MAN

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

- - -

I have seen The Invisible Man. I know that sounds silly, but so does the play. It looks all right, fitted out by Judith Bowden with neat, pretty sets that put a new gloss on an old style: crowded split-level interiors and airy etched backcloths that hark back to the Edwardian theatre, when stories were stories and plays were melodramas. Fair enough, since Michael O'Brien's adaptation of H. G. Wells' pioneering science-fiction novel is set in and around an English Edwardian (well, late Victorian) village with the picturesque name of Iping. The program says it's in Sussex, which is not that far from London, but the inhabitants all speak in the thick, all-purpose brogue known to generations of British actors as Mummerset. To Canadians it comes less naturally, making it very hard to understand.

Well, you don't go to The Invisible Man for the acting, which is just as well, since most of it is atrocious. You go for the effects, and one of them is indeed a stunner. The title figure, who has been going around swathed like a mummy so that nobody will notice his lack of a body (he doesn't want his invisibility to be visible), is swarmed by the villagers and revealed to have a hole where his head should be. They all gasp, and so do we. But most of the other magic tricks in Neil Munro's production are about furniture moving around, apparently of its own volition. This is smoothly done, and it must have taken ages for the technicians to get right, but that doesn't make it especially exciting to watch.

The invisible man is James Griffin, a brilliant scientist who is the victim of his own genius. Having worked the voodoo on himself, he has no means of reversing it, and while trying desperately to find a cure he has to cope with the hostility of his fellow men, who fear him as they would fear anything unknown. Even on a more mundane level he finds invisibility not all it's cracked up to be; you may be able to play all kinds of pranks on other people but you can't stop them from bumping into you, and it's painful. Progressively embittered, he plans to use his powers to achieve universal domination (today West Sussex, tomorrow the world!) and thereby to avenge himself on all who ever slighted him, notably the girl who turned him down in college and the plodding fellow student who had the impudence to marry her. In a program note, O'Brien claims to have added to the novel by making Griffin a working-class prodigy whose prickly arrogance got him banished, first from his school debating society and then from the school. Not having read the book, I take his word for that. But judging from the program note (by a Wellsian scholar, Nicholas Ruddick), most of the vital elements were already in place, including Griffin's egomania, hubris and frank ambition to institute a reign of invisible terror. Also, apparently, a mixture of styles that O'Brien has all too faithfully reproduced. It may have worked on the page, but the stage version swings clumsily between broad farce (never Munro's strongest suit as a director), portentously crude psychology with a dash of politics and plodding detective fiction. It's especially bad when the wires cross. The invisible man's chief adversaries are a quartet of yokels who spend most of their time huddled together in the alehouse snuggery. (This may partly explain the lifelessness of their acting. They barely have room to breathe.) Later on, when the full force of the law is turned on Griffin, these fellows are at the head of the chase. It's hard to get a thrill from a manhunt when the principal hunters are village idiots.

I said the acting didn't matter, but I lied. Acting always matters; and if the play drags the actors down, the actors do it to the audience. The only specks of conviction come from Wendy Thatcher as the pub proprietress, when she isn't either mumbling or gabbling; from Neil Barclay, in a few moments of good, clean camp; from Bernard Behrens, who has all of two minutes on stage and uses them; and from Jeff Meadows, who as virtuous hero and all-around straight man, makes a decent show of being decent. The invisible himself is Peter Krantz, who whether playing the tormentor or the tormented, seems to have checked in his personality along with his corporeal being. To be fair, the script does manage a neat twist at the end, the kind that's just predictable enough to be satisfying.

- In repertory until October 29. 1-800-511-SHAW

2006-06-01-separating-the-men-from-the-b:
CORIOLANUS

Festival Theatre, Stratford

- - -

Shakespeare's Coriolanus hates being called a boy, though his enemies have good reason for doing it to him. For a man with a large and unashamed expanse of bald, shiny dome, Colm Feores Coriolanus makes a remarkably convincing boy. The boyishness is psychological rather than physical. This least empathetic of heroes is an invincible Roman soldier -- a human war-machine -- who despises anyone not born into the officer-class and reserves especial venom for the poorer and hungrier of his non-combatant fellow citizens. They in turn divide our sympathies by being both fickle and shrewd. They certainly have the protagonists number; right at the start they attribute his military exploits to his wanting to please his mother and to be proud. (I didn't actually hear them do it. A chapter of accidents made me miss the first couple of scenes of the Stratford Festival's opening production, but I cannot imagine that these vital lines were cut.)

Feores Coriolanus actually -- and accurately -- combines intolerable arrogance with agonizing modesty. His body language comes in two dialects. Upright and unforgiving on the battlefield -- which can include his native senate-house when people disagree with him -- he goes gawky, gangly and weak-at-the-knees when obliged to listen to speeches in his honour. (What he says, roughly paraphrased, is "I was just doing my job.") He also, unlike some Coriolani I have seen, has a sense of humour, though its a very circumscribed one. When forced to put on a ragged gown to solicit popular votes for the consulship, he feels as ridiculous as he looks, and he turns the joke against himself but also savagely against the people. Most of his playfulness, though, is reserved for his mother Volumnia, the controlling matron who made him what he is. She is as arrogant as he, but unlike him she has the instincts of a politician. (It's currently tempting to liken Coriolanus to Stephen Harper, but it's impossible to imagine him belonging to a party, let alone leading one. He may be aloof , but he isnt ideological about it.) She knows, as he doesnt, how to temporize; and when she tries to get him to do it, it puzzles him. For her part, though her pride in him is absolutely genuine, she enjoys her power over him; indeed, in Martha Henry's performance, she revels in it. And since mother and son have been playing these games for years, there is a shared joy in their mutual dependence.

The crisis comes when Coriolanus, banished from Rome, makes common cause with the national enemy and marches back to destroy the city. All pleas for mercy fail, until his family is sent to plead with him. And Volumnia gets through to him by appealing not, as earlier supplicants have done, to his pity, but by making him feel on some level ridiculous, like a helpless child. She doesn't, in this performance, seem to care that much about Rome, but she cant stand her sons disobedience to her. And he can't stand disappointing her. In breaking him down she, knowingly or not, signs his death warrant. She also, drawing on her last maternal reserves, exhausts herself, spiritually as much as physically. Whatever the reason, at her last supposedly triumphal appearance she's shaking like a leaf. Its the most powerful moment in the play.

Nothing Feore does quite matches it. His characterization is outstandingly lucid and intelligent, and his classical chops are in excellent shape. He is fine in moments of lip-curling irony; hear him repeat the words must and "shall," as if incredulous that anyone should have the impertinence to make such demands on him; fine too in moments of prophecy since this Coriolanus, once banished, does to a certain extent grow up, developing a wry sense of fatality. Its the moments of regression that lack their proper scale; the outbursts of volcanic rage, fuelled by pride and heedless of danger, that breach all dams and bring, in inexorable succession, disgrace and exile and death. Maybe Feore really is too mature an actor to play this boy. I don't mean he's too old. I mean hes too watchful.

Antoni Cimolinos production achieves the same partial success as its hero. It conveys a sense of history on the move -- moving fast too, with one scene merging seamlessly into the next on a Festival stage reduced to its barest and most satisfying essentials. Crowds look good on it and solitary figures look even better, with help from Gil Wechsler's lighting and from Santo Loquasto's costumes, which have an original, sculptural line. There is also a fair, or unfair, amount of generalized hubbub; relationships are well stated, but they dont put down roots. This is especially true of the heros protracted dance with Aufidius, his rival, ally and nemesis; and especially frustrating since Graham Abbey, making clearest sense of some of the most convoluted passages in Shakespeare, sounds ready for anything. Paul Soles is ingratiating as the wily old Menenius, and especially fine in his mixture of pique and pain when his errand of mercy is slighted. Robert King stands out as the toughest and wittiest of the Roman crowd as do a pair of senate officers, for similar reasons, and another pair of enemy sentries. Best of all the supports is Bernard Hopkins as the oilier and more articulate of the two demagogues who engineer the hero's enforced exit and get bitten by it. He and the title character barely deign to speak to one another, but there's a real current between them and between the things they stand for.

- In repertory until Sept. 23. 1-800-567-1600

2006-06-02-a-hinton-what-s-to-come-in-th:
NAC's artistic director returns to Stratford with contrasting pieces

Peter Hinton used to think that the essence of theatre lay in acting, so he became an actor. Later he thought that it might reside in directing, so he started to direct. Later still he decided that the most important thing was writing, so he began to write plays. He has kept the latter two talents running in tandem, and they've established this soft-spoken man as one of the most provocative talents in the Canadian theatre, an Anglophone in an artist-showman mould we more usually associate with Quebec.

His playwrighting debut was maybe the most elaborate ever seen on a major Canadian stage: The Swanne, a fantastical-historical- allegorical trilogy about events leading up to the accession to the British throne of the young Queen Victoria, told largely from Hinton's highly individual version of Victoria's own point of view. It took him a decade to write. Quite apart from the research involved, it took him, he told me with a laugh, "10 years to learn how to write." It was staged over three years -- 2001 to 2004 -- at the Stratford Festival, and he directed it himself. "Writing," he says, "is about creating problems. Directing is about solving them." He had to solve mountainous problems of his own creation, and he did it spectacularly well. He returned to Stratford last year with a darkly imaginative production of the musical Into the Woods, and he's back again this season in both his capacities. He directs John Webster's The Duchess of Malfi (opening today), a Jacobean tragedy whose luxuriant excesses should suit him perfectly, and he also stages a contrastingly modest piece of his own, Fanny Kemble, a solo piece, starring Domini Blythe, about a pioneering 19th-century actress.

And if that's not enough, he's also the newly appointed artistic director of the English theatre company at the National Arts Centre in Ottawa, with a self-imposed mission to take the "national" part of that title seriously -- not in the sense of doing every kind of play, or being all things to all people, but of, in his words, "encouraging artists across the country, from British Columbia to Halifax." He wants to attach Canadian writers, including First- Nations writers, to his companies; make co-productions with other companies "an absolute boon;" and give a big central space to "Canadian theatre groups that are lauded around the world but are relegated here to 200- or 300-seat houses." His first season, starting this fall, will consist, almost unprecedentedly for a major residential theatre, entirely of new Canadian work. In his second he's focusing on the classics. And working towards that, he has a workshop program planned for the end of this year exploring the neglected plays of Shakespeare's predecessors, contemporaries and successors. Which brings us back to The Duchess of Malfi.

A baroque play, I suggested, using the term rather loosely to suggest something unruly and extravagant, but Hinton went along with it. "I love the Jacobean theatre. It's high theatre -- high horror - - that still demands great emotional truth from the actors. We've talked a lot in rehearsal about not going either over the top or under the top: about how to keep that razor-balance." As Jacobean plays go, The Duchess ("an incredible play," Hinton says, as directors do) isn't all that neglected. It's been done at Stratford once before, in 1971, in a legendary production by the late Jean Gascon. It was, Hinton notes, "the first play performed by Shakespeare's own company after his death," and they did it not in the open-air Globe but at the roofed-in Blackfriars -- a theatre "with 400 or 500 seats, roughly the same as the Tom Patterson," which is where the new Stratford production is happening. And Webster took full advantage of his setting and of its technology; some of the greatest and most terrible scenes happen in the dark as, in a metaphysical sense, does the whole play. Hinton has a cast of old Stratford hands, headed by Lucy Peacock (Richard Monette, Stratford's artistic director, has long thought of the play as a possible vehicle for her) as the widowed Italian duchess who incurs the wrath of her brothers, a duke and a cardinal, by marrying beneath her, and is tortured -- more mentally than physically -- and eventually murdered for it. "It's wonderful," Hinton says, "to look at the play with actors who know their Shakespeare. They keep saying, 'This is just like Shakespeare,' then they run up against something that's quite unlike him.

"In Shakespeare, when you get a couplet at the end of a scene, it sums up and reinforces what has gone before. In Webster, the couplet actually increases the complexity of the scene." The style is unpredictable: "Characters jump from verse to prose, with no reference to their social status. The play is full of ambiguities." We sympathize with the Duchess, obviously, but Hinton also links her to the Jacobean genre of the "lusty widow," women sexually experienced and financially independent, regarded by authors and audiences with as much nervousness as admiration. They're rebels. ("The Duchess," Hinton notes, "has huge issues with God.") The character we most identify with is the nominal villain, ex-galley- slave Bosola, the Cardinal's hit man and fall guy who kills the Duchess and spends the rest of the play trying to avenge her. "Webster has the ability to make us like people who are so evil." Even Ferdinand, the Duchess's ducal brother. whose sadism can only be motivated by incestuous passion, "is in such pain, you feel for him." The mystery is in the characterization rather than the narrative. "So often in a new play a playwright will want to withhold a great secret. Webster lays it all out immediately." Hence the galloping excitement with which these plays begin, and which the best of them maintain.

In that sense they connect with Hinton's own teeming achievement in The Swanne, though he says -- suprisingly, but persuasively -- that his own play has "a more gentle heart; it's more Dickensian." Webster presents us with a cruel world that's morally in free fall. It feels -- as people have been saying for 400 years -- very modern.

robertcushman@lycos.com

2006-06-07-legends-of-the-falstaff:
HENRY IV PART ONE

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

- - -

After 13 years running Stratford, Richard Monette remains underrated as a director of Shakespeare. He isn't a purveyor of grand concepts, but you can usually keep those anyway. Few in Canada are as good as he at animating both a stage and a text. Henry IV Part One is a great play that can get off to a very bad start, opening as it does with an expository royal council scene -- all names and nobles and bulletins from the battlefield -- that could be an unconscious parody of the entire history play genre. It's transformed here by showing us Henry, the would-be crusader king, taking the sacrament before buckling down to worldly affairs. He switches instantly, in Scott Wentworth's sonorous and penetrating performance, from earnest and devout to calculating and suspicious, the two moods infected by one guilty conscience. It poisons his mind against his son Prince Hal, and also against Hal's opposite number, the rebel Harry Hotspur, whom, Henry shamefacedly admits, he prefers. The admission here is at once so wistful and so emphatic that it gets a laugh, surprising and satisfying.

The great insight of Monette's production is that the play does not exist in watertight compartments marked "comic" (prose, Falstaff) and "serious" (verse, everyone with a title); both halves are both. Good classic juveniles don't come along every week, or even every year, and Adam O'Byrne, the gangling, impetuous youth who plays Hotspur, is a revelation. We laugh at him, sympathetically, in his first scene where the efforts of his elders to involve him in some serious conspiring are frustrated by his inability to keep his tongue off his own grievances. Everything they say sets him off on some new tangent. I've waited for decades to see the humour in this scene released; here it finally is, in torrents. We laugh with Hotspur when, with unflagging accuracy, he makes deflationary fun of his grandiloquent ally Glendower (Raymond O'Neill). There's a deadly point to the frivolity: We've just seen these men down on their hands and knees, poring over an outsized map of England, squabbling as to how they'll carve up the land. It's called counting your chickens. It's also called a terrible "look-out" for the country if they win. None of this makes O'Byrne's Hotspur any less gallant or, to those he loves, loving. Slain by Hal in single combat, he dies a great death; his adversary holds on to him so that he delivers his last words on his feet, a great improvement on the traditional speech from the floor.

It's a famous irony that Hotspur, who hates poetry, consistently delivers the most ringing verse in the play. Less noted is that he, who contemptuously calls Hal "the merry madcap Prince of Wales," is actually the more madcap of the two. Hal, the part-time pub- crawler, uses frivolity while Hotspur lets it use him. David Snelgrove gets Hal's earnest opportunism well enough; indeed, he touches most of the character's bases. But he strikes few sparks off them, and his return to his father -- the turning-point -- goes for nothing. As for his surrogate father, James Blendick gives Falstaff a fruity voice, a gentlemanly demeanour and, courtesy of wardrobe, an imposing belly, all as you would expect. There is little excitement here, but at least what there is comes in key places: The disparaging speech about honour, the tall story of the 11 buckram men grown out of two and the tavern masquerade in which Falstaff and Hal alternate the roles of king and prince. Blendick delivers a flavoursome impersonation of Wentworth's mournful monarch and there is an overall sense of the characters' worlds about to collide and disintegrate. The lesser rogues are more diverse than usual: Gadshill (Keith Dinicol), an imitation Falstaff with an eyepatch, Bardolph (Barry MacGregor), liquored beyond human hearing, and even the shadowy Peto (Tim MacDonald), given some identity as an eager apprentice.

There are also some things I could do without. The Shakespearean effect I most hope never to see again is the one in which a group of plotters freeze in their conversation while a troop of hostiles crosses the stage, and then start up again at exactly the same volume. Or any volume. I would also like some day to see people entering a tavern without laughing uproariously and then making a literal song-and-dance about it. And there are some things I missed: Falstaff, in defiance of a hallowed stage direction, is denied the chance to strike a blow or two before running away like his fellow highway-robbers. But the robbery itself is delightfully staged, the thieves parading by like pious pilgrims before beating up the travellers. And if you think that disguise is mean, you should see what happens in the real battle, the king dressing his nobles up in his own colours so they will attract the death-wounds intended for him. I've never seen this deception so graphically illustrated before. And this king is really pious.

- In repertory until September 24. 1-800-567-1600

2006-06-07-please-sir-may-i-have-some-me:
OLIVER!

Festival Theatre, Stratford

- - -

It's tempting to imagine a really dark production of Oliver!, one that would put the twist back into Oliver Twist. Dickens novel is, after all, one of the most horrific in the language, a non-stop chronicle of crime and child-abuse, and Lionel Barts epic crowd- pleaser of a musical can't altogether prevent cheerlessness from breaking in; at times it even seems to welcome it. Not for long, admittedly, and even the most determinedly misanthropic director would probably be defeated by the change of gear halfway through the first act, when the show goes merrily ahead into streets-of-London- type overdrive. But we can still continue to dream and, up until that point and in a few places later, Donna Feore's Stratford production allows us our nightmares.

We certainly believe in the starving workhouse children of the opening, even if an inappropriately festive bout of ring around the rosey interrupts their otherwise-unimpeachable yearning for Food, Glorious Food. Olivers fateful asking for more is accorded full dramatic value, as is his grotesque enslavement to the local undertaker; though its a shame, when a funeral procession makes a spectral appearance at the corners of the stage, that it isn't made clear that it's a childs coffin theyre following.

Terror can co-exist with comedy; it generally does in Dickens. Bruce Dow's Mr. Bumble and Mary Ellen Mahoney's Widow Corney, complacent and commanding, respectively, are splendidly matched, first in song, then in marriage. Equally effective, on a smaller scale, is Kyle Blair as Noah Claypole, the undertakers sneak who may be the nastiest piece of work in the entire story. Oliver himself is splendidly played, and soaringly sung, by Tyler Pearse, a nine-year-old who seems completely unfazed by the instant transitions hes required to make from terror to defiance to all- around wholesomeness. The designer, Santo Loquasto, sets the mood with a giant, threatening drop-curtain and reinforces it with a giant, threatening and very mobile bridge.

Around, above and underneath it the director mounts an admirably stage-filling production, though her choreography as the show goes into cockney knees-up mode and declines into a stock succession of kicks and twirls. The optimistic choral reprise of Oliver's Who Will Buy is devalued when the entire urban population reappears in gleaming white so that we'll know how happy theyre all feeling.

The song itself, though, is an especially felicitous example of Barts capacity for speaking showbiz like a native; he makes us believe in simplified emotions by believing them himself. He can give Bill Sikes a stock "I am a villain" song that still offers the actor the chance of something more: A chance here seized upon by Brad Rudy who, in taking it quietly, makes it sound genuinely psychopathic. He can give Nancy (here clad, as in all productions, in hot traditional harlot's red) the infectious It's a Fine Life, which seduces us with its swing and snap, and then throw it back at us, an act later, as a surprisingly grim and complex trio. He can also write Nancy what must count, I suppose, as one of the great bad songs, As Long As He Needs Me. It really is bad: One musical phrase endlessly repeated, though fitted out with a different lyrical cliche every time. But it always stops the show, and Blythe Wilson gives it the appropriate, lung-bursting treatment. She makes nothing of her dialogue, though, and even in her songs falls into the classic error of talking lines she could be singing, as if this made them funnier or more affecting. Outside of patter songs, it never does.

Barts greatest liberty, of course, was to turn Fagin, the crafty, cringing devil whom Dickens habitually dubs the Jew and who in the novel prompts Sikes to murder, into a lovable old rogue who wouldnt hurt a fly. It's sentimental, it's shameless and its wonderful. And it is so because its true to the book -- if not to what Dickens put into it, then to what generations of readers have taken out. We all screen out Fagin's monstrosity and remember his charm and his humour. It's like My Fair Lady reclaiming the romance in Pygmalion. And Bart, East End Jewish himself, connects with his own roots by making the comedy ethnically idiomatic ("so at my time of life I should start turning over new leaves?") as the original never did. Through that, he achieves a comic richness both of characterization and, to coin a word, performability. Colm Feore revels in both, whether lurking at the edge of the crowd, leaping into its centre or leaving it behind to explode all over the stage, physically and vocally, in his showpiece Reviewing the Situation. Like most Fagins nowadays, he plays down the racial aspect, at least until his last moment, when he plonks his hat on his head, turns upstage and exits into the sunset. Feore's Coriolanus, the evening before, had ended on a funeral pyre. That makes two nights in a row that this actor has gone out in a blaze of glory.

- In repertory until October 29. 1-800-567-1600

2006-06-08-meet-the-transparents:
THE GLASS MENAGERIE

Avon Theatre, Stratford

- - -

Did you take in the Century of Progress? the Gentleman Caller asks the crippled, and cripplingly shy, Laura Wingfield. Laura didn't; nor is she ever likely to. The whole concept represented in the name of that exhibition, the idea that so excites her brash, well-meaning visitor, has passed her by. As, to a lesser extent, it has forsaken her mother, Amanda, the former Southern belle, reduced in late 1930s St. Louis to selling subscriptions for the Ladies Home Companion. As for son and brother Tom, the aspiring writer who is the plays narrator and its only other character, he's torn: Aware of the present ("Guernica!"), straining towards the future, lured by the past. Though of course, since, as he tells us, the play is memory, it's all the past, including the future.

Miles Potters production of Tennessee Wiliams The Glass Menagerie faithfully incorporates all the atmospherics that the author specified, but it's still the hardest-edged, least wispy memory-play imaginable. It's hypnotically gripping, every moment charged; the first night held the auditorium in a pin-drop silence broken only by a laughter that was surprisingly strong and frequent. Most of it was raised by Seana McKenna, whose Amanda is bracingly efficient and startlingly devoid of nostalgia. When she harks back to the gallant days of her youth she does, indeed, note the decline in manners and in her own level of comfort (her current apartment, as designed by Peter Hartwell, is uncompromisingly shabby). But she takes it as the way of the world; she certainly doesnt wallow. This is much at odds with all the fragile, flighty Amandas one has seen or read about, but there isnt a moment at which you can catch McKenna playing against the text. So maybe the legend is wrong; maybe we've been confusing Amanda with that other early Williams heroine, Blanche DuBois, who trumpeted her Dixie upbringing as the repository of higher values. Then again, maybe Blanche herself wasn't quite as breakable as weve liked to think. Williams himself said that she would never run short of kindly male strangers to depend on.

Something is lost, though -- not so much in the character of Amanda as in the knock-on effect on the fugitive Tom. Instead of fleeing from a smothering mother and all she represents, hes merely escaping a strong, nagging woman to whom he can give as good as he gets. Steven Sutcliffe plays him excellently, with delicacy and shamefaced wit and the occasional biting outburst of frustrated anger. There is excess baggage on this character, and I think it's the author's fault. Tom admits that memory -- a metaphor, I suppose, for the dramatists art -- makes him an unreliable narrator, but we have nothing against which to measure his unreliability. The play is rooted in autobiography, but an audience can hardly be expected to come to the theatre primed with the facts of the authors life. Certainly the original audience couldn't have done so; in 1945, when the play was premiered, Williams was new and unknown; he wasn't Eugene ONeill, rounding off a career as Americas top playwright by dishing the dirt on his family. It has to be Tom Wingfield's memory we're concerned with, not that of Tennessee Williams. And since this Tom doesnt have much reality outside of his role as chorus, theres something frustratingly circular and closed-in about the process. To put it another way, Tom acts as if the play's about him, but the dramatic facts don't bear him out.

He talks as if its about Laura. The last, legendary epiphanic line is directed at her, or at the memory of her: "Blow out your candles, Laura." Oddly, though, we dont see very much of her in the earlier parts of the play; we spend more time hearing about her family's worries about her, her with her collection of glass animals and her obsessive playing of the Victrola. But we do finally get to her scene with the Gentleman Caller, one of the most pitch-perfect duets in modern drama, a wonderfully tactful presentation of tactlessness. Matthew MacFadzean, stocky and crew-cut, is the breathing image of the former sports hero, current apostle of progress and self-confessed "stumble John." He is genuinely admiring of Laura, wanting to help, stirred into kissing her, then admitting he's engaged, and breaking her glass unicorn and also her heart. Only maybe he doesnt; maybe he only breaks ours. As Sara Topham plays her, Laura is hurt, but not beyond healing; her protestations that it really doesnt matter ring unexpectedly true. It's surprising, because earlier she's veered towards the historical reality of the authors sister, who spent most of her adult life in a mental institution. But she now emerges as her mothers daughter: a possible survivor. And McKenna, dropping the last trace of Amanda's affectations in angry, selfless concern, helps make it moving. Our knowledge of what really happened does, I must admit, add to the poignancy, just as Tom's protestations that he isnt a drunk take on an added sour dimension by our awareness of how much Tennessee himself became capable of putting away. This is having it both ways, but as the possibility is there we may as well take advantage of it. Its a relief, overall, to see Williams rescued from the sentimental swamps, and a treat to see the rescue so immaculately performed.

- In repertory until October 22.

2006-06-08-ye-olde-curiosity-fop:
LONDON ASSURANCE

Avon Theatre, Stratford

- - -

Designers dont usually take curtain-calls, but the Stratford first night of London Assurance presented a special case. Desmond Heeley, one of Stratford's (and London's and New Yorks) finest, was celebrating his 75th birthday. He had also done a bang-up job on this particular show, an early Victorian piece in the grand English tradition of comedy of manners. It moves from the house of a metropolitan swell to a rambling country estate, glimpsed both inside and out. Heeley evokes both locations with his characteristic blend of the sumptuous and the airy. His costumes, similarly, range from the comfortably homely to the eye-poppingly fantastic. It was good to have a chance to applaud him.

Unfortunately, there really isnt too much else to applaud. But - - keeping for a moment to the good stuff, and still on the subject of curtain-calls -- Brian Bedford, who both directs and plays the leading role, seems already to be taking one at his very first appearance. That is not a criticism. The character he plays, Sir Harcourt Courtly -- an ageing buck left over from the age of Beau Brummell -- has lived his life on the assumption that his mere physical being is God's gift to men, and especially to women. To preen and to pose are as natural to him as breathing. Probably more natural, given the tightness of the stays into which he must lace himself to preserve his figure as he advances in age. That's not even to mention the weight of the rouge, the powder and the monstrous black wig he has to carry, or the waistcoats that include a plum-coloured creation whose fruitiness you can practically taste.

Dion Boucicault, the young playwright who had a first-time hit with this play in 1841 and went on to many others in a variety of veins, puts Sir Harcourt through some time-honoured hoops. Basically, he takes the mans urban self-satisfaction (or London assurance) and exposes it to shocks. Its bad enough that, wooing an 18-year old for her money, he has to journey into the wilds; once there, he is confronted by his own son, who insists so emphatically that he is somebody else that his father is compelled to believe him. Bedford plays gorgeous variations on a single theme of nose- wrinkling incredulity. His technical virtuosity is, as usual, kept strictly within the parameters set by the play. He also plays the man's decency; unlike some of his Restoration ancestors, Sir Harcourt is vain but not vicious. When made a fool of, by himself or others, he knows how to climb down. He ends the play with a heartfelt assertion of the true nature of a gentleman and does it, for all his previous absurdity, beautifully. Has anybody ever thought of casting Bedford as Falstaff?

If the character goes, in the end, for less than he should, that's because Bedford the director hasnt provided Bedford the actor with much of a context. Apart from the star, the designs and a handful of sterling supports, this is a sad affair in which the disciplined self-awareness of the central performance has notably failed to trickle down to the majority of the unwashed. A variety of servants, tricksters and pretenders are misplayed by actors who all but wink at the audience while going through some laborious routines. The idea may be to acknowledge that they are actors playing stock roles in a stock play, but conscious artifice needs far more rigour than this and it sells this particular play short. To take the worst -- because most prominent -- example: Sean Arbuckle, the excellent Worcester of Henry IV, gets no handle on Dazzle, a sponger from nowhere, who cascades through the play on sheer self-confidence until someone at the end speaks for us all by asking "who is Mr. Dazzle?" The moment is a send-up in itself, a comment on all the unaccountable dandies who populate period comedies. Boucicault was a shrewd operator, a man who here plundered all his predecessors back to Shakespeare (and was to be quarried in turn by The Importance of Being Earnest) while creating something warm but unsentimental of his own. It seems here like a bad play, a mere collection of familiar intrigues; a shock, too, for anyone old and lucky enough to have seen the crack Royal Shakespeare Company production (it once played Toronto) that rediscovered it and to which Bedford himself plays generous tribute in the program.

The consolation prizes include a pleasant pair of lovers: Sara Topham as one of the plays real inspirations, a bespectacled bookworm who thinks she has no illusions about romance; and Adam O'Byrne as her sheepish suitor, whose multiple identities confuse even him. More emphatically --much more emphatically -- Seana McKenna is all top-hole and tally-ho as Lady Gay Spanker, a fox- hunting beauty who arouses Sir Harcourt's wayward passions even while the sheer outdoorsiness of her personality perplexes him to death. Even better, indeed with a touch of comic poetry as he ties himself up in verbal and emotional knots, is Brian Tree as her husband, Dolly, whom she treats as an adored household pet and who, after a brief fling at self-assertiveness, relapses contentedly into subservience. What do you know? A happy marriage.

- In repertory until October 21. 1-800-567-1600

2006-06-09-royal-lady-pulls-audience-ove:
THE DUCHESS OF MALFI

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

- - -

Anyone familiar with The Duchess of Malfi will grasp what I mean when I say that certain scenes in Peter Hinton's production are so dark you can't see your severed hand in front of your face. For those who aren't: John Webster's Jacobean tragedy concerns an Italian noblewoman, a young widow who incurs the murderous wrath of her brothers, a duke and a cardinal, by marrying a second time and marrying beneath her. They arrest her, imprison her and subject her to a prolonged regime of mental torture. This includes turning off the lights and placing the aforementioned hand in hers; showing her a waxworks exhibit of hanged bodies and telling her that they are the corpses of her husband and eldest son; and filling her room with the inmates of the local madhouse. Finally, they take pity on her and have her strangled, along with her waiting-woman and her two remaining infants.

In this magnificently atmospheric production, we don't see these two children, but we do see their tiny coffins afterwards. The sight brings home exactly what has been done. The garroting of the Duchess is carried out in merciless, efficient detail. The effect is horrific but it isn't sensational. It is what the story demands and no more. (A true story, by the way, or so the Jacobeans thought. It even gives a date, 1504. Did I mishear, or has the production changed the date to 1623, when the play was first published?) The same goes for the mad scene, filled with music and literally naked menace, and for the pitch blackness whose last descent is on the play's concluding massacre. The Duchess' death isn't the finish of the play; its last section finds her jailer and chief executioner, Bosola, an ex-galley slave with a discontented scholar's sensibility, repenting and seeking revenge on his employers. He succeeds, to the extent that they both die, but he also brings about his own death and that of Antonio, the Duchess' husband, whom he had hoped to save. It was, he says to the surviving courtiers, "such a mistake as I have seen in a play." It is, indeed, a farce that you don't laugh at. It's also, as Bosola himself knows, just.

Self-awareness runs through the play. T.S. Eliot's poem about the death-obsessed Webster who "saw the skull beneath the skin" is quoted in all the handbooks, but it may be more important that he heard the beating mind as well. Hinton's production, in black-and- silver designs by Carolyn M. Smith, is wonderfully alive to the sights of Webster's world; it is equally alive to the sounds, hauntingly assembled by Peter Hannan to reflect an author whose favourite image seems to have been the screech owl. The most important sounds, though, are the shifting moods of the text, the way in which passion, despair and metaphysical wit keep treading on one another's toes. This production knows when to roar, when to whisper, when to laugh, and when to be still. It is extraordinarily of a piece. The actors are white-faced, an effect that seemed intrusive in Hinton's production of Into the Woods, but works perfectly here. And he picks up superbly on details. The Duchess' invocation, in her farewell to Antonio, of the classical ferry across the River Styx inspires the staging of the whole scene in a boat crammed with aristocratic refugees. The Cardinal mentions a ghostly old woman who appears at moments of family doom; the text briefly supplies a gossipy old bawd: they are here combined into a living memento mori, sitting in wait for us as we enter the theatre.

About the only lapse in style is the scene after the Duchess' death when Bosola, a conscience waiting to happen, goads Ferdinand, the incestuously-driven Duke, into an awareness of what he has done, pushing him from the jealous edge of madness into the abyss. Both actors rant and rush it; the rhythm of the scene goes, so do the modulations, and so, incidentally, does the double cynicism of Bosola's demand to be paid and Ferdinand's crazed offer to buy him off with a pardon for the murder that he himself instigated. It's unfortunate, since this may be the greatest scene in the play, but it isn't destructive.

At any rate, Scott Wentworth's Bosola comes safely out the other side; sardonic, melancholy, mercurial, jovial and blisteringly honest, he is master of all the play's moods. None of the other performances matches his, except perhaps Laura Condolln's maid who goes biting and scratching to her death. Peter Donaldson's Cardinal is authoritative but hardly haunted; Paul Essiembre's Ferdinand is petulant rather than possessed; and Shane Carty's Antonio is just dull. He may suffer, though, from the director's conviction that the Duchess, even in love, is always the great lady, always in command. This unfortunately plays into the schoolmistressy side of Lucy Peacock's personality; this Duchess hardly seems to need a lover, let alone to marry one. She lacks mischief. She is very fine in captivity, rising above her persecutors, but she doesn't have much to rise from.

For once in my life, though, I can forgive individual performances for the sake of everyone's adherence to a magnificent conception (as opposed to a mere concept). Some things may be fainter than one would like, but nothing goes missing. Webster's plays, maybe more than those of any other playwright, demand that a production create a world. This one does, and right up to the ominous last-line coronation of the Duchess' and Antonio's surviving son -- who must be the youngest, smallest child ever allowed upon a professional stage -- it never lets go.

- The Duchess of Malfi runs at the Tom Patterson Theatre until Sept. 23. 1-800-567-1600

2006-06-10-everyone-is-racist-or-homopho:
robertcushman@lycos.com; Romance runs through June 10 at the Berkeley Street Theatre Upstairs, 416-368-3110

David Mamet's Romance -- a title for which I cannot supply even the most fanciful interpretation -- has acquired a reputation for being verbally unbuttoned even by Mamet's standards. One sits through its first, very entertaining, scene wondering exactly why. We are in a New York courtroom where a chiropractor (not, whatever the prosecution may say, a chiropodist) is on trial for some misdemeanour whose nature is never disclosed but that seems to involve a trip to Hawaii. The accused is an expert at deflecting or not seeming to understand any questions that are put to him, while the prosecuting and defending counsel are constantly at one another's throats over points of order. The judge, meanwhile, is rather out of it, since his hay-fever medicine makes him drowsy, which means he can't remember whether he's taken it or not, which means he takes more. He orders an adjournment.

This is vintage Mamet, all misunderstandings and misdirection and overlapping staccato dialogue, and also all male. It's given a new focus by the legal setting, which just about mandates verbal duels and purposeful obfuscation. It almost seems as if the former poet of junk shops and real-estate scams has found his ideal metier, even if the formal atmosphere means that the language has to stay uncharacteristically clean.

But then, as the defendant angrily confers with his mouthpiece who never wanted him to take the stand in the first place, things change. The chiropractor, we suddenly learn, is Jewish, and all of a sudden the lawyer is calling him on it. "You people," he says, "can't order a cheese sandwich without mentioning the Holocaust," to which his client smartly replies, "we people don't eat cheese sandwiches." He also starts insulting the lawyer's own faith -- "an Episcopalian? What's that, a Catholic with a Volvo?" -- and soon the two are exchanging every racist jibe and obscenity in the book. It may not be too plausible, not in these circumstances and on such slight acquaintance, but it's certainly funny and oddly liberating. Besides, we tell ourselves, Mamet is dealing with ugly essentials, not polite surfaces. And to prove that uptight prosecutors can be just as hypocritical as uptight defenders, he takes us into the home of this one, who turns out to be a closet queen with a live-in boyfriend who resents him for a) keeping their relationship secret; and b) burning a pot roast.

Here comes the wider angle. Out on the streets a peace march is - - well, whatever is the opposite of raging. "So many people," says the judge, whom the protest has delayed on his way to work, "but I suppose that's the nature of a parade." It's occasioned by the rare presence in town of an Arab-Israeli peace conference. This gives the defence an idea; the chiropractor will give peace a better chance by relaxing the delegates' spines. Will the judge grant permission? Who, given the stakes, could say no? Especially as his honour has switched to another medication, one that releases all his inhibitions. Under its influence he reveals that the judicial life ("sentencing people to death and having a reserved parking space") isn't always as cool as it looks. He wants to do the decent thing, whatever it is, though it leaks out that he himself has been an occasional child molester and golf-course anti-Semite.

Indeed everybody onstage turns out to be racist or homophobic or both. Somehow the question gets aired of whether Shakespeare was gay or Jewish. ("No Christian," says the chiropractor, conceivably speaking for his author, "could write that well.") The only group that everybody ostentatiously refuses to slam is Muslims. The joke about political correctness -- and sheer bloody fear -- has some truth, I suppose, but it comes across as very heavy-handed. Nor is the play much helped by a closing spate of far-fetched coincidences. Not that we're supposed to take them seriously, but the sudden switch from intellectual farce to narrative farce suggests desperation. Anyway, the point seems to be that if chaos and prejudice prevail even in a moderately well-intentioned courtroom, what hope can there be for the world? And so it proves.

A wise man once wrote that you can laugh and laugh and still leave unsatisfied, and so it is here. But that's better than leaving unsatisfied without having laughed. And if the targets here are obvious, the jokes are mostly good and occasionally inspired. The Toronto production, a maiden directing effort by Irene Poole, has great brio, with Don Allison giving an especially joyous performance as the judge. David Ferry has a devilishly innocent twinkle as the defendant, and as the opposing attorneys Paul Eves and Stewart Arnott are a right pair of professional barracudas, falling privately apart at the seams. Brendan Gall plays the houseboy for pique, which seems to be what's required. Christopher Stanton adds to the throng of licenced maniacs in a last-minute appearance as a doctor, and Steven Manuel is excellent as the court bailiff, one of those rewarding roles that starts as a solicitous functionary and then sprouts wings of its own. As he sits reading the sports pages while Jew and Christian hurl abuse at one another, you wonder what, if anything, is going on in his mind. It turns out something is, and it isn't comforting.

- - -

DEAD AIR!

Mysteriously Yours

2026 Yonge St. - 416-486-7469

The plot and characters of the new Mysteriously Yours show are the same as the plot and characters of all their previous shows. But this time there's a new wrinkle; this, as its subtitle says, is a musical murder mystery that sharpens the element of parody, here directed at old-time network radio presenting cowboy stars in things with titles like Withering Heights. (A Brontesaurus?) The songs are neat and all the cast have voices, including Jean Daigle doing his customary interactive turn as both corpse and sleuth. Indefinite run.

OLIVER!

Festival Theatre

Stratford - 1-800-567-1600

Donna Feore directs a stage-filling production of Lionel Bart's epic crowd-pleaser of a musical, one that even manages in its opening scenes, and sometimes later, to sneak in some of the nightmare atmophere of Dickens' original non-stop chronicle of crime and child abuse. Bart, whose genius was instinctive if short-lived, spoke showbiz like a native, resulting in a self-believing score in which even a rank bad song like As Long As He Needs Me sort of works. Colm Feore revels in Bart's comical Fagin; Tyler Pearse's Oliver is splendidly acted and sung; Bruce Dow and Mary Ellen Mahoney are perfectly matched workhouse tyrants. In rep through Oct. 29.

HENRY IV,

PART ONE

Tom Patterson Theatre

Stratford - 1-800-567-1600

Richard Monette's production understands that the prose and verse parts of this great play are equally comic and serious. Adam O'Byrne's gangling, impetuous Hotspur is an especial revelation, witty in himself and the cause of wit in others (to quote Part Two). Scott Wentworth's sonorous King is both calculating and devout, two faces sporting one guilty conscience. Falstaff and Hal are less exciting, but there are many vivid minor performances and some brilliant strokes of staging. In rep through Sept. 24.

THE HEIRESS

Royal George Theatre

Niagara-on-the-Lake

1-800-511-7429

Tara Rosling gives an extraordinary performance, rising to tragedy, as Henry James's shy, plain heroine. Mike Shara, smooth and gauche at the same time, is the suitor who tantalizingly may not be faking it. Taut direction by Joseph Ziegler, superb design by Christina Poddubiuk. In rep through Oct. 7.

10 DAYS ON EARTH

Berkeley Street Theatre

26 Berkeley St. - 416-368-3110

In Ronnie Burkett's new puppet-play, a mother's love is felt, overwhelmingly, through its forcible removal. Darrell, a 50-year- old mentally challenged man, is orphaned but doesn't know it. The effect is heartbreaking, though the supplementary material, despite Burkett's technical virtuosity, feels like padding. Through June 24.

ARMS AND THE MAN

Festival Theatre

Niagara-on-the-Lake

1-800-511-7429

Jackie Maxwell's production of Shaw's anti-romantic comedy is cute as a whole row of buttons; this has its charms but ends up selling the play short. Peter Hutt and Patrick Galligan give entertaining performances, but the exaggerated Balkan sets and costumes dominate the evening. In rep through Oct. 29.

HIGH SOCIETY

Festival Theatre

Niagara-on-the-Lake

1-800-511-7429

The show of the movie musical of the play (that was also a movie). It never worked, and this busy production is particularly coarse. The augmented Cole Porter score is made up not of songs the characters just have to sing but of songs it's not quite impossible they might; it's dehydrating. Dan Chameroy and the sets are good. In rep through Nov. 19.

THE LORD OF THE RINGS

Princess of Wales Theatre

300 King St. W. - 416-872-1212

At its best, it's wonderful; at its worst, it's far better than doubters ever thought it could be. Scenically and technically, it's a marvel; and the adaptation of Tolkien's trilogy is outstandingly intelligent. Indefinite run.

2006-06-12-a-disappointment-for-canadian:
Well, The Drowsy Chaperone won a lot of things -- more than any other musical this season -- but it didnt win the Best Musical Tony. That went to Jersey Boys, the jukebox musical about Frankie Valli and the Four Seasons. Jersey Boys, as brash as The Drowsy Chaperone is wide-eyed, arrived at the Tonys as joint favourite for Best Musical Award. Both, though, came in as underdogs, or at least as outsiders.

Jersey Boys ends with its four heroes being inducted into the Rock 'n' Roll Hall of Fame and affirming that because it comes from the people, this award counts for more than anything at the Oscars or the Emmys. They dont mention the Tonys. That could have been tact on the writers part. It could have been superstition. Either way, it seems to have paid off.

It, too, had a Canadian component in the shape of its director, Des McAnuff (well, Canadian-raised; he works out of California). He didn't win, but John Lloyd Young as Frankie Valli won for Best Actor in a Musical and Christian Hoff as his cohort Tony de Vito for Best Supporting Actor.

Those last two prizes were warning signs that the Chaperone, unlike in the show itself, was going to end up as the bridesmaid and not the bride. It was a disappointment for reasons that go beyond local pride and national history. It has to do with Bob Martin's starring role as the droll narrator identified in the program as Man in Chair, a rrole for which he had received a best actor nomination. "Theres a certain heart to the show -- people identify with the Man in Chair," said Martin, after picking up the Tony that he did win for Best Book of a Musical, at least partially on behalf of "that group of people who create musical-parodies in Toronto." Don McKellar, his co-author and co-winner, reinforced the point that the show, in effect, makes Canadians of the entire theatre audience. That is to say, all the people who sit at musicals, gawping at the glamour and wishing that life were more like them (the musicals, that is, not the people), find a surrogate in the onstage musical- theatre nerd who watches a show coming to life in front of him, and ends by becoming part of it.

The Chaperone did win for its writing, not just the book but for the score by Lisa Lambert and Greg Morrison. Casey Nicholaw, the shows U.S. director and choreographer, surprisingly failed to win in either category, but the piece's stylish look did get celebrated in prizes for sets (David Gallo) and costumes (Gregg Barnes). So both the show's Toronto origins and its New York makeover got recognition.

The national group that really cleaned up was the British, largely on account of one superb show. Alan Bennett's play The History Boys, in a National Theatre production, won its expected prizes for best play, best direction (Nicholas Hytner), best actor (Richard Griffiths), best supporting actress (Frances de la Tour) and best designer (Bob Crowley) while John Doyle won for best director of a musical for his barebones actors-as-musicians Sweeney Todd and Ian McDiarmid for best supporting performance in Faith Healer.

Otherwise, a richly deserved Lifetime Achievement Award went to Hal Prince, though no one thought to mention that two of this year's three Best Musical Revival nominees were Tony-award winning shows that he helped originate: The Pajama Game and Sweeney Todd.
2006-06-15-make-music-not-war:
SOUTH PACIFIC

Avon Theatre, Stratford

- - -

I find that, for a musical I don't much like, I like South Pacific quite a lot. From a distance, when Im listening to a cast album or remembering the movie or contemplating individual songs, it strikes me as the stodgiest and least amusing of the big four Rodgers and Hammerstein shows. But on the rare occasions when I get to see it on the stage, I am conquered by its craft and awed by its self- belief. Oscar Hammerstein and Joshua Logan, his collaborator on the book, welded three James Michener short stories into a seamless narrative about sailors and civilians waiting for their chapter of the Second World War to get started, and it sweeps you along. Richard Rodgers wrote his most ostentatiously romantic score - - every number is some kind of love song, or at least some kind of sex song -- and it wraps you up in the tapestry.

The shows particular glow was best described by the director and critic Harold Clurman in his review of the original 1949 production; he wrote that when Mary Martin as Nurse Nellie Forbush sang that she was in love with a wonderful guy, one murmured not "who cares?" but congratulations, congratulations, congratulations, to you both. Cynthia Dale, whose Nellie is the best thing she has done at Stratford, induces a similar response, getting right inside the poundingly happy tune without forcing a note. Nellie's role is unusually constructed, in that her two biggest numbers come practically back to back; A Wonderful Guy appears hot on the heels of the equally delightful I'm Gonna Wash That Man Right Outta My Hair, and acts as a counterweight to it. First comes the heroines declaration of independence to her friends in the showers; then, after shes dried off, her ecstatic recantation. We go on a small journey with her, and neither stage of it would work half as well without the other.

That trip is itself part of a longer one that Nellie takes in a show that's also a simplistic but powerful parable about culture shock and tolerance. Dale's role in last years Cat on a Hot Tin Roof may have been a stretch for her, but it bequeathed to her a pert Southern accent that sits beautifully on this musicals little girl from Little Rock, floored by the revelation that her French lover was formerly married to a Polynesian -- and has two small children to prove it. Nellie gets to sing other charming songs, like the sweetly raucous Honey Bun and the surprisingly tricky Cockeyed Optimist, but the emotional peak of Dale's performance isn't musical at all. It comes when she meets Liat, the bewildered native sweetheart of Joe Cable, the young lieutenant who has gone to his death with his "carefully taught" racism still unresolved, and takes the heartbroken girl in her arms. Its the moment in which Nellies own dam of prejudice finally bursts. In this production it's rather clumsily staged, but my throat still lumped.

If Nellie's numbers find Rogers and Hammerstein at their sprightliest, the solos for Emile de Becque, her middle-aged Gallic flame, find the team dusting off their funeral attire; the lament This Nearly Was Mine is stately, and the supposedly joyous Some Enchanted Evening positively elephantine. Out of context these songs bore me, but within it they work. Theodore Baerg sings Emile excellently, and if his acting tends to the stolid, its never offensively so. Laird Mackintosh, as Joe, also sings better than he talks, but since his big song is Younger than Springtime, which sits beautifully in the middle of the shows great divide, that's all right, too. Grace Chan is a good Bloody Mary, though she never reconciles the character's twin aspects of heartless bawd and hearty comic relief. Ive seen this musical described in reputable print as the teams funniest, but I find that baffling; the show's comedy is formulaic. It's a tribute to Bruce Dow that he finds as much in the role of Luther Billis, a Sergeant Bilko with a soft centre, as he does. Douglas Paraschuk supplies bamboo sets that are evocative, though less of the actual South Pacific than of the Hawaiian room at a theme hotel.

Both of this years Stratford musicals have been staged by director-choreographers, though neither show had even a choreographer-choreographer in its credits when it was new. Michael Lichtefeld keeps the action of South Pacific crisp and the steps plausible; when he stages jokey routines for the second act camp concert, they are such things a cast of imaginative amateurs might conceivably come up with. Did I say "camp" concert? When the male chorus sing Theres Nothin' Like a Dame, it's hard to take their itchy frustration seriously; after all, theyve got each other. Theres a larger problem, though not unrelated; except for a few moments of urgency from Brian McKay's tetchy Captain Brackett, there is little sense that there's a war on, a phoney war until half-way through Act Two, but still a war. Some film footage of planes taking off is too meagre, too late. Admittedly the writers dont give much to go on; admittedly, too, a recent London production that tried hard to fill in the gaps seemed, by most accounts, merely to be trying hard. There are one or two lines -- about the doubtful chances of war bringing a better world -- that ring uncomfortable bells, but theyre quickly forgotten. The show is a product of post- war confidence, though not of post-war complacency, and that is connected with a confidence about how to write musicals. It makes love better than it makes war, and its love story is honestly moving. In its time South Pacific was considered a daring show. It isn't that now, but it's still surprising.

- In repertory until Oct. 28. 1-800-567-1600

2006-06-15-yeah-well-our-actor-is-a-musi:
A couple of years ago there was a best musical Tony award race between the critically dismissed Thoroughly Modern Millie and the critically praised Urinetown. Millie won, because it was thought that it would be the more saleable title on the road, the word "title" being taken very literally in this case.

The word around New York before last Sunday's Tonys was that history was about to repeat itself with Jersey Boys, a tribute to Frankie Valli and The Four Seasons loaded with name-recognition, beating out The Drowsy Chaperone, a more salubrious title than Urinetown but even more mysterious -- and Canadian at that. And so it proved in the end.

Jersey Boys is a mainstream show, even though it claims not to be. And Chaperone is a show that thrives on oddity, even while purporting to celebrate the mainstream. The only thing the two shows have in common is that they make their audiences very happy.

Jersey Boys, to judge from the performance I saw the night before the Tonys, is playing to a largely local crowd that just happens to come from the next locality. The house was crammed with New Jersey citizens, cheering every local reference and getting to their feet not just after numbers but during them.

That doesn't mean that Jersey Boys wont travel. It probably will. The Four Seasons music is still a force, and the show has plenty of energy, though that isn't exactly a rarity on Broadway. But it isn't very good. Its a jukebox musical that tries hard to be something more.

Its hard to write about the music business without falling into cliche. Most of the time, the show is stuck with trying to relate pop songs, generalized by definition, to specific lives and situations. Even the great songs fall short. There's a real rush when the boys launch into their first big hit, Sherry, but it only lasts a moment. And so it goes with their succeeding masterpieces, Big Girls Don't Cry and Walk Like a Man, which follow on the stage even more rapidly than they did in real life. The songs are apparently judged too sacred to be turned into production numbers, so the actors just face front and sing them, with some barely relevant Pop Art drawings projected onto the unexcitingly ugly set as some kind of gesture towards visual interest.

They sing them well; but they cant compete. The excitement about these numbers in the pre-Beatles 60s was not just that they had better tunes than most doo-wop but that they were funny. Nick's solemn low notes, chiming in at grotesquely unexpected moments, were just as important as Frankie's high ones, and the show cant duplicate the effect.

Thats despite excellent vocalizing by John Lloyd Young (winner of best actor in a musical), who makes Frankie's character nearly as angelic as his voice; ironic that the real Valli should in later life have earned a regular role on The Sopranos, a show that casts something of a shadow over this one. That's especially the case with the would-be wise guy Tommy, excellently played by Christian Hoff (best featured actor in a musical) who has a great rapport with the audience.

Its not as great, though, as the one established in The Drowsy Chaperone by Bob Martin, who should have won best actor and who has the house totally under his control, in the way that only a shy person transformed by the lights can manage. This show isnt just narrated by Martin's character, Man in Chair; it's about him, and the show-within-the-show -- the imaginary 1928 musical comedy with the same title -- that he conjures into flesh-and-blood existence by playing its music is entertaining less in itself than in what it tells us about him. Its fun because he thinks it is; its not just a case of his enthusiasm being infectious, he is infectious. And somehow the book (by Martin himself and Don McKellar) keeps finding new ways of spinning out what is, on the face of it, a very slender conceit.

I've gone through stages with this show. I didn't see it, obviously, in its first incarnation as a wedding present to Martin and his bride Janet Van De Graaff; I wasnt invited. Nor did I see its first public outing on the Toronto Fringe. I did see the first full-length version at Theatre Passe Muraille, and hardly liked anything about it except Martin himself. I then saw Daniel Brooks rewritten, recast and delightfully absurd production at the Winter Garden, and was enchanted.

There have been further extensive revisions for the Broadway production, especially to the score; and though I wouldn't swear to it, I suspect that some of them have been for the worse. I certainly remember getting more pleasure in Toronto out of Greg Morrison's music and especially out of Lisa Lamberts lyrics. Or maybe its just that the Broadway production values make you expect more. Casey Nicholaw's direction and choreography are as stylish and inventive as could be wished; likewise David Gallo's sets and Gregg Barnes costumes. The performers are uniformly excellent; the only Tony went to Beth Leavel, who, in the title role that definitely isnt the lead, meets all the demands of being imperiously sozzled. But the star turn is definitely Sutton Foster, who goes through a full vocal, terpsichorean and acrobatic repertoire while protesting, I don't want to show off.

That's a great idea for a number. In fact, theyre mostly great ideas for numbers. But the songs themselves never reach the plateau graced by The Boy Friend or Dames at Sea, of being as good as the things theyre spoofing. Sometimes they don't even seem to know the rules; writers the show specifically invokes, for instance, would never have fallen back on invented words when faced with the need for a quadruple rhyme. Even the book sometimes falls short; the silliest musical of 1928 might well have let the boy lose the girl in the way shown here, but it would have found a more ingenious way of getting them together again. The numbers are intoxicating without being satisfying. But this bubbly at least means well. Like love, as described in the show's best lyric, it "would never purpose to offend." And in the end it isnt about the songs, its about the Man in Chair, who at one terrified moment denies that he likes musicals because he doesn't want the embarrassment of having to define his tastes, but in the end rises -- literally -- above it, gets swept away -- again literally -- by it. In a way they were right to deny Martin best actor in a musical.

What he actually is, is best actor as a musical.

- Jersey Boys is at the August Wilson Theater, New York, 212-239- 6200. The Drowsy Chaperone is at the Marquis Theater, New York, 212- 307-4100. Indefinite runs.
