2006-06-17-endings-droop-in-the-dust-sou:
robertcushman@lycos.com; The Importance of Being Earnest runs through Sept. 2 at the Young Centre, Distillery District, 416-866- 6666.

All of the characters in The Importance of Being Earnest are convinced that they are right. They may sometimes be checked by circumstance, but as far as they're concerned that's circumstance's fault. They go straight on in pursuit of their aims, be those aims marriage or money or muffins. This universal single-mindedness is what makes Oscar Wilde's comedy a farce: a farce of manners, one of a kind. It seems to be an extremely difficult quality for contemporary actors, bred on hesitation and ambiguity, to encompass. That impression is strongly reinforced by the new production from Soulpepper, which is shockingly below this company's standards.

The play was first staged in 1895, which also turned out to be the year of Wilde's downfall. Ben Barnes, the director here, has set it in the 1920s. This enables Patricia Fagan, whose Gwendolen is much the best performance, to look very fetching in a cloche hat. Otherwise the updating is at best irrelevant and at worst ridiculous. And before you accuse me of being an old reactionary who only wants to see Shakespeare done in doublet and hose: Few of Shakespeare's plays are tied to a specific time and place, and none of them to his own; they were born anachronistic. Plays that depict solid, identifiable societies -- which includes the majority of English comedies -- can be successfully transported, but only if the new setting connects in some way with the old.

Wilde's play depends on its characters' acceptance of rigid social and sexual conventions; the younger ones may find small ways of bending the rules, but they are still unquestioning parts of the system. Just 30 years later, this had changed; a world war helped. Youth rebelled and didn't care who knew it; anything went. To see the difference dramatically, look at Wilde's plays and look at Noel Coward's, with their flirtatious flappers. Wilde's young ladies are predatory but they are also demure, and the contrast is a large part of the humour. Samantha Espie's Cecily looks as if she would fit very nicely into a production of Hay Fever; she is hopelessly at sea in Earnest.

In fact, arguing this production's conception is almost beside the point, since the execution is so sloppy. John Gielgud once said that Earnest has almost too many funny lines. Well, that isn't a problem here. Even the wretched Shaw Festival production a couple of years ago got more laughs than this one does. It's tone-deaf; or perhaps I should say rhythm-deaf. Actors take breaths in the middle of lines, or let their endings droop in the dust, or come down heavily on the wrong words, or address their remarks to the wrong people or to no people at all. The cumulative effect of this is to make the play all but meaningless.

It's a structure of language (another thing that differentiates it from other farces), and poised, ornate language at that (another thing that makes it look out of place in the '20s, when casualness was all). It isn't just a collection of detachable epigrams; that aspect of the play can degenerate into a kind of nervous tic, but there isn't nearly as much of it as people think. The ceaseless verbal paradoxes create a world, an absurd one in which a tale of imaginary invalids and of babies left in handbags at railway stations becomes perfectly logical, but also a confining one in which the attempts to subvert the proprieties only testify to their overriding power. It's the world by which Wilde himself was shortly to be destroyed.

Obviously there's more to a successful production of Earnest than just getting the words right. They have to be turned into modes of communication between the actors, and this production does at least seem to have that in mind, especially in the scenes between Kevin Bundy's Jack Worthing and Damien Atkins' Algernon. Bundy, who usually plays losers, is happiest in the moments of frustration, of which Jack has more than any other character (i.e. he's the hero). Assurance is more of a stretch cfor him, but he shows signs of getting there, and in a better-orchestrated production he might actually arrive. Atkins' willowy Algy has the right attitude, as a young man obsessed with finding an appropriate verbal and physical pose, but he's the worst gabbler of the bunch. Fagan's Gwendolen, wielding pertness and preciousness as erotic weapons, is absolutely on the button in the first act, and though she loses focus later on she is, definitely, her mother's ruthless daughter.

As for mama herself, Nancy Palk's Lady Bracknell has the blessed abil- ity to deliver a long sentence without choking on it, and her censoriousness is beyond reproach. But she can't link it to a sense of unquestioned and unquestioning privilege, though she brought the trick off very handily in last year's Olympia. Like everyone else in this show she sounds, at some level, apologetic. (And her costumes don't let her take full advantage of her height; they seem to be showing off, rather than showing her off.) Nor do the other veterans supply as much as one would hope. The attraction between Canon Chasuble and Miss Prism is virtually non-existent. Oliver Dennis's canon does supply a nice sense of pedantic self-satisfaction; Brenda Robins seems, to judge from her wig and her teeth, to have taken Lady B's description of Prism as "a female of repellent aspect, remotely connected with education" excessively to heart. This, I think, is unnecessarily self-denying of her.

David Storch plays both the valet and the butler, and it says something that the production's most joyful moment comes when he peels off his moustache to change from one servant into the other. Maybe Barnes wants to destroy the play. That would explain Peter Hartwell's set, which wishes the same drab wallpaper on two separate rooms and, most bizarrely, a garden. It also incorporates two long, sliding library ladders that people keep climbing whatever the locale, which I suppose may count as a unifying device. Other props include a handbag too small to hold either a baby or a three-volume novel, and a cake stand that would seem ungenerous in 1895, 1929 or, if you go to the right hotel, 2006.

Random bursts of stylization that fall short of actual style (a recurrent problem at Soulpepper) include having Cecily, who should be talking to Algernon at the time, pick up a tennis racquet to hit imaginary balls while sound effects check in from the wings, and having Jack conduct his final search for the handbag onstage rather than off, thereby littering the floor with debris over which the actors have to pick their way to take their curtain calls. This supersedes what would otherwise have been the coup de grace: having the entire cast join in Jack's concluding line about having discovered the vital importance of being earnest. It isn't about them; it's about him. For the 100th time: There's no point in making fun of a farce. It got there first. Not getting this play right may be a misfortune; it happens to a lot of people. Getting it so insistently wrong looks like carelessness. Or that's the most optimistic interpretation.

Colm Feore's Coriolanus is outstandingly lucid and intelligent, his classical chops in excellent shape. He has two separate body languages for a hero who combines intolerable arrogance with agonizing modesty. 2006-06-19-a-lean-mean-meta-play-machine:
We have now had nearly a quarter of a century to decide whether The Real Thing, Tom Stoppards 1982 play about love among the playwrighting class, is the real thing. The jury, as far as I am concerned, is still out. The original London production and its New York remount left me disappointed that Stoppard should have settled for writing the kind of play that lesser dramatists write better. A revival in 1999, again in both cities, changed my mind completely; it was leaner, sexier, more passionate, far more moving and probably funnier. The new Soulpepper production, directed by Diana Leblanc, falls somewhere between the two. My admiration for the play remains largely intact, but some of my doubts have returned.

The play's central character is Henry, a playwright. Henry leaves his wife Charlotte, an actress, for Annie, another actress, currently married to Max, an actor. This is particularly messy because, when we first meet them all, Charlotte and Max are co- starring in Henry's latest West End play, the ironically titled House of Cards; I never thought to ask this before, but one thing Stoppard doesnt tell us is whether the double break-up meant that House of Cards had to fall early, or whether all concerned smiled gamely and went on taking the money. Anyway, Henry, who in the course of this play is dubbed "the last romantic," is devoted to Annie and to the idea -- no, the fact -- of being in love with her. She has equivalent feelings about him; but their ideas about what constitutes a trusting relationship, and especially about the importance or otherwise of sexual fidelity and the inevitability of jealousy, arent always in sync.

Henry has other passions. They include early '60s pop music, especially the Crystals and the Righteous Brothers, and the precise and rigorous use of the English language. He's enraged when people use it sloppily for political purposes. His pet example is a certain Private Brodie, a young Scots soldier arrested for trying to set fire to a monument as an anti-missile protest, and a favourite cause of Annies. While in jail Brodie writes a terrible play -- terrible by Henrys lights anyway -- and Henry, to please Annie, agrees to make it presentable. All these elements are juggled and cross- lighted to make an intriguing pattern.

We actually get to see a scene from House of Cards. But it isn't like a parody of your typical boulevard adultery play. It seems like a boulevard adultery play as it would be written by Tom Stoppard, and a very entertaining one, all badinage and reversals. The Real Thing itself isn't like that; theres only one joke that counts as vintage Stoppard. But, joking apart, all the characters talk as if theyre in a Stoppard play. They're unstoppably articulate, and that's a problem since this one, unlike his others, comes on as naturalistic.

Henrys later speeches about love as trust and dependence are very eloquent. Albert Schultz delivers them beautifully. Earlier on, his soft-spoken, soft-bearded Henry is less fluent and less convincing. That surface naturalism may have led him astray; in the plays most celebrated speech -- comparing an effective prose-style to a well-sprung cricket-bat -- one is conscious less of what the character is saying than of his effort to find the right persuasive words to say it. And there wouldn't be an effort; not on that subject, not for him.

Most damagingly, there is little chemistry between him and Megan Follows' Annie, and without that spark the play loses much of its emotional charge.

In a generally good cast, C. David Johnson is wonderful as Max, baffled and belligerent; dramatic geometry says he, as Henrys second wifes first husband, must loom large at the beginning and then disappear, and his absence seems a terrible deprivation.

- The Real Thing runs through July 29. Tickets: (416) 866-8666

2006-06-20-less-excess-spell-success:
There seems to be a rule, one more stringent than for any other Shakespeare play, that productions of Much Ado About Nothing may be set in any historical period other than the one in which it was written. The new Stratford version is set -- or rather costumed, since the stage itself is, for the most part, timelessly bare -- in 1910. That's unusually precise, but I know it's true because the program tells me so. Left to myself, I'd never have worked it out, but that's because I have no dress sense. "Edwardian" is about as close as I'd have got, and I can't even guarantee that.

So much for when. The next question is why. My first guess was that we're running out of periods for Much Ado and that this one hadn't been used yet. My second had to do with the presence in the play of soldiers, soldiers ostensibly from Spain but billeted in Italy, who treat war as something of a joke -- a joke that, only four years later, would have died beyond hope of resuscitation. And my third had to do with the character of Beatrice, the play's heroine, whom Lucy Peacock plays, very effectively, as a refugee from Bloomsbury with a talent -- or at least a taste -- for watercolouring. This immediately sets her apart as a commentator and observer, possibly a caustic one; it also enables Peter Donaldson as Benedick, her sparring-partner and destined mate, to get even further into her bad graces by absent-mindedly defacing one of her canvases. Tellingly, he isn't just embarrassed by this; he's terrified.

Seeing him manoeuvred into her favour, and seeing her welcome him there, are this production's chief pleasures, as they are the play's. Donaldson and Peacock play beautifully together. He is a bluff barker of a misogynist; Benedick says with an appealing mixture of pride and shame that he was "not born under a rhyming planet," and indeed he speaks barely a line of verse in the entire play. His medium is lightly cynical prose, arias often with a casual, self-deflating sting in their tail. Donaldson times these throwaways to perfection; the show has something in common with this season's Henry IV in that both can make us laugh anew at passages that were always meant to be funny but usually aren't.

Beatrice has an equivalent, and more celebrated, line about her natal planet: "A star danced and under that was I born." Peacock interprets it as a shaft of light in a surround of melancholy. That isn't especially original -- in fact, it's how it's generally done - - but she does it very well. Benedick says, more than half admiringly, that Beatrice is "possessed with a fury," and her love here is a refuge from anger. It's fitting that the two should come together when her fury burns hottest: when she has seen her young cousin Hero rejected at the altar by her betrothed, Claudio, and his friends. This whole church scene has been staged with unusual economy, and exceptionally well, and its aftermath finds Beatrice incensed at Claudio, at men in general and at Benedick, until he consents to share his anger. Which he does, giving himself power and dignity. She, in turn, comes to share his laughter, which was always there anyway. It's very satisfying. Shakespeare probably envisioned the couple as younger than this (though older than the innocent Hero and the callow Claudio,) but casting them mature is a good modern habit. You get actors with the wisdom and technique to carry the play off.

This production was originally directed by Stephen Ouimette; when he fell ill at the dress rehearsal stage it was taken over by Marti Maraden. Whoever did what, the result is one of the least showy -- but most entertaining and humane -- of recent Stratford Shakespeares. The plotters who engineer Benedick and Beatrice into discovering their love are suavely led by Shane Carty's Don Pedro, who also deals very tactfully with his encounter with the sad, funny old men (Gary Reineke and Paul Soles) whom he has temporarily robbed of a niece and daughter. The schemers, without even good intentions to recommend them, are captained by Wayne Best's Don John, whose opening stab at politeness makes the entire household visibly uncomfortable. Thom Marriott as the minor villain Borachio makes, especially in repentance, an indelible impression -- as this actor always does. Or nearly always; he's in the cast of London Assurance, but I didn't realize it until he turned up at the curtain-call.

Robert Persichini doesn't get much mileage out of Dogberry's malapropisms, but he succeeds -- with invaluable assistance from Bernard Hopkins as his partner Verges -- in the more important task of establishing the constable's unshakable complacency and making it endearing. My last bouquet goes to Jacob James, whose singing of ‘Sigh No More, Ladies’ is magical.

There seems to be a rule, one more stringent than for any other Shakespeare play, that productions of Much Ado About Nothing may be set in any historical period other than the one in which it was written. The new Stratford version is set -- or rather costumed, since the stage itself is, for the most part, timelessly bare -- in 1910. That's unusually precise, but I know its true because the program tells me so. Left to myself, Id never have worked it out, but that's because I have no dress sense. Edwardian is about as close as I'd have got, and I cant even guarantee that.

So much for when. The next question is why. My first guess was that were running out of periods for Much Ado and that this one hadn't been used yet. My second had to do with the presence in the play of soldiers, soldiers ostensibly from Spain but billeted in Italy, who treat war as something of a joke -- a joke that, only four years later, would have died beyond hope of resuscitation. And my third had to do with the character of Beatrice, the play's heroine, whom Lucy Peacock plays, very effectively, as a refugee from Bloomsbury with a talent -- or at least a taste -- for watercolouring. This immediately sets her apart as a commentator and observer, possibly a caustic one; it also enables Peter Donaldson as Benedick, her sparring-partner and destined mate, to get even further into her bad graces by absent-mindedly defacing one of her canvases. Tellingly, he isnt just embarrassed by this; hes terrified.

Seeing him manoeuvred into her favour, and seeing her welcome him there, are this production's chief pleasures, as they are the play's. Donaldson and Peacock play beautifully together. He is a bluff barker of a misogynist; Benedick says with an appealing mixture of pride and shame that he was "not born under a rhyming planet," and indeed he speaks barely a line of verse in the entire play. His medium is lightly cynical prose, arias often with a casual, self-deflating sting in their tail. Donaldson times these throwaways to perfection; the show has something in common with this seasons Henry IV in that both can make us laugh anew at passages that were always meant to be funny but usually arent.

Beatrice has an equivalent, and more celebrated, line about her natal planet: A star danced and under that was I born. Peacock interprets it as a shaft of light in a surround of melancholy. That isn't especially original -- in fact, it's how its generally done - - but she does it very well. 2006-06-29-closing-a-shock-but-not-a-sur:
Kevin Wallace, the British producer of The Lord of the Rings, blames the show's early Toronto demise on the critics. He may well be right. As he says, if youre being asked to shell out $120 for a theatre ticket, you need the affirmation." In this case the Toronto critics, or most of them, were decidedly non-affirmative.

Personally, I can plead not guilty. I liked the show. But Ive been in the opposite position too often to deny my colleagues their right to disagree. Nor do I think it's true that critics from outside Canada were uniformly more enthusiastic than the locals: The New York Times was vitriolic, and as for the London critics --well, it depends on who you read: The Times was enthusiastic, The Daily Telegraph the reverse. The Guardian was favourable, but I wrote that one so it probably doesn't count.

There were, I think, enough positive responses to have persuaded anyone who read all the reviews and judiciously compared them, that this was a show worth taking a chance on. But of course such people dont exist. Most rely either on the one paper they read or, more crucially, on a hunch, a general, undocumented sense that a particular show has been praised by everyone.

There are shows that prosper hugely no matter what the critics may have said. Some recent examples in Toronto are Beauty and the Beast, The Lion King and Mamma Mia. These are all shows for which the audience went into the theatre humming the tunes. The Lion King was an imaginative production, while the other two shows were deplorable, but it really didnt matter. Audiences went because they wanted more of the same.

The Lord of the Rings didn't have that advantage. It may have looked pre-sold; it was based on a hugely successful book that had been turned into three hugely successful movies. But those movies weren't musicals, so the show lacked a crucial element of built-in reassurance.

If people had trouble believing in the possibility of staged Tolkien, they had even more trouble crediting the idea of staged Tolkien with songs. What they did know about the book and the films were that they were long, and this made them nervous.

John Karastamatis, director of communications for Mirvish Productions, which presents the show in Toronto, said people would phone the box office asking if it were true the show lasted nine hours. The first preview actually lasted five; by the time of the official first night it was down to three and a half, but psychologically the damage had been done.

The closing in September is a shock but not a surprise. The shock is partly due to the announcements coming just two days after Torontos Dora awards, for which The Lord of the Rings had been nominated in a record 15 categories and won seven. Now, the Doras don't have anything like the commercial clout of the Tonys. Still, one doesn't envision the producers meeting the morning after and saying, "All those prizes; well have to close.

Obviously, the decision must have been taken earlier, and there have been mutterings of the shows departure for months, practically since it opened. In fact, according to Karastamatis, it hasn't been losing money. But neither, playing at 70% or 80% of capacity rather than the hoped-for 90%, has it been making enough to arouse confidence that it could run happily through the summer when audiences tend to dwindle. The final blow, ironically, was the announcement of the show's London opening next May at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane. The elaborate Toronto sets and machinery are being shipped to Britain, for extensive reworking. This will give the Canadian investors, who include the province of Ontario, a stake in the London production and even a chance to recoup their investment.

What does the shows Toronto failure mean to the Canadian theatre? Artistically, its sad and a blow to morale. We are losing an imaginative and adventurous production, which audiences, when they actually saw it, enjoyed. For the Mirvishes (who are the commercial theatre in Toronto), it must mean confirmation of the lesson already taught by the disappointing showings of The Producers and Hairspray: the days of the guaranteed hit musical with an open- ended run are over.

The pattern now will be to bring in touring productions for limited periods and bring them back if they take off. This is already happening with Wicked, and they must be hoping that it will happen again with Spamalot. This in turn means that the days in which Toronto was a city that Americans would visit just to see shows are gone. SARS and 9/11 put a dent in that, and the rise in the Canadian dollar and the increased tourist-friendliness of New York have reinforced it. The theatre may be an adjunct of our tourist industry, I doubt if it can ever be the basis of it.

To the other theatres and theatre companies in the city -- Soulpepper, CanStage, Tarragon and right on down the line -- it will make no practical difference at all. They're structured, rightly, to play to locals.

To most Canadian theatres outside Toronto, it will mean even less. The exceptions perhaps are the Stratford and Shaw festivals, which are dependent on tourists, especially Americans. But according to Antoni Cimilino, Stratford's executive director, people who are devoted to classical theatre, come every year, and may take in a whole week of plays.

But the end of The Lord of the Rings does cast what Tolkien's characters would call a shadow. It's psychological. As Cimilino says, We needed this to be a success, to shine a spotlight on our theatre."

2006-06-30-as-every-schoolboy-jokes:
THE HISTORY BOYS

Broadhurst Theatre, New York

Alan Bennett made his playwrighting debut around 1968 with a comic allegory of England's past and present, set in a boys' school and entitled Forty Years On. Forty years further on, he's back at school, and with comparable intentions. The History Boys was staged to acclaim at London's National Theatre and has now moved, with its original cast and production, to New York, where it has received more raves and just about every award available. It deserves all the praise and all the prizes.

Bennett focuses on a rite of passage that was built into the British education system until a few years ago. Bright teenagers would take their final state exams and then return to high school for a further term, one devoted to preparing them for university entrance. If they had their sights set on Oxford or Cambridge, the pressure was greatly increased; come December, they would have to travel to one of these institutions to take its individual set of entrance exams. (Less prestigious places made do with existing marks, and maybe the occasional interview.) For the candidates this meant a strange couple of months of being academically force-fed while feeling personally freer and more intellectually alive than at any time before or quite possibly since.

At least that's how I remember it, and it's what Bennett has brilliantly recaptured here. He shows eight budding history specialists, attending a northern English school in the 1980s, whose headmaster is set on improving the place's position in the higher education league-tables. Opposed to him -- philosophically, temperamentally and in just about every other way -- is a pudgy, near-retirement English teacher called Hector (that's his surname and his nickname) who has the boys for General Studies, which he joyously translates as Useless Knowledge and which he values because it's useless. ("I count examinations, even for Oxford and Cambridge, as the enemy of education. Which is not to say that I don't regard education as the enemy of education, too.") Under his tutelage, the boys learn poetry (by heart, a central part of Hector's philosophy), but also learn about old movies, of the Now Voyager and Brief Encounter vintage, and about old songs. There are performances in this play of Bye Bye Blackbird and Bewitched that are more poignant and more entertaining than songs from any new musical in years. This happily confirms my old theory that songs in plays are greeted as unexpected bonuses, not to mention welcome respites from all that talking, while songs in musicals, being what you expect, indeed what you're there for, are always at heavy risk of being disappointing.

I've seen it objected that children of the '80s would never have known those songs. The answer is, they would if Hector had been teaching them. (And they do sing Pet Shop Boys as well.) It's not that the boys uncritically worship Hector -- far from it -- but he engages their curiosity and, most crucially, their sense of humour - - a faculty more acutely alive at that age than at any other; when you're eighteen and intelligent, everything seems funny. It can drive adults mad and it can, when employed as a collective weapon, be cruel. Hector gets to feel the pain of that but also reap its benefits. In one glorious sequence he conducts a miniature experiment in French immersion; the boys get to improvise a scene in that language, set in any workplace they choose, but using only "the conditional or the subjunctive." They choose a brothel. Then the headmaster walks in and, with supreme quick-wittedness and the absolute minimum of physical alteration, they change the scenario to a field-hospital from the First World War.

As well as this, the funniest scene in ages, the play boasts what may be the most moving. Hector is conducting a one-on-one poetry class with a withdrawn boy named Posner. ("I'm a Jew. I'm small. I'm homosexual. And I live in Sheffield. I'm fucked.") Shyly, Hector puts out his hand. The gesture isn't reciprocated; Posner has his own doomed crush on the most confident boy in the class, Deakin. And in fact the real emotion in the scene is somewhere else; it's in the passion Hector infuses into analyzing a poem by Thomas Hardy. It's what he's about, and it's why he's a good teacher in -- the play would have us believe -- a doomed tradition. Hector's own gayness consists in giving selected students a lift on his motorbike and fumbling with them en route. Bennett himself, the laureate of frustration, has questioned how much gratification there could possibly be through gauntlets, but it's enough to get Hector sacked.

His successor is already in waiting, an ambitious young historian named Irwin, delegated to get the boys into Oxbridge. He seizes on their impressive store of Useless Knowledge -- what he, to Hector's despair, calls "gobbets" -- and suggests they use them to spice up their essays. Despite appearances, the two men are not actually polar opposites. Both are more or less covertly gay -- though the scene in which Irwin is effectively seduced by Deakin, who prefers girls but is an all-around flirt, is the least convincing in the play. More significantly, Hector's love of the subjunctive is reflected in Irwin's recommendation to flout accepted conventional historical wisdom in favour of what might have happened; reflected, though, in a distorting mirror so that it becomes assembly-line contrarianism. It's an approach, as we learn in a series of flash- forwards, that carries him far: into a career as a presenter of BBC history programs and then into politics, advising on the uses of paradox (as in "the loss of liberty is the price we pay for freedom"); taught under Thatcher, he flourishes under Blair.

The play keeps jumping between past, present and future, between enactment and commentary. It keeps you on your toes, but it never confuses. Nicholas Hytner's production backs up the onstage action with grainy video footage that brings the whole school indelibly, and often hilariously, to life. The fluency of this production, its quicksilver mastery of mood, is exhilarating, and so is the precision of the performances. There isn't a false note in the show. Richard Griffiths, a master of quiet comedy that transpires of quiet heartbreak, is the embodiment of Hector, solid but sagging. Less spectacular but equally real is Stephen Campbell Moore's Irwin; even his TV commentaries, an acting-trap, hit exactly the right understated note. As a female teacher (some things in British boys' schools have obviously progressed) Frances de la Tour, whose specialty as a young actress was being nasal and gawky, is now nasal and acidulous; she brings down the house practically every time she opens her mouth. But then she does have the wisest lines; take your choice between "one of the hardest things for boys to learn is that a teacher is human, one of the hardest things for a teacher to learn is not to try and tell them," and "I have not hitherto been allotted an inner voice", her comment on both the play she's in and the system it's in. Also, to Hector, "a grope is a grope, it's not the Annunciation;" to the world in general, "the chief enemy of culture in any school is always the Headmaster." That's a bit sweeping, perhaps, but my own English experience suggests that it's 66% true. Certainly Clive Merrison's beleagured technocrat of a principal makes it seem very plausible, not least when paying tribute to Hector in words ("he opened a deposit account in the bank of English literature") that desecrate everything Hector stands for. And not only is it hard to imagine this play done by non-British actors; it's hard at the monent to imagine it done by British actors other than these. The eight boys are astonishingly good, individually and as a group.

To be honest, the writing gives only four of them much chance to be individuals, so an epilogue in which we learn of their subsequent careers has only half its intended impact. Indeed, the entire state- of-the-nation aspect is only fitfully effective; as indeed was the case with Forty Years On. But the more immediate picture is perfect; and if the bittersweet ending doesn't quite justify itself in terms of structure, it does so overwhelmingly in terms of character and atmosphere. It's tempting to put the show in the embarrassment-of- riches category, except that there's nothing embarrassing about it. But as for richness and sheer pleasure: I doubt that there is currently a better example, anywhere, of what the theatre is for.

2006-07-01-shakespearean-play-is-a-dream:
It's attracted less attention than the pending extinction of The Lord of the Rings, but the Royal Bank Festival of Classics, at Coronation Park in Oakville, has ceased operations. This year's promised production of The Merchant of Venice will not be happening. This is sad news. It had one of the most enchanting natural settings of any of the open-air theatres around Toronto, and some of its productions -- Diana Leblanc's Twelfth Night, Michael Shamata's Love's Labour's Lost and, last year, Miles Potter's A Midsummer Night's Dream -- have been outstandingly enjoyable. And with that magic lake in the background, I was just waiting for them to do The Seagull.

The Resurgence Theatre Company in Newmarket also has an enchanting liquid setting; at least it did last time I was there two years ago. After a year's break, Resurgence has resurged but in another part of the forest, or at least the park. It has had to re-pitch its tent (I mean that literally) out of sight of water, but with the back of its stage now giving on to a breathtaking avenue of trees. It cried out to be used for ceremonial entrances, or at least for entrances, and it was disappointing that it never was.

There is nothing else in David Ferry's production to be disappointed by. It is yet another Dream, that manages not to be yet another Dream. The director, who thinks I'm a purist, informed me cheerfully when I arrived that I was going to hate it, and I can see why. It begins with the words "you have to wake up early for your mom's wedding tomorrow;" and you don't have to be a scholar to guess that that line was not written by Shakespeare. It's spoken by a nanny to a little boy whose name, aha, is Will and whose parents (one natural, one adoptive) have been fighting, despite the impending happy day. The nanny reassures him, and leaves him reading a book that looks suspiciously like a copy of the play. He, of course, proceeds to dream it. His nanny reappears as Puck, his mom and dad are Titania and Oberon and he himself becomes the Changeling Child over whom the fairy king and queen are fighting a custody case. He doesn't seem to be overly worried about it. He has a high old time; when he isn't being a wide-eyed spectator, he's nudging the other actors into position or placing important props in their hands. He's played, with great command, by Robert Dunsmore-Van Wart.

This is a very physical production. One expects the four-sided lovers' quarrel to be acrobatic, but Irene Poole, a self-propelling human missile, may be the first Hermia to spend half her time lying horizontal in mid-air, supported by the unwilling hands of one or other of her menfolk, and thrashing furiously. Hermia is not generally reckoned to be one of the great Shakespearean heroines, but Poole is the second actress in my experience (Kristin Thomson was the first) to make her seem practically the centre of the play. She turns her trademark intensity to comic ends. This is a Hermia who, when informed in the first scene that she will have to choose between death and the cloister, milks her situation for all the tragic dignity she can get; who, when bidding farewell to her Lysander with "me must starve our sight ... till morrow deep midnight," blows him a heavily dramatized kiss; and who, when awaking to find him vanished, is mocked by echoes that might have strayed in from The Duchess of Malfi.

Maev Beaty's Helena, pouting with frustration, matches her in furious funniness, and the prescribed contrast in their statures ("her height, forsooth," rages Hermia, as if this were the last straw) could hardly be more graphically or wittily exploited. Lysander (Christopher Morris, scarily dismissive when he falls out of love) and Demetrius (Tim Campbell) do remarkably well with their lesser material; they share, once under the influence of Love Potion whichever-it-is, a delightful inability to pronounce the name "Hermia" without turning it into some kind of guttural obscenity. The horizontal-hold effect is used, by my count, just once too often, but that's more than forgivable. Indeed the whole quarrel scene, which in some productions can seem to go on forever, is as disciplined as it's inventive. Behind all the gymnastics, each of the actors keeps a steady thought line going.

The fairies are played with Jamaican inflections and varying degrees of success. Cara Ricketts' Titania is a sensuous delight, Jamie Robinson an Oberon who gives "I know a bank" a hip-hop beat and whose authority comes and goes along with his comprehensibility, and Lisa Codrington a Puck who needs to calm down and take several breaths. Still, the doubling of the fairy king and queen with the mortal rulers Theseus and Hippolyta makes more sense than usual. Both couples are visibly navigating toward a happy ending, and we're glad when they get there. Stuart Wilber brings off the unusual feat of playing Peaseblossom, Cobweb, Moth and Mustardseed, all at the same time. Technology helps.

Art Hindle, like many Bottoms before him (if you follow me), ceases to be amusing when he's underneath his ass's head, but in his natural state he's very engaging. He's one of your quiet, assured Bottoms, rather than one of your raging egomaniacs, but conscious of his rights. Alon Nashman's anxious Quince knows, when casting him for Pyramus, that the best way is to appeal to his masculinity. "Pyramus," he says, "is a sweet-faced man," ignoring the adjective to stress the noun.

There's a great and instructive contrast when Quince is compelled to turn from director to actor and deliver the prologue to Pyramus and Thisbe; he can hardly get the words out. Though when he gets round to outlining the plot, he's helped out by a silhouette show. I've never seen that before. Brendan Gall's Flute the bellows-mender looks as if he would be exceptionally good at his job, though how many Elizabethans would have needed to have their bellows mended on a regular basis has always puzzled me. And Don Allison is a nicely fretful Starveling, though his real triumph comes as the heavy father Egeus who, it seems, can hardly wait to see his daughter mewed up or married off. Asked to select a fate for her, Death or a Maiden, he'd probably vote for death. You end up thinking, as at all good productions of A Midsummer Night's Dream, that this must be the best play ever written.
2006-07-04-the-tsar-crossed-lovers:
LOVE AMONG THE RUSSIANS AND THE MAGIC FIRE

Court House Theatre, Shaw Festival, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

THEATRE REVIEW

This year's lunchtime show at the Shaw Festival brings together two of Chekhovs early one-act farces, or "vaudevilles," as he called them. The Bear, which leads off, was the first he wrote and is probably the best-known. This is its third production in these parts in the last five years. Its popularity stems from it being the most endearing kind of love story: the kind about two people who are obviously destined to get together but who, on first encounter, cannot stand one another.

The bear of the title is a landowner called Smirnov, a man bereft of social graces, who comes to collect a much-needed debt repayment from Popova, who is also a landowner. (Who isnt in Chekhov?) Popova refuses to hear him, as she is much too busy mourning her late husband. He was apparently an all-out cad, but now that he's dead she intends to devote herself to his memory in the hope that this will give her a moral leg up in the afterlife. Smirnov, hopping mad at her intransigence, goes so far as to challenge her to a duel. She accepts, on condition that he show her how to fire the pistols. By now, of course, he is hopelessly smitten and so, equally of course, is she. He proposes. Widowhood is forgotten. There is another primal theme at work here: the triumph of life over death. Or, to put it in traditional comic terms, the folly of making idealistic vows -- of chastity or of eternal fidelity -- that will inevitably be mugged by reality

Eda Holmes' production is a high-voltage affair, with songs thrown in, though it isnt a musical. (There is, however, a musical of The Bear. Its called A Night in the Ukraine, and it's the play as it might have been done by the Marx Brothers. Smirnov is transformed into a shyster lawyer, played, of course, by Groucho: My father named me Serge; he really wanted a suit. Popova is Margaret Dumont, and her servant is Chico, who says of his bereaved employer, "she's-a more than unhappy, shes-a housebroken." I recommend it.) Morwyn Brebner has provided a lively translation, up- to-date to a fault. Smirnov, pondering the ethics of shooting at a woman, justifies it by saying that after all women can vote; they can join the army. In Tsarist Russia? I dont think so.

Blair Williams, known in this vicinity as an impeccable high comic, drops his customary suave facade while retaining all his technical skill; his Smirnov goes from unassuageable anger to complete erotic capitulation, with no visible break, in about 20 minutes. Diana Donnelly's widow-with-all-the-trimmings -- she looks great in black -- navigates emotional hairpin bends with similar insouciance; this is the best thing she has done at Shaw (or anywhere else, for all I know). Physically as well as temperamentally, they make a towering team; William Vickers, as a servant in a constant state of intimidation, gives a general impression of scurrying around between their legs.

The second half of Love Among the Russians is another farce, called The Proposal. This comes from Russia with rather less love. A shy landowner called Lomov attempts to pop the question to Natalya Stepanovna, another landowner's daughter. And she might very well have him -- truth be told, shed probably have anybody -- only he never gets to ask, since they start quarrelling, first about the precise boundaries of their respective territories and then about the precise qualities of their respective dogs. This pair, too, may well be a predestined match, but it isnt because of their attractive characteristics; their squabbles and misunderstandings get monotonous. This is less the fault of the play than of Holmes' production; the vocal and physical energy of the previous play here deteriorates into mere shouting and gesticulation. Donnelly and Vickers reappear, as Natalya and the father who will do almost anything to get rid of her. An additional actor, Martin Happer, play the suitor; this spoils the symmetry of the double-bill but permits a series of impressive comical contortions; the performance is, in fact, a continuous pratfall. This half of the show has its due quota of laughs, but they're compromised by a general sense that its all very hard work.

Most autobiographical plays are as much fun as leafing through somebody elses souvenir album. The exceptions are those in which the author's memories have been rigorously edited and fitted into a frame. The classic examples are Long Day's Journey into Night and The Glass Menagerie, the first of which compresses the anguish of years into 24 hours and both of which confine their attentions to a mere four characters. And even in those cases the least vital person on stage is the surrogate writer.

Lillian Groag, the American author of The Magic Fire, takes the opposite tack. She does fit her story into a limited time-span, but she fills her stage with characters, most of them from the same family. She actually chooses to sprawl. She tried, she tells us, to write "a novel directly for the stage," which considering the difficulties of putting a novel on stage in any circumstances, seems foolhardy. I share her preference for large-cast plays over small (they are, for obvious reasons, generally less boring) but when the cast consists of the authors own relatives, the form is an open invitation to self-indulgence.

Groag, in her program note, is coy about the extent to which her play actually is autobiographical, but there seems little reason for it to exist if it isnt. We are told that Groag was born and grew up in Argentina and then moved to the United States. This is also the trajectory described by her narrating character, who has the not dissimilar name of Lise Berg and who spends the evening looking back on a two-month period in Buenos Aires in 1952, in the course of which she turned seven and Eva Peron died. Lise has an Austrian immigrant father and an Italian immigrant mother, plus a stageful of aunts, uncles and grandparents, who in turn spend a lot of time reminiscing and squabbling over their extremely cultural roots; they are all heavily into opera. The audience in its turn spends a lot of time trying to work out which of the characters is related to whom, and how. Meanwhile the play lacks a central character or, if that's too old-fashioned a concept or a focus. The grown-up Lise talks as if the point of it all is the effect it had on her and on her subsequent development, but we learn virtually nothing of what that development was. We're told, in passing and with no details, that she became an actress and was twice unhappily married; thats all. Tara Rosling, who plays her, is reduced to patrollling the edges of the stage, trying not to sound literary and occasionally succeeding. Sometimes she gets to harangue her younger self, who is peppily played by Lila Bata-Walsh but seems no different from the precocious kid of a hundred other plays. There are hints that her recollections are mere nostalgia and not to be trusted, but unreliable memory is only an interesting subject when you care about the person doing the misremembering.

It ties in, though, with the conversation of Lises elders, who, as the play hardly ever stops informing us, are nostalgics to a person. How many times -- it feels like hundreds -- do we need to be told that their devotion to high European culture is a defence mechanism that encourages them to shut out the world around them? (The title refers to the ring of fire that surrounds Wagner's Brunnhilde, and there are hints that Lise is in some way similarly encircled, but that's just something the characters say; its never dramatized.)

We are in the last stretch of a three-hour evening before it occurs to Lises father to compare the dictatorship in his adopted country to the one that he fled Austria to escape. The Bergs refer to Eva as "that woman," and there is an unintentionally hilarious moment when, without so much as coming in on the middle of a sentence, they turn on the radio at the precise moment her death is announced. It's like a Tom Stoppard parody. Lise, in her own emigre's epilogue, speaks of the U.S. as a country where Fascist dictatorships are the stuff of Broadway musicals. The implicit condescension seems doubly unwarranted when you consider a) that the play tells us less about Peronism than Evita does; and b) that when the author has one of her characters say "its all just politics, nothing to do with us", shes quoting that more celebrated escapist, Sally Bowles from Cabaret, practically verbatim. It's a dim, self- important play; and though Jackie Maxwell stages it well, especially a long dinner-table scene that's something of a tour de force, the acting is all over the place. A bevy of the Shaw Festivals top character ladies (Sharry Flett, Goldie Semple, Patricia Hamilton, Donna Belleville) do their stuff in self-contained little bursts, going on and off like light-bulbs. Each seems to be in a play of her own. Jennifer Phipps is in a world of her own, which is something quite different; shes also in a class of her own, which is something else again. She follows her saintly Rebecca Nurse, an unsentimental jewel of a performance that got squeezed out of my review of The Crucible, by playing an irascible old lady from the Italian side of the family who seems to have selective dementia and is still furious with Mussolini; she can exude wit, just by thrusting out her chin. She shares an accent with Michael Ball who, as her son, alternates entertainingly between long-suffering and explosive. Both these actors are flesh and blood, as, more quietly, is Waneta Storms as a maid whose brother is a political fugitive; she only falters when her professional competence overcomes her sisterly concern too efficiently to be credible.

Other compensations include Ric Reid, a quiet tower of strength as Berg pere, and Dan Chameroy who, as a high-up fascist moonlighting as family friend, continues his impressive progress from musical-comedy hunk to subtle and authoritative dramatic actor. As his opponent, an outspoken liberal journalist, Jay Turvey is cruelly miscast but puts up a good fight. The play violates the Shaw's supposed policy of producing plays written either during or about their patron's lifetime. So of course, and more spectacularly, does The Crucible. But thats worth breaking the rules for. This isnt.

- Love Among the Russians is in repertory until Sept. 24. The Magic Fire is in repertory until Oct. 8. 1-800-511-SHAW.

2006-07-07-the-food-of-life-as-served-wi:
This is Illyria, lady: a seaport and spa located, according to the new Stratford production, somewhere on the coast of India, in the days of Queen Victoria. Shakespeare's Duke Orsion is now a nabob, in emotional, and maybe even cultural, thrall to the resident English, as represented by the Lady Olivia. She comes on like an imperious Raj widow, mourning not a husband she has lost but a brother.

Leon Rubin's production of Twelfth Night is the latest instalment in his ongoing project of refreshing the Shakespeare canon by resetting the plays in exotic, usually Asian, climes. The benefits, this time, are local rather than general. They include lush, lived-in settings (by John Pennoyer) and sinuous dancing (by Keira Loughran) that makes the food of love seem spicier than ever, but they don't extend to supplying the play with a political context, probably because it can't accommodate one.

The Venice of The Merchant of Venice, even the Messina of Much Ado About Nothing (which has in the past been brilliantly staged in a British Raj setting) are comparatively realistic locations, with interacting social levels. lllyria is geographically in the Balkans, but to Shakespeare it seems to have been just a name, another in his line of shadowed Arcadias. There doesn't seem to be anything to it beyond Orsino's household and Olivia's, and though he theoretically runs the place the only tension between them is erotic. When the twins, Viola and Sebastian, are washed up on shore to wreak havoc with the local libidos, they seem to have come from nowhere. They are -- and here the production's choice of locale does have a point - - like breaths of fresh air in a hothouse.

Most of the play takes place at Olivia's place, a crowded establishment whose cross-currents are charted here with exceptional clarity. The rich texture may owe something to the geographical transplant; the set-up, as Shakespeare wrote it, is plainly Elizabethan English, so there's no great stretch in making it Victorian Colonial. It probably owes more, though, to the wit of director and actors. The chatelaine herself is played by Seana McKenna who is, to put it bluntly, older than most Olivias. (Or at least than most recent Olivias. Once upon a time, Olivia regularly used to be played by Viola's mother. How's that for overtones?)

Instead of a self-cloistered ingenue violently awakening to love, we get a worldly woman who's not as aware as she thought she was and can laugh at herself even as she totters. It doesn't necessarily make more sense to have Olivia played as a mature woman, but it's certainly a bonus to have her played by a mature actress, one as alert as McKenna to both the wit and the absurdity and as adroit as communicating both. Dana Green's Viola is an excellent foil for her, empathizing, from a distance, with her fraternal loss and then confronting her like a blast of common sense with a smile attached.

It's also easier than usual to believe that Olivia and Sir Toby Belch live in the same house and that they're actually related. They meet seldom, and he's always drunk when they do, but in these encounters they communicate an authentic blend of acceptance and distaste. Thom Marriott's Toby, someone's cashiered younger brother, is genial enough, a bully who can actually fight, but there's real calculating nastiness in him, especially in his dealings with Don Carrier's endearing Sir Andrew who, as befits his name and very much in line with the realities of the Raj, is Scottish; the yellow costume (Olivia's least favourite colour) in which he, like most Andrews, is haplessly got up is a plaid, the ancestral tartan perhaps of the clan MacAguecheek. He also plays what Toby, departing somewhat from the text, describes as "strange instruments;" they are of course bagpipes. He is the only Andrew I have seen to be permanently jealous of, and wounded by, Toby's success with Maria, who flirts with him at their first encounter and ignores him afterwards.

Diane D'Aquila is a commanding Maria, her relationship with Toby growing through each scene. Andrew Massingham's Feste is clever and melodious, though a white Indian mask (he's supposed to be the bridge between the two cultures) obscures not only his face but his personality. Brian Bedford has played Malvolio at Stratford twice before; his comic virtuosity -- when reading the fatal letter or when strutting cross-gartered -- remains intact, but it's underpinned this time by a sharp sense of class. This steward has worked his way up, and he despises those who haven't. (They return the compliment.) In specs and curlers, he exudes sniffiness. But he's serious; and when he's duped and tormented, though we don't actually feel sorry for him, we do feel. His is both the funniest performance of the evening, and the most disturbing. At least it appears to be heading in the latter direction, as does the whole production, until they both get derailed. The ultimate culprit here seems to be Sanjay Talwar's performance of Orsino, which so fastens on the character's self- pity and self-love that he comes out spineless. It becomes even harder than usual to understand what Viola sees in him. When called upon for passion in the last act, he supplies only petulance. This weightlessness infects the entire scene, so that the twins' reunion and the pairings are neither as joyous or as moving as they should be. McKenna adopts the fashionable deflationary reading of Olivia's "most wonderful" when faced with two objects of her affection.

Frankly she doesn't need it -- she has enough laughs under her belt - - but anyway she doesn't have much to deflate; journeys end in lovers' meetings, but there isn't much of an arrival.

There is a lovely autumnal staging of Feste's last song, in which the various stanzas actually apply to the people in the play, leading to a sharp reversal of fortune as between the clown and the avenging steward. It's plainly meant to chill our blood but it comes too late; we've been primed to laugh and there hasn't been enough to stop us. The production is far more successful with the play's fun than with its pain. But if you have to err on one side, the funny side's the right one.
2006-07-08-regrets-of-the-master-of-the-:
If the term "theatre of the absurd" accounts for anything, it accounts for Eugene Ionesco, whose plays, farce with a dusting of nihilist philosophy, came violently into fashion in the 1950s, slipped quietly out of it in the '60s and have been creeping back again over the past decade. The centrepiece of this renaissance has been The Chairs, which premiered in Paris in 1952 when it managed to bewilder even the French, was revived there in triumph in 1956 before taking off to conquer the world. In 1997, it was a surprise success all over again in London and New York. I'm not sure that it's his best play, but it makes an excellent calling card, functioning as it does on so many interlocking levels.

It's the play about the old couple, each of them 90-plus, who live on top of a very high building -- conceivably a lighthouse, certainly overlooking some kind of waterway -- where the Old Man is caretaker. He has a message to give to the world; and he and the Old Woman, a faithful helpmate, summon an Orator, whom we see, to deliver it, and a large audience of celebrities and others to listen. We don't see them, but -- an image that has made the play's fortune -- we do see the chairs they sit upon: 56 of them in the new Soulpepper production, all dragged and arranged on stage by the tireless couple themselves. You can see why these parts are generally cast far younger than they're written.

The Old Man has regrets and thwarted ambitions, as who has not, and he has of course had plenty of time, and plenty of space, to accumulate and brood upon them. As both he and his wife say, repeatedly, he could have been a grand master, a chess master, a master of the revels, a master builder, a master don as opposed to just a mastodon (these are all my own suggestions, but I think they're in the spirit of the text), or at least master in his own house; instead he's just -- these are his own words -- "master of the mop and bucket."

All these reiterations are the kind of thing that made Ionesco famous, demonstrations of the meaninglessness of language, or at least of its ability to deaden our responses, and of the supposed inability of human communication actually to communicate. It's an unproved case, though everybody lapped it up in, roughly, the years between existentialism and Vietnam. Prone to redundancy and sloppy thinking though we may all be, this isn't really the way people talk, and the more virtuoso Ionesco's puns and patterns become, the more tiresome become their pretensions to comment on either the social system or the human condition. Just as wordplay, it's fun if over-extended, though the new translation by Martin Crimp, the current go-to guy in England for translating anything, strikes me as less flowing and felicitous than the traditional one it's replaced. I think this is what's known as putting a Crimp in the style.

However: This is also a play about a marriage, and here the repetition does have a point. It underpins a deeply observed portrait of fretfulness and consolation, a mutually supportive, mutually exploitative relationship that's long been on automatic pilot. As the Old Man's confidence grows, and as his imaginary audience swells (it includes an Emperor), he moves, with absolute logic, from regret to resentment, and from there to outright paranoia. He spills out accusations, very persuasive-sounding ones, against all the people who blocked his advancement. His wife's contribution is to jolly him up while urging him to make the most of his last opportunity. It's hers, too; when company calls, she flirts like there was no tomorrow (a reasonable assumption in the circumstances), while maintaining a pose of outraged virtue.

This is where Jim Warren's production comes into its own. Its great virtue is that nobody seems to have told it that the play is Absurd. Oliver Dennis and Kristen Thomson play the couple absolutely for real, he dapper and hopeful and bitter, she bustling and buxom, if sagging. Just as Waiting for Godot always works best in productions that take the metaphysics for granted and concentrate on the interaction of two guys at the side of a road, so this one flowers as a day in the lives, that happens to sum up all of the days that have gone before. Of course, most marriages don't last this long, at least not with both partners sentient, but this is what it would be like if they did.

The two actors are also whizzes at the farcical mechanics, which gets us to yet another level. The accumulation of the chairs, shoved on stage at breakneck speed through the multiple doors of Sue LePage's admirable set, is a theatrical treat in itself, quite apart from what it may actually mean. As to that, there are two interpretations. The most popular holds that the guests are a delusion, comparable to the Old Man's conviction that he has the key to all humanity's problems, if only humanity would listen.

But this does seem to be laying things on with a trowel, and it's equally possible to believe that the guests are really there and that the chairs are only theatrical shorthand for their presence. Certainly the way Thomson chats them up, or hawks programs, had me believing, as did the perfect timing of their imaginary entrances, each prolonged (those doors again) until you could swear you actually see them. And if the spectators are real, then the failure of the imposing Orator (Kevin Bundy) actually to orate, is all the more poignant, while the self-immolation of the couple who dive through separate windows -- portholes, really -- into the depths far below, is all the more logical. They have prepared for their moment and, whether they truly anticipate its being a triumph or a disaster, they have nothing left to live for. The resultant muted splash, craftily delayed, is a highlight of Richard Feren's sound score, a vital asset from the first foghorn to the last hubbub.

I have a personal theory, quite unsupported, that the murky waters below used to be the Seine. This is, among other things, an end-of-the-world play, or at least an end-of-French-civilization play, unfolding in a barren room comparable to the hecatomb setting of Samuel Beckett's Endgame. So we have yet a fourth level, a blend of the political and the apocalyptic. (We need an Ionesco word for that. Apoliticalyptic, perhaps.) It doesn't hold too much water, holy or otherwise, since Beckett writes theatrical poetry, while Ionesco deals in whimsy. This production, featuring two outstandingly likeable actors, probably accentuates that; Ionesco has been called "an antic poet of despair," but the antics here outpace the desperation. That, though, is a reasonable choice. It plays to the interpreters' strengths but it also, whatever he himself may have wanted to believe, does honour to the author's.

- The Chairs is in repertory through Sept. 6 at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts, 416-866-8666.

2006-07-10-playing-the-race-bard:
THEATRE REVIEW

HARLEM DUET

Studio Theatre, Stratford

Shakespeares black Othello married a white woman, and his play has much to say on how her white friends felt about it. It tells us nothing about the reactions of his black friends; it doesn't even tell us if he had any. Djanet Sears' Harlem Duet is a response to that, a recasting of the Othello situation in which the Moor has become a black New York academic. His Desdemona is now simply Mona, an unseen, though not unheard, white colleague. Very much seen and heard is Billie, Othellos former partner, driven to frenzy by his desertion. Most of the play happens in the Harlem apartment that Othello and Billie used to share, and where she now lives alone.

The time is the present, mostly. There is the occasional, very effective, flashback within the main action. There are also brief fragments of a couple of parallel stories, set in the past, and performed by the same actors who play Othello and Billie. These also take place in Harlem, and both similarly show a black man leaving a black woman for a white. One is set at the time of the Civil War, with the black couple initially wondering whether to light out for the fabled freedom of Canada; the other takes us to the 1920s, where a black actor with classical ambitions but condemned to appear in demeaning racial sketches (he actually has to put on blackface) incurs the murderous wrath of his about-to-be-ex.

Sears play, much feted in Toronto in 1997, earns its Stratford revival, directed by the author, on grounds both textual (it's superbly written) and contextual (Shakespeare and all that jazz, the jazz being nearly as important as the Shakespeare). It does not, though, sit very happily in the festival's Studio, a small but steep auditorium with a thrust stage inhospitable to domestic drama, which this essentially is, and to the kind of buttoned-down acting it naturally summons forth. Some of the performances are lacking, and one of the crucial images -- the stripping-down of a home -- doesnt count for much in a setting that never looked lived-in in the first place. The historical scenes arent well placed, physically or emotionally. They're fairly confusing, even in the text. They do set off some internal sparks, some of which illuminate the main story, but not enough to justify the distraction. A tale isn't necessarily richer for being told three times, especially when its an explicit variation on one that already exists.

Harlem Duet does more than supply a new context for the Othello story. It also spins out variations on the plays existing elements. Some of these are just facile nudges; this Othello has his Iago, an offstage white colleague who presumably had something to do with tempting him. Others cut deep; if Shakespeare's Othello might be seen as an outsize representation of a black man "trying to pass, then that is certainly how Billie comes to regard her Othello; the more he seems to reject his heritage, the more she embraces hers. And then there's the matter of the handkerchief, the strawberry- spotted one that Othellos mother passed on to him, with magic in the web" -- a phrase that Sears manages, without any incongruity, to incorporate into her own dialogue. Her Othello gives it in turn to each of his women. Shakespeare tells us that "a sybil in her prophetic fury sewed the work; Billies given name, we learn, is Sybil, and in her fury, prophetic or otherwise, she soaks the napkin in old poisons, carefully researched (Billie," says a marvellously skeptical friend, "if this kind of stuff truly worked, Africans wouldn't be in the situation we're in now.) and gives it to her Othello and his new bride. The old Othello was the agent of revenge; this one is its victim. Billie, meanwhile, seems the reincarnation of an even older tragic protagonist, though one of whom the play makes no explicit mention; in her passion, in her vengeance, in her sorcery, even in the means she uses against a smooth-tongued deserter, Billie is Medea.

Unlike Medea, she isnt a monster. All the plays clever allusions, all the magic in its web, wouldn't mean much if the central relationship didn't hold in its own right, and if the dialogue, however highly charged, didnt make sense as conversation. There is still a sexual current between this couple, and its complications can be bitingly funny; the personal is definitely political, as the two hurl accusations about their shared past, about their finances (she supported him through college, he cant or won't do the same for her), about colour and race. Billie has a wonderfully rebellious speech on this last equation: Who called us Black anyway? It's not a racial category, it isnt even the colour of my skin." Momentarily she seems in the same camp as Othello who, among other things, casts strong, elegant doubts on the idea of affirmative action; but then, as Billie more or less points out, having climbed that ladder himself he can afford to throw it away.

Nigel Shawn Williams is an excellent Othello, both in his shifty troubled contemporary form and in the occasional intimations of his tortured namesake. Karen Robinson doesnt have the lightest touch of any actress in the world, but her power, which includes an aggressive wit, does fine for Billie. Barbara Barnes-Hopkins as Billie's landlady and Sophia Walker as her supportive sister-in-law have entertaining moments but they don't fill the space. The remaining character is Billies long-absent father who arrives half- way through, looking to mend fences; hes come in from Nova Scotia and is actually called Canada. (There was a famous black American actor named Canada Lee, and in a play as steeped in theatrical lore as this one, I'd be surprised if that didn't mean something.) Walter Borden doesnt give him much more than muted geniality, but I doubt if its his fault that the play begins to fall apart when he comes on. The whole conception of the character is sentimental, despite some initial skirmishing, and the play's Canadian content seems like an add-on. There is a tie-in, of course, with the yearnings of the Civil War couple for Canada, and specifically for N.S.; but that's a whole other play. There's already more than enough going on in this one.

- In repertory through September 22. 1-800-567-1600

2006-07-12-spam-by-me:
To bring Monty Python and the Holy Grail to the stage, Eric Idle had to convince his colleagues, raid the back catalogue and reinvent the musical

Eric Idle says, when asked, that he is not an ex-Python. "I always deny that. I say Graham's an ex-Python." That would be Graham Chapman, the one who died: an ex-Python in the same way that the Norwegian Blue is an ex-parrot. Im more of a former Python. You cant escape it till you're dead. There's no end.

He warms to his theme. "Are you an ex-Beatle? No, youre a Beatle." Well, if youre Paul or Ringo. That's your game. You're a Liverpool player. Youre reminded of it every day. People yell at you in the street.

And what, I asked him over a King Street lunch in Toronto, do they yell at you?

"Hello, Mike, I love your travel books." That would be Michael Palin, whose most visible pursuits post-Python have been a notable series of TV globetrotting shows that afterwards went into volume form. He and I are always mixed up because we play the same kinds of roles. Well, they were the two Pythons with the greatest air of scrubbed innocence. In a raddled sort of way, they still are. "And they say, You're John Cleese's little friend, arent you? They yell all sorts of things. Like, 'Hello, Monty.' "

Cleese, as actor and writer, went from the anarchy of Python to the traditional farce of Fawlty Towers and A Fish Called Wanda, diversifying along the way into pop psychiatry and health education. He seems to have become the closest thing to a reluctant Python; he wasnt in the last TV series. The two Terries, Jones and Gilliam, have done direction. Of them all, Idles career has been the show- busiest, culminating -- at least to date -- in his authorship of the hit Broadway musical Spamalot. Which is what brought him to Toronto, where the touring production opens officially on Sunday.

Spamalot is based on Monty Python and the Holy Grail, which Idle says has always been the most popular of the team's movies. What, not Life of Brian? Apparently not: People love the Judean Liberation Front scenes -- as well they should -- but maybe a picture that ends with a mass crucifixion was never going to be a popular favourite. Grail has now been a hit with several generations. "Everyone knows the story, has seen the movie. They see it in college. It feeds into the whole Dungeons and Dragons thing."

In fact it was while he was working on a CD-ROM thing of Grail in the States that it occurred to Idle: "If you can adapt it as a game, it would make a very good musical." It was clear that a Python reunion tour -- a perennial pipe dream of Idle's though not necessarily of all the others -- was never going to happen. A musical seemed a promising idea to pursue instead. Then came the sobering thought: Ill have to deal with all the Pythons. When he did contact the other four, they gave their consent, though it seemed obvious that "they didnt think it would work. They were concerned to distance themselves; I'd be exposed as a charlatan, trashing their legend." Now that the show is on, and a huge success, they love it.

Idle himself wrote the show's book and lyrics, and collaborated on the music with John Du Prez. He is, in truth, the only one of the Pythons one can easily imagine doing a musical. He was responsible for most of the songs that cropped up in the TV shows.

But as far as turning Holy Grail into a musical: Well, it sort of starts with Gilbert and Sullivan. Jonathan Miller came to me in 1986 and said, Would you like to be in The Mikado, at the English National Opera? I said, 'What are you going to do with it?' He said, Well, Im going to get rid of all that Japanese nonsense for a start.' So I said, 'Count me in, because a Japanese-free Mikado has got to be something worth seeing. He played Ko-Ko, the Lord High Executioner, and "I just had the best time, because theres a tradition that you can rewrite the Little List Song, and I'd rewrite it every night. And I thought, well this is it, musical comedy is a form I really enjoy, something that's really appropriate for me. So Ive been trying to reinvent musical comedy ever since then."

When he did it, he caught a wave. The Producers had revived the fashion for funny musicals, something that had lain largely dormant during the long years of the British Ascendancy. In Spamalot, Idle and Du Prez seem to be lampooning their more solemn compatriots with The Song That Goes Like This, a number that everyone takes to be a parody of an Andrew Lloyd Webber ballad, though Idle swears it isnt. He has also raided his own back catalogue for Always Look on the Bright Side, the Life of Brian finale number that has fitted into any number of celebratory scenarios from mass crucifixions on.

To create the stage show, all the roles Idle had played in the film were combined into his major one of Sir-Robin-the-not-quite-as- brave-as-Sir Lancelot; similarly, all of Michael Palin's original roles have been collapsed into that of Sir Galahad.

In the musical, King Arthur is definitely the star part. Tim Curry originated it on Broadway; Simon Russell Beale, the British classical actor, took over from him, and will be playing it again later this year in London; Michael Siberry, another British classical actor, plays it in Toronto.

Simon plays him like a man who doesn't really believe he has a horse, Idle says. "Siberry plays him with dignity." Theres one other obvious casting choice thats yet to be realized. At some time I'd like to have a shot at playing Arthur myself. I've been tempted to do it for a few weeks in London. Only for a few weeks, since he and his wife and children live in California. Cleese lives in California, too, but one gathers they dont do much socializing; it is, after all, a very big state.

American resident or not, Idle can still talk and feel like a Broadway-struck Englishman. "Its a 30-year period since we did the movie. And now we're doing this show on 42nd Street. It's very moving."

- Spamalot begins previews tonight at Toronto's Canon Theatre. 416-872-1212
