2006-07-15-double-the-fun-in-high-park-t:
Theatre critics are resigned, given the ubiquity of open-air theatres in and around Toronto, to being exposed to A Midsummer Night's Dream on an annual basis. What other play takes you so far into the woods? Nor is it any great surprise to find regular alfresco productions of As You Like It, set chiefly in a forest, or even of Twelfth Night, which generally looks good in a garden. And they're all love plays, which go well on a summer evening.

The Comedy of Errors would seem a less likely proposition, being a predominantly unromantic farce that happens entirely in built-up areas. All the same, it has turned up here three times in as many years. There was a straightforward production by Miles Potter in Oakville, a spookily imaginative one by Richard Rose in Barrie, and now, as this year's Dream in High Park, we have a lively but uneven version directed by Kelly Thornton.

This is the play about two sets of identical twins, masters and servants, separated since infancy, each being continually mistaken for his double in the course of a single day in Ephesus, the town in which one pair dwells and to which the other has journeyed from Syracuse in hopes of effecting a grand reunion. (Mysteriously, it never occurs to the visiting pair that they have stumbled on exactly what they were looking for. But then, most farce depends on people failing to ask obvious questions.)

The new production comes heralded by directorial declarations about the play being, underneath all the knockabout, a search for identity, both individual and familial. But this doesn't emerge much from what we actually see on stage and, to the extent that it does, it adds nothing to what we have seen in earlier productions.

The final reunions of the Antipholus brothers, their father and mother (also long-lost) and the long-serving and long-suffering Dromio siblings are touching and even healing, but then they always are. And stress is laid on the nervousness of the boys from Syracuse when faced with inexplicable happenings in a town with a reputation for witchcraft (the residents, under similar provocation, merely get angry), but as that's written into the text in letters practically of neon, it hardly counts as a revelation.

Another of the production's announced angles simply doesn't fly. It's about the cities of Ephesus and Syracuse being in a state of what the director has called "a trade war," though it's really more of a reciprocal hostage-taking situation. But that's just a device to get the play started.

Indeed, the Ephesus the production actually shows us seems to be rather a liberal society; at least, it allows an alien under sentence of death to wander around, alone and unescorted, playing Shenandoah on the mouth-organ. By the end -- this is hardly a spoiler -- he will have been reprieved, by Ducal dispensation. This makes Errors the first of several Shakespearean comedies in which a ruler, invariably a Duke, starts the play by threatening the letter of the law and ends by abrogating it; others are Dream, Measure for Measure and The Tempest. But in this play at least, the gesture has no wider charitable significance; there's no suggestion that future Syracusan trespassers in Ephesus, or vagrant Ephesians in Syracuse, will from now on be let off with a caution.

It's difficult anyway to think of this production's Ephesus as a society; its inhabitants sport gaudy coiffures and multi-coloured costumes that are apparently meant to suggest the day after tomorrow, but look more like a fancy-dress parade. The set, meanwhile (I question whether open-air productions should have sets, but the High Park ones always do), is all-purpose exotic, with beaded-curtain entrances that make even supposedly respectable homes look like low-profile bordellos; Antipholus of Ephesus appears to have set up house in the pink-light district, and the female population is notable for its high proportion of masked temptresses.

Farce and fantasy are not the same thing; indeed, you could make a good case for their being polar opposites. And, clinging to the old-fashioned idea that though farce may be nonsense it should never be nonsensical, I'd question the idea of casting the Antipholi with one black actor and one white, as the plot depends on their being indistinguishable. (That's without even getting into the biology of it.) It isn't as if the production doesn't want us to notice how everybody else looks, not with that design scheme. And since the colour-blindness doesn't extend to the Dromios, both of whom are white, it doesn't even count as a convention.

Still, all four twins are admirably played. This production may be hit-and-miss, but its hits are palpable. Kevin Hanchard, apart from being the clearest and supplest speaker, makes an amusingly supercilious Antipholus of Syracuse, as much offended as alarmed by the sorcery into which he thinks he's stumbled. Alex Poch-Goldin is a contrastingly cool opposite number, volatile but still able to see the sophisticated joke in being barred from his own door.

That door, the only solid one in town, is both free-standing and delightfully mobile. It gives, all things considered, the wittiest performance of the evening, though the two Dromios run a close second. They are played by Anthony Malarky, who's especially excellent, and Bradley Brackenridge (they even have appropriate names for clowns), and have their finest moments unknowingly aping one another from either side of that door, like Groucho and Harpo in Duck Soup.

Christine Brubaker spins out a spectacular comic-melodramatic cadenza as the jealous Adriana, unleashing on the brother to whom she isn't married all the reproaches she has been saving up for the one to whom she is. She ends it squirming on the floor, though I think she throws in just one squirm too many. Niki Landau plays her conciliatory sister with a pink parasol (goes with the decor) and an unmelted-butter demureness; her performance doe-sn't get much beyond that point, but then neither does the writing. Both actresses suffer, individually and as a team, from having to play most of their scenes on a balcony, high up and far back.

Other performances are patchy, and the production's comic invention never really snowballs; we never find ourselves laughing helplessly. But we do laugh, respectably often; while the ending, as it should, makes us smile. The two Dromios have spent most of the evening cracking jokes while being cuffed by their masters; finally, they are left alone to take pleasure in one another's company -- "I see by you I am a sweet-faced youth" -- and to exit, "hand in hand, not one before another." That's nice.

- The Comedy of Errors runs at the Dream in High Park through Sept. 3; 416-367-1652. Pay what you can.

2006-07-18-opening-knight:
MONTY PYTHON'S SPAMALOT

Canon Theatre, Toronto

- - -

Some people chop trees; they're lumberjacks and they're all right. The Monty Python boys, who taught us this and much else, are intellectual lumberjacks; they chop logic. It's an old English tradition, but one that the Pythons took to new heights with their sequences of insanely intense argument, their erudition worn at dangerously rakish angles. Some of these sublimely funny dialogues light up Monty Python's Spamalot, the stage version of Monty Python and the Holy Grail. Many of them, indeed, are taken from the movie word for word. There is, pretty near the beginning, the one in which a couple of sentinels debate, from opposite apertures high up in a medieval keep, the respective wing capacities of the European and the African swallow for carrying coconuts from the Caribbean to King Arthur's Britain, where the natives use them to provide sound effects for horses' hooves. Quite soon after that, there's the one in which an oppressed peasant named Dennis, questions, from an orthodox Marxist perspective, the right of Arthur to rule over him or anyone else. ("It's always class with you, isn't it?" sniffs Dennis' mother for whom, plainly, Dennis is not Che Guevara, just a very naughty boy.) Dennis is especially scornful of the king's claim to derive his legitimacy from the Lady in the Lake or, as he puts it, "some tart in a pond" holding a sword. Even if the sword is called Excalibur.

There are also passages that, though they don't derive from the film, are fully worthy of it. After the voice of God (played by the voice of John Cleese; shrewd casting, that) has commanded Arthur and his team to seek the Holy Grail, the knights fall to questioning the omniscience of a Deity who can't keep track of his own tableware. That hits the authentic, wildly literal note. Which, since founding Python Eric Idle wrote it, is no surprise. Idle is responsible for the show's book, lyrics and, in collaboration with John Du Prez, music. Monty Python's Spamalot is a musical -- a spoof musical. In a way, that's a logical progression, since the movie was a spoof epic. But there is a difference. There were not many mock-Arthurian pictures before Holy Grail. (Or since, if it comes to that.) Just about every musical we see now is a parody musical, to the extent that there is little in the form left to make fun of; if song-and- dance shows are self-evidently ridiculous, why go on writing them?

As with The Producers (which used parody but wasn't one), the stand-out number in Spamalot is a carry-over: Always Look on the Bright Side of Life, which isn't quite as funny when the people singing it aren't being crucified, but is still irresistibly jaunty. I Am Not Dead Yet is cute, sung by a man refusing to be loaded onto a plague cart, and The Song That Goes Like This is a hilarious take- off of an Andrew Lloyd Webber ballad, even if its authors protest it isn't, which in turn makes you wonder why the staging incorporates a collapsing chandelier. But most of the numbers seem like intrusions, even though the writers and the director, Mike Nichols, have tried to make the idea of "being in a musical" part of the concept. It culminates in something called You Won't Succeed on Broadway, which is about musicals being mainly done by Jews. Well, Jews used to write most of them (not so much any more) but they've never mono- polized the performance of them, nor would most audiences care one way or the other; and though I salute Idle for rhyming "Gentile" with "percentile" this number doesn't so much stop the show as stop it in its tracks. It drives its one joke into the ground.

That's another thing. The great strength of the Python TV shows, carried over with remarkable success into the movies, was their speed. When an idea was exhausted, they moved unceremoniously on to the next. A musical is ceremonious, almost by definition. And though the stage cast do a lot of doubling, they can hardly be expected to recover the do-it-yourself exhilaration of half-a-dozen writer- performers doing all the parts. Nor do the present touring company put much of an individual stamp on their roles. (The starry Broadway originals may well have done.) Michael Siberry's Arthur is closely patterned on Graham Chapman's baffled authority in the movie, only with geniality standing in for ineffability. His bluffness kept reminding me of Ross Petty, who might be ideal Canadian casting; and indeed the show, which includes audience participation and a singalong, not to mention mock-medieval decor, does sometimes suggest a superior Petty panto (as opposed to Wicked, which was like an inferior one.) The various knights are hard to tell apart but Jeff Dumas, strongly resembling Baldrick from Blackadder, is delightful as Patsy the put-upon squire who wields the coconuts that, in a nice touch, also come in useful for providing tap-dance noises.

This is not a show with great opportunities for women, a point repeatedly made by the only one present, Pia Glenn, whose Lady in the Lake is a vociferously frustrated diva fashioned after Eartha Kitt. Again one wishes that the show would stop making jokes about musicals and get back to making jokes about Arthur and his knights, especially as those jokes are very good ones. When this show is funny, it's explosively so; and it finishes better than the movie whose ending, it must be confessed, was a cop-out. (It actually involved cops.) There is what the show's author might characterize as a rather high nudge nudge, wink wink quotient; it's hard not to wince when an audience of devotees starts applauding before a favourite scene starts; comedy is supposed to be about surprise. On the other hand, only an arrant churl could resist an opening fish- slapping dance, especially as it turns out to be sublimely irrelevant. Some of the show is the purest Python, even if it isn't the full Monty.

- Until Sept. 10. 416-872-1212.

2006-07-19-things-are-bound-to-get-a-bit:
THE BLONDE, THE BRUNETTE AND THE VENGEFUL REDHEAD

Studio Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

There are more characters than you might expect from the title of the Australian play The Blonde, the Brunette and the Vengeful Redhead but fewer players. The author, Robert Hewett, has written a play built around a single incident, to be performed by a single actress, who is however required to play seven roles, with seven different hair-colourings. It is, obviously, a succession of monologues, which could easily be a recipe for boredom. In fact it turns out to be compelling and even moving. It is also, in its Stratford production, superbly performed. Lucy Peacock does the honours and, even allowing for the lack of on-stage competition, walks deservedly off with them.

To start with the title roles: The carrot-topped avenger is a suburban housewife whose dark-haired friend and neighbour informs her that her husband is carrying on with a flaxen floozie. The wife seeks a confrontation, with dire results. The catastrophe spreads outwards, and we get to meet some of the others caught up in it: an English doctor on an emergency ward who finds herself with a personal stake in one of her cases; a bereft young boy; an aged female friend, sympathetic but judgmental, even in the act of refusing to pass judgment; and the husband, who seems to deserve all the terrible things that get said about him. And there is still another character, never heard from but much spoken of, whose development over a period of years turns out to be crucial.

The action has been transported from Australia to Canada with only one textual glitch. (The doctor says that her colleagues call her "that Pommy bitch". That is not a phrase we use around here. Not the adjectival part of it anyway.) The implication, plausible enough, is that this is a story that could happen anywhere, or at least in any place with shopping malls. That is not in itself an earth-shattering observation, but in Geordie Johnson's production, designed by Michael Gianfrancesco, it's given a powerful reality by a pitiless series of video stills, projected while the actress, in silhouette, changes costumes and, of course, wigs. There is a constant counterpoint as the writing and performance particularize the characters in an environment which, if not certifiably dehumanizing, is certainly anonymous.

There are times when the play skirts caricature, notably with the nosey neighbour who turns out to have her own sexual agenda, and whose censorious hypocrisy, though certainly funny, is a little too complete to be credible. (How enviable to be that free of doubts about yourself.) And there may be some sentimentality in the depiction of the boy, whose situation can hardly fail to pull at your heart and so should, by the highest standards, be treated as rigorously as possible. He also muddies the convention. The others seem to be speaking their thoughts; he seems to be talking to someone.

Peacock, in fact, is required to play not just a variety of roles or even of moods, but of styles. Her triumph is, among other things, one of brinkwomanship, since she never undersells a character but never overstates an emotion. Her most obvious tour-de-force is of course as the husband, who is introduced in an outstandingly witty piece of staging befitting what turns out to be a devastating portrait of a man whose capacities for self-delusion, self-interest and self-pity outstrip even those of the lady next door. (It's consoling to reflect that this merciless unveiling of male solipsism was actually written by a man.) The unavoidably light vocal texture actually lends an edge; Brecht would have approved.

But it's the Vengeful Redhead herself who cuts deepest, even though on first encounter, she doesn't seem capable of depth. She's placid, level and accepting: strenuously so. And it's all too believable that, when she does lash out, terrible things will ensue. If a central theme emerges through the monologues, it's repression and its consequences; it gives a face, or faces, to the production's emphasis on urban (or suburban) anomie. The redhead is the only character given a second speech, which here translates as a second chance. It's about wisdom through endurance; it's spoken by a person we barely recognize as the one we first met, but put the two together, add in the complete breakdown and reconstruction of a personality, and it's credible. It may be presumptuous to say so but in her plumbing of this last scene Peacock seems to grow, not only as an actress, but as a woman.

The play has anecdotal rather than universal force, but that's enough to be going on with. After a succession of plays, monologues and others, that make demands on our respect by advertising their authenticity, it's quite a relief to find one that is written, unabashedly, from the outside.

- In repertory until Sept. 24. 1-800-567-1600

2006-07-22-production-and-play-have-good:
The Greeks didnt only invent the Western theatre. They also invented the Western open-air theatre. Philosophers Walk, by the University of Toronto law faculty, may not quite be the Theatre of Dionysus, but it certainly has an appropriately evocative name. For the past three summers, the Canopy Theatre Company has challenged the city's Shakespearean monopoly with an alfresco Attic tragedy. This year it's Oedipus Rex, the big one.

The Canopy company is a barely professional outfit, mainly composed of recent theatre-school graduates, and this production (which I saw at its one and only preview) has no chance of qualifying as a transcendental experience. Not that Ive ever seen a production of Oedipus that did. This one is the story delivered pure and simple, with a few unfortunate flourishes. But once youve accepted that, it becomes rewarding and even engrossing.

To dispose of some of the oddities first: The set consists of a rostrum, approached by several shallow steps and, right at the top, a very steep one. The actors, who after all are mainly young and agile, take the latter obstacle in their stride, but it has to be an ungainly stride. It seems especially hard on Oedipus himself in the throes of his final humiliation. He's blinded himself, and has to be helped around the stage. He's taken the blame for everything, like a good tragic hero. Hasnt he suffered enough? Surely the least he deserves is a reasonably level playing field on which to take his medicine.

There are five Doric columns on top of the platform, and another three scattered around below. Theres also a sacrificial flame, burning all on its own, and a few lampposts, which obviously come with the property but blend in surprisingly well. The total effect is all-purpose classical, a style that also extends to the costumes, and especially to the white sheets worn by members of the chorus.

The chorus is, as always, a problem. The solution attempted by Andrea Wasserman's production is to naturalize and colloquialize them as much as possible. It doesn't look like that at the start of the show; when we first see them the actors are wearing flimsy white masks. But it turns out that the chorus is doubling as the plague- stricken population of Thebes (usually theyre Elders, whose status seems to entitle them to some kind of pestilence-immunity package), and theyre dragging themselves, or one another, to the royal palace, groaning. Their condition once established, the masks come off, though the complaints and lamentations go on. Timing is everything, and it obviously isn't the production's fault that the sequence looks like the "bring out your dead" number in Spamalot, minus the laughs. Well, almost minus the laughs.

Even in the main body of the play, this chorus has no intention of staying choral, not if that means staying on the sidelines. Sophocles play is, among other things, the first detective drama to have come down to us, and it may well be the best, with very superior twists. Oedipus relentlessly probes the facts surrounding the late King Laiuss murder and the remarriage of his widow, Jocasta, and discovers that he himself has done it; he unwittingly killed his father and, as all the world knows, went on to unwittingly marry his mother. Though he didn't have a complex about it. And jokes about how much Oedipus loved his mother (does anyone remember Never on Sunday?) are invariably as ignorant as they are cheap. Oedipus didn't know.

Now the same foul temper that led Oedipus to regicide also leads him, in the course of his investigations, to level paranoid accusations at those he feels are against him, chiefly his brother- in-law, Creon, and the prophet Tiresias. And in this production, the chorus joins in the mudslinging, sometimes appropriating some of the kings own lines to do it. At best theyre sycophants, at worst they're a lynch mob. The intention, obviously, is to turn them from commentators to participants: to, a dreaded word in this context, humanize them. But there's something amateurish in the sound of all that jeering, something very lets-get-in-touch-with-our-feelings- and-make-it-up-as-we-go-along. It would take far more experienced actors to make all this ad-lib chattiness convincing, though I doubt that more experienced actors could easily be persuaded to try.

The soloists, who would seem to offer severer technical challenges, actually fare far better. Paul Kits Oedipus is a brash, impatient young man with an incorruptible conscience and a helpfully loud voice; this may not amount to great tragic acting, but it covers the basics. Joel Grothe is similarly vigorous as Creon, though it's a shame that the two are much the same age; Creon should surely be older. Some maturer actors do helpful work: John Illingworth as a de facto chorus leader (a.k.a. Priest of Zeus), Albert Masters as an amusingly bumptious Messenger from Corinth, Peter Higginson doubling a piteous old Shepherd with a powerful Tiresias. That's the most accomplished performance of the evening.

Lada Darewych has trouble finding a tone and personality for Jocasta, but thats understandable. Mother? Wife? How old is she supposed to be? Maybe one shouldnt ask such questions, but in a production that makes gestures to realism, they're inescapable. And even as written, her reactions -- she guesses the truth before anyone, and counsels against pursuing it further -- are the most accessible of any in the play. She's tired of living in a myth, governed by fates and oracles, but she cant escape it. The men embrace it, but it doesnt spare them, either. Greek tragedy presents the ineluctable tendency of things to go wrong, which is why we both need it and resist it, and this one does it more starkly than any. Everyone involved has good intentions, and it avails them nothing. That, at least, comes through.

- Oedipus Rex runs through Aug. 5 at Philosopher's Stage on Philosopher's Walk.

2006-07-28-self-indulgence-and-a-suppres:
DESIGN FOR LIVING

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

Gilda, Otto and Leo have Central European names, though they themselves seem to be English. It's hard to be sure because they spend their time hopping in and out of countries, as well as in and out of one another's lives and beds. They are the trio of Destiny's Tots whose gay goings-on, and sad goings-off, are the subject of Noel Coward's Design for Living. Coward wrote the play in the 1930s as a vehicle for himself and his close friends -- and America's favourite married acting team -- the Lunts. It bears the marks of its origin in the demands its characters make on our attention, time and tolerance. The implication is that we have to care, because they're stars. However, one of the best things about Morris Panych's fine production at the Shaw Festival is that it doesn't indulge them. Another, stemming paradoxically from the first, is that it wins our sympathy for them.

At the beginning of Act One, Gilda, an interior decorator, is living with Otto, an artist, in his studio in Paris , but has just spent the night with Leo, a playwright. Otto is very upset when he finds out, and storms off, though it's an open question as to which of the two he is more jealous of. Probably he doesn't know himself; the three seem to have been together, in one formation or another, for years. Act Two finds Gilda shacked up in London with Leo, now the much-courted author of a hit play. Otto arrives and history repeats -- or, if you prefer, reverses -- itself. Gilda, appalled at the havoc the three of them are wreaking, walks out on the arm of Ernest, art-dealer and long-time friend and admirer, leaving the two boys (that really does seem to be the right word) to be furiously angry at one another, and then to reach a mutual accommodation by way of getting elaborately and hilariously drunk. Act Three shows us Gilda in New York, a great professional success in her own right. She's also married to Ernest, an arrangement that Otto and Leo flatly refuse to take seriously. They descend like a pair of not-so- heavenly twins (they spend much of the act in matching pyjamas), stake a joint claim to Gilda, and waltz off with her. Or, more accurately, Ernest waltzes off without her, even though it's his apartment.

In a way the play is a reprise-with-variations of Coward's Private Lives, although instead of two people who can't live with or without one another, we have three. This dilutes the humour (the drunk duet is the only really funny scene in the play) but expands the pain. There are other gains and losses. Both sets of characters share their author's preference for living anywhere but England, but while we never find out how Private Lives' Elyot and Amanda finance their cosmopolitan lifestyles, the later trio are at least shown to have jobs. We don't, however, learn much else about them; we have to take a lot on trust, including the vital assumption that they are made for one another. This may well be a legacy of the original casting. The roles are empty vessels for the stars to fill up, which in turn may account for the play's uncommon length. Each of them had to be given sufficient room to shine. Or rather to talk; because while Private Lives shows us its squabbling protagonists in action, some of it quite violent; their descendants in Design for Living seem to have one of those relationships that consists mostly of discussing the relationship. They don't, however, talk about how it affects them as individuals so much as how their bisexual menages a trois affects them in relation to the rest of the world. They end up with the declaration that they've found something that works for them, if not for anyone else. Their isolation makes them seem defensive, and also strangely innocent.

That, at least, is how it comes out here; and it's much preferable to presenting the threesome as cast-iron sophisticates, forever scoring points over the unworldly and unworthy squares. Ken MacDonald gives us a succession of skewed and skeletal sets, outsize windows through which we glimpse the Eiffel Tower, Big Ben and the Empire State Building, each one bent at an angle suggesting that if it had its druthers it would be in Pisa. But when it comes to the acting, Panych's production forswears brittleness, and with it any attempt to persuade us that the characters are wittier or more glamorous than they actually are. This does have its drawbacks in some of the stock comedy scenes (a sequence involving a Cockney maid's doomed attempts to answer the phone falls noticeably flat) but it works wonders for the emotions. Nicole Underhay is Gilda ungilded: Not one of her lines comes out as a wisecrack. She is instead a handsome, generous woman who for much of the play is scared of whom she may be hurting. By avoiding obvious star tactics, she emerges as a star.

Her two partners are more mischievous, David Jansen's Leo the more insistently (sometimes over-insistently) so, Graeme Somerville's Otto graver and more easily injured, the play's nearest approach to a thoughtful commentator. A key factor in keeping the leads human is the presence of a worthy antagonist, in the shape of Lorne Kennedy's Ernest, a wonderfully unselfish performance. He isn't a buffoon; he isn't a prig; if he were either we'd suspect the play of loading the dice, and take against it. He's sensible and he's dignified; he's also humourless and, as the boys fatally detect, sexless. So he has to go, which he does after finally losing his cool and unleashing a moralistic tirade -- though I think the production loses its own cool, not to say its magnanimity, in having him make his exit underneath a funny hat.

This being a 1930s boulevard comedy, the homosexuality is kept under wraps, at least at dialogue level; but they're thin wraps, easy for a modern production (and audience) to pierce; this one does so with enthusiasm, with the drunk scene spiralling into erotic knockabout. That's's how it ends; it starts as a display of professional as well as personal jealousy. The subject of success, its penalties and rewards, is much on the play's mind -- autobiographically so when Leo-the-lionized gets to reading and commenting on his first-night reviews and when he meets the press (Harry Judge as a young reporter who conducts an interview as if it were a police interrogation). That raises the question: How well does this secondary theme fit in with the main one? And it prompts the answer: Hardly at all. Coward had various things on his mind and, in airing them, he wrote a frankly self-indulgent play about frankly self-indulgent people. But he knew what he was doing, and did it with wit, and he made a vital moral point: Those who indulge themselves by indulging themselves do less harm than those who indulge themselves by suppressing others. Its time may have come again.

- In repertory until Nov. 18. 1-800-511-SHAW

2006-07-29-one-needs-an-identity-the-oth:
robertcushman@lycos.com; I Am Not a Dinner Mint closes tomorrow at Harbourfront Centre Theatre, 416-973-4000. Bird Flu Over the Cuckoo's Nest runs indefinitely at Second City, 416-343-0011.

Trey Anthony, who wrote Da Kink in My Hair, has said that one of the most gratifying aspects of its success was the way it cut across race and colour lines. White women came up to her and told her that her play, set in a hairdressing salon with an exclusively black staff and clientele, expressed their thoughts and feelings as well. With her new play, I Am Not a Dinner Mint, written in collaboration with Rachel-Lea Rickards, Anthony has taken the logical next step. She has a cast of five women, of whom three are black and two white. The step after that, of course, would be to open up the stage to the other half of the human race. But one thing at a time.

Of course, no play is under any obligation to be about everybody. What it does have to be, though, is about somebody, and here I Am Not a Dinner Mint falls down. It doesnt have the unity of setting, or the vestiges of plot, that helped give Da Kink an identity. Its mostly a series of self-contained soliloquies, whose only formal unity comes from the title, a dinner mint being defined as the small refreshing afterthought one enjoys after a really good meal." This apparently is how men think of women; even how some women think of women. Whatever the underlying truth of that, the image itself is far-fetched and when the performers invoke it at the beginning and end of the show, it sounds forced.

We have a series of complaints ("I have been treated like a dinner mint) bookended by affirmations (I am not going to be treated like a dinner mint"). The play is subtitled "the crap women swallow to stay in a relationship, and much of it, as you would expect, deals with the speakers' experiences with their partners, male or female. But the show's view of what constitutes a relationship turns out to be remarkably, even meaninglessly wide. It can encompass a womans relationship to her employers, or even to the work itself, not to mention the loss of it. But theres nothing specifically female about being fired, or even about hating your job while you have it.

The show certainly isn't whining or self-pitying. It is, most of the time, very good-humoured, not often funny but still vivaciously cheerful. There's some music, and one of the acting quintet, Graziella Mastrangelo, is also a singer who can hit some startling high notes. But the two most powerful items, the two after which you feel that you have met a person, are the starkest. In the first, Aktina Stathaki plays an overburdened mother who, all too believably, loses it. The second gives us Rickards, the co-author, as half of the only black couple on the Bridle Path, caught in a confounding vortex of privilege and abuse; shes a trophy whos also a punching bag, and she projects her rage and confusion outward. Some of the show's earlier takes on women and men have incorporated self-deprecation and made it amusing; Rickards' turn explores its consequences, and makes them kink-in-my-hair-raising.

The shows current run is a brief one with no trappings, obviously intended to lead, as happened with its predecessor, to greater things. There are certainly scenes in it worth developing. At the moment, though, its less a play than a cross between a cheerleaders' rally and a consciousness-raising session.

Or a revue. Which brings us to that form's leading local practitioners, Second City. Their latest show is called Bird Flu Over the Cuckoos Nest: one in a long line of groan-provoking titles, though this one has a modicum of relevance. The show does contain a number about avian flu. Its a calypso, sung -- in what may be a historic fusion of West Indian rhythm and East Indian voice -- by Anand Rajaram, a performer who excels at being simultaneously woeful and forceful. He sings it to a very aggrieved chicken, a non- verbal role that nonetheless gives the tousle-haired and impeccably beaky Matt Baram his second-finest hour. His finest comes as a scootered cop, berating stationary members of the audience for exceeding the speed limit and answering a call to an incident at Jane and Finch with a flat I don't go there."

The show's opening promises political satire and its closing behaves as if theres actually been some. In between, though, it delivers nothing of the kind -- also par for the course at Second City -- except for a long Bush-Harper sketch that stubbornly refuses to tell us anything we havent heard before. In general, this show is a steepish step down from the standard of its immediate predecessor, but it does have its share of goodies. Best of all, it has Naomi Snieckus, a comedienne with a face that sumptuously accommodates every variety of shock and delight, as a mother hacking into her son's MSN account to converse with two of his friends; for once a revue number doesn't run out of surprises, for us or for her. Snieckus also shines as a woman who answers a telephone survey about eggs, opts to answer her questions in French and lives to regret it. There were two understudies on at the show I saw, and they got to share a sketch, about two people who share a cab, post office- party. They did very well: David Raitt as an embarrassed underling desperately making conversation as if his life, not just his livelihood, depended on it ("There are many movies. Some with Dudley Moore. Most without."); Ashley Botting shooting him stony glares. She also sang the best of the few songs, something called I'm Getting More Like My Mother Every Day. It might, with a rhythmic makeover, fit very neatly into I Am Not a Dinner Mint.

Colour Photo: Courtesy of Second City / From left to right: Lauren Ash, Jim Annan, Scott Montgomery, Naomi Snieckus and Matt Baram in Bird Flu Over the Cuckoo's Nest, playing at Second City.
2006-08-05-brian-is-resurrected-monty-py:
robertcushman@lycos.com

I am intrigued by the prospect of Not the Messiah, the oratorio based on Monty Python's Life of Brian and composed by the Spamalot team of Eric Idle and John Du Prez, which, it was announced this week, is coming to us next year as part of the new Toronto arts festival, Luminato. Though I don't know about these names. Why can't they just call it the Toronto Festival? It doesn't seem to have hurt Edinburgh.

Anyway, I'm taken by the oratorio idea because I've always preferred Life of Brian to Monty Python and the Holy Grail. So I am pleased that, in the wake of Spamalot, we will be getting the sit- down version; indeed, not only getting it but originating it, with the Toronto Symphony conducted by its very own director, and Idle's very own cousin, Peter Oundjian.

I'm much taken, too, by Idle's promise that it will be "funnier than Handel, but not as good." The world may well need a funny oratorio, though it's hard to be sure since it's probably never had one. Anyway, it seems a safe prophecy, on both counts, and a very Idle thing to say. Or a very Python thing to say. Or, to come right down to it, a very British thing to say. It ties in with Idle's first-night speech at the Canon when he thanked Toronto audiences for "opening your arms -- and your legs" to the Python team when they still were a team and toured here in the early '70s.

There's always something refreshing about the demeanour of British performers at showbiz junkets. You see it particularly at the big award ceremonies. They rarely, when victorious, thank God or their mothers, and they always seem somewhat amused by the whole enterprise. The balance of arrogance and self-deprecation is hard to bring off, and Americans, though they sometimes try, can never manage it.

I'm never sure that Americans get British toughness or even, at the root, British humour. (Canadians? They're in between. Like honest brokers.) It doesn't stop them rhapsodizing over British entertainers. Idle himself has said that the Pythons owe their cult status to America, but that may be because the Americans thought them more whimsical than they actually were. It's like the Beatles. For many of their countrymen, the Beatles' defining moment had little to do with music. It was when they appeared at the Royal Variety Performance, and John Lennon told the audience in the (comparatively) cheaper seats to clap; "the rest of you," with a look at the Royal Box, "just rattle your jewellery." That kind of cheerful disrespect -- which wasn't that cheerful underneath -- didn't travel, not in the way that lovable mop-toppishness did. And when the group grew spiritual pretensions, they became perfect transatlantic exports. It's tempting to blame America for bringing out the worst in the Beatles, and, ultimately, for ruining them.

America didn't quite have that effect on the Pythons. (After all, John Cleese went on to write the misanthropic farcical masterpieces that were Fawlty Towers. Years later there was an attempt to produce an American version, which the networks felt compelled to enrich with "human interest." I'm sure they didn't set out to desecrate the originals. They just couldn't help themselves.)

But I suspect American fans embraced the silliness of Python, while ignoring the intellect. What really made the TV shows was the shamelessly intelligent way in which their creators mixed their surrealist skills with their university education. Your typical Python sketch found most of the cast in drag as housewives at a laundromat, trying to put a phone call through to Mrs. Jean-Paul Sartre to check on a detail of her husband's philosophy. I'm not claiming that that's as hysterical as the dead-parrot number, but it's as characteristic. It isn't, though, something that the fans keep quoting.

I was surprised when Idle told me that Holy Grail had always been more popular than Life of Brian, but I shouldn't have been. Brian isn't just a Biblical send-up, as Grail is an Arthurian send-up; it has something to say about human gullibility. (I remember Cleese being emphatic about this in a TV discussion with Malcolm Muggeridge, the English cultural mandarin and late-life religious zealot, who wearily dismissed the movie. Wearily dismissing things was his trademark.) So maybe it was born to be an oratorio, and especially one with that double-edged title, which manages to spoof Handel while quoting the film's most famous line. It's almost as if they'd planned it, decades in advance.

And maybe, by the same token, Spamalot -- whose title is probably only a coincidental spoof on the Lerner and Loewe Camelot, but is a purposeful homage to the processed-meat product that Python has kept fresher than any refrigerator -- was born to be a musical. After all, there were, just as in The Producers, already two musical numbers in the movie waiting to be staged. One is the minstrel's song of the Brave (and Multiply Mutilated) Sir Robin, which makes it on to the stage unscathed, unlike its subject. The other is Knights of the Round Table, a small mock-production number in the movie and a big mock-production number on the stage. The size and the mockery, though, cancel one another out. In the film the number is effectively cancelled out by having Graham Chapman's Arthur say, immediately after it's over, "No, let's not go to Camelot; it seems like a silly idea." That's funny, and very Python. But you can't do it in the theatre, not with the audience's applause providing a buffer zone. That's Broadway. That's America.

With the rage for putting famous movies on stage, I have to wonder if anyone is planning to turn the Marx Brothers' masterpiece Duck Soup, the last word on war, into a musical. I hope not, but I have to admit that it is, well, a sitting duck. It, too, has two numbers already in place, and they could easily be supplemented with other songs by the same composers. (Bert Kalmar and Harry Ruby, if you're wondering.) And the Marxes themselves aren't strictly inimitable. And you can bet that, however good its intentions, any stage production would forfeit the movie's anarchic inconsequentiality, and probably its satiric bite as well. Tame the Marx Brothers? But it's already been done, by MGM: the studio to which the brothers moved after their early classics at Paramount (which culminated in Duck Soup) and which fitted them out with hearts of gold and romantic subplots. The audiences bought it, too. It isn't just the British to whom American show business can do it. It can Americanize Americans as well.

Colour Photo: Peter J. Thompson, National Post / Eric Idle, seen here bowing at a performance of Spamalot, brings Not the Messiah to Toronto in 2007.
2006-08-10-incredible-ibsen:
ROSMERSHOLM

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the Lake, Ont.

THEATRE REVIEW

The Shaw Festival production of Rosmersholm is a revelation. I say this with feeling since, of all Henrik Ibsen's plays, this is the one I have always had the most trouble taking seriously. It concerns John Rosmer, a former pastor whose family has, for generations, been the most influential in the neighbourhood -- and also the most conservative. He has now forsaken both his religious and political beliefs, under the influence of Rebecca West, a young woman who moved into his house to help care for his sick wife, Beata, a troubled lady who drowned herself shortly before the play began.

Gradually, the play being one of the showpieces of Ibsen's cat- and-mouse dramaturgy, it's revealed that Rebecca was responsible for Beata's death. She had wanted Rosmer for herself and persuaded Beata that Rosmer loved her in return and that Beata herself stood between her husband and his happiness. Too late, Rebecca realizes that her own idealism, her belief in freedom and progress, has misled her. She is a murderess. She must atone.

Rebecca attributes her awakening, not to her own conscience, but to her exposure to the high moral tone of the Rosmer household. This is represented on stage by the massed portraits of the current Rosmer ancestors, gazing down on the present incumbent, each more unforgiving and censorious than the last. Or so, in the current production, we must imagine. In Peter Hartwell's economical design, the portraits are a series of empty frames, plus a single video still representing a couple of Rosmers past who look forbidding.

Ibsen wrote this play in the 1880s, and set it in his native Norway. Director Neil Munro has placed it "somewhere in Europe between the wars," though the time shift is hardly noticeable, and the shift in place not noticeable at all. No audience will sit through an Ibsen play believing that it could happen anywhere but Norway, and Munro virtually admits it by keeping the play's name intact, even while anglicizing it in the dialogue to "the House of Rosmer."

But though the generalized updating is unnecessary, some specific changes are very helpful, especially where the play's politics are concerned. It may come as a shock to hear Headmaster Kroll, Rosmer's brother-in-law and polemical antagonist, described as a leader of the Christian Right, but that is what he is after all, even if the term itself is anachronistic for both the 1880s and the 1930s. Here, for once, we discover what the "advanced ideas" in an Ibsen play actually are and why the characters are so passionately for or against them.

Rebecca is habitually played in the grand manner, as if she were a consolation prize for an actress who isn't getting to play Hedda Gabler this year. Waneta Storms plays her more intent, believing in her cause, biding her time but poleaxed by the revelation that her lover, in the years before she came to Rosmersholm, was also her biological father. The matter is confined to one scene but it tears Rebecca apart; it's the only point at which Storms storms, and it's enough. At the very moment when Patrick Galligan's Rosmer, the kind of open-faced paragon with whom any faction would want to burnish its image, admits he wants her physically, it becomes impossible for her to accede. Giving both participants a family curse may be adding incest to injury, but nobody could say that Ibsen starves his actors of motivation. Storms and Galligan play superbly together, and even better with Peter Hutt's magnificent Kroll, a role usually reduced to a pompous, bloodless caricature. Hutt, while never stinting on smugness and intolerance, grants him a point of view that's serious and sincerely-held, complicated by a deep personal involvement -- philosophical, familial, sexual -- with the people he's up against. He conveys, subtly and speedily, extraordinary shades of feeling.

This has been an up and down and in-between season at the Shaw, but the ups -- The Heiress, The Crucible, Design for Living, most of Too True to Be Good and now this -- have been spectacular.

- In repertory through Oct. 7. 1-800-511-SHAW

robertcushman@lycos.com

Black & White Photo: Shaw Festival / Waneta Storms and Patrick Galligan defy convention and turn their backs to the audience in this stellar adaptation of Ibsen's most difficult play.
2006-08-10-star-crossed-lovers-need-a-li:
ANTONY AND CLEOPATRA

Shakespeare in the Rough, Withrow Park, Toronto

- - -

Some plays defeat the best of intentions. I was set to be impressed by Ruth Madoc-Jones' production of Antony and Cleopatra, just on the basis of its line-by-line lucidity. It's one of those Shakespeare productions in which the actors seem to know both what they're talking about and who they're talking to. More than that, there's an engaging feeling of gossipy intimacy about the early scenes here, the ones devoted less to Antony and Cleopatra themselves than to their entourages. But gossip alone won't get you through this play. It also needs grandeur.

I don't mean scenic grandeur, or even numerical. The standard editions credit the play with 34 named characters and 42 separate scenes, but the text can be (and here has been) intelligently cut, and the minor people sensibly combined or doubled. Nor do the extremely casual conditions of Withrow Park -- a space rather than a stage -- do the play any harm. As usual at Shakespeare in the Rough, the wide, deep spaces stretching beyond the main playing area provide evocative pictures. Some of them are sketchy, but it's helpful to be reminded of Rome when we're in Egypt and of Egypt when we're in Rome.

But none of this matters very much without stars -- not star names, necessarily, but star presences. Antony and Cleopatra is a play about stardom -- maybe the first ever. Its two protagonists have the free-spending habits of stardom; Antony, who gives kingdoms as presents and finally throws away an empire, is insanely generous, materially and emotionally, and Cleopatra, far more canny and cautious in what she gives away, finally learns generosity from him. If that largesse isn't there in them, we have no reason to care; and the play becomes an elaborate chronicle, pointlessly spun out. That is what happens here.

One lead performance is stodgy, the other unformed. Sean Dixon's Antony is sometimes good at anger, but the passion that eventually terrifies Cleopatra, leading her to fake her own death and so provoke his, is nowhere to be found. Lesley Dowey's Cleopatra isn't frightening enough either; the messenger who brings her the news of Antony's marriage ought to be lucky to escape with his life, but here he seems in no danger whatever. This Cleopatra can be flirtatious, but she isn't technically up to all those words, especially the awesome flood of them in her last scene. It's a promising performance, but in this context an insufficient one.

Some supporting players do well, most of them in omnibus roles that gather several characters under a single umbrella. Thus, Richard Lee gives an incisive account of several Egyptian functionaries, all called Alexas, while Brett Christopher does as much for a bunch of Roman officers answering to the name of Agrippa. Christopher Morris is excellent as Enobarbus, the Roman soldier half- seduced by the pleasures of the East, although when he gets into deeper waters -- tormenting himself for deserting his master, Antony -- he merely treads them; but by this point the whole production seems to have lost its grip. The passions at stake are simply too much for it. So are the politics. Gregory Prest has almost no handle on the ultra-cool Octavius Caesar, but then he's let down from his very first entrance, when the director has him chasing after his ineffectual colleague Lepidus rather than the other way around. Maybe I was being too generous about this production's intelligence. It's also plagued, as shows at this address often are, by a theme song, something about eternal love; the words are by Ezra Pound, but it's still banal. It's sung, like an Andrew Lloyd Webber theme, at the beginning of the play, at the half-way point, and at the end. Can't they tell how demeaning that is?

- Until Sept. 4. Pay what you can. 416-556-6226

robertcushman@lycos.com
2006-08-26-singers-of-jazz-and-big-band-:
Some half-dozen years ago there was a Broadway musical titled Swing! which was, according to your level of cynicism, an authentic tribute to the jazz and big-band music of the 1930s and 40s or an attempt to cash in on what was, at the turn of the millennium, the latest retro-craze. Either way, one of its highlights was a performance of Blues in the Night by Ann Hampton Callaway, a performer previously known as a cabaret singer-pianist, one of the few in modern Manhattan to make a steady living. She has now released a CD (on Telarc) of which that song is the title number and the centrepiece.

Technically, Callaway is an awesomely proficient singer, with range and control in the Sarah Vaughan league. (She looks awesome, too; a towering brunette.) She's a songwriter as well as a singer, and one of the staples of her club act has been the construction on the premises of a brand-new song from a series of ideas submitted by the audience. Impressive the first time you hear it, this rapidly loses its appeal at subsequent encounters; once you know she can do it, you know she can do it.

A more formal number of her own, that she must have been doing at least since the '70s, when I first heard her, is The Im-Too-White- To-Sing-the-Blues Blues, in which she laments that, despite her double-barrelled surname, she is related neither to Lionel nor to Cab. The song is on the new CD, and its self-consciousness is multiplied tenfold in a setting apparently designed to present her as a big-band blues singer in the Chicago or Basie tradition; shes either protesting too much or admitting too much.

Backed by the Diva Jazz Orchestra, who are what used to be known as an all-girl band, she storms her way through a bunch of Harold Arlen tunes: Stormy Weather, When the Sun Comes Out and the title track. She can do them all right, but it all sounds like an imitation, based on a prefabricated idea of what a jazz singer should sound like, and with no particular relation to the songs themselves. She's best when she turns down both the pace and the volume and delivers a breathtaking Willow Weep for Me that touches tragedy (not just "bluesy" but certifiably blue) and, as a closer, The Glory of Love, a corny tune with a surprising habit of turning up trumps. Here she goes back to her roots as a cabaret singer, one who has brushed up against jazz and found it productive.

- - -

Callaway ranks, by current standards, as a veteran. Barbara Lea, who has been at it, mainly in New York, since the '50s is an institution. At least she should be. Her career, which got off to an excellent start, stalled when this music fell out of fashion in the 60s, and she has become a cult performer, though with none of the preciousness or extravagance that phrase usually implies. Shes nobody's diva; she is instead a singer puritanically devoted to the shape and meaning of the songs: not an obviously subtle singer like Peggy Lee or Blossom Dearie, whose quietness signals that something combustible is going on under the surface, but a subtly subtle singer.

She seems to be singing no more than the plain sense of a lyric, but then will alert you, with an unexpected emphasis, of a tiny shift in rhythm. Her new CD (available from barbaralea.com), Black Butterfly -- named after an obscure Duke Ellington song that's a strange choice of title cut for a decidedly WASP lady -- teams her, too, with a crisp and sometimes sonorous big band, led by an old collaborator, pianist and saxophonist Loren Schoenberg.

Lea, in her 70s, sometimes wavers on the long notes, but she can transfix you with a punched-out syllable, especially when the subject is loss. The albums principal fault is its almost unwavering solemnity; Lea has a delicious sense of humour, but its not much called-on here, though she can put herself into a delightful period frame, as on Ellington's Just Squeeze Me and Irving Berlin's All by Myself, both duets with Schoenberg. The triple highlights are When They Ask about You, an old song new to me (and an apparent precursor of Dont Get Around Much Anymore), the best-ever vocal of Thelonious Monks Round Midnight, recreated as a tone poem, and a barebones reclamation of an even more overdone song, Come Rain or Come Shine, which here becomes all about need. Since the death of Rosemary Clooney, Lea sings this repertoire better than anyone.

- - -

Small labels keep the voices of lesser-known singers in this area available, and also cast new light on the famous ones. Harbinger Records is one of them. They offer two volumes of Ethel Merman singing her famous songs and others, like My Funny Valentine, that you would never expect her to do in a million years. (She does it very nicely.)

The performances are drawn from private recordings, demos (including the original Gypsy) and nightclub performances, and in this altered ambience, even the warhorses come up fresh.

Susan Johnson, a lesser-known Broadway belter (The Most Happy Fella) with a more sophisticated sense of humour, has a disc in the same series, and it's a delight, especially the discovery of an unknown (to me, anyway) Cole Porter song, I've Got Somebody Waiting. And there is another devoted to the cabaret doyenne Mabel Mercer, including a few songs she never recorded commercially.

My only disappointment in the Harbinger catalogue is the disc I anticipated most, The Land Where the Good Songs Go, dedicated to the Broadway lyrics of P.G. Wodehouse. Too many of these wonderfully conversational songs are weighed down with portentousness and stripped of sparkle. There is some nice singing, though, by classical singer turned nightclub thrush Sylvia McNair, and the point is conclusively made that Wodehouse, God's Englishman, was also America's first great lyricist.

Black & White Photo: KRT File Photo / Harbinger Records offers two volumes of Ethel Merman, left.
2006-08-30-the-food-of-life-as-served-wi:
Theatre Review

TWELFTH NIGHT

Festival Theatre, Stratford

- - -

This is Illyria, lady: a seaport and spa located, according to the new Stratford production, somewhere on the coast of India, in the days of Queen Victoria. Shakespeare's Duke Orsion is now a nabob, in emotional, and maybe even cultural, thrall to the resident English, as represented by the Lady Olivia. She comes on like an imperious Raj widow, mourning not a husband she has lost but a brother.

Leon Rubin's production of Twelfth Night is the latest instalment in his ongoing project of refreshing the Shakespeare canon by resetting the plays in exotic, usually Asian, climes. The benefits, this time, are local rather than general. They include lush, lived- in settings (by John Pennoyer) and sinuous dancing (by Keira Loughran) that makes the food of love seem spicier than ever, but they don't extend to supplying the play with a political context, probably because it can't accommodate one.

The Venice of The Merchant of Venice, even the Messina of Much Ado About Nothing (which has in the past been brilliantly staged in a British Raj setting) are comparatively realistic locations, with interacting social levels. lllyria is geographically in the Balkans, but to Shakespeare it seems to have been just a name, another in his line of shadowed Arcadias. There doesn't seem to be anything to it beyond Orsino's household and Olivia's, and though he theoretically runs the place the only tension between them is erotic. When the twins, Viola and Sebastian, are washed up on shore to wreak havoc with the local libidos, they seem to have come from nowhere. They are -- and here the production's choice of locale does have a point - - like breaths of fresh air in a hothouse.

Most of the play takes place at Olivia's place, a crowded establishment whose cross-currents are charted here with exceptional clarity. The rich texture may owe something to the geographical transplant; the set-up, as Shakespeare wrote it, is plainly Elizabethan English, so there's no great stretch in making it Victorian Colonial. It probably owes more, though, to the wit of director and actors. The chatelaine herself is played by Seana McKenna who is, to put it bluntly, older than most Olivias. (Or at least than most recent Olivias. Once upon a time, Olivia regularly used to be played by Viola's mother. How's that for overtones?)

Instead of a self-cloistered ingenue violently awakening to love, we get a worldly woman who's not as aware as she thought she was and can laugh at herself even as she totters. It doesn't necessarily make more sense to have Olivia played as a mature woman, but it's certainly a bonus to have her played by a mature actress, one as alert as McKenna to both the wit and the absurdity and as adroit as communicating both. Dana Green's Viola is an excellent foil for her, empathizing, from a distance, with her fraternal loss and then confronting her like a blast of common sense with a smile attached.

It's also easier than usual to believe that Olivia and Sir Toby Belch live in the same house and that they're actually related. They meet seldom, and he's always drunk when they do, but in these encounters they communicate an authentic blend of acceptance and distaste. Thom Marriott's Toby, someone's cashiered younger brother, is genial enough, a bully who can actually fight, but there's real calculating nastiness in him, especially in his dealings with Don Carrier's endearing Sir Andrew who, as befits his name and very much in line with the realities of the Raj, is Scottish; the yellow costume (Olivia's least favourite colour) in which he, like most Andrews, is haplessly got up is a plaid, the ancestral tartan perhaps of the clan MacAguecheek. He also plays what Toby, departing somewhat from the text, describes as "strange instruments;" they are of course bagpipes. He is the only Andrew I have seen to be permanently jealous of, and wounded by, Toby's success with Maria, who flirts with him at their first encounter and ignores him afterwards.

Diane D'Aquila is a commanding Maria, her relationship with Toby growing through each scene. Andrew Massingham's Feste is clever and melodious, though a white Indian mask (he's supposed to be the bridge between the two cultures) obscures not only his face but his personality. Brian Bedford has played Malvolio at Stratford twice before; his comic virtuosity -- when reading the fatal letter or when strutting cross-gartered -- remains intact, but it's underpinned this time by a sharp sense of class. This steward has worked his way up, and he despises those who haven't. (They return the compliment.) In specs and curlers, he exudes sniffiness. But he's serious; and when he's duped and tormented, though we don't actually feel sorry for him, we do feel.

His is both the funniest performance of the evening, and the most disturbing. At least it appears to be heading in the latter direction, as does the whole production, until they both get derailed. The ultimate culprit here seems to be Sanjay Talwar's performance of Orsino, which so fastens on the character's self- pity and self-love that he comes out spineless. It becomes even harder than usual to understand what Viola sees in him. When called upon for passion in the last act, he supplies only petulance. This weightlessness infects the entire scene, so that the twins' reunion and the pairings are neither as joyous or as moving as they should be. McKenna adopts the fashionable deflationary reading of Olivia's "most wonderful" when faced with two objects of her affection. Frankly she doesn't need it -- she has enough laughs under her belt - - but anyway she doesn't have much to deflate; journeys end in lovers' meetings, but there isn't much of an arrival.

There is a lovely autumnal staging of Feste's last song, in which the various stanzas actually apply to the people in the play, leading to a sharp reversal of fortune as between the clown and the avenging steward. It's plainly meant to chill our blood but it comes too late; we've been primed to laugh and there hasn't been enough to stop us. The production is far more successful with the play's fun than with its pain. But if you have to err on one side, the funny side's the right one.

- In repertory until Oct. 28.

Black & White Photo: Stratford Festival / Diane D'Aquila as a commanding Maria, Don Carrier's endearing Sir Andrew Aguecheek and Thom Marriott's genial but nasty Sir Toby Belch.
2006-09-02-from-slings-to-stratford-what:
The powers at the Shaw and Stratford festivals must sometimes wish life could be more like Slings & Arrows. The third season of this delightfully incestuous TV series ended last Monday with some choice slices of wish-fulfillment. The season centred on the attempts of Geoffrey, artistic director of the New Burbage Shakespeare Festival, to mount a production of King Lear starring Charles Kingman, an aged actor who had dreamed his entire life of playing the king. One thing Charles neglected to mention until after signing the contract was that he was dying of cancer. The combined effects of his condition and his drug regime led to the cancellation of not one but two first nights and finally to the canning both of the show and of Geoffrey himself.

At the last minute, however, Charles rallied and the company, in defiance of the new Burbage regime, mounted Lear for one night only, in a church hall. Everyone wept, Charles got through the performance triumphantly and died immediately afterward in his dressing room, crowning his career as he would have wished.

There were, of course, overtones. The fragments of Kingmans King Lear that we got to see and hear were sublime. This was not surprising since Charles was played by William Hutt, and for most Canadian theatregoers -- with no disrespect to the other fine actors who have recently played it (Christopher Plummer), are about to play it (William Webster) or are rumoured to be playing it (Brian Bedford) -- Hutt is Lear. He has played the role three times at Stratford alone, the last time when he was pushing Lear's own age of 80, a rare achievement indeed.

Obviously Hutt isn't Charles, if only because he survived playing Lear to play Charles; still, we never lost the delighted sense of who we were watching. He was wonderful as the old actor, his comic timing intact, and still had some surprises to spring as the king. In one scene, a rehearsal of the great "reason not the need speech, he really let fly at the actress playing Regan. She was shocked; the rest of the company gazed on apparently fascinated but actually aghast. It turned out Charles had gone off his meds, but the rage was still perfect Lear. I expected Geoffrey to tell him to keep it in, and was very disappointed when he didnt.

Its uncertain how closely the New Burbage is based on Stratford. Obviously there are resemblances. This season even had one of the senior actors talking about how he had been with the operation ever since it started in a tent. I don't know how long ago that was supposed to have been but, though the Burbage now apparently boasts both a main and a studio stage, its repertoire seems no larger than Stratford's was in its first season under canvas 53 years ago. Just two shows: Lear and a solemn new musical called East Hastings, a low- rent Rent that became a surprise hit. Somewhat confusingly, we were asked both to laugh at the awfulness of the musical itself, courtesy of some dead-on parodies, and to sympathize with the author of it, when an incompetent director (Don McKellar, eyes glinting with charlatanry and pretention) set about making it even worse.

So, a great Shakespearean actor, with a matchless blend of experience and freshness, shows how it should be done, and passes on the torch. A play works magically in an improvised set-up, away from big stages and big organizations, and everyone loyally rallies round. (Shades of The Cradle Will Rock.) The philistines prosper materially, but inside they really hate themselves. I laughed and cried in all the right places. Like I said, wish-fulfillment.

In the real world, I doubt that the salvation of our classical festivals lies in their taking vows of poverty. They need to be richer, both in the scope of what they do and in the amount of funding they receive to do it. I dont think they have to give up doing musicals; I would like them to stop feeling obliged to do musicals. The well-documented decline in tourism, meaning American tourism, is a setback but it could also be an opportunity; it seems ridiculous, after all, for Canadas major institutional theatres (they aren't national theatres) to measure their success on their appeal to foreigners. Their primary aim should be to make Canadians happy; if that's achieved, and properly reported and promoted, the visitors will come back. (Some might even come from Europe, where they are gluttons for it.)

It would be nice to see our marketers of culture, especially in Ontario, treat our theatre as something of international importance, rather than something to be jokily apologized for. Much cultural advertising seems to be saying not you will enjoy this," but "dont worry, it wont hurt." Stratford and Shaw have in fact much to shout about. This year, Stratford's Duchess of Malfi and the Shaw's Rosmersholm are revelatory reimaginings of great, tough plays.

And we should certainly be celebrating our actors, what I call the super-ensemble that stretches out from Toronto, through Ontario and across the country. Even into TV: It was very much in evidence in Slings & Arrows, which, apart from those already mentioned, featured scintillating work from Stephen Ouimette and from Susan Coyne who, as writer, actress and producer, accumulated a dizzying five credits per episode. I'm taking it for granted, by the way, that this season has been the last; there was something very epiphanic about it. But if Geoffrey and his team come back and retake New Burbage from the usurper, I think the play they should be looking at is Richard III.

robert.cushman@ hotmail.com

2006-09-09-when-alan-rickman-played-the-:
The films that most interest me at the Toronto International Film Festival are Canadian, or part Canadian, but there are things about them, and people within them, that reach beyond our borders.

I have an unprofessional stake in the Anglo-Canadian Snow Cake: The extras include three members of my own family, one of whom -- I am told on good authority -- gets a close-up. (I shan't dare blink.) But I'm intrigued too by the story and setting: The relationship between a haunted man, recently out of prison, and the autistic woman whom he befriends after being involved in her daughter's death in a car crash. The mother lives up in Wawa, Ont., and it sounds like an ideal meeting of psychological and meteorological extremes. (Filming in Wawa proved to be no piece of any kind of cake. Much of the film was shot in Toronto.)

What really hooks me is the casting. The stars are Alan Rickman and Sigourney Weaver, in a set-up about as far removed as possible from their previous teaming in Galaxy Quest. I've been a fan of Weaver's for years, and I suspect that her snow woman will prove a more enlightening and less Hollywooden study of autism than Dustin Hoffman's Rain Man.

I've been a fan of Rickman for even more years; to be precise since 1962, when I was in my last year at a West London grammar school and nabbed the title role in a production -- well, a rehearsed reading -- of the modern cult classic Serjeant Musgrave's Dance. Playing Annie, the barmaid (it was an all-boys school) was a younger boy whom I'd never met before. I'd like to say that I immediately knew myself to be in the presence of a future star, but I was probably thinking more along the lines of unfair competition. Looking back, though, I realize that many of the qualities that have contributed to that stardom -- the aquiline face and voice, the irony, the authority, the all-pervading mournfulness -- were already present, and served him just as well when playing an angry, vulnerable young woman as they did in his more familiar later guises of decadent aristocrat or sneering villain. In fact, some of his adult performances that I've most liked (and Snow Cake may well turn out to be another of them) have fallen outside those categories: his courteous gentleman in Sense and Sensibility and, in a surprisingly successful Irish transplant of Chekhov's The Seagull at London's Royal Court Theatre, his world-weary novelist formerly known as Trigorin.

That's one screen performance and one on stage; and it both interests and impresses me that, though it's obviously the films that have made him famous, he's managed to maintain a foot in both. Maybe it's because of my job, maybe it's because of our old association and my subsequent witnessing of his stage career which, after a late start, took off steadily and fast, but I think of him as a theatre actor who also does movies. If you want to do this, it helps to be British, since Britain has a theatrical culture and something of a film industry; Americans, under pressure both commercial and geographic, usually have to choose between.

Compare Rickman's career with Weaver's; she trained at the Yale Drama School (her resume includes being one of the original chorus of amphibians in Stephen Sondheim's The Frogs) but she is stamped as a film actress, just like her fellow Yalie Meryl Streep. Streep does do stage from time to time -- she's doing Mother Courage in Central Park at the moment -- but it always seems at best a diversion, at worst a gesture.

In Canada, of course, the option hardly arises, or only in a stark form; you want a big movie career, you leave the country: to live, like Christopher Plummer, or just to work, like Colm Feore. Otherwise there's stage leavened by TV, with the chance of an occasional movie, homegrown, visiting or -- as in this case -- both. The supporting cast of Snow Cake includes such pillars of Toronto acting as David Fox and -- cast as a couple -- the two writer- performers of Slings & Arrows, Mark McKinney and Susan Coyne. McKinney became a Canadian star in TV and stand-up comedy, Coyne in classic and contemporary drama. It's a pleasant convergence.

Sarah Polley is something else, a child star on stage and TV who grew up to become an all-rounder: a valued actress in Canadian (read small-budget) movies, a political activist, a director in her own right. Away from Her, her first feature in that capacity, has impeccable Canadian credentials: Atom Egoyan, no less, as executive producer, an Alice Munro story as source. And it is crammed with Canadian acting talent. Some are resident: the veteran-bordering-on- iconic Gordon Pinsent; Toronto theatre's cherished Kristen Thomson; Michael Murphy, whose sardonic judge was my favourite thing on This is Wonderland.

What is most surprising about stage-to-screen transitions is the ease with which certain apparently un-starlike British actors have made homes for themselves in American movies: the tough clowns like Bob Hoskins and Alfred Molina, and even less expectedly, the sensitive neurotics like Pete Postlethwaite and Tom Wilkinson. Some of them have even achieved that Holy Grail of British actors: being cast in American movies as Americans. Rickman bridges the two traditions; he's a character man but he's also a romantic, or rather an anti-romantic so intense that he ends up romantic. I feel rather proud to have been in at the start.

Rickman typifies British aptitude for theatre/movie crossover.
